title:
MANAGEMENT: IDEAS INTO ACTION/FRED ANDREWS;
A Man of Words Is Still Partial to One: Loyalty
body: IN the 90's, a tough, impatient decade that has given loyalty a drubbing, Frederick F. Reichheld has always been loyalty's champion in business. Mr. Reichheld produced the hard numbers showing that a seasoned employee, treated properly, was two or three times as productive as someone just in the door. No one ever questioned that customer loyalty was a good thing. But precious few companies actually understood how powerful a lever a committed customer was. Mr. Reichheld, a management consultant at Bain & Company in Boston, had the tally: A company that keeps just 5 percent more of its customers from sliding away could lift profits by 50 percent. Times have changed, but he still preaches that loyalty, an old-fashioned virtue, is fundamental to business success on the Internet. This season Amazon.com, for one, with its obsession with serving customers, is singing Fred Reichheld's song. Everyone understands that e-commerce economics requires enormous expenditures upfront to attract a clientele. This holiday season was a critical test of which e-tailers could win out in pulling customers to their sites. But that's only a start. Those customers have to stick around. The Internet measures a site's "stickiness" in minutes; profitability is reckoned in years. According to preliminary research by Bain and others, it will take three to four years of loyal patronage just to break even on what is now being spent to drag customers in the door. "The economics of loyalty just gets applied so much more powerfully," Mr. Reichheld said in an interview on Dec. 17. "If you think about the true economics of an Internet business: they've got this big acquisition cost, and then they've got a potential annuity of income if they treat people right and earn their loyalty." Mr. Reichheld believes the Internet has enormous potential for serving customers better, with richer information, interactive relationships and innovative services. "There are so many creative things you can do for the customer's lifetime experience," he said, "lots of ways to create a unique, distinctive and much better customer experience." From what he has seen so far, however, "very few" companies are going to be able to hold their customers for three to four years. Acquisition costs for the pure Internet e-tailers are "going up like crazy," he said, while the customers they attract tend to surf from one retail site to another. "They're snagging fundamentally disloyal butterfly kinds of customers," he said. The preliminary research on consumers' Internet shopping habits and projected loyalties shows some traditional merchants like Lands' End and L. L. Bean doing very well. Their customers are Velcro, not Vaseline. "I'm pretty convinced that the existing firms, as they add Internet capabilities, are going to cream pure-play Internet," Mr. Reichheld said. Some traditional merchants enjoy customer retention rates 10 to 20 percentage points higher than their newer competition. Normally, trailing the competition by 20 points in customer loyalty "is enough to put you out of business," he noted, adding that "10 points is very weak returns." Mr. Reichheld's core doctrine is engraved in stone: Companies that cultivate loyal customers, loyal employees, loyal investors, consistently outperform their competition. Mr. Reichheld first built a Bain practice and then a philosophy on that observation. "One, it all starts with trust," he said. "If you don't earn your customer's trust, you won't make money on the Internet. Two, unless you have superior economics -- a strategy for building real economic advantage -- you're not worthy of trust. Three, customer selection is more vital than ever. There is so much churn out there." Mr. Reichheld is an idealist and a perfectionist. On average, he notes, American companies lose roughly half their customers in five years, half their employees in four. The huge expense of replacing them offends his perfectionist streak. And the emerging career pattern of workers jumping from employer to employer strikes him as a sad failure. It is "sheer hogwash" to preach that message to young people, he said. "A great company is where you want to end up and spend most of your life," he said. "Most of life is a search for people and institutions worthy of your loyalty and commitment. People yearn for that. That's why the Marines are not short on recruiting." At 47 and financially secure, Mr. Reichheld has retired from client engagements. His Bain partners made him the first Bain Fellow, a half-time senior position that permits him to concentrate on extending his loyalty research. He gave a score of speeches this year, and he is three-quarters through writing a book on corporate leadership. "This idea of treating people right, principled relationships -- it doesn't just happen naturally," he said. "It takes leaders who have the ability to put others' interests ahead, to take a long time frame, and to bring things into that framework." Every year or so, most recently in October, Mr. Reichheld assembles a a circle of chief executives from companies he admires. The collection is as varied as Intuit, Vanguard, Harley Davidson, Chick-fil-A, Northwestern Mutual Life, State Farm, A. G. Edwards, Enterprise Rent-a-Car, ServiceMaster and Bright Horizons Family Solutions. That circle provides sketches from life for his book on leadership -- far-sighted executives like Scott Cook of Intuit, Benjamin F. Edwards III of A. G. Edwards and S. Truett Cathy of Chick-fil-A. "These businesses structure themselves in a way that would make it logical that you would commit to them," Mr. Reichheld said. "The way people are treated, the principles they run on, the real results, are worth that commitment." Among other things, "they align people's interests, so that if the team wins, they drag along everyone who contributed." His favorite instance is Chick-fil-A, the fast-food chicken chain, which is based in Atlanta. Its store operators put up only $5,000 and pay the parent company 15 percent of sales for various services. Above that, parent and operator split all the profits 50-50. Incomes of $100,000 or more are common; a handful of operators earn $300,000 or more, typically from two outlets. By contrast, the competition might pay $40,000 or $50,000. "Chick-fil-A -- they celebrate when their people do well," Mr. Reichheld declared. In his view, Mr. Cathy, who founded Chick-fil-A, got it exactly right: "There is no way in heaven he can get rich unless his store operators get rich." And Mr. Cathy is quite rich. Four years ago, Mr. Reichheld's first book, "The Loyalty Effect" (Harvard Business School Press), debunked the notion that loyalty was dead. It also put loyalty economics on the map. It showed, for instance, that when a brokerage house improved its retention of brokers to 90 percent from 80 percent, it more than doubled the potential value of a new hire. For one credit card company, a 5 percent increase in customer retention translated into a 75 percent increase in the average customer's lifetime value to the company. Typically, a customer generated $40 in profit the first year, $106 in the 10th and $161 in the 20th. Customers who stick around tend to buy more, are much cheaper to serve, bring in friends as referrals, and accept premium pricing. Over the years, that all compounds. "In the old world," Mr. Reichheld said, "you can have medium loyalty and still make a buck," protected by a convenient location or the customer's lack of information. In the Internet world, there will be no place to hide, no substitute for earning high loyalty. "The economics are going to be obvious," he predicted. "People are going to be forced to do the right thing or get out of business." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: No matter what else changes, Frederick F. Reichheld says, "If you don't earn your customer's trust, you won't make money on the Internet." (Rick Friedman for The newyork Times)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
The Beautiful and the Panned
body: Before any look back at the creative output of Madison Avenue in 1999, let's get this out of the way: Dot-com. Dot-com. Dot-com. Dot-com? Dot-com! As the year raced by, the advertising frenzy for Internet marketers, offline as well as online, built to a fever pitch. Alas, the frantic efforts to get consumers to notice the dot-coms produced some of the most tasteless ads ever to appear in the mainstream media. Mercifully, the vulgarity was sometimes eclipsed by hilarity, as discerning advertisers and agencies realized that the funny bone can often be the human anatomy's most sensitive part. What follows is a recap of the bright lights and burned-out bulbs of the year. The shining moments are first, in alphabetical order. AMAZON.COM The holiday television campaign for Amazon.com presented a chorus delivering paeans to online gift shopping in an affectionate sendup of early 1960's variety series like "Sing Along with Mitch." The jest was cleverly reinforced with period editing techniques and production values like the cheesy graphics superimposing song lyrics on screen. The subtle message: using high technology can be as easy as following the bouncing ball. Agency: FCB Worldwide, part of True North Communications. CRACKER JACK To reintroduce Cracker Jack snacks, now owned by the Frito-Lay unit of PepsiCo, a commercial conveyed the spirit of fun that once epitomized the venerable brand by deftly delivering wry sight gags. The best: a pony emerging as the prize from a make-believe package, the "really big bag." Agency: Goodby, Silverstein & Partners, part of the Omnicom Group. DOCKERS Though Levi Strauss cannot find the right formula to sell its denim jeans to younger shoppers, the company has reinvigorated sales spiels aimed at that market for Dockers khaki pants, with commercials ably blending sex appeal, music and humor. In one spot, the buff, boyish hero was doused repeatedly in a dunk tank to show how Dockers stand up under repeated washings. This campaign stood up under repeated watchings. Agency: FCB. GAP What is it about khaki slacks that inspired creativity? In addition to Dockers, Gap Inc. delighted consumers with a khaki campaign, this one a sequel to "Khakis swing," perhaps the best spot of 1998. As attractive dancers sashayed to go-go, country and soul tunes, viewers wondered whether "Khakis waltz" or "Khakis polka" would come next. Gap's holiday campaign also used music and dance to good effect as models cavorted to an odd medley of "Sleigh Ride" and "Ice, Ice Baby." The theme, "That's holiday," however, may have created a credibility gap among grammarians. Agency: in-house. M&M's The antics of the anthropomorphic characters that peddle the M&M's line of candies for a unit of Mars Inc. were never more delicious than in a commercial featuring the comic actor Patrick Warburton. This spot, like others in the series, toyed with the advertising convention of food products wanting to be consumed; Mr. Warburton admonished three M&M's noshing from bags corresponding to their flavors. "You don't eat your own kind," he scolded. "It's unnatural." Even after they switched bags, he remained unmollified, muttering a line that ought to become a "Seinfeld"-style catch phrase, "That's just disturbing." Agency: BBDO newyork, part of the BBDO Worldwide unit of Omnicom. MTVIt was a remarkable year for promotional campaigns by and for the MTV cable network owned by Viacom Inc. Commercials created in-house celebrated the power of music to overcome adversity. Spots by FCB spoofed so-called blaxploitation movies of the 1970's with soulful verisimilitude. Wacky ads by Fallon McElligott newyork City about an imaginary dysfunctional family named Jukka reminded viewers of MTV's off-kilter sensibilities. And a public service campaign, "Fight for your rights," made a powerful statement against hate crimes with a spot by Public Interest Productions for the Gay, Lesbian and Straight Education Network, which featured Judy Shepard, mother of the murdered student Matthew Shepard. MONSTER.COM A brilliant commercial, for the Monster.com job search World Wide Web site operated by TMP Worldwide, broke through the dot-com clutter without crudeness. The spot presented preternaturally prescient children voicing incongruously unambitious vocational aspirations: "I want to have a brown nose," "I want to claw my way up to middle management," "I want to be a yes man." It was a shrewd way for Monster to claim to be the source for the job you always really wanted. Agency: Mullen Advertising, part of the Lowe Group unit of the Interpublic Group of Companies. NIKE It was, as they say in sports, a career year for Nike Inc. after several seasons of inconsistent advertising. A stunning commercial saluted the dedicated jock, the core Nike consumer, with an unflinching presentation of scarred and injured athletes, who were serenaded with the song "You Are So Beautiful." Spots promoting the unitedstates women's soccer team captivated viewers with their dry wit. Baseball spots spoofed home-run mania by encouraging pitchers to learn to hit ("Chicks dig the long ball") and attributing superhuman powers to Ken Griffey Jr. Agencies: Goodby, Silverstein, soccer; Wieden & Kennedy, the rest. ONLINE TRADING Campaigns for three online stock brokerage services were effective as well as entertaining, a rare feat in the overcrowded dot-com domain. Spots for Ameritrade by Ogilvy One Chicago, part of the Ogilvy & Mather Worldwide unit of the WPP Group, took an audacious tack, using a geeky young pitchman who uttered phrases like "Let's light this candle" to liken investing online to rebelling against the Establishment. Commercials by Goodby, Silverstein for the E*Trade Group used the soft sell to remind investors that knowing when to buy may be less important than knowing when to sell (e.g., when that movie studio whose stock you own begins believing its own hype). And TD Waterhouse defied expectations with a campaign by Emmerling Post that actually forged strong connections between celebrity endorsers (Jackie Chan, Geena Davis, Phil Jackson) and the service they peddled. VOLKSWAGEN A commercial for the VW Passat, sold by Volkswagen of America, pleased viewers with its double punch lines. The spot depicted a man flirting with a woman whose car is stopped next to his at a traffic light. Punch line one: The man has a child in the car with him. Punch line two: She has a child in her car, too. Are they would-be adulterers? Single parents, free to flirt? A married couple driving separate cars? Look for the sequel, "Ships That Passat in the Night." Agency: Arnold Communications, part of Snyder Communications. Now here are 10 points of darkness, also alphabetically: AT&TPaul Reiser, unfunny in the final seasons of "Mad About You," also rings up wrong numbers in a campaign to promote long-distance calling plans for the AT&T Corporation. In the worst commercial, for the One Rate Seven-Cent Plan, he mercilessly mocked an actor speaking with a British accent. It's madness for ads aimed at international callers to portray xenophobia as a virtue. What's next, a campaign featuring John Rocker? Agency: Young & Rubicam Advertising. BUD LIGHT A surprising spate of tacky spots during Super Bowl XXXIII foreshadowed what consumers endured the rest of the year. For instance, Anheuser-Busch resorted to bathroom humor in a spot about two shoppers choosing between buying Bud Light beer or toilet paper. Agency: DDB Chicago, part of the DDB Worldwide unit of Omnicom. CNET A provocative campaign for Cnet Inc., a producer of online and television programming about computers and technology, was deemed so deplorable, it came to symbolize the excesses of dot-com advertising. If the commercial about a man's unexpected encounter with a proctologist didn't offend you, the spot with the fetal pig probably did. The outcry was loud enough to force Cnet to replace the campaign -- and the agency that created it, Citron Haligman Bedecarre. FORD FOCUS Live commercials for Focus, a new compact car sold by the Ford Motor Company, were dead on arrival. The freshness and spontaneity promised by Ford executives before the spots ran proved harder to find than Toyotas in Michigan, primarily because the TV networks required that scripts be submitted in advance. It didn't help that the production values made the spots appear taped. Agency: J. Walter Thompson, part of WPP. GAP Not every Gap campaign was a winner. Commercials urging "everybody" to wear cords, leather and vests were as dispirited as their khaki and holiday counterparts were energetic. The casts behaved like zombies who had exchanged their personalities for Gap gift certificates -- or jobs at Gap stores. Agency: in-house. HOTJOBS.COM According to an extravagant commercial, the "hot" in Hotjobs.com, an Internet employment service, referred not to the heat generated by the jobs available on its Web site but to the scantily clad young actresses, secretaries and bimbos that men can meet at work. Now there's a sure-fire strategy: alienate half your potential customers. Agency: McCann-Erickson Detroit, part of the McCann-Erickson World Group unit of Interpublic. JUST FOR FEET An appalling, insensitive commercial for an athletic footwear chain named Just For Feet stunned Super Bowl viewers. The spot showed a black Kenyan runner being treated like an animal, hunted, captured and drugged by white-hunter types. Just For Feet executives apologized and discontinued the commercial, blaming the agency, Saatchi & Saatchi Rochester, and suing for malpractice. Just For Feet recently filed for federal bankruptcy protection, encouraging those who believe karma is shaped like a boomerang. PEPSI ONE The Pepsi-Cola Company unit of PepsiCo is oh-for-two with campaigns for Pepsi One, a reduced-calorie soft drink. The introductory spots in 1998 were derided for a bombastic star turn by the brand's pitchman, Cuba Gooding Jr. A replacement this year, lamely copying the cult film "Reservoir Dogs," fared no better. The bad Mr. Gooding soon vanished from the campaign faster than his turkey, "Instinct," vanished from theaters. Pepsi-Cola executives denied he was dismissed. Sure, and Pepsi One outsells Coke. Agency: BBDO newyork. 7UP Cadbury Schweppes, desperate to recoup from two failed campaigns, ran commercials for its 7Up soft drink, carrying the theme "Make 7Up yours," that were replete with awful double entendres. It was a sad, shameful comedown for a brand once sold as a tasteful friend: "You like it. It likes you." Agency: Y.& R. Advertising. TRICON It was harder for Tricon Global Restaurants to generate sales from a campaign centered on "Star Wars: Episode I -- The Phantom Menace" than it was to find fans of Jar Jar Binks. Commercials that brought together characters representing the three Tricon fast-food chains -- KFC, Pizza Hut and Taco Bell -- proved sillier than Carrie Fisher's hairdo in the original "Star Wars." That helped doom the promotion, which "actually slowed momentum" for Tricon restaurants, the company's chairman conceded. But then, what else could be expected from spots showing a Colonel Sanders lookalike fighting alien invaders with a "talking" chihuahua and a perky young Pizza Hut employee? Agency: TBWA/Chiat/Day, part of the TBWA Worldwide unit of Omnicom. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: MONSTER.COM -- Mullen Advertising's spot for the job search Web site, right, has children express ambitions like "I want to be a yes man."; CRACKER JACK -- To reintroduce the venerable snack, Goodby, Silverstein's commercial, below, showed the prize from the "really big bag."; MTV -- Winners for the cable network included Fallon McElligott's dysfunctional Jukka family, above.; GAP/HOLIDAY -- An in-house campaign by the retailer, above, blended music and dance well.; GAP/CORDS -- An ad, left, urging viewers to wear cords featured a zombie-like cast.; TRICON -- TBWA/Chiat/Day's ad with characters from 3 chains, far left, fell flat.

title: Time of Turmoil at Willy Loman & Co.
body: For months, at work and in bed at night, Bob Carr agonized over the exodus of his insurance customers to Web sites that offered the same products at lower rates. Since 1980, he had sold pension plans and 401(k) programs to businesses for the Equitable Life Assurance Society, often making more than $100,000 a year in commissions. But by last year, his income had shrunk to an annual rate of about $60,000, mostly because of competition from insurance-related Web sites like Quotesmith.com. "It came to the point where I couldn't sleep and I couldn't envision myself getting up each morning and finding new clients," said Mr. Carr, 53, who lives in Westfield, N.J. So in November 1998, he quit in disgust, even though he had no job lined up. For six months, he searched for a sales position that would be "immune" from the Internet. Finally, in May, he landed one, with Parker Interior Plantscape, a company in Scotch Plains, N.J., that designs floral landscapes for office buildings and hotels. Now, instead of debating the benefits of whole-life versus term policies with customers, Mr. Carr consults with companies on whether palm trees or ficus will thrive better in their atriums. While acknowledging that he has no green thumb, Mr. Carr says he also has no fears that customers will abandon him for the Internet. "Nothing can happen that can cause me to lose sleep," he said. These days it is not just car dealers and retail clerks who fear for their jobs as the World Wide Web encroaches on their territory. Increasingly, people in traditional corporate sales jobs like insurance, hotels and newspapers and magazines are debating what will become of them as online selling takes off. Many of them, seeing what they view as the writing on the wall, are bailing out before they have to. Eventually, many will have to. Sales of business-to-business products through Internet-based corporate networks are expected to increase from at least $95 billion this year to $500 billion in 2002, according to the GIGA Information Group in Cambridge, Mass. That would eliminate the need for many of the calls that corporate sales representatives make to purchasing managers. "The lone-ranger salesman is getting rarer and rarer in the business-to-business world," said Neil Rackham, a consultant who wrote "Rethinking the Sales Force" (McGraw-Hill, 1999). "Face-to-face selling is very expensive, and because of that the Willy Loman becomes an expensive way to tell your customers about your product." The Internet poses a long-term threat to the entire sales profession, one of the biggest parts of the American economy. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, America's 14 million sales representatives make up 12 percent of the work force. Robert Davenport, a vice president with Hay Management Consultants in Jersey City, says that percentage has held steady for nearly 15 years, but he and others predict that it will fall into the single digits within five years, meaning that several million jobs, mostly in retail, will disappear as consumers switch to buying online. So far, corporate sales representatives have weathered the storm. But once big corporations get their online selling systems up to speed, or once the economy inevitably turns sour, John DeVincentis, a consultant based in Solebury, Pa., said, "then we will see some bloodletting." Michael Pusateri, who spent 10 years in sales for Marriott hotels, working as a vice president for sales and overseeing the company's e-commerce business, is also among those who have chosen not to wait and see how the new economy might affect their careers. In April, he left Marriott to join Proxicom, a Web development company in Reston, Va., as head of sales and marketing. He says he was lured to the new industry more by its income potential than by any immediate fears of losing his hotel job. Still, as he debated making the change, he remembers asking himself, "Do I stay in the marathon and get the silver ring, or do I jump now and try to get the brass ring?" He jumped, and it looks as if he got the gold ring. Since he joined Proxicom, where he has stock options, its stock has shot up from $13 to more than $90 this week. "If I lived my whole life at Marriott, I never would have made that much money," said Mr. Pusateri, who is 40. Stephen Powell took the leap from hotel sales to an Internet company, too, but for different reasons. He had spent 26 years working at hotel chains like Loews and Sheraton. But as more companies were swallowed up in mergers, his sense of loyalty to his employer was replaced by a dread of losing his job, and when Sheraton, a division of Starwood Hotels and Resorts, asked him to relocate from Atlanta to the newyork area, he took a buyout instead. Three months later, he became vice president for global sales at PlanSoft, an Internet company that provides hotel information for companies planning corporate meetings. Since then, Mr. Powell, 49, has persuaded several other experienced hotel sales representatives to join him, including Susie Lichenstein, who spent 13 years with Sheraton. "I'd rather be on this side of the fence than working in sales for a hotel company," said Ms. Lichenstein, who is based in Raleigh, N.C. "Once this type of product takes off -- and it could be 5 years or 15 -- you probably won't need all that manpower on the other side of the fence." That sense of uncertainty weighs heavily on some career decisions. Mr. Carr had misgivings about leaving Equitable, which he says treated him well, but he knew that the Web's impact on his income would intensify. "I'm middle aged," he said, "so the question becomes: Do I do something now and be comfortable and earn a good living, or do I try to hang on and get to 55 or 57 and it's too late to start something new?" He has not soured on the Web, though. He is using his new knowledge of plants to help design Parker's first Web site, and he has done some shopping online, though he admits to a twinge of guilt. "Some other salesman is suffering," he said, "because I can make my choice on the Internet." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Michael Pusateri joined Proxicom, a Web developer, after 10 years in sales at Marriott. title: Controls Sought For Drug Sales On the Internet
body: Clinton administration officials said today that they would ask Congress to regulate the growing sale of prescription drugs over the Internet. White House officials said President Clinton would ask for legislation requiring online drugstores to get approval from the Food and Drug Administration to operate. In addition, they said, he will ask Congress to beef up the agency's investigative powers and increase the penalties for online sales of prescription drugs without prescriptions. The proposals would also make it easier to stop online sales of unapproved drugs, counterfeit drugs and products promoted with fraudulent claims. No federal certification is now required for online pharmacies, and operating in cyberspace, many of them do not get the state licenses that are required of traditional drugstores. Policing online stores and their sales of prescription drugs has been difficult, federal officials say.  Dr. Jane E. Henney, the commissioner of food and drugs, said Mr. Clinton's proposal would create civil penalties of up to $500,000 for selling prescription drugs to an individual without a valid prescription or for operating without federal certification. Federal officials said they now had difficulty prosecuting online pharmacies, and they complained that fines were usually limited to $1,000 for a violation. Because so many online pharmacies are not licensed, it is hard to estimate their numbers. The National Association of Boards of Pharmacy, which represents state licensing agencies, said there were at least 400 online pharmacies, including many that prescribed drugs for customers who simply filled out questionnaires. To get F.D.A. certification, online pharmacies would need licenses in the states where they did business, would have to comply with state laws affecting pharmacies and would have to employ licensed pharmacists. As part of his budget request next month, White House officials said, Mr. Clinton will seek $10 million to hire 100 people and upgrade computer technology to investigate Web sites suspected of illegally dispensing prescription drugs. In an interview tonight, Dr. Henney said the proposals would screen out disreputable pharmacies and make it more difficult for people to get drugs they should not be taking. "The object of the whole proposal," she said, "is to make sure there's a strong safety net for patients." Dr. Jeffrey E. Shuren, a medical officer at the F.D.A., said the agency was investigating more than 200 Web sites suspected of selling unapproved drugs or selling approved medications without valid prescriptions. Under Mr. Clinton's proposal, the F.D.A. would be given the power to issue administrative subpoenas compelling online pharmacies to provide records for federal investigators. The administration said it would protect patients' privacy, but did not give details. William A. Hubbard, a senior associate commissioner at the agency, said: "Online pharmacies come and go daily. Some are fly-by-night operations. Some are located overseas." In a document describing its plan to regulate online pharmacies, the White House says the new federal rules would, in effect, piggyback on state regulations on the practice of medicine and pharmacy and would not replace them. If, for example, an online pharmacy based in Florida sold prescription drugs to consumers in newyork, the pharmacy would have to comply with licensing requirements in both states, federal officials said. President Clinton plans to announce his proposals this week. A White House official said: "Internet pharmacies are not all bad. Sometimes you can get access to quality prescription drugs at lower prices in a more convenient way over the Internet. The president's proposals are intended to target the bad apples who purvey fraud on the Internet." To order from an online pharmacy, a customer uses a computer to visit the company's Web site. Many sites offer information about drugs and diseases. Reputable companies insist on getting a prescription from the patient or the doctor. A recent study by doctors at the University of Pennsylvania said it was alarmingly easy for consumers to get prescription drugs without seeing a physician or a pharmacist. States have traditionally regulated the prescribing and dispensing of drugs, the study said. But several states have found it difficult to locate and prosecute online violators because the prescriber, seller and buyer may be in different states. Several state attorneys general have filed lawsuits against Web site owners, charging violations of state laws -- for example, providing drugs without a local pharmacy license or mailing drugs to minors. In some cases, drugs are sent from online pharmacies overseas, so it is difficult for federal and state authorities to take action against them. The Pennsylvania study found 86 Web sites that sold Viagra, the anti-impotence drug, without requiring a doctor's visit or a prescription. Twenty-two of the sites appeared to be based outside the unitedstates. Dr. Matthew E. Naythons, who is vice president of one of the best-known online pharmacies, PlanetRx .com, based in South San Francisco, questioned the need for more regulation "We are licensed to dispense drugs in all 50 states," Dr. Naythons said. "There are sufficient rules and regulations at the state level to govern the practice of online pharmacy. Legitimate pharmacies conform to those state regulations. To layer on another level of regulation, at the federal level, would seem to be unnecessary." Contrasting his company with some of its competitors, Dr. Naythons said: "At PlanetRx, we dispense medication. We don't prescribe it. We are like your neighborhood pharmacy, but we have 35 million to 40 million branch offices through desktop computers. We want to speak to your physician in every case, to verify your prescription, unless we get it through themail." But, he said, other companies are not always so scrupulous. "Some online pharmacies -- rogue sites -- prescribe and dispense," Dr. Naythons said. "You can log on, complete a brief questionnaire online and get Viagra or other drugs without seeing a doctor in person." The Food and Drug Administration established a Web page last week to give consumers information about buying drugs and medical products online. The agency's Web site is at www.fda.gov. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Dr. Jane E. Henney, the commissioner of food and drugs, talks of a "strong safety net for patients." title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Italian Directory Publisher Offers to Buy Office Supplier
body: Seat Pagine Gialle S.p.A., the Italian publisher of yellow pages that has expanded into online businesses, has offered to buy Buffetti S.p.A., which operates a chain of office supply stores, for 708.4 million euros ($718 million) in cash and stock. Seat's bid, made on Friday, would create a big European company in the growing market for electronic sales, focusing not only on individual retail purchasers but also on professionals, like doctors and lawyers, and small and midsize companies, which abound in Italy. It would be the latest step in the accelerating spread of electronic commerce, as companies pick partners to gain products, expertise and capital. Tiscali S.p.A., an Italian company that, like Seat, helped to pioneer free Internet access in Continental Europe, said last week that it was spending $101 million to acquire control of two French telecommunications companies: Nets S.A., which operates a glass fiber cable linking London and Paris, and A Telecom S.A., a provider of local phone service with potential Internet uses. Lorenzo Pellicioli, the chief executive of Seat, said that Buffetti, which has also been expanding online, "complements Seat in developing the Internet for professionals and small and midsize companies." Seat, based in Turin, in northern Italy, acquired Virgilio, one of Italy's leading Internet search engines, earlier this year. Its acquisition of Buffetti would be the next step in a strategy that it expects would lead to online operations accounting for at least 10 percent of revenue by 2002. Through Virgilio, Seat now offers links to companies selling products online and search tools for phone numbers. Seat expects its online businesses to account for 40 billion lire ($20.9 million) this year, compared with 27 billion lire ($14 million) in 1998. Buffetti, based in Rome, has been pushing out of its traditional over-the-counter sales and into online selling and has diversified the products it offers. Buffetti sells books and software online, and announced plans earlier this month to join an undisclosed partner in the financial services industry to sell insurance and banking products through its network of about 1,200 stores in Italy. The alliance with Seat will enable Buffetti to sell products online and give Seat access to Buffetti's ability to deliver products without using the unreliable Italian postal system. Shares of Seat rose 0.517 euro today, or 18 percent, to 3.43 euros. Buffetti rose 3.64 euros, or 26 percent, to 17.51 euros. In recent weeks, shares in Internet companies have surged on the Milan stock exchange as investors in Europe and abroad poured money into companies operating in telecommunications and related technology. Swept by this fever, shares of Seat rose more than 75 percent over the last month. In trading before Christmas, Seat was worth about 22 trillion lire, or $11.5 billion, roughly 80 times its profits. Yet analysts said its price could continue to rise. In a report earlier this month, Lehman Brothers Securities raised its price target for Seat to 3.05 euros, or $3.08, from 1.82 euros, and maintained an outperform rating for the stock. Based on share prices on Thursday, the last trading day before the bid was officially made, each package of 500 Buffetti shares, the minimum amount the Milan stock exchange buys and sells, would bring about 44 euros, or $44.57, in cash, and 2,735 shares in Seat. That represents a premium of almost 16 percent to Buffetti's closing share price. Though Internet use in Italy lags behind that in many other European countries because of the low number of households with computers and sparse familiarity with English, the Web's dominant language, experts expect it to surge in coming months as the sale and leasing of computers grows and Internet content in Italian increases.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: After Shaky Starts, News Organizations Gain Confidence on Web - Correction Appended
body: Minutes after The Seattle Times disclosed on Dec. 17 that a man with the makings of a fertilizer bomb in his car trunk had been arrested in Port Angeles, Wash., news sites across the World Wide Web were sprinting to deliver details. But no other site gave the Port Angeles arrest a showcase to match MSNBC.com, the news Web site that for the last year has consistently commanded the largest audience. A picture of the Seattle space needle dominated the home page, overlaid with the headline "Y2K Plot?" In slightly smaller type were the words "NBC News: Officials fear suspect was part of plan to bomb Seattle." A report by NBC correspondents popped up with links to the Web site of NBC's Seattle affiliate, KING-TV. Another link took the reader to a video report by an NBC correspondent. Another led to a map showing where, according to law-enforcement authorities, the suspected terrorist Osama Bin Laden had been active. The MSNBC.com report was an archetype of a new journalistic form and of the emerging values of general news sites as run by major news organizations. These include speedy, professional crafting of original material, multimedia options, clean packaging -- and lots of self-promotion. As they move from a cyberchildhood of experimentation and starry-eyed possibilities into a sometimes awkward adolescence on the Web, the nation's largest news organizations are getting more sure-footed. And as the news site with largest audience, MSNBC.com, a partnership of General Electric's NBC and Microsoft, is emerging as an exemplar of the new medium's new self-assurance. The site is also in sync with those who believe the verb "to brand" is not a neologism but an imperative; MSNBC.com puts the logo of one of its parents, NBC, on everything in sight. Meanwhile its other parent, Microsoft, puts links on its Web sites to let some of the biggest audiences anywhere on the Internet know that MSNBC.com is the place to go for news. "MSNBC is heavily branded," said Tim McGuire, who, as the senior vice president for new media at The Minneapolis Star-Tribune, is a professional connoisseur of online news packaging and a student of what does and does not work in news delivery on the Web. "When we come out the other side of this tube we're in, the big brands will be fine." But the site does not ride just on NBC's name or Microsoft's muscle. "One of the keys to this whole thing," Mr. McGuire said, is "using the information that plays to the medium's strength." "They've done some interesting things and are creating a new medium," he said. Of course, as he and other newspaper journalists say, broadcasters are more used to supplying continuous news updates. Among MSNBC.com's innovations, according to its editor, Merrill Brown, are elements like short news clips on breaking developments, taped in the site's offices in Secaucus, N.J., and a navigation scheme that creates direct paths among scores of pages on the site. Like CNN Interactive's sites, which MSNBC.com dethroned as the Web's most-visited news organization earlier this year, it is also quick to provide supplemental interactive graphic material. A recent example was an elegant montage that showed how genetic researchers deconstructed the DNA on chromosome 22. "The goal from the beginning has been to package the experience, instead of giving people endless lists of things -- which for many other news sites is the norm," said Mr. Brown, who has been editor in chief of the site since its start in 1996. But MSNBC.com does not live by content alone. The site's ties to the behemoth sites of Microsoft, which funnel news-hungry audiences its way, are the envy of its rivals. According to MSNBC.com's statistics, about a third of the site's traffic comes from the pages of MSN.com, the Web sites of Microsoft Network. In October, according to Media Metrix, a Web audience measurement firm, MSNBC.com had more than seven million "unique" visitors -- a measure of how many different computer users visited the site, regardless of how many times each may have returned. The October figure topped a previous high for news sites that MSNBC.com reached in July, the month that John F. Kennedy Jr.'s sudden death drew record news audiences on the Web. The October figure outstripped its rival CNN.com by about one million unique visitors -- though Scott Woelfel, the general manager of CNN Interactive, a unit of Time Warner Inc., says that CNN.com's visitors typically view more pages a visit than MSNBC.com's audience does. MSNBC.com, with a staff of about 185, has achieved its No. 1 rank chiefly by making deals with an array of partners. The list includes The Washington Post and Newsweek, the crime reporting site APBnews.com, the technology news provider ZDNet and a site specializing in cancer news called oncology.com. For partners like The Washington Post, MSNBC.com has an enviable heft. Chris Ma, the senior vice president of Washingtonpost.Newsweek Interactive, said, "We felt that we very much needed a partner who lived in this world to help shepherd our brand and our product into a multimedia realm." Newspapers with national reach, like The newyork Times and Gannett's USA Today -- which has the biggest audience of any newspaper, both in its print and online forms -- find their sites evolving with ambitions similar to those of the successful broadcast groupns' sites, like MSNBC.com, cnn.com and abcnews.com, a unit of the Walt Disney Company. They want to provide quality information and video across subjects that include financial news and science and sports, and they are trying to decide how best to do it. In the last two months, both The newyork Times and The Washington Post have moved to the 24-hour news cycle, establishing links with newsroom editors who channel dispatches to the sites during the day. The Times on the Web has also updated financial reports filed by a small financial news staff, operated by TheStreet.com, a Web operation in which the newyork Times Company has a 6.3 percent stake. Steve Coll, the managing editor of The Washington Post, said in a recent interview, "We see the Web as another edition of the newspaper." But, he added, "it is incumbent on us to make sure that as we add editions, we maintain a commitment to the same quality of work." Richard J. Meislin, the editor in chief of the Times's unit Times Company Digital, said: "Our gut instinct is going to be that people come to The newyork Times for news that is the quality of the newyork Times newspaper and they would like to have that throughout the day." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Business Day yesterday about Internet sites run by major news organizations referred imprecisely to the operations of the staff that provides financial news updates to The newyork Times on the Web and TheStreet.com. The staff is a joint venture of The newyork Times and TheStreet.com -- not operated solely by TheStreet .com, in which The Times also has a financial interest. Correction-Date: December 28, 1999, Tuesday Graphic   Photo: MSNBC.com commands the largest audience of news Web sites. Merrill Brown is its editor and chief. (Peter Yates for The newyork Times)(pg. C8)  Chart: "Pulling Ahead of Its Rivals" While the fortunes of other general news Web sites have been up and down, MSNBC's site has, over the last year, outdistanced many of its competitors. title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Many Year 2000 Worriers Starting to Close Up Shop After devoting months and sometimes years to raising consciousness about potential Year 2000 disruptions, many prominent worriers are folding up their tents. For example, Peter de Jager, the Canadian programmer who became a Year 2000 Paul Revere in 1993, has put Year2000.com, the popular Internet site he created, up for sale at eBay.com. "The crusade part of this is just about over," said Edward Yardeni, a Wall Street economist who still thinks there is a 70 percent chance that Year 2000 breakdowns will usher in a worldwide recession. "Now it's just a matter of what happens. There's no point in being alarmist anymore."    Page C4. More Moves Seen for 'This Week' Inside ABC News, staff members viewed last week's dismissal of William Kristol, the conservative commentator, as perhaps only an initial move in what most conclude is a long overdue reshaping of the network's faltering Sunday morning discussion program, "This Week." David Westin, above, the president of ABC News, removed the show's longtime executive producer in September. But ratings have continued to decline, and many producers and correspondents at the network think the main problem is the absence of a single anchor.    C8.  Web Retailers Discover Warranties Until recently, online buyers were spared the hard sell for extended service warranties. Now, retailers are looking more closely at warranty options. Not only can extended warranties generate more profit than the products they cover, but they give online merchants the chance to bolster what has generally been an anemic record of post-sale support. Helps to Wire East Timor While aid workers help East Timor's people build an economy and government from the ruins of the province, the United Nations Development Program sent an official to bring the World Wide Web to the capital and to begin designing the kind of national data network that is fast becoming vital to participation in the new information economy.    C2.  TV Station Adopts Web Format A cable television channel in Canada is trying to blur the lines between TV and the Internet. Its news screen has seven different fields of information, including stock prices, weather updates, headline news and a rotating selection of shots of area roads so that people can check traffic conditions. The idea is to provide information quickly, and so far the format seems to be successful in attracting viewers.    C8.  Publisher in Israel Is Indicted In the latest development in a circulation war gone wild, a newspaper publisher in Israel, Ofer Nimrodi, was indicted on charges of trying to arrange the murder of a witness against him in a wiretapping scandal.    C2. title:
E-Commerce Report;
More Internet merchants are awakening to a lucrative revenue-enhancement possibility: extended warranties.
body: FOR many consumers, there is nothing to love about buying extended service warranties. First comes the hard sell at the cash register, typically punctuated with a horror story about someone who was "saved by the warranty." If customers reject the warranty, the horror story lingers. If they accept, they contend with the aftertaste of a $200 high-pressure purchase. Until recently, online buyers were spared that experience, as most World Wide Web merchants had neglected to offer extended service plans. Now, however, retailers are looking more closely at warranty options, for several reasons. Not only can extended warranties generate more profit than the products they cover, but they give online merchants the chance to bolster what has generally been an anemic record of post-sale support. And if one believes the rhetoric of e-commerce sites offering extended service plans, the Internet may even make the buying process palatable for consumers. "There's no salesman in a plaid suit saying 'Hey, buy this warranty,' " said Rich Pournelle, vice president for marketing at WarrantyNow, which offers extended warranties in partnership with e-commerce sites. "The customer is much more in control." WarrantyNow and RevBox are among the first companies to offer warranties online, and though their businesses differ in significant ways, the basic approach is the same. Both companies provide Web retailers with the technology to sell extended warranties and to offer consumers a secure site where they can keep track of the warranties and get help with service. Through WarrantyNow, for instance, Wristwatch.com customers can buy a two-year, $70 extended warranty on a $1,500 Breitling 867 watch, covering theft or breakage due to "normal use." When buyers choose the coverage, they can record their warranty on WarrantyNow's Web site, where they can also process a repair claim or find local repair shops. According to Ron Goedendorp, WarrantyNow's chief executive, the company offers broader support for more complex products, like computers or consumer electronics. In those categories, customers can call a toll-free number or send an email message to get technical support. Mr. Goedendorp said that the company, which began operations in July, had signed up 13 merchants -- including Onvia.com, Wristwatch.com, and Miadora -- and 60,000 repair companies in the unitedstates. That network, he said, covers 97 percent of the ZIP codes in the country, and spans an array of product categories, including lawn equipment, fitness equipment and personal electronics. RevBox, WarrantyNow's chief competitor, began operations last month, and so far has signed up two merchants, according to James Wu, the company's chief executive. It, too, covers a wide range of product categories, and it has 33,000 repair shops within its network. Mr. Wu said that RevBox also offered warranties on products not sold at merchant partners, as long as those products were still covered by the manufacturer's warranty when the extended service plan was purchased. Mr. Wu said that the company would stress two features as it vied for consumers and merchant partners. First, he said, the site and its merchant partners would compete aggressively on price. Second, it would offer extensive additional information about product warranties and user manuals. Analysts and executives said retailers typically earn profit margins of 30 percent to 75 percent on extended warranties. Mr. Wu declined to say what margin RevBox would seek, but he said that the company's merchant partners would charge significantly less than other retailers. For example, the company recently offered a two-year extended warranty on a Compaq Presario 1685 notebook computer for $80, while CompUSA and WarrantyNow charged $199 for a similar plan. "We're an Internet company," Mr. Wu said. "We're funded to be aggressive." RevBox will also try to differentiate itself by offering more information on its Web site. Customers are automatically registered on the RevBox site when they purchase an extended warranty from a merchant partner, but they can also register other purchases at the site, regardless of where or when they bought the product or whether they bought a warranty. Once they have registered the model numbers of various products on a personalized Web page, customers can then avail themselves of warranty information on 55,000 products, as well as 10,000 user manuals from more than 5,000 manufacturers. "It's taken a lot of work to develop that," Mr. Wu said. "I suspect it'll take a long time for any competitor to catch up." Notably, RevBox also plans to chronicle the breakdown history of those products, and offer that data to customers as a way to research future purchases. Both RevBox and WarrantyNow are selling what amount to wholesale insurance and service plans. When WarrantyNow users make a claim on a damaged product, for instance, they are actually relying on one of several "third-party administrators," which for years have offered post-purchase support services to offline retailers. The warranties of those third-party administrators are themselves underwritten, typically by large insurers. RevBox, on the other hand, resells the warranty and service offering of one company, Federal Warranty, a unit of the Fortis Group. The extended warranties offered off line by retailers like Macy's, Tandy and CompUSA often originate with Federal Warranty, Mr. Wu said. Since RevBox plans to sell warranties at prices below Federal's other partners, he said, "it's a bit of a delicate situation." Both the prices and the approach of online warranty sites could change the way consumers approach extended service plans, said Robert Brown, the chief marketing officer for Techsumer, a company selling consumer electronics and computers online at www.techsumer.com, and selling extended warranties through RevBox. "Let's be real honest," Mr. Brown said. "Everybody knows that not all warranties will be redeemed, so we recognize there's the opportunity for profit here." But the lower prices from RevBox will not necessarily translate to lower revenue for retailers who sell the warranties, he said, because lower prices should translate to higher sales volume. Mr. Brown cited other factors that he said boded well for higher online sales. Not only would consumers be more informed about warranties when they buy, for example, but the online services of sites like RevBox mean consumers would be less likely to lose track of warranty slips, and more likely to stay informed of the warranty's benefits, he said. "We might get more people opting in to these warranties, so even if there's a higher redemption rate, our net revenue could be higher as a result," he said. More important, Mr. Brown said, is the fact that extended warranties allow Web sites to offer "better customer service, by educating them about what the products do, and giving them options for additional support if they have an issue." According to Chris Martins, an analyst with the Aberdeen Group, this realization in itself is a big step forward for Internet retailers. "A lot of the original focus in e-commerce was up to the sale; after that, the attitude was 'It'll get handled,' " Mr. Martins said. "This allows retailers to provide a more complete sales experience, as well as give themselves a revenue opportunity -- which they could use." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Ron Goedendorp, chief executive of WarrantyNow, said the company, which sells extended warranties on products from lawn and fitness equipment to jewelry to personal computers, has signed up 60,000 repair companies covering 97 percent of ZIP codes. (Peter DaSilva for The newyork Times)

title:
Market Place;
Technology Bankers Work To Give Merrill A Silicon Shine
body: WHEN the Goldman Sachs Group and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter announced upbeat earnings news last week, a cheer could be heard in Silicon Valley. There, both Wall Street investment banks have flourished, riding the wave of dot-com companies that have enriched themselves by offering shares to a rapacious public or selling out to each other. But in recent years, another big Wall Street name has been conspicuously scarce in the Silicon Valley gold rush: Merrill Lynch. The firm's sideline status has been puzzling, given that as much as one-quarter of the revenue generated by investment banking departments these days comes from advising technology companies on mergers and public stock offerings. So why has Merrill largely missed out on technology bankers' big bull market? To hear Merrill Lynch explain it, the firm has not missed out at all; it simply got a late start. Tom Davis, executive vice president of Merrill's corporate and institutional client group, said the company was only three years into a multiyear effort to expand its technology presence worldwide. "We are at the beginning of what is a long secular shift in the economy," Mr. Davis said. Of Merrill's strategy, in particular, he said, "I think we are at the early stage of this game." Of course, technology executives have heard that before. When Merrill set up an office in Palo Alto, Calif., in 1996, it was the third attempt to crack Silicon Valley's clubby community, after abortive efforts in the 1980's and early 1990's. Mr. Davis said the company had been too busy expanding other departments to focus much on technology in those days. Given its relatively late start, Merrill has made a respectable showing this year. According to Thomson Financial/Securities Data, Merrill ranked fourth in taking new technology companies public in 1999, as measured by the amount of money raised. That is a far cry from 1997, when it did not even rank among the top 20. Merrill's total of $2.2 billion in technology underwriting this year, as calculated by Thomson, gave the firm a market share of 7.8 percent through Dec. 22. Those numbers do not tell the full story, though. That is still only about half the market share of more influential rivals like Morgan Stanley, Credit Suisse First Boston and Goldman Sachs -- which rank first, second and third, respectively, in Thomson's lineup. And with the exception of the Internet Capital Group, a Merrill loyalist that invests in Internet concerns and which Merrill took public in August, Merrill has yet to attract the roster of superstar companies that their larger competitors have. Investors in Goldman and Morgan have been handsomely rewarded this year, in part, because of their prowess in the technology sector. Goldman's share price is up 53 percent since the firm went public in May; Morgan's is up 85 percent for the year. Merrill's share price, though, is up only 17 percent. "It is not clear to me that they are going to make strides quickly enough," Steven Galbraith, an analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein & Company, said of Merrill. The concern, Mr. Galbraith said, is that by the time Merrill might catch up in technology, the market will have moved on to the next hot sector. Some analysts have said that when merger talks between Merrill and the technology investment boutique Hambrecht & Quist broke down two years ago, Merrill missed a ripe opportunity to increase its presence in technology underwriting. Merrill suffered blows, too, with the loss of high-profile executives like its president, Herbert M. Allison Jr., a favorite in Silicon Valley who left the firm earlier this year and joined the ranks of political fundraisers, and, more recently, Scott Ryles, head of technology investment banking, who had helped build that practice. Mr. Ryles left last month to become chief executive of a new online investment bank backed by Charles Schwab. What is more, Merrill has not been a believer in the "star system," Mr. Galbraith said. Having a name-brand stock picker, like Mary Meeker, the celebrated Morgan Stanley analyst who helped put that Internet practice on the map, is essential, he argues. On that count, though, Merrill may now be trying to cultivate a rising star. In February, it hired a 33-year-old CIBC Oppenheimer analyst, Henry Blodget, who went way out on a limb last year by predicting that Amazon.com would hit $400 a share -- a target the stock not only reached but surpassed. Hiring Mr. Blodget, who has quickly gained a Silicon Valley following, is simply one indication of the way Merrill Lynch has expanded its technology research effort, said Steve Milunovich, the firm's global team coordinator for technology research. "I'm a big believer that changing perception is hard," Mr. Milunovich said. "Our perception is probably better outside the valley than in the valley." Certainly, Merrill's perception problem was not helped by comments one of its top executives made about the Internet last year. A Merrill vice chairman, John Steffens, was criticized after newspapers quoted him as saying that online trading was akin to gambling and a "serious threat to Americans' financial lives." Some in Silicon Valley took umbrage, suggesting that if Merrill did not understand the impact of the Internet on its own business, how could it understand theirs? When Mr. Steffens, who is known as Launny, subsequently began extolling the Internet, the perception that he was scrambling to recover from a faux pas only seemed to make matters worse. Mr. Davis said that Merrill had not lost a piece of business because of Mr. Steffens's comments. But others at the firm wonder how much potential business landed elsewhere. "We got tarred for that," Mr. Milunovich said. "There's no question that Launny's comments hurt." One of Merrill's best technology credentials has been serving as a mergers-and-acquisitions banker to the networking giant Cisco Systems. Merrill got the job because it is one of Cisco's largest equipment customers. Cisco has an in-house team that does most of the heavy lifting on its transactions, but Merrill has retained the client on merit. "They do a nice job and we've been pleased with the level of service," said Mike Volpi, Cisco's senior vice president for business development. Still, Merrill's career as a merger adviser has hit some snags. Merrill had a very close relationship with the At Home Corporation, a provider of high-speed Internet service for cable television subscribers. Merrill had helped take At Home public and arranged for subsequent financings. So it was not surprising the firm was tapped to advise At Home on its $6.7 billion stock-swap merger in January with Excite Inc. But the night before the Excite@Home merger was to be announced, executives at Excite noticed a problem: the total that At Home would pay in stock was lower than the agreed-to price. In effect, a miscalculation had been made in the documents, and At Home's board of directors had to be reconvened to vote again on the correct amount, according to George Bell, president of Excite@Home and the former chief executive of Excite. "We were up until 4:30 a.m., they fixed it, and we announced that morning," Mr. Bell said. "Because it wasn't our company, I can't say it was the bankers' fault." Whoever was to blame, industry executives say such last-minute mishaps are rare. Thomas Jermoluk, who had been At Home's chief executive, could not be reached for comment. But people involved in those talks say he and executives from the AT&T Corporation, which owned a large stake of At Home, were enraged at the time. And when the merged Excite@Home, led by Mr. Jermoluk, announced its acquisition of BlueMountain.com recently, it was not Merrill that was hired to advise on the deal. Mark Shafir, who is in charge of Merrill's technology merger department in San Francisco, was hard pressed to comment on the mixup with Excite and At Home except to say the terms were "discussed and vetted" with executives and their lawyers. "Unfortunately, there must have been some misunderstanding," he said. If the technology boom continues, as many analysts expect, Merrill may now bear watching. Executives there say that the firm's technology effort for the first time has the full backing of Merrill's management. And if the company can transform indeed itself into the stock-offering powerhouse that it is in other industries, the next few years could improve Merrill's standing in Silicon Valley. "Perception," Mr. Davis said, "lags reality." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "One Bull That Is Not Stampeding" Morgan Stanley Dean Witter's stock has soared this year, as has Goldman Sachs since going public in May. But in a great year for the markets, Merrill Lynch's performance has been rather ordinary.
