title:
MEDIA;
Toronto TV Station Adopts Web-Page Format
body: The Internet continues to change the face of the conventional media. Take the Toronto television market, where for the last 18 months viewers have been able to catch up on the news by turning to a 24-hour cable television station that looks more like a World Wide Web page than a traditional video screen. The cable station is Cable Pulse 24, or CP24, a subsidiary of Chum Limited, a Canadian broadcasting company. Its news screen has seven different fields of information, including stock prices, weather updates, headline news and a rotating selection of shots of area roads so that people can check local traffic conditions. A recent study by Rocky Mountain Media Watch, a media watchdog group that is often critical of local news coverage, praised CP24 for offering "without doubt, the most information-packed newscast in North America." The screen's resemblance to a Web page is not coincidental, Stephen Hurlbut, the station's vice president and general manager, said. "We want to blur the line between the news channel and the Web site," he said. The station plans to start a Web site in January. The idea is to give people information quickly. "It's designed for people who have busy lives," Mr. Hurlbut said. "They turn it on and get their 15-minute hit and they go off to work. This is utility TV for people in this city." So far, the format seems to be successful in attracting viewers. A year and a half ago, CP24 started out with about 800,000 people a week watching it. It now has a weekly audience of 2.2 million, making it the leading news channel in its market, Mr. Hurlbut said. Ratings have not yet translated to profits, though. The significant capital investment needed to start the station and the additional personnel needed to run it have kept CP24 in the red. But Mark Rubinstein, a senior vice president at Chum Television Channels, said that the new format offered the best possibilities for future business growth. "We are hoping we can turn this into a model of how television and the Web can be packaged and sold," Mr. Rubinstein said. "Our expectation is that new media and business opportunities will outstrip the traditional revenue channel." Mike McKean, associate professor of broadcast journalism at the University of Missouri, sees CP24 as a trailblazer. "As you start to see media converge and stations begin broadcasting digitally, you'll see more stations with that sort of information on the screen," he said. "People will have the option of turning those types of things off, especially as it becomes more interactive." And while he conjectures that older viewers may be more resistant to such approaches, he says that the television medium must adapt to the times. "There are many ways for the general audience to get information now, often more tailored to their needs," Mr. McKean said. "Television has got to figure out a way to present information in an appealing way." Not everyone agrees that television will be able to match the Web. Edward Tufte, author of three books on information design and professor emeritus at Yale University, says that dividing the screen up is helpful, but multiple fields of information on a TV screen cannot compete with the interactive features of the Web. "The really good channels on the Web just far outperform nearly any kind of television way of conveying information -- except moving information," Mr. Tufte said. "For data, the Web has been so much more effective." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo/Chart shows format used by Toronto television station.

title: U.N. Agency Is Bringing Timor Online (Horsemen in Mongolia, as Well)
body: With a legacy of violence and a quarter-century of repressive Indonesian rule, East Timor lacks almost all the essentials: adequate drinking water, health care, a working educational system. To that litany of need, add a contemporary essential: Internet access. So while aid workers help East Timor's people build an economy and government from the ruins of the province, the United Nations Development Program this month dispatched an official from Malaysia to bring the World Wide Web to the capital, Dili, and to begin drafting blueprints for the kind of national data network that is fast becoming vital to participation in the new information economy. "The network is the key," said Gabriel Accascina, manager of the United Nations Development Program's Asia-Pacific Development Information Program, who visited East Timor this month. "It's the one enabling factor today that is basically changing the way people think, changing the way governments operate and giving opportunities that weren't there before." For the Timorese, the information superhighway so often cited in technologically advanced places was a distant bit of geography early in September, when pro-Indonesian militias responded to an Aug. 30 vote for independence by laying waste to the territory. Now, everything -- the buildings, the port, the civil administration and the schools -- must be rebuilt, a task being overseen by the United Nations transitional administration in East Timor. The process could take take two or three years. While it is going on, a nation is to be created using the Internet as one of its building blocks -- something of a first. Mr. Accascina said the initial step was to establish an Internet connection from Dili via satellite to Singapore, giving the United Nations staff reliable access to email service. The next task, he said, would be to import the computer equipment needed to develop the first Web site operating from East Timor. The United Nations created the Asia-Pacific Development Information Program in 1997 to foster the use of information technology for social and economic development. From its headquarters in Kuala Lumpur, the program tries to help Asian governments and community groups develop their own information structures and adopt the policies and legislation for entering the electronic marketplace. There is a lot of work to do. Though Tokyo, Singapore and hongkong compete with each other as centers of Internet innovation, most of Asia still lacks either the telephone lines or the computers needed to get online. Only eight of every 1,000 Asians outside Japan use the Internet, according to estimates by the International Data Corporation, compared with 320 of every 1,000 Americans. "In countries like India and China, people can't afford to go online, and the geography makes laying down the infrastructure a pain," said Pete Hitchen, an International Data analyst in Singapore. Other obstacles abound. "There's regulation, there's infrastructure, there's language, there's a cultural thing as well," he said. Giving destitute countries the ability to tap into the Internet's American-style tumult may seem of dubious benefit. But Mr. Accascina says that Net access is an urgent priority in a continent that is home to nearly three quarters of the world's poor. Not only does the Internet create the potential for long-distance education and medical help, it enables producers in remote areas to offer goods and services on the global market, providing them a louder voice. Mr. Accascina, a 46-year-old Sicilian, followed a zigzag path to his role as the United Nations Development Program's high-technology missionary. The son of an engineer and a lawyer, and a certified pilot, he worked for the World Health Organization in India in the late 1970's. In the mid-1980's, Mr. Accascina went to California. He worked briefly for Microsoft, set up his own computer consulting firm and developed an interest in digital video. A software project for Unicef turned into a full-time job shooting a documentary in Albania, and in 1994 a stint in Fiji. In 1996, he joined the United Nations Development Program. The world organization, he said, hopes to eventually hand over to an East Timor government a fiber optic digital network that merges voice telephone calls with data transmissions. "This will be a great opportunity to leapfrog technology," he said. And although East Timor's homes and buildings were largely destroyed, Mr. Accascina said the militias left a surprising degree of infrastructure intact. Dili's power plant was torched, but electricity has been restored, he said. The cellular phone network seems to be operating. Attempts to burn down Dili's technical institute also failed, Mr. Accascina said, leaving behind laboratories and classrooms that he hopes will soon house an academy to train networking engineers -- part of a program that the Asia-Pacific Development Information Program began in August with Cisco Systems. The East Timor project is one of several by the agency that have started to bring the computer age to remote populations. In October, it helped set up the first Internet connection on Tuvalu, a self-governing atoll in the South Pacific. In June, workers from the United Nations Development Program helped establish the first Internet service in Bhutan, just as the Himalayan nation got its first television station. "For a landlocked country, information is a good commodity," said Henrik Holde at the development program's office in the capital, Thimphu, where efforts are under way to set up an Internet cafe. With per-capita incomes in the $400 range, few Bhutanese can afford Internet access, much less a personal computer. But by using microwave signals to carry the Internet to community centers in villages separated by mountains, Mr. Holde says health workers can take advantage of information on disease, and rice farmers can get better information on prices in India and Bangladesh. In contrast, Mongolia's people are spread over a largely flat area almost as big as Alaska, and most Mongolians live as nomadic herders. But thanks to heavy subsidies from the old Soviet Union, more than four of five Mongolians can read; periodically horsemen ride into a town to sell their meat and read newspapers flown in from the capital, says Atsushi Yamanaka, information and communications technology officer at the United Nations Development Program in Ulan Bator. The flights ended with the fall of Communism, so the United Nations has helped establish community email centers for the newspapers to be downloaded and printed out. Borderless communications is already paying off in India, with an increasing number of Western companies moving some back-office and data-processing functions there to cut costs or offer round-the-clock services, said Mark Leigh, president of business communications systems at Lucent Technologies in Singapore. GE Capital International Services, for example, performs some transaction processing outside New Delhi and Swissair, British Airways and Lufthansa have moved some data processing to Bombay. Still, there are those who doubt whether access to the global network will really benefit people who have yet to own a telephone and whose craftsmanship, however considerable, has not prepared them for the vexations of troubleshooting the personal computer. Realities like these have stymied past efforts in Africa and Latin America. Internet advocates reply that failure to set up networks for the poorest countries only keeps them poor. "You can't exclude these countries just because they're backwaters," Mr. Hitchen of the International Data Corporation said. "The Internet is becoming so important on a basic economic level you have to start looking at Internet adoption as a measure of development like you would televisions and telephones." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The United Nations' information program chief in East Timor, Gabriel Accascina, by a satellite dish. His first priority is email access. (Gabriel Accascina)

title:
ECONOMIC VIEW;
A Governor Leads the Charge Against Taxing the Internet
body: TO listen to Gov. James S. Gilmore III of Virginia, a conservative, tax-cutting Republican, the escalating debate over whether to make the Internet a permanently tax-free shopping zone is no contest. He brushed aside concerns that state and local sales tax revenue would dry up as shoppers fled the malls for the Web. He suggested that traditional retailers should stop whining about unfair competition from the Internet and start viewing the technology as an opportunity to build new markets. And he said the best economic strategy is to nurture the potential of the Web to preserve the competitive advantage that is the basis of the America's current prosperity. "I don't have the slightest interest in destroying the tax base of cities, states and counties," Mr. Gilmore said in an interview. "But there is an interesting philosophical debate going on here. Some politicians are basically saying that you have to have fairness and a level playing field. Since we're going to have a sales tax, we have to apply it to the Internet." That, Mr. Gilmore said, is precisely the wrong approach. "Government is entitled to the revenue it needs to provide services, but it is not entitled to reach into new areas to get revenues it doesn't need," he said. "Government is not entitled to a taxation windfall just because a new industry has emerged." If there were any doubts that the Internet is reshaping the economy in fundamental and far-reaching ways, they were dispelled this year, as dot-com stocks drove Wall Street, as the stodgiest of corporations embraced the power of the Web and as technology-driven enhancements in business efficiency startled Alan Greenspan and his colleagues at the Federal Reserve. But economic policy makers are only beginning to respond, and the political parties are just starting to recognize the potency of technology-related issues. No issue has had a higher profile in recent months than tax-free cybershopping, a perk (or quirk) of electronic commerce that millions of consumers enjoyed for the first time this holiday shopping season. Online shoppers usually must pay for shipping, but rarely pay any sales tax on goods bought from companies that do not have physical presence, like a store or a warehouse, in the state where they live. The issue has come up regularly in the presidential campaign. Both Al Gore and George W. Bush have said they favor extending the current moratorium on Internet taxation while the matter is studied, but are concerned about the fallout for state finances and traditional retailers. Most of Mr. Bush's Republican rivals want to make the moratorium permanent. It is a tough issue, raising questions of fairness and ideology without providing much middle ground on which a compromise can be built, and there are passionate voices on both sides. But no one argues the case against Internet taxation more vociferously or with greater certitude than Mr. Gilmore. He has built his political identity on tax cutting, and the state he governs is home to one of the most successful technology corridors outside California, with America Online among his many Internet-dependent constituents. Mr. Gilmore was chosen by Republican leaders in Congress to be chairman of a national commission studying the issue. Its latest meeting, this month in San Francisco, reached a deadlock between members who think applying sales tax to electronic transactions is both proper and technically feasible and those, like Mr. Gilmore, who think it would be a mistake and would anyway be too complicated to enforce. FOR starters, Mr. Gilmore said, there is no sign that online sales are coming at the expense of traditional retailers or are eating into state and local tax revenues. "The statistical data will have to come later," he said. "But at this point you only have to look into the stores and the malls and ask, 'How's business?' Business is booming. There is no evidence I can see that sales tax revenue is down or that commerce in traditional bricks-and-mortar retailing is down." The governor's message to traditional retailers, especially local stores, is to stop fighting the Internet and embrace it: "It's wonderful for small business. It's a dynamic development that gives small-business people the ability to broaden their bases and compete with big business." Mr. Gilmore acknowledged the importance of ensuring Internet access for the poor, so online commerce and its benefits will not flow only to those who can afford computers and monthly service fees. His bottom line is that because no one can foresee precisely how electronic commerce will develop or what its economic effects will be, the best policy is to bar the door to Internet sales taxes. But that same uncertainty might equally argue for a more flexible approach, one that does not prejudge where technology will drive an economy now changing in ways no one yet fully grasps. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING;
Behind a Thudin an Internet Stock Price
body: WHEN the InterTrust Technologies Corporation, went public on Oct. 27 at $18 a share, it was a model for a successful Internet start-up. A maker of software used to manage the sale of digital content like music, InterTrust has a clever business plan, strong partners and respected management. The shares took off, closing at $187.25 on Dec. 8, buoyed by positive analyst reports from three of the four brokerage firms that underwrote the offering. All investors had to do was wait for the bump-up in the share price when a fourth underwriter, Citigroup's Salomon Smith Barney, issued its report on the stock. Then, a bombshell. On Dec. 15, Salomon issued its report. But instead of serving up a buy rating, as underwriters almost inevitably do when starting coverage of a stock they helped to underwrite, Salomon gave the stock what it calls a 3S rating -- the equivalent of a lowly "hold." Hold is precisely what shareholders did not do. They sold with a vengeance, sending the stock down $33.375 in one day, to $121.6875, a plunge of more than 20 percent. The stock now trades at $124.8125. In the momentum-fueled world of Internet stocks, the event offered a reminder of how investors can punish those that receive anything less than exuberant plaudits. But it also offered insight into how analysts deal with the challenge of valuing companies in the evolving Internet market -- and the discomfort that some of them have with the notion of using those valuations to determine their recommendations. Richard Zandi, the Salomon analyst who wrote the report, praised the company's management, business model and potential to dominate its market. Indeed, Mr. Zandi says InterTrust's net margins may eventually rival those of Microsoft -- more than 40 percent. In the end, he says, his hold rating came down to his price forecast. According to his calculations, InterTrust should be trading at $170 a share in 12 months. Since the company was already trading at $155 at the time of the report, he concluded that it was already "valued to the vision." To arrive at his target price, Mr. Zandi estimated InterTrust's future market, prices, margins and eventual growth rate, and discounted the resulting earnings. Even a tiny change in one of the estimates could have had a huge effect on his price target. Indeed, valuing early-stage companies like InterTrust is, in the words of one analyst, "more art than science." And that is one reason that the other, bullish analysts disagreed with Mr. Zandi. For his part, Todd Raker, an analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston, Intertrust's lead underwriter, said he had moved away from assigning target prices to early-stage companies because of the uncertainty. "Doing a pure valuation call on early-market stocks is a very difficult task to achieve with any level of confidence," he said. "I think what investors should be focused on is finding very attractive business models that generate a lot of cash." Mr. Raker uses discounted cash flow analysis in his reports. But rather than coming up with hard numbers, he computes upper and lower limits on variables like market size and then comes up with a range of possible values for the stock. He estimates that InterTrust is worth from $58 to $200 a share -- an exceedingly wide range. He says his current rating, a strong buy, is justified because he believes his analysis to be conservative and because the stock is trading within his range. In another report, Raimundo Archibold, an analyst at J. P. Morgan, another underwriter, calculated a relative valuation for InterTrust. He took a class of similar companies, looking at their revenue multiples and long-term growth rates. That showed InterTrust shares could hit $214 in the near term and $562 in the next 12 months -- although he does not characterize those numbers as official price targets. (The fourth underwriter, Soundview Technology, called price forecasts "a challenge" but nevertheless cited a price target of $250.) MR. ZANDI said he had no regrets. "One thing I hear from people who wring their hands at these valuations is that it's ludicrous," he said. "But you have to do it -- you have to decide whether to buy and sell these things." He added that Salomon requires its analysts to assign price targets to stocks they cover. Some investors who are focused on the Internet are throwing up their hands at nebulous valuations. Peter Doyle, a co-manager of the Internet Fund, said he and his staff did their own research. "We don't really use Wall Street research in any measurable way, he said, "because the research tends to be very subjective." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: "Off Target?" tracks closing prices of InterTrust since Oct. 27. (Source: Bloomberg Financial Markets)

title:
INVESTING;
Quietly, Dot-Coms Rewrite Rules on Office Romance
body: A DATE. That's what Kate Hayes wants for New Year's Eve. Someone to clink Champagne glasses with. Someone to kiss at the stroke of midnight. So Ms. Hayes has been doing something she had vowed she would never do: She is actively pursuing a mate through work. For the past few months, she has told everyone she meets -- clients, colleagues, her superior -- that she is available. "I am so in the millennium-date fret mode," said Ms. Hayes, who is 25 and a director at Hireminds.net, an Internet and Web staffing specialist in Cambridge, Mass. "Some of my colleagues interview people who are prospective clients, and if I'm not representing them then I think I can date them. I feel out the situation: 'Hey, I heard about this party, why don't you go, it would be a great way for you to meet people.' " Ms. Hayes is among many young people at Internet and high technology start-ups using the workplace as a launching pad to find love. Not content with redefining other aspects of workplace culture, dot-com companies, often populated by the young and dedicated, are throwing out corporate rules that discouraged dating and fraternization among employees. But they are finding that writing the new conduct codes, which often allow relationships between a boss and an employee, is not so easy. People have always found romance on the job. According to a 1988 report by the Bureau of National Affairs, a private research group in Washington, one-third of all relationships begin in the office. And in a 1994 survey of of 485 managers and executives from Fortune 500 companies, the American Management Association found that 74 percent said it was all right to date a co-worker. Among the dot-com set, workplace dating is almost de rigueur. "For such a long time people would discourage any social interaction at work, but a lot of corporations are realizing that this is a dedicated work force, extremely hard workers," said Tiffany Shlain, 29, founder and director of the Webby awards, the Oscars of the Internet. Saying she was "a bit old-fashioned on a lot of things," Ms. Shlain added that she could see why allowing dating was necessary. "I've always cared to make sure my staff enjoys their work environment," she said. "You have to cater more to the needs of the people working for you. It would be cold-hearted and nearsighted not to create an environment they want." Mara Engel, a senior public relations manager at Excite@home, in Redwood City, Calif., agreed. "Dating isn't encouraged here per se, but it's definitely a social environment," she said. "It's not exploited -- people aren't running around holding hands and making out in the bathrooms -- but it exists. You really get to know people and you're working toward the same goal and it fosters romance. People work 10 hours a day in some cases. Your work becomes your life." Like their forerunners in Silicon Valley, many Internet companies hold happy hours or keg parties at the end of the week attended by both upper management and underlings. Partly because most people in such companies are around the same age, the boundaries of behavior can be blurry. JAMIE ARMISTEAD met his wife, Katherine, at Interactive Planet Inc., a privately held Internet development company in Atlanta. He was the senior account manager; she was an account manager. They sat about 10 feet apart. "Technically I was her boss," Mr. Armistead said. The company had only about 15 employees, "so there was some sensitivity to dating in the office," he said. The couple kept their romance secret until it became clear that it was becoming serious. Finally, they went to lunch with their boss -- Mr. Armistead's former college roommate -- and came clean. "I expected to lose my job," Mr. Armistead recalled. "It was his company, and he cared a great deal. His concern was being able to portray a professional work environment to our core client base. He didn't want us to work on the same accounts in case we had personal problems. It could have gone either way, but he said, 'Well, you're both very professional.' But he made it clear that we wouldn't be working on the same project." (Both have since moved to other companies.) According to Ethan Winning, a management consultant in Walnut Creek, Calif., who specializes in employee handbooks, policies and procedures, only about 10 percent of companies have written policies on dating and fraternization. But most employers, worried about sexual harassment claims, discourage managers from dating subordinates. They may also separate couples, transferring one person to another part of the company, requiring one to report to a different manager or even asking one to resign -- especially if they marry. At Internet start-ups, where there are often fewer than 30 employees, such moves can be impractical. And some employers have another rationale for allowing dating: they believe that happy employees are productive, too. But some workers and companies have found that the new attitude can cause problems. Lori Park and Lisa Bongiorno each recently filed a $10 million lawsuit in newyork State Supreme Court against Juno Online Services of Manhattan and a senior manager. Each woman contended that the company allowed a sexually hostile environment and that she had been sexually harassed by a manager. Ms. Park, 25, who was a software engineer at Juno, said she dated Matthew Battles, a senior vice president, for the year and a half she was there. Ms. Bongiorno, 28, who was an account executive, said she was romantically involved with the senior vice president for strategic marketing, Jordan Birnbaum. "When I first got there I didn't want to be involved with dating in the office," Ms. Bongiorno said. "But I was told that once I got used to the Juno environment, I would soon see that dating was acceptable and encouraged." She worked at Juno from February 1997 through February 1999, when she was dismissed. She blames Mr. Birnbaum. Mr. Birnbaum and Mr. Battles declined to comment last week, according to the company's public relations representative, Howard Rubenstein Associates. In a statement, Juno's general counsel, Richard Buchband, denied all accusations in both suits. He said that Ms. Bongiorno's case was dismissed in October on technical grounds and that it was without merit. He said Ms. Park had been treated in a "professional and lawful" manner; Ms. Park's suit is pending. "Our firm has strict policies and procedures to protect our employees against any mistreatment in the workplace," Mr. Buchband added. Ms. Bongiorno is appealing her suit's dismissal. Ms. Park, who now works at another Internet company, said she had been terrified to break up with Mr. Battles for fear of losing her job. "A lot of people were dating within the company, and it's a bad idea because people treat you differently," she said. "I felt that everyone was trying to get on my good side or say things to me to get to Matt. You can't legislate workplace dating, but I wouldn't do it again. It makes your private life totally public and if your lover is more important than you, you never know what they're going to do to you. And it's your livelihood and your career." MR. WINNING, the management consultant, called dating within an office "the worst idea you can possibly come up with." "Companies, in general, don't want to talk about this," he added. "They'd rather talk about their salaries than dating." Mr. Winning, who has written behavioral guidelines and rules of conduct for dot-coms and high-technology companies, wishes that more young companies would adopt written employment policies. "They think they're very progressive in Silicon Valley, Boston, newyork or Minneapolis," he said. "They're all very young and they don't care what their employees do." He said couples should be aware of the pitfalls of intra-office dating. "You can always say that a dating relationship interferes with the work flow," he said. "You know how catty people are, what the rumor mill is like. And the breakup of a relationship -- marriage or not -- can tear an organization apart. The company does have a right to protect its interest, even without a written policy." Right now, however, there are other things on the minds of many young people -- like the more pressing issue of a New Year's date. "I go to tons of Cyber Brew parties and I always mention that I'm single," Ms. Hayes said. "I can put a spin on it that makes it business-related, so it's also business-motivated for me, because when I go to a party I'm socializing but also networking. Even if it's a bum date, I still get work." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Katherine and Jamie Armistead kept their romance a secret at Interactive Planet Inc. in Atlanta. Eventually, they told their boss, who discouraged work on the same projects. (Jenny Thomas for The newyork Times)

title:
Practical Traveler;
Tighter Security For Web Buyers
body: THE Internet has been a boon for wired travelers with the patience and savvy to surf for good deals, but it can also leave unwary travelers in a highly precarious position. This year, for example, a technical administrator for an Internet service provider in Seattle discovered that hundreds of Web sites had left their customers' credit card information completely exposed to anyone with an Internet connection. Among those sites was a travel company that arranged trips to Cancun; so not only could thieves use the card but they could also find out a family's travel plans and visit the empty home while they were away. Executives of travel Web sites are quick to point out that no such thefts have been reported, but the mere threat continues to vex Internet users. Jupiter Communications, a newyork-based research firm, says that 17 percent of online shoppers surveyed are "extremely reluctant" to use credit cards online. But the situation is improving, as technology companies and travel sites continue to roll out features and policies meant to protect customers from fraud -- and as consumers become more accustomed to online buying. The most popular travel sites now give customers myriad ways to pay for tickets and secure reservations, while also paying the first $50 of any fraudulent misuse of credit cards (credit card issuers are liable for the rest). And every reputable online travel site features secure sockets layer (SSL) transactions, which encrypt credit card data while in transit, virtually guaranteeing safety. Safe 'Neighborhoods' "On the Internet you can't tell when you're in the bad part of town," said Terrell B. Jones, president of Travelocity (www.travelocity.com), which announced a merger with Preview Travel (www.previewtravel .com) in October. "Everything looks just about the same, so we have to convince people we're a safe place to do business. And that's especially true when you're selling a $280, nonrefundable electronic ticket. People don't want to make a mistake." Mr. Jones said that Travelocity saw a measurable difference in sales last year when it posted a notice telling consumers that they would not be liable for the first $50 of any credit card misuse, if the card issuer did not cover it. "We also told consumers they could call in their credit card numbers if they weren't comfortable giving them online," he said. In addition, the company allows consumers to mail or fax credit card numbers to secure reservations. "Somehow people think a fax is an unbreakable secure encryption system, which it isn't, but that's O.K., it's what they're comfortable with," he said, noting that about 50 people a day phone or fax their numbers. Analysts and executives say it is now common for the better-known travel sites to offer the option to phone or fax credit-card numbers. But most travel sites will not honor a personal check. Airlines cannot hold seats based on a personal check because it can take several days for bad checks to be reported, during which time the airlines cannot sell the seats to other buyers. "And they don't want a 7-year-old booking a flight on the Concorde, which happened once," Mr. Jones said. Travel sites are also sweetening the pot to encourage reluctant shoppers to part with their credit card numbers online, mostly because sites know how much cheaper it is to process a reservation online. Companies can pay $25 or more in overhead every time a customer service representative answers the phone. Thus the deluge of online travel incentives: the Hotel Reservation Network (www.hoteldiscount.com), a Dallas-based service that books hotel rooms nationwide, is offering rebates up to $50 this month for reservations made completely online; through April 30, United Airlines (www.ual.com) is giving 3,000 miles upon each customer's first online booking, plus the standard 1,000-mile bonus for each online purchase. Sites are offering other forms of encouragement as well -- most notably convenience. Online travel companies have made it easier than ever to complete transactions, in part because they now offer a degree of personalized service that's almost unsettling. For instance, Expedia (www.expedia.com), Travelocity's chief competitor, allows registered users to create a file of travel preferences for everyone in the family, including frequent flier numbers, seating and food preferences, disabilities and age (in case anyone qualifies for discounts). Expedia will also store a user's home airport the first time a trip is booked through the site, which, when combined with the travel preferences and credit card information stored by Expedia, can whisk users through a reservation in three to four clicks. Travelocity boasts the same capability, and both sites go to great lengths to assure that personal information will remain confidential. Travelers who are either too leery of storing personal information on multiple travel sites or don't want to spend the time typing it in are candidates to use an increasingly popular online technology called the "digital wallet." These wallets allow users to store their information either on their computer or on a secure Internet site, where it can be used to fill in forms with one click. Two of the more popular wallet devices are offered by eCode (www.ecode.com) and Gator (www.gator.com), each of which provide the service free. ECode, based in Santa Clara, Calif., stores a user's personal and credit card information -- as well as log-ins or passwords for sites requiring registration -- on the company's secure server. Whenever users confront a blank form on any site, they click a button and their relevant information is instantly sent -- encrypted -- to the site. Gator, which has compiled hundreds of thousands of users in a few months, stores your information on your computer. Frequent travelers must store it on laptops to use a digital wallet on the road. Downloading a Wallet With both Gator and eCode, users must spend a few minutes downloading the wallet software, which does not work with a Macintosh. Wallets only help fill out the transaction forms -- ticket returns or any other issues arising from the purchase must be handled directly with the merchant. And these wallets don't yet store the more-complete dossier of information that travel sites typically do. But that may change quickly, as technology improves. "Our vision is for Gator to evolve into a general purpose assistant," said Jeff McFadden, the company's chief executive. "So if you're on United Airlines' site looking to book a trip to Bermuda, Gator could recognize that and say 'Hey, would you like me to check all the rest of the airline sites for a better rate?' " Gator, based in San Mateo, Calif., was begun last year by Mr. McFadden and a team of entrepreneurs, who began offering the service to consumers in June. Since then, Mr. McFadden said, the company's electronic wallet has been downloaded by hundreds of thousands of people. ECode is used by more than 100,000 people, said Rohit Chandra, the company president, who founded the firm in 1997. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Robert Neubecker)

title: The Internet Wears Out Its Welcome
body: E-NUFF already. It is the surest sign that the Internet is totally mainstream: Everyone is tired of it, not just the sleep-starved workers at dot-com startups, but everyone -- man and beast alike. Turn on the television and you are assaulted by an endless parade of jabbering advertisements for e-commerce companies. Newspapers are so bloated these days with ads for dot-com marketers that dogs across the nation must be loosening their teeth and straining their necks to fetch them. The latest sign of the times was Time magazine's selection last week of Jeff Bezos of Amazon.com, the big online retailer of everything from books to toys, as its "Person of the Year." Time's cover headline declares, "E-commerce Is Changing the Way the World Shops." Inside is a large picture of Mr. Bezos' face, doctored with a white "e" inserted in his left eye. "An Eye on the Future," says the accompanying headline. Though Mr. Bezos is worth $10 billion, he doesn't really care about the money, Time says. And a Time reporter says that Amazon's workers are "all imbued with this giddy faith that their best days lie ahead of them." Innovations in technology and communications -- the telegraph, telephone, automobile, airplane and others -- have often touched off waves of optimism and exuberant claims about how the new thing is going to transform society. In the 1920's, for example, as the airplane moved beyond the Red Baron stage and started to become used for carrying civilian passengers, there was a lot of talk of every household having a personal airplane in its garage. That strain of euphoria was called "air-mindedness." Technology historians remain skeptical that the Internet age can match the period from about the 1880's to 1910 in terms of its impact on people's lives. Inventions and new products from that period of technological dynamism included Bessemer steel making, refrigeration, the light bulb, the phonograph, the telephone, the radio, the automobile and the airplane. Still, the historians say, there does seem to be one truly distinctive feature about the present. "I don't think there has ever been anything like the Internet and cyberspace craze in terms of media hype," said Robert C. Post, a technology historian and a former curator at the Smithsonian Institution. The use and abuse of a single vowel -- "e" -- also seems without precedent. And I.B.M. is largely to blame. Since Lou Gerstner took over in 1993, I.B.M. had been trying to give its image as a mainframe dinosaur a makeover. By 1995, it was apparent that the Internet was the future, and the company began promoting itself first as an expert in "network-centric computing," then "network computing" and then "Internet solutions" -- before settling on "e-business" in fall 1997. Rivals scoffed at first, and then scurried to copy I.B.M. when the marketing campaign caught on. By now, all the Internet stories seem familiar -- of dot-com millionaires, or billionaires, of young people fleeing business schools, investment banks and consulting firms to join the Internet gold rush. Mike Ruettgers, the president of EMC, which sells the big data storage equipment used by so many e-commerce companies, was rummaging through his briefcase recently and pulled out a family picture. It showed his daughter at newyork's Metropolitan Museum of Art, where she worked. Still there? "Nah, she's 24 and went off to join a dot-com company like everybody else," Mr. Ruettgers replied in a tone that suggested he was belaboring the obvious. Things could get more interesting if, as some analysts predict, there will soon be a Darwinian winnowing among dot-com companies who have bet so much of their venture capital money on ads to try to become brand names during the do-or-die holiday season. The winners will play on, while the losers will have little to show for it and scant chance of raising more money. "These companies are burning enormous amounts of cash, and there will be a massive shakeout in the new year after it becomes clear who did well and who didn't," said Michael Hansen, an e-commerce specialist at the Boston Consulting Group. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The restroom at Alt.Coffee, a newyork cyber cafe. (Fred R. Conrad/The newyork Times)

title: These Mobile Computer Doctors Do Make House Calls
body: INEVITABLY, whenever Sydney Stanton's children and grandchildren come to visit the same thing happens. "After they leave, my computer is not the same," she said. "They change everything around. This last time I couldn't find my address book." It is not that Ms. Stanton's children are computer incompetents. On the contrary, her son runs a computer graphics business in London, and her granddaughter is a science journalist. Ms. Stanton, a freelance writer in Rye Brook, N.Y., is also computer competent, yet when faced with a recalcitrant computer and a deadline, she puts in an emergency call to the Computer Tutor-PCI in Bronxville. "Within two hours Rick Harder arrived and fixed everything," she said. "He specializes in Macintosh, so when I needed a new modem, he helped me select it, and he installed it. I call him my computer doctor." But unlike most doctors, these computer specialists make house calls, including to Manhattan and Fairfield County. Jim Mulcahy, the company president, and Mr. Harder, his associate, call on customers in their office on wheels, a black sedan with the company's logo and a license plate that Mr. Mulcahy is especially fond of: C DRIVE. But fixing computer problems is only one of the things Computer Tutor does for clients. The company also helps customers buy the right computer for their needs and teaches them how to use it. Ann Petersen of Bronxville was not exactly computer challenged either. She was comfortable doing word processing on her Macintosh, but she and her husband, Hollis, travel often, and when she wanted to go on the Internet to search the Web for travel and tourist information, she had to upgrade. "I was frantic that I'd lose all my data when I upgraded from Mac to a PC," she said. "But Jim did it for me without a hitch. Then with Jim I upgraded again, to Windows 98 and gave my hand-me-downs to my husband." Not long ago, she explained, her husband was happy with only his typewriter. "He didn't want anything to do with a computer," she said. "Then, surprisingly, when I gave him my old Mac, he was happy with it -- for a while." Eventually, she said, Mr. Petersen became so enamored with the capabilities of her PC that he was spending more and more time at her computer researching the stock market. "I could never get on the Internet," she recalled. "In the interest of saving our marriage, we got a second PC, and it was easy -- no tears -- with Jim's help." Help, priced by Mr. Mulcahy, is $75 an hour in Westchester south of Route 287, then it increases to $90 north of Route 287. Calls to Manhattan or to Westport are billed at $100. Mr. Mulcahy said that one of the most important services his company provides is very basic. "We start at the beginning by helping people buy their computers from one of the big mail-order houses," he said. "It's done via a three-way conversation lasting from 45 to 60 minutes. We ask a lot of questions, quizzing the customer carefully, so we can advise him on what is right for him. Then we call Dell or Gateway or Compaq and place the order for the computer, which will come in approximately 15 percent less than buying it retail at a store." The growth of the computer mail-order business has been so strong it has caused major retailers like CompUSA, based in Dallas, to cut down on hardware inventory and close some of its stores, Mr. Mulcahy said. "Rick and I both worked at CompUSA in Norwalk," he said. "And we saw a lot of customers who were very new to computers and needed a lot more than the technical information we could give them on the selling floor. People didn't know much about installation, and they certainly didn't know how to solve the problems that occur two or three months down the road." Mr. Mulcahy said he felt he had discovered a niche that had the potential for a business. He reasoned that his service would have to be mobile, since on-the-spot repairs were essential. He forged ahead, financing the startup with credit cards in the amount of $8,000. The business turned a profit in the first year, encouraging him to expand. Mr. Harder, a graphics artist, and an Apple expert, joined him as an associate. Ideally, tutoring starts shortly after the computer has been delivered. Home-based offices account for about 70 percent of Computer Tutor's business. About half the company's customers are people older than 50, including several clients in their 80's and a woman older than 90 who wanted "to keep up with the times." Not everyone who telephones can become a Computer Tutor client, however. "We ask questions," Mr. Mulcahy said. "And not everyone qualifies." For example, people like the man who wanted to activate his son's computer, abandoned 10 years ago. "We tell him, It's not worth it," Mr. Mulcahy said. For on-the-spot software repairs, he uses a $40 set of computer tools, but he emphasized, "I make most repairs using what's in my head, not the tools." Hardware is another story. "We don't do it, but we arrange for the computer to be picked up and delivered," Mr. Mulcahy said. And for the problems that cannot be solved, Mr. Mulcahy will call manufacturers' help lines himself. "There's a reason we recommend companies like Dell and Compaq," he said. "They have good technical support, and we can always reach them on the phone." Business is 80 percent repeat, the majority of customers like the Petersens coming from recommendations from friends. "I saw the car outside a neighbor's house," Mrs. Petersen said. "When I checked it out, my neighbor gave the service very high marks. I agree. Without my upgrade I never would have found a two-day excursion in Burgundy, called France in a Glass, on the Internet. We took it, and it was wonderful. With Jim Mulcahy on call, I'm becoming a computer whiz, and it's a lot of fun." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Rick Harder, above, and Jim Mulcahy of Computer Tutor-PCI, left, fix computer problems at clients' homes. Mr. Mulcahy stores equipment in his car. (Photographs by Rebecca Cooney for The newyork Times)

title: Increasingly, Traditional Retailers Take That Internet Plunge
body: As it joined the stampede to the Internet in July, the electronics retailer Circuit City Stores devised a way for its online customers to avoid a major source of e-commerce anxiety. Any shopper who fretted over whether an item would arrive on time could order a gift online and then pick it up at the store. Like a number of other Internet innovations, Circuit City's "express pickup" system did not always function perfectly this holiday season. But it underscored the growing realization in the retail industry that far from being in conflict with each other, e-commerce and earthbound retailing can often operate in tandem. After standing on the sidelines for an agonizingly long time during the explosive growth of Internet commerce, many traditional retailers have recently jumped onto the Web with both feet, trying to capitalize on some of the advantages they enjoy over their virtual competitors. National chain stores, after all, do not have to build brand awareness from scratch with expensive advertising. They already have thousands of customers. And when it comes to returning an item, they have sensed that most consumers prefer to do it in person, not through themail. (Of course, online retailers have advantages of their own -- for now, at least -- like access to plentiful capital without having to show earnings.) As the holidays approached, many traditional retailers began to see that the Internet could serve as an additional distribution channel for their merchandise, and stopped worrying about cannibalizing in-store sales. "The point is to give your customers a choice, so they can decide where they want to shop and when they want to do it," said Eileen M. Leary, an analyst for State Street Research in Boston. Ultimately, according to Michael E. Hansen, co-chairman of the e-business practice at the Boston Consulting Group, "the consumer wants to shop in both channels, and wants to have a seamless experience." Knowing this, some leading retailers, including Home Depot and Wal-Mart Stores, which is introducing a new Web site, have elected to move slowly rather than risk disappointing customers with a premature and poorly designed site. But the number of traditional retailers that have taken the plunge is big enough now that analysts are starting to identify those they believe will be most likely to succeed online. At or near the top of many lists are chains that came to the Internet with extensive experience in catalogs and mail order, which share with Internet retailing the crucial need for reliable delivery. A widely cited example is Williams-Sonoma, the kitchenware retailer, which opened its Web site for business Nov. 1 and racked up $1.5 million in Internet sales in its first month. "They know how to get the product to the customer in a timely fashion," said Brian S. Postol, an analyst for A. G. Edwards in St. Louis. Other retailers used to catalog sales expected to thrive on the Internet include Staples and Office Depot in stationery and office supplies, and Victoria's Secret, the lingerie retailer owned by Intimate Brands. Unlike most retailers, Victoria's Secret does not offer its Internet customers the option of returning items bought on the Web site at its stores. But the relative privacy of shopping on the Web appeals to men who find browsing in a lingerie store uncomfortable. Among department-store chains, two have taken sharply different approaches to the Internet. Federated Department Stores, parent of Bloomingdale's, Macy's, Stern's and other chains, signaled a big foray into e-commerce when it bought Fingerhut, the catalog company, in February. Several analysts said that Fingerhut's expertise in order fulfillment gives Federated an online edge. But some wondered if the Internet lends itself to buying sportswear, suits and dresses, and said that Federated's Web sites so far do not offer enough depth of selection to sustain customer interest. By contrast, Nordstrom, which began as a shoe store, is emphasizing depth, not breadth, on its new shoes-only site, www.nordstromshoes.com. The company says that the site lets customers choose from among 20 million pairs of shoes. The new site, which may be a prototype for other specialized Nordstrom sites, leaves many analysts skeptical, but Dorothy S. Lakner, of CIBC World Markets, is optimistic about its prospects. Since 30 percent of the company's catalog sales come from shoes, she said, the company "knew that people would buy shoes without trying them on." Analysts point to Costco as the general merchandise retailer to watch on the Web, because of its success in selling merchandise online that is not carried in its sprawling stores, including items like jukeboxes, pool tables and even diamond jewelry. Some may find it hard to imagine buying a $70,000 ring online from a warehouse store, but Costco seems to inspire an unusual level of trust in customers. "They are known for having good-quality items," said Michael J. Shea, an analyst at D. A. Davidson in Great Falls, Mont. "And you know you're getting the best deal." Not all analysts say Costco's online product strategy makes sense. Daniel T. Binder of Brown Brothers Harriman faulted the company Web site's limited selection. "The beauty of the Internet," he said, "is being able to offer a greater breadth of product, which they don't do." But like other retailers, Costco has found that the Internet presents a low-cost opportunity to promote its products and establish a bond with customers. For now, like many "click-and-mortar" retailers, Costco's revenues from the Internet are fairly insignificant: It expects just $60 million in online sales in the fiscal year ending in August, a pittance next to overall sales of $27.5 billion. And the portfolio managers who are buying the stock, including Ronald E. Elijah of the RS Value and Growth Fund, said that the company's fundamentals are the attraction, not its Internet performance. Analysts and investors, though, may have doubts about any large retailer that fails to have an e-commerce strategy, though. "We worry about the ones that don't understand it, that are holding out," Mr. Elijah said. "They're going to get challenged." http://www.nytimes.com

title: The Internet's Gift Is a Wider Bazaar
body: The 1999 holiday season has shaped up as the time when Internet shopping solidified its place in mainstream culture, measured both by the number of purchases made on-line and by the values Wall Street is assigning to cyberstores. According to the market research firm Bizrate.com, holiday sales at e-commerce sites are up more than 400 percent over 1998, with total American Internet sales this year expected to reach $6 billion. The conventional explanation for the rapid growth of e-shopping is that the Web offers convenience, low prices and speed. But while it's nice to shop at home in your bunny slippers, e-commerce is no improvement on catalogue sales in that particular kind of convenience. Christmas gift items are often competitively priced at a store that's 20 minutes from home. And, as Malcolm Gladwell pointed out in a recent newyorker article, delivery of the average Web purchase takes four days -- exactly the time that catalogue purchases have taken to arrive since express delivery became standard in 1994. So why are so many Americans flocking on line? The answer is in a defining attribute of the Internet itself: it's not only convenience that attracts us to the Web; it's also connectedness. First and most obviously, the on-line superstores like Amazon and Buy.com connect us to inventories with a breadth that would make the old Sears, Roebuck blush. No store could reasonably stock so many goods, and no retailer could send a catalogue of them. But beyond the sheer magnitude of possible purchases, the Web also connects us to products and information in more subtle ways. Consider the difference between a visit to your average real-world chain book store and a click into Barnesandnoble.com or Amazon. A book on Amazon is viewable from an array of different perspectives: its sales rank, quotes from recent reviews, star ratings, reader comments, personalized recommendations, and often interviews with the author and excerpts from the book itself. And the page on which the book is listed is always connected to the universe of related data available elsewhere on the Web. What supplementary information greets the real-world bookstore browser? The offerings are slim at best: the promotional information included on the book jacket and the humans at the information desk, who tend to traffic in I.S.B.N. numbers more than thoughtful recommendations. Granted, we encounter other shoppers in stores, but how many of us have bought a book based on a recommendation from one of them? The difference between these two shopping experiences -- the vast, accessible on-line store and the limited envelope of the bricks-and-mortar version -- gets to what is missing in most descriptions of on-line commerce. The Web remains uniquely suited to presenting data from multiple perspectives and letting users jump easily from one perspective to another. That was true when a high-energy physicist was originally developing the Web as a platform for sharing academic research, and it's true today for the 15-year-old Nebraskan contemplating the purchase of a Britney Spears CD. On-line shopping also keys into the spontaneity that derives from Web connectedness. A colleague's memo about a new book flashes on the computer screen during the workday, or a sibling sends word of a new recording in an email, and without leaving your cubicle or picking up the phone, you've already bought a copy. Shopping becomes seamlessly integrated into life in front of the computer screen. The most seductive impulse-buying opportunities in consumer history have arrived with so-called one-click ordering that lets repeat customers place orders without even having to drag out their credit cards. Buying becomes an effortless, almost money-free experience, with a which is why Amazon is putting maximum legal muscle into protecting its one-click patent. In time, the rise of e-commerce could threaten the extravagant rituals of the shopping mall and department stores, which are even now reinventing themselves to keep up with consumer demands for a more multidimensional experience. After all, shopping as pure recreation -- something you block off an entire Sunday afternoon for -- didn't become a mainstream pastime until the 20th century.  The instant connectedness of the Web may well usher it back to the margins in the 21st. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Retailers Look Back and See Online Shopping Is Gaining
body: Online holiday shopping is increasingly gnawing at the business of traditional retailers this year, with preliminary indications that seasonal Internet sales may nearly triple from last year. Visa, which represents about half the nation's credit card spending, estimates that Internet shoppers using its cards will have spent $1.47 billion this November and December, 179 percent more than in those months last year. In the overall retail market, that figure is still small -- 1.79 percent of Visa's total retail sales, up from 0.76 percent last November and December. And with the economy buoyant and retail sales expected to rise an overall 6 percent this holiday season, the big store chains have yet to see the Internet take a substantial bite out of their sales. But the overall trends may mask a more troublesome phenomenon for those retailers, experts say, as stores find that their best customers are the quickest to move online. "The retailers are feeling the pain because the fattest part of their market is moving online," said Mel Bergstein, chief executive of Diamond Technology Partners, a Chicago consulting firm. "The guys online don't buy the $10 gifts. They're the big spenders." And this year there are more of them. A newyork Times/CBS News poll of 1,026 adults Dec. 17-19 found that 17 percent had bought gifts over the Internet this holiday season or planned to do so, compared with 7 percent who said they had last year. The growth in Internet holiday spending reflected in the Visa data is at the high end of industry forecasts. Various analysts had predicted online holiday sales would be up 61 percent to 219 percent this year. American Express said its online retail sales had increased roughly 200 percent from last year's holiday season, although it would not provide precise numbers. (MasterCard said it did not track online sales.) Of course, sales were bound to increase given the blitz of television advertising by Internet stores over the last month, many offering deep discounts and free shipping. And some wonder whether the rapid growth might taper off, were Wall Street to demand that Internet companies ever turn a profit. "It's easy to give away stuff for free," said Toby Lenk, the chief executive of eToys, a fast-growing Internet store. "A lot of dot-com start-ups and wannabes are spending more in advertising than they are taking in sales, and they are discounting heavily. You've got to question the viability of that business model." To others, though, the rapid growth in Internet shopping this holiday season reinforces the predictions that the share of online shopping will continue to rise. "What we have seen so far is the tip of the iceberg," said Gerry Sweeney, a vice president of Visa's electronic commerce unit. "By 2003, we believe that 10 percent of our volume will come from the Internet." With that potential threat, this year many of the best-known names from the country's malls and mailboxes have opened up major stores on the Internet as well. And early measures show that some of the traditional players have attracted a lot of traffic, with their well-known brands and the convenient potential of returning unwanted items to their stores. Surveys show that Toys "R" Us, KBKids, the Gap, Costco, Wal-Mart Stores and Lands' End along with Barnes & Noble, already a Web veteran, appear to have significant growth in traffic. But there is some evidence that while many traditional retailers are attracting visitors to their Web sites, the Internet-only stores are doing a better job of making sales. Next Card, a credit card company, notes that based on its tally of sales, a greater percentage of the people who visit eToys, an Internet-only toy store, make purchases than visitors to Toysrus.com. And the average purchase is $65 for eToys and $45 for Toysrus.com. Even so, Toysrus has attracted far more sales than it can handle. On Wednesday it said it would give $100 gift certificates to customers who might not receive toys by Christmas. It declined to say how many customers were affected. Toysrus was not alone. EToys and KBKids were among the stores that left some parents giftless for Christmas. Still, the problems faced by the online toy companies spoiled what many people said was otherwise a very satisfying experience shopping on the Internet. The newyork Times/CBS News poll found that of those who shopped for gifts online, 62 percent said the experience was better than shopping in a store; 25 percent said it was the same, and 8 percent said it was worse. The online shoppers cited the convenience, lack of crowds and the speed of shopping as the main benefits over traditional stores. The biggest effect of the Internet appears to be in the toy market.  Analysts estimate that 1 to 2 percent of the $16 billion in holiday toy sales will occur online; last year the figure was well under half of 1 percent. "Toys are the perfect category for online shopping," said Katherine Borsecnik, a senior vice president at America Online, where toys and other children's merchandise have been the top selling category this holiday season. "No one likes to go to a toy store between Dec. 15 and Christmas, and a Pokemon from an Internet site is no different than a Pokemon from a Toys 'R' Us store." Of course, the online sales are not just at the expense of retail stores. While traditional mail-order catalog sales are still greater than Internet sales, the catalog business is growing slowly, and some merchants are reporting tough going. Lands' End, for example, said sales fell by 18 percent in the first five weeks of the fourth quarter. At the same time, the rise in online buying is proving a boon to the delivery business. The Postal Service says that Priority Mail shipments are up 8 percent this holiday season, largely because of Internet businesses. It has had to charter an additional 100 airplanes. Federal Express says its volume is up about 20 percent this holiday season, in part because of electronic commerce. United Parcel Service says that Internet companies are driving a volume increase and that many of its biggest customers are now online stores. Putting an overall dollar figure on holiday e-commerce is far from a science. Since Visa represents about 54 percent of card spending in the country, its data suggest that about $3 billion is being spent on online retail purchases in the last two months of the year. But Visa cautions that the numbers may slightly underestimate sales levels because some merchants with both traditional and online business may not be identifying Internet sales separately. And while nearly all purchases from online stores are made by credit card, many purchaes on auction sites like Ebay are by check. Market research firms have been predicting online sales for the holiday season as high as $6 billion to $9.5 billion, but their methodologies and definitions may vary significantly from those of Visa. Many rely on surveys of consumers and merchants rather than actual transaction records. The National Retail Federation estimates that total retail sales over the holiday season will be $185 billion. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Open for Business" The number of people shopping online this holiday season has more than doubled from last year and they are making bigger purchases. title:
Selling Online, Delivering on Bikes;
Low-Tech Courier Services Thrive On Growth of Web-Based Retailing
body: Here at the high noon of holiday shopping in Manhattan, the future of the e-commerce revolution is increasingly dependent on a low-tech, often-despised grunt: the bicycle messenger. Newly belted with two-way radios and data pagers, tracked by sophisticated routing software, these two-wheeled e-liverers are more in demand, more highly paid, better trained and, well, better uniformed than ever before. They call themselves riders, and only they can prevail on an island where gridlock is the black hole of the traditional delivery van, in a time when an exploding number of imperious dot-commerce customers want service in less than one hour. And the riders know it. "They need us, all these people that want things faster than ever," said William Hightower, 33, a courier for Kozmo.com who was poised to hurl his 21-speed Trek mountain bike on yet another dangerous delivery run. "And now we ride all day." Idealized in the 1980's for their rebel glamour, bicycle messengers found themselves superseded in this decade not only by the fax machine but also the ubiquitous email attachment. They have also been excoriated in the City Council, singled out by the mayor's quality-of-life crackdowns and stigmatized by terrorized pedestrians. But now the city's couriers are enjoying a renaissance as new Web-based retailers -- including Kozmo.com, Urbanfetch.com and Barnesandnoble.com -- are employing them as shock troops in a struggle with traditional brick-and-mortar video outlets, food purveyors and retail stores. (Even those merchants are going virtual, and employing more messengers.) "No matter how high-tech these companies are, their products are still going to be delivered in Manhattan on the back of the guy on the bike," said Denyse Barbay-Burgess, vice president for marketing at the Earlybird messenger service in Manhattan, which is delivering book orders for Barnesandnoble.com. "newyorkers are the busiest people in the unitedstates, and we're catering to their needs for convenience and instant gratification," said Joseph C. Park, the chief executive of Kozmo.com, which employs 300 messengers in Manhattan and Brooklyn Heights to provide free delivery of anything from a package of Twizzlers ($1) to a Toshiba DVD player ($319). And so at Earlybird, "we're up 15 percent thanks to e-commerce," Ms. Barbay-Burgess said. "In the last few months," she said, "we've been bombarded by dot-com companies that want to crack the newyork market." Earlybird has dedicated more than 100 of its 300 messengers each day just to deliver 600 to 800 orders for Barnesandnoble.com that used to be schlepped by postal or parcel delivery trucks. "It is not more expensive to us," Jonathan Bulkeley, chief executive of the online bookstore, said of the newyork pilot project, "and it's a way for us to stand out from the crowd" of competitors that ship by snail mail. At first, the Internet challenged the messenger business "because every time someone sent an email document attachment, we lost a delivery," said Robert Kotch, owner of Breakaway Courier Systems in Manhattan, which fields 120 messengers serving 3,000 city accounts, many of them dot.companies. "But e-commerce was a godsend to us," Mr. Kotch said. "It came just at the right time." More than 300 newyork messenger companies compete for business worth about $700 million, estimated Bill Goodman, director of the newyork State Messenger and Courier Association, a trade group. Cruising the city is an army of as many as 10,000 unlicensed bicycle, van and foot messengers. (The vans are for bulky items like DVD players.) About 5 percent of couriers are women, Mr. Goodman said. The going messenger rate is $6 to $10 per delivery, at least $5 less than it was a decade ago, because of severe competition, Mr. Goodman said. Full-time bicycle couriers can log more than 30 miles a day on shifts that last 8 to 10 hours. They are paid $300 to $800 a week. Those employed by Kozmo.com and a few other e-tailers are allowed to accept tips, and can make $15 to $60 a night. Thanks to Internet commerce, "We've been pulling our hair out to find people to work for us," Mr. Kotch said. Nate Kretzschmar, 26, a delivery supervisor at Kozmo.com who paid his dues as a bicycle messenger, agreed. "It's definitely a messenger's market now," he said, adding that the Internet companies "are beginning to take all the best riders." Unless the e-house of e-cards collapses, the demand for messengers will keep surging. Earlybird is recruiting more Manhattan couriers, and Mr. Park said Kozmo planned to expand its pool to 1,000 riders by the end of next year. These days, seasoned street warriors are getting bonuses and benefits unheard of a few years ago. Earlybird offers a 10 percent bonus for trips on rainy days, a $500 bonus for six months of perfect attendance, and 401(k) retirement accounts and contributory health insurance. In delivering a 50,000-item inventory ranging from Palm organizers to gift certificates at the restaurant Daniel, Urbanfetch.com "has a strictly enforced no-tipping policy," said Ross L. Stevens, the company's chief executive, "because customers are uncomfortable about how much to tip on a DVD player," he said. To compensate for its no-tipping ukase, the company offers a cornucopia of incentives to its 100 couriers so "they can make more than $800 a week," Mr. Stevens said. Urbanfetch.com, like a growing number of competitors, uniforms its couriers (in green, white and black). And many companies now put messengers through intensive delivery training sessions "because that one moment of interaction makes or breaks the experience for our customers," said Mr. Park (whose messengers at Kozmo.com wear orange, green and navy blue). The training strategy reassures many customers. "Usually bike messengers are kind of a crazy crew, pierced and tattooed, but Kozmo.com has some very good guys," said Jarom Fawson, 26, a computer consultant who lives in the West Village and places Internet orders every other week. The courier industry hopes that the city's newfound need for riders will upgrade their image. "Messengers have been stigmatized, but to make the city work, you have to have them," Mr. Goodman said. "It's a tough job, it's a big city, and it's crazy out there." The streets they ride are indeed mean. So far, 34 bicyclists have been killed this year in the five boroughs. Although the Police Department cannot say how many were messengers, most are believed to be. "Even several of our bicycle officers have been injured on their bikes," said Inspector James Hegarty, commander of the Traffic Control Division. Riders are prey to the bristling side-view mirrors of passing vehicles and to lane-changing drivers. "I've seen taxi doors suddenly open up on riders, and it took their fingers right off," said James Douglas, 19, a Kozmo.com messenger who was waiting recently in the dispatch room of the warehouse at 111 East 12th Street -- a bare-bones space filled with shipping boxes that everyone calls the lounge. Riders are also under intense pressure from the police. Responding to citywide complaints about bicycle messengers, the Police Department doubled its Manhattan Traffic Task Force last year from 10 to 20 mountain-biking officers. The heightened enforcement came after a man was struck and killed on a sidewalk by a food deliveryman on a bicycle in 1997. Mr. Goodman drew a distinction between couriers and the riders who inhabit the bottom of the food chain, delivering takeout orders for tips on wobbly balloon-tire bicycles with wire baskets. Those riders provoke "the No. 1 quality-of-life complaint by the people who reside and do business in our community," said Capt. Michael E. Shea, commander of the 20th Precinct in Manhattan. Not long ago, messengers had a transgressive chic that was mainstreamed by entertainments like "Quicksilver," the 1986 Kevin Bacon film, and "Double Rush," the 1995 CBS series about a Manhattan bicycle-messenger service. Despite Hollywood, plenty of newyorkers seem to prefer not to share an elevator with a messenger. "If you want to know how discrimination feels to minorities, just be a bike messenger," Mr. Kotch said. "The guy at the front door takes one look at you and tells you to go around to the back." And since it is Manhattan, they get some extraterrestrial requests that attempt to push them where no messenger has gone before. One regular Kozmo.com customer keeps specifying deliveries from "a cute, naked messenger" in his email requests. "That's one we haven't entirely fulfilled," Mr. Kretzschmar said. But some veteran messengers cannot get enough of the riding rush. "It's a thrill riding on the streets; you're addicted," said Andrew Terrelonge, 38, a messenger for 10 years, the last 2 at Earlybird. "There is nothing like it," agreed Jose Arroyo, 33, a courier for 12 years. "I even ride on my day off when it's nice." That's with his wife, Maisie, and the oldest of his four children, Junior, 12, and Justin, 9. For others, the romance, such as it is, lies in their pay envelopes. "For me, it's quick cash while I'm going to school," said Danny Barrera, 24, a part-time business student at Queensborough Community College. Perry Benes, 22, from Haifa, Israel, found himself in Greenpoint, Brooklyn, five months ago and started riding for the money, he said. "Another few months," he added, "and I'll have enough to go to South America." But for a majority of riders, the glamour fades after five years, said Mr. Kotch, 42, who spent a couple of years as a messenger himself. "Then you get tired of sucking down diesel exhausts." These days, he is content to lug a folding bicycle onto New Jersey Transit for his trip to work so that he can pedal to Canal Street, where his courier company plays its part in keeping the new Internet economy clicking right along. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Bicycle delivery service is a growth industry in newyork.
