title: A Resurgence of Blacksmithing
body: TO understand blacksmithing's current appeal, forget about Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's village smithy under the spreading chestnut tree with his arms like iron bands. Instead, suggests Brian Gilbert, consider the lowly kitchen spatula. Everybody has one. "I have one, too," Mr. Gilbert of Chattanooga, Tenn., wrote by email, "except mine is handmade, and if you take the time to notice, has decorative touches that make it really nice to hold. It's a pretty piece, there's not another exactly like it anywhere else in the world, and I'm proud of it." Mr. Gilbert is editor of The Hammer's Blow, one of two publications of Abana, the Artist-Blacksmith's Association of North America, which was founded in 1973 in Lumpkin, Ga., by 20 blacksmiths attending a convention. Ten years later, membership was 2,250, and today, it is 4,500, with more than 300 joining each year, according to Abana's Web site, www.abana.org/index .html. There are more than 50 Abana chapters, including chapters in Australia and New Zealand and some on university campuses where decorative arts and metalworking are taken seriously. On the site, one can subscribe to Abana's two newsletters, The Hammer's Blow, with many how-to hints, and The Anvil's Ring, which showcases new creations. There is also an online store. Blacksmithing is most often associated with shoeing horses, an association not all blacksmiths care for, said Jim McCarty, who edits The Anvil's Ring. "I know many blacksmiths who would not like to admit this," Mr. McCarty of Taos, Mo., wrote by email. "They wear pins with a horseshoe covered by the 'Ghostbusters' symbol as a sign of disdain for the mere shoer of horses. The fact is had they not continued their trade, blacksmithing would have died." Farriers, blacksmiths who specialize in shoeing horses, kept the old traditions alive, Mr. McCarty said. "The farrier saved blacksmithing," he wrote. "While the need for blacksmiths to make tools, repair farm equipment and forge household items ended around World War II, there has never been a time when the services of the farrier were no longer needed." A second reason for the resurgence of blacksmithing, he wrote, was the efforts of the Sixties generation to rediscover lost arts. And there were revered teachers like the late Francis Whitaker, who died in October at age 92 and whose contributions are outlined in a special page in Abana. You are not going to learn blacksmithing without doing it in person, but the fraternity will be glad to give you plenty of online help. Blacksmithing has its own Web ring, and one of its sites, anvilfire.com, has a How Do I Get Started in Blacksmithing page with many suggestions, including these: Sign up for a welding course at a local college or trade school. Buy a few books, recommended online. Join Abana. "Start to look for equipment and scraps of steel to experiment with or to build equipment. Be imaginative. Don't get stuck on setting up a classic 19th-century shop!" The site also posts basic information on hammers, tongs, forges and anvils, as well as how to buy out-of-print blacksmithing books. The Blacksmith's Compendium, sponsored by the Celtic Knot, has an Frequently Asked Questions list of sorts, indexed from Abana (www.celticknot.com/elektric /compendium/guide.shtml). Topics include anvils and anvil repairs, "blacksmith's elbow," chain mail, blade steels, Damascus steel and "Coal: A Brief Primer." For a blacksmith's page for women, try www.blacksmithchic.com. "In many ways, women make better blacksmiths," Mr. Gilbert wrote, "since they often have less upper body strength. They cannot force the iron to move as easily as a large man could, so they work smarter, often with better hammer technique and control than the average male." Perhaps the most enthusiastic and charming site is the Blacksmith's Virtual Junkyard (www.keenjunk.com), the creation of Neil Winikoff, 79, of Bellevue, Wash., a former writer for industrial magazines and a blacksmithing devotee for 30 years. Interspersed with pictures of Cassius, his junkyard dog, and audio of appropriate rock songs are a joke page, how-to pages for beginning and advanced metalworkers, listings (you want to contact a smith in Sri Lanka?), a sketchbook page for drawings and ideas, and an online junkyard. Blacksmithing sites are far removed from any guild-style secrecy. "The near loss of this art form isn't lost on today's smith, either," Mr. Gilbert wrote by way of explanation. "Some of the original founding members of Abana are still around. These 30 or so people realized that secrecy was death, and they freely shared all that they knew, and encouraged others to do the same." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: HAMMER AND TONGS -- A revival of blacksmithing has given rise to a number of Web sites, like those of (left to right) the Artist-Blacksmith's Association of North America; anvilfire.com, with tips on how to get started; and for women, blacksmithchic.com.

title: Filmmaker Says U.S. Suppressed His Work
body: Last summer, as he contemplated the news media's coverage of plans for New Year's Eve, Michael Zieper, an independent filmmaker, conceived a script that would explore the themes of distrust for the government and public anxiety over the new century. What if, he wondered, the unitedstates Army were to incite an enormous race riot at the stroke of midnight on Dec. 31, as the streets become darkened by computer-related power failures? What if it were to happen in Times Square? Mr. Zieper's musings became the subject of "Military Takeover of newyork City," a six-minute film he produced and posted on the Internet in October. Yesterday, the authorities' response to the film became the subject of a federal lawsuit. Acting on behalf of Mr. Zieper, 39, and Mark Wieger, 38, an independent Web site operator, the American Civil Liberties Union filed a suit claiming that the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the unitedstates attorney's office in newyork used coercion to suppress the film, which was made as if it were a secret military training tape of ways to provoke a Midtown riot. According to the suit, an F.B.I. agent and an assistant unitedstates attorney pressured Mr. Wieger to block access to the movie's Web site -- www.crowdedtheater.com -- telling him by telephone in November that they did not want any more people viewing it, and that his business could suffer if he did not comply with their wishes. Mr. Wieger at first agreed to the request, deleting the film from the Web on Nov. 15. But about 10 days later, after being inundated with complaints from Internet users, he restored the movie to his server, where it remains available for viewing, albeit with a new link Mr. Zieper designed to explain that it is fiction. Mr. Zieper, who lives in New Jersey, and Mr. Wieger, who lives in Michigan, said that the government had not inquired further about the movie since it was restored to the Web. The suit claims that the F.B.I. and the unitedstates attorney's office violated Mr. Zieper's and Mr. Wieger's rights to due process and free speech by pressuring them to restrict access to the film without any court review of the film's contents. It seeks unspecified monetary damages, lawyers' fees, and a court declaration that "Military Takeover of newyork" is constitutionally protected. "We want to make it very clear today that we applaud the F.B.I.'s effort to fight real threats of terrorism, including those that surround the millennium," said Ann Beeson, a lawyer with the Civil Liberties Union. "But censoring artists is certainly not the way to make people safe this New Year's Eve." Both the F.B.I. and the unitedstates attorney's office declined to comment. "Military Takeover of newyork City" has only one character: an army officer whose face is never seen. He is merely a voice talking over a tape of Times Square traffic, telling his soldiers what their missions will be on New Year's Eve. The officer's plan is simple. A woman will falsely claim that she was raped. Soldiers in civilian clothes will circulate through the crowd and spread rumors and fear. And as computer glitches cause power failures and confusion, the crowd's unease will erupt in violence and chaos, forcing the military to "sweep and clear" Manhattan. "This is how it all goes down; I'm going to walk you through it," the officer says, and then he does, giving each of his team members instructions in blunt, sometimes profanity-laced language. Mr. Zieper and the A.C.L.U. say that the film is meant to provoke serious discussion of serious issues: the public's concerns about millennium-related problems, the depth of the nation's racial problems and distrust for the government. And they say the film was made in the spirit of Orson Welles's "War of the Worlds," a 1938 radio drama about an alien invasion that some listeners mistook for a newscast. Emily Whitfield, a Civil Liberties Union spokeswoman, said the government had overreacted. "It's akin to them hearing about 'The Blair Witch Project' and running off into the woods to hunt down the witch," she said. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
An Internet Vision in Millions
body: Charles Zhang is a young man in a hurry. Mr. Zhang, the 35-year-old founder of one of China's hottest Internet companies, Sohu.com, swept into his office here the other day amid a flurry of ringing mobile phones and scampering aides. He was late for another meeting, he quickly explained to a visitor. Could the interview be put off for an hour? Better yet, could he chat by cell phone on the way to his appointment? Eventually, Mr. Zhang found time to sit down in a conference room, ignoring his co-workers pacing outside the glass door. "When I started this company two years ago," he said, "we were working in complete obscurity. Now it is so much like Silicon Valley. It happened so suddenly." China's Internet industry has tantalized outsiders ever since the country's Communist leaders made it clear that they welcomed the digital revolution. But in the last six months, the novelty has mutated into a kind of obsession. With the number of online users tripling in 1999, to nearly seven million, the Internet in China looks like a here-and-now opportunity. Foreign technology companies, venture capitalists and investment banks are all angling for pieces of it. Although Mr. Zhang happens to work in the capital of China, not far from Tiananmen Square, he might as well be in San Francisco, Seattle or any other place where starting a dot-com company seems like a ticket to instant riches. His life has become a whirl of salesmanship as he seals joint ventures, drums up money from investors and prepares his company to go public. It is not that Chinese online companies make any money; as in Silicon Valley, they wear their losses like a badge of honor. Nor is China anywhere close to being a mass market. Its entire online advertising business generated about $12 million in revenue this year. A recent Gallup survey found that just 14 percent of China's 1.2 billion people had even heard of the Internet -- let alone used it. And yet, foreign investors are betting that China will soon have one of the world's biggest Internet markets, perhaps second only to the unitedstates. As they have in other Chinese industries, foreigners with stars in their eyes are rushing to finance a handful of home-grown companies that they believe will be this country's eBays and Yahoos. "If you look at potential Internet usage in China, the numbers are absolutely staggering," said Gordon G. Chang, a partner who advises Internet companies in the Shanghai office of the law firm Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison. "Of course, it leads people to do silly things." China.com, a hongkong company that operates a little-visited World Wide Web site on the mainland, set off the current stampede in July when it raised $84 million in a stock offering on Nasdaq that valued the start-up at $1.5 billion. Sina.com, a Beijing-based company that operates the most popular Chinese site, raised $65 million in September and hopes to sell shares on Nasdaq next month. Mr. Zhang's Sohu.com, best known for its search engine and electronic directory, has raised more than $10 million from investors like Intel, Dow Jones and Hang Lung, a hongkong property developer. It, too, hopes to issue shares on Nasdaq in the first half of 2000. Farther down the road is Netease, a Beijing company that runs Web sites and online auctions of goods ranging from computers to cameras. Indeed, China's entire Internet industry has become an auction of sorts. Executives like Mr. Zhang, Daniel D. Mao, the chief operating officer of Sina.com, and William Ding, the founder of Netease, have all listened to bankers from the Goldman Sachs Group, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter and other firms tell them what lavish multiples their companies will trade at after they issue stock. "V.C." -- which once suggested Viet Cong in East Asia -- now stands for venture capital. "People are talking about V.C.'s, strategic-round financing, stock options, market cap, management teams," said Mr. Zhang, a Beijing native who spent nine years in the unitedstates and has a Ph.D. in physics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. "It's all this American management jargon." Relentless news coverage, which lionizes young technology executives as fearless pioneers, has added to the expectations. People like Mr. Zhang and Edward Zeng, the founder of Sparkice.com, are celebrities in China. And they behave that way, according to their rivals. "Some overseas Chinese came back here with swelled heads," said Wang Yan, 27, general manager of Sina.com. Mr. Wang, who studied law in France and returned in 1996, is not lacking in confidence himself. The prospect of a rich payday is so palpable in the offices of China's young Internet companies that some experts fear money may corrupt the industry. While they acknowledge that high salaries and rich stock options will attract bright young people, they say that the founders of the companies are spending too much time hustling for cash, and too little creating real businesses. "You cannot look at Silicon Valley and not be influenced by it," said Duncan Clark, a partner at BDA China, an Internet consulting firm in Beijing. "The question is whether all this money is going to spoil the industry." The culture of Wall Street has already caused management strains at Sohu. Several senior employees left last year after complaining that Mr. Zhang had refused to share ownership. Mr. Zhang said it was too early to grant stock options in 1998 because Chinese employees did not grasp the concept. He said he began handing out options this summer, and they are now very popular. A visit to Sohu's offices shows that the gap between Northern California and north China is not easily bridged. With its young, sweatsuit-clad programmers hunched over PC's and Apple Macintoshes, the company looks like any other start-up. But sitting in the middle of the office is a time clock that employees must punch daily. With more than a hint of jest, Victor Koo, the chief financial officer of Sohu, said, "We view ourselves as a Silicon Valley company with Chinese characteristics." Many companies have dealt with the growing financial demands by recruiting American-trained Chinese, like Mr. Koo, to handle fund-raising and investor relations. Mr. Koo, 33, has degrees from the University of California at Berkeley and Stanford University, where he was a classmate of Mr. Mao of Sina.com. Netease is typical in its evolution. Started in 1997 by Mr. Ding, a soft-spoken engineer from Ningbo, near Shanghai, it sold email servers to Internet access providers. Later, the company developed its own Web sites, specializing in email and chat rooms. When it began drawing interest from foreign investors, Mr. Ding thought that his English was not good enough to handle presentations. So he recruited two American-trained Chinese executives, Helen He and Oliver Kwan. Mr. Kwan, who worked for an asset management firm in newyork, said he was attracted to a career in finance by the movie character Gordon Gekko, the flamboyant, if ethically challenged trader in "Wall Street." But he said he was also impressed by Americans' unlimited access to computers. When Mr. Ding approached him about returning to China to join Netease, he traded in his pinstriped suits for rumpled chinos. Now, Netease is making the transformation from a software provider to a large-market Internet company. The company has completed two rounds of financing, raising nearly $20 million. And it is mentioned, along with Sina.com and Sohu.com, among the most promising candidates for an initial public offering. But Mr. Kwan said he was putting the brakes on expectations of a quick sale. "We need a C.E.O.; we need a good management team," he said. "If you do an I.P.O. before you're ready and you miss your revenue projections for one quarter, the market will cut your stock price in half in a day." While the influx of foreign-trained Chinese has given these companies a veneer of financial sophistication, some people contend that it has shifted the focus away from creating services that appeal to customers. "People never ask you about your new products," Mr. Ding said. "They only ask you, 'When is your I.P.O.?' " At the moment, Sina.com seems likely to be the first mainland Chinese company to issue shares -- as early as January. The company, formed by the merger of an American Internet company that catered to overseas Chinese and a Beijing concern, operates a popular Web site here, with an estimated five million page views a day. Sina.com has more than a million registered users. Sina.com had hoped to offer its stock this fall, but delayed it because of sudden uncertainty in the Chinese Internet market. In September, China's top communications official unexpectedly reaffirmed the long ban on foreign investment in telecommunications. The announcement unnerved the foreign partners in all these companies, and temporarily chilled the market. The trade agreement between the unitedstates and China in November eased those fears. Assuming it is approved by Congress, it will by 2002 open the door to foreign ownership of up to 50 percent of Internet content companies, and by 2006. up to 49 percent of Internet service providers. But the Chinese official, Wu Jichuan, has made it clear that Beijing can tie up foreign investors in cumbersome licensing procedures. Then, too, there is the question of how much freedom the Beijing government really plans to give the Internet. Sina.com and Sohu.com both offer news on their sites and have partnerships with Western media companies like Dow Jones and Reuters. But both these Chinese companies, in response to government pressure, have dropped nonfinancial foreign news. Beijing has also warned them not to provide links to the Web sites of foreign news organizations. For Mr. Zhang, staying out of trouble is a simple matter of knowing the boundaries. "It works if you are cooperative and don't underestimate the government's intelligence," he said. "If you become too confrontational, the government feels like it's being insulted and it will shut you down." Mr. Zhang insisted that officials in Beijing could not halt the growth of the Internet in China, even if they wanted to. And he said he did not feel hemmed in by political constraints. "Besides," he said with a wave of his hand, "the Internet is not just about political issues; 99 percent of it is about people's lives." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: World Wide Web enthusiasts searching out Chinese sites on personal computers at a Beijing exhibition early this month. title: It's Make-or-Break Season at One Young Online Company
body: Jonas Lee has a Harvard M.B.A. and he worked for a blue-chip management consulting firm. But no business school course or consulting firm project, he now knows, can possibly prepare you for the daily frenzy at an Internet start-up, particularly during a make-or-break holiday season. Mr. Lee is the 33-year-old president of GiftCertificates.com, an online marketer of gift certificates. He ticks off a laundry list of minor mishaps including running out of glue sticks used to seal envelopes at 2 a.m. ("You go to every all-night convenience store you can find") and trying to fix an ink-choked printer that was ruining envelopes at 3 a.m. ("You race out to the 24-hour Home Depot in Queens and get a little vacuum cleaner"). The fortunes of GiftCertificates.com, like those of so many Internet retailers, will be determined largely by how well it copes with such mundane matters as order handling, packing, shipping and answering customers' questions over the phone. And that means deftly managing and motivating the people who do this work -- not M.B.A.'s or techies, the expected dot-com denizens, but mostly high school graduates. This is the home truth about e-commerce as the Internet becomes more mainstream -- that so much of it is old-fashioned "commerce" instead of the technological wizardry of "e." GiftCertificates.com occupies two floors of a building on Seventh Avenue and 35th Street in Manhattan's garment district. Most of the management team, the Web site designers and software programmers are on the sixth floor, while the customer-service, order-tracking, packing and shipping operations are two floors up. The eighth floor hums through three shifts, round the clock, with workers fielding customer calls in one room and tracking, packing and shipping gift certificates in another room. Work in the order room is called "feeding the green dragon," because the small conveyor belt that ferries gray trays filled with gift-certificate orders has a green metal frame. The floor is home to workers mainly in their teens to 30's, mostly black and Hispanic, graduates of the city's public high schools. They are paid hourly wages, and many are hired just for the holiday season. Jeans and sweatshirts are the order of the day. Two workers have brought their radios, one tuned to a hip-hop station, the other playing classic soul. Such hires have brought the GiftCertificates.com payroll to roughly 140 people, more than double its size three months ago. Among the temporary workers is Sparkle Taylor, 19, who says she has had seven or eight jobs in the last two years. Ms. Taylor, a customer service representative, sits at a personal computer, wearing a headset and navigating through information on the company's Web site to answer questions. Some callers want information about the more than 200 retailers and restaurants whose gift certificates the company offers. Others are newcomers to online shopping and simply want someone to talk them through the process of buying by computer. Ms. Taylor has done telephone work before, selling long-distance service for a phone company and doing surveys for a market research firm. "That was all outbound -- people can get very hostile," she said. "In customer service, they need you. I like it here." Like other temporary workers at GiftCertificates.com, she said the company was paying pretty good wages -- $12 an hour in customer service and $10.50 an hour in order fulfillment. The holiday season also provides an audition for permanent jobs. "My short-term goal is to have them keep me full time," said Ms. Taylor, who joined the company three weeks ago. If the company does well, Mr. Lee said, the plan is to keep a payroll of 100 to 110 people, meaning about half of the temps would be offered permanent jobs. "The stars have already been identified," Mr. Lee noted. "You can tell who really cares, especially in a wartime situation like this." Jose Camacho, who works in the order fulfillment room, is a permanent worker at the company and a veteran by the standards of GiftCertificates.com. He joined at the end of August, leaving a job as a purchasing manager in an art supplies store. Three months later he was promoted from fulfillment representative to supervisor. "Yep, I'm moving up the ladder," said Mr. Camacho, 28, during his 4 p.m. to 1 a.m. shift last Wednesday. "I've been here almost four months and it feels like four years," he added, offering a shop-floor view of Internet time as hiring, training and production go on all at once. Motivational signs alongside the conveyor belt encourage workers to "Do Us Proud" and show the target number of orders to be handled hourly at each station. A sign above the urinal in the men's room reminds them of the "Eight Steps" in the fulfillment process; a day earlier, there were "Seven Steps." When a new shipping record was set last week, each worker in the department was given a $25 bonus on the spot -- in gift certificates. (The eighth-floor work force is proof that personal affluence and technological literacy do not necessarily go hand in hand. Even though Ms. Taylor does not yet own a personal computer, she has two free email accounts, which she uses from friends' computers or from work. Mr. Camacho learned of the job opening at GiftCertificates.com one Sunday evening while browsing through online classified ads using his WebTV.) To further motivate its employees, both management and hourly, GiftCertificates.com is offering stock options to every full-time worker, as many Internet start-ups do. "You bet the stock options are a big deal to me," said Amaryllis Diaz, 28, a supervisor in the customer service department. Ms. Diaz left a customer-service job at an industrial printing company she had held for years. Like others in operations at the Internet start-up, who are typically paid annual salaries of $20,000 to $40,000, she said she wanted to "get in on a company that had a lot of potential, just as it was taking off." "It just seemed more exciting than my other job," she said. She views stock options not as the equivalent of a winning lottery ticket -- as they can be for the founding executives of a start-up -- but as potentially providing a modest nest egg. "I've got two kids," Ms. Diaz said. "It could be a nice bonus." The financial calculus of joining an Internet start-up was more complicated for the 10 members of the management team at GiftCertificates.com. If things go well, the payoff for them could be many millions of dollars, but the risk can be greater, too, at least in the near term. Michael Stephenson, the company's 35-year-old chief financial officer, abandoned a roughly $1 million-a-year job as an investment banker at Merrill Lynch in August to go to GiftCertificates.com, where his salary is about one-tenth as much. Leland Harden, 37, the executive vice president for business development, walked away from $5 million in unexercised stock options, at current prices, when he left a larger Internet company in April. When they speak of why they came on board, they sound very much like Ms. Diaz. "You can try to think it to death all you like, but, heck, you really do it for the adventure," Mr. Harden said. It has been a shared adventure this holiday season on the eighth floor. Every member of the management team pitches in to take shifts "picking and packing" in the fulfillment department. So do family members, including Mr. Stephenson's wife, Cathy, who is expecting the couple's first child on Christmas Eve. Special steps have been taken for the eighth-floor employees. Last week, for example, a masseuse was brought in to ease the strain on the weary necks and shoulders of those picking and packing at a frenetic pace. Mr. Lee is often there, packing envelopes, picking trash off the floor and offering words of praise and encouragement. "A big part of my job is being a cheerleader, doing things for people and showing them you care," he said. "If you don't, there is a real potential for an upstairs-downstairs, us-and-them mentality to set in. We can't afford that." With only two days left till Christmas, GiftCertificates.com stands a chance of being one of the emboldened survivors of the Internet winter of 1999. Its goal for the holiday season was about $20 million in sales, and a steady surge of orders recently has made that target seem attainable. "A few weeks ago, I was worried that we wouldn't hit it," Mr. Lee said. "It's been a nail-biting experience." His anxiety is explained by the pace at which money is going out the door. GiftCertificates.com, which raised roughly $24 million this year in venture capital, plans to spend $12 million in the last three months of the year on advertising alone -- in newspapers and magazines, on billboards and buses, and over the radio, featuring the actress Sophia Loren as the Web site's spokeswoman. The venture backers are optimistic but not patient. William Ackman of Gotham Partners, a New York investment firm and a large shareholder, observed, "We'll know whether this company succeeds or fails before long, sometime next year." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Jonas Lee of GiftCertificates.com shows Felicia Brown how to handle phone orders. (Richard Termine for The New York Times)(pg. C1); Sparkle Taylor, left, hopes her temporary position at GiftCertificates.com becomes a full-time job after the holiday season. The company brought in a masseuse, right, to provide relief to busy workers. (Photographs by Richard Termine for The New York Times)(pg. C5)

title: Looking for Winners in a New Category
body: GiftCertificates.com is one of a handful of Internet start-ups trying to build an online marketplace for gift certificates. The Web retailing category, analysts say, may well prove to be a good niche business for the winners. "One or two of these companies could emerge with businesses of a couple hundred million dollars annually over the next 5 or 10 years," said Ken Cassar, an analyst for Jupiter Communications. "But I can't see one of these companies ever becoming a multibillion-dollar business." The business thinking behind a company like GiftCertificates.com is that gift certificates are a sizable market -- more than $11 billion a year -- that is waiting to be transformed by the Internet. Like books or records, gift certificates are something that consumers do not necessarily have to inspect in person before purchasing. And for most retailers, gift certificates represent a couple of percent of yearly sales. "For most retailers, gift certificates are an afterthought," said Jonas Lee, the president of GiftCertificates.com. "For us, it's the only thought." Retailers do tend to view gift certificate Web sites as a complement to their bricks-and-mortar businesses instead of as a threat. "We see working with them as a way to drive business to our stores -- a person who receives a gift certificate walks through our doors to use it," said Michele Cerwin, a marketing executive at Chanel Inc., one of the more than 200 retailers and restaurants that offer their certificates on GiftCertificates.com. Executives at GiftCertificates.com talk of helping to transform the image of their product from a last-minute option into "a new category, more of an everyday expression of love and affection," said Bertina Ceccarelli, executive vice president for marketing. The company's offerings are shipped in a variety of packaging, from gold envelopes to a velvet case with a ribbon. Web resellers like GiftCertificates.com buy their certificates from retailers at a 10 to 20 percent discount from their face value -- a discount retailers are willing to offer because many consumers either don't use the full value of the certificates or go to a store to use a gift certificate and then buy additional merchandise. GiftCertificates.com and Giftpoint.com, analysts say, seem to be the early leaders. In November, the most recent month for which data is available from Media Metrix, a Web traffic monitor, Giftpoint.com had slightly more visitors than GiftCertificates.com, and both were well ahead of other rivals, including Flooz.com and Webcertificates.com. More important than window shoppers, of course, are buyers. In November, GiftCertificates.com showed the largest gain in online purchases of any Web site from the previous month, up 462 percent, according to Nextcard, which tracks the Internet buying of 100,000 Visa card holders. Still, its previous sales were modest, so it is not yet clear how significant or lasting such a surge will prove to be.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Man Arrested In Bomb Threat To City Tunnels
body: The authorities posted police officers and bomb-sniffing dogs at several tunnels leading into newyork City yesterday morning after a New Jersey man posted a threatening message on the Internet saying that a van filled with explosives would be left in a tunnel leading into the city, officials said. Federal agents later arrested a Newark man, Renato DeSousa Flor, and charged him with having sent the threatening message to a chat room operated by America Online. Although no explosives were recovered at Mr. Flor's home, the authorities had taken the threat very seriously and earlier in the day had assigned the police to check trucks entering the Holland and Lincoln Tunnels from New Jersey. America Online contacted the authorities after reading the threatening message, and members of the Joint Terrorism Task Force arrested Mr. Flor at his home, according to a Federal Bureau of Investigation statement released last night. The Internet message had been posted early yesterday to an email address used by Mr. Flor, according to the criminal complaint. In the complaint, Special Agent Jeffrey A. Farrar of the F.B.I. said the message warned the F.B.I. and C.I.A. that a blue van with explosives, accompanied by two cars, would be parked sideways in the middle of a tunnel. "Then the driver will get inside one of the cars and exit the tunnel," the message said. It is unclear from the complaint whether the threat had specified a particular tunnel, but the F.B.I. statement said the message had specified the Holland and Lincoln Tunnels. The complaint said Mr. Flor had admitted sending the email message. The rapid response to an Internet threat was an indication of how carefully the authorities are taking security precautions for the millennial New Year's Eve celebration. But newyork officials have said they have not received any credible threats against the city. "There are no guarantees against terrorism when you live in a free society," Police Commissioner Howard Safir said at a news conference yesterday. "But I believe that we are doing everything humanly possible to make sure that it is a safe and enjoyable millennium celebration for everybody." Mr. Safir said 35,000 police officers, double the usual number, were assigned to work during the celebration, which will last until 6 a.m. on New Year's Day. In addition to confiscating open containers of alcohol, Mr. Safir said the officers would look out for people carrying "packages, knapsacks and briefcases that may be suspicious." In addition, he said, "we will be doing lots of sweeps with both dogs and other equipment to make sure that all of the venues that are going to be used are safe." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
ONLINE SHOPPER;
Click and Heat, Thawing Optional
body: I NEVER met an artichoke I didn't like. Of course, that could be because I never tasted an artichoke -- or an avocado or even hollandaise sauce -- until college. I had a lot of pent-up demand, after growing up in a house where the recipes tended more toward "weenie stew," the specialty of a family member who wishes to remain nameless (I'll call her Mom). To make weenie stew, slice a package of franks into a pot of canned whole tomatoes. Add some canned corn (stop reading here if you feel queasy), then bring to a boil. For my introduction to other cuisines, I thank my friend Mary O'Doherty, widely considered one of the best cooks ever to coax heat from the cranky electric stoves that plagued the off-campus apartments in Bloomington, Ind., in the early 1980's. Mary must also live with the knowledge that the powerful cravings she unleashed led me as a penniless freshman to shoplift guacamole (marked an outrageous $2.54). I still crave three Mary O'Doherty-worthy meals a day. However, the constraints of my current life style -- imagine the phone ringing and the dog throwing up on the dining room rug as three little girls of varying heights clutch at my legs and, in synchronized whines, blame me for the invention of long division -- often eliminate the leisurely hours I would otherwise devote to cooking. So I was excited recently to learn that on the Internet I could buy meals -- or substantial entrees that needed only a loaf of crusty bread to attain the status of supper -- over the Internet. The meals would arrive on my doorstep, ready to be stored in the refrigerator or freezer until minutes before eating. It all sounded appetizing, but specialty food may be one area where the Internet and my expectations are hopelessly ill-matched. The current proof that online shopping works is that whatever you ordered arrives relatively on time and with a minimum of calls to the shipping department. But as any gourmand knows, the proof of the pudding (not that I ordered pudding) is in the taste. With New Year's Eve coming up, I decided to hunt for appetizers. Over two weeks, I ordered from four online retailers -- www.tamale.com, www.customcreationfoods.com, www.cookexpress.com and www .koshermeal.com. (The site www.cookexpress.com announced late yesterday that it was suspending operations although it may resume delivering meals in the new year.) All items arrived when promised, within 48 hours, packaged securely inside Styrofoam containers and cooled by either dry ice or little freezer pillows. With great excitement, I took an inventory of my loot: black bean soup, squash flan and root vegetable medleys. But for someone who once turned to crime for a $2.54 container of dip, the shipping costs were expensive, adding a hefty surcharge that ranged up to a whopping $27 for each order at Koshermeal.com. When I phoned Stefan Strehler, co-owner of Custom Creation Foods, to complain, he said the problem was one of perception, by which he meant my perception. "You pay to get any food delivered," Mr. Strehler said. "A nine-inch pizza that comes to the door costs you $15, and then you tip the driver $2, and you have paid $17 for a pizza that cost the company $1 to make." All four companies met my convenience test: the food could be served within 30 minutes. Three companies shipped frozen foods that tasted fine after being defrosted in the microwave and heated. (I ignored the recommendations to thaw at room temperature. If I had that much foresight, I wouldn't need to go on the Internet in search of cheese blintzes.) And the fourth, CookExpress, sent the raw or partially prepared fresh ingredients for a chicken dinner and enclosed instructions on how to finish the meal. My only regret as I handled the plump, juicy pieces of chicken was the recipe. Dutifully, I coated the pieces in oil, salt and pepper, then roasted for 30 minutes on a cookie sheet. The result: bland. Couldn't the company have included a sprig of rosemary, a clove of garlic or even the hint that a cast-iron skillet would produce a browner skin? Many of these foods would not have passed the O'Doherty taste test. I did not enjoy the kosher meals, for example: the salmon entree was not as fresh as I would have liked, and the rib-eye steak was tough. But for the target customer -- a business traveler, for example -- the concerns might be different. "We offer large portions, it's wholesome, and the food gets there and is waiting in the hotel," said Bill Pinkerson, owner of Royal Palate Foods in Inglewood, Calif., which runs Koshermeal.com. The best foods came from Custom Creation Foods, where items were partially cooked, highly seasoned and then frozen quickly before being mailed. The technique was successful when it came to the tuna cakes, flavored with ginger and lemongrass. The soups were a little salty, but let me point out that the saltiness has not stopped me from having several portions, including a piping hot cup of the shrimp and corn soup that I am eating right now as I type. The jalapeno and cheese "nibblers" ($6.46 for a two-pound bag containing 30 to 34 appetizers) were certainly good enough to serve at a New Year's Eve party. So were the tamales from Pedro's Tamales in Texas. And in the context of party food, the tamales' biggest drawback -- their near-microscopic size -- could be a plus. In fact, I could eat a dozen. At $59.95 for six dozen (including shipping), they could add up. But not for me. On New Year's Eve, I'll honor my food roots. No, not the weenie stew. I'll be dipping artichoke leaves into hollandaise sauce. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Prepared foods are sold at sites like CookExpress (above), Koshermeal .com (left), Custom Creation Foods (middle left) and Pedro's Tamales.

title: On the Net, Curiosity Has a Price: Registration
body: NO matter where you go on the Internet these days, it seems you won't get very far without first registering, signing in or becoming a "member," all of which require that you provide your name, your email address and other personal information. Many computer users shy away from registering at such sites out of concerns about privacy and spamming. But others don't bother simply because registering is a time-consuming pain in the neck. "I wish people wouldn't require log-ins for sites that don't really need it," said Rhonda Hyslop of Washington, who spends about an hour online each day. "There are two or three sites I've actually signed up for, but unless they provide me with really good information, I'm not going to bother," she added. Access to the further reaches of a site typically requires you to register by picking a user name and a password, then entering line after line of personal information, which can take several minutes. The quest for an unreserved user name is one example of how an Internet site throws a wrench into what should be a quick and easy task. In some cases, if a desired user name is already taken, the site will send the surfer back to a blank page to enter not just a new user name but also every other piece of information relinquished on the first go-round. "A lot of the time that the Internet was supposed to save you by not having to run to the newsstand or to the library is being lost by what you have to do to get into it," said Joseph Riser, a marketing consultant in Los Angeles. "You end up registering for these sites that you might not ever use again," he said, "but getting beyond the first page is often not worth the effort." Greg Peters, president of Vignette, an Internet consulting firm in Austin, Tex., said: "It often seems like Internet companies are more interested in the data than in the person who's actually coming to the site. You have to gain someone's trust before you throw a form in their face. It's like trying to kiss on the first date." Approximately one in five people will register at a site to get beyond the first few pages of information, according to a recent survey of 10,000 Internet users conducted by Forrester Research of Cambridge, Mass. The firm also recently published a study predicting that electronic businesses would spend between $1.5 million and $2.1 million in 2000 to redesign sites, in part to address usability issues. "Everyone is focusing on being first to market right now," said Nora King, vice president for interactive services at Xcelerate, an electronic commerce consulting company in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., "but if companies can't master customer profiling in a way that maintains credibility and integrity, they won't stay in business." Until then, one of the most effective solutions to registration overload is Enonymous.com's Enonymous Advisor, a software program that stores personal information on a person's computer and automatically plugs it into the appropriate registration boxes upon the user's request. The program, which is available free for downloading at www.enonymous.com, is distinct from similar software in that it rates the privacy policies of thousands of Web sites and reveals the ratings to the surfer in pop-up windows whenever a new site is visited. The person can then decide, based on the rating, whether to register. Blue Mountain Arts, the electronic card company, is one of the few popular sites that does not require registration. That is because it believes the information that is handed over online is not always valid, said Karen Davidson, vice president of marketing and sales. "Whether it's out of privacy concerns or not, we find that a lot of people give out information that's only partially correct anyway, so for now, we don't require it," Ms. Davidson said, although Blue Mountain Arts may change its policy after Excite@Home completes its acquisition of the company. "If it's used in a good way, and not just turned over to an advertiser, we don't have a problem with that," she said. But for patient users, the benefits of taking the time to register make the process worthwhile. "I've never considered registering any deterrent," said Roger Asbury of Fairbanks, Alaska, who is registered at several news and community sites. "It gives me some semblance of confidence that someone can't post a message using my name. Some of the places I visit don't have a lot of members, so they really know me by the name I use, which lends to the sense of community there." News and community groups that users can customize are other perks that make registration worth the effort, Mr. Asbury said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: To get very far at many of the popular Web sites, visitors are required to register.

title: Sites That Measure Candidates' Views Against Your Own
body: CANDIDATES seeking a presidential nomination are already campaigning heavily, and voters are trying to determine, by viewing debates and political advertisements, whom they support. This political season, they have an alternative online. You can register your opinions on various issues, hit a button and see which candidate's views match yours. Curt Anderson of Ashland, Ore., who set up a candidate selector at www.selectsmart.com, said he took on the task to "cut through negative ads and the hyperbole of presidential Web sites." Since his candidate selector went online in September, up to 30,000 individuals have visited the site each day. Mr. Anderson, a marketing director for Darex, an industrial tools manufacturer, built his first online selector in 1996 to help clients choose industrial tools. Then, on his own, he created a selector on the Web for dog breeds that he licenses to an online pet supply company. For the candidate selector, Mr. Anderson scoured news reports to collect candidates' positions on issues like free trade and campaign finance reform. He said he tried to keep the language of the questions neutral, and although some users have accused him of left-wing or right-wing biases, many have been satisfied. "If I were still in the classroom," wrote a visitor to the site's message board, "I definitely would have my students access this page." One of the prevailing topics of discussion on the site's bulletin board is whether a vote for a third-party candidate would be a wasted vote; many users have been surprised to find that they have selected third-party candidates. The more extreme position a user states, the more likely the selector is to choose a third-party candidate. "His test is structured so that they kick you to extremes," said Michael Cornfield, a research professor at George Washington University who studies online politics. "If you choose one of the stronger positions, it weights it three times as much." Mr. Anderson's system does not hide its methods. The site discloses the scoring system and the methodology by which candidates are selected. Experts in political uses of the Internet say that disclosure is a critical component of candidate selectors online. They warn that if the concept catches on, it could be manipulated by campaigns and interest groups to favor specific candidates. Kathleen deLaski, director of political and government programming for America Online, helped develop a selector for AOL called President Match. Developed with CBS News, President Match is expected to be completed in January, but a test version at www.presidentmatch.com is available to anyone. Ms. deLaski and Professor Cornfield recommended that voters watch for several factors to identify credible selectors online: neutral wording of the questions, a listing of all the candidates, full disclosure of the group or individual behind the selector, a privacy policy and an explanation of the computation process. With those considerations in mind, Ms. deLaski said she hoped that President Match would enhance the way voters make decisions. Selectors, she said, help a voter "to step away from your preconceived notions." "It stacks the candidates up on your a la carte issue positions," she added. "We're not recommending that people use this as their only tool for voting, but it might help people cut through the sound bites." Harry Browne, who was the Libertarian Party's candidate for president in 1996 and is seeking the nomination for 2000, learned about the SelectSmart site from a steady stream of email from voters who discovered his campaign through the site. But when Mr. Browne took the test himself, he found that he came up with only an 83 percent match to his actual views. So Mr. Browne, submitted position statements to the site, as did three other candidates. It was worth his time, he said, because the site is spreading awareness of the Libertarian Party. "These were people who were ideological strangers, who said, 'I didn't know anything about the Libertarian Party,' " Mr. Browne said. With this sort of selection method, he added, "I would think that over time, we would get a lot of new people. The Internet is very, very good for us." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: FLAT TAX, ANYONE? -- Sites like SelectSmart.com and AOL's President Match let prospective voters plug in their views on various issues and compare them to the candidates' positions.

title:
Spam Your Way to a Good Education;
Online Application Forms Add to College Admissions Frenzy
body: A FEW years ago, applying to college meant staring at blank forms, fighting with the typewriter, applying liberal amounts of Wite-Out and -- after proofreading those precious pages for the 20th time -- packing them in 8-by-11 envelopes and sending them through the unitedstates Postal Service. This year, for more students than ever before, that ritual is history. As deadlines loom this month, an increasing number of college-bound students are sitting in front of computers, filling in blanks on digital applications, crossing their fingers and clicking the button that says Submit. Xap.com, a company that develops online applications, reports that more than 100,000 applications have been processed through its computers in the last two months. The University of California system, which created its own Web forms, has drawn nearly 19,000 online applicants this year. "It's what students are expecting and demanding," said Chris Munoz, associate provost for enrollment management at the University of Dayton in Ohio, a college that received almost 50 percent of its applications via the Web last year. So far this year, Mr. Munoz said, 68 percent of applications have arrived online. Hundreds of other colleges are offering Web-based applications, too. About 77 percent of colleges now provide online applications, according to a November survey of more than 400 admissions offices by the National Association for College Admission Counseling. Nearly three-quarters of those offices said their systems allowed applications to be sent over the Web. Others can be downloaded and then printed or saved to a disk, which can also bemailed to admissions offices. Jennifer Angenend and Lauren Bogue, seniors at St. Agnes Academy in Houston,raved about online applications. They said that in addition to having avoided the trouble of finding a typewriter, they had had the benefit of software that filled in rote information -- name, address and Social Security number -- after they had entered it once. "It's so much more efficient," Ms. Angenend said. That efficiency, which most students tout as the best part of applying online, may be playing a role in a larger trend -- the tendency of students to apply to more schools, especially if they are aiming for selective institutions. A decade ago, many guidance counselors say, high school seniors with good grades typically applied to four, five or six schools. In recent years, the counselors have seen the same type of students send applications to at least 8 schools, if not 10. The increase in applications should primarily be attributed to the intensely competitive college admissions process, many admissions counselors and consultants say. Statistics from the National Center for Education Statistics project that the number of high school graduates next spring will be the largest since 1983 and say that the percentage of students going to college -- 66 percent last year -- is at record levels. Although some colleges are planning to respond to the influx by admitting more students, most Ivy League colleges and other selective institutions say they intend to maintain their class sizes. That means more students competing for the same number of slots. "There is a frenzy," said Debbie Skelly, a guidance counselor at St. Agnes. To compensate, students who hope to attend selective schools say they are applying to more top-tier colleges and more backup schools than they originally planned. In many cases, they credit the technology with making it possible. Ms. Angenend, for example, is applying to 11 schools. Three of them -- Texas A&M University, Tulane University and the University of Pennsylvania -- did not offer electronic versions of the honors applications she wanted to submit, so she filled out the forms by hand. Harvard University had no online option for submitting the application, so she downloaded the application, which she plans to fill out on a computer, print and send through themail. But the Internet played a major role in Ms. Angenend's decision to apply to the other schools, she said, including Boston College, Bowdoin College in Maine, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Stanford University and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in newyork. "I had not considered applying to M.I.T. before I realized that they had an online application," Ms. Angenend said. Bowdoin, Boston College and Rensselaer also became options only after she found she could apply to them electronically. After painstakingly filling in three paper applications and writing essays by hand (like most of her peers, Ms. Angenend does not own a typewriter), Ms. Angenend decided she was spending too much of her time trying to cramp her handwriting into the forms' little lines. She said she cringed at the thought of completing many more without the assistance of software. Andrew Walther, a senior at Lafayette High School in Williamsburg, Va., also attributed several of his college choices to the fact that the schools offered applications online. When he first started looking at schools, he went to Web sites for the University of Florida and Florida State, where he discovered he could apply online. He did, finishing the applications (which didn't require essays) in less than 20 minutes each. A few days later, he said, he found that the University of Maryland at College Park had an online application, too -- one that would enable him to save his work and come back to it later. "I wasn't planning to apply to College Park," Mr. Walther said. "But I did it in just two afternoons." Application fees, of course, deter most students from submitting dozens of forms online. Fees range from $15 to $65, and most Ivy League colleges charge at least $50. But Bernice Munsey, an educational counselor in Arlington, Va., said many parents are starting to see those costs as minuscule compared with the price of tuition and the importance of getting into a good school. "The most common parent comment I get," Ms. Munsey said, "is, What's a few more dollars for a few more applications?" Such comments make some admissions officers wonder whether a combination of anxiety and technology may spur an influx of applicants who are less than serious about attending. But in many cases the swelling ranks of applicants are cause for cheer, they say: After all, colleges like to brag about their selectivity. The more applications they get, the more they can reject. And the higher their selectivity, the better chance they have of landing a coveted spot in annual college rankings, which use those selectivity numbers in their ranking formulas. Many admissions officers say it is too early to tell whether online applications will have any significant impact on college selectivity. The number using technology is clearly increasing, they say, but the majority of applicants still use paper. Some do not have Internet-connected computers at home. Other high school seniors are choosing to fill out some, if not all, of the forms on paper -- even if they have the means to go online. Jason Chan, a senior at Clements High School in Sugar Land, Tex., is an example. He is filling out some forms by hand and printing others onto paper with the best quality he could find. "I've paid attention to every detail," said Mr. Chan, whose first choice is Brown University. "I'm trying to stand out any way I can." But some schools -- like Virginia Tech in Blacksburg, Va. -- tell students that they would actually prefer applications to be completed over the Internet. A few, like the University of Dayton, have even waived the application fee for those who use the Web. Some graduate schools, like the Sloan School of Management at M.I.T., will accept only applications sent online. Guidance counselors predict, too, that students may become more inclined to take the technological route as the admissions season comes to a close. Mr. Walther of Lafayette High School, for example, envisions doing more online applications when January deadlines have passed and nervousness kicks in. "I definitely see myself going through the Web and finding all the ones that have February deadlines," Mr. Walther said. "If I can do it in an afternoon, why not have five more schools to get into?"  Avoiding the Paper Crunch -- Steering Your Digital Data to the Admissions Office  THE fastest way to find college application forms online is to go to college Web sites. Nearly every college in the unitedstates has created an online admissions area by now, and many of them include forms customized for their institutions. The most advanced applications can be filled out and submitted over the Internet; others are available online but must be downloaded to your computer and then printed or saved to a disk. If you are a classic procrastinator and have not yet made your college choices, you may want to browse lists of schools that offer online applications. Several college-oriented companies are happy to oblige. Many of them require you to set up an account first, usually by providing at least your name, your e-mail address and a password. Here are a few to get you started:  APPLY: www.review.com Software created by the Princeton Review enables students to download applications that automatically include basic information they provided upon registering. The company has customized applications for nearly 700 colleges.  COLLEGEQUEST: www.collegequest.com Offers electronic versions of two standard types of applications accepted by more than 1,000 colleges, about 100 of which can be submitted via the Web.  COLLEGENET: www.collegenet.com Provides customized online applications for more than 400 undergraduate colleges, as well as graduate programs.  EMBARK.COM: www.embark.com Offers customized online applications for more than 75 undergraduate colleges, as well as graduate programs. Also offers online versions of standard applications accepted by 300 colleges.  XAP.COM: www.xap.com Creates online applications for consortia of private colleges or multicampus universities in California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Texas and Wisconsin. In newyork, almost every public and private college is part of the system, which can be entered by going to NYMentor.edu. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Myron Achbach, right, admissions director at the University of Dayton, with a computer tape that could hold 10 years' worth of admissions data and file cabinets with applications from 1997. title:
The Neediest Cases;
Donating With a Mere Click of a Mouse
body: The notion of donating to charity this time of year may evoke images of tossing change to a sidewalk Santa, but with so many daily transactions now done with a click of a mouse, it is no surprise that the Internet has become an increasingly popular way to give. For charities, the attractions of online giving are obvious: it is fast, there is no need for expensive solicitations and it has the potential to tap into that growing, curious group of users known as Web surfers. Those who give say they appreciate those same qualities of speed and convenience. Not to mention that the novelty is making donors of Web surfers, and vice versa. Michael C. Wolf, 61, a retired dental school instructor who lives on the Upper West Side, bought his first computer last month, and soon made a contribution to The newyork Times Neediest Cases Fund. "I thought, 'Neat, I have to learn to use the thing, and I'm going to make a contribution anyway," he said. "So, I might as well have some fun experimenting with it online." The Neediest Cases Fund, which raises money for seven newyork City charities, created a Web site this year for donors using a credit card at www.nytimes.com/neediest. With his online contribution behind him, Mr. Wolf has begun making travel reservations on the Web and says he likes the ease of donating online, as well as the frequent-flier miles he earns on his credit card. Brenda J. Udoff, 76, bought her first computer in the 1980's for $5,600. By now, she is on her third machine, which she used this month to make her first online donation. "I was looking in the newspaper for the address to send it the old-fashioned way and I saw the Web address, so I tried it," she said. "It went so smoothly that I told my friends." Much the way that online shopping gained prominence last year, donating online seems to be coming of age this year, and operators of online charity sites have praised the medium as being unrivaled for quick emergency fund-raising. In August, the American Red Cross, on its site, www.redcross.org, raised $138,000 in a single day to assist earthquake relief efforts in Turkey, and $40,000 over six days this month for flood relief in Venezuela. The nonprofit organization this year has raised $2.5 million online. The online auction is also being increasingly adapted for charity use. TraceUrban.com, a new online magazine, has raised almost $50,000 this month by holding online auctions of donated designer dresses and art for AIDS relief in Africa, said Claude Grunitzky, the magazine's founder. Entrepreneurs are also seeking out charities that are not on the Internet to help them reach online donors. Webcharity.com conducts auctions of donated goods for nonprofit charity groups, with the site charging buyers a 10 percent premium. It has raised more than $160,000 this year for a variety of charities. In addition, standard e-commerce sites have begun to combine with nonprofit charities. Shop2give.com, for example, gives a percentage of its online sales profits to a charity that the buyer chooses. Many smaller charities benefit from the ease of advertising online and the Internet's widespread audience and teaming up of different sites through online links. America Online's philanthropy portal, www.helping.org, for instance, has information about 620,000 nonprofit organizations. Qpass, an Internet commerce company, handles the online donations to the Neediest Cases Fund free of charge. Donors may choose 1 of 14 donation amounts, from $5 to $5,000. Personal and payment information is taken but not shared with other sites and is secured during transmission with the same encrypting process used for most standard e-commerce transactions. Through yesterday, there were about 300 online pledges to the fund for a total of about $78,000. The Neediest Cases Fund predates the Internet a bit. It was established in 1912 by Adolph S. Ochs, who bought The Times in 1896. The newyork Times Company Foundation, a private charity, administers the fund. The fund raised a record $6.7 million in its 1998-99 campaign, and the foundation's president, Arthur Gelb, said he hoped that this year's totals would "dramatically increase because of this method of donating."  HOW TO HELP  Checks payable to The newyork Times Neediest Cases Fund should be sent to P.O. Box 5193, General Post Office, newyork, N.Y. 10087, or any of these organizations:  BROOKLYN BUREAU OF COMMUNITY SERVICE 285 Schermerhorn Street, Brooklyn, N.Y. 11217. Box 4100, newyork, N.Y. 10261-4100  No agents or solicitors are authorized to seek contributions for The newyork Times Neediest Cases Fund.  The Times pays the fund's expenses, so all contributions go directly to the charities, which use them to provide services and cash assistance to the poor.  Donations may be made with a credit card online, courtesy of the Qpass digital commerce service, at www.nytimes.com/neediest. Online donors receive a free trial subscription to the crossword puzzle of The newyork Times on the Web.  Contributions to the fund are deductible on Federal, state and city income taxes to the extent permitted by law.  To delay may mean to forget.
