title: Web Sites Bloom in China, and Are Weeded
body: On a recent evening, Zhang Aijing sat at her terminal at the Internet division of People's Daily, watching comments drop from cyberspace into the Communist Party newspaper's chat room. Ms. Zhang is an "editor" assigned to "anchor" discussions, and her responsibilities include weeding out comments overly critical of the party. With a click of her mouse, ugly thoughts disappear. She had just posted a notice on the site about a Western reporter's visit and was watching intently to see what came in. After all, unpredictable things happen here, where party propaganda meets cyberspace and, as if to underscore that point, a screen saver flashes smiling images of Diana, Princess of Wales, her wedding and Prince William nearby. "The U.S. is a killer -- we can't forget May 8," comes the first reply, referring to the day last spring when NATO forces bombed the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade. Most Chinese reject NATO's explanation that the attack was an accident. More angry comments tumble in. But soon another message hits the screen: "I want her to know that we Chinese people don't like our government." And another: "The Communist Party doesn't let Chinese people read newspapers from overseas." The comments stand. "We try to let the people speak," said Jiang Yaping, who heads the Internet division, with a shrug. "We are the main newspaper of the party, so of course there are limits. But it would take something stronger than these to be removed." With the ambivalent blessing of the government, locally produced Web sites and chat rooms have spread rapidly here in the last two years, giving China's estimated seven million Internet users a forum for public debate and discussion -- even a degree of dissent -- that previously was unavailable. On the local Internet, Chinese are exposed to information and opinions that could never appear in the tightly controlled Chinese media, on topics like the crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in Tiananmen Square on June 4, 1989, and the mistreatment of people with AIDS. Local governments are even using Web sites to poll residents about policy issues, like bus fares. "The Internet is changing China," said Minxin Pei, a researcher at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington. "Now we have people voting in cyberspace who cannot vote in political space. That will certainly have an effect." It is a delicate balancing act for China's leaders and for the commercial Web sites. They must preserve the sense of freewheeling openness that makes the Internet so popular while maintaining the control over information and dissent that the Communist government requires. For the government, the Internet has been, at times, a useful tool: after the embassy bombing in Belgrade, for example, chat rooms gave Chinese an outlet for their anger. But it is clearly a double-edged sword. The banned Falun Gong spiritual group, whose leader is now based in newyork, has frequently used email and the Internet in its campaign for legal recognition and to help mobilize its followers, although its Web sites are now blocked. This month, Information Minister Wu Jichuan announced that government ministries would monitor Internet sites, but did not elaborate on what form that monitoring would take. "We will not allow the introduction of trash that is harmful to the people," he said. To experts it is no surprise. "I expect that the government will be very deeply involved in regulating the Internet for two reasons," said Kenneth DeWoskin, a partner at PricewaterhouseCoopers who spoke at a recent conference on the Internet at Beijing University. "The Chinese government has always had a strong interest in managing information. And also, the government has a strong commercial interest in the Net; it's a major owner." But control over a multi-headed, constantly morphing creature like the Internet is difficult to achieve, as Chinese censors have already learned. Although the government restricts access to a number of foreign Web sites, many technically savvy Beijingers know how to get around the barricades. To get to The newyork Times on the Web or to sites related to Falun Gong, for example, Chinese who know the proper codes can dial a device called a proxy server, which effectively masks the identity of the site being visited. Some government officials use proxy servers to read the Times Web site. But domestic Web sites face a great deal more direct pressure, from readers hungry for the broadcast of more information and from a government that wants less. Sina.com is one of China's most popular Web sites, featuring a creative blend of features, sports and entertainment. It runs celebrity chat rooms, where Internet surfers can "meet" people like the film director Zhang Yimou. This fall it made waves by displaying China's first online birth: surfers could follow the prenatal development and birth of a real baby called Dian Dian. But one of Sina.com's special strength is news, and that requires especially deft handling. Unlike China's newspapers and magazines -- which are owned and controlled by the government -- Sina.com is the product of a private Chinese company, the Stone Group. "We are not under the media control of the Chinese government," said Paul Jin, executive deputy general manager of Sina.com in Beijing. "Still, we have to be very careful." "We have to make sure that every article is suitable to the Chinese government," Mr. Jin added, noting that the Sina.com's mainland China Web site contained different offerings from its Chinese-language Web sites overseas. "We make our own judgments. News here has great value, but it also has risks." When it started up just over a year ago, Sina.com included dispatches from foreign news agencies, including Agence France-Presse and Reuters. But after the government reiterated that its own newspapers were not permitted to use text directly from foreign news organizations, Sina.com dropped the practice as well. Today, it writes some of its own dispatches but mostly buys copy from the Chinese press. Many private Web sites in China avoid news that has not been sanctioned by the government, especially political news, even though urban Chinese are inveterate news junkies and there is great market demand. Even though the Dow Jones Company is a major shareholder in Sohu.com, popular Chinese general-interest Web site, the site offers only Dow Jones's business and financial news, not its broader news service. But it is in the chat rooms that the dicey stuff appears. "We don't worry too much about news items," Mr. Jin said. "It's the chat rooms that make us really nervous. Especially around sensitive days, like June 4, we have to screen very carefully, since you never know what will appear." At Sina.com and People's Daily, the goal is to review all comments within minutes after they drop and remove those deemed inappropriate. The People's Daily chat room got government permission to go online on May 8, the day of the embassy bombing in Belgrade, provoking an outpouring of popular anger. The chat room had already been months in planning. The government "thought that people had a lot to say at that time," said Mr. Jiang, explaining the timing, "although some people criticized us for allowing this kind of discussion." Since then, he said, leaders have becoming increasingly supportive of the enterprise, since the chat room, which gets more than 2,000 visitors a day, gives citizens a chance to vent their anger and also for China's officials to stay in touch with popular opinion. But the heated chat room debates that occurred on many Chinese Web sites in the month after the bombing showed that the Internet could buttress, but also occasionally undercut, government policy. In early May, for example, most of the entries were attacks on the unitedstates, NATO and President Clinton, reflecting the widespread view that the Chinese Embassy had been deliberately chosen as a target. But by the end of the month, the anniversary of the June 4, 1989, crackdown in Tiananmen Square was fast approaching. Along with thousands of patriotic entries, a few more controversial thoughts occasionally made their way online -- if only for a few minutes. On the chat room Netease, which was devoted to the embassy bombing, one person ventured: "June 4 is coming. What do you think?" The events of June 1989, when tanks moved into central Beijing, killing hundreds of civilians, are among China's ultimate political taboos. More recently, in a People's Daily chat room on AIDS run by an expert from the Health Ministry, viewers got official statistics (via the expert) as well as a embarrassing account (courtesy of a Net surfer) of how a Chinese deputy health minister had been heckled as he left the stage at a recent International AIDS meeting in Malaysia. Chinese take advantage of the relative anonymity provided by the Internet to say things they might not utter in other public forums. Although it is theoretically possible for a chat room to tell what phone number a comment is coming from, many Chinese gain access to the Internet through Internet cafes and it would be difficult to connect a particular comment with a particular individual, experts said. Many experts say that the quick growth of the Internet will push the Chinese media to be more open -- and that it has done so already. "The Internet is very international, and with the Net you really cannot construct obstacles to prevent people from knowing things," said Mr. Jiang, of People's Daily. "So often it's better that we inform people about something rather than have them learn about it elsewhere. But we stand on behalf of the Chinese government, and in some areas it better for us to keep quiet." For the foreseeable future, the Chinese government will certainly continue to try to exert control over the beast that has been unleashed. But monitoring every entry in every chat room will become increasingly cumbersome as the number of Internet users in China grows. "That is a problem for us," Mr. Jiang said. "Right now we don't know just what we will do." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Wrong Call on Bell Atlantic
body: The Federal Communications Commission's approval of Bell Atlantic's application to enter the market for long-distance service in newyork State looks more like a bow to political pressure than to consumer protection. The 1996 Telecommunications Act requires that for Bell Atlantic to gain permission to go after the long-distance customers of AT&T and other competitors, it must first open up its own network of wires and switches so that these competitors get a fair shot at wooing Bell Atlantic's customers for local service. Bell Atlantic comes close, but does not pass some key tests. The commission could have held up approval for a couple of months until Bell Atlantic showed it was fully ready. But having already turned aside several previous applications from Bell companies, it responded to pressure to prove the '96 act was creating competition by finally approving one. The danger with compromised standards is that Bell Atlantic could wield its power to wall off its local market even as it moves to crush competitors in long-distance and Internet services. Bell Atlantic owns the only telephone wire into most homes and businesses. The '96 act requires that Bells rent their wires, switches and other equipment to AT&T and other potential competitors so that they can reach local customers, offering them an attractive combination of local, long-distance, Internet and wireless services. Then the act invites Bell to offer the same services so that customers would get a battle for their business. The commission's job is to ensure that Bell Atlantic does not use its chokehold over its network to create problems for customers who ask to switch to AT&T, MCI Worldcom or others. Under the heavy thumb of the newyork Public Service Commission, Bell Atlantic has taken tremendous strides over the past 18 months or so to comply with the '96 act. The state authority even had an independent company, KPMG Peat Marwick, create a fictitious telephone company, placing orders to see if Bell Atlantic met its demands for equipment rental. The state authority also kept track of actual orders placed by MCI and others. Bell Atlantic made an excessive number of mistakes, even putting a few customer phones out of order when it switched their wires. It also fumbled too often when providing equipment for high-speed Internet access and renting its entire network of switches and wires to competitors. Despite these shortfalls -- each correctible within a couple of months if not weeks -- the state authority recommended to the F.C.C. that it approve Bell Atlantic's application. The Department of Justice, scrutinizing the state's data, disagreed. Yesterday the commission waved Justice's objections aside and settled for what Bell Atlantic had already achieved, threatening stiff penalties if its performance deteriorates after it gains entrance into long distance. Having acted prematurely, the commission faces two challenges. The first is to carry out the threat to hammer Bell Atlantic with fines if its actions prevent competitors from serving their customers as well as Bell Atlantic serves its own. The second is to make sure that every other application by a Bell company to enter long distance is held to no lower standard than has been set for Bell Atlantic in newyork. If it does both, the commission might still create the strong competition that Congress promised and consumers expect. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Ex-Student to Get New Trial In Internet Sex-Assault Case
body: An appellate court yesterday ordered a new trial for a Columbia University graduate student who was convicted in 1998 of kidnapping, torturing and sexually abusing a Barnard College student he had met over the Internet. The court said the trial judge had wrongly invoked the state's rape shield law to bar explicit email messages the woman wrote to the man before they met. The former doctoral student, Oliver Jovanovic, 32, has always maintained that his encounter with the woman, then 20, was consensual. He has served 20 months of a 15-year prison sentence. Prosecutors, who could appeal the decision to the state's highest court, the State Court of Appeals, declined to comment on the ruling yesterday. It was unclear whether Mr. Jovanovic's accuser, who spent six days on the witness stand in the trial, would be willing to testify again. And legal experts said they had not yet had time to review the decision and could not say what effect it would have on the use of the shield law in other rape cases. Enacted in 1975, the law was intended to encourage rape victims to come forward by restricting which aspects of their sexual history could be made public by defense lawyers in a trial. For example, the law states that evidence of an extramarital affair is irrelevant at a rape trial. But other sexual conduct, such as a prior sexual relationship between the accuser and the accused, can be presented to the jury. Writing for the majority, Judge David B. Saxe of the State Supreme Court harshly criticized Justice William A. Wetzel's decision to use the law to prevent the jury from seeing four email messages the woman sent to Mr. Jovanovic. "Given the highly intimate nature of some of this information," Judge Saxe wrote, "the statements, as a practical matter, should be viewed as the equivalent of 'prior sexual conduct with the accused.' " The decision was not meant to undermine the rape shield law, the ruling said. But in a dissenting opinion, Judge Angela M. Mazzarelli warned that the ruling would make it easier for defense lawyers to sully the reputations of rape victims. He said the ruling "would only serve to turn the clock back to the days when the main defense to any such charge was to malign the complainant." But the majority held that Mr. Jovanovic's trial had been unfair. Judge Saxe said the trial judge's failure to admit the email messages as evidence or to allow defense lawyers to ask the young woman about sadomasochistic relationships she may have had, had an "enormous" impact on Mr. Jovanovic's ability to defend himself. The court ruling included the email messages; in one, sent two days before the attack, the woman wrote Mr. Jovanovic that she was dating a sadomasochist. "Now I'm his slave," she wrote, "and it's painful, but the fun of telling my friends 'Hey, I'm a sadomasochist' more than outweighs the torment." In a subsequent email, the woman responded affirmatively to a question from Mr. Jovanovic about whether she was "submissive." In another, she used the slang term for a submissive partner in a sadomasochistic relationship to describe herself. "As the case stood, Jovanovic was precluded not only from bringing out the degree to which the complainant seemed to be inviting sadomasochism," the judge wrote, but from exploring the possibility that she was "a less-reliable narrator of events than she appeared to be at trial." Relatives and friends of Mr. Jovanovic's, who have lobbied for a reversal of his conviction, hailed the ruling yesterday as long overdue justice. Sabina Jovanovic, his mother, said she had spoken with her son yesterday and hoped to have him home for Christmas. "He is very much relieved, just relieved and happy that this one stage is over," she said. "It's been a trip to hell and back." The case stirred debate about the safety of anonymous meetings over the Internet. According to his accuser, Mr. Jovanovic lured the woman on a date after an extended email correspondence, tied her to a futon in his Washington Heights apartment, and tortured her for more than 20 hours. The woman said Mr. Jovanovic had threatened to kill her, bit her until she bled, burned her with wax and beat her with a stick. But Jack Litman, a defense lawyer, accused her of making up a story about what was a consensual sexual encounter. http://www.nytimes.com

title: SportsLine.com Sells a Unit To a Venture Led by Athletes
body: A new venture led by John Elway, Michael Jordan and Wayne Gretzky agreed to buy the online retailing business of SportsLine.com, publisher of the CBS SportsLine World Wide Web site, the companies said today. The venture, MVP.com, has formed an online advertising pact with the CBS Corporation and expects to set up an online retailing site for sporting goods next year. Mr. Elway, who led the Denver Broncos to two National Football League championships before retiring earlier this year, is MVP.com's chairman; Mr. Jordan, the former National Basketball Association superstar, and Mr. Gretzky, the National Hockey League's all-time leading scorer, also serve on the board. SportsLine's founder and chief executive, Michael Levy, will join them on the seven-member board. John Costello, a former senior executive vice president for Sears, Roebuck & Company who has been appointed chief executive of MVP.com, will serve on it as well. MVP.Com is also backed by Benchmark Capital, a Silicon Valley venture-capital firm, the Galyan's Trading Company, a sports retailer, and Gaylan's controlling investor, Freeman Spogli & Company. Under its pact with MVP.com, SportsLine will receive $120 million in guaranteed cash payments over 10 years plus an equity stake in the start-up. MVP.com will acquire and assume all operating responsibilities for SportsLine's electronic commerce business. MVP.com will receive $85 million in advertising, promotion and other considerations for four years from CBS, which holds a stake in SportsLine. CBS will get an undisclosed stake in MVP. Shares in SportsLine.com, which is based in Fort Lauderdale, rose 87.5 cents, to $63.25, in Nasdaq trading today.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Help for Web Pharmacy Users
body: The Food and Drug Administration started a Web site today to help patients buying drugs and medical products on the Internet to ensure that they are coming from legitimate sources rather than dangerous quacks. The site, which is reachable from the drug agency's home page (www.fda.gov), is part of what the agency calls a "much more aggressive" effort to police Internet medicine. It includes instructions for consumers to report any suspicious sites and to alert the agency quickly if they suffer serious side effects or injuries from products bought online. It can be difficult to tell the difference between legitimate online drugstores and those that sell illegal products -- some dangerous, others a waste of money, the agency warned. For example, it recently uncovered illegal at-home AIDS tests sold over the Internet that did not work. And it said a 53-year-old Chicago man died after taking Viagra ordered over the Internet, instead of seeing a doctor who could have advised him that he was at risk for heart disease that made the impotence pill dangerous. The drug agency says that consumers can make sure an online pharmacy is legitimate by checking the Web site of the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy (www.nabp.net). And it urges consumers not to buy prescription drugs without a real prescription from a physician they know. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
OUTLOOK 2000: AN EPITAPH FOR THE 20th CENTURY;
A Time of Energy And Enterprise And E-Everything
body: When eight well-known executives were asked to sum up the most important characteristics of the last 100 years in an epitaph for the 20th century, they invariably talked about the powerful impact of technology in all its myriad forms: the airplane, television, computers and the Internet. "Before this century, science did not matter to the average person," said Franklin D. Raines, the chairman and chief executive of Fannie Mae, the world's largest nonbank financial services company. "In this century, science is changing our lives fundamentally." But as much as these business leaders, who hailed from entertainment and financial services and industry, praised the huge advances in technology over the last 100 years, they expressed concern about how technology could be used and the double-edged nature of change. The dark side of the passing century was hinted at by the comic creator Stan Lee's rendition of Mongorr, a despot eager to infiltrate our world to take advantage of the new technology. But, in as epic terms as any battle waged between superheroes, Robert E. Rubin, the former Treasury secretary, also talked about the stark contrasts of the last 100 years: the huge advances made and the devastation wrought by the ability of people to hurt one another. "Human nature has remained a constant," he concluded. Many of the executives were also quick to note the substantial divide that exists between those who have benefited from the prosperity of the last 100 years and those who have not. "The haves and have-nots are getting further apart," said Lawrence A. Bossidy, the chairman of Honeywell, the industrial giant created by the recent merger of Honeywell, the maker of electronic controls, and AlliedSignal, a diversified manufacturer. As the chairman of Stan Lee Media, a publicly held company based in Encino, Calif., Mr. Lee is participating directly in the revolution being created by the Internet. "I've been in comics, radio, television, animation, movies and now the Internet," said Mr. Lee, who is one of the people responsible for such memorable superheroes as Spider-Man and the Fantastic Four and plans to bring a new generation of different superheroes and villains to the Internet in short animated episodes. Television and the Internet, in particular, have achieved enormous global reach, Mr. Lee says. People who once lived in isolation are exposed as never before to what is going on in the rest of the world. "There are no hicks anymore," he said. But Mr. Lee is genuinely worried about how this technology is used. Like Mongorr, one of Mr. Lee's new characters, there are those who may use the Internet to harness hatred. "I'm hoping that the closer we come together, the more that will fade away," he said. When Mr. Bossidy of Honeywell thinks about the 20th century, he ticks off the numerous advances in electronics: the cathode ray tube in televisions, the microchip and the various iterations of computers that allow work to be done rapidly, leading to huge improvements in productivity. The advances in medicine -- the cure of diseases like scarlet fever and new treatments for heart disease and cancer -- are also striking, Mr. Bossidy said. "People feel better; they don't just live longer," he said. But the role of the corporation has also undergone significant change, he argued, as companies have become much more efficient. "Corporations used to be run exclusively by dictators," said Mr. Bossidy, who spent more than three decades at General Electric before joining AlliedSignal, where he became chief executive in 1991. "Now you have to lead and be prepared to serve," he said, and employees have the freedom to contribute. Increasingly, governments and other organizations will rely on a corporate model to improve how they operate, according to Mr. Bossidy. He also believes that companies will be asked more and more to address social issues like education, not in privatizing them but in marshaling resources. But Mr. Bossidy was wary of trying to guess what other innovations the next century might bring. Just as few foresaw the Internet, "most of the changes in the 21st century will not be predicted," he argued. Mr. Rubin, who is as well known on Wall Street as he is in Washington, takes an even-handed approach in assessing the century. Once a top official at Goldman Sachs, he is now the chairman of the executive committee of the board for Citigroup, the nation's largest financial services company. "It has been a period of tremendous advance," Mr. Rubin said, noting how much of the global population has benefited from technology. But he is quick to point out the last century's episodes of war and violence as well as the use of technology for mass destruction. Globalization has also remarkably changed how we live, he noted. "I think we are far more interdependent today than we were 100 years ago," economically, environmentally and geopolitically, Mr. Rubin said. He, too, is concerned about the gulf between those who are enjoying this century's tremendous prosperity and those who are not but understand what they are missing. The challenge, he said, will be to see how the tension between sovereignty and the growing global interdependence is handled, and he believes the unitedstates must decide what role it should play. "There is a tremendous struggle between those who believe that the U.S. should play a major leadership role and those who believe in some fashion that we should turn inward and turn our back," he said. David H. Komansky, the chairman and chief executive of Merrill Lynch & Company, takes a strikingly more optimistic view. "Be bullish," he argued, not about financial markets but in viewing the strides made in the past 100 years. Despite world wars, the Great Depression and other economic turbulence, there have been significant improvements in the standard of living, medicine and technology, he said. "I think we are on the doorstep of a truly global life style that will benefit every person in every part of the world," Mr. Komansky said. The power of instant communication -- the ability to make a telephone call anywhere in the world or tune into CNN to see minute-by-minute broadcasts of war -- has created a world that is linked almost in real time, Mr. Komansky said. Globalization, he argued, has transformed businesses like Merrill Lynch, which two decades ago was primarily a domestic firm. Today, more than a third of its business is conducted outside the unitedstates, and Merrill employs 65,000 people in 44 countries. Managing the huge variety of people from different ethnic backgrounds becomes more of a challenge, he said. "I think the phenomenon of globalization is in its very early days," Mr. Komansky predicted. But he said he was confident that civilization would continue to make great progress. "The future is much brighter than the past," he said. The head of Fannie Mae, the country's largest provider of home-mortgage financing, Mr. Raines is keenly aware of how much more accessible capital -- in the form of mortgages, credit cards and loans -- is today than it was before a variety of government programs created in the aftermath of the Great Depression to help homeowners, farmers and small businesses. Then, "the Government was involved in pushing capital out into the economy and making it much more available to the individual," Mr. Raines said. While the private sector has taken over much of that role -- and Fannie Mae is now a publicly held company -- the continuing spread of capital has helped create "a huge wealth effect" in the unitedstates, according to Mr. Raines. But Mr. Raines, the first black chief executive of one of the nation's largest 100 corporations, also spoke of the "century-long effort" to promote equality and "integrate black America into society." Corporate America has also taken part in that effort, he said, and he pointed to the advancement of several black executives within the last few years. "Ten years ago, you couldn't think about it," he said. Mr. Raines also talked about those who have been left behind in what is known as the wealth gap. "The democratization of wealth has not been complete," he said, and he voiced concern that the nation could lose its commitment to that goal during the next 100 years. Michael D. Eisner, the chairman and chief executive of the Walt Disney Company, was reluctant to pontificate, but he, too, emphasized the transforming power of technology. The 20th century "has been a triumph for human expression," he said. Communication has been transformed, he said, from what was once largely face to face to something that is now both instant and universal for people around the globe. No matter how effective books and other printed forms of expression were in creating change, the widespread adoption of television and the Internet has fundamentally changed how we express ourselves, he said. While the next century may see advances that make such communication even more efficient and ubiquitous, it cannot make communication faster, Mr. Eisner noted. "You can't go faster than instant," he said. Mr. Eisner, who suggested that philosophers and psychiatrists were more adept at thinking about the implications of this change, shied away from predicting where this instant human expression, allowing anyone to say anything to nearly anyone else, would lead. Either global democracy or totalitarianism could result, he said. Martha Stewart, the entrepreneur whose sense of style led to the creation of her own media and merchandising empire, Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia, worries that we are already witnessing the drawbacks of the new speed at which we conduct our lives. While she applauded the advances of the 20th century in technology, science and medicine, "advancement in the study of the humanities, in art and in cultural endeavors, seems to have been less progressive, especially in the second half of this century," she argued. The result of the widespread adoption of the telephone, faxes, e-mail messages and computers has been the inability to think creatively, Ms. Stewart said. Answering e-mail has taken the place of writing a great novel. Her own life has been consumed by the Internet, she said, and technology has allowed her to do any number of jobs at once. "It's insane," she laughed, but she said she was also saddened by the widespread implications of this speed. She is also concerned about the social impact of the technology, which she described as taking away physical contact, from seeing someone directly or talking to them on the telephone. "It is much more introverted living," she said. What she hopes is that the next century will provide more time for people to reflect. As people get used to the technology, they may learn to dominate it. And she hopes that we remain sensitive to the challenge of making technology accessible to all, although she is confident that will happen. "Computers are going to be cheap," she said. "Everyone is going to have them." As the chairman and chief executive of America Online, one of the best-known providers of access to the Web, Stephen M. Case enjoys a key vantage point on the development of the Internet. The proliferation of telephones and cars, the television, the computer and the Internet created an increasingly mobile society, Mr. Case said. Businesses were opened up, and people could be on the move without losing all ties to family and friends. "Suddenly, anything was possible," Mr. Case said. The result, according to Mr. Case, has been the American century. "It was a time of unprecedented opportunity," he argued, as technology, coupled with the spread of democracy and the relative prosperity and security of this period, allowed people to explore new areas. "Technology was a real driver because it created not just whole new industries, but it has also reshaped our lives," Mr. Case said. But he acknowledged that the challenge faced by society is in making sure everyone has access. "It is not about dropping computers" into places where people have difficulty taking advantage of the technology, he said, but about developing an integrated approach to making sure they have the tools and wherewithal to use the computers. Mr. Case believes, however, that the Internet journey is only beginning and that there is much to learn yet about how it will affect this country and the world. "I do think the next century is going to be the Internet century," he said, and the next decade or two will be defined by the changes wrought by the new medium. The Internet has the ability to transform all aspects of what we do to gather information, shop, communicate or be entertained. "It is very, very empowering," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: FRANKLIN D. RAINES (Carol T. Powers for The New York Times); ROBERT E. RUBIN (Reuters); STAN LEE (Kim Kulish for The New York Times); MARTHA STEWART (Timothy Greenfield-Sanders/Outline); MICHAEL D. EISNER (Associated Press)

title:
OUTLOOK 2000: ECONOMY & INDUSTRY;
Goodbye Cold Calling; Hello Cross-Selling
body: If families continue to sit down together for dinner in the 21st century, they should be able to enjoy their meals with fewer interruptions. The stream of unsolicited phone calls from sales people and stockbrokers pitching everything from stock tips to credit card insurance should ebb as financial services companies develop more sophisticated ways of selling their products and services, industry executives and consultants say. They see the dreaded "cold call" being replaced with the new industry buzzword, the "cross sell" of services to people who are already customers of another business of a company. In the wake of the historic changes made by Congress this year in laws that separated commercial banks, investment banks and insurance companies, a wave of consolidation is expected among financial services companies, creating more conglomerates like Citigroup, the first company in the unitedstates to combine an insurer with a commercial bank, an investment bank and a securities brokerage firm, the experts say. "If history and the experiences in other countries are a guide, the structural changes that will follow will be of great significance," said Jerome Kenney, an executive vice president who plots corporate strategy for Merrill Lynch & Company. "Our own internal forecast is, if you go out five years, there will be very few independent securities firms." Only the biggest firms on Wall Street, like Merrill, Goldman Sachs Group and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company, will be able to avoid being gobbled up by commercial banks and insurance companies, industry analysts predict. Most small and midsize brokerage firms, especially Internet-based trading firms that are competing on price, will be acquired or will fail, said James Punishill, an online financial services analyst at Forrester Research in Boston. Electronic trading with low commissions will remain commonplace, as it has become in the last several years, but it will not be profitable enough to sustain a big business, analysts say. The new conglomerates that are expected to compete with Citigroup will look more like what Europeans call universal banks, Deutsche Bank of Germany or UBS of Switzerland, for example. They will provide the full spectrum of financial products and services under one roof, or in the case of Citigroup, under one red umbrella. But once companies pay huge sums to acquire the heft needed to remain competitive in a global market, they will face the challenge of making those acquisitions pay off by selling more products and more types of products to their growing lists of customers, and they will do so in a market that is being redefined by the Internet. So far, the track record of cross-selling financial services is spotty, at best, and the growth of the Internet adds to the challenge, as new competitors spring up all over the World Wide Web, offering bargain prices. Some are well-disguised units of traditional players, like Wingspanbank.com, an online bank created by the Bank One Corporation. Bank One's management has taken pains to hide the connection, hoping to lure customers with higher rates on certificates of deposit without cannibalizing the bank's existing business. That strategy is not a proven winner yet, but online banking is just starting to catch on and analysts expect its use to increase rapidly as more online banks appear and customers of traditional banks switch over to the Internet. Widespread acceptance of the Internet as a medium for researching and shopping for financial services has complicated efforts to cross-sell. Consumers no longer need to rely on banks and brokers for information about financial services and prices. Insurance companies have succeeded at cross-selling different types of insurance by offering package deals, like selling auto insurance at attractive rates to customers who also buy a homeowner's policy. Citigroup and Merrill also claim to have had success in selling home loans to customers of their brokerage units. But, over all, there is no convincing evidence that people want to keep all their assets in one place or to buy a wide variety of financial products from a single source. "A lot of these big deals will fail ultimately because they're not generating the top-line growth," said Peter Davis, a financial services consultant with Cambridge Group in Manhattan. "They have to start cross-selling, and that cross-selling has to occur around an understanding of their customers. Cold calls and statement stuffers won't cut it." For examples, Mr. Davis pointed to the comparative records of banks that are the products of one or more mergers and those that are not. Both types of banks, he said, sell about 2.1 products, like certificates of deposit, per customer. "There really is no difference in performance," he said. Once a merged organization cuts out overlapping costs, the only way to make a merger pay off is to increase revenue. So inevitably conglomerates will seek to do so by trying to get their customers to buy more from them or invest more with them. The problem is that consumers have easy access to lots of information -- some would say, too much -- about purveyors of financial services, their prices and offerings. In the future, they will be more likely to shop around, mostly online, before buying investing or borrowing money and will be less susceptible to unsolicited sales pitches of any kind. Wall Street is already adapting to the new times. Merrill Lynch; Salomon Smith Barney; Morgan Stanley Dean Witter and other big brokerage firms are turning their sales forces away from stock promotion and toward money management. Most firms are concentrating their sales efforts on omnibus accounts that charge an annual fee based on an account's assets, instead of on the number of transactions executed. In theory, the rise of the fee-based brokerage account will allow the brokers to focus their attention on finding new clients and providing them with advice about how to meet their financial goals. The switch should also make the earnings of brokerage firms more predictable and make their stocks more attractive to investors. "The traditional broker, we think, is a thing of the past," said Ruediger Adolf, senior vice president at the American Express Company. "The way you can add value, in our belief, is through understanding the goals of an individual customer in a holistic way and developing strategies of how they can get there." American Express and other financial services companies have accepted that a significant number of investors, not just young people with relatively few assets, want to handle at least some of their financial dealings themselves. Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley and others have introduced online trading services, with commissions as low as $29.95, to appeal to those people. That is the same basic price that Charles Schwab charges, but considerably higher than E*trade's low rate of $9.95. American Express undercut them all when it recently started offering free stock trades to customers with big account balances. Analysts see those moves as an acknowledgment that the execution of stock trades, once a core offering on Wall Street, is fast becoming a commodity. In essence, brokerage firms are saying, "Let us manage your money for a fee, and we'll throw in the stock and bond trades." Forrester Research predicts that after the price war that is raging among dozens of online brokerage firms, about 75 percent of them will either be acquired or fail within five years. Now that the most aggressive traders have migrated to the Internet, online brokerage firms are all expected to suffer a significant decline in growth, although overall growth of online financial services will accelerate, Forrester predicts. Mr. Davis says the execution of simple stock trades is just one of many financial services that can be carried out electronically and yield only slim profits; others are basic term life insurance and the brokering of standard home mortgages. Consequently, he said, the livelihoods of thousands of people who now sell those services are threatened by the Internet. "Most existing players in personal financial services won't be successful online," Mr. Davis said, citing their expensive networks of offices and salespeople. Brokerage firms have taken to the Internet largely as a defensive measure. They found they were losing too much of their customers' money to firms that offered electronic trading, such as Charles Schwab, E*trade and Fidelity Investments. John L. Steffens, a Merrill Lynch vice chairman, told Merrill brokers recently that customers had moved $9 billion to eight leading online brokers. "The big thing becomes choice," Mr. Kenney, of Merrill, said. "What had heretofore been a bundled product until Schwab came along is going to be unbundled and offered in multiple forms." Mr. Kenney said that wealthy people would continue to demand the personal attention of an adviser, or team of advisers, but they would expect many transactions, such as the paying of monthly bills, to be handled automatically. In exchange for a fee that amounts to a slim percentage of the assets they keep at the firm, they will expect sound advice and guidance delivered electronically, over the telephone and, occasionally, in person, he said. Other customers will purchase one or more of the firm's services a la carte, paying only for research on certain industries or advice on how to allocate their assets. But firms will offer the best value to people who keep at least $100,000 in a fee-based account. "That is the cutoff everybody is using, and they're not raising the amount," Mr. Kenney said. "Five years from now, it's still going to be $100,000. For a middle-class income plus some assets, there's going to be an extraordinary amount of services available from the best firms for a reasonable amount." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Going Online With Personal Finance" An increasing number of people will use the Internet for online financial services. the number of households managing their bank accounts online is expected to increase steadily over the next few years, as are the total assets in online financial accounts.  Graph tracks the number of households with online bank accounts, in millions, projected through 2003.  Graph tracks assets in online brokerage accounts, in trillions, projected through 2003. title:
OUTLOOK 2000: ECONOMY & INDUSTRY;
Health Care Consumers Can Expect Change, and a Shock or Two
body: Americans who have complaints about the health care system may soon be in luck -- or maybe not. Many health care professionals expect the medical system in the unitedstates to be overhauled so remarkably during the next two decades that many patients will not be able to recognize it. While such a notion may excite some consumers -- who hasn't fantasized about the death of health maintenance organizations? -- others will no doubt be riled by new procedures that actually provide less medical care and coverage than before. "The one thing that is sure to happen is a lot of change across the whole health care industry," said Dr. David B. Skinner, the chief executive of the newyork Presbyterian Hospital. "A better quality system has started, but it is going to take several decades to develop." Consumers should brace themselves for a few shocks. Many patient advocates and Democratic representatives in Congress would like a government-sponsored health care system, similar to many of those in Europe. But some health providers -- notably the pharmaceutical companies -- snarl at the mention of more government involvement, given the likelihood of a federally mandated reduction in drug prices. "The insurance of last resort is the government," said Joseph Zammit-Lucia, the chief executive of Cambridge Pharma Consultancy in newyork, which advises drug companies. "But you never know what insurance you may be able to buy in the future." Even if health care in the unitedstates remains in private hands, change will be dramatic. One of the biggest changes during the next 10 to 20 years is expected to be the increasing role of the patient in choosing his or her treatment. Instead of relying only on their doctors' advice, consumers will also use medical information from the Internet and prescription-drug ad campaigns. "Currently, health care is professional-driven," Mr. Zammit-Lucia said. "But with the Internet and consumer ad campaigns, I will know about as much about my illness as the doctor does. I'll use him as a professional adviser, similar to how I use a financial planner now." Patients will also get their medications in new ways. Health experts are confident that drugs will routinely be bought through the Internet, including treatments for serious conditions. Pharmacists, long the prime instructors of how medications should be taken, will dole out more advice in cyberspace, especially as consumers become brand loyal to their health care Web sites. Medications are also likely to change. Scientists predict that hospital-bound treatments like chemotherapy may eventually be administered as pills that can be taken at home. Patients will also have more choices about how they take their medications, such as through injection, patch, nasal spray or inhaler. "It's realistic to believe that cancer will become a chronic illness," said Dr. Scot Remick, head of clinical trials at the University Hospitals of Cleveland. "We're not curing all cancers yet, but patients will be able to live longer with a good quality of life." The increasingly enormous amount of medical knowledge will also change patients' visits to their doctors. Using models of a person's gene structure, scientists will soon be able to tell which infants can be expected to develop certain illnesses -- including some cancers and diabetes -- and what medicines have little risk of side effects. Doctors say that breakthroughs in genomic technology will allow consumers to know what diseases they are likely to get and what measures to take to prevent them. Yet patient advocates worry that the insurers may use genomic information to deny or limit coverage. "In a brave new world, it is frighteningly realistic to imagine an insurance industry that knows more than it should about the lifestyle and family history of every American," said Diane Archer, president of the Medicare Rights Center, a consumer advocacy group in newyork. "Through health profiling, an insurer can refuse affordable coverage to everyone with a perceived health risk." Dr. Charles M. Cutler, chief medical officer of the American Association of Health Plans, a trade group representing managed care companies, said that insurers would use genetic information not to deny coverage but to provide better care. He noted that some illnesses can be diagnosed now during pregnancy, but insurers have still provided coverage to these infants. That's hardly the last of a consumer's worries. During the next 20 years, Americans will have to deal with increasingly large and powerful health care organizations. Almost all of them will demand higher prices. The consolidation that has swept the drug industry -- with Pfizer and American Home Products battling now to acquire Warner-Lambert, and Zeneca Pharmaceuticals of Britain buying the Swedish drug giant Astra last year -- will continue until there are a handful of companies, each with 10 percent of the global market, double their current share. Only five companies currently have more than a 4 percent share of the worldwide pharmaceutical market, according to I.M.S. Health, an industry consultant. Cambridge Pharma forecasts that, as a result of more costly technology, drug prices will increase to 30 percent of medical expenditures in the unitedstates during the next 20 years from 10 percent at present. "Consumers are going to have to pay for routine drugs out of their own pockets" as insurers scramble to control costs, predicted Mr. Zammit-Lucia, citing generic painkillers as an example. "What will happen is that insurance will only pay for what is not affordable." By most accounts, H.M.O.'s will not live long into the next century, but many health care experts are not sure what type of insurance will take their place. Everyone agrees that traditional indemnity plans are history, even though consumers are demanding an unrestricted choice of doctors. "The problem with managed care is that it became so intrusive in the relationship between patient and doctor," said Dr. Thomas R. Reardon, president of the American Medical Association. "The H.M.O.'s were spending more money than they were saving. We have to find a method to provide appropriate care. But that may not mean all the care the patient wants." One thing on which health care experts agree is that the insurers of the next two decades will be substantially larger than any of the entities that have preceded them. Several doctors predicted that H.M.O.'s would eventually be replaced by large hospital systems, with local clinics and hospices, that contract with employers to provide medical insurance and treatment. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Merck's consumer advertising campaign for Vioxx, above, is aimed at arthritis suffers who want to experience "everyday victories" over their pain. The company is also pitching Zocor, above for lowering blood cholestorol levels.

title:
OUTLOOK 2000: ECONOMY & INDUSTRY;
Key Forces for Business Success, Creativity and a Local Touch
body: For five years now, a klatch of management scholars and forward-looking executives have met at the Sloan School of Management at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to ponder a question: What will be tomorrow's model for business success? Their collective answer goes well beyond the usual suspects, the likes of Dell Computer, Amazon.com, Qualcomm or Priceline -- all commonly hailed as prototypes for the age of the Internet. Instead, this business academy with its dazzling virtuosity in technology seems at pains to reassert that technology is not enough. "Success takes a balance of forces; technology is not always necessary and is almost never sufficient," said Michael S. Scott Morton, professor of management. Dr. Scott Morton has been co-director of M.I.T.'s initiative on Inventing the Organizations of the 21st Century, a research project involving a score of scholars and engaging dozens of companies in its deliberations. A specialist in corporate strategy, Dr. Scott Morton maintains there is less than meets the eye in the Internet land rush. He sees more activity than results from the celebrated Web start-ups. In the long run, he expects "the bigger and longer-lasting impacts" will come from established companies that successfully reinvent themselves in imaginative ways, using technology to enlarge their fundamental business vision and to support an inspired work force. To be sure, this leaves a great variety of possibilities, and the roughly 200 executives and scholars who met in mid-November for a valedictory summing-up of the five-year inquiry heard a good many of them. Tomorrow's model company might be gigantic, or it might be tiny -- either possibility was seen as entirely consistent with the power of the Internet. Tomorrow's company might be in continuous flux, its operations put together and pulled apart like a Lego toy. The model enterprise might be acutely sensitive to its physical and human environment, or it might be lean and terribly mean, asking no loyalty and offering none. But within the forest of possibilities, there seemed a consensus on several broad principles: *Highly decentralized systems will be far more important than they are today. Not a soul took issue with that. A great many companies have concluded that if they are to move quickly and adroitly, as many decisions as possible should be made by those closest to the customer. *Activities -- not organization charts -- will become the key building blocks in business. As outsourcing and alliances become even more common, basic functions like recruiting or training or sales promotion may be turned over to outside specialists. So product design, an activity, will remain essential, but not necessarily an in-house design department. *Companies, large or small, will be both global and local. To compete effectively, global giants will require the local touch. And with the borderless Internet, even small businesses will reach customers around the world -- and face global competition, as well. The M.I.T. covey's most celebrated member is Peter M. Senge, who wrote "The Fifth Discipline" a decade ago and touched off a corporate quest to create the "learning organization." Speaking by video hookup from Paris, Dr. Senge said he now expected "environmental sustainability" to become a cornerstone of corporate strategy. "Waste is an artifact of the industrial age," he declared. "Nature actually has no waste -- none." One of Dr. Senge's models for tomorrow is Xerox, which designs new copiers for remanufacture, having discovered it can save money in building new copiers by reprocessing parts from old ones. Another is Interface Inc. of Atlanta, the nation's largest maker of commercial carpeting, which has made a signature commitment to "sustainability" through recycling and waste reduction. (Its Web site at www.interfaceinc.com is as lofty and luminous as a New Age greeting card: "More than just a carpet company, we represent peace of mind.") The idea, one Interface executive wrote, is "to deliver better service and increased value, not more stuff." Its Terratex, Solenium and Deja Vu fabrics and flooring are made from recycled materials. Its ReEntry program reuses or recycles customers' old carpeting. "We guarantee your old carpet won't end up in a landfill, period." In looking for companies with foresight and imagination, Dr. Scott Morton singled out Schneider National of Green Bay, Wis., the nation's largest full-load trucking company and a pioneer in using Qualcomm satellite technology to direct its fleet. Schneider has transformed itself from a routine over-the-road hauler to a sophisticated carrier that provides an essential service in today's manufacturing economy. It provides "just in time" parts delivery, guaranteed, come hell or high water, for customers on the nationwide scale of General Motors. Schneider has also expanded its conception of its business. Through subsidiaries, the company will design, install and run logistics systems for other companies, including owning and operating dedicated fleets. It buys and finances trucks for others, and it matches loads to available trucks for more than 1,000 carriers. Dr. Scott Morton credits the creativity and courage of Donald J. Schneider, president and chief executive. Mr. Schneider, true to character, credits the company's 17,000 "talented associates." Thomas W. Malone, a professor of information systems and Dr. Scott Morton's co-director, veered from the more traditional models of his two colleagues and expressed a vision that is drenched in the power of the Internet. But he was less taken with the current fervor over e-commerce than with what he saw as a more profound change, a coming golden age for "microenterprises." As the communication costs fall to next to nothing, "essentially everyone" can be well enough informed to make good decisions, he said. That power will be a boon to the highly motivated, the creative, the innovative. He expects a vast Internet marketplace in business services to take shape, enabling the smallest businesses to rent the talents and capabilities to compete with the largest companies. Large portions of the business economy will consist of very small enterprises, as few as one to 10 talented people, and that sector will take on the radically decentralized character of the Internet. Dr. Malone's prototype enterprise is TopsyTail, a tiny Dallas-based company founded a decade ago to produce a plastic hair-styling tool. Relying on a score of vendors, from design firms to injection molders through fulfillment houses, TopsyTail has produced more than $100 million in sales at retail with only three employees (a chief financial officer, a marketing director and a general assistant). Its latest product is a collapsible foam-lined cowboy hat to prevent "hat hair and hot heads." Its founder, Tomima Edmark, who once sold large systems for I.B.M., says she turned to extreme outsourcing by hunch and by necessity. She champions the technique as an inexpensive, fleet-footed way to bring out a product. "I always felt it would work," she said in an interview, "I needed to ramp up quickly, and I didn't have much money." Ms. Edmark assembled her network of TopsyTail vendors the old-fashioned way -- by phone, personal contact and trial and error. But her newest venture is more purely Internet: a Web store to sell brands of women's underwear online, starting in February. Outsourced as usual, the site is being built by a New Jersey webmaster. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Schneider National pioneered the use of satellite technology to direct its fleet. (Schneider National)
