title:
The Web: New Ticket to a Pink Slip;
On the Job, the Boss Can Watch Your Every Online Move, and You Have Few Defenses
body: ONE day early in October, 40 employees of the Xerox Corporation, working in locations across the unitedstates, received unwelcome news: They had been caught in the act of surfing to forbidden Web sites, nabbed not by managers or fellow employees but by software designed to monitor their online indiscretions. The software recorded every Web site they had visited (many of which, it turned out, were related to shopping or pornography) and every minute they had spent at those sites. "This was up to eight hours a day in inappropriate visits to Web sites," said Bill McKee, a spokesman for Xerox. "Obviously they were not doing their job." The 40 workers were fired immediately, but they were not the only ones being subjected to the watchful eye of the monitoring software. In fact, the Web use of every one of Xerox's 92,000 employees -- in countries around the world -- is routinely monitored by the company. The surveillance is no secret, Mr. McKee said. Xerox workers have come to expect that they are being watched. Employees at companies elsewhere should begin to expect the same: In 1999, at least 45 percent of employers said they monitored their employees' phone calls, computer files or email messages, according to the American Management Association. That number, based on a survey of more than 1,000 human-resources managers at corporations of varying sizes, is up from 35 percent two years ago. The monitoring is necessary, employers argue, because of the changing nature of the workplace. Supervisors must keep tabs on which workers are wasting company time by surfing to entertainment Web sites, which ones are sending email messages that create a hostile environment for women or members of minority groups, and which ones are distributing company secrets or jamming their networks with bulk email. Balancing that desire for control with an employee's rights to privacy has never been easy. Even before the arrival of the Internet, courts have heard cases of employers who search through desks or listen to voicemail messages. A spattering of laws, including state and federal wiretap laws, have tried to offer some guideposts. Under the federal wiretap law, for example, an employer cannot listen to an employee's personal telephone conversations unless the employees have been notified that their conversations are monitored and unless the monitoring is required for business purposes. Now questions of privacy have moved to the electronic realm -- where laws related to workplace surveillance are nearly nonexistent. And so far, less than a dozen lawsuits that raise questions about an employer's right to read email messages or track Web site use have made their way to courts.  In several of these, judges have ruled that employers can do what they want with computers they own. Some judges have said that as long as employees are warned that they may be watched, they should not expect any privacy in their online interactions. But some privacy advocates, labor organizations and lawyers consider those arguments still largely untested. A person's home life and work life are increasingly intermingled, they argue. At what point is it reasonable to expect at least some privacy when using a company's computers or network? "You can't define privacy as whatever the employer wants it to be," said Craig Cornish, a lawyer who specializes in issues related to workplace privacy. "Then it's no right at all." For now, the issues revolve around technology that enables employers to watch and record what flies over their networks. Recent developments in software may add further complications: companies can now record and view everything a person does on a computer, from typing in a word-processing document to opening an image file. One new product, called Spector, surreptitiously takes digital snapshots of whatever appears on the screen, as often as every few seconds. "Your employees will hate Spector," the Web site for the software declares, "because Spector records everything." Although Spector was just released this month, John Yatsko, a security consultant for J & J Consulting in Erie, Pa., has already installed it at a plastics manufacturing company that he would not name. "If you need evidence you want to take to the police, Spector is great for that," Mr. Yatsko said. Most employers are less heavy-handed. They say they won't routinely read email messages. And they will typically look at Web traffic among a pool of computers without focusing on individual use. But if something looks suspicious, they say, they have a right to dig into an employee's electronic records. "You have to take appropriate steps to make sure the resources are put to appropriate business use," said Alan Hodel, a spokesman for Compaq Computer, one of 4,800 companies that use a filtering and monitoring product called Websense. Employers' fear of sexual-harassment lawsuits is one of the greatest forces driving the monitoring movement, according to companies that sell filtering and monitoring software. If employees are surfing to pornography sites, said John Carrington, president of Websense Inc., "it's like having porno magazines all through your office." If blocking and monitoring software is in place, Mr. Carrington said, "a company can say, at least we tried." Many companies that track Web use say they also watch to make sure that employees are getting their work done. In a recent survey of about 1,200 employers by Vault .com, a company that publishes reports about workplace issues, 54 percent reported that they had caught employees browsing Web sites that were not related to work. In response to the perceived abuse of resources, many companies have posted policies outlining what use of email and the Web is permitted and what is not. Xerox, for example, flashes a message on the screen every time employees log on. It tells them not to use the Web for anything but work. As in the Xerox case, the repercussions of violating those polices can be drastic: In a survey commissioned by Websense of 200 human-resources officers in midsize and large companies, one in three reported that their company had fired employees for misusing the Internet. A few cases noted in the survey, taken in November, stemmed from shopping, stock trading, gambling, sports and computer games. But the vast majority involved pornography. Just this month, for example, The newyork Times Company fired 23 employees in a central processing center in Norfolk, Va., for distributing pornographic images via email, according to Nancy Nielsen, a spokeswoman for the company. The action was not a result of monitoring but was in response to an employee complaint. "A lot of people were made very uncomfortable" by the distribution of the material, Ms. Nielsen said. So far, only a handful of employees have argued in court that an employer's electronic surveillance invaded their privacy. Not one case, according to Mr. Cornish, who has been following the subject, has been tried by a jury. Some experts suspect that if the employees had faced a group of their peers, they may have found a more sympathetic audience. In addressing judges, however, employees have failed: not one has ruled in their favor. The case of Mark L. Simons, a former employee of the Central Intelligence Agency, is one example. In 1998, Mr. Simons was convicted of possessing child pornography after a network manager detected that his workstation had called up several pornographic Web sites. While Mr. Simons did not dispute the facts of the charges against him, he argued in court that the agency's search of his computer was unlawful because his employer initially looked at his hard drive without involving the police, who would have had to obtain a search warrant. "If the employer was looking through his computer for a legitimate business reason, he wouldn't need a warrant," argued Marvin Miller, Mr. Simons's lawyer. "But this was a criminal investigation." The judge in the case, James C. Cacheris of the unitedstates District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, was not persuaded. The agency, Mr. Cacheris wrote in his opinion, had made clear to its employees that they were only permitted to use the company's Internet service lawfully. And he agreed with the employer's argument that the agency has a right to monitor its networks to make sure that its systems are secure. Mr. Simons has appealed the ruling. Mr. Miller is not the only lawyer to wonder about the fairness of such reasoning. Those who specialize in employee rights question whether employers can unilaterally claim the right to monitor what happens on their computers. Just because the computers and networks are the employers' property, they argue, does not mean that they have a right to read everything that crosses the computer screens. "A logical extension of that," said Mr. Cornish, who is co-chairman of an American Bar Association subcommittee on workplace privacy, "is the argument that you're using our bathrooms, therefore we get to put a camera over the stalls." Everett L. Bobbitt, a lawyer in San Diego, said he recently took on a case in which an employer took the ownership argument too far. He represented a police officer who said he had been fired after his employer searched his computer and found a file showing he had visited www.whitehouse.com, -- a pornographic Web site. The police department argued that it had a right to go through the officer's computer files partly because it owned the computer. But the police officer, whom Mr. Bobbitt would not name, insisted that he had meant to type www.whitehouse.gov -- the official White House site. He sued for wrongful termination and eventually settled the suit for $100,000. The employer had no right to go through the officer's files simply because they were on the company's computer, Mr. Bobbitt argued. "It was just a fishing expedition," he said. Beyond such cases, some privacy advocates wonder about the larger impact of electronic surveillance on how people live their lives. "More and more of us are working in a mixed work-and-home environment," said Beth Givens, project director of the Privacy Rights Clearinghouse, an advocacy group in San Diego, Calif. People are using their computers for making medical appointments, sending messages to loved ones or filling out forms for car insurance. "Any monitoring needs to take that into account," Ms. Givens said. "There are many individuals who would feel they have a reasonable expectation of privacy." Even everyday information-gathering -- like visiting political Web sites or checking the news -- may be thwarted if workers are worried about being watched, Mr. Cornish said. "Surveillance has a chilling effect," he said. "To what extent is this going to choke off an informed citizenry?" At the very least, many lawyers argue, employers should warn their employees that their email may be read and their Web use may be monitored. Last summer, the American Management Association issued a memo to its 10,000 member companies, urging them to make their employees aware that their electronic actions and communications "are subject to recording and review." But not everyone thinks such policies should be required. In California, Gov. Gray Davis recently vetoed a a bill that would have prohibited companies from secretly monitoring their employees' email or personal computer records. He argued that the law would unduly burden companies. At least employees have time on their side. Employers who choose to scan through employee files, email and Web logs are in for hours of extra work. A joke circulating on the Net, written by a 28-year-old named Joe Lavin, puts it this way: A manager installs monitoring software on his employees' computers. Right away he starts reprimanding them for playing video games, downloading Pamela Anderson photographs and sending offensive email messages. But in the end, it is the manager who is fired. "He was in the past a very effective manager," the joke goes. But lately "he has been merely sitting in his office all day, spying on other employees."  Tools of the Trade  MONITORING -- Tracking Web site visits and their duration with software. SEARCHING -- Sifting through servers for email messages sent and received. VIEWING -- Taking electronic snapshots of employees' screens.  A Few Parameters  What Employers Can View at Work THE increasing pervasiveness of surveillance technology has led many employees to wonder just how much privacy they can expect anywhere in the workplace -- whether on their computers or in their file cabinets. The questions are not always easily answered, but a few guidelines can be drawn, according to people who follow employment law. In many cases, experts say, the details of a particular situation -- such as the presence of locks on drawers -- will determine what is considered an unlawful intrusion. Whether the employer is part of the public sector also matters: Public employers are held to standards set in the Fourth Amendment, which protects people against unreasonable search and seizure by government officials. And policies set by an employer can make all the difference in determining what level of privacy is reasonably expected. The following list may provide a rough idea of which areas of the workplace are typically considered private, and which are not -- according to several lawyers' interpretations of privacy laws and court rulings.  PURSES AND BRIEFCASES -- As a general rule, employers have no right to go through a purse, briefcase or piece of luggage that has been brought into the workplace, according to a 1987 ruling by the unitedstates Supreme Court, O'Connor v. Ortega.  DESKS AND FILE CABINETS -- The drawers of desks and file cabinets are also typically off limits to employers -- as long as employees have not been given notification that their drawers are subject to monitoring and as long as the drawers are locked and not shared by others. This interpretation, too, is based upon the Supreme Court's 1987 ruling.  PHONE CONVERSATIONS -- In most cases, in accordance with federal wiretap laws, employers may not listen to an employee's personal conversations without their knowledge. But many exceptions apply: An employer may listen to the phone conversations of telemarketers, for example.  VOICE MAIL -- Employers may gain access to voice mail messages if they have a business purpose for doing so, and especially if they have told their employees that the messages may be monitored.  email AND WEB USE -- Most employees should not consider their office email to be private, nor should they assume that their employers are not looking at logs of the Web sites they have visited. Only a handful of lawsuits regarding workers' email and Web privacy have made their way to court. So far, judges have been ruling overwhelmingly in favor of the employers, especially if employees are told not to use the company networks for anything but work. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Craig Cornish, above, a lawyer, specializes in protecting workers' privacy rights. John Carrington, chairman of Websense, makes software that blocks access to Web sites. (Gaylon Wampler for The newyork Times; inset, Robert Burroughs for The newyork Times)(pg. G8); (Brian Stauffer)(pg. G1)

title:
Where the Risk Is Riskier Yet;
A New Breed of Venture Capitalist Scouts Latin America
body: Upon arriving in the big Amazon port of Belem several months ago, Patricia Moles, the manager of a venture-capital fund, was faced with an unusual investment-related decision: whether to continue by boat to the hearts-of-palm plantation in which her fund was hoping to acquire a minority stake, a trip that would take 12 hours, or to rent a propeller plane. "Time was a must so I chose the plane," said Ms. Moles, 33, a native of Mexico, whose Brazil-based employer, Banco Axial, looks for investments in environmentally friendly companies. Although her trip was off the beaten track of the briefcase bankers who stick to financial centers like Sao Paulo, it was indicative of a new investment trend that is sweeping Latin America. Venture capitalists are searching the region for opportunities in young companies, much as they have been doing in Silicon Valley. Many of these financiers like the challenge of nontraditional investments -- organically produced hearts of palm, for example, grown from custom-selected and -germinated seeds that generate a continuing supply of palm stems. Yet most venture capitalists investing in companies with a Latin American focus, like those providing seed money to ventures in the unitedstates, are seeking out high technology -- particularly Internet-related companies. The quest is complicated by the often precarious nature of Latin American economies as well as the relative lack of advanced technology, along with the generally frenetic nature of the young Internet industry. The growth of venture-capital investing is part of the wider trend of private equity investors focusing on Latin America, a huge market. Though the region has quickly embraced the Internet, it still has a long way to go in terms of wealth and technology to catch up with the richest industrial nations. Unlike earlier waves of investment, most of which came from abroad or were state-sponsored, the venture-capital investments of the last few years have pitted some of Latin America's richest people against foreigners, particularly from the unitedstates. Among the Latin Americans are Juan Navarro, president of the Exxel Group, one of Argentina's largest privately owned companies; Jorge Paulo Lemann, founder of Garantia, a big Brazilian investment bank now owned by the Credit Suisse Group, and Carlos Slim Helu, chairman of Telefonos de Mexico. Then there are the people who work for, or are partners in the venture-capital funds controlled by these investors. Antonio Bonchristiano is an example of this new breed. Six months ago, Mr. Bonchristiano, 32, was a partner in a fund that is part of GP Investimentos, an investment group based here, whose owners include Mr. Lemann. His task was to seek out an appealing Brazilian Internet company and buy it. What he came up with was BookNet, an online bookseller similar to Amazon.com, and GP acquired a controlling stake. In something of an unusual twist, Mr. Bonchristiano became the company's chief executive, switching roles from venture capitalist to entrepreneur. Using his knowledge of the game, he then went to newyork to drum up additional money, and returned with $14.3 million from firms like Warburg Pincus and individual investors like Henry R. Kravis of Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Company. BookNet was renamed Submarino, and now the company's headquarters here is brimming with 50 employees working 14-hour days and relieving stress at a couple of pinball and foosball machines. The company has opened offices in Spain, Argentina and Mexico, and aims to become the leading online shopping destination in the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking world. "This is dreamlike for me as a Brazilian," Mr. Bonchristiano said in English polished during his undergraduate years at Oxford. "Brazil was colonized for so long, either economically, intellectually or technologically, and the Internet is changing that. With new access to investment and technology, the playing field is leveled." Latin America's capitalist structures are still considered relatively backward, though. Domestic stock markets are riddled with labyrinthine regulations that make it hard to buy or sell securities. And some investors, including Dennis Rodrigues, a partner in the Sao Paulo-based firm FIR Capital, see the evolution of domestic capital markets as the key to the success of venture-capital investing in Latin America. But other investors, as well as many entrepreneurs, are drawn by the possibility of leapfrogging local exchanges and listing their companies on markets in the unitedstates, nearly always Nasdaq, hoping for some of the paper wealth made possible by a market fascinated with dot-coms. Going public on Nasdaq is a lot easier with help from people who have generous sources of capital and who also know the American regulatory environment. That is where venture capitalists from the unitedstates come in. Among the most active of these is Chase Capital Partners, part of the Chase Manhattan Corporation. Together with Flatiron Partners of newyork, Chase Capital Partners has invested in five Internet companies that focus on Latin America. The largest, StarMedia Network, a newyork-based portal company for Spanish and Portuguese speakers worldwide that also provides Internet access in some Latin American countries, has been its biggest success so far. After StarMedia went public earlier this year, the initial investment by Chase and Flatiron of $29 million grew to well over $300 million. While some venture operations, like GP Investimentos, often seek to acquire control of companies, others, including Chase, have invested in Latin America in a way that is closer to the traditional Silicon Valley model of providing seed capital to small companies that then proceed through several rounds of financing before going public. Usually, this model involves the purchase of a minority stake in the company, through which management direction is provided but not dictated. "Being a venture capitalist in Latin America largely involves adapting what has worked in the unitedstates to what is realistic in countries like Mexico and Brazil," said Susan Segal, head of Latin American operations for Chase Capital Partners. E-commerce, for instance, is as strong a lure in the region as it is in the unitedstates, and has accounted for some of Chase's bets -- like its recent investment in Mercado Livre, an Internet company hoping to reproduce online some of the fervor of a boisterous open-air market. The Boston Consulting Group estimates that revenue from electronic commerce in Latin America will grow to $3.8 billion in 2003 from $167 million this year. Yet while most signs point to the growth of purchases over the Internet, and of Latin American Internet use in general, obstacles to such rosy outcomes remain. According to a report by the International Data Corporation, weak credit card processing operations, the high cost of basic Internet service and precarious and costly shipping networks will inhibit the spread of e-commerce. And the use of computers and even telephones in the region is still relatively low, a limiting factor for all Internet businesses. For instance, in Brazil, Latin America's largest country, there are an estimated 12 telephone lines for each 100 people, compared with more than 50 lines for every 100 people in the unitedstates. And the entrepreneurial culture that speeds the creation of start-ups in the unitedstates is different in Latin America. "Some entrepreneurs that are used to sealing deals with a handshake don't realize that a lot of rigorous detail is needed to put together a venture-capital deal," said Lisa Krochmal, a lawyer in the Buenos Aires office of Morrison & Foerster, an American firm active in new technology deals. Another concern is the erratic nature of the Internet industry itself. As in the unitedstates, most young Internet companies in Latin America lose money. This, coupled with the boom-and-bust cycles of Latin American economies, makes some investors wary of betting on the region's young companies. "A lot of people are going to get burned when they realize that transforming an interesting idea in Brazil into a stock appealing to retail investors in the U.S. is no piece of cake," Mr. Rodrigues of FIR Capital said. Still, where some people see obstacles, others see opportunities -- opportunities that require capital to realize. Aiming to bring Internet access to people without a phone or a computer, an American, Terrence Danial, helped found NetKiosk, a Buenos Aires-based company that sells stand-alone units equipped with a PC that allows users to surf the Net for a fee. In addition to sales of the units, which are put in places like hotel lobbies, NetKiosk hopes to gain revenue from selling advertising that appears on the units as well as on the company's portal page. But NetKiosk has had trouble attracting seed money. "In my view, venture capital in Latin America still has a long way to go," said Mr. Danial, adding that the seed-money industry is not as well developed in the region as it is in the unitedstates and that potential backers are often warier of taking risks. "A lot of investors are still seeing things from traditional business mind-sets," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Antonio Bonchristiano, above (Paulo Fridman for The newyork Times), the online bookseller Submarino's chief, breaks his 14-hour days at the pinball machine. At a coconut plantation in Brazil's Tocantins state, Patricia Moles of Banco Axial joins Edmund Baruk, a project co-sponsor. Ms. Moles also dabbles in hearts of palm. (John Forgach)  Graph: "Reeping Rewards in Latin America" StarMedia Network is one of the first start-ups with a focus on Latin America to get Silicon-Valley-style cash and management help from the unitedstates. Chase Capital Partners and Flatiron Partners together invested $29 million to help the company go public. That investement was worth roughly $360 million yesterday. The graph shows the stock price since May 1999. (Source: Bloomberg Financial Markets)

title: How Small-Town Standards Can Block a Big-City Class
body: Last spring, Raymond Stefan Pultinas and his students set up a Web site dedicated to the classic novel "Invisible Man," Ralph Ellison's angry and satiric commentary on black life in America. Along with links to historic reviews by Saul Bellow and Irving Howe, the students began posting their own impressions and compositions, inviting reaction not just from their peers but from the outside world. It was, Mr. Pultinas said, a wonderful success, and encouraged even the students who never spoke up in class to join free-wheeling conversations. "One of the beautiful things about this project was that the technology and the use of the Internet had the potential for expanding the conversation," Mr. Pultinas said yesterday. This fall, Mr. Pultinas, a teacher at DeWitt Clinton High School in the Bronx, tried to duplicate the experience, but met a roadblock. Time after time, as students tried to type in their messages -- original compositions in Ellison's voice, excerpts from his novel, sometimes using profanity and racial epithets, sometimes not -- they were met by the words "Access Denied." What had happened is a lesson out of some of the novels in Mr. Pultinas's class in advanced literary criticism -- Ray Bradbury's "Fahrenheit 451," perhaps, and Big Brother in George Orwell's "1984." It is a textbook case of how school systems across the country are dealing with the wide open world of the Internet. They are buying commercial filtering programs and using predetermined settings that decide what children can and cannot see. Those settings are based on objections submitted to the software companies by officials and educators across the country, and so they tend to reflect the standards of the more cautious communities. Conservative, Bible-Belt communities like Conway, S.C., are helping to set the standards for what students in more cosmopolitan places like newyork are allowed to see. When the situation first came to light in newyork in early November, Schools Chancellor Rudy Crew promised to train teachers to modify the commercial filtering program, I-Gear, that the Board of Education had adopted. Dr. Crew's director of technology urged teachers to call his office for help. But Mr. Pultinas said his calls to the technology office in the last two weeks were answered by a man named "Joe" who refused to give his last name, said he would try to help, but changed nothing. Pam McDonnell, a spokeswoman for the board, said yesterday that Dr. Crew had formed a filtering-standards committee composed of union representatives, technology experts and parents, that will look at situations like the one at DeWitt Clinton. Board of Education officials said they adopted I-Gear because of its flexibility: it can distinguish "breast" from "chicken breast," for example. The flexibility was cited as a selling point by the manufacturer, Symantec, in Cupertino, Calif., but unless local school officials customize the filter, it relies on 23 predetermined, or default, settings. Those are "super categories" of prohibited sites set by the company, ranging from "news" to "intolerance." In newyork, teachers complained that at first the I-Gear filter banned the last chapter of John Steinbeck's "Grapes of Wrath," The newyork Times, The Daily News, CNN and abortion-rights sites but not anti-abortion sites. Symantec officials have insisted that the filter does not reflect judgments about issues like abortion, but its customers, like school officials in Hory County in rural South Carolina, said that because they recommend sites to be filtered out, such idiosyncrasies might creep in. Michael Cherry, technical systems administrator for the Hory County schools, is the main arbiter of what is allowed or not allowed on the Internet in the county's schools. Mr. Cherry described his community as "deep in the Bible Belt," and said he tried to use that standard as his guide. He spends about a third of his day, he said, reviewing computer printouts showing Web sites that his students and teachers have tried to reach. He looks for offensive content that slips through the filter. He can trace each record to a single user at a single machine. The material can be used to discipline students or teachers who use the Internet for noneducational purposes. "I can sit anywhere in the world, if I can get on the Internet, and I can see where anyone has been," Mr. Cherry said. When he detects a site that he thinks should be banned, he passes it on to Symantec. Mr. Cherry said Symantec had adopted some of his suggestions, like banning a site that enabled users to exchange letters with prisoners. A high school of 1,100 students, he said, averages 800 violations per day; about half are attempts to download games, which is against school rules, and just a handful involve pornography, he said. "We took the approach to lock it down, and then loosen it up as we needed it," he said. newyork used much the same reasoning, assuming that schools would be grateful for "half a loaf" when they had nothing before, said Chad Vignola, the board's lawyer. But DeWitt Clinton was accustomed to almost the whole loaf. A year ago, U.S. News and World Report magazine named it one of America's 96 outstanding high schools. The school wired its 10 computer labs to the Internet two years ago, well before most newyork school did, and paid for the connection. But when the board offered to provide centralized Internet service this year, the school was only too happy to save the money, said Michael Greene, the school's technology specialist. The results have been disappointing, Mr. Greene said, because students must share the Internet connection with central administrative functions like recording attendance. Now, in addition to the restrictions created by the filter, the increased traffic is drastically reducing student access to the Internet. A year ago, all 340 computers in the school computer labs could be connected to the Internet at once, Mr. Greene said. Now only 60 or 70 can, "if we're lucky." Mr. Pultinas said it was unclear why some students were blocked from posting messages on the class Web site (www.dwchs.com/classes/litclass /literary.htm). While some of the messages contained profanity, others did not. "It's erratic," he said. Sherine Cummings, one of Mr. Pultinas's students, wrote a letter of protest to Dr. Crew. "Ask yourself this," she wrote. "How are we as young adults supposed to grow up maturely and independently in the world, when we still have people trying to hold our hands through the whole experience?" http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: In Room 306 at DeWitt Clinton High School, Raymond Stefan Pultinas, right, taught Ralph Ellison's "Invisible Man." In Room 149, a computer filter denied access to his students trying to use the class Web site's material on the classic novel. (Photographs by George M. Gutierrez for The newyork Times)

title:
IDEAS INTO ACTION;
It's Not the Product That's Different, It's the Process
body: MARSHALL McLUHAN wrote 35 years ago that the medium is the message, a puzzling perception that turned out to be profound. Today, a great many business thinkers, in one way or another, seem to be saying something similar: In the new economy, the process is the product. Set aside the electronic gadgetry. Are the other things we buy -- the cars we drive, the shoes we wear, the trips we take -- all that different from what they were when the other George Bush was president? Not really. The shirts and skirts and jackets we wear today are pretty much the same as the ones that hung in our closet a decade ago. But the ways they are produced -- all the steps from textile plant to doorstep delivery -- have been overhauled, in a forced infusion of information technology. In the 1990's, the apparel industry saved its skin by bringing off a process revolution all but invisible to the consumer. Something similarly invisible is taking shape now with the Internet. Who could possibly escape the squall of dot-com retailing this season? But largely out of sight, the Internet is also devising the institutions that will enable businesses to deal with one another in radically different ways. Corporate America seems to have concluded that the train -- the Internet Express -- is leaving the station. The foundations of a new business order are being laid right now. And unless companies respond in kind, they will wither like towns on the Great Plains that failed to attract the early rail lines. Richard R. Roscitt, the new president of AT&T's huge Business Services arm, made his reputation building complex Internet-based networks for corporate giants. He thought he saw the makings of a business revolution in the Internet several years ago, but he is astounded at how quickly it came. "You would have to have had a crystal ball," he marveled in an interview last week. The commanding heights of business have come alive to the power of networking as a pervasive way of doing business, Mr. Roscitt said.  Established giants are shifting critical functions to the Internet, at least to their roped-off corner of it. Merrill Lynch has embraced online trading, Citibank sends trillions of dollars a day across the Net. The Internet is pumping "the lifeblood of the organization," Mr. Roscitt said. "The stakes are much higher." The chronic weakness among automakers has been a development process that moves at a turtle's pace. Now AT&T is building an Internet network for General Motors that will enable G.M. to bring cars to market more quickly. The five-year, $350 million project will link G.M. design centers, factory floors and dealerships the world over and allow them to perform continuously as though they were side by side. In "Blown to Bits" (Harvard Business School Press, 1999), Philip Evans and Thomas S. Wurster, partners at the Boston Consulting Group, argue that communication via the Internet has become so cheap and so powerful -- and still no end in sight -- that it will shatter today's business order. They predict it will force every business in America to pick apart the processes that lie behind its products and consider putting the chain back together in novel ways. It has always been costly to convey thorough, reliable, timely, rich information. That reality protected those who could afford to play. On the Internet, the cost will all but dry up. And once pure information is cut loose from the expensive physical means of delivering it, whether a printing plant and a fleet of trucks or a dedicated network of mainframe computers, the value of all those old arrangements comes into question. In the new economy, information will substitute for goods. Branch Rickey once remarked that luck was the residue of design. Mr. Evans and Mr. Wurster write that "inventory is merely the physical correlate of deficient information." Not nearly as epigrammatic, but it is a powerful thought: The more known about what customers want, the less the need to tie up money in expensive (and perishable) stock. The process replaces the product. Exactly that notion about inventory drove the remaking of the American garment trade. Apparel makers, under searing pressure from retailers like Wal-Mart, used computer links and the sharing of sales and production data to create a discipline of speedy response. They successfully met the simultaneous demands of "lean retailing" for both lower inventories and a much greater variety of goods, at lower prices and in smaller, more frequent deliveries. The story of how information technology enabled the American garment industry to triumph over low-cost competition overseas is told in "A Stitch in Time" (Oxford University Press, 1999) by Frederick H. Abernathy, John T. Dunlop, Janice H. Hammond and David Weil. Laser technology permitted the key innovation: the bar code, which tracks demand at the cash register and the status of goods at every earlier stage. That system in turn required computers and software to monitor thousands of prices and millions of items. But the industry also had to abandon old thinking and invent a new way for handling goods, the bustling hub known as the modern distribution center. "A distribution center," the authors of "A Stitch in Time" remark dryly, "is the antithesis of a warehouse." Goods sit in a warehouse; they speed through a distribution center on conveyor belts, racing from supply trucks at inbound bays to delivery trucks at outbound. And yet nothing would flow until everything fit. The industry had to hammer out common standards at every juncture, from the bar-coding itself to labels on shipping cartons to uniform price tags and garment hangers. That history came before the Internet, but the pattern is instructive. The new order will require not only lasers and computers but also, like lean retailing, fresh thinking about old processes and new arrangements of bricks and mortar. The apparel rebirth relied on expensive computer systems tying giant retailers more tightly to selected suppliers. By contrast, the Internet will be open and cheap, accessible to a host of new and smaller suppliers. Uniform standards, essential in every era, now define the day. The Internet itself consists of agreements to communicate in a certain way.  New protocols are being added industry by industry. With every added layer, the Internet connects new realms and thousands of new participants.  Mr. Evans and Mr. Wurster of Boston Consulting say that in many ways this standard setting is more profound than the dazzling technology. Mr. Roscitt of AT&T says it is the only way to fly. "Internet protocol is what everyone's going to jump on," Mr. Roscitt said. "No one in their right mind would build anything not based on that." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart/Illustrations: "Reinventing an Industry" American apparel makers were a fading force until they learned to view their product as a process of harnessing information along a chain that runs from the factory floor to the retail counter.  Bar codes identify items so they can be tracked as they move through the supply chain. At the cash register, they monitor demand and sharpen sales forecasts.  Computer systems and software connect retailers to their suppliers, keeping track of thousands of orders and millions of items, from textile plant to final sale.  The modern distribution center is a bustling hub that funnels goods quickly from apparel makers to retail stores.  Uniform standards permit goods from many producers to flow smoothly through the system. They range from computer codes to shipping labels to garment hangers. (Illustrations by Sarah Slobin/The newyork Times)

title:
MY JOB;
I Write Copy for a Web Start-up
body: A few weeks ago, I abandoned the sinking ship of newspaper journalism and hopped aboard a pirate vessel, the Internet. Instead of writing news for a venerable newspaper, I'm now providing content for a Silicon Alley start-up founded by two 20-somethings. My fellow reporters and I often grumbled about the long hours, low pay and humdrum assignments at the Philadelphia daily where we toiled on the suburban beat. Yet, when I told them where I was going and added that, yes, at the tender age of 27, I'd be receiving stock options, I saw sellout in their eyes. Sellout? Maybe. But in journalism, you have to work your way up the ladder for years. After all, your bosses have worked their way up the ladder. So, you put in time at newspapers in states like Iowa and Louisiana, and then maybe you have a shot at a staff job on a newspaper in newyork or San Francisco. In the new economy, if you're smart and confident, you don't have to wait in line. You can be whatever you want to be. There are no ladders and no pigeonholes. My new bosses at InfoRocket, an online information-auction company where users pay other users for answers to their questions, seemed excited about my arrival. Experiment with the copy, they told me. We trust you. So I admit it: I was probably rubbing it in when I told my newspaper friends that InfoRocket's co-founder, Matt Cassin, 24, was wearing shorts during my interview. And that irreverent employees had scrawled site models and quotes like "Revolt Against Time" in black ink on the office's white walls. (I later learned this was because the walls were to be torn down.) But it wasn't just the casual atmosphere that struck me; what bowled me over was the sheer energy of the place. People were coming and going, banging away furiously at the keyboards, shouting across rooms. At one point, Teo Montoya, 25, the other co-founder, stumbled into the room unshaven and disheveled. He had been up all night writing code, but that didn't stop him from sitting down with me for an hour to talk about everything from my favorite movies to the "new information paradigms." I hate to say it, but the hectic pace made me wonder if this Internet start-up didn't resemble a newsroom back in the heyday of newspapers. I belonged here, I told myself. I didn't have a computer or a desk for the first three days, and it took even longer to get a telephone. But on my first day the company ordered pizza and my 13 colleagues and I sat around the conference table. "O.K., team," said Matt. "How is everything going? Do we need to discuss anything?" We really didn't, but we did anyway. I was forced to reveal my most embarrassing moment. (Losing my bathing suit while water-skiing, if you must know.) Now, I'm hard at work planning the email newsletter I'll eventually be writing for our users. "I have lots of ideas," I say. "We'll take 'em," my colleagues reply. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: DEIRDRE SHAW -- Internet Wordsmith (Jeffery A. Salter/The newyork Times)

title: Oracle 2nd-Quarter Results Beat Analyst Expectations
body: Shares of the Oracle Corporation soared this evening in after-hours trading. The gains came after the company reported second-quarter earnings that beat estimates and defied predictions of a slowdown in software sales as corporations focused on Year 2000 computer problems. Analysts' expectations were dampened in September, when Oracle's first-quarter earnings just met estimates and revenue growth fell short. Oracle executives, at the time citing a seasonally weak quarter and a few big sales that slipped past the closing date, predicted a strong year. Today's results were sweet vindication for them. "This was the Y2K quarter, and I expected it to be tough," said William Epifanio II, an analyst with J. P. Morgan. Oracle's database and big applications like accounting and human resources, he said, are exactly the kind of software purchases analysts had expected corporations to defer. "They defied Y2K," he said, "and I think from this point forward we can expect even better performance. With everything happening in e-commerce, the market is moving in Oracle's direction." Oracle reported after the close of the Nasdaq market, where its shares had dropped 2 7/8, to 76 15/16. But in after-hours trading, they jumped 7 1/16, to 84, and were expected to lift opening stock prices tomorrow. For the quarter ended Nov. 30, Oracle earned $384 million, or 26 cents a diluted share, up 40 percent from $274 million, or 19 cents ashare, last year. Revenue grew 13 percent, to $2.32 billion, compared with $2.06 billion a year earlier. Analysts had expected per-share earnings of 22 cents, according to First Call/Thomson Financial. Oracle said revenue from software licensing grew 18 percent year over year. Database software sales increased 17 percent, to $651 million, while applications software sales grew 31 percent, to $168 million. Services, which include education, consulting and support, rose 10 percent, to $1.4 billion. "It's the sixth quarter in a row that we've improved our margins," Jeff Henley, Oracle's chief financial officer, said in a telephone interview. "That's something we think will continue as we convert to an e-business." Oracle's chairman and chief executive, Larry Ellison, said six months ago that the company would transform itself into an Internet company by moving most sales to the Worldwide Web, replacing multiple computer systems around the world with central Internet-based servers and procuring supplies electronically. His goal was to cut $1 billion in costs within 24 months. Oracle also updated its products, including its core database program, Oracle 8i, and all applications to operate over the Internet, so that users need no software except a Web browser. Oracle also says it is the only vendor now offering a complete suite of business applications, including both back-office programs, like human resources and accounting, and front office, like sales force management and purchasing. "Maybe you can just buy it all from Oracle and it all works together and it all works over the Internet," Mr. Ellison said in a conference call with analysts. "My summary for the quarter is, 'Gentlemen, you ain't seen nothing yet.' "  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
AMR's Spinoff of Its Stake in Sabre Could Lure Airline Investors
body: In a move that could touch off investor interest in airline stocks, the AMR Corporation said yesterday that it would spin off its 83 percent stake in the Sabre Holdings Corporation, the travel reservation company. Analysts praised the deal, noting that AMR, the parent of American Airlines, could better control rising fees that are associated with booking tickets. Computer reservation companies, like Sabre, have continually raised their fees, leaving carriers little room to negotiate. "This is the right move for AMR," said Samuel Buttrick, an airline analyst with PaineWebber. "We fully expect airlines to become more aggressive and innovative in finding ways to reduce reservation fees. Privately, airline executives have been fuming over these fee increases." In the divestiture, valued at $6.2 billion, AMR will distribute its 107 million Sabre shares to its shareholders. Each AMR stockholder will receive about 0.7 share of Sabre for each AMR share. Sabre will also pay $675 million in dividends to its shareholders, including AMR. Investors were enthusiastic about the deal. Shares of AMR increased $4.75, or 7.5 percent, to $68.50. Sabre Holdings rose $2.875, or 5.5 percent, to $54.75. With American Airlines shedding Sabre, analysts expect the carrier to have more leeway in lowering its cost of selling tickets. Other companies that own stakes in computer reservation companies -- notably UAL, the parent of United Airlines, and the Northwest Airlines Corporation -- are also expected to sell their holdings, which would create more competition in the industry. The airlines have been increasingly successful in selling tickets to customers over the Internet and forcing reductions in fees from travel agents. But carriers that owned stakes in computer reservation systems have felt compelled to use the companies. Analysts are hoping that the spinoff of Sabre, which was reported yesterday in The Wall Street Journal, will attract more investors to the airline sector. Many of the stocks have increased about 10 percent since increases in fuel prices pushed them to 52-week lows in late summer. Despite the stocks' recent gains, analysts remain bullish that the momentum has only just begun. The airline sector is projected to trade at about seven times 2000 earnings, compared with 25 times earnings for the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index. "The whole airline sector is undervalued," said Candace Browning, an airline analyst with Merrill Lynch. "There will be more short-term negatives. There is going to be a slowdown in traffic, due to Y2K. Everybody in America is going to stay home." Some analysts said that AMR's stock was a good value. They expect the stock to trade at about six times earnings next year, making it one of the cheapest in the airline sector. The company has become more focused on its operations. AMR said yesterday that it would use its share of Sabre's $675 million dividend to invest in its core airline business. Mr. Buttrick thinks that AMR will hit $82 a share by spring, a 19.7 percent gain from yesterday's closing price. But even with AMR's projected gain, two other large airline stocks are expected to outperform it. Delta Air Lines has diversified, buying a 5 percent stake in Priceline.com, which tries to offer Internet users the lowest prices on goods and services. Mr. Buttrick said that shares of Delta, which closed yesterday at $50.0625, should reach $74 in the spring. That move would give investors a 47.5 percent gain. Continental Airlines is also expected to perform well. The airline, projected to trade at about eight times 2000 earnings, should reap more revenue from its North Atlantic routes, where excess capacity hurt profits this year. Analysts also noted that Continental had made inroads in the newyork market, taking market share on some routes from its competitors. According to Mr. Buttrick's calculations, Continental Airlines' stock should reach $52, a 25 percent increase from yesterday's closing price of $41.5625 a share. Analysts were divided about the financial prospects of Sabre. Most agreed that without its ties to AMR, the company would be more likely to obtain contracts from other carriers.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Dow Closes Lower on Worries Over Long-Term Interest Rate
body: Stocks fell yesterday, hobbled by a drop in the technology sector and a jump in long-term interest rates on news that shoppers went on a big spending spree last month. The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 32.42 points, or 0.29 percent, to 11,160.17. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index fell 12.05 points, or 0.85 percent, to 1,403.17. The Nasdaq composite index plunged 86.51 points, or 2.36 percent, to 3,571.66 after racking up 23 record closes in 31 trading sessions. "The Nasdaq is at long last starting to go down," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at the First Albany Corporation. "You could attribute it to profit taking set in motion by very sharp declines in the bond market as there is a growing concern that the economy remains too strong," he said. Internet stocks, which helped push the Nasdaq to a series of record highs over the last four weeks, fell sharply. The price of the 30-year Treasury bond plunged 1 11/32, to 97 21/32. The bond's yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, rose to 6.30 percent from 6.20 percent on Monday on worries that the Federal Reserve may have to raise interest rates again to slow the economy's growth. In another sign of a speeding economy, the government reported retail stores perked up in November, beating forecasts, as shoppers hit stores after the Thanksgiving Day holiday in the traditional run-up to Christmas. The Commerce Department said total sales soared 0.9 percent, to a seasonally adjusted $255.8 billion -- nearly twice the 0.5 percent increase forecast by Wall Street economists -- after a gain of 0.3 percent in October. The jump in bond interest rates rattled financial stocks. Among the Dow components, American Express was off 6 to to 160 1/2, and J. P. Morgan & Company was off 3 5/16 at 131 1/4. Citigroup was down 1 13/13 at 53 1/2. The Labor Department reported that inflation was still subdued, with the Consumer Price Index up only 0.1 percent in November. Excluding food and energy, the index rose 0.2 percent. Among Internet stocks, America Online was off 5 3/8 at 88 7/16 and Amazon.com slid 6 7/8, to 95 5/8. Semiconductor stocks fell after Solectron, a custom electronics maker, slumped 9 1/8, to 82 5/8, on disappointing quarterly results. Analysts said a shortage of components had hurt Solectron, and fear about the shortage dragged down chip makers. Among them, Intel, a Dow component, was off 1 1/4 at 72 13/16 and Texas Instruments Inc. was off 9 5/16 at 96 5/8. Microsoft rose 2 1/16, to 98 11/16, on speculation that there was a settlement of the government's antitrust suit against the company. Microsoft said the rumors were "unfounded." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average over the past year.
