title: Computer Consultant to Buy USWeb in a Stock Swap
body: Whittman-Hart Inc., a computer consulting company based in Chicago, said today that it had agreed to acquire USWeb/CKS, a company based here specializing in Internet design and marketing strategy, in a stock swap valued around $5.87 billion. The two companies said they would create the largest Internet professional-services concern in the world. But Wall Street reacted negatively to the deal, sending the stock of both companies plummeting. Shares of Whittman-Hart closed at $54.50, down $24.8125, or 31 percent, in Nasdaq trading. Shares in USWeb also fell, if less starkly, to $43.8125, down $7.0625, or 13.9 percent. Thomas Rooney, an analyst with Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, reduced his rating on Whittman-Hart's stock to market perform from buy, while Gary Dean of J. C. Bradford lowered his recommendation to buy from strong buy. Still, some analysts said the deal made strategic sense. Although Whittman has built a large, profitable business managing computer systems for midsize companies, primarily in the Midwest, it has only lately added Internet-related services. USWeb was one of the first companies to specialize in Web site creation, and with the acquisition last year of CKS, added expertise in marketing and strategy. Buying USWeb gives Whittman strong Internet services, these analysts say. But unlike Whittman, which earned $18.8 million, or 35 cents a share, in 1998 on revenue of $307.6 million, USWeb had a loss of $188.3 million on revenue of $228.6 million. Analysts point out that much of USWeb's growth has come through a series of acquisitions and may not be sustainable. The company has acquired about a dozen consulting firms since it was founded in 1995 by a group of former Novell executives. According to the terms of the deal, each share of USWeb/CKS will be exchanged for 0.865 share of Whittman-Hart stock. After the merger, USWeb/CKS stockholders will own roughly 57 percent of the combined company and Whittman-Hart stockholders, roughly 43 percent. Robert Bernard, the chairman and chief executive of Whittman, will be chief executive of the new company. Robert Shaw, USWeb's chief executive, will be chairman. USWeb experienced a degree of incredulity when its original chief executive and co-founder, Joseph P. Firmage, was forced to resign in January after publishing accounts of his meeting with an alien from outer space. Mr. Firmage, 29, remains a major shareholder. Another co-founder, Sheldon Laube, left in August to create Center Beam Inc., a company offering personal computers, wireless networks and software by subscription. But USWeb still has clients like Harley-Davidson and Apple Computer.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
NTL to Buy Cablecom in a $3.7 Billion Deal
body: NTL Inc., Britain's largest cable concern, expanded its foothold in Continental Europe today with a $3.7 billion deal to buy Cablecom Group, Switzerland's leading cable television operator. The purchase gives NTL 1.28 million subscribers in Switzerland, accounting for 53 percent of the cable market there, according to the two companies. As part of the deal, NTL also will get Cablecom's SwissOnline subsidiary, one of the most popular Web sites in Switzerland. NTL, a six-year-old telecommunications company based in newyork that operates mainly in Britain, has gone on a European shopping spree within the last six months, betting that cable delivery of entertainment, telephone and Internet services to homes will become an increasingly important business in Europe. Backed by influential shareholders that include France Telecom and Microsoft, NTL bought Cable and Wireless P.L.C.'s consumer cable, telephone and Internet units in Britain, as well as France Telecom's 1G networks and Ireland's largest cable company, Cablelink. Those acquisitions, along with the purchase announced today, have put NTL in direct competition with United Pan-Europe Communications, or U.P.C., which is based in Amsterdam and has followed a similar path. NTL's chief executive, Barclay Knapp, who is from Nebraska, has pursued a strategy that combines bundling telephone service, cable television and Internet access into a single service, much as AT&T has sought to do with its acquisition of Tele-Communications Inc. "In terms of our overall European strategy, it is particularly important to have acquired a network at the very heart of Europe," Mr. Knapp said in a statement about the deal. Analysts said the acquisition would benefit both NTL and Cablecom because it solidified NTL's position in Europe while it would make Cablecom more competitive at home. Terence Sinclair, an analyst at Salomon Smith Barney in London, said the deal brought NTL "one of the best run, competitively and operationally strong cable companies in Europe at a low price." Mr. Sinclair, who rates NTL stock as a buy, said the acquisition gave NTL "an opportunity to consolidate its position, not just as the leading U.K. player but as the most athletic competitor to U.P.C. across Europe." While most analysts praised the deal, investors sent NTL's share price down $6.375, to $113.375, on the Nasdaq stock market. Analysts said investors were nervous that NTL might have to issue more shares to finance the acquisition of Cablecom. NTL already has about $7.7 billion in debt. NTL said that Morgan Stanley Dean Witter and Chase Manhattan Bank would finance $2.3 billion of the purchase price and said it was assessing a number of proposals to finance the balance of the purchase price.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Reuters in Deal With Dow Jones
body: Reuters Group P.L.C. said yesterday that it had reached a five-year deal to be the principal financial data supplier to the publications and news wires of Dow Jones & Company. Terms of the agreement were not disclosed. Under the deal, Reuters will be the primary source of financial pricing information for The Wall Street Journal, The Asian Wall Street Journal, The Wall Street Journal Europe and Barron's. Reuters data will also be used on The Journal's online edition and the dowjones.com Web site. Robert Crooke, a Reuters spokesman, said Reuters data would be used to calculate Dow Jones international financial indexes and for foreign exchange rates. Reuters data will not be used to calculate the Dow Jones industrial average, Mr. Crooke said. The agreement will allow Dow Jones "to consolidate multiple systems, streamline vendors and save millions of dollars each year while actually improving product quality," said Blair Worrall, executive director for process redesign at Dow Jones. The deal is separate from Factiva, the Reuters and Dow Jones joint venture, and is separate from the October 1998 agreement allowing Reuters financial services customers to subscribe to Dow Jones news wires as an optional service through Reuters terminals. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Wall St. Is Flush With Cash But Also Green With Envy
body: Even by the inflated standards of high finance, Wall Street is overflowing with holiday cheer this year. Investment banks have set aside $13 billion to pay bonuses, 20 percent more than last year, with pay packages above $10 million no longer a rarity. Yet among Wall Streeters the mood has changed. One industry veteran bemoaned the "opportunity cost" of remaining a financier in the Internet age. Others are leaving to join online start-ups, technology companies and venture capital firms, the pillars of the new economy, where they sometimes take home more than their old bosses from Day 1 -- and, they say, have more fun. For the first time since Wall Street became the surest professional path to riches during the frenzied 1980's, those with the biggest paydays are former investment bankers. Like Timothy Weller. He is the talk of the Street, but mostly because he no longer works there. Last summer, Mr. Weller, 34, left Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, where he was a middle-ranking analyst tracking the telecommunications business, to join Akamai Technologies, which provides networking services for the Internet. Akamai, based in Cambridge, Mass., enticed him to sign on as chief financial officer by selling him 1.05 million shares, valued then at $2.63 million, and even lent him the money to buy them. Gratification was quick: when Akamai went public in October, its stock soared from $26 to $230. Mr. Weller's stake is now worth $240 million. But that could change if the share price falls. And companies often place restrictions on when shares can be cashed in. Few bankers will reap such gains, but many are still taking their chances on the Internet. One-time masters of the universe say banking has become prosaic, with the heavy demands no longer producing unrivaled rewards. Bankers now ogle online entrepreneurs the way lawyers and accountants once envied Wall Streeters. "It used to be that investment bankers were at the cutting edge," said Mark Long, who as a banker for Credit Suisse First Boston helped some of America's hottest Internet companies go public. "Today, bankers are just hired guns." During a trip last summer to promote the Internet start-up Intraware to potential investors, Mr. Long, 32, accepted his client's offer to become a vice president, joining shortly before it went public. If Intraware does well, Mr. Long stands to earn considerably more than he did as a banker, thanks to stock options. But that is only one reason he left. "You get tired of sleeping 45 minutes a night," he said, "to sell someone else's business." With profits for financial firms and bonuses for bankers at all-time highs, there is certainly no looming crisis on Wall Street. Even those who leave banking often do so with trepidation, fearing that inflated Internet stocks could come crashing down. The Internet's impact has been more psychological than financial. The pressure to earn Internet windfalls shows up in little ways, as with the rising stock analyst who says he has lost bidding wars for Upper East Side apartments and adds, only half in jest, that $10 million does not buy much of a condo these days. The online lure is also enhanced by ex-bankers who have changed careers seamlessly. Jeff Bezos worked on Wall Street until he founded Amazon.com, and that trend keeps gathering steam. Mr. Bezos, now many times a billionaire, hired a number of other former bankers and made them Internet retailers. Analysts and deal makers involved in technology, telecommunications and the Internet readily change hats and become financial officers or strategic planners at start-ups, often bringing along former colleagues. Some defectors compete directly with their old firms. At least three new online investment banks and several Internet stock and bond trading companies, all planning to use the Internet to steal business from traditional investment banks, are led by people who learned the business from the inside. Robert Lessin, chief executive of Wit Capital, an online investment bank, and formerly a top officer at Salomon Smith Barney, has poached a long list of bankers from Salomon, Merrill Lynch and other firms. "It's like I'm a banker but I get to wear casual clothes," said Kate Cornish, 28, who left Salomon for Wit a few months ago. Especially susceptible are those three to five years out of business school -- on the cusp of devoting a career to a firm, but young enough to start fresh. "They say, 'I want to be a multimillionaire by the time I'm 30, but if I stay at Morgan Stanley, it may take me until I'm 50,' " said Joseph Perella, Morgan's head of investment banking. Americans, he added, want "instant gratification." In reaction, Morgan Stanley has started offering stock to some newly hired bankers. BancBoston Robertson Stephens, a leading technology banking firm, has lost 10 bankers to Internet clients this year. The firm recently took 300 employees to a weekend retreat to help build esprit de corps and to aid retention, though firm officials said it was not a response to this year's attrition. Investment bank recruiters once acted like bouncers, accepting only the best. Goldman Sachs still finds plenty of eager applicants, says Peter Kiernan, a senior partner who oversees hiring from business schools, but now, he said, "if you expect to back up a truck and load the top 10 people in a class, you're going to be disappointed." Business school graduates think entrepreneurial jobs are the wave of the future, he said. He now tries to convince people that they can be entrepreneurs within an investment bank, which can be a tough sell. "One thing you don't do is try to sell against the Net," he said. Not long ago, Wall Street did not have to try so hard. With the rapid growth of stocks and bonds and the explosion of mergers, securities firms were seen as controlling the levers of America's economy. Investment banking, offering top dollar, consistently ranked as the No. 1 or No. 2 career choice for top business graduates. Popular culture followed the money. "Wall Street," the movie, and "Bonfire of the Vanities," the novel, created a stereotype of shark-like bankers and traders. In the early 1990's, investment banks were seen as the engines of globalization, financing road projects in China and privatizing phone companies in Brazil. While corporate America merged and consolidated, bankers raked in record fees. But the Internet, like an electronic black hole, has stolen all the gravity. Securities firms seem to have less to do with creating Internet companies than they did with arranging restructurings or sending capital abroad. And through the Silicon Valley looking glass, Wall Street egos can appear almost humble. Scott McNealy, chief executive of Sun Microsystems, wrote an Op-Ed article in The newyork Times last summer extolling the value that entrepreneurs create in the economy and belittling the "nonjobs" of bankers. In "The New New Thing," Michael Lewis, who a decade ago chronicled Wall Street hubris in "Liar's Poker," portrays today's financiers as desperate grovelers who shovel money at Internet entrepreneurs in hopes of profiting from their creative instincts. Investors seem no different. They have pumped up the stocks of Internet-friendly finance companies so much that a recent survey of the wealthiest people in finance, compiled by Institutional Investor magazine, found that the richest financiers often double as Internet entrepreneurs. Charles Schwab, the founder, chairman and chief executive of the No. 1-ranked Internet broker, has seen his Schwab stock holdings soar to almost $5.8 billion, making him the second wealthiest person in finance after Warren E. Buffett. J. Joe Ricketts, chairman and co-chief executive of Ameritrade, the No. 7 Internet broker, has stockholdings of almost $2 billion, eclipsing the combined stockholdings of the leaders of Morgan Stanley, Merrill and Goldman. Until recently, headhunters rarely tried to lure bankers away from Wall Street. But dot-com fever has changed that. When Priceline.com decided in June to go after an investment banker to fill a senior post at a unit it expected to take public shortly, it asked Cynthia Remec, an executive recruiter, to round up candidates the same day and set up interviews the next. Ms. Remec frantically phoned 20 bankers to fill this tall order. Within hours, to her surprise, she found 15 eager to hop the train to Stamford, Conn., Priceline's headquarters, for an interview. Priceline hired one of them, Anne Maffei, a former banker at J. P. Morgan, as a senior executive at Webhouse.com, its grocery-shopping affiliate. Bankers and analysts on the front lines of the new economy sometimes make especially easy pickings. Though the work hours of Internet entrepreneurs are legendary, many bankers say the life compares favorably with the burden of arranging public offerings and mergers. "You feel like lead oar in 'Ben Hur,' " said Bill Burnham, a top analyst for Credit Suisse First Boston who left to join Softbank Capital, an Internet-focused venture fund. "No one works harder than a tech banker or has less control over his life." The lure of stock options is also potent. Thomas Casey, 47, left as co-head of global telecommunications and media at Merrill Lynch to head corporate development, among other things, at Global Crossing, a new company that is building a fiber optic network for Internet traffic. At first, the move was a roll of the dice. He left behind a hefty pay package -- $3 million to $5 million a year at his level. When he started at Global Crossing, he took a huge pay cut. But he got options on 2 million shares when the stock was valued at $2 a share. Those options are now valued at nearly $90 million. "On Wall Street, you are not going to be so rich that your children and grandchildren would never have to work again," Mr. Casey said. "But you have that opportunity if you go to a start-up." Mr. Casey said money was only one motivation. "Ultimately, I wanted to be in a position where I participated directly in creating something substantial," he said. Today, some Wall Street firms are responding aggressively. Nearly all the big ones have taken stakes in online trading companies, including virtual stock-trading forums known as electronic communications networks. Most now allow clients to buy and sell securities on the Internet. Several analysts predict that Wall Street's willingness to compete online will slow the growth of purely online rivals -- and perhaps stem the outflow of seasoned bankers. But John Hewitt, a longtime Goldman vice president who helped execute that firm's efforts to modernize its technology, still sees the biggest securities firms as being stuck in another era. He recently left Goldman to become president of Knight/Trimark, which has used technology and low fees to lure stock-trading business. Mr. Hewitt, 48, said he long expected to retire as a Goldman employee. But the more he learned about the Internet, he said, the more it gnawed at him -- to the point that he raised his hand for the Knight/Trimark job during a business dinner with Ken Pasternak, the chief executive. "All the Wall Street firms, Goldman included, have become so successful that they have a vested interest in the status quo," Mr. Hewitt said. "The more I thought about it, the more I felt I had to go somewhere that had a sense of speed and that wasn't afraid of the future." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Mark Long, 32, left his banking job to join Intraware shortly before the company went public. "Today, bankers are just hired guns," he said. (Peter DaSilva for The newyork Times)(pg. C12)  Graph: "Bonus Time" The graph shows newyork City Comptroller's office estimates of Wall Street bonuses (in billions) since 1995 (pg. C12)

title: Candidates Eager to Negotiate Cyberspace and Cyberissues
body: "Yours," Senator Orrin G. Hatch of Utah admonished Gov. George W. Bush of Texas during the first of the Republican presidential debates earlier this month, "is not user friendly." As political zingers go, it might have been a bit lame. But that Mr. Hatch would use precious air time to criticize an opponent's Web site as "pretty tough to use" is only one indication of how the presidential candidates are confronting the Internet and technology generally, both as substantive issues and pervasive cultural forces. They are raising money over the Internet. They are raising money from people who have grown rich from the Internet. They are debating how best to nurture the potential of the Internet while shielding children from pornography and consumers from potential misuse of data about them. And in the early stages of the first Internet-era national election, they are eager to let voters know they are as comfortable with a mouse as the next guy. "The pace of candidate education is nearly as rapid as the pace of technological development," said Representative Christopher Cox of California, a Republican who is one of the few true techies in Congress. Vice President Al Gore long ago dropped his paternity claim to the Internet. But Mr. Gore, who can sometimes be spotted with a Palm Pilot clipped to his belt, dropped into the CyberStop Cafe in Washington last week and with reporters and photographers watching sent an email message to Bill Bradley, his rival for the Democratic presidential nomination, questioning his opponent's stand on Medicare. Mr. Bradley has held electronic town hall meetings. And the Republican candidates have gone back and forth about technology issues regularly during their debates. "In not very many years, politics has moved from a lot of smoke-filled rooms and ward bosses giving out turkeys to constituents to dueling emails," said Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, a Democrat with a strong interest in technology issues. "This is an extraordinary transformation in politics. To reach the swing, independent voters who are going to decide about the 2000 elections you've got to talk about these issues." The most politically charged of the issues may be whether and how to apply sales taxes to electronic commerce, and it is shaping up as a test of the candidates' views on the Internet in the economy and society. Most governors and many local government officials are worried that as business migrates from Main Street and the mall to Amazon.com and Ebay, state governments will face a fiscal crisis, since online retailers for the most part are not required to collect sales taxes, the primary revenue source for states. But in Washington, there is support in both parties for making the Internet a permanently tax-free shopping zone. A government commission studying the matter seems headed toward a deadlock. The issue is particularly tricky for Mr. Bush, who is trying to establish his antitax credentials but shares the concerns of other governors that revenue losses from a shift to tax-free Internet shopping could leave states in a bind and hurt traditional retailers. Mr. Bush favors extending a moratorium against Internet taxes while the issue gets further study. Mr. Bush's unwillingness to come out definitively against Internet sales taxes is being exploited by his rivals, who are suggesting obliquely that Mr. Bush is soft on taxes and maybe a bit of a Luddite to boot. "The Internet should not be taxed," Senator John McCain of Arizona said. He extolled the Internet as "the greatest thing that's happened to the world," and compared its impact to a combination of the printing press and the industrial revolution. "The governors are incredibly short-sighted when they want to tax this baby in its cradle," Mr. McCain said. Mr. Hatch said it was "far overblown to think that the fact that people buy over the Internet is going to reduce Main Street U.S.A." But the politics of technology can be complicated. Despite his message to Washington to "keep the government's mitts off" the industry, Mr. Hatch has been a supporter of the federal antitrust case against the Microsoft Corporation. He has been raising campaign funds from executives at some of Microsoft's rivals. Steve Forbes, by contrast, says the Microsoft case is a waste of time and money, because the pace of change in the software business will render moot any court judgment. The scramble to raise money from technology companies almost guarantees that candidates will continue to pay attention to the issues on the industry's mind. Mr. Bush had raised $1.73 million from people affiliated with technology and communications companies through Oct. 15, while Mr. Gore had raised $1.54 million from them, Mr. Bradley $770,000 and Mr. McCain $500,000. But the candidates seem fascinated and intrigued by the technology's potential to affect the world, not just dot-com companies. Defending his support for bringing China into the World Trade Organization, Mr. Bush cited the Web's potential to communicate democratic values even in the face of opposition from a repressive regime. "Imagine if the Internet took hold in China," Mr. Bush said. "Imagine how freedom would spread." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
E-Commerce Report;
On the Web, Pricing Errors Can Be Costly in More Ways Than One
body: WHEN traditional retailers mistakenly label an item the wrong price -- for instance, marking a $99 item $9.90 -- they might have to apologize to a customer and give a quick lesson in decimals to a clerk. On the Internet, they have to be prepared to either lose face or part with a lot of money. Amazon.com is the latest Web site to confront this problem. Early last week, it received a slew of visits from people who read newspaper advertisements listing a Toshiba DVD player for $199.99. When customers saw the actual retail price listed on the site, $249.99, Amazon faced a no-win situation: either honor the advertised price and lose money, or explain the mistake and risk losing the customers. Amazon ultimately decided to sell its stock of DVD players at the advertised price, limiting customers to two per order. "What else can you say --it was an error," said Paul Capelli, an Amazon spokesman. Mr. Capelli declined to say how many players the company sold or how much money it lost in all. "What's important is we're taking a customer-centric approach to the solution," he said. Internet retailers are coming to grips with the notion that pricing errors can be far more costly online than in traditional stores. Thanks to chat rooms, email and shopping bots like MySimon and DealTime, which survey prices on products offered at thousands of sites, such mistakes rarely remain a secret for long. What is more, Web merchants have made a habit of slashing prices to startling levels to attract customers, so those same merchants cannot appeal to the reasonable expectations of their customers when a pricing glitch happens. Buy.com ran afoul of those expectations earlier this year when it listed a $588 Hitachi computer monitor on its site for $164. Buy.com began taking the orders, but after realizing the error, the company agreed to sell only what it had in stock at the time to the first customers who ordered at the lower price, then refused to honor the other orders placed. The company is now in the midst of a class-action lawsuit based, in part, on its handling of the matter. A more innocuous version of this happened to Ashford.com, a seller of luxury goods, which earlier this month posted five watches for sale priced at $0.00 -- with free shipping, no less. The company said consumers understood Ashford.com's decision not to give away the timepieces, given their combined value of $11,332, but the resulting bad press did little for the start-up's image. According to Mary Lou Kelley, Ashford .com's vice president for marketing, the pricing mistakes were the result of a system used to set up its merchandising pages before they were published on the site. Under that system, which has since been scrapped, items were given $0.00 prices until the correct number was entered. Ms. Kelley said the company posted a disclaimer on its site, stating that it was not responsible for pricing errors, but she added that the company would evaluate such situations case by case. "We'll do whatever we can to make customers happy, short of giving watches away," she said. Not only is it more costly for Internet retailers to make such mistakes than their off-line counterparts, but Web merchants are far more prone to commit such errors, said Erik Brynjolfsson, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Sloan School of Management. Mr. Brynjolfsson recently completed a study of Internet pricing, and found that Web merchants changed their prices "much more frequently" than brick and mortar stores. "It's much easier to change prices on the Net, and the benefits are much greater, because of shopping bots," Mr. Brynjolfsson said, noting that even 1 cent price reductions can give companies greater exposure on price comparison sites. "But that presents a big opportunity for mistakes." However, and this news will not endear him to bargain hunters -- Mr. Brynjolfsson said pricing errors would decrease with time, "as pricing technologies and systems get more accurate." "But in the short run," he said, "these companies have to discover the kinds of really stupid things they can do." Michael Anthony, chief executive of Brookstone, said the company relied on a team of "four to five people" to verify prices on its site, in the company catalog and in Brookstone's stores. "It also helps that we have one price on our items, no matter how you buy them, so there's less of a chance of a mix-up," he said. When a pricing error does occur on his site -- a situation that has yet to happen, Brookstone "will appeal to the reasonable expectations of our customers," Mr. Anthony said, adding that "most people are reasonable." Then again, he said, "there are so many crazy pricing schemes on the Internet that a lot of people wouldn't be sure what is a reasonable price, so we'd have to look at each situation differently." Indeed, the concept of reasonable pricing on the Web has all but disappeared with the advent of free computers, free Internet access and merchants who have not been compelled by Wall Street to focus on profits. That, in turn, has made it more difficult for consumer advocates to deal with such cases. The Federal Trade Commission generally occupies itself with unfair business practices like so-called bait-and-switch pricing and cedes issues of pricing errors to state jurisdictions. State contract laws, meanwhile, typically protect merchants who make a genuine error in pricing. But other watchdog organizations may set higher standards. The Better Business Bureau Online, for instance, is drafting a new set of standards for Web merchants who want to post the organization's seal of approval on their sites. The current version of the draft requires merchants to "comply with all commitments, representations, and other promises made to a consumer." Whether that statement would require a merchant to sell a DVD player for $100 as a result of an advertising error, however, is an open question. "We're open to feedback on this one," said Russ Bodoff, the Better Business Bureau Online's chief operating officer. "It's a difficult issue, because the Internet presents real questions around this area of consumer expectations." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Don Blate, right, a Brookstone area manager, helped a customer on the phone find a product on the company's Web site. Brookstone relies on a team of employees to verify that prices posted online are correct. (Chang W. Lee/The newyork Times)(pg. C14)

title: Entertainment Internet Venture Gets a Chief
body: Kenneth P. Wong, former president of Walt Disney Imagineering, Disney's technology research and development unit, has been named chairman and chief executive of Pop.com, the recently announced collaboration between Dreamworks SKG and Imagine Entertainment to create and distribute entertainment on the Internet. Pop.com, which is expected to begin in the spring, will offer three- to six-minute segments that it calls "pops," a combination of digital films, animation, live events and interactive games. Because it was formed by prominent Hollywood artists and executives -- Steven Spielberg, Jeffrey Katzenberg and David Geffen of Dreamworks and Ron Howard and Brian Grazer of Imagine -- and because it is being largely financed by Paul G. Allen's Vulcan Ventures, Pop.com fast became one of the most visible attempts in Hollywood to come to terms with entertainment in the digital age. Mr. Wong recently left Disney after an eight-year career that saw him rise from senior vice president at the Disney Development Company to executive vice president of the Imagineering division in 1995 and its president in 1996. As head of the division, he oversaw such projects as Disney's recently opened Animal Kingdom in Florida, its Times Square Studios, Tokyo DisneySea, Disney's California Adventure and two Disney cruise ships. Mr. Wong was "the architect of unprecedented growth at Imagineering," Mr. Katzenberg said, "and we are excited to work with him to build Pop.com into a successful enterprise in the exploding Internet marketplace." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Metro Matters;
E-Commerce: Buyers Gain, Cities Lose
body: AT the schoolyard flea market on Columbus Avenue yesterday, one jewelry vendor was talking to another. "With a click, they get everything, even delivery," she said. "I'm telling you, you may not realize it yet, but that's our competition. The Internet." That isn't the half of it. Internet shoppers get more than convenience with a click. They get substantial savings. Like flea market buyers, they often save the sales tax. And compared with flea markets, electronic commerce -- e-commerce -- is a global phenomenon. So in this season of resolutions, prognostications and conspicuous consumerism, a prediction: the traditional retail sales tax will soon be seen as so unfair that it may even go the way of the subway token. E-commerce is becoming the new shopping mall. It now accounts for less than 4 percent of all retail sales but is growing exponentially. Holiday cyberspace sales tripled last year to $2 billion and are expected to triple again this year, to $6 billion. That includes a lot of unpaid taxes. Technically, cybercustomers are supposed to pay a "use tax" equivalent to the sales tax, but Internet merchants, like catalog-order businesses, do not have to collect the tax if they ship to a state in which they do not have a physical presence. "That's giving somebody 8 1/4 percent off on every sale, it really is," said Alice Bergman, owner of West Side Kids, a toy store on Amsterdam Avenue at 84th Street. Online companies, with their relatively small overhead costs, can already offer lower prices than traditional stores. "If they are not paying taxes, we will really feel it," said Ms. Bergman. So will the more than 6,500 American cities, towns, counties and school districts that depend on sales taxes to pay for services and pay down their debts. newyork City, for instance, collected $3.2 billion from sales taxes in the last fiscal year -- 15 percent of its total tax collections. "If this type of e-commerce continues to remain untaxed, local governments are going to have to radically revise their tax structure," said Abraham Biderman, a former city finance commissioner. "I'm not talking about something at the margins. The whole system will have to change." Either government services will be cut, or other taxes will have to be raised or found -- local income taxes, property taxes or, as in Europe, value-added wholesale taxes. WITH so much at stake, the political debate has begun -- encouraged by lobbying and campaign contributions from online companies. Gov. James S. Gilmore III, Republican of Virginia, who is chairman of a national advisory panel on e-commerce tax policy, would exempt online purchases from sales taxes. So would Senator John McCain of Arizona, the Republican presidential contender. Gov. George W. Bush, the Texas Republican, recommends putting off any decision, pending more study. Vice President Al Gore says wait for the Gilmore panel to report to Congress in April. The White House calls the Gilmore proposal potentially damaging to localities and traditional retailers. The bipartisan National Governors Association, worried about local and state treasuries, wants to make every Internet purchase subject to traditional sales taxes. It would let a private technology company monitor sales of participating merchants and help the states collect the revenue. Here in newyork, elected officials have only begun to look at this issue. Gov. George E. Pataki and City Comptroller Alan G. Hevesi, speaking through aides, say they favor a tax-free Internet, to maintain a favorable business climate for Web companies. Neither explains how retail stores could compete. Mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani's position is unknown; as is often the case, his press office did not return phone calls. Mark Green, the public advocate and next mayor if Mr. Giuliani becomes a senator, says he is still studying the matter. "I don't envy the next governor and mayor," he said with a laugh. Ah, but envy the consumers, who know a good thing when they see it. How, practically speaking, can governments hope to collect taxes from national and even global cyberspace purchases when nobody pays taxes even at the flea market in the schoolyard on Columbus Avenue and 76th Street? Up at West Side Kids, Alice Bergman is enjoying a good season. Her customers are loyal, and they like the personal attention a small shop offers. But with catalogs, discount chains and now e-commerce, she's worried. She has substantial overhead costs, a window to dress, sales clerks to train -- and taxes to collect on every sale. "Why," she asked, "should we have to pay taxes if they don't?" http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
On Wall Street, newspaper companies make a comeback, partly on the strength of the Internet.
body: IMAGINE what would happen if the people who made the old Miller Lite commercials tried their magic on newspaper stocks. The script might go something like this: (Two hotshot analysts are arguing.) ANALYST A: Newspapers are a stodgy cyclical business! ANALYST B: Newspapers are a sexy Internet business! ANALYST A: Stodgy! ANALYST B: Sexy! (Enter soothing portfolio manager.) PORTFOLIO MANAGER: Relax, folks. Newspaper companies are stodgy and sexy. They're two, two, two stocks in one. That more or less describes events last week, when newspaper companies' stocks jumped 10 percent or more. The numbers seemed to please both those who cared about cyclical trends and those enamored of Internet highfliers. Company by company, the executives reported to investors at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette's media conference that the stodgy cyclical business was thriving. And company by company, they reported that revenues from their Internet properties were growing exponentially and indicated levels of investment in online properties that reflected their commitment to the new online marketplace. Wall Street's reaction could be seen in the way the stock prices climbed in the week. Dow Jones & Company ended the week with its stock price at $69.0625, a gain of 42 percent since the beginning of January and 10.5 percent for the week. The newyork Times Company's stock closed on Friday at $46.4375, up 12 percent for the week and 35 percent for the year. And the Tribune Company's stock closed at $57, up 14 percent for the week and 71 percent for the year. "The bottom line on 1999 for newspapers is that the Internet has gone from a negative to a positive," Douglas Arthur, an industry analyst with Morgan Stanley, said. Pointing to the dot-com advertising bounty in newspapers, he said the Internet was driving ad revenues. "It's reaffirming the role of newspapers as an ad medium," he said. "And the franchise value of the content that newspapers have." A year ago, he added, "there was this really negative karma around the newspaper stocks, even though business was good." Not now. Just to underline the point, the Standard & Poor's newspaper publishing index, which in the first quarter languished while Internet stocks soared, no longer moves in a different direction than do the indexes of online stocks. The newspaper index has climbed 31 percent since the beginning of the year, and last week, when it gained 7.3 percent, it was moving roughly in tandem with TheStreet.com's index of Internet stocks, which moved up 9.8 percent last week. In part, the new synchronicity between newspaper and Internet stocks reflects the Internet advertising. "These dot-coms take this money, and they don't build factories, they build audiences," said Douglas Arthur, an analyst with Morgan Stanley. "They have to build them through mass media. So newspapers are re-emerging on a secular basis as a very effective mass media in local markets." USA Today, the Gannett Company's flagship, which now has the highest circulation in the industry, "is getting the highest share of print dot-com spending," Lauren Rich Fine, an analyst for Merrill Lynch, wrote. That newspaper's advertising revenue through November was up 16 percent, compared with a year earlier. But other industries were spending on newspapers as well. Financial advertising helped push advertising volume in Dow Jones's Wall Street Journal up 30.5 percent in November, compared with the 1998 month. For the first 11 months of the year, The Journal's advertising volume was up 15.2 percent. Advertising revenue at The newyork Times was up 20.7 percent in November, compared with November 1998, and 10.6 percent for the year to date. USA Today has brought in 16 percent more revenue in 1999 than it did for the comparable period in 1998. At The Los Angeles Times, owned by a the Times Mirror Company, ad revenue increased an average 9 percent in October and November over the comparable 1998 period. And at Knight Ridder's San Jose Mercury News, one of the industry's most disturbing trends -- the loss of high-margin help-wanted classified ads, apparently to competing Internet sites -- reversed itself in the second half of 1999. Help-wanted revenues were up 25 percent in October and 21 percent in November, compared with those months in 1998. So there is good news from a cyclical point of view. But for those who use Internet math, which counts increasing revenues as a plus (for obvious reasons) and increasing losses as a plus (because they reflect a degree of commitment to new technologies and new markets), the numbers were even better. Knight Ridder announced that it would consolidate its Internet properties into a unit called KnightRidder.com, which will be managed separately from its newspapers and may compete with them for advertising. Dow Jones executives indicated they expected online businesses to generate $150 million in revenue this year. Gannett executives said they expected $40 million in Internet revenues in 1999, and said that 15 of its sites, including usatoday.com, the most-visited newspaper Web site, were running profits for the year. The Times Company's online unit, Times Company Digital, is expected to post revenues of $29 million to $31 million in 1999 and to incur operating losses of $20 million to $22 million. Next year, executives said, revenue is expected to reach $49 million, and losses $40 million to $60 million. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Are Newspapers Internet Stocks?"
