title: Getting to the Land of Oz Is Easier on the Internet
body: LYMAN FRANK BAUM, a gentle man with a gift for storytelling, was entertaining his sons and their friends in Chicago one day in 1898. He began a tale about a girl named Dorothy and how she met a scarecrow. "Where did they live?" a small voice asked. As the account goes, he looked at his two file drawers, A-N and O-Z. Next year is the publication centennial of America's greatest fairyland, one that Baum created without the Grimms' horror or ugliness or moralizing. The International Wizard of Oz Club (www.ozclub.org) is already hard at work on a celebration July 20-23 at Indiana University at Bloomington. There will be scholarly papers (27 and growing), performances of early Oz plays and films, an exhibition of rare Oziana and perhaps a Russian Oz author -- Russians may not have invented the Emerald City, but they and others are still expanding it. Jane Albright of Kansas City, Mo., vice president of the club and the organizer of the centennial, wrote by email that her interest in Oz had begun with a dozen Oz books before she had even known how to read. "I simply opened them and fell in love," she wrote. "The sense of place Baum created in Oz was as tangible to me as Kansas -- I was raised in Topeka. I've yet to encounter any other fantasy land as utterly convincing." Club members, and the countless fans who learned to read and loved to dream on the Oz books, grieve that so many people know only about a movie. There's a reason for that, and it makes Oz online doubly important. The Oz books can be hard to find without a Web guide. They have often been unpopular with teachers and librarians -- for having no formal educational purpose, for not preaching, for being too funny, too irreverent, too easy to read, too imaginative, too undignified. Baum's style is simple and often repetitive; it is his imagination that is spectacular. The voluminous Wonderful Wizard of Oz Web site by Eric Gjovaag (www.eskimo.com/tiktok) has a history of Oz, information about the centennial convention, lesson ideas for teachers, a message board and Oz updates. Its 19-chapter Frequently Asked Questions about Oz provide an exhaustive resource for every conceivable aspect of Oziana in print, and on stage and screen. Mr. Gjovaag's site debunks two of the most frequent false rumors about Oz. No, there is not a hanged man in the forest scene in the movie, and no, Baum did not set out to write a parable about populism. That myth arose from a 1964 article in the magazine American Quarterly by a high-school teacher, Henry M. Littlefield, who used Oz as an allegory to teach about the populist movement and the election of 1896. Mr. Littlefield has since written that there is no evidence that Baum intended a political message. The Emerald City of Oz site (www.emeraldcityofoz.com) has an extensive on-line library, with both summaries and full text, of the Oz books by Baum and by his successor as "Royal Historian of Oz," Ruth Plumly Thompson, as well as the artist John R. Neill and later successors. The Oz Library (homes .acmecity.com/oz/baum/123) includes the text of 21 Oz books, plus many illustrations, as well as the complete script for the 1939 movie. Jim's Wizard of Oz Website (www.geocities.com/Hollywood /Hills/6396/index.html) has a good deal of magic itself. On its Mouse overs Page, the movie's main characters are shown as they appear in Kansas. Rolling the cursor over them turns them into their Oz equivalents. The official Warner Brothers Wizard of Oz movie site is www.thewizardofoz.com/index.html. As for the synchronicity between the movie and Pink Floyd's 1973 album "Dark Side of the Moon," which members of the rock group have denied is intentional, try www.xnet .com/arkiver/synch/dsotr.shtml. Piglet Press (www.halcyon.com /piglet/index.htm) produces and sells audio versions of many Oz books; its Web site has many online listening selections. Piglet Press also has a wonderfully illustrated cross-referenced Oz encyclopedia. Try it out using one of the best names in Oz: the Lord High Chigglewitz. The Piglet index will remind you that his real name is Larry and he is the chief Fuddleperson in Fuddlecumjig (in the north of the Quadling country). He uses his jigsaw-puzzle skills to piece together the Fuddles, who fly apart at the slightest provocation . . . oh, never mind. Just read "The Emerald City of Oz." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The International Wizard of Oz Club site celebrates the Oz books.

title:
HOLIDAY GIFTS;
When Antiques Follow Function
body: THE old wallpaper roller, inherited from my father, was the first tool I treasured. Its wooden handle was worn, and when I wrapped my hand around it, it was as comforting as a wooden shift knob on a '66 Camaro. Besides its patinated handle, it had a curved head of orange Bakelite, which was gentle in delicate corners -- it didn't rip the paper the way the new hard and heartless plastic ones do. Alas, although I treasured it, I am irresponsible. The wallpaper roller was lost. But I know where to find another one. All kinds of wonderful old tools -- cheap and not so cheap -- can be found in a lot of places these days: country auctions, flea markets, swap meets and, maybe best of all, the Internet. I just missed a set of five Bakelite-and-wood wallpapering tools, which sold for $9 on eBay, the online auction site. Last week, eBay had a whole box of wallpaper tools at a starting bid of $5. Unfortunately, they were new, which the seller seemed to think was their main selling point. But often old tools (the ones labeled "antique" seem to be expensive) are made better, and, many of us believe, work better, too. Just this week, eBay was peddling vintage wallpaper presses from Maine (to imprint a "wallpaper look" on walls, the seller said); Bakelite pottery tools in orange, red, green and amber; planes made of Brazilian woods; and a rosewood-handle mortise gauge trimmed in brass. If you are buying a gift, it doesn't matter if you don't know what a mortise gauge is -- as long as the carpenter you love wants one. This is not the same as buying a tie: ask for a list of specific tools, and then ferret them out. And if you don't know an awl from an ax, the Internet may be the best, cheapest place to search for old tools -- implements with provenance and patina. Just take your list and enter the key words: for a 14-inch steel-blade back saw, you enter "back saw" and see what comes up. On eBay last week, a set of Lutz drafting tools from Germany, arrayed lovingly in a polished hardwood box, sold for $15. A set of chip-carving tools went for $6.61. An old L. L. Davis 26-inch wooden level trimmed in brass brought $53.65. An antique rosewood Stanley No. 96 brass-bound level sold for $358.34, with 24 people bidding. (There's that word "antique.") I've done some buying and selling on eBay recently, and, generally speaking, the items I bought were pretty much as described and arrived soon after my check cleared. Shipping charges are usually detailed in the item description. If you have questions, be sure to ask before you bid; eBay makes it easy to send email to the seller. But suppose you can't find what the Christmas boy or girl wants? For the real collector, there is www.mjdtools .com, run by Martin J. Donnelly, a 44-year-old amateur carpenter. A few years ago, Mr. Donnelly went to a hardware store looking for a saw and could find only one, with a handle cut out of a single piece of plywood, priced at $28. "I couldn't bear to buy it," Mr. Donnelly said. Later, he found himself at a local auction bidding $15 for two saws made in the late 1800's. They had rosewood handles with bushels of wheat carved on them. "Driving home, I had to stop the car and just look at them," he recalled. Although www.mjdtools.com (or www.oldtools .com, www.toolsrules.com, www.tooltimer.com or any number of other sites) is full of esoterica (an early cooper's compass for $225; an Atwater's Tiger wrench for $265; a Goodell-Pratt No. 4 gear-driven hand drill for $550), Mr. Donnelly said plenty of good old tools are floating around for $5 to $10. And they are practical. Like the Bakelite wallpaper roller, many of these tools work better than new ones. Many are heavier and don't drift on a workbench like newer ones. (Garrett Wade in newyork sells new tools made to old designs, at much higher prices than originals you might find on eBay or in a bin at a country auction -- but then, they're brand-new.) Take pliers and prying tools. Fifty years ago, they were made in dozens of shapes, unlike the one-size-fits-all versions now sold in hardware stores. It was easy to assemble a collection in no time. I have a collection of old pry bars, including a long, thin handmade bar of spring steel. It's perfect for removing old moldings; I got it for 75 cents at a tag sale. Old planes, because their metal and wood parts were fitted by hand, often have more adjustments -- useful for fine woodworking. As an example, Mr. Donnelly cited Stanley's skewed-blade rabbet plane, a specialist's tool on which the cutting iron is set at an angle, indispensable for cutting figured woods. "It's the best rabbeting plane ever made," he said. Because such planes aren't made anymore, and because carpenters need them, "they bring even more money than if they were only sought by collectors." He added that he doesn't happen to have any in stock at the moment. The planes usually bring $300 to $400. But the thrifty should not despair. Small, ordinary tools like bevel gauges, planes and wood-handle hammers and screwdrivers might sell for $1 to $5 at a flea market or swap meet. I once bought a small wood and iron plane for $3 in an antique-junk shop in North Scituate, R.I. The plane is a gem: it's handy in small places (sometimes you can even plane a sticky door without taking it off the hinges), the blade is easy to sharpen and, well, it feels very good indeed. And the old rock maple, polished by decades of use, is a joy to look at. Why would anyone ever buy plastic again? http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: THE COMFORT OF OLD TOOLS -- Gifts for a handyman, picked up for less than $5 apiece. (Tony Cenicola for The newyork Times)

title: Microsoft and Ericsson To Create WirelessVenture
body: Ericsson of Sweden and the Microsoft Corporation will create a joint-venture company to market and deliver mobile email and other Internet services for wireless network operators, the companies said yesterday. Ericsson, the world's third largest mobile phone maker, will own a majority of the new venture. Under the terms of the deal, Ericsson will provide its Wireless Application Protocol to Microsoft and will adopt Microsoft's Mobile Explorer, a new version of its Internet browser, in future cellular phones. Ericsson officials said the partnership did not mean that the company would use Microsoft's Windows CE operating system in its wireless devices at this time, although they did not rule anything out. Microsoft said it expected to start shipping Mobile Explorer in the middle of next year. On Nasdaq today, Microsoft's stock closed at $91.8125, down $1.1875. Shares in Phone.com, a Redwood City, Calif., company that already produces browser software for cell phones, fell $12.625, or more than 8 percent, to $142. In Stockholm, a 12 percent rise in the shares of Ericsson led the Swedish market to an unusual daily gain of 5.82 percent. Analysts said the deal should help Ericsson regain market share lost to Motorola and to Nokia of Finland, and it represented another significant step in Microsoft's efforts to be a major competitor in wireless networking. Microsoft has entered into a similar joint venture with Qualcomm, called Wireless Knowledge, and has made a number of acquisitions of companies with wireless technology or software. "Even Microsoft can't jump-start the wireless-data industry single-handedly," said Alan Reiter, president of Wireless Internet and Mobile Computing, a consulting firm in Chevy Chase, Md. "This is one step in Microsoft's attempt to be a major player in wireless data, but it's certainly not going to be a slam-dunk." Microsoft and Ericsson officials said their venture would concentrate on building, marketing and deploying products that use Microsoft's Windows NT Server and Exchange programs and Ericsson's infrastructure and mobile Internet technologies. "The mobile Internet is part of Ericsson's vision of convenient and user-friendly information access and wireless email," said Kurt Hellstrom, the company's president. Ericsson officials said the partnership with Microsoft did not diminish the company's commitment to Symbian, a consortium it set up with Psion, Nokia and Matsushita of Japan, in part to keep Microsoft from realizing the kind of dominance in the wireless industry that it achieved in personal computer software. Symbian has created a standard operating system, called EPOC, for wireless devices. Juha Christensen, Symbian's executive vice president, said he did not see the deal as a threat. "Obviously, every time we see people with a competitive offering, we get a little apprehensive," he said. But in this instance, he said, "We don't have a competitive offering," adding, "In the long term it's very difficult for anyone who wants to play in the corporate space to avoid Microsoft because they own all the desktops." Still, analysts said this deal, coming on the heels of a recent one in which Nokia agreed to use the operating system of Palm Computing, presented trouble for Symbian and its operating system. "This is Strike 2," said Andrew Seybold, an industry consultant in Boulder Creek, Calif. "Symbian, instead of being on the inside looking out, could be on the outside looking in." But he noted that none of the wireless partnerships to date were exclusive deals. "Nobody knows what the winning combination of wireless communications and information service is going to be," he said. "This is all posturing." For Microsoft, the link with Ericsson provides credibility in winning deals with major wireless carriers. "Microsoft, in order to be competitive in the wireless arena," Mr. Seybold continued, "has to get into the carriers' back-end infrastructure some way because that's where all the smarts are. Ericsson is a trusted back-end supplier." David Readerman, a managing director of Thomas Weisel & Partners, said the sheer numbers in the wireless market made it attractive to Microsoft even if it would never achieve the dominance it has in desktop computing. "Certainly in Europe, the installed base of handsets is soon to exceed the installed base of PC's," he said. "This may not represent the classic annuity stream for Microsoft, but they need to be there. It's a major strategic move."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: New Law Touches Off Suits Over Names in Cyberspace - Correction Appended
body: It has been less than two weeks since President Clinton signed a new law banning "cybersquatting," -- registering trademark names as Internet addresses in the hope of selling them at huge profits. But trademark holders around the country are already filing lawsuits to win the rights to names they consider their property. In California, New Zealand's America's Cup team today won a temporary injunction preventing two New Zealand men who own the americascup.com domain from using it for a Web site. Harvard University accuses two men of trying to auction off a number of Harvard-related domains, and the National Football League has sued a man who runs NFL-related sites that it says violate the league's trademarks and promote gambling. All three suits cite the anti-cybersquatting legislation that was signed into law Nov. 29 as part of the omnibus budget bill. Opponents of the law say large companies will use it to grab domain names, as Internet addresses are known, away from small companies and individuals with legitimate claims to the addresses. But even they see a bright side to the suits. "I argued against the law," said A. Michael Froomkin, a University of Miami law professor. "But now that we have it, I guess we will all win by getting some convergence on what the standards are." The law was also opposed by the Clinton administration, which feared it would undermine attempts by the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, or Icann, to cut the number and cost of international lawsuits over cybersquatting by consigning trademark-related disputes to arbitration. Icann was picked by the administration last year to take over management of the Internet's domain name system. It has already approved rules for assigning trademark disputes to international arbitration centers. Those rules, however, only apply to domain names dispensed by newly created registrar companies. The vast majority of the more than five million domain names already assigned with the popular .com, .net and .org suffixes were distributed by Network Solutions, a Herndon, Va., company that until this year had a monopoly over those domains. Only domains that Network Solutions assigns after Jan. 1 will be subject to Icann's rules. The first dispute under the Icann process was filed last week with the World Intellectual Property Organization. The names of the parties have not been made public. The Icann rules were intended to give trademark holders recourse against cybersquatters who were, in effect, using domain names to extort money from trademark holders, or in some cases to intentionally mislead or misdirect consumers. But trademark holders said the rules were not enough. They persuaded Congress to pass the law, which allows them to sue cybersquatters for possessing domains and to seek up to $100,000 in damages. The America's Cup suit was filed by Quokka Sports, a company handling the Web sites for the New Zealand America's Cup yachting team, the same day the law was signed. The New Zealand team first began trying to wrest americascup.com from two Auckland men, Arron Brett and Justin Nicholas, in June, but the dispute has been tied up in litigation in New Zealand ever since. Quokka's lawyer, Terry Gross, today persuaded a federal judge in San Francisco to issue an injunction barring the use of the americascup.com domain until it can be determined whether the address should be turned over to the America's Cup New Zealand team, which as the current holder of the cup also holds the trademark. Mr. Gross insists that it is a clear-cut case of cybersquatting, that the men were using the trademark to attract advertisers and to misdirect people looking for the official America's Cup site, americascup.org. The lawyer representing Mr. Brett and Mr. Nicholas, however, insists the case is an example of trademark holders trying to abscond with a legitimately owned domain name that the plaintiff covets after failing to register it. The lawyer, Peter Dengate-Thrush, said: "These young entrepreneurs are being singled out unfairly. How are they going to defend themselves in California?" On the East Coast, meanwhile, Harvard filed a suit Monday in unitedstates District Court in Boston, contending that Michael Rhys and Michael Douglas registered 65 domain names that use the words Harvard and Radcliffe. The men are accused of violating both cybersquatting and trademark infringement laws. Harvard says that after the names were registered through Network Solutions at its standard $70 rate, the defendants put the names up for auction on a Web site that is called HarvardYardSale.com, asking thousands of dollars per name. Also on Monday, the National Football League filed suit in U.S. District Court in newyork City, accusing Ken Miller of Clearlake Park, Calif., and his Web sites -- NFLtoday.com, NFLtoday.net and NFLtoday.org -- of violating a number of trademark and anti-cybersquatting rules. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Business Day yesterday about lawsuits seeking Internet addresses held by others referred incorrectly to the effect of international rules on addresses registered by Network Solutions Inc. before Jan. 1, 2000. Beginning on Jan. 3, those addresses will be subject to the rules intended to protect trademark holders. The addresses will not be exempt from them. Correction-Date: December 10, 1999, Friday Graphic   Photo: Two Team New Zealand ships race last month in a bid to qualify for America's Cup competition. New Zealand's America's Cup team has gone to court to bar the use of the Web address americascup.com. (Reuters)

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Conspicuous Consumption For the Internet Generation
body: Looking for just the right gift for that new Internet millionaire on your Christmas list? Something that says both money and technology? The Financial Literacy Center, in conjunction with the Henry Ford Museum and Berner Machine Labs, has just the ticket, or ticker: an exact replica of Thomas Alva Edison's original 1870's Universal Stock Ticker. Exact, that is, but for three things: It will set you back $35,000, it gets its market data from the Internet and it is a decidedly useless, if arguably delightful, anachronism, more sculpture than tool. Any serious day trader can get financial data much more quickly, conveniently and inexpensively by using a portfolio service on the Internet. And when the day is over, the trader can walk out the door without sweeping up several hours' worth of ticker tape. The Financial Literacy Center, which says it "provides innovative, educational and motivational products to help people use money effectively in their lives," is justifying this pricey piece of nostalgia by limiting first-year production to 300 tickers and by assembling what it calls a "dream team" of craftsmen to reproduce the machine. The team consists of two machinists, a historian, a computer specialist, a violinmaker (he studied old wood finishes) a woodworker, a printer and a "jack-of-all-trades." Confounding categorization, the replica is described as a "meticulously crafted, working replication" with "a glass dome cover and a beautifully handcrafted mahogany pedestal." But hidden inside that pedestal is a "plug-and-play computer interface" that also enables the ticker to spit out sports scores and personal messages. So, if it helps, think of it as a $35,000 pager. Orders -- or rather, "reservations" -- are being taken online at www.edisonstockticker.com.ROB FIXMER http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Tonga Is Set to Go Online To Stake Its Millennium Claims
body: While there is some debate about which piece of inhabited land will be the first to greet the new millennium, the Pacific islands that make up the Kingdom of Tonga seem to have a reasonable claim to the honor. At the stroke of midnight in Tonga on New Year's Eve it will still be 5 a.m. Eastern Standard Time. To mark the occasion, San Francisco-based Forthenews.com will offer live Webcasts of the Tongan millennium celebrations. "They don't have a broadcast TV station in Tonga, but they're doing some very sophisticated things with the Internet," said Alan Shulman, president of Forthenews.com. "Tonga has been virtually ignored by all the millennium committees." At the stroke of midnight, Tongan time, Dr. Shulman said, the Real Video feed to his company's site, www.forthenews.com, will show King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV praying in front of a choir of 10,000 Tongans. Another part of the site will feature a series of millennial firsts from the yet-to-be-created Hall of Firsts within Tonga's Royal School of Sciences. Among the planned features are the first cup of coffee, the first kiss, the first profit and loss statement. Dr. Shulman will auction the rights to perform some of them. "Some duffer is going to want the first golf swing," Dr. Shulman said. "It will be the highlight of their life." Finally, the site will also train one of its Webcams on a personal computer to, as a company announcement puts it, demonstrate to the world "the reality of Y2K problems, at least in Tonga."   IAN AUSTEN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV of Tonga

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Web Portal for the Arts Promotes Genre-Hopping
body: Culture vultures have a new place to nest on the Internet. ArtandCulture.com, a portal site for all things aesthetic, was scheduled to make its debut today on the Web. Each of its 1,000 entries on artists, performers and cultural movements is accompanied by an incisive essay and a small set of links to related Web sites (www.artandculture.com). Although the entries are categorized by artistic discipline, the site's goal is to encourage visitors to explore subjects beyond their usual enthusiasms. Marc Lafia, the site's founder and editorial director, said, "The great thing about the computational platform is that it lets you put Rabelais next to William S. Burroughs." The entries are assigned descriptive labels like "intimate" and "bubblicious." Stephen Sondheim, the site says, is bubblicious. title:
NEWS WATCH;
Web Site Helps Disabled Work and Communicate
body: Moving the Internet a step closer toward fulfilling its promise to be all-inclusive, We Media, a three-year-old company serving the disabled and their families, recently unveiled a full-service Web site aimed at that market. At first glance, www.wemedia.com appears much like many other commercial or service sites, with lots of information and links to shopping. But each mouse click beckons users to explore a range of offerings, including education, employment, travel and financial services made to appeal to the needs of the disabled. Cary Fields, co-founder of We Media, said that as many as 54 million Americans considered themselves disabled, a group that he said had more than $1 trillion in spending power. Being able to buy groceries, bank and communicate with friends and family by way of the Internet is especially important for the disabled. The site also offers users free email and computer-based long-distance phone calls over the Internet. Portions of the site, like the We Media magazine, have special software that enable users with impaired vision to hear rather than read the site. Alexander Spinelli, We Media's chief technology officer, said the company is being "very aggressive in its ongoing effort to make it completely accessible."   MICHEL MARRIOTT http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: New Toy Ideas Dance in the Heads of Precocious Inventors
body: As the holiday season marches on, children fill their wish lists with action figures, Furbies and the oh-so-popular Pokemon. Next year there may be a new item on those lists: Mr. Itchy Pants. The wiggling stuffed doll, which sings "I've Got Ants in My Pants," was chosen from 40 finalists as a grand-prize winner of a toy invention contest for children. It is expected to be manufactured and sold in time for next year's holiday season. Mr. Itchy's creator, 11-year-old Nadia Smith of Voorhees, N.J., based the doll on a variety of acquaintances. "There is a boy in my class who never sits still, so we named him Mr. Itchy Pants," she said. Mr. Itchy's waggling eyebrows were inspired by another friend. Among other phrases, the doll asks, "Hey, do you think you can help me out?" and says, "I'm still itchy!" The prototype, made from five knee-high nylon stockings, is autographed on the stomach by its creator. Nadia said she never thought her idea would take first prize, and was in tears of joy and surprise after receiving the award. Her mother, Ellen Smith, remembers that her daughter was reluctant to attend the event. She says she would say, "No, Mom, everyone's going to laugh." Now, Nadia advises other children to "try hard and never give up." She will receive a $10,000 college savings bond, as well as 7 percent of the royalties from the doll. The ants-in-the-pants doll was one of several humorous toys spotlighted in a gathering on Saturday in Manhattan. A clay prototype submitted by Natalie Perach, 11, of Farmington Hills, Mich., showed a monkey that smashed a banana in its face if the listener did not laugh at its jokes. The Monster Spy Truck, designed by 6-year-old Scott Klein of Antioch, Calif., came with a hidden camera behind the windshield and could be used for several undercover purposes. "There is a remote control to drive it," Scott wrote in the description, "and then you can take a picture of your sister without her noticing." His sister, Erinn, 3, was unavailable for comment. There was the House for Change by Rebekah Glickman-Simon, 8, of Boston, a doll house bank that divides a child's money into Savings, Spendings and Charity. Rebekah got the idea for the house when her parents increased her allowance, with the condition that she organize her fortune. "I only had glass jars for my money," she said. Her doll house has room for all her change, as well as a closet to stash that other childhood treasure, candy. The contest was divided into two age groups, 8 and under and 9 to 12, with 20 finalists chosen from each group. The runners-up were Daniel Fremont, 8, of Palo Alto, Calif., and Megan Griffin, 11, of Englewood, Colo., each of whom will receive a $2,000 college savings bond. Daniel won for his Robopet, a cone-shaped remote-controlled pet robot that wheels around and talks. "I just thought about what children would like," he said philosophically. Robopet "will follow you, and if it crashes into something it will say, 'Ouch.' " Megan's design was the Karaoke Hair Care Brush, which plays music and features a microphone so kids can sing along. "My friend's younger sister has a toothbrush that plays music and you sing to it," she said. "I thought it would be neat to have a hairbrush that did it." Megan, with wavy, waist-length hair, admits she already uses her hairbrush as a microphone when jamming to the radio with friends. The grand prize for inventors 8 and under went to Nicholas Englisis, 7, of Morganville, N.J., who created a doll with a picture-frame face where a child can put a snapshot of a friend. Nicholas suggests that his My Favorite Friend doll come with a disposable camera to take the pictures, as well as trading cards that can be personalized with information on the friend. Also, the doll should have different types of hair. "You can change the hair," he said, "if your favorite friend changes." Matthew Page, 8, of West Monroe, La., creator of the action-figure Karate-Chop Kenny, had lots of ideas on marketing. "Who knows," Matthew wrote in his proposal, "there may be a movie of him, and it will be good! And maybe a comic book to come with it!" Another idea came from Jay Lonski, 10, of Shelby Township, Mich. His bath-time boat, the Tubtanic, is designed to break up when it hits the side of the tub and dump lifeboat-shaped soap into the water. "If I win, I am planning on making a sister ship called the Sudsoapia," Jay said, "and when it travels along, liquid soap comes out the back." The contest was sponsored by Amazon.com. Jeff Bezos, the company's founder, was a judge. "We wanted to do something to celebrate toys, to celebrate innovation, and to celebrate kids," he said. The two grand prize toys will be manufactured and sold online through Amazon.com Toys. Seven percent of the royalties will be put in a college fund for the winners. The four other judges, in addition to Mr. Bezos, were: the Olympic skating gold medalist Katerina Witt; Lonnie Johnson, inventor of the Super Soaker water gun; Richard Levy, a developer of the Furby doll; and Thomas Edison Sloane Jr., a veteran of the toy industry and a great-grandson of Thomas Alva Edison. The gathering also featured a sticky Velcro Wall and Human Bowling. Each child appeared onstage to introduce his or her toy. "It was very emotional to see the kids come up and introduce their toys, and say, 'I invented this,' " Mr. Bezos said. Although the event featured fun and games, the presence of the toy manufacturers showed that toy making is also a serious commercial endeavor. After the ceremony, Mr. Levy, who has developed more than 100 toys and other products, said the children showed creativity that is often lost in adults. "I just hope they stay like this, because they don't know what can't be done," he said. Mr. Johnson, whose Johnson Research and Development, in Atlanta, focuses on toys, said of Nadia Smith: "I wonder if she understands how much her life has changed this day. Mr. Itchy Pants has the potential to make her a millionaire." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
ONLINE SHOPPER;
Christmas Trees (Not for Downloading)
body: IF I am a snob about Christmas trees, blame my mother. When I was small, she would march through the tree lot, suspiciously searching for crooked trunks, missing branches and needle loss. In her quest to acquire the biggest, fullest, freshest Scotch pine, she was not above examining candidates already reserved for other customers. One year she fell in love with a particularly graceful specimen slated for the nuns at a nearby convent. She bribed the lot owner $10 to snip off the "reserved" tag. All those trees were competing against a memory: the Christmas tree of 1945, when my mother was 4 years old. The war had ended, but tree lights were still scarce, at least in the secluded hills and hollows of eastern Kentucky, where she grew up. So my grandfather, a mechanic, brought home taillights, headlights and reflector lamps from the shop and attached them to the branches. The next morning a new doll sat beneath, bathed in an eerie red and orange glow. "Prettiest tree we ever had," my mother insists. And so, because I am my mother's daughter, I believe a proper Christmas tree is six and a half feet tall and too bushy to fit anywhere except right in front of the big picture window. It is lighted by strings of old-fashioned, oversize colored bulbs that give off an eerie glow (probably because half their paint has been scratched off over the years). Not to be picky, but the foil angel suspended in a glass ball should hang six inches above the miniature creche in a beaded eggshell. You can imagine, then, that I was pretty nervous about buying a Christmas tree over the Internet. First I telephoned four purveyors of online trees -- www.xmas-trees.com, www.freshchristmastrees.com, www.echristmastrees.com and www.evermontproducts.com/eVermontChristmastrees/index.html -- to grill, er, ask a few questions about how they could possibly shoulder the responsibility of choosing the right tree, much less pack and ship such a fragile item to my house within three to five business days via United Parcel Service. All four assured me they would handpick only the finest tree, painstakingly pack it in a long cardboard box and guarantee a replacement if I was not satisfied. I could order ahead and specify a delivery date, or, if I procrastinated, I could pay extra for speedier delivery. Gayle Cormier, who operates eVermontProducts.com, vouched for the packing process. "I had one in a box for five days," she said. "It looked like a cube at first. Within an hour, it regained its shape." To prove her point, Ms. Cormier mailed a six-and-a-half-foot balsam fir to me. It arrived within three days and, yes, regained its shape within three hours. The only problem was that it was a fir. Now, I know some people want a fir, and all four online tree sellers offer them in heights from three feet to seven feet and at prices from $59.95 to $107.95 including shipping. And I don't even mind that some people like a fir, even if Scotch pines -- my family's choice -- are so obviously more beautiful and festive. Why, there even used to be a fir family on my block. Of course, this family also believed in "theme" tree decorations. One year, the decorations consisted of clumps of purple balls that looked like gigantic bunches of fever-dream grapes. To get a Scotch pine, I had to narrow my choice to Xmas-trees.com, a Web site operated by Guy Frederick, who grows trees on a farm near Cadillac, Mich., that once belonged to his grandfather. To maintain freshness, Mr. Frederick recommended unpacking the tree right away, sawing one-half inch off the bottom of the trunk and sticking it into water. "You don't want problems with needle retention," he warned. As if I could forget the year my father burned out the motor on the vacuum cleaner while trying to suck unretained needles out of the trunk of the car. I ordered, specifying a height of five and a half feet to six and a half feet, which costs $50, including shipping. I requested that the tree be delivered on Dec. 3. That afternoon, my daughters sat in the big picture window, waiting for the U.P.S. truck and bickering over whose year it was to hang the carved wooden camel with the jeweled saddle. By suppertime, they gave up. But then, right after we lighted the Hanukkah candles (yes, we celebrate both), the tree arrived. It looked like a cube. But by the next morning, the tree had opened into a beautiful cone shape. It had, however, one problem. It was not bushy. It was so slender and elegant that it would have looked better in designer clothing than in the suddenly ridiculous old-fashioned lights. I phoned Mr. Frederick, who said I should have noted my bushiness preference on the order form's Comments section. "People specify all kinds of things -- down to the inch -- and we stand there in the barn holding the order form while we pick one out," he said. Next, I phoned my mother. After ascertaining that the tree had a strong, high branch on which to hang the glitter-frosted Mad Hatter ornament, she suggested -- somewhat to my horror -- that I change the lights. A thinner tree could work if I put aside the traditional fat-bulb lights with a string of tiny white lights, which my mother always called "Italian lights" because she first saw them in a spaghetti restaurant in the 1960's. "Substitute Italians for standards," she told me. The difference was remarkable. "Prettiest tree ever," my oldest daughter said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing

title: RealNetworks Plans Venture
body: RealNetworks Inc. plans to announce a partnership with WebGlide today to market, develop and distribute a technology that enables high-quality streaming of "synthetic" video even over dial-up modem connections. RealNetworks said it planned to integrate WebGlide with its own technology for delivering video over the Internet. As part of the agreement, RealNetworks said it would take a minority stake in WebGlide and that RealNetworks' chief executive, Rob Glaser, would join Web Glide's board. The integrated product, called Utopia, enables companies to create synthetic video, which is computer-generated animation, often integrated with snippets of actual video or photographs, and deliver it to consumers on the Web in real time in a highly compressed format. The technology is expected to be used to develop e-commerce sites where users can interactively browse through a virtual store or to deliver 3D video advertisements. The product "creates a user experience that from a visual standpoint has the same impact that you associate with natural video," Mr. Glaser said. While WebGlide technology can be viewed over a standard Web browser, users will also have to use RealNetworks' player software to get audio synchronized with the video and some of the interactivity. The companies plan to release a test version in the first half of 2000.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
Shares End Lower on Profit Taking as Dow Drops 38.53
body: Stocks closed mostly lower yesterday as investors took a break from recent buying sprees in the technology sector and failed to find reasons to buy stocks in the broader market. The Dow Jones industrial average fell 38.53 points, to 11,068.12. Broader stock indicators gave up early gains and closed with modest losses. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index declined 5.29 points, to 1,403.88, while the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite index fell 0.84 point, to 3,586.08. Brian G. Belski, chief investment strategist at George K. Baum & Company, described the choppy movements in the Dow and the S.& P. 500 as "backing and filling." Those gauges are pausing after a steep run-up, he said, trying to muster strength for the next push higher. The Nasdaq, pausing after its recent surge, ended a string of four consecutive closing highs. On Tuesday, the index rose 40.91 points, to 3,586.92, setting its 20th closing high since Oct. 29, largely because of a 23 percent gain by shares of Yahoo, the Internet search company. Yahoo was added to the S.& P. 500 after the close of trading Tuesday, a move that pushed its stock price higher as index fund managers bought shares. Yesterday, though, Yahoo fell as investors collected profits from its steep ascent. Investors continued to seek other technology shares that have performed well this year. Shares of Hewlett-Packard and Amazon.com rose. But market leaders like Dell Computer and Intel slipped. "The market has been correcting in a very quiet way," said Barry Hyman, senior equity analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum. While the largest technology stocks have bounded higher in recent weeks, most stocks have languished. That trend is partly a result of the calendar: As portfolio managers polish their holdings for end-of-year reports, they buy the best-performing stocks and shed any laggards, Mr. Hyman said. Bill Miller, president of Legg Mason Fund Advisor, said that as the year ends, investors seem to be applying stricter standards to the Internet companies that have dominated the market for much of 1999. "There's a high degree of expectation, but many of these companies don't have business models that are sustainable," he said. Mr. Miller singled out Amazon.com and America Online as companies that have fortified their business plans and attracted enough customers to prove their merit on Wall Street.  Treasury Prices Slip By Bloomberg News Treasury bond prices fell yesterday, snapping a three-day advance that drove yields to a two-week low, on concern that economic growth might prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again in the months ahead. Corporate and government agency debt sales, including a $1 billion offering by Procter & Gamble, drew investors away from Treasuries, as did declines in European bonds, traders said. The price of the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 12/32, to 98 21/32. The bond's yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, rose to 6.22 percent, from 6.20 percent on Tuesday. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average over the past year. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
BB DO New York breaks down why, when, where and how young adults get information.
body: NEW study by BBDO newyork of consumers' perceptions of the media says that newspapers have the most traditional image of all media and that the Internet has replaced television as the favored medium for escape. The method used by BBDO newyork might at least be partly responsible for the conclusions. To conduct the study, the agency, whose clients include Campbell Soup, FedEx, Mars, the newyork Stock Exchange, PepsiCo and Visa, interviewed 104 adults, ages 22 to 34, in eight markets across the unitedstates in September. The relative youth of the group might have influenced their perceptions of the newest medium -- the Internet -- as well as their thoughts on one of the oldest, newspapers. BBDO newyork is a unit of BBDO Worldwide, whose parent is the Omnicom Group. This possible bias notwithstanding, the study appears to confirm beliefs previously held by advertising and marketing executives on the roles various media play. Karen Olshan, executive vice president and director of strategic operations at BBDO newyork, said the study stemmed from the notion "that if the medium is the message, then the consumer's view of a given medium could contribute to or detract from the image of an advertised brand." It looked at the reasons consumers use each medium; who consumers think uses each medium; and the psychological rewards consumers say they get in using each medium. Respondents said they used the Internet for escape and mental stimulation and to obtain specific information on travel, business and health issues. Users were perceived positively, as young career-oriented adults. Respondents said using the Internet gave them feelings of innovation, intelligence, creativity, power and accomplishment. Respondents said they read magazines for information on current fashions, recipes and health issues and to reward themselves. They perceived magazine readers as being physically attractive; they also said reading magazines gave them feelings of sexiness, self-esteem, luxury and creativity. According to Ms. Olshan, magazines "have the most aspirational image among all major media." She added: "People go to them to reward themselves. Sitting down with a magazine takes time; it implies you have time. It's a nice feeling, a relaxing thing to do." The study found that respondents watched television for entertainment, to end the day or to spend time with family. Viewers were perceived largely as homemakers and families, while respondents said watching TV gave them feelings of happiness, comfort and fun. Radio was perceived as a background medium, to be listened to first thing in the morning or while doing other things. Listeners were seen as young and hip, while respondents said radio gave them feelings of peacefulness, relaxation, inner harmony and youthfulness. Respondents said they also read newspapers first thing in the morning and to obtain in-depth news, financial and sports information, and movie reviews. Readers were perceived as middle-aged or older, more often male than female. Respondents said reading newspapers gave them feelings of tradition, stability, security, maturity, respect and intelligence. Ms. Olshan said these findings suggested that TV was an ideal medium for advertising products that entertained or were associated with fun, like soft drinks, candy or amusement parks. Magazines make the most sense, she said, for luxury products and beauty and fashion brands, while newspapers are suited to advertising for technology and e-commerce companies. Marketers using the Internet must address consumers' desire for mental stimulation and escape in their advertising, she added, while radio advertising must find a way to move its messages from the background to the foreground. Over all, Ms. Olshan said it was important for marketers to consider the image of a medium when deciding where to advertise because this can reinforce the desired image of a brand. Elizabeth Silver, senior vice president for advertising and brand management for Visa USA, said she was pleased the Internet "had a well-developed profile in the study." She added, "I'm glad to see its profile has moved beyond geeky guys, that there's mainstream stuff going on." She also said the study had confirmed her intuition about the use of different media, but that it "was not changing my life." The most noteworthy section of the study, according to Jim Spaeth, president of the Advertising Research Foundation, was its definition "of the appropriate slice of the pie for the Internet" -- something he said he had not seen measured or documented before. Other observers were more skeptical of BBDO's findings, however. Roger Lavery, a professor at the Adcenter at Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond, warned: "They need to be careful making this all too tidy. Marketers like things tidy, but unfortunately, the world isn't that way." Erwin Ephron, a media consultant in newyork, called the study's findings "very superficial," and questioned the size and age of the group surveyed. BBDO newyork executives said they were likely to do surveys of consumers who are younger and older than those polled in September.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Two Years Before the Mast (and the Computer)
body: IF wind, weather and luck hold out, the crew of the Makulu II, a 43-foot sailboat-turned-cyberspace-classroom, is expected to complete a two-year voyage around the world on Saturday by sailing into a Florida marina not far from where it started. But that news would hardly be a surprise to the thousands, perhaps millions, of students and the simply curious who have been following the crew's exploits and explorations by way of email and the crew's Web site. Unlike mariners of old, the six young men and women on board, who look more like Ralph Lauren models than ship-weary sailors, have been using computer technology to take anyone with access to the World Wide Web along with them -- virtually, of course. They have shared practically everything online, like digital pictures of their underwear drying in the sea breeze and weekly log entries describing their adventures, as well as funeral rituals in Southeast Asia, Carnival celebrations in Gibraltar and a solemn tour of a former slave-trade house on an island off the coast of West Africa. And there have been the dispatches, sometimes routine and sometimes hauntingly honest, uploaded to the Net from the Makulu II. "Crossing from Senegal to Brazil in this season is proving more difficult than we thought!" reads one of the weekly updates posted on the Makulu II's Web site, www.reachtheworld.org. "We did NOT find the wind that we hoped would carry us southwest to Brazil. As a result, we have changed our plan and are heading directly to Trinidad, a 2,200-plus-mile passage that could take as long as 40 days." The interactive adventure has all been done in the cause of education -- that of the crew and, most important, of the students who are part of a global network of classrooms linked to the Makulu II over the Internet, said Heather Halstead, the 25-year-old creator and co-captain of the project. The crew receives as many as 200 messages a month from students and teachers. They are part of a project that would not be possible without the relatively low-cost computer-assisted communications available today, Ms. Halstead. "I've always been into teaching my whole life," Ms. Halstead said in an interview in newyork, where she was taking a break from the voyage to visit her family and some of the project's participating schools. "And I always knew I wanted to sail around the world." And despite the obvious fun Ms. Halstead and her crew have had, the pictures and dispatches that have been streaming from the crew have hardly been the stuff of vacation postcards. Instead, Ms. Halstead, with the help of a group of educators, created a curriculum center online that helps classroom teachers use the experiences of the Makulu II crew to learn and teach about world cultures and more. There have been lesson and activity guides that have covered, among other subjects, African art and gravestone art, world languages, origin myths and astronomy, cartography and weather forecasting. The sailboat uses satellite-assisted navigation and communications, which include an on-board telephone and email. But the services are expensive, she said. The telephone, which uses a technology called side band radio that bounces signals off the atmosphere, costs about $5 a minute, and email costs almost a penny per character, Ms. Halstead said. The crew also uses much cheaper email systems at cybercafes when it can find them on land, she said. By communicating directly with Ms. Halstead, a sixth-grade class was able to persuade the Makulu II crew to swing by Singapore to complete a fact-finding itinerary; another school asked the crew to ask middle school students in the Cook Islands about their lives here; still another school used the Makulu II to chat with children in a Thai fishing village. "It was a wonderful experience for my students to be able to feel a connection to real people as they studied the classroom maps," said Pat Palazzolo, a ninth-grade teacher at the Upper St. Clair High School in Clair, Pa. "My students were fascinated by the idea of people not much older than themselves involved in such as adventure." Combining her interests in education and circumnavigating the planet was far from easy for Ms. Halstead. Shortly after graduating from Dartmouth in 1997 with an honors degree in American social history and education, Ms. Halstead decided that she would indeed do just that. The product of an affluent newyork family, Ms. Halstead was able to use money she inherited from her paternal grandfather -- the inspiration for the voyage -- to buy the yacht, with the idea of recovering the money by selling the boat once the trip was completed. But buying a oceangoing vessel was only the beginning. She created the Reach the World Company, a nonprofit group that became the organization base for the voyage and related educational projects. Then in quick order, she said, she had to teach herself how to insure a boat (something that would come in handy during the trip), equip it so she could communicate with students and teachers, and select a crew. Finding a co-captain was simple. Ms. Halstead, who as a child was terrified of boats, later fell in love with them at a summer sailing camp she attended in the British Virgin Islands. Eventually, she became an instructor and developed, she said, the confidence to believe that she could sail around the world. Sailing was also in her blood. Her father, Clark Halstead, sails, and her maternal grandfather was a cruise director and merchant marine. As an instructor at the sailing camp, Ms. Halstead met Marc Gustafson, an instructor and an able sailor. Together, she and Mr. Gustafson, who is 22 and a graduate of Elon College in North Carolina and the Chapman School of Seamanship in Stuart, Fla., are the Makulu II's skippers. The co-captains' first two days at the helm of the Makulu II (which in Zulu roughly means "big mama") were not promising. In trying to move the boat to a marina where the voyage would begin, Mr. Gustafson ran it aground three times -- hard -- along Florida's intracoastal waterway from Titusville to Fort Lauderdale before he got the feel of the sailboat. "That was a disaster," Ms. Halstead recalled. "We were discouraged, to say the least. We're like, we're never going to get out of Florida. It's funny to look back on it now." Crew members have numbered more than two dozen friends, relatives and other volunteers who have sailed passages on the Makulu II of varying lengths. The current crew has been onboard for a semester. Each is required to contribute $1,000 a month to help cover the cost of the voyage. Other costs are covered by donations and grants to Reach the World. "We really didn't believe she was going to pull it off," her mother, Carol Halstead, said with a chuckle. "But we kind of encouraged her. Now the fact is that she is making it happen and it is awe inspiring." Shawn McCullough, 29, a former wilderness ranger from Boulder, Colo., with little ocean-sailing experience, joined the crew in the fall. He said he had been sold on the idea shortly after speaking with Heather Halstead and remembering how "she was constantly sparking, never letting the fire die out" of the project. "The idea that excited me most," Mr. McCullough said, was having a child be able to write to us on the ocean and say, 'Can you take a picture of the sunrise in the middle of the Atlantic?' " Ms. Halstead knows the feeling. Having taught in challenging environments before, from the backwoods of Colorado to the bush in Kenya during a semester break from college, she said she had been moved to create the floating classroom on the Makulu II to help teachers and students explore the world and its people. "We've been out there long enough to see what the connections are between different regions," she said. She has been able to see traces of different languages from the east coast of Africa to the Middle East and various movements in dances in widely separated cultures in the South Pacific, for instance. "I've sort of had this idea of the world being an overlapping of concentric circles, of cultural influences," Ms. Halstead said. "It's really there. I love that." And while she and her crew have had trouble, including ripped sails and serious engine trouble 50 hours out of Trinidad, the Makulu II is expected to reach the Florida coast on schedule. When it arrives, Carol Halstead said, she will be both proud and relieved. "They have learned so much," she said of the voyage, "but it has been a school of hard knocks." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: SAILING ON -- Heather Halstead is nearing the end of a two-year voyage around the world one that has been shared with thousands of students and others through the Internet. The project's Web site includes a log of the journey, photographs - including some of the boat, Makulu II - and maps detailing the route. (Marilynn K. Yee/The newyork Times)  Map of the world shows Heather Halstead's route.

title:
WHAT'S NEXT;
Legal Squabbles in Path of Internet
body: ONE of the recurring dreams of technology utopians is the idea of the celestial jukebox. It's a metaphor for the Web of the future in which individual terminals will have access to great digital warehouses in the sky packed with petabits of digitally stored CD's, books, television shows and any other copyrighted information or entertainment imaginable -- all for micropayments too small to pinch the wallet. The idea is that consumers of the future will pay a few dollars or cents -- or even a fraction of a cent -- to watch an episode of "I Love Lucy," listen to an aria by Bryn Terfel or view a missed Chemistry 101 lecture, deliverable on the spot to home or office. There are already companies like 1ClickCharge or Qpass that let people run a chit or bill a credit card for single, low-cost items. Some experts say companies like these will become part of a gigantic business that will make it easy for consumers to buy information or entertainment in small segments. As technology changes, the celestial jukebox will surely become possible. In fact, it may be that the stickiest issues will involve legal, not technical, questions. "The juggernaut is moving -- there's an internal market logic to the celestial jukebox," said Paul Goldstein, a law professor at Stanford University and author of "Copyright's Highway: From Gutenberg to the Celestial Jukebox" (Hill & Wang, 1994). "But first there are hurdles to deal with." The hurdles Dr. Goldstein and others speak of are the tangled legal issues of patents, trademarks, trade secrets and copyrights -- known collectively as intellectual property issues. "Intellectual property used to be a relative backwater, a fairly quiet territory," said Rory J. Radding, a partner at the Pennie & Edmonds law firm in Manhattan. "But the Internet has made it red hot, right up there on the radar screen." Mr. Radding is chairman of the newyork State Bar Association's committee on intellectual property on the Internet. Some of the intellectual property issues associated with the Internet involve the protection of copyrighted materials, like music and books. New encryption methods are being developed to prevent the unauthorized distribution of such material over the Internet, but one question is how much encryption should be used to prevent piracy without at the same time stifling a market. Patent disputes can involve the methods used to conduct business over the Internet, not just the material being sold. The business-methods issue arises from a ruling in July 1998 by the unitedstates Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which ruled that companies could patent such methods. In that case, the method involved a computer system for managing portfolios. For 100 years, courts had held that business methods themselves could not be patented, said Barry D. Rein, a partner at Pennie & Edmonds, but the 1998 ruling ran counter to that idea. Many Internet companies promptly started filing patents for their methods, and some of them then sued other companies for infringement. Amazon.com, for instance, won a patent for "one-click ordering," an express service that lets customers place orders without re-entering financial information each time they buy. Amazon.com subsequently sued Barnesandnoble.com for its one-click "express lane" method, saying it infringed on Amazon.com's one-click patent. Amazon won the first round in this dispute: last week a Federal District Court judge in Seattle issued a preliminary injuction ordering Barnesandnoble.com to stop using the one-click system because of Amazon's patent claim. The issue is significant because companies often use similar software to do business online. "Any new entrant into commercial space on the celestial jukebox has to worry about its business plan being cut off at the knees by a patent infringement lawsuit," Dr. Goldstein said. "This issue could effectively bring e-commerce to a halt." Paul Hagen, a senior analyst at Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass., said companies who spend fortunes to set up retail Internet sites might be given pause by the specter of patent infringement suits. "They won't keep on investing unless that money is protected," he said. "And when you have a patent on such a vague process, you can completely chill an entire marketplace." Many people in the field say the law alone is not going to solve infringement issues.  "Intellectual property owners will look for alternatives to the legal system," said David Post, a law professor at Temple University who originated one of the first Internet law courses. "If I'm sitting on $100 million in intellectual property, I'm not going to wait around for the complex legal world to sort itself out." Dr. Post predicted that in the recording industry, encryption would be the solution to intellectual property problems. "The recording industry will eventually succeed in promulgating standards that will allow them to encrypt files so they can't be accessed without contractual terms and conditions," he said. Lisa Allen, an analyst who is the lead author of a Forrester report called "The Intellectual Property Mess," said encryption would take the owners of intellectual property rights only so far. "Rights owners can't rely on technology alone to stop infringement" if they are going to be able to compete in the e-commerce market of the future, she said. "If you don't want to miss out on $3.2 trillion in commerce worldwide by 2003, you're going to have to think of other solutions," she said. Ms. Allen draws a parallel with the fight the movie industry had over VCR's because it thought the devices would hurt its business. "If this had continued, the industry would have missed out on a new revenue stream," she said. Dr. Post recognizes the complex problems of intellectual property rights on the Internet, but he is confident that the age of the celestial jukebox will arrive anyway. "I can't sell you access to my course for a few pennies yet, but the arrow is clearly pointing in that direction," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Mary Ann Smith)

title: Automakers Turn Over Their Data Traffic to a New Operator
body: A privately held California company announced today that it had bought the assets and operations of the auto industry's private data network, the latest in a series of corporate moves as automakers begin switching their vast purchasing systems to electronic commerce. The General Motors Corporation and the Ford Motor Company are developing software to set up electronic marketplaces next year on the once-obscure network. These marketplaces could be used to conduct bidding and to place purchase orders for auto parts and even for services, like health care for employees. G.M. plans to use its software on the Internet as well. Ford hopes to do so but has concerns about whether Internet transactions will be safe from hacking. DaimlerChrysler A.G. is still studying plans for electronic purchasing. The Automotive Industry Action Group, a technology consortium of G.M., Ford, DaimlerChrysler and 1,600 of their auto parts suppliers, sold the network's computers, software, patents, copyrights and brands to the Science Applications International Corporation, a company based in San Diego. It will manage the Automotive Network Exchange, as it is known, although auto industry executives will remain on the network's governing committee. Terms of the sale were not disclosed. Doug Buchanan, a steel executive on one of the industry group's committees that designed the Automotive Network Exchange, said the data network's sale was necessary because the group did not have the large sums needed to expand the network. "S.A.I.C. brings some deep pockets to the table," he said. The group said it planned to add new features to the data network, including video conferencing. Automakers believe the data network offers tighter security than the Internet. Users have special phone lines to the network's computers, although there are plans for dial-up access next year. Automakers are working on ways to take bids for multimillion-dollar auto parts contracts over the public Internet, but are wary that rivals might figure out a way to steal competitive information. Whatever system is used "has to be secure, because none of us want to be able to see each other's product development plans as they're buzzing through the lines," said Mark Baughman, Ford's manager of supplier electronic commerce. David Barnas, a G.M. spokesman, said that the company believed it could safely conduct electronic commerce with suppliers over the Internet and did not need to rely exclusively on the elaborate security of the Automotive Network Exchange. The Automotive Network Exchange connects the automakers' computers to those of 250 suppliers; 200 more suppliers have applied to join the data network. The network is already used to exchange confidential computer blueprints of future car models and to transmit bids for auto parts contracts. Automakers also use the network to send hourly updates of assembly plant activity to suppliers, who then send auto parts in time to be installed on vehicles. The data network is expanding into other industries tied to the automakers. Hospitals and health care insurers in southeastern Michigan will start using the network next spring, said Dennis McCafferty, vice president for product development at the Greater Detroit Area Health Council. Tracy Trent, the S.A.I.C. senior vice president for e-business, said the company hoped to bring other industries onto the network, including electronics manufacturers. The S.A.I.C. is owned by its 36,000 employees, and is best known for its purchase in late 1997 of Bell Communications Research, the research arm of the regional Bell telephone companies. The group, which had $4.7 billion in revenue last year, also designs military and scientific computer systems.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Court Bars Release of Judges' Financial Data
body: Days before an Internet news service was to put the financial disclosure forms of all 1,600 federal judges on the World Wide Web, the chairman of a special committee of judges has blocked the release of the information and says the panel will review the matter this week. Karen Redmond, a spokesman for the Administrative Office of the Courts, said that while the information had been generally available to people who applied as individuals, several judges had become concerned that a wholesale dissemination of it could threaten their security. As a result, William J. Zloch, a federal trial judge in Florida who is chairman of the Committee on Financial Disclosure for the Judicial Conference, the governing body of the federal courts, ordered last week that the release of the records to the Internet service, APBnews.com, be barred. In addition, Judge Zloch put a hold on some three dozen other such requests, from individuals and groups, and called a meeting for Friday in Washington, where the committee, composed of 15 sitting judges, will discuss the issue. Like high-ranking officials in both the legislative and executive branches, federal judges have been required by law since 1979 to report all family assets within broad ranges of estimated worth. Ms. Redmond explained that till now, a request by an individual for a judge's financial disclosure form led to the judge's being notified before the information was released. Then, under legislation adopted by Congress last year, a judge who considered the applicant a possible security threat could have the file edited to eliminate information that might be used to locate him or his family. If the financial disclosure data was instead put on the Web, Ms. Redmond said, those who see it could not be screened as they are now. "We're very concerned about the security of the procedures," she said. All this seems overstated to Bob Port, a senior editor at the APBnews service, whose site features criminal-law issues. "On its face, the security concerns sound reasonable," Mr. Port said. But in fact, he said, there is little information in the forms that could be used to threaten a judge. The forms do not show home addresses or telephone numbers, for instance, although among the things that officials are obliged to disclose on them are the general locations of assets like mountain or lake cottages that produce income. Mr. Port also said the practice of notifying judges of the identity of those seeking access to the forms only discouraged people like litigants and lawyers, who, he said, had a legitimate need to see them, to check for judges' conflicts. The issue was joined when Mr. Port and his colleagues at the service, having come up with the idea of putting all the federal judges' financial forms on the Web, asked for them last fall. Mr. Port said the Web posting had seemed like a helpful thing to do, as it would allow lawyers and litigants to look at the forms "without being intimidated by the knowledge that the judge would know they had requested it." The news service's request involved an enormous amount of copying. On Nov. 1, APBnews.com mailed a check for $2,516 to the Administrative Office of the Courts to cover the cost of copying 12,580 pages of documents. "We had everything ready to put it into the system this week," Mr. Port said. "We had equipment to scan the pages and everything." The debate touches on judges' special role as officials whose very job often causes them to inflict bitter disappointment on criminal defendants and on either of the warring parties in civil suits. In addition, there is a kind of cultural reluctance among judges, in which they generally consider themselves entitled to greater privacy than those in the other branches of government. "They have a long history of being reluctant to give out information," Mr. Port said. "I understand that it's an invasion of privacy, but unfortunately they're in public service, they have a job for life, and this comes with the territory." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Metro Business;
Avon Will Enhance Its Presence on Web
body: Avon Products Inc. will spend more than $30 million next year to build a new avon.com Web site, which will showcase its entire product line, including cosmetics, gifts, clothes and jewelry, the company announced yesterday. The new site will open in June, with IBM as its technology partner. Avon, based in newyork, has operated an avon.com site since 1997, but only about 10 percent of the more than 4,000 products that the company sells are available. The site will be designed to help Avon's 500,000 sales representatives in the unitedstates increase their business by enabling them to sell online through their own personalized Web pages, which they will develop in partnership with Avon. The representatives will be able to conduct all aspects of their Avon business online, including ordering, getting the status of accounts and making payments. Avon will also sell products directly to consumers if they choose not to buy from a representative. Other direct sellers, including Amway and Tupperware, have moved their businesses onto the Internet in the last year. But all have had to come up with a way to link their sales representatives and the Web. In addition to its Web site plans, Avon also said yesterday that it would begin its first global advertising campaign next year, spending as much as $90 million, double what it has spent this year on advertising. http://www.nytimes.com

title: 'South Park' Creators Plan Cartoon Series for the Web
body: In the latest examples of how Hollywood is trying to turn the Internet into an entertainment venue, the creators of the television show "South Park" have said they have agreed to make a series of 39 short cartoons for the World Wide Web. The cartoons, which will be different from South Park, will be distributed starting next March on Shockwave.com, an entertainment Web site run by Macromedia Inc., a software company. Trey Parker and Matt Stone, the creators of "South Park," will receive equity of less than 10 percent in Shockwave.com, which is being run as a separate subsidiary of Macromedia and is expected eventually to issue its own shares to the public. Many people in the entertainment and computer industries, from Steven Spielberg to unknown animators and directors, are distributing or planning to distribute cartoons, television programs and movies through the Internet. Still, it is unclear how successful this will be as a business. Mr. Stone said he and his partner were attracted to the Web by the freedom it offered to go beyond the language and content restrictions of television. "We're definitely excited to push those limits," he said. He said he and Mr. Parker had turned down offers to do Web programs in the past because the Internet technology was so crude. "It's really just now the technology made it possible to do cool stuff on the Web, especially in animation," he said. While much of the Web-based entertainment is derived from television, movies or comic books, Mr. Parker and Mr. Stone will create new characters and a new series that will be seen first on the Internet. If a creation succeeds on the Web, it might then be sold or distributed to TV networks or movie studios, having already built up an audience. "What we can deliver from the get-go are millions of viewers," said Mike Simpson, executive vice president of the William Morris Agency, which represented Mr. Stone and Mr. Parker. This could become a much less expensive and risky way to develop new shows than making full-length pilots, he said. Mr. Parker and Mr. Stone will retain the copyrights to their work, although Shockwave.com will share in revenues even from television programs or movies based on the Internet characters, according to Rob Burgess, chairman and chief executive of Macromedia, which is based in San Francisco. "We think it's a watershed deal with Hollywood," he said. The animations will be two to five minutes long and will be viewable using Macromedia's Flash software, which the company says is already on 200 million computers. One of the barriers to entertainment on the Web is the poor video image quality and long transmission times. But that is not as big a problem for animation because software like Flash allows cartoons with near television quality to be transmitted reasonably fast. Image quality is even less of a factor for the crude type of animation in "South Park." Shockwave.com last week received investments totaling $44 million from Sequoia Capital, the venture capital firm that backed such companies as Cisco Systems and Yahoo, and from Jim Clark, the entrepreneur who started Silicon Graphics and Netscape Communications. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Matt Stone, left, and Trey Parker, will make cartoons for a Web site run by Macromedia. Mr. Stone said the two were attracted to the Web by the freedom it offered to go beyond the restrictions of television. (Reuters)

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Yahoo Shares Lead Way as Nasdaq Hits Record Close for 4th Day
body: Technomania continued in the stock market yesterday, as the Nasdaq composite index rose to a fourth consecutive record, partly because of a huge jump in the price of shares of Yahoo. But other indexes struggled, and ended lower. Trading volume was heavy. Led by a second big drop in the price of Coca-Cola, the Dow Jones industrial average slumped 118.36 points, or 1.05 percent, to 11,106.65. A number of Wall Street analysts downgraded Coke's stock yesterday, a day after the company's chairman and chief executive said he would resign his positions in April, an announcement that stunned the business world. Shares of Coca-Cola closed at $60, down $4. Since M. Douglas Ivester said he was leaving the company, the stock has lost 7 percent of its market value. A bad day for drug stocks contributed to a slide in the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index, which closed at 1,409.17, down 14.16 points, or 1 percent. For the most part, the performances of the Dow and S.& P. were eclipsed by continued brisk demand for the technology shares that dominate the Nasdaq composite index. Issues like Cisco Systems, Ciena and Yahoo pushed the index up 40.91 points, or 1.15 percent, to 3,586.92. Volume on the newyork Stock Exchange was 1.09 billion shares and more than 1.5 billion shares traded on the Nasdaq. Much of the session was dominated by Yahoo, the Internet media company that at the close of trading became part of the S.& P. The imminent addition of Yahoo to the index prompted mutual funds that mimic the composition of the S.& P. to sell shares of the 499 other companies to make room for Yahoo. Yahoo will have a far bigger weighting than the company it is replacing, Laidlaw Inc. Shares of Yahoo have been rising steadily since Nov. 30, when Standard & Poor's said Yahoo was being added to the index. But analysts were stunned by what happened yesterday: Yahoo's shares closed at 347, up 66 1/4. "In a week, almost $42 billion in Yahoo's market capitalization has been created out of thin air," said William Meehan, chief market analyst at Cantor Fitzgerald. "The only news has been that the stock is being added to the S.& P. index." Stocks that are added to a widely used index like Standard & Poor's generally rise after the decision is made to put them in. But the 54 percent gain in Yahoo's shares in the last week is a seismic reaction. Henry Herrman, chief investment officer at Waddell & Reed in Overland Park, Kan., which has some $27 billion under management, called the run-up in Yahoo's stock unbelievable. But in the next breath he added that for a while yet technology shares are likely to appreciate further. "On a performance basis, everybody is forced to put more money into technology," he said. "Right now, technology is nearly 30 percent of the S.& P. 500 and people are talking about it going to 40 percent." "I have this vision of the Nasdaq as a diver that is about to jackknife," he added. "But I don't think we will visit that issue until sometime next year." It was a bad day for big drug stocks and health company issues.  Bristol-Myers Squibb fell 2 5/8, to 66 13/16. Eli Lilly dropped by 23 85/128, to 66 53/64. And Johnson & Johnson slumped 3 5/16, to 93 3/8. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average over the past year.
