title: Times Adds 2 Critics To Film Review Staff
body: The newyork Times has appointed two new film critics to review the growing number of new releases, Joseph Lelyveld, the executive editor, announced yesterday. The critics, Elvis Mitchell, 41, of The Fort Worth Star-Telegram, and A. O. Scott, 33, the Sunday book critic at Newsday, will assume their duties next month, joining Stephen Holden, who has been a staff critic for The Times for 11 years. The three will share responsibilities, with Mr. Holden in particular also writing regular critical essays in the Arts & Leisure section on Sundays, Mr. Lelyveld said. Janet Maslin, the newspaper's senior film critic, announced on Sept. 21 that she was leaving the paper after 22 years. Mr. Mitchell, The Star-Telegram's film critic for two years, previously reviewed films for The Los Angeles Herald-Examiner and The Detroit Free Press. For the last 15 years he has also been an entertainment critic for "Weekend Edition with Scott Simon" on National Public Radio. He was also host of the film-related interview program "The Treatment" for KCRW, Santa Monica's public radio station, and the host of the Independent Film Channel's "Independent Focus" program. In addition Mr. Mitchell has written on movies for Rolling Stone, GQ and Interview magazines. He was brought up in Detroit and attended Wayne State University. Mr. Scott, before joining Newsday last April, wrote for The newyork Times Book Review, The newyork Review of Books, The Nation and The newyorker. He has been an editor at The newyork Review and Lingua Franca and has been a regular contributor on culture and politics to the Internet magazine Slate. A recent article in Slate on Martin Scorsese drew him to the attention of The Times, Mr. Lelyveld said. Mr. Scott has a B.A. in literature from Harvard and a master's degree in English from Johns Hopkins University. Mr. Lelyveld said the increase in critics was a response to the growing number of movie releases. In 1990 The Times ran 325 movie reviews; so far this year the number is 375. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Two Makers of Communications Gear to Announce Products
body: As the communications equipment industry continues to advance at a white-hot pace, two small companies intend to announce today the development of products meant to broadly increase the flexibility of big communications networks. Sycamore Networks Inc., which had an enormously successful initial public stock offering in October, intends to announce the development of a communications switch that is possibly the first to use light instead of electricity. Ennovate Networks Inc., which has been underwritten primarily by Japanese conglomerates and venture capitalists, intends to announce that Psinet, one of the biggest Internet carriers, will be the first customer for Ennovate's main product, which allows corporations to tie far-flung offices together with so-called "virtual private networks." Ennovate anticipates that it will make an initial public stock offering next year. Though the Sycamore and Ennovate products differ widely, the companies' announcements will each highlight the importance that major communications carriers are placing on delivering flexible services rather than raw capacity. Such capacity is largely becoming a commodity, forcing big carriers to offer customized services that relate directly to their corporate customers' core operations. That requires new sorts of equipment. Technically, the new Sycamore product could prove revolutionary. Optical technology has been widely used for at least a decade to transmit torrents of data between fixed points. But the network "intelligence" that figures out what goes where has remained electrical, increasing its complexity and preventing carriers from manipulating light waves as finely as they might like. Sycamore's product may solve those problems, allowing communications carriers to direct different light waves to different places with mere keystrokes. That could allow carriers to provide big communications links to companies on demand and for flexible amounts of time. Sycamore intends to announce that iaxis, a small, new carrier in Europe, has agreed to try the new product. Ennovate's product allows a corporate customer to construct national or perhaps global networks that appear to be based on private, dedicated communications lines. In reality, that company's data will travel intermingled with those of other enterprises, reducing costs, but Ennovate's product will help keep each traffic stream separate and secure. Executives close to the deal said that Psinet has agreed to purchase $15 million worth of equipment from Ennovate over four years. That is a relatively small number, but small numbers have not hurt Sycamore. The company posted only $11 million in revenue in its last fiscal year and it now has a market value of about $19 billion. Sycamore's technology, however, is more far-reaching than Ennovate's and Ennovate, based in Boxborough, Mass., is unlikely to reach that sort of valuation. Shares of Sycamore, based in Chelmsford, Mass., closed yesterday at $247.125, up $7.625, in Nasdaq trading. http://www.nytimes.com

title: AT&T Revamps to Win Local Phone and Internet Gains
body: In a series of far-reaching announcements yesterday spanning the realms of finance, management and regulation, the AT&T Corporation fleshed out its plans for going after the regional Bell companies' markets across the country. As expected, the long-distance communications company announced a change in financial structure, a broad new wireless communications initiative, sweeping changes in its top executive ranks and a deal to open its cable television systems to outside Internet service providers. Disclosed at a meeting with hundreds of analysts in newyork, the initiatives were meant to convince Wall Street and federal regulators that AT&T is serious about providing better returns to investors and new choices for consumers in local phone service and high-speed Internet access. More important, the announcements are meant to convey that the company has the wherewithal to make those things happen. As expected, AT&T announced plans to issue a tracking stock for its fast-growing wireless unit that would trade separately from AT&T's common stock, which is among the most widely held in the nation. AT&T also said it would deploy a new "fixed wireless" technology to provide local phone service and quick Internet access to millions of homes in the unitedstates. Wireless, however, will not provide AT&T's main foray into the local communications business, which the company had to give up when it split under court supervision in 1984. AT&T has invested more than $100 billion to become the nation's No. 1 cable television provider and plans to use cable to deliver high-speed Internet access and local telephone service. AT&T's cable strategy, however, has run into criticism because in acquiring Tele-Communications Inc., it inherited a contract giving the Excite@Home cable modem venture exclusive rights to provide high-speed Internet service until 2002. Other Internet providers, led by America Online Inc., say that the arrangement is unfair and that AT&T should open its cable systems to other Internet providers. AT&T has continued to stand by its exclusive deal with Excite@Home, of which it is the largest shareholder, but the company has tried hard to convince regulators and the Internet industry that it will happily strike deals with other Internet service providers after 2002. As expected, AT&T yesterday announced a broad, if somewhat vague, agreement with Mindspring, a big Internet provider, and with the chairman of a Federal Communications Commission advisory group regarding the principles that AT&T will follow in dealing with Internet providers. Those principles include an agreement by AT&T to provide its customers with a choice of Internet providers; to allow users to customize their "start page" on the Web, often considered valuable advertising territory; and to allow users unfettered access to all Web content without additional charges from AT&T. The agreement, outlined in a public letter to William E. Kennard, chairman of the F.C.C., is clearly meant to forestall any regulatory attempts to force AT&T to open its cable systems. Municipalities including Portland, Ore., which must approve the transfer of cable licenses from TCI to AT&T, are trying to pry open AT&T's systems, though Mr. Kennard has said the federal government, not states or cities, has jurisdiction over any such policies. Accompanying the strategic and financial moves were announcements of sweeping management changes to implement them. As expected, John D. Zeglis, AT&T's president, was named chairman of the newly independent wireless unit. Daniel E. Somers, AT&T's chief financial officer, was named chairman of the cable unit, succeeding Leo Hindery, who left the company in October and yesterday was named to head a division of Global Crossing. Richard R. Roscitt, head of the AT&T unit that runs the networks of big business customers, was named chief of AT&T's overall business-services division. Executives close to AT&T said that the company was still negotiating with Charles H. Noski, the No. 2 executive at the Hughes Electronics unit of General Motors, to succeed Mr. Somers as AT&T's chief financial officer. The executives said an agreement could be announced soon. Kathleen Earley, who previously ran the company's Internet operation, was named to a new post overseeing all AT&T data communications offerings for business customers. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Former Executive From AT&T Re-emerges at Global Crossing
body: Adding yet another big name to Global Crossing's already crowded executive suite, Leo J. Hindery Jr., recently of AT&T, said yesterday that he would become chairman of the Global Crossing unit that maintains Web sites for corporate customers. Mr. Hindery added that Global Crossing intended to announce plans early next year to spin off the Web unit that he will run as a separately traded company. Mr. Hindery, a former newspaper executive, rose to prominence as the No. 2 executive at Tele-Communications Inc., the big cable television carrier. After AT&T, the biggest long-distance telephone company, agreed to acquire TCI last year in a bid to offer local phone service and high-speed Internet access using cable lines, Mr. Hindery essentially kept his job as the head of AT&T's new cable unit. But Mr. Hindery, 52, and his sometimes aggressive management style clashed with C. Michael Armstrong, AT&T's more measured chairman. Mr. Hindery appeared to chafe under AT&T's highly formalized management structure. He resigned in October. (Yesterday, as expected, AT&T named Daniel E. Somers, previously the company's chief financial officer, to succeed Mr. Hindery at the helm of the cable unit.) Since October, the cable and telecommunications industries have been awash in rumors about Mr. Hindery's plans. Many executives expected him to step back from active management and instead invest in a small portfolio of start-ups. Instead, he has decided to join Global Crossing, the undersea cable upstart that recently acquired the Frontier Corporation, formerly Rochester Telephone. At Global Crossing he joins Gary Winnick, the company's chairman and a former associate of Michael R. Milken, and Robert Annunziata, who ran AT&T's business-services unit briefly before agreeing to become Global Crossing's chief executive. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Losing Pounds by Surfing, on the Web
body: It was probably inevitable that the World Wide Web would bloom with sites for dieters. But to the surprise of professional dietitians, many of these sites have turned out to be not only popular but effective. From fee-based ventures like eDiets.com to free ones like Cyberdiet.com, a cornucopia of sites has sprung up in the last year or two to provide nutrition and diet advice. Many offer services that are otherwise found through private dietitians or diet companies like Weight Watchers, including personalized feedback and support from a group of fellow dieters. In one of the first studies of the effectiveness of online dieting, preliminary research at Brown University suggests that "the Internet seems to be a great vehicle for what has proven successful in face-to-face programs," in the words of the principal researcher, Deborah Tate, a graduate student completing her doctorate in clinical psychology. The study, to be completed early next year, compared two groups of overweight people. Members of the first group, who were given Web-based information about dieting, lost an average of 3 pounds in the first 12 weeks of the program. But members of another group that interacted on the Internet -- who reported on their meals and exercise, had questions answered, got email from professionals and posted messages on bulletin boards -- lost 9 pounds in the 12 weeks. "Additional information alone, while helpful, doesn't appear to be enough," Ms. Tate said. Felicia Busch, a dietitian in St. Paul, who is a spokeswoman for the American Dietetic Association, an 82-year-old organization of food and nutrition professionals, says online dieting offers easy access to information and support from the privacy of the dieter's home or office. And Judith Dodd, a former president of the association, is on an advisory committee that helps rate about 200 online nutrition sites for the Tufts University School of Nutrition. The service, itself on the Web at www.navigator.tufts.edu, gives high marks to a number of dieting sites. For example, it calls Cyberdiet.com "an oasis of sane, fun and well-presented nutrition information." Ms. Busch and Ms. Dodd say that in some cases there is no substitute for an individual counselor, who can give personalized recommendations and take a more exact diet history than might be possible on the Web, and who may be covered by insurance. A dieter with special needs "may be flirting with danger online," Ms. Dodd said. Still, she added, Tufts's high-ranked sites "are a really good starting point" and provide quick answers to dieting questions. The trend to online information and advice comes at a time when Americans are heavier than ever. "People are driving 10 minutes to find a spot in front of the health club so they don't have to walk too far," Ms. Busch said. One of the most aggressive commercial sites, eDiets.com, has offered nutrition, exercise and motivation advice for two years. It is fairly typical of the online diets. New users, who sign up for $70, are asked to fill out a simple profile, on topics like binge eating, desired weight loss and amount of exercise they get. That results in a computer-generated schedule for weight loss: a 12-week plan, with meal plans and shopping lists, that is adjusted to reflect the diet's progress, reported weekly. EDiets, based in Florida, has had about 50,000 paying customers in two years, the company says. Its chairman, David Humble, said he turned to the Net when he discovered that it offered an opportunity "to change lifestyle as opposed to a quick diet that inevitably doesn't work in the long term." The company has a dozen employees, including dietitians and psychologists, and sends out free newsletters by email to 700,000 subscribers. EDiets offers "the general supervision of the dietitian, but not the one-on-one with a dietitian," Mr. Humble said, adding: "But also not the costs associated with that. Three months of supervision online costs less probably than a single visit to a dietitian off line." The company says active participants report losing 1.8 pounds a week; at that rate, members should reach a goal of losing 20 pounds in three months, a period that dietitians say is long enough for behavior changes to become ingrained, and for people to determine why they had a problem in the first place. Women from 25 to about 50 make up the largest group of users of the site, but eDiets is also trying to develop special areas for men, vegetarians and people with specialized diets. The company says it tries to screen people whose health makes online dieting unwise, including those with diabetes. With the benefit of anonymity, people can confide the fears that keep them from succeeding. Cyberdiet.com, based in California, insists that it is not primarily a diet program, because that "means you are either on something or off something," said Timi Gustafson, a co-founder. "I don't believe in diets," he said. "I believe in helping people adopt a healthy lifestyle." Cyberdiet offers eight-week weight-loss programs, free, with special menus, in four calorie ranges, modulated for diets those who need to restrict their intakes of sodium, cholesterol, dairy or other foods, and for people with problems like diabetes, hypertension and heart disease. It also has a 12-week exercise program, and workout drills. The free site was started by Ms. Gustafson, a registered dietitian, and Cynthia Fink as something of a public service, and was acquired this year by Mediconsult.com, which provides information online for people affected directly or indirectly by chronic illness. The site has lively message boards. One, for people trying to lose 100 pounds or more, attracts 1,500 messages a week. It is so popular that 40 of the dieters met in Chicago this summer to make friends in person with people they had met online. Another site, eFit.com, offers 30-second video demonstrations of exercises. For now, established weight-loss companies like Jenny Craig and Weight Watchers are not yet jumping into the online market. Both companies have Web sites, but they are mainly informational, used to draw dieters to their established programs. But the success of their online competitors clearly has their attention. Les Koll, senior vice president of marketing at Jenny Craig, said of eDiets, "We are watching them very closely." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Among the most aggressive commercial dieting sites that have sprung up on the Web is eDiets.com. The site offers advice on nutrition, exercise and motivation for a fee.

title:
Metro Business;
Cable TV Group Buys Into Salon.com
body: Rainbow Media Holdings, a subsidiary of Cablevision Systems and the operator of the Bravo cable television network, said yesterday that it would acquire a 10 percent stake in the Internet magazine Salon.com in exchange for 10 years' worth of advertising valued at $12 million. Salon.com will issue 1.11 million common shares, worth about $7.56 million, to Rainbow Media, and will develop a weekly television series to appear on Bravo next year. Its reporters and columnists will appear on three Rainbow channels seen in the newyork area. The deal reflects a growing trend toward alliances among entertainment and Internet companies to add content and sell advertising across different media. Cablevision of Bethpage, N.Y., is the largest cable television company in the newyork metropolitan area. It also operates American Movie Classics and the MSG Network, which features sports events from Madison Square Garden, through Rainbow Media. Salon.com includes columnists like the humorist Garrison Keillor and the feminist writer Camille Paglia on its network of 10 Web sites. The companies will offer advertisers packages of advertisements to be shown on both companies' Web sites and on television, and they will promote each other's sites and exchange programming and news content. Rainbow also holds a controlling stake in Madison Square Garden Properties, which includes the arena, the Theater at Madison Square Garden and the newyork Knicks basketball team and the newyork Rangers hockey team. NBC, a unit of General Electric, owns about 25 percent of Rainbow. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Borders Events to Go Digital In Deal With Net Start-Up
body: Borders.com, the online spinoff of Borders Group, the nation's No. 2 bookseller behind Barnes & Noble, has struck an alliance with an Internet start-up to create virtual entertainment from thousands of author lectures and appearances at Borders bookstores. Called Borders Vision, the bookstore events will become video material for Centerseat, a digital company based in newyork that was founded in the spring and is developing Internet programming that will mix filmed scenes with opportunities to order products. For example, filmed segments of a Borders appearance by J. K. Rowling, the author of the popular Harry Potter children's books, will be shown online along with separate promotions for the books, which can be ordered at the same time. "We're talking about moving the Borders brand name into an entirely new arena," said Rich Fahle, a spokesman for Borders.com. "I don't know where this will go, but we're creating a digital media version of Borders that we're pretty excited about." He estimated that Borders holds as many as 90,000 events featuring authors and artists. Centerseat plans to introduce its new Web site, Centerseat.com, which it calls "an integrated entertainment, information and commerce experience," early next year. Over the last few months, the company has been signing deals with an eclectic assortment of personalities to develop its Internet programming. The Prague Symphony Orchestra and the State Opera of Prague agreed in October to create programming for Centerseat, as did Ken Robinson, host of the Travel Minute radio show. In November, Centerseat announced programming deals with George Hirsch, a chef who was also the host of a series on grilling for PBS, and James Hong, an Asian-American actor who will be the host of a martial arts show and a celebrity cooking show, "In the Kitchen With James Hong." Centerseat was founded by its chief executive, Scott Harmolin, who sold his company, Icon CMT, to Qwest Communications last September in a $185 million stock trade. http://www.nytimes.com

title: AT&T's Move May Provide Sharper View OfLeadership
body: The early jockeying to succeed AT&T's chairman, C. Michael Armstrong, begins in earnest today. At a meeting with hundreds of investors and financial analysts today in newyork, AT&T intends to announce the most sweeping management changes since Mr. Armstrong took over two years ago, according to executives close to the company. Although Mr. Armstrong is only 61, his mandatory retirement at age 65 in four years may not seem so far away for any of the company's senior managers hoping to emerge as his successor. While it is not at all certain that the company will tap an insider to succeed Mr. Armstrong, the company's history suggests that Mr. Armstrong's lieutenants stand an excellent chance to rise to one of the most prominent executive jobs in the world. With today's management announcements, the roster of internal hopefuls will include John D. Zeglis, Daniel E. Somers and Richard R. Roscitt. And it may very likely include Charles H. Noski. Mr. Noski is president of General Motors' Hughes Electronics subsidiary, but is said to be Mr. Armstrong's favorite candidate to become AT&T's chief financial officer. Before joining AT&T, Mr. Armstrong was chairman of Hughes and knew Mr. Noksi there. Late yesterday, AT&T was still negotiating with Mr. Noski, however, and it was unclear whether Mr. Noski and the company would come to terms in time for an announcement today. Separately, in a move intended to mollify its regulatory critics, AT&T also plans to announce an agreement today with Mindspring, the big Internet service provider. The agreement will outline how Mindspring might eventually be able to offer Internet access over AT&T's cable television systems. Until now, AT&T has been criticized for an arrangement that gives the Excite@Home Corporation exclusive access to its cable systems through 2002. The Mindspring agreement lays the groundwork for outside companies to gain such access in the future. In a third announcement, AT&T also intends to say today that it will split off its wireless business as a separately traded tracking stock. That move may include issuing billions of dollars in new shares of the wireless company. A tracking stock is an investment vehicle that can allow big companies to highlight the financial value of a business unit, without relinquishing ownership of that business. Investors in a tracking stock can buy and sell them like regular shares, but the stock does not represent an actual separate ownership stake in the business it tracks. Taken together, the three initiatives represent the latest part of Mr. Armstrong's continuing effort to change AT&T, the nation's No. 1 communications company, from the lumbering long-distance telephone behemoth he inherited to the nimble communications dynamo he envisions. An AT&T spokeswoman declined to comment on the plans. Of the executives involved in the shuffle, Mr. Zeglis, the former lawyer who is AT&T's president, will retain that title while also being named head of the newly separate wireless unit. Mr. Zeglis's main challenges at the wireless unit will be to continue its robust growth and to mount a new initiative to offer Internet access and local phone service to as many as 10 million unitedstates homes using an innovative wireless technology known within AT&T as Project Angel. One person close to the company said on Friday that if Mr. Zeglis succeeds, he could become a shoo-in to succeed Mr. Armstrong. Mr. Somers, currently AT&T's chief financial officer, will be chosen to lead the company's far-flung cable television unit, succeeding Leo Hindery, the former Tele-Communications Inc. executive who recently resigned from AT&T. In moving from a staff job as AT&T's chief financial officer to run the most critical unit for the company's future, the cable business, Mr. Somers could also be seen as trying to burnish his operational credentials. If AT&T's multibillion-dollar cable strategy fails to live up to its promise of offering interactive television, high-speed Internet access and local phone service across the nation, nothing else will be able to bail out the company. Mr. Roscitt, chief executive of AT&T's fast-growing unit that runs networks for the company's largest corporate customers, will be named head of the unit that oversees all the needs of business customers. When Mr. Armstrong arrived at AT&T in the fall of 1997, he did not bring any other senior executives with him. If the company and Mr. Noski come to terms, he would be AT&T's most significant executive hire from outside the company since the arrival of Mr. Armstrong himself. While Mr. Zeglis will initially retain his title as president, his move to the wireless unit and Mr. Somers's move to AT&T's cable headquarters near Denver would seem to vacate duties that might prompt Mr. Armstrong to hire a chief operating officer, executives close to the company said. Those who might be disappointed by today's management announcements would appear to include Daniel Hesse, currently chief executive of AT&T's wireless unit, and Michael Keith, president of AT&T's business services unit. According to executives close to AT&T, Mr. Hesse will report to Mr. Zeglis and will run the wireless unit's consumer segment. Mr. Keith, who is essentially losing his job to Mr. Roscitt, is set to move to the wireless operation, where he will have responsibility for selling wireless services to business customers and for the new residential wireless initiative. Mr. Hesse won praise for basically remaking the wireless business with AT&T's Digital One Rate plan, which eliminates roaming charges and long-distance fees. But his reputation suffered as AT&T consistently underestimated demand for its wireless services in big markets including newyork City, leading to service problems. Mr. Roscitt is a hard-charging executive who colleagues say was enraged last February when he was passed over in favor of Mr. Keith to run the company's business-services unit after the departure of Robert Annunziata in February. According to executives close to the company he has now won the job, at least in part because he put himself in the running for chief executive jobs at other companies, and AT&T did not want to lose him. On a level just below these top management changes, Kathleen B. Earley is set to be announced as AT&T's new "Internet guru," according to an executive close to the company. Ms. Early, currently president of AT&T's Internet division, will assume overall control of the company's diverse data communications operations. http://www.nytimes.com
