title:
Compressed Data;
A Dot-Com Takes Aim At Market for Green Power
body: Add another product to the lengthening list of things you can buy with a mouse click. Now it's green energy: power derived from windmills, solar panels, anything that does not pollute the air. GreenMountain.com plays middleman between wind farms and other clean sources of electricity and consumers who want to feel guilt-free when they flick an electric switch. Its business plan is based on the premise that, given a choice, consumers and businesses will want to buy electricity that was generated in environmentally sound ways. And energy deregulation, which mandates that local utilities will have to deliver power from competing sources across their existing grids, is making that choice now possible. So far, GreenMountain.com, although based in South Burlington, Vt., operates only in Pennsylvania and California, which were among the first states to embrace deregulation. But it has its eye on New Jersey for next year, and is ready to mount marketing blitzes as other states deregulate. Hence, the dot-com label, which the company adopted last year, changing its name from Green Mountain Energy Resources. It wants to do most of its selling, billing and customer communication through its Web site, and the old name did not create that visceral pull that prompts customers to log on. "We wanted to signal that we are a modern company that's using the most efficient and environmentally friendly means to do all our business," Dennis Kelly, the company's chief executive, said. CLAUDIA H. DEUTSCH http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
A Pet Site That Wants To Know All About Your Dog
body: Consumers wary of the information that Web sites gather about them have one more reason to lose sleep: an Internet company now wants to compile dossiers on their dogs. PogoPet.com, which rolled out last week, is the latest entrant in the increasingly cluttered category of pet Web sites. The difference between this venture and its competitors, company executives say, is that PogoPet will compile personal data on a pet owner's dog or cat and use it to deliver information tailored to that pet. "I have a Labrador, and I sometimes forget to administer heartworm pills, and I feel a lot of anxiety and guilt about it," said Stacey Estrella, PogoPet's chief executive. Ms. Estrella said the site, which serves only dog and cat owners, would ease such worries by sending email reminders about a pet's medical needs. Of course, to avail themselves of such services, consumers must first provide some information, including the age, breed and favorite activities of the pets. PogoPet never shares personally identifiable data about a user's pets others, Ms. Estrella said, and will instead deliver advertisements on behalf of marketers while keeping the user's identity secret. It is a policy that will doubtlessly go far to placate owners -- not to mention some dogs who may not want to go public with that pesky halitosis problem. BOB TEDESCHI http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Personal messages for dogs and cats.

title:
E-Commerce;
For the employer, theprocrastinator and, of course, the merchant: online holiday gift certificates.
body: TO some, gift certificates represent a cop-out on the part of gift givers -- a way to foist the shopping responsibility onto the recipient. To others, they are the ideal gift -- subsidized shopping that spares others the guilt and drudgery of returning something they hate. And for e-commerce executives, gift certificates are one more way to seize a greater share of the holiday-shopping dollar from traditional stores. At least half a dozen Web-based ventures have been rolled out in recent months, whose sole purpose is to sell gift certificates. Around the same time, Internet retailers are hastening to offer their own electronic versions of gift certificates. Helping propel the trend, executives say, is the immediate gratification provided by the Internet. "People who are online want instant feedback," said Tracy Wan, president of the Sharper Image Corporation, which plans to begin offering digital gift certificates on its site today. "They don't want to pick something out, get it wrapped, call someone up and actually walk it over," Ms. Wan said. "And people who receive one online can apply it instantaneously." Online gift certificates are nothing if not fast. At Amazon.com and Buy.com as well as Sharper Image, buyers can have a certificate emailed to the recipient, complete with a brief message, within hours. The recipient can then redeem it at the site by using the certificate number listed in the email message. Flooz.com, a Web-based start-up, also offers this sort of speed. It sells a kind of scrip that is the equivalent of a gift certificate for customers to use instantly with its Internet merchant partners, including Fogdog Sports and Babystyle.com. So far, though, many online retailers do not have the technology to send gift certificates electronically. Rather, they typically sell traditional gift certificates online, then mail them to recipients, who can redeem them online or offline, depending on the retailer's policy. And a new Internet business category has emerged in connection with this process: gift certificate stores. Companies like Giftpoint .com and GiftCertificates.com allow shoppers to buy certificates from hundreds of merchants in categories ranging from cigars to restaurants, and have the certificates packaged in a variety of ways. On GiftCertificates.com, for instance, a standard holiday card to accompany the gift certificate is free, while fancier cards cost $2.50, and gift boxes cost $6.95. The company also offers a so-called super certificate, which the recipient can redeem for a gift certificate at any of the site's merchant partners. Jonas Lee, chief executive of GiftCertificates.com, said the company purchases the gift certificates at wholesale prices, then sells them at face value to customers. In an effort to distinguish itself from the thousands of other dot.com advertisers shouting from the airwaves in the next few weeks, Mr. Lee said his company would spend $9 million this holiday season in radio and print ads. Sophia Loren has agreed to act as the site's spokeswoman for several years -- in exchange for an equity stake in the company. "Everything I've been doing for two-and-a-half years leads up to the next 30 days," said Mr. Lee, who expects more than $20 million in sales this season. "To me, this is it." If companies like Mr. Lee's are to achieve sustained growth, they will have to overcome competition from an unlikely source -- their merchant partners, who are forging ahead with their own efforts in electronic gift certificates. Retailers like SharperImage.com and OmahaSteaks.com are happy to get additional gift certificate sales through GiftCertificates.com and its ilk. But if they can email their own certificates and allow them to be redeemed at their own Web sites, they can avoid selling them at a discount through the wholesalers. "It's an issue of customer service as well as an effort to capture that piece of the business that others are capturing," Ms. Wan of Sharper Image said of her company's new virtual gift certificate service. Ms. Wan, whose company still sells paper gift certificates through GiftCertificates.com and Giftpoint.com, said setting up its own online delivery and redemption system was "not a huge issue." It mainly involved integrating the accounting and processing structure that already exists offline with the new online certificates. The process took less than 60 days and cost less than $100,000, she said. Industry analysts and executives said that gift certificates benefited retailers in other ways. First, they cut down on returns, as people select only items they want. Gift certificates also offer retailers the chance to draw interest on the shopper's money, as there is typically a lag between the time the certificate is bought and when merchandise leaves the store. And there's another big bonus for the retailer: Recipients often spend less than the face value of the gift certificates -- or fail to redeem them at all. "That's sort of the dirty little secret of gift certificates," said Ken Cassar, a Jupiter Communications analyst. As for consumer acceptance of online gift certificates, "there's certainly a heavy demand in the offline world," said Mr. Cassar, noting that gift certificates represent 3 percent of conventional retail sales. "In the next year or two, consumers will gravitate toward proprietary gift certificates because that's what they're used to," he said. "But in the long term, the potential is with the networks," Mr. Cassar said, alluding to the gift certificate sites that sell on behalf of several retailers. "They offer far more utility, because you can redeem them at a number of merchants." Perhaps the real long-term opportunity in the gift certificate category is with businesses, not consumers. According to Doug Nielsen, chief executive of Giftpoint.com, businesses buy about half of the $15 billion spent on gift certificates each year to give to employees, clients and suppliers. "They prefer to give gift certificates instead of cash because they know the person won't blow it on the light bill," he remarked. To capture that market, Mr. Nielsen built a corporate sales team, and created customized Web pages on his site for corporate clients. "This is going to be a building process," he said. "We know it will take awhile." In the next few weeks, though, executives expect gift certificates to be the province of the last-minute shopper. "They're fabulous because you can give a gift literally at the last minute and still come out looking good," said Todd Simon, senior vice president of Omaha Steaks. Mr. Simon said Omaha Steaks.com would have electronic gift certificates on the site early next year, but for now offers paper certificates through several gift certificate sites. "It's a great last-minute gift opportunity that hasn't existed before," he said. Ms. Wan of Sharper Image agreed. "You could do it on Dec. 25 if you wanted, although you might have to give $100 instead of $50," she said, alluding to the guilt premium that the late giver might feel impelled to pay. "But it's the thought that counts, right?" http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Todd Simon, senior vice president of Omaha Steaks, which is currently using paper certificates available from gift sites and expects to have online certificates early in 2000. (Kent Sievers for The newyork Times)

title:
Media Talk;
Entertainment Web Site Will Offer News Hybrid
body: Financial news and information sells on the Web, but can entertainment news sell, too? Today, a handful of magazine-industry expatriates will announce the plans for their new Web venture, Powerful Media, a company that has attracted advance attention because its founders are from the core of Manhattan's ever-churning, self-scrutinizing media world. Kurt Andersen, former editor in chief of newyork magazine, and Michael Hirschorn, former editor in chief of Spin, will serve as co-chairmen. Deanna Brown, former publisher of Brill's Content, is chief executive; James Cramer, co-founder of TheStreet.com is a financial backer. They have lured their staff -- with the promise of ample salaries and stock options -- from the ranks of Variety, The Wall Street Journal and ESPN.com, among others. Powerful Media will produce a Web site that "is neither a conventional consumer magazine, nor a straightforward trade publication, but combines the virtues of both," Mr. Andersen said, adding that it will offer frequently updated, comprehensive news about the entertainment and media industries, along with longer pieces about, well, powerful media. The site, founded on a $5 million cash infusion from the venture capital firm Flatiron Partners, has 15 employees now and expects to have 50 editorial staff members in newyork and Los Angeles by its spring start-up, Ms. Brown said. Mr. Andersen said parts of the site will be free; others will require a subscription fee. The site's premise, he said, is that "at this moment and obviously for some time to come, that all these worlds of entertainment are morphing together and interconnecting and merging, so people who are in books need to know about movies, and people in movies need to know about music, and bringing a global authoritative intelligence to those realms seems like an intelligent thing to do." Mr. Andersen added that while the trade publications report deals, they rarely assign investigative pieces, which Powerful Media will assign -- along with the constantly updated flow of information. How large is the market of media insiders and fanatics? About 100,000, the site's founders say. Mark Mooradian, a media analyst with Jupiter Communications, said rapidly updated information is a hot commodity in the entertainment community. "The sooner you have information in those industries, the better," Mr. Mooradian said. Variety, The Hollywood Reporter, Advertising Age, Publishers Weekly and other trade publications do have Web sites. "But they are not moving at Internet pace right now," he said. "Their offerings are clearly offshoots of their traditional publications." He said, however, once they sense a new competitor, "I would think they would mobilize rather quickly." Peter Bart, editor in chief of Variety, was unperturbed by the news. "I feel that to succeed with that game plan would require such an enormous staff -- and a sophisticated staff -- that it is way beyond their resources," he said. "I think what they are going to do, frankly, is make big promises, and strike out." ALEX KUCZYNSKI http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Kurt Andersen will be co-chairman of an entertainment news Web site. (Ozier Muhammad/The newyork Times)

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Enforcer for the Electronic Marketplace
body: The market for selling merchandise over the Internet -- everything from books and CD's to groceries and Pokemon toys -- is already well established as e-tailers head into what is expected to be a pivotal holiday season. But many analysts expect that 2000 will see huge growth in another kind of electronic commerce -- all-digital products like documents, recorded music and videos that exist only as computer files and are delivered directly from a Web site to the consumer's hard drive. J. P. Morgan Securities, for one, predicts that the market for digital content will reach $275 billion by 2003. One company well positioned to capitalize on that market is the InterTrust Technologies Corporation of Santa Clara, Calif., whose initial public offering in October was one of the year's hot Internet issues. The company specializes in technology that protects the copyrights of digital content by preventing illegal copying. It also tracks the material's distribution and manages the finances involved in buying and selling it. Although InterTrust's products are still in the testing phase, the company already has deals with media heavyweights like the largest record company, Seagram's Universal Music Group, and the storage media division of Bertelsmann A.G., which manufactures CD's and CD-ROM's. Both have agreed to use InterTrust software to protect various kinds of digital material from being illegally copied. And its deals with content providers have led to complementary agreements with companies like MusicMatch, Diamond Multimedia and Creative Labs that sell software or portable devices for playing digital music. Initially, much of the demand for InterTrust's products has been driven by the recording industry, whose urgent concerns about music piracy on the Internet led to the formation early this year of the Secure Digital Music Initiative. S.D.M.I. aims to produce universal standards for preventing the pirating of digital music, and it says it will not endorse any single proprietary technology. Even so, InterTrust is an active member of S.D.M.I., and its technology is widely expected to play a leading role in the music industry. Still, InterTrust faces stiff competition. The company's activities in the digital music market, for example, put it on a collision course with other popular music-management technologies, including Liquid Audio, and with Microsoft's Windows Media Audio compression format. In the document-publishing market, InterTrust will be bumping up against giants like Xerox, which has introduced a digital-rights management system based on Java, and Hewlett-Packard, which plans its own document-management effort. And several niche companies have developed their own protection plans. But Victor Shear, InterTrust's chief executive, predicts that his company's broad array of patents, coupled with its focus solely on digital-rights management, will enable it to take on all comers. "It is an area that requires a huge amount of single-minded focus," Mr. Shear said. "Having it as a side project or add-ons or dependent on other agendas will not allow for an efficient system." Moreover, InterTrust derives power from its partnerships, as indicated by the contracts with Bertelsmann and Universal. Each company has promised to designate InterTrust's products as its preferred digital-rights management technology and to promote its adoption by other companies. Those deals "put it in position to dominate the digital distribution space for the major labels," Aram Sinnreich, an analyst at Jupiter Communications, said. Such prospects might seem unusual, given that InterTrust's products have yet to be tested in the marketplace. But InterTrust's partners say its technology is particularly attractive. "What InterTrust does is facilitate business models we find very advantageous as a content company," said Larry Kenswil, president of global commerce and advanced technology at Universal.  "What we've liked about them from the beginning is that they thought long and hard about how people do business." Johann Butting, chief executive of Bertelsmann's unit for digital rights management, praised InterTrust technology for working across all the company's media products. "We will go to great lengths to have as few platforms as possible," he said, "and will try to get our clients to use InterTrust." Bertelsmann is also one of the world's leading publishers of books and magazines, and its record label, BMG, is second only to Universal in market share. The BMG division has not yet signed a deal with InterTrust, but analysts and industry executives say a deal may be imminent, given InterTrust's relationship with Bertelsmann. On the manufacturing side, InterTrust recently signed a deal with Cirrus Logic to build security directly into chips for portable music players, cell phones, hand-held devices and home stereos. InterTrust's digital commerce system, known as the MetaTrust Utility, packages content with rules governing its usage in encrypted files known as DigiBoxes, which can be downloaded from Web sites or passed among friends. To open a DigiBox file, a user must install InterTrust's InterRights Point Software, to be distributed by content companies. The user's credit card information is locked into the software, and payments, specified by the usage rules of the DigiBox, are automatically deducted. Managing payments and tracking use falls to third-party clearinghouses. National Westminster, Mitsubishi and Reciprocal are among the companies that have signed on as clearinghouses. One of InterTrust's major challenges will be to maintain the security of its system. InterTrust executives acknowledge that like any such system, their security is not perfect. But they expect it to be robust enough to prevent widespread piracy. Currently, InterTrust earns revenue only from licensing fees and software support. But in the future, the company expects that its main revenue will come from a fee ranging from 0.6 percent to 2 percent for each transaction using InterTrust technology. InterTrust closed at $149.6875 on Friday, more than eight times its offering price of $18 in October. In the quarter ended Sept. 30, the company had revenue of $363,000 and an operating loss of 25 cents a share. J. P. Morgan, which lists the stock as a buy, expects total revenue for 1999 to be $1.4 million and that InterTrust will become profitable in late 2001. One potential hazard is growing concern about online abuses of consumer privacy. InterTrust's technology enables publishers to collect usage data on protected content. While InterTrust does not collect this data directly, it does collect fees each time one of its partners sells demographic information. "If they want to collect information for sale, our only requirement is that they tell users what they're doing," David Van Wie, InterTrust's international chairman, said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Victor Shear, InterTrust chief executive, says the company's patents will enable it to dominate what could be a very competitive market. (Thor Swift for The newyork Times)

title: Web Domain to Be Assigned For PalestinianTerritory
body: Palestine, still struggling for international recognition as an independent state, will soon gain official status of another sort with the designation of its own piece of real estate in cyberspace. The Internet's international coordinating authority, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, said on Friday that it had received and expected to grant an application to give the Palestinian National Authority its own two-letter suffix, or domain, on the Internet. The domain -- .ps -- would enable the Palestinian group to register Internet addresses like, say, yasirarafat.gov.ps. The .ps domain will join the list of the 243 so-called country-code domains that have already been assigned to countries and territories around the world. It will be the first new domain added to the Internet since administration of its addressing, or domain name system, was handed last year from federal contractors to the private, nonprofit Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, widely known as Icann. The Commerce Department, which is overseeing the transition to private administration of the Internet, would have to give the final approval to the addition of .ps to the Internet's address system. But people close to the process said the department was not expected to block it. The Palestinian application is not complete. But Michael M. Roberts, Icann's president, said he expected the process and final approval to be completed soon. Icann officials declined on Friday to identify the person whose name was listed on the application without the applicant's permission. But people close to the process indicated it was an official in Yasir Arafat's Palestinian National Authority. Clinton administration officials were hesitant to discuss the pending application. But Mr. Roberts said there would be no basis for turning it down. Middle East politics aside, he said, Palestine has been added to the United Nation's list of country codes that is used for assigning telephone area codes. In the past, the telephone list was used by the late Jon Postel, one of the Internet's founding fathers and the original administrator of its numbering system, as a guide for granting Internet country codes. Mr. Postel had said that he had specifically chosen that list to keep politics out of his process for deciding what constituted an official country or geographical territory. "We don't regard this as a controversial issue," Mr. Roberts said. "The delegation of a country code does not create a political weapon. All it does is create a way for names to be assigned within that top level domain." He said, however, that it does emphasize the need for Icann to begin formulating uniform rules for the two-letter country codes. Until now, Icann's focus has been on introducing competition in the lucrative business of registering domain names in the popular and largely commercial international domains of .com, .net and .org. It has also adopted policies for resolving disputes over trademarks used as words to identify those domains. Mr. Roberts said the .ps application, as well as indications by the European Union that it would seek to get a regional .eu domain, had emphasized the need to focus on the country code issues. The delegation of country codes in the past was handled strictly by Mr. Postel, who in most cases gave the codes to the corresponding countries, but in some instances gave them to commercial or academic interests. "Postel made some very pragmatic decisions about how to get the Internet going in certain countries," Mr. Roberts said. "There's not a lot of bureaucratic consistency there." Although Icann and the Clinton administration were initially hesitant about the politics of granting Palestine its own country code, Peter Dengate-Thrush, a New Zealand trademark attorney and active member of Icann's constituency of country code interests, said there had been no opposition that he had seen in the Internet community. He noted that countries like Libya had their own codes. And territories like American Samoa and land masses such as Antarctica also have independent Internet designation. And Mr. Roberts said Israel had long had its own active domain. Still, Mr. Dengate-Thrush acknowledged: "Diplomats often look to strange symbols. But all they're doing is creating a domain space that will add efficiency to the Internet." But he agreed with Mr. Roberts that establishing policy guidelines for country code domains is the most pressing issue Icann faces. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Computer Doctors Who Make House Calls
body: INEVITABLY, whenever Sydney Stanton's children and grandchildren come to visit the same thing happens. "After they leave, my computer is not the same," she said. "They change everything around. This last time I couldn't find my address book." It is not that Ms. Stanton's children are computer incompetents. On the contrary, her son runs a computer graphics business in London, and her granddaughter is a science journalist. Ms. Stanton, a freelance writer in Rye Brook, is also computer competent, yet when faced with a recalcitrant computer and a deadline, she puts in an emergency call to the Computer Tutor-PCI in Bronxville. "Within two hours Rick Harder arrived and fixed everything," she said. "He specializes in Macintosh, so when I needed a new modem, he helped me select it, and he installed it. I call him my computer doctor." But unlike most doctors, these computer specialists make house calls. Jim Mulcahy, the company president, and Mr. Harder, his associate, call on customers in their office on wheels, a black sedan with the company's logo and a license plate that Mr. Mulcahy is especially fond of: C DRIVE. But fixing computer problems is only one of the things Computer Tutor does. The company offers clients a full range of services, from helping them buy the right computer to teaching them how to use it. Ann Petersen of Bronxville was not exactly computer challenged either. She was comfortable doing word processing on her Macintosh, but she and her husband, Hollis, are inveterate travelers, and when she wanted to go on the Internet to search the Web for travel and tourist information, she had to upgrade. "I was frantic that I'd lose all my data when I upgraded from Mac to a PC," she said. "But Jim did it for me without a hitch. Then with Jim I upgraded again, to Windows 98 and gave my hand-me-downs to my husband." Not long ago, she explained, her husband was happy with only his typewriter. "He didn't want anything to do with a computer," she said. "Then, surprisingly, when I gave him my old Mac, he was happy with it -- for a while." Eventually, she said, Mr. Petersen became so enamored with the capabilities of her PC that he was spending more and more time at her computer researching the stock market. "I could never get on the Internet," she recalled. "In the interest of saving our marriage, we got a second PC, and it was easy -- no tears -- with Jim's help." Help, priced by Mr. Mulcahy, is $75 an hour in Westchester south of Route 287, then it increases to $90 north of Route 287. Calls to Manhattan or up to Westport in Fairfield County are billed at $100. Mr. Mulcahy said that one of the most important services his company provides is very basic. "We start at the beginning by helping people buy their computers from one of the big mail-order houses," he said. "It's done via a three-way conversation lasting from 45 to 60 minutes. We ask a lot of questions, quizzing the customer carefully, so we can advise him on what is right for him. Then we call Dell or Gateway or Compaq and place the order for the computer, which will come in approximately 15 percent less than buying it retail at a store." The growth of the computer mail-order business has been so strong it has caused upsets among major retailers like CompUSA, based in Dallas, to cut down on hardware inventory and close some of its stores, Mr. Mulcahy said. "Rick and I both worked at CompUSA in Norwalk," he said. "And we saw a lot of customers who were very new to computers and needed a lot more than the technical information we could give them on the selling floor. People didn't know much about installation, and they certainly didn't know how to solve the problems that occur two or three months down the road." Mr. Mulcahy said he felt he had discovered a niche that had the potential for a business. He reasoned that his service would have to be mobile, since on-the-spot repairs were essential. He forged ahead, financing the startup with credit cards in the amount of $8,000. The business turned a profit in the first year, encouraging him to expand. Mr. Harder, a graphics artist, and an Apple expert, joined him as an associate. Ideally, tutoring starts shortly after the computer has been delivered. Home-based offices account for about 70 percent of Computer Tutor's business. About half the company's customers are people older than 50, including several clients in their 80's and a woman older than 90 who wanted "to keep up with the times." Not everyone who telephones can become a Computer Tutor client, however. "We ask questions," Mr. Mulcahy said. "And not everyone qualifies." For example, people like the man who wanted to activate his son's computer, abandoned 10 years ago. "We tell him, It's not worth it," Mr. Mulcahy said. For on-the-spot software repairs, he uses a $40 set of computer tools, but he emphasized, "I make most repairs using what's in my head, not the tools." Hardware is another story. "We don't do it, but we arrange for the computer to be picked up and delivered," Mr. Mulcahy said. And for the problems that cannot be solved, Mr. Mulcahy will call manufacturers' help lines himself. "There's a reason we recommend companies like Dell and Compaq," he said. "They have good technical support, and we can always reach them on the phone." Business is 80 percent repeat, the majority of customers like the Petersens coming from recommendations from friends. "I saw the car outside a neighbor's house," Mrs. Petersen said. "When I checked it out, my neighbor gave the service very high marks. I agree.  Without my upgrade I never would have found a two-day excursion in Burgundy, called France in a Glass, on the Internet. We took it, and it was wonderful. With Jim Mulcahy on call, I'm becoming a computer whiz, and it's a lot of fun." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Rick Harder, left, and Jim Mulcahy of Computer Tutor-PCI, above, who fix computer problems at clients' homes. Mr. Mulcahy getting his equipment out of his car. (Photographs by Rebecca Cooney for The newyork Times)

title: County Arms Itself to Battle Internet's Messengers of Hate
body: AT first glance, it looks like any other Web site aimed at children. Big, colorful letters spell out "Kids." Children are welcomed and told to "feel free to take a look around and have fun." Activities are offered, including coloring and crossword puzzles. But a closer look at the word clues for the puzzles reveals a sinister agenda: Four across: "Your first (blank) belongs to the White Race. Nine across: Racial Loyalty is the (blank) to our racial survival. Fourteen across: Equality among the Races is a (blank). Fifteen down: The (blank) are the deadliest enemies of the White Race. The answers to those clues -- given on another page of the children's site -- are as follows: loyalty, key, myth and Jews. The games are part of a Web site (www.wcotc.com/ kids) of the World Church of the Creator, one of more than 2,000 sites run by extremist groups. The ending of the welcome message to children says, "Have Fun! RAHOWA," which another page explains is an acronym for racial holy war. The children are also offered a shooting game -- by clicking on a linked site -- which shows visuals of the Pope being blasted full of holes by rifle shots. Still another site offers a point system for killings -- the highest level obtainable is that of an Aryan warrior. These Internet sites may have been created thousands of miles away. But the World Church of the Creator, based in Peoria, Ill., as well as the National Alliance, a neo-Nazi group with headquarters in Hillsboro, W.Va., are both known to have members here in Westchester, according to local law-enforcement officials. Recruiting by the extremist groups -- as well as their potential to spread propaganda and incite violence among children and adults -- has increased exponentially with their presence on the Internet, presenting new challenges to the county's effort to combat hate crimes locally. In an attempt to keep abreast of the latest tactics in fighting bias crimes and to pool resources with others around the unitedstates, County Executive Andrew J. Spano recently sent a team of county law-enforcement officials to the National Institutes Against Hate Crimes training seminar at the Simon Wiesenthal Center in Los Angeles, an international Jewish human rights organization dedicated to preserving the memory of the Holocaust and fostering tolerance. Since its return, the delegation has been working closely with the county executive to develop a comprehensive plan to fight hatred. "Our zero-tolerance attitude toward hate crime in Westchester County is just the beginning," Mr. Spano said. "I have always believed that the Internet is a powerful tool to bring people together and to govern. But these Web sites are the flip side of that power. We haven't been devoid of programs for hate crimes in Westchester County. But we need everyone involved in a coordinated, holistic program." The team that trained in Los Angeles included District Attorney Jeanine Pirro, Deputy County Attorney Kathie Davidson, Judge Anthony A. Scarpino Jr. of State Supreme Court in White Plains and representatives from the county's Probation and Public Safety Departments. Mr. Spano will coordinate the new program and will also continue to lobby for a hate crimes bill, legislation that would prescribe tougher penalties for bias-related offenses. newyork is one of nine states without such a law. Mrs. Pirro, who in 1997 established a hate crimes unit in her office, said that pushing for a hate crimes bill would also be a priority for her. She said the hate crimes unit is constantly busy. "We've seen explosions in Westchester," Mrs. Pirro said. "We've seen stabbings. We've seen people assaulted. We've seen people who just open their own door and have someone say to them, 'I don't like people like you living in my country. Go back to where you came from.' This is a real problem, and it is not something that we're anticipating. It is something that we have to deal with today." Last month, arrests were made in Ardsley after anti-Semitic messages were sent on the Internet to local high school students. Other incidents in Westchester include the arrest of aLewisboro man who had spray-painted swastikas on a Pound Ridge house (the police later found a 12-inch pipe bomb and bomb making equipment in the defendant's home), the arrest of a Dobbs Ferry man who had drawn a swastika and the initials "W.A.R.," said to stand for White Aryan Resistance, on a building there and the spraying of the phrases "Kill All Jews" and "Holocaust in Orienta" on houses in that Mamaroneck neighborhood. Though the cases of anti-Semitism received the greatest attention, the district attorney's office has many cases pending that concern race and sexual orientation as well as religion. Law-enforcement officials say that fighting hate crimes is different from combatting other types of crime. First, the criminals themselves are different, in that they often do not believe that they are doing anything wrong. Mrs. Pirro said: "With hate crimes and domestic terrorism, the person believes he is of a superior race or a superior religion. Therefore, there is no gap between his values and his ethics. They believe that what they're doing is right, and they will do it again. It's a unique kind of crime and a unique kind of criminal." And because of the proliferation of extremist Web sites, local law-enforcement officials must combat in Westchester what is being encouraged from afar. "When you think of the 150 million to 200 million people on line, you get an idea of the potential for propaganda," said Mark Weitzman, director of the Wiesenthal Center's Task Force Against Hate and a speaker at the conference. "Extremists can now go literally from their own home, where they don't have to expose their own identity. They can pretend to be whoever or whatever they want to be, and they don't have to run the risk of losing their jobs or taking their hoods off during a demonstration. Yet they can reach into any school, any home, to any child's mind that is online." The team tackling the problem includes not only the executive branch of county government with its prosecutorial staff, probation officers and public safety officials but also the judicial branch. Judge Scarpino said that he hopes to teach others about what he learned during the training. "The courts have to be ready to adjudicate these matters," he said. "When they have these cases coming in front of them, they have to have the background to understand what is going on and the depth of the problems that are out there." Probation officials are considering new types of sentencing options, which may include community service with the groups at which the defendant's hatred was aimed. Programs that teach tolerance to elementary and middle school children are another part of the approach. Westchester was the first county in newyork, New Jersey or Connecticut to send a team to Los Angeles. The travel expenses of the participants were subsidized by the Wiesenthal Center, which received a $1 million grant from the federal Justice Department to conduct the seminars. As they work on new strategies, the team will also be able to continue to use the center's Web site, where local law-enforcement officials can compare notes with others nationwide and contribute to a shared database of hate-crime information. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
IN PERSON;
A Cyber Cop Who Slams Back
body: IRREVERENT yet strict, just over six feet tall and husky, Mark Herr is the hockey-playing anti-nerd who created the state's first precinct of cyber cops to patrol the Internet. No pocket protector on the 41-year-old Mr. Herr, an assistant state attorney general and director of the division of consumer affairs. He is known as a hacker for two reasons: the way he takes down Net criminals and ice hockey opponents alike. "I play to win," Mr. Herr said in a recent interview. "I am not a physical person by nature, not a touchy-feely person. On the other hand, I have no problem slugging someone on the ice." He also has no fear of hauling frauds into court. Since being appointed by Governor Whitman 1994, Mr. Herr has pioneered lawsuits against all sorts of frauds on and off the Internet. He has brought suit in Superior Court against 20 telephone companies -- including the Heartline Company of Texas and the National Accounts Company of New Jersey -- for the practice of fraudulently switching customers from one company to another, called slamming. To date, more than $1 million in restitution and $1 million in penalties have been collected, he said, and more cases are pending. In addition, he has filed a suit -- still pending -- against Coral Communications of Florida for adding charges to bills for service a customer has not ordered, known as cramming. And currently he is developing a suit against a public utility board -- he will not say which one -- for "energy slamming." With a staff of more than 500 of various racial and ethnic backgrounds, Mr. Herr has also implemented an Hispanic Outreach Program, working with Latino newspapers and translating Consumer Affairs information into Spanish. Still, Mr. Herr is best known in political circles for creating in 1994 the post of Internet police officer, who works under the Division of Consumer Affairs. He reasoned that residents of New Jersey -- who spend much of their time commuting to newyork and Philadelphia -- would find the Internet irresistibly convenient for shopping, banking and financial trading. Yet those same conveniences would also make e-buyers in the state easy prey for online charlatans, especially during the holiday shopping season. "I think you really had to have your head in a bucket not to realize that e-commerce and the Internet were going to be a big deal," Mr. Herr said. "Looking at what we had, I decided we wanted to be out in front of the wave rather than drown in it." At the time, he said, his colleagues in the attorney general's office did a lot of "eye rolling" but went along with his plans with an air of amused tolerance. "After last Christmas and the explosion of e-commerce and the resulting fraud that has sprung up," he said, "they see where I was going." Mr. Herr went on: "Crimes on the Net went from piddling chain letter scams to big-time fraud almost overnight. It's the holidays and of course I want to believe in the inherent goodness of people, but I know that out there on the bell curve of humanity are a certain percentage of dirt balls trying to rip people off. I'm here to stop them." From former neighbors in Hopewell to the parents of the children he coaches in ice hockey to colleagues, the book on Mr. Herr is fairly consistent: like him or not, people say Mr. Herr is driven, honest -- and a little dangerous. "He left a good impression on Hopewell," said Linda Hellfish, Borough Council secretary. "I never hear a bad word about him, but I did hear he had a lot of energy. He was very passionate and got very involved while he was here." Raymond Disch, a Democrat who served with the staunchly Republican Mr. Herr on the Borough Council, said that while they had their differences, it was difficult not to like his fellow councilman. "He has a view of politics that is twisted in a good way," said Mr. Disch, who runs Power Works Energy Consultants in Trenton and lives in Hopewell. "I think his humor was wasted on the bureaucracy. He should make a career as a TV pundit." A fellow hockey coach and Princeton resident, Nick Hare, characterized the act of interviewing Mr. Herr as "very brave." "He's nonstop," Mr. Hare said. "He's coaching four teams right now." Despite his John Wayne-like passion for justice and rounding up the bad guys, Mark Herr did not start out to be a cyber cop. At the age of 41, Mr. Herr's career and life choices have been an odd mixture of religion, journalism, law and politics. He is a fan of Jimmy Buffett and has a soft spot for his lumbering, 100-pound golden retriever named Tort. Born in Newark as the eldest of three children, he comes from five generations of Presbyterian ministers, which he says gives him "the blessing of hundreds of years of repression." For his part, Mr. Herr is a deacon at the Nassau Presbyterian Church in Princeton, and his children sing in the choir when not being terrors on the ice. "When God is the family business, everything else seems really lightweight," he joked. His mother died in 1986 and his father, the Rev. Ernest Herr of Belle Harbor, N.Y., ran the King's Lawn Presbyterian Church in Brooklyn until retiring in 1989. His brother and sister both live in Dallas; his brother went into the pizza business, and his sister became a wife and mother. "I wanted to make a difference and I agreed with my father, who always told us that regular people have a better chance at influencing those around them than ministers," he said. "They lead by example in a normal life instead of being a minister where everyone expects you to be perfect all the time. There's a lot of pressure in ministering." At first, Mr. Herr chose to pursue a career in journalism. After graduating from Colgate in 1979, he earned a master's degree at the Columbia University School of Journalism in 1982. He worked for newspapers in New Jersey, and was the State House bureau chief for the United Press International until 1985. "I got tired of standing out in the freezing cold to ask people questions for stories that didn't really matter or make much of a difference," Mr. Herr said. "The outdoors is not my thing anyway." In 1985, he became a speechwriter for Gov. Thomas H. Kean and at the same time attended night school at Seton Hall University Law School. He earned his law degree in 1990. "My wife will tell you that the two best words in the English language are juris doctor because when parties change over it means you have a real job and real skills and can do something socially useful with yourself if politics is not an option at that point," Mr. Herr said. Mr. Herr then went to work for Cohen, Shapiro, Polisher, Shiekman and Cohen, a law firm in Lawrenceville, until being appointed to his current post in 1994. Through all the career changes one constant has remained -- hockey. All his adult life he has skated on amateur teams, coaching children's leagues and raising his two daughters and two sons to be lean, mean hockey machines. His wife, Rachel, an accountant, is also no stranger to politics. She filled her husband's unexpired term as a Republican council member in Hopewell Borough, which he had to vacate upon accepting his appointment. "It was a good experience over all, but I did spend the term getting screamed at once a month and learned about small-town politics," Mrs. Herr said. The following year she ran for the same seat, but lost to her Democratic opponent. "Mark is the better politician," she conceded. Mrs. Herr added: "He would love to be running for Congress right now, but it was a family decision not to, because we could never afford to raise four children on what he would make. The children and how they are brought up are the most important thing in the world to Mark." As assistant attorney general and director of the Division of Consumer Affairs, Mr. Herr earns $96,000 a year As a congressman he would earn $130,000 yearly but would have to support an additional residence in Washington and pay commuting costs. "The bottom line is that the cost to the family is too high because in the end I would be missing out on my children's childhoods," Mr. Herr said. "That's too high a price to pay." Mr. Herr and his wife lost one son 1997, shortly before his first birthday because of a birth defect that caused his small intestine to fail. "He was on a respirator and we were asked to make the decision to take him off," Mr. Herr recalled stoically. "They couldn't save him. There was nothing they could do but prolong the wait for a month. It was a choice between letting him stay alive for a month, on machine, or let him go on his own." Sam died in his father's arms shortly after the machines were disconnected. "It's the kind of thing that either breaks you, or in some bizarre way makes you stronger," he said. To handle the crisis, the family took to the local ice rink to skate through their grief. "It was very therapeutic to just keep putting one foot in front of the other over and over, day after day," he said. "Skating is what we all do, so as a family it made perfect sense to mourn that way." As a father he classifies himself as protective rather than prudish for his practice of banning the Internet from his home and limiting television to only a few select programs and music to "oldies only" radio. The one and only computer in the top cyber cop's house is in the kitchen, where it is very public and "a child can't go sneaking off into chat rooms." "I'm an old-fashioned guy and I don't want to find myself explaining things to my 9-year-old daughter that I don't feel comfortable talking about," he said. He then added: "That protectiveness is not dissimilar to my job. The governor has entrusted me with the protection of the people of this state and I take it very seriously." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Mark Herr, who has brought lawsuits against telephone companies for bilking customers, has been policing the Internet for fraud since 1994. (Frank C. Dougherty for The newyork Times)

title:
Journal;
The Strange Legacy of Matt Drudge
body: In a move that would have incited headlines less than two years ago but barely rated column items two weeks ago, Fox News Channel ended the brief TV career of the first New Media journalistic superstar, Matt Drudge, by "mutual consent." Attention should be paid to this cautionary tale, and not for the reasons you might expect. As those whose memories haven't entirely purged Monicagate will recall, Mr. Drudge is the fedora-wearing grandstander whom many, I included, once feared as the Devil of journalism incarnate. He published malicious rumors as fact and, with the new-fangled speed of the Internet at his back, browbeat some insecure Old Media news organizations into repeating them. He hijacked scoops from other reporters. He boasted about his lack of education and his contempt for professional standards. So what if he got some stories wrong, prompting a major defamation suit? He got some big ones -- including The Dress -- right. Likening himself to John Peter Zenger while addressing the cowed mainstream media at the National Press Club, he spoke of how the Internet was "going to save the news business" because "every citizen can be a reporter, can take on the powers that be." Those were fighting words, though they're all but forgotten now, a mere 18 months later. Mr. Drudge's most cherished post-Monica scoop, an alleged Bill Clinton love child, defied his strenuous efforts to make it fly, and drudgereport.com itself now is swamped by other Web sites of partisan gossip and standard news links (witness lucianne.com). When Fox yanked Mr. Drudge's weekly show, he cried censorship (of a fetal photo), but since when does a Rupert Murdoch enterprise muzzle right-wing ideologues? There was no public outcry supporting the defanged Drudge because not enough people cared. Ratings for his show had already fallen by 30 percent. According to Media Metrix, which monitors Web traffic, the Drudge site, which ranked 228 at the time of his Press Club speech, is now at 636. Journalistic watchdogs should be overjoyed at their nemesis' ignominious exit from the tube. We should be thrilled that he no longer has the power to terrorize the nation's news cycles with his apocalyptic bulletins. But the decline in Mr. Drudge's stature is in some ways a barometer of permanent changes in the media culture that may make us look back on his brief reign as national press mascot as a relatively innocent time. Mr. Drudge was in power long enough to change the mainstream press for keeps -- and not for the better. But some of his downfall is due to rapid changes in the press that he didn't see coming, that affect all journalists and news consumers -- and of which he is as much an impotent victim as the rest of us. How he changed the press is self-evident. The elevation of rumor and gossip to news is now ubiquitous in mainstream media; few except professional worrywarts bother to complain any more. No Internet impetus is needed when both TV and print routinely recycle intimations of alleged drug use by George W. Bush without any sourcing (or accusers), and embroider any gun massacre (workplace or school) or celebrity death (such as John Kennedy Jr.'s) with spectacularly entertaining theories before there are facts. We're so inured to speculation in the name of news that it's become a constant white noise. No Matt Drudge, however incendiary his or her own "scoops" may be, could possibly shout loudly enough to be heard over the now-permanent din. But what also hit Mr. Drudge is the historic sea change he thought he could buck: the continued consolidation of news into a handful of huge conglomerates. Whatever errors he made in his Washington coverage, they were nothing compared with his wildly mistaken conviction that any citizen can be a reporter in the new democratic era of the Internet. Even during the short time since Mr. Drudge arrived on the scene, the consolidation of the news business has accelerated (witness the marriage of CBS and Viacom), and the Internet, like every other medium from magazines to broadcast networks, is being annexed too. The Web's most heavily visited news-and-information site is MSNBC. It is not only a consortium of two of the world's largest corporations, Microsoft and General Electric, but it's still growing: it just sealed a major new partnership with The Washington Post and Newsweek (replacing a far less extensive MSNBC alliance with The Times). On the Web, as in other media, MSNBC's closest competitors are such fellow behemoths as Time Warner (CNN) and Disney (ABC, ESPN), and, to a lesser degree, the major national newspapers. Though there are plenty of Drudge wannabes on the Internet gassing on many subjects, people turn to the Big Boys, not amateur citizen reporters, for news. The liveliest independent journalism sites spawned by the Web, such as Salon and Feed, are not so much primary news sources as havens for sharp commentary and analysis, like print magazines such as The newyorker or Harper's. The good news about giant corporations owning most major news operations, whatever the medium, is their resources. If they choose -- and this is a big if in some cases -- they can bankroll the journalistic talent, depth and enterprise to cover non-tabloid stories from Kosovo to Pluto. This is why consumers turn to them, after all, and why their brands mean something. The bad news is that they leave little oxygen for the maverick, independent journalist who really might use the freedom Mr. Drudge talked about to challenge the powers that be. Worse still is the potential for conflicts of interest -- through sins of omission, commission or synergy. Should G.E., Microsoft, Viacom or the rest suppress stories that affect their multitudinous businesses, our press is free in name only. Should such corporations pimp for their own products under the guise of "news," it's not journalism -- it's advertising. How can we tell when these giants are up to no good? We're on our own. Sure, there are press critics calling attention to some of these transgressions, but the circulation of journalism reviews, from Brill's to Columbia's, is modest. Even "The Insider" -- a star-laden, enthusiastically reviewed, widely publicized Hollywood account of the "60 Minutes" capitulation to Big Tobacco -- has failed to catch on. One ominous explanation was offered by a studio executive to Bernard Weinraub of The Times this week: "The fact is, most people . . . assume that the media is corrupted by big business." Do these same people assume that media critics are corrupted? I asked Howard Kurtz, who covers the press for both The Washington Post and CNN, how the public can judge his work given that he is in some way affiliated, thanks to the octopus-like entanglements of his employers, with seemingly half the media outlets he must critique. After noting that he was "uncomfortable" with the new Post-MSNBC alliance because "it adds to the perception there are a lot of big corporations in bed together," Mr. Kurtz vowed: "I'm going to be just as tough on NBC and MSNBC as I've ever been. But I don't blame folks for being skeptical. . . . We're talking about a profession that many people already view with disdain." Short of unlikely government antitrust measures, it may be left to market forces to police the press in our new jungle of conglomerate journalism -- for money talks louder to corporations than even the most articulate press critic. However disdainful Americans may currently be of big media, they still consume the products and vote daily with their remotes, mouse clicks or subscription payments. Watching ABC News's "This Week" panelists enthuse over "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire" a couple of Sundays ago -- with nary a mention that it helps pay their salaries -- I wondered if it was inane Disney cheerleading like this that in part has driven audiences (and newsmakers like George W. Bush, who favored NBC's Tim Russert that morning) to competitors. Conversely, the Web magazine Slate may gain readers' loyalty with its not-in-the-tank coverage of its parent company, Microsoft. Long before his recent travails, Mr. Drudge predicted, "Eventually they'll all throw me back in the Internet after they chew me and spit me out." He called that one right at least, and his departure from Fox is nothing if not a particularly ruthless example of the market at work. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawings

title: Amazon Wins Court Ruling to Protect Patent on Order System - Correction Appended
body: Signaling that many common features on Web sites can be patented, a federal judge has ordered Barnesandnoble.com to stop using a "one click ordering" system that Amazon.com patented. Judge Marsha J. Pechman of Federal District Court in Seattle issued a preliminary injunction late Wednesday in a case filed in October by Amazon, the online store that pioneered many now-common techniques for retail sales on the Web. Patent lawyers say it is rare for such injunctions to be issued in patent disputes. But the judge ruled that Amazon's case "demonstrated a reasonable likelihood of success on the basis of merits." Moreover, she wrote that Amazon would face "irreparable harm" if it did not have exclusive use of the one-click feature during the holidays, when as many as 10 million people are expected to shop online for the first time. This is the first ruling in what experts expect to be a flurry of disputes over patents related to Internet sites. Already Priceline.com has sued Microsoft, contending it violates Priceline's patented method for consumers to name their own price for hotel rooms. Barnesandnoble.com introduced its "Express Lane" one-click ordering system in May 1998. Experts say they expect many more such suits as patents filed over the last few years are granted. "This injunction is going to send shockwaves through boardrooms across the country," said Robert Greene Sterne, a patent lawyer with Sterne, Kessler, Goldstein & Fox in Washington. "Internet companies that have not been filing for patents, for whatever reason, are going to be in a tough spot." At issue in this case is a feature on Amazon's Web site, introduced in September 1997, called "one click ordering." It enables customers to click on a single button on a screen to order an item. To use the feature, customers must have previously registered their names, addresses and credit card information. But the judge did provide an alternative for Barnesandnoble. She ruled that the patent specifically incorporates methods to purchase an item over the Internet "using only a single action." The judge wrote: "The evidence indicates that Barnesandnoble.com can modify its 'Express Lane' feature with relative ease. For instance, infringement can be avoided by simply requiring users to take an additional action to confirm orders." Jonathan Buckley, the chief executive of Barnesandnoble, said the company would soon replace its one-click system with one that requires two clicks to order. He said this would be part of an improved system that the company had planned to introduce next year. After clicking the first button, next to the name of a book, the customer will now see several options, such as a choice of shipping addresses. Clicking on one of those will complete the order. Nonetheless, Barnesandnoble said it would immediately appeal the preliminary injunction and that it ultimately expected to win the case after a full trial. Barnesandnoble.com is a publicly traded company, although the majority of its shares are controlled by its parent, the Barnes & Noble bookstore chain. It has marketing relationships with other sites, including The newyork Times on the Web, which refers potential customers to Barnesandnoble.com through advertising links on its books section.  http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Business Day yesterday about a patent dispute between Amazon.com and Barnesandnoble.com misstated Barnes & Noble's ownership stake in its online affiliate. The bookstore chain controls about 40 percent of the Internet company's stock, not a majority. The article also misspelled the last name of Barnesandnoble.com's chief executive. He is Jonathan B. Bulkeley, not Buckley. Correction-Date: December 4, 1999, Saturday

title: New York Times Editor Named To Miami Herald's Top Post
body: The Miami Herald ended a six-month search for a new editor yesterday with the announcement that Martin D. Baron, the night editor at The newyork Times, will become executive editor on Jan. 1. Mr. Baron's post at The Times will be filled by Craig R. Whitney, a former foreign editor and longtime foreign correspondent who most recently was Paris bureau chief. Mr. Baron's hiring was welcomed at The Herald, which has endured years of cutbacks, shrinking circulation and a declining reputation. Journalists at the paper and critics in the industry have accused The Herald's corporate parent, Knight Ridder, of being more interested in profits than in good journalism. When the search for a new editor went on for months after Douglas Clifton resigned in May to be editor of The Plain Dealer in Cleveland, there was fear in the newsroom that Knight Ridder wanted someone who would further deplete the staff. But Mark Seibel, the assistant managing editor for metropolitan news at The Herald, said Mr. Baron's selection was a good sign. "People were very relieved to finally have the search over and were pleased that it is a guy with some bona fide journalism credentials," Mr. Seibel said. Mr. Baron said he believed that the paper, which already had high standards -- it won the Pulitzer Prize for investigative reporting this year -- could still do excellent journalism within its budget. "It is already a wonderful newspaper," he said. "They have an investigative tradition, a tradition of elegant writing and of service to the community, and just need to do more of it." Mr. Baron, 45, started as a reporter at The Herald in 1976 and left three years later to join The Los Angeles Times. He was the assistant managing editor who ran its Orange County edition when he left in 1996 to become the night editor at The newyork Times, with the formal title of associate managing editor. Alberto Ibarguen, The Herald's publisher, said he was drawn to Mr. Baron because Mr. Baron had worked in the kind of competitive environment The Herald faced as its core readers moved to suburbs. The Herald's daily circulation peaked at 442,560 copies in 1985. Last year The Herald and its Spanish-language sibling, El Nuevo Herald, had a combined circulation of about 381,000. "It is not any editor who can come into this town at this newspaper and make a positive difference, but I believe he can," said Mr. Ibarguen, who said he wanted to meet profit goals by expanding rather than cutting. "I believe he is going to fiercely defend the interests of the newsroom, and nothing does more for the morale of the newsroom than that." Writers at The Herald said that finally having an editor would help reverse the perception that the paper was no longer the powerhouse that won eight Pulitzers in the late 1980's and early 1990's. In the last two years, about 90 journalists have left the paper, which has a newsroom staff of 410. "We are tired of people saying we are down the toilet, because we don't feel that way," said Dave Barry, the paper's humor columnist and a Pulitzer Prize winner. "So I am glad we have a new editor. Of course, it has never been clear to me what editors do, but I am glad we have one." Mr. Whitney, 56, who joined The Times in 1965, will be an assistant managing editor. He has been an assistant managing editor previously, and bureau chief in Washington, Moscow, Bonn, London and Saigon. "We are happy for The Herald, for American journalism and for Marty, but we hate to see this exceptionally strong and focused leader leave our newsroom," said Joseph Lelyveld, the executive editor of The Times. "At the same time, it's hard to think of anyone who has a richer set of experiences on this paper than Craig. It gives me great peace of mind to know that he will be the person in charge in those last hours when the paper is coming together." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Martin D. Baron, left, of The newyork Times, is to become executive editor of The Miami Herald. He will be replaced by Craig R. Whitney. (The newyork Times)

title: They Soar. They Dive. They're One-Day Wonder Stocks.
body: CALL it the one-day wonder. It is the latest manifestation of Wall Street's speculative fever, one that moves at turbocharged speed with ample help from the Internet and cable television. A one-day wonder is a long-dormant stock that leaps from a low price to a very high one in the course of a single day, or at most two. There is talk that a new product is a killer that will soon dominate a hot industry. The trading volume can be huge, perhaps several times the number of shares in existence. Internet chat rooms and cable television shows focus on the stock. Analysts are found to explain its attraction. The chief executive may turn up to discuss his high hopes for his new product. Then, just as suddenly, the price collapses. In a day, most of the gains are lost. Over a period of a few days or a few weeks, the price returns to its previous low level. The speed is what distinguishes such moves most from those of past speculative markets. In those days, it could take weeks for an obscure stock to get attention and build enthusiasm. Few people could monitor minute-by-minute trading and there were limits to how many people could be reached in a day by promoters pushing a stock. Now speculators can see moves instantly and then leap in quickly while paying commissions far below those of years past. Consider the case of V-ONE. It is a stock that has been around since going public at $5 a share in 1996. Its sales peaked in 1997, and it has consistently lost money. Its auditor -- since fired -- warned early this year that it might not be able to continue as a going concern. Nasdaq threatened to delist it unless it raised more capital. For months it traded around $3 a share, although a product announcement briefly pushed it over $5 in early September. It was just after that run that the company came up with the capital needed to stay on Nasdaq. It raised $8 million in a private offering of preferred stock with warrants. For every $26.25 in preferred that a buyer took, he or she got 10 warrants to buy V-ONE common at $2.625 a share. The price surge came last week. V-ONE announced that it was ready to ship an Internet-security product that is compatible with Red Hat's version of the Linux computer operating system. (Red Hat is a wonder, but not of the one-day variety. It went public at $14 a share in August, topped $50 the first day of trading and now is at $210.) V-ONE shares leaped from under $4 to a high of $15.50 on Tuesday, closing at $13.50. At 60 million shares, volume was triple the number of shares outstanding. By yesterday, the price was down to $7.84. It's a good bet that some of the investors in the September deal sold on Tuesday. Perhaps V-ONE's fortunes will finally turn, and its latest product will provide the success that has heretofore eluded it. In Internet chat rooms discussing the stock, however, that was not the principal issue being debated. There was talk that the stock had to rise because all the available shares had been bought. Close attention was paid to coverage of the stock on CNBC and CNNfn. Insults were exchanged between speculators who were buying the stock and those who were selling it short. The most illuminating comment came from a trader who wrote that V-ONE could be another Ariel Corporation. Ariel was then trading around $12 a share, a few days after jumping from $4 to $57 on the strength of an announcement of plans to offer an Internet-related product. The writer was not, however, being critical. He believed he could get in on V-ONE's rise and get out before the fall. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the daily closing price if V-One shares since November.

title: Big Names Lead in Holiday Internet Sales
body: Already, Internet merchants as a group are having a merry holiday. Over the Thanksgiving weekend, numerous online vendors, including Yahoo and Toysrus.com, reported their biggest days of the year. Internet retailing accounts for only a tiny portion of total Christmas spending, but it is growing rapidly, tripling by the year. Shop.org, the industry association of Internet retailers, released a survey yesterday of its members predicting that about $9 billion will be spent on the Internet between Nov. 1 and Dec. 31. Though the various sites do not provide weekly sales figures, it is possible to track traffic. According to Media Metrix, Ebay, the auction site, ranked No. 1 in visitors among e-commerce sites for the week ended Sunday. Amazon.com was a close second. The National Retail Federation has projected that retail sales will increase 6 percent this year over last year, and, through the season, Media Metrix will provide weekly data on the top e-commerce sites, along with the big gainers and losers. Such data should provide clues on which businesses will emerge triumphant from the Christmas season. The most popular sites in the last week included several toy sellers. Amazon, Toysrus.com, and etoys.com are in a tight race for dominance of the Pokemon and Barbie clientele on the Web. But Toytime.com had the biggest jump in traffic, with a 127 percent increase from its average over the previous three weeks. Still, it recorded less than a third of the traffic of Toysrus.com. Also on the list of fastest growers were KBkids.com, the online outlet of KB Toys, Wal-Mart.com, etoys.com, fingerhut.com., a subsidiary of Federated Department Stores, and bestbuy.com. "It was all about toys," said Doug McFarland, a senior vice president of Media Metrix. Of particular interest has been the fast rise of Toysrus.com. Last year at Christmas, the giant toy retailer was an also-ran in the Internet world. Not two months ago, it looked like persistent management troubles for the mother chain would doom it to an embarassing finish again. Its ability to bounce back appears to be further testimony to the power of a well-known name to draw consumers to the web. While the list of top sites for the last week was dominated by companies that have only Internet commerce and eschew real stores, the gainers list contained many sites that have been created by stores, with such land-based giants as Wal-Mart.com and Bestbuy.com climbing fast. The real test will be how the pure Internet retailers stack up on service this season. Many shoppers are buying on the Web for the first time and are tentative at best. Amazon.com hit a glitch when riots hit downtown Seattle on the eve of the World Trade Organization summit. Amazon was forced to close the telephone portion of its customer service operation from 5:30 p.m. on Nov. 30 until the following morning because its answering center was in the area closed by a curfew. An Amazon spokesman, Bill Curry, said that the sudden shutdown did not affect sales and that by the end of yesterday Amazon had cleared a backlog of calls. Until the public companies provide additional details on their sales for the end of the year, traffic will be the primary tool to gauge how they are doing. Internet traffic measurement -- like television ratings -- can be a controversial science. Companies with Web sites often complain that independent monitors produce numbers that vary significantly from their own count. But Media Metrix, which bases its numbers on the patterns of a panel of 50,000 users of the World Wide Web both at home and at work in the unitedstates (the largest panel used by any of the monitoring groups), is widely recognized as a leader in this field. The firm uses a meter that connects to the computers of participants in its panel to directly monitor every click the browser makes in real time. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Table: "Top E-Commerce Sites" Internet sites with the highest average number of daily unique visitors* for the week ended Nov. 28.
