title: Design Is Selected for Times Capsule
body: After a yearlong competition in which 48 designers, architects and engineers were asked to contemplate the future, a design by a Spanish architect, Santiago Calatrava, has been chosen for The newyork Times Capsule. The vessel, in which artifacts from this century are meant to be preserved for the next 1,000 years, will be displayed this morning to reporters and invited guests at the American Museum of Natural History, where it will be on view to the public beginning on Saturday. The capsule will also be featured this Sunday in The Times Magazine, which conducted the competition. Mr. Calatrava, a bridge designer who is also a sculptor and student of mathematical topology, likened his capsule to a flower. Based on a series of marble sculptures that explore the formal properties of folded spheres, the origami-like module can be opened in segments to contain 50 cubic feet of storage. The capsule, five feet high and weighing two tons, was made of stainless steel at A.R.T. Research Enterprises in Lancaster, Pa., at a cost to The Times of $60,000. Mr. Calatrava's design, along with proposals by 13 of the 21 finalists, is the centerpiece of "Capturing Time: The newyork Times Capsule," on view at the museum through March 26. At the close of the exhibition the capsule is to be sealed for permanent display at the museum, possibly outdoors. The newspaper intends it is to be reopened in 3000. The competition began in January when editors from the magazine convened a panel of experts in preservation, geology, archival materials and "deep-time messaging," efforts at communication across the centuries. Forty-eight designers were approached. Competitors were told they could be either practical or fantastic in their creations, and some submissions were too fanciful to produce. The judges maintained that the capsule needed aesthetic appeal to make it worth preserving. Proposals ranged from Maya Lin's spiral of trees planted on the mathematical relationship known as the Golden Section, a proportion found in classical architecture and nature, to the Ocean Group's "Adrift," in which nine capsules would be airdropped on the Antarctic ice shelf and eventually released into the oceans through global warming. Jaron Lanier, with his colleagues Dr. David Sulzer and Lisa Haney, proposed to translate every 1999 issue of the magazine from its electronic digital code into genetic code and then affix it to the DNA of a cockroach, which could breed throughout newyork City. In addition to objects suggested by residents of the unitedstates, India, France, Zimbabwe and Brazil, the capsule will include all six of the magazine's millennium issues, printed on acid-free archival paper and microengraved on a nickel HD-Rosetta disk, which is about two inches wide and can be read with a microscope. The contents will be placed in subcontainers filled with argon gas that will be suspended in thermal-gel insulation. Once sealed, the capsule will be mounted on a reflective base of flowing water. The winning design and finalists were selected by a panel of judges drawn from The Times, including the editors of the magazine's final millennium issue; Herbert Muschamp, architecture critic; Julie V. Iovine, design reporter; and Pilar Viladas, the magazine's design editor. The finalists on display at the museum, in addition to Ms. Lin, Mr. Lanier and the Ocean Group (a collection of designers from Finland, Norway and Germany who practice in a paperless office in cyberspace), are Antenna Design, Cooper Union, Caples Jefferson, Wes Jones, Pentagram Design Inc., Morphosis, and Greg Lynn and Jeffrey Kipnis, all from the unitedstates; Droog Design of the Netherlands; Kenji Ekuan of Japan; and Dagmar Richter of Germany. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The newyork Times Capsule, designed by Santiago Calatrava, is a module resembling a flower. (Edward Keating/The newyork Times)

title: From Reindeer to Noisemakers, Party Supplies on the Internet
body: YOU don't have to stumble over a department store Santa to realize that the holiday season has arrived, often bringing with its annual rituals of gift-giving and celebration some degree of stress. But in the last days of the 20th century, harried shoppers are increasingly finding some relief by mouse-clicking their way through virtual store aisles rather than braving shopping malls in flesh and blood. The creators of Celebrate Express.com, a new online party planning and merchandise service, are hoping anyone considering holiday entertaining will make that easier, too, by going to www.celebrateexpress.com. The concept is simple. Anyone with access to the Internet can browse through the site, picking up free planning and menu tips and suggestions for, to name a few, Christmas, Hanukkah and New Year's parties and gatherings. One page is dedicated, for instance, to alcohol liability issues and car services to get guests safely home. But key to Celebrate Express.com is the selling and delivering of themed party goods, said its co-founder, Jan Jewell. The company is betting that people will shop its site rather than making a trip to the party goods store. A typical Celebrate Express package, a "golden reindeer dinner for eight," includes eight invitations, dinner and dessert plates (bearing a leaping reindeer), cups, plastic stem glasses, knives, forks, spoons, similarly themed napkins, confetti, baskets, a reindeer-print table cover and even a papier-mache gold-colored reindeer. Cost: $64.95. Similar packages are designed around the Star of David, the approaching millennium and many other nonholiday themes. Celebrate Express.com also sells packages for anniversaries, baby showers, dinner parties and other events. A tailgating package for football games is in the works, Ms. Jewell said. Ms. Jewell estimated that the entertainment and party goods industry is a $9.4 billion market. "We feel that it's definitely a market worth playing in," she said. And Celebrate Express.com is certainly not playing in that market alone. A simple search on the World Wide Web for party planners reveals scores of businesses doing similar work. But many are small operations. Some of the bigger players are eParties (www.eparties.com), iParty (www.iparty.com) and Great Entertaining (greatentertaining/ge /cda/). Celebrate Express is actually an offshoot of Ms. Jewell's mainstay party planning service, Birthday Express. Based in Kirkland, just outside Seattle, Birthday Express was started six years ago, a year after Ms. Jewell's son, Sebastian, was born severely premature. When he reached his first birthday, healthy and happy, Ms. Jewell said she and her husband, Mike, started looking for a way to celebrate children. Birthday Express, of which Mr. Jewell is the chief executive and Ms. Jewell is its "chief creative officer," has almost 600,000 customers, most of them women. Ms. Jewell said her company had helped to give birthday parties for more than three million children this year with themes ranging from Barbie to Barney, from "The Wizard of Oz" to "Star Wars." "And," she said, "we're still growing." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: NAPKINS INCLUDED -- Celebrate Express sells party-supply packages for all occasions.

title: It's Often Hard to Find Help Behind the Cybercounter
body: ROBERT LOCASCIO left his computer, took the elevator downstairs and walked into the corner Starbucks, not just for coffee and a muffin but as a way to illustrate how badly the Web treats its customers. "What's the difference between Frappuccino and cappuccino?" Mr. LoCascio asked a young man behind the Starbucks counter. The young man giggled and squirmed a little, then answered, "Frappuccino is sweet." And he briefly compared the two coffee drinks. Back upstairs in front of his computer screen, Mr. LoCascio logged onto the Starbucks Web site (www.starbucks.com) and tried to get the answer to the same question. Looking through the site for a while without any luck, he went to the search engine, where he typed "frappuccino." No documents were found. So he sent an email message asking the question he had asked the man behind the counter, then waited for a reply. "This is why only 1 to 2 percent of people who visit a site online wind up buying anything -- and why at least 90 percent of the people who enter the brick-and-mortar Starbucks buy something," Mr. LoCascio said. "What if I had walked in the store with my question and the man behind the counter had said, 'Write it down and come back in an hour'?" Mr. LoCascio has had his share of bad experiences with online shopping. In fact, he said, "I started my company because I was a frustrated shopper." The company he started is LivePerson.com, which makes it possible for Web sites to have their customers chat via written notes in real time with customer service representatives (liveperson.com). It is one of a growing number of businesses that try to help e-commerce companies address the problem of providing customer service, but the problem is not going away. "The state of online customer service is bad, and getting worse" said Cormac Foster, an analyst with Jupiter Communications, an Internet market research firm. "Companies are still focusing on acquiring customers, not servicing them." Everyone seems to have a different definition of good customer service: Some see it as synonymous with good salesmanship, others say it means ensuring contact with a real person, while others say it means solving problems, responding quickly and correctly to all inquiries or following up after a purchase. Regardless of the definition of good customer service, many seem to agree that the Net does not have it. "The last holiday season, there were some real problems with Internet shopping," said Scott Silverman, who oversees Internet retail issues for the National Retail Federation. Those problems included late deliveries and customers' inability to track purchases or get answers to questions, he said. Many companies responded at the time by promising better customer service. But Mr. Foster said that had not happened. "Either it was all a lot of lip service, or they underestimated the demand," he said. "Traffic is getting worse." Part of the companies' failure, in other words, may be due to their success. Most analysts estimate that sales will total anywhere from $6 billion to $12 billion this season, three to four times what they were last year. Part of the problem may have to do with online culture. "The whole industry was built on the concept that we can get rid of people -- it would be a huge savings," said Lixuan An, vice president of LivePerson. Mr. Foster said he believed that customer service would continue to be poor. "We're not too bullish heading into this holiday season," he said. He is the principal author of a Jupiter study that reported the results of sending a simple email inquiry to 125 sites. Twenty-five were retail merchants, and 25 were travel companies; the rest were split evenly among financial services, online publications and companies that use their sites to promote, but not sell, their products. Almost half of the sites took at least five days to respond, or never responded, a significant increase over the rate reported in a survey a year ago. But even if the overall picture is discouraging, Mr. Foster said, some retailers are improving their service. "Some sites are taking the initiative and making things happen," he added. The service offered by various sites was ranked in a third-quarter survey of some 100,000 Internet users by Harris Interactive. "Our survey shows that iQVC and Amazon dominate in a number of product categories," said Julia Resnick, who oversaw the survey. "The top-rated sites across all categories include Lands' End, Gap, Christianbook, VitaminShoppe and Clinique." It was not an accident that three of the top sites sell clothing. "Clothing, music, video, books and health and beauty tend to be benchmarks for customer service," Ms. Resnick said. She added that sites selling "electronics, computer software and hardware -- places where people need a lot of assistance -- have more challenges in servicing the customers because of the complexity of questions." One company that is frequently mentioned as innovative is Lands' End, a clothing company that offers immediate responses to typed inquiries (www.landsend.com). It also has technology that allows a company representative to show a customer a specific item by taking charge of the customer's browser to call up a page on the site. Another Lands' End service, called Shop With a Friend, makes it possible for a woman in newyork, for example, to go online with her grandmother in Wisconsin to choose a sweater for a gift. Miadora, an online jewelry store, has moved beyond text-based customer service by offering a voice-chat option (www .miadora.com) for people making purchases at the site. The conversations are handled by computer microphones and speakers. It remains to be seen, however, whether voice chat will be technologically feasible or become a popular service. Mr. LoCascio has some suggestions for people who shop online. "To judge if a site is going to have good customer support, ask them what their return policy is," Mr. LoCascio said. "Will I have to take a day out of my life? Will they pack it up for me? Can I use the box they sent it in? Will they send someone to pick it up, or will I have to do that? I would also go to the customer service area and interact with them, send them an email or a chat and see what response I got." More than four hours after Mr. LoCascio had sent Starbucks a question via email, the company replied with an obviously automatic email response. It told him how to find about a half-dozen products on the Starbucks Web site, including Frappuccino. It did not say, however, how it differs from cappuccino. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Companies like LivePerson, started by Robert LoCascio, are offering to help Internet companies improve their customer service. (Richard Perry/The newyork Times)

title:
LIBRARY;
Hockey, Behind the Mask and on the Web
body: OF the four major-league sports in North America, hockey has the best trophy, the most exciting playoffs -- there is more tension in a Calgary-Edmonton divisional semifinal than there has been in all 30 Super Bowls combined -- and the most inspiring championship ceremony. Players from the winning team skate around the arena and take turns hoisting the Stanley Cup overhead, which is somehow preferable to the baseball ritual of running around a shrink-wrapped locker room and spraying Tim McCarver with Budweiser. What hockey doesn't have is respect, or at least not the respect it craves. In the unitedstates, the sport remains a distant fourth behind football, baseball and basketball and locked in the regional cable-television rotation with five-pin bowling and swamp buggy racing. In response, a schism has opened in the hockey world between the internationalists, who want hockey to become part of the global entertainment business, and the isolationists, who believe that hockey belongs to Canada and the parts of the unitedstates that resemble Canada and who don't really care what the Sun Belt or the rest of the world thinks. For now, the internationalists are winning. The National Hockey League's official site (www.nhl.com) publishes the usual game reports, player statistics and bland articles. But it also includes links to a page on European hockey players -- an acknowledgement that the league currently draws players from 18 countries and that many of today's best players come from Europe -- and a page on the league's Diversity Task Force. The task force, an attempt "to introduce children of diverse ethnic backgrounds to the game of hockey," is a tacit acknowledgement that hockey, despite players like Grant Fuhr and Mike Grier, remains a poor draw among African-Americans. If NHL.com suffers from basketball envy, then the Exploratorium Science of Hockey site (www .exploratorium.edu/hockey/) suffers from baseball envy. The curveball may have physical qualities worthy of debate, but just about everybody agrees that colder rinks have better ice and that knowing an open-ice hit delivered by Eric Lindros produces 6,232 joules of energy doesn't make it hurt any less. For a very different view of hockey physics, you can look up the Hockey Enforcers' Web ring, for pages dedicated to hockey goons and their trade. Despite the efforts of the league to minimize fighting to sell hockey to a family audience, goons do serve a function in hockey -- they use their fists to stop other players from using their sticks. As the old joke goes, it's a good thing hockey players don't realize they're standing on knives. The Web ring seems to have only one page so far, Steve's All Canadian, All Hockey, All Fight Page (www.angelfire.com/ab/steevstuff /fights.html). It offers photos, some crude animation, a poll and a special citation for Steve's favorite goon, Rocky Thompson of the Calgary Flames. "Look at Rocky pound his opposition into the ice" screams the site. Look at our marketing strategy go up in flames, the league office says. The patron saint of fighting and of hockey isolationists everywhere is Don Cherry, the flamboyant former coach of the Boston Bruins and Colorado Rockies. He has cultivated an enormous following in Canada and the unitedstates through his Coach's Corner segment during Saturday night hockey broadcasts. Deeply suspicious of the league and shamelessly patriotic, he could easily be dismissed as hockey's answer to Pat Buchanan if not for his superior knowledge of the game and his underlying decency. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation makes Coach's Corner available on the Web (cbc.ca/sports/hockey/hnic /coach.shtml) in both audio and video formats. For an art-historical perspective on hockey, several sites, including Chip's Puck Page (www.geocities .com/Colosseum/Sideline/7959 /hockeypucks.html) and My Ever Increasing Puck Collection (www.cjnetworks.com/%7Estallion /pucks/puck.html) features photographs of, you guessed it, hockey pucks. The Painted Warrior Web site (users.aol.com/maskman33 /classicnf.html) contains an archive of goalie mask designs dating from the 1950's. Goalie masks started out as protection for injured goalies. By the early 1970's, they had become a form of theater and, like masks in Greek drama, they revealed as much as they concealed. Ken Dryden, the imperturbable goalie for the Montreal Canadiens, wore a mask that resembled a sardonic grin. Jacques Plante's mask had an eerie mathematical perfection. Gerry Cheevers, a Bruins goalie who sometimes skated out of the way of slap shots, painted fake stitch marks across his mask wherever the puck made contact. Current mask designs, sadly, tend to feature cartoon dinosaurs and air-brushed fangs -- a letdown for the longtime fan but perfect, no doubt, for the global marketplace. title:
NEWS WATCH;
Dell's Webcentric PC's In Anything but Beige
body: Starting next Tuesday, consumers can surf the Web through Sedona orange-colored glasses. Following in Apple Computer's footsteps away from the traditional putty tower, the Dell Computer Corporation is going after what it refers to as the "cyber-psyched" market with the Webpc (www.webpc.com), a low-cost, colorful desktop PC designed for easy Internet access. Measuring 6 inches wide and almost 11 inches high, the new PC's are about one-third the size of a regular desktop and come in five anti-beige colors: Tahoe blue, Sedona orange, Sea Island teal, Red River red and Napa purple. Printers and external floppy drives can also be ordered in complementary colors. "We developed the Webpc for people whose lives revolve around Internet activity and who want a system that's easy to buy, use and support," said Bob Kaufman, a spokesman for Dell. "They also want something that looks good in their house." Prices will start at $1,000 for a system that includes an Intel Celeron 433-megahertz processor, 64 megabytes of RAM, a 15-inch monitor, an HP-610 printer and one year of Dellnet Internet service. Flat panel displays are available for an extra $850. Features specifically designed for Internet use include an instant-on button for booting up the PC quickly, a keyboard that lets users customize keys for direct access to email and favorite Web sites and a key that runs a system health check and connects to Dell's online tech-support.   CATHERINE GREENMAN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
ONLINE SHOPPER;
Searching for Fashion Advice? You May Be Sorry You Asked
body: DO I need a personal shopper? Recently I showed up at a party in a dress that frankly looked like underwear. I would like to believe that an expert personal shopper would prevent me from repeating that sort of fashion tragedy. So I arrived at www.boo.com eager to meet Miss Boo, an online personal shopper who wore a neat ponytail and lipstick that matched the red of her shirt. I understand that Miss Boo is nothing more than software. While she may look like a person, raising her eyebrows encouragingly as I shop, in reality she is programmed to persuade me to buy. Of course, a few weeks ago I also understood that a sweater set and wool pants would have been more appropriate party wear than a black dress that looked like a slip. Or at least warmer. But like many shoppers, I abandon objectivity at a mall entrance. My subconscious takes over, and I find myself involved in convoluted plots that remind me of dreams. I try on outlandish items like boas and subsequently buy black satin pumps instead of the boring loafers I need. Later, I analyze the shoes; they remind me (in a Jungian way) of a pair my mother wore to parties when I was very small. Being such a repressed (and extravagant) shopper should make me an ideal candidate to buy clothes from online retailers like Boo.com, with sites that seem like fantasy theme parks to tap into your deeply buried personal preferences. At Boo.com, the software can learn something of my tastes by keeping track of the items I examine on the site. Other sites, like www.landsend .com and www.alwaysinstyle.com, will dispense fashion advice based on my measurements and coloring. Still, I have been reluctant to buy clothes online. It turns out that this is common; nearly half of the 2,399 Internet users surveyed in August by the market researchers at the NPD Group said they wouldn't do it either, and 85 percent of those polled said they worried about buying clothes they couldn't try on. When I phoned Jay Herratti, president of Boo.com's North America division, he said tools like Miss Boo would make me feel more connected to online clothes. "She helps to create an environment where shopping for clothes is fun," he said. So I braved Boo.com's sluggish site (do not try this with a modem slower than 56K; the site also isn't available to Mac users yet) to click on clothes -- zooming in on a pair of Converse One Star sandals ($37) that really tempted me with the quality of stitching around the soles. Then, as I considered a pair of $200 sneakers, described as "a classic 70's-inspired football style trainer," I glanced at Miss Boo, hoping she would chide, "Two hundred dollars for sneakers that would make you look like that girl in sixth grade who wore nylons with culottes?" Instead, she advised, "Hey, Cinderella, show yourself in regal footwear and arouse the envy of all those Prince Charmings." So much for Miss Boo. She clearly could not be trusted. I wondered, though, if things would be different at a site that had personalized information about me. So I went to the Lands' End site, which generated a human figure shaped vaguely like me (based on measurements I provided) and fashion advice that I immediately knew to be brilliant: "You can add variety to your wardrobe because you look good in everything." I felt smug until I "looked good" in a long pleated skirt and a sleeveless blouse that my high-school Spanish teacher might have worn. Realizing that in real life that outfit would look ghastly, I had to admit the truth: I had fibbed about my measurements to create a more idealized me. Blaming the site for encouraging me to behave so vainly, I left immediately. Next, I entered more truthful information at Always in Style -- and was rewarded for my candor by a recommendation to buy "large size" separates from Lane Bryant. I phoned Doris Pooser, who created the site's Personal Profile feature, to ask why she thought I wanted to look like my grandmother in the red suit she wore to my cousin's wedding. The site, Ms. Pooser said, was still in beta and Lane Bryant was one of the few retailers whose clothes had been entered into the database. I'll try to shop there again, but not until after Jan. 1, when it makes it official debut with at least 12 brands. "In March," Ms. Pooser added, "we hope to add teen fashion." That reminded me that I wanted a new pair of jeans, maybe hip-huggers like the ones my favorite baby sitter wore in 1971. I went to the mall to get them. It was a good thing, too, because I had to try on eight pairs before finding some that fit. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Boo.com, above, offers clothing, accessories and optional commentary from Miss Boo, a virtual personal shopper, about shoppers' choices. At the Always in Style site, left, shoppers can receive a personal profile.

title: Unraveling the Mysteries of Sherlock Holmes
body: WHAT would Sherlock have thought of the Internet? Its spreadsheets would have been invaluable time-savers (for correlating soil colors and granulations by London neighborhoods, for instance; or trouser threads by manufacturer and tailor). He would have found it quite useful as a library and a correspondence tool, if only for cataloging and exposing the mistakes of others. As a code-breaker, it would have been entirely unnecessary; his own intellect was enough. As biography, he would have declared it absolute rubbish. But that is only what Sherlock Holmes himself would have thought. For more than a century, Holmes devotees have been enthusiastically filling the gaps left by the incomplete journals of Dr. John H. Watson, Holmes's friend and chronicler, and they have lost no time putting their speculations online. Sherlockian trivia is legendary, and since "obsessive" would be Holmes's middle name if he had one, there is no shortage of Web sites. One of the most comprehensive sites is at Yoxley Old Place (www .geocities.com/sherlockian /index.html), compiled by "Fred Porlock," who is also the host of a Baker Street Web ring. From Yoxley, one can find information on everything from The Baker Street Journal, the quarterly publication of the Baker Street Irregulars, perhaps the most famous Holmes society, to collectable and trivia sites. One can also link to "A Matter of Attention" by Greg Stoddard, an essay contending that Holmes suffered from attention deficit disorder, and to "Was Sherlock Holmes Autistic?" by A. Michael Maher. "The Detective in Montana," by Bruce A. Trinque, concludes that both Holmes and Watson served incognito in the Seventh Cavalry and survived the Battle of the Little Bighorn. In "The Truth About the Speckled Band," L. M. Klauber, a herpetologist, writes that there is no such Indian reptile as a "swamp adder," that Watson misunderstood Holmes as usual and that, in fact, the villain in the case had made a hybrid, crossing a cobra and a Gila monster. "Fred Porlock" is the nom de Doyle for Rick Freeman, 40, a Canadian civil servant who lives in Chatham, Ontario. "When I first began Yoxley, there were only a handful of sites with a lot of Holmes/Doyle content, but that has grown so quickly that it is hard to keep up," Mr. Freeman wrote in an email message. "I say I have over 1,200 links on my site, but I don't know really how many anymore." Non-English sites are growing especially fast, he added, noting Holmesiana in French, German and Polish. (Yoxley Old Place, incidentally, is the name of a house in the Holmes short story "The Adventure of the Golden Pince-Nez," which takes place not far from Chatham, England.) Whether touring Holmes Web sites or actual British sites, one should be aware of the Game. The Game is not what's afoot; it is a premise of Holmesian research. Mr. Freeman explained: "Those who follow the Game 'believe' Holmes was real, Watson wrote the stories and Sir Arthur Conan Doyle was merely the literary agent who brought them forward for publication. Doyleans dislike the Game intensely and say it takes away the credit Doyle should get for Holmes as well as his many other works. I don't speak for all Sherlockians, but personally, I think we all know what a genius Doyle was." Other issues can turn the chat lines red-hot, Mr. Freeman wrote. One is original stories, most of which can be downloaded off the Web, versus pastiches. (For a list of public-domain stories, see watserv1 .uwaterloo.ca/credmond/canon .html as well as Yoxley.) "People either like and accept well-written pastiches or hate every one," Mr. Freeman wrote. Another is choosing the best Holmes actor and best film. On the other hand, should Holmes be enjoyed only in book form? Just how many times was Watson married? (Doyle is not consistent.) Were Holmes and Watson gay? (The majority say no, but there are strong opinions for each side.) As for the source of Holmes's enduring popularity, "Personally, I think it has to do with Doyle's writing style," Mr. Freeman wrote. "Doyle began to hate Holmes, even killing him off in the early 1890's so he could get on with his 'important' work. Since he didn't take Holmes seriously, he was a bit careless with details and continuity (which makes for a lot of what 'the Game' entails). However, he wrote about the times in a way that brings them back to life for many. "You don't just read the stories; you're transported back in time and become part of the story." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Webcams Focus On Day Care - Correction Appended
body: SUZY O'MARA of Hoover, Ala., watches her 18-month-old daughter, Morgan, all day long. That would not be unusual if Mrs. O'Mara was a stay-at-home mother, but she works full time as a claims adjuster at the State Farm Insurance Company in Birmingham, and her daughter spends her days at the Samford University day care center in the city. The computer on Mrs. O'Mara's desk is hooked to the Internet, where she can see what is on a Web camera trained on her daughter's classroom at the center. Not that Mrs. O'Mara watches all the time. But she said she checked in about a dozen times a day. "If I'm on hold, or on call with a customer, and what I'm saying is pretty routine, I can click over and see what's going on," Mrs. O'Mara said. Some days, she added, work takes precedence and she doesn't log on at all. The day care center at Samford University is among about 150 centers nationwide that offer Internet-based systems that allow parents to watch their children through Web cameras in the classroom. The Web monitor at Samford is run by the university, and access to the service is free to parents. But most parents with access to day-care Webcams pay $15 to $25 a month for the service. There are more than 120,000 licensed day care centers nationwide and a half-dozen companies wiring day care centers with Web cameras. The oldest of these, Watchmegrow.com, of Bellevue, Wash., has been in business since 1996. The company's founder, Eric Foster, said it hooked up its first center, the Children's Courtyard in Dallas, in 1997. Other day care Web camera companies include ParentWatch (www.parentwatch.com), which is based in Manhattan and has wired 70 centers, and San Diego-based KinderView (www.kinderview.com), which has cameras in 21 day care centers, including the one at the Naval Station in San Diego. These companies say they have contracts to serve 580 more centers. But technology is costly -- about $13,000 for a system -- and wiring is slow. Though the number of current installations of Web camera systems is small, day care center administrators and day care Web camera company owners say that word of the new technology is out among parents of young children and that more and more of them are seeking centers offering the service. About 30 percent of all parents in the centers with Web cameras have signed up, and they are logging on at least six times a day, on average, for 15 minutes at a time. Parents who are watching say the service is the balm that soothes their guilt about leaving their children in day care for stretches as long as 12 hours daily. Though day care centers have open-door policies for parental visits, parents say they simply can not take advantage of them. Watching their children on Web cameras is the next best thing. Initially, parents log on to make sure their children are safe and happy, that the day care staff is providing quality care. After parents and children are broken in and comfortable with the arrangements, parents say checking in makes them feel closer to their children and lets them talk to their children later about the specifics of their day. Instead of asking their children how their day was, they can ask about the letter of the day, the book they read or the funny dance they did with the teacher. Adam Aronson, a former banker who has no children, said he started ParentWatch because he believed that parents would use the systems to monitor day care providers. But day care directors and administrators did not like the suggestion that they needed surveillance, so ParentWatch now describes its Webcams as a way to foster goodwill between day care centers and customers. Some services offer video, others a still image that is updated every three seconds. Both kinds of systems work in much the same way. At least two cameras are installed in every classroom. One camera is trained on the table area and the other on the floor, a favorite gathering place for preschool children. No cameras are pointed at diaper-changing stations, bathrooms or administrative offices. Subscribers can log on only by using a password. Most systems allow parents to log on for a limited amount of time per camera, anywhere from 5 to 15 minutes, before being logged off. ParentWatch assigns one password per user, while other companies allow one password per family. Since passwords can be shared among extended family members, some grandparents also enjoy the routine, albeit one-way, contact. Ray Hodgen of Atmore, Ala., peers into his 2-year-old grandson's day care classroom in Noonan, Ga., four times a day. "It's a chance to see him grow up and see how he's taken care of at the day care center," said Mr. Hodgen, who added that most of the time his grandson is playing or reading a book. "You see so many things on TV about how children are mistreated." ParentWatch and another service, ToddlerView (www.toddlerwatch.com), also offer information for parents and sell child care items on their Web sites. Although the systems have been set up for parents, Cheyenne Roedell, the owner of Scripps Exploring Academy in San Diego, said they protected the day care center's staff as well. The Scripps center uses the KinderView system. "Sometimes the imagination can create things that aren't quite like they were but cause everyone a great deal of distress," Ms. Roedell said. "With KinderView, you can check in and see what the norm is." Other day care providers who were initially wary of the cameras say they have been pleasantly surprised. One such person is Janet Pasteka, director of the Kiddie Academy in Hillsborough, N.J., which offers ParentWatch. She said she had thought the Webcams would become an administrative headache. Ms. Pasteka envisioned a flood of phone calls from overly protective parents. But she said the frantic "Billy fell down and is crying" calls have not happened. To her surprise, the system helps parents reaffirm that their decision to place their children at a particular day care center was the right one, by letting them see what actually happens during the day. Sharon Lynn Kagan, a senior associate at the Yale Bush Center, a public policy institute that studies child care issues, said: "I believe the movement toward this kind of surveillance is indicative about parental concerns about safety and quality of child care centers in America. You can put eight million of these things in centers and there's still going to be skepticism." Ms. Kagan is also the president of the National Association for the Education of Young Children, an organization that has not taken a formal position on the use of Webcams in day care centers. Ellen Galinsky, the president of the Families and Work Institute and author of "Ask the Children: What America's Children Really Think About Working Parents" (William Morrow & Company, 1999), said parents were more likely to put their energy and dollars directly into a child care program of their choosing to establish familial bonds with the centers than to lobby for better child care over all. And while parents may initially check in on the day care center to ensure that the providers are doing their jobs, Ms. Galinsky said that parents were using the Webcam systems mostly because they are fun. David Hudak would agree. Mr. Hudak, an accountant whose 3-year-old daughter attends the Kiddie Academy in Hillsborough, N.J., said he logged on to ParentWatch to see her at least six times a day. On some days, he encourages his clients to take a peek at his daughter eating her peas and carrots at lunch or coloring a picture of a giant cookie. He says he expects to keep watching when his 4-month-old daughter starts attending the center in December. Still, Mr. Hudak regards the service as a novelty, worth the $25 a month only until his interest wanes. "In the long term, I'm not going to want to pay $25 a month to watch my child when I'm paying day care to do that," said Mr. Hudak, who added that he had not told his wife, Lynn, of his decision. Mrs. Hudak, who works as a dietitian at St. Peter's University Hospital near the day care center, said she was so happy with ParentWatch that she believed it should be installed in public schools. "As a parent, you always have a longing to see your children," Mrs. Hudak said. Even though the day care center has an open-door policy, she said, she is usually too busy at work to take advantage of it. Now her daughter asks when she leaves for day care whether Mrs. Hudak will be watching. But Mrs. Hudak wants to hear her daughter as well. "Whoever invented this," she said, "tell them I would love to have sound." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Circuits on Dec. 2 about the use of cameras in day care centers for monitoring over the World Wide Web referred incorrectly to the first such use of the devices, known as webcams. Both Watchmegrow.com and the Simplex Knowledge Company report that they installed their first day care systems for testing in September 1996; thus Watchmegrow.com is not acknowledged as the oldest company in the field.
