G1); WEBCAM VIEW -- David Hudak, below, is a parent who watches the Kiddie Academy in Hillsborough, N.J. (Photographs by Norman Y. Lono for The New York Times); REASSURANCE -- A Webcam behind 18-month-old Morgan O'Mara at day care helps Suzy O'Mara, below, stay in touch. (Photographs by Steve Gates for The New York Times)(pg. G6)

title:
WHAT'S NEXT;
Satellites May Clear Logjams on Net
body: IN THE beginning, the Internet provided email and that was good enough. Now, the world is obsessed with turning the Internet into a video distribution system. That is putting an incredible strain on resources, and several companies are re-engineering some of the old television infrastructure to relieve the pressure. The fundamental problem is that the Internet was designed to ship data from one computer to another. It handles this one-to-one transfer with remarkable agility and reliability. But when many people want to get copies of the same file, problems emerge, whether it is the latest video of an earthquake from the CNN Web site or the latest security patch for Windows. Sending many similar files at once, often called multicasting, requires the Internet to carry thousands of copies of the same data and do thousands of times the work to accomplish it. The cost of multicasting goes up with every new viewer who wants to watch. An alternative is to take equipment meant for broadcasting and use it for multicasting. For example, companies can pay to use satellites that carry television signals for networks like NBC and use them to send data meant for the Internet. Doug Humphrey, president of SkyCache, which is based in Laurel, Md., said, "A multicast is just a fake broadcast. It's not as good. The one thing that satellites do better than anything is broadcast. It goes up once and comes down on every square inch of the country." So his company broadcasts video to what he calls "the edge" of the Internet, local offices of Internet service providers like AOL or Earthlink. These are often known as POP's, or points of presence, and are located in thousands of different communities so customers can connect to the closest one with a local phone call. The I.S.P.'s link their POP's with vast fiber optic networks, or backbones, which carry the information between the POP's and the various Web servers. The latest video from CNN, for instance, would stream out from Atlanta to all the POP's where dial-up customers had requested a copy of the latest news. If the news was exciting, this demand could be quite heavy and require sending copies to all the local POP's. That might overload the fiber optic backbones leaving Atlanta; they might not be big enough to handle requests from 2,000 or more POP's. Companies like SkyCache; IPPlanet, based in Israel; and iBeam, in Sunnyvale, Calif., are three of many trying to lighten this load by using satellites. They take one copy of the data and bounce it off the satellite so the signal lands on one-meter-wide dishes on the roofs of POP's throughout the world. One satellite broadcast can transmit copies to all the POP's on the edge of the Internet. Mr. Humphrey estimates that SkyCache's link becomes cost-effective when someone wants to move 15 or 20 copies of the same file, a number that is much smaller than the number of POP's in the country. This use of satellites began with feeds of smaller files years ago. Both SkyCache and IPPlanet, for instance, are selling a service that delivers a constant stream of the Usenet newsgroups to local POP's. The thousands of discussion groups, with names like alt.sport.air-hockey or comp.risks, consume gigabytes of bandwidth a day. Downloading the information from a satellite saves the cost of running extra fiber optic lines to carry the traffic. Now the satellite companies are rushing to add streaming video to the services they offer. Many companies that tried to broadcast across the Internet quickly discovered that the signals often got bogged down in the middle as the signal traveled to the edges. The "middle" is the fiber optic network that links the POP's -- a vast web of shorter connections that are bound together by traffic directing computers known as routers. Data moving from Los Angeles to newyork, for instance, may move through 20 to 50 fiber optic links. At the end of each link, a router must choose the optimal path for the data. At each decision point, the data can slow down or even stop if the router is bogged down. Data streams carrying video information are particularily sensitive to delays caused at the routers. email handling software, for instance, can wait for delays or ask for the information to be resent if it is lost along the way. Video software, on the other hand, must balk and display a blank screen if the data do not arrive on time. These companies are trying to simplify the trip by sending the data over their satellite link, avoiding the routers and their potential delays. IBeam, for instance, places frequently used data on its own servers at POP's throughout the country. These servers keep copies of the data sent to them over the satellite link and send the information out to the local dial-up customers. That saves the time it would otherwise take to send the request to the Internet. Many other companies are experimenting with putting servers at POP's. Akamai, based in Cambridge, Mass., is placing its servers at POP's to carry up-to-date copies of high-traffic Web sites. Akamai recently leased some of SkyCache's satellite time to speed the updating process. Tom Gillis, vice president for marketing at iBeam, said his company was also installing servers at POP's. The company can download video streams to these servers and save a great deal of money compared with the cost of sending information over the fiber network. Sending 1,000 copies of a music video to viewers over the fiber backbone would cost about $67, Mr. Gillis said, but iBeam would be able to deliver the copies for about one-third of that price using satellites. He also promises that his system will insert customized advertisements into each stream, producing even more revenue. "Satellite is the ultimate broadcast medium," Mr. Gillis said. "We can deliver to thousands if not millions of users at a fixed cost." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Mary Ann Smith)

title:
BUSINESS TRAVEL;
Business fliers worldwide are increasingly using the Internet to research and book their flights.
body: BUSINESS travelers worldwide are increasingly embracing the Internet to research and book their flights, an annual survey by the International Air Transport Association has found. Almost two-thirds of the survey's approximately 1,000 respondents from Europe, North America and the Asia-Pacific region said they used the Internet to find flight information, a 50 percent increase over the survey's results from two years ago. In some cases IATA compares the current results with year-earlier figures, in others with figures from 1997. Not surprisingly, North American business travelers -- who made up approximately one-third of the group surveyed -- were the heaviest users of the Internet for flight research; 70 percent of this group said they went on-line to do research, an increase of 27 percent over 1997. Such use grew at an even greater rate among European travelers (an increase of 68 percent over 1997) and Asian travelers (an increase of 63 percent). Over all, the number of travelers using the Internet to actually book a trip has almost doubled, from 9 percent in IATA's 1998 poll to 17 percent this year. One in 10 of those surveyed said they made flight reservations online weekly, one-fifth use the Internet monthly to book, while almost 40 percent make online bookings every few months. The number of respondents who said they expected to use the Internet to make travel plans in five years' time also increased significantly, rising from 39 percent in 1997 to 51 percent this year. The IATA survey also found the following: *Some two-fifths of travelers have used electronic tickets, a 60 percent increase over 1997. *Two-thirds of respondents favor airport check-in desks over automated check-in and curbside check-in.  *Delays are business travelers' greatest concern. Delays on short-haul trips in particular were cited by 52 percent of respondents this year, up from 36 percent in 1998. *Almost two-thirds of travelers said they were willing to try a no-frills airline for short-haul flights, while 37 percent said they were "very willing" to do this. *More than two-thirds of respondents said they did not use in-flight business services like telephones, faxes and computer data ports on their last long-haul flight. When these were employed, the telephone was used most. Rating in-flight entertainment activities, respondents said they watched films the most; they also said they watched news programs and read in-flight magazines. *Airline schedules are the most important factor when choosing long-haul economy-class flights, respondents said, followed by frequent-flier programs, low fares, seat comfort and audio systems. Norman Sherlock, executive director of the National Business Travel Association, a trade group whose members are corporate travel managers, questioned the survey's projections on future use of the Internet. He predicted that corporations would not allow their employees to go online to make reservations "until airlines satisfy their concerns about individuals booking on the Internet and observing travel management policies."  Airline Update Northwest Airlines is offering a new online booking program to small and medium-size corporations that features incentives including free tickets and upgrades, elite frequent-flier program status, airport lounge memberships and travel management aids. UAL's United Airlines is giving a bonus of 25,000 miles to participants in its frequent-flier program who stay at least 10 times at Regent International Hotels by Dec. 30, 2000; each stay must be a minimum of three nights. Travelers also must register with Regent and pay the corporate room rate. British Airways established a Web site on London as a destination (londontraveller.com) that contains in-depth information on the city from a variety of travel guidebooks, as well as data on the newest restaurants, bars, clubs, theater and art exhibits. Visitors to the site can also buy airline tickets and book hotel rooms.  Finding Your Way "I'll Never Get Lost Again," by Linda Grekin (RDR Books, $12.95), promises to help readers improve their sense of direction. It explains why ordinarily competent people become easily disoriented, and offers helpful tips to those it calls "directionally challenged." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Have Laptop, Will Upload for Dinner
body: Mike Phillips wanted to go home. An animation artist, he had worked in newyork for MTV and in Berlin for a film studio, but he couldn't get Barrie, a town 60 miles north of Toronto, out of his mind. "I missed being able to drive a short distance to the wilderness," said Mr. Phillips, 25. So, despite the paucity of animation work there, home he went this year and began trolling the Internet for work. That is how he discovered eLance, a jobs bazaar (www.eLance.com) where freelancers can list their skills and search for work. And though he named a price that was more than 50 percent above what a newyork employer wanted to pay, he landed an assignment. Mr. Phillips is the beneficiary of an economic boom that has driven unemployment in the unitedstates to its lowest level since astronauts were landing on the moon and has made employers desperate for skilled workers. To cater to them, an entirely new kind of job fair is springing up, run not out of a convention center but in cyberspace. ELance and its rivals are the information-age equivalent of the medieval town square where workers-for-hire called out their skills. Today's job seekers do the same, but through their computer keyboards. And whether they are computer programmers in Atlanta or Finnish translators in San Diego, they can find work without traveling. For their part, employers gain access to a new pool of freelancers without having to give them office space or fringe benefits. Across the economy, said Berrud Sheth, the chief executive of eLance, "the supply is sitting all over the world, and demand is where it is," often unable to move. Though small, the sites tap into three of today's hottest employment trends: the rise of outsourcing, the Internet revolution and the surge in people working at home as telecommuters or small-business owners. The biggest jobs bazaar is Monster Talent Market, a part of Monster.com, the most popular Internet job-hunting site. After five months in business, Monster Talent Market says it has signed up 110,000 independent contractors and more than 7,500 employers. By contrast, one of the newest players in the field, FlexMind.com, is deliberately elitist. The Massachusetts start-up wants to register only students at a dozen or so of the most selective universities in the country, assuming that employers would love to hire them for part-time assignments and that the students who otherwise might have to wait tables would jump at the chance. "It's a nice way for a company to have a low-commitment preview of an employee," said Julius Mokrauer, chief executive of FlexMind. In FlexMind's first two months, about 500 students and 40 companies -- including American Express and barnesandnoble.com -- have registered on the site, Mr. Mokrauer said. He left his job as a trader at Lehman Brothers to start the company last year after hiring a Harvard law student for $35 an hour and realizing what a bargain that was for his employer. FlexMind charges employers 20 percent of whatever they are paying to the freelancer. ELance, which is now free, will begin charging companies, and perhaps freelancers, next year. Monster charges employers about 10 percent but no more than $1,000. At eLance and FlexMind, it is the freelancers who do the bidding; at Monster, it is the employers. Other Web sites, like FreeAgent.com, simply list job openings for freelancers and their resumes for employers but do not allow auction-style bidding. With so many job openings going begging these days, the freelance Web sites can be a boon to employers. Susan Patnaik, for example, was having trouble finding an artist in newyork to illustrate a graphic novel -- a type of comic book for adults -- that she was producing. She had called artists she knew and asked for recommendations but was striking out. So she listed the assignment on eLance for $350. Bids started arriving the next day, and she chose Mr. Phillips, even though he wanted $550, because she was impressed with the samples she had downloaded. Presto: talent-hungry Ms. Patnaik had her worker, and job-hungry Mr. Phillips had his 25-hour assignment, even though they live hundreds of miles apart, do not know anybody in common and may never meet. Of course, $550 is hardly enough for Mr. Phillips to live on, and thus far he has not landed any other jobs through eLance. On average, only four or five deals are made each day on the site, the company said. From an employer's perspective, the sites can create as many problems as they solve, since virtually anyone can post a resume. On eLance, Mr. Phillips said, "It seems like there are a lot of young, inexperienced artists applying for jobs." And HotJobs.com, a rival to Monster, does not offer an auction site, the company says, because its clients -- big companies -- have shown little interest. But there are a few big success stories. Benita Kenn quit her job as a public-relations manager for a California technology company this year to spend more time with her folk band. She put her resume on Monster Talent Market and got two jobs. The first, with a golf merchandise site, began in August and is just ending, while the other, with a seller of personalized T-shirts and mugs, began in October. Ms. Kenn has been working an average of 20 hours a week at pay that she says is typical for a public-relations consultant. (That would be about $100 an hour, people in the industry said.) Still, she uses her old contacts because she said she cannot rely solely on the auction site. "Ideally, there would be hordes of people bidding for me," Ms. Kenn said. "But that's not where it's at at this point." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Mike Phillips lives where he wants, in Barrie, Ontario, and seeks job assignments by way of cyberspace in the field of animation art. (Phill Snel for The newyork Times)

title:
MANAGEMENT: IDEAS INTO ACTION;
Merger Mania Got You Down? So, Start Thinking Small
body: WE might be forgiven for concluding that everything in corporate America is getting bigger and bigger. The global couplings in autos, oil and gas, financial services, telecommunications and now pharmaceuticals sometimes give the impression that the business world is driving toward an acquisition apocalypse. When the dust settles, we will all draw a paycheck from the same employer. Now comes Thomas W. Malone to file a minority report. Dr. Malone is a professor of information systems at the Sloan School of Management at Massachusetts Institute of Technology and an alumnus of Xerox's creative Palo Alto Research Center. For five years, he has been co-director of a major-league effort to think about what shape the company and the workplace will take in the new century, now only a month away. In his view, the century will bring a new golden age for small enterprise and a new springtime for individual creativity in business. Communications in the Internet era will be so powerful, so rich, so cheap that even the smallest enterprises, already nimble, will be armed with the information they need to compete with corporate giants. He expects an economy in which companies as small as 1 to 10 talented people can thrive. Newborn Web businesses are already swirling like snowflakes. How long before they carpet the ground? Dr. Malone summarized his views last month at a valedictory gathering of M.I.T.'s initiative on Inventing the Organizations of the 21st Century, an extensive research effort he cofounded in 1994. The project (at the Web site ccs.mit.edu/21c) has drawn in two dozen scholars and numerous companies, with financing from British Telecommunications, A. T. Kearney, National Westminster Bank, Union Bank of Switzerland and a consortium of Norsk Hydro and other Norwegian business interests. Dr. Malone's talk in Wong Auditorium on the M.I.T. campus amounted to instructing the elephants on the mouse. The assemblage was mostly a roll call of big companies trying to peer over the horizon, among them Ford Motor, DaimlerChrysler, Fidelity Investments, State Farm, Polaroid, Intel, Sun Microsystems, Compaq Computer, PricewaterhouseCoopers, Andersen Consulting and the Naval Undersea Warfare Center. (One mouse in the crowd, tiny Sohodojo of Raleigh, N.C., billed itself as "a nanocorp" and lamented the tax disadvantages of working out of the home.) Dr. Malone's term is "the e-lance economy," a play on the word "freelance." He expects a business landscape in which much of the work that large corporations now do will be done instead by "temporary companies" -- ad hoc combinations of small specialist firms that come together to tackle a single project and disband upon its completion. At the heart of that economy will be a vast electronic marketplace in business services, already taking shape. Small companies will be able to rent the design, manufacturing and marketing muscle now available only to big businesses. Small talent pools will be free to focus on what they do best. Dr. Malone likes to talk about TopsyTail, a tiny Dallas-based producer of hair and fashion accessories founded a decade ago. Relying on a score of vendors, from demand forecasting through manufacturing and order fulfillment, TopsyTail has produced more than $100 million in sales at retail with three employees. "I am not good with employees, I am good with vendors," TopsyTail's energetic founder, Tomima Edmark, said in an interview on Monday. Outsourcing to the limit not only fits her managerial personality, she said. It also provides instant, inexpensive expertise in a consumer business where the race is always to the swift. Her next step is a Web store, HerRoom.com, to sell women's underwear online, starting in February. The seeds of an economy of microenterprises are everywhere. Dr. Malone sees them in the surge in outsourcing; in the popularity of telecommuting; in the proliferation of virtual companies; in the erosion of the Fortune 500 as the premier employer; in the legions of people who opt for freelance or part-time work. He sees the same trajectory inside large companies, which increasingly work through project teams, joint ventures, ad hoc alliances, internal markets and independent business units. In some familiar industries, the e-lance economy has long been the norm. "It is the way that films get made," Dr. Malone said. "It's also the way that we make buildings." Decades ago, the major Hollywood studios had everything under one roof. Today, a coalition of artistic and technical talents is assembled piece by piece. The studio does the financing and manages marketing and distribution. Almost everyone believes that the next century will see greater decentralization of business decision-making. There the debate begins. Will the Internet foster an economy of small enterprises, or will it make it possible to build a global empire far more extensive than anything known today? Is the prototype Edward Jones, the investment firm, with more than 5,000 local offices united by cutting-edge communications and an engrained culture of serving the careful long-term investor? Or is it the cottage industry of thousands of independent financial advisers who rely on Charles Schwab for their transaction needs and tap the Internet for endless sources of financial analysis? Many experts, including some at the M.I.T. conference, say that economies of scale and new efficiencies in harnessing corporate learning favor the larger-and-larger structure. They say that only the largest will be able to assemble and manage the costly information engines needed to power a global empire.  And huge companies like BP Amoco are devising new systems to organize and index the vast business savvy that exists within their ranks but today is tacit and untapped. "My bottom line is very simple -- if we look at 2010, we will find bigger organizations, bigger and bigger and bigger," John F. Rockart, the director of the Center for Information Systems Research at M.I.T., said in a video presentation at the conference. It used to be that the cost and sheer difficulty of communications increased geometrically with a company's size. But with more powerful electronics and better data management, "that's going away," Dr. Rockart said. "Size will no longer be an inhibitor." Dr. Malone contends that it is easier to think about flattening the corporate hierarchy by chopping away at middle management and empowering underlings -- all half-measures in his view -- than it is to grasp the workings of a vast network of many, many small players under no central direction or control. (Some people call that a market.) But his model of creativity and efficiency is not merely a leaner, flatter company. Instead, he said, consider the celebrated Linux operating system, which was developed and perfected by thousands of volunteers after Linus Torvalds posted his early efforts on the Internet and invited all and sundry to have a go at them. Or consider the Internet itself. Dr. Malone invariably draws smiles when he asks if the Internet could conceivably have been developed by AT&T, with the normal panoply of corporate procedures and clearances. "There's literally no one in charge of the Internet," he said at the conference, "no one who can shut it down, no one who can keep you from connecting with it." Fundamentally, it is a collection of interaction protocols, a set of rules for exchanging information. "Anyone who follows those rules can basically play any role they want." "No one controls the Internet," he wrote in the Harvard Business Review. "No one's in charge. No one's the leader. The Internet grew out of the combined efforts of all its users, with no central management. The Internet had to be self-managed." This is the idea: No one organization can match a thriving marketplace of ambitious talents for creativity and innovation. So why shouldn't a General Motors, instead of being wedded to its in-house battalions of engineers, open its needs to innumerable design enterprises from outside? That is the open architecture that propels Silicon Valley. Why not tap it to build cars? http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Thomas W. Malone, a thinker about the shape of the company and the workplace in the new century. (Rick Friedman for The New York Times)(pg. C14)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
True North will acquire Stein Rogan, a shop that specializes in digital communications companies.
body: AN agency company that was early to explore cyberspace is expanding again in the fast-growing realm of digital communications, acquiring a newyork shop specializing in online and offline advertising for dot-coms. True North Communications in Chicago, the world's No. 7 agency company with estimated billings of $12 billion, is buying Stein Rogan & Partners in newyork, which has estimated capitalized billings of $75 million from clients like Apartment.com, Blackboard.com, Cars.com, Flycast, Mail.com and FasTV.com. Stein Rogan, with 70 employees, will operate as an autonomous unit of True North, which also owns traditional agencies like FCB Worldwide, Bozell and Temerlin McClain. The top managers of Stein Rogan, which also has a small office in Chicago, will continue leading the agency. They include Tom Stein, president, and Mark Rogan, executive vice president and creative director. The deal for Stein Rogan, which started in 1986 as Stein Kilpatrick & Rogan, is indicative of the intensification of efforts by Madison Avenue to meet the challenges posed as the Internet remakes advertising, marketing and the media, particularly in competing against upstart startups. Giants like True North, the Omnicom Group, the Interpublic Group of Companies and the WPP Group are responding with strategies that range from acquisitions to investments in independent new-media shops to opening digital units within their traditional agencies. "Omnicom probably has the largest list of dot-com clients," said Michael J. Russell, an analyst who follows the advertising industry for Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in newyork, "but Bozell has Datek and FCB has Amazon.com." Omnicom and True North lead among the biggest agency companies in estimated revenue to be derived from dot-coms in 2000, by Mr. Russell's estimates, at about 3 percent of the total, compared with about 1 percent for the others. The mad dash to capitalize on the dot-coms is not limited to agencies. For instance, NBC, part of General Electric, is combining several of its online operations with the portal Web site Snap.com and Xoom.com, an electronic commerce company. The combined company, named NBCi, began trading yesterday on the Nasdaq Stock Market. The True North cyberholdings include R/GA Interactive and 50 percent of Modem Media.Poppe Tyson, the digital agency that began as two interactive units of FCB and Bozell before being combined and eventually sold in an initial public offering. And DoubleClick, the giant Web ad network, started in 1995 as the Internet sales group of Poppe Tyson. "With the explosion of e-commerce companies seeking to brand themselves online and offline, it's obvious not every one is going to win," said David Bell, chairman and chief executive at True North. "Tom and Mark are experts in placing their chips on those that are." Mr. Bell discussed the acquisition in an interview yesterday; the formal announcement is to be made today. Terms of the deal are not being disclosed, though recently agency acquisitions are being made for prices equal to about one year's revenue. Stein Rogan's 1998 revenue was $12 million and its revenue for the first six months of 1999 was $11 million, according to estimates by IQ Interactive News, a weekly supplement to the trade publications Adweek, Brandweek and Mediaweek. The 1999 figure placed the agency 24th among the top 50 interactive agencies ranked by the supplement. "We're ready to move on to bigger and better things," said Mr. Stein, 43, "and True North is going to help us get there." "We'd started out as a general advertising agency but took those capabilities and focused ourselves in 1995 as 'the information agency, using interactive media as a marketing venue," he added. "We saw an opportunity that today involves building brands in the Internet space in entertainment, education, finance, e-business of all sorts." "And there's going to be a tremendous continuing intensity of activity in that space," Mr. Stein predicted. "There will be not just a lot of dot-com advertising on the Super Bowl, but all through the first quarter." "I'm exaggerating a little bit to say one or two business models come across our desks every day," he added, "and every one we see is ramping up for 2000." Mr. Rogan, 44, echoed his colleague's optimism, but noted that the growing popularity of the Internet brings more dot-com campaigns, which makes it increasingly difficult "to break through the clutter." "So what you do for dot-com brands has to be done a lot smarter," he added, "and in Internet time." As an example, he cited the work Stein Rogan has produced for Cars.com, an automotive Web site operated by Classified Ventures, a consortium of large newspaper companies. The campaign sought to balance the needs of car shoppers with the needs of car dealers, who are the site's primary revenue source. "We needed to build a value proposition for Cars.com with consumers," Mr. Stein said, "but at the same time not alienate dealers, who pay the freight." So rather than proceed with a campaign carrying the theme "Drive home a better deal," the Cars.com ads carry this theme: "Car shopping the way it should be. Simple." And the offline ads for Cars.com, on television and in newspapers, "have the look and feel of the Web site," Mr. Rogan said, by including "a lot of screen shots" and even "duplicating the browser frame" computer users see. "The creatives fight that," he added, "saying, 'People know they're going on the Web.' But there's nothing wrong with a product demonstration." http://www.nytimes.com

title: What's in a Cybername? $7.5 Million For the Right Address - Correction Appended
body: In what is believed to be the highest price ever paid for an Internet address, a company here is paying $7.5 million for the rights to the domain name business.com. The price is more than twice the previous known record for an Internet domain name -- the $3.3 million the Compaq Computer Corporation paid last year to buy altavista.com, the name of its search engine. Compaq purchased the address from a man in San Jose, Calif., who had registered the name to use for his software company. The seller of business.com, a Houston entrepreneur named Marc Ostrofsky, bought the name in 1997 from an Internet service provider in Europe for $150,000. His sale today is the latest example of a kind of land-rush mentality on the Internet, in which speculators and entrepreneurs have been staking claims to domain names, the cyberspace equivalent of real estate, in hopes that the addresses will appreciate in value. The purchaser of the name business.com is Ecompanies, an "incubator" that aims to start numerous Internet companies. It will use the name for what it says will be a broad directory of Web services available to businesses that it plans to start next year. Jake Winebaum, a co-founder of Ecompanies, said the price was not too high for a brand name, given that Web-based companies are spending more than $1 million for a 30-second commercial during the Super Bowl to make their names known. "We actually think the name means a lot," said Mr. Winebaum, who ran the Walt Disney Company's Web business before starting Ecompanies earlier this year with Sky Dayton, the founder of Earthlink Network, an Internet service provider. "It captures what I think we're building," he added. "I would rather have it like that than trying to spend a lot to figure out what the brand stands for." Jaime Friedman, an Internet analyst with Goldman, Sachs, said business-to-business electronic commerce could be a $1.5 trillion business in five years. Given the potential, he said, "to have one of the marquis names in that business could be a favorable return on invested capital." But Allen Adamson, managing director of Landor Associates, a leading consultant on branding, said such generic names lack lasting value. "It's a huge amount of money for something that might be a commodity in six months," he said. "Owning generic domain names will not be a long-term play in branding and marketing." Anyone can register a domain name not already in use for $70 for two years from Network Solutions, a company chartered by the government to supervise the system. Speculators and entrepreneurs, sometimes called cybersquatters have taken to registering names that might be wanted by others in hope of selling them for a big profit. Some names are being sold through Web auction sites. But million-dollar deals are rare. The name wine.com was purchased for $3 million; Wallstreet.com for $1.03 million; and drugs.com for $823,000 according to GreatDomains.com, a Web site that provides a marketplace for buying and selling domain names. But most prices are far less. An entrepreneur in California demanded that Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company pay $75,000 for a name the brokerage firm wanted to use for its online stock trading service. Morgan Stanley offered to pay $10,000. Mr. Ostrofsky owns the Multimedia Publishing Corporation, which publishes telecommunications magazines and ran trade shows. He sold those businesses recently to Primedia for $35 million and said he planned to use that money to start Web companies. He was planning a business-oriented Internet site using business.com but also was willing to sell the name and shopped it around. "You've got to know when to hold them and when to fold them," he said, adding that he believed Mr. Winebaum would do a better job developing a Web site than he would.  He and Mr. Winebaum said there were several bidders for the domain, though they would not identify them. Mr. Ostrofsky, 38, said he owned more than 100 domain names, most obtained for just $70. When he paid the $150,000 for business.com, he said, "I had more than my fair share of people telling me I was out of my mind." Mr. Ostrofsky said he had previously sold the name eflowers.com to Flowers Direct for $25,000 plus 50 cents from every transaction made on the site. As part of the deal, Mr. Ostrofsky's wife will get flowers once a month for the rest of her life. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Business Day on Wednesday about the sale of the Internet domain name Business.com for $7.5 million and an article on June 5, 1997, about a previous sale of the name for $150,000, described the seller in the 1997 transaction incorrectly. The company, Business Systems International of London, installs corporate computer systems; it is not an Internet service provider or a software company. The 1997 error was discovered after a reader noted a discrepancy between the articles. Correction-Date: December 6, 1999, Monday

title: No More Giveaway Computers. Free-PC to BeBought by eMachines.
body: As it turns out, there is no such thing as a free PC. Free-PC.Com, one of the most audacious experiments in advertising, said yesterday that it would no longer give away computers and Internet access. Rather it has agreed to be acquired by eMachines, a maker of low-cost personal computers that intends to use Free-PC's software to put advertising on the screens of its computers and to collect data about what users do. Free-PC's original business plan was to give away computers in exchange for being allowed to send on-screen ads to its users and to gather data about users' Internet surfing and PC use habits. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. Both Free-PC and eMachines are private, although eMachines has filed for a public offering that it hopes to complete early next year. The sale reflects a sharp turn around for Bill Gross, the chairman of IdeaLab, a Pasadena, Calif., company that has been involved in dozens of Internet start-ups, including eToys, Goto.Com and Ticketmaster-Citysearch, as well as Free-PC. Mr. Gross, a peripatetic entrepreneur, once boasted that Free-PC would someday be bigger than Microsoft, according to people he had tried to recruit as investors. His idea was to turn the computer from an appliance into an advertising-sponsored medium, much like network television. To get a computer from Free-PC, users were to fill out a detailed financial and demographic survey. Strips on two sides of the screen were always filled with advertising. And everything done with the computer, including which Internet sites were used, would be monitored so that advertisers could aim ads specifically. Analysts said that Free-PC needed to take in $30 a month per user in advertising to cover the cost of providing the computer and Internet access. That is a high hurdle, particularly with such a small base of users. More than a million people applied to get the free PC's, but as of yesterday the company had delivered only 30,000 machines. Mr. Gross said that he had not been looking to sell the company, but that when eMachines approached him he decided that selling would be more lucrative than a business model that was developing very slowly. "We believed that to get the business model to work we needed at least one million users," he said. "We were scaling as fast as we could, but at 10,000 a quarter, we couldn't get to one million fast enough." In the year since it sold its first computer, eMachines has become one of the largest PC makers in the country by focusing on machines in the $400 to $800 price range. Since several Internet service providers are now offering $400 rebates for people who commit themselves to three-year contracts, its lowest-cost models appear to be free. Of course, the user then must typically pay $22 a month for Internet service. Free PC's Internet service was also free. Stephen A. Dukker, the founder and chief executive of eMachines, said the company had no interest in giving away computers. "Our business model has caused people like Packard Bell and I.B.M. to throw in the towel," he said, alluding to recent decisions by those companies to pull out of the low-end PC market. In October, eMachines was the No. 3 computer maker, after Compaq Computer and Hewlett-Packard, with 12.4 percent of the market, according to PC Data. From the start, eMachines assumed that the market for computers would come to resemble wireless telephones, where the phone is typically given away and subsidized by the monthly fees. But in recent months, it shifted its strategy to focus more on opportunities to use computers as an advertising medium. Already, it charges advertisers to put icons on the computer desktop or even buttons on the keyboard that link to a certain Web site. Now, eMachines will use the Free-PC software to place advertising on users' screens as well. The advertising will take up less screen space than it does on the Free-PC computers, and in contrast to the Free-PC arrangement, users will have the option to not see the advertising. EMachines hopes, however, that they will keep the ads in place by linking them to a "tool bar" with buttons that will make it easy for new users to navigate the Internet. This software, moreover, will send data about the computer users back to eMachines to use for advertising selection. The company declined to say what data would be collected but said that at first it would be less than Free-PC gathered. Ultimately, however, eMachines says it hopes to persuade at least some users to allow their activities to be monitored. Indeed, even if the user does not agree to have any data collected or any advertising on the screen, eMachines will still be able to profit. Whenever the user connects to the Internet, its software will still be able to place new advertising icons on the desktop or to change the advertiser linked to each keyboard button. The company is largely controlled by two Korean electronics makers, the TriGem Corporation and Korea Data Systems. In the first half of the year, it lost $3.9 million on sales of $351 million. http://www.nytimes.com

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Stock Market's Success May Hinder Future Rally With about a month left in the millennium, the three main stock gauges are poised to record annual returns of more than 10 percent each for the fifth consecutive year -- an unprecedented streak. But the wealth generated by those gains may also pose the biggest threat to a repeat performance in 2000. If the gauges keep rising, some economists argue, the stock market will continue to fuel consumer spending, which could prompt the Federal Reserve to raise short-term interest rates. Higher rates could spook equity investors if they conclude that the economy and earnings growth will finally slow significantly. Market Place.  Page C8. Music TV Shows May Have Peaked The enthusiasm for music-based television mini-series is starting to cool, largely because the most ambitious music project this fall was undone by ABC's rampaging -- and inexpensive -- "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire" game show. CBS promoted "Shake, Rattle and Roll," a fictionalized journey through the early rock 'n' roll years, heavily and scheduled it on the first Sunday in November. But "Millionaire" pushed the mini-series to a poor first-hour rating, and the show never recovered. CBS has no music-based movie projects on its development slate, although NBC has "The 70's" ready for May. And it may commission a film on the 50's rocker Little Richard.  C19.  The Architect of a Wireless Empire Christopher Gent, the chief executive of Vodafone AirTouch, has moved with dizzying speed to fulfill his vision of a company that would operate the world's largest wireless network, positioning it smartly for the future. But his hostile offer for Mannesmann was rejected by the company's supervisory board.  C2.  Online Ad Crowd for Super Bowl The scramble by Internet companies to increase recognition of their brand names by advertising in traditional media outlets will accelerate on Super Sunday. Dot-coms are paying record prices -- an estimated average of more than $2 million for each 30-second commercial during the Super Bowl, which is at least 25 percent higher than the 1999 rate. Stuart Elliott: Advertising.  C22.  Hanson of Britain Bids for Pioneer Hanson, the British building-materials producer, said that it had offered to buy Pioneer International of Australia for $2.51 billion to strengthen its global position.  C5.  Dispute Over Customized Music A growing number of Web sites are offering customized music programming. What the listeners are not hearing is a behind-the-scenes dispute between the sites and record labels over how much these sites should reimburse record labels each time they play recordings owned by the labels. Fallout From 'Y2K: The Movie' After the broadcast of "Y2K: The Movie," in which computing's millennium glitch leads to industrial apocalypse and sets off a nuclear meltdown, a manager at Charles Schwab in San Francisco rushed to calm the gullible. In an email memo to employees, a manager involved with Schwab's Year 2000 preparedness effort, assured employees the Year 2000 movie "would not be the typical scenario."
