title: Cisco to Offer More Details On WirelessTechnology
body: A new wireless technology is about to join the contest to provide high-speed Internet connections to homes and businesses. Cisco Systems, a leading Internet technology company, plans to brief analysts and reporters on Wednesday about a new approach to wireless communications that would be offered as soon as next year to provide both voice telephone service and Internet access. The technology is meant to be a nonmobile -- or fixed -- wireless alternative to the telephone industry's high-speed digital phone lines and cable television industry's Internet modems. Cisco's briefing will be the first detailed plans to follow an announcement last month by the company, Motorola and 10 other equipment makers and service providers who said they would create an industry-standard format for sending Internet data over a long-existing, little-used set of microwave frequencies. That frequency band, known as multichannel multipoint distribution services, or M.M.D.S., was set aside years ago for a form of wireless subscription television that was meant to compete with cable television but never really caught on. More recently, M.M.D.S. has been seen as a way for telecommunications giants like Sprint and MCI Worldcom to compete with the regional Bell operating companies to provide direct connections to local telephone customers. Now Cisco and other equipment makers are trying to push M.M.D.S. into a full-blown voice and Internet-access technology. Use of the M.M.D.S. frequencies requires licenses from the Federal Communications Commission. But the commission has also set aside wireless frequencies in a band called the Unlicensed National Information Infrastructure. This second, unlicensed frequency band is meant to encourage experimental uses of the airwaves without the expense of buying or applying for licenses. Because Cisco's technology will also work with this unlicensed band, the company predicts that smaller Internet service providers and communications companies will be able to quickly enter and compete in the market for high-speed -- or broad band -- Internet access at relatively low cost. "Fixed broad-band wireless access will change the world of telecommunications as profoundly as mobile telephony," said Dale R. Pfau, a financial analyst at CIBC World Markets in San Francisco. Cisco executives predicted that consumers would be able to buy broad band wireless transmitter-receivers -- known as transceivers -- for less than $500 by the end of 2000. At the heart of the Cisco-led alliance's plans is a new wireless approach developed by a Silicon Valley designer, which deals with a thorny problem known as "multipath interference" that has long bedeviled communications engineers. At certain frequencies, wireless communications systems must contend with echoes from secondary signals that are reflected from buildings or hills and that arrive at the receiver slightly after the original signals. Television broadcasts, for example, have long been plagued by the phenomenon, commonly known as ghosting. The problem became an intriguing challenge to Greg Raleigh, a longtime Silicon Valley engineer, who in the early 1990's returned to Stanford University to study for an advanced degree. Mr. Raleigh realized that with the vast amounts of computer power now available to perform signal processing it would be possible to transform multipath interference from a disadvantage into a benefit. Mr. Raleigh knew that, besides ghosting, there is typically a second drawback to fixed wireless communications: reliable transmissions require a clear line of sight between the transmitter and the receiver. That requirement poses special challenges to network designers attempting to reach tens of thousands of receivers in an urban area. But by using special encoding techniques, Mr. Raleigh reasoned, it might be possible to offer reliable two-way communications that would not require direct lines of site, but would instead use ghosting echoes as intentional signal paths rather than treating them as unwanted interference. With two of his Stanford classmates, Mr. Raleigh founded a company, Clarity Wireless, in an extra room in his home. There, they developed his theory into a technology called vector orthogonal frequency division multiplexing, or V.O.F.D.M. Cisco acquired Clarity Wireless in 1998 and recently decided to freely share its technology in an effort to quickly establish it as an industry standard. So far, besides Motorola, Cisco has secured commitments from Toshiba, Samsung, Texas Instruments and others to help develop components of the broad band wireless infrastructure. Cisco's is not the only approach in the M.M.D.S. broad-band data market, however. The company's wireless competitors will include Spike Technologies, ADC Telecommunications and Adaptive Broadband. But Cisco's prominence as an Internet technology vendor, along with the powerful alliance it has built, could give the company an inside edge, some analysts said. "There is no real leader as yet, but Cisco has quite a strong story," said Tim Luke, a financial analyst at Lehman Brothers in newyork. Still, some telecommunications analysts point out that M.M.D.S. occupies a relatively limited frequency band. That means, they say, that communications carriers would need to set up a large number of transmitters in order to subdivide a metropolitan area into numerous cells to allow the same channels to be reused in different parts of the region. Cisco executives nevertheless contend that broad-band fixed wireless technology can be a cost-effective alternative to cable modems and digital phone lines in urban areas. As for rural areas, Cisco says that broadband wireless will hold dramatic advantages over traditional wired or fiber optic networks, which can be costly ways to provide service in sparsely settled places. Certainly the Cisco alliance, if its technology proves viable, will be in a position to compete for the many companies and consumers that seem to have developed an insatiable appetite for Internet data communications bandwidth. Service providers like Winstar, Nextlink and Teligent have already developed a significant business providing so-called point-to-point broad-band wireless communications in urban areas. Those services permit corporations and buildings in urban areas to bypass local telephone and fiber optic communications links and connect directly to Internet providers or long-distance carriers or to connect to another branch office in the same metropolitan area. Cisco intends to make these point-to-point customers the first target for its new V.O.F.D.M. technology. In fact, later this month the company will begin selling a high-speed wireless system that will permit companies to extend communications between buildings over relatively short distances. The point-to-point wireless microwave equipment market, according to Mr. Pfau of CIBC World Markets, was about $2.56 billion in 1998 and is expected to grow to $5 billion by 2003. The more versatile point-to-multipoint market, which will develop for consumer and commercial applications, is forecast to grow to $3 billion in 2004 from less than $200 million next year. Mr. Raleigh, of Cisco, said that he believed the Cisco technology had a promising commercial future in part because of new radio spectrum that will be made available for interactive data applications. In Europe, for example, there will be soon be an auction for radio spectrum at the 3.5 gigahertz frequencies. Meanwhile, in the unitedstates, the Federal Communication Commission plans to auction spectrum for interactive data in the frequency band that until now has been used solely for ultrahigh frequency, or UHF, television.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
Internet Law Expert Returns to Antitrust Case
body: He's back. Lawrence Lessig, a 38-year-old Harvard professor and Internet law expert, has been recruited for the Microsoft antitrust case once again. When Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson prodded the two sides toward settlement talks and appointed a mediator on Nov. 18, he also said he wanted Mr. Lessig to write a friend-of-the-court brief on his behalf on the issue of technological tying. Mr. Lessig was removed from the case last year, after serving three months as a special master -- an outside expert with a broad mandate. Microsoft had protested, saying Mr. Lessig had a "clear bias" against the company. Without addressing the bias claim, an appeals court removed Mr. Lessig, ruling that the case was not an appropriate one for a special master. This time, Microsoft has not yet said whether it will object to Mr. Lessig. Reached last week in Berlin, where he has a research fellowship, Mr. Lessig said he was eager to weigh in on the subject of so-called product tying, which he called "the toughest issue in the case." Judge Jackson asked him to write a 50-page paper on it. The Government has accused Microsoft of tying its Internet browser to its monopoly product, the Windows operating system, in an illegal tactic to stifle competition. In his findings of fact on Nov. 5, Judge Jackson echoed the government's accusation. But antitrust experts say the tying issue could be vulnerable on appeal, and that an appeals court in a related case last year said Microsoft should be free to fold browsing software into Windows if there was a "plausible claim" of consumer benefit. Mr. Lessig isn't saying, but antitrust experts expect him to make the intellectual case for taking software tying seriously. "Code is law" is the Lessig refrain. In his new book, "Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace" (Basic Books), he suggests that the technological architecture of software is an appropriate subject for government scrutiny, though traditional regulation would be misguided. "My argument is not for some top-down form of control," he writes. "My claim is not that regulators should occupy Microsoft." Mr. Lessig's views are difficult to dismiss as simply anti-Microsoft. He gives more weight to the competition Microsoft faces, for example, than did Judge Jackson -- who found that the Linux operating system was a fringe technology and not likely to challenge Microsoft anytime soon. "By 1998," Mr. Lessig writes, "it had become apparent to all that Linux was an important competitor to the Microsoft operating system."   STEVE LOHR http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Lawrence Lessig, a professor at Harvard University.

title:
E-Commerce Report;
Nightmares Before Christmas
body: FOR many Internet retailers, success this holiday shopping season rests on the shoulders of the customer service team or the technical support staff -- whose job it is to keep a Web site from crashing. But for executives of Bluefly.com, a discount apparel merchant, success rides on the back of a Himalayan mountain goat -- the source of Pashmina. Pashmina has turned to be the season's must-have fabric -- a cashmere blended with silk to produce shawls and scarves of great warmth, and even greater cachet. Bluefly executives had decided to build the site's holiday promotions around their Pashmina items, but they hit a slight snag when, two weeks ago, they sold out. "Everyone's walking around asking when the Pashmina's coming in because everything's on hold until then," said Jonathan Morris, Bluefly's executive vice president. "It's like the Furby of the fashion world." Such glitches are but one version of the nightmares before Christmas that may be haunting many an e-commerce executive the next month. Some Internet retailers, including Toys "R" Us, have already had problems on their sites, while others are struggling to fill open seams in their order processing and customer service systems. But ready or not, the e-tailing rush is under way. Internet shopping surveys indicate that online holiday spending started in earnest the 10 days before Thanksgiving. Forecasts call for more than 20 million holiday shoppers to click up $6 billion or more in purchases: triple last year's holiday total. And while retailers focus on this year's action, they know that any breakdowns will jeopardize next year's sales. Last Friday, some Web sites were already straining to keep up with demand. KBkids.com, a partnership of KB Toys and BrainPlay.com turned away some shoppers because it was overloaded for parts of the day. And both eToys and Amazon.com said they were already out of some Pokemon toys. "The difference between Christmas '98 and '99 online is that last year, there were simple failures, like sites not working properly, that consumers were relatively O.K. with because everyone had the same problems," said Ford Cavallari, executive vice president of Renaissance Worldwide, a strategy consulting firm. "This year consumers expect more, and a lot of sites won't be able to deliver." While nearly every e-commerce executive interviewed acknowledges losing sleep over holiday-shopping jitters, the ones with the worst insomnia are probably the retailers who are entering their first season. "The first thing that pops me out of bed in a bad dream is a major critical system failure where the site goes boom," said Michael Clebnik, chief executive of BuyItOnline.com, a new online mall. "I think that's true for any company that's going through its growth stages like us, where we're not in a financial position to spend tens of millions to say 'Here, buy as many servers as you need so we can scale to the size of Yahoo.' " Mr. Clebnik, who began operations in May, said he planned to add servers -- the workhorse computers that support the site -- in sufficient numbers to ensure a 50 percent buffer between peak traffic and total system capacity. He has also set up a backup database for customer order and billing information, in case the first database fizzles. "We have to do it," he said. "Any loss of confidence in our system is critical." Even for more experienced e-commerce sites, like Garden.com, this is a worry. Garden.com, a purveyor of cut flowers and gardening supplies, has three holiday seasons under its belt. But this year the company has added more sophisticated features to its site -- like the ability to recognize each returning customer and display a personalized page. "So not only is our traffic going up, but what customers do while they're on the site is hitting our database more," said Cliff Sharples, Garden.com's chief executive, adding that the company spent between $2 million and $3 million in August for a systems upgrade to handle the increased usage. John Hnanicek, chief information officer of eToys, said his company spent "in the seven figures" last month on a system that gauges the site's performance every 20 seconds, and alerts executives to any performance lags. "It lets me sleep well because I know I'll get a phone call if there's anything to worry about," he said. So far, at least, there have been no nocturnal calls. More pressing for Mr. Hnanicek and others, perhaps, is the issue of so-called fulfillment -- actually processing and shipping what the customer has ordered. According to Jupiter Communications, the top Internet retailers can each expect to process 58,000 orders each day, and they will have to impress upon warehouse workers the urgency of picking, packing and shipping as if the entire business were at stake. Instilling that sense of mission can be difficult, however, when the fulfillment workers are third-party vendors, as is so often the case with e-commerce companies. "That's one of the fun things about eToys," said Mr. Hnanicek, who spoke from Fingerhut's Provo, Utah, warehouse, which handles a large percentage of eToys's shipments. "When we talk to the staff here, we can ascribe a little higher meaning to the stuff we sell, because they're bringing Christmas to kids. It's not like we're selling auto parts." Mr. Morris, of Bluefly, which is based in newyork, said his site's fulfillment and marketing anxieties should subside within a week, when a shipment of several thousand Pashmina scarves and shawls is expected to arrive at the Chicago company, Marketing Out of the Box, that handles Bluefly's fulfillment. Beyond that, he said he is most concerned about preparing the customer service staff -- "especially in the early in the season, because there's a chance for repeat purchase and good word-of-mouth." Accordingly, Bluefly's 10 full-time and three part-time customer service representatives will be bolstered by employees from other departments to cover the expected 400 daily inquiries by telephone and email during the holiday rush. "Don't be surprised if you call customer service and I pick up the phone," Mr. Morris said. "I'm not sure you want that, but it may happen." Within the realms of fulfillment, customer service and site performance, there is an almost endless list of places where a site can fail, said Mr. Cavallari, of Renaissance Worldwide. He cited at least a dozen areas of vulnerability, including the failure of systems to allow an order to be modified once it has been placed. Another shortcoming is the inability of many sites to recognize when a customer has typed a zip code that either does not exist or does not correspond to the shipping address. Most alarming, perhaps, is the fact that in the age of "fully-integrated, end-to-end software solutions," some sites are still typing in customer orders by hand. "You'd be surprised at how many sites are rekeying data," said Mr. Cavallari. "At least half of all commerce sites are duct-taped and glued in a similar manner." While new e-commerce companies can expect to suffer from rookie mistakes, traditional retailers are not invulnerable. "A lot of older retailers with 10-year old warehouse database systems are trying to link their Web pages to them, and they're using the duct tape and glue approach," Mr. Cavallari said. Given that approach and the difficulty of keeping up with every aspect of critical systems, he said, "It's scary when you think about all the places where a site can break down." Hilary Billings, chief executive of RedEnvelope.com, an online gift retailer founded in 1997 and formerly known as 911Gifts.com, said to gird against any last-minute failures the company recently simulated a peak traffic day. She declined to provide specifics, other than to say that the test went well. "Now we just have to do it when the real peak day comes," she said. Ms. Billings expects that day to be Monday, Dec. 20, as last-minute shoppers try to beat the express-delivery deadlines. To handle the strain, Ms. Billings said the company had sought to inject as much flexibility into its systems as possible. "We can get more fulfillment space, more customer service reps, and more inventory if we need to," she said, noting that the site can serve 10 times the number of visitors it served last year. "Still, this is the scariest holiday season I've ever faced in my history as a retailer," said Ms. Billings, who previously worked seven years for Pottery Barn's catalog and retail operation. "There are just so many unknowns." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The busiest online retailers can each expect to process 58,000 orders a day in the holiday shopping rush. Brenda Bowers, an eToys employee, wraps a gift that has been ordered by a customer over the Internet. (George Frey for The newyork Times)(pg. C16)  Drawing (Tom Bloom)(pg. C1)

title: Internet Equipment Maker Planning to Make a $4.3 Billion Acquisition
body: Redback Networks, a maker of equipment to help Internet service providers transmit data more easily, is acquiring Siara Systems for about $4.3 billion in stock, company executives said yesterday. Redback makes a box called a subscriber management system that helps Internet service providers -- like telephone companies and cable operators -- send data quickly over high-speed broad band networks. In buying Siara Systems, Redback hopes that the optical networking equipment and software Siara is developing will turn Redback into one of the first one-stop shops for products needed to run the next generation of computer networks. Optical networking, which makes it easier to send more information quickly across broad band networks, is all the rage among technology companies in Silicon Valley. Some of those companies are paying astonishing prices for enterprises that have no products or revenues but that hold promise in the race to offer high-speed Internet access to homes and businesses. Cisco Systems, for one, raised eyebrows recently when it agreed to buy the Cerent Corporation and Monterey Networks, two networking concerns, in deals with a combined value of more than $7.5 billion. And several public companies are already developing products in this field, too, including Sycamore Networks. "We're all taken aback by where the valuations are," said Dennis Barsema, Redback's chief executive. "Cisco's payment for Cerent was sort of a new benchmark." But what Redback is really paying for is talent -- 170 engineers -- and the promise that their ideas will be more market-worthy than those of their competitors. Siara sells no products but is expected to begin testing some in the middle of 2000. "Redback is a very bold company," said Mr. Barsema, who will remain as chief executive in the combined company. "We think this is a key strategic move to broaden the reach into the new access market." Redback, which is based in Sunnyvale, Calif., recently sold shares in one of the most watched initial public offerings of the year. On Friday, Redback's stock closed down $3.1875 a share, at $137.375, in Nasdaq trading. A combination with Siara, a privately held company based in Mountain View, Calif., would give it a market value of $11.2 billion and, Mr. Barsema said, increase the available market for the combined company's products 10 times. Siara was formed in July 1998 by a group of engineers who had left Cerent. During the last 16 months, Siara has hired 170 engineers and several high-level executives from competitors like Lucent Technologies, Cisco, Advanced Micro Devices and Nortel Networks. One of Siara's first proponents was Vinod Khosla, a general partner of Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers, the venture capital firm, and co-founder of Sun Microsystems, who will become a director of the combined company. Mr. Khosla has had a golden touch this year. Not only was he the driving force behind Cisco's acquisition of Cerent, but he was also a key supporter of Juniper Networks, a maker of telecommunications gear. "A couple of years ago, we adapted a vision of how to build a next-generation network," he said in an interview yesterday. "So we started building these companies around how we thought networks should be built. The fact that they are valuable is because they had one, two, three years of development. Now that vision is being validated." Executives for the two companies began negotiating their agreement three weeks ago, though Mr. Bersema said they had previously discussed a merger as much as nine months ago. One of the key things that Vivek Ragavan, chief executive of Siara, said he wanted to ensure, though, was that his executives be treated as equals in any transaction. He said that access to Redback would give his company a better idea on about how to develop products that customers can use. The combined company will keep the Redback name; Mr. Ragavan will be named president of the combined operation. Once the merger is complete, Redback shareholders will own 62 percent of the new company and Siara stakeholders will own 38 percent. The boards of both companies have approved the transaction. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MEDIA;
Web Sites and Recording Labels at Impasse on Fees
body: A growing number of Web sites are offering customized music programming -- song sets created in response to the personal tastes of listeners. What the listeners are not hearing is a behind-the-scenes dispute between the sites and major record labels, in which tens of millions of dollars may be at stake. The basic issue is how much these Web sites should reimburse record labels each time they play recordings owned by the labels. Months of discussions between trade groups representing the two sides recently petered out, so the issue is set for arbitration next year. Meanwhile, some Webcasters have been negotiating individual royalty licenses with the recording industry. Because the sites are permitted to continue playing music until arbitration is completed, the issue may seem insignificant to the growing number of Internet listeners. But the question may not be so insignificant to investors in the Web sites, which include Launch Media, NetRadio, SonicNet (owned by Viacom's MTV) and Spinner.com (owned by America Online). The royalty fees paid to the record industry ultimately could become a substantial business expense. The stage for the royalty dispute was set in late 1998, when Congress passed and President Clinton signed the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. Like broadcast radio stations, Webcasters are required to pay licensing fees to copyright owners through Ascap or BMI, which collect royalties. But on the assumption that digital distribution raises additional intellectual property issues because it allows for high-quality copying, the new law requires Webcasters to pay a licensing fee to record labels that is not required of broadcasters. The law did not set a rate for royalty payments by the Internet companies but did provide for arbitration if the two sides could not reach an agreement. Trade groups for both sides say the negotiations, which began early this year, never went much beyond exploratory talks. Now, the two sides are scheduled to file position papers next month with a three-person arbitration panel to be appointed by the unitedstates Copyright Office. A request by the recording industry for a deadline extension, filed last week, is still pending. People involved in the discussions between individual Web sites and record companies have said the royalty percentages being asked by the labels range as high as 15 percent of a site's gross revenues. Lobbyists for the Web sites say they are arguing for as low as 1 to 2 percent. There are also open questions about how a Web site would even measure revenue for purposes of royalty payments -- whether the count would include advertising, transactions or subscription revenue, or some combination of the three. Steven M. Marks, senior vice president for business affairs for the Recording Industry Association of America, which is representing major record labels, declined to say what percentage the industry hopes to secure in the arbitration process. But he said the figure should reflect the music's value to the Web sites. "They're paying for the right to build a business using the content that's been created by record companies and artists," Mr. Marks said. The Web companies, meanwhile, contend that they already are putting money in the pockets of the recording industry because they are helping to spur album sales. Further, the sites argue that the royalties should only be paid on revenue directly related to the use of a copyrighted song, such as from a banner advertisement displayed while a song is played. "We're paying for a performance right, we're not paying for the right to be in business," said Jonathan Potter, director of the Digital Media Association, a trade group that includes many of the large music Webcasters. Mr. Potter said the recording industry had approached individual Webcasters asking for 15 percent of gross revenues. What both sides agree upon is that customized, Internet-based "radio" is a growing force. The concept is that Web sites poll listeners for their music preferences, both artist and genre. The sites then create hundreds of radio "stations," each reflecting the musical tastes of a narrow category of visitors to their sites. The categories listed under Vintage Rock on Spinner.com, for example, include British invasion, psychedelic and surf. A survey published two weeks ago indicates that online radio listening is popular among college students.  Webnoize, an online publication covering the new media music industry, found that of 4,000 students surveyed, 63.4 percent were interested in Internet radio for niche programming. "There's going to be a great demand for these services," said Joanne Marino, editor in chief of Webnoize, who said Web communities like Yahoo or Geocities may find it necessary to add a personalized radio component to compete. Mr. Marks from the Recording Industry Association of America, said the record industry had signed "many" licensing deals with Webcasting companies, but declined to provide a figure. The association provided the name of only one company with which it had reached a deal: Musicmusicmusic Inc., which operates a service called RadioMoi. Besides that agreement, Mr. Potter of the Digital Music Association said he knew of no other such licensing deals yet. He contends that the record industry wants to make it seem that more deals have been signed to induce Webcasters to negotiate individually, rather than as a group through arbitration. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Arbitration over royalty fees has been scheduled for next year between Web sites that play music over the Internet and record labels.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
The Super Bowl is attracting a crowd of new competitors.
body: IF Beethoven were commissioned to rewrite his Fifth Symphony for Super Bowl XXXIV, he would undoubtedly begin this way: "Dot, dot, dot, com. Dot, dot, dot, com." The mad scramble by Internet companies to increase recognition of their brand names by advertising in traditional media outlets will accelerate on Super Sunday, typically the biggest day of the year for Madison Avenue. Dot-coms are paying record prices -- an estimated average of more than $2 million for each 30-second commercial during the game, which is at least 25 percent higher than the 1999 rate -- to elbow their way into the ranks of mainstay Super Bowl advertisers like automobiles, beers, credit cards and soft drinks. For the first time, a dot-com, the E*Trade Group, will even sponsor the halftime show, until now the province of purveyors of prosaic products like lunch meat. "The dot-coms need to generate awareness and attention, to introduce themselves to the public, to get noticed by Wall Street," said Joe Mandese, editor of The Myers Report, a media industry newsletter. "What better way to do that than the ultimate advertising event?" To be sure, the big gamble by the dot-coms that the exposure gained during the game on Jan. 30 will be worth the expense could be proved wrong. If the performance of their pitches is deemed sufficiently weak, what was intended as a shrewd business move could backfire badly. Not only might those dot-coms not be back for Super Bowl XXXV, they might not be in business by then either. "There's going to be a major-league shakeout," said Gene DeWitt, president and chief executive at DeWitt Media in newyork, which buys commercial time and ad space for advertisers. "They all seem to have decided it's live or die, spending gobs of money," he added. "There's a kind of desperation to it." Of the estimated 30 companies buying commercial time during the game, which will be broadcast by ABC, a dozen or so will be dot-coms. That is four times as many as last year. In fact, that is more than have appeared during all previous Super Bowls combined. The estimated 125 million American viewers of Super Bowl XXXIV will see commercials for companies like Angeltips.com, Computer.com, Kforce.com, Ourbeginning.com, Pets.com and Screaming Media, all seeking to draw traffic to their Web sites or sell various online goods and services. "The Super Bowl is the one time of the year when the viewers look forward to the commercials," said Jon Mandel, co-managing director at Mediacom in newyork, the media services arm of Grey Advertising. "It's a one-of-a-kind event," he added, "reaching everybody: men, women, children, pets. If you're trying to stand out, it's the place to be." Grey is creating a Super Bowl commercial for Kforce.com, a job search Web site owned by Romac International that is formally known as the Knowledge Force Network. "It's a very intense, hyperconcentrated atmosphere for these companies, some of which you've heard of and some of which are coming in cold," said Ted Sann, co-chief executive and chief creative officer at BBDO newyork, part of the BBDO Worldwide unit of the Omnicom Group, which will create Super Bowl work for the Charles Schwab online brokerage division as well as advertisers without dots like Federal Express, PepsiCo and Visa. "There's a potential for confusion because the dot-com category will be so cluttered, so they're going to have to differentiate themselves on the spot," he added. "If they don't have an execution that's incredibly good, absolutely riveting, they'll just be throwing the money away." And what money it is. The estimated average of more than $2 million for each 30 seconds of commercial time compares with the estimated average of $1.6 million charged by the News Corporation's Fox Broadcasting unit for each 30-second spot during Super Bowl XXXIII. "If ABC could add a fifth quarter, they'd do it," Mr. DeWitt said. Because of the demand from dot-coms, as well as the overall strength of the advertising market, commercial time during the game is almost sold out, though nine weeks remain before kickoff. Reflecting that bull market, ABC is selling some of the last commercial slots left for prices estimated at $3 million each. "The dot-coms recognize they need that quick and effective reach to drive people to their sites," said Marv Goldsmith, president for sales and marketing at the ABC Television Network in newyork, part of the ABC unit of the Walt Disney Company. "And several are coming in on a competitive basis, reacting to each other." For instance, besides the Kforce job search Web site, which is a newcomer to the Super Bowl, two other job-search sites are buying spots -- Hotjobs.com and Monster.com, part of TMP Worldwide. Both are returning from last year. "It's obvious why we're back: the Super Bowl really worked for us," said Dean Harris, senior vice president for marketing at Hotjobs.com in newyork. "It drew traffic to our site and grew our business." But this year will be tougher. "Last year, people hadn't been asked to remember as many dot-com brands," said Edward Boches, chief creative officer at Mullen Advertising in Wenham, Mass., Monster.com's agency that is part of the Lowe Group unit of the Interpublic Group of Companies. "Now it won't be as easy as putting a name up on the screen with a dot-com after it." "You're going to have to give people a real reason why, make them take a course of action," said Mr. Boches, whose agency is also creating a spot for Oxygen Media, a Web site and cable TV network aimed at women. "That puts more pressure on the advertising." Julie Wainwright, chief executive at Pets.com in San Francisco, said, "You have to have a strategy, a point of differentiation." The commercial for Pets.com by the San Francisco office of TBWA/Chiat/Day, part of the TBWA Worldwide unit of Omnicom, will emphasize the Web site's breadth of merchandise as well as its mascot, a sock-puppet dog. The creative content of most dot-com commercials tends to be frenetic, cheeky, sometimes deliberately provocative, to help the spots stand out. That affects not only the other dot-coms but also other advertisers. "When you know the commercials will be interesting, different, contemporary, exciting, it keeps you on your toes," said Tony Ponturo, vice president for media and sports marketing at Anheuser-Busch in St. Louis, which for the 12th consecutive year will be the exclusive beer advertiser during the Super Bowl. "It makes you lean forward and make sure you're sharp as well. "Our estimates are that there's $500 million to $700 million of dot-com money in the marketplace," he added. "That's huge, more than the beer category." If by some chance the commercials for brews like Budweiser and Bud Light fare poorly with viewers and critics on Jan. 30, Anheuser-Busch will open for business come Jan. 31. That may not be true for some dot-coms. "There'll be smart money out there and there'll be dumb money out there," said Michael Sievert, vice president for marketing at E*Trade in Menlo Park, Calif. "Unlike the 'newbie' entrants in the dot-com marketing craze, our approach is investment, not expenditures. "The dot-com clutter in some cases helps us because we're one of the top four e-commerce brands," he added. "The more focus and attention on the Internet space, the more focus and attention there is on the leaders." E*Trade will spend an estimated $3.8 million on its halftime show sponsorship and accompanying commercials by Goodby, Silverstein & Partners in San Francisco, part of Omnicom. "We all have a concern whether or not this pays off," acknowledged Jorge Cauz, senior vice president for Britannica.com in Chicago, which will run a Super Bowl spot created by Deutsch Inc. in newyork. "But we feel we're taking a calculated risk." He added: "Most dot-com brands were not here two years ago, a year ago, the day before yesterday. We have a brand that's 231 years old, so we're not coming to the dot-com environment as a fly-by-night. The fact we're Britannica will make people ask 'What are they doing on the Internet?' " Whither the clamor for Super Bowl commercial time if the dot-com boom goes bust? What primarily determines whether rates rise or fall is the health of the general economy. And for now at least, as Mr. Mandese noted, "there's still huge demand from existing advertisers" like "direct-to-consumer pharmaceuticals, telecommunications and financial companies." CBS, which is to broadcast the Super Bowl in January 2001, has traded equity stakes in several dot-coms for commercial time. Some of those spots could certainly run during Super Bowl XXXV. That inspired Mr. Mandese to predict "the first deal for an advertiser to trade equity to a network specifically for a Super Bowl spot." And of course, Super Bowl mishaps are not confined to dot-coms. Take Just for Feet, a retail chain that was a first-time Super Bowl advertiser last January. Its commercial was roundly criticized as offensive. Then problems like an ill-timed expansion and changes in footwear fashion led the company to file for Federal bankruptcy protection. The result: the first Super Bowl spot from Just for Feet may very well have been its last. "You don't have to be a dot-com to be stupid," said Mr. DeWitt of DeWitt Media. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Dot-coms Take the Field" Dot-com advertisers will be blitzing the Super Bowl the same way they have been recently flooding other television programming. A dozen or so dot-coms have been identified thus far as buyers of commercial time during Super Bowl XXXIV. That is far more than have appeared during all previous Super Sunday games -- combined. title: Vodafone's Chief Executive Has an Empire on Which the Sun Never Sets
body: To a backdrop of glittery chandeliers and somber marble pillars in a financial-district conference room, Christopher Gent, the smooth-talking chief executive of the world's biggest mobile phone company, was outlining his designs on German rival Mannesmann the other day when, unusually, he seemed to stumble over a word. Mr. Gent, the chief executive of Vodafone AirTouch, was discussing the web of deals that girds the globe's wireless networks, and he was talking about companies already under his control. What emerged, though, was not "companies" but "countries" -- as if, in this era of corporate hubris and consolidation, boardrooms have supplanted nations in creating the empires that will rule the digital millennium. That may seem to be a lot of freight to load onto a simple slip of the tongue, of course. But, considering that Mr. Gent (pronounced JENT) was discussing global expansion and control, an observer might be forgiven for sensing imperial overtones. As in the lands that Britain still ruled when he was born 51 years ago, the sun never sets either on Mr. Gent's realm of wireless networks from the unitedstates to Australia, or on his ambition to expand his empire. This year alone, with dizzying speed, Mr. Gent has moved from the $60 billion acquisition of AirTouch last January, through a summer dominated by negotiating a joint venture with Bell Atlantic -- which he outbid to secure AirTouch -- to create the biggest wireless network in the unitedstates. Now, spurred by Mannesmann's own imperial effort to acquire Britain's No. 3 wireless operator, Orange P.L.C., Mr. Gent has moved on to history's largest takeover bid: a roughly $127 billion all-stock mammoth of a hostile move on Mannesmann. Success by Vodafone would give the combined companies stakes or control in 25 countries with full or partial access to the mobile phone use of 73 million people -- including the biggest cellular markets in the unitedstates. This evening, Mannesmann's supervisory board -- the equivalent of a board of directors -- met in Dusseldorf, Germany, and, as expected, voted to reject Vodafone's takeover offer. German news reports indicated that several board members had wanted the company to consider negotiations, but Mannesmann's chairman, Klaus Esser, adamantly ruled that out. Mr. Gent declined to be interviewed. But in his recent conference-room remarks he said that if the hostile bid succeeded, "we will operate the largest wireless networks in the world; this combination puts us in pole position for the wireless data and Internet future." Not only that, a combination with Mannesmann would position Vodafone to challenge oil giant BP Amoco as Britain's largest company, with a market value of more than $250 billion -- quite a rise for a company that began life less than a decade ago as a fledgling contender in the untested mobile phone market. And most of that expansion has come in the brief two years and 11 months since Mr. Gent took over as chief executive. Yet, the man behind the imperial vision somehow remains elusive, showing a regard for personal privacy as steely as the determination of his deal making. The Vodafone official biography of Mr. Gent simply skips from his appointment in 1985 as an executive of Racal Electronics -- the parent of Vodafone before it was spun off in 1988 -- to his becoming chief executive of Vodafone in 1997. Initially, he secured the company's dominance in Britain's rough-and-tumble mobile phone business before venturing into mega-mergers. "He put his own backyard in order before some of the bigger deals," an aide said. The official biography makes no allusion to his family or social life, beyond his love of tennis and cricket. Publicly, at least, Mr. Gent offers a seamless image of unflappability: even barbed questions comparing radiation from mobile phones to smoke from cigarettes as a health hazard fail to ignite a spark of anger or defensiveness and are rebuffed with well-rehearsed counterarguments. Newspaper articles note that he drives an Aston Martin sports car, but associates say playboy connotations or a quest for ego-tripping celebrity are wide of the mark for a man with a young son from a second marriage that he wishes to shield from publicity's glare. "He does have a car like that, but I suspect it gathers dust in the garage," said a business associate who spoke in return for anonymity. "It's not like he's driving it around all the time. He works too hard. He's not a mega-ego kind of guy. He has a lot of confidence, but he doesn't feel the need to show off." So what does drive him? Of course, it could just be money, although that does not seem to be the entire story. In a recent ranking compiled by The Sunday Times of London, Mr. Gent emerged only as Britain's seventh best-paid chief executive with a basic salary of $1.07 million, multiplied eightfold by stock incentives and bonuses to $8.57 million. Most of his recent stock option disposals, his aides say, were related to paying for his divorce from his first wife. He remarried earlier this year and lives with his second wife, Kate, in a large house on about two acres in the Lambourne Valley -- horse-rearing country close to Vodafone's rambling corporate headquarters, according to Mike Caldwell, Vodafone's head of corporate communications. It is a token of Vodafone's helter-skelter growth that the headquarters occupies a staggering 58 separate buildings at Newbury, west of London. In class-ridden Britain, achievement is gauged not only in pounds and pence, but in the ability to crash the barriers that -- certainly in Mr. Gent's formative years -- would have divided the upper crust from the rest. "His father died when he was quite young; he didn't go to college and he's very driven to achieve a high level," the business associate said. "In Britain, people often find it very difficult not being from a particular background. He's cut through all that." In some ways, that makes Mr. Gent rather similar to an old friend of his, former Prime Minister John Major. Both left school to go to work in their teens -- Mr. Gent as a trainee bank manager, Mr. Major as a clerk at an insurance brokerage. Both sought a political niche in the Young Conservatives, of which Mr. Gent was national chairman from 1977 to 1979. Both, too, project the manner of a new, meritocratic elite. "The beautiful white collars and striped shirts, the tailoring -- he does have a slightly patrician air," said a financial analyst who has observed Mr. Gent's presentations and who spoke on condition of anonymity. And, like Mr. Major, Mr. Gent deploys what is most kindly described as a dry, even acerbic, wit. Asked at a recent news conference what mechanism he would use to put his merger proposals to Mannesmann's supervisory board, he snapped back, "It's known as a letter." For the record, Mr. Gent has said he believed that revenue from voice, data and Internet uses was the key to unlocking profit from technological advances that are supposed to give wireless devices much greater speed and capacity. "We believe that the future of telecommunications is wireless," he said. That is only one belief that has put him at loggerheads with Mannesmann, which aims to build its empire on a combination of fixed-line and wireless technology. Protesting Mannesmann workers last week publicly compared Mr. Gent's appetites for expansion to those of a shark. Indeed, in plunging into the cosseted world of German labor relations, he may well have underestimated the likely resistance of Mannesmann's 130,000 workers to what protesters called "the wild predator" from a company called "Voodoofone." There is no doubt that, in launching his bid, Mr. Gent has shown himself willing to do battle across one of the great divides of corporate Europe. It is an effort that calls not just for business acumen but also for the diplomatic skills to persuade German politicians, industrialists and workers to countenance the first ever cross-border raid on Germany Inc. Whatever the German image of Mr. Gent as a predator, though, he has been a more reactive than a proactive aggressor. In both big merger battles this year, Mr. Gent was initially caught off balance. News that Bell Atlantic was competing for AirTouch came through last January when he was away in Australia watching a match by his beloved English cricket team, which Vodafone sponsors. And, last month, he was at dinner when word reached him that Mannesmann was close to a deal with Orange -- a move that would turn Mannesmann from being Vodafone's most important European partner into a direct competitor on its British home turf and a challenger for European domination. So how did he react? "Furious would be too strong a statement," said Vodafone's Mike Caldwell. "Nonplused would be more like it because he thought we were in the friendly camp with Mannesmann." Thus, when Mr. Gent resolved to make his hostile bid, "most people accept that as far as he's concerned it was a very difficult decision to make," said Nigel Hawkins, a telecommunications analyst with Williams de Broe brokerage. "He didn't choose the battleground or the timing." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Christopher Gent, chief executive of Vodafone AirTouch, is leading the world's largest takeover battle against Mannesmann. (Reuters)  Chart: "A Busy Year of Deal Making" If Vodafone succeeds in its bid for Mannesmann, it would cap off an extraordinary year for the company.  Graph tracks daily closes of American depository receipts of Vodafone AirTouch since January 1999.  JAN. 15 -- Vodafone agrees to buy AirTouch for $60 billion, outbidding Bell Atlantic. SEPT. 21 -- Vodafone AirTouch signs a multibillion dollar agreement with Bell Atlantic to combine their unitedstates wireless operations. (Source: Bloomberg Financial Markets stock price )

title: Amazon's Risky Christmas
body: MAZON.COM has ordered 181 acres of holiday wrapping paper and 2,494 miles of red satin ribbon -- just in case. It has stocked its shelves with 10,000 copies of the Pack the Pig game and a few extra table saws. And it has built four new automated warehouses that give it the capacity to pack, wrap and ship nearly a million boxes a day. "This is the fastest expansion of distribution capacity in peacetime history," gloated Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon.com, the most popular store on the Internet. This holiday season, Mr. Bezos said, Amazon will send more packages -- perhaps in excess of 15 million -- to more people than any mail order company in the country. But this holiday season -- in which millions of people will do their first online shopping -- Amazon will also have far more competition than ever. Buy.com has become the No. 2 online store, based on sales of $397 million so far this year, selling computers, books, electronics and more, at prices generally far lower than Amazon's. And in every category, Amazon faces specialized competitors that have become smarter and stronger: Barnesandnoble.com in books, Amazon's original product line; eToys, Toys "R" Us and KB Toys in toys; 800.com and Circuit City in electronics; and Sears, Roebuck in tools. Those and hundreds of other companies are spending so much money on advertising this Christmas that the true winners on the Internet so far have been the television networks. And this year, many traditional retailers have overcome their fear of cannibalizing in-store sales to promote their Web sites. "We can do things that Internet-only companies can't," said Srikant Srinivasan, chief executive of KBkids.com, an Internet toy store controlled by KB Toys. "Our name is plastered over all of the stores. We have access to exclusive merchandise the store carries. And if you don't like a toy, you can just walk into your nearby mall to return it." KB and many other big companies are now willing to lose money to build their online units -- just as most Internet companies do. KB will spend $43 million to promote its online store this Christmas, compared with $30 million for its bricks-and-mortar store chain. Still, analysts expect Amazon to post fourth-quarter sales of $450 million to $600 million, enough to remain the No. 1 online store, as it has been since it began four years ago. Indeed, despite the competition, Amazon has actually increased its share of online retail sales every year, according to Jupiter Communications. But the stakes for Amazon this Christmas are not simply whether it will survive or even stay on top. Rather, Amazon must validate a strategy that is the biggest gamble on the Internet: aiming to be the store that sells most anything to anyone. Last Christmas, Amazon sold only books, music, videos and a handful of gift items, but it still nearly imploded trying to keep up with the volume. So far this year, Amazon's sales have nearly tripled, and the site now offers toys, electronics, tools and building supplies. It also runs auctions of everything from rare books to attic junk, operates a mall of other stores called zShops and owns big chunks of other online retailers like Drugstore.com and Pets.com, which are linked to its site. "Amazon ruled the last two Christmases," said Chip Austin, former president of the online bookstore at Bertelsmann, the German publishing group, which merged its Internet efforts in the unitedstates with Barnesandnoble.com last year. "But I'm not sure they will be able to broaden themselves as much as they want to." He says the company risks spreading itself so thin that it will be trumped by companies that specialize in each of the product lines it sells. "If I buy a buzz saw at Amazon and don't get the same kind of service I got on books, I'll say, 'That's it, they've stretched too far, and I'll buy my dog food and buzz saws somewhere else,' " said Mr. Austin, now a venture capitalist. Mr. Bezos has four weeks to show the world that he can do for buzz saws what he has done for books. His tactics are the same as his long-term strategy: Think big and control everything. That is why he ordered far more inventory -- and far more paper in which to wrap it -- than even his most optimistic forecasts would suggest. That is why he built his own warehouses, when most online stores farm out the packing, wrapping and shipping. And that is why he decided at the last minute to triple his advertising and marketing budget to $90 million, making sure he isn't drowned out by the competition. In the last year, Amazon has more than doubled its staff, to 5,000, and quadrupled the computer power that runs its Web site. Of course, thinking big means spending big, and Amazon is burning through the $1.5 billion it raised on Wall Street at an ever faster pace. In 1999, Amazon is expected to lose $550 million on sales of $1.5 billion. But Mr. Bezos is clear: if the choice is between ordering enough ribbon to be sure he won't run out, or being conservative to avoid costly overstock, he will always choose the extra ribbon. "You could say we will disappoint some small fraction of people but we will make a lot more money," Mr. Bezos said. "But if you disappoint people, you lose brand reputation, and that's worth a lot more to us right now than money." In 2000, Amazon wants to expand even more than it has this year. It is aiming at many more merchandise categories, though it may lose more money on the new initiatives just as the bookstore starts to turn a profit. Wall Street will keep financing Jeff Bezos's dream store, analysts say, so long as Amazon continues to astound investors with growth. And that is why there is so much pressure for the company to decisively exceed Wall Street's fourth-quarter forecasts. "The question for Amazon is whether they can hit the ball out of the park again this Christmas," said Nicole Vanderbilt, an analyst with Jupiter Communications, a research firm in newyork. "The danger for them is that they aren't No. 1 in all of the new categories they have entered. And they have been heavily rewarded up to now for seeking growth opportunities." RAPID growth, of course, is a blessing and a curse. In each of Amazon's four holiday seasons so far, it has nearly buckled under the pressure. "We were woefully unprepared when we started in 1995," Mr. Bezos acknowledged. "We were so dumb we didn't have any packing tables and wrapped packages on the concrete floor." By 1997, so many buyers swarmed to Amazon's Web site that the company had to turn away customers, posting a notice to try the site later. "We would rather lock people out of the store than have the gifts show up December 26th," Mr. Bezos said. Each year, the near-death experience emboldened the company. Early in 1998, Mr. Bezos decided that Amazon should not be just a bookstore, but an everything store. "The most frustrating part of shopping is not being able to find what you are looking for," Mr. Bezos said. "Two years ago, we realized that if we could solve that problem and provide truly universal selection, we could build an important and lasting company." Amazon, however, almost didn't last through Christmas 1998. It was so unprepared for the holiday volume that executives and office workers were ordered to work second shifts every day for three weeks, packing boxes or answering customers' email messages. "We saw the number of orders starting to increase and then everyone gasped," recalled Andrew N. Westlund, Amazon's vice president for warehouse, transportation and engineering. "We were starting to run out of gift wrap, and finding additional wrapping paper right before Christmas is tough." Amazon squeaked by, processing most of the orders on time. It found some substitute wrapping paper, if not in the best designs. But even before that experience, the company decided that things had to change in 1999. "On December 22, I pulled back and started to think about Christmas for this year," Mr. Westlund said. Within a week, the company decided to build five modern warehouses, one each in Nevada, Kansas and Georgia and two in Kentucky, at a total cost of $300 million. With more than three million square feet of space -- including two older, low-technology warehouses in Seattle and Delaware -- Amazon will have the capacity to handle more than $10 billion in sales, analysts estimate. BUT by operating its own warehouses, Amazon forfeits the leverage that allows companies like Yahoo and eBay to run Web sites that serve millions of people without ever having to stock anything with three dimensions. Most online stores find other companies to hold and ship their goods. "I want to hire designers and database specialists and people who are high productivity," said David Friedensohn, chief executive of BigStar Entertainment, an online video store. "I don't want 1,000 hourly workers sitting in a warehouse wrapping presents. There are plenty of people bidding for that business." But at Amazon, Mr. Westlund said that if it hired another company to handle distribution, it would risk losing the advantages of innovations aimed at serving customers better and more efficiently. "We would be the teacher and then they would offer those services to our competitors," he said. Building five automated warehouses is difficult enough, but the company decided that four of them had to be operating by Christmas 1999. Typically, building one such warehouse takes 18 months. Making the job much worse, the warehouses needed to handle a wide range of merchandise -- so wide, in fact, that Amazon didn't know what it would be. "My job was to leap ahead of the marketing people by building a facility that was so broad that when the company's visionaries say 'take a sharp turn,' we can do it," Mr. Westlund said. "I joked that we might sell log splitters. Now, with table saws, we're pretty close." As the warehouses were being built, the company was deciding which products to add next. The likely prospects were toys and consumer electronics, as both had been good sellers among Amazon's gift selections the previous Christmas. The initial plan was to introduce these "stores" on the Web site in the fall. By March, however, the company decided to open them in July, so it could work out the bugs before Christmas. (The home improvement section was added to the planned Christmas lineup in early fall, mainly to take advantage of the experience of Joe Galli, Amazon's new president, a veteran of Black & Decker. Tellingly, Amazon got it up and running in just 60 days.) As soon as the toy and electronics stores opened, planning for how the holidays would be handled on the Amazon site began in earnest. To David Risher, Amazon's senior vice president for merchandising, that was quite an accomplishment. "In 1997, we started thinking about Christmas in November," Mr. Risher said. "In 1998, it was October. We started thinking about Christmas this year in June." A TEAM was deployed to create new features for the site to encourage gift-giving. One is a system that lets shoppers put together a big order, for example, then send each item, tagged with an individual message, to a different address. Amazon also built a wish list -- much like a wedding registry -- that lets people tell the world what gifts they want to receive. In the early days, Amazon's innovative features -- like the ability to order a book with one mouse click -- put it far ahead of the competition. This year, however, other sites now offer most of these features, so Amazon must ensure that its engineering experience makes its versions better, or at least that its reputation makes customers think they are better. The quirky personality of Mr. Bezos, who has taken to granting some wish-list wishes himself, may also win the hearts of some customers. "I like to type in a random name, say 'Smith' in newyork, and buy them a little thing off their list," said Mr. Bezos, who owns about $10 billion of Amazon stock. "It's more fun than feeding parking meters." There are now weekly Christmas war-room meetings, devoted to making contingency plans for any breaks in Amazon's elaborate chain. If the Delaware warehouse runs out of a given book, for example, Amazon will send it by air express from Nevada, even if the customer paid for surface freight. Amazon would not say how much that plan would cost, but it warned Wall Street that such extra shipping expenses would contribute to its wider-than-expected losses this quarter. "Ten years from now, no one will remember whether Amazon.com spent an extra $100,000 upgrading shipping from the West Coast to the East Coast," Mr. Risher said. "All that will matter is whether electronic commerce gave people a good or bad experience." Moreover, Amazon figures that it has enough people this year that executives won't have to work the graveyard shift packing boxes. But just in case, everyone at headquarters has signed up for the equivalent of the Army Reserves at one or another of Amazon's facilities, to be called in if needed. EACH online store, meanwhile, has been adding merchandise and preparing holiday promotions. About two weeks before Thanksgiving, a dozen top managers of the toy department, all in their 20's and 30's, assembled in a conference room at Amazon's new headquarters, a retrofitted Art Deco hospital that looms over a hill on the edge of downtown Seattle. The conference table, like all the company's desks, is made of a door bolted to two-by-fours, a deliberate message of frugality to employees of a company that is losing hundreds of millions of dollars a year. First there was a status report. "Video games are rockin'," said Harrison Miller, 38, general manager of the toy store. Just a week earlier, Amazon added a selection of 3,500 video games, three times the selection of a typical electronics store. Much of the discussion centered on how to fit links to all of the company's special features and promotions onto its already crowded pages. They found space for a big promotion for a catalog that features classic wooden trains and blocks. The meeting ended with the reading of a top 10 list -- actually, two of them: the top 10 things that people search for in Amazon's toy section and, more important, the top 10 search terms that bring a customer no results. Topping the first list, to no one 's surprise, is Pokemon, the Japanese characters that delight children and perplex anyone over 15. Next are dolls, Nintendo and other video games and Furby. The group spends more time on the other list: No. 1 on it is "Pokedex." "Anyone know what that is?" Mr. Miller asks. Someone replies that it is an electronic organizer listing the attributes of the hundreds of Pokemon characters. An executive is assigned an "action item" to find a supply as soon as possible. No. 2 is "Pokeman," a misspelling. The site will be reprogrammed to send searchers to the Pokemon page. Search lists are among the most powerful ways in which online retailers can outpace traditional stores in responding to customers. There is no easy way for Toys "R" Us, for example, to keep track of toys its customers can't find in its stores. But Amazon can log each one and work to get it in stock. That helps to explain one of the stranger aspects of Amazon's strategy: zShops, the new listing of the products for sale by 3,500 small merchants. Many analysts worry that Amazon risks sullying its reputation if some of the shopkeepers to which it refers customers do not offer top-notch service. But Mr. Bezos says Amazon wants people to see the company as the place to start searching for anything they want to buy, and the auctions and zShops bring to the site thousands of items that it doesn't yet stock. Amazon earns a commission on each sale and collects rental fees from vendors. Perhaps more important, it gets to compile a list of exactly what all its customers want, and that will help it choose the categories to enter next. SITTING in Fernley, Nev., next to nothing but scrub grass and a small flat casino, Amazon's warehouse is a vast beige building with two dozen loading docks. It looks so big that if Amazon ever decided to sell jet planes through its Web site, they could be stored and shipped from this facility. For now, the warehouse holds more than a million types of items -- towering piles of toys, stacks of big-screen televisions and shelves with enough books to fill a university research library. Every item has a bar code that is scanned 17 times from the moment it arrives on the loading dock to the time it is shipped away, so that special computer software (written by Amazon) can always keep track of where it is. That is more scanning than necessary, but, as always, the company is willing to overdo it just to make sure orders don't get lost. "Efficiency and productivity lie in our future," said Mr. Galli, Amazon's president. The warehouse is already a wonder of automation. On the third level, for example, is a box of about a dozen Raggedy Ann dolls with a red light in front of it. When the light goes on, it means that someone, somewhere in the world, has gone to Amazon's Web site and ordered the doll. Quickly, a worker comes by, picks out a doll, puts it into a green cart and deposits it on a conveyor belt that rushes through the vast warehouse. The doll moves from belt to belt until it drops into a long chute-like bin, one of 2,000 used to assemble orders. As the conveyer moves, other items for the same customer also fall into the bin. When the order is complete, another light flashes below the bin, and a worker puts all the binned items into a box, which then travels down another series of belts through machines that pack it, tape it, weigh it and affix a mailing label. Yet more conveyers carry it directly into a truck at one of the loading docks. But the warehouse is still working out some problems. One morning about two weeks ago, the shrink wrapper, which encloses books in plastic to protect them during shipping, wasn't quite getting the wrap to shrink. And one of the devices that affixes shipping labels onto boxes as they flow past was malfunctioning. But, in general, the place was humming. Boxes flowed off the assembly line, this one headed for California, the next to Japan. And the holiday rush was under way: Amazon had started mailing out discount coupons to its better customers, and orders were up 60 percent from a week earlier. "Over the next month, I'll really know what Santa Claus feels like," said Michael Perkins, the warehouse manager. "I can't disappoint those kids." Despite all the automation, one crucial step must be completed by hand: gift-wrapping. Alongside the conveyor belts, the company is busily building more than 150 tables equipped with rolls of wrapping paper, piles of boxes and spools of the red ribbon. "The standard for our deluxe gift wrap is that it has to be better than your mom would do for you," Mr. Bezos said. "That's just hard." The task of teaching hundreds of workers how to wrap 30 gifts an hour falls to Kathy Van Woert, known back at headquarters as "the gift-wrap goddess of Fernley." She left her longtime job in an office supply company last March to join Amazon.  Until then, she had never bought anything online. Now, after volunteering to be the gift wrap trainer, she spends two hours with each new wrapper, explaining how to use the wrap sleeve and tie the satin bows. "It's just like tying your shoe," Ms. Van Woert says helpfully. OF course, if people don't order their presents, especially toys, from Amazon, there will be enough extra paper to make this part of the Nevada desert look like an installation by the artist Christo. And toy sales may be difficult to build, given the name recognition of Toys "R" Us and the early lead in online selling taken last year by eToys. Indeed, Amazon's research shows that even though the company has been adding new product types for more than a year, consumers stubbornly associate it only with books. "We have a huge challenge," Mr. Bezos said. "Do we have the best toy store? Yes. Do people know it? No." Amazon is sending $10 gift certificates for toys to many of its past book buyers. And two of its quirky new television commercials -- featuring a chorus of balding lounge singers -- focus on toys. To drive the point home, Mr. Bezos concocted a publicity-grabbing contest called "Toy Quest," which invites children to design their own toys. The winning toy will be manufactured and sold next year by Amazon. "I can't contain myself," Mr. Bezos said, with his trademark belly laugh. "It's just amazing how creative some of these little kids are. We might have the best-selling toy ever." In a funny way, Mr. Bezos has won a very similar contest. Wall Street has put up the money to realize his dream for the most "amazing" and "creative" store that sells everything. Now the warehouses have been built and the ribbon has been bought. There's only this Christmas, and maybe a few more, to find out just how big Amazon.com can be. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Ready to fulfill everyone's wish list, including the company's own, two Amazon.com employees, Greg Mitchell, at left, and Emily Montion, worked on customer orders at a new distribution center in Fernley, Nev. (Photographs by Cathleen Allison for The newyork Times)(pg. 15); Amazon's automated warehouse in Nevada holds more than a million different items.
