title:
GRASS-ROOTS BUSINESS;
OfDolls and Online Dollars
body: TWENTY-NINE, single and childless, Dmitri Gurevich may seem an odd man to be plotting an assault on the fantasy life of young girls. But soon, his Web design studio in this city's thriving "cyberdistrict,"on the South Side, will roll out a new Internet-based service that he hopes will transform the way that girls play with -- and buy -- dolls. The new Web site, called iDolls, lets girls design their dolls from scratch, choosing facial features, clothes and accessories in any of 69 billion possible combinations. Paid for with a parent's credit card, an ordered doll is manufactured to specifications in China and shipped to the customer within two weeks. "This is the beginning of an attempt to create a whole new set of options for girls," said Mr. Gurevich, who immigrated from Russia in 1990 and founded his company, Double Decker Studios, three years later. "This is not a set piece. This is a revolutionary thing." Although not the first doll Web site, iDolls is a mold-breaker, using technology to overturn conventional marketing notions in the industry. Mike Collins, president of iDolls, noted that dollmakers like Mattel have spent millions of dollars developing and promoting specific doll characters like the Barbie and Friends line or the American Girl historical figures made by the Pleasant Company, a Mattel subsidiary in Middleton, Wis. Mr. Collins contended that iDolls' approach, with its huge range of possible designs and no set characters, represents "the future of doll play." This notion of giving power to young shoppers is the latest trend in an increasingly expensive and sophisticated drive to tap a market that is growing in numbers and buying potential: girls 8 to 12 years old. These girls have emerged as a prime target for companies from camera makers to entertainment conglomerates. Their impact is visible in the strong ratings of television shows like "Buffy, the Vampire Slayer," and they are credited with much of the success of films like "Titanic" and "Mulan" and pop groups like the Spice Girls, 'N Sync and the Backstreet Boys. The 8-to-12 group of girls, now numbering more than 15 million nationwide, is also having more impact at the shopping mall. Retail chains like Limited Too have sprung up specifically to address the $5 billion-a-year market in preadolescent girls' clothing. And mainstream cosmetics marketers like Bath & Body Works (owned by Intimate Apparel Inc.), Avon and Estee Lauder have introduced lipstick, blush and accessory brands for girls. Perhaps the most impressive brick-and-mortar expression of niche marketing to girls may be the Pleasant Company's American Girl Place, a 35,000-square-foot retail outlet in downtown Chicago. The sprawling emporium of dolls and girls' clothing opened a year ago and features a tea room, live entertainment and elaborate displays about the historical characters upon whom the Pleasant Company bases its dolls. In its first year, American Girl Place counted more than 750,000 visitors; the store has become a tourist destination. LOOKING ahead, the real action for dollmakers seems to be in cyberspace, where, perhaps surprisingly, preteenage girls appear to outnumber preteenage boys. Two-thirds of girls in the 8 to 12 group have access to a computer, compared with only 58 percent of boys, according to surveys by the Zandl Group, a newyork market research firm. And girls seem to use the computer differently, according to Irma Zandl, one of the firm's principals: they generally prefer to treat it as a communication device or a way to exercise their imaginations, rather than as a platform for playing competitive or shoot-'em-up games, the preferred mode for boys of similar ages. "They like designing things," Ms. Zandl said. "They are checking out looks and outfits -- like playing with dolls in a more sophisticated and contemporary way." Mr. Collins of iDolls said he believes these characteristics will give his company's business model an online edge over vendors like the Pleasant Company, where he worked until Mattel acquired it in 1995. Companies like Mattel are stuck in the past, he said, selling girls a story of a 1980's vintage, while Barbie herself reflects "an essentially 50's image of girls." MATTEL doesn't see it that way, of course, and its quintessential California-girl flagship product is putting up a fight in cyberspace. Despite Mattel's well-publicized financial woes -- its stock price has fallen by more than half in the last two years -- the company has maintained a strong hold on computer software for girls, with Barbie-related CD-ROM's accounting for 6 of the 10 best-selling titles last year. Its year-old Barbie.Com Web site, which features a "my design" program that allows some customization of Barbie dolls, averages more than a million hits a month. "This brand is very vital," said Adrian Fontenella, president of Mattel's Barbie Girls division. Noting that the Barbie brand continues to bring in about $1.5 billion in annual sales, or roughly 30 percent of Mattel's total revenue, Mr. Fontenella dismissed the suggestion that Barbie was outdated: "People like to advertise a perception about our being old, but reality tells you something different." Ultimately, the fate of the dollmakers is in the hands of the young shoppers themselves. Laurie Meyer, 27, a Web page designer brought to Double Decker by Mr. Gurevich to give the iDolls site a feminine feel, thinks the power of computer technology will make girls impatient to exercise control and make choices far beyond what even the most flexible traditional dollmaker can offer. "When I was that little, nothing like that existed," Ms. Meyer said of iDolls. "This has opened a whole realm of activity" for preteenage girls, she added. "It creates a new world of imaginary play. You can design them -- and you can own them. It opens all kinds of doors." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Julie Peters shops with daughters Stephanie, 4, and Katrina, 8, at the American Girl Place in Chicago. The store features a tea room, live entertainment and elaborate displays about its dolls based on historical figures. (Steve Kagan for The newyork Times)

title:
Ideas & Trends;
Searching for the Search Engines of Meaning
body: I can't remember what I was looking for; it was something easy to find on the World Wide Web, a fact or a song lyric or a recipe. The original search topic was quickly forgotten when the search engine replied with a non sequitur: "Altavista knows the answer to this question: What is the meaning of life?" When had the search for Web sites turned into the search for meaning? How many clicks away was the meaning of life? And what else did Altavista know? I selected the answer. A message appeared: "Unable to connect to the site. The site is down, overloaded, or unreachable. Try connecting again later." Overloaded, no doubt. Maybe someone had figured out the meaning of life and posted it on the Web, and Altavista had found it for me. Maybe users had generated the question. Surfers in the throes of inner questioning could have asked it. Readers of the "Hitchhikers' Guide to the Galaxy" could have asked it, remembering the supercomputer in the book that spends years pondering the meaning of life and finally says the answer is: 42. Once, Internet search sites served as helpful road maps. With advances in artificial intelligence, one day they might be brilliant secretaries. But today, they are in a state of transition, slouching toward the human, growing more philosophical. Mixing mechanical and personal elements, they have turned into accidental wisefolk, spiritual advisers and drive-by psychoanalysts. In the Renaissance, poets drew parallels between geographical maps of newly discovered lands and the landscapes of the human body and soul. Today, the newly discovered lands are virtual places where users may seek themselves. A spiritual pilgrimage used to mean having to leave the house, but with the Web getting more metaphysical, seekers can pursue truth right at their desks. Surfers began asking the major questions online five years ago, when visionaries noticed the Web was a city built without a map and launched Web directories like Yahoo and search engines like Lycos, Infoseek and Altavista. In the beginning, the goal was clear: to serve as tour guides in a foreign land. SEARCH engines send a "robot" known as a "spider" or "crawler" to scan Web sites. The spider feeds data into an index. Software then sorts and ranks indexed information. Yahoo uses human indexing rather than mechanical indexing, with individuals mapping out the territories of cyberspace. Such sites have spawned imitators and "metasearchers" -- search engines that search other search engines. Today more than 3,000 engines scan, search and "spider" other sites, holding up virtual lanterns and giving directions, waiting for the day they will have the technology to behave with real intelligence. Meanwhile, they approximate intelligence and sometimes end up sounding like a maddening cocktail party guest or an idiot savant. Altavista has always had a stunning number of Web pages indexed -- estimated today at more than 250 million. But that wasn't enough. This spring, the folks behind the curtain decided that Altavista should speak English. The Queen's English. Altavista had licensed the technology from the "Ask Jeeves" search engine (www.ask.com). That engine, of course, is modeled after the ingenious, efficient butler from P.G. Wodehouse's fiction, casting the user in the role of Bertie Wooster, the cheerfully incompetent narrator who couldn't find socks already on his feet. Users would type questions in English -- "What is the highest mountain in Uzbekistan?" -- and Jeeves would answer or raise a related question: "Jeeves knows the answer to these questions: 'Where can I go mountain-climbing?'; 'Where can I ski in Aspen?'; 'What is Uzbekistan?' " Sometimes Jeeves came off like an infuriating salesperson, trying to sell you sandals when you specifically asked for rain boots; sometimes he would surprise you. THE personalities of these engines were clear: Jeeves spoke English, Altavista spoke full-text search indexing. Jeeves liked questions, Altavista liked phrases in quotation marks. Jeeves seemed like an aging, avuncular know-it-all, Altavista seemed like the woman who keeps winning Double Jeopardy. Their technology-sharing agreement made for strange bedfellows. Indeed, it is unnerving when Altavista claims to know things -- using the same sentences that Jeeves did, without a helpful smiling cartoon to suggest personhood. But it is comforting to think the answers to the big questions are just a click away. One Web site -- answers.com -- attempts to indulge this fantasy. Instead of referring to other sites as search engines do, answers.com gives answers right there -- to such questions as "Does extraterrestrial life exist?" "Where do babies come from?" and "Can you kiss your own elbow?" When answers.com launched, the site charged for individual answers depending on the difficulty of the question, starting at $1.79 for an easy answer, and up to $11.99 for custom research. "What is the meaning of life?" was the site's most popular question in 1997 and cost $1.79. It turned out that people want the answers to the big questions but they don't want to pay for them. So the site now answers questions for free, as developers prepare for a re-launch in December, when answers.com will license its technology to other companies, using the interface to help weed through frequently asked questions on corporate Web sites. Individuals will still be able to ask the pressing questions at no cost. WHEN asked for the complimentary answer to the meaning of life, answers.com replied, "When you find out, let us know!" One hopes that the $1.79 answer had more substance. Recently, the most popular question has been "Why is the sky blue?" The site deals with the topic deftly. It also handles the classic, "If a tree fell in a forest, and no one was around to hear it, would it make a sound?" The answer explains how physicists and philosophers can have different definitions of sound. Perhaps the oddest free answer offered to me came one autumn day when Altavista performed a search on some dry academic question and then added, "Altavista knows the answer to this question: Am I in love?" This question only raised more questions. Who was Altavista, anyway? Ideally, the engine was a mind-reader able to give different answers to each emotionally conflicted user. Or was Altavista itself in love, and sure of it? And who wrote the question? Had the programmers anticipated that it might be asked? Or was the engine spitting out a question that had originated with a user? If so, who was this poor soul who yearned for romantic advice from a computer? Computers have already created poetry and art. Futurists say that one day supercomputers will know loneliness, lobby for legal rights, and learn how to feel. But if we teach computers how to know and how to feel, can we teach them to know how they feel? That's an entirely different lesson, one that human beings can barely process themselves. If Altavista is in love -- and I imagine Jeeves wouldn't be right for her anyway -- and if she really knew it, artificial intelligence will have reached a new high. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
INVESTING;
One Way To Play Start-Ups
body: FOR Internet investors, early-stage investment is the holy grail. The goal is to buy into emerging companies that are poised for runaway growth because of promising business plans or technology. Few retail investors can get access to companies at that stage, and even procuring shares of initial public offerings can be all but impossible. But an alternative is evolving: the publicly traded incubator company. Such businesses, the best known of which are CMGI Inc. of Andover, Mass.; the Softbank Corporation of Tokyo; and the Internet Capital Group of Wayne, Pa., offer the enticing growth potential and some of the risk of early-stage investing, along with the benefits of diversification. "This is a new and very compelling business model, because what these incubators are offering is something between a corporate parent and a V.C. firm," said Henry Blodget, an analyst at Merrill Lynch, referring to venture capital firms. Roger McNamee of Integral Capital Partners, which invests in technology companies, added: "They have been a great way to turbocharge any portfolio." CMGI, Softbank and Internet Capital buy positions in Internet-related businesses, typically exerting varying degrees of management control while developing partnerships and synergies among the companies. The incubators offer investors broad exposure to the Internet. While some of their investments are in public companies, many are still private, which means that the incubator stands to benefit if an I.P.O. goes well. So far this year, the incubator business model has rewarded shareholders lavishly, with CMGI and Softbank returning 450.7 percent and 1,023.5 percent, respectively, through Friday, versus 142.5 percent for TheStreet.com Net index. Internet Capital, which went public on Aug. 5 at $12 a share, closed on Friday at $169.125. Valuing the stocks is tricky, since earnings are not particularly meaningful and many of the holdings are private: analysts tote up the estimated value of their holdings and ask whether the stocks deserve a higher price. The answer almost always seems to be yes, and the market has agreed. Each of the big three incubator companies has its own twist on the business. Under David S. Wetherell, its chief executive, CMGI has long been considered a blue chip. CMGI's portfolio has majority and minority stakes in more than 50 companies. Phil Benyola, a research associate at Raymond James Financial, a brokerage firm, estimated that 10 to 15 of CMGI's companies would go public over the next 12 months. One likely winner is Alta Vista, the search engine company in which CMGI holds an 83 percent stake; Mr. Benyola expects it to go public by the end of March at a price that would put its value between $5 billion and $7 billion. Phil Leigh, vice president at Raymond James, said that despite its run-up, he thought CMGI was reasonably priced. "It has always looked like CMGI is overvalued, but when these companies engage in I.P.O.'s, then everything seems to fall in place," he said. On Monday, CMGI announced a new fund for investing in business-to-business Internet start-ups, and its stock climbed 17.4 percent for the week, to $146.625. Raymond James's 12-month target price on CMGI is $159. Internet Capital has always focused on business-to-business e-commerce investments since its founding in 1996. Its companies are mostly in far earlier stages of development than CMGI's: just 3 of the 40 or so in which it is invested are public, making it riskier than CMGI. STILL, Forrester Research in Boston expects business-to-business e-commerce to grow from $43 billion in 1998 to $1.3 trillion in 2003, versus just $108 billion in e-commerce directed at consumers. "It's our top pick," said Eric B. Upin, an analyst at BancBoston Robertson Stephens referring to Internet Capital. He declined to give a price target, but said "there's a huge upside." Softbank, once primarily a computer distributor, has stakes in more than 100 companies worldwide and plans to expand that number to 780 in five years. It uses its global network to turn its unitedstates holdings into foreign businesses. Typically, it takes a unitedstates company's business model and clones it in a foreign market. For example, it leveraged its 31 percent stake in Yahoo by starting Yahoo Japan, which began trading separately in 1997 and is now that country's No. 1 portal. Softbank also has stakes in Buy.com, InterTrust and E-Loan, among others. Ralph Wanger, whose Acorn Fund held 235,000 Softbank shares as of June 30, said, "Anyone who is going to study the company will conclude that Softbank is the premier growth company in Japan." Juliette Chow, an analyst for Lehman Brothers in hongkong, said the stock, which closed on Friday at 76,400 yen, should hit 100,000 yen in a year. Some newer incubators are likely to go public soon. Analysts say two examples are Idealab of Pasadena, Calif., and Divine interVentures of Chicago; officials of both companies were not available for comment on Friday. As for the current incubators, a cooling Internet sector could punish them severely. "They are really leverage plays on the market for Internet stocks," Mr. McNamee said. "If that market goes down, these will get pounded all the way down." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (David Klein)  Graphs: "Venture Capital Is King" Change in share prices since Dec. 31, plotted on comparable percentage change scales. title:
MARKET INSIGHT;
Will Retailers Learn the E-Commerce Dance?
body: AS car doors open and slam shut in shopping-mall parking lots across America, it is clear that the buying season has begun. The noise is music to the nation's retailers, the bricks-and-mortar people who do business in real stores instead of in cyberspace. And the stakes are high: the rule of thumb is that just under half of a retailer's annual profit is realized in the fourth quarter. According to estimates from the National Retail Federation, total sales for the holiday season will top $180 billion this year. Still, compared with other sectors, the so-called broad-line retailers have received a cool reception from investors. This year, the Standard & Poor's retailing index is up only about 8.6 percent through Friday. Michael Exstein, a retailing analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston, talked last week about retailing, e-tailing and the holidays. Following are excerpts of the conversation.  Q. What sort of an early read are you getting on Christmas?  A. On the surface, people are very nervous. There has been a notable slowdown in business since mid-October, which nobody can explain. So there is some concern out there that Christmas won't come. But it will come. Retailers understand that Christmas comes later every year because customers understand that retailers won't run out of merchandise, and if they wait long enough, prices sometimes come down.  Q. What would constitute a good selling season for the companies you follow?  A. For the majority of the dozen general merchandisers I follow, if they get a 3 percent to 4 percent gain, that will be a very good Christmas, and those sorts of gains have been the norm rather than the exception for the past few years. A gain of less than 2.5 percent would make it a bad season.  Q. Switching gears a little, how are big retailers reacting to the emergence of e-tailers? A. Most retailers are not worried about the impact of the Internet on their businesses. They are worried about structural change. And there is not a retailer out there today who knows how much structural change will take place because of e-commerce. I break down the retail world in terms of how they are dealing with the whole e-commerce issue into four categories: embracing, evolving, reinforcing and considering. So far, there are two companies that have embraced e-commerce aggressively: Federated Department Stores and Nordstrom. Federated spent $1.7 billion to buy Fingerhut, and has created Web sites for Macy's and Bloomingdale's and an online catalog for Macy's. Nordstrom adopted a different strategy and developed its capabilities in-house. They knew the catalog industry infrastructure could be leveraged as e-commerce developed. Today, their online catalog does about $200 million in sales. Last August they sold off 15 percent of the online catalog to venture capital interests. At the same time they created Nordstrom Shoes, the world's biggest online shoe store.  Q. This is a brutally competitive business, even without e-tailers. Are there potential problems out there that worry you?  A. Consumer installment debt has started to accelerate again, and I worry about that, because that is the last thing that keeps spending going. I also worry about overbuilding. When times were flush in the past, companies would build new stores, and when things got bad they would either slow the pace of building or close stores. Right now companies are building stores. Over all, the industry increased capital spending by 21 percent in 1998, and as of the first quarter of this year it was projected to be up another 11 to 12 percent.  Q. The market has not been kind to most of these stocks. Why?  A. What you are seeing is that the market is reacting very, very rationally, and is sorting out the winners and the losers. Wal-Mart has been a good stock this year. In part, the performance is based on a tremendous amount of skepticism that traditional retailers will be able to fashion a competitive response to e-tailing. My response to that is that companies like Federated, Nordstrom, Wal-Mart and Sears are not sitting idly by, and while they may not get it perfectly, there is a lot to be said for offering both traditional retailing and e-tailing. Infrastructure matters. Customer service will matter. It is not just a one-way flow of goods.  Q. So which stocks do you like?  A. I like four: Federated, Wal-Mart, Nordstrom and Zale's. The thing that unifies those four stocks is that they have continuing growth in market share and margin opportunities. There is not much room to raise prices in this industry. But there is room to source better, have differentiated product and to continue to improve efficiency. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Michael Exstein

title: M.B.A. Boom Fades as Candidates Seek Instead the Rewards of the Internet
body: Michael Hyatt was dutifully following a traditional path for a future corporate executive. After college, he joined a consulting firm, where he advised blue-chip companies like AT&T, General Motors and I.B.M. He then applied to a few business schools, gained admission to Stanford, the most selective of them all, and prepared to enroll this fall. During the summer, however, he took an eight-week job helping a friend who worked at a small Internet company in Southern California, and when it ended, Mr. Hyatt, 28, was hooked. So shortly before he was to sit down to his first finance class, he called Stanford to say thanks anyway: he wouldn't be showing up in Palo Alto after all. "You need to do this now, before it's too late," Mr. Hyatt said of working for an Internet start-up. "If you wait two years, there's going to be consolidation in the industry. Right now, you have a chance to stake out your own claim." As many of the nation's most talented young workers rush to stake that claim, business school has suddenly lost some of its luster. That has had a significant impact on applications to some top schools, particularly those that tend to attract the entrepreneurially minded. In the last year, applications to Stanford, M.I.T., Dartmouth, Michigan and the University of California at Berkeley, have dropped as much as 11 percent. On other elite campuses, like Northwestern and Carnegie Mellon, applications have leveled off. Some less prestigious universities have seen steep declines. More students are also dropping out after the first year of the two-year M.B.A. program to remain with companies where they worked over the summer. And driven in part by the generally strong economy, the number of Americans taking the standardized admissions test for business school has fallen sharply in recent years. The changes are a significant departure from the attitude toward the M.B.A. degree earlier in this long economic expansion. For the past decade, until last spring, applications increased at every elite school virtually every year, turning the M.B.A. program into one of the hottest areas of higher education. Today, however, many potential students worry that two years is too long to be studying marketing and operations, and, unlike those aspiring to be lawyers or doctors, they do not need a degree to practice their craft. Much as William H. Gates decided in 1976 that starting a software company was more important than graduating from Harvard College, they are eager to get moving. Among the prizes they seek are the stock options available to the first employees of a start-up -- even if it means forgoing the six-figure salaries that M.B.A.'s often command. Behind the eagerness is a broader anxiety shared by many investors and executives that the current Internet bull market could be at or very near its peak. That perception is encouraging companies to go public at a record pace to take advantage of current valuations, for example, and making stock prices gyrate. Many people in their 20's and 30's also question whether the ivory tower is the place to learn about the emerging Internet world. "There's an urgency that this is happening so fast that you've got to be in it to really learn it," said George Daly, dean of newyork University's Stern School of Business. Applications to N.Y.U. dropped slightly last spring after rising an average of 15 percent in each of the previous three years. To attract students and recruiters, schools are overhauling curriculums to offer more Internet courses and even creating majors devoted to the subject. Some schools have increased advertising budgets and stepped up their own recruiting to compete with companies trying to lure skilled workers. And for the first time in their histories, schools are seeing groups of students leave after their first year, perhaps abandoning the $25,000 or so investment many had made in a year of tuition. Twenty-five of the 765 members of the M.B.A. class of 2000 at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, for example, did not return this fall, and almost all now work for Internet start-ups, a spokesman for the school said. In response, some schools are considering more liberal leave-of-absence policies, while others, including Pennsylvania and Northwestern, have dusted off little-used rules to allow students to take up to five years off. Around the country, said Donald P. Jacobs, Northwestern's dean, "people are wringing their hands" about the departures. Professor Jacobs said he expected most students to return eventually. Though there are no statistics that offer a definitive reason for the changes, many observers said the Internet was a major culprit. More broadly, a low unemployment rate and an almost insatiable demand for high-skilled workers in corporate America has left people who would normally be pondering an M.B.A. quite happy in their current jobs. Administrators also pointed to demographic factors, noting that the number of people in their late 20's is shrinking slightly, and added that the recent M.B.A. boom and the resulting lowered acceptance rates might be intimidating potential applicants. Over all, the number of Americans taking the standardized business-school admission test has fallen 17 percent in the last four years, according to the Graduate Management Admission Council, which administers the test. That decline is exaggerated by the fact that the test, in its new computerized format, is no longer offered on college campuses, discouraging undergraduates from taking it. Still, top schools typically consider only applicants with at least two years of work experience, and the number of test-takers has dropped in almost every age group since 1995, according to the council. Not every school has seen interest wane. Fueled by the six-figure salaries many graduates fetch and the continued growth in the number of foreigners who want American business degrees, applications to some schools are still rising. Applications to Harvard, for example, rose 5 percent last year, and at Columbia, where one-third of the student body hails from other countries, they increased by almost 10 percent. Duke and the University of Chicago also saw increases. But at top schools renowned for attracting entrepreneurs and technology experts -- like Stanford and Berkeley -- the number of applications fell or was unchanged last spring. Many people who traditionally apply to those schools now feel an urgent need to work at an Internet start-up, said Sally P. Lannin, a former Stanford administrator and currently the president of M.B.A. Strategies, a Minnesota-based consulting firm for business-school applicants. By contrast, Harvard, Columbia and Chicago -- while turning out many entrepreneurs as well -- are among the schools that aspiring investment bankers consider first. Patty Benson, 26, is one of the nonapplicants. Like Mr. Hyatt, she had been following the usual course for ambitious people who want to work in corporate America. Ms. Benson majored in economics at Colby College in Maine, landed a plum job at Bain & Company as a consultant, and started to think about business school. Then the online explosion interrupted her thoughts. "All these companies are growing very, very fast," Ms. Benson said. "I wanted to be in on it." So she applied to Internet companies rather than business schools and ended up moving to Seattle two months ago to work as an assistant product manager in Amazon.com's books division. "I love it," she said. Just as she imagines a business school to be, she added, "it's filled with a lot of very smart, enthusiastic people." Even on campuses where applications have declined, school administrators say their schools continue to thrive. The most prestigious still admit only about one in eight candidates. Graduates are snapped up by consulting firms and investment banks -- and, increasingly, Internet start-ups. The heightened competition has forced some more traditional companies to offer new perquisites, like leaves of absence, in addition to starting salaries that sometimes reach $150,000. "The market for M.B.A.'s is very exciting," Professor Jacobs of Northwestern said. "As long as we don't become irrelevant to what's happening in the marketplace, I think we're fine." To stay relevant, schools are quickly creating new courses and changing lesson plans in existing classes to include Internet business. Earlier this month, Wharton announced that it was adding an e-commerce major, effective immediately, with 50 faculty members teaching courses. At the University of Chicago this fall, two staff members had to stand outside a 9 a.m. Saturday Internet course on the first few days of class to prevent students not enrolled from sitting in on the lectures. Still, a decline in the number of applications can be a serious matter for graduate schools, particularly in the M.B.A. world, where schools compete aggressively with one another. Such a drop can force admissions officers to be less selective in selecting a class, has the potential to drop a school's ranking in U.S. News & World Report's influential annual survey and can require a school to spend more money promoting itself. Some less elite schools, which are often unknown in other countries, are faring the worst. At Tulane University, they fell more than 40 percent over the last two years, though the assistant dean for admissions, John Silbernagel, said he thought the pool was still of similar quality. At the University of Iowa's Henry B. Tippie School of Management, where applications dropped by more than a quarter last spring, the acceptance rate rose to 37 percent, from 28 percent in 1998. In response, the school has tripled its advertising budget and continued a recent push to send more unsolicited mail to people who take the admissions test, said Mary Spreen, the school's director of M.B.A. admissions and financial aid. "It has caused some concern," Ms. Spreen said. "When you have a larger applicant pool, you're able to attract a higher-quality class." But business school can be a tough sell in the current, frenzied Internet environment. Many potential students hope to be among the early employees of a company, who typically receive a larger batch of stock options at a lower price than employees who join later. When Mr. Hyatt left his consulting job, at Mercer Management Consulting, for a summer stint at Winfire, which designs Internet software, it had 10 employees. It now has 40. Had he attended Stanford and joined after graduation, the company would have had 150 employees, he estimated. The influx of venture capital even allows some Internet start-ups to offer high salaries, in addition to options, noted Mr. Hyatt, who said he was making more than $100,000 as the director of product management at Winfire. The changing attitude toward the M.B.A. is particularly striking in Silicon Valley, a new center of American business and yet a place where business school has suddenly become less popular. Applications to Berkeley's program dropped by 11 percent last spring. At Stanford -- where school employees came up with the idea that led to the creation of Cisco Systems and whose graduates include top Internet executives like Scott McNealy of Sun Microsystems -- they fell 6 percent. These days, students worry that their chances of emulating such titans will decrease if they wait two years to start work. Many of the start-ups are also making a big push to keep employees who have been at their jobs for two to seven years, traditionally a period of high turnover, Jacques Leger, a human resources consultant with Watson Wyatt in San Francisco, said. "Now, with two years of experience, you're considered a prime candidate with lots of experience," Mr. Leger said. Students notice the difference. "The opportunity cost of going to school has gone up dramatically," said Cheryl Proctor, a second-year M.B.A. student at Berkeley, who watched some of her classmates quit this summer while many others work part-time jobs during the year to maintain contacts, she said. Ms. Proctor herself spent last summer at a small Internet company in San Francisco that asked her to stay when her internship ended. "They made it really tempting," she said. But business school, she added, "seems like a safe bet." Many school administrators predict that applications will start rising again everywhere as the Internet industry matures. One possible sign of resurgent interest in M.B.A. programs is already being seen: a small rebound in recent months in the number of Americans taking the admissions test. "There is a gold-rush mentality" to the Internet, said Paul Danos, dean of the Amos Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth. "A lot of potential students will make the wrong decision. Everybody thinks they're all going to strike it rich, and it's just not going to happen." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: After an eight-week summer job at a small Internet company in California called Winfire, Michael Hyatt, 28, opted against getting his M.B.A. from Stanford. title: Busy Season Begins for Merchants
body: Ed and Kathy Blasco kicked off their holiday shopping today the same way they have for the last 15 years: they headed for the Country Club Plaza in Kansas City. The Blascos were set to enjoy the balmy weather and the Christmas songs being played by a live band, but they did not plan to make many purchases. "If we get ideas today, we may very well do online shopping," Mr. Blasco said. They intended to take advantage of an online retailer's free shipping offer on a playground set for their 1-year-old granddaughter and said they had already bought a doll on Ebay.com. With unemployment at record lows and the stock market flying high, economists and retail analysts have been predicting that Christmas 1999 will be very strong indeed. Sales of merchandise, excluding autos, will reach $184 billion for November and December, up 6 percent from last year, predicts the National Retail Federation. So the real issue is not whether Americans will shop, but where. The Internet is growing rapidly, and estimates vary on just how big a chunk the virtual vendors will divert from stores. Estimates of holiday sales on the Web run from $6 billion by Forrester Research to $12 billion by Ernst & Young, numbers that are comparatively small, but at least twice last year's. The day after Thanksgiving, known as Black Friday because merchants historically have relied on sales leading up to Christmas to move them from the red into the black, is no longer the busiest shopping day of the year. (That honor is now held by the days nearest Christmas Eve, as Americans conditioned to sale shopping delay buying as long as possible.) Still, the Thanksgiving weekend does send millions of families to the mall and provides a snapshot of how the season will shape up. Early reports indicate that online shopping is fast becoming as much a holiday tradition as strolling along eating chestnuts and gawking at decorated store windows. And at least on the first day of the holiday shopping season, there were sporadic reports of service trouble on the Web (KBkids.com was down much of the day and offering $5 off coupons to appease consumers), while merchants on the ground were doing a better than expected job of making visitors comfortable. At Crate & Barrel's flagship store on Michigan Avenue in Chicago, there were more clerks than people at 10 a.m., including a full-time janitorial staff that was meticulously polishing escalators and handrails almost the minute they were marred by fingerprints. Kay Barker, of Carmel, Calif., who was visiting Manhattan, stocked up on perfume and sweaters at Bloomingdale's and then waited while her son tried on clothes at Banana Republic. She was like many other shoppers in offering praise of newyork sales clerks. "The personnel have been very patient with all the crowds," Ms. Barker said. Despite heightened attention to customer service and warm weather that encouraged shopping outdoors, many Americans still chose to stay home and bathe in the light of their computer screens, much to the delight of cybermerchants. "From what we can tell by traffic to our Web site as of noon, today will be the No. 1 day for our Web site all year," said Mike Goldstein, chief executive of Toys "R" Us. Amazon.com, which sells books, music and toys, reported a sales increase of 267 percent over Black Friday last year. And Richard Rogowski, a spokesman for Yahoo!, said, "This is our biggest day of the year so far. We are getting almost five times as many orders on Yahoo! stores as we got last year on Black Friday." At Outpost.com, a supplier of high-technology gifts, big sellers included DVD players and flat-screen computer monitors. "It is very darn good this week," said Bob Bowman, Outpost's chief executive. "We already have orders exceeding last year. We will do north of a million today." Consumers were drawn, Mr. Bowman said, by the offer of free overnight shipping and a promotion that rewarded a shopper every 15 minutes with a gift appropriate for Internet surfing, like a bathrobe and a pretzel-popcorn snack. But the increased traffic did not come without a price. In the week leading up to Black Friday, many Web shoppers complained that sites were responding slowly and that some did not take orders at all. Among the most troubled were the toy sites, with Toys "R" Us and Etoys having down time during the week, and KBKids.com suffering badly today. Because Internet retailers must ship goods, they tend to hit their Christmas peak a little earlier than traditional merchants, who can provide cash-and-carry gratification. Perhaps this explains why reports from stores were mostly positive but a bit mixed. "It was a slow start, to tell you the truth, because there was not one big toy this season," John Konarski, president of the International Council of Shopping Centers, said this morning. "There was no reason to get up at 4:30 in the morning and wait on line." Consumers strolling the avenues in the big urban centers reported that they had every intention of spending lots of money and plenty of it in plain old stores. And there were signs everywhere that retailers were not going to cede sales readily. Many stores were already promoting big markdowns, and in what may be a service emphasis inspired by a fear of the Internet, most had salespeople clamoring to help browsers. Sue and Brad Briddell, who traveled from Toledo, Ohio, to shop in Chicago, had only praise for the service they had found on Michigan Avenue. The two had been out of their hotel and on the hunt by 7:30 a.m., and by mid-morning had already visited Marshall Field's and Old Navy and had fingered the parachute flight pants at Express. The couple did not find the stereotypical scarce or gruff sales help. Both said they had been served well. "Oh, it has been fantastic," Ms. Briddell said. "Everyone's been very up and very friendly." Whether stores can maintain that first-day polish will be the question as the shopping season gathers steam. The Web's popularity might be changing the world of shopping, but certain things remain constant online or off. Discounted merchandise or anything Pokemon was a good thing today. Jeff Tauber, chairman and chief executive of Cybershop, an online merchant specializing in toys, apparel and housewares, said, "We are definitely exceeding last year's numbers, and this day last year was one of our top three or four days of the entire year. People are always looking for a good deal." Among Cybershop's specials was a $99 bundle of Pokemon paraphernalia, including trading cards, the coveted Pikachu plush animal, a pencil set and a key chain. In Atlanta, more than 50 shoppers rushed to the electronics department to buy Pokemon items when Target, the low-price division of Dayton Hudson, opened its doors at 7 a.m. While shopping at Target, Starla Littleton and her niece Shelly Park used walkie-talkies to make their trip more efficient. "She goes to get one thing, and I go to get another," Ms. Littleton said. They kept in touch as one checked out the Pokemon display and the other headed to the Furbie Babies. Meanwhile, the department stores, which offer mid-range prices and few toys, were rather empty before midday. Diana Brown, who was shopping at Barney's in newyork with a couple of girlfriends, said that just before her excursion she had heard that today was Black Friday. "We thought, 'Oh, no,' " Ms. Brown said. "But it's not bad at all." Cathy Joiner, of Nashville, who was fingering Pashmina shawls at the Bloomingdale's on 59th Street, while her husband, Don, looked on, said, "I was here last year, and it was a whole lot worse than this." But if the fashionable clothiers were worried, they did not admit it. In sales, "we are up double digit above last year," said Judy Collinson, the Barney's Inc. general merchandise manager for women's wear, "and we don't even expect this to be one of our biggest days." Ms. Collinson said that luxury items selling well included Fendi purses, shearling jackets and Pashmina shawls, which run up to $3,000 for the hand-embroidered variety. "Our customers purchase things on the Internet," Ms. Collinson said firmly, "but not the things they buy from us." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Crowds of shoppers kept retail employees busy yesterday. When Jasmin Brown, right, reported to work at Bloomingdale's in newyork, she was asked to help a customer even before she removed her coat. (Edward Keating/The newyork Times); Jean DiMarco of Lawrenceville, N.J., struggled to keep two carts of gifts under control yesterday at the Wal-Mart store in Lawrenceville. (Associated Press)

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Nasdaq Reaches Another Record During Light Trading
body: The Nasdaq stock market sprinted to another record yesterday, as investors gave Internet retailers a boost at the traditional start of the holiday shopping season. But stocks over all had a mixed performance in light post-Thanksgiving trading. And in the bond market, prices fell for a fourth consecutive session, dragged down by weak overseas bond markets and strong economic numbers that have prompted fears of rising inflation. The price of the 30-year Treasury bond dipped 13/32 , to 9818/32 . The bond's yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, rose to 6.23 percent from 6.20 percent on Wednesday. The Nasdaq composite index rose 27.31 points, to 3,447.81, for its 16th record in the last four weeks. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index dropped 0.46 points, to 1,416.62, and the Dow Jones industrial average fell 19.26 points, to 10,988.91. For the week, the Nasdaq composite index added 78.56 points, and is now up 57.24 percent so far this year. The Dow Jones industrials dropped 14.98 for the week, while the S.& P. 500 slipped 5.38. "A tremendous pocket of strength in technology is pulling up the Nasdaq," said Richard McCabe, chief market analyst at Merrill Lynch & Company. But he cautioned that over all, the declining stocks are outpacing those advancing, which should raise a cautionary note for investors. Stock gains were held back by inflationary concerns related to a Commerce Department report yesterday that Americans' personal income in October posted its biggest jump in more than five years, and rose more than twice as fast as spending. Personal income, which includes wages, interest and government benefits, surged by 1.3 percent in October. It was another sign of the nation's economic strength, which added to bond-market jitters that the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates again early next year to hold down inflationary pressures. Trading was listless as the stock market closed at 1 p.m. yesterday, three hours earlier than usual, as traders were on a holiday weekend schedule. Benefiting from the traditional kickoff of the holiday shopping season on the day after Thanksgiving, the online retailer eToys rose 3 3/8, to 67 13/16, along with Amazon.com, up 7 1/16, to 94 1/4. Toys "R" Us gained 1 1/4, to 18 3/8. Wall Street has high hopes for brisk online selling in the next month. Leading the Dow was AT&T, up 4 1/4, to 57 7/16. The company, the largest unitedstates long-distance phone concern, is reportedly considering selling stock in its wireless unit. Technology concerns benefited from institutional investors buying the year's hottest equities so that those issues are included in their year-end portfolios, Mr. McCabe said. "Strength is begetting strength and for no particular fundamental reason," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average over the past year.
