title: EBay Is Told That It Sells Nazi Items
body: The online auction service eBay Inc. has come under fire previously for letting people bid on pornography and firearms. Yesterday, it encountered more problems when a group that monitors anti-Semitism complained about the sale of Nazi memorabilia. A letter sent to the company by the Simon Wiesenthal Center in Los Angeles said items that "glorify Nazism" were being auctioned and noted that the sale of such items was illegal in Germany. "My goal here is not to get eBay indicted," said Rabbi Abraham Cooper, associate dean of the center. "My goal is to keep eBay from selling Nazi memorabilia in Germany." A spokesman for eBay, which is based in San Jose, Calif., said that the company already prohibited the sale of such items in Germany because they are outlawed there. But he said it generally polices the sales of banned items only after receiving complaints from users. In addition, the spokesman said, the service expects users in Germany not to violate their country's laws and thus would not technologically block such sales. Last week, Amazon.com said it would stop selling Hitler's "Mein Kampf" to customers in Germany, citing German laws prohibiting sales of hate literature. The move came after the Wiesenthal Center filed legal complaints against Amazon and other Internet booksellers in August. Unlike Amazon, eBay does not handle or ship the items sold on its site. A search for listings containing the word "Nazi" on eBay yesterday returned nearly 3,000 items. They included a Nuremberg rally postcard for $24, items described as "Five Beautiful Large Nazi Death Notices!!" for $40, and a Nuremberg rally flag for $550. http://www.nytimes.com

title: John G. Stewart Book Executive, 80
body: John G. Stewart, former manager of The newyork Times Book Division, died on Tuesday at his home in Rumson, N.J. He was 80. He had a brief illness, his wife, Linda, said. Mr. Stewart was born in Dobbs Ferry, N.Y., grew up there, graduated from Phillips Academy in Andover, Mass., and, in 1940, from Harvard College. He was a pilot in the Army Air Corps in World War II and got a master's degree in 1947 from the Columbia School of Journalism. He worked for what is now United Press International and This Week magazine before becoming an editor for The newyork Times Sunday Magazine in 1957. He became the manager of The newyork Times Book Division when it was established in 1963. In its first three years, the division issued more than 50 titles in collaboration with 25 publishers; it became Times Books and was later sold to Random House. Later he held a variety of positions at The newyork Times Company. He retired in 1992. His marriage to Helen Markel ended in divorce. In addition to his wife, Linda, he is survived by a sister, Jane Heckman of Lombard, Ill.; his son and daughter from his first marriage, Mark, of Monmouth Hills, N.J., and Jennifer Stewart of Studio City, Calif.; three stepchildren; and 12 grandchildren. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
For People Shopping Online, Survey Strikes Cautionary Note
body: If you believe all the television commercials, online shopping will be an effortless and satisfying experience this holiday season. But a couple of recent reports suggest that dealing with Web-based stores can be anything but. In a survey conducted by Jupiter Communications, an Internet research company, at least 40 percent of retail Web sites did not respond to email requests for help. Another survey, which polled consumer agencies, showed that many Internet-based shops had disappointed and angered customers by sending goods late or not shipping them at all. Those numbers are worse than in earlier years, analysts say. In the third quarter of 1998, the Jupiter survey found, only 28 percent of Web retailers failed to respond to email requests that had been sent, anonymously, from Jupiter researchers. And the National Association of Consumer Agency Administrators, which based its conclusions on data collected through the end of 1998, said that the number of complaints related to Internet transactions or Internet service had increased by 39 percent since 1997. Jupiter found a gulf between the companies that are ready for the holiday rush and those that aren't. Of 25 online shops the company tested, 15 responded to email messages within one day, while 10 took longer than five days to respond. (Among 100 Web sites outside retail sales, 46 percent failed to respond to email requests.) Some of the problems encountered by consumer agencies went much further than a lack of response to email. Wendy Weinberg, a spokeswoman for the national consumer group, said that people had complained about undisclosed shipping charges, packages that arrived weeks later than expected and purchases that turned out to be fraudulent. She advises people to look for traces of the nonvirtual world before pulling out the credit card. "At least check if there is a phone number listed on the Web site first," she said.   LISA GUERNSEY http://www.nytimes.com

title:
ONLINE SHOPPER;
Taking Care (Use Plastic) on Foreign Sites
body: HERE are a few things I know about the raw-milk camembert cheese that a French company called Fromages .com sells online. First, milk is ladled carefully into vats. Then it matures into creamy yellow rounds that get coddled, like newborns in a hospital nursery, until at the age of 21 days they reach the peak of taste. Now we get to one important thing I do not know: how that peak tastes. That is because raw-milk cheeses that mature in less than 60 days may harbor dangerous bacteria; they are illegal in the unitedstates. So American shoppers who arrive at www .fromages.com are steered instead to a truncated list of federally approved cheeses. As for the list, the Roquefort, the Saint-Marcellin and the Reblochon sounded fine -- like the camemberts, they are stored in a temperature-controlled cellar until ready to eat, then shipped overnight to customers around the world. But the site's soulful descriptions of 116 cheeses convinced me that I wanted nothing less than the distinctively runny camembert, ripened "to the very heart." So I phoned Marc Refabert, the director of Fromages.com. But he said, simply: "I am very sad that I cannot send it. To my point of view, for the person who does not have the chance to have this cheese, it's a pity." If he had not rubbed it in like that, my initial response might have been more graceful. In any case, I would like the record to show that any subsequent comments I might have made along the lines of "Listen, Refabert, who would it hurt if you just shipped me one little bite?" were entirely in jest. I changed my mind anyway, after I phoned the unitedstates Food and Drug Administration, where a spokesman told me that the listeria bacteria in contaminated raw-milk products killed 425 people a year in the unitedstates. Resigned to a healthy fate, I returned to Fromages.com to instead order a (legal) camembert made from pasteurized milk. Waiting for my cheese, I had time to reflect on the fact that this is just one of the many compromises that American shoppers are going to have to make as a growing number of overseas merchants go online. "A lot of countries are rushing to catch up to where the unitedstates is in e-commerce, and that means that shoppers are going to run into this more and more," said Bob Laity, an Andersen Consulting managing partner who advises overseas Web sites. "If you saw a nice ivory bracelet on a French Web site, would you know that it is illegal to import? What about a product that is classified as food in one country, but as drugs in another?" The simplest answer is that if you question a product's legality, do not buy it. While government officials acknowledged that they simply could not inspect every single parcel, the last thing you want is to be the unlucky shopper whose shipment of fresh meat or endangered species of plants or Cuban cigars is seized on the docks. I cannot even begin to contemplate the headache involved with trying to get a refund. In fact, if you need any sort of customer service -- if you want to return a damaged item, if you have questions about shipping or import tariffs -- you can expect problems, Mr. Laity said. "The unitedstates as a country is way ahead on customer service, so if you are buying overseas, anticipate difficulties if everything is not all right with the purchase. How do you straighten it out, when the dot-coms in Europe don't come from an environment where customer service is as widely considered important?" One way to protect yourself is to pay by credit card; you can always dispute the charge. Even better, some overseas Web sites will calculate your credit card payment in unitedstates dollars. For instance, at www.chinesejade.com (a jeweler headquartered in hongkong), at www .aviapress.com (a Russian seller of aviation-related books) and at www .indiagiftcenter.com (in India), buyers make credit card payments through CCNow of Delaware, which processes credit card transactions for about 7,000 merchants, 30 percent of whom are overseas. That method worked well for me when I recently bought a poster from a hongkong art dealer who happened to be a CCNow client. The seller calculated a final price (including shipping costs) in dollars and informed me that no duty was owed. (A unitedstates Customs spokesman told me that duty was assessed on purchases over $100 unless they fell into duty-free categories like books, antiques or paintings.) As soon as CCNow processed the $15 transaction, the seller mailed me the poster. I still do not know how much my cheese will cost me, however. Fromages.com estimated that the total, 455 francs, would be about $63. However, when I phoned American Express two days later to find out how much my account had actually been charged (currency exchange rates can fluctuate several times in the course of a single day), I learned the transaction had not been posted -- and might not be for up to 30 days. Luckily, the cheese itself arrived much sooner, lovingly wrapped in protective silver foil and nestled in a bed of torn paper strips. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Margaret Riegel)

title: Reaching Out for Help, or to Help
body: WHEN Bonnie Frascatore was confined to bed for seven months during a high-risk pregnancy, the high point of each day came when she switched on her computer. Every day, she received email from a woman who had experienced a pregnancy just as difficult. Through email, she found compassion that was not always available at home -- and she did not have to contend with making her house or herself presentable for a visitor. "It was nice to write what I wanted to write without having a family member say, 'Oh, get over it,' " said Ms. Frascatore, who is 36 and lives in Amsterdam, N.Y. In fact, when she went into labor in March, she insisted that her family send an email note to the woman, a volunteer with a nationwide support group. "At the hospital, the first thing I said to my husband was, 'I forgot to email!' " she recalled. Since then, Ms. Frascatore has become a volunteer with the same online support group, the Sidelines National Support Network (www .sidelines.org), and she sends email messages each day to other women with high-risk pregnancies. Her experience as a virtual volunteer is becoming more common as nonprofit groups learn to organize helpers who want to contribute to society from their keyboards. Jayne Cravens, manager of the Virtual Volunteering Project (www.serviceleader.org/vv) at the University of Texas at Austin, has identified more than 250 organizations nationwide that have started such programs. They range from small grass-roots environmental groups to large educational organizations that coordinate the online mentoring of students. "People say, 'I want to help, but I want to do it by computer,' " Ms. Cravens said. Her project tracks groups that allow volunteers to work via computer and also provides training in setting up programs. Three years ago, when the program started, the nonprofit world resisted the notion of using the Internet. "The idea of working with unseen volunteers -- people think, 'I'm never going to see these people, and the Internet is crawling with pedophiles,' " Ms. Cravens said. But as perceptions of the Internet matured, she said, organizations became more open to the concept. In some cases, outreach would not be possible without the Internet. Last year, the San Jose Children's Musical Theater created a production called "Pulse: The Rhythm of Life" by drawing disabled and seriously ill children into the process as online volunteers. Tegan McLane, director of the Theater as Digital Activity program (www.sjcmt.com/TADA!), created characters based on composites of the children who volunteered as online consultants. For example, producers asked the children what kinds of challenges an 11-year-old character named Thomas with bone cancer would face. The children were asked what episodes would unfold in Thomas's life and what his dreams and fears would be. When the songs and dialogue for the production were written, they were posted on a Web page for the children to critique. Ms. Cravens is compiling more examples. She sees the Internet as an important catalyst for getting people involved in causes. "I'm sick to death of stories about how the Internet is making people lonely and cranky," she said. "If anything, I've noticed the Internet is getting people out more." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: HANDS ACROSS THE ETHER -- Help for women with high-risk pregnancies.

title:
STATE OF THE ART;
Not Born To Be Wired
body: WHEN Apple introduced the iBook several months ago as the portable version of its popular iMac desktop computer, one of its more intriguing features was a built-in radio antenna that in theory enabled the iBook to connect to the Internet and share files with other Macintosh computers without wires. But like the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence project, which scans radio emissions coming from deep space for patterns that might indicate alien intelligence, and perhaps even explain the Pokemon phenomenon, the antenna in my iBook picked up only static. Apple finally released the missing components last week to allow the iBook to communicate with other silicon-based life forms: the $299 AirPort base station and the $99 AirPort wireless networking card. They were well worth the wait. The AirPort wireless networking system is confirmation that there is intelligent life in the computer industry. The AirPort networking technology enables two or more AirPort-equipped computers to share files and Internet connections via radio waves at distances of up to 150 feet, even through walls and ceilings, at speeds of up to 11 megabits per second. That is faster and easier than any wire-based networking scheme I've tried at home, including prototypes of a 10 mbps system, the Home Phoneline Networking Association Version 2.0 kit for PC's. Two Macs, each with an AirPort card, can swap files and share system resources and can be used for multiplayer games. With the base station, up to 10 (or maybe more) Macs equipped with AirPort can share a high-speed Internet connection. That is so important, and it has such potential to change the way we use computers and information appliances around the house, that I'm compelled to repeat it in a different way: I'm sitting outside the house on the deck, with an iBook on my lap, enjoying a glorious autumn day, reading the current e-news, checking email, doing a little bit of holiday e-shopping and writing this column. There are no wires, cables or extension cords in sight. As the stars come out, I simply stroll back into the house and continue working from the sofa in the living room. Now I know how my dog must feel. I'm not supposed to be on the sofa, at least not with a computer. Computers have been banned from the living room, mainly for aesthetic reasons. But with no wires and power cords, and an easily carried iBook, no one will know. Along with the health and happiness of my family, a championship for the Yankees and my digital subscriber line high-speed Internet service, AirPort is at the top of my list of things to be grateful for this Thanksgiving. The iBook itself is a bit of a puzzle, however. How odd it is to finally receive intelligent radio transmissions from Out There, only to discover that they emanate from a device that vaguely resembles an orange or blue toilet seat. Technically, the iBook is a clamshell design of translucent, ice-colored plastic with rubberized hot tangerine or cool blueberry accents. Apple designed it for students and for consumers buying their first portable PC's. The iBook has many clever features, including an extraordinary six-hour battery, a powerful PowerPC G3 microprocessor, a rugged case with a flip-up handle, a plush, full-size keyboard with comfortable wrist wrests, and the AirPort radio antenna embedded in the translucent plastic surrounding a big, bright, colorful display screen. At $1,599, the price measures up admirably against other laptops in its class. It also has some turkey features, however, including a base configuration that offers just 32 megabytes of RAM and a 3.2-gigabyte hard disk. Apple says the iBook weighs 6.6 pounds, which may be true on Mars. Here on Earth, my scale said it was 8 pounds. The stingy helping of RAM means that only one or two application programs can be active at once and that the processor will be hobbled by frequent hard disk access. But Apple wanted to keep the iBook's price down, and it chose to spend its money on things that cannot be upgraded easily, like the Thin Film Transistor screen, the keyboard and the AirPort system. Because of the AirPort system, I have been carrying the hefty iBook everywhere I go in the house. Upstairs, downstairs, in the kitchen, in the living room, on the deck, in the garage -- everywhere I went, the iBook stayed in touch with its D.S.L.-connected base station or, in computer-to-computer mode, to another AirPort-equipped iMac in my office. AirPort is based on a new wireless networking protocol called I.E.E.E. 802.11, which has been adopted widely within the computer industry. This week, in fact, Dell introduced a line of 802.11 wireless networking products for its corporate computers. Apple, however, is the first to bring 802.11 to the consumer world, at down-to-earth prices. In theory, Windows-based machines that adhere to the 802.11 standard will eventually be able to network wirelessly with Macs. For now, however, AirPort wireless home networking is a luxury for Mac owners only, and then only for Macs that have antennas and can accept the AirPort wireless networking card. Those include all of the iBooks, all of the newest iMacs (but not the original ones) and all of the desktop G4 Macintoshes except the bottom-end 350-megahertz model. Apple says current PowerBook portables, the larger and more powerful siblings of the iBooks, and older G3 Macintoshes can be added to an Airport network with an optional WaveLAN network card from Lucent, which co-developed the AirPort system with Apple. The cards cost $179 or $199, depending on features (www.wavelan.com). Lucent says the cards can also add Windows-based PC's to an AirPort network, but I did not test that claim. Older Macs, including the recent G3 blue-and-white desktops, are essentially out of luck. They can be hard-wired, via Ethernet cable, to an AirPort base station. The AirPort base station resembles a silver flying saucer from a 1950's science fiction movie. It is stylish enough to leave on the desktop. The base station contains both a 56K modem and a 10BaseT Ethernet port for connection to a high-speed local area network, D.S.L. or cable modem. The real value of the base station is in sharing a fast Internet connection. Cable and D.S.L. connections are always on, so connections from a remote AirPort-equipped computer are instant. If the Internet connection is by dial-up modem, connecting from a remote computer works just as it does from a wired computer. Clicking on the browser or email software tells the base station to dial into the Internet service provider. AirPort works only with I.S.P.'s that adhere to common Internet protocols, which includes just about all of them except America Online. So if you connect to the Internet through AOL's dial-up system, you will need another I.S.P. for the AirPort Internet connection. Once connected to the Internet through AirPort, it is easy to log onto AOL and use all its resources, including email. Wireless networking is going to be profoundly important, and I hope other PC makers follow Apple's bold lead in making 802.11 connections a standard feature. Another wireless standard called Bluetooth will show up in products next year to allow small appliances, phones, computer peripherals and consumer electronics devices to communicate automatically. We will soon be bombarding the universe with more radio and infrared emissions than ever before. It seems appropriate, then, that another profound application making its debut this year involves radio waves arriving from the other direction. More than 1.4 million Internet-connected personal computer owners in 224 countries have teamed up to donate their otherwise unused computing cycles to help create the world's largest ad hoc supercomputer. The common goal is to help the SETI@home Project at the University of California at Berkeley search for extraterrestrial intelligence (www .setiathome.ssl.berkeley.edu). Since the project began in May, these PC's have collectively contributed 120,000 years' worth of computing time to analyze radio emissions from outer space, said Dan Werthimer, the project's chief scientist. They have not bagged any aliens yet, Dr. Werthimer noted. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
Storing Your Life in a Virtual Desktop;
Web-Based Storage and Software Reinvents an Old Idea, the Network Computer
body: COLIN S. BRADY is one of those executives whose office is a computer screen, whether it is the one on his home computer, his work computer or his laptop. So last July, when both his laptop and his home computer crashed irreparably within a four-day period, it was as if two-thirds of his office had been destroyed. By all measures, Mr. Brady should have been in a panic. Instead, he remained calm. His work had been saved in what he called his "safe deposit box in the sky," an online area that had been serving as his virtual desktop. Within a few days, he had a new laptop and had logged onto a Web site called Visto.com to retrieve his documents. "It was a professional lifesaver," said Mr. Brady, a recruiter for TMP Worldwide Executive Search. If last year's buzzword was Web portal, this year it is the virtual desktop, also known as the roaming desktop, the Internet desktop, and, in some circles, pervasive computing. In 1998, portals were heralded for their ability to give people a central place to find personalized news, sports and stock quotes from any computer on the Internet. Today, virtual desktops are being promoted for their convenience, but they take "personal" a step further: users have constant access to their files, their address books, their calendars. "All the information you ever wanted to look at will be available at any time, anywhere," said Kevin Herrboldt, director of engineering for Cyrus InterSoft of Minneapolis, which is offering virtual desktop software called Speiros. "You will no longer say, 'I have to go home and download that information from my computer.' " So far, virtual-desktop services are mostly available in bits and pieces. Some companies offer online storage, while others provide Web-based calendars or photo albums. A few companies, like MyFamily.com and Bungo.com, have tried to put those services in one package. The newest services, which are still being tested, provide spreadsheet or word-processing programs. The programs do not need to be loaded onto a computer's hard drive. They can simply be borrowed or rented from companies like Cyrus InterSoft or Desktop.com, which keep the applications on servers and operate them over the Internet. So far, that concept seems to appeal mostly to users who have lightning-fast connections. But just as portals have not become essential for most computer users, virtual desktops may not live up to their promise either. How many people, for example, actually manage to keep the physical elements of their work and their private lives -- to-do lists, calendars, projects, phone numbers -- in one place? "Companies are of the viewpoint: this is where you'll put your stuff, and that's what people will want to do," said Keith Dawson, editor of an email newsletter, Tasty Bits from the Technology Front. "It's not clear at all that that's what people want to do." Concerns about security, reliability and privacy, not to mention bandwidth, may keep some people from adopting the virtual desktop, Mr. Dawson said. "I don't think it's the next big thing," he added. "I think it's a small thing that may not work." Most people say they do not want to depend on just one computer. Many users, in fact, are already using an ad hoc version of the virtual desktop: They send documents to their home computer as email attachments, then use email to transfer them back to work. Or they set up roaming email accounts, like Hotmail, that allow them to check their messages from any Web-connected computer, like those at airport kiosks. Still, it is sometimes difficult to maintain a "home base" -- one place that contains the latest version of files. Some newly updated documents, for example, might be sitting on the computer at home when they are needed on the laptop or at work. Now imagine, the advocates of virtual desktops say, if those files could always reside in something like Mr. Brady's "safe deposit box in the sky." The latest changes would always be retrievable because the documents would be stored on servers maintained by companies that make a business of keeping that data safe. That vision has been bandied about for years among computer manufacturers and information-technology enthusiasts. Computer historians would argue that the vision was a reality before the days of personal computers, when people worked on dumb terminals that were connected to mainframes. In the consumer market, the idea is more recent. In 1995, Oracle began developing a device it called the network computer, a stripped-down machine that tapped into a more powerful network. Oracle's chief executive, Larry Ellison, predicted in 1997 that network computers would outsell PC's by 2000. Today, most analysts agree that the network computer is as good as dead. But the companies jumping into the virtual desktop movement are not discouraged. In fact, many of them argue that as soon as their software gains acceptance among consumers, the idea of a network computer will probably take off. This time it will be called a Net appliance, a device like a cell phone or handheld computer. "Not only can you go to any computer," said Sam Fahmy, president of Bungo.com, one of the virtual-desktop companies, "you'll have a handheld device that has a consistent interface." That means that the user will see a familiar-looking desktop, no matter what computer is used. So far, most of the virtual desktops run on a Web browser like Netscape or Internet Explorer. Users create desktops by setting up their user ID's and passwords. Then they upload files from their computers into the servers maintained by the desktop companies. Entering data into Web-based calendars and address books can often be done on the fly, using fill-in-the-blank forms. Desktop.com provides online calculators, applications that make graphs of stock quotes and notepads that act as word processors. Cyrus InterSoft, the company making Speiros, is taking a different approach. It is abandoning the Web interface and marketing a stand-alone product that acts something like a browser, except that is specifically designed to maintain the security of personal documents and run applications like spreadsheet programs. "The Web was meant to be a place to broadcast public information," said Mr. Herrboldt, of Cyrus InterSoft. "It was never meant to provide a secure location for storing information." The company is hoping to add Speiros to Internet computers that are in airport kiosks. It believes that people will be willing to download Speiros onto their laptops and computers because they are already accustomed to downloading the latest version of Netscape for Web browsing. But dial-up users, beware: Trying to maneuver around a full-service virtual desktop, whether using a Web browser or another piece of software, can be a chore. If loading a simple Web page can take minutes using a dial-up modem, imagine the agony of using a word-processing program that runs over the Web from a server thousands of miles away. Even over a speedy T-1 line, the process can be like typing underwater. Those who have adopted some form of virtual desktop (often those in areas with broadband Internet access) use them as communal spaces as much as personal ones. Once information resides on a networked server, outside a private hard drive, anyone with a password can gain access. The online desktop becomes part virtual bulletin board, part virtual conference room. For example, Stuart Fullinwider, an investor in Bungo.com who lives in Denver, uses the service to publish a schedule of his son's ice hockey games, which other team members can also use. John Blair, a 40-year-old resident of Longview, Wash., puts photographs of his late father on a virtual desktop he built using MyFamily.com. His 10 brothers and sisters, who are scattered around the country, can log in and add their own. Last summer, the group planned a reunion using the service. "It's caused a lot more interaction," Mr. Blair said. The family-and-friends benefit is not lost on virtual-desktop companies. Capturing an audience, particularly one that multiplies with every group enlisted, can translate into lucrative advertising revenue and commissions on e-commerce products. "The service can wrap you in more closely and make you loyal," said Mr. Dawson, the newsletter editor. "If your stuff is there, you are going to stay." Just how much stuff people will put in their virtual desktops is an open question. Marlene Cupit, a 60-year-old resident of Hurst, Tex., stores family stories on a MyFamily.com site that nearly 80 family members can enter. Because of the password protection, she said she was confident that no one else could gain access. The family even uses the site to talk about financial matters. Others may be less trusting. "I think people will use these for nonsensitive data," said Bob Rankin, an editor of Tourbus, an email newsletter. But they will demand high levels of security, he said, for more private material. "Especially," he added, "after the first highly publicized hacking incident." All the virtual desktop companies promise that their customers' documents are safe; many have encrypted the materials and most of them boast about their back-up procedures. But often the files are only as private as people's passwords, which are often not as safe as people think. "It's very difficult to make these services bulletproof," Mr. Dawson said. Human psychology comes into play as well. Some observers argue that people want to be able to point to a machine, Zip disk or floppy disk and say: Here is where the information resides. "I like having my data on my hard drive," Mr. Rankin wrote in an email message. Even Mr. Brady, the executive who swears by his "safe deposit box in the sky," backs up his data. He uses a Visto.com utility that automatically synchronizes his data every day and then sends copies to Visto.com for safekeeping. "I always have the latest stuff on all three machines regardless of which machine on which I originally did the work," Mr. Brady said. After all, virtual-desktop companies may say that their services are available "anytime, anywhere," but that "anywhere" comes with a caveat: you must be connected to the Internet. Until it becomes practical to log on for hours while flying at 30,000 feet, Mr. Brady will do much of his work off line, from a document stored on his hard drive.  Site-Seeing: Virtual Desktops An Internet Corner To Call Your Own It started with email: Companies like Hotmail.com and Yahoo offered people an online space to keep their email so they could gain access from any Web browser. Now the concept has moved to other desktop services, from online calendars to word-processing programs that run over the Web. Companies are sprouting up to offer the services, which are free -- in exchange for your glances at the sites' advertisements. Here is a sampling of sites:  CALENDARS AnyDay.com SuperCalendar.com When.com  FILE STORAGE @backup.com freedrive.com i-drive.com xdrive.com  PHOTO ALBUMS GatherRound.com Photoloft.com  ALL OF THE ABOVE Bungo.com eCircles.com MagicalDesk.com MyFamily.com Visto.com  ALL OF THE ABOVE, PLUS APPLICATIONS LIKE WORD-PROCESSING PROGRAMS CyrusIntersoft.com Desktop.com MyWebOS.com http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: NO NEED TO PANIC -- Thanks to a roaming desktop, a server maintained by an Internet company, Colin Brady did not lose files when two of his computers crashed. (Richard Perry/The New York Times); LOOKING AHEAD -- Concerns about security and privacy might hinder the adoption of the virtual desktop, said Keith Dawson, editor of Tasty Bits from the Technology Front. title: Whitney Biennial May Include Digital Artworks
body: In what may come to be viewed as a milestone for digital artists, the Whitney Museum of American Art is preparing to include Internet-based artworks in its biennial survey of American art next spring, say to artists and others familiar with plans for the exhibit. When the exhibition opens on March 23, as many as 10 digital works, ranging from interactive Web sites to multimedia narratives that can be read online, are expected to be displayed. The artists selected for the Whitney Biennial are not scheduled to be announced until mid-December. Mary Haus, a spokeswoman for the museum, declined to discuss details of the biennial until that announcement had been made. She said no final list of participating artists has been made. During the last year a few intrepid museums have augmented their gallery shows with, at most, a token Web-based piece or two. Despite the controversies it has provoked in recent years, the biennial remains a signal event in the art world, and the inclusion of digital art could legitimize the young genre. Steve Dietz, the director of new-media initiatives at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, said, "This potentially recognizes that Net-based art is no different than other contemporary art." Maxwell L. Anderson, who joined the Whitney as its director in September 1998, has been responsible for a number of digital-art initiatives, including the Art Museum Image Consortium, an online database of fine-art reproductions for research use. For the museum's two-part exhibition, "The American Century: Art and Culture, 1900-2000," the Whitney mounted an ambitious Web version of the exhibition. The challenge of how to present digital works in a public space when they have been designed for individual viewing on a computer screen has thwarted the acceptance of Internet art. Some works require live Internet connections, which are not always practical in a gallery. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Concerns Raised Over Encryption Report
body: As the Clinton administration began circulating its long-awaited plan yesterday for easing export controls on encryption technology, industry representatives and privacy groups said the proposal fell short of promises made by the White House two months ago. The draft, floated to industry representatives and groups, puts into writing the plans that Vice President Al Gore announced during a trip to Silicon Valley in September to ease the administration's controversial controls on the data scrambling technology. Encryption is widely used to keep computer data and online communications like email private. But while the draft represents a substantial easing of licensing controls, privacy advocates said it did not go as far as Mr. Gore had promised. Ed Gillespie, who heads Americans for Computer Privacy, a lobbying group that favors lifting all controls on the export of encryption, said: "Two months ago we were looking at a clean lifting of export restrictions. Now we are looking at a complicated mass of regulations." But Mr. Gillespie also noted that the proposal was only a draft. Indeed, administration officials said they would continue seeking industry input before publishing their final rules in December. The industry's biggest concerns lay in complicated and ambiguous language placing restrictions on products sold to governments. Those reviewing the draft said they were unsure how the restrictions would affect the ability of American companies to compete with companies overseas. Among the proposal's defenders was Stewart Baker, a partner with the Washington law firm of Steptoe & Johnson and a former National Security Agency counsel who was part of the committee that advised the administration on how to change encryption export policy. "In some respects, it's better than promised," he said. "In fact, there's a part of me that wants to say, 'You've been upgraded from a prop plane to a Concorde, and now you're going to complain that you didn't get a window seat?' " William A. Reinsch, the under secretary of commerce who heads the Bureau of Export Administration, said the administration both expected and welcomed the criticism. "My objective was to put forth a good-faith effort that reflects what was said in September," Mr. Reinsch said. "This is a genuine work in progress, and we intend to take their criticisms to heart." The administration has for years fought attempts to eliminate export controls on encryption, in part because the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the National Security Agency contend that encryption makes it easier for terrorists and criminals to conceal their activities. Under the old rules, strong-encryption products needed a license to be exported. The new plan lifts license and review requirements for many mass market products but still requires Commerce Department reviews in a number of circumstances. Laura Ipsen, senior government affairs manager for Cisco Systems Inc., the leading maker of networking equipment, said there was "clearly more work to be done." "We have concerns about restrictions on telecommunications and Internet service providers," she said. "We will continue to work with the administration and Congress to achieve the landmark encryption reform promised in September, which this overly complex draft falls short of achieving."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Edible Gifts, a Click or a Call Away
body: WHAT started as a trickle of mail-order food sources on the Internet last year has turned into a torrent, making it difficult to sort out the delicious from the dreary. So this year, instead of just thumbing through catalogs and magazines and taking suggestions from friends, colleagues and perfect strangers, I have also prowled the Web to seek out the best food gifts for the holidays. With few exceptions I did not find much that is newer or better than I would have by my old methods, but my searching and test-shopping could save you time. Most of the 24 mail-order sources listed below have their own Web sites, but not all of them are interactive. Some simply provide a little information and direct the shopper to order by email, phone or fax. The boutique food business is still largely small time, and some of the one-person operations have only recently stuck a foot into the chancy waters of the cyberworld. And when they do, they are not always better than good old catalogs. Some sites take so long to navigate that you could drive to the store and be back with your purchases before you've found what you want online.  Often the quality of the photos is poor. In ordering online, be careful when giving credit-card information. You know you are in a secure area when the URL box in your browser reads "https" instead of "http." And be sure to get a confirmation on your order, either on the Web site itself or by email. In some of my dealings companies said they never received the order. And I never received the food. The Web sites are all still too primitive to deal with custom orders. If they offer a gift basket with five items and you want five different items, you will still have to phone the company or email it to see if something special can be created just for you. Some of the sites, like ChefShop.com, which has unusual and excellent food, do not even have a place where the buyer can provide special instructions for delivery, like "leave at front door without signature." Sometimes it is not easy to find what you want. Grace's Marketplace is located at fultonstreet.com, and to find Grace's you have to click on three different places. What's more, a panettone ordered directly from Grace's is much less expensive than the same panettone ordered on the Web. At one Web site I kept checking a quicker -- and more expensive -- form of delivery but to no avail. I finally had to call the company, making double work. If you want something delivered by a certain date, always phone. If a Web site has no warehouse, the order goes to a middleman, adding time to delivery. In shopping I found that no single system worked all the time or was as fast as the phone. Until there is someone at the other end who can instantly answer questions, the Internet will never be better. On the other hand, if you like to order at 3 a.m., the Web is the perfect medium. Here are my choices of food gifts for the holidays. Unless otherwise noted, orders can be placed on the Web site, and shipping is extra. The last date orders are accepted for Christmas delivery is included. The oatmeal cookies from the BELLOWS HOUSE BAKERY -- are so buttery and packed with plump raisins they could pass for homemade. Two-plus pounds, $30.90, including shipping. P.O. Box 818, Walpole, N.H. 03608; (800) 358-6302; bhbakery@sover.net; cutoff, Dec. 17. Unless you catch your own, there is no better way to sample exquisitely fresh seafood than by ordering from BROWNE TRADING --. Sweet, delicate peekytoe crab is $9.50 for seven ounces; Maine sea scallops (after Dec. 1) are $25 a pound, and sushi-grade yellowfin tuna is $36 for two pounds. 260 Commercial Street, Portland, Me. 04101; (800) 944-7848; www.Browne-Trading.com; orders: markgrobman@browne-trading.com; cutoff, Dec. 20. CHEFSHOP.COM -- has excellent taste: Any or all of these selections would make someone happy. The English Biscuit Sampler, containing Duchy biscuits bearing the stamp of Prince Charles, is $18.99 for one seven-ounce box each of ginger, almond and lemon flavors. June Taylor's Mostly Marmalade Basket contains one jar each of delightfully tart organic grapefruit and Meyer lemon marmalade (11 ounces), blood-orange marmalade and Santa Rosa plum Conserve (8 ounces each) for $32.99. The Peanut Sauce Basket holds two 11.5-ounce jars of Vong spicy peanut sauce, for $19.99. And LuLu's Gift Basket for the Cook, by Restaurant LuLu in San Francisco, contains one each of a smoky romesco sauce, peppery roasted tomato harissa and intense olive tapenade, each in a six-ounce jar, plus one each of the restaurant's delightfully perfumed white truffle and lavender honeys, in nine-ounce jars, for $44.95. 1435 Elliot Avenue West, Seattle 98119; (877) 337-2491; www.chefshop.com; orders: shopkeeper@chefshop.com; cutoff, Dec. 15. CHEESECAKE MOMMA -- makes organic cheesecakes for people who didn't think they liked cheesecakes. The berry, pumpkin and espresso, all with cookie crusts, are not too sweet but exceptionally creamy. A six-inch cake is $32; a nine-inch cake, $47; both include shipping. 200 Henry Street, Ukiah, Calif. 95482; (707) 462-2253; momma@pacific.net; cutoff, Dec. 16. For sheer indulgence no one beats D'ARTAGNAN --. Its goose liver terrine, silky and rich, comes in 9.5-ounce or 1 1/2-pound sizes at $75 a pound. A 3.5-ounce container of butter thickly studded and perfumed with black truffles is $6.50. Nine ounces of the perfect breakfast sausages made with chicken and dried apples is $5.95. Orders over $200 are shipped free. 280 Wilson Avenue, Newark 07105; (800) 327-8246; www .dartagnan.com; orders:christine @dartagnan.com; cutoff, Dec. 20. A tea cake made with Meyer lemons and buttermilk from DIVINE DELIGHTS -- would be just right after one of those overindulgent holiday dinners. A two-and-a-half-pound cake is $31.50, including shipping. 24 Digital Drive, Suite 10, Novato, Calif. 94949; (800) 443-2836; divinede@wenet.net; cutoff, Dec 20. For the jaded palate, the FANCY FOODS GOURMET CLUB -- is offering smoked salmon either pastrami-style or flavored with pesto, each $20 a pound. 330E North Stonestreet Avenue, Rockville, Md. 20850; (800) 576-3548; www.ffgc.com; orders: ffgc@ffgc.com; cutoff, Dec 12. Panettone is the traditional Italian Christmas yeast bread, and GRACE'S MARKETPLACE -- offers one that is very fresh, sweet and filled with raisins and fruit. On the Web site, a 1 pound 10 ounce panettone is $19.95; ordered directly from Grace's, it is $12.50. 1237 Third Avenue (71st Street), newyork 10021; (888) 472-2371; www.fultonstreet.com (click on "gourmet grocer," then "sweets, coffees and teas"); cutoff, Dec. 21. THE GRATEFUL PALATE -- provides lemon or lime curd, deeply flavored with bits of peel, that tastes like homemade. Each jar weighs 6.5 ounces and costs $7.95. 601 Del Norte Boulevard, Unit G, Oxnard, Calif. 93030; (888) 472-5283; www.gratefulpalate.com; order@gratefulpalate.com; cutoff, Dec. 15. The many fine choices from GREATFOOD.COM -- include addictive Killer Pecans with a spicy kick (a 16-ounce tin for $22.50); superb Muscovy duck breast (either drake at 1.7 to 1.9 pounds for $40.50 or duck at 14 to 16 ounces for $48.95); chunks of creamy Danish blue cheese in delightfully herbed oil (six 10.5-ounce jars, $25.95); and a 6.5-ounce jar of smooth and lemony artichoke lemon pesto with a five-ounce package of dipping crackers for $13.50. 2731 Eastlake Avenue East, Seattle 98102; (800) 841-5984; www.greatfood.com; orders: customerservice@greatfood.com; cutoff for perishables, Dec. 17; nonperish ables, Dec. 10. Now you don't have to live in California to enjoy the sweet and delightfully perfumed Meyer lemons from KATZ & COMPANY --. Two pounds in a handsome 13-inch Italian ceramic bowl decorated with lemons cost $49, zester included. Katz also sells a 12.7-ounce bottle of organic Meyer lemon olive oil, to drizzle on salads or to use as a simple marinade, for $18. 101 South Coombs Street, Suite Y-3, Napa, Calif. 94559; 800-676-7176; www.katzandco .com; cutoff, Dec. 15. LINDA GRISHMAN CHOCOLATES -- combines dark rich chocolate with bits of espresso beans in irresistible Dashing Through the Snow crunch bars. A package of 12 is $28.90, including shipping. P.O. title:
Stores at the Mall Try To Reclaim Christmas;
Retailers Face E-Commerce Challenge
body: As Internet retailers crow that the country is about to have another e-Christmas, brick-and-mortar stores are striking back. Take wish-list programs, first promoted by online sites as the perfect Internet holiday convenience; they are now being usurped by traditional shopping destinations. A me-generation update of the bridal registry, the wish list allows any acquisitive consumer to record gift choices by simply checking size, color and model number. Dan Swaab, a 29-year-old architect, recently put a black pullover from the clothing outlet Butch Blum and a customized picture frame from a store called Fireworks, among other items, on his list. But instead of signing up on a computer site, he did so at the University Village shopping mall outside Seattle, which has been providing forms since the beginning of November for visitors to fill in as they visit their favorite boutiques. The completed lists can be dropped off at locations throughout the complex and are entered into a database (at no cost to shoppers) that is available both on the mall's Internet site and at kiosks.  Mr. Swaab, who says he is familiar with the Internet but "not a full-bore browser," sees no advantage to doing a wish list solely on the Internet. "Returns can be such a hassle," he explains. "This way I've tried everything on." Even if online sales this Christmas reach the high-end predictions of $12 billion, traditional retailers will ring up about 14 times that amount. But mall merchants need to do more than hold their own during the season that accounts for much of their profits for the year. Retailers know they are facing a pervasive stereotype that real-world holiday shopping is a parking and service nightmare. So to make sure Americans do not stay home in front of their computers to buy gifts, stores are beefing up basics like customer service and displaying innovative incentives that range from cash to psychics who select something for hard to please in-laws. The holiday season always brings out a creative streak in merchants, and that has been accented this year by fear. Since the economy remains strong, the official outlook for Christmas 1999 is very bullish -- the National Retail Federation predicts total sales will be about $184 billion, up 6 percent from last year. But the growth in retail sales slowed in October and November, suggesting that consumers might not be as willing to dip into their pockets to satisfy their appetite for DVD players and pashmina shawls. For merchants who rely on Christmas foot traffic for a large chunk of the year's sales, the potential softening of consumer demand has combined with heightened Internet hype to put them on edge. Although most merchants and malls will not admit having such Internet fears for the record, retail analysts say the early rush to put decorations in the windows and the ever-earlier markdowns show that retailers on the ground are feeling pressed. "Mostly traditional retailers are acting very defensively about Christmas," said Wendy Liebmann, president of WSL Strategic Retail, a consulting firm. "They feel that all the talk on the Internet is going to drain them." Among the most interesting retailers to watch this season are those whose livelihoods are most directly challenged by the Web. The Web site of Borders Group is a footnote in the battle between Amazon.com and Barnesandnoble.com to dominate cyberspace book sales, but the chain is rolling out holiday ideas to remain competitive for in-store sales. This season, Border's stores will hold art-and-crafts workshops where children can make bookmarks out of construction paper and crayons. The chain will also hand out booklets of appropriate quotations for book inscriptions for the wit impaired. For example, shoppers giving books on personal finance are advised to copy a quote from Mark Twain, "The lack of money is the root of all evil," onto the front flap. "We wanted to be an extra resource for our customers this year," Ann Binkley, a company spokeswoman, said. Malls, which have the most to lose if shoppers decide to avoid their crowds and parking headaches, are also being creative. Gurnee Mills outside of Chicago has set up a Psychic Aid Station, where "tried and tested" clairvoyant Joanna Ammons will conduct free readings to help shoppers with holiday gift ideas every Saturday to Dec. 18. Ms. Ammons, who says she has successfully predicted 94 marriages, 74 divorces and 8 lottery/casino lucky winnings in the first six months of this year, only requires the name and date of birth of a loved one to divine the perfect stocking stuffer. Other malls owned by the Mills Corporation will have "procrastination stations" where Mrs. Claus will be on hand to offer last-minute gift suggestions and maps, as well as milk and cookies. Naturally, Santa will be there, too. As an extra incentive to shoppers, the mall is offering to take photos of their children to create postcards that can be sent free to anyone in the country. Even retailers that have been doing well with consumers are looking for new twists to make their stores more appealing. Target, the stylish discounter owned by the Dayton Hudson Corporation, has opted for a very direct kind of consumer gratification: money. Each day in November and December, a user of the Target credit card will win $2,000 as part of a "2000 'til 2000" promotion. And Banana Republic, a unit of Gap Inc. and a formidable Internet presence itself, is taking its cut at luring the technology generation by providing services like free cell phone recharging and a download to Palm Pilot devices that includes a top 10 list of attractions near its flagship stores in urban centers. Employees of the Electronics Boutique chain will be roving the aisles with hand-held cash registers in 30 of its Northeastern stores. Seth Levy, the company's chief information officer, calls the new system "a line buster." He adds that the devices, which are equipped to take credit card sales, create an intimate transaction. "If I can talk to you face-to-face in front of the register, we feel it is a closer relationship than if there is a four-foot block of wood between us," Mr. Levy said. Beyond the innovations, improved convenience is a mantra among the stores this season, as they are determined to combat the perception that the Internet is less annoying for shopping, according to J'Amy Owens, president of the Retail Group, a Seattle-based consulting firm. For example, Toys "R" Us Inc., the big retailer that has taken a thrashing at the hands of disenchanted consumers in recent years and faces fierce online competition from Amazon.com and Etoys.com, has put special effort into polishing its performance for this all-important season. Starting in June, the retailer sent sales associates through a training program at the Disney Institute to teach them to be more responsive to requests and more informed about the products. Big department stores, which some say are difficult to shop in because entering, reaching the gift and exiting can be tiresome, are again focusing on "bundling" -- the practice of choosing gifts, prewrapping them and putting them out front where consumers can grab them on the go. For example, Provenance, a vitamin and herbal retailer newly available on the cosmetics floor at Macy's, has packaged groups of products in iridescent fabric and given them names like Peace and Holiday Survival, which contains an enzyme dietary supplement. Bloomingdale's will be experimenting with a new kiosk technology that allows visitors to bypass the sales staff and do everything from search for a product to complete a purchase through the interactive machines. "Retailers show that they are not going to roll over and die on the customer service sword," Ms. Owens said. "The real surprise this season is that the traditional retailers are going to clean the clock of the e-retailers. I am predicting a lot of online flops." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Besides traditional holiday displays, stores are using innovations like mobile clerks, bottom, who can complete transactions. title: Tables Are Waiting On the Internet
body: A HIGH-STAKES movement is taking shape in the newyork restaurant world. In the last six weeks, three instant online reservation services have opened for business. About 20 others are in various stages of gestation, and many observers, including Tim Zagat, are watching the battle with great interest, because whoever wins in newyork is well positioned to dominate national online restaurant reservations, a business that some industry analysts estimate to be worth as much as $2 billion a year. Making reservations online potentially has many advantages for the diner, like an end to the frustration of either being put on permanent hold or confronted with an endless busy signal, and the ability to make a reservation at any time, 24 hours a day. Eventually, the services promise, all a client will have to do is log onto the site, select a restaurant and a time, and reserve with a few clicks of the mouse. Reservations are free, but often the restaurant pays a fee to be on the site. But "eventually" hasn't quite arrived. Last weekend, I attempted to make reservations using the three instant-reservation sites that are up and running and cover newyork: Foodline.com, OpenTable.com and Restaurantrow.com. Only a handful of restaurants have signed on so far, and there are glitches in each of the three systems. Sometimes it was quicker -- and more reliable -- to pick up the telephone and call a restaurant directly. Although in one case, I was able to secure a reservation that I could not by phone. The instant-reservation sites are the next step in the evolving business of reserving on line. Since 1997, sites like Savvydiner.com, a national restaurant reservation site, have simply acted as middlemen between the diner and the restaurant -- you request a reservation on the Web site, and they make the call. A confirmation could take an hour or more. Over the last few months, a number of restaurants, including Tavern on the Green and the Russian Tea Room, both owned by Warner LeRoy, have started taking reservations over the Internet on their own Web sites. But the new sites are different: they want to work the way Moviefone.com does, with a large selection of establishments and immediate confirmation. Reservation requests are sent electronically to an electronic "book" at the restaurant; if there is an opening, the customer gets an email. "Large selection" is key. For any service to succeed, it will need a vast number of restaurants in its newyork database alone. The city has 20,000 restaurants, after all. Mr. Zagat, the restaurant guide publisher, is eyeing the reservations business with more than casual interest. He believes that both diners and restaurants would want to deal with only one Web site, which makes the online business a "natural monopoly." "Many may wade into the fray, but only one will emerge," said Mr. Zagat, who is exploring links with these sites. On Saturday, Foodline had only 24 "coming soon" restaurants and four available on its Web site. OpenTable had 16 "coming soon," one "back soon" and one available. Restaurantrow had seven available. Others in development include RSVIP.com, Dinel23.com, Reservemytable.com and Reserveatable.com. The potential is clearly there. In August, 480 guests booked online for Tavern on the Green, said Karen Bailey, a spokeswoman. By October, the number had grown to 1,114. But even so, restaurants are not flocking to sign up. One reason is the cost. OpenTable charges each restaurant it serves between $500 to $1,000 for installation and customization of the computer hardware, plus $100 to $200 a month for the Internet connection (depending on the size of the venue), plus $1 a reservation. Foodline charges $200 for its Internet connection, plus $1 a head. Restaurantrow does not charge restaurants, but it has limited access to tables and intends to build other business partnerships with the data it acquires through the service. In October, Mr. Zagat met with the representatives of 100 or so newyork restaurants to talk about the opportunities and pitfalls of online reservations. He warned that some systems that offered services free in the beginning might not be free in two or three years. Most of all, he said, any system should protect customer confidentiality. These Web sites could use a restaurant's database of addresses, phone numbers, dining frequency and other proprietary information. Derickson K. Lawrence, the group president of Restaurantrow, based in Rye, N.Y., acknowledged that ownership of this information might be a bone of contention in the future. He said the information might be shared in the future with, say, a theater near a restaurant that is trying to draw in moviegoers. But for the time being, many restaurant owners are waiting to see which company and which system will win out. Jean-Claude Baker, an owner of Chez Josephine in Midtown, said he would not accept online reservations, because "it takes away from the personal touch." Richard Coraine, the director of operations for the Union Square Hospitality Group, which runs four restaurants in Manhattan -- Tabla, Eleven Madison Park, Gramercy Tavern and the Union Square Cafe -- said: "What we sell is hospitality and graciousness. There is no substitute for a kind, human voice on the phone." Stephen Hanson, the president of B. R. Guest Inc., which owns seven restaurants, including Blue Water Grill, Ocean Grill and Park Avalon, said that so far, none of the services appear to be the front runner. "All these companies are about the same ability," he said. "None has developed a system that works for the restaurateur. I need an automatic wait list, so that I can call a person immediately if I should get a cancellation. I need something that will drive people into my seats." Over the weekend, when I logged onto OpenTable, based in San Francisco, I found one newyork restaurant available: Lola in Chelsea. The seven at Restaurantrow, based in Seattle, were the Four Seasons, Jean Georges, La Cote Basque, Moomba, La Grenouille, the "21" Club and Trata. I used Foodline, a newyork City company with four restaurants on its site: Calle Ocho, the Globe, Onieal's Grand Street and Rain. I picked Rain, the one on Third Avenue, which was described as an affordable Pan-Asian restaurant with quiet wood booths. I was intrigued to read that I would be surrounded by people in "casual chic." But mainly I chose it because it was the only mid-price restaurant on the Upper East Side where I could get a table online. It was not easy. After registering -- with my name, address, phone and credit card numbers, information required on all the sites -- I requested a table for two at 5:30 that night. But the server kept giving me earlier times, like 4 p.m., and later times, like 6 and 6:30 p.m. I found it hard to believe that there were no 5:30 tables open, and so I kept trying, off and on, for an hour. Finally, I picked up the phone and called the restaurant. A woman with a cheery voice answered and immediately put me on hold. When she returned a minute later, she took my reservation request -- 5:30 p.m. Saturday -- and it was done. Elapsed time: 2 minutes 30 seconds. Paul Lightfoot, the president and chief executive of Foodline, attributed the glitch to newness, since the restaurant had been online for only a week. He said Foodline, which just sold a percentage of its business to Ticketmaster Online-CitySearch for $5 million, hopes to have 600 newyork restaurants online within a year. Next, I gave OpenTable a try. The site is very spare compared with Foodline's, which is buzzing with information: links to a wine column, a recipe column, local food events, a spirits column. Here, I just clicked and a map of the unitedstates appeared with eight cities highlighted on it. I clicked on newyork and there was one restaurant listed: Lola. Still, I proceeded by clicking to find out about its hours, location, executive chef, and a description ("an elegantly casual restaurant featuring American cuisine").  If you like what you see, you click "reserve now," and type in the day, time and number of people in your party. If your time is available, you click to make your reservation. If it is not, the times nearest the one you requested are given. I clicked on my time: that evening at 7:30. The reservation was confirmed through email. I then made a phone reservation, which took the same amount of time, about two minutes. Finally, I tried to scale the Himalayas of the restaurant world by making a reservation at an exclusive place. Restaurantrow was my sherpa. I clicked on its home page and clicked "Top Table," the instant reservation link, and then clicked on Moomba. My first three times were not available. Unlike Foodline and OpenTable, which can conceivably book all seats in a restaurant, Restaurantrow is allotted a certain number of tables at the restaurants it handles, usually four or five a week, said Mr. Lawrence, the company's group president. As a result, you might call a restaurant and be told there are no available tables, then go online and secure a reservation. But even online, Moomba lived up to its reputation. It was fully booked. I clicked on "time" and found a line of other restaurants in the system with available tables: Jean Georges for two, four and six at 5:30, 6 and 10:30 p.m. With information on the screen, I called the restaurant at 3, asked if a table for two was open at 5:30 and was told it was booked. I went back online and made a reservation for two at 5:30 p.m. One of the allocated tables was still available. Once you reserve through Restaurantrow, you are subject to a $25 penalty if you do not give at least 24 hours' notice that you are not showing up. When I was making reservations, there was no way to cancel online, but they have since added a feature that allows you to cancel by email. Both OpenTable and Foodline have buttons on their sites for cancellations, and email confirmations are given. OpenTable asks customers to cancel at least 30 minutes in advance on the day of the reservation. The Foodline cancellation policy says a $20 penalty will be imposed for not showing up or not canceling, but it does not say when you must notify them to avoid the charge. Tavern on the Green and the Russian Tea Room also charge a $25-a-person no-show fee, but only for patrons who reserve online, not by phone. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos (pg. F10)  Drawing (Ed Koren)

title: email and the Internet Brighten Nursing Homes
body: It may not quite be the fountain of youth, but experts say nursing home residents, even frail ones, take to computers quickly and can revitalize their lives through email and the Internet. "The Internet is a window to life," said Dr. David Lansdale, a geriatrics expert from Stanford University. "It's an elixir for these people." Dr. Lansdale, who advocates communal email and Internet access for every nursing home, was one of several experts to raise the issue here at a weekend meeting of the Gerontological Society of America. He said mastery of email and Internet techniques could help overcome what he called the four plagues of the institutionalized elderly: loneliness, boredom, helplessness and the decline of mental skills. "We want to promote relationships," he said. "Getting connected is bringing people back to life." Dr. Lansdale directs a program called LinkingAges that teaches nursing home residents how to use email to communicate with distant family, old friends and health care providers. The 12-week course ends with a graduation ceremony, and encourages participants to share the email they receive from relatives. He told of a woman in her 90's who mastered the lessons and got this message from a granddaughter: "Dear Grandma, I can't believe you just sent me email. You're the coolest grandma in California." Group dynamics of a nursing home can improve the program's success. One resident might exclaim, "Hey, I can do this!" and other residents will be emboldened to make the effort themselves, Dr. Lansdale said. People who master the technology gain confidence that spreads into other aspects of their lives, and many take pride in helping teach the skills to their fellow residents, he said. "You have opened up the heavens to me," Dr. Lansdale said he was told by one resident who is confined to a wheelchair. Douglas McConatha, a sociologist from West Chester University in Pennsylvania, said he observed improved morale and a drop in depression among nursing home residents who were given Internet training as part of a study he conducted. "It took maybe two training sessions," he said. "You turn them loose in this environment, and a large portion of them flourish. They learned so fast they outpaced the 20-year-old college students learning with them." Dr. McConatha advocated expanded online education programs aimed at attracting retirees both as students and as instructors. He described one such program, Circle of Learning, that encourages elderly people to offer courses based on their lifetime experience, on topics from personal finance to hobbies. One man is teaching a course about his Italian grandmother, Dr. McConatha said. "We can now capture the knowledge of our elders and transfer that wisdom to future generations," he said. Only 25 percent of Americans over age 60 own a computer, compared with 50 percent for the rest of the population, according to research by Microsoft and the American Society on Aging. One of the keys for expanding Internet use by the elderly is to make equipment and Web sites more accessible to them, Dr. Lansdale said. Among changes needed are increased print size on some Web sites and easier-to-use keyboards. http://www.nytimes.com

title: SBC Makes Deal to Transfer Internet Customers to Prodigy
body: SBC Communications Inc., the regional telephone giant, said yesterday that it would transfer all of its residential Internet customers to the Prodigy Communications Corporation, the online service that has long been overshadowed by America Online, in return for a 43 percent stake in Prodigy. SBC, which does business as Ameritech, Pacific Bell and Southwestern Bell, said Prodigy would assume day-to-day management of SBC's 650,000 residential and small-business Internet customers. SBC also said it had agreed to make Prodigy its Internet service for consumers and small businesses. Based on Prodigy's market value yesterday of almost $2 billion, the 43 percent SBC stake would be worth about $900 million. The current primary shareholders, Telmex of Mexico and Carso Global Telecom, will hold about one-third of Prodigy. SBC will control just three of the nine Prodigy board seats, but it will have a veto over major acquisitions and the hiring of key executives. Last month, SBC said it would spend $6 billion to deploy high-speed Internet systems throughout its service region, which covers more than one-third of the unitedstates population. SBC intends to deploy a technology called digital subscriber line, or D.S.L., which uses standard telephone wires to transmit digital data at speeds many times that of those using normal modems. The D.S.L. announcement reflected the company's confidence that it could profit from the exploding demand for Internet access, particularly at high speeds. But none of the Bells have had wild success as retail Internet providers, perhaps because their brands are so throughly associated with voice telephone service. In yesterday's deal, SBC agreed to market Prodigy's service exclusively and to deliver 1.2 million new customers to Prodigy, based in White Plains, over the next three years. If Prodigy consumers use D.S.L. lines, Prodigy will pay SBC for the use of those lines. Consumers who use normal lines will almost always be able to choose an independent Internet provider. SBC executives said yesterday that not only would the deal give them access to Prodigy's brand but it would also give them access to Prodigy's stock as a potential currency for future acquisitions. SBC's stock generally trades as a multiple of projected per-share earnings. Because of the potential for dilution, that can make it difficult to use SBC stock to acquire Internet companies that may not have earnings. "This shields us from significant earnings dilution if we decide we want to grow that business substantially," Stephen A. McGaw, an SBC managing director for business development, said in an interview. Referring to a widely used tool for valuing stocks, he added, "If you run a discounted cash flow of some of these Internet companies, you can't come near to what's ascribed in the market. Having a currency there is a big help." Prodigy was advised in the negotiations by Bear, Stearns & Company. SBC was advised by Goldman, Sachs & Company. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
Technology Issues Continue to Help Nasdaq Index Climb
body: Technology stocks continued their rapid ascent yesterday, carrying the Nasdaq composite index to its 14th record in the last 17 sessions. Gains in Internet stocks and big companies like Microsoft and Intel helped to fuel the advance. Despite the gains in Nasdaq stocks, the other main stock gauges were mixed. "It is a surprise to a lot of us to continue to see the market act the way it is acting," said Ned Collins, head stock trader at Daiwa Securities America. "It continues to beat all expectations." At the close, the Nasdaq composite index was up 23.31 points, to 3,392.56. Since the start of the month, the index has gained more than 14 percent. Big gains in several old-line blue chips, including Coca-Cola, AT&T and I.B.M., helped to push the Dow Jones industrial average up 85.63 points, to 11,089.52. But the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index slipped 1.06 points, to 1,420.94. And the Russell 2000 index of small companies dipped half a point, to 460.77. Microsoft, a component of all three main market gauges, was the biggest positive influence in yesterday's session, traders said. The stock jumped 4 3/16, to 90 3/16, after Federal Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson, who is presiding over the government's antitrust case against the company, named a mediator last week to try to help reach an out-of-court settlement. "The news from Microsoft is probably the most positive corporate news out there," said Arthur Hogan, chief market analyst at Jefferies & Company in Boston. Trading was brisk yesterday, but is likely to slow as the Thanksgiving holiday nears. The stock market will be closed on Thursday and will be open for a half-day on Friday. More than 873 million shares were traded on the newyork Stock Exchange. On the Nasdaq market, 1.2 billion shares changed hands. Coca-Cola was among the best-performing Dow stocks. The company jumped 4 7/8 a share, to 65 3/8, after a Merrill Lynch analyst issued a positive report on the company's prospects next year and raised his rating on Coke shares. AT&T was also a big winner, rising 5 7/16, to 52. And I.B.M. gained 4 1/16, to 108. Among Internet stocks, Exodus Communications jumped 17 3/16 a share, to 118 3/16, after the company, which manages Internet sites for other companies, announced a two-for-one stock split effective Dec. 14. It is the third time the company has split its shares this year. Electronic Arts rose 14 9/16, to 106 9/16, after the video-game publisher said it had signed a deal to provide all content to America Online's games site. A rise in long-term interest rates, prompted by a jump in spot oil prices, did not help financial service stocks. Shares of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter fell 1 9/16, to 122 13/16. Citigroup dropped 1, to 55 1/2. And Chase Manhattan fell 1 1/8 a share, to 81 7/8. The rise in oil prices, though, did little to help big oil company stocks. The Royal Dutch/Shell Group, an S.& P. component, fell 5/8 a share, to 62 3/4. Mobil declined 1 1/16, to 103 7/8. And BP Amoco lost 1, to 59 7/16. "The immediate effect of a sharply spiking oil price is negative for the majors," Mr. Hogan said, "because they hedge their positions for a long ways into the future. Also, these companies are much more diversified than they used to be. So it doesn't go hand in glove that a spike in oil prices is good for the majors."  Treasury Yields Jump By Bloomberg News Treasury bond yields rose yesterday to their highest level this month, as surging oil prices and a drop in the dollar raised concern about quickening inflation. Bond prices fell for the fourth time in five sessions, as investors became increasingly concerned that the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates again in coming months to curb inflation. It raised rates last week, the third time in five months, and said that risks to sustainable growth persist. "With the resurgence in world growth and higher oil prices, we have higher rates to look forward to," said Christopher Sullivan, chief investment officer of the United Nations Federal Credit Union. The price of the 30-year Treasury bond fell 12/32, to 99 5/32. The bond's yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, rose to 6.19 percent from 6.16 percent on Friday. title:
VITAL SIGNS: RESOURCES;
For Latest on AIDS Therapy, Click Here
body: For people who have AIDS, or the infection that causes it, information can be the most important weapon of all. Now it has become easier to get. A new Web site offers doctors and patients a wealth of information, regularly updated, about various H.I.V. therapies that are approved or are still in the experimental stages. The Web site should improve access to what has long been a valuable resource for fighting the disease: the H.I.V./AIDS Treatment Directory, published since 1985 by the American Foundation for AIDS Research. The Web site (www.amfar.org/td/) offers users the ability to search a database of clinical studies of experimental therapies, which may be especially useful for patients who are not responding to conventional treatments. People using the Web site can anonymously enter information about where they live and the specifics of their conditions, like their blood counts. They will then be told which programs may be the most appropriate. The site also contains links to published studies. Unlike the print version of the directory, which was updated twice a year, the Internet one will be changed continually. But the print directory will still be published and be available free to patients. The foundation is a nonprofit group that says it has spent more than $161 million to fight AIDS, mostly by helping to finance almost 1,800 research teams. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
Survey Finds Resistance To E-Shopping for Clothing
body: Merchants with high hopes for peddling cashmere and embroidered denim jeans on the Web this season and into the future may be in for a shock. Nearly half the Internet users in a recent survey said they never planned to buy clothing online, according to NPD, a market-research company based in Port Washington, N.Y. Significantly, this aversion to making clothing purchases on the Web extends not only to Internet users who have never bought clothing online but even to those users with years of experience, NPD said. More than 40 percent of experienced Web users in the survey -- many of whom had bought a fashion item online and had a good experience -- said they would avoid buying apparel on the Web in the future. "We are putting up a yellow flag here," said Mike Hand, president of NPD apparel services. "We thought apparel would be $13 billion a year by 2003 on the Web, which is the equivalent of catalog. Now I don't think it is going to make it." The study, which is based on information collected online in August from a sample of 2,399 people selected to be representative of the nation's Web users, found that consumers' reservations about buying apparel online have been difficult to overcome. Eighty-five percent of those polled for the NPD study said they were concerned about not being able to try on the clothing before buying it; return policies were an issue for 70 percent. So far the retailers that are most successful at receiving online sales are specialty sites that focus just on clothing, like Gap.com or LandsEnd.com, according to NPD. Sites like Comcast's QVC.com or Federated's Macys.com, which have many product categories, may attract more visitors.
