But nearly three-quarters of consumers polled for the study said they had made their most recent online apparel purchase at a specialty site. The study also supported the growing notion that the Web might be most effective as an adjunct to -- not a replacement for -- brick-and-mortar selling. Almost half the online buyers said their most recent purchase of clothing from the Internet was made in addition to purchases made off line. "At this point in time, the Internet is hardly stealing apparel sales away from traditional stores," Mr. Hand said. "To the contrary, one of the main reasons for buying clothing online, besides convenience, is because consumers cannot find the items in regular stores."   LESLIE KAUFMAN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
E-Commerce Report;
Seller beware:A new kind of software tool makes it easier for Internet surfers to track down the lowest on-line prices.
body: E-COMMERCE companies have enough to worry about when it comes to competitive pricing, as Internet shoppers can visit price-comparison sites like mySimon and DealTime.com to search for savings. Now, shoppers do not even have to click away to another site to find better prices. Several companies have developed a new breed of so-called agents -- software tools that work with Web browser software, offering shoppers better deals on whatever merchandise they happen to be viewing on a Web page. For an off-line analogy, imagine someone infiltrating the checkout line at OfficeMax and telling people they can save money on the same products at Staples. Agent companies like ClickTheButton, DealPilot and R U Sure have developed software that scans various shopping sites for price and delivery data, then sorts it (most often by price). In some cases, the agents also gather information about product availability, shipping costs and the length of time it takes to receive the item. Once a user has downloaded software from one of these agent services, though, the software is activated any time the Web browser is open. Someone surfing the Web with ClickTheButton, for instance, sees a bull's-eye icon in the corner of the screen. By clicking on this icon while viewing a Web page about a particular product, a price comparison page appears listing competitors' prices for the item. Last week, while on an Amazon.com page featuring the book "Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets," a ClickTheButton search yielded price information from 15 retailers. Six of them, including Amazon, offered the book for about $9, plus $3 for shipping. One site, 1Bookstreet.com, offered the book for $10.77, with no charge for United Parcel Service ground shipping. Such results essentially mirror those of shopping comparison sites, but there are two fundamental differences between the browser-based services and the shopping comparison sites. First, the browser-based agents typically monitor a shopper's habits, thereby allowing the services to make relevant offers at the right moment. Second, merchants do not have to pay to be included in at least two of these services -- a significant departure from shopping comparison sites, which generally charge merchants fees to be listed in prime positions. And although one might expect merchants to mount a counter-assault against technologies that effectively hijack their sites, Internet retailers have reacted to them with a surprising air of resignation. "These things are both intriguing and a little bit scary," said Michelle Rubin, director of affiliate marketing for the music seller CDNow. "I think they will become more sophisticated in the future, to give consumers a fuller picture of what's important at a store beyond prices. But right now it's a very freewheeling, competitive environment out there, and it's just hard to stop stuff like this." Bill Curry, an Amazon spokesman, was even more sanguine. "We're comfortable with people making price comparisons, and qualitative comparisons as well." Based on the current rate of consumer adoption, at least, Amazon and its competitors may not have much to worry about. ClickTheButton.com is among the oldest of the bunch, having rolled out in March. It now has over 100,000 active users, Cheyenne Ehrlich, the company's chief executive, said in an interview last week. "But we just started our marketing campaign this week," he said, adding that the company's goal is to obtain two million users by the end of next March. ClickTheButton scans information from 233 of the most visited retailers in six categories: books, electronics, hardware and software, movies, music and toys. Users download the software -- a process that takes less than a minute on a 56-kilobit modem -- and register with the company so it can monitor the user's shopping habits. Mr. Ehrlich said the company made money from a few different sources, including referral fees from some retailers that obtain customers through ClickTheButton. Given the wealth of data the company can collect about its users, ClickTheButton could conceivably gorge itself at the trough of dot-com advertising, but Mr. Ehrlich said it would abstain. "I'd take this data in aggregate and maybe tell Amazon where to price their goods in order to get a certain percentage of people to move from Barnes & Noble, but I don't want ads," he said. "Nothing we do will let companies get back to users." Another new company, Dash, has a somewhat different approach. The company takes advantage of retailer affiliate programs, which pay referral fees to sites that funnel sales their way. Dash essentially serves as an intermediary: a software tool directs shoppers to Dash's partner retailers, and Dash collects referral fees whenever a purchase is made at one of its 100 or so partner sites. Dash then passes those fees back to consumers with a monthly check. For instance, when someone is shopping for goods on the Gap.com, a message will appear on the toolbar at the bottom of the browser telling users that they can "save 5 percent when you shop at J. Crew instead." Users can then click directly to J. Crew's site and shop as they would normally, knowing they eventually will get a 5 percent rebate check from Dash. Notably, if Gap signs up with Dash, J. Crew and other competitors will not be permitted to display competing coupons when the user is on Gap's site. At any time, however, users can click an icon on the toolbar and view the savings available through competitors in the Dash network. According to Daniel Kaufman, Dash's chief executive, the service capitalizes on both the greed and the fears of merchants. "The greed factor is that any company loves the idea of advertising at a competitor's checkout aisles," he said. "The fear factor is that if they don't work with us, their customers will see a competitor's ads. In the end, fear and greed overcomes the negative effect of paying a discount on every sale." The company earns referral fees from retailers in addition to what it pays back to consumers, Mr. Kaufman said, and by allowing companies to target users with specific offers. "If I'm United Airlines, I can target someone who flies to Orlando four times a month, business class, on American," he said. Mr. Kaufman hastened to add that merchants "never know who is getting a message," since Dash is the conduit. As with most of the other browser-based shopping comparison services, Dash posts a lengthy privacy policy on its site. (Dash hired Jason Catlett, a well-known privacy advocate, to develop its privacy policy.) Analysts are mixed on the promise these technologies hold. "Give them credit for the idea," said Melissa Bane, an e-commerce analyst with the Yankee Group. "But the trick here is to get people to download these things. That's still a real barrier." Ken Orton, chief strategist for Cognitiative, a consulting firm, was more skeptical. "People go to a site for a reason, and to be sold off of that in the middle of the experience is not a likely scenario," he said. Mr. Kaufman of Dash is predictably optimistic that both consumers and merchants will warm to this technology. "This is perhaps the best way for consumers to capture value when shopping," he said, noting that the service has 20,000 users after just two weeks in business. As for Dash's relationship with retailers, Mr. Kaufman said partner merchants could enjoy sizable sales advantage over competitors. "So we're in a pretty serious love fest right now." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Jorgen Wahlsten, left, Cheyenne Ehrlich and Peter Kamali of ClickTheButton.com have more than 100,000 users of their comparison-shopping software, which scans pricing information from 233 of the most visited on-line retailers. (Edward Keating/The newyork Times)

title: Excite@Home to Separate Cable and Content Divisions
body: Under pressure from investors to clarify its business strategy, Excite@Home has decided to draw a distinction between its Internet access business and its media-content business by creating a separate tracking stock for the media assets, the company said today. The company said it would file the necessary documents with the Securities and Exchange Commission in the first half of next year and distribute the new stock in the third quarter. The company was created in May by the merger of the Web company Excite and the At Home Corporation, a cable Internet-access company. At the time of the merger, its stock was trading around $63 but has sunk as low as the mid-30's in August. On Friday, the shares closed at $52.3125, up $2.125. Executives at Excite@Home said the tracking stock was meant to signal that the company saw a difference between the information content and Internet access portions of its business. AT&T, which is Excite@Home's largest investor, has a 26 percent equity stake in a class of shares that gives it a 56 percent voting stake. AT&T has persistently signaled discomfort at the coupling of the content and cable business. "There has been an overhang on the stock that is the result of speculation about the outcome of our discussions on the strategic direction of company," Thomas A. Jermoluk, chairman and chief executive of Excite@Home, said in an interview today. "We believe we have achieved strategic alignment." Mr. Jermoluk said the decision was not a precursor to a more formal spinoff of the media assets into a separate company. In fact, he noted that S.E.C. rules would preclude such a spinoff for several years, once the company issued a tracking stock. Excite@Home presently receives 65 percent of its revenue from its media assets, which includes the Excite Web portal available to anyone on the Internet; a high-capacity @Home Web portal for cable subscribers; MatchLogic, a direct marketing company and Enliven, a multimedia advertising company. The balance of the revenue comes from subscription fees from cable Internet-access customers, of which it had 840,000 at the end of the third quarter. The company's third-quarter revenue of $112.6 million slightly exceeded analysts' forecasts, and was nearly double revenue of $57.8 million in last year's third quarter. Excite@Home lost $498.6 million in the most recent quarter, largely as it took charges associated with the merger. By 2002, the company expects to see a shift in the balance of its revenue, with 45 percent coming from the media assets. The board's decision to issue the tracking stock, reached last Wednesday, comes against a backdrop of uncertainty and a fast-changing marketplace for Excite@Home. In 2002, exclusive contracts will begin to expire with AT&T, Cox and Comcast, which until then are obliged to use Excite@Home for the cable-modem services offered on their cable television systems. Cox and Comcast each own 8 percent of Excite@Home. AT&T has already said that it would consider opening its systems to competing Internet access providers once the Excite@Home contract expires. AT&T has faced a heavy lobbying effort on that issue by a coalition of Internet access providers, including America Online. Mr. Jermoluk asserted that the media side of the business was moving so quickly that a separate tracking stock would put the company in a better position to react to competitive changes. The tracking stock, he said, might be used for making acquisitions of other media businesses without diluting the shares representing the Internet-access cable business. "In order to be competitive in the world of the Net we need to be able to move quickly, and to have a full range of strategic options," Mr. Jermoluk said. "One of the key reasons for the structure is that it allows us to pursue all options without diluting the interests of our cable partners." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Holiday Target For Music Sales Over Internet Won't Be Met
body: After scrambling to adopt a technical standard for sales of music online, record companies and hardware makers last summer said they had paved the way for Christmas sales of portable digital players. But the holidays are ringing in a reality: neither the tunes nor the players will be in place to make this the first big "digital music Christmas." Underscoring the delay, Sony Electronics, a consumer electronics bellwether, last week introduced its digital music player, the Memory Stick Walkman, but said it would not be for sale until January. Meanwhile, major music companies say that the delay in adopting standards -- along with logistical challenges -- has forced them to abandon their one-time goal of making much of their music available over the Internet by Christmas. The delays suggest the complexity of the still evolving technical standards being developed by the recording industry's Secure Digital Music Initiative, and they hint at continued uncertainty for consumers. They also reflect competing interests. The music companies fear that insecure digital players will lead to rampant piracy of music downloaded from the Internet, while the consumer electronics industry sees the digital players merely as heir to the portable cassette and compact disc player. In fact, a final agreement on the first phase of the specifications being developed by the Secure Digital Music Initiative, or S.D.M.I., is not even scheduled to be signed until next week. Initiative officials plan to meet in Maui, Hawaii, on Dec. 1 to sign a contract with Aris Technologies Inc., which makes a key screening technology for the portable devices. Hardware vendors have sought to play down the delay, suggesting that a single holiday shopping season lost will make little difference in a still-nascent market. At the same time, some say they are disappointed that they were pushed to adopt and comply with standards but will not reap the benefits. This delay hurts the "credibility of S.D.M.I.," said Chris Smith, portable audio program manager for Creative Labs. His company makes the Nomad II, a portable player initially due out by Christmas but now scheduled for distribution in the first quarter. When S.D.M.I. was formed, he said, "our stated goal was to have specifications by June 30 so we could create products for Christmas." The consumer electronics manufacturers said their concern had been mitigated by the fact that their competitors' digital players would not be on the shelves either. "Our goal was Christmas," a spokeswoman for Sony said, "but in the grand scope of things, missing one Christmas isn't going to make or break us." More than two dozen portable digital players that record music on tiny hard drives are already on the market. But those players are not yet fully compatible with the technical standards, and it is unclear how many of them will be able to be upgraded once the new standards are in place. If they ultimately cannot meet S.D.M.I. specifications, they will not be able to play the newest music -- either downloaded from the Internet or "ripped" from compact discs. What has made the issue so pressing from a music industry perspective is that the downloading of music from the Internet has gathered momentum. College students in particular, a huge music audience, have taken advantage of the Internet to trade, download and listen to music online in a format called MP3, opening both a massive opportunity and a potential Achilles' heel for music companies. The great fear of the music industry -- and of some musicians -- is that the existing MP3 technology makes it possible for people to trade and distribute music freely, in blatant violation of copyright laws and possibly costing the companies tens of millions of dollars in lost sales. The industry in turn regards the portable players as the paraphernalia of music piracy because people will theoretically have even more incentive to pirate music if they can copy, store and play it on easy-to-use portable devices. The recording industry's trump card is its vast catalogs of popular music. Its promise to make this content available over the Internet is what has lured the device manufacturers to cooperate in S.D.M.I. Without the content, the conventional wisdom goes, the market for the devices will not thrive. Both the recording and consumer electronics industries expressed optimism in June that they would meet the Christmas target. At the time, a coalition of more than 100 companies from the two industries agreed to the first S.D.M.I. specifications, which were designed to eventually preclude the portable devices from playing pirated music in the MP3 format. That first specification, called Phase I, stopped short of preventing piracy but would have enabled the players to be upgraded once the record industry settled on a secure format for the delivery of music. Theoretically, these Phase I compatible players would screen incoming music and prevent the devices from playing illegally obtained songs. But despite the agreement in principle to Phase I specifications, S.D.M.I. did not settle on the Aris screening technology until Nov. 12. And, in fact, the final contract is not slated to be signed with Aris until the Dec. 1 meeting in Maui. Mr. Smith, with Creative Labs, said the S.D.M.I. committee did not expect licensing the technology from Aris to take so long. The delays were so great that when Creative Labs begins selling its Nomad II sometime in the first quarter next year, it will not initially be Phase I compatible. To make it compatible, consumers will eventually need to download software from the Internet, though it is not entirely clear what incentive consumers will have to download the software. The same is true of players expected from Sanyo, Toshiba and Sharp, among others. Meanwhile, opponents of S.D.M.I., which has been criticized as a record industry initiative to maintain control of music distribution, contend that the latest delays underscore much larger problems. "S.D.M.I. is dead -- it's dead as a door nail," said Robert Kohn, chairman and cofounder of emusic.com, an online music site that sells songs in MP3 format. "There's no document from which any of these companies can develop specifications. They've developed a framework, not specifications." The music companies themselves are facing delays, partly because of S.D.M.I. delays and partly because of technical logistics in preparing their music for online distribution. Laurie Jakobsen, a spokeswoman for Sony Music Entertainment, which now offers limited downloads of music for promotional purposes, said that Sony would be pushing back commercial distribution of music online "because of S.D.M.I." "We'll do more as soon as there players out there," she said. Jay Samit, senior vice president for new media for EMI Records, said there were also simple, practical matters to contend with. For example, he said, the record companies have discovered that they must explore how and whether each artist contract permits the distribution of music over the Internet. "We're going as fast we can," he said. "We are moving through mounds of paper." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY: Digital Commerce;
After a year on the credibility trail, a columnist finds that the Internet industry is still dangerously self-indulgent.
body: FINALLY, the Internet's growing lack of credibility among consumers is becoming a cause celebre. Just last week, two organizations -- one grass roots, the other representing industry -- announced their intentions to bring some balance and intellectual rigor to a debate that has been almost completely lopsided toward unfettered growth at any cost. One of the groups, People for Internet Responsibility (www.pfir.org), is a global, nonpartisan network. It says its mission is to make the voice of consumers and citizens heard at a level equal to that of the corporations and governments that have vested interests in how the Internet is run. The second, an industry organization called the Internet Policy Institute (www.internetpolicyinst.org), says it wants to provide an antidote to the "noise, hype, rumors, marketing, I.P.O.'s and the hopes of starry-eyed start-ups" on the Internet by providing the first independent, objective analysis and research about the global network's development and use. Granted, several of the institute's backers have made billions in that starry-eyed Internet economy, which raises the specter of a fox with a mouthful of feathers guarding the henhouse. Nevertheless, it contends that it will not lobby "or otherwise actively advocate or represent the interests" of Internet companies. As it should be, of course. But then, I'm not objective about the subject. Aside from writing this column, I have also been on the public-speaking circuit for nearly five years, keening about the sorry state of credibility online and championing a code of conduct for publishing. And after having spent much of the last year doing research and interviewing Internet companies about disclosure and credibility practices, I wonder how much change any industry-based organization can effect without real, outside pressure from either consumers or the law. Based on conversations with nearly 40 Internet publishers, vendors and researchers, it seems that the revenue-starved Internet economy is far more willing to risk consumer wrath and rejection than to voluntarily adopt a meaningful code of conduct or to reveal too much about how it conducts its business. Although the initial focus was online journalism -- "Freedom of the press belongs to those who own one," said A. J. Liebling, and pretty much anyone with a computer and an Internet account fits that bill -- it became clear almost immediately that any standards code would have to extend more broadly. Portals, search engines, commerce sites, independent artists, universities and researchers had all become "publishers." And while most journalists understand that with publishing comes accountability, the "accountability" quotient was almost completely absent on the Web at large, in almost every area, from consumer privacy to customer service to disclosure of conflicts of interest. Unlike print and broadcast media, for example, most Web sites feel no particular need to distinguish between what information is paid for by sponsors and what is not. In fact, next to labeled advertising, the sale or barter of a hypertext link on a Web page is probably the most fundamental value exchange for those conducting business on the Internet. When a commercial link is in or near a news story, credibility advocates -- rightly aghast -- call the practice "transaction journalism." But the concept might better be called transaction publishing, because it applies virtually across the Web. Transaction publishing is neither fundamentally good nor evil. In fact, the ability to directly link pieces of information, whether transactions or content, is the defining feature of the Web. But precisely because the link is so powerful a metaphor, it is particularly incumbent upon online publishers to give users full disclosure -- as much context as possible to judge the substance, value and credibility of the links they explore. This seems self-evident. Yet almost nowhere on the Web can users easily find even the most basic contextual information, like a company's physical location or telephone number. Or who or what company owns and runs the Web site. Or what business(es) it is in and how it makes money -- a fact that is not always obvious for Internet businesses like portals, which derive revenue every which way they can. Most commercial sites offer news and a search engine, but often do not provide the source of the news -- nor do they volunteer whether specific key words or links are sold and, if so, to whom. And despite widespread privacy concerns, they are rarely upfront about what personal information they collect and what they do with it. It is evident from consumers' concerned reactions to paid product endorsements on Amazon.com and DrKoop.com and to the more recent revelation that RealNetworks was secretly vacuuming up users' personal data without permission, that this wholesale disregard for the truth is generating confusion and alarm. But amazingly, the specter of the online marketplace collapsing as consumers sprint for the doors is not a sufficient impetus for companies to clean up their acts. "There is an ideal confusion in the mind of the consumer today," said the chief executive of one Internet company, who was granted anonymity -- as were all the interview subjects -- in exchange for candor. "It's good if the consumer doesn't know whether he's buying the watch from Casio's site or from us." Then there was the marketing executive who spoke of a project in which a prominent business publication worked closely with marketing executives for his client, a big technology vendor, to design a Web page. The idea was to make the links, which led directly to the advertiser's site, exactly match the magazine's editorial style. "I was horrified," he said. "No one seemed to understand that once a consumer clicked on that link and found out that it took them directly to an ad, their credibility was shot and they'd never get it back." The many interview subjects who did support strong disclosure standards for the Internet tended to be lawyers, researchers and others who were concerned with long-term effects on the credibility of the Internet as a medium. The rest are apparently banking on the "ride this horse till it drops" strategy. And considering the amount of activity that their bad behavior is generating, they may not have long to wait. The burning question is what is going to bring them down? And who will they take with them? http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Internet Makes an Easy Target For Lobbyists and Lawmakers
body: When it comes to cyberspace, the mantra of politicians vying for the title of most e-friendly, Republicans and Democrats alike, has been "Hands off and go slow." Yet lawmakers have already passed a laundry list of bills that leave the federal government's fingerprints all over the Internet, and more are in the pipeline. The efforts include inventing rules against the peddling of Internet addresses, granting legal standing for digital contracts, proposing bans on the Internet programming known as Webcasts, prohibiting online gambling and regulating "spam," the junk mail of cyberspace. And that is just a partial list of e-era legislation this Congress has passed or is considering. Some are the products of politicians seeking a hot issue. But others are being promoted by the same companies that originally insisted on self-regulation or by traditional lobbying powerhouses and special interest groups taking advantage of Internet fever to promote laws that protect their niches. The business groups backing the growing list of bills defend them as necessary rules of the road for electronic commerce. Watchdogs, however, see a disturbing anticonsumer trend in much of the legislation that could have long-term negative effects -- not only on Internet users but on the very companies that are now scurrying for new legislation. What is more, digital laissez-faire seems to be applied arbitrarily. While laws to protect business interests like intellectual property and digital contracts have been on the fast track, proposals to lay out basic protections for consumer privacy online have been pushed aside as unnecessary and contrary to the need to keep cyberspace unencumbered. "I characterize it as short-term-advantage thinking with long-term implications," said Jerry Berman of the Center for Democracy and Technology, a nonprofit group in Washington that aims to work with industry to establish responsible Internet policy. "My view is that the Internet is going to get hurt, consumers are going to get hurt, and since all things come around, different industry parts of the Internet are going to get hurt." But Rick Lane, who handles e-commerce affairs for the unitedstates Chamber of Commerce, and Harris Miller, executive director of the Information Technology Association of America, disagree. "There are certain rules of the road that we need legislation to establish," Mr. Lane said. "And the rules of the road that are being created are an incredible empowerment tool for consumers." And Mr. Miller argues that rules governing things like privacy are not necessary because Internet companies know that their customers -- with "just one click of a mouse" -- will move from a Web site they do not trust to one that offers them basic consumer protections. Mr. Berman says the trend has moved away from true self-regulation to "leave it alone -- except for this, except for that." "Every company says, 'except for this,' " he said. "And maybe that exception makes sense, but it should only be done after careful scrutiny." In 1996, Mr. Berman said, after watchdog and industry groups united to fight the Communications Decency Act as a form of unconstitutional censorship, Internet business associations set up the Internet caucus to educate Congress about the complicated issues presented by the global network and the need to legislate carefully. "But what has happened is a number of these issues have not gone through the process," he said. "And I am unhappy and disappointed that regardless of what side the different industry players are on, they are moving their agendas without this kind of scrutiny." Indeed, one key Internet bill to outlaw so-called cybersquatting -- the ransoming of .com, .net and .org Internet addresses using famous names or trademarks -- was worked out largely in closed meetings and passed last week as an attachment to the omnibus spending bill. Critics of the measure argue that it will give trademark holders unprecedented rights to Web names at the expense of individuals and small businesses and that it could have a chilling effect on free speech. It could also threaten the authority and credibility of the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, or Icann, a still tenuous and experimental oversight board chosen by the Clinton administration last year to oversee the distribution of Internet addresses, known as domains. Icann recently established its own rules on cybersquatting, but the powerful Motion Picture Association of America and other trademark groups, unsatisfied with the rules, pushed for stronger protections. Despite the increased willingness by lawmakers to put their names on anything touted as friendly to e-commerce, Representative Christopher Cox, a California Republican who championed the first comprehensive Internet deregulation bill, the Internet Tax Freedom Act, said most of the Internet legislation pending in the 106th Congress was premature. "Government simply doesn't have the answer at the moment," Mr. Cox said, noting that evolving technology could eliminate the need for rules over domain name disputes and problems like spam. "That is not to say there is not a distinction between good and bad laws," he said. "But by and large, as a policy matter, regulation of the Internet should be put on hold because the subject of the regulation itself is not yet settled." But as technology companies increasingly make their presence felt in Washington, the trend is not likely to go away. America Online, one of the companies most vocal in calling for a hands-off approach to the Internet, is pushing legislation that would force cable companies to open their high-speed Internet lines to competition. The auction site eBay is pushing a database protection bill opposed by the rest of the high-technology pack, which fears that it could limit access to Internet content. Complicating the increasing dissension among high-technology companies, lobbies like the banking and insurance association are pushing their own agendas. Such an alliance earlier this month turned a bipartisan compromise for giving digital signatures the legal weight of their ink-and-paper counterparts into a broader law that would eliminate many record-keeping and consumer notification laws. In the end, House Democrats who had supported the administration's push for the narrower bill voted for the broader measure anyway. "I thought it was very alarming and pretty surprising," said Margot Saunders, managing attorney for the National Consumer Law Center. "Here we had a debate on the House floor for four hours where the leaders were saying to their colleagues that this bill hurts all Americans, it does not help electronic commerce. Yet you had this huge block of middle-of-the-road Democrats completely ignore what their own leadership was saying." "It was clearly a matter," she added, "of everybody being scared to death to vote against the high-tech industry." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Representative Christopher Cox, Republican of California, says most of the Internet-related legislation that has been considered by the 106th Congress is premature. (Shana Raab for The newyork Times)(pg. C1)  Chart: "The Internet Bills Before Congress"  Digital Signatures BILLS: HR-1714, S-921, HR-1320, S-761, HR-439 PURPOSE: Five bills that, in varying ways, are meant to give signatures rendered in digital form the legal weight of their ink-and-paper counterparts. STATUS: Among these, the House has passed a bill that would authorize digital contracts and eliminate some traditional paper record-keeping. A narrower bill has passed the Senate.  Cyber-squatting BILLS: S-1255, HR-3028 PURPOSE: To outlaw speculative trafficking in the domain names used for Internet addresses. Allows civil claims of up to $100,000 for the bad-faith registration of trademarks as Internet addresses. STATUS: A compromise version of the two bills was added to the spending bill approved by Congress.  Database protection BILLS: HR-1858, HR-354 PURPOSE: To provide new legal protections for information collected in computer databases. HR-1858 would provide narrow protections for the compilations, but not the facts in the databases. The other bill would provide broader protections. STATUS: Both bills are pending before the full House.  Internet filtering BILLS: HR-2650 PURPOSE: To require schools and libraries that receive federal Internet funds to install filtering software on computers used by children. STATUS: Pending.  Online alcohol and gun sales BILLS: HR-2031, S-577, HR-3020 PURPOSE: To outlaw the sale of guns or alcohol over the Internet. STATUS: Bill to ban online alcohol sales has passed the House and been referred to Senate Judiciary. House legislation to outlaw gun sales online is pending.  Internet gambling BILLS: HR-3125, S-692 PURPOSE: To outlaw gambling on the Internet. STATUS: Passed in the Senate; pending in the House.  Online privacy BILLS: HR-1685, HR-313, S-809, S-1901 PURPOSE: To set basic rules for protecting consumer information collected online. STATUS: Pending in committees.  Junk e-mail BILLS: S-759, HR-3113, HR-1910 PURPOSE: To regulate and limit unsolicited commercial e-mail. STATUS: Pending in committees.  Internet access BILLS: HR-2637, HR-1686, S-877, HR-2420 PURPOSE: To increase competition in Internet access and give consumers better access to high-speed Internet services. STATUS: Pending in committees.  Encryption BILLS: HR-850, S-798, S-854 PURPOSE: To relax the administration's export controls on data-scrambling technology used to secure online communications. STATUS: Pending.  Comprehensive Internet package BILLS: HR-1685 PURPOSE: The bill would require cable operators to open their broadband Internet lines to competitors; prohibits use of false return addresses in e-mail solicitations; promotes the use of digital signatures; requires companies to create privacy policies and then post and comply with them. STATUS: Pending in House committees. (pg. C5)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Point-and-click with a personal touch: Internet company offers customized computer cursors.
body: A SMALL Internet company is hoping that the adage about tall oaks growing from little acorns also applies to cyberspace, as it seeks big results from turning perhaps the tiniest place on a computer screen into advertising. The company is Comet Systems in newyork, which has developed a proprietary technology for commercializing cursors, the arrows that point and click their way through the Internet. On Web sites where marketers have bought ad space, computer users who have installed Comet software can be offered customized cursors. The Comet Cursors are colorful miniature billboards in fanciful shapes that can range from Pokemon characters and Energizer bunnies to telephone directories and "Star Trek" spaceships. They also come in generic forms with themes like pets, holidays and sports. The Comet efforts are indicative of the so-called rich media applications being introduced to increase interest in online pitches, particularly the banner ads that tend to be as dull as, well, arrow-shaped cursors. "The test of any rich-media product is how effective it is at getting more customers and creating more brand awareness," said Marissa Gouck, an analyst at Jupiter Communications in newyork. "The trick is to keep it something special," she added, "because often, the more ubiquitous it becomes, the less effective it becomes." Research by Millward Brown Interactive, a unit of the WPP Group, that was commissioned by Comet and sponsored in part by four large advertisers showed that differentiated cursors can significantly increase the ability of computer users to recall seeing ad banners and their desire to click through to read the ads. "It struck me that if the cursor could change contextually with each site you visit, the advertising impression would remain with you," said Jamie Rosen, recently promoted to chairman at Comet from president, "because it's a way of stamping a personality onto a site." Mr. Rosen founded the company in 1997 with Dean Margolis, the chief executive, who left during the summer, and Tom Schmitter, the chief technical officer. "Like any new technology, the problem with putting an image in the cursor space is one of education, getting people familiar and comfortable with it," said Ben Austin, marketing director at Comet. "But invariably, every time we show it to people, they become believers." The Comet technology is used on more than 55,000 Web sites, by the company's count, with licensees that include AT&T Worldnet; the Comedy Central cable network, jointly owned by Time Warner Inc. and Viacom Inc.; Mattel, and the Warner Brothers Online unit of Time Warner. Under an agreement signed last month with 24/7 Media in newyork, a product named the Cometized Banner, which automatically serves branded cursors when an ad banner is clicked through, will be delivered across the 24/7 ad network. Campaigns with commercialized cursors have appeared on Web sites operated by AltaVista, Lycos, theglobe.com and Yahoo, sponsored by marketers like BellSouth, Energizer and Toshiba. "We incorporated the Comet Cursor into our own site, Energizer .com," said Harriet Blickenstaff, a spokeswoman for the Eveready Battery Company in St. Louis, a division of Ralston Purina. "It captures the fun and surprise of the bunny." "In terms of driving people to the site, the results were inconclusive," she added. "But we would still deem it successful because it fits our strategy, our tone, our spirit." The arrival of advertising in yet another Internet space could generate a backlash among critics of the increasing commercialism of communications, who could complain, to paraphrase the outcries of the defeated villains in melodramatic old movies, "Cursors, foiled again!" But "the nice thing about the Comet Cursor is that the user has to make an active choice to get it," said Beth Suitt, advertising manager of BellSouth Intelliventures in Atlanta, referring to the need to download the software, known as a plug-in. "It's more of an opt-in experience instead of being put in your face without permission," she added. "That gives advertisers an opportunity to stick to users' minds without being intrusive." The plug-in aspect can be a minus as well as a plus if users are wary of the time it takes to download the Comet Cursor from sources like www.cometsystems.com and www.cometzone.com. "We pay for the sins of our predecessors," Mr. Rosen said, laughing, "when people see a download and think it's going to crash their computers." But Comet plugs the plug-in process as brief, lasting less than 10 seconds. (If you try it late on a Friday, when your computer is choking as colleagues file articles on deadlines for Saturday, Sunday and Monday, it may take five minutes.) So far, by Comet's estimate, 15 million computer users have downloaded the plug-in. "It's a neat little application that improves response rates for advertisers," said Will Margiloff, advertising sales director at theglobe.com in newyork, which has developed promotions with holiday themes using Comet Cursors. "We'll continue to use it with almost every promotion we do going forward." But can the commercialized cursor become more than just a promotional ploy? "There's definitely a gimmicky aspect to it," Ms. Gouck at Jupiter said. "The approach Comet has is pretty good, but technology can go only so far. "I've seen some great executions of the Comet Cursor and I've seen some awful ones," she added. "A lot depends on the creative capabilities of the advertiser." And Comet's technology initially proved more popular with individual home pages and small-business sites than with marketing giants. For example, none of the four large advertisers from the Comet survey have used the technology so far. "We were pleased with the results," said Gretchen Briscoe, a spokeswoman for one advertiser, Procter & Gamble in Cincinnati. "The cursor drove awareness and people remembered the brand, but we've got no plans going forward to use it." Let's hope P.& G. rethinks its reticence. Who wouldn't relish the chance to see a Comet Cursor shaped like a can of Comet cleanser? http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: New technology can turn cursors into miniature billboards. (Comet Systems)

title:
BRIEFS;
Dog Is Sold Viagra on Web, Leading to Fraud Charges
body: A sting operation that resulted in charges for allegedly selling Viagra to a police officer's dog over the Internet is one of several cases being brought by the state Division of Consumer Affairs. "In New Jersey, a person is ten and a half times more likely to be ripped off at ballpoint than at gunpoint,' said Mark Herr, director of the state Division of Consumer Affairs. "E-commerce has exploded in the last 18 to 24 months." Last Monday Mr. Herr said that Barbara Arkelian and Darren Baker of the Highlands were charged with fraud for allegedly selling Beanie Babies, Furbies and Bruce Springsteen tickets in the internet but not delivering. Millenium Interactive Technologies Corp. (formerly Exeter Financial Services Corp.) and five sales agents and officers were charged in Superior Court in Essex County with allegedly selling unregistered stock in the company thorough unregistered agents. The suit alleges that the officers pocketed more than $850,000 of the more than $1 million that was taken in during sale of the stock. In addition, Kmeco International was charged in Superior Court in Middlesex County with dispensing the prescription drug Viagra to a dog owned by an officer of the Division of Consumer Affairs.   LISA SUHAY http://www.nytimes.com

title:
C.E.O ROUND TABLE;
Online Pioneers: The Buzz Never Stops
body: SPEED. Sleep. Greed. Recruiting. Role models like Thomas Edison and Ayn Rand. Losing money, yet turning away capital. New-found wealth and an ensuing change in lifestyle -- or not. Those were some of the topics on the table when four chief executives from dot.com companies -- Candice Carpenter of iVillage, a women's Web site; Fernando J. Espuelas of StarMedia Network, a Spanish- and Portuguese-language service; Kevin O'Connor of DoubleClick, an on-line advertising network, and Stephan J. Paternot of Theglobe.com, a shopping, news and business information site -- gathered late one afternoon early this month at The newyork Times for a wide-ranging discussion about managing in the Internet age. These pioneers from Silicon Alley, an area in the Flatiron district of Manhattan that is populated by many fledgling Internet companies, were joined in the two-hour discussion by Saul Hansell, Patrick J. Lyons and Judith H. Dobrzynski of The Times. As founders of young companies, each executive had experienced the adrenaline highs and the growing pains that accompany the transformation of an idea into a business and then into a publicly traded company. They don't worry about nonexistent earnings in a topsy-turvy environment where not producing a profit is, for the moment, a virtue. For them, the bigger pressure is to build organizations -- fast -- before opportunities slip away. Following are excerpts from the conversation.   JUDITH H. DOBRZYNSKI  Q. What's the difference between running the kind of company you run and running a big company?  CARPENTER Speed. Leading in conditions in which speed is a very big factor. It puts a lot of additional pressure on all the systems.  And you have a lot of very young people, and you're teaching them to be managers at a very accelerated pace without a lot of formal programs.  PATERNOT Tying into that is just the idea of keeping your entrepreneurial spirit. Things are shifting fast enough that you need to be able to jump into any new idea, shift your company into it and move at light speed.  ESPUELAS I would say the absence of a road map. Not that any business is particularly easy, but when there's nothing that you can follow except your instincts and the little bit of data you're able to gather in this context of a lot of speed, I think there's a lot of intuition that goes into these kinds of very fast-moving environments.  O'CONNOR In large corporations, you need to spend a lot of time quantifying what the market's going to look like and how you're going to go about it and what the expenses are going to be. And here it's very much speed, it's intuition, it's trying to figure out, "Is this a big market or a small market?" If it's a big market, you go after it. You spend a tremendous amount of money and you go after it quickly.  Q. What's the first thing that's sacrificed in the name of speed?  O'CONNOR Facts.  CARPENTER Sleep. We're trying to really come up with graded solutions to burnout caused by exhaustion. We have people who have been at this for four years in our company and we have to figure out a way to get them to learn how to completely refresh themselves in short increments of time. I've stood at the elevator with people going on vacation and actually taken the laptop and the cell phone out of their hands and said, "Great, now you can actually have a vacation." The only way to truly regenerate yourself enough to be truly creative and inventive again is to be unwired at times in the year and to be in the other part of the world.  Q. Do any of you have programs for dealing with burnout?  PATERNOT Sometimes it's frequent rotation of some of your stars. You'll often find that in your company you have a few stars, and if you leave them in the same position too long they'll burn out. And, quite frankly, you don't want to lose them.  CARPENTER We're starting a sabbatical program. It's for people who've been there three years who would love to be there 20. We're giving them a month to go and just do whatever they want. Sleep probably will be at the top of most people's list.  ESPUELAS Are you going to take it yourself?  CARPENTER Yeah, I am. I have to, otherwise no one else will take it.  O'CONNOR We have a very strong policy that people can move to wherever they want to move. Any job in the company's open. So we try to force rotation, because doing the same thing, day in and day out, tends to cause burnout.  Consciously Reaching Out  Q. Tell us a little bit more about how you're managing growth so far.  ESPUELAS I travel all the time. And I try to talk to as many people as possible. We do monthly all-hands meetings and we actually Web-cast them simultaneously and have people call in and try to have an ongoing dialogue. And now we're doing things which I never thought we'd ever do. We're going to create an employee newsletter. We're doing a lot of things that I used to scoff at when I worked at other companies. What I've also found is that things I said two years ago are now on a plaque, and that people are still acting the same way: "But Fernando said that." Yeah, but that was two years ago.  Q. Is communication a common problem?  PATERNOT Absolutely. We've seen ourselves have to increase the rate of communication dramatically. When we started four or five years ago, it was a group of 20 to 25 people. My partner Todd Krizelman, co-chief executive and I could just make decisions very quickly, hoping everybody can keep up. But eventually it starts to hurt you more when you get to 200, and people in departments don't understand what's going on. And we've had to deal with a lot of organizational changes over the last year, but everybody understands why we're doing stuff.  O'CONNOR We start off with a week of training. It's a week of indoctrination for every employee -- whether you answer the telephone in the German office or you're a vice president, it doesn't matter. You sit, you learn what we do, why we do it, what's the core culture of the company, so everybody's got a good, firm foundation.  Q. How do managers who have worked at large companies fare in your kinds of companies?  O'CONNOR On average, they've fared pretty well. You've got to pre-screen them very carefully. You tend to get people who expect to have two assistants. But our first test is, we make them take a pay cut. If they won't take a massive pay cut, you've pretty much got them pegged.  Q. Do they have options, though, on the other end?  O'CONNOR Absolutely.  CARPENTER The structure that I've seen be the most successful is a solid infrastructure of senior managers from big companies, very seasoned, very good at creating structure. That gives you room to promote people with less management experience, and have someone to go to when wisdom and time around the track is the issue.  Mountains of Resumes  Q. How hard is it to find employees? Are strangers handing you resumes as soon as they find out who you are?  O'CONNOR I probably get 10 resumes myself a day. We probably get, as a company, 100 resumes a day. There's a lot of talent that wants to get in, that absolutely wants to get into the dot-com company. To get great, smart people is always tough. But it's relatively easy for a dot-com company.  ESPUELAS We have two realities. One is in the U.S., which mirrors that. But in Latin America, it's totally different: There's no such thing as us. There's a lot of big companies that are owned by families, so the best you can hope for is to work for so and so, as opposed to being one of the owners of the company. So in Latin America we're able to really tap into really great people who don't have an equivalent to go to.  PATERNOT Even though we get a hundred resumes a day, we're at a point where we're trying to find the perfect person to fit this type of software development. It's easier for us to find people in marketing and sales, because newyork has a lot more of these people and they're easy to train. But finding the right technical person, whether it's for infrastructure or for software, we still find it tough. These people can command huge salaries from the banks. And finding a seasoned database manager, for instance, can mean that you have to pay huge cash, because some of these people want the options and they want the cash, and they're not going to leave their cushy job at Goldman Sachs unless you throw it all at them. The fact is, if you're a well-known dot-com company, it helps immensely over the unknown dot-com companies and over a lot of the other companies.  How to Set Priorities  Q. Do you find that your thinking about the way you run your company changes over time?  ESPUELAS For the last two years, I've been thinking about, well, what happens in 10 years and what happens in 20 years? Which is kind of a ridiculous thing to think about on the Internet.  O'CONNOR Most start-ups go through the struggle of going from an entrepreneurial environment to professionalization. Making that transition from a total entrepreneurial world with no rules to where you've got to have systems; you've got to have order.  PATERNOT You have to learn to delegate. Todd and I were completely attached to the product, had to test everything ourselves. We were the chief Q. A.  quality assurance guys. Eventually, you have to stop that. As much as I still use the product now, when I have to use it, I want to be able to rely on 50 people who think about this more than I do and who know it better than I do.  O'CONNOR On the flip side, I still spend half my time with new products -- because that is the entrepreneurial side and new products are the key to rejuvenating the company, growing the company. We set out to create a big company.  Q. Did you, from the beginning, do something differently than other start-ups might have done, because you were planning for growth?  O'CONNOR Definitely. I was fortunate because I started my first company right out of college. So I went through the "how you could have done things differently and better." We tried to avoid all the mistakes. I was building the human infrastructure, getting the people who could build their own business and leverage. When I look at DoubleClick, we're actually a collection of about 50 companies: People who were running their own thing, whether it's their own country, and there were 22 countries, or we have a bunch of business units with people running their own businesses. The thing we most tend to look for in people is intelligence and -- I call it -- athleticism: people who love to compete, don't like to lose.  ESPUELAS I don't think anybody stumbles onto a big company. You have to visualize where you're going. You don't know the path necessarily, but there's a goal. There's something I always think about and try to get people to think about. I'm not a martial-arts guy, but when you break a board with your hand, what they teach you is that if you were able to project the energy, not on the surface of the board, but behind the board, you will break it. And you can break three boards, then four boards. But if you aim it for the surface, you will break your hand. And that's a little bit of what you dream about. You have to make choices accordingly. When we were looking for venture funding, and we were out of our money and we got offered by not-so-great V.C.'s venture capital firms who wanted not-so-great terms, we knew we'd never go there. So we held out. And we got good funding.  CARPENTER I can think of a number of examples where we turned down advertisers, we turned down money, because to do otherwise would create a precedent which would limit us later. And as a very tiny company, it's very scary to do or have to do it. And once you do it, it inspires everybody.  Of Churchill, and Branson  Q. Other chief executives want to be Jack Welch of General Electric. Is there any model you think about?  ESPUELAS I spent a lot of time learning how Winston Churchill ran the Second World War. I bring that up as a metaphor -- not having information, not having clarity, the stakes being very high. Of course, the stakes he had to deal with were somewhat higher than what we have to do. But that was part of the encouragement -- to think that something so important could be managed, and all the mistakes that were made and the chaos of the moment. And the other thing, which he said, which I love as a philosophy, is: You don't have to get it right all the time. You just have to get it right 51 percent of the time, and that will carry you through. And that's a very, very liberating philosophy.  CARPENTER I admire two people.  Steve Ross, who turned a funeral parlor into one of the great media empires in the world Time Warner . He did it by empowering people tremendously. And he was a bit of a cowboy, but that's the only way you get from a funeral parlor to one of the largest media companies in the world. When you were in the room with him, you would want to just get up and run and help him to fulfill this vision. And then in the dot-com world, I personally admire Tim Koogle chief executive of Yahoo so much. I think Yahoo has an elegance in the way they do things. They never sacrifice. They're the only portal that never charged money for carriage. And they did it because they only want to have the very best content. They want to invite the best people in. Everything they've done has been for long-term greatness. There's all these fancy dot-com buildings down in Silicon Valley. And you go to Yahoo and it's so very understated. We send our architects out there to visit it because, we said, this is the model. And the employees love it because they really thought about how the employees could have a great day there.  PATERNOT Todd and I have the same idol: Richard Branson founder of the Virgin Group -- just his philosophy of wanting to be a successful businessman and having fun while doing it. And he's one of those guys that's really built up one of the best-recognized brands in the world. And after reading his book, "Losing My Virginity," you can see how he's had a lot of similar experiences to what Todd and I had. Seeing how he started from some inexperienced young guy and turned it into some major media empire. And seeing how this man embodies the brand, Virgin, is extremely inspiring. Todd and I have always had a philosophy since we started, that we're only doing this as long as we have fun. The day that you're just doing it for the money, that's the day we get out.  O'CONNOR Mine's more historical. Edison was a horrible C.E.O. but a hell of an innovator. He pretty much innovated the 21st century. And then Ayn Rand.  CARPENTER Yeah. Champion of capitalism.  O'CONNOR Her philosophy of capitalism and the individual is just how we pretty much run the company. I think Koogle is great. I think Steve Case chairman of America Online is amazing. How many times did people write Case off? And he's always come back. Gates Bill Gates of Microsoft is an incredible entrepreneur that everyone really respects -- an entrepreneur who was successful in transitioning from an entrepreneur to building a phenomenal company.  Q. Can you imagine out a couple of years? If you have a 10,000-person organization, is it going to be like every other 10,000-person organization?  CARPENTER No.  O'CONNOR There's nothing wrong with big companies. We all want to become one. And we all want to create a company that stands the test of time. Look at the great companies: General Electric -- what they do is something to be idolized. Disney -- they keep innovating. I.B.M. -- we all want to be like that. But we all want to stay away from the bureaucracy.  ESPUELAS I'm sure that some Internet companies will become stodgy old media companies in the next five years. The challenge is: How do you maintain that freshness and how do you organize yourself and how do you develop a culture that it doesn't matter whether you're 500 or 5,000 or 50,000 people? At Microsoft, they have 30,000, 40,000 employees. They move fast. They have that drive. That's cultural.  The Price of Profits  Q. How long do you think you can exist without producing profit?  O'CONNOR It's clear what the market's telling us. They want to give us a lot of money, so we take it and we invest. Why? We look back, and what was the biggest mistake that we made? We should have invested even more money. We should have lost more money. Why? Because this is the biggest thing that's ever hit. Market share is everything. But it depends on what stage the company is in. People are going to start expecting profits from us in the next one to two years.  PATERNOT The reason we all lost money and all went crazy for this is because we realized how big it could be. And it's worth losing the money for the sake of becoming that much bigger down the long road. And I think that investors traditionally, by default, will say "yes, we'd prefer a profitable company," but not if they know it's at the expense of getting that company to be way bigger a little bit further down the road.  ESPUELAS Things have changed. In '96 when we started our company, nobody knew if anybody could make a profit on the Net. And now we look and we see that there are certain models, in our case the advertising model, and the e-commerce models, that actually can be profitable. The biggest risk is that we under-invest, as Kevin said, because this won't come again. And if we don't own that waterfront before everyone else, somebody else will. We don't want to be in a situation next year having to buy someone for a billion bucks that we could have invested $25 million to build or buy them when they're little. We have invested over the last two years much more in building our brand than the advertising revenue available in the whole of Latin America. Now we're either very stupid or clever and I'd like to think that we're clever, because it means that we are now capturing more than our fair share of that revenue opportunity. Q. How much longer will it be before people begin to say "wait a minute"?  CARPENTER Off the Internet, media companies take five to seven years to become profitable. Everybody knows that in the media business.AOL took eight years, because they were early. Let's say Yahoo took four and a half. So that kind of defines it. Part of what's interesting is that many of the investors came out of technology. They don't have models of the dynamics of a media company. They're applying a different model and then wondering, "Gee, this doesn't look like anything I've seen," but it's not like the world has never seen it before. You can look at media models and see exactly where we all are on the curve, because it's a business where you do spend a lot up front to build brand, to build advertising-revenue generation capability, and then your revenue starts scaling past it.  O'CONNOR It is starting to happen. The scary thing that's happened is what's coming out public today are companies that have no revenue.  Q. How do you pay your employees?  ESPUELAS We pay good salaries, but fair salaries within the norm for that kind of job in other industries. And then we try to get people to really think about the stock being their major compensation. Q. Does everybody have stock?  ESPUELAS Yeah, after I believe it's six months -- after your first review -- everyone gets stock options.  PATERNOT Same policy exactly.  Q. At a couple of your companies, the stock price today is a quarter of where it once was. Does that linger as a question in the hallways?  PATERNOT You've got to have open communication with your people. You've got to tell them not to look at your day-to-day stock price, but at the same time they deserve to have an explanation and understanding of where things are going in the long run. Give them enough vision so that it's their decision: "Well, I don't care what the stock's at today, I think that we had a great internal story, and a year from now I think things could be way better; I'm going to stick around."  CARPENTER At the time of the I.P.O., we pulled out the stock charts of five companies and we said, "Well, here's what you're in for." The pattern was so ridiculously consistent.  Risk vs. Executive Reward  Q. Many big-company chief executives think you're overpaid. The whole world thinks they're overpaid. Are you overpaid and are they overpaid?  O'CONNOR Am I working a million times, or whatever it may be, smarter than someone else? No. Am I overpaid? No. It is what it is.  ESPUELAS We win when the stockholder wins and not otherwise, which is a perfect alignment of value.  PATERNOT If those traditional media types all want to complain about it, they can always start their own Internet companies and take a chance, and I think they'll realize what the risk-reward ratio is.  CARPENTER It is a little bit like the lottery, because the person brought in to run eBay hit the lottery. She, Meg Whitman, is great, but she would be the first to say she got really lucky. The risk of walking away from what's known and guaranteed and starting over in one room that you're sharing with eight people, in retrospect, looks like no big deal. But when you do it, you're taking a big risk. Our culture happens to reward that behavior, which is one reason it's a great country. My old media colleagues say, you know, "damn, this is really annoying that you guys went and did this," but there's something in you that allows you to go take that risk. It wasn't guaranteed. In the end, it could have been worth absolutely zero.  Q. Do you worry that the Internet economy isn't a fair economy, that you have to be lucky to get rich in it?  O'CONNOR No, I think the market's very discriminating, and customers are very discriminating. PATERNOT In many senses, it's this wealth creation -- even though sometimes I don't like the fact that a lot of people are jumping into this industry to make a buck -- that is driving every single business out there to want to give it a chance. No one disputes that the Internet, in some way -- business to business, business to consumer -- is improving the lives of consumers.  Wealth, but No Time  Q. What do you tell people who want to be entrepreneurs about your lives and the impact that sudden wealth has had on your lifestyle?  O'CONNOR I tell everyone just to pursue what you love. If you pursue what you love, you're either going to put in the effort, and you become the best at it, and then you're going to create a successful company, and lots of money, and do well and have fun, or you're going to die poor and happy because you pursued what you love.  ESPUELAS I was just meeting with entrepreneurs talking about this in Argentina and saying: Forget the money. You probably won't go public. You probably won't be able to raise money. You're probably going to die as a company, so you have to focus on the fundamentals. What is it that you're going to do that's going to change the world? And if you pick something that changes the world really well and you do it very well, then you'll make money off of that.  CARPENTER You have to have leisure time to change your lifestyle, and no one has leisure time yet, so I don't see people rushing out and capitalizing on the money to change the way they live. Everyone's too busy building a franchise right now. Obviously, this is going to create huge shifts in wealth. And I think it's going to open up charitable giving in a wave that we haven't seen for 50 years that's going to change this country dramatically. I did go out and buy a few Versace gowns. It was really therapeutic. And I've just bought a little fur jacket, and all of that's really fun, but at the end of the day, that all takes time, and I basically have to go back to work and keep building.  Q. Do you have time to follow politics? What do you want from Washington?  O'CONNOR I think the Internet is changing the world like no other system -- in such a short period of time -- that it's causing industries to become entrenched in wanting to limit the Internet. People want to stick their hands on the Internet through regulations, so I think we're all finding ourselves spending a lot more time educating governments and senators and Congress people to make sure that they understand.  PATERNOT A coalition has been formed -- Netcoalition.com -- that is specifically for the purpose of having someone there, including the C.E.O.'s of those member companies, going to Washington and speaking with senators, just educating them, so that eventually, when they do make a policy decision they haven't made it completely out of thin air.  CARPENTER We're involved in politics on the consumer side. We have each of the presidential candidates coming in to do a town meeting in which the questions are not created by the people of iVillage but are filtered up through the membership. It's just having this fabulous rejuvenating impact on democracy that we haven't even seen the beginning of yet.  O'CONNOR Platform for libertarianism worldwide, you're going to see it worldwide. That's my theory.  To Change the World  Q. Is there a difference in culture between now and the 1980's? Are we just a "greed-is-good.com" culture or is anything different motivating people now?  ESPUELAS At least in the first couple of waves of the Internet, you'll find a lot of people who think they're actors in a play to change the world, which is very different than money for money's sake. We're not investing in glamour and luxury; we're investing in our product and our people and basic business stuff. So I think the culture is very different.  PATERNOT If you look at the movie "Wall Street" as the quintessential example of that, nothing really new was being created. We're in positions here where I think the reason there is wealth is because we're doing something completely different than playing with money. We are literally shaping, in some way, the way people are going to live and the way businesses are going to run.  CARPENTER I was talking to someone about this whole thing, about why this thing grabs hold of you. And then you feel like you don't have it; it has you. For some reason, some number of people have been tapped on the shoulder, like 'you're going to be part of this thing that is going to be born.' There is nothing that's going to stop this particular transformation. It is great sometimes. Other times, it's just so consuming that you wish you could just dial down and have 60 percent of the experience. But that's not available. You're either in, tapped, put to work, on the road crew, or probably you're not in. There is no kind of convenient, "this really works for my life." And I think that's probably when any big transformation happens -- it just sort of puts people to work in the service of itself.  Q. Kevin is burning to say something.  O'CONNOR It's something I probably shouldn't say, because it's contrarian. I think that without question there's a real temptation for some really bad things to happen. And you start to see signals of it. We had the highest turnover in our Silicon Valley office. I'll talk to an employee who's leaving the company and saying: "Love the company, love the compensation, love DoubleClick, love everything, but I'm going to go and really throw my hat in the ring with a hot new start-up over here. The guy next door made $20 million. I've got to make my $20 million or I'm a failure." So you start to see greed. Money creates greed, and greed creates corruption. And you're going to see more and more of this. You're going to see bad companies. Wherever there's an incredible, immense amount of money, there's going to be bad people.  CARPENTER As long as the pie keeps rapidly expanding, everybody's going to be really good friends and get along really well. When it starts really getting to be a battle for market share, it'll be a different story.  No Fun in the Fishbowl Q. What do you all really hate about being a chief executive? ESPUELAS Having to be "on" all the time. Everyone you meet sees you through that optic. So much so that now, unless it's a business context, I never say what I do. I always work for "a Latin American company."  PATERNOT That's exactly what I do as well. A nameless company. The biggest change I saw to the negative is going from a private company to a public one. All of a sudden you have to be that much more careful with the random people that you meet, because sometimes you'll start off in a perfectly casual conversation and before you know it, you realize that person's just wanting to know where your stock's going next week. That can get annoying. It's constantly feeling like sometimes you're being taken advantage of by people who do know who you are, and you just want to be anonymous. You don't want to necessarily be a public profile 24 hours a day.  Q. Is there anything else you dislike?  CARPENTER Travel. Today, being a C.E.O. means an enormous amount of travel. Often, you go somewhere and you talk for an hour and it's critical. You have to do it, but you think, "God, this whole thing took me 12 hours and it was an hour of something that actually happened." We can be more and more productive on planes with computers, but travel takes a huge personal toll.  ESPUELAS I arrived this morning in Miami at 5 from Buenos Aires, had a press conference at 8:30, gave a speech at 9:30 and got on a plane at 11 to come to newyork . Something I don't think is at all a positive is that the C.E.O. figure has become a bit of a starlet. Literally, there's probably 30 people or more in our company who could have done that speech today, and done it much better than I, since I was half dazed anyway. But people want to meet you, and that makes a difference. Sometimes it is a bit overwhelming.  O'CONNOR To me, it's just family. You just don't get to see them. Wife can understand, but two kids, two young kids, they have a tough time.  Q. Will you still be the chief executive of DoubleClick when you're 60?  O'CONNOR The board willing. Hopefully, I'll drop dead behind my desk of old age and the board doesn't shoot me. So far they like me, though.  Q. You envision that kind of career?  O'CONNOR Yeah, if the board thinks I'm the best person for the job, then, yeah, I'd love to keep it.  Q. How about the rest of the panel?  ESPUELAS Sixty's a long way away. I love what I do. I can't imagine doing anything else, but I've also seen people who've been at the same job for 20 years, and it's not pretty. I'd like to also think that I'm imminently replaceable, that within the 700 people we have in our team are at least 100 that could have my job. I like to think that anybody can replace me and that that should be everyone's desire at our company, that they should want my job and that they should work for it and get it. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos (pgs. 1&14)(Photographs by Richard Perry for The newyork Times)  Charts  KEVIN O'CONNOR DoubleClick THE EXECUTIVE Age: 38 Previously founded ICC, a software company in Atlanta. Received an engineering degree at the University of Michigan. THE COMPANY Started in 1996, DoubleClick is an Internet advertising network company. It creates and sells database technology and information that lets advertisers reach specific kinds of consumers. Went public IN February 1998  FERNANDO J. ESPUELAS StarMedia Network THE EXECUTIVE Age: 33 Born in Uruguay and educated at Connecticut College. Has a background in advertising and worked at AT&T. THE COMPANY Founded in 1996, StarMedia is a Spanish-and Portuguese-language media company. It offers news, Web channels and e-commerce services to residents of Latin America. It is also an Internet service provider. Went PUBLIC IN May 1999  CANDICE CARPENTER iVillage THE EXECUTIVE Age: 47 Former president of QVC as well as Time Life Video and Television. Has an M.B.A. from Harvard. THE COMPANY Started in 1995, iVillage provides Internet services for women, offering information and networks about everyday issues like working, baby care and health. It also lets other companies market products to members. Went PUBLIC IN March 1999  STEPHAN PATERNOT Theglobe.com THE EXECUTIVE Age: 25 Studied business and computer science at Cornell University. THE COMPANY Mr. Paternot and his co-founder and co-chief executive, Todd Krizelman, also 25, founded the company while still in college. Theglobe.com started as chat rooms and a network for teenagers; it now offers shopping, news and business information. Went PUBLIC IN NOVember 1998. (pg. 14)

title: Connecticut's Corner of the Web - Correction Appended
body: QUIRKS and all, Connecticut's presence on the World Wide Web is a bit like a leisurely bicycle ride though the emerald hills of Litchfield County: every turn brings an unexpected delight, or yet another endless byway under construction. Hundreds of towns and private companies operate sites to guide Web surfers through the often intricate process of finding just the right destination or service. Some accomplish the task better than others, and finding the best overall site is no easier than trying to agree on the best pizza joint in New Haven. Many Web sites are well worth visiting, but very few combine the many threads that tie together Connecticut's patchwork of cities, commuter suburbs and bucolic small towns. Is there a quintessentially Connecticut site? Perhaps, but it is best to first sample several of the many sites that make up Connecticut's corner of the World Wide Web. Tourism is the main draw at many Connecticut sites, and the first stop on the meandering Web trail is Bethlehem, where a cottage industry centers on the town postmark. Since 1938, the local post office has been applying decorative rubber stamps, called cachets, to Christmas cards either mailed from the post office or sent there for forwarding. (The address is Postmaster, Bethlehem Post Office, 34 East Street, Bethlehem, Conn. 06751.) The Bethlehem Web site displays all of the cachets, which are numbered, and gives a brief history of the postal tradition. The main town site is simple but polished, and has plenty of links to churches, civic groups and town departments. Clearly we are on the right track. For big-city sites, start with Hartford. Clicking on the branches of the Charter Oak -- a little anemic compared to the mighty oak on the new 25-cent Connecticut coin -- sends surfers off to sundry city departments and related links. Some of the departments' pages seem like investment prospectuses, but others are more useful for the public. Bridgeport's site has a bit of the spirit of a former mayor, P. T. Barnum, with a conspicuous link to a large portrait of the current mayor ("Joe Ganim -- Portrait of a Leader") backed in a royal hue of purple. The links to city services are plentiful, but some, like the one for the airport, lead to dead ends. Aside from municipal sites, a handful of private Web pages contribute to an overall picture of life in Connecticut. Web surfers who enjoy the horse-pulling contest at the Durham Fair may be interested in Tractor Parts Unlimited of Bozrah, which specializes in antique tractor restorations. Several completed projects are shown, and it is easy to imagine the gleaming red and silver 1964 Massey Ferguson 35 plowing fields in Tobacco Valley. Such small sites abound, some more flavorsome than others. Mystic Pizza modestly capitalizes on its tie to the 1988 movie that began the career of Julia Roberts.
