The Mark Twain House in Hartford was a bit difficult to find using the usual Internet search tools, but it eventually popped up on a site managed by Trinity College. For a nautical theme, the Electric Boat Corporation maintains a list of every nuclear submarine ever built in Connecticut. In Pomfret and nearby communities, genealogists have transcribed cemetery markers and headstones as part of a nationwide project known as USGenWeb. It's remarkable to think that someone meticulously transcribed each headstone and memorial marker, and even more fascinating that a vast network of volunteers is doing so all over the country. Unfortunately, listening to "Here Comes the Sun" played ad infinitum makes it tough to stay at this site for long. Connecticut sports fans' loyalties have long been torn between newyork and Boston. The joint Web site for Watertown and Oakville complicates matters by following the career of a hometown hero, the former Mets first baseman Rico Brogna, as he makes good with the Phillies. A passer-by might mistake this for a site in Bucks County, Pa., rather than near Waterbury. But it appears to be updated often, and even high school scores are fresh. This is the archetypal small-town sports site, focusing on a region that would otherwise be ignored by larger sites. Raw information about the state can be gleaned from the University of Connecticut, which has made an astounding amount of mapping data available at no cost. Posting these expensive federal files is a real public service, and the collection of antique maps is a logical starting point for anyone interested in the history of Connecticut. Look under "Quad Level" for modern maps and aerial photos; the files designated J.P.E.G., for Joint Photographic Experts Group, can be downloaded and then viewed with a Web browser. Special mapping software is needed to view most of the other files. Dozens of smaller Connecticut schools have Web sites, some with charming surprises. The Gilbert School in Winsted is private but serves as a public school for the towns of Winchester and Hartland under the terms of a trust established by the school's founder. If anyone doubts the provisions of the trust, William L. Gilbert's last will, dated 1890, is posted, including the admonition that "no teacher, scholar or inmate shall under any condition be admitted or receive the benefit of either of said institution who shall use tobacco in any form or spiritous liquors as a beverage." Many school Web sites fall into disrepair as students graduate and underclassmen go off on their own projects. Staples High School in Westport manages to keep its professional-looking site fairly up to date, complete with search capabilities and prominent copyright notices. Updating a school Web site consumes vast tracts of time, making student efforts even more impressive. Under the "non sequitur" Web site category, the musical group Inka Antares, based in Weatogue, plays the regional Andes music of South America. The Tibetan Association of Connecticut also maintains a site, suggesting that our finalist must have an international touch. Which Connecticut Web site takes all of these threads and best weaves them into a single tapestry that is unmistakably Connecticut? For a good candidate, look to Chester (founded 1692, population 3,600). This town's unpretentious site is a combination commons, town meeting and barber shop waiting room, with an impressive number of links to other Chester-related Web pages. Yes, there are a bunch of Chester sites, and not all in Connecticut. Take, for example, the Chester International Links Association. It seems that town residents visit other places named Chester, and residents of the other Chesters reciprocate. Such travels are duly noted on the Web. Recently, Mike and Sally Sanders told of their journey to Chester, England, the mother of all Chesters, and a trip to Chester, Nova Scotia, was being organized. The various town Web sites are also linked, making a unique international Chester network. Even the Connecticut version of Chester has more than one Web site. Chester's rather dry alternate is part of the state's municipal Web site network, known as the Municipal Public Access Initiative, but it is out of date and not nearly as entertaining to browse. It does, however, have a motto: "Chester. We know where it is!" The genuine town site is a mixture of municipal housekeeping and community and business guides of a richness that belies the town's tiny population. Under "ordinances and special acts," is recorded the resolution that separated Chester from Saybrook in 1836 and, with relief for sports fans, the repeal of the ordinance that prohibited Sunday baseball. Town demographics revealed that in 1990 there were 13.9 students per teacher in the town schools and 253 town residents who commuted to work in Essex. At last count there was one bank, and the crime rate was about one quarter of the state average. But this site tells a lot more about Chester and Connecticut than mere numbers. Dozens of photographs include a picture of the tiny Chester train station (it's smaller than the men's room at Grand Central Terminal), and other local Web sites linked here include the National Theater of the Deaf and an elementary school project to study Chester Creek. Activities large and small are chronicled, giving the site the flavor of a small-town newspaper. There is a slightly unvarnished sense of community here that most commercially inspired municipal Web sites fail to capture, and perhaps there is also a wistful sense of the New England that tourists expect to find and residents fondly remember. Quite a lot for a small-town Web site.  Bookmark These Addresses, Please Here are addresses for the Web sites in the article. title: Elliott M. Sanger, 77, a WQXR News Producer
body: Elliott M. Sanger Jr., a news producer for WQXR, the radio station owned by The newyork Times, and a corporate relations executive for The newyork Times Company, died on Friday at his home in Manhattan. He was 77. The cause was non-Hodgkins lymphoma, said his wife, Joan Sanger. In a career that spanned four decades at The Times, Mr. Sanger held a variety of positions at the newspaper and at WQXR, which his father, Elliott M. Sanger Sr., helped begin in 1936. It was bought by The Times eight years later. When The Times was closed by a 114-day strike that began in late 1962, Mr. Sanger directed a project to put nonstriking correspondents on the air. The project won a George Foster Peabody Award, and it proved so popular that it continued after the newspaper resumed publishing. For the next seven years, Mr. Sanger headed a staff of news writers in the Times newsroom who worked with reporters and editors for assignments on the air. In 1970, Mr. Sanger became the executive producer of "Insight," a nightly program of news analysis moderated by Clifton Daniel, a former managing editor of The Times, who interviewed correspondents about the top stories of the day. In 1973, Mr. Sanger joined the corporate relations department of the Times Company and became manager of corporate relations in 1980. He retired in 1987 but continued working for The newyork Times Company Foundation. Elliott Maxwell Sanger Jr. was born in Manhattan and graduated from Columbia College in 1943. He served in the Army, landing in Normandy a few days after D-Day. In addition to his wife, Mr. Sanger is survived by his mother, Eleanor N. Sanger of Manhattan; a brother, Kenneth E. Sanger of White Plains; his daughter, Elizabeth Sanger of Larchmont; and two grandsons. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING;
Old-Fashioned Growth Stirs Interest in Borders
body: WITH all the attention being paid to the online rivalry between Barnes & Noble and Amazon.com, could the smartest buy actually be the shares of the beleaguered Borders Group? That is what investors in Borders are hoping. Last Monday, some of them were cheered by what the market perceived to be good news: Borders, the bookseller based in Ann Arbor, Mich., hired a new chief executive: Gregory P. Josefowicz, formerly president of Jewel-Osco, a division of Albertson's, the supermarket giant. News of the appointment sent Borders shares up 6 percent in one day. Mr. Josefowicz replaced Philip Pfeffer, who resigned in April after only five months on the job, during which the stock price languished; Mr. Pfeffer previously was chief executive of Random House. Even before the appointment of Mr. Josefowicz, however, the strong market position and cash flow of Borders had begun to attract value investors. The company operates 284 Borders Books and Music superstores, nearly 900 Waldenbooks mall stores and about 40 bookstores overseas. It had $2.60 billion in sales last year, not far behind Barnes & Noble, at $3.01 billion, and far ahead of Amazon, at $610.0 million. Driving Borders's growth are its superstores and international outlets. Despite the jump last week, Borders shares are still down more than 42 percent since Dec. 31; they are now at $14.375. The stock is trading at just 10.5 times analysts' estimated earnings of $1.37 a share for the year ending January 2001. Barnes & Noble, by contrast, is trading at over 15 times next year's earnings estimates. Amazon is expected to post a loss for its 2001 fiscal year. "At these prices, I'm buying," said Alan Snyder of Snyder Capital Management of San Francisco, who since June has nearly doubled his stake in Borders, to 3.6 million shares -- about 4.6 percent of the company's outstanding stock. Other big buyers include Lazard Freres, which quadrupled its stake this year, to 3.43 million shares as of Sept. 30. And the largest shareholder, Dreman Value Management, which owns more than 10 percent of the outstanding shares, has been adding to its position. David Dreman, chief investment officer, said he is looking for the stock to rise by at least 50 percent over the next 12 months or so as Borders implements a new Internet strategy and resolves its management turmoil. "Borders is an excellent bookseller that got slammed because it was late to the Internet," Mr. Dreman said. Many investors are optimistic about the company's use of the "clicks and mortar" strategy, in which walk-in customers use a Borders intranet site to search for titles and order books once they are in the store. Borders partisans say this combination of traditional and online retailing may help the company sidestep online price wars. Though it has tried to compete on the Internet, the Borders site, Borders.com, runs a distant third to Amazon and Barnes & Noble, in part because the company did not begin generating sales from it until late 1998. Online sales accounted for less than 1 percent of revenue in the third quarter. The site has also been a drag on earnings -- the reason that Borders posted a third-quarter loss of 2 cents a share on Thursday. But the company's all-important superstores had healthy growth in same-store sales -- for those open at least a year -- of 6.6 percent. Without the Internet operations, Mr. Dreman said, he figured that Borders would be in a position to post full-year profits of $1.30 a share. Instead, analysts polled by First Call/ Thomson Financial estimated that it would earn just $1.16 a share. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: The graph shows the Borders Group share price, plotted weekly since January 1999.

title:
The Way We Live Now: 11-21-99: Word & Image;
Comehither.com
body: So how come my television screen and newspapers are filling up with come-ons for dot-coms? Besides cars and telephones, the ads on "Ally McBeal" are pushing eToys.com and petstore.com and drugstore.com. Dot-coms flash on my screen between murders and disasters on the 11 o'clock news. Ads in The Times shout Yahoo and Excite and eBay and E*Trade and ask me to think AltaVista every time I dream of Michelangelo's ceiling. Quite remarkably, it seems the New Media have suddenly decided to enrich the Old. Or, if you prefer irony in your paradox, the Old Media are greedily wolfing down the poison that will hasten their destruction by the New. Paradoxically, too, most of the dot-com companies still lose money on every sale, which means that the more successful their ads, the greater their losses. Indeed, they are bidding up the cost of commercials in what could turn out to be a giant Ponzi game: they are spending huge sums obtained from venture capitalists and stock-market gamblers on ads that can only increase their so-far unprofitable business and deficits. And they can only hope that the added traffic will cause investors to send them still more money. That Peter-to-pay-Paul rondo is only one reason to wonder precisely what business the dot-coms are in. Mainly, even the best-known, like Amazon, Yahoo or America Online, are looking to tattoo their names on the minds of surfers while they evolve every season into a new enterprise. For example, Yahoo and AltaVista began life as sophisticated "search engines," which quickly scour the Web to produce an index of documents answering your questions. Ask about Shakespeare's sonnets or sourdough bread, and they can instantly cough up texts, recipes and relevant commentaries. Instead of charging a fee, the search engines thought they could get rich from ads posted alongside their findings. But the appearance of many competitors (Hotbot, Excite, Google, et al.) soon ruined their prospects. A further challenge was posed by the success of America Online, with its colorful array of public and proprietary goods and services. It became popular by also providing email, chat rooms, bridge games and live reports on the price of stocks or airline seats. And once it, too, made itself into a search engine, AOL became an all-purpose Web gateway, a network of networks financed not just by advertising but also by a flat monthly fee from millions of subscribers. That was only the beginning of the Web's evolution. Other gateways soon appeared and charged less than AOL. And searchers like Yahoo became gateways for no charge at all. Almost all these "portals" now offer news, email and a cascade of services like tax advice, movie schedules, bill paying, games, clubs, calendars, football scores. For income, they look not to fees or even ads but to the growth of dot-com commerce -- their sales of goods and commissions for sending customers to other merchants. Imagine a future, then, in which virtually every Web site is linked to every other. Read a news or feature story about a lovely resort and with a few clicks of a button you can locate a suitable airline schedule, order the tickets, choose a car rental and hotel, reserve golf time and restaurant tables and maybe also order babysitters, guidebooks and the appropriate wardrobe. What AOL and the other gateways currently long to become is your port of entry to this vast commercial net. Some dot-coms may be content to sell a single line of goods or services -- videos, tulip bulbs, lipsticks or banking and bill paying. Some may grow like Amazon.com, which is fast becoming a department store offering not only books but also electronics and computers, CD's and videos, toys and drugs. And like Amazon, they may also compete with eBay, which brokers auction sales of both gems and junk among its customers. Once enmeshed in the Web, every dot-com will relate to every other. Merchants find it useful to post complementary news and advice. And companies offering news and advice grow eager to link themselves to the sellers of goods and services. E*Trade.com, for example, began life as a stock market charging only small commissions. But it soon added headline news about the economy, business articles and discussion groups, a bookstore and shopping service and most recently a one-button connection to a full-service telebank. Similarly, The newyork Times and other newsmongers will lure you with reading matter but hope to pay for it by directing you not only to ads but also to purchases inspired by your reading. Potentially, every site on the Web can be a portal to all other sites, just as in the air age every American city can be a gateway to our country. The ultimate competition among the dot-coms will be for a place in the subconscious of every Web user. But while the Web stores must build warehouses and employ order fillers, the grandest portals will exist only virtually and collect from you every time you pass Go. Think of stocks and you may begin your Web journey on E*Trade. Think of news and we hope you'll reach for Nytimes.com, for The Times and most other publications also expect to be Net portals for communities of like-minded readers whom they can sell to Web advertisers and merchants. So even in these primitive stages of Web commerce, the struggle for name recognition has grown fierce. A few name-brand dot-coms are hoping to end up with outsize reputations as Net ports, attaining the stature that actual ports like newyork, London and hongkong achieved as centers of commerce. Since every Web site can blossom into a great portal, the richer ones are throwing all their resources into ads that might distinguish them from the pack. They want to be famous in the old world even before they are well defined in the new. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
VOWS;
Oksana Katsuro and Douglas Hopkins
body: LAST January, when Oksana Katsuro first encountered Douglas Hopkins, she was living and working in Obminsk, Russia, and dreaming of an escape. Ms. Katsuro, who is 26 and nearly six feet tall, with butterscotch-color hair, was earning the equivalent of $20 a month designing computer programs to track nuclear materials at a government institute. She occupied a tiny dormitory room there, and like most people she knew, she barely scraped by financially. "I mostly ate potatoes from my mother and my sister's gardens," she said. "Sometimes, my mom went to the forest and picked mushrooms and marinated them." Eating in a restaurant severely stretched her budget. Starting a family was out of the question. "Even my girlfriends who are married don't have children because they can't afford it," she said. At the institute, Ms. Katsuro spent a lot of time exploring the Internet, sometimes conversing with Americans on One & Only, an international matchmaking Web site. Then she began corresponding regularly with Mr. Hopkins, who was fascinated to find highly educated Russian women on the site, including a laser physicist and a lawyer. "Tens of thousands of Russian women are on the Internet trying to leave and better their lives," observed Mr. Hopkins, who at 53 was eager to marry and settle down. In person, he is reed thin, beautifully spoken, Old World in his tastes and unorthodox. He switches careers often and gracefully, having worked as a fashion photographer in newyork and as a volcanologist for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, climbing and measuring erupting volcanoes. Ten years ago, he started Douglas Hopkins & Company, a perfume maker based in his wood-panel duplex on the Upper East Side. Many of his products are inspired by remedies dating back centuries and are packaged like perfumes in a Parisian apothecary. (He describes his perfume Zazou as "the California scent with a hint of sanity.") By email, Ms. Katsuro and Mr. Hopkins discussed aromatherapy, computers, volcanoes and her former marriage, which ended in divorce three years ago. "Sometimes, I got six letters from Doug a day," Ms. Katsuro said. "I spent all my weekends reading and writing." While he said her messages were funny and full of "the proverbial Russian soul," he imagined her as "in her 40's and rather drab-looking." "Beautiful women generally have an ego, and there was nothing like that in her letters," he said. "Then, one day, she very modestly asked if I wanted to take a look at her home page. I was shocked! It was like opening a Ford model book. So I lost no time at all. I went to Russia as quickly as I could." Many people tried to talk him out of going. "My whole family thought I was nuts," he said. "My father said, 'Mark my word, someone will do harm to you in the Moscow airport.' " The couple spent four days together in Russia in April. On the second day he proposed marriage, and she accepted. On the third day, they kissed for the first time. In June, he went back with an engagement ring. "Russians have no hope," he said. "They really don't believe in tomorrow at all. But when I gave Oksana the ring, I could see in her eyes that she believed." In August, she moved to newyork, and on Nov. 6, they were married in a civil ceremony in a friend's antiques-filled Manhattan loft. The bride, who wore a white dress as short as a tennis outfit, hopes to become a mother soon. "I'm proud of myself, that I managed to do this, that I had the energy and courage," she said. "My father, who died a year and a half ago, taught me that we are born in order to bring up our children and give them all the knowledge and education we can. So, for me, it's like I'm doing what I was supposed to do. I'm on the right road." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: MANHATTAN, NOV. 6 -- Top, the bride and bridegroom at a friend's loft, where they were married. Above, young guests at the reception. (Photographs by Aaron Lee Fineman for The newyork Times)

title: F.C.C. Approves Line Sharing for Data Carriers
body: The Federal Communications Commission voted today to require major regional phone companies to share their lines with data carriers, a move that may make high-speed Internet service more readily and cheaply available for residential customers. The agency ordered that dominant carriers like SBC Communications and Bell Atlantic share their lines with competitors that provide high-speed data service. Under current rules, customers of data carriers like the NorthPoint Communications Group, the Covad Communications Group and Rhythms Net Connections Inc. usually must install a second phone line to provide high-speed Internet access. So-called line sharing could reduce the monthly fees data carriers have to pay for transmitting over telephone lines. The dominant carriers already use line sharing when they offer their own high-speed Internet service. Both groups of carriers use a technology known as digital subscriber line, or D.S.L., that offers high-speed data service over ordinary phone lines by transmitting in a range of frequencies above those used for voice communications. "This decision should help to decrease our members' cost of providing D.S.L. and other advanced services," said Russell Frisby, president of a recently established trade group of local carriers called the Competitive Telecommunications Association. Major carriers called the ruling an unneeded benefit to the upstart data carriers. "There is no need for corporate welfare that gives one sector of a very competitive industry an unnecessary advantage," said Bruce Posey, senior vice president of U S West. Companies like Covad, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif., typically provide Internet services to small businesses, but will be able to tap into the residential market more easily if they can use existing telephone lines. Shares of Covad, which have risen more than 60 percent in the last month, were down 62.5 cents, to $64.6875; NorthPoint, based in San Francisco, was up $81.25 cents, to $35.9375, and Rhythms, based in Englewood, Calif., was up $4.1875, to $43.50, all on Nasdaq. Among the regional Bell companies, U S West was a fraction higher but the others were lower. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
FILM REVIEW;
In This Version of Cyberutopia, Show and Tell Lasts All Day
body: Amid the hue and cry about how the Internet is destroying personal privacy, few have pointed out that for certain cyberfanatics that erosion is cause for rejoicing. Computer gurus like Justin Hall, the bratty, motor-mouthed exhibitionist who is the focus of Doug Block's intriguing but disorganized documentary, "Home Page," see no need for personal privacy once the utopian electronic community of their dreams is established. The world Mr. Hall imagines is a kind of virtual commune that recalls the headiest collective fantasies of the hippie counterculture but is situated in cyberspace instead of the real world. When first glimpsed, Mr. Hall is an undergraduate at Swarthmore College in 1996, where he is a cybercelebrity who operates a home page visited daily by 7,000 people. Dressed in psychedelic finery, his blond hair teased into a pointed tower, he is the very model of latter-day hippie proselytizer. On his page, which consists of a daily journal and photographs of him and his friends, Mr. Hall literally lets it all hang out, revealing himself in nude photographs (he is a soft-featured, girlish-looking boy with an impish grin) and disclosing the most intimate details of his personal history and his relationships with a series of women. Mr. Hall is only too eager to confide to the camera that his father was alcoholic and committed suicide, that he was brought up by a succession of nannies and that he has had nine years of psychotherapy. The film follows Mr. Hall from Swarthmore to San Francisco, where he teams up with his mentor, Howard Rheingold, the author and World Wide Web visionary, to help begin a Web site called Electric Minds whose goal is the establishment of a virtual community. Their relationship is far from harmonious, and Mr. Hall tests it by sneakily revealing his mentor's background as a writer of purple-prosed cyberporn. Mr. Hall is the most vivid and messianic figure in this movie's portrait of a loosely knit band of computer fanatics who use the Internet to explore the boundaries of communication and human relationships. In the film's halfhearted subplot, Mr. Block establishes his own home page, in which he writes a confessional journal, talks his elderly parents into going online and interviews his wife, Marjorie Silver, and young daughter, Lucy, about the effects of computers on their lives. The more people Mr. Block interviews, the more the film, which opens today at Cinema Village, seems to reinforce cliched images of computer nerds as brainy neurotics who resort to sophisticated high-tech mind games to try to surmount discomfort in their own bodies. The relationship of Julie Petersen, her husband, Jim, and her boyfriend, Patrick Farley, is offered as a utopian paradigm for cybersexual liberation. While Julie traveled across the country with Patrick, they related running accounts of their affair on their personal home pages. Jim insists that he was grateful for their accounts because it was "better than living in the dark." But as Carl Steadman, one of the movie's few voices of reason, observes, endless communication doesn't change human nature. "People disagree," he admits. "And you very well might not like your neighbor's opinions." Sitting in front of a giant teddy bear, Mr. Steadman, the boyish founder of his own satirical Webzine, continues: "We've gone from this state where the Web was going to offer the perfect communications medium where everyone could talk to everyone else and their differences would be erased to this fallout where it's not as we planned, and the Net is not going to provide what we wanted it to provide, and it's not going to make us rich. There's no revolution at hand."  HOME PAGE  Written and directed by Doug Block; director of photography, Mr. Block; edited by Deborah Rosenberg; music by Elephant Ears; produced by Mr. Block, Jane Weiner and Esther Robinson; released by Copacetic Pictures, Home Box Office and ZDF Arte. At the Cinema Village, 22 East 12th Street, Greenwich Village. Running time: 102 minutes. This film is not rated.  WITH: Justin Hall, Lucy Block, Doug Block, Patrick Farley, Julie Petersen, Jim Petersen, Howard Rheingold, Judi Rose, John Seabrook, Marjorie Silver, Josh Silver, Carl Steadman and J. Carew Kraft. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Justin Hall has little use for privacy in the documentary "Home Page." (Copacetic Pictures/HBO)

title: Microsoft Drops Instant Message Fight With AOL
body: Microsoft has backed off in its battle with America Online over instant messages on the Internet, saying the latest version of its MSN Messenger service will not operate with AOL's Instant Messenger. Microsoft contends that America Online's latest attempt to block MSN Messenger from working with Instant Messenger involves "a very serious security bug" that could allow computer code to be run on a personal computer without the computer user's approval or knowledge. "To provide an update to MSN Messenger service that would continue to enable interoperability, Microsoft would need to put our own users at risk in a similar fashion," Yusuf Mehdi, director of marketing for Microsoft's Consumer and Commerce Group, said on Wednesday. Ann Brackbill, a spokeswoman for America Online, said, "We're glad they have decided to respect the security and privacy of our members and users." Concerning Microsoft's allegation of a security bug, she said: "We said four months ago that it was a fake issue, and it still is a fake issue today. We would never do anything to compromise the security of our users." Microsoft first released its Internet chat software in early August, challenging America Online's dominance of the market. One advantage that Microsoft promoted was the ability to work with America Online's software, allowing MSN customers to exchange instant messages with America Online users. America Online immediately complained that Microsoft engineers had hacked into its proprietary network and blocked Microsoft from linking to its software. Microsoft redesigned its chat software to bypass America Online's block, but was then stymied again and again as America Online continued to put up blocks. Mr. Mehdi denied Microsoft had "lost" the battle to America Online. "There are no winners," he said. "Consumers will win when an industrywide instant messaging standard is in place that ensures all users the ability to message with others regardless of which service they're using." As of last month, America Online had 45 million people signed up for the messenger service, while Microsoft said today that it had 4.5 million users. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Delivering the Goods: No Simple Solution
body: E-COMMERCE is like comedy. Coming up with ideas is easy; delivery is hard. If the explosion in online shopping had taken place in 1959 instead of 1999, getting packages delivered might have been easier. In 1959, many homes still had milk boxes. "There's sort of a disconnect," said Carter Griffen, a co-founder of Mental Physics, an e-commerce systems company, based in Vienna, Va., that is hoping to profit from the situation. "The front end of e-commerce -- placing an order -- is very sexy, very easy. Receiving the order, however, is problematic." His company is one of a few promoting the idea of a jumbo mailbox for online parcels. After recently purchasing the patent rights to Smartbox, a roll-up household parcel container that was invented by a Kansas City, Mo., dry cleaner but never made it to market, Mental Physics is developing a series of locked, reinforced boxes of various sizes that will sit outside houses. To allow access to all delivery services, the yet-to-be-named devices will be wired to the Internet. When the box owners make an online purchase, special software will create and transmit a code for each order. A delivery driver can punch in the code on a keypad to unlock the box and make the delivery. Another company, Streamline .com, has at least one variation of that idea already in place. The company, which runs errands and delivers a variety of goods to suburban customers outside Boston and Washington, installs boxes with a full-size refrigerator-freezer and two room-temperature shelves in the basement or garage of customers as part of its service fee of $30 a month. To allow its drivers access to the boxes, Streamline also fits keypad locks on its customers' doors. About 3,700 houses now have Streamline's boxes, according to the company. But there is a widespread belief that any kind of superbox for parcels will be a hard sell and perhaps unworkable outside spacious suburbs. Even Streamline is developing portable dry ice containers that it will leave outside the houses of customers who will not, or cannot, accept more permanent boxes. It's a solution that has been used for decades by Omaha Steaks, a mail-order giant turned e-commerce merchant. "I just don't see boxes working right now," said Elaine Rubin, chairman of Shop.org, a trade group for online retailers. "I've got enough bikes, baseball bats and other junk in my garage already. I don't need a big box in there as well. Outside, it's an eyesore. And how often do people order online, anyway? About three times a month." Figuring out where parcels can be safely sent is an issue that buyers from ordinary mail-order catalogs, which outsell online merchants by a wide margin, have long encountered. Jill Frankle, director of retail research at Gomez Advisors, said she expected online buyers to use the same kinds of solutions for the next three to four years. "The current system works for most people," Ms. Frankle said. For many people, Ms. Frankle suggested, a solution is getting packages delivered at work. While she knows of no firm data that support her view, Amazon.com's "purchase circles" lend it at least some anecdotal support. To help its customers make choices about books, music CD's and videos, Amazon creates best-seller lists grouped around shipping destinations, including corporate offices. While some of those lists are filled with books that are probably work-related (Boeing's is heavy on engineering and computer tomes, and the most popular book on Microsoft's list is the latest offering from its chairman, William H. Gates 3rd), many strongly suggest that either a lot of niche book clubs are meeting in cubicles or offices have become a handy delivery spot for Amazon's boxes. The top seller at the Gillette Company is Bret Lott's "Jewel," a novel about a child with Down syndrome, which is followed on the list by Thomas Harris's novel "Hannibal." At Nabisco, the cookie and snack maker, diet books figure prominently. Alan Amling, the director of e-commerce for United Parcel Service, has no doubt that many of the boxes its brown vans deliver to offices are either online or catalog purchases. While he is not aware of any companies that have complained to U.P.S. about being overwhelmed by employees' holiday shopping, Mr. Amling said, "As volumes continue to increase, it would make sense that some employers would object." Ms. Rubin, of Shop.org, anticipates that as online shopping increases, the answer to delivery problems will come from the delivery companies themselves, who might start allowing customers to schedule delivery times, particularly after work. "I think that's more reasonable," she said. Mr. Amling said such schemes would not be viable for some time. Until then, he said, solutions depend on drivers' initiative. "Our drivers," he said, "have a relationship with their customers that allows them to know who wants us to leave the package under the lawn chair and who wants it on the front porch." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Randy Jones)

title: Digital Players Break New Ground - Correction Appended
body: IT was only a year ago that Diamond Multimedia introduced the Rio PMP300, the world's first portable MP3 music player, and spurred an audio revolution in downloaded music. This year, there are more than a dozen variations on the theme, portable players offering features like FM-radio tuners and easy-to-use controls. More important, the players -- costing from about $200 to $400 -- are moving toward improved storage capacity so they can carry more tunes. Most players store no more than 64 minutes of high-quality music. So far, fewer than a million MP3 players have been sold in the unitedstates. But audio market analysts and MP3 player makers say they expect sales to be brisk this holiday season and beyond. One reason is that mainstream America has begun discovering digitized music on the Internet. Every day, about 17 million MP3 files are downloaded. Unlike previous portable players, MP3 players have the significant advantage of having no moving parts. As a consequence, they are practically skip- and flutter-proof and the batteries they use last longer. And the sound is near CD quality. The rage for MP3 has manufacturers scrambling to ride the next digital wave. In the spring, Samsung Electronics plans to introduce an MP3 player that will play not only downloaded music files but also still pictures and video from the Internet. In a nod to the widening popularity of online music and portable devices that play it, Packard Bell NEC recently introduced the NEC Home Music Studio system, a personal computer that is designed to capture, manage and make digital music. Built-in software allows it to download and upload music to and from an MP3 player. Yet, there is no guarantee that MP3, which is a format for compressing and storing digital audio signals, will continue to be the compression format of choice. Sony has introduced a digital player that uses its own audio format. And there are other software approaches to storing digital music on the way from major players like Microsoft, I.B.M., Liquid Audio and AT&T. But a Betamax-style demise of MP3 may be years off, some analysts say. In the meantime, one MP3 maker, Creative Labs, is hedging its bets with its new Nomad II, a digital player equipped to adapt to whatever audio format is winning the day. Of course, such future-proofing comes with a cost: about $100 more than the price of its nearest competitor.  1. SONY CD WALKMAN D-EJ01 Sony's CD Walkman D-EJ01, a sleek, slick and shiny update of the portable CD player, looks as if it might have fallen off the starship Enterprise. Breaking with classic clamshell design, the D-EJ01 does not open; it loads CD's with a slide-in mechanism and plays them with remarkable fidelity and power. Besides being reasonably shock resistant, the $349.95 player also promises 62 hours of continuous playback with NiMH rechargeable batteries.  2. SKIPDOCTOR SkipDoctor is a $34.99, handheld, hand-cranked device that lives up to claims that it can repair damaged optical discs, whether they are CD's, CD-ROM's, DVD's or game discs like those used in Sega's Dreamcast. SkipDoctor is best used to repair troublesome scratches, and is reliable and fairly simple to use.  3. PANASONIC DVD-L50 PORTABLE DVD/CD DVD-L50 Portable DVD/CD player by Panasonic is nothing less than a home theater that can fit in the palm of your hand. Amazingly compact, the $999 player opens to reveal a five-inch L.C.D. color screen and half-dollar-size stereo speakers linked to a fully functioning DVD/CD player. Films are remarkably sharp whether they are seen on the player or are piped to a television with supplied patch cords.  4. REPLAYTV 2001 The first of several new tapeless video recording devices to arrive this year, ReplayTV lets you watch a "real-time recording" of a live program, put it on pause to answer the phone or grab a snack, then return to pick up your viewing where you left off, even as the recording continues. The ReplayTV 2020 model ($699) records up to 20 hours of television programs on a hard disk drive and enables couch potatoes to create their own television channels based on their favorite themes -- not just series names like "Star Trek" but also "fishing" or "Michelle Pfeiffer." It requires a phone jack to download the latest program schedules each night, but in doing so it also automatically resets the clock. The era of the flashing 12:00, alas, is over.  5. SONY MDR-IF330RK CORDLESS HEADPHONES MDR-IF330RK cordless headphones by Sony ($129) are designed for anyone who wants to have his sound delivered without being tethered to its source. The headphones, which also connect to home audio systems, televisions and VCR's, provide a solid sound with good deep bass capacity. Its transmitter, which promises 100 hours of (rechargeable) battery life, has a range of 24 feet.  6. AUDIOVOX MP DJ The lower-cost MP DJ by Audiovox is a late but notable entry into the MP3 music player category. Tiny, even by MP3 standards, the MP DJ has a startling sound nonetheless. Taking advantage of its odd, stop-watch shape, the MP DJ has a large liquid crystal display and logically placed controls. The $179.95 player comes with 32MB on board and can be upgraded with additional memory. Even the download software that comes with it is cute.  7. SRS LABS WOW THING WOW Thing by SRS Labs is a makeup-case-size device that when plugged into a personal computer's sound system creates stunning power and 3-D sound effects -- on the cheap. Costing $29.95 and sold only on the Web at www.wowthing.com, the device is simple and effective.  8. CREATIVE LABS CD-RW BLASTER 8432 CD-RW Blaster 8432 by Creative Labs is a handy and, better yet, speedy way to use a personal computer to create or copy CD's and CD-ROM's. The $299.99 CD writer and rewriter is among one of the fastest and lowest priced devices of its kind. It can record 60 minutes or 545 megabytes of data in under nine minutes.  9. AUDIBLE.COM MOBILEPLAYER For those who want to take the author Frank McCourt on the road, Audible.com, which offers thousands of downloadable versions of books on tape available for PC's and P.D.A.'s, also makes the MobilePlayer. The 2-megabyte device can hold two hours of audio and comes with a cradle for downloading. Alone, the player is $99; the player is free when you purchase $9.95 of content from Audible.com every month.  10. RIO 500 DIGITAL AUDIO PLAYER The more powerful version of the planet's first MP3 player, the new Rio ($269) is elegant and packed with 64MB of memory that can be expanded with an additional memory card to 96MB. The Rio 500 connects to computers (PC's running Windows 98 and Macs) by way of a U.S.B. port and a much improved download software. Most of all, its sound is rich, full and detailed.  11. SONY MINIDISC MZ-R55 After a year on the market, MiniDisc MZ-R55 by Sony is still the finest and smallest digital device to record and play back prerecorded music. While it is barely larger than the 2.5-inch-square blank minidisc, the device can faithfully record up to 74 minutes of music on the disc from practically any source. Handsome in its metal skin, the $349 MZ-R55 produces a sound that is true, full of dynamic range and relatively skip free.  12. SONY GLASSTRON PLM-S700 PC PLM-S700 PC Glasstron virtually allows wearers to carry a large screen in their pocket. A pair of hyperhi-tech wraparound glasses by Sony, the Glasstron, which cost $2,599, can render computer graphics or the output of any audio-visual device with an S-video high-speed connection in the privacy of the glasses. The effect creates the impression of a 30-inch screen being viewed from about 6 feet away. Headphones are included.  13. I2GO EGO EGo by i2Go is the first MP3 player on the market that is designed specifically for use in the car. Appearing like the sport utility vehicle of pagers, the $299 eGo can hold just more than one hour of near CD-quality music on a 64MB memory card. The unit can be mounted in the car by way of a cassette adapter.  14. YAMAHA @PET RP-U100 PC RECEIVER Yamaha's solution to the blight of poor off-the-shelf PC audio systems, this $500 minitower packing 30-watts per channel is designed to stand between the computer and its speakers. Using home-entertainment-center style enhancements, the receiver can deliver a no-nonsense surroundlike sound, just right for enjoying the latest DVD movies or computer games. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  A caption in Circuits last Thursday with an article about portable music and multimedia players misidentified a model of the Sony Glasstron, a device that looks like sunglasses and is used to view entertainment or game videos. The player shown was the PLM-A35, which costs $599, not the PLM-S700 PC, which is $2,599. Correction-Date: November 25, 1999, Thursday Graphic   Photos (Photographs by Tony Cenicola for The New York Times)

title: For Online Shoppers, a Virtual Mall as Big as All Cyberspace
body: Here is a sampling, by no means complete, of popular places to shop online, with examples of what each sells.  Books  AMAZON.COM: www.amazon.com -- The granddaddy of book sites has branched into home electronics, music and zstores, an online bazaar for businesses and individuals. BARNESANDNOBLE.COM: www.barnesandnoble.com/ -- The retailer's online division sells books, magazines and calendars, and it offers downloadable titles for the Rocket eBook.  BOOK BUYERS OUTLET: www.bookbuyer.com/ -- An online store for books, games, software and hardware.  ADVANCED BOOK EXCHANGE: www.abebooks.com -- A source for out-of-print titles. The site has 5,300 book sellers and 15 million titles.  BORDERS: www.borders.com/ -- The home page offers books, music and videos, and, like other online bookstores, Oprah's latest pick.  1BOOKSTREET.COM: www.1bookstreet.com/ -- This site sells books only, but it also has a mystery magazine called Hard Evidence.  POWELLS: www.powells.com/ -- This retailer has rare titles and used hardcover and paperback editions, and it offers recommendations from independent book sellers.  Clothing  ASHFORD.COM: www.ashford.com/ -- The store offers accessories like leather bags, sunglasses and jewelry. It also offers watches, new and vintage, including a Rolex watch from the 1950's for around $2,700.  BLUE FLY: www.bluefly.com/ -- Blue Fly offers discounts on designer apparel and accessories, from long-sleeve shirts by Sweetpea to glassware by Mikasa, with short profiles about most of the designers.  BROOKS BROTHERS: www.brooksbrothers.com/ -- The quintessential men's store has dressed Presidents Lincoln and Kennedy, and heartthrobs like Clark Gable and Cary Grant, and the store takes credit for introducing the argyle sock to America.  LANDS' END: www.landsend.com/ -- Everyday fashions, even school uniforms, for everyone. There are images in full color, sizing charts and even an interactive on-screen body image for women to try on various outfits.  L.L. BEAN: www.llbean.com/ -- The Maine retailer sells lots of cozy winter clothes at this time of year, in addition to outdoor gear like sleeping bags rated to minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit and aluminum snowshoes.  SHE GETS DRESSED: www.shegetsdressed.com -- This online boutique has a small selection, but enough to outfit a woman in the workplace.  Computers  APPLE: www.apple.com/ -- The iMac and the iBook are featured along with software and peripherals for the personal computer that offers an alternative to a Windows-based system.  COMPUSA: www.compusa.com/ -- Everything a shopper would find in a Comp USA store, from books to computers. Customers can build a computer or look for a deal on existing systems.  DELL: www.dell.com -- All sorts of computers, from desktop to notebook, which can be built to customer specifications. There are also refurbished computers that come with the same guarantees as the new models, and peripherals and accessories.  GATEWAY: www.gateway.com/ -- The Gimbels to Dell's Macy's, Gateway offers similar products and services, including limited labor and parts replacement. Like Dell, it also has digital cameras and scanners.  Stores and Malls  HARRODS: www.harrods.com/ -- The British department store sells apparel, electronics and toys. And then there are the store's own blends of tea and tins of biscuits.  IMALL.COM: www.imall.com -- This shop-by-category site is made up of small merchants like the NY Sock Exchange, www.nysockexchange.com/, and the Power Marketing Group, www.imall.com/stores/ pmg/pmg.html, which sells "The Belle Figure Liposome Reducing System," an herbal product to help customers lose "excess fat."  MACY'S: www.macys.com/ -- The home page for the all-American department store features fashions, furnishings and fragrances.  FOOD CHUKAR CHERRY COMPANY: www.chukar.com/ -- Chukar sells trail mix, chocolates, preserves and sauces, but its signature product is fruit: three kinds of dried cherries, plus dried blueberries, cranberries and strawberries.  GREAT FOOD.COM: www.greatfood.com/ -- Foods, searchable from appetizers to vegetables. A shopper can also search by choosing the type of meal being planned, including cocktail party, romantic meal and tailgating.  MO HOTTA MO BETTA: www.mohotta.com/ -- Hot and spicy sauces of all kinds, from Mean Mama Jamma's Zombie Juice to Crazy Charley Bar-B-Cue Sauce, with a chart that ranks the fiery products.  PACIFIC COOKIE COMPANY: www.pacificcookie.com/ -- The classic cookies like chocolate chip, oatmeal and lemon drop, plus chocolate cherry pecan and "mint condition," a double chocolate cookie with green mint chips.  HOME FURNITURE.COM: www.furniture.com/ -- The furniture is sold like in a store, arranged by rooms. Consumers can use a search engine to choose styles, colors and a price range, everything but sit on the couch.  GARDEN.COM: www.garden.com/ -- The site offers 20,000 products, including seeds, bulbs, plants and trees, garden furniture, tools and books on garden design and getting started.  KITCHEN CLASSICS: www.kitchen-classics.com/ -- Cooks can fill a kitchen with products like pots and pans, knives, mixers, food processors, cookbooks, utensils, cutting boards and measuring cups, and, if they are in Phoenix, they can take some cooking classes.  S. TIMBERLAKE: www.stimberlake.com/ -- This Bethel, Maine, company, one of hundreds of small furniture companies online, offers reproduction Shaker tables, benches, chairs, tables and dressers.  Toys  ETOYS.COM: www.etoys.com/ -- Customers can search by age, brand name and categories like make believe, dolls, stuffed toys and radio control. There are sections featuring 50 favorite toys for each age group and finds from small toymakers.  SHOP HEAVEN.COM: www.shopheaven.com/ -- Shop Heaven sells various products, including toys, and it has a search feature that many aunts, uncles and grandparents will appreciate: the ability to search for gifts for teenagers.  TOYSMART.COM: www.toysmart.com/ -- Toysmart sells toys designed to promote learning and imagination, like Brio wooden train sets, rattles to encourage motor development and products from Go Fly a Kite. The site has articles and tips for parents, kids and teachers. Software -- BEYOND.COM: www.beyond.com -- Beyond.com, like other sites, sells software and computers, books and handheld items. The site is organized by category, with many software titles, articles and information, and a breakdown of software by publisher.  ZDNET: www.zdnet.com/ -- ZDNet is an all-purpose site, with reviews and information on shopping, Internet, computers and technology. The shopping section offers an outlet store, auction links, a holiday guide and lots of products.  Sports  FOGDOG: www.fogdog.com/ -- In addition to equipment for the usual sports, Fogdog offers products for cheerleading, fishing, motocross, diving and wrestling.  GEAR.COM: www.gear.com/ -- This store sells brand-name sporting gear from specialty companies, including Bolle, the North Face, Swiss Army, Fila, Wilson, Rossignol and Timberland.  SHOP SPORTS: www.shopsports.com/ -- In addition to sports clothing and gear, this store lets fans shop for team clothing and collectibles, videos and books, fitness equipment, software and vitamins. There is even a page to buy balls for almost every sport. title: In Bots We Trust? - Correction Appended
body: THE agents are ready for service. The question is, whom will they serve? For years, futurists have said that the World Wide Web will enable automated shopping robots, or bots, to instantly scan hundreds of merchants to help penny pinchers find the best goods at the lowest price. And there have been some comparison shopping services, but they have often been on small sites started as hobbies or technology demonstrations. Often users found searches that turned up either nothing or too many, often irrelevant items. But now, just in time for the holiday shopping frenzy, there is a new generation of bots to help shoppers sort through the expanding array of merchandise on the Web. The biggest services, like America Online and Yahoo, have them. And some of the little startups, like mySimon (www.mysimon.com) and DealTime (www.dealtime.com), have raised money and are upgrading their sites with more products and better searching technology. There are comparison services for special areas, like Cnet Shopper for computers (shopper.cnet.com/) and DealPilot for books and music (www.dealpilot.com/). And even Amazon.com (www.amazon .com), the giant of electronic commerce, has just introduced its "all product search" shopping agent, which will help people find out who carries items that Amazon does not stock. Many of these can help shoppers save time and money. But buyer beware: that shopping agent is probably a double agent, with loyalties to someone other than the consumer. The evidence: many of the sites, like mySimon and Cnet Shopper, have stopped automatically listing items with the lowest cost first. They put items from advertisers first unless the user requests otherwise. America Online and Disney's Go Network will not even list merchants that do not pay for exposure. And even services that loudly proclaim that their shopping listings are unbiased, like Frictionless Commerce on Lycos (www.frictionless.com/), still take payments from merchants for sending customers to their stores. The only bot that does not take money from merchants appears to be Amazon. But to no surprise, its search engine skips Barnesandnoble.com and other big competitors. The other shopping agent companies say they have no choice but to take money from the very merchants they are trying to compare. After all, shoppers show little interest in paying fees to see unbiased comparisons. "Our customer, in terms of who pays the bills, is the merchant," said Josh Goldman, chief executive of mySimon, one of the more popular shopping sites. "The technology is very cool that can bring product information and prices to consumers, but it's very threatening to merchants. They think comparison shopping is a threat to their brands and a threat to their profit margins." So Mr. Goldman changed the site so that merchants can pay to add their logos and information about their promotions and special services. Moreover, instead of listing products with the lowest price first, it gives priority to these paying merchants. At first, merchants tried to block the shopping bots. And even now, Ebay is blocking sites like AuctionWatch and Bidder's Edge, which want to compare its auctions with those of other auction sites. But most merchants now largely accept the comparison sites as another source of customers. Although Amazon, the best-known name, does not actively cooperate with other shopping agents, neither does it block them from searching its site. Buy.com (www.buy.com), a site devoted to selling computers, books and other goods at near break-even profit margins, got many of its initial customers through shopping bots. And even some merchants that are not the cheapest in the market are embracing the shopping agents, particularly those that de-emphasize price shopping. "We believe that the comparison services are a good thing," said Greg Drew, chief executive of 800.com (www.800.com), a site that sells consumer electronics. "But I work to make sure the C.E.O.'s of those sites understand that for complex products, like the ones we sell, there are other factors besides price, like service, after-purchase support and whether the merchant is an authorized dealer." The 800.com site has bought preferred placement on sites like mySimon and Bottomdollar.com. But online shopping analysts say that as customers begin to understand that many sites are now favoring advertisers, there may be a backlash. "If the search result is sorted by price, it doesn't leave any room for editorial misdeeds," said Ken Cassar, a shopping analyst with Jupiter Communications. "But as soon as they alter the sort order to one that is not relevant to the consumer, they raise questions of integrity. And in the long run, users will gravitate to the sites that are the least biased." Mr. Goldman says mySimon is providing a better service to consumers than most other agents, because it lists 1,800 merchants and most of them do not pay the company anything. "The fact that we list everyone in the world we can think of, whether they pay us or not, says we are the only bot that can claim to be unbiased," he said. "Does someone say the Yellow Pages is biased because one plumber has a quarter-page ad with a picture of their truck and their phone number in big type?" But in fact shopping bot users seem to respond to these promotions the way Yellow Pages users will often call the plumber with the big ad. For example, only 21 percent of the users of the Cnet Shopper site select the button that sorts listings by price, with the cheapest first. If they do not, advertisers who paid to have their logos displayed are listed first, followed by those that paid for bold listings. "I was shocked" by how few people sort by price, said Kevin McKenzie, the co-head of electronic commerce at Cnet. "But a lot of people will pick a branded listing even if it is way off the lowest price." Cnet hopes to get half its revenue from selling listings on the shopping site. Unlike mySimon, Cnet and many other sites will not even list merchants unless they agree to some sort of payment. This is actually a benefit for both consumers and merchants, argued Kevin D. Brown, the head of shopping strategy for Inktomi, a company that operates the shopping search for a variety of sites including Disney's Go Network, Time Warner's CNNfn and Merrill Lynch. "Consumers don't want 100 undifferentiated merchants," he said. "And we can say to companies that are nervous about comparison shopping that we are not overloading a category, so you have a good shot of getting to a consumer." America Online, which operates the busiest shopping mall on the Internet, just introduced a new service that lets users search and compare more than one million items. But all those items are sold by the 275 merchants who pay millions of dollars a year to be on its shopping channel. Patrick Gates, the head of AOL's shopping service, argues that customers will find all the goods they want. "It's the 80-20 rule," he said. "The brands we have online drive the majority of the business." But there are notable exceptions. Since Barnes & Noble is the exclusive bookseller on AOL, Amazon, the No. 1 Internet retailer, never shows up in AOL's product search. AOL's search does not give certain merchants priority over others. But neither does it give users the option to sort results by price. The only criteria for listing is the company's proprietary "relevance" ranking. "We are not hearing a lot of demand for price comparison from our customer base," Mr. Gates said. "People want to find the products they are looking for." Yahoo's shopping search also emphasizes those merchants who pay to be in the Yahoo Stores mall. But unlike AOL, which caters to the richest merchants, Yahoo Stores is mainly a way for mom-and-pop businesses to go online with relatively low cost. Thus a search on Yahoo Stores is likely to turn up unusual items at small vendors but will miss many of the largest online merchants. Unlike AOL, however, Yahoo offers a second search option. After a user looks at all the offerings of its stores, it will offer to search other nonpaying merchants on the Web. Even as the big portals get into the comparison shopping business, there is a generation of new services that purport to be the better bot, often by claiming to be more objective. One example is Frictionless Commerce, an offshoot of M.I.T. research, which lets users describe what they are looking for based on a number of criteria. So shoppers can say whether they want the cheapest price, the most liberal return policy or the strictest privacy policy. Search results will be ranked based on these factors and cannot be influenced by advertising. But if a merchant that it lists has an "affiliate program" that pays for referring customers, Frictionless will sign up and take the money. DealTime is a service that lets users camp out on the steps of merchants, waiting for prices to fall. Users enter what they want to buy and the price they want to pay, and DealTime will e-mail them as soon as it finds someone offering that price. Advertisers, however, are listed first on its site. Another new approach is shopping bots that hover in the background as a user surfs the Web. Once a user finds something, say, a book on Amazon, the bot will search other sites for better deals. These services are just being introduced by ClickTheButton (www.clickthebutton.com/) and by DealPilot, among others. Cheyenne Ehrlich, the founder of Click TheButton, says that he does not know yet how his year-old company will make money, but that it will probably try to earn some sort of commission for introducing buyers to sellers. But for now, the company does not exclude nonpaying merchants, and it will always list items with the cheapest first, he said. "People who use comparison services don't want to go through four screens to find the lowest price," Mr. Ehrlich said. "The people who say that price doesn't matter all have stock options and don't care how much they pay for things." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Circuits on Thursday about shopping robots that offer online price comparisons, referred incorrectly to Bottomdollar.com. Internet merchants can pay the company for advertisements on its site only; they cannot pay to have their products put at the top of lists of search results. Correction-Date: November 22, 1999, Monday Graphic   Illustration (Mary Ann Smith)(pg. C1)  Chart: "Home Shopping Net" Comparison shopping programs on the Web, often called shopping bots, offer a selection of prices for any given item. But, merchants often pay for listings, and the lowest price may not be listed first. Chart provides some examples of what the bots produce, but the products listed may not be available immediately. (pg. G25)

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
German CourtOverturns Pornography Ruling Against Compuserve - Correction Appended
body: Overturning a verdict that has horrified the Internet industry in Germany for the last two years, a Bavarian court ruled today that the former top executive of Compuserve's German subsidiary is not guilty of distributing pornography. The decision is a big victory for online services, which had viewed the case as a crucial legal test of their legal responsibility for material that customers might obtain from the Internet. Two years ago, a Munich court convicted the executive of Compuserve Deutschland, Felix Somm, of distributing pornography because customers could use Compuserve, a unit of America Online, to download child pornography from Internet sites in the unitedstates. Compuserve had argued that it was helpless and had tried to block German customers from a long list of pornographic sites. But a local court in Munich dismissed that defense, ruling that Compuserve could have done more. It sentenced Mr. Somm to two years of probation and fined him 100,000 marks, or about $180,000. A state court in Munich overturned that verdict. Invoking a new multimedia law passed shortly after Mr. Somm had been convicted, the court ruled that Mr. Somm could not have done much more than he did and could not be held responsible. Mr. Somm is "a slave of the parent company," said the court's chief judge, Laszlo Ember. Taking note that Mr. Somm had briefly tried to block access to a number of Internet sites, later giving up because the blockade proved unmanageable, Judge Ember said Mr. Somm had done all he could. Lawyers for Compuserve in Germany were ecstatic about today's ruling. "On the eve of the new millennium, the German judiciary has disposed of another explosive waste product," said Ulrich Sieber, a law professor who prepared much of Compuserve's defense. Besides exonerating Compuserve in Germany, he said, the decision eliminated a major source of legal uncertainty for the online industry across Germany. Though it came as a relief, legal experts said the decision was not entirely unexpected. At the time Mr. Somm was first convicted, in November 1997, the German Parliament had not yet passed a multimedia law that was intended to shield online services from liability for material that simply traveled over their networks. The issue is identical to one that has been at the center of heated political debate in the unitedstates: To what extent should a company that provides access to the Internet be held responsible for material that it does not own or control but which flows over its network? Germany has been more aggressive than almost any other Western nation in trying to police the Internet. The federal government maintains lists of illegal Web sites, some of which contain pornography and some of which support violent or neo-Nazi activities. Mr. Somm, who is Swiss, has since left Compuserve and now runs a small company of his own. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  Because of an editing error, an article in Business Day on Thursday about a German court ruling that overturned a former CompuServe executive's 1997 conviction for distributing pornography on the Internet misstated the dollar equivalent of the 100,000-mark fine he had paid. It was about $55,550, not $180,000. Correction-Date: November 20, 1999, Saturday

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
N.T.T. Plansto Cut 21,000 Jobs in Effort to Be More Nimble
body: Nippon Telegraph and Telephone, one of the world's largest phone companies, officially confirmed today that it planned to eliminate 21,000 jobs and sharply curtail investment over the next three years in an effort to enhance its competitiveness. The announcement had been expected; unions representing N.T.T. employees leaked word of the plans a month ago. Nonetheless, the cutback is a strong sign that measures undertaken by many Japanese businesses to become more efficient are pressuring even the most stalwart companies to change. N.T.T. was once the government-owned monopoly for domestic telephone services. Now, smaller competitors like DDI and Japan Telecom as well as foreign companies like Cable and Wireless and British Telecom are pressing N.T.T. to cut costs and change its ways. The company was recently forced to cut the price of a flat-rate Internet access service to roughly $75 a month at current exchange rates, almost half the price it had originally intended to charge. Others have plans to charge even less. SpeedNet, a joint venture of Tokyo Electric Power and Microsoft, is hoping to offer consumers a $48 monthly Internet access service, and Sony is moving to offer wireless Internet access service in big cities. N.T.T.'s job cuts will be done Japanese style, through attrition, hiring freezes and what is known as shukko, or pushing excess workers onto affiliates. N.T.T., which has 224,000 employees throughout its affiliates and subsidiaries, said it would send employees only to growing affiliates, like the NTT Mobile Communications Network and NTT Data. Junichiro Miyazu, the president of N.T.T., made it clear that the company had no intention of adopting Western-style tactics in job elimination. "Sales at NTT East and West are falling, but we will keep people there who we hired when we were making money from the telephone business," he said, referring to the two entities under the N.T.T. umbrella that provide local fixed-line service. The company's plans to cut capital spending by 900 billion yen, about $8.5 billion at current exchange rates, underscored the economy's heavy dependence on government spending. Last week, the government announced an $18 billion economic stimulus package, but if companies like N.T.T. continue to keep a lid on spending, it may have to come up with a similar size package sometime next year. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Need for Computer Experts Is Making Recruiters Frantic - Correction Appended
body: The managers at Vivid Studios, a Web site consulting firm here, are accustomed to calls from employment recruiters trying to poach their technical staff. But the day a suitor telephoned looking for Nevil was a new low. Vivid's receptionist assured the recruiter that it would be difficult to put Nevil on the line. And with good reason. Nevil is a black Labrador retriever. Thanks to the booming technology-based economy, companies' long-standing scramble for qualified technical workers has taken on an air of desperation lately. A severe shortage of engineers who design hardware and software and create Web pages has led companies and their recruiters to try all sorts of tricks, like the Nevil-seeking entrepreneur who called each name listed on Vivid Studio's Web site. Recruiters are known to send email to all the engineers at a company, offering to beat their existing salaries. At dawn, recruiters scour Internet job-placement services for the most recently posted resumes before a competitor makes contact. At restaurants, they pull business cards from fishbowls in which engineers had placed them hoping to get a free lunch -- not a job offer. "I was going to a funeral recently, and a friend said, 'Don't recruit,' " said Noelle Tardieu, a recruiter who works under contract for Silicon Valley companies. Weddings, however, are another matter. Ms. Tardieu says she reads the marriage announcements in the newspaper to find names and titles of prospective recruits. So it follows that the heavily courted engineers and other technology-trained employees are cashing in. Salaries in specific high-demand areas, like Web site programming and development, have gone up 18 to 20 percent the last year, said Eric Campbell, vice president for human relations at Docent Inc. of Mountain View, Calif., which makes software for corporate training. "We wind up six months after we hire an engineer having to fight off offers for that same engineer for more money," he said. "It's become a very predatory environment." One big change in recent years is the extent to which stock options have become part of the package. Fifty percent of junior technical employees now have stock options, up from 35 percent three years ago. To seal deals, recruiters offer candidates overseas airline tickets, increase vacation time to four or five weeks from the usual two weeks for starting employees or toss in 11th-hour signing bonuses that can range from $5,000 to $20,000. Other perquisites now seem commonplace: employees can redesign offices or cubicles, bring pets to work, work at home and dress casually -- even at interviews. Longtime recruiters and compensation experts say the scramble for talent is the most intense they have ever experienced. "It's a free-agent market and the folks out there know it," said Mark Edwards, president of iQuantic, a compensation consulting firm in San Francisco. "I haven't ever seen companies be more flexible in how they attract and retain folks." The fervent demand for technology employees often funnels down to the recruiters, where it comes out in a spigot of offers, cajoling, creativity, relationship building and, occasionally, ambulance chasing. Indeed, when the rare layoffs do occur at a company involved in a merger or experiencing a downturn, recruiters wait in the parking lot to scoop up the discards. "I bag 'em and tag 'em," said Sandra C. Chroman, a recruiter in Silicon Valley, adding that recruiters fight over junior techs in the parking lot. "I joke that I keep engineers bound and gagged in my trunk and just drive around the high-tech companies and drop them off on the lawn," she said. If only it were that easy. Ms. Chroman said she had heard all the tricks of the trade and used a few of them herself. One tactic, she said, is to walk into high-technology companies, make friends with the receptionist through small talk, explain she wants to send everyone in the company a mailer and then walk out with a company phone list. "Receptionists will give you people's home phone numbers," Ms. Chroman said. "It's amazing what some people will give you." But lately Ms. Chroman, like many other recruiters, is looking outside Northern California for talent, notably at companies and universities in Canada and Mexico, where engineering candidates are not in as much demand as they are here. In addition, thanks to the North American Free Trade Agreement, their citizens are not required to obtain visas. Another place often visited by recruiters is cyberspace. Comfortable with technology, engineers looking for better offers post their resumes on a growing number of Internet job services, like monster.com, where recruiters in turn look for the latest talent that may be willing to switch employers. "I check it every morning at 6," said Mara Flores, a contract recruiter for Fujitsu Software, who said she also used a program called a Web crawler to search the Internet for newly posted resumes from engineers. But if demand for engineers has been tough on companies, it has been good for the recruiting business. Well over 1,000 recruiters operate in Silicon Valley, Ms. Tardieu estimated, a number that includes freelance recruiters, recruiters who work for agencies and contractors who sign on with specific companies. Ms. Flores said it was not uncommon for an aggressive recruiter, even with only a few years experience, to earn $100,000 to $200,000 a year. The leeway given to recruiters by their client companies varies. Some companies conduct the financial discussions themselves; in other cases, they provide some flexibility, or recruiters insist upon it -- in working out signing bonuses, for instance. And despite some seeming cutthroat tactics, the recruiters appear to treat one another cordially, even with a sense of brotherhood. There are few stories of back stabbing. Recruiters say they rarely hear of competitors disparaging one another or using dirty tricks to steal a candidate. More often, the battle simply comes down to who can best marry a willing candidate with a job opening and enticing benefit package. The phenomenon is not confined to Silicon Valley, with at least 350,000 openings nationwide for programmers, systems analysts and computer scientists and engineers, according to a 1998 study by Virginia Tech and the Information Technology Association of America, a trade group. Today, the association reports, one of every 10 information technology jobs remains unfilled. "We have the same trouble in Boston, newyork, Dallas and Chicago," said Mr. Campbell of Docent. At a recent job fair in Mountain View, in the heart of Silicon Valley, Hewlett-Packard said it had hundreds of jobs available in the Bay Area and thousands worldwide. The story echoed at booth after booth of prospective employers; easels and binders full of jobs, from administrative assistant to patent lawyer, but mostly engineers. A sign at the booth of Kaiser Electronics, a military contractor, sought to lure candidates with the promise of "Every Other Friday Off." For the candidates, the experience can be both flattering and overwhelming. Samir A. Batla, 29, worked as an engineer at Ernst & Young in San Francisco until he decided four months ago that he wanted a new job. He posted his resume on monster.com and within days had heard from 11 recruiters. Various sales pitches ensued, and the price tag escalated. Mr. Batla expected to earn $70,000 to $80,000, but he found his sticker price soon soared to $85,000 to $100,000. He said he was offered stock option packages that could have made him a millionaire if the company went public and its stock continued to climb. The recruiters sought to sell him on intangibles, too. Some tried to sell him on the value of working at a smaller company, others at a larger, more established office. They talked to him about the culture of the prospective workplace, and this turned out to be an important hook for Mr. Batla, who said money was only one criterion. Another was attire. "I decided I wouldn't work at any company if I had to dress up for the interview," Mr. Batla said. Ultimately, he settled on Vivid Studios, the Web design company. "To the interview, I wore blue jeans and a collared shirt -- what do you call those, polo shirts?" he said. The people interviewing him, he said, "were wearing shorts, T-shirts and sandals -- I felt overdressed." He took the job with the title of senior engineer. Vivid Studios, onetime home of Nevil, the Labrador retriever, also knows what it is like to lose employees. The dog's owner, Dan Lederer, 40, quit Vivid recently to pursue a quieter life with his family in Plainfield, Mass., population 550. Mr. Lederer, a Web site designer who said he was hounded by recruiters while working at Vivid, is now freelancing and says he seems to have found a recruiter-free zone in the Berkshires. "If you don't want to be called, it's nice to be out here," he said. Still, Mr. Lederer said he would not mind hearing from a recruiter who could offer him a job with money, benefits and one other perquisite: permission to work remotely from his home on 13 secluded acres. "With the pay and the whole scenario working out, yeah, sure," he would entertain offers, he said. These days, it might not seem so much to demand; he and Nevil may be getting more offers than they can handle. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  Because of an editing error, a front-page article on Thursday about the recruiting frenzy for technical talent in Silicon Valley referred imprecisely to the immigration status of Canadian and Mexican workers. Visas are indeed required, though under the North American Free Trade Agreement, provisions are less restrictive for Canadians and Mexicans in some jobs than for other foreign workers. Correction-Date: November 22, 1999, Monday

title: Niche Sites Offer Chance to Create or Personalize Gifts
body: ONLINE shopping may be a good way to avoid the shopping-mall parking lot, but it does not guarantee that you will avoid the homogeneity of the shopping-mall experience. In fact, the likelihood that you will give or receive The Gap's latest V-neck sweater style (boiled lamb's wool with a ribbed trim at the cuffs) is sure to increase this year, as online shoppers from even the most remote places click on trusted brands. But although Web portals channel shoppers to the same high-profile stores, the Web itself offers an antidote to the herd mentality. Tiny, family-run stores abound -- many of which suggest gifts that you would never find at J. C. Penney or the retail shops that surround it. Online niche shops allow you to buy monthly deliveries of caviar for your friends, for example. There is at least one shop where you can order aerial photographs of your grandparents' favorite national park. The Internet also makes it easy to personalize gifts. Fill in a Web form about your child to order a custom-printed book or a song sung in your child's honor. Pick your favorite tunes from an online database and have them put on a custom CD. If you know what you are looking for, you can find these shops by plugging key words into search engines. If you are starved for ideas, here are some sites to try: PERSONALIZED CHILDREN'S BOOKS www.booksforme.com/ w3ent.com/abcpersonalized.htm www.kidcartoons.com/ BooksForMe creates books with heroes whose names are the same as those of the children who are reading the stories. To order, parents must fill out a form, entering the child's name, age, birthdate, town and other details related to the story.
