"My Space Adventure," one title, will put your child in command of a backyard spaceship on its way to the planet Love. BooksForMe will also insert your child as a character in more traditional books like "Bambi" and "Mother Goose." Each book costs $12.95. Like BooksForMe, ABC Storybooks obtains its books from a single publisher, Create-a-Book, in Gulf Breeze, Fla., and acts as distributor. ABC Storybooks' custom books feature holiday themes, including Christmas and Kwanzaa. Some, like "The Magic Little Christmas Tree," are pop-ups to boot (though these are personalized with stickers inserted on each page instead of integrated text). Prices run from $12.95 to $19.95 each. KidCartoons takes the custom concept to another level. The artists at KidCartoons will create comic-book covers, comic books and cartoon videos based on a child's photograph. The site is operated by K Design, a computer graphics company in Brentwood, N.Y. Prices are $9.95 for the comic-book covers, $14.95 for the comic books and $19.95 for the cartoon video.  PERSONALIZED CHILDREN'S SONGS www.kidtraxsongs.com/ www.cakencandle.com/ If print is not enough, several companies will put a child's name into song. At the Kid Trax Creations site parents can order a 17-minute tape containing five songs that mention their child's name more than 30 times. A cassette and song-book set costs $12.95. At the site for Cake and Candle Cassettes parents may order a personalized lullaby, a birthday song or Christmas carols that mention the child's name 18 times. The tapes cost $8.50 each.  PERSONALIZED SONGS FOR ADULTS www.giftsongs.com/ www.psycholaborations.com/ www.giftsongs.com/ P.S. I Love You, the Personalized Song Company, creates professionally recorded CD's or cassettes of custom songs. The company's president, Mark Baker, has composed tunes for the Temptations and other groups. Now he will write a song for you or your loved ones. Cassette tapes cost $39.95 each; CD's cost $49.95 each. For something heavier in a personalized song, consider a "Psycholaboration" with Pat DiNizio, lead singer for the pop-rock band the Smithereens. Mr. DiNizio will turn lyrics into personalized songs. Enter your own lyrics, prose or poetry into the order form on his Web site; choose a type of music -- rock, folk, disco -- and the format -- cassette, CD, MP3. The result costs $350.  OTHER CUSTOM GIFT IDEAS www.wrappedup.com/ Looking for an alternative to Christmas cards? Wrapped Up, an online retailer in Bay Minette, Ala., will wrap chocolate bars with a label of your choice. Select clip art from the Web site or request a custom graphic for an additional $25. Chocolate choices include Hershey bars, Mr. Goodbar and small KitKats, most of which cost $1.35 each with the custom wrappings. Not responsible for melted arrivals.  www.edier.com/special/occasion /multimedia.htm Some day, traditional photograph albums -- full of static snapshots and devoid of sound and video -- will seem awfully dull. A small company called Edier Developer produces multimedia CD-ROM's of events in a person's life, based on videotapes, audio recordings and still photographs that are sent to the company's studio. (In most cases, music used for the CD-ROM's has to come from Edier's own collection so that the company steers clear of copyright violations and royalty payments.) Edier Chiong, the founder, said that he decided to make a business of personalizing CD-ROM's after Hurricane Andrew swept through Miami, where Edier Developer is based, in 1993. "It wiped out most of the pictures we had," Mr. Chiong said. But if they had been saved on a CD-ROM, he said, "We wouldn't have lost those pictures."  www.tide-in-stitches.com/ If you know grandparents who like to brag about their grandchildren, they just might like a sweatshirt embroidered with the children's names. Ruth Andrick has been doing personalized embroidery for more than 12 years from various addresses and recently opened an online shop. The sweatshirts for grandparents are her best sellers. "I wish I had kept track of every single kid's name I have put on these shirts," Ms. Andrick said. "It's got to be in the millions." That includes names of children born years after a sweatshirt was made. "I'm constantly adding names on ones I've done before," she added. Adult-size sweatshirts with up to three names cost $30 each; each additional name costs $3.  www.unique-sports.com/ Your sports-obsessed friends cannot be true fans if they don't have a helmet lamp -- that is, a table lamp, complete with shade, that extends from a real football or baseball helmet base. You can order them for your friends, featuring their favorite team's logo, from this site. Baseball lamps cost $150; football, $165. Other gifts include the Good Sport Snack Machine (a gumball machine adorned with plastic props apropos of your favorite sporting event) and framed photographs of professional scoreboards that have been altered using photography software to digitally show a person's name in lights.  www.musicmaker.com/ College students might have the time to sit around hitting Record and Pause buttons as they create custom cassette tapes for their friends, but most other people don't. MusicMaker.com offers a much faster alternative on line for CD's. The site provides a database of more than 200,000 tracks from more than 100 music labels. And it does so legally, by paying royalties to the artists whose works are selected. MusicMaker offers suggestions of song combinations as well, like "Space Age Spectaculars" for the "Star Trek" set, which includes soundtracks from movies like "Star Wars," "The X-Files" and "2001: A Space Odyssey."  terraserver.microsoft.com/ How about something special for your security-minded friends: an aerial photograph of their house, captured by American or Russian satellites. If they live in a big house, in a city or suburban area, there is a chance that such a photograph exists. You can search for it using the TerraServer, a site that offers a database of aerial and satellite photographs from the unitedstates Geological Survey and SPIN-2, a Russian-American satellite venture. Before beginning your search, however, you may need to know the latitude and longitude of your friends' homes. The TerraServer suggests going first to MapBlast .com, which provides that data after you enter a street address. The TerraServer is also a source of aerial shots of famous geological sites, like Niagara Falls. Prints of the photographs range from $7.95 to $24.95. TerraServer's newest product is a CD-ROM of satellite photographs of Area 51, the military zone in Nevada that has been the subject of conspiracy theories and supposed alien sightings.  silver.chartshop.com members.aol.com/Ipredict7/ Astrologers and psychics are attuned to e-commerce. IVillage.com's astrology expert, Kelli Fox, suggests buying an in-depth destiny report (or a family, love or career report) for yourself or as a gift at Chartshop.com. One offering is the Love Potential Profile, which includes a compatibility report and a monthlong romantic forecast. Joyce Luciano, who is described on her Web site as "a professional psychic with 38 years of experience," gives private readings in an AOL chat room. To encourage newcomers, she has cut her prices to $35 for a half-hour for first-timers.  GIFTS THAT KEEP COMING www.of-the-month.com/ www.greatclubs.com/ www.cigarmonthclub.com/ www.beermonthclub.com/ www.chocolateofthemonth.com/ Judging by their number, gift clubs for fine-food lovers and "of the month" clubs appear to be thriving online, and most offer gift memberships. Of-the-month.com sells deliveries of cheese or cheesecake, coffee or caviar, soap or seashells and many other items. Other sites cater to popular sins, like beer and cigars. Chocolate is one of the most common offerings. What better way to kick off your friend's New Year's resolution than to send two pounds of toffee?  www.enews.com www.magmall.com/ Magazine subscriptions have always been the gift of choice for those who would rather avoid shopping, gift-wrapping and standing in line at the post office. Now you can order gift subscriptions online instead of waiting for an annoying subscription card to fall out of the next magazine you open. Enews.com sells subscriptions to more than 850 titles and features a page called the Magazine Matcher, which suggests magazines for animal lovers, military buffs, computer fans and more. MagMall.com offers 900 titles and enables users to search for gift subscriptions by price range.  BEYOND GIFTS  ww.cardsupply.com/ www.preciousyou.com/ www.americangreetings.com/ www.photoloft.com/ www.amazingmail.com/ If the thought of picking out and addressing holiday cards is already bringing out your inner Grinch, you'll be pleased to hear that the Internet can make the task easier, without necessarily making it less personal. If you order cards from CardSupply.com, you can click through categories like "interfaith" or "snowflake, stars" to narrow your search for boxes of cards to be delivered to your home. You can also order custom envelopes with your return address. The Precious You site specializes in holiday cards with pockets or corner mounts for attaching family photographs. American Greetings offers a slightly less personal option: pick out a card, type in a greeting and the company will mail it. PhotoLoft.com lets you upload a digital photo, then select a greeting-card style and type in a message and your recipient's postal address. To save more time, you can also upload your address book to the site. PhotoLoft will create the photo-finished cards and mail them via second-day air, saving you that visit to the post office. Or you can send them free by e-mail. Prices for the snail-mail service start at $1.22 a card, featuring designs for Christmas, Hanukkah, Kwanzaa and other major holidays throughout the year. If you don't mind a postcard format, a slightly less expensive alternative is offered through Amazingmail.com. For 99 cents a card (or less if you buy in bulk), the site will send a postcard via the postal service with your own photo (or one of theirs) on one side and a personal message on the other. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (David Suter)

title:
ONLINE SHOPPER;
It's Beginning to Look a Lot Like Panic
body: THIS was how my holiday shopping began this year: As we were driving home the other day, my 8-year-old middle daughter leaned forward into our car's front seat airspace, brushed her bangs from her eyes for the 10th time that hour and said: "Dad, you're Jewish, and so are Zoe and Clementine and me. We celebrate Hanukkah. So why do we get presents on Christmas, too?" My husband said, "Because your mother grew up with Christmas, and she loves it." To which Ella replied wearily: "Dad, how many times have I told you? You should have stopped to think, before you married her, about how confusing this was going to be for us kids." Truthfully, Ella, sorting out which holidays to celebrate can be very confusing even for the adults in our family. The uncertainty manifests itself in our annual holiday shopping system, which I would describe in general terms as a belligerent refusal to confront either an impending holiday or the need to shop for it until, say, the day before. This is followed by a frazzled dash to an overcrowded mall where we buy the children gifts for both Hanukkah and Christmas, although spoiling them only results, apparently, in even more cheekiness. That is why I vowed to change this year by doing all my holiday shopping early and online. But holiday shopping does not migrate to the computer screen so easily. The British anthropologist Daniel Miller has theorized, after all, that shopping for those closest to you is an intimate way to define your relationship to them. Holiday shopping, therefore, is fraught with far more painful emotional overtones than buying groceries or toothpaste. "What people are really obsessed by are a few close personal relations, with partners, children and so forth," he told me recently. "The consequence of the physical act of shopping for those people is that you confront and define your relationships to them." Exactly what I hoped to avoid. I wanted to bypass the sensations of touching, of smelling, of wondering if a certain fuzzy grayish blue sweater the exact color as Ella's eyes would be a more appropriate gift for Hanukkah or for Christmas, then wondering darkly if my decision would be symbolic of an unconscious ambivalence toward -- oh, let's not get into it here. Instead, let's just say I was looking forward to a comparatively clinical approach. Online, I could point, click, enter some emotionally neutral information about the expiration date of my credit card. By changing the rules of the ritual, I hoped to transform the fundamental nature of the shopping experience itself. Here is what happened: I BOUGHT NO CHRISTMAS TREE ORNAMENTS Why is this significant? Because I always buy Christmas tree ornaments. In other words, the kinds of things I bought online were different. If I were wandering through real stores redolent with holiday smells of candles and potpourri and the subtle pressure of carols piped into the sound system, I would have made holiday-related impulse purchases. Instead, I bought safe things that I didn't need to see or to touch to appreciate, like books and board games that I played with as a child. Later, I found out that this pattern of buying is typical. "You're a living example of my research, I must say," said Eugene Fram, a professor of marketing at the Rochester Institute of Technology in upstate newyork, who has conducted two studies of online shoppers' habits in the last five years. "You're in cyberspace, and cyberspace is cold. So online shoppers buy safe products, those without risk of color, fabric, style, complexity. A book is a book is a book." Of course, safe does not have to mean boring. I bought bottles of invisible ink, a set of pens to tint black-and-white photographs and a cardboard playhouse with walls you can color, all from Flax Art and Design (www.flaxart.com), a San Francisco art supply store that I would not have stumbled into except online. I STARTED SHOPPING EARLIER THAN EVER And instead of a single shopping marathon, I shopped a little bit each day. It was so easy to do without leaving my desk. Even so, I still couldn't beat the crowds. For instance, when I visited www.mujionline.com, a Web site that was set up to attract overseas holiday shoppers to the Japan-based Muji department store, two of the three items I wanted were sold out -- in early November. only when I tried to add them to my shopping basket do I learn they were unavailable. At www.toysRus.com, the crowds were so thick one recent afternoon that it took me an hour to get onto the site's Big Book page, where the company is offering first-time buyers $10 off purchases of $25 or more through Nov. 20. Once there, I found problems. The price on one item, a Play-Doh Super Value set, did not match the price in a print catalog that I received in themail a few days earlier. So I didn't buy it. Also, the site was so sluggish that it took me 13 minutes to successfully place two items into a shopping basket, and then it took an additional 17 minutes to complete the order. This could be because, as a company spokeswoman explained to me later, 62 million people received the same catalog that I did, causing the site's traffic to increase 1,000 percent in a single week. Good for Toys "R" Us sales? Maybe. But very annoying for me. Even more ominous, online shortages and traffic jams are expected to get worse. "Shop early, because I think there will be some major problems with fulfillment of orders; a lot of these virtual retailers and distributors will not be able to handle the movement of goods in a timely fashion," said Jack Gifford, a professor of marketing at Miami University in Oxford, Ohio. "I just bought two pieces of software online from Microsoft -- who should be good at this -- and there's a 40-day wait. I probably could walk into a real store and get it today. "Some online businesses are starting with a storefront, but don't have the fully integrated back-room systems that real stores would. They're madly building warehouses to try to catch up. But that takes time." So, as the holidays loom closer, follow the advice of Nick Karris, a senior analyst at Gomez Advisors, which publishes reviews of online merchants at www.gomez.com. "Ask yourself, is this a credible site?" Mr. Karris said. "How long has it been in business? And ask yourself, do they have a clear policy on how they are going to support me if I have to return something or if I have a question?" I SAVED MONEY Comparison shopping was so much easier to do online, where I could check out a dozen or more merchants' prices in a half-hour. And I found that the selection was much better. For instance, when I went hunting for Playmobil dollhouse furniture, I learned that I could beat the price advertised at www.etoys.com by $5 by bidding on the same item at www.ebay.com. Of course, the Ebay item was not new from a store. But it did arrive in a never-opened box that looked just like new. And I saved in other ways. While shopping for books to ship to five nieces and nephews, I found that the prices were virtually identical at www.amazon.com and at the www .barnesandnoble.com site. Since Barnesandnoble.com was offering free shipping the second week in November (an incentive for early shoppers that may not be repeated this holiday season, a spokesman said), I did my research on Amazon, where its software knows my preferences, then placed the order with Barnesandnoble.com. My savings: $7.75. A few days later, however, follow-up email from Barnesandnoble.com listed shipping charges. I called the site's toll-free number; a polite customer service representative apologized for what he described as a system error and credited my account. I BEGAN TO CRAVE HUMAN CONTACT Well, what I really missed was advice from helpful sales clerks. So I went to www.thegift.com, which has a Gift Finder assistant to help shoppers make selections. The site's chief executive, Jeff Swearingen, had told me in a phone interview that after I entered information about the recipient, the tool would search through a database of about 500 gifts to come up with a list of 30 that would be appropriate. So I told the Gift Finder the recipient of the gift (my husband), his age (over 20) and how much I wanted to spend (any amount). That last answer was a lie, of course, but to put a price on love (one of the other options was "$20 or less") seemed a little cold, even for me. Then I got hung up describing the recipient's personality traits; none of the eight choices, ranging from "homebody" to "dainty and demure," conjured a mental image of my husband. I settled for "career-minded," but the recommended gifts all sounded too impersonal, so I gave up. I mean, what would your husband say if you handed him a three-pound tin of jumbo cashews ($28) and called it a gift? The problem here, and at a number of other sites that steered me toward merchandise sold by their merchandising partners, was that the selection was too limited. It made no sense, to me, to retreat to the restrictive setting of Internet shopping malls that showcased a limited number of retailers, like www.bocado .com and www.foofoo.com. I BOUGHT JUST AS MUCH FOR MYSELF AS USUAL Maybe more, come to think of it, because more of the things I wanted were available online than, say, if I had been standing in the science-kits aisle of a local toy store. Online, I bought a wooden artists' mannequin and a political poster from the Cultural Revolution that depicts cheery Chinese farmers walking home from work. So far. I have completed about half of my holiday shopping online. While the experience has been, for the most part, pleasant -- I'm convinced that I am living in the golden age of shopping -- it has not changed the fundamental nature of the shopping experience. No, Ella, it did not miraculously make everyone in our family Jewish. It didn't even give us all the same last name. Nor did it help me decide which holiday would be more appropriate for someone to receive a heather-gray V-neck sweater from www.delias.com (free shipping on orders of more than $40). When I reported my conclusions to Professor Miller at University College London, he said that maybe I had expected too much. "I've just finished a new book about the use of the Internet," he said, "and I found that it makes far less difference than people seem to expect. When the telephone first came out, we thought it would change basic relationships. Instead, it's just a tool." At least the tool made it easier to buy two sweaters. http://www.nytimes.com

title: So Easy to Buy, Such a Struggle to Return
body: WHILE hauling merchandise back to the store after the holidays is an inconvenience, digging up receipts, finding addresses and boxing up items to ship back to an Internet retailer thousands of miles away can be an off-the-charts hassle, so much so that many shoppers simply do not return items they bought online. "It usually takes me a couple of months before I get around to sending it back, and after a while, it becomes too late," said Ruth Hereford of Las Vegas, who shops regularly at NetMarket, CDNow and Amazon. "For something that costs $20, it's just not worth packing it up, putting some note in it and going to the post office." What's in store for Web gift-givers and recipients after all the wrapping paper's been stuffed into recycling bags? Most reputable online retailers give a consumer 30 days to return a product for a refund, a store credit or an exchange, but the similarities in their "100 percent satisfaction guarantee" return policies often end there. Although Amazon.com, for example, will grant a full refund, minus the cost of shipping and handling, other online purveyors of CD's, software and consumer electronics will penalize shoppers for opening packages or for not returning items right away. Insight (www.insight.com) and Egghead (www.egghead.com) are two of many retailers that charge restocking fees of 15 to 20 percent on the price of an item, including taxes. Both Insight and Egghead will levy the fee if the product is not returned within 15 days. Unless the merchant has sent the wrong item, shipping charges for returned items are always the consumer's responsibility. If the buyer has documentation showing that something was sent by mistake, most retailers will cover the cost of shipping it back. For that reason, it is important to keep a printed confirmation of the order form that the retailer sends via email and to pass it along to the recipient of the gift. Debra Martinez, chairwoman of the newyork State Consumer Protection Board, advises against purchasing any insurance offered toward the safe delivery of a product. "If it breaks on the way over, it's their responsibility," she said. If the product does arrive damaged, and it was purchased with a credit card, Ms. Martinez said, a consumer may have recourse through the credit card company. People who buy and return new PC's and other computer equipment will confront a hurdle in the return process known as the Return Merchandise Authorization number. In most cases, a consumer must call the customer service number listed in the packing materials or on the company's Web site to get an authorization number and attach it to the returned item before sending it back. Consumers must get a Return Merchandise Authorization number before the manufacturer's deadline, which can range from 15 to 90 days from when the product was received. The authorization number helps ensure that a merchant is not being sent merchandise bought elsewhere. "Especially in the consumer electronics industry, merchants have to be careful that people are returning what they say they bought," said Richard Chin, a spokesman for Amazon, which now sells computer-related equipment. "It also allows customer service to understand why it's being sent back." If a product is defective when it arrives or breaks during use, some electronics companies will offer the customer a refurbished replacement unit. Palm Computing, for example, gives each customer an option: After mailing back a P.D.A., the customer can wait up to several weeks for repairs or can accept a refurbished device as a permanent replacement. Regardless of how necessary return authorization numbers are, getting them can be challenging. Some companies make their customer service numbers difficult to locate on their Web sites or, worse, require the buyer to write a letter to customer service to get a Return Merchandise Authorization number. The good news for Internet shoppers is that many online clothing and home-furnishings retailers also operate brick-and-mortar storefronts. Banana Republic, Gap, Eddie Bauer and Barnes & Noble will permit customers to return items they bought online at actual retail stores. But for those who must ship items for a refund or exchange, the two most viable delivery options are through United Parcel Service and the Postal Service. If the item is sent via U.P.S., the merchant will often enclose a return label that can be attached to the box. The U.P.S. Web site (www.ups.com) is equipped to calculate return charges based on package weights and geographic distances, and shipping tags can be bought with a credit card and printed out. Although the Postal Service has started an electronic merchandise return service called Returns@ease that allows customers to pay for and print out merchant return labels, only Altrec.com, an outdoor clothing and equipment retailer, has signed on to use the system. Neither U.P.S. nor the Postal Service Web options provide an easy solution for those who need to return merchandise in large packages from their homes. U.P.S. charges about $10 for each pickup; shipping is an additional charge. Express couriers like Federal Express and Airborne Express will make pickups, but they can charge much more than $50 for pickup and shipping, depending on the shipment's size and weight. And although a Postal Service letter carrier will accept packages for sending out, "within reason," said Robert Anderson, a spokesman for the Postal Service, a more likely situation is that shoppers will draw on their dwindling reserves of holiday cheer and head to post offices themselves. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Niculae Asciu)

title:
STATE OF THE ART;
How Fast, How Much
body: AFTER nearly a quarter-century of intense research by many of the greatest technical and marketing minds on the planet, personal computers still force the average consumer to decipher an eyeball-glazing catalog of technical mumbo-jumbo like this, from a recent newspaper advertisement: "ATX w/300 Watt PS, 48x CD Rom, 9.1 GIG LVD U2W 2MB Buffer, 128MB PC100 ECC RAM, Intel PIII 500 w/Fan, 8 MEG ATI Xpert 98 AGP, 3Com 905TX 10/100 NIC. . . . " No wonder the Apple iMac has been such a popular computer. Until recently, the most daunting task for iMac buyers has been choosing a color: Blueberry? Grape? Tangerine? Some day, probably early in the next millennium, most computers will be as easy to buy as the iMac. The recent emergence of so-called information appliances, Web pads, smart phones and new-generation PC's is encouraging. There will always be people whose socks roll up and down in excitement when they see a list of technical specifications for a new PC, just as there are those who care passionately about the cubic inches, cylinders and horsepower of an automobile engine, or the combined slugging percentage and on-base average for baseball players. For many people, especially professionals, the megahertz and megabytes are worthy of intense scrutiny. For the rest of us the goal is merely to get the best deal on a personal computer that will meet our computing and communications needs, and budget, for a few years before it becomes obsolete. To make that choice easier, I offer a guide to buying a personal computer. Keep in mind that almost any personal computer sold now has more than enough power to handle tasks like word processing, email, keeping a calendar, managing a contact file, balancing the finances, playing games, running educational software and so on. But the real value of a PC is not as a calculating engine but as a communications device. Sending and receiving email has become the most commonly cited task for personal computers, followed closely by doing research on the Internet. An Internet connection harnesses the resources of millions of computers worldwide and transforms an ordinary desktop PC into the most powerful and versatile knowledge machine available to the average person. Increasingly, even traditional disc-based computer applications like educational software and games are being enhanced by online links to the Internet. So no matter what computer you choose, get a modem. To oversimplify it, a modem is the telephone that a computer uses to call the Internet over regular phone lines. Specifically, get a 56K modem, often called a V.90 modem. Better still, for those who plan to spend a lot of time online and who have access to a high-speed cable or digital subscriber line (D.S.L.) Internet service, get an Ethernet card. Cable and D.S.L. are the two leading options for connecting to the Internet at speeds many times faster than a 56K modem. Such services require something known as a Network Interface Card, or N.I.C. An Ethernet card fits the bill. Macintoshes come with Ethernet cards.  BRAND NAME -- The differences in actual components used by the major manufacturers are minimal. Any decent byte mechanic can screw together off-the-shelf components to make a PC that works just as well as one assembled by a multinational corporation. The real issue is how well the PC maker deals with you before, during and after the sale. Experienced PC users who need no hand-holding can find good deals from clone shops. For beginners, I recommend staying with one of the big companies, even if it costs a bit more. In the most recent PC Magazine survey of service, reliability and support, only I.B.M., Dell and a smaller vendor, Quantex, earned Readers Choice "A" ratings for desktop computers. I.B.M. and Sony topped the list for notebook computers.  WINDOWS VERSUS MACINTOSH -- The choice between these operating systems is almost religious in nature. Mac users are in the minority but believe that they are a click closer to heaven. Windows could be described as a digital code version of a Hieronymous Bosch painting, but it has a monopoly on PC sales, or so the judge says. Both systems are more complicated and unstable than they ought to be. Once you get online, it matters less and less. And now for the more specific stuff.  MICROPROCESSOR -- There are no practical, functional differences between the market-leading Intel and Advanced Micro Devices chips, or the less common Cyrix chip, for that matter. Intel makes two flavors, the basic Celeron, which is a good value for home PC's, and the advanced Pentium III, which is favored for games, multimedia and more demanding professional applications. The Advanced Micro Athlon chip is an impressive performer and represents the most serious challenge to Intel's hegemony. Do not buy anything slower than 350 megahertz unless you plan to replace the PC soon. Do not buy anything faster than 600 MHz unless you are spending someone else's money or are seriously into video and playing games.  MEMORY -- RAM, or random access memory, is system memory. When people ask how much memory your computer has, RAM is what they usually want to know. Typically measured in megabytes, RAM is like your own memory: It works great when you are awake (the power is on), but evaporates when you go to sleep (the computer is shut down). More RAM is better, because it means the processor does not have to run to the filing cabinets so often, which slows things down. So if you can afford it, pile it on. If the budget is tight, it is better to upgrade the RAM and downgrade the processor. Do not buy less than 64 megabytes of RAM. Get 96MB if you can, or 128MB if you have used the word "multimedia" in a sentence more than once this week. Another important kind of memory is called Level 2 (L2) cache, which mainlines data to the processor at high speed and improves system performance. The important thing is that there be an L2 cache. The amount, usually measured in kilobytes (for example, 512KB), falls under the more-is-better rule, but any is better than none. Video or graphics memory is another type. Make sure your system has at least 4MB of this kind, or, if games and multimedia are important, 8MB. Some larger monitors need more than basic video memory.  STORAGE -- If you are like me, it is imperative to write things down lest they be forgotten. That is where storage comes in. Most personal computers come with a hard disk drive, whose capacity these days is typically measured in gigabytes (GB). Do not get less than 6 GB. If you plan to save a lot of digital photographs or MP3 music files, or are a compulsive pack rat, go for 10 GB or more. Almost all computers today come with a CD-ROM drive. Some PC makers tout their CD-ROM speed, like 40X or 48X, but in general anything over about 20X is superfluous. If you can afford it, consider replacing the CD-ROM drive with a DVD drive. It does everything a CD-ROM drive does, including playing CD audio discs, but it also transforms the PC into a DVD movie player. Hard disks fail, although not as often as they used to. Inevitably, they fail when you forget to make a backup of your data files. Backing up your files is the computer equivalent of brushing and flossing your teeth, only more important. Floppy disks are fine for backing up a handful of important files, but now that hard disks are measured in gigabytes, it would take a bushel of 1.44MB floppies, and hours of time, to make a dent in one's backup duties. Instead, get a Zip drive, which stores 100 MB on a relatively cheap, removable disk. Zip drives get the job done. For more fun, however, get a CD-RW recordable drive. But I'm running out of space, so that will be discussed in a future column.  MONITOR -- The new standard is 17 inches. Once you have opened a bunch of World Wide Web pages, you will understand why anything smaller is a pain. If desk space is tight, or if budgets are loose, consider a new flat-panel monitors. A 15-inch flat panel offers the same screen size as a 17-inch conventional monitor.  PORTS -- The computing world is shifting to Universal Serial Bus (U.S.B.) as a common standard for connecting printers, scanners and other peripheral devices. The U.S.B. connections are faster and easier than the older serial and parallel ports. But then remember to buy U.S.B. peripherals.  COMPAQ PRESARIO 5900Z-700 For the inveterate gamer, this Compaq computer, with a 700-megahertz Athlon processor, includes 128 megabytes of RAM, a high-speed 27-gigabyte hard disk, a 10X DVD drive, a 4X CD-RW (rewritable) drive, 32 MB of graphics memory on a Creative 3-D Blaster TNT-2 Ultra graphics card, a 19-inch monitor, a Klipsch Promedia THX surround-sound speaker system and a D.S.L. modem. All for $2,912 on Compaq's Web site.  DELL DIMENSION XPS T500 For the budget-conscious, this $1,339 system includes a 500-MHz Pentium III processor, 64 MB of RAM with 512 kilobytes of Level 2 cache, a 6.4 GB hard drive, 16 MB of video memory on a Voodoo 3 graphics card, a 48X CD-ROM, a 17-inch monitor, Harman Kardon speakers, a 56K modem, a floppy drive and a year of Net access -- backed by Dell's reputation for reliability.  SONY SPRESSA CRX100E/X U.S.B. CD-RW DRIVE This versatile drive is not the flashiest, but it does everything well. It backs up as much as 650 MB of data on a blank CD-R (write-once disc) or CD-RW disc, writes CD-audio discs (including a CD labeling system) and reads any disc that can be read by a CD-ROM drive, including Photo CD. This external U.S.B. version lists for $399 but can sell for much less; it works with Windows and Mac machines. If you want to burn your own music CD's, this is a hot burner.  ITOUCH KEYBOARD Logitech's Internet keyboard ($39.95; wireless version $99.95) lets you open email or search the Net with one touch of a button.  MICROSOFT INTELLIMOUSE EXPLORER With its sleek silver-and-gray body and glowing-red underbelly and taillight, this mighty mouse is unlike anything else out there. It uses optical sensors to find its way around with greater precision than any conventional mechanical mouse. The big difference is that it uses a tiny video camera instead of a more traditional rolling ball and scans any surface (except glass) 1,500 times a second, which translates into high-precision control of cursor movements. The Intellimouse Explorer has five buttons, including a scroll wheel, which makes it an ideal mouse for World Wide Web browsers. Web pages rarely fit in one screen, and a scrolling wheel means that the user doesn't have to mouse over to a scroll bar and click up or down. The Explorer works with Macs as well as Windows, and it costs $74.95. It has no mechanical or moving parts, and it doesn't accumulate the belly-button lint that causes mechanical mice to skip, get stuck or lose their bearings.  I.B.M. T-55A 15-INCH FLAT PANEL MONITOR Flat-panel monitors are sleek and stylish, but they are at least triple the cost of conventional C.R.T. displays. This "stealth black" beauty, a $1,249 work of desktop sculpture, offers brilliant images and as much usable screen space as a 17-inch C.R.T. but takes up only one-third the desk space (and saves energy). There is no glare and no compromises on color or image sharpness.  MONSOON MM-1000 It may seem odd to hear 3-D sound from what are almost 2-D speakers, just one inch thick, but this system (two flat-panel satellite speakers and a subwoofer) punches it out while taking up minimal desk space. Music fills the room, jets zoom overhead and monsters creep up behind you, courtesy of Sonigistixs sonic imaging technology. This system sells for as little as $150 online.  DIAMOND VIPER V770 ULTRA Based on the nVidia Riva TNT2 Ultra processor, this 3-D/2-D graphics card ($179) is the ultimate game and video engine for Intel and AMD computers. It has 32 MB of high-speed graphics memory and 4X AGP (graphics card) performance (for up to 100 frames a second), and 32-bit rendering and 32-bit Z-stencil buffering. The result: nonpareil 3-D game play.  APPLE IMAC DV DV or not DV? That is the question when trying to choose among the three new models of iMacs from Apple. You could go for the $1,299 iMac DV (digital video) in one of five colors or, if your budget permits, the stylish gray iMac DV Special Edition at $1,499. The slot-loading DVD drive lets iMac DV owners use CD-ROM discs, play CD audio discs and even watch DVD movies. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos (Tony Cenicola for The New York Times)(pg. G10)  Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)(pg. G1)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Leading Media Companies Forming Joint Web Venture
body: An unusually broad news-sharing arrangement is bringing together some of the nation's leading media companies in a venture to share news reports on their Web sites. The venture includes the nation's leading broadcaster, the most popular news site on the Web, one of the country's most prominent newspapers, the No. 2 weekly newsmagazine and an all-news cable channel. The announcement was made by major subsidiaries of NBC News, MSNBC and the Washington Post Company and represented one of the most significant developments in media alliances responding to the challenge of attracting audiences in the narrowcasting era of cable TV and the Internet. Their companies' World Wide Web outlets will receive daily lists of planned articles from the partners and have access to the final news reports. Yesterday, a Washington Post report on travelers' reluctance to fly on New Year's Eve was on MSNBC.com. Many details remain unsettled. But the executives of the news organizations said yesterday that the journalism of the Washington Post, NBC News, Newsweek and MSNBC will be available on both MSNBC.com, Washingtonpost.com and a planned new site, Newsweek.MSNBC.com. Some exclusive reports will be held back until after they have been published or broadcast. In addition, WRC-TV in Washingtin, which is owned and operated by NBC, a unit of General Electric, will share news reports with each other on their respective online outlets. Advertising revenue from the collaborative ventures will be shared, the executives said. And in the coming election year, NBC, MSNBC and MSNBC.com can supplement their coverage with the reports of The Washington Post's respected corps of political reporters. MSNBC and MSNBC.com are joint ventures of NBC and Microsoft. The Washington Post Company owns Newsweek. Tom Wolzien, an analyst with Sanford C. Bernstein & Company who had been a producer with NBC News, said yesterday that the effort to aggregate high-quality journalism on a Web site could quickly broaden that site's audience -- and its appeal to advertisers. "What we've got, both with the Web but also with TV and cable, is a recognition that depth of content, depth of proprietary content, counts," he said. "As you move into an advertiser-supported Internet, 'your' site needs to have more proprietary content than 'mine.' " Collaborative reporting among some of the news organizations has also been discussed, executives said on a conference call yesterday. "There will be discussions about shared presentations of news between NBC and The Washington Post," said The Post's executive editor, Leonard Downie Jr. "We have no idea what form it will take. This is new territory." The alliance between the news outlets of NBC and the Post Company is one of many arrangements that have turned competing news organizations into partners. Some arrangements have supplemented earlier alliances and others have superceded them. For instance, now that reporters for The Washington Post and Newsweek will be appearing on Brian Williams's MSNBC news broadcast, reporters from The newyork Times will not. But yesterday's agreement leaves intact the broader pre-existing partnership between Dow Jones, the Wall Street Journal's parent, and CNBC, the financial news cable channel owned by NBC. The Journal's reporters regularly contribute material to CNBC. In return, Dow Jones is paid a licensing fee and shares in the advertising revenue. Articles from The Journal are also posted on the MSNBC.com site. The newyork Times has been exploring ventures with other news outlets, like ABC, which is owned by the Walt Disney Company. "We've talked to them about a whole range of things, including a limited collaboration on campaign coverage and some cooperation in television and Internet news," said Bill Keller, the managing editor of The Times. "It's all at the talking stage at this point," he added. "We haven't signed any formal agreements." In the world of the Web, alliances are the rule as media giants seek partners to help them compete in myriad online niches. This week, Pearson P.L.C., the parent company of The Financial Times, said it would take a stake in a major owner of the financial news Web site Marketwatch.com. That site is also partly owned by the CBS Corporation, and its journalists appear on some CBS news programs. The newyork Times also holds a 6.3 percent stake in TheStreet.com, another financial news site. Several reporters at TheStreet.com's offices in Manhattan's financial district file reports throughout the day both to The newyork Times on the Web and to TheStreet.com. Each of the news organizations in the alliance that was announced yesterday will retain editorial control over its publications or news broadcasts. Editors at the Web sites receiving material from partner newsrooms, however, cannot edit the material without consultation. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE POP LIFE;
Don't Worry? Yeah, Right
body: This week's No. 1 pop album, "Breathe," by the country singer Faith Hill, extols the virtues of true love, faith in God, the smile of a stranger and the eyes of a child. Though there may be little that is recognizably country on this album of slick pop-rock ballads with a CD booklet that looks like a Victoria's Secret catalog, it does have one thing in common with the earliest commercial country successes more than 70 years ago: It is the sound of pop's rear guard marching, waving the flag of traditional values in a society complaining about their disappearance. But on Tuesday afternoon, pop's rear guard received a lecture from the front line. Pressing a panic button, the Country Music Association convened what it called a town meeting -- its first in 10 years -- of record label presidents, songwriters and some 500 others in the business. Executives from Manhattan and Los Angeles flew in to discuss two changes that have punctured the vacuum that is the Nashville music business: the Internet and consolidation. One of the most significant developments in the record business in the 90's has been the emergence of a third region to rival the dominance of newyork and Los Angeles. The South Coast, as it is called (despite a frequent lack of proximity to the ocean), rose when Garth Brooks started an unprecedented country music boom in the early 90's. That rise solidified when Master P and his No Limit label in Louisiana helped turn the South into rap's creative center. But with this new national prominence, Southern music empires have lost their immunity to outside business influences. In a shrinking record industry, what affects newyork and Los Angeles causes bigger waves in Nashville. The town hall meeting was divided into two halves. First, for two hours, the gathering was told not to fear the coming of the Internet. That message came from Hillary Rosen, the formerly fearful chief executive of the Recording Industry Association of America; Marc Geiger, the ever-enthusiastic chief executive of the Internet site Artist Direct Network; Phil Ramone, the producer and founder of N2K Entertainment; and others. Then another panel of experts told the audience not to fear the consolidation that has constricted the record, concert, radio and publishing businesses in recent years. But in telling their colleagues not to be scared, panelists ended up inciting more fear. Though Ms. Rosen asserted that Internet music piracy was under control, she was speaking to a songwriting town, for which issues of performance rights, licensing fees and the breakdown of royalty payments on the Internet have not yet been worked out satisfactorily. Crash Craddock, the president of 37212, the first Internet company to open on Music Row here, was the first audience member to protest, complaining that traditional radio stations didn't have to pay licensing fees to play music. But his Internet radio stations, even though they have no sources of revenue like advertising, will be required to pay fees to the recording association for transmitting music. The consolidation segment of the meeting was even more ominous, with executives fooling no one by saying that layoffs were good because they allowed the newly unemployed to become independent entrepreneurs. "I'm on a binge to try and buy radio stations," said Larry Wilson, the chief executive of Citadel Communications, which already owns more than 160 stations. He went on to explain that it was wonderful that a company can own "six or seven stations in one market." This was probably not very reassuring to record executives who complain that country-music stations have become too limited and closed-minded in making additions to their play lists. It was interesting, however, to observe that broadcasters feel the same way about Nashville; radio executives complained that they were desperately in need of new country superstars, but that Nashville kept churning out copycat singers who all sounded the same. By the day's end record executives and radio programmers had proven themselves to be two mirrors facing each other, sending the same reflection back and forth ad infinitum. What country may really need is someone to point one of the mirrors in another direction. And this is where the Internet comes in. "Based on what they were saying, radio is going to have less and less superstars because radio is playing less and less new artists," Mr. Craddock said. "That concerns me. But they also said that as the trees grew bigger, there'd be a lot of nuts to pick up. And I feel like a squirrel with my cheeks full of nuts. Because the Internet will be a place for people to hear the music that's not on the radio." And this is where the new Faith Hill record comes in. "I've seen walls that could never be broken," she sings, "come tumbling down." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: At the Country Music Association meeting, from left: Phil Ramone, the producer; Jeff Green of the association; Ed Pierson of Warner/Chappell; and Marc Geiger, the chief executive of Artist Direct Network. (Chris Berkey for The newyork Times)

title: Where the Wired Consumer Can Give as Well as Receive
body: E-COMMERCE may do many things, but wiping out world hunger won't be among them. Nonetheless, the anticipated droves of consumers heading online this holiday season may come across a proliferation of charity malls and other Web-based programs that offer opportunities to donate to a worthy cause. "Internet shopping is good for philanthropy," said Mark Rovner, director of CMS Interactive in Arlington, Va., a Web consultancy for charitable organizations. "People who've bought five or more items online are more likely to give online as well." One of the most prevalent and convenient ways holiday shoppers can make donations while they shop on the Internet is through charity malls, including iGive.com, 4Charity.com and Greatergood.com. These sites are set up to let consumers buy products from leading online merchants and designate a charity to receive a percentage of the money spent. When a shopper registers at iGive (www.igive.com/html/intro.cfm), for example, then heads to the American Greetings site to buy a stack of Christmas cards, American Greetings will contribute up to 15 percent of the purchase price to a selected cause. The charity mall model also extends to portals that do not necessarily have philanthropy as their focus. When shoppers register at Zipple.com, for example, a new Jewish portal (www.zipple.com), a percentage of the proceeds from the products they buy at Zipple links will be donated to Jewish charities like the Jewish Federation of Chicago and the Jewish Federation of newyork. Although the idea of giving till you drop may have an appeal, some charity malls keep part of the proceeds to pay for their overhead. In addition, many online merchants who participate in such programs require minimum purchases before the charity receives its portion of the proceeds. As a result, experts say there are more effective ways to donate money. "It remains to be seen whether any of the charity portals are going to reach critical mass," Mr. Rovner said. "I think the Internet's real promise is for facilitating direct relationships with the charities themselves." But proponents of such online charitable programs say even incremental sums of money gathered from consumers while they shop online are worth seeking out. "It's money that wouldn't otherwise be going to the charities to begin with," said Dan Langan, a spokesman for the National Charities Information Bureau in Manhattan. "If they can give while shopping at L. L. Bean, that's all to the good." In addition to the charity malls, a number of sites let shoppers direct rebates, gift certificates and rewards to charitable organizations. * Dash.com, a virtual mall at www.dash.com where 100 retailers offer 5 percent to 25 percent discounts on their products, will give consumers the option of donating the money saved to one of four charities: the American Cancer Society, Greenpeace, the United Way of America or the World Wildlife Federation, beginning Thanksgiving Day. Dash charges no administrative fees, and the charities receive the entire amount of the discounts, said Andrew Surwilo, Dash's vice president for partnership marketing. * GiftSpot.com (www.giftspots .com/Giftspot/default.asp.) sells gift certificates for retailers, including eToys and Sharper Image. Shoppers can apply the full amount (or the change) to charities like the American Lung Association and Easter Seals. * ClickRewards.com, a site that uses air miles as a reward for consumers who shop at one of 60 retail partners at www.clickrewards.com, will match every dollar donated to CARE, Dads and Daughters, Rainforest Action Network, the Special Olympics and Unicef with two ClickMiles, which are redeemable for frequent-flier miles and upgrades at nine airlines. * MyPoints.com rewards its members by giving points for responding to retail advertisements on its site (www.mypoints.com /index.html). Members who usually apply their points toward gift certificates to retailers like Macy's and Barnes & Noble can turn their points into cash to be donated to the American Red Cross or the Toys for Tots Foundation through the end of December. Online catalogs produced by smaller nonprofit groups like the Heifer Project (catalog.heifer.org) and World Vision (www.worldvision gifts.org/worldvision/appeals.nsf /stable/agc) allow shoppers to make donations in someone's name as a gift without having to shop at another online retailer. The Heifer Gift catalog features a selection of animals, birds and trees that can be bought for a family in need in any of the 60 countries it sponsors. At the World Vision site, shoppers can sponsor a child, buy animals or donate money toward the distribution of clothing and food. Other gift catalogs, including One Nest.com (www.onenest.com), which goes live in December, and World2Market.com showcase and sell artwork, jewelry and crafts made by artisans around the world (www.world2market.com). Both organizations work with nonprofit organizations to help artisans establish businesses over the Web. Shoppers who are low on funds or just browsing can head to the Hunger Site (www.hungersite.com), where it's not necessarily the thought, but the click that counts. Hitting the Donate Free Food button will call up a page of banner advertisements from companies including Games2Learn and ProFlowers. Each company pays the Hunger Site a half-cent every time its advertisement appears, enough to buy a quarter-cup of rice for the United Nations World Food Program, which serves 80 countries. The combined sponsors add up to about three cents for each click, ultimately generating 100 tons of food each week, said John Breen, a computer programmer in Bloomington, Ind., who opened the site in June. Before you participate in any online giving program, the National Charities Information Bureau recommends searching the Web site for clearly stated privacy policies, detailed descriptions of how the money is sent to the charity and information on how to get in contact with the charities directly. The bureau provides reports on each of the charities it evaluates. Consumers can go to its Web site (www.ncib.org) or call (212) 929-6300 to order reports for $9.95 each. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Will Gift Lists Click?
body: THOSE who agonize over what to give far-flung nieces and nephews for the holidays or what to buy the friend who is a compulsive gift-returner can now instruct the would-be recipients to simplify the shopping process by setting up an online gift registry. Gift registries are usually associated with weddings and with the question: "Is the gravy boat still available?" On the Internet, gift registries, including Wish.com (www.wish.com), WishClick.com (www.wishclick.com) and Wish-List.com (www.wishlist.com), to name a few, have sprouted in the last year, all with the goal of being the single online destination for gift recipients, gift givers and the online retailers who can satisfy the needs of both. Except for slight variations in selection and processing, the sites work essentially the same way. A shopper registers, chooses a category like clothing, peruses products from a variety of retailers and creates a wish list. In most cases, the registry site sends the person to the retailer's site to view the product, then links the shopper back to the registry when a product has been selected forthe list. The wish list is stored at the site, and the list creator alerts friends and family members. The gift giver can then go to the site, enter the person's name or email address and view the wish list. Each time someone buys an item on a list, the registry site receives a 5 percent to 15 percent commission from the retailer. Wish.com and NetGift.com (www.netgift.com), two sites focusing on strong retail partnerships, have agreements with more than 300 retailers. "Instead of trying to drive people to our site, we're driving them to other well-known sites," said Randall Greg, a spokesman for NetGift, whose goal, he added, is to register two million users by year end. Other sites, like IveBeenGood.com (www.ivebeengood.com) and eWish.com (www.ewish.com), list retail partners but also encourage shoppers to wish for products anywhere on the Internet. Della.com, the expansion of the Della & James online bridal registry into an all-occasion gift site, is taking a slightly different approach. In addition to partnering with name retailers like The Gap and Neiman-Marcus, Della showcases products from many stores and processes the purchase transactions at the Della site (www.della.com), instead of having the consumer go to the retailer. Many retailers, including Amazon (www.amazon.com), CDNow (www.cdnow.com) and eToys (www.etoys.com), have their own registries, which gift buyers can view by typing in the recipient's name or email address. Buyers from the eToys registry can get a 10 percent discount for the holidays. Although a list of must-have toys might be fun for children, it remains to be seen whether adults will warm to the idea. Even consumers accustomed to shopping online are squeamish about wish lists. "I'm not one of those people who feel comfortable asking someone for a gift," said Lyle Rutschman, a toy collector in Wichita, Kan., who regularly buys Star Wars figurines online. "It just feels a little like begging." Mr. Rutschman instead uses wish lists at eToys and Toytime.com (www.toytime.com) as a way of reminding himself of what he plans to buy. "Outside of weddings, it's going to be difficult to make it fly for adults," said Ken Cassar, a digital commerce analyst at Jupiter Communications. "There's no gratification for the buyer, who is essentially an order fulfiller." Of course, registries can just about obliterate any sense of surprise. Because many registries notify the list maker once a product has been bought, a child with access to a registry can perform the electronic equivalent of peeking through the wrapping paper. To avoid this, parents should set up the wish lists and have any email notifications about gift purchases sent directly to them. Families that are already accustomed to list-making are most likely to benefit the most. "Our family writes up wish lists on paper every year anyway," said Kathy Truesdell, of Austin, Tex., who plans to register at eWish.com this year. "It's always very painstaking work, so this seems like it might make it easier." Wendy Mincer, of Dallas, also plans to use an online registry this year, and to tell her family about it. "Swinging steaks may be a delicacy where my brother's from, but I don't want any more," she said, referring to a regional dish also known as Rocky Mountain oysters -- deep-fried calf, lamb or buffalo testicles. "This is a way of giving him other ideas." http://www.nytimes.com

title: 13 on Staten Island Accused In Internet Sales of Illicit Drugs
body: Thirteen members of a Staten Island gang were arrested yesterday and charged with arranging sales of designer drugs like Ecstasy over the Internet, police officials said. This is the first such online drug ring uncovered in newyork City, the officials said. Detectives who had been investigating the gang began looking into the sales in December after they received a tip that members were selling drugs through America Online chat rooms, officials said. Inspector James P. McCool, commander of the Gang Investigation Division, said that the 13 members of the gang, called the Gods of Mass Destruction, were arrested on drug sale and possession charges. Five other people, relatives of the gang members, were arrested on similar charges when investigators searched their Staten Island homes, officials said. "It's the first time we have seen" such drug sales in newyork, Inspector McCool said, but he added that it was inevitable that people would begin selling drugs on the Internet. The police called the investigation "Operation You've Got Jail." Inspector McCool said that detectives from the computer crimes unit, using fake user names, logged into public chat rooms on America Online where the gang members arranged sales of Ecstasy, hallucinogenic mushrooms, Special K and other drugs popular at night clubs and among high school and college students. The detectives then set up meetings at bars and clubs and behind shopping centers in which undercover narcotics officers bought more than 800 Ecstasy pills. Some of the drug sales also took place in the Staten Island Mall, near a Y.M.C.A. and a Burger King on Richmond Avenue, and in front of the defendants' homes, officials added. The Staten Island District Attorney's office helped investigators obtain the assistance of America Online in confirming the identities of the sellers. Investigators are still trying to determine who supplied the drugs to the gang and did not disclose which chat rooms were being used to set up the sales. Five of the gang members were indicted by Staten Island grand jury on Nov. 10, according to records that were unsealed in criminal court yesterday. In addition to what was bought, investigators said, five searches yielded 1,000 Ecstasy pills, 24 boxes of Special K, a pound of hallucinogenic mushrooms, steroids, 2 ounces of crack cocaine and 8 pounds of marijuana. The detectives also seized 10 rifles, 5 shotguns, a handgun, a Nissan Pathfinder, a Ford Contour and $7,000, officials added. In one instance, when investigators searched the home of 19-year-old George Pezulick Jr. on Delmar Avenue in the Annadale section, they ended up arresting his parents, MaryAnn, 41, and George Sr., 44, and his sister, Jaclyn, 16. Officials said the three said tried to hide or destroy drugs that were in the house. Inspector McCool added that the defendants, all of whom lived in southern Staten Island, had easy access to computers. "This is a group that worked in a middle-class, upper-class neighborhood in Staten Island, not your obvious area for street gangs," he said. Police officials said the gang, whose name comes from the villains in an animated Japanese film, began while its members were in high school. The gang members, now between 18 and 22, started off as graffiti vandals and graduated to assaults and selling, officials said. William L. Murphy, the Staten Island District Attorney, called this case an example of how "we need to work as a community to protect our young people from online exploitation." "I cannot say it enough, please monitor you're child's online activity," Mr. Murphy added. "Chat rooms are where many young people can commit crimes or become victimized." http://www.nytimes.com

title: As E-Giving Sites Spring Up, Some Say It's Donor Beware
body: ARASH of new Internet sites is promising to make it easier to support worthy causes. Want to do a little good when you shop? Shop-for-a-cause sites like iGive.com and Greatergood.com say they will send part of the price of whatever you buy to your favorite organization. Interested in making a donation over the Internet? There are several sites like GiveForChange.com and Charitableway.com that say they will shepherd your gift to a charity, sometimes for a fee. Other sites, like Helping.org, created by the Internet powerhouse America Online through the AOL Foundation, are positioning themselves as clearinghouses for potential donors who want to learn more about charities. Helping.org, a nonprofit Web site, offers information on more than 620,000 charities. While the potential of the Internet to generate new money for charities and educational institutions is vast, few of these sites have been in operation for long, and some are just getting off the ground. The majority are profit-making businesses, hoping to earn money by taking fund-raising fees or keeping part of the commission paid by retailers whenever the site sends a shopper their way. They account for a tiny fraction of individual giving. Because these sites have different business models and distinct philosophies, consumers need to make sure they understand how each one operates, said William P. Massey, the president of the National Charities Information Bureau, a charity watchdog in newyork that has been following the online activity. Among the sites there are significant differences about which charities are included and how much money ends up going to a specific cause. Many charities also allow donors to give through their Web sites, and some, notably the American Red Cross, have had considerable success fund-raising over the Internet, appealing to donors at times of specific need, like after a hurricane. The challenge for the sites that serve as middlemen, many of which do not have the backing of well-established charities or companies, will be to win the confidence of consumers and charities alike, according to Carol Cone, the chief executive of Cone Inc., a marketing research company in Boston that recently completed a study of cause-related marketing on the Internet. "The sites just have to be built with credibility and authenticity, unlike almost anything else," Ms. Cone said. If consumers do not trust the sites, they will not use them. "The sites really don't have credibility; they don't deserve it," said Michael Kieschnick, the president and co-founder of Working Assets, a San Francisco company that provides credit cards and long-distance service, donating a percentage of the revenues to help support progressive causes. In October, the company started ShopForChange.com and a second site, GiveForChange.com, to allow individuals to generate more revenue for those causes. Because there has been such a proliferation of sites, consumers should be wary. While sites may promise to send money to a charity, it may never get there. "This makes this new industry a potential source of fraud," warned Jay D. Hair, the former chief executive officer of the National Wildlife Federation and an executive vice president of Greatergood.com, at a recent conference on e-philanthropy in Washington. Deciding which site to use is not easy, even if consumers are comfortable that the money will go where it was intended. Buying cosmetics from Avon over the Internet would generate twice as much money for a cause from 4charity.com, which says that it sends all commissions generated by its shoppers to charity, than from iGive.com, which takes part of the commission. Greatergood.com promises to send at least 5 percent of the purchase to your cause, which is still less than what 4charity.com sends. Potential donors who have a cause in mind might think twice about using some of the sites, and might be better off simply sending a check. GiveForChange.com, for example, takes a 10 percent fee for every donation. Charitableway.com, a new business that is focusing on Internet fund-raising for charities through employee giving programs and other means, promises to take less than 10 percent of any donation, although it recently received matching funds that allow it to send 101 percent of donations to charity through January 2000. Helping.org says it will forward the money without charge, except for credit-card fees. HOW all this fund-raising over the Internet should be regulated is the subject of considerable debate. The charities and sites serving as middlemen have different views about what they are obligated to do under state law. Givers looking for advice about which charities merit their money may be disappointed. Helping.org says it does not want to be a screening mechanism, preferring potential donors to do their own homework, while iGive.com lets its shoppers nominate causes. Other sites tend to sign up charities that are willing to work with them and pay their fees. In contrast, Working Assets says that, in essence, it is endorsing the charities on its sites. The company's directors choose progressive charities based on evaluations by the Tides Foundation, a San Francisco group devoted to social change. "Our filter is really important," Mr. Kieschnick said. In the coming months, many sites will go dark as entrepreneurs find they cannot make money with some business models, and consumers gravitate to others. Some early sites have already been absorbed into other businesses. "There's going to be a huge shakeout," Ms. Cone said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Matt Collins)

title: Desktop Discount Shopping, The Newest Perquisite
body: First came corporate day care centers. Then it was concierge services that pick up employees' dry cleaning or deliver groceries for a fee. Now comes the virtual discount mall, offering workers everything from books to car insurance at up to 10 percent off, right on their office computer screens. In the latest attempt to please workers without giving them big raises, some of the nation's largest companies are trying to make shopping of all kinds both cheaper and easier for their employees. It is part of an explosion of soft benefits, which, unlike the hard perquisites of health insurance and retirement plans, cost employers almost nothing. With unemployment at a 29-year low and people working longer hours, executives see the programs as a way to lift workers' morale. They also assume that employees who do their shopping in cyberspace will spend less time ducking out of the office to run errands. At the least, Susan R. Froid, a senior human resource manager at Microsoft, said, employees "don't have to spend all their free time figuring out what they're going to do -- it's an easy decision to make." That was the pull for Lisa Rose, who works on hiring and training for Sylvan Learning Systems, an education company in Baltimore. When she heard about the offers, she logged onto Sylvan's Web site and bought medical insurance for her 6-month-old Labrador, Ewing, who is named after the newyork Knicks center whom her husband idolizes. The cost, $16 a month, is deducted from her paycheck. She also bought roadside insurance that covers towing, locksmith service and travel planning for $4.16 a month, not even bothering to compare the insurer's prices with AAA's. "It was so easy for me to sign up, and I don't have to pay another bill every month," she said. The trend has picked up in recent weeks, with such corporate giants as AlliedSignal, Hallmark Cards, Nordstrom and Northwest Airlines connecting their internal Web sites to virtual malls where merchants sell everything from Hickory Farms sausage to MCI Worldcom long-distance service. The pioneers for such plans include Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing, Blue Cross/ Blue Shield, Boeing and Microsoft. "It's so difficult to attract employees, and the retention side is getting more difficult," said Joe Demarte, the vice president for human resources at Nordstrom, the department store chain, which employs 40,000 people. The discounts are the latest addition to a benefit package that includes adoption advice and discounts on legal services. The virtual malls are an Internet-age remake of the old corporate discount card that gave employees free tickets to a nearby amusement park or a few dollars off at the local florist. The World Wide Web, however, allows workers in satellite offices to take advantage of the discounts. It also enables employers to negotiate deals for a much wider array of products, including expensive items like insurance and mortgages. The Internet discounts are part of a wider move toward offering more soft benefits to placate time-burdened workers. In 1994, for example, only 8 percent of companies made car insurance available to workers through company-sponsored plans. Next year, the portion should rise to 35 percent, according to Hewitt Associates, a management consulting firm in Illinois. The virtual malls are typically operated by Internet start-ups, which charge employers nothing for the service and build password-protected links from the corporate intranet sites to, say, toysrus.com. In exchange for what amounts to advertising on the Web site and in company brochures describing the program, merchants then offer the 5 percent to 10 percent discounts and pay a few percentage points of each sale to the Internet companies. The trend is even creating a new niche of e-commerce. Employeesavings.com received a $5 million investment earlier this year from Benchmark Capital, which previously financed eBay and Webvan. By early 2000, employeesavings says its plans will cover two million people. And Rewards Plus, which sells only financial products, expects its annual sales to more than double to $9 million this year, as it increases its work force by 25 percent each quarter. The programs are not without their downsides. Not all employees have Internet access, and those who do not -- some Nordstrom sales clerks or Northwest flight attendants, for example -- are often the ones who need the discounts the most because they make less money. (Companies say, however, that some of the discounts are available over the phone or at local stores.) Web shopping is also a potential threat to productivity, giving workers a company-approved reason to procrastinate. Already, the peak time for Web traffic and many consumer e-commerce sites is the middle of the workday, when people have access to high-speed corporate Internet connections. But human resource managers said they were not worried. "This isn't something where you're going to go out and play for hours," Mr. Demarte said. "It probably isn't any different from what they already do" by making personal phone calls. And it may be cheaper. Robert A. Arrison, 41, a computer systems administrator at Aramark Inc., the Philadelphia food service company, was shopping for homeowners' and auto insurance a year ago. He checked the rates of Allstate Insurance, which had sold him a previous policy, and Allmerica Financial, which participated in his company's discount plan. By going with Allmerica, he said, he saved almost $200 a year. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Ms. Rose also bought medical insurance for $16 a month for her Labrador, Ewing.; Lisa Rose bought roadside insurance at work on Sylvan Learning Systems' Web site. (Marty Katz for The newyork Times)

title:
Foreign Affairs;
Next, It's E-ducation
body: The two most telling stories about the 10th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall actually ran in the business sections of The newyork Times and The Washington Post. One was a short article in the back pages of The Times that reported that the number of adults using the Internet in the U.S. had surpassed 100 million, meaning that roughly half the U.S. population is now online. The other article, in The Post, noted that Amazon.com was shipping an extraordinary number of copies of Adolf Hitler's racist manifesto, "Mein Kampf," to buyers in Germany. It is illegal to sell "Mein Kampf" in bookstores in Germany or publish it there. But as we move from the world of Borders books to the world of borderless books, a k a Amazon.com, Germans can order "Mein Kampf" online and have it delivered by mail, and their government is powerless to stop it. Indeed, Amazon shipped so many copies of "Mein Kampf" to Germany that over the summer Hitler made Amazon's top 10 best-seller list among German buyers. What these two little stories tell is that 10 years after the fall of the Berlin Wall a whole other set of walls is starting to fall, as we move deeper into the Internet revolution. And this is not simply an American phenomenon, nor, as the "Mein Kampf" example illustrates, will it automatically bring out the best in people. So what comes next? With the first phase of this wall-destroying Internet revolution -- the email and e-commerce phase -- now fully under way, I posed that question to John Chambers. Mr. Chambers runs Cisco Systems, which makes the routers that run the Internet. Beware: He has an obvious stake in touting the Internet. But note: His past predictions have proved extremely accurate. Mr. Chambers argued that the second phase of the Internet revolution -- businesses absorbing the Internet and using it to relate to one another -- was now just taking off, and that this was going to be a monster market. There is barely a C.E.O. in the developed world who in the last six months hasn't said to himself: "Oh my God! This Internet thing is real. Somebody call me an Internet doctor and wire me up." Once a C.E.O. understands that absorbing the Net into every aspect of his or her business "is the only way they are going to survive," said Mr. Chambers, "they are going to be spending big bucks on it. That's why I believe that Y2K will be short-lived, and after that we are going to see one of the best years the computer industry has ever seen." So now that commerce has moved to the Net, and the Net is moving into business, what comes after that? "Education," said Mr. Chambers. "The next big killer application for the Internet is going to be education. Education over the Internet is going to be so big it is going to make email usage look like a rounding error" in terms of the Internet capacity it will consume. What will drive it will be the demands on companies, in an intensely competitive global economy, to keep improving productivity. E-learning, insists Mr. Chambers, if done right, can provide faster learning, at lower costs, with more accountability, thereby enabling both companies and schools to keep up with changes in the global economy that now occur at Net speed. Schools and countries that ignore this, he says, will suffer the same fate as big department stores that thought e-commerce was overrated. If universities move properly, they will offer the ideal combination of online and instructor-led learning, argues Mr. Chambers. But if universities don't reinvent their curriculums and how they deliver them, for an increasingly Net-driven economy, many students, particularly in information technology fields, "will go to schools online," he says. Many big firms -- Cisco, G.E., I.B.M., AT&T -- are starting online academies to train new employees and to constantly upgrade the skills of existing ones. "Unlike in the industrial revolution when you had to be in the right country or city to participate, in this new era capital will flow to whichever countries and companies install the best Internet and educational capabilities," says Mr. Chambers. Governments and unions will be powerless to stop this capital flow, which will affect the global balance of economic power. Although the technology exists today, this revolution will take about 10 years to be fully in place. But, insists Mr. Chambers, "it's coming next." http://www.nytimes.com
