title: Gates Advocates Competition, but He Has His Doubters
body: As William H. Gates opened his annual speech at the Comdex technology conference, he tried to portray Microsoft as a company that wanted to give consumers choices in how they use computers and get on line. But many of those attending expressed doubts about whether Microsoft was truly embracing the idea of competition. Hundreds of thousands of technology professionals, from software developers to network managers, have descended on this city to attend Comdex, the huge conference that has been showcasing new business computing technologies for 20 years. More than 7,000 of them swarmed into the ballroom where the Microsoft chairman presented his keynote address on Sunday night, eager to hear his reaction to the strong attack embedded within the findings of a federal judge this month in a government antitrust case. But aside from a couple of joking references to lawyers, Mr. Gates steered clear of any direct references to the case. Instead he jumped among several topics, from the ways software can help businesses manage hardware failures to how Web sites and non-Web programs could seamlessly exchange data. Mr. Gates, whose company has defined the personal computer era, also heralded the dawn of a less PC-centric age, when people will use several different mobile devices -- like Internet-enabled cell phones and personal digital assistants -- to gain access to the Web. He stressed that people will have a choice of Internet devices. "No one will dominate over the other," he said. At the same time, he painted a picture of a world in which Windows software would run on any device. And today, as mobs of people huddled near Microsoft's booth awaiting its opening, several shook their heads when asked whether they sensed the dawn of an era in which Microsoft would lose its dominance. "He's trying to deflect the monopoly situation he's facing," said Charles Shepperd, director of information systems for Plastics Plus, a company in Auburn Hills, Mich. There may be many new companies, and many new products evolving, Mr. Shepperd said, but "I don't think anybody is going to be able to catch up" to Microsoft. Dan Gervais, director of research and development for a start-up company called RealLegends.com, said that Microsoft's "deep pockets" would keep it in its dominant position for several years, regardless of the outcome of the Microsoft trial. As he sat crosslegged on the convention floor, Mr. Gervais pulled out his hand-held device, a personal digital assistant called a Cassiopeia, which runs on one of Microsoft's operating systems, Windows CE, which Mr. Gates cited in his speech as a platform of the future. Windows CE represents, in fact, an area in which Microsoft does have formidable competition. The Palm, from 3Com, is the personal digital assistant of choice, Mr. Gervais noted, and does not use a Windows operating system. He also predicted that voice-recognition software might someday replace the Windows graphical interface. Still, he said, it will probably be 10 years before "there will be a lot more choices." Some attendees pointed to Linux, the operating system of the so-called open-source movement, as another potential competitor to Microsoft. In fact, many at the conference, while bemoaning a Microsoft monopoly, also hailed Linux's latest successes. For the first time, the organizers of Comdex, Ziff-Davis, opened a parallel conference called the Linux Business Expo to give Linux developers a central place to display their wares. The halls were not nearly as crowded as those near Microsoft's booth, but hundreds of people streamed by to look, for the first time, at new programs like a Linux version of Word Perfect from Corel. "There is a lot of momentum," said Andy Wolf, a business development manager for Andover.net, the parent company of SlashDot, a pro-Linux Web site. "But I don't necessarily think it will become bigger than Microsoft." But several of those interviewed noted the quandary inherent in such competition. Because Linux is a free system, whose code can be manipulated by anybody, it also breeds variation. Instead of having one standard system upon which everyone can build applications and use documents, Linux may have differing branches depending on how it is altered by individual developers. Microsoft, on the other hand, stands for standardization -- there is one system that can be built upon without any fear of incompatibility. To Ryan Priest, a Microsoft-certified systems engineer who came to Comdex partly to hunt for a job, Microsoft's standards are not something that should be simply dismissed: "It boils down to, how can you use it? Everybody can develop things that are compatible with Microsoft. With other platforms, you're going to have problems." He added: "Competition is good. But you also want stability." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: William H. Gates, Microsoft's chairman, speaking at the annual Comdex computer conference in Las Vegas. He said his company wanted to give consumers choices in how they used computers and got on line. (Associated Press)

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
Shares Close Little Changed Ahead of Fed Panel Meeting
body: Stocks closed little changed yesterday as investors waited for today's Federal Open Market Committee meeting that will decide the direction of interest rates. "People were reluctant to take a stand one way or another for fear of being surprised by the Fed meeting when they just have a few hours to wait," said Michael Holland, chairman of Holland & Company in newyork, which manages $50 million. The market was hindered by Microsoft, which fell after a report in Barron's said the software company could be worth almost one-third less if antitrust enforcers broke it up. "All the stuff going on with Microsoft is giving the market pause" because the company is so large, Mr. Holland said. "It can stop the upward movement of the market." The Dow Jones industrial average dropped 8.57 points, to 10,760.75. The Nasdaq composite index declined 1.61 points, to 3,219.54. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index fell 1.67 points, to 1,394.39. All three market measures moved between small gains and losses during the session.  Eight stocks rose for every seven that fell on the newyork Stock Exchange. Some 793 million shares traded on the Big Board, about average for the last three months. The Ameritrade Holding Corporation rose 4 7/16, to 26 7/16, and TD Waterhouse Group rallied 2 3/8, to 19. The discount brokers said they would form an online investment bank with the Charles Schwab Corporation in an effort to sell more shares of initial public offerings directly to retail investors. Schwab rose 2 1/4, to 43 1/4. Microsoft dropped 2 1/8, to 87 1/16, its eighth decline in nine days. David Readerman, an analyst at Thomas Weisel Partners in San Francisco, told Barron's the value of the company's three major operations -- its Windows-related business, development and applications, and the Internet -- adds up to about $355 billion, 31 percent below its current market value. Microsoft shares have fallen 5 percent since Nov. 5, when the judge found that Microsoft used its monopoly to squash competitors. The finding opened the way for sanctions that could include breaking up the company. Global Crossing Ltd. rose 4 1/4, to 42 7/8, after saying it would form a $1.2 billion venture with Hutchison Whampoa Ltd. to offer Internet-related services in hongkong and later in mainland China. Oak Industries soared 19, to 68 3/4, after Corning Inc. agreed to buy the telecommunications equipment maker for $2 billion in stock and debt. Corning, the maker of fiber optic cable, will exchange $75 of its common stock for each Oak share. The offer represented a 51 percent premium to Oak's closing price of 49 3/4 on Friday. Corning fell 3 1/4 to 87 1/8.  Treasuries Are Flat By Dow Jones Treasuries were little changed in quiet trading yesterday, as most market participants stayed on the sidelines ahead of today's meeting of Federal Reserve policy makers. The benchmark 30-year Treasury rose 4/32, to 101 13/32. The bond's yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, fell to 6.02 percent from 6.03 percent on Friday. Trading activity was said to be on the cautious side yesterday. Both investors and dealers are wary of building new positions in bonds because it is still unclear whether the policy-making committee will raise interest rates. The decision will be announced around 2:15 p.m. "Very few people are willing to take any risk" by creating new positions ahead of the committee meeting, said Yasunori Sugi, a trader at Fuji Bank Ltd. in newyork. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
When dot-coms want to build up their images, they hitch their Web sites to a star.
body: REMEMBER Carl Sagan's sing-song declarations about space being filled with billions and billions of stars. Cyberspace is now becoming filled with stars, too, as a lengthening list of dot-com marketers center their ads on celebrities. Famous faces and voices are peddling Web sites, e-commerce companies, PC's, search engines and e-tailers -- almost anything interactive- or Internet-related. They range from immediately recognizable (Donald Trump) to nostalgic favorites (Barry White) to hip semicelebrities (the singer Seal). The trend is not unexpected if dot-com advertising is considered to be mimicking the model established by pitches for traditional products like packaged goods. The initial phase is to inculcate the name, usually by repetition and spelling: "Remember, that's w-w-w-dot-beauteesoap-dot-com. And don't forget, 'beautee' has three E's." Then comes the phase of differentiating one brand from another, particularly in categories in which the participants are proliferating. And what better way to do that than renting some star power -- a device known as borrowed interest. If Amos and Andy could make Americans brush with Pepsodent and Ozzie and Harriet make them snap pictures with Kodak film, why can't Sophia Loren make shopping at www.giftcertificates.com chic and Joyce Brothers make buying computers at www.cozone.com seem like a no-brainer. "Consumers are inundated with dot-com this and dot-com that," said Joseph Park, chief executive at Kozmo.com in newyork, a company specializing in so-called urban delivery services. "One of the key challenges is to build credibility." "A celebrity subconsciously brings credibility and legitimacy to whatever claims are being made," he added. A humorous television commercial for Kozmo.com by DiMassimo Brand Advertising in newyork presents Lee Majors as a contemporary version of Steve Austin, the character he played on "The Six Million Dollar Man" in the 1970's. "Dot-coms are using celebrities to bring the familiar to the world of the unknown," said Kathy Delaney, partner and executive creative director at Deutsch Inc. in newyork. "Most of these dot-com companies are brand-spanking new," she added. "The celebrities lend immediate recognizability." Deutsch is introducing a TV and print campaign for the Encyclopaedia Britannica's Web site (www.britannica.com), featuring Seal, Ms. Taylor, Norman Mailer, Anjelica Houston and Francis Ford Coppola. "Celebrities are brands, and their brands can drive brands," said Richard Kirshenbaum, co-chairman at Kirshenbaum Bond & Partners in newyork, an agency with many dot-com clients. "The latest thing is the merging of commerce and entertainment to create content that consumers remember," he added. "So if content equals entertainment and celebrities equal entertainment, therefore content equals celebrities." In some instances, the stars have an obvious link to the dot-coms they promote. For example, a campaign for Barnesandnoble.com presents authors and entertainers whose books and compact discs are sold at its Web site (www.bn.com). In addition to Mr. White, the husky-voiced singer, they include the mystery writer Sue Grafton, the law novelist Scott Turow and the chef-turned-scribe Emeril Lagasse. "We're not using a spokesperson who may or may not like the product," said Carl Rosendorf, senior vice president at Barnesandnoble in newyork. "Our spokespeople are the product. "The relevance of the person is most important here," he added. "At the same time, we're giving the buying online process some personality and style." The campaign was created by the newyork office of TBWA/ Chiat/Day, part of the TBWA Worldwide unit of the Omnicom Group. "For us, the celebrities are relevant to where we're spending most of our money," said Len Short, executive vice president for advertising and brand management at Charles Schwab in San Francisco. Because Schwab "bought time in some key sports properties," he added, the brokerage firm's commercials include the football players Jason Sehorn and Shannon Sharpe and the tennis players Mary Joe Fernandez and Anna Kournikova. "The celebrities put us in the event," Mr. Short said, "but the point isn't celebrities. It's that we show them to be surprisingly intelligent about investing" -- because they are Schwab customers, natch. The Schwab spots are created by BBDO newyork, part of the BBDO Worldwide unit of Omnicom. "Just to get a celebrity for celebrity's sake may bring a bit of attention to a brand, but it does little or nothing for the brand in the long term," said Ted Sann, co-chief executive and chief creative officer at BBDO newyork, which is known for star-infused campaigns for PepsiCo brands like Frito-Lay and Pepsi-Cola. "It's exactly the same as for general brand advertising," he added. "There has to be a brand positioning before you hire a celebrity, which the celebrity has to fit. That was the case with Cindy Crawford and Ray Charles and Michael J. Fox for Pepsi and Diet Pepsi." How then does Ms. Loren fit with Giftcertificates.com? "In a media environment that's so cluttered, especially this season, you've got to hit as hard as you can," said Mark Paviluk, vice president and group management supervisor on the company's account at Grey Advertising in newyork. "And what could be more impactful than the most beautiful woman in the world, who appeals to everyone from the housewife in Des Moines to the Chanel shopper in Manhattan," he added. For Cozone.com, a unit of Comp-USA, a campaign features Mr. Trump, Dr. Brothers and the basketball star David Robinson, all depicted as fish out of water: Mr. Trump, for example, taking a pottery class, and Dr. Brothers on a turkey shoot. "Celebrities often get used too much in advertising," said Edward Boches, chief creative officer at the Cozone.com agency, Mullen Advertising in Wenham, Mass., part of the Lowe Group unit of the Interpublic Group of Companies. "The idea here is that just because the celebrity is good at one thing, it doesn't necessarily mean he or she is good at other things, like buying computers," he added. Finally, sometimes stars are part of campaigns because they are stakeholders in the companies. Whoopi Goldberg, for instance, is a part-owner in a gift certificate Web site, Flooz.com, so she appears in the advertising by Hanft Byrne Raboy & Partners in newyork. And members of the N.F.L. Quarterback Club -- present and past players like Bernie Kosar of the Cleveland Browns, Warren Moon of the Kansas City Chiefs and Ricky Williams of the New Orleans Saints -- will be featured in a campaign by Organic in newyork for Pseudo Programs, an Internet broadcaster that uses streaming media on a Web site (www.pseudo.com). Pseudo has scheduled a live show on the site at 11 a.m. Eastern time today to promote its coming QB Channel. "This is not an endorsement deal," said Jeanne Meyer, senior vice president for marketing at Pseudo in newyork. "The Quarterback Club is making a cash investment and Bernie Kosar is joining our board of directors." Wait a minute. That's another trend, executives who appear in ads for the companies they own. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
Hand-Held WirelessData Gets a Flat-Rate Test
body: A spinoff of 3Com's Palm Computing division plans to say today that it will test a flat-rate wireless service offering nationwide access to the Internet and email. The OmniSky Corporation, based in Palo Alto, Calif., will in partnership with AT&T offer a small radio modem that attaches to Palm V hand-held computers. The company said it would begin a test program in December for 5,000 users of the popular hand-held digital organizer. At the end of March, it plans to follow with commercial service for a flat monthly fee. The new service is based on AT&T Wireless Services' cellular digital packet data network and is intended to offer a range of services similar to that now provided by Palm's wireless Palm VII hand-held computer and a growing range of pagers and cell phones connected to the Internet. Many of those plans, though, have been criticized because they are priced by use based on the amount of data, in bytes, the user sends or receives. That plan has proved unpopular with the Palm VII; consumers have had difficulties estimating how many bytes they consume in any given month, and corporate users complain that it makes budgeting for wireless use of the Palm VII almost impossible. The new service will be free during the company's four-month test period after the 5,000 Palm users buy a $299 modem. The company said it had not yet determined the monthly price but said it would be less than $50 and could possibly be as low as $30 for regional service. "This is about real Internet access," said Patrick McVeigh, chief executive of OmniSky. "A lot of people have tried this in the past, but we believe we've hit on the right value proposition." Mobile wireless data devices have long been objects of desire in the industry, but have been slow to take off. Companies like Radiomail and Wynd Communications stumbled in the early 1990's, when broad consumer demand for "email on the go" never developed. "This is a good first step," said Andrew Seybold, publisher of Andrew Seybold's Outlook, a newsletter on mobile computing. OmniSky was formed in June this year by executives from 3Com and Infoseek; it has financing from 3Com and Aether Systems, a maker of wireless Internet technology. JOHN MARKOFF http://www.nytimes.com

title:
E-Commerce Report;
Letters to Santa are no longer necessary. Wish lists, complete with sizes, can be posted on the Web.
body: ELECTRONIC-COMMERCE companies have long been accused of wishful thinking. Now they're selling it. Wishlist.com, Wishclick.com and OhIWish.com have joined a lineup of other e-commerce start-ups in the suddenly cluttered field of online gift registries, where people post lists of their preferred gifts in hopes that friends and family members will take their not-so-subtle hints. The element of wishful thinking in this trend goes beyond the obvious pun, however. For these sites to succeed, they will have to convince consumers to scrap the traditional mode of receiving mystery gifts gracefully -- no matter how awful they are -- and instead announce to the world exactly what gifts they want, down to the sizes, colors and retailers. Purveyors of gift registry sites argue that consumers are ready to make that change -- are prepared, in effect, to push gift giving closer to a barter exchange, as in "give me this, and I'll give you that." But they also acknowledge that consumers will need a bit of monetary incentive to test this new approach. And the amounts gift registries are shelling out to users are testimony to just how much they and their e-commerce partners stand to gain if this bit of consumer behavior can be altered. Until now, online gift registries have been confined to wedding sites -- like The Knot and Williams-Sonoma's Wedding and Gift Registry -- or specific retailers like Recreational Equipment Inc. -- better known as REI -- and Crate and Barrel. In recent months, however, several all-occasion registry sites have emerged that amass products from multiple retailers. Typically, users post their wish lists on the registry site, which offer different mechanisms to disseminate the lists to friends and family -- an email greeting card is the most common approach. For instance, on Della.com, which last week expanded from a wedding registry to an all-occasion site, users send email greeting cards to potential gift givers with messages like "All modesty aside, here's what I want," and "Here's what I sent to Santa . . . hint, hint" along with their lists. Gift buyers can then either come directly to the gift registry site to buy the goods, or follow links to retailers affiliated with the registry. When an item is bought, the purchaser is usually responsible for eliminating that item from the list on the registry site. One of the most well-financed companies in this category, Della.com offers items from eight well-known retailers, including the Gap, REI and Amazon.com, which owns a 20 percent stake in the company. It has plans to have 50 retailers by mid-2000. Users click on items on the site to add them to a "wish center," a page on Della.com's site that lists a person's wishes and general hobbies, clothing sizes and favorite colors. Or, they can select an item from far-flung Web retailers and post the item's address on the list. Once someone has purchased a gift, he or she can delete the item from the list. For retailers and registries, at least, there is a lot to like about this approach to gift buying. The gift registries collect a referral fee from retailers each time someone buys a gift from a retail partner. Those fees -- in the range of 5 to 15 percent -- mirror those of affiliate programs, whereby sites make money by sending customers to e-commerce partners. But because registry sites include multiple retailers, that money can quickly amount to meaningful revenue. Retailers, meanwhile, acquire customers for a fraction of what they pay through other means, like advertising or paid placement on Yahoo, Lycos or other portal sites. Retailers have also embraced the idea because it helps reduce one of their biggest headaches: returns. Internet retailers who continue to struggle with fulfillment issues exult at the prospect of shipping a package with a virtual guarantee that it will not be dropped back on their doorstep a week later. Beyond that, gift registries collect data about specific items that consumers want; the sites can then share that information with retailers and marketers if users agree to allow it. Even if consumers do not agree to share their personal information, however, registry sites can collect statistics about what products their customers like, giving them bargaining leverage with potential retail partners and advertisers. The attraction for consumers, industry executives say, is that the services make buying gifts easier. "The reason why it'll catch on is that it solves a fundamental problem," said Rebecca Patton, chief executive of Della.com. "People want to buy better gifts." Like other gift registries, Della.com faces two basic obstacles to instant consumer adoption: getting customers to register and getting them to circulate their wish lists. And like other gift registries, Della.com has a simple strategy to overcome those hurdles: money. Those who create a Della.com wish list are entered into a weekly sweepstakes for $2,300 worth of items they have registered for, and those who send their wish lists to 10 people to Della.com receive a $10 gift certificate for purchases at Amazon.com. Wishclick.com, meanwhile, gives users a $50 gift certificate when they persuade 10 people to register on the site -- and those people get $10 gift certificates for joining. IveBeenGood.com gives users a $25 gift certificate for sending their list to five people. Online registry executives admit that money will only get them so far -- particularly this holiday season. "I think it'll be a while before lots of people register for their birthdays and send the list to everybody they know," said Ms. Patton, of Della.com. "Right now, this is usually initiated by the person who's buying the gift, so this builds on existing behavior. So this season will be for introducing people to it. Next year it'll grow." Ravi Gururaj, president of IveBeenGood, is slightly more bullish. "Our research shows that consumers are yearning for technology like this," he said. "I think it's like e-commerce in general. We'll see a certain amount of growth this Christmas, but next year it'll be almost ubiquitous." Registry executives also said the rate of adoption would be increased by well-known e-commerce sites, like eToys and Victoria's Secret, that have added wish list features on their own. Noting that Amazon.com also just added a wish list feature, Scott Sangster, chief executive of Wishclick.com, said that "almost 100 percent of consumers somehow create a wish list -- be it verbally, written or emailed." "So they get it," he said. "Now they're just looking to improve on the process." Analysts tend to agree. "These sites are viable, there's no question," said David Sanderson, head of Bain & Company's e-commerce practice. The practice of consumers registering for wedding and baby gifts "is absolutely transferable to other events," he said, adding, "The reason people shop online is convenience, so if there is a more convenient way of dealing with gifts, customers will come and they will respond to that." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Jessica Herrin, a founder of Della.com, reviews design elements for its Web page. Della.com expanded from a wedding registry to an all-occasion site. It offers items from eight retailers, including Amazon.com, which owns a 20 percent stake in Della.com. (Peter DaSilva for the newyork Times)

title: Granddaddy of Computer Trade Shows Is Remaking Its Global Gigs
body: Comdex, the Las Vegas exhibition that is the king of computer trade shows and the jewel in the crown of its sponsor, ZD Events, opens today for the 20th consecutive year. In those two decades, Comdex has grown from a humble gathering of technology fans into the flagship in an international armada of trade shows. Even now, ZD Events is erecting booths in Israel for the opening of the first Comdex/Israel 99 show on Nov. 30 and mapping logistics for the third Expo CommChina South, which opens the same week in Guangzhou. A week later, it's the fourth annual Comdex India show in New Delhi. The sun, it seems, never sets on the ZD Events empire. Virtually every week, somewhere in the world, the company is setting up or tearing down a computer trade show. Today, ZD Events produces 100 shows, including 22 Comdexes, in 25 countries, and this year it is adding a show in Greece as well as in Israel. Next on its list of target markets are Sweden, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and Turkey. Comdex in Las Vegas is the undisputed top dog, the world's largest computer trade show. ZD Events says it expects the event, which attracted 4,000 computer enthusiasts and dealers in 1979, to draw roughly 202,000 people this year. They will trek through a million square feet of exhibition space in search of the next trend in computing technology. While that turnout would mark a decline from the show's peak of 215,000 in 1996, Comdex remains a cash cow for ZD Events and the biggest brand in the computer trade show business. But a huge transition is under way for Comdex. The glory days of the one-size-fits-all computer show are past, replaced by smaller, more focused gatherings -- an enormous and still-growing crop of executive seminars and single-subject conferences. As the high technology industry enters the post-PC era in which the Internet is king, it is hardly surprising that a decidedly PC-centric trade show would face substantial change. "Where people get their information is changing," said Alan Meckler, who founded the popular series of Internet World shows before selling to Penton Media Inc. last year. "The problem that Comdex has is that the PC is finished as an innovator." And with the Internet supplying customers with up-to-the-minute product information and industry news, they no longer must attend conventions to stay up to date. Even at Internet World's newyork show, which soared to 70,000 attendees in only a few years, attendance is flat, Mr. Meckler said, adding, "Niche shows are the rage now." ZD Events is already beginning to reinvent the show, even dubbing it "dotComdex" in its recent marketing campaign. "It's part of our branding campaign to try to put Comdex at the epicenter of all decisions about technology relating to the Internet economy," said Peter Shaw, executive vice president of ZD Events, which is part of Ziff-Davis Inc., the leading publisher of computer magazines. Thanks to its magazine publishing roots, ZD Events can offer technology companies something its competitors are hard pressed to match: packaged deals that include both a trade-show presence and advertising in some of the largest computer magazines in the business, said Mandana Hormoiza, an analyst at Lazard Freres & Company in newyork. At the same time, ZD Events is building a research and development unit called ZD Studios, charged with creating new, typically highly focused events for corporate clients like Sun Microsystems, for which it produces the JavaOne show. Still, the company is not about to abandon its general shows just yet. "We see there's a trend toward vertical industry events," Mr. Shaw said. "But if you look around the globe, every country with an information technology industry, except for the U.K., looks to have a center of gravity with a Comdex show that covers a broad spectrum." The Comdex brand has undergone transitions before. In 1995, the Interface Group, the company that founded the show, sold its trade show division to Softbank, the Japanese conglomerate, for $800 million. Within a year, Softbank also bought a majority stake in Ziff-Davis, eventually merging the two operations. Today, Softbank owns 70 percent of Ziff-Davis, which operates ZD Events as one of five units. Ziff-Davis stock, which went public in May 1998, has fluctuated widely in price in the last year -- from just above $8 a year ago to a high of $29 last March and a closing price of $17.1875 last Friday on the newyork Stock Exchange. Another Ziff-Davis unit, ZDNet, tracks its stock separately. In July, after Softbank announced that it would focus on Internet-only companies, Ziff-Davis said that it had hired investment bankers to help it sell off its business units. Softbank has already sold off Ziff-Davis's market research business to Harte-Hanks for $101 million in cash. Mr. Shaw said several potential suitors had expressed interest in buying all or parts of Ziff-Davis, though he declined to name them. Though Ziff-Davis has been steadily losing money the last few years, its losses have narrowed recently. For the third quarter, the company lost $14.9, compared with a loss of $27.6 million for the quarter last year. Revenue rose 10 percent, to $232 million. The company's trade show division accounted for much of the improvement; 23 percent of Ziff-Davis's revenue came from ZD Events. Besides Comdex, ZD Events' other big brands include Network+Interop, which is geared to network managers, and Seybold Seminars, a series of shows related to desktop publishing. But the division's future growth, say both analysts and Ziff-Davis officials, lies in ZD Studios. Despite uncertainty over its ownership, ZD Events continues to open new shows abroad, typically with local business partners familiar with the trade show landscape. In India, for example, the show organizer is Business India Expositions, an 11-year-old event management company. Without a local partner to arrange the show, ZD Events officials say, the risk of making a cultural gaffe or other business mistake is too high. In South America, for example, ZD Events has learned there is no point in presenting a keynote address in the morning because no one will show up until noon. "We think globally, but we try to act locally," said Jason Chudnofsky, chief executive of ZD Events. For local attendees, the draw is the big-name speakers from Silicon Valley that the Comdex brand is able to attract. The benefit for ZD Events is that its foreign shows tend to feed its unitedstates operations. As foreign companies learn the advantages of trade show marketing, Mr. Chudnofsky said, they start making the trek to the unitedstates. For American technology companies, consultants and analysts who attend ZD Events' overseas shows, the international circuit can be costly and exhausting, but many say it is worth the effort. "I send people to nearly all these events," said Howard Anderson, founder of the Yankee Group market research firm and most recently a venture capitalist. "It seems like it's one long, endless caravan." A caravan that starts and ends in Las Vegas. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart/Map: "Globe-Trotting" ZD Events, sponsor of trade shows all over the world, is constantly adding to its list of target markets. Map of the world shows sites of future ZD Events trade shows. (Source: Ziff-Davis)(pg. C1)  Graph: "Profits Prove Elusive" Ziff-Davis has been generating less revenue and losing more money. title: Net Investors Wary About Trade Talks With China
body: As the unitedstates and China continued marathon negotiations today on China's possible entry into the World Trade Organization, nobody watched the to-and-fro more anxiously than entrepreneurs and investors in the Internet. China's Internet industry has been in a state of suspension since September, when the nation's top communications official suddenly reaffirmed a longstanding ban on foreign investment in Chinese Internet service providers. While any trade agreement was not expected to deal specifically with the Internet, analysts said it could clarify Beijing's stance toward its bubbling online industry. For restless cyberspeculators, such clarity could not come soon enough. Intel, Yahoo and other American companies rushed into partnerships with Chinese Internet providers before Beijing's warning. But new deals are being held up as investors try to guess the intentions of the Chinese official, Wu Jichuan, the minister of information industries. "It has cast a big shadow over the industry," said Duncan Clark, a partner at BDA China, an Internet consulting firm in Beijing. "People think of it as unfinished business." Mr. Wu said he would issue new rules on foreign investment by the end of the year. A trade agreement could have a decisive influence on those regulations because it is expected to open China's telecommunications sector to outsiders. Mr. Wu has cited the existing ban on foreign ownership of telecommunications providers as the justification for keeping foreigners out of the Internet. "I find it very hard to believe there could be a W.T.O. deal at the same time China is imposing a complete ban on foreign investment in the Internet," said Gordon G. Chang, a partner who advises Internet companies in the Beijing office of the law firm of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison. Part of the problem in predicting China's Internet policy is that it crosses industry boundaries and intrudes into politically sensitive areas. Internet service providers, which connect users with state-run gateways to the global Internet, could be opened up as part of an agreement to open state telephone companies. But Internet content providers could face stricter regulations, like those put on the film and publishing industries. Beijing continues to block a handful of foreign Web sites, and the authorities have begun warning Chinese Internet providers not to provide links to news services on foreign Web sites. Some analysts say China could strangle the industry in its crib if it does not allow in foreigners. Although the number of online users in China almost doubles every year -- it is projected to grow from 2.4 million in 1998 to 16 million in 2003 -- China needs software technology from the unitedstates to develop more sophisticated businesses in areas like electronic commerce. "Even a momentary dip in enthusiasm in China will put it behind," Mr. Clark said. "It's like a hothouse flower: if you break the window and let in the cold air, you will kill it." Left unsaid is that China's Internet entrepreneurs could miss out on a rich payday. China.com, a hongkong-based Internet provider for the mainland market, raised $84 million in a recent stock offering on the Nasdaq exchange that valued the company at $1.5 billion. Mainland Web companies with names like Sina.com and Sohu.com had hoped to reap similar riches from the market. Publicly, the entrepreneurs are keeping up a confident front. They say they are plowing ahead with plans to raise capital and find foreign partners. They say Mr. Wu's recent dictum was part of a power struggle between conservatives and liberals in the Communist Party. And they say the government will come to accept the futility of trying to control a medium as anarchic as the Internet. "The attitude of most investors is, 'We're going to ignore this. Eventually Beijing will lighten up,' " said Hanson Cheah, the executive director of Asia Tech Ventures, a venture capital firm here that specializes in Internet companies. But he added, "If we're wrong, we're dead." Such caveats may be wise, given China's tense political climate and Beijing's mounting suspicion that the Internet can be used as a tool for subversion. Despite a sweeping crackdown on a spiritual movement known as Falun Gong, the government has been unable to prevent its members from using the Internet to spread news throughout China. The Chinese authorities recently arrested a student in northeastern China after he posted information about Falun Gong on the Internet. Beijing's ambivalence toward the Internet may benefit Taiwan and hongkong, which are far more hospitable to foreign investors and share a common language with their mainland neighbor. America Online recently announced a partnership with China.com to introduce an America Online service in hongkong. The company hopes to break into the mainland, but for now, it regards hongkong as a reasonable staging ground. Not all Chinese Internet entrepreneurs think open markets are an unqualified benefit. Edward Zeng, the founder of Sparkice I-Com Ltd., a three-year-old e-commerce venture in Beijing, said that letting in foreign companies without any restrictions could squash some nascent local companies. "AOL has the money, the technology and the global consumer base," Mr. Zeng said. "If they want to set up an AOL China, nobody could compete with them." The more likely possibility, he acknowledged, is that America Online would choose a Chinese partner to set up such a service. Mr. Zeng's own company is building an e-commerce business to sell Chinese products to consumers overseas. And he is scouting for foreign partners, a process that he says has been slowed down by the worries about China's Internet policy. So like the political bosses in Beijing, Mr. Zeng is torn. He believes that China's Internet industry would grow faster if it were open to foreigners. But he worries about small local companies like his. In addition to his global venture, Mr. Zeng runs a string of Internet cafes and is starting a domestic e-commerce business. He plainly does not relish the prospect of competing against Amazon.com or Ebay. Mr. Zeng, who spoke to Mr. Wu at a conference in Shanghai in October, said the minister's statements about the Internet had been misunderstood. Mr. Zeng said he believed the government's goal was not to seal off China's Internet business, but to set the stage for controlled development. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Lobbyist Turns to Internet To Influence Policy Makers
body: Richard Cook has never forgotten his frantic years as a young Congressional aide in the 1960's. The challenge of the job, which required constant research to track dozens of issues, has not changed since then, but the tools have. Now, as a lobbyist for the satellite company PanAmSat, Mr. Cook has started a campaign on the Internet that is directed toward busy Congressional aides. He contends that PanAmSat's competitors are outspending him 5 to 1 on the issue of privatization of access to satellite services and that the Internet is giving his client a better chance for equal access to important Congressional offices. To run the campaign, he hired Robert Arena, who handled the online side of Bob Dole's presidential campaign in 1996, as well as Internet campaigns for two governors, Christine Todd Whitman of New Jersey and George E. Pataki of newyork. Mr. Cook's tactic is a departure from conventional Internet campaigning, in which the goal is to generate hundreds of email messages to Congressional offices to show support for an issue. Mr. Cook's campaign, which is built around a Web site called satellitereform.org, is designed to influence only the influential. "This is much more powerful" than a grass-roots campaign, Mr. Arena said, "because this gets information in the hands of people who make the decisions." Statistics support the notion that the Internet paves the way to Congressional aides. A survey by the Holm Group in 1998 found that 88 percent of staff members in Congressional offices check the Internet for information every day. The target audience for Mr. Cook's campaign amounts to no more than 200 people. The Web site, with its spartan, easy-to-download design to accommodate busy policy advisers, serves as an online briefing book that changes when the issues change. It is augmented by email updates after each Congressional action that are subtly worded to reflect the perspective of PanAmSat. "The test for this site is, can they look at it and in 15 or 20 minutes come up with a one-page memo to their senator or Congressman?" Mr. Cook said. Considering the complexity of the issue, that goal is not easy to achieve. As the government moves to privatize access to satellite service that was once controlled by a quasi-governmental body called Intelsat, several companies are lobbying for the best terms under the changes. The battle is so contentious that the companies involved do not even agree on how many lobbyists are working on the issue. Mr. Cook said PanAmSat had devoted six or seven lobbyists, but that his competitors, Lockheed Martin and Comsat, between them have put 20 to 30 lobbyists on the case. His estimates of his competitors' staffing, he said, came from two decades of experience directing lobbying efforts for Lockheed Martin. Charles Manor, spokesman for Lockheed Martin Global Telecommunications, said both his company and PanAmSat had registered 19 lobbyists. He said Mr. Cook inflated the figures. PanAmSat, Mr. Cook said, wants to push for rapid privatization. The company's perspective came through in a recent email update to Congressional aides about a new bill for privatization. "This bill," it said, "promotes competition, opens foreign markets and creates new business opportunities for U.S. companies and high-tech jobs in the U.S." Mike Rawson, a key policy adviser for Senator Conrad Burns, a Montana Republican who is the author of influential legislation in the area, said he found Mr. Cook's Web site and email updates to be "a great resource." In the thick of battle, said Mr. Rawson, who tracks 20 to 30 issues in the telecommunications field, he would check the Web site every few days to keep up. "I found it to be an extremely smart use of resources," he said. Sheila Krumholz, who tracks lobbying for the Center for Responsive Politics, a watchdog group, described the Internet lobbying tactic as "a frugal and public-minded thing to do." "It seems like a cost-effective way of doing business and one that would benefit the issue," she said. Mr. Cook said the low-cost method would "enable some fairly small organizations to do something innovative and catch up with the well-financed organizations." Of course, he predicted that the largest lobbying efforts would embrace the idea just as quickly. "I think it's going to radically change lobbying in Washington and state capitals," Mr. Cook said. "There won't be a lobbying effort in a year's time that doesn't have a component of this." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: As the unitedstates gets ready to privatize access to satellite service, PanAmSat is offering its perspective on a Web site, satellitereform.org.

title:
INVESTING;
Latest Lure On the Web: Free Trades
body: THE price war among online brokerage firms has escalated so rapidly that the stock trade has gone from being a commodity to a come-on. As commissions for executing stock trades sank lower and lower, Wall Street experts said it was only a matter of time before somebody started giving away trades. Well, that time has come: the American Express Company on Monday began promoting an online brokerage service with commission-free stock purchases for anybody who deposits $25,000. That offer, which American Express officials say is not temporary, has caused a lot of head-shaking in an industry that already abounds in gimmickry. To entice investors, online brokers are tossing in everything from trips to Hawaii to $100 bills. "It's getting very messy," said Stephen D. McDonald, chief executive of TD Waterhouse Group, an online brokerage firm that charges $12 for some trades. "Next thing you know, we'll be giving away toasters." There are no small appliances on the immediate horizon. But the firms have started so many giveaways that even their executives have trouble keeping track of what is being dangled before investors' eyes. Last week, DLJdirect, the online brokerage arm of the investment bank Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, was using ads on financial Web sites, making two offers simultaneously to new account holders: investors who knew where to look could choose to accept a credit of $100 or six months of free Internet access, which would be paid in the form of a $120 credit. E*Trade Group went a little further this month when it started offering $150 to customers of a competitor, the Discover Brokerage Direct unit of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, for switching to E*Trade. That was double the offers of $75 that E*Trade and Discover had made for opening accounts. Ameritrade, an Omaha-based firm that charges $8 for some trades, is trumpeting an offer that may be worth more than those that E*Trade and DLJdirect have on the table. In exchange for opening a new account, customers can get two round-trip plane tickets to London, Mexico or Hawaii. The catch is that the tickets are free only after a customer pays for a nondiscounted, seven-night stay at certain hotels. "There's a lot of crazy things going on in terms of marketing and account acquisition," said James Marks, an analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston. Online brokerages are spending so much money on advertising and promotion for very similar services, he said, that they find themselves "in a position like American Express where you have to come up with almost a gimmick that isn't sustainable." Mr. Marks recently turned cautious on the stocks of some on-line brokers, including Ameritrade and E*Trade. Although he was an early proponent of heavy marketing spending, he now fears that some online brokers are spending far too much to acquire new accounts. This summer's slowdown in online account activity, he said, raised doubts about whether the online brokers could continue their growth pace. Shares of some of them, which ran up sharply in the first half of the year, are now about 50 percent off their highs, despite a rally on Friday. "The accounts that these guys really want are the investors that will take out margin loans," or borrow to buy stocks, Mr. Marks said. But advertising low-margin interest rates does not attract customers the way free trades or other promotions do, he said. AS cluttered as the landscape has become, American Express managed to steal the spotlight, if only briefly, by creating a new business model for the brokerage industry. While some of the biggest Wall Street firms are struggling to shift from commission-based models to fee-based models, American Express has decided to charge neither commissions nor fees. "We thought that this is kind of an interesting way we can differentiate ourselves," said Ruediger Adolf, a senior vice president at American Express. While Mr. Adolf prefers not to describe the free stock trades as a loss leader, American Express is giving away a service that costs it at least several dollars to provide. Mr. McDonald estimates that it costs the biggest and most efficient brokerage firms at least $8 to carry out a stock trade ordered electronically. The cost for firms that have to pay others to execute and process their trades could run as high as $25, he said. "We make money in other ways," Mr. Adolf said, referring to the interest that American Express earns on the cash in customers' accounts and on loans that customers take to buy stocks. "With traditional brokers, this would be a very, very dangerous game because you fundamentally are cannibalizing your main business." In other words, American Express has nothing to lose by giving away trades -- except money. Mr. Adolf declined to say how much American Express expected to lose on the commission-free trades, but on the whole, he said, "we think we absolutely can make money in this business." The company is not making all stock trades free. Customers with at least $100,000 in their accounts pay no commissions, but those with less than $25,000 in their accounts pay $14.95 a trade. For the people in between, American Express came up with an interesting twist: they can buy stocks without paying a commission, but must pay $14.95 each time they sell shares of a company. That move, unusual for a brokerage, comes directly out of the mutual fund playbook. Many fund companies let investors buy fund shares without a sales charge, but charge one when the shares are sold. A key component of the plan: Mr. Adolf said American Express did not want to attract the type of investor for whom free trades would be most appealing -- the hyperactive trader. What could sound better to somebody who spends his days buying and selling stocks than an account that charges no fee and no trading commissions? Instead, American Express, like some other financial services firms offering low-priced trades, preaches long-term investing. "We do not subscribe to very aggressive trading strategies, particularly day-trading," Mr. Adolf said. To head off a rush of day traders, American Express has put in a speed bump: Even those customers with $100,000 will have to pay $14.95 to sell a stock the same day they bought it. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Cartoon (Chris Murphy)

title: Christie's Rules Out Joining Mass-Market Web Ventures
body: Christie's said yesterday that it had decided against joining forces with an online giant like eBay or the Walt Disney Company's Go.com to offer its auctions online and that it had merged its six-month-old Internet unit into its marketing department. Christie's archrival, Sotheby's, announced an alliance with Amazon.com five months ago, but after months of discussions, Christie's officials said they had concluded that a link with a giant online retailer risked diluting the Christie's brand name. Instead, the officials said, Christie's will update Christies.com, its Web site, so that over time it will be able to offer its clients online bidding for all its auctions. "We made a decision to protect the integrity of our brand name," said Edward Dolman, Christie's managing director in America, when asked why the company chose not to link up with ebay or Go.com. "We made the decision not to go after high-volume, low-value merchandise with a separate team of business-getters because it didn't make commercial sense." Christie's has decided to concentrate its energies on the high end of the business rather than going after the mass market as the Sotheby's-Amazon.com alliance has done. "It would potentially take us in the wrong direction," Mr. Dolman said. "We seek greater efficiency and market share at the top end of the business." Mr. Dolman added that he believed that the company's change of focus would better protect the core of Christie's business, selling multimillion-dollar fine and decorative arts. "It will make us increasingly more competitive," he said. Christie's plans could not be more different from Sotheby's, an unusual situation for two companies that for more than 100 years have slavishly copied each other's strategies. While Christie's sees the online business as an extension of its existing auction business, Sotheby's $25 million investment in the online business is intended to broaden its client base by offering millions of Internet users an enormous sampling of merchandise, from low-end poster art to jewelry and eventually even fine art. Sotheby's has put together a team of more than 100 people to work on its Internet business, which is scheduled to start sometime before the end of the year. It has also signed up 4,600 dealers who have agreed to sell exclusively through Sotheby's.com. Its link with Amazon means Sotheby's will be starting two Web sites before the end of the year: Sothebys.Amazon.com for lower-priced merchandise and Sothebys .com for more traditional auction fare. Both will offer goods vetted either by the dealers selling online or by experts at the auction house. Christie's will not have to worry about vetting merchandise for the Internet since everything it auctions has already been authenticated by its own experts. Mr. Dolman declined to say just how much money Christie's planned to invest in upgrading its Web site.  But over time, he said, the firm will not only have the capability to hold online auctions, but it will also be able to offer multimedia viewing capabilities for every item offered for sale, email chat rooms with specialists, and virtual reality tours of its exhibitions. To do this, Mr. Dolman said, Christie's expects to spend tens of millions of dollars. Christie's has already begun to test online auctions. In June, it used the Internet to sell 100 guitars that belonged to Eric Clapton, and last month, it held a live Webcast of a sale of Marilyn Monroe's property. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
CONNECTIONS;
Off the Page and Onto the Screen: An Encyclopedic Mirror of What?
body: In the early years of this fading millennium, two words often appeared in encyclopedia titles: "speculum" (mirror) and "imago" (image). Encyclopedias were meant to reflect the world while also giving it shape. And what enormous mirrors they were! One Chinese encyclopedia from the 13th century filled 240 volumes. The German-language General Encyclopedia (1818-89) reached volume 167 and was never even completed. These textual universes were also meant to reflect the divisions and categories of the surrounding world. The 10th-century Arabic encyclopedia, Mafatih al-'Ulum (Key to the Sciences), was split into two sections: indigenous knowledge (including jurisprudence, secretarial duties and history) and foreign knowledge (philosophy, logic, alchemy). One 12th-century European encyclopedia devoted an entire section to a chronicle of events since Satan's fall. The Enlightenment changed the categories, but not the ambition. Francis Bacon, in the plans for his encyclopedia, intended "to commence a total reconstruction of sciences, arts, and all human knowledge, raised upon the proper foundations." Until a few hundred years ago, merely alphabetical organization was considered to be, in Coleridge's words, a sign of "impudent ignorance" that presented the world as a "huge, unconnected miscellany." Forgive the encyclopedic introduction. I have been reading the 25,000-word entry on encyclopedia in the Britannica. Last month -- after sales of the $1,500 set dropped 80 percent in the early 1990's, stumbling into the Internet era a few years ago with a failed paid subscription site and being sold to a Swiss financier -- the Britannica, the oldest and largest English encyclopedia, became freely available on the Internet (at www.britannica.com). Britannica is changing from an encyclopedia into a "portal," an entry point into the Web, including news (from The Washington Post), weather, stock quotes and email. Advertisements, tailor-made for encyclopedia entries, will provide income. There will also be be "e-commerce" deals and an online store. Britannica wants to become an Internet brand. This may have some advantages. Jorge Cauz, Britannica's senior vice president for marketing, says a 100-member editorial staff is setting up three-year cycles of continuous revision. About 50 percent of the text will remain intact over time; the total text will end up being larger by about a third, and "broader topical references" will be included. But the very nature of the encyclopedia may also change. From its first edition (1768) in Scotland, the Britannica's world mirror was formed out of meticulously molded smaller ones. In its 14 editions, the Britannica published classic entries: Swinburne on Keats, John Muir on Yosemite, Freud on psychoanalysis, Houdini on conjuring, Einstein on space-time. The Britannica's alphabetical organization, far from creating "a huge unconnected miscellany," became a sign of both humility and grandeur: humility because it acknowledged that no system could encompass the world in all its complexity and grandeur because it asserted that there was still a way to present that immensity for human delectation. But about a decade ago this model changed; it has been most clearly reflected in Microsoft's CD-ROM encyclopedia, Encarta. The new structure of knowledge is not conceptual or alphabetical. It is technological. "Features" organize the encyclopedic world: time lines, panoramic views, videos, audio snippets, virtual tours, games. Encarta's actual content, in fact, often seems an accompaniment to the razzle-dazzle technology. Monthly updates are available on the Internet for a subscription fee and each year has seen welcome improvements. But most of the text comes from Funk & Wagnall's and Collier's -- decidedly second-rate encyclopedias. So don't expect Encarta to be too revealing about "encyclopedias," for example (an entry gives incorrect dates for the Britannica). Even a subject close to Encarta's technological heart -- the "Internet" -- is oddly treated; the Encarta 2000 edition has little information after 1997 and a sidebar is offered from an antediluvian 1994 entry. Patchwork and miscellany seem more common than systematic interpretations, a symptom perhaps of hypertext and multimedia obsessions. But the new technology isn't a problem in itself. It can provide unusual opportunities to search, listen and watch, as in the fascinating new release of Encarta Africana (Microsoft), with its surveys of black American and African culture. And there are times when the technology, even if imperfectly applied to a dated text, is still of great use, as in the invaluable CD-ROM of the Encyclopedia Judaica (Judaica Multimedia). Even Britannica's own CD-ROM uses technology to illumine the text. The danger comes when technology, instead of being a tool, determines the content. For Britannica, though, the greatest risk may be not in technological excess, but in Internet access. If income depends on e-commerce, will emphases change to court clicks? Will as many resources be devoted to a rarely consulted scholarly entry on, say, Baroque opera as to a popular and commercially supported entry on, say, rock music? Right now, the Web site offers a "Britannica.com happening" featuring "psychedelic rock": "turn off your mind," it urges, "relax and float downstream." If systematic changes take place -- and the company insists they will not -- the new categories of knowledge won't be in history or divinity or the alphabet; they will be in revenue and click count. Britannica.com would be constantly creating itself in response to the demands of its readers. That sort of speculum might accurately reflect the current universe, but not quite in the way the creators of great encyclopedias had in mind. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A Web page of the Encyclopaedia Brittanica, one of the reference books available on the Internet.

title: Election Panel Clears a Use Of Web Sites By Campaigns
body: Federal regulators said on Wednesday that Web sites created by independent supporters of a candidate do not count as campaign contributions, partly clearing a murky area of election law. The Federal Election Commission said it would consider homemade Web sites to be a form of volunteer activity. Links from an independent site to an official campaign site are also not considered contributions unless the manager of the independent site normally charged for links, the commission said in an opinion. The opinion was a response to an inquiry from the presidential campaign of Gov. George W. Bush of Texas. The Bush campaign raised the questions out of concern that if links and Web sites built by supporters qualify as contributions, then those expenses could cause the campaign to be fined for exceeding contribution limits. The Bush staff had been discouraging supporters from building such sites in recent months. Benjamin L. Ginsberg, a lawyer for the Bush campaign, called the opinion "a very sane and rational way to approach this." "It will allow people who want to help the campaign to help the campaign," Mr. Ginsberg said. "It will let political participation on the Internet gain strength." The commission also exempted individuals whose online activities were unknown to the campaign, and the opinion stated that the campaign had no obligation to police the Internet to track that activity. Those who have tracked the commission's approach to Internet campaigning said the decision shows a more relaxed approach. "That's good news for us," said Michele Hoferitza of Syracuse, Utah, who has organized a group of Web sites built by Bush supporters. While the opinion makes clear that campaigns are not responsible for the Internet activities of supporters, the legal status of those same people who create sites encouraging the election or defeat of a candidate remains uncertain. In past interpretations, the commission has ruled that such people could be required to register as political action committees if they spend at least $250. That issue remained beyond the scope of the questions placed before the commission by the Bush committee. "They have yet to address the individual who is doing this and spending large sums of money," said Joe Sandler, a Democratic lawyer who specialized in election law. From the perspective of the commission, Mr. Sandler said, "some guy sitting at home sending email or building a home page, we're going to treat him as a volunteer and not worry about." http://www.nytimes.com

title: In E-Politics, Clinton's Former Adviser Still Plays by Own Rules
body: One of the best-known veterans of old-fashioned hard-ball politics, Dick Morris, has turned to the Internet and shaken up e-politics. Mr. Morris's method of working the Internet involves asking visitors to vote yes or no on issues featured on his Web site, which converts the votes into thousands of email messages that are sent to elected officials. That technique has provoked outrage among longtime Internet political experts, who say it should be the visitors to the Web site who are selecting the issues, not Mr. Morris. They also object to his flooding elected officials with thousands of email messages that could obscure the correspondence sent by individuals. The experts characterize Mr. Morris as a member of the old guard who is blundering into a medium he does not understand. The Internet venture has also brought Mr. Morris, a former adviser to President Clinton, into a dispute with the White House over whether staff members there had blocked email sent from his Web site, Vote.com, which went online Oct. 31. In an email message sent on Friday to users of his profit-making Web site, Mr. Morris wrote that the site had sent more than 82,000 email messages to the White House in a week. He said that after an initial rush of messages, the White House had blocked all email from Vote.com, then set its computer "to accept only 70 emails per hour from our site." A White House spokesman, Barry Toiv, said email from Mr. Morris's Web site had never been blocked. Further, Mr. Toiv said, the practice of slowing email is a standard method of deterring the "mail bombing" technique used by hackers to cripple Web servers. In his message on Friday to users of his site, Mr. Morris wrote: "What an odd response from an elected administration to hearing the views of those who vote. It appears that the Internet administration is burning the bridge to the 21st century." But in a telephone interview on Monday, Mr. Morris said he saw "that the White House did have a point." He added that he had started rounding up the votes cast by users on the site on a variety of issues and consolidating them in packets of 1,000, to be delivered in a single email message that lists all the individuals' email addresses. Nevertheless, Mr. Morris has called the routing of individuals' votes on issues to elected officials online "a megaphone that gives an opportunity for anyone who wants to be heard." But political strategists who specialize in use of the Internet denounce that practice. "From the perspective of the Internet, this just adds to email gridlock," said Joe Rodota, the founder of an election-oriented Web site, FAQvoter.com. Mr. Morris's presentation of issues for voters to consider also runs counter to the spirit of the Internet, said Mr. Rodota, whose profit-making site allows voters to set the agenda by allowing them to address questions to candidates. The site runs all questions as received. "This is exactly what a Washington insider would think the Internet is all about," Mr. Rodota said of Mr. Morris's site. "They control the information that flows to the voter, and the content is heavily controlled." Mr. Morris responded by saying: "They believe we're undermining the goal of electronic democracy by exercising it. My question to them is, why the hell haven't you done this yet?"  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Users Now Exceed 100 Million
body: The number of adults using the Internet in the unitedstates has surpassed 100 million, a market research report said this week, with surfers becoming increasingly savvy about ways to use the Web. The Strategis Group, a Washington-based market research firm, said in its Internet User Trends study for mid-1999 that one half of all adults in the unitedstates now use the Internet. The figure is up from 65 million in mid-1998. "Not only is half of the population online," said Jeff Moore, an analyst with Strategis, "Internet users are more experienced and have become significantly more sophisticated in their use of the Internet as a tool for communication, commerce and learning." Strategis said 77 percent of Internet users send emails with files or attachments every week, a task that was difficult to impossible for many novice users. The average user sends more than six emails a day, and the proportion of total users who surf daily has risen to 60 percent among home users and 69 percent among work users. More than 20 percent have created or updated a Web page in the last three months, the study found. The International Data Corporation, another market research firm, said it expected the number of Internet users in the unitedstates to grow to 177 million by the end of 2003. Worldwide, IDC said, the number of users is expected to grow to 502 million by 2003, from more than 142 million in 1998. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Lands' End Sales Warning
body: Lands' End Inc., themail-order and online apparel retailer, set off a 30 percent decline in its stock price today by warning that it expects its sales to decline in the next few quarters as it cuts the size of its catalogs to focus on the Internet. The warning came as the company posted third-quarter results that were better than expected. Its shares fell $24.8125, to $58.50. "The reason has to be management's comment that sales in the fourth quarter will be flat to slightly down," said Kevin Silverman, an analyst with ABN AMRO. Lands' End said it expected a decline in sales in the fourth quarter and in the first half of next year as a result of its decision to reduce the size and circulation of its catalogs. The circulation cuts, which are being made to eliminate unprofitablemailings and to manage the company's shift from print to e-commerce, will continue through the first half of fiscal 2001, the company said. Lands' End plans to reduce circulation of its primary monthly catalogs by 5 to 10 percent through the first half of next year, compared with a 20 percent reduction in the second half of fiscal 2000. The company said it earned $8.8 million, or 28 cents a diluted share, in its third quarter, which ended on Oct. 29. A year earlier, Lands' End earned $347,000, or 1 cent a share. Securities analysts surveyed by First Call/Thomson Financial expected the retailer to report earnings of 25 cents a share. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft and Tandy in Internet Agreement
body: The Microsoft Corporation announced a strategic agreement with the Tandy Corporation yesterday to spotlight Microsoft's Internet products and services within Tandy's Radio Shack stores. As part of the deal, Microsoft will make an equity investment of $100 million in RadioShack.com, Tandy's recently started online store. Links to the online store will have premier placement across all of MSN, Microsoft's Internet service, including eShop, MSN's online shopping service. Tandy will create a Microsoft "store within a store" in each of its 7,000 retail outlets. Microsoft will provide money for fixtures, PC's and the design of the in-store boutique areas, which are expected to be completed late next year. The boutiques will feature Microsoft products and services, including MSN Internet Access, WebTV, Windows CE-based handheld devices, MSN mobile solutions and Microsoft home networking. Radio Shack salespeople will sign up customers for MSN Internet service, including a version of MSN co-branded with Radio Shack, and will offer installation. Radio Shack will earn an undisclosed portion of Microsoft's revenues from the Internet customers it signs up. The agreement dispells rumors that Tandy was planning a similar agreement with America Online, under which the online service would be Radio Shack's preferred Internet service provider, or I.S.P. Although Radio Shack stores feature personal computers made by the Compaq Computer Corporation that come loaded with AOL software, customers will not be aided in subscribing to AOL, but they will be encouraged to sign up with MSN, said Leonard Roberts, Tandy's chairman, president and chief executive. "The economic model with Microsoft definitely won out," Mr. Roberts said in a telephone interview. "While we went looking for an I.S.P. partner, what we needed was a total connectivity partner. The logical and only choice was Microsoft." Microsoft shares closed at $89.625, up $2.50, in Nasdaq trading; Tandy shares gained $6.25, or 9.59 percent, to close at $71.4375 on the newyork Stock Exchange. America Online shares slid $2.75, to close at $143.25, in Nasdaq trading. Analysts said the deal was a win-win that would help Microsoft spread its Internet business to a mass market. At the same time, they said it would establish Radio Shack's credentials as an online services provider, much the way its partnership with Sprint helped make it a powerhouse in cellular phones, where it claims 70 percent of retail sales. "The resurgent Tandy has done a beautiful job with the store-within-a-store concept for Sprint and Compaq, and I think Microsoft recognized that," said Seymour Merrin, president of Merrin Information Services. "It's really a unique entity, Radio Shack, and this sort of thing will play very well there. This should be a win-win, and the customer can't lose." Microsoft and Tandy have actually had a close relationship dating to the early days of the personal computer, when the then-fledgling software company provided a version of the Basic programming language for the TRS-80, an early PC. Microsoft also created the simple operating system and applications for the Radio Shack Model 100, a pioneering notebook computer. Waxing a bit nostalgic on a conference call with securities analysts, William H. Gates, Microsoft's chairman and chief executive, recalled, "That was one of the last projects where I got to write the majority of the code myself." But Steve Ballmer, Microsoft's president, said in a telephone interview that it was Radio Shack's more recent track record that made the partnership attractive. "We know Radio Shack well, but we had to be reminded that Radio Shack is really a unique entity," he said, noting the small size of the stores, and the training the salespeople receive. "They really work with a partner to tell a story."  http://www.nytimes.com
