title: Allstate Poised to Sell Insurance Over Telephone and Internet
body: In a major shift in sales strategy, the Allstate Corporation said yesterday it would begin selling auto and homeowners' insurance and other coverage over the telephone and the Internet. The company, one of the nation's largest insurers, said it was not abandoning its force of 15,200 agents. But it expected them to continue selling and to provide service for customers who wanted personal attention after buying coverage through the new methods. Even so, Allstate's embrace of the new technology -- the first major insurer with a large sales force to fully do so -- means the dawning of a new day for the agents. The company's trend toward converting its agents to independent contractors -- who pay for office expenses and health insurance, instead of being Allstate employees -- is accelerating; by July, there will be virtually no agents on staff. That will mean less job security for the 6,500 agents who are still in process of changing to independent contractors. But company executives said that it would also mean opportunities for higher commissions, more freedom to expand and, for the first time, the ability for agents who are retiring to sell their book of clients to another agent rather than simply pass them along without a farewell profit. In another jolt to its employees, Allstate, whose shares are down significantly from a year ago, said yesterday that it would cut 4,000 back-office positions, about 10 percent of its administrative staff, from its payroll by the end of next year as part of a plan to reduce operating expenses by $600 million annually. Edward M. Liddy, the chief executive of Allstate, said the savings would roughly equal the new expenses of setting up the telephone and computer operations and promoting them nationally. Allstate and other major insurers, have been watching the rapid growth of smaller companies like Geico, a Berkshire Hathaway subsidiary that sells its policies only over the telephone, and the Progressive Corporation, which uses the phone, the Internet and independent agents. Traditional insurers have tried to figure out how to use the new sales approaches without inciting rebellions among their agents. Allstate believes it has struck a balance by, for example, promising to pay local agents a commission of 2 percent to 3.5 percent for Internet and telephone sales of auto policies to customers in the agents' territories. In exchange for those commissions -- which compare with commissions for an auto policy of about 8 percent for staff agents and 10 percent for independent contractors -- the agents will be expected to help any client who asks for information or submits a claim. In addition, customers who give their approval will be referred to local agents; the agents will receive full commissions on any sales they develop as a result. Even so, analysts said, many agents may interpret Allstate's move to phone and Internet operations as their own company creating competition for them. "I would imagine a lot of agents will hate this deal," said Brian Sullivan, the editor of Auto Insurance Report, a national newsletter based in Dana Point, Calif. Ronald W. Frank, an analyst at Salomon Smith Barney, said that the company and the agents had come to an inevitable turning point, with little choice but to follow customer demand. "If the customer wants to do business over the Internet, the agent isn't going to see that business no matter what," he said. "The agents have to realize they're competing with the Internet whether they like it or not. " One factor that may temper any sense of competition between the company and its agents is that Allstate plans to offer its insurance at one price, regardless of how the customer buys it. Geico boasts it can save clients as much as 15 percent on auto coverage, partly because it pays no commissions to agents. Many companies offering policies on the Internet have yet to pass along to customers the benefit of lower operating expenses. But analysts say that is likely to become the trend. What has driven the rapid growth in insurance sales over the phone and Internet has been convenience and, in many cases, lower prices. Allstate is betting that customers will value its brand name and the services of its agents and claims representatives more than a rock-bottom price. "The key question no one can now answer for sure," said Weston Hicks, an analyst at J. P. Morgan Securities, "is to what extent homeowners' and auto insurance are becoming commodities in which the only thing people care about is price." http://www.nytimes.com

title: 'Cybersquatting' Measure Attached to Satellite-TV Bill
body: Hoping to fend off a threatened veto of a controversial bill to outlaw speculating in Internet addresses, or "cybersquatting," Congressional leaders have attached it to a bill on satellitetelevision that has already passed the House and is awaiting a vote in the Senate. The revival of the anti-cybersquatting legislation as part of the Satellite Television Home Viewers Act is a big victory for the Motion Picture Association of America and other groups that have sought to protect trademarks online. The bill passed the House Tuesday night by a vote of 408 to 8. The Internet language was inserted into the satellite bill because the White House had threatened to veto anti-cybersquatting legislation. But the administration favors the satellite bill as a way to help satellite-TV companies compete with cable operators. Senator Phil Gramm, a Texas Republican, may have thrown a monkey wrench into that strategy, however, by threatening to block final passage of the satellite bill because he opposes a financing provision. The Internet speculation language would allow trademark holders as well as politicians and athletes -- groups that increasingly have been the targets of cybersquatters -- to take civil action against anyone who registers celebrity names or trademarks as Internet addresses with hopes of reselling them at a profit. Trademark holders would be able to sue cybersquatters in the nation where the domain name was registered and seek up to $100,000 in damages. Those provisions were sought by the Motion Picture Association of America and other groups representing trademark holders, who say their members have spent millions of dollars in recent years buying the rights to domain names, which cost only $70 to register. Cybersquatters routinely register movie titles, company names or the names of products, then demand large sums to turn them over to trademark holders. Personal names would also be protected, although those suits could not seek monetary damages. Among the proponents of that language was Senator Orrin G. Hatch, the Judiciary Committee chairman and a Republican presidential candidate, who earlier this year was solicited by cybersquatters who had registered names that could be used for campaign Web sites, like hatch2000.com. Opponents of the legislation say they fear its impact on Internet free speech and worry that it would put at a disadvantage small companies that might have a legitimate claim to the same name or word as a larger company's registered trademark. "The bill will increase the problem of reverse domain name hijacking, where someone who covets a domain name but has no legal claim to it tries to coerce the domain name owner into handing over the domain name," said Carl Oppedahl, a Colorado trademark lawyer. There have already been several highly publicized cases of reverse domain name hijacking, including that of a young boy nicknamed Pokey who almost lost pokey.org to the toy company that owned the rights to the Gumby and Pokey characters, and a young girl named Veronica whose Web site was sought by Archie Comics. "The $100,000 is going to be used to intimidate people," said A. Michael Froomkin, a University of Miami law professor who has been closely following international attempts to crack down on cybersquatting. "In a lot of these cases, the mom-and-pop type operations will just go quietly." Michael Heltzer, government relations manager of the International Trademark Association, said groups like his were only trying to control the "bad-faith actors." "We were looking for an effective and evenhanded piece of legislation," Mr. Heltzer said. The White House last month opposed the cybersquatting legislation, saying it preferred to see rules governing such disputes set by the global network's executive body, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, or Icann. Icann is the nonprofit entity picked by the Administration last year to run the Internet's domain name system. The group recently enacted a rule that sends all claims related to trademarks to arbitration panels. The idea of the Icann policy is to reduce the cost of litigation and make sure there is a uniform set of rules that can be applied worldwide. Icann officials have declined to comment on the Congressional bill. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Do You Know Who's Watching You? Do You Care?
body: CALL L. L. Bean, the clothing and outdoor gear company, don't identify yourself in any way, place your order, and see what happens. If you have shopped there before and you're calling from your home telephone number, the folks there know it -- even if you've blocked Caller ID. They know where you live. And they have your credit card number. In the course of the transaction, the cheerful sales clerk on the other end of the line will happily recite that information to you, letting you dispense with the tedium of giving your full credit card number or spelling your street name. This is not a new development. L. L. Bean has had such caller-identification technology in place for years. But the company began using it openly with customers only recently, in the belief that they would no longer be spooked, said Rich Donaldson, an L. L. Bean spokesman. That's not to say that L. L. Bean executives think that people are ready to give up their privacy. To the contrary, L. L. Bean believes that, as always, people are willing to share private information with those they trust, and it believes that it has its customers' trust. The company may be right. It reports that customers love the convenience. In fact, one recent caller was so charmed by the personal treatment that she thought the saleswoman recognized her voice. "That's a trusting relationship with that business," said Marc Rotenberg, executive director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a privacy advocacy group in Washington. Mr. Rotenberg said L. L. Bean's customers had faith that the company would not abuse the information by reselling it. So much for blind faith. Even L. L. Bean recently began exchanging customers' names and addresses (but not other kinds of personal information) with other companies, which captures perfectly the complications and contradictions of a giant policy issue: What are the acceptable limits to privacy? For all the attention it gets, privacy is an elusive concept. It means something different to everyone, and when it comes to behavior, both as consumers and as citizens, people draw the line at different points on the privacy spectrum. At one extreme are the privacy fundamentalists, who denounce the potential abuse on the part of direct marketers and their increasingly sophisticated personal-profiling techniques. Privacy absolutists abhor supermarket discount cards and are vigilant about keeping their names off lists of any kind. One person who vigorously guards his privacy is Jason Catlett, president of Junkbusters, a Web site that helps people protect their privacy online. He shops on the Web but from a small number of sites. He also loves the convenience of buying from catalogs, but he minimizes the number of companies he purchases from so he can keep a low profile in marketing databases. When shopping online and offline, Mr. Catlett often renders his address a little differently so he can track who has sold his name to others against his instructions. He owns credit cards -- four, to be exact -- but pays for many things with cash. He steers clear of supermarket discount cards, which require surrendering not only his address and telephone number but also, every time the card is used, details about his shopping patterns. And he never fills out warranty cards. "A warranty card is the fast track to junk mail central," he said. At the other end of the spectrum are people who simply don't care who knows what about them. They figure that privacy is a thing of the past anyway, so why fight? Most Americans, however, seem to fall somewhere in between. They are willing to part with personal information as long as they get something in return, and as long as they know what is to be done with the information. They are happy to carry supermarket discount cards. They are annoyed when they get new computers and must re-enter all the information needed for one-click ordering at Amazon.com. These same people, however, are highly protective of their medical records and are generally appalled when they learn of clandestine data collection practices. The recent news, for instance, that Real Networks had been tracking the musical tastes of people who use the RealJukebox software to play CD's on their computers generated indignant messages all over cyberspace. Mindy Zuckerman, a freelance producer of corporate events in San Francisco, is one of those who pick and choose their privacy issues. Ms. Zuckerman has discount cards from her neighborhood Safeway and Lucky supermarkets. Both are imprinted with her real name. Yet when she sends contributions to charities, she includes a note requesting that her name and address not be distributed. She occasionally shops over the Internet. And when she called to order flowers recently from Flowers U.S.A., which she uses frequently, she was surprised that she was asked for her credit card number. She assumed the store already had it. It bothers Ms. Zuckerman that her Social Security number is her identification for her health insurance, and she has asked her bank to use a different means of identification. She doesn't mind the cameras that record license plates at parking garages. Yet she owns a shredder, and she shreds anything with her name on it. "I don't imagine people are dumpster-diving in Noe Valley," she said, referring to her neighborhood in San Francisco. "But I'm originally from newyork. Maybe I just brought my paranoia with me." The idea of privacy as something entitled to legal protection was most famously expressed in 1890, when Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis, writing in the Harvard Law Review, defined privacy as "the right to be let alone." While Warren and Brandeis were more passive, appropriate for their era, the information age called for a new formulation. In 1967, Alan F. Westin, a privacy expert who is a professor emeritus of public law and government at Columbia University, gave the concept a more assertive thrust when he defined privacy in "Privacy and Freedom" (Atheneum) as the right of individuals to determine for themselves when, how and to what extent information about them is communicated to others. Since Dr. Westin came up with that description, the gathering of information about individuals has become far more widespread and automatic. Such information is continually being recorded, while computers are busy merging, purging, sorting and selecting information to produce personal profiles and pieces of direct mail that are tailored to consumers' habits. What used to be easily protected private information is now there for the taking, thanks not to changing attitudes but to changes in technology. Thousands of computers linked to the Web track individual patterns of online buying and behavior, which are translated in turn into highly sophisticated marketing strategies. "The World Wide Web is direct marketing on steroids," Mr. Catlett said. "With the Web, the process of gathering information on consumers and messaging them with new offers is vastly accelerated in speed and reduced to a very low cost." Privacy advocates say it's fine to be practical like Ms. Zuckerman, as long as you really know what is being done with the information you give away. "The missing piece here is that consumers aren't always being told the consequences of all the data collection," said Robert M. Gellman, a privacy consultant in Washington. But people differ in their attitudes toward data collection. Dr. Westin said that for the 25 years or so that he has been conducting public opinion surveys (usually financed by corporations), the general breakdown of how people draw the line when it comes to their privacy has remained the same: roughly one-fourth of the population is vigilant about its privacy, and roughly the same number of people are indifferent. About 55 percent of those he surveys are what Dr. Westin called privacy pragmatists, people who want to know what benefits are in it for them if they allow information about themselves to be collected. These pragmatists also want to know what risks they are running and what safeguards are in place. If they trust the organization asking for the information, Dr. Westin said, they are more likely to surrender information. Mr. Rotenberg, of the privacy information center, is skeptical about those findings, arguing that people's desire for privacy may change at different times in their lives, or even in the course of a day. For that reason, he favors legislation that would give individuals control over the use of their personal information. Mr. Gellman said supermarket discount cards were a good example of the kinds of privacy trade-offs many people were willing to make. Roughly 27,000 food stores in the nation provide cards that offer discounts or other promotions to customers who sign up; those customers' personal information can then be linked to records of what they buy.  More than half the customers of those stores have signed up for the cards, and more are signing up every day, according to the Food Marketing Institute, a trade group in Washington. "The supermarket loyalty card is the least intrusive of any kind of loyalty promotion," said Todd Hultquist, an institute spokesman. "Stores want a better grasp of what's selling and when, and when to do certain promotions." Mr. Gellman isn't so sure. He said that while preferences in canned tuna may be fairly innocuous, other purchases may be more private. "If a woman goes to a supermarket on Saturday and buys a pregnancy test kit, then buys prenatal vitamins the next week, it's a reasonable inference that she's pregnant," Mr. Gellman said. "And what if she hasn't told anyone?" Jerry Kang, an acting professor of law at the University of California at Los Angeles, agreed. "There is widespread ignorance or misinformation about how personal data is used in the database marketing industry and in the information collection process in cyberspace," he said. "Privacy doesn't mean information quarantine. It just means individual choice. People need to know up front what will happen to their personal data before they engage in these market transactions." Mr. Catlett of Junkbusters said that was called fair information practice. "There is no reason for information to be handled in an unfair and unsafe manner," he said. Earlier this week, a group of Internet advertising and data-profiling companies announced that those companies would give customers notice that information was being collected as well as the option to refuse to have that information used for profiling. Mr. Catlett, Mr. Rotenberg and other privacy advocates say that such self-regulatory efforts have failed in the past and that the Federal Trade Commission should recommend legislation that would establish a code of fair information practices, which they say would include an individual's right to get access to personal information held by others and would require a person's consent before such information could be disclosed to others. They also said online profiling should be halted until legislation is enacted. "The right to see information about you shouldn't be something given to you out of the goodness of the company's heart," Mr. Catlett said. "You should have a legally guaranteed right to it." Then there are people like Larry Engel -- so blase on the subject that they are lost causes to privacy advocates like Mr. Catlett. Mr. Engel, a documentary film maker and professor of film at Columbia University, belongs to the minority of people who are indifferent about the amount of information known about them. "I love the idea of marketers knowing my shopping habits," he said. "And look, if I'm going to be be spammed on my e-mail, I'd rather be spammed by people who at least have a clue." Mr. Engel loves the convenience of one-click ordering at Amazon.com and the identification feature at L. L. Bean. He loves it when he calls the front desk from a hotel room and hears, "Yes, Mr. Engel, how can I help you?" And the many ways he can be located? "I don't care if it's the government or a marketer or my wife, my brother or my accountant -- I'm happy to be located," he said. "Because the way I look at it, I don't care if people know where I am. It's my choice as to whether I respond." Surveillance cameras, Mr. Engel said, like those at intersections, are a bit trickier, but he said that over time, people would probably not care. "Will a camera on every street corner lead to Big Brother? No," he said, "it will probably lead to more gossip." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: LOOKING OVER HIS SHOULDER -- Jason Catlett, president of Junkbusters, a site that helps people guard private information, uses several strategies to guard his own privacy. (Edward Keating/The newyork Times)(pg. G1); WATCHDOG -- Marc Rotenberg, executive director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, advocates legislation to give consumers more control over their personal data. (Shana Raab for The newyork Times); TAKING CARE -- Mindy Zuckerman doesn't always worry about privacy, but shreds papers with her name on them. (Peter DaSilva for The newyork Times)(pg. G8)

title: 'Modernism' Pieces to Be Sold Online
body: FOR collectors who are yearning for a 1920's Jean Dunand bronze bowl or a 1930's French lacquered desk lamp but who can't get to the "Modernism" show, which opens today at the Seventh Regiment Armory, pieces from the show will be auctioned on the Web at www.icon20 .com. The auction began yesterday and will end on Sunday at 3 p.m. Fifty of the 78 show exhibitors contributed an item to the auction. The Dunand bowl on a slender pedestal base, offered by Sandi Berman, the owner of Deco Deluxe in newyork, has a $3,500 reserve. "I chose the bowl because Dunand is a known name, and I didn't have to ask the world for it," she said. Frank Rogin, another Manhattan dealer, offered a 1950's floor lamp with a conical shade suspended from a curved ash frame ($3,500 reserve). Reserves for objects in the auction range from $300 to $25,000, while items in the show are priced as high as $100,000. Some exhibitors did not participate in the auction because they are among the 4,500 dealers in the unitedstates and Europe who have signed contracts with Sothebys.com, which will handle online auctions for Sotheby's, perhaps by the end of December. The Sotheby's contract forbids a dealer from auctioning on other sites wares valued at more than $300. For Icon20, which went online last week, the "Modernism" auction is its first event. It won't be taking a commission, but 5 percent of the winning bids will go to the Children's Defense Fund. The site will focus on 20th-century design, selling books and listing museum shows and exhibitions. What Icon20 will not do is live auctions. "We wouldn't be able to keep up," said Usha Subramaniam, its president, who is a former decorative arts specialist at Christie's. "The technology isn't there. Online, you can go through 20 lots an hour. Live, 100 lots an hour."   ELAINE LOUIE http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
J. Crew Web Goof Results in Discount
body: Want a cashmere sweater from J. Crew for $18? For several hours this week, J. Crew's Web site, www.jcrew.com, inadvertently listed a $218 cashmere sweater for $18, leading several hundred e-shoppers to quickly add the item to their digital shopping carts in hopes that the pricing glitch would go unnoticed. J. Crew officials soon discovered the mistake on the site and removed the item. But did the sly surfers who ordered the $18 sweater really get away with a $200 discount? For about 24 hours, that seemed to be the case. Then, the email message arrived. "Big mistake!" said Emily Woods, chairwoman of J. Crew, in an email message to customers. "I wish we could sell such an amazing sweater for only $18. Our price mistake on your new cashmere zip turtleneck probably went right by you, but rather than charge you such a large difference, I'm writing to alert you that this item has been removed from your recent order." The company is allowing customers who ordered the sweater at $18 to reorder it for $118.80 to $130.80 depending on the size through a special address on the Web site. But that plan could also run into trouble because anyone who knows the address can buy the sweater at the discount.   ANDREW ROSS SORKIN http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Lifetimes of Memories Preserved on CD-ROM's
body: A new Internet company is betting its existence on a truism: People like to talk about themselves. The company, Life.com, has recently released a CD-ROM called My Life that encourages people to assemble their memories, thoughts and long-held secrets into a multimedia memoir. My Life asks people to select a electronic cards from 230 categories, like "Creativity" or "As a child." Each card poses questions that range from practical to probing. One asks: "What is the flat-out stupidest thing you have ever done?" "We went through a lot of research to make the questions interesting in and of themselves," said Kent Ertugrul, the company's founder. Life.com, whose employees now number 60, spent five years and $2.8 million coming up with 50,000 questions and building the software around them, he added. Users can enter responses by typing them or recording them using their computer's microphone or Webcam. The software also allows the inclusion of scanned snapshots and home movies. For information that is provided with dates, My Life creates timelines. The CD-ROM, which is now available in stores and online at www.life.com for $69.95, also enables people to publish their memoirs to a password-protected Web site, so that relatives and friends can participate or just take a look. While Mr. Ertugrul acknowledges that not everyone has the time, or inclination, to log their life on a computer, he says he believes that a market exists for people who want to be nudged toward introspection -- or at least preserve their memories for posterity. "There isn't a lot out there that really resonates emotionally," Mr. Ertugrul said. "This is emotional. It's deeply personal."   LISA GUERNSEY http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
NEWS WATCH;
New Web Service Offers Portable Bookmark Lists
body: For regular Web users, browser lists of bookmarks or favorites are personal bibliographies. Unlike lists on paper, unfortunately, browser lists of Web addresses cannot easily be transferred between computers, at the home and the office, for example. Blink.com is hoping to persuade users of multiple computers to move their personal lists of greatest hits from their browsers to Blink.com's Web-based service. "We think of ourselves as Hotmail for bookmarks," said Ross Garon, the company's chief operating officer. When a subscriber registers for Blink's advertising-supported service, the company's software automatically copies the subscriber's favorites list from the browser. Then, users of Microsoft's Internet Explorer browser download a tiny screen icon (the Blink Bar) that can be clicked on to add future entries. Users of Netscape Navigator must use a slightly less convenient program (the Blinker) that lurks in the background of the active screen. Blink's favorites lists can be organized into categories and can include site descriptions. The lists can also be searched using keywords. If they wish, users can also share their lists with specific subscribers to the service or the world at large. And because Blink lists are accessible only with a password, Mr. Garon said, they are more private than browser-based lists.   IAN AUSTEN http://www.nytimes.com

title: Online Journalists Keep Their Eyes on Daily Numbers
body: OLD-media journalists measure their mettle in scoops and Pulitzers. New-media reporters and editors have another gauge of success or failure: hits. By counting the hits or, more accurately, page views, on their Web sites, online magazines like Salon, Slate and The Industry Standard can track not only how many people are reading them but also for how long people are reading any given article. In a business that has never quite been able to nail down the habits of that elusive consumer -- the reader -- no old-fashioned focus group can match the hard binary data of the Internet. And for ink-stained wretches -- now repetitive-stress-injured wretches -- who are already prone to a certain amount of professional neurosis, a little knowledge may be a dangerous thing. "It was utterly shocking coming from a newspaper with a 700,000 circulation," said Joshua Quittner, who had been a technology columnist at Newsday before starting a Web site called The Netly News for Time-Warner in 1995. "Because I had the feeling that when I wrote a story in the newspaper, 700,000 people read it. Which was, of course, untrue. On a Web site, not only do you know how many people are really reading your stuff every week, so do your editors." Even more "horrific," added Mr. Quittner, who is now managing editor of Time Digital, a print supplement to Time magazine, is the fact that "it's not uncommon for people to spend something on the order of 20 seconds on a page." Not quite the mind-meld of reader and writer that journalists fantasize about when tapping out their deathless prose. But that only makes hit statistics more addictive. Like authors who check their books' Amazon.com rankings on an hourly basis, editors and writers at Salon receive a daily count -- the equivalent of overnight ratings in television. "We devour them avidly," said Gary Kamiya, Salon's executive editor. "It's become an addiction, actually. One of the things I look forward to is calling them up and seeing how we did." Craig Offman, a correspondent in Salon's newyork office, said of the routine, "Basically, you get a morning tally and you check it immediately." And as in the world of television, this ratings tally has equal power to elate and deflate. Being near the top of the list -- say, 20,000 hits for a Salon cover article -- is a validating high. Appearing at or near the bottom of the list -- 2,000 to 3,000 hits -- can have the opposite effect. "It's like in high school and you've auditioned for the school play," Mr. Offman said. "You look at the cast list and your eyes just slowly move down." Predictably, what scores big numbers is not lengthy exegeses on foreign policy. It's sex, incendiary opinion columns and almost anything about the Internet. Articles concerning Linux software benefit from what is known as the Slashdot effect. Slashdot is a Web site favored by Linux enthusiasts that provides links to Linux mentions all over Web. So if Salon or The Industry Standard runs an article on Linux, the links automatically increase hits. Obsessive "Blair Witch Project" linkers have the same effect. Mark Gimein, who covers technology for Salon, knows the pain of ratings anxiety. "Sometimes you see a story of yours did really poorly and then you think, 'What went wrong?' " he said. "You think, 'Gee, why are people reading the slapdash commentary I pulled together in an hour over this great story that I took 23 weeks to report?' " This summer, Salon ran an article studying the behavior of teenage girls online. It was an analytical, not particularly sexy article, but the headline included a reference to oral sex and readership was correspondingly high. Also this summer, Salon announced that it was giving a prostitute her own column. Tactics to increase circulation are hardly new to the newspaper trade. And magazines routinely base editorial decisions on expected newsstand sales. But some keepers of journalistic ethics worry that the instantaneous reader surveys will bend online magazines to the mercenary will of their business sides and encourage pandering to sex-obsessed technogeeks. "It's a publisher's dream and a journalist's nightmare," observed James Poniewozik, formerly Salon's media critic and now television critic at Time. James Ledbetter, a media critic for The Village Voice before he became newyork bureau chief of The Industry Standard, said that "when the investment bankers and shareholders are breathing down your neck to maximize traffic," online magazines inevitably became obsessed with hits. "If you put sex in the headline, you're guaranteed twice the number of hits," Mr. Ledbetter continued. "If you put oral sex in the headline, you're guaranteed the highest possible returns. So what you have measured is that people will click on the term 'oral sex,' and that's not journalism." Mr. Kamiya acknowledged that Salon happily gratified its readers' taste for lurid headlines and "libido-tweaking" material, "within reason and where appropriate." But he said the magazine did not shy away from far less sexy book reviews, foreign news or dry political articles. Advertisers are looking for "lots of eyeballs," he said, but "advertising doesn't dictate any of our editorial policy." Asked if pressure was put on Salon writers by their editors to deliver those eyeballs, Mr. Kamiya said, "We've joked about having page views connected to cubicle sizes." Michael Kinsley, editor of Salon's higher-brow competitor, Slate, called the ability to count page views "insidious." He looks at the numbers out of "malicious curiosity," he said, but does not share them with his staff because, he added, "writers are delicate flowers." Nor does he believe that the numbers have any real value. "The traffic that goes to one particular article may or may not reveal how important that article is to you or your readers," he said. "The click rate doesn't measure the intensity of somebody's interest." He drew an analogy to his days as editor of Harper's magazine: "We had a crossword puzzle. Only 5 percent of the readers went to the puzzle, but for that 5 percent, it was the reason they got the magazine." All kinds of tricks are used to measure traffic on the Web. Salon lays out its articles with plenty of blank space, so the reader has to click through three or four pages to get to the end. Each click is measured as a page view. Slate articles, on the other hand, are designed in a continuous scroll -- a single page view. The Time Digital Web site also adds up "unique users," Mr. Quittner said. A person who goes to the site and reads 27 articles still counts as only one user. Mr. Quittner recalled fondly the "golden days" of Web-based journalism when he and his young staff at The Netly News, which became the Time Digital site last year, would lure readers by any means necessary. One enterprising Netly employee set up a fake Web site purporting to be the world's biggest collection of links to pornography sites. Users would click on a link to Tokyo Topless and get a Netly article on the news of the day instead. "For a couple of months the page views went through the roof," Mr. Quittner recalled. "And a lot of those people ended up being some of our most loyal readers." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: THAT CLICKING SOUND -- Michael Kinsley, editor of Slate, says the ability to count page views is "insidious." (Therese Frare for The newyork Times)

title:
ONLINE SHOPPER;
For the Young And the Hip, And Only On the Web
body: I AM looking over some notes I jotted down the other day while visiting a new Web site called Troublewear.com. "It's really pimp," I wrote. "This is tite, I'm ready for a killer whack. Click and buy, dude. Just do it." It took me roughly an hour to come to my senses after my initial foray into Troublewear, a high-energy world of online youth culture that celebrates surfer lingo, blaring music and the sort of jerky green graphics that remind me of Wired magazine circa 1995. How did I get there in the first place? To translate my notes: I wanted to buy my brother a really cool ("pimp") birthday present to divert attention from the fact that it would arrive several days after his actual birthday. When I heard about the extreme-sports theme of Troublewear (www.troublewear .com), the site's selection of logo-laden men's shirts ($10 to $17) sounded like just the thing for my brand-conscious brother, a devoted adherent of such extreme sports as mountain biking, in-line skating and baby-sitting for his nieces. Troublewear.com also calls itself the first extreme-sport brand to be marketed solely on the Internet. The company joins a growing number of new brands -- www.ingredients.com started an Internet-only line of scented bath products last week, for instance -- that are taking advantage of the lower overhead online, where proprietors don't have to rent physical space to display their wares or hire sales clerks to sell them. At first glance the site was pretty pimp. There's a Lingo Lounge to explain the site's jargon, a chat and bulletin board area and a rich collection of Quicktime video "killer klips," featuring such extreme sports footage as a motorcycle rider nicknamed Shed Guy jumping over prefabricated tool sheds. But when I actually tried to buy something at Troublewear, the site suddenly didn't seem quite so clean and pure ("tite"). For instance, the images of the clothes for sale weren't actual photos that showed models wearing the shirts. They were simple line drawings of the shirts. You could zoom in on the logo -- and yes, zooming was a killer whack feature -- but in the end it was still impossible to tell what the clothes looked like. Would it be a tight or loose fit? How high was the neckline? The color choices looked more like the blocks of paint in a set of children's watercolors than like fabric hues. My brother is somewhat picky. Fanatically loyal to such tried-and-true brands as the Gap (he likes the fit) and J. Crew (he owns one of the largest documented collections of the cotton chambray checked shirts), he has demanding standards when it comes to color and texture. Shopping for him is as adventurous as trying an extreme sport for the first time. Sometimes I think it might be less nerve-wracking to jump a motorcycle over a row of prefab sheds than to choose just the right cotton blend with contrasting ribbed trim. In the case of Troublewear.com, I started sketching and gave up. I phoned Troublewear's founders to complain that the site seemed to put far more emphasis on creating an online haven for extreme-sports enthusiasts than on its retail operation. That, I was told, was the whole point. "With this kind of brand, you have to create a community first," said Rob Shively, the company's vice president of marketing. He explained that Troublewear is aimed at shoppers aged 12 to 21. "The generation that we're trying to appeal to is very fickle and they're very elusive," he said. "They know when they're being sold something and they're very cynical about advertising. If they think that a brand is selling out, that it's just about making money, they won't buy it anymore." If you buy the questionable premise that kids are cynical about advertising (that's why they wear it on their chests), you can see the reasoning behind Troublewear.com's strategy. It's far easier to control the image of the brand by limiting the marketing and distribution process to the Internet. That way, there's no chance that the company's clothes will end up on the 50 percent-off rack in an un-pimp mall store. That also explains that the problem with the site wasn't the crude line drawings of shirts. It was me. Maybe I'm a little too old for Troublewear.com. The company's president, Don Kerkes, was too polite to come right out and say it, but he did point out gently that "we felt blending extreme sports with the Internet really targeted the younger customer." So I decided to turn my back on all extreme sports except bargain hunting. That's how I ended up buying my brother a nice lamb's wool V-neck sweater from the J. Crew Web site. In the catalog, the sweater cost $49.50; online, the price was $39.60. When I called J. Crew's toll-free number to make sure there was no mistake, a customer service representative (who sounded, reassuringly, slightly older than me) said that J. Crew, also eager to take advantage of the savings of doing business online, was offering discounts on selected items to encourage shoppers to use the site. And I know the fit will be killer. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: HIGH ENERGY -- Troublewear.com seeks to attract extreme-sports fans with its own brand of clothing.; PLAYING IT STRAIGHT -- J. Crew has a more traditional Web site.

title: Picking the Right Data Superhighway - Correction Appended
body: THE key to happiness in the Internet age is bandwidth. Bandwidth, bandwidth, bandwidth. Fat pipes, capable of sucking down Web pages, music files, video clips, email and other forms of digital information and entertainment from the Internet in the blink of an eye. A data spigot that is always open, without busy signals and without the kinds of delays and service interruptions that drive most computer users mad. Bandwidth -- a measure of the flow of information, in bits, that moves over a given distance in a period of time -- is the most important factor in the development of new types of services on the Internet, more so than increases in personal computer processing power or new types of Internet communications devices. Until recently, high-bandwidth connections to the Internet were available mainly to businesses and certain lucky people willing and able to pay hundreds or even thousands of dollars a month for so-called broadband Internet access. But with the development of cable modems, digital subscriber line (D.S.L.) modems and satellite data services, several million Americans now have access to high-speed, broadband data services. You can tell who they are by the smug looks on their faces. I know, because I see the face of a bandwidth glutton in the mirror each morning. I am rich in bandwidth, wallowing in a broadband trough. In recent months I have had the luxury of using not just one broadband connection in my home office but three: a cable modem, a D.S.L. modem and a satellite modem. I've been testing them to see which one to keep, a decision that sooner or later a lot of Net surfers are going to make. Now, only a small percentage of Americans live in the right geographic or service area to get any one of these services, and even fewer -- perhaps 1 percent, according to market reseachers -- have a choice of two. But by the grace of whatever digital deities watch over the Internet, my house in Austin is in a rare sweet spot, where cable, D.S.L. and satellite coverage overlap. I also had I.S.D.N. (integrated services digital network, which essentially combines the capacity of two phones lines), but I had it ripped from my house when its cost and complexity far outstripped the modest speed improvements it offered over regular dial-up phone service. My files are downloaded in a snap. Web pages pop onto my screen. I do not think twice about downloading video clips or MP3 music files. Multiplayer network games and home videoconferences suddenly become practical. But the thing that changes everything is the fact that the Internet is always on, whenever I want it. My biggest nightmare is that I will wake up someday and have to connect to the Internet using -- the horror, the horror -- an old-fashioned 56K modem on a dial-up telephone line. Here is an example: Earlier this year, the movie trailer for "Star Wars: Episode I -- The Phantom Menace" was made available for downloading from the Internet, but it was a 25-megabyte file. The fastest conventional modems available today, at 56K, can download nearly 56,000 bits per second. There are 8 bits in a byte, and, because of way binary numbers are counted, 1,048,576 bytes, or 8,388,608 bits, in a megabyte and roughly 200 million bits in a 25-megabyte file. In the time it takes to do the calculation of how long it would take a regular modem to download the file, it would already be done via a cable or D.S.L. modem. Alas, I cannot put all three broadband services on my expense account indefinitely, so I have to choose. Following is a discussion of the three broadband options, and what went into my decision.  Cable The black coaxial cable that carries cable television signals to tens of millions of households can also handle high-bandwidth data connections. Analysts expect cable to become the dominant method for high-speed Internet connections at home, in part because cable already passes by the majority of houses in the country. But older cable systems were designed to be only one-way, sending video to the home, so cable providers have to upgrade their systems to give them the two-way capabilities needed for Internet access. The top speed of a cable modem, at least in theory, is about 30 million bits per second (30 mbps), but a more realistic expectation is around 1 mbps. It can be a bit faster, but considering that most of us connect a cable modem to a 10-mbps Ethernet card, 30 mbps is a pipe dream. Uploading is somewhat slower, but that is usually not a problem for most home users. More important is that cable downloading can be even slower, depending on how many of your neighbors are also using the neighborhood cable pipe at the same time. It is a shared service. If you have the local cable line all to yourself, you can easily top 1 mbps. But if all of your neighbors have cable modems, things can slow down so much that you might actually yearn to have your dial-up modem back. If one of your cable-using neighbors starts running a Web server out of the home, you can imagine neighbors marching with torches and pitchforks. The two leading cable data services, Time Warner's Roadrunner and AT&T Cable's @Home, forbid residential customers to run Web server computers on the network. Remember, however, that the practical speed of any broadband network, no matter what its theoretical speed, is limited by the slowest link on the network. If you link to a popular site that is congested, or to an obscure site that may be attached to the Internet through the equivalent of a hand-cranked computer, your multimegabit broadband connection will slow down accordingly. My monthly cable data fee is $44.95 because I also subscribe to the cable company's standard (as opposed to basic) television services. If I were not already a cable television customer, I would have to become one to get the data services, taking my monthly cost to a minimum of about $65 a month. With my extra television channels, I'm now paying Time Warner $85 a month, which includes the rental of the cable modem. Adding email addresses for family members costs $5 a month each. If I want to have a home page on the Web, it is $5 extra per month. There was a setup and installation charge of $130, but periodic promotional deals cut that price in half. It took several frustrating exchanges with the local company before technicians finally came to my house. Over all, the installation process was about what I had come to expect from my cable company: a logistical nightmare. Besides the Jekyll and Hyde speed issues that affect cable modems, a big drawback is that cable customers have no choice of Internet service providers. America Online and other popular I.S.P.'s are challenging the cable companies in court to open cable services to competition, but for now, it's either Roadrunner or @Home. Time Warner is my local cable company, and Roadrunner is the only choice I have for cable I.S.P. service. Another concern is data security. Because it is a shared network, any of your devious neighbors with the technical expertise to run a network sniffer can intercept data packets from your computer. That is highly unlikely, but it is a risk. Try this: Lie to your neighbors, telling them that hackers came in over your cable modem and wiped out your bank accounts. Mention that you have heard that D.S.L. service is more secure. Then you will have the cable network all to yourself.  D.S.L. D.S.L., which stands for digital subscriber line, enables high-speed Internet connections to houses and small businesses over the same copper telephone lines that handle voice and fax calls. It does not interfere with voice traffic on the line, however, so one person can make or receive calls while another is using the same line to connect to the Internet. A big advantage, therefore, is that D.S.L. does not require the installation of a second phone line or cable service. Its big drawback is that the service degrades quickly as a function of distance, so customers are limited to a geographic radius of about 3 miles from a telephone company's central office (technically, about 17,500 feet). The phone company first checks to see if your nearest central office offers digital service, then checks to see if you live close enough to it and finally checks the actual line to see if it can handle D.S.L. bandwidth. If everything checks out, the phone company will send out a crew to install a splitter, which splits voice and data traffic on the line. A splitterless form of the service is also in the works. There are many kinds of D.S.L. The most common for residential service is the asynchronous kind, A.D.S.L., or A.D.S.L Lite, which offers slightly lower data speeds. On an A.D.S.L. line, information is uploaded to the Internet at one speed, typically 128 kilobits per second, but downloaded at much higher speeds, typically 384 kilobits per second (kbps) to 1.544 megabits per second (mbps). The downloading speed is most important for most people, so it is fair to say that downloading with D.S.L. is anywhere from 7 to 25 times as fast as with the fastest dial-up analog modems. Unlike cable modem users, who share a line, each D.S.L. subscriber has a dedicated line to the central office. Therefore, the speed is more constant and predictable. The top speed of a D.S.L. modem is basically determined by how much money you are willing to spend and how close you live to the central telephone office. I live 200 yards from a central office, and my basic D.S.L. service regularly achieves more than the minimum speed of 384 kbps downstream and often hovers near the 1.5 mbps maximum; it is 128 kbps upstream. It costs about $70 a month, which includes the telephone company line charge of $39 a month, the fee of the Internet service provider, three email addresses and other services for which the cable company charges extra. I also paid $212 for a cable modem and a network adapter card. I leased the modem instead of buying one outright because I wanted to make sure it worked with the D.S.L. equipment at the phone company. My monthly fee is high compared with other D.S.L. offerings around the country. In general, you can expect to pay $30 to $50 a month for basic service. While D.S.L. cannot compete with cable in terms of speed during the day, when most of my neighbors are at their offices and I have the cable line mostly to myself, it is routinely faster than cable in the evenings, when my neighbors are sharing my cable pipe. I can increase my guaranteed D.S.L. performance to a minimum of 384 kbps upstream and 1.544 mbps downstream by paying $170 or more a month. The performance at this level is almost comparable with the speeds of T-1 lines, which many companies use to operate Web-based businesses. T-1 service typically costs $1,000 a month or more. Other forms of D.S.L. service can promise speeds up to 50 mbps, but at monthly prices that would probably exceed your mortgage payment. As with cable, my D.S.L. connection is always on.  Satellite Satellite data service has so much promise, especially for people in areas not served by D.S.L. or cable. But satellite also has many challenges. The Web is an interactive medium, while satellite is intrinsically a one-way medium (most of us do not routinely communicate with satellites). To send mouse clicks and typed commands to the Internet, you have to have an open telephone line in addition to the satellite connection. Satellite service requires the installation of a receiver dish antenna, which is about the size of a garbage can lid and costs $200 to $400. The dish has to have a clear line of sight to the satellite, which in the New York City area is typically in the southwestern sky. The installation and alignment of the dish is not for technological sissies, and I highly recommend paying the extra $200 to $300 for professional installation. Once installed, moreover, the data signal can be knocked out of whack by high winds or other bad weather conditions. I signed up for Hughes DirecPC satellite data services as part of a package with Compaq Computer. Compaq, like many other PC makers, is trying to make it as easy as possible for its customers to be ready for broadband access. Besides the dish and installation cost, monthly satellite data service costs $30 to $130 a month, depending on how many hours you spend on line. The $30 plan is good for a measly 25 hours a month. The $130 plan allows up to 200 hours a month (versus unlimited time with cable or D.S.L. service). Satellite data services may someday be ubiquitous and reach speeds of 45 mbps, but for now the maximum speed is a relatively pokey 400 kbps. More users can mean slower speeds and, occasionally, busy signals when you're trying to connect with the local satellite I.S.P. So far, so bad. The guys who wired my satellite system were apparently receiving their orders directly from deep space. Despite my request that they mount the dish on the side of the house and not drill holes in my roof, I now have a dish bolted through my roof. Satellite is a swell choice for people who cannot get cable or D.S.L. service, especially people who live in remote areas. But a satellite broadband connection requires a phone line, and that can be a major problem if you live in Whitefish, Mont., and the nearest satellite I.S.P. is a long-distance call away in Bozeman.  Decisions If you spend only a few minutes on line every day, switching to a broadband modem may not make much financial sense. But if you find yourself spending more time connected to the Internet each day and becoming more impatient with busy signals and the time spent waiting for pages to load, a broadband connection may be the solution. Satellite was scratched off my list first. If I lived in an area where satellite was my only choice, I could live with it. But since I have a choice, satellite isn't it. I'm still going to use an analog modem because it is impossible to take my cable modem and D.S.L. modem with me on trips. The choice, then, comes down to two contenders, cable and D.S.L. Either is vastly more satisfactory than a regular modem, and if I had no choice and had to take one or the other, I would still consider myself very fortunate, no matter which one I had. The speed is nice, but more than that, I have come to rely on the always-on connection. There are no busy signals, no delays in getting online, no screeching, beep-boop modem sounds and no interruptions if I stay idle longer than the service provider thinks is necessary. Despite cable's theoretical speed advantage, the actual performances of cable and D.S.L. are comparable. Therefore, the determinants come down to price and, to a lesser extent, to security, the choice of I.S.P. and reliability. If I had to choose -- and economics dictate that I must -- I would keep D.S.L. Performance is steady and reliable. From the start, the phone company has been easier to deal with than my cable company, although both could improve their customer service skills. Naturally, many people have drawn exactly the opposite conclusion. They found their local phone company impossible to deal with and had no trouble with cable. It all depends on the skills and temperament of the local service providers. The best tactic, as always, is to ask neighbors and friends who have local broadband access about their experiences. title:
REVIEW;
A Web Page Kit Full of Tools for Beginners
body: COMPLETE WEB STUDIO 2.0 (Sierra Home; $79.95; Windows 95, 98 and NT 4.0.) IT seems everybody has a Web site these days -- businesses, television shows, grandmothers and pets. If you're feeling left out, Sierra Home has recently released its Complete Web Studio 2.0 software for home users. The program is designed for people who just want to make a Web site on their own, without having to marry an HTML manual or invest in high-end Web development programs like Adobe's GoLive or Macromedia's Dreamweaver. Web Studio not only makes creating a Web site about as easy as pointing and clicking, but it can also make uploading the site to the Web a breeze, even for nontechnical users. Actually, "dragging and dropping" might be a more appropriate comparison, because that is what you pretty much do to create a page with Complete Web Studio. The program, on two CD's, comes with more than 37,000 graphics, photographs, backgrounds, animations, sounds and page templates. If you have spent any amount of time on the Web, you have probably run into your fair share of truly hideous and poorly designed sites. Many of them are most likely labors of love from people still learning this relatively new medium. The Web Studio program gives you a generous number of templates that you can select and modify to your own tastes. The overall look of the templates is quite conservative, but there seems to be one for every occasion, including graphically appropriate blueprints named such things as "A history links page!" and "A page about your auto collection!" Perhaps in an attempt to cover all bases, the template file also contains such narrowly focused themes as "A page about Grandpa in the war" and "A page for your Japanese exchange family." To make a Web page with the program, you simply pick a template or start with a blank work space, and then drag and drop desired page elements into place. Tiny samples of all potential page parts are arranged on a multilayered, tabbed palette next to the main on-screen work space. To add a colorful background to your page, click on the sample and drag it onto the main window. You can type in and style your own text, add your own pictures or choose from the vast array of clip art and stock photos. Some of the clip art and backgrounds included look a bit amateurish, but there are scads of others to choose from. You can shift and move items around on the canvas and even place things like hit counters and calendars on your page. Web Studio allows you to drag and drop links from your browser's Bookmarks or Favorites file, and you can easily add more pages to your site to link to the first one you have created. Once you have completed your site, Web Studio will convert your creation to HTML and save your file and all its parts in a folder. The program is fairly intuitive to use, but if you do have questions, Web Studio conveniently comes with multimedia tutorials to explain the steps and a 110-page manual. As software manuals go, this one is fairly understandable, although it tries to water down some subjects too much. In Chapter 6, which explains how to get your newly made site off your hard drive and onto the Internet, the manual refers to File Transfer Protocol, or F.T.P., as "Friendly virTual Postman." Although the manual's index gives the proper rendering, it is somewhat aggravating to see abbreviation abuse in a program aimed at nontechnical users who are probably easily confused as it is. But on the subject of F.T.P., users don't really have to know what it is anyway, because the Web Studio's Upload Wizard takes the headache out of uploading the finished site to the Web for all to see. The Upload Wizard allows you to post the page by typing in a user name and password and clicking with the mouse a few times. The program contains a database of many popular Internet service providers that provide free Web space to their members (like America Online, MindSpring and Xoom), which provides an even faster shortcut to uploading. Complete Web Studio 2.0 also includes two other programs: SnapShot Express, a picture-editing application, and iCollect, which lets you download entire Web sites for offline browsing and study. A recent version of Microsoft's Internet Explorer browser, required for the program's Help files, is included on one of the CD's as well. To install Web Studio, at minimum you will need a PC with 16 megabytes of RAM, a Pentium-class 100-megahertz processor, a CD-ROM drive and 50 megabytes of hard drive space. Web Studio runs better with 32 megabytes of RAM, though, and the standard install needs 160 megabytes of hard drive space. All in all, Complete Web Studio works well in its mission of bringing easy site creation to the nontechnical masses. Using the software is vaguely reminiscent of tossing items into a shopping cart in an enormous supermarket -- except instead of a week's worth of meals, you have a complete Web site when you're done.
