title:
E-Commerce Report;
Web site publishers and advertising agencies square off on ownership of data on customers.
body: ON the Internet, where information is king, some of the most valuable information is data about user or customer behavior. Of this, one of the most closely followed measurements is so-called click data, which focuses on who has clicked on an advertising banner or some other particular link. Web site publishers, advertising agencies and companies that buy those ads have relied heavily on that data to build their businesses, and until now they have been generous about sharing it freely with each other. Now one of the Internet's biggest advertisers is raising the question of whether that data belongs to anyone but the advertisers, and the resulting debate could shape the future of the advertiser-publisher relationship. According to executives within the Internet advertising industry, I.B.M. is testing new techniques of serving its ads to Internet users in a way that prevents publishers from knowing who clicked on I.B.M. ads displayed on their Web sites. I.B.M., these executives say, may then withhold the click data from publishers unless they can be persuaded to do otherwise. An I.B.M. official declined to comment about the proposed policy, saying it was premature to speculate. Indeed, industry executives said the company had merely floated the idea of claiming ownership of click data. But the I.B.M. talk has brought the issue of data ownership to a head, and given new impetus to a debate that has loomed as one of the most important facing the industry. "This is just the tip of the iceberg; and the bottom of that iceberg is the issue of who owns the data," said Michael Donahue, executive vice president of the American Association of Advertising Agencies. "The ad agencies don't want to be cut out because they want access to that data. The advertisers say, 'It's my money, so it's my data,' and the publishers say, 'That ad is part of my site's content, so it's my data.' " The possibility of losing access to click data has sent a shiver up the spines of Web site publishers, who rely on these statistics to gauge the effectiveness of advertising and to gather information about the buying interests of their users. That data is tremendously valuable to publishers, who can command high advertising fees for showing, for example, a mortgage company's ad to someone who has recently clicked on an advertisement for a realtor. Publishers also fear that if I.B.M. assumes such a stance, other advertisers will follow suit. Beyond I.B.M.'s considerable spending power -- industry executives rank the company as one of the top three advertisers on the Internet -- it has been influential in shaping industry policies. I.B.M. spearheaded an effort earlier this year, for instance, to force Web site publishers to post privacy statements or lose the company's advertising. Internet advertising executives cite two potential justifications for withholding click data. For one thing, their traditional relationship with print publishers and television and radio networks suggests that the data belongs to advertisers. The ad buyers generally do not share the results of advertising campaigns with networks or print publishers when those media run so-called direct response advertisements -- for example, a commercial that invites viewers to call an "800" number to buy a product. Advertisers acknowledge that Internet publishers play a far more active role in bringing qualified buyers to their doorstep than other media. But they also make the point that the Internet ultimately resembles the direct response model, so they could be justified in handling the data in a similar manner. Of equal importance for some advertisers is the suspicion that publishers and other companies that deliver ads are not above selling click data to an advertiser's competitor. These companies espouse a so-called Chinese wall policy dictating, for instance, that publishers do not sell information about people who clicked on one car company's ad banner to another car company. But industry executives say that there are violations. "I don't think it's pervasive, but there are people doing it," said Kevin O'Connnor, chief executive of Doubleclick Inc., an Internet advertising network. "And advertisers want to put a stop to it." According to industry executives who spoke on condition of anonymity, I.B.M.'s new advertising approach enables it to deliver ads from its own server computers -- a departure from the norm, since advertisers generally rely on publishers or third-party advertising companies like Doubleclick and Flycast to deliver ads on their behalf. Moreover, the way the ads are coded prevents publishers from tracking who clicked on I.B.M.'s ad banners. Most other advertisers, of course, lack the technological wherewithal to deliver their own ads or to otherwise separate publishers from click data. But publishers fear other advertisers could eventually deliver their ads in a manner similar to I.B.M.'s new technique. Or, even if they lack the technical expertise to block access, advertisers might seek either to contractually prevent publishers from using that data or to force publishers to pay for it. Industry executives say that I.B.M. is sensitive to concerns about causing a ripple effect, having staked a good measure of its business future on the growth of the e-commerce industry. But as the company joins others in pouring millions of advertising dollars into the Internet economy -- and as the value of customer data continues to rise -- I.B.M. may decide that now is the time to establish a precedent on the matter. According to Vivienne Bechtold, director of interactive marketing for Procter & Gamble, the issue could force advertisers to re-evaluate the role of publishers in helping to build ad campaigns. Ms. Bechtold, who is also a member of a coalition of Internet advertising and publishing leaders known as the Future of Advertising Stakeholders, or FAST, stressed that Procter & Gamble had not determined its own position on the issue. "I can understand why I.B.M. would consider this stance," she said. "On the other hand, the dynamics of the Internet raise the question: If we share the data, would advertisers benefit more from that collective expertise than if we treated them in the traditional, customer-supplier way?" Ultimately, she said, "advertisers could adopt a hybrid approach, where we choose to share with some, while with others, we treat it in the traditional way." Other trends are complicating the matter, including the tendency of advertisers to establish so-called "pay for performance" deals with Web sites. In those agreements, a publisher's payment is often based on the percentage of users who click on ad banners, so advertisers would naturally disclose click data to publishers. Other advertising deals remain on a "CPM" model, whereby advertisers pay a set rate, typically in the $25 range, for every thousand banners shown on a site. But about half of Internet advertising deals are a combination of pay-for-performance and CPM, so disputes over who owns the data could quickly muddy the waters. Publishers, meanwhile, are using so-called "collaborative filtering" technology to aim ads at consumers on their sites -- and can offer even more precise targets when they know what ads their customers are clicking on. Indeed, according to Anil Singh, chief sales and marketing officer for Yahoo: "We can target clusters of our audience that have a higher propensity to click on certain types of offers. That's a great service for advertisers. If we were unable to collect data in that effort, it would hurt the services we could offer our clients." At the same time, a growing number of advertisers are choosing to deliver their ads through third-party servers like Doubleclick and Flycast, which also rely extensively on click data. Those companies have much at stake as well. "Are we willing to step back and not have access to the data?" asked Doubleclick's Mr. O'Connor. "I'm not so sure. It could very well not be a good thing for the advertisers." At the center of this issue is Rich LeFurgy, chairman of the Internet Advertising Bureau, an industry group that represents Internet publishers. Mr. LeFurgy, who is also the chairman of FAST, said the advertising bureau and I.B.M. were seeking common ground. "They understand our position, we understand theirs," he said. "But this is stuff that's not to be underestimated in terms of its importance and implications." Internet publishers, however, have little leverage in the debate, in the view of Jim Nail, an analyst with Forrester Research. "Advertisers are ultimately the source of all the money, so they hold the trump card in this," Mr. Nail said. "If they want to do it, they can." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Rich LeFurgy, left, the chairman of the Internet Advertising Bureau, an organization that represents publishers, discusses online direct marketing with Shane Moore of MyPoints.com, a shopping Web site. (Don Hogan Charles/The New York Times)

title: I.B.M. to Offer PC's in Color, With Brand Name, Next Year
body: I.B.M. will introduce business personal computers with new designs and a new brand in the first half of 2000 to try to revive its money-losing PC unit, the company said here today. The desktop PC's will be the first models of a new brand that has not yet been named. One new PC will be encased in a flat-screen display and will cost $500 to $1,000, I.B.M. said. I.B.M.'s PC unit lost almost $1 billion last year and $311 million before taxes in the first nine months of 1999. Last month, I.B.M. said it would stop selling home PC's through unitedstates retailers and instead focus on sales online. The business models "are an attempt to put some sparkle into the brand and generate revenue growth," said Roger Kay, an analyst at the International Data Corporation in Framingham, Mass. I.B.M. will run an advertising campaign costing more than $100 million to accompany the spring introduction of three desktop PC's, the company said. While competitors over the years have burnished their personal computers with new brand names, I.B.M. has until now stuck with calling its business machines "PC" followed by a model number. "There was a hole in the brand," Mr. Kay said. The I.B.M. brand has lost some of the cachet it commanded when the company created the mass market for personal computers in the early 1980's. I.B.M. was the fifth-largest PC maker in the unitedstates in the third quarter, increasing its shipments only 6 percent from those in the period a year earlier, according to International Data. Over all, PC makers' shipments for the quarter jumped 24 percent. The all-in-one, flat-panel PC could prove especially popular below $1,000, Mr. Kay said, adding: "That would be like pulling a rabbit out of a hat. People want the flat panels -- they're better in every way except price." But Mr. Kay also said that the company might have trouble keeping up with demand because flat panels would be in short supply until 2001. The flat-panel model will use parts from desktop PC's, which are cheaper than the notebook computer components used in rivals' models, I.B.M. said. The new personal computers will be smaller, thinner and lighter and will come in different colors, Mr. Kay said. They will include automatic links to the Internet, chat groups and an I.B.M. center where users' questions can be answered and software can be updated. The Internet features may not appeal to companies that want to limit employees' access to World Wide Web sites unrelated to business, Mr. Kay conceded. New Thinkpad notebook PC's and computers that display applications run on powerful server computers will come later. The notebooks will be wirelessly linked to corporate networks and will communicate with devices such as hand-held computers and cellular phones. http://www.nytimes.com

title: New Technology Investment Fund Says It Has Raised $600 Million
body: Redpoint Ventures, a technology-focused venture capital firm created in August through the combination of Brentwood Venture Capital and Institutional Venture Partners, plans to announce on Monday that it has raised $600 million in its first fund -- an amount thought to be the largest effort for a first-time technology fund. Redpoint, based in Menlo Park, Calif., plans to specialize in Internet businesses, including companies devoted to broad-band -- or high speed -- telecommunications technology for Internet use. Redpoint has already made commitments to several investments, including a $15 million stake in Reflect.com, a Web-based, customized beauty business started by Procter & Gamble, which contributed $35 million. Tim Haley and Geoff Yang, Redpoint managing directors, are on the board of Reflect.com. Internet companies that received venture financing from Redpoint's predecessors include Excite@Home, Ask Jeeves, Tivo, Xylan, Stamps.com and WebTV. According to the research firm Venture Economics, the $600 million commitment to Redpoint makes it the largest first fund raised by a technology-focused venture capital firm. While in part this reflects investors' interest in new Internet companies, it is also attributable to the fact that Redpoint is the combination of two well-known firms rather than an entirely new entity. Brentwood was founded in 1972 in Southern California, while Institutional Venture Partners was founded in 1980. "The whole premise of this is we're not starting a new fund; we're building on the platform that I.V.P. and Brentwood had put in place," Tom Dial, a Redpoint managing director, said. "In no case would we have been able to raise a fund this large without the history of the two funds and the partners." In their August announcement, Institutional Venture Partners and Brentwood said they would combine their efforts in Redpoint, as well as a second firm, Palladium, which will be devoted to biotechnology and other investments related to health care. With the explosion of the Internet, many diversified venture capital funds have found it hard to reconcile the fast pace and potentially huge returns of Web start-ups with the longer time frames and often smaller returns on new drug companies. Some have virtually abandoned life sciences investments, but Sam Collela, Institutional Venture Partners' founder, has insisted that venture capital will have a continuing role in health care. He will be a managing director of Palladium, while playing a smaller role at Redpoint. "When you have a diversified fund, there's just less synergy around the table when the partners get together to talk about these deals," Mr. Dial said. "There's a real advantage to having six or seven partners around the table, all of whom are really knowledgeable about the Internet. It just lifts the dialogue." Redpoint's institutional investors are all previous investors in Brentwood Venture Capital and Institutional Venture Partners, including ARCO, the Carnegie Corporation of newyork, Duke Foundation, Ford Foundation, Harvard University, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, the Mutual Life Insurance Company of newyork, Princeton University, Rockefeller Foundation, Stanford University, Pfizer Inc. and Yale University. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Now Putting A Big Stamp On the Era Of the Internet;
Pitney Bowes Is Updating The Business of Business Mail
body: The three phrases flash in rapid succession on the United Illuminating Company's Web site: No stamps. No checks. No fees. Since July, the words have alerted the southern Connecticut utility's customers that they can now get and pay their electric bills with a click of the mouse. Slowly, but steadily, the customers are doing just that. "It's been slow, maybe, but I'm certain that it will take off," said Edward J. Drew, the United Illuminating executive who runs the Internet billing project. By rights, that prospect should terrify the folks at Pitney Bowes Inc. After all, United Illuminating is one of Pitney's biggest customers, and every electronic bill the utility clocks is a bill not sent through a Pitney postage meter, or processed through Pitney's customized bulk mailing systems. So does that make Pitney -- universally thought of as a print-on-paper player -- a dinosaur? Not quite. It was Pitney that helped United Illuminating design the electronic billing program, runs its bill-paying Web site and is aggressively looking to teach other big customers the ways of e-commerce. As Michael J. Critelli, Pitney's chairman, sees it, Pitney's business is messages, however they are relayed. And he figures Pitney, based in Stamford, Conn., can make good money providing the water wings for companies that are learning to swim in Internet waters. "The Internet can deliver data much faster than the old ways, and we want to help customers use it as a tool," he said. Pitney is not billing itself as an Internet specialist per se. But in recent years copiers, fax machines, postage meters, envelope stuffers -- in effect, all the hardware that Pitney sells -- have moved from stand-alone machines to digital devices that are plugged into computer networks. Pitney already has a cadre of software writers who specialize in moving documents around in a digital environment. So, for Pitney, Internet applications represent a difference of degree, not kind. Moreover, Pitney is making ample use of Internet-savvy partners. Working with Tumbleweed Communications, Pitney has introduced iSend, a service that uses encryption, passwords and tracking features to guarantee the privacy and delivery of email. ISend was originally aimed at law firms and other small businesses that traffic in sensitive documents. But Pitney has now teamed with SAP, the huge software company, to market an industrial-strength version that would enable corporations to track hundreds of secure files as they move on the Internet. Separately, Pitney is ready to roll out ClickStamp, which will let customers buy postage from the Web. Two start-up companies, Stamps.com Inc. and the E-Stamp Corporation, under Postal Service authorization, already have set up similar sites that are beginning to attract small-business customers. But Pitney is suing both for royalties, claiming that each uses patented Pitney technology. And some financial analysts say that Pitney, with an established brand name and a big budget to promote it, has a better-than-average chance of catching up. "I'd guess they could grab 35 percent of the market before long," said B. Alexander Henderson, an analyst at Prudential Securities Research. And Pitney has plunged modem-first into the so-called e-tailing market, as a supplier to companies that sell goods on the Web. For example, Pitney is pushing a version of iSend to Internet merchants as a way to confirm orders and generate bills. And it has developed software to help e-tailers plot out the best way to deliver products to their customers. "We used to think of shipping as a service you offered warehouses; but these days a shipper is anyone who realizes there's stuff in the garage that they can auction online," said William T. Shannon, vice president of product planning for Pitney's small-business division. So far investors seem skeptical that Pitney can pull off its metamorphosis into an Internet player. "Pitney is pushing a lot of hype on their Internet capabilities, but when you crunch the numbers they are not getting a lot of revenues," said James W. Lundy, a research director at Gartner Group, a research firm in Stamford, Conn. On Oct. 19, when Pitney released third-quarter results, its shares plunged $4.4375, to $50.25 -- well off a price above $70 as recently as July.  Pitney's earnings were well ahead of the corresponding period last year, but analysts say that shareholders were disappointed that revenues had increased just 8 percent. Pitney shares closed at $44.875 on Friday. Although Pitney executives say they expect Internet-related products to eventually yield 30 percent of revenues, e-commerce still remains a tiny part of Pitney's sales. The bulk of revenues continue to come from postage meter rentals, financing, bulk mailing systems, and services like running mail rooms and handling direct marketing. Analysts say investors have been wary of Pitney's shares because of concerns that the Internet will make inroads into basic mailing products. But Pitney's Wall Street fans -- and there are many -- say such worries are unfounded. "The Street psychology may be negative, but their fundamentals are outstanding," said Jonathan Rosenzweig, an analyst with Salomon Smith Barney. And the electronic markets that Pitney is chasing are potential blockbusters. While older meters required a trip to the post office to buy refill postage, modern meters can be reloaded by telephone. In both cases, the Post Office, not Pitney, sells the postage. But Pitney charges higher rentals for newer digital meters, which it says are more convenient to use. And the company will offer, for a fee, to buy the postage for customers and reload the meters remotely. The International Data Corporation, a research firm in Framingham, Mass., expects the online market to account for $1.5 billion of postage sales in three years. On the billing front, Forrester Research Inc., a firm in Cambridge, Mass., predicts that electronic billing will account for 13 percent of all consumer bills in five years. But the pursuit of those markets has Pitney navigating uncharted, and fiercely competitive, waters. No one yet knows, for example, whether businesses will prefer to download postage directly from the Web -- the method used by Stamps.com -- or whether they will prefer using a lock-box device, as the E-Stamp system requires. The lock box hooks onto a customer's computers and stores downloaded postage, which the customer can print out without connecting to the Internet each time. Pitney, operating under the names ClickStamp Online and ClickStamp Plus, is offering both methods. That means it can hedge its bets until the market chooses one approach over the other, but it also means Pitney must spread its marketing and research dollars pretty thin. As for electronic billing, Pitney runs the risk that the market will veer away from being biller-centric -- companies billing all of their customers electronically -- to a payer-centric model in which customers pay all of their bills at a single Web site. While Pitney has pursued the biller-centric business, bill consolidators like Transpoint, CheckFree and Spectrum are now offering payer-centric services to consumers. Even some early electronic billers suspect that the one-stop-shopping approach may be the model that makes it. "We may want to look at that option in the future," said Mr. Drew of United Illuminating. Pitney is keeping its options open here, too. It is talking to bill consolidators about alliances, and to banks about payer-centric Web sites. "We want to run Web sites that handle billing for all of a bank's customers," said Karl Schumacher, general manager of the Pitney division that handles high-speed mailings for huge companies. Perhaps the biggest question mark of all is whether Pitney can successfully woo the small businesses that make up the fastest growing market for Internet services. Because small businesses typically have had no need for postage meters or mail room management, few have dealt with Pitney in the past. To court them, in September Pitney came out with PitneyWorks, a compendium of products that includes Personal Post, a digital postage meter and scale aimed at low-volume users; various Web-related shipping and direct marketing software programs and services, and a line of credit for postage. Pitney is also counting on ClickStamp to generate small business traffic. "There are eight million small businesses out there using stamps, and until now we had no way to get to them," said Marc C. Breslawsky, Pitney's president. "If we can get those customers into our store, we can sell them profitable items like iSend now, and upgrade them to digital meters as they grow." Those upgraded products may not all be Internet related. Unlike the Internet start-ups it now competes with, Pitney has a stable of conventional products that yield a steady cash flow to support its Internet forays. Indeed, although its stock may be slumping, its sales and earnings have been solid. Its 1998 revenues of $4.22 billion were 8 percent higher than 1997's $3.92 billion, while its net income of $576.4 million was up 10 percent from the prior year's $526 million. Pitney postage meters still dominate the United States market, despite solid competition from digitally savvy companies like Neopost and Francotyp-Postalia A.G. of Germany. And analysts expect Pitney to garner 30 percent of the international postage meter market by 2004, up from just about 14 percent now. Companies numerous and huge, including U S West, Cigna and General Motors, are using Pitney's equipment to address, stuff, stamp and mail bills and customized literature. Many others have hired Pitney to run their mailing operations. In either model, the client provides Pitney with demographic information about customers, and Pitney sees to it that, say, a young family's bill comes with an insert promoting products for children, while a retired widow's bill might include data on care for the elderly. "The Internet has certainly not lessened the importance of personalized content inside an envelope, or of customized printing on the outside," Mr. Critelli said. Even with paper mailings, computer networks are playing a role. Pitney now sells systems that help companies glean custom-tailored mailing lists from e-commerce Web sites, and use them for direct marketing -- or, in the case of smaller businesses, hire Pitney to handle the mailing for them. It has database products that double check the accuracy of addresses and their listed occupants against post office records, so as to guarantee error-free mailing lists. And, it is testing a system at the General Motors Acceptance Corporation's mail room in Detroit whereby Pitney will scan some of the nonpersonal incoming mail into a computer, and deliver it to employees electronically. "Paper isn't going away, and only Pitney has the bricks and mortar products to offer a hybrid approach," said Mr. Lundy, the Gartner analyst Pitney has even figured out a novel way to get the float on a customer's money. Pitney set up a chartered bank in Utah in 1998. Then last June, Pitney's Financial Services division started offering free postage, representing about a 2 percent discount on postage costs, to customers who put a lump sum into a reserve account at the Utah bank. Pitney draws from the reserve to pay the customer's postage bills to the Post Office as they are accrued. That, in essence, gives Pitney access to funds at well below its usual 6 percent cost of capital. "We've effectively coupled financial services with postage transactions, which means we're borrowing less expensively," said Matthew S. Kissner, president of Pitney's small business and financial solutions unit. Pitney will offer the discount to ClickStamp users as well, a move that analysts say may help pull small businesses to Pitney's site -- and in turn, help the company trade them up to more lucrative products. It is that kind of cascading effect that keeps many analysts in Pitney's corner. "They are in prime position to transition small and home office people from stamps to metering to full mail services," said Mr. Henderson, who has kept a strong "buy" recommendation on Pitney stock for three years. "They're using the Internet as a trojan horse to pull in other services." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: From its stamp device, at right, from 1902, to digital meters like the one above, Pitney Bowes has helped companies manage their mail. title: Republicans Plan to Offer A Party Line To the Internet
body: In an effort to raise money, embrace supporters and bypass the news media, the Republican National Committee plans to begin offering subscriptions in January to a "family friendly" Internet service that will deliver the party's messages directly to supporters. Party officials say they plan to market Internet access to registered Republicans, political donors and subscribers of political publications -- a target audience of as many as eight million people. The program is to be announced tomorrow in Washington. Big contributors will qualify for free subscriptions to the service, while other supporters will pay the standard Internet access fee of $19.95 a month. The party will receive a small portion of those monthly subscription fees as donations. Party leaders will not say how much they will take, but they say the greatest benefits of the plan will be political. Unlike Web sites, which require some degree of active effort before they are viewed, the Internet service allows the party to send specific messages to supporters whenever they connect to it. "When Al Gore double-speaks on his record on the nuclear test ban treaty, we'll get our response in their hands the same minute as it reaches a state party chairman," said Larry Purpuro, deputy chief of staff for the Republican committee and director of what is called the e.GOP program. Though the Democrats are considering proposals from several Internet companies to offer a dial-up service, Joe Andrew, national chairman of the Democratic National Committee, said such a service would be "a very minor part" of the party's online strategy. The Democrats, Mr. Andrew said, are more interested in building "communities of interest" online using tools like Web sites and email. Mr. Andrew said the strategy of offering Internet service was "irrelevant but for the dollars" and illustrated the Republicans' approach to politics. "They need money, and they win by raising money," he said. "We need people who believe in our issues." Subscribers to the Republicans' Internet service, in addition to instant access to the party's stance on current events, will receive an email address, GOPnet.com, that identifies their political affiliation. They will also get to see where, as donors, their money goes. Subscribers will receive previews of the party's television advertisements and political mailings, and the chance to participate in members-only political discussions online. The Republican service will be family friendly, Mr. Purpuro said, because pornographic Internet material will be filtered. The concept of a party-sponsored Internet service resolves a troublesome issue for political parties in the Internet era. Party officials have been concerned that their role as purveyors of political information would be threatened in a world in which everyone can be a publisher. "This is a good example of a 19th-century institution trying to adapt to a new battleground," said Bruce Bimber, director of the Center for Information Technology and Society at the University of California at Santa Barbara. Further, the Internet service corresponds with the Republican Party's tradition of treating membership like a club, said Michael Cornfield, a research professor at George Washington University who studies online politics. "This is a bid for parties to gain a part in people's lives the way they did before the decline of the machines," Professor Cornfield said. The major parties are joining more and more groups that are establishing Internet services for their members. Banks, sports teams and even the rock star David Bowie have set up "affinity services" for their customers and fans. The A.F.L.-C.I.O. recently introduced an Internet service for its members. The downside for groups that offer these services is that consumers might blame the groups for technical problems, not the Internet companies that run the machinery. The Republicans' service, for example, will be run by Big Planet, a national Internet service provider. "You'll have people saying, 'I was using the Republicans' service, and it wasn't any good,' " said Zia Daniell Wigder, an analyst for Jupiter Communications, an Internet research firm. "The customers don't know who to blame." Political parties also face legal issues in providing Internet service. Federal election laws impose limits on parties' roles in promoting candidates. For example, a party can present information about polls and newspaper editorials, but if party officials explicitly direct the public to vote for or against a candidate, the act counts as a campaign contribution. The Internet complicates the legal issues further. The Federal Election Commission is currently dissecting a number of Internet-related questions, including whether a link from one Web site to a campaign site can count as a contribution. If such practices do qualify as contributions, then the act of promoting a candidate on the Internet service can be counted against how much cash the party could give to a campaign. Also, under campaign finance bills currently moving through Congress, raising money through subscriptions to an Internet service could be banned altogether. Such funds qualify as "soft money," which would be prohibited under at least one bill awaiting action. "If something like that happens, we'll have to go back to the drawing board," said Thomas J. Josefiak, chief counsel for the Republican National Committee. "If the law changes, we have to change everything." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY: Digital Commerce;
The future of online commerce must be built on credibility. And yet, companies continue to squander the public's trust.
body: IF dot-com companies are really trying to inspire consumer confidence as they embark upon what could well be their make-or-break holiday season, they must be taking oxymoron pills. Under the hot light of recent scrutiny, their increasingly questionable business practices are becoming public, casting long overdue doubt on the credibility of much of the commercial Internet. The fact that the Internet allows people and companies to misrepresent themselves with impunity is well known to online veterans, who after years of sending and receiving April Fool's gags and imitation news releases look askance at everything they get online unless they can verify its source. But the juggernaut that is now the consumer Internet has foisted an avalanche of half-truths, lies-by-omission and outright fraud on a new, more naive online population. Unsophisticated Net users rarely question who or what is operating behind their computer screens and, thus, are far easier to snooker. Their complacency is not completely unwarranted. The Internet, particularly the Web, looks a lot like a computer version of print or broadcast media. But it is neither. As a rule, it has not adopted the kinds of standards and practices that are assumed in traditional media, where advertisements and paid announcements are labeled and conflicts of interest are, at least in theory, disclosed as a matter of course. These disclosures are what provide readers, listeners and viewers of traditional media the context to judge what they read, hear or see. But it is not incumbent upon today's commercial Internet, either by tradition or law, to provide such context. The online credibility issue first hit the international news in early 1999, when Amazon.com was called to task for accepting money from publishers for its purportedly independent book reviews. Since then, more examples of online half-truths and lies have come to light. Most recently, The newyork Times and USA Today both reported that a "fashion photographer" was starting an e-commerce auction Web site, selling fashion models' eggs to would-be parents. He is also, apparently, an established merchant in soft-core pornography, a fact that came to light after the global publicity the stories had generated. A few months ago, DrKoop.com, the Web site of the former surgeon general, Dr. C. Everett Koop was publicly embarrassed for taking commissions on products and services sold through the site without disclosing such financial arrangements. Changes were made on the site in response to the criticism. Less visible but just as pernicious are the growing numbers of "comparison shopping" sites for products on the Internet, sites that do not disclose the methods by which their listings are derived. Although some of these sites are supported solely by advertising revenues, many listings are based on which companies paid to be listed with them. Equally rankling are the portals and search engines that deliver Web addresses, ostensibly in response to a consumer's query but in reality based on paid key words. Advertisers buy key words from portals to make it to the top of the search-results list -- the functional equivalent of companies that name themselves "AAAAAAAcme" for telephone directories -- but portals rarely tell their users of the practice. "People have to assume that there is an advertising influence on almost all the content they see online," wrote the online newsletter eMarketer in March 1999, shortly after the Amazon story broke. "For instance, here is what comes up on a search for 'digital camera' on Lycos: A (paid) banner for digital cameras; a (paid) link to an online bookstore offering books on cameras; the (unpaid) search result links." This is business as usual to people who know how the industry works, but not to consumers, as seen in the Federal Trade Commission's struggle to investigate hundreds of claims of fraudulent practices and sites on the Internet. In May, the F.T.C. held a workshop to educate online companies about disclosure regulations and, in particular, to inform them that existing consumer protection laws did in fact apply on the Internet and to explain how the laws would be enforced. Some Internet companies are doing a good job of disclosure and, in fact, are using it as a selling point for their services. For example, the online bill paying service Paymybills.com makes virtually all information about its service, its company, its policies, partners and business practices available within two clicks of its home page. "We're in the business of consumer trust," says John Tedesco, the chief executive of Paymybills.com. "We consider the language on our site to be a legal contract with our customers. If it ever leaked out that we didn't abide by our policies, it would destroy our business. So we clearly disclose, and we hold by them." Contrast this with Amazon.com, which promised after its paid-reviews debacle to make the company's policy more visible. Amazon has buried its disclosure at the very bottom of its lengthy "Site Guide" page, beneath a link called "Co-Op Disclosure" -- not exactly a descriptive title, or the first place a consumer might look for such information. Credibility of online information is a growing concern both within and outside the industry. Several organizations -- including the Internet Content Coalition, the Online Privacy Alliance and the Pew Charitable Trusts (in which this writer participated) -- have addressed credibility by producing advertising and privacy guidelines and projects focused on disclosure. Most recently, Ziff-Davis founded an industry group called the Council for Internet Commerce (www.commercestandard.com) to try to improve the customer experience online by implementing standards for disclosure of business practices. James Hake, founder and chairman of the project, said that the level of agreement between the 200 companies that voted on the first draft of the standard was "so high that I need to go back and make sure they really meant it." He added, "I'm afraid they might have been answering from the point of view of what the consumer wants to hear, instead of what they were actually willing to do." But if today's practices continue for much longer -- or, as eMarketer put it, if the question as to what's fact and what's for sale is not made clear to consumers -- the use of the Net as a commercial medium could drop precipitously as consumers realize they are being gamed. If dot-coms think it is too much trouble to implement disclosure practices, they will soon discover it is a lot more trouble to win back consumer trust once it is lost. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title:
U.S. VERSUS MICROSOFT: THE INDUSTRY;
Silicon Valley Cites Concern Amid Glee on Microsoft Case
body: In Silicon Valley, the nation's high-technology capital, Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson's powerful findings in the Microsoft antitrust case have been received with a sense of vindication but also ambivalence. In issuing his findings of fact on Friday evening, Judge Jackson delivered two implicit yet unmistakable messages to the industry. Yes, he found, there is indeed a "Microsoft problem" in the computer business, and the software monopolist's bullying tactics hurt consumers and undermine innovation. He also found that there was nothing special about the software industry. For purposes of antitrust, he found, this high-technology world was not much different than any other bricks-and-mortar business. So any satisfaction in Silicon Valley that the judge shares the locally prevailing view of Microsoft is offset by concern that his document is a step toward greater government intervention in the high-technology economy. The judge's findings are not a final ruling in the case, but they will almost certainly serve as the framework for the outcome of the case -- either in court or in an out-of-court settlement between the Microsoft Corporation and the government. "This document does change the landscape," said Jim Breyer, managing partner for Accel Partners, a venture capital firm here. In short, the judge's framing of the facts increases the prospect of mandated changes in Microsoft's corporate behavior, if not more sweeping measures that, in theory, could include breaking up the company. And the Justice Department affirmed today that it had not ruled out seeking any of those options.  Page A23. Much has changed in the computer business since the government filed its sweeping antitrust suit against Microsoft in May 1998. But industry executives here say the issues raised in the trial are still crucial to the nation's high-technology economy. It is true, they note, that most of the venture capital and entrepreneurial effort in Silicon Valley these days is focused on Internet start-ups. At these start-ups, the software and electronic commerce services are built to work on the Internet's World Wide Web rather than being bound to Microsoft's Windows operating system. Such an evolution has become known as the post-PC era, which some experts say is already aborning and beyond Microsoft's control as people increasingly tap into the Web using everything from hand-held devices to TV set-top boxes. Still, the personal computer remains the primary avenue to the Web, and that promises to continue for years. And the federal antitrust case focuses largely on how Microsoft may have used the market power from its Windows monopoly to try to stifle the challenge from Internet software. Whether Microsoft can use its dominance in personal computing to give it the upper hand in the Internet era, industry executives say, will be an important policy issue for years. "Some people think we're in some post-PC era, but we're not, and this issue really matters," said John Doerr, a partner in Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers, a leading venture firm that has backed both Internet start-ups aligned with Microsoft and leading Microsoft rivals like Sun Microsystems and America Online. Still, there are aspects of Judge Jackson's findings of fact that give people here second thoughts. The judge's sweeping castigation of Microsoft's business practices deals largely with how the company's restrictive contracts thwarted efforts by personal computer makers, Internet service providers and others to promote, distribute or use the products of rivals. But in his findings, Judge Jackson made some fine-tuned judgments about the software business. He found that the computer operating system and Internet browsing software were separate products. Microsoft, however, chose to fold its browsing software into Windows -- and in a separate but related case, a Federal appeals court said Microsoft was free to do that as long as it could make "any plausible claim" of business efficiency or consumer benefit from doing so. Judge Jackson went further. He found that by putting its browser in the operating system, Microsoft made Windows 98 unnecessarily buggy. That decision, he wrote, "unjustifiably jeopardized the stability and security of the operating system." Just what does and does not belong in a computer operating system can make for fascinating and impassioned debate among software programmers. But the idea of a federal court or the government second-guessing such decisions is one that makes many industry executives and experts leery, even those who are critical of Microsoft. "Everyone in the industry is uncomfortable with the choke hold that Microsoft has," said Hal R. Varian, dean of the school of information management and systems at the University of California at Berkeley. "But they are also uncomfortable with having the government get involved in software design decisions." To be sure, industry executives are not shy about offering solutions for curbing Microsoft's power, and have done so since before the suit was filed. They run the gamut from restricting Microsoft's power to write restrictive contracts to forcing the company to publish its software protocols to breaking up the company. Nearly all the proposed solutions are problematic. Breaking up the company by separating the Windows operating system business from Microsoft Office productivity programs, for example, runs the risk of merely creating two monopolies instead of one. Microsoft's market share in programs like word processing, spreadsheets and presentation software is even higher than its share of the operating system market. Mandating that Microsoft openly publish the underlying "source" code for Windows -- another sweeping potential sanction mentioned -- runs the risk of reducing Microsoft's incentives to innovate because other software companies, at no cost, would get the technology Microsoft had invested to build. "The fundamental challenge for the government and the courts is to come up with a set of remedies that really do help consumers instead of doing more harm than good," said David Yoffie, a professor at the Harvard Business School. Yet many industry executives agree on what the policy goal should be in dealing with Microsoft: keeping the basic technology standards an open, public resource in the Internet era. Common technology standards have been catalysts for the growth of industries for centuries. "The personal computer industry has benefited greatly by the establishment of technology standards, but they happen to be owned by Microsoft," observed Richard Shaffer, principal of Technologic Partners, a consulting firm in newyork and San Francisco. "And for the Internet and electronic commerce to flourish, we need standards for security, payment and software protocols. But the objective has to be that nobody -- no single company -- becomes the next Microsoft in this new world." Esther Dyson, editor of Release 1.0, an industry newsletter, added: "From a policy standpoint, what you want to do is create an environment of dynamic instability where everyone, including Microsoft, has to innovate constantly to move forward without getting the government deeply involved. You don't want Microsoft controlling the industry, but you don't want the government controlling it either." Microsoft's top executives cringe at the suggestion that they control the key technology or the pace of innovation in computing -- in the PC era or any other. "There is no control," Steven A. Ballmer, the president of Microsoft, said. "If customers don't want to upgrade to the next version of Windows, they don't have to. And if anybody wants to innovate on top of us or alongside us, they can." In an interview, Mr. Ballmer said the rise of new technologies like Web-based software and the Linux operating system represented a cataclysmic change in the software business. "We have no guaranteed position in this new Internet era," he said. "To me, it sure doesn't feel like we control things." More and more, Microsoft's challengers hope that Mr. Ballmer proves to be correct. In his findings of fact, Judge Jackson found that Microsoft's grip on the industry would not be loosened any time soon by Linux or another rival operating system, BeOS. The judge called both "fringe" technologies and found that neither posed a challenge to Windows in the foreseeable future. "I loathe Microsoft, and there's no question it's a monopoly," said Eric Raymond, a programmer, author and Linux evangelist. "But I think Judge Jackson underestimated the competitive threat that Linux presents." Jean-Louis Gassee, founder of Be Inc., maker of BeOS, said he founded his company because he felt Microsoft's grip on the industry was loosening. The Microsoft suit and the rise of Linux, he said, "made it possible to consider a fringe operating system" -- and, he added, to consider the possibility that it could make inroads against Microsoft. After the judge's findings, he says, his chances could improve. "It's a staggering document," he said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Web Audio Network Plans New Delivery System Today
body: RealNetworks Inc., the multimedia Internet company, plans today to announce a new network delivery service and a new version of its media player, called RealPlayer 7. The new service will include a daily program listing called Take 5, which will inform Internet surfers about multimedia offerings around the Internet. It will also include a message service to alert users of the company's RealPlayer software of late-breaking multimedia events during the day. Rob Glaser, founder and chief executive of RealNetworks, said the company had already distributed 85 million copies of its RealPlayer software for PC's, which is used for playing multimedia programming transmitted over the Internet. RealNetworks executives said that besides the daily Take 5, the new network service would include a more comprehensive roundup of multimedia programming on the Web to be called the Real.com Guide, which would serve as a reference and search directory for Internet audio and video programming. "We've integrated a network of services," Mr. Glaser said. The company will have more than 100 broadcast and Internet media partners for the service, he said, and the guide would list multimedia programming from networks like ABC, BBC, CBS, Fox and NBC, as well as Internet-only media companies. The new RealNetworks service is certain to intensify the company's competition with Microsoft, which has recently begun to work more closely with the recording industry to attempt to set technical standards for managing digital rights. Microsoft has also cut deals with Creative Labs and Cirrus Logic to build support for its audio standard into portable music players. Another matter RealNetworks, based in Seattle, must now face is that it is moving toward competing directly with America Online, Yahoo and Broadcast.com. This shift could push some of the largest Internet portal companies away from the RealPlayer standard. RealNetworks is also trying to address user-privacy concerns expressed last week after new reports that the company's RealJukebox software, which can record and play compact disks as well as download digital music from the Internet, continually reports personal information about its users to RealNetworks. After that disclosure, the company released a software patch on its Web site to prevent the RealJukebox program from relaying personal information about users to the company or to any third party. Executives said they would begin a review of the company's privacy practices. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Commercial Property /The Market;
Office Space Is Scarce, and Getting More Expensive
body: WE are already seeing triple-digit rents at the upper end of the midtown market," said an ebullient Steven Swerdlow, the senior managing director of CB Richard Ellis's newyork office, referring to the $100 a square foot annual rents reported for the buildings at 712 and 767 Fifth Avenue. Mr. Swerdlow cautions that stratospheric rent levels are likely to be confined to a few trophy buildings on Fifth Avenue and 57th Street, but he said the figure expresses the tone of the office market in Manhattan: space is scarce and it is getting more expensive. The strength of the market is such that some real estate executives say it may prompt something not seen in this decade, new construction without a government subsidy. The situation is the result of a booming economy that has produced nearly 79,000 private sector jobs in the city over the last 12 months. Unlike past expansions that were largely fueled by the financial services industry, much of the current growth is the result of industries that did not exist in previous cycles, such as new media and other Internet-related activities. The importance of these companies, and the telecommunications firms that are also multiplying, cannot be underestimated, said John Powers, an executive managing director of Insignia/ESG, the real estate services company. Through the end of September, he said, these companies accounted for 35 percent of the space leased this year in Midtown South and 12 percent of the space downtown. William G. Cohen, an executive vice president of Newmark & Company Real Estate, said the new computer-based companies are transforming whole neighborhoods. Many are lumped together under the rubric of "dot com" after the last part of their Internet addresses. "The dot com's are driving the Park Avenue South and Garment District markets," he said. "They are all out there looking for 10,000 square feet in move-in condition." Examples of these transactions include Media Matrix, which took 10,000 square feet at 250 Park Avenue South at 20th Street; Fortune City.com, which signed up for 22,600 square feet at 500 Seventh Avenue at 37th Street, and Screaming Media, which took 26,000 square feet in the Starrett-Lehigh Building at 601 West 26th Street. These companies are largely selling the skills of their highly educated, generally younger employees, and they go to considerable effort to recruit and retain them. Many are attracted to the culture and nightlife of big cities, a bonus for newyork. A recent national survey commissioned by Cushman & Wakefield, the real estate services company, found that "computer services professionals chose newyork more frequently than any other city when asked where they would most like to work." Broader measures of leasing activity showed the strength of the market as well. "The Manhattan office market posted strong results in the third quarter and is now poised to end the decade with the lowest vacancy rates and highest asking rents since the early 1980's," according to the Cushman & Wakefield report. And because there has been little new building in Manhattan in the last decade, the report noted that the upward part of the real estate cycle is likely to be extended. The overall vacancy rate in Manhattan fell to 7.4 percent in the third quarter, the lowest rate in the decade, with space in Class A buildings even tighter at 5 percent, according to the report. The average asking rent increased to $39.44 a square foot annually from $32.89 at the comparable time in 1998. Average asking rents in midtown broke the $40-a-foot barrier, increasing to $41.57, while those in Midtown South -- once not considered a prime office district -- are expected to top $30 a square foot before the end of the year. Average asking rents downtown are already over $30 a square foot, reaching $32.95 in the third quarter. ASKING rents only tell part of the story, since other lease terms have an effect on the total cost of a deal. Funds provided by landlords for the construction of interior space -- called work letters -- have been shrinking and the period of free rent growing steadily shorter, brokers say. "Work letters have been declining from $50 a square foot a few years ago to $30 and under now," Mr. Powers said. "That adds to rent," he said, because tenants have to bear more of the cost of building their space. In the early 90's, when landlords were almost desperate to lure tenants, a year to a year and a half of free rent on a 10-year lease was common. Now. he said, "tenants are lucky to get the time of construction" during which they are not actually occupying the space and are paying rent somewhere else. Although office rents seem lofty compared to those in the mid-1990's, they have just recovered the losses of the early part of the decade, real estate executives say. "Nominal rents are back to the 1980 level," said Mr. Swerdlow. "Adjusted for inflation, we are still not back to that level." Averages are useful for tracking trends in the market, but they also obscure localized developments by blending the highs and lows of a market. More important, some real estate executives say, is the fact that rents in some parts of Manhattan have reached the level where nonsubsidized new construction is economically feasible. "It takes rent of about $65 a square foot to justify new construction without a subsidy and we have just gotten there in some parts of town," said Thomas Falus, president of Cushman & Wakefield's newyork metropolitan area operations. He noted that the new buildings in the Times Square area and the ones planned at Columbus Circle all involved assistance from government entities. "We have over a dozen clients who are looking to do something with land that is dormant or underutilized," he said. "There is a lot of land in the pipeline and the question is whether it will be developed in an orderly fashion over the next 24 to 36 months or come out in a rush." He said it would be useful if 4 million to 5 million square feet of office space were built over the next few years, noting that it would add only about 1 percent to Manhattan's inventory. The capital markets are prepared to finance new construction as long as certain conditions are met, said John D. Lyons, the executive managing director of Granite Partners, a real estate finance company.  "The capital is there to finance new construction as long as it is a quality project with ample preleasing," he said. Unlike the early 1980's, when lenders were willing to finance new construction on a purely speculative basis, today's investors want a high level of assurance that the buildings will be occupied once completed, he said. And while real estate investment trusts have diminished as a factor in the market, another class of investors, known as opportunity funds, has arisen to take their place.  "Opportunity funds have raised $29 billion in capital in the first three quarters of this year," he said. "REIT's at their height in 1997 only raised $37 billion." REIT investment in the city has declined by 12 percent since the third quarter of 1998 while private investors increased their presence in the city by 27 percent, accounting for almost half the total office transactions through the third quarter. With the leasing market strong, buildings in Manhattan have held their value or increased in price. According to Granite, buildings in Midtown South increased 7 percent to an average of $157 a square foot over the same time last year, while those in midtown held at $197 a square foot and those downtown remained at an average of $122 a square foot. While declining vacancies and rising rental rates are good news for owners of property, the situation can be difficult for brokers whose business depends on finding space and making deals. "This is a very frustrating market to work in," said Robert Emden, an executive managing director of Grubb & Ellis who specializes in midtown properties. "You have to canvass the market to find out where space is going to become available before it hits the market. Once it is on the market, it's old news." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Steven Swerdlow of CB Richard Ellis's newyork office notes triple-digit rents at top of midtown market. (Frances Roberts for The newyork Times)

title:
JERSEYANA;
That Old Crescent Moon
body: The approach of the new millennium has made for some strange bedfellows, one of the strangest being people surfing the Internet in search of outhouses to adorn their suburban gardens. Welcome to the quirky side of Y2K, where Spam is what's for dinner and privies on line are all the rage. Whether people are buying outhouses because they fear the collapse of the indoor plumbing system or because they long for kitschy history we may never know, but the fact remains that they are moving fast. "New Jersey Historic Outhouse Available! Color red, a small window on one side, no cutout design in door. Very sound and sturdy," read the advertisement on the Outhouses of America Tour Web site, placed by Bob Shafto of Falmouth, Me., last January. According to Mr. Shafto, the ad drew dozens of takers, from Maine to California. In the end, the circa 1850 privy went free of charge, to a couple who live near Trenton and needed a trendy new potting shed. The privy was part of a farm in Hazlet owned by Mr. Shafto's aunt, Margurite Ludwig, who had sold it to a developer and moved to a senior care center in Navasink. The farm was going to be demolished. "I'd heard people were interested in outhouses and I figured this piece of history should be saved," Mr. Shafto said in a telephone interview. "I wasn't doing it for money, although people were willing to spend a great deal of money and effort to get the thing to their home." Privies are selling for $400 to $4,000. New Jersey, with its creeping suburban sprawl threatening older home sites, has become a fresh source of outhouses. The state's outhouses, old and in disrepair or spruced up with paint and flower boxes, have become icons adorning not only lawns but also merchandise. "We have puzzles, wooden and tin outhouse night lights and books and we just sold out of them all for the third time since September," said Marilyn Schmidt, who owns Buzby's General Store in Chatsworth.  Jersey privies grace calendars, coasters, post cards and jigsaw puzzles as well as a half-dozen Web sites. The Outhouses of America Tour on the Internet, run by John Loose of Michigan, features Jersey privies. His site also offers trivia, jokes and cartoons. One featured outhouse on the "tour" is in Brick Township in Ocean County at the Havens Homestead Museum. Mr. Loose explained that the privy was built by a local Boy Scout troop to go with the circa 1830's museum house "because the original met its end when a young boy and his twin brother decided to experiment with methane gas by lighting matches in the outhouse." Possible virtual tour additions include Double Trouble State Park's outhouses in Toms River and the Old Stone Store privy in Manahawkin, both in Ocean County. "We've had privies here since the turn of the century," said Bill Bulger, historic preservation specialist at Double Trouble. "The park is undergoing a lot of changes and upgrades, being on the New Jersey Coastal Heritage Trail. Although we have now closed the outhouses they're here to stay. They are part of the time period of the park that we're trying to push." Since the demand has outstripped the supply -- there are only so many little shacks with a crescent moon on the door to go around these days -- replicas are being built and sold. The Red Top Market in Burlington County sells privies along with produce by the roadside on Route 70, while the Hammonton stretch of the White Horse Pike is dotted with the narrow structures. Tom Sankowicz of Lake Pine in Burlington County wanted a tool and boat tackle shed to stand behind his new lakeside home. Being handy with a hammer and saw and recalling the old gas station his uncle used to run in Tuckahoe, which had an outhouse, he was inspired to build a privy. "I remember that the outhouse was a real highlight of the place," Mr. Sankowicz said of his uncle's garage. When he was making plans for his new home he thought "a traditional shed would be ugly and an outhouse would make it more interesting." The spiffy new privy stands proudly facing Lake Pine with two brightly colored canoes propped on either side. "Boaters passing by the house recognize what it is by the crescent moon on the door and you can just see they get a laugh out of it," he said. "It makes an interesting conversation piece." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Bob Faisst, a retired plumber in Devonshire, makes outhouses. As with the one above, they are often used for storage rather than their original purpose. (Photographs by David Hunsinger for The newyork Times)

title:
MARKET INSIGHT;
Bidding War To Uncork Drug Stocks
body: REDD FOXX, the comedian, once observed that health nuts were going to feel stupid someday, lying in the hospital dying of nothing. It is difficult to call a business with more than $130 billion in sales worldwide dead, but until the end of September drug stocks did not have much life: as measured by the Amex Pharmaceuticals Index, from the start of the year through Sept. 29 the group was down more than 14 percent. The stocks started to wake up in October. Last week, investors became even more interested when Pfizer made an $82.4 billion bid for Warner-Lambert, casting doubt on Warner's friendly merger agreement, worth more than $70 billion, with American Home Products. Until recently, Larry N. Feinberg, managing partner of Oracle Investment Management, which manages about $600 million in hedge funds and private equity exclusively in health care companies, was not buying drug stocks. He is now. Mr. Feinberg took some time last week to talk about the industry's problems and prospects. Here are excerpts from the conversation.  Q. In the mid-1990's drug stocks were crushed by fears about the Clinton health plan and then roared back. What has ailed them this year?  A.  Drug stocks have lagged this year because of economics, politics and the Internet. From an economic point of view, fears of rising inflation have not helped, because if interest rates are backing up, then price-earnings multiples are suspect. A political issue is the biggest cloud over the industry, and one of the keys there is the Medicare prescription drug benefit. There is a big political push to get the elderly covered for prescription drugs. This fear of government regulation implies possible price controls by the government. The Internet has caused concerns about drug utilization and benefit management. Historically, the thing that has been really striking about the health care industry is the lack of information flow. Now we are entering a period where a number of companies are hooking up health information systems with doctors. The net impact of that is that drug utilization will get controlled more, and cheaper drugs, where applicable, will be used more often.  Q. It seems these are real concerns. Yet you are positive on drug stocks. Why?  A.  We are past the bottom and are beginning to turn up. For demographic and technological reasons, the health care industry will be the world's great growth industry. I believe we have entered a tremendous new product cycle. At the moment we have new drug categories like osteoporosis, breakthrough drugs for certain cancers. The first two flu drugs have just been approved. These are huge new markets that are opening up, and we are just at the tip of the iceberg. The next big wave will be based on genomics, as we get more answers to what genes turn on and off and why that happens. That will lead to customized drug therapy. Even if the effort to curb costs intensifies, expensive drugs are not going to go away. If they are better than generics, paying for them is still better than putting people in the hospital.  Q. What is your sense of the struggle for Warner-Lambert?  A.  Both Pfizer and American Home Products are good fits with Warner-Lambert. American Home Products has a great drug pipeline. Warner-Lambert doesn't have much of a pipeline, but it has good products. The Pfizer bid, which will be hard for American Home Products to match, is more of a strategic combination in that it gives Pfizer a better position in the cardiovascular business. But the real key to this is that this is the trigger that will open the floodgate to further mergers.  Q. Which companies are more likely to combine than others?  A.  Anybody who wants to get bigger is a candidate, so you could include everybody in the industry. There are tremendous cost savings to be realized. The most obvious merger candidates are those that need help, a list that includes Novartis, SmithKline Beecham and Pharmacia Upjohn. I wouldn't put it past Merck to do a deal. In the next five years there will be fewer, bigger players.  Q. So which stocks do you like?  A.  We own Bristol-Myers Squibb, which has a great drug pipeline, American Home Products and biotechnology companies like Amgen, which is selling at a multiple comparable to the drug companies but is spending twice as much on research and development. Aside from the drug companies, the big opportunity for investors is business-to-business commerce in health care. Companies in this area include Medical Manager, CareInsite, which has the former management team from Medco Containment; Healtheon; and IDX Corporation. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Feinberg

title:
U.S. VERSUS MICROSOFT: PART 3 OF 7;
Setback for a Software Giant: Key Sections of Judge's Findings of Fact
body: Excluding Navigator From the OEM Channel  BINDING INTERNET EXPLORER TO WINDOWS  The Status of Web Browsers As Separate Products Consumers determine their software requirements by identifying the functionalities they desire. While consumers routinely evaluate software products on the basis of the functionalities the products deliver, they generally lack sufficient information to make judgments based on the designs and implementations of those products. Accordingly, consumers generally choose which software products to license, install, and use on the basis of the products' functionalities, not their designs and implementations. While the meaning of the term "Web browser" is not precise in all respects, there is a consensus in the software industry as to the functionalities that a Web browser offers a user. Specifically, a Web browser provides the ability for the end user to select, retrieve, and perceive resources on the Web. There is also a consensus in the software industry that these functionalities are distinct from the set of functionalities provided by an operating system. Many consumers desire to separate their choice of a Web browser from their choice of an operating system. Some consumers, particularly corporate consumers, demand browsers and operating systems separately because they prefer to standardize on the same browser across different operating systems. For such consumers, standardizing on the browser of their choice results in increased productivity and lower training and support costs, and permits the establishment of consistent security and privacy policies governing Web access. Moreover, many consumers who need an operating system, including a substantial percentage of corporate consumers, do not want a browser at all. For example, if a consumer has no desire to browse the Web, he may not want a browser taking up memory on his hard disk and slowing his system's performance. Also, for businesses desiring to inhibit employees' access to the Internet while minimizing system support costs, the most efficient solution is often using PC systems without browsers. Because of the separate demand for browsers and operating systems, firms have found it efficient to supply the products separately. A number of operating system vendors offer consumers the choice of licensing their operating systems without a browser. Others bundle a browser with their operating system products but allow OEMs, value-added resellers, and consumers either to not install it or, if the browser has been pre-installed, to uninstall it. While Microsoft no longer affords this flexibility (it is the only operating system vendor that does not), it has always marketed and distributed Internet Explorer separately from Windows in several channels. These include retail sales, service kits for ISVs, free downloads over the Internet, and bundling with other products produced both by Microsoft and by third-party ISVs. In order to compete with Navigator for browser share, as well as to satisfy corporate consumers who want their diverse PC platforms to present a common browser interface to employees, Microsoft has also created stand-alone versions of Internet Explorer that run on operating systems other than 32-bit Windows, including the Mac OS and Windows 3.x. In conclusion, the preferences of consumers and the responsive behavior of software firms demonstrate that Web browsers and operating systems are separate products. Microsoft's Actions In contrast to other operating system vendors, Microsoft both refused to license its operating system without a browser and imposed restrictions -- at first contractual and later technical -- on OEMs' and end users' ability to remove its browser from its operating system. As its internal contemporaneous documents and licensing practices reveal, Microsoft decided to bind Internet Explorer to Windows in order to prevent Navigator from weakening the applications barrier to entry, rather than for any pro-competitive purpose. Before it decided to blunt the threat that Navigator posed to the applications barrier to entry, Microsoft did not plan to make it difficult or impossible for OEMs or consumers to obtain Windows without obtaining Internet Explorer. In fact, the company's internal correspondence and external communications indicate that, as late as the fall of 1994, Microsoft was planning to include low-level Internet "plumbing," such as a TCP/IP stack, but not a browser, with Windows 95. Microsoft subsequently decided to develop a browser to run on Windows 95. As late as June 1995, however, Microsoft had not decided to bundle that browser with the operating system. The plan at that point, rather, was to ship the browser in a separate "frosting" package, for which Microsoft intended to charge. By April or May of that year, however, Microsoft's top executives had identified Netscape's browser as a potential threat to the applications barrier to entry. Throughout the spring, more and more key executives came to the conclusion that Microsoft's best prospect of quashing that threat lay in maximizing the usage share of Microsoft's browser at Navigator's expense. The executives believed that the most effective way of carrying out this strategy was to ensure that every copy of Windows 95 carried with it a copy of Microsoft's browser, then code-named "O'Hare." For example, two days after the June 21, 1995 meeting between Microsoft and Netscape executives, Microsoft's John Ludwig sent an email to Paul Maritz and the other senior executives involved in Microsoft's browser effort. " O bviously netscape does see us as a client competitor," Ludwig wrote. " W e have to work extra hard to get ohare on the oem disks." Microsoft did manage to bundle Internet Explorer 1.0 with the first version of Windows 95 licensed to OEMs in July 1995. It also included a term in its OEM licenses that prohibited the OEMs from modifying or deleting any part of Windows 95, including Internet Explorer, prior to shipment. The OEMs accepted this restriction despite their interest in meeting consumer demand for PC operating systems without Internet Explorer. After all, Microsoft made the restriction a non-negotiable term in its Windows 95 license, and the OEMs felt they had no commercially viable alternative to pre-installing Windows 95 on their PCs. Apart from a few months in the fall of 1997, when Microsoft provided OEMs with Internet Explorer 4.0 on a separate disk from Windows 95 and permitted them to ship the latter without the former, Microsoft has never allowed OEMs to ship Windows 95 to consumers without Internet Explorer. This policy has guaranteed the presence of Internet Explorer on every new Windows PC system. Microsoft knew that the inability to remove Internet Explorer made OEMs less disposed to pre-install Navigator onto Windows 95. OEMs bear essentially all of the consumer support costs for the Windows PC systems they sell. These include the cost of handling consumer complaints and questions generated by Microsoft's software.Pre-installing more than one product in a given category, such as word processors or browsers, onto its PC systems can significantly increase an OEM's support costs, for the redundancy can lead to confusion among novice users. In addition, pre-installing a second product in a given software category can increase an OEM's product testing costs. Finally, many OEMs see pre-installing a second application in a given software category as a questionable use of the scarce and valuable space on a PC's hard drive. Microsoft's executives believed that the incentives that its contractual restrictions placed on OEMs would not be sufficient in themselves to reverse the direction of Navigator's usage share. Consequently, in late 1995 or early 1996, Microsoft set out to bind Internet Explorer more tightly to Windows 95 as a technical matter. The intent was to make it more difficult for anyone, including systems administrators and users, to remove Internet Explorer from Windows 95 and to simultaneously complicate the experience of using Navigator with Windows 95.  As Brad Chase wrote to his superiors near the end of 1995, "We will bind the shell to the Internet Explorer, so that running any other browser is a jolting experience." . . . Although users were not able to remove all of the routines that provided Web browsing from OSR 2 and successive versions of Windows 95, Microsoft still provided them with the ability to uninstall Internet Explorer by using the "Add/Remove" panel, which was accessible from the Windows 95 desktop. The Add/Remove function did not delete all of the files that contain browsing specific code, nor did it remove browsing-specific code that is used by other programs. The Add/Remove function did, however, remove the functionalities that were provided to the user by Internet Explorer, including the means of launching the Web browser. Accordingly, from the user's perspective, uninstalling Internet Explorer in this way was equivalent to removing the Internet Explorer program from Windows 95. In late 1996, senior executives within Microsoft, led by James Allchin, began to argue that Microsoft was not binding Internet Explorer tightly enough to Windows and as such was missing an opportunity to maximize the usage of Internet Explorer at Navigator's expense. Allchin first made his case to Paul Maritz in late December 1996. He wrote: I don't understand how IE is going to win. The current path is simply to copy everything that Netscape does packaging and product wise. Let's suppose IE is as good as Navigator/Communicator. Who wins? The one with 80% market share. Maybe being free helps us, but once people are used to a product it is hard to change them.  Consider Office. We are more expensive today and we're still winning.
