title: Web Retailers Empty Wallets On Advertising
body: Send.com is buying its 15 minutes of fame right now. The year-old Internet gift site has raised only $10 million in venture capital financing so far, but it has committed to spend $20 million for television advertising on such top-rated shows as "Ally McBeal," "Frasier" and "Monday Night Football" the next two months. Its budget would be substantial for even a big retailer like Amazon.com, which is said to have spent $17 million on television for all of 1998. But for tiny Send.com, which has no profits and negligible revenue, it is stunningly audacious. Although he has borrowed against investors' pledges of more capital to pay for his ad spending spree, Send.com's chief executive, Michael Lannon, sees little choice. "Not every company is going to survive this Christmas," he said. "We are treating the next eight weeks like an election campaign. Both we and our investors believe that customers are going to vote on who the leading gift site is, and only one candidate wins." Convinced that this Christmas season will be make-or-break, e-retailers are in a costly race to bring their names to consumers through TV advertising. There is little evidence that such exposure in a crowded market will prove to be a cost-efficient way to attract new customers. In fact, when Amazon.com recently indicated it would triple holiday marketing to more than $100 million, the move gave stock analysts pause and sent its stock price plunging. Moreover, in some cases, the start-ups are buying air time at the expense of other important business components, like customer service, inventory and simple Web design. But many companies say they feel compelled to spend everything they have (and more) and hope the financial markets will refill their coffers after the holiday. In all of 1998, Internet companies -- including portals, online brokerage firms, as well as e-retailers -- accounted for $323 million in TV ad spending, according to Competitive Media Reporting, an advertising monitoring service. In the first half of this year, they spent about $400 million on TV, and media buyers estimate spending in the second half will far surpass that level and push the sum for the year well past $1 billion. Though retailers and other gift sites are leading the charge, almost every site seems desperate to register with consumers in the end-of-year buying crush. Total Internet sales of products and services like travel are expected to be $6 billion in November and December, according to Jupiter Communications. "A lot of e-tailers have sold their souls to the TV networks, gambling that they can drive massive customers through the site through mass advertising," said David Cowan, a partner in Bessemer Venture Partners, a Silicon Valley firm that has helped finance such Web start-ups as eToys and MotherNature.com. "This season will be a proving ground for the TV networks to flex their muscles as the true portals of e-commerce." As more Internet companies feel the need to match their competitors' presence on television, the cost of being a noticeable player spirals upward. "The price of entry for an annual plan might be $40 to $50 million a year -- $8 to $10 million a quarter," said David Smith, the principal in Mediasmith Inc., a San Francisco agency that plans and buys ad time for interactive firms. "That is a lot of money." To put that in perspective, an established retailer typically spends 3 to 4 percent of its revenue on advertising, according to Burt Flickinger III of Reach Marketing, a consulting group in Westport, Conn. Gap Inc., one of the nation's largest retailers with $9 billion in expected 1999 revenue, allotted $157 million for television advertising last year, reports Competitive Media. And Gap is ubiquitous on TV. Nordstom Inc., the department store chain with more than $5 billion in revenue last year, just announced its biggest national TV and print campaign ever. The $17 million effort will promote, what else, Nordstromshoes.com, its newest Internet retailing site. Of course, the feeding frenzy has been a boon to the old media concerns that Internet companies tend to mock as dinosaurs. Newspapers, magazines and radio stations have all seen a generous flood of media dollars. But TV outlets, with their relatively high rates, have been swimming in them. At the major networks, the cost of 30-second ads on top programs like "E. R." and "Monday Night Football" come at a substantial premium over last year, partly on the strength of Internet demand. For 30-second spots on the Super Bowl, average prices rocketed from $1.6 million on Fox TV last January to $2 million for ABC's broadcast in January 2000. CBS Inc. has been trading on the desperation of Internet companies by offering television time in exchange for stock in those ventures. "We've been swapping equity for branding," said a company spokesman, Gil Schwartz, who said the network now had stakes in 13 companies. Four of the companies -- including Marketwatch.com and Med scape -- are publicly traded, and CBS's total stake is worth more than half a billion dollars, Mr. Schwartz said. The obsession with television is a new and unproven strategy among Internet companies. Even a year ago, most Internet companies concentrated their ad dollars online. "Last Christmas, merchants were allocating 70 to 80 percent of their marketing budgets online largely at portals," said Ken Cassar, a digital commerce analyst at Jupiter Communications, a new-media consulting firm. "Today, that is flipped, with the majority being spent on traditional media and most in television." Several factors have led to the transformation of marketing across the industry. There is a general belief that online advertising through banners and portals like Yahoo! and America Online is ineffective. This last year, Internet companies have enlisted executives from marketing giants like Pepsi and Procter & Gamble, which have a history of using television to increase customer awareness of their branded products. But most important, television in particular is perceived as a king maker based on a few Cinderella stories last year. In its first year in business, eToys, a Web-based toy seller, did $2 million in sales. Then the credit card consortium Visa U.S.A. decided a good way to support e-commerce in general during the Christmas season was to air an ad showing children snuggled in bed as parents clicked away at the site to get their presents. eToys' revenue jumped to $23 million in the fourth quarter. Last year, though, there was relatively little "dot com" advertising on TV. Now the ads flow together one after another through the commercial breaks. Robert Levitan says getting a brand out to consumers is much tougher now than when he co-founded iVillage, a community site established in 1995. Now, he is chief executive of Flooz.com, which essentially allows shoppers to buy a gift certificate that can be redeemed at select Internet sites. The site calls its currency flooz, which is emailed to a recipient. "Earlier on, if you made a big noise and were provocative that was enough," he said. "Now everyone is provocative and irreverant." To rise above the din, Mr. Levitan is betting roughly half the company's $16 million in funding on marketing in the next 10 weeks. He also gave up a significant share of stock options (he won't say how many) to Whoopi Goldberg to engage her as spokeswoman. The uncertainty of using advertising to rise above the din is heightened because so many young Internet companies are beginning their TV ads in a big national push without testing them in smaller markets. Send.com, for example, had done only radio commercials before it jumped into the national television market. In addition, industry consultants suspect some Internet retailers are short-changing key operations, like improved Web design that will keep shoppers coming back. "Several times," said Jakob Nielsen, a Web designer in Silicon Valley, "companies have called up and said basically: 'We have this ad campaign planned. It is $20 million. We have already shot the commercial and booked the air time. It is running in three weeks. But we have discovered our Web site is no good. What should we do?' " "The answer is, you are sort of doomed," Mr. Nielsen said. Even if everything runs smoothly -- if customers arrive and they find good service -- some Wall Street analysts are beginning to question whether such big expenditures can be a cost-effective way to attract new customers. Amazon.com's stock plunged after it indicated it would spend heavily to keep up with the Joneses because its cost of acquiring new customers will continue to go up even though stock analysts had expected it to finally turn south. But if Wall Street is signaling that it is worried about costs, Internet retailers are turning a deaf ear. Peter Neupert, the chief executive of drugstore.com, an online pharmacy that has spent heavily on ads, estimates that it cost his site $63 in the third quarter to acquire each new customer. "We expect that number to go up -- not down,"' he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Whoopi Goldberg in a television spot for Flooz.com. title: CD Software Said to Gather Data on Users
body: RealNetworks' popular RealJukebox software for playing CD's on computers surreptitiously monitors the listening habits and certain other activities of people who use it and continually reports this information, along with the user's identity, to RealNetworks, said a security expert who intercepted and examined data generated by the program. In interviews last week, company officials acknowledged that RealJukebox, which can copy music to a user's hard drive and download it from the Internet as well as play it, gathers information on what music users are playing and recording. Dave Richards, RealNetworks' vice president for consumer products, said the company gathered the information to customize services for individual users. He and other company officials insisted that the practice did not violate consumer privacy because the information was not being stored by RealNetworks nor distributed to other companies. But privacy advocates and security experts interviewed last week were unanimous in condemning the practice, calling it a violation of the privacy of the 13.5 million registered users of RealJukebox, almost all of whom have given the company their names and email addresses. Even if the company's use of the data is benign, these experts said, the practice is unacceptable because of the secrecy: RealNetworks, one of the largest distributors of audio software on the Internet, does not inform consumers that they are being identified and monitored by the company. The information that RealNetworks gathers is extensive. According to Richard M. Smith, an independent Internet security consultant from Brookline, Mass., who discovered RealJukebox's monitoring functions, each time the program is started on a computer connected to the Internet, it sends in the following information to the company: the number of songs stored on the user's hard drive; the kind of file formats -- RealAudio or MP3 -- the songs are stored in; the quality level of the recordings; the user's preferred music genre, and the type of portable music player, if any, that the user has connected to the computer. Officials at RealNetworks said most of this information was used to offer music selections to users based on their preferences. All this information is combined with a personal serial number known as a globally unique identifier, or GUID, which is assigned to each user when he or she registers the software. RealJukebox is distributed only on the Internet, and users are instructed to register -- giving the company their names, email addresses and ZIP codes -- when they install the software. What is more, if RealJukebox is used with its default settings, it automatically loads each time a CD is inserted in the CD-ROM drive, and if the computer is connected to the Internet, the title of the CD is sent, together with the GUID, to RealNetworks. "Either they have been dazzlingly careless with their treatment of personally identifiable information or they are completely disingenuous," said Jason Catlett, founder and president of Junkbusters, a privacy watchdog organization. "Which is worse? If they are not disclosing what they are doing, that is unconscionable." Some other CD player programs also assign GUID's to each copy of the software. The difference lies in what they do with it. The Microsoft Corporation, for example, says that the unique identifier in its Windows Media Player is used for such things as purchasing multimedia from a Web site. It is not routed through Microsoft, nor does Microsoft require users to register, and it does not gather information through Media Player, said a spokesman for Waggener Edstrom, a public relations firm that represents Mircrosoft. The fact that RealJukebox is gathering this information is not mentioned in the long privacy policy the company posts on its Web site. Nor is it acknowledged in the licensing agreement that users must approve when installing the program. David Banisar, a lawyer in Washington who specializes in Internet law, said that RealNetworks' surveillance practices could violate various state and federal statutes, including the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. "It's a new type of case that hasn't been brought before," he said. "But I think it's a pretty good case." Mr. Banisar argued that RealJukebox could be considered a "trojan horse," a legitimate program that contains hidden instructions to perform illegitimate functions. Company officials said on Friday that the registration procedure for the free version of RealJukebox did ask for personal information, including name and email address, but they said that users could skip the registration and still use the program and that RealJukebox would stop prompting users to register after five attempts. Some customers, they said, had stumbled on this fact and had declined to register. However, customers who purchase RealJukebox Plus, a version with enhanced features that RealNetworks sells online for $29.99 with a money-back guarantee, cannot avoid registering since they must type in a unique serial number to install the program. And in this case, RealNetworks also gathers credit card and mailing address information before it assigns the number. Mr. Richards of RealNetworks said the reason the program tallied the number of songs a user had recorded was to enable the company to determine whether the user was "naive" or "sophisticated." This better enables the software to steer sophisticated users toward its advanced features, he said. But this seemed at odds with a statement by Steve Banfield, RealNetworks' general manager of consumer products, who said the company was gathering only "aggregate usage" information about users of the software. Privacy experts said the kind of information being gathered by RealJukebox had the potential to be used to detect copyright violations. Mr. Banfield said that to his knowledge, the company had no plans to allow information about individual users to be used in this manner. But Mr. Catlett of Junkbusters said that such information could be subpoenaed under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. "This usage and tracking information is a way for them to collect intrusive profiles about people and possibly set up prosecutions for copyright infringements," he said. Like some 250 other such programs, RealJukebox licenses the right to use a database of CD titles and tracks that is compiled and maintained by a company called CDDB. This enables the software to display the title and tracks of a CD moments after it is loaded into the computer. To do this, the program must send out information to CDDB every time a user plays a CD. But unlike other popular programs, RealJukebox routes the information through its own servers and tags it with the GUID, which uniquely identifies the user. Mr. Banfield said the information went to CDDB via a proxy server, a computer that masks certain data, to protect the privacy of RealJukebox user@real.com. Mr. Banfield painted RealNetworks as a defender of consumer privacy, asserting: "Everyone else who uses that database sends them their email address. We don't." Ann Greenberg, senior vice president of marketing and business development for CDDB, said last week that her company "strongly encourages but does not require" email addresses or any other identifiers than enable the company to tally unique users of its database. She said the addresses were purged every four days. But she said it was not fair for RealNetworks' to blame CDDB for gathering personal information. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The RealJukebox Plus Web site collects information on what music users play and record. This screen is set up to play Beatles songs. (pg. C10)

title:
Compressed Data;
Revamped Britannica Site Is Swamped by Demand
body: The maiden voyage of the free Internet-based version of Encyclopaedia Britannica is shaping up like the Encyclopaedia Titanica. On Oct. 19, Britannica opened a revamped version of its Web site, Britannica.com, offering free access to the entire contents of the encyclopedia. Trouble is, the company was unprepared for the influx of traffic, which promptly caused the site to crash. Nearly two weeks later, the site still is not up, and it is not expected to be accessible until at least the middle of this week, when the company increases its computer capacity. Instead of seeing encyclopedia content, site visitors last week were met with a note from Don Yannias, chief executive of Britannica Inc., which is based in Chicago. "We were simply unable to handle the demand," he wrote, adding that reaching sufficient capacity "is a big job but we're committed to getting there as fast as we can." Yesterday, even that letter of explanation was removed, replaced by a notice that the site was "Coming Soon." How could Britannica be so unprepared, given that it is no Web novice? The company has been online since 1994 with a fee-based research service -- $5 a month before the recent remodeling -- and a licensing program for educational organizations. In a matter of speaking, Britannica officials blame the messengers. They said they had vastly underestimated the amount of media coverage the site's revamping would create. The grand reopening generated some 850 articles and Internet accounts worldwide -- including front-page coverage in five of nine daily newspapers in Britain, said Kent Devereaux, Britannica's senior vice president for product development. Mr. Devereaux said that international visitors helped contribute to levels of traffic that were "orders of magnitude" higher than the hundreds of thousands of daily visitors the site was accustomed to. He said late last week that the company still was not certain how many visitors it had received and was analyzing the traffic data. MATT RICHTEL http://www.nytimes.com

title:
E-Commerce Report;
All that some retailers want before Christmas is a functional site.
body: THE e-commerce train is about to leave the station for the second meaningful Internet shopping season, and when it does, plenty of disappointed retailers will still be standing on the platform. Stores like the Limited, Home Depot, Tiffany, Williams-Sonoma's Pottery Barn, the Sports Authority and Gap's Old Navy are joining a host of newly formed Internet companies in watching the calendar move closer to Thanksgiving and the start of the online buying binge. Some of those retailers are working around the clock to open their sites within the next two weeks, but others are taking a "wait till next year" approach. There are a variety of reasons that some retailers will miss this holiday season, analysts and executives say. Established companies wary of sullying their brands with a weak Web site are proceeding with extreme caution. Start-ups, on the other hand, often underestimate the difficulty of building a good site and miscalculate how long it will take. And everyone is struggling to find enough programmers, designers, marketers and fulfillment specialists to get the job done quickly. "A lot of this comes down to simply believing that building a site is an easy thing to do," said James McQuivey, an analyst with Forrester Research. Part of the $10 million cost of building a first-rate site is hiring people like developers, he said. "But guess what -- everybody else is, too," he went on. "Some companies have been looking for vice presidents of e-commerce all year. Then you have to build the site, handle fulfillment, customer service call centers, and on it goes." Elaine Rubin, an e-commerce consultant and chairwoman of Shop.org, an industry trade group, said companies that handle fulfillment and other tasks for Internet retailers "are to this day getting calls from people looking to get up before Christmas." Most of those calls are coming from those with no previous e-commerce experience, she said. "The ones with experience know some of the steps," she added, "and they typically started planning their launch in the early spring." Which makes it all the more puzzling that many deep-pocketed, experienced retailers that witnessed the e-commerce surge last year will not make it online this year. According to Jon Ricker, chief information officer of the Limited, the company started planning the online rollout of its brands -- including the Limited, Limited Express and Victoria's Secret -- in mid-1997. So far, only Victoria's Secret is up and running; neither the Limited nor Limited Express will have an e-commerce site running this year. "We refuse to do damage to our brand," Mr. Ricker said. "The lure of additional Christmas revenue just isn't worth the risk." Though it is easy to say that traditional retailers are lagging behind because they are not yet able to operate at Internet speed, Mr. Ricker said bigger retailers had more at stake than Internet start-ups and were justifiably more cautious about risking their reputations with a site that may not be ready for prime time. "And for a large retailer like ourselves with a global presence and global sourcing," he said, "there's a lot more to consider as you put the model together." In addition, larger retail corporations with a single e-commerce division can do justice to one brand's debut on the Web at a time, said Shelley Nandkeolyar, vice president for e-commerce at Williams-Sonoma. The company will introduce its site for Williams-Sonoma (www.williams-sonoma.com) today, as scheduled, Mr. Nandkeolyar said, but other company chains like Pottery Barn and, appropriately enough, Hold Everything, will have to wait. "We had some hard negotiations between the brands about who would launch when, but it made most sense to do it this way," Mr. Nandkeolyar said. The company started the Williams-Sonoma Wedding and Gift Registry (www.wswedding.com) earlier this year "to help us learn about how to launch e-commerce," he said. "Now the Williams-Sonoma site is going up, and in short order next year we'll bring the rest online," he said. If executives like Mr. Ricker and Mr. Nandkeolyar sound less than mortified at the prospect of leaving some of their brands on the e-commerce shelf this year, they may have good reason, analysts said. Despite the Web retail hyperbole, holiday sales this year will amount to only $4 billion, according to Forrester Research. "So I don't think the opportunity cost is huge," Mr. McQuivey of Forrester said. "But can you live without the confidence it inspires in Wall Street, or in the boardroom, or the cachet it generates with consumers who see you on the Web?" Mr. McQuivey asked. "I think the opportunity costs are more intangible." Of course, retailers that miss the rush will also have to work harder in the future to win customers away from stores that make the holiday deadline and perform well. Mindful of this, executives like Dick Sabot, chairman of Eziba.com (www.eziba.com), are determined not to let November pass without getting started. The company, which will sell handmade goods from around the world, is expected to go live within the next week -- thanks in part to an unexpected source of pressure. "We had to decide in August on advertising placement," Mr. Sabot said, noting that recent ads in magazines essentially committed the site to rolling out soon. "If it wasn't for the discipline that imposed on us, it's hard to imagine how we would've forced ourselves to get it done. Looking back, it was a fairly audacious thing to do." Another crucial factor in making the opening happen on time was persuading e-commerce service providers to work with them. It was no easy task, since fulfillment and Web site development companies and advertising agencies were buried with work offers even in March, when Eziba started building its site. "We had to go in there early and win the competition," Mr. Sabot said. "And then we had to convince them to internalize our deadline." Mr. Nandkeolyar of Williams-Sonoma said he had to guard against "scope creep" in the seven months it took to build the Williams-Sonoma site. Six weeks ago, for instance, one member of the site development team suggested building more content into a section devoted to seasonal event planning. "We thought we could do more, but it would require pages and pages of programming, and that would jeopardize the launch date," he said. "We couldn't get enough production, since we're in the Bay Area and everyone's trying to launch by Nov. 1. So we'll just have to build it out over time." Even those that have managed to start operating on time are often doing so quietly, in hopes of ironing out any wrinkles in the system before the holiday deluge hits. Jim Finkelstein, president of Luxuryfinder.com (www.luxuryfinder.com), a purveyor of the pricey that went live late last month after eight months in development, said he simply did not publicize the rollout. "We're prepared for the rush, but we just want to make sure we've got everything right," Mr. Finkelstein said. "That's why you try to get up a couple of months before the holidays. And that's why it's smart for companies who couldn't launch by the fall to wait until next year. If you want to create something that will last, you have to go about it the right way." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Jeremiah Thompson, software engineer for Eziba.com, fell asleep in his office after working long hours on the Web site, which is expected to go live within the next week. (Photographs by Terri Cappucci for The newyork Times)

title: Signatures on Cyberspace's Dotted Line
body: What began as a seemingly simple attempt to stimulate electronic commerce by giving so-called digital signatures the legal weight of their ink-and-paper counterparts has erupted into a partisan political battle in Congress that opponents fear could wipe out some basic consumer protections. Digital signatures refer to various technologies including encryption, fingerprint readers and stylus pads that are used to verify one's identify in cyberspace in order to certify contracts that are agreed to over the Internet. They are accepted as legally binding in some states and localities, but not in all. The legislation was originally meant to create a uniform federal law recognizing the validity of digital signatures. But lately, it has been expanded in ways that critics say would work against consumers. At issue are the thousands of state and local laws that require institutions like banks and insurance companies to keep certain paper records and to notify customers by mail of certain situations, including default on their credit card debts or loans; if there are changes to the terms of a financial agreement, like the amount of a monthly payment, or if a home mortgage is being foreclosed on or an insurance policy canceled. Under the legislation pending in both the House and the Senate, such companies would be able to make those notifications electronically, instead of by mail, if the contracts were made online instead of on paper. The companies would also be relieved of a number of paper record-keeping rules. Supporters say the measures would enable companies and their customers to realize the full benefits and conveniences of electronic commerce. Not only would the legislation make it easier for consumers to complete transactions from home, they say, but it would cut down on paper and mailing expenses, helping reduce the shipping costs that are passed on to customers. But opponents fear that the proposals will allow companies to sidestep longstanding consumer notification laws. Consumers, they say, may not know that the fine print of their contract eliminates the requirement for traditional notification. Or they may simply never get crucial information if their computers break down or they change their Internet service provider or email address -- which typically has no forwarding-address procedure as postal mail does. Or, the opponents argue, companies can include contract fine print requiring that consumers periodically check a World Wide Web site for updates on their agreements, a kind of provision many may overlook or forget. "It's bad public policy," said Andrew J. Pincus, general counsel for the Commerce Department. "It's also bad for the Internet. If the online world is not safe for consumers, what does that do to the future of electronic commerce? It goes in the tank." The Commerce Department had given approval earlier this year to a bill on validation of electronic signatures by Senator Spencer Abraham, Republican of Michigan. The department's support came after he agreed to reduce its scope so that the bill would be temporary, applied to the handful of states that did not already have laws recognizing the legality of electronic contracts. The idea was that Mr. Abraham's measure would expire once all states adopted a uniform digital-signature standard that has been recommended by a national group of lawmakers, state officials and lawyers. But the bill that Senator Abraham tried to bring up for a vote last week was substantially different from that compromise and included provisions that would pre-empt a number of state and Federal laws. So Senator Patrick J. Leahy, Democrat of Vermont, blocked its consideration, saying that Mr. Abraham had reneged on a carefully drawn compromise and was trying to pass off a substitute as the same bill that had been supported by the Clinton administration. Similar legislation is pending in the House, introduced by Representative Thomas J. Bliley Jr., Republican of Virginia and chairman of the House Commerce Committee. The National Conference of State Legislatures issued a a statement last week saying that the Bliley bill "would eviscerate consumer protections" and eliminate record-keeping requirements that allow state and federal oversight agencies to do their jobs. Lobbyists on both sides of the argument spent much of last week working with legislators, trying to help work out the differences in the House and Senate bills. Changes made on Friday to the House bill tried to address consumers' concerns by adding provisions to clarify that state and federal consumer-notification laws still applied, and that notification requirements could be made electronically only if the consumer had agreed by using a form separate from the credit or loan agreement. The revised House bill would also state that insurance cancellation notices, home foreclosure and utility-disconnection warnings would still have to be sent by mail. But consumer groups and the administration remain staunchly opposed to both bills, which could go to the floor for votes this week. "Yes, they've made a lot of changes," said Margot Saunders of the National Consumer Law Center. "But the problem is not the examples they have addressed. The problem is the whole game." Ms. Saunders said that exempting foreclosure notices did not get to the underlying matter of all the warning notices that would precede that final document -- and which would not come by regular mail in the case of contracts that had been completed electronically. "The big difference between electronic information and written information is that it costs money and takes extra effort for consumers to receive electronic information," she said. Chris Larsen is the chief executive of E-Loan, an online loan center in Silicon Valley that is working with an industry group, the Electronic Financial Services Council, to get the legislation passed. He said he was perplexed by the administration's opposition to the Bliley and Abraham bills. "We clearly see this as an aggressive pro-consumer issue," Mr. Larsen said, "because it allows online disclosure that allows better disclosure to consumers at a lower cost." He said companies were not trying to get around consumer protection laws, but simply wanted to bring their businesses into the electronic age. Mr. Larsen said his company had processed some $2.3 billion in loans online. Enabling more of the transaction to take place electronically, he said, results in lower interest rates. "We are not talking about changing any of the disclosures that are required at the state or federal level," he added. "We think all those protections are essential to consumers. We just want to be able to deliver that electronically." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Combatants over consumer signature protection include, from left, Representative Thomas J. Bliley Jr. and Senators Spencer Abraham (Photographs by Associated Press) and Patrick J. Leahy (Stephen Crowley/The newyork Times). The administration opposes versions headed for floor debate.

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Motorola to Offer a Chip That Can Support a Variety of Cell-Phone Standards
body: With an eye toward the convergence of the Internet and next-generation digital cellular networks, Motorola plans to announce a new chip design on Monday that is meant to support a wide range of cellular telephone standards while offering more computer-like features. The new chip family is part of Motorola's effort to move its chip production beyond supplying the company's own cell-phone business and toward competing directly in the cellular market with chip makers like Texas Instruments, Royal Philips Electronics and Qualcomm. "We've been extremely quiet; now we want people to know we're open for business," said Mario Rivas, the general manager of Motorola's wireless subscriber systems group. This year, 225 million cellular telephones will be sold worldwide, accounting for the sale of $10.7 billion worth of semiconductors, according to researchers at the International Data Corporation, a market research firm in Mountain View, Calif. But in 1999 the market has already begun to shift toward data and Internet-related features. Earlier this year, for example, the Sprint Corporation began offering a variety of phones, made from a variety of components, that enable Sprint subscribers to perform rudimentary types of Web surfing. By next year, according to the market research firm Jupiter Communications, almost half of all wireless phones sold will have built-in Web-browsing capabilities. The new Motorola system, which will be known as the DSP56690 baseband processor, will come with both a microprocessor and a specialized digital signal processor capable of handling a variety of cellular telephone technical formats. Unlike Japan and Europe, which mainly have single cellular telephone standards, the unitedstates remains a hodgepodge of competing cellular formats. Motorola said its new chips would make it possible for a telephone designer to build a single device capable of working with a variety of cell phone standards. But the company said it expected the new processor's "universal" architecture to enable a manufacturer to use the same basic design for a variety of phone models that would each be intended for use with a specific transmission format. "The average consumer really doesn't travel that much," Mr. Rivas said. "He just wants his phone to work transparently." Motorola's biggest challenge in its new strategy is finding a way to sell its chips to companies with which it competes as a maker of cellular handsets. The new chips, which will be available in volume in the first quarter of next year, have a variety of data-oriented features, including the ability to run Web browsers and the Java programming language widely used on the World Wide Web, as well as allowing for connections to display screens and the USB serial ports by which a variety of devices can be connected to personal computers. Japan and Europe are now advancing rapidly toward deployment of so-called 2.5 G wireless data networks that will handle both data and voice, but not full multimedia. The unitedstates is farther behind, but high-speed wireless data networks with bandwidth up to approximately 150 kilobits will begin to become available late next year in this country. "A lot of this is going to be driven by the Internet," said Allen Leibovitch, program manager for semiconductor research at International Data. The new Motorola chip is also designed to work with the Global Positioning Satellite receiver chips that the Federal Communications Commission is requiring as part of future wireless emergency 911 service. But cellular phone carriers are eager to develop new commercial "location-based" services as well. In the future, Web sites are expected to be able to automatically tailor information to a cellular data phone user, based on where the telephone is. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Procter & Gamble Adds Deutsch to Its Roster
body: Deutsch Inc. in newyork is joining the agency roster of Procter & Gamble, the world's largest advertiser. Deutsch has been named agency of record for Reflect.com, the Internet company formed in September by P.& G. and two venture capital funds, Institutional Venture Partners and Redpoint Ventures. Deutsch will create advertising for Reflect.com, a Web site (www.reflect.com) that will sell customized women's beauty products and services. Gretchen Briscoe, a spokeswoman for P.& G. in Cincinnati, said the decision came after a review that included agencies on and off the company's agency roster; she declined to identify the other participants. Denis Beausejour, vice president for global marketing at P.& G. and the Reflect.com project leader, praised the "entrepreneurial spirit" of Deutsch as well as its "creative and strategic skills." Deutsch joins two other agencies working for Reflect.com: Rapp Collins Worldwide in newyork, part of Omnicom Group, for direct marketing, and Critical Mass in Calgary, Alberta, 50 percent owned by Rapp Collins, the interactive agency of record. In a related development, Deutsch resigned the account of the Biore line of skin-care products sold by the Andrew Jergens Company in Cincinnati, a unit of Kao. Deutsch had handled the brand since Biore's introduction in 1997, but Jergens and P.& G. are competitors. Jergens did not announce a replacement for Deutsch; Bozell in newyork, part of True North Communications, handles the Jergens and Curel brands for Jergens. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MARKET WATCH;
Over the Rainbow With Amazon.com
body: PAY no attention to those losses behind the curtain. Thus spake management at Amazon.com, the great and powerful, the Internet sweetheart stock. And for years, investors obeyed, focusing instead on Amazon's impressive revenue growth as a reason to pay dearly for the stock. The more money the company lost, the higher its stock seemed to go. Last week, however, things appeared to change in the Land of Internet Oz. Investors appear to be looking closer at Amazon.com and they do not like what they see. For example, cumulative losses at the five-year-old Internet retailer now exceed $550 million. Attitudes started changing late last Wednesday when Amazon.com, perhaps the most beloved of Internet stocks, reported its third-quarter earnings and fourth-quarter outlook in a conference call with shareholders. The company said that while its revenues more than doubled, its net loss in the period was $197 million, up more than fourfold from the $45 million it lost in the same quarter last year. Amazon also warned that it would not be profitable until 2002, well beyond analysts' hopes, and said it would spend $250 million to promote its Web site this Christmas. In the past, euphoric investors would have propelled the stock on a doubling in sales. But on Thursday, the shares plunged 6.5 percent on the news, wiping out $1.6 billion of Amazon's market value. And on Friday, the stock slipped again, to 70.625. For the first time, Wall Street analysts, who had been schooling investors in the "ignore losses" view, expressed frustration with Amazon management over the company's ballooning losses. Five analysts lowered their ratings on the stock, including Henry Blodget, Merrill Lynch's Internet guru who said in a report that investors would soon become "as tired as we are of endless postponement of gratification." Clearly, Amazon's numbers don't paint a pretty picture. Customer growth has slowed from 60 percent in the fourth quarter of 1997 to 22 percent in the most recent quarter. Revenues per customer have declined from $40.32 in the third quarter of 1997 to $27.16. Amazon has long said that a decline in revenues per customer is to be expected since not all shoppers buy each quarter. The company instead points to growing repeat orders as an indication of brand loyalty. The most recent period had a 72 percent repeat order rate compared with 55 percent two years ago. Interestingly, revenues per new customer have declined almost 20 percent from $51.68 in 1997 to $41.51 today. At the same time, cost per new customer has risen 10.2 percent, from $32.73 to $36.08. This is not the kind of progress most shareholders want to see. Amazon.com is not the only Internet company experiencing increasing costs to acquire new customers. In the most recent quarter, Ameritrade, one of the nation's largest Internet brokerages, greatly increased its costs associated with signing up new clients. These costs almost tripled from $157 per customer in the third quarter of 1999 to $451 in the fourth quarter. Irritation with Amazon's continued unprofitability among brokerage analysts, some of the very same folks who helped push Amazon's stock to a split-adjusted $105.0625 a share last April may indicate that Wall Street will be less inclined to help the company feed the beast with the proceeds from fresh stock and bond offerings. This is worrisome. In the last year and a half, Amazon has collected $1.75 billion from investors, money that it is now breezily spending on marketing and acquisitions. If this flow of funds is cut off, then the party is really over. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph compares Amazon.com revenue and costs per new customer since 1998.

title:
MY MONEY, MY LIFE;
Twentysomethings' Lament
body: THE almost overnight success of the Jerry Yangs of America has made them the symbol of my age group, replacing the goofy Adam Sandler image that once defined Generation X. But Silicon Valley success stories like that of Mr. Yang, the 30-year-old co-founder of Yahoo, have given my parents' generation the wrong impression that all young people are -- or even want to be -- wealthy owners of the Internet companies commonly called dot-coms, investors in dot-coms or Wall Streeters who arrange stock offerings for dot-coms. The reality for most of us, of course, is not all that different from what the older generation faced: most of my friends and I -- just a few years younger than Mr. Yang -- remain mired in college loan debts and struggle to make ends meet as we try to figure out what we will do with our lives. A few of my friends who are analysts or traders or Internet entrepreneurs live in Manhattan penthouses and dine daily at restaurants where they are seated back-to-back with celebrities. On the other hand, after three years spent traveling and working for news organizations and as a freelance writer in hongkong, I recently returned to my parents' home in suburban newyork and commuted to my job in the city. Usually, I dined out of a brown bag at lunch time. And while other twentysomethings may be chauffeured to the office or arrive in their Porsches, I drove my two-door Toyota to the train station each dawn, where I was likely to run into a classmate from high school who had also returned to the nest. They, too, arrived at the parking lot in second-hand cars and with brown bags. Primarily, we commiserated about life at the entry level: the hours spent monitoring fax machines and fixing cappuccino makers. Most of us studied liberal arts in college or were aspiring actors or writers; Java, margin calls and E*Trade were foreign territory -- not because they were out of our reach but because we had chosen not to take that path. Of course, it's hard to stay grounded when high-tech nerds are becoming poster boys for our generation and making it onto the most-wealthy lists. It's even worse when people who are old enough to know better look at us as if something has gone awry because we are not making six figures. A few weeks ago, a middle-aged man I met at a party was stunned when I told him I was a writer. "That's weird. Isn't everyone your age starting their own dot-com," he asked, implying that I was either incredibly ignorant or hopelessly idealistic. AND at a family gathering, soon after I began working as a producer at a dot-com, the hefty dinner bill was sent my way. Everyone assumed I was well-fixed because of my job, and too proud to disappoint them, I clenched my teeth and handed over my credit card. In fact, most young people live ordinary lives. Many of my friends have chosen lower-paying jobs like research assistants, teachers, social workers and even extras in films because they love what they do and understand that for most of us the ladder of success must still be climbed rung by rung. Even those of us making our livings from the Internet mostly live ordinary lives. At the dot-com where I worked until recently, there were plenty of younger workers who ate stale pizza and hunted for roommates. My stint in HTML-land came to an end as soon as I realized that money, titles, successful initial public offerings, corner offices and Porsches were important things, but not important enough to sustain me beyond my 40's if that wasn't where I wanted to be. In fact, I'm already planning a trip to Asia in a few weeks, and I'm planning to continue to make my living as a writer -- even if it only pays me peanuts. At least my relatives won't expect me to pick up the tab again. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Lisa Haney)

title: Need a Cartoon? There's a Bank for It
body: YOU can't help smiling when visiting the spacious warehouse of an office of the Cartoon Bank overlooking the Hudson River here. "When you need to get serious about being funny" is among the company's slogans. Familiar newyorker cartoons dot the walls. And in the hallways are three- and four-foot cardboard cutouts of cartoon figures from newyorker cartooning perennials like Roz Chast, James Thurber, William Steig and Robert Mankoff. And here is the gregarious Mr. Mankoff himself, The newyorker cartoon editor, a resident of Hastings-on-Hudson and the president of the Cartoon Bank, who can hold forth on everything from the critical elements in forming a growing business -- "You need all kinds of milk to go with the coffee machine, from whole to skim to half-and-half" -- to the challenges of being a newyorker cartoonist, all of which underlines the serious business taking shape here. The Cartoon Bank calls itself the world's largest storehouse of cartoon humor. A division of The newyorker magazine, this computer-digitized archive of cartoon images is available for a variety of purposes, from corporate presentations and advertisements to textbooks, Web site "cartoons of the day," greeting cards and gifts. The Cartoon Bank's Web site (www.cartoonbank .com) allows anyone to search for a favorite cartoon by artist or subject, which people are doing in ever increasing numbers. The Cartoon Bank's Web site gets about 100,000 hits a day, with the average hit lasting 10 minutes -- "years in Internet time," as Mr. Mankoff said. Last year's revenues topped $2 million, double that of the previous year, he added. The biggest customers, Mr. Mankoff said, are Web site designers, corporate publications and textbook companies. And of particular interest, he said, are cartoons about computers and pets, including the all-time Cartoon Bank best seller, which combines the two -- a July 5, 1993, Peter Steiner work, with one poker-faced dog telling another, "On the Internet, nobody knows you're a dog." Increasing revenues have created the opportunity for Cartoon Bank staff members to pursue Mr. Mankoff's longtime goal of digitizing every one of The newyorker's 60,000 or so cartoons. At this point, there is quite a way to go; completed so far is everything back to the mid-1980's and selected cartoons from before then. Meanwhile, the Cartoon Bank continues to develop more Web-related, greeting card, calendar and even apparel agreements. Recent developments include supplying cartoons to the Web sites petsmart .com and barnesandnoble.com. "There's a wide range of ways that we can work with specific companies," said Andy Pillsbury, the Cartoon Bank director of new business development, who joined the business in July after years of working in Silicon Valley in San Jose, Calif. "This is a product with real cachet," said Mr. Pillsbury, who lives in Chappaqua. "It's sophisticated humor that can really add to a Web site's identity. It can keep people coming back to their site." The core of the Cartoon Bank's collection of more than 85,000 cartoons is many of the cartoons that originally appeared in The newyorker over the magazine's 75-year history. Long noted for its smart, urbane drawings, The newyorker, as Mr. Mankoff put it, "is to cartoonists what God is to religion." But it really was not until 1991 when Mr. Mankoff started the Cartoon Bank out of his home that cartoonists had much of an avenue beyond the 15 or 20 cartoons chosen weekly by The newyorker. Mr. Mankoff estimates that for every cartoon he actually has placed in The newyorker, he has done perhaps 30 or 40 cartoons that used to go nowhere further than the editor's rejection pile. Mr. Mankoff reasoned that there would be a market both for cartoons that appeared in the magazine and for work by the same artists, which, for whatever reason, the magazine turned down. Built in was artist protection; all images have copyrights and cannot be used without permission of the artist. "In the beginning, I didn't really have a business plan, beyond a feel that there would be a market for this work and that this thing would work," said the 55-year-old Mr. Mankoff, who has been The newyorker cartoon editor for two years. "It was my 'Field of Dreams.' If I made this thing, I felt people would come to it, just as they do to the cartoons. I figured it would work out in some way. "I said to my cartoonist friends that here we are leading this freelance life where we live and die by what The newyorker accepts, while producing 15 to 20 ideas every week. I thought it would be great if other people had access to our work as well." For Jack Ziegler, a fellow newyorker cartoonist who lives in Las Vegas, "It's a great thing to have a venue so people can actually see and use work that wasn't published in The newyorker." Speaking on the telephone from his home, he continued, "This way, the drawings that actually appeared in the magazine and elsewhere get a second wind. Bob really wants to see people do well, and part of his rationale is that being a magazine cartoonist these days, you don't make a lot of money at it. Bob likes being able to help." Mr. Ziegler is typical of the handful of the cartooning elite whose work is available through the Cartoon Bank. More than 600 of his cartoons are stored there, far more than have actually appeared in The newyorker. It is not that the Cartoon Bank actually changes the work habits of the typical newyorker cartoonist; it just means more options. "I still sit down every week and do a bunch of drawings, and I still gear everything to The newyorker," Mr. Ziegler said. "But with the Bank, the drawings have more life." That is the idea, said Mr. Mankoff, who knows firsthand of the challenges of the cartooning life, having been a freelancer for so many years. A native of Queens, he dropped out of a City College of newyork doctoral program in experimental psychology in 1974 to become a cartoonist, a decision, he says, that was "greeted by astonishment and disdain by my parents." "Actually, what happened is my pigeon died," Mr. Mankoff said. "I had miscalculated in a psychology experiment and the pigeon I was experimenting on didn't get enough to eat and just keeled over. I took that as a sign that I should move on." So he did, and three years later, Mr. Mankoff sold his first cartoon to The newyorker. After running the Cartoon Bank from his home for perhaps two years, Mr. Mankoff moved the business to his studio in Yonkers and then to Hastings in 1997, which was about the time he sold the business to The newyorker. Then, in April, the Bank relocated to its current site in a building that dates from the 1920's. Despite the challenges of running a business, Mr. Mankoff continues to draw cartoons. "It's harder, no doubt about it," he said of trying to maintain a dual career as cartoonist and editor and business executive. "Sometimes, I look back nostalgically at the days of cartooning full time and doing things like looking under the bed or changing your shirt for ideas," he said. "Yes, it's tough keeping all the balls in the air. That's the price you pay for juggling." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Robert Mankoff, The newyorker cartoon editor and president of the Cartoon Bank in Dobbs Ferry. Below, a July 5, 1993, Peter Steiner work. (Susan Farley for The newyork Times); (Peter Steiner From The newyorker)(pg. 11); Web site of the Cartoon Bank, which has a Dobbs Ferry office. (pg. 1)

title:
ON MY...YAHOO;
DAVID FILO
body: He doesn't sleep under his desk any more, but David Filo, the co-founder of Yahoo, the world's most popular Web site, spends a lot of time in his cubicle at the company's headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif. Several times each day, Mr. Filo uses one of his company's most popular creations -- My Yahoo -- to keep up with what's going on in the world. My Yahoo lets users create a page with their most used features in one place. Mr. Filo has a typical mix of news headlines, stock quotes and links to some of Yahoo's various services, like its instant message network. And Mr. Filo has modified the page to keep tabs on some of his interests like sports and jazz. But he concedes these areas are more reminders of his passions in earlier days. These days, Mr. Filo, who shares the title of "Chief Yahoo" with Jerry Yang, is more likely to use the site to keep an eye on Internet stocks and to check quick facts. "I use it a lot for the yellow pages and phone number lookup," he said. Like many computer users far less technologically savvy, Mr. Filo says he has the nagging feeling that there is more he could do with his own invention. "We started out with simple things like news and stocks," he said, "but now there are a lot of things on it that I don't know what they are." SAUL HANSELL http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: STOCK QUOTES -- Mr. Filo owns 23.4 million shares of Yahoo. MOVIE SCHEDULE -- "That's the closest theater to my house." CALENDAR -- "When I remember, I enter things I can't afford to forget. But I have a lot of things written on pieces of paper." BOOKMARKS -- Several computer sites, Yahoo's game chat room and the Onion, a satiric weekly. WEATHER -- "Around here, the weather is not very interesting."

title:
Political Briefing;
Seeking New Rules For a Campaign Tool
body: Few things have had more influence in recent years on the way political campaigns are run in this country than the Internet. In fact, the effect has been so great that the Federal Election Commission thinks it is time to set some rules and guidelines. "Candidates, parties and political action committees have apparently concluded that the Internet is a powerful campaign tool with the potential to significantly influence the outcome," the commission said in a statement issued on Thursday. But so far, there are few guidelines to follow as the nation crosses this new frontier, as the commission called the Web. Candidates now raise money, spread their messages and organize via the Internet. Just about every candidate has a Web site and hardly a campaign manager can be found who is not pondering some even more inventive use. So the commission is asking for comments on how -- and, for that matter, whether -- it should regulate the new tool. "The commission is grappling with the new area of technology and the application of campaign law to it," Scott Thomas, the chairman, said in calling for questions, suggestions and observations from campaign workers and the public. "We would be well served," he added, "to get the questions answered as soon as possible." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Akamai Technologies Stock Surges on FirstTrading Day
body: Shares of Akamai Technologies Inc. soared yesterday in the fourth-hottest initial public offering ever, underscoring investor enthusiasm for a new Internet technology that speeds up delivery of Web pages to computer users. The red-hot investor reception bestowed yet another staggering valuation on a small, money-losing Internet company. Akamai closed at $145.1875 on Nasdaq. It was initially priced at $26 a share and opened at $110. The stock's 458 percent surge from its initial price is the fourth-largest ever, according to the Securities Data Corporation, a financial market researcher. Theglobe.com, the No. 1 ranked initial offering, rose 606 percent on opening day. Foundry Networks rose 525 percent and Marketwatch.com rose 474 percent. Akamai sold nine million shares to raise more than $1.3 billion. Its closing share price gave Akamai a market value of more than $13 billion -- even though Akamai had sales of just $1.3 million and lost $28.3 million in the first nine months of this year. "Akamai" (pronounced AH-kuh-my) is the Hawaiian word for intelligent, clever and cool. Formed last year in Cambridge, Mass., the company offers Yahoo and other Web destinations a service that delivers the most image-intensive portions of their Web pages -- like advertisements with colorful moving images -- through a speedier route than the public Internet. The service answers a common complaint that graphic-intensive Web pages take too long to download and can cause computers to crash. This is particularly important to Web site advertisers that use elaborate images to promote their products. To provide the service, Akamai owns a global network of 1,475 powerful computers that in essence let Web clients use a private network instead of the Internet's crowded public system to transmit images. Demand for such a service is "immense," said Ullas Naik, an analyst with FAC Equities/First Albany, a Boston-based investment firm. "It's going to keep growing significantly." Companies that have invested in Akamai include Apple Computer Inc., Cisco Systems Inc. and the Microsoft Corporation. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Slayings Bring Speculation On the Internet
body: In the real world, the world of flesh and blood and families, mourners were grieving yesterday for two stock promoters shot to death Monday night in a New Jersey mansion, while investigators continued to comb the house for clues about who had killed them. In the alternate world of the Internet, where the two men had pitched small stocks on their Web site -- stockinvestor.com -- people who did not even know the men were also searching for clues, coldly speculating about their deaths on investment bulletin boards, including one with a special section devoted to the killings. The two worlds of Maier Lehman, 37, family man and felon, and Albert Alain Chalem, 41, charmer and wheeler-dealer, seemed far apart yesterday, the day Mr. Chalem was buried. But those worlds may have collided violently. One focus of the investigation is their business dealings, including the possibility that the two men recently became involved in a bitter battle over the stock of a small company called C3D Inc., whose partisans and detractors have been slugging it out on the Internet. The fledgling company says it has an innovative new computer technology, to be demonstrated soon, but its most salient feature is a stock price that has zoomed from $1.75 in April to more than $22 yesterday. Traders who were betting that the price would fall say that they have told investigators that Mr. Chalem was helping them, and that they feared that he and Mr. Lehmann had been killed because of that help. Law enforcement officials and stock regulators must determine whether this is a hot tip or the kind of paranoid fantasy not unknown in the no-holds-barred world of the small, risky securities known as penny stocks. There could also be a money motive for the speculation. Any public mention of such a small company, pro or con, can have a huge effect on the price of its stock, and both company boosters and critics may have a lot of money at stake. On each of four days last week, more than 100,000 shares of C3D changed hands, most at prices above $20. C3D officials said they had never heard of Mr. Chalem or Mr. Lehmann. "These people may have been doing penny stock -- and our company is one that is a hot company," said Eugene Levich, the chief executive of C3D. There are many possible motives for the slayings, including the men's personal lives and their other business ventures, and the investigation remains in its early stages. Robert A. Honecker Jr., the First Assistant Monmouth County Prosecutor, who is handling the investigation, said yesterday that the search of the business records of the two victims was continuing. The police hope the records will contain clues to both the killer and the motive, but, he said, "As of now, we don't have anything more to report." Small companies with hopes of high-tech breakthroughs long fascinated Mr. Lehmann, said Alexander Novak, a newyork lawyer who knows the family of Mr. Lehmann's wife, Tamar. Mr. Novak said he first represented Mr. Lehmann almost a decade ago, when Mr. Lehmann was running a video equipment business in newyork called Not Just Videos, and became involved in an insurance swindle to which he ended up pleading guilty. More recently, Mr. Novak said, "He would go around the world and find these very interesting high-tech ideas in companies that were fairly incompetent about raising money and try to promote the stock and match the money with other people." Mr. Lehmann's activities in promoting one of those companies in 1997 got him in trouble with the Securities and Exchange Commission, which sued him in 1998, alleging he manipulated the stock of Electro Optical Systems. Without admitting or denying the charges, Mr. Lehmann agreed to pay $630,000 in fines and restitution in the case, which remains under criminal investigation. But Mr. Lehmann was also generous, giving away some of the money he made from his illegal activities to those in need, Mr. Novak said. Mr. Lehmann felt remorse after his crimes, his lawyer added, saying, "Sometimes even likable guys do something wrong." And Mr. Lehmann was very likable, handsome and charming, his friends say, and though he does not appear to have attended college, quite smart. "I see him at the pool, in his tank top, a good-looking guy smiling," a friend recalled. Mr. Lehmann, who was born in Manhattan and whose family later moved to the Rockland County town of Monsey, N.Y., was described by many as religious. He had attended a yeshiva and more recently spent time in Israel studying the Torah, said Rabbi Moshe Weinberger of Congregation Aish Kodesh, an Orthodox synagogue in Woodmere, N.Y., where Mr. Lehmann had lived for the last several years with his wife and five children. "He was extremely devoted to his study of the Torah and we often spoke about it and spirituality," the rabbi said, adding that he never once heard Mr. Lehmann discuss his business. Mr. Chalem was also bright and charming, according to several acquaintances. Mr. Chalem, who lived with his longtime girlfriend in the Colts Neck mansion where he and Mr. Lehmann were killed, had attended the University of Miami and lived for a while in Fort Lee, N.J. "He impressed me as being a gentleman, and everyone really liked him," said one friend, who said Mr. Chalem had invested in real estate. In the 1980's, Mr. Chalem owned Spectrum Ink in Clifton, N.J., according to state records, and in 1989, he began to work at the Heartbreak Hotel at the Hunter Mountain ski resort in the Catskills, according to a brief resume he filed with securities regulators when he registered to work in the brokerage business. That resume also lists a two-year stint at a contracting concern before he joined A. S. Goldmen, a brokerage firm in Iselin, N.J., that prosecutors contend was a criminal enterprise. In July, the Manhattan District Attorney indicted the company, its principals and many employees -- though not Mr. Chalem, who was cooperating in the investigation, law enforcement officials have confirmed. While he was at the brokerage firm, Mr. Chalem bought Allen's Acres, a motel in Hampton Bays on Long Island. Shortly thereafter, Clean-X-Press, a San Francisco company that said it was in the dry-cleaning business, issued a news release announcing that it had bought the motel for $2.4 million, and would lease it back to Mr. Chalem. There is no evidence the deal went through. And if the announcement was intended to boost the company's stock price, it failed. The shares, which then traded for about $2, now go for less than a penny. Irate investors have sued, and investigators have been examining both Clean-X-Press and the brokerage firm that promoted it, which has been linked to organized crime. And for people who have lost money though penny-stock debacles like Clean-X-Press, sympathy for stock promoters, even dead ones, can be hard to come by. On Silicon Investor, a Web site favored by stock mavens, a new section devoted to the killings includes a comment from someone who goes by the screen name Max. "Harsh as it may seem," Max wrote, "if the killer or killers were scam victims, then I hope they never get caught." http://www.nytimes.com

title: A.M.A. and 6 Others Set Up Medical Internet Company
body: The American Medical Association and six other medical societies said yesterday that they had created an Internet company that, starting next year, will publish consumer information on health care and help doctors set up their own medical Web sites to communicate with patients by email. Medem Inc., a for-profit company, enters a crowded field of Internet medical information companies that includes DrKoop.com, Healtheon and Medscape, as well as 17,000 other World Wide Web sites devoted to health care information. Dr. Edward Fotsch, a former emergency-room physician from Sausalito, Calif., who is Medem's chief executive, said doctors need a reliable source of information for patients, and by bringing together seven medical societies, the company would provide it. Some medical Web sites provide information that "is great, some is so-so and some of it will probably kill you if you follow it," Dr. Fotsch remarked. Doctors, he said, "certainly don't have the time to read every page of information from an Internet start-up company." "If you are going to refer patients," he continued, "you have to have confidence in that information, sight unseen." Officials of Healtheon and Medscape said their medical information was developed under the same standard that Medem proposes to use. "In terms of who trusts what, our track record shows we are trusted," said Dr. George Lundberg, editor in chief of Medscape, which he said had 300,000 doctors and 1.2 million other users. Dr. Lundberg, a former editor of the Journal of the American Medical Association, noted that he was instrumental in formulating those standards. Healtheon said it was "the pre-eminent source of trusted content for physicians and consumers." Dennis Upah, chief operating officer of DrKoop.com, said his site had become the leading medical information Web site by posting medical content reviewed by other doctors. Medem will get its editorial content through a separate, nonprofit organization called called Medem E, a separation intended to insure its integrity, said Dr. William Mahood of Abington, Pa., an A.M.A. trustee. Five percent of Medem is owned by a charity, called the Medem Trust, that will use its profits to provide health care to the poor, Dr. Fotsch said. While Medem is owned by the seven medical societies, Dr. Fotsch said he expected other professional societies to join, with groups representing osteopaths and chiropractors to apply to be owners. "The board wants to be inclusive," he said, adding that the company's charter banned only tobacco companies from involvement. Eventually, he said, ownership stakes may be sold to investors or even to the public. The imprimatur of major medical societies, representing more than 400,000 of the nation's 650,000 doctors, is likely to help Medem attract both advertisers and providers of health care services. It may also have links to other sites like Healtheon, which wants to digitize the paperwork now required of doctors and patients to collect insurance payments, issue and renew prescriptions, and store treatment records. Until last week, Dr. Fotsch was a vice president of Healtheon, which was hired by the medical societies to draw up the Medem business plan. In addition to the A.M.A., the other Medem owners are the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology; the American Academy of Ophthalmology; the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists; the American Academy of Pediatrics; the American Society of Plastic Surgeons, and the American Psychiatric Association.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Amazon Says Its Losses May Grow Next Quarter
body: Amazon.com, by far the biggest merchant on the Internet, reported yesterday that its losses in the third quarter were slightly less than analysts had expected. But the company also warned that it expected to lose far more than it had previously indicated in the fourth quarter, as it tripled its spending on marketing and advertising to compete vigorously this Christmas. That strategy indicates how quickly Amazon has moved from David to Goliath. When it started in 1995, it was an upstart bookseller taking on Barnes & Noble. Now it offers a wide range of merchandise, including electronics, and is host to auctions and storefronts for other merchants. Which means it is now hearing footsteps. Jeffrey P. Bezos, the company's founder and chief executive, said Amazon had to defend itself from the hundreds of newer Internet stores, flush with cash from venture capitalists and public stock offerings. "All you have to do is watch "Ally McBeal" to see that every commercial is a dot-com company," Mr. Bezos said in a conference call yesterday with analysts. "We don't know if we need to triple our marketing spending, but we know we don't want to take the chance." Amazon declined to say how much the marketing blitz would cost, but analysts estimated it would be well in excess of $100 million in the next three months. Much of the spending, Mr. Bezos said, would be in the form of discount coupons, typically in the form of email messages, inducing its customers to make purchases in its newer product areas. Amazon has become the archetype of the classic Internet business model: lose lots of money to grow very quickly. But even as other Internet pioneers, like Yahoo, have started to make a profit, Amazon's losses have continued to widen -- even as its sales and customer base make it a big business in its own right. In the third quarter, the company lost $197 million on sales of $356 million. A year earlier, it lost $45 million on sales of $154 million. This year's third-quarter loss included $111 million in costs the company said were one-time charges related to acquisitions, investments and stock-based compensation. Excluding these charges, on an operating basis, the company lost 26 cents a share. That is slightly better than the 28 cent loss that analysts had expected. Even so, analysts yesterday expressed frustration that Amazon had significantly changed its forecast for the fourth quarter. "They had indicated that their losses would decline, ever so slightly going forward," said Lauren Levitan, an analyst with Robertson Stevens. "Now they tell us that won't be the case." Amazon's stock, which fell $5.31 to $75.93 in trading yesterday on the Nasdaq, fell even further in after-hours trading, to $72.75. Faced with repeated questions by analysts about why the company was not moving more quickly toward profitability, Mr. Bezos said that the company keeps discovering new business lines it wants to enter. "The further we go into this, the more we find new things to do," he said. "We think it would be really foolish to slavishly commit to plans we made in the past." The company did say that in the fourth quarter it expected its book business in the unitedstates to become profitable for the first time and that products other than books would likely approach half of all sales. Analysts seized on that prediction -- the first ever in which Amazon used the word "profit" -- as some consolation to investors who are wearying of Amazon's ever widening losses. "If you can see books are profitable, you may be willing to believe the model works and they will be able to duplicate this in other areas," said Henry Blodget, an analyst with Merrill Lynch. Mr. Blodget said he expected the company's shares to decline further, as all but the true believers among investors get out of their positions. "They have said from the very beginning they are going to invest everything for the long term," he said. "If you think this is just words, then sell." Amazon said it expected sales to increase significantly in the fourth quarter, but it also predicted the gain would be entirely offset by the increase in marketing spending and additional increases in the cost of inventory, warehouses and shipping. Amazon is spending more than $300 million to build seven automated warehouses around the unitedstates. Mr. Bezos conceded that warehouses would not be operating at peak efficiency and that the company would have to cover the delays by paying for express shipping. The company also said it had nearly quadrupled its inventory from the beginning of the year, to $118 million, and would increase it even further to make sure it had goods on hand for the Christmas peaks. While Mr. Bezos conceded that if the company's forecasts were wrong, it might have to take big markdowns to sell excess inventory, he added, "We want to minimize the risk we will let down customers." http://www.nytimes.com
