title:
DOWNTIME;
Wide-Ranging Movie Sites Offer the Rare and Offbeat - Correction Appended
body: BLOCKBUSTER last week announced that it would offer movie rentals over the Internet by the middle of next year and said it was evaluating ways to transmit movies into people's homes on demand. But you don't have to wait until then to order movies over the Internet and have them delivered to your door. There are already a number of videotape and DVD movie rental sites on the Web, many offering the kinds of films you would never see at a chain video store. The selections range from high art and film rarities to exploitation films and vintage pornography. A quick search of the Internet turned up six on-line video rental stores and nine DVD rental sites. Some are simply extensions of brick-and-mortar video stores; others are Internet-only businesses. Some, like Net Flix, are well financed and slick; others appear to be shoestring, amateurish operations. All function in a similar way, allowing some kind of search through a trove of films that can be ordered on the site for delivery by mail. Of the 15 sites, most people could eliminate DVD Rent right off the bat -- it offers film and music rentals and sales throughout Australia. And DVD Wave and Video Ltd. no longer rent movies, even though their Yahoo listings say they do. Laser Discovery required a security deposit of $500, which seemed excessive -- wasn't that the total shooting budget for "The Blair Witch Project"? The video sites offered more eclectic film collections than those that handle DVD's, in part because some of the more offbeat movie titles are not yet available in the DVD format. But as a group, the video sites had the least consumer-friendly policies. Best Video (www.bestvideo.com) promises a broad selection but charges $16.99 per rental -- pretty steep, considering that a video at the local Blockbuster is less than $4. Several video rental stores did not include a return mailer or return postage in the cost of the rental. In the time it takes to wrap up a video and wait in line at the post office, a movie lover could watch an entire film festival. Both Facets Video (www.facets .org), which also required a $35 membership, and Rick's Video, (www.ricksvideo .com), which charges $19.95 for up to three tapes or DVD's, do not offer the convenience of a return mailer. Two other video sites do not offer return postage, although they do have intriguing film collections. One is Video Vault (www.videovault.com), which has a delightfully tacky Web site. It lives up to the slogan "Guaranteed Worst Movies in Town" with rentals like Ed Wood Jr.'s "Glen or Glenda," as well as the film Siskel and Ebert used to cite as among the worst ever made, "I Spit on Your Grave." The second, www.videowasteland.com, specializes in horror, exploitation and B movies. One of them is "Skeeter," which features giant mutant killer mosquitoes -- a movie certain to be in demand in newyork after the events of the summer. Home Film Festival charges a $6 rental fee and a minimum shipping fee of $4.30 (www.homefilmfestival.com). There is also a $9.95 membership fee, bringing the total to $20.25 for the first video. That's a lot of money, but Home Film Festival could come up with a hard-to-find cult classic like, for example, "The Harder They Come," starring the reggae singer Jimmy Cliff, so it might be worth it to a real film buff. An order for membership and the movie was placed about 6 P.M. on a Friday. On the following Monday, an email message confirmed that the membership had been processed but said "The Harder They Come" was not available. It was an expensive movie not to see. But later, a 215-page catalogue showed up with finds for cinemaphiles like "Absolute Beginners," starring David Bowie, and "Zou-Zou," starring Josephine Baker. Things went better with the DVD providers. The King Kong of DVD sites is Net Flix (www.netflix.com). The site has a wide selection -- it was the only DVD site of those surveyed to have the hard-to-find 1970's Richard Lester costume romp, "The Three Musketeers," and the even-harder-to-find sequel, "The Four Musketeers." The site is also loaded with viewing suggestions. Leonard Maltin, the film reviewer, has a page where he recommends five films each month. Net Flix also packages films into fairly random collections of five or so movies. The cover of "Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil" on the main page, is linked to the Southern Charm collection, which includes "Cat on a Hot Tin Roof," "Sling Blade" and "Eve's Bayou," but not "In the Heat of the Night." The main page is so jammed with films that it's a little busy, and the box cover shots are postage-stamp size when viewed on a 17-inch monitor. No membership is required at Net Flix, but the site offers discount packages. The Marquee service, for a monthly fee of $15.95, sends viewers four films a month with no due date, late fee or shipping charges. There are also package deals of 10, 25 and 40 disks that offer discounts of about 50 cents on each rental, once shipping is figured in. Single rentals are $3.49 per disk plus a shipping fee of 95 cents. There is also a flat fee of 99 cents per order, for a total cost of $5.43. An order is quickly followed by an email confirmation, another to say the DVD's have been shipped, a third when it's time to send them back and a fourth when they are received. Disks ordered about 6 P.M. on a Friday arrived on Tuesday. A stamped return mailer was included. The major downside to Net Flix is the marketing blitz an order sets off, including automatic subscriptions to three electronic newsletters. DVD Overnight (www.dvdovernight .com) has a streamlined opening page, with video box pictures that are a little larger than most. And the rentals are a reasonable $3 per disk with a flat shipping fee of $3, return included, whether you rent one disk or six, the maximum. The site carries mostly new releases, which means that you would need to search for all but the most common classic films elsewhere. But DVD Overnight has one thing that neither Blockbuster nor Net Flix has: pornographic movies. And that means you should be careful surfing the site with children. The site suffers the occasional technical glitch. Clicking on "Toxic Avenger 2," for example, sent the surfer to "Magical Mystery Tour." But DVD's ordered on a Friday appeared by Wednesday in good shape, with a return mailer that was easy to use. The Digibuster home page (www .digibuster.com) has a do-it-yourself look, with a champagne glass background and a very prominent link to a different Reuters entertainment news article each day. There is also a link to India Weekly, with which it must be allied, because India Weekly appears on the credit card receipt for rental DVD's. In fact, there is a special link to movies from India. The site has a small selection, about 150 DVD's, and most are the sort of movies that would have been featured on the wall at a Blockbuster months ago. But it is among the least expensive: disks are $1.99 plus $1.49 handling and shipping for each one, for a minimum of two disks. An order was followed by an email confirmation, and the movies showed up in a few days. DVD Cache (www.dvdcache.com) has a Web page that proved a little cranky, at least on a Netscape browser -- it loaded slowly, and sometimes without a scroll bar. But the site was fairly easy to shop, partly because it offers only about 350 titles, including a total of 6 Westerns and 5 classics. The scroll bar was not the only technological problem. Using the search engine to look up "Costner" turned up several films, but not "Silverado," with Kevin Costner, even though it was in stock. Rentals are $2.99 each, with a flat $4 shipping fee for up to six DVD's. If you order six, the shipping is free. But the return mailer must be postmarked seven days after the shipping date -- most other sites allow a lenient seven days from the time the movies arrive. If you are willing to put up with the occasional technical glitch and to wade through some hard-to-browse pages, these on-line sites offer a broader array of films than you are likely to find in any single store. All you need for your own film festival is the popcorn -- which is also available for delivery on line. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  A chart in Circuits on Thursday with an article about renting videotapes and DVD's online misstated the number of movies available at the DVD Overnite site. It is 1,200, not 12,000. Correction-Date: November 2, 1999, Tuesday Graphic   Photos: CLICK AND WAIT -- Sites like DVD Overnight, Home Film Festival, Video Vault and DVD Cache send films by mail. title: Egg Auction On Internet Is Drawing High Scrutiny
body: Days after a new Web site auctioning models' services as egg donors made a wide-ranging publicity splash, some are questioning whether the auction is for real, or just a ploy to attract Internet traffic. Clay Shirky, a professor of new media at Hunter College, wrote Tuesday in an on-line publication, The Silicon Alley Daily, that he had paid to join the site, called Ron's Angels, so that he could investigate it and had sent email inquiries about bidding but received no reply. Mr. Shirky and others questioned whether Ron Harris, the photographer who founded the site, actually intended to market the site not as an egg auction but as an erotic venue much like others he has run. The site charges $24.95 a month for the opportunity to bid on donor eggs and to get more information on the models. By last night the site also featured an advertisement for an on-line pharmacy offering drugs for impotence, baldness and obesity. A spokesman acknowledged yesterday that Mr. Harris had run a number of erotic sites on the Web, but said he had been closing them and was serious about auctioning off eggs. The fledgling site's staff has been so swamped by interest from news organizations that it has had no time to answer inquiries, he said. The newyork Times published an article on Saturday about the site and the reactions of infertility specialists. On Monday, an article in USA Today included interviews with two prospective egg donors and a woman who said she had bid $42,000 for one model's eggs. This week The Washington Post, The Boston Globe and on-line publications have published articles citing skepticism about the site's authenticity and Mr. Harris's motives. By Tuesday, the number of models shown as potential donors on the Ron's Angels site had dropped to three, from eight last week. Mr. Harris's spokesman, who spoke on the condition that he not be named, said that in view of the publicity and debate about the site, five models had asked to be removed, at least temporarily. But he said the site planned to add donors within days. The spokesman said he could not immediately make the three remaining models available for interviews, and attempts yesterday to reach the two models quoted in the USA Today article were unsuccessful. The site has drawn outraged criticism from infertility groups and specialists, who condemned it for turning human eggs into a commodity that would go to the highest bidder. Infertility clinics routinely offer egg donor profiles, sometimes on line, but they generally pay no more than $5,000 to the donors, and the money is meant to compensate them for their discomfort and time, rather than for the genetic material itself. Mr. Harris's other Web ventures have sometimes attracted scrutiny.  The Better Business Bureau in Los Angeles, where Mr. Harris is based, said it had received two complaints from subscribers displeased with the content and service provided by Eros Entertainment Inc., one of Mr. Harris's businesses. A spokeswoman for the local office of the Federal Trade Commission said it was undertaking no suits against Mr. Harris or his companies. The Internet, however, carried ample records of complaints against Mr. Harris for "spamming" -- bombarding news groups on the Internet with advertisements for his soft-porn sites. Many of the sites attributed to him and listed as "rogue" sites by spam fighters are defunct. Also on the Internet, on a site called 4porn.net, is an interview with Mr. Harris from 1996 that quotes him discussing his sites, calling himself an artist rather than a pornographer. "If you get your genes into the next generation, you win," he said then. "The only reason you are here is to breed, to transmit your DNA." Though Professor Shirky harshly criticized reports on the site that took it at "face value," he also said he could believe that Mr. Harris was sincere in his ideology and in the Web site's mission. "I don't think this is a hoax," he said, "I think it's a public relations stunt." Mr. Harris does hope that the site will generate interest in a book he has been writing on his views about genetics for the last 20 years, his spokesman said, but "this is not a publicity thing." Ultimately, the spokesman said, accusations that the site is a hoax can be disproved only if bidders agree to go public about the deal after the current bidding period ends on Dec. 31. "All I can say is, stay tuned," the spokesman said. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Live From Las Vegas, A Concert on the Internet
body: As the Internet grows, bigger stunts are needed to attract attention. It's hard to imagine what will top the on-line iBash that the new streaming video company, Pixelon, will stage this weekend. The company plans to call attention to its new ability to send full-screen, live pictures over the Internet by giving a party in Las Vegas, hiring acts like the Who, the Dixie Chicks and Faith Hill and broadcasting their performances live. The show begins at 2:30 P.M. on Friday, Pacific standard time, and ends at midnight. Pixelon is a small, tightly held start-up company that is reaching out to the public with a big gesture to demonstrate how its Web-based solution could replace old-fashioned television. Michael Fenne, Pixelon's founder, said that the company was able to shrink the size of the data stream to about 100,000 bits per second, about a third of what the standard, MPEG, would use to represent the moving pictures. The solution represents several years of serious mathematical research into how to represent images on the screen with the least amount of data. The company is also investing heavily in placing proprietary technology at the local substations to which home computers would connect. These points of presence, or POP's, are getting a huge bank of disk drives to hold video for delivery on demand as well as a satellite link for picking up live events like the Las Vegas concert. The new system also includes a technology that will tailor the advertisements shown to the demographic information about a viewer. If the scheme works as planned, a 23-year old man who used the Pixelon network to tune into a talk show like "Oprah" would still see advertisements for a forthcoming monster truck rally and wrestling festival.   PETER WAYNER http://www.nytimes.com

title:
ONLINE SHOPPER;
A Little Something for You, and for Humanity
body: I HOPE I am not the first person to tell you that you do not need a hemp linen pillow stuffed with buckwheat hulls. So what if it has a zipper for easy hull removal? Never mind that the photo on the Ethical Shopper home page made this $24 pillow look deeply comfortable (www.ethicalshopper.com). No, you don't need it and I don't need it. Nor do we need to buy a wool passport bag from Nepal ($9), a pet collar made with natural hemp webbing ($7.95) or an earth-tone potpourri box with a lid handle shaped like a frog ($14). So why am I lingering over the product descriptions ("Liven up your bathroom with these bright colored all-natural, herbal soaps") at Ethical Shopper? Perhaps because the people behind it and other "ethical shopping" sites like Ecomall and Enviroshop are no fools. They know that for many consumers, the act of shopping isn't just about what they want to own but also about what they want to be. And so if I clicked the Order button, perhaps I would become socially and environmentally conscientious, someone who supports, say, the earthenware-producing efforts of an Indonesian women's cooperative. I could also buy products that show my support for animal rights, human rights, employee rights, community rights. Also, I try not to litter. As you can probably tell, I didn't arrive at Ethical Shopper with anything but disdain for something I saw as a marketing gimmick. Even for someone who likes to shop as much as I do, it would seem the height of self-delusion to equate the process of buying useless trinkets with responsible behavior. Shopping, in fact, is the kind of activity I engage in to avoid behaving in a morally responsible fashion. If I truly cared about animals, for instance, wouldn't I stop gazing at the picture of the hemp pet collar long enough to take my dog out into the yard for some training to reiterate the importance of not running in front of cars? Ethical shopping sites play upon that exquisitely painful combination of lust and guilt that only shopping elicits. I was on line, happily imagining how the potpourri box would look on the shelf in the bathroom when all of a sudden, my mind flashed on the sad image of a chocolate Labrador retriever limping around the neighborhood in a hip cast. Guilt won. And if I had been browsing among the limited wares in a small gift shop in the real world, I would have simply walked out. But on line, where shopkeepers aren't limited by the amount of physical space available to store inventory, the varied wares of countless independent retailers are displayed enticingly on a single Web site. And impulse buying is much easier when all you have to do is click. I realized this when in my haste trying to log off, I accidentally clicked instead on Eco-Supermarket and saw that the Ethical Shopper was selling Annie's Homegrown Macaroni and Cheese. I usually buy cheaper, inferior brands, the ones with artificial colorings and artificial flavorings and actual preservatives, because Annie's costs $1.49 a box at my local supermarket. But here was an opportunity to get a case of 24 boxes of the comparatively delicious Annie's brand at nearly $1.35 per box ($27, plus $5.30 for shipping) and yes, the bunny pasta shape was available. To reassure myself that 14 cents per box was a significant saving, I applied my Starbuck's standard: let's see, 14 cents times 24 boxes equals slightly more than two cups at Starbuck's. Just think of all that free coffee I would be drinking next week. Did I need 24 boxes of macaroni and cheese? Of course not. But I did need to believe, temporarily, that I could be the sort of mother whose children could finish dinner without having the telltale evidence of orange chemical residue on their lips. I made a quick side trip to compare prices at the Annie's Homegrown Web page (www.annies.com). I could order the identical item for $30 including shipping -- $2.30 less than the Ethical Shopper price. Then it hit me: Since the Ethical Shopper charges a flat-rate shipping fee, the answer was to purchase more things, spreading out the shipping costs. Did I forget to mention that I had been eyeing a bamboo-strip book journal ($12), with paper made from Himalayan bark? With two daughters who are diary-keeping fiends, I was bound to purchase some journals somewhere out there in the world of shopping. Why not buy socially responsible ones? Comparison shopping. Flat-rate shipping. Coveting Himalayan bark-paper diaries. Somehow I didn't feel I was really in the spirit of ethical shopping. But as I found out later, talking to one of the Ethical Shopper's co-founders, Rachel Prishkolnick, on the phone, that is exactly the reason shoppers end up buying environmentally friendly products. "If you're going to buy a certain item anyway," she said, "and you're given the choice of buying a product that's socially conscious over something that's not, where's the dilemma? There also is an increasing knowledge of our environment and the damage we've done and how that affects us." So buying from one of the growing number of on-line purveyors of socially conscious products fills a great shopping need: the ability for me to believe simultaneously in behaving selflessly (supporting socially conscientious companies) even while I selfishly get what I want. In other words, I could buy what I wanted and, in some small way, what I wanted to be. Of course, the experience cost me $56.30, and we will be eating macaroni until it makes us cry. But at least I didn't get hulls all over the bedroom floor. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: QUIET SLEEP? -- A buckwheat-hull pillow could be equated with a clear conscience.; "Ethical shopping" sites are selling products like herbal soaps and organic pasta.

title: Police Look Into Business Dealings of 2 Slain Stock Promoters
body: The two partners in an Internet stock promotion operation who were found shot to death on Tuesday inside a mansion here were linked to "shady" business dealings and may have been killed to be silenced, the Monmouth County Prosecutor said today. One victim, Albert Alain Chalem, 41, who lived in the mansion in this wealthy suburb, had worked for the brokerage A. S. Goldmen, which was indicted in July in newyork on several charges of stock manipulation and illegal trading; the firm has denied the charges. The other victim, Maier Lehmann, 37, of Woodmere, N.Y., paid $630,000 in penalties and refunds to investors last year to settle a regulatory complaint accusing him of fraud and securities registration violations. The case remains under criminal investigation by Federal prosecutors. The two men, shot execution style, were found on the marble floor of the foyer of the $1.1 million home by two friends of Mr. Chalem's at 1 A.M. Tuesday. Mr. Lehmann apparently died of a single shot, while Mr. Chalem was shot several times, suggesting that he had tried to get up after being shot. Cell phones belonging to the two men were lying nearby, and are being analyzed. The house was otherwise undisturbed, and money has been dismissed as a direct motive. "If someone swindles you out of money, what you want is your money back," John Kaye, the County Prosecutor, said. "You don't murder them, because then you don't get your money and you get caught. So my operating belief is that there was something more here. It was probably related to the victims' business activities, and the killer or killers feared something else more than the loss of money." Mr. Kaye called the two men's business practices "shady" but said investigators did not know of any illegal operations involving the Web site the men maintained. That site, www.stockinvestor.com, that provided free stock quotes but also recommended that investors buy certain small and obscure stocks, known as penny stocks. Just a little buying or selling can cause big changes in such stocks' prices, which is why the number of Web sites devoted to them has soared, despite warnings from securities regulators that many of these sites are vehicles for stock fraud. Aggressive penny stock promotions have been a chronic problem for regulators for more than a decade, and have proliferated during the current stock market boom. But until the last few years, these cases have rarely involved violence or threats of violence. Investigators spent today hauling away vanloads of evidence from the mansion, including paper files and computers. The computer hard drives have been sent to the New Jersey State Police laboratories for analysis and duplication, Mr. Kaye said, and Federal investigators, including officials from securities law enforcement agencies, are helping to sift the financial records taken from the house. No weapon was recovered, said Chief Kevin A. Sauter of the Colts Neck Police Department. Investigators appeared to be focusing on Mr. Chalem, if only because the slayings took place at his home. But given his involvement in a case under criminal investigation, Mr. Lehman may also have had knowledge that would have made someone want to silence him, Mr. Kaye said. "We have lots of evidence and lots of leads and lots of suspects, because lots of people didn't like these people," he said. Securities and Exchange Commission records give Mr. Lehmann's wife's name as Tamar, and a phone number for a Tammy Lehmann is listed in Woodmere, N.Y. The number was connected to a fax machine. Mr. Chalem is listed in his most recent regulatory filing as living in East Hampton, N.Y., at 20 Cross Highway, but Chief Sauter said the broker had moved to Colts Neck in the spring. The white brick mansion sits on about 10 acres on Blue Bell Lane, with a circular drive surrounding a fountain. It was bought in the spring for $1.1 million by Russell Candela, of Brooklyn, who is the father of Mr. Chalem's girlfriend, Kimberly Scarola, 39. Ms. Scarola, who lived with Mr. Chalem, was in Florida when the shootings took place, the prosecutor said, and returned to New Jersey today and was questioned. Mr. Kaye said the two men's Internet site was listed in Web registration documents as having its headquarters in Panama City. But the site's administrative contact was listed as Moos Gabor, with a Budapest telephone number. "They did stock promotion over the Internet and in mass mailings," Mr. Kaye said. "A lot of these things involve stocks worth around $5 and a lot of them violate S.E.C. rules." Stockinvestor's site today offered two stocks, apparently technology-related, that sold for less than $10 a share. Penny stock operations have proliferated in newyork, New Jersey and Florida. Mr. Chalem and Mr. Lehmann had been involved in the seamier side of the securities business, according to regulatory records. From 1994 through early 1996, Mr. Chalem worked for A. S. Goldmen, a now defunct brokerage firm, according to records maintained by Federal and state securities regulators. Goldmen, which specialized in selling tiny stocks to unsophisticated investors, has a long history of regulatory and legal problems. In July, the firm, which had offices in Iselin, N.J., as well as in Florida and newyork, was indicted along with its owners and more than two dozen brokers by a Manhattan grand jury. Robert M. Morgenthau, the Manhattan District Attorney, said the firm and its employees manipulated stocks, lied to investors, forged documents and made unauthorized trades; lawyers for the firm have denied the charges. Last spring, Mr. Lehmann, without admitting or denying the charges, agreed to settle a separate complaint by the S.E.C. involving a company called Electro Optical Systems. According to the commission, he was one of a large group of people who conspired to inflate the price of the fledgling company's stock by promoting it on the Internet and by issuing false press releases about it; investors lost about $10 million in the scheme, according to the S.E.C. Legal proceedings in the case have been put on hold because of a pending Federal criminal investigation, S.E.C. officials said earlier this year. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Two Internet stock promoters who were killed execution style on Tuesday were found in the lobby of a mansion in Colts Neck, N.J., a wealthy suburb in Monmouth County. (Laura Pedrick for The newyork Times)

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Those Dark Corners of the Web: Sites for Horror and the Occult
body: HALLOWEEN is a holiday with ancient roots that span many cultures. The modern observance is thought to be a mixture of influences from the Celtic festival of Samhain, Pomona Day in ancient Rome and the Christian holidays of All Saints' and All Soul's Days. In tune with its varied ancestry, Halloween sites on the Web range from serious to silly. If you're looking for a quick supply of Halloween information, go to the obvious address, www.halloween .com. A hefty collection of links resides there, and you can find everything virtual from haunted houses to ghost stories and Halloween jokes. Information about witches, both fictional and modern Wiccan, abounds. A link to an electronic tour of Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia is there as well, for those who want a historical digression. Another plentiful source of spooky lore is the Halloween on the Net page (www.holidays.net/halloween). In addition to a virtual pumpkin patch to tromp through, the site has a section devoted to Los Dias de los Muertos -- the Day of the Dead, a traditional Mexican holiday. It is celebrated Oct. 31 through Nov. 2 to honors one's ancestors. Although a holiday with the name Day of the Dead may sound a bit morbid, it is actually a rather joyful time of remembrance in Mexico, with parades and family gatherings. Halloween seems to be a natural time to look up the writer J. K. Rowlings's ubiquitous Harry Potter, with his adventures and tales of adolescent witches and wizards. In addition to starring in three best-sellers, the young wizard-in-training has his own official home on the Internet www.scholastic.com/harrypotter, and the site has a few features that do more than sell the books. Children can play trivia games and download a Harry Potter screen saver ( available for both Windows and Macintosh). The site also contains discussion guides and a reading circle where readers can post comments and share their thoughts. Scary.com (www.scary.com) is a horror Web site that offers plenty of G-rated thrills and chills. A character named Shriek the Bat (who even has his own playable theme song) leads children through the fully interactive site, which includes a jam session by a mummy band and a point-and-click haunted house. The site features original Web cartoons -- one of which is "Dead Run," the tale of a boy who really, really wants to be a vampire. The cartoons are created by Spunky Productions, which also has shows with non-Halloween themes at its main site, www.spunkytown.com. The cartoons are created in Macromedia's Flash program and new episodes appear regularly. Children can click on a character in midshow to get more information and can email jokes from the program to friends. And there is a bonus for parents: the Web cartoons can be watched at any time of year. And for those who are too shy -- or too cool -- to scream on the big night, www.americangreetings.com is offering free electronic Halloween greetings that will send the screams of seven celebrities, including Gillian Anderson from "The X-Files," to the email boxes of your friends and family. For every scream sent, American Greetings says it will make a 10-cent donation to the Starlight Children's Foundation, a non-profit group dedicated to helping children with serious illnesses. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Shriek the Bat presides over Scary.com, in the spirit of Halloween.

title:
STATE OF THE ART;
Faster And Faster, But Why?
body: ANOTHER generation of faster microprocessors is about to arrive in the stores, just in time to spark a new wave of holiday technology lust among the pocket-protector crowd. Faster chips are introduced every few months. We all know that the hot new PC chip that is the champion of the silicon raceway today will become in just a couple of years the desktop equivalent of the embarrassing old clunker that leaves oil stains in the driveway. But as always, the most significant result of the introduction of new chips is that they inevitably lead to a price war, and that usually translates into cheaper yet better computers for consumers. Even though costs are rising for memory chips and other PC components, this week's processor price wars between the Intel Corporation and its main rival, Advanced Micro Devices, are expected to offset most of those increases and keep PC prices steady before Christmas. Almost any PC sold today, even those costing less than $500, have enough processing power to perform the basic computing tasks that consumers ask them to do, like connecting to the Internet for email and on-line shopping, playing simple games and writing business plans for new Internet start-ups. Getting more processing power for the same money is a welcome bonus. But for a few more advanced applications, like 3-D graphics, high-end computer games, professional graphics, rocket science, software development, digital video editing, speech recognition and downloading streams of bootlegged music files from the Internet while doing the computer equivalent of standing on one foot and balancing spinning plates on a stick, the faster the microprocessor the better. To appeal to that audience, the Intel Corporation this week introduced 15 new and enhanced Pentium III microprocessors based on an advanced production technology called Coppermine. Nine of the new Coppermine Pentium III chips will be used in desktop computers, with speeds ranging from 500 megahertz to 733 megahertz, or millions of cycle per second. Computers built around these chips are expected to cost $1,200 to $2,500. Three chips will be used in notebook computers, with speeds of 400, 450 and 500 MHz. Three more, at speeds of 600, 667 and 700 MHz, are to be used in powerful workstations and servers that consumers rarely see. Coppermine has nothing to do with the copper manufacturing process developed by I.B.M. as a superior replacement for aluminum in microprocessors. Rather, it is Intel's code word for a new 0.18-micron manufacturing process. A micron is a millionth of meter, so 0.18 microns is extremely small. Earlier Pentium III and Pentium II chips were made using a 0.25-micron process. By squeezing the Pentium III's 28 million transistors into less space, the new Coppermine Pentium III chips are smaller, faster and cooler. Faster is better for obvious reasons, and smaller chips not only allow smaller and more stylish devices, but they also consume less power, which means that they do not get as hot. Smaller, cooler chips that use less power are ideally suited for portable PC's. The new manufacturing process allows Intel to integrate the main processing unit with a high-speed memory subsystem called a Level 2 cache, all on the same die. Until now, the L2 cache was on a separate chip. The 256 kilobytes of full-speed, integrated cache on the Coppermine chips improves their performance significantly, Intel says, outperforming twice as much cache memory on a separate chip. That's the easy part. Unfortunately, Intel made this a very confusing introduction. After months of hype, Intel failed to deliver a new supporting chip set, called the i820, that the company said was to have been the underlying platform for getting the highest performance from the new Coppermine processors. The i820 chip set is needed to allow the new Pentium III to take advantage of a high-speed memory subsystem called Rambus. The jury is still out on the value of the Rambus technology for consumers. Rambus memory modules are much faster, but also much more expensive, than current memory technologies. Intel now says the i820 chip set will be sent to PC makers before the end of the year. To add to the confusion, some of the new chips work only with a slower, 100-MHz system bus -- the data path between the processor, the memory and other system components -- while others work only with a faster, 133-MHz bus. Some work with either. Also, some of the new chips appear to compete with earlier Pentium III chips at the same clock speed. Some consumers will need help telling them apart without opening the computer case. The net effect is that there is a lot of confusion about the new chips, even among industry analysts with advanced engineering degrees. Consumers who do not need to buy a new PC right away may want to wait until the smoke clears. High-end-PC users, including game fanatics, may want to wait until computers arrive with the i820 chip set, which also includes support for a new graphics standard called AGP 4X. Technological esoterica aside, the Coppermine chips will allow Intel-based machines to keep up with computers based on the exceptionally fast Athlon processor from Advanced Micro Devices, which is, at 700-MHz, the current speed champ and darling of the 3-D game community. Long considered the Salieri to Intel's Mozart, AMD makes microprocessors that run Windows software just as well as Intel's chips do, but at lower cost. AMD has vowed to keep prices 25 percent below Intel's for comparable chips. AMD plans to move to the 0.18-micron process next year. Both Intel and AMD have publicly demonstrated 800-MHz chips, and both have said they will push speeds beyond 1 gigahertz by the end of next year. Why does this matter? Faster chips must be evaluated in three distinct ways. One, do they allow me to do interesting new things that I could not do before? In some cases, yes, but remember that it takes time for software developers to take advantage of the faster chips, and by the time they do, prices are usually lower. Two, is it worth spending more now for the fastest PC chip? Buying the fastest processor available may prolong the useful life of the computer, but not by that much. Other important PC components evolve as well. In terms of value, it often makes more sense to buy a lesser computer and to plan to replace it sooner. And three, will a faster chip save me at least 4 minutes a day? There are 1,440 minutes in a day, but there is something magical about 4-minute chunks of time. According to "Faster," a new book by James Gleick, Americans spend an average of 4 minutes every day just booting up and shutting down a Microsoft Windows-based personal computer. Americans spend an average of 4 minutes a day filling out government paperwork. And coincidentally, they spend an average of 4 minutes each day having sex. Few Americans yearn for more time to fill out government forms or to watch Windows booting. But I would be willing to spend the money on a new computer if it allowed me to devote more time to more interesting pursuits. Most Internet users spend much more than 4 minutes a day waiting for their computers to retrieve email, download graphics and audio files, and display Web pages. Investing in a cable or D.S.L. connection would in theory have a more profound impact on their romantic lives than getting a faster processor. On the other hand, if the Internet was faster and less frustrating to use, people might spend more time in front of the computer screen than they probably should. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: House Passes Measure on Internet Domain Names
body: The House of Representatives passed legislation today to crack down on cybersquatting, the practice of buying up popular words as Internet addresses in the hopes of reselling them to companies and trademark holders at a hefty profit. The bill was passed on a voice vote despite an effort by opponents to slow down action on the proposal. A similar version has already been passed in the Senate. "This legislation will make cybersquatters think twice before trying to profit off the hard work of others," Representative J. C. Watts Jr. of Oklahoma, the House Republican conference chairman, said of the bill by Representative James E. Rogan, a California Republican. Civil libertarians, however, are concerned that the proposals, which now go to a House-Senate conference committee, will trample on free speech on the Internet. In an email campaign over the weekend, the Association for Computing Machinery, a group of computer professionals, circulated a message to get Internet users to urge members of Congress to vote against the bill, arguing that it would "grant sweeping new powers for trademark holders and undermine the rights of domain name holders, Internet users and small businesses." The group also said the legislation would undermine a policy recently adopted by the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, which was picked last year by the Clinton Administration to oversee administration of the Internet's addressing system. That policy aims to reduce court battles over domains by establishing a uniform international arbitration system for resolving such disputes. Both the House and Senate bills outlaw "bad faith" registrations of Internet addresses, or domain names, that use movie, book or product titles or the names of large companies that might later be interested in using those addresses to build an Internet presence. Some companies have paid hundreds of thousands of dollars to get coveted Internet addresses away from those who had registered them. Other companies, however, have refused to pay what they consider to be the equivalent of a ransom, and have instead taken squatters to court. In the House and Senate bills, bad faith is defined as using an Internet domain name that dilutes or is identical or confusingly similar to a trademark. The House bill gives courts the power to revoke a pirated domain name, and authorizes damages of up to $100,000 to be paid to a plaintiff. The Senate bill also establishes criminal penalties for repeat offenders.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: In High Technology, the Grind Evolves
body: In May 1994, Jeff Treuhaft, 25, joined a little Silicon Valley start-up called Mosaic, later to be renamed the Netscape Communications Corporation. The pace was brutal -- 18 hours a day, seven days a week in the early months -- but the work was exhilarating. "The really tough part was that my son was 9 weeks old when I started at Netscape," he recalled. Five years later, Mr. Treuhaft has two more children and a tidy nest egg from the sale of Netscape this year to America Online. Like many former Netscape executives, he is stepping back from the front lines of the Internet business, working part time as an investor and adviser to a few start-ups. Suddenly, Mr. Treuhaft finds himself free to play with his children, feed them lunch, even tag along on a school field trip to the pumpkin patch down the road. "It seems mundane stuff," he said, "but when you finally get a chance to do it, you appreciate it." At Microsoft, Netscape's main rival in the infamous Internet browser battle, some have made similar personal choices. Brad Silverberg, a former senior vice president, took a sabbatical in the summer of 1997 to decompress after directing Microsoft's hurried march to catch up and then gain leadership in the Internet software business. He took a solo bicycle trip through the Canadian Rockies, spent time with his wife and two children and thought about all the personal things that had been shunted aside for work. "Time is the one thing you cannot get back," said Mr. Silverberg, 45, who now works part time as an investor and adviser to start-ups. The trade-off choices made in so many American households of personal life versus work, time versus money, are magnified in the Internet economy. The time pressure is so intense because a lead of just a few weeks or months over a rival can be a huge competitive advantage in the Internet land rush. And the financial rewards for the front-runners can be astronomical. Still, if the Internet is going to be a transforming technology, like electricity, it must spread throughout the economy and society, as it finds new uses and new customers. That process, inevitably, will take time. It means carefully building big Internet businesses, not just starting them. Internet "cruising speed" will become a valued skill and a competitive edge. For both companies and individuals, that means pacing, in one way or another, in a race that is becoming more a marathon and less a sprint. As the Internet economy matures, high-technology companies are expanding programs and policies intended to help harried workers balance their personal lives and the demands of work. A greater use of flexible hours, part-time work, day care, sabbaticals and longer vacations are all part of that effort. According to the Radford division of the benefits firm Aon Consulting, average vacation time offered by high-technology companies has steadily increased in recent years. Forty-one percent even offer full vacation benefits to new recruits during their first year of employment, and 10 percent of Silicon Valley companies now offer sabbaticals, Radford reports. Cisco Systems, for example, gives all new hires four weeks of vacation at the start. After surveying its employees last year, Cisco is building a day-care center on its corporate campus in San Jose. "We found supply was low, demand was high and more and more high-tech companies are doing something in child care," explained Peggy Lynch, manager of benefits for Cisco. Two years ago, I.B.M. introduced a program allowing people to work part time while still getting the benefits and opportunities of full-time employees. One person in the program is Marie Wieck, director of XML technology, a hot new field of Internet software programming. Ms. Wieck, 39, works 32 hours a week now instead of the 60 she used to. She still travels, but she typically is in the office only three days a week, giving her more time to spend with her two young daughters. "I'll keep doing this as long as it makes sense both for the business and for me," Ms. Wieck said. Yet it is in Internet start-ups, not established companies, where the work regimen is the most grueling. The hours are still long in today's second-generation Internet start-ups, but the perspective of the young programming whizzes does seem to have changed a bit. Lou Montulli, 29, was one of the first engineers at Netscape. After Netscape was sold, he moved on to another Internet start-up, Epinions.com. "I really like the energy of a start-up," he said, "because it's an environment where you can really make a difference as an individual." But these days, Mr. Montulli is working 70-hour weeks instead of the 120 hours he often did at Netscape -- a single-minded commitment to work that he acknowledges contributed to the break-up of his marriage, to the daughter of Jim Clark, a co-founder of Netscape. "I'm just not emotionally equipped to work like that anymore," he said. "I have a life." For people with children, however, 70-hour workweeks may not be their idea of balancing work and personal lives. And the stock-option wealth created by many high-technology companies has given people like Mr. Treuhaft and Mr. Silverberg the financial freedom to do what they call "serial balancing" -- shifting from stints of intense work to time off or part-time work, and back again. "Balance is a very difficult thing to achieve, at least in parallel," Mr. Silverberg said. "To achieve great things in one's career typically takes a tremendous amount of focus and dedication. I've tried to achieve 'balance' in a more serial way, so that hopefully it will even out over the long haul. And thanks to Microsoft, I have the freedom to do that." In Silicon Valley, Mr. Treuhaft takes a similar approach to his period of part-time work, viewing it as a recess. "I don't think I'd call this my career," he said. "It's more catching my breath, while still pedaling the bicycle." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Jeff Treuhaft has more time for his children after leaving Netscape and stepping back from the front lines of the Internet business. (Peter DaSilva for The newyork Times)

title: The Co-Founder of Netscape Is an Entrepreneur Once Again
body: For some people in Silicon Valley the garage still holds more allure than the board room. Marc Andreessen, a co-founder of Netscape Communications, said today that he would be the founding chairman of Loudcloud Inc., a company to be based in Menlo Park, Calif., that is for the time being housed in a single warehouse-like room. The company will develop software to help companies get their businesses on the Internet quickly. In choosing to lead a start-up, Mr. Andreessen is eschewing both his recent corporate role as chief technology officer of America Online, which acquired Netscape last year, and becoming a venture capitalist, the currently popular career route among successful entrepreneurs. In an interview today, Mr. Andreessen said that he was reveling in being back in a world that was closer to the legendary Silicon Valley garages in which Hewlett-Packard and Apple Computer were born. "Our philosophy is that we're cheap and we're proud," he said. Mr. Andreessen, who is 28 years old and whose personal wealth has been estimated at several hundred million dollars, said he had set up his start-up in an extra room at a semiconductor equipment company. The new company so far is self-financed. Its management team consists of three Netscape executives: Ben Horowitz as chief executive, Timothy Howes as chief technology officer and In Sik Rhee as chief strategist. Mr. Andreessen will be the full-time chairman. He said he had flirted with several offers to become a venture capitalist but had ultimately rejected that path in favor of hands-on entrepreneurism because "I think it would get very frustrating only being able to get so far involved." Indeed, Mr. Andreessen's decision to take an operating role comes as many of the Valley's venture capital firms have bemoaned a dearth of experienced managers in technology industries. "There's a real issue in finding a good C.E.O.," said Joe Schoendorf, a venture capitalist at Accel Partners in Palo Alto, Calif. "At the end of the day, you still have to run a business," he said. "We love great ideas, but if we look at our top 10 successes, in each case they are ones which have been started by great management teams." Loudcloud is almost certain to have major competitors, perhaps including giants like I.B.M. and the Microsoft Corporation. But Mr. Andreessen said he believed that the explosive growth of Internet commerce would only accelerate the market for Loudcloud's technology. He said that more detailed announcements about the company's strategy, products and customers would be made early next year. "Our DNA is going to be software," he said. "We're not going to be consultants, and we're not going to build Internet data centers." At the same time, Mr. Andreessen predicted that the traditional software industry would face increasingly perilous times as the Internet changes the way software is purchased, used and distributed. "Software will become more important in the future, but at the same time, the software industry will be less so," he said. In addition to Loudcloud, Mr. Andreessen said, he had made investments in two other start-ups: ReplayTV, a digital television recording system, and Accompany, an Internet consumer purchasing company. Mr. Andreessen stepped down as America Online's chief technology officer last month, just seven months after the company acquired Netscape. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Marc Andreessen is returning to the life of an entrepreneur. (Associated Press)

title: Dreamworks and Imagine Plan an Internet Venture
body: In what its principals say is a first glimmer of the rapidly approaching digital entertainment world, executives at Dreamworks SKG and Imagine Entertainment said today they would join to create a new Internet entertainment company and World Wide Web site offering short films, streaming video, live events, games, performance art, continuing series, "nonlinear interactive features" and whatever else they can think of. Dreamworks, a studio formed by Steven Spielberg, Jeffrey Katzenberg and David Geffen, announced the partnership with Imagine, a film and television production company headed by Ron Howard and Brian Grazer. They vowed that the new company, to be called Pop.com, would be operating by early spring. The company is to have offices in newyork and Los Angeles, and the announcement of its first chief executive will be made shortly, Mr. Spielberg said. Pop.com is being financed by Vulcan Ventures, the investment vehicle of Paul G. Allen, the Microsoft co-founder who is already a major Dreamworks investor. Vulcan has committed $50 million for the initial phase of the project, Mr. Katzenberg said. For that, Vulcan will get 50 percent of the company; Dreamworks and Imagine will split the other half. When it goes on line, Pop.com is to offer a daily menu of interactive shorts it calls "pops," most running between 30 seconds and 6 minutes. The emphasis will be on comedy, but no genre will be ignored, Mr. Spielberg said, and each "pop" will come with its own chat room and instant- messaging capability. "They have to be so seductive and ultimately addictive that people don't click out after one click," Mr. Grazer said. Mr. Spielberg and Mr. Howard, both film directors, said they intended to contribute their own "pops" to the site, though they added that initially much of their work would be to encourage others to get involved and to nurture the work of fledgling digital artists. "This is an emerging and evolving new format," Mr. Katzenberg said. "The analogy I keep coming back to is 25 years ago when you had this wonderful style called music and someone said, let's turn it into an audio and video experience, and out of that was born MTV. We believe we are at that time and moment now for the Internet." Today's announcement is indicative of the scurrying in Hollywood in recent months to find ways to understand and capitalize on the sweeping technological advancements in on-line and digital film making and use it to shape the entertainment world of the future. Also, Mr. Howard said, they want to have some fun. "This is kind of freewheeling, less about narrative drive and all the discipline we have to live with when we make a movie and more about the exploration of interesting new ideas," he said. "I think we're going to able to entice a lot of really talented people to do some work with us." The "pops" presented on the site might also be the seeds of other, larger projects, from video games to television series to feature films. "I certainly see this as like a large, fertile field," Mr. Spielberg said. "You can harvest all sorts of spin-offs, just from whatever germinates. It could be a book, a piece of music, a movie -- who can say?" As word of the venture began to make the rounds in Hollywood and among investors, most executives and analysts said they wanted to reserve judgment until they could see exactly what was planned, and how it might differ from other, perhaps smaller, Internet sites offering digital films. "How do they promote it?" asked one entertainment analyst. "It's very nice to digitize films and put them on the Internet, but where is the value in it for investors? I guess my initial reaction is, 'yeah, so?' " Digital movie making -- sometimes called microcinema -- is a relatively small but growing movement of small-scale film makers using the cheaper and rapidly evolving digital technology to make short films and exhibit them on the Internet. The October issue of Wired magazine listed more than a dozen Internet sites offering short digital films, among them Atomfilms -- which exhibits shorts that are festival favorites or Academy Award nominees, and counts as its partners the HBO and Warner Brothers Online units of Time Warner -- and the Bit Screen, which offers short first-run films and episodic series of 10 minutes or less. Pop.com will be different, its founders say, in the scope of its ambitions, the people associated with it and the strategies it will use to turn a profit. They intend it as a money-making enterprise. "We definitely see this as an advertiser- and sponsor-supported business," Mr. Katzenberg said. In coming weeks, Pop.com plans to talk with Madison Avenue executives about ideas for advertising on the Web. "In the same way that we have to really discover these new forms, Madison Avenue is going to have to reinvent the way it advertises to this kind of viewer," Mr. Katzenberg said. "Each step that is being taken in this world today is a first step. All of us, individually and collectively, are on as big a learning curve as you can be on. There are no rules, and there is no proven formula for success in this as yet." Mr. Spielberg said the venture did not intend to corner the market in digital film making or to muscle out weaker competitors. "I think there will be many stimulating sites in the future," he said. "There will still be movies, and there will still be TV," Mr. Grazer added. "We're not thinking we're changing the world. We're just trying to be a part of the sensibility of this new medium." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Excite@Home To Acquire Bluemountain - Correction Appended
body: Excite@Home will pay up to $1 billion to acquire Bluemountain.com, a privately held electronic greeting card company with little revenue but millions of loyal users. Although a top-rated site on the Web, Bluemountain.com does not actually sell anything. It was created in 1994 by two former hippies, Stephen Schutz and Susan Polis Schutz, to be a "spiritual and emotional center for the Web." The couple, owners of the Blue Mountain Arts Publishing Company, a successful paper greeting card and poetry publisher, decided to give away E-greeting cards. Using only word-of-mouth as advertising, Bluemountain .com swiftly grew to be one of the most consistently popular sites on the Web. And that popularity is what attracted Excite@Home, which is majority-owned by the AT&T Corporation and serves as a gateway, or portal, to the Internet. Excite@Home predicted that the acquisition would increase its audience by 40 percent, to encompass approximately 34 percent of Internet traffic. With a 34 percent share, it would pass the Disney portal Go.com for fifth position, right behind Lycos but still a long stretch from dominant players like America Online, Microsoft and Yahoo. In the short run, the combined audience will allow both sites to raise their rates for advertisers. Additional revenue will also come from opening up Bluemountain to sales of items like flowers, chocolates and gifts. Stock analysts generally praised the move, and Excite@Home's stock gained 75 cents, to close at $39.8125, as the overall market and technology stocks generally fell. Under the terms of the agreement, Excite@Home will issue approximately 11 million new shares, valued at approximately $430 million, and $350 million in cash. If Bluemountain.com meets certain targets for holiday traffic, it will get as much as $270 million more in the acquirer's stock. Excite@Home's long-term strategy is to be a leading planner in broadband -- high-speed Internet access over cable television. @home, which focuses on the cable business, acquired Excite to create a narrow-band Internet presence and said that it had similar intentions with Bluemountain. "We recognize the importance of making the narrow-band end of the funnel as robust as possible explicitly for the purpose of converting those users to broadband eventually." said George Bell, Excite@Home's chief executive. Devotees of the Bluemountain site use its cards for everything from celebrating Robert Burns Day to proposing marriage to far-away lovers. According to MediaMetrix, an Internet audience measurement firm, it now ranks 14th among sites on the Web. Although they have been approached for more than a year by numerous companies, the Schutzes said they had declined to sell because they wanted to keep creative control. But costs forced their hand. "As we got more and more popular, it got extraordinarily expensive," said Ms. Polis Schutz. "We had 300 servers and 86 employees. We could not handle it anymore." Excite@Home, which started the bidding process more than a year and a half ago, made its third offer a few months ago, just as the Schutzes were concluding they had to sell. The family was impressed that Excite offered many of the features they wanted to incorporate ---like a calendar, date book and gift registry -- and would have paid to develop themselves. They also clicked with Mr. Bell, whose colorful past includes a long stint as an independent documentary producer for organizations like National Geographic and the Discovery Channel. "The Excite@Home team are understanding about the nature of our community, and we are confident they will continue to be good stewards into the future," said Jared Schutz, who is Stephen and Susan's oldest son and executive director of Bluemountain. Stephen will continue as editor in chief of Bluemountain for at least another year, under the terms of the deal. While making a commitment to Bluemountain's community, Excite@Home savors the site's untapped commercial potential. "The beauty is you have roughly a million people ordering cards everyday, and most all are for events that have gifts," said Arthur Newman, an Internet analyst at Schroders. Yahoo ran into trouble when it tried to bring a more commercial approach to Geocities, a similar acquistion in 1998. A site where users could make their own Web pages free, Geocities had lots of loyal customers who revolted when Yahoo tried to force members to relinquish copyright on their Web creations. Bluemountain was spun off from the publishing company earlier this year. Both companies are privately held by the Schutz family, but Ms. Polis Schutz said the benefits of the merger would be widely felt. "Every musician, every artist, every employee has options," she said. "We are thrilled for them, that they are going to be rewarded for their incredible dedication." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  Because of an editing error, an article in Business Day on Oct. 26 about the acquisition of Blue mountain.com by Excite@Home misstated the stake held by AT&T in Excite. It is 26 percent; AT&T is not the majority owner. Correction-Date: November 4, 1999, Thursday Graphic   Photo: Bluemountain, an Internet card company, is owned by Susan Polis Schutz, left, her husband, Stephen Schutz, and their son Jared, right. (Kim Kulish for The newyork Times)(pg. C10)

title: New Alliance Will Promote Wireless Access to Internet
body: A group of leading technology companies said yesterday that they would form an alliance to create products that would allow consumers to get high-speed Internet access through a wireless system within the next year. The consortium -- which is led by Cisco Systems Inc., the giant Internet networking company, and Motorola Inc., the maker of wireless telephone products -- is essentially backing an alternative to delivering broadband Internet access through underground cables and wires. The race to bring broadband Internet access to consumers has led to several alliances that promise to deliver that kind of service through satellites, cellular telephone networks and standard cable and telephone lines. Now, the group headed by Cisco and Motorola is trying to provide a cheaper and more effective solution to digging up the ground and laying cables: They want to deliver data, voice and video services over the airwaves and directly into buildings and homes that are affixed with antennas or the equivalent of a satellite dish. "This is the technology that is going to take the fixed broadband wireless market into the next millennium," said Steve Smith, director of marketing in the broadband wireless business unit at Cisco Systems, which is based in San Jose, Calif. "This gets consumers Internet access without tearing up the ground." Officials at Cisco Systems said yesterday that a group of 10 companies -- Motorola, Texas Instruments, Broadcom, Bechtel Telecommunications, Samsung, Toshiba, LCC International, EDS, KPMG Consulting and Pace Microtechnology -- had agreed to create and develop products that use a Cisco technology, one that is equipped to deliver Internet service over a radio frequency called MMDS. Aware that the AT&T Corporation was moving into cable television and developing a system capable of delivering high-speed Internet access through its cable services, MCI Worldcom and Sprint have spent about $1 billion in the last few years to buy many of the companies that owned the licenses to the MMDS radio spectrum. Three weeks ago, MCI Worldcom agreed to acquire Sprint in a $115 billion merger. If the technology is successful, it appears that Internet service providers will be able to choose among cable operators, wireless service providers and perhaps even satellite operators like Teledesic L.L.C., which is developing a kind of "Internet in the Sky" technology, a multibillion-dollar plan backed by the cellular telephone pioneer Craig McCaw and William H. Gates of Microsoft. Cisco Systems and Motorola are also backing something called LMDS, which is another radio frequency that offers broadband access, mostly to businesses. According to Cisco officials, however, the MMDS system is more effective in crowded urban areas and is more easily available to everyday consumers and the mass market. Robert Edwards, a spokesman at Motorola, which is based in Schaumburg, Ill., said yesterday that the company was backing both the LMDS and MMDS technologies and working to develop a large portfolio of offerings so that big technology companies and consumers could have a wide range of alternatives to getting broadband access. The companies involved in the agreement yesterday said that the ability to deliver high-speed broadband access through a wireless system would also rapidly accelerate the introduction of broadband services to rural areas and urban centers, and do so more easily and inexpensively. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
The PC Industry Shows Strong Growth
body: The personal computer industry is continuing to show significant global growth, with third-quarter shipments of machines increasing by 23.2 percent over the comparable quarter last year, according to a Dataquest report to be issued on Monday. Dataquest, a market research company based in San Jose, Calif., cited strong growth in all regions of the world and lower prices as the foundation of the continued surge in computer shipments, which totaled 28.5 million in the quarter. Compaq Computer remained the world's largest PC maker with a 12.8 percent market share, although that figure was down from 13.4 percent last year. Compaq shipped 3.65 million computers during the quarter, according to Dataquest. In contrast Dell Computer, the No. 2 PC company, whose sales have grown along with the rise of Internet commerce, expanded its market share from 8.2 percent to 10.8 percent, shipping 3.07 million computers during the quarter. Behind the two leaders were three other computer makers based in the unitedstates: I.B.M., Hewlett-Packard and Gateway. Dataquest analysts said that companies like Compaq, Hewlett-Packard and I.B.M., which have typically sold to customers indirectly, had experienced slower growth than those like Dell specializing in direct sales over the Internet. Despite Compaq's global leadership position, it dropped behind Dell in sales of machines within the unitedstates. That was a milestone for Dell, according to Dataquest. For the third quarter, Dell's domestic market share rose to 17.1 percent, up from 13.4 percent a year earlier -- a growth rate of 56.5 percent. Compaq's domestic shipments, meanwhile, rose only 24.9 percent, as its unitedstates market share edged up to 15.3 percent, from 15 percent a year earlier. Meanwhile, I.B.M.'s overall market share sank to 7.6 percent, from 8.4 percent in last year's third quarter. Last week, the company announced that it was exiting the retail market and in the future would sell its personal computers via the Internet. Dataquest said that the quarter was unusual because of the rise of computer memory prices, a trend whose impact had been felt most directly by Dell, but also by many of the other computer makers, in terms of lower profits margins. Dataquest said that Gateway's new partnership with America Online, announced last week, was an example of a shift to a "next-generation PC economic model," which would shift the emphasis in competition beyond high inventory turnover. title:
E-Commerce Report;
Consumer products are being reviewed on more Web sites, some featuring comments from anyone with an opinion.
body: TRADITIONALLY, advice on consumer purchasing decisions has been the province of print publications like Consumer Reports, PC Magazine or Car and Driver. While many of these publications have moved their content on line, the growth of the Web has empowered another source of buying advice: the neighbor, cousin or uncle who just bought a particular item and is more than willing to share an opinion. Internet retailers and some publishers have already capitalized on this instinct by allowing users to post opinions about products the companies sell or review. But a handful of companies are hoping to take the age-old effectiveness of word-of-mouth recommendations one step further, by creating independent Web sites that give common folks and bona fide experts a forum for their opinions and users a way to rate the pundits. While some of these sites are charging users for qualified help, most are looking for more creative ways to balance their books and keep users coming to the site. The company that has generated the most recent buzz around this idea is Epinions, which was started in the summer by several well-known Silicon Valley venture capitalists. It is far from the first company to provide users with opinions on what to buy, but it has been a force behind some changes in how these sites approach their business. The cornerstone of the Epinions service, for instance, is that it both rewards and rates product reviewers, in hopes of giving them enough incentive to provide useful opinions. Anyone can sign up to give advice on products that fit into the site's 12 categories, and prospective shoppers can browse through the reviews and rate them on a scale from "not useful" to "very useful." To build credibility -- and eliminate suspicions that they are merely company shills in disguise -- advisers can build a page on the site with photos and personal information. The payoff is aimed at both the reviewer's wallet and ego. Reviewers earn royalties of from one to three dollars for every 10 times their review is read by an Epinions member, and their picture might be featured on the front page of the site if their reviews are widely read. According to Nirav Tolia, a company co-founder, the site relies on a so-called "web of trust" in which users, reviewers and advisers tend over time to be matched up with people whose opinions they have come to trust. "It mimics the way word-of-mouth works in the real world," Mr. Tolia said. When word-of-mouth recommendations result in a sale, Epinions earns an undisclosed referral fee from merchants who pay to have links displayed in areas where their product categories are discussed. Epinions also earns money by displaying banner advertisements on its pages, and can charge higher advertising rates than general information sites -- between $30 and $70 for every thousand banner ads displayed -- since advertisers know they are reaching buyers more qualified than the general surfing public. Mr. Tolia said the company also earned money by licensing its service to other E-commerce sites like Lycos, which included the Epinions service in the new Lycoshop. "It's hard to find people who've actually walked the same path you're walking when you're looking for a product," said Jeff Bennett, vice president for E-commerce at Lycos. "Epinions is very good when it comes to that." Other sites, like Productopia.com and Deja.com, have offered recommendations from users for months, building expansive archives of reviews across hundreds of categories of goods. But those sites do not compensate contributors for their opinions -- at least not yet. Tom Phillips, Deja.com's chief executive, said the company planned to use both a rating and a reward system for reviewers in the near future. The reward system "could involve ego gratification," he said, rather than financial incentives. "There's a way to do both successfully." Roger Neal, Productopia's chief executive, said his company had no plans to compensate consumers who post reviews, since it already pays professional product reviewers to post recommendations on its site. "We'd rather have people doing it for the normal reasons they post on message boards," he said. One question about the business model of these sites is whether the quality of the user reviews is enough to attract a lot of visitors on an ongoing basis. Mr. Phillips, of Deja.com, acknowledged that the responses can be mixed, but said the current quality of reviews on his site "is pretty good." "You certainly get some three-word reviews that are insipid," he said, "but anyone who's put any effort into it usually has something worthwhile to say." Another issue is objectivity. These sites purport to be more objective than retailers that offer user opinions. But some question whether sites that accept commissions, referral fees or advertising can deliver worthwhile information, even if it is provided by individuals with no vested interest in the products. "Since these sites derive revenue from transactions that result from people responding to an opinion, it ultimately raises a question of bias," said Andrew Bartels, an E-commerce analyst with Giga Information Group, a consulting firm. Unscrupulous sites could prominently display reviews that favor certain products, for instance, and gain higher transaction fees for those products. "It could be that the only way to get true, unbiased opinions is for users to pay for it," Mr. Bartels said. But Mr. Phillips, of Deja.com, disagrees. "I don't buy that argument," he said. "We have no incentive to do anything except try to make this valuable for consumers. The primary relationships we have are with marketers who sell all of the products across a category, so we don't do any better on one product versus another." At least one company is betting that consumers are willing to pay for advice, although the services offered generally do not focus on purchase decisions. Exp.com, introduced last month, enables consumers to buy advice and services on topics ranging from career planning and tax shelters to what type of roses to plant. According to Mark Benning, the company's president, the site allows users to rate the performance of its advisers, and takes a 20 percent cut of whatever the advisers charge. The service is unusual in that users contact the expert with a specific question or request, and negotiate a fee before the advice is given. "So they get a much more personalized response," Mr. Benning said. It remains to be seen, however, whether the arrangement will pay off for those who offer their services for sale. Cathy Walworth, for instance, is a horticulture consultant and columnist in Idaho who joined Exp.com in the late summer. She said demand has been light, even though she often charges as little as $5 for a short consultation -- and sometimes gives flower-buying advice for free. "Let's be real here: At that rate, I'm not going to Europe any time soon," she said. "But I got into this business to help people." Exp.com's motives, on the other hand, are decidedly more profit-minded. Mr. Benning said he was optimistic that the company could operate in the black., given what he has seen so far. "We've done thousands of transactions in just a month," he said. "We're pretty pleased with that." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Cathy Walworth, a horticulture consultant, provides advice on Exp.com, one of a growing number of free and fee-based Internet sites that provide consumer advice. (Andy Arenz for The newyork Times)

title: Putting Investment Road Shows on the Internet
body: In the two weeks before they issue stock to the public, company executives often make an exhausting round of meetings across the country, sometimes the world -- in what is called a road show. Money managers with billions of dollars at their disposal get a chance to speak face to face to the people to whom they plan to entrust some of that money. And in question-and-answer sessions, they can see how well a chief executive knows the business and how he performs in the spotlight. But this longtime practice of giving sophisticated investors a preview, and sometimes useful nuggets of information beyond the public documents, is being challenged now that Webvan, an on-line grocer, has postponed its initial stock offering. Webvan was forced to delay its plans a few weeks ago after a reporter for TheStreet.com listened by telephone to a road-show presentation and reported that the company had made significant statements not included in its public filings. The issue is on the radar screen of the Securities and Exchange Commission. In remarks last week, the S.E.C.'s chairman, Arthur Levitt, said that road shows should not be forums for providing a different look at a company than what is in its prospectus. But the debate is part of a larger issue: the unequal disclosure of material information. In his remarks, Mr. Levitt stepped up an attack on selective disclosure, a practice in which companies brief some analysts about financial data, like earnings details, before the public release. He urged companies to let all investors take part in conference calls about important information. In the Webvan episode, the fact that it involved an Internet company and Internet reporter is almost incidental. And yet the Internet does figure into the rising debate over who should be invited to these road-show meetings and what material should be disclosed. After all, on-line trading is encouraging more and more people to take an active role in their stock-market investments. And use of the Internet allows the distribution of financial information to be quicker and wider than ever before. Until now, only so many people could fit into a conference room for a road-show meeting. And even a telephone conference call, it could be argued, might become too expensive and disruptive if a large number of individuals were to chime in. But these days, so-called Webcasting technology can enable anyone with an Internet connection to listen in on a conference call, if the company wants to make it public -- as many Internet-savvy companies have begun to do with their quarterly-earnings calls to analysts. In the case of initial public offerings, securities law does not preclude individuals from taking part in road shows. But it does make far-flung participation virtually prohibitive, because S.E.C. rules permit more liberal discussion of a company in person than they do when communication is by radio, television, phone or the Internet. Companies that have filed for a public stock offering must publish all information material to their business in public documents. But they may clarify or elaborate in oral communications. As a former S.E.C. official put it, the companies add "melody to the lyrics" of the prospectus in the road show. Written communication is limited to what appears in the prospectus -- hence the term "quiet period" to refer to the time just before a new stock offering. And yet, some companies have successfully appealed to the commission to let them broadcast their road-show presentations by phone and on a limited basis over the Internet. Congress gave the commission broad power to change the rules three years ago, and the S.E.C. is now proposing that companies have the same latitude in broadcast communications that they have in oral communication during the so-called quiet period. The proposals are part of a controversial overhaul of rules governing new stock offerings, which has been opened to public comment. The proposals would not require such public access, but would allow it. Supporters of the current system say that opening road shows to everyone could cause chief executives to clam up, for fear that their comments may lead to shareholder lawsuits. This new wariness, this argument goes, might be a subtle but key impediment to new companies' ability to raise capital.
