In essence, the debate pits an information-age drive to give all investors equal access against many companies' desire to conduct private forums with the sophisticated investors who dominate the financial markets. "What we're seeing is a collision between the traditional idea of a quiet period and the pressure being put on the system by technology," said William R. McLucas of the Washington law firm of Wilmer Cutler & Pickering, a former S.E.C. enforcement director. Advocates of more openness say individuals should have a chance to perform exactly the same sniff test on a new stock that big investors do. David L. Menlow, editor of the newsletter IPO Frontline, said television interviews with chief executives after a company comes out of its quiet period, appearances that can often move stock prices, are a clear indication that investors do place importance on how a company's leader looks and sounds. And that, Mr. Menlow said, is evidence they could gather earlier if they had access to the road show. Mr. Menlow says it is not unusual for companies, as Webvan did, to offer nuggets of information that could prove useful to any investor. "Why should the institutions have the advantage?" he said. "I'm incensed the investment banking community has gone unchallenged. It and the S.E.C. have exercised complete control and kept out the media and small investors." But opponents of opening up the road show say the prospect raises two practical considerations. First, individual investors listening to the meetings may not have the sophistication to distinguish salesmanship from salient material. In the prospectus, the risks of the venture are completely laid out, but they typically are not spelled out in a road show. This, in turn, leads to the concern about the possible proliferation of lawsuits. If investors feel misled during a road show by an executive's implication, wink, nod, or other suggestion of success, and the stock plummets, plaintiffs' lawyers could get plenty of extra work. That is why big investors tend to worry that opening up a road show would force executives to stick to the script of the prospectus, and hinder the ability of institutions to get the information they need to make investment decisions. Alfred R. Berkeley, president of the Nasdaq market, who says he has attended several hundred road shows, generally favors broader access. But he said any change had to be incremental, adding, "My concern is that the demand for mouths to open will actually have the effect of causing mouths to close." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: An Internet link to a company earnings call for securites analysts.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: Digital Commerce;
In the Internet rat race, greater value seems to be put on devising the next business plan than on making it work.
body: THE desire to cash out big is not a new motivating force in the technology industry. But what is striking about today's Internet economy is how much of that money lust is focused on selling business plans for their own sake, rather than planning viable businesses. This trend may have already sown the seeds of its own demise. "I call it 'the millennial pause,' " said Richard Miller, a veteran Silicon Valley strategist and investor who is distressed at the frenetic coupling of people with half-baked ideas and those with an overabundance of money to finance them. "It's the industry's saturnalia." In ancient Rome, the seven-day festival honoring the god Saturn took place at the end of each year. Its ostensible purpose was to pause long enough to resynchronize the lunar and solar calendars. But in fact, it was a lengthy debauch during which Romans enthusiastically engaged in all manner of licentious and excessive behavior. What one considers licentious in the networked economy is a matter of personal taste, of course. But excessive -- that is something everyone apparently agrees on these days. "M.B.A.'s aren't going to class anymore; they're taking two-year sabbaticals to write business plans," said Ann Winblad of Hummer Winblad Venture Partners in San Francisco. Her firm has reviewed as many as 1,000 business plans in a single month, and looks at 5,000 to 7,000 of them a year. "Business school has become business-plan school," she said. "Students go there, find a team and start creating a company." Unfortunately, precious few are the next Amazon.com. The overwhelming flood of plans are "products for Wall Street, not real businesses," said Yogen Dalal, a general partner with the Mayfield Fund venture firm in Menlo Park, Calif. "The opportunities we're seeing today are a real disappointment," agreed William Davidow, a 20-year veteran of the venture game and a general partner at Mohr, Davidow Ventures in Menlo Park. "Many companies being founded today don't even have a single product," Mr. Davidow added. "I know a guy on the board of a company where the engineering manager was quitting. The company was public, but the product hadn't shipped yet. The engineer had already vested 1 percent of his stock, and had done the same thing at four companies in a row. He never completed a single project in any of them." Yeah, yeah, so one company hired the wrong guy. O.K., so maybe four companies hired the wrong guy. Cry me a river, right? Who is really hurt? In a market flooded with easy money and profit taking, victims are hard to find. But as Wall Street and individual investors continue their process of reality checking the true worth of Internet companies, some industry executives believe that the flakiness of the work force is only one reason to believe that the entire Internet economy is becoming a giant Ponzi scheme. Certainly the description appears to fit. In today's well-known Internet "business" model, the equation is that some venture capitalists are willing to give, say, $1 for a dot-com's 75 cents of value. A dot-com's first round of venture money might be $1 million. A second round could be $10 million. The final, pre-I.P.O. investment might be $30 million -- then it goes to the public market to be valued at $100 million. A remarkable example of overvaluation is Blue Mountain Arts, the greeting-card Web site with a $1 billion valuation, 10 million users and virtually no revenue. Just as "every success sows the seeds of its own destruction," said Mr. Davidow, the very interconnectedness of the Internet, which created such incredible opportunity, has also created the massive instability in the economy that it has spawned. "The Internet creates vast amounts of 'near-money,' " he said. "Near-money tends to be things that can be translated into money very quickly. Where it used to be that it was very expensive to sell stocks, for example, and it took time to sell them, what the Internet has changed is that stocks are now near-money -- you can sell them very quickly; they're extremely liquid." This change, Mr. Davidow asserted, is one of the reasons Alan Greenspan, the Federal Reserve chairman, is concerned about the tremendous overvaluation of the stock market. "All these institutions had physical constraints on the speed at which money moved through the system," he said. "When that constraint is gone, stock equals money, and the method that you once used to control the money supply is gone, too." Closer to home, the ability of entrepreneurs and investors to pull cash out of companies quickly and with impunity may soon begin to crumple those Internet businesses that can no longer get free money from investors or the public markets. "These companies have voracious, unsustainable cash requirements," Mr. Davidow said. "And their business models are based on cash being available. It's not even a Ponzi scheme, because there's nothing downstream to pay off the investors." And by nature of their interconnections -- Internet businesses are nothing if not linked to each other, by their swapping of advertising "revenue," their reliance on each other to drive each other's businesses, their critical need for cash to acquire customers -- a few crumpled companies could quickly turn into a big tumble for the successful businesses in the networked economy. As one investor put it, "The point is that they will pull down the good companies with them." So much for the millennial pause. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title:
Ideas & Trends;
A Cyberspat Makes History
body: THIS month marks the 30th anniversary of the Arpanet, the Internet's predecessor. Then again, maybe it doesn't. The University of California at Los Angeles was ground zero for the Arpanet. Then again, maybe it wasn't. This anniversary of the Internet has been a particularly contentious one. Vice President Al Gore's misstatement to CNN last spring that he "took the initiative" in inventing the whole thing was roundly ridiculed by anyone with an inkling of the network's true origins. But in recent months, several more genuine contenders have stepped forward to stake a claim to this or that invaluable piece of the invention, giving rise to a number of public spats. As barbs fly and longstanding friendships disintegrate, figuring out just who did what when is more difficult than ever. I know about this problem at close range. In 1993, when I began researching a history of the Arpanet, the story seemed a relatively straightforward one. I scoffed when one of the Net's many fathers said to me one day: "Why are you even trying to write a history? No matter what you write, it won't be the real story." While that may be true of history in general, anyone who tries to write the real story of the Internet right now will encounter a welter of contradictory material. Now graying, the scientists who took part in building the Net are busier than they ever were, not inventing new technologies but telling their side of the story to reporters, putting up time lines and history pages on their Web sites and shooting off email messages. The goal, of course, is not to get rich but to secure a spot in history. "What we're witnessing is a case of history getting revised in real time," said Peter J. Denning, a computer science professor at George Mason University who took part in the development of the Internet but has remained a largely silent observer. "We are watching the process of myth-making as it happens around us. Eventually certain people will emerge out of the myth and lots of what's been accomplished will be ascribed to them, even if they didn't do it personally." The revision of history while the principal participants are still alive is not new. The author Stephen E. Ambrose said he grappled with the phenomenon recently when writing about the construction of the transcontinental railroad 130 years ago, an immense project in which dozens of luminaries like Senator Thomas Hart Benton and the industrialist Leland Stanford had a hand. "You should see how those people fought each other," he said. "They would write letters to The Railroad Journal, or Horace Greeley's paper, saying, 'I'm the one who first suggested it's possible to build a railroad across the country.' " To try to sort it out for himself, Mr. Ambrose relied on a well-established body of literature. His advantage was not having to fend off calls from Leland Stanford's p.r. agency. Nevertheless, he found no consensus. "I threw up my hands," Mr. Ambrose said. "Don't ask me who first thought of it. I could give you a lot of entries into the race." Alan Brinkley, a professor of history at Columbia University, says it's a common problem. "History is constantly being revised in informal ways, in popular culture and in private conversations," he said. "There are always many different versions." What's new, Professor Brinkley said, isn't the revisionism as much as the presence of the Internet as a revisionist's tool, providing an easy way to spread one's own version of events. The latter-day equivalent of fighting it out in letters to the editor is to spam the world with your take, using the Internet as an amplifier. Whoever is fastest with the send button, whoever has the lengthier "cc" list, is most likely to rise above the din. Scholars are wondering if the Internet will make the process of historical inquiry more difficult. "The word definitiveness comes to mind," said Neil M. Postman, a professor of communications at newyork University. "Print is more definitive. Books preserve information. The Internet moves information. So with information on the move, appearing and disappearing, and without gatekeepers, it diminishes the credibility of claims." Not only do electronic versions of events have a way of drifting more quickly and easily into the public's consciousness, but they underscore how quickly other information can disappear from the record. In the case of the continuing paternity battle over the Internet, Professor Denning pointed to 1989, a more subdued time in the Net's evolution, when a symposium commemorating the 20th anniversary of the Arpanet took place at U.C.L.A. Back then, the Net was still relatively obscure and there was nothing much at stake. In attendance were the very men slugging it out today. A transcript of the event has them lavishing one another with praise and credit. But that transcript exists not on the Internet but on paper tucked away in the archive of the Charles Babbage Institute of Computer History in Minnesota. Whatever remaining solidarity there might be among the Net's founding fathers is increasingly strained. There is one contingent that stands by early September, when the network got its first node, as the birth date of the Arpanet. Others continue to claim it was late October, when the first electronic bits passed from U.C.L.A. to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute, about 300 miles to the north. Some profess to have invented packet-switching, the data transmission technology that made it all possible. Still others claim to have had the idea for a network in the first place. FOR his part, Professor Brinkley does not believe the Internet will hamper historians' ability to gather facts. "I don't think the Internet has reinvented history," he said. "It's just expanding and complicating it a bit. History is always contested, and over time frivolous claims get discounted, and more serious claims get more attention, and eventually there's a consensus around a particular answer. You won't have the open-ended disputes that are going on today." Time may also slow the rush for recognition. Every so often, the Internet is not glorified but blamed -- for inflation, for the slump in dot-com stocks, for widening the gap between haves and have-nots. "When the true dark side comes along, you won't see people scrambling to take credit for that part," Professor Denning said. "It will be, 'That's not the part I had anything to do with.' " Maybe they'll say that was Al Gore's part. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Cartoon (Nancy Carpenter)

title:
INVESTING;
How to Play The Internet, With Apple - Correction Appended
body: MAYBE it's time to look at Apple Computer Inc. in a different light: as an Internet stock. As Apple points out in advertising for new versions of its popular iMac computer, 90 percent of iMac owners are connected to the Internet -- an astonishingly high share -- and most of them got wired the first day they owned the machine. So maybe Apple is an Internet platform company. Consider also that the latest versions of the Macintosh operating system contain a metasearch tool called Sherlock that links to powerful Web engines, like Alta Vista, Infoseek, Lycos and Hotbot, and prioritizes their results. In MAC OS 9, Apple's latest version of the operating system, which shipped last week, the improved Sherlock 2 channels make searching easier and more powerful by grouping similar sources together and returning more relevant results. It also adds a shopping channel. So maybe Apple is an Internet portal company. Add the vast number of sites running video using Apple's Quicktime technology, or created on Macintoshes running Web-designing tools like Adobe's InDesign and you have a liberal sprinkling of Internet pixie dust. But even with the 80.6 percent run-up in Apple shares this year, to $73.9375 on Friday, they still trade at a discount to those of other personal computer manufacturers like Dell Computer or Gateway, let alone to a pure Internet play like Yahoo. Apple has a price-to-earnings ratio of 23.2, versus 53.9 for Dell and 45.1 for Gateway. (Yahoo's market capitalization is over 100 times trailing 12-month revenues; its P/E ratio is not considered meaningful, because its net income is so small.) With numbers like these, some analysts say there is still strong potential for an increase in Apple's stock price. Apple has been on a roll since its co-founder, Steven P. Jobs, returned in 1997 as interim chief executive. The successful launch of the iMac a little over a year ago was followed by splashy rollouts of the G3 desktop machines, new G3 Powerbooks and the iMac's portable cousin, the iBook. Just when it seemed that Mr. Jobs and company could walk on water, they stumbled in the third quarter, announcing a shortfall in earnings early because of inadequate chip supplies for the new G4 desktops and flat-panel displays for the iBook. Unable to get the fastest versions of the G4 microprocessor in time, Apple cut the speed rating of the new G4 machines by 50 megahertz without cutting prices. Then, in a move that surely tested even devoted Mac loyalists, the company canceled existing orders, only to reinstate them later for anyone who ordered before Oct. 13. Apple managed to beat analysts' revised estimates, as well as its own predictions, by 6 cents a share for the fourth fiscal quarter and predicted a strong December quarter. Of 20 analysts polled by First Call/Thomson Financial, which tracks company earnings, six rated Apple as a strong buy, six as a buy, seven as a hold and one as a weak sell. Lou Mazzucchelli of Gerard Klauer Mattison in newyork is among those calling it a strong buy, with a 12-month price target of $90. "There's more growth to come," Mr. Mazzucchelli said, "and if you look at how much negative perception there is still in the market, that shows you the potential." Apple's prospects as an Internet play are an added bonus for what is already a robust growth story, said Mr. Mazzucchelli, noting that the company received orders for 150,000 iMacs in the three months after its introduction, but booked 250,000 orders for the new models in just one week. "Apple's not talking about it," he said, "but should they find a way to leverage their immense Internet installed base, which is growing at a huge rate, you can make a case for at least part of the business to be valued as an Internet company." Apple executives have been coy about possible Internet service offerings, saying only that they have nothing to say now. But other experts are bullish on Apple's Internet prospects. "I don't think Apple can reinvent itself, but I do think it can rejuvenate itself via the Web," said Geoffrey Moore, president of the Chasm Group, a Silicon Valley consultant. "Moreover, as the market migrates from product to service, Microsoft isn't getting it.  Steve might get it," he said, referring to Mr. Jobs and adding that a truly distinctive Apple Internet service could prove a winner if it attracts enough Mac users. "How much money would Mac loyalists part with? I think quite a lot, if the experience were truly Mac-like," he added. FOR now, Apple is busy adding loyalists through the iMac. The company is establishing the iMac as the slickest platform for surfing the Web, much as the original Macintosh was the clear choice for desktop publishing or today's Wintel machines are the standard for running Microsoft Office. Apple has established its Internet status "in very subtle ways," said Daniel Kunstler, an analyst with J. P. Morgan, who also has a 12-month target of $90 on the stock. "They haven't beat you over the head saying 'we're an Internet company,' " he said. "They've done it with their platform, and, suddenly, with the launch of the new iMacs, it dawns on everybody. Their claims are not overstated and they're really starting to pan out." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article last Sunday about investing in Apple Computer for its Internet potential misidentified an Adobe Systems software program that contributed to the popularity of Apple's Macintosh computers among designers of Web sites. It is GoLive, not InDesign. Correction-Date: October 31, 1999, Sunday Graphic   Drawing (Robert Zammarchi)  Graph: "Moving Up" Shares of Apple Computer have doubled over the past year. They jumped sharply earlier this month after the company beat analysts' estimates for third-quarter earnings. The graph shows Apple's net income and the Apple share price since October 1998. (Source: Bloomberg Financial Markets)

title: Putting the W's in www
body: Weaving the Web The Original Design and Ultimate Destiny of the World Wide Web by Its Inventor. By Tim Berners-Lee with Mark Fischetti. 226 pp. San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco. $26. Tim Berners-Lee, the 44-year-old English physicist who created the World Wide Web, is precisely the kind of hero that a relatively simple invention with profound social and economic consequences should lay claim to. He is not just creative but democratic, diplomatic, polite and generous with credit and praise. Those traits are what make his book, "Weaving the Web" -- a dry but important account of how, when, where and why he cooked up the Web -- well worth reading. It is a book written by the ultimate good guy. The Web, it should be pointed out, is not the Internet, which began 30 years ago as a Government-sponsored network research project and is now a vast matrix of communications lines and routing hardware and software used by 200 million people around the world. Berners-Lee started the World Wide Web as a set of protocols for transferring, linking and addressing documents to send over the Net. Without the global reach and open technical standards of the Internet, the Web could never have proliferated as it did. The story of the Web starts in 1980, when Berners-Lee, a young consulting physicist at the CERN physics laboratory near Geneva, grew frustrated with existing methods for finding and transferring information. So he wrote a program called Enquire, after "Enquire Within Upon Everything," the title of a book of Victorian advice that fascinated him as a child. He wrote Enquire as a series of links for keeping track of information on one CERN computer. Early in his story, Berners-Lee gives a glimpse into his views of how the mind works, which in turn informed the Web. "I liked the idea that a piece of information is really defined only by what it's related to, and how it's related," he writes. "There really is little else to meaning. The structure is everything. . . . The brain has no knowledge until connections are made between neurons. All that we know, all that we are, comes from the way our neurons are connected." When his consulting contract ended, Berners-Lee left CERN and gave the disk containing the Enquire code to someone there, explaining that it was a program for keeping track of information. Apparently, Enquire didn't make much of an impression, as that eight-inch disk got pushed to the back of a drawer and eventually disappeared altogether. That could have been the end of the story if Berners-Lee had not returned to CERN a few years later. By 1988 he was again noodling over a way to approach documents the way the brain works -- associatively. This time, he based his program on hypertext, a nonsequential layering of information whereby words and phrases in a document can be highlighted to let readers skip from one source to another rather than read in a traditional linear fashion. In Berners-Lee's scheme, each document would have an address by which it could be referenced. Berners-Lee wrote the code for a trio of protocols, and named them HTTP (hypertext transfer protocol), HTML (hypertext markup language) and U.D.I.'s (universal document identifiers). U.D.I.'s eventually became U.R.L.'s, or uniform resource locators, the abbreviation that most of today's Web users recognize. For the name of the system itself, he toyed with a few ideas. First came Mine of Information, or MOI, which seemed too egocentric. Then came the Information Mine, or TIM, which was even worse. Finally, he settled on World Wide Web. The first Web server (a computer that holds Web pages) was up and running on Berners-Lee's own desktop computer at CERN by Christmas Day 1990. He also wrote the original browser, a program for gaining access to and reading information on the Web. Using the HTTP protocol, computer scientists around the world began making the Internet easier to navigate by inventing point-and-click browsers. One browser in particular, called Mosaic, created in 1993 at the University of Illinois, would help popularize the Web, and therefore the Net, as no software tool had yet done. Berners-Lee goes out of his way to make it clear that he was not the only one to have done all the work. He credits a colleague at CERN, Robert Cailliau, not only with helping to champion the Web cause when others were indifferent but with much of the technical work as well. Dozens of others get mentioned, too, which makes the book seem at times like an especially tedious Academy Award acceptance. At other times, however, the story is fascinating. Berners-Lee tells of a 1993 meeting with computer scientists at the University of Illinois. Present at the meeting was a student named Marc Andreessen, who together with a University of Illinois staff member named Eric Bina had created Mosaic. From the beginning, Berners-Lee sensed that Andreessen was approaching the meeting as if it were a poker game. Unlike meetings with other browser developers, this one had "a strange tension to it," he writes. The group in Illinois seemed intent on renaming the Web as Mosaic. This irked Berners-Lee considerably. Andreessen, of course, went on to commercialize Mosaic as Netscape and become one of the Internet's first young multimillionaires. A lingering disdain for Andreessen and his unwavering focus on Mosaic, as if it were the Web itself, is a thread throughout that brief section of the book. Unlike Andreessen and others who decided to cash in on their Internet-related inventions, Berners-Lee took the high road. In 1994 he moved to M.I.T.'s Laboratory for Computer Science and started the World Wide Web Consortium, a group whose mission is to insure that the foundation of open standards he laid for sharing and identifying information endures. Berners-Lee devotes much of the latter part of the book to describing his hopes for continued open standards as the Web becomes increasingly commercialized. At times "Weaving the Web," written with Mark Fischetti, is plodding and reads a bit like an interview transcript. At other times it's sloppy. Some names are misspelled, and at one point Berners-Lee himself seems to confuse the Internet and the Web. Still, nothing should detract from the role Berners-Lee played in taking a relatively obscure computer network and making it into a mass medium. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
The Nation: Encyclopedia Green;
The High Road at a High Cost
body: AS Internet users stampeded to visit the Encyclopaedia Britannica's sleek new Web site last week, the venerable intellectual icon was nearly road kill on the information highway. Britannica.com is busily adding computers to handle the more than 10 million people who tried to peruse its site. But the company also faces a much bigger question: Will its vaunted reputation for rigor be compromised by its decision to give free access to its vast stores of knowledge? In the first half of this decade, annual sales of the familiarly bound volumes plummeted by roughly 80 percent as Britannica miscalculated, refusing to produce a cheap, computer-based version of the storied publication that most adults in America used in school and from which many cribbed at least one science report. While Britannica was charging up to $2,000 for a 32-volume edition of books, Microsoft was often giving away CD-Rom versions of its Encarta encyclopedia to buyers of new computers. When Britannica produced a CD-Rom, it was $1,000 initially versus $50 retail for Encarta. And when Britannica first joined the World Wide Web, it did so with a subscription-only site, charging a fee for access in a medium where nearly all information sites are free. Now, Britannica.com has joined the Internet mainstream with a free site that is supported by the sale of advertising and by links to an array of products for sale. But whether the new economics of the Internet age will allow the Encyclopaedia Britannica to support itself as a living document, constantly updated and renewed, is unclear. "They certainly face an uphill battle," said Thomas S. Wurster, a vice president at the Boston Consulting Group and co-author, with Philip Evans, of "Blown to Bits: How the New Economics of Information Transforms Strategy" (Harvard Business School Press), which is expected to be published next year. "Britannica was always thought of as a trusted adviser, known for its rigorous quality," Mr. Wurster said. "But on the Internet, others, like Yahoo, have a better identity with core users. Because Britannica will no longer be getting any revenues from their content, their success will very much depend on whether they can attract eyeballs to the site," and therefore be able to charge advertisers higher rates. THE fact that the main competitors for Britannica.com are not other encyclopedias but on-line services like Yahoo and America Online is not lost on Britannica. By offering free content, it removes any advantage gained by serviceable but generally lesser products like Encarta, based on the old Funk & Wagnalls encyclopedia. And Britannica.com includes not only its entire encyclopedia but also articles from magazines like The Economist, Esquire and Sports Illustrated, news links, stock quotes, an Internet search service, links to Barnes & Noble's on-line bookstore and other commercial sites. "Our intention is to be the premier knowledge destination site," said Kent Devereaux, senior vice president for product development and editorial at Britannica.com, based in Chicago. "We have found that the entire definition of the encyclopedia has to change. If that puts us into the same space as Yahoo and America Online, so be it." Working to insure that its intellectual edge is not lost will be, in addition to the traditional team of Britannica researchers, a second group of content specialists. Their focus will be preparing weekly updates on current events -- a vast improvement over the biennial updates of the old print version -- plus taking advantage of the Internet's audio and video capabilities. While adding researchers, it has eliminated the door-to-door sales staff that accounted for most of the cost of the printed version. The overwhelming response to Tuesday's unveiling of Britannica.com showed that the name Britannica retains its cachet in this country and around the world. If Britannica.com can continue to attract a passionate audience among the information generation, it will serve as a stellar example of how companies that are late adapting to new technologies can end up on top -- if they have a superior product. But such a brainy product must still compete in a medium based on entertainment and commerce as much as information. And just think what might have been: Even if Britannica.com eventually completes an initial public offering of stock, it will probably never catch up to Yahoo's $46 billion market value. For succor, Britannica.com might consult its own Web site. The Encyclopaedia Britannica has no entry for "business failure." But type in those words on its search engine and a visitor will be offered the chance to buy a potentially helpful book -- titled "When Things Go Wrong: Organizational Failures & Breakdowns." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Cartoon: A cartoon of the encyclopedia's printer and editor, Andrew Bell and William Smellie. (From "The Great E.B." by Herman Kogan University of Chicago Press, 1958 )

title: Amazon Sues Big Bookseller Over System For Shopping
body: Amazon.com has filed suit against its rival Internet book and music seller Barnesandnoble.com, accusing it of illegally copying Amazon's patented checkout system and demanding an immediate end to its use. The suit, filed on Thursday night in Federal District Court in Seattle, is the latest chapter in a storied and sometimes litigious rivalry. But if Amazon.com is successful in the suit, it could have broad ramifications for the development of E-commerce. Retailers that use variations of the popular "one click" checkout method, which allows customers to make repeat purchases with one click of the mouse instead of having to fill out credit card and billing information with each shopping trip, could be forced to desist or pay a licensing fee to Amazon.com. Amazon stopped short of saying that was its goal, but the possibility was not lost on it. "This litigation just goes to Barnesand noble.com," said an Amazon spokesman, Bill Curry. "But we clearly have a patent, and this is a sign we want to protect our intellectual property." Amazon started using one-click technology in September 1997, but did not receive a patent for it until Sept. 28 this year. Barnesandnoble has offered Express Lane, its one-click checkout, since early 1998. "The one-click feature is one of Amazon.com's signature strategies for differentiating itself from the competition and building loyalty among its customers," Amazon wrote in its complaint . Customer loyalty is especially important to Amazon now, as the company is expanding well beyond its original book format to electronics and toys and all manner of items in hopes of becoming the Internet shopper's primary destination. Arguing that the infringement is causing irreparable harm, Amazon is seeking monetary damages and an immediate injunction preventing Barnesandnoble.com from using Express Lane. Barnesandnoble.com called the lawsuit an attempt to retaliate for its growing popularity. "We believe the allegations to be completely without merit, and we will vigorously defend our position," said a spokesman, Gus Carlson. "Traffic to our Web site was up substantially today because of the publicity. We thank our competitor for the incremental sales." The two mammoths of book-selling have a colorful history of feuding that includes both threatened and actual litigation. In 1997, Barnes & Noble Inc., the parent company of barnesandnoble.com, filed suit against Amazon claiming that its slogan, World's Largest Bookstore, was false advertising. The suit was settled out of court with neither side paying damages. In turn, Amazon made threatening noises when Barnes & Noble tried to acquire the distributor Ingram Book Group. The deal was canceled, and litigation was never initiated. Lawyers and patent experts differ on the strength of Amazon's case, but agree that the effect could be far reaching. "If this patent did hold up, it could put a damper on Internet growth," said Ken Cassar, a digital commerce analyst at Jupiter Communications, an Internet research firm. He estimates that half the retail sites on the Web have an "automated wallet" -- a process that stores billing and address data for repeat customers. E-commerce companies are increasingly turning to patents to protect their business interests. Last week, Priceline.com filed a patent infringement lawsuit against Microsoft saying that the software giant's Expedia.com site had copied its model of allowing customers to bid for plane tickets and hotel rooms. "This is just the first of what will be a bloody round of patent wars on the Web," predicted David Kline, author of "Rembrandts in the Attic: Unlocking the Hidden Value of Patents," to be published by Harvard Business School Press in January. Patents covering software or programming related to Web sites are the fastest-growing sector at the unitedstates Patent office, said Robert Greene Sterne, of the Washington-based intellectual property law firm of Sterne, Kessler, Goldstein & Fox. He said the suits might over the long term give a real advantage to Web companies that were the first to build technological applications that everyone else wants. "The early-comers' commerce to the space may be able to generate a lot of profits through licensing to later-comers," he said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: On Web, Models Auction Their Eggs to Bidders for Beautiful Children
body: To the horror and disgust of mainstream infertility groups, a longtime fashion photographer has begun offering up models as egg donors to the highest bidders, auctioning their ova via the Internet to would-be parents willing to pay up to $150,000 in hopes of having a beautiful child. "It screams of unethical behavior," Sean Tipton, spokesman for the American Society of Reproductive Medicine, said of the Web site, www.ronsangels.com, which was already up on the Web today and is to be officially started on Monday. Infertility specialists deplored the Web site as exactly the kind of "commodification" of human egg donations that they hope to avoid. Just this spring, signs of movement in that direction came when a couple advertised that they would pay $50,000 for an egg from a tall, athletic, top-college student with high College Board test scores. The photographer, Ron Harris, justifies the egg auction as a natural outgrowth of the urge that people have to mate with genetically superior people and produce babies with evolutionary advantages. That is particularly true, he said, in a society whose "celebrity culture" worships beauty. "If you could increase the chance of reproducing beautiful children, and thus giving them an advantage in society, would you?" he asks on the Web site. In a telephone interview today, Mr. Harris, 66, described the objections to egg auctions as politically correct. Since not all women are the same, he said, what they are paid for their eggs "should be a price that floats based on perceived value." Mr. Harris's melding of Darwin-based eugenics, Playboy-style sensibilities and eBay-type commerce struck some infertility specialists as the most worrying sign yet of where the partly unregulated field of assisted reproduction may be going. Shelley Smith, director of the Egg Donor Program, a center in Los Angeles, said: "It's frightening and horrible, and the worst part for me is to think there might be something worse still beyond our imagination. It seems to escalate, and ever since the Internet it seems to snowball more rapidly, this depersonalization of people and selling of eggs." Ms. Smith and others said that as far as they knew, Mr. Harris's Web site was legal. Federal law forbids trafficking in human organs but not in sperm and eggs, they said. Research by Mr. Harris's lawyers reached the same conclusion. The Web site has already received a serious bid of $42,000 from a couple who found it through a search engine, Mr. Harris said. The models receive the full bid price, and Rons Angels takes a commission of an additional 20 percent. The bid price includes no medical costs, the site specifies, and the site takes on no medical functions. But it does list scores of specialists who might be willing to perform the procedure once an agreement is reached. Confidentiality is strongly guarded in such cases. In the case concerning the $50,000 offer, the brokers who arranged it say they are not at liberty to divulge how it turned out. Mr. Harris said the models could not be interviewed today because of an exclusive agreement with another newspaper until the site is opened on Monday. But each of the eight models whose photographs appear on the Web site offered their reasons in print for selling their eggs: They ranged from "to not be dependent on a man" and "to support my 4-year-old son" to "I want to help others." Several models were from other countries, and one said her goal was "to move to the U.S.A." Mr. Harris is probably best known as the creator of Aerobicise, a best-selling 1980's exercise video featuring models in leotards, and "The 20 Minute Workout," a television show with similar appeal. He has been a fashion photographer for 40 years, he said, and also done some television directing for Playboy. The use of donor eggs by infertile couples remains relatively uncommon. Resolve, the National Infertility Association, says that about 1,700 babies were born from procedures involving egg donation in 1996. Those numbers have been growing only slightly since then, experts say. But the compensation for egg donors is a burning issue these days, including a discussion by the ethics panel of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and a meeting here this week of Resolve, which brings together patients and practitioners to support and educate infertile people. Members of both organizations said they had recently discussed Mr. Harris's Web site, which has been posted in various forms for about two months, as an example of the kind of thing that has to be stopped. "Things like this need immediate attention -- the thing is, where is the appropriate avenue?" asked Diane Aronson, the executive director of Resolve. It is routine for egg donation centers to offer would-be parents an extensive profile of the egg donor, including photographs and descriptions of their talents and personalities. Several post donor catalogues online, and West Coast centers report a surfeit of donors, though they say there is a shortage in the East, particularly in newyork City. But mainstream infertility groups deem it acceptable only to choose an egg donor based on her traits and then compensate her -- usually from $2,500 to $5,000 -- for her time, inconvenience and discomfort. (Donors receive hormone shots to hyper-stimulate their ovaries, and have a dozen or so eggs removed with a needle.) The groups tend to frown on anything that seems like actually trying to buy extra-nice genes -- though the line does seem blurred. "Basically, what it comes down to is we're selling human tissue, and somewhere along the line we've got to bring ethics into it," said Karen Synesiou, director of Egg Donation, a private company in Beverly Hills, Calif. "I don't know where the line is because I want to balance the needs of the infertile community versus society at large, but I think a bidding game crosses the line." In response, Mr. Harris said it was "very unfair to put a limit on a girl's ability to make money." And seeking to pay all women the same, he added, "is like saying all women are the same, which is not the case." While trafficking in eggs is not illegal, it is distasteful enough that eBay, the giant auction Web site, specifically bans offering eggs for sale, as well as the auctioning of sperm and other human body parts (though hair is allowed). Ms. Synesiou and others said that in addition to other concerns, mating with a model might bring tremendous disappointment to some couples if the genetic dice rolled the wrong way and their child turned out to be unattractive. And it would be very hard for the child who failed such expectations. "It's the same as couples who go to the genius sperm banks," Ms. Synesiou said. "How will the child feel when the child's no genius?" Nancy Etcoff, author of "Survival of the Prettiest: the Science of Beauty," (Doubleday, 1999) noted that acquired characteristics like dyed blond hair and lips made plump by collagen are not inherited. Parents' quest for beautiful genes resonates powerfully with a growing body of academic research into the possible evolutionary reasons that certain physical characteristics, from hip-to-waist ratio to symmetrical faces, are considered desirable and beautiful. Mr. Harris, Dr. Etcoff noted, seemed to "put his own spin" on such evolutionary research. Indeed, in an editorial on the Web site, Mr. Harris quotes a study that looked at personal ads to determine the "market value" of mate choice, and found that men wanted youth, beauty and social skills, while women who had those qualities wanted rich, good-looking and young men. "This is Darwin's natural selection at its very best," Mr. Harris wrote. "The highest bidder gets youth and beauty." A bit later, he wrote: "It is not my intention to suggest we make a super society of only beautiful people. This site simply mirrors our current society, in that beauty always goes to the highest bidder." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The Web site Rons Angels, which offers models as egg donors to would-be parents who bid the highest so they can have a beautiful child.

title: Big Consultants Woo Employees by Offering a Piece of the Action
body: Help wanted: Prestigious firms, already offering six-figure salaries, will now let employees take up to two months off each year or get special access to Internet investment funds. This, in essence, is what the world's top consultants are resorting to as they battle the tide of E-commerce that is stealing many of their best job candidates and employees from college campuses and even the corner office. In a range of initiatives just under way, the consulting firms are trying to hire and keep people by emphasizing the advantages of a secure job while also trying to copy some of the perquisites of a start-up. McKinsey & Company, which for years has had its pick of business school graduates, has decided to offer its associates access to Internet start-up investments intended to mimic the growth potential of stock in a new business. Among other options, the plan could include letting the junior consultants buy stakes in investment funds, possibly including venture-capital funds, that would not normally be open to them. Or, they might buy stakes in a pool of McKinsey clients that have given the firm equity instead of paying cash, said Anil Kumar, a McKinsey director and one of the leaders of @McKinsey, its electronic-commerce practice. Details will be made final within two months, he said. Mercer Management Consulting is telling consultants this week about new work rules under which Mercer will help them design a new business plan, and even leave the firm to carry it out. The rules will also allow consultants to take up to two months a year to do anything from enrolling in a class to climbing mountains. "Historically, it's been all the major consulting firms and all the major investment banks going after the best and brightest," said James Down, vice chairman of Mercer. Now that E-commerce firms have joined the fray, Mr. Down said, "we certainly have lost some very good people." Indeed, turnover rates have risen at many big consultants, including McKinsey. In September, George T. Shaheen, chief executive of Andersen Consulting, the industry's largest firm, quit to head up the tiny Webvan Group, an Internet grocery business in Foster City, Calif. At the same time, the firms are having to work much harder to woo M.B.A.'s who consider their heroes to be the Amazon.com founder Jeffrey P. Bezos or the Yahoo co-founder Jerry Yang more than titans like Jack Welch or Warren E. Buffett. "It almost seems like it's the new gold rush," said Douglas McCracken, managing director for the Americas at Deloitte Consulting, which this week began an ad campaign to promote its month-old E-business unit, "where everyone is going to dot.coms, expecting to get stock and get rich." The new initiatives indicate just how attractive the start-ups have become. Consultants for years have prided themselves on their workaholic schedules, boasting about 14-hour days in far-away cities. Now, to keep employees happy, Mercer is telling people to take long vacations, with benefits but not pay, if they feel like it. In addition, Mercer is saying to employees who are interested in one day starting their own company that it will help them plan, put them in touch with venture capital firms, and perhaps even invest in the business. The firm will also set up some consultants with "externships" -- one- or two-year assignments in outside companies from which they conceivably might not return. "It's a big, big change," Mr. Down said. McKinsey had long been wary of accepting equity in any of its clients, lest it find itself so tied to one company that a rival would not hire the firm for a different assignment. Even as Bain & Company made big profits after starting Bain Capital, a private equity firm, in 1984, McKinsey partners shunned such a move, concerned it might call their independence into question. Bain says its two units do not share information. But for the last 18 months, McKinsey has accepted small stakes in start-up companies that could not otherwise afford its fees. That gives it entry to the Internet world and makes it more attractive to M.B.A.'s, Mr. Kumar said. Now the firm is considering allowing its own associates to invest blindly in those equity stakes. "We don't want the best talent to feel they don't have a vehicle to join in this wealth creation," Mr. Kumar said. "For McKinsey, these are very radical moves," said Susan Webber, a former McKinsey consultant and now president of Aurora Advisers. The investments, even if blind, raise the prospect of conflict-of-interest problems because consultants would assume that the firm, and perhaps even themselves individually, owned a piece of any start-up for which it had done work. That, in turn, could make rival start-ups uncomfortable about hiring McKinsey. Mr. Kumar said McKinsey was taking only small stakes in other companies and that it planned to sell its shares as soon as it was financially prudent to do so. He also said consultants would not know which start-ups they owned a piece of, adding, "We want to adhere to the highest standards of professionalism." Virtually all the other major consulting firms also accept equity stakes from small companies that lack the cash to pay fees. The firms hope that having a significant E-commerce practice will allow them to hire and keep people who are interested in technology and may one day decide to join a start-up. Lisa Overton is the kind of candidate the firms are hoping to woo. A 28-year-old student at Columbia Business School, she worked for a high-technology investment firm before going back to school and then spent last summer at an Internet company. Now she is applying to Bain and McKinsey, while also trying to start her own E-commerce business and talking to other start-ups, she said. "It was always understood that the best students would want to go to consulting, and there was no serious competitive industry," Ms. Overton said. Today, however, "everyone is getting completely intoxicated" thinking about the Internet, she said. The trend is particularly evident at Harvard Business School, where a graduating class of 800 once included some 300 consultants. In 1996, 35 percent of M.B.A.'s took such a job, compared with 16 percent who went into high technology or venture capital, the school said. Last spring, the portion going into the new fields doubled, to 32 percent, while the share of consultants dipped to 29 percent. Of course, the recruiting and retention battles should be kept in perspective. Consulting is still the most popular job for graduates of the top graduate business school programs, and the firms are growing, causing them to hire more people than in previous years. Attrition "has been rising, and it's related to E-commerce," Mr. Down of Mercer said. "But we're not devastated or panicking."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Big Day Looms In Stock Offer By DeveloperOf Optic Links
body: When Cisco Systems Inc. agreed to acquire the Cerent Corporation in August for almost $7 billion, many everyday investors had a common reaction: What is Cerent? They may well have a similar feeling today because another small company, little known beyond Wall Street and the tightly knit communications fraternity, Sycamore Networks Inc., appears set to make a big financial wave, only this time investors will at least have a chance to catch it. Sycamore is expected to raise more than $280 million in an initial public offering today. Last night, the issue was priced at $38 a share, which would give the company a market value of about $3 billion. It is possible, however, that by the end of today Sycamore's value will surpass even the price paid for Cerent. Anticipation surrounding Sycamore's offering has been mounting on Wall Street for weeks because the company is perhaps the leading member of a new breed of companies, including Cerent, that are developing the next generation of optical networking technology. It is also the first to offer stock to the public. The explosion in demand for data communications generally and for Internet services specifically has required old-line communications carriers to retool and expand their networks and has prompted new carriers to design their networks for data from the ground up. After the development of suitable optical fibers in the 1970's, initially by Corning Inc., the major long-distance carriers deployed fiber optic transmission systems in the 1980's to replace older copper-wire systems, largely as a way to cut costs. As companies like the Nortel Networks Corporation of Canada and Fujitsu of Japan developed ways to transmit more and more pulses a second, the Ciena Corporation, which went public in 1997, helped lead perhaps the biggest qualitative leap in optical technology in two decades: transmitting multiple wavelengths, or colors, of light simultaneously over a single fiber. Today, the dominant optical communications technology is known as Sonet, for synchronous optical network, and though the latest Sonet networks can transmit billions of bits of digital information a second, they are inflexible in some ways. While optical technology has been widely used to transmit large amounts of data from one point to another, the network intelligence that determines what goes where and that creates services that people actually use has remained stubbornly in the domain of semiconductors and copper wires. Not coincidentally, the new breed of optical communications companies has come along to help change that just as the big communications carriers realize that the data explosion requires them to revamp their networks. "There really is a connection between what investors read about the Internet and the growth and opportunity for these optical companies," said Mary Henry, a communications equipment analyst for Goldman, Sachs. "It's really the explosion of data traffic driven by the Internet that requires this migration to optical technology." Most consumers now think about network bottlenecks in terms of what is often called "the last mile," referring to the slow data links to most unitedstates homes. But as more consumers get high-speed access to cyberspace through cable modems, the high-speed phone line connections known as digital subscriber lines, or perhaps wireless links, that will place additional demands on core communications networks. "The stone wall is an access problem today, like you and I not being able to get access at the speeds you want," said Frank Dzubeck, president of Communications Network Architects, a networking analysis and consulting firm in Washington. "When we get it from D.S.L. or cable modems, it pushes the stone wall back into the network. If you can't make the developments to handle that, you're left with the same problem." Among those developments are new ways to add and remove traffic from traditional Sonet fiber optic systems more efficiently, technologies that could allow future networks to be designed in ways that are more flexible than the somewhat rigid ring configurations required by Sonet and, eventually, communications switches that operate totally optically. The roster of companies trying to develop these technologies is well known to venture capitalists and to the bigger communications companies like Lucent, Nortel, Cisco and Ciena that have been acquiring their peers, but to few people outside the industry. In addition to Sycamore, based in Chelmsford, Mass., the roster includes Astral Point, Chromatis, Corvis, Optical Networks Inc., Qtera and Tellium. "At the basic technology level, the challenge is: Can you get the basic product done, in a quick time to market and hit your price point?" said Richard W. Barcus, Tellium's president. "The second layer of accomplishment is: Can you establish relationships with the customers, the service providers, and can you articulate the value of your products to help them solve their problems?" As Sycamore articulates its value to both customers and investors, its hurdle has been made much lower by the pedigree of its top executives, Desh Deshpande and Daniel E. Smith. Mr. Deshpande and Mr. Smith were the top two executives at the Cascade Communications Corporation before that company was acquired by Ascend Communications Inc. in 1997 for $3.7 billion. Cascade's products proved critical to Ascend and were perhaps the main reason Ascend was subsequently acquired by Lucent for $20 billion. Citing "quiet period" regulations related to its stock offering, Sycamore declined to comment. The company hopes to complete its initial product line by releasing a fully optical switch in the first half of next year and appears close to announcing an agreement with Siemens of Germany under which Siemens will help distribute Sycamore's products internationally, according to executives close to the companies. Sycamore's two customers so far are Williams Communications Group Inc. of Tulsa, Okla., and Millennium Optical Networks Inc., a small local communications company in newyork.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: What's in a Web Address? Maybe a Lawsuit
body: Executives of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company have been boasting this week about their new on-line stock trading service and the head start they got on their competitors on Wall Street. But when it came to the Internet address they desired, somebody got a jump on them. Depending on who is telling the story, that somebody is either a 17-year-old schoolboy who created a Web site to share his passion for mountain-bike racing, or an opportunistic "cybersquatter" who registered dozens of Internet addresses in a scheme to exact ransoms from big-name corporations. Typing in the domain name, or Web address, that Morgan Stanley coveted takes a Web surfer not to its electronic brokerage but instead to what appears to be a site dedicated to mountain biking. It carries a photo of a helmeted cyclist under the title Mud Sweat's Downhill World. Ivan Wong, a senior at a private high school in Los Altos, Calif., said he created the site at www.msdwonline.com and named it after Mud Sweat & Gears, the shop that sold him his mountain bikes. "Me and my friends saw other sites on the Net," he said, sitting with his parents in the dining room of their spacious home in Hillsborough, north of Silicon Valley. "We wanted to start our own -- with a bunch of pictures and videos and stuff." Morgan Stanley filed suit in unitedstates District Court in Manhattan, contending that Mr. Wong's Web site infringes on the firm's trademarks. Morgan Stanley is asking a judge to stop Ivan from using the domain name. From a distance, it seems a touching anecdote about a boy who stumbled into the path of a profit-seeking juggernaut. But turn the page and the story veers away from David and Goliath into a tale more fitting in this "get rich with a click" era. It turns out that a company set up by Mr. Wong's father, Sau Wong, has registered dozens of domain names, many derived from the names of investment banks. Among them: goldmansachsdirect.com and jpmorganonline.com.  In Morgan Stanley's view, the case is a blatant example of cyber squatting, the practice of registering Internet addresses -- at $70 each for two years -- in hopes of reselling them to companies or organizations that have a commercial use for them. Some companies have paid hundreds of thousands of dollars, but others, like Morgan Stanley, have gone to court to obtain addresses that they claim are rightfully theirs. In a motion filed this week in its lawsuit, Morgan Stanley contended that "the defendant in this case has targeted MSDW and the newyork investment banking community with particular precision and malice." But instead of walking away, as many cybersquatters do when they are sued by corporations, Mr.  Wong is holding his ground. "We've hired three teams of attorneys to fight this," his father said. Ivan Wong said it was coincidental that the site had a name so similar to Morgan Stanley's main site, www.msdw.com. "It was pretty ironic how they would have the same name as us," he said. Sau Wong's company, Smart Ideas, registered www.msdwonline.com in May, several weeks before Morgan Stanley officials settled on a new name for their on-line brokerage. In late July, a marketing executive discovered that the obvious domain name for the new unit was already taken. So the securities firm had to introduce its overhauled electronic brokerage, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Online, yesterday with a not-so-intuitive address on the World Wide Web, www.online.msdw.com. Representatives of the firm located the apparent owners and began negotiating with on-line correspondents they believed to be Ivan Wong and his 18-year-old brother, Ben. They offered to pay what a company representative called a "reasonable fee" for the domain name. The response that came by an electronic message: "Give us an offer we cannot refuse." Morgan Stanley quickly bid $10,000, a sum that Alejandro Levins, who was representing Morgan Stanley, described to one of the boys as "a nice bag of money for a guy your age," according to documents Morgan Stanley filed in court. Suddenly, the tone of the on-line negotiations hardened, according to the court documents. The sellers demanded $75,000 for the domain name and when Mr. Levins balked, he received a message that said: "By the way, you are not dealing with a kid. I am the father of Ben and Ivan. I am an entrepreneur myself." Another dispatch to a Morgan Stanley executive, apparently from Sau Wong, opened with this note, "As you may not be aware, some 'useful' domain names can fetch as much as six (6) figures or more." It went on to describe Smart Ideas as "an innovative and forward-looking company" that had "registered many relevant domain names covering some of the major competitors of your parent company." "Our rationale," it continued, "is that all brokerage houses, which do not have on-line trading today, will eventually provide that service." Mr. Wong then lowered his asking price to $50,000 and later offered to throw in another domain name his company had registered, morganstanleydirect.com. Frustrated, Morgan officials rescinded their offer of $10,000 and filed suit on Aug. 13. In court documents, executives contend that the biking theme that now appears on the Web site did not appear there until 10 days after the suit was filed, "in a transparent attempt to conceal its fraudulent ransom scheme." They now think they were dealing all along with Sau Wong, who says he is a computer-chip engineer who has worked in Silicon Valley for 25 years, not either of his sons. But Mr. Wong and Ivan tried to dispel that notion in an interview, saying the idea of registering domain names had been Ivan's from the start. Ivan said he had read an article that said the people who register domain names can sometimes profit from them. "In school, we learned about freedom of speech," he said, adding that one of his teachers had told him that if you got a Web site first, "you can sell it." Asked how a 17-year-old came up with the names of so many investment banks, like Goldman, Sachs, Ivan said his father gave him the ideas. "I have a Goldman Sachs account," Mr. Wong said. Both Ivan and his father insisted that they did not solicit buyers for any of the domain names. "We are not beggars," Mr. Wong said. "We do not need to beg." Cybersquatting has created a storm of legal controversy. Trademark holders are getting more support from the courts and from the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, known as Icann, a nonprofit corporation that oversees the registration of domain names, legal experts said. So many disputes over the rights to domain names have landed in court that Icann is trying to set up a mandatory arbitration system to settle them. There is also legislation before Congress intended to strengthen the rights of trademark holders to claim Internet addresses and to seek damages against squatters. In one recent case, a Canadian boy, 16, incurred the wrath of Apple Computer Inc. when he registered the domain name www.appleimac.com after Apple introduced its iMac personal computer. He said he would use it to draw traffic to his Web-based business but would consider selling it. But after hearing from Apple's lawyers, he renounced ownership of the name. Still, some judges don't see speculating in domain names as so harmful, said Pam Samuelson, a professor of law at the University of California at Berkeley. "One could say that cybersquatting is just another example of American ingenuity," she said. "These people are going out and creating things that somebody else might find of value. In a sense, they're entrepreneurs." Ms. Samuelson said that "This doesn't seem to be an open-and-shut case" of trademark infringement. The trademark in question, MSDW, is relatively new -- Morgan Stanley merged with Dean Witter in 1997 -- and not that famous, she said. A Federal statute enacted in 1995 was expressly aimed at stopping cyber squatters from diluting the value of established trademarks. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Ivan Wong, 17, the owner of a sought-after Internet address. (Peter DaSilva for The newyork Times)

title: AOL Exceeds Expectations; Agrees to Invest In a PC Maker
body: Expanding its growing domain into the PC market, America Online punctuated a stronger-than-expected earnings report yesterday by announcing that it would invest $800 million in Gateway Inc., taking a 5 percent stake in the maker of consumer computers. The investment will be made over two years and will be paid for in part with $180 million in America Online stock. In return, Gateway will offer America Online membership to new PC customers. Many computer makers already bundle America Online with all their new machines. But the marriage goes far deeper than those agreements. As part of the deal, Gateway will move the 600,000 subscribers of its own Internet access service, Gateway.net, to the America Online network, in effect putting two competing services onto the same network infrastructure. Eventually, America Online, already the world's largest Internet service provider, or I.S.P., will handle all network operations, billing and customer service functions, Gateway officials said. Gateway said it would commit $85 million to market its products on America Online and would market AOL's products and services in nearly 200 Gateway retail stores. News of the deal was released as America Online reported net income of $184 million, or 15 cents a share on a diluted basis. The results exceeded analysts projections of 13 cents a share. The company announced its earnings after the close of the regular trading day which ended with the shares at $118, a rise of $2.75, on the newyork Stock Exchange. In after-hours trading, the shares fell slightly. In separate conference calls with reporters, American Online and Gateway asserted that their deal represented an inevitable convergence of hardware makers and Internet providers. For example, they said they planned to use the partnership to develop and deploy high-speed Internet technologies. Jeff Weitzen, president and chief operating officer of Gateway, said the deal with America Online, the world's largest Internet access provider, did not amount to an admission of failure for Gateway.net. He said the service had added 200,000 subscribers this quarter, equal to the growth it had last quarter. He sought to differentiate Gateway's Internet offering, which is more of a direct pipeline to the Internet, from America Online, which offers more proprietary content, including chat rooms, news services and shopping channels. "AOL is more of a mass-market prepackaged service," he said. "Gateway.net is a more personalized service." Some industry analysts said, however, that the deal had the markings of throwing in the towel on Gateway.net, despite the seemingly healthy growth in recent quarters. "If you think about it," said Brian C. Oakes, senior Internet analyst with Lehman Brothers, "it sounds like Gateway is saying, 'We gave it a good run. Let's do a good deal and get out of the I.S.P. business.' " This is the largest investment by America Online in a PC maker, but it is hardly a unique strategy, and the company has made substantial investments in other hardware companies. For instance, it invested $1.5 billion in Hughes Electronics, the General Motors unit that makes satellite receivers and direct television. At the same time, Robert W. Pittman, the president of America Online, said the latest deal showed the clear convergence of PC makers and the Internet industry. "The big reason people are buying computers is so they can go on line," he said. America Online's earnings report underscored the fact that it knows something about consumers' rush to get on line. Continuing its unmatched growth, the company reported that it added 1.1 million subscribers worldwide in its first fiscal quarter, which ended Sept. 30, for a total of more than 18 million. Its subsidiary, Compuserve, has 2.2 million subscribers. America Online attributed the growth in revenue and profits to strong performance in several of its brands -- including the on-line service itself, the ICQ chat service and Compuserve -- and in particular to a continued growth in revenue from advertising and electronic commerce transactions. The company said revenue from advertising, E-commerce and other nonsubscription-based revenue rose to $350 million, compared with $175 million in the quarter a year earlier. Its quarterly subscription revenue rose to $995 million, compared with $723 million for the first fiscal quarter last year. The growth came in a period in which there were increasing competitive pressures on the company: growth in low-cost services, including free I.S.P.'s and broadband access, notably cable modem services. And there was some concern that America Online would face competition from itself, in the form of its subsidiary, Compuserve, which it has marketed aggressively in the last several months. Critics have said America Online could cannibalize its namesake service by making Compuserve too attractive. But company officials argued yesterday that the growth in both Compuserve and America Online showed that those fears had not been borne out. "If they're cannibalizing anything, it's Earthlink and Mindspring," said Mr. Oakes of Lehman Brothers, speaking of two competitors that recently agreed to merge. Stephen M. Case, the company's chairman, said the earnings augur a bright future for America Online, which began 10 years ago this month. "We've made a lot of progress in the decade," he said. "But most people still aren't connected, so the big opportunity during the next decade is to make the transition to a connected society."  http://www.nytimes.com
