title: Creator of the Fantastic Four Is Ready to Spin More Tales on Line
body: NEXT to his superheroes, Stan Lee has the most recognizable name in comic books. The longtime writer and editor for Marvel Comics helped create, among others, the Fantastic Four, Spider-Man, the Silver Surfer and the X-Men. In his 60-year career, he has become perhaps one of the best-read authors in the unitedstates. But ask Mr. Lee about his effect on popular culture, not to mention his influence on the literacy of a couple of generations' worth of comic-book readers, and his voice takes on a hushed, disbelieving tone. "I'm constantly amazed to meet people who grew up reading these things," he said. Now, at age 76, Mr. Lee wants to spin his own Web. In December, his site will introduce a new comic-style story called "The Seventh Portal," Mr. Lee's first new series since assuming the publisher's seat at Marvel in 1972 (www.stanlee.net). Mr. Lee, who is writing all the plot lines for "The Seventh Portal," said that the five-minute episodes would offer "the equivalent of a 10-page comic, but with a lot more detail and a lot more going on." The series is about an international team of beta-testers who are transported through the Internet into another dimension, where they gain superhero powers and battle the evil Mongorr. "The idea is that there are seven portals that lead to other dimensions," Mr. Lee explained. "Mongorr has conquered the other six; the seventh leads to Earth. It's up to these heroes to keep him from finding it." Mr. Lee made his career in pen and ink, and he hopes that his on-line comics stimulate renewed interest in the paper kind, too. Comics publishers could use the help. Marvel's bankruptcy, in 1996, was only one symptom of an industrywide slump, which occurred after a brief speculative boom in the early 90's. Sales are back to where they were 10 years ago, but most observers agree that comic books have been hurt -- and even supplanted -- by home video games and the arrival of the Internet, technologies that are aimed squarely at comics' core audience. Like Slate and Salon, original magazines that first appeared on the Web, comic books have been quietly developing on line since 1996, with artists and writers experimenting with the form in a variety of ways. The Web comics range from reproductions to blends of comics and animation, but few have thus far attracted much notice. "The nice thing about it is that it's a wide-open field," said Buddy Scalera, the on-line editor of Wizard, a comic book fan magazine. "Nobody has come out on line with the definitively must-read comic book that everybody is talking about. If anybody could do it, it probably would be Stan Lee." Marvel's characters landed on America Online in 1996 in a series of weekly Cybercomics, and the stories have evolved on the Web with tales of Spider-Man, Wolverine and several others. (Cybercomics are also available, after free registration, at www.marvelzone.com.) New episodes were recently scaled back to a monthly basis, said Marvel's president and chief executive, Peter Cuneo, and will be tied in more directly with Marvel's newsstand offerings. Part of the difficulty facing writers and artists who produce on-line comics is recreating the comic book's particular blend of words and pictures. Utilizing Macromedia's Shockwave software, Marvel's Cybercomics have the polish of comic books. Readers guide the action by clicking through word balloons and following panels. Although complete with animation, sound effects and music, the Cyber-comics "are still very much in the comic book or strip genre," Mr. Cuneo said. The result is a cross between comics and animation. For example, in a panel from "Doom Control," a Marvel series currently running on Macromedia's Shockwave site (www.shockwave.com), Dr. Doom's "mechanism for seizing mental control" takes over the roof of the Chrysler Building. The building juts into the frame at an off-angle, and weird electrical impulses are seen and heard crackling from the device. Ron Mann, director of the documentary film "Comic Book Confidential," said he was very interested to see the development of on-line art and storytelling. "The page is completely different on a computer screen," he said. "You can endlessly scroll down. The screen itself is a frame." Mr. Mann has experimented with rendering comic book panels on line. The CD-ROM version of "Comic Book Confidential" includes reproductions of seminal comic books on big pages that can be moved for different views, as well as background information on major artists, including Mr. Lee and his long-time collaborator, Jack Kirby. Still, Mr. Mann said, "because there are too many bad comics on line, it is harder to find the good comics." One Web-only comic that has sparked interest within the comics industry is a companion site to the film "The Matrix" (www.whatisthematrix.com /cmp/comic_index.html). Comic-book-style stories are evolving in the gap between the hit movie and its planned sequels. Current tales are by writers and artists from Dark Horse, DC and Marvel. Scott McCloud, a comics creator, theorist and author of "Understanding Comics," a comic book about comic books, has created several strips on line (www.scottmccloud .com) that explore the outer reaches of single Web pages, including Choose Your Own Carl, a reader-guided comic strip long on nonlinear narrative and short on flash. "Comics are a kind of temporal map," Mr. McCloud said. "As you move from one inch to the next, you're actually moving from one moment to the next. That's a really powerful idea, and a really simple one." It's also one that may not be preserved in on-line comics, he said. "The moment you have broadband, you can have full animation," he said. Can on-line comics ever match the vitality that sprang from Mr. Lee's dialogue and Mr. Kirby's panels? No matter how close they come, of course, the industry feels secure with its books. "A computerized piece of art is going to appeal to different senses," said John Jackson Miller, editor of Comics Retailer. "It almost takes you out of the realm of literature. Getting comics to work on the screen takes a transformation of what the thing is into something different." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Stan Lee and Krog, one character in "The Seventh Portal," an on-line comic-style story by Mr. Lee, a longtime writer and editor for Marvel Comics. (Kim Kulish for The newyork Times); Part of an Internet strip called "My Obsession With Chess" by Scott McCloud.

title: New Privacy Rules for Children's Web Sites
body: The Federal Trade Commission today unveiled tough new privacy rules for Web sites for children, detailing how privacy policies should be posted and how companies must comply with a new law that will prohibit them from collecting personal information without parental permission. The rules, which were approved 4 to 0, were written to carry out the Children's On-Line Privacy Protection Act passed by Congress last year. They were praised by privacy advocates, who said the commission rejected intense lobbying by some companies to keep the rules loose. The rules, which will take effect in April, are expected to have a dramatic effect on hundreds of popular Internet sites aimed at children. The sites typically offer free on-line games and other entertainment in exchange for personal information valuable to marketers. The law requires that all Web sites that gather information from children under 13 first gain "verifiable parental consent." But Congress left it up to the trade commission to define how that test could be met. A number of companies had argued that email from a parent was sufficient, saying that other methods were too costly for small start-ups. But privacy advocates said that email was too easy to forge. The commission rules have a "sliding scale" that allows Web sites to vary how they gain permission, depending on what information is being gathered and how it is used. For example, Web sites will be required to use more reliable forms of consent, like postal mail, fax, credit card or tamper-resistant "digital signatures" before children can participate in chat rooms or give out personal information that will be made available to third parties. But for information that is only used internally by the Web site collecting it, the operators will be able to accept email from parents, as long as the companies take steps to confirm the parent's identity, like a follow up email or a telephone call. After two years, the sliding scale will expire in favor of more secure electronic forms of consent. "The bottom line is that it looks remarkably good," said Jason Catlett, president of Junkbusters Corp., a privacy advocacy group based in New Jersey. "They made a number of changes to the draft rules, and despite intense lobbing of industry for loopholes, they seem not to have created any substantial ones." Kathryn Montgomery, executive director of the Center for Media Education, a Washington research and advocacy group, said the commission "has done a very thorough and conscientious job of developing rules that will be both flexible and effective." Industry representatives also said they found something positive in the new rules. "The F.T.C. did a good, balanced job," Ron Plesser, a lawyer who worked with the Direct Marketing Association and other groups, told the Associated Press. "Everything's a compromise -- it's not all great for industry, but it resolves some major concerns." In addition to detailing what companies must do to gain parental consent, the commission will mandate that children's Web sites post a prominent link to a notice of its information-collection practices on its home page and at each area where personal information is collected. Robert Pitofsky, chairman of the commission, said the new rules achieve "one of the commission's top goals -- protecting children's privacy on line." "It puts parents in control over the information collected from their children on line, and is flexible enough to accommodate the many business practices and technological changes occurring on the Internet," he said. The Children's On-Line Privacy Protection Act was passed by Congress after an F.T.C. survey in March 1998 showed that 89 percent of Web sites collected personal information from children, but only 24 percent posted privacy policies and only 1 percent asked the children to get their parents' permission before sending information about themselves. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
ONLINE SHOPPER;
Bulk Buying Adds the Suspense of Auctions
body: FOR me, the concept of bulk buying has always conjured up images of cold warehouses filled with shoppers wrestling with mammoth containers of mayonnaise or struggling toward their cars under the weight of a pallet of canned green beans. A new breed of on-line shopping sites offer a novel twist on bulk buying, a version that doesn't involve lugging around six-gallon drums of peanut butter. Sites like Mercata, Accompany and (scheduled to start next month) Act Big -- are bringing shoppers together to form groups to make large-volume purchases on hundreds of items, like computer equipment and baby supplies. Although each site operates differently, the principle is the same: the more shoppers who agree to buy a certain item, the lower the price goes. For instance, last week at Accompany (www.accompany.com), the first five shoppers who wanted to buy Nintendo Gameboy Color could pledge to purchase it for $56.95 apiece. If 10 buyers pledged, the price would drop further. To reach Accompany's rock-bottom price, $49.95, a minimum of 21 buyers would have had to pledge. Then everyone, even the shoppers who had signed up back when the price was higher, would have paid only $49.95. The caveat? The price may never drop; in fact, on the half-dozen items I monitored at both sites last week, only one dropped (by less than $2). And, I had assumed, once I pledged to buy an item, I was committed to buy. In any event, the risk didn't seem great. The opening prices (before any bulk discounts) at the Accompany and Mercata sites seem competitive with other available prices, both off and on line. But there are hidden costs. Accompany's Gameboy cost an extra $4.99 for shipping and 35 cents for insurance. (Accompany plans to offer free shipping until the end of the year.) Since Accompany's items are shipped directly from suppliers, a shopper who lives in a state where a supplier is located would have to pay sales tax. I decided to try out Mercata (www.mercata .com), which offers free shipping and ships items from warehouses in Pennsylvania and Washington, so I could avoid the sales tax, as well. Mercata was also enticing new shoppers with $50 of credit that could be used to pay up to half the price of any item. (Mercata also offers some products at discounted, non-negotiable prices.) Mercata advertised a 32-inch JVC set (model number 32050, with all the features my gadget-addicted husband craved) for $744.80, well below the manufacturer's suggested price of $849.99. And the price could conceivably go even lower if enough buyers signed on. Plus, with my new-shopper credits, I could drop the price to $696.50. I wavered for three days, returning to the site to check to see if the price dropped; it never did. I then began to wonder how many other shoppers like me were out there, unwilling to be the first ones to take the plunge. I suspected there were quite a few, which was confirmed by Jonathan Ehrlich, Accompany,'s vice president of marketing, who said that two kinds of buyers frequent bulk sites: people who really, really want a specific product and people who want it only if it's a great deal. The first kind of buyer helps drive down the price. If too many of the people who visit the site are like me -- customers who hover but do not commit -- the price will never drop. The lesson here would seem to be this: unless you're comfortable with the first, undiscounted price quoted on a bulk site, you shouldn't pledge. Restless, I began some comparison shopping. One on-line merchant, Intec, advertised a price of $630 and was coincidentally headquartered in Hicksville, N.Y., near where I live. I phoned Intech's toll-free number and reached Ken Yokel, the company's president, who told me that I could avoid shipping costs by picking up the television at the company's nearby warehouse. Mr. Yokel also offered me an additional 5 percent off the purchase price if I paid in cash. Total, with sales tax: $647.88. Smug about finding a good deal, I invited my friend Nancy Bendit (widely considered the best bargain shopper of her generation) along to witness my triumph. Instead, she was present as I was humiliated twice: first when the television would not fit into my Honda Civic without first being unpacked from the box and later when I panicked that the hulking monster was bigger than my cabinet. ("You didn't measure?" she asked. Nancy carries a tape measure on her key ring.) At that point, I realize that I had come full circle, standing behind a chain link fence in a warehouse, waiting to take delivery of an unseen item. It was not, however, a complete defeat for bulk-buying sites. Unknown to me when I first used Accompany, the site offers Buyer Flash, which will notify you if the price drops to a certain level. Mercata will allow hoverers to make conditional bids -- you pledge to buy an item at a certain price, and if it drops to your price, you must buy. Otherwise, you don't have to buy. The larger point about bulk sites, about all on-line shopping, is that whether you are shopping on line or off, if you start your search on the Internet, you will be much better informed and can potentially arm yourself with a target price to use as leverage. The same JVC model was marked $749 at a P. C. Richards store a mile from the warehouse; when I told a salesman I could get it cheaper on the Internet, he dropped the price to $680.89 including sales tax. Forget the days when shoppers lived in a great information vacuum, at the mercy of local retailers with limited selection and confusing pricing policies. If I sound cocky, it may be because the 32-inch television fit in my cabinet. With a quarter-inch to spare. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Margaret Riegel)

title:
REVIEW;
Safe Places to Survey Quakes
body: MAJOR earthquakes aren't occurring more frequently now than they have in the past. It just seems that way, given the recent earthquakes in Turkey, Greece, Taiwan and Mexico, which have produced a succession of all-too-familiar images: collapsed buildings, rescue crews hunting through rubble and victims being pulled from the wreckage. Many people in the unitedstates have their own reasons for reflecting upon the subject: last Sunday, for example, was the 10th anniversary of the devastating Loma Prieta earthquake in Northern California, and it came just one day after a quake shook Southern California. Although earthquakes make compelling television, the Web is a better place to learn about them. Some earthquake Web sites are a natural fit for the medium, neatly combining the original purpose of the Internet (linking scientists together) with the advantages of the Web (presenting information in a broadly accessible way). Through them, the public now has easy access to almost instantaneous updates about earthquakes occurring anywhere in the world, descriptions of seismic activity in particular regions, explanations of how faults and plate tectonics work and retrospective looks at individual earthquakes. A good starting point is the site run by the National Earthquake Information Center (earthquake.usgs .gov), a division of the unitedstates Geological Survey. The Current Earthquake Information link leads to the most notable feature of the site: the center's Near Real-Time Earthquake Bulletin "Finger" List, a continually updated list of the 21 most recent substantial earthquakes. The list gives the epicenter of each earthquake, the time it occurred and its magnitude. Clicking on any quake produces a set of relevant maps that highlight the epicenter and indicate the area's major faults. In some cases, a written description supplements the raw data. Hours after the tremor that shook Mexico on Sept. 30, for instance, a posted summary noted that the effects of that powerful jolt, as big as the Taiwan quake, were diffused partly because the epicenter was far beneath the earth's surface -- an atypical occurrence for earthquakes caused by the Cocos plate off Mexico, which have produced some major disasters in recent decades. Certain portions of the earthquake center's site are technical and intended for seismologists, but the General Earthquake Information section is meant for the lay reader.  Several links describe how earthquakes are measured. (A 7.0 quake, like the one that struck Southern California on Saturday, releases 30 times as much energy as one measuring 6.0, for example.) Others provide a history of seismology, list major historical earthquakes and discuss earthquake preparedness. There is also an earthquake database, searchable by region. Major earthquakes "have remained fairly constant throughout this century," the site says, "and have actually seemed to decrease in recent years." Scientists detect more minor earthquakes than ever before, it says, but only because more seismograph stations have been placed around the world. Other sites also provide a mixture of quake updates and background information, although they all rely upon the earthquake center's data to do so. A rare privately run site doing that is called Seismo-Watch (www.seismo-watch .com). One attraction of Seismo-Watch is that its Special Earthquake Reports contain more complete descriptions of major earthquakes than the earthquake center's site does, even detailing how residents perceived them. It also produces weekly regional surveys of seismic activity, with better maps than the center's. Seismo-Watch is, however, a commercial site, so only some of these are free. Similarly, a university consortium, the Incorporated Research Institutions for Seismology, has developed its own update system (www.iris.edu), using the N.E.I.C. as a source. The Seismic Monitor link on the home page displays an interactive, real-time global earthquake map; clicking on it produces lists of earthquakes by date in the past 30 days. This format seems cumbersome, but buried beneath the surface is a surprise: graphic animations illustrating the different types of faults. (The direct address for this is www.iris.washington.edu/seismic /events/faults.html.) The companion site to the public television series "The Savage Earth," produced by WNET in 1998, also shows how faults move (www .wnet.org/savageearth/earthquakes /index.html). Through a series of animated clips, it depicts various types of faults, the propagation of earthquake waves and even the way the earth's surface shakes during a quake. The unitedstates Geological Survey has posted a 10th-anniversary retrospective (quake.wr.usgs.gov /study/LomaPrietaAnniversary) about the Loma Prieta quake. It gives a dire warning: "The next big earthquake in the San Francisco Bay Area may come sooner than you think." That is hardly reassuring for people with close ties to the region. But when it happens, at least they will know where to find a quick and accurate report. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Reuters)

title: I.B.M. Plans to Stop Selling Its PC's in Retail Outlets
body: I.B.M., which helped touch off a boom in computer retailing when it introduced its personal computer nearly two decades ago, said yesterday that consumers in North America soon would not find its PC's in stores; they will have to buy them on the Internet. After Christmas, the International Business Machines Corporation will sell its Aptiva line of consumer desktop computers only on the World Wide Web. Its popular Thinkpad laptops will still be available in stores, and it will continue to sell corporate computers -- a much larger business for I.B.M. -- through dealers, as well as directly from the company. It is abandoning retail stores for its PC's because, like other computer manufacturers that sell through brick-and-mortar outlets, I.B.M. has been losing ground to companies that sell directly to customers, like the Dell Computer Corporation and Gateway Inc. I.B.M.'s PC division lost $1 billion last year and $240 million in the first half of this year. To stem the losses, I.B.M. is paring the business, cutting costs and focusing on its more profitable divisions. Two weeks ago, the company said it would lay off as many as 1,000 of the 10,000 employees in the personal-computer division, many of them involved in selling computers to consumers. Starting in January, I.B.M. said it would emphasize sales of Aptivas on its own Shopibm.com site in addition to selling through some Internet dealers, like ValueAmerica.com. "We can't figure out how to go through retail and have us make money and have the retailer make money on a consistent basis," said David M. Thomas, the executive in charge of I.B.M.'s personal systems group. He said that consumers represented about $2 billion of the company's $17 billion in PC sales but that the consumer line "consistently loses more money than any other." Already, I.B.M.'s share of the consumer market is far smaller than industry averages. Ziff-Davis Infobeads estimates that in 1999, 41 percent of desktop computers and 19 percent of portable computers were sold to home users. Mr. Thomas said that the consumer market had been tough for I.B.M. because it has been dominated by very low-cost machines, where profit margins are much thinner than I.B.M. needs to support its expensive infrastructure. Moreover, retailers demand expensive support, such as subsidizing the cost of unsold models, he said. Mr. Thomas said these problems were mainly limited to the unitedstates and that I.B.M. continued to sell well through retail outlets in Asia. The company would keep selling in such outlets in overseas markets, he said. Analysts also say that I.B.M. has been inconsistent in its approach to the consumer market and has often been late to spot industry trends, especially new lower price levels. "I.B.M. reminds me of a 747 that takes off, climbs to 40,000 feet then does a nose dive and pulls out just before it crashes," said Mathew Sargent, an analyst with Ziff Davis. He said that I.B.M. had recently fallen to fourth place in the retail market, with an 11 percent share, after Hewlett-Packard, Compaq and an upstart, E-Machines. I.B.M. hopes that Internet sales will prove more lucrative. Selling directly to consumers delivers higher profit margins, and even when the sale is made on another retailer's Web site, the PC is often shipped directly from I.B.M. to the consumer, reducing the cost of distribution. Moreover, I.B.M. said that Internet buyers typically spend more on computers and need less technical help than those who buy in stores. Mr. Sargent said that based on its track record, I.B.M. would find its Web-only strategy difficult. "On paper, it's the right thing to do, but in practice it won't work," he said. "I.B.M.'s Web site is horrible. Customers find it very difficult to order, and that just won't hold up when they are competing with Dell and Gateway." Trink Guarino, a spokeswoman for I.B.M.'s PC unit, said the company understood that its Web site needed work. "By the first quarter, it will be greatly improved," she said. She said that I.B.M. would promote Aptiva sales on its Web site with a $20 million advertising campaign in the first three months of 2000. Executives at Hewlett-Packard and Compaq said yesterday that they had no intention of pulling their computers out of retail stores. "Over the last four years, the consumer business has been very healthy for Compaq," said Michael Larson, the head of Compaq's consumer unit.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MANAGEMENT;
Internet Strategy Becomes a Must at the Top
body: No one asked Emmanuel A. Kampouris whether he could surf the Web when he was named chief executive of the American Standard Companies in 1989. Nor did anyone at the LTV Corporation question Peter E. Kelly about the marketing potential of the Internet when he was named president of the company in 1991 and became a front-runner for the top job. For that matter, the World Wide Web did not even exist when John F. Welch Jr. took over the General Electric Company in 1981. But anyone eager to succeed those chiefs had better be as familiar with the Internet as their predecessors were with mainframes and PC's. "Now that E-commerce has joined quality, globalization and services as a companywide initiative, it's a good bet that the next C.E.O. will be savvy about the Internet," said Bruce Bunch, a spokesman for G.E., which is bracing for Mr. Welch's retirement in December 2000. It was more than a wager at American Standard, a maker of bathroom fixtures and air-conditioning equipment. Just this month it tapped Frederic Poses, president of the Allied Signal Corporation, to succeed Mr. Kampouris, who also will retire next year. American Standard recently began selling to distributors on the Web, and Mr. Kampouris had told recruiters to put "conversant with the Internet" up there with integrity and leadership as major qualifications for his job. "We wanted to be sure that all candidates understand that you have to invest in the Internet, even if it detracts from next quarter's earnings," Mr. Kampouris said. "Allied Signal has been moving heavily toward the Internet, so it seems clear that Fred Poses is committed." These days, even old-line industries are realizing that cyberspace is crucial to their future. Few expect their chiefs to design Web pages or be power Web surfers. But they want leaders who recognize that a workable Internet strategy goes straight to the bottom line. "Even if they don't specify Internet savvy by name, they are asking for it," said Gerard R. Roche, chairman of Heidrick & Struggles, a search firm. "They say: 'The world is moving at warp speed; get me someone who's comfortable with that.' Since the Internet is the major revolution of today, I wouldn't dream of providing a candidate who doesn't understand it." For now, lack of demonstrable Internet skills is rarely a deal breaker. "The Internet is such a new phenomenon that it would be too limiting to mandate hands-on experience," said Thomas J. Neff, chairman of unitedstates operations for the search firm Spencer Stuart. "Sure, it's a plus, but industry experience and ability to lead teams rank a lot higher." Still, Mr. Neff expects that within two years he will routinely ask candidates about their Internet experience. Similarly, Jeffrey E. Christian, chairman of the executive-recruiting firm Christian & Timbers, expects the proportion of non-Internet companies demanding Internet expertise to grow from 30 percent today to 60 percent in just six months and to 100 percent three years from now. "It is the C.E.O. who must understand how Internet strategies blend with overall strategies, and who must line up strategic alliances and joint venture deals," Mr. Christian said. "And it is the C.E.O. who has to keep a sales force motivated even as you build E-commerce vehicles that will eliminate their jobs." Twenty years from now, such people will be plentiful. The candidates of that era are probably in their 20's or 30's today, and the Internet is as seamless a part of their lives as a microwave oven or CD player. But few will be seasoned enough to head a Fortune 500 company anytime soon. That worries Mr. Kelly, 57, who became chairman of LTV in February. LTV, which buys and sells steel on line, has incorporated Internet awareness into every aspect of management development. "Our 25- and 35-year-old up-and-comers find all this stuff natural," he said. "It is the 45-to-55-year-olds we worry about. Those that argued against selling on the Net certainly hurt their chances in the succession plan." Recruiters say that the lack of home-grown Web knowledge is a key reason that companies go outside for top-level talent. Mr. Christian said he had a mandate to fill in that gap when the Hewlett-Packard Company hired his firm to find a chief executive to replace Lewis E. Platt. And he noted that Carly Fiorina, who got the job in July, had racked up a lot of Net-based experience at Lucent Technologies, her former employer. Chief executives, many in their 50's or 60's, often must be content with recognizing, not generating, good ideas. It never occurred to Michael R. Bonsignore, the 58-year-old chief executive of Honeywell Inc., to give customers access, for a fee, to the company's equipment-testing software on a Honeywell Web page. But when younger people suggested it, he jumped on it. Now Honeywell, which recently agreed to merge with the much larger Allied Signal Corporation, has invited customers to use another Honeywell Web site, dubbed myplant.com, as a chat room to exchange ideas. The hit rate is high enough, Mr. Bonsignore says, that more than 100 companies have paid Honeywell a fee to advertise on the site. Mr. Bonsignore, who will head the merged company, expects significant hands-on Internet ability from his own potential heirs. "My successor will have had to demonstrate that he or she had used the Internet to create value," he said. "And it's not too early to identify the people who should be on the radar screen." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Emmanuel Kampouris, chief of American Standard, knows his bathtubs and the value of the internet. (Norman Y. Lono for The newyork Times)

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
A WholeOther Type of E-Trade
body: SINCE the first cave man exchanged his favorite club for a neighbor's animal pelt, barter has been an accepted form of commerce. Now some Internet companies have turned themselves into virtual trading posts, making barter a way of life. Consider Sportsline USA, whose sports-related Internet site is relentlessly promoted during broadcasts of football games and other sporting events on CBS, the television network that owns a stake in Sportsline. In the first half of this year, nearly a fifth of Sportsline's $24 million in revenue involved no cash payments. Instead, Sportsline gave to other companies that amount of advertising space on its site in exchange for advertising and other services and goods on their World Wide Web sites. These types of exchanges have become so common that they may be skewing the financial picture for the Internet industry. Since these new companies rarely have profits, revenues are often the key determinant of their value. Strong revenue growth, thus, can translate into higher stock prices. Barter accounted for more than 10 percent of revenue at Internet companies including Ivillage, Salon.com, Earthweb, Verticalnet and Edgar Online in the second quarter, the companies reported. Over all, it represented 7 percent of the $693 million in Internet advertising recorded in the first quarter of the year, double the percentage of just three years ago, according to a survey of Internet advertising conducted by PricewaterhouseCoopers and the Internet Advertising Bureau, a trade group. Some Internet analysts say these numbers are far too low. Were companies to take into account deals in which two Internet companies simply agree to scratch each other's back -- selling equal dollar amounts of advertising to each other for cash -- barter would account for more than 15 percent of all Internet ads, the analysts estimate. In few cases do investors have any idea how big barter has become. Most companies that include barter deals in their reported revenue, like Sportsline, do not mention the practice in their earnings news releases. Only by reading far into a company's quarterly report to the Securities and Exchange Commission would an investor find disclosures about such transactions. The S.E.C. requires companies to break out the deals if barter accounts for 10 percent or more of revenue. "Something about the practice doesn't smell right to me," said Robert A. Olstein, portfolio manager of the Olstein Financial Alert fund, a $350 million mutual fund that tries to find undervalued stocks by parsing companies' financial statements. "It may be O.K. according to generally accepted accounting principles, but I'm not sure anything truly economic is happening in these transactions," he said. "I like to see independent transactions where cash is exchanged, and the company that receives it can consciously decide where to spend every dollar." Major accounting firms all sign audited financial statements of Internet companies that recognize some barter transactions, giving the practice legitimacy. And the exchange of advertising is important to companies trying to get their names before the Web-surfing public. But because of the peculiar characteristics of the Internet business, accountants and securities regulators are taking a closer look at the issue. On Monday, the S.E.C.'s chief accountant, in a letter to the Financial Accounting Standards Board, requested that the board's special task force on emerging issues take up the issue of accounting for barter transactions, calling it one of four "Priority Level 1" issues that accounting and securities regulators face. Accounting for barter transactions has long been governed by an old rule that says the deals must be recorded at the "fair value" of the goods exchanged. Fair value of advertising is easily determined for established media companies that sell nearly all of their advertising space for cash. But an Internet company may now collect payments on only a small fraction of its space. Much of the rest goes unused, so exchanging a part of it with another Internet company has little downside. "In some cases, I don't know what fair value is on the Internet," said George Neble, a partner in the high-technology practice in Arthur Andersen's Boston office. "Current practices by companies are all over the place. Given the infinite amount of space on the Internet, I think you have to demonstrate that you can get cash for these spots from independent parties and that you have a pattern of doing it." Mr. Neble added, "Valuations for these companies are being driven by revenues, and barter creates the potential for distortion in a company's revenues." Lynn Turner, the S.E.C.'s chief accountant, says he, too, has grown uncomfortable with some companies' extensive use of barter. "We want to make sure that the information being reported gives investors a true notion of what is really going on with revenues and that they are reliable numbers," he said. "We're always concerned that someone will push the envelope too far." While most Internet companies engage in some form of barter, some refuse to recognize those transactions as revenues. "Personally, I think it's fraudulent," said Alan M. Meckler, chief executive of Internet.com, which runs a network of Web sites, electronic newsletters and discussion groups. Mr. Meckler has been around the Internet for almost as long as the Internet has been around. And as the former publisher of Internet World magazine, the organizer of Internet trade shows and the creator of the on-line magazine Iworld, he is no stranger to the arenas of publishing and advertising. But when he looked into the vortex of barter transactions for Internet advertising, Mr. Meckler said he saw a sort of black hole. "No company would possibly take barter for something they could sell, unless they were getting something back that is worth more," he said."What's more, advertising on the Internet has no shelf life -- and if it has no shelf life, it has no value that should be recognized as revenues." Though Internet.com engages in some "immaterial" amounts of barter, it does not record any revenues or expenses for those transactions. Most barter transactions are recorded as even exchanges, meaning that equal dollar amounts of revenue and expense are recorded. Thus, the transactions do not affect a company's bottom line, its cash flow or taxes. But companies that recognize barter transactions generally say they are valid because they both give and receive something of value. Barter helps young companies, because it gets a company's name and brand in front of more people without expending any cash. Salon.com, the on-line magazine, said that barter rose to 16 percent of revenues in the year ended March 31, up from 7 percent the previous year and zero percent the year before. "Salon believes that these barter transactions have been important to the establishment of the Salon brand and expects to continue to engage in these transactions in the future," the company said. Not all companies appear at ease with the recognition of barter revenues, though. In Sportsline's case, CBS, its largest shareholder, gets royalties of 15 percent of revenue -- calculated by excluding any revenue received in the form of barter. Larry Wahl, a Sportsline spokesman, declined to discuss why barter accounts for so much of the company's revenue. "We don't disclose anything additional with regard to barter, even our rationale, beyond what's in our financials," he said. Typically, a company that barters advertising records two transactions of equal value. For the advertising space on its own site that it gives away, a company records a given dollar amount of "expenses." At the same time, it records an equal amount of "revenues," representing the value of the ad space on another company's Web site that it received in exchange. Some companies report that barter is quite important to their financial health. Ivillage, a Web site dedicated to women's news and information, said in an S.E.C. filing that it "is dependent on barter transactions which do not generate cash revenue," but which still accounted for 20 percent of 1998 revenue and 12 percent of its $14.6 million in revenue in the first half of this year. Jason Stell, a spokesman for Ivillage, said that because the company broke out the amount of its barter transactions, "people can take that into account when they do their models" to value the company. For many Internet companies, preserving precious cash is nearly as important as getting their brand name in front of Internet users. "Many Internet companies don't have the resources to purchase content or advertising and promotion," said Debbie A. Simon, a vice president at Houlihan Lokey Howard & Zukin, a Los Angeles investment banking firm, who specializes in Internet transactions. "So we definitely are seeing an increasing trend toward barter deals." But a liberal use of barter can work against companies, said Rich LeFurgy, chairman of the Internet Advertising Bureau. "If you're willing to barter, it's hard to sell ads at the full rate," he said. Peter Petrusky, director of the new-media group at PricewaterhouseCoopers, said that though barter has doubled as a percentage of total Internet ad spending in the last three years, he believed it would fall back to about 5 percent, as larger companies come to dominate the industry's ad spending. Other analysts are not so sure. Marissa Gluck, an advertising analyst for Jupiter Communications, thinks barter makes up a far larger percentage of on-line advertising -- at least 15 percent, or up to three times the trade group's estimate. "There is a significant chunk of revenues out there that are probably barter, where it looks like money is changing hands," Ms. Gluck said, but where in fact two companies simply buy equal amounts of advertising on each other's Web site. "It's a somewhat insidious practice that is hard to track." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo  Chart: "Virtual Money" For many Internet companies, barter transactions where no cash is involved, like advertising swaps, account for a significant share of revenue. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
It's agency hunting season for everything from beauty products to boysenberry jam.
body: MARKETERS of products as disparate as cosmetics sold on line and jams sold in supermarkets are naming or changing agencies. Reflect.com the Internet company formed last month by Procter & Gamble, selected Rapp Collins Worldwide in newyork to create campaigns aimed at driving traffic to its Web site (www.reflect.com), which will offer customized women's beauty products and services. Billings have not been determined. Rapp Collins, part of Omnicom Group, will work with Critical Mass in Calgary, Alberta, the interactive agency of record for Reflect.com. Rapp Collins, which has worked on projects for P.& G., has collaborated with Critical Mass on assignments for Mercedes-Benz USA; last week, Rapp Collins acquired 50 percent of Critical Mass. "There's a really interesting partnership between Critical Mass, the leader in understanding how to use the Internet to develop one-to-one E-commerce, and Rapp Collins, with its skills in relationship marketing and data mining," said Nathan Estruth, a marketing director at P.& G. in Cincinnati who is co-leader of the Reflect.com start-up team. The campaigns will appear in off-line and on-line media. There will be print ads in magazines like Cosmopolitan, Entertainment Weekly, Jane, Martha Stewart Living and Vogue; direct marketing efforts likemailing consumers foldable cubes inscribed with beauty imagery, and so-called viral marketing in the form of email postcards consumers can send to friends. The campaigns carry the themes "Create your own beauty" and "It's the image of you." P.& G. has teamed with two venture capital funds, Institutional Venture Partners and its successor, Redpoint Ventures, to start Reflect.com, which will be based in San Francisco rather than in Cincinnati. In an agency change, J. M. Smucker of Orrville, Ohio, which sells jams, jellies, fruit spreads and other products under brand names like Smucker's, Goober and Magic Shell, is parting ways with Leo Burnett U.S.A. in Chicago after five years. Competitive Media Reporting, a unit of VNU N.V. that tracks ad spending, estimated spending last year at $10 million to $15 million. Smucker and Burnett, part of the Leo Burnett unit of Leo Group, described the parting as amicable and a mutual decision. "We and the agency believe it is in our collective best interest to seek out a new marketing partner to help us achieve our future business objectives," said Tim Smucker, the company's chairman. Brenda Dempsey, a spokeswoman for Smucker, said the company would begin a review to select a new agency but declined to identify participants or give a timetable. Turning to other changes, two banks are shifting accounts in decisions that affect three agencies. Fleet Boston, the company formed after the acquisition of BankBoston by Fleet Financial Group, named Hill, Holliday, Connors, Cosmopulos in Boston, a unit of the Interpublic Group of Companies, the agency of record on its brand, retail and corporate advertising assignments, with billings estimated at $50 million. Arnold Communications in Boston, a unit of Snyder Communications, had handled those tasks for Fleet Financial, while Hill, Holliday had been the agency for BankBoston. "Early on, we were a little concerned about that," said Karen Kaplan, executive vice president at Hill, Holliday, who will oversee the account, "but over the course of the last seven months, as we worked on a branding project, we won out." Three Arnold sibling shops will continue handling direct marketing, design and sports marketing assignments for Fleet Boston. Arnold quickly rebounded in the banking category, landing the account of PNC Bank in Pittsburgh, with billings estimated at $25 million. PNC is leaving the Southfield, Mich., office of Doner, which had been its agency for only six months, for the Washington office of Arnold and siblings that include Circle.com, which will handle interactive work. "We had started a brand project earlier this summer with Arnold," said Denise Johnson, chief marketing officer at PNC, who formerly worked at Arnold, "which led us to feel maybe we should put all our business at one agency." Doner, meanwhile, landed two accounts with combined billings estimated at $25 million, potentially compensating for the PNC loss. One, awarded to Doner Canada in Toronto, was the account of Blockbuster Entertainment Canada, part of Viacom, with billings estimated at $10 million. The Doner Southfield office handles Blockbuster in the unitedstates. The Canada account had been handled by Bensimon Byrne D'Arcy in Toronto, part of the D'Arcy Masius Benton & Bowles Communications unit of MacManus Group. And the Doner office in Newport Beach, Calif., was awarded the first account of Intellifutures in Aliso Ciejo, Calif., a company that plans to introduce an on-line futures and options trading service in the first quarter of 2000. Those billings were estimated at $15 million. Finally, Celebrity Cruises in Miami, part of Royal Caribbean Cruises, awarded its domestic account, with billings estimated at $35 million, to Saatchi & Saatchi in newyork, part of Saatchi & Saatchi P.L.C. Harris Drury Cohen in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., the Celebrity agency for two years, resigned in August. The decision came after a two-month review that had been narrowed to Saatchi & Saatchi and three other finalists: Bozell in newyork, part of True North Communications; Ogilvy & Mather Worldwide in newyork, part of WPP Group, and West Wayne in Atlanta, which will continue to handle the collateral domestic advertising duties for Celebrity. Lieber Levett Koenig Farese Babcock in newyork, which has an alliance with Saatchi & Saatchi, will handle the direct marketing duties.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Candidate on the Stump Is Surely on the Web
body: The modern campaign headquarters is no longer a rented storefront decorated with bumper stickers, bunting and empty soda cans. Increasingly it has an annex open any hour of the day or night, at an address starting with www. If in 1996 a candidate could prove hipness simply by posting an electronic version of a campaign brochure on the World Wide Web, White House hopefuls for 2000 are learning to use their Internet sites to raise money and rally troops. The Web page is the new whistle-stop, a way for candidates to carry their messages daily to more people than they can reach on the campaign trail. By posting everything from their baby pictures (as George W. Bush has done) to their favorite Bible stories (an offering from Elizabeth Dole), candidates are using the Internet as a fireside chat room, to portray themselves as just plain folks. The sites also provide a new conduit for cash: Bill Bradley has towered over the opposition in on-line fund-raising, while the Steve Forbes campaign created a way for Web surfers to crash a recent $1,000-a-plate gala -- for a small fee, of course. No one is suggesting that the Internet has come of age as a medium of political influence, as television did most notably with the Kennedy-Nixon debates of 1960. But with 67 million Americans on line, up from 7.5 million four years ago, it has become a new variable in campaign calculus. "It used to be said the candidate had to have a good message, a good ground game and enough money to wage a good air game on TV," said Rick Segal, the Internet strategy adviser to Mr. Forbes. "This is the first cycle that it can be proven that a candidate needs to have a good on-line game as well." That game includes producing fill-in-the-blank email that backers can send to all their friends in support of the candidate, and gathering campaign contributions requiring just a few mouse clicks. And for all that, the sites are a relative bargain -- Mr. Bush spent $57,000 on his over the last seven months -- with candidates hiring Web consultants, contracting with private companies or allowing volunteers to create and maintain them. Lately the sites have not only conveyed the campaigns' messages but also made news: Governor Bush last month became the first Presidential candidate to make updated lists of campaign donors available on line, and Senator John McCain of Arizona got under the skin of fellow Republicans by using his site to single out examples of Congressional pork. Howard Opinsky, Mr. McCain's press secretary, affirmed the Internet's growing campaign role, saying it was "almost like the 51st state." "It has no boundaries," Mr. Opinsky said. "The Internet has progressed from a billboard to a two-way street, and I think it's probably good in the end for the political process." To be sure, Web pages -- unlike television or radio commercials, which to the public can seem unavoidable -- depend on the initiative of people to look for them. But such surfers are valuable visitors: Mr. Bradley's campaign says that on an average day his site brings in about $7,000 and is seen by 5,000 people, more than he might encounter in a day on the trail. Mr. Bradley's campaign workers try to drum up traffic to his site by displaying the address on every lectern he uses. And Mr. Segal has worked to make sure the Forbes site is indexed in Internet search engines, thereby increasing the probability of surfers' stopping by, and is placing advertisements on news and financial Web sites. At the same time, as the Internet grows in popularity, candidates are cutting down on printed campaign literature. The Forbes campaign, for example, says it is sending out fewer newsletters than it would have in pre-Internet campaigns, because the Internet is a faster and less expensive medium. And more than in a television advertisement, the candidates are able to convey their personalities through their pages. The aura of digital friendliness that results can either charm or repel prospective supporters. Mr. Bradley's site, for example, includes recipes for dishpan cookies, oatmeal icebox cookies and butterhorns, from Rosalie Dunker, Dede Herrell and Em Aubuchon, who baked for his campaign kickoff in Crystal City, Mo. Governor Bush has baby pictures of himself and his daughters on his site and mentions his family's dog, Spot, and three cats, India, Cowboy and Ernie. One Presidential hopeful even sells his gospel recordings on line, at www.hatchmusic.com (a site separate from that of his campaign), where one can download snippets of Senator Orrin G. Hatch singing "The Cross Before the Crown." At www.AlGore2000.com, technologically savvy voters are rewarded with a message from the Vice President that is embedded in the source code, the programming blueprints of a site. "Thanks for checking out our source code!" the candidate -- or a group of Gore techies -- writes, describing plans to improve the code. "The fact that you are peeking behind the scenes at our site means you can make an important difference to this Internet effort." In another innovative move, the Forbes campaign blended virtual reality with real reality by inviting 400 computer users to an on-line version of a $1,000-a-plate bash in June at the Waldorf-Astoria in newyork. For $10 each, plugged-in supporters saw live video of the festivities, and typed messages back and forth with Mr. Forbes and others in attendance. Later that night his address was seen on a free Webcast by about 1,800 people, 600 more than at the live event. In many respects, the partnership between established candidates and the wild, wild Web is uneasy as they plumb the possibilities of this new technology. "Campaigns are a tight, disciplined, focused message delivered in a focused way, reducing chance, variables and conflict to a minimum," said Phil Noble, president of PoliticsOnline of Charleston, S.C., a company offering Internet expertise. "The Internet is about millions of voices colliding, all at the same time, about all kinds of things in a near-chaotic pattern." But candidates recognize that the Internet is an effective way to get their messages across and to keep the prospective voter's attention. Studies have shown that campaigns can usually get 45 seconds of a voter's attention by phone or 30 seconds in a television advertisement, compared with eight minutes through a Web site, said Emilienne Ireland, president of Campaign Advantage, an Internet campaign-services company in Bethesda, Md. And more than ever before, the candidates' pages are used to bring in contributions. Mr. Bradley's campaign says it has raised over $770,000 through his site, 4 percent of its total contributions. (According to a survey by PoliticsOnline, Mr. McCain had raised $260,000 on the Internet through September; no other candidate had brought in more than $100,000 through the Net.) Of the half-million people who have visited the Bradley site since last December, 14.4 percent have filled out a form to get involved, and 1 percent have brought out their credit cards or checkbooks to contribute, said Lynn Reed, a consultant to the campaign. "The Bradley campaign has been real effective in the overall strategic use of the Net," said Jonah Seiger, co-founder and principal of Mindshare Internet Campaigns, consultants in Washington. "They raised a great deal of money and a great deal of press attention, suggesting they clearly have a better strategic sense of the Net than the Gore campaign does, considering that Gore is so identified with the Net. Here they're doing something that is really going to hit Gore where it hurts." But Andrew Sather, senior vice president at Sapient, Internet consultants in Cambridge, Mass., who redesigned the official White House Web site, cited the Gore campaign's use of the Web to let visitors interact with the candidate, through electronic town halls, where people can pose questions about anything from class size to the income gap. The Bush campaign has used its site to gain credentials for the Texas Governor as a Net-savvy candidate, notably with the decision last month to begin posting a list of all his contributors, even those who gave less than $200. "This gives Americans the opportunity to look for themselves at the broad-based support Governor Bush is receiving," said Scott McClellan, a campaign spokesman. About 100,000 people have dipped into the 1,750-page listing so far, he said. At the same time, just as readers of Web pages get more information about their candidate, the candidate gets more information about them, helping a campaign organize its ground troops. Several Web watchers pointed to what the Forbes campaign calls electronic precincts as a canny use of the Internet: In a political version of multilevel marketing, a campaign volunteer brings in a handful of other volunteers, who in turn bring in more. The first volunteer, the E-precinct captain, is rewarded with special briefings, on-line video presentations, a chance to meet the candidate and real-world recognition. "It's something that's growing in its own viral kind of way," said Mr. Segal, the Forbes adviser, who added that the campaign had about 5,000 E-precincts, a few with as many as 5,000 members each. The Forbes campaign keeps tabs on where its E-volunteers live and what kind of volunteering they would like to do. Using similar information, the Bradley campaign was able to send email to 5,000 supporters in the Northeast, encouraging them to take part in a weeklong canvass in New Hampshire this summer. "We were able to get 300 folks, free," Ms. Reed said. "If you had to make phone calls for the same return, it might not be worth it." With all those electronic addresses and ZIP codes flowing in from supporters to Webmasters, some Internet experts have become concerned about what is done with this information. To reassure supporters, the Gore site posts this disclaimer: "We do not share our volunteer lists with any other site or any other entity." Chuck Todd, managing editor of The Hotline, a daily Web-based political newsletter published by The National Journal, predicts that the watershed event of the Internet's new power will most likely occur in a primary campaign, in a small or particularly well-wired state. "The way, in the past, there was a last-minute TV barrage, there will be a huge Internet campaign to swing votes toward a candidate," he said. Some analysts say the Internet may not show its full potential as a political tool until 2004 at the earliest, when high-speed Internet connections become more common and zapping messages to particular groups of voters has been refined to an art. "The potential watershed moment will be when Al Gore can make sure his pro-choice abortion ads are only seen by moderate, pro-choice women," Mr. Todd said. "That's what the Internet allows, targeting and identifying voters by household." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos (pg. Also available is a Dinner Party Kit, for holding a soiree to introduce friends to the Bradley candidacy.  George W. Bush WWW.GEORGEWBUSH.COM His site features video clips of the announcement of the formation of his exploratory committee, back in March, and records of campaign donors. The site is available in Spanish, as is Al Gore's.
