title:
E-Commerce Report;
In the holidayselling season, knowing when traffic peaks will be a key to success.
body: PART of what has made E-commerce one of the most compelling spectator sports of the year is this fact: No matter how much experience executives have had running multimillion-dollar companies in other industries, when it comes to Web retailing, many of them are still making things up as they go along. A case in point is anticipating and preparing for changing traffic patterns on the World Wide Web. While traditional retailers can say precisely when and why their customers arrive -- and can maximize their efficiency accordingly -- Internet merchants have frequently been caught by surprise in the past year by traffic surges. As E-commerce merchants brace for their second meaningful holiday shopping season, however, they are beginning to decipher some of the rhythms of their Internet shoppers. Namely, while Web traffic in general becomes heavier as the day goes on, many Internet retailers report that traffic is actually heaviest during the middle of the day, between 2 P.M. and 3 P.M. E.S.T. -- suggesting that workers blessed with high-speed Internet connections remain anchored to their desks at lunch time, sandwich in one hand, mouse in the other. So, with the holidays rapidly approaching, some retailers are shoring up their sites' technological infrastructure and hoping they have enough capacity to handle the midday traffic smoothly. Others, meanwhile, are looking beyond the back-office technology issues into marketing opportunities presented by the 9-to-5 set. For that matter, not every retail site is subjected to the same midday shopping rush, analysts and executives said, since other factors help determine the peaks as well. The type of goods sold and the type of consumer the company attracts, for example, can also affect a site's traffic patterns. "Lower-consideration purchases like books, gifts or flowers are much more likely to be made during the daytime hours, since people tend to see those things as a task that can be done quickly," said Melissa Shore, an analyst with Jupiter Communications. "With things like computers, people will do a lot of research and then go home and talk it over with their significant other or see if it's compatible with their system, then go on line and buy it." Travelocity, a travel site owned by the AMR Corporation that recently announced a merger agreement with Preview Travel, peaks at 3 P.M. E.S.T, according to Terrell Jones, Travelocity's president. "There are a lot of busy dual-income families who can't book something at night, when most travel agents are closed," he said."And the high-speed access at work certainly has an effect." But marketing is also a factor, Mr. Jones said. Preview Travel advertises heavily on America Online, which has heavier traffic during the evening hours. "So Preview's activity tends to be later also. We're on Yahoo, which tends to peak earlier in the day," he said. Handling those peaks, of course, requires resources. Just as brick-and-mortar stores plan for heavier shopping times by scheduling more staff, Internet retailers need to rely on more technology and personnel to get them through the rush. The great fear of all Web merchants is that a traffic surge will catch them by surprise -- landing them in the inauspicious company of Ebay, Toysrus.com and E*Trade as examples of sites that have occasionally failed to handle their own peak loads. But even if a surge in users does not result in a system crash, it can slow down the performance of a Web site sharply and alienate potential customers. "Our primary concern is making sure we can handle all the traffic that doesn't come evenly," said Gabe Fried, manager of research at Toysmart, an on-line toy retailer. That job, he said, is complicated by the fact that traffic trends can change quickly in response to marketing efforts, like an early-morning promotion Toy smart recently began with Sesame Street. The campaign yielded "a rather large shift in our peak hours and processing hours," Mr. Fried said, but with beneficial results: the site's traffic is now distributed more evenly through the day. "That's better for us because it means less of a load on our servers," he said, "and better for users because the fewer of them we have at one time, the faster the site is." Web sites with less predictable traffic patterns could be in for a long holiday season, said Jeff Nickerson, a partner in the electronic business practice at PricewaterhouseCoopers. "Last holiday season, there were a lot of sites that were shocked, and the consumers were a bit forgiving," he said. "This time around, there are so many more merchants that if stuff doesn't perform well, sites will lose money big time." More aggressive Web retailers, meanwhile, are looking into ways to cash in on Internet users' lunchtime shopping habits. Brookstone, which sells through its Web site, catalogues and stores, is planning a radio advertising campaign that may include lunchtime advertising, a spokesman said. Others are considering scheduling more banner advertisements to be displayed on various Web pages during lunchtime. Unlike radio and television broadcasters, however, not every Internet publisher -- not even America Online -- has the technological means to serve a banner ad for a specific time slot. But the technology is available. The Internet advertising company Doubleclick enables the 8,000 sites in its network -- and others that license the company's technology -- to serve ads whenever they want, a company spokeswoman said. Thus far, she said, the service has been most popular with financial advertisers, which typically want their ads to appear mainly between 8 A.M. and 8 P.M. "You could argue that, yes, it does matter," said Mr. Nickerson, of PricewaterhouseCoopers. "People are more likely to buy during these times than in other parts of the day. It's like the Internet rush hour." Since so many people are shopping at work, one would expect the companies already involved with workplace Internet access to seek a piece of the action. According to Ms. Shore of Jupiter, they may get it. She predicted that E-commerce sites will start joining forces with companies that set up intranet sites for corporations. "Let's say Amazon partnered with Peoplesoft, which puts together a customized intranet for Time Warner," she said. "Amazon could get massive exposure to Time Warner's employees, and Time Warner could get discounts from Amazon that they could pass onto their employees as a benefit. It makes sense for everyone." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Gabe Fried, research manager at the on-line retailer Toysmart, says a "primary concern" is making sure the site can satisfy customer demand at all times, even when traffic is heaviest. (Rick Friedman for The newyork Times)

title:
Media Talk;
Will Journal's Managing Editor Go to CNN?
body: Paul E. Steiger, the managing editor of The Wall Street Journal, is considering an offer from CNN to take the helm of the network's financial news outlets -- including the troubled CNNfn financial network -- which have been without their own leader since the departure of Lou Dobbs in June. Mr. Steiger's talks with the network, a unit of Time Warner Inc., have been going on in stutter-step fashion for weeks, according to people who have spoken with both parties in the negotiations. Mr. Steiger, The Journal's top newsroom executive, has discussed the scope and authority of the new job with CNN's president, Ted Turner. He has discussed his options with Peter R. Kann, the chief executive of Dow Jones & Company, The Journal's parent. If he decided to make the switch, Mr. Steiger, who is 57, would be leaving the command of about 600 journalists at the nation's premier financial newspaper, whom he has led for the last seven years, to assume control of a staff of 300 at both CNN and CNNfn. The financial network reaches fewer than one-fifth of the 68 million homes reached by its chief rival, CNBC. And since Mr. Dobbs left to start his own World Wide Web site, the lines of authority over CNN's financial coverage have been unclear. But if Mr. Steiger made the move, he would follow a newspaper-to-cable-TV path blazed by Tom Johnson, CNN's chief executive, who was the publisher of The Los Angeles Times in the early 1980's -- a period when Mr. Steiger was that newspaper's business editor. The job of heading both CNNfn and the financial news segments of the main cable channel and its Web site "is truly an international job, when there are few international jobs left," said one person who has talked to both sides in the negotiations. Figuring in Mr. Steiger's calculations may be the fact that it has been rare for any managing editor of The Journal to move to the top of the corporate ladder at Dow Jones. Mr. Steiger referred telephone calls about his discussions to Richard J. Tofel, the Dow Jones spokesman, who, when asked for a comment, would say only "Pass." Sue Binford, a spokeswoman for CNN, also declined to comment. But the assumption that Mr. Steiger was about to leave permeated The Journal's newsroom Friday. Among the names mentioned as possible successors are Daniel Hertzberg, who is one of two deputy managing editors, and, from elsewhere inside Dow Jones, Steven Swartz, editor in chief of Smart Money, and Paul Ingrassia, the president of Dow Jones Newswires.   FELICITY BARRINGER http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
Media Talk;
Worth Strives to Be Internet-Oriented
body: Pssst . . . Hey, you -- rich guy. Need a house in the Hamptons? A Gulfstream jet? Want to buy one on line? W. Randall Jones thinks that wealthy Americans are willing to shop on line for everything from charter flights to duplex apartments -- and he's shifting the focus of his magazine company to do just that, joining the wave of publishers turning their attention to the Internet. Mr. Jones said last week that Capital Publishing, the company of which he is chief executive, will now be known as the more Internet-oriented Worth Media. Early in 1998, Mr. Jones had said he wanted to expand his print fief -- which then consisted of Worth, Civilization, Equity and The American Benefactor. But late last year, Mr. Jones folded The American Benefactor and this year he said that the quarterly Equity would be published twice a year. "I looked at how we could expand this company," Mr. Jones said. "If you're running a magazine and it's cooking on all burners, you could get a valuation of twice the revenues. When you're doing that with a working Internet strategy, you can get 200 times revenues." With a $5 million investment from Dawntreader, an Internet venture fund, Mr. Jones will build what he calls "a platinum portal for the rich" -- Worth.com, which he will introduce next spring. "If you think of a day or a week in the life of a wealthy person, we want to be the portal they go to to meet all their needs," Mr. Jones said. One impact of the reorganization: Joe Armstrong, Capital's group publisher and a former publisher of newyork and Rolling Stone, has resigned. "I am still in love with print," Mr. Armstrong said, "and I really want to be in a company where print is big and important, the principal focus. Call me a fish swimming against the tide."   ALEX KUCZYNSKI http://www.nytimes.com

title: SBC Communications to Offer High-Speed Internet Connections
body: Firing the latest salvo in the local telephone industry's battle against cable television providers, SBC Communications Inc. intends to announce today that it will spend $6 billion in the next three years to deploy high-speed Internet systems, people close to the company said yesterday. Within three years, SBC intends to offer high-speed cyberspace links to 80 percent of its customers using a technology called digital subscriber line, or D.S.L., which uses normal telephone lines. SBC recently completed its acquisition of the Ameritech Corporation, the Midwestern telephone giant, making SBC the local phone provider for about a third of the nation's roughly 100 million households. That deal made SBC the nation's No. 1 local telephone company, at least until the Bell Atlantic Corporation completes its merger with the GTE Corporation. During the last few years, the cable television industry has taken the lead in delivering continuous high-speed Internet links to unitedstates consumers, now serving perhaps one million households. Encouraged by the prospects of using cable systems to deliver not only Internet access but also interactive television and local phone service, the AT&T Corporation has agreed to spend more than $90 billion to become the No. 1 cable carrier. The big local phone companies appear to have paid more attention to merging with one another and fighting regulatory battles to win entry to the long-distance market than to the cable industry. They now appear to have deployed D.S.L. to fewer than 100,000 customers. But that may be changing. Bell Atlantic recently began offering D.S.L. in newyork City and SBC under its new plan intends to double the percentage of its customers with access to the technology. In its last D.S.L. announcement, in January, SBC committed to offering D.S.L. to only 40 percent of its customers. According to analysts and executives close to SBC, the company plans to spend about $4.5 billion on D.S.L. systems provided mostly by Alcatel of France and on replacing some copper lines into local networks with fiber-optic systems. The other $1.5 billion will be spent mostly on deploying advanced transmission systems in the core of the company's network, using a technology called asynchronous transfer mode. The technology splits communications into small pieces called cells. While spending on the new plan, known as Project Pronto, could dilute SBC's earnings during the next few years, executives close to the company expect the project to generate $3.5 billion in annual revenue and $1.5 billion in annual savings by 2004. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Tax Returns Of Charities To Be Posted On the Web
body: The detailed tax returns that charities file annually with the Federal Government are to be posted on the Internet beginning today, giving quick and easy access for the first time to comprehensive details on how charities use their money. "This is, by far, the most important development ever in making charities accountable and making their finances transparent," said Virginia Hodgkinson, a founder of the National Center for Charitable Statistics in Washington, who spent two decades trying to make financial data on charities widely available. The cost of exposing charity finances to widespread scrutiny is being financed by charities themselves -- notably the Ford, Kellogg and Mellon foundations -- and the Web site is operated by another charity, Philanthropic Research Inc. of Williamsburg, Va. The scrutiny of all charities, these organizations say, will ultimately bring major changes to the financial practices of the $700 billion charitable world, just as increased public access to financial data of publicly traded companies has transformed the business world. Donors will be able to compare quickly the Cancer Research Institute in newyork, which spends 91 percent of its revenues on research, with the Walker Cancer Research Institute of Aberdeen, Md., which spends 83 percent on raising funds. "We are on the verge of a whole new era of nonprofit accountability," said Arthur W. Schmidt Jr., president of Philanthropic Research, the charity that is posting the so-called information returns, Form 990's, on the Web. "The 990 will move rapidly from being this obscure, obnoxious reporting document to something informative and acceptable and transform itself into a useful document," Mr. Schmidt said. For a half-century, all charities, which fall under Section 501(c)(3) of the tax code, as well as most other nonprofit organizations, like trade associations, have been required to file 990's with the Internal Revenue Service. The returns include detailed information, like how much of the money taken in goes directly to charitable services and how much to pay individual top officers, directors and consultants. But few people, even among nonprofit executives, were aware that the 990's are public records. Often, the only way to get copies of returns was from the I.R.S., which typically involved delays of up to six months. A small industry of charity watchdogs has long used the 990's and other documents to rate the performance of charities for donors, though only a narrow segment of the charity world was ever scrutinized. Since June, Congress has required all charities to make their 990 returns readily available. The law, however, has been widely ignored by charities, many of which delay, claim ignorance or just refuse to comply, according to tests conducted this year by students at Baruch College in newyork, Evergreen State University in Seattle and other schools. Now anyone with Internet access can examine these returns. Ron Williams, the official in charge of the project for the I.R.S, said: "Right from day one we thought it was an excellent idea. Congress wants the 990's open to the sunshine, and wants them available as quickly and easily as possible." Unlike the simple pie charts that charities often include in solicitations to show how they use gifts, these returns show how much revenue came from donations, fees and government; list the organization's debts and investments, and detail overhead and fund-raising costs. The first 140,000 of the 220,000 or so returns are available now, without charge, at www.guidestar.org, and the rest will be posted before year-end. The most recent returns will be posted, mostly for 1997 and 1998, though some dating to 1992 will be included for charities that have not filed since then. The site also provides a synopsis of each charity's finances and an explanation of the Form 990. (Congress does not require 990 reports from several hundred thousand other charities -- religious organizations, Federally chartered organizations like the Red Cross or groups with less than $25,000 in annual revenues.) The site will soon include a data base with each of the hundreds of individual facts on each Form 990, allowing computerized comparisons of charities by type, size and location. Over the years, as the data base grows, it will also allow examination of long-term patterns. While anyone can view the reports, a minority of Americans probably will, said Russy D. Sumariwalla, co-head of the Aspen Institute's Nonprofit Sector Research Fund. The site's main value, he added, will be in the scrutiny that nonprofit executives will apply to peers and competitors, which he said should result in more efficient use of charity dollars. The Urban Institute, the Washington researcher that runs the National Center for Charitable Statistics, is giving the I.R.S. nearly $1 million over five years to enable the agency to scan the five million or so pages of charity returns annually onto 400 CD-ROM's. (By comparison, the entire Encyclopaedia Britannica easily fits on just one.) The I.R.S. needed the cash infusion to do the work because, after years of budget cuts, some of its charity records were a shambles. The Ford, Rockefeller Brothers Fund and other foundations have made grants to Philanthropic Research to have each line on each Form 990 keypunched into a data base. Philanthropic Research must raise $2 million a year to continue the data entry until the I.R.S. accepts electronically filed reports from the charities, now scheduled for 2007. Separately, a handful of charities have followed the lead of the California Community Foundation in Los Angeles in posting their own 990's on the Internet. In addition, a variety of Web sites run by nonprofit specialists active in the cyberaccountability movement have posted small collections of 990's, such as one devoted to AIDS charities, and the attorneys general of California, Minnesota and 13 other states have begun posting 990's and similar reports by charities in their states. But none of these efforts comes close in scale or comprehensiveness to the Guidestar site. Mrs. Hodgkinson, the charity statistics expert who laid the groundwork for the Web site effort, said the increased access should benefit donors and legitimate charities alike. "My goal was for the public to be able to get that information in a minute because the more transparency charitable organizations have the better," Mrs. Hodgkinson said, adding, "and, I believe, transparency will result in more contributions." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Arthur W. Schmidt Jr., president of Philanthropic Research, holds a year's worth of tax returns from charities on approximately 350 CD-ROM's. (Timothy Wright for The newyork Times)(pg C9)

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Using Consumer LoyaltyMay Be a Boon For Profit-Hungry Net Service Providers
body: Before his favorite football team started an Internet service, Brett Fennell jumped from one on-line service to another. But when the Baltimore Ravens offered Internet access with premium information about the team, Mr. Fennell found a provider he plans to keep. Not only does he get a chance to buy tickets ahead of the general public, but he also receives statistics about the team before the numbers reach the newspapers -- a great advantage in his fantasy football league. Mr. Fennell, a 29-year-old who develops E-commerce strategies for Airtouch Cellular in Atlanta, said the service allowed him to choose the information that would be sent to him on line. "I didn't really like all the sales pop-up stuff that came with all the other services," he said. "The Ravens information is what I want to get hit with." But while Mr. Fennell's email address and start-up page end with raven.nfl.com, the Internet service provider, or I.S.P., he logs into is PSINet. The Ravens are one of about 30 organizations that have deals with PSINet to market an Internet service under the organizations' own names. Tapping into consumers' loyalty to a group, a school, a team or myriad other organizations or institutions could prove a boon to profit-starved Internet service providers. Some analysts and executives predict that in coming years these so-called "affinity I.S.P.'s" will become the dominant way Internet services attract subscribers. The attraction for the affinity groups is that they get a useful marketing tool, and if they attract enough subscribers, they earn a slim profit on each subscription. Any entity with followers, from church groups to rock stars, is a likely candidate. David Bowie was one of the first celebrities to create an Internet service; part of the appeal for subscribers is that he drops in for on-line chats from time to time. Though the models vary, in most cases the affinity groups receive their Internet service at a wholesale rate, then make money on subscriptions by charging customers a higher rate. The affinity groups also take a percentage of profits from products sold through the service. Affinity I.S.P.'s represent a major savings in marketing costs for Internet providers, reducing typical marketing costs of between $100 and $150 to enroll each new subscriber to nearly nothing. What is more, increased subscriber loyalty can also cut the high cost of churn. These days, Internet service providers can count on losing one subscriber out of five in the course of a year. "Today, it's all about the customer relationship," said Zia Daniell Wigder, an analyst for Jupiter Communications. "All of these players are trying to lock in the customer relationship." Early research shows that Internet users welcome the concept. More than 47 percent of on-line households would switch to an affinity service if offered incentives, according to a consumer survey conducted by Jupiter Communications in March. That is why AT&T and the Concentric Network Corporation, like PSINet, are aggressively courting partners for affinity services as a way to compete with America Online, which has more than 18 million subscribers and 40 percent of the domestic market. "We're deadly serious about this being a very important part of our Internet strategy," said Bruce Jackson, vice president of Global Offering Management for AT&T. The company recently helped begin two high-profile affinity programs: free Internet access from United Parcel Service and a Spanish- and Portuguese-language Internet service for Star Media that crosses national boundaries in Latin America. The Baltimore Ravens hope to build community through their own Internet service. "We kind of view it as the ultimate fan club," said Kevin Byrne, a spokesman for the team. "We're going directly to our best fans without going through the filter of the media." In fact, the service is marketed as a way for fans to get news about the team before it hits the newspapers. Subscribers are offered the same level of information as the news media receive. And in addition to priority access to tickets, they can chat with coaches and players. The Ravens, now in their fourth season, have built a large audience to whom the Internet service can be marketed. The first target group was the 25,000 season ticket holders, followed by leads from the 70,000 tickets that go to single-game ticket buyers. For each subscription, the team receives $1 a month. So far, since April, fewer than 5,000 people have signed up for the service. But the appeal has gained momentum since July, when the team offered subscribers live video feeds from training camp. During a three-day trial, 1,000 people downloaded the live feeds. So far, the I.S.P.'s that have moved aggressively into the affinity market appear to have attracted a small proportion of their total subscribers through such partnerships. PSINet's 30 groups, including the Ravens, have brought in what one executive described as "the high tens of thousands" of new customers. Concentric, which has been in the affinity business since 1997, reports bringing in 70,000 subscribers that way, while AT&T says it has signed on about 120,000 subscribers through affinity services. Affinity groups, however, face potential pitfalls. Generally they must guarantee to sign up a minimum number of subscribers to secure discounted rates. If the groups fail to deliver the subscribers in six to eight months, the rates increase. "Ten thousand would be a runaway success for an affinity," said Harry Lalor, director of wholesale management for PSINet. "We ask for 5,000." With fewer subscribers than that, he said, the model is not feasible. What is more, if the email server crashes, customers are most likely to blame the group whose name is on the service. Nonetheless, more and more organizations are willing to take those risks. Ted Parker of Lubbock, Tex., started a small affinity service with several Internet partners last year. Mr. Parker put $3 million into the company, a filtered service called Clean Web, and targeted the Christian market. After spending $1.5 million on magazine advertising, he attracted only 5,000 subscribers. Now he is changing his marketing strategy. He is putting together a deal to provide a specialized affinity Internet service for Women of Faith, a national women's Christian organization similar to Promise Keepers. The numbers look encouraging: the organization has 600,000 members, and 67 percent of them use the Internet. Considering this kind of potential, Mr. Parker recently presented a plan to investors that showed a way to deliver 500,000 subscribers in five years. He could approach that figure just by signing a deal with Women of Faith. "If they are successful in converting a lot of them over," he said, "it doesn't take a lot of time to reach those kinds of numbers." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Brett Fennell says there are benefits to getting on line through the Baltimore Ravens. (Thomas S. England for The newyork Times)  Graph "Service Options" In a recent survey, some consumers said they would be willing to buy Internet access from companies that are not primarily in the information business. Here are the types of businesses that con-sumers said they would buy from.  Non profit -- 36% Airline -- 24% Warehouse-style store -- 11% Credit card company -- 10% Sports team -- 8% Bank -- 5% Other -- 6%  (Source: Jupiter Communications)

title: Autobytel Brings On-Line Auctions to Consumers
body: Auctions are one the oldest ways to sell cars and other commodities, but now they are getting a modern twist -- on the Internet, of course. Autobytel.com, an Irvine, Calif., on-line car-buying service, began its auction service earlier this month, selling new, used and collector cars. An Autobytel competitor, Autoweb.com, is testing an auction option for used cars in California. And Ebay, which sells all kinds of products on line, auctions collector cars, but not new and late-model used cars. Autobytel practiced on-line auctioning a few months ago with a dealer-to-dealer service before expanding to consumers. The Autobytel auction service allows vehicles to be sold by one consumer to another or by a dealer to a consumer. Autobytel has 3,000 dealers that pay monthly to have Autobytel customers shop on line with them. Consumers can place a minimum bid, program in a maximum bid and order the system to bid in certain increments. The consumer can then track the bidding on line. To promote the opening of its auction service, Autobytel has put the 1996 black Saab 900SE convertible used in the "Seinfeld" television series on the block. Bids will be accepted through Oct. 21 on the Seinfeld Saab, with the proceeds going to Citymeals-on-Wheels USA. In addition to selling vehicles, Autobytel has added an auto parts and accessories auction conducted by the Fairmarket Auction Network. Autobytel has added other services to its on-line auction. These include enlisting CCC, a chain with more than 15,000 body shops, to inspect and certify vehicles put on the auction for $69.99 each. On-line bidders can view the interior, exterior and mechanical components of vehicles up for auction. Autobytel insures the transfer of paperwork and money from buyer to seller, and it has an arrangement with Movecars.com, comprising more than 95 transportation companies, to deliver vehicles to buyers. Roadside assistance is available on every used vehicle sold at auction and will be free to the first 1,000 buyers. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Foreign Affairs;
Reality Bytes
body: Is this a story we will read sometime in the next year? newyork (NYT) -- The Dow Jones industrial average dropped 1,266 points today after Amazon.com announced that it had inadvertently made a profit. After years of having persuaded investors that its business model called for it to consistently lose money until it had built up its market share, Amazon stunned Wall Street by announcing earnings of 1 cent per share this quarter on sales of $1.1 trillion, or 10 percent of U.S. G.D.P. The reason these earnings rattled Wall Street was that investors began to realize that no matter how big Amazon's market share became its profit margins were going to remain razor thin because it is now competing with everyone -- not just booksellers. And therefore its market capitalization -- the company is valued at more than Fort Knox -- was simply not sustainable. "Pie in the sky is always great as long as the pie remains in the sky," said one Wall Street broker, "but when the pie actually comes down to earth and you get to see what a real slice looks like -- well, you have a problem. Amazon's whole strategy was to keep the pie in the sky. But now they've blown it by accidentally making a profit." The Seattle-based Internet retailer issued a statement following its quarterly earnings report, saying: "The Amazon board wants to apologize to shareholders for completely missing its quarterly loss target and inadvertently making a profit. The board has been assured by management that this problem will be rectified in the coming quarter. Amazon intends to increase both its advertising budget and the number of books it will sell at a loss to insure that it returns to unprofitability by the next quarter. Our shareholders can rest assured that our primary goal remains market share and our business motto remains: 'Amazon.com: We took the 'E' out of P/E.' " Said one Wall Street Internet analyst: "Look, I believe the Internet changes everything. I've taken the Kool-Aid. But I think the question of whether Jeff Bezos Amazon's founder will ever make the massive profits that his stock price implies is really uncertain." It will depend on at least three things, the analyst said. The first is, Are Amazon's competitors dead or are they just behind? Has Mr. Bezos killed Wal-Mart, Barnes & Noble, Best Buy, Borders, Toys "R" Us and Circuit City -- all of which he is now competing against? Or, has he just showed them the power of the Internet as a retailing tool and all these brick-and-mortar companies will now become clicks and bricks? "If that is the case," the analyst said, "all Amazon will have done is to build market share for the day when its rivals catch up. If it hasn't made money up to now, with its huge head start on the Internet, how is it going to make big money when the others catch up? The cost of switching from Amazon to another retailer is zero on the Internet. It's just one click. Wal-Mart hasn't even come into cyberspace in any serious way yet -- and those guys are meaner than junk-yard dogs. You think they're going to let Amazon just put them out of business? No way." The second thing Amazon's future depends on, said this analyst, is what inning we are in. If we are still in the first inning as far as Internet retailing is concerned, maybe Amazon, or another Amazon soon to be born, will come up with yet another innovation for using the Internet to sell things at a profit. But if we are already in, say, the fifth inning, if the basic Internet revolution in retailing is now in place and the rest is just execution, then the Wal-Marts will eventually learn to execute. Amazon might still be a winner -- it is a phenomenal marketer -- but not a winner-take-all. The third unknown, the analyst said, is whether Amazon can use its high stock price to buy one or more already profitable brick-and-mortar retailer in order to go head to head with Wal-Mart. At first people thought all business was moving to the Net; now they see that the Net is moving into business. The next big merger wave will be between virtual companies and real ones. "I swear, I thought Bezos' actual plan was to skip making a profit and go directly from being an I.P.O. to being an N.G.O. for distributing books cheaply," said another analyst. "I don't know what Amazon's future is as a company -- but as a charity, wow! What a write-off machine! It could have been called 'Unicef.com.' Really, who's given away more kids' books at cost than Amazon? Bezos had a chance to be Andrew Carnegie -- without ever making a dime. Now he's blown it by making a profit and forcing everyone to look at Amazon like, well, a real company. I mean, who needs that?" http://www.nytimes.com

title: Tracking Down Pedophiles Gains Impetus
body: JEANINE PIRRO, the county's District Attorney, was fuming. It was bad enough that Patrick Murphy, 45, of Port Chester, a former Pepsico executive, had been indicted for sodomy and having sex with a 15-year-old boy, but he was also HIV-positive. "The way the law reads now, that's only reckless endangerment, and he could be out on the street in seven years," Mrs. Pirro said. Frustrated, she slammed down the Murphy folder, vowing to propose tougher penalties for an act that could result in death. But equally troubling to the District Attorney on a recent afternoon was a second file of photographs from the Internet of adults having sex with children. In recent months, the efforts by the District Attorney's office, the major case squad of the county police and local police departments to crack down on pedophiles have begun to pay off, bringing to light the activity of those who stalk Internet chat rooms in search of underage victims. On Wednesday, the District Attorney's office announced that five people were indicted in connection with illegal sexual activity with underaged Westchester youths after they met in an Internet chat room. One of those indicted is Robert D. DeRosario, 36, who is a suspect in a separate murder case involving a child, according to the Dobbs Ferry police. In the indictment on Wednesday, Mr. DeRosario, a Yonkers resident who was also previously charged under three pending indictments with having committed acts of sodomy, sexual abuse and related offenses against nine Westchester youths, is now charged with sodomy, endangering the welfare of a 16-year-old Yonkers youth and endangering the welfare of a 15-year-old whom he met on the Internet. He is also charged with 12 counts of attempted bribery of a witness and 12 counts of tampering with a witness. Walter Salvatore, 39, was indicted for disseminating indecent material to a minor and allegedly sending nude photographs of himself over the Internet to a 15-year-old Westchester resident. William Chidester, 58, Guy Ebersole, 39, and George Noll, 36, were indicted separately on counts of sodomy and endangering the welfare of minors after meeting them in Internet chat rooms. Mr. Chidester served on the school board in Sommers from 1992 to 1995. The investigation is ongoing, the District Attorney said, but lawyers for the accused say the District Attorney's office is being overzealous. Several years ago, Mrs. Pirro assigned two Assistant District Attorneys and two undercover agents to a new high-technology unit addressing illegal on-line activities. "Kids aren't just on the phone these days, they're on the Internet," Mrs. Pirro said. In recent years, Mrs. Pirro has said "a computer is the best weapon a pedophile can have." Pedophiles' activities and the ruthlessness with which pedophiles prey on juveniles have astounded both an unsuspecting public and law enforcement officials. The District Attorney said that in almost 17 years as a prosecutor she has not become inured to the variety of child molestation cases she sees. "After all this time, I'm still shocked," she said, "but then I grew up in Elmira, so I guess I still have hay in my hair." Most recently, seven men accused of using on-line chat rooms to arrange off-line rendezvous with someone they thought was a teen-age boy, were arrested on Sept. 22 by the District Attorney's office. Undercover agents posing as 15-year-old boys entered chat rooms on America Online and responded to the pedophiles' requests to meet them. "We reminded them that we were just 15 and that we hadn't done this before," Kenneth C. Citarella, chief of the High Technology Crimes Bureau, said. He also explained that the undercover agents responded only to the pedophiles' advances and avoided entrapment. He said pedophiles tend to work quickly, adding that "they now don't spend six months gaining a victim's trust." From the time the acquaintance is struck up on the Internet to the actual meeting can be a matter of hours. "They're brazen," Mr. Citarella said. "They want to meet right away, this afternoon." The men who were arrested late last month ranged in age from 26 to 53. They were from Queens, Manhattan, Harriman, Lake Peekskill, Happauge, Mount Vernon and White Plains. Some were arrested when they arrived for an intended sexual encounter -- including three who were arrested at spots in White Plains, where each was supposedly picking up a teen-ager. Others were arrested at their homes. Each suspect was charged with one count of attempting to disseminate indecent materials to minors, a felony. Also, a search warrant was executed at the residence of each of the defendants, and their computers were seized and examined by the District Attorney's office. Mr. Citarella said his bureau employs special software to find hidden and even deleted files. In analyzing the activities of pedophiles, the Assistant District Attorney said pedophiles often hold on to transcripts of conversations and sometimes pornographic photos -- which later turns out to be incriminating evidence -- seeking to "memorialize their acts." In another case two weeks earlier, a former chief of staff to a Yonkers Mayor became the subject of a sting. It is alleged that James Surdoval, 42 -- who was chief of staff to Terence M. Zaleski, a former Yonkers Mayor, and an economic development officer for the city at the time of his arrest -- performed a sex act with a 15-year-old boy after having on-line conversations with him and picking him up at his home. Mr. Surdoval was charged on Sept. 7 by a Westchester County grand jury with third-degree sodomy and endangering the welfare of a child. He was released on $20,000 bail. Neal Comer, a White Plains lawyer representing Mr. Surdoval, said that when his client rejected the advances of the boy, the youth threatened to accuse him of pedophilia and then "made good on the threat." Mr. Surdoval, who pleaded not guilty to the charges against him, has denied any sexual contact with the boy. "Even if my client is acquitted, which I fully expect him to be," Mr. Comer said, "how does he get his life back? The answer is, he probably never will get it back all the way." Mr. Comer also said that while the District Attorney was "making a big issue" of protecting children from men who go on the Internet to prey on youths, some teen-agers are actively seeking sexual experiences with men and are the instigators. Under state law, however, someone under 17 is not considered legally capable of giving consent to a sexual act. Another man arrested at the same time was Mr. Murphy, a former public relations executive at Pepsico in Purchase, who allegedly performed multiple sex acts with the same boy over a two-month period. He was charged with 18 counts of third-degree sodomy, one count of endangering the welfare of a child and one count of third-degree reckless endangerment. The latter charge was for allegedly committing the sex acts without the use of protective measures -- while being HIV-positive and without telling the boy of the disease. He too was freed on $20,000 bail. It is not known if Mr. Murphy and Mr. Surdoval knew each other or knew of each other's contacts with the Westchester boy, whom they contacted and saw independently, the District Attorney's office said. Psychologists explain that 95 percent of pedophiles -- the overwhelming majority are men -- are people with recurrent fantasies or urges that are culturally deviant. Patricia Singleton, a clinical psychologist in Mount Kisco, has described pedophiles as immature, often loners and either not married or experiencing difficulties in establishing close adult relationships. While pedophiles have often sought careers in teaching, the ministry and Scouting, the Internet has opened new territory for them, enabling law enforcement officials to go on-line to ferret them out. Mr. Citarella said that many on-line pedophiles hold traditional jobs. In the case of Anthony R. Stabile of Floral Park, an undercover volunteer posing as a 14-year-old girl for the District Attorney's office met the pedophile on America Online. In a series of chat conversations, the 38-year-old Mr. Stabile, who was unemployed, inquired about the girl's sexual experience and described what he wanted from her. He was arrested by investigators in April 1998 when he arrived at the Galleria Mall in White Plains for their meeting. Mr. Stabile, who kept notes in his home of on-line chats, according to the District Attorney's office, was convicted last May 4, after a jury trial, of attempting to disseminate indecent material to a minor. A defense lawyer, Robert J. Collini, who practices in Brooklyn and who represented Mr. Stabile, said on Wednesday that it is difficult to select a nonbiased jury in many pedophile cases "because society is so indocrinated that even when they just hear these types of allegations, they become highly prejudiced." He said also that the publicity in an "overenthusiastic press" given to such cases, especially the Internet cases involving pedophilia and the new technology, has also prejudiced the public. "There's a 'let's nip this in the bud' mentality, a vigilante attitude that comes into play when anyone is accused of this crime." Mr. DeRosario, who was awaiting trial for allegedly molesting five boys, was charged with 44 counts of sodomy, sexual abuse, child pornography and other offenses in the molesting of four other boys between 13 and 16 whom he supposedly met in an Internet chat room. Mr. DeRosario is the subject of a continuing investigation into the killing of Orlandito Rosario Maldonado, 12, whose body was found in a shallow grave along the Saw Mill River Parkway in January, Chief George Longworth of the Dobbs Ferry Police said. The chief also said that Orlandito was last seen in the apartment building where Mr. DeRosario lived. The Maldonado investigation, Chief Longworth added, "is growing daily." Refusing to give details about the case, the police chief would say only that three Dobbs Ferry detectives and three detectives from the Major Crime Squad of the county police, in conjunction with the District Attorney's office, were working on the case and "investigating thousands of items" of evidence. "We're interviewing a lot of people DeRosario had contact with and other suspects," Chief Longworth said. "I can't be any more specific." He also declined to say what caused the death of Orlandito Rosario Maldonado. Mr. DeRosario is in the custody of the Westchester Department of Corrections. Tying together the recent cases, Mrs. Pirro said that charges against Mr. Surdoval and Mr. Murphy stemmed from a continuing investigation into the murder of Orlandito. She too would not be more specific.  Suggestions for Protecting Children TO prevent children from becoming victims of on-line pedophiles, the District Attorney's office recommends that parents and guardians: Be aware of what your children are doing on line. Do not be afraid to become involved, the office says. At home, set up your Internet connection in the family room, den or kitchen instead of children's bedrooms so you can watch and learn what children are doing on line. Periodically, monitor their activities. Teach children rules for Internet use. Children are told not to talk to strangers, but often they are not warned about meeting someone they contact on the Internet. A child should never provide personal information (name, home address, phone number, school name or on-line password) to anyone. They should also be taught not to accept electronic information on line (like E-mail files or Web addresses) from strangers. Some of those files could contain pornographic images. Warn children not to chat with strangers on line unless an adult is there to supervise. Tell children to access only chat rooms that are appropriate for their age group. Remind them that if someone says something that makes them feel uncomfortable, they should not respond and should alert a parent or teacher immediately. Protect passwords. Younger children should never be allowed to log on by themselves. Screen what a child can access on the Internet. Screening will protect children from offensive, inappropriate or dangerous materials, according to the District Attorney's office. Many Internet and on-line services provide screening software. Never allow a child or teen-ager to fill out an on-line profile to be used in chat rooms. Predators often scan the Internet looking for their young victims. If you or your child has been sent offensive material on the Internet, contact your Internet provider immediately. Also, if you have reason to believe that someone has been involved in inappropriate, criminal or sexually explicit dialogues with a child, contact your local police department or the Westchester District Attorney's Office. The telephone number for the High Technology Crimes Bureau is 285-3460.   ELSA BRENNER http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Jeanine Pirro with Kenneth C. Citarella of High Technology Crimes unit. (George M. Gutierrez for The New York Times)(pg. 12); James Surdoval, above, and Patrick Murphy in police pictures. (pg. 8)

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
CYBERSCOUT
body: MAPPING SOFTWARE It's easy to forget these days, but a computer does more than connect to the World Wide Web. You can use it to write an actual letter inquiring about room rates, print it out and, if you remember how, put it in an envelope, attach a stamp and drop it into a mailbox. You can buy software with information on destinations, descriptions of hotels, parks and resorts, or maps that you can make for yourself. The software, like a printed article, is fixed in place when it is published, unlike a Web site, which can be constantly updated (theoretically, anyway). One of the earliest mapping programs, DeLorme's Street Atlas USA, came out on CD-ROM in 1991. The seventh version of the program was published this fall, and it is almost too rich with possibilities: There are 8 menus across the top of the screen, 19 icons under the menus and 6 additional icons to the right of the windows where you type in the start and finish of your trip. A full installation of the Atlas takes up around 256 megabytes of hard-disk space, and you still must have the CD in its drive. I punched in newyork City as my starting point and the New Jersey town I live in as my destination. Detailed maps appeared on the screen, taking me through the Holland Tunnel and along a reasonable path, though the Lincoln Tunnel would have been my choice. I had to scroll through many maps on a 15-inch screen before I got home. There the town was, with little blue rectangles marking such points of interest as Dunkin' Donuts. (Version 7.0 adds almost 3 million "points of interest," most of them more interesting than that.) I entered my address, and a little "home" symbol appeared in what seemed to be the right place, although without the street name. Going into one of the icons at the top of the screen, I typed in the ZIP code of a friend who lives in San Francisco. In a moment, a map of that part of the city appeared. I typed in his full address and the "home" snapped onto the map on the correct block. Street Atlas USA 7.0 is compatible with the global positioning satellites used for navigation systems in cars, and will work out a new route if the driver goes off track (and is traveling with a computer). If you have a Palm or Windows CE handheld computer, you can transfer maps and routes to them. The program works with Windows 95, 98 or NT 4.0 and should be widely available for less than $45.  INFORMATION PLEASE www.gogoinfo.com You can go on the Web for travel information without getting bogged down in making reservations. Gogoinfo has names, phone numbers and often links to Web sites of airlines, cruise lines, lodgings, trains and buses, as well as destinations, attractions and travel publications. The Attractions section contained casinos, museums, parks and ski areas. Other sources included phone numbers for the Federal Aviation Administration consumer hot line and the Thomas Cook Currency Service.  OFFICIAL SITES Every state, and virtually every city, has an official Web site that provides the ABC's for travelers. Since I was in gogoinfo anyway, I linked to several of them from there. The San Diego Convention and Visitors Bureau, www.sandiego.org, was typical, with listings of lodgings, shopping, dining spots and maps. The Austin, Texas, Convention and Visitors Bureau, www .austin360.com/acvb, describes the city as the "live music capital of the world" and, appropriately enough, quotes Willie Nelson as saying "it's a great place to live." All these sites provide an easy entry to trip planning as long as you bear in mind that their purpose is promotion, not objective information.   L. R. SHANNON http://www.nytimes.com

body: Dow Jones Industrials Drop On New Fears of Inflation The Dow Jones industrial average and other stock market gauges plunged after an inflation report showed the biggest monthly increase in nine years in prices at the producer level and Alan Greenspan, the chairman of the Federal Reserve, alarmed investors by warning that the stock market might be more risky than many people now believe. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Co. BuysMassachusetts Paper for $295 Million and Posts Rise in Profit
body: The newyork Times Company bought The Worcester Telegram & Gazette yesterday for $295 million, expanding its reach in Massachusetts, where it already owns The Boston Globe, and making a major investment in the newspaper industry, which is currently buoyed by record advertising. The industry's boom was reflected yesterday in the Times Company's earnings report, which showed net income for the third quarter rising 9.2 percent, to $60 million, on revenue of $729.7 million. The revenue total was 6.9 percent above the 1998 third-quarter total of $682.7 million. Operating profit, excluding such special items as the cost of work force reductions at The Boston Globe, rose 11.2 percent, to $112.8 million from $101.4 million, an increase spurred by a 9.9 percent increase in newspaper advertising revenue, which rose to $460.9 million. Excluding the special items, the company earned 36 cents a diluted share, one cent above the consensus estimate reported by First Call/ Thomson Financial. The company's purchase of the Worcester newspaper, with a daily circulation of 107,000 and a Sunday circulation of 134,000 in central Massachusetts, ended a lively competition among at least seven newspaper companies bidding for the remaining newspaper properties of the Chronicle Publishing Company, which sold its flagship, The San Francisco Chronicle, this summer to the Hearst Corporation. One rival bidder, according to those who participated in the negotiations, was the Community Newspaper Company, which is based in Needham, Mass., and publishes dailies in Framingham and Milford, Mass., as well as more than 100 nondaily newspapers around the state. Another was the Denver-based Media News Group Inc., which owns five dailies in northern and central Massachusetts. The competition among bidders reflects the desire of newspaper companies to consolidate, or cluster, their holdings in one geographic area, to gain efficiencies in everything from printing and distribution to advertising sales. Nancy Nielsen, a spokeswoman for the Times Company, said that the company forecast economies in joint advertising sales between The Globe and The Telegram & Gazette as well as centralizing of newsprint buying, accounting and record-keeping. According to one person who has inspected the paper's financial statements, the $295 million price was about 13.5 times the 1998 cash flow of The Telegram & Gazette -- a multiple well below that paid by Pulitzer Inc. to Chronicle Publishing for The Pantagraph, a newspaper in Bloomington, Ill., that has a circulation of 49,600. Eight days ago, Pulitzer announced its acquisition of The Pantagraph for a purchase price of $180 million, representing a multiple of roughly 19 times 1998 cash flow, according to one newspaper company adviser who had seen the financial information circulated by Chronicle Publishing. But the Worcester acquisition was still a strong reminder of the prices newspapers can command these days. "The Worcester price is just reflective of the very strong state of the newspaper marketplace," said Owen Van Essen, the president of the newspaper brokerage firm of Dirks, Van Essen. He also said that newspapers the size of The Telegram & Gazette that dominate their markets -- the newspaper reaches 43 percent of the homes in Worcester County -- do not come on the market often. Mr. Van Essen added, "There is bullishness in newspaper companies" -- a comment bolstered by recent increases in the share price of some newspaper companies. The Times Company, Knight Ridder, Dow Jones & Company and Times Mirror Company all hit 52-week highs within the last week. The Worcester purchase, however, had little effect on analysts' views of the activities of the Times Company, particularly since the cash outlay for the deal is dwarfed by the $376 million the company has spent to repurchase its stock this year. Two analysts, Lauren Rich Fine of Merrill Lynch & Company and Kevin R. Gruneich of Bear, Stearns, used the same word -- "nonevent" -- to describe the Worcester newspaper purchase. Both analysts focused instead on the resurgence of advertising revenue at The Boston Globe, which took in $114.4 million in ad revenue in the third quarter, a 9.8 percent increase over the corresponding period in 1998. The newyork Times newspaper took in $260.5 million in the period, an increase of 10.9 percent. "The most pleasant surprise was the upward pivot in Boston Globe advertising," Mr. Gruneich said. He added that he also saw "some awfully good momentum at Times Company Digital" -- the division of the company that includes Web sites like nytimes.com and boston.com. The number of registered users of The newyork Times on the Web rose to 8.7 million, an increase of 900,000 over the June 30 figure. Times Company shares closed yesterday at $40.4375, down 56.25 cents and off more than $2 from the record high of $43 reached on Monday. http://www.nytimes.com

title: 4 More Charged in Inquiry Into Pedophiles' Use of Net
body: In a continuing investigation into the possible use of the Internet by pedophiles, four more men, including a former school board member in Somers, N.Y., were indicted today on charges of having sex with boys they met through the use of a computer. The investigation by the Westchester County District Attorney's office, which has produced 10 indictments involving 7 defendants and 11 victims, stems from the investigation into the unsolved slaying of a 12-year-old Yonkers boy whose body was found in January. Authorities have not indicated that any of the defendants were involved in the death of the youth, Orlandito Rosario Maldonado. More arrests are expected as interviews with victims lead to additional suspects, the authorities said. One of the four defendants whose arrest was announced today, William Chidester, 58, served on the Board of Education in Somers from 1992 to 1995. Mr. Chidester was indicted on three counts of sodomy in the third degree and one count of endangering the welfare of a child and accused of having oral sex with a 15-year-old at the youth's home after they met on the Internet. School officials in Somers received the news of his arrest with dismay.  Richard L. Braudell, Superintendent of the Somers Central School District, said, "My only comment is one of sadness for any victims, just sadness at this whole situation." Two neighbors said Mr. Chidester was married. Last month, a high-ranking Yonkers city official and a former public relations executive for Pepsico were indicted on charges of sexually molesting a Westchester teen-ager. At a news conference today, District Attorney Jeanine F. Pirro also announced additional charges against Robert D. DeRosario, 36, a Yonkers resident who has been previously described by authorities as the chief suspect in the death of the Maldonado youth but has not been charged with the slaying. He had been previously charged with sexually molesting and sodomizing nine boys, and today he was charged with sexually abusing two more boys, 15 and 16, as well as with trying to bribe and tamper with witnesses. The dead boy, whose body was found in a shallow grave beside the Saw Mill River Parkway in Dobbs Ferry, was last seen in Mr. DeRosario's apartment, the police have said. Officials said they widened their investigation to include pedophiles' use of the Internet after they found evidence in Mr. DeRosario's apartment of his solicitation of minors over the Internet. Some of the suspects arrested today were familiar with one another through their use of the Internet, and some of the indictments involved the same victim, Ms. Pirro said. She said her office has sometimes been frustrated by the unwillingness of "several victims" to testify.  "There are still some families who believe they can go on with their lives and sweep this under the carpet," she said. Ms. Pirro said pedophiles' use of the Internet was increasingly common. "They are roaming the Net everywhere," she said. "This is a new area of crime, and parents need to be aware of the fact that pedophiles are reaching out to their children in the privacy of their own homes through the computer." "Years ago it was through a video arcade or in a park -- an actual physical meeting." Also arrested was Walter Salvatore, 39, of Phoenix and Staten Island, on charges of disseminating indecent material to a minor in the first degree and endangering the welfare of a child. Authorities accused Mr. Salvatore, who is being held in Arizona, of sending nude photographs of himself over the Internet to a 15-year-old in Westchester and then soliciting sex with him on line. Extradition proceedings for his return to Westchester have begun. Another defendant, Guy Ebersole, 39, a theater worker of Pelham, N.Y., was indicted on three counts of sodomy in the third degree and one count of endangering the welfare of a child. Mr. Ebersole is accused of having oral sex with a 15-year-old in his Pelham home after meeting the teen-ager over the Internet. The fourth defendant, George Noll, 36, a truck driver in Thornwood, N.Y., was indicted on six counts of sodomy in the third degree and one count of endangering the welfare of a child. Mr. Noll is accused of having oral and anal sex with a 15-year-old boy in Mr. Noll's apartment and his car. At an arraignment today, Judge Peter M. Leavitt of Westchester County Court set bail at $15,000 each for Mr. Chidester and Mr. Ebersoll and $25,000 for Mr. Noll. None of the men charged today were accused of forcing the teen-agers to have sex, but because the boys were minors, the law does not recognize any consent they may give. Today's arrests were based on statements from boys. Earlier arrests involved a sting, in which agents from the District Attorney's office posed as underage teen-agers. Neither prosecutors nor court officials were able to provide the names of the defendants' lawyers. http://www.nytimes.com

title: A Plan for Trading on Wireless Phones
body: An on-line brokerage firm, the Ameritrade Holding Corporation, and Sprint PCS Group, the nation's largest all-digital wireless telephone network, said today that they had forged an agreement that would enable their customers to trade on line over the wireless network of Sprint PCS, a unit of the Sprint Corporation. The agreement will also let customers of the companies get access to their investment accounts and receive stock information on the Sprint PCS Wireless Web. The two-way transaction service is the first of its kind through wireless phones and is expected to be available in late October. Customers of Sprint PCS, which is based in Kansas City, Mo., who have an Internet-ready Sprint PCS phone will be able to get access to their Ameritrade account at no extra charge as part of any Sprint PCS Wireless Web service plan -- starting at less than $10 a month when added to an existing voice plan of $29.99 and higher. Once an Ameritrade account is called over a Sprint PCS phone, all Ameritrade fees apply in the same manner as if a customer were using a desktop computer for standard on-line brokerage services -- now $8 for each stock-market order. Sprint PCS operates the largest 100 percent digital, 100 percent PCS nationwide wireless network, serving more than 4,000 communities. http://www.nytimes.com

title: For Indian Nations, Virtual Trade Routes
body: ON a recent trip to visit the Catawba Indian Nation in Catawba, S.C., Dan Umstead, a member of the Oneida Nation of central newyork, was shown centuries-old pottery of Oneida design excavated there, some 800 miles from home. For members of the six-nation Iroquois Confederacy, which includes the Oneida, it was once common to travel half a continent on foot to trade with other Indian nations. That trade became much more difficult in the 19th century, when many tribes were moved to reservations. As some Indian nations, thanks in large part to gambling, have flourished economically again in the 1990's, nation-to-nation trade has become a hot topic among tribal leaders. The modern version of nation-to-nation trade involves goods ranging from T-shirts to computers, and the trade routes are virtual rather than physical. The marketplace is the Internet. Mr. Umstead, for example, is the Oneida's manager of Internet services. At a meeting in June of leaders of the United South and Eastern Tribes, or USET, a nonprofit intertribal organization, Mr. Umstead unveiled the Nation to Nation Trade Forum, an on-line bulletin board (bbs.oneida-nation.net) aimed at connecting the organization's 23 member tribes to discuss trade. "The USET committees thought that the idea of reaffirming these traditional trade ties between nations was good," Mr. Umstead said. "But let's take it a step further, into the 21st century." The Web site even has a fill-in-the-blank model of a bilateral trade agreement; it is available for downloading, although that service has had no takers so far. Keller George, president of United South and Eastern Tribes, estimates that 60 to 70 percent of the organization's member tribes are on line. Those who are not, like the small Gena band of Choctaw Indians in Alexandria, La., who are currently starting a deck-chair business, can market their products to different Indian nations through the tribal organization's Web site. "We're just trying to get back to the basics of how the Indian people a long time ago did nation-to-nation trade, by finding out what products they had to offer," Mr. George said. "Then it was done on a more personal basis, but today I think we can do it with technology." One tribe that is not on line yet but plans to be by the end of the year is the Unkechaug tribe of Long Island, which sells its organic coffee to the Oneida of both newyork and Wisconsin and to the Winnebago tribe in Nebraska. The coffee is already available on line at Allnative.com, a Web commerce site (www.allnative.com) owned by the Winnebago that also sells Indian-made crafts, computers and clothing. "There is significant production and development going on in Indian country," said the Unkechaug chief, Harry Wallace. "There is also a significant marketing ability." A hurdle facing both Mr. Wallace and Mr. George is the potential for on-line fraud. How can the Indian traders be sure that they are dealing with people who are in fact American Indians? The use of passwords has been discussed, but Mr. George says he is not worried about the future of his new venture over all. "Our people have been survivors because we've been able to adapt to whatever was there for us," he said. "We've gone from using natural resources to using technology. If we don't take advantage of the technology that is there for us today, then shame on us." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: Incognito Spinmeisters Battle On-Line Critics
body: THE scene unfolds on the Internet every day: a pack of outraged consumers takes over the discussion in an on-line forum with heated criticism of some offending product, perhaps a brand of stereo speakers. Then someone asks, If these speakers are so awful, how could the company have moved from No. 10 to No. 2 in the last year? After that, the criticism in the forum fades. It would be fair to suspect, in a case like this, that the participant who raised the question that turned the criticism around worked for the company that made the speakers. In fact, a small industry is emerging among consultants who specialize in spinning on-line discussions to favor the positions of companies and interest groups. Shabbir J. Safdar and his business partner, Jonah Seiger, regularly adopt pseudonyms and participate in on-line discussions on behalf of some clients. Their firm, Mindshare Internet Campaigns, in Washington, specializes in running the Internet side of advocacy campaigns. It offers the spin doctor service as part of the package. Some firms, in keeping with a traditional practice in public relations, recruit scientists and other experts to voice clients' perspectives in on-line discussions. Matthew Benson, a senior director at the Washington public relations firm Bivings Woodell, and Ken Deutsch, vice president of Internet strategic communications at Issue Dynamics, a public affairs firm in Washington, have specialized for years in steering experts to on-line forums on behalf of clients. Without question, these practices have made people taking part in on-line discussions suspicious. Questions about participants' identities and affiliations are becoming more common. In recent months, for example, on-line discussions about the registration of Internet domain names have been packed with revelations that some participants have received backing from companies affected by the issue. Jay Fenello, who, until recently, was president of Iperdome, a domain name registration company in Atlanta, has weighed in regularly in 10 on-line discussion groups against the policies of the Government-backed group that is deciding the future of the registrations. Until he closed the company in September to become a full-time consultant, he usually signed his messages by identifying himself as president of Iperdome. But his opponents recently posted messages saying that Mr. Fenello has also been working as a consultant for Network Solutions, the company whose monopoly on domain name registrations is being dismantled. In response, he acknowledged the tie but played down its importance, saying his opponents were using it just to discredit him. "It's something that I freely admitted," Mr. Fenello said. "It's just like Presidential politics. When something can be used as a weapon, it is. "I challenge anybody to detect any changes in my statements when I was working with Network Solutions and when I was not. Everybody in this debate is somehow funded by somebody." Whether companies' efforts to sway opinions on the Internet, surreptitiously or openly, ultimately improves the quality of on-line discourse or damages its credibility is debatable. Some argue that the practice of spinning discussions is less chilling than it is for companies to sue their on-line critics -- just as lawsuits once became a tame alternative to dueling. Not that companies have stopped turning to the courts. David Sobel, general counsel for the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a nonprofit research group, said the center had identified 20 cases in recent months in which companies had filed defamation suits against on-line critics. "It wouldn't surprise people who frequent these discussion groups to know that there are people being paid to say good things about a company," Mr. Sobel said. "That tradition comes with the territory of the Internet. What traditionally hasn't come with the territory is getting hauled into court." When compared to litigation, Mr. Sobel said, even using deception to try to turn around criticism on line is "a better approach." "The antidote to speech," he added, "is more speech." Because participants in Internet forums are becoming more suspicious, they are quick to challenge anyone who seems to be hiding an affiliation. In August, for example, people participating in a discussion of broadband Internet access started questioning Audrie Krause about her ties to AT&T, a major company concerned with the issue. Ms. Krause, a consultant in San Francisco, had presented herself in such discussions as a consumer advocate and argued against Government regulation. In a telephone interview, Ms. Krause said she did "Internet outreach" for a political consulting firm whose client is AT&T, but that the work "really isn't relevant to the position I'm taking." "The work that I'm doing that's funded by specific interests is very aboveboard," she said. Her opponents argue otherwise. Jamie Love, director of the Consumer Project on Technology, a nonprofit group, said forum participants were uncomfortable with Ms. Krause's ties. "She always stands up and says, 'As a consumer advocate, this is the position I take,' " Mr. Love said. "You should say, 'As a lobbyist for AT&T, this is where I come out on it.' " Tora Bikson, a senior scientist at the Rand Corporation who has studied on-line discourse, compared the practice of influencing on-line discussions with "pump priming" in public meetings, in which politicians plant supporters in the audience to ask friendly questions. The practice on the Internet is "more distressing," she contended, because people in the audience may expect questions to be planted in public meetings but may not be aware that perspectives are being planted in on-line settings. "If you don't know there are ringers and spin doctors," Dr. Bikson said, "that immediately damages the credibility of the forum. People could end up damaging the medium because everybody does want it to be this open medium." On its face, the fear of the power of on-line critics may appear to be unjustified. On-line discussion lists and forums tend to reach only several hundred people at most. But opinions formed in even the most obscure electronic byways can reach the mainstream quickly. Consultants who monitor forums for companies consider on-line discussions to be an early warning system for consumer complaints and public perceptions. At best, the consultants can strangle misinformation in the electronic cradle. "If participated in properly," said Mr. Benson, at Bivings Woodell, "these can be vehicles for shaping emerging issues." He and other consultants approach on-line forums cautiously. When deciding whether to intervene in a discussion, Mr. Benson said, they weigh a number of factors: How serious a forum is it? Do influential people frequent the discussion? How much reach does the forum have outside its own boundaries? Are the critics considered influential by the group, or are they merely considered annoying? The hardest part of the job, many consultants say, is to encourage companies to use restraint in their responses. "You see a lot of companies overreacting," said Mr. Deutsch, at Issue Dynamics. "They don't realize that not everyone is influential. They want to fight out every opponent on every discussion list they see." The easiest situation to handle is when critics of a company are posting blatantly inaccurate information. In those cases, consultants encourage representatives of the companies to respond openly and set the record straight. That strategy worked well earlier this year for Steve Mihaylo, chief executive of Inter-Tel, a digital communications company based in Phoenix. On a Yahoo message board read by many of the company's large shareholders, critics were ripping into the company's employees and marketing practices. When the criticism of individuals became too personal, Mr. Mihaylo stepped up to defend them. In his first posting, he wrote, "There is so much misinformation and just plain bad manners on this message board that I thought this might be a refreshing way to bring some objectivity to this process." The tone on the message board changed immediately. All the participants started addressing the chief executive of the company that they had just been trashing as Mr. Mihaylo. The virulence of their questions diminished. But consultants warn that in some cases, a company only fans the hostility by issuing a statement openly. In cases like that, consultants may enter the discussion using false identities or by misrepresenting their interests. But the tactic is risky -- so risky that some firms stick to recruiting outside parties like scientists or other advocates for a company's position to get involved without disclosing the company's role. The potential for trouble is why Mr. Safdar, of Mindshare Internet Campaigns, recommends a light touch for companies when they intercede in on-line discussions. "If you walk into a discussion that is ripe to go a certain direction and you ask a question and the crowd is ripe to go that direction, that's all you have to do," he said. "You say, 'If they were evil, would they do this?' " But to gauge a group's dynamics requires long-term monitoring. Bivings Woodell, for example, employs a division of four or five people dedicated to monitoring. "You have to sit somebody in front of the computer," Mr. Safdar said, "and they have to develop a cultural memory for the issues they're following." Such labor-intensive work can command large fees. Mr. Safdar said he had heard of companies running up bills of hundreds of thousands of dollars for a year's monitoring and intervention. "I've seen some big price tags," he said. "I've seen clients who were very, very worried and would plunk down large sums of money." Consultants describe the subterfuge as a way to balance discussions and defend the truth in a medium where facts can prevail. Within that framework, they argue, the practice is healthier for Internet discussion than a rash of lawsuits. "A lot of them want to sue," Mr. Deutsch said of clients who approach his firm. "It's a whole new ball game, and you can't operate that way anymore. How a company treats organizations and individuals on the Internet will affect how the public will perceive the company." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Steve Mihaylo, chief executive of Inter-Tel, calmed a recent heated Internet discussion of his company. (Jeff Topping for The New York Times); People in on-line discussions are often suspicious of company officers or consultants who join the debates. Jay Fenello, a consultant, regularly participates in such forums. (Alan S. Weiner for The New York Times)(pg. G9)  Drawing (Randy Jones)

title: In Wired World, Much Is Free at Click of a Mouse
body: For years, marketers have known that one word, more than any other, can spur people to action. The magic word, of course, is "free." And the wheels of commerce have long been greased with free samples, free trial issues, free toasters at the bank, or free tote bags with every bottle of perfume. But those are Cracker Jack prizes compared with what is happening these days on the Internet, where the slogan is quickly becoming: buy nothing, get everything free. With hundreds of Internet start-ups hellbent on immediate visibility and rapid growth, the giveaways have moved beyond information, like magazine articles and stock quotes, into products and services that could otherwise cost hundreds of dollars. Consumers can download a word-processing program or a recording of a hit single, sign up for a new phone number to receive faxes and voicemail, or even call long distance -- all without paying a penny. Some sites will set you up in business with your own on-line store free, if you can think of something to sell that people will pay for. If you want to take advantage of this costless cornucopia but are not yet wired to the Web, don't despair. A bunch of companies want to provide free Internet access. FreePC.com hopes to give away a computer, too. And if you need to communicate with your militantly unwired Uncle Waldo, postage4free.com will send you a stack of stamped envelopes, gratis. "You name it, and there is a start-up somewhere that wants to give it away free," said James Breyer, the managing partner of Accel Partners, a Silicon Valley venture-capital firm. All this comes at a price, of course. Those free envelopes are covered with advertising, and so are most of the other free offers.
