A Satellite Model For Streaming Media
body: As the Internet moves to broad band, the market for Internet audio and video, so-called streaming media, is expected to explode. But congestion associated with this bandwidth-hogging traffic can crash Web sites, drown out conventional traffic and degrade the quality of the sound or picture. And so iBEAM, a start-up backed by the likes of Intel, hopes to address these problems with an ambitious plan to deliver high-quality streaming media over the Internet. The company, based in Sunnyvale, Calif., begins formal operations this week. It relies on a cable-television distribution model: using satellite broadcast technology to take a single stream of data and direct it to a network of server computers spread around the Internet. The audio and video can be either delivered live by satellite or stored on servers for delivery on demand. The iBEAM servers are at the edges of the Internet. So its satellite approach, while not a remedy to congestion problems, at least avoids the costs and congestion associated with so-called Internet backbone networks. "Our hope is that we will be as big as traditional media," said Tom Gillis, iBEAM's assistant vice president for marketing. Rather than charging Internet service providers for the service, iBEAM intends to charge only the content providers, which would then recoup their expenditures with advertising revenues from iBEAM's targeted advertising service. The company has already equipped 60 Internet service providers with servers capable of Web casting to a total audience of 300,000, with 90 more installations expected later this year. Many content providers have signed on, including BBC and Bloomberg News, Mr. Gillis said, adding that MSNBC, Sony Tristar, Warner Brothers and Warner Interactive were expected to join soon. Mr. Gillis also said that iBEAM was in talks with the three big television networks. Some analysts said that while iBEAM's approach was clever and its partnerships impressive, they did not expect the satellite distribution model to prevail in the long term. "It's exciting, but it's a stopgap," said Michael Kleeman, an independent telecommunications industry consultant. But for now, iBEAM has received more than $60 million in investments from companies like Intel and Liberty Media and venture capitalists like Accel Partners and Crosspoint Venture Partners, and is close to announcing investments with Microsoft and Sony, Mr. Gillis said. SARA ROBINSON http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: iBEAM aims to offer streaming media.

title:
E-Commerce Report;
Turning small businesses' Internet dreams into reality.
body: COMPANIES hoping to do business on the Web are being bombarded with more solutions than ever -- all promising to provide services that address the problem of how to set up shop on line. And within the E-commerce sphere, the segment that "solutions providers" seem to think needs the most help is the small business category. In fact, they may be right. According to the unitedstates Small Business Administration, only 30 percent of the nation's 24 million small businesses accept orders on the Web, and far fewer can process credit card transactions. But as more of those companies develop a full-scale Internet presence -- and as everyone who ever had a lemonade stand decides to sell something on the Web -- E-commerce software and service providers are competing more furiously for market share. One increasingly popular approach is to offer "all-in-one" E-commerce packages, in which merchants pay a nominal monthly fee for software that enables them to build a site that is then hosted by a third party -- sparing the client the cost of Web servers and fast Internet connections. Analysts say such services generally fall short of providing everything businesses need to succeed on the Web, which is, of course, what many promise to do. Still, all-in-one packages have proven to be a good way to test the Internet waters, according to many business people who have used them. And as more competitors enter the market, analysts say, the quality of low-priced E-commerce services should improve. Rosa Simon, for one, can attest to the wide array of low-cost E-commerce packages available. Last year, Ms. Simon decided to build a Web site, www.blindsdepot.com, to extend the reach of her window treatments business, which she had previously run by herself selling door to door. A technology neophyte, Ms. Simon looked first at one of the market leaders in one-stop E-commerce setup, Yahoo Stores. As with other companies, Yahoo enables users to build a Web site in minutes by filling out a series of forms on line. For $100 a month, digital entrepreneurs can post their store on Yahoo's site and offer as many as 50 products for sale. The more products offered for sale, the higher Yahoo's monthly fee. Like its competitors, which range from established companies like I.B.M. to Internet service providers like Hiway Technologies and other portal sites, Yahoo offers a host of additional features. It aggregates orders and sends them via fax to the store owner for processing, encrypts credit card numbers during processing and offers a shopping cart feature, so customers can pay for multiple products at once. What Ms. Simon could not get from Yahoo -- or any E-commerce provider, for that matter -- was placement high up on the results pages of search engines. Seeking more shoppers, Ms. Simon opted for an all-in-one package provided by iMall, which guarantees placement on its shopping site, www.imall.com. When that also failed to generate sales, she built a store using software provided by Concentric Network, an Internet service provider that hosted the site for $50 a month, and she set about learning how to manipulate the search engines for better placement. However, the Concentric software tools were somewhat limited for her purposes, Ms. Simon said, so she spent about $500 to build a more sophisticated site with Shopsite software, from Open Market. With the help of a consultant, she also learned how to increase her site's visibility on search engines. The payoff, at last, came in March, when sales started to roll. "I'm making much more than before," Ms. Simon said, though she would not disclose specific numbers. "And I'm working much less." Jack Staff, chief economist with Zona Research, a unit of Intelliquest, said "there are literally dozens of features that are needed to make an E-commerce site work well" beyond those offered by the one-stop E-commerce companies. Among other things, Mr. Staff said, small businesses need technologies to analyze customer activity on the site, gauge the effectiveness of advertisements, personalize the site for each visitor, build incentive programs, offer coupons and instant discounts, confirm orders and returns and automate email responses. "And then the real issue becomes how to get well known with consumers," Mr. Staff said. In this regard at least, E-commerce service providers feel their customers' pain. According to Andrew Beebe, chief executive of Bigstep.com, which provides E-commerce services to businesses, profitability and visibility are difficult to achieve in this category. "There are a lot of people doing this," he said, "and they're making a lot of noise." As for profitability, Mr. Beebe said his company, which began operations last month, "is not making any money at all right now." The plan, at least, is to provide free help to small businesses starting E-commerce sites, then sell them more advanced technology services along the lines of what Mr. Staff, of Zona, described. With 20,000 small businesses currently signed up and hundreds more being added daily, Mr. Beebe said he can negotiate discounts from E-commerce technology providers and extract a margin with every sale to his customers. "But this really is going to be a tight margin game," he said. That is especially likely if his competitors keep driving the price of services down. "Every time someone else thinks they're going to sell something, we're going to give it away," said Serge Wilson, chief executive of Freemerchant.com, which provides E-commerce services completely free of charge. Mr. Wilson, whose company has signed up 20,000 merchants, earns money by offering suppliers like the Office Max retail chain access to Freemerchant store owners. Mr. Wilson sees his service as an ideal entree for people who are not sure they want to commit thousands of dollars to an Internet business. "A certain percentage of our merchants will never sell successfully," he said. "It takes the right product, and time and effort." It also takes more expertise in a given category than many E-commerce newbies are willing to develop, said Larry Erlich, founder of Domainregistry.com, who provides consulting services to small businesses. "Almost without fail, the people who try to start an E-commerce site try something they have absolutely no expertise in," he said. "They're usually involved in a business they could probably make some money with on the Web, but they want to do something else. It's clicks and wishes." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Rosa Simon, of Huntington Beach, Calif., runs her Blindsdepot.com Internet company from her home. Despite some initial difficulties, she says that her business has grown sharply. (Ed Carreon for The newyork Times)

title:
MEDIA;
Web Catches On With Fleet Street
body: Peter Martin, a senior editor, strides briskly through the newsroom of The Financial Times, gesturing to a bank of computer terminals where journalists craft the news for FT.com, the paper's Web site. In a matter of months, Mr. Martin tells a visitor, that relatively small unit will be gone, replaced by something much more innovative that, far more extensively than at any other British paper, will erase what he calls the ideological barrier between on-line news and the printed word. In its place, he says, will be a redesigned, integrated newsroom where journalists will work to feed both the Web site and the distinctively salmon-colored British newspaper. And that is not all, says Mr. Martin, whose title is deputy editor and editorial director for the FT Internet Businesses. The Web site will be reinvented as a full-fledged Internet portal, featuring a search engine for business readers, diary and email capabilities and expanded use of columnists and analysts to provide an early peek into their thinking. "We envisage it becoming a global business portal," Mr. Martin said. In many ways the development at The Financial Times, which expects to hire as many as 100 new staff members and spend up to $70 million on its on-line expansion this year alone, reflects both a broader push by its owner, Pearson P.L.C., to wring global value from its flagship, blue-chip brand name, and a response to growing competition from a range of business-oriented Web sites like TheStreet.com., in which The newyork Times is an investor. But The Financial Times's ambitious expansion is also being played out against a familiar backdrop. As Britain's broadsheet papers look to the Web, their traditional, no-holds-barred competition has taken a new turn and the fabled wars of what used to be known as Fleet Street have spilled into cyberspace. These days, visitors to the former Fleet Street's Web sites can expect to be enticed not simply by a rehash of the day's headlines but by a broader palette, including what George Brock, managing editor of The Times of London, calls "rolling journalism," driven by the same urge for speed as are news agencies like Reuters, Bloomberg News or The Associated Press. Indeed, Britain's on-line broadsheet newspapers are promoting a range of interconnected offerings -- all advertising-driven -- designed to lure just about everyone from job seekers to movie buffs to highflying executives. And they are not just competing with each other. "On line, the British are competing head to head in a firmly competitive market where we are also competing with the broadcast media," said Danny Meadows-Klue, publisher of the electronic version The Daily Telegraph (www.telegraph.co.uk). "Our competitive landscape is no longer just newspapers. It's TV, radio, specialist sectors like football, where we are competing with football clubs' own home pages." Of course, the former Fleet Street is not alone. Internet service providers from Compuserve to Yahoo already offer real-time news feeds from big news agencies. Newspapers in the unitedstates, including The Washington Post and The newyork Times, are seeking not just to provide up-to-the-minute news agency feeds but also to deploy editorial staffs of their own working alongside print journalists. Never was that changing relationship between the Web page and the printed page more obvious than after last week's London train crash -- the worst in over four decades -- which confronted editors with what, for some journalists, has become the central puzzle, or even threat, presented by their on-line editions: how to serve readers with breaking news and early analysis without undermining the value of the following day's printed pages. Within three hours of the crash, said Simon Waldman, editor of Guardian Unlimited, the Guardian newspaper's network of Web sites, "we had everything up" on the Web site -- including photos and eyewitness accounts that would ordinarily have been kept for the next day's printed editions. Mike Mr. Butcher of New Media Age, an industry newsletter, said: "One thing that newspapers have swallowed now is that the Web does not significantly eat into circulation. People use it in a different way. People don't really read articles in any depth on line. It's a different medium." Distinctions between what is happening in the British press and among American newspapers are manifold. For one thing, unitedstates newspapers are rooted in a stronger regional tradition, compared with the scramble for national dominance that distinguishes British newspapers. And they were generally quicker to go on line than their British counterparts. unitedstates newspapers benefited not just from the much cheaper unitedstates telephone rates, which encourage Internet use, but also from a much bigger potential market. "Web revenue is not the same and that explains the different speeds at which things have tended to develop," Mr. Brock said. Thus, ad revenue from British papers' on-line operations was a measly $31.3 million last year. But, according to many on-line managers, that represented an increase of some 140 percent from 1997. Some sites, like The Daily Telegraph, with six interconnected sites, are building networks for students and travelers to win over a new generation to replace an aging readership. Such is the desire to avoid being left out that The Independent (www.independent.co.uk) recently lured Web experts away from rivals like Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation, which owns The Times of London, to redesign its Web site in an effort to increase the number of visits to individual Web pages -- known here as page impressions -- from a 3.6 million a month. The Times of London (www.the-times.co.uk), too, is promising new features. It draws some 12 million visits a month -- roughly the same as The Financial Times, which reckons that some 40 percent of its on-line usage comes from the unitedstates. And, with five interlinked Web sites catering to news junkies, job seekers, movie fans and others, The Guardian's Guardian Unlimited (guardianunlimited.co.uk), begun in January, is pressing to expand beyond its roughly 10 million visitors a month. The Financial Times's aggressive strategy has raised some doubts among industry experts, particularly since it says it will be looking to advertising, not subscriptions, to provide revenue. Noah Yasskin, an analyst at Jupiter Communications, said the recruitment of 100 people "sounds like a lot of bodies for the British advertising market to pay for." And Jamie Wood, European media analyst at J. P. Morgan, said he was "not sure that Pearson has worked out" where the expansion fits in the overall strategy of a company whose activities include book publishing, television, business information and educational publishing. But Mr. Martin has an answer. "The risk from doing nothing is much higher," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Peter Martin, an editor at The Financial Times, aims to transform the paper's Web site into a full-fledged Internet portal. (Carlos Lopez-Barillas for The newyork Times); British newspapers have extended their tradition of stiff competition into cyberspace.

title:
Seizing the Initiative on Privacy;
On-Line Industry Presses Its Case for Self-Regulation
body: By the stilted linguistic standards of government reports, the Federal Trade Commission gave the on-line industry a pistol whipping in June 1998. After reviewing the privacy practices of World Wide Web sites, the commission told Congress that the industry had "fallen far short of what is needed to protect consumers." Only a tiny fraction of Web sites, the F.T.C. noted, told people what the sites did with the personal information they collected -- names, email addresses, credit card numbers. Even fewer sites offered consumers any choice about how their personal data were used, allowed them to access the data or gave assurances of its security. Industry self-regulation, the F.T.C. concluded, was not working. Its scathing report increased the chances that Congress would enact sweeping Internet privacy legislation. And the findings hardened resolve in Europe to reject the American self-regulatory approach to privacy on line, a dispute that threatened to escalate into the first Internet trade war. Christine Varney, the commission's Internet expert until she left in August 1997, had long warned the industry that if it did not move to shoulder responsibility on privacy, the Government would surely step in. Suddenly, that threat seemed imminent. Yet, two months before the F.T.C. report was released, a group of companies had already taken a collective first step toward trying to shore up the Internet industry's credibility on privacy, fend off regulation and deflect a trade war with Europe. On April 17, 1998, some 60 lawyers, lobbyists and executives gathered in an 11th floor conference room at I.B.M.'s Washington office, representing several companies that included America Online, I.B.M., Hewlett-Packard and Microsoft, plus a few trade groups like the Direct Marketing Association. There was a sense of urgency at that afternoon meeting. "We realized we had to make a lot of progress in a short time on the privacy issue," recalled Marc Berejka, Microsoft's manager of government affairs. The group formed that day, the Online Privacy Alliance, now has nearly 100 corporations and associations as members, and it has done a remarkable job in turning the public debate over Internet privacy in the industry's direction. And in a switch of roles of the kind so unremarkable in Washington, the person heading the industry alliance, as its legal counsel and spokeswoman, is Ms. Varney, the same F.T.C. commissioner who led the Government's efforts to safeguard privacy on the Internet. Her success, privacy advocates say, has been as a Washington insider guiding a shrewd campaign of persuasion and not, as the industry alliance asserts, in prodding on-line companies to adopt meaningful privacy policies. But even her critics admire her work. "Christine Varney has been enormously effective in her role -- she's a cheerleader for an industry self-regulatory approach that she believes in," said Marc Rotenberg, executive director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a civil liberties advocacy group. "The problem is that you now have the Government taking its lead from industry on the privacy issue." Judgments about the Online Privacy Alliance vary. But there is no disputing that the group has strengthened the standing of those who believe that a hands-off approach is the wisest Internet policy. The group has blunted the drive for broad Internet privacy legislation or strict Government regulation. Its efforts have won praise from the F.T.C. And the group has even made headway on impressing Europe's trade negotiators. "The jury is still out as to whether self-regulation will work, but there is no doubt that the industry has made a lot of progress on the Internet privacy issue in the last year or so," said Robert Pitofsky, chairman of the F.T.C. "And if the industry keeps making as much progress as it has recently, I don't see how you can really argue that we need legislation." The 43-year-old Ms. Varney, who served as secretary to the Cabinet in the Clinton White House before joining the F.T.C. in October 1994, is a lawyer at Hogan & Hartson, a Washington law firm, where she is building an Internet-law practice. Her pedigree made Ms. Varney very attractive to the companies assembling the industry privacy group. "She was perfect," said Jill Lesser, vice president for domestic public policy for America Online Inc. "She had really pushed this issue at the F.T.C., so she had credibility with Government and with consumer groups." Ms. Varney has no qualms about her labors on the industry's behalf. She sees her role as a continuation of her work as a privacy advocate and not as a compromise of the principles she espoused during her Government service. She is not opposed to regulation per se, Ms. Varney says, and she urged the industry alliance to get ahead of its critics by pushing for a privacy law tailored for children. The industry group did encourage Congress to enact the Children's On-Line Privacy Protection Act of 1998, passed last October, which requires Web sites to obtain parental permission before collecting any personal information from children under 13. In most cases, however, Ms. Varney believes regulation should be a last resort, filling the breach if the private sector fails, especially in Internet markets, which change so quickly, undermining the effectiveness of traditional regulation. "I think we can have a market-driven approach to privacy on the Internet," she said. "And, at least, this experiment with self-regulation is worth doing. Let's see if the marketplace can do it." There are encouraging signs of progress. In early 1998, when the F.T.C. surveyed 1,400 commercial Web sites, only 14 percent gave users any notice of how they handled personal information. In early 1999, a Georgetown University survey of some 360 heavily trafficked Web sites -- a study requested by the F.T.C. and paid for by the industry -- found that 66 percent gave users some notice of how they handled personal data. "That 66 percent is pretty astonishing from where we were a year ago," Ms. Varney observed. "From my perspective, that means that self-regulation is working." But privacy advocates point to other numbers as evidence that self-regulation is failing. They note, for example, that the 1999 Georgetown survey also found that only 10 percent of Web sites included the four touchstones of what the F.T.C. calls "fair information practices": notifying users of the sites' data collection practices; giving users a choice of opting out; giving them access to personal data, and assuring them that their personal data were secure. The same four principles also serve as the basis for the Online Privacy Alliance's voluntary guidelines, but critics say the principles are too vaguely worded, giving companies too much leeway, to protect consumers. "And those policies are just window-dressing unless they are backed up by a credible system of enforcement," said Deborah Hurley, director of Harvard University's Information Infrastructure Project. The industry has financed independent privacy monitoring organizations, like eTrust and BBB Online. Even so, enforcement remains an issue for privacy groups and in negotiations between the unitedstates and Europe. To date, much of the development of privacy practices on line has been by the marketplace, responding to complaints, often by the thousands. In 1997, for example, when word spread that America Online planned to pass along customers' telephone numbers to telemarketers and other direct-sales merchants, the big Internet service provider heard a consumer outcry -- and quickly dropped the plan. Likewise Amazon.com, the big on-line bookstore, ran into a backlash last month when it posted "purchase circles," which showed the book buying habits of users from selected companies and universities. Some users found this a breach of privacy without consent and asked to be removed. After asking employees for their reaction, Louis V. Gerstner Jr., chairman of the International Business Machines Corporation, received 5,000 email responses within hours. More than 90 percent objected to having their book-buying habits as a group disclosed on line. I.B.M. was removed from the book-purchase circles. Later, Mr. Gerstner wrote to Jeff Bezos, chief executive of Amazon.com, saying, "I'm certainly not going to tell you how to run your business, but I do urge you to view this as an enormously important issue." Some on-line privacy issues have surfaced case by case. Last year, for example, a customer service representative at America Online told a Navy investigator the real name of a naval officer who had identified himself by the screen name "Tim" and listed his marital status as "gay." Later, America Online reached an out-of-court settlement with the officer and adopted new policies to protect the privacy of its customers. America Online's thousands of customer service representatives are now given special "scenario training" to insure that they do not give out private information about users without those users' consent or a court order. This trial-and-error, market-driven approach to privacy, Internet executives note, has often resulted in stricter practices than those, for example, of the credit card and catalog industries. Besides, they add, a rapid response system for customers is built into the Internet, where email complaining and chat room organizing can punish companies more quickly and more severely than Government regulations can. "At the end of the day, good privacy policy is good business for us," said Robert Pittman, president of America Online. "It's very important to our members. We've learned that anything you do, you have to think through the prism of privacy. "We're not always perfect," Mr. Pittman added. "But if we miss something, our members tell us in one big hurry." Most on-line consumers, apparently, are willing to fend for themselves on the increasingly commercial Internet. A survey by Privacy and American Business, a research firm, found that 86 percent of 460 adult Internet users questioned earlier this year said they wanted to be able to essentially "trade" their own personal information with Web sites -- as long as they were properly informed about how their data were used and were offered benefits for doing so. Mr. Pitofsky, the F.T.C. chairman, points to those survey results as the reason he is "willing to be patient to see if self-regulation works." Yet many people argue that some basic legislation to protect individual privacy on the Internet is inevitable -- and that it could both benefit consumers and stimulate the growth of E-commerce by fostering greater public trust in doing business on line. Such sentiments extend well beyond the traditional champions of Government intervention like privacy advocates and consumer groups. Tim Berners-Lee, the British physicist who created the basic software for the Web, is the director of the World Wide Web Consortium at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. His consortium is working on privacy-enhancing technology, software that holds a person's privacy preferences and can communicate and bargain on an individual's behalf over the Internet. Still, Mr. Berners-Lee said: "On privacy, I don't think that self-regulation is enough. In America, I believe that the lack of regulation means that the corporate marketers have too much power." That power seems certain to increase in the near future. The spread of Internet technology will result in a data collection network of previously unimagined reach as telephones, televisions, cars and appliances -- not just personal computers -- are connected to the global digital network before long. And the rapidly developing fields of data-mining and profiling software will enable corporations to increasingly slice and search through this ocean of data to identify personal patterns of buying and behavior -- and make inferences, accurate or not, about a person's likely behavior. The unnerving prospect, according to Paul Saffo, a director for the Institute for the Future, is that "we will all be players in what could be a fairly inaccurate virtual Truman Show." At stake, technologists say, is far more than who gets which Internet marketing pitches. Profiling, they say, could be employed to determine who gets -- and who is excluded from -- all kinds of opportunities like jobs, housing and education. The F.T.C. is also studying the use and potential abuse of increasingly powerful Internet software. The commission has scheduled a public workshop on "on-line profiling" in November. Digital red-lining, Ms. Varney says, is an evocative term and a troubling concept. "There's no question that this technology could be hugely invasive," she said. "But it could also be enormously empowering by allowing individuals to make their own choices and by saving us all time and money. Particularly in the future, we will face more difficult decisions and trade-offs. But I think that argues for leaving those decisions to the marketplace for privacy as much as we can." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Christine Varney was the Federal Trade Commission's Internet expert until she left to join an alliance dedicated to staving off Government privacy rules. (Shana Raab for The New York Times)(pg. C1)  Chart: "Guidelines vs. Requirements" Industry groups contend that self-enforced guidelines are sufficient for protecting privacy on the World Wide Web. But privacy-rights groups want legal requirements -- not industry self-policing. Here is a comparison of some ways the two groups would protect the privacy of personal data collected on the Web. ACCESS  The Industry Suggests -- Companies should take "reasonable steps" to insure that personal data are "accurate, complete and timely."  Privacy Groups Demand -- Individuals should have "the right to see personal information" that a company has collected on them -- and to correct inaccuracies.  CONSENT  The Industry Suggests -- Users must be given the "opportunity to exercise choice" over how their personal information may be used when such use is "unrelated to the purpose for which the information was collected."  Privacy Groups Demand -- Individuals should have "the right to control the use" of their personal information. Such information should not be "used or disclosed for other purposes without the consent of the individual or other legal authority."  DATA SECURITY  The Industry Suggests -- Companies should take "appropriate measures" to insure the reliability of personal information and take "reasonable precautions" to protect from its loss or misuse.  Privacy Groups Demand -- Companies "must institute reasonable security safegaurds" against risks including "loss, unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification and disclosure."  (Sources: Online Privacy Alliance; Center for Democracy and Technology)(pg. C8)

title: A Leader's-Eye View Of Leadership
body: LAWRENCE A. BOSSIDY spoke of the value of hiring those who have failed. L. Dennis Kozlowski shook his head at the "absurd" valuations of Internet companies, while Charles B. Wang talked about having dot-com envy. Shelly Lazarus defended the $80-million-plus pay package that Hewlett-Packard recently awarded its new leader. Early one Monday morning in late September, these four chief executives -- Mr. Bossidy of Allied Signal, Mr. Kozlowski of Tyco International, Mr. Wang of Computer Associates International and Ms. Lazarus of Ogilvy & Mather Worldwide -- gathered over coffee at The newyork Times to talk about leadership and how they do their jobs. All are featured in a recent book, "Lessons from the Top: The Search for America's Best Business Leaders," (Doubleday/Currency, 1999) written by Thomas J. Neff and James M. Citrin, two executive recruiting consultants from Spencer Stuart in newyork. Mr. Neff and Mr. Citrin also joined the discussion, as did Reed Abelson, Alison Leigh Cowan and Patrick J. Lyons of The Times. The four chief executives brought different perspectives to the two-hour discussion. Mr. Bossidy, who has more than four decades of business experience, helped turn around Allied Signal and is currently merging it with Honeywell to create a company with $25 billion in sales. Mr. Kozlowski has guided Tyco through the purchase of more than 100 companies since he took over as chief executive in 1992. At Computer Associates, one of the world's largest independent software concerns, Mr. Wang managed the transition from founder to the leader of a company with more than $5 billion in annual sales. And while the agency that Ms. Lazarus runs is not an independent or public company -- the London-based WPP Group acquired it in 1989 -- it has long been one of the most successful advertising agencies in the world. Much of the discussion focused on the challenge of managing people: the fierce competition for talented employees, the need to communicate effectively, the growing demand for a healthier balance between work and life outside the workplace. The four also frankly discussed compensation, and all noted the importance of their own actions in conveying the values of the companies they lead. Following are excerpts of the conversation. REED ABELSON  Making Their Mark  Q. What kind of thoughts do you have about the legacy you're going to leave behind? Is it just to have the biggest company? BOSSIDY -- It isn't size that is as important to me as to have the employee base be convinced that we were always willing to change a lot of things, that the company had some edge. KOZLOWSKI -- We went out and did a reverse acquisition of ADT a couple of years ago where we had to charge our shareholders capital gains on the deal. It was a pretty unpopular decision with shareholders and even with my board. I hope to exemplify leadership in a way that we're willing to do things that are unpopular. WANG -- I don't know if legacy is defined only in business. If I could be remembered for something, it's probably how I raised my kids and what else I did. As much as we think we're very important, I think we forget there's probably somebody in our ranks who thinks they can do it better and probably can do it better. Our job probably is to make sure that they have the right values. LAZARUS -- I inherited a legacy, which came home very much to me when David Ogilvy died. We had a memorial service, and thousands of employees returned who hadn't worked for the company in 20 and 30 years because the emotional connection to what David founded was so remarkable. So I see my job much more is to keep that alive. WANG -- Why wouldn't you make your own legacy? LAZARUS -- Well, because it's marvelous, because it's founded on a set of values. It's not founded on a personality, on an individual. And it's a set of values that are all about excellent people and excellent work and all about recognizing individual contribution. I've stayed for 28 years because I believe in all those things.  Success and Succession  Q. The book "Lessons from the Top" is clearly a reflection in time. As we approach 2000, what qualities and skills will your successors need? BOSSIDY Trying to stay ahead of the game, trying to work with a work force which is far more independent than it was when I started and trying to be responsive and keep those organizations at the leading edge will be the challenge. I mean, you could be a C.E.O. 10 years ago and never have talked to your employees. You talk to them every day now. This notion of C.E.O. and C.O.O.  chief operating officer , which I think is awful, will go in the next 10 years. It's a bad thing under a set of circumstances that doesn't envision transition immediately, because it separates two jobs that should be joined. KOZLOWSKI -- I agree that the C.O.O. concept is a dangerous one in most companies, because it really separates the C.E.O. from the operating groups. WANG -- You know, maybe by the traditional definition of what the C.E.O. or C.O.O. does, what their job function is, perhaps you can say that. But maybe I'm fortunate. I know who the next C.E.O. is: He's my C.O.O. But he doesn't really operate in that traditional sense. We do things together. He happens to have the unfortunate task of doing everything I don't like to do. If you asked him, he'd probably tell you he can run the company better than I can. And I hope he feels that way, because that's what makes somebody who should be the C.E.O. LAZARUS -- The thing that keeps me up at night is the scarcity of talent. In my industry, we keep recycling the same eight people. There's so much opportunity for young people now -- the world of the Internet and start-ups and dot-coms, and 28-year-olds making $50 million overnight. The challenge for us is to figure out how to keep those people long enough that they are ready to become C.E.O.'s. BOSSIDY -- I think there's more talent than ever before. The trouble is, it migrates to narrower places. A few years ago, if you didn't go to a consulting firm, you weren't essentially in the main. Now if you're not with a dot-com you're basically not allowed to the party. KOZLOWSKI -- There are 20-year-olds coming out of college now, and out of graduate school, that are far brighter and have a far greater perspective of the world than anybody did in my class. But there's another thing that's happening, too: Really talented, bright people are starting to question the life styles that are involved in this kind of work. LAZARUS -- Absolutely. I think we're going to have to get much more flexible and open-minded about how we -- I don't even say employ people -- but how we source resources. Because there are people who are now saying, "I'll give you X number of hours a week but I am not signing up as a full-time employee." Q. Can you give us an example of the flexible arrangements you find yourself making? LAZARUS -- Well, we have a man who wants to live in Penelope, Tex., where he has a ranch. I'd make him a creative leader in my agency; he doesn't want to do that. He said: "I will sell you 40 percent of my time. And I will also retain the right to refuse an assignment if I don't want to do it." He has done a brilliant job for us, absolutely brilliant. If I can get five more of him, if I get a hundred more of him, I would take them. BOSSIDY -- You've also got to be careful that the only people you retain aren't those who are risk-averse and don't want to do the dot-com situation. So I say to our people: "Let's go get some people from the dot-coms right now. They're failing every day. But at least they showed the interest and the courage to take some risks." Q. So failure can be a good thing? BOSSIDY -- I used to hire real estate people. I always hired ones that had failures. I wanted the person who had lost a lot of money for somebody else to come work for me. You don't reward -- you don't praise -- failure. But it can be a wonderful thing in terms of what you learn. Q. Even if the failure is very public? BOSSIDY -- I think every failure needs to be analyzed. Why? What happened? And sometimes you've got to stand up, yourself, and say, "I was a part of that and I have as much responsibility for it as anybody does. Now, let's make sure we don't make that same mistake again when we develop another product." WANG -- I think what you've got to do is take the blame. I mean, ultimately you give all the credit to your people and you take all the blame. We tell our people we're no smarter than any other company in the world. The problem with all the other companies seems to be, they may spend five times the amount of time to make decisions, spinning about what went wrong: "It's really not my fault." And all of that time could have been used to make decisions. So if we could just cut out all the spinning, then we'd have that much more time. KOZLOWSKI -- Any time you're going to try something, at whatever level, there's always a risk of failure. BOSSIDY -- And if you study it for three months, or study it for a day, probably the percentages are about the same. Embracing the Internet  Q. These days, one primary reason that chief executives seem to fail and are shown the door is the Internet. KOZLOWSKI -- I don't see the Internet as being the demise of C.E.O.'s. There are a couple of examples, maybe, but C.E.O.'s usually trip over themselves. They make slow decisions or bad decisions or invest the money in the wrong way or don't have a focus -- aren't quick out of the box. LAZARUS -- I think the healthiest thing that's coming out of this whole Internet phenomenon is that the good C.E.O.'s are rethinking the whole way they go to the market. So it's not the Internet per se. I think that becomes sort of like a distraction. But because you have this new capability -- this new way to distribute, inform, communicate -- the good companies are stepping back and saying, "What does this mean about the whole way we go to market?" BOSSIDY -- One of the things I try to do is get everybody in the company involved on the Net in some way -- manufacturing people, more outsourcing; purchasing people, more global sourcing. And you can use it as a way to reinvent the company. You get a whole new set of excitement; some new people come to the fore. You do some things experimentally that you would never do otherwise.  E-Communicating Pros and Cons  Q. You all lead large organizations. How do you stay in touch with your employees? WANG -- Get a good C.O.O.! BOSSIDY -- There's such a thing as the E-mail now. And you have an easier time communicating with anybody than ever. You can issue E-mails, you can get E-mails, all the time. And I think it's essential that you do. LAZARUS -- But I also think there's no substitute for face-to-face. BOSSIDY -- I agree. LAZARUS -- Something happens when you are in the room with people with whom you work, trying to solve a problem together or just listening to them. And the E-mail becomes more meaningful after the trip with the face-to-face. KOZLOWSKI -- We have 140,000 employees in 80 countries. And it takes a lot of face-to-face time, a lot of travel on my part, to be able to articulate our goals and where we're going. But I really like showing up. You know, I really like being there and being able to have a dialogue like this. BOSSIDY -- If you aren't willing to communicate and if you're not good at it, you're at a disadvantage. You have to do even more than you've ever done before in whatever way you do it, but it's something that you ought to do every day, someplace. KOZLOWSKI -- Employees are far more willing to critique -- openly critique -- the C.E.O. than ever before. BOSSIDY -- That's better than having it only in chat rooms. LAZARUS -- I agree. WANG -- I don't have E-mail. I force my people to get in touch with me. And it takes an effort. And it must be important, then, too. And I travel a lot. Once a year we also bring all our field people together for what we call a kickoff. We spend a week of basically bringing them all up to date on what's happened. But as you get bigger, you still have to force the issue of thinking small, because otherwise you end up in a bureaucracy that can choke you.  Fair Play in the Numbers Game  Q. What about that other constituency: the institutional investors, the analysts? WANG -- My C.O.O. deals with Wall Street. KOZLOWSKI -- I spend 10 percent of my time communicating with investors. BOSSIDY -- One of the things I think C.E.O.'s do is understand who your constituents are, and one of them is share owners. You've got customers, you've got employees, you've got suppliers, you've got share owners, you've got communities in which you live. You've got to spend time with all of them.  Q. Does paying attention to the share owners make you too short-term at times? KOZLOWSKI -- You absolutely have got to deliver what you promised in the short term. And you've got to have a strategy in place worrying about two years from now. I pretty much know what the next year and a half will look like and have a forecast in place that I'm very confident in. LAZARUS -- I'm actually sitting here thinking this is probably the only benefit of having been acquired hostilely by an English company.  Q. We have seen very good managements run into trouble when they surprise analysts. But then, maybe truly good managements never surprise analysts. BOSSIDY -- You're better off to run it on the basis that you avoid those surprises to the fullest possible extent. NEFF -- You could probably get away with one surprise. KOZLOWSKI -- I don't agree. BOSSIDY -- No. The price is immediate. KOZLOWSKI -- Yeah. You miss earnings by a penny and you can lose $3 billion of market value the same day.  Q. Doesn't that increase the temptation to have a little bit in the back pocket to make sure you're going to make your numbers? KOZLOWSKI -- It increases the temptation of making sure you give appropriate guidance to Wall Street as to where you think you're coming out. You can't manage earnings. There are very specific accounting rules and S.E.C. rules now that preclude one from going that route. But it really is terribly important to have good communication and good visibility of your own businesses, so that you can become, and are, and continue to be a predictable company. WANG -- I don't know if you really can be that predictable. There are a lot of things beyond your control. We do so many deals a year. Some of them can slip by a few days. You don't know until almost the -- actually, till the last day of the quarter, many times. Q. You see a company that makes its numbers for 15 years in a row. Do you suspect they're just lucky enough to be in a very predictable business, or do you suspect that the chief executive is good at making the numbers? KOZLOWSKI -- I think they're good. I think companies like G.E. are good. They're well-run companies.  That Urge to Merge  Q. This is a golden age for mergers. Do you see that changing? BOSSIDY -- I think it depends on two things: What's the interest rate environment and what's the stock market going to be? I think there's benefit to being big. To Charles's point, I think you want to be as big as you can and run it as small as you can, as a way to be quick. KOZLOWSKI -- When interest rates fluctuate, pricing usually comes down on companies to be acquired and you're more inclined to use some combination of stock and cash in those deals. I would expect, for any horizon I can see, a Tyco that would continue to be quite active. BOSSIDY -- Dennis, let me ask you a question. What's going to happen to your view if pooling of interests, a method of accounting for mergers is eliminated? KOZLOWSKI -- I think what we attempted to do with Raychem -- where we could have pooled Raychem and shown another penny or two a share but where we used half stock and half equity -- is the kind of deal that you're going to see going forward. However, part of the proposal is showing earnings before the amortization of goodwill. Then you have the best of all worlds. And there are so many unintended consequences of poolings, limitations that the S.E.C. puts on you -- not being able to sell off things that you don't want to have, on the purchase of your own stock -- I think it's almost a good thing that poolings will be eliminated. It will protect us from ourselves. BOSSIDY -- I agree. I think there's going to be a lot of furor expressed on the potential elimination, but I don't think at the end of the day it's going to have much impact.  A Brave New World?  Q. Does this unprecedented period of prosperity herald a "new economy," or are you afraid that it's got to end pretty soon? WANG -- I think we are in a new economy. I think we've gone through this kind of industrial age, the marketing age, and now we're really in an information age. And I think the people we call the knowledge workers are expected to have more information and make decisions faster. KOZLOWSKI -- It's a true global economy now, too, that just didn't exist five years ago, where you're buying and selling on a worldwide basis, and your competitor now may be in Indiana, or your competitor may be in Brazil, or your competitor may be in Germany. Plus, the information technology that you have available to you now allows you to see a lot of things on a real-time basis that you weren't able to see five years ago. Q. Is the business cycle gone? KOZLOWSKI -- No, probably not. In business, as far as I know it, the good times get bad and bad times get good. Maybe there are longer cycles now. BOSSIDY -- I think, too, there's another factor, which doesn't mean that markets won't, over time, change. I think the U.S. has a big competitive edge now. We have taken a lead in the information technology. We've taken the lead in Internet. I don't say that we're destined to always have that advantage, but I do think in the last number of years we've moved faster than the Europeans, we've moved faster than the people in the Far East. Q. So higher price-to-earnings ratios are justified? BOSSIDY -- I think on a global basis, yes. You know, markets are smart. Q. What about the Internet valuations? Do you all wish you had dot-com at the end of your company's name? KOZLOWSKI -- No. Some of it is absolutely absurd. WANG -- I wish we had dot.com. We do so much business on the Internet, but traditionally, the perception has been that we are a plumbing company, what's behind it. Our software manages the largest Web sites in the world, and we have more security software than any other independent software company. And yet our valuation is not a dot-com. LAZARUS -- Once you relax the profit requirement, you know, it's very different. And we have clients coming in who are new dot-com companies who say, "We have an advertising budget of $70 million, $80 million," and you sort of press them on the economics. I just saw where Etoys today is going to invest 70 percent of their sales last year in advertising in the next three months. I mean, it's madness. BOSSIDY -- But you know, therefore, that's going to stop. LAZARUS -- It's got to stop. BOSSIDY -- But I do think that the medium will continue. Tom, what percentage of your placements have been Internet placements in the last 12 months? NEFF -- In terms of current assignments in the U.S., it's into the double digits. It's probably approaching 15 percent, currently. So we've had over 100 active search assignments for Internet C.E.O.'s.  Q. Many a brilliant marketing campaign aims to familiarize the public with these new Internet names. What about the companies that possess the old great names? LAZARUS -- Well, I think they have an advantage if they use it. Sears, which is one of our clients, as a name for the old catalogue company, as a place that you trust to get merchandise, is brilliant. But they've got to get onto it or Amazon.com is going to become the retailer of the year 2000. I mean, because I don't think they're stopping at books. WANG -- I really believe that an established business should look at a hybrid type model instead of thinking of this as a separate, distinct silo. Imagine if you could get on line, buy books and at the end of your whole order, you have a choice: send it to me or go drive through a drive-through window at Barnes & Noble and pick up my package. BOSSIDY -- And yet, it's ironic that because of Amazon.com, Barnes & Noble's got a better household recognition than ever before. So the question is: Can you capitalize on that?  The Chief as Superstar  Q. Last week George Shaheen surprised all of us by jumping from Andersen Consulting, which he ran with an iron fist, to the Webvan Group, the Internet grocery vendor. Out of his mind? KOZLOWSKI -- He has the opportunity to make a whole lot of money over there, from what I've read. So, you know, it's like the risk somebody pointed out before: if he has a shot at $100 million or thereabouts, it's probably a reasonable place to go. And he's probably a pretty capable executive, so it's a risk worth taking.  Q. Do the media exaggerate the extent to which the C.E.O. is the company and the company is the C.E.O.? KOZLOWSKI -- I've thought about that a lot, and I think the difficulty you have is it's hard to talk about a company -- that Allied Signal did this or Tyco did that. BOSSIDY -- I think you ascribe brilliance too soon. I mean, you take a Jack Welch of General Electric for 20 years -- he deserves it. He's come through good and bad times and always has done well. But I don't think you should do it in terms of a year or two. I mean, you might want to see them season a little.  Q. What about C.E.O. compensation? There is some concern that while the market's been doing wonderfully, C.E.O.'s have made out more than handsomely. BOSSIDY -- The press had something to do with that. They didn't like salaries and bonuses, so they said, "You ought to put more of your income at risk." And so the corporations did, and now they're complaining about that. But when I get asked in my own audiences, I say: "I make a lot of money. And take on a lot of risk." And then I say, "Our savings plan is up $2.5 billion since I came." That doesn't mean just me -- the whole company has made a lot. And the people who own the stock in the company make a lot of money. KOZLOWSKI -- I do not receive one single penny of bonus unless my earnings per share grow over 20 percent a year. However, I do start accruing restricted shares of stock, and I make an awful lot of money in the stock. We pay taxes on that, and our compensation is totally in line with the shareholders. And one could look at it and say, yeah, we truly are overpaid, but a lot of it's been the appreciation of the stock market. WANG -- It's been noted that I got a $600-and-some million grant. But people don't realize this was a plan that was approved by 86 or 87 percent of the shareholders. If we brought a value of $18 billion to shareholders, I would think then we'd earned a bonus. It was a five-year plan with a seven-year tail. KOZLOWSKI -- You got a $600 million grant? I'm glad I'm not your shareholder. BOSSIDY -- I wouldn't mind being your adopted kid. LAZARUS -- I had a fascinating conversation last week with someone who was absolutely outraged by Carly Fiorina's pay package when she recently signed on at Hewlett-Packard . And I said, "Yes, but why would she have come otherwise?"  Q. It's often said that at a certain level it no longer matters how much any of you make, that you would be doing just as good a job for $100 million less or $20 million less. KOZLOWSKI -- Yeah, all my meals are paid for, for as long as I'm around. So, I'm not working for that any longer. But it does make a difference in the charities I ultimately leave monies behind to, and it's a way of keeping score. BOSSIDY -- Hewlett-Packard doesn't have a habit of going out and paying exorbitant salaries, so they wanted her Ms. Fiorina to run the company, and that's what the market was, and she got the market price. How can you be critical of that? LAZARUS -- I don't even know her, but I think she would have considered herself foolish if she left all that money on the table. Why would she do that?  Setting an Example  Q. Do employees and other stakeholders in the companies look to activities outside the executive suite as signals about the chief executive's leadership and values? WANG -- I think charity is a personal thing. We also recognize the company is also a member of the community and the world at large. What I try to do is encourage my people to give. If you're an employee of C.A., if you give $1, C.A. will match $2 for it. So this way we really push them to give more. BOSSIDY -- I think, though, there is an issue as to how much time a C.E.O. should spend doing other things. I think you're hired to run the company. That doesn't mean you should be ignorant of what's going on in Washington, but you ought to go down there selectively as opposed to weekly. I don't think you can get involved in a whole bunch of charities. I think you can get involved in a charity and then spend some time, and influence it, and try to make it better. But the more I see C.E.O.'s fragment their time doing a lot of other things, I think, the less successful they're going to be. LAZARUS -- I'd like to answer your question in a somewhat different way, because I think I'm always asked these questions about balance and how do you retain women. How I spend my time and how I communicate my own values and my own priorities does have a very significant impact on the employees in my company. So that when I stay out for three months for maternity leave, I am well aware that that makes it all right to take maternity leave. And if the C.E.O. isn't going to the school play, and the C.E.O. is canceling his vacation, and the C.E.O. is not coming home to be at his 6-year-old's birthday party, well then, the rest of the company knows how they're supposed to behave.  Q. We still haven't seen too many cases of women with small children running large organizations. WANG -- Why is it different for women? I raised my three kids. One of them is 28 years old. And I raised them while I was building Computer Associates. Now I have two more kids. One's 6 and one's 1 year old. I go to the school play. I'm the one that goes to the parent-teacher conference.  Q. There is a widely cited statistic that two-thirds of the men who work, are married and have children, have wives who stay at home, but hardly any working wives with children have stay-at-home husbands. WANG -- My wife works. She works for C.A. She has 4,000 people reporting to her. KOZLOWSKI -- So she is your successor? WANG -- No, she's not. She's too nerdy! BOSSIDY -- I've had nine children. There's no reason why you can't be president and do a lot of the things as the kids grow up. I did. And I do think the hardest deal in the world is for a woman to have two or three young kids, to work when their spouse works. That is just physically exhausting. That takes a toll after a while. And I don't know what we in business have done yet to be able to resolve that. KOZLOWSKI -- We've tackled it a little differently in the last couple of years, where we've put about 8,000 of our managers through diversity training, approaching all types of issues, from creating a culture where a man or a woman can work from the home, to being much more flexible in their abilities to make contributions to a company, to being supportive of maternity leaves before Congress mandated them. And I think you really need to do that, because if not, you're going to eliminate an awful lot of talented people out of your pool of resources. LAZARUS -- The smart C.E.O. has to do that. Why would you give up 50 percent of the population when talent's a scarce resource? BOSSIDY -- I tell people: "Don't come in here on Saturday and Sunday unless something special is going on, because all you're going to do is become a bore. I mean, do something, music or whatever you like, but for heaven's sake, grow." They'll say, "How many Sundays do you work?" I work a couple of Sundays a year, only because something special is happening.  Q. What is the one thing about being a chief executive that you would change with a wave of your hand, if you could? KOZLOWSKI -- I'd probably eliminate the jet plane, so that we wouldn't be expected to be in so many different places so often. Jets have really destroyed civilization. WANG -- One thing is, don't perceive us C.E.O.'s as some kind of higher order of human beings. I really want to work with people and not have a meeting where everybody is, "He's here, so I've got to be on a different kind of behavior." I wish they would just relax. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: C.E.O. title:
Ideas & Trends;
In E-Commerce Frenzy, Brave New World Meets Old
body: WHEN Amazon.com declared two weeks ago that it was beginning a bold campaign to become an Internet shopping bazaar, Wall Street applauded. And why not? Amazon, a corporate poster child of the New Economy and pioneer of on-line retailing, would be collecting money from any business, large or small, that wanted to set up shop under its cyber-tent. Besides, Amazon really needs the cash. Its losses are mounting, as they are for most Internet merchants. But, Amazon explains, the red ink merely underlines the scale of its ambitious investment for future growth. And what is Amazon spending so lavishly on these days? Building a high-tech bunker of supercomputers or hiring battalions of software wizards? No, Amazon is spending much of its money on a half-dozen huge warehouses across the country. The New Economy is increasingly coming face-to-face with the old: Net code hackers and money hustlers meet the members of Bricklayers Local 247. The hot, new fields of the Internet economy suddenly include distribution and logistics, the humdrum backstage of business. Indeed, as electronic commerce moves into the mainstream -- an estimated 17 million American households will purchase on line this year -- it has prompted a new appreciation for the business skills of the old bricks-and-mortar world. Customers, it seems, still have decidedly off-line standards of service. They demand timely delivery of goods and the ability to easily return merchandise that proves disappointing, for example. The on-line retailers who come up short on those fronts, industry analysts predict, will be casualties in the coming consolidation among on-line retailers -- a Darwinian winnowing expected to begin during this year's Christmas shopping season as winners are sorted from losers. "A lot of the dot-com retailers are going to fold after their venture capital money runs out," observed David Pecaut, a senior vice president of the Boston Consulting Group. Curiously, the biggest winners in on-line retailing could well be today's department stores, discount chains and specialty stores. In fact, 62 percent of E-commerce sales are accounted for by bricks-and-mortar and catalog companies that also have begun on-line ventures. Within five years, Mr. Pecaut expects that share to rise to 85 percent as companies like Wal-Mart, Nordstrom and Sears improve their performance on the World Wide Web. THE reason, he says, is that their assets from the "legacy world" -- well-known brands, distribution networks, stores and purchasing power -- will prove to be advantages, and increasingly so in electronic commerce. The leading on-line brands like Amazon and Ebay, for example, came onto the marketplace a few years ago as innovative newcomers, when cyberspace was far less crowded and Internet brand-building was far less costly. The chance of an Internet start-up gaining that kind of brand recognition today, Mr. Pecaut says, is slim. "For marketers, the superior economics in the future are going to come from the old standards of business -- and not just being on line," he said. The new catch phrases of modern retailing have embraced that notion: multi-channel retailers, integrated shopping and 360-degree marketing. All are meant to convey the concept of servicing -- or assaulting -- the consumer on many fronts, on line and off. Some Internet companies are even using their high-priced shares as currency to buy bricks-and-mortar counterparts. For example, the on-line auctioneer Ebay purchased Butterfield & Butterfield, a San Francisco-based auction house founded in 1865, for $260 million in stock earlier this year. The statistics for on-line retail sales, and projections of future revenue, show meteoric growth. Yet a closer look at the numbers suggests how much traditional retailing retains its hold, despite the rapid, up-from-zero growth of E-commerce. On-line sales in the unitedstates will rise sharply this year to $20 billion and jump to $185 billion by 2004, according to Forrester Research Inc., a technology research firm in Cambridge, Mass. Still, the $185 billion figure, even if it proves accurate, would represent only 7 percent of the nation's retail sales in 2004, the firm maintains. The rise of the Internet has clearly created not only new wealth but a new sense of economic opportunity. "The essence of the new Internet economy is its ferocious speed, the faith that this is a big deal and the uncertainty that it will pay off," said Thomas Eisenmann, an E-commerce expert at the Harvard Business School. The economic payoff from Internet technology will almost surely come first in an area that gets the least attention: its use as a low-cost communications technology to automate all kinds of business transactions. "The Amazons of the world get all the press, but the real growth in electronic commerce in the next five years is going to be in the business-to-business market," said Peter Schwartz, chairman of the Global Business Network, a consulting firm. FUELING that growth will be companies using the Web instead of faxes, telephones and face-to-face meetings to handle the "back office" tasks involved in trading with their corporate customers and suppliers. Forrester Research projects that the business-to-business market could reach $1.5 trillion by 2003. But even the Internet-assisted overhaul of dealings among businesses in the next few years represents an evolutionary instead of a revolutionary step. Much of the anticipated transformation amounts to doing the same chores more efficiently because of new technology -- as was true with the telephone and, before that, the telegraph, which has been called "The Victorian Internet," in a book published last year (Walker & Company) by Tom Standage. And if the past is any guide, the surest corporate winners in the E-commerce business may be the suppliers of basic tools and services for the Internet: computers, software and technical know-how. That, at least, seemed to be the lesson of the last great gold rush in California. It was the general stores and saloons, not the miners, that pocketed the steady money. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Working the old-fashioned way at Amazon.com's distribution center in Seattle. (Dan Lamont for The newyork Times)  Graph: "WindowShopping.com" On-line shopping is expected to grow dramatically, yet it will remain a small portion of total retail spending, and growth should level off. Graph tracks total U.S. online retail revenues, online shopping as a percentage of total retail, and new online shopping households added each year for 1999 through 2004. Data is tracked from 1999 through 2004. All figures are projection. (Source: Forrester Research)

title:
MUTUAL FUNDS REPORT;
Swimming Against an Ebb Tide
body: IT was a lackluster, disappointing third quarter for most mutual funds, but there were notable exceptions -- many of them helped by investments in innovative companies in the telecommunications, semiconductor and biotechnology industries.  And smaller growth stocks in general outpaced bigger, value-oriented issues in the three months ended Sept. 30, helping those funds that tilted in that direction. Here, stock-pickers of three top-performing funds for the quarter look back at what made their funds such standouts -- and offer a glance ahead. A Disciple of Growth New technology created the winners in the $145.2 million Strong Enterprise fund, a mid-cap growth fund.  It returned 19.5 percent for the quarter, taking the No. 1 place among domestic diversified equity funds.  "We try to identify the leading companies in rapidly growing industries," said its manager, Andrew S. Cupps, 29, "companies that can capitalize on opportunities in a changing world." One of his biggest winners was Sandisk of Sunnyvale, Calif., which makes what is in effect the film used in digital cameras -- the chips on which images are stored. Two million digital cameras have been sold since their commercial introduction in 1998, said Mr. Cupps, adding that sales of 28 million units are forecast for 2002 -- "and every one goes out with a Sandisk chip." The company, he added, also makes chips that enable portable music players like the next-generation Sony Walkman -- due in January -- to play music downloaded from the Internet. "There was no market at all for these several months ago," Mr. Cupps said, "and now they should sell several million units." Sandisk, whose stock rose 44.9 percent in the quarter, also makes chips that are built into personal digital assistants designed by Compaq Computer and Hewlett-Packard, he said. Another winning stock was Broadvision, of Redwood City, Calif., a maker of software for companies doing business on the Internet. Its stock rose 80.4 percent in the quarter. Broadvision software lets companies like American Airlines offer personalized Web sites, Mr. Cupps said, by helping them identify individual customers and then offering special deals geared to their spending patterns. He also made money in Millennium Pharmaceuticals, a biotechnology company in Cambridge, Mass., that specializes in genomics. Its stock rose 80.6 percent in the quarter. The company's research on human genes "can help pharmaceutical companies discover drugs more quickly and in a more targeted fashion," Mr. Cupps said. Millennium is currently focusing on the genetic roots of obesity. Looking ahead, he remains optimistic. "A small group of big technology stocks and next-generation stocks have been very strong, but a whole generation of software stocks are down because of Y2K and other concerns." he said, adding that the market could resume its upward move "if the economy slows down, and there's some indication that this is happening."  A Monster Bet on Chips How did the $265.1 million Northstar Special fund, a small growth fund, earn its No. 5 place among domestic diversified equity funds for the quarter? Through investments in semiconductor stocks, which made up 20 percent of the fund's portfolio, and contributed mightily to its 17.4 percent return. "Semiconductor companies are secular growth vehicles that went through a slowdown last year, partly because of the Asian crisis and global recession, and began to come out of it this spring," said the fund's manager, Mary Lisanti, 43. "What's helping now is the strong demand for personal computers because of the Internet, cheap PC pricing and personal digital assistants." One of her biggest winners was PMC-Sierra, a Burnaby, British Columbia, manufacturer of semiconductors used in telecommunications equipment; its stock rose 56.9 percent. The company is highly profitable and is "always considered one of the class acts in the business," Ms. Lisanti said, adding that it weathered the recent downturn better than most of its competitors did. "It's a value-added player as opposed to a commodity provider," she said, because of the specialized nature of its chips. Another hit was Harmonic Inc., a Sunnyvale, Calif., company that makes fiber optic systems for delivering voice, data and video over cable satellites and wireless networks.  The company, whose stock rose 127.7 percent in the quarter, uses a technology called wave division multiplexing that lets it expand fiber capacity by splitting light waves. "It allows you to make a 2-lane road into a 10-lane road," Ms. Lisanti said. She also made money in Applied Micro Circuits, a San Diego designer and maker of semiconductors used in broadband communications. "It has leading-edge chip-manufacturing technology that it developed for the military, which always sent tons of data around the world," she said.  "Now they're producing it commercially at a competitive cost." The stock rose 38.6 percent in the quarter. What's ahead for the market?  "This year is the exact opposite of last year, when you wanted to own the big safe havens," Ms. Lisanti said. "Now you want the opposite -- more industrially oriented companies, to benefit from the economic recovery overseas." She expects an inflation rate in the 2 to 3 percent range through year-end and long-term interest rates of 6 to 7 percent.  Thinking Small, Really Small "We try to identify the most dynamic companies in the microcap universe that are also exhibiting above-average relative price strength," said Tom Callan, 39, co-manager with Bill Wykle, 62, of the $141.9 million Blackrock Microcap Equity Portfolio. In the third quarter, he found those stocks among emerging biotechnology and wireless communications companies. The fund returned 17.7 percent in the quarter, earning it the No. 4 place among domestic diversified equity funds. Among his biggest winners was United Therapeutics, a biotechnology company in Silver Spring, Md., that produces UT-15, a new version of a hypertension drug. UT-15 is administered intravenously, using a tiny portable pump instead of the awkward refrigeration unit that its predecessor required, Mr. Callan said. "It's a big step up in ease of delivery," he added. He originally bought shares in the June initial public offering. The stock was up 143.2 percent for the quarter. He also made money in Trimeris, a Durham, N.C., company that is developing a new class of AIDS drug, called T-20, that blocks the H.I.V. virus from entering T-cells, Mr. Callan said, adding that it can be used when combination therapies and protease inhibitors are ineffective. The stock was up 15.1 percent for the quarter. Another winner was Price Communications, a newyork company that provides wireless service, mainly in Georgia and the rural South, and which benefited from accelerating growth in its number of subscribers. "The average revenue per user has remained stable, even though rates have dropped dramatically across the board," added Michael Carey, 30, a co-manager of the fund. The stock rose 75.4 percent in the quarter. As for the future, "the market is trying to find a new level of equilibrium," Mr. Callan said. He is cautiously upbeat. "In the best-case scenario," he said, "third-quarter earnings, which should be strong, will dominate the news and that should lead a rally through year-end." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Tom Callan, a co-manager of Blackrock Microcap Equity, says he scours the world of microcaps for "the most dynamic companies."
