title: Nike, Long Wary of E-Marketers, Links With Web Retailer
body: Nike Inc., which has consistently blocked Web-only stores from selling its goods, has reversed its stand and will let Fogdog Sports, an on-line sporting goods dealer, sell the full Nike product line. But Nike extracted a high price for the right to buy its shoes: Warrants to acquire 12 percent of Fogdog's shares. Nike is the first of the big athletic shoemakers to forge a pact with a retailer that sells goods only on the Web. And its imprimatur may cast a favorable light on Fogdog, a three-year-old company with less than $10 million in annual sales. Fogdog, based in Redwood City, Calif., filed for a public stock offering on Friday just as the Nike deal was closed. "Nike is the 800-pound gorilla in the industry," said Timothy Harrington, Fogdog's chief executive. He said that the company's growth had been slowed because, until now, the only Nike goods it had been able to offer so far had come from other retailer's overstocks and other unofficial channels. Now, Fogdog hopes it can recoup the cost of the deal from consumers -- who will find a broader selection -- and more importantly from investors, who may see the Nike swoosh logo as an indicator of the potential of Fogdog's stock. This is not the first time an Internet start-up has given away stock to a supplier in order to validate its business model. Before going public early this year, Priceline.com, the offer-your-own-price shopping site, gave warrants for about 10 percent of the company's shares to Delta Air Lines. The sporting goods category, which has been slow to develop on the Internet, has seen a flurry of activity this year. Most notably a small Philadelphia company called Global Sports arranged to create on-line stores for a half-dozen large sporting goods retailers, including Sports Authority, Athlete's Foot and Sports Chalet. Michael Rubin, the chief executive of Global Sports, said he thought Fogdog's strategy was flawed and risky. "I would never in a million years give any stock in my company to a manufacturer," he said. "What will they say when Reebok and New Balance come and say, 'What percentage do we get?' " Mr. Harrington said that Nike was the only manufacturer to which it would give such a deal. "Nike is the only company with double-digit market share," he said. Until now all of the big footwear brands declined to sell their wares to Internet stores. Their position was similar to the rationale of other manufacturers with high-end brands, including Sony and Ralph Lauren, that had not wanted to risk diluting the value of their brands by distributing them through inexperienced entrepreneurs using untested technology. "We saw a lot of on-line retailers who were not putting the right emphasis on product presentation," said Mary Kate Buckley, the Nike vice president who looks after its Internet strategy. What is more, Nike thought that it would have to limit the number of on-line retailers much more tightly than it did for local stores. And so the company wanted to choose Web dealers carefully. "Our bricks-and-mortar partners offer a convenient location where customers can feel the product quality and try products on," she said. "When you move to the Web, you present products in two dimensions, take away the local convenience. So we were concerned that over time if everyone is selling the same thing on-line, the only difference would be price." So Nike moved slowly, first by allowing some of the larger chains of bricks-and-mortar sporting goods stores -- like Venator Group's Foot Locker and Copeland Sports, a California chain -- to sell Nike products on their Web sites. But even this was tentative. Nike recently stopped selling to Copeland's Shopsports.Com. "They were not meeting our marketing standards," Ms. Buckley said, but she declined to elaborate. Meanwhile, in June Nike started selling about half of its various shoe models and 20 percent of the rest of its products directly to consumers through the Nike.com Web site. Recently, when Fogdog came back to Nike with another of its steady stream of requests to distribute the Nike line, Nike was intrigued. Fogdog said it would maintain its policy of not discounting products below the manufacturers' suggested minimums. Moreover, Nike judged that Fogdog was becoming the leading on-line company in the category. "A lot of people were showing us business plans, but Fogdog was out there executing for three years," Ms. Buckley said. And Fogdog offered Nike a portion of its stock just before the public offering. In return, Nike agreed to give Fogdog the support it gave to big chains, including preferred prices, technical information, joint marketing and other promotions. Nike will continue to expand its own sales effort through Nike.com, but it agreed not to sell to any other pure Internet company, including all of sites being developed by Global Sports, for at least six months. Mr. Rubin of Global Sports said he believed that Nike would soon choose to support his venture, too. "Our six partners are all among Nike's top 20 accounts," he said. "Nike needs to support them, and they need to be on the Internet in order to survive in the 21st century." Ms. Buckley acknowledged that this arrangement was sure to cause some consternation among Nike's other retailers. But she predicted that it would ultimately be accepted. "We think this is a big commitment to sporting goods retailing," she said. "The sporting goods industry has been slow to adapt to the Web. This will be a jump-start." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Fogdog will add the Nike brand to the list on its Web site under a deal that will give the footwear maker the right to a 12 percent equity stake. (pg. C2)

title:
TECHNOLOGY: E-Commerce Report;
Many Internet companies have focused on attracting customers. The bigger challenge is fulfilling orders.
body: COMPANIES involved in E-commerce have achieved most-envied status in the late 1990's business world with their riches from initial public offerings, gaudy marketing budgets and news clippings that laud them as pioneers of an industrial transformation. Given the glamour, then, it is not a little ironic that the most important issue facing the industry is the retail function with the least board room cachet: order fulfillment. Picking, packing and shipping products was difficult enough in recent years for Internet retailers who had no experience in such matters. But with consumers' expectations rising and E-commerce companies preparing to ship a wider array of merchandise to customers this holiday season, distribution issues loom even larger than before. "This is emerging as a huge issue," said John Hagel, who leads the E-commerce practice for McKinsey & Company, the consulting firm. "And it's a real bottleneck to growth. Too many companies started with the assumption that the challenge was getting people to buy things, when, in fact, the real challenge is getting it to them." According to Forrester Research, an Internet consulting firm, Web retailers will ship roughly 230 million packages this year -- mostly during the holiday season. Large companies like PlanetRx and Etoys ship more than 1,000 packages daily, while the industry behemoth, Amazon.com, ships more than 10,000 a day. And last week, the research firm of Jupiter Communications predicted that the busiest sites, including Amazon, CDNow and Barnesandnoble.com, may each reach 58,000 transactions a day in November and December. That process is rife with potential pitfalls and inefficiencies. In their infancy, most merchants simply took customers' orders, had them handled by a distributor and hoped that the items were in stock and shipped on time to the right people. In those days -- which, in some cases, extend to today -- customers could all but count on email telling them their ordered items were out of stock or would be shipped late. Competition is starting to halt such practices. To gain customer allegiance, Internet merchants are seeking more control over the shipping process. In many instances, most notably in the case of Amazon, they are building huge warehouses of their own near major shipping hubs. But because a high-technology distribution center can take two to three years to complete, Internet merchants are scrambling to find third parties to handle distribution for them. Two leaders in this category are Federated Department Store's Fingerhut Business Services Inc. and Hanover Direct's Keystone Fulfillment Inc. Keystone handles fulfillment for Mercata, KBkids and Dress Barn, while Fingerhut does the same for Wal-Mart Stores, Levi Strauss and Etoys, among others. Fingerhut's 1.2-million-square-foot distribution center in Provo, Utah, will employ as many as 1,200 workers during the holiday peak, processing orders, shipping items and handling returns. To the dismay of many E-commerce executives, such arrangements entail far more than simply writing a check and getting back to the business of planning the company's initial public offering. Because consumers are increasingly demanding so-called real-time inventory -- which includes access to information about product availability and shipping status -- distribution warehouses must be closely wired to the merchant's Web operations. Third-party distributors, however, typically have their own electronic tracking and ordering systems, which require painstaking efforts to link with the retailer. "For every order, we have to pass information to their system," said Louis Zambello, senior vice president of Etoys, which recently began shipping products from Fingerhut's Utah warehouse. "The warehouse then has to pass it back to us for confirmation," Mr. Zambello said. "When the item ships, that information goes to us for confirmation. When they get inventory in stock, that also has to go to our system, and if you do anything special for the customer, it has to flow from you to the outsourcer, back to you for confirmation." Integrating the retailer's computer system with the distributor's, he said, "takes dozens of people on both sides working long hours." Mr. Zambello added, "The misconception is that outsourcing is easier, but it's just different." Though Etoys and Fingerhut would not disclose the costs associated with building warehouses or maintaining outsourcing relationships, Rakesh Kaul, president and chief executive of Hanover Direct, said the costs for both options could be steep. Companies can expect to pay between $60 million and $80 million to build a one-million-square-foot warehouse, Mr. Kaul said, while they would pay a third-party distributor roughly 10 percent of each sale to fulfill their orders. In building distribution centers of their own, E-commerce companies "have to bear in mind fixed costs," he said. "It's like owning a 747," Mr. Kaul said. "You have to be big, or fortunate enough to fill it, because if you don't fill it and operate all the time, you're guaranteed to lose money." Mr. Hagel of McKinsey agreed. "Unless you do high volume, it doesn't make sense to build this capacity in the long run. There are significant economies of skill and scale in these businesses," he said, referring to third-party distributors. Gaining assistance from fulfillment experts will be even more critical, Mr. Hagel said, as E-commerce companies evolve. Not only will Web retailers increasingly seek to sell products abroad -- an exercise that presents logistical nightmares -- but they will also be pushed by consumers to even greater levels of service, including customized products. More immediately, though, Mr. Hagel said, Internet retailers are complicating matters by broadening their product selection in an effort to increase the amount spent by each customer. That means potentially shipping multiple items from multiple points, using different shippers. "On one hand, I understand the importance of that as a way to derive more revenue from customers," Mr. Hagel said. "But on the other hand, if these companies think they've been challenged by fulfillment issues to date, it's nothing compared to what's coming." If nothing else, the sudden ascendancy of fulfillment is vindicating a segment of the business world that has long suffered from a lack of respect. "We used to be those guys in the dirty suits out there," said John Buck, president of Fingerhut Business Services. "Would you believe that fulfillment is the darling of the day? It's actually stunning to me." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Fingerhut's distribution center near Provo, Utah, handles orders for Etoys. Clockwise from far lower left, products arrive from toy makers; a worker checks an invoice and begins preliminary sorting; at an automated bin, a worker receives items for a customer's order, which is boxed and sent by conveyor to two workers, who prepare it for shipping. (Photographs by George Frey for The newyork Times)

title:
Foreign Affairs;
Little Brother
body: Last summer I visited Chicago and stayed at a large chain hotel. In the morning I went down to swim in the pool, and I put my room key in my bathing suit pocket. I then proceeded to lose the key in the pool. So I went back to the front desk and asked for a new key. "Can you show me a picture I.D.?" asked the desk clerk. "No," I said. "I'm in my bathing suit! I have no I.D." "No problem," said the clerk. She typed a few things into her computer, and then looked up at me and asked, "What are the ages of your two daughters?" My daughters weren't with me. But I had stayed in this hotel a year earlier with them. I correctly answered the clerk's question about their ages and she handed me a new key. But I couldn't help wondering: What else do they have on me and my family in that little computer, and whom are they selling that info to? Last week, I got a letter from an old friend, Richard Day, whom I met in Beirut in 1982 but had lost contact with. Richard, a consultant, now lives in Dubai and his letter said the following: "I found your address on a People Search site on the Internet. I was amazed that for a mere $59 I could order a complete background search on you that included, among other things, a complete listing of your assets. I kept my $59, but it made me wonder what all of this is really coming to. Your daughters and my sons can check each other out in ways that you and I never dreamed were possible." And it's just the beginning. Rule No. 1 of the Internet is this: We are all connected, but nobody's in charge. That is, the Internet is Orwellian in its reach, but there's no Big Brother. Instead of Big Brother, there are a lot of Little Brothers. Beware of the Little Brothers. They are going to be the problem. The Internet super-empowers individuals, Web sites, corporations and even hotels -- the Little Brothers -- so they can amass huge amounts of information outside of any government supervision. Some of these Little Brothers will use that personal data responsibly; others won't. A study by the Center for Democracy and Technology found that less than 10 percent of all Web sites respected the O.E.C.D.'s privacy guidelines, which stipulate that people have the right to expect that any personal data they submit over the Internet will not be used without their consent, that they have a right to correct any errors and to assume the data will be protected from abuse. How we deal with the Little Brothers should be a campaign issue. There are lots of ideas. One of the most thoughtful comes from Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig, in his upcoming book, "Code, and Other Laws of Cyberspace." Mr. Lessig argues that people suffer from the illusion that however cyberspace is right now is how it must always be. It can't be changed. It's a place to be discovered, not shaped. But cyberspace was not handed down by God. Its architecture is shaped by people with certain interests, who are, as we speak, "designing the hardware of cyberspace in ways that are determining the freedom and privacy that you and I will have there," says Mr. Lessig. The architecture of cyberspace is highly influenced by commerce and government, "both of which have an interest in knowing as much as they can about what people are doing and where," says Mr. Lessig. "So it's not an accident that the emerging Internet architecture makes it easier to track people and collect private data, because tracking people is what governments like and collecting private data is what commerce likes." Government, argues Mr. Lessig, can't legislate privacy on the Internet, but it can create incentives for people to build privacy filters and other safeguards into the Internet. "Let's say the government says that data about you is your property and the only way that someone can take it away is by negotiating with you," he said. "That would create an incentive for Web designers to make it easier for each of us to negotiate about our personal data -- what we want to give up for free, what we want to be paid for and what we don't want to give up at all." I don't know that Mr. Lessig has the right answer, but I am certain he's asking the right question: How do we get better governance in cyberspace, when there is no government in control there? Issues such as the right to privacy are core values from our Constitution and Founding Fathers. Are we moving into an age when such values will only be respected on land, but not in cyberspace? If the Constitution ends where the Web begins, well, beware of Little Brother. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING;
An Internet Stable Is Ahead of the Pack
body: DURING a summer of Internet flame-outs, the stock of Internet Capital Group was noteworthy for streaking higher. Internet Capital, a holding company in Wayne, Pa., that owns stakes of between 10 and 50 percent in a portfolio of 36 mostly private Internet-related companies, sold an 11 percent stake in itself to the public on Aug. 4, at $12 a share. Despite the ugly recent environment for Internet stocks, the shares finished their first day of trading at $24.4375 and are now at $91.125. That gives the company a stock market capitalization of $11.3 billion, versus $8.08 billion for CMGI, the Internet holding company in Andover, Mass., to which it is often compared. Even with that run-up, the stock has continued to receive some favorable notices. Henry Blodget, an Internet analyst at Merrill Lynch, which was lead manager for Internet Capital's offering, has called it a "must-own" holding for long-term investors. The stock, he said, "allows public-market investors to invest at private-market prices." Nearly all of Internet Capital's "partner businesses," as it calls its holdings, are engaged in so-called business-to-business commerce on line. And many Internet experts say it has enormous growth prospects. Forrester Research in Boston expects business-to-business E-commerce to grow from $43 billion in 1998 to $1.3 trillion in 2003 -- far above the $108 billion it expects in E-commerce directed at consumers. Bob Turner, chief investment officer of Turner Investment Partners, a money manager in Berwyn, Pa., who bought shares at the offering, said the company's "built-in diversification" is key to investing in business-to-business E-commerce, "where winners and losers are especially tough to identify." The company was founded in 1996 by Walter W. Buckley 3d, now 39, who is chief executive, and Kenneth A. Fox, 29, a director. Both were employed at Safeguard Scientifics, an information technology firm with an impressive record in starting technology companies; Safeguard is Internet Capital's largest shareholder, with a 14.3 percent stake. Internet Capital's largest holding, Verticalnet, went public in February at $16 a share and is now at $32.4375. It has 47 industry-specific on-line sites for commerce. A big advantage of business-to-business E-commerce is scale. "It's a higher-margin, higher-impact business," said Charles Finnie, managing director at Volpe Brown Whelan, the San Francisco investment bank that was a manager for the Verticalnet underwriting. A typical transaction, he noted, can be thousands of dollars, compared with, say, $15 for a book. Internet Capital may have advantages in attracting start-ups. It has devoted 40 percent of its current budget to amassing in-house expertise to help such businesses get off the ground. Because it owns only part of its businesses, their entrepreneurs can keep big positions and share in future growth. Still, some Web-stock investors have stayed on the sidelines, seeing that Internet Capital trades at more than 11 times analysts' estimates of net asset value. Moreover, management expects to incur operating losses for several years. Jay Tracey, manager of the Oppenheimer Enterprise fund, does not own Internet Capital shares, saying the company's businesses -- some with little more than a trickle of revenue -- are just too young to evaluate. "I may not be giving them enough credit for the individual properties," he said, "but their companies are very early-stage." Mr. Blodget, for his part, predicts the shares will reach $125 within two years, on his assumption that Internet Capital, through its stakes in its partner companies, will account for 1 to 3 percent of all business-to-business E-commerce. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: "Eyes on E-Commerce" plots Internet Capital Group stock price, daily closes, since its I.P.O. at $12.

title:
MARKET WATCH;
Wary of the Internet? Just Try to Avoid It
body: THE major stock indexes gave up a lot of ground last week on fears that a stumbling dollar might reignite inflation and dampen enthusiasm for unitedstates equities among foreign investors. The Dow Jones industrials lost 4.8 percent on the week; the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index fell 4.3 percent. Technology stocks were hit after Steven A. Ballmer, Microsoft's president, allowed on Thursday that a "gold rush" mentality had driven the shares to absurd heights. The Nasdaq composite, down 4.5 percent on the week, is still up 25 percent this year. If Mr. Ballmer thinks shares of technology companies are overvalued in general, what must he think of Internet issues in particular? Although these stocks are well off their highs, their prices are mighty rich when judged against their earnings, if they have any. Many investors, hurt by plunging Web stocks -- or interested in owning companies that actually make money -- have sworn off E-shares. But it is increasingly difficult for investors to escape the Internet altogether. By virtue of their incredible market performance, shares of Internet companies play a big role in the major stock indexes, and contribute greatly to their peregrinations. Like it or not, investors in index funds are exposed to Internet stocks -- something that many of those investors may not realize. Prudential Securities recently analyzed a host of indexes and the contribution that Internet stocks make to them. The firm considers a company to be of the Internet species if it does or will get significant sales from the Web. More than 300 qualified, ranging from Amazon.com, E*Trade Group and CMGI to lesser-known companies like Digital River and Proxicom. Among the major indexes, the Nasdaq composite, not surprisingly, has the greatest exposure to the Internet, with 239 Web-linked companies making up 49.2 percent of its market value. The Russell 2000, the benchmark for small-capitalization stocks, includes 103 Web companies, accounting for 5.1 percent of its value. (The Internet component of the Dow industrials is not in the study, because Dow Jones would not give Prudential the information it needed.) And here is a shocker for index-fund investors: Internet companies account for 25.9 percent of the value of the S.& P. 500. Steven DeSanctis, director of small-cap research at Prudential, said the presence or absence of Internet stocks in seemingly comparable indexes has skewed some benchmarks' moves. The fact that the Russell 2000's weighting in Internet stocks is three times that of the S. & P. Small Cap index may help explain why the latter is down 3.4 percent for the year, while the Russell is off 1.1 percent. Of course, some Internet stocks are priced more wackily than others. But investors should know how much these shares contribute to the market indexes' moves today. Mr. DeSanctis said that on Aug. 31, when the S. & P. 500 was up 8.41 percent for the year, Internet-related stocks had contributed almost two-thirds of that gain. Many Internet stocks are up this year, and so continue to lift the indexes they dominate. But there is no guarantee that their effects on these indexes will remain salutary. Increased Internet exposure has another effect on these indexes: heightened volatility. Seat belts, anyone? http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: "On Line?" The graph shows the percent of market value that represents Internet companies as of June 30

title:
PERSONAL BUSINESS;
The On-Line Trader Is Becoming the New Big Man on Campus
body: SHORTLY before 9 A.M. on Sept. 17, an alarm sounded on Derek O'Banion's personal computer -- the signal that Vitria Technology, an Internet business software developer, had begun its first day of trading on Nasdaq. Vitria, offered at $18, soared to $45 but quickly dipped. Mr. O'Banion pounced, buying 200 shares at $43.375, watching them rise to $46, and then selling when they slipped to $45.50. Ten minutes and a $425 profit later, he was back in bed for another half-hour of sleep before his 10 A.M. introductory fiction-writing class. With the school year in full swing, Mr. O'Banion, a senior at the University of Puget Sound in Tacoma, Wash., is one of thousands of college students who fit on-line stock trading into already busy schedules of lectures, exams and keg parties. Younger versions of the office workers who sneak in trades while the boss isn't looking, more students are checking prices and shifting their portfolios between, and sometimes during, classes. "I don't expect it to conflict, but if it does, once in a while I can miss a class," said Mr. O'Banion, 21, a computer science major. "It's not like I haven't done that before." Most undergraduates grew up with personal computers and saw the stock market soar throughout their teen-age years. And they have easy access to financial news and research in their dormitories, fraternity and sorority houses and campus computer rooms. Many students appear to be taking a relatively safe approach to on-line investing. Mustafa Gultekin, a finance professor at the University of North Carolina, said that of about 70 students in the undergraduate investing club last year, only two were day-trading. "That's a sure way to lose money," he tells students. Indeed, last month, the North American Securities Administrators Association reported that 70 percent of day traders lose money. GOMEZ ADVISORS, a research firm in Lincoln, Mass., that follows the on-line brokerage industry, said a July survey of on-line traders showed that about 548,000, or nearly 11 percent of the nation's 5.12 million on-line traders, were 25 or younger. While the firm could not say how many of those under-25 traders were students, it reported that nearly 5 percent, or about 25,000, were placing orders from schools, mostly universities. About 61 percent, or 305,000, were placing orders from home, a number that could also include some students. Gomez found that, like their older counterparts, nearly half of the younger on-line traders had long-term, or at least 10-year, investing strategies. But nearly 23 percent of them invested on line primarily for fun or challenge, compared with 13 percent of their elders. Mr. O'Banion is more active than most students, making as many as 20 trades daily since he opened an on-line account last spring with MB Trading of El Segundo, Calif., using $10,000 he inherited. While his portfolio has grown about 40 percent, he has lost and recouped thousands of dollars along the way, he said. He has cut down on his trading since spending $1,000 in commissions shortly after he started, even with discounts for frequent traders. For Mr. O'Banion, the thrill of the moment and the dream of great riches are why he continues to day-trade -- and why he focuses on initial public offerings of Internet stocks.  "When you get into an I.P.O., your heart starts racing, because you could make or lose a lot of money real fast," he said, shortly after making his Vitria Technology trades. Because he concentrates on the first few hours of trading, beginning at 6:30 A.M. on the West Coast, Mr. O'Banion said investing does not usually cut into class or study time. Other students spend more time following the market than trading in it. Rodger Bucchianeri and Jeffrey Monat, 21-year-old seniors and roommates at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, opened on-line accounts two years ago. They watch CNBC and get stock quotations from Bloomberg terminals in campus buildings. Mr. Bucchianeri also carries a pager that displays stock prices and news, which he monitors during his classes. Louis Cohen, a senior business major at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, has made three or four trades a week since opening his on-line account with E*Trade at the beginning of this year. His portfolio started with stock in blue-chip companies like Philip Morris and Merck that he received as gifts from his parents and grandparents, beginning in first or second grade. He now has $15,000 to $20,000 in the market, mostly in long-term holdings, but with $2,000 to $3,000 allocated to making short-term moves. Mr. Cohen, 21, consults with Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity brothers who are also interested in stocks, and he is in close touch with his older brother, Lawrence, a day trader in Forest Hills, Queens. "If he sees something I should look into, he'll send me an instant message, and I'll do the same with him," Mr. Cohen said. FOR many student investors, managing an on-line portfolio is training for a career on Wall Street or in the broader business world. Mr. Bucchianeri, who has already done internships with Paine Webber, J. P. Morgan and Bear, Stearns, regards his early start in investing as a chance to take risks that he might shun later. As he put it, "I can afford to lose it all, so I'm looking for the high gains." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Derek O'Banion, a student at the University of Puget Sound, trades stocks on line from his dormitory. (Daniel Sheehan for The newyork Times)

title:
PRIVATE SECTOR;
Delectable Options On the Grocer's Shelf
body: George T. Shaheen, the chief executive who helped build Andersen Consulting into the world's largest consulting firm, said last week that he was leaving to become the chief of Webvan Group, an Internet start-up in Foster City, Calif. It wasn't the first offer Mr. Shaheen received recently. Last year, he was wooed for a top job at E.D.S., but turned it down. So why leave the firm just as its protracted battle with its sister accounting firm, Arthur Andersen, is coming to a head in final hearings next month? One answer: stock options. Webvan, an on-line grocer that plans to go public, has offered Mr. Shaheen a stake of at least 3 percent, which could soon be worth tens of millions of dollars if the offering is successful. But that certainly is not assured. While Mr. Shaheen is a whiz when it comes to information technology and electronic commerce, it's not clear what he knows about grocery shopping beyond what he might have picked up from his parents, who ran a grocery store near Peoria, Ill. His wife, Darlene, said this week that he has accompanied her to the local market, Draeger's in Menlo Park, Calif., on a few occasions. Now, she said, the family will be buying its groceries on line.   MELODY PETERSEN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Shaheen

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Seeing the Future of Print In a Universe Gone Digital
body: The consensus at a forum this week on the future of print journalism in the digital era was that there would be a future, in part because readers continued to see value in the printed page. For a couple of decades now, publishers have been warned that the digital age could make newspapers and magazines -- and perhaps their staffs -- obsolete. But at the forum, sponsored by CSC Vanguard, a consulting arm of the Computer Sciences Corporation, even those who are developing ways to deliver information electronically said the printed page would persist. "On-line services will coexist with print for the foreseeable future and maybe forever," said Stephen B. Shepard, editor in chief of Business Week, at the gathering of about 75 reporters, editors and publishers from newspapers, trade journals and magazines. "It isn't an all-or-nothing proposition we are facing."  The Electronic Threat Industry analysts have seen the proliferation of electronic services like America Online and Compuserve and the increasing popularity of the Internet, the global web of computer networks, as a growing threat to print media. More and more newspapers and magazines are making deals to have their publications, or other information they generate, distributed on electronic services. And the cost of delivering information electronically continues to decline while the cost of delivering printed materials continues to rise. Further, it has been asked why computer users, with information at hand from nearly 50,000 computer bulletin boards, a vast array of data bases and their 20 million fellow users of the Internet, still need newspapers or editors. "We're at a point in time where everything has gone digital," said Nicholas Negroponte, director of the Media Laboratory of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. "That has consequences we don't understand yet." He noted that engineers recently demonstrated the capability of delivering 50 gigabits, or billions of bits, of data over fiber optic networks, which means that the entire 104 years of The Wall Street Journal could be delivered electronically in half a second.  Value of Journalists But Roger F. Fidler, director of the Knight-Ridder Information Design Laboratory in Boulder, Colo., argued that such a profusion of information would make editors and reporters all the more valuable. "The idea that all this information will be out in cyberspace and people will select what they want is insane," he said. "There is no business model for that. Who will pay for it?" Others agreed. "Those of us who produce content will be in demand," said Marshall Loeb, who is about to retire as managing editor of Fortune magazine. "The marketplace value of journalists and editors who master content will rise significantly." Rich Karlgaard, editor in chief of Forbes ASAP, a technology supplement to Forbes magazine, noted that the first discussions of the paperless office occurred in 1980. But by the end of the decade, as desktop publishing proliferated, "we had four times the amount of paper being created in offices as in 1980," he said. Others pointed out the portability advantage of print. Michael Treacy, an independent business consultant, noted that newspapers and magazines were an "anywhere, anytime device." Forum participants said people enjoyed folding, scanning and turning pages of newspapers and magazines -- or saving articles without having to sign on to a computer. The editors agreed that, in the long run, an electronic newspaper might be preferable to what Paul E. Steiger, managing editor of The Wall Street Journal, called using "dead trees." But they said the move must be driven by consumer demand. Mr. Treacy said, "We can take money out of the pulp and printing-press process, but are these forms of electronic distribution something that people are prepared to pay money for?" Editors also saw drawbacks in trying to sell advertising, which continues to support newspapers and magazines, in an electronic medium like the Internet, where advertising is considered taboo. A model for the future blending of electronic and print information may be found at Wired, an 18-month-old magazine that chronicles the impact of an increasingly computerized society. Louis Rossetto, its editor and publisher, said Wired had embraced the Internet, publishing the Internet addresses of all its editors and writers and encouraging electronic dialogue with its readers to supplement the publication. "We're already in the interactive world," he said. "This is not a transient thing."

title:
The Executive Computer;
For Befuddled Newcomers, Easier Access to the Internet
body: TO the uninitiated, navigating the Internet can feel like sailing the Pacific without a chart or compass. Users may reach land eventually, but whether it's their intended destination is another matter. That's because the global web of computer networks known as the Internet arose from scientific and academic computing based on the notoriously arcane Unix software operating system, which can require users to memorize all sorts of complex network commands. But suddenly, dozens of companies seem to be offering graphical interfaces to the Internet, using on-screen icons and a point-and-click mouse to disguise the command-line complexity of the network. Companies like Notis Systems Inc., based in Evanston, Ill., and the Pipeline, based in newyork, offer easy point-and-click access to the Internet. Next week, MKS Inc. of Waterloo, Ontario, plans to start selling graphical interface software for Internet users. And next month, Netcom On-Line Communication Services Inc., based in San Jose, Calif., plans to introduce a software package called Net Cruiser, which the company says will put even first-time users directly onto the Internet in less than 10 minutes through Netcom On-Line. Dozens of other companies, including startups and commercial on-line services and software publishers looking for business opportunities, are working to connect the millions of less-technical users who are clamoring for easy access to cyberspace. "The difference between having an interface for the Internet and not having an interface is, for 99 percent of us, the difference between using the Internet and not using it," said James Gleick, president of the Pipeline, an Internet access service. There is another, not insignificant reason that dozens of software companies are betting that there will be plenty of customers for these programs, which are generally priced between $100 and $ 200: with commercial software comes technical support -- someone to call for users who lose their way on the Internet. When it comes to Internet "front-ends," as these products are called, there are as many approaches as there are software programs in the labs. Some are simply interfaces, while others are Internet services. But all seek to reduce the many steps it takes to establish a direct Internet connection -- and, when connected, to send and receive electronic mail and find the way through the 7,000 or so discussion groups, known as "news groups" in Internet parlance. But there is one caveat: setting up a system to run some of these programs is not for the faint of heart. Some require the installation of a TCP/IP stack -- byzantine software that lets a computer connect to the Internet through the TCP/IP protocol, or set of communications instructions, that is an Internet standard. Most of them require a SLIP (serial-line Internet protocol) or P.P.P. (point-to-point protocol) connection, which is available by subscribing to an Internet access service -- unless a user works at a company, university or other organization that operates its own Internet server computer. (To their credit, software publishers that sell the front-ends usually will help users find the best SLIP or P.P.P. providers for their needs). These are not necessarily provided by dial-up Internet service providers like the Well in Sausalito, Calif., or the World in Brookline, Mass. So, users already endeared to such a service may end up having to subscribe to a second access provider to use a front-end. For Macintosh users, it is unfortunate that most current and imminent commercial programs are for PC's running Windows. Experienced users of the Internet have had a graphical interface for years in Mosaic, a software program developed by the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois, which can be downloaded free over the network. Using Mosaic, users can browse the World Wide Web, a collection of published documents and services that is one of the fastest growing parts of the Internet. Its hypertext links allow users to quickly jump from one document to another, regardless of where those documents are, by simply clicking on the highlighted hypertext words or phrases. And the documents found through Mosaic can contain multimedia and graphics, in addition to simple text. Users who have navigated the Web without Mosaic will be amazed at how gracefully Mosaic does the dirty work. But Mosaic has its limitations.  While the program is easy, outfitting a PC with all the parts necessary to run it can be daunting. There are no instructions and no on-line help systems to help solve problems. "With the Windows version, the same computer user who would find it so easy to use is probably likely to have trouble installing it," said Jae Allen, project coordinator for the National Center for Supercomputing Applications. But a handful of ambitious software developers hope to change that. The supercomputing center has licensed Mosaic to a half-dozen companies that plan to bring out commercial products that fix the bugs and iron out the quirks, and the center is in the final stages of negotiating with many other companies. By this time next year, users should be able to choose from a variety of commercial Mosaic programs. Quarterdeck Office Systems, the Santa Monica, Calif., maker of the QEMM memory manager program, hopes to have a commercial Mosaic product out by the end of the year, complete with everything a novice needs to get started on the Internet for less than $100. The same is true for Spry, a software company in Seattle that is jointly developing a $149 product called Internet-in-a-Box with O'Reilly & Associates, a book publisher in Sebastopol, Calif. But some of the most promising interfaces take a different tack from Mosaic. Perhaps the most intriguing new interface is the Pipeline, an Internet communications service that went on-line for the users of Windows in December. The programs has a simple point-and-click interface, reducing many complex functions to a single click, and it uses the image of a notebook to help users organize news group searches. The Pipeline interface does not require chores like obtaining a SLIP connection, and it is an interface that works on Pipeline's own Internet service and other access providers, like the Hooked service in San Francisco, that have licensed it. Other programs take other approaches. Notis Systems, a unit of Ameritech, has built a $129 front-end to Gopher, the searching tool that helps users find and retrieve files on server computers throughout the Internet. But installing and configuring all the pieces is a tedious process. Cyberdesk, from Cybercorp Inc. in Atlanta, is a $179 communications package that can function as a front-end to all on-line services, including the Internet. This program may be ideal for users of multiple electronic services who are tired of connecting to each one separately. Cyberdesk will call the Internet service along with other electronic services at specified times and retrievemail and news group messages that can be read off-line. Of the on-line services, the Delphi Internet Services Corporation, based in Cambridge, Mass., provides the most comprehensive built-in access to the Internet, including news groups, Gopher, and World Wide Web. Delphi is working on improvements to its interface, which uses menus but is not truly graphical. America Online, the fast-growing on-line service based in Vienna, Va., recently began providing access to some Internet functions, including electronic mail and news groups. Although America Online's Internet functions are limited, new features are expected this summer. Not insignificant is the fact that with America Online, a user's connection to the Internet is established without any additional software and makes use of the graphical user interface that has made America Online so popular among network novices.  Compuserve, too, is working on Internet access, and hopes to make it available by the end of the year. But not everybody is so optimistic that easy-to-use front-ends will make the Internet more hospitable to the average computer user. "Graphical front-ends are not the panacea of the newcomer to cyberspace," said Daniel Dern, author of "The Internet Guide for New Users." "These interfaces make it easier to use Internet tools and let the user more easily understand what the Internet is," Mr. Dern said. But, he added, they can also help users get more quickly to the Internet's true bottlenecks, like traffic jams and a lack of adequate indexing of material. But even if newcomers to cyberspace find they quickly bump into the limitations of the Internet, it is remarkable that they got there at all. And because of this new class of software, that's more than many of them are doing today. Graphic   Drawing

title: Arizona Lawyers Form Company for Internet Advertising
body: In a move that is certain to increase the turmoil on global computer networks, two Arizona lawyers said yesterday that they had formed a company with the goal of making commercial advertising pervasive on the Internet. In doing so, they shunned a plan, announced earlier this week by two other companies, to create specific advertising zones on Usenet News, a popular network that is connected to the Internet, a global web of computer networks. The advertising zones, which would require advertisers to pay a fee to place their messages on the network, would theoretically allow the estimated 20 million Internet users to choose to view ads. The new advertising company, called Cybersell, was started by Laurence A. Canter and Martha S. Siegel, husband-and-wife partners in the immigration law firm of Canter & Siegel in Phoenix.  Focus of Criticism Mr. Canter and Ms. Siegel have been the focus of intense criticism on several computer networks since April 12, when they posted an advertisement offering their legal services on thousands of Usenet bulletin boards, called news groups, without regard for the interests of the specific news groups. The first product Cybersell will advertise throughout the Internet is "a health product, super-oxygenated water," Ms. Siegel said yesterday. "You drink it, and the fact that it has additional oxygen gives you additional energy and promotes the healing process," she claimed, adding that the ads would be ready "within days, certainly within two weeks." The Usenet is one of the largest networks within the Internet, read by an estimated 10 million people. Most of the computers comprising the Internet and Usenet networks are privately owned.  Violation of Tradition The act, while not illegal, violated long-held traditions against random placement of any type of messages on news groups. Such scatter-shot messaging is known as "spamming." Each Usenet participant pays, either directly or indirectly, for the data he or she receives. In contrast, the cost to spam an advertisement in thousands of news groups, where it is potentially read by hundreds of thousands of computer users, is typically less than $50. The first advertisement spamming by Mr. Canter and Ms. Siegel resulted in tens of thousands of complaints -- even death threats -- from Usenet readers. Electronic vandals jammed the law firm's telephone, facsimile and computer systems for days. But Ms. Siegel said the law firm made so much money from its ad -- offering, for $95 per person, to help foreign nationals fill out free applications for unitedstates Government "green card" work permits -- that it decided to continue with the ads.  An Alternative Proposal In response to the outcry, the Internet Company of Cambridge, Mass., and the Electronic Newsstand of Washington, both of which provide Internet services, announced that they would create "an acceptable channel" on Usenet where companies could place commercial advertising, product information, promotional offers and price lists. "Unsolicited advertising on the global Internet is as acceptable as junk fax is in the real world," said Robert Raisch, president of the Internet Company and chairman of the Electronic Newsstand, a joint venture of the Internet Company and the New Republic magazine. The Electronic Newsstand hopes to become a main distributor of books and magazines on the Internet. The advertising channels would be grouped under a broad "market" directory on Usenet, with many subdirectories created for different products and services. Mr. Raisch said companies that advertised on the market news groups would pay the Internet Company a fee to do so, and that 25 percent of the fees would be set aside to subsidize Internet services for all users.  Veterans Cite Other Ads Some network veterans said advertising was already accepted on the Internet, as long as it was done in accord with the wishes of the Internet community. "There are plenty of existing groups that have appeared spontaneously and organically," said Edward Vielmetti, vice president of MSEN, Inc., an Internet service provider in Ann Arbor, Mich. "They appear around existing discussion groups with a ready audience. That appears to work phenomenally well." In an interview yesterday, however, Ms. Siegel rejected the idea of special advertising zones, and said Cybersell would post its messages to all Internet users. "I think it's too limiting," she said of the advertising zone proposal. "Advertising has to take its place on the Internet, just as it has in other media -- newspapers, TV and radio." "What these people are planning to do is relegate ads to some sort of black hole off in a corner," she said.

title: New Venture in Cyberspace By Silicon Graphics Founder
body: James H. Clark, the former Stanford University professor who founded Silicon Graphics Inc. and turned it into a leader in the work station market, has formed a new company aimed at what he sees as computing's next big trend: navigating cyberspace. Mr. Clark is the co-founder of the company with Marc Andreessen, a 22-year-old computer designer who helped create a program called Mosaic for retrieving information from the Internet, a global web of computer networks used by an estimated 20 million people. Mr. Clark's new company, called the Mosaic Communications Corporation, and based in Mountain View, Calif., has also hired six other members of the original Mosaic development team from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Mr. Andreessen, a former student there, has been a part of the National Center for Supercomputer Applications at the university. Mr. Clark said that he had turned to the young Mosaic team because they had the clearest vision of how to commercialize the Internet, a chaotic system of networks developed by university and corporate researchers. "I know there are a bunch of people looking for the gold in the Internet," Mr. Clark said. "These guys have already been there and found it," he said of his new team. In the last 18 months Mosaic has become a phenomenon even by the standards of the computer industry, in which logarithmic growth curves are routine. Mosaic enables computer users to navigate the Internet and retrieve information by simply pointing and clicking with a mouse. More than one million copies of Mosaic are already in circulation. The program is available free to individual users who can download it over the Internet, and many companies -- like Mr. Clark's -- are now seeking to develop commercial versions with additional features. Mosaic has touched off an outpouring of new technology development, corporate investment and excitement because it has made the resources of the network accessible to people who lack technical expertise. On the thousands of "server" computers on the Internet, information is stored as documents that may include text, graphics, video clips and sound. Documents in turn may have "hypertext" links -- highlighted words or phrases pointing a user to information on other computers. Mosaic enables users to click on the hypertext links, retrieving information instantly from dozens of machines around the world.  Built on the Web Mosaic is built upon a system known as the World Wide Web, developed by Tim Berners-Lee, a researcher at the Cern international physics laboratory in Switzerland. What began as an electronic library system for a group of physicists has turned into an international bazaar. Corporations are using the Web to store huge volumes of technical data, making it instantly accessible to their customers. Other companies are planning to use it for commercial ventures as diverse as business-to-business purchases or even home shopping. Newspapers are using it to publish electronic dailies. Mosaic is being heralded as the way to bring buyers and sellers together on the Internet. "Clearly somebody has to figure out how to get around on the net," said Denise Caruso, editorial director of Technology and Media, a newsletter in San Francisco. "That's a huge market."  Will the Internet Be Paved? In the last year there has been a spirited debate between those who argue that the Internet is only a placeholder for a future commercial information network to be built by cable and telephone companies, and those who believe that the Internet will inevitably become the nation's data highway. Mr. Clark said he was squarely in the Internet camp. "I believe that the Internet is the information highway," he said. "I'm religious about this. I don't think it's cable television." Larry Smarr, the director of the National Center for Supercomputing Applications, said he was comfortable with the idea of having young researchers leave academic organizations to start new ventures. "Jim has told us that he got his first team of people from Stanford Univeristy to create Silicon Graphics," Mr. Smarr said, "and he is getting his next team from the University of Illinois."
