title:
Sound Bytes;
An Electronic Salon, in N.Y.
body: AS a graduate student in newyork City in 1989, Stacy Horn discovered the Well, a computer conferencing system based in Sausalito, Calif. She was so smitten with the virtual community created by the Well that she decided to found her own on-line community in newyork the same year. Using two personal computers as "hosts" and a handful of telephone lines to receive calls from other computers, she began with 20 people and five areas of discussion. Since then Echo -- the system name she chose, which she later decided stood for East Coast Hang Out -- has attracted more than 2,000 members in 50 discussion groups. The system is supported by user fees of $19.95 a month for up to 30 hours of use, with discounts for students. Ms. Horn, Echo's president, is considering starting Echo in other cities, possibly Austin, Tex., New Orleans or Minneapolis. Besides being an electronic home for many people, Echo is a place where users experiment with the intersection of computing and television. Every Thursday at 11 P.M. on a program called Electronic Neighborhood on Manhattan Cable, viewers can read Echo keyboard conversations displayed on their screen, and listen to a separate three-way telephone conversation. Question: Why did you start Echo? Answer: I loved the idea of an electronic salon with a newyork attitude. I liked the Well in California, but I wanted to do things differently. I'm an artist and so I wanted more discussions of arts and culture, and fewer discussions of computers. Q: Was it expensive to get going? A: Not at all. I had been working at Mobil Oil and I quit when they moved to Virginia. I used my severance pay to start the system. It's just text, so today we run Echo with two 486-based computers that we're planning to upgrade to Pentiums. I employ two part-time people. We have 35 phone lines and we're planning on adding 10. We also have a high-speed connection to the Internet. Q: Is this a substitute for community in the traditional sense? A: It's another tool for creating community. People are always grouping around something. This is a new tool and it's a thousand times more efficient and richer. Ms. magazine is taking over the women's forum. The Village Voice has their own conference, and the Whitney Museum is starting a conference on American Art. Q: Echo isn't an exclusively male hangout? A: Forty percent of our users are women. Q: How does that make Echo different from conventional bulletin board and conferencing systems? A: I wish I had a good answer. Everyone says there's a different flavor. Not only are there more women on Echo. Now they're talking and not lurking. As a result it's more civilized. Q: When Echo began growing quickly, did you feel like you were losing a child? A: There was definitely a little while where I felt like, "Wait a minute, this is mine." But it freed me at the same time. It's very similar to what parents go through. Q: Have people tried to buy Echo? A: A number of people have approached me. It would be great to have a partner so I could have the capital to expand and improve Echo. But there hasn't been anyone I thought was a good match.  STACY HORN  Born: June 3, 1956, Norfolk, Va.  Education: Bachelor of Fine Arts, School of the Museum of Fine Arts of the Boston Museum of Fine Arts; master's degree, interactive telecommunications program at newyork University.  Noncomputer reading: "A Natural History of the Senses," by Diane Ackerman.  Ideal escape: The movies.  Hobby: Swing dancing.  Family: Single.  Pets: Two cats.  Other interests: Has written an unpublished novel.  Computer: Two Intel-based 486's running Unix, and a Macintosh SE.

title:
On-Line Romance;
Office Workers Feel Cupid's Byte
body: Burke Stinson and Nancy J. Smith, husband-and-wife executives at A.T.& T. in New Jersey, conducted a prolonged courtship through interoffice email before their wedding last year, sending sometimes two or three notes and love letters a day in an outpouring that eventually totaled more than 400 pages of confessional, epistolary romance. "It's such a thrill to bare one's soul right on the screen, see it, save it, re-reread it, then swallow hard and push the send button," Ms. Smith said. "A wonderful combination of old-fashioned courting and at the same time, up-to-the-minute technology." The office romance, long a staple of pulp fiction and real life drama, has been updated. As computer networks have linked larger numbers of employees inside companies, and between companies, and as electronic mail has become more accepted as a means of internal corporate dialogue, lovers and other email experts say that bytes and blips have become yet another means for the endlessly inventive human heart to make connection. No statistics exist, of course, about how many people inside company or government offices have found each other in this way, but sex researchers, psychologists and computer buffs say that judging by the flow of anecdotes, the phenomenon is as old as email itself, and affairs of the heart and the keyboard are becoming more common. "The starting point for any relationship is proximity," Naomi B. McCormick said. "Computers give you an opportunity for electronic proximity." Ms. McCormick is a professor of psychology at the State University of newyork at Plattsburgh and president elect of the Society for the Scientific Study of Sex. "People do use the information highway to start new relationships or to make a new relationship more intimate." To be sure, this is a cool medium, and ultimately that may be the appeal: No lingering glances across the desk that can be misinterpreted, no unwelcome visual or physical component at all in fact, until and unless an electronic conversation grows into something more compelling. "People are much more cautious because they've been sensitized about sexual harassment, and we have this information highway that people are becoming more familiar with," said Lisa A. Mainiero, a professor of management at Fairfield University and the author of "Office Romance: Love, Power and Sex in the Workplace." "You put the two together and you have a natural vehicle for office romances to take place." Like human sexuality itself, electronic dalliance can take innumerable forms. Last year at a Midwestern manufacturing company, for example, in a case recounted by Dr. Mainiero, a woman began receiving anonymous messages on her computer. Eventually she confronted her suspect, an engineer, who immediately confessed. They were still dating at last report. In another instance, she said, an employee who dumped an office lover turned on her computer every day to find it loaded with pitiful pleas and electronic entreaties stacked up like a dead letter file. In a recent dial-in computer forum on sexuality, a woman lamented: "My husband demands compusex." About 55 percent of the 2,000 largest companies in North America now have some version of electronic mail, up from 30 percent in 1991, according to an industry trade group, the Electronic Messaging Association, which projects growth in the use of email of 19 percent a year through this decade. Its use in many companies is also climbing rapidly. At places like Apple Computer or Microsoft, email has become an internal nerve system for employees to stay in touch, collaborate or just plan lunch. Equally important, communications experts say, is that email tends to encourage a certain kind of writing: much more personal and informal than old-style memo writing or even telephone conversation, often full of hyperbole and exaggeration, and often lacking in judicious thought about how the message might be perceived. All things, in other words, that make people open up, or least seem open to others.  It Doesn't Take Much "The great thing about email is that somebody can send you a two-line message and you can get an idea of their wit from reading just two sharp lines," said Monica Harrington, a public relations manager at Microsoft, the computer software company. Mrs. Harrington met her husband, Mike, a software engineer at the company, through email. She also made the first overture: an electronic invitation to play racquetball. "I knew he'd lose, and he did," she said. Lee Sproull, a professor of sociology in the business school at Boston University, who has written a book about how email is transforming the modern office, said that electronic writing loosens inhibitions specifically because all the visual and physical reminders of status are removed: You think, you type and off it goes. "Just as the telephone produced its own form of communication, so will email," she said. Veterans of email romance say it also makes relationships fundamentally different when they do evolve into real love. "It's a backward relationship, inverse," said Will Thompson, an electronic technician from Salt Lake City, who met and fell in love last year through an Internet contact that grew from a casual conversation into a passionate intellectual dialogue. He and his friend, Susan, a doctor who lives in Los Angeles, met there last Thanksgiving. "We're still learning how each other squeezes the tooth paste," Mr. Thompson said. "But we know what the reaction will be to some crisis or abstract thing. It's almost like we've been married for a couple of years." Some people seem to find their voice in email. Mr. Stinson and Ms. Smith at A.T.& T. both said they found it awkward to speak to each other on the phone, so much had the keyboard become their medium. She was working in Pennsylvania for the company, while he was at the headquarters in Basking Ridge, N.J. "For an unknown reason we are comfortable with each other, comfortable in the sense that we don't hold back too much during these exchanges," Mr. Stinson wrote in a note to her. "But we both, to some degree, worry about being able to continue the -- what? -- the attraction when/if our eyes meet again." Beyond the cooing, however, privacy experts say that high-tech romance is in some ways riskier than the old-fashioned kind. There are no laws about when email messages may be legally opened and read by employers, for example, and most companies maintain that since they own the computer system -- and could perhaps be held responsible if an employee began using email to harass a co-worker sexually or conduct an illegal business -- they can monitor all email. email lovers also risk exposure from co-workers, who might find a particular note interesting enough for wider circulation. An overly persistent email suitor also risks his or her intentions being taken as a form of harassment, though a spokeswoman for 9 to 5, the National Association of Working Women, said that email sexual harassment is so rare as to be a nonissue. Some people believe that the age of innocence for electronic love may already be over. "With all the sexual harassment danger, it's a risky business," said Geoffrey Bryan, a lawyer in Los Angeles who met his wife, Martha, in the late 1980's through a Macintosh users forum on Compuserve, the computer networking company. They were married in 1991. "Whatever sequence of events that led to that would be much more difficult to have happen now," he said. Graphic   Photo: "A wonderful combination of old-fashioned courting and, at the same time, up-to-the-minute technology, " said Nancy J. Smith of her courtship with Burke Stinson via interoffice email. The couple, sitting in their home in Madison, N.J., were married last year. (Norman Y. Lono for The newyork Times) (pg. 22)  Chart: "LOVE ON-LINE: Courting by Computer" Excerpts from the email courtship between Burke Stinson and Nancy J. Smith. Ms. Smith: "I looked ona map and the midpoint between Madison, N.J., and Camp Hill, Pa. is Schwencksville, just south of Allentown. They have a pretty nice truck stop there. If you like cabbage and pigs stomach, served with enormous mounds of mashed potatoes, that's the place for you. How about Philadelphia?" Mr. Stinson: "Philly in December . . . Leaves off the trees and shrubs. Grass gone brown . . . Look, it all comes down to what "personalities" we become when we're with each other - how we make each other feel, act and respond. So barren elm trees and chilly drizzle won't matter." Ms. Smith: "Being one who doesn't recognize danger, I'll keep moving forward." Mr. Stinson: "We haven't run the other way . . . If you do drive past that Schwecky place, do pick up a sweatshirt or something. Then , some day, let's meet there."  (pg. 22)

title: Junnosuke Ofusa, Long the Manager For Times in Tokyo
body: Junnosuke Ofusa, the Japanese journalist who managed the Tokyo bureau of The newyork Times for nearly six decades, died today in Tokyo. He was 86 years old. Mr. Ofusa suffered a heart attack, said his son, Nobuo Ofusa. He was hired in 1930 by the first bureau chief for The Times in Tokyo, Hugh Byas. The Japanese Government, which in prewar days suspected Mr. Ofusa was a spy, later honored him.  A Reporter and Interpreter He worked with more than 20 bureau chiefs and correspondents assigned to Tokyo, acting as reporter, interpreter and fixer. "He was a lovely man whose devotion and courage on behalf of The newyork Times were an inspiration," said Arthur O. Sulzberger, the chairman and chief executive officer of The newyork Times Company. When the Japanese authorities decided that Mr. Byas, who was British, was a spy, Mr. Ofusa said that he, not Mr. Byas, had collected statistics about Japan's industrial output, then a military secret, and the officer interrogating him backed down. The next bureau chief, Otto D. Tolischus, was arrested on the day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor. For months Mr. Ofusa took food and clothes to Mr. Tolischus in prison, until he was sent to the unitedstates in a prisoner exchange. When the American occupation army swept into Tokyo in 1945, Mr. Ofusa greeted the arriving correspondent, Lindesay M. Parrott, with a smile, saying: "I did my best to defeat your country. But now the war is over." Mr. Ofusa became a well-known figure in journalistic circles, with entree to political and business leaders. After his formal retirement in 1987, he held the post of senior adviser to The Times's Tokyo bureau. Mr. Ofusa is survived by his wife, Tama, his son, two daughters and seven grandchildren.

title:
SUNDAY, MARCH 13, 1994;
Slipping Through the Net
body: Are you information-poor or information-rich? Is there an entrance ramp to the data highway near you? Or are you that new creature, an information hermit? Palo Alto is at one extreme. The town has just gone on line by making some of its records accessible on the Internet. In the future it will offer more records and services. And who in town is on the Net? As much as half the population is, according to estimates. That doesn't mean half the population has computers, or modems. Half the population has computers, modems and Internet access. Chicago is another matter. First Chicago and Michigan National and U.S. Bancorp recently introduced full on-line banking services for customers with Microsoft Money 3.0. What's their market? First Chicago estimates that 25 percent of its customers have computers and that 10 percent of those computer owners have modems. Compared with Palo Alto, Chicago is a informational hick town. And then there's Wainscott, N.Y. Bill Henderson, who runs the Pushcart Press in Wainscott, has founded with Doris Grumbach and Henry David Thoreau (in spirit) the Lead Pencil Club, which proudly describes itself as "a pothole on the information highway." Members take a vow of abstinence from email, voicemail and faxes. They do, however, make photocopies of their (typed) manifesto, which warns that if technophiles have their way, "We will have raced at incredible speeds on the information superhighway to reach our final destination -- Nothing." The club is against many things. It is for "direct human contact" and, of course, pencils. Letters to the club can be sent to P.O. Box 380, Wainscott, N.Y. 11975. No Internet address available.

title: Big Cable Company to Offer A High-Speed Internet Link
body: Continental Cablevision Inc., the nation's third-largest cable television company, said yesterday that it had begun offering a high-speed link to the Internet data network over the same coaxial cables that carry television channels into the home. Although several other companies are testing the delivery of two-way data services over cable television systems, Continental is believed to be the first to begin selling the service commercially. Its partner is Performance Systems International of Herndon, Va., the country's largest Internet service provider. The Internet connection is initially available only to Continental customers in Cambridge, Mass., but company officials said it would eventually be offered to nearly three million customers nationwide. Continental, based in Boston, provides cable service to Westchester County, N.Y., and in California, Idaho and Michigan. However, at a rate of $125 a month for residential customers, and higher for business customers, the service is unlikely to displace the MTV's and the Home Box Offices at the top of a 500-channel hit parade, even in Cambridge, the sort of academic-technical redoubt where enthusiasts consider Internet access more important than the telephone. Joshua Harris, president of Jupiter Communications, a market research firm in newyork City, was skeptical. "Cable customers barely want to pay $9.95 a month," he remarked, noting that customers can already get access to the Internet's electronic mail, information research and file-transfer services over regular phone lines for less than $25 a month through service providers like the Pipeline, Panix and Delphi Internet services. David M. Fellows, senior vice president for engineering and technology at Continental, defended the $125 monthly rate, saying coaxial cable can carry 500,000 bits of information a second, compared with an average of 9,600 bits a second on a regular pair of twisted telephone wires. In such quantitative terms, the difference between a twisted pair of telephone wires and coaxial cable might be seen as the difference between a garden hose and a fire hose. To take advantage of the trial service, computer owners in Cambridge must have an Ethernet card, which is the most common type of adapter that connects personal computers to office networks. A special cable modem is then required between the Ethernet port and the thicker, coaxial cable that carries the television signals. The modem allows two-way data traffic over what is normally a one-way line. Several other popular on-line information services are conducting trials with cable delivery. The Prodigy Services Company of White Plains, which says it has two million customers, is testing two-way cable delivery in El Cajon, Calif., with Cox Cable Communications of Atlanta. Compuserve Inc. of Columbus, Ohio, which says it has 1.7 million subscribers, has a two-way cable test under way in Exeter, N.H., also in conjunction with Continental Cablevision.  Tiny Trial Groups The test programs are extremely limited, with fewer than a dozen families in each trial. Until more households are added, it is unknown how the cable systems will perform under the heavy traffic loads now experienced on telephone lines. Although cable can carry more information, the question is whether the higher performance it promises can be sustained when there are hundreds or thousands of users. At the same time, telephone and data-communications companies are constantly expanding the capacity of twisted-pair phone lines and speeding the installation of fiber optic lines, which also offer data-transfer speeds fast enough to handle video signals. "Cable is a kludge," remarked Mr. Harris of Jupiter Communications, using a computer term for an inelegant solution to a technical problem. "The market is aching to have everything in full motion, and cable is sort of a middle-of-the-road solution."

title: Strangers, Not Their Computers, Build a Network in Time of Grief
body: It was all too familiar a newyork story. A gunman, after robbing a topless club in Times Square, turned and fired at his pursuers. A stray bullet instantly killed a bystander in a nearby store. The victim, David Alsberg, was a 42-year-old computer programmer. He left behind a wife, a young son, and hundreds of grieving friends in both of the neighborhoods in which he lived: one in Astoria, Queens, and the other in the electronic community called cyberspace. Although most of them had never met him in the real world, his cyberspace neighbors from around the nation mourned Mr. Alsberg's death with an on-line wake that lasted weeks, commiserating through their personal computers. Using modems linked to telephone lines, they met in the same electronic forums where, just before his killing a few days after Christmas, Mr. Alsberg had been involved in a passionate debate on handgun control. Much more than a mere crime statistic, Mr. Alsberg has come to symbolize the new social dynamic of computer networking. In a world where physical contact is impossible, Mr. Alsberg's cyberspace neighbors consoled each other over the senseless loss of a mutual friend. And in their collective grieving, they demonstrated an impulse for togetherness that is as modern as the digital age and as old as humankind. For as more people become citizens of cyberspace, they are forging relationships that many describe as being as rewarding as their face-to-face friendships. When Mr. Alsberg's cyberspace mourners learned that he had no life insurance -- he had been laid off several months earlier from his programmer's job at Citicorp -- they decided to begin soliciting recipes to compile an electronic cookbook. Proceeds from sales, once they begin, will go to a trust fund for the Alsberg family. There are no hard numbers for the population of cyberspace, although it has recently been estimated at 30 million to 35 million -- if one counts all the computer networks in offices, the networks that subscribers pay for like Compuserve and Prodigy and Minitel of France, the thousands of privately run electronic bulletin board services, and the global network of networks called the Internet. Alone, the Internet has 15 million to 20 million individual addresses -- although it is not known how many of those are in regular use. But the hundreds of thousands of messages posted each day on the Internet indicate an active user universe. And the vitality of relationships on these data networks appears to dispel the notion of computer users as loners and social misfits who prefer the cold glow of video tubes and the precision of binary logic to the warmth and unpredictability of human relationships. Like frontier neighbors who come together for barn-raisings, for worship, for dances and for funerals, the residents of cyberspace often display a sense of communal support that surprises newcomers. "Those who scoff at the notion of electronic community sometimes suggest that it is inhabited by classic lonely guys, get-a-life types," said Jim Seymour, a computer consultant in Austin, Tex., who had often chatted with Mr. Alsberg on the Ziffnet on-line information network, although they never met.  Artificial Intimacy This new type of computer-based relationship -- some might call it artificial intimacy -- is catching the interest of psychologists and sociologists. One cannot travel very far on the data networks without coming across new communities, new friendships and spontaneous acts of kindness among strangers, phenomena that sometimes seem to be all too rare "in the real world" -- or I.T.R.W., as it is known in the shorthand of cyberspace. Sara Kiesler, professor of social and decision sciences at Carnegie-Mellon University in Pittsburgh, said she first noticed the phenomenon more than a decade ago while studying the Arpanet, a scientific and academic network that has since evolved into the Internet. "Although the network was originally supposed to connect people with computers, what they really spent their time doing was connecting with one another," Professor Kiesler said. It may be hard for many people to imagine developing a close emotional relationship with someone with whom one merely corresponds, although such things do happen in real life. Pen pals do fall in love, and friendships are made and lost over the telephone. But in cyberspace the exchanges are still mainly in text. Even so, it is common to hear stories of people laughing or weeping while they interact with others through the computer screen, of people so attached to their on-line relationships -- they become addicted to the net -- that they seek counseling.  Various Groups Form On most larger commercial services as well as on the global Internet, people form all sorts of groups based on a shared need for information and emotional support. There are forums for cancer patients, for people with AIDS and for people who do not have AIDS but carry H.I.V., the virus that causes it. There are network groups for victims of sexual abuse -- and even a support group for recovering abusers. Other communities range from the broad (one has the Internet address "soc.culture.feminism") to the narrowly drawn ("DEAFBLND," coordinated by a computer at the University of Kentucky, for those with dual sensory impairment). One of the most popular, and broad based, network gathering spots is the Internet Relay Chat service, the cyberspace equivalent of citizens' band radio, where people gather for free-ranging discussions on a virtually limitless array of topics. It was on I.R.C., as it is known, that Internet night owls gave live reports about the recent Los Angeles earthquake and its aftermath. News, good and bad, travels fast in cyberspace. Brendan P. Kehoe, an affable, 23-year-old computer whiz in Mountain View, Calif., was severely hurt in an auto accident on Dec. 31 while visiting in Newtown, Pa. Mr. Kehoe is well known on the Internet, having written "Zen and the Art of the Internet," an introductory guide to cyberspace. Within hours, word of Mr. Kehoe's accident spread throughout the global web of Internet connections, passing from one friend to the next in the cyberspace equivalent of jungle drums.  Flood of Get-Well Cards The next day, Mr. Kehoe's housemate and co-worker, Jeffrey Osier, flew to Pennsylvania from California and set up a laptop computer in a motel room across from the hospital, the University of Pennsylvania Neurological Trauma Center in Philadelphia, where he posted regular Internet updates on Mr. Kehoe's condition. Get-well cards, mostly electronic but also on paper, flooded in. Messages arrived in Spanish, Japanese, French and Russian, reflecting the global nature of the network. Dozens of people offered financial help, with more than $1,000 sent so far. Others, reflecting the Internet's heritage among university and scientific researchers, sent research papers about brain injuries, gleaned from medical data bases. When Mr. Kehoe emerged from the coma and began speaking in numbers, rather than words -- a condition known as aphasia -- people who had suffered from similar symptoms, or knew others who had, began sharing anecdotes about what Mr. Kehoe and his family could expect in the months ahead. Mr. Kehoe, who is regaining his normal speech, said he intended to answer every get-well message. But the task is hampered by a broken shoulder that he says has reduced his typing speed to a mere 110 words a minute from his pre-accident pace of 150.  Mother Goes On Line He also has to fight for access to the computer. While recovering, he is living in Augusta, Me., at the home of his mother, Alice Kehoe, a local radio disk jockey who became so interested in the on-line community that she now spends an hour a day chatting with friends on the Prodigy network. Another case: Last May, the moving van taking Mike Godwin's belongings to Washington from Cambridge, Mass., caught fire en route and most of his belongings were destroyed. "I felt immensely uprooted and alone" in a new city with a new job, Mr. Godwin recalled. "I didn't know my new neighbors in Washington, but I knew who my cyberspace neighbors were." Mr. Godwin turned to his neighbors on the Well, an electronic community of about 8,000 users, operated by Bruce R. Katz, a private investor in San Francisco. When Mr. Godwin expressed particular concern over the loss of his books, which he had been collecting since youth, another Well resident, Elliot Fabric, suggested that he post a list of the books that had been destroyed. He did so, "and for the next six months, not a day went by that I didn't get a book, or a box of books, in the mail," Mr. Godwin said. The Well is unusual in that it has a strong geographic locus, the Bay Area, which allows members to meet "I.T.R.W." if they choose. "We rent a nice site under the Golden Gate Bridge once a month and sort of see what happens," said Gail Williams, conferencing manager for the Well. Attendance sometimes approaches 500 people. It is common at such encounters for people to be surprised by the physical appearance of people they know only by streams of text. In cyberspace, physical disabilities, racial or ethnic differences, socioeconomic stratas and even gender issues tend to disappear. Mr. Kehoe, recovering from his auto accident, said he now saw a different dimension of cyberspace. "I knew I had a dozen really close friends, but oh, it just really amazes me," Mr. Kehoe said. "It occurs to me now that even though they're just E-mail addresses on screen, there are real people behind them. It's really neat, especially when you realize that the people who are into it aren't just computer weenies." Graphic   Photo: Brendan P. Kehoe is recovering at his mother's house in Augusta, Me., since being severely hurt in an auto accident on Dec. 31. He has gotten floods of electronic get-well cards from his friends on the Internet. (Gary Guisinger for The newyork Times) (pg. D2)

title: Motorola Set to Announce A Palmtop Communicator
body: Motorola Inc. is expected to raise the standards in palmtop computing and wireless communications this week with the introduction of a device that combines the two emerging services. The Envoy personal communicator, to be shown on Monday, lets users send and receive information through Ardis, the nation's largest wireless network. The device, expected to retail at about $1,500 when it reaches stores this summer, can also be linked by wire to telephones, computers and peripherals. This will let users tap into on-line information services, exchange files with personal computers, or use a printer or keyboard. Envoys can also "talk" with each other through an infrared transceiver, exchanging messages that can be enlivened with animation and sound -- either the user's voice or packaged effects. It also includes software for taking notes and keeping track of schedules and expenses. "First-generation products fell short -- they didn't really deliver on communications," said Cheryl Beck-Ruff, the Envoy project manager. Computer industry analysts praised Envoy's communications abilities and its combination of hardware and software. "These are communication devices that put you in touch with more than other people," said Paul Saffo, a director of the Institute for the Future, a consulting firm in Menlo Park, Calif. Envoy is the latest product in the field of personal communicators. The hand-held devices, which are linked by wire or through a wireless network, communicate by voice, fax, electronic mail and other ways, and also manage personal information. One of the earliest of the products, Apple Computer's Newton Messagepad, was upgraded on Friday with improved handwriting-recognition capabilities. People in the industry have been eager to see the Envoy because it is the first product on the market to include software by General Magic of Mountain View, Calif., which was formed by Motorola, A.T.& T. and the Sony Corporation. Users operate the Envoy by tapping on-screen boxes or an on-screen keyboard with a finger or electronic pen. They can also jot down a note and transmit it as written, but Envoy -- unlike Apple's Newton -- does not recognize handwriting. That is because handwriting recognition has not advanced far enough, said Curtis Sasaki, manager of product marketing for General Magic. The original Newton was criticized for inaccurately reading handwriting. Envoy links users to Ardis, a network owned by Motorola and I.B.M., through a built-in wireless modem and a two-way wireless radio modem. Ardis links with RadioMail service, enabling users to communicate with anyone with an Internet address.

title: George Tames, Photographer, Dies at 75
body: George Tames, a news photographer for The newyork Times whose work for nearly half a century changed the way Americans looked at Presidents and political power, died here today while undergoing heart surgery. He was 75. His photographs chronicled 10 Presidents from Franklin D. Roosevelt to George Bush, countless members of Congress and visiting statesman from Churchill to Khrushchev. President Eisenhower chose two Tames photographs for official portraits, and a third became the basis of a 6-cent Eisenhower stamp. The photo for the stamp was a characteristic Tames shot, taken of Eisenhower in 1953 in an unguarded moment as the President was delivering a radio-television address announcing that a truce had been agreed to ending the Korean War. Over the years Mr. Tames also won awards and citations for dramatic action shots of a farmers' protest and a civil rights march and a still life of the Lincoln Memorial. He joined The Times in 1945 after six years with Time magazine. That was the era of the large Speed Graphic camera, whose film holder had to be changed after each shot. He retired from The Times 40 years later in the era of the 35-millimeter camera with high-speed shutters and large, fast lenses.  Kennedy at His Desk Mr. Tames was a keen student of Washington's changing political culture; early on, he developed an instinct for capturing dramatic moments on film. One of his most widely known photographs showed a silhouette of President Kennedy from the back, leaning on his desk in the Oval Office and appearing burdened by the weight of his job. It was the kind of picture that Mr. Tames could find and shoot because of his ability to develop easy and informal access to the powerful. "Mine was an unofficial role in his political kingdom," Mr. Tames recalled in his memoir, "Eye on Washington," published in 1990, "that of jokester and bringer of news, rumors and spicy Capitol Hill gossip." Knowing that Kennedy often worked standing up because of an injured back and that his door was often open, Mr. Tames saw the President bent over, reading something in a newspaper. "I deliberately underexposed," he said later. "I wanted the blackness, the mood that I saw with my eye."  'Posterity's Spy' In a tribute two years ago on the occasion of the National Press Club's Fourth Estate award to Mr. Tames, Ken Burns, the documentary film maker, spoke of Mr. Tames's work as "pictures that last, that speak eloquently, that have and will endure, that clearly are the DNA of our political story in the last 50 years." Mr. Burns said Mr. Tames was "posterity's spy -- a mole -- penetrating farther and much deeper into our political landscape and psyche than any reporter who hangs on words has." George Tames was born on Jan. 21, 1919, a few blocks from the Capitol. He was the son of Greek-Albanian immigrants; his father was a pushcart peddler. In the Depression, when the large Tames family depended heavily on relief, President Roosevelt was venerated in their back-alley home, his photograph placed alongside those of St. George and the Virgin Mother next to candles on an icon stand. George was introduced to the Capitol early in his life. He had to go to work after completing the 10th grade, beginning as an office courier for Time-Life, a job that took him back to Capitol Hill. The work of news photographers attracted him, although in those days they were not allowed to roam the corridors of Congress. But he was soon permitted to make photographs of individual members of Congress, and before the end of World War II he was among a small number of photographers permitted to take pictures of President Roosevelt.  Truman Was His Favorite Although Mr. Tames had a deep affection for Kennedy, President Truman was undoubtedly his favorite, not the least because he was the first to treat photographers with respect. Mr. Tames relished the recollection of the day Truman "made White House photographers first-class citizens" by freeing them from a tiny West Wing chamber they called the Doghouse and giving them entree to the press room. Mr. Tames recalled Truman telling a foreign dignitary: "I am President of the most powerful nation in the world. I take orders from nobody, except photographers." Memorable Tames images conveyed not only the flavor of the capital but also of people who were making headlines: Lyndon B. Johnson as the Senate majority leader, bending Senator Theodore Francis Green of Rhode Island backward over a table to influence him; Vice President Hubert H. Humphrey in a moment of silence he called for when the assassination of the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was announced; President Nixon, pulling on a sock at a golf club; Truman grinning broadly over his 63d birthday cake.  Font of Anecdotes Mr. Tames had a wiry build and always seemed to be on the move around a city he loved. He was a tireless raconteur, telling anecdotes he had shared with the high and mighty, capped with a raucous laugh. This was a part of the persona he cultivated that made him popular not only with the politicians he covered but also with his colleagues. They celebrated him at 14 retirement parties, starting in 1986, after which everyone lost count. But Mr. Tames did not really retire. He went on shooting pictures as a freelance, mainly for The Times, and when a colleague or a colleague's child got married, he happily volunteered to make the wedding pictures, asking only for the cost of the film and permission to dance with the bride. He was usually the life of a party. "He's the champion," Cornell Capa, a former Life photographer, said a decade ago. "He beats everybody." In a tribute to Mr. Tames, Wally Bennett, a longtime Washington photographer for Time, said today: "He knew all the players in the political game. He did his background work. He had a marvelous eye. He used his knowledge to make marvelous photographs that will be in the history books." Mr. Tames is survived by his wife, the former Frances Faye Owens; two sons, Chris, of Nags Head, N.C., and Michael G., of Manteo, N.C.; three daughters, Pamela T. Goodman of Wilson, N.C., Kathryn Tames-Walton of Springfield, Va., and Stephanie, of Statesboro, Ga., and five grandchildren. Graphic   Photos: In his half-century career as a news photographer, George Tames (William E. Sauro/The newyork Times, 1985) chronicled 10 Presidents, including John F. Kennedy, whom he photographed leaning on his desk in the Oval Office burdened by his job, and Lyndon B. Johnson. Mr. Johnson, as Senate majority leader in 1957, was at his persuasive best in a conversation with Senator Theodore Francis Green of Rhode Island. (Photographs by George Tames/The newyork Times)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Satellite Service Will Extend the Reach of Bloomberg Radio
body: His all-business-news radio station in newyork had barely turned one year old when Michael Bloomberg decided to celebrate by going national with it. The decision was easy, because the radio station, WBBR-AM, can tag along at no additional expense on the satellite service that Mr. Bloomberg is leasing to start a 13-hour-a-day television service of business news. Along with the video channel, called Bloomberg Direct, which will be part of GM Hughes Electronics' satellite-to-home broadcasting service, will come an audio channel carrying WBBR. A subscriber to the satellite service, which will start about May 1, will be able to hear the station through a television set, with the screen blank, or by connecting a radio to the system.  A Station of Many Uses The audio channel is just one more unusual way in which Mr. Bloomberg is taking advantage of the radio station he bought (the former WNEW-AM, at the frequency of 1130) in the fall of 1992 for $13.5 million. Mr. Bloomberg is the founder of Bloomberg Financial Markets, which provides computerized financial data to business customers, and Bloomberg Business News, a news service that reports and interprets the data. Another innovation from Mr. Bloomberg is to put the radio programming inside the computer terminals he leases to business customers for $1,000 a month. The terminals are used to retrieve and display all the data gathered by Bloomberg Financial Markets -- and the Bloomberg software runs only on the Bloomberg hardware. But more than 20,000 of Bloomberg's 34,000 terminals now have built-in speakers for the radio programming. Because WBBR broadcasts a digitally encoded signal, it can be captured and stored electronically on the Bloomberg computer system, then played on demand. If a broker, instead of typing a stock symbol on the keyboard, types in "WBBR," the terminal displays a menu of recent radio programming, like the most recent market report, news broadcast, weather or traffic report, or perhaps Alan Greenspan's speech of the day. Hit the number of a menu item, and the selection is replayed. WNEW-AM, which played big band music and crooners, attracted about 1.6 percent of the listening audience in the newyork area. Since WBBR began broadcasting on Jan. 3, 1993, the station's share, as measured by the Arbitron Company, has averaged about three-tenths of 1 percent. While others in the radio business deride the station and its paltry ratings, Mr. Bloomberg, in the time-honored fashion of stations with low Arbitron numbers, prefers to bash the rating service. "The people who listen to my station, investment bankers and the like, don't take the time to talk to market researchers on the phone, or to fill out Arbitron phone diaries," Mr. Bloomberg said in a recent interview at his Park Avenue office. To prove his point, Mr. Bloomberg has commissioned "qualitative ratings" from Accuratings of Chicago, a relative newcomer that is offering its services to radio stations as a way of getting beyond the raw numbers of Arbitron to measure the wealth, education and buying habits of radio listeners. Many classical-music stations also use qualitative ratings, hoping to demonstrate that they, too, have an attractive audience in terms of buying power and taste. "A bigger percentage of WBBR's listeners have bought a new car in the last six months than at any of the top 20 stations in newyork," Kurt Hanson, the president of Accuratings, said. "A bigger percentage of WBBR's audience went to graduate school than of any station in newyork except that of WQXR," the classical-music FM station owned by The newyork Times Company, he said. Whatever Accuratings may show, and however tony the advertisers WBBR attracts -- at rates of $500 a minute in morning drive time to $150 in off hours -- executives at newyork's all-news stations, which Mr. Bloomberg likes to call "all-crime" stations, are happy to sneer in return. "We don't look at them as competition," said Scott Herman, the vice president and general manager of WINS-AM, the all-news station owned by the Westinghouse Electric Corporation. In the latest Arbitron ratings, WINS had 3.9 percent of the listening audience, or 13 times that of WBBR. "They're not in the business of attracting listeners," he said of WBBR. "He's just trying to sell his data." At WCBS-AM, Harvey Nagler, the director of news and programming, said the countermeasures that his station took when WBBR began broadcasting had proved unnecessary. "When we first heard about WBBR, we started a small-business report that airs twice a day," he said, "and we increased what we were doing off-air. Four times a year, we rent a hotel hall and do breakfasts for the community with well-known figures to talk about business and economic issues." But aside from losing two part-time employees to Bloomberg, Mr. Nagler said, WBBR had had no effect on WCBS, which had 2.9 percent of the audience in Arbitron's latest ratings.

title: Appeals Panel Revives Suit Against The Times
body: The unitedstates Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circiut today revived a lawsuit against The newyork Times by a reporter who said the newspaper libeled him when it published a critical review of his book. The court said the author, Dan E. Moldea, may pursue his claim that a review of his book "Interference: How Organized Crime Influences Professional Football," which appeared in The newyork Times Book Review in September 1989, harmed his career and invaded his privacy. Mr. Moldea's suit had been thrown out in January 1992 by Federal District Judge John Garrett Penn, who said that the Book Review had stated "an unverifiable opinion, and is thus not actionable under libel law." But in the 2-to-1 opinion handed down today, Judge Harry Edwards wrote for the court that the statement that Mr. Moldea's work was sloppy "has obvious, measurable aspects when applied to the field of investigative journalism." Judge Edwards wrote that it made no difference that the statement appeared in a book review rather than a news article. His opinion, joined by Judge Patricia Wald, said the court was not judging the merits of Mr. Moldea's claim. Chief Judge Abner Mikva dissented, saying, "If the statement that Mr. Moldea wrote a sloppy book is defamatory, so would be a statement that Bette Midler wore a sloppy dress, or that Oliver Stone made a sloppy film." Nancy Nielsen, a spokeswoman for The Times, said: "We are very disappointed in the majority's ruling, which we feel has been wrongly decided because it does not give sufficient constitutional protections for expressions of opinion in a review. "We are considering asking the entire court to review the decision. In any event, there are many strong defenses which were not raised on this preliminary motion, and we remain confident that the case will be dismissed before trial."

title: I.R.S. Tries On-Line Tax Filing
body: In a test that glimpses the potential of the emerging national information network, the Internal Revenue Service said yesterday that taxpayers in nine states would be able to file their 1993 Federal tax returns by personal computer over telephone lines. The test program, which involves Midwestern and Southwestern states, is the latest attempt by the I.R.S. to streamline the tax process and reduce the amount of paper it handles. In another experiment this year, more than 300,000 single taxpayers in seven test states have already filed Forms 1040 EZ by entering the data on the keypads of their touch-tone telephones, the I.R.S. reported. There are several advantages to electronic filing. The I.R.S. said that taxpayers due refunds would get them in no more than three weeks, or even sooner if they choose to have them deposited directly into their bank accounts. Typically refunds take four to eight weeks for returns filed by mail.  Accuracy an Advantage Accuracy is another advantage. Returns that are received on paper must be keyed into mainframe computers at the I.R.S. by human typists, which often results in errors, an I.R.S. spokesman acknowledged. Electronic returns do not require retyping, so there is "virtually no chance" for transcription errors, he said. Taxpayers who file electronically will receive a confirmation by return electronic mail that their forms have been received, or a notice that more documentation is required. The new electronic filing systems do not entirely eliminate the need for paperwork. Taxpayers still must provide their legal signatures on a paper Form 8453 OL (the OL stands for On Line) and include paper copies of W-2 forms and supporting documentation. Computer experts said the technology needed to create and authenticate electronic signatures may not be widely available for several years.  Data Security at Issue Representatives of both the I.R.S. and the Compuserve Information Service, which will be used to transmit the returns, said their systems were secure from data eavesdropping. However, computer security experts said that the transmission of tax returns over public networks raised concerns about privacy and data security. "There isn't a chance in hell that I'd file my tax return over Compuserve or any other network," said Winn Schwartau, a computer security consultant in Seminole, Fla. "It sure looks like a lot of plain text traveling around." Plain text refers to computer data that have not been encrypted, or scrambled, to prevent unauthorized reading. In recent months, the security systems of thousands of computers on the global network known as the Internet have been penetrated by data thieves who have captured unencrypted messages. There is no evidence that Compuserve, which is owned by the commercial tax preparation company H & R Block, or Internal Revenue Service computer systems were affected by the widespread break-ins on the Internet.  Forms Can Be Retrieved In the program displayed yesterday, Compuserve subscribers are able to retrieve official I.R.S. documents and forms, research tax questions, purchase tax preparation software and have it delivered electronically, ask questions of tax experts, compare notes with other taxpayers, and, for taxpayers in the nine test states, file their own returns over the Compuserve network. The states are Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas and Wisconsin. The returns will be sent first to Compuserve's mainframe computers in Columbus, Ohio, then to a commercial tax company in Rome, Ga., and finally to the I.R.S.'s electronic forms center in Austin, Tex. Compuserve's estimated 1.7 million subscribers pay a minimum monthly fee of $8.95 for access to basic services and additional fees, ranging up to $9.60 an hour, based on the amount of time connected to special services. Within that cost, subscribers -- even those who choose not to file electronically -- can retrieve official I.R.S. forms and publications, which they can print out.  Software for Sale Taxpayers can also use the Compuserve system to buy the tax preparation software needed to use the filing system. The popular programs, Taxcut, Turbotax and Macintax, each cost $39.95. There is an additional fee of $14.95 for taxpayers to file their Federal tax returns using the Taxcut program, and $19.95 to file using Turbotax or Macintax. In comparison, H & R Block estimates that the average fee for tax preparation and filing in one of its walk-in offices is about $50. A less sophisticated form of electronic filing has been available in previous years, but only through I.R.A.-authorized tax preparation services and other commercial intermediaries. People who prepared their own return could take paper copies or a computer disk to the centers for transmission. The I.R.S. expects more than 10 million returns to be filed through these indirect services this year. The use of electronic mail systems to send sensitive information, including tax returns and medical data, raised concerns among privacy advocates. "Once you realize the increasing sensitivity of the information we send electronically, the importance of encryption increases," said David L. Sobel, legal counsel to an organization called Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility. Mr. Sobel said the new I.R.S.-Compuserve agreement was likely to focus attention on the Clinton Administration's efforts to establish a nationwide data encryption standard based on computer chip called Clipper. Computer and civil rights organizations oppose it because the Government holds the key to open and read any Clipper-encrypted message.

title:
Technology;
How to Keep Bandits from 'Snarfing' Your Passwords
body: WHEN the alarm finally went off 10 days ago, electronic bandits on the global web of computer networks known as the Internet had already made off with thousands of user passwords, the supposedly secret codes that act as keys to public and private computer networks around the world. No one knows how many passwords were stolen after the break-ins started last summer, but officials at the Government-sponsored Computer Emergency Response Team say tens of thousands of computers around the world have been put at risk of being attacked by the intruders, not just on the Internet but on any computer network attached to it. "A network of computers, especially one as extensive as the Internet, is not as secure as a stand-alone computer," said Michael DeFazio, executive vice president and general manager of the Unix Systems Group subsidiary of Novell Inc., one of the leading network software companies.  "With a stand-alone computer you can limit access in physical ways, putting it in a locked room guarded by people with guns, if you want. You can't do that on a global network." But there are technologies that can greatly reduce, if not eliminate, the types of break-ins that have occurred on the Internet in recent months, security advisers say. Data encryption, one-time password generators, "fire- walls" and a user-authentification system called Kerberos are all cited as effective ways to decrease the risk of password theft. Last week, a Mountain View, Calif., computer company posted its version of the Kerberos program on an Internet "server" computer, making it available without charge to any American or Canadian network that wants it. The company, Cygnus Support, hopes to recoup its investment by selling support services to companies that use the program. Used alone or in combination, Kerberos and the other techniques make it harder to steal passwords, or can render them useless if they fall into the wrong hands or can virtually eliminate their use on the network. Security experts say that once a break-in is discovered it is relatively simple to expunge password-grabbers from affected computers. At that point, it's a matter of changing passwords and patching the hole in network security that allowed the intruders to enter the system. But those steps alone are not enough to reduce the risk of damage from such password pilfering in the future, the experts say. For example, one small company that was an early victim of the Internet bandits cleaned its system and ordered everyone to change passwords. A short time later, technicians discovered that the intruders had planted another hidden program that was designed to recognize the "change password" request and steal the new one. Passwords are "the biggest single source of security problems on any networked environment, not just the Internet," said William Yundt, a director of Barrnet in Stanford, Calif., one of the first commercial Internet service networks to be attacked in the latest wave of break-ins. Here are some proposed solutions:   Data Encryption Data encryption is the high-tech equivalent of the secret decoder rings one used to find in cereal boxes. It is used primarily to hide the contents of sensitive information files, such as those containing financial data, medical records and classified material. A data file or password is scrambled using a special "key," or set of instructions, and it is difficult to unscramble unless the recipient has the same key. Encryption works well between two people who arrange ahead of time to use a common key, but it becomes cumbersome on an open network where there are millions of users and thousands of different types of computers. So the Government and various groups are proposing an encryption standard for use throughout the network. In fact, a strenuous debate is under way over which data encryption standard to support. The Clinton Administration wants one called Clipper, which is technically sophisticated but has a "trap door" designed into it that the Government contends it needs for national security and law-enforcement purposes. Groups concerned about potential invasion of privacy oppose the Clipper standard, arguing that the Government would hold the key needed to read everyone's electronic mail.  One-Time Password Generators Hardware solutions include electronic "tokens" that generate new passwords every minute. There are also "challenge response" systems that require a user to provide a unique code generated by a device similar to a pocket calculator. The advantage is that such systems generate one-time-only passwords that change every 60 seconds or so, and thus become invalid at the end of the user's session. The drawbacks, which must be weighed against potential benefits, are that such systems add complexity and cost. The password generators typically cost $35 to $100 or more depending on features, and some sort of synchronized password-authentification software is required on the "host" computer. The most popular such device in use today is the Secur ID, made by Security Dynamics Inc. of Cambridge, Mass.  Firewalls For higher levels of security, some organizations install "firewalls," typically a highly secure computer that acts as a buffer between the Internet and all the other computers within a company. The firewall system is effective because it presents only a single point of attack to be monitored and defended. Many companies place their firewall computers in a physically secure room. Firewalls are not widely used because the firewall barrier works both ways, limiting access to the outside world while blocking intruders from coming inside.  Kerberos Several computer security experts cited the Kerberos system as the most effective way to prevent passwords from being "snarfed" by network eavesdroppers (to use the digerati's term of art for snatching passwords). The Kerberos architecture eliminates the need for clear, unencrypted text passwords to be passed over the network. The process, described in the accompanying chart, appears complex, experts concede. But so does the inside of a door lock, and people still lock their doors. In practice, using Kerberos adds a single step to the computer network log-on process, and it insures much greater security. Will the Internet, or other networks, ever be completely secure? "It's a difficult thing to accomplish," said Mr. Yundt, who supervises the networks at Stanford University. "You can create an effective technology, but to embed it in every platform and application, in a way that it is globally used, takes a matter of years."    SOME PASSWORD DO'S -- AND DON'TS PASSWORDS are effective only to the extent that they remain secret. And security experts say they rarely stay secret for long, because most people fail to heed sensible password rules. The rules apply not only to passwords used on computer networks, but also to those used with most other networked systems, like the personal identification numbers used with automatic teller machines and the calling-card numbers used for charging long-distance phone calls. Here are ways to avoid being "snarfed": 1. Don't choose words that can be found in a dictionary, English or otherwise. Computer crackers often use "brute force," employing automated programs that test every word at lightning speed. 2. If possible, use at least eight characters. The longer the password, the harder it is to guess. 3. Use a mix of letters and numbers, and include special characters if possible. On systems that are "case sensitive," mix upper and lower case letters. The password "K2jw&#69" is harder to guess than "loverboy." 4. Don't use obvious, guessable passwords. License plate numbers, birth dates, Social Security numbers, pet names, sports teams and other familiar terms may be easy to remember, but they are also easy to guess. 5. It may seem obvious, but don't write your password anywhere people can find it. Don't keep it in your wallet or purse with your bank card, or in the desk drawer next to your computer. 6. Change passwords frequently, the more often the better. The best systems require a new password each time a user signs on. 7. Watch out for people looking over your shoulder. Professionals use telescopes in airports and near public phones. 8. Never "lend" your password to someone else, for any reason. 9. Never tell your password to anyone over the phone. Thieves posing as computer administrators say it's surprising how many people are willing to divulge their passwords to strangers. 10. Report any unusual "log on" experiences immediately to the system administrator. If you feel your password may have been compromised, tell the administrator right away. PETER H. LEWIS    A PASSWORD PILGRIM'S PROGRESS The Kerberos system uses multiple "keys" to protect computer networks on the Internet without exposing users' passwords to possible interception. Here's how it can work:  Step 1 Our hero -- call him Pete -- contacts the Acme network service company and gets a special password called a "secret key."  Step 2 Later, when he wants to use Acme as a gateway to the Internet, Pete sends a message to Acme's authentication computer.  Step 3 The computer sends Pete an encrypted response -- an electronic package of information that can be read only with Pete's "secret key."  Step 4 The response contains a temporary key good for this session only and an encrypted ticket that will expire if he doesn't use it soon.  Step 5 Pete sends two things back to the Acme computer: the ticket, as evidence that Pete is Pete, and an encrypted message coded with the temporary key, as further evidence that Pete is indeed Pete.  Step 6 Our hero receives a second encrypted ticket and decodes it with his temporary key.  Step 7 And here's the ticket! Pete sends it over the Internet to, say, NASA's computer data base of satellite maps, requesting access. The NASA computer queries Acme to verify that Pete has a valid ticket. Acme confirms that Pete is authorized to use the network, and NASA opens its gates. At no time does Pete's "secret key" go over the network to risk interception.

title:
COMPANY REPORTS;
Times Co. Reports Loss in Quarter Despite Operating Gain
body: The newyork Times Company reported improved operating earnings for the fourth quarter and all of 1993 yesterday but said a reduction in the value of its forest products operations and the expected cost of a planned staff reduction at The newyork Times newspaper resulted in a net loss for the quarter. The company reported a fourth-quarter loss of $24.1 million, or 23 cents a share, compared with a loss of $3.7 million, or 5 cents a share, in the final quarter of 1992. For the year, the company reported net income of $6.1 million, or 7 cents a share, in contrast to a loss of $44.7 million, or 57 cents a share, in 1992. The results for both years reflected a number of special factors. Excluding the special factors, the company said, earnings for the year would have been 93 cents a share, up 40.9 percent from 66 cents a share in 1992. For the quarter, earnings would have been 38 cents, up 90 percent from 20 cents a year earlier.  Revenues Increase Revenues for the year rose 14.1 percent, to $2.02 billion, and for the quarter 35.8 percent, to $636 million, largely reflecting the acquisition of The Boston Globe in October. The company did not detail The Globe's contribution to revenues and profits. The Times Company issued 36.4 million class A shares in its acquisition of The Boston Globe on Oct. 1 and bought back 10.3 million shares in the second half of the year. The earnings announced yesterday exceeded estimates that the Times Company made public on Dec. 6. The gain, the company said in a statement, came from stronger operations at its newspaper group and a lower-than-anticipated tax rate because the company was able to reduce its liability by carrying forward tax losses from previous periods. The earnings were announced after stock markets closed yesterday. Earlier, the Times Company's shares ended at $26.25, down 37.5 cents, on the American Stock Exchange.  Advertising Linage Up Advertising linage at The newyork Times increased 7.8 percent in the fourth quarter, and 1 percent for the year, the company said. At The Boston Globe, the gains were a more impressive 9.7 percent for the quarter and 4 percent for the year. The newspapers' circulation was little changed from 1992, with The Times selling an average of 1.2 million copies on weekdays and 1.8 million on Sundays and The Globe 504,600 on weekdays and 814,500 on Sundays. Among the company's 30 smaller newspapers, advertising rose 3.8 percent for the quarter and 3.9 percent for the year, primarily because of an increase in advertising inserts, the company said. At the Times Company's magazine group, which produces 21 magazines, operating profit more than doubled, to $4.9 million, in the fourth quarter and rose 24.2 percent, to $12.3 million, for the year. The company said weak advertising for consumer packaged goods hurt its women's magazines. At the broadcast/information services group, operating profit rose 41.5 percent, to $5.8 million, for the quarter and 31.1 percent, to $19.4 million, for the year. Higher local advertising revenues at the company's five television stations accounted for the gains, the company said. The broadcast group also operates WQXR-FM and WQEW-AM in newyork; the information services group includes The newyork Times News Service, The Times Syndicate and TimesFax.  $47 Million Charge Taken The forest products group lost $47 million in the quarter and $51.9 million in the year, after a special charge of $47 million in the 1993 fourth quarter. Without the charge, equity in operations would have been even in the quarter, compared with a loss of $2.5 million in 1992; for the year the loss would have been $4.9 million in 1993, down from a loss of $8.7 million in 1992. The charge reflected a writedown of the company's investment based on current market conditions. These were other factors that affected 1993 earnings: *A $30 million pretax charge to cover severance and related costs from planned white-collar staff reductions at The newyork Times. *A $5.4 million pretax charge to cover severance and related costs from voluntary early retirements in The Times's composing room. *A $5.6 million tax expense because a change in Federal taxes increased the corporate income tax rate by one percentage point, to 35 percent, retroactively to Jan. 1, 1993. *A $3.7 million adjustment in advertising and circulation rates after last March's huge snowstorm disrupted deliveries of The Times. Graphic   Table: "The newyork Times Co. (A)"  b-After an after-tax charge of $47 million, or 44 cents a share, for the quarter, and 56 cents for the year, which included other items, against equity in operations of the Forest Products Group to write down the company's investment in the group to reflect current operating conditions and economic factors in the industry. Exclusive of the write-down, equity in operations of the Forest Products Group for the latest periods was break-even in the fourth quarter, and a loss of $4.9 million for the year. The 1993 year also included tax expense of $5.6 million, or 7 cents a share, of which $600,000 was related to the Forest Products Group, because of new legislation, which increased the Federal corporate income tax rate to 35 percent from 34 percent retroactively to Jan. 1, 1993; it affected the deductibility of certain costs and caused the company to remeasure its year-end 1992 deferred tax balances to reflect the higher tax rate. c-Net loss, which was after charges of $33.4 million after tax, or 43 cents a share, reflecting net cumulative effect of mandated noncash accounting changes for income taxes, post-retirement and post-employment benefits.
