title: A Rise in Internet Break-Ins Sets Off a Security Alarm
body: Citing computer-security violations of unprecedented scope, security experts have issued a warning that unknown assailants have been breaking into scores of government, corporate and university computers connected to the global Internet communications network. Saying that it had been "flooded" with reports of computer break-ins in the last week, the federally supported Computer Emergency Response Team broadcast its warning late Thursday night over the Internet, a web of computer networks used by an estimated 15 million people in the unitedstates and abroad. Sophisticated software, secretly planted on various computers throughout the Internet, has allowed unknown intruders to steal passwords and electronic addresses from legitimate users, computer security experts said yesterday. Although there were apparently no reports of significant damage to big computer systems on the Internet, and although similar attempts to breach Internet security systems have been fairly common in the past, the sheer volume of the reported security violations caused alarm among some computer administrators. The attacks also underscored the vulnerability of computer networks at a time when more and more companies and consumers have begun using them to communicate and conduct business. "This potentially affects tens of thousands of computer accounts," said Terry McGillen, a spokesman for the Computer Emergency Response Team, a group of security experts at Carnegie-Mellon University that serves as a clearinghouse for Internet security issues. "We now know that an unknown number of intruders have the information they need to get access to thousands of additional computers, including entire networks." In theory, the intruders could use the stolen information to gain access to government, educational, commercial and private files on unprotected computers connected to the Internet. Depending on the type of password captured, an intruder could also damage, alter or erase files shared by thousands of users on a network. Security experts say it is impossible to assess the motives of the intruders, but the attacks will force thousands of computer system administrators to do the costly and time-consuming work of inspecting and cleaning their systems. Officials of the response team declined to name specific institutions affected by the break-ins, although the University of Texas and Rice University were among the organizations that identified themselves as having found evidence of the intruders. The response team said last night that reports were still being analyzed to determine whether the intruders had used the captured passwords with malicious intent, or whether they were merely pranksters trying to "crack" the system. The organization advised computer administrators to review their systems and to make sure users changed their passwords frequently. Some computer security officials said that because of previous security problems on the network, the latest wave of break-ins posed little real risk to sensitive information. "Most prudent organizations no longer keep sensitive or classified information on any computer attached to the Internet," said David Fisher, computer security manager for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Ames Research Center in Mountain View, Calif. He said NASA had not experienced any unusual increase in computer security violations in recent days.  'Trojan Horse' Program According to a response team advisory sent to Internet computer sites late Thursday night, the latest wave of attacks involves a "Trojan horse" program that primarily affects certain versions of computer operating system software produced by Sun Microsystems Inc. and Solbourne Computer Inc. A Trojan-horse program appears to be harmless to a casual observer -- if it is noticed at all. But it contains a more sinister program that in this case secretly captures the password and account information for anyone trying to gain access to the computer from a remote site. The information is stored and can be retrieved later by the person who planted the Trojan horse program in the computer. The technique has been used to steal information on the Internet since the mid-1980's, said Cliff Stoll, an astrophysicist and author in Oakland, Calif., who discovered such a scheme, conducted by East German spies, on computers used by unitedstates Government researchers. He recounted the tale in the book "The Cuckoo's Egg." Mr. Stoll said the current outbreak was apparently more widespread than anything in the past.

title:
BUSINESS TECHNOLOGY;
Even in Cyberspace, Overcrowding
body: For a world that is theoretically infinite and without boundaries, cyberspace appears to be straining at the seams. In the computer-age equivalent of the Gold Rush, thousands of people are signing up each month for access to the worldwide web of computer networks and electronic information services -- known as cyberspace -- where strangers can chat, mail can be exchanged, groceries can be ordered and home banking can be done to name only a few possibilities. Lured by triple-digit annual growth rates, hundreds of businesses are emerging to offer services, ranging from billion-dollar corporations that want to provide entertainment, shopping and information networks, to technically savvy teen-agers who are among those providing the computer and phone line connections needed for individuals and businesses to link up. But the intense interest in computer networks is creating headaches for the technicians and frustrations for customers, who increasingly must deal with sluggish overloaded systems. In fact, last night, the 600,000 subscribers of a popular information service, America Online, received an unusual apology from Steve Case, the company's president, who said the service would postpone efforts to attract new customers. "Nobody goes there anymore, it's too crowded," joked Raymond L. Boggs, an analyst at BIS Strategic Research in Norwell, Mass. "The real question is whether they are growing so fast that the infrastructure will collapse."  Backbone Is the Internet There is no real danger that the global network will fail, experts say. Its backbone, the Internet, a chaotic web of thousands of connected computer networks that give users access to information and data bases, as well as a way to communicate with each other, began as a military communications system designed to survive a nuclear attack -- and made it through the recent Los Angeles earthquake unharmed. (By popular demand, the Internet was opened to the public, although most people pay a gatekeeper to facilitate access.) The real threat to the nation's information infrastructure may not be nuclear bombs, but the constant pecking of millions of little personal computers. Spurred by plunging prices for the computer equipment necessary for connecting to the electronic world, and by an Administration that has made the electronic infrastructure a national priority, new customers are "logging on" by the thousands each week. The population of the Internet, for example, is growing so fast that its unofficial demographers lost count recently at about 15 million. Because there is no central authority for the Internet, no one knows for sure. Mr. Case of America Online disclosed that as the service's population doubled from 300,000 last summer, a decision had been made to deny access to some customers at peak hours, at least temporarily, to avert further system deterioration. Mr. Case also wrote that America Online was postponing efforts to attract new customers and delaying the introduction of some new services that could sap system performance. "The huge increase in usage has put some strains on our system," he said. Mr. Case said this had happened even though his company, based in Vienna, Va., rushed to add computer capacity, beefed up its telephone network resources, added dozens of technical support people and billing representatives, and doubled the programming staff in an attempt to keep up with the growth. Capacity is taxed not only by the number of new subscribers but also by the growing demand for advanced system features like faster data-transfer rates, control systems that use pretty graphics instead of plain computer text and new engines that make it easier to search for a particular piece of data. The higher technical demands, coupled with the steep growth in subscribers, has most service providers scrambling to keep up, adding more phone-line capacity, mainframes and data storage. Tiny service stations, for those who do not want to navigate cyberspace alone, are popping up around the globe to capitalize on the increased traffic. "It's kind of crazy," said Smoot Carl-Mitchell, president of Zilker Internet Park, which recently opened 16 telephone lines in Austin, Tex., to offer customers access to electronic mail, news and other services on the Internet. "The total cost of the hardware to get into business was less than $15,000." "Maybe you shouldn't let that out," said Mr. Carl-Mitchell, a former Austin city councilman, "or everybody and his dog will be setting up as Internet service providers in their kitchens."  High School Businessman Or spare room. Scott Drassinower, a commercial provider of Internet access in White Plains, operates his growing high-tech business when he's not attending classes at Ardsley High School. He is 15 years old. "After school, usually the first thing I do is put my books down, check my email to see if there are any pressing problems that demand immediate attention, and then I do my homework," he said. As might be expected, he uses the Internet's vast information resources when he is researching his school reports. Despite the logistical pitfalls and ballooning expenses for service providers, there is no shortage of billion-dollar companies eager to enter the fray. So far this year, Apple Computer Inc., the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, many of the Baby Bells, the Ziff-Davis Publishing Company and several other large businesses have disclosed plans for starting new information services. Novell Inc., the largest provider of computer networking software for businesses, is said to be preparing to give its users easy access to the Internet, which could swell the population of the Internet by millions of users. The Microsoft Corporation, best known for its personal computer software, is reportedly working with companies in the entertainment and cable television industries to create a new interactive information service. "Gates is basically looking for another million-plus-unit market, and the desktop computing paradigm is coming to an end," said Mary Modahl, a senior analyst with Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass., referring to William H. Gates, the chairman of Microsoft. "There aren't many virgin desktops out there to find any more, so Gates looks at the home as the largest possibility." And he is far from alone in hoping to make money along the back alleys and cul-de-sacs of the information highway. "The pie is growing fast enough for all to enjoy, but at some point there will be too many entrants," said Russell Williams, vice president and general manager of the Delphi Internet Services Corporation, an on-line information service owned by Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation. "Too many people are asking for that $10 to $15 commitment from customers each month." Many customers, if not most, subscribe to more than one on-line service. It is not uncommon today to see as many as six or seven different electronic mail addresses printed on a business card or letterhead. The evidence suggests that people are indeed finding the on-line services more compelling. Home computer users responding to a survey taken by BIS Strategic Research in December reported that they spent 8.5 percent of their total computing time connected to remote data bases, a category that includes the on-line services. A year ago, the figure was 4.2 percent.  Pricing Changed But it is difficult to predict where those figures may go next because several of the big services have recently changed their pricing structure. The Prodigy Services Company, a joint venture of Sears, Roebuck & Company and the International Business Machines Corporation, which has about two million users, and Genie, a service owned by General Electric, which has an estimated 100,000 users, were the last big commercial services to offer unlimited access to the networks for a fixed fee. Both recently abandoned the flat-fee approach in favor of a metered system that assesses charges based on the amount of time the user is connected. As competition heats up, prices are coming down. Compuserve Information Services, a subsidiary of H& R Block, which claims to have about two million subscribers, has announced that it will cut its prices sharply on Feb. 6. Apple's new service, called eWorld, effectively matched Compuserve's reduced rates. In general, it still costs an average of $4 to $5 an hour to use the popular commercial services, although many services offer special rates that can reduce the fees to as little as $1 an hour for the most frequent users. Such a frequent user is Boris Rapport of Anaheim, Calif., a 59-year-old financial planner and part-time college professor. Mr. Rapport said he spent about three hours each weekday connected to various on-line services, especially Prodigy. His wife, Shirl, said she used the system perhaps an hour a day. Asked to describe how they spent their 20 or so hours a week in cyberspace, Mr. Rapport recited a list: They visit various electronic bulletin boards, send and receive electronic mail, get stock market information, do most of their banking and read on the computer screen most of what they once read in their daily newspaper. But they also turn to cyberspace for a sense of community. "I have a fairly rare illness called celiac sprue, and there are 40 or 50 of us on the bulletin boards," Mr. Rapport said. He and others who suffer from the gastrointestinal disorder share diets, drug information and discuss how to function in society with that disorder, he added. "As a result of that, I've had to learn how to do cooking and baking, so I also spend time on the cooking and baking bulletin boards."  Letters to Politicians Mrs. Rapport enjoys writing electronic-mail letters to politicians. (Even the White House has its own electronic post office.) Prodigy ran a live, 30-second television commercial during the State of the Union address last Tuesday, asking Prodigy subscribers to log on and assess Mr. Clinton's performance in an instant poll. Within an hour, more than 5,000 people had registered their opinions. A big question is whether the growing public and commercial interest in cyberspace is indicative of a sustainable trend, or whether it is a fad fueled by media accounts and the novelty of personal computer-based communications. "I have read that the average duration for someone to stay with a given service is something like 25 months," said Lisa Johnson, a technology analyst with Link Resources in New York City. " It's like when you buy the exercise bicycle, and the interest wanes after a while," but there could be a big hook to keep users in cyberspace. Trials are already under way that link computer-based information services to the television. Graphic   Photos: With people rushing onto computer networks, entrepreneurs like Scott Drassinower, 15, of White Plains, left (G. Paul Burnett/The New York Times), and Smoot Carl-Mitchell and Jack Quarterman, right, in Austin, Tex., are starting new service businesses. (Lisa Davis for The New York Times)

title:
The Executive Computer;
Curtain's Rising on a Third Generation of On-Line Services
body: THE fashionable joke floating around the Internet last week was that the "information superhighway is just like CB radio, but with more typing." There is no disputing that computer networks and on-line services -- spurred on in part by Vice President Al Gore and his promotion of the "national information infrastructure" -- are currently the nation's biggest craze. At Demo 94, a personal computer industry conference held here each year, a new generation on-line services was on exhibit last week. The offerings won't be commercially available until later this year, but many of the technologies have already emerged in experimental form on the Internet, the global network of networks used by more than 15 million people. And last week there were also fresh indications that the Internet is gaining commercial momentum, as major publishers begin to offer genuine commercial services over the net. The first generation of on-line services, which emerged in the late 1970's were based on connecting one's "dumb" terminal -- a personal computer using terminal-emulator software -- to a mainframe computer. Problems included a slow response time and a monitor display limited to simple screens of text. The second generation -- services like those from the Prodigy Services Company and America On-Line -- have used the increasing power of the personal computer to speed up the interaction and give a simpler and more graphical interface to the user. The next generation of on-line technology, exemplified by the new Interchange service that the computer trade publisher Ziff-Davis announced last week, are starting to emerge as computers grow more powerful and communications links get faster. The new systems promise to change the way users interact with remote central computers and, more significantly, are for the first time beginning to hint at an experience that rivals traditional print publishing. "This is truly the third generation in on-line technology," said Stewart Alsop, editor of Infoworld, a rival personal computer newspaper that has agreed to be distributed over the new Ziff-Davis service. "It begins to remove the notion of remoteness that came with earlier services." Indeed, the erosion of the old mainframe-to-dumb-terminal model of tele-computing appears to be giving way rapidly. Earlier this month, General Magic, a Mountain View, Calif., software developer, unveiled Telescript, a communications language that will provide the foundation of A.T.&T.'s Personal Link on-line service, scheduled to begin later this year. With Telescript, a computer user has no idea of "connecting" to a remote service at all. Instead, a program called an agent travels from the user's computer through the network, looking for information or even making purchases, based on commands given by the user. Ziff-Davis is the largest publisher of computer magazines, and the Interchange service, which will be commercially available for Windows-based personal computers in the fall, offers its readers a way to read their favorite publications on-line, as well as the ability to join communities of other personal computer enthusiasts and download software and other information. By itself that doesn't appear to be any more than what is available on existing on-line services, including Ziff-Davis's own Ziffnet which is accessible through Compuserve. But the Interchange system moves a step forward in taking advantage of the client personal computer. It offers the ability to view true "compound" documents that include graphics and images, rather than simple windows of scrolling text. It also offers multi-tasking, which means that you can start to download a document or a program in one part of the system and then go on to browse information in another part while the download is taking place. Interchange, scheduled to go on-line next fall, makes extensive use of "hyper text" links between different pieces of information -- a feature that is widely accessible in the Internet, but not available in more tightly compartmentalized commercial systems. As Interchange is designed, this means that it is possible to read a news article about a new computer system and then click on a pointer to read reviews about the same machine that are stored elsewhere. No pricing information was available for Interchange, but the service will be sold via a fixed monthly membership fee for a specific number of hours, with additional hours sold on a metered basis. The idea, said Michael Kolowich, president of Ziff-Davis Interactive, is to avoid the high costs that Prodigy encountered when it found that the service it envisioned as shopping in an electronic information-retrieval mall instead turned into a electronic community center where users chatted on-line for hours and hours, paying only a monthly flat fee. Prodigy subsequently changed to a pricing system pegged more closely to actually on-line time. "You don't want to get into the trap that Prodigy got in when their best customers became their worst customers," Mr. Kolowich said. Another intriguing commercial venture introduced at Demo 94, was a joint venture between Dow Jones's electronic Dow Vision news service and Wais Inc., a small software and services company. Dow Vision, which includes the Wall Street Journal and a variety of other newspapers and financial information, will be made available through Wais via the Internet for a monthly license or subscription fee.  Next year, the service will also include The newyork Times News Service, under an agreement signed last month by The newyork Times Company and Dow Jones. The Wais version of Dow Vision should be a good example of third-generation on-line service. Users won't log in to Dow Jones at all. Instead they will be able to use a variety of "client" programs on their personal computers to more easily browse through and retrieve specific information from the Dow Vision data base. These client programs, which include Wais's own, as well as two free public-domain programs known as Gopher and Mosaic, display information in windows on an Apple Macintosh or on a Windows-based personal computer. The software eliminates many steps for the user, making many disparate data bases seem to be a single information bank. Retrieving specific stories is done by pointing with the mouse and clicking on a particular headline. Dow Jones officials said the Wais joint venture is an experiment with electronic distribution over the Internet. For example, in a manner similar to the way newsstands work today, it will be possible to make the headlines of the day's top stories available for free for anyone on the Internet to browse. People who wanted to read the article, however, would have to pay for the "publication." "We're looking at this as a way to learn about the Internet," said Greg Gerdy, assistant director of Dow Vision. "The Internet is still the wild wild West." The big question of course is one the publishing world hasn't answered yet: Will electronic news services steal subscribers from traditional print publications? Ziff-Davis executives said they hoped theirs would represent a obvious synergy between print publications and on-line services. "There are some things that print does well and some things that electronic media do better," said Mr. Kolowich of Ziff-Davis. "But we expect our print publications to be around for a long, long time." Graphic   Drawing

title:
THE EARTHQUAKE: Trapped;
Airborne in Bed: A Building Collapses, Leaving 15 Dead
body: By ELIZABETH KOLBERT Erik Pearson heard a loud explosion and felt a jolt like a bomb. Still on their bed, he and his wife then fell 12 feet through the ceiling of the apartment below. "We were airborne," said Mr. Pearson, a 27-year-old nursing student. "I heard the glass break from the glass sliding doors. Our apartment came down and pitched diagonally." The door was jammed shut, the couple said, but they climbed down to safety off their once third-floor, now second-floor, balcony. But at least 14 other residents of the tan stucco apartment complex, the Northridge Meadows, did not. They died as building suffered some of the worst damage of the earthquake today and its residents bore the brunt of the casualties. The building, half a block from California State University at Northridge, housed many college students. An identical building next to it, the Northridge, buckled but did not collapse. The Meadows, a three-story, 164-unit apartment complex near the epicenter of the quake in the San Fernando Valley, looked like a cardboard box that someone had stepped on. In several sections of the building, the first floor no longer existed; it lay crushed beneath the two other floors. Windows had popped out of their frames, balconies dangled at odd angles and entire walls buckled.  Famous From Now On Until 4:31 A.M. today this sleepy middle-class section of Los Angeles, about 20 miles northwest of downtown, was known only for its tree-lined branch of the California State University. From now, it will be known as the epicenter of a devastating 6.6 earthquake. Simply put, city officials said the 14 deaths made this building the site of the largest number of earthquake fatalities in the city's history. John William, 36, a survivor who lived on the first floor, managed to slither to safety by following a small path of light to a crack in the building's foundation. "I pushed open the crack in the wall; my fiancee and I were pressed together, and we squeezed ourselves free," said Mr. William, who had cuts on both hands and arms. "I felt like we were going to lose circulation at any minute. "I was hearing moans and whining and banging from people pinned in the other apartments. I'm not exaggerating: the second floor is now in the dirt. There is not two inches of room in my apartment." Residents described a scene of panic in the hours before dawn as people tried to climb from their balconies or pick their way down dark staircases that had been torn apart by the quake.  Search for Bodies This afternoon, many residents of the complex were still milling around in front of the ruined building, at 9565 Reseda Boulevard, as firefighters, sweaty and exhausted, continued to search the debris. Eight hours after the quake, firefighters held out little hope that anyone still trapped would be found alive, but they said they were inserting electronic listening devices into the rubble that could pick up sounds as soft as human breathing. Earlier, they brought in dogs trained to find survivors in building rubble. There was no power in the area, most of the shops were closed and, in an incongruously festive gesture, people up and down the street had taken to eating half-melted ice cream cakes from a nearby Baskin-Robbins. The force of the tremor ripped apart homes, businesses, roads and utilities, leaving thousands of people without water, power or shelter. Reseda Boulevard, a main thoroughfare, resembled a war zone: broken water mains flooded streets; gas permeated the air, fuel for numerous fires that were controlled by the late afternoon. Traffic lights were knocked out, and accidents occurred throughout the area. Many of the community's 20,000 residents camped out in front of their damaged apartment buildings and houses, sleeping on blankets and lawn chairs and clinging to whatever items they were able to salvage in their haste to exit. All afternoon, aftershocks, some quite strong, could be felt throughout the neighborhood. With each one, more people moved into the street to stay clear in case more windows shattered. Capt. Robert De Feo of the Los Angeles Fire Department said the shearing motion of the quake had twisted the three-story building, causing the floor to collapse into the parking garage below. In what is perhaps the most stunning evidence of the quake's force here, the building now stands two stories high, surrounded by other three-story buildings. In addition to the university students who lived here, many Northridge Meadow residents were elderly and had to be coaxed from their apartments after the quake hit. Mike Kubeisy, a 34-year-old photographer who lived on the third floor, said he had broken into several apartments through the windows and forced the elderly residents inside to climb out over the broken glass. "They were scared," he said. "I was scared There was water and blood everywhere. I thank God I'm standing here." Mr. Pearson, who is trained in emergency medical treatment, also helped pull several people from the wreckage. He said he and four groups of five men each spent the morning throwing fire hoses up to the upper floors and climbing up to carry residents down. At one point, he said, he heard a woman on the first floor faintly cry for help. She was pinned face down on her bed by a wooden beam. Mr. Pearson went to get help; by the time he got back, three minutes later, she was dead.  Screaming for Help Syd Dalven, a 35-year-old retiree who lived in Apartment 135 on the first floor, said she had awakened to find herself pinned underneath the walls and ceilings of her apartment. "Everything caved in on my bed, so I started screaming for help," she said. "Luckily, four guys heard me and pulled me out." Sitting on the curb in front of her demolished apartment building, Ms. Dalven rubbed her legs, which had to be treated for minor scrapes and bruises. "This means nothing," she said. "I'm alive." Police and fire officials were not releasing the names of those who were killed in the building collapse, pending notification of relatives. Captain De Feo said that in addition to the 14 people who were killed, eight had been taken to hospitals for treatment of injuries, some of them serious. The Northridge Meadows was built in 1972, and fire officials said they had no reason to believe that it did not meet building specifications imposed after a large earthquake struck the same area in 1971. They also said they had no idea why this apartment building had collapsed, while others nearby suffered only slight damage. Several residents of the complex pointed out that the apartments that had collapsed were built over the parking garage and therefore may not have had as firm a foundation.  Signs From Better Times This afternoon, the small lawn in front of the complex was strewn with mattresses, furniture and piles of clothing, pulled there as part of the rescue efforts. Little red banners, which had been hung in happier times, fluttered in front of a wooden sign advertising "Luxury Resort Living" complete with "Jacuzzi, pool, putting green, sauna, BBQ, tennis court and billiard room." One-bedroom apartments in the complex rented for about $600 a month, residents said. This afternoon, the police were not allowing residents back into the complex, and many bemoaned the fact that they had left in their pajamas and now had no clothes to wear. Annette Grossman, a retired department store clerk who said she was in her 70's, was standing in front of the building in her nightgown and bathrobe. She said the quake had thrown her out of bed and onto the floor. "I threw the pillow over my head and prayed for it to end," she said. It took a half-hour for neighbors to reach her in her second-floor apartment and pull her out through the window. "I just feel lucky," she said. That also went for her neighbor, a man in his 80's. It was more than four hours after the quake hit when the rescue teams pulled the man from his apartment. He looked up at the bright blue California sky, she said, and "his first remark was, 'Isn't this a beautiful day.' "

title: Gore Preaches, and Practices, the Techno-Gospel
body: The Vice President strode into his office, took a seat at a Compaq personal computer and briskly pecked out a confident greeting. "Welcome to the White House," Al Gore typed. "Let's get started." Thus did Mr. Gore, displaying excellent work station posture and impressive typing skills, become the first Vice President to hold a live interactive news conference on an international computer network. The session Thursday, just two days after he delivered a much-publicized speech describing the Clinton Administration's vision of the "national information infrastructure," demonstrated that Mr. Gore practices the techno-gospel that he preaches. He may be only No. 2 at the White House, but Al Gore appears very much to be the Virtual President of the electronic Commonwealth of Cyberspace. It is Mr. Gore who has become the point man in the Administration's effort to build a national data highway, much as his father, former Senator Albert Gore, was a principal architect of the interstate highway system a generation or more earlier.  An Electronic Vox Populi The questions on Thursday came not from journalists but from a diverse group of people scattered over cyberspace from California to France. Following is the first query scrolled onto the Vice President's screen, one green line at a time, errors and all:  QUESTIONER Mr VP . . . I am from Hammond IN What are your views on These Virtual Communities . . . and Are you currently involved in iany[sic] networks? The response, after a small technical glitch froze Mr. Gore's computer in midsentence:  GORE I'm back. Sorry. Anyway, we have a kind of "virtual community" here in the White House that gets a lot of work done but we have not yet established the myriad links outside that we hope to soon. The Administration's first official hands-on foray into cyberspace -- the on-line world of computer networks, accessible to anyone with a personal computer, a modem and a telephone line -- was not profound on substantive policy questions. No bold initiatives were proposed, and no existing proposals were detailed. It was not particularly smooth either, lacking the fluidity of spoken communication and magnifying trivial typing errors. Nor was it noteworthy to the technological elite -- so accustomed to thinking about a future in which a simple exchange of computer text pales beside the promise of interactive video images and digital sound flowing over Internet, the vast global network of networks and the prototype for the national data network that Mr. Gore envisions. But as popular technological history and White House lore, Thursday's interactive computer conference may rank with President Franklin D. Roosevelt's appearance at the 1938-39 newyork World's Fair on a newfangled contraption called television. It took another decade for television to reach the public on a broad scale, just as it may be a decade before computer networks are commonplace. The physical locus of the news conference was in the Vice President's office in the West Wing of the White House, but the conversations actually took place in one of several mainframe computers in Columbus, Ohio, operated by the Compuserve Information Service. The conference, sponsored by U.S. News Online, the electronic version of U.S. News & World Report, used the most advanced ground-based and satellite networking systems. (This did not prevent the session from being interrupted when the father of a young fellow in Huntington, W. Va., inadvertently picked up a phone receiver while his son was chatting with the Vice President.) The meeting took place in a cyberspace "convention center" set up by Compuserve. Unlike most other on-line discussion groups, which can support a few dozen participants at most, this convention center had the capacity for hundreds of users. Previous appearances in Compuserve's virtual convention center have been made by Oliver North and the rock performer Lou Reed.  A Sellout Crowd Still, said Debra Young, a spokeswoman for Compuserve, Mr. Gore's popularity in cyberspace was unprecedented. The 300 slots for the conference were filled, first-come, first-served, within minutes after it was announced the previous week on Compuserve, as were 600 spectator slots, which allowed people to view the dialogue text as it appeared but not to ask questions. Scores of computer users who could not gain access tried posing their questions on the U.S. News Online forum in advance. Questions came to the Vice President from as far as Sweden, where Anette Brannstrom wanted to know if the information superhighway was to be "an all-American thing," and as near as Karen Jackson at the Bureau of Land Management in Washington, who concluded her question with this postscript: "I'm deaf so this type of conference is a miracle for me." Janine Janson, 6, of Deer Park, L.I., had hoped to ask "Dear Mr V.P. Gore" if he could "bring some more compters to my school so I can comminate with children from other places." Joe Pagano of Roseland, N.J., wanted to say, "Al, you are the coolest VP to date for providing leadership in organizing the NII" -- the national information infrastructure. But they did not get the chance. The conference moderator, William F. Allman, a senior editor at U.S. News & World Report, chose questions at random from a live message queue that jammed as soon as it was opened. One by one, keystroke by keystroke, the Vice President received the electronic supplicants trooping into the White House, just as his predecessors did more than a century ago -- well before the age of metal detectors -- when the White House executive offices were open to ordinary people petitioning the President and his aides. Through cyberspace, it was open once again on Thursday -- if only for 45 minutes.  Invasion of the Techie Generation Yet in those 45 minutes, the computer-toting Clinton Administration stood in sharp contrast to the previous White House, where technology sometimes appeared to be a source of puzzlement and mystery. Mr. Clinton has been known to receive electronic-mail messages and respond to them off-line, when he has time. Two years ago, President George Bush displayed genuine wonder when, at a campaign stop at a supermarket, he saw a clerk feeding prices to the cash register by waving products over a relatively common bar-code reader. Mr. Bush did make an attempt to learn how to use a personal computer in 1991. He took pride in his accomplishment, according to a White House press release put out the next day, which quoted Mr. Bush as saying: "Today I learned to turn one on. I pushed a button down there, and a little one up there with green on it, and out came a command for someone I had written." The White House has taken a technological leap under Mr. Gore, who as a senator was known for his eagerness to embrace technology issues that many of his colleagues were reluctant to tackle. Mr. Gore's electronic-mail address is now "vice-president@whitehouse.gov." He has a Macintosh Powerbook Duo notebook computer that is kept in a "docking station" on his desk when he is not toting it around. The machine is wired into a network. He has another Macintosh at home, which makes the Vice President stand out in the White House, which is otherwise dominated by I.B.M-compatible machines. Yet he showed no hesitation when confronted with a non-Apple computer that was used for Thursday's on-line conference. All the other computers in the West Wing use Microsoft Windows software. Let history show that Mr. Gore's own desktop computer apparently does not adhere to Energy Star, the Environmental Protection Agency's program to reduce electricity used by computers, which the Administration has promoted and which many computers now on the market are certified for. That would seem to be a rare techno-lapse for the author of "Earth in the Balance," Mr. Gore's 1992 book on environmental issues. But otherwise, Mr. Gore presents himself as a model citizen of computing.  Room for Diversity When one questioner on Thursday said that he was handicapped, Mr. Gore quickly noted that the woman who operates the White House Forum on the Compuserve network, Georgia Griffith of Lancaster, Ohio, is deaf and blind. (The Clinton Administration has no formal relationship with the forum, although White House officials occasionally participate.) "There will be many opportunities for the disabled to use their minds productively on networks," Mr. Gore noted. And when his aides signaled that his time in cyberspace was up, the Vice President typed: "Thanks. I loved it. I'm just sorry that it is impossible to answer everyone. Let's do it again sometime soon." Graphic   Photos: A computer exchange between Vice President Al Gore and a participant in the Vice President's on-line news conference last week. (Compuserve Information Service)(pg. D4); Vice President Al Gore in his office last week as he took part in a live news conference by computer network. Mr. Gore has become point man in the Clinton Administration's effort to build a national data highway. (Associated Press)(pg. D1)

title: Internet Users Get Access To S.E.C. Filings Fee-Free
body: In a two-year experiment that begins today, documents filed electronically to the Securities and Exchange Commission from public companies will be available to users of Internet, a global network of computer networks. Documents obtainable on the service include annual reports, 10-K filings, proxy statements and other information valued by traders and investors. These documents are already available electronically through commercial data suppliers, including Mead Data Central Inc. of Dayton, Ohio, but the new Internet service is the first to make them available without additional charges. The new service is the most ambitious experiment so far by the Clinton Administration to make much Government information widely available to the public at minimum cost. Although access to Internet itself can be costly, millions of people can tap into it through commercial, Government and educational computer networks. Once a computer user is connected to Internet, a giant global network that links millions of large and small computers so they can share information, there is typically no extra fee for document transfers.  Financed by Taxes "We have a policy that Government information ought to be made available at only the marginal cost to provide the information," said Tom Kalil, who coordinates science and technology policy at the White House's National Economic Council. "We view this type of information dissemination as one of the ways we can address the info 'haves and have-nots' issue. Since taxpayers have already paid for it, the idea of making it available was appealing." The cost of providing the S.E.C. data to Internet users is being underwritten by a National Science Foundation grant to the newyork University Business School. In turn, the contract for operation of the computer data bases is with a not-for-profit company, the Internet Multicasting Service of Washington.  Coordination With S.E.C. Carl Malamud, the principal of Internet Multicasting, said the S.E.C. is charging $78,000 a year to supply his company with data tapes of each day's filings. The fee, he said, basically covers the cost of the tapes and messenger fees. Mr. Malamud said the S.E.C. has projected that as many as 50 gigabytes of data -- 50 billion characters of information -- will be supplied each year. An average S.E.C. document contains about 3,000 characters, he said. Mr. Malamud said that although they offered the same raw data, his Government-subsidized service is not in conflict with commercial information services like Mead Data. In return for its higher fees, Mead Data provides search software that makes it easier to find a particular document, and it guarantees its customers access to the data within minutes of the time the document is filed. "Our data is 24 hours later than theirs, and we are not massaging the data to the extent that Mead is," Mr. Malamud said, although a goal of the experiment is to fashion easier search and retrieval mechanisms for the raw S.E.C. data. Also, only 50 Internet users can gain access to the S.E.C. data base at one time, he said, cautioning that "if you were betting your business on getting a document right away, you shouldn't bet on us." Computer users with access to Internet can get more information by sending an electronic-mail message to "mail[at]town.hall.org" requesting help. Those without Internet access can telephone (202) 628-2044.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Newspapers Race for Outlets In Electronic Marketplace
body: The rapid development of electronic information technologies has placed the American newspaper industry at a crossroads. New methods of delivering information to desktops and living rooms are threatening the economic foundation of the $45 billion newspaper industry, historically one of the most lucrative and influential of American businesses. Newspaper companies are racing toward electronic media of all kinds in an attempt to pre-empt the competition. Last week alone, three ventures were announced. The Los Angeles Times said it was starting an electronic shopping service with Pacific Telesis, and The Philadelphia Inquirer, owned by Knight-Ridder Inc., said it was going into the television news business with its own local evening newscast. The Washington Post and the Oracle Corporation also agreed to an alliance to develop an electronic publishing service, which they are expected to detail today. [Page D7.] Increasingly, newspaper executives and industry analysts recognize that computer, telephone and cable hookups have opened paths for new vendors to compete cheaply in the sale of news and other information. "With the digital age (apparently) fast approaching, the newspaper industry has been racking its communal brains figuring out how not to be left behind," Tod A. Jacobs, a newspaper securities analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein & Company, wrote in a recently published study of the industry's future. Some on-line computer services now carry news updates and financial information, like stock market reports, that do not originate at newspapers. Perhaps most threatening to the newspaper industry, electronic buying and advertising services are already competing for advertiser dollars that traditionally went to big daily newspapers. Without the need for costly presses and newsprint, or fleets of delivery trucks, it is now economically feasible for the new vendors to sell everything from world and national news reports to neighborhood listings and restaurant reviews, Mr. Jacobs and others said. On-line services have already opened a new market for wire services and various suppliers of niche information. And entrepreneurs are working feverishly to find new ways of collecting information to sell.  A Franchise Challenged Some in the newspaper industry are convinced that paper-and-ink dailies will never die. But the likelihood that they will be challenged as primary providers of daily information has captured the industry's attention. James Longson, the vice president for technology at the Tribune Company, owner of The Chicago Tribune and other newspapers, gave this tongue-in-cheek explanation when asked why newspaper executives are rushing into electronic ventures: "Because everybody else is," he said. "Everybody can't be wrong, can they?" More seriously, Mr. Longson said, "There will be some segment of the audience that will prefer to receive their information electronically; if we don't meet that need, someone else will." Some newspaper executives argue that if they move quickly, newspapers can establish themselves in new media as suppliers of "brand name" information that they sell at premium prices, the way Procter & Gamble sells soap. Toward that end, newspapers are starting on-line editions, data base marketing businesses and telephone information services. They are struggling to harness newspapers' strengths as the owners of vast stores of information.  'Evolution' of News Providers When he announced the television venture last week, P. Anthony Ridder, the president of Knight-Ridder, one of the country's largest newspaper companies, said the move represented a step in his company's "evolution from print to a full-service information provider." Many executives at large newspapers are expressing similar sentiments as they try to avoid becoming "road kill" on the information highway, to borrow a warning phrase coined by Jeff Greenfield, a political and media analyst for ABC News. The newspaper industry still has vast wealth and enormous power, and many analysts say that it has years, perhaps even decades, to fight to retain its place as a primary source of current information. But there is an emerging consensus that newspapers face a challenge that may be as fundamental as previous threats from television, radio and other competitors for Americans' attention.  Costs No Longer Prohibitive Electronic delivery of information could negate the newspaper industry's biggest financial protection, Mr. Jacobs said. For decades, the enormous cost of newspaper printing plants and delivery systems served as a barrier to many potential rivals. The stock market has been enthusiastic about non-newspaper companies that are aiming for multimedia riches, according to the newspaper securities analysts at J. P. Morgan Securities Inc. But some analysts contend that the new information suppliers cannot yet compete meaningfully with newspapers. "It will take many years and much capital for such companies to usurp the traditional newspaper information franchises," the Morgan analysts said in a recent report. Newspaper executives do not like to hear talk about usurping their franchises, no matter how far off. But entrepreneurs are already carving away parts of the newspaper industry's revenues.  Computer Classifieds An example is classified advertising. A fledgling industry is already offering various types of ads by telephone or computer, providing users with quick access to information. Some services let a potential buyer of a used car, for instance, specify the desired make, model and year without having to pore over thousands of listings. Newspaper companies are involved in some of the new ventures. Industry analysts and newspaper executives differ on the extent of the new competition and on how quickly the industry must move against it. But in the last year, most big newspaper companies and many small ones have sharply accelerated their own electronic ventures. Whether the financial commitments are large or small, it is clear that newspapers are struggling to protect what they consider special relationships with their communities. Competing information vendors, they say, will have difficulty matching ties that developed over generations. Still, significant hurdles face the industry as it tries to reshape its business. Here are a few of the challenges facing newspaper executives in their race against the digital clock: Is the newspaper a forgotten friend? To take advantage of reader loyalty in the electronic age, newspapers must have reader loyalty in the first place. Veronis, Suhler & Associates, a firm that provides investment banking services to media companies, recently calculated that the hours Americans spend with their newspapers is dropping. By 1997, it said, the average American will devote about 165 hours a year to reading a newspaper, down almost 11 percent from 185 hours in 1984. The slippage is occurring while time spent on activities like watching videos is increasing sharply. If readers are jilting newspapers, is there any reason to believe the romance will be rekindled electronically? Will consumers pay more for newspaper information? Even at 50 cents a day, some analysts say, Americans essentially view newspaper news as costing nothing. And that is exactly what they want to pay for it -- even electronically. With many newspaper executives concluding that traditional advertising revenues may never return to the lucrative levels reached before the stock market crash of 1987, an unanswered question of many new newspaper businesses is how to make the ventures pay. Is the electronic glass half full or half empty? A strength that newspapers are said to bring to electronic ventures is credibility as carriers of advertising.  But old advertising patterns have been eroding for some time. Direct-mail companies and a host of broadcast and print rivals have been grabbing newspaper advertising dollars. In retailing, Wal-Mart Stores Inc. rewrote some industry rules in the 1980's partly by slashing the amounts spent on newspaper advertising. Newspapers compensated somewhat for retail advertising losses by increasing the percentage of their revenues derived from classified advertisements. But even classified ads fell sharply after the market crash of 1987. And now, Morgan's analysts say new electronic information ventures by cable and telephone companies "could be a long-term threat" to traditional classifieds. On the other hand, the Morgan analysts conclude that newspapers participating in these ventures see electronic classifieds as "a new product opportunity." Where should newspapers place their electronic bets? Though newspapers may seem nearly prehistoric next to electronic gizmos, a sometimes overlooked fact is that newspapers, the biggest segment of the communications business, rake in large amounts of cash. Even during the tough times of the last few years, the nespwpaper industry's average profit margins have remained respectable -- 12 to 14 percent, according to Veronis, Suhler -- and consistently higher than those in the communications industry as a whole. Moreover, with most newspaper markets beginning to show signs of economic recovery, those profit margins are expected to climb. Newspaper publishers "are poised for positive earnings surprises in 1994," Michael A. Kupinski, a securities analyst at A. G. Edwards & Sons in St. Louis, said. That means that some of the country's leading newspaper companies will have fat rolls of cash to invest. Mr. Kupinski recently predicted that with costs down and advertising starting to rebound, profit margins at major newspaper companies were likely to head toward pre-recession levels of 21 percent or more. Mr. Jacobs of Bernstein & Company recently calculated that over the next four years the Gannett Company, the largest newspaper company in the country, was likely to have about $1 billion in cash available for investment, while the Tribune Company was likely to have $700 million and Knight-Ridder about $600 million. In effect, the old dinosaurs have enough money to reinvent themselves before there is any real danger of extinction. The issue is whether they will make the right choices about investing in the new forms of electronic information delivery. As Mr. Jacobs put it: "The billion-dollar question, of course, is: What'll they do with all that dough?" Graphic   Graph: "What's Driving the Newspaper Industry" shows newspaper advertising, spending and profit margin statistics. (pg. D6)

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
Dutch Buyer Acquires BPI
body: BPI Communications L.P., the publisher of Billboard magazine and The Hollywood Reporter, has been acquired by VNU, a Dutch media conglomerate, for $220 million, the two companies announced yesterday. VNU acquired the company from a group of investors made up of BPI management, Boston Ventures and The newyork Times Company. The Times Company acquired its one-third interest in BPI Communications last year through its acquisition of Affiliated Publications Inc., the publisher of The Boston Globe. Besides Billboard and the Hollywood Reporter, BPI publishes 17 magazines, including Adweek, a trade publication. Through its book division, Watson-Guptill, it publishes specialty books under five imprints. It also puts out 20 annual directories and operates computer-based communications and information services. The company's annual sales total $130 million, and it employs 800 people at 19 offices worldwide. VNU, or Verenigde Nederlandse Uitgeversbedrijven B.V., is the largest producer of mass circulation publications in the Netherlands, owning magazines, regional newspapers, broadcasting interests and computer data bases. VNU has expressed an interest in expanding in the unitedstates, where the bulk of its current holdings are in data bases. The Times Company said it expected to receive net proceeds of approximately $55 million when the sale of BPI is completed in the first quarter.  For financial reporting purposes, the company said, no gain or loss will be recognized on the transaction.

title: Live, Via Compuserve: It's On-Line With Al Gore
body: In a hands-on demonstration of the "information superhighway" technology he has been promoting, Vice President Al Gore conducted the first computer-based news conference from the White House tonight. He made history and only a few typographical errors. Mr. Gore, appearing comfortable at the computer keyboard and displaying more than a passing acquaintance with the electronic realm known as cyberspace, spent 45 minutes reading and responding to typed questions that scrolled down his screen from unseen questioners from California to France.  Real-Life Questions The questioners were not journalists. And with the exception of a single question on the strife in Bosnia, all the questions concerned the Administration's proposed "national information infrastructure" and its possible effects on people's everyday lives. The unseen questioners revealed their diversity. "I'm handicapped and spend a lot of time on the Net," wrote Larry H. Lewis from Alta Loma, Calif. "Hello from Reynoldsburg, Home of the tomato!" typed in Ben Huntoon, apparently from Ohio. In all, about 900 computer users were crowded -- electronically speaking -- into the the news conference, which Mr. Gore conducted from his White House office in the West Wing. It was sponsored by U.S. News & World Report, which has an electronic version that is carried over Compuserve Information Service, an on-line network for personal computers.  Quiet and Mostly Competent With the exceptions of his clicking keyboard, the reading of the questions by Mr. Gore and his typed responses for the benefit of a dozen onlookers in his office and countless others watching via C-Span, the news conference seemed eerily silent by White House standards. The questioning was interrupted only a few times by apparent technical glitches. In an exchange, for instance, with Aaron Dickey, a 23-year-old student in Huntington, W. Va., the questioner's message dissolved into garble. "Line snoise sorry," the student typed. "Line noise was my father picking up an extension, Mr. VP, sorry. [grin]" "I think it was my fault," the Vice President said. His words reached the student's ears as quickly as the electrons sped across the computer network from the the White House to Compuserve's mainframe computer in Columbus, Ohio, and then on to West Virginia. And even in cyberspace, a certain deference to the executive branch obtains. "No, sir," the student wrote, "it was my father, not your fault."

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times to Seek Cost Savings Including Some Cuts in Jobs
body: After six years of sharp declines in advertising, The newyork Times reported yesterday that it had a "tiny -- but nonetheless real"-- advertising gain of 1 percent for 1993, compared with 1992. But in a memorandum to the staff, the newspaper's publisher, Arthur Sulzberger Jr., said that while The Times's financial picture "has stabilized, we still find ourselves facing serious difficulties" that will force the newspaper to seek cost savings, including a reduction in its white-collar work force. The newyork Times Company yesterday announced a special pretax charge of $30 million (approximately 19 cents a share) for the fourth quarter of 1993 "for severance and related costs resulting from anticipated white-collar staff reductions." It had earlier projected 1993 earnings of $59 million to $67 million, or 70 cents to 80 cents a share. Mr. Sulzberger said that the newspaper had lost more than a third of its advertising volume since the 1987 stock market crash and that despite signs of an improvement in the economy, "there is little to suggest that much of this lost linage will return." Because of increased competition for fewer advertiser dollars, Mr. Sulzberger said, the newspaper "must respond to diminished revenue by rethinking the way we operate" and reducing costs without affecting the quality of the newspaper. He said the newspaper would seek savings, including reductions in the number of white-collar employees and managers. He said that the newspaper would try to achieve the reductions through voluntary measures, but that he could not rule out the possibility that some employees "will have to leave with severance packages." Nancy Nielsen, the spokeswoman for The Times, said the newspaper would evaluate all categories of white-collar employees, including those in the newspaper's newsroom, as it determines where reductions would be made.  Union Involved The newspaper's contract with the newyork Newspaper Guild, the union that represents white-collar and some other employees, expired on March 31. Negotiations are continuing. The Times has contracts through the year 2000 with its production unions. Mr. Sulzberger's memorandum noted that the newspaper had reduced its staff by about 10 percent over the last six years, with most of the reductions coming from the craft employees. Mr. Sulzberger said it was "reasonable to assume" that the newspaper would need a similar reduction over the next few years from white-collar employees. The Times made its announcement after the stock market closed yesterday. Earlier, the Times Company's class A shares ended trading at $29.125, up 37.5 cents, on the American Stock Exchange.

title:
SUNDAY, January 9, 1994;
Lost in Cyberspace
body: There he was, as cyber as you can get without being a punk, best-selling author of "The Hitchiker's Guide to the Galaxy" series, having an identity crisis -- well, a virtual identity crisis. Douglas Adams, or some digital embodiment of somebody who claimed to be Douglas Adams, was on the Internet. He has been on the Internet longer than most. And immodest though it may be, he will sometimes check in with alt.fan.douglas-adams.  That, for non-cyberspeakers (to whom nets are something to string across the Seine), is a Douglas Adams fan club. At the club, however, people started challenging him, saying that Adams was not who he said he was. Queried by email about this disturbing situation, a person claiming to be Douglas Adams replied, via email: "It just seemed annoying. Why would anyone want to go to elaborate lengths to pretend to be me, and why should I have to defend my identity? Then someone started sending abusive notes to members of the 'alt.fan. douglas-adams' list, and making it appear that they came from me." Adams had to post messages arguing that he was indeed himself, and pointing out that he hadn't been sending the unpleasant notes. According to Adams (you have to give him the benefit of the doubt if you want to stay sane), only in the groups devoted to his work or to science fiction is he challenged. Elsewhere he's more easily accepted. "Maybe it's just that there is no particular reason for someone to pretend to be me on the 'sci.nasal.membranes.rhinoceros' group. . . . Or maybe it's just that people who hang around on SF-related newsgroups are more than usually predisposed to traffic in fantasies, conspiracies and paranoid delusions." In one of his messages trying to quell the identity brouhaha, Adams asserted: "I will not get involved in any pointless debates about who I am. I know who I am, and if you have a problem with that, then it stays your problem." Good for him, whoever he is. And stay tuned for some real confusion when the net welcomes Philip Roth.

title: Testing the High Hopes for TV Shopping
body: Just when it seemed as if all the pizazz had gone out of retailing, when financiers and technocrats had replaced the merchant princes and price had become the only weapon with which to compete, the era of electronic selling dawned in America. Well, sort of. Electronic retailing has been around for more than a decade, mostly in the form of mercilessly cheerful televised hucksters pushing cubic zirconia and tacky knickknacks, or as lists of airline, theater and movie schedules and fares called up on computer screens. A few companies -- notably J. C. Penney, Dayton Hudson and Sears, Roebuck -- tried their hand at selling via cable television and failed miserably, unable to compete with the down-market, high-volume cable programmers QVC Network Inc. and the Home Shopping Network. But along came Barry Diller, the Hollywood phenomenon who bought a controlling stake in QVC. And suddenly in 1993, retailers, most of whom secretly adore celebrity of any sort, fell in love with electronic selling.  Necessity Meets Opportunity Despite the failures of the past, most retail companies now say they think home shopping in some form will play a crucial role in their future. Macy's, Spiegel, Saks Fifth Avenue, Nordstrom, Wal-Mart Stores, F.A.O. Schwarz, Lillian Vernon and legions of manufacturers have jumped on the bandwagon, even though the form that the new retailing will take is unclear at this point. It was a case of necessity colliding with opportunity. Analysts estimate that retailers could close about 30 percent of their existing store space and no one would notice. So future growth for companies other than Wal-Mart, Home Depot and a handful of others will have to either be seized from competitors in an expensive battle, or come from new venues. And developments in technology, backed by strong companies with deep pockets like Time Warner, Bell Atlantic and Tele-Communications, are opening new channels of interactive distribution far more sophisticated than the home shopping of today, which is little more than a televised catalogue with sound -- and no chance to browse through the pages. No one expects that kind of electronic retailing to last long. While Home Shopping Network and QVC have grown explosively in less than a decade, they have failed to attract the affluent consumers most retailers want. A study by Deloitte & Touche showed that the average household income of television shoppers was $34,900, compared with a total retail market average of $38,000.  'There's No Limit' Retail experts say that enticing those with bigger wallets to shop electronically is -- as the best merchants have long known -- a matter of presentation. "Once we get true interactivity combined with interesting programming, there's no limit to what can be done," said Walter K. Levy, a retail consultant. Mr. Levy envisions a day when a consumer will have a box on top of her television that will allow her to call up a customized selection of merchandise, much like a personal shopper in today's department stores. She might ask to look for a gift for her husband, for example, priced from $25 to $50. Using the machine's keys, she will create a selection of choices without leaving her armchair. She will be able to view the merchandise from all angles and, in the case of clothing, be able to see it on a model who roughly matches her husband's body size and coloring. When she makes a selection, she will punch in her credit card number, hit the order key and within 24 hours, have the gift at her home. The question is how long it will take to develop such a system. Communications companies have been testing primitive interactive systems for several years with mixed results. Consumers so far have shown scant interest in using their television sets to order things like library books, videotapes and food.  Experiment in Florida Time Warner is gearing up for an interactive cable experiment to begin in April in Orlando, Fla., which will be closely watched by retailers. Apple Computer mailed out 30,000 compact disks last month that contained catalogues from retailers like Tiffany & Company, Land's End and Williams-Sonoma that can be used in CD-ROM drives and let consumers browse, much as they thumb through conventional catalogues. And TV Macy, R. H. Macy & Company's 24-hour shopping cable channel, is scheduled to begin next fall. It is expected to take home shopping to a new level by mixing programming and entertainment with selling. Julia Child, for example, might whip up saumon en croute using utensils and kitchen wares that would be for sale. Or a Macy's sales clerk might demonstrate different ways to tie scarves. While the industry is keeping a close eye on those developments and others, some companies are more cautious than others. Leslie Wexner, for one, the legendary merchant who is chairman and chief executive of the Limited Inc., has said he would be content to enter the electronic arena after some other retailer had proved it worthwhile. And so far, ventures into electronic retailing other than the Home Shopping Network and QVC have been disappointing. J. C. Penney poured an estimated $170 million to $200 million into two different electronic shopping experiments in the late 1980's and early 1990's only to withdraw after deciding the systems were unlikely to add considerably to its bottom line. One experiment, the J. C. Penney Home Shopping Network, reached 15 million homes in 725 markets but found it could not compete with QVC, which was on in many of the same markets. The other Penney test, Telaction, offered more elegant merchandise than was generally available on QVC or Home Shopping but also failed to attract shoppers.  Saks and QVC The shot in the dark that started retailing's stampede to the airwaves was Saks Fifth Avenue's announcement last summer that it had entered an agreement with QVC to sell one of its house brands on the network. But Saks has not renewed its contract with QVC, although the two companies are still negotiating. The sophisticated retailer found it could not make a profit from home shopping unless QVC lowered its commission rate or Saks itself found a cheaper way of making its clothing. Nonetheless, Philip B. Miller, Saks's chairman and chief executive, said he thought electronic retailing, whether on QVC or in another arrangement, would be a big part of Saks's future. "We very much want to continue to explore this medium and be a part of interactive cable television shopping," Mr. Miller said in a recent interview. "The experience has been invaluable in terms of what we've learned about this new way of selling. Now we have to figure out a way to produce some return on investment."
