title:
IDEAS & TRENDS;
Staking a Claim on The Virtual Frontier
body: FOR the hardy bands of pioneers who staked out the first electronic communities in the early 1970's, the sprawling web of computer networks known as cyberspace had the anarchist, individualist feel of an electronic frontier. Now the Net, as it is called, is feeling the pressures of suburbanization, as efforts to commercialize it are creating the electronic equivalent of neon signs and endless avenues of strip malls. With a computer connected to the net it is already possible to read a magazine or newspaper, buy an airline ticket or just hang out in the cybernetic equivalent of a bar or tavern (without virtual beers). But the commercialization of the net is only in its infancy and corporate America is suddenly in a mad rush for new digital markets. This week, for example, both A.T.&T. and Apple Computer Inc. plan to unveil nationwide on-line systems that will offer electronic shopping and other commercial services, joining the explosive growth of existing companies like Prodigy, America Online and Compuserve. Moreover, computer network use is about to burst out of the home office and den and into the family room as cable companies explore ways to send interactive computer data directly to special boxes that will sit on top of television sets. Soon it will be possible to glide electronically through vast virtual shopping malls or to turn your television into a digital cineplex. Computer networks have created thousands of virtual communities that have been the basis for a participatory democracy, creating fast friendships for millions of people around the world. But now it seems the pace of commercialization is in danger of overwhelming the original spirit and intent. Many of the network pioneers are distressed that the fragile and anarchic culture that they have cultivated is about to be trampled by a horde of digital pitchmen hawking their wares. "I'm in mourning," said Mark Seiden, a computer consultant based in Belmont, Calif. "We once had our own code of honor. Now there's a land grab going on in cyberspace. I'll just have to put up bigger walls and get better alarms." The commercial glitz is in sharp contrast to the computer universe first established as the Arpanet -- an experimental network connecting research centers funded by the Pentagon -- which later expanded into the global system known as the Internet. As the network grew, a kind of frontier ethic emerged, characterized by an outspoken congregation of computer experts and scientists, many dedicated to the free flow of information. Until now any company or newcomer who dared break the code of behavior, by offering services for sale, would be "flamed" -- deluged with caustic electronic mail messages questioning the morals, behavior, and even the intelligence of the interloper. But many of these pioneers are finding that their voices and even their electronic communities are being drowned by the "newbies," neophyte users who know nothing of the manners or morals of cyberspace. Some parts of the network are slowing to a crawl because of sheer overload. Many long-time users are finding their favorite discussion groups glutted and their electronic mailboxes filled with junk mail. Last month the American Association for the Advancement of Science sponsored a conference on the legal and ethical aspects of computer network use and abuse at the University of California at Irvine. Some of the researchers who attended said that the emergence of a commercial cyberspace not only threatens the virtual communities of the Internet but will also weaken communities and neighborhoods in the real world as more and more people spend their days and nights in front of computer monitors.  'What Walmart Started' "Cyberspace is going to finish what Walmart started," said Richard Sclove, the executive director of the Loka Institute, a public policy research center in Amherst, Mass. "Interactive shopping via computer networks is going to put more traditional downtowns and more mom-and-pop stores out of business." Still, not everyone is grieving over the passing of the original net culture. Geoff Goodfellow, a computer hacker turned entrepreneur, believes that commercialism is actually a healthy sign. As a Silicon Valley teen-ager in 1974 Mr. Goodfellow dropped out of high school, becoming what he describes as the first street urchin on the data highway, spending his days at SRI International, one of the first ARPAnet sites. More recently he has founded Radiomail Corp., a wireless electronic mail business that routes messages from mobile computers over the Internet. "Some of the net purists would characterize the evolution as the malling of cyberspace," he said. "I think it shows that there's a healthy marketplace out there. That's a good thing, it will be just like wandering around Times Square -- remember, there's money to be made in Times Square." Others believe that the pioneering days are over and that network culture must inevitably grow up and meet the mainstream of society. "The original Internet culture was a real vibrant counterculture," said Carl Malamud, the author of "Exploring the Internet: a Technical Travelogue. "But there is nothing worse than hippies 20 years later." Nevertheless, the fierce race to stake out territory in cyberspace is sure to change the shape of the sleepy electronic commons. Already there is crowding and pushing. Recently, Wired magazine and the Women's Information Resource & Exchange squabbled over each company's network addresses. Wired is wired.com while the Resource & Exchange is wire.net, too similar in the opinion of the magazine's attorneys. Despite the land-rush mentality, some network pioneers believe that the vibrant cyberspace communities are resilient enough to resist the flood of new commercial services. The most significant tradition in the two-decade-old Internet culture is the free sharing of information -- a powerful force that corporations will find difficult to overcome. "For every greedy guy who shows up on the network trying to make a buck, there will be people around with something of equal value that's available for free," said Michael Roberts, a vice president of Educom, a consortium of university computer network users. "That will do a lot to thwart the greed." Graphic   Illustration: (Robert Zimmerman)

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MP3.COM TO ACQUIRE ONLINE EVENT-PLANNING BUSINESS
body: Internet music retailer MP3.com Inc. said yesterday that it would acquire the online event-planning company seeUthere.com for about $150 million. Shares of MP3.com surged $9.755, to $35, in Nasdaq trading. SeeUthere.com provides online ticketing, customized World Wide Web sites, invitation and response management and sales monitoring for events. MP3.com, which is based in San Diego and went public in July, operates a Web site with more than 250,000 songs from about 40,000 artists. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MEDIA 100 EXPANDING ITS VIDEO-EDITING SOFTWARE LINE
body: Media 100 Inc., a maker of software that allows broadcasting over the Internet, agreed to buy Digital Origin Inc. for about $87 million in stock. Each Digital share will be exchanged for about half of a Media 100 share, or $14.44, a 67 percent premium to Digital's closing price Monday. Shares closed unchanged yesterday at $27. Digital, which is based in Mountain View, Calif., makes software for digital video camcorders. The combined company would offer software that lets personal computer users capture, edit and stream video on the World Wide Web using a single application. Media 100 is based in Marlboro, Mass. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
WORLD BUSINESS BRIEFING: AMERICAS;
ARGENTINE INTERNET
body: A new Argentine start-up, i.cero, which plans to go online Jan. 10, said it would offer free Internet access. "Connecting is totally free, for good, and with no restrictions on when or for how long people are connected," Juan Manuel Dapcich, i.cero vice president, said. The company said it sought an audience between 14 and 30 years of age, and would make money on advertising and eventually, on electronic commerce. Horacio de la Fuente, the company's president, said it would operate Brazil, Mexico, Colombia and Ecuador next year. http://www.nytimes.com

title: A Book of One's Own
body: To the Editor: Steven Johnson and Eric Liftin ("The Internet's Gift Is a Wider Bazaar," Op-Ed, Dec. 25) praise online booksellers because they offer shoppers other people's opinions of books. But what these superstores lack is access to the book itself. In a real-world bookstore, readers can thumb through a copy, read any page that catches their interest and form their own opinion of the book. Obviously, independent thinking is anathema to booksellers, who simply want the public to buy what they want to sell.  VIRGINIA M. DONNELLY newyork, Dec. 26, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title: Dow Jones Agrees To Sell a Division
body: Dow Jones & Company, the publisher of The Wall Street Journal,said yesterday that it would sell the business that produces Investment Advisor, Asset Management and Property magazines and the newsletter Realty Stock Review to Wicks Business Information. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but Dow Jones said it expected to record a gain on the sale. The closing is expected next month. Dow Jones said it signed a letter of intent to sell Dow Jones Financial Publishing as part of its program of divesting itself of noncore assets. "We are very excited to bring these high-profile titles into our expanding portfolio of financial publications," said Douglas Manoni, president and chief executive of Wicks Business Information, an affiliate of the Wicks Group of Companies.  "These properties are well positioned to exploit the growing affluence in America." Asset Management is aimed at sophisticated investors and professional investment managers, while Property and Realty Stock Review are intended for real estate investment trusts and commercial real estate markets.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Metro Business;
Internet Company Sued
body: CMGI Inc., an Internet company whose shares have increased more than tenfold this year, has refused to honor an employment contract providing a former president of NBC Television with at least $50 million worth of company stock, a federal lawsuit alleges. In court papers filed in Manhattan yesterday, the plaintiff, Neil Braun, says CMGI hired him in February to help develop a "strategy for becoming the pre-eminent broadcaster of entertainment on the Internet." CMGI, based in Andover, Mass., runs several venture capital funds investing in Internet companies. In addition to an annual salary and a bonus of $300,000, Mr. Braun says he was promised an option to buy 122,000 shares of CMGI stock over four years, as well as 3 percent of the shares in a subsidiary firm, iCAST Corporation, which he was to run. Mr. Braun says he developed a plan to present audio and video entertainment over the Internet but was fired in November because of "friction" with CMGI's chairman, David Wetherell, who is also named in the suit. Mr. Braun says he was told at the time that he would receive only a year's worth of CMGI and iCAST options. A CMGI spokeswoman said the company had no comment. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
IN MY...BRIEFCASE;
MICHAEL C. RULTTGERS
body: THE president and chief executive of EMC, Michael C. Ruettgers, 57, can be thought of as one of the Internet's leading plumbers. EMC, based in Hopkinton, Mass., makes the sophisticated storage systems used by so many big Web sites and by corporations for storing data. It has been a lucrative, if lower-profile, niche of the information technology business for years: EMC and Dell Computer are vying to be the best-performing stock of the 1990's, both up about 70,000 percent for the decade. "I meet C.E.O.'s all the time who say, 'EMC, great stock,' because it's in their personal portfolios," Mr. Ruettgers said. "They are surprised when I tell them they are also customers."   STEVE LOHR http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Michael C. title:
PRIVATE SECTOR;
At Least E-Tailing Works in High Places
body: Even President Clinton, for the first time, shopped online this holiday season. Not surprisingly, he hasn't reported the delivery problems that some constituents have had. From his antique wooden desk in the Oval Office, using a Compaq laptop, the president ordered gifts last Monday from two Web sites, said Nanda Chitre, a White House spokeswoman. He bought horsehair bracelets from a Web site, www.lakotafund.org, that benefits the Oglala Lakota Nation in South Dakota. And he bought a book, "Children from Australia to Zimbabwe," which invites children to experience what it is like to grow up in other countries, from www.world2market.com. The gifts were sent to the White House, Ms. Chitre said, using the special ZIP code that routes mail to the presidential residence. Elsewhere in Washington, Vice President Al Gore (who once claimed to be the father of the Internet) also bought gifts online this holiday season. But a spokesman declined to disclose details, saying that Mr. Gore did not want to look as if he were endorsing specific sites. The first lady, Hillary Rodham Clinton, shopped the old-fashioned way this year, according to a spokeswoman.   JOHN FILES http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Bill Clinton

title:
PRIVATE SECTOR;
Keeping an Eye on a Rival?
body: The competition in Brazil's Internet industry is getting really heated, thanks to Bob Wollheim, president of the Brazilian subsidiary of StarMedia Network, the newyork-based Internet company that focuses on Latin America. He recently rented the side of an apartment building near the Sao Paulo headquarters of its largest rival, Universo Online, for a monster billboard of StarMedia's logo. "Now when those guys stand up from their desks to look out the window, they'll be reminded of the competition," Mr. Wollheim said, chuckling audibly. Caio Tulio Costa, UOL's managing director, was not amused. "It's a waste of their investors' money," he said.   SIMON ROMERO http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
JUNO SHARES FALL ON NEWS OF AN ADDITIONAL STOCK SALE
body: Juno Online Services Inc., whose shares surged more than fourfold this week after the company offered free Internet access, said yesterday that it would sell additional shares, sending its stock down nearly 25 percent. Juno fell $15.0625, to $46.1875. Juno, based in newyork, said on Monday that it was shifting its strategy to offering free access from building a fee-based subscriber service. The company, which is controlled by the hedge fund manager David Shaw, wants to build revenue through increased online advertising. Juno has 500,000 paying subscribers and 2.4 million users who receive its free email service. It did not say how much stock it intended to sell.   http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NEW XEROX BUSINESS GROUP WILL FOCUS ON THE INTERNET
body: The Xerox Corporation said yesterday that it had formed an Internet business group to enhance its Web-based business activities and Internet-related technologies. The group will add more interactive communications to Xerox's Web site. Michael Miron was named president of the new organization. Mr. Miron previously served as senior vice president for corporate business strategy and development. Xerox, based in Stamford, Conn., makes copiers, printing systems and software. It had revenue of $13.79 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Starbucks to Open 400 More Coffee Shops
body: Starbucks Corporation said today that it planned to spend about $300 million in its current fiscal year to open at least 400 coffee shops. Starbucks also spent $28.3 million to invest in two Internet ventures, Talk City Inc., which runs chat rooms, and Living.com Inc., which sells furniture and other products, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Howard Schultz, the chief executive, has been investing in online companies that sell household goods to widen Starbucks' visibility on the Internet market. At the same time, Starbucks has continued to expand its main coffee-shop franchise while entering supermarkets and other outlets with packaged and bottled coffee and ice cream. Starbucks, based in Seattle, opened 460 stores in its most recent fiscal year, which ended on Oct. 3. It did not specify in the filing where it would open the new stores. It operates more than 2,600 coffee shops worldwide and sells whole-bean coffees in supermarkets and online. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INCOMING;
Last-Minute Log-On
body: To the Editor: Last year was so great I decided to do all of my holiday shopping online this year. Unfortunately, all I have experienced this year is shipping delays, items back ordered, items that arrive and look nothing like their picture, customer service apathy, and just utter, utter frustration.  HEATHER ARNET newyork, Dec. 22, 1999  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INCOMING;
Working Off the Clock
body: To the Editor: I hope that those companies that remind their workers not to use the company computer for personal business also post signs at their exits reminding employees not to think about work once they leave the office ("The Web: New Ticket to a Pink Slip," Dec. 16). I'll be the first to admit that I write personal emails, shop and look for information on hobbies while I'm at work. I frequently think about the best way to handle work issues while I swim after I leave the office. Employers need to be realistic about human nature, and keep their focus on whether employees are getting the job done, not how they go about doing it.  ANDY SLOAN Goldens Bridge, N.Y., Dec. 16 http://www.nytimes.com

title: Editors' Note
body: A front-page article on Dec. 11 about the rise in Internet-related patents referred to one recently granted to LinkShare, a newyork company. The article said the patent gave LinkShare the right to block other Web sites from using an arrangement in which they earn commissions from purchases by users they refer to online stores. The article described the LinkShare patent as a technique for doing business, a claim with potentially broad implications, rather than a narrow technological innovation. The article should have attributed the description of the patent's breadth to LinkShare. No legal claims have yet arisen, and LinkShare's competitors say they feel the patent has a more limited scope. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Taxing Internet Sales
body: To the Editor: Re "Retailers and Governors Attack Proposal to Make the Internet a Tax-Free Zone" (Business Day, Dec. 16): For several years, many states have been transferring the tax burden from upper- to lower-income citizens by substituting increases in retail sales taxes for property, business and income taxes. Now that the Internet offers the public an escape from this pernicious device, there is pressure to force e-merchants to tax customers on behalf of the states. If the Internet remains happily tax-free, perhaps brick-and-mortar retailers around the country will pressure their legislators to return to more equitable means of taxation.  ART HILGART Kalamazoo, Mich., Dec. 16, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

body: Federal agents today arrested an 18-year-old man who they say used the Internet to send a threat that led officials to close Columbine High School in Littleton, Colo., on Thursday and today. title: Help E-Commerce Grow
body: To the Editor: A Nov. 30 letter about the policies of the World Trade Organization and positions taken by Microsoft stated that the W.T.O. seeks to "make Internet commerce tax-free." In fact, the W.T.O. has only a moratorium on tariffs for transmissions over the Internet. But it has taken no position on taxes, like sales or value-added taxes, relating to online purchases. Microsoft is one of many companies supporting this policy and urging extension of the tariff moratorium, because we believe that this results in lower prices for consumers, helps e-commerce grow and avoids discrimination against suppliers in international trade. It's important to note that the W.T.O.'s position does not alter individual countries' internal tax structures and certainly does not make Internet commerce "tax free."  BRAD SMITH General Counsel, Worldwide Sales and Support, Microsoft Redmond, Wash., Dec. 6, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

The problem is, the EWonders Web site misspelled "grammar" -- writing it "grammer." EWonders fixed the mistake, after a reporter pointed it out. title:

Frontiers in Marketing I: Not Just a Pretty Face
body: The assignment: Find a marketing gimmick that can make a business-to-business Internet start-up stand out from all the noise. Why not go for the old reliable celebrity endorsement, and borrow a little sex appeal from a famous entertainer? Apparently, that is how RuPaul, of all people, happened to land in Silicon Valley, of all places, last Tuesday: as celebrity endorser for WebEx, a San Jose, Calif., company that provides meeting services over the Web. The idea has a certain logic. There being no other towering transvestite an average person may be able to name without prompting, it is fair to say RuPaul knows a thing or two about standing out. And dot-com start-ups have been successful with off-the-wall ad ideas before. But where Outpost.com and others have tried bizarre non sequiturs like imitation gerbils shot from a cannon, Web-Ex at least squeezes a pun from RuPaul's presence: "Meetings used to be a drag." WebEx said it would spend most of its $25 million in new venture capital on the ad campaign. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Connected Parents
body: To the Editor: The article "Webcams Focus on Daycare" (Dec. 2), explains how parents can watch their children for 15 minutes at a time for up to six times per day. If these parents can afford to spend 90 minutes of their working days watching their children on a Web site, wouldn't the time be better spent together as a family?Parents would feel closer and more connected to their children and less guilty about leaving them by utilizing their time more appropriately. Rather than creating more guilt-free ways to detach themselves from the lives of their children, parents should be seeking ways to connect with their children more intimately.  Child care centers should be advocating more on-site parental involvement. It would appear that these parents have the time.  LAURA ENSLER Brooklyn http://www.nytimes.com

title: Grace in Cyberspace
body: To the Editor: Re "E-Etiquette" (Op-Ed, Dec. 6): One would think that Letitia Baldrige had just discovered computers and email. Not only has email been around for more than 20 years, but online manners (known by most users as Netiquette), like other social norms, have been developing and debated since the early days of the Internet. Improved etiquette is probably lacking more in today's political discourse than on the Internet. In the time it takes to read Ms. Baldrige's rules, Internet users will have written, read, ignored and discarded hundreds of messages from friends, family members and strangers with appropriate social grace.  DANIEL FARKAS Pleasantville, N.Y., Dec. 6, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:

Ticker-Tape Cachet
body: Often stuffed into a pocket with a fleeting glance, that business card might bear a closer look. Internet companies like Xceed (XCED) and Fashionmall.com (FASH) have begun adding stock ticker symbols to their cards, eliminating the need to flip through Dun & Bradstreet. "I definitely get some interesting comments because of it," said Nancy Fermaglich, 29, an account executive at Fashionmall.com. "At my age and the crowd I'm around, it's very impressive to work for a public company, especially a dot-com one." Scott Mednick, a former graphic designer who is now the chairman and chief strategic officer of Xceed, came up with the idea when he was chairman of Think New Ideas (THNK), a marketing company. "The ticker symbol on the card reminds people that this company is one that's already traded as opposed to one where you're betting on the future," he said. But wearing your symbol on your sleeve can also advertise a company's clever credo. The Internet service provider Internet America, for one, proudly displays its GEEK symbol on its cards. Lesson for discerning night crawlers: read the fine print.   LARRY SMITH http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: (Lisa Haney)

title: Lure of Internet Success
body: To the Editor: M.B.A. candidates are dropping out of business schools and flocking to Internet companies not just to follow the money (news article, Nov. 28). They are looking to carve a niche in an industry they know is changing business around the world. On the Web, there are few barriers to entry. Almost every dot-com company is working hard to get a first-mover advantage because the only sustainable advantage will be name recognition and a place among well-used "bookmarks." But once the Internet bloom falls off the rose, the success of Internet companies will depend on satisfying the customer, increasing the company's value, running effective operations and managing people well: things you learn in business school.  FREDERICK W. WINTER Pittsburgh, Nov. 30, 1999  The writer is the dean of the Katz Graduate School of Business, University of Pittsburgh. http://www.nytimes.com

title:

body: A leading privacy advocacy group filed a lawsuit today that seeks to force the National Security Agency to release its records on potential government surveillance of the Internet communications of American citizens. The lawsuit, filed in federal district court here by the Electronic Privacy Information Center, seeks the public disclosure of internal documents discussing the legality of the agency's intelligence activities. The filing was prompted by various news reports in the last year that indicated that the agency was coordinating a global surveillance system known as Echelon. The current issue of The newyorker magazine reports that it took the agency only 11 months to fill what was expected to be three years' worth of planned storage capacity for intercepted Internet traffic. In response to the lawsuit, the agency issued a statement saying that it "operates in strict accordance with U.S. laws and regulations." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Even the Strong Succumb
body: To the Editor: In "Editor Explores Unintended, and Negative, Side of Technology" (Nov. 25), Stephen L. Talbott explains how considering the computer one's "enemy" provides a sense of freedom. Mr. Talbott has a love-hate relationship with technology because he is dependent on it. One does not need to rebel against something to forgo it. I have chosen from the beginning not to spend much time online, to play computer games or to use the computer for daily activities. It has been easy as so much technology is simply reinventing the wheel. Though technology pervades our lives, when to use it can be an active choice. There are limits, however. Like Mr. Talbott, I wrote the draft of this letter longhand. But I felt obligated to send it via email.  SHEILA FEIT Syosset, N.Y. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DELL COMPUTER TO SELLMACHINE FOR BASIC WEB ACCESS
body: The Dell Computer Corporation, the leading direct seller of personal computers, introduced the Webpc yesterday, a slimmed-down machine intended to let novice PC users get online quickly. The Webpc is Dell's first attempt to attract inexperienced computer buyers. The new device, which comes in five colors and resembles a coffee maker, costs less than $1,000. That includes a 433-megahertz Celeron processor from Intel, a 15-inch color monitor, a CD-ROM drive, a printer and one year of Internet access through Dellnet, the company's service. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Company Dismisses 23 Over email
body: The newyork Times Company dismissed 23 employees at an administrative center in Norfolk, Va., yesterday for violating the company's email policy, a company spokeswoman said. The workers -- men and women in a variety of departments and functions -- were among 200 employees at a center that processes invoices, pay and benefits for the company's various divisions. An unspecified number of other employees received disciplinary warning letters over the incident, which involved internally circulated email, the company said. The company would not elaborate on the basis for the dismissal except to say that the employees had violated a policy specifying that "computer communications must be consistent with conventional standards of ethical and proper conduct, behavior and manners and are not to be used to create, forward or display any offensive or disruptive messages, including photographs, graphics and audio materials." The company had dismissed "a person here or there" over email violations in the past, but never a group of such size, said Nancy Nielsen, the company spokeswoman. http://www.nytimes.com

body: CULVER HOLDINGS P.L.C., Cardiff, Wales, said its subsidiary, WorldTravel Direct, had acquired the travel company Powerflyer.com Inc., San Jose, Calif., to expand its Internet-based travel business.  PAPA JOHN'S INTERNATIONAL INC., Louisville, the fourth-largest unitedstates pizza chain, bought Perfect Pizza Holdings Ltd. of Britain for about $33 million as part of its international expansion plans. QWEST COMMUNICATIONS INTERNATIONAL INC., Denver, a long-distance phone company that operates a fiber optic network, won a five-year contract to be host of Passport New Media's network of children's Web sites. title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ALTAVISTA IS BUYING RAGING BULL, FINANCIAL WEB SITE
body: The AltaVista Company, an Internet search service that is controlled by CMGI Inc., will buy the closely held financial Web site Raging Bull, adding 1.7 million users to AltaVista and making it the ninth most visited Web site. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. Raging Bull, based in Andover, Mass., has received financing from CMGI, a venture capital company. CMGI bought a majority stake in AltaVista, based in Palo Alto, Calif., in August and plans to sell shares in the company to the public next year. Shares of CMGI, also based in Andover, rose $14.875 each, to $161.25, in Nasdaq trading. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING: DIARY -- FUNDS WATCH;
Baron's Internet Play
body: Baron Capital of newyork, which currently offers a trim lineup of just three mutual funds, apparently is bullish enough on the growth prospects for the Web to become the latest money management firm to start an Internet fund. In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company said it expected the fund to begin operations on Feb. 29, 2000. It said the fund would invest both in emerging Internet companies and in more mature "bricks and mortar" businesses that it expects to benefit from the Web. The fund, called Baron iOpportunity, will be managed by a team of advisers, but the filing did not disclose their names. Ron Baron, chief executive, is known for taking substantial positions in small and midcap companies and holding on to them for years; as a result, his funds' turnover is usually light. How will such a style mesh with the volatile world of the Web, where today's hot stock can easily be tomorrow's road kill? "We're not traders," said Morty Schaja, chief operating officer at Baron. "If we don't see long-term competitive advantages we won't invest."   RICHARD TEITELBAUM http://www.nytimes.com

WORLD BUSINESS BRIEFING: AMERICAS;
INTERNET ACCESS EXPANDED
body: In a move that advances the plans of companies like the Microsoft Corporation and Organizacaoes Globo, Brazil's government will allow pay-television providers to provide Internet access. The authorization is likely to shake up Brazil's fast-growing Internet industry. Microsoft was one of the first foreign companies to make a commitment in Brazil's high-speed Internet market by investing $126 million in a subsidiary of Globo. Simon Romero http://www.nytimes.com

title: An Excite@Home Deal With Compaq
body: Excite@Home said today that consumers would be able to sign up for its @Home high-speed Internet service through the Compaq Computer Corporation, a maker of personal computers. By visiting the Web site of Compaq, Excite@Home said, consumers could sign up for @Home and arrange for installation. Excite@Home said that consumers could also buy Compaq Presario computers with network cards for connection to its Internet service, which runs on TV cables. Excite@Home, based in Redwood City, and Compaq, based in Houston, agreed last November to develop systems for Compaq customers. Besides teaming with cable TV operators to offer Internet access, Excite@Home operates the Excite.com Internet portal and search engine. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Privacy Concerns
body: To the Editor: I read with great interest the article on electronic privacy. Netizens must be ever vigilant in ensuring that overreaching governments do not hamper the development of private solutions to privacy issues. For instance, a proposal by the National Governors' Association to tax Internet sales would preclude the kind of anonymous digital cash systems discussed in "A Cloak for Shoppers' Web Dollars" (Nov. 11). Consumers would be required to verify their locations for tax-collecting government agents each time they make a purchase, which would make anonymous digital cash incompatible with online shopping. The National Governors' Association proposal would invade the authority of Congress over interstate commerce and lay the framework for a dangerous tracking and taxing system that could rapidly expand into both a national sales tax and national database of consumer purchases, both online and off. Decisions about privacy should be left to consumers, not tax-happy statehouses and other big-government lobbyists.  JAMES PLUMMER Washington, Nov. 12, 1999  The writer is a policy analyst for Consumer Alert, a nonprofit group. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Superhighway Encounters
body: To the Editor: Although the article on broadband Internet access mentioned that some people find the local phone company difficult to deal with in getting a D.S.L. Internet connection, that was an understatement. I had an I.S.D.N. line that I wanted converted to a D.S.L. line. Bell Atlantic said the switch would take three weeks. Instead it took more than two months during which time I could neither receive nor send fax messages on my other phone line. My Internet service was disrupted for weeks, then ended up being completely unavailable. I spent at least 100 hours on the phone. I had to stay at home on three occasions for service people. The line was installed only after I had spent close to two hours on the phone while a Bell Atlantic worker in Albany talked to engineers in newyork City. While I held on, they were able to get the line running. My advice is to give great thought to choosing a high-speed Internet service.  MARCO S. SONNENSCHEIN newyork, Nov. 15, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title: America Online Deal With Intuit
body: America Online Inc., the top Internet service provider, and Intuit Inc., the maker of the popular Quicken financial software, said yesterday that they would provide an online bill-paying service to AOL's more than 19 million subscribers. Terms of the five-year agreement were not disclosed. Intuit will be the exclusive provider of bill tracking and payment services for America Online's flagship service and the AOL.com World Wide Web site, starting early next year. America Online is offering the service as the number of households using the Internet to pay bills is expected to increase tenfold to 18 million by 2003. About 55 percent of consumers who use the Internet said they would be interested in paying bills online, according to a study from Roper Starch Worldwide and America Online. Intuit and America Online will let utilities, credit card companies and other billing companies present bills online to their customers using encryption technology. The service will also be available to users of America Online's CompuServe service. America Online has not determined yet whether a fee will be charged. Intuit is the top maker of personal-finance software. http://www.nytimes.com

title: News Corp. Weighs Investing in Health Site
body: The News Corporation is in talks to invest cash and other assets in the Healtheon/WebMD Corporation for a large minority stake in the Internet health-information company, its chairman and chief executive, Rupert Murdoch, said yesterday. Mr. Murdoch, who did not elaborate on how much the News Corporation would spend, said an investment would include "some cash and some advertising." Last month, the companies said they were in talks about a series of transactions aimed at developing global Internet and branding services. Negotiations are going "very well," Mr. Murdoch said in newyork after the first annual shareholder meeting of Fox Entertainment Group, the News Corporation's unitedstates media and entertainment affiliate. Fox will make several "significant" announcements about its Internet business in the "next few months," Mr. Murdoch said without elaborating. The News Corporation wants to strengthen its existing Fox Internet sites, which include FoxNews.com and FoxSports.com. Early next year, it will introduce a revamped version of its Fox.com site. Shares of Healtheon/WebMD rose $2.1875, to $40.75. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Nike to Sell Custom-Design Shoes on Web
body: Nike Inc., the world's largest athletic shoemaker, said this week that it would sell custom-designed men's and women's shoes to American customers over the Internet. Consumers can place orders for customized Air Turbulence running shoes and Air Famished cross-training shoes at the Web site Nike.com under the program that started today, Nike said. The program allows customers to select colors and add an eight-character identification, like a name or a number, to their shoes. They can view models of the shoes before making a final purchase, the company said. The shoes will sell at regular retail price plus a $10 custom-design fee and shipping costs, Nike said. Nike will take a maximum of 400 orders a day. Nike will eventually use custom-design information to help design its regular shoe offerings, Mary Kate Buckley, vice president of Nike.com, said. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Greenfield Opening An Internet Unit
body: The Greenfield Consulting Group in Westport, Conn., is starting Digital Idea, an Internet research consulting company. Peter Mackey, 43, managing director at Greenfield, will be president at Digital Idea, joining Jim Hood, 47, executive vice president, who came to Digital Idea from the Lord Group in newyork, a joint venture of Dentsu and Young & Rubicam Inc., where he had been chief executive. Other executives at Digital Idea include Virginia Gray, 44, managing director for branding and marketing at Digital Idea, who had been vice president for marketing and public relations at Cox Communications in Atlanta, and Edward Martin, 33, managing director for consumer insights, who had been vice president for global insights and information and manager for customer experience at the Citibank unit of Citigroup in newyork.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DIGITAL INSIGHT AGREES TO PURCHASE NFRONT
body: The Digital Insight Corporation agreed yesterday to acquire NFront Inc., another provider of Internet banking software to community banks, for about $439 million in stock. Digital Insight will swap 0.579 share for each share of NFront. Shares of Digital Insight, of Calabasas, Calif., tumbled $9.75 each, to $40.375, in Nasdaq trading, where shares of NFront rose $2.5625, to $21.3125. Digital Insight, which reported revenue of $11.8 million for the quarter that ended on Sept. 30, said that after the merger it would have about 645 financial institutions as clients. NFront, based in Atlanta, reported revenue of about $5 million for the fiscal year that ended on June 30. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
GOTO.COM, INTERNET SEARCH SERVICE, BUYING CADABRA
body: GoTo.com Inc., an Internet search service, said yesterday that it would acquire Cadabra Inc., which provides comparison-shopping services, for $250 million in cash and stock to expand its electronic-commerce offerings. GoTo.com will pay $8 million in cash and $242 million in stock for closely held Cadabra. GoTo.com offers to help guide Internet users to products, prices and other features so it can match up merchants and advertisers with its Web site visitors. The company, based in Pasadena, Calif., offers an Internet search service where merchants pay for listings. Cadabra is based in San Mateo, Calif. GoTo.com's shares fell $2.625, to $105.625. http://www.nytimes.com

title: InfoSpace.com Acquisition
body: A provider of maps and directories to Web sites, InfoSpace.com Inc., agreed today to buy closely held eComLive.com Inc. for about $33.5 million in stock to add real-time services like video conferences. InfoSpace.com will exchange 355,618 shares of its common shares for all of eComLive.com's shares and options. EComLive.com, based in Fremont, Calif., offers Internet-based services including multimedia broadcasting. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Internet Companies Agree to Merger
body: Two Internet companies that are minority owned by the Interpublic Group of Companies have agreed to a deal. Nicholson NY, an electronic business development company with clients like Motorola, the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Reader's Digest Association, agreed to be acquired by Icon Medialab International in Stockholm, an Internet consulting company, for Icon shares valued at about $68.5 million and a possible additional payment if certain sales and profitability goals are met next year. Nicholson NY, with almost 100 employees and projected net revenue in 1999 of $10.5 million, will become the newyork office of Icon Medialab under the name Icon Nicholson. The office will remain under the leadership of Tom Nicholson, 52, chief executive, and Chad Gallant, 37, managing director; Mr. Nicholson will also become chief creative officer for Icon Medialab. Trade publications have reported that Interpublic may be considering combining its various Internet agencies and holdings into a publicly traded unit. Interpublic owns 20 percent of Icon Medialab and 25 percent of Nicholson NY.    http://www.nytimes.com

title:
PRIVATE SECTOR;
Bidding for the Auctioneer Is Right Up Their Alley
body: Haven't seen enough of Meg Whitman, the high-profile chief executive of on-line auctioneer eBay? If profiles in Business Week, Glamour and Vanity Fair left you begging for more, maybe you should consider bowling. Earlier this month, Butterfield & Butterfield, the old-time San Francisco auction house that was recently acquired by eBay, auctioned off a bowling date with Ms. Whitman and two eBay employees. Twenty-nine bids were submitted over 10 days to raise money for the San Francisco chapter of the American Red Cross. The first bid was a mere $75, but, like everything related to the Internet, the price soared, to $11,600. The lucky bidder? A group from Yahoo's auc tion team paid for the fun of dropping pins and what the auction's description called a "less than swanky meal" with the eBay group. With their combined billions, they might as well just buy the alley.   LAURA M. HOLSON http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Meg Whitman

title:
PRIVATE SECTOR;
Online, or Else
body: The latest advice on cyber-etiquette: unplug your old office equipment if you're dealing with people who make their living from the Web. Brewster Kahle, chief executive of Alexa Internet, which he recently sold to Amazon.com for nearly $300 million, recently told the newyork Infotech Forum that he communicates with his lawyers and accountants over the Internet, thank you. "If they fax us anything," he warned, "we look for a new one." He's not kidding. email addiction is a key test for lawyers or accountants wanting his business. "Everyone says they have email, but many do not live on it," Mr. Kahle said, in an exchange of emails. "We only want to deal with those that cannot live without an email fix no matter where they are or what they are doing." http://www.nytimes.com

title:

body: Trim your tree with a T-Rex. The Peabody Museum shop has Christmas ornaments adorned with the heavies of the dinosaur age, with images taken from the 110-foot-long mural by Rudolph F. Zallinger that was painted in the museum's Great Hall in the 1940's. Eeach glass bulb is hand-painted from the inside out with tiny brushes inserted through the opening at the top. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Editor JoiningTimes
body: William Norwich has joined The newyork Times Magazine as editor of a new supplement, "Style and Entertaining," which will make its debut Nov. 5, 2000. He will also edit Entertaining features for the weekly magazine beginning Feb. 13. Mr. Norwich, who has contributed to Fashions of The Times, was editor at large at Vogue magazine and an editor at Conde Nast House & Garden. He wrote an around-the-town column for The Daily News in newyork until 1991, then wrote a column for The newyork Post until 1993. His Style Diary, a report on fashion, interior design and manners, appears weekly in The newyork Observer. His novel, "Learning to Drive," was published by Grove/Atlantic in 1996. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ACCRUE TO ACQUIRE NEOVISTA FOR $140 MILLION
body: Accrue Software Inc., a maker of Internet analysis software, agreed yesterday to buy the closely held NeoVista Software Inc. for about $140.3 million in stock to move into electronic direct marketing. Accrue will pay 2.4 million shares of its common stock. The purchase will push Accrue, which is based in Fremont, Calif., into the fast-growing market for electronic direct marketing. Accrue's Insight software gathers information from data moving over the Internet and analyzes the activities of Web site visitors to see how effectively a site holds a customer's attention. Accrue's shares rose $2.3125 yesterday, to $58.4375. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ZIFF-DAVIS TO SELL UNIT TO WASSERSTEIN FOR $172 MILLION
body: Ziff-Davis Inc., the publisher of computer magazines, agreed yesterday to sell its ZD Education unit, a provider of Internet training, to the investment bank Wasserstein Perella Group Inc. for $172 million in cash. Ziff-Davis, which publishes PC Week, has been shedding businesses to improve its stock price. Wasserstein plans to use ZD Education to offer more online services to corporate customers that want to use the Internet to sell products. Ziff-Davis, which is majority owned by the Softbank Corporation of Japan, said it was not selling SmartPlanet.com, a World Wide Web site that offers courses on how to set up Internet sites. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Calendars Made for Sharing, For the Online and Handheld Set
body: The Internet calendar craze has moved to handheld devices. WeSync.com not only lets you create an online calendar but lets you share it with family and friends by synching it to a Palm Pilot or any other device running the Palm Operating System. Companies have been using shared online calendars for several years, but the concept is just now moving to consumers. "We think that it will be valuable to have family members share data about their activities," said Pete Grillo, president of WeSync.com. "The service takes on the aspect of an electronic bulletin board because each person who has permission can update the shared calendar." The WeSync software also lets you view multiple calendars on a Palm device. You could create a business calendar, one for the family and one for golfing buddies, listing tee times. The software, available on the company's Web site (www.wesync.com), is free, but it runs advertisements on your PC during synchronization. No ads are loaded on the handheld device. "We don't want to do anything to adversely affect the Palm user's experience," Mr. Grillo said.   STEPHEN C. MILLER http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
KnightRidder.com Selects an Agency
body: KnightRidder.com, the new Internet business unit of Knight Ridder in San Jose, Calif., has awarded the first account for Real Cities, a network of regional Web sites, to the Salt Lake City and San Francisco offices of Euro RSCG/DSW, part of the Euro RSCG Worldwide unit of Havas Advertising. Billings were estimated at $20 million. The decision came after a three-month review that had been narrowed to Euro RSCG/DSW and three agencies in San Francisco. The Web sites of Real Cities, which include Bayarea.com, Twincities.com, DFW.com, and Miami.com will be featured in local print ads that begin today; television commercials are to start early next year.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
WORLD BUSINESS BRIEFING: AMERICAS;
AMERICA ONLINE IN BRAZIL
body: Moving to tap Brazil's fast-growing Internet market, America Online began its first Portuguese-language service in Brazil, Latin America's largest economy. America Online will lend its brand name and technology to the venture, while its partner in Latin America, the Cisneros Group of Venezuela, will inject $100 million of investment. America Online plans Spanish-language services in Argentina and Mexico. Simon Romero http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ARIBA IS BUYING AUCTION SOFTWARE MAKER
body: Ariba Inc., the largest maker of Internet procurement software, agreed yesterday to buy the closely held TradingDynamics Inc. for $400 million in stock, adding E-commerce products and services to help create Internet exchanges. Internet exchanges bring together groups of buyers and sellers online for greater buying power. TradingDynamics makes software that lets customers create any kind of auction, reverse auction or bid-ask exchange. TradingDynamics was founded in 1998 and now has more than 50 employees. Ariba stock surged $13.375 a share to close at a record $210.125 in Nasdaq trading. Ariba announced the acquisition after the close of regular trading. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
INTERNET CONCERN AGREES TO BUY NET EFFECT SYSTEMS
body: Ask Jeeves Inc., an Internet search provider, agreed yesterday to buy the closely held Net Effect Systems Inc. for $288.1 million in stock, adding a live-help service for searching the World Wide Web. Ask Jeeves will exchange 1.835 million shares for Net Effect, based in North Hollywood, Calif. Net Effect investors will own 5.5 percent of Ask Jeeves. Ask Jeeves's service allows users to find information on the Web by phrasing queries in conversational English. It said the acquisition of Net Effect would enable it to link customers to live experts who can answer questions either by email or telephone. Shares of Ask Jeeves, based in Emeryville, Calif., rose $8.75 each, to $167.75, after soaring to $184.375 earlier in the day. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
WORLD BUSINESS BRIEFING: ASIA;
HONGKONG INTERNET VENTURE
body: One of hongkong's four fixed-line telecommunications operators, Hutchison Whampoa Ltd., and Global Crossing Ltd., a Nasdaq-listed Internet service provider, said they would form a $1.2 billion venture to offer Internet-related services in hongkong. The new 50-50 venture, to be called Hutchison Global Crossing, will provide links to Global Crossing's global network. Global Crossing will provide Hutchison $400 million of convertible preferred shares, international telecommunications capacity rights on its global optical fiber network and other data-related cable capacity that it values at $350 million. It will also invest $50 million cash. http://www.nytimes.com

title: U.S. Court Blocks Disney Use of 'Go' Logo
body: A Federal District Court has temporarily blocked the Disney Corporation's use of its Go.com logo, a company with a similar logo, GoTo.com, said today. Earlier this month, Disney said it expected to complete acquisition of the Internet search service Infoseek on Wednesday, when its Buena Vista Internet Group and Infoseek will be combined to form the Go.com Internet portal. The logo for GoTo.com, which links consumers to Internet advertisers, is a green circle on a yellow background with the words "Go" and "To" printed in the circle. The Go Network's Web page, www .go.com, features a green circle with a yellow background and "Go" printed inside the circle. Disney vowed to appeal the decision, which prohibits the logo's use pending a full trial. "Since we are confident that our logo does not impinge on that of any other," said a Disney spokesman, John Dreyer, "we are very disappointed in the ruling." Mr. Dreyer said the ruling did not affect the use of the name Go. Infoseek said the injunction would take effect on Monday. GoTo.com has been using its logo since December 1997. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Hitler Online Sale Is Sparking Protest
body: The Internet auction of silver pieces believed to have been owned by Hitler is prompting protest, the local branch of the Anti-Defamation League says. Lobster forks, ice cream spoons and a cigarette box are among dozens of items being sold by a Georgia family that acquired them through a member who was a soldier in World War II. "We think it would be perverse if an individual bought a fork or a setting and invited people over so they can show them their Hitler plates or cigarette box," said Jay Kaiman, the league's Southeast director. Great Gatsby's, an Atlanta auction house, is conducting the auction, which continues until Thursday. The auction house's manager, Maxine Hyland, said there had been "very few complaints" about the Hitler items. They are among hundreds of items available in Great Gatsby's first online auction. Other items include four original works by Pablo Picasso and the original 16-millimeter master print of the Beatles movie "Let It Be." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING: DIARY;
Muni Offering on Web Pays Off
body: Pittsburgh officials said last week that they had received twice as many bidders as expected for the city's sale of $55 million of general obligation bonds, offered directly to investors online. The sale was conducted over MuniAuction, a Web site that allows underwriting firms to bid for bonds. While selling munis over the Internet is not unique, Pittsburgh's sale was the first to allow mutual funds, insurers and other institutional investors to bid against the securities firms for bonds. Generally, underwriters bid for bonds and then sell them to institutions at a markup. "Clearly, this is the way the muni market is going," said Ellen McLean, Pittsburgh's finance and budget director. http://www.nytimes.com

title: GTE to Waive Some Fees on Net Service
body: For the remainder of 1999, GTE will waive installation fees for high-speed Internet service for its customers in 17 states. The telephone company said this week that it expected the move would draw customers to its digital subscriber line service. The fees vary widely, with some as high as $340, GTE said. Business and residential customers who order the service usually pay installation fees to their local phone company and Internet service provider. GTE said its local phone-service customers who order the service from one of 248 partner Internet service providers would not be charged for installation. In addition, the company said, its phone customers who order through a subsidiary Internet service provider, GTE.net, will not be charged a one-time $50 Internet access fee. GTE charges $49.95 or more a month to provide high-speed Internet service. Roughly 60 percent of GTE's local phone customers live or work where the service is available. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DYNAMICWEB TO ACQUIREEB2B FOR 25 MILLION SHARES
body: DynamicWeb Enterprises Inc., which helps companies do business over the Internet, agreed to buy the closely held eB2B Commerce Inc. for 25 million shares, worth $118.8 million at Thursday's closing price, and a $15 million investment from eB2B. EB2B runs commerce networks between manufacturers and retailers. DynamicWeb gains eB2B's business-to-business technology, while eB2B gets DynamicWeb's customer base. The new company, to be called eB2B Commerce Inc., will have 30 million shares outstanding. EB2B's president and chief executive, Peter J. Fiorillo, will retain those roles. DynamicWeb's president and chief executive, Steve Vanechanos, will become chief technology officer. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Amazon to Offer Its Own Credit Card
body: Amazon.com Inc. will introduce its own credit card early next year, which could bring the money-losing Internet merchant as much as $150 million in fees in the next five years. Amazon, based in Seattle, said today that it would offer the cobranded card with NextCard Inc., which specializes in issuing credit cards on the Internet. NextCard shares rose sharply on the news, climbing $9.375, to $41, in Nasdaq trading, where Amazon was up $1.1875, to $72. This was the second big announcement to come from Amazon this week. On Tuesday, Amazon.com announced it would begin selling home improvement goods, computer software and a wider array of video games on its Web site. Amazon already offers books, music, videos, toys, electronics and greeting cards, as well as hosting auctions. While Amazon is the biggest merchant on the Internet today, it has yet to make a profit. Analysts think that Amazon may form other alliances like the NextCard deal to offset some of the losses from its other businesses. Amazon.com's 13 million customers will be able to get online approval for cards, account alerts and electronic statements and bill payment. The cobranded card will also include customized e-commerce services. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Batch Grocery Orders Online
body: To the Editor: I have been shopping with Netgrocer for nearly three years, with extremely good results ("Buying Groceries Online? Forget About Lamb Shanks," Online Shopper, Nov. 4). The article gave the impression that the shipping cost is more linear than it is. Ms. Slatella's $26 order cost $5.99 to ship in that zone. On the other hand, an order up to $99.99 would have cost only $1 more, and for another two bucks, one could have paid for shipping an order up to $199.99. The trick is to batch the orders to save on shipping.  CHERYL SHONBORN Rumson, N.J., Nov. 4, 1999  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
BEA SYSTEMS TO BUY THEORY CENTER FOR $100 MILLION
body: BEA Systems Inc., the largest developer of so-called middleware software, agreed yesterday to buy the closely held Theory Center of Boston for $100 million in stock and cash. It will absorb Theory Center's 42 employees. BEA Systems, which is based in San Jose, Calif., said the acquisition would help it create e-commerce software to help its customers conduct business over the Internet. It said the move complemented its acquisition last year of the closely held Web Logic Inc. BEA Systems shares rose $4.875, to $66.25. The news was announced after the close of unitedstates markets. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Snippets to Remember: The Fall of the Wall
body: Here's something the Internet didn't have a role in: the fall of the Berlin Wall. But making up for lost time, the Web has an abundance of sites that pay homage to the event, which occurred 10 years ago this week. The National Archives and Records Administration has a small exhibit on its Web site (www.nara.gov/exhall/originals /kennedy.html) with a reproduction of a handwritten cue card from President John F. Kennedy's "Ich bin ein Berliner" speech near the wall on June 26, 1963, and a typewritten card from President Reagan's 1987 address in which he implored Mikhail Gorbachev to "tear down this wall." A more personal look at the wall can be found at Chris De Witt's Berlin Wall page (www.appropriatesoftware.com/BerlinWall /welcome.html), which includes essays and photographs by Mr. De Witt, a Briton. And The Berliner Morgenpost has the sad tale of Chris Gueffroy at (www.go-on.de/bm /international/inhalt/0499/wallvictim.html), the wall's last victim, who was shot to death less than a year before the wall came down.   HENRY FOUNTAIN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
WORLD BUSINESS BRIEFING: EUROPE;
BRITISH TELECOM CUTS RATES
body: Moving closer to offering flat-rate pricing for Internet calls, British Telecommunications P.L.C. said it would again cut the cost of Internet calls. The cuts will let Internet-access providers charge its clients a flat rate for access to the Internet by January. Industry experts say that Internet use in Britain and throughout Europe has been stifled because most local phone calls are metered by the minute. Andrew Ross Sorkin http://www.nytimes.com

title:

PRODIGY TO BUY RIVAL FLASHNET COMMUNICATIONS
body: The Prodigy Communications Corporation, an Internet-service provider, agreed yesterday to buy the rival FlashNet Communications for about $124 million in stock. Prodigy, based in White Plains, will exchange 0.35 share for each FlashNet share outstanding, or $8.66, based on Prodigy's price on Friday. The offer is 13 percent less than FlashNet's closing price on Friday. The purchase is Prodigy's third since it first sold shares to the public in February. Its subscriber base will expand to more than 1.5 million with the addition of the Fort Worth-based FlashNet's 244,000 customers. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Metro Business;
A Conduit to Phones, TV and the Internet
body: An unusual telecommunications company began operating yesterday in Hartford, offering a conduit for high-speed telephone and Internet access in Connecticut. The company, Gemini Networks, is installing hundreds of miles of high-speed cables -- the same kind used by cable television -- on utility poles. But unlike conventional cable or telephone networks, which are primarily used by their owners, Gemini will offer no services of its own. Instead, it will open its network to any company wishing to offer Internet access or local telephone or long-distance service, and let customers at home connect to the network at no charge, officials said. Gemini would be paid by the companies using the network to deliver services. "We're going to be building a brand-new network that ultimately will be nationwide in scope," said Arnold Chase, the company president. Building an open network for use by other service providers has never been tried before, he said. Gemini plans to build a pilot project by next year in West Hartford, Avon and Farmington. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Utopia
body: To the Editor: Re "Social Safety Net" (column, Nov. 3), by Thomas L. Friedman: Forgive me for being a little skeptical about the ability of Internet technology to provide the answer to eliminating poverty. The use of micro-loans is an impractical and improbable theory that will not be realized in the near future. It is doubtful that the micro-loan market will appeal to large commercial banks because of the cost of the paperwork involved. The reduction of this cost will admittedly make a venture into the micro-loan more desirable, but it sounds as if this may be only a pipe dream. MOJDEH MALEKAN newyork, Nov. 3, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet for Research?
body: To the Editor: The notion of James A. Kadamus, a deputy commissioner of education for newyork State, that public libraries should stay open later to provide access to the Internet, demonstrates how little library collections are appreciated ("For Research, Students Now Head to Barnes & Noble," Education page, Nov. 3). The Internet offers few classic works on any subject. While it has its virtues, it mainly offers unreviewed and probably otherwise unpublishable misinformation, trivia and ephemera. If children cannot find up-to-date collections of printed books, periodicals and reference works in school and public libraries, they are better off doing their research at a good bookstore.  ALBERT HENDERSON Bridgeport, Conn., Nov. 3, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title: Cybersegregation?
body: To the Editor: It was dispiriting to read Henry Louis Gates Jr.'s Oct. 31 Op-Ed article, "One Internet, Two Nations." Somehow, he has managed to find discrimination and black victimization in a medium that is totally democratic and color-blind. Also, using a loaded word, "cybersegregation," is not helpful. The Internet is similar to civil rights legislation: it's an opportunity, not a guarantee.  SHEILA MASSEY FRIEDLI Madison, N.J., Nov. 3, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Door Is Wide Open to Blacks
body: To the Editor: Re "One Internet, Two Nations" (Op-Ed, Oct. 31): I gasped when I read this statement in Henry Louis Gates Jr.'s article: "Few African-Americans have been compelled to sign on to a medium that offers little to interest them." Little to interest them? The World Wide Web is the greatest source of knowledge and information that has ever existed. Everything is on the Web: sports, music, movies, television, geography, merchandise of every description, and practically every hobby and special interest known to man. Type in "Malcolm X" or "Hank Aaron" or "the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr." or "Aretha Franklin," and you will undoubtedly be hit with a tidal wave of information. If Mr. Gates is right, there is an immense money-making opportunity waiting for the first entrepreneur, black or white, who builds a compelling African-American Web site.  ROBERT CHANDLER Beverly Hills, Calif., Oct. 31, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (William van Roden)

title:

UNISYS LOOKS TO INTERNET TO INCREASE PROFIT
body: The Unisys Corporation, a computer services supplier, said yesterday that it expected more than half of the revenues of the $7-billion-a-year company to come from the Internet within about three years. At a news conference, the Unisys chairman and chief executive, Lawrence A. Weinbach, announced a portfolio of Internet services and aggressively priced products aimed at winning a piece of the Web market and aiding the company's flagging financial performance. Pennsylvania-based Unisys, the product of the 1986 merger of two mainframe computer makers, is seeking to move into more profitable service areas after struggling for years with flagging growth. Unisys stock fell $1.375 yesterday, to $21.75. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Digital Video Camera Is Freed Of Its Tether to the PC
body: Cams -- tech slang for tiny video cameras for personal computers -- have been popping up in all sorts of shapes and styles. The latest, Video Blaster Webcam Go, is the first to free itself from its wired connection to the PC. Created by Creative Labs, this $150 digital-camera-to-go can snap individual pictures and snippets of motion pictures, all of which are easily uploaded to the Internet or attached to email. The camera can also be used to set up video conferences, and, detached from its wired base, it can be used like a point-and-shoot digital camera. With four megabytes of on-board memory, the camera delivers 90 good-quality 640 x 480 images (or you can get more than 200 images at a much lower resolution) in Internet-ready JPEG format.   MICHEL MARRIOTT http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: The Internet Road Hog
body: To the Editor: Voice chat sounds like good clean fun ("The Web Discovers Its Voice," Oct. 21). But the dismaying revelation in the article is that commercial long-distance telephone companies have begun using the Internet to transmit their phone calls, presumably in full duplex, where both parties can talk and listen simultaneously, as with a normal long-distance connection. If that practice becomes widespread, it will devour an undue share of Internet bandwidth. It takes far more data packets to transmit a sentence of digitized voice than to transmit the same sentence in ordinary, typed-in text. How much of this can the Internet backbone handle without markedly slowing down for other users? I'm no purist on the commercial use of the Internet, but it was never designed for routine bandwidth-hogging commercial uses like commercial telephony.  WARREN WETMORE Hazel Crest, Ill., Oct. 25, 1999   http://www.nytimes.com

body: Stamps.com Inc., an Internet postage company, agreed to buy the closely held Iship.com for about $305 million in stock to create a one-stop Internet mailing and shipping source. Stamps.com will exchange eight million of its shares for the shares, warrants and options outstanding of Iship.com, which is based in Bellevue, Wash. After the merger, customers will be able to buy and print stamps, compare rates among shippers and arrange for package pickup and tracking from one Web site. Stamps.com, based in Santa Monica, Calif., is one of two companies licensed by the Postal Service to allow customers to buy and print stamps on the Internet. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Carriers Sued by GTE
body: The GTE Corporation, a local phone company and Internet carrier, said today it had filed an antitrust lawsuit against the AT&T Corporation and the Comcast Corporation about deals the two companies struck on behalf of their Internet service provider, Excite@Home. GTE's suit contended that the companies required their high-speed Internet clients to use Excite@Home, thwarting competition. Excite@Home called the suit absurd, noting GTE's dominant position as a provider of local phone service in some markets. GTE and other phone companies offer high-speed Internet access over phone lines. Under current law, the carriers cannot require their customers to buy Internet services from them. AT&T and Comcast require clients to buy Internet service from Excite@Home even if they prefer another provider. The cable companies say that the rules do not apply to them and that the deals are needed to pay for improving service. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
POLITICAL BRIEFING;
McCain Welcomes Rival To Web Site
body: This being the age of the computer, almost every Presidential candidate has a site on the World Wide Web, some fancier than others but all of them overflowing with self-serving biographical data and the latest on what the candidate is thinking and doing. For example, pull down the Web site for Senator John McCain, www.mccain2000.com, and the Arizona Republican serves up . . . click here for the latest speech . . . or here for today's campaign schedule . . . or here to make a donation . . . or here if you are from the Bush campaign . . . or . . . say what? Just trying to "make it easier for the Bush campaign to surf our site," a note to users explains. As the Senator's computer people tell it, the McCain site received more than a million "hits," or visits, in the first half of October, with more than 4,500 of them coming from the Bush campaign, twice as many as from any other visitor. The Bush people counter that they have "better things to do than spy on who's using our Web site." http://www.nytimes.com

title:

INTERNET SERVICES CONSOLIDATION VALUED AT $287 MILLION
body: Critical Path, an electronic-mail service provider, agreed yesterday to buy Isocor, hoping to strengthen its position in the growing market for Internet messaging services. Shares of Isocor soared 71 percent, jumping $7.375 each, to $17.625, in Nasdaq trading. Critical Path's shares fell $3, to $47. Under the deal, stockholders of Isocor, which is based in Santa Monica, Calif., will receive 0.4707 share of Critical Path for each Isocor common share, putting the deal's value about $287 million, based on Critical Path's closing price on Wednesday. Critical Path, which is based in San Francisco, provides email messaging systems for corporate customers, Internet service providers, Web host companies and portals. http://www.nytimes.com

title: S.E.C. Settles On-Line Stock Auction Case
body: The Securities and Exchange Commission said this week that it had settled charges against three men who tried to sell stock at the Internet auction site Ebay. The S.E.C., saying this was the first time it had filed charges based on a sale of securities in an on-line auction, issued cease-and-desist orders against the three. It said they agreed to settle the case without admitting or denying the charges. Ebay was not accused of wrongdoing. Ebay's auction site is known for offering around-the-clock auctions for a wide variety of items. But on-line stock auctions are illegal, the S.E.C. said. Helane Morrison, district administrator in the San Francisco office, said in a statement that securities laws "apply in cyberspace, just as they do elsewhere." The three men who had been accused were Richard Davis, 28, of Duncanville, Tex.; John R. Hoff, 24, of Hudson, Wis., and Louis Sitaras, 37, of Jupiter, Fla. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Reuters Drops onDisappointing Results
body: The British media and information company Reuters Group said today that its third-quarter sales were little changed from a year ago, disappointing analysts and sending its stock down sharply. Reuters cited lower levels of trading activity, mergers and acquisitions among its customers and a slowdown in demand as clients upgraded their computer systems to avoid problems involving the year 2000. Slower revenue growth from its Instinet electronic equity brokerage services was also a factor. Reuters sales amounted to £763 million, or $1.27 billion, for the three months ended on Sept. 30, compared with £761 million a year earlier. Analysts had expected sales of £770 million to £780 million. The revenue slowdown, which hit the Reuters trading systems particularly hard, is likely to worsen in the fourth quarter, the company said. But it said profits should still increase in the second half of the year. Reuters reports its profits semiannually rather than quarterly. The company's American depository receipts fell 13 percent, dropping $8.375 each, to $57.50, in Nasdaq trading. http://www.nytimes.com

title:

Encyclopedia Britannica on Line, But Its Site Is Quickly Overrun
body: The Encyclopedia Britannica, once sold door to door, is now coming in through the Internet. This week, Encyclopedia Britannica said all 32 volumes would be available at www.britannica.com, free of charge. The site will also feature news feeds, magazine articles and a list of Web sites chosen by Britannica's editors. Within days of the opening of the site, however, the Britannica servers were overrun, leaving millions of grade-school term papers in limbo.   BRUCE HEADLAM http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Garden's Lush New Site Offers Thousands of Plants
body: You shall probably never see a Web site as lovely as a tree, but a new site might come close. The newyork Botanical Garden in the Bronx is putting digitized images of 75,000 plant specimens on the Web (www.nybg.org/bsci/hcol/vasc). The plants, like the Macleania pentaptera pictured here, are type specimens -- individual plants used by botanists to identify a species -- and the high-resolution images will allow scientists to examine them for taxonomy. So far, the garden has posted 2,500 images from its collection, which includes specimens from all over the world, some more than 100 years old.   BRUCE HEADLAM http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: Web Site Removes Charities' Tax Reports
body: The Web site where the tax returns of 190,000 charities were posted on Monday pulled most of the returns off the Internet yesterday after discovering that the names of donors and the amounts they gave were included in three tax returns. The donors' names were supposed to be withheld by the Internal Revenue Service when it scanned the charity tax returns onto CD-ROM's for the Urban Instititute in Washington and Philanthropic Research Inc., a charity in Williamsburg, Va. Federal law requires charities to report the names of donors and the amounts they gave to the Internal Revenue Service but allows charities to withhold these details when releasing their Form 990 tax returns, which are otherwise public records. Arthur W. Schmidt Jr., president of Philanthropic Research, which operates the www.guidestar.org Web site, said he hoped that all of the returns, minus any donor information, would be reposted today. He said that less than 1 percent of the returns scanned by the I.R.S. might have included donor names. By law, charities may keep donor names and amounts confidential, but some charities publicize the names of their donors. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Britannica Free To Web Users
body: The Encyclopaedia Britannica, afraid of becoming just a dusty relic of the precomputer age, announced today that it was making its 32-volume set available free on the Internet. From a-ak (an ancient East Asian music) to Zywiec (a town in Poland), the encyclopedia is being offered in its entirety at the company's retooled World Wide Web site: www.britannica.com. The 231-year-old company dropped door-to-door sales three years ago and hopes now to make money selling advertising on its site. The move may have been inevitable in an era when students doing homework are more likely to get their information from a computer than from a book. The privately held company would not disclose revenue figures, but sales of its print volumes -- which cost $1,250 a set and are now sold mostly to schools and other institutions -- have experienced a steep decline, Don Yannias, chief executive of Britannica.com., acknowledged. Free encyclopedias are only part of the lure of the new Web site. It will also offer current information from newspapers, news agencies and 70 magazines as well as email and financial market reports. http://www.nytimes.com

body: Metricom Inc., a provider of wireless Internet services, agreed yesterday to rent space on 500 communication towers from the Crown Castle International Corporation for as much as $126 million over 10 years as it prepares to offer its high-speed data service nationwide. Crown Castle, which is based in Houston and owns and manages more than 7,000 communication towers in the unitedstates, said it would receive $1,500 to $2,100 a month per tower, depending on location. The service, which the company wants to offer in 46 markets by mid-2001, allows users to connect to the Internet and corporate data networks at speeds faster than traditional computer modems. http://www.nytimes.com
