title:
COMPANY NEWS;
FINGERHUT TO FILL WAL-MART AND ETOYS ON-LINE ORDERS
body: Federated Department Stores Inc. said yesterday that its Fingerhut direct mail unit would fill Internet orders for Wal-Mart Stores Inc., the world's largest retailer, and Etoys Inc., a leading on-line toy store. Financial terms were not disclosed, but Will Lansing, chief executive of Fingerhut, said Wal-Mart and Etoys were the largest of the company's 22 clients. Fingerhut, acquired by Federated earlier this year, provides Web and phone order processing and order fulfillment, warehousing and shipment, payment processing, customer service and merchandise returns. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Stock Fraud Admitted
body: An employee of Pairgain Technologies Inc. pleaded guilty today to securities fraud that involved posting a false news report of an acquisition on the Internet to drive up the company's stock price. The employee, Gary Dale Hoke, an engineer at the company's Raleigh, N.C., plant, pleaded guilty to two counts in an agreement with Federal prosecutors. Mr. Hoke, who was scheduled to go on trial July 6 on five counts, faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and fines up to $1 million on each count. Under Federal sentencing guidelines, he is expected to get a much shorter sentence of 10 months to 16 months, an assistant unitedstates attorney, Christopher Painter, said. Mr. Hoke remained free on $50,000 bond. Federal prosecutors described him as a midlevel engineer in electronics development at Pairgain, a telecommunications equipment manufacturer. Prosecutors said the hoax was executed without the knowledge of company officials. Mr. Hoke planned the ruse for about two months and had intended to profit from it, but apparently got "cold feet" when he saw all the attention his bogus report was getting, Mr. Painter said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Privacy Groups See Danger in a Merger
body: Leading privacy advocates today blasted the $1 billion merger of the Internet advertising firm Doubleclick Inc. with the Abacus Direct Corporation, a consumer data collector, arguing that the combination would collect far too much personal information about consumers. The nonprofit Electronic Privacy Information Center and the privacy-oriented Web site Junkbusters (http://www.junkbusters.com) said they would probably ask regulators to block the deal if the companies proceeded. Combining Doubleclick's ability to follow on-line surfers around the Internet with Abacus's vast data base of names, addresses and phone numbers collected from direct mail vendors would "severely undermine" privacy, the groups said in a letter to the companies that was also sent to the Federal Trade Commission and top members of Congress. "This would represent a surveillance machine of unprecedented breadth and depth, posing unacceptable privacy dangers to the public," the groups added. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Squinting at a Web Book
body: To the Editor: That publishing new dissertations has become increasingly difficult ("Hoping the Web Will Rescue Young Professors," Arts & Ideas pages, June 12) is not just an acknowledgment of the obstacles to becoming a tenured professor but also a reminder that research is becoming increasingly specialized. Rather than exploring new subjects, we are extending old ones, often to the point that they are completely inaccessible to those not in the field. Web publishing is a great way to distribute these esoteric works, but who wants to squint at the computer screen to read? Until reading becomes easier, these digital publications are no better than books collecting dust.  DAN FLEDER Philadelphia, June 12, 1999  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Squinting at a Web Book Academic Tool;
Academic Tool
body: To the Editor: Re "Hoping the Web Will Rescue Young Professors" (Arts & Ideas pages, June 12): It should be noted that Internet search engines are becoming far more sophisticated. On one, I typed, "What is the text of the Gettysburg Address?" and the response was a Web page that included drafts of the address, translations in 28 languages and the only known photo of Lincoln at Gettysburg. The Internet is an extremely powerful tool when you know how to use it, and search engines are growing more user-friendly and less likely to locate Internet trash. My son wants to major in history, and I stress that he will not succeed until he masters the Internet.  JEFFREY K. BAUMANN Vernon Hills, Ill., June 12, 1999  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Squinting at a Web Book;
Accessible to All
body: To the Editor: Re Robert Darnton's "No Computer Can Hold the Past" (Op-Ed, June 12): By serving as an alternative source of original documents, the Internet already plays an important role in preserving the past for everyone, not just scholars. Not only can I find ancient works, but I can also search these texts for particular words or phrases, and yes, I can cut and paste them instead of retyping them. The Internet has also made documents like the Congressional Record and Supreme Court decisions more accessible to everyone. Mr. Darnton argues that researchers lose an important tactile experience when they use source material from the Internet. However, don't researchers already lose this experience when they use ancient sources in other languages? And do we really need to touch materials like the Congressional Record?  JONATHAN WALLACE newyork, June 12, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

body: To the Editor: "Office 2000 Is Well Connected" (June 10) is the kind of fluff I don't need or want to read. Why not compare Office 2000 to Corel's 2000 office suite? That would be useful. title: Scholars' Tool or a Web of Lies?
body: To the Editor: Robert Darnton's June 12 Op-Ed article on the use and abuse of Internet sources for historical research was a welcome dose of reason. There has been a rising chorus of alarm that students are dumping undigested content from the Internet into research papers, but I see little difference between this and any misapplication of source material. Bad scholarship is the fault of the scholar, not his sources. As the director of a Web site that chronicles the history of Seattle, I know that historical content on the Internet is extremely uneven and the quality of the material is equally wide. For researchers, the Internet should serve as a front door, not the last word. Web sites can help by publishing information about books, institutions and other Web sites where users can obtain further information.  WALT CROWLEY Seattle, June 12, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
June 6-12;
Goodbye, TV. Hello, Net.
body: When Lou Dobbs, whose name is synonymous with televised financial news from his 15 years anchoring CNN's "Moneyline" and his founding of the CNNfn network, resigned to join an Internet start-up called Space.com, his colleagues were baffled. Some said he had tired of ego-clashing with other top executives at CNN. Some said he saw the money some Web entrepreneurs were making, and wanted his chance to make a mint. Overlooked, Mr. Dobbs said, was a simpler notion: He is a space nut. He is also fully Net-savvy, having helped create CNNfn.com, the leading business-news website. Mr. Dobbs denied interest in another television job, saying, "My full commitment is to the launch of Space.com on July 20 and to the operation of the best Internet site on space."   LAWRIE MIFFLIN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Lou Dobbs.

title:

Jordan Shows His Hand
body: Having dealt his way out of a job by turning Westinghouse, the appliance maker, into CBS, the network, Michael H. Jordan has dealt his way back into another job, and in a manner in keeping with the times. Last week, the Clarant Worldwide Corporation, which aims to help major corporations and new Internet ventures do business on line, filed for a $150 million-plus public offering, for 30.7 percent of the company, with Mr. Jordan as chairman. Clarant, based in Dallas, will be formed from eight companies that it has agreed to acquire. Mr. Jordan yielded the top CBS job to Mel Karmazin, a far more experienced broadcasting executive, on Jan. 1. It turns out, however, that Mr. Jordan has learned a thing or two about matters digital. He has been on the Dell Computer board since 1992 and on the Marketwatch.com board since last June. He is also involved in ventures ranging from Webcasting to Internet document encryption. Mr. Jordan will leave the company's operations in the hands of Guillermo G. Marmol, Clarant's chief executive and founder. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Corrections
body: The Advertising column in Business Day on Monday, about software that can prevent "banner" ads from being displayed with Web pages, referred incorrectly to limits imposed by some sites on such ads. Yahoo, America Online and many other site operators have restricted the file size -- not memory size -- for banners on their sites. The column also misstated the purpose of the tiny files known as cookies, transmitted from some Web sites. A cookie labels the user's computer for identification if it later connects to the same site; the cookie does not collect data about the user's activity on the Internet. http://www.nytimes.com

title:

body: Not everyone is upset by the recent volatility in Internet stocks. Consider the Kansas City Board of Trade, which began trading futures contracts on the ISDEX index of 50 Internet stocks last Tuesday. "That's what we want," said Michael Braude, president of the board, best known for its wheat futures trading. As for volume on the Internet futures, the first such contracts available, Mr. Braude said he was pleased. "It's about exactly where I predicted," he said. title: Making I.S.P. Choices
body: To the Editor: At the very end of your I.S.P. article (May 20), you hinted at one step to stop junk mail from reaching your email address: get a new email address. Here are three steps to prevent your email address from being accessible on the Internet. Step 1: Get a new email address. This address will be your main one, and yes, you will have to inform all of your friends and family. Step 2: Get a second, free email address. This address can be another user name on the same I.S.P., or it can be a free email address from providers like Juno, Excite, Rocketmail and Hotmail. Step 3: Every time you must input your email address on the Internet, or fill out an on-line form that requests your email address, simply input your second address.  NOAH CHINITZ New Rochelle, N.Y., May 25, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title: NEWS WATCH
body: The Internet must be a community because now you can tell on your neighbors. The F.B.I. and the National White Collar Crime Center announced recently that they were creating an Internet Fraud Complaint Center on line this summer. Anyone who sees signs of on-line identity theft, email pyramid schemes or any other Internet-based criminal activity will be able to file a report on the Web site. "The Internet is so vastly different that it requires a new way of looking at crime," said Richard L. Johnston, director of the center. The Anchorage Daily News reported recently that a disgruntled employee tried to hold his company's database hostage. The employee, Gregory Todd Erkins, a computer systems operator for a small real-estate firm, sealed up the company's records behind a firewall and demanded $2,500 for their release, the police said.  Mr. Erkins was later arrested on charges including extortion. "It was just like if somebody broke into your home and you feel extremely violated," Linda Garrison, the company's co-owner, told The Daily News. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
I.B.M. Devises a Program To Enliven On-Line Ads
body: Can banner ads be effective or even (gasp) interesting? I.B.M.'s new media group thinks so and, to that end, has released a new Web development tool called Hot Media. Hot Media uses Java applets to let Web developers put animation, audio and video into banner ads and on-line catalogues that don't require users to download or configure plug-ins. "A banner ad with Hot Media can get loaded in the browser and running with only a 15K download," said Bill Pence, director of development for I.B.M.'s Internet media group. Banner ads garner click-through rates as low as 0.5 percent, Mr. Pence said. Tests using ads intended to take advantage of the new tools found that number jumped to 5 percent to 8 percent, he said.   STEVEN E. BRIER http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Remembering American Soldiers on a Virtual Wall
body: Nothing on the Internet can replicate the experience of standing in front of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, scanning the thousands and thousands of names of American soldiers inscribed on the black granite wall. But if you cannot get to the capital, or want a quick way to find a specific name this Memorial Day, several sites offer the wall on the Internet. You can view the Virtual Wall that the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund has opened on line (www.thevirtualwall.org), browse the Wall on the Web that was posted by an Atlanta resident named Tom Holloway (grunt.space .swri.edu/thewall/thewallm.html) or search a Web-based database designed by a Vietnam veteran named Chris Shepard (www.no-quarter.org). America Online includes a similar area, under the keyword Wall. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Associated Press)

title: Not So Friendly
body: To the Editor: I thought "Computer Designed for Granny Offers a Friendly Interface" (May 20) was an insult to everyone considered somewhat senior. We do not turn into idiots with the passage of time. I am a woman in her 70's who has been using a computer for more than three years without any of the problems mentioned. I have many friends who are also capable of reading manuals and figuring out icons and how to navigate menus. I think an apology is in order for the patronizing tone and for complete insensitivity.  TERIE GELBERG Roslyn Heights, N.Y., May 20, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:

Big Demand Overwhelms New Genealogy Web Site
body: The Mormon church's new genealogical Web site was overwhelmed by demand today, forcing its partner, I.B.M., to add a backup computer to handle Internet traffic. The site, www.familysearch.org, was down for six hours because the pipeline into the I.B.M. computer servers became clogged, said Elder D. Todd Christofferson, executive director of the church's Family History Department. The Web servers for the site are equipped to handle peaks of 30 million to 35 million hits a day and 25 million hits day after day, Mr. Christofferson said. "From all we can tell, the site can handle all that's coming its way," he said. "But the gate into the servers had to be widened." Before the six-hour hiatus, the site that puts part of the world's biggest genealogical database on line was being hit at a rate of 30 million a day. Today was the day it officially opened. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Barnesandnoble.com Raises $450 Million
body: Barnesandnoble.com Inc., the on-line bookseller owned by Barnes & Noble Inc. and Bertelsmann A.G., raised $450 million yesterday in an initial stock sale that tapped into investors' belief that the company will challenge Amazon.com Inc. The newyork-based company sold 25 million shares at $18 each. That was at the top of the range of $16 to $18 that had been set by Goldman, Sachs & Company and Merrill Lynch & Company, which handled the transaction. The sale represented an 18 percent stake and gave the company a market value of $2.52 billion. Investors expect barnesandnoble.com to be a strong competitor to Amazon.com, the No. 1 Internet retailer, said Ben Holmes, president of ipoPros.com, a research firm in Boulder, Colo., that specializes in initial public offerings. "A lot of people are looking at this as a potential slugfest between barnesandnoble and the incumbent Amazon," Mr. Holmes said. "It's about time. There needs to be a serious contender in that space, and barnesandnoble provides that." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Can Claim A Browser Majority
body: In a turnaround, a survey shows that almost 60 percent of companies say they now use the Microsoft Corporation's Internet browser -- a trend that could be a Pyrrhic victory for the software giant. Microsoft's push to persuade consumers to use its software rather than the browser made by the Netscape Communications Corporation is at the core of the Government's antitrust trial, which is scheduled to resume on June 1. A survey in October by Zona Research Inc. that was cited in the trial indicated that 60 percent of companies used Netscape's software. A Microsoft lawyer, John Warden, argued that the earlier survey "completely undermines the Government's case." But the new survey by Zona of 308 corporate technology professionals showed that 59 percent identified Microsoft's browser as the one they "personally use the most at work." The results put Microsoft in the awkward position of playing down a survey that trumpets the company's own success. A spokesman, Jim Cullinan, argued today that the results show only which browser the professionals used personally, not necessarily which browser was used by all employees. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Chancellor Mediato Form Internet Units
body: The Chancellor Media Corporation said today that it would form three Internet business units to offer its programs and other services electronically. The radio and billboard company, based in Irving, Tex., also said it would change its name to AMFM Inc. and would continue to pursue Internet alliances. Chancellor said a new AMFM Interactive Inc., or AMFMi unit, will develop and manage local Web portals for its radio stations. The company said AMFMi already had a trial under way in Philadelphia. AMFM.com will offer streaming media services and create Internet-only radio stations. Chancellor said AMFM.com's primary source of revenue would be the sale of audio and video commercials and sponsorships, electronic commerce revenue sharing with AMFMi and the sale of video conferencing and other Web-casting business services. Finally, its AMFM Equities unit will develop promotional partnerships with new media and Internet concerns that will exchange air time and other forms of exposure for equity in small, start-up companies. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Official Leaving Times Co.
body: Stephen Golden, president of the forest products group of The newyork Times Company, said yesterday that he would resign on June 30 to pursue a law degree and a master's degree in American Indian studies at the University of Arizona.  Jennifer C. Dolan, who has served as controller for the forest products group, was named acting director. Mr. Golden, 52, has been a vice president of the company since 1990 and has additionally headed the forest products group since 1994. He joined The newyork Times as a reporter in 1966, leaving the next year for a series of posts in radio and television. He rejoined The Times in 1976, serving as a manager in several departments. Mr. Golden is a member of the family that owns the controlling shares of the Times Company and is a first cousin of the chairman, Arthur Sulzberger Jr. Mr. Golden's mother, Ruth S. Holmberg, is a former director of the company and a sister of its chairman emeritus, Arthur Ochs Sulzberger. http://www.nytimes.com

body: LYCOS INC., Waltham, Mass., an Internet search directory, said it would purchase up to a 9 percent stake in the closely held on-line auctioneer Fairmarket Inc., Woburn, Mass., for undisclosed terms.  DEAN FOODS CO., Franklin Park, Ill., a dairy processor and distributor, said it would dismiss 200 workers and take an $8 million charge against earnings to close an Indianapolis-based plant.  BELL MICROPRODUCTS INC., San Jose, Calif., a distributor of semiconductors and computer products, said it would buy some assets of Future Tech, Miami, a high-tech components distributor, for undisclosed terms. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AMAZON.COM TAKING 35%STAKE IN INTERNET GROCER
body: Amazon.com, a leading Internet retailer specializing in books, music and videos, is moving into groceries. The company said yesterday that it was paying $42.5 million for a 35 percent stake in Homegrocer.com, which operates an on-line grocery-delivery service around Portland, Ore., and Seattle. The investment will allow Homegrocer to speed up its national expansion, the companies said. Homegrocer hopes to be operating in half a dozen cities by the end of the year, according to its chief executive, Terry Drayton. Homegrocer, based in Bellevue, Wash., takes orders over the Internet and delivers the products to customers' homes. Amazon is based in Seattle. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
EBAY TO BUY ON-LINE BILL PROCESSOR AND A CAR AUCTIONEER
body: Ebay Inc., the No. 1 on-line auctioneer, agreed yesterday to buy Kruse International, auctioneers of collectible cars, and Billpoint Inc., a provider of on-line payment services, for a combined $275 million in stock. Ebay is expanding the variety of goods it handles as competition in the on-line auction business intensifies from Amazon.com Inc. and other new entrants. Last month, Ebay said it would buy the Butterfield & Butterfield Auctioneers Corporation, a San Francisco-based auction house, for about $260 million in stock, adding high-priced art and other collectibles to its service. Billpoint is based in Redwood City, Calif.  Kruse International is based in Auburn, Ind. Both companies are closely held. The stock of Ebay, which is based in San Jose, Calif., fell $8.875 a share, to $189.5625. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Music Concern Files With S.E.C.
body: MP3.com, which runs an on-line site from which consumers can download music, has filed to raise $115 million through an initial public offering. The San Diego-based company, which boasts the singer-songwriter Alanis Morissette among its shareholders, said today that it had more than 56,000 songs from more than 11,000 artists available at its Web site: www.mp3.com. Consumers can search, sample and download from the collection free of charge, MP3.com said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company's revenue comes from on-line advertising, sponsorships and by selling CD's on line, the filing said. The company reported a net loss of $357,538 on revenue of $1.1 million in 1998. It had a net loss of $1.4 million on revenue $665,785 in the first quarter of this year. http://www.nytimes.com

THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Ogilvy Interactive Wins a Grand Clio

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
SECURITY FIRST TO BUY2 ON-LINE BANKING CONCERNS
body: The Security First Technologies Corporation agreed yesterday to buy two on-line banking companies for $1.4 billion and also formed a strategic alliance with Intuit Inc. Security First will buy the Brussels-based FICS Group N.V., a privately held software company specializing in corporate-finance solutions, and the Edify Corporation, a Santa Clara, Calif., on-line banking software company. Security First, an Atlanta-based developer of Internet applications for financial products, will issue 20 million shares for the FICS deal, which is valued at $1.08 billion based on Security First's closing price on Friday. Under its agreement, Intuit, which is based in Mountain View, Calif., will invest $50 million for about 971,000 shares of Security First. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Ebay and Skytel In a Venture
body: Ebay Inc., the No. 1 on-line auctioneer, and Skytel Communications Inc., the second-largest unitedstates paging company, plan to introduce a service that lets customers monitor and participate in auctions away from their computers. The free service will notify Ebay users through their pagers, cell phones and electronic organizers when they have made a winning bid and when their items sell. It will begin in July and be expanded later to allow users to increase bids using wireless devices. Existing Skytel customers will be able to sign up for the service through the Ebay World Wide Web site. Ebay and Skytel, based in Jackson, Miss., will also offer an Ebay-branded paging service to customers who currently do not have a pager or wireless device that can receive email or text messages. The package will include a text pager with prepaid service, a personal toll-free number and an email address. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Health Network Interests Dell
body: The Dell Computer Corporation and two other companies are seeking to invest as much as $30 million in Drkoop.com Inc., the on-line consumer health care network co-founded by the former Surgeon General, C. Everett Koop. Dell, the Quintiles Transnational Corporation and FHC Internet Services L.C. have each "expressed interest" in acquiring Drkoop.com common stock, according to a registration statement filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. These expressions of interest are nonbinding, the filing said. Nevertheless, Drkoop.com will reserve $10 million of stock for each of the potential investors as part of the company's coming initial public offering. The Web site run by Drkoop.com, based in Austin, Tex., provides users with health care information on topics like acute ailments and nutrition. The site also offers access to medical data bases. The company recorded revenue of $404,000 during the first quarter of 1999, almost 10 times the $43,000 in revenue generated during all of last year. Drkoop.com generated a net loss of $30.5 million during the first quarter. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Charles K. McWhorter, 77, Aide to Nixon
body: Charles K. McWhorter, an aide to Vice President Richard M. Nixon and later a lawyer for A.T.&T., died on Tuesday at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston after being injured on May 1 in a car accident on Cape Cod. He was 77 and lived in Manhattan and Los Angeles. Mr. McWhorter was a legislative assistant to Vice President Nixon from 1957 to 1961 and joined A.T.&T. as an executive assistant and attorney shortly afterward. He retired in 1987. In 1968, after Nixon had been elected President, Mr. McWhorter turned down an offer to work in the White House, saying he preferred to remain in newyork. He accepted an appointment to the National Council on the Arts instead. Mr. McWhorter was born on Feb. 22, 1922, in Lewisburg, W.Va. He graduated from West Virginia University and in 1949 received a law degree from Harvard University. He also served in the Army during World War II and the Korean War. A onetime president of the Young Republican National Federation, he was active in Republican politics throughout his life. He is survived by a sister, Susanna Reckerd of Claremont, Calif. http://www.nytimes.com

title: TheStreet.com's New Shares Soar
body: Shares in TheStreet.com tripled in their first day of trading yesterday as investors piled into the Internet news service promoted by its co-founder, James J. Cramer, a hedge-fund manager and financial columnist. Shares of the company rose $41, to $60. The surge gave the three-year-old, money-losing company a market value of $1.41 billion. TheStreet.com's backers include The newyork Times Company and the News Corporation. The company, which produces financial news and analysis on its World Wide Web site, had 51,000 subscribers at the end of March, up 59 percent this year. title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NTL, A CABLE TV CONCERN, WINS FRENCH CONTRACT
body: NTL Inc., a newyork-based company that provides cable television and Internet services over advanced broadband fiber networks to 25 percent of the homes in Britain, moved into the Continental European broadband market yesterday after it won a competitive tender for control of France Telecom's 1G Networks. 1G Networks, which NTL will acquire for 350 million francs ($57 million), provides multichannel television services in four areas of greater Paris totaling 176,000 homes and 90,000 homes in Toulon. NTL will hold exclusive licenses to provide analog and digital television services over 1G Networks. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Intel Sets Up Fund for Internet Research
body: The Intel Corporation said today that it had set up a $250 million fund to invest in companies developing Internet applications for the company's new microprocessor technology. The new architecture, called IA-64, processes 64 bits of data at a time, rather than the 32 bits of earlier chips, and uses other design tricks to carry out multiple tasks at once. Intel, based in Santa Clara, plans to begin producing the first IA-64 processor, named Merced, in mid-2000. Intel said investors of the Intel 64 Fund include the Compaq Computer Corporation, the Dell Computer Corporation, the Hewlett-Packard Company, Silicon Graphics Inc. and the NEC Corporation. Such funds are used by Intel, and other high-tech giants such as Cisco Systems Inc. and Lucent Technologies Inc., to invest in companies that can make their products more useful. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Mexican Tycoon Buys Stake in CDnow
body: Carlos Slim Helu, Mexico's leading industrialist, has added to his Internet holdings through the acquisition of a 5.3 percent stake in the on-line music retailer CDnow Inc. An investment group that includes Mr. Slim and his family's holding company, Grupo Carso, filed papers with the unitedstates Securities and Exchange Commission saying they hold 947,000 shares of CDnow common stock. Their stake has a current market value of $17.5 million. The Slim family portfolio already includes controlling interests in Telefonos de Mexico S.A., the telecommunications giant, and Prodigy Communications, the Internet access provider. Purchasing CDnow shares gives the family a stake in one of the Internet's most promising areas of retailing. Unlike many Internet stocks, CDnow shares have struggled this year. After trading near $25 early in February, CDnow fell as low as $13.25 on April 19. It rose $1.3125 today, to $18.0625. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Bookstore Extinction
body: To the Editor: The small booksellers who have complained that Frank McCourt, the author of "Angela's Ashes," sold out to big bookstores because he appeared in a television commercial for Barnes & Noble should realize that their businesses are headed for certain extinction (Making Books column, May 6). Even farm subsidies didn't keep family farming alive; they just helped big farmers gobble up small ones. Owners of independent bookstores should try to capitalize on their strengths by becoming authors, editors, reviewers, boutique publishers or Web site proprietors. With the electronic book just down the road and the on-line store already upon us, the ability to run a small retail outlet will be the least marketable of their skills.  JOHN CHATTERTON newyork, May 6, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
BARNESANDNOBLE.COM HOPING TO RAISE $300 MILLION
body: Barnesandnoble.com, the on-line retailer jointly owned by the bookseller Barnes & Noble and the German media conglomerate Bertelsmann A.G., said yesterday that it hoped to raise about $300 million in an initial public offering. It plans to sell 25 million shares, or about 18 percent of the company, for about $12 each. A date has not been set. title:
Filtering the Web Won't Protect Kids;
Foiling the Snoops
body: To the Editor: A May 3 news article points out that parents are using filters on their children's Internet accounts, restricting passwords and reading email. The problem is that young people may establish Internet accounts unknown to their parents. They may also log on to the account of a friend who is willing to lend them a password. Children can also use Hotmail accounts that give them access to a permanent email address from any computer with an Internet connection. For parents to learn what their children are doing on the Internet, they may check the hard drive on their children's computers for history files, temporary Internet files and files containing cookies left by Web sites visited. However, the browser and operating system provide simple methods of erasing these files without a trace. The best solution is to help young people learn how to deal with bad ideas. I suspect the process should be quite explicit and begin very early.  RICK SAUSE Tigard, Ore., May 3, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title: Have Laptop, Will Travel
body: To the Editor: The article "A Home Page Away From Home" (April 29) reported on some ways that long-term travelers can use the Internet to stay in touch with family and friends. Our company, High Adventure Travel (www.airtreks.com), offers a Web-based journal to travelers who buy their around-the-world tickets from us. Each traveler's page offers an itinerary, contact information and room for messages and reports from the road.  JAMES PILAAR President, Airtreks.com San Francisco, April 29, 1999   http://www.nytimes.com

title: Lucent Is Planning A Wireless Portal
body: Lucent Technologies Inc. said today it had licensed Custom Netcenter from America Online's Netscape Communications division in an effort to develop an Internet portal for wireless phones and hand-held personal organizers. Lucent's new portal, named Zingo, is to serve as a starting point on the Internet for traveling professionals and a testing ground for wireless equipment providers. By applying the Netcenter software to wireless equipment, Lucent can broaden its scope. For example, an executive arriving in a city new to her could have driving tips on avoiding traffic jams instantly available from the Internet, displayed on a personal digital assistant or in a text-to-speech format on a mobile phone. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Dane N. Bath Picture Editor, 58
body: Dane N. Bath, a former picture editor of The newyork Times and The Chicago Tribune, died on Wednesday at Lenox Hill Hospital in Manhattan. He was 58 and lived in Parsippany, N.J. The causes were cardiac arrest and complications related to diabetes, his wife, Patricia, said. He attended the Universities of Maryland and Wisconsin and worked for newspapers in Wisconsin and Iowa. He was with The Tribune from 1965 to 1973, rising from reporter to picture editor and then graphics editor. He was picture editor of The Times from 1973 to 1981. Later, he founded dnb Media, a public relations and political consulting firm. Besides his wife, he is survived by a son, Dane 3d, of Queens, and a brother, Michael, of Franklin, Wis. http://www.nytimes.com

title: I.B.M. Set to Focus on Small Businesses
body: The International Business Machines Corporation said yesterday that it would spend $100 million on a new marketing campaign aimed at small businesses. The campaign will begin today with an eight-page insert in major newspapers and a new Small Business Center link on I.B.M.'s Web site. I.B.M. said the program would offer small businesses, or companies with fewer than 100 employees, products and service through multiple channels, including the Internet and telephone sales. "We want to establish an ongoing relationship with small business on a global basis," Peter Rowley, I.B.M.'s general manager for global small business, said in a telephone interview.  "We want to have products that they want to buy." Earlier this year, I.B.M. introduced the 300 GL, the company's first commercial desktop PC designed specifically for small businesses, and a new marketing relationship with American Express to provide products at discount to small-business card holders. Under the new small-business program, I.B.M. will offer low-cost leasing, with approval within an hour, and products and services to help customers do business on the Internet. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Violent Games, Violent Deeds?;
What Libraries Do
body: To the Editor: Lynne Gomez's May 2 letter criticizing the American Library Association's decision not to advocate Internet filtering indicates a misunderstanding of the historical role that libraries play in providing access to information. Libraries are not passive warehouses of information. Tens of thousands of library and information professionals manage resource collections to meet the needs of all members of their communities, including children. In this regard, children's access to inappropriate information is not a new problem. The implication of the library association's position concerning Internet filtering is that professional judgment rather than impersonal software should determine what material is appropriate in local libraries.  STEVEN L. MAC CALL Tuscaloosa, Ala., May 2, 1999  The writer is an assistant professor, School of Library and Information Studies, University of Alabama. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING: DIARY;
Coming Soon From CMGI: More Internet Offerings
body: David Wetherell, chief executive of CMGI Inc., the Internet-venture fund company, said he expected about a dozen of CMGI's portfolio of 36 companies to go public in the next 12 months. Engage Technologies, which makes online marketing software to help identify Web audiences, and Silknet Software Inc., which makes software for on-line marketing and customer relations, are two of the candidates for initial public offerings. CMGI, based in Andover, Mass., had a 4,622 percent cumulative return on realized investments of its @Ventures fund for the 36 months ended April 26, Mr. Wetherell said, speaking last week at the Hambrecht & Quist Technology conference in San Francisco. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: David Wetherall

title: We Have Gone Too Far to Protect Internet Speech
body: To the Editor: Re "Some Enter the Fast Lane to Get Access to the Web" (front page, April 28): Broadband is not just the next big thing in the evolution of the Internet, it is an enabling technology that allows users to realize the full potential of the communications revolution. Consider this: High-speed Internet access would enable schoolchildren trapped in classrooms with inadequate teachers to close the skills gap by enrolling in distance-learning classes taught by more capable teachers in other parts of the country. And through telemedicine, residents of medically underserved communities could "visit" the offices of better doctors whose offices are located hundreds of miles away.  FAYE M. ANDERSON Washington, April 28, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Andy Rash)

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MARKETWATCH.COM TO PAY $166 MILLION FOR BIGCHARTS
body: Marketwatch.com Inc., a Web-based provider of business news, agreed yesterday to acquire Bigcharts Inc. of Minneapolis, one of the 10 most visited financial Internet sites, for about $160 million in stock and $6 million in cash. Marketwatch.com is to exchange about 2.175 million shares of its common stock and pay $6 million in cash for all outstanding Bigcharts stock. Marketwatch.com, based in San Francisco, is a joint venture between CBS Broadcasting Inc. and the Data Broadcasting Corporation, a financial information provider. Marketwatch.com's shares slipped $1.125, to $72.50. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
SHAW IN $312 MILLION DEAL FOR FUNDY COMMUNICATIONS
body: Shaw Communications Inc. said yesterday that it planned to buy Fundy Communications Inc., for $312 million, including $102 million of class B shares. Fundy, a privately held company in Saint John, New Brunswick, operates cable television systems serving 192,000 subscribers, mainly in New Brunswick. With Fundy's fiber backbone network, Shaw said it would be able to introduce digital cable and high-speed Internet access service in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. title:
COMPANY NEWS;
RCN TAKES 47.5% STAKEIN JUNIORNET FOR $47 MILLION
body: The RCN Corporation, a provider of telecommunications services based in Princeton, N.J., said yesterday that it had acquired a 47.5 percent stake in the Juniornet Corporation, a commercial-free on-line learning service for children that was introduced last month, for about $47 million in cash. At the same time, Juniornet bought RCN's Lancit Media Entertainment subsidiary, which creates children's television programming, for about $25 million in cash. title:
INTERNATIONAL BRIEFS;
Korea Telecomto Raise Internet Service Speed
body: The Korea Telecom Company, South Korea's largest telephone company, said yesterday that it would invest 350 billion won ($297 million) to increase tenfold the speed of its Internet service, Kornet. The state-run company will spend 70 billion won to speed its backbone network speed to one gigabit a second. Giga switches, or central operators, will be installed in 35 cities across the nation to increase the speed of intercity Internet service. Kornet, the nation's largest Internet service provider, has about 488,000 personal and corporate subscribers. It posted a profit of 3.8 billion won last year. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Phone Company In Internet Deal
body: Intermedia Communications Inc., a local telephone company, said this week that it planned to expand its deployment of high-speed Internet access services through two strategic alliances. Intermedia, based in Tampa, Fla., said it had formed alliances with Rhythms Netconnections Inc. and the closely held Northpoint Communications to deliver so-called digital subscriber line in large markets nationwide. The service delivers high-speed on-line connections using copper phone lines. Gene Noble, Intermedia's vice president for data services, said the company was deploying the service in 16 markets in the East and South. The alliances with Northpoint and Rhythms will expand Intermedia's coverage to 17 more cities, including San Francisco and Chicago, in about 90 days. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
A Merger Deal By 2 Internet Firms
body: Two World Wide Web sites that are aimed at the advertising-agency industry are being combined. Warp 10 Technologies, which is based in Toronto and operates Adsgallery.com, is acquiring Portfolios Online, which is also based in Toronto and operates Portfolios.com. Financial terms of the deal were undisclosed. Under the agreement, Adsgallery.com will house the content of both Web sites. Michel Neray, 41, now the chief executive at Portfolios Online, will become the marketing director at Warp 10. Marvin Igelman, 36, will remain president and chief executive at Warp 10.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: What Can We Do About Web Hate?
body: To the Editor: Thomas L. Friedman (column, April 27) suggests more parental involvement as the solution to the problem of unlimited choices for children on the Internet. Perhaps, but parents can only act as an effective censor for so long, and the pictures and ideas that are the precursors of violence and hatred are entrancing to some people, even those brought up by loving parents. The Web makes living in a world of email, chat rooms and glowing images easy. People get hooked, as in a cult. Students need to be able to identify harmful ideas that lead to cynicism, isolation and bitterness. We should be teaching logic and philosophy in the public schools.  KURT COOPER Tucson, Ariz., April 27, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
What Can We Do About Web Hate?;
An Internet Inferno
body: To the Editor: Thomas L. Friedman's April 27 column about the Internet as a powerful interactive technology with no editor reminds me of the cautionary note expressed years ago by Vartan Gregorian, the former president of the newyork Public Library, concerning the implications of electronic information. Recalling T. S. Eliot's description of Hell in Dante's "Inferno" as a place "where nothing connects with nothing," Mr. Gregorian warned that the information overload we are experiencing made possible by electronic technology can foster not only absurdity and alienation but also a critical loss of knowledge and judgment. How we encourage citizens to find coherent meaning and knowledge informed by the humanistic tradition in this new digital era is a major challenge of our time, requiring a complete rethinking of our institutions.  JOHN BOYER Newark, April 27, 1999  The writer teaches journalism and media studies at Rutgers University. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
What Can We Do About Web Hate?;
No Need for Bans
body: To the Editor: Thomas L. Friedman, in his April 27 column on the Columbine High School shootings, says the Internet can be both "an incredible knowledge tool and an incredible microphone for hate," but he refuses to acknowledge any purpose for assault weapons other than to "kill other human beings." In fact, assault weapons can stop or deter the killing of innocent people when used with the same "personal judgment and responsibility" that Mr. Friedman acknowledges are "critical" when surfing the Web. A total ban on weapons is no more justified than a total ban on objectionable Web sites.  MAURICE JAY BAUMGARTEN Miami Beach, Fla., April 27, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NOTEBOOK;
Textbooks on the Internet
body: Linking textbooks to the Internet has formidable problems: Web addresses may become obsolete, sites may decline in quality and they are beyond publishers' control anyway. The National Science Teachers Association has one solution, which it has named Scilinks. Web watchers -- teachers and specialists in particular fields -- find and screen Web sites related to various concepts found in a textbook: threatened rain forests, for example. A student can go to Scilink's Web site (www.scilinks.org), type in the code published next to the key phrase in the textbook and link to age-appropriate Internet recommendations. Holt, Rinehart & Winston is the first publisher to contract with Scilinks, for two textbooks due this year in environmental science and chemistry. Holt, a subsidiary of Harcourt General, plans seven or eight more, said Bill Talkington, Holt's president.   MICHAEL POLLAK http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AMAZON TO BUY ON-LINEBOOK SITE AND 2 OTHER COMPANIES
body: The on-line book and music seller Amazon.com said yesterday that it would buy three Internet companies for a total of $645 million in stock. The Seattle-based company will acquire the privately held Exchange.com, which runs two Internet sites that match buyers and sellers of hard-to-find books and music. Amazon also said it would take over privately held Accept.com of Redwood City, Calif., which develops ways to simplify Web transactions. The third company is the privately held Alexa Internet of San Francisco, which has a Web service that provides supplemental information about Internet sites as they are browsed. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MICROSOFT TO BUY JUMPNETWORKS, WEB CALENDAR SERVICE
body: The Microsoft Corporation said yesterday that it would acquire Jump Networks Inc., making the MSN service the latest Internet giant to add a Web-based personal organizer to its portfolio. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. Like other such services, Jump, which was founded last year, allows users to store their personal calendars, address books and to-do lists free on a central server, which then can be reached over any Internet connection. Microsoft executives said they planned to integrate Jump with the MSN network. Microsoft's shares rose $2 each, to $88. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
TELESCAN TO BUY INVESTOOLS IN $49.2 MILLION STOCK DEAL
body: Telescan Inc., an on-line financial-information company, agreed yesterday to buy the closely held Investools Inc. for $49.2 million in stock to increase its Internet investment advisory business. Telescan will pay about 2.4 million shares for Investools, based in Redwood City, Calif., and which has annual revenue of about $3 million. Investools provides investment newsletters and advice to subscribers via the Internet. Telescan, with 1998 revenue of $15.5 million, develops and operates Internet sites and on-line networks for the financial, publishing and entertainment industries. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
Taking to the Road With a New Internet Pitch
body: He is flush from the recent initial public offering of iVillage.com, in which he got insider stock as a participant in the Web site's Armchair Millionaire section. Now, Lewis Schiff, a newyork-based Internet marketer, is touting his latest venture, Invest-o-rama, an on-line listing of some 10,000 financial information sites on the World Wide Web. Mr. Schiff recently bought into Invest-o-rama, which was started four years ago by Douglas Gerlach, and hopes to use the billboard to attract other investors to help expand the site. Mr. Schiff paid $20,000 for a 14-foot-by-48-foot billboard ad, which went up on April 15 and is strategically placed along Silicon Valley's most traveled artery, Highway 101. "I want to make sure the most influential people know about what we're doing," he said. For the next two weeks, at least, if they are driving on the highway, they couldn't miss it if they tried. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Anne Dowie for The newyork Times)

title: London Theater
body: To the Editor: I was surprised by the 23 percent surcharge Anita Gates paid for tickets ordered over the Internet. She would have paid much less had she used Good Show! London Theatre and Booking Service (www.goodshow.com). Good Show! charges a flat $25 fee for two plays with a maximum of six tickets per show. For each additional show there is a $10 fee, again for a maximum of six tickets. The site provides reviews of everything in London, including the West End, the Royal Shakespeare Company (both London and Stratford), and the National Theater, plus fringe productions. I am a regular London visitor, generally once a year from mid-December to mid-January, and try to fit in as much theater as possible during my stay. I have yet to find any Internet site as comprehensive and price competitive as Good Show!  STEPHEN C. SCHAEFER San Pablo, Calif. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
EXODUS IS BUYING COHESIVE TECHNOLOGY FOR $100 MILLION
body: Exodus Communications Inc. signed a definitive agreement late on Wednesday to buy Cohesive Technology Solutions Inc., based in Palo Alto, Calif., for $100 million. Cohesive is a privately held professional services company with expertise in networking, Web applications like E-commerce, and technology solutions. The acquisition will position Exodus as a provider of computer services for running large corporate Internet sites. The stock of Exodus jumped $19.8125 yesterday, or 23.5 percent, to $103.8125, in Nasdaq trading. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
First, the 'Free' PC; Now the 'Free' Server
body: In the spirit of a new breed of companies offering "free PC's" -- tempered with the reality that there's invariably a catch -- a Silicon Valley company says that it plans to start distributing "free" server computers. Encanto Networks Inc., a computer hardware and services company in Santa Clara, Calif., said last week that starting in June it will give away "free Internet servers" -- network hubs that small businesses could use for supporting email, operating Web sites or conducting electronic commerce.  The catch: users must agree to spend $69.95 a month for two years of Internet access from Encanto and software that can be used to develop and host a Web site. That brings the two-year cost of a free server to $1,680. Encanto, a start-up company, is pitching its services as a means for small businesses to participate in E-commerce without having to make a big investment. A new server purchased from Encanto would cost $1,495 but would not include Internet access, which varies widely in cost, said Tom B. Blaisdell, the company's vice president of marketing.   MATT RICHTEL http://www.nytimes.com

title: Netscape Registration Up
body: Netscape, maker of the Web browser, said today that membership of its central Web site, Netscape Netcenter, had surpassed 15 million. The company, a unit of America Online Inc., the No. 1 Internet access provider, said Netscape had attracted one million new registrants in the four months that ended in March. America Online completed its $10 billion buyout on March 17. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Filtering the Filters
body: To the Editor: How sad to read that the Internet monitoring service Cybersitter ("Sticks and Stones Can Hurt, but Bad Words Pay," April 8) includes "gay rights" as an objectionable term. Apparently, the inclusion of the phrase in any Web site earns it censorship in customers' homes. Gay rights is not an appropriate subject for children? I think that there is no more appropriate topic for the young. The seeds of bigotry are sown in childhood, and rooting them out early is a parent's duty.  Most people seem to think that a discussion about gay rights with children need include a much-dreaded explanation of gay sex. But, the themes in such a discussion can be the same as those used in talking about racism or sexism. Further, does the company see something naughty or arousing -- that I don't? -- about a basic struggle for equal rights in employment or housing? Perhaps the prurience that Cybersitter so eagerly seeks to ban comes from within.  ED BOLAND newyork, April 13, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NET.BANK STOCK SOARS 48 PERCENT AFTER NEWS OF SPLIT
body: The Internet bank Net.bank Inc. said yesterday that its board had approved a 3-for-1 stock split. Shares of Net.bank soared 48 percent, or $76.516, to $235.016, in Nasdaq trading. The stock traded at $10.75 in October. The bank has no branches and says it can offer depositors good rates because its costs are lower than those of conventional banks. The split will apply to shareholders of record on April 23, and the additional shares will be issued May 14. Net.bank's chief executive, D. R. Grimes, estimated it could have as many as 55,000 accounts by the end of the year, based on current growth, according to a report Monday in the on-line financial information service Stockhouse.com. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ZAPATA PLANS TO SPIN OFF ITS ZAP.COM INTERNET BUSINESS
body: The Zapata Corporation, the fish-meal processor that added an Internet operation to its business, said yesterday that it planned to spin off its Internet unit, the Zap.com Corporation, in a future stock offering. Zapata said it would offer its shareholders the right to buy one Zap.com share for $8 for each Zapata share they hold. Up to 13.612 million shares of Zap.com are eligible for sale if all rights are exercised, making the offering worth $109 million. Zapata will still control Zap.com after the offering because it holds 10,000 preferred shares. Last year Zapata purchased two Internet magazines, Word and Charged, and announced its intention to turn Zap.com into an Internet portal. The main business of Zapata, which is based in Houston, is the production of marine protein for animal feed. Its shares fell $1.6875, to $10.375, yesterday on the newyork Stock Exchange. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Broadcast.com Loss Less Than Expected
body: Broadcast.com, a provider of multimedia events over the Internet, said today that its first-quarter loss was less than expected, as more companies used its service for events like conference calls. Broadcast.com, which is being acquired by Yahoo Inc., had a loss from operations of $3.4 million, or 9 cents a share. The company had been expected to lose 12 cents a share, according to the average estimate of analysts surveyed by the First Call Corporation. Revenue more than doubled to $10.3 million from $4.5 million. Broadcast.com, which is based in Dallas and like many Internet companies has yet to earn a profit, agreed on April 1 to be acquired by the No. 1 on-line directory Yahoo for about $6.1 billion in stock. Some analysts expect Internet multimedia programming to grow in popularity as high-speed Internet connections become more common. Meanwhile, Broadcast.com is aiming at companies seeking to cut costs and reach a broad audience by airing conference calls, product introductions and other events on line. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
EQUITEX TO BUY FIRST TELEBANC AND OPEN A WEB BANK
body: Equitex Inc. said yesterday that it would acquire the First Telebanc Corporation in a stock deal that could enable it to open its own Internet banking operation by the summer. Equitex, based in Englewood, Colo., is aiming to take advantage of efforts made by First Telebanc's Net1Bank N.A. subsidiary to develop a Web banking site. It said it had signed a letter of intent with the bank holding company in Boca Raton, Fla. Specific financial terms were not disclosed. Equitex shares closed $5.5625 higher at $23.4375. Equitex, which already owned 9.9 percent of First Telebanc, said it would change its name to the Net1Bank Corporation once the deal was complete. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Salon Magazine Buys a Virtual Community
body: Salon, the on-line magazine, has acquired the Well, one of the Internet's first virtual communities, providing a larger customer base and a place to hone its image as a marketplace for new ideas. No purchase price was disclosed for the deal announced today, as both the Well and Salon are privately held. Salon magazine, owned by Salon Internet Inc., became Salon.com after buying the domain name www.salon.com from a Texas hairdresser on Monday. The Well, short for the Whole Earth 'Lectronic Link, features more than 200 on-line conferences on topics ranging from politics and sex to the Grateful Dead. It will remain a separate business under its new owners, said Andrew Ross, vice president for business development at Salon.com. Mr. Ross said he planned to market the Well's conferencing system, which costs $10 to $15 a month, to Salon.com readers to help increase the Well's membership of 7,000 people, built over 14 years. Salon.com has 1.2 million members. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AT HOME REACHES TWO CABLE INTERNET AGREEMENTS
body: The At Home Corporation strengthened its position in the unitedstates and Japan yesterday with two agreements that promote Internet access via high-speed cable lines. The Japanese cable operator Jupiter Telecommunications and the Sumitomo Corporation, which owns 60 percent of Jupiter, agreed to join At Home in setting up At Home Japan. Jupiter and Sumitomo will deliver the cable Internet service to their combined 5.1 million subscribers, representing more than 10 percent of Japanese households. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DUPONT TO INVEST $220MILLION IN ALLIANCE WITH WEBMD
body: DuPont said yesterday that it would invest $220 million in an Internet health care program with WebMD Inc. WebMD, which began in October, offers doctors and consumers information about medicine and managed care. The deal will help DuPont, the nation's largest chemical company, increase its life-sciences business. Last month DuPont said it would issue a new class of stock to track the performance of the business; it also plans to expand the unit through alliances and acquisitions. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Memory vs. Storage
body: To the Editor: As a computer consultant, I strive to educate my clients on the difference between memory and storage ("Memory Takes New Shape," April 1). Memory refers to RAM, while a hard disk or a floppy disk is storage. The error message "out of memory" does not mean you need a larger hard disk. If you fail to save your work, you will not find it "somewhere in memory."  LYNN UNDERWOOD newyork, April 2, 1999  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times PromotesExecutive
body: Thomas E. Helling, group director for the corporate and financial advertising teams at The newyork Times, was named vice president for advertising sales yesterday. The promotion was announced by Jyll F. Holzman, senior vice president for advertising. In his new position, Mr. Helling, 42, will oversee a wide range of advertising categories at The Times, including financial services, media, packaged goods, technology and books. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
PRODIGY TO START INTERNET SERVICE FOR SPANISH SPEAKERS
body: The Prodigy Communications Corporation will offer a Spanish-language Internet access service to Spanish-speaking households in the unitedstates. The service will provide both customer service and technical support for Spanish-speaking customers and will be supported with Spanish-language advertising, news and links to other Hispanic Web sites and services. Visitors will be able to search the Internet with Spanish-language search engines. The service will first be promoted in commercials on Spanish-language television stations in Miami and Chicago, The Wall Street Journal reported yesterday, and the marketing campaign will later be expanded to other American cities. Other companies offer Spanish-language content on line but focus mainly on subscribers outside the unitedstates. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
THEGLOBE.COM IN $43 MILLION DEAL FOR ATTITUDE NETWORK
body: Theglobe.com Inc., a company that lets Internet users set up home pages, said yesterday that it would acquire the game-related Web publisher Attitude Network for about $43.1 million in stock. Theglobe.com will also assume $5.1 million in debt. Theglobe.com, based in newyork, now has 9.3 million registered users and said it would gain an additional 2.3 million in the acquisition, most of them in the demographic group that advertisers covet -- 18- to 44-year-olds. Attitude Network publishes sites for computer game enthusiasts. Theglobe.com, derives most of its revenue from advertising and subscriptions. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Metro Business;
'Star Wars' on Line
body: More than a month before the highly anticipated opening of the movie "Star Wars: Episode 1," Cable television's SCI FI Channel and Internet hub Lycos Inc., announced an exclusive agreement yesterday to sell Star Wars merchandise at a Web site, the SCI FI Store. Visitors to The SCI FI Store (www.scifistore.lycos.com) will be able to buy in advance officially licensed merchandise, including action figures, books, clothing and gifts. While merchandise will not be released to any retailers until three weeks before the film's mid-May opening, the SCI FI Store will offer on-line shoppers items in advance. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Deal on Internet Content
body: Yahoo Inc. announced an agreement today with Online Anywhere, a unit of Motorola Inc. that provides Internet content to a range of personal computer, wireless and other hand-held devices. Terms were not disclosed. Online Anywhere, based in Santa Clara, enables Internet content to be distributed to televisions and portable computers in a format specific to those devices. The agreement includes such Yahooservices as email, calendar, stock prices and weather. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
Bypassing Louvre Lines With On-Line Tickets
body: Visitors to Paris can now avoid long lines for entrance to the Louvre. Advance tickets are available on the Internet through Ticket Web, an Oakland-based on-line ticketing company. The tickets, good for admission any time until Jan. 31, 2000, to the Louvre's permanent collection, can be purchased at www.ticketweb.com or through the Louvre's Web site, www.louvre.fr. Tickets are also available at (510) 594-1400; fax (510) 594-1401. Ticket Web accepts Mastercard and Visa. Ticket holders enter through the Richelieu Passage, a separate entrance between the Place du Palais Royal and the Cour Napoleon. Prices for March -- the price is updated the 1st of each month, based on the exchange rate -- were $7.50 for entrance before 3 P.M. and $4.50 after 3 P.M. and on Sunday (the first Sunday of each month is free). There is a service fee of $1 an order and $1.60 a ticket. The Louvre is open daily except Tuesday from 9 A.M. to 6 P.M., and until 9:45 P.M. on Monday and Wednesday. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Wake-Up Calls at Home, Complete With Advertising
body: Thanks to the Internet, deep sleepers can get the same wake-up service they enjoy at hotels for free at home. But they'll have to put up with the dulcet tones of early morning marketing. A new Web site, www.mrwakeup.com, allows people to program in their phone numbers so they can be called back at a specified date and time. A computer then places the call, and the recipient is greeted with a synthesized computer voice intoning a reminder that it is time to rise. In addition to wake-up calls, the service can be programmed to provide short news blurbs, weather updates, horoscopes and 125-word reminders that the recipient types in; they are read by a text-to-voice synthesizer. The service is free, with a catch. Each call begins with a message from the call's sponsor; among the sponsors during the two-month old consumer test are Amazon.com and Starbucks. Eduardo Yeh, president of iPing, the newyork company behind the site, said he was planning to offer different voice types for the call.  "Soon you'll have a variety of voices, including female, one like a comedian and someone who sounds crazy, like nuts," Mr. Yeh said. http://www.nytimes.com

body: The stock of Abovenet Communications Inc. rose more than 32 percent today after the company, a provider of Internet connectivity services, said it would split its shares 2 for 1. The split would double the number of shares, to 27.2 million, but halve the value of each. The new shares will be issued on May 7 to holders of record as of April 14. OFFICE DEPOT INC., Delray Beach, Fla., the office-products retailer, acquired the remaining 50 percent of its Japanese operations from its joint-venture partner, Deo Deo Corp., for about $28 million. title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NETTAXI TO BUY PLUS NET TO UPGRADE ON-LINE COMMERCE
body: Nettaxi Inc., a World Wide Web community, agreed yesterday to buy the closely held Plus Net Inc., for about $70 million in stock to capitalize on Plus Net's advanced-search and comparison-shopping capabilities. Nettaxi said details of the transaction, including the total number of shares the company, which is based in Campbell, Calif., would issue, would be made final later this week. Plus Net, based in Los Angeles, brings Internet search, email and commerce technologies to Nettaxi, which plans to offer its subscribers the option to buy and sell goods from personal Web sites they create through Nettaxi. title: E*Trade Acquiring Another Web Site
body: E*Trade Group, the No. 3 on-line brokerage firm, said today that it had agreed to acquire Clearstation Inc., a financial World Wide Web site with 90,000 registered members. E*Trade, based in Palo Alto, said it would pay an undisclosed number of shares for Clearstation, which is based in San Francisco. The site being purchased, www.clearstation.com, was opened in July 1998 by Doug Fairclough, an Internet software developer, and Kris Skrinak, a former Wall Street trader and financial software developer. It offers technical and fundamental analysis tools, including message boards, personalized alerts and the ability to track multiple portfolios of stocks. E*Trade has gained almost one million registered members for its free Web site, www.etrade.com, since September 1998 as it tries to gain market share in the Internet brokerage industry. title:
INTERNATIONAL BRIEFS;
British Bookseller Plans Internet Service
body: W. H. Smith Group P.L.C., Britain's largest book retailer, said yesterday that it would set up a free Internet access service through a venture with the Microsoft Corporation and British Telecommunications P.L.C. Users will be able to buy books, music and videos. The move counters a free service begun by Dixons Group P.L.C. last September. The British Internet retail market is expected to grow to $5 billion by 2003 from $380 million last year. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
CNET BUYS KILLERAPP FOR $46.7 MILLION IN STOCK
body: CNET Inc. said that it had acquired the Killerapp Corporation, a closely held Internet media company based in Fremont, Calif., for about $46.7 million in stock. CNET, a producer of Internet network and television programming based in San Francisco, said it had exchanged 500,000 of its shares for the company. title: Arab Web Censorship
body: To the Editor: The Saudi Government has made no secret of its censorship of its citizens' access to the Internet ("The Internet's 'Open Sesame' Is Answered Warily," Riyadh Journal, March 18). But this is only the most recent such effort by a Middle Eastern government to block the flow of data in cyberspace. Iran and Bahrain block Web sites by political opposition movements; the United Arab Emirates blocks a site by a gay activist group, ; and Tunisia blocks sites by human rights groups. For more than a year Bahrain detained an engineer it suspected of emailing information to dissidents overseas. Elsewhere, governments have made Internet access too expensive for all but a small elite. Governments should not trample on international law protecting the right to receive and exchange information.  HANNY MEGALLY newyork, March 19, 1999  The writer is executive director, Human Rights Watch, Middle East and North Africa Division. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Arab Web Censorship;
Pakistan Is Wired
body: To the Editor: "The Internet's 'Open Sesame' Is Answered Warily" (Riyadh Journal, March 18) implied that the Internet is banned in many Muslim countries, and is just now slowly being introduced in some of them. But the examples cited include only a few Middle Eastern countries and Iran. In Pakistan use of the Internet has grown quickly over the past five or six years. And Malaysia was planning a "cybercity" to attract business before the recent economic crises there. Even in Bangladesh, nonprofit organizations are providing Internet access to the poor. Conservatives all over the world are concerned about the effect of pornographic, racist and propaganda on the Web, including the unitedstates, where Congress passed the Communications Decency Act before it was declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in 1997.  SHAHBAZ CHAUDHARY Ann Arbor, Mich., March 18, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
March 14-20;
Candidacy on the Net
body: The multimillionaire publisher Steve Forbes formally announced his candidacy for the Presidency, becoming the first contender to announce on the Internet. In his second campaign for the Republican nomination, Mr. Forbes cast himself as the unconventional choice, telling visitors to his Web site, "You and I are entering the information age -- and the Washington politicians are stuck in the Stone Age." In 1996, Mr. Forbes made his mark hawking the flat tax, which he still wants, but he devoted his opening speech to positioning himself as anti-abortion and as a supporter of religious conservatives. Although Mr. Forbes sank $36 million of his personal wealth into a lost cause last time, he is expected to be a force in shaping the political dialogue, win or lose. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Steve Forbes.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
IVILLAGE STOCK ENDS HIGHER THAN OFFERING PRICE
body: The stock of iVillage Inc., the Web site devoted to women's issues, closed yesterday at more than three times its offering price after the first day of trading. The shares jumped to as high as $100 each before closing at $80.125 in Nasdaq trading. iVillage had priced 3.65 million shares at $24 each late on Thursday, after having raised the range last Tuesday to $22 to $24 from $12 to $14. Goldman, Sachs was the lead underwriter for the issue. iVillage is similar to Yahoo, Excite and other popular Internet portals, except that its content is aimed at women, from career and parent tips to horoscopes and chat rooms. http://www.nytimes.com

title: CMGI to Split Shares
body: CMGI Inc., an Internet venture fund company, said today that it would split its shares 2 for 1. CMGI will split its shares May 27 to shareholders of record May 13, pending shareholder approval. It is the second split since December by the company, which has seen its shares more than triple in value since the start of the year. CMGI, which is the largest shareholder of the No. 3 Internet search service Lycos Inc., drew a spotlight last month when its chief executive said he would not support Lycos's pending acquisition by USA Networks Inc. Shares of CGMI fell $5.375 each, to $175.375. http://www.nytimes.com

body: A chart in Business Day on Tuesday, summarizing the approches of Internet stock trading companies, showed an erroneous screen to illustrate E*Trade. The screen belonged to a different company, known as e-trade. Here is that section of the chart corrected.  E*TRADE A broker that emerged purely as an Internet company.
