title:
NEWS WATCH;
Instant Postcards And Fast Food
body: Say cheeeese -- burger! Last month, Peter Allen Abramson, a Burger King franchisee who turned his Manhattan restaurant into the world's first cyber-burger joint, augmented his bank of 20 Internet-surfing computers with five Big Picture video cameras from the 3Com Corporation. The cameras, linked to the Internet through special high-speed lines that are also supplied by 3Com, enable munchers to zap their images -- in the form of an email post card -- to anywhere that the World Wide Web reaches. Neil Clemmons, vice president of consumer marketing for 3Com, called the idea "revolutionary." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
NBC and 24/7 In Marketing Deal
body: The NBC unit of the General Electric Company and 24/7 Media Inc. in newyork, a Web advertising company, have signed a three-year agreement to collaborate on television and Internet marketing plans for local advertisers. As part of the deal, NBC will take a small stake in 24/7 as 24/7 and NBC-Interactive Neighborhood, an on-line network of NBC stations featuring local community information, create ad packages for the local NBC stations and their Web sites. A nationwide sales staff based at the NBC stations and 24/7 offices will sell the ad packages. The alliance is part of NBC's efforts to find new revenue streams apart from traditional sales of commercial time.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
LOTUS PACIFIC TO BUY STAKE IN TURBONET COMMUNICATIONS
body: Lotus Pacific Inc., which offers on-line trading services and Internet access through television sets, agreed to buy 81 percent of the cable modem maker Turbonet Communications for $80 million in restricted stock as it seeks to broaden its customer base. Turbonet will not be able to sell the stock until it has annual revenue in excess of $30 million and pretax annual profit of $6 million. Turbonet, based in San Diego and partly owned by the Toshiba Corporation, currently has annual revenue of about $2 million. Lotus Pacific, based in Piscataway, N.J., offers Internet access though TV set-top boxes in hotel rooms. http://www.nytimes.com

title: College Web Surfers Need the Library, Too
body: To the Editor: Nate Stulman (Op-Ed, March 15) inserts a healthy "byte" of caution into the discussion of classroom technology. New technologies clearly offer great opportunities for learning and research. In my introductory courses, for example, I suggest Web-based resources to help with researching and writing papers. The problem is that while offering a great time-saving resource for collecting information, the new technologies do not easily teach students how to search in a discriminating manner or how to think critically about the information they download. Our enthusiasm for cyber-pedagogy should not prevent us from at least recognizing its potential negative impact on students who are far more likely to have surfed the Web than to have visited a library before they enter college.  MARK CASSELL Kent, Ohio, March 15, 1999  The writer is an assistant professor of political science at Kent State University. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
College Web Surfers Need the Library, Too;
Live and Learn
body: To the Editor: As a undergraduate I understand Nate Stulman's point that our fellow students spend way too much time on the computer ("The Great Campus Goof-Off Machine," Op-Ed, March 15). But Mr. Stulman's notion that universities are doing a disservice by providing Internet access -- which will revolutionize the way we live -- is downright foolish. High school and college students get in car accidents all the time; does that mean they shouldn't drive? The bottom line is that college life is a learning experience, a time in which students learn to live independently and to acquire self-discipline. I spend a lot of time on the Internet, and maybe I should be doing my schoolwork instead. But I have also learned to limit my surfing time, spend hours studying, and learn to enjoy life.  PAUL HOGARTH Berkeley, Calif., March 15, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
College Web Surfers Need the Library, Too;
World at Our Fingers
body: To the Editor: The Internet is not merely a tool for "finding simple facts," as opposed to one for doing serious research, as Nate Stulman claims, but the ultimate tool for fact-finding ("The Great Campus Goof-Off Machine," Op-Ed, March 15). Through the World Wide Web services my university subscribes to, I can read the thousands of different journals that are on line, covering AIDS research to international policy theory. The academic applications of the information available are endless. Contrary to Mr. Stulman, computer science or math majors are not the only students who need computers other than for email and word processing. The Internet has changed the way that research can be done in any field.  DAVID SCHWARTZ Medford, Mass., March 15, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
YAHOO TO OFFER CREDITCARD SERVICES THROUGH BANK ONE
body: Yahoo Inc., the No. 1 Internet directory, signed an agreement with the Bank One Corporation and the First Data Corporation to offer credit card processing services to on-line stores featured on Yahoo's Web site. Yahoo said it was working with Banc One Payment Services, a joint venture of First Data and Bank One. Terms were not disclosed. Yahoo began its store service last year, allowing retailers to design and set up Web sites that let people buy and sell goods on the Internet. The credit card service will help Yahoo merchants establish and process credit cards within 48 hours of setting up shop on the Web, instead of the usual wait of as long as six weeks. Yahoo rose $3.4375 a share, to $179.4375. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
BUSINESS: DIARY;
PuttingEvolution On Fast-Forward
body: The corporate chief who has created more shareholder value ($300 billion plus) than anyone not currently accused of monopolistic practices acknowledged in a newyork appearance last week that he is a "Neanderthal" when it comes to computers. But that executive, John F. Welch Jr. of General Electric, is determined that each of his company's businesses will leap from the Stone Age to the 21st century when it comes to making the best use of the Internet. The pace of the Internet's growth, seen in the surge of on-line retail sales at the end of last year, caught him by surprise, Mr. Welch acknowledged to an audience at the 92d Street "Y." Among the company's many units, he credited only NBC with making good use of the new medium.  MSNBC, the cable channel, is owned by NBC and Microsoft; the chairman of Microsoft, William H. Gates, is one of Mr. Welch's golfing buddies. G.E. is seeking ways to use its own Internet interests as currency to buy or invest in other Internet businesses. Instead of dipping into its $4.3 billion cash hoard to make acquisitions, Mr. Welch said, "we have to have seven more dot-coms, so we can trade our paper with somebody else's paper."   ALLEN R. MYERSON http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Welch

title: On the Internet, Bigger Is Better
body: To the Editor: Thomas L. Friedman's March 9 column, his second in two weeks on Lyle Bowlin, implies that anyone can compete against the big companies using the Internet. Well, yes, especially if he or she can get a columnist of The Times to provide free publicity. Those who can't will face the clutter of thousands of competing small fry, as well as the advertising clout of the big fish.  EDWARD GOLDSTEIN Brookline, Mass., March 9, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Karen Caldicott)

title: Yahoo in Venture With Mannesmann
body: In a move to catch the growing European market, the Internet media company Yahoo Germany joined forces yesterday with Germany's second-largest telecommunications service provider to ease access to the Internet. Yahoo's pact with Mannesmann Arcor is an attempt to expand its service in the country, which has 8.4 million German-speaking Internet users. Beginning May 1999, the new Yahoo Online service will be available via Yahoo's home page, a Mannesmann statement said. Clicking on the Yahoo Online icon dials a Mannesmann Arcor number and the user is directly connected to Yahoo Germany's starting page. On-line users visiting Mannesmann Arcor's Web site will get free access to Yahoo's German and all international Web services. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Yahoo Inc., based in Santa Clara, Calif., is among the most widely used sources of information and discovery on the World Wide Web. http://www.nytimes.com

title: More Foreign Papers
body: To the Editor: Curious people will enjoy the newspapers mentioned in "Foreign Paper? Try Its Site" (March 4), but my favorite was not included. It is The Electronic Telegraph, the Internet version of Britain's Daily Telegraph (www.telegraph.co.uk). I like to get the British view of American news, and I find that we are no longer two peoples separated by a common language. Much of what I read in the British news section of that paper could have happened here. The site is well designed, with many links to Web sites that give valuable background information about the subject matter in different articles.  GAIL ENID ZIMMER Fair Lawn, N.J., March 5, 1999    http://www.nytimes.com

title: Skepticism as a Tool
body: To the Editor: In "Whales in the Minnesota River?" (March 4), the article about approaching Web sites with skepticism, it says that many librarians "are learning to navigate the world of the Web, and they may just point an information-hungry consumer elsewhere." Librarians have always been on the leading edge of organizing and evaluating Internet resources, and if they sometimes steer users away from the Web, that is because the best information resource may be off line. Each research query requires a unique solution, and the Internet is one tool of many.  MONICA BERGER newyork, March 4, 1999  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Chinese Books For Sale on Line
body: An Internet-based bookstore began operating today in Beijing, offering more than 160,000 Chinese titles, according to the Compaq Computer Corporation. Compaq, based in Houston, said the enterprise, known as Beijing Book Center Online and developed by Compaq China and the China Information Highway Corporation, was opened in Beijing by Compaq's president, Eckhard Pfeiffer, and the Vice Mayor of Beijing, Lin Wenyi. China Information Highway will handle technology deployment, systems integration and infrastructure. Compaq will provide servers, along with technical support. "E-commerce is the focus of the information industry and the star of 21st-century businesses," Mr. Lin said. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
METRO NEWS BRIEFS: NEW YORK;
Spitzer Seeks Laws Protecting Web Users
body: Legislation to make it easier for Internet users to maintain on-line privacy and to fend off unwanted email was proposed yesterday by State Attorney General Eliot L. Spitzer. Concern about computer and software systems capable of discerning personal information about Web users has been increasing. The Manhattan Democrat said his bill would prevent companies from selling information about Web users without authorization. A companion bill is aimed at protecting users from mass transmissions of junk email. Mr. Spitzer would require marketers to provide identifying information with email and give consumers the chance to decline future transmissions. http://www.nytimes.com

title: On-Line Commerce Deal
body: Imall Inc. said today that it would buy an on-line credit card processing company, Pure Payments Inc., in a stock deal valued at about $6.2 million. Imall, based in Santa Monica, is one of the largest virtual shopping malls on the Internet. The transaction will allow merchants on Imall to reduce the number of steps it takes to add processing of credit card payments to their on-line stores. The deal is valued at about $6.2 million based on Imall's closing stock price on Monday. Imall's shares rose 50 cents today, to $14.25, in Nasdaq trading. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Executive Nominated for Times Co. Board
body: The board of The newyork Times Company has nominated Henry B. Schacht, former chairman and chief executive of Lucent Technologies Inc., for election as a director at the Times Company's annual shareholder meeting on April 15. Mr. Schacht, 64, retired last year as chairman of Lucent, the communications-equipment maker, based in Murray Hill, N.J., that was spun off from the AT&T Corporation in 1996. He had stepped down as chief executive in 1997. Before joining Lucent in 1995, Mr. Schacht had been chairman and chief executive of the Cummins Engine Company, which he first joined in 1964 as a vice president. Last month, the Times Company announced that Raul E. Cesan, the president and chief operating officer of the Schering-Plough Corporation, had also been nominated for election as a director at the shareholder meeting next month. Two current directors, William O. Taylor and George L. Shinn, are retiring. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Henry Schacht, board nominee.

title:
INVESTING: DIARY;
No Stopping the On-Line Parade
body: Investors keep funneling record numbers of stock trades through the Internet, and average trading volumes are expected to rise at least 25 percent in the first quarter of this year, an industry analyst said last week. Buoyed by heavy trading in shares of Internet companies, on-line brokerage firms should process an average of 425,000 trades a day in the first quarter, up from 340,000 a day in the fourth quarter of 1998, said the analyst, Bill Burnham of CS First Boston. The projected 25 percent increase in on-line trading is less than the 34 percent gain reported in the fourth quarter. That is because Mr. Burnham expects a slight decline in March, based on current trends. "It's a conservative estimate; actually brokerages are now running at a 30 percent growth rate," he said, adding that trading volumes were trailing off slightly in February after a very strong January. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ALCATEL AGREES TO BUYASSURED ACCESS FOR $350 MILLION
body: Alcatel S.A., Europe's No. 2 phone-equipment maker, made another foray into the unitedstates Internet technology market yesterday by agreeing to buy the closely held Assured Access Technology Inc. for $350 million in cash. Assured Access, based in Milpitas, Calif., makes remote access devices that let phone companies and Internet service providers sell services that allow people to dial into a computer network from remote locations, like homes and airports. Earlier this week, Alcatel agreed to buy the Xylan Corporation, which makes data-networking equipment for corporate networks, for $2 billion in cash. Shares in Alcatel, based in Paris, rose 4.8 euros, to 113.9. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
VERIO TO PAY AMERICA O NLINE FOR WEB SERVICES DEAL
body: The Internet-service provider Verio Inc. will pay America Online Inc. at least $42.5 million to become the on-line service company's exclusive operator of Web sites for businesses. America Online will also get a share of future revenue in the deal, which includes a Verio and America Online Web site that will offer Verio Web services and Internet commerce products, the companies said yesterday. Verio will receive on-line advertising and promotion of the venture. Verio shares rose $4, to $36.50, while America Online's fell 81.25 cents, to $86.25. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DELL COMPUTER OPENS SUPERSTORE TO EXPAND WEB SALES
body: The Dell Computer Corporation opened an on-line superstore yesterday for consumers to buy electronics and computer-related products. The Wall Street Journal reported the move yesterday. The store, which can be found at www.gigabuys.com, offers shoppers more than 30,000 computer-related products from many leading brands, the company said. Dell sells more than $14 million in products each day over the Web, 25 percent of the company's business. It plans to do 50 percent of its business on line by the end of 2000, officials said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Paine Webber Takes Kingland Stake
body: Paine Webber Group Inc., the nation's fifth-largest brokerage firm, said yesterday that it would take a 25 percent equity stake in the Kingland Companies, an Internet software developer, for $13.5 million. Kingland, the parent of the Kingland Systems Corporation, helped Paine Webber develop software to link its brokers' computer screens with its trade and account processing operations in 1997. "We wanted to make sure we continue our relationship with Kingland," Bob Silver, Paine Webber's director of operations, service and systems, said in a telephone interview. "It also gives us more insights into the on-line financial services market." Kingland, based in Mason City, Iowa, develops a range of browser-based systems for brokers, insurers and banks, including BankAmerica, Wachovia and the on-line investment bank Wit Capital. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AT&T PLANS TO DIRECT CAPITAL SPENDING TO THE INTERNET
body: The AT&T Corporation said yesterday that it wanted to stop investing in traditional long-distance telephone systems by next year. In a conference call with reporters, Frank Ianna, president of AT&T's network operation, said the company intended to stop buying long-distance switches for traditional telephone calls made by Lucent Technologies Inc. and would redirect its annual capital spending of about $6 billion toward products based on Internet technology. He added that the company would continue to buy other Lucent products. AT&T also said yesterday that it would participate in a group formed by Lucent, Motorola and other companies to promote new uses for the Internet, such as services that read email over the phone. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MICROSOFT BUYS 5% STAKE IN DIALOGIC AND EXPANDS PACT
body: The Microsoft Corporation said yesterday that it would buy a 5 percent stake in the Dialogic Corporation for $24.2 million and enter a $20 million licensing and service pact with Dialogic to expand in telecommunications. Dialogic, which electronically links telephones and computers, will receive the $20 million over four years for product development, support and licensing of its products. The agreements expand the companies' previous joint development of standards for Internet voice transmission and could make it easier for software developers to write programs for voice transmissions over the Internet, voice recognition and call centers, analysts said. Shares of Dialogic rose $3.125, to $34, while Microsoft fell $3.1875, to $148.5625. http://www.nytimes.com

title: CMGI to Acquire Internet Profiles
body: CMGI Inc., an Internet venture capital concern, said today that it would buy the closely held Internet Profiles Corporation for an undisclosed price and would use it for expansion into the Internet traffic-tracking business. CMGI said it would merge Internet Profiles, based in Redwood City, Calif., with Engage Technologies, a business it already owns. Engage sells technology that allows companies to profile Web site visitors. Internet Profiles measures traffic to Internet sites. CMGI said the acquisition would give Engage additional research services, allowing the combined company to integrate audience information with actual site traffic. It will also help position Engage to meet the increasing demand for on-line advertising and marketing information, CMGI's chairman and chief executive, David Wetherell, said in a statement. CMGI, based in Andover, had revenue of $91.5 million in 1998. Shares of CMGI rose $10.75 yesterday, to $133.375. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Ebay Stock Falls On U.S. Inquiry
body: The on-line auction site Ebay, which has already gained the attention of newyork City consumer officials, now says it is under Federal investigation for "possible illegal transactions." The company issued a terse release about the inquiry late Friday, withholding details about the substance "to protect the investigations," but saying that it was "fully cooperating." It said an unspecified branch of the Federal Government requested company documents on Jan. 29. The company's stock split 3 for 1 yesterday, and closed at $323, down $11 from Friday. Two weeks ago, Ebay announced that it would ban the sale of firearms on the site, effective this Friday. That move came in response to a report that weapon sales, governed in the off-line world by a complex set of rules that differ from state to state, were impossible to monitor in the geographically boundless on-line community. Officials at the company have also confirmed in recent weeks that they are cooperating with the newyork City Department of Consumer Affairs, which is investigating accusations of fraudulent activity on the part of a seller of sports memorabilia through Ebay. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Latest Land Rush: Virtual Real Estate
body: To the Editor: In his description of the ease with which someone can start his own Internet business, Thomas L. Friedman (column, Feb. 26) misses the subtle distinction between giving your customer a choice and helping him choose. The Internet magnifies these subtleties until, providing the retailer has a successful formula, there is a correlation between one's Internet address and a given product. The end result is the creation of virtual real estate, like being able to buy the corner of Broadway and 34th Street for your product. What Internet speculators seem to understand is that this real estate is currently available -- but it won't be forever.  STEVE PLOTNICKI newyork, Feb. 26, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Metro Business;
On-Line Bank Gets Cash
body: Wit Capital Group Inc., an on-line investment bank, said yesterday that Capital Z Financial Services Fund II L.P., which counts the insurance industry executive Steven Gluckstern as a partner, had taken a $25 million stake. Wit Capital, based in newyork, said it would use the funds to start an after-hours stock-trading system for individual investors and build its business of raising money for companies over the Internet. Capital Z, also based in newyork, is to name two members to Wit's board of directors. In a news release, Mr. Gluckstern said after-hours trading represented "an untapped avenue." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
PRIVATE SECTOR;
All in the (Jordan) Family
body: Vickee Jordan Adams, a senior vice president at Ketchum, a public relations agency, has been named director of corporate communications at Dow Jones & Company. Ms. Adams, 40, is the daughter of Vernon E. Jordan Jr., the Washington lawyer and Presidential confidant, who has been a member of the Dow Jones board since 1982. She will report to Richard J. Tofel, the company's vice president for corporate communications. "I have known her for many years," Mr. Tofel said. "Hiring her was entirely my idea." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Frontier May Spin Off Local Phone Business
body: The Frontier Corporation said yesterday that it was exploring a range of restructuring options, including spinning off its local phone operations and creating a separate stock for its Internet business. Frontier, the former Rochester Telephone, has spent the last 18 months revamping in an effort to distance itself from its past as a stodgy public utility and to be perceived as a fast-moving modern communications company. Frontier provides local, long-distance and wireless phone service and has made aggressive moves to build data-transmission and Internet businesses. In 1998, it posted revenue of $2.6 billion, up 9 percent from the year before. Joe Clayton, Frontier's chief executive, said it was a "distinct possibility" that the company would split itself into parts. "We could conceivably do both," Mr. Clayton said, referring to the issue of a so-called tracking stock for the Internet business and a spinoff of the local telephone business. The company emphasized that no decision had been made yet, and that it might decide to keep all its units together. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Gateway Plans to Offer Free Net Service
body: Starting Friday, Gateway 2000 Inc., the No. 2 direct seller of personal computers, will offer customers one year of free Internet service when they buy machines costing more than $1,000. Buyers will get 150 free hours of Internet use a month through gateway.net, the company's on-line service. Each hour beyond that will cost $1.50, the company said on Wednesday. "We talk with more than 50,000 people every day and understand that most of them want a computer so they can get on the Web," Gateway's chief executive, Theodore W. Waitt, said in a statement. Gateway also said that it had bought a 20 percent stake in NECX, a closely held on-line seller of computers and other electronic products, for about $21 million. The companies plan to start an Internet site called Spotshop.com to sell Gateway products. Gateway said it had the option to make an additional investment in NECX in the future. Gateway sells its PC's directly to consumers over the telephone and Internet. The North Sioux City company also sells its machines through its chain of Gateway Country Stores. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Metro Business;
Chase Is Offering On-Line Banking
body: A Chase Manhattan official said yesterday that the bank would start offering banking services over the Internet, becoming the last of the nation's seven biggest consumer banks to do so. Online Banking Report, an industry newsletter based in Seattle, said that about 300 banks had provided the service before Chase, the second largest bank in the country. Wells Fargo started Internet banking in 1995 and more than 600,000 customers now use it, the most among American banks. Chase's service allows customers to check their account balances and transaction records, transfer money between accounts and pay bills. The bank started Internet banking services in 1997, but only for businesses, which had to use the bank's software and could not bank over the Web, which offers consumers access from virtually any computer without the need to maintain software. The bank will promote Internet banking through broadcast and print advertisements, and does not plan to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on Internet marketing agreements with popular Web sites, unlike one of its competitors, said Bruce Zimmerman, senior vice president and manager of Chase's Internet services. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
BEYOND.COM AGREES TO BUY SOFTWARE DISTRIBUTOR
body: The Beyond.com Corporation, an Internet-based computer software retailer, said yesterday that it had agreed to buy its closely held rival Buydirect.com for about $143.4 million in stock. Beyond.com, based in Sunnyvale, Calif., is gaining Buydirect.com's expertise in distributing software through programs over the Internet. While this technology is not widely used by consumers, many analysts expect it will boom as high-speed Internet access becomes more common, cutting down on the time it takes to download a program. Shares of Beyond.com rose $1.8125 yesterday, to $26.5625. Buydirect.com is based in San Francisco. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Metro Business;
Web and Video Link
body: The on-line service provider Prodigy Communications Corporation will post entertainment information from the video rental chain Blockbuster Inc. on the Internet, and Blockbuster will offer free Prodigy software under an alliance the companies announced yesterday. Prodigy, based in White Plains, said subscribers would receive a customizable page with information from Blockbuster about entertainment, video releases and specials. Blockbuster, in turn, will market the service and distribute free Prodigy Internet software to its members in nearly 4,000 Blockbuster stores. "Consumers can get a fast and reliable Internet connection through Prodigy, surf the Web and get exposure to Blockbuster.com offerings," Gena Kay Sedlak, Blockbuster's vice president of technology, said in a statement. Blockbuster will initially offer free co-branded Prodigy Internet CD-ROMs to its members, with the service costing $9.95 each of the first three months and $19.95 each of the following months in the first year of service. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
FEBRUARY 14-20;
On-Line Magazine Free, Again
body: Ten months after deciding to charge readers $19.95 a year, the publisher of the on-line magazine Slate announced in an email notice to subscribers that the magazine is now available free on the World Wide Web. The fee was an important test of one facet of Internet commerce: Would readers pay to read a magazine -- even a really good one -- on line? The answer, for now, is no.   ALEX KUCZYNSKI   http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MERRILL LYNCH TO PURCHASE D. E. SHAW UNIT
body: Merrill Lynch & Company confirmed yesterday that it had signed a definitive agreement to buy D. E. Shaw & Company's Internet technology unit as part of a plan to compete in the on-line trading business. Financial terms were not disclosed. Merrill Lynch said it expected to begin on-line entry of some customers' orders for securities and mutual funds in the next few weeks. The Wall Street Journal reported yesterday that Merrill Lynch was likely to pay $25 million to $35 million for the unit, D. E. Shaw Financial Technology L.P. Merrill Lynch intends to offer investors services, including trading, at roughly the same fees it now charges for securities sold through brokers, The Journal reported. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Filtering the Internet
body: To the Editor: "Free Speech and the Internet" (editorial, Feb. 16) rightly points out that it is difficult for lawmakers to avoid trampling on the First Amendment in their efforts to shield children from offensive material on the Internet. But you give the impression that filtering software would avoid infringements on free speech, and you do not mention an important court decision from Virginia. In the Loudoun County case, a Federal judge struck down as unconstitutional the use by a public library of filtering software that would have prevented adults from having access to First Amendment-protected speech. The software blocked Web sites that might be inappropriate for children but are in no sense obscene and outside protection. Filtering software has its place in the home, but its use in public libraries is at best suspect.  GINO J. SCARSELLI Associate Legal Director A.C.L.U. of Ohio Foundation Cleveland, Feb. 17, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
PROVIDIAN ACQUIRES GETSMART.COM FOR $33 MILLION CASH
body: The Providian Financial Corporation, the nation's biggest issuer of credit cards backed by deposits, said yesterday that it had bought Getsmart.com, which operates an Internet site where consumers can apply for loans, for $33 million in cash. Getsmart.com allows consumers to comparison-shop and apply for credit card, mortgage, home equity and personal loans from about 100 lenders on its site. It drew eight million visitors and processed 500,000 applications in 1998. Providian also established a new division to build its Internet businesses. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Drug ExecutiveNominated For Times Company Board
body: The board of The newyork Times Company has nominated Raul E. Cesan, president and chief operating officer of the Schering-Plough Corporation, for election as a director at the Times Company's annual shareholder meeting on April 15. The company also announced that two current directors, William O. Taylor and George L. Shinn, were retiring from the board. Mr. Cesan, 51, was named in November to his current position at Schering, a pharmaceuticals and health care products company based in Madison, N.J. He joined Schering in 1977 as director of finance and administration for the company's Latin American region. He later held positions of increasing responsibility, including president of operations in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and was appointed president of Schering-Plough International in 1988. In 1992, he became president of Schering-Plough Laboratories and president of Schering-Plough Pharmaceuticals in 1994. Mr. Taylor, 65, is chairman emeritus of the Globe Newspaper Company and a former publisher of The Boston Globe, now owned by the Times Company. Mr. Shinn, 74, is a consultant and a former chairman and chief executive of First Boston. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Raul E. Cesan

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
New Times VicePresident
body: The newyork Times has appointed Yasmin Namini vice president for circulation marketing. She will help direct sales and marketing efforts for the newspaper. Ms. Namini, 38, was previously group director of circulation marketing, planning and product management. She joined The Times in 1984. She received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of Maryland in 1981 and a master's degree in applied statistics from Villanova University in 1989. http://www.nytimes.com

title: A Niche Market on Line
body: To the Editor: I read "Buying is Only a Click (Oops!) Away" (Feb. 11) and wanted to share my experience. Through Ebay, I was able to find a woman who has been supplying me with chipped plates, which I use to make mosaic picture frames, mirrors and other items. A cyberspace twist for a cottage industry.  MARSHA EDELL Larchmont, N.Y., Feb. 11, 1999  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ETOYS FILES FOR A $115 MILLION INITIAL PUBLIC OFFERING
body: Etoys Inc., an Internet seller of toys, games, videos and software, filed for an initial public offering that could raise as much as $115 million. The company, based in Santa Monica, Calif., started its virtual store at www.etoys.com in October 1997. By last December, Etoys was the No. 5 most-visited Internet retail site, with about 3.9 million individual shoppers, according to the Web market watcher Media Metrix Inc. Etoys did not say the number or price of its common shares in the offering, which it filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission yesterday. The $115 million estimated offering value was provided only as a basis for calculating the registration fee. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Softbank Trims Its Yahoo Stake
body: The Softbank Corporation, Japan's top software distributor and a shareholder in dozens of Internet ventures, said today that it had sold a $410 million stake in Yahoo Inc. to finance new investments. Softbank's unitedstates holding company sold three million shares in the world's most-visited Internet directory, reducing its stake to 28 percent from 30 percent and recording a capital gain of $390 million. The one-time gain will drag the company out of the red, tripling its group profit to 32 billion yen ($271 million). The company, which has accumulated several billion dollars in paper gains on a series of early investments in Yahoo and other fast-growing Internet services, said it planned to set up a new fund to add other on-line ventures to its portfolio. The sale of Yahoo shares will offset a drain on earnings by its American affiliate Ziff-Davis Inc. that will necessitate a $57 million revamping charge.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
For the Refrigerator, A Silicon-Chip Treat
body: The Internet refrigerator has long been a kind of Silicon Valley joke (killer app: crispy lettuce) but don't tell that to the people at Electrolux. In tandem with the software company ICL, the appliance manufacturer recently unveiled a prototype of the Screenfridge, a fridge-freezer equipped with a touch screen and a bar-code scanner. The touch screen has an Internet link, including email, and the scanner can be used to swipe items, entering them directly into a Web shopping list. "After PC modems and interactive TV, we were looking for the most appropriate room in the house for electronic commerce," said Sion Roberts, ICL's vice president for interactive retailing. "The kitchen is the focus for the household community." The Screenfridge will be tested in Europe this year, and the companies are working on a separate screen-only unit that can sit on the doors of existing fridges "like a giant, modern-day fridge magnet." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: Health Web Site Makes CNN Deal
body: CNN News Group, a unit of Time Warner Inc., said today that it had invested an undisclosed amount in the closely held Web MD and signed an agreement to exchange news and advertising with the company, an on-line medical information service. Financial details were not disclosed. Under the agreement, Web MD committed itself to a three-year, multimillion-dollar ad campaign across six CNN cable television networks. Web MD will be promoted on CNN Web sites, television and radio. CNN will use information from Web MD's Internet site, including health news and reports on medical research. The Atlanta-based Web MD provides medical research and health news, insurance verification and medical-supply data to the Web pages of doctors and consumers. Time Warner, based in newyork, rose $2.375 today, to $63.50. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
METRO NEWS BRIEFS: NEW YORK;
Motor Vehicles Office Plans TV's for Patrons
body: Officials at the State Department of Motor Vehicles announced plans yesterday to install television sets at 27 district offices around the state that customers can watch while waiting for service. The 27-inch monitors will show news, sports, lottery, weather reports, traffic safety messages and information on how to conduct business at the agency. Pegasus Internet Communication Inc. of Jericho, was awarded the contract. CBS has agreed to broadcast the news programming, said Sam Carino, an owner of Pegasus. Advertisements will pay for the program, and the department will get a 15 percent commission. The service is to begin March 1 at eight offices in Albany, newyork City and Long Island.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
February 7-13;
Internet Reality Check
body: If investors in high-flying Internet stocks secretly suspect they are playing with Monopoly money, there was some evidence to back up the fear last week. Lycos, a modest Internet gateway with a stock price in never-never land, said it was merging with the electronic shopping units of USA Networks, including Home Shopping Network and Ticketmaster -- a business with 20 times the revenues. In other words, little Lycos had made it to the big time. This was the payoff. Or so it would seem. The trouble is that investors said, wait a second: This isn't an Internet stock anymore! Lycos, they realized, would now be a very measurable part of an earthbound company, and they quickly shoved their money back in their pockets. Lycos shares plunged 26 percent in a day.   HUBERT B. HERRING http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING: DIARY;
For Internet Users, Safety Is an Issue
body: What worries Internet users when it comes to trading stocks on line? Safety, first and foremost, according to a poll by CBS News and cbs.marketwatch.com. The survey, conducted between Jan. 27 and Feb. 2, found that security was the No. 1 concern of 35 percent of the 876 respondents. Execution of trades was the next-biggest worry, cited by 10 percent. Traditional publishers should take note: The quality of financial data available on the Internet was only the No. 3 concern, cited by just 6 percent. (Three percent cited all three.) Indeed, 80 percent of respondents said financial news and information available on the Web was as reliable or more reliable than that available from traditional sources. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
CENDANT PLANS TO SELLTHREE OF ITS INTERNET COMPANIES
body: The Cendant Corporation, the hotel franchiser, said yesterday that it planned to sell three of its Internet companies: Rentnet, Bookstacks Inc. and Match.com. The units have been marginally profitable, Cendant said, but they are not beneficial to its core businesses. The company also plans to invest in its Internet membership businesses, which are unprofitable, but are integral to its individual membership businesses. Cendant said it would seek strategic partnerships with major Internet players. Separately, Cendant reported operating earnings of 22 cents a diluted share yesterday after the close of trading, compared with 13 cents in the period a year earlier, beating expectations of 20 cents. Earlier, its shares closed down $1.1875, to $19. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Birder's Eye View Helps In Tracking Migration
body: From the 19th to the 22d of this month, bird watchers nationwide can use the Internet to help the National Audubon Society track the winter bird migration. The Audubon Society, along with Cornell University, is seeking volunteers in the second annual "backyard bird watch" to report their daily sightings to the Web at birdsource.cornell.edu. Taking birding information on line will allow scientists to digest and publish the daily sightings more quickly, said John Bianchi, spokesman for National Audubon Society, based in newyork. "As results come in, we'll publish them on a map," he said of the bird-watching updates. "It will be just like election returns." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: Shaw Sells Part of Its Cable Stakes in U.S.
body: Shaw Communications, the second-largest cable television operator in Canada, said here today that it had sold stakes in two American companies, the At Home Corporation and Terayon Communications Systems, for $80.6 million (Canadian), or $54.1 million (unitedstates), to capitalize on huge share-price gains. Shaw indicated it had a combined gross profit of $70 million (Canadian) on the sale of 375,000 shares of At Home, the leading provider of high-speed Internet access over cable lines, and 250,000 shares of Terayon, a cable modem system maker. Shaw invested in the two companies as it began offering Internet access to its cable subscribers. It continues to hold more than 3.8 million shares and warrants in At Home and 3.4 million shares and warrants in Terayon. Shaw said it would realize a pretax profit around $45 million (Canadian) from the sale of At Home after accounting adjustments, including an employee-incentive program. It did not disclose its pretax profit on Terayon. In Toronto trading today, Shaw's class B shares fell 60 cents, to $42 (Canadian). On the Nasdaq market, At Home rose $3.75, to $96.125, and Terayon gained $2.375, closing at $35.75. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Government Plans to Track Internet Sales
body: The Commerce Department said today that it would begin tracking sales on the Internet, which it called "a major indicator of the nation's economic health." But even as the Government pointed to figures showing that consumers spent $9 billion last year on the Internet, it warned that growth of electronic commerce would wane unless shoppers trusted that personal information would be kept private. "I wouldn't want people selling information about which books I buy, or what records I buy," said Robert Pitofsky, chairman of the Federal Trade Commission. "The Internet is probably going to grow, anyway. It's just not going to grow as fast until these concerns are addressed." "Consumers have to feel as comfortable doing business in cyberspace as they do on Main Street," added Commerce Secretary William M. Daley. Mr. Daley said his agency would begin tracking sales over the Internet separately from figures for catalogue sales. But he said complete figures for last year and this year would not be available until next summer. The F.T.C. has criticized the on-line industry for its failure to protect privacy rights. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
National News Briefs;
Anti-Abortion Web Site Shut Down by Provider
body: An Internet service provider has shut down an anti-abortion Web site that an Oregon jury on Tuesday said constituted a threat to abortion providers. The move on Thursday night came a day after the creator of the Web site, Neal Horsley, said he planned to add video cameras at abortion clinics in five American cities as well as in England and Japan to monitor activities for the Web. The Web site included the names and addresses of abortion doctors. Three of those doctors were killed, most recently in October when a sniper shot Dr. Barnett Slepian in his home outside Buffalo. Dr. Slepian's name on the Web site was crossed out that same day. Mindspring, which provided the Internet space for the Web site, said it shut it down for violating "appropriate-use policies." A Federal jury ruled on Tuesday that the site constituted a threat to abortion providers and awarded the plaintiffs $107 million in damages. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Wit Capital Hires Analyst
body: The Wit Capital Corporation, the brokerage firm that pioneered the sale of stock over the Internet, said yesterday that it had hired Jonathan Cohen, a Merrill Lynch analyst, as its director of research. Mr. Cohen followed Internet companies for Merrill Lynch. He was named to Institutional Investor's All-American Research Team in 1996, 1997 and 1998, Wit Capital said. He will continue to follow Internet companies and will build a group of analysts to provide research to Wit's individual investor clients, the firm said. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
LIBRARY/TAX SOFTWARE;
Before You Buy - Correction Appended
body: Here are some things to consider before buying tax software:  Make sure the software works on your computer. -- Many tax packages have demanding system requirements. Make sure you get all the forms you need.  Make sure the program handles your state returns. -- Not all programs handle all states. State software can cost extra.  Look for a program that will import data you already have. -- If you used tax software last year or use personal financial software, some programs can make use of that information.  Compare with Web-based programs. -- Using the Web to prepare taxes can cost less than using software, but Web software tends to be slower than a desktop package, have fewer features or both.  Never pay list price. -- You can save money with discounts and rebates, and it is often cheaper to download software from the Web. You can deduct the cost on next year's return.   STEVEN E. BRIER http://www.nytimes.com Correction  A chart in Circuits yesterday about buying tax preparation software referred imprecisely to the deductibility of the cost. Tax preparation expenses can be claimed as a miscellaneous deduction from income on the next year's return, but such miscellaneous deductions can be taken from the taxpayer's income only to the extent that their total exceeds 2 percent of adjusted gross income. Correction-Date: February 5, 1999, Friday

title: Live Victoria's Secret Show Jams Web Site
body: Victoria's Secret broadcast its annual Spring Fashion Show over the Internet yesterday, but it was not prepared for the number of people who tuned in to watch. The computers failed as millions of Web surfers tried to log on. The Web site was sluggish, the video of the 14-minute show was often jagged and the sound cut out. "That says to me the technology is not up to snuff," said Wendy Hargle, a computer technician in Berkeley, Calif., who tried to view the show. "Someone did not anticipate the level of interest." She thought many people might have tried to grab the good seats early, so to speak, by logging onto the Web site and keeping their connections open, thus preventing others from logging on. The fashion show was one of the first large-scale live video events in which a corporation invested money and prestige. Victoria's Secret is owned by Intimate Brands Inc. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Technology for Blind Users Even Reads the Internet Ads
body: This week I.B.M. started selling technology that allows blind users to hear the World Wide Web. Called Home Page Reader, the software, which costs $149, uses a speech synthesizer not just to read the text on a given Web page but also to describe the graphics and even advertisements. Other screen readers are capable of reading Web-page text. But Paul Luther, a manager with International Business Machines' special-needs unit, said the Home Page Reader was designed specifically with the Web in mind and tailored to reading pages built in HTML. "If there's a picture of a person on bicycle, the Home Page Reader will say, 'There's a picture of a person on a bicycle,' " he said. "Then the blind user can say, 'I'm not interested in this,' and move on." (And when there's a banner advertisement, it will probably say: "Loading, loading, still loading. Go take a nap; I'll call you in 20 minutes.") http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Web Surfers Starting to Look Like Just About Everyone Else
body: The universe of Web users might need a group therapy session to come to terms with the latest assessment of their state: collectively, they have grown average. That is the essence of a new survey from the Pew Research Center for the People and the Press, based in Washington. The study found that the demographics of Web surfers, and their interests, had evolved strikingly in the last two years and now more closely resembled those of the general public. It seems that the single most-sought-after news item on the Net is the weather; today, 64 percent of users log on to learn about the weather, up from 46 percent two years ago. Andy Kohut, director of the Pew Research Center, said the changes reflected the changing demographics of the Web. "The ways the Internet is being used are more ordinary," he said. "The kinds of people who are using it are more typical and ordinary." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS;
Ebay Expands Auctions
body: Margaret C. Whitman, the chief executive of Ebay Inc., an on-line auctioneer, said the company had started offering auctions in Canada and Britain, expanding its service outside the unitedstates for the first time. The new services started operating last week, said Ms. Whitman, speaking at the NationsBanc Montgomery Securities technology conference in San Francisco. Ebay, which lets individuals and small businesses buy and sell items ranging from coffee pots to antique dolls on the Internet, makes money by charging listing fees and taking a portion of each sale. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
THEGLOBE.COM TO BUY AZAZZ.COM FROM FACTORYMALL.COM
body: Theglobe.com Inc., an Internet company that lets people set up free Web pages, said it would buy Azazz.com, an on-line department store, for about $18.5 million in stock to accelerate its move into electronic commerce. Theglobe.com will issue 307,000 shares to Azazz.com's parent, factorymall.com Inc., and will assume all the outstanding options and warrants of factorymall.com. Shares of theglobe.com fell $5.9375 yesterday, to $60.125. The company went public at $9 a share on Nov. 13. Azazz.com, based in Kirkland, Wash., offers a variety of goods and provides the help of a representative while the user is shopping on the Internet. Theglobe.com, based in newyork, currently provides connections to other on-line retailers of merchandise, including flowers, gift baskets and software. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Frank Rich Getting Dual Role at Times
body: Frank Rich, whose column has appeared on The newyork Times's Op-Ed page twice a week since January 1994, will write longer articles for the page and become a regular contributor to The Times Magazine. This arrangement was announced yesterday by Arthur Sulzberger Jr., publisher of the newspaper. Times editors said the new arrangement was a response to Mr. Rich's desire to write essays and articles lengthier than the 700-word Op-Ed format would permit. Starting in June, he will write a 1,400-word opinion article for the Op-Ed page every other Saturday. He will also write articles and commentaries for the magazine on a variety of subjects. Joseph Lelyveld, the executive editor, said Mr. Rich would "continue to be a major cultural critic in every possible sense." Mr. Rich joined The Times in 1980 and served as its chief theater critic for 13 years before becoming a columnist. Journal, Mr. Rich's 700-word column, will appear until Feb. 13. He will then take a four-month leave to finish a memoir for Random House and will return in June. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Ex-Chairman Sued by Internet Company
body: Michael Schulhof, the former chief executive of the Sony Corporation of America, is being sued by World Online International, the Dutch Internet company of which he was chairman until being dismissed on Jan. 11. The lawsuit, which was filed by World Online and its majority shareholders on Friday in state Supreme Court in Manhattan, contends that Mr. Schulhof and a company he controlled tried to steal business from World Online and that Mr. Schulhof used his World Online credit card to pay for a visit from a prostitute. The suit also said he made inappropriate comments to the company's investment bankers about sex clubs and prostitutes. Mr. Schulhoff and Ochill Investments N.V., a company he controlled, are also being sued in Amsterdam, said John Goldman, a lawyer for the firm that is representing plaintiffs. World Online's biggest shareholder, Rotonde, a subsidiary of the Sandoz Family Foundation, is expected to file another suit in Amsterdam today. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
TRADING IN NEW INTERNET COMPANY IS HALTED
body: The Securities and Exchange Commission suspended trading in the securities of USA Talks.com Inc., a start-up Internet telephony company, after its shares almost quadrupled in less than a month, to a market value of $1.3 billion. The agency said questions had been raised about "the accuracy and adequacy of public information" about the company, including questions about the status and extent of its business operations. Trading in the securities of five other high-flying companies was also halted by the S.E.C. While USA Talks.com has 25 million shares outstanding, fully diluted the actual number of free-trading shares is only about 600,000, said the company's president, William Ervine. Its shares last traded at $52.25. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Download Songs, Then Pay Sony
body: Sony Music Entertainment is studying a plan to allow Internet users to download music for a fee and record it onto minidisks, a company spokesman said today. Under the plan, customers would be charged according to the number of songs downloaded or the playing time of the music, the newspaper Asahi reported. The company is still conducting feasibility studies on the project and no decision has been made, said Kyouhei Akai, a Sony Music Entertainment spokesman. Potential problems include acquiring the rights to the music to be sold through the Internet, he said. Sony Music Entertainment's parent company, the Sony Corporation, has been aggressively pursuing new recording technologies including the minidisk. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Bubble Is Ready to Burst
body: To the Editor: Let's hope that the quest for creating durable companies rather than converting stock into cash is what drives the big shareholders in the Internet stock boom (news article, Jan. 25). If not, we will all be in trouble, both for the negative social impact of doing things simply for the money and for the economic woes that will be felt by investors and noninvestors alike. If a hot new Internet company's major shareholders decide to cash out quickly, the stock price will likely plummet. Wall Street knows that perception is reality. And from that perception, the reality would be disastrous: other investors unloading Internet stocks, analysts and brokers panicking that the Internet bubble had burst, and shock waves in the marketplace.  ADAM WEINER Boston, Jan. 26, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
FRANKLIN MUTUAL ADVISORS REDUCES STAKE IN DOW JONES
body: The investor group Franklin Mutual Advisors Inc. has cut its holdings in Dow Jones & Company to 5 percent, or 3,678,100 common shares, from a 5.4 percent stake reported in a 1997 filing in which it also disclosed its intention to press Dow to shed its Telerate division. MICROSOFT TO INVEST IN DUTCH CABLE-TELEVISION COMPANY

title:
NEWS WATCH;
New Domain Names Set a Record in 1998
body: Internet users who registered a domain name in 1998, the first step in publishing a Web site, were in good company. Network Solutions, the Herndon, Va., registrar of .com, .net, .org and .edu names, said it logged a record 1.9 million new domain names in 1998, nearly double the 1997 total of 960,000. The biggest number of these came from the unitedstates, followed by Canada and the United Kingdom. The states with the largest number of registrants were California, newyork, Florida and Texas, which a Network spokeswoman, Cheryl Regan, said was probably some reflection of both the size of those states and of the Net savvy of their populations. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Group Moves to Limit Internet Music Piracy
body: In a move designed to cut down piracy of music on the Internet, three dozen software and hardware companies and on-line retailers plan today to endorse the use of a so-called certificates of authentication that would accompany songs and albums distributed digitally. Record companies and other authorized sellers of licensed music would be able to include the certificates, which would appear on a computer monitor when users open a music file, said Gerry Kearby, chief executive of Liquid Audio. His company makes on-line audio software and is a leader of the new group, the Genuine Music Coalition. Various factions in the record industry, including musicians and executives, are pondering ways to cope with what they say is rampant proliferation of pirated music files on the Internet. Mr. Kearby said the certificate will not prevent illegal copying, but is meant to help publicize the names of licensed dealers, provide links to their World Wide Web sites, and perhaps deter users from making unlicensed copies of music. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
January 17-23;
An On-Line Auction With Cachet
body: The name Sotheby's usually brings to mind a collector snatching up a multimillion dollar artwork with the flick of a wooden paddle. Not any longer. Sotheby's announced it would join the Internet auction craze. At first, only items valued at less than $10,000 will be offered on the Internet www.sothebys.com but prices will climb once the technology allows close inspection of the merchandise. Seeking to deflect fears that it might become a cheesy home shopping network, Sotheby's promised that the on-line goods would come only from the auction house or reputable art dealers.   TERRY PRISTIN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Sotheby's offering last year.

title:
January 17-23;
Hacker Destroys U.S.I.A. Web Site
body: The intruder was mean as well as clever. Not content just to invade the Web site of the unitedstates Information Agency and leave a cryptic message, he (or she) knocked the site off the Internet. By week's end, computer experts at the agency, which oversees a variety of cultural and educational-exchange programs, were still trying to restore the site and promising better security. The intruder called himself "Zyklon," perhaps after Zyklon-B, the gas used in Nazi death camps.   DAVID STOUT http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AT&T SAID TO WEIGH SALE OF INTERNET ACCESS BUSINESS
body: The AT&T Corporation may be selling its Internet access business to the At Home Corporation, a deal that analysts say would give At Home greater muscle to compete against America Online Inc. The Wall Street Journal reported yesterday that AT&T is considering the sale of its Internet access business to At Home. In exchange, AT&T would get about $1 billion in At Home stock. AT&T will have even greater control of At Home after it completes its pending $48 billion acquisition of At Home's largest shareholder, the cable television giant Tele-Communications Inc. Neither AT&T nor At Home would comment on the report. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
TOYS 'R' US GOES ON LINE IN BRITAIN
body: Toys "R" Us Inc., the world's largest toy retailer, said yesterday that it had started a free Internet service in Britain to increase on-line sales. It becomes the second retailer in the world to offer free Internet access. The move follows the success of Freeserve, started by Dixons Group P.L.C., an appliance retailer, in September, which has since become Britain's largest Internet service provider. Toys "R" Us aims to make money from advertising and Internet commerce as more people shop on line. The British market for Internet retail sales is expected to rise to $5 billion by 2003. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Value America in Filing
body: Value America Inc. filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission for an initial public offering, marking the Internet retailer's second attempt at a first-time stock sale. The Charlottesville, Va., company will seek to sell five million common shares at $15 to $17 each, according to documents filed with the S.E.C. The proceeds are estimated at a net of $72.9 million if the shares sell for $16 each. , http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
COMPAQ CUTS PER-SHAREPRICE OF DEAL FOR SHOPPING.COM
body: The Compaq Computer Corporation yesterday said it was cutting the price of its tender offer for the on-line retailer Shopping.com by 75 cents a share, to $18.25, after receiving new information about a higher number of common shares and convertible securities outstanding. Compaq, the No. 1 personal computer maker, agreed last week to buy Shopping.com for $19 a share in cash, or $220 million. The total value of the newly structured deal remains $220 million, a Compaq spokesman said, because Compaq cut the price for each share in proportion to the number of additional shares that were identified after the original agreement. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Enron to Provide Fiber Optic Feed
body: The Enron Corporation, one of the nation's largest energy companies, and Real Networks Inc. formed an alliance to deliver high-quality video to Internet providers and companies over Enron's fiber optic network. Enron, which had 1998 sales of $31.3 billion, said today that its on-line venture would use Real Network's software, which lets users gain access to sound and video through their computers. Financial terms were not disclosed. The deal was first reported in The Wall Street Journal. Enron, based in Houston, will deliver live and on-demand feeds over its network at multiple speeds. The company introduced its fiber optic Enron Intelligent Network today. The network is being tested in eight cities and is part of the 15,000 mile fiber optic network. "We will have the product with Real Networks commercially available in newyork, Chicago, Washington, Dallas, Houston, Portland, San Francisco and Los Angeles in April," said Steve Elliott, the chief financial officer at Enron Communications Inc., a unit of Enron. Enron shares rose 93.75 cents, to $66, while Real Networks fell $1.50, to $55.75, along with other Internet stocks. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Sun Microsystems' Earnings Grow 22%
body: Sun Microsystems Inc., one of the biggest makers of computers that run the Internet, said today that fiscal second-quarter earnings rose 22 percent, fueled by robust sales of its powerful machines. Profit before a charge rose to $272.3 million, or 67 cents a diluted share, from $223.2 million, or 57 cents, in the corresponding period a year earlier. Sun was expected to earn 66 cents in the quarter ended Dec. 27, the average estimate of analysts polled by the First Call Corporation. Shares of Sun, which also declared a 2-for-1 stock split today, have almost doubled in the last three months on optimism that the market for computers used by Internet service providers and for sites on the World Wide Web will remain hot. Sun's sales rose 14 percent, to $2.78 billion from $2.45 billion. "The market for high-end servers is robust," Phil Rueppel, an analyst with BT Alex. Brown, said. He rates Sun shares "buy." Sun, based in Palo Alto, reported earnings after the close of regular trading. Its shares fell $7.125, to $98.25, amid concern that it might have trouble meeting optimistic earnings forecasts because it switched to a new system for handling its orders, manufacturing and distribution.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Overseas Internet Users Protest High Cost of Access
body: Internet users in Brazil said on Wednesday that they would stage a cyberstrike: They pledged to refuse to log on to the Internet for the day to protest the high cost of Net access. The cyberstrikers in Brazil join Web surfers who have engaged in "Internet strikes" in Germany, France, Spain, the Czech Republic, China and Poland. Often organized by students and academics, the strikes are meant to protest high access charges, which can mount to hundreds of dollars in monthly Internet bills. In Brazil, supporters said that as many as 500,000 of 2.2 million Internet users would participate in the boycott, The Associated Press reported. In most countries the protests are aimed not at the service providers, but at the national telecommunication companies, which are sometimes state-owned monopolies. In China, protesters there said they would boycott the Internet every Sunday this month. The monthly cost of basic access in China runs $30 to $43, which is more than a quarter of the average monthly income, according to The Guangzhou Daily, a newspaper. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
SBC TO OFFER HIGH-SPEED INTERNET ACCESS BY YEAR-END
body: SBC Communications Inc. said yesterday that it planned to offer high-speed access to the Internet to 8.2 million residential customers and 1.3 million businesses by the end of the year. SBC, based in San Antonio, will offer Asymmetrical Digital Subscriber Line access, which uses traditional copper telephone lines to deliver fast Internet service. The technology, which requires special equipment and installation, is the response by Bell telephone companies to cable modems, which deliver fast Internet access via coaxial cable lines. http://www.nytimes.com

title: COMPANY BRIEFS
body: BIG ENTERTAINMENT INC., Boca Raton, Fla., an Internet-based seller of entertainment merchandise, agreed to acquire the Times Mirror Company's Hollywood Online Inc. unit, which operates a Web site for movie and celebrity information, for $31 million in stock. YAHOO INC., Santa Clara, Calif., the Internet directory company, agreed to offer its Internet services on the new Aptiva personal computers of I.B.M.  BOEING CO., Seattle, the world's largest maker of jets, agreed to launch 28 satellites for Globalstar Telecommunications Ltd., newyork, to help complete its satellite-based global telephone network. Terms were not disclosed. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
TICKETMASTER ONLINE-CITYSEARCH TO BUY AUCTIONEER
body: Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch Inc., which offers entertainment-event tickets and city guides over the Internet, plans to buy the closely held Internet auctioneer Cityauction Inc. for about $54 million in stock so it can offer local auctions of bulky items or items difficult to transport. Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch, owned by USA Networks Inc. and based in Pasadena, Calif., plans to integrate the auctions into its network of guides of about 19 cities and regions in the unitedstates, Scandinavia and Australia. Cityauction, based in Palo Alto, Calif., had listed about 115,000 auctions as of Dec. 31. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Dell-GTE Internet Accord
body: The Dell Computer Corporation, the largest direct seller of computer systems, made an agreement today with a unit of the GTE Corporation to integrate GTE.net's Internet access service into Dell personal computers. The deal will enable Dell customers to choose GTE as their access provider when they log onto the Internet. Dell is based in Round Rock, near Austin, Tex.; GTE is based in Stamford, Conn. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
Letting Your Fingers Reserve a Campsite
body: Camping reservations for the most popular National Park areas can be made on the Internet, using a Visa, Mastercard or Discover credit card. The secure Internet address is reservations.nps.gov. The site, which was launched Jan. 5, provides data, including what is available, for 23 parks and 3 tours. Bookings may be made five months in advance. The service operates from 10 A.M. to 10 P.M., Eastern time. Reservations can still be made by telephone; the number for most campsites is (800) 365-2267; for Yosemite, it is (800) 436-7275, and for Carlsbad Caverns, Mammoth Cave and Frederick Douglass tours, (800) 967-2283. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
Ski Web Site Lists Resorts, Snow Reports
body: Winter-sports enthusiasts can now plan their vacations at www.skiresorts.com on the Internet. One feature of the site, begun in late October, is an online booking directory for more than 400 resorts throughout the world that allows comparison shopping and room reservations. The site also includes information about weather, snowfall, lift ticket prices and trail maps. In addition, about 2,000 vacation properties, including hotels, condominiums and rental homes, can be reviewed and booked directly. Twice-daily snow reports are provided for some 500 mountains, with hourly weather updates for more than 1,500 places.. Information about lodging, dining, transportation, child care and activities is available for featured ski towns -- currently Vail and Aspen, Colo.; Lake Tahoe and Mammoth, Calif.; Park City, Utah; Jackson Hole, Wyo.; Sun Valley, Idaho, and Whistler in British Columbia. Discounts are offered regularly on the site, and last-minute travelers can sign up for email alerts of special deals. A related site, www.mountainzone.com, provides news about skiing and snowboarding. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
RITE AID AND GENERAL NUTRITION AGREE TO AN ALLIANCE
body: The Rite Aid Corporation and the General Nutrition Companies, a retailer of vitamins and mineral supplements, have agreed to form a strategic alliance that includes opening GNC stores within Rite Aid stores and selling vitamins on line. Under the agreement, Rite Aid, the drugstore chain based in Camp Hill, Pa., is to open 1,500 GNC stores within Rite Aid stores in the next three years. The companies also plan to develop and market a new vitamin and nutrition brand, Pharmassure, supported by $30 million in advertising in the first year. The new line of vitamins and supplements is to be sold on the Internet and at Rite Aid's 3,900 stores and GNC's 3,650 stores, starting in the fall. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Times Makes Appointment
body: The newyork Times said yesterday that Kenneth G. Hackett had been named vice president for national circulation. Mr. Hackett, 48, will be responsible for the newspaper's circulation across the country, including single-copy sales, home delivery and national expansion efforts. Mr. Hackett is returning to The Times after having served as vice president for sales and distribution for the North American edition of The Financial Times since last April. He began his career at The newyork Times in 1984 and held several positions in the circulation and advertising departments. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Cisco Planning a Multimedia Network
body: Cisco Systems Inc., the computer-networking company, is expected to announce on Thursday its strategy for blending Internet data with voice communications to reach consumer households. The company, which is based in San Jose, Calif., will discuss plans to create a high-speed broadband network for digital cable subscribers of Tele-Communications Inc. The new network is to combine Internet, phone and video services over a single cable line. Cisco is the largest maker of the router systems that are used to direct Internet traffic. The company has been developing a new generation of products to permit those systems to handle voice and video as well as computer data. It plans to use the Consumer Electronics Show, now under way in Las Vegas, Nev., to introduce an alliance of 32 phone, cable, Internet service and consumer electronic companies that will support the new technology. The new network technology will become available to consumers as TCI upgrades its cable networks around the nation to support Internet data. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MINDSPRING IS IN $245MILLION DEAL WITH ICG
body: Less than a year after acquiring Netcom, a big Internet service provider, for $284 million, ICG Communications Inc. said yesterday that it had agreed to sell most of Netcom's operations to Mindspring Enterprises Inc., another Internet provider, for $245 million in cash and stock. For ICG, a new local phone carrier, the deal ended a mostly disappointing experiment in providing retail "dial up" Internet service. While ICG kept Netcom's network of roughly 45,000 modems, it sold Netcom's unitedstates customers to Mindspring. J. Shelby Bryan, ICG's chief executive, said he hoped to sell Netcom's overseas units within a few weeks. ICG's shares dipped 18.75 cents yesterday, to $22.9375. But Mindspring's shares leaped by $8.5625 each, to $75.125, as the deal increased its customer base by around 60 percent. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Dance Is Enhanced On an Interactive Site
body: An innovative display of dance and digital technology has found a home on the Web. Ghostcatching, "a virtual dance installation," features original movements by the choreographer Bill T. Jones that have been captured and digitally manipulated by a new media studio in newyork called Riverbed. The Ghostcatching Web site (www.cooper.edu/art/ghostcatching) offers an interactive view of the installation. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: MOVING IMAGE -- A compilation of scenes from the Ghostcatching Web site.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Surf the Net by Telephone? That May Be Possible Soon
body: Several high-tech companies are working on a "telephone browser" that will enable users to surf the Internet by speaking into the telephone. For instance, a user could ask for basic information, like sports scores or the temperature, and the software will translate that into a data query and retrieve the information from the Net. The telephone browser combines voice-recognition programs from Lucent Technologies and data-mining software from Spyglass, a provider of software and services for making devices work with the Web. Wayne Yurtin, director of business development for Spyglass, based in Naperville, Ill., said a commercial product could be available within a year. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Netscape Site Numbers Up
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation said yesterday that more than 10 million individuals had subscribed to its Internet portal site, Netscape Netcenter. The company, which is based in Mountain View, Calif., said it had more than doubled its membership rate since July. Netcenter is a World Wide Web site that serves as an access point to the Internet. In 1998, Netscape Netcenter added 18 business and consumer channels and 16 services, including free electronic mail. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
3 AppointmentsMade at Distribution Unit of Times Co.
body: The newyork Times Company has appointed a president and two senior vice presidents at City and Suburban, its wholesale distribution subsidiary in Long Island City, Queens. The president is Roland A. Caputo, 38, currently production group director and manager of the newspaper's printing plant in Edison, N.J. Reporting to him will be John G. Daly, 48, as senior vice president for sales and operations, and Phyllis Calvano, 42, senior vice president for finance and administration. Mr. Daly had been named vice president for national circulation at The Times in April, and Ms. Calvano had been the assistant controller of the newspaper since 1994. City and Suburban distributes The Times, 56 other daily newspapers and 104 other publications to more than 8,000 news dealers in the newyork area. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
America Online Loses in Court
body: A Federal judge has rejected a request by America Online Inc. for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to block Worldnet Service AT&T from using the Internet phrases "You Havemail," "Buddy List" and "I M," AT&T said today. America Online uses a similar phrase, "You've Got Mail," to inform subscribers that email has been sent to them. Buddy List and I M are used by the AT&T I M Here instant messaging service, which is available free to AT&T Worldnet Service users. The ruling, by Chief Judge Claude Hilton of the Federal District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, came in a hearing on Dec. 24. "We realize this is just the first round, but AT&T is confident we will also prevail at trial," said James Cicconi, AT&T's general counsel and executive vice president for law and government affairs. A representative for America Online could not be reached immediately. America Online must now proceed with the case on a regular schedule. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Dec. 27-Jan. 2;
On-Line Shopping Takes Off
body: Early holiday sales figures for Internet retailers were stronger than even the most bullish predictions of a month ago. One consumer survey suggested that on-line sales would reach $5 billion. That would be four times the total sales last year between Thanksgiving and Christmas and twice expectations for this year of $2.3 billion in sales. While the data were preliminary, they sent many electronic-commerce stocks soaring. LESLIE KAUFMAN  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
PERSONAL BUSINESS: DIARY;
On-Line Searches For Off-Line Work
body: The Internet is no longer just for technophiles, and neither, it seems, is on-line job-hunting. A growing number of services are catering to job seekers of all types, offering everything from on-line classified ads to aptitude evaluation questionnaires and resume advice. And a new study suggests that most people searching the World Wide Web for employment opportunities are not looking for jobs involving computers and software. Career Mosaic, a Web employment site, analyzed key terms typed in by job seekers who conducted 15.1 million searches of its data base between July and September. The word that came up most often was "manager" (or "management"); only 3 of the 10 most frequently used terms -- "engineer," "computer" and "programmer" -- were specifically technical. Other search terms in the top 10 were sales (No. 3), marketing (4), finance (5), accounting (6), assistant (8) and human resources (10). Over all, the company said, the survey illustrates the Web's increasingly mainstream place in the workaday world.   ALAN KRAUSS http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
GENESIS TO SELL 20 BRANDS ON EXCITE AND WEBCRAWLER
body: The catalogue sales company Genesis Direct Inc. reached an electronic commerce agreement with the world's second-largest Internet search company Excite Inc. The deal brings more than 20 Genesis catalogue brands to Excite and Webcrawler Web sites. Shares of Genesis Direct, based in Secaucus, N.J., jumped 39 percent, gaining $2.8125 each, to $9.875, in Nasdaq trading. The deal brings Genesis products, including the multisports Web site proteam.com, to Excite's Internet site and to its affiliate site Webcrawler. The agreement also allows for Excite, based in Redwood City, Calif., to have promotions in Genesis Direct catalogues and merchandise shipments, as well as other sales and promotions.
