title: Digital Music
body: To the Editor: The articles on the MP3 compressed music format ("Internet Music, to Go" and "Music to Feed New Player: Some Free and Some Legal," Dec. 24) underestimate the danger this format poses to the music industry. The first article says that "MP3 music on the Rio sounds better than FM radio," and the second says the music sounds "at least as full-bodied as a cassette on a Walkman." The truth is, the MP3 format is indistinguishable from the CD format. Try a blind taste test comparing an MP3-compressed song with its original on CD, and you will find that you cannot distinguish between the two, even if you have great equipment and great ears. The music industry has good reason to be quaking in its boots.  JASON FREIDENFELDS Madison, N.J., Dec. 24, 1998

title:
NEWS WATCH;
A Virtual Pilgrimage Is Complete With Souvenirs
body: Let the word go forth: the little town of Bethlehem is open for E-commerce. A new Web site, Jesus2000.com: Virtual Pilgrimage to the Holy Land, sells religious trinkets, artifacts and mementos via modem (www.Jesus2000.com). It touts itself as "The Holy Land's Largest Shopping Mall on the Internet," which may seem audacious given that it opened just last month. The company behind the Web site, Vector Holdings, is already in discussions to find an underwriter for a public offering, said Alexander Barak, a Vector board member. Speaking from Israel, Mr. Barak said the Luxembourg company was made up of international investors and was nondenominational. He said the company planned to create similar Web sites offering merchandise related to other religions, and had reserved the domain name www. Haj2000.com to sell Muslim merchandise. "What Yahoo is to search, we want to be to church," he said. Thom Calandra, editor in chief of CBS Market Watch, on on-line site for investors, said it might sound ambitious for a young company to announce plans to go public after starting a single Web site. But given the demand for Internet stocks, he said, heaven only knows what could happen. Graphic   Photo

title:
NEWS WATCH;
New Contest Is Melding Stock Frenzy and the Web
body: On-line marketing and the frenzy of interest in the stock market combine in a new Internet-based contest that promises to pay out a very real $20 million grand prize. The catch is that to win, you must guess all six numbers in a given week's Friday close of the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the last 8 of 10 numbers in the closing volume. This is a task that makes mastering the state lottery look easy, winning in Vegas downright simple or figuring out what makes Internet stocks rise and fall a piece of cake. The odds? "In the billions," conceded Chuck Seidman, chief executive of Real Time Media, a company in Haverford, Pa., that produces the sweepstakes site, www.prizes.com, where the "Beat the Street" contest is scheduled to go live in mid-January.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Starcom to Open An Internet Unit
body: Starcom Media Services in Chicago, the media services agency owned by the Leo Burnett Company, said yesterday that it would open Starcom IP, a unit focusing on media planning and buying on the Internet. Rishad Tobaccowala, 39, was named president of Starcom IP. He had been president at Giant Step in Chicago, a Burnett unit that designs Web sites and advertising for the Internet. At Giant Step, Adam Heneghan, 29, chief operating officer, will take on the additional duties of president; Eric Heneghan, 31, continues as chief executive.

title: U.S. Relaxes Rules on Encryption Sales
body: The unitedstates Commerce Department said today that it had issued rules relaxing unitedstates export limits on data-scrambling technologies, considered vital for secure electronic commerce and Internet communications. These rules, which become effective on Thursday, carry out the policy changes announced in September by Vice President Al Gore. They end the need for licenses for sales of powerful encryption products to companies worldwide in several key industry sectors after a one-time review by the Commerce Department. The new rules virtually eliminate restrictions on selling powerful computer data-scrambling products to subsidiaries of unitedstates corporations. The rules relax controls for encryption products sales to health and medical organizations in 46 countries by almost all foreign subsidiaries of unitedstates companies as well as non-unitedstates companies. Privacy advocates have criticized the plan for helping big companies while ignoring concerns of ordinary Internet users.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
SURGE COMPONENTS AGREES TO PURCHASE ORBIT NETWORK
body: Surge Components Inc., a maker of electronic products, said yesterday that it had agreed to buy the closely held Orbit Network Inc. for about $66 million as it sought to expand its business on the Internet.  Surge, based in Deer Park, N.Y., said it planned to exchange 25 million shares for Orbit, based in Novato, Calif., which connects consumers with travel suppliers using the Internet and other networks. The acquisition will help Surge build its business on the Internet as a link to leisure and international travel suppliers. The company also sells electronics products on the Internet. Surge's shares soared $1.53125 each, to $2.625, in Nasdaq trading.

title: RCN to Combine Internet Services
body: The RCN Corporation, which provides telecommunications services in the Northeastern unitedstates, said today that it would combine its four Internet service operations into a single concern under the common brand name RCN.com. In the last year, RCN's number of Internet customers has gone from virtually none to nearly 500,000 through four major acquisitions and strong internal growth. RCN will now merge its providers of Internet service -- Erol's, Ultranet, Javanet and Interport -- into one entity that uses RCN's fiber optic network. Shares of RCN jumped more than 54 percent today, rising $7.25 each, to $20.625, in Nasdaq trading. Each new RCN Internet customer will be given an rcn.com domain name or email address. Internet service to existing customers of Erol's, UltraNet, Javanet and Interport will not be interrupted, and these customers will be able to retain their current email addresses. RCN offers both dial-up and high-speed Internet services as well as local phone, long distance and cable television in several markets from Boston to Washington.

title:
THE MARKETS;
Shift in S.& P. 500 Listing
body: America Online Inc., the No. 1 on-line service, will replace Venator Group in the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index effective after the close of trading on Dec. 31, S.& P. said. Internet stocks have been among this year's best performers, and the industry has experienced explosive growth in the last few years. The 500-stock index, the benchmark against which professional money managers are judged, currently has no Internet stocks. America Online, with a market capitalization of $63 billion, will be larger than all but 38 of the companies in the S.& P. 500. Venator, formerly the Woolworth Corporation, has a market capitalization of $924 million.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Micron Spot Goes To Internet First
body: Micron Electronics Inc. in Nampa, Idaho, is introducing a commercial that is to appear first on the Internet and then on television. The spot, created by Bam in Austin, Tex., will feature Jeri Ryan, who plays the character Seven-of-Nine on the series "Star Trek Voyager." The spot, part of a campaign carrying the theme "New rules, new tools," is to be introduced next Monday on the Micron Web site (www.micronpc.com), then run the next day on TV during the coverage of the Micron PC Bowl college football game.

title:
National News Briefs;
On-Line Alcohol Ads Lure Youths, Study Says
body: Web sites promoting alcoholic beverages too often contain cartoons and other elements that could appeal to those too young to drink legally, a report says. The report, issued last week by the Center for Media Education, an organization based in Washington that monitors electronic media, is an updated look at the status of on-line alcohol and tobacco promotion. The group first issued a study about the subject in March 1997. Major alcohol beverage companies are a growing commercial presence on the Web, with more than 35 brands represented. Center researchers, who examined 77 alcohol product sites from August to October, found that 62 percent included features that young people might find attractive, like cartoon figures, games and "youth oriented" language.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AT HOME TO PURCHASE INTERNET ADVERTISING PROVIDER
body: The At Home Corporation, an Internet service provider, said yesterday that it had agreed to acquire the closely held Narrative Communications Corporation, a provider of Internet-based advertising, in a stock deal valued about $89 million. At Home will use Narrative's Enliven software and technology to create advertisements for the World Wide Web. At Home, based in Redwood City, Calif., provides Internet access through coaxial cable. At Home will issue between 1.34 million and 1.55 million shares of its common stock to acquire Narrative, based in Waltham, Mass.

title:
METRO NEWS BRIEFS: NEW YORK;
Man Accused of Abusing Boys He Met on Internet
body: A Howard Beach man who the police say used the Internet to lure young boys to a Long Island park has been charged with two counts of sexual abuse, the police said. The man, James W. Cleary, 36, was arrested on Thursday at his home by the Nassau County police, who said that he communicated with 10- to 12-year-old boys over the Internet and then met them at Wantagh Park in Nassau County. Mr. Cleary sexually abused at least two boys at the park on Nov. 11, the police said. Mr. Cleary was arraigned yesterday, said Edward Grilli, a spokesman for the Nassau County District Attorney. He pleaded not guilty; bail was set at $1 million.

title: Times Company Promotes Two
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that Raymond E. Douglas had been promoted to corporate chief information officer and that Ellen Taus, the company treasurer, had received the additional title of vice president. Mr. Douglas had been vice president for systems and technology. Ms. Taus has been treasurer of the company since 1997. Mr. Douglas, who is 49, joined The Times in 1990 and is a graduate of Michigan State University and the Advanced Executive Program at the Newspaper Management Center of Northwestern University. Ms. Taus, who is 40, graduated from Northwestern University and has an M.B.A. from Columbia University. She had previously worked in the corporate finance department at R. H. Macy & Company.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Cancel the Red Alert; It's Just Rudolph
body: In addition to its cold war responsibility of tracking enemy missles, the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or Norad, has kept a close watch on the whereabouts of Santa Claus for 44 years. For the second year, Norad will plot St. Nick's progress on its Web site. The site (www.noradsanta.org), also offers some nifty looks at Norad's tracking equipment and an explanation of the Milk and Cookie Theory, which projects that Santa will eat 60,000 tons of cookies on his rounds this year. So, yes, he needs milk. Graphic   Photo

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Trivial in Name Only: 80's Game Headed for the Web
body: Trivia question: What popular board game has found a new home on the Internet? Hint: It made its debut in 1982, enjoyed huge sales and frequently caused players to bemoan the names of forgotten state capitals, curse categories like "Arts & Entertainment" and "People & Places" and sometimes to yank out their own hair trying to remember some detail from high-school science. Yes, that game known as Trivial Pursuit is slated for the Web. Sony Online Entertainment said it had reached an agreement with Hasbro Interactive to publish an on-line version on the Sony game page next year. The game's appearance on the Sony site begs a different question, namely, what is Sony, a movie house, entertainment company and consumer electronics maker, doing in the on-line game business? In an effort to promote the brand name, the Sony site, www.station.sony .com, offers numerous free games, including on-line Jeopardy and Wheel of Fortune.

title:
Paid Notice: Deaths
HIGGINBOTHAM, A. LEON, JR.
body: HIGGINBOTHAM-A. Leon, Jr.  The partners, associates and staff of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison express profound sorrow at the passing of our Senior Counsel, Judge A. Leon Higginbotham, Jr., a great lawyer, wise jurist, dedicated public servant, admired colleague and beloved friend. Judge Higginbotham will long be remembered for his deep commitment to social causes, his wise counsel and his many accomplishments. His death is a profound loss to all who knew and loved him and to the nation at large. We extend our deepest sympathies and condolences to his wife, Evelyn, his sons, Stephen and Kenneth, his daughters, Nia and Karen, and all the other members of his family. HIGGINBOTHAM-A. Leon, Jr. The newyork Times Company, its Board of Directors and its employees note with sadness the death of A. Leon Higginbotham, Jr., a member of our board since 1993. We will miss Judge Higginbotham's formidable intelligence, sound judgement and unfailing integrity. We will remember fondly his wit, warmth and humanity. We express our heartfelt condolences to his family. Arthur Sulzberger, Jr., Chairman The newyork Times Company

title: Advancing On Line
body: To the Editor: The article "Soaring Prices Spur a Revolt in Scientific Publishing" on Dec. 8, did not mention the main force changing academic publishing: the Internet. In many fields, research is published first on the Internet, in the form of preprints and technical reports posted to scientists' Web sites. By the time an article is published on paper it is often already old news. Academic journals serve important roles as archivers, editors and enforcers of academic standards. But these functions can be replaced by on-line publishing, cheaper and more efficiently.  NELSON MINAR Cambridge, Mass.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BRIEFS;
Wolters Kluwer to Split Stock 4 for 1 Next Year
body: Wolters Kluwer N.V., Europe's biggest tax and legal publisher by revenue, said yesterday that it would split its stock 4 for 1 next year, restating share value in euros to conform with Europe's new single currency. Shareholders will receive four shares with a nominal value of 0.12 euro for each existing share with a nominal value of 1 guilder. The split will occur a few weeks after a shareholders meeting on April 15. Wolters Kluwer said its American depository receipts would also be split 4 for 1 at that time.

title: Finding Jobs at Ski Resorts
body: To the Editor: Thanks for the section on Web sites of interest to skiers ("Hitting the Virtual Slopes All Year Round," Nov. 26). The lead article mentioned that some Web sites include ski-area jobs, but no specific sites were listed for that. One very helpful place that brings together job seekers and employers in the snow-sports industry is www.skiingthenet.com. It includes detailed descriptions of vacancies listed by resorts, ski shops, suppliers, food services and other operations, as well as copies of resumes of potential employees and interesting links to the Web sites of some employers who include information on opportunities in their organizations.  JOHN ANDREW Ridgewood, N.J., Dec. 4, 1998

title:
Metro Business;
On-Line Insurance Move
body: Hartford Financial Services Group said on Tuesday that it would join with Juno Online Services to sell auto and homeowner insurance on the World Wide Web. The company, which offers property and casualty insurance, said the five-year agreement with Juno, an Internet service provider, would let Juno users receive information and price quotes for insurance coverage on line. Hartford Financial said that it hoped to reach the growing number of people who use the Internet to shop for financial services. The company's Affinity Insurance Center in Farmington, Conn., which processes claims for its independent alliances with banks and organizations like the American Association of Retired Persons, will manage the on-line business.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Perhaps We Should Be Amazed That It Can Surf the Web at All
body: Since 3Com announced its newest version of the popular Palm Pilot, the Palm VII, it has been criticized by some users for offering only limited Web access. That access, called Web Clippings, allows Palm users to see updated, albeit abridged, information from 22 corporate Web sites through a wireless connection. Joe Sipher, director of wireless products for 3Com, of Santa Clara, Calif., said the company had concluded that it would be too costly and unwieldy to offer full Web access on its personal digital assistant. "Try hooking into the Web on a Windows CE device," he said. "It's a terrible, terrible experience." The information available through Web Clippings is restricted to that which is well suited for the Palm's small screen and very slow access speed of 8 kilobits per second. For instance, Etrade will allow access to stock quotes, but not trades; the Yahoo function will allow telephone and address searches, and USA Today Online will provide a digest of news and sports. The service is not designed to offer general Web access, nor is it cheap. The wireless access will cost $9.99 a month for about 6 transactions a day, or $24.99 for up to 18 a day, Mr. Sipher said.

title:
Metro Business;
Cable Access to Internet
body: Cablevision Systems Corporation said yesterday that it would be capable of offering high-speed Internet access over cable modems to about 714,000 homes by the end of the year, up from 370,000 in September. Cable modems allow subscribers to connect to the Internet at speeds much faster than traditional phone lines can provide. Since Cablevision introduced the high-speed access late last year, about 1.9 percent of eligible Cablevision customers have signed on, and in some Connecticut markets like Westport as many as 5 percent have done so. Cablevision, which is based in Woodbury, N.Y., and other cable operators are starting to offer new services, including residential telephone hookups and digital television, to generate revenue. Optimism for these services has helped increase Cablevision shares, which have risen 93 percent so far this year. The cable-modem service costs customers about $30 to $40 a month, and Cablevision expects to be able to achieve margins of about 40 percent to 50 percent, said Frank Golden, the company's vice president for investor relations. Cablevision has 3.4 million cable customers primarily in three core markets, newyork, Boston and Cleveland.

title: Shares of Ubid Have Strong Trading Debut
body: The on-line auction company Ubid Inc. began trading yesterday, with the shares closing at $48 -- far above the $15 offering price. Coming on the heels of several run-ups by Internet initial public offerings the last month, Ubid was able to price the offering beyond the original estimated range of $12 to $14. Ubid sold 1.6 million shares through its lead underwriter, Merrill Lynch. It has 8.9 million shares outstanding after the offering. The offering generated $24 million for use in marketing and brand development. Ubid, based in Elk Grove Village, Ill., was formed about a year ago and began holding auctions last December. It specializes in sales of computer products, home electronics and other leisure-related goods. For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Ubid reported a net loss of $3 million on revenue of $24.1 million, according to the prospectus.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
An Alliance With Netscape Will Add to AOL's Web Power
body: The Microsoft Corporation as the Internet's monolith? Think again. A new analysis of America Online's plan to buy Netscape might spare Microsoft the on-line-monopoly moniker. If the buyout goes through, Web sites owned by AOL will become by far the most dominant gateways to cyberspace, according to the survey, by Cyber Dialogue, an Internet research firm based in newyork. The company's report says that after an AOL-Netscape alliance, one in every three American adults would start each Web experience from an AOL-owned site. These sites would include AOL's proprietary service, used by 14 million people worldwide, AOL's home page on the Web and Netscape's Netcenter portal. That dominance won't be without challenges, however, said Thomas E. Miller, vice president of Cyber Dialogue. In particular, he said, AOL would have to fuse two vastly different cultures -- the newbies and neophytes of AOL with the relatively more sophisticated surfers who regularly log onto Netcenter. "The attitudes of the two audiences are really quite different," Mr. Miller said. "The challenge is going to be how to blend them."

title:
NEWS WATCH;
History Buffs' Hangout
body: The Internet may be paving the way to the future, but a Web site that now proclaims itself a "portal" is all about the past. The History Channel, which treats cable-TV viewers to a generous helping of all things past, reopened its Web site on Nov. 30 as a gateway for people with a yen for history. The site, www.historychannel.com, includes an archive of articles, audio and video clips, and exhibits. It also has topical features like This Day in History and an Internet-wide search engine that it advertises as "the best search in history." Graphic   Photo

title:
Metro Business;
NBC Buys Internet Stake
body: General Electric Company's NBC said yesterday that it would buy a minority stake in iVillage.com, the No. 1 on-line network geared toward women, for an undisclosed price to strengthen its place on the Internet and among female audiences. Village will get on-air promotion from NBC and on-line distribution on NBC.com and Snap.com, an Internet search directory jointly owned by NBC and Cnet Inc. Snap and iVillage will put three new sites on Snap.com related to parenting, family and health issues, and Snap will be featured on each of iVillage's 12 Web sites. NBC wants to strengthen its on-line presence as more people divide time between television and the Internet. In particular, the network said it wanted to capture a larger portion of the female audience. newyork-based iVillage, founded in 1995, has more than 77 million page views a month.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
New Program For Geocities
body: Geocities, which offers free personal Web pages to computer users, is introducing what is being described as its first major integrated communications program. The program, which includes print, Internet and radio advertising and a new corporate identity, begins tomorrow. The work is the first from Young & Rubicam Inc. in newyork, which was awarded the account, with billings estimated at $15 million to $20 million, in October. Y.& R. units including Young & Rubicam Advertising, Wunderman Cato Johnson, Landor Associates and Brand Dialogue are bringing out the program, which is centered on a new theme describing Geocities as "a virtual population explosion." The ads and corporate identity effort introduce a lower-case letter "g" to promote Geocities. The letter, with a dot inside to represent an eyeball, becomes a character displaying several moods. "We are convinced this effort will increase our visitor traffic," said Thomas R. Evans, president and chief executive at Geocities in Santa Monica, Calif. Geocities has 2.9 million users, or "homesteaders," who have created an estimated 22 million pages of personalized content in the company's on-line community.

title:
November 22-28;
Urge to Merge
body: Side by side they seem to be the corporate odd couple of cyberspace: America Online, a middle-brow service catering to on-line newcomers, and Netscape Communications, the Internet software pioneer founded by whiz-kid programmers. But America Online purchased Netscape for roughly $4.2 billion in stock. The worlds of media and technology, industry analysts say, will meld together more and more in the future, so merging these two companies may well make sense. In a side deal, America Online announced a joint marketing and software development alliance with Sun Microsystems to reassure Netscape's programmers.   STEVE LOHR

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
EARTHLINK SHARES RISEON REPORT OF BID BY SPRINT
body: Shares of Earthlink Network Inc. rose 37 percent yesterday on a report that the Sprint Corporation, the third-largest unitedstates long-distance telephone company, may buy the remaining 71 percent of the Internet-service provider it does not already own. Earthlink shares jumped $19.50, to $71.875, in Nasdaq trading. The Dec. 7 issue of Business Week magazine reported in its "Inside Wall Street" column that unidentified people expected Sprint, which is based in Kansas City, Mo., to break an agreement signed in February that prohibits it from buying Earthlink for 39 months. Robin West, a money manager for the New Mexico State Investment Council, estimates Earthlink is worth $4.8 billion, or $120 a share.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
LUCENT TO BUY 80% OF WAVE ACCESS FOR $50 MILLION
body: Lucent Technologies Inc. agreed yesterday to buy the remaining 80 percent of the closely held Wave Access Ltd. for $50 million in cash, giving Lucent, the No. 1 North American phone equipment maker, a technology for sending data on wireless networks. Lucent, based in Murray Hill, N.J., paid $6 million in May for a 20 percent stake in Wave Access, based in Raanana, Israel. Lucent expects to take an unspecified charge for research and development at Wave Access. Wave Access's technology lets wireless users send and receive information over the Internet.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Viewing Windows By Using Windows
body: The seasonal tradition of creating lavish holiday displays in department store windows went digital this week when Bloomingdale's flagship store at 59th and Lexington Avenue began Webcasting its famously magical windows. Teaming up with the 3Com Corporation, Bloomingdale added images of the holiday windows (updated every 30 seconds) to the store's Web site (www.bloomingdales.com). Tomorrow, live pictures of children visiting Bloomingdale's Santa will be added to the site. Graphic   Drawing

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Visits to News Sites Decline, For Understandable Reasons
body: Major news organizations may wince at first glance at the latest figures on the decline in popularity of their on-line sites. According to Media Metrix, an on-line research company that compiles monthly figures on Internet usage, in October, MSNBC attracted 5.1 million visitors, down from 6.4 million in September. CNN dropped to 4.6 million from 7.1 million; USA Today to 3.3 from 3.9 and The newyork Times on the Web to 1.6 million from 1.8 million. Did the nation suddenly become less interested in daily events? Only temporarily, said Doug McFarland, senior vice president of Media Metrix. He said the declines seem so large because they follow a sharp rise in September, fueled by the publication of the Starr report and other revelations about President Bill Clinton and Monica Lewinsky. Graphic   Photo

title: Searching the Net
body: To the Editor: As a reference librarian, I read with interest the adventures of finding information on Algonquin crafts ("A Needle in the Internet Haystack," Nov. 19). I would like to take issue with the comment: "We never could have found this list at the library." Most libraries have Internet connections, and the librarians I know are experienced Internet searchers.  ELISABETH OLIU Metuchen, N.J., Nov. 19, 1998

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DOW JONES TO DISMISS 118 WORKERS TO REDUCE COSTS
body: Dow Jones & Company said yesterday that it would cut costs by dismissing 118 employees, closing offices and using an outside company to handle subscription telemarketing for The Wall Street Journal and Barron's. The move is part of a plan to stem rising expenses as Dow Jones faces an uncertain advertising market. The newyork-based publisher said it expected to take an after-tax charge against fourth-quarter earnings of about $2 million, or 2 cents a share, mostly for severance and closing offices. The job cuts, affecting about 1.4 percent of Dow Jones's work force, will be made at nine sites in eight states. Dow Jones shares fell 81.25 cents, to $49.125.

title: Library Can't Filter Internet, Judge Rules
body: In a decision supporting unfettered access to the Internet in public libraries, a Federal judge struck down yesterday the Loudoun County, Va., library's policy of using filtering software on all computer terminals. "Such a policy offends the guarantee of free speech in the First Amendment and is, therefore, unconstitutional," the judge, Leonie M. Brinkema of Federal District Court in Alexandria, Va., said in the decision. Judge Brinkema wrote that the use of the filters, made by a private company, to limit Internet access was also a form of prior restraint on distribution of speech and asserted that "a defendant cannot avoid its constitutional obligation by contracting out its decision making to a private entity." Judge Brinkema issued a permanent injunction against the filtering policy, but the decision leaves unanswered whether it would be constitutionally acceptable to use filters on terminals that are set aside for children. Loudoun library officials made no statement about an appeal. About 15 percent of libraries have installed filters on at least some of their terminals, according to a recent survey from the American Library Association.

title: Barnes & Noble Loss Exceeds Estimates
body: Barnes & Noble Inc., the largest unitedstates bookseller, reported a loss in its third quarter that was wider than expected as expenses at its fledgling Internet unit offset higher sales at its chain of bookstores. Barnes & Noble reported a loss of $4.59 million, or 7 cents a diluted share, compared with net income of $65,000, or zero cents a share, a year earlier. It had been expected to post a loss of 3 cents a share for the quarter, which ended on Oct. 31, the average estimate of analysts polled by the First Call Corporation. The costs of marketing and developing the barnesandnoble.com Internet site have exceeded sales at the unit, which lost $12.1 million, or 18 cents a share. The site competes with a bigger rival, Amazon.com, which is also losing money. Barnes & Noble earlier this year cut its forecast for revenue from the on-line unit to $65 million from $100 million, and analysts said they did not expect the site to be profitable before 2001.

title: Federal Judge Blocks Internet Smut Law
body: A Federal judge yesterday temporarily blocked a new Federal law intended to shield children from on-line pornography. Free-speech advocates had asserted that enforcement of the measure, which was to have gone into effect today, could violate the First Amendment. The judge, Lowell A. Reed Jr. of Federal District Court in Philadelphia, issued a temporary restraining order blocking the law for 10 days, until Dec. 4. Full hearings on the matter are scheduled for Dec. 8 and 9. Judge Reed is likely to extend the order until the hearings are held, said Ann Beeson, a lawyer for the American Civil Liberties Union, which is fighting the law. The law, the Child On-Line Protection Act, would make it a crime for operators of commercial Web sites to make certain types of graphic material available to those under 17 years old. The suit challenging the act was filed on Oct. 22, hours after it was signed into law by President Clinton. The case is being brought by 17 on-line publishers, retailers and other organizations.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
VERIO LOWERS HIWAY TECHNOLOGIES BID TO $257.2 MILLION
body: Verio Inc., the Internet service provider, said yesterday that it would pay $257.2 million in cash and stock for Hiway Technologies under an agreement revised after a 37 percent drop in Verio's share price. Verio, based in Englewood, Colo., agreed in July to buy Hiway, which runs Web pages for companies, for $329 million. Verio has now increased the cash portion of the agreement to $176 million from $101 million, but decreased the number of common shares it will pay to 4.92 million from 8.67 million. Verio had an initial stock offering in May at $23 a share. It closed yesterday at $16.50, up 31.25 cents.

title: Macy's Says It Will Revive Web Sales Site
body: R. H. Macy & Company, the department store chain, is restarting its two-year-old site on the World Wide Web, macys.com, offering a broader product selection from a variety of departments with new customer-friendly features. Macys.com's president, Kent Anderson, said he expected the Web site's sales this holiday season to be four times what they were last year. He declined to give a sales figure at the store, a division of Federated Department Stores Inc., but said macys.com is expecting to be profitable in 2001 or 2002. Mr. Anderson said macys.com would offer convenience to shoppers but would not use a promotional pricing strategy like Macy's department stores. Goods that a shopper orders are expected to be shipped by United Parcel Service of America within 72 hours of the order, he said. I.B.M. is working with macys.com in developing the Web site and featuring it in advertising.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
If You Can't Get Enough Talk, Tune Into New Internet Shows
body: Talk shows are undeniably successful staples of television and radio. So it's not surprising that Talkspot is attempting to adapt the format for the Web. Talkspot (www.talkspot.com), following the lead of Web-based audio services offering music, has four channels aimed at different tastes that are delivered using Real Audio. The topics are familiar to even a casual talk show listener: astrology, politics (mostly conservative), parenting advice, weight loss and, on Channel Z, off-color shock-jock humor, "where everything is politically incorrect and proud of it!" James Golden, Talkspot's vice president for programming and host of two shows, acknowledged that one potential attraction of Web talk was that it could not be curbed by the Federal Communications Commission. "Much of Channel Z pushes the borders," said Mr. Golden, a former producer of Rush Limbaugh's radio show who appeared on the air under the name Bo Snerdly. "However, we have standards here too." As in conventional broadcasting, listeners can also pitch their views or question guests through toll-free phone lines.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Sony Offers On-Line Jukebox With 'Pay as You Play' Service
body: The jukebox is back -- on the Internet. Sony Music Online's new site, a partnership with Real Networks, has a "pay as you play" structure, allowing users to choose songs and play them through their computers. The songs selected from the site (www.sonymusic.com/jukebox) can be played an unlimited number of times in a 24-hour period. Users with credit cards can purchase "tokens" at 10 for $2.50, 22 for $5 or 50 for $10. The songs (about 200 on line today and up to 500 promised) are all from the Sony catalogue. They range from pop favorites by Michael Jackson and Bob Dylan to chestnuts from Mott the Hoople's "All the Young Dudes" and "Nature's Way" by Spirit. The site will allow Sony to track users according to time of day, music type and ZIP code. Sony's vice president for new technology and business development, David Waldman, said the data would be used to determine listening patterns.   CHARLES BERMANT

title:
INVESTING: DIARY;
More Internet Offerings Waiting in the Wings
body: Investors kicking themselves for not being in on last week's initial offerings of Earthweb and Theglobe.com -- which finished the week up 378.6 percent and 605.6 percent, respectively -- may want to keep this thought in mind: There's more where those two came from. Nineteen Internet companies tracked by Commscan L.L.C., a newyork research firm, plan to tap the public market, hoping to raise a total of $826.9 million. Five of the companies have already set tentative schedules. Among them is Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch, an on-line provider of event ticketing and local city guides. It hopes to raise $63 million in an offering planned for early December. Other big names on the list include Prodigy Communications, the Internet access provider, which hopes to raise $86.3 million, and Marketwatch.com, a Web-based news provider, which hopes to bring in $34.5 million. Neither has set a specific time for its offering. Through Thursday, Commscan said, 30 Internet companies had raised a total of $1.6 billion this year, returning an average of 74 percent.   RICHARD TEITELBAUM

title: Primark-Dow Jones Pact
body: The Primark Corporation agreed today to buy Dow Jones & Company's Edgar Direct unit, which electronically publishes Securities and Exchange Commission filings, for an undisclosed price. Primark, based in Waltham, Mass., a provider of financial and economic data, is buying Edgar Direct through its Disclosure Inc. unit, according to a Dow Jones statement. Edgar is the S.E.C.'s electronic system for company filings. Dow, the newyork-based publisher of The Wall Street Journal, said it was cutting 30 jobs by selling Edgar Direct and restructuring its Federal Filings unit, which reports on filings to the S.E.C. and other Government agencies.

title: Auction Universe Is Sold
body: Classified Ventures L.L.C., an Internet services company financed by eight leading media companies, bought Auction Universe today from the Times Mirror Company. Financial terms were not disclosed. Classified Ventures is financed by Central Newspapers Inc., the Gannett Company, Knight-Ridder, the McClatchy Company, The newyork Times Company, Times Mirror, the Tribune Company and the Washington Post Company. Auction Universe provides on-line auction services through a network of over 30 newspapers and other media properties.

title: A Worthwhile Investment
body: To the Editor: Last June, for her 90th birthday, we gave my mother-in-law Web TV, the inexpensive television hookup to the Web. We have noticed a transformation! While my mother-in-law has always been a very intelligent, "with it" woman, her 89th year had been difficult because she suffered a small stroke, which left her befuddled and forgetful, something she found infuriating and embarrassing. Over the last five months, the befuddled thinking and vague language have completely disappeared, and my mother-in-law's eye and motor coordination is normal (she could barely type the first few weeks). Furthermore, a whole world has opened up to her: she's discovered interesting sites like the National Gallery and cowboy poetry. Most important, she is connected to all her grandchildren and children, who now copy her on everything. She's in the loop! We're all thrilled.  SUESAN W. TAYLOR Palo Alto, Calif., Nov. 6, 1998

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NETSCAPE AGREES TO ACQUIRE ATWEB FOR $95.1 MILLION
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation, the No. 1 maker of Internet browser software, said yesterday that it planned to buy the closely held Atweb Inc., an on-line Web site services company, for about $95 million in stock and options. Netscape, based in Mountain View, Calif., said it would issue 3.36 million shares to buy all of Atweb, which is based in Sunnyvale, Calif. That values the transaction at $95.1 million based on Netscape's closing price of $28.3125, up 18.75 cents. Atweb provides services that help small businesses communicate and advertise on the Web, as well as set up Web sites.

title: Vietnam Memorial Names to Be on Internet
body: The 58,196 names etched on the polished black granite of the Vietnam Memorial wall here will be posted on the Internet, along with statements from their families, Vice President Al Gore said today. "The Vietnam Veterans Memorial Web site will be up and running at midnight on Veterans Day," Mr. Gore told a group of veterans in the Roosevelt Room of the White House. "For 15 years, people have come to the Vietnam Wall to run their hands across the names and remember those who never came home," Mr. Gore said. "Now, anybody who can run their hands across a computer keyboard will be able to make contact with those names." The new Web site, a joint project of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund and Winstar Communications Inc., will be made available in two stages. Users will be able to visit the Web site (www.thevirtualwall.org), choose a veteran's name and, in many cases, hear recordings from family members or friends. In January, the Web site will have a "virtual wall," a re-creation of the Vietnam Memorial wall.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
SOFTBANK EXPANDS ITS STAKE IN BUYCOMP.COM BY 9.9%
body: The Softbank Corporation, Japan's largest distributor of computer software, has purchased 9.9 percent of the closely held Buycomp.com for $40 million as it expands its investment in the world's largest Internet computer retail outlet. Softbank bought the stake in Buycomp.com, which is based in Aliso Viejo, Calif., on Sept. 30, Buycomp said, adding to the 10.25 percent stake purchased in August by Softbank's technology unit for $20 million. Buycomp, which sells computer software, hardware and related products on the Internet, said it would use Softbank's investment to expand into new on-line markets.

title: COMPANY BRIEFS
body: CMGI INC., Andover, Mass., an Internet venture capital firm, said it had acquired a stake in Virtual Ink, Cambridge, Mass., a start-up company developing a low-cost system that allows computer users to hold meetings over the Internet. Financial terms were not disclosed.  GT INTERACTIVE SOFTWARE CORP., newyork, a publisher of games for personal computers, is buying Onezero Media Inc., Boston, a closely held company that runs an Internet site about entertainment, for about $15 million in stock. SUN CO., Philadelphia, the oil refiner and chemical company, will change its name today to Sunoco Inc. in an effort to improve name recognition.  SUNGLASS HUT INTERNATIONAL INC., Coral Gables, Fla., said it would buy back up to eight million shares of its stock.

title:
Compressed Data;
Lifetime Internet Access Faces Uncertain Future
body: Just how long is a lifetime on the Internet? About 21 months, if you ask Atbigger.net. In early 1997, the San Jose, Calif., Internet service provider promised unlimited lifetime Internet access for a one-time fee of $59, plus another $10 for a lifetime email account. Nearly 20,000 people believed it, hoping to rid themselves forever of those pesky $19.95-a-month access fees. But as it turns out, the company did not have the technology, or the management, to succeed. Last week, company executives filed for bankruptcy. But at the last minute, a buyer appeared: Brigadoon.com, an Internet service provider in Bellevue, Wash., paid an undisclosed sum for the company's assets and has vowed to keep the company alive.   LAURIE J. FLYNN Graphic   Photo

title:
October 25-31;
Stock Promoters Charged
body: The Securities and Exchange Commission accused 44 stock promoters of fraudulently promoting more than 235 tiny companies on the Internet. It was the first nationwide sweep of stock fraud on the Web. The promoters, mostly little-known individuals working from their homes or for small public relations companies, often touted stocks on Web sites and bulletin boards, and in Internet newsletters. They made recommendations but often failed to disclose that the companies had paid for the promotions, a violation of anti-fraud regulations, the S.E.C. said. DAVID BARBOZA

title: AT&T Plans Internet Sales - Correction Appended
body: The AT&T Corporation said today that it planned to sell At Home Corporation's high-speed Internet access separately from At Home's on-line information services. The move would let customers access the Internet through At Home via cable lines and pay other companies like America Online Inc. for information. AT&T's chief executive, C. Michael Armstrong, said that the plan would be similar to agreements America Online had to sell its content to customers of other Internet access providers. Correction  A brief report in Business Day on Friday about AT&T's plans for the At Home on-line network misstated the sales arrangement. C. Michael Armstrong, AT&T's chief executive, said that while At Home's Internet access and information offerings would be sold as one service, other companies could connect to the network to offer At Home customers their services. He did not say At Home's Internet access would be sold separately. Correction-Date: October 31, 1998, Saturday

title: America Online Adds 40 Retailers
body: America Online, the world's largest on-line service, said yesterday that it had added 40 new retailing partners, including Toys "R" Us Inc., to the shopping section of its on-line services, bringing the total to 11O. America Online, with 13 million members, has said 95 percent of the retailers who have agreements to sell on its service renew those partnerships. It noted that most of the agreements with its retailing partners extend to its Web site, www.aol.com, and to its Compuserve on-line service. The announcement appeared to be stoking the company's stock, which rose $2.125, to $124.125. Among the other new partners added to what America Online calls its Shopping Channel, are the retailer Macy's, which is owned by Federated Department Stores Inc. and the apparel maker Bugle Boy.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Boy Scout Handbook Adds A Page About the Internet
body: For the first time, "The Boy Scout Handbook," that trusty life guide used by almost 100 million boys throughout the century, will include a page on the Internet. "You might already be using the Internet for school work, hobbies, or simply for enjoyment," says the handbook, which is to be released early next year. "For all of its benefits, though, the Internet can also present hazards you should know about and avoid." The 11th edition of the handbook -- the first revision this decade -- cautions users never to disclose personal information like addresses and telephone numbers. It also urges youngsters never to agree to meet anyone they have encountered on line unless a parent or guardian accompanies them. In other words: Be prepared.   MICHEL MARRIOTT

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Momentum Awards For Work on Internet
body: Several Internet-related companies and executives were honored for leadership and innovation at the 1998 Momentum Awards ceremony. The companies are Ebay in Sunnyvale, Calif.; Home Shark in San Francisco; Link Exchange in Palo Alto, Calif.; Priceline.com L.L.C. in Stamford, Conn., and Travelocity in Fort Worth, which is operated by Sabre Group. The executives are Mary Furlong, chief executive of Third Age Media in San Francisco, and Seth Godin, chief executive of Yoyodine in newyork, now part of Yahoo Inc. The E-Marketer of the Year Award went to Cisco Systems Inc. in Sunnyvale. The Turbo-Agency of 1998 Award, for the Internet advertising agency that has done the most for media technologies, went to Modem Media.Poppe Tyson in Westport, Conn., part of True North Communications. The awards are sponsored by seven organizations including @d:tech, owned by Conexmar in Richmond, and ChannelSeven.com, part of X-ceed Inc. in newyork.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Internet Research Firm Sells Stake to Nielsen
body: Another consolidation in the Internet research field occurred yesterday as Nielsen Media Research in newyork acquired what was described as a significant equity stake in Net Ratings Inc., an audience research company in Milpitas, Calif., and combined the two companies' audience-measurement systems for the Internet. Financial terms were not disclosed. The deal "moves the entire industry closer to the day when strategies for using the Internet can be based on accurate, reliable and consistent information," said John A. Dimling, president and chief executive at Nielsen Media Research. The combined measurement service, called Nielsen Net Ratings, will be led by Dave Toth, 42, president and chief executive at Net Ratings.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Odiorne Wilde Wins Salon's Account
body: Salon, an on-line magazine operated by Salon Internet Inc. (www.salonmagazine.com), has named Odiorne Wilde Narraway & Partners in San Francisco as the first agency to handle its account. Billings were estimated at $1 million to $2 million. Patrick Hurley, marketing director at Salon in San Francisco, said a two-month review of the account had also included Blazing Paradigm in San Francisco.

title: 3 Leaving at Wells Fargo
body: Three top executives at Wells Fargo & Company are leaving the bank because of the pending merger with the Norwest Corporation of Minneapolis.The executives are Joseph Stiglich, 51, who is a vice chairman and head of the retail branch network; Michael Gillfillan, 50, who is a vice chairman and the bank's credit chief, and Dudley Nigg, 51, who is an executive vice president and the manager of on-line banking.

title: Teach Children to Be Internet Filters
body: To the Editor: In "Censorship or Common Sense" (Op-Ed, Oct. 19), Roxana Robinson implies that to be opposed to the use of Internet filtering software is to be opposed to any action protecting children from certain Web sites. This may be true for a few extremists, but most of us simply have a problem with the method of filtering currently in use. As a mother I firmly believe that schools and libraries have a responsibility to prevent children from accessing certain Web sites. But simply installing filtering software on all computers is not a solution because these software programs are arbitrary and do not work as they claim. For example, although my Web site, which is about attention deficit disorder, contains no sexual content, it has been blocked by "Surf Watch" because the server I use contains one Web site that was determined to contain sexually graphic material. If filtering software is to be used, adults and children with adult permission should be given passwords that allow access to blocked material. And makers of filtering software should not be allowed to arbitrarily block all Web sites from a particular server.  TERESA GALLAGHER Shelton, Conn., Oct. 19, 1998

title:
National News Briefs;
Suit Filed to Block Internet Smut Measure
body: Attacking an hours-old Federal statute intended to restrict children's access to pornography on the Internet, a coalition of 17 organizations filed suit yesterday in Federal District Court in Philadelphia to block the measure, which they say violates the free speech provisions of the First Amendment. The measure, the Child Online Protection Act, was a small part of the budget bill passed by Congress this week and signed by President Clinton on Wednesday. It does not take effect for 30 days.

title: Filters vs. First Amendment
body: To the Editor: "Library Grapples With Internet Freedom" (Oct. 15) mentioned the Loudoun County library filtering litigation. That case, in which I am a plaintiff, argues that filtering software is overbroad, blocks numerous innocent and socially valuable sites and cannot pass the strict tests imposed by the First Amendment. The Web site of the Censorware Project, an advocacy organization that opposes the use of blocking software in public institutions (www.censorware.org), contains a complete record of the Loudoun case and information on blocking software.  JONATHAN WALLACE newyork, Oct. 15, 1998

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Merry-Go-Round View of Baseball Stadiums
body: When the final out is called, when the TV crews have packed up, when the last baseball die-hard has been pulled from the bleachers by the authorities, Yankee Stadium will take on the serene quiet of its natural state. And that is the way visitors will find it at the Web site of Be Here Inc. (www.behere.com), a Silicon Valley technology company that makes technology to display 360-degree images on the Internet. The site features 360-degree images of both Yankee Stadium, in the Bronx, and Qualcomm Park, the stadium the San Diego Padres call home. The images, taken from various points inside the stadiums, pan through an arc of 360 degrees. Graphic   Photo:

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Survey Will Track Internet Audiences
body: The question is not whether people are tuning in to radio programs over the Internet -- they are, albeit not in mass numbers. The question is whether the listeners count. Toward that end, The Arbitron Company, which measures traditional radio audiences in local markets, last week announced plans to modify its surveys to track which of the station's listeners tune in over the Internet. The new plan is a joint effort between Arbitron NewMedia and RadioWave.com Inc., the interactive radio subsidiary of Motorola. There are 1,708 radio stations worldwide with streaming audio, up from 763 a year ago, said BRS Media, an Internet radio consulting agency. But thousands of others -- among them, the CBS Corporation owns about 160 radio stations and has a policy against streaming audio -- have abstained, in part because they want to be able to measure audiences accurately.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Videophone Call-Ins On a Cable TV Channel
body: The Internet has made it possible to perform all sorts of tasks without leaving the house -- banking, working, even dating. Credit ZDTV, a fledgling 24-hour cable channel with programming focused on computer issues, for using the Net to make a virtual community out of yet another group: the studio audience. The network, based in San Francisco, urges viewers to call in to its programs using Internet-based videophones, which transmit not just voices, but faces. "Larry King says, 'We'll go to Altoona, Pa., for our next call,' and you'll hear the caller," said Greg Derbin, senior vice president for Programming and Production at the network. "With ZDTV, you'll see the caller." To encourage wider participation, ZDTV will give away up to 10,000 videophones, called Netcams because they transmit their audio and video signals over the Internet. From Oct. 26 to 31, it plans to give away one videophone every hour on its Web site, Mr. Drebin said. ZDTV, which is owned by Ziff-Davis and began broadcasting in May, reaches eight million homes. Graphic   Photo

title: Internet Sports News Deal
body: The Internet directory company Excite Inc. said today that it entered a deal for Sports Line USA Inc. to be the exclusive provider of sports information to its Web site. The deal covers sports news as well as scores, columns, news analysis and other services. Excite will continue to sell all the advertising on its sports channel, one of several "channels" it offers focusing on different subject areas. However, Excite and Sports Line will share revenues from the channel, including advertising and merchandise sales. The revenue- sharing pact also provides for certain minimum guaranteed payments Excite will make to Sports Line.

title: Internet Watchdogs
body: To the Editor: No parent wants to leave children vulnerable to on-line pornographers (Op-Ed, Oct. 19). But are Internet filters, which block access to the national Planned Parenthood Web site, really the best way to protect them? If we want young people to be informed about the most common sexual health threats they face, like teen-age pregnancy and sexually transmitted diseases, then placing Internet filters in public library computers is a very bad idea. Published reviews of some of the leading Internet filters show that they block access to many responsible sites. Some parents might wish they could shield their children from all discussion of sex. But even if the Internet didn't exist, would that be possible? Should local libraries be expected to drop subscriptions to newspapers and magazines? A healthier solution is to start an age-appropriate dialogue with young people about sexuality and values that would help them make responsible choices. An uncensored Internet can be part of the solution, not part of the problem.  BONNIE MC EWAN V.P. for Communications, Planned Parenthood Federation of America. newyork, Oct. 20, 1998

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NETSCAPE TO BUNDLE REALNETWORKS PRODUCT IN BROWSER
body: Stock prices for both Realnetworks Inc. and the Netscape Communications Corporation rose yesterday after Realnetworks said it would bundle its Realplayer software with a new version of Netscape's Web browser and its Web site. Realnetworks already distributes the software through the Microsoft Corporation's Web browser, which competes with Netscape. Shares of Realnetworks, based in Seattle, rose $2.50, or 7 percent, to $37.375, and shares of Netscape, based in Mountain View, Calif., rose $3.50, or 17 percent, to $23.75.

title: Internet Filter Makes Bad Censor
body: To the Editor: Roxana Robinson (Op-Ed, Oct. 19) argues that the protests over filtering Internet access are "tangled up in false cries of censorship." Yet Internet filtering is a much more tangible form of censorship than, say, choosing which books to stock in limited shelf space, because the Internet is unlimited; filters actively censor only those materials that some individual deems harmful to children. And therein lies the problem: Who decides what is harmful? Violent pictures may be deemed harmful, but nobody would argue that children shouldn't learn about the Holocaust. Some might consider nudity inappropriate, but nobody would suggest that teen-agers shouldn't see Michelangelo's "David." Yet most Internet filters can't make these simple distinctions.  JOHN ROSENTHAL newyork, Oct. 19, 1998

title:
NEW YORKERS & CO.;
Home Delivery, Off the Internet
body: newyorkers are used to picking up the phone and having whatever they fancy wrapped up and hot-footed to their doorstep. Now they need just pick up their fingers with the debut last month of the Homedelivery Web site. After arriving at the site -- http://homedelivery.com -- shoppers can choose "In my neighborhood," entering their ZIP code for a list of stores with hand delivery, or select "Anywhere" for a list of merchandise categories, like books or flowers or tobacco. They can then choose from a number of retailers that fill mail orders. Shoppers also pick a method of payment (cash on delivery or credit card) and get an electronic receipt by email. The idea grew out of something Ari Friedman, the company's president and founder, said he wanted for himself. Though the plans are in an embryonic stage, he said he plans to expand the site to serve other American cities.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Cartoon Characters Give Web Sites Their Master's Voice
body: New software called Agent 7 can help personalize a Web site with an animated character that speaks in one's own voice. Agent 7, by 7th Level Inc. (www.7thlevel.com), provides cartoon characters that can be assigned specific mannerisms like pointing and waving. After a message is recorded into a WAV file with the PC's microphone, Agent 7 will lip synch the character to a vocal track and convert the creation to Web-ready animation. Agent 7 characters can also be embedded into Microsoft Powerpoint, Word and Excel files. Anyone for spreadsheet serenades? Graphic   Drawings (7th Level Inc.)

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Using Internet Polls To Predict Election Results
body: It remains to be seen whether the Internet, as a grass roots medium, will revolutionize politics, but political pollsters hope it will at least help them predict the outcome of elections. In the latest effort to determine whether the Net is a viable medium to gauge voter predilections, Harris Black International and Excite are conducting four on-line polls on the Nov. 3 elections. The polls will track the sentiments of registered voters in senatorial and gubernatorial races in 16 states. The information has significance to Harris Black internally. The oft-quoted polling company wants to determine whether Internet polls can approximate the accuracy of telephone polls. Whereas each Harris Black telephone poll reaches more than 1,000 people a month, each of the new political polls will reach 80,000 voters, said George Terhanian, director of Internet research for Harris Black. There is a potential benefit for consumers: fewer telephone calls from pollsters during dinner. (Note to pollsters: please try to get the telemarketers to follow suit.)

title: COMPANY BRIEFS
body: ALLSTATE LIFE INSURANCE CO., a unit of Allstate Corp., Northbrook, Ill., agreed to reinsure and administer about 21,000 variable annunity contracts worth a total of $1.3 billion managed by Lincoln National Corp., a financial services company based in Fort Wayne, Ind.  GOODNOISE CORP., Palo Alto, Calif., an Internet record company, agreed to buy Nordic Entertainment Worldwide, Napa, Calif., and Creative Fulfillment Inc., Santa Monica, Calif., both Internet music sellers, for undisclosed terms. GORDON BROTHERS GROUP, Boston, announced a strategic merger with DJM Asset Management, newyork, a company specializing in real estate acquisition and sales services for retailers.  BEST BUY CO., Eden Prairie, Minn., a consumer electronic retailer, said it would buy back as much as $100 million, or about 3 percent, of its outstanding stock.

title: Congress Passes Anti-Piracy Bill
body: Legislation intended to protect books, music, computer software and other works from Internet pirates cleared its last congressional hurdle today, winning unanimous approval by the House of Representatives. The Senate approved the measure last week. It will now go to the White House, where President Clinton is expected to sign the bill into law. The main provisions of the legislation would shield telephone companies and on-line service providers from liability when a customer illegally transmits or posts copyrighted works on their networks. The bill is a compromise involving the telephone industry, on-line service providers and Hollywood producers and writers. The competing interests had been haggling for more than two years over the issue of when and under what circumstances a company would be liable for copyright infringement. The legislation would also make it a crime to circumvent technological protections used to prevent copying of copyright-protected works. The bill also retains the "fair use" principal -- which lets schools, libraries and others make limited copies of copyrighted works.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
New Chief for Times Magazine Group
body: Leonard P. Forman has been named president and chief executive officer of The newyork Times Company's magazine group, the company announced yesterday. Formerly senior vice president for corporate development, Mr. Forman, 53, succeeds James W. Fitzgerald, 59, who will serve in an advisory role as chairman of the magazine group for one year. Mr. Forman will be responsible for the magazine group's publications: Golf Digest, Golf World and Golf Shop Operations. He will report to Russell T. Lewis, president and chief executive officer of the Times Company. The Times Company publishes The newyork Times, the Boston Globe, 21 regional newspapers and three magazines. It also operates television and radio stations as well as news, photo, graphic and electronic publishing services. Graphic   Photo: Leonard P. Forman. (John Abbott for The newyork Times)

title:
PRIVATE SECTOR;
Other Alums May Take the Hint
body: Never one to shirk the limelight, Michael R. Bloomberg has rounded off his gift-giving to Johns Hopkins University at an even $100 million. Mr. Bloomberg, the colorful -- some say egotistical -- founder of Bloomberg L.P., says he will add $45 million to the $55 million he contributed three years ago. That makes him the "largest single donor by double" to the Baltimore school, a spokesman for Johns Hopkins said, adding that Mr. Bloomberg, head of its $1.2 billion fund-raising drive, is "putting his money where his mouth is." Mr. Bloomberg says most of the new money will go to undergraduate financial aid. "Even though the economy is softening and markets go down, we still have to educate kids," said the author of an autobiography entitled "Bloomberg by Bloomberg." Last year, he gave a similarly high-minded reason for his original gift, but couldn't help adding that the donation generated "great publicity for my company and the university."   GERALDINE FABRIKANT Graphic   Photo: Michael R. Bloomberg

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
PENTON MEDIA TO ACQUIRE MECKLERMEDIA FOR $274 MILLION
body: The business media company Penton Media Inc. agreed yesterday to acquire the Mecklermedia Corporation for about $274 million in a move that bolsters Penton's position on the Internet. Mecklermedia, whose products include the Internet World and Ispcon trade shows, owns several prized Web site names, including Internet.com, which contains a network of 18 Web sites. Penton Media, which was spun off from the Chicago-based Pittway Corporation in August, offered to acquire Mecklermedia's common stock for $29 each. The shares of Mecklermedia, based in Westport, Conn., jumped about 30 percent, gaining $6 each, to $26.1875, while Penton slipped 43.75 cents, to $13.125.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ZIFF-DAVIS TO SHUT 3 MAGAZINES AND CUT 350 JOBS
body: Ziff-Davis Inc., a major publisher of computing magazines, said yesterday that it would discontinue three publications and cut 350 jobs, or 10 percent of its unitedstates work force. The newyork-based company will stop publishing Internet Business, Equip and Windows Pro. Instead it will focus on stronger products like PC Magazine, PC Week, the Comdex trade show and its ZDNet technology Web site. Costs associated with the restructuring will lower fourth-quarter earnings by $50 million to $60 million, before taxes, the company said. Shares of Ziff-Davis fell 28 percent, falling $1.6875 each, to $4.25, on the newyork Stock Exchange.

title: Dow Jones Profits Are Down by 4%
body: Dow Jones & Company's profits slipped 4 percent in the third quarter, as the company, the publisher of The Wall Street Journal, incurred nearly $10 million in costs to cut jobs at its Ottaway community newspaper group. Dow Jones announced yesterday that it had earned $25.6 million, or 27 cents a diluted share, in the quarter that ended on Sept. 30, down from $26.8 million, or 28 cents a diluted share, a year earlier. Revenue dropped 30 percent, to $443.6 million from $636.3 million, mainly reflecting the sale of its Dow Jones Markets financial information service in May. Dow Jones also suffered from softer advertising as companies have felt the pinch of Wall Street's recent downturn. Severance costs for the 220 job cuts at Ottaway slashed 10 cents a share from the recent quarter's profits. Dow Jones was also hurt by higher newsprint prices and Asia's economic troubles. The results were in line with lowered expectations announced last week by Dow Jones, based on weaker September advertising at The Journal and Barron's magazine. Shares of Dow Jones fell $1.75, to $42.5625.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
General Consumers Are Similar To Those Plugged Into Web
body: It sometimes seems there are two parallel universes, one with tech-savvy Netizens on the front lines of the digital revolution, and one with plain old folks who think calculators, in-person conversation and paper-based organizers work just fine. One new study finds those universes are not as far apart as they appear. Interactive Solutions Group, a division of Market Facts Inc., finds that the general consumer population and Internet users "mirror one another in most buying habits." The study of 3,000 households found that when the group of Internet users was controlled to reflect the demographics of the general population, those surveyed had similar responses to questions about life styles, travel, health issues and media habits. Interactive Solutions Group, which researches buyer habits on the Web, hopes that the survey will demonstrate to major corporations that they can rely on the validity of marketing surveys taken via the Net. MATT RICHTEL

title:
NEWS WATCH;
THE DOCTOR IS IN
body: Think of it as a doctor's office with the world's largest waiting room. America's Doctor Online is a new service provided to members of America Online. Found on AOL's Health channel, America's Doctor Online (keyword: amdoc) will provide AOL users with free access to certified primary-care doctors, either through email correspondence or through real-time conversations in chat rooms. "AOL is always talking about the on-line community." said Dr. Scott Rifkin, the service's founder. "To have a community, you need medical information. I just thought there ought to be docs talking to users." There are no diagnoses, prescriptions, record-keeping or follow-ups. The more than 40 ADOL doctors can offer only general information.

title: Potential of the Internet
body: To the Editor: These days we read daily that the Internet is the most powerful educational tool the world has ever seen.  Yet, the uses on which most people have focused are its massive storage capability and its role as a research tool. These uses will not transform education. To take advantage of its power, the Internet must be more than a larger library or place to put Web pages -- as valuable as these uses are. The power of the Internet is in its human potential. By connecting us as global citizens and local community members, we learn better. We open ourselves to new ideas, and in turn, shape the thinking of others through diverse input. We and our students are empowered to apply learning within our societies and in the global community in ways that can impact positively on lives and environments.  EDWIN H. GRAGERT newyork, Oct. 1, 1998  The author is director of the International Education and Resource Network.

title: Yahoo Reports Robust Growth
body: The on-line directory company Yahoo Inc. reported another quarter of robust growth today, helping restore some investor confidence to the volatile Internet sector. Yahoo said it earned $16.7 million, or 15 cents a diluted share, in the third quarter, up from $681,000, or 1 cent a diluted share, in the period a year earlier. The earnings were above the 9 cents a share that most analysts had been forecasting. Sales rose to $53.6 million, from $18.1 million. Yahoo shares, which fell sharply yesterday, regained some of the lost ground in after-hours trading, following the release of the third-quarter numbers. Yahoo, which had closed the regular session down $10.4375, to $114.375, was trading at $116.50 after the earnings report. Yahoo, the Internet service of choice among office workers and a close second to America Online Inc. in the at-home market, has been a bellwether for the entire group of on-line businesses.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
LYCOS PLANS $83 MILLION STOCK DEAL FOR WIRED DIGITAL
body: Lycos Inc. agreed yesterday to acquire Wired Digital Inc., a privately held Internet company, for $83 million in stock. In the deal, Lycos will issue additional stock equal to any Wired Digital cash on hand at the time of closing. Wired Digital, based in San Francisco, provides Internet-based products and services, including Hotbot, a so-called spider search engine. Lycos, based in Waltham, Mass., provides Web navigation as well as business and consumer electronic commerce products. Lycos said its Angelfire home pages and Mailcity email applications were now offered to all Hotbot and Wired Digital users. Lycos's stock fell $1.8125 a share, to $30.125.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Trade Group Forming For Internet Issues
body: A group of Internet marketing and promotion executives have formed the Internet Direct Marketing Bureau in newyork, a trade organization that will address such issues as email advertising and on-line privacy. Paul Grand, 30, chief executive at Word of Net Promotions in Sherman Oaks, Calif., is heading a steering committee for the association, which will hold its first meeting on Nov. 11 in Scottsdale, Ariz. The new group plans to elect a chairman, president and vice president and hire an executive director in the next year.

title: Bell Atlantic Sets Fast Web Access
body: The Bell Atlantic Corporation said yesterday that it had begun offering high-speed Internet access in Washington and Pittsburgh, supported by marketing alliances with computer companies, to meet the demand for faster connections to computer networks. The company, the largest local phone company in the unitedstates, also announced a partnership with Cnet Inc.'s and NBC's Snap Internet search directory. NBC, which is owned by the General Electric Company, first invested in Snap in June. Bell Atlantic's service, using asymmetric digital subscriber lines or A.D.S.L., offers Internet connections up to 250 times faster than standard modems. It can simultaneously handle data and regular calls on the same line. Local phone companies are scurrying to offer faster Internet access to meet consumer and business demand and compete with cable companies offering very high-speed connections via cable modems. Bell Atlantic said it had alliances with Apple Computer Inc., the Compaq Computer Corporation, the Dell Computer Corporation and CompUSA Inc. to market the service. Bell Atlantic's A.D.S.L. service starts at $59.95 a month.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Executive Is Named At New York Times
body: Michael G. Williams has been appointed vice president and chief information officer of The newyork Times. His appointment was announced yesterday by Janet L. Robinson, the newspaper's president and general manager. Mr. Williams, 42, had been vice president for information technology and chief technology officer at the Seagram Company's Spirits and Wine Group. He had been at Seagram since 1992, previously serving as chief information officer of Seagram Asia-Pacific and in other communications management positions. Before that Mr. Williams worked for the Aetna Life and Casualty Company and the Emery Air Freight Corporation in telecommunications. Mr. Williams will be responsible for the development and maintenance of business and publishing systems, the production of all Times products printed by outside vendors, the newspaper's data center and the administration of some business customer functions. He will report to Richard H. Gilman, senior vice president for operations. Graphic   Photo: Michael G. Williams

title:
BUSINESS;
Treasury to AllowSales by Telephone
body: Investors will be able to buy unitedstates Treasury bills, notes and bonds by touch-tone telephone starting tomorrow, the Treasury Department announced last week. To use the service, an investor must have a Treasury Direct account with the department's Bureau of Public Debt. An account can be established by requesting a form from one of the 12 regional Federal Reserve banks or through the Treasury's Internet site on the World Wide Web, www.publicdebt.treas.gov. Once a customer gets an account number from the Treasury -- a process that usually takes about two weeks -- the customer can dial (800) 943-6864 to find what securities are available and follow instructions for buying them.

title: Avoiding Log-Offs
body: To the Editor: Regarding Keith Johnson's letter (Sept. 24) about staying on line while using AOL: Go to www.jimjams .com, where you can download a product called Absolutely on Line (free trial) that will send a signal to your ISP that you are active.   RICHARD GORDON newyork, Sept. 25, 1998

title:
NEWS WATCH;
New Web Radio Will Show Animation to Go With Music
body: Somewhere around the nexus of MTV, radio, the Internet and the late-night laser show at the Planetarium exists FlashRadio, which its marketers are calling a new concept in radio. FlashRadio (www.flashradio.com), which is scheduled to make its debut today, presents five channels of different music themes, including pop, alternative and urban. The added touch is that while the music plays, the monitor fills with a continuous animation show (the images are not tailored to the individual songs, but to the channel's "mood"). The station is the product of a joint effort between Sonicnet (www.sonicnet.com), the popular music entertainment site; Macromedia (www.macromedia.com), which makes animation software, and the Intel Corporation. Nicholas Butterworth, the 30-year-old president of Sonicnet, a division of TCI Music, conceded that there were already a lot of radio stations on the Internet. "They have been great to listen to, but boring to watch," he added. How much fun FlashRadio will be to watch may depend on the speed of your processor. Mr. Butterworth noted that a Pentium II processor was needed for optimal viewing. That is a vast minority of home computers.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
This Space Available on AOL Starting for a Mere $25,000
body: For the Web surfer who has everything, the new Neiman Marcus Christmas catalogue offers an exclusive spot on the menu of America Online. The price tag: just $25,000. Actually, that is the minimum bid in the auction for the spot, which AOL calls a "keyword." Typically, these keywords are saved for general categories like Sports or News or are sometimes used to advertise on-line events for celebrities like the Spice Girls. The keyword up for auction will be the first assigned to a regular Joe or Jane, albeit one with some big green to toss around. The winning bidder will get a new computer (perhaps not a big bonus for someone with $25,000 to spare on a Web site) and help in designing the content to which the keyword will be linked. There are some restrictions, however, in that the bidder can use the keyword to link only to personal content, not to business material. The keyword will be active for one year. "It's like a vanity license plate," said Ginger Reeder, a spokeswoman for Neiman Marcus Direct, who knows how to wring an analogy out of the information superhighway metaphor.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
WOLTERS KLUWER U.S. TO ACQUIRE OVID TECHNOLOGIES
body: The Wolters Kluwer U.S. Corporation, a wholly owned unit of the big Dutch publisher Wolters Kluwer N.V., said yesterday that it had agreed to buy the electronic information provider Ovid Technologies Inc. for about $200 million. The companies said that Wolters would buy all shares outstanding of Ovid, which is based in newyork, for $24.59 a share in cash. Ovid's shares were unchanged yesterday at $20. The deal was announced after the close of trading.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
BEA SYSTEMS TO BUY WEBLOGIC FOR $192.5 MILLION IN STOCK
body: BEA Systems Inc. agreed yesterday to buy the closely held Weblogic Inc. for $192.5 million in stock, based on Friday's closing price, giving the corporate software maker Weblogic's Internet technology to add to its product line. BEA will issue 7.7 million shares to buy the San Francisco-based company. BEA, based in San Jose, Calif., said it would include Weblogic's software in its own products, which let companies process such transactions as airline reservations over different types of computers in a network. Weblogic's Internet technology will let BEA's customers also handle transactions over the Web, the companies said.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
PRODIGY COMMUNICATIONS PLANS PUBLIC OFFERING
body: The Prodigy Communications Corporation, an on-line service that has shed its extensive content services to focus on providing Internet access, announced yesterday that it would sell shares in a public offering. The news came on the heels of a highly successful public offering by Ebay Inc., an on-line auctioneer whose stock soared more than 163 percent in its first day of trading on Thursday. Prodigy said the size of its offering had not been set. It said the timing of the offering would be determined by market conditions, but that it did not expect to come to market before November.

title: AT&T-Yahoo Partnership
