body: The AT&T Corporation has expanded its marketing partnership with Yahoo Inc., the No. 1 Internet search directory, to create a co-branded Internet service. AT&T had agreed with Yahoo in May to market its phone services on Yahoo's directory. The new service will be called Yahoo Online, powered by AT&T Worldnet Service. The Yahoo Online service will be available at an introductory subscription for $14.95 a month, the companies said.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DELL, AT&T AND OTHERSOFFER INTERNET PACKAGE
body: The Dell Computer Corporation teamed with the AT&T Corporation, Excite Inc. and SBC Communications Inc. yesterday to offer a package of Internet hookups intended to attract the growing number of people who buy personal computers mostly to get on line. Terms were not disclosed. Buyers of Dell computers will be offered Internet service through AT&T and then will be taken directly to an Excite site on the Web. The move by Dell, the No. 1 direct seller of PC's, follows similar offerings from the Compaq Computer Corporation and Gateway Inc. SBC Communications said that starting early next year it would offer Dell users faster A.D.S.L. technology, which speeds the delivery of Internet content over regular phone lines.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
FIRST INITIAL STOCK SALE IN 4 WEEKS RAISES $63 MILLION
body: Ebay Inc., operator of an Internet auction site, raised $63 million yesterday in the first initial stock sale in four weeks. The company, in San Jose, Calif., sold 3.5 million shares at $18 each, the top of the $16-to-$18 range set by the lead underwriter, Goldman, Sachs & Company. The initial offering gave the three-year-old company a market capitalization of $715.3 million and its 31-year-old founder and chairman, Pierre M. Omidyar, a stake worth about $274.1 million. Ebay shares are expected to do well as they begin trading today, analysts said, even though the initial offerings market has been battered for months.

title: Downloading on AOL
body: To the Editor: Michelle Slatalla, the writer in "A Second Look at AOL, the Refurbished Ellis Island of the Net" (Sept. 17), was fortunate that her return to AOL was courtesy of her current Internet service provider. She mentions a long download, but at least with her I.S.P., it was uninterrupted. Any AOL download longer than 47 minutes is interrupted by a message that asks, "Do you wish to stay on?" If you're not around to answer, AOL simply boots you off. Downloading from AOL requires you to stay at the screen, or at least be around every 47 minutes. Ms. Slatalla even mentions a conversation with an AOL representative who seemed surprised that millions of people had sat through the download. Nobody with a decent I.S.P. sits through a download. You go off and do something else for a while, or go to bed, while the download proceeds automatically. When it's done, your computer hangs up after a reasonable amount of idle time.  KEITH JOHNSON newyork, Sept. 18, 1998

title: Land Lines for Data
body: To the Editor: One important use of the standard phone line not specifically addressed in "Cutting the Cord" (Sept. 17) is Internet service. The majority of Internet users connect to their service provider via a standard phone line. When Internet service providers that are not centered around land lines (like providers of cable modems or I.S.D.N. lines) become less expensive and more popular, the billions of fiber optic lines in the land will become less useful. That will take another huge bite out of the land-line market.  DAVID MARCINKOWSKI Cranford, N.J., Sept. 22, 1998

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Portable Music Player Uses No Tape or Disk -- Just RAM
body: A popular way to buy, trade and download music on the Internet may now become even more popular. The Rio PMP 300, created by Diamond Multimedia Systems of San Jose, Calif., is a portable music player that is about the size of a pager and does a lot more than beep. A departure from Walkman-like music players that use cassette tapes, compact disks or mini-disks, the Rio can store up to 60 minutes of digital-quality music directly into its 32 megabytes of memory. Because it can handle only music that is compressed in the MP3 format -- used to record and play music distributed on the Internet -- the Rio comes with software that also permits users to convert music on CD's into the MP3 format. A major feature of the Rio, which is expected to ship to retailers next month with a suggested price of $200, is that it cuts the tether that has previously tied MP3 music listeners to their computers. Other advantages: the tiny Rio can run for 12 hours on a single AA alkaline battery, and during a recent demonstration it proved to be highly resistant to flutter and skip, something that just might cause the hearts of some mobile music lovers to skip a beat themselves.   MICHEL MARRIOTT

title:
NEWS WATCH;
The Purple Moon Store
body: Purple Moon, the software company whose "friendship adventures" cater to pre-teen-age girls, is getting ready to entice budding shoppers into getting adventurous with their weekly allowance. On Oct. 1, Purple Moon will post an on-line shopping center on its Web site (www.purple-moon.com), featuring backpacks, CD-ROM's, watches and other items related to the narrative world of characters in the Purple Moon games.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DISNEY AND INFOSEEK TO CREATE NEW INTERNET DIRECTORY
body: The Walt Disney Company and the Infoseek Corporation said yesterday that they were developing a new Internet directory called Go Network, to be introduced later this year, as the world's No. 2 entertainment company looks to reach a bigger on-line audience. The move, reported yesterday by The Wall Street Journal, follows Disney's agreement in June to buy a 43 percent stake in Infoseek, which has the fourth-largest Internet search and directory service. The companies said the new site would build on Infoseek's current service. Shares of Infoseek rose 81.25 cents, to $21.3125; Disney fell 43.75 cents, to $25.125.

title:
INVESTING: DIARY;
For Yahoo, the Growth Mantra Goes On and On and On
body: Investors searching for signs of life in the stock market, and for the technology sector in particular, need look no further than their Internet search engine. While thousands of stocks are trading at 25 percent or more below their recent highs, shares of Yahoo, which closed at $90.4375 on Friday, are up 430 percent from their one-year low and off just 12.8 percent from their high on July 7. There is more good news. On Thursday, at a conference sponsored by Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities in San Francisco, Yahoo's management told portfolio managers that the company's operating profit margin was likely to increase by more than one-third by this time next year. That means that the 16 to 26 percent operating margins that Yahoo said it expected when it went public in mid-1996 should increase to a range of 30 to 36 percent. On Wednesday, Yahoo delivered the same message to a conference sponsored by Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette in newyork. That day, Yahoo shares jumped nine points.   EDWARD WYATT

title:
NEWS WATCH;
An Internet Filter Is Eager To Zap the Starr Report
body: At least one software company is bragging that it can do a highly effective job of keeping the work of Kenneth W. Starr, the independent counsel, from reaching your home computer. Seeking to capitalize on the goings-on in Washington, the company, Cybersitter, fired off a press release late last week announcing that its filtering software of the same name could keep children from viewing the salacious details in Mr. Starr's report. Cybersitter is one of a handful of programs marketed to parents and teachers as a way to keep children from viewing lurid content and hate speech. Marc Kantor, vice president for marketing at Cybersitter, which is based in Santa Barbara, Calif., said that the program would not filter out documents just because they included the word "sex" but that it was programmed to filter out content that mentioned oral sex or included discussions of sexually explicit activity. Asked if the software might inadvertently prevent students from learning about important civic matters, Mr. Kantor said he urged parents not to rely solely on the software but to read the document and make their own decisions about the suitability of its content.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
You Can Surf Together But Who Gets to Drive?
body: Who's ready for a browser built for two? Hip Bone Software of Palo Alto, Calif., recently released Co-navigator, a Java applet that permits individuals sitting at separate computers to surf the Web together (www.hipbone.com). The software, which takes only a couple of seconds to download, enables two or more computers to communicate so their users see the same Web pages. When one person moves to a U.R.L., the browsers on the other computers follow. For now, Hip Bone is giving away the software on its Web site. Dan Rolla, a co-founder of Hip Bone, said the company hoped that the technology would become so popular that it would be able to license versions of the software, sell advertising space on Co-navigator and sell data on the habits of joint Web surfers. So who gets to control the browser when there is a disagreement over a destination? Whoever types in a U.R.L. first, Mr. Rolla said. Sounds as though this could make battles over the television remote control seem like child's play. Graphic   Photo

title: Writers' Consolation
body: To the Editor: I was pleased to see that Alberto Manguel's "Writers' Wish List" (Op-Ed, Sept. 8), on the technological consolations for the slow-selling author, ended with Mr. Manguel's turning back to Thomas Love Peacock and a less mechanical way of coping. Almost 40 years ago, when my first and only novel was busily not selling, I copied a passage from Oliver Goldsmith's "Vicar of Wakefield" that I handed to anyone who asked how the book was going: "I published some tracts . . . myself, which, as they never sold, I have the consolation of thinking were read only by the happy Few."  GERALD WEALES Philadelphia, Sept. 9, 1998

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
QWEST COMMUNICATIONS TO BUY ICON INTERNET SERVICE
body: Qwest Communications International Inc., which is building a nationwide network based on Internet technology, has agreed to acquire the Icon CMT Corporation, an Internet-service provider, for $185 million in stock. The shares of Icon soared 44 percent, gaining $3.25, to $10.50, in Nasdaq trading. Qwest's stock was unchanged at $28.8125. The acquisition of Icon will allow Qwest, based in Denver, to offer a broader menu of Internet-related services to large corporate clients. Qwest's fiber optic network is robust but lacks the heavy traffic volume of such rivals as MCI and AT&T. Icon, based in Weehawken, N.J., sells Internet access, Web hosting and network-management services to large businesses.

title: Sulzberger to Retire As Museum Chairman
body: Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, chairman of the Metropolitan Museum of Art for 11 years, will retire from that post by early next year, the museum has announced. Mr. Sulzberger, who is chairman emeritus of the newyork Times Company, reaches 73, the mandatory retirement age for a trustee, in 1999 and is advancing his departure by several months to make the search for his successor concurrent with the museum's search for a new president, the Metropolitan said. In addition, Mr. Sulzberger announced the election of a noted art collector, Karen Bassine Cohen, who has a special interest in French 19th-century works, as an honorary trustee of the museum.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Accounts
body: * Auction Universe, newyork and Yalesville, Conn., an on-line auction Web site owned by the Times Mirror Co., named two agencies to handle accounts with combined billings estimated at $10 million. Romann Group, newyork, will handle traditional advertising and Modem Media. Poppe Tyson, newyork, part of True North Communications, will handle creative and media placement for on-line advertising. Also, R/GA Interactive, newyork, another unit of True North, was named to handle Web site design. * Chasetel Wireless Communications, Chattanooga, Tenn., to Johnson Group, Chattanooga, as the first agency to handle its account. Billings were estimated at $4 million. Johnson Waterhouse, Chattanooga, will handle public relations.

title: COMPANY BRIEFS
body: HARSCO CORP., Harrisburg, Pa., a maker of gas-containment sytems, agreed to buy the high-pressure valve division of Amcast Industrial Corp., Dayton, Ohio, a metal fabricator, for an undisclosed price.  INFOSEEK CORP., Sunnyvale, Calif., will pay Microsoft Corp. $26 million for a two-year exclusive agreement to provide Internet search and directory services on WebTV, Microsoft's Internet-television service. UNITED NATURAL FOODS INC., Dayville, Conn., a distributor of natural foods, agreed to buy the closely held Albert's Organics Inc.. Bridgeport, N.J., a distributor of organically grown produce. Terms were not disclosed.

title: Mindspring to Buy Sprynet
body: Mindspring Enterprises Inc. said today that it would buy Sprynet, an Internet service provider, from America Online Inc. for about $35 million to $45 million in cash. Mindspring, an Atlanta-based Internet service provider, said it had agreed to purchase Sprynet's subscriber base of about 180,000 customers as well as the customer support and network operations. Mindspring said the final purchase price would be determined by the number of subscribers who transfer.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Ad Sales Executive Named at The Times
body: Denise F. Warren, who has spent the last 20 months as director for marketing, planning and research in the newyork Times advertising department, will become vice president for advertising sales, the newspaper announced yesterday. The promotion gives Ms. Warren, 34, responsibility for overseeing a variety of advertising categories -- including help wanted, general classified, real estate and home furnishings advertising -- which together account for roughly a third of the newspaper's advertising revenue, said Nancy Nielsen, a spokeswoman for The newyork Times Company. Ms. Warren joined the company in March 1988. After working as a financial analyst in two departments and as a business manager for group advertising sales at the company's women's magazine group, Ms. Warren joined the newspaper in July 1994 as a project manager in the strategic planning department.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
X-ceed Acquires Mercury Seven
body: X-ceed Inc. in newyork has acquired Mercury Seven Inc. in newyork, a development and consulting company that specializes in on-line services for Internet industry professionals. Terms were not disclosed. Mercury Seven, which operates an on-line network at www.channelseven.com, will become an autonomous unit of X-ceed. Bob Risse, 37, continues as chief executive and Kevin Labick, 28, continues as president. Both will join the management board of X-ceed, which has been expanding its interactive operations and recently hired Scott Mednick, former chairman and chief executive of Think New Ideas Inc., as co-chairman and chief strategic officer. Also, Mercury Seven said that it would join with Adknowledge in Palo Alto, Calif., to introduce Turbo List (www.turboads.com), a directory of Web sites that accept so-called rich media advertising formats, the more elaborate types of on-line pitches that many marketers are adopting.

title: Successful Searching
body: To the Editor: I enjoyed "Desperately Seeking Susan OR Suzie NOT Sushi" (Sept. 3). Anyone still having trouble finding information quickly on the Web might try some of the simple tricks I use: Go to the source. If you want the latest gross domestic product data for Jordan, call up the monthly statistical bulletin of the Central Bank of Jordan (www.cbj.gov.jo/docs/ mainme.html). Add the magic word "resources." If you are looking for information on "economics," for example, type in "economics resources." That often leads you to pages containing pointers to the best Web resources on the topic.  ERIK T. MUELLER newyork, Sept. 4, 1998

title: INTERNET'S IMAGE PROBLEM MAY DEPRESS USERS
body: To the Editor: The findings by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University associating Internet use with depression are not so unexpected (front page, Aug. 30). With the growth of pornography on line, the extensive news media coverage on Internet-related sex crimes and the general characterization of Internet use as a sport for geeks, cyberspace is suffering from an image problem. I wonder whether our notion that cyberspace is not "real" space, combined with our fear of technology overtaking every aspect of our lives, has added to the bad reputation that the Internet has recently gained.  JI CHAE Berkeley, Calif., Sept. 3, 1998

title:
INTERNET'S IMAGE PROBLEM MAY DEPRESS USERS;
On-Line Candor
body: To the Editor: I'm surprised that no one has suggested an obvious reason why Internet users might report slightly elevated levels of depression (front page, Aug. 30): Remote interaction tends to reduce inhibitions against expressing one's feelings, resulting in the phenomenon known as flaming, as well as more positive expressions of emotion. Thus, Internet users may simply be reporting their feelings more candidly than those who have not been exposed to the medium.  KEVIN SAUNDERS Ithaca, N.Y., Sept. 3, 1998

title:
INTERNET'S IMAGE PROBLEM MAY DEPRESS USERS;
The Web as Community
body: To the Editor: Re "Sad, Lonely World Discovered in Cyberspace" (front page, Aug. 30): As a parent of a child with diabetes and another who is predisposed to diabetes, I have made wonderful and enduring friendships on the Internet. The chat room on a Web site devoted to children with diabetes allows me and other parents of children with diabetes to air our frustrations in dealing with this chronic illness. The site allows us to help one another get the best medical care for our children and feel less alone in our daily struggles. We have a purpose for our connection. In many ways the Internet has given me back my life, and I'm sure it has done the same for others in similar situations.  ELLEN H. ULLMAN Boca Raton, Fla., Sept. 3, 1998

title: Does the Internet Bring Us Down?
body: To the Editor: If alienation on the Internet is the problem (front page, Aug. 30) one solution is obvious: use computers in a socially rich environment, like a public library. Using the Internet at your local library provides a healthy balance between private computing and public discourse. Moreover, libraries offer a rich array of information and pleasure reading outside of a computer screen. As more and more libraries offer comfortable chairs, espresso bars, children's programs and Internet access, libraries may become the post-millennium social centers.  KAREN SCHNEIDER Albany, Aug. 31, 1998

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
A Trans-Atlantic Cable Network Deal
body: A consortium of telecommunications operators signed a $1.5 billion project today for a new fiber optic cable link between Europe and the unitedstates intended to cut waiting time on the World Wide Web. More than 50 telecommunications operators signed contracts for the TAT-14 cable that will have a capacity of 640 gigabits and could carry 7.7 million simultaneous telephone calls. About 80 percent of its capacity will be allocated to Internet and multimedia traffic. The network is a 1997 initiative of 11 carriers: AT&T, British Telecommunications, Cable and Wireless, Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom, KPN of the Netherlands, MCI Communications, Pacific Gateway Exchange, Sprint, Swisscom and Telia. KDD Submarine Cable Systems of Japan, a unit of the Kokusai Denshin Denwa Company, is the main supplier of the project. The TAT-14 cable will link five European countries -- Germany, Britain, Denmark, France and the Netherlands -- with the unitedstates. It will span 22,000 miles and is expected to be completed and in service by the end of 2000.

title: Yahoo to Join Stock Index
body: The Internet search-engine company Yahoo Inc. will replace MCI Communications in the Nasdaq 100-stock index after MCI completes its merger with Worldcom Inc., the Nasdaq stock market said today. The Nasdaq index is a weighted index of 100 of the largest nonfinancial stocks listed on Nasdaq, based on market capitalization. Yahoo shares were up $5.75 each today, to $78.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
INKTOMI TO ACQUIRE C2B TECHNOLOGIES IN $90 MILLION DEAL
body: The InktomiCorporation, a company that provides search engines for computer users, said yesterday that it would acquire the privately held C2B Technologies, a developer of software for on-line comparison shopping, in a stock deal worth about $90 million. The purchase is Inktomi's first move into the growing on-line commerce market. C2B's software gives shoppers access to prices, industry commentary on products, user reviews and other information. Inktomi will acquire the outstanding stock of C2B for about 1.8 million shares of Inktomi common stock, with a market value of about $90 million, and will assume all outstanding options and warrants. Both companies are based in San Mateo, Calif. Inktomi's stock was up $2.375 yesterday, to $51.375, in Nasdaq trading.

title: Zapata Hires Wall St. Firm
body: The Zapata Corporation, a onetime oil driller trying to break into cyberspace, said today that it had hired Salomon Smith Barney, the Wall Street firm, to evaluate its financial alternatives related to its Internet business. Zapata has said it will split into two companies, separating its Internet operations from its food and packaging businesses. The company has not disclosed terms of the Internet deals it has signed to date.

title:
METRO NEWS BRIEFS: NEW YORK;
Queens Man Charged In Internet Sex Case
body: An electrical engineer from Queens used the Internet to arrange sexual liaisons with children and transmit child pornography, and he also sexually abused a 4-year-old girl, prosecutors said yesterday. Martin Schraier, 42, of Howard Beach, has been charged with sexual abuse, attempted sodomy, promoting an obscene sexual performance by a child and receipt and transmission of images depicting sexual conduct by a child, said Richard Brown, the Queens District Attorney. He was accused of using the Internet to transmit images of children as young as 5 who were engaged in sexual acts, Mr. Brown said. If convicted, Mr. Schraier would face up to 15 years in prison. In a statement, Mr. Brown also said Mr. Schraier sexually abused a 4-year-old girl, but no additional information was immediately available on that charge. The police seized Mr. Schraier's computer, disks and other material on Friday.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
CISCO SYSTEMS AGREES TO PURCHASE AMERICAN INTERNET
body: Cisco Systems Inc., the top maker of equipment to link computers, agreed yesterday to buy the closely held American Internet Corporation for about $56 million in stock to further its push into the lucrative market for providers of telephone, cable and Internet services. American Internet's products make it easier to install and set up television set-top boxes and cable modems to hook consumers up to the Internet. The acquisition is in keeping with Cisco's strategy of buying technology and engineering talent it does not already have to push into new markets. Shares of Cisco, based in San Jose, Calif., rose 12.5 cents, to $102.75, in Nasdaq trading.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Turning a Cursor Into an Ad But Mainly Just for Laughs
body: To view the newest form of advertising on the Web, you don't have to point and click. Just point and look. Comet Systems, a newyork company, has begun licensing software that can turn the cursor itself into any graphic or animation. Comedy Central, one of the cursor's early adopters, now offers the technology on its Web site to PC users (www.comedycentral.com). Visitors can surf with a cursor that looks like the animated character Kenny, from the show "South Park," or "Dr. Katz" from the show of the same name, or the comedy network's logo. Visitors to the site must first download the free Comet Systems software, which takes little more than 10 seconds (www.cometsystems. com). The year-old Comet Systems is marketing its malleable cursor as a way for companies to get their messages across in a pointed fashion. For instance, the 1-800-Flowers site is going to feature a cursor that morphs into a price tag when it is scrolled over certain sale items; other times is a red rose beside the numbers "1-800." Graphic   Photo

title: Times to Buy More Shares
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that its board had authorized spending as much as $575 million to buy back additional shares of the company's class A common stock. So far this year, the company has bought about six million shares for $201.2 million. The shares, which touched a 52-week high of $40.6875 on July 6, closed yesterday at $30.75, down 18.75 cents, on the newyork Stock Exchange.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
TMP WORLDWIDE TO BUY AUSTRALIAN RECRUITER
body: TMP Worldwide Inc., one of the world's largest recruiters and the owner of the Monster Board job-search Internet site, will buy the Australian recruiter Morgan & Banks Ltd. for $209 million in stock. The stockholders of Morgan & Banks will get no more than 0.1124 share and no less than 0.07025 share of TMP stock for each share held, based on the currency exchange rate at closing. Shares of TMP jumped $2.3125 yesterday, to $36.125; they have soared more than 51 percent in the last 12 months. TMP, based in newyork, is betting that buying Morgan & Banks will bolster its intern-to-chief-executive strategy as more people turn to the Internet for jobs and employees.

title: Gates Pinpoints Date of Browser Decision
body: William H. Gates, the chairman of Microsoft, asserts that his company began work on an Internet browser for its Windows operating system on April 5, 1994 -- two days before the incorporation of Netscape Communications, the company that would become its Internet rival. Mr. Gates pinpointed the date for the first time in an interview published today in The Seattle Times. The date is significant because a key allegation in the Government's antitrust lawsuit against Microsoft is that the software giant decided to bundle its browser, called Internet Explorer, with Windows to give Microsoft an unfair advantage over Netscape in the marketplace. Mr. Gates asserted in the interview that the decision to develop a browser was made during an executive retreat. "I said, 'Hey, we're going to get it integrated into the operating system,' " Mr. Gates said. In an April 16 memo, he gave executives responsibility for putting together browsing technology for Windows and proposed that Microsoft develop a Web site, he said.

title:
August 9-15;
Internet Privacy Deal
body: When new members fill out an on-line application form for the popular World Wide Web site Geocities, they are asked to reveal personal information about education, income, occupation and personal interests. Not to worry, Geocities promised on the site's registration page: "We will not share this information with anyone without your permission." But the Federal Trade Commission found that Geocities had misled more than two million subscribers by passing the information to advertisers and others. In the Federal Government's first Internet-privacy enforcement action, the F.T.C. approved a settlement with Geocities under which the site has to disclose how it intends to use the personal information it collects.   JOEL BRINKLEY

title: U.S. Cites Violation Of Internet Privacy
body: The Federal Trade Commission said that a popular site on the World Wide Web had lied to more than two million subscribers when it told them that it would not disclose personal information it had collected from them. In the Government's first enforcement action to safeguard privacy on the Internet, the commission said it had reached a settlement with Geocities, the company that runs the site, to stop making such promises. "Geocities misled its customers, both children and adults, by not telling the truth about how it was using their personal information," said an agency official. The company admitted no wrongdoing and was not fined for its actions. But it did post a new statement about how it uses the information it collects, including age, education, occupation, income and personal interests. Article, page A15.

title: Corrections
body: An article in Business Day on Monday about a patent awarded for an Internet auction system misidentified the court whose ruling last month helped pave the way for the new patent. It was the unitedstates Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which hears appeals from district courts in patent, trademark and copyright cases, not the unitedstates Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.

title: Netscape Names A New Executive
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation said Sunday that it had named a former Oracle Corporation executive, Barry Ariko, as chief operating officer in the latest move in the company's effort to redefine itself as a leading software company. Mr. Ariko, previously executive vice president and a member of the executive management committee at Oracle, had been given much of the credit for that software giant's sharp growth in sales in the last few years. Netscape said it had hired Mr. Ariko to fuel its enterprise software business, which is increasingly a main focus as the company seeks to offset the decline of its Internet browser. Although it is perhaps still best known for its browser, Netscape also makes a range of so-called enterprise software products, which are intended to help other companies do business over the Internet. Netscape's stock jumped $6.125 a share today, to $31.1875, in Nasdaq trading.

title: Apple Chooses Earthlink for iMac Service
body: Apple Computer Inc. has chosen Earthlink Network Inc. as the default Internet service provider for its new iMac home computers. Users who choose Apple's one-step Internet setup will be hooked up with the Earthlink Network, which will waive its usual $25 setup fee and give 30 days of free service to iMac buyers. Apple, intent on strengthening its position in the home computer market with a low-priced machine, plans to start selling the iMac on Saturday. The machines, expected to sell for $1,299, are Apple's first new line of home computers since the Performa was introduced in 1992. Earthlink, based in Pasadena, Calif., said more than 20 percent of its members use Apple Macintosh computers.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
SCIENTIFIC-ATLANTA STOCK UP 14% ON NEWS OF TCI ORDER
body: Scientific-Atlanta Inc. said yesterday that Tele-Communications Inc. had ordered "substantial quantities" of advanced digital-cable control boxes, with deliveries to begin later this year. Terms of the contract, the first that TCI, the second-largest unitedstates cable-television operator, has placed with Scientific-Atlanta, were not disclosed. Scientific-Atlanta's shares rose $2.9375 each, or 14 percent, to $23.9375. The Explorer 2000 set-top box, which TCI initially plans to distribute in Salt Lake City, can handle interactive applications for consumers, including Internet access, video on demand and electronic banking. They also can provide telephone service using the Internet.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ZAPATA GARNERS 31ST DEAL TO BUY AN INTERNET CONCERN
body: The Zapata Corporation, the fish-oil and meat-casings company that recently formed a business to focus on the Internet, agreed yesterday to buy the closely held Attitude Network Ltd. of Naples, Fla., to add computer-game software and news to its Web site. Terms were not disclosed. Attitude Network's six sites, which include Happy Puppy, are among the most popular computer-game sites on the Internet, according to Media Metrix, which tracks Web site visits. The deal brings to 31 the number of Internet sites and electronic-commerce businesses that Zapata's Web unit, the Zap Corporation, has agreed to buy. Shares of the Houston-based Zapata fell $1.4375, to $15.6875.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
A Half-Million Pictures to Beautify Your Words - Correction Appended
body: Bill Gates has established himself as the Lorenzo de' Medici of digitized art through his privately held company, the Corbis Corporation, which has amassed the rights to 23 million images and photographs. Now, through a partnership with Compaq's Alta Vista search service, Mr. Gates is throwing open the gallery doors to the public. The Corbis Picture Collection allows users to browse or search through more than 500,000 images from the collection (www.corbis.com). The Create a Card function at the Corbis site or through Alta Vista (www.altavista.com) allows the use of those images to create and send an email postcard. There are already many other E-postcard services, of course, but none with access to Corbis's images, which include Leonardo's Mona Lisa, the picture of Albert Einstein sticking out his tongue and 19 photographs of Mr. Gates himself. Corbis's Create a Card is free to users. The benefit for Corbis is very likely to be increased traffic for the company's site, which features other services that produce revenue, like its print shop, a travel service called Tripview and Corbis's imaging-licensing division. Correction  An article in Circuits yesterday about the Corbis on-line picture collection misstated the Web address of the Alta Vista search engine. It is: www.altavista.digital.com Correction-Date: August 7, 1998, Friday Graphic   Photos.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Financial Support for Sites With a Unique Point of View
body: Somewhere on the World Wide Web, among the gritty personal home pages and the glitzy sites offered by corporate giants, are pages that forge new ground -- and the Web Development Fund wants to know about them. The fund, a nonprofit group, has just opened its second call for entries for projects that will tap into the "public interest and creative use of the medium," said the fund's founder and director, Marc Weiss. Crystallizing the potential of the Web to organize people, and getting users to think about challenging issues, are two criteria for sites that the fund seeks to support. Proposals will be accepted until Sept. 13. A look at the guidelines, as well as a list of sites financed in the last year, are available at www.weblab.org.LISA NAPOLI

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Japanese Senior Managers Are Lagging in Internet Access
body: Remember a couple of years ago when Americans believed that Japanese business could do no wrong? Neither does anybody else, apparently. The newly formed legions of Japan-bashers can look for more ammunition in a recent study on Internet usage. According to a survey by Andersen Consulting, only 71 percent of Japanese executives have access to the Internet, the lowest level among senior management in nine of the world's leading economies. American executives led the field, with 99 percent having access to the Internet, followed by executives from Canada (98 percent), France (91 percent) and Britain (91 percent). Only 13 percent of Japanese executives were reported as "comfortable" or "familiar" with the Internet, compared with 46 percent of American executives, although the Japanese were much more likely to use email (69 percent) than their counterparts in Germany (55 percent).   BRUCE HEADLAM

title: Web Shopping Tangles
body: To the Editor: "Internet Shopping: A Mixed Bag" (July 30) neglected one very compelling reason to buy on line: access. Not all of America lives equidistant between two malls. On-line shopping offers a tremendous breadth of goods not available locally at any cost -- much less the discount one often finds. Want some truffles from the French village of Sainte Alvere (www.sainte-alvere.com)? How about caviar from Azerbaijan (www.caviar.tic.cz) and a nice chianti from the Castello di Monterinaldi (www.monterinaldi.it)? You can find these offerings on line. I'd also have to take issue with the contention that the Internet is no bargain. Neither is newyork -- unless you know how to shop. On-line coupons, classifieds, auctions, comparison shopping: all these elements combine to offer a very rich, but not expensive, virtual shopping experience.  JOSEPH LOWERY newyork, Aug. 3, 1998  The writer is author of "Buying Online for Dummies" (IDG Books Worldwide, 1998).

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
New York Times Puts An Account in Review
body: WQXR-FM and WQEW-AM in newyork, the radio stations owned by The newyork Times Company, placed in review their account, which has been handled since 1990 by McCaffrey Ratner Gottlieb & Lane in newyork and a predecessor agency, McCaffery & Ratner. Billings were estimated at $500,000. Gina Dona, marketing and promotion director at WQXR and WQEW, said McCaffrey Ratner would be invited to compete for the account, and added that she was seeking other agencies to participate, too. A decision is expected in October.

title: Ex-Investment Banker Charged
body: Michael Lissack, a former Smith Barney Inc. investment banker, has been charged with using the Internet to harass executives at his old firm by posting messages that solicited phone calls to the company's headquarters and, in some instances, to the homes of executives. Mr. Lissack, 39, was arrested and arraigned by the Manhattan District Attorney's office earlier this week. The complaint says one Internet message asked for support for "Little Jim, a friend's 6-year-old just diagnosed with terminal liver cancer," and listed the Salomon Smith Barney address of James Boshart, the firm's vice chairman for investment banking. Mr. Boshart was bombarded with gifts and calls from well-wishers. The complaint charges that responses to the posting "tied up the telephone lines at Smith Barney causing Smith Barney to become annoyed and alarmed." A hearing is set for late August. Neither Mr. Lissack nor his lawyer could be reached for immediate comment. Salomon Smith Barney declined to comment.

title: Hollywood Entertainment to Buy Reel.Com
body: The Hollywood Entertainment Corporation, the second-largest chain of video rental shops, said yesterday that it had agreed to buy Reel.Com Inc., the largest service selling videos over the Internet. The price is $100 million, of which $30 million is in cash and the remainder in stock. The deal represents an expensive about-face for Hollywood Entertainment, which turned down a chance to invest in Reel.Com last year at a much lower price. "We thought we could do whatever they did better ourselves," Mark J. Wattles, the chairman and chief executive of Hollywood, said yesterday. "Then I started using the Internet and found that it takes more than prices next to products to sell things." Reel.Com, which was founded by Stuart Skorman, a former video store owner, has 60 people writing movie reviews and a number of ways to help people find movies that suit their tastes. Hollywood hopes to link the Web site to its list of the names and movie-rental habits of its 25 million members. This will help it find prospects and recommend to them the sort of movies they would like. As part of the deal, several of Reel's major backers will invest $67.5 million in Hollywood.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
VERIO BUYING HIWAY TO EXPAND ITS WEB SITE OPERATIONS
body: Verio Inc., a provider of Internet services, said yesterday that it would buy the closely held Hiway Technologies Inc. for $329.7 million in cash and stock to expand its business of operating Web sites. Verio will pay $101 million in cash and issue 8.67 million common shares for Hiway's outstanding shares. Its shares rose $2.625 yesterday, to $29. Shareholders of Hiway, which is based in Boca Raton, Fla., and employs 275 people, will own about 19 percent of the combined company. With the acquisition of Hiway, Verio, based in Englewood, Colo., will operate more than 150,000 Web sites.

title: S.E.C. Sets Up Unit to Fight Internet Fraud
body: Responding to the growth in securities fraud over the Internet, the Securities and Exchange Commission announced today that it had established an Office of Internet Enforcement. "While the Internet has many benefits, a small group of thieves is trying to hijack unsuspecting investors on the information superhighway," said Richard Walker, the S.E.C.'s director of enforcement. Securities fraud using the Internet has grown in recent years along with the bull market on Wall Street. Mr. Walker said that the commission had already brought more than 30 cases involving Internet fraud. Schemes have included fictitious stock offerings, stock price manipulation, frauds aimed at specific ethnic or religious groups and pyramid schemes in which funds from new investors are used to pay off promised returns to other investors. The S.E.C.'s on-line Enforcement Complaint Center now receives more than 120 reports a day of possible securities fraud over the Internet. The new Internet office will be headed by John Stark, now the commission's special counsel for Internet projects in the Enforcement Division. Jay Perlman, a senior attorney in the S.E.C.'s chief counsel's office, will be his deputy.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
HARCOURT UNIT BUYING GARTNER TECHNOLOGY TRAINING UNIT
body: The Harcourt Brace unit of Harcourt General Inc. agreed to buy Gartner Group's information technology training unit and will merge it into its NETg operating unit. Harcourt said Gartner Group would receive an 8 percent equity interest in the combined entity, plus other considerations, though it did not disclose the purchase price. The combined company will have revenue of more than $100 million in the fiscal year 1999, Harcourt said. Gartner Group, in Stamford, Conn., is a management consulting firm. Harcourt General, of Chestnut Hill, Mass., is a multimedia publisher and service provider.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
TELEFONOS DE MEXICO TO BUY STAKE IN PRODIGY SERVICES
body: Telefonos de Mexico S.A., or Telmex, Mexico's largest telephone operator and largest Internet service provider, said it planned to buy a 20 percent stake in the Prodigy Services Corporation for $49 million to secure a presence in the unitedstates Internet service provider market. The investment would be carried out by injecting new capital in Prodigy, the on-line service company, and by buying minority stakes from Prodigy's shareholders. Prodigy, controlled by Carso Global Telecom S.A. of Mexico, is the fourth-largest Internet service provider in the unitedstates with 450,000 customers. Carso Global also owns a 15 percent stake in Telmex.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
TEL-SAVE IN TALKS TO BE BOUGHT BY AN INTERNET COMPANY
body: Tel-Save Holdings Inc., which is based in New Hope, Pa., said yesterday that it was in talks to be acquired by an Internet company. Daniel M. Borislow, the chairman and chief executive of Tel-Save, would not name the suitor or say how soon he expected an agreement. The company's president, Gary McCullough, said the unnamed Internet company was attracted to Tel-Save, which sells long-distance phone services to subscribers to America Online Inc., because of Tel-Save's experience on the Internet. Tel-Save's stock fell $1.125, to $15.9375, in Nasdaq trading.

title:
National News Briefs;
Senate Votes to Prohibit Gambling on the Internet
body: The Senate voted today to try to shut down the billion-dollar Internet gambling industry, calling it addictive, a corrupting influence on the young and a source of crime. Senators voted 90 to 10 to ban all forms of gambling on the Internet, including the interactive, pay-to-play casino-style games offered by about 140 sites on the World Wide Web. Most are operated by businesses based overseas. The measure would extend to the Internet -- and to new technologies involving microwave transmission and fiber optic cable -- the current Federal ban on interstate gambling on sports by telephone or wire.

title:
Metro Business;
Internet Supermarket Moves Into New York
body: Peapod Inc., a leading Internet supermarket business, announced yesterday that it would begin to offer its service in the newyork metropolitan area later this year. Peapod, which takes orders for grocery and drugstore products over the Internet and delivers the merchandise to customers' homes, said it would start in Long Island, where it will have a warehouse. In early 1999, the company plans to expand service to northern New Jersey with a second warehouse, and hopes to begin in newyork City, Westchester County and Connecticut in the future. Peapod, whose Web site is www.peapod.com, now operates in seven metropolitan markets in the unitedstates.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Prodigy Opens On-Line Classes To Teach Software Programs
body: Prodigy Internet has established an on-line learning center, offering training classes for popular applications from Microsoft, Adobe, Lotus and others. Prodigy said the classes could reduce the time and costs associated with training by using the Internet as a delivery mechanism and using animation and real-time audio technology. The company has developed a synchronized multimedia file format to deal with the choppiness and poor quality found in most Internet multimedia files. Users will need to download and install a program to read the files. Training is available on about 40 programs, and more will be added, a Prodigy spokesman said. The learning center courses are available only to Prodigy members. A week of access to one tutorial costs $9.95; a year's access to the entire catalog costs about $200.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
LERNOUT & HAUSPIE IS IN $71 MILLION DEAL FOR GLOBALINK
body: Lernout & Hauspie Speech Products N.V. has agreed to buy Globalink Inc. for about $71.1 million in stock. Lernout said late on Monday that it would pay $5.60 a share for all of Globalink's 12.7 million shares outstanding. Globalink, based in Fairfax, Va., provides language translation software. The company had 1997 revenues of $14.7 million. Lernout & Hauspie, based in Belgium and Burlington, Mass., develops speech-recognition equipment. The company had 1997 revenues of $99.4 million. Shares of Globalink rose 18.75 cents, to $4.8125.

title: A Double-Edged Scalpel
body: To the Editor: The article about 9-year-old Robert Lord's recovery ("Can the Internet Cure the Common Cold," July 9) makes a strong case for patients using the Internet to discover potentially lifesaving information. Physicians all too frequently rely on memory and intuition to determine what's wrong with a patient and what to do about it. We should expect physicians to use currently available information tools that easily and quickly bring virtually all biomedical knowledge to bear on a patient's specific health problem.  DANIEL PAGE Falmouth Me., July 14, 1998  The author is executive director of the Health Commons Institute, which sponsors projects on how computer technology can improve health care.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
POINTCAST WITHDRAWS PLAN FOR PUBLIC STOCK OFFERING
body: Pointcast, the leading purveyor of "push" technology, which delivers World Wide Web information to consumers rather than forcing them to forage through the Web to find it, said yesterday that it had withdrawn its planned initial public stock offering to pursue a possible sale of the company or another venture. Pointcast offers users free software that downloads news and advertising from the Internet and displays it on their computers. David W. Dorman, the chief executive, said Pointcast had developed new software that combines news, electronic mail and shopping opportunities and is of interest to companies racing to become the portal -- or front door -- for Internet users. He declined to say which companies the concern was negotiating with.

title:
CURRENTS: HOME ACCESSORIES;
Click on Chopsticks And Chrysanthemum Plates
body: Rather push a mouse than a shopping cart? Home accessories are available at www.rabidhome.com, including lacquered chopsticks ($24 for four), a yellow bowl ($12.50) and Chrysanthemum plates ($48 for four), with advice and images to help shoppers coordinate. "We're trying to make buying on line more than a one-dimensional experience," said Doug Livingston, one of the Web site's creators. Graphic   Photo.

title: Cellularvision to Sell Bandwidth to Winstar
body: Cellularvision USA Inc. agreed yesterday to sell to Winstar Communications Inc. almost two-thirds of the radio spectrum bandwidth it uses to provide wireless television and Internet services in newyork City. Under the deal, Winstar would pay $32.5 million to acquire 850 of the 1,300 megahertz of continuous local multipoint distribution services, or LMDS, spectrum that Cellularvision holds under a license from the Federal Communications Commission. Winstar's newyork City holdings would total 1,750 megahertz. Winstar would also lend Cellularvision $3.5 million when lenders' consents were obtained and an additional $2 million when shareholders' approval was granted. LMDS is the wireless equivalent of fiber-optic cable. It uses small rooftop antennas and receivers to transmit television and high-speed Internet service. Winstar provides local telecommunications services via networks of rooftop radios and antennas. It had revenue of $47.4 million in the quarter ended March 31. Cellularvision delivers television and Internet access via wireless technology to newyork City residents. It had revenue of $1.4 million in the quarter ended March 31. Both companies are based in Manhattan.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
THE LEARNING COMPANY SELLS A CANADIAN BUSINESS
body: The Learning Company, the large educational software maker, said yesterday that its Canadian unit had sold its Canadian income tax software business to a unit of Wolters Kluwer N.V., the Dutch publisher, for $45 million in cash. The Learning Company unit, Softkey Software Products Inc., sold the tax-preparation business to CCH Canadian Ltd. The Learning Company, based in Cambridge, Mass., said it wanted to focus on instructional and entertainment titles. Proceeds from the sale will help pay for recent acquisitions.

title: COMPANY BRIEFS
body: ZAPATA CORP., Houston, said its Zap Corp. Internet subsidiary had agreed to acquire Coolchat Inc., Pleasanton, Calif., a free Web chat site with 300,000 members. Terms were not disclosed.  R. R. DONNELLEY & SONS CO., Chicago, a printing company, said the 450 employees at a Lackawanna County, Pa., printing plant might lose their jobs as the company considered its long-term future. TIGER MANAGEMENT L.L.C., newyork, a hedge fund run by Julian Robertson, and an affiliate reported that they hold a 10.1 percent stake in Federal-Mogul Corp., Southfield, Mich., a manufacturer of auto and truck parts.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
SOFTBANK OF JAPAN IN $400 MILLION ON-LINE DEAL
body: The Softbank Corporation, Japan's largest software distributor and an investor in on line companies, agreed to pay $400 million for 27.2 percent of E*Trade Group Inc., the biggest Internet-based brokerage firm.  Softbank paid $25.56 a share for 15.6 million new shares of E*Trade. E*Trade last traded at $24.50, down $1.0625, before trading in the stock was halted. E*Trade is the latest addition to Softbank's collection of Internet companies. The Tokyo-based company increased its stake in Yahoo Inc., the most-visited Internet directory, to 31 percent earlier this week. It also owns 35 percent of Geo Cities, a World Wide Web-based community, and 71 percent of Ziff-Davis Inc., a media company specializing in computers and software.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BRIEFS;
Europeans Clear Worldcom-MCI Deal
body: European regulators yesterday said they cleared Worldcom Inc.'s proposed $37 billion takeover of the MCI Communications Corporation on condition that MCI sell off its Internet businesses. The ruling by the European Union's executive Commission, which was widely expected, added that the buyer would have to be approved by both European and unitedstates regulators and that it might appoint a trustee to oversee the divestiture. It said the sell-off was needed to insure that the two long-distance phone giants did not dominate the market for Internet connection services to retail customers and Internet service providers.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
A.D.S.L. Lines of BellSouth To Start Including Mac Users
body: BellSouth plans to tap into the Apple market as the phone company speeds up its rollout of the A.D.S.L. high-speed Internet connection. When the company, which provides local phone service in the southeastern unitedstates, first announced its rollout of A.D.S.L. (asymmetric digital subscriber line) technology in May, it focused on Windows computers. But the company then received what it called a huge demand for the service from Macintosh devotees, something that caught its attention. "By working directly with Apple, we are bringing the Mac version of BellSouth.net Fast Access A.D.S.L. service to market much more quickly," said Andrew Dietz, director of product marketing for BellSouth.net Services. By focusing on Mac users, BellSouth hopes not only to increase market penetration but also to promote its service to the wider on-line community. "We also are extending BellSouth's lightning-fast capabilities to an important group of computer users, who we believe are highly likely to have Internet access and be evangelists for new Internet services," Mr. Dietz said.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
VERIO BUYS TABNET, WEB SITE CREATOR, FOR $45.5 MILLION
body: Verio Inc., an Internet service provider, acquired Tabnet, which helps in setting up World Wide Web sites, for $45.5 million in cash. Verio said it would also pay as much as $43.2 million if Tabnet meets certain levels of revenue and cash-flow growth, through December. Verio, based in Englewood, Colo., has bought more than 30 smaller Internet service providers since 1996. With Tabnet, it gets a large collection of registered Internet, or "domain," names as well as Tabnet's advertising agreements with top Internet sites. Verio, which went public in May at $23 a share, holds more than 55,000 domain names. Its shares rose 12.5 cents, to $27.25.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
VERISIGN BUYS SECURE IT, RIVAL IN INTERNET SERVICES
body: Verisign Inc., an Internet security company, said yesterday that it had acquired the closely held Secure It Inc. for about $69.1 million of stock. Verisign, based in Mountain View, Calif., issued 1.67 million shares to buy Secure It, a 20-month-old company based in Norcross, Ga., that provides Internet security consulting, testing and educational services to clients.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ZAPATA STOCK DOUBLES AFTER COMPANY SPLITS
body: The Zapata Corporation is splitting into two entities: Zapata, which includes the company's marine protein and food packaging business, and the ZAP Corporation, consisting of its Internet operations. Wall Street welcomed the deal. Shares of Zapata, which is based in Houston, more than doubled, soaring $11.625 each, to $21.50, on the newyork Stock Exchange. As part of its plan to focus on Internet business, ZAP will offer links to electronic-commerce businesses. ZAP formally announced it would acquire 21 Internet sites and electronic commerce businesses that would be integrated into ZAP.com, the new company's Web site. Zapata also said it would buy back, over time, up to five million shares, or 21.5 percent, of its stock.

title: Hate on the Web
body: To the Editor: Why aren't concerns about hate on the Internet part of the discussion on Internet self-governance (Business Day, June 29)? As the Internet grows, so do hate sites, reaching potential numbers unthinkable just a few years ago. People opening their email can be bombarded by unsolicited hate messages. Young people exploring the Web can unsuspectingly log on to virulent hate sites, like those of the Ku Klux Klan and the White Aryan Resistance. This new medium provides untold opportunities. However, as the medium of choice for hatemongers, the Internet also provides us with the challenge to do something about this problem.  ABRAHAM H. FOXMAN Natl. Dir., Anti-Defamation League newyork, June 30, 1998

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
QUALCOMM TO SPIN OFF SOME WIRELESS PHONE COMPANIES
body: Qualcomm Inc. said yesterday that it planned to spin off its investments in land-based wireless operating companies into a separate publicly traded company. Qualcomm, based in San Diego, makes digital wireless systems and Internet products. Stockholders will receive one share of the new company for each four Qualcomm shares. Qualcomm will receive a warrant to purchase up to 18 percent of the new company's shares over a 10-year period. The new company will own Qualcomm's interests in ventures in Mexico, Russia, Ukraine, Chile and Australia as well as Chase Telecommunications Inc. in the unitedstates. Qualcomm will provide financing in the form of a $250 million secured line of credit and $10 million in cash.

title: Microsoft Settles Lawsuit Over Trademark
body: The Microsoft Corporation settled a trademark lawsuit today, agreeing to pay $5 million for the right to continue using the name Internet Explorer for its World Wide Web browser. On the second day of a Federal jury trial in a Chicago, Microsoft reached a settlement with lawyers for Synet Inc., a defunct Illinois software company that said it had the the right to the trademark. "We are confident that we would have won the case on the merits, but we are pleased to put this issue behind us," said Mark Murray, a Microsoft spokesman. As part of the settlement, Microsoft takes over Synet's pending application to register Internet Explorer with the Patent and Trademark Office, but Mr. Murray said he was not sure whether the software giant would complete the registration. Microsoft lawyers argued at the trial and in court papers that Internet Explorer, far from being an exclusive Microsoft property, was merely a descriptive term for software that allows users to roam through cyberspace. But a decision from the patent office favored Synet's application.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
New Mexico Internet Law Is Ruled Unconstitutional
body: So far, laws that seek to protect minors from Internet pornography haven't passed muster with the Constitution. On Wednesday, a law was to take effect in New Mexico that would have made it a misdemeanor to "knowingly or intentionally" transmit sexual content, including "actual or simulated nudity, sexual intercourse or any other sexual conduct" to a minor. Late Tuesday, however, Judge C. LeRoy Hansen of Federal District Court in New Mexico issued an injunction, declaring that the legislation violates the First, Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. The decision should come as no surprise. In June 1997, the unitedstates Supreme Court overturned the Communications Decency Act, which would have made it a felony to send "indecent" material to minors.   MATT RICHTEL

title:
NEWS WATCH;
This Elephant Can Remember All of Those Lost Web Pages
body: Want to recall that fabulous Web page you found yesterday? You know, the one you forgot to list in a bookmark? If that happens to you often, you might be suffering from internesia (the inability to remember important Internet information). For people suffering from internesia and those with Web bookmarks that can fill a disk drive, help may be on the way. Elephant Tracks, a new downloadable program (www.elephantsoftware.com), watches where a Web browser goes and allows users to retrace their footprints. The program was written by Ed Staub, a 44-year-old programmer who said he had found himself suffering from internesia around New Year's. "I had this problem and looked for a solution," Mr. Staub said. "I couldn't find it, so I wrote this." Elephant Tracks indexes the words on Web pages that are viewed. When someone needs to look up an earlier page, the index for that page can be searched. "It is an infallible extension to a fallible memory," Mr. Staub said. Elephant Tracks for Internet Explorer costs $24.95. A version for Netscape Navigator should be ready in September.   STEVEN E. BRIER

title:
June 21-27;
Ruling Goes to Microsoft
body: Microsoft scored a major legal victory when a Federal Appeals Court ruled that the software giant could bundle anything it wanted with its Windows operating system, as long as the combination benefited customers. That issue was at the core of the Justice Department's longstanding lawsuit against Microsoft -- and the new suit, filed last month by the Department and 20 states. The Justice Department vowed to press on.   JOEL BRINKLEY

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
Bag-Tracking By Phone or Web
body: If your luggage was lost on a Delta Air Lines flight -- "delayed" is Delta's euphemism -- there is now something to do other than call an 800 number and listen to recorded messages. The airline has added a feature to its Web site that allows a traveler to learn the status of the bag search. But it can be tracked on the Web only after a passenger arriving at an airport reports the bag missing, describes it and its contents and receives an identification code for what Delta calls a property-irregularity report. On the Web site, www.delta-air.com/baggage, passengers enter their names and the report identification code. The site might then respond that the bag is being delivered to a particular address at a specified time. Or it might report that the bag is still being sought. For those without access to the Web, the number to call is (800) 325-8224.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Popular Target: Family Trees
body: The Web is an obvious destination for the genealogically inclined, and its popularity among family tree makers was underscored earlier this week when AT&T released the results of a survey: nearly one-third of those responding said they had used the Internet to seek family roots. In a survey of more than 5,400 AT&T Worldnet Service subscribers, one out of every 12 respondents said they had a family-tree Web page. Of those who did not, nearly 70 percent said they would like to create one. April Helm of Savoy, Ill., a professional genealogist who, with her husband, Matthew, maintains several Web sites on genealogy, pointed to the convenience of the Web as the principal reason for the explosion in interest in genealogy. "People are finding the Internet is a good tool for researching their family because it saves them from having to leave their house to find records," Ms. Helm said. At the same time that AT&T released its survey, it announced a genealogy page on the AT&T Worldnet Service Web site (www.att.net/find/ genealogy). The AT&T Genealogy Page features links to genealogy resources and family-tree software. The company has hired the Helmses as its resident genealogy experts.

title: Web Sites for the World
body: To the Editor: The article "The Web Reflects a Wider World" (June 18) has many implications. Those wanting to do international business on the Internet will need to consider their approach to the language issues you raise, as some are already doing. It is clear that many non-native English speakers browse the Web in English, at least some of the time. These people make up a huge market, and very few are fully bilingual. Owners of English-language Web sites who want to address this market should make sure that the English they use is clear, simple and international. And clear, simple English will be easier to translate to other languages when the time comes -- if it hasn't already.  ALAN ACTON London, June 23, 1998  The author is the chief executive of Acton Web Export (www.actonwebexport.com), which translates Web sites.

title: British Concern Drops MCI Suit
body: Cable and Wireless P.L.C. dropped the breach-of-contract lawsuit today that it had filed against the MCI Communications Corporation to secure its bid to buy all of the long-distance company's Internet business. George Cary, a lawyer for the British telecommunications company, notified a Federal court here that Cable and Wireless was no longer pursuing the case. After initially agreeing to sell Cable and Wireless its wholesale Internet business for $625 million, MCI now is seeking to sell the rest of its Internet services to win approval from regulators of its $42 billion takeover by Worldcom Inc. The lawsuit accused MCI of breaching its sale contract by soliciting offers for the balance of its Internet business without giving Cable and Wireless the opportunity to first bid on the properties. unitedstates District Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson refused last Friday to grant a Cable and Wireless request to prevent MCI from discussing the Internet sales with other prospective buyers. Since then, Cable and Wireless has said it was having discussions with MCI but refused to say whether it was negotiating to purchase the Internet assets.

title: INSIDE
body: Falsehoods at Boston Globe Patricia Smith, an award-winning columnist, was asked to resign because she had fabricated people and quotations in her writings. Page A18.  Disney Gets Gateway to Web Walt Disney will buy a stake in Infoseek, becoming the latest big media company to make a deal to control an access point to the Web. Page D1. A Striver Is Accused A man who had battled schizophrenia, earning a law degree and contracts for his life story, was charged with murdering his fiancee. Page B1.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Cruise the Internet and Download Your Own Zamboni?
body: It's a sure sign that electronic commerce has come into its own when Zambonis go up for sale on the Net. The Zamboni Model 100 Ice Rink Resurfacing Machine will soon be offered for $9,995 at Sportsite.com, say officials at the site (www.sportsite.com). A warning: The tractor's not included. Graphic   Photo.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
2 Associations To Join Operations
body: The Internet Advertising Bureau in newyork and the Internet Local Advertising and Commerce Association in Oakland, Calif., said yesterday that they would combine operations under the bureau name. The more than 50 members of the association, which represents broadcasters, newspapers and others involved in local Internet services, will become bureau members, bringing the bureau's total membership to more than 300. The bureau will also form a Local Advertising Committee to be headed by Jim D'Arcangelo, 45, a founder of the association who is president of NFO Ad:Impact in Stamford, Conn. Rich LeFurgy, senior vice president for advertising at Buena Vista Internet Group in newyork, a unit of the Walt Disney Company, will continue as chairman of the bureau. Also yesterday, the bureau released figures for Internet ad revenue, showing that revenue in the first quarter of 1998 totaled $351.3 million, up more than twofold from $129.5 million in the corresponding period of 1997. And the bureau presented its first annual Marketer of the Year Award, which went to the Intel Corporation for leadership in the use of the Internet as an effective marketing tool.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DOW JONES TO INVEST $232 MILLION IN WALL STREET JOURNAL
body: Dow Jones & Company said yesterday that it would invest $232 million in The Wall Street Journal to expand pages and color capacity. In a speech yesterday to securities analysts, the chief executive of Dow Jones, Peter R. Kann, said the program would allow The Wall Street Journal to expand its daily pages to 96 pages, from 80 pages, and that it would be capable of increasing the number of color pages of advertising to 24 pages, from 8 pages. He said the new capacity would be fully in place by 2001.

title:
JUNE 7-13;
Ruling on On-Line Privacy
body: It was not the retirement that Master Chief Petty Officer Timothy R. McVeigh had wanted. But after America Online violated its in-house rules and disclosed to a military investigator that the sailor had posted an electronic message describing himself as gay, Mr. McVeigh said he was left with little choice but to go. The Navy had originally planned to discharge Mr. McVeigh without retirement benefits. But after a Federal judge's ruling that the Defense Department had violated its "don't ask, don't tell" rule in investigating Mr. McVeigh's sexual orientation, the Navy agreed to provide him with full benefits and pay his legal fees. America Online reached a separate settlement and agreed to pay damages to Mr. McVeigh for violating his privacy; the sum was not disclosed.   PHILIP SHENON

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
CABLETRON TO GET HIGH-TECHNOLOGY-EQUIPMENT MAKERS
body: Cabletron Systems agreed yesterday to pay $58.5 million for two businesses that develop equipment for high-speed Internet access. Cabletron is paying $25 million in cash or stock for the 65 percent that it does not already own of the Flowpoint Corporation, a privately held company in Los Gatos, Calif. It will pay $33.5 million in cash for the Ariel Corporation's Communications Systems Group, based in Cranbury, N.J. Cabletron Systems, based in Rochester, N.H., makes network switches, remote access products and network and system management software.

title: Appropriate Name for WWW
body: To the Editor: I am also frustrated by the lengthy verbalization of the WWW abbreviation for World Wide Web ("Wanted: Web-Site Addresses That Won't Twist the Tongue," May 28). I would like to propose a conflation of the word "treble" and the letter "W" to form the term "trouble-you." It rolls nicely off the tongue and, in many cases, aptly describes the experience of navigating the Web.  KEN GRUNSTRA Santa Cruz, Calif., May 28, 1998

title:
INTERNATIONAL BRIEFS;
Wolters Kluwer to Buy Plenum Publishing
body: Wolters Kluwer N.V., the big Dutch publisher, said yesterday that it would buy the Plenum Publishing Corporation of newyork for $258 million in cash to bolster its research-oriented scientific publishing unit. The offer equals $73.50 a share for Plenum, publisher of The Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology. It is the latest in a string of takeovers by Wolters Kluwer, which in March ended plans to merge with the British-Dutch rival Reed Elsevier P.L.C. Graphic   Graph tracks daily closes of Plenum Publishing, since June 1.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
YAHOO BUYING VIAWEB, A WEB-MARKETING SOFTWARE MAKER
body: The Internet directory company Yahoo Inc. agreed yesterday to buy the privately held software maker Viaweb Inc. in a stock deal valued around $49 million. Yahoo, which is aiming to broaden its offerings, expects to incur a one-time charge of about $45 million in its second quarter relating to technology acquired in the deal. It plans to issue about 455,000 common shares in exchange for all Viaweb shares, options and warrants outstanding. Viaweb, based in Cambridge, Mass., has 21 full-time employees. It makes software for building and operating on-line commerce Web sites. Shares of Yahoo, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif., jumped $4.375 yesterday, to $109.375.

title:
Metro Business;
Internet Service Planned
body: The Bell Atlantic Corporation of Manhattan will offer high-speed Internet access in Washington, Pittsburgh and Philadelphia in September as it taps into demand for fast Internet connections. Bell Atlantic will extend the service to the Hudson River area of New Jersey in October, and newyork and Boston next year. It will sell the service to consumers and people who work at home for $70 to $190 a month for unlimited use. Bell Atlantic said the technology it will use transmits information over phone lines as much as 250 times faster than the typical modem. The move to provide high-speed Internet services follows the GTE Corporation, the No. 3 local phone company, which said in April that it would offer such services in 16 states. The Internet-access market will grow to $38 billion in 2002, from $6 billion last year, according to Forrester Research, a technology market data researcher.

title: Web Index to Cater to Latin Americans
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation and Starmedia Network Inc. plan to start an Internet guide for users in Latin America. The companies are trying to capitalize on the growth of Internet use in Central and South America, which they said was outpacing other regions. An index of sites geared toward Latin Americans will be posted on Netscape's Netcenter Web site in August. Under a two-year agreement, the Spanish- and Portuguese-language versions of Netscape's Web browser will include a prominent link to Starmedia's site, which is used by about 500,000 Latin Americans a month. Netscape, which makes the Navigator Web browser, has been adding content on its Web site through similar agreements. It recently agreed to offer content from the site of Cnet Inc., a popular source of computing and technology news and other services. Ed Gyurko, a spokesman for Starmedia, which is closely held and based in newyork, said the agreement was valued at more than $2 million.

title: Girl Zone for Hip Girls
body: To the Editor: In response to "Offering Curious Girls Room for Exploration" on May 21, I would like to point out the omission of Girl Zone, a popular Web zine "where every girl is cool." Girl Zone (www.girlzone.com) is affiliated with American Association of University Women and Women's Sports Foundation. Girl Zone is the most comprehensive, hip site on the Web for girls today! Girls 11 to 16 love to shop, talk, whine, celebrate, learn, compare and share their experiences in their own zone. Check it out!  MARY JO REALE S. Burlington, Vt., May 27, 1998

title: NEWS WATCH
body: Gateway announced a new computer purchasing program yesterday. For about $50 a month, you get a customized PC, software, unlimited Internet access and "obsolescence protection." But the program -- called Your:)Ware -- is fairly restrictive. It allows anyone who buys a new Gateway computer through the program to trade in that computer no sooner than two years, and no later than four years, after the sale. The customer can apply the wholesale value at the time of the trade-in only toward a new Gateway computer. And the customer pays shipping. No haggling. Be:(Ware might be a more appropriate name. "It's a good idea, poorly executed," said Rob Enderle, an analyst at Giga Information Group. Another innovation that Gateway flirted with briefly last week was sending its customers over to Dell. The chief executive at Dell, Michael Dell, said he had been surprised when someone pointed out to him that if you clicked on the technical support button on the Gateway Web site, you were routed to the support page at Dell.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Barnes & Noble Adds Software To Expand On-Line Bookstore
body: Software is not the first thing that springs to mind at the mention of Barnes & Noble, the nation's leading purveyor of books. But the company is betting that it can change that. As part of a major overhaul of its on-line bookstore (www.barnesandnoble.com), Barnes & Noble announced yesterday that it had opened a software superstore with 1,000 software titles. The titles include exclusive distribution rights to the much-anticipated new game, Incoming, and software like Adobe's new Photoshop 5.0, which comes with an accompanying book. Some of the bundled products will be offered at a discount, but the rest of the software will not. The software page also features a collection of 25 new titles chosen by Intel and designed for Pentium II processor-based computers, like Monster Truck Madness II from Microsoft. Barnes & Noble already sells software at a handful of its retail stores. But some analysts are skeptical of the on-line move. Chris Shipley, editor and publisher of Demoletter, an industry newsletter, pointed out that other on-line software vendors, like Software.net, with 30,000 titles, were already well established.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BRIEFS;
Europe Criticizes MCI-Worldcom Deal
body: The European competition chief, Karel van Miert, lashed out on Monday at the $37 billion merger between Worldcom Inc. and the MCI Communications Corporation, saying that any overlap between the two unitedstates companies in the Internet market should be eliminated. A chief concern is that the combined entity could control Internet service prices. Worldcom owns Uunet, a powerful Internet service provider. This is the second time in less than a week that Mr. van Miert has criticized the merger, which needs regulatory approval in the 15-nation European Union, where the companies do substantial business. The deal is also being reviewed by the unitedstates Justice Department. At stake in the antitrust investigations on both sides of the Atlantic is the two partners' combined holding of the critical Internet backbone to transmit data and to interconnect Internet service providers. A rival company, the GTE Corporation, which has filed a lawsuit to stop the merger, has argued that Worldcom and MCI would together control 50 percent to 60 percent of Internet traffic. But the two partners say their market share will be only about 20 percent based on revenue.

title: Internet Monopoly?
body: To the Editor: Robert E. Hall (Op-Ed, May 20) misses the mark when he claims that Microsoft's practice of bundling a variety of software packages has been a "boon for consumers" because they get free software with Windows. It is highly unlikely that consumers who have "free" Internet access through Internet Explorer will seek other browsers, like Netscape's. The more consumers accept what Microsoft has chosen for them as their means of access to the Internet, the less competition will exist for that access. Lack of competition always harms consumers. Once Windows 98 hits the market, Microsoft's monopoly of the operating system business will result in its gaining a monopoly share in the market of Internet access.  JANET ARNOLD HART San Carlos, Calif., May 24, 1998

title: Microsoft's Futurism
body: To the Editor: Going after Microsoft for some of its business practices is probably a good use of the Justice Department's time (front page, May 19). Yet the Government in some ways shows a surprising lack of understanding of where computing is headed. Most Internet connections are conducted over slow phone lines. However, faster connections are just beginning to become widely available. As high-speed cable connections proliferate, the distinction between a user's computer and the Internet will disappear. So it is appropriate for an operating system to manage the computer's relationship with the Internet. This will not be perfected in one shot, but incorporating an Internet browser in the operating system is a good start and shows that Microsoft is headed in the right direction. Microsoft and most other computer companies have a history of giving the consumer more and more for less and less. It seems foolish for the Justice Department to object to this.  MICHAEL G. WORAM Brooklyn, May 21, 1998

title: If Microsoft Loses, Consumers Will Win
body: To the Editor: Robert E. Hall ("Antitrust Excess?", Op-Ed, May 20) too hastily concludes that the antitrust suit against Microsoft may not benefit consumers. He neglects the possibility that Microsoft's tie-in of its Web browser is a means of preserving its monopoly on operating systems. Windows has maintained its high market share in part because it supports more software applications than any potential rival. But competing browsers like Netscape can act as alternative "platforms" to which applications can be written. Consumers could soon choose an operating system other than Windows and still have access to a wide range of software.  GREGORY SILBERT New Haven, May 20, 1998

title: Times Company Directors Vote to Split Stock 2 for 1
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that its board had approved a 2-for-1 split in its class A and class B shares and an 11.8 percent increase in the quarterly dividend. The additional shares will be issued July 1 to shareholders of record on June 17.
