The quarterly dividend will be increased to 19 cents a share, based on the number of shares before the split, from 17 cents a share, on both classes of stock. The class A shares reached a 52-week high of $74.3125 yesterday, before retreating to close at $72.9375, down 18.75 cents on the day. The last stock split, also 2-for-1, was in September 1986. The stock split is subject to approval by a majority of class B shareholders, who will vote on a proposed increase in the number of authorized shares of both classes at a meeting on June 16.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Kodak and AOL Plan To Offer Photos on Web
body: In a bold move designed to revive its digital photography operation, the Eastman Kodak Company announced this week that it had joined with America Online in a service to be introduced in the fall. Kodak will permit AOL's 12 million subscribers to drop off rolls of films at any of about 30,000 photo-processing shops in the unitedstates. Once the film is developed, the images can be digitized and sent to their owners over the Internet as email. The service will be called You've Got Pictures, a twist on AOL's familiar digitized voice that beckons users to open their electronic mailboxes. In addition to sending pictures over the Internet, the service will also let users store their photographs in virtual albums as well as send them to others as email. Kodak, which posted $500 million in losses last year in its digital operation, has already turned to the computer chip manufacturer Intel to help it come up with a digital camera that might catch the consumer's eye. The company also bought Picture Vision, an on-line competitor, netting some 40,000 customers in the process.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
BELLSOUTH TO OFFER HIGH-SPEED INTERNET ACCESS SERVICE
body: The BellSouth Corporation plans to announce today that it will offer high-speed Internet access using a new technology to three million customers by the end of the year. The new technology, known as ADSL, for asymmetric digital subscriber line, allows Internet data to flow through normal telephone wires at speeds up to 30 times faster than are allowed by today's fastest consumer modems. BellSouth, which is based in Atlanta, plans to offer the service in seven markets -- including Atlanta, Charlotte, N.C., and Raleigh, N.C. -- by the end of the year. The service will cost $59.95 a month plus one-time installation and equipment fees that total $299.90.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NETSCAPE AGREES TO LICENSE ITS SOFTWARE TO CITIBANK
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation agreed to license its electronic commerce software to Citibank, as Netscape focuses on the corporate software business. Netscape said Citibank had a permanent license to use its CommerceXpert line of software that allows the financial institution to conduct business over the Internet. Financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed. Netscape's CommerceXpert software suite lets companies automate procurement, on-line sales and customer service over the Internet. Citibank, owned by newyork-based Citicorp, already offers some on-line-banking services that will be expanded using Netscape's software. The bank also plans to use the software to broaden its electronic commerce among corporations and consumers.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
KODAK AND AMERICA ONLINE TO OFFER PHOTOS VIA INTERNET
body: The Eastman Kodak Company is expected to announce today that it is joining with America Online to offer developed photographs via the Internet. Starting this fall, America Online subscribers who drop film off with participating retailers can, for the charge of from $5 to $7, have small versions of their pictures uploaded directly to America Online within 48 hours. The America Online subscriber can put the pictures in on-line photo albums, and can electronically order prints. America Online, Kodak and the retailers will split the profits from the extra fees and from reprint orders. The system uses technology created by Picturevision Inc.; Kodak owns 51 percent of Picturevision, and America Online plans to buy 10 percent of the remaining shares.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
LUCENT SELLS MAPPING UNIT TO BANYAN SYSTEMS
body: Lucent Technologies Inc., a maker of telephone equipment, sold its Maps On Us Internet map unit to Banyan Systems Inc., which plans to add the maps to its on-line phone directory. Lucent's technology, which gives Internet users street maps and directions, is used by the AT&T Corporation's Worldnet Internet division as well as USA Today and Nintendo. Banyan, which makes software for voicemail and messaging products and is based in Westborough, Mass., will take a $1 million to $1.5 million charge this quarter for research at the unit. Other terms were not disclosed. Banyan also acquired Lucent's Maps On Us Web site.

title: 2 Web Ventures End Merger Plan
body: Citing incompatibilities in cultures and technology, Citysearch and the Zip2 Corporation, two of the leading developers of local World Wide Web sites known as city guides, have called off merger plans that were announced April 3. The dissolution of the merger plans prevents formation of what some industry analysts have seen as a potential juggernaut in providing local news, maps and entertainment guides on the Internet. Zip2, Citysearch, and its two main competitors in the city directory business, Digital Cities from America Online and Sidewalk from the Microsoft Corporation, seek to attract local advertisers to the Internet, a market that is expected to be among the largest in electronic commerce. But beyond attractive surface similarities, serious differences emerged soon after the merger was announced, according to executives in each company. Zip2, based in Mountain View, Calif., has been more of a technology company, providing local newspapers with the software to publish on line and to create local "yellow pages"directories. Citysearch creates its own city guides, sometimes as a partner with existing media.

title:
Being 13;
On-Line Confidential
body: LeonardoDiCapriofan: 'I think I like getting to know Internet people -- 'cause even if they were ugly or had a disease, that wouldn't matter. I would like to get to know people better starting from the inside.' SuperKat: 'Yes. Here in Idaho there is a lot of prejudice against religions and minorities. On the Net, you don't run into that as much. I've seen a little of it on line. But when I do, I tell everybody to shut up and leave.' The screen names were changed when this article appeared. (Photographs by Eve Fowler)

title: Allied Signal Buys 2 Concerns
body: Allied Signal Inc. said today that it would acquire two closely held companies to bolster its specialty chemicals and plastics businesses. Terms were not disclosed. Allied Signal agreed to buy Web Technologies Inc., a maker of plastic packaging for electronics, and Pharmaceutical Fine Chemicals S.A., a Swiss maker of chemicals used to manufacture drugs, owned by an investor group led by Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. Allied Signal, the maker of Prestone antifreeze and Fram oil filters, has been building up the two businesses amid slumping demand for its automotive products. Allied Signal fell 75 cents today, to $43.6875. The company's plastics and fibers division generated revenue of more than $2 billion in 1997, while specialty chemicals had sales of $1.5 billion. Overall Allied Signal sales were $14.5 billion, led by aerospace and electronics products. Pharmaceutical Fine Chemicals, based in Lugano, Switzerland, has more than 500 customers in 50 countries and had sales of $110 million last year. It employs 354 people and operates two production and research facilities in Italy and one in the Bahamas. Allied Signal said Web Technologies had annual sales of about $25 million.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
USWEB AGREES TO ADD GRAY PEAK, A NETWORK CONCERN
body: The USWeb Corporation, an Internet strategy and professional-services concern, said yesterday that it would buy Gray Peak Technologies, a closely held network solutions company in newyork. The deal will be completed through an exchange of stock valued at $80 million to $100 million. USWeb said that by combining with Gray Peak it would be able to offer clients a single source for strategic Internet solutions, security expertise and network services. Shares of USWeb, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif., rose $1.8125 yesterday, to $23.375

title: Internet Tax Ban Is Called Biased
body: The affluent would receive a tax break at the expense of people of modest means if the proposed moratorium on taxing sales made over the Internet becomes law, the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a liberal research group in Washington, said in a report this week. The Internet Tax Freedom Act would ban state and local taxes of sales made over the Internet for up to six years. Sales taxes account for one-quarter of all state and local government revenues, the center said. "Higher-income households who are able to afford the computers, Internet access subscriptions and credit card accounts that are a precondition of being able to buy goods and services" could avoid sales taxes if the act becomes law, the budget center said. This would create pressure to raise sales tax rates, the burden of which, it said, "would fall most heavily on lower-income households without the resources to get on line and avoid them." President Clinton has endorsed the legislation, which has drawn opposition from a variety of state and local government organizations worried about erosion of their tax base.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Web Site Designed to Let Free Speech Ring Out
body: Proponents of free speech may have found a new window of expression on the Internet with a Web site that is dedicated to posting censored and banned writing on line. The Digital Freedom Network, working with numerous international human rights groups, has collected writings from more than a dozen countries where free expression has been supressed, a spokesman for the network said. The site (www.dfn.org) includes the words of a Kenyan activist, Koigi wa Wamwere; of two Chinese former political prisoners, Bao Ge and Wei Jingsheng, and poems by Raul Rivero, a former journalist in Cuba. "Despite continued persecution, these dissidents have continued to speak out, sometimes without knowing if the world would hear them," said Bobson Wong, the network's executive director. Now, he said, millions may hear them.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Sulzberger Family Sells Some Times Co. Shares
body: Four members of the Sulzberger family, including two directors of The newyork Times Company, said yesterday that they had sold more than one million shares of stock in the company, taking in more than $76 million. The sale was disclosed by the sellers, Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, 72, the company's chairman emeritus, and his sister, Dr. Judith P. Sulzberger, 74, also a member of the board; Marian S. Heiskell, 79, and Ruth S. Holmberg, 77. . "Today's action is part of the family's overall financial planning, which continues in an orderly manner," Mr. Sulzberger said in a statement. The sale, of 1,080,000 class A shares, represented less than 7 percent of the family's holdings and was equal to about 1 percent of the company's outstanding shares. The family controls the company through the ownership of class B shares, which are not traded and have super-voting rights. The company's class A shares fell $1.125 yesterday, to $70.9375, on the newyork Stock Exchange.

title: Is Timbuktu Ready to Go on Line?
body: To the Editor: Thomas L. Friedman is right when he says that the Internet can help Africa leapfrog into the global economy (column, May 5). Thanks to the Internet, one field in particular stands to benefit greatly: science. The Internet will connect African scientists to the kind of specialized information that once resided exclusively in expensive books and printed journals. They will also have access to on-line meetings and symposiums. And with email they can stay in touch with colleagues around the world and stay current on the latest findings and developments. The Internet is no panacea, but it can help make the playing field between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres a little more level.  WILSON GRABILL Princeton, N.J., May 5, 1998

title: AT&T and Lycos Enter 3-Year Pact
body: The AT&T Corporation and the Internet navigation company Lycos Inc. announced a three-year pact today to develop and offer new Web-based consumer communications services and sell AT&T offerings via Lycos's Web site. The stock of Lycos, based in Waltham, jumped $5.25 a share, to $68.625. Shares of AT&T rose $1.3125, to $62.0625. Financial terms were not disclosed, although Lycos's president, Robert J. Davis, said AT&T would be paying his company for promoting AT&T services on Lycos's Web site. AT&T and Lycos plan to provide advanced services that will combine Web-based technology with traditional telephone services, the companies said. In one service being tested, a person taking part in an Internet chat would be able to convert the keyboard-based session into a voice conversation, the companies said. In another, a person could find someone on an on-line directory, click on that person's name and automatically set up a phone call.

title:
Paid Notice: Deaths
MCLEAN, JANET G.
body: McLEAN-Janet G. Newspaper Librarian, 82, who retired in the late 1960s as a librarian with the Washington bureau of the newyork Times, died of breast cancer April 26 at her home in the Lewisdale neighborhood of West Hyattsville. She was a native of Chicago who performed as a piano soloist there as a teenager. Her family moved to the Washington area in the early 1940s. Mrs. McLean graduated from the Eastman School of Music at the University of Rochester, where her orchestral and piano works were performed while she was a student. She went to work for United Press as a librarian in 1957 after her husband, journalist Hector F. McLean died. Mrs. McLean was organist & choir director at St. James Episcopal Church in Rockville. Survivors include two daughters, Nancy Suniewick of Kensington and Judith McLean of Lewisdale; a sister, Nancy Stephens of Ocean View, Delaware, and Key Largo, Florida; and three grandchildren. McLEAN-Janet. The newyork Times records with deep sorrow the passing of Janet McLean, associated with The Times from 1963, until retiring in 1984.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
LYCOS BUYS A MAKER OF CUSTOMIZED SEARCH SOFTWARE
body: The Internet search directory Lycos Inc. said yesterday that it had acquired the Wisewire Corporation, whose software allows Internet users to do customized searches, for $39.75 million in stock. Wisewire, a closely held company based in Pittsburgh, makes software that searches Web sites and picks out areas preferred by a user. That allows users to cut the time spent searching for information. Share of Lycos rose $6.125 each, or 11 percent, to $61.8125. Lycos, based in Framingham, Mass., ranked eighth in March among Internet users, according to Media Metrix, which tracks Internet use.

title: Finding Books on the Web
body: To the Editor: Thank you for your feature on Web sites that sell books ("Browsing Books in Cyberspace," April 23). You neglected to mention those that sell used, out of print or hard to find books. One very fine one is www.abebooks.com. Another site, www.mxbf.com, searches seven different sites, including Abebooks and Amazon, for used and out of print books. This allows you to compare pricing and condition without having to search each site individually.  DAVID PERKINS newyork, April 23, 1998

title:
NEWS WATCH;
MSNBC Leads for the Month As the Top Web News Site
body: MSNBC, the on-air and on-line mixed marriage of Microsoft and NBC, was once again named this week the No. 1 general news site on the World Wide Web. The monthly ratings, measured by Media Metric, a PC Meter company, are based on March figures that tracked, using a sample group, the overall size of the audience and the number of times each person visited the news site (www.msnbc.com). The site, which has an audience of four million, has been the ratings champion in 14 out of the 21 months since it began, MSNBC spokesmen said. According to Media Metric's figures, MSNBC drew 4.8 percent of the Internet users last month, compared with 3.3 percent for two competitors, CNN Interactive (www.cnn.com) and USA Today's on-line site (www.usatoday.com).

title:
NEWS WATCH;
When email Words Pall, A Program Can Add Pizazz
body: Want to spark up your electronic mail? If writing lively prose just isn't enough, the folks at Novita Communications say they have the answer: Novita Liveletter 1.1, software that can make email, the most popular use of the Internet, multimedia. The program, which became available this week on the Internet (www.novita.com) for $29.95, promises to let users add a range of colors and fonts to their email, along with recorded voice clips, animated images, personal photographs and even playable games. The company says Liveletter can also grab and customize any page on the World Wide Web and send it as an email message. "We don't want to change people's habits, just make them easier and more effective," said Julien Nguyen, the chief executive of Novita Communications, of Santa Clara, Calif. A free trial version of Liveletter is available either on a CD-ROM or downloaded from the Novita site. But the trial software, Mr. Nguyen said, will not operate after 30 days.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Accounts
body: * eToys, Santa Monica, Calif., a unit of Idealab, to Kalis & Savage Advertising, Pacific Palisades, Calif., as the first agency to handle advertising for the Internet toy store. Billings were estimated at more than $1 million.

title: Real Networks Is Set for Software Release
body: Real Networks Inc., the largest independent publisher of software for sending and viewing video and audio on the World Wide Web, today introduced a new version of its technology, known as Real System G2. The new software is intended to move the Internet a step closer to competing directly with television and radio, by offering higher-quality audio and video delivery systems for personal computer users. With the support from a number of Internet broadcasters, including CNN, ABC, Fox, ESPN, CBS Sportsline, The Wall Street Journal, Cnet, Sony and Warner, the new Real Player software allows computer users to retrieve on-demand programming via the Internet. Until now, attempts to receive audio and video streams of information by the World Wide Web have been disappointing because of problems ranging from congestion to limited bandwidth.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AMAZON.COM IS IN DEALS FOR THREE INTERNET COMPANIES
body: Amazon.com Inc. said yesterday that its board had approved a 2-for-1 common stock split, payable on June 1 to shareholders of record on May 20. Separately, the on-line retailer of books and music, said it had acquired three leading Internet companies: Bookpages Ltd., Telebook Inc. and Internet Movie Database Ltd. Amazon.com expects Bookpages, (www.bookpages.co.uk), one of Britain's largest on-line bookstores, and Telebook, (www.telebuch.de), Germany's No. 1 on-line bookstore, to be part of the company's expansion into Europe. Internet Movie Database, (www.imdb.com), an on-line repository for movie and television information, is expected to support Amazon's entry into on-line video sales. The company will incur charges of about $55 million.

title: Earnings Higher At US West Unit
body: US West Communications Group said today that its first-quarter earnings rose 2.4 percent on strong sales of Internet services and demand for more phone lines. The company, the phone and data communications unit of U S West Inc., reported net income of $347 million, or 71 cents a diluted share, up from $339 million, or 70 cents, before charges a year earlier. The local phone company beat the average estimate of 69 cents from analysts surveyed by I.B.E.S. International Inc. U S West is profiting as more customers sign up for its Internet-access and data services and buy additional phone lines for the hookups. Revenue increased 4.8 percent, to $2.71 billion from $2.59 billion. The company said earnings growth was hurt by costs of building its digital wireless phone business and spending to hook competitors into its network. U S West increased its number of phone lines by 4.1 percent from a year earlier to 16,259. Volume, or minutes of use on its network, rose 6.3 percent, to 17,345, in the quarter.

title: Of Internet Inequality
body: To the Editor: Re "Racial Divide Found on Information Highway" (front page, April 17): The real situation is probably worse than the data in the study indicate, since the information was collected by a telephone survey. Yet 18 percent of black households lack phones (the same for Hispanic homes), while more than 95 percent of white homes have them. So the survey contains a bias. Universal access to the Internet is unlikely to be realized. More than 60 years of Federal policy devoted to achieving universal phone service has not prevented the maldistribution of the older technology. In a country that now appears to have a declining interest in equity considerations, it will take a substantial political revolution to lead to a different result for computers and the Internet.  PHILIP L. BEREANO Seattle, April 21, 1998  The writer is a professor of technical communication, University of Washington.

title: Appeals Court Is Disputed
body: To the Editor: In "It May Be Boilerplate, but Read Before You Click" (April 16), about "click through" contracts, you say that I sold data on the Internet.  The article described a case involving an Internet contract in which an appeals court ruled against Matthew Zeidenberg's use of data from Pro CD.  This is not the case. I gave all listings away for free. The way I was planning to make money was by selling banner ads on my search pages. This error did not originate with you but with the appeals court. The facts as revealed in the lower court indicated that I never sold the data. The appeals court decision is available on line (www.law.seattleu.edu/ chonm/Cases/procd2.html). Incidentally, there is now a bill in Congress that would overturn the results of the case since some members of Congress have realized the damage it has done to the copyright law.  MATTHEW ZEIDENBERG Madison, Wis., April 16, 1998

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
7TH LEVEL ENDS AGREEMENT TO BUY PULSE ENTERTAINMENT
body: The internet software developer 7th Level Inc. said yesterday that it had canceled its pending acquisition of Pulse Entertainment Inc. The shares of 7th Level fell $1.5625 each, to $7.6875, on the Nasdaq stock market. Since announcing plans in November to acquire privately held Pulse Entertainment, 7th Level, based in Dallas, has turned itself from a games developer to a supplier of services and software for a wide variety of entertainment, consumer and business customers. Under the original terms, 7th Level would have issued about 21 million common shares to Pulse shareholders.

title: How Soon We Forget
body: To the Editor: Such nostalgia in the April 16 issue of Circuits! One story quoted a fellow reminiscing about the struggles of making Internet phone calls "the old way" back in 1995 ("Internet Phone Calls, No Computer Necessary"). Another paid homage to the quiet closing of those cybercafes that became popular way back in, let's see, the mid-1990's ("The Sad Ballad of the Cybercafe"). And there was the piece about the founders of crayon. net, who developed one of the early services for customizing daily news pages ("A Free Personal Shopper for Internet News Hounds"). That was in the pioneering Web days of, well, 1995. One of the young crayon.net founders even noted their site has been a free service "for a really long time." It all points up the accelerating pace of change in digital technology. And it reminds me that at the incredibly early date of April 1994 -- just four years but seemingly a cyberlife ago -- we were having serious debates in NASA Public Affairs about whether to allocate any resources to a public presence on the Web. (Turns out we got it right.)  GEOFF VINCENT Alexandria, Va., April 16, 1998  The writer is the former deputy head of NASA Public Affairs.

title: NEWS WATCH
body: BOOLA BOOLEAN -- Dartmouth College in Hanover, N.H., is the most wired campus in America, according to an annual survey by Yahoo's Internet Life magazine. The magazine rated 100 schools on the extent to which they have integrated computers into college life. Dartmouth dethroned last year's champion, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, which fell to third behind Dartmouth and the New Jersey Institute of Technology in Newark. AMERICA'S PROMISE -- Gen. Colin L. Powell will be the on-line guest on Monday at 9 P.M. E.D.T. on America Online (keyword AOL Live). General Powell will discuss his year-old volunteer group, America's Promise, which aims to help the country's estimated 15 million at-risk youth.

title: Shakers on the Net
body: To the Editor: In response to Stuart Semmell's letter about the Shakers mentioned in "Horse and Blender, Car and Crockpot" (April 9), the seven Shakers of Sabbathday Lake, New Gloucester, Me., are alive and well and (www.shaker.lib.me.us) living on the Internet. The Shakers are neither technophiles nor technophobes. They accept new technology in a remarkably tranquil and un-neurotic manner, to the degree that they believe it will help them realize their aims as a religious community. When I visited the Shaker Library a few months ago, Sister Frances, the community leader, spent a few laughing minutes with me surfing the Web on their computer.  JOEL COHEN Amesbury, Mass., April 17, 1998  The writer, Boston Camerata music director, says he recorded spirituals with the Shakers for "Simple Gifts" (Erato).

title: Next to Gates, Rockefeller Shines
body: To the Editor: Re "Racial Divide Found on Information Highway" (front page, April 17): The most important difference in the likelihood of Internet use is of income, not race. As you report, among blacks with incomes over $40,000, computer ownership and Internet access are roughly the same as that of whites in the same income group. You also report that blacks with incomes of less than $40,000 are less likely to have access to the Internet than their white counterparts. However, there are many more whites than blacks in the unitedstates, so at low income levels there are more whites lacking access to the Internet than blacks.  ALBERT ADATO Valhalla, N.Y., April 17, 1998

title: U S West Will Offer a TV-Internet Service
body: U S West Communications said today that it would offer a new service in the Phoenix area providing digital television and high-speed Internet access over existing phone lines, beginning this summer. U S West, the regional Bell company based in Englewood, Colo., also said it had reached an agreement with the Phoenix Suns to carry the basketball team's games by television and on-line services beginning in 2003. Under the arrangement, viewers will receive all 41 home games and home playoff games with their basic U S West video package. The new digital TV and Internet service, to be called U S West Telechoice, will offer a sharper picture, compact disk-quality sound and access to telephone features like caller identification while watching TV. It will first be offered in Phoenix this summer and expand to other markets in 1999, U S West said. Under the deal with the Suns, U S West will also sponsor and pay part of the cost of a new five-story pavilion adjoining the America West Arena where the Suns play. The 130,000-square-foot pavilion will feature entertainment, dining, meeting facilities, and office and retail space.

title: Executive Shuns Pay
body: James Barksdale, president and chief executive of the Netscape Communications Corporation declined virtually his entire pay package last year, as the company lost money amid pressure from its rival, the Microsoft Corporation in the Web-browser market. According to the company's annual proxy filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Mr. Barksdale did not take a salary or year-end bonus for 1997.

title:
IN BRIEF;
N.J.I.T. Ranks High As a 'Wired' College
body: The New Jersey Institute of Technology in Newark has won the ranking of the second "most wired" college in the unitedstates, behind Dartmouth, from Yahoo! Internet Life Magazine. N.J.I.T., listed in seventh place last year, moved up in this year's ranking of 400 schools, which was announced last week. Every N.J.I.T. student gets a computer and an email account. Students can not only drop and add courses on line but can also register for Rutgers University classes at the Newark campus, and Rutgers students can register on line for N.J.I.T. classes. At least 60 percent of the N.J.I.T. classes involve computer work. Four television studios on campus allow classes to be broadcast for "distance learning," which is used by one third of the 8,000 students, Saul K. Fenster, the institute's president, said. Students also can get assignments and lessons and leave questions and comments for instructors in "any time, any place" classes designed for students and teachers to participate at different times through their computers. "N.J.I.T. is what higher education is going to look like 10 years from now," Dr. Fenster said.   KAREN DeMASTERS

title: New Finance Chief At New York Times
body: James L. Terrill, who has played a role in the financial management of various departments of The newyork Times Company, has been named the newspaper's chief financial officer. Mr. Terrill, 52, served as controller of the newspaper from January 1994 to December 1996, when he was appointed a vice president. Mr. Terrill has also served as executive vice president and chief financial officer of the Wilderness Society, which he left to rejoin The Times in 1993. Between 1977 and 1989, he had a variety of jobs at the Times Company, serving as business manager of the newspaper's news department and as group controller for the Times Company's western regional newspapers and for its information services division. Graphic   Photo: James L. Terrill.

title: Finding Even More Ways To Listen to Your Computer
body: To the Editor: As an Internet radio fan, I recommend M.I.T.'s Web site, with links to more than 4,000 radio stations worldwide (wmbr.mit.edu/stations/ list.html).  MADALYN MARGOLES newyork, April 10, 1998

title: That Soggy Stable
body: To the Editor: Many thanks to "It's Confirmed: Web's Size Bogs Down Searches" (April 9) for a magnificent malaprop! The article compares the task of searching the Web to shoveling the "Aegean stables." What a picture! The Augean stables tackled by Hercules were reputed to be among the filthiest in the world (and did require the force of a river to clean them out). But to shovel out a stable in the Aegean Sea?  MARA ELLIOTT Delmar, N.Y., April 9, 1998

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Publisher Moving To Geocities
body: Thomas R. Evans, who has held top publishing titles at three magazines owned by Mortimer B. Zuckerman, said yesterday that he would leave to join the Internet company Geocities as chief executive. Mr. Evans, 43, has been president and publisher of U.S. News & World Report and Fast Company magazines as well as president of The Atlantic Monthly. At Geocities, Mr. Evans will succeed David Bohnett, 42, the founder, who will continue as chairman. Geocities, based in Santa Monica, Calif., generates revenue through advertising, electronic commerce and the sale of member services. Mr. Evans will be based in newyork and Santa Monica. At the Zuckerman magazines, a successor to Mr. Evans has not been named.

title: The Net's Real Riches
body: To the Editor: The Internet has been compared with the California Gold Rush of 1849. But there was more than gold at stake in the Gold Rush. When it was over, California had a new transportation network: steamships and railroads spanning America. Today, that transportation infrastructure is one reason California leads the nation in retail and wholesale trade. Will the Internet rush of the 1990's bear similar fruit, an information infrastructure of high-speed fiber optic lines? It would be wise to be longsighted and not miss the real point in the rush to find gold on the Internet.  ERIC S. NYLUND North Bend, Wash., April 6, 1988  The writer is the author of the book "Signal to Noise" (Avon, 1998).

title:
NEWS WATCH;
White House Easter Eggs To Roll on the Internet
body: The White House is scrambling to make the annual White House Easter Egg Roll, scheduled for Monday, a technological eggstravaganza. The day's events on the South Lawn will be broadcast live (www.easter.earthlink.net) on the Internet for the first time. Earthlink Networks, one of the country's largest Internet service providers, has wired the White House so hundreds of thousands of children worldwide can see and hear the Easterlink festivities using streaming audio and streaming video from 10 video cameras on the White House lawn, and there will be links to an assortment of other educational and Government resources. To see famous bureaucrats and celebrities posing for digital pictures and to hear them reading from storytelling stages, Easterlink visitors must have a recent, Java-enabled copy of either Netscape Navigator or Microsoft Internet Explorer. The software is free and available for downloading from the Easterlink site. Attorney General Janet Reno will be one of the storytellers. It is not known whether her story will be compatible with Internet Explorer.

title:
THE MARKETS;
Profits at Dow Jones Rise 37% in Quarter
body: Dow Jones & Company reported yesterday that it had a 37 percent jump in first-quarter net income to $34.7 million, but repeated that it expected to take a significant charge against earnings in the second quarter, when the sale of its Dow Jones Markets unit is expected to be completed. The size of the expected second-quarter charge was not disclosed. The company, which publishes The Wall Street Journal, said earnings per basic share were 36 cents, up from income of $25.4 million, or 27 cents. The first-quarter profits included a gain of 11 cents a share from the sale of the company's interests in WBIS+, a television station in newyork City, and in Texas Monthly magazine. Profits in the first quarter of 1997 included a four-cent gain from selling its American Demographics unit. Excluding the one-time gains, Dow Jones's first-quarter profits matched the First Call consensus estimate of 25 cents a share.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Makes Appointments in Circulation
body: John Daly, an executive who spearheaded The newyork Times's move to broaden its reach by making distribution agreements with 123 newspaper distributorships around the country, has been named vice president for national circulation at the newspaper. Mr. Daly, 47, who has worked in circulation since joining The Times in 1983, is currently director of circulation sales development. The company also announced that Lauretta Prestera, a vice president for advertising for the last four months, is returning to the circulation department as vice president for newyork circulation. Ms. Prestera, 50, joined The Times in 1980 and has worked in various posts in the circulation department.

title: Excite to Acquire Advertising Site
body: Excite, the Internet search service, has agreed to buy Classifieds2000, a World Wide Web site that posts classified advertising, for $48 million in Excite stock. Like its larger rival, Yahoo, Excite wants to transform itself from simply a jumping-off point for Web surfers to a broader service with a variety of features that keep users lingering and reading its advertising. Local services, like classifieds and telephone "yellow pages" listings, represent big draws for users and large pools of potential advertising, said George Bell, the chief executive of Excite. Classifieds2000 allows individuals to post listings without charge, but charges fees to display classified ads from businesses. It also sells so-called banner advertisements, which are displayed prominently on Web sites. Helped by a surging stock price, Excite has made several acquisitions over the last year, using its own shares as currency. In October, it bought Netbot, a provider of Internet shopping software, for $35 million in stock. Then in January, it spent $89 million in stock for Match Logic, which provides demographic information to Internet advertisers.

title: Making the Web Speak
body: To the Editor: On the guidelines for making Web pages accessible to the blind and visually impaired ("Carefully Designed Pages Can Make All the Difference," March 26), it should be noted that there is a program that allows any Web site to become instantly accessible for those with ocular disabilities. Hear the Web Speak, sponsored by the Productivity Works, offers Web site designers and managers a downloadable link to the award-winning pwWeb Speak technology. This technology provides a speaking Web browser that translates the HTML code of the Web pages and allows the blind to navigate through the text and links on the page with ease. More information on Hear the Web Speak is available at the Productivity Works site (www.prodworks.com).  PHIL HALL newyork, March 26, 1998

title:
THE MARKETS;
Deals Lift Lycos Stock
body: The shares of Lycos Inc. rose almost 16 percent today after the Internet-search directory company said it had received contracts worth $30 million over several years, more than all the revenue it had last year. The stock rose $6.875, to a high of $51.125. Some 1.6 million shares were traded. Lycos makes its money by providing advertising space on its Web site and licensing its search technology to other companies.

title: AT&T to Eliminate Flat On-Line Fee
body: The AT&T Corporation said yesterday that it would eliminate its flat monthly fee of $19.95 for unlimited Internet access, in the latest industry move to curb the onslaught of users straining the global network. Starting on May 1, AT&T will charge an extra 99 cents for every hour that people spend on line exceeding 150 hours of monthly use, in addition to the $19.95 fee. AT&T, with 1.2 million customers, is the nation's largest provider of Internet-only service. The move is another crack in the industry's move to flat rates two years ago. In February, America Online Inc., the largest Internet service also offering its own on-line programs, increased its monthly $19.95 fee for unlimited access by $2 for its 11 million customers, saying it needed to upgrade its network. "The Internet has arrived as a mass medium and usage is soaring," said Dan Schulman, head of AT&T's Worldnet service.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
QWEST AGREES TO BUY DUTCH INTERNET SERVICE
body: Qwest Communications International Inc., an expanding Denver-based telecommunications power, said yesterday that it had agreed to buy the Dutch Internet services provider EUnet for $154.4 million in stock and cash. Qwest said it sought EUnet to take advantage of an expected explosion in demand for on-line services across Europe. EUnet had 1997 revenue of about $55 million. It expects 1998 sales to exceed $75 million. Qwest's stock rose 87.5 cents, to $40, in Nasdaq trading. Earlier this month, Qwest bought LCI International Inc. for $4.4 billion, creating the fourth-largest unitedstates telephone company.

title: House Clears Way for Bill on Internet Tax
body: State, city and county government leaders announced today that they had reached agreement on a bill to mediate the thorny issue of taxing Internet services and commerce. Under the bill, which is expected to be voted on by the House of Representatives in the next few weeks, no new taxes could be placed on Internet service providers or other businesses involved in Internet-related commerce for three years, although existing taxes could remain in place. But there is no guarantee that taxes will ever be levied, and there are significant differences between it and a Senate version. During the three years called for in the House bill, a commission of local, state and Federal leaders would recommend a means to tax Internet transactions -- as well as traditional mail order sales. The recommendations would be forwarded to Congress for action. Gov. Michael O. Leavitt of Utah said he was pleased that under the bill there would be no taxes of Internet transmissions. Governor Leavitt, a Republican, negotiated the agreement on behalf of the National Governors' Association with the bill's sponsor, Representative Christopher Cox, Republican of California.

Mr. Shelton, 52, will oversee the company's diversity, management development and management performance programs. He will report to Cynthia H. Augustine, senior vice president for human resources. Mr. Shelton joined The Times in 1967 and has held jobs in sales, budget analysis and circulation. Since August 1995, he has been vice president for distribution. Graphic   Photo: Charles E. Shelton.

title: Battling Junk email May Become Easier
body: Sendmail, the most popular software used to deliver email on the Internet, is getting a powerful set of tools to fight the junk mail known as spam, which is increasingly clogging cyberspace and filling mailboxes of Internet users with unwanted promotions on subjects as diverse as get-rich-quick schemes and pornography. The new version of Sendmail, to be announced today by its creator, includes a variety of anti-spam features, including the ability to reject mail from known spam addresses and a mechanism that will force spammers to disclose their real Internet addresses. Internet experts said the improvement could seriously crimp the ability of promoters to fire off millions of advertisements each day in the form of email messages. Business Day, page D1.

title: No Hiding on the Web
body: To the Editor: "Frank Racial Dialogue Thrives on the Web" (front page, March 8) mentions the "almost impenetrable anonymity" or "illusion of anonymity" people enjoy when posting messages on a discussion forum, but doesn't elaborate on this misconception. Every electronic message leaves a digital footprint. Although most people may not know, or want to know, how to trace an email address, government agencies or even a dedicated hacker can do so in an instant by decrypting the header information. Actually, America Online addresses are the easiest to trace, especially with a warrant; in the case of a perceived threat to national security, even anonymous remailers can have the sender's address decrypted. So blabbermouths, beware! You never know who's monitoring your cyber-pearls of wisdom.  RENEE PALMER newyork, March 8, 1998

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
CMG INFORMATION ACQUIRES ACCIPITER FOR $35 MILLION
body: CMG Information Services Inc. said yesterday that it had bought closely held Accipiter Inc. for $35 million in stock, adding technology that tracks on-line users to its Internet ventures. CMG, a direct marketer that invests in Internet companies, will combine Accipiter with its Engage Technologies unit, which sells market research on how people use the World Wide Web. CMG intends to use Accipiter's technology to increase advertising revenue at its ventures. The technology lets on-line advertisers change the ads that Web surfers see based on user profiles. Shares of CMG, which is based in Andover, Mass., fell 81.25 cents, to $57.75, in Nasdaq trading.

title:
LIBRARY/WINE;
And Don't Forget . . .
body: THE World Wide Web site of the Wine Spectator (www.winespectator.com) is an impressive starting point for on-line wine resources. The magazine's text is only one issue behind the newsstand, and there is a free searchable database of 15,000 reviews, with tasting notes and ratings, covering the previous two years. There is a Wine Basics section with essays on tasting and varietals, country-by-country descriptions of wines and more. Folksy and friendly, Robin Garr's Wine Lovers' Page (www.wine-lovers-page.com) includes a huge volume of resources, highlighted by Mr. Garr's "Quick Wine-Tasting Course," a collection of articles he wrote for The Louisville (Ky.) Courier-Journal. There are also tasting forms, a glossary, vintage charts and bulletin boards for discussions. Other magazines worth visiting on the Web include Smart Wine Online (smartwine.com) and Wine Enthusiast (www.winemag.com). All sites, of course, have links to other sites, increasing the chances of finding pleasant surprises like Corkscrew.Com (www.corkscrew.com), devoted to a San Francisco Bay Area couple's 20-year passion for collecting corkscrews.

title: Students and Laptops
body: To the Editor: It is interesting to hear that the newyork program does not provide Internet access (". . . With Liberty and Laptops for All?" Feb. 26). In my view, email and World Wide Web access are critical components of technology use in schools. Laptop computers really are a cheaper alternative for most students. For my son, the school district is struggling to provide enough labs. At the same time, students and their families are investing heavily and repeatedly to provide access so school work can be completed at home. A laptop computer program would eliminate duplicate acquisition of resources that tend to sit idle when the student is at school -- or, for the school, idle in the evenings when students are at home.  RAY BROWN Mayville, N.D., March 3, 1998  The writer is vice president for academic affairs at Mayville State University.

title: 'The Web Made Me Do It'
body: In "'The Web Made Me Do It"' (Feb. 15), Jack Shafer implies that raw reportage via the Internet is somehow more truthful than information processed by editors bent on protecting "corporate America." He attributes this purification of Internet data to "disintermediation," suggesting, for instance, that Matt Drudge's reports are somehow credible because they are "straightforward" and that Drudge has "something original to say." Many crackpots have original ideas. Originality is no test for veracity. And Drudge's sanctimonious posturing smacks of the Linda Tripp school of ethics. If Drudge were really disintermediated, he would drudge up rumor and innuendo on all public figures, politically right, left and center. Drudge, by editing himself, is just as intermediated as those editors Shafer decries.  Jeff Johnson Indialantic, Fla.

title: Applause for WebTV
body: To the Editor: The biggest attraction of WebTV ("WebTV Offers Cheap Web Access, but Consumers Are Wary," Feb. 26) is its convenience. We have a computer, but it is not very handy to use for email or the Internet because it is in its own room rather than where my wife and I are likely to be. We considered getting a laptop, but to use it would require taking it to the phone line. WebTV overcame these problems. I hooked it up to the TV in our bedroom, which is connected to two other TV's in other parts of the house. Now whenever we are in a room with a TV, we can send mail or surf the Net.  R. W. WINSOR Wilmington, Del., Feb. 27, 1998

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Internet Bureau Locates in New York
body: The Internet Advertising Bureau, an association for on-line advertising, has established a headquarters and named its first director. The association, which has more than 175 members, is locating its headquarters in newyork. Frank Dudley, president of FX Dudley Communications in newyork, becomes director of the bureau. Mr. Dudley, 36, will be responsible for overseeing operations like membership service and recruitment as well as supervising the association's Web site (www.iab.net). In addition, Rich LeFurgy, 41, was re-elected chairman of the association for 1998. He is senior vice president for advertising at ABC News/ ESPN Internet Ventures, a unit of the Walt Disney Company in newyork. Richy Glassberg, 34, vice president and general manager at Turner Interactive Marketing and Sales in newyork, part of Time Warner Inc., was re-elected vice chairman.

title:
Science Watch;
Total Eclipse on the Web - Correction Appended
body: One of nature's most majestic and benign spectacles, a total solar eclipse, will sweep across the Caribbean on Thursday morning, relieving a few thousand lucky tourists of the need for sunblock for a few minutes, anyway. Flights and cruise ships to the region were long ago sold out but stay-at-homes can still get in on the action via the Internet. Scientists from NASA's Sun-Earth Connection Education Forum, San Francisco's Exploratorium and Discovery Online will be teaming up to broadcast images of the eclipse, along with demonstrations, interviews and background reports on the Web. There will be two broadcasts, each switching back and forth between a studio at the Exploratorium and an expedition site in Aruba. The first, at 4 P.M. tomorrow, will present background information about eclipses and solar research. The second, starting at 6 A.M. on Thursday, will include live sights and sounds of the eclipse itself. Fans of the dark side should point their browsers to www.explorator ium.edu/eclipse. DENNIS OVERBYE Correction  A brief report in the Science Watch column yesterday about a solar eclipse that will sweep across the Caribbean tomorrow misstated the times of two broadcasts on the Internet about the event. The first, at 10 p.m. today (not 4 p.m.), will offer background information. The second, at noon tomorrow (not 6 a.m.), will include live views of the eclipse. Times are Eastern standard. Correction-Date: February 25, 1998, Wednesday

title:
PUBLIC LIVES;
Magazine Drives
body: FRANCIS FORD COPPOLA's Zoetrope magazine has found a novel way to get feedback on material it might publish. Starting next week, it will ask anyone who uses the Internet to send in short stories to read and rate five other submissions. "It's like a writers' workshop," Mr. Coppola said as he celebrated the magazine's first anniversary at the TriBeCa Grill. But a planned demonstration had to be called off. "As with all technology," he said, "it broke."

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
SPRINT AND EARTHLINK PLAN MERGED INTERNET VENTURE
body: The Sprint Corporation and Earthlink Network Inc. said yesterday that they planned to combine their Internet access operations in a joint venture that will give Sprint a 30 percent stake in Earthlink. The deal is valued up to $230 million. Earthlink, which is based in Pasadena, Calif., will gain Sprint's 130,000 Internet Passport subscribers, raising its customer base to 600,000. Sprint, based in Westwood, Kan., will pay $24 million in cash and provide a $100 million line of credit to Earthlink. In return, Sprint will receive 4.1 million convertible preferred shares and begin a tender for 1.25 million Earthlink shares at $45 a share. Shares of Earthlink jumped $8.125 each yesterday, to $46.75.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
WAVERLY IN DEAL TO BE ACQUIRED BY WOLTERS
body: Waverly Inc., a medicine and science publisher, agreed yesterday to be acquired by the Dutch publisher Wolters Kluwer N.V. for $375 million, but the price disappointed Wall Street and Waverly's stock tumbled. Wolters Kluwer is offering $39 a share. Shares of Waverly, which is based in Baltimore, slid $8.25 each, to $39. Wolters Kluwer said it had an agreement with Waverly's founding family and other stockholders representing a majority of the outstanding shares to acquire their stakes. The offer was conditioned on Wolters Kluwer's receiving tenders of at least two-thirds of Waverly's common stock, Waverly said.

title:
National News Briefs;
Man Is Convicted Of Internet Hatemail
body: A Federal jury here has convicted a man for a hate crime over the Internet. The jury on Tuesday found Richard Machado, 21, guilty of civil rights violations for using electronic mail to threaten 59 Asian students at a West Coast college. "The decision of the jury has precedential value," a prosecutor, Mavis Lee, said today. "This case demonstrates that you're not insulated from crime liability all of a sudden because you happen to be logged on the Internet." In his messages, which he signed "Asian Hater," Mr. Machado threatened to hunt down and kill the students. He said he blamed his poor grades on Asian students who he felt raised the grading curve. Mr. Machado's lawyer, Sylvia Torres-Guillen, said an appeal was planned.

title:
IN BRIEF;
School Declines to Discipline Boy for Computer Comments
body: A Bergen County eighth grader was recently discovered to have written derogatory and sexually explicit comments about his teachers on the Internet, but the school authorities decided last week not to discipline him because he did the writing at home. A Mahwah boy at Ramapo Ridge Middle School wrote descriptions of eight teachers and two administrators on his own Web site from his home computer. The work was later discovered by another student on a computer at school. The boy, who has not been identified by the police or the school, apologized to the teachers, and his parents vowed to supervise his computer time at home more vigilantly. A letter sent by the superintendent to all the parents asked each of them to do the same. "There are rules on what is allowed if it is done in school or on school property," said Murray Blueglass, the school superintendent. Since this was something done at home, it is beyond the school's jurisdiction, he said. Police maintain that they or the school could file charges against the youth, Mahwah Captain Raymond McGill said, but if the teachers are not going to pursue it, neither will they.   KAREN DeMASTERS

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
LYCOS BUYS WEB SITE WITH A MILLION CUSTOMERS
body: Lycos Inc. said yesterday that it had acquired the closely held Tripod Inc. for $58 million in stock, adding an on-line community to its Internet directory service. Tripod, based in Williamstown, Mass., is a Web site that offers members free publishing tools to create their own Web sites and content on topics like media, work, money, health and sports. Lycos, which is based in Framingham, Mass., said the acquisition added almost one million members and was an attempt to reach 18- to 34-year-old consumers. Lycos said the purchase would make it the fifth-most-visited Web site.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
EGGHEAD WILL CLOSE STORES AND SHIFT TO INTERNET SALES
body: Egghead Inc., a pioneering computer industry retailer that has struggled for years, said yesterday that it would close its remaining 80 stores and shift entirely to Internet sales. Citing years of declining revenue and operating losses, the company, based in Spokane, Wash., said it would change its name to Egghead.com Inc., eliminate about 800 of its 1,000 jobs and try to capitalize on the explosive growth of Internet commerce. For Egghead, which was founded in 1984 and once had more than 200 stores and 2,500 employees, the shift is the latest in a series of restructurings. Its stock fell $1.375 a share, to $6.375.

title: New Data Method Sought for Internet
body: The Universal ADSL Working Group formally announced on Monday that it would develop a new way to send data over the Internet into consumers' homes, greatly increasing the speeds at which it is possible to browse the World Wide Web. The group expects wide deployment of the technology by the end of 1999. The companies that are members include Microsoft, Intel, Compaq, Ameritech, Bell Atlantic, BellSouth, GTE, SBC Communications, Sprint and U S West. Under the group's proposal, installation would be no more complicated than current phone installation and cost about $45 a month. ADSL, or asymmetric digital subscriber line, is a technology that uses existing phone lines for high-speed Internet access up to 30 times faster than today's modems. A new modem would be required, and telephone companies would need to install new equipment, but consumers would be able to transmit the complete works of Shakespeare in five seconds or watch movies on line.

title:
January 18-24;
Power Surge
body: Internet users tired of waiting to download information from cyberspace could get a big boost in the foreseeable future. Compaq, Intel and Microsoft have joined forces with most of America's big local telephone companies. The result should enable users to receive information up to 30 times faster than before. The new technology may be available by Christmas or mid-1999.   SETH SCHIESEL

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
PSINET REJECTS OFFER FROM USINTERNETWORKING
body: Psinet Inc. said its board rejected an offer from USinternetworking Inc. to buy at least a 51 percent stake in the company for $10 a share in cash. The offer price was 19 percent, or $1.5625, higher than Psinet's closing price of $8.4375 on Wednesday. Psinet, an Internet service provider, said the proposed offer was "inconsistent" with its business plan, including its alliance with IXC Internet Services Inc. USinternetworking, based in Washington, is a company whose stated purpose is to acquire Internet-related companies. It is run by Christopher S. McCleary, the former chief executive of Digex Inc., an Internet service provider that was bought by Intermedia Communications Inc. last year. Shares of Psinet rose 56.25 cents, to $9.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
RCN TO BUY ULTRANET AND EROL'S INTERNET
body: The RCN Corporation said it would buy Ultranet Communications Inc. and Erol's Internet Inc. for $110.5 million in cash and stock, as it seeks more Internet customers in the lucrative Northeastern unitedstates with the goal of selling them phone and cable service. Erol's and Ultranet are both closely held providers of Internet-access service. RCN, a cable, local and long-distance phone and Internet company, said it would pay $35 million in cash and $48.5 million in stock for Erol's, and $7.8 million in cash and $19.2 million in stock for Ultranet. RCN will add about 325,000 Internet customers with the addition of Erol's, based in Boston, and Ultranet, based in Springfield, Va. Shares of RCN, based in Princeton, N.J., rose $3.50 yesterday, to $39.75.

title: Intel Offers Software to Cut Web Delays
body: The Intel Corporation introduced software yesterday to help Internet service providers eliminate some of the delays that plague users of the worldwide computer network. Intel will sell the software, Quick Web, for an undisclosed price to Internet service providers, which connect users to the World Wide Web. Intel said it was negotiating with the 30 largest Internet service providers and had already signed up three of them. Quick Web is Intel's latest product to try to increase use of the Internet, which could mean more sales of personal computers that use Intel chips. The company, the world's largest maker of microprocessors for personal computers, also makes a digital camera that lets people make video phone calls and send still images over the Web. An Internet service provider, Netcom On-line Communication Services, agreed to introduce the software product on Feb. 1 after about 700 of its users helped test it, Intel said. Users will pay a premium for the service, probably $5 a month, and Intel and the on-line service provider will both get a percentage of that. Users will have to change one setting on their browsers to benefit from the new technology.

title: Internet Sales Climb for Barnes & Noble
body: Barnes & Noble Inc. is expecting sales at its Internet book-selling site to reach $8 million in the current quarter, helped by the holidays. The company also said sales in the fiscal year that begins this month are expected to exceed $100 million. The sales forecasts come as Barnes & Noble moves to expand its Barnesandnoble.com site, which offers books for as much as 40 percent off the list price. Since the site was introduced in May, sales have doubled in each of its three quarters of operation, as the number of customers using the service rose to more than 250,000, the company said. Barnes & Noble said sales during the holiday season ended Jan. 3 were $5.6 million. During the site's first quarter of operation, sales were $2.1 million and in its second quarter, they were $4 million, the company said. Barnes & Noble also said it would increase advertising and marketing efforts during the next year to encourage more sales. Barnes & Noble, based in newyork, is the largest unitedstates bookseller, with 484 superstores and 555 stores in malls. Its mall stores include the B. Dalton Bookseller, Doubleday Book Shops and Scribner's Bookstores chains.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Internet Ad Monitors In Strategic Alliance
body: Two companies are combining units that track advertising spending on the Internet as they agree to a strategic alliance. The Intermedia Advertising Solutions unit of Competitive Media Reporting in newyork, owned by VNU USA, will acquire the Adspend Data Report from Jupiter Communications in newyork. Terms were not disclosed. Adspend will be combined with Intermedia's Interwatch service to create a data base with information on ad spending on more than 325 World Wide Web sites. Joseph Philport, president of Intermedia, and Gene DeRose, chairman and chief executive of Jupiter, said the alliance would involve cooperative ventures between Competitive Media, which tracks ad spending for advertisers, agencies and media, and Jupiter, a leading Internet consulting company. Jupiter estimates that on-line advertising will total $1.4 billion in 1998, double the estimated $700 million spent in 1997.

title: INSIDE
body: Russian Reformers Set Back Two reformers, both Deputy Prime Ministers, were stripped of some duties, indicating that power struggles are continuing in Moscow. Page A4. Germans to Eavesdrop Moving to combat crime, Germany took a step toward allowing the police to bug private homes for the first time since the Nazi era. Page A4.  A Case of On-Line Privacy A veteran sailor has filed suit to fight the Navy's plan to dismiss him after obtaining his America Online user profile saying he was gay. Page A6.  Democrats Avoid a Split After strains between the White House and Representative Richard Gephardt, relations are improving, averting a messy split. Page A9.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Company Names New Vice President
body: Cynthia H. Augustine has been named senior vice president for human resources of The newyork Times Company. Ms. Augustine, right, will be responsible for all human resources functions, including compensation, employee benefits and organizational development, effective Feb. 16. She is currently a partner in the law firm of Sabin, Bermant & Gould, where she specializes in employment law. She was a lawyer in the Times Company's legal department from 1986 to 1993, working primarily in employment relations, labor relations and employee benefits. A 1979 graduate of Sarah Lawrence College, Ms. Augustine, 40, also graduated from Rutgers Law School in 1982. That same year she began her legal practice with the law firm of Pitney, Hardin, Kipp & Szuch in the employment law department. She is admitted to practice law in newyork State and New Jersey and is a member of the American Bar Association. Graphic   Photo.

title:
METRO NEWS BRIEFS: NEW JERSEY;
At Web Site, Whitman To Discuss State of State
body: Gov. Whitman's State of the State Message on Tuesday will be available on the Internet, the Governor's office said. People who reach the site will be able to watch the Governor as she delivers the speech, read the text of the address and use an email form to send in responses. The site will also contain a trivia quiz about New Jersey, said Julie Plocinik, a spokeswoman for the Governor. The Governor is scheduled to begin at 3 P.M. Information about the State of the State will be available at New Jersey's web site: www.state.nj.us. Graphic   Photo: Gov. Christine Todd Whitman plans to reach Internet users during her State of the State Message. (Associated Press)

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
QWEST TO CARRY APEX INTERNET DATA FOR $260 MILLION
body: Qwest Communications International said yesterday that it would transmit Internet data for Apex Global Internet Services on its fiber optic network. The deal is valued at $260 million, but Qwest could get as much as $575 million over the life of the 20-year contract, said Robert Woodruff, Qwest's chief financial officer. Qwest, which is based in Denver, will receive a 19.99 percent stake in Apex, and Apex, based in Dearborn, Mich., will make monthly cash payments to Qwest. Qwest is building a 16,000-mile fiber optic network. Its shares rose 43.75 cents yesterday, to $65.9375, after gaining $5.125 on Monday, when it obtained a 288-mile fiber optic cable in the Northeast.

title:
METRO NEWS BRIEFS: NEW JERSEY;
State Plans Millions For Internet in Schools
body: The Education Department said yesterday that it would give $3.75 million to 40 school districts this year to expand Internet access. The state will spend an additional $4.2 million this year to train teachers in technology, as well as $40 a student to support distance learning by computer, said Julia A. Stapleton, director of the State Office of Educational Technology.

title:
National News Briefs;
Campaign Money Papers Posted on the Internet
body: The Federal Election Commission has begun publishing digital images of campaign finance records on its Web site, allowing those with access to the Internet to look up reports on many Federal candidates, political parties and political action committees. Until now, the F.E.C. had the reports -- which list donor names, how much candidates and parties raised and how much they spent -- available for viewing only at its public records office in Washington. This new addition to its Web site will broaden public access to campaign finance information, the agency said. There is no fee for looking at the reports. All 1997-98 reports filed by political action committees, political parties, Presidential and House campaigns are available for viewing. Reports dating to 1993 for PAC's, parties and Presidential committees will be available in the coming weeks as will 1996 reports for House candidates. Senate campaign reports are not available. The Web site address is http://www.fec. gov.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Internet Phone Service Pact
body: A telephone company owned by Ronald S. Lauder, the cosmetics heir, said yesterday that it had reached an agreement to sell phone service that travels over the Internet to members of Japan's largest on-line service. The company, RSL Communications Ltd., based in Bermuda, intends to announce the agreement today with a subsidiary of Fujitsu Ltd.. The unit, known as Nifty, has about 2.5 million subscribers. The agreement will enable Nifty customers to make international telephone calls over the Internet using RSL's technology.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MICROSOFT ACQUIRES HOTMAIL, AN email SERVICE PROVIDER
body: The Microsoft Corporation said yesterday that it had acquired Hotmail, a Sunnyvale, Calif., company that provides a free Web-based email service. Hotmail will become part of the Microsoft Network on-line service that is available free to Internet users. Financial terms of the purchase were not announced. Hotmail's technology gives members access to a permanent email address from any PC with an Internet connection. Hotmail has more than nine million users worldwide.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
PSINET CUTS OFFER FOR ISTAR INTERNET BY 38%
body: Psinet Inc. lowered its takeover offer for Istar Internet Inc. yesterday by 38 percent, to $21.8 million (Canadian), or $15.3 million (unitedstates), in cash in the wake of a 61 percent drop in Istar's stock price since a Nov. 10 agreement between the companies. Psinet will bid 75 cents (Canadian), or 52.5 cents (unitedstates), a share for the money-losing Istar. Its original bid was $35 million (Canadian), or $24.5 million (unitedstates), in convertible preferred shares. Istar's shares tumbled to 61 cents (Canadian) from $1.59 (Canadian) after Psinet made its offer. Yesterday, Istar's shares rose 11 cents (Canadian), to 72 cents (Canadian), while Psinet fell 31.25 cents, to $4.84375.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Co. Appoints Technology Officer
body: Raymond E. Douglas has been named vice president of systems and technology for The newyork Times Company. Since 1993, Mr. Douglas, right, has been a vice president of The newyork Times with responsibility for the newspaper's publishing systems and business information systems. He played a major role in the newspaper's changes in the last year, as The Times introduced color to its news sections and added daily sections. In his new position, Mr. Douglas, 48, will oversee information systems and technology for the entire company. He will report to Michael Golden, vice chairman and senior vice president of the Times Company. In addition to The newyork Times, the company publishes The Boston Globe, 21 regional newspapers and 3 magazines; it operates television and radio stations and news, photo and graphic services as well as electronic publishing and new-media businesses. Mr. Douglas joined The Times in 1990 as a pre-press manager. Previously, he had been systems director at USA Today. Graphic   Photo: Raymond E. Douglas

title:
Updates/Media;
Wall Street Journal Plans A Daily London Edition Beginning in January
body: The Wall Street Journal Europe plans to begin a special daily edition for London in January, a spokesman for the newspaper's parent, Dow Jones & Company, said this week. The concept is similar to that of the five regional editions of The Wall Street Journal in the unitedstates. But those are weekly editions, which consist of four extra pages of regional news. The Wall Street Journal Europe has a circulation of 66,000; 13,000 in Britain.

title:
December 14-20;
The New Computer Talk: Mum's the Word.
body: The nation's biggest information companies hoisted a flag in the wars over computer privacy. They said they would voluntarily and automatically remove some personal information -- a person's Social Security number, date of birth, unlisted telephone number and mother's maiden name -- from non-public sources in the data bases now sold to the public. Such information will still be available through public records and to law enforcement agencies. If consumers want to eliminate even more basic information -- like their names, addresses and aliases -- they will have to contact the companies. The move seems to have quelled calls for new privacy legislation -- for now.   KATHARINE Q. SEELYE

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
4 Times Executives Get New Jobs In Advertising and Circulation
body: The newyork Times announced several executive changes in its advertising and circulation departments yesterday. The newspaper said the changes, effective Jan. 1, were intended to build on the paper's gains in those areas the last year. Lauretta Prestera, a vice president for circulation with responsibility for home delivery, will move to the advertising department as a vice president. Ms. Prestera will direct sales for a wide range of advertising categories in the metropolitan newyork region, including consumer electronics, real estate and fashion. Ms. Prestera's home delivery responsibilities will be taken over by Harold F. Woldt Jr., now circulation vice president for sales and marketing. In turn, John O'Reilly, president of City and Suburban Delivery Systems, a wholesale-distribution affiliate of The Times, will become a circulation vice president, taking over Mr. Woldt's marketing and sales responsibilities while also retaining responsibility for City and Suburban. Donna C. Miele, now a vice president and project administrator with a background in human resources management, will join the circulation department in the new position of vice president for customer service. Graphic   Photos: The newyork Times announced new responsibilities for Lauretta Prestera, Harold F. Woldt Jr., John O'Reilly and Donna C. Miele.

title: McCaw to Resume Chief Executive Duties at an Internet Company
body: A co-founder of Teledesic L.L.C., Craig O. McCaw, will take a more active role in running the company, which is building an "Internet in the sky," as he resumes the job of chief executive. Mr. McCaw, who is chairman, will share the chief executive duties with Steve Hooper, a longtime McCaw associate. The current chief, David Twyver, 51, will join them on a three-member executive committee. Mr. McCaw's resumption of chief executive duties, which he had until a year ago, reflects the determination of the company, based here, to stick to an ambitious timetable for creating a 288-satellite network. The network is to provide Internet access, video-conferencing and voice communication for companies. The first satellite is to be launched in 2001 and service is to begin in 2002. Mr. McCaw and William H. Gates, the Microsoft Corporation's founder and chairman, each own one-third of Teledesic. Boeing owns 10 percent, and the remaining shares are in private hands.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Thomson Science Unit Sale
body: The Thomson Corporation, the Canadian information and publishing concern, will sell its Thomson Science publishing unit to the Dutch publisher Wolters Kluwer N.V. Terms were not disclosed. Thomson Science publishes scholarly books and journals and has operations in London, newyork and Philadelphia. The transaction excludes its German operation.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
WINSTAR SAYS IT IS BUYING GOODNET FROM TELESOFT
body: Winstar Communications Inc. said yesterday that it was the buyer of Goodnet, an Internet access provider, from the Telesoft Corporation for $22.5 million. Winstar will pay $3.5 million in cash and the rest in common stock. Winstar, a wireless telecommunications provider, said it expected Goodnet's 1998 revenues to be double its current annual revenues of about $8 million. Winstar, based in newyork, had 1996 revenues of $68 million. Telesoft, a Phoenix-based telecommunications systems services company, said on Wednesday that it was selling Goodnet but did not disclose the buyer.

title: Setback for Microsoft
body: Microsoft was ordered to separate, at least temporarily, its Internet browser software from its industry-dominating Windows operating system. The order, issued by a Federal judge, is a setback for Microsoft in its long-running antitrust battle with the Justice Department. Business Day, page D1.

title: Telesoft to Sell Its Internet Unit
body: The Telesoft Corporation said yesterday that it had agreed to sell its Internet subsidiary for more than $20 million. It said that a phone company based in the newyork area had agreed to acquire its Goodnet unit and that the deal would be announced this morning at the Internet World convention in Manhattan. Telesoft, of Phoenix, did not identify the acquirer. Goodnet is a small Internet service provider with about $10 million in annual revenue that serves both retail and corporate users. Telephone carriers have rapidly been acquiring Internet companies as they seek to offer a full bundle of voice and data services to their customers. The trend began with the acquisition of Uunet Technologies, one of the largest, by MFS Communications in April 1996 and has since been moving down market. This summer, GTE agreed to acquire the BBN Corporation. In October ICG Communications agreed to buy Netcom On-Line Communications Services.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
3 Are Chosen For Hall of Fame
body: The American Advertising Federation in Washington has selected three executives to be inducted into the Advertising Hall of Fame. The honorees are: the late Gertrude R. Crain, the chairwoman of Crain Communications Inc. who died last year; Alex Kroll, chairman emeritus of Young & Rubicam Inc., and Paul Schrage, the former senior executive vice president and chief marketing officer at the McDonald's Corporation. They will be honored at a luncheon at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel in newyork on March 31.

title: Mideast Goes on Line
body: To the Editor: While many Arab societies have been virtually walled off from the information and financial-market revolutions taking place around the world, the "silent invasion" of the Internet in the Middle East that Thomas L. Friedman talks about (column, Dec. 8) is threatened. Several Mideast and North African countries are clamping down on what they perceive as politically and socially subversive on the World Wide Web. Internet providers are required to set up software blockades to censor material. A case in point is Etisalat, the only service provider to the United Arab Emirates, which through a "proxy cache server" cuts out sites deemed immoral. The problem is that if the software is programmed to block keywords like breast or sex, information about Middlesex County in England, breast cancer research or even a recipe for chicken breasts would be blocked. It is crucial that the Internet be regarded in conservative societies not as a danger to be feared but as a vehicle for knowledge.  ALI HOUISSA Ithaca, N.Y., Dec. 8, 1997

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
INTEL TO ACQUIRE 4.9% STAKE IN CMG INFORMATION SERVICES
body: The Intel Corporation agreed to buy a 4.9 percent stake in CMG Information Services Inc., a direct marketing concern that also invests in Internet companies. Terms were not disclosed, but the stake would be worth about $13.5 million on the open market. CMG shares surged 19 percent, gaining $4.625, to $28.50. Shares of Intel rose 87.5 cents, to $78.4375, as almost 10.1 million shares were traded. CMG, based in Wilmington, Mass., has a majority stake in Lycos Inc., which makes a widely used Internet browser. Intel, the semiconductor giant, is based in Santa Clara, Calif. CMG said the two companies would explore Internet business opportunities.

title: Newsprint Stakes Are Sold
body: Dow Jones & Company and the Washington Post Company said that they have sold their matching 35 percent stakes in two newsprint and timber companies to their partner, Brant-Allen Industries, for a total of $226 million. Dow Jones and Washington Post said that the sales of their interests in the Bear Island Paper Company and the Bear Island Timberlands Company would result in fourth-quarter gains of $28 million. The Bear Island companies produce 225,000 metric tons of newsprint annually and own 130,000 acres of timberland in Virginia.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AXENT TECHNOLOGIES TO ACQUIRE RAPTOR FOR $250 MILLION
body: Axent Technologies Inc. agreed to acquire Raptor Systems Inc. for $250 million in stock. Axent, based in Rockville, Md., provides network security software and services. Raptor, based in Waltham, Mass., specializes in software known as a firewall, which connects a company's internal computer network with the public Internet without compromising security. Under the deal, Axent will swap four-fifths of a share for each Raptor share outstanding, issuing about 12.8 million shares. Raptor shares dropped $1.125, to $14.625, and Axent fell $1.75, to $19.

title: Shares of At Home Up 8%
body: The stock of the At Home Corporation rose nearly 8 percent today after the company said it would offer high-speed Internet access service for business travelers staying in hotels. At Home, which is based here, offers high-speed Internet connections via cable modems. It will work with Fourth Communications Network Inc., an Internet service provider that specializes in hotels, to develop the service, the companies said today. Shares of At Home gained $1.625, to $22.25, on the Nasdaq stock market.

title: Netscape Says Browser Has Been Big Seller
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation says the number of users of its Netscape Communicator software has topped 25 million since the product began shipments in June.
