The company cited the figure as evidence that momentum continues to accelerate behind its products despite stiff competition from the industry titans like the Microsoft Corporation, which provides a rival Internet browser, and the International Business Machines Corporation's Lotus unit. Netscape said more than 68 million individuals had tried or used its products. "The adaption rate was as fast as we were seeing in our previous versions" of Netscape's earlier browser products, David Rothschild, Netscape vice president of client products, said on Wednesday.

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
Tours of Historic Places On the Internet
body: The National Park Service has begun to post on the Web tours of buildings and sites listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Three city itineraries and one regional itinerary are already available. The on-line tours of the cities -- Chicago, Baltimore and Seattle -- use photographs, maps and written descriptions. The Chicago itinerary introduces 25 buildings, including early skyscrapers, stylish houses, and buildings central to the history of blacks in the city, like the Eighth Regiment Armory, the first built for a regiment commanded entirely by blacks. The regional itinerary available on line is "Along the Georgia and Florida Coast," featuring 51 sites from Savannah to Key West. The itineraries can be found through the National Park Service's Web site, www.nps.gov, under Links to the Past, or through the National Register Travel Itineraries home page, www.cr.nps.gov/nr/ tourism.html. Graphic   Photo: Fort Jefferson, a Civil War prison in the Gulf of Mexico, off Florida. (Len Kaufman)

title: Apple Books $500,000 in Orders on Line
body: Apple Computer Inc. said today that its new on-line store for selling products over the Internet received more than 4.4 million "hits" and booked more than $500,000 in orders in its first 12 hours of operation. "We're thrilled by this immediate customer response to our Apple Store and new G3 computers," Steven P. Jobs, the company's co-founder and interim chief executive, said. "Apple is really 'thinking different' about the way we do business." On Monday, Apple introduced a new line of PowerMacintosh computers and some major changes in the way it makes and sells its products, including the addition of an on-line store. The Apple Store, at http://www.apple.com on the Internet, is part of a new distribution strategy, to give customers a greater choice in how they buy Apple products. The strategy also includes building systems to exact customer specifications and using more common parts, thus lowering product inventories and manufacturing costs.

title: Browser Short At Microsoft
body: In trying to convince the Government and the public that there is plenty of competition in computing, the Microsoft Corporation has consistently pointed to the Internet. It may dominate the market for PC operating software, Microsoft says, but the Internet is a wide-open frontier. But it was not open enough yesterday for anyone trying to view Microsoft's court filings, posted on the company's World Wide Web site, with the competing browser, Netscape's Navigator. Until about noon,only those tapping into the site (www.microsoft.com/corp info/11-10Filing.html) with Microsoft's Internet Explorer could view the documents. It was an honest if embarrassing mistake, according to Microsoft. It seems an inexperienced Web programmer responsible for the documents put up seven errant characters in hypertext markup language used for stitching documents onto the Web. Since Microsoft employees use only the company browser, no one at headquarters in Redmond, Wash., learned of the problem until a flood of complaints landed, mainly from reporters. As a result, Microsoft will now use both Microsoft and Netscape browsers for Web site testing, a spokesman said.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
PSINET TO BUY ISTAR INTERNET FOR $25 MILLION
body: Psinet Inc. said yesterday that it had agreed to acquire Istar Internet Inc. for about $25 million in Psinet convertible preferred stock. Combining Istar with Psinet's Canadian operations would create a business with annual revenues of more than $34 million, making it the largest Internet service provider in the Canadian marketplace. Under the agreement, Istar shareholders would receive nonvoting, 8 percent cumulative convertible Psinet shares. Up to one-third of the shares of each holder would be convertible on or after April 1, 1998; July 1, 1998, and Jan. 1, 1999, into Psinet common stock.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Judge Backs a Dow Jones Libel Award
body: A Federal judge in Houston let stand a $22.7 million libel judgment against Dow Jones & Company that stemmed from a 1993 article about a Houston brokerage firm that appeared in The Wall Street Journal, the company's flagship newspaper. In March, a Federal jury awarded the brokerage firm, MMAR Group Inc., which is now defunct, $222.7 million in the case, including $200 million in punitive damages. But in May, Judge Ewing Werlein Jr. of the Federal District Court in Houston cut the award to $22.7 million. Dow Jones had asked the judge to either grant a new trial or "greatly reduce" the remaining award, which represented compensatory damages to MMAR. But in a 38-page decision handed down yesterday, Judge Werlein let the compensatory damage award stand. "We expect shortly to appeal," Dow Jones said in a statement. "We remain optimistic that this judgment ultimately will not withstand the scrutiny of the courts."

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Internet Profiles To Acquire a Rival
body: There was a significant consolidation in the field of Internet audience measurement yesterday as the Internet Profiles Corporation in Redwood City, Calif., said that it had agreed to acquire the technology and other assets of a rival, Netcount L.L.C. in Los Angeles. Terms were not disclosed. Internet Profiles, known as I/PRO, will purchase the products and intellectual property of Netcount and offer its services to Netcount customers. I/PRO and Netcount are now used to track visitors to more than 400 World Wide Web sites that I/ PRO executives estimated account for more than 70 percent of advertising spending on the Web. The deal calls for Netcount employees to help I/PRO in converting Netcount customers to I/PRO products and services; Netcount is expected to end operations on Monday. Plans call for the agreement, subject to the approval of the boards of both companies, to be completed by mid-December. I/PRO customers include AT&T Worldnet and NBC. Netcount customers include Hollywood Online, NBC and Warner Brothers.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
GARTNER ACQUIRES 32% STAKE IN JUPITER COMMUNICATIONS
body: The Gartner Group Inc. said yesterday that it had bought a 32 percent stake in the privately held Internet market research firm Jupiter Communications L.L.C. for $8 million. Founded in 1986, newyork-based Jupiter Communications provides analysis and strategic planning consulting to the consumer Internet market. The companies said there would be no changes to Jupiter's management. Gartner Group, based in Stamford, Conn., provides information technology advisory services, measurement, research, consulting and training.

title: Corrections
body: A front-page article on Saturday about Net Day, a volunteer effort to provide Internet access to the nation's schools, misstated the number of students who graduated last year from McClymonds High School in Oakland, Calif. It was 71 of the 81 students in the senior class, not 16 of 150 seniors.

title:
Metro Business;
Interactive Data to Move
body: The Interactive Data Corporation, a unit of Pearson P.L.C., which publishes The Financial Times newspaper, has agreed to lease three floors encompassing 58,000 square feet of space at 100 William Street, at the intersection of John Street. The company, which provides computerized financial data to institutional investors, is expected to move in early 1998 from its present 40,000 square feet at 14 Wall Street. Executives of Sylvan Lawrence Company, which owns and manages 100 William Street, said the value of the lease was more than $18 million. Andrea H. Loew, general counsel for Interactive Data, said about 190 people would occupy the new offices. Interactive Data's decision to expand in the downtown financial center is another indicator of how well the once-moribund area has rebounded, brokers say. According to the Insignia/Edward S. Gordon Company, a real estate brokerage and management company, leases have been negotiated for 6.5 million square feet of space in the downtown area in the first three quarters of the year, almost double the 3.34 million square feet leased in the same period last year. JOHN HOLUSHA

title: Microsoft's Illogic
body: To the Editor: Re "The Justice Department v. Microsoft: The Evidence and the Answers" (Business Day, Oct. 27), on Microsoft's demand that its Internet browser be present in all shipped systems: In its defense, Microsoft said, "Ford would not allow one of its dealers to pull the factory installed engine out of a Mustang and substitute a Chevy engine." The analogy is flawed. First, the Internet browser does not "drive" the computer. Second, auto retailers will allow the customer to pull the factory-installed stereo system from a delivered car and will give the customer a credit. If anything, Microsoft's argument works against it.  RICHARD A. LOWENSTEIN Westport, Conn., Oct. 27, 1997

title:
INTERNATIONAL BRIEFS;
Reed Elsevier to Sell Consumer Magazines
body: Reed Elsevier P.L.C. said yesterday that it planned to sell its British consumer magazines unit as it prepares to merge with Wolters Kluwer N.V. of the Netherlands. Reed Elsevier, a British-Dutch publishing company, aims to complete the sale of the unit -- IPC Magazines, the market leader in Britain with more than 70 titles -- by early 1998 when it also hopes to seal the merger with Amsterdam-based Wolters Kluwer. The deal excludes the New Scientist weekly, which complements the group's position as the world's biggest publisher of scientific journals. Titles for sale include TV Times, Woman's Own, Classic Car, Country Life, Shooting Times, New Musical Express and Loaded. IPC had sales last year of £314 million ($514 million) and pretax profits of £63 million ($104.4 million).

title: Microsoft Monopoly
body: To the Editor: Clyde W. Crews Jr. (letter, Oct. 24) asserts that if Microsoft's browser tie-in were detrimental to the computer industry, "Dell, Gateway and Compaq could collectively demand relief." And what bargaining power does Mr. Crews see in the hands of the computer manufacturers? Can they threaten Microsoft with a refusal to license Windows? Microsoft's monopoly power, and its threat to extend that power into the Internet, makes the Justice Department's actions necessary. Jonathan Novack's statement (letter, Oct. 24) that a browser is a "legitimate addition" to Windows ignores the nature of the problem and why Microsoft is eager to act. Microsoft does not have control over the Internet, but it does have the opportunity to use its monopoly power in operating systems to gain that power. Control over access to the Internet will lead to control over Internet protocols, and Microsoft doesn't want anyone but itself to have such dominance.  SCOTT ROTHSTEIN Massapequa, N.Y., Oct. 27, 1997

title:
October 19-25;
U.S. Cites Microsoft In Antitrust Case
body: The Justice Department has decided to enter the Internet browser war. Moving aggressively against the Microsoft Corporation, antitrust prosecutors sought a court order to block the company from forcing computer makers that use its popular Windows 95 operating system to also use its less popular, but steadily growing, browser software. Attorney General Janet Reno said Microsoft had tried to leverage its monopoly over operating software to squeeze out competitors in the unfolding struggle for control over the World Wide Web. Microsoft said it had not done anything improper and would contest the challenge. The dispute is not likely to be resolved for months, and may not end by the time the company introduces Windows 98, the next version of its operating system, next year.   STEPHEN LABATON

title: Microsoft Is Being Punished for Its Success
body: To the Editor: Re "Metaphor Monopoly" (Op-Ed, Oct. 23): The Justice Department's complaint is that Microsoft requires computer manufacturers to bundle Internet Explorer 4.0, the World Wide Web browser, with the Windows 95 operating system. So? Products have been bundled at least since the toy surprise inside Cracker Jacks. Reviews consistently show Internet Explorer 4.0 to be a superb product, free to grateful consumers who retain their option to download competing products. Most important, Microsoft isn't impervious, as antitrust superstition holds. If the "tie-in" of the operating system and browser were detrimental to the health of the computer industry and competing software, the computer manufacturing giants Dell, Gateway and Compaq could collectively demand relief at the next contract renegotiation with Microsoft. There is no role for the Justice Department here: markets can police themselves.  CLYDE W. CREWS JR. Washington, Oct. 23, 1997  The writer is a fellow in regulatory studies at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

title:
Microsoft Is Being Punished for Its Success;
'Download the Patch'
body: To the Editor: Attorney General Janet Reno's action against Microsoft is unjustified ("Metaphor Monopoly," Op-Ed, Oct. 23). In fact, Microsoft wants computer manufacturers that load Windows 95 on their machines also to load the Internet Explorer browser because almost all systems support is found on the World Wide Web. The first thing I am told when I call almost any manufacturer with a computer-related problem is, "Download the latest patch from our Web site." Microsoft is providing the ability to do this with a free, value-added product. However, some may argue that you get what you pay for and decide to purchase a browser with features that are suitable to their needs.  CARL L. FENLEY San Diego, Oct. 23, 1997

title:
Microsoft Is Being Punished for Its Success;
The Browser's Ascent
body: To the Editor: "Justice Moves Against Microsoft" (editorial, Oct. 22) asserts that Microsoft, by bundling its Internet Explorer browser with its Windows 95 operating system, is in violation of a 1995 consent decree. If it were still 1995, that would be true. In 1997, however, this is no longer the case. Two years ago, a World Wide Web browser was just an amusing application program that allowed the user to "surf" the Web for interesting pages to view. Today, however, small businesses and major corporations are converting many of their Windows-based programs to this new Web environment and running them directly in their browsers instead of in Windows. In the near future, the browser may well replace the Windows operating system entirely. As such, it fully qualifies as a legitimate addition to Microsoft's Windows 95 operating system and is clearly exempt from the 1995 agreement.  JONATHAN NOVACK Princeton, N.J., Oct. 22, 1997  The writer is a software design consultant.

title: Two Booksellers Settle Lawsuits
body: Barnes & Noble and Amazon.com have settled lawsuits against each other concerning sales of books on the Internet, the companies said yesterday. The rival booksellers said that neither party admitted wrongdoing of any kind, and neither paid damages. The companies said they "simply decided that they would rather compete in the marketplace than in the courtroom." Amazon.com and Barnes & Noble have been fighting for on-line bookselling supremacy for months. Amazon.com sells books solely over the Internet, while Barnes & Noble also operates 462 stores nationwide. In May, Barnes & Noble sued Amazon.com for false advertising following the claim by Amazon.com that it was "the world's largest bookstore." Amazon.com countersued, contending that Barnes & Noble competed unfairly by improperly failing to charge sales taxes on books sold over the Internet.

title: U.S. Is Vulnerable on Internet, Report Says
body: A report concluding that the nation is vulnerable to electronic attacks was delivered to the White House today by a Presidential commission. The classified findings and recommendations of the Commission on Critical Infrastructure Protection said the danger of computer attacks that could shut down communications and power grids was real and required early action. The report recommended stepping up research, educating people about the problem and revising existing laws to insure protection against attacks through the Internet. P. J. Crowley, a White House spokesman, said a task force of representatives from Government agencies would review the report and make recommendations.

title: Excite to Acquire Netbot for $35 Million
body: Excite Inc. has agreed to buy Netbot Inc., which makes software for finding and buying products on the Internet, for $35 million in stock, to attract more shoppers to the directory's site. Excite plans later this year to add Netbot's Jango software to its Internet search service to make it easier for consumers to shop on line. The closely held Netbot, based in Seattle, was founded last year by two University of Washington professors. Excite, which is based in Redwood City and is the No. 2 Internet directory behind Yahoo Inc., last month revamped the shopping area on its site and has signed agreements with on-line merchants including Amazon.com Inc. in an effort to increase revenue by promoting merchants and taking a cut of their sales. Consumers use Netbot's software to search merchant Web sites and data bases to get product information, comparative reviews and prices. The software is designed to make it easier and faster to find products on the Web.

title: Dow Jones Looks At Troubled Unit
body: Dow Jones & Company is considering whether to continue with a $650 million plan to revamp its troubled Dow Jones Markets financial information service and is reviewing options for the unit. A Dow Jones spokesman, Richard Tofel, said yesterday that company management and the board of directors were "engaged in a review of that plan and various alternatives concerning Dow Jones Markets." Mr. Tofel would not specify what those alternatives might be, but said that Dow Jones had not been displeased with the unit's performance. Mr. Tofel said there was no time schedule for the review, which came as the company was considering its budget for next year. Dow Jones shares, which had been trading lower most of the day, rallied after the announcement to $47.50, up 37.5 cents, on the newyork Stock Exchange. In January, Dow Jones disclosed the plan to overhaul the business, formerly known as Dow Jones Telerate, which provides electronic financial data such as bond prices. The business has fared poorly amid strong competition, dragging down the company's earnings and stock price.

title:
New Jersey Daily Briefing;
Whitman Web Site in Spanish
body: Spanish-speaking voters with Internet access can now get the same information on Gov. Christine Todd Whitman's re-election campaign as their English-speaking counterparts. Since Saturday, a Spanish translation of Governor Whitman's campaign Web site has been available on the World Wide Web at www.christie97.org, campaign officials said. Campaign officials for State Senator James E. McGreevey, the Democrat who challenging Mrs. Whitman, said they publish Spanish-language fliers but do not translate the campaign's Web site, www.mcgreevey97.com. "We just don't have the cash," Cathy Ellis, a spokeswoman, said.   ALAN FEUER

title: Greenburgh Offers Help To Animal Shelter
body: Thank you for the article about the Elmsford Animal Shelter (Sept. 14). The town of Greenburgh, which worked closely with animal shelter officials to get the new state-of-the-art, 1,100-capacity shelter built, hopes to work with Elmsford Animal Shelter officials to reduce overcrowding. We plan to make available to animal shelter officials an Adopt a Pet category on our Web site: www.town.greenburgh.ny.us. The Internet site offers photos of adoptable pets and updates about some pets that need a permanent home with a caring family. It's my hope that this Adopt a Pet Web site will help the shelter respond to concerns about overcrowding and also continue their important work.  PAUL J. FEINER Town Supervisor Greenburgh

title:
Metro Business;
Bills Delivered on Line
body: Customers of the Chase Manhattan Corporation and the CheckFree Corporation will be able to receive and pay bills via the Internet next year, as part of a plan to expand the bank's on-line services. Chase, the largest bank in the nation, already allows customers to pay bills on line. It said it is the first bank to offer the bill delivery service. Customers will access merchants' bills on Chase's Web site. "The merchants will save on the rendering of paper statements, so it reduces their costs quite dramatically," said Ken Herz, a spokesman for Chase. "It will also be convenient for our customers." The electronic billing will be available in the first quarter of 1998. CheckFree, of Norcross, Ga., provides services and products to the electronic commerce market.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Web Genesis Picks Kirshenbaum Bond
body: Web Genesis Inc. in newyork said yesterday that it had named Kirshenbaum Bond & Partners in newyork as the first agency of record to handle integrated marketing for the Globe, its community Web site. Billings were estimated at $5 million to $8 million. The decision came after a six-week review that began with six agencies and had been narrowed to Kirshenbaum Bond and one other finalist, CKS Site Specific in newyork, part of the CKS Group. The Globe, aimed at males between the ages of 18 and 24, reports that it has more than 670,000 registered members for its chat, home page and email services. Advertisers on the Web Genesis World Wide Web site (www.theglobe.com) include the BellSouth Corporation and the Microsoft Corporation. Kirshenbaum Bond's compensation will be based on helping the Globe gain subscribers and advertisers, said Susan Berkowitz, advertising and marketing director for the site and Web Genesis.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
YAHOO ACQUIRES ON-LINE DIRECTORY AND email CONCERN
body: Yahoo Inc. said yesterday that it would acquire the privately held Four11 Corporation, an on-line communications and directory company, for $92 million in stock. It will use the company's Rocketmail technology for a free, Web-based electronic mail service starting today. Yahoo is best known for its Internet directory, which is the most popular means for finding information on line. But the company has been working to become a broader source of information. The company, based in Santa Clara, Calif., has been looking for a way to provide email and decided to acquire Four11 and its Rocketmail service, which has 750,000 registered users, said Jeff Mallett, Yahoo's senior vice president for business operations. Yahoo shares rose $1, to $56.75.

title: I.B.M. Introduces a Home Page Creator
body: A service to help small businesses run electronic stores on the World Wide Web for less than $60 a month was introduced today by the International Business Machines Corporation. The service, the I.B.M. Home Page Creator, would make it easier and less expensive to create Web sites that allow businesses to interact with customers, suppliers and employees over the Internet, the company said. The Home Page Creator packages several tools to provide a "fill in the blanks template" for creating interactive Web sites. It can also be used to put together electronic catalogues, and some packages allow businesses to process credit cards and checks on line. I.B.M. said it currently cost "tens of thousands of dollars" to hire someone to maintain a business Web site. "That's a big investment," said an I.B.M. spokesman, Steve Wittenborn. "Small businesses often do not have their own expertise to do it on their own."

title: Bell Atlantic Internet Pact
body: The Bell Atlantic Corporation said yesterday that it had picked equipment by Farallon Communications as the router for its Internet access service. Bell Atlantic Internet Solutions said that its integrated services digital network/local area network service packaged with Farallon's Netopia router was priced at $115 a month for unlimited Internet access, based on a three-year contract.

title:
WEDDINGS;
Tara Vent, John Tucker
body: Tara Lynn Vent, an assistant district attorney in the Bronx, and John Brian Tucker, a news anchor for both Bloomberg Radio and Bloomberg Television in Manhattan, were married yesterday in Middletown, N.J. The Rev. Barbara Rambach, a United Methodist minister, performed the ceremony at the Monmouth Hills Club. Ms. Vent, who is 31 and is keeping her name, graduated from newyork University and received her law degree from Yeshiva University. She is a daughter of Norma T. Vent of Manahawkin, N.J., and the late Arthur W. Vent, who headed the maintenance and service division of the Serge Elevator Company in Wood-Ridge, N.J. Mr. Tucker, 35, graduated from Fairleigh Dickinson University. His parents, Joan D. Tucker and Dr. Thomas N. Tucker, live in Middletown, where his father is a dentist.

title: Suspect Apparently Has a Web Site
body: A site is posted on the World Wide Web under the name of the 15-year-old suspect charged with murdering and assaulting an 11-year-old New Jersey boy. The site is devoted largely to the Smashing Pumpkins rock group. The author, who identified himself as Sam Manzie, 15, of Jackson, Ocean County, N.J., said he had been born in California and had also lived in Florida, North Carolina, and Monmouth County, N.J. The page included an October 1996 picture of its author and excerpts from several essays he wrote in the spring of 1997. In one essay, he discussed the question of which of the two cartoon characters Beavis and Butt-head would win if they fought: "Butt-head seems to be the dominant one of the two characters. Butt-head is also the stronger one and the one who inflicts more physical abuse on the other," he wrote. "There are a few instances, however, where Beavis will be struck by Butt-head repeatedly, will get pushed over the edge, and will burst into a paroxysm of violence against Butt-head. Thus, it can be concluded that although Beavis gets more injury inflicted upon him, he would win in a fight."

title:
INTERNATIONAL BRIEFS;
Australia Prices Stake In Telecommunications
body: The Australian Government's asking price for one-third of its telecommunications company, the Telstra Corporation, will be between $12 billion and $14.2 billion (Australian), or $8.6 billion and $10.2 billion (unitedstates), the Government said yesterday. The shares will be sold to institutions and individuals at prices between $2.80 and $3.30 (Australian) each. At least 70 percent of the 4.29 billion shares sold will go to Australian investors, with the application process to start soon. Australia is one of several countries selling all or part of their telecommunications carriers, raising money and forcing the companies to become more efficient to compete with rivals.

title: Citicorp and First Union Buy Into Integrion
body: Citicorp and the First Union Corporation agreed yesterday to buy stakes in Integrion Financial Network, an electronic banking and payment venture owned by I.B.M. and 16 North American banks. Integrion, formed in January, distributes consumer electronic banking and bill payment services to 10 of the 15 largest banks in North America, representing 75 percent of households. The companies did not disclose the financial terms. "We intend to be a leader in the electronic commerce industry," said William Fennimore Jr., Integrion's managing director. It is the latest partnership for Citicorp, which has abandoned its strategy of developing proprietary systems as it works to develop large-scale electronic banking services for its customers worldwide. In recent months, Citicorp opened a site on America Online Inc., hired the Mining Company to develop Internet banking sites and invested in Security First Network Bank. First Union, of Charlotte, N.C., has also moved aggressively to create a "cyberbank" that would supplement branches. The sixth-largest unitedstates bank is developing Internet, direct-access computer and telephone banking services.

title: New York Times Company Promotes Three Executives
body: Laura J. Corwin, corporate secretary of The newyork Times Company, has been promoted to the additional position of vice president. The company also said that Ellen Taus had been promoted to treasurer from assistant treasurer and that R. Anthony Benten had been elevated to assistant treasurer from director of treasury. Ms. Corwin has been corporate secretary since 1989 and corporate counsel since 1993. She joined the company in 1980 as a lawyer and became assistant secretary in 1983. As treasurer, Ms. Taus will continue to report to Diane P. Baker, the senior vice president and chief financial officer who had previously held the post. Graphic   Photo: Ellen Taus, left, and Laura Corwin have been named to new positions. (Tyler Hicks)

title:
Government Plan Threatens Patients' Privacy;
Social Security on Line
body: To the Editor: Contrary to Stanley A. Spiegelman (letter, Sept. 10), the Social Security Administration's decision to use the Internet to provide earnings and benefits information is not headed for failure. This information is a valuable tool for retirement planning. When privacy concerns were raised, the agency took steps to strengthen security on the site, including holding public forums that solicited the views of experts on privacy, consumer advocacy, computer security and commercial Internet use. As a result, the Internet site will have security improvements sufficient to protect individual privacy.  SAWL WOOLFSON newyork, Sept. 11, 1997  The writer is a public affairs specialist, Social Security Administration.

title:
NEW JERSEY DAILY BRIEFING;
Child Pornography Charge
body: An executive of the Avon Products Corporation was charged yesterday with receiving and distributing child pornography over the Internet, officials said. Eugene Byrnes, 47, of Kinnelon, the company's vice president of workplace management, is accused in a Federal indictment of using the America Online computer network to send and receive 24 pornographic photographs of children.

title: Amex Goes Live On the Internet
body: For those who want to get a taste of Wall Street without actually having to go there, the American Stock Exchange has this alternative: a live video of the trading floor available via the Internet. The exchange said that the service, which was inaugurated yesterday on the exchange's Web site (www. amex.com), is the first live broadcast of a stock exchange in the unitedstates. On the first day, between 30,000 and 50,000 people visited the Web site, three times the number that the Web site has usually drawn. The Web site has five cameras offering live pictures and sounds from the trading floor between 9:30 A.M. and 4:30 P.M. It also offers live market reports at 9:30 A.M. and 4:30 P.M. and educational videos on how the exchange works.

title: Social Insecurity?
body: To the Editor: Your Sept. 4 front-page article describes the Social Security Administration's plan to permit access to benefits information through an Internet site. This is the second time in less than a year that the agency will open its confidential files to Internet users. It is headed for failure. Agency officials seem to be undeterred by the horrendous state of affairs on the Internet, including break-ins of credit card and other confidential data bases by hackers. Moreover, incidents of break-ins by bank and corporate criminals are often not disclosed. The "verification code" and other safeguards will not stop illicit programmers from attacking the agency's World Wide Web site. It is frustrating that agency bureaucrats are so ill advised. While they advertise questionable staff savings, they have subordinated the more compelling need to protect private information that is entrusted to the agency.  STANLEY A. SPIEGELMAN Pelham Manor, N.Y., Sept. 5, 1997

title:
IN BRIEF;
Landing Soon at Airports: Links to Cyberspace
body: The Port Authority is studying 16 proposals for installing computers with Internet access in the airline terminals at Newark International Airport and the other two newyork City area airports. For a fee, passengers could use their waiting time to log on to a computer and check email, confirm reservations or reach Web sites, said Robert E. Boyle, the Port Authority's executive director. Computers connected to the Internet have been in place in the two business service centers at LaGuardia Airport, where other business equipment is available, since May 1 and have been well received, Mr. Boyle said. Whatever company is selected to install the computers would determine fees and a time frame for installation. The computer terminals are expected to be installed this fall at all three airports, said Allen Morrison, a Port Authority spokesman, who said the three metropolitan airports would be the first in the nation to offer the service. Whether the Port Authority will share in the revenue from the service will depend on the agreement between the winning company and the Port Authority Board of Commissioners.   KAREN DeMASTERS

title: Wiley to Sell Legal Unit to Dutch Publisher
body: John Wiley & Sons Inc. has agreed to sell its Wiley Law Publications division to Wolters Kluwer N.V. of the Netherlands for an undisclosed amount. John Wiley said the sale would allow it to concentrate on its core divisions, including educational, scientific, technical and medical and professional-trade publishing. After the proposed sale of the division, which could close in early fall, the Wiley Law publications will become part of Aspen Publishers of Gaithersburg, Md., a Wolters Kluwer American company. Wiley Law Publications is based in Colorado Springs. John Wiley's sales for the fiscal year that ended on April 30 were $432 million, while Wolters Kluwer reported sales for 1996 of about 4.315 billion Dutch guilders ($2.12 billion).

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
UUNET TECHNOLOGIES ACQUIRES NLNET OF THE NETHERLANDS
body: Worldcom Inc.'s Uunet Technologies unit, an Internet service provider, said yesterday that it had bought Nlnet of the Netherlands for an undisclosed amount of stock. The acquisition of Nlnet, a Dutch Internet service provider, would allow Uunet to provide a wider group of networking services to businesses in Europe, the company said. Uunet connects corporations to the Internet and to their far-flung offices. The closely held Nlnet, which will be renamed Uunet NL, controls 66 percent of the business market in the Netherlands.

title:
Paid Notice: Deaths
GOLDSTEIN, JOYCE
body: GOLDSTEIN-Joyce. Former Head Nurse at the newyork Times newspaper (retired 1980) passed away at the Wood River Retirement Community in Bensalem, PA on August 19, 1997. Mrs. Goldstein was 76. Wife of the late David Goldstein, also retired (1969) from the newyork Times newspaper. Mrs. Goldstein was President of the National Association of Industrial Nurses. She was the daughter of John and Edna (nee Nave) Nelson. Joyce is survived by three brothers, Retired Col. Carl A. Nelson of Colorado Springs, CO; John W. Nelson, Jr., of Mountaintop, PA; and Frank L. Nelson of Emporia, KS. Also several nieces and nephews. Tomlinson Funeral Home, Bensalem, PA.

title: THE MEDIA BUSINESS
body: The newyork Times Company has applied to list its class A shares on the newyork Stock Exchange and expects the shares to begin trading on the Big Board on Sept. 25. The company's class A shares currently trade on the American Stock Exchange; the class B shares are not publicly traded.

title: Lycos Expects Patent on Web Index Method
body: Lycos Inc. said today that it expected to receive a patent for Web-data indexing technology in the next few months and was preparing to demand licensing payments from other Internet-search companies using the technology. The patent covers so-called spidering technology used by Internet directories to gather information from the 30 million World Wide Web sites, Lycos said. Lycos, based in Framingham, said it planned to enforce its patent aggressively when it is granted in three to four months. Two of Lycos's rivals -- the Infoseek Corporation and Excite Inc. -- said they saw little overlap in the software Lycos said was patented and their technology. Shares of Lycos rose $1.6875, to $33. Excite fell 56.25 cents, to $22.375. Infoseek fell 68.75 cents, to $8.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
CUC REDUCES PRICES FOR BOOKS MEMBERS BUY ON LINE
body: CUC International Inc.'s on-line book unit disclosed price cuts yesterday aimed at stealing market share from Amazon.com Inc. and Barnes & Noble Inc. in the fledgling industry of electronic book selling. CUC's Book Stacks Unlimited said it would increase discounts to 40 percent off the suggested retail price for hardcover books and 30 percent off for paperbacks. The discounts apply to members of Net Market, CUC's electronic shopping site, and to members of the Frequent Buyer Club of Book Stacks. Shares of CUC fell 37.5 cents, to $24.375, while Amazon.com stock dropped 31.25 cents, to $27.8125. Barnes & Noble stock fell $1.875, to $45.625.

title:
New Jersey Daily Briefing;
Internet Gambling Criticized
body: Expressing alarm at a rising rate of gambling on the Internet, unitedstates Representative Frank A. LoBiondo, whose district includes Atlantic City, says it should be banned, in part because it poses risks for fraud and abuse, The Associated Press reported yesterday. He said that he planned to introduce legislation to ban such gambling when Congress returns next week. More than 120 gambling sites operate on the Internet, Mr. LoBiondo said. The sites, he said, are open to swindles like winnings that never get paid or games of chance that are rigged. Advocates for the Internet gambling industry, much of which is based overseas, argue that Congress should consider regulations instead of an outright ban.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
INTEGRION FINANCIAL ACQUIRES VISA'S INTERACTIVE UNIT
body: Integrion Financial Network said yesterday that it had acquired the assets and operations of Visa Interactive, the remote banking subsidiary of Visa International, the credit-card organization. Terms were not disclosed, although the companies said Visa International had received stock in Integrion, an interactive banking provider for financial institutions. Integrion, a closely held company, said the deal added more than 60 financial institutions to its customer base.

title: Corrections
body: The TV Sports column on Tuesday, about Mets games that were blacked out on cable television in some areas because of a dispute between Time Warner newyork City Cable and Sportschannel misstated the reason Sportschannel added 25 Mets games to its schedule. Sportschannel exercised an option in its contract with the Mets; the reason was not that Channel 9 no longer wanted to keep the games.

title:
Updates/Media and Technology;
Survey Finds More Internet Users Sign On When Away From Home
body: More people are signing on to the Internet from outside their homes, offices or schools, according to a study released by MCI Librarylink, a collaborative project between the American Library Association and the MCI Communications Corporation to connect public libraries to the Internet. The percentage of all computer users who hooked up to the Internet using what are called alternative points of access -- computers in places like libraries, community centers, churches, stores, cafes, museums, hospitals, hotels or airports -- increased from 7 to 12 percent between spring 1996 and spring 1997. Nielsen Media Research compiled the study based on a survey conducted in the unitedstates and Canada. The study was commissioned by MCI Librarylink, which is financed by MCI Communications and which has connected 27 libraries to the Internet since 1995, to gauge interest in alternative access points. Internet users were defined in the study as those who had used the Internet in the last six months. The majority of respondents who said they had used an alternative access point in that time said they used public libraries.   SHELLY FREIERMAN

title:
Metro Business;
$20 Million Invested In Internet Company
body: Demonstrating confidence in newyork's fledgling new-media industry, Michael Egan, the chairman and former owner of Alamo Rent-a-Car, invested $20 million last week in Web Genesis, a company that runs a popular Internet site. The deal, which gave Mr. Egan a minority stake in the company and the title of chairman, was one of the largest investments ever in a newyork new-media company, said Mark Mooradian, group director of consumer content for Jupiter Communications, a new-media research firm. Web Genesis was founded in 1994 in Ithaca, N.Y., by two Cornell University students, Todd Krizelman and Stephan Paternot, and moved to Manhattan earlier this year. It is best known for The Globe (www.theglobe.com), which offers a "virtual community" of chat rooms, personal ads and discussion groups and has more than 600,000 registered users. Ed Cespedes, managing director of Dancing Bear Investments, Mr. Egan's investment company in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., said the deal reflected Mr. Egan's desire to "create a virtual community and reach a mass audience" as a possible base for, among other things, selling products on-line. DAVID W. CHEN

title:
New Jersey Daily Briefing;
Charge in Internet Sex Case
body: A 39-year-old unemployed computer engineer from Long Branch was charged yesterday by Federal prosecutors with taking sexually explicit photographs of a 14-year-old girl whom he had met in an Internet chat room in June. The man, Richard C. Crandon, drove to the girl's home in Coon Rapids, Minn., on Monday to bring her to New Jersey, but left her at a bus stop in State College, Pa., the next day after learning that her mother had reported her missing, said Lieut. Patrick M. Joyce of the Long Branch police. When the police arrested Mr. Crandon at his home Wednesday, they found photographs of the girl partly nude and charged him with endangering the welfare of a minor, Lieutenant Joyce said. TERRY PRISTIN

title:
Metro Business;
Internet Service Expanding
body: The Bell Atlantic Corporation said yesterday that it would offer Internet access to customers in newyork and New England. It had promised to extend the service to Nynex customers as part of its $25.6 billion merger with Nynex. Bell Atlantic.net, as the service is known, costs $19.95 a month for unlimited access or $6.95 a month for five hours, plus $1.95 for each additional hour. The service is already available to customers in Bell Atlantic's original mid-Atlantic service region. Nynex and Bell Atlantic completed their merger last week after receiving final regulatory approval from the Federal Communications Commission.

title: Forbes Buys a Custom Publishing Unit
body: Forbes Inc. has purchased the custom publishing division of The newyork Times Company for an undisclosed price. The unit, which is separate from The newyork Times Company's magazine group, creates publications for clients. The titles include Beyond Computing, for the International Business Machines Corporation, and Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts, for the luxury hotel chain. The custom magazine field is dominated by Time Inc., a unit of Time Warner Inc., and by the American Express Company. Forbes's American Heritage magazine has been involved in custom publishing for clients like International Paper and General Motors. But Forbes itself is new to the business. Last year, The newyork Times custom publishing division had revenue of about $13.7 million.

title:
New Jersey Daily Briefing;
Cost of Net Access Estimated
body: Bringing Internet access to all of New Jersey's schools and libraries would cost $2.8 billion over the next five years, according to a report issued yesterday by an agency that is studying the issue. The Division of the Ratepayer Advocate filed the report, titled "Before 2000," with the Board of Public Utilities as part of a proposal to create a $40 million public-private fund to provide discount telephone and wiring services to schools and libraries, said Mally Becker, a spokeswoman for the Ratepayer Advocate. The State Department of Education's goal is to have one computer equipped with Internet access for every five schoolchildren in New Jersey, and six computers for every library in the state, Ms. Becker said. New Jersey schools currently provide one computer for every nine students, she said. The Board of Public Utilities will begin hearings on the proposal next month, she said.

title:
Looking Glass;
On the Web, Winning Isn't Everything Isn't Everything but Awards Are Everywhere
body: To W. Edwards Deming, the famed management guru, awards meant that only one person would be a winner, and the rest losers. The on-line community has found a way around that problem: Give out awards for just about anything. The Cool Site of the Moment award alone generates hundreds of winners a day. The first World Wide Web award, according to on-line lore, was the Cool Site of the Day award (no relation to the Cool Site of the Moment). That was in 1994, when there really was only one cool site a day. The daily award then developed into the coveted Cool Site of the Year award, complete with ceremony and publicity. In 1997, dozens if not hundreds of individuals, organizations, new media companies, old media companies, trade publications and other Web sites are offering.   KRIS GOODFELLOW Graphic   Charts:  From the People http://cool.infi.net/ csoty/index.html  AWARD -- One site among them is chosen as Cool Site of the Year. Other awards include coolest personal sites and coolest design. SPONSOR -- Infinet owns Cool Site of the Day; Kodak and G.T.E. sponsor the awards. CRITERIA -- From a short list of Day winners, Web surfers vote for the coolest one. NOMINEE --"This is one of those dreams you have when you are a young, Web geek," said Derek M. Powazek of "The Fray," a personal Web site. "But I'm going to lose to 'The Onion.' "  From the Extremely Earnest http://www.gii.com  AWARD -- Global Information Infrastructure (GII) Award in 11 categories, including entrepreneurship and volunteerism. SPONSOR -- Softbank Forums, a media company, with support from politicians such as Vice President Al Gore and House Speaker Newt Gingrich. CRITERIA -- A site must show that it has had some impact on broader society. "This is not a digerati insider thing," said James Hake, chairman of the GII Awards. WINNER -- Starbright World Project won the Next Generation award for its virtual play space for seriously ill children in nine U.S. hospitals.  From Traditional Media http://www.naa.org/ edge.html  AWARD -- Digital Edge, given to newspaper Web sites at various circulation levels. SPONSOR -- Newspaper Association of America. CRITERIA -- Innovative conversion of newspapers to the Web. WINNER -- The Sun Herald, in Port Charlotte, Florida, won for its community focused site. For example, in a county with a very high concentration of senior citizens, the site offers it users a write-your-own-obit page. "The award was wonderful for staff morale," said Ronald duPont Jr., the Internet editor.  From Trade Magazines http://www.webbyawards.com  AWARD -- Webby Awards in 15 categories including best art and design, politics and law, books and mags and money. SPONSORS -- The Web magazine and about 30 media, software and technology companies. CRITERIA -- Writing, design, links to other sites and overall "flair." "As with anything, it's very subjective," said Tiffany Shlain, organizer of the awards ceremony. WINNER --"It's always nice to win an award," said Michael O'Donnell, president and publisher of Salon magazine.  From Left Field http://www.coolcentral.com  AWARD -- Cool Site of the Hour. SPONSOR -- Anthenia Associates, Web publishers. CRITERIA -- Coolness as assessed by "experts," according the site's creators, Andrew King and Robert Peyser. WINNER --"The silliest award we ever got was for "Cool Site of the Hour," said Omar Wasow of newyork Online. "I think we won the Monday 3 A.M. award or something. True joy."

title: Macabre On-Line Game Prompts Apology
body: Virgin Net, a London-based computer on-line service owned by Virgin Airlines' chief, Richard Branson, has apologized after a game based on the massacre of 16 children and their teacher in Scotland was found on an Internet site accessed through Virgin Net. Ivan Izikowitz, technical director of Virgin Net, said that the company did not know the Web site contained such offensive material and removed it as soon as it was discovered. Families of the people killed by a gunman, Thomas Hamilton, on March 13, 1996, in Dunblane, Scotland, were outraged at the game. It invited players to shoot at children and those who hit all the targets with the fewest bullets were awarded a fictional accolade. "I don't understand how someone could put something like this on the Internet for entertainment," said Rod Mayor, whose wife Gwen died protecting the students. The game was placed on a site created by one of the 6,000 people who access the Internet by subscribing to Virgin Net. Mr. Izikowitz said the subscription of the unidentified person who created the massacre game had been terminated.

title:
BASEBALL;
Mets TV Broadcasts Stopped
body: A blackout of 14 Mets cable games by Time Warner's newyork City systems began abruptly at 10:40 last night, midway through the Mets-Rockies game from Denver. Viewers suddenly saw a screen that read: "We regret that SportsChannel is blocking us from showing the Mets game." The blackout was to begin with the 9 P.M. start of the game but was delayed because SportsChannel had problems blocking the signal from the satellite that beamed the game. Earlier yesterday, Time Warner refused a SportsChannel request for its systems to switch to a second satellite carrying alternate programming, insisting that SportsChannel was contractually obligated to block the game's signal. The dispute arose because SportsChannel is carrying 100 Mets games this season, up from 75 last year, and Time Warner has refused to pay for the extra telecasts at the price being demanded by SportsChannel. Time Warner has carried 11 of the 25 games, without paying. But on Thursday, Time Warner said it would carry no more.

title:
Metro Business;
Dow Jones Markets To Open New Office
body: Dow Jones Markets, the financial data division of Dow Jones and Company, is setting up a 150-person office in Manhattan to develop new products as part of an effort to turn itself around, the company said yesterday. In January, under pressure from minority shareholders upset by the poor performance of the company's stock, Dow Jones announced plans to invest $650 million over the next three to four years to overhaul Telerate, which it renamed Dow Jones Markets. Telerate has been losing market share to Reuters Holdings P.L.C. and Bloomberg L.P. In April, as part of that effort, Dow Jones Markets formed a technology and marketing alliance with the Microsoft Corporation. The new office at 195 Broadway will house about 50 people who now work at Telerate's complex at Harborside Financial Center in Jersey City, as well as close to 100 new employees. Dow Jones, represented by Cushman & Wakefield, rented 35,920 square feet at 195 Broadway, at Fulton Street, on a three-year sublease from the Cigna Insurance Company, which has 10 floors in the building, owned by Peter S. Kalikow. Cigna was represented by the Williams Real Estate Company. DAVID M. HALBFINGER

body: Killings in South Africa The cycle of revenge that has long constituted political discourse in South Africa's KwaZulu/Natal Province had seemed to be abating, but it has reappeared with new intensity in recent months.
