title:
SUNDAY, AUGUST 10, 1997;
EEZ HYPER
body: The Government can't tell us what to do, scoffs Marc Silverman. His Montreal computer store, Micro-Bytes, recently received a ding from Quebec's Office de la Langue Francaise, ordering the retailer to change its predominantly English Web site to at least equal parts French and English. Provincial law allows English translations in commercial publications, but requires that French retain equal prominence. Silverman pointed out that the law does not mention cyberspace, but compromised anyway -- Micro-Bytes Web pages are now available in both tongues. As a protest, he has left one English-only page that rails against the O.L.F. For its part, the O.L.F., ever vigilant, now wants to expand its charter to cover the Web.

title:
COMPUTING'S NEW ALLIANCE;
Microsoft Unit in Deal With Competitor
body: WebTV Networks, an Internet access provider that was recently acquired by Microsoft, is expected to announce today that it has reached an agreement with one of Microsoft's major on-line competitors, CitySearch. Microsoft operates Sidewalk, a World Wide Web site that is similar to CitySearch, a guide to different cities throughout the country. The deal calls for CitySearch to provide content for WebTV's AroundTown area, which will feature entertainment and food listings. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. "The Web is really the home for strange bedfellows," said Adam Schoenfeld, an analyst with Jupiter Communications. "But I give Microsoft style points for doing deals that at least give the appearance that there is an open playing field." Still, it is unusual that Microsoft has not included Sidewalk, which also has arts and entertainment listing among other things, on WebTV instead of CitySearch. "We are trying to offer the best consumer experience possible," said Aaron Mata of WebTV. "CitySearch provides the service for our audience." "If it was a mission-critical venture, Microsoft wouldn't let this happen," Mr. Schoenfeld added.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MICROSOFT BUYS VXTREME FOR INTERNET AUDIO AND VIDEO
body: The Microsoft Corporation said yesterday that it had acquired an Internet start-up company, Vxtreme Inc., to let companies send sound and video over the Internet. Terms were not disclosed. Vxtreme, based in Sunnyvale, Calif., makes software that allows streaming, or the continuous delivery of audio and video to personal computer users. The move follows Microsoft's agreement to license similar technology from Progressive Networks Inc. and to take a 10 percent nonvoting stake in that company. The acquisitions help Microsoft put its stamp on the nascent market for on-line broadcasting. Microsoft shares rose $1.75, to $143.3125.

title:
Metro Business;
The Zipper Returns, Clearer and Faster
body: After being dark for two months, the zipper will resume flashing the day's news in Times Square today, its operator, Dow Jones & Company, said yesterday. The zipper, which wraps around the 22-story building at One Times Square and has been displaying headlines since 1928, has been upgraded to make it clearer, faster and more reliable, the company said. The 369-foot ribbon of moving words will be illuminated by 235,000 amber light-emitting diodes, instead of the old 12,400 incandescent light bulbs, which were hard to read in bright sunlight. Dow Jones has operated the zipper since June 1995.

title: Babel on the Internet
body: To the Editor: In creating his own Internet lexicon, Kyle Shannon, founder of Agency.com, says that only the ideas matter, not the words (news article, July 24). Really? Communication is impossible without common terminology. Mr. Shannon is trying to fix something that isn't broken. And at least one of his terms would confuse things. Instead of "home page," which he feels implies a single point of entry, he would like to use "gateway." But gateway already has other meanings in Internet technology. He might have discovered that with a little research into the established structure he so easily disdains.  GERRY FIFER newyork, July 25, 1997

title:
Updates/Media and Technology;
On-Line Guide To Music Offered By MTV and Yahoo
body: MTV Networks, a unit of Viacom Inc., and Yahoo Inc. announced the introduction of their much anticipated World Wide Web music guide, Unfurled, this month. The music cable network and the Web directory service teamed up to create the new site, which will offer music fans a comprehensive directory linking users to music-related Web sites. Unfurled will also have daily music news, event listings and industry gossip. The site features a directory of more than 1,100 performers and bands that links users to sites about their favorite artists. Unfurled (http://www.unfurled.com) also features local entertainment listings and a directory for musicians with links to Web resources and information about equipment, instruments, and even studio space.   ANDREW ROSS SORKIN

title:
Metro Business;
Citicorp to Add Web Site
body: Citicorp said yesterday that it had hired a newyork company to build "virtual communities" on the Internet as a new way to communicate with customers worldwide. The newyork City bank signed an agreement with the Mining Company, a creator of Web sites, to let customers of Citibank, a unit of Citicorp, access information and communicate with each other through bulletin boards, email and "chat rooms." The agreement will let the bank "build on existing customer satisfaction and loyalty and attract new customers all at the same time," said Edward D. Horowitz, Citibank's executive vice president in charge of advanced technology. The Mining Company is a unit of General Internet Inc., a closely held newyork company.

title: Internet as Equalizer
body: To the Editor: There is one inaccuracy in A. J. Jacob's otherwise amusing piece on the unsung virtues of snail mail (Op-Ed, July 19) -- no Macintosh user will ever send email that reads "i'm on macintosh. can't download it." The glory of the Internet is that it's platform independent, to use computerspeak, or color-blind, to use English. With a modem and a phone line, a 10-year-old box running Unix can talk to a $4,000 computer, just as a Windows machine can talk to (and exchange information with) a Macintosh.  PAMELA REEVES newyork, July 19, 1997

title:
Update/Media and Technology;
Excite To Offer Free email Service Over World Wide Web
body: Excite, the popular World Wide Web directory service, is expected to announce today that it will offer a free Web-based electronic messaging service on its site. Mailexcite will offer users a free email address and account that will be accessible via http://www.mailexcite.com. "We are trying to make Excite a daily habit," said Joe Kraus, senior vice president of Excite Inc., based in Redwood City, Calif. On-line users who sign up will be assigned an email address. Users of the Excite service will be able to check their email from any computer using a Web browser. The company plans to support the service with on-line advertising.   ANDREW ROSS SORKIN

title:
New Jersey Daily Briefing;
Campaign on the Net
body: Most campaigns slow down in the heat of the summer, but voters itching for the governor's race to pick up speed can now turn to the Internet. Governor Whitman unveiled a campaign web site yesterday that offers video and audio clips as well as the text of speeches, position papers and a biography. The web page, at www.christie97.org, even shows supporters how to make their own campaign buttons. Mrs. Whitman's Democratic challenger, State Senator James E. McGreevey, of Woodbridge, has been on line since February.   TERRY PRISTIN

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
T/SF COMMUNICATIONS CONSIDERS A $124 MILLION BUYOUT
body: The T/SF Communications Corporation said yesterday that an undisclosed buyout firm had offered to buy the company, which is a casino industry publisher, for more than $37 a share, or more than $124 million. T/SF said it would put on hold plans to buy about two million of its shares for $37 apiece and become a private company. T/SF, based in Tulsa, Okla., publishes a magazine called International Gaming and Wagering Business and newsletters covering the casino industry. T/SF said it would give the buyout firm a few weeks to look at its books and make a final offer. The company's stock jumped $1.875 a share yesterday, to $37.875, on the American Stock Exchange.

title: Internet Will Become Its Own Watchdog
body: To the Editor: I disagree with Eli M. Noam's conclusion in "An Unfettered Internet? Keep Dreaming" (Op-Ed, July 11) that the Internet "will not create a new regulatory system." Mr. Noam is correct that national governments will probably seek to regulate the Internet by concentrating on people and institutions rather than on signals, but he is wrong to conclude that this will subject the Web to regulation like that for other media. Punishing a local institution, like a service provider, for content originating in another country risks isolating the regulating government. Recent proposals for reorganizing the registration of Internet domain names provide possibilities for a new regulatory system. Withdrawing a domain name is equivalent to banishing someone from the Internet. The same private, transnational system that registers domain names can also make and enforce rules. It can become a new type of "government," joining the nongovernment organizations, private financial networks and treaty-based institutions that represent new forms of regulation.  HENRY H. PERRITT JR. Chicago, July 14, 1997  The writer is dean of the Chicago-Kent College of Law. Graphic   Drawing (Gale)

title:
Updates/Media and Technology;
Hughes Plans To Introduce Satellite Dish
body: Hughes Network Systems -- which manufactures a "pizza size" home satellite dish, Digital Satellite System, that receives DirecTV and USSB digital television -- is expected to announce today that it will introduce a digital satellite system that will be able to receive both television broadcasts and high-speed Internet access through one dish. The new dish, Direcduo, is the first of its kind and is expected to be priced between $899 and $999. Current owners of the Digital Satellite System will be able to upgrade with a $599 add-on product that will allow them to receive high-speed Internet access 14 times as fast as with a standard telephone line. Hughes Network, part of the General Motors Corporation, is based in Germantown, Md. It also manufactures an Internet-only satellite system, Direct PC. The company will offer an option to upgrade that dish to include television broadcasts.   ANDREW ROSS SORKIN

title:
Updates/Media and Technology;
Internet Analyst Joins Venture Capital Firm
body: J. William Gurley has joined Hummer Winblad Venture Partners, a venture capital firm, as its fourth partner. Mr. Gurley was previously an Internet financial analyst at DMG Technology Group, a division of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the investment banking arm of Deutsche Bank. As an analyst, Mr. Gurley attracted a following based on a series of articles about the Internet market that appeared both on line and in Fortune magazine. "He brings a big intellect and a big following," said John Hummer, who founded Hummer Winblad in 1989 with Ann Winblad. Mr. Gurley was previously an equity research analyst at CS First Boston. He has also worked at Compaq Computer and Advanced Micro Devices. Hummer Winblad's first $35 million fund eventually returned more than $250 million to investors. The firm, which focuses exclusively on software investments, has financed such companies as Powersoft, Arbor, Scopus and Wind River.   JOHN MARKOFF

title:
Updates/Media and Technology;
Sprint to Offer N.F.L. Net Access
body: The Sprint Corporation and the National Football League hope to attract football fans to the Internet with a special version of Sprint's Internet access service that is expected to be announced today. Named the "N.F.L. Edition" of Sprint's Passport access system, it will deliver subscribers to a special home page on the World Wide Web with links to football-related information, including the N.F.L.'s Web site and the site of ABC's "Monday Night Football." Subscribers will also be offered special promotions and contests from both Sprint and the N.F.L. throughout the season. The offering is part of Sprint's efforts to win subscribers to its standard Internet access service by focusing on specific interest groups. In addition to the N.F.L., Sprint has programs with the publishers Simon & Schuster and Macmillan. A deal in which compact disks were given away at Blockbuster video stores ended earlier this year. Sprint will begin making the N.F.L. Internet service available this summer via a toll-free number and as part of promotions for the sale of season tickets by the football league.   LAURENCE ZUCKERMAN

title:
Updates/Media and Technology;
Targeted Advertising On Times Web Site
body: The newyork Times Electronic Media Company will announce today that it is introducing a new marketing technology to its World Wide Web site aimed at helping on-line advertisers reach specific audiences. The newyork Times on the Web (http://www.nytimes.com) will use an electronic data base system that will enable the Web site to display different ads to different on-line users, based on a user's demographic profile. The newyork Times on the Web gathers this information when people register to use the Web site. The demographic information includes age, gender, income and zip code, which the data base will tie to identifiable email addresses. Using these data, the company said, the Web site will be able to match advertisers with prospective customers. The company said it had 1.7 million registered users of its Web site.   ANDREW ROSS SORKIN

title: Don't Regulate Internet
body: To the Editor: Eli M. Noam (Op-Ed, July 11) says the Internet industry is inconsistent in its libertarianism. He says "it" liked the Government subsidies that created it, "it" fought for regulated cheap access to phone networks, and "it" supports subsidies for school and library Internet access. But there is no "it" to the Internet. There is no one in charge. The main reason Government agencies want to regulate the Internet is to collect taxes. If they tax it, they control it. If they control it, they ruin it.  DAVID KRISTOPEIT Racine, Wis., July 11, 1997

title:
Metro Business;
Web Company Lands Deal
body: Snickelways Interactive, a Web consulting company based in Manhattan, has signed an agreement with Alnet, an Internet company in Turkey, to develop on-line products for the Turkish market. The deal is worth between $2 million and $3 million, said Andy Howarth, Snickelways' president. It is the largest deal ever for the Manhattan company and the first one with an international company. Snickelways, which was founded in 1991, has developed Web sites and provided technology consulting for clients like American Express, Fruit of the Loom and Microsoft. Alnet, which was founded in 1996, is Turkey's second-largest Internet service provider. The first joint project will be the development of an on-line inventory tracking system for one of Turkey's largest shipping ports and storage centers. The tracking system will enable wholesale businesses to go on line and find out immediately the status and location of their orders. DAVID W. CHEN

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Quarterly Profit Falls Sharply at Dow Jones
body: Dow Jones & Company said yesterday that its second-quarter profit fell by nearly a third, with operating income at its troubled financial information unit virtually evaporating. Second-quarter net income dropped 32.9 percent, to $34.9 million, or 36 cents a share, from $52 million, or 54 cents a share, in the second quarter of last year. Revenue for the three-month period ended June 30 rose 1.6 percent, to $640.7 million from $630.6 million. Dow Jones, which publishes The Wall Street Journal and Barron's, saw a rise in operating income from its print publications and television operations. But operating profit at its financial information services unit, which includes Dow Jones Markets, Newswires and Global Indexes, fell nearly 100 percent, to a barely break-even level of $169,000, compared with $40.3 million a year ago. Revenue dipped 4.5 percent. Dow Jones said in January that it planned to invest as much as $650 million in the next three years to strengthen the unit, formerly known as Telerate. Some money managers who have taken sizable stock positions in the company, including Michael Price, have pushed Dow Jones to sell or spin off the unit.

title:
Updates/Media and Technology;
Internet Tax Relief From Massachusetts
body: Amid a national debate over how -- and how much -- to tax the commerce that is done in cyberspace, Massachusetts is moving to repeal one tax that would have hurt the state's booming Internet companies. Lawmakers there are likely to pass a bill exempting Internet service providers from the tax by the time the House breaks for summer on July 15, Speaker Thomas Finneran said this weekend. The measure would exclude Internet accounts from the same 5 percent telecommunications sales tax now paid on telephone bills. It has widespread political support, including that of Gov. William F. Weld. Repealing the tax would place the state's more than 70 Internet service providers on equal footing with competitors in tax-free states like California, Washington, Florida and newyork.

title: Clinton and Internet
body: To the Editor: Qualified congratulations are due the policy adviser Ira C. Magaziner and the rest of the Clinton Administration for taking a largely hands-off approach with regard to taxation and regulation of the Internet and electronic commerce (Business Day, June 30). Let the Internet thrive and grow, and we'll position the unitedstates at the forefront of the information economy in the 21st century. For once, Washington seems to be resisting its we-know-best impulse to regulate. I'm cautiously optimistic that deeds will follow words and that, in this case, President Clinton will prove Ronald Reagan wrong. ("If it moves, tax it. If it keeps moving, regulate it. And if it stops moving, subsidize it.")  MARC D. BEAUCHAMP Falls Church, Va., June 30, 1997

title: Internet Filters Can't Do Librarians' Job
body: To the Editor: "To Screen or Not to Screen: Libraries Confront Internet Access" (Business Day, June 23) discusses the use of filtering technology in public libraries to block access to objectionable sites on the Internet. This filtering technology creates more problems than it solves. Making it work requires some remote company -- rather than the library itself -- to keep up-to-date lists of objectionable sites. This is not how libraries work. Libraries allow access to what they themselves have approved as suitable. Depending on community standards, they often choose not to stock materials like pornography. What libraries need, therefore, is technology to treat the Internet in exactly the same way they treat their other resources, which would enable them to create their own age-appropriate data bases of approved Internet sites.  STEVEN WINNETT Brighton, Mass., June 23, 1997 Graphic   Drawing (Laurent Cilluffo)

title:
Internet Promotes an Informed Drug Debate;
Everything at a Click
body: To the Editor: The Internet contains information about myriad topics, so it is not surprising that you could find material for your June 20 front-page article on the drug culture that is flourishing on the Internet. I decided to test your findings by doing my own search. Using a search engine, "marijuana" produced 8 category and 128 site matches. These ranged from support groups for those who wish to recover from marijuana addiction, to discussions of the medical uses of marijuana, to "pothead" Web pages and even to a government report from the Netherlands assessing the drug policy there. The beauty of the Internet arises from its completeness.  THEODORE W. WILCOX Rochester, June 24, 1997

title: Microsoft in On-Line Billing Venture
body: The Microsoft Corporation and the First Data Corporation said yesterday that they had formed a company that would allow consumers to pay bills over the Internet, a move aimed at speeding up the use of the global computer network for business. The joint venture, called MSFDC, would allow consumers to receive and pay bills using personal computer home banking software or through banks' sites on the World Wide Web. The new company, to be based in Denver, would be equally owned by First Data, of Hackensack, N.J., and Microsoft, of Redmond, Wash. The companies said that they planned to test the service later this summer and introduce it early next year. Financial terms were not disclosed. The agreement is aimed at promoting the Microsoft software that banks, merchants, consumers and billers use, and at giving First Data, a credit card processor, a part of bill payments made over the Internet, analysts said. MSFDC would compete with similar offerings from Intuit Inc., the Checkfree Corporation and Integrion, a banking group led by I.B.M..

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DUTCH COMPANY BUYS PUBLISHING CONCERN FROM DISNEY
body: Wolters Kluwer N.V., the Dutch publishing company, said yesterday that it had acquired the unitedstates company NILS Publishing in Chatsworth, Calif., from the Walt Disney Company, which has been selling publishing assets. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. Wolters said NILS had annual sales of $25 million and 135 employees. The Dutch company said that the acquisition was part of its strategy to strengthen global legal publishing activities and that NILS would become part of CCH Inc., its unitedstates business and finance unit that specializes in tax and business law publishing.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
CISCO IS BUYING 2 COMPANIES FOR ABOUT $200 MILLION
body: Cisco Systems Inc., which is based in San Jose, Calif., and is a supplier of Internet transmission equipment, agreed yesterday to buy the privately held Ardent Communications Corporation for about $156 million in stock. Cisco had previously held a minority equity stake in Ardent, which is also based in San Jose and is a maker of products for integrating voice, video and data on computer networks. Cisco also said it would buy Global Internet Software Group for about $40.325 million in cash and take an undisclosed minority stake in the parent company, Global Internet.Com Inc. Global Internet Software Group specializes in security solutions for Microsoft Windows NT networks.

title:
New Jersey Daily Briefing;
Man Is Guilty in Internet Case
body: A 47-year-old man from Ohio pleaded guilty in Federal court yesterday to enticing a 13-year-old New Jersey girl he met on the Internet to send him pornographic videos and photos of herself. The man, Paul Brown Jr. of Cleveland, posed as a 15-year-old boy, prosecutors said, and gained the girl's confidence over more than a year of email messages and phone calls. He faces up to five years in prison.

title: Dow Jones Markets Names New Officers
body: Dow Jones & Company has filled two crucial jobs in an effort to remake Dow Jones Markets, its troubled electronic markets information service. But the position of technology director, who will lead the service onto the Internet, has not yet been filled. Gregory E. Smith, 41, has been named senior vice president for content and Debra Isenberg, 45, will become senior vice president for marketing. Mr. Smith is the founder and former head of Indepth Data Inc., an information system on the taxable bond market that Dow Jones acquired last week. Ms. Isenberg has been a marketing vice president at AT&T since 1994. In January, Dow Jones announced a three-year, $650 million effort to rebuild Dow Jones Markets, formerly called Telerate, from a desktop to an Internet-based information system. The service has lost market share to systems from Bloomberg and Reuters.

title:
WEDDINGS;
Susan Antilla, Dennis Leibowitz
body: Susan Antilla, a financial columnist for Bloomberg News and Bloomberg Television in newyork, was married yesterday to Dennis H. Leibowitz, a senior vice president and securities analyst for the broadcasting, cable television and wireless industries at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, the newyork investment bank. Sydney Greenberg, a justice of the peace, officiated at the couple's house in New Canaan, Conn. The bride, 43, who is keeping her name, graduated from Manhattanville College and received a master's degree in journalism from newyork University. Her previous marriage ended in divorce, as did the bridegroom's. She is the daughter of Gloria M. Claudet of New Fairfield, Conn., and the late Oscar Antilla. Her mother retired as a broker for Emile Rellstab Real Estate in New Rochelle, N.Y. Her father was a factory worker in Larchmont, N.Y. Her stepfather, Henri L. Claudet, retired as a videotape technician for CBS-TV in newyork. Mr. Leibowitz, 55, graduated from the University of Pennsylvania. He is a son of Frieda Leibowitz of Las Vegas, Nev., and the late Irving Leibowitz, who was the editor of The Lorain (Ohio) Journal. Graphic   Photo: Susan Antilla. (Steve Friedman)

title:
Metro Business;
Woman Sues Bloomberg
body: A former female sales executive sued Michael R. Bloomberg and his privately held companies yesterday, accusing them of sexual harassment. In the lawsuit filed in unitedstates District Court in newyork, the former executive, Sekiko Sakai Garrison, who now lives in Seattle, contended that "sexual harassment and sexual degredation of women at Bloomberg was pervasive." The lawsuit also accused Mr. Bloomberg of harassing Ms. Garrison by making offensive remarks. Ms. Garrison is a former sales representative for Bloomberg, a financial information company in newyork, according to court papers. Neither Mr. Bloomberg nor his lawyers were available for comment. The companies are Bloomberg L.P. and Bloomberg Inc. Ms. Garrison was employed by Bloomberg from January 1989 until she was dismissed in May 1995.

title:
How to Track Down Collegiate Cyber-Cheaters;
Beware Web 'Cookies'
body: To the Editor: Frank Rich ("howdydoody.com," column, June 8) points out the true dark side of the World Wide Web. The Internet is a perfect medium for marketers to reach into the lives of young people and manipulate them in ways that television never could. By the clever use of "cookies" (tracking technology inserted in your computer without your knowledge by Web site advertisers), marketers can track your (and your child's) Web journeys, using the data they obtain to create a cyber-profile. Some Web browsers (like Netscape) allow you to elect to be warned when a "cookie" is about to be placed and refuse it. But most people are either unaware of this feature or don't recognize the danger in letting someone look over your shoulder as you travel the Web.  SHELDON L. TARAKAN East Hills, N.Y., June 8, 1997

title:
Metro Business;
Dow Jones Unit in Move
body: Dow Jones & Company has leased 71,000 square feet of office space at Two World Trade Center, the Port Authority of newyork and New Jersey said yesterday. The 10-year lease is valued at about $23 million. Dow Jones Markets, the company's financial and business information unit, will move its marketing operations to newyork from Harborside Financial Center in Jersey City. The company will occupy two floors in the 110-story tower, which is owned by the Port Authority.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
INTUIT TO PAY $40 MILLION FOR 19% STAKE IN EXCITE
body: Looking for ways to expand its financial services on the Internet, Intuit Inc. agreed yesterday to pay $40 million to buy a 19 percent stake in Excite Inc., the Internet search site operator. The companies also entered a seven-year agreement to develop sites on the World Wide Web where customers can get financial news and information to manage their finances. Intuit will buy 2.9 million shares of Excite, or 19 percent of the company's shares outstanding, for $13.50 each. The companies announced the agreement after the market closed, but Excite's stock had already risen $2.25, to $15.375. Intuit shares closed down 50 cents at $24.50. Intuit is best known for Quicken, the electronic personal finance program.

title:
Metro Business;
Station to Carry Bloomberg
body: The Paxson Communications Corporation agreed to broadcast Bloomberg Television programming on its new newyork City television station, giving Bloomberg its long-sought entry into the city's market. Financial terms were not disclosed. Bloomberg Television, operated by Bloomberg L.P., a provider of financial news and information, will be carried on WPXN-TV 31 from 6 A.M. to 6 P.M. weekdays starting June 30 under a one-year contract, the companies said. WPXN will broadcast Fox Sports News and live sporting events at other times. Paxson agreed to buy WPXN last month from Dow Jones & Company and the ITT Corporation for $257.5 million.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AMERICA ONLINE AND CUC SHOPPING SERVICE FORM VENTURE - Correction Appended
body: America Online Inc. and the discount-shopping service CUC International Inc. are joining forces. Under a three-year agreement, America Online, the Internet access provider, will receive $50 million in fees plus potential other payments from a revenue-sharing arrangement. CUC is expected to generate more than a million annual memberships for America Online, which is based in Dulles, Va. America Online will promote CUC services on line and by direct mail to America Online subscribers. CUC, based in Stamford, Conn., is best known for restaurant coupon books often sold by churches and other nonprofit groups. Much of its $1 billion-plus annual revenue derives from fees it charges its millions of customers, typically $49 a year. Correction  A brief report by Dow Jones in some editions of the Company News column of Business Day yesterday about an alliance between America Online Inc. and CUC International Inc. understated CUC's annual revenue and misidentified the company whose membership is expected to surge because of the alliance. CUC's revenue exceeded $2 billion in its most recent fiscal year; it was not merely $1 billion-plus. In addition, it is CUC, not America Online, that expects to gain a million annual memberships. Correction-Date: June 12, 1997, Thursday

title: Virtual Term Papers
body: To the Editor: Some students will always seek dishonestly to use another's work ("On the Internet, Term Papers Are Hot Items," front page, June 8). A greater percentage of students, however, may be confused, caught between new sources of information and traditional classroom expectations. Thus a greater problem than catching plagiarists is teaching honest students how to use the Internet and how to document their sources properly. My solution is to require papers to be submitted electronically, along with a list of World Wide Web site references. This way I can click along as I read the paper. This format is more efficient than running around the college library, checking each footnote.  EUGENE DWYER Gambier, Ohio, June 8, 1997  The writer is a professor of art history at Kenyon College.

title: An On-Line Bookseller Goes Off Line, Too
body: Cbooks Express, an on-line computer bookstore, is expanding into more conventional territory, buying four bookstores operated by Computer Literacy Bookshops Inc. The upstart electronic bookstore is moving in the opposite direction of the nation's leading bookseller, Barnes & Noble, whose bookselling Web site had its debut this month. Chris MacAskill, who founded Cbooks more than a year ago in his Mountain View, Calif., garage, will lead the merged companies as president and chief executive. He said his company decided to expand into bricks and mortar because it was clear that customers still yearned to touch and skim books. With the companies' combined revenues of about $20 million, Mr. MacAskill said, "We're hoping to expand into more locations and put up internet terminals in all the stores." Cbooks has grown rapidly, with 40 percent of its orders coming from foreign customers. But so far it has failed to post a profit. Cbooks' name will change to Computer Literacy (Bookshops+Online), capitalizing on the brand name popularity of the 14-year-old computer bookstore chain. Three of the stores are in Silicon Valley in Northern California and the fourth is in Tysons Corner, Va.

title: An Accord With Total News Is Reached
body: In a legal settlement expected to bring changes in the way content is viewed on the Internet, a Web site has agreed to stop displaying the content of six news providers with its own ads. In the settlement, the site, operated by Total News Inc. (http:// totalnews.com) agreed to stop putting borders -- known as frames -- around content provided by the news organizations, including CNN and The Washington Post. The Total News site links to 1,350 news sites worldwide, but keeps a frame of its own advertising wrapped around the other sites. In February, the six news companies sued Total News in Federal District Court in Manhattan, accusing the company of trademark and copyright violations. Under the settlement, Total News can continue to link to the more than 100 Web sites managed by the six companies, but must do so directly.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NEW MICROSOFT FORMAT TO BE COMPATIBLE WITH NETSCAPE
body: The Microsoft Corporation said yesterday that it would make its "push" technology compatible with software from the Netscape Communications Corporation, in a move intended to simplify Internet standards. Push technology provides continuous content to Internet users through "channels," much like data over a television. Microsoft said a change in its channel definition format would allow software publishers to write in a single format that would work both with its Internet Explorer version 4.0 and with Netscape's Netcaster client software, due out this summer.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Washington Post Co.'s On-Line Venture
body: The Washington Post Company will team with Citysearch Inc. to develop a new site on the World Wide Web for Washington, D.C., area news and information. The announcement, which is to be made today, marks The Post's first major initiative on line since it withdrew from a partnership with ABC News and The National Journal in March. The three had run a respected site on national politics called Politics Now. The new site will be owned and administered by the Post company's electronic media subsidiary, the Digital Ink Company, while Citysearch will contribute technological expertise. Citysearch is a small company based in Pasadena, Calif., that has developed sites that feature information on leisure activities in Austin, Tex., newyork City and Salt Lake City. The company has financial backing from the venture capital arms of companies including the AT&T Corporation and Goldman, Sachs & Company. The Post company would also make an investment of undisclosed size in Citysearch. Citysearch is the Microsoft Corporation's foremost competitor in the electronic market for local information. Microsoft is expanding its spending on a chain of local entertainment guides on the Web called Sidewalk.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
BELL ATLANTIC TO OFFER FASTER INTERNET ACCESS IN 1998
body: The Bell Atlantic Corporation said yesterday that starting in mid-1998 it would be able to offer Internet access over telephone lines at speeds 100 times as fast as those that are available today. Using a technology called Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line, or A.D.S.L., Bell Atlantic will upgrade its phone network to carry data at speeds of up to six megabits a second. But other than awarding a contract for the technology to the DSC Communications Corporation of Plano, Tex., Bell Atlantic disclosed little about when or where the new service would be available. After failing to deliver on its ambitious plans to enter interactive television, the company now avoids such predictions.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Accounts
body: * PSINet, Herndon, Va., to Arnold Communications, McLean, Va., for the commercial Internet service provider, whose account had been at Woolward & Partners, San Francisco. Billings were estimated at $3.5 million.

title: Amazon.com Stock Sale Raises $54 Million
body: Amazon.com Inc. sold shares today at $18 each in a $54 million public offering, according to Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, which is managing the sale. The Seattle-based Internet bookseller sold three million shares for more than the expected range of $14 to $16 a share. It will have about 23.9 million shares outstanding after the offering. On Tuesday the company increased the size and the price range for the offering from 2.5 million shares at a range of $12 to $14, a sign of healthy demand. The offering has attracted considerable interest because Amazon.com is one of the first companies to exploit the Internet as a medium for commerce. The public offering values the whole company, which will trade on the Nasdaq, at about $429 million.

title: Art as a Virtual Feast
body: To the Editor: Re Michael Kimmelman's May 2 Critic's Notebook discussion of art on the World Wide Web: Browsing the Web for art nourishment may depend on one's starting level of knowledge, expectation and purpose. I am a self-taught learner. I marvel at the world's museums placed before me. Yes, sometimes confusion reigns, as Mr. Kimmelman says. Imagine my frustration one night when I had to close down my computer while in the Vatican Museum Web site because I couldn't get out! Not all art Web sites may be totally nourishing, as Mr. Kimmelman says. But they provide a good hors d'oeuvre.  NANCY GELBER Toronto, May 3, 1997

title: CHRONICLE
body: SIR PAUL McCARTNEY is giving the Internet a spin. At least a million fans have signed up to pose questions to the former Beatle in a 90-minute on-line chat to be televised live on VH1 in the unitedstates, Britain and Germany on May 17. The channel calculated that it would take two years to answer all the questions. "It's an awful lot to ask of anyone," Sir Paul told Reuters yesterday. The Web site visit by the onetime denizen of Penny Lane and Abbey Road marks the release of "Flaming Pie," his first album in four years. Questions may be sent to http:// vh1.com or http://flamingpie.com.    LAWRENCE VAN GELDER

title: Microsoft Sued By Ticketmaster
body: Ticketmaster Group Inc. filed suit in Federal court here today accusing the Microsoft Corporation of "electronic piracy" for providing links to Ticketmaster's Web site from its entertainment guide on the Internet. The suit seeks to stop Microsoft from letting users hook up to the Ticketmaster site from Microsoft's "Seattle Sidewalk" guide. Any Internet user can look up Ticketmaster's listings and, using a personal computer, buy tickets to entertainment events. But users who hook up to the site from Microsoft's guide can make their transactions without receiving information on policies and service information offered by Ticketmaster. The suit takes aim at the common Internet practice of providing free links to other companies' Web sites to enhance the attractiveness of a company's own site. The suit contends that Microsoft should have first signed an agreement with Ticketmaster. But Microsoft said that it had no plans to disconnect the link to Ticketmaster or to other outside services available from its on-line guide.

title: Chase Offers Free On-Line Banking
body: Chase Manhattan Bank said yesterday that it was offering its own free on-line banking service, as the nation's largest bank competes for a growing share of the tellerless market. A new Chase Online Banking software package became available to customers last week with free, unlimited use. The system is based on Windows technology, an improvement over its 10-year-old DOS-based Excel system, which Chase stopped promoting long ago. Chase will continue to let customers bank on line using Intuit Inc.'s Quicken or the Microsoft Corporation's Money personal finance programs. But until last week, Chase charged for on-line banking services: $10.95 for Excel and $2.95 a month, plus 50 cents for each bill payment, for Quicken and Money users. Chase continues to charge customers for use of Quicken and Money, but gives away the software. Of its 1.5 million individual and small-business checking accounts in the newyork metropolitan area, Chase has about 75,000 on-line banking customers, almost all through Quicken and Money. Chase hopes to have 250,000 customers using its proprietary system by the end of the year and hundreds of thousands more by the end of 1998.

title:
COMPANY REPORTS;
NETSCAPE COMMUNICATIONS (NSCP,NNM)
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation said yesterday that its earnings more than doubled in the first quarter, exceeding expectations, amid continued demand for Netscape software that sets up corporate computer networks using Internet technology. Net income rose to $7.94 million, or 9 cents a share, from $3.59 million, or 4 cents a share, in the comparable period a year earlier. Revenue jumped to $120.2 million from $56.1 million. Wall Street expected the company to earn 8 cents a share, based on the average estimate of 17 analysts surveyed by I.B.E.S. International. The company, which is based in Mountain View, Calif., said demand grew for its server products, which are used to relay information within networks. The company said demand for its software during the quarter was spurred by wider use of email and groupware, which is used to exchange documents between employees within corporations. Netscape shares in the last four months have fallen 53 percent amid concern about competition from Microsoft and from the Lotus unit of I.B.M. The second quarter is considered key as Netscape ships new products, including more sophisticated email and groupware, to compete with those companies. title:
COMPANY NEWS;
POINTCAST AND EXCITE SET TO DISCLOSE PARTNERSHIP
body: Pointcast Inc., a privately held company that broadcasts news and information to about one million desktop computers through its Pointcast Network, plans to announce today that it has formed a partnership with Excite Inc., an Internet search company based in Mountain View, Calif. Excite will create a directory for a new Pointcast channel, called Connections, that will give Pointcast's customers access to information from more than 1,000 World Wide Web sites. In addition, Excite will become the search service Pointcast customers first see when they venture onto the Web from the network. Pointcast, which is based in Cupertino, Calif., also said it would embrace the Recreational Software Advisory Council's system to rate the content of Web sites.

title: Netguide Is Connected
body: To the Editor: I couldn't agree more with Po Bronson that some of the site fallout on the World Wide Web can be attributed to "the Internet's new maturity and profitability" and that it's good news that advertising revenues are still growing (Op-Ed, April 11). However, contrary to news reports, Netguide Live, the on-line Web directory whose plug Mr. Bronson said was pulled, is alive and connected at http://www.netguide.com/. CMP Media Inc., practicing the sustainable economics Mr. Bronson refers to, has moved Netguide Live's headquarters from San Francisco to the company's headquarters in Manhasset, L.I. The product will unveil a new design while maintaining its identity.  BARBARA KERBEL Vice President, CMP Media Inc. Manhasset, L.I., April 11, 1997

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
2 NEW INTRANET PRODUCTS JOINING I.B.M. SOFTWARE ROSTER
body: The International Business Machines Corporation announced new entry-level software yesterday aimed at helping small businesses or corporate departments establish internal computer networks, or intranets. The two new products will be sold by I.B.M.'s Lotus Development unit and will be available later this year. They are part of a new framework integrating all of I.B.M.'s Internet software. The first product, code-named Lotus Go, is Web-server software, which is the foundation of an intranet. It will compete with products from the Microsoft Corporation and the Netscape Communications Corporation as well as with software available free on the Internet. The second new offering, called Domino Mail, adds email, on-line discussion and scheduling features to a web server.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NCR SET TO INTRODUCE SERIES OF PRODUCTS FOR INTERNET
body: The NCR Corporation is planning to introduce a series of new Internet-related products on April 28, the company said yesterday. NCR, which was spun off from the AT&T Corporation earlier this year and is based in Dayton, Ohio, has been slow to embrace the Internet because it has been trying to reverse years of losses under AT&T. Scott Swain, an NCR executive, said the new products would extend existing NCR technology to the World Wide Web. For example, NCR's cluster technology will enable large businesses to operate Web sites 24 hours a day. Other products will enable banks to offer customers home banking using simple Web browsers and let telephone companies offer customers access to their bills on line.

title:
April 6-12;
Social Security Goes Off-Line
body: The Social Security Administration last week pulled the plug on an electronic information service, concerned that it could have violated privacy rights by divulging people's income and future benefits. "The Internet is a new world," John J. Callahan, the Acting Commissioner of Social Security, said as he shut down an agency Internet site that supplied information about individuals' personal income and retirement benefits. In the next two months, he will solicit advice from experts and the public on what to do. Many taxpayers wanted easy access to the information to help them plan for retirement, Mr. Callahan said. But that also meant that to get the information, any computer user needed only to supply the name, address, telephone number, place of birth, Social Security number and mother's maiden name for the person whose records were sought.   ROBERT PEAR

title: Guatemala
body: To the Editor: Congratulations for recognizing Guatemala as a wonderful destination and for mentioning Ken Johnson of Guatemala Unlimited as a resource. You have neglected, however, to provide contact information. Guatemala Unlimited may be reached at (800) 773-3350, on the Net at Guatemala1@aol.com or on the Web at  http://members.aol.com/guatemala1/html/guatunl.htm. Mr. Johnson's service is efficient, prompt and highly reliable. This is especially important to those of us who travel on the cheap. Ken has been making my arrangements for several years now.  BRIAN QUINBY Aurora, Ill.

title: New Categories Approved for Internet Sites
body: The growing demand for Internet addresses has spawed a new set of on-line tags. All Internet addresses in the unitedstates now end with one of six domain names: .com for businesses; .org for nonprofit organizations; .net for networks; .edu for educational institutions; .gov for governmental bodies, or .mil for the military. Under changes approved on Tuesday, seven endings will be added: .store for businesses offering goods; .info for information services; .nom for individuals who want personal sites; .firm for businesses or firms; .web for entities emphasizing the World Wide Web; .arts for cultural groups, and .rec for recreational or entertainment activities. The change will not affect existing names, only future applications. The endings were proposed by the International Ad Hoc Committee, a group of 11 representatives of Internet, legal and other international standards groups. They were approved by five organizations that help oversee the Internet functions.

title: MTV to Transmit Internet Videos
body: Viacom Inc.'s MTV unit said yesterday that it would broadcast music videos to consumers' personal computers using technology developed by the Intel Corporation. MTV will use Intel's Intercast to provide two hours of video programming daily beginning Friday. MTV's sister station, M2, will also transmit Intercast programming. Intercast allows consumers to watch video and receive data from the Internet on their computers at the same time. For example, viewers would be able to watch a music video and receive news about the artist and album. NBC, Cable News Network and others also provide Intercast programming.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DOW JONES APPEALS $222 MILLION LIBEL JUDGMENT
body: Dow Jones & Co. asked a Federal judge to overturn a record $222.7 million libel judgment, contending that it would have a "staggering effect" on journalism if allowed to stand. Lawyers for the plaintiff, MMAR Group Inc., said the jury's verdict last month "easily passes constitutional muster" and should be approved by unitedstates District Judge Ewing Werlein. MMAR, a now-defunct securities firm, charged that it was forced out of business by a 1993 article in The Wall Street Journal, which Dow Jones publishes.

title: Government Shouldn't Rule on Internet Content
body: To the Editor: Sara Butler (letter, March 28) makes a crucial error in her defense of the Internet indecency legislation: indecency is not the same as obscenity. While Ms. Butler is unable to imagine a project that would require material the Government would term indecent, I can think of several. A report on the transmission of AIDS through sexual intercourse or one on abortion might contain material that could be termed "indecent" under more than one set of community standards. In fact, a paper discussing J. D. Salinger's "Catcher in the Rye" might well violate such standards. A paper detailing Holocaust atrocities might also be affected by this legislation. Contrary to Ms. Butler's assumptions, and those of many other individuals throughout the country who have seen no reason to oppose this law, indecency refers not only to pornography but also to any sexually or otherwise explicit material, without regard to artistic or social merit. Additionally, laws already governing distribution of pornography to minors can and have been applied to cases involving the Internet. No new legislation is needed to accomplish this.  JON LASSER Baltimore, March 28, 1997

title:
Updates: Media and Techonology;
Internet Bookstore Files To Sell Stock to Public
body: Amazon.com, a popular Internet bookstore and a rare cyberspace success story, has filed with securities regulators to sell 2.5 million shares to the public in an initial offering. The offering will include 375,000 additional shares to cover unexpected demand for the stock, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Amazon.com, based in Seattle, expects the shares to be sold initially at $13 each. Proceeds are estimated at $33.9 million after paying fees associated with the sale. Amazon.com will have about 23 million shares outstanding after the offering, and the offer price values the company at $299 million. Amazon.com was founded in July 1995 by Jeffrey P. Bezos, a former investment banker.   DOW JONES

title:
DEATH IN A CULT;
On Line: Designers
body: The path that led police to the bodies of 39 men and women this week started with the Interact Communications Group, a successful Web development firm that had subcontracted design work to a group of men who identified themselves as both space aliens and monks. The interactions of the firm and the cult members are described in the CyberTimes section of The newyork Times on the Web: www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Needs Decency Rule to Shield Young
body: To the Editor: Kristen Farron (letter, March 23), in arguing against the Government's setting up decency rules for the Internet, says "it is the parents' responsibility to watch their children, not the Government's." Would Ms. Farron abolish laws forbidding the sale of cigarettes and alcohol to minors because "it's the parents' responsibility to watch their children"? Because it is impossible for parents constantly to monitor their children, especially as their children get older, sometimes the community, and government, must serve in loco parentis. Ms. Farron is also afraid that she will not have access to the material she needs for school work. Like Ms. Farron, I am a high school student. I recently used the Internet to complete a science project on muscular dystrophy, and the Internet was indeed an invaluable tool. But I cannot imagine a school project that would require material that the Government would term indecent. As wonderful as the Internet is, it is not sacred. There is no reason that the laws that govern the distribution of other "indecent" material to children in the form of magazines and videos should not apply to the Internet as well.  SARA BUTLER newyork, March 25, 1997

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
CISCO IN STOCK DEAL FOR NICHE COMMUNICATIONS COMPANY
body: Cisco Systems Inc. disclosed yesterday that it had acquired a Silicon Valley start-up company, Telesend Inc., that makes technology that allows phone companies to offer high-speed Internet access connections. The acquisition, which was completed early this month in a stock swap, called for the exchange of Cisco shares for all of Telesend's outstanding stock and options. The company did not disclose further financial details. Telesend has developed a technology known as Integrated Services Digital Network Digital Subscriber Line, which relieves congestion on telephone voice networks caused by rising Internet use. Cisco's stock was up $4.50 yesterday, to $52.375.

title: President Named By Servicenet
body: Servicenet, an Internet commerce joint venture of Andersen Consulting and the BBN Corporation, has named John M. Whiteside as its president. Until last week, Mr. Whiteside, 41, was general manager of I.B.M. Global Network after a stint as a vice president at the MCI Communications. Servicenet intends to establish itself as an Internet utility for business, charging fees for data transmission just like any other utility, Mr. Whiteside said. To date, Servicenet's revenue has been only a few million dollars, he said. Temporarily based in Minneapolis, Servicenet was formed in June. Servicenet expects to work with big Andersen accounts like the British Petroleum Company and the Dell Computer Corporation as well as BBN accounts like the AT&T Corporation and America Online Inc., Mr. Whiteside said. "Companies do not have to build their own networks" for using the Internet for business, he said. Servicenet intends to pitch its 24-hour-a-day service to large accounts. While rivals like the Electronic Data Systems Corporation compete with Andersen and Internet specialty providers, there is no utility currently providing total Internet service to business, he said.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DOW JONES TO SELL DEMOGRAPHICS UNIT TO COWLES MEDIA
body: Dow Jones & Company said yesterday that it had agreed to sell its American Demographics Inc. unit to the Cowles Media Company for an undisclosed price. The unit consists of American Demographics and Marketing Tools magazines, the newsletter Forecast and a catalogue of books and CD-ROM's. A subsidiary, Cowles Business Media, will operate American Demographics, which has been owned by Dow Jones for about 15 years. Cowles Business Media, based in Stamford, Conn., also publishes Cable World, Directory World and Catalog Age magazines. Dow Jones, based in newyork, publishes The Wall Street Journal and operates the Telerate financial information service.

title: Internet Indecency
body: To the Editor: Re your March 20 news article on the Supreme Court's debate on decency rules for the Internet: I agree totally with the computer industry's lawyer. Who is the Government to decide what is decent? It is the parents' responsibility to watch their children, not the Government's. I am a high school student who uses the Internet for projects. What will happen when I have a science report and need the Internet? Will the material I need be absent because some Government official says it is "not decent"? Let's hope not!  KRISTEN FARRON Flushing, Queens, March 20, 1997

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
I.B.M. SETS ITS SIGHTS ON A MAJORITY STAKE IN NETOBJECTS
body: The International Business Machines Corporation has agreed to buy a majority interest in Netobjects Inc., a closely held provider of software for creating World Wide Web sites on the Internet. I.B.M. said that Netobjects, based in Redwood City, Calif., would continue to be run independently, with its chairman and chief executive, Samir Arora, at the helm. It will also continue to provide software that is compatible for all brands of computers, I.B.M. said. Terms were not disclosed. Netobjects sells Netobjects Fusion, software for creating web sites that can operate on computers running the Microsoft Corporation's Windows system as well as the Macintosh system made by Apple Computer Inc.

title: Court Weighs Rules On Internet Decency
body: Preparing to decide the fate of the Government's effort to regulate sexually explicit material on the Internet, the Supreme Court heard two starkly different descriptions of the global computer network. In spirited questioning, the Justices pressed lawyers to explain how the law would protect children from offensive images and messages, without making criminals out of parents who make the Internet available to their children on home computers. Article, page B10.

title:
Metro News Briefs: NEW YORK CITY;
Planned Parenthood Wins Suit Over Name
body: A Federal judge blocked a Web site operator yesterday from masquerading under the Planned Parenthood name to attract readers to his anti-abortion home page. Judge Kimba Wood barred Richard Bucci from using the trademark of the Planned Parenthood Federation of America Inc. or anything that would cause visitors to his site on the Internet to think he was related to the group. Planned Parenthood, which operates 900 health centers nationwide, is the world's largest voluntary reproductive health care organization. In a statement, the president of Planned Parenthood, Gloria Feldt, called the ruling a "victory for truth in cyberspace." A message left for Mr. Bucci at his Syracuse residence was not immediately returned. Mr. Bucci hosts "Catholic Radio," a daily program broadcast on WVOA radio in Syracuse. On Aug. 28, Mr. Bucci registered the Internet domain name plannedparenthood.com with Network Solutions Inc., a company that handles the assignment of domain names on the Internet. Planned Parenthood responded by filing a lawsuit in Federal court in Manhattan to shut down the Web page.

title:
Updates: Media and Technology;
New Commercial Service Will Provide Real-Time S.E.C. Corporate Filings
body: In the split-second world of financial trading, speed is only slightly less valued than smarts. A fledgling news provider, Internet Financial Network (http://www.ifn.com), plans to introduce a product this week with ample helpings of both. It is called Instant News Service. And if it does not completely live up to its ambitious name, it comes impressively close as it absorbs complex corporate filings from the Securities and Exchange Commission and spits out brief, headlined excerpts. The service uses a proprietary computer program, rather than people, to sift the filings. That could make the new service faster than its human competition. I.F.N.'s Edgarwatch product, named for the S.E.C.'s electronic data base, has been providing real-time commission releases since last year. But it does not help make them any more intelligible on first glance. Clifford T. Boro, I.F.N.'s president, says the service will give traders and fund managers enough of an edge to justify its cost, which will be at least $10,000 a year. I.F.N.'s principal owners are the Data Broadcasting Corporation and Travelers Group Inc.   SETH SCHIESEL

title:
Updates: Media and Technology;
U.S. Supreme Court To Hear Arguments On Internet Decency Law
body: In a historic case about free-speech rights in cyberspace, the Supreme Court of the unitedstates will hear arguments on Wednesday involving a new law that severely restricts indecent material on the Internet. The Court will consider an appeal by the Clinton Administration, which is defending the law that bans the dissemination of sexually explicit material to anyone younger than 18.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
U.P.S. IN TRACKING DEALS WITH INTERNET SEARCH COMPANIES
body: United Parcel Service of America Inc. has reached agreements with the Infoseek Corporation, Lycos Inc. and Yahoo Inc. to provide U.P.S. on-line utilities on the Web sites of the Internet service companies. U.P.S. said in a statement that beginning yesterday, users of Infoseek, Lycos and Yahoo would be able to track U.P.S. packages, find drop-off centers and download U.P.S. on-line tracking software from the search-engine companies' Web sites. U.P.S. said it expected to double its Internet tracking activity.

title: Web Ads Require Children's Critical Response
body: To the Editor: Parents should not be surprised that alcohol and tobacco companies are using the World Wide Web to pitch products to young people ("On Web, New Threats Seen to the Young," front page, March 7). For simple demographic reasons, these industries want to replace older consumers, and the young are the easiest replacements to acquire as well as the most profitable. But we need not simply submit to this trend or to the cartoonish Web pages used to lure children. Government censorship is controversial and problematic, and industry self-censorship would be slow in coming and weakened by conflicts of interest. But there is another response: education. Parents and educators have begun to teach children to be savvy about movies, television and print advertising. Children should now be taught about the Internet and given the tools to discern the informative, or simply entertaining, from the hip pitches that disguise something potentially harmful.  MEG MILNE MOULTON WHITNEY RANSOME Concord, Mass., March 10, 1997  The writers are directors of the National Coalition of Girls' Schools.

title:
METRO NEWS BRIEFS: NEW YORK CITY;
Man Is Hospitalized After Fight at The Times
body: An employee of The newyork Times was hospitalized and another was arrested on assault charges early yesterday morning after an altercation between the two men broke out in the sub-basement of the newspaper's building at 229 West 43d Street, the police said. James Dillon, 40, was charged with second-degree assault, the police said, after he attacked a colleague, Bernard O'Reilly, with a cutting tool. Mr. O'Reilly, 41, was taken to St. Vincent's Hospital and treated for a wound in his side. A hospital spokeswoman said he was released yesterday morning. Both men work for the newspaper's production operations, and a Times spokeswoman said the two had been suspended. The police did not disclose the nature of the dispute.

title: CBS to Acquire 22% of Sportsline USA
body: CBS announced yesterday that it would acquire a 22 percent stake in Sportsline USA Inc., an Internet media company, in a deal valued at more than $100 million. CBS executives described the deal with Sportsline as evidence of the network's aggressive plans to build a stronger presence in the on-line business. Peter A. Lund, president of the CBS Television Network, said the partnership was "a vital first step" in the network's Internet strategy. CBS, a unit of the Westinghouse Electric Corporation, is paying for its stake mainly in in-kind advertising and promotion. The network executives declined to say how much, if any, of its contribution would be in cash. CBS has an option to increase its ownership of Sportsline to 33 percent in the next five years. The option, if exercised, would be a cash investment. Sportsline, a leading on-line sports service, will change the name of its site on the World Wide Web to CBS Sportsline. The Internet address of the site will also change, to http://cbs.sportsline.com.

title:
Metro News Briefs: NEW YORK STATE;
Minister Gets Probation In Pornography Case
body: A Baptist minister who copied child pornography images off the Internet received three years' probation in exchange for his guilty plea to a reduced charge. Charles David Hess, must pay a $1,000 fine, forfeit his home computer, not have any unsupervised contact with children under 17 and undergo counseling. Mr. Hess, 47, the former minister at the First Baptist Church of Hamilton, was arrested in January. Computer technicians at a repair shop had found 30 pornographic images of children in his computer and notified the state police. Mr. Hess pleaded guilty on Monday in village court to a reduced obscenity count, a misdemeanor.

title: Microsoft Offers To Fix Software
body: The Microsoft Corporation offered a software fix today for a security flaw that was discovered by a Massachusetts college student in some versions of its Internet Explorer browser. "We're strongly recommending that people download this patch" from the Internet, a Microsoft spokesman said.  "It's the only way to be secure." The company said no one had reported problems because of the security flaw -- which could allow someone to put damaging programs on a computer's hard drive from the Internet.

title: Internet Address Authority Facing Lawsuit
body: World Wide Web page design company is challenging the Internet's tradition of consensus, suing the group that rules on electronic addresses. Christopher Ambler of Image Online Design of San Luis Obispo, Calif., says the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority reneged on a deal giving him permission to register addresses ending in .web. Every computer on the Internet has an address issued by the authority. Although the authority is responsible for the overall naming system, responsibility for registering and tracking numbers and names is handled by a private company, Network Solutions of Reston, Va. In the suit filed last Thursday, Image Online Design said it had been authorized in July by an authority spokesman, Bill Manning, to register addresses ending in .web for $25 each. But Mr. Ambler said the authority backed out when a plan was announced to change the current system for assigning Internet addresses by adding seven new endings, including .web or .store.

title:
Updates: Media and Technology;
Times Company to Sell A Publishing Unit That Does Custom Work
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it had decided to put its NYT Custom Publishing unit up for sale. The division produces custom-designed magazines for customers including I.B.M. and the Massachusetts Office of Travel and Tourism. The division had revenue of $13.7 million last year. The Jordan Edmiston Group Inc., an investment bank that specializes in publishing and information transactions, will assist in the sale. The custom publishing unit is not part of the Times Company's Magazine Group, which has nine consumer and trade sports magazines, and a sports marketing operation.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AT&T TO END OFFER OF 5 FREE HOURS OF INTERNET SERVICE
body: The AT&T Corporation said yesterday that it would end its introductory offer to long-distance customers of five free hours a month on its Worldnet Internet access service on March 31. In its place, AT&T will establish an hourly pricing plan. Worldnet will continue to offer unlimited access for $19.95 a month, AT&T said. Starting March 31, AT&T will offer long-distance customers who sign up for Worldnet and expect to spend a limited amount of time on line a monthly rate of $4.95 for their first five hours and $2.50 for each additional hour. Long-distance customers who signed up before March 31 will continue to get their first five hours free for a year.

title: On the Internet
body: To the Editor: I was pleased to see Susan Spano's Frugal Traveler column "Planning a Trip, Fingers Crossed" (Jan. 19), because planning a trip is almost as much fun as taking it. In addition, the column is my favorite in the Travel section. However, I do believe that Ms. Spano understated the value of using the Internet. It has an infinite amount of useful travel information and enables one to request even more brochures from local tourist agencies, as well as up-to-date information on weather and events. For example, when planning a trip to Florida, I was able to review the spring-training baseball schedules. The most promising aspect of the Internet is being able to make contact with the people of an area. Before leaving for Alaska with my son, I sent email to the University of Alaska and asked to stay in its dormitories. The reply was negative, but a faculty member did offer to meet with us when we get to Fairbanks.  HOWARD STOLLER Albany Graphic   Drawing (Nikki Middendorf)

title: New York Times Company Announces a Promotion
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that James C. Lessersohn had been promoted to vice president for corporate planning. Mr. Lessersohn, 41, who had been managing director for corporate planning, has worked on strategic planning and acquisitions since he joined the company in 1987. Mr. Lessersohn's previous positions were with The Boston Globe and its former parent, Affiliated Publications, which was bought by The newyork Times Company in 1993, and The Daily News of newyork.

title: Times Company Plans Stock Buyback
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that its board had authorized spending of as much as $150 million for the repurchase of class A shares. Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, the chairman and chief executive of the company, said that the repurchased shares would be used for stock-based employee benefit plans and other corporate purposes. Last year, the company spent $43.8 million to buy 1.4 million class A shares. In 1995, the Times company spent $46.3 million for 2.1 million class A shares. In 1994, it spent $235.2 million to buy 10 million shares. The Times Company also declared a quarterly dividend of 15 cents a share on its class A and class B shares. The dividend was raised in November for the first time since 1990, to 15 cents from 14 cents. The company set a quarterly dividend of $1.375 for each share of the 5.5 percent cumulative prior preference stock.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Co. in On-Line Pact
body: The newyork Times Company announced an agreement with America Online Inc. yesterday to expand the on-line provider's exclusive use of news and features from The newyork Times, including original material developed by The Times. The new features, which will be available to the eight million subscribers of America Online, will include an expanded version of Science Times, a new People electronic page, crossword puzzle chat rooms and a monthly "theme" crossword puzzle that will appear only on the electronic service. Officials of both companies said that the measures were intended to satisfy the growing demand for exclusive content and services as the on-line market expands. Apart from the exclusive elements, The Times's news report is also available from its own site on the World Wide Web, at http://www.nytimes.com.

title: Microsoft Notified Of Texas Inquiry
body: The Microsoft Corporation, which has fought a series of Federal antitrust investigations, now faces an inquiry by Texas state officials into its Internet products. While Texas may not individually present a serious danger to the software-industry leader, antitrust lawyers say the state investigation could ratchet up the pressure on the unitedstates Justice Department to take action in its investigation. Both the Federal investigation and the state investigation involve questions about whether Microsoft is using its dominance in the market for personal computer operating systems to gain unfair advantage in the competition for Internet browsers or other software and on-line products. Microsoft confirmed today that the Texas Attorney General's office got in touch with it on Monday. The Texas request comes as the Justice Department is in the midst of a wide-ranging antitrust review of complaints by the Netscape Communications Corporation and other industry rivals, which say Microsoft is unfairly using its leading position in computer operating systems to stifle competition for World Wide Web browsers and other Internet software.

title: Sign Is Leased By Dow Jones
body: Dow Jones & Company signed a 10-year lease to continue operating the electronic headline sign in Times Square, known as the zipper, the company announced yesterday. The lease runs until the end of 2006, with a renewal option for five years, said Roger May, a Dow Jones spokesman.

title: Dow Jones Nominates 7 Directors to Board
body: Dow Jones & Company said yesterday that it had nominated seven directors, four of them new candidates, and cut the size of its board. Dow Jones, the publisher of The Wall Street Journal, said Carlos Salinas de Gortari, a former president of Mexico, would not stand for re-election. Three members will resign because they have reached the mandatory retirement age of 70. The nominees are Harvey Golub, chief executive of American Express; Frank N. Newman, chief executive of Bankers Trust; William C. Steere Jr., chief executive of Pfizer, and Leslie Hill, a member of the controlling Bancroft family. She replaces Martha Robes, her cousin, who is leaving the board after 16 years. Standing for re-election will be David Li, Jane MacElree and James Ottaway Jr. Carl Valenti, a Dow Jones senior vice president, will resign. Shareholders will vote at the company's annual meeting in April. Dow Jones will reduce the size of the board to 15 directors from 17.

title: Family Member Quits Dow Jones
body: An outspoken member of the family that controls Dow Jones & Company has quit his job there. William Cox 3d, who had been in charge of sales and marketing for Dow Jones Global Indexes, has been unhappy with the performance of Dow Jones stock, which sits below highs set more than 10 years ago. Mr. Cox's resignation was reported yesterday in The newyork Post. Dow Jones said the resignation letter was dated and received yesterday. Mr. Cox, 41, told the newspaper that he had decided he should move on after 18 years at the company, which publishes The Wall Street Journal. He said he would continue to push for improvement in Dow Jones shares. A message left at Mr. Cox's office seeking comment was not immediately returned. A recent article in Fortune magazine reported that Mr. Cox and one of his cousins, Elisabeth Goth, were displeased with the situation at the company.

title: Journal Rejects Ad From Rival
body: The Wall Street Journal has rejected an advertisement from Fortune magazine promoting Fortune's recent piece on a shareholder revolt at The Journal's parent company, Dow Jones & Company. The advertisement noted that a prominent money manager increased his Dow Jones stake after reading an article in Fortune. But Journal advertising representatives told Fortune's head of marketing, John Needham, on Monday that the chief executive of Dow Jones, Peter R. Kann, had refused the advertisement, Mr. Needham said. "It appeared that the senior management of Dow Jones is interfering directly in the operation of the Journal," Mr. Needham said. Roger May, a Dow Jones spokesman, responded by saying only that "the Journal chose not to run this particular ad by a competitor."

title: Curtain Set to Drop On AT&T Web Site
body: The AT&T Business Network Web site that offers a wealth of business information will be closed down, the Internet company that runs it under license from the AT&T Corporation said yesterday. Jennifer Christensen, a spokeswoman for Nets Inc., the operating company, said the Web site (http://www.bnet.att.com), which remained active yesterday, was no longer being updated daily. The site is to disappear entirely by the beginning of April, she said. Last week Nets told employees that it would close the Web site and cut 54 of the company's 304 jobs. The company said yesterday that it would seek additional investors but was not ready to make an initial public offering. Ms. Christensen saidmore work was needed to prepare for a public offering. Nets, among whose biggest shareholders is Jim P. Manzi, former chief executive of the Lotus Development Corporation, is planning to build a business-to-business electronic commerce operation to help maintenance and repair organizations buy parts.

title: Rockwell to Sell High-Speed Chip
body: The Rockwell International Corporation said today that it planned to begin production shipment of its new high-speed modem chips this month. Rockwell's K56 modem chip sets allow Internet users to connect to the Internet over conventional telephone lines at almost twice the currently available speed. The U.S. Robotics Corporation has developed a competing technology called x2. To date Rockwell and U.S. Robotics have not worked out standards for the two technologies to be interoperable. Rockwell said it had shipped samples of the K56 modem chips to more than 130 customers and was on schedule to begin production this month, as planned. It said demand for early samples of the K56 chips had been strong, adding that the first modems using the technology should be in retail stores in March.

title: Internet Prank Riles Cronkite
body: Walter Cronkite says he considered suing when he found a fabricated tale on a homepage on the World Wide Web that carried the title "Walter Cronkite Spit in My Food." The man who had put together the homepage, Tim Hughes of West Carrollton, Ohio, pulled it on Thursday, posting in its place a notice saying, "It was never my intention to hurt anyone." Mr. Cronkite, the longtime CBS anchorman, said in a telephone interview from Chicago on Thursday that he had been stunned several months ago when he spotted the page, which included an image of himself and an accompanying fable about a tipsy, cursing Mr. Cronkite accosting Mr. Hughes and his wife at a Florida restaurant. "I punched up 'Cronkite' just to see what was on the Internet and stumbled on this scurrilous article," Mr. Cronkite said. "The whole thing is just so outlandish. I don't think I've ever spit in my life." Mr. Hughes, 28, an Internet applications developer, admitted that he made the whole thing up.

title: Internet and Literacy
body: To the Editor: In "Techno-Paranoia in the White House" (Op-Ed, Jan. 25), David S. Bennahum says that "the Internet has come into its own as a news source," yet most people lack the more active kind of literacy skills required to make sense of it. As someone who handles technical support calls from Internet users, I am shocked at the lack of literacy and reading comprehension skills in those those I help. They can't enjoy the benefits of the Internet and are left wondering what it's all about while they point at pictures and click. This is bad for democracy and fodder for dictatorship.  GREGG SQUIRES newyork, Jan. 25, 1997

title: 3-Company Pact on Internet Technology
body: The 3Com Corporation, the Cascade Communications Corporation and the International Business Machines Corporation are cooperating in an effort to provide systems that will speed access to the Internet and intranets. In a joint statement yesterday, the companies said the cooperative effort would allow enterprises that use the Internet and the providers of network services to deploy new voice, video and graphics applications. The new systems, scheduled for delivery for production networks in the second half of this year, will integrate technologies from the three companies.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
National Campaign For New York Times
body: A national campaign for The newyork Times will begin on Sunday, the Times Company said yesterday.
