The campaign, with a budget of $20 million, is part of efforts to build a broad brand image for The Times as it undertakes significant expansion plans this year that include new editions for readers in New England and the Washington area. Television, radio and print ads will carry the theme "Expect the world." The campaign was created by the newspaper's longtime agency, Bozell Worldwide, a unit of Bozell, Jacobs, Kenyon & Eckhardt in newyork.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
CITYSEARCH TO ANNOUNCE JOINT VENTURE IN AUSTRALIA
body: Citysearch, an Internet start-up based in Pasadena, Calif., plans to announce partnerships today with two of Australia's largest media companies to offer on-line services in Sydney and Melbourne. Citysearch said it would work with John Fairfax Holdings, publisher of the newspapers The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age in Melbourne, to supply local news and other information, and BIG Color Pages, a directory publisher, to provide data on local businesses. Service will start in Melbourne this summer and in Sydney shortly after.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MOTOROLA BUYS STAKE IN INTERACTIVE MEDIA COMPANY
body: Motorola Inc. said yesterday that it had acquired a stake in Worldgate Communications Inc., which offers users access to the Internet over cable-television networks. For $4.95 a month, Worldgate offers its customers access to the Internet through their television sets, remote controls and cable-television converters. Unlike traditional Internet access services, no computer or modem is needed. Motorola did not disclose the size of the investment or how much of the equity of Worldgate, based in Trevose, Pa., it had acquired. Shares of Motorola, with headquarters in Shaumburg, Ill., rose 75 cents, closing at $68.25.

title:
NEW JERSEY DAILY BRIEFING;
Discussing Farmers' Futures
body: Some of New Jersey's 8,800 farmers have begun cultivating plots in cyberspace, selling soybeans on the Internet and designing Web sites. But too many others still rely on the rotary telephone, state agriculture officials say. Using technology on the farm is the subject of the general session at the state agriculture convention that opens today at Harrah's Casino Hotel in Atlantic City. About 1,000 people are expected to attend the two-day conference.

title: America Online: The Internet Reacts - Correction Appended
body: Since America Online, the world's biggest computer on-line service, introduced a new flat monthly access charge last month, the number of people trying to dial in to it has soared, causing many frustrated customers to encounter busy signals when trying to connect. Last week, customers filed lawsuits in several states accusing the company of selling a service that it could not provide. America Online has acknowledged the problems and pledged to add capacity and provide better access in the near future. The company's promises have not satisfied all its customers, however, though some subscribers have defended the service. Some Internet bulletin boards and World Wide Web sites have been created to exchange criticisms about the service provider. Here are some comments that were posted in the last few days to a Usenet bulletin board that uses an unflattering word to describe the quality of America Online's service. Each of these comments was confirmed by its author, whose original grammar and punctuation has been preserved.   DYLAN LOEB McCLAIN Correction  A chart in Business Day on Jan. 20 reproducing criticisms of America Online's service that were posted on an Internet bulletin board referred incorrectly to a comment by Jeffrey Ray Roberts of Kansas City, Mo., who said he was disconnected while trying to reserve airlines tickets. The comment did not relate an actual experience; it was intended as a parody. Correction-Date: February 1, 1997, Saturday Graphic   Chart provides quotes of AOL users.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
WPP Acquires Stake in Peapod
body: WPP Group in London acquired less than a 10 percent interest in Peapod Inc. in Evanston, Ill., which offers on-line shopping and delivery to consumers in six cities. Terms were not disclosed. The deal calls for WPP and Peapod to join in advising advertisers on home shopping. That joint effort will be headed by Eric Salama, 35, group director for strategy at WPP in London, and Tim Dorgan, 44, president of Peapod Interactive, Peapod's marketing services division in Evanston. The investment is the most recent by WPP in a variety of interactive media and marketing ventures.

title: Software Alliance for Corel and Netscape
body: The Corel Corporation and the Netscape Communications Corporation, seeking to steal some thunder from the Microsoft Corporation, announced this week an alliance to meld office productivity software with enhanced Internet capabilities. Corel said it had licensed Netscape Communicator -- Netscape's new email and browser software -- with the aim of integrating it with Corel's Wordperfect Suite 8 and Corel Office Professional 8. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. The announcement was also intended to take some of the limelight off Microsoft's planned glitzy introduction of its Office 97 software package on Thursday. The marriage of Netscape's Internet software suite and Corel's word processor and other software tools is part of a growing marketing trend in which Internet browsing and communications are brought together with other computer applications in a seamless package.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
TELEPORT IN STOCK SWAP FOR INTERNET SERVICE PROVIDER
body: Teleport Communications Group said yesterday that it had agreed to buy the Internet company Cerfnet Services Inc. from General Atomics for $68.3 million in stock, based on yesterday's closing price of $32.50 a share. The combined company will provide telephone, Internet and World Wide Web services, primarily to business customers. Teleport will issue 2.1 million shares to buy Cerfnet, which is based in San Diego and provides Internet services to more than 6,000 corporate customers. Teleport Communications, based in Staten Island, is owned by several cable television companies, including Tele-Communications Inc., Cox Communications and the Comcast Corporation.

title: No New York Tax On Internet Access
body: Gov. George E. Pataki said today that Internet access services would be tax-exempt in newyork. The move would make newyork the first state in the country to provide such exemption, although other states were wrestling with the issue, a spokesman for the state tax department said. In addition, companies in newyork that provide on-line services and that accept advertising from companies outside the state will not have to pay sales tax on the revenue from those ads, the spokesman said. Some providers had feared that by carrying advertisements for mail-order companies outside the state, they would be subject to sales tax. The exemptions are intended to make newyork attractive to Internet providers, Mr. Pataki said, adding, "newyork must encourage the new-media industry to continue to expand and thrive in our state." Kevin Quinn, the tax department spokesman, said the plan did not require legislative approval because the services were outside the existing tax code. He also said that Connecticut, Massachusetts, Tennessee and Texas were taxing services and that Nebraska had a partial tax.

title: The Times Announces Two Appointments
body: The newyork Times announced the appointment of Dennis L. Stern yesterday as vice president for human resources. He will be responsible for the paper's news as well as business departments, which formerly maintained mostly separate personnel functions. The appointment, effective on Monday, was announced jointly by Joseph Lelyveld, executive editor, and Janet L. Robinson, president of the newspaper. Mr. Stern, 50, has held editing positions on The Times's national and metropolitan desks, and most recently served as associate managing editor for newsroom administration. A graduate of Haverford College with a law degree from newyork University, he joined The Times in 1981. He had been metropolitan editor of The Washington Star and earlier worked at The Miami News and The Associated Press. The Times also announced the appointment of Mr. Stern's predecessor, Donna C. Miele, as vice president and project administrator. She will serve as the newspaper's liaison to a corporate-level project centralizing and overhauling The newyork Times Company's personnel and accounting systems.

title: I.B.M. Sees Business on Internet Improving
body: The International Business Machines Corporation expects its Internet-related business to break even this year as electronic commerce becomes more popular. Mark Greene, vice president of electronic payments and certification with I.B.M., said today that many of the company's hardware and software products would become profitable after heavy investment in 1996. "Over all, the mix is moving from substantial investment to balanced investment and revenue," he said at the Internet World '97 conference. "We are encouraged that we are turning the corner." Mr. Greene said I.B.M.'s most successful Internet products were Net.Commerce, software that lets merchants do electronic transactions, and World Avenue, an electronic mall service. He estimated that $900 million of business was done over the Internet in 1996. Mr. Greene said he expected Internet sales to hit $3 billion to $4 billion this year and $1 trillion by 2000.

title: Zenith's Internet TV Plans
body: The Zenith Electronics Corporation, which makes television and video products, said it was joining with the Oracle Corporation and the Netscape Communications Corporation to offer new Internet TV products. Zenith said it planned to offer Internet television products with interactive capabilities based on software from Network Computer Inc., a unit of Oracle. Zenith also said it planned to collaborate on consumer-based Internet software and services with the consumer affiliate of Netscape.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NORTHERN TELECOM SELLS 25% OF INTERNET COMPANY
body: Northern Telecom Ltd. said yesterday that it had sold 25 percent of its newly formed Internet security company, Entrust Technologies Inc., to a group of institutional investors for $26 million. The investors include Olympus Partners, J. P. Morgan & Company, Societe Generale S.A., T. Rowe Price Associates and Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Inc. Northern Telecom, a phone equipment maker based in Mississauga, Ontario, said it was selling the stake to let Entrust have more freedom in choosing partners other than Northern Telecom and in selling its technology. Entrust provides software used to scramble and identify information on the Internet.

title: Shift at Dow Jones Union
body: The Independent Association of Publishers' Employees, a labor union representing 2,500 workers at Dow Jones & Company, announced today that it would affiliate with the Communication Workers of America, becoming a local of that union, effective Feb. 1. Members of I.A.P.E. work for various Dow Jones subsidiaries, including The Wall Street Journal, Barron's, Dow Jones Information News Service and WBIS-TV in newyork. Dow Jones's main offices are in newyork and South Brunswick, N.J.

title:
OUTLOOK '97: MEDIA & TECHNOLOGY;
WHAT HAPPENED: The Browser War Rages On
body: Microsoft dedicated 1996 to the Internet as it sought to catch up to Netscape Communications for control of the Internet browser market. Microsoft quickly introduced new versions of its browser software and turned the Microsoft Network into an Internet access company. Netscape fought back with its own updates and still controls about 80 percent of the browser market. Graphic   Photo (Andre Lucero)

title: Sybil Primis, 87
body: Sybil Primis, the mother of Lance R. Primis, the former president and chief operating officer of The newyork Times Company, died yesterday at South Nassau Hospital in Oceanside, L.I. Mrs. Primis, who lived in Valley Stream, L.I., was 87. Mrs. Primis, the former Sybil Schiller, was born in Brooklyn and educated in the newyork City public school system. She married in 1932 and reared three children. Besides her son Lance of Holmdel, N.J., she is survived by her daughter, Sondra Plotkin of Valley Stream, and her son, Dr. Ronald Primis of East Meadow, L.I.; seven grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.

title: Nissan Plans to Sell Cars on the Internet
body: The Nissan Motor Company of Japan will start to sell passenger cars on the Internet next summer, the Japanese business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported Saturday. Internet users will be able buy a car from home, using electronic catalogues on Nissan's home pages on the World Wide Web, the daily reported. Nissan will advertise "Internet car" models, variants of existing models for sale exclusively on the Internet, the Nihon Keizai said. Nissan intends to sell Internet cars less expensively by cutting promotion costs, like advertising and marketing. The company's car home pages will feature color images and detailed information on the models on sale and will offer an electronic mail information service. Nissan is the first Japanese car maker to announce Internet car sales but is expected to be followed soon by other domestic motor giants, the business daily reported.

title: Internet Traffic Jams May Have a Helpful Side
body: To the Editor: "An 'All You Can Eat' Price Is Clogging Internet Access" (front page, Dec. 17) says that the trend toward flat-rate pricing has been "damaging for the hundreds of small Internet service providers who once had the market to themselves." That's not necessarily so. Rather, the frustration of dealing with a national Internet service provider like America Online, which offers unlimited access at $19.95 a month, may be a terrific opportunity for small, local service providers. I recently switched to a local service provider and for $30 a month I never get busy signals. When I call for assistance a knowledgeable human being answers the phone. I get 20 megabytes of space for Web pages and file transfers. And I have noticed a considerable speed increase in Internet access. Check with a computer buff or the Yellow Pages for a local provider: Small is still beautiful.  JOHN HILGERDT Asheville, N.C., Dec. 18, 1996

title:
Internet Traffic Jams May Have a Helpful Side;
Phone Bill Blues
body: To the Editor: The Dec. 17 front-page article on clogged Internet access told only half the story. The other culprit to Internet congestion and access abuse is the free or low flat-rate local telephone calls Americans take for granted. In most European countries, even local calls are billed on a time-connected rate. In France, if one is lucky enough to have a local access provider, a call costs five cents a minute. If one has to call farther than 62 miles, the rate jumps to between 30 cents and 47 cents per minute. Both rural and urban Internet users therefore are more concerned with their phone bill than they are with their Internet subscription rates. If this scarce resource is being overused, charging for local calls in North America would cool overheated demand and shift the billing burden from long distance users -- who I believe are subsidizing cheap local service.  PETER STOCK Toronto, Dec. 16, 1996

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
3 at Times Are Promoted to Vice President
body: Three business executives at The newyork Times have been promoted to vice president, Janet L. Robinson, president and general manager, announced yesterday. Scott Heekin-Canedy, group director of strategic planning, will become the newspaper's vice president for strategic planning. Mr. Heekin-Canedy worked in The Times's circulation department from 1987 to 1989 and rejoined its financial planning department in 1992. Alyse Myers, promotion director, will be vice president for promotion. Ms. Myers has worked in the advertising and promotion departments of The Times since 1979. In her most recent position, she directed promotion for the celebrations of the centennial of Adolph S. Ochs's purchase of The newyork Times. James L. Terrill, controller, will add the title of vice president. Mr. Terrill first joined the Times Company in 1977 as controller for an educational division. He later served as business manager of the news department and as an executive director overseeing finances in the production department. The promotions take effect Jan. 1.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MERRILL LYNCH REDUCES INTEREST IN BLOOMBERG TO 20%
body: Merrill Lynch & Company said yesterday that it had sold one-third of its 30 percent interest in the financial information and media company Bloomberg L.P. to Bloomberg Inc. and recorded a pretax gain of about $155 million on the sale. The brokerage firm estimated that it had paid about $39 million for its 30 percent interest in Bloomberg. Bloomberg Inc. is the investment vehicle controlled by Michael Bloomberg, who is chief executive of the limited partnership. Merrill Lynch, which first invested in Bloomberg in 1985 and increased its stake to 30 percent by 1990, said it would remain a partner and major customer of the company, which provides financial information, analysis and news through 67,000 terminals worldwide.

title:
THE NEEDIEST CASES;
Immigrants Aided From the Start
body: A Christmas night encounter in 1911, when Adolph S. Ochs, publisher of The newyork Times, was moved to help an impoverished immigrant, inspired the creation of The newyork Times Neediest Cases Fund. The fund has helped immigrants ever since. In what remains a city of immigrants, the fund's 85th annual appeal is under way. The money raised goes to seven agencies that aid needy newyorkers -- immigrant and native-born alike. The stories of some beneficiaries, from Ukraine, Cuba and Georgia, are told here today. Articles, page 65.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Co. Sees '96 Profit Gain
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it expected to report higher earnings for 1996 compared with the previous year. Diane P. Baker, the Times Company's chief financial officer, told a gathering of securities analysts in Manhattan that the company expected to earn $1.78 to $1.88 a share for 1996, after subtracting nonrecurring charges and revenues from accounting changes, employee severance costs and the sale of real estate. The estimate is a rise of more than 25 percent over 1995 earnings of $1.41 a share on the same basis, she told the Paine Webber conference. The Times Company owns The newyork Times, The Boston Globe and regional newspapers as well as magazines and broadcast stations.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MCI TO CLOSE MUSIC RETAILING BUSINESS
body: The MCI Communications Corporation plans to close its one-year-old music retailing business and an on-line shopping service, saying people liked to window-shop but were not buying, company officials said yesterday. The long-distance telephone company entered the $12 billion music retailing business in November 1995 with an 800 number that let people sample and buy their favorite recordings. It spent around $10 million developing and promoting the service, the company said. Company officials said plenty of people called the music service dubbed 800 Music Now, but they were not buying.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Trade Groups Propose Web Banner Guidelines
body: Two trade organizations that represent buyers, sellers and producers of Internet advertising issued the first voluntary guidelines yesterday for creating banner ads on the World Wide Web. The Coalition for Advertising Supported Information and Entertainment and the Internet Advertising Bureau said they hoped the recommendations would help simplify the creation and placement of the ads. There are now more than 250 sizes of banners, the small sign-like ads that appear on World Wide Web sites. To reduce that proliferation, the guidelines propose eight "voluntary model banner sizes." Newspapers and other traditional media have standardized their ad space units in much the same manner. The coalition, known as Casie, is a joint effort of the American Association of Advertising Agencies and the Association of National Advertisers. The ad bureau, formed this year, has more than 125 members.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MICROSOFT BUYING NETCARTA, A DEVELOPER OF WEB SITES
body: The Microsoft Corporation, the software giant, agreed yesterday to buy the Netcarta Corporation, which makes Web management and navigation tools for computer networks, for $20 million in cash. The acquisition of Netcarta, based in Scotts Valley, Calif., will give Microsoft a comprehensive product for developing Internet Web sites and internal corporate networks called intranets. Netcarta is a unit of CMG Information Services Inc., based in Wilmington, Mass. Microsoft stock rose 12.5 cents yesterday, to $81.875, in Nasdaq trading of 15.7 million shares. CMG Information Services climbed $1.75, to $19.125, also on Nasdaq.

title: On-Line Sales Soar for Cisco
body: Cisco Systems Inc., the leading producer of internetworking equipment, has made $75 million in electronic sales since it went on line less than five months ago with Cisco Connection Online, the company's World Wide Web site for business users, according to a story in the current issue of Communications Week. Cisco executives reached on Friday confirmed the report. The officials also said that their goal was to conduct 30 percent of all sales transactions on the Web by the end of the company's fiscal fourth quarter in July 1997. At the current rate, those Web sales could be worth as much as $1.77 billion, which would make Cisco the world's leading electronic merchant. Cisco said the company also planned to sell the technology it uses for electronic commerce to customers. Though the Internetworking Product Center, as Cisco calls its sales site on the Web, is new, Cisco is no newcomer to Internet sales. In Cisco's early days, when it had no sales force, nearly all of its sales came from word of mouth, often via electronic mail.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
New Publisher at Boston Globe
body: William O. Taylor will step down as publisher of The Boston Globe in April, and his place will be taken by his younger cousin, Benjamin B. Taylor, the newspaper announced yesterday. William Taylor, who is 64, started at The Globe in 1956 as a production assistant and became publisher in 1978. Benjamin Taylor, 49, will become the fifth member of the Taylor family to head The Globe as publisher since the paper was founded in 1872. The Globe is now a subsidiary of The newyork Times Company. The incoming publisher joined The Globe in 1972, and has worked on both the news side, as a reporter and editor, and for the paper's business offices. Mr. Taylor became executive editor in 1988 and was named president in 1993. He will continue as both president and publisher after his new appointment takes effect on April 1, the paper said. Benjamin Taylor's father, John I. Taylor, was president of The Globe before he died in 1987. Graphic   Photos: William O. Taylor; Benjamin B. Taylor

title: Microsoft Names New Leadership Group
body: The Microsoft Corporation has formed an executive committee to replace its office of the president as its top decision-making group. Two senior vice presidents, James E. Allchin and Brad A. Silverberg, are joining the new committee. Other Microsoft executives on the committee are: William H. Gates, the company's chairman; Steven A. Ballmer; Robert J. Herbold; Pete Higgins; Paul A. Maritz; Nathan P. Myhrvold, and Jeffrey S. Raikes. Mr. Allchin and Mr. Silverberg will take on additional product responsibilities. Mr. Allchin will head the personal and business systems group that includes the Windows division, server applications division and associated marketing functions. Mr. Silverberg will run the applications and Internet client group, including the desktop applications division; Internet client and collaboration division; tools division; Web authoring product unit; developer relations, and associated marketing operations.

title: America Online Revises Price-Change Plan
body: America Online users nationwide will receive more time and information to consider a new pricing plan as a result of an agreement with the Attorney General of Washington. The agreement, announced on Friday, came after talks over America Online's plan to automatically switch subscribers to a $19.95 flat rate on Dec. 1 unless they advised the company they wanted to keep the current basic plan -- $9.95 a month for five hours and $2.95 an hour thereafter. The state Attorney General, Christine Gregoire, contended that the plan violated the state's consumer protection law. Under the agreement, the company will notify subscribers with an electronic message when they log on to the service. Customers who are automatically switched to the new plan on Dec. 1 can change back to the original through March 31 and get a refund for the difference. The new choices are: a standard $19.95 monthly plan offering unlimited use of America Online and the Internet; a $9.95 rate for unlimited access to America Online, for those who already have an Internet connection; and three hours of the service a month for $4.95, with additional time at $2.50 an hour.

title:
Technology Is Only as Good (or Bad) as Its User;
Patrolling the Web
body: To the Editor: I read with interest Hubert H. Humphrey 3d's Nov. 19 Op-Ed article about gambling on the Internet. The ability to gamble away the rent from one's living room will, no doubt, have no shortage of horror stories. But more than a third of web sites are offshore; it's not called the World Wide Web for nothing. How does Mr. Humphrey propose to enforce laws against on-line gambling? Should F.B.I. agents look over our shoulders whenever we log on?  RAYMOND M. HICKS 3D newyork, Nov. 21, 1996

title: Times Co. Raises Dividend to 15 Cents
body: The newyork Times Company announced yesterday that its dividend payment would be increased for the first time since 1990. The quarterly dividend on the company's two categories of common stock, class A and class B, will increase to 15 cents from 14 cents. The dividend is payable on Dec. 16, to shareholders of record on Dec. 3. Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, the chairman and chief executive, said that the dividend increase reflected the company's improved operating performance and the board's confidence in the company's financial performance in the future. Class A shares of the Times Company, which are publicly traded, rose 37.5 cents yesterday, to $37.875, on the American Stock Exchange.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Compuserve May Curb German Operations
body: Compuserve G.m.b.H. said today that it might transfer its administrative operations out of Germany because of Government moves to force Internet companies to control pornography on their networks. The German unit of the world's second-largest on-line service would continue to offer services in Germany but shift its headquarters to a country that does not hold on-line companies responsible for obscene material on the Internet, a spokeswoman, Doris Kretzen, said. A law under consideration in Germany's lower house of Parliament would require on-line companies to block access to child pornography, neo-Nazi materials or extremist pictures or writing. Compuserve, which is second to America Online as a provider of on-line services, has balked at such proposed legislation, saying it would require the company to "censor" much of the Internet. Compuserve, which is substantially owned by H & R Block , provides on-line information, electronic mail and Internet access to more than four million subscribers in 140 countries. Its 500,000 European customers include 335,000 in Germany, and its German operations employ 250 workers.

title: Microsoft Sees Big Internet Loss
body: Microsoft says it will probably lose more than $1 billion over the next three years on its Internet and news services before they broke even. Last week, Steven A. Ballmer, an executive vice president, forecast a loss of $300 million to $400 million in the coming year for on-line ventures and deficits of that size or slightly less for two years after that. "They've told us they mean to spend on the Internet and that they want to make these projects work," said Jamie Kiggen of Cowen & Company. Stock investors do not seem fazed. Microsoft shares are up 60 percent from a year ago, when it said it would assault the Internet market. Still, the Internet has not proved it can generate substantial amounts of revenue. "If a company like Microsoft can't make money on the Web, it doesn't look good for the Internet," said George Colony, head of Forrester Research. Microsoft's biggest push this year will be the updated version of its MSN on-line service, due for release this month. The service was redesigned after an unsuccessful debut and will use more innovative Internet technology. It has already forced America Online to adopt flat rates.

title: Internet Browsers In Lotus Products
body: The Lotus Development Corporation said today that it planned to ship its next generation of products with Internet browsers manufactured by both the Microsoft Corporation and the Netscape Communications Corporation. "Today's customers want openness, interoperability and simple delivery of product," Jeff Papows, the president of Lotus, said. "This is another step in Lotus's strategy to integrate Notes clients with a variety of browser applications and browser components." The move comes as Lotus's workgroup software has faced a threat from lower-cost Internet technology. Lotus, a division of the International Business Machines Corporation, said it would ship the Netscape Navigator 3.0 with selected Lotus products. Lotus Notes 4.5 is scheduled for shipping by the end of the year. It is the first Lotus product planned for shipment with Netscape's Navigator browser. Lotus will also ship the products with Microsoft's Explorer 3.0 browser, which competes with Netscape's more widely used Navigator.

title: On Latin Web Site, How to Say 'Whoa!'?
body: To the Editor: "Et Tu, Cybernetica Machina User?" (Business Day, Oct. 28), your fine article on the Latin speakers' group on the Internet, excited some sparks in the eyes of my wife, who was a Latin major in college. So, as your article advised, we duly sent the message "Subscribe Latine" to listserve@plearn.edu.pl. Caveat emptor. After our message was accepted, my emailbox quickly had 16 messages in it, all in Latin, and the tide of correspondence continues even into the fourth day. Apparently new subscribers get on the list for all correspondence the site receives. Since Rule 1 on the site is that all discussion must be in Latin and Rule 2 is that when in doubt, refer to Rule 1, I must figure out in Latin how to say stop, gratia, or else get a country-sized mailbox. Ergo, caveat emptor, et cetera, et cetera.  HAROLD FOWLER Walnut Creek, Calif., Nov. 1, 1996 Graphic   Drawing

title: Times Union Accepts Pact
body: Local 6 of the newyork Mailers Union announced yesterday that its members had ratified a four-year agreement with The newyork Times that will give 200 workers lifetime job guarantees and give the newspaper more flexibility to print in the Northeast outside the newyork region. George McDonald, the local's president, said 195 mailers had voted for ratification and 171 against it in Thursday's vote. He said those favoring the pact had been swayed by the job guarantees while opponents had disliked the pay freeze in the agreement's first year. In ratifying the pact, the union, whose members assemble and bundle the newspaper, agreed to end an arbitration in which it had challenged The Times's right to print in the Northeast outside newyork. The newspaper plans to begin printing in January at plants near Boston and Washington. Half of the newspaper's 400 mailers won lifetime job guarantees in 1992, and under the agreement each of those 200 will receive a $10,000 bonus.

title: COMPANY BRIEFS
body: GENESCO INC., Nashville, a footwear maker and retailer, said it would close its Hohenwald, Tenn., boot factory, laying off about 180 employees. The company will take a $1.7 million charge in the third quarter.  WOLTERS KLUWER N.V., Amsterdam, a publishing company, has agreed to buy Blessing/White Inc., of Princeton, N.J., a provider of professional training in the unitedstates and Britain, for an undisclosed sum.  WOOLWORTH CORP., newyork, is selling its interest in a chain of German costume jewelry and accessory stores, Rubin G.m.b.H., to Bijou Brigitte Modische Accessoires A.G., for undisclosed terms.

title: Netscape Stock Sale Planned
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation and four of its shareholders plan to sell five million shares, raising as much as $235 million, according to a Securities and Exchange Commission filing. The maker of the popular browser for the World Wide Web part of the Internet expects to sell two million shares, while shareholders plan to sell three million. The company will sell them for as much as $47 each. The company filed with the S.E.C. after the close of trading today. Shares fell 25 cents today, to $46.125. The selling stockholders paid about $2.25 each for the shares before the company went public little more than a year ago, Netscape said. After the stock sale, there will be about 86.5 million common shares outstanding. The company plans to use proceeds for working capital and general corporate purposes. Adobe Systems Inc. is selling half of its 1.79 million shares. Knight-Ridder is selling all of its 888,892 shares, Hearst is selling 23 percent of its 888,892 shares, and TCI International, a unit of Tele-Communications Inc., is selling 1.02 million shares.

title:
NEW JERSEY DAILY BRIEFING;
Catching Up on the Web
body: After a late start, the state government sites on the World Wide Web are seeing brisk traffic, officials said Friday. The sites for Gov. Christine Todd Whitman and 19 state departments have been averaging 38,000 visits a day, said Amy Collings, a spokeswoman for the Treasury Department, which oversees the sites. The figure is a count of pages accessed, not of individual users. The Web sites, which offer information on state jobs, pollution and tourist sites, can be reached through the address http:// www.state.nj.us.ANDY NEWMAN

title: Slate Delays Fee for Readers
body: Slate, the Microsoft Corporation's on-line magazine of political commentary, has decided to delay charging its readers a subscription fee for another three months. Slate announced the move on its World Wide Web site last week in a note to readers from the editor, Michael Kinsley. Slate began publication on the Web in June. It had planned to charge readers $19.95 a year, beginning Nov. 1. But the free period will be extended until February because Microsoft has been unable to develop a workable on-line billing system, Rogers Weed, Slate's publisher, said. Some analysts said they were surprised that a software problem would delay subscription plans for Microsoft. Others noted that the decision simply emphasized that software for Internet commerce was very different from personal-computer software. About 35,000 people now regularly read Slate, a weekly, Mr. Weed estimated, while its roster of advertisers includes the FMR Corporation's Fidelity Investments, and the auto makers Toyota and Ford.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
U.S. ROBOTICS SHOWS A NEW, FASTER MODEM
body: U.S. Robotics Inc. displayed a new modem yesterday that can transmit information faster than existing devices, speeding up customers' connections to on-line services and the Internet. The new modem can send data at 56,000 bits a second, leapfrogging current models that transmit at speeds up to 33,000 bits a second. The new modem is expected to be available in January. U.S. Robotics is not the only company that has the technology, though. Lucent Technologies Inc. introduced a chip yesterday that offers the same speed and expects to ship the chip in the first quarter of 1997. Rockwell International Inc. also displayed its own 56,000 bits-per-second chip.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Group to Study On-Line Users
body: NFO Research Inc. in Greenwich, Conn., said yesterday that it had formed a panel of more than 50,000 households to provide data about consumers who use interactive and on-line media and to conduct interactive market research. The panel, named NFO//net.source, is being described as offering a representative sample of households that use the Internet, the World Wide Web and services like America Online, Compuserve and Prodigy. NFO said the panel would be available in January.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AIRLINE RESERVATIONS UNIT'S STOCK GAINS SHARPLY
body: The stock of Sabre Group Holdings Inc., the AMR Corporation's airline reservations and information system, closed 17 percent higher than its offering price on its first day of trading on the newyork Stock Exchange. The initial public offering by AMR, the parent of American Airlines, of 20.2 million shares of Sabre, or about 16 percent of the company, was priced at $27 a share. The stock closed at $31.625, after almost 10.2 million shares were traded. The offering raised about $662 million for Sabre, which intends to expand further into the information services business, where it faces stiff competition from computer systems companies like the Electronic Data Systems Corporation and the Computer Sciences Corporation.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Cybersites for News And Entertainment
body: Two companies have disclosed plans for Internet initiatives that are both scheduled to begin Monday. The Mecklermedia Corporation will introduce an Interactive Advertising Report on its Iworld magazine (http://netday.iworld.com/iar). The report will offer news, analysis and data aimed at agencies, advertisers and Web publishers. Tristan Louis, publisher of Iworld in Westport, Conn., said that Mecklermedia was talking to large computer advertisers about becoming sponsors of the report. And American Cybercast in Marina del Rey, Calif., in which companies including the Creative Artists Agency, Grey Advertising and the Intel Corporation hold stakes, will start a World Wide Web network (http://www.amcy.com) that combines two episodic series with their own Web sites, the Spot and Eon-4, with two new offerings, the Pyramid and Quick Fix Theater. Advertisers like Apple Computer Inc. that have sponsored the two series will continue; new sponsors will include Intel, the Toyota Motor Corporation and the Visa USA unit of Visa International.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AMR RAISES OFFERING PRICE FOR RESERVATION SYSTEM
body: The AMR Corporation raised the initial public offering price for its Sabre Group Holdings Inc. unit to as much as $545.4 million in a sign of strong investor demand. The parent of American Airlines raised the share price for the initial offering of its reservations system to between $25 and $27 each, according to an amended Securities and Exchange Commission filing. The company had expected to sell shares for $20 to $23 each to raise as much as $464.6 million. AMR plans to sell a 15.8 percent stake in Sabre through an offering of 20.2 million class A common shares. AMR would continue to hold 107.3 million class B shares. Under the revised prices, AMR will receive about $495 million after expenses if the shares sell for $26 each.

title: Dutch Publisher's Deal
body: The Dutch publisher Wolters Kluwer N.V. has acquired the French publisher Groupe Liaisons Investissements for an undisclosed sum. Groupe Liaisons is a 30-year-old publisher that specializes in social and fiscal law, transport and pharmacology. It also publishes material on agriculture and tourism and has distribution and audiovisual activities. The company, which is based in Paris, has annual sales of about $79 million and employs some 400 people.

title: Europe Online Returns as a Nonprofit
body: The former on-line information service Europe Online S.A., which shut down in August after going bankrupt, returned this week as a nonprofit organization promoting Europe on the Internet. "Europe Online is now a navigation service, a European gateway to the Internet," Candace Johnson, president of the company's board, said. The association, to be called Europe Online Asbl, is sponsored by Luxembourg P&T, the state telecommunications company, and was founded by former Europe Online S.A. employees. Europe Online Asbl said it was providing consumers with a user-friendly interface, easy navigation and information retrieval service for the Internet in various languages. It does not provide Internet access itself, but acts as a framework for information and content providers in Europe to put their content on the World Wide Web part of the Internet. Ms. Johnson said a number of Internet service providers had shown interest in incorporating Europe Online in their services. Membership dues and sponsors will finance the association's activities. The old Luxembourg-based company shut down in August after last-ditch talks with Deutsche Telekom and others failed to keep the operation running.

title: Executive Changes
body: DATA BROADCASTING CORP., San Mateo, Calif., named Mark Imperiale to the new positions of president and chief operating officer.  DIBA INC., Menlo Park, Calif., an Internet appliance start-up, appointed Albin Moschner, a former chief executive of the Zenith Electronics Corp., vice chairman. Mr. Moschner will be opening an office in Chicago.  HUGHES ELECTRONICS CORP., Los Angeles, a unit of General Motors, named Steven Dorfman to the new position of chairman of its telecommunications and space unit. LIZ CLAIBORNE INC., North Bergen, N.J., appointed Denise Seegal, a former executive at Calvin Klein, president of its women's apparel company, succeeding Paul Charron, who continues as chairman and chief executive.

title: Executive Changes
body: DATA BROADCASTING CORP., San Mateo, Calif., which provides financial market data to individual investors, said Mark Imperiale had been appointed president and chief operating officer. Mr. Imperiale, the chief financial officer, will hold that title until a replacement is hired.  HOLIDAY INN WORLDWIDE, newyork, a unit of Bass P.L.C., said Timothy Lane, its chairman and chief executive, had resigned after less than seven months because of a dispute with the parent company. Bryan D. Langton, who had held those positions earlier, was named to succeed him on a interim basis.  INTERNATIONAL FLAVORS AND FRAGRANCES INC., newyork, said Brian Chadbourne will take over as president on Jan. 1. Mr. Chadbourne, a former fragrance manager for the company's North American division, is replacing Hugh R. Kirkpatrick, who is retiring.  TEXAS INSTRUMENTS INC., said William B. Mitchell, its vice chairman, would retire at the end of the year. His retirement follows the naming of James R. Adams chairman and Thomas J. Engibous president and chief executive. The posts were filled after the death of Jerry R. Junkins in May.

title:
NEW JERSEY DAILY BRIEFING;
State Jobs, but Not on Paper
body: As one of the economy measures in Gov. Christine Todd Whitman's current budget, the state has stopped publishing a list of vacant Civil Service jobs. The list is available over the Internet, but two Democratic legislators say that is no help to many job-seekers who do not have access to a computer. Only 15 of the state's 400 libraries offer Internet access, the New Jersey Library Association said. Dropping the printed job bulletins saved the state $100,000. But two Assembly members, Shirley K. Turner of Ewing Township and W. Reed Gusciora of Princeton, urged yesterday that the bulletins be restored.

title:
POLITICS;
On Line: Issues '96
body: An Internet site devoted to Issues '96 is now available to computer users at http:// www.nytimes.com/issues. A collaboration by The newyork Times on the Web and National Public Radio, the site includes news coverage and background material on major campaign issues, as well as forums for discussion, interactive quizzes and links to other Internet resources for voters.

title: Don't Let Anyone Tax Internet Transactions
body: To the Editor: Your Sept. 19 Business Day article on a Treasury Department conference to address concerns about electronic money laundering and counterfeiting on the Internet raises important issues. But except for Treasury Secretary Robert E. Rubin's reference to tax evasion, you barely touch on the issue of taxing Internet transactions. Our Government and others must not go too far in regulating electronic commerce. With millions of dollars at stake, revenue-starved countries will be clamoring to tax transactions conducted over the Internet. Proposals to tax these transactions will not work. Location and jurisdiction as criteria for taxation of transactions will only create new tax havens. Another flawed policy would be to impose a regional tax on income earned worldwide or to apply a value-added tax, which would be almost impossible to enforce. Congress and its foreign counterparts need to hear about the promise of electronic commerce as well as the need to protect it through coordinated tax policies. It is better to err on the side of underregulation.  NILESH K. SHAH Costa Mesa, Calif., Sept. 23, 1996  The writer is a partner of KPMG Peat Marwick, accountants.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
LUCENT PLANS TO MAKE INTERNET PHONES ACCESSIBLE
body: Vowing to make voice and video communication over the Internet as easy to use and accessible as the telephone, Lucent Technologies Inc. introduced a business venture yesterday and several products intended to bring Internet communication into the mainstream. Lucent, the former equipment unit of the AT&T Corporation that is based in Murray Hill, N.J., said it would offer a set of products that enables high-quality voice, music and video communications over the Internet to become more widely available to businesses and consumers.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
People
body: * Paul Bonington, publisher of Web Week and Web Developer magazines, Westport, Conn., owned by the Mecklermedia Corp., was promoted to senior vice president and group publisher of the Mecklermedia magazine group. He assumes responsibilities from David Egan, the group's president and chief operating officer, who resigned.

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
Caution Urged on Offer Of International License
body: An organization called the Pan American Auto Travel Association, with a post office box in San Juan, P.R., is offering international driving permits by mail through a site on the World Wide Web although the unitedstates Department of State has authorized only two organizations to sell these permits in the unitedstates: the American Automobile Association and the American Auto Touring Alliance. Under the original United Nations convention, permits are valid only when issued in the country where the driver is licensed; the Pan American group's permits are issued by the Automobile Club of Nicaragua, according to Bob Cahill, who describes himself as owner of the Pan American club and the Nicaraguan auto club. The Web site is at www.driving-permit.com. The A.A.A. has sent a notice to its member clubs urging them to warn clients against the Web site offering. The price is $65 for a four-year permit; the two authorized groups charge $10 for one year. An international driving permit is valid only for drivers already holding driving licenses. Mr. Cahill, interviewed by telephone, said he found it unnecessary to ask applicants for the numbers of their driving licenses or the issuing state.

title:
Independent Booksellers Defy the Cyberniche;
Preservation on the Net
body: To the Editor: The graphic that accompanied "Getting a Read on Bookselling in Cyberspace" (news article, Sept. 2) neglected to mention the World Wide Web site of the Antiquarian Booksellers' Association of America. It is http://www.abaa-booknet.com. The site offers access to dealers in rare and out-of-print books. More than 175 of the 450 members of the association are on line, and many have catalogues and educational material available at their web sites. With so many books going out of print rapidly, used- and rare-book dealers are a vital component of the book market.  CAROL MALTBY Olivebridge, N.Y., Sept. 4, 1996  The writer is a partner in Wilsey Rare Books.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Accounts
body: * Dow Jones & Co., Princeton, N.J., to Hill, Holliday, Connors, Cosmopulos, Boston, to handle circulation marketing for The Wall Street Journal, which includes direct-response and image advertising. Those duties had been handled by J. Walter Thompson newyork, a unit of WPP Group. Billings were estimated at $10 million.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DIGITAL EQUIPMENT PLANS TO SPIN OFF ITS ALTAVISTA UNIT
body: The Digital Equipment Corporation said yesterday that it planned to spin off 20 percent of its Altavista Internet Software unit, which offers Altavista, a popular World Wide Web search tool. Altavista is considered one of the most powerful Internet "search engines," with access to more than 30 million Web pages. Lehman Brothers, Cowen & Company and J. P. Morgan & Company will manage the offering. Rival Internet search engine companies Yahoo and Excite have gone public in the last year, but both stocks have declined since their offerings.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NETSCAPE AGREES TO DEVELOP BROWSER FOR APPLE
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation has agreed to develop a new version of its Netscape Navigator Web browser to support two Apple Computer Inc. products, the companies said yesterday. The Apple products are Cyberdog, Apple's Internet suite, and Open Doc, a software design architecture. The Navigator is the leading browser software for conducting searches on the Internet's World Wide Web computer network. Apple, based in Cupertino, Calif.. said it has been incorporating Internet access directly into the Macintosh operating system and other applications so that computer users do not require separate stand-alone software to access the Internet.

title: Congressional Bills Belong on the Internet
body: To the Editor: Representative Rick White has introduced a resolution (H.R. 478) that would make important House documents available to citizens on the Internet. This resolution deserves our support. Although valuable legislative information has been placed online by Congress, committee prints and amendments to existing bills are generally not available to ordinary citizens. However, these documents are made available to lobbyists who often play a role in the drafting and revision of legislation. This constitutes an unfair and unwise impediment to an open democratic process. Without access to timely and accurate information about emerging legislation, we are forced into a defensive position as citizens. This was demonstrated in January when the only source of up-to-date drafts of the telecommunications bill was through the Regional Bell Operating Company's Internet site. It's time for Congress to do everything possible to bring all stakeholders into the process.  TIMOTHY R. QUIGLEY newyork, Aug. 22, 1996

title: Novell Introduces an Intranet Product
body: Novell Inc. has introduced new Intranetware software intended to establish the company in the growing market for internal corporate networks known as intranets. Novell has been a leader since 1983 in conventional networking software but has fallen behind Netscape Communications and Microsoft in the competition for intranets, which are private networks that function like the Internet's World Wide Web. Novell's Intranetware is a full-service access product for businesses of all sizes. It builds on the features of the company's Netware 4.11 network software. The latest product offers a high-performance Web browser and server software -- the software needed to access and publish Web pages -- and is intended to take advantage of the latest standards for surfing the Internet and using far-flung corporate networks. The company provides software for an estimated one million networks with 55 million users. It said Intranetware is compatible with existing Novell network software and will allow companies to preserve previous investments in network software. Novell, based in Orem, Utah, did not give prices for the software, which it plans to release in the fall.

title: Genie Online Is Acquired
body: The IDT Corporation has bought Genie Online Service, a small Internet company that provides electronic discussions and games, from the Yovelle Renaissance Corporation. Terms were not disclosed. The sale comes seven months after Genie's founder, the General Electric Company, sold the service to Yovelle. Genier was one of the first companies to offer Internet services when it was created in 1985. The service had about 20,000 customers in the unitedstates.

title: Flaw in Microsoft Explorer
body: The Microsoft Corporation's Internet Explorer 3.0, its much-promoted new software for browsing the Internet, has a flaw that affects its performance on some World Wide Web sites, a company executive says. The new version of the browser, introduced last Monday to compete with the Netscape Communications Corporation's Navigator, had been downloaded for free by more than 100,000 people by Friday, said Bill Koszewski, a Microsoft product manager. The flaw is a bug in the software that will slow users trying to access certain Web sites that require the user's name and a password, Mr. Koszewski said. Instead of saving the password and automatically resubmitting it when needed, the new browser requires users to retype their password each time they link to a new page on that site, he said.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Accounts
body: * Web TV Networks, Palo Alto, Calif., to Rubin Postaer & Associates, Santa Monica, Calif., as the first agency to handle the account of the on-line television service. Billings were estimated at $6 million to $8 million.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Internet Access to Homes Via TV Cable
body: Time Warner Cable will begin deploying Internet access service to its cable TV subscribers next month, starting with its systems in Akron and Canton, Ohio. The company has been testing Internet access through cable lines in Elmira, N.Y., for several months. Many other cable companies are also testing Internet access services. Data can be delivered at a much higher speed through a TV cable than through a telephone line. Owners of personal computers must obtain new modems to use cable for connecting to the Internet. In Akron and Canton, Time Warner Cable will offer modems from Motorola Inc. as part of its service, which begins on Sept. 10. It is expected to cost about $40 a month.

title: MFS Shareholders Approve Uunet Purchase
body: The MFS Communications Company said this weekend that its shareholders had approved the company's $2 billion acquisition of Uunet Technologies Inc., an Internet access provider. The merger of MFS, a telecommunications company based here, with Uunet, which is based in Fairfax, Va., is expected to take effect on Monday, MFS said. "MFS can now serve as a single source for a full range of voice, data, video and Internet services," James Q. Crow, the chairman of MFS, said in a statement. "Because there is substantial overlap between our networks, the merger was especially compelling from the start," he said. MFS did not provide details of the vote. Under terms of the merger that were announced when the plan was made public on April 30, each share of Uunet common stock will be exchanged for 1.78 shares of MFS common stock.

title: Times Expands Circulation Push
body: As part of an ongoing push to expand its circulation around the country, The newyork Times has entered into separate agreements with a dozen other newspapers to deliver The Times in their respective cities. The Chicago Tribune will begin delivering The Times today; the agreements with the other papers have different starting dates, and include different arrangements for delivery to homes and newsstands. The delivery agreements with the newspapers will help The Times broaden its distribution in Chicago and in parts of Colorado, Florida, Texas and Washington State.

title:
DIARY: COMPUTERS;
email, Voicemail, Telephone, Whatever
body: Visitors to the Macworld convention in Boston last week tried out Internet Phone, which allows computer users to make long-distance phone calls over the Internet. Last year, some 400,000 people regularly used the Internet to make calls, but that number may jump to 16 million by 1999, according to a forecast by the International Data Corporation.

title:
MOVIES AND THE WEB;
Good News For Consumers, Too
body: To the Editor: The greatest attributes of Internet communication are its decentralizing and democratizing features. Outsiders can now, for the first time, distribute work widely without needing approval from the large companies that guard access to commercial arenas. This is welcome news for independent film makers, as Peter M. Nichols's article notes ["For Some Directors, the Web Is Their Studio," July 28]. It is equally happy news for consumers whose taste runs outside the mainstream. A new day is dawning for artists and their fans.  RALPH HUMMEL Huntington, L.I.

title: Transit on the Web
body: To the Editor: After navigating my way to work from Queens the morning of the E train subway fire (news article, Aug. 3), I wasn't sure if the trains were back to normal when I was ready to return home. I kept calling the Metropolitan Transportation Authority's information line, but it was busy, so I decided to check the M.T.A. Web site. The schedule information that I found had not been updated in two days. With today's technology, why can't the M.T.A. offer more efficient Internet service to its customers?  SUSAN PRICE Kew Gardens, Queens, Aug. 3, 1996

title:
INTERNATIONAL BRIEFS;
Reed Elsevier Profit Rose in First Half
body: The publisher Reed Elsevier P.L.C. said yesterday that its pretax earnings rose 12 percent in the first half of 1996, driven by growth in existing businesses and continuing strong sales at its Lexis-Nexis electronic data base unit. Reed also said that it had agreed to pay £100.5 million, or $155 million, in cash for Tolley Publishing of Britain. The profit at Reed was £416 million, compared with £370 million a year earlier. The company is a 50-50 venture of Reed International of Britain and Elsevier of the Netherlands.   (Bloomberg Business News)

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MICROSOFT TO USE VERIFONE SOFTWARE IN INTERNET SYSTEM
body: The Microsoft Corporation announced an agreement yesterday with Verifone Inc., a maker of automated transaction systems, to incorporate Verifone software into Microsoft's Internet commerce product, which is to become available in the fourth quarter. Microsoft, which is based in Redmond, Wash., said it would include Verifone's so-called virtual point-of-sale software in the system. The software is intended to allow merchants doing business over the Internet to let customers safely make purchases from their personal computers, using credit cards. Verifone is based in Redwood City, Calif.

title: Times Reporter Is Honored
body: Joseph Durso, a longtime baseball writer for The newyork Times, received the 1996 J. G. Taylor Spink Award for baseball writing today at the Baseball Hall of Fame induction ceremonies. Durso, who now covers horse racing for The Times, has been an editor and writer for the paper since 1950 and a sportswriter since 1964. In presenting the award to Durso, Jerome Holtzman of The Chicago Tribune, the president of the Baseball Writers Association of America, said Durso's writing possessed an "uncommon elegance and grace." Durso is the author of 13 books, including biographies of Casey Stengel, John McGraw and Lou Gehrig, and a history of Yankee Stadium. Herb Carneal, a broadcaster for the Minnesota Twins for the past 35 years, received the 1996 Ford C. Frick Award.

title: News Corporation Revamps Internet Units
body: The News Corporation said today that it was realigning its Internet-related businesses, refocusing and expanding the entertainment-related offerings available through its Iguide Internet site and establishing a new company to offer technology services and software to the Internet industry. "By more closely aligning our Internet Web sites with News Corporation's content in news, entertainment and sports, and leveraging our technological capabilities in this way, we will be exceptionally well positioned to participate fully in the growth of the Internet industry long term," president of news technology, Greg Clark, said in a statement. The technology-related parts of the News Corporation's Internet business will be consolidated and operated by the new company, News Internet Services, or N.I.S., which will provide software and technology services to both third-party and News Corporation companies. NIS will be headed by Bharath Kadaba, executive vice president for Internet services of the News Corporation's technology group. The News Corporation's Iguide will emphasize News Corporation content, focusing on TV Guide On-line, entertainment, sports and news.

title: Ex-Sybase Executive Named Inktomi Chief
body: The Inktomi Corporation, a start-up Internet technology company, said today that it was naming David Peterschmidt, the former chief operating officer of Sybase Inc., to the post of chief executive. Inktomi said the appointment of Mr. Peterschmidt, who is 49, was a further step in efforts to bring the power of supercomputing technology to applications on the Internet. Inktomi was founded by its chief technology officer, Eric Brewer, and a former graduate student, Paul Gauthier, who jointly developed its technology at the University of California at Berkeley. The technology is intended to link desktop computers into a "network of work stations" with supercomputing capabilities. With Hotwired, the Internet arm of Wired magazine, Inktomi created Hotbot, an Internet search engine with a system that uses parallel processing, a type of supercomputing.

title: New Executive At Times Co.
body: Donald S. Schneider, a lawyer and longtime personnel executive, is joining The newyork Times Company as senior vice president for human resources. Mr. Schneider, 49, comes to the Times Company from the North American division of the Bertelsmann Entertainment Company, a division of Bertelsmann A.G., the German media giant, where he has been vice president for human resources since 1993. Before that, he had been a human resources executive for more than 20 years at Frank B. Hall & Company, Citicorp and General Electric. At the Times Company, Mr. Schneider will be responsible for all human resources functions, including employee benefits and compensation, management development and organizational structure. His appointment is effective Aug. 12. Mr. Schneider graduated from the State University of newyork at Buffalo in 1968 with a bachelor's degree in business administration, and from Syracuse University College of Law in 1972. Graphic   Photo: Donald S. Schneider

title: Intel Introduces Phone Software
body: In its quest to make the personal computer an indispensable tool, the Intel Corporation introduced software today that it said would make it easy to place long-distance phone calls over the Internet. The company said the Intel Internet Phone software was the first to allow users of different types of computers and software to connect. The software works on PC's running the Microsoft Corporation's Windows 95 operating system. Intel has also signed 120 companies that have agreed to use the standard in new products. Jeff Pulver, who wrote the "Internet Telephone Toolkit," which is expected to be published soon, and is chairman of the Voice on Internet Coalition, said Intel's breakthrough was that the software was based on open standards, and so could spur the use of the Internet for telephone calls. To insure its success, Intel is offering free copies of the software starting Wednesday on its World Wide Web site, http: //www.intel.com/iaweb/cpc. Mr. Pulver said use of the Internet to provide telephone service began when Vocaltec Ltd., a New Jersey start-up company, introduced a product in 1995.

title: Verisign Security System Is Selected by Visa
body: Visa International Inc. said yesterday that it had chosen Verisign Inc. to verify the identity of credit card users when they make purchases using the Internet. The bank credit card association is hoping that Verisign's so-called digital certificates will provide added security for purchases on the Internet, where transactions can be vulnerable to computer hackers. Verisign will operate the service for Visa, which in turn will make it available to Visa member banks. "By offering digital certificates through Verisign, Visa is working to enable its members to move cost effectively into the electronic commerce marketplace," a Visa official, Steve Herz, said.

title:
OLYMPICS;
A Site for Computer Users
body: Starting tonight, additional Olympic coverage is available to computer users from The Times's two services -- The newyork Times on the Web, at http://www.nytimes.com, and @times on America Online, including these highlights:  *Results, color photos and audio, updated during the day.  *Forums for on-line discussion with Robert Lipsyte, Times columnist.  *A daily journal by Pat Connolly, former Olympic athlete and coach.  *A collection of Times previews and coverage of the 1996 Games, and retrospectives from previous Olympics.  *A special Olympic crossword and trivia quizzes.  * An interactive calendar of events, and links to related sites.

title: Corrections
body: The Advertising column in Business Day on July 8 about Newsweek magazine's World Wide Web sites misstated the address of one site, Newsweek International. It is http: //www.newsweek-int.com.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
America Online Forms Alliance for News
body: America Online Inc. said today that it had teamed with the Tribune Company to expand the local news and services it offers to 88 local markets on the Internet. The venture, dubbed Digital City, already operates in Washington, Boston and San Francisco, providing America Online members with information on local news, weather, sports, traffic conditions and local events. Tribune will help America Online begin local information services in Chicago, southern Florida and Hampton Roads, Va., where Tribune currently publishes newspapers. Financial details of the alliance were not disclosed, but The Wall Street Journal reported the venture was expected to require a $100 million investment. Chicago-based Tribune is expected to take a 20 percent stake in Digital Cities, putting up roughly $20 million, The Journal said. The Digital Cities initiative was started last fall by America Online, based in Dulles, Va.

title: What Price Cable's Internet Gift to Schools?
body: To the Editor: It is with astonishment that I read your July 14 editorial endorsing the cable television industry's decision to give schools high-speed Internet access. Even those who once trumpeted the information age have begun asking the difficult questions ignored by the software companies and media conglomerates so eager to get us all connected. It is strange that you take the cable industry's "gift to schools" at face value, failing to hint at what might be transmitted over the cables. Will it be free, open and democratic information, or will those who can afford to produce the glitziest, highest-resolution and fastest-downloading products have a monopoly? Will this new medium be bilateral and participatory in the tradition of classrooms, or unilateral and unresponsive in the tradition of television? Will there be advertising? Compare the contents of cable television today to what was promised 20 years ago as a beginning inquiry. It would be ignorant to deny the importance of the Internet or to try to halt its progress. However, some skepticism would be in order concerning this farming-out of education to commercial interests.  KONRAD SIEWIERSKI Sunbury, Ohio, July 14, 1996

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ORACLE TO DISCUSS DETAILS ON INTRANETS
body: The Oracle Corporation plans to provide details today about its strategy for software that would allow corporations to build intranets, following both the Microsoft Corporation and the Netscape Communications Corporation. Based on Internet technology, intranets permit corporations to distribute information more efficiently to employees and to build corporatewide messaging and conferencing systems. Oracle executives said the company, based in Redwood Shores, Calif., had an advantage in such areas as the distribution of video and text retrieval as well as database retrieval and transaction processing. Computer-industry analysts believe that the market for corporate intranets will be at least as lucrative as the current Internet market.

title: Netscape Program to Get Tighter Security
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation said today that the Government had granted the company permission to distribute within this country a version of its popular Navigator browser software containing substantially stronger encryption technology. Coding software is used by Internet browser programs to provide secure channels to transmit information like credit-card and banking data. Current unitedstates rules limit software exports to products with mathematical encryption keys of up to 40 bits in length. Computer experts in the unitedstates and Europe have shown that such key lengths are vulnerable to attack by networks of fast computers. Under the agreement with the Government, Netscape will, beginning on Tuesday, place versions of its software with a 128-bit key on its site on the World Wide Web. unitedstates citizens living in this country will be able to download the software to their computers. Netscape, which is based in Mountain View, Calif., said that the longer mathematical key would make scrambled information significantly more difficult to decode.

title: Have We Forgotten Pinko Space Aliens?
body: To the Editor: While it may turn out in a sequel to "Independence Day" that Microsoft was behind some intergalactic conspiracy to market Windows 2000 (editorial, July 10), the concern expressed by Jeff Greenfield of ABC about computer compatibility in the 1990's may not be so far-fetched. If you appreciate the technology of the Internet and the World Wide Web, it's not to hard to imagine a hacker from an alien civilization desiring to create and connect to the Galaxy Wide Web, if only to observe a cross-section of terrestrial intelligent life rather than to destroy it. Furthermore, given the rush to merge the communications businesses with computing, compatibility of most information technology may not be far off. After all, E. T. did phone home.  DANIEL FARKAS Pleasantville, N.Y., July 10, 1996  The writer is chairman, information systems department, Pace U.

title:
Careful Employers Should Curb Internet Access;
Dire Consequences
body: To the Editor: Walter Olson (Op-Ed, July 7) highlights the growing danger of harassment charges brought by employees offended by racial or sexual messages they encounter on the Internet. As a principal shareholder in a small company that provides Internet access, I am concerned that my company will someday be forced to censor the ideas available to its customers to avoid paying lottery-size damages to offended employees. Lower courts in California and New Jersey have held that harassment laws allow anyone, not simply employers, to be sued if certain speech "aids" or "abets" the creation of a "hostile work environment." This has potentially dire consequences for Internet access providers, since their product is speech, and workplace clients generate most of their revenue.  LARS BADER newyork, July 9, 1996

title: GTE, With Uunet, Signs On to the Internet
body: GTE, the largest local telephone company, introduced a national Internet access service yesterday with help from Uunet Technologies Inc., which also connects the big on-line services to the global network. GTE follows other big phone companies into the Internet access business, moving a bit more slowly to avoid the explosion in supply that hurt other providers, notably AT&T. GTE first tested Internet services in the Dallas-Fort Worth area last winter. It decided to form a partnership with Uunet nationwide because of that company's network and performance record. Financial terms of the relationship were not disclosed. Uunet connects more businesses to the Internet than anyone else, using higher-capacity lines than are typically available to consumers. GTE will charge $19.95 a month for unlimited dial-up access to the Internet, and give customers a second billing option of $8.95 a month for five hours of access plus $1.95 for each additional hour -- rates comparable to those charged by other providers.

title: A Start-Up Gets Licensing Deal
body: Sony Electronics Inc. and the Philips Consumer Electronics Company have decided to license technology from a Palo Alto, Calif., start-up company, Webtv Networks,for a set-top box for viewing the Internet Webtv was founded in June 1995 by three former Apple technology developers, Steve Perlman, Bruce Leak and Phil Goldman. The company plans to provide low-cost Internet information to home television users, who will initially connect their television sets to the Internet and retrieve information. The device can be controlled either by an infrared hand-held controller or an optional keyboard. Webtv officials said their goal was to offer a more "TV like" experience for viewing Internet web sites. They said their licensees were planning to bring out products this fall and that prices would likely be below the $500 target for the so-called network computer. Webtv has backing from a number of venture capital firms and from Paul Allen, the co-founder of Microsoft, and Marvin Davis.

title: Brewer Plans a Stock Offering on Internet
body: The Spring Street Brewing Company said yesterday that it planned to raise $3.3 million through an Internet stock offering, joining a handful of entrepreneurs using the global computer network to sell shares directly to the public. The brewing company, which is based in newyork, said it filed plans with the Securities and Exchange Commission for approval to sell about 1.2 million shares at $2.75 each to investors through the company's home page on the World Wide Web. Investors wishing to purchase shares must reach Spring Street's Web page, fill out the application and send their payments directly to the company. A company spokesman said it hoped for S.E.C. approval to offer the shares within two months. The microbrewery first offered shares last year through an initial public stock offering promoted on the Internet and on six-packs of its Wit beer. It was the first stock offering conducted through the Internet. By offering stock via the Internet, the company says it lets investors buy shares without paying commissions to Wall Street underwriters.

title: Helping Stop Crime Via a Police Web Site
body: newyorkers can now help the state police solve crimes via the Internet. The state police began a site on the World Wide Web today, offering mug shots of the state's "12 Most Wanted" suspects, as well as information about three unsolved crimes. "We're asking the public to help the police fight crime," said Lieut. Col. Ray Dutcher of the state police. "The more information we can get out, the bigger advantage we have in fighting crime." Information on developing investigations can also be updated much more quickly on the Internet than through television or newspapers, Colonel Dutcher said. The site, http://nyslgti.gen.ny.us/nystate/NYSP/, also provides a history of the state police, addresses of state police offices, crime statistics and information on how to become a state trooper.

title: Publisher Burda to Sell Europe Online Stake
body: The German publisher Burda G.m.b.H. said today that it planned to sell its 36 percent stake in Europe Online S.A., an Internet service provider. Burda said it had been pressing Europe Online to change its management structure to streamline decision making. "We feel that it is no longer economically viable to keep putting capital and creativity into a project that is so complicated to navigate," a spokesman for Burda, Philipp Welte, said. He said Burda planned to concentrate on developing its own Internet service for the German market. Officials of Europe Online, who insisted on not being identified, said the company, which is based in Luxembourg, was negotiating with potential investors.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
INDIVIDUAL BUYS NEWS SERVICE FOR $38 MILLION
body: Individual Inc. said yesterday that it had acquired Freeloader Inc. for about $38 million in cash and stock. Freeloader, based in Washington, is a personalized news service that retrieves information from the Internet's World Wide Web and delivers it to the personal computers of subscribers. Individual, based in Burlington, Mass., paid $2 million in cash and 1.9 million common shares for all Freeloader stock outstanding. Individual's stock fell $1.50 a share, to $15.75, in Nasdaq trading. Individual plans to integrate Freeloader's technology with its other customized news services.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
BBN TO SELL MAJORITY STAKE IN SOFTWARE UNIT
body: The BBN Corporation, a provider of Internet access, agreed yesterday to sell a majority stake in its software-making unit, the BBN Domain Corporation, to an investment group led by ABS Capital Partners, which will buy $36 million worth of preferred stock in Domain. BBN, which changed its name late last year from Bolt Beranek & Newman, said it would retain a minority interest of 15 percent of the voting stock of Domain, which is based in Cambridge, Mass. ABS Capital, which is privately held, is based in Baltimore.

title:
TV NOTES;
WNYC-TV Signs Off
body: The public television station WNYC-TV ceased to exist this week, replaced by WBIS-TV, the new outlet formed by ITT and Dow Jones, the partnership that purchased the license of WNYC-TV from the city of newyork for $207 million. So far, the new station has been running only old sports events from the Classic Sports Network. Its new programming format begins in the fall. The two partners will supply the programs: business news all day, from Dow Jones, and sports events in the evening, from ITT, the owner of Madison Square Garden and its principle residents, the Knicks and the Rangers. Roger May, a corporate spokesman for Dow Jones, said yesterday that both teams would appear on WBIS, along with some entertainment programming supplied by ITT, including shows from Caesar's Palace. The switch-over to WBIS took place on Monday. It followed months of opposition from several groups that fought to keep their regular programs, many in foreign languages, on the channel.

title: Psinet to Sell Consumer Internet Division
body: Psinet Inc., one of the country's largest Internet service providers, said yesterday that it would sell its consumer Internet subscriber base of about 100,000 customers and a support center to Mindspring Enterprises Inc. of Atlanta for $23 million. The deal will allow Psinet, based in Herndon, Va., to concentrate on its more profitable corporate customers. Psinet had offered individual Internet access accounts under the Pipeline and Interramp brands. Psinet said it would provide partial financing for the deal until Mindspring can hold a second stock offering this year. Psinet has also been hired by Mindspring to continue providing network services to Pipeline and Interramp customers.
