Mindspring has about 30,000 subscribers in nine Southeastern states and the District of Columbia. Mindspring's principal shareholder is ITC Holding Company of West Point, Ga., formed by two independent companies, the Interstate Telephone Company and the Valley Telephone Company. Shares of Psinet rose 20 cents, to $11.625. Shares of Mindspring rose 50 cents, to $11.125, in Nasdaq trading.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
EXCITE AND MCKINLEY TO COMBINE INTERNET DIRECTORIES
body: Excite Inc. said yesterday that it had agreed to acquire the McKinley Group, the creator of the Magellan Internet guide, in the first consolidation of leading Internet directories. The companies said the deal, valued at $18 million, would position Excite as the second-largest Internet search and directory service, behind Yahoo Inc., which pioneered the concept two years ago. Excite, based in Mountain View, Calif., said that the deal would combine its reviews of 60,000 sites on the World Wide Web with 40,000 on Magellan. Under the preliminary agreement, Excite will trade 1.2 million of its shares for the closely held McKinley, based on its stock price in the last 30 days, and assume an unspecified amount of debt. Shares of Excite fell 25 cents, to $8.25, well below their initial public offering price of $17 a share in April.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Ad Group Begins New Media Award
body: The Coalition for Advertising Supported Information and Entertainment, a joint venture of the Association of National Advertisers and the American Association of Advertising Agencies focusing on the new media, plans to begin an annual awards competition for effective advertising and marketing on the Internet and the World Wide Web. The Casie Awards will be presented for the best interactive advertising campaign and the best advertiser Web site. The initial awards will be announced during the 1996 annual meeting of the advertiser association, Oct. 4-7 at Amelia Island, Fla.

title:
100 YEARS (1896-1996);
A Life of The Times: 4 Shows
body: How the old New-York Times became the modern newyork Times is a story that began in 1896 when a publisher from Tennessee, Adolph S. Ochs, bought the newspaper, dropped the hyphen and, without fear or faintheartedness, began a revolution in daily journalism. The details of Ochs's purchase, and the history of The Times and its century, are told in exhibitions that open today and tomorrow at four newyork cultural institutions. The Museum of Natural History's exhibition of science writing in The Times was reviewed yesterday. The other shows focus on photography, at the Museum of Modern Art; and the Times and Ochs archives, at the Pierpont Morgan Libary and the newyork Public Library.

title: Cybergold Plans New Marketing Approach
body: In an effort to use the Internet to cut out the middleman between advertiser and consumer, a new company, Cybergold Inc., plans to announce Monday an on-line approach to marketing and advertising that will permit advertisers to pay potential customers for reading their ads. A start-up venture founded by the veteran Silicon Valley entrepreneur Nat Goldhaber, Cybergold is creating a World Wide Web site that will permit companies to pay for "attention." Users will be sought to join the no-fee service, fill out a questionnaire and then receive fees that are a cross between currency and coupons that can be spent on services and merchandise, on-line connection time to subscriptions or merchandise purchased directly from some other Internet sites. Mr. Goldhaber, the president of a joint venture between Apple Computer Inc. and I.B.M., said he believed that advertisers would be attracted by the ability to reach a targeted audience and the assurance that their message was being received. "We've created the first marketplace for attention," Mr. Goldhaber said.

title: Times Expects Steady 2d-Quarter Earnings
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it expected its second-quarter earnings, excluding a one-time gain on a real estate transaction, to approximate its results in the comparable 1995 quarter. The latest results will include a charge against earnings for employee severance. In the second quarter of 1995, the Times Company earned 45 cents a share. The company said the expected results for the latest quarter were in line with management's expectations. Wall Street had been forecasting about 49 cents a share in the second quarter, based on the average estimate of nine analysts surveyed by Zacks Investment Research. Shares of the Times Company fell 37.5 cents yesterday, closing at $30.75 on the American Stock Exchange. On Tuesday, the Times Company said it had sold a building at 110 Fifth Avenue in Manhattan for an undisclosed price; the company did not disclose the gain from that sale.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Softbank Awarded Interactive Work
body: Two companies have named Softbank Interactive Marketing in newyork to handle interactive advertising accounts. NBC Interactive Media, which oversees the on-line activities of the NBC unit of the General Electric Company, named Softbank to sell advertising and sponsorships on its Olympic World Wide Web site (http://www.olympic.nbc.com). And the Netscape Communications Corporation in Mountain View, Calif., which provides software for the Internet, selected the media sales division of Softbank Interactive to handle sales for technology, business-to-business and financial services accounts on Netscape's Web site. Softbank Interactive is a joint venture of the Softbank Corporation, Interactive Marketing Inc. and Network 1.0.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AMERICA ONLINE TO SELL ADVERTISING FOR NETSCAPE SITE
body: America Online Inc. said yesterday that it and the Netscape Communications Corporation were forming an unusual arrangement in which America Online sales representatives would also sell advertising space on Netscape's World Wide Web site. Netscape has one of the most popular sites on the Web, allowing visitors to download its Navigator software, which helps users browse the Web. Analysts said they expected the deal to bring in more revenues for America Online.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MCI AND INTEL TEAM UP TO SELL WEB PRODUCTS
body: The MCI Communications Corporation and the Intel Corporation teamed up yesterday to sell a combination of products and services that are aimed at helping businesses publish information on the World Wide Web. MCI planned to market the product, called NetworkMCI Webmaker, to small and medium-sized businesses. At a starting price of about $10,000, businesses could purchase preconfigured computers, based on Intel's Pentium Pro chip, and software to establish a secure Internet presence. MCI and Intel hope to save companies the trouble of assembling various communications links, computers and other products themselves.

title:
NEW JERSEY DAILY BRIEFING;
Web-Ripened Tomatoes?
body: People with visions of 4.5-pound tomatoes dancing in their heads ought to put their plants in the ground now if they hope to grow New Jersey's biggest tomato, Joe Heimbold, who has organized the state's annual tomato-growing contest since its inception in 1978, said Saturday. This year, Mr. Heimbold is offering growers help by way of a page on the Internet. Mr. Heimbold's web site is http:// www.njtomato.com. The winner will be announced on Aug. 24.   TERRY PRISTIN

title: On Line: A Bosnia Gallery
body: "Bosnia: Uncertain Paths to Peace," an interactive photo essay and international discussion examining the aftermath of the war in Bosnia, begins today on the Internet as a special report by The newyork Times on the Web. The project, available at http://www.nytimes.com/bosnia, features a gallery of 150 pictures by the French photojournalist Gilles Peress that chronicle the last weeks of the siege of Sarajevo in February and March and the exodus of Serbs from the city's suburbs. In addition, for the next month, The Times on the Web will offer on-line discussion groups on a dozen themes related to war and peace in the former Yugoslavia. The forums, open to all Internet users, will be led by hosts including Madeleine K. Albright, unitedstates delegate to the United Nations, and scholars, artists and other experts. A collection of background material, including audio reports, maps, chronologies, links to Internet resources and recent Bosnia coverage from The Times, will also be available.

title: Correction
body: An article on May 19 about software that permits voice communications over the Internet referred incorrectly to the technology of the leading commercial on-line services. Because of technical changes, Compuserve and America Online now permit users of some computers to communicate by voice.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
IDT IN FINAL NEGOTIATIONS TO TAKE OVER ECONOPHONE
body: The IDT Corporation, which provides international telephone and Internet services, said yesterday that it was negotiating the final terms of a deal to acquire Econophone Inc. Econophone, a closely held newyork City-based company, provides full telephone services in the unitedstates and long-distance service in Britain. It had annualized telecommunications revenue of about $50 million as of June 3. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. IDT, based in Hackensack, N.J., said its strategy was to bundle telephone service with Internet access and expand its overseas Internet operations.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Buys Distributor
body: City and Suburban Delivery Systems Inc., a subsidiary of The newyork Times Company, said yesterday that it had bought Imperial Delivery Service Inc., a newspaper wholesaler that distributes newspapers and other periodicals throughout Long Island and Westchester and Fairfield counties. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed. City and Suburban is the major distributor of The Times in metropolitan newyork. John R. O'Reilly, City and Suburban's president, said in a statement that the acquisition would allow the company to expand its newspaper delivery, sales and merchandising coverage to roughly 85 percent of the greater newyork market.

title:
Currents;
A New Web Site For Coping Parents
body: PARENTS of children with disabilities now have a central clearing house on the Internet. Last month, the Waisman Center, a research center for mental retardation at the University of Wisconsin at Madison, introduced its Family Village Web site. Designed to put parents in touch with one another, it has resources for 400 conditions, from autism to spina bifida. Pam Wilson, who lives in Renton, Wash., has a 12-year-old son with Down's syndrome and diabetes. Ms. Wilson has found comfort through the site, chatting with another parent whose child also has both disabilities. Through the site, Linda Rowley, its project director, donated her son's outgrown wheelchair to a girl in Poland. (LOT Polish Airlines flew it to Warsaw for free.) The address is http://www.familyvillage.wisc.edu.

title:
SPORTS PEOPLE: TELEVISION;
New Station Chooses President
body: CAROLYN WALL has been named president of WBIS+, the business and sports channel owned by ITT, co-owner of Madison Square Garden, and Dow Jones & Company, that will be in operation by the end of the year. The station, formerly WNYC-TV/Channel 31, will carry financial programs, entertainment, plus some Knick and Ranger games that would be on the MSG Network, and some Yankee games that are now broadcast by WPIX-TV. "We have a mix of programming that lets us be broadly viewed, powerful names with brand recognition and we're a local station, which gives us immediacy," said Wall, a former general manager of WNYW-TV/Channel 5. WBIS will be run at first as a local station; later, its owners plan to make it a nationally distributed cable superstation. The purchase of WNYC was protested by viewers who feared the loss of its unique ethnic programming.

title: Bettina Bancroft, 55, a Dow Jones Director
body: Bettina Bancroft, a former director of Dow Jones & Company, which publishes The Wall Street Journal and Barron's magazine, died on Tuesday, at her Los Angeles home. Ms. Bancroft, who was 55, also had a residence in Manhattan, where she was involved in foundation work. The cause was cancer, her husband, Andrew Klink, said. A great-granddaughter of Clarence W. Barron, who bought Dow Jones in 1902 from a co-founder, Charles H. Dow, she became a director in 1982 to represent the Bancroft and Barron family descendants. She retired from the board in April, but remained a director of the Dow Jones Foundation. In addition to her husband, she is survived by her mother, Bettina Gray of Rancho Santa Fe, Calif.; a daughter, Elisabeth Goth of Del Mar, Calif.; three brothers, Christopher Bancroft of Denton, Tex., Hugh Bancroft 3d of Aspen, Colo., and William P. Liscomb 3d of Carlsbad, Calif., and a sister, Kathryn Kavadas of Waban, Mass. A previous marriage, to Michael R. Goth, ended in divorce in 1974. A son, Michael B. Goth, died in 1990.

title: Investors Bid Up Internet Stock
body: Shares of Open Market Inc.  more than doubled yesterday in the first day of trading for the developer of software to expedite Internet commerce. The stock soared $21.875 from its initial public offering price of $18 a share, closing at $39.875 in Nasdaq trading. Open Market, which is based in Cambridge, Mass., sold 4 million shares at $18 to raise $72 million. The sale represents a 15 percent stake. Open Market provides server computers and software that let businesses and individuals clear and execute business transactions on the global computer network. Incorporated in 1993, Open Market had a loss of $13.9 million last year on $1.8 million in revenue. The company had $3.7 million in cash at Dec. 31. Advance Publications Inc., the parent company of the Random House publishing giant and Conde Nast magazines, owns 1.7 million Open Market shares. The Tribune Company of Chicago owns 1.8 million shares. Shikhar Ghosh, a founder of Open Market and its chairman, owns roughly 3.6 million shares.

title: AT&T Worldnet Growing
body: The AT&T Corporation has signed up 150,000 people for its Internet access service, the company said yesterday. It was the first specific statement from AT&T on the progress of the service, which was announced on Feb. 27 and went into operation on March 14. "We were surprised and delighted by this huge response," the vice president of AT&T Worldnet service, Tom Evslin, said in a statement. AT&T provides its long-distance customers with up to five hours of free on-line access a month; it charges $20 a month for unlimited use.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
CHARTER COMMUNICATIONS TO ACQUIRE OVERLOOK
body: Charter Communications International Inc. agreed yesterday to buy Overlook Communications International Inc., a closely held long-distance provider, for about 40 percent of its stock, worth about $55 million. The merger would give Overlook access to the Latin American market through Charter's satellite links and would allow Charter to expand its domestic Internet-access business to Atlanta, said David Olson, chairman and chief executive of Charter. Charter's shares jumped $2.75, to $9.25, in Nasdaq trading. The shares, 92 percent of which are held by insiders, have risen from a low of 37.5 cents in December, when Mr. Olson and other investors activated the shell company by purchasing an Internet service provider. Overlook buys long-distance service in bulk.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times National Edition To Expand Sunday Sales
body: The newyork Times will begin publishing an early version of the national edition of its Sunday newspaper, to be printed at midday on Saturdays, for distribution outside the Northeast. The move, starting this weekend, is aimed at making the Sunday newspaper more widely available across the country. The early national edition is expected to be distributed on Saturday afternoons and evenings to some airports and major newsstands and the next morning to many more cities and towns. In addition, The newyork Times Company said yesterday that the newspaper would print a later version of its Sunday national edition, to be distributed on Sunday mornings in major cities outside the Northeast. This edition will go to press at 11 P.M., Eastern time, enabling it to include late news and sports scores.

title: Times Co. in Deal to Buy 2 TV Stations
body: The newyork Times Company announced yesterday that it had reached a preliminary agreement to buy television stations in Oklahoma City and Des Moines from Palmer Communications Inc. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. The stations, both NBC affiliates, are KFOR-TV in Oklahoma City and WHO-TV in Des Moines. The cities rank 43d and 72d, respectively, among the nation's television markets. Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, chairman and chief executive of the Times Company, described the acquisitions as "another step in our business strategy to increase our holdings in electronic media." The acquisition will bring to eight the number of network-affiliated television stations in the Times Company's broadcast group, which also includes two radio stations and a video production company. In addition to broadcasting, the Times Company publishes The newyork Times, The Boston Globe and 21 regional newspapers and has interests in magazines, news and photo services and electronic publishing.

title: Internet Monitors Can Aim at Workers
body: A software program intended to help network administrators spot anyone using Internet resources to an unusual degree can also be used to monitor an employee's cyberspace activities. Optimal Networks of Mountain View, Calif., plans to release a test version of its monitoring software that will track every World Wide Web site, news group or file-transfer location an employee visits, and record the size of each file downloaded. "We're giving employers something like an itemized phone bill," John Graham-Cumming of Optimal said. "The spinoff is that they can see what the employees are doing." Sequel Technology of Toronto is testing a program specifically intended to monitor employee Internet use called Access Manager.

title: Psinet Opts to Focus on Higher-End Market
body: Psinet Inc., the Internet access provider based in Herndon, Va., said Friday that it was reorganizing its business to focus on higher-cost consumer Internet access, in a move responding to the AT&T Corporation's entry into the market. Psinet said it would stop providing its $9-a-month Pipeline service, but it would keep its $19 and $29 monthly services, with a new service aimed at experienced Net users. As a result, the company said it would lay off 15 percent of its work force, or about 85 employees, because focusing on the higher end of the market required a smaller work force. William Schrader, chairman and chief executive of Psinet, said that he did not expect any charges to earnings as a result of the action and that he expected the move to benefit third- and fourth-quarter earnings. He also said that many analysts had been predicting that with AT&T's entry into the low-end consumer Internet access market, with its five free hours a month, many consumers would leave their current Internet access providers for AT&T.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Arnold Snares A Nynex Account
body: The Nynex Information Resources unit of the Nynex Corporation in Middleton, Mass., named Arnold Communications in Boston as the first agency to handle advertising for Big Yellow, an on-line shopping directory on the World Wide Web that is operated by Nynex Information Technologies. Though billings were not disclosed, Advertising Age estimated them at $10 million, with the potential to increase to more than $50 million "in coming years." Arnold was awarded the account after a four-month review that also included Hill, Holliday, Connors, Cosmopulos in Boston and three agencies in newyork: Kirshenbaum Bond & Partners; Poppe Tyson, a unit of Bozell, Jacobs, Kenyon & Eckhardt, and Warwick Baker & Fiore. And the A. T. Cross Company in Lincoln, R.I., the marketer of pens and pencils, named Pagano Schenck & Kay in Boston as its agency of record after that shop had worked on a project for the Metropolis line of pens. Billings were estimated at $7 million to $10 million. Hill, Holliday, Connors, Cosmopulos had served as agency of record for the last seven years; Pagano Schenck was selected without a formal review.

title: Cyberspace for All
body: To the Editor: Your May 6 Business Day lead feature is right: age has no limits in cyberspace. As a 63-year-old grandmother, I have taught myself hyper text markup language, the World Wide Web coding scheme, and am designing sites for the Web. The possibilities are unlimited for any age to learn this technology. Your piece suggests that we seniors are not into this new field. We are.  CAROL HENRY Southbury, Conn., May 6, 1996

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
DIANA SHARES RISE ON WORD OF INTERNET DEAL
body: The shares of the Diana Corporation rose by one-third yesterday after the company's Sattel Communications unit agreed to supply communications lines for Internet services to the Concentric Network Corporation for undisclosed terms. With the agreement, Diana became the latest stock investors have embraced amid the frenzy over the Internet. "Breathe the word 'Internet' around a stock and anything can happen," said Tom Pincince, senior analyst at Forrester Research. The shares rose $17.25, to $66, on the newyork Stock Exchange before trading was halted. Sattel will supply high-speed communications lines and services to about 21 sites in the unitedstates for Concentric Network, which is based in Cupertino, Calif.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
America Online Gains on Report
body: The shares of America Online Inc. climbed yesterday, assisted by a report that it planned to team up with a Japanese company to offer Internet access service in Japan by the end of the year. The Kyodo news agency in Japan reported over the weekend that America Online would form a joint venture with Mitsui & Company to offer Japanese-language Internet services. An America Online spokeswoman declined to comment. Shares of America Online rose $5.25, to $67.875, in Nasdaq trading of more than three million shares. The company expects to have more than a million subscriptions in Japan in the next two years, Kyodo reported. The Japanese on-line companies, the Nifty Corporation, a joint venture of Fujitsu Ltd. and the Nissho Iwai Corporation, and PC-Van, a unit of the NEC Corporation, each have about 1.5 million subscribers, it said. Kyodo quoted industry sources as saying that America Online planned to expand into India and Australia.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
EDIFY STOCK DOUBLES ON FIRST DAY OF TRADING
body: The stock of the Edify Corporation closed yesterday at more than twice its offering price after its first day of trading. The company, a software concern in Santa Clara, Calif., sold 2.5 million shares at $15 each late on Thursday. The stock opened yesterday at $31 on the Nasdaq stock market, rose to $34.50 and finished the day at $33.75. Edify develops software that lets companies provide automated services through the Internet, Web browsers, telephones and electronic mail.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
FORMER CHIEF OF DELPHI ON-LINE SERVICE BUYS IT BACK
body: Three years after the News Corporation bought the Delphi on-line service, the former chief executive of Delphi has bought it back for an undisclosed price. The executive, Dan Bruns, who left Delphi two years ago, led a team of entrepreneurs who jumped at the chance to buy it back earlier this year, around the same time as the News Corporation's Internet joint venture with MCI Communications fell apart. Mr. Bruns announced his return to Delphi subscribers, whose numbers have been dwindling, on line this week.

title:
Sunday April 28, 1996: YUMMY ALGAE IS NETTED;
Skimming The Pond
body: You can't buy Super Blue Green Algae in stores. It and related pond harvests produced by a company called Cell Tech in Klamath Falls, Ore., are sold only by 300,000 independent distributors, much the way Amway sells soap. But you can find the algae that is fished out of Upper Klamath Lake and hawked as a nutritional supplement on the Internet. For salesmen once constrained by door knockers, the Internet has proved fertile ground. In fact, it has engendered a new breed of peddlers, who may or may not be licensed to sell what they're selling. Many of the supposed Cell Tech distributors who have taken to the Net in droves, proselytizing about the benefits of Aphanizomenon flos-aquae at $14.50 and up a bottle, aren't authorized distributors at all. The company says it has approved just 20 distributors to use sites on the World Wide Web and is in the process of rooting out the hundreds of impostors who have set up shop on line.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
SPYGLASS TO BUY 2 INTERNET BROWSER COMPANIES
body: Spyglass Inc. said yesterday that it was buying Surfwatch Software and the OS Technologies Corporation, bolstering its position as a leading developer of Internet browser software. Spyglass, based in Naperville, Ill., confirmed it had a definitive agreement to acquire Surfwatch for $12.6 million. Surfwatch, which sells software that allows PC users to block out undesirable Internet sites, is a privately held company based in Los Altos, Calif. Privately held OS Technologies develops and licenses World Wide Web conferencing technologies. Terms of that deal were not disclosed. Surfwatch will become the core of the Spyglass West Coast research and development organization. OS, based in Townsend, Mass., will become part of Spyglass's East Coast unit.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Accounts
body: Wit Capital Corp., newyork, to Mezzina/Brown Inc., and M/B Interactive, newyork, to handle advertising and marketing and develop World Wide Web programming for the investment bank and brokerage firm, in exchange for Mezzina/ Brown's receiving an undisclosed equity stake in Wit. The billings were not disclosed.

title: Lexis-Nexis to Carry Bloomberg Services
body: Lexis-Nexis, one of the world's largest providers of on-line information, and Bloomberg L.P. are expected to announce today an alliance that will provide Bloomberg's business news and daily market summaries to more than 750,000 Lexis-Nexis subscribers, beginning in the second half of this year. Bloomberg's news and analysis services are currently sent electronically to more than 55,000 specialized computer terminals used by brokerages, newspapers and other business news consumers. Under terms of the deal to be announced today, the same Bloomberg information, delayed 12 hours, will be made available to Lexis-Nexis subscribers for a fee that has not yet been determined. The addition of Bloomberg news services is the latest in a string of alliances for Lexis-Nexis, whose customers are primarily in legal, business or government offices. In the past year, Lexis-Nexis, a Dayton, Ohio-based division of Reed Elsevier P.L.C., has also agreed to carry information provided electronically by the Dun & Bradstreet Corporation and CNN, a unit of the Turner Broadcasting System. The financial terms of today's agreement have not been disclosed.

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: FLATBUSH: UPDATE;
Library Is On Line
body: The Brooklyn Public Library took a fledgling step onto the information superhighway last week when its Flatbush branch began offering Internet access to the public. The library system purchased a dozen computers for the Flatbush branch, at 22 Linden Boulevard, with a $150,000 donation from Bill Gates, the chairman and chief executive officer of Microsoft Corporation. Mr. Gates made a virtual appearance at the library over a modem hookup when the computers came on line last week. The Flatbush branch, open every day but Sunday, is the first of the Brooklyn Public Library system's 60 branches to offer free Internet access to the public. The Business Library in Brooklyn Heights allows only library staff to search the Internet.   SOMINI SENGUPTA

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
COMPAQ IN CLOSER TIE WITH INTERNET SECURITY CONCERN
body: The Compaq Computer Corporation will incorporate network security software by Raptor Systems Inc. into its computers, the companies said yesterday. In Nasdaq trading yesterday, shares of Raptor rose $3.375, to $32.625. Financial terms of the arrangement, which builds on an existing relationship, were not disclosed. But Raptor stands to grow rapidly if Compaq deploys its software broadly. Raptor lost $2.6 million on $3.9 million in sales last year. Compaq intends to use Raptor's EagleNT software in machines that companies want to work with both internal corporate networks and the Internet.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
BELL & HOWELL TO USE THE INTERNET FOR ITS MEETING
body: Bell & Howell Company said yesterday that it would supplement its first annual shareholders meeting in Ann Arbor, Mich. with a first-of-its-kind session on the Internet. The Skokie, Ill., supplier of information-access products will provide a live interactive audio feed of the meeting on May 16 to shareholders who connect electronically through its site on the World Wide Web (http://www.bellhowell.com).

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
BELL ATLANTIC TO OFFER INTERNET ACCESS
body: The Bell Atlantic Corporation jumped on the Internet bandwagon yesterday, saying it would offer access to the global computer network next month. The Baby Bell, which is based in Philadelphia, signed a licensing agreement with the Netscape Communications Corporation for Internet browsing software. It also said it planned to offer a version of the Microsoft Corporation's on-line service, Microsoft Network. Bell Atlantic joins the AT&T Corporation, the MCI Communications Corporation and the Nynex Corporation in establishing an Internet strategy. Bell Atlantic shares rose $1.25 each, to $61.25. Netscape gained $3.25, to $52.50.

title: Utility Entering A New Business
body: The Central and South West Corporation won approval today from the Federal Communications Commission to be the first electric utility to enter the telecommunications business under the new telecommunications law. The recently enacted law shatters 62-year old barriers and permits local and long-distance phone companies, cable-television operators, and TV broadcasters to invade each other's turf. It also permits electric utility companies to offer phone, cable-TV and other communications services. Central and South West, based in Dallas, said it could eventually offer cable-TV, phone, electronic banking, Internet access and other services over its own fiber optic lines, or lease spare space on the lines to other telecommunications companies. "As a company, we haven't ruled anything out," said Mark Menezes, the director of Federal agency relations. "We're looking at all of our options." The company operates electric utilities in Arkansas, Texas, Louisiana and Oklahoma.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Herald Tribune Appoints Editor
body: Michael Getler, the deputy managing editor of The Washington Post, will become the executive editor of The International Herald Tribune in July, the Paris-based newspaper announced yesterday. Mr. Getler will succeed John Vinocur, a former reporter and editor for The newyork Times, who has run the news operations of The Herald Tribune for 10 years. Mr. Vinocur will become the newspaper's senior correspondent, reporting in Europe and Asia. Mr. Getler, 60, will join The Herald Tribune after a 26-year career at The Washington Post. Over the years, his reporting assignments included covering military affairs and national security, and stints as a foreign correspondent in London and Bonn. Mr. Getler has served as The Post's foreign editor, as an assistant managing editor for international news and as deputy managing editor. The International Herald Tribune, founded in 1887, is owned jointly by The Washington Post Company and The newyork Times Company.

title:
New Jersey Daily Briefing;
Flaw Is Found in Netscape
body: Researchers at Princeton University have uncovered a security flaw in the programming language used in the popular Netscape Internet browser system. Because of the flaw, a site could be rigged so that the personal Internet files of someone visiting that site could be deleted or made public, Edward Felten, an assistant professor of computer science, said yesterday. Sun Microsystems, the company that developed part of the Java software, where the flaw was found, has issued a warning to users.   TERRY PRISTIN

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Softbank Raises Stake in Yahoo!
body: The Softbank Corporation, a Japanese computer software distributor, will increase its investment in Yahoo! Inc., an Internet search engine company. But a company spokesman declined today to comment on a Japan newspaper report that said Softbank would increase its stake to more than $60 million from around $2 million at present. He said the exact amount had yet to be decided. Yahoo! earlier this week filed documents with unitedstates securities regulators for a public stock offering that would raise $31.2 million. Yahoo!, based in Sunnyvale, Calif., provides an easy way to search the enormous amount of information on the World Wide Web. There are several dozen similar companies but only a few with as prominent a presence on the Internet. The company's stock offering document takes 11 pages to list the risks of the Internet directory business, one of which is a limited operating history. Yahoo! was incorporated in March 1995 and did not begin generating advertising revenues until last August. Softbank is a distributor of software and operates computer industry trade shows and publications.

title: Atlanta Tickets Going on Sale
body: A total of 135,000 tickets for Olympic events previously announced as "sold out" -- including gymnastics, basketball and volleyball -- will go on sale by phone and on the Internet beginning at 9 A.M. Saturday, the Atlanta Committee for the Olympic Games said today. Phone and Internet orders must be charged to a Visa card. Phone customers may call the ticket line at (404) 744-1996. The Internet ordering system is available at http:// www.atlanta.olympic.org. The tickets became available after the Atlanta committee completed its review of seating charts at the Omni, where volleyball will be contested; the Georgia Dome, site of gymnastics and basketball, plus several new venues under construction. The seats were originally "identified as potentially not available for sale because logistical and physical planning inside the venue might have resulted in obstructed views or the elimination of seats," said Scott Anderson, managing director for games services. Seats have become available for every session of volleyball, plus 33 of the 46 sessions in basketball and 19 of the 25 gymnastic sessions.

title: Don't Let Publishers Stifle Internet Access
body: To the Editor: As the Internet's capacity for data transmission increases and multimedia technology improves, it will become as easy to copy music, photos and movies as it is to copy text now (front page, March 18). How can government hope to prevent copyright infringement without encroaching upon individual privacy rights? It cannot. Content providers must accept the loss of those customers willing to pirate content and concentrate on packaging their product with enough value added so that wealthier customers remain willing to pay.  STEVEN D. LAVINE Los Angeles, March 19, 1996

title: Macromedia in Deal To Acquire Iband
body: Macromedia said this week that it was acquiring Iband Inc., a developer of Internet Website development tools in a stock deal valued at $32 million. Macromedia said it would take a $1.9 million charge in the current quarter to cover merger-related expenses. Based in Campbell, Calif., Iband is the developer of Backstage, a family of tools for building dynamic Websites. With the Iband acquisition, Macromedia is extending its Web publishing product offerings with a suite of integrated tools.

title: Corrections
body: A table with the Taking In the Sites column in Business Day on Monday about investment information on the World Wide Web misstated the electronic address for one finance-related offering, Research Magazine Online. It is: http://www.researchmag.com

title: Netscape Tie To Compuserve
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation broadened the reach of its popular Navigator World Wide Web browser program today by entering into a distribution agreement with Compuserve Inc., the world's second-largest on-line computer service. Users of Macintosh and Windows-based computers who subscribe to Compuserve or its separate Internet access provider, Sprynet, will be able to download Navigator at no charge beginning this spring. Jeff Shafer, spokesman for the Columbus-based subsidiary of H & R Block Inc., said Compuserve's goal had always been to provide its subscribers with the most comprehensive array of options possible. He added that Compuserve would welcome any company that developed a popular Internet browser, if subscribers asked for it.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
YAHOO INTERNET SERVICE PLANS A PUBLIC STOCK OFFERING
body: Yahoo, which operates one of the most popular directories on the World Wide Web of the Internet, announced yesterday that it would sell shares to the public for the first time. The initial public offering would be the latest in a flurry of sales by Internet-related companies over the last year. In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Yahoo said that it would offer 2.6 million shares and that it expected the price to be $10 to $12 a share. Yahoo was incorporated only last April. Yahoo's directory makes Web browsing easier, and the service has more than 800,000 users a day.

title: Apple Computer Stock Declines
body: Apple Computer Inc.'s stock slid to a 52-week low today after the company canceled a teleconference with computer industry analysts at which it had been expected to discuss its Internet strategy. Instead, an executive at Apple's Internet group said that the teleconference was to have focused on its troubled eWorld on-line service and that it was canceled to allow the company to complete its plans to shut down eWorld. The company disclosed on Friday that it would shut down the service on March 31. Apple's stock fell 62.5 cents in Nasdaq trading, closing at $26.25 today. Some analysts had expected Apple to disclose details of its full Internet strategy at the teleconference and were concerned when it was canceled. But the Apple executive said the company had no plans to disclose its Internet strategy until a later date. Subscribers of eWorld were told today that their electronic mail would continue to be handled for three months after the service is shut down. They will also receive copies of Apple's Internet kit. The eWorld service, which was introduced in June 1994, has attracted fewer than 200,000 subscribers.

title: Apple to Close Its On-Line Unit
body: Apple Computer Inc. has decided to discontinue its once-heralded on-line service, eWorld, on March 31. The move was announced yesterday in a memorandum to publishers on the service. Apple had said late last year that it planned to increase its presence on the Internet's World Wide Web but had not yet decided whether or how to mesh its on-line service into that effort. The memo makes clear that eWorld will cease operations. "Apple has made the decision not to move eWorld to an Internet-based service, but rather to discontinue the eWorld on-line service and greatly expand Apple's presence on the Web," the memo stated. Apple declined to comment yesterday. In an interview in late February, Gilbert F. Amelio, Apple's new chief executive, said the service might be discontinued. "Does the world really need another computer on-line service?" he asked. eWorld has not shown the growth of other on-line services, like America Online Inc. and Compuserve.

title:
Currents;
Internet Surfers Master Art of Cyber-Haggling
body: CALL it virtual antiquing. Instead of early-morning prowls along West 26th Street, some collectors browse and bargain for treasures through email chat. Arielle Greenberg, 23, of Long Island City, Queens, posted a message the other day in rec.antiques.marketplace, an Internet news group. Her message read "subject: wtb 1920's hats," and she included her email address. The essential lingo is "wtb" (want to buy), and "fs" (for sale). Two days later she heard from a man in Tempe, Ariz., who sent her two Victorian, hats, " not in great shape, but I've never seen anything like them," Ms. Greenberg said. She offered $35 for both, postage included, and mailed off a check. Ms. Greenberg also helped a fellow cyber-haggler find a McCoy lily-pattern pitcher (above) in Waterloo, Iowa, for $25, not the $85 it would fetch in the East. Another friend plays the spoon market: "wtb yellow Bakelite soupspoons."

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Co. Appointment
body: The newyork Times Company has promoted Gordon Medenica, 44, to senior vice president and group publisher for its Magazine Group, the company's chairman and chief executive, Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, announced yesterday. Mr. Medenica will assume his new position on Friday. He will become publisher of Tennis magazine and will also oversee the group's special services, which include foreign licensing, electronic media, custom publishing and related products. In addition, he will manage human resources for the Magazine Group. Mr. Medenica, who joined the Times Company in 1982, has been vice president for operations and planning since 1993.

title: Times Co. Appointments
body: The newyork Times Company's Magazine Group has named four vice presidents, its president, James W. FitzGerald, announced. Robert Carney was promoted to vice president for special services, which includes foreign licensing and electronic media, from director of those operations. Theresa McCann, formerly national travel and resort manager for Golf Digest, was named vice president and director of sales for Golf Digest Information Systems. Donna Doherty, editor of Tennis magazine, and Robert Sauerberg Jr., controller of the group, added the title of vice president.

title: COMPANY BRIEFS
body: BAY NETWORKS Inc., Santa Clara, Calif., a maker of computer networking equipment, agreed to acquire Performance Technology Inc. of San Antonio, a closely held maker of a hardware and software package that provides Internet access, for about $13 million in cash. STUDENT LOAN MARKETING ASSOCIATION, known as Sallie Mae, which buys and sells student loans, said its Sallie Mae Servicing Corp. unit would close its student loan servicing center in Tampa, Fla., by the end of June and dismiss its 160 employees.

title: CHRONICLE
body: ARTHUR OCHS SULZBERGER, chairman and chief executive of The newyork Times Company, plans to marry ALLISON COWLES on March 9 in a small family ceremony in Spokane, Wash. Mr. Sulzberger, 70, is also chairman of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. His wife, Carol Fox Sulzberger, died in August. He was publisher of The newyork Times from 1963 until 1992, when his son, ARTHUR SULZBERGER JR., became publisher. Mrs. Cowles, 61, is the widow of William H. Cowles 3d, who was president and publisher of The Spokesman-Review and The Spokane Chronicle until his death in April 1992. She is a director of the Seafirst Bank and chairwoman of the advisory board for the Spokane campus of Washington State University. The two families have a newspaper connection going back to the early 1900's, when Adolph S. Ochs, Mr. Sulzberger's grandfather, and W. H. Cowles, grandfather of Mr. Cowles 3d, were members of the Associated Press board.   ELAINE LOUIE

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ORACLE AND VERIFONE TO PURSUE ON-LINE PAYMENT SYSTEM
body: The Oracle Corporation, the giant data base software developer, and Verifone Inc., the largest developer of credit-card verification systems, will announce an alliance today to create a secure payment system for consumers and businesses on the Internet. The system will combine Oracle's Webserver software with Verifone's secure payment software to give merchants, banks and other financial providers an on-line payment system. The companies will also incorporate the Verifone Pay Window software into Oracle's Power Browser, its free browser for surfing the Internet's World Wide Web. Verifone's Pay Window software will provide transaction options and make the Power Browser easier to use.

title: On-Line Software Deal
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation has agreed to integrate software from Aurum Software Inc. into its popular Navigator software to help companies track sales leads from their sites on the World Wide Web. The companies said today that they would announce the agreement on Tuesday. Aurum's software enables companies to merge sales leads coming from their Web sites into their current internal sales and marketing systems. Financial terms were not disclosed.

title: Crime Statistics on Web
body: Data on the nation's homicide and drug-use rates and other crime statistics are now available on the Internet computer system, the Justice Department said on Friday. The Bureau of Justice Statistics said it had established a home page at: http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov/bjs/. The information available through the Internet site includes crime rates and reports on subjects like violence against women, capital punishment, drugs and crime, gun use in crimes and prison populations. The data go back through the mid-1970's and will be updated.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
SOFTBANK BUYS A STAKE IN CYBERCASH
body: The Softbank Corporation of Japan said that it had bought a 9.9 percent stake in Cybercash Inc. for $15.2 million. Cybercash, based in Reston, Va., makes technology intended to make it easier to shop over the Internet, using encryption software to safeguard credit-card data. Softbank, a rapidly expanding distributor of software and publisher of computer magazines, said it saw the stake as a way to enter the Internet business. Softbank bought the shares yesterday, on their first day of trading on the Nasdaq market. Cybercash shares rose 64 percent from the offering price, to $28.25.

title: A World Wide Web Screening Program
body: The researcher credited with starting the World Wide Web says he will offer a free screening program to people who want to keep objectionable material from entering their computers from the Internet. Tim Berners-Lee, director of the World Wide Web Consortium at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said he would rather see parents control their children's access to the Web than have Government censorship. "The Web is a universal information medium of great importance and potential, and it should not be constrained by government fiat," he said in an interview published today in The Boston Herald. The telecommunications law signed by President Clinton on Thursday has a provision banning "indecent speech" on global computer networks. Civil liberties group have already filed suit to block enforcement of those provisions. Mr. Berners-Lee said his filtering software, which any computer user could install on a PC, would be available in three months. Heidi Strup, a spokeswoman for the Christian Coalition, said the program "definitely would be a useful tool for us."

title:
February 4-10;
China's Grip on the Net
body: Not many people use the Internet in China yet, but their numbers are growing, and the proof is in the Chinese Government's decision to control the Internet more tightly. The Government issued regulations last week not to block Internet use but to steer the flow of electronic information through officially controlled ports that can be monitored. The regulations stipulate that the Government can penalize anyone for sending or receiving anything it deems harmful to public order. But the Goverment is most concerned with keeping Internet providers under its direct supervision. No one knows how many Internet users there are in China; estimates range from 30,000 to 100,000 people. Relatively few homes in China have a private telephone or a computer, and most users either work at a university or at a computer company. But if the Government's anxiety is any sign, then that too is changing.   SETH FAISON

title: Clinton's Budget Available on the Internet
body: For those interested in taking a closer look at President Clinton's budget proposal for the 1997 fiscal year, the White House Office of Management and Budget has posted a copy on its Internet site. The electronic posting of White House budget documents began in 1995, and since then they have been accessed at the site more than 25,000 times. The Internet site offers the same budget information as the printed version, available from the Government Printing Office at a cost of $1.75. The O.M.B. plans to update the site again in March, when the President will flesh out his budget proposal with details, and then as often as supplemental data become available. After the March submission, the budget office will also offer the budget in CD-ROM form, just as it did in 1995, when it sold more than 800 copies. The World Wide Web site address is http://www.doc.gov/BudgetFY97/index.html, or ftp.doc.gov/ pub/BudgetFY97 for those using file transfer protocol.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MICROSOFT PURCHASE INVESTIGATED BY U.S.
body: The Microsoft Corporation's acquisition of a fledgling World Wide Web software company, Vermeer Technologies Inc., is being investigated by Federal antitrust regulators, the Justice Department said yesterday. The investigators are looking at whether the purchase will hurt competition on the Internet's World Wide Web. It is unusual because it involves such a small company in the emerging and competitive market for Web software, antitrust lawyers said. Since last year, Federal officials have been examining the company's entry into the market for on-line information services. The Justice Department investigation of the Vermeer acquisition was first reported yesterday by The Wall Street Journal.

title: China Issues Rules To Monitor Internet
body: The Internet is just starting to grow in China, and the authorities are trying to keep it firmly in their grasp. Yesterday, China issued a new set of rules to regulate Internet use, the latest in a recent series of moves to assert control over the flow of information in the country. Rather than try to choke off Internet access, the rules appear to steer the flow of electronic information through officially controlled ports so that it can be better monitored. Article, page A3.

title: America Online Expands Service
body: America Online Inc., the leading unitedstates on-line service, has started AOL Canada, extending its international reach. The new service from America Online, which is based in Vienna, Va., plans to feature Canadian content and also provide email and access to the Internet, the company said. Key partners in the new service include Citytv, a Toronto-based television producer; MuchMusic, Canada's first national music television channel, and Shift magazine. Intuit Inc., which makes the popular Quicken financial-management software, will provide access to new kinds of financial information, America Online said. Canadian subscribers will have access to the content offered on America Online's German, British, and unitedstates services. All America Online subscribers will have access to the full Canadian service, the company said. Separately, AOL named William Razzouk as its president and chief operating officer. Mr. Razzouk was formerly chief operating officer at the Federal Express Corporation and fills a newly created position at America Online.

title: Dow Jones Reports 3% Rise in Earnings
body: Dow Jones & Company, the publisher of The Wall Street Journal, said yesterday that net income rose 3 percent in the final quarter of 1995, held down by a 50 percent rise in the cost of newsprint. Earnings were $60 million, or 62 cents a share, up from $58.2 million, or 60 cents a share, in the comparable quarter a year earlier. Revenue rose 8 percent, to $612.1 million from $566.6 million. For all of 1995, profit climbed 6.4 percent, to $189.6 million. "This was another year of solid progress for Dow Jones with earnings rising for the fourth consecutive year," said Peter R. Kann, chairman and chief executive officer. "Significantly, this gain was despite a very sharp increase in newsprint prices, strong competition in all areas of our business and our strategic decision to invest heavily in expanding our existing businesses and building new ones." Dow Jones' share price gained 2.2 percent on the newyork Stock Exchange yesterday, rising 87.5 cents, to $39.875.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BRIEFS;
China Drafting Rules On Internet Links
body: China's State Council, striving to embrace the Internet but not its pornographic and political content, adopted unspecified draft rules yesterday governing links to overseas computer information networks. In an executive meeting led by Prime Minister Li Peng, the council reiterated its provisional approval for global computer links, the official New China News Agency reported. Officials declined to provide a copy of the draft rules or disclose their contents. Chinese insiders have said the rules will probably set limits on which organizations can offer public Internet access, order the screening of who can secure such access, and try to mandate the use of technology to filter out offensive materials.   (Reuters)

title: I.R.S. Forms On the Web
body: Hoping to cut down the telephone volume of taxpayers seeking help with their returns, the Internal Revenue Service has created a home page on the World Wide Web. According to the General Accounting Office, only 8 percent of calls placed during last year's filing season got through to the I.R.S. The agency, whose budget was cut this year, does not plan to hire more people to handle telephone inquiries. Among the features of the I.R.S. home page are an area for down-loading 600 tax forms and publications, a summary of changes in tax rules for 1995 and summaries of 150 tax topics and answers to frequently asked questions. Both summaries are accessible through a keyword search. The agency's World Wide Web address is http:/www.irs.ustreas.gov.

title: Times Delivery in Florida
body: The newyork Times has reached an agreement with The Sun-Sentinel of Fort Lauderdale, Fla., to distribute The Times in Broward and Palm Beach Counties in Florida. The Sun-Sentinel, which is owned by the Tribune Company, will begin single-copy sales today and home delivery in March. William L. Pollak, executive vice president for circulation at The Times, said the newspaper was in discussions with other newspaper companies around the country to establish similar delivery arrangements.

title: New Java Chief Expected at Sun
body: Sun Microsystems Inc. is expected to announce today that Alan E. Baratz, former chief executive of the News Corporation's Delphi Internet Services Company, has been named chief of Sun's Java software business unit. Mr. Baratz, who is 41 years old, would be assuming a job that has been handled on an interim basis by Sun's chief scientist, Eric Schmidt. Java is a highly regarded technology that works with various makes and models of computers and software and is designed to greatly enhance the capabilities of computer networks, especially the Internet's World Wide Web. Many other software companies have licensed Java since Sun introduced it seven months ago. Mr. Baratz will be running a business unit that currently has some 70 people but has the mission of "growing like crazy," according to Sun's chief executive, Scott McNeely. Mr. Baratz was director of strategic development at I.B.M. before joining Delphi Internet Services in 1994. Since last summer, when the News Corporation merged Delphi with the MCI Communications Corporation's on-line business, Mr. Baratz has been the News Corporation's executive in charge of developing new technology-related businesses.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
COMPUSERVE LOOKS TO RESTORE INTERNET SEX GROUPS
body: Compuserve Inc. said yesterday that it planned to restore access to 200 sexually oriented Internet discussion groups as soon as it found a way to block them from subscribers in Germany. Last week, Compuserve, a unit of H & R Block, blocked all access to the groups after German prosecutors said the material violated the country's pornography laws. The company, whose subscribers get access to the Internet by paying monthly fees, said it did not have the capability to screen out German subscribers. The discussion groups are places on the Internet where computer users can post messages for all to see.

title: No Supranational Control for the Internet
body: To the editor: Re ("Unmuzzling the Internet," Op-Ed, Jan 2), Jaron Lanier's reaction to potential muzzlings: It might appear from this advocacy of a fanciful technology to thwart Internet censors that the author is an unalloyed champion of liberty. Not so. By declaring the Internet to be an international phenomenon beyond the control of any nation, Mr. Lanier is once again surfacing the proposal that nations must bow down to some supranational authority -- presumably run by what he refers to as "Stewards," who would regulate and control everyone involved. Perhaps some collection of multinational trading companies would fit the bill. As has been the case since the late 18th century when Jeremy Bentham first wrote about unleashing personal freedoms while being paid by the leading slave- and drug-trading "steward" enterprise of the time -- the British East India Company -- such proposals have carried a consistent double message. Wanton abandon in everything small; oligarchic tyranny in everything large.  Then and now, liberty has had no greater enemy.  MARK STAHLMAN President, New Media Associates newyork, Jan. 2, 1996

title: Irony Seen in Germany's Ban on Internet Smut
body: To the Editor: Those who have ventured into the seedier areas of virtually any large European city may be aware that Germany has long been a major source of some of the most bizarre and extreme pornography on the planet. Thus it is, to say the least, ironic that Compuserve should be forced to block access to more than 200 allegedly "pornographic" on-line discussion groups on the ground that their content violates German pornography laws ("On-Line Service Blocks Access to Topics Called Pornographic," front page, Dec. 29). Considering the open and widespread availability of pornographic materials in Germany (not to mention the vast quantities exported), I am astonished to discover that that country has laws restricting pornography. In fact, one shudders to contemplate just how perverse the offending discussion groups would have to have been to alarm the German authorities.  G. M. WATSON Vancouver, B.C., Dec. 31, 1995

title: Where the High-Tech Jobs Are
body: While jumping on the Internet bandwagon seems to be the latest rage, the second-largest fad for the computer industry is coming up with ever-sillier nicknames for the areas that house their home offices. Silicon Valley was one of the first, but that has spawned Multimedia Gulch (the area in San Francisco known for web site and CD-ROM development), Siliwood (the meeting place of technology and Hollywood somewhere slightly north of Silicon Valley) and Silicon Alley (newyork City's attempt to claim a piece of the multimedia pie.) Boston is known for its Route 128, a rough aggregation of companies like Digital Equipment and the Lotus division of I.B.M., Texas has Texas Instruments and the software companies in Austin, and Washington state has Bill Gates and his friends. Minnesota is a surprising blip on the map, but further inspection reveals that Control Data, Honeywell, 3M and other hardware and software companies make their home in that state. The maps are a broad indicator of computer employment. The computer industry is projected to be one of the three top job-creating fields in the next decade. title:
New Jersey Daily Briefing;
The Internet Aids in a Search
body: A Seattle woman is using the Internet to help a Chatham family search for a 23-year-old hiker who disappeared in Turkey in mid-September, The Associated Press reported yesterday. The mother of the missing man, Donald George Ziegler, has tried to find him by customary means. She alerted the State Department, the unitedstates Embassy in Ankara and the unitedstates Consulate in Adana, Turkey. But Becki Bump, a hiking partner of Mr. Ziegler's, decided to try a more unconventional method. She said she had received 30 responses through cyberspace, including some from Turkey. The messages were supportive, she said, but no one had spotted her friend.

title: 3 Banks Join Software Project
body: Meca Software said today that three banks would join the BankAmerica Corporation and the Nationsbank Corporation in a venture to make software for on-line banking services that use personal computers. The three are First Bank System Inc., Fleet Financial Group Inc. and the Royal Bank of Canada. BankAmerica and Nationsbank bought Meca, publisher of the personal finance program Managing Your Money, about eight months ago. The three banks will own portions of Meca, which is based in Fairfield.

title: Talk Radio's Support
body: To the Editor: I know these are tough days for The newyork Times. Your circulation is falling. Your editorials go unheeded by the President of the unitedstates. It takes energy and effort to not cover monumental Republican successes. I feel your pain. But "Talk Radio's Conservatives Enlist in the Budget Battle" (front page, Nov. 18) asserts: "Some of the hosts, like Rush Limbaugh, have begun urging listeners to call the White House with their complaints." I did not give out the White House phone number, or urge listeners to call it -- especially to "complain." My program is totally based on uplift, optimism and good cheer. For only the third time in my seven-year national radio broadcast, I gave out the Capitol Hill switchboard number, for listeners who wanted to convey to Republicans encouragement and support. I did this in an attempt to counter the weight of anti-Republican fervor in the mainstream media -- including the venerable newyork Times.  RUSH LIMBAUGH newyork, Nov. 20, 1995

title: A.P. Is Expanding Its On-Line Service
body: The Associated Press said yesterday that it would offer multimedia news packages on line, and an electronic archive of its articles to its members next year. The new service would repackage, for use on the Internet's World Wide Web, the same text, photographs, audio and video that the A.P. currently distributes to more than 1,500 print and broadcast subscribers. Because the A.P. is a cooperative made up of most of the country's daily newspapers, the Web pages and archive will only be accessible through subscribers' Internet sites. "We are not going to be in the business of competing with our members," said James M. Kennedy, the editor who will direct the A.P. Multimedia Services department. The archive, which is expected to go on line in the second half of 1996, would allow subscribers to search for A.P. articles going back 10 years.

title:
World News Briefs;
Britain Jails Designer Of Computer Viruses
body: The first person in Britain to be convicted of creating and planting computer viruses was jailed today for 18 months after being prosecuted under the 1990 Computer Misuse Act. The defendant, Christopher Pile, a 26-year-old computer expert, dubbed himself the Black Baron and copied computer programs and games before infecting them with a virus and putting them back into computer networks. They were picked up by users of the Internet, who infected their own systems. Judge Jeremy Griggs said in a court ruling in Exeter, in southwestern England, that millions of dollars' worth of damage could be caused by the viruses. "Those who seek to reap mindless havoc on one of the vital tools of our age cannot expect lenient treatment," he said. The prosecutor, Brian Lett, said many of the viruses were detected within days of use. But they could not be defined and purged because of a cloaking device Mr. Pile had used.

title:
IN BRIEF;
Applying to N.J.I.T.?All You Need Is a Modem
body: High school seniors who want to attend the New Jersey Institute of Technology in Newark can stash their typewriters in the closet. From now on, they can complete and send applications for admissions on a computer. The institute is the first school in New Jersey to computerize its application process. Students can find the institute's electronic application by accessing its home page on the World Wide Web, located at http://www.njit.edu. Students can fill out the application form on any computer that can connect to the World Wide Web. But the Postal Service still plays a role -- applicants must send a $35 fee before their application is processed. They must also send an official copy of their high school transcript and standardized test scores. About 20 students have filed applications through the web site. Kathy Kelly, director of admissions, predicted that by the year 2000, half the applications to the institute would be by computer.   ABBY GOODNOUGH

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
INTUIT TO BUY PROVIDER OF MUTUAL-FUND DATA ON INTERNET
body: IntuitInc., the maker of Quicken personal finance software, yesterday agreed to buy Galt Technologies Inc. of Pittsburgh, a leading distributor of mutual fund information on the Internet, in a stock deal valued at more than $9 million. Galt Technologies runs a service called Networth that distributes information of 65 mutual fund companies on the Internet's World Wide Web. The acquisition would allow Quicken users to use their home personal computers to download prospectuses and other information for mutual funds through the Quicken Financial Network, Intuit's new Web site (http://www.intuit.com/quicken).

title: Cunningham Benefit
body: An "Out Surfing With Merce" benefit party for the Merce Cunningham Dance Company is to take place on Tuesday at 7 P.M. at @ Cafe, 12 St. Marks Place, East Village. Highlights of the event include a question-and-answer session with Mr. Cunningham on the Internet Chat Box and the opening of the company's Home Site on the World Wide Web. title: Mourning Rabin On Line
body: Condolences and poems about Israel were sent across the Internet on Sunday, hours after the assassination of Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin. More than 3,000 other people sent their condolences via modem to a new Internet location set up four hours after Rabin's death. "In the condolences book we invite the world public to enter their names, all of which will be passed on to the Rabin family," said a creator of the site, Joel Leyden. A short biography of Rabin is also available at the site. Netking, Israel's largest Internet site, created the location Sunday and hopes to keep the site going for months, Mr. Leyden said. The Rabin site address is http:// www.netking.com.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Acquisition by Golf Digest
body: Golf Digest/Tennis Inc., a wholly owned subsidiary of The newyork Times Company, has acquired PAR Golf Systems Inc., a company based in Portland, Ore. PAR provides computerized tee time reservation networks and automated pro shop business systems, which provide pro shops with point of sale, inventory, purchasing and member billing information. The terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The business will be operated by Golf Digest Information Systems Inc., a new subsidiary of Golf Digest/Tennis Inc.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times and Dow Jones Expand On-Line Pact
body: The newyork Times and Dow Jones & Company announced yesterday that they had expanded a licensing agreement, signed in March 1994, under which Dow Jones distributes news articles from The newyork Times to customers of its on-line services. Starting in January, the new terms allow Dow Jones to distribute the most recent 90 days of Times articles to its news retrieval, news wire and news clipping customers in North America. Previously these customers could receive Times material on the day of publication only.  The expanded agreement also licenses Dow Jones to offer customers overseas the full data base of The Times, dating from 1981. James E. Patterson, vice president of NYT Business Information Services, said the arrangement would provide improved service to existing customers and "will help us to increase revenue by reaching new marketplaces, especially in the financial communities in Europe and the Far East."

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MACROMEDIA'S MULTIMEDIA TOOL FOR INTERNET
body: Macromedia Inc., which develops software for animators and graphic artists, demonstrated a technology yesterday to let developers create interactive material, including animation and sound, for the World Wide Web. Sun Microsystems Inc. has a competitive programming language, Java. Macromedia's Shockwave requires no programming and is intended to help build home pages on the Web with motion and sound like television. Shockwave's multimedia material can be converted to run on the Web using a point-and-click program. Macromedia's stock soared $6 a share yesterday, to $36.25, in Nasdaq trading.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NETSCAPE CUTS PRICES ON ITS INTERNET SOFTWARE
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation said yesterday that it had cut prices as much as 57 percent on some Internet server software because of a more competitive market. Its server software is used to publish and relay information on the Internet. The company, based in Mountain View, Calif., is known for its browsing software but plans to get most of its profits from the more expensive server software and said it wanted to speed up acceptance of its servers to lock in its position in the market. Netscape's shares gained $7, to $88.50, in Nasdaq trading yesterday.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BRIEFS;
Fujitsu and Sega Plan Computer Network
body: Fujitsu Ltd. and Sega Enterprises Inc. will set up a computer network offering on-line video games and shopping services that users of Sega's home video player can gain access to via their televisions. The link is the latest move by Sega to bring it closer to the personal computer world. The two companies said yesterday that they would begin a service in Japan in March that would link Sega's Saturn game player to Fujitsu's Nifty-Serve personal computer network, which is similar to American commercial on-line services. Sega and Fujitsu plan to add on-line games and shopping services later. No money will change hands in the deal, and the service will be available only in Japan.   (Bloomberg Business News)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
BPA to Expand Auditing to the Web
body: BPA International, which audits the circulation of business and consumer publications, plans to expand its auditing to measure use of sites on the World Wide Web belonging to publications whose circulations it also measures. BPA, which is based in newyork, said last week that it expected to complete its initial interactive audit early next year. BPA will work in conjunction with the Internet Profiles Corporation in San Francisco. The BPA audit is meant to verify traffic at Web sites with registered and unregistered users; among those BPA intends to audit are sites created by CMP Publications in Manhasset, L.I.

title:
WEDDINGS;
Laura J. Corwin, J. Portis Hicks
body: Laura J. Corwin, the secretary and corporate counsel of The newyork Times Company, was married on Wednesday to J. Portis Hicks, a senior partner in Boulander, Hicks & Churchill, a newyork law firm. A town registrar performed the ceremony at the Palazzo Cavalli in Venice. Ms. Corwin is keeping her name. She graduated from Brown University and received a Ph.D. in English from the University of Pennsylvania and a law degree from Yale University. She is the daughter of Sally and Joseph Corwin of Newton, Mass., who are partners in Corwin & Corwin, a Boston law firm. Mr. Hicks graduated from the University of Michigan, from which he also received his law degree. He is the son of the late Mildred Portis Hicks and Livingstone P. Hicks. The bridegroom's father owned the former Livingstone Porter Hicks Advertising in Detroit. The bridegroom's first marriage ended in divorce.

title: Intuit Plans a Financial Service on Internet
body: Intuit Inc. plans to set up a financial service on the Internet, using technology from the Netscape Communications Corporation and the Concentric Network Corporation. Customers will be able to use Quicken 96, the updated version of the company's flagship banking software, to get free access to the company's Internet site. The Quicken Financial Network will offer product information, personal finance advice and direct connections to Intuit's financial partners. The site, on the Internet's World Wide Web, is Intuit's answer to the Microsoft Corporation's two-month-old on-line service, analysts said. In May, Microsoft called off a planned purchase of Intuit because of antitrust concerns at the Justice Department. Computer owners who use the updated version of Quicken, scheduled for release Thursday, will get free direct access to the service. Concentric will provide the connection to the service. Customers will be able to use Netscape's Navigator software.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MICROSOFT TO TEST PRODUCT SALES ON INTERNET
body: The Microsoft Corporation said yesterday that it was starting a pilot program to test sales of software over the Internet. The company said it was in negotiations with a group of several retailers for a test of electronic sales that will begin shortly and run through the end of the year. Microsoft products that will be for sale at wholesale prices as part of the program include Microsoft Word and Microsoft Flight Simulator. But analysts said the experiment would have little appeal, because of the long download time required for most programs on standard telephone modems. "The reality is that very few people buy software electronically, especially the first copy," said Jeffrey Tarter, editor and publisher of Softletter, an industry newsletter.

title: On-Line Bank Set to Start
body: The Security First Network Bank, which was formed to conduct banking on the Internet, said yesterday that it would make its first transaction tomorrow morning at a news conference in newyork. Security First, a unit of Cardinal Bancshares Inc., received approval earlier this year from the Office of Thrift Supervision to become the first bank operating on line. Security First's chairman, James Mahan, who is also chairman and chief executive of Cardinal, said that the approval allowed Security First to accept deposits from customers nationwide. Mr. Mahan said that Cardinal was close to filing a registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission to spin off Security First to Cardinal shareholders and that he expected it to do so by the end of this week.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
MICROSOFT TO BUY MINORITY STAKE IN INDIVIDUAL INC.
body: The Microsoft Corporation has agreed to buy a minority stake in Individual Inc. and use its news product on the Microsoft Network so customers can create personalized news searches. Financial details were not disclosed, but Microsoft would be represented on the board of Individual, a privately held company based in Burlington, Mass. Using what the company calls inews, subscribers to the Microsoft Network will be able to set criteria for filtering through news sources and then directly receive news on specified topics. The Microsoft Network, introduced with the company's Windows 95 operating software, gives users access to offerings from more than 200 content providers, on-line news groups, the World Wide Web and news and information.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
UUNET OFFERS TO BUY INTERNET ACCESS PROVIDER
body: The shares of Uunet Technologies Inc. rose yesterday after it offered Monday night to buy Unipalm Group P.L.C., Europe's largest Internet access provider, in a $154 million stock swap. Uunet shares rose $1.875 to close at $40.875 in Nasdaq trading. Uunet, which provides Internet access to the Microsoft Network users, offered to acquire Unipalm after two months of negotiations. Under the offer, which has been recommended by Unipalm's board, Uunet said it would exchange 0.1671 share of its common stock for each ordinary share of Unipalm, valuing each Unipalm share at $6.83.

title:
OCT. 1-7: Instant Funds;
Two Donors Give Millions To Two Universities
body: At a time when Government is cutting money for higher education, two universities got some good news from private donors last week. Michael R. Bloomberg, founder of Bloomberg L.P., a news and financial information company, gave $55 million to Johns Hopkins University, where he is vice chairman of the board and head of a $900 million fund-raising drive. And Jon M. Huntsman, chairman of four large, privately held chemical companies, gave $100 million to the cancer research center at the University of Utah. Mr. Huntsman, who lost his parents to cancer and has had two kinds of cancer himself, had already given the center $10 million. "As people become aware of what others are doing, they rethink what they are doing," said Helmer Ekstrom, president of the American Association of Fund-Raising Council Trust for Philanthropy.   KAREN W. ARENSON

title: Oracle Plans a PC With Video Feature
body: The Oracle Corporation said today that it planned to offer by mid-1996 a low-cost computer that would provide video access to the Internet. The new product, called Web TV, "will be available by the end of the first quarter, or in the second quarter," Lawrence J. Ellison, the company's chairman and chief executive, said at the Telecom 95 telecommunications-industry conference here. "It will video-enable the Internet," he said. Mr. Ellison said Web TV would be available through an Oracle set-top box costing $500. Cable access would cost about $30 a month in rental charges. Web TV is planned to allow subscribers to download video on high-quality lines from servers. "We are talking to different content suppliers so that they can offer their servers to Web TV," he said. Oracle, which is based in Redwood City, Calif., announced various other deals today, including one with Philips Electronics N.V. of the Netherlands to enhance electronic mail services, and another with Telefon LM Ericsson/Hewlett Packard Telecommunications on integrating a telecommunications package with Oracle equipment.
