title: America Online Looks at Yahoo
body: America Online Inc., the nation's largest on-line service provider, is in talks to acquire Yahoo, the maker of one of the most popular Internet directories, The San Francisco Chronicle reported today. An America Online executive confirmed the negotiations, but a spokeswoman said no deal was imminent, the paper said. An acquisition of Yahoo, a start-up company based in Mountain View, Calif., would augment America Online's established directories, which allow users to search the graphical portion of the World Wide Web by using key words, subjects or phrases. Yahoo, which was created by two Stanford University students, Jerry Yang and David Filo, is in the process of starting to sell advertising space on Yahoo Web pages as a way of generating revenue.

title: Compuserve's Internet Service
body: Compuserve Inc. announced a service today that links computer owners directly to the Internet, stepping up competition in the Internet-access market. Customers will be able to make a local call to dial up the worldwide network without going through the Compuserve service. The new service, Spryte, will be available at the end of the year. Spryte is intended for customers who want to use the Internet alone without subscribing to an on-line service. It is another step in the oldest on-line company's expansion onto the Internet. The H & R Block Inc. unit already offers Internet access through the Compuserve service. The growing number of Internet-access providers is threatening customer growth at on-line services, analysts say. Some are striking back. In addition to Compuserve, several other on-line companies have announced plans to provide direct Internet access. Over the last year, Compuserve has made investments in Internet technology, buying Spry Inc. for $100 million last spring. Software developed by Spry will be used to let customers navigate the Internet.

COMPANY NEWS;
GENERAL MAGIC LICENSES TECHNOLOGY TO FRANCE TELECOM
body: General Magic Inc. of Sunnyvale Calif., said yesterday that France Telecom had licensed its Telescript technology, enabling the French company to offer an easier to use and more powerful software interface for users of its Minitel on-line system. In 1994, the Minitel electronic marketplace, available throughout France, was used by 18 million users to gain access to the 26,000 merchants who participate in the service, the company said. Telescript technology helps computer users begin electronic searches and retrieve specific types of information.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
On the Internet Without a PC
body: Philips Electronics N.V. said today that it would introduce a service in Britain this month that offers access to the Internet through television and telephone. Instead of a personal computer, the new Internet access uses a television, a CD-I player and a so-called Internet starter pack that includes a telephone modem. The Internet is a global computer network that offers data, graphics and video images. It allows access to information provided by others and to send and receive electronic mail. Philips said the service would be offered by a subsidiary of its Philips Media unit called CD-Online. The service will be available in other European countries next year. The CD-Online system will include an on-screen keyboard that can be operated through a remote control with a joystick. Philips said it was considering offering a small separate keyboard later. The Internet starter pack will cost about 260 guilders ($163). CD-I players, which can play movies, music, video games and interactive encyclopedia, have been sold since 1993.

title: S.E.C. Opens An Internet Site
body: The Securities and Exchange Commission began operating a World Wide Web page on the Internet today, offering free access to its vast electronic library of corporate records. The new Web page (http://www.sec.gov) resolves a lingering controversy about public access to the so-called Edgar data base, which stands for Electronic Data Gathering Analysis and Retrieval. The documents, including corporate annual reports and statements about big investors buying or selling holdings, are extremely valuable. A cottage industry has developed here distributing the nearly 12 million documents filed annually with the S.E.C. to Wall Street investment banks and law firms. An experiment financed by a 1993 National Science Foundation grant allowed the Internet Multicasting Service to distribute the S.E.C. documents on the Internet. The S.E.C. decided to sponsor free access to the documents, which are delayed one day. The Web page also includes electronic libraries of S.E.C. enforcement cases, essays on how investors can protect themselves in the markets, telephone numbers for state securities regulators, rule filings and speeches by S.E.C. commissioners.

title: Netscape Says Microsoft Sought 20% Stake
body: The chairman of the Netscape Communications Corporation said today that the Microsoft Corporation had sought a 20 percent stake in the maker of popular Internet browser software. James Clark, the chairman, said Netscape rejected the offer, which he criticized as an attempt by Microsoft to try to control another software company. "It is not in Microsoft's bones to cooperate with other companies," Mr. Clark said. A Microsoft spokesman, Greg Shaw, declined to comment on whether Microsoft had made an offer, except to say: "We aren't in current discussions." Netscape said that Microsoft sought the stake as well as a seat on Netscape's board in return for software code Netscape wanted from the Windows 95 operating system.  Speaking at a conference here, Mr. Clark said Netscape had asked Microsoft for the code before the release of Windows 95 so it could include certain features in its new Internet browser and server software for Windows 95 users. Mr. Clark said Microsoft responded that it would share the code only if Netscape gave it the 20 percent stake and a seat on Netscape's board.

title: Hackers Alert Netscape to Another Flaw
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation said today that a third flaw had been discovered in its Internet access software by a group of computer hackers who call themselves the Cypherpunks. The hackers -- computer users and mathematicians who try to discover weaknesses in computer software and networks -- found a design flaw that can shut down Netscape's Navigator browser software, which helps people travel on the Internet. Two American college students last week broke Netscape's software security code, a design flaw that could jeopardize financial transactions done using Navigator. A month earlier, a French hacker broke a different Netscape security code. "We are learning a lot from these problems," said Michael J. Homer, vice president of marketing at Netscape. Shares of the company, which sold its first stock to the public last month, rose $4.25 today to close at $67 in Nasdaq trading. The latest flaw found by the hacker group is a programming error in Netscape software used to navigate the World Wide Web, a part of the Internet made up of photos, sounds and drawings.

title: House Takes Its Turn on Internet Censorship
body: To the Editor: Draconian censorship of the Internet is imminent, and nobody knows about it. A counterpart to Senator Jim Exon's infamous Communications Decency Act lurked in what is called a "managers' amendment" to the House version of the telecommunications bill. Accordingly, new Internet speech crimes, related, as usual, to expression about sex, could bring up to five years in prison. Managers' amendments are presumed to be for housekeeping matters, and when the House voted, apparently some members were unaware of this one's contents. You fail to report that these restrictions passed as part of this bill. House Speaker Newt Gingrich got much recognition for saying, several weeks before the vote, that he thought such legislation was "a violation of free speech and a violation of the right of adults to communicate with each other." But does anyone suppose this got by without approval? Who, after all, is the real manager of the House? The press needs to alert us about this, especially since the telecommunications bill will soon be considered by a House-Senate conference committee.  LEANNE KATZ Executive Director, National Coalition Against Censorship newyork, Sept. 7, 1995

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Mecklermedia Picks A Group President
body: Mecklermedia, a publisher and interactive media company in Westport, Conn., has named Jeffrey Dearth to the new position of group president of its magazine and World Wide Web site division. Mr. Dearth, 44, was previously president of the New Republic Corporation in Washington and chief executive of the Electronic Newsstand, which markets magazines on the Internet. At The New Republic, Joan Stapleton, 42, the publisher since 1988, was promoted to the additional position of president, assuming responsibilities from Mr. Dearth.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Appoints 3 To Circulation Jobs
body: Three senior executive appointments in the circulation department of The newyork Times were announced yesterday by William L. Pollak, executive vice president for circulation. Charles E. Shelton, 49, was named vice president for distribution. He will oversee development of delivery from the newspaper's printing plant under construction in College Point, Queens, and from planned new printing operations in the Boston and Washington areas, as well as national wholesale and third-party distribution. Mr. Shelton had been vice president for circulation sales. Lauretta Prestera, 47, was promoted to vice president for circulation, where she will supervise home delivery and customer service. She had been group director for distribution. Harold F. Woldt Jr., 48, was promoted to vice president for circulation for sales and marketing. Mr. Woldt joined The Times last year after nine years with Newsday.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NEXT COMPUTER'S WEBOBJECTS JOINS INTERNET RACE
body: Next Computer Inc. introduced software yesterday that allows programmers to create sites on the World Wide Web of the Internet. While companies like the Netscape Communications Corporation and the Microsoft Corporation offer programs to browse Web sites, the new Next software, Webobjects, is intended to allow software developers to create Web sites that respond to the person pointing and clicking on the site. "Ninety-nine percent of Web server-pages today are static," or pages of published information that do not change until it is updated, said Steven O. Jobs, the chief executive of Next. Mr. Jobs, a co-founder of Apple Computer Inc., started Next in 1985.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
G.E. Selects Meta4 For Internet Work
body: The General Electric Company of Fairfield, Conn., has named Meta4 Digital Design in Jersey City as its Internet agency of record. The billings were not disclosed. Meta4 was awarded the account, which includes re-creating and maintaining G.E.'s presence on the World Wide Web, after a two-month review that was narrowed to that agency and three other finalists whose names were not disclosed.

title: So What's a Web Browser, Anyway? - Correction Appended
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation introduced itself to Wall Street last Wednesday with an initial public offering that rocked the stock market. The price of Netscape shares soared from $28 to $74.75, settling at $58.25 by day's end and $52 by week's end. Netscape has created what many Internet users consider the best Web Browser. Browsers allow people with a low tolerance for computerese to click-and-jump through the dense data fields. The tour winds people around a region of the Internet called the World Wide Web. Correction  A chart in Business Day on Monday explaining Web browser software, which helps users navigate the World Wide Web of the Internet, misstated a source for the data. It was Icon International Inc., not Icons Inc. Correction-Date: August 17, 1995, Thursday Graphic   Charts/Diagrams illustrate how Netscape facilitates navigation within the Internet and compares usage of browsers during November 1994 and July 1995. (Sources: Interse; Icons, Inc.)

title:
IN BRIEF;
How 27 Teachers Spent Summer Vacation: Net-Surfing
body: It may be years before every school in New Jersey has access to the Internet, but some teachers are preparing now. This summer, 27 teachers from around the state learned how to cruise the Internet and take advantage of its offerings at the Information Superhighway Academy. The academy, a five-day seminar in Piscataway, was sponsored at AT&T and the state Department of Education. The teachers, from 10 of the state's poorest school districts, will take what they learned back to their schools in September. A team of AT&T employees will help them set up computers in their classrooms. AT&T will provide the schools with used computers and other equipment. Each school will be assigned a mentor who will provide technical advice to teachers for a year. The academy was a pilot program that AT&T hopes to expand to other states next year. Participating districts included East Orange, Elizabeth, Hoboken, Irvington, Jersey City, Newark, Phillipsburg, Plainfield, Union City and West newyork.   ABBY GOODNOUGH

title:
International Briefs;
Reed Elsevier's Profit Rises 11.4%
body: Reed Elsevier, the British-Dutch publishing company, said first-half pretax profit rose 11.4 percent on a strong contribution from Lexis-Nexis, which it acquired last year for $1.5 billion; higher sales of scientific products, and advertising growth. Sales increased 20 percent, to £1.8 billion ($2.9 billion). Pretax profit rose to £370 million ($592 million), from £332 million ($531 million) in the first half of 1994. Excluding the impact on earnings of divestments, last year's first-half pretax profit was £281 million ($450 million). Nigel Stapleton, financial director of Reed Elsevier, said: "The major contributor in acquisition terms was Lexis-Nexis. The results for Lexis-Nexis were up more than 50 percent against the same period last year." Reed International P.L.C. of London and Elsevier N.V. of the Netherlands each own 50 percent of Reed Elsevier, which was formed in 1993.   (Bloomberg Business News)

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
E.D.S. AND SILICON GRAPHICS PLAN INTERNET ALLIANCE
body: Electronic Data Systems Inc. will use Silicon Graphics Inc.'s hardware and software to help other companies develop presences on the Internet's World Wide Web, the companies said yesterday. Financial terms of the alliance were not disclosed. The World Wide Web is a system for gaining access to information in a graphical format on the Internet, the global computer network. E.D.S., which is a subsidiary of the General Motors Corporation, will combine its strengths in computer systems integration with Silicon Graphics' expertise in advanced visual computing systems and World Wide Web technology, the companies said. Silicon Graphics is based in Mountain View, Calif.

title: A Video Phone For the Wrist
body: Philips Electronics N.V. said today that it was developing a video telephone that could be worn on the wrist and would offer users access to the Internet. The gadget is being called a wrist communicator. Philips, the Dutch electronics company, said scientists at its semiconductor division plan to develop a working model by the year 2002. "The basic technology to make it already exists within Philips," the company said. The key element of the wrist communicator would be a video telephone, including a small camera, the company said. It would also include a radio, a television and a computer that connects users to the World Wide Web -- an information service on the Internet, the global computer network, that can display graphics and video images. Philips said the product might also be equipped with voice recognition technology that would make buttons redundant. "The finished product could end up purely as a flat screen mounted on a band around the wrist," the company said. Philips is one of Europe's largest electronics companies, with annual sales of more than $38 billion. It sells consumer electronics, small home appliances, televisions and industrial electronics worldwide.

title:
NEW JERSEY DAILY BRIEFING;
Selling a Military Base, On-Line
body: Internet surfers are used to surprises, but maybe not information touting the real estate benefits of a military base. Hudson County and Bayonne officials are signing up for a new on-line service of the unitedstates Commerce Department's Office of Economic Conversion that is designed to attract business interest and replace lost jobs at military bases targeted for closing -- specifically, the Military Ocean Terminal in Bayonne. "Basically, what we do is we help the communities design their own Internet home pages," Dr. Erik Pager, the director of the Economic Conversion Office, said yesterday. "The system includes site maps, videos -- the basic information that a developer would need to know," he added. Robert C. Janiszewski, the Hudson County Executive, said that the Bayonne information terminal home page could be on-line within 30 days.   JOE SHARKEY

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Sponsors Sign Up For On-Line Service
body: The Yahoo! Corporation, which operates a popular directory of sites on the World Wide Web, said yesterday that it had signed five initial sponsors as part of a plan to redesign the service and become advertiser-supported. Yahoo!, based in Mountain View, Calif., identified the sponsors as the Internet Shopping Network in Palo Alto, Calif.; the MCI Communications Corporation in Washington; Mastercard International in newyork; NECX in Peabody, Mass., a computer reseller, and Worlds Inc. in San Francisco, an on-line software company. As part of their sponsorship, the logos of the companies will rotate daily as banners through the Yahoo! list of the five most frequently used Web sites. In a related development, the Reuters New Media subsidiary of Reuters Holdings P.L.C. yesterday signed a one-year agreement with Yahoo! to supply an on-line news service that will be supported by advertising. Reuters will receive a share of the revenue from the ads displayed on the Reuters news pages.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
INTERNET PROFILES SELECTED TO AUDIT WEB USE
body: Hoping to become the Nielsen rating service of the Internet, the Internet Profiles Corporation of San Francisco has been selected by Playboy Enterprises, the Netscape Communications Corporation, Ziff-Davis Publishing, a unit of Forstmann Little & Company, and several other media companies to provide independent auditing of World Wide Web users. The companies will use data compiled by Internet Profiles' I/Audit program to determine electronic advertising costs, sell advertising space and evaluate the effectiveness of ads on the Web. Several companies have announced plans to provide such services, but Internet Profiles, a privately held company known as I/Pro, is the first to gain a following among big Internet publishers.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
PEARSON TO BUY SECURITIES INFORMATION UNIT
body: The Dun & Bradstreet Corporation said yesterday that it had agreed to sell its Interactive Data Corporation unit, which provides historical and analytical information on financial securities, to the Financial Times Group of Pearson P.L.C. for $201 million in cash. Dun & Bradstreet, which is based in newyork, said that it expected to record a pretax gain of about $90 million on the sale. As part of the deal, Pearson signed a five-year agreement to cooperate with Moody's Investors Service, the credit rating agency owned by Dun & Bradstreet, to create a data base of companies listed on stock exchanges around the world. Interactive Data had operating profits of $13.6 million on sales of $66.8 million in 1994. Pearson, which is based in London, publishes The Financial Times.

title:
WEDDINGS;
Susan McLellan, Donald F. Harris
body: Dr. Susan Redman McLellan, an owner of Lenox Hill Veterinarians in newyork, was married yesterday to Donald Frederick Harris, the systems manager in corporate human resources for The newyork Times Company. The Rev. Dr. Robert E. Heffner performed the Lutheran ceremony at the West Kortright (N.Y.) Center. The bride, 50, graduated from the University of Illinois at Champaign-Urbana, from which she also received her degree in veterinary medicine. She is a daughter of Agnes Redman of Montrose, Colo., and the late Capt. Emil Redman, a Navy chaplain. The bridegroom, 53, graduated from Ohio Wesleyan University and received an M.B.A. from newyork University and a Ph.D. in philosophy from Columbia University. He is a son of the late Barbara and George Harris. The bride's previous marriage ended in divorce, as did the bridegroom's.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
ENCYCLOPAEDIA BRITANNICA ENTERS INTERNET PACT
body: Encyclopaedia Britannica reached an agreement earlier this week with Time Warner Inc.'s Pathfinder Internet subsidiary to integrate and market its reference works on the public computer network. Computer owners with access to the World Wide Web portion of the Internet will be able to reach Britannica Online through Pathfinder. Topics in the on-line version of Encyclopaedia Britannica will contain links to other information on the World Wide Web. For instance, an article on viruses will be linked to a data base at the University of Wisconsin, where more timely information will be available. In addition, editors will try to link related articles.

title: Apple Planning On-Line Shift
body: Apple Computer Inc. plans to release an upgraded version of its eWorld on-line service with expanded access to the Internet. eWorld, available for users of Apple's Macintosh computers, competes against such similar but larger services as Prodigy, CompuServe and , giving users access to news, financial information and entertainment. The service has also included electronic mail. Apple said Friday that the new version of eWorld lets Macintosh users get information from UseNet newsgroups, electronic bulletin boards on which people can post messages on a huge array of subjects. The new eWorld also lets subscribers get software available over the Internet. Access to the World Wide Web is expected to be available next month. The Web, the fastest growing part of the Internet, links many thousands of text and graphics-based documents, letting computer users move quickly and easily from one to another. The revised eWorld also includes improved multimedia capability, enabling faster and better use of photos and video.

title: Corrections
body: Because of an editing error, the Digital Commerce column in Business Day on June 5, about an effort by some cable operators to offer connections to the Internet and on-line services, misstated the ownership of one company that is developing modems for such connections, the General Instrument Corporation. It is independent, not a unit of Forstmann Little & Company. Forstmann Little, an investment firm, acquired General Instrument in a buyout in 1990. In 1992, shares of General Instrument were sold to the public, and Forstmann Little has since reduced its holding to about 15 percent.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AT&T AND BOLT BERANEK TO OFFER INTERNET SERVICES
body: The AT&T Corporation and Bolt Beranek & Newman Inc. agreed yesterday to provide businesses with services for access to the Internet. The terms of the deal were not disclosed. The companies said the venture would generate more than $120 million over three years for the BBN Planet Corporation, a unit of Bolt Beranek. AT&T, based in Basking Ridge, N.J., will supply knowledge of the communications needs of businesses, as well as physical and technical resources. Bolt Beranek, based in Cambridge, Mass., will provide the Internet services. Shares of Bolt Beranek rose $9.125, to $27.625, on the newyork Stock Exchange, while shares of AT&T gained 12.5 cents, to $52.875.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Co. Deal Is Off
body: The Gannett Company said yesterday that it would not buy The Daily Commercial, a newspaper in Leesburg, Fla., from The newyork Times Company. Gannett said on May 8 that it had reached an agreement in principle to buy the paper, which in 1994 sold 31,700 copies a day during the week and 34,500 on Sundays. But the companies said yesterday that they could not agree on the terms of the sale. They declined to provide further details. The Times Company, which bought The Daily Commercial in 1971, will continue to try to sell the paper, said Nancy Nielsen, a spokeswoman for the company.

title: Eavesdropping On the Internet
body: In the midst of its debate on the comprehensive telecommunications legislation, the Senate took the better part of a day last week to debate, and then to pass, an amendment making it a felony to knowingly transmit indecent material over a computer network accessible to people under the age of 18. Within the multiplicity of Internet newsgroups, people have been discussing the legislation with a mixture of frustration and outrage for months. The Amendment, sponsored by Senator Jim Exon, a Democrat of Nebraska, was approved in the Senate by a vote of 84 to 16, provooking reactions ranging from all-caps fury to disdaini to approval. A selection of messages about the amendment is reprinted on the screens to the right. They are sent by individuals whose aliases, or screen names, are not necessarily their real names. Not all of these messages are reprinted in their entirety, though original spellings and punctuation are preserved. While these messages were selected from Usenet news groups and America On-line's forums as indicated, many were sent to several newsgroups simultaneously.

title:
NEWS AND TOPICS: IN BRIEF;
A New Route to the Internet In Northern New Jersey
body: Internet users in Northeastern New Jersey have a new choice for a local access carrier. The Intac Corporation has installed new high-speed fiber-optic telephone lines to expand internet service to businesses in Bergen, Essex, Passaic and Union Counties and newyork City. Intac (short for internet access) provides installation and maintenance of phone lines and modems, and backups of hardware and software to corporations, electronic bulletin boards, newspapers, schools, hospitals and nonprofit organizations. Mike Hauan, the president of Intac, said the new lines would allow companies to tap into information on products, annual reports and other services available on the Internet. Intac also offers individuals email and access to local and wide-area networks and the World Wide Web. The email address is mjh@intac.com; the telephone number is (201) 944-1417.   GEORGE GENE GUSTINES

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Accounts
body: * Internet Services Co., Vienna, Va., a division of America Online, to Miller/Kadanoff Direct, San Francisco, as the first agency to handle marketing strategy and branding. The billings were estimated at more than $1 million for the rest of 1995. * Casino Morongo, Cabazon, Calif., to Di Zinno Thompson Integrated Marketing Solutions, San Diego, as the first agency to handle television and radio advertising. The billings were estimated at $1 million.

title: Money Laundering Fears
body: The Internet computer network and other computer technology has helped turn money laundering into a worldwide activity valued at more than $300 billion a year, a unitedstates expert on financial fraud said last week. "We feel a lot of nervousness as a result of new technologies, such as Internet, which permit anonymous international cash flows," said Stanley Morris, director of the unitedstates Treasury's agency that fights money laundering. The London Stock Exchange warned last week that the Internet posed a growing danger for the future regulation of financial markets.

title: Do Movies and Rap Go Too Far?
body: To the Editor: Re "Lyrics From the Gutter" (Op-Ed, June 2): Bravo to William J. Bennett and C. DeLores Tucker for having the courage to take on Time Warner, the megacorporation that promotes the ugly, misogynist garbage masquerading as "music." I fear, however, that asking a gigantic money-making machine to have a social conscience is akin to asking pigs to fly.  HELENE BENARDO Bronx, June 2, 1995

title: Only a Mirror
body: To the Editor: I agree with William J. Bennett and C. DeLores Tucker (Op-Ed, June 2) that there is much vulgar music being played, and also wish that record labels would show self-restraint. Rather than causing violence by glorifying it, is it not possible that this music is only representing the feeling of many young people in today's urban environment? Music can be a powerful expression of people's feelings and the times they live in. Mounting pressure on corporations might "clean up" the airwaves. However, let us not neglect the real battle -- to improve the conditions for those young people, so they will hum a different kind of tune.  DANIEL B. MAINZER Framingham, Mass., June 2, 1995

title:
CURRENTS;
On-Line Performance Art
body: IMAGINE a fusion of MTV, alternative radio and edgy P.S. 122-style performance art. That's the funky downtown vibe of Visual Radio Inc., a new arts and entertainment service that integrates on-line and CD-ROM technologies. The service provides a monthly disk that contains a visual sampler of the performances of more than 100 artists -- musicians, poets, film makers, dancers -- nationwide and also provides access through the Internet or to a direct-dial bulletin board. Terrence Peck designed the service with a Romanian architect, Lucian Andrei. On the computer screen, Mr. Andrei created a loft performance space with a spotlighted stage (below) on which tiny animated performance artists can each present two-minute cameos with the click of a mouse. Visual Radio costs $9.95 a month; (800) 555-7234. The Internet address is http://www.visualradio.com/.

title:
Most Wanted;
An Internet Provider Becomes a Hot Stock
body: It was a big week for hot initial public offereings in high tech, with no fewer than five of them leaping as soon as public trading began. But the hottest of them all was Uunet Technologies, a company that provides access to the Internet, and is partly owned by Microsoft. It closed Friday at $27.50, 96 percent above the offering price of $14. The company has never made a dime, but hjopes to change that after Windows 95 is issued by Microsoft, using Uunet (pronounced you-you-net) to provide access to the Internet computer network. title: Barron's Announces Finn as New Editor
body: Dow Jones & Company said yesterday that Edwin Finn Jr., managing editor of Barron's magazine, had been promoted to editor of the business and financial weekly. Mr. Finn succeeds James Meagher, editor since March 1993, who was appointed executive editor of the Dow Jones Magazine Group, a new position at the company. Mr. Meagher will work with Jim Ottaway Jr., president of the group and senior vice president of Dow Jones, on new magazine ventures. In addition, Richard Rescigno, assistant managing editor of Barron's since 1991, was promoted to managing editor. Mr. Finn, 40, has been managing editor of Barron's since rejoining Dow Jones in March 1993, where he started his career in 1980 as a national copy reader at The Wall Street Journal. In the early 90's, he was editor of American Banker.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AMERICA ONLINE TO BUY TWO SMALLER COMPANIES
body: America Online Inc. plans to buy two smaller computer products companies that will expand its publishing and Internet presence, the commercial on-line service said yesterday. The company said it would acquire the multimedia and Internet publishing and production companies Medior Inc. and Wide Area Information Servers Inc. America Online would acquire Medior for about 825,000 shares in stock, or about $31 million. The company would acquire Wide Area Information Servers for about 400,000 shares, or about $15 million. Shares of America Online gained $1 yesterday, to $36.75, in Nasdaq trading.

title: Another Internet Stop For New Jersey Surfers
body: To the Editor: In his May 14 article "Have you Hugged Your Computer Today?" David W. Chen surfed right past one of the best New Jersey Internet resources, EdeZign Group's New Jersey Home page at http://www. ezweb.com. It contains information on festivals in New Jersey, charitable events, beach and casino information and other items of interest. Our entertainment listings, focusing on the greater Princeton area, also cover restaurants, comedy clubs, nightclubs and coming musical and theatrical events. BILL LYON Vice President, EdeZign Group Pennington

title: An Internet Site For 'Batman'
body: Warner Brothers is relying heavily on the Internet to promote the release of its "Batman Forever" movie next month. The studio, a unit of Time Warner, created a site on the World Wide Web for computer owners to view clips from the movie, hear portions of its soundtrack and read promotional material. The web site is found at http://www.batmanforever.com. The Web site for "Batman Forever" is believed to be the first devoted to a single film.

title: Pulitzers Chairman Is Named
body: Peter R. Kann, the chairman and chief executive of Dow Jones & Company, which publishes The Wall Street Journal, has been elected chairman of the Pulitzer Prize Board. The board also elected three new members: William B. Ketter, the editor and vice president of The Patriot Ledger in Quincy, Mass.; Rena Pederson, vice president and editor of the editorial page of The Dallas Morning News, and William Safire, columnist for The newyork Times.  Members of the Pulitzer Prize Board serve a maximum of nine years; chairmen are elected annually. The announcement was made yesterday by George Rupp, the president of Columbia University, which awards the annual prizes on the board's recommendation. Mr. Kann succeeds Meg Greenfield, the editorial page editor of The Washington Post, and Burl Osborne, the publisher, editor and chief-executive officer of The Dallas Morning News, who served as co-chairmen of the board.

title: COMPANY BRIEFS
body: HALLIBURTON CO., Dallas, an oilfield equipment and service company, plans to sell a part of its Brown & Root Inc. subsidiary, NUS Training Corp., that provides industrial training products and services.  MEDALLIANCE INC., Nashville, formerly ImageAmerica Inc., which operates diagnostic imaging centers, said it would sell its 70 percent stake in a partnership that owns its Little Rock, Ark., imaging center for about $12.5 million in cash.  SUN HEALTHCARE GROUP INC., Albuquerque, N.M., a health care concern, purchased more than eight million shares, or about 15 percent, of Ashbourne P.L.C., a British nursing home group. Sun paid $19 million for the stock, purchased from current Ashbourne shareholders.

title: COMPANY BRIEFS
body: DATA BROADCASTING CORP., newyork, which provides financial market news and data, completed the sale of its Shark Information Services unit to a subsidiary of Automatic Data Processing Inc. for about $18 million in cash plus the assumption of about $2 million in debt. MARITRANS INC., Philadelphia, a tugboat and barge concern, plans to repurchase up to 1.8 million of its 12.5 million common shares outstanding.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Gannett Buying Times Co. Paper
body: The Gannett Company has reached an agreement in principle to buy The Daily Commercial, a newspaper in Leesburg, Fla., from The newyork Times Company, the two companies said yesterday. The terms of the sale were not disclosed. The Times Company said in March that it was discussing the possible sales of The Commercial and six other small regional newspapers, in line with a strategy of concentrating on and acquiring larger regional newspapers and investing in electronic media. The Commercial's circulation is 31,700 daily and 34,500 on Sundays. After the completion of the sale, which is expected to occur early next month, the Times Company will own 27 regional newspapers along with The newyork Times and The Boston Globe. Gannett would then have 83 daily newspapers, including USA Today.

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
Finding an ATM On the Internet
body: Visa or Plus cardholders can find information on the Internet about accessible automatic teller machines throughout the world. The Visa/Plus International Locater Guide can be accessed through the Visa home page on the World Wide Web -- http://www.visa.com/visa/. By selecting Ireland, for example, a user will learn that Irish pounds may be obtained with a Visa or Plus-marked card at more than 600 machines associated with six financial institutions. The guide does not cite individual cities or street addresses. The locater guide also provides diagrams and information about ATM locations at six airports: Frankfurt, Los Angeles, Oslo, Singapore, San Francisco and Tokyo. The company plans to add airports to the network each month, furnishing information on 50 airports by the end of the year.

title: Delphi Internet Plans to Hire 750 People
body: The Delphi Internet Services Corporation said today that it expected to hire more than 750 people to work in new offices in newyork and the Boston area. The newyork office, at 620 Avenue of the Americas in Manhattan, is meant to help the company make inroads into the unitedstates publishing market. The company is also opening up a new office in Lowell, Mass., to relocate its Cambridge, Mass., headquarters. The new locale will house the company's software development, operations and member services departments and the company's new data center. Delphi is a subsidiary of the News Corporation Ltd., a media company that is headed by Rupert Murdoch and is based in Sydney, Australia. The parent company's businesses include newspaper, book and magazine publishing, commercial printing, theatrical and television programming and airline broadcasts.

title: 3 Big New Customers for Open Market Inc.
body: Open Market Inc. will announce today that three major media companies will use its software and services to provide content and conduct business on the Internet. A privately held company based in Cambridge, Mass., Open Market said it had signed agreements to provide technology to the Tribune Company, Advance Publications and the Time Inc. unit of Time Warner. The Tribune Company and Advance Publications said they had also made investments in Open Market and would name directors to the company's board. "The active participation of these companies in Open Market is a tremendous asset as we continue to build complete, innovative electronic solutions for the publishing industry," Shikhar Ghosh, Open Market's chief executive, said in a statement. Time said it would use Open Market's Integrated Commerce Environment to support registration and future commercial activities on its Pathfinder Internet site. Pathfinder offers text, photos, audio and video from Time, Sports Illustrated, Warner Books and other Time Warner divisions.

title: Times Co. Promotion
body: The newyork Times Company has promoted Steve Rago to vice president for strategy and new business development in the company's Information Services Group. In his new position, Mr. Rago, who is 44 and previously served as the group's director for new media, will head the new media/new products unit of the group. He will also assume responsibility for strategy and the development of media products and services throughout the division, the company added.

title: Prodigy to Provide Fast Internet Service
body: The Prodigy Services Company signed an agreement yesterday with three regional Bell companies that will provide much faster access to its on-line service and the Internet computer network via digital phone lines. Prodigy, a joint venture between the International Business Machines Corporation and Sears, Roebuck & Company, said its members in San Jose and Woodland Hills, Calif., in Boston and in Nashville would be the first to connect to the service using a digital phone line called Integrated Services Digital Network, or I.S.D.N.. The service is provided by the BellSouth Corporation, the Nynex Corporation and Pacific Bell, a unit of Pacific Telesis Group. With I.S.D.N. lines, members can gain access to Prodigy, the Internet and rapidly download files, video and graphics. I.B.M. is providing a consumer-grade I.S.D.N. modem called the Wave Runner, priced at $495 for Prodigy members, beginning in May. The regional Bell operating companies will charge members on their monthly bills to install and maintain an I.S.D.N. line, which can handle two telephone lines at the same time. There are no additional Prodigy charges to gain access to I.S.D.N.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Infomercials Coming To the Internet
body: The infomercial, the program-length television commercial that poses as a program, is making its way onto the Internet. Williams Television Time in Santa Monica, Calif., an agency specializing in infomercial advertising, said yesterday that two infomercial clients would introduce by the end of the month "extended informational" commercials on the Internet, the worldwide computer network. Katie Williams, chief executive of Williams Television, identified the clients as Philips Consumer Electronics, a unit of Philip Electronics N.V., for its CD-i compact disk interactive system, and Proform, a unit of Icon Health and Fitness, for its fitness equipment. Each Internet infomercial would be about 15 to 20 pages long, she said, and accompanied by photographs; they will appear on a new site on the World Wide Web, the Sports Ticker, in conjunction with the Interactive Connection in newyork.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
New Travel Service for World Wide Web
body: The newyork Times Company and Advance Publications Inc., owner of Conde Nast Publications and Random House, said yesterday that they would cooperate to create a travel information service on the World Wide Web of the Internet. The new service, to be called Travel Connect, is expected to begin limited operations in June. Plans include the electronic publication of selected travel articles and photographs gathered from Times Company publications, Conde Nast Traveler magazine, Fodor's Travel Guides and other publications owned by Advance. The material will be offered to computer users without charge, and will be linked to other travel-related information sites on the World Wide Web, a multimedia Internet service. Although the participating companies will share space on the Web on a home page, a screen that serves as an index for their services, each company will develop, operate and sell advertising separately in the electronic venture. Material from the Times Company will include a library of columns from the Travel section of The newyork Times, as well as material from the company's leisure magazines, which include Golf Digest, Tennis and Sailing World.

title:
COMPANY REPORTS;
Dow Jones Profit Increases 15.6%
body: Dow Jones & Company, which publishes The Wall Street Journal, said yesterday that its profits were up 15.6 percent in the first quarter of the year compared with the corresponding period last year, helped by an increase in earnings from its financial information services. Net income for the quarter was $46.4 million, compared with $40.2 million in the first quarter of 1994. Operating earnings at the business publishing segment, which includes print publications, television and the business information services group, fell 42.5 percent because of a write-down of a lease and costs related to the start-up of European television operations. title: Times Ads Available Over America Online
body: Beginning today, the three largest Sunday classified advertising sections of The newyork Times will be available through the week to subscribers of the America Online computer service. The new service is accessible from the main screen of @times, The Times's on-line service, and includes the help wanted, real estate and automotive advertisements from tomorrow's newspaper. Several newspapers, including The Chicago Tribune and The San Jose Mercury News in California, already offer classified advertising on line. But Steve Rago, director of The newyork Times Company's new media unit, said the new @times service "should be faster and easier to use, because it exploits new software tools." He said subscribers would be able to narrow their searches of classified advertising to particular automotive makes and models, for example, or to real estate listings in particular towns. The Sunday classified advertisements will be posted on America Online for a test period of about six months at no additional charge to advertisers or on-line subscribers.

title: New Prodigy Price Plan
body: The Prodigy Services Company said yesterday that it had developed an alternative pricing plan for subscribers of its on-line service, lowering the cost of access to the Internet, the global computer network. The plan offers 30 hours of monthly access to Prodigy, including the broader Internet, for $30. After 30 hours, the service costs $2.95 an hour. For people who do not use the Internet as much, Prodigy will continue to offer its original pricing structure, a $9.95 fee for five hours of access with additional hours priced at $2.95 each. Prodigy, which is based in White Plains, is a joint venture of the International Business Machines Corporation and Sears, Roebuck & Company.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Company to Buy a Video Stake
body: The newyork Times Company has agreed to acquire a majority interest in Video News International, a global video news-gathering service for television and cable networks, the two companies said yesterday. The terms of the deal were not disclosed. Founded two years ago, Video News International employs more than 35 journalists in the unitedstates and other countries. It specializes in what is known as small-format television news reporting, using a journalist equipped with a small video recorder instead of the four-member camera crews frequently deployed by large stations and television networks. As a result, production costs are significantly lower. The company's clients include "The MacNeil/Lehrer News Hour" on public television; "Nightline," the news program broadcast by ABC, and the British Broadcasting Corporation. "We are excited to be getting in on the ground floor of this emerging form of video news production," said Lance R. Primis, president and chief operating officer of the Times Company. "Video News International is another building block in our television development strategy."

title: I.O.C. Going on Internet
body: The International Olympic Committee is hopping on the information super-highway. Its executive board said today that the I.O.C. will be linked to what Director General Francois Carrard called the "wild world of Internet" by June. The I.O.C. will be a server on the worldwide computer network, offering historical information on itself, the international federations and the Games themselves.

title: Prodigy Official Joins MCI
body: The MCI Communications Corporation said yesterday that it had hired Scott Kurnit, executive vice president of the Prodigy Services Company, to lead its new on-line services unit. As head of the MCI Information Services Company, Mr. Kurnit will oversee several hundred employees who operate its Internet access service, World Wide Web site and on-line shopping area. He will also direct the new-media venture that was announced last week between MCI and the Public Broadcasting Service.

title: Times Settles a Suit Over Pressroom Hiring
body: A Federal judge approved a settlement yesterday requiring The newyork Times Company to increase its hiring of women and minority workers in its pressroom to resolve a lawsuit brought by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission against the company and the pressmen's union. Judge Robert P. Patterson Jr. of the Federal District Court in Manhattan determined that the settlement satisfied antidiscrimination laws. The settlement sets a target that calls for 25 percent of the pressroom's casual workers to be members of minority groups and women in 10 years. The consent decree affects freelance applicants who show up at The Times's Manhattan plant at 229 West 43d Street, applying to mop floors, clean printing machines, move stacks of compacted papers and perform other odd jobs. When the equal opportunity commission sued The Times and the newyork Newspaper Printing Pressmen's Union No. 2 in 1992, the casuals pool consisted entirely of white men, except for one person at the bottom of the list. The commission asserted that the application process favored friends and relatives of permanent workers who are union members. In 1992 the union had no blacks, Asians or women.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
An On-Line Service From USA Today
body: USA Today is jumping on the electronic bandwagon with an on-line service offering news, sports scores and casual chat with reporters and editors. Other features are electronic bulletin boards and a fantasy baseball game, offered for an extra charge. The service, which will begin on April 17, will be available on the Internet for $14.95 a month for three hours of use, and $3.95 for each additional hour. Although the Internet is generally free, users must gain access to the USA Today service through special equipment from Compuserve Network Services, a unit of H & R Block Inc., and software from USA Today, which is owned by the Gannett Company. Readers subscribing to USA Today on line will receive Compuserve's Mosaic browser, which is software for obtaining information on the Internet's World Wide Web, and a local telephone number.

title: Times Co. to Issue Debt
body: The newyork Times Company is planning to raise $250 million by issuing notes and debentures to pay off debt. According to the offering notice, which was issued on Friday, the notes and debentures will be used to repay $162.3 million in debt related to newspaper acquisitions in 1985 and $50 million to pay off debt issued by Affiliated Publications Inc., the parent company of The Boston Globe. The Affiliated debt was guaranteed by the Times Company in connection with its 1993 purchase of The Boston Globe. The remainder of the $250 million will be used for general corporate purposes. Of the total, $125 million is being offered in notes due 2005 and $125 million in debentures due 2025.

title:
International Briefs;
Profit Increases 16% At Reed Elsevier
body: The big Western European publisher Reed Elsevier said yesterday that its profit surged 16 percent in 1994 and that its newly acquired Lexis-Nexis unit was outperforming expectations. Pretax profit for the company, formed two years ago from the marriage of Reed International of Britain and Elsevier of the Netherlands, rose to $983 million, from $847 million in 1993. Disregarding special items, the increase was a little better yet -- 17 percent, at the top end of market forecasts. Revenue rose 9 percent, to about $4.8 billion, an increase of 4 percent, excluding acquisitions. The company expressed optimism about its prospects and said it expected to take price rises in paper and printing costs the middle of this year in stride.   (Reuters)

title: COMPANY BRIEFS
body: CAMPO ELECTRONICS APPLIANCES AND COMPUTERS INC., Harahan, La., a retailer, ended its discussions to acquire Gregg Appliances Inc., Indianapolis, for $52 million in cash and stock.  DATA BROADCASTING CORP., newyork, agreed to sell Shark Information Services Corp., which provides stock market information, to Automatic Data Processing Inc., Roseland, N.J., for $20 million. MOBIL CORP. , Fairfax, Va., said Continental Plastic Containers Inc., a unit of Continental Can Co., Syosset, L.I., would supply nearly all of its motor-oil plastic containers produced in the unitedstates under a five-year, multimillion-dollar agreement.  PHILIPS ELECTRONICS N.V., Eindhoven, the Netherlands, said it expects to complete an agreement to buy the securities systems business of Burle Industries, Lancaster, Pa., through its Philips Electronics North America Corp., newyork, for an undisclosed sum.

title: Times Company May Sell 7 Small Newspapers
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it was in discussions for the possible sale of seven of its small regional newspapers. Among the papers are five dailies with a combined circulation of about 71,600 copies: The Daily Corinthian in Corinth, Miss.; The State Gazette in Dyersburg, Tenn.; The Daily Commercial in Leesburg, Fla.; The Lenoir News-Topic in Lenoir, N.C., and The Messenger in Madisonville, Ky. Also involved in the discussions are two weekly newspapers: The Banner-Independent in Booneville, Miss., and The York County Coast Star in Kennebunk, Me. The Times Company declined to identify the potential buyers involved in discussions, pending an agreement in principle. "These discussions are consistent with our corporate strategy, which is to concentrate on and acquire larger regional newspapers and invest in more electronic media," said Lance R. Primis, president and chief operating officer of the Times Company. The company also publishes 21 other regional newspapers, along with The newyork Times and The Boston Globe.

title: Netcom Names a President
body: Netcom On-Line Communication Services Inc. said today that it had named David W. Garrison as president and chief operating officer. Mr. Garrison was formerly president of Skytel, a division of the Mobile Telecommunications Technologies Corporation. Mr. Garrison's main tasks will be to increase the number of Netcom subscribers and improve customer service, the company said. Netcom, based here, provides consumer on-line services, including links to the Internet. It went public in December. It had been looking for an executive to handle day-to-day operations and manage growth. Netcom said the addition of Mr. Garrison, who will also join the company's board, will prepare the company for its next phase as a public company. Earlier this month, Netcom appointed two executives to its network and customer-support operations.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Cable Venture
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that its television station in Fort Smith, Ark., KFSM, had started two local cable news channels that each carry advertising aimed at a specific region. The two cable channels, each known as News Channel 5, provide news around the clock by simulcasting live news programs from KFSM and replaying them until the next live news broadcast. One channel appears on a Fort Smith cable system, while another appears on a northwestern Arkansas cable system. Advertisers can reach viewers in either or both areas. "This is the first television station in the country to launch two local cable news channels with separate advertising zones," Nancy Nielsen, the spokeswoman for the company, said yesterday.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Appointment
body: The newyork Times has named Jyll F. Holzman vice president for advertising sales, effect March 20. Ms. Holzman, 42, will be in charge of advertising sales for The newyork Times Magazine. She will also coordinate advertising sales for The Times involving fashion products, jewelry, home furnishings, cosmetics, sporting goods and packaged goods. Most recently, Ms. Holzman was associate publisher for the Walt Disney Company's Family Fun magazine. Before that, Ms. Holzman was advertising director for Child magazine when it was owned by The newyork Times Company.

title: On-Line Deal Being Sought
body: Deutsche Telekom A.G. announced plans today that could soon put millions of Germans on the Internet and also said that it was in talks with the Microsoft Corporation about a possible on-line computer venture. The new service, to be called Telekom On-line, will offer its subscribers full access to the Internet computer network and German-language computer services ranging from home shopping to on-line publications, including many magazines. The previous system, Datex-J, which is now considered archaic, is a text-based computer network that requires its users to memorize and type in lines of text. But new services that use a Windows format, allowing users to point to an item and choose it, have become popular and spurred the growth of on-line services. Deutsche Telekom will distribute free software for Telekom On-line to all Datex-J users. The users will also receive full access to the Internet, email with an Internet address and a range of other services.

title: Times Stock Buyback
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it would spend up to $50 million to buy back shares of its class A common stock in the open market and in private transactions. The latest stock repurchase follows a $100 million repurchase plan announced on Oct. 20, 1994, that has substantially been completed. The Times Company's shares gained 12.5 cents yesterday to close at $21.625 on the American Stock Exchange.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
FIDELITY TO OFFER SERVICES ON WORLD WIDE WEB
body: Fidelity Investments said yesterday that it would offer a range of information services to users on the World Wide Web, a string of data bases available through the global maze of computer networks known as the Internet. Fidelity, the nation's largest mutual fund company, hopes to allow users to trade mutual fund shares, but not for at least another year until Federal regulatory concerns are met, a spokeswoman for Fidelity, Mary Ruth Moran, said. Fidelity is the first mutual fund company to provide financial information on the Internet, said Joel Maske, a spokesman for Galt Technologies in Pittsburgh, an independent distributor of mutual fund information to networks. But mutual fund companies, including Fidelity, already offer information on other on-line services, like Prodigy.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
COMPUSERVE PLANS TO OFFER WIDER INTERNET ACCESS
body: Compuserve Inc. said yesterday that it was within 60 days of offering the World Wide Web and other Internet services to some of its 2.6 million on-line information service customers. The company, a division of H & R Block that is based in Columbus, Ohio, will make the Internet services available to computer users with "dial P.P.P." Internet connections. Such connections are typically more complex than those made to standard commercial information services and are usually made through companies called Internet service providers. Only a relatively small number of Compuserve's customers are thought to have dial-P.P.P. connections.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Cable News in Florida
body: The Sarasota Herald-Tribune, a daily newspaper owned by The newyork Times Company, and Comcast Cable Communications, a unit of the Comcast Corporation, have agreed to create a 24-hour cable news channel in Sarasota and Charlotte counties in Florida. The Herald-Tribune will produce the programming for the channel, which is expected to begin operations by summer. Comcast will distribute the channel on its Sarasota cable system and will produce a daily local talk show.

title: Internet Users Consider Spamming a Hostile Act
body: To the Editor: Most of us who read and administer the newsgroups at Internet sites do not equate "spamming" with "excessive crossposting," as your Jan. 11 article on email does. A crossposted article is a single electronic file that can be viewed from any of the several newsgroups (discussion areas) to which it has been sent. Today's software lets readers avoid seeing a widely crossposted article more than once -- in the first group where they find it. Crossposting is frowned on only when it is excessive and off-topic. It is a less serious offense than spamming. A spammed article is one that has been posted separately to many newsgroups. Each appearance represents another file that has to be transmitted to and stored on the thousands of computers all over the world that carry that newsgroup. Because the software sees each appearance as a different item, readers encounter it over and over. This waste of resources is what makes spamming so unacceptable to netnews readers.  MARA CHIBNIK Administrator, Public Access Networks Corporation newyork, Jan. 12, 1995

title: Dowd Is Named a Columnist
body: The appointment of Maureen Dowd as an Op-Ed page columnist of The newyork Times was announced yesterday by the paper's publisher, Arthur Sulzberger Jr. Ms. Dowd, a member of the Washington bureau of The Times and a columnist for The newyork Times Magazine, will move to her new post around midyear. "Maureen Dowd has long been one of the most original reporters and compelling writers in American journalism," Mr. Sulzberger said. "She has shone in all her roles at The Times, both in newyork and in Washington. I know she will be an important, fresh voice on our Op-Ed page." A native of Washington, Ms. Dowd, 42, is a graduate of Catholic University there. She joined The Times as a metropolitan reporter in 1983 after writing for The Washington Star and Time magazine. She moved to the Washington bureau in 1986 and to the White House beat two years later. Graphic   Photo: Maureen Down. (The newyork Times)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Books for Sale On Internet
body: HarperCollins Publishers, a division of the News Corporation, said Friday that it had begun offering more than 10,000 books and software titles for sale through the new Online Bookstore of the Delphi Internet Services Corporation. The bookstore, which can be searched through personal computers by title, author or category, offers a wide range of books, the publisher said. The service was introduced Friday at the Consumer Electronics Show here. Delphi Internet members have unlimited access to browse, sample and order books, software, and other merchandise on line, HarperCollins said. All orders are placed on line, with credit card transactions through Delphi Internet's customer service department, and mailed from HarperCollins's warehouse center in Scranton, Pa.

title:
OUTLOOK 1995: TECHNOLOGY & MEDIA;
Lurking On-Line: The Electronic Eavesdroppers
body: Each day, millions of people log on to computer networks to discuss their lives with complete strangers, whether on safe subjects like pet grooming, lurid topics like foot fetishes or emotionally wrenching issues like alcoholism or child abuse. But for every person chatting in one of these conversations, many more are eavesdropping -- a practice known in the electronic community as lurking. Lurking used to be one of the on-line world's most disdained practices. But just as the Internet community has been forced grudgingly to accept millions of new arrivals to the neighborhood, so has it been forced to accept lurking as an inevitable consequence of all those curious, shy or nosy newcomers. Of course, in most live on-line "chat" areas, it's nearly impossible to go unnoticed. Entering an on-line chat room signals your arrival to others (at which point you can decide to jump into the conversation). On computer bulletin boards, however, where conversations are simply a series of postings and responses, anyone can browse unnoticed. On the Usenet, a collection of thousands of message boards on the Internet, there may be as many as 100 people browsing for every participant.  LAURIE FLYNN Graphic   Chart: "Information Back Alleys" Probably the busiest sphere in cyberspace is the collection of thousands of discussion groups known collectively as Usenet. Orginally a communications system for computer scientists, Usenet can now be found on most commercial computer services, like American Online. Usenet "news groups" -- basically, computer bulletin boards -- are each devoted to a highlyspecific topic. Despite the opportunity to discuss virtually any subject known to human kind, however, a listing of the 10 most popular Usenet news groups indicates that many cybernauts have only a few things on their minds. title: America Online Acquisitions
body: America Online Inc., the fast-growing computer on-line service, said today that it had acquired Booklink Technologies Inc. and Navisoft Inc. in tax-free stock deals valued at $47.7 million. Booklink, based in Needham, Mass., makes worldwide web browsers, which are tools used to search bulletin boards on the Internet, the global web of computer networks. Navisoft, based in Hillsboro, Calif., makes tools for publishing on the Internet. America Online, based here, said the acquisitions were expected to strengthen its strategic initiative of popularizing the Internet for publishers as well as consumers.

title: LIFTOFF
body: Regarding the last sentence of "Liftoff," there is no need to worry about the young. Our children introduced many of us to computers, and they are jetting off on the Internet ahead of us. The rest of Frankel's essay is wonderfully, umm, uplifting.  JEAN PORTELL Brooklyn

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
A NAME CHANGE IS PLANNED FOR MEAD DATA CENTRAL
body: The new owner of Mead Data Central plans to change the company's name to Lexis-Nexis, making reference to the names of its on-line database products. Reed Elsevier P.L.C. is expected to make the change when it completes the acquisition of the electronic legal information and news retrieval company. Reed, an British-Dutch publishing company, said on Oct. 4 it would pay $1.5 billion to the Mead Corporation of Dayton, Ohio, for the data unit. The companies hope to complete the deal by the end of the year. Lexis offers on-line legal information, and Nexis offers electronic retrieval of text from a wide range of newspapers and magazines. It had sales of $551 million in 1993.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
AMERICA ONLINE STOCK UP AGAIN ON ACQUISITION PLAN
body: Shares of America Online Inc., the computer on-line services provider based in Vienna, Va., rose again yesterday after it said on Monday that it planned to buy Advanced Network and Services, a major architect of the Internet. The acquisition is part of America Online's strategy to expand its access to the Internet, the global web of computer networks. The stock rose $2.875 yesterday, to $43.75, on Nasdaq. On Monday, the shares gained $4.125.

title: Disney Drawn To the Internet
body: The Walt Disney Company is entering cyberspace with a new marketing service on the Internet computer network. Called Movie Plex, the interactive service allows users to see previews and clips of Disney films, read about the making of films, check the release dates of individual films by country, learn about special events and premieres and play movie trivia games. The service is divided into two parts, one for the general public and one for journalists.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Film-Preview Channel Set
body: The newyork Times Company and the Torstar Corporation, the parent company of The Toronto Star, said yesterday that they were developing a cable network called the Popcorn Channel. The companies said the network, which is scheduled to start at the end of the first quarter of 1995, would show previews of new motion pictures. In addition, it will use the bottom portion of television screens for local movie theater listings, showing when and where movies are playing near subscribers' homes. The companies have not yet decided how local the listings will be, a spokeswoman for the Times Company said. The channel will also sell movie- and entertainment-related products, and offer ticketing services. The companies declined to say how much they were investing in the network.

title: Louis J. Kleinklaus; Radio Engineer, 83
body: Louis J. Kleinklaus, a retired chief engineer of WQXR and WQXR-FM in newyork who helped to shape FM stereo broadcast standards, died last Friday at Fair Oaks Hospital in Fairfax, Va. He was 83 and lived in Manassas, Va. He suffered a brief illness, said his stepdaughter, Virginia Heal of Manassas. Mr. Kleinklaus was the engineer in 1961 when WQXR-FM, the classical radio station of The newyork Times Company, became the first in newyork City to broadcast in stereo. The changeover took place under new FM-stereo standards set by the National Stereophonic Radio Committee, on which he served, in 1959 and 1960. He joined the Times Company's broadcast unit in 1940 and was chief engineer from 1951 to his retirement. He is also survived by two sisters, Fabiola A. Kleinklaus of Kerrville, Tex., and Loretta McGowan of the Bronx, and two stepgrandchildren.

title: CHRONICLE
body: A. M. ROSENTHAL, the former executive editor of The newyork Times and a columnist for the newspaper, will receive the Light of Truth Award from the International Campaign for Tibet for his efforts to expose the plight of the Tibetan people. Mr. Rosenthal is recuperating from cardiac surgery, so his son ANDREW ROSENTHAL, the newspaper's Washington editor, will accept the award on Thursday at the Marriott Marquis Hotel in Manhattan. SENATOR DANIEL PATRICK MOYNIHAN, Democrat of newyork, is to speak at the dinner, which will be sponsored by nine organizations involved in refugee affairs. The award is a butter lamp from the private collection of the Dalai Lama. When told that a butter lamp, which is used for religious observances, is traditionally lit by yak butter, Mr. Rosenthal said, "That's not on my diet."

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
Textbook Publisher Sold
body: The Dutch publisher Wolters Kluwer N.V. said today that it would acquire a legal and business textbook division from Simon & Schuster, a unit of Viacom Inc. Financial details of the purchase of Prentice-Hall Law and Business were not disclosed. The unit will operate under the imprint of Aspen Law and Business, part of Wolters Kluwer's American subsidiary, Aspen Publishers.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
NEW CHIEF NAMED FOR WARNER BROTHERS RECORDS
body: Danny Goldberg, a former writer for Rolling Stone magazine who went on to become a music industry executive, was named chairman and chief executive of Warner Brothers Records, the company said yesterday. As expected, Mr. Goldberg will succeed Mo Ostin, who will step down Jan. 1 after 25 years in the post and take a consulting position with Time Warner. Mr. Goldberg has been president of Atlantic Records, a Time Warner subsidiary, since January. He joined the company in 1992 as senior vice president. A political activist, Mr. Goldberg was chairman of the American Civil Liberties Union Foundation of Southern California and currently serves as the foundation's president. Warner Brother is based in Burbank, Calif.

title: Appointments By Times Co.
body: The newyork Times Company announced several appointments yesterday in its information services division, which includes The newyork Times News Service and Syndication Sales Corporation as well as Times On-Line Services and NYT Custom Publishing. Patricia A. Ecke, publisher of TimesFax, was promoted to vice president, specialized publishing. James E. Patterson, director of The newyork Times Index and Times On-Line Services, was named vice president, business information services. Richard W. Stockton, general manager of NYT Custom Publishing, was appointed vice president for the operating unit. Vincent R. Cimmino, group controller, was named vice president, finance, for the information service group. Henry Scott, group director of new-business development, was promoted to vice president for new media and new products. Erich G. Linker Jr., senior vice president for group sales at The newyork Times Magazine Group, was named vice president for marketing of the information services division.

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY: HOTELS;
Interactive Business
body: A new program on the Internet means personal-computer users will soon have an alternative to phone calls and brochures when planning a stay at hotels run by companies like Hyatt, Hilton and Forte. Travelweb, advertised as the hotel industry's first interactive electronic travel catalogue, provides PC users with detailed color photographs and information on rates, restaurants, local attractions and other amenities at participating hotels. By the year's end, PC users should be able to book reservations directly on their computers as well. At present, reservations can be made by calling (800) 233-1234. The free service, available to anyone using the Internet's World Wide Web, can be accessed by logging in www.travelweb.com. Though initially Travelweb is offering information only on 16 Hyatt resorts in the unitedstates and the Caribbean, 87 additional Hyatt properties will be included before the year ends. And next month, Travelweb should extend to properties of other members in Thisco, a large reservations system that includes ITT Sheraton, Best Western and Marriott.   TERRY TRUCCO

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Stock Buyback For Times Co.
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that its board had authorized the repurchase of up to $100 million of its class A common shares. The stock repurchase program is the company's second in a year. The Times Company said yesterday that it had spent all of the $150 million authorized under a program announced on Oct. 21, 1993. Under the board's latest authorization, purchases may be made from time to time on the open market or through private transactions. The Times Company said the repurchased shares would be used for the company's stock-based employee benefit plans and for other corporate purposes. The company's class A common shares closed yesterday at $22 each, down 37.5 cents, on the American Stock Exchange.

title: New Golf Travel Service
body: The newyork Times Sports/Leisure Magazines, which publishes magazines that include Golf Digest and Golf World, said yesterday that the group would introduce a travel division that offers one-stop shopping for customized golf travel. The travel club, called the Golf Digest Resort and Travel Club, is scheduled to be in operation on Nov. 15 and will be open to all interested consumers. With one toll-free phone call, members would be able to book resort or lodging accommodations, tee times, instructions, flights and car rentals.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
PIPELINE IN AGREEMENT TO MARKET INTERNET SOFTWARE
body: The Pipeline Company, an Internet service provider in newyork, reported yesterday that it had reached an agreement with Intercon Systems Inc. of Herndon, Va., to market Pipeline's proprietary Internet access software internationally to corporate, academic and commercial customers. The agreement is one of the most ambitious attempts to establish a standard software control panel for nontechnical users of Internet, the global information network.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Electronic Newspaper
body: The Gainesville Sun, a Florida newspaper owned by The newyork Times Company, has agreed to publish an electronic edition in cooperation with the College of Journalism and Communications at the University of Florida. Students will prepare the electronic paper, which will offer versions of articles to be published in The Sun the next day. The service, known as SUN.ONE, will have advertising and will be offered at no charge for 30 minutes a day. Unlimited usage can be purchased for flat fees starting at $6.66 a month. Customers must have a personal computer and modem.

title: To Our Readers
body: The newyork Times last week increased the size and spacing of the type used in news articles, in letters to the editor and on the Op-Ed page. The goal of the change is ease of reading. The change is most noticeable on news pages inside The Times, where white space has been added between lines of body type. Previously, extra spacing was largely confined to the front page and the editorials. In the next few weeks, the change will be extended to Sunday sections; article typography will then be consistent on all standard-size pages. For comparison, the previous two paragraphs are set in the old type style. This paragraph and the next two are in the new style. The Times's typeface remains Imperial, designed by Edwin W. Shaar in the 1950's and adopted by this newspaper in 1967. In printers' terminology, the former size was 8 1/2-point (1 point equals about 1/72 inch of height). The new size is 8.7-point. More important to legibility is the spacing between lines. That measurement -- from the base of one line to the base of the next -- was previously 8.8 points inside the newspaper; now it is 9.6 points uniformly.
