title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Executive to Join Times
body: Harold F. Woldt Jr., a senior executive at Newsday, will be joining The newyork Times later this month as deputy circulation director, The newyork Times Company announced yesterday. He will report to Charles E. Shelton, vice president for circulation, and will be responsible for circulation sales and operations -- including home delivery and customer service -- throughout the unitedstates. Mr. Woldt, 47, is the senior vice president for circulation and distribution at Newsday. In his nine years at the Long Island-based paper, Mr. Woldt developed the circulation strategy for newyork Newsday, an edition that is primarily sold in Brooklyn and Queens.

title:
WEDDINGS;
Susan P. Jeffery, Matthew S. Fine
body: Susan Penhallow Jeffery, a communications consultant in White Plains, and Matthew Stuart Fine, the sales manager of the multimedia division of Dow Jones & Company in newyork, were married yesterday in Salisbury, Conn. The Rev. Dr. Charles Bevan performed the ceremony at St. John's Episcopal Church. Mrs. Fine, 28, graduated from Mount Vernon College. She is a daughter of David E. Jeffery of Charlevoix, Mich., and Sarah P. Jeffery of Shelton, Conn. The bride's father is the owner of an insurance agency in Charlevoix. Mr. Fine, 34, graduated from the University of Pennsylvania. He is a son of Wilma C. Fine of Harrison, N.Y., and the late C. Robert Fine. His mother, a former vice president and recording director for Mercury Records in newyork, is the producer of the Mercury "Living Presence" classical music series. His father, who was a sound production engineer in newyork, won two Grammy Awards.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Sports Service For Computers
body: The Sports/Leisure Magazines Group of The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it would develop with the Unet 2 Corporation an on-line sports network for computer users. The companies said they planned to start the service, to be called the Sports/Leisure Online Network, by the beginning of 1995. Magazines of the Times Company that will be available on the computer network include Golf World, Tennis, Snow Country, Cruising World and Sailing World. Subscribers to the network will be able to communicate with one another, receive instructions from experts in a particular sport and look at classified advertisements. Unet is an electronic publisher that specializes in on-line consumer services.

title: Times Raising Weekday Price
body: The newsstand price of The newyork Times on weekdays will be raised to 60 cents from 50 cents within the newyork metropolitan area, the newspaper announced yesterday. The change in price, which will not affect the price of home delivery or of the Sunday newspaper, takes effect Sept. 12, said Nancy Nielsen, a spokeswoman for The Times. The price increase is necessary because of an increase in the cost of newsprint, Ms. Nielsen said. The 50-cent newsstand price of The Times has been in effect since September 1991.

title:
WEDDINGS;
Roseann DeJoseph, Thomas Cavallaro
body: Dr. Roseann Judith DeJoseph, a dentist in Huntington, L.I., was married yesterday to Thomas James Cavallaro, a senior financial analyst at The newyork Times Company in newyork. The Rev. Francis Black performed the ceremony at St. Helen's Roman Catholic Church in Howard Beach, Queens. The bride, 28, will be known as Dr. DeJoseph Cavallaro. She graduated from Adelphi University and received a D.D.S. degree from the State University at Stony Brook, L.I. She is the daughter of Leona DeJoseph of Howard Beach and the late Joseph DeJoseph. The bride's father was a production manager at Jonathan Logan, the women's clothing manufacturer, in newyork. Mr. Cavallaro, 30, is a certified public accountant. He graduated cum laude from St. John's University in Queens, from which he also received an M.B.A. He is a son of Johanna and Albert F. Cavallaro of Westbury, L.I. His father teaches mathematics at Great Neck South (L.I.) Public High School.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
British Golf Magazines Sold
body: A British publisher, EMAP P.L.C., has acquired three British golf magazines from The newyork Times Company. EMAP said it paid £11.25 million ($17.4 million) for the magazines: Golf Weekly, Golf Industry News and Golf World (U.K.). As part of the deal, the Times Company will work with EMAP to develop joint advertising sales in the unitedstates. The three publications will be allowed to reprint articles from Golf Digest, an American magazine owned by the Times Company. Last month, the Times Company announced a separate deal to sell the British publications to IPC Magazines, a unit of the British-Dutch publisher Reed Elsevier P.L.C. But a final agreement was never reached, the Times Company said. EMAP, which had revenue of £362 million ($560 million) for the fiscal year that ended in March, has interests in consumer and trade magazines, newspapers and broadcasting, mainly in Europe.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Co. Appointment
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it had named Jacqueline M. Leo director of magazine and media development. She will be responsible for developing new products across the company's lines of business, which include magazines, newspapers, broadcasting and information services. Ms. Leo had been editorial director of the Times Company's Women's Magazines Group, but that division was sold recently to Gruner & Jahr USA Publishing. Ms. Leo joined the Times Company in 1987 as editor in chief of Child. In 1988, she was appointed editor in chief of Family Circle magazine, before being named editorial director of the magazine group in March.

title: Doubts on Internet
body: Some experts contend that far fewer people use the Internet web of computer networks than the 20 million to 30 million generally estimated.  But there is widespread agreement that the number of users is growing rapidly, perhaps doubling each year. Business Day, page D1.

title: Digital Focuses On Internet Use
body: The Digital Equipment Corporation said today that it had formed a unit to provide services and products geared toward customers who rely on the Internet in their businesses. The company, a computer maker based in Maynard, Mass., said its Internet Business Group would sell products to provide security against unwanted prowlers on the Internet and provide software to make it easier to navigate the amalgam of global computer networks that make up the Internet. Digital, which has been struggling through restructuring and financial losses in recent years, will also use the unit to market its products. Internet users can "test drive" the company's advanced Alpha microprocessor and get information about other Digital products, a spokeswoman said.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
Executive Changes
body: DELPHI INTERNET SERVICES, Cambridge, Mass., a unit of the News Corporation, appointed Dr. Alan Baratz chief executive. HAMBURGER HAMLET INC., Sherman Oaks, Calif., named A. Shawn Holder president and chief executive, succeeding Jack A. Lavine, who had held those positions on an interim basis. Mr. Lavine has been named to the post of executive vice president and chief financial officer.

title:
SUNDAY, JULY 24, 1994;
'Wanted' Posting
body: No need to run to the post office. "Wanted" posters are now on line. The Air Force Office of Special Investigations made Internet history on June 24 when its computer crime officers posted a "Fugitive Sought!" message to several news groups. The Air Force and the Okaloosa County, Fla., sheriff's office are trying to track down Edward Jon Zakrzewski, an Air Force sergeant who allegedly killed his wife and two daughters. The posting included a description of his car, a blue 1992 Geo Prism, and his license number, and noted that he had Internet access. His on-line ID: zakrzews. If you have information about him, contact the Air Force at masseyd@eglin.af.mil or (904) 882-2152/5565, or the Okaloosa sheriff at (904) 651-7400.

title: Alfred E. Clark; Reporter, 80
body: Alfred E. Clark, a reporter for The newyork Times for more than 40 years, died on Tuesday at St. Clare's Hospital. He lived in Manhattan and was 80 years old. The cause was cardiac arrest, said his wife, Frances. Mr. Clark started at The Times as a copy boy in 1932 while a student at Stuyvesant High School and later at St. Peter's College in Jersey City. After becoming a reporter in 1941, he covered a wide range of subjects, especially crime, the police and politics in the city. He was a former president of the Newspaper Reporters Association and a member of the Inner Circle of political writers and of the Silurians, a group of veteran newspaper reporters and editors. He retired in 1983. He is survived by his wife of 43 years.

title: Executive Changes
body: BANKERS TRUST CO., newyork, named Bluford H. Putnam managing director and chief strategist of its global investment management group.  DATA BROADCASTING CORP., newyork, named Mark Imperiale executive vice president and chief financial officer, succeeding Stephen W. Ellis, who assumes the new position of executive vice president of administration. FUTURE HEALTHCARE INC., Cincinnati, named Keith A. Cheesman chief financial officer.  OM GROUP INC., Cleveland, a producer and international marketer of value-added, metal-based specialty chemicals, appointed Eugene Bak president and chief operating officer.  RIGGS NATIONAL BANK, Washington, appointed Fred Bollerer president and chief executive.

title: Carl Barnett; Newspaper Foreman, 76
body: Carl Barnett, a general foreman for the delivery department of The newyork Times for more than 30 years, died on Saturday at St. Francis Hospital in Roslyn, L.I. He was 76 and a resident of Port Washington, L.I. The cause was cardiac arrest, his wife, Mary, said. Mr. Barnett was born in Manhattan and reared in Pelham Bay, the Bronx. He joined The Times in 1945 as a truck driver after serving with the Navy Seabees in the Pacific during World War II. In 1949, he was promoted to general foreman, the top position in the delivery department at that time. He left the position in 1979 to work in the circulation department. He retired in 1980. In addition to his wife, he is survived by a son, Carl Bryan of Ojai, Calif.

title:
COMPANY REPORTS;
DOW JONES & CO. (DJ,N)
body: Dow Jones & Company reported yesterday a 15.6 percent increase in earnings for the second quarter. Despite the rise, the price of the company's shares declined on the newyork Stock Exchange. The reported earnings of 46 cents a share were at the low end of analysts' estimates, which had ranged from 46 cents to 52 cents a share. The company reported that it earned $46.02 million in the second quarter, up from $39.81 million, or 40 cents a share, in the corresponding period of 1993. Total income rose 7.6 percent, to $524 million from $487 million. The company said revenues from its business publications segment, which includes The Wall Street Journal, increased 4.7 percent, to $219 million, even though advertisiing linage at The Journal showed a decline of 2.7 percent in the quarter. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Retirement At The Times
body: Michael E. Ryan, a senior vice president of The newyork Times Company, has retired after 38 years with the company, Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, the chairman, announced yesterday. Mr. Ryan, 56 years old, will be a consultant to The Times, handling special assignments. He had supervised legal matters and the company's forest products division. His many areas of responsibility since 1967 have also included corporate development, administration, finance, broadcasting, cable, real estate, human resources and public relations. Commenting on Mr. Ryan's departure, Mr. Sulzberger said: "Mike and I grew up together at The Times. Much of what we today take for granted is due in no small measure to Mike's vision and hard work. He was instrumental in guiding us in the transition from a private to a public company, and his stamp is on many of the acquisitions we later made. I shall miss my day-to-day contact, but I am gratified that he will be available for special assignments."

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Dow Jones in Vietnam
body: Dow Jones Telerate Inc. has announced that it will introduce its financial information services in Vietnam. The service monitors prices from world financial markets, financial news and market analysis. The introduction of Telerate's products will be sponsored by the Vietnamese Government. Terms were not disclosed. Dow Jones Telerate is a unit of the newyork-based Dow Jones & Company, which publishes The Wall Street Journal and Barron's.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Begins On-Line News
body: The newyork Times Company and America Online started a service yesterday to give computer users access to an electronic data base of articles and information from The newyork Times. People who subscribe to the service, which is called "@times," will have access through their computers to the main news articles of the day from The newyork Times News Service. But the two companies said the main feature of the service would be an entertainment guide that included a range of reviews and articles on cultural as well as arts and leisure activities in the newyork region. It will include information about the theater, movies, books, restaurants, art exhibitions, music performances and sports events as well as an archive of reviews from The Times. The service is interactive, meaning subscribers to the service can post messages to electronic bulletin boards to discuss a variety of topics. In the future, the companies said, users will be able to hold discussions through the service with some writers at The Times. Information about subscribing to the service, which is available seven days a week, can be obtained from America Online at (800) 827-6364.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Honors
body: * Jacqueline Leo, senior vice president and editorial director of the Women's Magazines Group at The newyork Times Company, was named to receive the 1994 Human Relations Award by the publishers division of the American Jewish Committee. Ms. Leo will be honored at a dinner on June 22 in newyork.

title: Sega to Begin Cable Ventures
body: Sega Enterprises Ltd., a leading Japanese game maker, said today that it would soon begin joint ventures to distribute game software through cable television in both Japan and the unitedstates. Subscribers to some cable networks in Japan will be able to receive Sega game software through their cable system and play the games on their television sets for 3,000 yen ($28) a month, Hiroyuki Mori, a Sega spokesman, said. Sega Digital Communications, the company that will distribute the new service, will be set up on July 1, the spokesman said. The venture will provide about 30 different game software titles each month. It will be the first such game-software distribution company in Japan, Mr. Mori said. He said Sega would start a similar distribution business soon in 12 or more unitedstates states and territories through a joint venture with Time Warner and Tele-Communications Inc. More than 70 percent of households in the unitedstates subscribe to cable television, but in Japan only 132,000 households get cable, which is mostly limited to locally operated channels.

title:

Resume Service Ends for Times
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it would no longer participate in an electronic resume distribution service called Fastrak. The newyork Times announced in November that it would offer a new interactive system for employers to advertise jobs and for prospective employees to send resumes. The service, which began in January, had a strong response from users, the company said. The Times said the company that developed the system, Information Kinetics Inc. of Chicago, was ceasing to provide the service. Officials of Information Kinetics could not be reached for comment yesterday. The Times, however, said yesterday that it was exploring the possibility of another, broader system in association with The Chicago Tribune.

title: INFORMATION FUTURE: OUT OF CONTROL
body: In "The Information Future: Out of Control" (May 1), James Gleick claims that "the Internet is like a town that leaves its streets unmarked on the principle that people who don't already know don't belong." I know of no other community whose inhabitants are so willing to help everyone, friend and stranger. Many of the Internet resources contain documents, known in Internet jargon as F.A.Q.'s (frequently asked questions), to help the newcomer learn how to get around. Pleas for help to the myriad mailing lists, bulletin boards, forums and the like bring many, usually instant, replies. The Internet is democratic and welcoming, which, in part, accounts for its incredible growth.  HOWARD L. FUNK Former Executive Director, Internet Society Katonah, N.Y.

title:

body: Janet L. Robinson, a vice president for advertising at The newyork Times, has been named to the expanded position of vice president and director of advertising. Ms. Robinson, whose appointment is effective today, will be in charge of overall advertising sales at the newspaper in addition to her current responsibilities for national advertising and for The newyork Times Magazine. Ms. Robinson will report to William L. Pollak, executive vice president for sales, who said her new responsibilities reflected a reorganization of the sales and marketing departments. Ms. Robinson, who is 43, became a vice president last year after serving as a group senior vice president for the advertising sales and marketing unit of The newyork Times Company Magazine Group since January 1992 and vice president for the group since September 1990. Ms. Robinson joined the Times Company in 1983 as an account executive at Tennis magazine. She was the national resort and travel manager of Golf Digest/Tennis from 1985 to 1987 and the advertising director of Tennis from 1987 to 1990. title: Internet Commercials Are O.K., but Be Polite
body: To the Editor: The problem with Laurence Canter's advertisement over the Internet (Business Day, April 19) was not that he used the Internet for commercial purposes. Commercial usage is legal. The real problem is that he posted his message to thousands of news groups unrelated to the topic. I teach an introduction to Internet for faculty and staff at Swarthmore College; one thing we discuss is Netiquette: using the Internet politely. That means choosing a news group designed for the type of information you intend to post. Mr. Canter bombarded Internet users with the same message in every conceivable news group. That's the electronic equivalent of ambulance-chasing, and it is rude and destructive.  ANDREW J. PERRIN Philadelphia, April 19, 1994

title:
SUNDAY, APRIL 24, 1994;
Purse by Any Other Name
body: Comment read on the Internet: "Electronic Purse? No real man is going to be caught dead using such a thing. Give me electronic gold or electronic silver." This bit of macho pique was touched off by the word "purse" in a news release from an international consortium organized by Visa. The group is developing standards for a worldwide digital money card that would have a computer chip to register how much money it "holds." Users would load the card with money at a bank cash machine and then spend it on gasoline, groceries, food, telephone calls and other items wherever the equipment existed to handle the card. The question is, Why a purse and not a wallet? Albert Coscia of Visa says the term has no great meaning or marketing purpose. It's a term that evolved in Europe and "is widely used in the payment card industry." A purse is simply something to hold money, and male net-nerds may just have to get used to it.

title: Henry Gemmill; Newspaper Editor, 76
body: Henry Gemmill, a former managing editor of The Wall Street Journal, died on Sunday in Washington. He was 76 and had homes in Washington and Franklin, Me. His family said the cause was heart failure. Mr. Gemmill was managing editor of the Journal from 1950 to 1954. A 1939 graduate of Yale University, he began his career with Dow Jones in 1942 as a reporter in the Washington bureau of The Journal and was subsequently news editor, Washington bureau chief and chief of European correspondents. He was also editor of The National Observer, a weekly publication of Dow Jones and Company, from 1971 until it ceased publication in July 1977. He retired from Dow Jones at the end of that year. He is survived by his wife, Ann-Mari; two daughters, Elisabeth Izenour of Philadelphia and Ann-Maria Gemmill of Tacoma Park, Md., and a son John, of Guilford, Conn.

title: Military Jitters Over Internet
body: Fearful that computer hackers could invade Pentagon data networks, officials of the Defense Department are moving to limit military links to the Internet, the backbone of the emerging advances in information technology, a computer magazine said yesterday. Network World said a plan to add a protective gateway to Milnet, the worldwide military data network, has touched off an uproar among computer users inside and outside the Pentagon. A brief notice from the Defense Department's network planning group said the gateway was to be introduced early in 1994, the magazine said, though the plan has not yet been carried out. A spokeswoman for the Pentagon had no comment on the report but said the department closely monitored computer security. "We are looking at ways to protect the network against hackers and viruses," she said. Network World said critics of the plan argued that the security gateway could not handle the volume of electronic mail and data that now flows daily between Milnet and Internet users around the world. They questioned why less drastic security measures commonly used by industry to protect computer networks had apparently been rejected by the military.

title: Cisco and Motorola Make Wireless Deal
body: Trying to deliver high-speed Internet links without wires, Cisco Systems Inc. and Motorola Inc. plan to announce today that they have agreed to acquire a subsidiary of the Robert Bosch Corporation of Germany that is developing advanced wireless technology. Cisco and Motorola do not plan to disclose terms of the agreement, but executives close to the deal said the price would be substantially less than $1 billion. That would be in line with other recent acquisitions by Cisco, which has made a string of deals but none for more than $265 million since 1996, when Cisco acquired Stratacom Inc. for $4.7 billion. Cisco, the No. 1 maker of data networking equipment, and Motorola, a big maker of cellular phones and equipment, plan to buy a Bosch unit based in Richardson, Tex., that has between 100 and 200 employees. The unit is trying to make products to transmit large amounts of data between stationary fixed antennas using a wireless technology. One of the hottest battlegrounds in the communications industry has become the competition to offer high-capacity data links to consumers and small and medium-sized business customers. The AT&T Corporation has bet more than $90 billion that it can offer advanced communications packages using cable television systems, for example. The Baby Bell local phone carriers, MCI Worldcom and others, meanwhile, are focused on so-called digital subscriber lines, a new technology that increases the data capacity of normal phone lines. The dark-horse technology in this race has been wireless. Wireless mobile telephones have become popular, but no company has yet succeeded in broadly and profitably delivering torrents of Internet data using wireless links -- whether mobile or stationary. With the Bosch deal, Motorola and Cisco want to make high-speed delivery of stationary wireless data possible. "This really strengthens our position in high-speed Internet access," said Donald J. Listwin, a Cisco executive vice president. In acquiring the Bosch unit, Cisco and Motorola intend to form a new company called Spectrapoint Wireless. Motorola will own 81 percent of Spectrapoint and Cisco will own 19 percent. Cisco began developing technology in cooperation with Bosch about a year ago, but found that potential customers wanted not only technology, but also financing and help in deploying wireless equipment. Partly to address those needs, Cisco turned to Motorola and in February Cisco and Motorola announced plans to spend $1 billion jointly for a period of up to five years to develop wireless products. One challenge to Spectrapoint in the unitedstates could be in finding customers. Teligent Inc. and Winstar Communications Inc. were the first two unitedstates companies to try to broadly deliver voice, video and data services using stationary, or fixed, wireless technology. But Teligent has already committed itself to use mostly wireless equipment from the Nortel Networks Corporation of Canada while Winstar is working closely with Lucent Technologies. Potential new customers, including Nextlink Communications Inc., which is backed by Craig O. McCaw, the cellular phone pioneer, are on the horizon, however. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
Voicemail and Faxes Add Intrigue to email Offer
body: Free email may be about to become a lot more interesting. A small start-up company called Onebox.com plans today to start a new service on the Web that combines free email with free voicemail and free incoming faxes. If the company can iron out some bugs in its service, if its business model holds up and if the technology can handle thousands of users, Onebox.com could find itself at the front of a new wave of Internet messaging. Free email, generally supported by advertising, has become common on line, through services like Microsoft's Hotmail.com. But Onebox.com goes further. Not only does it offer free email, but each user is to receive a free personal voicemail account. Onebox.com will start by offering local numbers only in Austin, Tex., and San Mateo, Calif., but even as a long-distance service it could find popularity among corporate road warriors. That is because the voicemail accounts can receive faxes as well as voice messages, which are listed in on-screen directories. The voicemail account is also accessible from a normal telephone, though the service will not be able to read email or fax messages to the user over the phone. "People have tried to solve unified messaging by doing a telephone approach, by stuffing everything into the phone," said Bill Nguyen, a company founder. "But we stuff everything into the Web instead." There were still some bugs last week, mostly with the fax capabilities. The fax display quality was low, printing faxes did not always work on command and figuring out how to send a fax to the service could be confusing. Nonetheless, Onebox.com has found at least one convert: Zdnet, a unit of Softbank, which has signed up as Onebox.com's first Web distributor.   SETH SCHIESEL http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Bill Nguyen is one founder of Onebox.com, which plans free voicemail and fax service. (Darcy Padilla for The newyork Times)

title: Disney Said To Consider Web Spinoff
body: The Walt Disney Company is considering a spinoff of its Internet-related operations, several people close to the discussions said yesterday. The details of any plan were not clear, but Disney has stakes in several Internet businesses that could become part of any spinoff. A Disney spokesman declined to comment. Still, analysts say that Disney is under pressure to raise its sagging stock price, which has been hurt recently by weak earnings from its television and film operations. For the second quarter, Disney said its profit fell 30 percent because of weaker home video and merchandising sales and higher costs at ABC. Despite those figures, shares of Disney rose $1.625, or 5.6 percent, on Friday, to $30.625, amid reports that Disney might either spin off some of its Internet operations or possibly buy back some stock. Disney's stock had been as high as $40.313 last July and had fallen to $22.50 by October. A year ago, Disney acquired 43 percent of the Infoseek Corporation, a service that helps guide users on the World Wide Web, in a deal valued at $900 million. Disney put up $90 million in cash and its ownership of Starwave, a company that creates elaborate Web sites. Disney had previously acquired Starwave in several phases from Paul Allen, the co-founder of Microsoft. The company's biggest venture is the sports site it operates on behalf of ESPN. Several of Disney's other businesses, including ABC, ABC News and Disney itself, have established Web sites, and one analyst speculated yesterday that Disney might swap those assets into Infoseek in exchange for a larger stake in the company. Infoseek executives could not be reached for comment yesterday. Disney already has the right to raise its stake in Infoseek to as much as 50.1 percent as part of an agreement to lend Infoseek up to $139 million over the first five years of the deal. Infoseek and Disney have also created the Go Network, Disney's answer to Yahoo, and other portals to the Internet. Disney could theoretically spin off some of its assets into a tracking stock, where underlying assets are owned by the parent company but the stock itself is publicly traded. But a spinoff might not be met as favorably on Wall Street as a stock buyback because Internet stocks have weakened and new offerings have lost some of their allure. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Market Place;
Notes on corporate culture and possibilities as MCI Worldcom meets two years after its creation.
body: JUST as legal concerns began to percolate last Wednesday about whether MCI Worldcom Inc. misled investors as it negotiated its deal to buy Skytel Communications, the company convened its first meeting for analysts and investors in more than two years. So much has changed in the telecommunications industry in two years that MCI Worldcom, the No. 2 long-distance carrier behind AT&T, did not even exist in 1997. Back then, an acquisition of MCI may not have even been a gleam in the eye of Bernard J. Ebbers, formerly chairman of Worldcom and now chief executive of the combined company, which was formed when Worldcom acquired MCI. So the four-hour series of presentations last week in Manhattan offered a useful update on a company that continues to grow far faster than AT&T, even if AT&T has recently grabbed more headlines through its move into cable television. And even if MCI Worldcom seemed to try hard not to make any news at the meeting, at least three salient points emerged:  AT&T-MCI RIVALRY IN DECLINE -- Ever since William G. McGowan took over MCI three decades ago, the company has defined itself as anti-AT&T. With AT&T starting off with 100 percent of the long-distance market, and MCI angling for a share, the two companies focused on many of the same corporate and residential customers. But over the last year, their strategies have significantly diverged. AT&T, fearful that the Bell local phone giants could soon ransack its stronghold in the consumer long-distance market, has agreed to spend more than $90 billion to become a cable television powerhouse. Thus, AT&T hopes to counterattack the Bells in local arenas. MCI Worldcom, by now, is far less dependent on residential customers, and so it has not had to respond to the Bell threat as has AT&T. As MCI discussed its investment plans at the meeting, the focus was not on household telephone service but on Internet and overseas expansion. Before acquiring MCI, Worldcom served hardly any residential customers, and none of the top former Worldcom executives seem particularly enthusiastic about consumer markets now. They have that luxury largely because they have Uunet, the No. 1 Internet service provider, which mostly serves businesses and other Internet service providers. AT&T is far behind Uunet. According to Boardwatch magazine, a trade publication, MCI Worldcom has 2,952 backbone Internet connections to AT&T's 382. AT&T is beefing up its business-services unit, and MCI Worldcom may one day propose a broad plan to offer communications bundles to consumers. But for now the two giants seem to be focusing most of their attention in separate directions.  DON'T CALL IT A TAKEOVER -- The polite word for what Worldcom did with MCI is "merge," but the real term is "take over." It is obvious that except for the sales and marketing operation (which is, to be sure, the unit that brings in business), former Worldcom executives are running the show and setting the strategic direction. After Mr. Ebbers opened Wednesday's conference, he was followed by three more Worldcom veterans: Scott D. Sullivan, chief financial officer; John W. Sidgmore, vice chairman and Internet czar, and Ron Beaumont, executive vice president for operations and technology. Despite persistent rumors that Timothy F. Price, MCI's marketing chief, is not getting along with his Worldcom brethren, no friction was obvious on Wednesday. In the somewhat tribal culture of the old MCI, Mr. Price generated more loyalty than perhaps any other MCI executive after Mr. McGowan, who died in 1992. And it may speak to Mr. Price's value that he is the most senior MCI executive who still appears publicly engaged in running the combined company. Mr. Price and two of his subordinates gave presentations at the meeting. So did Fred M. Briggs, the chief technology officer, who came from MCI and reports to Mr. Beaumont. But Bert C. Roberts Jr., MCI's former chairman, who is now chairman of the combined company, was not even at Wednesday's meeting. Perhaps even more telling, his absence did not seem to surprise anyone in the audience.  SPRINT SPECULATION ABOUNDS -- In comments made in the aisles and corridors, it became clear that at least some analysts and investors believe that MCI Worldcom ought to wind up acquiring the Sprint Corporation, the No. 3 long-distance carrier. "I've already built it into my model," an analyst joked. There would be two main benefits to such a deal. First, Sprint would give MCI Worldcom a nationwide wireless phone network. (MCI has no cellular business.) Second, Mr. Sullivan and his financial engineers could surely wring billions in costs from a combined MCI Worldcom-Sprint. The two companies do not appear to be in negotiations. But based on some aisle discussions Wednesday, it is clear that top MCI Worldcom executives have thought about it. They fear, though, that regulators would balk on antitrust grounds at the prospect of the top four long-distance carriers of a couple of years ago -- AT&T, MCI, Sprint and Worldcom -- becoming only two. But once the Bells jump into the long-distance market, those regulatory concerns may ease. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: "Flying High" tracsk daily closing stock price of MCI Worldcom, since the acquisiton that created the company. (Source: Bloomberg Financial Markets) Dai

title:
Media Talk;
Dow Jones JournalistsProtest Pension Cuts
body: Six weeks ago, a large group of journalists at Dow Jones & Company decided to assemble in an unusual venue -- the company's annual meeting -- to express their dismay over proposed cutbacks in their pension benefits. Last week, another group of Dow Jones journalists decided not to assemble in a usual venue -- the CNBC studios -- to make the same point. The quasi-boycott began when Robert Langreth, a Wall Street Journal science reporter and a member of the board of Local 1096 of the Independent Association of Publishing Employees, was instructed to keep his union button -- reading "I <heart> My Retirement Benefits" -- out of sight before CNBC's cameras started filming him on May 24. . Soon, a button boycott broke out. Reporter after reporter decided that there were better things to do than appear buttonless on CNBC. After all, when Dow Jones contracted to provide material to CNBC, the company assured reporters that their appearances would be voluntary. In the last 10 days, the number of volunteers plummeted. According to the accounts of five Journal reporters, Charles Gasparino and Rebecca Buckman rebuffed a CNBC liaison seeking to have them discuss their page-one article about Merrill Lynch's decision to offer on-line stock trading. Their editor, Larry Ingrassia, appeared instead. On Thursday, William Pesek, an economics correspondent at Barron's, which is owned by Dow Jones, declined to go on CNBC to talk about Alice M. Rivlin's resignation from the Federal Reserve Board. "It came out of nowhere," said a reporter participating in the boycott, who insisted that he not be identified. "It does reflect the anger and concern of a lot of people at the paper." Richard J. Tofel, vice president of corporate communications for Dow Jones, said the reporters' action had little impact on the Dow Jones contributions to CNBC. He noted that the Washington bureau chief, Alan Murray, had been on the air, as had the technology columnist, Walter Mossberg, and several reporters. "There is not a single story for which we have failed to produce somebody knowledgeable," Mr. Tofel said, "so the viewers have not missed anything." Except a chance to see some union buttons.   FELICITY BARRINGER http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The button that sparked a boycott.

title: Microsoft Binds Office Software More Tightly to Internet
body: The Microsoft Corporation's power and influence in the computer industry stems not only from its dominant Windows operating system, but also from its office productivity software. And on Monday, Microsoft will announce that it has begun retail shipments of a new version of its office productivity "suite," Office 2000, that all but eliminates the distinctions between a PC document and Internet data. Office 2000, which includes word processing, spreadsheet, presentation, data base, email, scheduling and other software functions, has a long list of new features -- almost all of which are intended to give PC users a set of software tools that deeply integrate Internet capabilities. At the heart of the integration strategy is Microsoft's adoption of the World Wide Web's basic document structure -- known as HTML, for hypertext markup language -- intended to make it easy to publish documents on the Web and perform what is known as "round tripping," or translating documents back and forth between Web and traditional Microsoft Office formats. "You're looking at the standard in the corporate world," Amy Wohl, president of Wohl Associates, a computer industry consulting firm, said. "The program has an enormous number of improvements in terms of features and integration with Windows and the Internet." And, depending on one's perspective, the business strategy and product capabilities of Office 2000 either underscore the urgency of the Federal antitrust trial that continues this week -- or make that trial even more irrelevant. One issue in the trial is whether Microsoft's hegemony in personal computer software has enabled the company to dominate other parts of the software industry to the point of exercising illegal monopoly power. Certainly, Office 2000 represents Microsoft's clearest example yet of subsuming Internet capabilities into one of the company's dominant desktop products. In any case, the arrival of Office 2000 on store shelves and in corporate offices this week will very likely unleash a tidal wave of revenue for the giant software publisher. Microsoft had already begun to receive income as part of a commercial test of Office 2000, including $400 million in the last quarter, which the company has said it will report as revenue once the product starts shipping in volume. Company executives said on Friday that they would not make any public statements about preshipment sales. But Ms. Wohl said she had been told that Microsoft had already received orders for 15 million copies of Office 2000. Traditionally, each new major product generation represents a crossroads for the software publisher, and industry analysts have repeatedly questioned whether computer users will continue to have an appetite for Microsoft's barrage of new features. With Office 2000, though, Microsoft executives said, they are confident they have addressed such concerns by insuring that Office 2000 documents will be compatible with documents created using the previous version of Office and by simplifying the program's control panel, or so-called user interface. "The best way to address the compatibility issue is by not having to change anything," Steve Sinofsky, vice president of Microsoft's office business, said. Mr. Sinofsky said the company had not tampered with Microsoft's existing file formats except in its Access data base program. And in the case of Access, he said, the company had tried to make the translation of data seamless to computer users. Despite such efforts, some industry analysts said computer users would be forced toward a new dimension of complexity by the shift to Internet-compatible documents. "This is very sophisticated code, and that's a troubling direction when you think of the history of PC's as tools that empower individuals," Jeffrey Tarter, publisher of the computer industry newsletter Softletter, said. "I'm not sure you're empowering people when you turn a simple word processing document into five pages of programming code." The code, which controls the appearance of a document like a Web page, is hidden from the user. The potential for problems arises if a user wants to manipulate the document in a way not anticipated by Microsoft's programmers. But Mr. Sinofsky said adding computer code to documents was not actually a new approach. He pointed to the popular Adobe Postscript format, which has long incorporated similar hidden complexity to give computer users control over the appearance of their documents. Microsoft executives also took issue with the widespread opinion among industry analysts that it would be corporate users, rather than people who use PC's at home or in small offices, who would find compelling reasons to upgrade to the new program. "I think the individual user will find Office 2000 useful because you can do things you just couldn't do before," Mr. Sinofsky said. He pointed to the ability to take pictures of one's children and publish them on a Web site for viewing by grandparents as an example of the kind of feature that would drive noncorporate users to the new product. This newest product rollout continues a process of integrating application programs that Microsoft began in 1990, when it introduced the first version of Office, bundling together its Word, Excel, Powerpoint and Mail applications. By 1993, with the introduction of Office 4.0, the integrated program had become the primary product, as opposed to the individual application programs. That integration strategy proved to be the key competitive edge in the battle to wrest the corporate market from companies like Lotus and, at the time, Wordperfect. Although the Justice Department has largely ignored the company's virtual office-suite monopoly in the current antitrust suit, the issue has come up in trial testimony given by Avi Tevanian, the Apple Computer Corporation's top software executive. In a deposition last year, Mr. Tevanian testified that Microsoft executives had threatened to cancel development of Office 98, the Apple Macintosh version of the Office suite, if Apple did not adopt Microsoft's Internet Explorer as its primary Web browser software. Microsoft executives responded that the Government was twisting the significance of its business negotiations with Apple. Still, even with its control of more than 90 percent of the retail market for office productivity software, Microsoft could find itself under increasing pricing pressure from the Corel Corporation, the feisty Canadian software publisher. Corel, which acquired the Wordperfect brand several years ago, began shipping a new product in April known as Wordperfect Office 2000. The program has received strongly positive reviews. Corel contends that it has 22 million users worldwide and said it was focusing on its current customer base by simplifying and adding Internet features to its new version. "We still have a massive installed base," Jimi Smith, director of brand management for Wordperfect Office, said. "These people have stuck with us for a reason. The entry-level version of Wordperfect Office has been selling for as little as $79 in major chains like Comp USA, Mr. Smith said. In contrast, the standard version of Microsoft's Office 2000 has a street price of $229. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: "Suite Success" Microsoft dominates the growing market for office productivity software.  Breakdown of office suite sales, April 1999 Microsoft -- 93% Corel -- 6% Lotus -- 1%  Graph also tracks retail sales of office suites, from 1995 to 1999. (Source: PC Data)

title:
TECHNOLOGY: E-Commerce Report;
As the number of their viewers declines, television networks are testing the Internet to sell products from their programs.
body: FOR television executives, the notion of sharing viewers with the Internet has been about as palatable as showing reruns of the news during sweeps week. But they also recognize that to take part in the dot.com sweepstakes, some sharing will be in order. Toward that end, each of the major networks has either formed partnerships with Internet companies or started Internet businesses of their own in the last year, and the broadcasters are expending valuable air time promoting these on-line ventures. Significantly, the television networks are looking at these arrangements as more than mere "content plays." Faced with a downward curve of network viewership and looking for ways to generate more revenue from every program, the networks are rapidly turning to the Internet to sell goods featured on sitcoms, mini-series and dramas. Although such sales have not yet had much impact on the networks' balance sheets, they could provide significant revenue in the future, some analysts say. Electronic commerce initiatives are "sort of the big idea that hasn't been lost on anyone in the TV business," said Frank Biondi, the former chief executive of Viacom, who is now a principal with the investment firm Biondi Reiss Capital Management. "It's particularly important for broadcasters, given their declining viewership, because they don't have a secondary revenue stream," he said. The merchandising effort began in earnest with NBC's broadcast of "Merlin" 14 months ago, when NBC sold videos of the mini-series by advertising a phone number during the program. But with consumers turning more to the World Wide Web to buy goods, the networks are increasingly turning there as well to sell their tie-in products. During NBC's recent mini-series "The 60's," for instance, the network sold nearly 50,000 CD's of the soundtrack over the phone, at $34.90 each. But an additional 15 percent of sales came from the nbc.com Web site, where viewers could buy not only the CD's but other 60's items, like lava lamps and tie-dyed T-shirts. Elisabeth Sami, NBC's vice president for business development, said the average sale on the Internet during the 60's event was significantly higher than by telephone. Compared with phone sales, Ms. Sami said, the Web can cultivate a return clientele. CBS sold thousands of copies of its "Joan of Arc" video on cbs.com after broadcasting the mini-series last month, said Dana McClintock, a spokesman. On a broader level, the network's stakes in Internet companies like Sportsline and Hollywood Online "will provide an array of opportunities" in E-commerce, Mr. McClintock said. "Right now, those opportunities are few and far between," he added, "but in the future there will be a lot of them." On ABC, a Walt Disney Company unit, cast members of the daytime talk show "The View" recommended books, music and movies appropriate for Valentine's Day in a February broadcast, leading to an undisclosed amount of goods being sold on the ABC Web site (abc.go.com) through on-line retail partners, like Barnesandnoble.com. And soon, the ABC soap opera "General Hospital" will feature cast members wearing T-shirts that can be purchased on ABC's Web site. The Fox Network has on-line offerings of a broad range of items related to several of its series, like wristwatches from "The X-Files" and T-shirts from "The Simpsons." Analysts and executives said it was too early to predict the potential size of the television tie-in market. "Like everyone else, we're revising our projections every few months," Ms. Sami of NBC said. She said that in the last 18 months, Internet sales had grown to 12 percent of total tie-in product sales from 3 percent, as the company put more emphasis on the Internet and on merchandise sales generally. Videos and CD's were the networks' entry-level products, but analysts say that apparel may be the most promising way to broaden Internet sales, because people have been buying items worn by their television heroes since the first Hopalong Cassidy gun-and-holster sets hit the market in the 50's. Aaron Spelling, the creator of the Fox series "Melrose Place," has been a particularly aggressive merchandiser. Mr. Spelling recently helped start the company AsSeen In.com, which enables viewers to visit a Web site and find products seen on Mr. Spelling's programs. They can visit a Web page depicting a room in a character's house, for example, click on the rug, then go to the Web site of the rug retailer. Executives of AsSeenIn.com declined to comment on the venture, citing the pending sale of the Spelling Entertainment Group to Viacom. But analysts say the Web site would most likely receive a commission for each sale. There are indications that fans of "Melrose Place," at least, are avid on-line buyers. After the series finale last month, 240 items from the set were auctioned on Amazon.com. The auction received nearly 10,000 bids and raised some $200,000 for charity, an Amazon spokesman said. (Among the most sought-after items was the headboard of the bed used by Heather Locklear's character. It sold for $3,050.) Analysts say the confluence of television, the Internet and E-commerce could provide significant revenue from certain groups of products. "I think especially in the area of fashion this could be successful, as well as with goods that are more impulse buys," said Michele Slack, an on-line advertising analyst with Jupiter Communications, an Internet research firm. "Women, especially, look for fashion guidance from characters like Amanda in 'Melrose Place,' " Ms. Slack said. "But they wouldn't just buy whatever computer she uses." Still, Ms. Slack cautioned, "this is a wait-and-see kind of thing," because only the staunchest fans would buy something simply because it was featured on their favorite series, and because relatively few people are yet buying goods of any sort on line. But Mr. Biondi was more optimistic. "I'm sure there is an audience," he said. "The only question is finding the right balance, and finding out what consumers are comfortable with." The E-Commerce Report appears on alternate Mondays in Business Day, and every Monday in the Technology section of The newyork Times on the Web: www.nytimes.com/tech http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Account Decisions By On-Line Services
body: Three on-line services have made decisions involving accounts. Firstsource.com in Santa Ana, Calif., an Internet-based computer product retailer that is part of En Pointe Technologies, named D'Arcy Masius Benton & Bowles Los Angeles, a unit of MacManus Group, as the first agency to handle its account. Billings were estimated at $20 million. The decision came after a two-month review that had been narrowed to D.M.B.& B. and three other finalists: Cole & Weber in Seattle, part of the Ogilvy & Mather Worldwide unit of WPP Group P.L.C.; Rieches Baird in Irvine, Calif., and TFA/Leo Burnett Technology Group in Chicago, a unit of the Leo Burnett Company. Altavista.com, the search engine owned by the Compaq Computer Corporation, is conducting a closed review for its first advertising campaign. Though billings were not disclosed, the bigger search engines spend tens of millions of dollars annually on brand advertising. Charles Rashall, vice president for marketing and advertising sales at Alta Vista in Palo Alto, Calif., said about six agencies, which he declined to identify, would participate, adding that he expected a decision in four to six weeks. The agency has to be "capable of reinforcing our brand leadership position," Mr. Rashall said. And Accutrade, an on-line brokerage firm owned by the Ameritrade Holding Corporation, awarded its account to Romann Group in newyork. Billings on the account, which had been at Doremus & Company in newyork, part of Omnicom Group, were estimated at $5 million to $10 million. Peter Ricketts, president at Accutrade in Omaha, said that the decision came after a monthlong review in which Doremus did not take part. The review was narrowed to Romann and a second agency, which he declined to identify. Accutrade was "looking for an agency with on-line discount brokerage experience," Mr. Ricketts said. Romann had handled the account of DLJ Direct, the Internet-based brokerage subsidiary of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, part of AXA's Equitable Companies. That account, with billings estimated at $30 million, was shifted in November to Kirshenbaum Bond & Partners in newyork.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Commercial Property/Environmental Conservation;
Economics, Pro and Con, of Making Buildings Green
body: TEN years ago one of the nation's premier environmental groups, the Natural Resources Defense Council, bought an old industrial loft building at 40 West 20th Street and decided to demonstrate its contention that constructing a building designed to be environmentally sound could be financially sound as well. Working with the architect Randolph Croxton, the council produced a design that emphasized energy savings through insulation and the use of natural light from windows and skylights that spread through the top three floors of the building, and distributed the light via an atrium and glass strips at the top of interior walls. This is in contrast to most conventional designs, where executive offices block light from outside and where interiors are blasted with artificial light that generates heat that requires the consumption of still more energy to cool. The installation also included the use of natural materials that do not exude toxic gases, and furniture made from nonendangered species of wood. The council estimates that it saves $65,000 a year in energy costs for its 25,000-square-foot national headquarters. Since the group deliberately used only products readily available in the market, the offices were intended to be an example to other designers interested in producing structures more in tune with the environment. It has had an impact on other environmental groups, with the Audubon Society and the Environmental Defense Fund building out their offices using similar materials and approaches. "We have had 5,000 design professionals and policy makers through here over the last 10 years," said Allen Hershkowitz, a senior scientist with the council. And it captured the attention of the Durst Organization, which has installed fuel cells, which convert natural gas into electricity without a flame, and photovoltaic panels, which convert sunlight to electricity, in its soon-to-be completed office building at 42d Street and Broadway. But other developers, even ones eager to be seen as progressive and green, say the economics of such technologies are still unfavorable compared to more conventional approaches. (Environmental advocates counter that this is so only because the production of raw materials enjoys billions of dollars of subsidy by the Federal Government, but developers and builders have to live in the world as it is.) In an effort to change that balance, at least slightly, the Pataki Administration has proposed a "green building" tax credit that could be claimed by building owners and tenants in newyork State who invest in measures to improve energy efficiency, improve indoor air quality and reduce the environmental impact of commercial and residential buildings in the state. The measure is backed by an unusually diverse coalition of business, environmental, labor and real estate groups, including the Real Estate Board of newyork. As currently drafted, the credit would be limited to $25 million, so a few big projects could drain the fund quickly. But advocates of the measure say the important thing is to establish the principle and seek greater funding later. This is evidently the first time legislation has been introduced to promote the use of environmentally friendly technology in the state's construction industry, said Deborah B. Beck, executive vice president of the real estate board. "I think it will happen and I hope it happens sooner rather than later, which means this year," she said. Timely passage is important, Ms. Beck said, because the industry is in the midst of a construction cycle, so the credit could influence projects now under way. Once the cycle passes, such a law would be just words on paper, she said. "Most developers are risk averse," she said. "They figure they are so far out on a limb with new development, they want to avoid anything that adds to costs. The credit would create a reason for conservative people to use new materials or use them in different ways." Ms. Beck said that there does not appear to be any organized opposition to the bill, but that it is difficult to distinguish this particular piece of legislation from all the other issues swirling around in the state capital. "It's just not easy to do given the political climate in Albany," she said. THE basic credit would be 5 percent of the capitalized costs for eligible types of construction with an additional 2 percent credit available if a base building and all its tenant spaces complied with the listed criteria. The bill is also written to encourage the use of fuel cells and photovoltaics, with a credit available for 30 percent of the installed cost of fuel cells and 100 percent of the cost of photovoltaics over the cost of ordinary building panels. Photovoltaics work by adding material that converts sunlight to electricity to the panels that shield a building in places where there are no windows. Environmentalists say the reason for the emphasis on fuel cells and photovoltaics is that both technologies are available now and the prospect of an increase in demand could spur investments in new plants to manufacture them, which typically lowers the costs of the products. To be eligible forthe credit a building could not use more than 65 percent of the power allowed by the state's Energy Conservation Construction Code and would also have to meet indoor air quality standards for the amount of ventilation and content of the air. This is ironic, because many designers and engineers say it was stiffer energy standards that led to the reduction in the amount of fresh air flushed through buildings, allowing toxic gases and particles to build to concentrations that made people sick. The eligibility criteria also include the use of building materials and finishes that have minimum percentages of recycled content and systems to handle waste disposal and reduce water use. According to a report prepared by the real estate board, the developer of a 500,000-square-foot building worth $110 million could qualify for tax credits worth over $7.5 million, under the provisions of the bill. The credits would be spread over five years in equal parts and would be transferable to subsequent owners and tenants. Naturally, the project would have to stay in compliance with the criteria during any years when the credit is claimed. John Gilbert, the chief operating officer of Rudin Management, which is building a headquarters building for the Reuters news and information company at 42d Street and Seventh Avenue, said environmental considerations have become part of quality construction. He said that when the Rudin family took an empty building at 55 Broad Street, rewired it for advanced telecommunications and filled it with high-tech tenants, the objective was to develop a "smart and ready building." Today, he said at a recent conference at the Natural Resources Defense Council, the goal for the Reuters offices at 3 Times Square is to produce a "green, smart and ready building." He said 3 Times Square is designed to save 30 percent of the energy consumed by a typical office building. But he said what happens to the tax bill may affect the decision on whether to go ahead with installations of fuel cells and photovoltaics. "The tax credit bill is very important when it comes to photovoltaics and fuel cells," he said. "The raw economics do not makes sense, but if you change the economics using the tax code, maybe they do." He said the building was being wired in such a way that it can accept power from either source as the economics improve and the technology advances. As a result, he said, the Rudin organization is not biting its nails waiting for legislators in Albany to take up the bill. "Because we're prepared to plug in these alternate energy sources, we can wait until the legislation passes or the technology becomes more efficient," he said. While the council benefited from the energy savings because it is its own tenant, Mr. Gilbert noted that electricity costs are typically passed on to tenants by landlords, so investment by a building owner to reduce power consumption is a dubious proposition, at least on the surface. But Robert Fox, a principal in Fox and Fowle Architects, who is doing both the Durst and the Rudin projects, said the benefits are real, if more subtle. Reducing power costs makes a building more attractive to tenants, who are concerned about their total cost of occupancy. "Durst and Rudin spent a lot of money on these buildings that they did not have to and the tenants are getting the payback," he said. But he said they are creating a desirable asset that will be attractive to tenants, particularly in tough economic times. "They will have full buildings in a bad market," Mr. Fox said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Model of the Reuters building, which is to rise at 42d Street and Seventh Avenue. John Gilbert of Rudin Management, its developer, said the goal was to produce a "green, smart and ready building." But specifics, he added, may hinge on whether the tax-credit bill passes. (Jock Pottle/Esto)

title:
INVESTING;
Still FeedingAn Internet Frenzy
body: THE ink on the first draft of the history of the Internet stock boom isn't yet dry, and the revisionists are already having their say. Even as Internet shares were tumbling from their highs, three of the companies backed by Accel Partners, a venture capital firm, went public last month. Though their net losses total $56 million, the three now have a combined market capitalization of $10 billion. "Astounding," James W. Breyer, the firm's managing partner, calls that performance, echoing the giddiness common in Silicon Valley when people talk about the Internet. But in the same breath, Mr. Breyer decries the shortcomings of the crop of new offerings following in his companies' footsteps. "We've had far too many low-quality companies go public," he scoffed. The recent market turmoil that has sliced the value of many Internet stocks in half is making investors more discriminating, he added approvingly: "Investors can more easily distinguish between companies building a long-term business and those which have been merely opportunistic." Ah, to be a master of the Internet universe and not only make business history, but spin it, too. As some of the air leaks out of the Internet stock bubble, the same people who manufactured the feeding frenzy -- the venture capitalists, entrepreneurs and investment bankers who have been the biggest promoters of the phenomenon -- are beginning to say it may have spun out of control. Stocks not ready for prime time were foisted on a welcoming public lusting for the big score, they now say. In Silicon Valley's effervescence the past few months, discretion lost out to greed. And yet even as they apply the rhetorical brakes to careening Internet mania, those same financiers are stepping on the gas, racing to bring companies to market before the Internet euphoria disappears. Some investment bankers say clients are asking them to pull together "road shows" -- in which executives pitch their companies to prospective buyers -- in little more than two weeks, half the usual time. And many of the bankers, supposed arbiters of a company's market-worthiness, are only too happy to oblige. "Right now it's hang onto the rocket ship and giggle all the way to the moon," said Mark G. Shafir, an investment banker at Merrill Lynch in San Francisco. Already, 59 Internet companies have gone public this year -- compared with 30 in all of 1998, according to Thomson Financial Securities Data, which tracks such numbers. Fifty-six percent of the 212 Internet and Internet-related companies filing plans to go public with the Securities and Exchange Commission since January 1994 did so in the last six months. May was the busiest month on record, as 35 companies registered with regulators. That pace concerns David Menlow, who, as the longtime president of IPO Financial Network, a firm in Milburn, N.J., that tracks new offerings, has seen his share of hysteria on Wall Street. Even he is stunned at the crush of companies rushing to go public since Internet stocks hit a record high in mid-April. Mr. Menlow's most recent newsletter is chock-full of comments on the new crop, and few are charitable. "Right church, wrong pew," he writes about one Internet-related medical concern. "Talk about swimming upstream," he says of a company that creates computer operating systems. The market for Internet stocks is still fertile, Mr. Menlow said, but companies like these will be judged more harshly in coming months, since the euphoria over the sector has ebbed. "Before, the window was wide open," he said. "Now the window has a fine mesh screen." Yet with Silicon Valley still working overtime to generate excitement -- and the transformative power of Internet innovation a genuine, powerful lure -- investors can be said to share a new caution only if their behavior is judged against the hysteria of the last few months. In January, according to Securities Data, initial public offerings of Internet companies averaged a first-day gain of 248 percent. By the end of May, with so many deals to choose from and appetites waning a bit, that gain had dwindled to 73 percent. Fearlessly, though, Silicon Valley financiers are developing ways to institutionalize the Web frenzy. Venture capitalists are demanding that shares of some new companies be sold on line, where Internet-hungry investors are abundant. And some neophyte investment firms see that as an opportunity to supplant the more established banks. Looked at innocently, they are aiming to democratize investment. Looked at cynically, they are looking to give every investor equal standing in the hype. Some Silicon Valley veterans believe it is time for some cooling. "I actually despair what is going on in the Valley," said Judy Estrin, chief technology officer at Cisco Systems, herself an entrepreneur who was a co-founder of three companies. "It used to be if you had good products and you took care of your clients and customers, you'd win. That's not enough anymore. Today it's more about marketing hype and rising above the noise level." That may be overly pessimistic. Most here are ecstatic at the speed and breadth of innovation that the Internet has unleashed. But for the financiers, one thing is certain, even with Web shares down: It doesn't get much better than this.  Grabbing for a Slice of Ebay Many of Silicon Valley's venture capitalists and investment bankers ply their trade in Menlo Park, not far from grassy pastures dotted with cows and an occasional deer. There, in the 2700 block of Sand Hill Road (more aptly named "Stand Still Road" when rush-hour traffic clogs the four-lane route), two of the fiercest competitors in investment banking have set up shop. A small, flower-filled courtyard separates the offices of rivals Morgan Stanley Dean Witter and the Goldman Sachs Group, their buildings connected by a covered walkway 100 yards long. It's an intimacy rare even in a place where deals are cut at Saturday-morning soccer games. "We have a pact not to go through the trash," joked Eff W. Martin, a Goldman partner, pointing at Morgan's offices through a slit in the window blinds. Still, the arrangements seem a bit cozy, as if what the bankers have in common -- their insider status in a very rich game -- trumps any antagonisms. Bradford C. Koenig, Goldman's co-head of high technology, employed the same nanny later hired by Rex Golding, a Harvard Business School classmate and his counterpart at Morgan Stanley. And it is not uncommon to see bankers from both camps schmoozing at the same Valley soirees. On Wall Street, investment bankers sit at the top of the financial pyramid; here they mainly play the role of courtiers. The true princes of finance are the venture capitalists, who invest in start-ups with the hope of a big payoff when a company goes public or is sold. More Internet venture dollars are chasing deals than ever before. Funds raised by venture capitalists have blossomed in the past four years, from $774 million in 1995 to $4.9 billion last year, according to the VentureOne Corporation. Jonathan Lee, an entrepreneur in Redwood City, Calif., who last September started a company called Corio that distributes business software over the Internet, said he was approached by no fewer than 20 venture capital firms, including the godfather of Silicon Valley venture capital, Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers. In the 1980's, "there wasn't a countervailing presence to the lunacy of the bankers," said Gary Rieschel, managing general partner at Softbank Technology Ventures, an early investor in Yahoo, the Internet directory service. "Now you have the lunacy of the venture capitalists to counter the lunacy of the bankers." Indeed, this decade's venture capitalists have much in common with bankers of a decade ago who hired publicists to promote themselves and their successes. In keeping with the spirit of the companies they finance, most have their own Web sites and are skilled at creating a buzz loud enough to rise above the Valley static. One of the more accomplished is Robert Kagle, a venture capitalist at Benchmark Capital in Menlo Park. Benchmark was an early investor in Ebay, the on-line auction company that has seen its share price climb more than 1,000 percent since going public last year. Mr. Kagle, 43, a Michigan native who, like many Valley veterans, moved to Palo Alto to attend Stanford Business School and never left, is self-deprecating. "Some venture capitalists see themselves as the center of the universe," he said. "We see it as a service business." Yet even as he shares credit with colleagues for his successes, Mr. Kagle is an adept salesman for the companies he backs. In a recent interview, for instance, he readily volunteered that he collects antique fishing decoys -- bought through Ebay, of course. And he strained to use the term "Ebaysian" ("pronounced e-BAY-ze-an," he said) no fewer than five times in a 35-minute telephone conversation. Why? It is his attempt to introduce Ebay culture -- which advocates the equal standing of every bidder -- into the new language of the Internet, a bit of manipulation that he doesn't deny and even laughs about. No other Internet company has been so hotly fought over as Ebay, and the story of its public offering suggests how eager bankers are to hook up with a company they think will be a winner. In May 1998, when Mr. Kagle and Ebay's chief executive, Meg Whitman, invited investment banks to pitch for the job of taking the company public, Goldman and Morgan jumped at the chance. Ms. Whitman had one peculiar demand: When they came calling, each bank had to bring an item bought on Ebay. A team of eight Goldman executives entered Ebay's headquarters, bags crammed with charts, market data -- and Tank the Armadillo, a Beanie Baby that Mr. Koenig had bought for his 7-year-old son, Austin, for $32.75 in an Ebay auction. Michael K. Parekh, an analyst, had a 25-year-old Parcheesi game that he had bought for $110. He also presented the Ebay executives with a sample research report before the Goldman team swept them off to dinner. "It was clear they would be a leader in this market," Mr. Koenig said, explaining the avid campaign. "The more time we spent on the site, we realized it was a whole new dimension in personal trading." Goldman's inventiveness struck a chord with Ebay, though Morgan Stanley was dogged, too. Its executives also logged hours on Ebay's Web site, buying fine French wine and a couple of piggy banks in which Ebay could stuff its newfound money. But "they didn't display as deep an understanding," Mr. Kagle said. And it cost Morgan the job. The bankers were devastated. "We walked out of the meeting right then and knew that it didn't click," said Mary Meeker, Morgan's celebrated Internet analyst -- "Queen Mary" to her fans, "Bloody Mary" to her detractors and a stock-moving powerhouse in the eyes of both. Ms. Meeker was convinced that Ebay would be a market leader, and after Morgan lost, she quickly went to work repairing the relationship. She spent hours getting to know Ms. Whitman, including a dinner at Logan Airport in Boston last July, one of several meetings over a period of months. In August, Ruth Porat, Morgan's co-head of global technology and Ms. Meeker spent an evening on the phone with Ms. Whitman, critiquing Goldman's road-show presentation. They suggested that the company demonstrate its users' enthusiasm better; as a result, Ebay created slides listing some of the thousands of items for sale related just to the baseball superstar Mark McGwire. Ms. Meeker also took the unprecedented step of publishing a favorable research report the day after Ebay began trading last September. (Analysts usually like to wait until the company has a track record before giving an endorsement.) Goldman was legally barred from talking up the stock for 30 days after the offering, Ms. Whitman noted, "so Mary became the one the press called. She became associated with Ebay." Morgan Stanley's hard work paid off. In March, Goldman lined up investors for Ebay's $1 billion secondary stock offering but was forced to share the business with Morgan. Goldman chafed at the concession but was powerless to prevent it. "Morgan earned it," Ms. Whitman said.  Marketing to the Mania If there is any question that technology is transforming business, investors need look only at the most staid rite of passage on Wall Street: going public. It used to be that for a standard 7 percent underwriting fee, bankers would herd management onto a chartered jet for a two-week road show, cram in 10 to 12 meetings a day with mutual fund managers and other investors and hope to end up with a list of interested buyers -- with a tiny portion of the stock reserved for mom-and-pop investors. Now, investors' mania for the stocks minted by Silicon Valley financiers -- along with the growing trend toward do-it-yourself investing on line -- has banks scrambling to find new ways to get stock in I.P.O.'s into the hands of individuals. And the new on-line banks, without armies of bankers and salesmen, expect to charge companies fees of 5 percent or less. "First you had the discount brokers," said Michael Moritz, a venture capitalist at Sequoia Capital in Menlo Park. "Now you have the emergence of the discount investment banker." Established firms like the Charles Schwab Corporation and DLJ Direct, the on-line affiliate of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, already distribute shares on line and help underwrite stock offerings. But the emergence of on-line investment banks -- like the Wit Capital Group of New York (which itself went public on Friday) and E*Offering, which is backed by Sanford Robertson, a co-founder of Robertson, Stephens & Company of San Francisco -- could open the process further, with new stocks available on a first-come, first-served basis. The most revolutionary concept is being championed by William Hambrecht, co-founder of another San Francisco investment bank, Hambrecht & Quist. Housed in a former warehouse in the city's design district, his firm, W. R. Hambrecht & Company, sells new stocks over the Internet in a so-called Dutch auction, with investors setting the price. Investors place bids for the number of shares they want at a price they are willing to pay. After a few weeks of bidding, a clearing price is set at the lowest offer at which all shares can be sold. Those bidding above the clearing price get all the shares they asked for. Investors bidding at that price may get only a percentage of the shares they want. Those who bid too low are shut out. The concept, while by no means proven, appeals to venture capitalists like Bruce Dunlevie, a partner at Benchmark Capital. "I think the trends favor it," he said. "It is the rise of the consumer in the I.P.O. market." But the mechanics may serve only to feed the frenzy further, encouraging overbidding. "If you guess the actual price, you run the risk of not getting stock," acknowledged Ian H. Zwicker, president of W. R. Hambrecht. Plus, it is unclear whether many analysts will follow the companies and offer investors needed guidance. Ravenswood Winery, the first company whose stock was auctioned this way, got a tepid reaction from investors. But most experts believe the logical users of Hambrecht's services are Internet entrepreneurs.  A Case of Caution If the market for Internet stocks remains weak, Silicon Valley may have no choice but to pause and catch its breath. That would please Mr. Lee, the founder of Corio. Corio's fiercest competitor, a Maryland company called USinternetworking, was grabbing headlines after its stock price shot up from $21 to a high of $60 on April 9, the day it went public. Though USinternetworking had $33 million in net losses and a still-developing business model, the first day's trading gave it an eye-popping market capitalization of $2.4 billion and, Mr. Lee worried, instant credibility. He was faced with a decision: Should Corio go public, too? It had promising sales but couldn't guarantee the same success in the coming months. And while Wall Street analysts may not require profits, they do demand predictability. "That doesn't come without processes, people and tools in place," Mr. Lee said. After an agonizing two-hour board meeting in April, the company chose to hold off. "We definitely felt the pressure," Mr. Lee said. "You get caught up in the hype. Given that we could do it, of course we thought about it. A lot of people do. We are fighting a clock." A month later, he doesn't regret the decision. USinternetworking's market capitalization has fallen to $1 billion, and investors who bought in the first day's euphoria are facing losses of more than 58 percent. "My philosophy is that an I.P.O. is a measure of doing something well," Mr. Lee said. He hesitated for a moment, reconsidering the thought. "But it's also about being at the right place at the right time." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: With its celebrated analyst, Mary Meeker, left, and investment banker, Ruth Porat, Morgan Stanley selectively takes Internet companies public.
