Barry Diller Keeps Redefining 'Convergence' … and Convergence Keeps Redefining Him
body: For much of the last three decades, to ask the question "What is the hottest fad in the media business?" is to invite the responding query, "What is Barry Diller up to now?" From his start as an ABC programmer, brainstorming movies-of-the-week in network television's heyday in the early 1970's, Mr. Diller always found ways to surf the trends of the moment. After subsequently running Paramount Pictures, he spent most of the 1980's building Rupert Murdoch's Fox Television into a viable alternative to the Big Three networks, mining the premise that there was a younger, hipper audience than ABC, CBS and NBC were delivering to advertisers. And then, in the 90's, running the home-shopping channel QVC and later the Home Shopping Network, he has demonstrated that advertising is not the only way to derive revenue from the remote-control constituency. From there, it was only a mouse-click or two to the realization that the Internet could be a lot like what some people used to call interactive TV. And so, Mr. Diller was soon extending the Home Shopping Network onto the World Wide Web. And then he was acquiring the electronic ticketing agent Ticketmaster and melding it with the city-guide Web company Citysearch -- even as he was also amassing a more conventional set of media holdings through his television empire, USA Networks Inc. All this past was prelude to Barry Diller's latest multimedia move. Last week he proposed a three-way shuffling of high-priced stock certificates through which Mr. Diller hopes to come out controlling a new company that would combine Lycos, a popular portal to the World Wide Web, with the electronic shopping holdings of his current company, USA Networks Inc. The new operation, to be called the USA Lycos Interactive Networks, would entertain, inform and sell things to people on line, on television and over the telephone. It was valued at $22 billion when it was announced on Tuesday, before Wall Street panned the deal, sending the shares of Lycos -- and the deal's prospects -- tumbling. That initial investor skepticism does not mean Mr. Diller will not carry out the plan, of course. After all, Mr. Diller's best-known enterprises previously, the Fox Network and QVC, were seen as media Siberias when he started. But he was able to fire up enough perceived heat, and real business value, to create the next media sensation. But the task of mastering both the style and substance of this deal will be Mr. Diller's toughest yet, since he has before never run something with as many disparate lines of business. "Barry has been brilliant in building the company," said John Tinker an analyst with Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities. "He has done O.K. in managing it. But now the challenge will be pulling all this together." Mr. Diller argues that the complexity of his new deal reflects a world in which media companies and retailers are increasingly intertwined. And significantly, given his continued interest in the convergence of old, passive media and new, interactive ones, USA Lycos would aim to make its money as much from retailing as from advertising. "I really do believe that there is a new convergence between information, entertainment and direct selling," he said in an interview last week. "Once you have the technology for interactivity, you can have direct selling and you can bypass the middleman." Mr. Diller's road to the media shopping mall began in 1992, as he was looking for a venture after leaving Fox. Mr. Diller first noticed QVC on the recommendation of a friend, the fashion designer Diane Von Furstenberg. He marveled at QVC's capacity to translate a focused hour of televised product pitching into a frenzy of phoned-in sales orders. So it was no accident that when Mr. Diller moved on to the Home Shopping Network, he became keenly interested the company's small outpost on the Web, the Internet Shopping Network, which was one of the first on-line computer stores. Mr. Diller decided that computers had too low a profit margin, and so he closed the store. But in its place he created First Auction, a site that offers some of the costume jewelry and collectibles sold on Home Shopping Network along with other merchandise like furniture, all of which have much higher profit margins. The auction format, which has also been successfully adopted by Web companies like E-Bay, has transformed shopping on the Internet from a utilitarian exercise in ordering to the blend of entertainment and sport that has made TV shopping channels so successful. First Auction's sales are now running at a $40 million annual rate, with few of the costs faced by Internet start-ups because it can use the warehouses and computer systems of the Home Shopping Network. But until now, Mr. Diller's efforts to link the Internet and television have been modest and limited to some First Auction promotions on the Home Shopping Network. Indeed, he has found few ways to cross-promote his company's television operations -- the Home Shopping Network and the USA Network, a cable channel specializing in original series as well as movies, and its sibling, the Sci-Fi Network. Each network, he says, has a very different profile -- with Home Shopping appealing to older women and USA going after a younger audience. Over all, however, analysts give Mr. Diller good, if not excellent grades, for his record of running the companies he has acquired. Since coming to the money-losing Home Shopping Network in late 1995, Mr. Diller has turned it around. Last year, cash flow -- or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization -- was $330.3 million and revenue of $1.07 billion. And yet, it trails QVC, which despite reaching one-third fewer homes is expected to report 1998 revenue of well over $2 billion and cash flow above $400 million. But making deals may well be Mr. Diller's most notable accomplishment lately. Take his purchase of Ticketmaster, in two transactions in 1997 and 1998. Shortly after gaining control of Ticketmaster, Mr. Diller realized that the company's small but rapidly growing Internet ticket sales site was as big as many of the Internet start-ups that were receiving huge valuations in the stock market. So he split off that business as Ticketmaster Online and merged it with Citysearch, a somewhat struggling effort to create Web-based local entertainment guides in major cities that had been started by an eccentric entrepreneur, Bill Gross. With a combination of good timing and sales panache, Mr. Diller was able to sell 10 percent of Ticketmaster Online Citysearch in December in a public stock offering at $14 a share. Its shares subsequently rose as high as $80, although they are now less than half that, closing Friday at $36.50. Still, USA's portion is worth about $1.6 billion, far more than the $610 million it paid for all of Ticketmaster. In fact, it is the high market value of Ticketmaster Online's stock that has given Mr. Diller the chips to raise his stakes in the Internet market. Mr. Diller was worried about other big media companies activities on line -- like the Walt Disney Company's effort to tie all of its media properties into one all-encompassing Internet portal, the Go Network.  Among many other things, Go intends to offer the sort of local information that Citysearch does. "We sat around watching what Disney was doing," Mr. Diller said, "and said if we don't get a relationship with a national portal, our desire to play a big game will be toast." Mr. Diller began talking with a number of portal providers, and three weeks ago started talks with Lycos, which had been conducting its own public search for a partner. At first, Mr. Diller proposed merging Ticketmaster Online Citysearch with Lycos. But the conversations soon expanded to include First Auction and then the rest of the Home Shopping Network -- along with the old-fashioned, telphone-sales portion of Ticketmaster. "We realized we had to put HSN in with all its merchandizing power and ability to be a real retailer on the Net," Mr. Diller said. The prospect of $1.5 billion in shopping revenue particularly appealed to Robert Davis, the chief executive of Lycos, which is based in Framingham, Mass. He has long prided himself on having a New England frugality that contrasts sharply with the Internet new math practiced by many of his Silicon Valley competitors. "Lycos, Yahoo, Excite and the rest have been all dependent on pure advertising revenue," Mr. Davis said in an interview last week. "We believe that by moving to having more commerce and transaction revenue, we can have real earnings fiber." And yet, the new game plan looked disappointing to holders of Lycos stock, which plummeted on word of the deal. Lycos shareholders had apparently hoped that the company would be acquired for a big premium, the way that the portal Excite recently sold itself to the Internet-cable company At Home for nearly double Excite's stock market price. Even CMGI Inc., the investment company that took Lycos public in 1996 and still owns 20 percent of it, hinted it might vote against the deal if the company's stock stayed low. By Friday, Lycos had bounced back somewhat. But it ended the week at $99.50, down 22 percent from its price before the deal was announced on Tuesday morning. And by week's end, even the initial enthusiasm of USA Networks' shareholders seemed to have faded, as the stock closed on Friday at $38 -- 12.5 cents higher than they were last Monday night. Mr. Diller contends that any recalcitrant Lycos shareholders simply do not understand the deal, which he said would give them something rare -- a stake in an Internet company with real revenues and earnings. As for the remaining pieces of USA Networks, Mr. Diller has definite plans to go on a shopping spree to build it into a bigger, more conventional media conglomerate. "You will see us looking for opportunities to add cable networks, broadcast stations and probably film production and distribution," Mr. Diller said. But Mr. Diller's history of testing the outer boundaries of new-media models suggests that he will not be content to concentrate solely on conventional film, cable and broadcasting. If he can get Wall Street to endorse last week's USA Lycos deal, Mr. Diller would control an Internet company with a market capitalization in excess of $20 billion. That would not only provide a solid platform from which to sell tickets and consumer products. It might also prove the perfect investment vehicle for picking up a few more on-line properties. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Barry Diller, an executive with a knack for finding the hottest media fad, on a terrace overlooking Central Park. Mr. Diller's latest move is to combine Lycos, a portal to the World Wide Web, with the electronic shopping holdings of his current company, USA Networks. (Suzanne DeChillo/The New York Times); Mr. Diller, as new chairman of Home Shopping Network, in late 1995. (Bill Serne)  Chart: "The Making Of a Multimedia Mogul" As a top executive at ABC television, Paramount Pictures and then at the Fox network, Barry Diller spent the 1970's and 80's in the conventional media. But during the 90's, Mr. Diller has become a deal maker who symbolizes the convergence of old media and new media.  Dec. '92 - Feb. '95 -- Shapes the home-shopping television network QVC Inc. into a telephone-based precursor to interactive TV. Aug. '95 -- Makes deal for control of Silver King Broadcasting, a chain of independent TV stations, having left QVC after its takeover by Comcast. Nov. '95 -- Returns to remote-control retailing in a deal to acquire Home Shopping Network, later combining it with Silver King into HSN Inc. May '96 -- Starts First Auction, a Web site for selling HSN merchandise. May '97 -- Acquires, through HSN, 47.5 percent of the telephone and on-line ticket-sales agent Ticketmaster -- the first step toward outright control. Oct. '97 -- Makes deal for HSN to acquire the USA Networks cable channels and Universal Television production unit from Seagram, which are subsequently combined into a new company, USA Networks Inc. Aug. '98 -- Agrees to merge Ticketmaster's on-line business with Citysearch, an operator of local cultural-events Web sites. Feb. '99 -- Announces deal with the popular Web portal Lycos to create a new Internet player, USA Lycos Interactive Network.

title:
Industry View;
How did a small company turn itself into a powerhouse of data storage systems? In part, through its marketing.
body: MUCH has been written about Cisco Systems Inc. and how it rose from obscurity to market prominence by providing the switches and routers that form the plumbing of the Internet. But there is another, more obscure, player that has reaped Internet rewards by producing a fundamental piece of technology. The EMC Corporation is to data storage what Cisco is to routers. But few outside of Wall Street and corporate data centers are familiar with this emerging technology powerhouse. Based in Hopkinton, Mass., on the far western reaches of metropolitan Boston's Route 128 high-technology belt, EMC dominates the $10 billion market for large data storage systems -- a market it wrested from I.B.M. EMC, which had revenue of $4 billion last year, provides the storage systems for corporate computer systems -- not only mainframes but also the power network server computers through which corporate America uses the Internet. And America Online, as well as 7 of the other 10 largest Internet service providers, employ EMC storage systems as their main data repositories. Although EMC was founded 20 years ago, it was only in the 1990's that the company rose to the leadership of the large data storage market -- a category encompassing both hardware and software that is expected to reach $35 billion by 2001, according to the re search house Dataquest. With the Internet creating a seemingly insatiable appetite for storage, and with corporate computing needs growing apace, EMC has seen its annual profits surge from $30 million in 1992 to nearly $800 million last year. Its stock -- which closed on Friday at $102.375, down $1.75 -- has been the second-best performer in the S.& P. 500 in the 1990's, with a return of more than 32,000 percent, second only to Dell Computer's 50,000 percent. Its stock market value, more than $50 billion, is larger than for companies like American Express, Boeing and Motorola. Part of EMC's success lies in its having embraced an approach that might be called radical marketing. Radical marketers emphasize listening to customers; creating a community atmosphere among customers, served by employees and salespeople who are expected to take a missionary's zeal to their work, and making marketing one of the top priorities of the chief executive. Successful organizations in a wide range of endeavors -- including Harley-Davidson Motorcycles, Providian Financial and Iams pet food -- have employed radical marketing techniques to overcome the larger advertising budgets and giant marketing machines of their bigger competitors. In the case of EMC, the tone was set by the co-founder and chairman, Richard J. Egan, and the chief executive, Michael C. Ruettgers, who joined the company in 1988.  As recently as 1990, EMC had no measurable share of the market for mainframe data storage. At that time, I.B.M. owned three-quarters of the market, in which the prevailing wisdom among information technology professionals was the aphorism that "no one ever lost his job by buying I.B.M." How quickly things can change. Today, EMC owns 35 percent of the market for large external storage systems, compared with a 22 percent share for the market's No. 2 company, I.B.M., which has now focused much of its attention on building smaller computer disk drives rather than the large data storage systems in which EMC specializes. How did EMC do this? To begin with, EMC helped convince customers that the data storage system was no longer a mundane peripheral to corporate computers but a technological weapon that the customer could put to strategic business use. For example, the catalogue merchant L. L. Bean, an EMC customer, found that it could process transactions sufficiently faster to add a full day -- and tens of millions of dollars in sales -- to its holiday shopping season and still promise delivery by Christmas. EMC's rise came on the wings of its Symmetrix storage systems, a product line that was introduced in 1990 and that drastically shifted the technical assumptions about data storage. Rather than follow I.B.M.'s model of writing millions of lines of complex software microcode to run these refrigerator-size electronic file cabinets, EMC engineers built storage devices made up of hundreds of small, off-the-shelf disk drives. The engineers were able to make these devices work together with a simple bit of microcode, and the company packaged them as smaller, cheaper, faster, more powerful and -- as it turned out -- inherently more reliable storage devices. That pioneering technology was known as RAID (redundant array of independent disks). And though it was invented at the University of California at Berkeley, EMC developed it into a commercially viable product that processed data faster than conventional storage devices and took up less floor space, too. I.B.M. had reaped 70 percent profit margins by selling "one size fits all" systems, much to the chagrin of corporate information-technology managers, who had long felt hampered by such limited and restrictive offerings -- and were often hard pressed to afford the systems, which might sell for $700,000 or more. EMC aimed to address such frustrations, seeking the advice of corporate computing managers and inviting them to a visitor center at EMC headquarters, where customers could regularly meet with engineers, see work in progress and offer suggestions. And to turn visitors into customers, EMC put the new systems into client sites at no charge for a few months of testing. The Unum Corporation, a large insurance company, used the free trial to process its year-end data, an enormous number-crunching effort that traditionally took two full weeks of computer time. Using EMC's system, the company completed the task in three days. The customer was sold. EMC executives referred to these as "puppy dog sales." Once the cute puppy was home, few cared to return it to the pet shop. It didn't hurt that initially at least, EMC's prices tended to be hundreds of thousands of dollars below I.B.M.'s. And over time, EMC learned to concentrate on the customers that could implicity help the company market its products. For example, some 9,000 banks in the unitedstates spend nearly $20 billion each year on information technology. EMC knows that the top five -- BankAmerica, Chase Manhattan, Citigroup, J. P. Morgan and Banc One -- account for nearly 40 percent of that spending. All are EMC customers. Winning them has helped the company turn the other top 25 banks into EMC customers today, and more of the nation's smaller banks are coming into the EMC fold each month. Grab the leaders and the rest generally follow. It's one of the premises of radical marketing -- the technology marketing model for the 21st century. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title:
MEDIA;
Slate Drops Its On-Line Subscription Fee
body: It was an important test of one facet of Internet commerce: Would readers pay an annual subscription rate of $19.95 for the privilege of reading a magazine on line? If the tale of Slate magazine, which is owned by Microsoft, is any indication, the answer is no. Ten months after deciding to charge readers $19.95 a year, the publisher of the on-line magazine announced in an email notice to subscribers that, as of last Friday, it would now be available free on the World Wide Web. Michael Kinsley, Slate's editor, said that the decision was not a setback. "Obviously, you don't like to reverse course," he said. "You try one thing, you try another. It's a stage in the learning process." In the email to subscribers, Scott Moore -- who was named publisher of the on-line magazine last Monday -- wrote that there were two reasons for the change. "First, the advertising market on the Web has continued to expand at a remarkable pace, " he wrote. "It roughly doubled in 1998 to about $1.8 billion, is predicted to grow to about $3 billion in 1999, and should continue a healthy 50 percent to 60 percent annual growth rate for the next several years." He explained that "the biggest problem with remaining paid was that doing so would restrict our advertising potential." "We're confident," he wrote. "that by making slate.com free, our audience will grow substantially and this will make us more attractive to advertisers." The second problem, Mr. Moore wrote, was that, on the Web, "paid subscriptions for content (other than smut and investments) simply have not grown as expected." Under the new arrangement, readers who pay $19.95 a year will get email deliveries and print-out editions, and have access to the archives and general bulletin board of Slate, services that will not be provided free. Bill Bass, an analyst at Forrester Research Inc., said that the issue was one of supply and demand. "Last year, I said this was the dumbest thing I had ever heard," he said. "There is so much free content on the Web that if you try and charge for it people won't go to you. There is too much substitutable content." He pointed to the fact that readers can look at Salon magazine, a Slate competitor, which is free. "It's like if Ford came out with a Taurus that cost $50,000. If I can get a Camry for $25,000, why would I pay $50,000 for a Taurus?" he asked. Mr. Bass added that only two areas on the Internet can charge for their services: financial and pornography sites. He said that financial sites like thestreet.com and The Wall Street Journal's Web site are popular because they offer specific advice that few other sites offer, and the subscription prices can be written off as business expenses. "The only wildly successful sites that charge have been adult entertainment," he said. "And people tend not to act economically rationally around adult entertainment." Patrick Keane, a senior analyst at Jupiter Communications, an on-line market research firm, pointed out the that there is also a psychological hurdle for consumers to overcome in paying for content on the Web. "People see their personal computers as a utility device, and they're going to pay for information that leads them toward a task, or that helps them with a purchasing decision," he said. "So consumers don't have a natural proclivity to pay for content on line." However, he added that the Internet is a maturing market. "After all," he said, referring to cable TV, "if somebody had told you in 1975 that you would be paying $40 a month for your television, would you have believed it?" In an editor's letter posted on Friday, Mr. Kinsley answered what he expected would be readers' questions about the decision. "It's painful," he wrote, "to think of turning away so many Slate readers from so much of our content -- not to mention the potential readers who don't come in the first place. The spreadsheet wizards figure that ad revenue from the increased traffic will more than compensate for the lost subscriptions." Slate's publisher, Mr. Moore, said that the paying subscribers number in "the high twenty thousands" and that the magazine was visited by 300,000 to 400,000 news users each month. Mr. Moore would not disclose Slate's ad revenue, which is charted by an internal group, MSN Advertising Sales. Slate was started in June 1996 and, after some false starts, began charging last March. It has remained something of a sideshow in Microsoft's Internet strategy, which in earlier stages emphasized entertainment programming or local information but is now focused on building traffic to a home page, MSN.com, that directs users to both content and electronic commerce. On its Web site Friday, Salon, which is published by Salon Internet Inc., crowed over the news, with a commentary headlined sardonically "Slate Rejoins the Web." Later, in an interview, David Talbot, the editor and chief executive of Salon, said that Slate's decision to charge readers "was a case of Microsoft's hubris" and "prevented other sites from linking to it, further restricting circulation." "When you charge, it prevents other sites from linking to you, which is how the Web grows, when you become integrated to other Web sites through links," he said. "When you hit a gate as a reader saying you have to pay, Web sites stop linking to you." Marisa Bowe, the editor of the on-line magazine Word, which is owned by the Zapata Corporation, said that she was not surprised at Slate's decision. "So far, no one has really been willing to pay to read anything on the Web," she said. "It's a little heartbreaking for me to say, but the Web magazines are just not as important, yet, as the print magazines." Mr. Kinsley said, "I think if she's going to be depressed about that, she's going to be depressed for a while." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Michael Kinsley, editor of Slate, Microsoft's on-line magazine, at his offices in Seattle last year. Slate has decided to stop charging subscription fees. (Therese Frare for The newyork Times)

title: Nasdaq Revives Proposal to Test Trading Halts
body: With continued volatility in Internet stocks, Nasdaq regulators are now moving to temporarily halt trading of the most wildly unstable shares. Frank G. Zarb, chairman of Nasdaq's parent, the National Association of Securities Dealers, has asked the association's board to consider testing trading halts for one year. A proposal to institute the use of trading halts was rejected just two weeks ago by a Nasdaq committee of market makers and brokerage firm officials that had studied the issue as a possible remedy to large daily price swings in Internet-related shares. But in the wake of recent warnings about on-line trading by the Securities and Exchange Commission's chairman, Arthur Levitt, and the disclosure by the newyork State Attorney General, Eliot L. Spitzer, that he would investigate the Internet trading industry, Mr. Zarb will now ask the association board to consider allowing halts. Association officials said the plan, which would also require S.E.C. approval, would allow Nasdaq to halt trading in a stock immediately "when there appears to be significant corporate news or when a company's security is experiencing extraordinary volatility, either of which is impacting the fairness and orderliness of the market." The enormous level of recent trading activity, Mr. Zarb said in a statement, has created "new issues of volatility and trading practices, issues that must be addressed by the exchanges and member firms to preserve the fairness of the market for investors." Advocates say that trading halts have worked at the newyork Stock Exchange and that they would stem the sharpest price moves of Internet-related stocks. But opponents contend that halts could increase volatility by causing investors to rush to make trades before a halt. A key issue that has not been resolved is what specific criteria Nasdaq officials would use before halting trading in a stock, said Bernard L. Madoff, a leading Nasdaq market maker and head of the Securities Industry Association trading committee. "It's something long overdue, and I think it would be a sensible way to deal with some of the volatility occurring in the marketplace," said Mr. Madoff, who expects that officials of both the association and the S.E.C. will approve trading halts. While the idea has been dismissed before, he said, "I think the circumstances in the marketplace today are such that there is so much volatility, and so many small public orders coming in, that it makes more sense." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Possible Bill Would Curb Posting Of Government Data on Internet
body: The chairman of the House Commerce Committee, Representative Thomas J. Bliley Jr., is considering legislation that would put limits on the types of publicly released government information that could be posted on the Internet. At issue are the "worst case scenario" plans for handling accidents that the Environmental Protection Agency is collecting from 66,000 chemical plants and chemical storage sites under the Clean Air Act. The information is to be released in June, and the E.P.A. originally intended to post it on its World Wide Web site. But Mr. Bliley and officials from intelligence agencies began objecting last year, saying such a move would create an Internet road map for terrorists. Environmental groups and community advocates, however, say easy public access to the data is necessary to help prepare for a much greater risk -- that of accidental spills of dangerous chemicals. The E.P.A. has dropped its plans to post the data on its Web site. But at a hearing on the matter Wednesday, Mr. Bliley said he remained concerned that environmental groups would obtain the information through the Freedom of Information Act and post it on their own sites. Mr. Bliley, a Virginia Republican, has not specifically said that he is considering legislation to limit what can be posted on the Internet. But a spokesman for Mr. Bliley said legislation on the issue was imminent. Several of his supporters questioned witnesses from the E.P.A. and the Federal Bureau of Investigation about terrorist concerns. And after the meeting, Mr. Bliley's office issued a news release contending that an official of the E.P.A. had agreed that the information "should not be posted on the Internet by the Government or any other party." A coalition of Internet advocacy groups has asked Mr. Bliley to reconsider filing legislation, saying that any proposals to limit the distribution of the data electronically would set a dangerous precedent for limiting public access to nonclassified Government documents. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
'Holy War' Over the Future of Wireless
body: Perhaps the most far-reaching battle in telecommunications these days is not being waged in board rooms or stock markets. It is being fought in places like the Mines Beach Resort and Spa outside Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. There, in a conference room not far from the ocean, representatives of 34 of the world's largest communications companies joined official delegates from 14 nations on Feb. 6 to try to forge a consensus on the next generation of wireless phones. That they failed was hardly surprising. For the last 18 months, the biggest players in the wireless business, both carriers and equipment makers, have been embroiled in what an AT&T spokesman describes as a financial, regulatory and political holy war for control of the wireless future. In six weeks, the International Telecommunication Union, a United Nations agency that set up the meeting in Malaysia, is scheduled to start approving international standards for wireless technologies for the next decade. But that process is being threatened by a general reluctance to compromise on arcane technical standards and in particular by intransigence on the part of Ericsson of Sweden and Qualcomm Inc., of San Diego, two big communications manufacturers that have feuded for years. The stakes are immense for both consumers and the companies. Over the next few years, most of the world's wireless carriers intend to introduce services that could prove technically momentous. With an emphasis on bringing high-speed data services to customers wherever they are, proponents of so-called third-generation wireless technology predict that the next wave of mobile phones will incorporate World Wide Web browsing and video conferences. Billions of dollars in revenue could await the companies that manufacture and sell the equipment that will make this happen. At the same time, a wave of consolidations is creating bigger and broader wireless carriers. Last month, for instance, the Vodafone Group, Britain's biggest wireless company, agreed to acquire Airtouch Communications of San Francisco, another huge wireless provider, for $60 billion. And as carriers extend their coverage, there is rising potential for callers to be able to use one phone, with one number, almost anywhere and at rates that are widely affordable. But to make that happen, the carriers, manufacturers and, to some extent, governments would have to agree on a single standard. Many industry insiders now think that will not happen. "The idea of one standard or a universal standard sounds good," said Jim Brewington, who runs the wireless business for Lucent Technologies, North America's largest communications equipment maker and a relatively neutral party in the dispute. "We would like to see it happen. I frankly don't think it's going to happen." Fabio Leite, a wireless counselor for the telecommunications union in Geneva, said, "We have a lot of reasons to be pessimistic." And even the adversaries concede that the fight, though couched in highly technical language, is really a political struggle. "If you're asking me is it a political issue or a technical issue, I'll say it's a political issue," said Keith Paglusch, a senior vice president of Sprint PCS, a big unitedstates wireless carrier that essentially belongs to the Qualcomm camp. "It really is a business/political issue." The roots of the row over third-generation wireless technology were put down in the early 90's, when it became clear that the first generation of wireless phones, analog cellular, was going to be replaced by a second digital generation known as P.C.S. -- personal communications services. At that time, Qualcomm was basically alone in advocating a wireless approach known as C.D.M.A., for code division multiple access. This works somewhat like the Internet in that it breaks messages into small bits, which are then scattered throughout the wireless telephone spectrum and reassembled at their destination. The idea that C.D.M.A., which was originally developed for military purposes, could be adapted to civilian use was heresy to many wireless engineers and their companies. Perhaps the most vociferous in its criticism was Ericsson, which had built a big second-generation wireless business on a competing technology called time division multiple access. That technology uses relatively narrow batches of wireless frequencies, which it then breaks up many times a second to convey many messages. It is in a lot of ways similar to a third technology in the wireless alphabet soup: GSM, or global system for mobile communication, which is the dominant second-generation standard in Europe and many other areas. It is largely associated with Ericsson but is also supported by Nokia of Finland, Siemens of Germany and others. Despite the engineers' early doubts, C.D.M.A., which was chosen by Sprint PCS and a few other carriers, turned out to work just fine -- and perhaps better than fine. So Qualcomm was upset when in October 1996, just as C.D.M.A. was emerging, Ericsson sued Qualcomm, charging that Ericsson held patents covering parts of Qualcomm's systems. The trial is scheduled to begin in April in a Federal court in Texas. Not much later, development began on the wireless third generation, and both Qualcomm and Ericsson chose to use C.D.M.A. technology for transmitting digital data at high speed. But in developing third-generation systems, Qualcomm and Ericsson seemed to have different agendas. Qualcomm wanted the new systems to be compatible with existing C.D.M.A. systems, so that carriers would not have to scrap their investments and Qualcomm could continue to sell second-generation C.D.M.A. with the promise that it could be upgraded. Ericsson, with no installed base of C.D.M.A. systems, did not appear as concerned with the compatibility issue. So with European partners, it developed a technology that is not compatible with existing C.D.M.A. services. It said it simply wanted the most robust, advanced system possible. But some unitedstates executives and officials smelled a plot after the European Union adopted a directive in December that appeared to force European carriers to use Ericsson's third-generation technology. Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright; Secretary of Commerce William M. Daley; Charlene Barshefsky, the unitedstates trade representative, and William E. Kennard, chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, sent a letter to the Europeans expressing concern over the policy. Last month, the European commissioner for telecommunications, Martin Bangemann, appeared to mollify American policy makers somewhat by saying that competing standards would not be barred from Europe. But suspicion remains. An American official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said, "It appears to some of us that our friends in Europe want to duplicate the conditions that allowed GSM to become the predominant global second-generation technology: Get it to market first, mandate it as a pan-European standard and make sure it's not backwards-compatible with existing wireless networks in North America." Ericsson and Qualcomm have now each claimed patent rights over each other's third-generation proposals, and the International Telecommunication Union says it cannot certify a standard until the property rights are settled. Qualcomm wants Ericsson to converge its standard with Qualcomm's in a way that grants existing C.D.M.A. operators thorough compatibility. Ericsson has so far refused, saying such convergence would yield a technically inferior standard. The end game may be a proliferation of multiple standards. For consumers, that could mean abandoning hope for a seamless global wireless network. Or it could mean higher prices if carriers and equipment makers have to offer many technologies to insure seamless global wireless systems. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Irwin M. Jacobs, chairman of Qualcomm, has pushed for one wireless standard . . . (Dave Gatley for The newyork Times); . . . while Sven-Christer Nilsson, president of Ericsson, has pushed for another.  Chart: "Competing Paths" With the equipment manufacturers Qualcomm Inc. and Ericsson of Sweden representing two divergent views, the wireless communications industry is debating the best technical format for the next, global generation of technology. Major allies: Nokia and Siemens

title: Ticketmaster and Microsoft Settle Suit on Internet Linking
body: Ticketmaster, a unit of Barry Diller's USA Networks Inc., has settled its two-year-old lawsuit against Microsoft. Although the parties agreed not to disclose the terms of the settlement, executives said the agreement did resolve the suit's central issue -- whether Microsoft's Sidewalk on-line city guides could bypass many of Ticketmaster's advertising-laden Web pages and link Sidewalk users directly to the ticket-purchase portions of Ticketmaster's site. Charles Conn, chief executive of Ticketmaster's Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch business, said that Microsoft had agreed to no longer link Sidewalk to pages deep within the Ticketmaster site, where visitors might not even realize they were using Ticketmaster's services. As a result of the settlement, the Sidewalk guides will now point visitors who want to purchase tickets directly to the Ticketmaster home page -- where Ticketmaster will have ample opportunity to bathe them in advertising. The two sides came to terms on Jan. 22, but had not announced the settlement. Mr. Conn disclosed the deal in an interview late last week. The case had been widely watched for its potential to establish a legal precedent on the intellectual property rights of Internet companies. But with an out-of-court settlement, the on-line industry remains without legal guidelines on the practice of so-called deep linking, of which Microsoft was by no means the only practitioner. Ticketmaster filed suit in April 1997 in a Federal court in California, arguing that Microsoft had "pilfered" its content and therefore diluted its value. At the time, Ticketmaster had recently signed a deal with Citysearch, which, like Microsoft's Sidewalk guides, provides information about local news, merchants and entertainment in various cities. In that deal Citysearch was essentially paying Ticketmaster for the right to do what Microsoft was doing free. Ticketmaster, which was acquired by Mr. Diller's company in 1997, merged its on-line division with Citysearch last September to create Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch. In its legal defense, Microsoft had argued that Ticketmaster's stance breached an unwritten Internet code in which any Web site operator has the right to link to anyone else's site. Microsoft also based its defense on what it said was its First Amendment right to publish public information. But with the settlement, those in the industry looking for the Federal court's guidance were disappointed. "I'm sure it's in the best interest of the parties, but for the purpose of providing meaningful guidance to the Internet community, this is the worst news I've heard all day," Jeffrey Kuester, an Internet law specialist and a partner in the Atlanta law firm Thomas, Kayden, Horstemeyer & Risley, said when told of the settlement. "We were hoping to hear some good, broad, general language from the court," Mr. Kuester said. "Now, do we know if deep linking is bad? Is linking to a main home page O.K.? Is it just not O.K. to link? We don't know." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Low-Key Lodging on Barbados
body: CHOOSING a room via the Internet? Really? Like accepting candy from a stranger, I thought at first after learning that some people do indeed pick out a hotel or apartment by tapping into cyberspace. But in July I found myself doing just that -- wandering around the Internet, searching for a hotel room on Barbados. The off-season rates were tantalizing, and, according to the Barbados Tourism Authority's Web site, the climate was not unreasonable, with highs in the mid- to upper 80's. My price range was under $100 a night, and I wanted my hotel to be a convenient base for touring Barbados's many cultural treasures, its graceful historic houses and tropical gardens. Island Web sites were plentiful and hotel choices bewildering. Suddenly the computer screen came alive with a spirited discussion of Barbados's beach resorts on a message board of America Online. No idle ramblings, these were declamations of loyalty to one gorgeous spot or another. The comment about Casuarina Beach Club -- "I'll never stay anywhere else" -- didn't equivocate. But who was the commentator -- a gabby satisfied repeat guest, the hotel marketing director or the owner's best friend? Two guidebooks gave the 160-room apartment hotel in Barbados's St. Lawrence Gap district pleasant reviews along with favorable comments about a neighboring resort, describing both in much the same way: good beaches, comfortable rooms. I called Casuarina and negotiated an off-season nightly rate of $82 plus 17.5 percent tax and service, for a studio with a garden view. Three weeks later, the taxi from the airport pulled up to a low-slung coral stone building in a tropical landscape that had the look of a manicured jungle, an anomaly on Barbados's busy, much-developed south coast, where the hotel is situated and where deforestation began centuries ago. Rocking chairs lined the driveway. The reception desk sat in front of a small lush courtyard. In the late afternoon light the lobby felt pleasantly cavelike. Comfortable couches and chairs were clustered in corners. Ceiling fans stirred the air. Vines tumbled out of large ceramic planters. My husband, Bernard, and I followed a walkway that meandered around two swimming pools and through tall trees and flowering shrubs, until we reached a four-story building. Room 325 had fresh white walls, white lamps and white tile floors brightened with a prim pink flowery bedspread. The matching curtains trimmed with a knife-pleated valance were suitable for a genteel English cottage in Devon but not out of place on British-flavored Barbados, where afternoon tea is a tradition. The white tiled bathroom was spotless, stocked with ample white towels and a hair dryer. There were no little bottles of lotions, no shower cap, just two fragrant bars of soap made in Dominica. The kitchenette was equipped with cutlery, crockery and cooking pots. The spacious balcony that overlooked the garden on the other side of our room's sliding glass doors was screened by palm fronds arching from trees in front of the building. The walls of the bedroom, kitchenette and bath were decorated with regional art, tropical pastel scenes and a ceramic relief of a woman's back. St. Lawrence Gap, a bustling stretch of coastal road, teems with night life but Casuarina's tranquil main dining room, filled with folk art, seemed just right after a bumpy plane ride. Bernard and I walked into the open-air restaurant under a tall roof sheltering pierced ceramic lanterns, aquariums, fish mobiles and wood carvings of octopus, seahorses and other creatures. Bernard commented that his grilled shrimp might have spent time in a freezer, but my grilled red snapper served with mashed potatoes and green beans was outstanding. The next morning as we ate breakfast, an iridescent blue-green hummingbird hovered among red hibiscus a few feet away. The moist banana bread and strong coffee were delicious. The 1,500-foot-long beach beyond the dining room was clean and beguiling, with turquoise water and mild surf. (Sometimes the waves are bigger, I'm told, and at other times it is very calm.) Tucked here and there in clearings in the luxuriant garden were chaise longues, a crib placed near one swimming pool, and a children's playhouse. We had wondered whether the hotel would have a gloomy, off-season air, but were reassured by the sounds of splashing and by the stream of guests -- Europeans, Canadians and Americans -- we met on the paths. The Casuarina, it turned out, was full. Bulletin boards announced some of the hotel's activities -- nature walks, bike rides, gallery visits, history lectures, water polo and bocce, among many others. But with just three days to explore the island, we hurried off to tour Sunbury Plantation House, built more than 300 years ago and rebuilt recently after a fire. Behind its two-and-a-half-foot thick walls, there was an appealing mix of antiques, maps, family heirlooms such as old christening gowns, and in the cellar, a collection of carriages. Before and after, we gawked at new hotel and condominium development in the south of the 166-square-mile island and along the more fashionable west coast. The highlight of the day was a walk through the Sunbury's grounds, a popular spot for island celebrations, where we stopped to sit in the shade of two giant bearded fig trees. During the next two days we visited Tyrol Cot Heritage Village, a fascinating small-scale version of Colonial Williamsburg, with artisans in reproductions of plantation workers' movable chattel houses, and strolled through the lovely Andromeda Botanic Gardens, with its winding paths and Egyptian papyrus, bromeliads and thousands of tropical plants. We looked at the newly restored wind-powered Morgan Lewis Sugar Mill, observed more hotel development and admired weathered old churches like St. John's, built in 1836, with Gothic arches and views of the rugged east coast. We lunched on one of the national dishes, tasty flying fish at the open-air Barclays Restaurant beside the beach. On all three days we returned to Casuarina too late for afternoon tea and too tired even to inspect the hotel's two tennis courts. At the Tuesday night party as we stood in line waiting for the free rum punch, we met Casuarina's energetic manager and co-owner, Sonia Cole-Wilson, when she sprinkled nutmeg into our tumblers. At the same time, sounding like a mother, she suggested we might want to dilute the rum with a bit more fruit juice. We did. In a brief chat about the hotel's eight-acre grounds, she told us the garden was her attempt to re-create a corner of her native Trinidad. Later that evening as a live band played and the party progressed, we shared a table with two German tourists, a teacher from Frankfurt and her mother. They were staying at the hotel three weeks. Why Barbados? we asked. And if they preferred warm places, why not someplace closer to Germany, such as Spain or Sicily? "We like the tropics," the teacher said. "A friend who used to live on Barbados told us about Casuarina. We've stayed here six times." One our last evening, we walked through the garden for a last look at the sea. On the dark beach we stumbled into a large telescope in front of a circle of chairs filled with children and their parents listening to an astronomer. We'd happened upon one of the hotel's regular lectures. Parents and children were asking questions about Chaos and peering through the telescope at the Milky Way. The scenario felt oddly familiar -- not too different from choosing a room via the Internet.  A homey haven Casuarina Beach Club, St. Lawrence Gap, Dover, in Christ Church Parish, (246) 428-3600 or (800) 742-4276 for toll-free reservations, fax (246) 428-1970, can be previewed on its Web pages at www.bajan.com (clicking on Barbados, then Hotels). Casuarina Web pages can also be reached through www.barbados.org, the official site of the Barbados Tourism Authority. Casuarina appears on a list that's billed as the island's "finest hotels," with links. Summer rates begin at $105 for a studio with a view of the pool or garden, plus the 17.5 percent tax and service charge. (I was able to pare that to $82, plus 17.5 percent, by calling the resort directly and asking for the corporate rate.) The same room rents for $190 during winter (until April 15) and $110 in spring (April 16 to May 31) and fall (Nov. 1 to Dec. 15). Beachfront rooms are $115 in summer, $125 in spring and fall, and $205 in winter. The 17.5 percent tax and service is additional. Larger units are also avail able. Meals are extra. The average cost of a dinner with a modest wine, dessert and coffee, was $28 including tax but not tip. Each morning, we skipped the tempting breakfast buffet, $16, to choose from the menu. We paid about $6 for a pot of coffee and two orders of the excellent banana bread. Barclays Rum Punch Bar and Restaurant, (246) 422-9213, is a rustic beachfront spot on the east coast road. The flying fish special served with rice and peas, salad and vegetables cost around $11. Lunch only. Open daily from around 10 A.M. to 6 P.M.   FRANCES FRANK MARCUS http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Lounging on the hotel's verdant grounds. On the beach, about 1,500 feet long. title: Web Sites Set to Transmit Images From Mars After a Craft's Landing Today
body: If all systems are go when the Pathfinder spacecraft comes to rest on the surface of Mars today and begins sending back images, millions of people will be able to watch what is happening live on the suddenly interplanetary World Wide Web. Anticipating that this weeklong event will generate a lot of interest, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is running the mission, has arranged for 25 Web sites to broadcast the images coming back from Mars simultaneously. The sites, all of which are identical, will be able to handle up to 30 million visits at a time. The Jet Propulsion Laboratory has set up a Web page that lists all the sites and lets Internet users choose the one nearest them to minimize the transmission time of images. In addition to the 25 official Pathfinder Web pages, there are a number of other sites that offer information about the mission and the planet. One such site belongs to the National Space Science Data Center, which is part of NASA. It contains photographs of Mars and information about the mission and the landing site. There is also a page of facts about Mars that will allow Internet users to find answers to questions like: How many days does it take Mars to orbit around the sun? (687) And what is Mars's mass as a percentage of Earth's? (11 percent) For those who barely remember the last visits to Mars of the Viking crafts in the mid-1970's and the Mariner missions of the late 1960's, they can explore them on a site created by the Johnson Space Center. It includes photographs of each of the craft and a couple of photographs taken by the Voyagers of Mars's surface. Spaceviews, an on-line publication about space exploration, offers dozens of photographs of Pathfinder, its robot explorer, called Sojourner, and the launching of the spacecraft last year. The site also has a section about the possibility of life on Mars and links to other Web sites, including a site about a future mission maintained by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The Lunar and Planetary Laboratory of the University of Arizona, which designed the imaging system on Pathfinder, has a Web site explaining how the camera works. It, too, has links to other Mars Web sites, for example, one called Mars Today that has a poster showing conditions on the planet and its relationship to Earth, updated daily. As might be expected, there are sites that have been created as teaching tools for children. One such site, from Passport to Knowledge, is organized in conjunction with a series of six broadcasts about the mission on PBS television stations. Children can send in questions to NASA scientists; some might be answered on two programs to be televised live on Sunday and Wednesday from 2 to 4 P.M. Eastern daylight time. title: Women Earn High Marks on a Web Test
body: Results of a World Wide Web navigating test, released yesterday by the MCI Communications Corporation and the Educational Testing Service, indicated that older women could find their way around the Web better than young men could. The Internet aptitude test, in which 16,500 Internet users participated, also reported that girls, who have often been said to be less computer-savvy than boys their age, scored higher than their male counterparts. "The actual variation in scores is rather small," said Vint Cerf, senior vice president of Internet architecture and engineering for MCI. "What is significant is that 60-year-old women can keep up with the younger guys." The test, called the MCI Great American Net Test, was offered as an interactive quiz on a Web site (http://www.nettest.mci.com). The anonymous exam tested users' ability to search the Internet. According to MCI, 650,000 Internet users visited the site, though only 16,500 completed the multiple-choice test. "I can see why people didn't finish the test," said Nate Zelnick, senior editor for Web Week, a trade publication. "It takes a long time." The average score on the test was 78.8 points, of a possible 100. Women outscored men and the national average, registering an average 79.91; men averaged 78.29. Women 60 years of age and older scored 71.38, outscoring boys 17 and younger -- thought to be the most advanced Web surfers -- who averaged 70.64.

title: Food Notes
body: Sauce for the Sirloin Smith & Wollensky, 797 Third Avenue (49th Street), has introduced its own steak sauce just in time for grill season. Horseradish gives the rich sauce a spicy bite. Smith & Wollensky Steak Sauce is $7.50 for 12 ounces at the steakhouse and Williams-Sonoma stores. This month, the restaurant will open a small retail shop to sell filet, T-bone and sirloin steaks for the sauce.  Farmers' Markets on the Net Starchefs, a Web site devoted to chefs, recipes, cookbook authors and other food-related subjects (www.starchefs.com), has added a directory of nearly 2,500 farmers' markets around the country. It is organized by state and city. Click on "Farm Fresh Markets" on the main menu. Fresh Poultry at the Door The Antzis Live Poultry Market, 1355 Amsterdam Avenue (126th Street), has started a delivery service for telephone orders to the Upper West Side, from 65th Street to 126th. The market sells chickens in several sizes, plus Long Island and Muscovy ducks, turkeys, guinea hens, quail, partridge, pheasants and rabbits. There is a $20 minimum for delivery. New customers will receive a 5 percent discount on orders over $20 and 10 percent on orders over $40. The delivery service is available daily, 8 A.M. to 3 P.M. All orders are C.O.D., cash only. The prices are based on live weight. A four-pound live chicken at $1.30 a pound, for example, will be reduced to about three pounds dressed, bringing the price to about $1.75 a pound. The poultry will be delivered in one to three hours. Fresh-killed poultry should be refrigerated but not cooked until about six hours after slaughter, to give the muscles a chance to relax and make the flesh more tender. For information: (212) 662-6773.  Off the Menu  Multilevel Noodles and Sushi In September, Li Ping, a partner in Kin Khao and Kelley & Ping, both in SoHo, plans to open Obeca/Li, a huge, multifaceted restaurant at 62-68 Thomas Street (West Broadway) in TriBeCa. Larry Bogdanow, who designed Union Square Cafe, is the architect for the 15,000-square-foot space on several levels. It will have a Japanese noodle bar, a tea bar, a sake bar, a sushi and oyster bar, an area for small plates that Ms. Ping calls "Japanese tapas," and French and Asian food at tables. The chef, Mitsuo Kikuchi, was previously at Cafe Seiyoken. Ms. Ping said the name was suggested by Odeon, a restaurant around the corner, TriBeCa and her own first name.  Homages to Women of the Stage Rebecca Charles and Mary Redding, chefs who were tired of being sequestered behind the stove, have just opened Pearl, a seafood restaurant, at 18 Cornelia Street (Bleecker Street). They have turned a narrow storefront into a simple restaurant, with most of the seating at two counters, thus forgoing formal waiters. A menu of chowder, steamers, lobsters and fish is $5.50 to $16. There is one table, which seats five. Pearl, as in the oyster byproduct, also stands for Pearl Goldsmith, Ms. Charles's grandmother, a onetime opera singer who lived on the Maine coast. Pearl Goldsmith is not the only performer to be celebrated in a new restaurant. The Evelyn, named for Evelyn Nesbit, a Floradora Girl famous for appearing on a red velvet swing, has opened at 380 Columbus Avenue (78th Street). The building, also called the Evelyn, was once a hotel owned by the family of Harry K. Thaw, who married Nesbit and murdered Stanford White, her former lover. The Evelyn, serving eclectic American food, replaces Phoebe's. It includes a lower-level lounge, once Alice's Underground, a secondhand clothing store.  Dining, 18th-Century Style Dinners based on 18th-century recipes are being offered on Saturday evenings from July 12 through Aug. 30 at Van Cortlandt Manor, a historic mansion in Croton-on-Hudson, N.Y. The events start at 4 P.M. with a tour of the mansion, followed by drinks at 5 P.M., then dinner, which ends at about 8 P.M. The cost is $50 a person. For reservations: (914) 631-8200, ext. 618.

title: Lotus Is Ready to Introduce Major Changes in Notes Program
body: The Lotus Development Corporation, responding to competitive pressure caused by new Internet technology, demonstrated major changes to its hallmark Notes program today that allow it to both read and create information for the World Wide Web. Most of the changes will be in a new version of Notes that goes on sale Jan. 1. Lotus also cut prices for the new version and other new Notes products. It will be possible to click onto the Web while reading electronic mail sent by a colleague in Notes. In addition, Web pages can be created using Notes. The steps are designed to keep Lotus, bought by I.B.M. five months ago in the software industry's largest takeover, as the leading seller of messaging and groupware programs, which combine electronic mail and sophisticated data bases.  "We view this as our turf," said Michael Zisman, chief executive officer of Lotus. "We are prepared to compete." A new kind of Notes for individual, or "client," computers was introduced today, called Notes Mail. It will sell for $55 each in quantities of 50. Another version, which interacts with data bases and is called Notes Desktop, will be cut in price from $155 to $69 each in quantities of 50. A programmable client, known simply as Notes, will remain at $275. Notes software for computers that serve several clients will cost $495 for a version that works on single-processor computers to $2,295 for one that works on very powerful computers. Lotus has been threatened by technical standards related to the Web that allow documents to be linked easily regardless of the computers involved, something that Notes first made popular. Those technical standards occur in Web programs, such as browsers, that are less expensive than Notes. Thousands of companies are incorporating Web standards in communications programs not just for the Internet but on their internal computer networks, something that has become known as an "intranet." "We see companies going off and believing they can build intranets less expensively than they can using Notes, and we want to address that by making our products more functional and affordable," Mr. Zisman said. The new products put Lotus at the forefront of major software producers that are changing their goods to embrace the global data network. Just last week, the Microsoft Corporation, the leading maker of personal computer software, outlined an Internet strategy but said it would be months before products were available. The Lotus announcement was surprising not only in scope but also in how close to market the products are. "It kind of takes the wind out of Microsoft's sails," said Amy Wohl, a technology industry consultant and newsletter publisher. "This is stuff that's almost ready to ship." Notes has emerged in the last three years as the most important Lotus product, surpassing the 1-2-3 spreadsheet and other office productivity tools on which the company was built. Notes was repeatedly cited by executives at I.B.M. as a key motivation for its $3.5 billion buyout of Lotus. Jeff Papows, the Lotus chief operating officer, said Lotus executives believed increased sales would make up for the revenue lost in the price cuts. "We expect to continue to grow this business in triple-digit rates as we have over the past three years," Mr. Papows said.

title: Report of High Internet Use Is Challenged
body: A Nielsen survey that concluded that there are more than 24 million highly educated and affluent adult users of the Internet in the unitedstates and Canada may have "significantly inflated" its findings, perhaps by millions, the study's principal academic adviser now says. The highly publicized findings of the Commercenet/Nielsen Internet Demographic Survey are based on fundamental flaws that render its conclusions invalid, said Donna L. Hoffman, a business professor at Vanderbilt University in Nashville. The survey was conducted by Nielsen, a unit of Dun & Bradstreet that performs marketing research, and paid for by Commercenet, a group of companies that hopes to foster computerized commerce. Other attempts to measure the size of the rapidly growing global computer network have found far fewer regular users, although numbers vary widely. And some of the conclusions of the Nielsen report surprised even the most ardent proponents of the Internet, while encouraging others to step up their efforts in electronic commerce. Among the Nielsen study's more surprising findings were that adults collectively spend as much time browsing the Internet each week as they do watching videocassettes, that 18 million adults use the Internet's World Wide Web and that 2.5 million people have bought goods or services on the Web. Paul Lindstrom, vice president of Nielsen Media Research in newyork, defended the accuracy of the survey -- which is being sold for $5,000 to $10,000 a copy to businesses --and played down the criticism from Professor Hoffman. "I wouldn't swear the absolute numbers in the study were the truth, quote unquote, but I'm absolutely certain we have better data than anything else out there for providing solid information on making decisions on where to go on the Internet," Mr. Lindstrom said. Cathy Medich, executive director of Commercenet, said she had relayed Professor Hoffman's concerns to Nielsen and was satisfied that Nielsen did the survey properly. The final report from the study was distributed last week to the more than 130 members of Commercenet, including such companies as American Express, Ameritech, Andersen Consulting, Bank of America, Federal Express, Netscape Communications, Sun Microsystems and Wells Fargo. Professor Hoffman and her partner, Prof. Thomas Novak, worked closely with Nielsen Media Research and Commercenet to design the survey, and she endorsed the preliminary report released on Oct. 30. But Professor Hoffman said that she had made the endorsement without having seen the raw data and that based on material Nielsen has since released, she believes "a big mistake has been made." For reasons she said would be apparent after Nielsen releases its raw data, the sample of 4,200 individuals surveyed by telephone last August tended to include people who were older, much more affluent and more highly educated than the population as a whole, at least based on 1990 unitedstates census data, Professor Hoffman said. People with lower incomes and less education -- and thus who were less likely to use personal computers at home or at work -- were underrepresented in the sample, she said. As a result, Professor Hoffman said, the population projections made from the survey sample were skewed significantly. She cited, for example, a conclusion in Nielsen's final report -- but not in the preliminary data -- that more than 40 million adults use commercial on-line information services. Other surveys put the number at no more than 10 million. Nielsen, according to Mr. Lindstrom, also pegged the number of America Online users at 10.5 million, when America Online itself claims 4 million subscribers. "I guess it depends on how you count," said Pam McGraw, an America Online spokeswoman. "It sounds very impressive." For his part, Mr. Lindstrom defended Nielsen's methods: "I wouldn't be prepared to say that because our data didn't match the census data, that the census was right and we were wrong. It's really making a comparison of apples and oranges." Mark Resch, general manager of business services at the Xerox Corporation's Palo Alto Research Center in California, said the participation of Professor Hoffman and Professor Novak -- both of whom are experts in data collection and analysis -- was critical to the success of the Nielsen study. "It will be a disappointment if her analysis is true," Mr. Resch said, "because it will mean we are still in the quest for a baseline Internet demographic." He said Xerox and other companies had high hopes for Internet businesses, but he also said that some companies were worried that the Internet might turn out to be "the CB radio of the 1990's." Others point to the sweeping changes caused by the Internet -- Microsoft, for example, repositioning itself last week as an Internet company -- and say that specific numbers are unimportant given the broader trends. "All estimates indicate the total numbers are growing and are doubling every year," said Eric Schmidt, chief scientist at Sun Microsystems, a Commercenet member. "So even if one study is twice as high as another, a year from now the market will get caught up." Commercenet said it would make the final report and raw data available to qualified academic researchers on Friday, but for now only Professor Hoffman and Professor Novak have seen the underlying data. Mr. Lindstrom of Nielsen questioned the expertise of the two professors and pointed to his company's reputation for careful polling and analysis. Nielsen plans to expand itsservices to include measuring traffic on World Wide Web sites. Graphic   Graph: "In Dispute" Donna L. Hoffman, a business professor at Vanderbilt University, says a survey of Internet users conducted by Commercenet and Nielsen was skewed toward older, more affluent and more highly educated people. Graph compares Nielsen's numbers with those of Dr. Hoffman. (Source: Professor Donna L. Hoffman)

title: What's Cooking In Virtual Kitchens - Correction Appended
body:
PATTI GREANEY, a no-nonsense maker of television commercials whose work bounced her from coast to coast, seldom had much time to cook for herself. But whenever she found a free moment to pull out the old pots and pans, her expectations of what she might whip up soared far beyond the recipes she had at hand. "I mean, if I take the time to cook, I hope what comes out on the other end is a fabulous piece," she said. So Ms. Greaney sought expert guidance. But, she said, she soon found that cookbooks were too boring, family recipes too mundane, and the world's greatest chefs were, well, generally about as approachable as divas at curtain time. In a flash of inventiveness that could have made Edison blush, she merged her hunger to prepare fine foods with her mastery of producing punchy nuggets of advertising copy. Two months ago, with the help of partners, she staked her claim on the Internet with Starchefs, a computer-generated open door into the lives of some of the world's most acclaimed chefs. Starchefs is one of the most entertaining and easiest to use of the emerging culinary sites on line. And it seems that cyberspace, that impossibly crowded computer web of information, is rapidly developing a sense of taste. Food, and practically everything connected to it, is a cyberspace hot spot, especially on the Internet's World Wide Web. Many food-related Web sites are visited electronically thousands of times a day. Shortly after Starchefs went on line this fall, it was receiving more than 500,000 visits a week. Gary Holleman, a chef and the author of "Food and Wine Online" (Van Nostrand Reinhold, 1995), said that as an indication of the popularity of food sites, when he searched the Internet for sites containing the word "culinary" late last year, he turned up nothing. When he repeated the search a couple of months ago, more than 800 sites popped up. As a consequence, even the most causal Net cruisers can visit fine restaurants, chat with master chefs, swap favorite recipes, browse vineyards and shop the culinary markets of the world with full-color sights and, in some instances, engaging sounds. "Food is a basic human need, so it's not very surprising that there's all this hubbub about food on the Net," said Judith L. Klavans, director of the Columbia University Center for Research on Information Access. But before anyone tosses out the toaster oven to make room in the kitchen for a new computer, consider a few cautionary notes. This gee-whiz electronic highway to the palate is, like much on the Internet, still being paved while it is being traveled by millions of people each day. So even the most experienced Web rovers are likely to stumble onto road clutter. For example, a recent listing of "cooking" sites using the Internet search engine Web Crawler included one dedicated to the misogynous humor of Andrew Dice Clay. Right now, says Martha Stewart, the house-and-garden guru, cyberspace offerings generally lack depth. "All of this is in its very, very early stages," she said. "I'm sure it will become more sophisticated and useful as time goes on." For at least the short term, she added, the printed cookbook is secure. One reason may be that the quality of the information -- and its presentation -- varies widely. Offerings can be text-only sites commonly found on electronic bulletin boards and in news groups like rec.food.recipes. There, submissions, or postings, are usually made by hobbyists and weekend cooks. It is strictly broil or bake at your own risk. But increasingly, professionals have set up more polished, smartly organized sites, like Virtual Vineyards, and on-line food and dining newsletters and magazines, like The Electronic Gourmet Guide, or EGG, and The Internet Epicurean from Conde Nast, the magazine publisher. And beware: while many Internet services like Starchefs are free, connections to the Internet are not. So just remember the meter is running during freewheeling expeditions to, say, Michael's restaurant in Santa Monica, Calif., to peek at its menus. Here is a look at some food finds in cyberspace. Resource Centers At Ms. Greaney's STARCHEFS, based in newyork, Net cruisers are only a click of a mouse away from up-close-and-personal profiles of chefs like David Burke, Mark Peel and Douglas Rodriguez. You can learn, for instance, that Mr. Rodriguez, the prince of Nuevo Latino cuisine at Patria restaurant in newyork, is 30 and counts the food processor among his favorite utensils. Besides the personal tidbits the service, like other sites, offers a repository of information on culinary careers and educational opportunities; special events like food festivals and restaurant excursions, and regularly updated lists of hunger-relief programs like City Harvest. THE CULINARY PROFESSIONAL'S RESOURCE CENTER is exactly what it sounds like: it is exhaustively thorough, and exacting. It is one of the best sources about food and dining in cyberspace. The center is also the home of the FOOD AND WINE ONLINE NEWSLETTER, which is edited by Mr. Holleman, the chef and product manager for Indian Harvest Specialtifoods in Bemidji, Minn. The resource center keeps electronic archives of the newsletter, which regularly features names, descriptions and cyberspace addresses for interesting and helpful culinary sites. The resource center also provides links to marketplaces and food and dining sites, like bulletin boards and data bases, and global fruit and vegetable prices. A click of a mouse can let users check out the menus of restaurants like the Grand Orbit Restaurant and Night Club in Brisbane, Australia, and Floogies Swamp Cafe in San Francisco. Magazines Besides the Food and Wine Online Newsletter, a number of outstanding electronic magazines, or e-zines, as they are called, are dedicated to food and dining. One of the most accessible for professional and amateur chefs is the popular ELECTRONIC GOURMET GUIDE. The guide features a food trivia game and an article on how to make a gingerbread house. It also has the top 10 best gifts for chefs. All the selections, from a $19.95 Italian truffle slicer to a porcelain, cooper and brass fondue pot for $149.95, were drawn from the deep shelves of Chip Fisher's Lamalle Kitchenware in newyork, which bills itself as the oldest such business in the unitedstates. Commercial Services The commercial on-line services like America Online, Compuserve and Prodigy, which charge for time spent on line, have their own food and dining sites. Some, like America Online's AOL DINER, are richly designed and well organized. This service offers a well-stocked data bank of information, from restaurant guides to ratings of after-dinner cigars. Prodigy offers far less, but nonetheless useful, food and dining information, including a bank of consumer reports, like an article on bogus health drinks. Practically all the services have chat rooms (electronic forums in which up to 24 users can communicate live through typed messages), marketplaces and bulletin boards. One of the newest and most extensive commercial on-line sites is INNTERREST -- or INNterREST, as its founders write it. They describes it as the "on-line and Internet solution for the global hospitality industry." It can be reached only through Bill Gates's fledgling Microsoft Network. And while it tends to favor food-industry types, like vendors and suppliers, it offers a flood of food facts. Shopping Two months ago, Cynthia Denny, went on line with FOOD OF THE WORLD, a cleverly constructed cyberspace mall of unusual and unheard-of foods, wines, coffees and micro brewery beers. Armed with a postgraduate degree in business and a special interest in food, Ms. Denny, a 30-something single mother, operates Food of the World from an office in Sacramento, Calif. Shoppers can peruse descriptions of a hearty spread of specialties like Maggie Gin's Asian Sauces and Mill Valley organic foods. Soon, she said, she will be marketing Frank Sinatra's Gourmet Italian Foods and adding Kashrus Magazine, a publication on kosher cooking, to her site. Founded in 1994 in Los Altos, Calif., VIRTUAL VINEYARDS combines the depth of a wine warehouse with the customer service of a corner liquor store. Founded by Peter Granoff with Robert Olson, his brother-in-law and a former computer executive, Virtual Vineyards assesses wines hand-picked by Mr. Granoff.  For those uncomfortable with sending credit card numbers through cyberspace, Virtual Vineyards also offers an "800" number for orders. Mr. Fisher of LAMALLE KITCHENWARE, which specializes in equipment and utensils for professional and high-end home kitchens, is currently putting his catalogue in cyberspace and is holding kitchenware forums on the Internet. "We usually answer lots of questions in a day," said Mr. Fisher, who also owns Fisher & Levy, a catering company, and two Mr. Chips ice-cream shops, all in newyork. Mr. Fisher said a sergeant major in the, Quartermaster Corps he had been corresponding with recently told him by electronic mail that he would have to sign off for a while. The reason? He was being shipped out as part of the American peace-keeping force in Bosnia. "That's instantaneous," Mr. Fisher said. HERE are some popular culinary sites, along with their Internet addresses. The Culinary Professional's Resource Center http://www.vnr.com/cul.html  The Diner's Grapevine http://www.dinersgrapevine.com  The Electronic Gourmet Guide http://www.2way.com/food  Food of the World http://www.w2.com/docs2/act/worldfood.html  The Internet Epicurean http://www.epicurious.com  Lamalle Kitchenware http://www.2way.com.food.egg  Starchefs http://www.starchefs.com  Virtual Vineyards http://www.virtualvin.com Correction  An article in The Living Section last Wednesday about food-related points of interest in cyberspace, with a listing of Internet addresses, referred incorrectly to Conde Nast's food site on the World Wide Web. It is Epicurious, at this address:
http://www.epicurious.com -- not the Internet Epicurean, at http://rampages.onramp.net/ ricsmith/epicure.html, which is an electronic magazine.
