title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Ziff-Davis In Deal With Web Provider
body: Hoping that their respective brand names will give each other a lift, the Ziff-Davis Publishing Company, a leading publisher of computer magazines, and the Yahoo Corporation, which operates one of the most popular directories on the Internet's World Wide Web, are expected to announce a partnership today, according to executives familiar with the deal. The agreement is said to call for Internet Life, a fledgling Ziff-Davis quarterly introduced in October, to be renamed Yahoo! Internet Life. In addition, the partners will apparently set up a site on the Web called ZD/Yahoo! Computing, which will be a guide to Web sites dealing with computer hardware, software and related topics. Ziff-Davis would be the exclusive agent for selling the computer-related advertising that appeared in the magazine as well as on Yahoo! and the ZD/Yahoo! site. Both Ziff-Davis and Yahoo declined to comment on the agreement, but a Yahoo executive who spoke on condition of anonymity said yesterday that the fast-growing company, based in Mountain View, Calif., hoped to use the alliance to distinguish itself from several other services that direct Web browsers to the thousands of sites available on the network. "Having our name on the newsstand has tremendous value for us," the executive said. "We have tremendous name recognition on line, but we need to get into the off-line channels, as well." Ziff-Davis Publishing, based in newyork, would also help Yahoo expand internationally, he said. Ziff-Davis presumably believes that the Yahoo name will help Internet Life rise to the top of the many new titles devoted to the World Wide Web, which is expanding rapidly. The two companies plan a joint news conference in newyork today. "This sounds like a good bit of branding, and that is what this business needs a lot more of," said Gary Arlen, an industry consultant. Since incorporating in April, Yahoo, which was founded by two 27-year-old Stanford University graduate students, has become one of the Internet's signature T-shirts-to-riches stories. The site has more than 800,000 visitors a day and has taken in more than $1 million since accepting its first advertisement in August. (Its Internet address is http://www.yahoo.com.) Last month, the company sold 12 percent of itself to five outside investors, including the Softbank Corporation, which recently agreed to buy Ziff-Davis Publishing for $2.1 billion. Ziff-Davis was also an investor. Together, the two stakes amount to about 5 percent of the company, which Softbank said cost $2 million, giving Yahoo a total value -- to these early investors, at least -- of about $40 million. Ziff-Davis Publishing dominates the market for computer magazines with PC Magazine, PC Week and other titles. The newly christened Yahoo! Internet Life will appear in print, on CD-ROM and as a site on the Web. The print version will appear on newsstands in February with a projected circulation of 100,000, according to people familiar with the companies' plans.

title: Microsoft Quietly Puts Together Computer Research Laboratory
body: Bill Gates may have been out on a book tour lately hawking his vision of everyone else's information-highway future in "The Road Ahead." But back at headquarters he has quietly assembled some of the industry's best and brightest computer researchers to help choose the paths that Microsoft itself should follow. They are seasoned travelers all, including Butler Lampson, the computer scientist who helped design the first personal computer, the Xerox Alto, in 1973 and the first office computer network technology, Ethernet, in 1976; C. Gordon Bell, the former Digital Equipment Corporation researcher who in the late 1970's led the development of what would become the world's most successful minicomputer, and Jim Gray, a pioneer developer of modern computer data bases. Others recently brought aboard are Jim Blinn, Andrew Glassner and Alvy Ray Smith, three of the most respected talents in the world of computer graphics research. Mr. Blinn came from the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory and Mr. Glassner from the Xerox Palo Alto Research Center; Mr. Smith is a founder of Pixar, the company responsible for the current hit animated movie "Toy Story." These hall of famers have been assembled over the last 12 months to bolster the activities of Microsoft Research, the software publishing giant's fledging research laboratory. The lab is part of Mr. Gates's concerted effort to make his company an innovator in computing's next generation. With the Internet rapidly shifting the industry's focus from desktop to network, prior success is no guarantee of future results. And as the world's dominant software company, Microsoft does not want to find itself stumbling the way the International Business Machines Corporation did during the industry's last big shift, when it relied too long on dominance in mainframe computing. But Mr. Gates's creation of this particular brain trust has raised questions from the outside about Microsoft's road ahead. By asking the people who invented previous generations of technology to lead the company into the future, is Microsoft looking down the information highway through the rear-view mirror? "The computer industry is preparing for the new life forms to emerge," said John Gage, director of the science office at Sun Microsystems, which is promoting its Java software language as an Internet technology that would make Microsoft's dominance of the desktop PC world largely irrelevant. "Is Microsoft going down a pathway that refines jellyfish when its time to leap to vertebrates?" "Not our guys," insisted Nathan Myhrvold, Microsoft's vice president of research and the executive who created the research laboratory four years ago. He notes that Microsoft has long been one of the most aggressive recruiters of new talent coming out of the nation's graduate and undergraduate computer science and electrical engineering programs -- young minds fertile with new ideas and insights. The goal in Microsoft's recruitment of wily veterans is to find people with proven experience in turning good ideas into products. "If you want to invent the future, the way to get the most positive odds is to get the smartest group of people you possibly can and make sure they're not mired in the past," Mr. Myhrvold said. "If you were going to find guys who won't get trapped in old paradigms, this is the group." One who knows he cannot afford to look backward is Mr. Blinn, who recently came to Microsoft after an 18-year career at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the California Institute of Technology, where he was acclaimed for having created some of the industry's most stunning computer graphics simulations. Mr. Blinn is part of a Microsoft team of researchers exploring new types of graphics technology for PC's that would bring greater 3-D realism. "The problems that are worth solving today," Mr. Blinn said, "are different from the ones that were worth solving 20 years ago." Microsoft's effort to beef up research comes at a crucial time for the world's most powerful software company, which succeeded largely by refining and marketing effectively technologies invented elsewhere. That was true of the original MS-DOS operating system for the first I.B.M. PC in 1981. Microsoft's Windows operating system was derived from technology pioneered by Xerox and Apple Computer. Now, as Mr. Gates himself declared in a speech last week, his company and the industry have entered "a second PC revolution -- the Internet." And if Microsoft has any chance of doing as well in this war as it did in the last, he knows he needs a first-class weapons lab. The research group itself has about 100 scientists and an annual budget of about $20 million for the main laboratory in Redmond and a smaller one in San Francisco. Besides graphics, the projects include natural language processing, speech recognition and vision systems. Other high-technology companies, like I.B.M. and Xerox, have traditionally had difficulty translating research results into products because of the cultural gulf between basic science and product development and marketing. But Microsoft's researchers recognize no such gap. "We've been successful in creating an atmosphere where there is a closeness between development and research," said Richard Rashid, Microsoft's director of research, who himself was a leading computer science researcher at Carnegie-Mellon University before coming to Microsoft four years ago. "These things have a very delicate chemistry." Its research emphasis on technology with near-term commercial applications has led some of Microsoft's competitors to suggest that in fact, Microsoft's Research Laboratory is too focused on its own advanced-product development. "This is product development," said Bob Taylor, a director of a Digital Equipment research laboratory based in Palo Alto, Calif. "How many computer science conferences are they at and how many papers do they publish?" And yet, other computer researchers are optimistic that the recent arrivals represent a turning point for the software community's most powerful citizen. "Unlike Apple and I.B.M., for example, Microsoft has taken but not given back much to computer science," said Nicholas Negroponte, the director of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Media Laboratory. "But these new people will change that." Jim Kajiya, another computer graphics researcher and former professor at the California Institute of Technology, said he decided to come to Microsoft after realizing he needed to shake up his stagnant academic career. Mr. Kajiya, who leads the graphics research team, said the company hoped to develop interactive 3-D computer graphics with the realism displayed in the movie "Toy Story." "I think you'll be very impressed with our three-dimensional graphics work," the pony-tailed researcher told a recent visitor. "But I've been instructed from the highest levels of the company that I can't show it to you yet." title: Secure Digital Transactions Just Got a Little Less Secure
body: The discovery of a vulnerability has shaken the computer security world's faith in the safe use of the data-security technologies on which most current and planned electronic banking, shopping and "digital cash" systems are based. The vulnerability has been found in a class of technologies known as public-key encryption -- designed to protect electronic transactions by scrambling data so they can be read only by people with the proper mathematical keys to the code. The flaw was identified by Paul C. Kocher, a 22-year-old researcher, who demonstrated in a paper a way that an electronic eavesdropper who is able to monitor the repeated process of unscrambling incoming messages could figure out the private key. It can be done, he says, by keeping track of the length of time, down to the microsecond, it takes to unscramble each message. The feat would be analogous to a burglar surreptitiously observing people in an office building as they punched in the security code of a door with a push-button combination lock. Even if the burglar could not see which buttons were being pushed, if he observed thousands of entries and timed each with a stopwatch, he might eventually be able to winnow down the possible number of combinations that could be entered within that precise time span. In theory, the burglar could then work through this list of possible combinations until he found the one that opened the door. Mr. Kocher's paper describes a type of attack -- not yet seen outside the lab -- in which a criminal using a PC could figure out the mathematical keys in minutes. Doing so might enable a network snooper to steal a consumer's computer banking deposit, siphon off a credit card number, read personal medical records or otherwise pilfer private data supposedly protected by the security technology. "If you're using an on-line system that is not explicitly guarding against this attack, you're going to be vulnerable," said Matt Blaze, a scientist at AT&T's Bell Laboratories who has studied Mr. Kocher's paper. Mr. Blaze is a well-known researcher in the field of codes and code breaking. Public-key encryption had been assumed to be so difficult to crack that only the brute force of a supercomputer could do it, and even then only if months -- or even years -- were devoted to the task. So highly has the Federal Government respected the technology's shielding power that its export is tightly controlled, for fear that the coding technique would enable foreign enemies and terrorists to conspire with impunity via computer. The newly discovered vulnerability does not affect various forms of private encryption technology between individuals or institutions communicating only with parties known to them, like the encrypted electronic funds transfers that banks perform with one another over secure computer networks. Rather, it is the electronic systems for use by members of the public that are the focus of the research paper, written by Mr. Kocher (pronounced KOTCH-er), who recently graduated from Stanford University with a degree in biology. Mr. Kocher's evidence suggests that while the basic coding technology in public-key systems still appears to be secure, those who install or use it without recognizing the newly disclosed, remarkably subtle vulnerability will put themselves or their customers at risk. Experts who have read the paper disagree over the likelihood of anyone's successfully mounting the type of attack Mr. Kocher describes. Nevertheless, his discovery of a chink in the best armor yet devised for digital commerce has presented scientists with the most sobering evidence so far that perfect security may be no more possible to achieve in the electronic realm than in the physical world of bank robberies and muggings at A.T.M. machines. "Kocher's paper is extremely important, and it will have enormous practical impact," Mr. Blaze said. "Everyone who is building systems in this category will have to re-evaluate their vulnerability." Everyone, in this case, is a broad group that includes anyone using, or planning to use, public-key encryption -- a technology designed to allow secure, private electronic interactions between and among members of the public. That includes most on-line shopping and consumer banking systems now in use or announced, as well as smart-card systems, like one planned by the unitedstates Postal Service, in which a digitally encoded credit-card-size device would hold electronic cash. It also includes various forms of "digital signature" systems, like one developed for civilian use within the Federal Government, intended to let recipients check the authenticity of documents sent over computer networks. "Many of the security systems that I am examining are good enough to keep out casual snoopers," said Mr. Kocher, who has worked as a security consultant for a broad range of influential software companies, including Microsoft, Netscape Communications and RSA Data Security, a provider of commercial public-key encryption software. "But they're failing catastrophically when it comes to protecting data against determined attacks." James Bidzos, chief executive of RSA Data, said he considered the danger cited by Mr. Kocher as more theoretical than real, but added: "We've never claimed that all this stuff is totally secure; the question is how much does it cost to attack it. It's important to remember that people can't become complacent." In public-key systems, the sender of an electronic communication uses software that automatically scrambles the information by encoding it through use of a publicly known numerical key. Decoding the scrambled transmission requires a private key, a number supposedly known only by the merchant's computer. Without this key, no outsider can unscramble the incoming messages. Breaking a public-key encryption code is not easy to do, Mr. Kocher acknowledges, and would require sophisticated knowledge by the criminal of how fast the software algorithms, or mathematical formulas, are calculated by a particular computer. Yet it can be done, he has concluded, and many experts say he is right. "Once you read his paper, you say, 'Oh yes, this is obvious,' " said Bruce Schneier, author of "Applied Cryptography," a textbook in the field. Security experts say the vulnerability can be corrected. One solution might be padding the elapsed time of the unscrambling process with random steps to make it difficult to determine how much time the real computation actually requires. But for systems already in operation, taking the precaution would require revisions whose cost and effort may be difficult to predict. "Among the people I'm working with about this," Mr. Kocher said, "there are lot of people who are panicking -- particularly for systems that cannot be changed easily." For future installations, designing safeguards against the vulnerability would be relatively easy, Ronald Rivest said. Mr. Rivest is one of the creators of RSA, a widely used standard for public-key cryptography, which he developed along with two other computer scientists, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adelman (the name RSA is based on the initial letters of their three surnames). He played down the impact of Mr. Kocher's findings. "This is an interesting kind of attack," Mr. Rivest said. "But it's not easy to mount." But any vulnerability undermines the security of an encryption system once it becomes known, cautioned Martin Hellman, a researcher at Stanford University and one of the developers of the first public-key encryption system in 1976. "In probably 99 percent of the cases this won't be a threat," Mr. Hellman said. "But if we don't protect against these rare cases, then the whole field of computer security will get a bad name." Netscape Communications, whose future depends on the public's faith in the security of on-line transactions, is so intent on ferreting out flaws that it recently offered to pay a $1,000 bounty to anyone finding a new security problem. On Friday evening, Netscape announced its first list of bounty winners, which included Mr. Kocher. The company has already modified a security component of its technology, known as the Secure Sockets Layer, to prevent the type of attack that Mr. Kocher first demonstrated at a university seminar on Nov. 29. title:
Taking In the Sites;
Celebrating Christmas With Latest Cybercards
body: For those who see cyberspace as the cold-blooded antithesis of a homey family Christmas, the idea of sending holiday cards through the Internet would surely be sacrilege. But for those who spend their lives at a keyboard and hate the tedious process of scrawling out dozens of cards, the Web offers some help this year. Several sites will let you design and send a card to your closest wired friends. So while you still may have to find a suitably sappy card for Aunt Gwen, at least the pain will be reduced. Probably the best starting point is the well-organized and amazingly thorough site called Holly & Sara's Christmas Page, which has useful links to dozens of sites, including several that do virtual greetings. The site was created by Melanie McCluskey, a housewife in Calgary, Alberta, and named for her two daughters. If a site could give off a holiday glow, this one would. The site itself is worth browsing, with links to shopping tips for virtual Christmas trees. For those cybergrumps, there is a link to the Grinch site that is full of drawings and the theme song from the Dr. Seuss classic. Ms. McCluskey, who has been inundated with requests from people to be linked to her site, said Christmas greetings in cyberspace are fine for people who like the wired world, though she sees why people would prefer real cards. "I would rather receive a card in themail," she said. "It's something you can display on the mantelpiece." One of the best card sites, which works consistently and easily, is from Thomas Cook, the travel service, where you can pick from an odd selection of eight images touting the joy of winter sports and greetings in several languages. After posting the card, Thomas Cook, a unit of the American Express Company, will alert your recipient and give him instructions to view the card. Most card services work this way, though sometimes the instructions are hard to follow. Another tourist company offering a site, this one with an environmental twist, is Asia Travel, which gives you a choice of 33 images and several greetings. The company says sending electronic cards will save trees, though it also seems interested in hyping some of its own travel destinations. The site seems to have worked out its recent technical problems. The most elaborate, if the most commercial, electronic greeting card site is part of Stoli Central, the Web site of Stolichnaya Vodka. Stoli makes up for some of the commercialism by giving donations to Literacy Volunteers of America for each card sent. The drawback is that the pre-fab cards are virtual advertisements for their vodka, though if you choose to build your own card with images and phrases they offer, including some in Russian, it can be nearly vodka free. The Stoli site is especially good for the chronically lazy and profoundly anti-Christmas crowd because you simply make one card and send all of your friends and family the password to view it. Of course people who still value the personal touch may think you have lost all humanity. And while it is easy enough to send the card, my brother, who was one of my recipients, could not get in to view it. Frustrating your nearest and dearest is definitely not in the holiday spirit. title:
TECHNOLOGY: CONNECTIONS;
Between the dream and the reality lies the shadow. Or is it the interface?
body: ONE of the eerie aspects of Bill Gates's new book, "The Road Ahead," in which the founder of Microsoft maps out a path toward technological redemption, is that the hopes in it seem so familiar. The book can often seem an old-fashioned print version of those high-tech rides that were such big successes at the newyork World's Fairs in 1939 and 1964. Hop on to see the homes, schools and businesses of the future. Those rides showed glimpses of moving sidewalks and staircases, self-steering electric automobiles, a city pulsing with personalized attention. Now, the veering cart driven by Mr. Gates -- hands inside, please -- rushes us by wallet-sized computers; houses like his own interactive manse-to-be -- the ultimate cocoon -- and schools where technological classrooms will massage each student's brain. Someday, Mr. Gates suggests, without even a hint of irony, we may even plug our central nervous systems into the Internet, the way the cyber-cowboys did in William Gibson's "Neuromancer." But this utopianism is based not on great promises of labor-saving devices or new mechanical inventions like those celebrated in the ride to Tomorrow, but on faster processing and better packaging of information, on the creation of "interfaces," a word used with abandon in Mr. Gates's book. Mr. Gates has made a good part of his fortune by creating computer interfaces, and today in pre-Gatesian utopia, the appeal of most software like Netscape's Navigator or Windows 95 is that it offers a new interface, a way to interact with that amorphous, ungenerous and untamed world that lies behind the computer screen. The interface is not, of course, a new idea. It is, technically, a surface forming a boundary between two bodies or spaces; it is the membrane that divides one world from another. In a pre-electronic, mechanical marketplace, the interface is what makes a machine usable by a human; it is primarily a matter of design. Human interaction with all kinds of objects requires the construction of interfaces -- from toilet seats to automobile dashboards -- contouring the object to suit our bodies and minds. But technology has transformed the meaning of the interface. It is no longer just the surface of cyber-objects, but their substance; it is not a practicality, but a necessity. The Internet, for example, is just a morass of data, dribbling out of servers around the world. It is unfathomably chaotic, mixing items of great value with cyber-trash, combining proposed bills regarding the fate of the National Endowment for the Arts with proliferating vanity pages from college students. The Web and the Internet would be completely useless without a grid; it would be like a city without any streets or transportation system. What the Internet requires is a way in which humans can give shape to that world and be shaped by it. That is why a Web browser like Netscape has so caught the imagination of investors. A browser cuts a path through the tangled growth and even creates a form of memory, so each path can be retraced. Such an interface actually constructs the substance: it makes the Web possible. In the country of the Internet, the browser provides both the streets and the car to navigate them. In fact, one of the smarter moves Microsoft has made in integrating the Internet into Windows 95 and its own Network is to blur boundaries between its software, its network, its browser and the Web itself. The Microsoft Network home page, for example, can lead one to Microsoft's own Internet page about the home (http://www.beta.home.msn.com/ access/home.htm), which brings together various sites on the Web, dealing with plant advice (from the Virtual Garden of the Time-Life Electronic Encyclopedia; http:// www.pathfinder.com), information on health (from the University of Iowa's Virtual Hospital;http://vh.radiology.uiowa.edu), or a compendium of college statistics (from the Princeton Review; http://www.review.com/index/html). Roads between these places are constructed and transportation provided; paths can lead from a photograph of the damage done by the Eastern tent caterpillar on flowering plum trees to the complete text of "John Barleycorn" by Jack London. And so the interface creates a new kind of malleable substance that seems to have little to do with the dark dystopias of technology that gave us tales like "Frankenstein" and "Brave New World." We have instead a rosy World's Fair vision, without threats or ambiguities. But the shadows can be found with a little searching. Ordinary machines like clocks, toasters, automobiles, are, after all, far more comprehensible than their cyber counterparts. For all their complexity, one part physically moves another; it is possible to open a watch or a steam engine and see how it works. We see causes and effects; actions have reactions; gravity works. This is a Newtonian universe. The brave new world of the interface is not. Open a computer and nothing moves at all (aside from a quaint fan). On a circuit board, there is no clear connection between an object's function and its appearance. There are no clear laws of cause or effect. Hardware provides the paths that information will take, but no substance. The interface is all. Who is not a bit anxious when faced with such strangeness? Even Mr. Gates admits that he will use ordinary mechanical light switches as backups to the computer operated sensors in his new house. Why then does he, or anybody else, think that the advances in interfaces and technology will lead us to a transformation of every aspect of life and bring on everything short of world peace? The World's Fair eventually comes to an end, and we are left to wrestle with the fractured connections that promise so much more than they can yet achieve. Graphic   Drawing.

title:
They Volunteered to Pull the Plug, But Will They Ever Do It Again?;
A Working Day Without 4 Computers
body: WHEN John Woram, a Rockville Centre author, discovered the Internet 10 years ago, it turned his working life upside down. Graduating from an electric typewriter, he has been surfing regularly, relentlessly, sometimes endlessly, for everything from shopping to checking up on his Web page to conducting serious on-line research. At the request of The newyork Times, Mr. Woramagreed to endure 24 hours without his computers. His inconveniences ran the gamut from the trivial to those he felt threatened his career. "I was surprised to find out how hard it was," he said when the ordeal was over. "I guess I'm really hooked on the technology." Mr. Woram, who bought his first computer in the late 1970's and whose seven books include "The PC Configuration Handbook," works out of a home office. One wall is lined with books and another has four computers of varying sizes, including one laptop. Normally, a haunting, flute-like sound pervades the room, signaling the arrival of new email. During his period of deprivation, the sound resonated over and over, but Mr. Woram did not reply. Without the computer, his productivity came to a standstill. He tried to write on his old IBM Selectric but since he could not find the typewriter, he made handwritten comments for later investigation. "I read a lot and scribbled little notes to myself," he said. "The only problem is that my handwriting is impossible to read." One frustrating part of the day was email withdrawal. Mr. Woram's latest book project is on the history of the Galapagos Islands, and he normally sends several queries a day to a guide in the archipelago off the coast of Ecuador. "I didn't bother to write a snail-mail letter to the Galapagos Islands that day," he said. "My contact works in an underfunded, understaffed tropical location without air-conditioning. For him to write back, he'd have to find a typewriter that works and paper and a stamp. It's just a heroic project to exchange a couple of letters, and by the time I'd get a response, I'd probably forget what I asked ." Rather than attempt the impossible, Mr. Woram waited until he was on-line again. In the meantime, he busied himself with other tasks. He went to work on a fountain that he had installed in his backyard. "It needs a little tweaking from time to time," he said, "so I worked on the valves." He also had time to clean out some cobweb-filled corners of his garage and to re-organize his office. Each of Mr. Woram's computers is progressively faster and serves a different purpose. "The problem with this computer stuff is that it works differently on different systems," said Mr. Woram, who runs different programs on different computers and later writes about them. His oldest computer, a Dell Omniplex, was purchased in 1994. It is set up with Windows 95 to see how that program runs on an older machine. In 1997, Mr. Woram bought a Dell Dimension, which he uses as his main machine. In 1998, he bought what he refers to as his "lapdog," a Dell Latitude CP, a laptop. Because it is portable, Mr. Woram uses it to demonstrate at the Long Island PC User Group class he teaches. "Since it's a fully functioning computer on its own, I often keep it running when I'm home." The latest computer, another Dell Dimension, was purchased a few months ago. It is faster than the older models, and is used to test Windows 2000. Each computer cost approximately $3,500. The greatest inconvenience on the computer-free day occurred when Mr. Woram had to drive his daughter to Kennedy International Airport. Although he had the option of making a phone call to the airline for the arrival and departure schedule, he declined. "I figured that if I called the 800 number, I'd have to play telephone tag and hit this button and that button to get what I wanted to know. You have to go through an endless routine, and it would've been so much easier to go directly to the Web site." So Mr. Woram took his daughter to the airport and promptly drove home. Shortly afterward, his daughter phoned to say that her flight had been canceled. Toward the end of the day, the author was looking forward to the end of his self-imposed computer blackout. "It was so frustrating," he said. "It was like that annoying feeling you experience on a holiday because you don't havemail service and you're waiting for a check." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Once upon a time, John Woram, a writer, used a typewriter. Now he is under the spell of the Internet. (Nancy Siesel/The newyork Times)

title: 2 Providers Of Net Access Set to Merge
body: Earthlink Network Inc. and Mindspring Enterprises Inc., two pioneers in the business of selling Internet access, announced a merger agreement yesterday, with hopes of more effectively challenging America Online. The merger, a $1.7 billion stock swap, creates a company with 2.8 million subscribers. It will be named Earthlink but will operate out of Atlanta, Mindspring's home. Earthlink is now based in Pasadena, Calif. The combined entity would leapfrog Internet services from AT&T and Microsoft to become the clear but distant second-place service provider in the unitedstates behind America Online, which has 18 million subscribers. "We're able to aspire to something that is more exciting than we could in the past," said Charles Brewer, who started Mindspring out of his apartment in 1994 and saw it grow into one of the top five Internet service providers in the country. "Our goal is to be No. 1 in the world," added Mr. Brewer, who will become chairman of the new company. The merger of two companies that symbolized success for the small Internet service provider underscores what some industry observers see as inevitable consolidation in the Internet access market. Yet, the number of small Internet service providers continues to grow, now standing at more than 5,000 in the unitedstates and Canada, and entrepreneurs are pursuing alternatives to the subscription-fee business model. Netzero, for example, is a growing advertising-based service that is free to consumers. The industry is also being changed by high-speed, or broadband, access with digital subscriber lines and cable modems. Such access threatens the dominance of the traditional dial-up service provider, while Earthlink, Mindspring and America Online are forming partnerships to offer these broadband technologies. But the real competition among service providers today is to add subscribers, and Earthlink and Mindspring insisted that their merger would allow them to do that more efficiently. The companies said they planned to merge back-office operations and to redirect some of the savings to marketing. "We're both spending a tremendous amount toward accelerated growth," said Charles Betty, EarthLink's president and chief executive who will be chief executive of the combined company. "We stepped back and said 'Wow, we should be doing this together.' " Earthlink projected adding 230,000 subscribers in the third quarter, while Mindspring will add roughly 80,000 new subscribers. As of March, each company had 1.1 million subscribers, according to Jupiter Communications, a newyork-based market research firm. For the second quarter, Mindspring reported revenue of $86 million and operating losses of $12.7 million, while Earthlink reported revenue of $78 million and operating losses of $28.5 million. The new company will trade under the Earthlink stock symbol, ELNK, on Nasdaq. Mindspring shareholders will receive one share of the new company for each share they hold, while Earthlink shareholders will receive 1.615 shares. Mr. Betty said the company would have a combined $500 million in cash to seed the marketing effort. He said the deal should be completed by the first quarter of 2000. Earthlink shares fell $1.125, to $42.375, on the Nasdaq stock market. Mindspring shares dropped $5.50, to $27.375.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Sets Shifts in Internet Strategy
body: The Microsoft Corporation disclosed several pieces of its new Internet strategy today, saying that it would offer the public a piece of its most successful on-line effort, the Expedia travel site; would significantly redesign its MSN portal, and would introduce a network computing device. Anticipating a world in which software will be sold as a service instead of a packaged good, the company said it would re-introduce MSN, shifting its focus to on-line communications, improved information searching and electronic commerce. The company also demonstrated its new low-priced network computer, the MSN Web Companion, which will deliver the MSN service beginning in mid-2000. The company said the device was part of an evolving business strategy -- going beyond its stranglehold on the PC industry to develop new ways to connect consumers to the Internet. The company called the new approach its "everyday Web" strategy and, in a complete turnabout, said it no longer had a dogmatic commitment to the PC platform. "The vision of the company is about software as a service," said Richard Belluzzo, group vice president for consumer and commerce business. "This fundamentally changes business models." As part of its new approach to the Internet, Microsoft said it planned to sell part of Expedia in an initial public stock offering. Expedia will become a separate company but will be majority owned by Microsoft. The company's stock plunged $4.875, more than 5 percent, to $91.188 as the briefing unfolded today -- not because of Microsoft's announcements but because its president, Steven A. Ballmer, told a gathering of business journalists that he believed technology stocks were overvalued. Later in the day, speaking at a company conference to outline Microsoft's Internet strategy, Mr. Ballmer sketched what he called a "Web services platform," built around "megaservices" like specialized messaging and email for use in building high-level electronic businesses it calls marketplaces. The company also demonstrated a new portal oriented to small-business and called Bcentral. Underlying many of the announcements was a deepening Microsoft reliance on the advanced Internet standard known as XML, a set of rules, or a protocol, that enables Web browsers to exploit the same information stored in data bases for a variety of commercial transactions and information gathering. Several analysts said that Microsoft would use XML to compete with Sun's Java language in many arenas on the Internet. Microsoft dispelled rumors that it would begin offering free access to the Internet. In fact, it said it planned to raise the price of its MSN access service by $2, to $21.95, and to add features while aggressively expanding its PC-bundling marketing efforts. The company deferred announcing pricing for its Microsoft Office suite of productivity software, saying that changes in its MSN strategy announced today would ultimately percolate through the entire company. One executive, Jon Devaan, said that America Online, while it leads MSN by a wide margin, is vulnerable. "Our research shows that as many as 50 percent of AOL members are extremely dissatisfied and would switch to another provider with better and more reliable service," he said. In an effort to make it easy for consumers to switch to MSN, the company has reduced the number of steps it takes to subscribe to MSN to six, less than a third of the steps it takes to subscribe to America Online's Compuserve subsidiary, Mr. Devaan said. The MSN Web Companion device "will raise a couple of eyebrows around the industry coming from the company that has been thought of as the PC company," admitted Yusuf Mehdi, director of marketing for the Microsoft consumer and commerce group. The company said that the MSN Web Companion would be based on the Windows CE operating system and would be tested later this year. It will be made by several manufacturers and will be discounted heavily as part of a subscription to MSN.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: NET SITES CO-OPTED BY PORNOGRAPHERS
body: The president of a company that produces a popular Internet game site for teen-agers was horrified last May when, trying to call up his site, he got instead a screenful of lurid sex scenes. Worse yet, he could not escape. Every time he tried to move on, he got more pornographic scenes. It turns out that his Web site was not the only one victimized. Some computer users searching for the Harvard Law Review, or trying to find sites about "Oklahoma tornadoes" or "news about Kosovo" or "child car seats," had the same experience. They were held captive by pornographic sites from which they could not figure out how to escape without turning off their computers. As many as 25 million Web pages, more than 2 percent of the World Wide Web, may have been affected by the Internet fraud, which investigators said was devised by an elusive Portuguese hacker and an Australian pornography company. American and Australian investigators described the fraud at a news conference here today and said that they had raided the offices of the pornography company on the east coast of Australia and had obtained an American court order to stop it. "These operators hijacked Web sites, kidnapped consumers and held them captive," said Jodie Bernstein, director of the Federal Trade Commission's Bureau of Consumer Protection. "They exposed surfers, including children, to the seamiest sort of material and incapacitated their computers so they couldn't escape." The scheme involved the cloning of legitimate Web pages, including such sites as Audi, Paine Webber and the Japanese Friendship Gardens. When computer users tried to reach those sites using the Alta Vista search engine, which indexes the Web, they were, in the new cyberspace parlance of investigators, "page-jacked" to a tawdry site run by the Australian company, known to its customers as Taboosisters.com, Kewl Images, Taboohardcore.com or Tabooanimals.com. When computer users tried to escape those sites by clicking on their browser's "back" or "home" buttons, they were instead directed to other pornography sites, or "mouse-trapped," investigators said. Investigators said the Portuguese hacker, Carlos Pereira, who cannot be found, and the Australian company pulled off the scheme by copying not only Web pages but also their so-called metatags. The tags, invisible to viewers, provide key words and code that are used to index the site for search engines. The defendants stood to make money from the scheme in three ways, the investigators said. They sold advertising on the Web sites, almost exclusively from pornography companies, based on the amount of traffic, and also offered viewers the chance to see more Web sites by paying for them. The Australian company also used the scheme to inflate the value of domain names, or Web addresses, by increasing the viewership of those addresses through the page-jacking and mouse-trapping. The company then tried to auction those domain names on an Internet site at hundreds of times their original cost. At the news conference at the Federal Trade Commission today, Australian investigators who spoke through an Internet video link from Canberra said they still did not know how much money had been made from the scheme. The Australian officials said they were considering civil or criminal charges against the company and had raided eight places, confiscating a variety of computers, routers and servers integral to the scheme. At the same time, a Federal judge in Virginia ordered many of the sites run by the company and the Portuguese hacker off the Web and directed them to stop copying legitimate Web pages. The contract for registering Internet names provides that disputes be handled in Virginia. American officials declined to give all the details of the episode, saying they feared copycats. Even though the suspects are all foreign individuals and companies, the officials said the unitedstates Government became involved in the case because many victims were Americans and American companies. The officials acted under the Federal Trade Commission Act, which prohibits unfair or deceptive practices affecting commerce. The content of the pornographic sites was not a legal issue. The authorities said the scheme was a relatively new kind of operation that did not involve traditional hacking, or the defacement of a Web page. Rather, it involved the improper diversion of consumers away from Web pages they were seeking. The inquiry began after Angel Munoz, the president of NewWorld.com, a popular Internet game site for teen-agers, was preparing for a meeting of his board last May to consider a sale of some of his company for more than $20 million. When Mr. Munoz tried to see how accessible one of the company's sites was by using the Alta Vista search engine, he was taken to a hard-core pornography site. When he tried to get out of the page by clicking the back and home buttons on his browser, more pornography sites appeared. "I was shocked," Mr. Munoz recalled in an interview today. One of Mr. Munoz's company lawyers complained to the Federal Bureau of Investigation in Dallas, which said it could do nothing about the case. But after the cable channel MSNBC reported the incident, the trade commission decided to start its own investigation. Trade commission officials said the Australian company took the pornographic sites down in June, but later in the summer put them back up. Investigators said that when they were up, Alta Vista received about 20 to 30 complaints each week. The complaints came from diverse quarters. They included students on the Harvard Law Review, mothers who had children on their laps when they were page-jacked, and one man who said he had nearly lost his job when his boss noticed he had lurid images on his computer screen. Executives at Alta Vista said in an interview today that pornography companies had repeatedly tried to trick computer users and that the company had taken steps to correct the problem by carefully monitoring their index and by offering filters that can be used to screen out objectionable sites. "We support wholeheartedly what the F.T.C. is doing in this area," said David Emanuel, a spokesman for Alta Vista. But Mr. Munoz said today that when he contacted Alta Vista, "They were not particularly helpful." Investigators say Mr. Pereira is well known in the small community of hackers and operated a site called Piratelynx.com. One official said today that Mr. Pereira had boasted of his ability to "control Alta Vista." But executives at Alta Vista said today that they had never heard of him. His whereabouts are unknown, although the Federal judge in Virginia, recognizing that he was all but certain to maintain a presence on the Internet, issued an unusual order that permitted the Government to serve him a summons by email. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Licensing Issue Stirs Up A Debate Over Using GIF's
body: Web developers, faced with the prospect of paying $5,000 for using an image-file format that has become a building block of the Web, are taking their anger public. The tiff is over GIF's. Most people who create Web pages are familiar with GIF's -- the slang term for digital images that carry the ".gif" extension and have been compressed using the Graphics Interchange Format. But most people are probably not aware that the programming code behind the GIF format is patented and belongs to Unisys, the computer company based in Blue Bell, Pa. In late July, Unisys quietly posted the new policy on its Web site. It requires any Web developers using GIF who do not have a GIF license to get one for $5,000. Several well-known imaging products, like Corel Draw or Adobe Photoshop, already come with Unisys licenses. But that is not the case for the vast majority of imaging software that can be downloaded free. Even people who simply use GIF's by copying images from other Web sites could be liable under the policy unless they can prove that the images were originally created using licensed software. In late August, several developers caught wind of the policy, and angry messages streamed into Unisys and into techie-oriented Web sites like Slashdot.org and Linuxworld. To many Internet denizens, the concept of patenting pieces of computer code is equivalent to patenting mathematical equations. They believe that such codes should be freely available. Oliver Picher, a spokesman for Unisys, said the company had no plans to go after people who have simply copied images and pasted them into their sites (although, he noted, copyright holders might have their own problem with that.) "We are not actually going out and tracking people down," Mr. Picher said. But he added that if developers created a popular Web site "with valuation in the billions, they might expect a phone call from us."   LISA GUERNSEY http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Need to Start the Wash? It's Just a Phone Call Away
body: A certain long-distance communications company lets you "reach out and touch someone," but the World Wireless Communications company is promising to let you reach out and control parts of your house through the World Wide Web. "The garage door on your home could be controlled by the browser on your desk at work," said Donald I. Wallace, the president of X-tra Web (www.x-traweb.com), the division of the company introducing the technology. The X-tra Web system works by attaching a tiny microcontroller called an X-Node to an appliance or machine. The X-Node then transmits data to an X-Gate, an Internet gateway, that then can be monitored from the Internet with a standard Web browser. "The X-Node itself has a little Web page in it, so we're actually giving the washing machine or the garage door its own little mini-Web page," Mr. Wallace explained. "It has its own I.P. address, just the same as any other Web page does. So all you have to do is open your browser, type in the I.P. address of your garage door and you would get back the status of the garage door." The system is designed to allow control or observation of things like automated teller machines, home appliances, office equipment, medical monitors and security systems over the Web. The X-tra Web technology is already being tested or used by a number of businesses, including a vending-machine company, a fast-food franchise and an engineering firm, but the company also has an eye on the consumer market. The devices are inexpensive, about $25 per X-Node and $150 for the gateway, and the company expects to see Web-enabled homes by early next year. And hey, it may just get the kids interested in housework -- just make sure little Tommy doesn't crash the dryer.   J. D. BIERSDORFER http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: Realnetworks, Realjukebox and Finally, It Seems, Real Money
body: Realjukebox is starting to earn some real money for its developer, Realnetworks Inc. Realnetworks, a Seattle company that makes software for sending audio and video over the Internet, will announce a series of alliances on Thursday with companies that will sell products or provide information to users of Realjukebox, a software product that allows people to copy, store and play music from compact disks on their personal computers. Checkout.com, the new Internet entertainment Web site co-founded by the Hollywood talent manager Michael Ovitz, will become the exclusive on-line vendor of compact disks and provider of entertainment information for users of Realjukebox. Another company, 800.com, will be the exclusive seller of electronic products, while MP3.com will provide music that users of Realjukebox can download free. Terms of the deals are not being disclosed. But industry executives said that Checkout.com would pay Realnetworks at least $8 million; the two other deals are somewhat smaller. Together the deals would represent a nice lift for Realnetworks, which had revenue in its latest quarter of $28 million and a net loss of $270,000. "Realnetworks is getting to a new level of scale in terms of the impact we have and our ability to derive economic benefit from it," said Rob Glaser, the company's chairman and chief executive. He said income from the agreements would be spread over several quarters. Realjukebox, which can be downloaded free over the Internet, has gained 10 million users since its introduction in May. The software allows users to store music from compact disks on their hard drives, to download music from the Web and to play back the music on their personal computers or download it to new portable digital music players. That large base of users is what made it attractive to Checkout.com, a new entertainment service that hopes the deal will drive users to its Web site as it fights to distinguish itself from numerous other on-line music vendors. "It's not like we're just throwing some ad banners out there," said Richard Wolpert, Checkout.com's acting chief executive. Checkout.com, a privately held company based in Beverly Hills, Calif., bills itself as an entertainment portal, providing information like biographies and concert reviews, in addition to selling compact disks. Its other big backer is Ronald W. Burkle, a billionaire supermarket entrepreneur. Mr. Ovitz and Mr. Burkle have purchased several Internet companies to augment their fledgling Internet empire. Realnetworks is also announcing a deal with Sony Music to allow consumers who play a forthcoming album by Rage Against the Machine on their computers using Realjukebox to download an unreleased track of the band's live performance at Woodstock this summer. Realjukebox users will also be able to preview three tracks from the record about a month before its scheduled release in early November. The announcements come as Realnetworks begins shipping the final version of Realjukebox. The 10 million downloaded until now have been beta versions.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Dell to Focus More on Consumers
body: The Dell Computer Corporation in Round Rock, Tex., said yesterday that it would significantly increase efforts to sell to consumers, seeking to expand beyond its core business customers, with ads and products bearing the brand "Dell4me." The new brand, accompanied by the theme "Your thoughts exactly," will be the focus of a campaign with a budget estimated at $30 million, which begins this weekend. The campaign is the first from the newyork office of Ammirati Puris Lintas, part of the Interpublic Group of Companies, which now handles the consumer, home office and small-business portions of the Dell account. BBDO Worldwide in newyork, part of the Omnicom Group, is the worldwide brand agency for Dell. The Dell4me campaign, which also uses the overall Dell theme "Be direct," plays down technical specifications of PC's sold directly by Dell, focusing instead on portraying Dell as "a partner to help you get the most out of technology," said Janet M. Mountain, vice president and general manager for the Dell Home Systems division. "It's more than a campaign," she added. "It's a whole change to our communications approach." The campaign includes pitches for a new digital music PC with Jukebox software, a PC meant to make it easier to create home pages on the Web and an on-line service and support resource named Ask Dudley, offered in a partnership with Ask.com, operator of the Ask Jeeves Web search engine. Dell is also selling high-speed cable Internet access through Excite@Home, the first time consumers can order that feature through a PC maker. The Dell4me name is intended to convey that Dell's direct-order system enables the company to "respond to what customers need," said Patricia A. Doyle, executive vice president and managing director for worldwide account and strategic services at Ammirati Puris. The brand was created after studying research conducted by Dell as well as consumer responses in focus groups, she added.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: 3 Brothers, 4 Months, 1 Fortune In an Early Success in Germany
body: SITTING at a makeshift confer ence table a white table top supported by cardboard boxes -- in the Spartan Berlin headquarters of Ebay Germany, the 26-year-old chief executive, Oliver Samwer, can barely contain his excitement as he outlines his company's spectacular and, in Germany right now, singular success story. It doesn't take long: Last September, he and his 24-year-old brother, Alexander, finished their respective university degrees and packed their bags to join their brother, Marc, 28, as interns in Silicon Valley. There they came across Ebay, the on-line auction site, and thought they saw a niche for a similar site in Germany. The brothers talked it over at Christmas, quit their internships and returned to Germany in January to start their own auction site on the Ebay model. They moved from their hometown of Cologne to Berlin, recruited three college friends (their 25-year-old chief financial officer, Karel Doerner, who worked at the consulting firm McKinsey & Company for two months, was the only founder with corporate job experience) and founded Alando.de in February. On March 1, the site went on line. Goldman, Sachs called on May 17 to say that Ebay was interested. Ebay's founder, Pierre Omidyar, flew to Berlin on May 21, and on May 30 -- less than a hundred days after founding the company -- the six 20-somethings sold Alando.de to Ebay for $43 million. Not surprisingly, the story has inspired a flock of other young German entrepreneurs to undertake E-based start-up companies. But it remains an exception. "Right now, E-commerce is taking place in Germany," said Alexander Artope, a co-author of the European Communication Council's report on the Internet economy. "But other than auctions, nothing's happening." Germany has more Web users than either Britain or France; it has one of the best telecommunications infrastructures in the world and is awaiting the drop in Internet toll charges that should follow the recent deregulation of its telephone industry. But industry insiders put Germany anywhere from eight months to five years behind the unitedstates in E-commerce development. Consumer reluctance to give out financial information over the Internet and unfamiliarity with credit card payment -- 80 percent of Germans do not have credit cards -- present significant barriers to Web browsing and buying. Add to this the conservative business practices of the traditional media publishing corporations that dominate Internet business in Germany (only one of the top 10 content providers offers Internet services exclusively, according to the New Media Report, based in Munich), and it is no surprise that in Germany, E-commerce has had a slow start. There has also been a shortage of the kind of hard-charging, baby-faced, overnight millionaires that have produced the dot-com mania fueling start-ups across America. Referring to Oliver Samwer and his colleagues, Scott Barnum, Ebay's international general manager and vice president, said: "In the German Internet-commerce world, these guys are very atypical. But they represent a new group of entrepreneurs that is trying to take hold. They are successful role models for entrepreneurs, and there haven't been that many success stories." That may be why this success story has entranced Germans. The young men have become German media darlings, and with scores of magazine articles and more than 15 television appearances under their belts, they have set off a wave of young start-ups. In the auction world alone, more than a hundred sites have sprung up since Alando, now called Ebay Germany. The founders offer consulting to fledgling entrepreneurships and have started Silicon City, a social networking group. "Alando helped raise the attention for E-commerce ventures on a large scale" in Germany, said Christian Bachem, an on-line strategy consultant based in Berlin. But, he added, Alando's copycat model "might be a viable trend in German E-commerce, but it does not at all represent the German E-commerce market." Oliver Samwer is enthusiastic about the nascent entrepreneurial community he has helped to create, saying that his own team would have welcomed the mentoring that it regularly dispenses to young start-ups. But he looks back with nostalgia at the skin-of-their-teeth route that the founders of Alando took, which included offering up their own childhood model trains at a fraction of their value to get the site going. "Mom," he said, "is still really sad about the trains." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Got rich quick: the founders of a German auction site, including brothers Alexander, Oliver and Marc Samwer, front to back on the right. (Ebay Inc.)  Drawing (Illustrations by Nannette Finkel Rebach)

title: A Feeding Frenzy Made for Consumers
body: IT'S hard not to look at all the money being made on Internet stocks and wonder, "How do I get my share?" Well, you could bet your life savings on a company started by teen-agers that has never had a dime of profit, with a stock that seems to follow the course of the Coney Island Cyclone. Or maybe you could dust off that recipe that was always such a big hit at the bake sale, open SuperFudgeBrownies.com, and then sell stock to all your friends on the P.T.A. Then again, you could plan to do all your Christmas shopping on the Internet. It may not have quite the thrills, but you're sure to walk away with a little of Wall Street's mad money. That's because so many Internet companies, and their investors, are so desperate to get big fast that they are almost willing to bribe people to shop with them. So the savvy cyberconsumer can find sites selling all sorts of items at or below cost, or with free shipping or all sorts of other giveaways and promotions. "You can get great values on line because of the venture capital frenzy and Internet stock frenzy," said West Shell 3d, the chief executive of Netcentives, which runs a system that lets Internet sites lure customers with frequent-flier miles. For example, E*Trade, the on-line stockbroker, is giving away as many as 25,000 of Netcentive's miles -- enough for a free ticket -- just for opening an account. "Everyone is spending the money from their I.P.O.'s to build their business," Mr. Shell said. Competition has already driven prices for digital video disks on line to as much as 40 percent below the suggested retail level. In many cases that means the price is well below the wholesale cost. And enough $15 coupons and free shipping deals have been fired in the bitter war between Drugstore.com and Planetrx.com that customers could well hoard a year's worth of free shampoo or toothpaste. "I need to establish and maintain our position of leadership, because whoever gets the lead is in the best position to keep the lead," said Peter Neupert, the chief executive of Drugstore.com. "If I can convince people to change their daily routines, the customers we get will be very valuable. People buy hundreds of dollars of these products every year, multiple hundreds if they use prescriptions." And so the logic goes across every conceivable category of merchandise. You name it and someone has started a Web site to sell it: Autoweb, Furniture.com, Ebags, Garden.com, Netgrocer, Pets.com, even Partyjunk.com, scheduled to be introduced this fall, for children's party favors. There are thousands more, and nearly all of them are planning to lose money for years. For on-line buyers, these good deals are still mixed with a lot of frustration. It's often hard to find a site that sells what you want. When you do, the sites can be slow and hard to navigate. If you place an order, too often the merchandise is not shipped correctly, intact and on time. And there is nothing that Silicon Valley has invented to let you tell by looking at a computer screen whether the sweater will be scratchy, or for that matter, what the color really is. A survey by Jupiter Communications, a newyork research firm, found that the portion of buyers who said they were very satisfied with their on-line shopping dropped to 43 percent this year from 63 percent last year. But whatever the qualms, more people are spending much more money on line every month. On America Online, the nation's largest Internet service, only 37 percent of its members had made an on-line purchase as of June of last year. Today, it is up to 62 percent, or nearly 11 million shoppers. Jupiter estimates that consumers will spend $15 billion in 1999. Of that, $6 billion will be spent this Christmas, double what was spent last year. In the short history of electronic commerce, Christmas sales have become an important benchmark for both the industry and for individual merchants. "Christmas is absolutely critical," said Timothy Harrington, the chief executive of Fogdog Sports, an on-line sporting goods merchant. "Amazon.com broke through the hype two years ago. Last year it was Etoys. We hope that we can become the next category killer." For both business and Wall Street, the question now is: how big can this get? Goldman, Sachs recently told clients it estimated that ultimately 15 percent to 20 percent of the nation's retail sales could flow over the Internet. And in many ways, business-to-business electronic commerce is having an even bigger effect and doing it faster, as everything from cattle farms to steel mills use the Web to link to suppliers and customers. No wonder investors are backing companies that look like they are growing fast, rather than those that are making a profit. To be sure, there may be a touch of irrational exuberance causing the stock market to value Etoys at $5.2 billion, far more than the $3.4 billion value of Toys "R" Us. Never mind that Toys "R" Us sells 400 times more toys than its upstart rival. Still, the growth in both Internet sales and Internet stocks have made electronic commerce the No. 1 topic of conversation in the board rooms of the world's largest companies. Executives who not so long ago wrote off the Internet as science fiction and then as an amusing little trend now see a tidal wave that threatens to swamp their businesses. That is, if it hasn't washed up their careers already. Herbert M. Allison Jr., the president of Merrill Lynch, and Robert C. Nakasone, the chief executive of Toys "R" Us, resigned in recent months, largely over disputes involving how to respond to on-line upstarts that started to steal the companies' best customers. And so this Christmas, the battle for the Web shopper will take on a second dimension. There will be even more start-up sites trying to establish their names in front of both consumers and investors, as Etoys did last year. But there will also be a host of big companies -- both retailers, like Nordstrom, and manufacturers, like Levi Strauss -- trying to win as much business on the mouse as they get at the mall. "For the mainstream retailer, the Internet was an interesting experiment last year," said Geoffrey E. Bock, a senior consultant with the Patricia Seybold Group in Boston. "Then E-Christmas blew the roof off everyone's expectations, and now it's a very important indicator of how you will do in the new economy." FOR established firms, it's hard to compete in the new economy when you are saddled with old-economy handicaps like investors who expect you to make a profit. That's why more and more companies are considering following the lead of Barnes & Noble, which took its Web site public so that it could be its own money-losing Internet company. It did this only after Amazon.com, by far the most successful on-line merchant, garnered more than 10 million customers. Indeed, Amazon's sales this year are expected to exceed $1.5 billion, which amounts to about half the total sales that Barnes & Noble rings up from its 1,000 stores. Now Amazon has expanded into music, toys, electronics and auctions and will soon add other categories. It can afford to do this because investors snapped up $1.25 billion of high-yield Amazon bonds earlier this year, even though the company does not expect to make a profit in the foreseeable future. For the same reason Amazon is feared in corporate America, it is being repeatedly emulated by the nation's entrepreneurs, who are trying to start the Amazon.com of this or that. Those business plans that win the blessing of Palo Alto's venture capitalists will be run down an assembly line that can turn an idea into a company almost as quickly as Henry Ford's River Rouge plant turned iron ore into cars. Typical is the story of Jessica DiLullo and Jenny Lefcourt, who in the fall of 1997 were first-year students at the Stanford Business School. Like most of their classmates, they talked of little else but what Internet company they could start. They decided to be the Amazon.com of wedding registries and spent the school year researching a business plan for a site they named Della & James, after the characters in the O. Henry story "The Gift of the Magi." By May, they had sold the idea to Kleiner Perkins Caufield and Byers, the influential venture capital firm that had backed Amazon. In just a few months, they had raised $5 million, hired an experienced chief executive and forged links to established retailers including Williams-Sonoma and Neiman Marcus. As everywhere, competitors abound, from newcomers like Theweddingchannel.com to established players like Macys.com. "Every category is being inundated," said Anthony Noto, an electronic commerce analyst with Goldman, Sachs. "No one wants to miss the boat." LOOK behind all this technical wizardry, however, and you'll see a lot of businesses that are staying together on little more than packing tape and a prayer. After all, it's much easier to make a pretty Web site, and advertise it on America Online, than to make sure you have the goods the site is offering in stock. "Last year was a wake-up call for everybody," said Katherine Borsecnik, the senior vice president in charge of America Online's shopping area. "People weren't prepared for the volumes that peaked about a week before Christmas." Julie Wainright, now the chief executive of Pets.com, said she learned her lesson when she spent a year running Reel.com, an on-line video store that was having trouble keeping track of its inventory and shipping orders on time. "When I got there, we had 50,000 customers, and 50,000 were mad at us," she said. Reel has since been sold to Hollywood Video. Starting over at Pets.com early this year, Ms. Wainright replaced the company's computer system with one that can handle 30 times its current volume. She leased a 120,000-square-foot warehouse to stock everything from Alpo to $200 Italian leather cat carriers, and she is hiring three shifts of people to staff it around the clock this Christmas. (Four out of five pets get a Christmas present from their owner each year, she said.) "Two years ago, people were really excited to try something new," she said. "But this year, the customers are completely unforgiving. They are not going to give you a second chance." This fall will also mark the debut of services known as electronic wallets that are meant to speed on-line shopping by automatically sending previously entered information about the shopper -- like credit card numbers and shipping address -- to the store. While Amazon.com has offered a similar one-click buy system for several years, the new systems, like Microsoft's Passport and America Online's Quick Check Out, are meant to offer the same convenience at many different stores. Last Christmas, many people who tried to shop on line found an even more basic problem: they couldn't find anyone selling what they wanted to buy. In some cases that was because they didn't know where to look.  But by this year, the big Internet guides, including America Online and Yahoo, will introduce new services that allow shoppers to search for a specific item at hundreds of on-line stores and see on one screen who carries it and what their prices are. But some companies -- especially makers of premium brands like Sony and Ralph Lauren -- won't sell most of their products to Internet stores. "When I first started, I had to put the kneepads on and grovel to get manufacturers to sell to me," Mr. Harrington of Fogdog said. Now it's getting easier, he said, but Nike, which is opening its own on-line store, still won't sell directly to Fogdog. Moreover, in categories in which the manufacturers have a lot of power -- like sporting goods, cosmetics and jewelry -- Internet retailers have been able to obtain merchandise only by promising that they won't cut their prices below what brick-and-mortar stores charge. "If I sell a Callaway Hawk Eye golf club for any less than $399, Callaway wouldn't sell to me anymore," Mr. Harrington said. S ECURITY is the other main concern that, according to surveys of Internet users, is keeping people from shopping on line. With so many sites appearing every day, it is hard to know the reliable merchants from the fly-by-nights, so many people are wary of sending their credit card numbers to anyone on the Internet. But a healthy suspicion, said David Medine, the associate director of the Federal Trade Commission, should make people more willing to use credit cards. "People should always use their credit cards when they buy on line because of the strong consumer protection laws that let you dispute charges on a credit card bill," Mr. Medine said. The most consumers will pay in case of fraud is $50. But use your head, too, he added, especially when looking at an offer that seems too good to be true. "The Internet has not lacked for scams," he said. "We've seen a lot of flashes from the past: chain letters, pyramid schemes and garden-variety business opportunity scams." So far, however, the F.T.C. has not classified the stock offerings of Internet merchants as illegal get-rich-quick schemes. But it's not at all clear that after the sales, the coupons and the barrage of dot-com advertising that will clog the airways this Christmas, how many of the new Internet stores will survive. "Right now everyone is investing in a lot of promotion and marketing to get customers," Mr. Noto of Goldman, Sachs said. "The key question is, what will happen when all the customers have been grabbed? In the long run, you have to take in more than you give away." But in the meantime, the shoppers will have a field day. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos (Firefly Productions/The Stock Market for The newyork Times); (George Diebold/The Stock Market)

title: A Food Site for Every Appetite, With Cookware to Boot
body: WHETHER you are a seasoned cook, a novice cook, a noncook, a wine lover, a beer brewer or somebody who simply wants to replace his metal sink strainer, there is an Internet entrepreneur waiting to walk you down the appropriate aisle. The number of food sites, which are rolling out at assembly-line speed, can be daunting. A review of more than 30 food and wine sites makes clear that the majority of them -- even those set up to inform and entertain people who have a serious interest in food -- have moved toward retailing in a big way. The Culinary Institute of America, for example, which had a cooking and recipe site for several years, has changed the site's name to Tavolo and sells a wide range of cooking equipment. Across the Web, it seems, posting recipes and food lore is fine, but pots and pans are the future. Which is not to say there aren't worthwhile gastronomic sites in cyberspace. Here are some of the more interesting ones that I have encountered.  EPICURIOUS.COM -- This site, which is owned by Conde Nast, is a supertanker on the churning digital sea, combining 10,000 well-researched recipes from Bon Appetit and Gourmet magazines and featuring articles, cooking techniques, cookbooks (including hard-to-find vintage books), descriptions of 10,000 wines, food chats and much more. The site is colorful, fun and easy to use. An expansion at the end of this month will add on-line food videos as well as the site's own cooking program, "Epicurious TV." Epicurious also recently began a site on Jewish food and cooking. The travel content of Epicurious has been spun off to a new site, Concierge.com.  TAVOLO.COM -- Formerly called Digital Chef and affiliated with the Culinary Institute of America, Tavolo began as a recipe site but now primarily sells kitchen equipment and specialty foods. Still, many of the recipes, developed by Culinary Institute teachers, are strong and clearly written; moreover, the entire site is user friendly. There are thematic recipes that change weekly: risotto, for instance, might be featured one week, with information about every grain of international rices, how they are harvested, how they are packaged, ways to cook them and scores of ways to season them. In addition, a daily quick menu can be easily extrapolated for the number of diners. It's especially useful for parties. Less welcome are the relentless commercial tie-ins, as recipes are paired with sales pitches for equipment (fish scaler, anyone?) -- though it does help that the equipment, cookbook and specialty food offerings are particularly thorough.  GLOBALGOURMET.COM -- Founded in 1994, this quirky and informative site is the brainchild of Thomas Way and Kate Heyhoe, who roared onto the gastronomic freeway early and have built a strong, entertaining site. When I called up some of the seasonal menus, I got more history and etymology about ingredients than I could digest in one sitting, but the recipes worked well. Among the many offerings are a column called "I Love Chocolate," another that offers diet tips, one called "Cooking With Kids" and a comprehensive cookbook store affiliated with the well-regarded Lisa Ekus Presents. Wine information is sketchy.  COOKING.COM -- Another largely commercial site, Cooking.com sells all kinds of kitchen equipment, along with recipes that use it (home juicers with recipes for drinks, for example). Some of the information comes from Fine Cooking magazine. A "Chef's Roundtable" is an interesting addition. Well-known chefs nationwide offer cooking tips on various subjects, like grilling fish and buying hot peppers (all with recipes). The site has a glossary of cooking techniques along with easy-to-follow recipes. But when I searched for two fundamental techniques, searing and braising, neither was included.  GOODCOOKING.COM -- For sheer volume, this is a site to be reckoned with; too bad much of it is sloppily organized and cluttered with information provided by product manufacturers. John J. Vyhnanek, an experienced chef and primary owner of the site, provides hundreds of recipes and cooking tips, but dishes are not listed in any apparent order. The main strength here is hundreds of links to other food sites, some of them useful, like Taste of Cuba, others obscure. Another site with a giant list of food-related links is Kitchenlink.com., which boasts more than 10,000 private and commercial food and cooking links.  WINESPECTATOR.COM -- This site from the Wine Spectator magazine is extremely well designed, colorful and staggeringly comprehensive. Magazine subscribers can get staff ratings of 77,000 wines from around the world; for others, the cyberglass holds about 15,000 ratings. The site also lists leading wine shops nationwide, previews auctions and allows visitors to seek wines by grape variety, region or name.  DEANANDDELUCA.COM -- Looking for white truffles from Alba or a Viennese pastry stand? This celebrated food emporium in Manhattan sells all kinds of specialty items, including caviar, cheeses, charcuterie, oils and vinegars and kitchen equipment. Although quality is consistent, bargains are rare. If you click on "recipes" you are led to the hefty Dean & DeLuca cookbook.  ZABARS.COM -- Another famous newyork City food bazaar, Zabar's also sells over the Web. Its selection is even larger than Dean & DeLuca's, and the site is easy to navigate. You will find lots of seasonal discounts.  BKSMITH.NET/RECIPETRADER -- The Recipe Trader is the culinary equivalent of chatting over the back fence.
