Visitors to the site can post their favorite recipes, request recipes ("I have some broccoli rape, what can I do with it?"), buy cookbooks (through Amazon.com) and read folksy features like "Mom's Cooking Tips." The fun factor here makes up for organizational shortcomings. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Anybody in There? Sites Strain To Build In Customer Service
body: CUSTOMER service is the key to business success on the Web. That is the conclusion of a growing number of experts in the field of electronic commerce. "Too many businesses think that it is enough to throw up a Web site and the money will start rolling in," said Craig Settles, the president of Successful.com, a consulting company in Oakland, Calif., and the author of "Maximizing Your Business Online" (ABS Group). "But keeping the customer happy is what generates repeat business." Satisfying customers, however, takes more than low prices, large selections and a customer-is-always-right return policy when the medium for your message --and your product -- is the computer. Web-based customer service involves giving customers control over all aspects of the interaction with the company through the computer, consultants like Mr. Settles said. That can include everything from product information to a human being typing responses in a chat window. Many of these experts think, however, that companies generally do not understand that the Web is a distinctive medium and that they must adopt a different approach when setting up Web-based customer service. "You can't maximize a New Age medium with Old World thinking," Mr. Settles said. Exceptions do exist, however. Some companies are trying to exploit the communications might and muscle of computer electronics to keep their customers in the fold; a few are trying to be innovators in the consumer relations field. "You need to provide some semblance of active, live, customer service," said Brett Renwick, the Internet site project manager for the Danone Group, which makes Dannon products in the unitedstates. But that service need not come from the company itself, he said. Mr. Renwick cited, for example, Liveperson.com, a company that provides other businesses with a support staff that can answer questions over the Internet. "Customers may be typing questions into the computer, but they are typing to human beings," he said. He thinks this kind of computer-linked, human-based customer support helps move sales along. Lawrence Holt, the chief executive of Quidnuc, a consulting company in London, said Web-savvy customers belonged to a "do-it-yourself" crowd: They thrill to being able to check the status of their orders as often as they want. Offer them easy, round-the-clock access to a package's routing, and "they come back repeatedly because they're now comfortable with your company," Mr. Holt said. Kenneth Stickevers, the vice president of Gateway.com, the Internet division of the computer maker Gateway, said the ability to track orders lured customers to visit the Gateway Web site. "A person will check on the status of an order five times over the two-week period it takes for the computer to arrive as opposed to one phone call during the same period before the Web," he said. Mr. Settles said that Federal Express generated brand loyalty and customer satisfaction while saving money on what it would have spent on a call center and other traditional support services by transferring its package tracking system to the Web. email is the most potent Web technology when it comes to customer service. For businesses, it is an inexpensive form of communication that can easily focus on specific customers and address their particular interests and needs. For customers, receiving email from the company about order status, sales, special discounts for repeat business and even a folksy newsletter can make them feel as if they are part of a family. First ask customers whether they want email from the company about products, updates and company news, consultants say. Giving consumers control over the volume of information they receive means they won't feel that they are being "spammed," or inundated with unwanted email. Once customers give the email go-ahead to Nordstrom, the retailer, known for customer service in its brick-and-mortar operation, provides a nifty email innovation for those who cannot find what they want in the electronic catalogue. Send a message to the store and someone will hunt down the product and send back news of the price, asking whether you want that lime green sweater after all. There are also personal shoppers at selected stores who deal only with the email requests and will contact customers either by email or by telephone. "Our goal is to provide our customers with a shopping experience that's on their terms," said Colleen Chapman, the Internet marketing director of Nordstrom.com. Cnet's News.com, which covers the technology industry, defines customer service in terms of a daily email of headlines and special features sent to its thousands of subscribers. It was one of the first to use this technique. "We started as an Internet news site and we had to build brand loyalty by making sure that our readers got the news as quickly as possible," said Jai Singh, News.com's editor. Now every major news site offers email delivery. Community is a much-used term in Internet circles. It generally refers to people with a similar interest gathering on the Web to exchange information. A company can "grow" a community, consultants say, using its Web site. "Just start a chat room," Mr. Settles said. Chat rooms allow customers to talk to one another honestly about products. These uncensored digital discussions, he said, can improve the company's image. "It gives the impression that the company is confident enough of its products to allow open discourse," he said. "It can also let a company spot potential problems early and respond to them quickly." Often, these chats can lead to product improvement, he said. Digital catalogues are another component of Web design that can translate into convenience for customers. In the mid-1980's, for example, the Buick division of General Motors started exhibiting at computer shows. Instead of exhibiting automobiles, G.M. representatives handed out computer disks. Potential customers could put the disk in a computer and see all the models, in every possible color. They could even calculate what a particular car -- with the desired features -- might cost. The computerized catalogue was a hit, and when the Web became a marketplace, Buick moved the concept on line. Other retailers have now adopted this "kick the electronic tires" model, which allows a potential customer to ask and answer questions electronically before buying. Phillip E. Risinger, the brand advertising manager for Buick, said the Internet attracted different buyers. "The Net was driving a younger buyer who might not have looked at a Buick before," he said. Another example of Internet power was demonstrated by a contest that Buick ran giving away a car a day for 45 days. People could call a toll-free number for a game card or download it from the Internet. "We got 300,000 phone calls, but more than a million people got game pieces over the Internet," Mr. Risinger said. In a few cases, companies have integrated Web-based customer service features into a larger strategy designed to guarantee that people have several routes through which they can get information about their purchases, answers to their questions and responses to their existing and anticipated needs. "Customer service is not an Internet strategy, it's a business strategy," Mr. Settles said. "Too many businesses treat the Web as a separate component; an adjunct, not part of the overall business plan that it should be." Integrated customer service is the philosophy at Gateway where, Mr. Stickevers said, a customer should be able to get the same level of service on the Web, on the phone and in the company's stores. "We're known for our customer support," he said. "It is what makes us different from other PC vendors." As such, it is considered a bulwark of the company's financial success. In 14 years, it grew into a multibillion-dollar Fortune 500 company. Gateway's integrated approach involves every method of customer contact. Mr. Stickevers said that a week after buying a Gateway computer, "you get a welcome package, complete with information about the company, discounts on additional purchases and ways to contact the company if you are not satisfied." Of course, a person can still get stuck in voicemail limbo at Gateway or be put on terminal hold while waiting to talk to a human being. "But if the reality doesn't match the vision, at least the company has a vision," Mr. Settles said. Too many companies do not, which means they are overlooking the real strength of the Internet and the Web, Mr. Risinger said. "The only reason to be on the Net is customer service and building relationships with your customers," he said. "Everything a company does should be to make customer service as simple as possible for shoppers." With the advent of the Web, he added, "there are so many opportunities for companies to serve their customers and serve the bottom line." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: A Ripe Target for Web Retailers, Teens Keep Heading to the Mall
body: TIM GEISENHEIMER, a computer savvy 15-year-old, has read most of the books of Iain Banks, the British novelist. But some of the surreal tales by the author are difficult to find in the unitedstates. So a few months ago, the adolescent newyorker checked in with Amazon.com, ordered what he wanted from England and paid for it with his mother's credit card. He gave his mother, Susan, cash when she received her statement. But she was aghast to discover the cost because the two paperbacks were shipped by air freight. "Have you any idea what it costs to send books out from the U.K.?" she asked her son. "Before you do it again, let's talk about this." So it is with teen-agers and the Internet. Many grew up wired and think on-line commerce is cool, but their parents, who worry about encouraging spendthrifts and protecting their own privacy, aren't as sure. With Web retailing still in its infancy, most sites for teen-agers make money from accepting advertising and selling market research to manufacturers. "We don't sell names," said Dan Pelson, the chief executive of Bolt.com, which provides forums and information for teen-agers, "but we do sell trends. We have more data on teen preferences than anyone in the world." According to Children's Business, a trade magazine, the sites encourage youngsters to "input information such as their names, ages, addresses, preferences, buying habits and even socioeconomic indicators" in an interactive format that doesn't always make it obvious that the teen-agers are taking part in a market research interview. The potential customer base of teen-agers for on-line retailing is huge. There are 70 million children in the unitedstates born to baby boomers since 1979. Marketers know them and love them as Generation Y or the Echo Boom, a cohort that is more than 50 percent larger than the 45 million strong Generation X. Roughly 30 million are 12 to 19, a figure that will rise to 33.6 million by 2005. Their spending power is enormous. Teen Research Unlimited, a market research firm, says that teen-agers commanded $141 billion in spending last year, up 16 percent from 1997, and each youngster spent an average of $84 a week. This teen-age population wave has crashed over the late 20th century's other big trend, the Internet. Find/SVP Research estimates that more than 20 million teen-agers will be on line by the end of the year. Once there, they will spend an average of a little more than seven hours a week on the Web, according to another researcher, Nielsen/Net Ratings. How do they pass their on-line time? Chatting with their friends by email, naturally -- two-thirds do that, consuming more than four of the seven hours. Shopping has yet to command anywhere near that investment of time. Teen Research Unlimited surveyed 2,000 12- to 19-year-olds last spring, and of the 14 on-line activities they listed, checking out merchandise to buy at a store was 12th (26 percent of boys and 23 percent of girls did that), and buying goods on line was dead last (13 percent of boys and 7 percent of girls said they had done that). Rachel Geller, a partner at Geppetto, another market research firm, concluded that the Web accounts for a relatively small $1.4 billion of spending by adolescents. Conversion rates, the industry term for turning an on-line window shopper into an on-line buyer, are still low. Web retailers do not release their figures, but across the Internet, the percentage ranges from one-half of a percent to 2 percent, meaning that only 1 in 50 browsers ultimately buys. Even so, like all Internet players, on-line merchants cannot resist extrapolating their growth into infinity, and sales estimates for the next century climb to 300 percent and 400 percent annual growth. But what the retailers really do know is that half these youngsters have after-school jobs; they make money and are willing to spend it. "Teen spending is a very growing and important category," said Linda Freedman, the vice president for marketing at Fashiontrip.com, a site for teen-age girls. "They have high discretionary income because they don't pay taxes or rent." The average on-line purchase is $38.35, according to Cheskin Research, and the goods that youngsters buy reflect what they buy off line at the mall: music, videos, accessories and clothing. Two of the most popular sites are Amazon.com and CDNow.com, though neither caters particularly to adolescents. Music, however, is probably the easiest thing for youngsters to buy on line. They can sample the audio -- try it on, essentially, before they buy -- so there is less chance that they'll wind up with something that has to be returned. Other popular Web stores are Delias.com, which has taken its famous catalogue for teen-age girls on line; Jcrew.com; Abercrombie.com, which has managed an amazing transformation from a frowsy purveyor of gun-check hunting jackets to a hip retailer for young men and women, and the ubiquitous Gap.com. This assortment should not be surprising because there is no more brand-conscious consumer than a teen-ager. These youngsters may not have a clue who they are, but the brands they wear tell the world who they would like to be. "For Christmas last year, my two brothers, who are 16 and 18, told me they wanted 'anything from Abercrombie & Fitch,' " said Renny Gleeson, the senior vice president at Iturf, the creator of Delia's on-line store. He noted that Brooke Shields and her Calvins brought name brands to the teen-age consumer 20 years ago, and brands have never looked back. In theory, on-line retailing could turn mall rats into cyberrats, but marketers are hesitant to say so. Instead, they comment on the tendency for virtual merchants to become brick-and-mortar merchants to reinforce their presence on the Web. For example, Delia's, which has five retail stores nationwide, expects to expand to 12 to 16 by the end of the year. Moreover, the mall is still a gathering place. Unlike the Internet, which most youngsters troll from home, the mall is somewhere they go to when they need to get out of the house. Ekaterina Walsh, a researcher at Forrester Research, said that while teen-agers say they plan to increase their on-line buying, less than 1 percent expect to forsake traditional stores. In addition, Web shopping has drawbacks. The most obvious is the one described by Mr. Pelson of Bolt.com: "Teens don't have the 16 digits." Only about 7 percent of teen-agers have their own credit cards. Everyone else has to borrow Mom's or Dad's. But Mom and Dad are worried about being scammed on line and prefer that their children order from catalogues over the telephone. An on-line survey by Jupiter Communications this year of 2,000 households reported that safety concerns about the Internet are also rising.  Seventy-six percent of parents said they were nervous about strangers their children might encounter in chat rooms or through email, and 68 percent said they feared invasion of their privacy through direct-mail solicitations. Concerns about protecting the personal and financial information of parents and children have given rise to a new solution for which retailers have high hopes, the "digital wallet." These sites let parents establish accounts from which children can draw to shop on line and limit the sites at which the money can be spent. The big three are Icanbuy, Rocketcash and Doughnet. The average Icanbuy account, for example, is $50, and arrangements can be made for grandparents, aunts and uncles to contribute as well. Forrester Research reports that only 5 percent of teen-agers who buy on line have reached for the digital wallet, but the technology, a little more than a year old, is still in its infancy. Shopping on the Web has other disadvantages. Purchasers can't try anything on, so they are frequently limited to accessories or items for which size doesn't matter. Even worse, teen-age shoppers frequently can't see what they are buying because the on-screen resolution, to use a technical term, stinks. A man's navy blue sweater at one on-line store was described as a V-neck, but the picture was so muddy, it looked like a crewneck, and shoppers have to take it on faith that the cargo skirt at another retailer has pockets. To rifle through a collection of dresses or khaki pants takes forever, because downloads plod along. Catalogues have much clearer photographs and drawings, and teen-agers can page through them faster. But these are problems that newer chips and faster modems will eliminate. The real experience that the Web cannot replicate is social. Shopping is something teen-agers do with their friends, especially girls who want to show each other how cool they look in the blue sweater they just found under a load of awful green ones. "The Net kind of takes away the whole experience -- the hunt, the get and the buy," said Eva Kuhn, 13, of newyork who browses on line but buys in the stores. "Web shopping is just too perfect" she said. "You type in 'gray cords' and there they are. It's not fun. The fun is the hunt." That's true, but the nature of the hunt changes on the Web. Teen-agers are extremely value-conscious shoppers, and they will comb the malls to get their favorite brands at lower prices. A growing Net-based economy is likely to push down prices because click-by-click comparison shopping is ultimately far less time-consuming. "We're building the Bolt economy," Mr. Pelson said. "I can go to a cell phone manufacturer and say, 'I've got 10,000 teens who want your phones, but you sell them for $75 and they'll only pay $45.' That's pricing power as well as buying power." That buying power exists, and teen-agers are just starting to flex it. Soon, the hunt will be on for the pricing power as well. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Thirteen-year-old Eva Kuhn says the fun of shopping "is in the hunt." (Ozier Muhammad/The newyork Times)

title: Beanie Baby Scams And Identity Thefts
body: THE world's flea markets, souks and bazaars have always been magnets for the criminally minded, from mountebanks and snake-oil salesmen to plain old-fashioned pickpockets. It should be no surprise, then, to learn that the global marketplace that has sprung up on the World Wide Web has drawn its share of crooks. By all objective measures, the rise of E-commerce has seen an accompanying rise in E-crime. Swindlers pose as merchants, taking people's money without ever sending along the wares. Then there are the technologically adept thieves, who have discovered on-line auction sites as a relatively safe and efficient way to fence their stolen goods. Most feared of all, perhaps, are the dreaded hackers who trespass in other people's networks, sometimes to vandalize, sometimes to steal data and, on occasion, to commit an especially pernicious crime that the authorities have started to call "identity theft": taking people's log-in names, passwords and credit card numbers to assume their identities and buy merchandise. None of this means that buying goods on the Internet has to be inherently dangerous. But if people want to avoid being cheated, law-enforcement officials and security experts caution, they must learn to recognize and avoid the risks of on-line shopping. Some of the best advice can seem counterintuitive. Consider the use of credit cards. One common fear expressed by people who may window-shop, but not buy, on the Internet is that it is risky to use credit cards on line. They worry that if they send their credit card information into cyberspace, it might be hijacked. But many law-enforcement officials and computer-security experts recommend that consumers use credit cards for on-line purchases as a precaution in the event they unwittingly do business with a bogus entity. They note that most fraudulent payments to on-line con artists are made by check or money order; some people even send cash. By using a credit card, they say, consumers can dispute fraudulent charges before they pay their bills. And in the unlikely event that a hacker steals a credit card number, Federal law limits liability to $50. So where, in the new and ever-changing world of E-commerce, does the danger lie? On-line auctions are among the riskiest forums, law-enforcement officials and outside monitors say. The Internet Fraud Watch, a monitoring group set up by the National Consumers League, reports that 68 percent of all the Internet-related fraud complaints it received in 1998 concerned auction sites. During the first six months of 1999, the group received 5,287 auction complaints, surpassing the 5,236 it received in all of 1998. The problem with on-line auctions is that their great advantage from a bargain hunter's perspective -- no middlemen -- is also their great disadvantage when it comes to security. So buyers must trust sellers to deliver what they promise. Needless to say, some sellers prove less than trustworthy. And they laugh all the way to the bank. "HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA," read a message that was posted on the Web in December 1996 by a man who California authorities now think used on-line auctions to defraud Beanie Baby fanatics out of thousands of dollars by pretending to sell stuffed animals that were never delivered. "All you people are really quite ridiculous. You make a deal via email, never see the person, never speak with the person and then get upset when you get ripped off. You must be a bunch of morons." The post ended, "I really hope, for my sake, that you all disregard the posting and continue as usual." The Beanie Baby scams continued until July, when the authorities arrested the man they say is responsible: James R. Denlinger Jr., 29, of San Jose, Calif., who was charged with computer fraud and conducting a false auction. He has pleaded not guilty. A closer look at his case, detailed by court records and the authorities, highlights some of the possible perils of on-line auctions. HE offered Beanie Babies on several small auction Web sites. Although he always listed his mailing address as a suite or an office room number, detectives say, he actually used private post-office boxes that he rented for short periods to collect the money. He always asked for checks or money orders. "He had a fleet of names, like Tom Richard and Ian Oerlin, that he would ask people to write checks or money orders to," said Detective Mike Hopkins, an investigator with the Sonoma County Sheriff's Department, who worked on the case. "But with a few strokes of the pen, Tom Richard could become James Richard Denlinger. And Ian Oerlin could become James Denlinger." On-line auction houses have taken steps to combat fraud. They recommend obtaining working phone numbers and verifying the physical addresses of sellers, possibly through on-line directories. Many auction houses advertise escrow services, which, for a small fee, will hold payments until the deal goes through to everyone's satisfaction. Several on-line auction houses offer services for person-to-person credit card payments. Some, like Ebay, offer insurance. And many have forums where customers can rate sellers. The only problem with that last safeguard is that many unscrupulous sellers rate themselves by disguising their email addresses and giving rave reviews. James Denlinger did, officials said. Quite a few thieves have looked at on-line auction sites and seen the perfect virtual fence, the way to sell their stolen property. Two men were arrested in newyork City in August on charges of trying to sell stolen cartoon art -- fittingly, an animation frame from Dr. Seuss's "How the Grinch Stole Christmas" -- on Ebay for $1,500. The winning bid was placed by an undercover detective, and the men were promptly arrested. IN Clearwater, Fla., a computer repairman was arrested in July after an undercover detective posed as a thief to sell the man stolen VCR's and then bought the VCR's back from him through an on-line auction site. "It's the perfect venue to commit crimes," said the detective, Javier Rosas of the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office. "Why go to a store where someone can recognize you or there might be a videotape to record you?" But the biggest fear of all, most law-enforcement officials and security experts agree, is identity theft. While an individual's liability is limited to $50 for lost or stolen credit cards, the aggravation and time it takes to repair damaged credit histories makes it nettlesome. Still, it is not necessarily a risk that Web shoppers run. The larger, more established sites use sophisticated encryption technology to protect their customers' credit card information. And while no encryption is impossible to crack, security experts say, it is so difficult and time consuming that it would hardly be worthwhile for a hacker to try to break into an individual email in transit just to get one card number. Most hackers would rather break into a corporate Web site to steal an entire database of credit card numbers. David Truog, an analyst with Forrester Research, a consulting firm in Cambridge, Mass., points out that it is easier for a waiter to steal a credit card number in a restaurant or for cellular-phone hackers to steal credit card numbers by eavesdropping on phone calls when people order from catalogues. When it comes to crime in the E-commerce arena, he said, "there's a legitimate reason for fear and trembling, but it should be the companies who are fearful because consumers are very well protected." And Dorothy E. Denning, a professor of computer science at Georgetown University who catalogued computer crimes in terrifying detail in her recent book "Information Warfare and Security," (Addison-Wesley), said that nothing in her research had dissuaded her from buying books on line. STILL, there are occasional horror stories. Recently, agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation worked on a case in newyork that they dubbed the Keystroke Snoopers. It involved a ring of people who used email to send a so-called Trojan horse, a disguised, malevolent computer program opened as an attachment, to thousands of people. This particular program captured all the keystrokes made by the people who received it. So the ringmasters were able to figure out the credit card numbers of people who ordered goods on line because they received a verbatim record of everything they typed on their keyboards before the card numbers were encrypted. The ring was made up of youngsters. "They made some purchases, but they seemed mostly interested in using the credit card numbers for pranks," said Edward M. Stroz, the special agent in charge of the computer unit in the F.B.I.'s newyork office. "One sent something like 16 dozen roses to somebody; another sent someone eight refrigerators." But law-enforcement agencies worldwide are gearing up to fight computer crime used for more malevolent purposes. In newyork City, Lieut. Christopher Malinowski pounds a cyberspace beat for the police. "Mostly, we find people are essentially doing the same old scams with new technology," he said. That is why the F.B.I. trains agents to handle garden-variety frauds perpetrated on computers, saving its computer experts for crimes unique to computers, like hackers who steal data. It is an ever-evolving field: new laws had to be drafted when investigators found in 1996 that they could not prosecute someone who stole data and emailed it across state lines under a statute prohibiting the interstate transportation of stolen property, because the electronic data were not considered "tangible." More laws are on the drawing board. "I constantly challenge myself to make sure I'm using the right analogy," Mr. Stroz said. "We're seeing new kinds of crimes, and if you start off with the wrong analogy, you can really get boxed into the wrong way of thinking about a problem."  'Buyer Beware' Goes for Web Shopping, Too  PAY BY CREDIT CARD -- If you don't get the merchandise, you can challenge the charge with the credit card company. Don't deal with cash-only sellers.  ENCRYPT, ENCRYPT, ENCRYPT -- Don't give your credit card number on line unless the latest security protocols are in place and you trust the company in question.  CHECK YOUR STATEMENTS -- Always review your credit card statements for billing errors or unauthorized purchases. correct problems immediately.  DO BUSINESS WITH COMPANIES YOU TRUST -- Only deal with companies you know and find to be reliable. Be sure you know what the company is and where it is.  PRINT OUT THE OFFER -- This way, you will have documentation if you need it.  WHEN IN DOUBT, CHECK IT OUT -- Ask the Better Business Bureau about the company's complaint record. However, fraudulent companies often come and go quickly, so the absence of a complaint record is no guarantee that a company is legitimate.  FOR AUCTIONS, TRY ESCROW -- For a fee, you can send payments to an escrow service, which will hold the money until everyone is satisfied with the sale.  KNOW WHOM YOU'RE DEALING WITH -- If you can't verify a seller's identity and figure out his or her real address and telephone number, don't do business.  FOR MORE INFORMATION -- Check for more tips at the Internet Fraud Watch Web site at www.fraud.org/ internet/inttip/inttip.htm, or the Federal Trade Commission's site, www.ftc.gov/bcp/menu-internet.htm. MICHAEL COOPER http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (David G. Klein)

title: Big Blue Casts Itself as Big Brother to Business on the Web - Correction Appended
body: AFTER years of working as a marketing executive for champagne houses like Taittinger and Veuve Clicquot, Rosemary Zraly decided it was time to branch out on her own. Like so many entrepreneurs in the 1990's, Ms. Zraly -- a consultant, lecturer and author -- headed for the World Wide Web. Her Web site, Champagnelady.com, is a decidedly modest foray into Internet commerce. It amounts to an advertisement for herself and an on-line shop for merchandise, including a book she has written and all manner of champagne paraphernalia, glasses, ice buckets, even earrings. No corporate powerhouses quake at the mention of her Web site. No Wall Street bankers are wooing Champagnelady.com, eager to sell its shares in a public stock offering. Yet Ms. Zraly's venture shows one side of the new economics of the Internet. "Anybody can afford to get into business this way," she said. "It's cheaper than my cable TV bill." Behind Ms. Zraly, pocketing a $60 monthly fee for running her Web site, is an unlikely partner -- the International Business Machines Corporation, the world's largest computer company. Its customers have long been its corporate peers on the Fortune 500, not tiny upstarts. Until a few years ago, that is, when the Internet took off and I.B.M. went with it in new and innovative directions. I.B.M. itself shows another side of the new economics of the Internet -- how a big, old-line company can turn the challenge of technological upheaval into a rejuvenating opportunity. I.B.M. has embraced the Internet in its products, practices and marketing -- from overhauling its mainframes into Internet computers to refashioning itself as an Internet leader with its giant "e-business" advertising campaign. The result has been a startling revival in I.B.M.'s prospects and image. A few years ago, I.B.M. was stumbling as the mantle of leadership in computing seemed to have passed to the Microsoft Corporation and the Intel Corporation, the technology standard-setters of the personal computer era. But the Internet changed the landscape again. The rise of the Internet -- a vast global network -- played to I.B.M.'s traditional strengths. It required powerful centralized computers to serve up data to millions of viewers. And I.B.M. adapted its big-iron computers to Internet protocols, recasting them as giant Web servers and the transaction-processing workhorses of electronic commerce. As the Internet moves beyond the experimental stage, as more and more companies actually run their businesses on the Internet, those systems must be robust, secure and up and running 24 hours a day, seven days a week. That level of reliability is second nature to I.B.M., and it is why airline reservations systems, national defense systems and the like depend on I.B.M. "We were moving in the right direction and, frankly, we were lucky as well," said Nicholas Donofrio, the senior vice president for technology at I.B.M. "The industry moved our way." Today, I.B.M. is a leading supplier of technology and know-how in the Internet era. The well-known names of this new world may be America Online, Amazon.com and Yahoo, but I.B.M. has emerged as the quiet giant of the Internet by serving as a kind of arms supplier for this new economy to companies of all sizes. In that role, it has plenty of competition from a wide range of companies, including Sun Microsystems, Hewlett-Packard, Microsoft and others. But none has risen as fast from what seemed to be so far behind not long ago. "I.B.M. is getting a real bounce from the Internet," said Stan Dolberg, a senior analyst at Forrester Research, a consulting firm in Cambridge, Mass. "It seemed a moribund company three or four years ago. But I.B.M. jumped on the Internet instantly, and it's been an innovator. It has surprised a lot of people." THE company estimates that roughly one-quarter of its revenue -- or $20 billion -- is driven all or in part by E-business demand. It defines E-business as companies grappling with Internet-related projects, from setting up a Web site to reach customers to handling most of its procurement over the Internet. I.B.M. has helped thousands of small companies get on the Web, and it runs their sites for fees that range up to $200 a month. By 2001, it hopes to have two million small-business customers. Yet it is the larger companies that remain I.B.M.'s bread-and-butter business. They often hire I.B.M. to help them use the power of Internet technology to revamp the way they deal with suppliers, customers and employees in an effort to lower their costs, focus their marketing and eliminate mountains of paperwork. These can be multimillion-dollar projects. Most of this work involves the economic infrastructure of companies dealing with one another -- known as business-to-business commerce. It is the business-to-consumer commerce of Amazon.com, Ebay and others that understandably gets the most attention. But streamlining business-to-business transactions will ultimately have the greatest effect on consumers in terms of prices and quality of service. Business-to-business dealings, analysts say, represent the biggest opportunity for Internet commerce over the next several years. Forrester Research estimates that consumer sales over the Internet will jump to $108 billion by 2003 from $3.9 billion last year. But that impressive increase is dwarfed by Forrester's projection for business-to-business commerce on the Internet, rising to $1.3 trillion by 2003 from $45 billion last year. And it is industry's "back office" -- procurement, accounting, order-processing and the like -- that economists are watching most closely for evidence that the spread of the Internet is leading a technology-based productivity payoff in the nation's economy. The evidence on that front is still inconclusive, but that could be because the use of powerful computing and Internet technology has not gone very far yet. Louis V. Gerstner Jr., the chairman of I.B.M., made that very point in a speech before industry analysts and professional investors in May. He bemusedly observed all the attention lavished on "these new dot-com Internet companies" by the media and Wall Street, before proceeding to his theme. "But I think of them as fireflies before the storm: all stirred up, throwing off sparks," Mr. Gerstner said. "But the storm that's arriving -- the real disturbance in the Force -- is when the thousands of institutions that exist today seize the power of this global computing and communications infrastructure and use it to transform themselves. That's the real revolution." Under Mr. Gerstner, I.B.M. has undergone its own internal transformation. Much of its sales, service, procurement and training are now handled on the Web. I.B.M. estimates that $3.3 billion of its sales last year were over the Web, or roughly five times those of Amazon.com. This year, I.B.M. plans to have Web sales -- mainly to corporate customers -- of $10 billion to $15 billion. The company figures it will save $600 million this year by letting customers find answers to straightforward service and technical support questions on specialized I.B.M. Web pages, thus freeing the time of its human support staff for more complex problems. By handling a portion of its internal training over the Internet instead of in classrooms, I.B.M. estimates it will save $100 million. And by procuring $12 billion worth of goods over the Web this year, I.B.M. says it will do away with about 5 million pages of paper forms. TO position itself as a company on the cutting edge of electronic commerce, I.B.M. began a major advertising campaign in the fall of 1997, promoting the notion of "e-business." The term was new then but has since become routinely used in newspaper and magazine stories and in the marketing campaigns of other companies. The I.B.M. ad campaign -- budgeted at $550 million worldwide this year -- has featured customers of all kinds, from body-pierced Web designers to Ms. Zraly to corporate titans. Its implicit message is that the Internet is not about just putting up a Web site, it is the technological starting point for a complex rethinking of how business is done. Trust us, we're I.B.M., we know more about business and complex technology than anyone else. Big companies like Ford, United Parcel Service, Charles Schwab and Bank One have chosen I.B.M. as their technology partner as they try to exploit the Internet to transform their businesses. Yet so have ambitious start-ups that are trying to change the economics of an industry, like E-Chemicals Inc. E-Chemicals, based in Ann Arbor, Mich., is an on-line marketplace for chemicals, founded by a group of former Dow Chemical employees and distribution experts. Its chairman is Yossi Sheffi, the director of the Center for Transportation Studies at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and its president and chief executive is Jim Alampi, the former head of one of the nation's largest chemical distributors. The chemical business is a $250-billion-a-year industry in the United States. E-Chemicals is betting it can make its fortune by streamlining the industry's fragmented distribution system, a jury-built setup based on industry directories, phone calls, faxes and relationships with distributors. Its on-line chemical marketplace lists 20 suppliers, including Dow Chemical and DuPont, more than 1,000 products and 600 registered customers. For suppliers, E-Chemicals offers a low-cost way to sell to small customers, right down to sales of a couple of 55-gallon drums. For smaller buyers, E-Chemicals promises to substantially level the playing field by offering the kind of lower prices usually available only to distributors' big customers. E-Chemicals can do that because of its lower expenses, operating as a kind of "virtual corporation" that uses subcontractors for much of its basic work. It has just 20 employees. Sun Trust Banks acts as its credit and collections department, and Yellow Freight serves as its logistics department. I.B.M. helped build its large Web site at www.e-chemicals.com and supplies much of its critical software. The site is hosted at a huge I.B.M. data center in Schaumburg, Ill. E-Chemicals says it chose I.B.M. because of its history of serving chemical-industry customers and its tradition of building and running computing systems that handle thousands upon thousands of complex industrial transactions. "For what we are doing, we're not talking about some on-line billboard where how it looks and the user interface are all that matter," Mr. Alampi said. "We're doing real commerce on this Web site," he said. "It has to be secure, and it has to be able to quickly increase the volume of transactions it can handle. I.B.M. can do that. And we don't want to have to buy computer hardware ourselves, so we let them handle all that by hosting the site. At E-Chemicals, our expertise is in the chemical business and distribution, and we want to stay focused on that." Saab Cars U.S.A., the American distribution arm of the Swedish auto maker, is putting in place a Web-based system that is a typical example of how existing companies are trying to use Internet technology to improve customer service. Most of its 210 dealers now have a new system, using mostly I.B.M. computers and software, for ordering parts and providing customer service and training. The dealers tap in from personal computers to Saab's database, and the early goal is to make dealer service more timely and efficient. YET the company is also working on creating more detailed, car-by-car data profiles that customers can use. With help from I.B.M., the company is building a vast "customer vehicle database" that will, for example, allow the owner of a used Saab to look up the repair history of that car. A person interested in buying a new Saab will be able to go to the company's Web site, look at the available models and arrange on line for the local dealer to deliver one for a test drive. "The goal is to serve customers better and ultimately sell more cars," explained Jerry Rode, the director of information technology for Saab. The Bank One Corporation, the nation's fifth-largest banking company, faces the classic Internet challenge of an enterprise with a vast brick-and-mortar network. It has more than 1,900 offices nationwide, serving more than 9 million retail customers. Bank One is making a big Internet push, both with its own Web site and by opening a virtual bank last June, Wingspan.com. John B. McCoy, the president of Bank One, succinctly summed up the thinking behind these moves: "I am not about to sit here and let someone take my business." I.B.M. is helping Bank One with its Internet strategy for gathering more customers. Wingspan.com is run from I.B.M.'s Schaumburg data center, selected for its reliability and knowledge of networks. But Bill Wallace, the top technology executive for Wingspan.com, also mentions one attribute that is surprising for a company once viewed as a dinosaur. "The Web is about speed," he explained, "and I.B.M. can move very quickly these days."  She Knows Her Bubbly, But Nothing About Bytes ROSEMARY ZRALY has a recommendation for personal computer makers. "They should give out Valium with the PC when you buy one," she said. "It's painful learning how to really use one." Ms. Zraly wanted to avoid having to master Web technology to get her on-line business, Champagnelady.com, up and running. That was why I.B.M.'s Home Page Creator service for small businesses appealed to her: it seemed to be a practically pain free way to start an Internet venture. I.B.M. helped her set up a Web site, which is run at I.B.M.'s data center in Schaumburg, Ill., outside Chicago. Ms. Zraly does not baby-sit for computer hardware or fret about software bugs or crashes. I.B.M. also handles most of the back-office plumbing of Internet business, processing the on-line transactions and credit-card verification. "All I have to do is ship the goods when I receive an order," Ms. Zraly said. The monthly fees for the I.B.M. small-business service range from $30 to $200, depending on the Web site's size. Ms. Zraly pays I.B.M. $60 a month. She can check the traffic on her site, update it or edit it from her home office in New York.  And Ms. Zraly has adapted to the Web's always-on pace. "My Web site is the first thing I check every morning and the last thing I see at night," she said."It's like living with another person, totally part of my life."   STEVE LOHR http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article on Sept. 22 in the special E-Commerce section, about business services provided by I.B.M., included a company erroneously among the 20 suppliers that sell their wares through an I.B.M. client, the E-Chemicals Web site. Dow Chemical is not among them. Correction-Date: September 30, 1999, Thursday Graphic   Photos: Jim Alampi, the chief executive of E-Chemicals. I.B.M. helped build the company's Web site, which is run from an I.B.M. center. (Jim West/Impact Visuals for The New York Times); "Anybody can afford to get into business this way," Rosemary Zraly says. (Ruby Washington/The New York Times)

title: Buy Here, and We'll Tell You What You Like
body: HOLLYWOOD agents, literary agents, real estate agents, travel agents -- now meet Internet agents. "Intelligent agent" programs and their kin, "shopping bots," are among the hottest new areas of electronic commerce. They hold out the promise of making shopping on the Internet better not just by finding lower prices but by matching products to the needs and tastes of individual consumers, as in the increasingly familiar, "If you like this, perhaps you'll like. . . ." While the term "agent" suggests a trustworthy representative dispatched into the wilds of cyberspace bazaars, bot conveys the image of a combative R2D2 scooting through the marketplace of some distant planet pricing used space cruisers. The reality behind the names is different: agents and bots are programs, routines, algorithms -- strings of complicated mathematical equations that are used to find and compare patterns. Marcus Zillman of Botspot, an agency that tracks software agents, predicts that in five years, bots will be involved in most on-line shopping. "Electronic word of mouth," is the phrase that Prof. Pattie Maes of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Media Laboratory uses to describe what some software agents bring to the party. Programmers less vividly call it "collaborative filtering." A pioneer in the field of software agents, Professor Maes has become one of the most visible and articulate proponents of this new type of program, which lets users learn by comparing their preferences with those of what she calls their "taste mates." Like a real estate agent or travel agent, a software shopping agent has responsibility for finding products and prices, Professor Maes said. One of the agent's responsibilities is to match the user's preferences. Software agents take initiative, learn from the habits of their clients and adapt to the market. At the M.I.T. Media Laboratory, Professor Maes founded and directs the Software Agents Group and holds the Sony Corporation Career Development Chair. Two of her many projects have led to commercial spinoffs that represent the two leading types of shopping bots. The first was Firefly, introduced in 1995, which helps make individual recommendations for taste-based products like compact disks, books and films. The other is Frictionless, which went into service in August on the Lycos portal and other Web sites. Frictionless is designed to shop for the best price and service on less-frequently bought products, like cars or camcorders. Firefly is Professor Maes's best-known spinoff. It was one of the first shopping bots to use intelligent agents and collaborative filtering. Developed in the early 1990's, Firefly's software began as a site called Helpful On-Line Music Recommendations, or HOMR, where users could receive guidance in finding music recommendations. Users rated a series of CD's to create individual profiles, which were compared with profiles of other users with similar tastes to generate suggestions for music the user might enjoy. "One of the beauties of these kinds of systems is that some notions we held before of how people fit into certain stereotypes are proven to be wrong," Professor Maes said. "On Firefly, for instance, the system kept telling us something that seemed strange. Ask what else classical music buyers like, and it would say the Beatles." In 1995, the HOMR project was spun off and incorporated first as Agents, then under the friendlier name Firefly. Other sites, including Reel.com, adopted similar techniques to help people choose films. Some licensed the software from Firefly. Then, in April 1998, Firefly was sold to Microsoft, guaranteeing its influence across one of the most powerful sets of on-line sites. Firefly and other collaborative filtering systems take advantage of the knowledge and tastes of customers. Sometimes the user fills in a form on line. At other times, the agent learns from a person's buying or browsing patterns, as tracked by software from companies like Doubleclick. A familiar nondigital comparison is with the Zagat Survey of restaurants, which is based on reports and ratings by diners. A new site, Deja.com, expands on this idea: "Consumer reporting from actual consumers" is its slogan. It offers information on a variety of products, including VCR's and computer printers. But true electronic word of mouth is more personalized, Professor Maes said. A college student might be presented only with the restaurants that fit his or her budget; a diner on a low-cholesterol diet might get a different list. Such recommendation options, including those produced by Firefly's competitor, Net Advantage for Barnesandnoble.com, are probably the most familiar of the new bots. Amazon.com for instance, offers Instant Recommendations based on past purchases. On its music pages, an agent is in effect tucked behind a button labeled "mood matcher." There, you can click on categories that include "party," "driving," "dancing," "Sunday morning" and "feeling depressed." Punch "depressed" and you will get subcategories like "got dumped" and "won't stop raining." Click "crashed your car" and the music suggestion is "All The Rage" by the Kronos Quartet. "This type of recommendation technology only works for domains where people buy on a regular basis," Professor Maes said. "It's good for areas where it is hard to put into words what it is you like or dislike. It's great for books or music, but not, say, for a car, which you might buy only every four to eight years." For those kinds of products, a different kind of agent technology, like Frictionless, works better. Frictionless also grew from Professor Maes's work at the M.I.T. Media Laboratory. It searches on-line shopping sites for products with specific features at the best price. For example, on Frictionless, someone interested in buying a laptop computer chooses among a set of user profiles, with names that include "road warrior," "budget shopper" and "telecommuter." Each profile provides a list of product features, among them weight, speed and memory, as well as information on the vendor relating to warranty, availability and delivery. To further personalize the search, the user can rely on the preset profile or edit it, rating factors like screen size and product warranty on a scale of "not important" to "very important." Frictionless is so named because it seeks to remove the friction from searching for and comparing products. The name could also refer to the friction that early shopping bots often encountered in dealing with on-line merchants. The first bot was Andersen Consulting's Bargain Finder, introduced in 1995. Current sites include Mysimon.com, Advantage and Bottomdollar.com. In the beginning, bots searched by price only, and many selling sites prohibited access to their price lists. The sellers wanted users to view their pages and advertisements directly. They also might have believed they were misrepresented by comparisons with other sites where prices might omit shipping or other costs. The current shopping bots are called second generation, which implicitly recognizes the limits of the first generation. Frictionless refers to its software as a "value-comparison engine," while its competitor, Mysimon, describes itself as a "virtual learning agent." One element of real-world shopping that on-line sites generally lack is the impulse purchase. Retailers have long celebrated the "serendipity factor." For example, the buyer browsing in a bookstore may be intrigued by a title he's never heard of while the CD shopper may pick up a disk by a Brazilian artist new to her and play it at a listening station. Can agents and bots be programmed for serendipity? "You can build in serendipity either in a narrow way, with a randomizer to make suggestions, or by giving customers things outside the current taste profile that are popular with some portion of their taste mates," Professor Maes said. Some users may feel their individuality challenged by the idea that others share their preferences; that something as personal as taste can be rendered in cold, hard algorithms. But the greatest concern is privacy. "This is a major issue that deserves public discussion," Professor Maes said. The more an agent knows about you, the more useful it can be. But while some shopping bot companies promise not to sell information to other companies, others give away their software and plan to make money from selling the information they gather on shopping patterns. A survey by Jupiter Communications, an industry tracking company, suggested that more than 60 percent of shoppers remained wary of giving information to an on-line site. Firefly hired an accounting firm to certify its privacy practices, and Professor Maes was an early backer of proposed industry standards for privacy. The so-called Platform for Privacy Preferences protocols are under discussion by the nonprofit World Wide Web Consortium and enjoy the support of Microsoft, MCI Worldcom, AT&T, I.B.M., Netscape, Oracle and other companies. BUT even if these standards -- which involve encrypting information and obtaining permission from consumers to transfer personal information -- become accepted, on-line shoppers may not feel comfortable. On Aug. 18, just two days after Frictionless went on line, Firefly's site vanished, swallowed by Microsoft's Passport shopping site, which will begin this fall. Many of Firefly's users were dismayed despite Microsoft's assurances that privacy and other policies would remain in place. Trust is vital to making software agents work well. For Professor Maes, agents have much more to offer than prices and suggestions, and many applications only now being dreamed of at M.I.T. expand the role of agents. Other future agents might be linked to smart appliances, and will order milk before it runs out. But Professor Maes likes to speak of agents leveraging the knowledge and experience of many people to help individuals. "Intelligence augmentation" is what she calls her next efforts. One of Professor Maes's projects at M.I.T. seeks to bring together people who have not met but have similar interests.  The program uses a survey of potentially sensitive information, like people's mail, their personal files or lists of their interests. It's easy to imagine how the program might be useful to link scientists around the world for academic conferences, but its working name suggests an even more dramatic matchmaking possibility: It is called Yenta. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Pattie Maes focuses on software agents at the M.I.T. Media Lab. (Asia Kepka for The New York Times)

title: Can Defendants Cry 'E-Sanctuary' and Escape the Courts?
body: THE prosecution of Kevin Jay Lipsitz, who was accused of trying to peddle magazine subscriptions from Staten Island, would have been a garden-variety consumer fraud case. But because it involved the Internet, it has become a watershed. Mr. Lipsitz's solicitations for low-cost subscriptions came in the form of spam, group distribution sent through email. But when 50 disgruntled consumers from newyork and around the world complained that they never got their subscriptions or received fewer issues than promised, the newyork Attorney General accused Mr. Lipsitz and his companies, including Krazy Kevin's Magazine Club and Tempting Tear-Outs, of violating the state's consumer fraud and false-advertising laws. Mr. Lipsitz responded that the newyork State court could not possibly have jurisdiction over the geographically limitless domain of the Internet and that, for similar reasons, it would be unconstitutional to apply newyork laws. But ruling in what she said was "a case apparently of nationwide first impression," Justice Diane S. Lebedeff of the State Supreme Court found that Mr. Lipsitz had sufficient connections to newyork to enable the state's courts to adjudicate the consumers' claims and that the state's laws did apply. "To place a realistic context on these matters and leave behind the rarefied air of cyberspace, the issues raised here would be the same if each involved a consumer individually sued in the Staten Island Small Claims Part," Justice Lebedeff wrote in June 1997. "There is no compelling reason to find that local legal officials must take a 'hands off' approach just because a crook or a con artist is technologically sophisticated enough to sell on the Internet. Invocation of 'the Internet' is not the equivalent of a cry of 'sanctuary' upon a criminal's entry into a medieval church." THE state of the law governing commerce on the Web is somewhere between the dusty streets of the Wild West and the decorous halls of the Supreme Court. As path-breaking as the Lipsitz case has become for local law-enforcement and consumer groups, it has only scratched the surface of the legal questions that are arising with the explosive popularity of the Internet as the world's largest bazaar.  While a trickle of court opinions in the unitedstates and abroad has begun to define the commercial rules for the Web by applying analogies from older principles, the medium has created problems that defy easy answers. Many other new technologies, like the telephone and television, raised a host of difficult legal questions. But the questions raised by the remarkably ubiquitous nature of the Internet are forcing an even more significant set of legal issues. In large part, these issues have arisen precisely because the law and the Internet are based on opposite notions. The law is inherently based on geographic boundaries, historically an effective way to impose a socialized order on human behavior. But the Internet knows no such boundaries and has prospered because of a kind of anarchy. The law can only work when the government or a private plaintiff can identify a wrongdoer as defendant. By contrast, the Internet thrives on anonymity. Economic realities have put a strain on the development of cyberspace law. Unlike the emergence of technologies like television or radio, the economic barriers to establishing a presence or business on the Internet are stunningly low. This has enabled many small businesses to use the medium to gain exposure to a marketplace that is potentially limitless. Not surprisingly, these differences between the law and the Internet, and between the Internet and older technologies, have led to the emergence of some legal issues that the courts have never before confronted. To take the case of Mr. Lipsitz, for instance, what would the judge have ruled if his business had been in New Zealand instead of newyork, or if he had not concentrated on newyorkers? If the court found a sufficient connection to apply its jurisdiction, whose laws should apply? And what kind of remedy would be available to newyorkers for a business whose assets lay offshore? More fundamentally, must a business that puts up a Web site abide by the laws and regulations of every jurisdiction around the world -- even those that may be inconsistent -- because anyone anywhere with a telephone, a computer and some basic software can theoretically read and respond to the site? "The Internet presents a problem of both overinclusiveness and underinclusiveness," said Henry H. Perritt, the dean of the Chicago-Kent College of Law and the author of a legal treatise, "Law and the Information Superhighway" (Aspen Law & Business). "For the seller, there is the potential of much conflicting regulation. But there is also an underinclusiveness problem in that this patchwork may prove not to be efficacious in providing a remedy for victims." At the Federal Trade Commission, the emergence of the Internet as a significant force in commerce has prompted a reassessment of every law and regulation to see how it could be affected. Officials have also held a series of conferences and meetings with representatives of companies and consumer groups, and with foreign officials, to begin to make sure that American consumers have the same protections on line that they enjoy off line in every area from advertising that is deceptive to warranties. But the F.T.C., which is widely regarded as being at the forefront of considering these issues, is only one small piece of a large, global equation, particularly because no international treaties directly address commercial issues and the Internet. "Right now the battle is pitched, with industry asserting on one side that the law of the originator controls and the consumer groups screaming on the other side that it's the law of the consumer state," said Ronald L. Plesser, a lawyer at Piper & Marbury in Washington who is involved in international conferences on the issue and who represents companies that are confronting it. "Both of those approaches have problems," Mr. Plesser said. "If you decide it's the law of the originator, then everyone will go to the state or country that has the lowest common denominator, putting their computer servers in those countries to minimize problems. But if you go with the law of the consumer state, you don't often know where that state is, and you wind up having to comply with a wide variety of different and conflicting rules." He added: "So we're in this murky midlevel right now. The seas and the oceans are forming around us, but if this were viewed like the creation of the universe, we're in about the fourth day." One way some companies have tried to avoid difficulties is by varying their Web sites. I.B.M., for instance, uses a different Web page for each of 167 countries, an approach that recognizes that the company has assets around the globe and that, by necessity, it must take steps to comply with many different rules. Many popular auction houses offer to protect consumers by indemnifying them for a fee and acting as mediators in disputes. Mr. Plesser and other industry lawyers have also suggested a self-regulatory approach through the establishment of basic rules for companies, which, if followed, would innoculate them from liability. But consumer groups and law-enforcement officials, while applauding that approach as a good first step, say it will not be enough. "We certainly welcome self-regulation and any effort by on-line businesses to be responsible corporate citizens in the same way they make those efforts off line," said Caitlin J. Halligan, the chief of the Internet Bureau at the newyork State Attorney General's office, which expects to receive about 2,000 complaints this year about issues involving on-line dealings. "But there are obviously situations where enforcement actions are appropriate when a company engages in fraudulent or otherwise unlawful activity," she said. "That's true whether the conduct is on line or off line." AS for transactions either between two consumers in a chat room or between a consumer and a company, Ms. Halligan advises people to take the same basic precautions that they would ordinarily take, recognizing the possibility that even more problems than usual can arise because of the nature of the Internet. "You also need to exercise the same, if not more, prudence than you do in an off-line transaction," she said, "particularly since you don't have the item in front of you while you are deciding whether to buy it." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (David G. Klein)

title: Coming Soon to a Web Site Near You: A Simpler Sales Tax
body: IF you are hoping that the Internet will become a tax-free zone, dream on. Business leaders know that would distort the economy, creating an uneven playing field that would benefit some companies while damaging their competitors. Also, state and local governments are not about to concede a chunk of their single biggest source of revenue, sales and use taxes worth $189 billion last year. But if you like the standardization that makes a Big Mac the same in Philadelphia and Provo, Utah, you will love what E-commerce is likely to do to your sales taxes. The patchwork of rules that makes a can of soda a taxable nonfood item in Ohio and a tax-exempt food in newyork is under attack from all sides in the debate over the taxation of electronic commerce. "The only certainty about E-commerce is that we will get simplification of the sales tax system," said Robert Cline, a state and local tax expert with the accounting firm Ernst & Young. Although the debate over Internet taxes is far from over, it is clear that the passage last year of the Internet Tax Freedom Act, which created a three-year moratorium on taxes specifically on Internet activity while a panel of political and business leaders studies the issue, has prompted new thinking about how a tax that arose in the Industrial Age can be made to work in the Information Age. Sales taxes took hold in the 1930's, promoted as stable sources of revenue in the Depression to pay for the police, teachers and other services. Today, 46 states, 4,831 cities, 1,511 counties and 139 school and special-purpose districts impose sales taxes, Mr. Cline said, which is only about one-fifth of the 30,000 jurisdictions cited by many advocates of a tax-free Internet. Nevertheless, Mr. Cline sees a serious problem because no map exists that matches every address to each taxing jurisdiction. Thus, a company selling over the Internet could have three customers in the same ZIP code, one of whom owes sales tax at the state rate, one who lives in a city with an added rate and one who lives in the same city and in a special district and owes a third level of tax. E-commerce and mail-order companies that operate in one state and ship to others have no incentive to create such a sales tax map because under current law they cannot be compelled to collect sales tax. A few companies, like Gateway, themail-order computer maker, routinely collect sales taxes from all customers. Creating a sales tax map is possible. J. C. Penney, which has stores in all 50 states and as a result must collect taxes on all sales from its Internet site and its catalogue, has built a detailed ZIP code database to determine the sales tax rate owed by every customer, said Jim Evatz, a Penney tax-compliance manager. "We feel that a level playing field is an issue," Mr. Evatz said of the advantage enjoyed by competitors who do not collect sales taxes. Stuart Feldman, the director of the I.B.M. Institute for Advanced Commerce, said, "It is not a big deal for a large firm to keep track of, or to get access to, what the tax rate is for clothing in New Jersey or even in a water district." The problem, Mr. Evatz and Mr. Feldman agree, is knowing which products and services are taxable. "No uniformity, no rhyme or reason, no plausible categorization," Mr. Feldman said of the sales tax. "When I lived in New Jersey, caviar counted as tax-free food, which I sort of thought missed the point." How, he asked, is everyone in E-commerce business to know "that purple sweaters are suddenly tax free -- this week only -- in Ulster County." One E-commerce committee of the National Tax Association, which has representatives from business, government and education, has suggested developing standardized product and services categories but allowing each jurisdiction to decide which will be taxed and by how much. Business members of the association said they wanted absolute national uniformity on what is taxed. E-commerce raises questions that extend beyond differences among the states and that will become increasingly important as Internet sales become global. For example, American-style retail sales taxes do not integrate well with the European-style value added tax. E-commerce also raises questions about who is to be taxed and where. In an age when tangible products were paid for at a cash register, the sales tax had the virtues of being obvious to the customer and easy to collect. E-commerce changes that. CONSIDER the problems posed by the sale of a book over the Internet. If the book is ordered from a catalogue and shipped across state lines, Congress could easily require a seller like Amazon.com to collect any sales tax and pay it to the state from which the book is shipped or where the bill is sent. The Supreme Court, in two major sales tax decisions, has told Congress that it has the power under the Constitution's commerce clause to require businesses to collect sales taxes for states to which they ship products, but Congress has never taken the hint. Taxes must be paid if the buyer lives in the same state as themail-order company, and many Web sites have a button to establish the tax payment. People who have products sent by mail owe use tax, the individual equivalent of sales tax, but hardly anyone obeys these state tax laws. In New Jersey, for example, only one in 500 people pay use tax. No state has made a serious effort to collect the tax. But where is the sales tax to be levied when a resident of Buffalo, while changing planes in Pittsburgh, downloads an electronic version of the book before flying to Oregon? Is sales tax due in Buffalo, where the bill goes? In Pittsburgh, where the product was acquired? Or is no tax due because the electronic book is read in Oregon? And what happens when a business buys a database, stores it on a computer in one city and then has its employees across the nation use it? Gerald D. Bair, the director of revenue and finance in Iowa, who has been involved with the National Tax Association project to define the issues on Internet taxes, said Congress would have to require companies to comply with all state and local tax laws, which he said would have to be simplified. Otherwise, he said, "states and local governments are going to have to stand up and attempt to enforce their use tax laws." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Connections That Are Fast, Faster, Fastest (and Even Faster)
body: JUST how many times can you watch the comets streak by the Netscape logo as the download goes on and on and on before you run out of the house screaming and go to the mall instead? That 14.4-kilobits-per-second feeling is one of the biggest hurdles on-line businesses face and one of the reasons that the phrase inevitably linked to the arrival of high-speed, so called broadband, Internet connections is: "will change everything." That revolution is actually, finally, kind of here, holding the promise of Internet connections that transmit information 10, 20, 30 or 100 times faster than those most commonly used in homes, at least for some customers in some areas, and at a higher price. One thing that is certainly changing is the confusion Web-hungry consumers face in deciding how to log on. At least when telephone companies began their marketing wars, everyone knew what long-distance service was. But how do consumers choose among technologies that are a scramble of initials, like I.S.D.N. or D.S.L., or companies with no-clue names like a newyork high-speed service enigmatically called Red? And how much is all that speed worth? Two competing technologies, cable modem and digital subscriber line, or D.S.L., are starting to offer Web users broadband service, which uses existing cable or telephone lines but has enough data-carrying capacity to feed the computer without interrupting telephone, fax or cable TV service. This means consumers can have an "always-on" connection, which means no more waiting to get on line. Broadband connections should make a range of Internet activities, including shopping, much faster, and to support ever-cooler on-line video and network computer games. These technologies, however, are more expensive than dial-up services and are available only in some areas. With a 14.4 kbps modem, a couple of pre-broadband options are available that let computer users dial up and browse without waiting eons for the J. Crew fall catalogue to download. Depending on the age and memory capacity of your computer, you can upgrade to a 28 kbps modem or a not-yet obsolete 56 kbps modem. You'll have to dig around to find a 28 kbps modem because large manufacturers, like 3Com, which owns the modem maker U.S. Robotics, no longer make them. But 3Com makes 56 kbps modems, beginning at around $100. Upgrades from a 28 kbps modem cost about $60. If 56 kbps isn't enough but you're not ready for broadband, the speed-demon technology of choice is the integrated services digital network, or I.S.D.N., line. This essentially combines two phone lines to move data twice as fast as one -- generally, 128 kbps. The downside of this technology is that you need to have two dedicated phone lines, which usually means you'll have to pay to have at least one extra line installed, and many I.S.D.N. services charge per-minute on-line fees. While pricing varies greatly among providers, fees can range from $30 a month plus per-minute charges of about 5 cents to a flat fee of $80 a month. You will also have to pay more than $100 for installation, and you may have to buy a modem. I.S.D.N.'s speed, however, has already been eclipsed by broadband technology. ONE such technology, the digital subscriber line, uses copper telephone wires to transmit Internet information at high speed. Because digital packets of Internet information sent over the copper telephone lines have a higher frequency than voice data, the Internet connection does not interfere with phone or fax use. A digital subscriber line costs about $100 to install and $20 to $400 a month, depending on the speed and service provider. Download speeds range from 384 kbps (three times the speed of I.S.D.N. lines) to a theoretical 8 megabits per second, although current computer hardware cannot run more than 3 Mbps, which is still more than 100 times faster than a 28 kbps connection. Sending information to the Internet is slower. D.S.L. technology comes in several flavors, so it is sometimes called x.D.S.L. The lack of standardization is one potential problem for introducing digital subscriber lines nationwide. (By the way, Red offers D.S.L. services, mostly to small business and telecommuters, along with I.S.D.N. and 56 kbps connections.) Cable modem technology, the main competitor to digital subscriber lines, uses cable TV lines to send and receive Web information. Cable modems usually cost $75 to $150 to install, and service costs about $40 a month. Possible speeds run from 3 Mbps to 10 Mbps, although, again, current computer hardware cannot run speeds faster than 3 Mbps. And just how much faster are these speeds? According to Excite@Home, the nation's largest cable modem service provider, you can download a quarter of a graphic-intensive page in a minute with a 28 kbps modem; with a cable modem, you can download 26 pages. One alternate technology, Hughes Network Systems' DirecPC satellite dish, downloads Internet information from a satellite link to a PC at speeds of up to 400 kpbs and is available to users anywhere in the unitedstates. A drawback of this technology is that it uses a regular dial-up line for sending information to the Web, so while you receive information quickly, you send it at a snail's pace. Although the price of the dish varies according to dealer, DirecPC units cost about $200, and monthly service charges range from $30 to $130. Bruce Kasrel, a senior analyst at Forrester Research Inc., said that there were about 200,000 D.S.L. subscribers and 1.2 million cable modem subscribers in the unitedstates, "probably a little less than 5 percent of U.S. Web users." But he predicted that by 2003, 27 percent of on-line subscribers would use broadband services. The providers of cable modems and digital subscriber lines each say they have the better technology, infrastructure and service package as they compete for a larger segment of the emerging broadband market. But according to William Lehr, the executive director of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Internet Telecom Convergence Consortium: "There's no pure technical basis for preferring one over the other. As far as effectiveness to the end user, there isn't an obvious difference, either." "The problem with D.S.L.," he added, "is that all the Bell companies are rolling out different versions, and it's not clear how much bandwidth they're going to offer." On the other hand, said Don Heath, the president and chief executive of the Internet Society, a nonprofit, international organization involved in setting Internet standards, "cable companies are not notorious for providing people with what they want." In March, PC Magazine reported that its tests showed that cable modem services generally outperformed digital subscriber line connections and were a better value, though it noted that service and performance could vary based on location, the distance between the test location and the service provider, the time and other variables. ONE of those could be what you might call the party-line factor. Because cable modem users share a cable line with everyone on their "node," essentially, everyone who gets cable in their neighborhood, performance decreases according to how many people are on line. Excite@Home disputes this, calling it one of the "top myths of x.D.S.L." in one company pamphlet. The A.D.S.L. Forum, a digital subscriber line industry forum, asserts that, unlike cable modems, D.S.L. connections are not subject to variations in performance depending on the number of users because D.S.L. technology uses individual phone lines instead of a shared cable line. But "that's not really true," Mr. Lehr said. "A lot of the distinctions that people make aren't really true," he said. "There are a number of myths. That D.S.L. is not shared is one of them. At a deep technical level, it's not clear which service will be better." The bigger practical hurdle is that most consumers don't have a choice of either service. "The world is made up of broadband haves and have-nots," said Michael Harris, the president of Kinetic Strategies Inc., a broadband research company.
