"The bottom line is they're lucky if they can get any of them," he said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Converting email From Spam to Steak
body: HANS PETER BRONDMO is building an Internet company squarely astride the most bitter cultural divide in the on-line world -- the war over privacy and email spam. There is possibly no more bitter issue for most Net-smart computer users and Web surfers than the tidal wave of digital junk mail -- known as spam -- that has accompanied the explosion of electronic commerce. When coupled with the tendency of every Web business to deploy data-mining software to chart each mouse click a visitor to a Web site makes, the Internet has increasingly become a battleground between digital-age marketeers and consumers. The email war and the ethical issues that commercial email raises hinge on the issue of "opt in," the use of a check box or other device to permit a computer user to decide whether to receive electronic mail and on what subjects. For example, a customer may want to be alerted to new books and compact disks by favorite authors and musicians or may want timely customer service information on an electronic device that he or she has bought. The new power and precision made possible by these Internet software technologies carry the potential for great abuses. "The important thing is whether or not it is genuinely opt in," said Tara Lemmey, the president of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit foundation here that focuses on civil liberties in cyberspace. "Then companies can get around spam and other issues as well." But it is just as easy to lose a potential customer when using commercial email incorrectly, Internet marketing experts say. "You can do great damage to your brand quite quickly," said Preston Dodd, an Internet analyst at Jupiter Communications, a market research company in newyork, "because your customer can respond to you almost instantly with a message like, 'Stop sending me these emails you blankety-blank.' " So Mr. Brondmo, who was born in Norway and graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Media Laboratory, is carefully picking his way through a potential minefield with Post Communications, the business he established in 1996 in a converted brewery in San Francisco's multimedia gulch. Today, Post provides clients with customized marketing programs based on software tools that blend traditional database marketing with email focused on specific consumers. Many Internet marketers are confident that email will transform the traditional direct-mail world, which came of age in the era of mainframe computers. Today's paper-based direct mail is based on information drawn from customer lists and demographic data. However, the precision and timeliness of mail-based direct marketing pale compared with the new world of on-line commerce. "In this business we get 90 percent of all of our responses in 48 hours compared to direct marketing, which takes six weeks," Mr. Brondmo said. Moreover, he argued, in building a relationship with a customer a company creates a much more powerful and receptive market. Selling to a new customer is 5 to 10 times more expensive than selling to an existing one, he said. That is because the marketing costs incurred in attracting new customers are extremely high compared with the cost of simply notifying existing customers that a new version of a product or a peripheral add-in is available. Mr. Brondmo contends that it is possible to stand the old $160 billion direct-mail marketing world on its head by honoring the Internet's cultural values of privacy and user control while using powerful server computers to identify specific customer preferences. "I don't believe there is a single customer in the world who wants a marketing relationship with a company," he said. "Customers want a service relationship." That subtle shift is one that has not caught on yet among direct marketers, who still use costly "campaigns" that send unsolicited mailings to millions of people. The direct-mail world has traditionally counted on the statistical assurance that it will obtain a 1 percent or 2 percent return from each mailing campaign. But in the digital world, where such campaigns are reviled as spam, there is an explosion of start-up companies creating a thriving industry variously known as digital direct marketing, on-line direct marketing or electronic direct marketing. In addition to Post, there is a variety of service providers and software application companies, like Digital Impact, Messagemedia, Media Synergy, Flycast, Connectify, Kana Communications and others, all trying to help companies build electronic relationships with customers. Many Internet commerce experts think that digital direct marketing is the future of electronic commerce on a much larger scale and that it will soon begin to displace other types of Internet advertising like banner advertisements. "The pace at which this thing is moving is remarkably fast," said Marc Singer, the author of "Net Worth" (Harvard Business School Press) and a co-leader of McKinsey & Company's Continuous Relationship Marketing business here. The reason, he said, is that electronic direct marketing is much more profitable than other on-line advertising strategies. He estimated that marketers who used banner ads spend as much as $1,500 a customer. In contrast, the per-customer cost of electronic mail marketing may be as low as $50 to $100. For Post's first client, the Palm Computing unit of the 3Com Corporation, the makers of the Pilot hand-held computer, email substantially changed the company's relationship with its customers by giving it more control. "When I saw what Post was doing, I remember coming back and telling my colleagues, 'I've seen the future of direct marketing,' " said Andrea Butter, who was then the marketing director for Palm's consumer business. With Post, Palm Computing, based in Santa Clara, Calif., created an email service program for its customers, asking whether they wished to receive occasional electronic messages about their Palm Pilots. Customers instructed the company on its Web page about the kind of communications that they wanted and how frequently they wanted email sent. The program was an instant success. The company had already compiled a large database of email addresses of its customers and 25 percent of them responded that they were interested in receiving email tips and marketing information. For Ms. Butter, the new program, which Palm named In-Sync, provided a clear way to save on staying in touch with her customers and to provide her with an avenue to advertise in a way in which the customers felt they were being served. "It turns the world upside down," she said. "A normal ad in a magazine is completely self-serving. As a marketer you have to realize that unless you can add value, the customer is likely to ignore you." Mr. Brondmo, who began his career as a software developer and has worked at Apple Computer and the video editing company Avid, among other enterprises, contends that the most important aspect of the new technology is that Post can transform a marketing relationship into a service relationship. Post's service can generate as many as 300,000 email messages an hour for a client, with far more individualized content than is possible in the off-line world. He says that if a company uses email effectively, it will have the opposite effect of spam. "The best possible email marketing campaign would be one where when the customer hasn't heard from you by midweek, he'll send you email asking why," he said. Post clients, like Music Boulevard and Harlequin Publishing, use the service to alert their customers to titles of interest. Wegmans, an East Coast supermarket chain and a Post client, is experimenting with shopping lists and recipes to build customer loyalty. For Ms. Lemmey of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, the intimate relationship that Internet marketers dream of raises other potential concerns that have not been addressed. WHILE there has been much glowing talk about the ability to determine user preference, so much so that it has been established as the Holy Grail of Internet marketing, there may be an unforeseen dark side, she said. "There is a fine line between targeting and redlining," she said. "What if an insurance company or an H.M.O. knows that you're reading about cancer or Alzheimer's disease on line? They may decide not to issue you an insurance policy or provide health care." She acknowledged that she did not know of such cases, but added that the discussion over the meaning of opt in was only beginning for the fledgling on-line direct marketing industry. "Just because someone says it's O.K. to use my personal information to target me doesn't say for how long," she said. Mr. Brondmo acknowledges that in the Internet world the values of the old direct-mail industry no longer apply. He says that if that new technology is to gain the confidence of the Internet generation, the companies will need to rethink their outlook. "I tell them, 'Ask not what you want to know about your customer, but rather what your customer wants to know about you," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Hans Peter Brondmo, the founder of Post Communications, and Cheryl Vedoe, the chief executive, hope to make consumers happy to see email. (Thor Swift for The newyork Times)

title: Deluxe Dilemma: To Sell Globally or Sell Haughtily?
body: CLICK on Gucci.com and what do you get? A Web site under construction. Point that browser toward Prada.com? There is a picture of a smoldering model, but no handbags are available for purchase. Perhaps, you think, a dress from Christian Dior.com? Oh, you crazy fool-for-fashion you. While bookshops blossom and drugstores multiply, luxury vendors have only tiptoed into the on-line space, which they perceive as a little too low rent. "The Web works well for standardized products, but with fashion you reinvent the product every six months, with new cuts and new fabrics that look different in different lights," says Godo Kraemer, the director of international public relations for Hugo Boss, summing up the Zeitgeist of the elite houses. The sleek suit maker whose creations cost as much as $1,200 at stores like Saks Fifth Avenue has plans for an informational site only. And although merchants certainly will not acknowledge it, there is also the Wichita (as in Kansas) problem. A large part of the cost of any luxury item is its exclusive image. "Perceived lack of demand drives supply," said Mike May, who follows the sector for Jupiter Communications, the Web research company. "The reason a Prada bag costs $450 is that you can only get it at a very few exclusive shops. If anybody in the world could buy a Prada bag, the name would lose some of its cachet." But members of the pashmina shawl set should not despair. The lures for luxury's prime-time players to join the Web rush are great. For one thing, counterfeit merchandise being sold on the Web is a growing problem, and what better way to frustrate virtual swindlers than to offer the merchandise through an official site. Technology is also improving. Pictures of clothing on the Web can lack texture and true color, but software advances will make it possible this fall to see the weave of the Irish cable sweater undulate in its full sumptuousness. There is also the alluring fact that the average Web user has twice the income of the average American. Top style houses are watching closely and have noticed that there are customers blithely willing to plunk down $30,000 for diamond stud earrings or $15,000 for a Queen Anne dresser at an auction site. Many are now investigating how to exploit the medium without angering the traditional retailers that are their biggest buyers. One option may be to design clothing lines to be sold only on the Internet. In the meantime, as Gucci and Hugo Boss dally, the Web is beginning to fill with lesser-known, but not lesser-cost, purveyors of couture, art and jewelry. People who want to shop for luxury goods now will probably end up at a site that is category specific. Everything from diamonds to antique automobiles has its own peddler. Nextmonet.com, for example, hopes to lead well-compensated professionals to their inner art collector. Most of its portfolio is from mid-career artists who are "underexposed," with works costing $2,000 to $7,000. Myrna Nickelsen, the site's chief executive and co-founder, describes her customers as "people who drive BMW's and are ready to graduate from posters but know nothing about art." Visitors to the site are not only introduced to artists and their works but are offered art history lessons and industry gossip. The other type of luxury site is a loosely knit front for a dozen or more upscale retailers. Bestselections.com is essentially a mall with a store roster that reads like a shopping diary for the international jet set. Shoppers at this site can browse by antique jewelry selected by Catherine Prevost, proprietor of a chic shop in the Knightsbridge section of London, or order million-thread count sheets from Roberta East Linens in East Hampton, N.Y. Styleclick.com offers a similar conglomeration-of-brands approach, but instead of retailers it features wares from manufacturers like Kenneth Cole, Anne Klein II and Trussardi Leather. A word of warning: such mix-and-match sites offer a limited amount of merchandise from their vendors, and often the poorer selection at that. "Thirty-five percent of our purchases are $500 or more," brags Maurizio Vecchione, Styleclick's chief executive. Maybe, but plenty of embroidered T-shirts for $32 can be had at his site as well.  Similarly, at Bagley Home, a farm antiques shop on Bestselections.com, it is easier to find chenille bunnies and beeswax candles than 18th-century armoires. Luxuryfinder.com, which is being introduced by the newyork social fixtures James Finkelstein and Pamela Gross this fall, aims at a more ambitious model: a luxury portal that is the equivalent of a social secretary for the wired billionaire set. The site will, of course, offer necessities like a Ghurka laptop carrying case for $1,295 and a bottle of Chateau Lafite at $10,000. Luxuryfinder.com, by the way, will eschew more common brands like Coach Leather, which Ms. Gross called "too low end." But Luxuryfinder will provide services like a calendar of society events and tips by Lord Charles Spencer-Churchill, a grandson of Consuela Vanderbilt, on how to behave like a British aristocrat. Such ambitious competitors have already shaken a few of luxury's big names out of their ennui. The luxury conglomerate LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton S.A., which owns couture houses like Christian Dior and Givenchy, plans to test the Web waters. In October, Sephora.com, the international cosmetics and beauty retailer, which is 80 percent owned by LVMH, will go live. The rest of the company's brands will follow. LVMH, which once saw the Web as a threat, now sees it as a matter of survival. "I don't think everyone knows for sure how big the market is, but the demographics are clear, the young affluent and aspiring affluent customer are already there," said Myron Ullman, LVMH's group managing director. "So we will be, too." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: Digital Dressing Rooms And Other New Twists
body: THE Internet has become a giant laboratory for new technologies intended to bring shoppers and sellers closer together, and consumers will encounter a much improved environment when they go shopping on line this fall. As befits a marketplace based on technology, electronic retailers, or E-tailers, as they are known, are hurling technological solutions against many of the most common criticisms of Internet commerce. These new technologies -- which include three-dimensional graphics, interactive customer service using text and voice, new payment systems, improved search engines and automated shopping agents called "bots" (for robots) -- are among the many tactics merchants will be using this year to capture the interest of shoppers. More important in the long term are the technologies designed to keep the loyalties of those who have already shopped at a site. Much of the new on-line shopping technology will be hidden from view, including software systems that will enable merchants to better track the personal spending and shopping habits of customers, reward frequent shoppers, manage inventory up to the minute, fill orders quickly and maintain continuing relationships with customers who, after all, can move to a competing Web site with a click of a mouse. Following are examples of some of the new technologies shoppers will see in the coming holiday season, or before. Some of the fancier technologies work best with fast Internet connections and powerful microprocessors, but most are designed to work with any standard PC and modem. Virtual shoppers still cannot pick up an item and examine it, but they can approximate the experience. The Sharper Image (www.sharperimage.com) has a "3D Enhanced" catalogue on line that enables customers with faster Internet connections and more powerful processors (Intel's Pentium III and AMD's Athlon chips, for example) to view images in three dimensions. Digitized images of many products can be rotated, just by clicking and dragging with a mouse, allowing them to be examined from any angle. The user can see the back of the item, for example, zoom in to see specific details and even manipulate the object to see how its lid opens or how it folds for storage. Lands' End (www.landsend.com) allows women to create a "personal model" on screen that approximates the shopper's physical proportions. Once the model's dimensions, hair style and skin color are established from a checklist, the shopper can send the model into a virtual dressing room to try on clothes from the catalogue. The model can be rotated to show how the clothes look from all angles, and the color of the clothes can be changed with a click. The site even recommends outfits that are flattering to the customer's body shape. The rising popularity of the Java software technology is allowing many sites to offer animated illustrations, which enable the customer to see, for example, how to assemble that new bicycle. Apple Computer's Quicktime and Microsoft's Media Player are among the multimedia tools that enable Web sites to include brief video clips and soundtracks, making the Web appear more like television than an electronic advertising brochure. Collaborative filtering, already used by popular sites like Amazon.com, is a technology that analyzes customers' buying patterns and preferences and makes recommendations based on the buying habits of other consumers with similar profiles. Anyone who enjoyed reading "Cold Mountain" by Charles Frazier, for example, can check to see what other books have been popular with people who were also fans of the novel. Another related approach, which will be used on many merchant sites this year, is to add electronic message boards or on-line community centers where consumers can compare notes with one another on line. Epinions.com, which will open for business later this year, appears to be obsessed with giving advice. It not only points consumers to what it considers the best expert reviews and information resources on the Web for any given product but also asks, and in some cases pays, regular consumers to add their own product reviews. Auction sites, led by Ebay, have become so popular that a new company called Auctionwatch (www.auctionwatch.com) is bidding to become the central site where buyers and sellers can come together to talk about tips and tactics and to share opinions on which auction sites are good and bad for certain items. Auctionwatch also plans to give sellers more tools to make it easier to sell items on line. Consumers are accustomed to buying small, common items like sweaters, books, and compact disks on line but may need more persuasion to buy larger and more expensive products like automobiles and furniture. Microsoft's Carpoint site was among the first to use panoramic, 360-degree digital images to enable on-line shoppers to examine the inside of many models. And Furniture.com (www.furniture.com) is enabling shoppers to arrange and rearrange room layouts on screen, to see whether that sofa will fit in the living room and whether it will clash with the fabric on the chairs. The company will even send fabric swatches through themail. Just as giant superstores -- the so-called category killers -- are gaining in popularity in the bricks-and-mortar world, so too are they gaining ground in the virtual world. Some sites, like CBS Sportsline (www.sportsline.com), plan to offer more than 200,000 products by this time next year. The problem with virtual superstores is that customers get lost amid hundreds of thousands of products. So several sites have turned to Ask.com, whose "Ask Jeeves" search engine enables people to type questions in plain English as opposed to searching for key words or phrases. The Ask Jeeves technology is being incorporated into shopping sites to make it easier for people to find what they are looking for. One is the consumer electronics site E-Town (www.etown.com), which uses the technology as part of its Interactive Decision Assistant, a software tool that is intended to guide consumers through the purchasing process in the same way a good sales clerk would. The system asks the customer a series of questions, including budget, and then recommends products. This may be the breakthrough year for intelligent agents, also known as bots or spiders. Bots are software programs that act autonomously on instructions from their masters. The first bots to gain wide acceptance from consumers came in the form of comparative shopping services like Bottomdollar.com. At such sites, the user types in the name of the product and the bots scurry forth to find the lowest prices available on the Internet, at least among the selection of stores that permits bots to gather information. THE next generation of bots, typified by sites like Netsage.com and Neuromedia.com, will not only be able to scour the Net for nuggets of information but also to execute simple or complex tasks, such as finding the lowest cost on a new VCR, buying it and having it shipped. Netsage's automated assistants -- like the animated paper clip that offers guidance in Microsoft Word's word processing software -- will eventually take photorealistic human form. Many shoppers, and merchants as well, are discovering that the hard part of E-commerce often comes after the sale. "Retailers still need to keep their eyes on the basics, things like customer service and fulfillment, and that's where things get sticky," said Fiona Swerdlow, a digital commerce analyst with Jupiter Communications in newyork City. "If the product is not delivered on time, if you are out of stock on an item and your site is still selling it, that's bad. If you can't provide good customer service, that's very, very bad. Retailers need to concentrate on the basics before getting caught up in the whiz-bang stuff." The next step is to enable customers to talk to service representatives using the Internet connection, with a microphone and speakers instead of a telephone. The technology, developed by Lipstream, is currently demonstrated on Excite's People and Chat service (www.excite.com/ communities/chat/voicechat/). Two or more people can open a Voice Chat screen and carry on conversations as they would using walkie-talkies, but without long-distance telephone charges. As voice technology proliferates, Internet businesses will enable customers to click a button on any given Web page to open a voice link with a service representative. In some cases, sites will offer a call-back button that lets consumers request that a service representative call them on the telephone at a certain time. One of the great marriages in commerce is the instant ordering made possible by the Internet and overnight delivery made possible by companies like Federal Express and Airborne Express. Last Christmas, shoppers discovered on some sites, like the one for the computer products dealer PC Connection, that they could place an order by midnight on Dec. 23 and have the item in hand by Christmas Eve. Several new companies, including Shipper.com (www.shipper.com), are experimenting with same-day courier fulfillment, meaning the customer can place an order and receive it the same day. The service is currently limited to the Los Angeles and San Francisco areas, with plans to expand to newyork City, Chicago and several other large cities in 2000. Will customers be willing to pay for rapid delivery? While some balk at the "hidden" charges for shipping and handling, others find it more convenient to pay than to spend the afternoon driving from store to store looking for an item. "At first I questioned whether we should even put $1.95 stuff in our store," said Daniel Head of CBS Sportsline. "What customer is going to spend $5.95 for shipping and handling for a $1.95 boat bracket? It turns out the customer was in newyork City, and $5.95 was a bargain when you consider the cost of a cab, or parking, and just the hassle of looking for the part in the city."  At High Enough Speeds, Possibilities Are Endless AS more customers go shopping on the Internet through high-speed connections at the office, or through new home services, on-line businesses will be able to deploy multimedia technologies featuring voice, video or both. Several years from now, as technology progresses, shoppers will most likely be able to shop in virtual reality stores, where they will be immersed in a three-dimensional world, able to roam simulated aisles looking at products on virtual shelves. Already, shopping on the Internet is expanding into real-world stores. Sales kiosks connected to the Internet allow some shops, like Radio Shack and the Gap, to offer customers access to on-line catalogues containing far more choices than can fit in the store. Coupled with new wireless Internet devices, like the 3Com Corporation's Palm VII handheld computer or the next generation of Web-enabled mobile phones, these new Internet technologies will transform shopping. In Finland, for example, consumers can already point their digital phones at a gasoline pump or vending machine and then dial an access code to have the purchase billed to their phone accounts. "I foresee shoppers walking through Wal-Mart with their connected Palm Pilots, comparing prices with other stores even as they walk down the aisles," said Peter Zandan, a founder of an Internet start-up company called Zilliant that is developing an assortment of smart software assistants.   PETER H. LEWIS http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawings (Ellen Weinstein); (Elaine Cardella)

title: Direct Marketers Find Some Familiar Ground
body: BEFORE there was anything electronic about commerce, there were companies selling goods directly to retail customers who could neither touch their purchases nor see those from whom they were buying -- the same businesses filling mailboxes with catalogues day after day. The catalogue companies pioneered innovations like database marketing, relationship marketing and advertising accountability. Then E-commerce arrived and the world changed. Today, it seems, everyone has a Web site. And everyone is trying to sell something to the public using the same one-on-one model that traditional direct marketers have been using for years. As a result, the pioneers in the field now see their markets threatened and their business models challenged. Or do they? While their track records are as varied as the businesses themselves, trends nevertheless are emerging. And, on the whole, it looks as if the traditional catalogue companies are adapting quite well to the age of electronic commerce. It stands to reason. For catalogue sellers, the Internet is a natural -- a "new medium for traditional direct marketing," as H. Robert Wientzen, the president of the Direct Marketing Association, calls it. Although fear of new technology made many of them slow to take to E-commerce -- at first their Web sites were little more than places to order their printed catalogues -- Mr. Wientzen said that 90 percent of his group's members were on line in some way and that 60 percent of them were selling. And they do not find the game -- or its rules -- that much different from what it was before. "It's just an extension of what we already do," said Mark Staudinger of Eddie Bauer Inc., a subsidiary of the catalogue company Spiegel Inc., based in Redmond, Wash. He is the vice president for the company's Interactive Media division, which was started in 1993, the proverbial dawn of the Internet age. Eddie Bauer has long followed what Mr. Staudinger called a "multichannel" approach to getting and keeping customers: catalogues, retail stores and, now, E-commerce. Total company sales were $1.7 billion last year, and though the company will not break out its figures any further, he said its Internet sales last year had increased 210 percent compared with 1997. Like Mr. Staudinger, officials at other catalogue companies say that most customers view the Internet as an additional means of communicating with sellers and not necessarily as a substitute for the others they have always used. "The Internet is just another option for our customers," said Thane Ryland, a spokesman for Lands' End in Dodgeville, Wis., which had $61 million in Internet sales last year out of a total of $1.37 billion. Rakesh Kaul, the president of Hanover Direct, goes further. "There is no such thing as a pure Internet customer," he said. Hanover, based in Weehawken, N.J., has 14 paper catalogues that are also on the Internet, including International Male, the Company Store and Tweeds. All of the company's customers are "hybrids," said Mr. Kaul, buying from catalogues and mailings and on the telephone and the Internet. Internet shopping, however, provides both buyers and sellers with capabilities that other media do not. Customers can even try on clothing purchases on line -- at least in a virtual sense -- by making use of features like Lands' End's "Your Personal Model," an interactive feature that enables women to build and store a three-dimensional model of themselves and select clothing that is flattering to their size and shape. But don't expect your mailbox to grow less cluttered. Despite the flash and dazzle of such Internet features, direct marketers agree that use of the Web remains a relatively ineffective way of getting new customers on board in the first place. There, time-honored techniques like direct-mail advertising and large-scale cataloguemailings remain the methods of choice. And that is something that gives the traditional catalogue companies a leg up on Internet-only, Johnny-come-lately operations that lack expertise in traditional media, said Andy Johnson, the president of E-commerce for Fingerhut in Minnetonka, Minn., a direct marketer of general merchandise, clothing and specialty foods. That does not mean that every company in the direct-marketing field is finding the transition easy. Clubs, like Book of the Month Club and its many imitators, are not. The club business model -- of which Book of the Month Club is probably the best known -- is quite different from that of the catalogues, which often sell their own exclusive goods. The clubs manufacture their products as licensees of the publishers and music companies that own the rights to them. The clubs, in turn, guarantee the publishers and music companies a minimum amount in royalties. All the products sold -- books and compact disks, for example -- can also be bought in retail stores or from on-line retailers. Historically, the clubs made money because of low unit cost and because members, lured by promotional offers, generally bought a significant number of books or compact disks. Sometimes that was because they agreed to a minimum commitment and because, until recently, most clubs followed a "negative option" model, in which customers automatically received a book or a disk if they did not return a card specifically rejecting it. For their part, members joined because they thought the clubs would be a good value and, very often, because the clubs offered them advice and expertise in choosing their selections. The music clubs also get a lift every time a new technology rolls around, like the audiocassette and, more recently, the compact disk. But consumer tastes are changing, as is technology. People do not necessarily want a long-term relationship with a club or an automatic selection. The "hot" technology in music these days is not a new kind of disk but the instant, direct Internet download. And because books and music lend themselves to direct marketing -- that is why the clubs started -- they have been the first products to be widely sold on the Internet by new on-line sellers like Amazon.com, which has been discounting aggressively. In response, many clubs have dropped their purchase commitments. Columbia House, a music club, decided to abandon the negative option in Play, a club begun in 1998 that already accounts for the majority of Columbia House sales, said Sharon Kuroki, the executive vice president for music marketing. Columbia House is also emphasizing specialization. By virtue of its ability to mine its database to determine what members have bought in the past, the club can market to each customer's specific taste. According to Ms. Kuroki, the result is 17 different "listening preference" categories, including three Latin and three Christian ones. By contrast, the catalogue companies are using their special strengths to survive. Many have also begun selling their back-office capabilities to direct-marketing neophytes that want to jump feet first into the Internet waters. Hanover Direct, for example, has opened a division called Keystone Fulfillment to service other marketers that do not have the infrastructure to enter E-commerce on their own. And there is Catalog City, which is owned in part by the Bear Creek Corporation in Medford, Ore., the parent company of Harry and David Orchards, themail-order seller of gift fruit. Catalog City allows hundreds of smaller operations to have a Web presence without investing in expensive technology, said Lee Lorenzen, Catalog City's president. The company's Web site, www.catalogcity .com, also features pages from catalogue companies that have a separate Internet presence but contract with Mr. Lorenzen's firm to expand their market reach. Fingerhut was so successful in promoting its ability to provide service to others that one of its customers, Federated Department Stores, ended up buying the company earlier this year. "As the retail industry sees itself maturing, there aren't a whole lot of places left to put stores," said Mr. Wientzen of the Direct Marketing Association, explaining the acquisition. "So direct marketers like Fingerhut are seen as a good way to expand." Fingerhut has taken over Federated's direct-marketing division, assuming responsibility for the direct-marketing businesses Federated used to run on its own, like Bloomingdale's by Mail and Macys.com. And it has recently contracted with Wal-Mart Stores Inc., the world's largest retailer, to handle its on-line sales. All of which means that everyone wants to be everywhere. And that, perhaps, is where the Internet has had its greatest effect on direct marketers: hastening a trend that had already begun in the 1980's and even earlier. Following the lead of companies like Eddie Bauer and Victoria's Secret, which went from catalogues to retail stores to the Internet, other direct marketers are now going from catalogues to the Internet and into stores at an ever-faster pace. And traditional retailers and catalogue companies are also acquiring one another at a breathtaking rate. Consider L. L. Bean, the enormously successful catalogue seller, which for 87 years had no retail stores except for its famous flagship in Freeport, Me. Lately, it has upgraded its Web presence; last spring, it announced its intention to open stores. Even the world of business-to-business marketing is not exempt from the trend. The office-supply retailer Staples last year acquired Quill, one of the nation's largest mail-order suppliers of office materials. And Staples's archrival, Office Depot, took over Viking, one of Quill's main competitors. It's all a "blurring of the traditional channels of trade," said Mr. Wientzen, with only one logical result. "Everyone," he said, "is becoming a direct marketer." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Lisa Adams)

title: Drugstores Scramble to Find Choice Corners in Cyberspace
body: NOW that the big pharmacy chains seem to have built facing drugstores at every intersection in America, the competition to sell aspirin, shampoo and antibiotics is moving onto the Internet just as aggressively. The idea has a lot going for it. From a practical standpoint, drugstore products are easy to ship. A pile of toiletries fits neatly in a relatively small package. And even the fruitiest of shampoos are nonperishable. More important to customers, on-line pharmacies can make it easier than ever to refill a prescription or shop around for the best deal in over-the-counter remedies. At some sites, detailed information about individual prescriptions and thousands of health care products is only a click or two away. The potential for persuading on-line customers to add a host of other, more profitable items to their prescription orders is so great that the market has grown crowded since the beginning of the year. Drugstore.com grabbed the media spotlight early as a result of its 40 percent backing by the on-line bookseller Amazon.com About the same time, Planetrx.com and Soma.com opened, sending the chain drugstores scrambling to bring their Web sites up to speed. But to get from here to there, retailers have discovered they need the blessing of the pharmacy benefit managers, the companies that manage prescription benefits for health insurance plans. That blessing is slow in coming. Pharmacy benefit managers arrange networks of pharmacies to fill prescriptions for the plans they manage and then reimburse the stores for prescription costs. Patients are more likely to shop at network pharmacies, where they can be sure their co-payments will be honored. So it behooves all pharmacies, on line and otherwise, to maintain contracts with benefit managers. On-line pharmacies are not being warmly received in these networks because of a turf war over mail-order prescriptions. The largest pharmacy benefit managers, Merck-Medico Managed Care, Express Scripts and PCS Health Systems, have long held exclusive contracts with their clients for 90-day mail-order business. Reluctant to give ground to new competitors, some are aggressively moving ahead with their own on-line pharmacies. If the fierce battle between Amazon.com and Barnesandnoble.com over the comparatively paltry $15 billion book market is any indicator of what is ahead, the on-line drugstore wars should be fierce. The pharmacy benefit managers' influence has already reshaped an industry that began early this year as a few high-profile on-line pharmacy upstarts and is now a complex array of independent ventures and strategic partnerships. "Right now there's a lot of push and shove," said Evie Black Dykema, an E-commerce analyst for Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. "Everyone's staking out their ground." The territory is huge. According to the National Association of Chain Drugstores, the retail drugstore industry is a $153.6 billion market. Chains account for about 60 percent of prescription drug sales, which total about $103 billion and are growing by about 10 percent a year, leading the president of Drugstore.com, Peter Neupert, to observe gleefully, "That's $10 billion in revenue just in new prescriptions every year." Drugstore.com and Soma.com figured out quickly that they would need powerful allies to gain access to that revenue. One week, Mr. Neupert was boasting of the superiority of his on-line store to real drugstores, and the next he was announcing a partnership with the Rite Aid chain. That deal gave Drugstore.com access to the 50 million customers served by PCS of Scottsdale, Ariz., the second-largest pharmacy benefit manager and a subsidiary of the Rite Aid Corporation, based in Camp Hill, Pa. Though Drugstore.com will remain an independent pharmacy, Rite Aid and PCS will have access to its site to make Internet sales. Just before that deal was announced in June, the CVS Corporation said that it was acquiring Soma.com for $30 million. As the country's largest drugstore chain, CVS, based in Woonsocket, R.I., has 55 million prescription customers and about 9,000 insurance providers. "We see the Internet as a logical, natural extension of our focus on convenience and value," said Larry Zigerelli, the executive vice president for corporate development at CVS. "Our Internet customers may choose to have their prescriptions mailed, or in the case of acute prescriptions, to pick them up in-store." While Mr. Zigerelli said that most pharmacy benefit managers had already worked out a mail option with CVS, some of the largest are holding out, choosing instead to carve out their own presence on line. Just last month, Express Scripts announced that it was transferring its fledgling E-commerce subsidiary, Yourpharmacy.com, to Planetrx Inc., which will become the exclusive on-line pharmacy for Express Scripts' 36 million members. In return, Planetrx will pay the company more than $11 million a year in fees. Express Scripts will continue to handle 90-day mail-order prescriptions, about 10 percent of its business, said Barrett Toan, the company's president and chief executive. But Planetrx will fill 30-day mail-order prescriptions for Express Scripts customers and try to sell them health and beauty products at the same time. Express Scripts customers who shop at other on-line pharmacies will have to pay full price if they want their prescriptions shipped. However, co-payments will be honored when they order prescriptions at a chain drugstore Web site, like CVS.com, and pick them up at a store. That retail store business, after all, is the lifeblood of the pharmacy benefit managers. "Certain products like antibiotics will always be the exclusive domain of the retail pharmacy," Mr. Toan said. "We don't see that changing." T he chains agree with that perspective but carry it one step further, arguing that their contracts with benefit managers extend to their on-line operations regardless of whether the prescriptions they fill are picked up at the store or shipped. "The 90-day mail-order prescription -- that is business the P.B.M.'s have today and that will remain," Mr. Zigerelli said. "The 30-day, 60-day, or sometimes even 20-day prescription -- that is business that we fill. We fully expect that all of our on-line customers will be able to receive their prescriptions by mail if they choose." No one is sure how this will play out. But David Restrepo, a health analyst at Jupiter Communications in newyork, speculated that the pharmacy-benefit managers would have to reach a compromise. Such an awareness is hinted at in the contract between Drugstore.com and PCS, he noted. While Drugstore.com will be the exclusive on-line vehicle for mail-order prescriptions for PCS, the contract leaves the way open for PCS to fill 30-day prescriptions for retailers who set up shop on the Internet. As for whether on-line pharmacies will supplant the corner drugstore, the National Association of Chain Drugstores is reserving comment. "There's no good way to determine their impact yet," said Phillip Schneider, the director of public affairs for the association. But Mr. Zigerelli does not expect much pain at CVS. He expects on-line pharmacy sales to account for no more than 10 percent of the industry's revenue over the next decade. And he said he expected the Internet to open new territory for CVS stores west of the Mississippi. Though many people will begin to buy their prescriptions and toiletries without going near their neighborhood pharmacy, partnerships between on-line and retail stores will continue to be crucial for reasons that have nothing to do with co-payments. No matter how many choices they have on line, some customers still will want to talk to a pharmacist in person. "The level of personal interaction is a lot more important in this category than in, say, books and CD's," said Erik Brynjolfsson, the co-director of the program on electronic commerce and marketing at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. "The on-line approach can bring in some cost-effectiveness, but what they lack is face-to-face human interaction." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: . . . across from this CVS store has hit the Internet with full force, producing a bevy of pharmacy sites. The brick-and-mortar competition that put this Duane Reade drugstore in Manhattan . . . (Photographs by Ozier Muhammad/The newyork Times)

title: Even Beyond the Big Guys, A Wealth of Auction Choices
body: EBAY, Amazon.com and Yahoo are the 800-pound gorilla and two 400-pound siblings in the auction business, but there are hundreds of similar sites. But despite a "build it and they will come" business plan, most of the sites have fewer than 200 items for sale at any one time; many have fewer than 25. A lot of sites are conducting promotional campaigns, including reducing fees, to attract a critical mass of users. Yet, in contrast to Ebay, many of the smaller person-to-person auctions out there remain a buyer's market -- if buyers are willing to scour skimpy listings for bargains. Some say Ebay has become so large that a fragmentation of auction sites into specialized niches is inevitable. The best bets for alternative auctions are actually companies and dealers who have decided to put their wares on line. Ranging from travel agencies to Hollywood film companies to wine dealers, these seller-operated auction sites have a guaranteed up-to-date selection of products. Here is a sampling of the nongorilla auction sites:  General Interest  WWW.AUCTIONWATCH.COM -- This is an auction lover's comprehensive all-purpose site. It gathers auction-related news articles and operates lively message boards on which auction aficionados gripe, praise and compare. An up-to-date list of more than 500 auction-oriented sites is well organized and simple to understand.  WWW.UP4SALE.COM -- Recently acquired by Ebay, Up4sale.com is a free auction, meaning that it charges no commissions and no listing fees for sellers. Other than toys and Beanie Babies, the most active categories, the listings are relatively sparse, making it a buyer's market.  WWW.AUCTIONUNIVERSE.COM -- For a general-interest auction, Auction Universe has some interesting features. For a $19.95 annual fee, the site will serve as an intermediary on all credit card transactions. The fee also buys $3,000 in insurance coverage and free listings. Paid members also receive a 1 percent discount on all purchases made on insured items.  Entertainment  WWW.SPORTSAUCTION.COM -- Sports Auction, which is operated by North Orlando Sports Promotions, sells autographed memorabilia and sports collectibles -- mostly photographs, baseball cards and autographed balls. Items are graded for their condition and come with letters of authenticity from North Orlando.  WWW.AUCTION.NEWLINE.COM -- New Line Cinema auctions off original props and wardrobe and promotional items from New Line films. "Austin Powers" items have been hottest of late; a car from "The Spy Who Shagged Me" recently sold for $121,000. A portion of all auction proceeds goes to the Legal Aid Society and Citymeals-on-Wheels in newyork.  Travel  WWW.SKYAUCTION.COM -- This travel agency Web site sells plane tickets and vacation packages to places all over the world. Rather than selling point-to-point destinations on specific dates, the agency generally offers a range of cities and dates. The more flexible the ticket, the higher the bids. Bidders should note that taxes can add a significant amount to the purchase price.  WWW.ADVENTUREBID.COM -- This site offers discounted vacations, including trips built around mountain biking, white-water rafting and safaris, and other packages for groups and individuals. Adventurebid.com works directly with tour operators, which are either trying to fill up spots on existing tours or to sell more tours.  Computers  WWW.BID.COM -- Bid.com focuses on selling refurbished consumer electronics and computer equipment with manufacturer-backed warranties. The moderate selection includes computers, monitors, digital cameras, phones, VCR's and televisions. Purchases can be returned within 30 days at a 15 percent processing fee.  AUCTIONS.CNET.COM -- The technology-news provider Cnet introduced an auction site in May for person-to-person technology sales. There are thousands of computers. There is also a 3 percent listing fee, plus additional fees if your item is to be highlighted on the site. Sales of Furbys are forbidden.  Hobbies  WWW.PHILATELISTS.COM -- A stamp lover's auction site, Philatelists Online offers dozens of auctions from accredited philatelic dealers and auction houses. Items range from beginner stamps for the new collector to expensive stamps for the investor. A recent high bid for a single 1875 30-cent stamp was $6,000. The dealers offer a range of historical, international and odd stamps and advice for beginners.  WWW.NUMISMATISTS.COM -- One of several hobbyist auction sites, Numismatists Online caters to coin and currency collectors with auctions from accredited dealers and auction houses. Items up for sale range from gold dollars to ancient Greek and Roman coins to other foreign currencies.  WWW.AUCTIONVINE.COM -- Auction Vine sells rare and interesting wines on behalf of accredited dealers. Recently, wines up for auction ranged from a Sonoma Russian River Valley Pinot Noir, which went for around $40, to a Bordeaux Graves Meritage from 1961, which went for more than $750. A recent high bid was two lots of 1870 Lafite-Rothschild for $11,000 each. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Nannette Finkel Rebach)

title: For a Perky Do-It-Yourself Web Site, the Price Was Right
body: HAVING your own electronic commerce Web site does not have to be hard or expensive. I know, because I helped my friend Dave Wolff -- who runs a coffee shop but doesn't know from Java -- put his business on line, with lots of links and pictures and other bells and whistles, for next to nothing. Since then, the price has gone down. And Dave still doesn't even own a working computer. Now that he's on line, Dave uses the Web to research sources of bagels and egg-cream syrup, lure customers in with special promotions and to sell coffee-related items. More important, the site is helping the coffee shop, the Fine Grind, act as a focal point for an otherwise scattered community of people interested in poetry, music and art in the rural area around Bel Air, Md., 45 miles north of Baltimore. And creating that kind of community was the fantasy Dave had in mind when he gave up his career managing an office high-rise to open a coffee shop. He had suspected that farm country might actually have some hip people who would enjoy exotic coffee and jazz but were not connected by any urban core or meeting place. The Internet was a logical way to try to reach them, but after espresso machines and air-conditioning, there was not enough money left for even Internet access, much less a computer. Having observed the trend toward free everything on the Web, we decided to see how far we could get noodling around without spending money. We got pretty far. Here's how: Once just search sites, outfits like Yahoo, Infoseek and Netscape are now trying to be all-purpose life crutches. Besides free stock quotes and free email, free Web sites are offered to get you to make these portals your on-line home. Each one is different. While Yahoo has great email and a customizable start page, Web pages built on its Geocities service have an advertising page pop up whenever anyone views your site. Netscape has a good start page and multifeatured Web site services, but its email system can get overloaded and is cluttered with ads unless you pay a fee. Netscape and Yahoo will forward copies of incoming email to a pager, handy for E-store owners on the run. Netscape and others will offer email-to-fax services for a fee. A new two-way pager, E-link, will even allow complete wireless sending and receiving of mail with Yahoo, Netscape or other mail services, for a portable E-store on a belt. Infoseek offers a simple, uncluttered operation, with Web-building kits ranging from basic to deluxe and no banner ads promoting its service on your Web page. To find dozens of other free Web-site places, just type "free Web site" into a search engine. Having your email and Web site at one stop may be convenient, but we opted for the sophisticated Yahoo mail and the uncluttered Infoseek Web pages. If you pay a company for Internet access, it probably already has a free Web space reserved for you, covered by your monthly fee. America Online has several Web kits on line for instant sites, as do many other Internet Service Providers. Building your page can be as simple as filling in a couple of lines of contact information on a template in basic on-line kits. When we registered for email at Yahoo and Web space at Infoseek, the only problem was thinking up names that had not already been taken that sounded like the Fine Grind. We had a site up and running in about 20 minutes, using Infoseek's most basic instant page. With a big "Welcome" graphic at the top, the store name and address, and an email link that when clicked brought up an automatic mail form to the Yahoo account. We thought it was pretty neat, especially for free. We started to use the email account immediately -- to find a way to have real bagels and chocolate egg cream syrup delivered from newyork. Dave ran down the street to the Harford County library a couple of times a day to check and send mail. He was on line. After a couple of weeks, though, we lusted for more: a site with our own text, our own art and pictures of products, and that didn't look too square. Maybe even moving images. We tried the next level up of Infoseek's kits, the Web Architect. We were able to put in our fill of pictures, links and text. By studying Web sites we admired and experimenting with design elements we found on line, we strove for site coolness. Other than a nonboring but authoritative type font and background, it seemed that the images were the key to not looking like an amateur. If you have art in your computer -- like photos of your business, products or logos -- you can add them to even the most basic Web kit. An entire universe of free pictures, animated drawings, backgrounds, borders, buttons and icons is available on line. We quickly learned that while it is possible to put many images on a page, each one makes the page slower. A good rule is to only put a few pieces of art on a page. If you need more, like for a catalogue, make more pages and place links to them on the first page. Remember to include contact information and a link back to the home page. Once we were confident that the site and mail really worked and seemed somewhat professional, we knew it was time to step up to what might appear to be the big time. We thought our site looked as good as some big-business ones, but something was missing.  What we needed was our own Web address, or a domain name. At the time, reserving a domain wasn't too hard, just a matter of paying $70, but finding one not already taken in the great land rush seemed tough. Making one actually work with a real Web site, though, was tough. Usually a domain-hosting company is hired to house both the name and the Web site. Searching for really cheap hosts, I stumbled on some companies that would inexpensively host the domain name and forward requests for it to any Web site we chose, like the free one we had already set up. They were virtual hosts. Fees were only about $50 a year. Some would also forward email requests, because when you get your own domain, you also get all the email addresses associated with it that you can think up. I chose Mydomain, because it forwarded both mail and Web-site requests and had reduced fees for additional domains (I was planning to set up my own site, too). Just recently, Mydomain announced it would do all this for free, which is a good price. It hopes to sell premium services to users, like advanced email management, to make money. You can search for available domain names and register them at many sites. The easiest place I have found to search is at EasyDNS (www.easydns.com), because when you type in "yourcompanyname.com," it also tries "yourcompanyname.net" and "yourcompanyname.org." It turned out that "www.finegrind.net" was available, astonishing because a Web nationwide yellow page look-up had turned up dozens of similarly named coffee joints. We registered it right away and received a $70 bill from Network Solutions a couple of weeks later. Other than Mydomain's service, which is now available for free, that was our only expense. Currently, the main page has 19 links, four small graphics, including a spinning cup of coffee, and a news ticker we put on by following cut-and-paste directions. The links go to Web sites related to Bel Air but especially to sites we thought people could really use, like live weather radar for our area and an interactive map to the store. One link goes to a page with an Internet Coupon we dreamed up to see whether anyone was paying attention. I copied a $50 bill from a clip-art site and superimposed Dave's picture on it with Photodeluxe, an amateur version of Photoshop that comes in the box with many digital cameras. And a couple of times a week, Dave has to quickly think up an Internet Special Item, like a free biscotti. Once a week, we update the schedule of art openings, music, poetry and the book club. Since submitting the site to the major search engines, email has come from six countries, some with orders. The previously dispersed and disconnected artists, urban refugees, former hippies, business people, farmers, poets and the just curious of Harford County are now visiting the site and the store, in person. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Dave Wolff at the counter of his coffeehouse, the Fine Grind, in Bel Air, Md. (Marty Katz for The newyork Times)

title: For This Supplier, the Sum of Its Parts Adds Up to Success
body: PEOPLE looking for fast-paced, cutting-edge careers tend not to think about manufacturing valves, maintenance products and replacement parts for industry. Even less exciting would be cataloguing and distributing such mundane wares, which is how W. W. Grainger Inc. makes a living. But Grainger is a good example of how even the most seemingly humdrum businesses are undergoing reconstructive surgery as E-commerce spreads through the economy. And Grainger's story shows how old-line industry stalwarts are not easy to shove aside in the business-to-business E-commerce sector, where reputations for reliability, speedy delivery and expert advice may be even more important than they are with consumer-product companies. Middlemen like Grainger, which is based in the Chicago suburb of Lincolnshire and had $4.43 billion in revenue in 1998, prosper by making life more efficient or less expensive for commercial buyers and sellers. The company says that about 80 percent of all American businesses are within a 20-minute drive of a Grainger branch. Grainger carries more than 4,000 different sizes and types of motors. It describes its lighting selection as "every light bulb known to man." In all, the company offers its 1.5 million customers about 210,000 products, and its red-covered catalogue (also in CD-ROM form), which runs to more than 4,000 pages, is one of the most widely distributed publications in business. Grainger consultants help businesses sort out purchasing policies, and some companies hire Grainger to make their purchasing decisions. But even relative giants like Grainger own a small piece of the pie. Businesses spend $300 billion a year in the unitedstates in Grainger's area of expertise: the equipment and services grouped into what is known as M.R.O., or maintenance, repair and operations. They spend $200 billion more managing the procurement offices, receiving operations and other activities that are needed to make those purchases. No wonder Internet entrepreneurs have smelled opportunity. Although it has happened less visibly than in the book and toy businesses and other consumer markets, Grainger's blue-collar world is also on the menu for upstart companies that are built around powerful software and visions of a new, Internet-based order. Investors clearly anticipate a revolution in business-to-business commerce. When Commerce One, which created an Internet marketplace for business buyers and suppliers, went public in July, its shares soared to $62 from $21 on the first day of trading. A few weeks earlier, its rival Ariba did even better, with its shares quickly jumping to $90 from $23. The market is also being shaken up by business-software vendors. For example, Project Software and Development, which is known for production-management software, has set up an Internet marketplace at www.mro.com. By combining orders for its clients, Project Software expects to negotiate lower prices. GIANTS like SAP and Oracle are also working on Internet-based procurement software that could streamline buying and encourage buyers to cut out middlemen whose computers cannot link to those software programs. Another group of vendors, including Freemarkets Online, is using the Internet to set up custom auctions. Instead of contacting manufacturers individually or checking Grainger's catalogue for prices and delivery terms, a buyer could tell Freemarket what it needs and let Freemarket set up an auction in which qualified suppliers bid for the contract. So, is Grainger, with its overhead of more than 15,000 employees and a network of more than 500 branches, in danger of being shoved aside? Hardly. When it comes to business-to-business electronic commerce, traditional industry leaders have huge built-in advantages, industry analysts say. Businesses are much more varied in their needs than, say, the book purchasers served by Amazon.com or Barnesandnoble.com. Many companies place a high value on proven distribution systems like Grainger's, which their employees know how to deal with, and on the expert advice that experienced middlemen can provide. "In the end, the bricks-and-mortar companies will win," said Barbara Reilly, the research director of E-business strategies at the Gartner Group in Stamford, Conn. That is, Ms. Reilly and other analysts say, assuming those companies adopt effective Internet strategies. Few have worked harder at doing that than Grainger, which has invested $35 million in a range of E-commerce initiatives. "We're focused on leading the evolution," said Donald E. Bielinski, a Grainger group president who is overseeing electronic commerce. That wave is too powerful for Grainger to exert much control over, but analysts say the company is doing a deft job of riding it so far. "At first I thought they were being defensive, but the more I look, the more I see offensive possibilities," said Russell Leavitt, an analyst at Banc of America Securities. Grainger set up www.grainger .com, its "digital storefront," in 1995. On-line sales jumped to about $9 million a month this summer from a little more than $3 million a month in the first three months of this year. Grainger calculates that 20 percent of the traffic on its site takes place outside normal business hours and that the average order is twice the size of the one received through traditional phone and fax contacts. The company followed up its Web site by developing Orderzone.com, a marketplace where customers can order not just from Grainger but also from leading distributors in other business segments. Orderzone leaves much to be desired for buyers who want E-commerce sites that are smoothly integrated with their own procurement-management systems. It offers one-stop shopping and payment but does not yet track deliveries, retain records of past orders or make it simple for buyers to compare competing products. Grainger says that thousands of companies have registered since Orderzone.com went on line in mid-May but declined to release early revenue figures. Mr. Bielinski said that a surprising number of big customers had signed on, apparently seeking experience with what could be a step toward a full-service marketplace. But the most intriguing piece of Grainger's E-commerce strategy has been its collaboration with many of the newcomers and large software companies like SAP, whose products and goals could make Grainger's life more difficult. Grainger has signed alliances aimed at insuring that as many software programs and Internet portals as possible link to its own site and to Orderzone.com. IT is a risky approach. The other players may make it easy for Grainger customers to move to other suppliers or, by joining orders from many customers at a portal like MRO.com, pressure Grainger to cut prices. But Grainger has done more than sign on as a supplier; it has also taken stakes in several other concerns, including Project Software and Commerce One. "Grainger is very Internet savvy," said Norman E. Drapeau Jr., the president and chief executive officer of Project Software. "They understand that some piece of their business may be cannibalized." As Grainger sees it, though, the explosion in pathways to its doorway will give it more chances to exploit its brand name and distribution system. "I have a real tough time with the word 'competitor' in the digital marketplace," Mr. Bielinski said. "There is so much room for cooperation. The potential payoff is huge." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: W. W. Grainger's distribution center in New Hyde Park, N.Y., has widgets of every kind. (Andrea Mohin/The newyork Times)

title: Hewlett-Packard Is in Deal To Lift Its Internet Presence
body: The Hewlett-Packard Company, long a laggard behind Sun Microsystems and I.B.M. in computer systems for electronic commerce, took a step toward strengthening its Internet presence with the announcement today of a deal with the Oracle Corporation to collaborate on developing and selling Oracle's electronic commerce software on Hewlett-Packard computers. Oracle said it would make HP-UX, Hewlett-Packard's version of the Unix operating system, a "strategic development platform" for all of Oracle's E-business software applications. In practical terms, this should insure that each new version of Oracle's software runs as well on Hewlett-Packard's computers as it does on machines made by Sun, Hewlett-Packard's archrival in the network and Internet server market. Oracle has long given priority to developing for Sun's Solaris variant of Unix. The endorsement of Oracle, the clear leader in software for electronic commerce, is key to Hewlett-Packard's Internet products, which it calls e-services. The benefit to Oracle is less clear, but it could give a lift to the company's new customer relationship management applications, or C.R.M., which manage tasks like sales contacts and service calls. Hewlett-Packard has agreed to use and co-sell the Oracle Sales component of Oracle's C.R.M. suite of software programs. Oracle has said it views C.R.M. as a major source of growth for the next decade. On a day of broad market downturns, Hewlett-Packard shares closed at $99.375, down $4.6875, on the newyork Stock Exchange, while Oracle shares closed at $44.50, down 62.5 cents, in Nasdaq trading. "We are together addressing the C.R.M. market first because it is the fastest-growing market today," Carly Fiorina, Hewlett-Packard's president and chief executive, said at a news conference at the company's Palo Alto, Calif., headquarters this morning. "This is a major shift from the way Hewlett-Packard has done business in the past when we were more of a Switzerland, partnering with everybody. Today we are making a clear choice." This was the first major announcement from Hewlett-Packard since Ms. Fiorina took the company's reins in July. It is part of a strategy articulated by Ann Livermore, president of the enterprise computing division, to announce a new strategic partnership every week, emphasizing deals intended to irritate Sun and I.B.M. and counter the perception of Hewlett-Packard as the also-ran of the Web. Nick Earle, Hewlett-Packard's senior vice president and chief marketing officer for the enterprise computing division, noted that the company's stock price had doubled since the e-services strategy was announced. "The Internet aura has been successfully applied to H.P.," he said. Analysts said the deal helped Hewlett-Packard at the expense of Sun, which every year sells billions of dollars worth of servers running Oracle's data base software. But Gary Bloom, Oracle's executive vice president, insisted that the company would not emphasize one hardware platform over another. "I don't think the close relationship with Sun has changed at all," Mr. Bloom said in a telephone interview. He said the major benefit to Oracle would be adding Hewlett-Packard's sales force to the marketing of its customer relationship management software. "I get a virtual extension of the Oracle sales organization," he said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: How to Talk Dot-Com Like a Webmaster
body: EVERY leap of technology brings its own leap of jargon. After all, it's an easy way for Early Adopters to distinguish themselves from I-Just-Learned-How-to-Program-My-VCR-and-Now-You-Expect-Me-to-Do-WWW-What? Adopters. Here's a guide to some of the more useful new terms.   GILES FELTON COOKIES Affiliates Sites that steer users to another E-commerce site in return for a percentage of any purchase; when you www.garliclovers.org site, for example, provides a link to something like www.garlicpeelersRus.com for a piece of the action. Click and mortar A business that combines traditional retail (brick and mortar) and on-line shopping. Cookies The coding placed on your hand drive that stores information abuot you and makes it available to the computers running Web sites that use passwords or offer personalized services. It is what makes all those My-whatever personalized sites possible. It also holds stunning potential for violations of privacy if someone hacks into My-whatever and steals your cookies' recipes. Data mining Every clock tells a story, but only after powerful software engines sort through the information collected from thousands of Web browsers. This information is stored in vast data warehouses and mined for a few nuggets about how to drive Web shoppers wild. E- The all-purpose Internet and Web prefix. It stands for electronic, though you could say any business that uses electricity has a right to that claim. But the E- is already familiar from email (which it does make sense to call electronic mail). Also, it sounds cooler than I-this or W-that. Guest book The polite (deceptive?) way for Web sites to get your email address and other useful facts that may be used to send you spam, as unwanted electronic mail has become known. HTML Hypertext Markup Language is the computer code in which Web sites are created. It is being supplanted by XML, or Extensible Markup Language, a more flexible system. Java This programming language makes a lot of the coolest Web effects, like animation, possible. Java is supposed to be "platform independent," so that programs written in it can run on any Windows, Apple or Unix computer equipped to use Java. Links Connections from one Web page to another. See how "window" is high-lighted in blue in "what light through yonder window breaks?" Click on it and you may find yourself at ww.al'sframesandglass.com MP3 Doesn't stand for anything. Scarier than y2K to much of the recording industry, MP3 is shorthand for a technology that can compress music files to a size that makes them easy to send over the Internet, where copyright laws can be difficult to enforce. Portals Sites that hope to attract you by offering to guide you to where you want to go are portals. But to keep you on their page, and reading the advertising they sell, they offer an ever-wider range of services like email and news updates with search engines. Yahoo and Excite are two fo the biggest portals. SSL Secure Sockets Layer, the dominant security protocol for Internet transactions and communications. Information being transmitted is encrypted, and only the user's Web browser and the computer server running the receiving Web site have the key. Shopping agents A form of bot (yes, from robot), the name given to programs that carry out their mission automatically. Shopping agents will search, with varying levels of skill, detail and perseverance for the best deal on whatever you tell them you want to buy. Stickness The marketing buzzword of the moment. A sticky site is one that keeps users glued to it, either through sheer intrinsic niftiness or by piling layer upon layer of more-or-less-related offerings, like stock quotes, weather updates or interactive whiz-bangs like sports trivia quizzes. URL Uniform Resource Locator. A site's Web address the thing that usually stars with www. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawings

title: In a Legal Gray Area, Blackjack Is a Click Away
body: KEVIN LACEY, a 41-year-old architect, was no gambler. He had never even been to Las Vegas, Nev. But when he saw a magazine advertisement about playing blackjack on the Internet, he was intrigued. Just for fun, he found the Web site, keyed in his credit card, played a few hands and won a couple of dollars. That was three years ago. Now Mr. Lacey is more than $60,000 in debt. "I've maxed out seven credit cards," said Mr. Lacey, who recently entered a gambling addiction program. "I've got to get this monster under control." Hundreds of "cybercasinos" have come on line since 1995, giving almost anyone with a computer and a credit card the chance to gamble. Americans last year wagered an estimated $1 billion on line in a form that thrives in a legal twilight zone as advances in technology have outpaced the law. These cybercasinos are based offshore, many of them on Caribbean islands, because gambling in the unitedstates requires specific legal permission. On-line casinos blur those legal boundaries. Is it illegal for a woman in Ohio, for instance, to place a bet with a cybercasino in Antigua? Does the betting occur in Ohio or in Antigua? Senator Jon Kyl, Republican of Arizona, has introduced a bill that would prohibit on-line gambling by giving judges the power to shut down Internet providers who give Web sites to cybercasinos. The Senate approved the measure last year 90 to 9, but it did not come to a vote in the House of Representatives before Congress adjourned. The bill is expected to come to the Senate floor again this fall. Mr. Kyl, the chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee's subcommittee on technology, said he thought that Internet gambling already violated the law against sports betting, which, although permitted in Las Vegas, was banned under the Federal Wire Act of 1961. But the law does not address nonsports betting. And the 1961 measure could eventually be irrelevant if satellite transmission or radio waves replace telephone lines. For now, some states have taken separate approaches, none of them altogether effective. Illinois and Louisiana have banned Internet gambling. Minnesota is studying whether on-line wagering could be regulated and licensed. And Missouri has taken court action against on-line gambling providers. Jay Nixon, the Attorney General of Missouri, has filed a Federal suit in Kansas City against the Coeur D'Alene Indian tribe in Idaho, contending that the tribe's lottery and bingo Web site violates Missouri's consumer laws, which prohibit the sale of illegal goods or services. The tribe, meanwhile, contends that the wagering is legal because it is based in a sovereign American Indian nation, where wagering is permitted. Missouri also filed suit against a Pennsylvania man for running an Internet gambling site. The man pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor charge last year and was fined $27,000. But prosecutions of Internet gambling remain rarer than a poker hand of four aces. Sue Schneider, who publishes an on-line magazine on computer gambling, Interactive Gaming News, said it would be impossible to stop people from wagering over the Internet. She said that more than 500 sites offered gambling. Instead, she said, states and the Federal Government should regulate the industry. Australia, she noted, has recently started to license on-line casinos. "You could regulate them just like you regulate any land-based gambling operation," Ms. Schneider said. Dianne Meyer, the publisher of Rolling Good Times On-Line, another Internet magazine that reports about on-line gambling, said a prohibition would drive the industry underground. That would leave consumers with no protection, she said. "This is an unregulated industry that desperately needs to be regulated," she said. But on-line gambling has relatively few defenders. In June, the National Gambling Impact Study Commission, created by Congress, called for a ban on Internet gambling. Most professional sports leagues, as well as the National Collegiate Athletic Association, have called for the prohibition of on-line wagering. The Las Vegas casino industry has called for a ban as well. Frank Fahrenkopf, the president of the American Gaming Association, which represents the casino industry, said he scoffed at the notion that his group's opposition to on-line gambling was rooted in a fear of competition. He said the industry's chief concern was that Internet gambling would tarnish all operators of casinos. Even those who support the ban, however, acknowledge that enforcement could be difficult. And the Internet providers have chafed at being forced to act as a sheriff expected to keep outlaws out of a virtual Dodge City. Acknowledging those concerns, the Kyl measure would relieve Internet providers of the responsibility to block on-line casinos in two instances: if it was technologically impossible to block access or if it was prohibitively burdensome to do so. While operators tend to be mysterious, surveys have gathered some information about users. On-line gamblers tend to be white men ages 20 to 40, often wagering on sports, said Kevin O'Neill, a spokesman for the Council on Compulsive Gambling of New Jersey. Sports betting is popular on the Internet, he said, "because everybody knows the outcome of a game -- you can't cheat on that." On-line casinos typically set up accounts with customers that debit a credit card. Losses are charged to the card, while winnings are tallied as a credit. Until now, it has been relatively easy for on-line casinos to open for business. Nearly two dozen of them are based in Antigua, where a license can be bought for $100,000 or less, and there are no taxes. Experts on gambling say on-line wagering removes most of the social barriers that inhibit gambling. There is no travel. And it can be done in private at home, so no one else has to know about it.
