Mr. Lacey, the architect who lost $60,000 to Internet gambling, said he started wagering on his computer as a way to forget off-line frustrations. "I found it as a means of escaping life's problems," he said. "I was in a bad marriage. And I had the early stages of Parkinson's." The gambling problem, he said, is a much fiercer foe than his health problem. "The Parkinson's, I can control that with medication," he said. "That gambling, that's a harder thing to control." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Kevin Lacey, whose on-line wagering left him $60,000 in debt, in the Compulsive Gambling Center's counseling room in Baltimore. (Marty Katz for The newyork Times)

title: In Brazil, Big Bank, Big Portal
body: BRAZIL'S 165 million people know the name Bradesco well: it belongs to the nation's largest bank. But now the company has used its considerable power to create Latin America's most comprehensive electronic commerce site at www.bradesco.com.br/comercio, which brings together more than 60 cyberstores. That number is expected to double in the next few months. To be allowed to operate on Bradesco's site, stores must accept the bank's rules. Bradesco not only determines who can participate, but also acts as a clearinghouse for every transaction in return for a percentage, paid by retailers. Because Brazilian consumers are fearful of credit card fraud, the bank issues a "digital certificate," allowing customers to make purchases without giving a credit card number over the Internet. The Bradesco site includes, of course, the usual purveyors of books and recorded music, Brazilian equivalents of Amazon.com or Everycd.com that can also be contacted independently if a shopper does not want to use Bradesco's services. But the site also contains stores that offer a remarkable array of other products: sporting goods, flowers, jewelry, toys, cosmetics, clothing and even vitamins. It has, in fact, succeeded in becoming the kind of dominant "portal" that the biggest players in the unitedstates -- Yahoo, Amazon.com, America Online -- can only dream of becoming. Whether or not it can keep its pre-eminent position, for now, its ability to bunch together competing stores under the same heading on the same site has been a boon to Brazilian consumers, allowing bargain hunting through comparison shopping. At the entry page, foreigners can click an icon for instructions in English and Spanish. But some of that text is less than idiomatic, and other headings have not yet been translated into English. Still, Bradesco's initiative seems to be making good on its promise to provide "the most secure, practical and economical way to shop via the Internet" in Portuguese. A recent study found that seven-eighths of all electronic commerce conducted in Latin America takes place in Brazil, and the Bradesco site is one of the main reasons why. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Latest Hit on Campus: Crescendo in E-Major
body: WHEN it comes to offering degrees, the halls of academia are not immune to fashion. Colleges and universities bank on blue-blazer classics like history and philosophy. But they also like to try what's hot every now and then. What's sizzling right now, given the successes of the dot-com crowd, is the E-commerce credential. In what many professors and administrators say is the fastest trend to take hold in the slow-changing world of higher education, colleges and universities nationwide are rushing to turn the study of business on the Internet into degrees, majors, minors, concentrations, specialties, certificates, fellowships and research centers. "While the University of Alabama does not have an E-commerce program yet, we are working full speed to set one up," wrote Bill Gerdes, a university spokesman, in an email response to a query about E-commerce degrees on the Tuscaloosa campus. There are as many variations on E-commerce instruction as there are institutions offering it. Of the dozen or so programs now available, some focus on Internet technology, with training in Web-site design, electronic data interchange and authentication technology along with marketing and consumer services. Others concentrate on entrepreneurship and the basics of running a business on the Web, including keeping tabs on finances and inventory. Some involve intensive curriculums and undergraduate degrees in subjects like computer science or finance. Others make fewer course requirements and would appeal to students who are not necessarily facile with computers. Carnegie Mellon University's graduate business school in Pittsburgh just introduced a master's of science program in electronic commerce that combines instruction in business and in computer science. The yearlong program, which began last May, costs $38,000 and, the university said, should enable graduates to build and run a company's on-line system from the floor up. The master's of science program at Marlboro College in Marlboro, Vt., which began in 1997, offers on-line instruction in basic Web design, marketing and strategic planning for Web businesses. The 11-month program requires students to be on campus every other weekend and costs $15,000. "We focus less on deep, technical infrastructure and more on teaching students to orchestrate Internet strategies," said Paul J. LeBlanc, the college's president. At the University of Florida in Gainesville, a certificate in E-commerce as part of a two-year M.B.A. program is awarded after completion of seven E-commerce courses that cover subjects like pricing of information services and products and one-to-one marketing over the Internet. Any student at LaSalle University in Philadelphia may qualify as an E-commerce "fellow" by attending two E-commerce courses; courses in other disciplines with an E-commerce component, or a seven-part lecture series. All fellows must write a 2,500-word research paper and work in the field -- for a company or a community service organization, for example -- for 40 hours. The fellowship designation appears on graduates' transcripts, and fellows walk away with portfolios of E-commerce work. Student interest in new E-commerce degrees and programs has been strong, university administrators say. Carnegie Mellon said it had received 180 applications, from which it chose its initial 37 candidates. Paul R. Brazina, the executive director of LaSalle's new Electronic Commerce Institute, said that 470 students had shown interest in applying to the institute's fellowship program, which is beginning this month. At Vanderbilt University in Nashville, 110 students, or a quarter of the M.B.A. candidates, have chosen E-commerce as either a concentration or specialty. Corporations are even more enthusiastic about E-commerce training than college and university administrators. Many companies think that employees with an intimate knowledge of modern computer technologies and E-commerce strategies might give them a competitive edge. Some companies are helping to sponsor E-commerce research centers, sometimes as a means for converting their business problems into case studies that students can try to solve. "The breadth of companies asking for E-commerce experience, from CS First Boston to General Electric, to start-ups, like Priceline.com, is amazing," said Robert F. Bonner, the director of the career management office at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. "A few years ago, companies would say E-commerce experience on a student's resume was 'nice to have.' Now they are saying, 'must have.' " Wharton, which started its Electronic Commerce Forum three years ago as a research center for corporations, students and faculty members, has stepped up plans to introduce an E-commerce major for graduate students this fall. School officials said they were also considering offering a master's degree in electronic business. Changes in salaries reflect the growing demand. Five years ago, a new Wharton graduate with experience in E-commerce could expect a starting salary of $62,000, not including a bonus or stock options, Mr. Bonner said. Today, those offers start at $80,000, about $10,000 more than other business fields. It is not just the computer literate who are making money. The academic foray into E-commerce has been profitable intellectually and financially. In most cases, the new programs have been a financial boon, bringing in tuition dollars and millions in grants to set up E-commerce research centers and faculty chairs. At Bentley College in Waltham, Mass., a new M.B.A. concentration, known as E-business, and a graduate-level certificate in electronic business have become part of a shift to technology in the entire business curriculum. School administrators said the change in focus had brought in $500,000 in additional tuition this fall along with at least $7 million in related grants and contributions for program support and development. Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta and Drexel University in Philadelphia have received $1 million each from corporations to establish E-commerce research centers. Both plan to offer E-commerce certificates or concentrations next year. The new programs also give colleges, universities and graduate schools a drawing card to attract accomplished students who help to improve the overall quality of their applicant pools. "E-commerce is moving so quickly that people don't have time to wait for experience to teach them," said R. M. Erik Gordon, the director of the Center for Retailing Education and Research at the University of Florida's business school. "The E-commerce credential sends the signal that someone knows something about E-commerce and that they've learned it in a focused and strategic way." But many professors and business executives dismiss E-commerce degrees and programs as more marketing ploy than academically sound initiative. "I object to the E-commerce degrees profusely," said Amit Pazgal, a marketing professor who teaches E-commerce at Washington University's John M. Olin School of Business in St. Louis. "I think it's a fad and that universities are just jumping on the bandwagon." At the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, Ryan Nelson, the director of the McIntire School of Commerce, said he turned down a professor's request to start an E-commerce program, arguing that the subject should be an integral part of the business curriculum. Edward A. Snyder, the dean of the university's Darden Graduate School of Business Administration, agreed. "E-commerce degrees are silly in the same way that teaching international business in a global economy is silly," he said. HARVARD and Stanford have one or more courses devoted to E-commerce, but Harvard, at least, says it has no plans for a separate concentration or E-commerce degree. "We have a good number of cases that focus on E-commerce throughout the curriculum," said Maura A. Byrne, a Harvard Business School spokeswoman. "But we are a school of general management. That's what it comes down to. Obviously, E-commerce is a hot and important industry to look at. But H.B.S. is about educating leaders and the best managers." Other objections to starting more E-commerce programs include a shortage of qualified professors and of comprehensive, up-to-date textbooks. Because technology is advancing so quickly, the few E-commerce textbooks, articles and case studies available quickly become obsolete. There is no shortage of faculty members willing to teach E-commerce courses, administrators say. They generally come from closely allied fields, like computer science or information technology; recent Ph.D.'s whose dissertations were in E-commerce; faculty "gear heads," who have pursued consulting or research on behalf of Web-based businesses, and "disciplinary migrants" -- young and midcareer faculty members looking for fields in which they can become pioneers and make their reputations. The challenge, administrators say, is finding faculty members who are more expert on computers than the students they will be teaching. With the E-commerce programs still in their infancy, it is unclear what real value they will have, many professors and corporate recruiters say. "Someone who has been exposed to a lot of dot-com successes and failures, even in an academic setting, would be viewed as more attractive, all things being equal," said Randall Kelley, a managing director with the executive search firm of Spencer Stuart in San Francisco and the head of its technology services practice. Michael P. Sherman, the executive vice president of the Fingerhut Companies, said, "I don't know exactly what an E-commerce degree is, but if it means more skills in the E-commerce area, we are interested." But Richard Alexander, who runs his own executive recruiting firm in Lawrenceville, N.J., said that until the E-commerce degree and its recipients established some kind of track record, "it has little credibility." "It's ludicrous right now," he said. "It's not the Web-site person that companies are looking for. It's the person who has strategic experience and can apply it." Still, students like James W. Walker see no downside to earning an E-commerce degree. Last May, Mr. Walker, a principal at American Management Systems, an information technology consulting firm in Denver, became one of five students from his company to join Carnegie Mellon's inaugural E-commerce class. "I looked at the program and was amazed at what they were doing," he said. "I saw that I could further my knowledge of the Internet and acquire the soft skills that many engineers lack. Those are skills I need to move up in management." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Beth Staples, left, a senior majoring in English, and Bonnie Sanville, a sophomore in nursing, have enrolled in the fellowship program at the new Electronic Commerce Institute at LaSalle University in Philadelphia. The institute's executive director is Paul R. Brazina. (Michael Branscom for The New York Times)

title: Make a Quick Purchase. Wait for the Delivery Man.
body: IT'S a fitting paradox for the on-line age that Internet shoppers can order up a virtual storm in minutes but have to wait days to get the goods. Buying on line, no matter how fast and convenient, still means relying on, and paying for, snail mail. Getting products out of the virtual shopping cart and into the home is a barrier to E-commerce growth, especially among the instant-gratification set. But the cost of home delivery and the hassle of waiting for it are enough to drive even patient consumers to the mall. And, of course, nobody ever returned a sweater on line. But like all things on line, this is changing. E-commerce has made home shoppers of many people who might never have ordered from catalogues or through toll-free numbers. That is forcing Internet retailers and the companies that deliver their goods to make the shop-pay-get experience more seamless. Home delivery, a hallmark of the early 19th century, is making a big comeback. Analysts say that means that whatever else happens in E-commerce, the delivery industry will be a big winner. "Industry leaders see these changes in distribution patterns, and begin asking who'll be hurt and who may benefit," said Anthony Gallo, a transportation analyst for Deutsche Bank Alex. Brown. "I think the easier answer is who benefits, and that is the package and parcel carriers with express service, like Fedex, U.P.S. and even the Postal Service, with its Priority Mail." But obstacles remain. "Delivery is not that simple," said Don Gilbert, a senior vice president for information technology at the National Federation of Retailers. "We know there will be some spectacular successes and some spectacular failures." Companies like United Parcel Service and Federal Express insist they are ready to handle any increases in home delivery that E-commerce may throw their way. Both companies have created software programs that allow retailers to integrate ordering, shipping and tracking with the retailers' Web sites. Another concern is the cost of shipping. A recently contemplated order of six items from the Web site for Toys "R" Us -- Toysrus.com -- totaled $101. Although there was no sales tax, shipping costs ranged from $10.50 for delivery in 7 to 10 business days to $29.40 for 3-to-5-day delivery to $39.70 for 2-to-4-day delivery. "We're beginning to hear about the abandoned virtual shopping cart," Mr. Gilbert said. "When you order on most sites, shipping costs aren't calculated until the very end. It scares lots of people away." Delivery costs can soar if every product is not ready to ship at once. "Some companies ship each item as it becomes available, and you end up paying each time," he added. "You could drop $42 on $50 worth of clothes by the time you're done." Mr. Gilbert said consumers should look for a check-off box instructing merchants to wait until all the items are ready to ship. That, of course, can create a further delay. Another problem is being at home to accept the packages. (Many companies forbid employees from receiving packages on the job.) A study of 1,600 consumers by Chilton Research Services in 1995 showed that while 65 percent reported waiting at home for deliveries, 25 percent refused to do so. Twenty-eight percent said that they would use home-delivery services if they had a secure way to receive goods. The survey was commissioned by David Porter, a dry cleaner in Kansas City, Mo., who invented the Smart Box, a discreet, secure and climate-controlled accordionlike compartment for groceries that can be installed on exterior walls. A coded keypad system allows delivery people to open it. "I came to realize one big reason more people weren't using E-commerce is because there's no safe place to leave packages," said Mr. Porter, who has obtained a patent for the Smart Box, which he estimates will sell for $300 to $400. About 75 percent of all E-commerce transactions are between businesses, which are accustomed to shipping large orders to a small number of places. But 44 million American consumers will order on line this year. While that amounts to only 1 percent of retail revenue, according to the National Federation of Retailers, it is enough to change the way sellers think about delivering the goods. E-commerce is new, and information about Internet-order fulfillment is scant. One study of the 1998 holiday shopping season, conducted by Zona Research in Redwood City, Calif., showed that 55 percent of 1,000 Web shoppers surveyed chose U.P.S. as their primary shipper, while 32 percent used the unitedstates Postal Service. Ten percent used Federal Express, with the rest split among other companies. Three kinds of companies now sell products to consumers over the Web: traditional stores used to having customers come to them (and that have little or no home-delivery experience); companies that sell through mail-order catalogues and toll-free numbers, and "virtual" companies designed for E-commerce, some of which promise same-day delivery in certain regions by using local couriers. In addition, about 150 Web auction sites, like Ebay, are increasing home-to-home deliveries, industry analysts say. Not surprisingly, mail-order companies have the easiest time moving to E-commerce. After all, shipping orders to individuals is their business. But many brick-and-mortar stores, whose strong points are brand loyalty and customer service, are starting from scratch. And the virtual companies, which were designed for Internet orders, often need to improve customer service. One solution is hybrids. Many traditional companies, for example, are teaming up with virtual ones. The virtual company might process the order and arrange with its partner to deliver it or have the customer pick it up or return it. ANOTHER idea for making home delivery more palatable was born in July, when Airborne Express began an experiment with the Postal Service. Airborne transports business-to-home shipments to any of the service's 24,000 centers within two days, and the Postal Service delivers them after that. In April, Ebay, Mail Boxes Etc. and iShip.com. announced a plan in which iShip.com would provide "upfront" information on shipping costs and options to Ebay buyers and sellers, who would be able to usemail Boxes Etc. stores for packing, shipping and receiving with a "hold for inspection" program to protect buyers. No matter what, technology is sure to continue changing the way products move from producers to consumers. For now, ideas like the Smart Box may be part of the solution. "At least," said Mr. Porter, the Smart Box's inventor, "until they can beam stuff directly into your home."  Smart Shopping, Even in Pajamas Here are some tips for getting what you want to where you want it, at a price that won't make you regret it.  SHOP AROUND Different merchants strike different deals with different couriers, so shipping costs can vary wildly.  PATIENCE IS CHEAP If you order more than one item, make sure everything is in stock and will be shipped at the same time, or else you could end up paying piecemeal for delivery, which is considerably more expensive.  PLAN AHEAD The Internet is generally not a good place for impulse buying and last-minute holiday shopping. Order in bulk when you can, and choose slower, less expensive shipping methods when possible.  DESIGNATE A RECIPIENT In many residential areas, where neighbors know, trust and sometimes even like one another, one household (usually with a stay-at-home adult) will agree to accept daytime deliveries for others on the block. Be sure the merchant and delivery company have your telephone number and that of the house that will accept delivery.  WEIGH COST VERSUS CONVENIENCE Sure, it's fun to order patio furniture at 3 A.M. in your pajamas. But sometimes it just makes more sense to go to the store. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: David Porter with his "Smart Box" folded up outside his home in Kansas City, Mo. (Roy Inman for The newyork Times)

title: Man Emerges, Still Breathing, After E-Cave Confinement - Correction Appended
body: AS humanity moves to the 21st-century method of grocery shopping -- over the Internet -- I see key limitations of old-style, walk-in markets. For one thing, they never told me that the banana is considered an herb because it lacks woody tissue. I pick up that fact when I click on "banana" while strolling the produce section of Webvan, an on-line grocer that advertises same-day delivery. As I fill my virtual basket, I bask in the advantages of on-line shopping, like copious product information, and in the absence of time-consuming shopping hassles, like finding a parking space or wearing pants. It is a Sunday night, and I have just sealed myself into an E-cave. For the next five days, I will order all sustenance and entertainment from the Net. I will hunker down in a bachelor pad in Palo Alto, Calif., armed with credit card and mouse. I will become the worst nightmare of OPEC and the makers of deodorant soap. I click my way to Webvan's checkout aisle to schedule a delivery time. Tomorrow morning would be great. Then, crisis. I'm told that deliveries are first come, first served. Webvan can deliver the same day, but the next available appointment is Wednesday night. Wednesday? By Wednesday, I could walk to the nearest market and back -- on stilts. I could buy groceries and take a two-day seminar on "The Banana: Animal, Mineral or Herb." E-commerce has revolutionized the selling of books, compact disks, travel and financial services and computer hardware and software -- commodities shoppers don't need to squeeze and prod to get a handle on. But will the on-line bazaar work for everyday survival, and as a means for daily upkeep of heart, soul, body, mind and, foremost, stomach? Or, put another way, as I stare at Webvan's offer of a delivery in 72 hours: When E-commerce fails to deliver, which parts of my computer are edible?  Monday Learning to Order Food In an Australian Accent In his quest for food, primitive man faced disease, pestilence and the woolly mammoth. I face slothlike delivery schedules. Undaunted by my Webvan disappointment, I set out on Monday morning to hunt and gather 21st-century style. I soon spot prey. A Web search turns up 69 sites offering "grocery delivery," including Groceronline, Netgrocer and Electrolley. I pop into and register at several sites, then head down the virtual aisles. But each time I go to check out, I learn delivery is either not available in my area or will take 3 to 10 days. Electrolley serves only Perth, Australia. Internet Home Delivery focuses on Florida's North Pinellas County. A harsh reality dawns: either I wait a week for food or move to Australia. By noon, frantic I'll star in the sequel to "Alive," I change strategies. I search on "food delivery, Palo Alto" and am led to Waiters.com, a service that takes on-line orders for local restaurants. At one spot I know, the Good Earth, I point and click through the menu. But I make rookie E-commerce errors, neglecting, for example, to complete registration forms. I inadvertently hit the browser's back button while trying to order a Danish. Two hours later -- it's 1:30 in the afternoon -- my $32 order arrives from the Good Earth. Hungry and having not seen another human being in nearly 24 hours, I practically hug Louis, the Waiters.com driver. This prompts some advice. "If I were you," he says, "I would have ordered over the phone. It's easier." If he only knew. All day, I have battled not just delivery schedules but a debilitating injury. I have hurt my left pinkie. I jammed it in a recent basketball game, and it's swollen and purple, like a mini-eggplant. If this sounds melodramatic, consider that in evolutionary terms, there is little worse than a crippled typing finger in the E-commerce age. I'm like a cave man unable to carry a club, a tiger without claws. I wince each time I type Q or A, two-thirds of the mother lode of all pertinent information on most sites. I speak of the "FAQ." I divine an answer: the cybermedic. A search for "medical advice" returns the names of dozens of doctors who offer virtual consultations. I even find a specialist, a sports orthopedist named Stuart Zeman. "Most people dread going to the doctor," his site says. "It can be expensive, inconvenient and stressful." Dr. Zeman's alternative is an email consultation for 10 bucks. Not only is he inexpensive, he's also concise. You get one paragraph to describe your malady, and the virtual physician's response runs only a few lines. (Somewhere, an H.M.O. executive is taking copious notes.) And so by the end of the day, I have scored several small E-commerce victories, including the fact that late in the afternoon, I have discovered an on-line grocer called Peapod. It was recommended not by a search engine but by Louis from Waiters .com. I arrange for a Tuesday delivery. When I go to bed, I have fed my brain with food, and I have tended to my corpus with medical advice. Tomorrow, feeling more seasoned in the ways of E-commerce, I will feed my soul. I will buy a golf course.  Tuesday Living Room Is Perfect For Sinking a 9-Footer Well, not an entire golf course, but at least an indoor putting green. This will permit me to test my E-commerce mettle, alleviate the boredom that accompanies an on-line, in-house life style and address one of life's pressing concerns, improving my golf game. My search-engine request on Yahoo spits out nearly 40 possible merchants, with names like Eagle Putting Greens and Chip-n-Putt. There are synthetic putting greens for the backyard, the home, the office, the home office and the backyard office. There are do-it-yourself kits, synthetic grass sold by the yard and pictures of children playing on elaborate miniature golf courses that can be constructed on large estates. It occurs to me that the Net is the world's biggest mall, a discount shopping strip that stretches from Finland to Fresno. But it's a double-edged sword; the vast product choices can make for a bottomless shopping experience. An obsessive-compulsive comparison shopper may wind up being carried away in a padded van. I settle on a shop called Big Moss Golf. This is partly because it feels like a local store and partly because it promises to bring my handicap out of the stratosphere. And partly because it has a toll-free number for customer service, and I'm starting to get a little lonely in the E-cave. "You'll have to work that out yourself," Tony Terisco says. He's the owner of Big Moss Golf who sells me on the Big Moss Original, a $159, nine-foot-long piece of carpet simulated to feel like grass with a golf hole at one end. "This will do more for your game than anything else in the golf industry," he promises. It dawns on me that it may be even more instructive to play actual golf. But I'm in no mood to quibble. I pay an extra $30 for overnight delivery. Just then, I receive a house call from my on-line doctor, Stuart Zeman. "You must get an X-ray," he prescribes in no uncertain terms. Leave the house? Never! I've got a reputation to uphold. I decide to seek a second opinion. I fire off an email to Dr. Michele Moore, who runs a site called www.askyour familydoc.com. She will give me a virtual bedside counsel for $25. As dusk settles, I'm feeling ever more optimistic about my E-commerce prowess. Except for one nagging concern: Have I started to go a little stir-crazy? Does part of me long for casual conversation in the express checkout lane, a little flirtation with the waitress, even an exchange of angry words at a stoplight? I quickly dismiss the notion. Frankly, I'm as sane at this moment as I've ever been. I am totally in control.  Wednesday An On-line Warrior Victorious in Battle Help. Send Prozac. Otherwise, I may torture and kill my neighbor. She's a nice enough young lady, but she's been practicing the piano for hours, repeatedly crashing down on the keys with hands like anvils. I look frazzled, with hair like Mozart's. But I will combat her, E-commerce style. My weapons are earplugs and aspirin. My destination is pharmaceutical sites. I settle on Planetrx.com and Drugstore.com, which are battling it out to be the next millennium's Long's and Walgreens, but without the bricks and mortar. I register at each site and check their delivery schedules. Then I take my budding skills to the next level -- I engage in a bit of hard-core price comparison. I open two browser windows and compare the sites side by side, checking response time, prices and product information. It is as if I were walking down an aisle with the products from the respective stores on each side of me. I am voting in real time with my mouse. The arrows favor Planetrx. Minutes later, I "walk out" with earplugs and Advil, opting for overnight delivery for an additional $10. While I'm at it, I check out the stores' aisles of bandage tape for my injured digit. Drugstore.com offers eight pages of athletic tape and gauze products. This is when I realize I've E-volved into a wily E-commerce veteran. I'm in and out of the drugstores in 10 minutes, far less than it would have taken to drive to a pharmacy. I've learned that E-commerce success depends on equal parts computer and modem but also confidence and experience. When I look in the mirror, I see a mouse-toting warrior, albeit one whose hair is standing on end, who is clad exclusively in boxer shorts. No shirt. No shoes. No problem. Flush with success, I endeavor an E-commerce challenge with an Olympic degree of difficulty. I'm going to use my modem to get my cat to stop throwing up. I've tried the normal remedies, like giving her soft foods and beer, but frankly, I inherited the cat from an ex-girlfriend and I never could figure her out -- the cat, I mean. I find a veterinarian to consult by email. But then I ascend further, pinpointing a service that in and of itself may illustrate just how far this new commerce medium has come: Kay Cox, on-line pet psychiatrist, www.getnet.com/petcouns/. Ms. Cox, a self-proclaimed "pet therapist and talent scout," offers on-line consultation for $40 an hour. I send her an electronic missive and assure the cat it will be O.K. Meanwhile, my own psychological salve has arrived -- my putting green. John Tuggle, the U.P.S. deliveryman, takes one look at me and says, "I think you need to get out of the house and go to the shopping mall." Hardly. I'm on a roll. I've used the Net to gather my food, tend to my body, my soul, my own sanity and that of my pet. Now I will endeavor the final frontier. I will tend to my heart. I will find love.  Thursday The Moment of Truth: Searching for Love "They" say it's hard to meet good people these days. "They" say it's tough to find a soul mate amid the cacophony of modern life. Well, they've never met Kitten664. This is the woman I am paired up with by Matchmaker.com. The on-line service concluded we may constitute a love connection by comparing our answers to about 50 questions like personal hobbies, income, height and weight and reading habits. Kitten664 and I matched on 54 percent of our answers, like the fact that we're both avid readers and own sport utility vehicles. Plus, we're both 5 feet 8 inches tall and weigh 160 pounds. It's true: I soon realize that among the criteria the company matches are our height and weight, which doesn't seem like a quality that either sex typically wants in a mate. In a second attempt at a dating service, I fill out a questionnaire on a site that promises to help me find my soul mate. But when I finish, it takes me to an advertisement for free, on-line pornography. I don't think this is a site I'd like to bring home to my mother. But there is good news on my penultimate day in the E-cave. The swelling in my pinkie has gone down. This is partly thanks to email from Dr. Moore, who advocates icing and elevating the finger. Also, I've ordered lunch with ease from Waiters.com -- without even needing to register because my registration is already on file. Plus, the cat has quit vomiting, even though the pet psychiatrist hasn't returned our emails. Sometimes the very suggestion of therapy inspires healing. And I'm starting to sink my putts. OPEC is in real jeopardy.  Friday A Little Wisdom Gleaned From Living Life on Line Just when I am feeling as if I may never need the outside world again, fate intervenes. My office calls and tells me I must go on an urgent assignment. My week in the E-cave is cut short. I will put down the mouse and pick up the car keys. As I do so, I reflect on the four days gone by. I have discovered that with a little practice and experience, the Net can yield some powerful dividends. Product information and diversity are unparalleled. The next time I need a sweater for my Irish setter and a pet sitter in matching attire, I'll toss aside the Yellow Pages and let my modem do the walking. Plus, there is extraordinary capacity to compare prices. When my local retailer advertises "the lowest prices on the planet or we'll give you your money back and buff your car," I'll print out some prices from the Net and drive them over. Then there's the downside. The on-line experience can be an isolating one. Some very important sense of community develops from shopping in the flesh, despite the hassles of driving, parking, fighting crowds and arguing whether you really have 10 or 11 items in the express lane. There are other bugs, too. Like sometimes an E-commerce site just freezes up, and frequently a site won't answer customer service emails for days. In either case, it's like walking up to a sales clerk in a store, asking a question, then having him glower at you before turning around and walking away. "Hey, I'm talking to you," I shouted at one point during the week to a frozen site. I may need a pet therapist myself. Ultimately, I conclude there are two basic and unassailable tenets of the E-commerce life: (1) you can order anything under the sun over the Net -- and in greater selection than in any other single venue on the planet, and (2) plan ahead, or you'll starve to death. One more thing. Once you do hunt and gather your food, once you navigate the registration and saunter confidently into the virtual checkout line of life, make sure to include one key facet of the old economy: find someone to eat it with. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article on Sept. 22 in the special E-Commerce section about ordering goods and services on the Internet referred incorrectly to the criteria of an on-line dating service, Match maker.com, for matching couples. The service does not pair people by height and weight. Correction-Date: October 6, 1999, Wednesday Graphic   Photos: But Don't Ask How Often He Changed His Clothes -- The things, large and small, that keep Internet-man going include: a bandage for a jammed left pinkie; cereal and milk (bananas optional); contact with the outside world, in this case represented by the Peapod delivery man, Sterling Crockett, and, of course, an indoor putting green for sharpening his golf game. Not shown is Kitten664, the match arranged for Internet-man by Matchmaker.com. (Photographs by Steve Castillo for The New York Times)

title: Night of the Living Bid: Four Tales From an Hour of Ebay
body: IT was just after 7:30 on a Monday evening in August, and Eric Clayberg, a 35-year-old software entrepreneur, was fixated on his computer screen. An auction on Ebay was minutes from closing, and Mr. Clayberg wanted to be the final bidder. Over the last month and a half, he had perfected his strategy, a nimble mix of patience, quick clicking and good timing. Every few seconds, Mr. Clayberg clicked the reload button on his Web browser to obtain up-to-the-second information about the item he wanted: a coin-operated arcade game called Taito Elevator Action. The price seemed to be stuck at $450, the result of a bid four hours before. Then it happened. Another bidder stepped in, offering $527.99. It was time for fast fingers. Mr. Clayberg clicked the bid button, frantically typed $537.99, hit the submit button and reloaded the page. His bid showed up with 13 seconds to spare. In previous Ebay sessions, Mr. Clayberg had learned that it typically took more than 20 seconds to enter a new bid. Even if someone else wanted the arcade game, it was too late. "I put in my final offer and it took," he exulted the next day. Mr. Clayberg is one of thousands of people who have been bitten by the Ebay bug. Since the on-line auction house opened in 1995, more than 3.8 million people have registered to participate and millions more have visited its site, www.ebay.com. In the second quarter of this year, gross sales topped $622 million. By the beginning of September, nearly 2.6 million items were listed on the site at one time. The site's popularity, some industry analysts say, is more than just a craze. The company and other sites that offer on-line auctions, like Amazon.com and Yahoo, are changing the rules of on-line commerce. They have redefined business for collectors, resellers, consumers and even shipping companies. Along the way, they have created ways for everyday people to connect with other everyday people who have the same interests, needs and must-have obsessions for items like coin-operated video-arcade games, circa 1980. "People are doing business in a way they really couldn't before," said Meg Whitman, the chief executive of Ebay, which is based in San Jose, Calif. "Out of this has grown a community." Watch the items for sale on Ebay and traces of the new E-commerce community emerge. Within that 7 o'clock hour in which Mr. Clayberg won his arcade game, for example, several other auctions were closing, too. They included a Minnkota speedboat motor, a piece of software designed to "double the speed of your PC in minutes," a computer with a 500-megahertz processor, a trio of Beanie Babies with American flags stitched into their cloth, a computer with a 450-MHz processor, a vintage Zeiss Ikon camera and 12 more sets of multicolored Beanies. Here are a few of their stories.  The Game Collector Mr. Clayberg, the software entrepreneur, telecommutes from his home in Middleton, Mass., to Portland, Ore. But in the evenings, you may find him in his basement, amid his arcade-game collection. As an avid collector, Mr. Clayberg created a personal Ebay Web page to keep track of the new games auctioned each week. That is how he found the Taito Elevator Action, a game on which he says he wasted much of his college years in the 1980's. (A secret agent uses the elevator to obtain documents and dodge bad guys.) He had seen pictures on the Ebay site -- bulky but beautiful, with colorful stickers -- and a seller's promise, declared amid multiple exclamation points, that the machine was in "good shape!!" When he first saw the game listed a week before, Mr. Clayberg bid less than $75, a low-ball offer. Each day he checked back and often raised his bid. He wasn't alone. By the close of the auction, the machine had received 58 bids from only 16 people. The same evening, 1,400 miles away in Tulsa, Okla., 30-year-old Dan Riggs was also poring over a computer screen, seeing how the bids turned out. Mr. Riggs was the seller of the Elevator Action game, one of nearly a dozen arcade games that his company, MVP Vending, had been trying to sell on Ebay that week. MVP Vending specializes in new and used arcade games and pinball machines, and most of the time Mr. Riggs is on the road in the Midwest, selling the games to restaurants and arcades. But over the last six months, he has decided to pursue some business on line, too, by auctioning some of his older machines on Ebay. Mr. Riggs does it, he said, for the exposure. Some of the Web pages that showcased his games have received more than 1,000 visitors. "That's the same as, say, 1,178 people coming into the shop," he continued. "You can't even compare that to the storefront." On Ebay, Mr. Riggs said, arcade games usually sell for more than what he would have charged in a traditional transaction. He said he thought the difference could be attributed to the cost of living. Someone in newyork, for example, might expect to pay a lot more than someone in Tulsa. Locally, Mr. Riggs would expect to sell a similar game for $450 to $500. "I met what I wanted to get for it about four days before the auction even ended," he said. Despite some prices that exceed those charged in stores, buyers are still flocking to on-line auctions, and sellers are finding them to be lucrative. On-line auctions have become the No. 1 place for many collectors to trade items, Mr. Clayberg said. "If you have a comic book collection for sale, you are not going to put an ad in your local paper," he added. Posting an item on Ebay can cost as little as 25 cents. Other arcade game collectors, he said, talk about Ebay constantly. They communicate through an email newsletter, exchanging bidding stories, information about new items and rumors about sellers or buyers who have bad reputations. On the same day that Mr. Clayberg was basking in victory, having bought his arcade game, he read comments about another bidding war, one that had turned ugly. In that battle, a different game had been bid upon every few minutes by a bidder who lived in the same town as the seller and who withdrew his bids at the last minute. Arcade game collectors grew suspicious, and many assumed that the bidder had been set up as a shill, someone who conspires with the seller to drive up prices. That game was offered for sale again later that week, but people were shunning the item, Mr. Clayberg said, "because they don't want to get scammed."  The Disappointed Seller Omer Erden, a 40-year-old Seattle resident, was the seller behind the computer with the 450-MHz chip being auctioned that same evening. Mr. Erden built the computer and for days had been watching the bids trickle in. The going price hovered around $600. Then, in the final seconds, it shot to more than $1,200 and closed at $1,376. "I couldn't believe it just doubled like that," he said in an email interview. Mr. Erden sent a congratulatory message to the highest bidder. But the sweet surprise soon turned sour.  "I received an email saying he didn't want the computer anymore and he was sorry he'd bid on it," Mr. Erden said. Dealing with bidders who back out is one drawback to Ebay and other on-line trading forums. Ebay cannot force anyone to follow through on a bid, other than to tell them that their bid represents a legal contract. Nor can it control sellers who suddenly decide not to sell. The site works on an honor system; the grease that turns the gears is the trust between two people who have never seen or talked to each other yet are willing to make a transaction. People who have to cope with flighty sellers and bidders do have one recourse: the site's feedback forum. Some criticize the forum as ineffective, but most Ebay users praise it as a salve for the uncertainty of anonymous transactions. Bidders and sellers are encouraged to rate each other on their professionalism and view each others' ratings. Mr. Erden did just that, giving a bad rating to the bidder who changed his mind. Then he sent an email message to the next highest bidder for the machine. He is still waiting. Meanwhile, he is dealing with what he calls a "humongous bill" from Ebay for listing items. Ebay charges sellers 25 cents to $25 for listing items and a commission for items that sell. Commissions depend on the value of the final bid and start at 5 percent for items that sell for less than $25.  The Business Owner Meanwhile, Albert Chidiac was also watching the action that evening. His company, a custom-computer store called Bear Solutions in Houston, was auctioning a fully loaded computer with a 500-MHz chip. Since his company started listing computers on Ebay three months ago, Mr. Chidiac said, his business has doubled. He attributes some of that to his Ebay feedback rating. He has received a 100 percent positive response from Ebay participants. "It's like a Better Business Bureau," he said. Mr. Chidiac had a better experience than Mr. Erden that night. After 42 bids, he sold the computer for $1,400. Within a few minutes, he received an excited email message from the winning bidder. After more email messages, the buyer called to provide a credit-card number and order parts that were not part of the initial offering. Bear Solutions, a company with seven employees, used free space on Ebay to put up a Web site advertising its business. The site offers information on Bear Solutions' function and products. This has given buyers the comfort of knowing whom they are buying from, Mr. Chidiac said, and has also translated into prime advertising space, with almost guaranteed Web traffic. "We've gotten calls from people saying, 'We'll send you a check for $3,000' and not think twice about it," he said. "We've had three businesses that have come through Ebay to purchase systems from us. One made a purchase and then called us back and purchased nine other ones."  A Dutch Auction About 6:15 central time that same night, Tracy Miller and Shirley Rankin were getting ready to leave their office at the Tharpe Company in Statesville, N.C., which runs employee-recognition programs. The two co-workers are friends who between them have collected nearly 300 Beanie Babies for themselves and their children. Ms. Miller, who estimates she has bought as many as 25 items on Ebay since she registered in May, had decided to check the site for new items that afternoon. She noticed that three Beanies coveted by her friend were on sale. In a few minutes, the two would have to leave the office and head home, where neither had high-speed access to the Internet. "I said: 'Shirley, I've got them right here. Do you want me to bid for you?' " Ms. Miller recalled. Ms. Rankin told her to go for it. The Beanies were being sold in a so-called Dutch auction, which offers several copies of the same item and, in the end, typically distributes them to multiple bidders. In this case, a toy distributor was selling 12 sets of three Beanies -- a butterfly called Flitter, a fish called Lips and a beady-eyed bear named Birthday Bear. They are highly prized because Ty Inc., the company that makes Beanie Babies, would distribute them only to a small number of retail stores. Dutch auctions can be confusing for new Ebay users; instead of the highest bidder winning the item, the highest bidders win the items but only have to pay the lowest amount that was bid among them. In the case of Flitter, Lips and Birthday Bear, for example, 50 people bid for the items. But only the top five bidders were successful. They included a person who bid $125 each for 10 sets, one who bid the same amount for just one, another who bid $125.01 for one, another who bid $127.75 each for two, and Ms. Miller -- acting for her friend -- who bid $130 for one. In the end, four of those five bidders got the number of sets they wanted. The bidder who wanted 10 sets won only the remaining 7. Under Dutch auction rules, the lowest bid of the highest bidders -- the $125 offered by the person who wanted all 10 -- was the amount that each bidder would have to pay. Ms. Miller -- who goes by QueenieBeanie3 on Ebay -- had become adept at Dutch auctions over the last few months. She knew that if she bid $130 and essentially outbid everyone else, her friend would be guaranteed to get one set of Beanies for less than the amount she bid. "A Dutch auction can be a pretty good deal," Ms. Miller said. The next day, when the two women came back to work, they logged on to Ebay and found that Ms. Miller's instincts were right. Ms. Rankin sent a money order for $125 to the seller by overnight mail. Flitter, Lips and Birthday Bear arrived three days later. Since then, Ms. Rankin has signed up for her own account on Ebay. Her latest purchase: a first-edition Beanie Baby called the Millennium Bear, with tags that have the word "millennium" spelled with only one "n." "They are now worth a lot because of the misspelling," said Ms. Rankin, who bought hers for $15.50. She has also been watching, she said, for Beanie Babies that her daughter, who is 18, would want to add to her collection. "Normally you'd spend a lot of effort," Ms. Rankin said, "Now it's so easy to sit at the computer and say, 'She needs this one.' " "Here in Statesville they sell them at a card shop," she added, "but they are so much cheaper over Ebay."  There Are 30 Seconds Left. Do You Really Need That Black Velvet Painting? EBAY enthusiasts usually have plenty of tips for newcomers. But before understanding the nuances, beginners need to understand the proxy bidding system. Most people assume that Ebay works the way a live auction does, with people calling out their bids (or, in this case, typing in bids) and waiting to see whether someone tops them. When you bid on an Ebay item, however, you are asked at the beginning to enter the maximum amount you would like to spend. A computer then acts as a proxy bidder, entering new amounts for your bid as needed, up to the maximum price you are willing to pay. Say, for example, that you have your heart set on a hard-to-find cookbook whose highest current bid is $4 and whose increments are set at 25 cents. You may be willing to pay as much as $6 for the book, so you would tell Ebay's computer system, your proxy, that your maximum bid is $6. The computer, however, would enter your bid as $4.25. If no one else bids, the item is yours -- for $1.75 less than you said you would pay. But if someone else bids $7, you will receive an email message saying that you have been outbid. You can always raise your maximum bid, as so many users end up doing, as excitement and previous judgment collide. Other hard-learned lessons from Ebay users include the following: WATCH FIRST "Don't buy the first thing you see," suggests Shirley Rankin, an Ebay user who collects Beanie Babies. "Be smart and shop." Pay attention to what types of items attract the most money and who is bidding on and selling them. One section of the site, called Going, Going, Gone, lists recent auction results. Browsing through it can give you an idea of the market value of your item. KNOW WHAT YOU ARE BIDDING ON Some sellers give more detail than others. You can send questions by email if something is not clear. Remember, a bargain isn't a bargain if you don't get what you wanted. CHECK OUT FEEDBACK RATINGS Ebay features a forum where buyers and sellers can rate each other. For each positive rating, a seller or buyer gets one point; for each negative rating, they lose a point. Although a few auction users warn that it is not possible to tell whether the ratings have been stacked, most Ebay users say that they trust the ratings and would never buy an item without checking them. THERE MAY BE A RESERVE PRICE Even if you are the top bidder for an item, you may not get it. Some sellers choose to set a reserve price -- the minimum amount for which they are willing to relinquish the item. The reserve prices are not listed publicly at the start of an auction, but bidders are usually notified during the auction when the reserve price has been met. Eric Clayberg, an arcade-game collector who uses Ebay, warns that some sellers appear to set a very high reserve price simply to see what the "pain threshold" is, without intending to sell the item. BE CAREFUL IN SENDING MONEY Do not send your credit card number in an email message that has not been encrypted. Many sellers will ask, instead, that you tell them your credit card number on the phone. Dan Riggs, a vendor of arcade games that are often sold on Ebay, frequently asks buyers to fax half of the credit card number and email the other half, so that if someone intercepts one message, the numbers are useless. Mr. Riggs also recommends that people send their money orders or checks by certified or priority mail so that packages can be tracked and records are available. If you are buying an expensive item, consider using an escrow service. Doing so will give you the chance to evaluate your purchase before letting go of your money and will reassure the seller that you plan to pay. Ebay recommends i-Escrow, which charges a fee of 6 percent on items worth $500 or less. Fees differ for higher-priced items. BEWARE THE ADRENALINE RUSH It may look like a must-have as the clock ticks down, but who knows how many similar items you may find for sale tomorrow. LISA GUERNSEY http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Shirley Rankin, left, and her daughter, Alaina, in a sea of Beanie Babies. Albert Chidiac doubled computer sales through auctions. (Photographs by Donna Bise (left) and F. Carter Smith for The newyork Times); When Dan Riggs, left, of Tulsa, Okla., put his Taito Elevator Action game up for auction, Eric Clayberg, right, of Middleton, Mass., won it with a last-minute bid of $537.99.
