title: One-Stop Site Offers Menorahs and Mates
body: FEEL like greeting Rosh ha-Shanah with a blast from a rabbinically approved shofar, made by Israeli hands from the horn of an Israeli ram? Would you like to share this iconic experience with a new special someone, preferably young, Jewish and open to prospects of marriage? Have we got a one-stop shopping deal for you: The bifurcated home page (www.agmonet.co.il) for an on-line retailer from Ramat Gan, Israel, can connect directly to Israstore, a five-year-old enterprise that says it is the oldest Internet purveyor of Judaica, or to the Jewish Singles Love Center, where hundreds of mate-seekers from 53 countries have posted short profiles and advertised their willingness to travel for romance. The Israstore offers a full range of modern and traditional mezuzahs and menorahs (including kinetic models with swiveling stems) plus Hebrew bibles and Haggadah booklets, for the traditional Passover dinner story, in English, French and Spanish. For those seeking a more decorous seder, there are gold-embroidered afikomen bags for the ceremonially hidden morsel of matzoh, the better for stealing away with. The site is also ideal for the always difficult task of picking a birthday gift for the Argentine soccer star Diego Maradona, with several finely crafted Hamsa, hand of God, amulets to chose from. The Love Center's current offerings, meanwhile, are 1,034 single Jewish men and 714 single Jewish women. Most are Israeli or American. And many do not seem all that demanding in their quest. Dagmar, 24, a k a Donna, of Herzliya, Israel, specifies that she wants a man, not a "fish." But Greg, 29, of Phoenix, a self-described fiscal conservative, firmly rules out women with "carry-on baggage" and "psychological disorders." Entirely in English, this site caters to the diaspora and Israel's "Anglo-Saxo" immigrants, the peculiar Hebrew term for all English-speakers. But it is also something of an anomaly as a full-service, well-established on-linemail-order house. In a country where every third household has an Internet connection and every crossroads its own chamber-of-commerce-style Web site, cyberretailing is still relatively undeveloped. That is changing, however, as local businesses begin to respond to on-line competition from abroad. For example: Israeli travel Web sites -- in both English and Hebrew -- offer hotel reservations at prices often below those posted for the same room on the sites of international chains. If the matchmaking prospers and at least one partner is in Israel, the Love Center site offers another useful service: same-day flower delivery. The shofar, by the way, will set you back $49; the company promises delivery almost anywhere within 12 days. A subscription to the on-line dating service, with that all-important "contact information," costs $38 for three months. http://www.nytimes.com

title: On-Line Trading Changes Landscape for Old-Line Brokerage Firms
body: LAST year, John (Launny) Steffens, the vice chairman of Merrill Lynch & Company, gave a speech at a computer trade show, warning of the financial risks of zealously trading stocks over the Internet. In March, he started doing it himself. Using the Internet meant he could place orders on weekends and when his financial consultant, as stockbrokers are known at Merrill Lynch, was out of town. "It was easier for me to do it and more convenient," he said in a recent interview at his office on the 32d floor of the World Financial Center. If anyone doubted the shift toward Internet investing, the trend became clear on June 1, when the nation's largest investment house, Merrill Lynch, announced that it was joining the Internet revolution. The firm said it would begin selling stocks on line for $29.95 a trade on Dec. 1, placing it in direct competition with discount firms like the Charles Schwab Corporation, which already offers Internet trading for that price. With Merrill Lynch lowering its drawbridge to accept cheap Internet trades, pressure mounts for other full-service brokerage firms to do the same. If they follow Merrill Lynch's lead, it will mean a move away from the tradition of brokers who advise and steer investors to stocks -- in return for a commission -- toward a world where consumers go on line to research, then buy, their own stocks. The question for consumers will be figuring out whether Internet trading is right for them and finding the cheapest, most reliable place to do it. The question for Merrill Lynch -- and by extension, the financial services industry -- is how it is going to pay for its gigantic infrastructure of brokers, sales staff and analysts if all the consumer cares about is finding a cheap and mechanically reliable place to trade. Already, on-line trading accounts for 37 percent of all retail trades, according to U.S. Bancorp Piper Jaffray, an investment firm. That percentage is expected to grow. A recent study by Gomez Advisors, a company that advises E-commerce companies, and Harris Interactive, an Internet market research company, found that 16 million more investors are likely candidates for on-line trading. But these rising numbers have been accompanied by costly glitches. One company's stock soared 38,000 percent after on-line investors bought it by mistake, using the wrong ticker symbol, Arthur Levitt, the chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, said in a May speech before the National Press Club. He also spoke of a woman who tried to buy $18,000 worth of stock but ended up owing more than $250,000 after the stock's price soared and her cancel orders didn't go through. Consumers need to be educated to prevent such gaffes, Mr. Levitt said. Investors must understand basics such as how to place a "limit" order, setting the maximum price they will pay for a rising stock, he said. And they need to factor in phone lines that can clog and systems that become overwhelmed, causing time lags in placing and canceling orders. The National Association of Securities Dealers, which operates the Nasdaq stock market, sent notices to member brokerage firms earlier this year with advice on how to educate consumers and on ways to design Internet systems to head off problems. But the bottom line is that those who buy on the Internet assume more responsibility for their investing behavior. COMMISSIONED stockbrokers were never objective advisers, said David S. Pottruck, president and co-chief executive of Charles Schwab, the discount brokerage firm, which has never used brokers to recommend stocks. They stood to gain financially by pushing stocks and investment products with large commissions, he said. But at least stockbrokers were trained on investments and worked under regulations requiring that they recommend only those stocks suitable to the client. Reputable brokers advised the unsophisticated against risky and expensive behavior, like rapid trading in and out of stocks. Investors who come up with their own stock picks must determine themselves whether a particular stock fits their financial goals and weigh the tax consequences of a trade. A way to alert buyers when they order a particularly inappropriate stock over the Internet may be developed, Mr. Litan said, but it is unlikely that an Internet brokerage firm would be required to refuse the order. The July shootings in Atlanta, where a day trader killed nine people at two brokerage offices after losing more than $100,000 in 15 days of trading, increased public awareness of the dangers of that particular form of investing. But people buying stocks from the comfort of home rather than at a day-trading office can also make big mistakes. Bill Bunke, 37, of Manhattan Beach, Calif., said he gave up his pool-maintenance business to trade stocks on line. In 18 months, Mr. Bunke said, he lost $25,000 of a $70,000 inheritance. "It was only $8 a trade, and by nature I like to gamble and it looked so easy to me," he said. "There were times I bought shares of a stock I'd never heard of before. I really got addicted." But others have taken a more deliberate approach and done well. Andrew Lohmann, a 36-year-old graduate student in Claremont, Calif., has never bought stocks any way but by using his computer. Since 1995, he has turned the $4,000 he decided he could afford to lose into $50,000 by buying stocks like Schwab and America Online. Robert Litan, who buys stocks over the Internet for some of the same reasons more than five million other Americans do, said, "It's so easy." He began investing on line in 1998, four years after investors first bypassed stockbrokers with the click of a mouse. But Mr. Litan is not just another guy in search of cheap Internet brokerage commissions, which average less than $16 a trade, a fraction of what a full-service broker would charge. As director of economic studies at the Brookings Institution, a research group in Washington, he knows that dangers lurk for naive Internet investors -- not to mention for the nation's 607,000 brokers, many of whom he thinks will soon be forced out of the job. Pouring a large chunk of one's savings into individual stocks isn't a good idea for the average investor, Mr. Litan said. Most people would be better off in mutual funds, managed by professionals, he said, rather than trying to decipher the analysts' reports increasingly offered by on-line brokers. But the real risk, Mr. Litan said, is to the livelihoods of brokers, who on average earned $168,726 in 1998, according to the Securities Industry Association. Some investors, particularly wealthy ones, will always be willing to pay to be coddled by a hands-on broker, he said. But "for the mass market, the traditional broker will become irrelevant," he predicted. Why pay high commissions for a broker's advice when most of them can't beat the market anyway? he asked. Merrill Lynch executives announced their move onto the Internet after traveling to Silicon Valley and Austin, Tex., early this year, where they heard from customers clamoring for on-line investing. At the same time, the company rolled out a second program it hopes will skim off investors who want access to Internet investing but are willing to pay for more personalized service. For a fee starting at $1,500 and increasing with the size of the account, Merrill will provide unlimited trading over the Internet or with a broker, as well as advice on stocks and financial planning tools. That program began July 1. Both programs come with checking accounts and debit cards. Merrill Lynch says it will continue to offer traditional, commission-based broker trades, with customers paying $35 to $105 in commissions for up to 100 shares, depending on the stock's price. "Some clients like the traditional relationship," said Susan Thomson, a Merrill Lynch spokeswoman. Investors with at least $50,000 to invest can also opt for professional money managers. Merrill Lynch executives stress that the change simply means its brokers will focus more on fee-based financial consulting and less on pushing stocks for a commission. Full-service brokerage firms have been moving in that direction for years, said Samuel Hayes, professor of finance at the Harvard Business School. Some brokers will continue to act like salesmen, he said, drawing in customers they then direct to the firms' fee-based investment products -- mutual funds, trusts and money managers. Merrill Lynch has stressed financial planning in training its brokers over the last decade, Miss Thomson said. Its certified financial management program, begun in 1980, was enhanced last year, she said. Whether consumers accustomed to thinking of brokers as salesmen will start seeing them as objective financial consultants remains in question, Mr. Litan said. "It wouldn't surprise me if the effort fails." BUT Mr. Steffens -- who got his start at the firm in its broker training program 36 years ago, and whose son, Andrew, is a Merrill Lynch broker in North Carolina -- predicts the ranks of Merrill's 15,000 "financial consultants" will grow, not diminish. "I would like to have 17,000 to 18,000 five years from now," he said. Still, even Merrill Lynch recognizes its brokers probably will be earning less, at least initially -- up to 18 percent less, by in-house estimates, Miss Thomson said. The firm has agreed to make up the difference for the next two years. In a West Coast office, a new Merrill Lynch broker said the firm's shift away from commissioned brokers toward fee-based financial consulting comes as no surprise. In-house, he said, old-style stockbrokers are viewed as dinosaurs. "And they went belly up and legs up." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: John Steffens thinks on-line trading will mean more jobs but lower salaries for brokers. (Merrill Lynch)

title:
PERSONAL FAVORITES;
DIANE VON FURSTENBERG, Fashion designer
body: Google.com (www.google.com) -- It's not officially out, but this is simply a great search engine. It's quick. It's fun to use. I want to check on a movie, read about an actor, find out who directed a particular film, this is where I look. It is very clever. Ebay (www.ebay .com) -- I haven't bought anything on Ebay, but I love cruising through it and seeing what's for sale. And I'm planning to do a major tag sale on Ebay. Wgsn.com (www.wgsn.com) -- Stands for Worth Global Style Network. I'm just starting to explore this Web site. It's a subscriber thing that a number of people in the world of fashion are starting to use. It looks like it carries the kinds of information that would be of particular interest to people in this field: trade show reports and calendars; photographs from major international shows, ready-to-wear and couture; photographs of shop windows from around the world -- all the major cities; new styles; new designers; what people are wearing. It really does sound like an amazing service. Amazon.com (www.Amazon .com) -- For books, I go to Amazon.com. It's fast; it's easy. I can find the titles I want and they are delivered to my door. Also, I am not addicted to cigarettes or alcohol or anything else like that. But even my family and friends make fun of the fact that I am constantly playing Solitaire on the computer. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Philip Greenberg for The newyork Times)

title:
PERSONAL FAVORITES;
STEVEN PINKER, Cognitive Neuroscientist, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
body: Amazon.com (www.amazon.com) -- Originally I scoffed at the idea that on-line shopping would significantly change people's buying habits -- "People like the social experience of shopping; they like to browse books and come across surprises; they like the look and feel of books, etc." -- until I actually bought something on line. Now, most of my book and CD shopping, I am ashamed to say, is on line. This behavior of mine pains me, because I do like the idea of local bookstores, and still patronize three of them in Harvard Square, just less often. But some new things really are a good idea. After Amazon, there is not one single site that I consistently patronize. Most of them (like the discount photo equipment stores that advertise in the back of Popular Photography) have really crummy Web sites, not in Amazon's league in terms of convenience or informativeness. But I do buy a motley collection of stuff on an ad hoc basis from individual Web sites that are not easily bought in stores. I bought a talc shaving stick from Electric Shaver Service (www.electricshaver .com) of Lincoln, Neb. I received a tiny sample of a talc stick with a travel razor and liked it very much -- it smoothed out the shave without making me smell like Austin Powers. But neither the 24-hour super-drugstores, nor the quaint old-timey drug stores in Harvard Square, carried the product. A drafting table was purchased from All-In-One Supply (www.allinonesupply .com), a drafting and architectural supply site in Lakewood, Colo. My wife and I searched for "drafting tables" on Alta Vista at 2 A.M., and the site turned up. The alternative would have been giving up a Saturday to drive around, look at a smaller selection and figure out how to get it home. And we bought a hard-shell suitcase (6 feet long) for a tandem bicycle from the manufacturer in Phoenix, Pedalpack (www.pedalpack.com). This is not an item that one easily finds in stores. I learned about it on a Web discussion group for tandem bicycle enthusiasts. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Bethany Versoy/W. W. Norton)

title: Present at the Creation (but Too Embarrassed to Admit It)
body: BACK before there was a dot-com on every bus and the word Internet could stir an Elvis-caliber frenzy in the hearts and minds of investors, I saw the light of the coming interactive revolution in the television control room at Silver Cup Studios in Queens. It was in the form of a roll-on personal waxer, which we sold on a shopping channel called Q2. As it was demonstrated on the upper lip of a production assistant, I, as the producer, sat and watched a computer tick off product sales. Thanks to the magic of a database, I could see how many people had called in to a customer service center in a distant city, and how many of them were buying the waxer. (I wished I could see exactly who they were and where they were from.) Had they not been buying, it would have been my job to whisper in the host's ear to move on to the next product. The goal was not to produce compelling television, which the production staff, hired from news programs, had been trained to do, but rather to move product off the shelves. Q2 was an experiment in upscale home shopping before shopping from home was cool. None of us could have known at the time that we were getting in-the-trench experience in a phenomenon that was to come of age just several years later and be better suited for a medium that barely existed. In 1994, only a fraction of the population was on line, and the notion of buying from a computer was about as strange as the idea that a computer could instantly link you to people and information around the world with one local phone call. In other words, very. At the time, most people were still suspicious about buying from a catalogue. While the merchandise buyers, who had come from retail establishments like F.A.O. Schwarz and Macy's, were thrilled to be part of this interactive television experiment -- ah, the glamour of TV! -- those of us who had come from the media were, frankly, embarrassed by our new careers. We had been lured by the promise of healthy paychecks. Even if the promise of creating something new had played a role, we didn't want to admit it. Also assuaging our perceptions was the involvement of Barry Diller, the media impresario who had invested millions of dollars of his own money in QVC, Q2's parent company, the electronic retailer known for its smiling show hosts and twirling cubic zirconium rings. (And not as well known to the public for its then more than a billion dollars in annual sales.) "We were little Barrys; Barry put the imprimatur on it that made it O.K.," said Candice Carpenter, the founding president of Q2 and perhaps its most famous alumnus. Her next job was on line, as the founder and chief executive of an early Silicon Alley start-up called iVillage, which many see as an early model of the future of E-commerce. "I was very embarrassed to tell people. I never said QVC. I said, 'I'm creating Q2 with Barry.' I was careful about identifying the job." After witnessing his friend Diane von Furstenberg sell thousands of dollars in merchandise in a single appearance on QVC, Mr. Diller suspended whatever disbelief he had in the medium and experienced a vision for a higher-end version of the channel. By investing in the original, he managed to pull off his experiment, basing it in newyork City, far from QVC central in suburban West Chester, Pa. The better to give it high-end cachet. The trouble was that Mr. Diller was, as visionaries often are, several years too early. Q2 was not carried in the markets it was created to serve. Most of the cable systems that carried it were in middle-American areas, which didn't appreciate the idea of artsy silver jewelry and other expensive boutique baubles sold on the air. Q2 was barely advertised, and the people who found it were either existing QVC customers -- not the right demographic -- or accidentally stumbled into our on-air store. And it takes many roll-on personal waxers, vertical turkey roasters and disco music boxed-CD sets to offset the cost of a TV production studio in newyork City. Another problem was that the Internet loomed. Though nascent efforts at on-line commerce existed on Prodigy, America Online and Compuserve, they were little more than petri dishes for what was to come. Once the World Wide Web started taking hold of the public psyche in 1995, the idea of shopping by modem came one step closer to reality. And, frankly, it beat the notion of sitting around waiting to view a special hour on exercise equipment scheduled for Saturday afternoon, when it was only Thursday night. "If you missed one of the shows, you missed out," said Mark Bozek, now the president of the Home Shopping Network, QVC's main rival, where Barry Diller now hangs his hat. Mr. Bozek has been on the cusp of the electronic commerce revolution since Mr. Diller hired him to work for QVC and then Q2. Though Q2 folded two years after it began, the lessons it taught were indelible. We couldn't help but be inspired by the power of interactivity as evidenced before us at Silver Cup Studios. We would beam to the world a product, prettied up and showcased in a television program in which its merits were demonstrated in every possible dimension allowed by the medium. And people would respond, calling in to discuss the product live on the air and, perhaps, even buying it. If it sounds like the Internet with training wheels, it was, though no one knew that at the time. Now, few people remember. Today, television shopping is the face of a broadband future, where set-top boxes allow shoppers to click a simple button and buy without getting off the couch. As merchants scramble to plot their on-line strategies, spending millions of dollars to set up Web sites and to market their services, it's hard not to think that the people at QVC and the Home Shopping Network are getting the last laugh. For years the subject of lampoons, both now have the opportunity to appear as geniuses in the landscape of electronic commerce. QVC's Internet arm, iQVC, was introduced three years ago, using the same computerized inventory and order delivery system as the parent channel. Sales totaled $44 million last year. "A lot of pure play Internet companies have had to spend millions upon millions advertising," said Steve Hamlin, the vice president of iQVC. "We have one of the best mediums to advertise, which is television." Both Mr. Hamlin and Mr. Bozek said the initial fears by the more conservative people in their respective companies that the Internet would erode sales in the core business have proved to be unfounded. "By having multiple channels, we've been able to get a more loyal customer who spends more money with us," Mr. Hamlin said. "It's not an erosion, but a service, a necessity in today's society." On a Saturday evening, watching that waxer demonstrated in the studio, it was hard to imagine that what we were offering was a public service, a necessary part of the larger commerce picture. But as the "24/7" mentality dominates more of our culture, it seems as if there could never have been a time when we couldn't roll out of bed and surf for the latest best seller, or depilatory, or whatever had touched off our dreams. Back in the days of Q2, Ms. Carpenter said, "Barry called it shopping for underwear in your underwear. He had the Internet in mind, even though it didn't exist yet." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A model displayed jewelry designed by Robert Lee Morris, seated with the host, Harriet Mays, in 1995 on the Q2 shopping channel. (Jay Brady)

title: Speed It Up, Webmaster, We're Losing Billions Every Second!
body: PETER GRANOFF knows how important it is to be slow. He is in a business where for centuries patience has not just been a virtue but also a necessity. He sells wine. The best wine can take years to make; even the very cheapest still must sit in its bottle for several months. "There's little way to speed that up," said Bill Newlands, Mr. Granoff's colleague. Indeed, Mr. Granoff said, "The whole point of wine is to slow life down. It has to do with community, with family, with friends, with relaxation over meals, with conversation. These are the ways in which we maintain our sanity." But Mr. Granoff sells wine over the Internet. He is a proprietor of a five-year-old company that last week changed its name to Wine.com (www.wine.com) but as Virtual Vineyards (www.virtualvineyard.com) was one of the earliest E-commerce sites -- "We were one of the first half-dozen sites to process credit cards over the Web," he said -- and one that is now faced with several new competitors. And so he would kill to save a second. "Site speed is of paramount importance," said Mr. Granoff, a master sommelier who suddenly sounds exactly like any of the hundreds of thousands of Web entrepreneurs. "We're constantly looking for ways in which we can leverage the technology. It's a never-ending process. Any E-commerce company worth its dot-com is engaged in a similar endeavor." That is why his company has hired Keynote, the first of a growing number of "Web-performance measurement companies," whose mission is to help get Web sites up to speed. "We really can't afford to be oblivious to this issue," Mr. Granoff said. Call it speed anxiety. Over the last year, an entire industry has sprouted up to measure, assess and suggest ways to improve "ease of navigation" and Web page design and to help avoid system crashes, which brought unwelcome headlines recently to Amazon.com and Ebay. On the Web right now, "performance" is almost entirely synonymous with speed -- the time it takes a customer to download the first page of a site, to link to another page or to buy something. Speed is so important for on-line brokers, whose livelihood depends on making many transactions throughout the day, that the Government may hold hearings on it; the General Accounting Office is researching on-line trading delays. The need is even more obvious for corporations whose reputation is based on the promise of speed, like Federal Express and United Parcel Service. All of these subscribe to Web-performance companies. It would be hard to find an E-commerce site that feels exempt from the pressure to go faster, whether it sells wine, art or long, leisurely novels. Art.com uses Service Metrics, another measurement company, and Amazon.com subscribes to Keynote, as does its main competitor in on-line book sales, Barnesandnoble.com, which also uses Gifwizard, Website Garage and Webcriteria. "Consumers are busy; they don't have time to wait 30 seconds to load," said Niel Robertson, a founder of Service Metrics, based in Boulder, Colo. "The idea is to get in and get out, to do it quickly. Companies live and die by this rule." Alistair Williamson, a founder of Webcriteria in Portland, Ore., added, "Even if your network is performing flawlessly, a speed bump -- a page that takes twice as long as a previous page -- could drive customers away." Umang Gupta, the head of Keynote, based in San Mateo, Calif., likes to say that "on the Internet, your competitor is just a click away." "If you go to Amazon.com or Barnesandnoble, there's not much difference in selection, in the look and feel of the pages," Mr. Gupta said. "You won't be able to tell the difference at 10 brokerage sites. The difference usually comes down to speed -- the speed of downloading or the speed of delivery." The Web-performance industry is not subtle about tapping into speed anxiety, speed envy and speed greed. Keynote commissioned Zona Research to conduct a study this year into "the economic impact of unacceptable download times." Titled "The Need for Speed," the report concludes: "On the Internet, the need for speed is a fact of life. In almost every way imaginable, speed rules." THE report cites the "eight-second rule," an unsubstantiated but widely held belief that customers will abandon their efforts to enter a Web site if download time exceeds eight seconds. It estimates that Internet companies in the unitedstates lose more than $4 billion each year from purchases that are not made because customers found Web sites too slow. It's easy to see E-commerce companies painting this in the starkest terms: an extra second costs $4 billion. Service Metrics has taken a more direct line of attack, monitoring the performance of specific companies within a particular industry during their most crucial periods. It looked at the performance between April 1 and April 15 of nine commercial sites designed to help with the preparation of income taxes: Yahoo Tax Center was the fastest, at an average of 1.65 seconds to download the first page; 1040.com was the slowest, at 13.97 seconds, and Quicken Tax Center's was in the middle, at 6.54 seconds. The report did not say which site was the most helpful, clear or accurate, or the most likely to prompt a tax audit. For Mother's Day, Service Metrics determined that the download time for FTD Flowers was on average two-thirds of a second faster than 1-800-Flowers. Victoria's Secret had the fastest average download time (2.81 seconds) and Hallmark the slowest (7.26 seconds). Godiva Chocolates was in the middle, at 3.37 seconds. Whether or not these marketing maneuvers have been effective -- out of the hundreds of thousands of E-commerce sites, Keynote claims only 1,500 subscribers -- it would be unfair to call them scare tactics. "The Webmasters are already scared," Mr. Gupta said. "It's important to be fast, and we're certainly investing in the site to make it run faster," said Dean DeBiase, the chief executive officer of Autoweb, which, along with Autobytel and Autoconnect, is one of the top car-buying Web sites. "Everyone has to do that." It's true that getting to a home page is slower than turning on the TV set, and buying something over the Web can be slower than buying it by telephone. It's also true that the numbers performance companies cite, like 7.26 seconds, assume optimum conditions for the user -- high-speed T-1 connections, for example, rather than regular phone hook-ups, which are two to three times slower. But it's still quicker, and for many people, more convenient, to go on line than to travel to an auto showroom or a local liquor store. So there is more going on than simply an objective measurement of time. Internet users have become rewired for speed. "When you talk about the Internet consumers," Mr. DeBiase said, "a bunch of words come to mind, and they all seem to start with I: 'impatient,' 'insistent,' 'informed.' " Speed is big these days. It's been the subject of an essay in Harper's Magazine, the topic of the first of Ted Koppel's "Brave New World" television programs and the focus of a new book, "Faster" by James Gleick (Pantheon Books), which ranges from MTV to microwaves to "multitasking," from instant polling to Type-A personalities, from fast forward to "speed" (amphetamines). Even the Metropolitan Transportation Authority in newyork City is getting into the act, issuing a recent report that buses in Manhattan travel on average an alarmingly inadequate 6 miles an hour compared with 16 miles an hour clocked by buses in other cities. HAS the Internet helped inspire all this, or simply reflected it? "It's a little of both," said Mr. Gupta of Keynote, who immigrated at 21 from India, where he grew up with neither a television nor a telephone. "There's a natural tendency for Americans to get things done fast, and they're willing to embrace new technology that makes it possible. Mr. Granoff notes that the Internet consumer's expectation of speed extends beyond download or transaction time to all aspects of the business, including inquiries by email. "I've had customers chew me out for not getting back to them within a few hours," he said. Wine.com likes to emphasize the convenience, friendliness and education it offers on-line customers, a gambit that seems common among E-commerce companies but may be particularly important to a company whose product is alcohol, given the tangle of state laws -- which may soon be exacerbated by pending Federal legislation -- that slows down distribution and delivery time. But if Mr. Granoff sees seven essential characteristics of a good wine, from intensity and sweetness to "complexity," Cyrus Khoshnevisan, his Webmaster, sees but three essential characteristics of a good wine-selling Web site, or of any Web site: "Can the users find what they want? Is it easy to understand? Is it fast?" Mr. Khoshnevisan's job focuses on the answer to the last question, and he uses Keynote to help him monitor the performance of the site, which is far more complicated than the average user might realize. Wine.com has two rooms full of about 20 powerful computer servers that run the site. Keeping a site up to speed is not just a matter of buying the latest and most powerful computers, though that certainly helps. It means maintaining a balance between the requirements of an alluring design and the restrictions of a limited bandwidth. A little cartoon of a popping champagne cork, Mr. Granoff said, is not worth waiting the extra time it would take to download it. It also means trying to anticipate slowdowns in the system caused by constant hazards like a malfunctioning computer in the network, overloaded traffic (illustrated famously by the release of the Starr Report on the Web) or something as mundane as a street repair crew accidentally cutting a fiber-optic line. Webmasters try to limit the damage by working on their connections, in several senses of the word. They often place their servers in different places across the country and use more than one Internet service provider to diminish the potential effect of any single glitch. They also chat up their service providers -- what is called "relationship management" -- so that when there is a problem, they are more likely to get action to put together the most efficient routing. Such networking requires data: the more specific information they have, the more the Webmasters know what to ask for. Keynote and Service Metrics are the only performance companies that have physically put computers in cities worldwide to measure the time it takes to download a page in each place, a service for which companies are paying anywhere from $700 to more than $1 million a year, depending on both the number of pages and the number of cities measured. Mr. Khoshnevisan checks not only the time for his Web site in 10 cities, but he also compares it with the Keynote Business 40 Internet Performance index, which Keynote compares to the Dow Jones industrial average. THE number indicates the average time over a business week it takes Internet users in 25 cities to get to the home page of 40 specific companies, chosen to be "a cross-section of the Web universe," said Dan Todd, who manages the index. This year, the weekly index, which is based on calculations every 15 minutes, has fluctuated between 8 and 5.5 seconds, providing a benchmark of comparison for other companies. This came in handy one day a few months ago, when Mr. Khoshnevisan noticed the data on his Web site indicated an alarming average of 15 seconds to download in Chicago. Because he saw that the average time in newyork was a normal 6 seconds and that the Keynote 40 was also at about 6 seconds, he knew it was not a systemwide problem. He contacted his Internet service provider and they pinpointed a single malfunctioning computer in the network, which they were able to bypass. Chicago download time was back down to 6 seconds within an hour. Another billion dollars in sales had not been sacrificed. The Webmaster might even have reached for a glass of wine, except that he doesn't drink. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Wine.com's Webmaster, Cyrus Khoshnevisan, left, and its master sommelier, Peter Granoff.
