title: The Flux in Pop Music Has a Distinctly Download Beat to It
body: A LOT of words have been used to describe David Bowie, but "conventional" is not one of them. So it is probably not too surprising that yesterday Mr. Bowie released his latest album -- "hours . . ." -- not in record stores but on the Internet. Just download in Liquid Audio or Microsoft Audio 4.0. Mr. Bowie is the most well-known artist trying to sell -- for about $18, the list price of a compact disk -- a full-length recording in a download format providing copyright protection. No one is sure how many people will pay that much for an unpackaged data file, even if it is the creation of a legendary rocker, and skeptics have suggested that the album's title refers to how long the download will take over an average modem. Whatever the reaction, Mr. Bowie's experiment is a response to changes throughout the music industry brought on by the popularity of MP3. Artists of every stripe are using the Internet to distribute audio in hopes of establishing a following, reviving a career or promoting new work. Since last year, the Internet has seen an explosion of legally downloadable music by prominent artists. New music is now regularly appearing on line from the major labels, which have co-opted the digital download trend as a direct-marketing gambit. The fourth quarter of 1999 is expected to see a record number of famous performers offering free audio samples on line to entice holiday purchases. The Red Hot Chili Peppers, Creed and Def Leppard recently began new albums with on-line previews designed to build anticipation before their release dates. As Chuck D of the rap group Public Enemy said in a recent interview: "The Internet happened to be a dog. You either pet the dog, or let the dog bite your leg." Last winter, it was not so easy for the artists who early on made their music available for downloading. At the time, Public Enemy and the Beastie Boys fought their labels' demands to remove MP3 files of their music from their Web sites. Meanwhile, the Recording Industry Association of America, the music industry trade group, was tracking down unauthorized MP3 distributors and formed the Secure Digital Music Initiative to establish standards for protecting copyrights. "We were this big band endorsing this thing the industry was trying to be united against," Mike D (a k a Mike Diamond) of the Beastie Boys told The Wall Street Journal in December. Chuck D -- Carlton Ridenhour -- put it more bluntly on Sonicnet.com: "The execs, lawyers and accountants who lately have made most of the money in the music biz are now running scared from the technology that evens out the creative field and makes artists harder to pimp." The Beastie Boys agreed to remove their MP3 files, live tracks recorded on tour, in December. But by April, their label, Capitol Records, had approved release of the group's remixes and video on its site. "The Beastie Boys are a good example of the industry's shifting mind-set on the Internet," said Hillary Rosen, the president and chief executive of the Recording Industry Association. They started out posting MP3 files on their Web site, "and getting a bit of hype out of having this public fight with their label," she said. "Their contract is up this year; they could have done anything." "Instead, they signed a new deal with Capitol for a $30 or $40 million advance," Ms. Rosen said. "They found that the existing system had a lot of advantages for them -- No. 1, that they got a lot of cash up front." A year ago, on-line proponents were saying that digital downloads would eliminate the need for record companies by allowing artists to take music directly to audiences. Instead, the rise of downloadable audio has spawned new companies like Emusic.com, Mp3.com and Atomic Pop that are pioneering Internet strategies for artist development, marketing and distribution. Less than a year ago, Michael Robertson, the chief executive of Mp3.com, was among those predicting the demise of major labels. Mr. Robertson now says "major labels are always going to be around." "They do play an essential part of the game," he said, "putting in a lot of marketing muscle to create a worldwide sensation like a Ricky Martin. But there is an Internet way of transacting business, of having artists deliver their music to fans, that the labels are going to miss out on." Mr. Robertson dubs his business model, "democratic access to the marketplace." "It's very different than the record labels who say, 'I'm going to pick a couple of bands and make those stars,' " he said. Anyone with a tape to upload can register with Mp3.com. Requests for the download will be automatically and continuously ranked against the rest of the songs on the site. "We don't take ownership of their music," Mr. Robertson said. "It's nonexclusive; they're free to work with anyone else. They're free to leave at any time. Those three points together make it a safe vehicle for artists." Al Teller, the founder and president of Atomic Pop, an Internet label, is a former chairman and chief executive of MCA and president of CBS Records. He speaks for underground and developing artists when he says, "There's an enormous frustration with how many artists get lost in the system and the cost of doing business there." Mr. Teller pursued Public Enemy after hearing of the group's differences with Def Jam Records over offering music for download. Atomic Pop then put the group's album "There's a Poison Goin' On" on sale through download in May, two months before the CD went to retailers. Atomic Pop, like other on-line labels, does not require artists to sign long-term contracts or relinquish ownership of their master recordings. Rather than offering artists an 8 percent to 12 percent royalty on sales, as the major labels do, on-line labels give artists a 50-50 net profit split. The arrangement eliminates exceptions like "free goods" (CD's given away for promotional purposes) that major labels use to whittle away the base on which royalties are applied. Business expenses for artist and label come off the top and must be documented. "To my mind, it's much more favorable to the artists," said Richard Grabel, a music lawyer with Grubman, Indursky & Schindler in newyork. Another frustrated performer was Greta Gaines. A former champion professional snowboarder and an aspiring singer-songwriter, Ms. Gaines signed with Giant Records in 1995. Soon afterward, Giant was reorganized and renamed Revolution Records. New executives replaced those who had promised to support Ms. Gaines. "I needed the faith and guidance of people who loved my music," she said. "They said, 'If you don't sell 250,000 units on your first single, you're out of here.' " Ms. Gaines completed an album for Giant/Revolution that was never released and asked to cancel her contract. "It was so damaging to me for so many years," she said. "Nobody would touch me." SHE continued to write and perform music, however. Three months ago, while preparing to release a debut CD on her own label, she posted three songs to Mp3.com as an experiment. The site, which does not charge for the service, also enables artists to get email directly from visitors who download their music. Gratified and surprised by listeners' responses, Ms. Gaines quickly revamped her postings to better represent the new album. In August, Mp3.com called to tell her that Alanis Morissette and Tori Amos had selected her to open on their tour, sponsored by the site. Now her single, "FireFly," is getting limited airplay at adult album alternative radio stations. "If I start selling records and my song starts doing well," she said, "it will be a complete revolution in the odds an artist has" of hitting it big. Ms. Gaines says she will not sign with a major label. "If I go on to have a major rock career, it will largely be based on the Internet," she said. They Might Be Giants, an indie rock duo, recently found itself with an album's worth of material while it was between label deals. So it sold "Long Tall Weekend" as an MP3-only release on Emusic.com. This provided a natural tie-in for a concurrent project, Radio TMBG, an Internet station programmed by the group. John Flansburgh, whose partner in the duo is John Linnell, said they assumed the MP3 album would serve merely as a way to connect with fans. "It's turned out to be just the opposite," he said. "We've probably gotten more media attention for this than our label CD release." It's a "strange, embryonic time," Mr. Flansburgh continued, comparing the advent of digital downloading to the rise of free-form FM radio in the late 1960's. "There's a tremendous amount of activity going on on a subcultural level," he said. "Meanwhile, the mainstream culture is still trying to figure out exactly what it is." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Among the artists who have made their music available on the Web: the Beastie Boys, top; the duo They Might Be Giants, and the singer-songwriter Greta Gaines. (Danny Clinch (top); Catherine McGann (middle); Lucas Mann)

title: The On-Line Consumer? Tough, Impatient and Gone in an Blink
body: FOR generations, American shoppers have been passive, long-suffering creatures, dutifully absorbing every whim and fancy that merchandisers cared to throw their way. Sure, the shopper might assert a kind of feeble will, refuse to open the wallet, mute the television remote, walk out of the store, even avert the gaze while cruising past yet another Calvin Klein billboard. But the truth was that we -- for like it or not, we are all erstwhile shoppers -- were at their mercy. And an entire psychology of consumer behavior was fashioned upon our meek, uncomplaining shoulders. The Internet changed all that. Psychologists and marketing experts are finding that on-line shoppers may be some of the same people who buy goods in the brick-and-mortar world, but their behavior is far different. Tough, mouthy, impatient, in control, they whiz through Web sites like the White Tornado through a dirty kitchen and vote their displeasure with a click of a mouse. And they talk back. For the first time, said Prof. Donna L. Hoffman, the co-director of the Electronic Commerce Research Center at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, "Consumers can provide content to the medium. I can have a Web site that says 'Company X Stinks' and there's not much anyone can do about it. That's profound. In fact, that's revolutionary." So revolutionary, it turns out, that researchers who have spent decades divining the laws that govern merchandising to a passive mass audience -- the so-called one-to-many model represented by television commercials, billboards and the like -- now have to start over, developing a radically different model that might be called "many to many," or even "any to any," since, as Professor Hoffman pointed out, anyone with access to a computer can have a voice. Consumer control, in the world of Internet retailing, means that customers are ready and willing to depart at any time, have a low frustration threshold and demand a high level of service in exchange for their loyalty. "It is increasingly clear that the consumer decision-making process is different," Professor Hoffman said. "And when we look at firms that are either making mistakes or not quite getting it right, in part it can be attributed to their not understanding that cyberspace is not a simulation of the real world. It is an alternative real existence." On-line shopping "went mainstream" during the last Christmas season, the number of shoppers jumping exponentially. Of the 100 million people in North America who use the Internet, surveys indicate that about 75 percent have made purchases on line. But customers in 1998 also were more dissatisfied than before. Experts attribute this to the ever-greater proliferation of Web sites and the fact that shoppers are no longer just those with computer expertise. Yet much remains unknown about exactly who these shoppers are, how they behave, what they like and don't like, and most important, what they will buy. "We're not even in the Dark Ages," Professor Hoffman said. "We're still in the cave." Somewhat easier to assess are the qualities that make the experience unique for consumers. One difference, said Paco Underhill, who wrote "Why We Buy: The Science of Shopping" (Simon & Schuster) and founded Envirosell, a marketing research firm that studies shopping behavior, is that a shopper on the Internet remains alone. "Somebody who steps out of an automobile or off the street to go shopping is looking to acquire goods, but they are also looking for the experience of being in public," Mr. Underhill said. "There are ways in which the on-line shopping experience does provide some sense of community -- you can set up chat rooms, reviews, customer commentary -- but your experience is still you and the screen, rather than you in public." David Schumann, the associate dean and professor of marketing at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville, agreed. "A fair segment of our society likes the human contact," he said, "and so on-line shopping really has not caught on for them yet, and may never." The lack of predictability and a tactile product also can create psychological obstacles for the would-be customer. In a store, Mr. Underhill said, "There's a doorway, there are aisles, there's a standardized checkout process and you have a pretty good idea of what you're in for as soon as you walk in the door." In contrast, he said, each Web site may require the customer to negotiate a different buying sequence. And while in the brick-and-mortar world, "you see it, you touch it, you feel it, you acquire it," in the on-line world, seeing is about as far as the consumer gets -- until the delivery truck arrives. As a result, on-line shopping sites appear most satisfying for shoppers who have a particular need and wish to search through a range of options, Mr. Underhill and other experts said, or for those who know exactly what they want -- a particular book or CD, for example. "What I'm a little tired of is the Web trying to be all things to all people," Mr. Underhill said. "It's not going to replace Kmart." Even when consumers have a particular product in mind, however, at the first hint of difficulty, they may look for the nearest door. "In the world of cyberspace," Mr. Underhill said, "everywhere is an exit. You have the capacity to bail out at any point, and an enormous number of people do." William Monroe, an interactive architect with Bowne & Company, a financial printing company, who has written about on-line purchasing, said that consumers initially like the fact that there are more options available for products on the Web, but then get frustrated if the information they need about a product is not available. "I bought an electric barbecue at a store," Mr. Monroe said, "and then went on line afterward and saw all these grills I didn't see in the store. But at the same time, what I encountered was a shopping environment that wasn't going to let me" find the necessary details about the merchandise. "Ultimately, I ended up buying a little side shelf," he said, "but I called the 1-800 number" instead of buying directly on the Web. Whether the Internet is more or less conducive to impulse buying is still a matter of disagreement. Mr. Underhill confessed that he bought a Doc Savage poster from Ebay recently, a spur-of-the moment decision. "I've been looking for a Doc Savage poster for a decade," he said. But other marketing specialists said that Web sites had yet to invent the equivalent of the checkout counter displays that tempt other shoppers, and they doubted that impulse would prove to be a significant motivation for on-line shoppers. While the rules of the shopping mall and street store may not apply in cyberspace, however, the bold, brassy shopping persona that is emerging on the Internet is already affecting the outside world, with consumers demanding more information and more choices, Professor Hoffman said. Consumers buying an automobile, for example, now expect to know not just the price but the true price, information available when buying on the Web. In a bookstore, they feel entitled to have at their fingertips a wide array of information about the books they are interested in buying. "Few people would drive from store to store and evaluate all the characteristics of every single offering," Professor Hoffman said. "But on the Web, those search costs go to close to zero, and that has profound implications for how you present these issues to consumers." Given the newfound pluckiness of on-line shoppers, that presentation had better be persuasive. Or somebody will be hearing about it. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Robin Jareaux)

title: Untangling the Grocery Web
body: WHEN I was a child, my mother used to phone the green grocer in the morning and read her shopping list to him. The groceries would arrive that afternoon, and my mother would tip the delivery boy a nickel (it was a long time ago). She paid the bill once a month. Supermarkets have mostly put an end to this convenience. But the modern version of grocery shopping by telephone is making its way onto the Internet. Right now, there are at least eight on-line grocers available to residents of newyork City, promising the service of the old-fashioned green grocer and the speed of the Internet: just click on to one of the Web sites, and check off the items you want. Then find everything bagged and waiting at your front door -- just as Mom did. But there's a big difference between then and now: then, it worked. Over the last month, I tried using all eight of these on-line grocery sites, and I found that many of them were not quite ready for prime time. Perhaps it is better to take the advice of the woman who called from the Associated Supermarket at 81st Street and First Avenue to verify the order I had placed through www.easygrocer .com: Why don't you just call us on the phone, and then you won't have to pay the $5.99 delivery fee? Easygrocer.com and keyfood.com offer one-stop shopping. Two other sites sell a limited amount of fresh ingredients (yourgrocer.com and netgrocer.com), another site sells only organic produce (urbanorganic.com), one sells only nonperishable items (wholefoods.com), one is more like the old-fashioned milkman, with milk, bread and a few other items (the Milkman, reachable through homedelivery.com), and the other provides all the ingredients needed to prepare a meal for two (cookexpress.com). Still, the concept of grocery shopping on line has possibilities. For example, priceline.com, the on-line merchant that lets shoppers name their price for a wide range of consumer goods, announced yesterday that it will start an on-line grocery service in newyork next month called Webhouse Club. Other newyork grocers, like Grace's Marketplace and Gristede's, are testing the Web waters. For now, most of the services require advance planning -- the deadline for orders is at least a day ahead, although easygrocer.com claims it will ship in as little as three hours. And then there are the glitches. One company, wholefoods.com, refused to accept my order, claiming incorrectly that I was ordering from a nonsecure server. Another, easygrocer.com, tried to deliver the order but would not leave it because I was not at home to sign the credit card receipt. A third, yourgrocer.com, wouldn't leave the order because there were perishables and I wasn't home (it would not entrust the order to my doorman). Ordering groceries is like ordering anything else on the Internet: you have to get used to it, and it helps if you're computer-literate. Or as Deborah Lewine, who telecommutes to her job as a writer for a video production company, said: "It's very time-intensive. I think it can take more time than going shopping. I could see that it would work better if you did it on a regular basis." It takes many, many clicks of the mouse and a number of false trails to find what you are looking for. Some sites do not describe the products in enough detail. Is that toilet paper one-ply or two? Many brands sold are obscure. Some have so many categories that it takes as long as it would in a 100,000-square-foot superstore. Most offer products in only a single size. Some sites move slowly; others force the user to click on another location to look at the shopping basket as it is filled. Some have no place to give specific delivery directions. When it comes to perishables, the shopper has to have an incredible reservoir of trust (others would call it naivete) that the virtual grocer will pick the ripest tomatoes, the tenderest beef and the freshest eggs just as the green grocer did for my mother. Delivery takes time. The quickest sites, like keyfood.com, are those based in the city. Urbanorganic.com requires ordering the previous Friday for delivery the following week. Yourgrocer.com delivers only three days a week, and orders must be placed by 5 P.M. the previous day. The on-line companies outside newyork City -- like wholefoods .com and netgrocer.com -- can take as long as four days to deliver, even by Federal Express. Two of the on-line grocers -- keyfood.com and yourgrocer.com -- did not tell me in advance that they did not have products I had ordered. They simply did not deliver them. Keyfood.com noted on the delivery receipt: "Sorry! No Perrier." But it neglected to mention that it had not sent the roasted turkey breast. (They didn't put it on the bill, either.) With one exception, the food cost more than it would have at my local supermarket, and that's before counting the shipping charges, which vary by weight when they come from out of town. newyork companies charged $5 or $6 for the service. The Milkman charged nothing for delivery, and neither did urbanorganic .com, although it charged a onetime $25 fee to join. The cost of food at netgrocer.com was high: $2.99 for a loaf of Arnold's whole-wheat bread, which was $1.19 at Food Emporium. One exception to the higher prices was yourgrocer .com, which sells in bulk and generally charges less than a supermarket. It's like Costco for carless newyorkers -- at least those who have the space to store 24 rolls of toilet paper. A dozen bottles of San Pellegrino water were $15.99, compared with $20.28 at the supermarket. Five quarts of Breyers vanilla ice cream were $8.49 at yourgrocer.com; two half-gallon containers (four quarts) were $9.98 at the supermarket. I had the most trouble when I ordered perishables. Unless your apartment building has a refrigerator to store your delivery, you probably have to be home when the groceries arrive. Otherwise, the delivery man may refuse to drop them off. That's what happened with yourgrocer.com. The delivery man called me five times between 6:35 and 8:05 P.M. to find out whether I was home. When he didn't get a response, he took the order back but agreed to return the next morning. The order from Associated Supermarket, made through easygrocer .com, produced a baffling phone call. The day after placing the order, I was told that the store had no pork tenderloin because "the butcher's gone home," that the store had only 10-ounce boxes of Cheerios, smaller than what I had ordered, and that it did not have the variety of toilet paper I had ordered. Then, I was told that the store would need a "physical imprint of your credit card." So, what was the point of ordering on the Internet? The woman on the phone wondered the same thing. At that point she consulted one of the owners and returned to say that the store didn't need a physical imprint for an Internet delivery. So, the order was processed. I was not at home when it was delivered, and the delivery man would not leave it because -- guess what? -- he said I had to sign the credit-card form. The groceries went back to the store. An order I placed with the Milkman, which said it delivers two days a week between 3 and 7 A.M., actually arrived at 2 A.M. Fortunately there was no milk in this order. The company says that if the apartment does not have a refrigerator, it rents or sells coolers in which perishables can be left with the doorman or at the front door. The most sophisticated of the companies I tried was cookexpress.com. But it isn't really a grocer so much as a meal planner: it sells all the ingredients for a complete meal for two, each item neatly packaged and numbered. The cooking directions are complete; the cook is required to provide very little besides pots and utensils. Next-day delivery is provided. A dinner for two cost $21 to $31; delivery for three such dinners was $17. The food was attractive and fresh, and if the seasonings were not what I might have chosen, they was easy enough to modify. When on-line grocers become as savvy, I may start pushing my virtual cart down the virtual aisles. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos (Margaret Reigel)(pg. F1); (pg. F11)

title: What Price Will Be Paid By Those Not on the Net?
body: THE latest Federal survey of who is using the Internet presented some sobering results. The "digital divide" is widening, the Commerce Department said in July, and the gap is on its way to becoming a "racial ravine." While more Americans of all demographic groups are going on line, black and Hispanic families are less than half as likely as white families to have access to the Internet from home, work or school. And even at the lowest income levels, the gap is great -- a child in a low-income white family is three times as likely to have Internet access as a child in a low-income black family and four times as likely as than a child in a low-income Hispanic family. It is clear that people without Internet skills are increasingly likely to be less competitive in school and in the workplace. But what about as consumers? Are they missing out on shopping opportunities and information? Are they likely to end up the captive customers of unwired retailers who will do what some inner-city grocery stores do now -- offer limited quality and selection at high prices? The answer is still up in the air. But there is cause for concern, experts say. "It's pretty easy to imagine that in a fairly short period of time, say within 10 years, to be a member of society and not be on line will be a little bit like living in Los Angeles and not having a car," said Paul Saffo, a computer industry consultant at the Institute for the Future in Menlo Park, Calif. "Their choices will be restricted, and they're going to pay a little more for things and they'll have fewer options," he said. "And it's not going to be one of these things where you see the digital homeless on the street, or sleeping on the steps of City Hall. It's going to be an invisible problem. The people who are digitally dispossessed may not even appreciate that they are dispossessed." For now, most experts agree, those excluded from E-commerce are not losing out on many price-cutting bonanzas. Best sellers may be 50 percent off at Amazon.com, but other books are not sold at such deep discounts there. Still, there are deals to be had, and not only through on-line auction houses. Some airlines offer discounts if customers buy tickets on their Web sites. And Mark Cooper, the research director for the Consumer Federation of America, said that long-distance telephone companies had been offering significant savings -- 7 cents a minute for customers who pay with credit cards on line, compared with 19 cents a minute for the average customer billed on paper. Analysts also predict that in a few years, so many companies will be selling on line that prices will become more competitive. But at the moment, the biggest plus for the on-line consumer is information and convenience. "Car sales are a good example," said Ann Winblad, a venture capitalist with Hummer Winblad Venture Partners. "People are going to car dealers armed with information to negotiate," she said. "They can ask for information on many sites on the Internet. Even if they are not buying on the Internet, they know what they should be paying. They know what things cost." Those shopping for compact disks can hear the music on line, read a review of an album, have a Web site like CDNow tell them what other artists they might enjoy and then walk into Tower Records and make an informed purchase. "It's very different from a store clerk -- they don't know you," Ms. Winblad said. Researchers who study the digital divide say they are puzzled by its persistence, especially after substantial computer price cuts and give-aways in recent years. James McQuivey, a senior analyst with Forrester Research, a technology research firm, said that because of affordable prices, the third of the population that earns less than $25,000 a year is expected to account for 11 percent of on-line retail spending by 2003, up from 6 percent now. But he said that would still pale in comparison to the group's off-line buying, which makes up 25 percent of retail spending. And, in general, he said, these consumers buy smaller impulse items, like compact disks. Donna L. Hoffman, a professor of management at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, said she was troubled that, according to her research and that of others, whites consistently have more Internet access compared with black people with comparable education and incomes. "There's something going on here," Professor Hoffman said. "Personal computer prices have dropped dramatically. And African-Americans' adoption of satellite technology and cable is dramatic. We think there are social and cultural factors that are influencing certain segments of society so they don't feel that they are interested in adopting PC's." Professor Hoffman said that one theory was that there is not enough that interests minority consumers on the Internet, something that may begin to change with the introduction this fall of www.bet.com, a Web site geared to African-Americans, which will include a store selling urban apparel, music and collectible items. But other Web sites focusing on black consumers say they have found it hard to draw shoppers. B. Keith Fulton, the director for technology programs and policy at the National Urban League, says the problem is complex, essentially a new frontier for civil rights. "There are two schools of thought," Mr. Fulton said. "One is that for African-Americans, our historical experience with automation has been one of disengagement and disenfranchisement. From the automation of plantations to industrialization in the North, whenever automation has come it's been to the disadvantage of African-Americans, so there is a lot of distrust there. Phones, cable TV, these are proven technologies." He said the "second school of thought says that for African-American kids, teachers aren't as well trained, schools don't have as many computers; kids aren't bringing the demand home for parents to get this device." With more transactions taking place on line, what will this mean to people who still shop in traditional stores? Some experts, like Professor Hoffman, think that off-line stores will be under pressure to improve services, if not prices -- both because of competition with on-line retailers and because of demands from Internet-educated shoppers. Retailers will have on-line divisions that they can use to augment their real-store services by, say, providing more information about items through a computer that customers can use in the store. But Mr. Cooper of the Consumer Federation is less optimistic. "Some think tank said this is not a case of haves and have-nots, but have-nows versus have-laters," he said. "The real problem is that the have-laters never catch up. You're going to be paying more for a long time if you don't get on line." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Preschoolers practice their mouse skills at the Essex County Child Development Center in Newark. (Thomas Dallal for The newyork Times); B. Keith Fulton heads the technology program for the National Urban League. (Jeffery A. Salter/The newyork Times)

title: What Sex Sites Can Teach Everyone Else
body: WHERE can an E-business struggling to fend off rising competition turn for a model of how to make money on the Web? To the entrepreneurs who were the first to make E-commerce pay and whose businesses are still the most profitable sector of the Internet: the on-line pornographers. Not only does the cyberskin game hold lessons for all sorts of on-line businesses, experts say, but pornography sites have pioneered technical and marketing developments that are at the heart of the business plans of many enterprises that would not be caught dead on the same server. "There are a lot of lessons to be had from the on-line porn's success on the Web," said David Zinman, the vice president for marketing of Adknowledge of Palo Alto, Calif., which charges site owners to gauge how well their on-line advertisements generate leads and sales. Mark Tiarra, whose on-line company, the Tiarra Corporation, creates advertisements and strategies for sex-oriented Web sites, said that compared with his clients and their competitors, "the nonadult side of the Web has always been a year behind the curve in marketing strategies." This innovative streak has been shaped by two realities: unlike many other Web businesses, sex sites have a product that people are willing to pay for but that almost anyone can produce. There would be no sex sites if sex did not sell. "Unlike major mainstream companies, sex sites had no off-line revenue stream," said Mr. Tiarra, who is also president of United Adult Sites, a trade organization of 500 on-line sex companies. "You have to make it on your own." Early on, visiting sex sites meant long downloads and slow video clips, but operators found ways to transmit large pictures despite narrow bandwidths. As the Internet became awash with sex sites, the operators scrambled to develop a way to use existing on-line technology to get pictures to Web surfers for the few moments they would land on a site. With income essentially based on speed of content flow, Web site designers began writing programs that tweaked technology to make pages and photos load more quickly to grab their share of the market. The resulting sites were not always coherent and flowing, but they delivered the product quickly, and that drew browsers and kept them from skipping to the next sex site. Creators of sex sites used tips and tricks in writing Web page scripts so that sexy selling points loaded onto the screen first before less appetizing elements, like sign-up fees. Most of the Web's sex sites make money by charging for entry to a video gallery, usually by a membership bought with a credit card. Many also carry paid advertisements for larger sites. Free sites profit by carrying links to other sites, which pay fractions of a cent each time a customer clicks through. With profits tied to traffic on the site, the battle for the most clicks was on. Some site operators designed tricks to lure casual surfers to accidentally visit sex sites. Some devised loops to repeatedly click onto sites, including manipulation of the back key to keep reloading a page. Stealth redirection techniques cropped up, including writing programs to create pop-up browsers that emerged as users left sites, creating a "no exit" barrage of windows and prompts. Web sites began feeding encoded key words for sites unrelated to sex into search engines, drawing unsuspecting browsers and causing pop-up advertisements to appear when certain key words were entered. They bought rights to commonly used names of Web sites with altered suffixes. For example, browsers seeking the Presidential Web site at www.Whitehouse.gov/ got a sex site if, by mistake, they typed in www.Whitehouse.com. Some sites began requesting credit card information as proof of age for "free trials," adding in fine print that membership charges automatically would begin afterward. Early on, Mr. Tiarra said, mainstream Web site owners were more complacent. "They were coming into this saying, 'Is this going to work?' " he said. "We came in saying, 'How am I going to make enough money to quit my job." Now, he said, mainstream companies are hiring designers of sex sites. "They're looking for successful strategies, so they're going to get the guys who had the most competitors," he said. Jane Duvall, who assesses sex-oriented sites, said there was a limit to what mainstream sites could copy from the pornographic ones. "The problem with copying porn sites is that sex is the compelling content, and you can never really compete with that," Ms. Duvall said. But for all the field's ferocious rivalry, sex sites offer lessons in the benefits of cooperation, too, said Ms. Duvall, a former newspaper advertising saleswoman who two years ago used $500 and an old Power Mac to set up her own Web site, Jane's 'Net Sex Guide, which reviews and rates sites. "We call it co-opetition, and you don't see it much on the nonadult sites," she said. "Even a link trade is a big deal. You're only sending away a user that is leaving anyway." Mainstream companies using click-through referrals should research the sex-site industry to learn how to avoid getting cheated, she said. The smaller on-line pornography sites formed larger networks offering comprehensive memberships and then splitting the profits -- resembling America Online's more recent decision to develop an electronic network that would allow members to shop at many retail Web sites with one credit account. They also formed large, free supersites, where each company would post its own click-through banner. Another example of the strategy of cross-linking or link-swapping was the formation of referral rings, networks in which sites refer customers to one another. Sophisticated tracking systems were then designed to count the referrals that became paying customers, so sites could reward one another with a percentage of the sign-up fee. This practice has been adopted by many mainstream sites, like Amazon.com and Beyond.com. "The on-line porn industry has driven Web technology just as it has with all new media," said Seth Warshavsky, the chief executive of the Internet Entertainment Group, a sex-oriented on-line company based in Seattle. "The adult industry entrepreneurs have been a lot more aggressive developing marketing strategies because they see a direct return on everything they put out," he said. "They're all players willing to take a risk to develop new marketing strategies, and only now are a lot of the mainstream on-line companies applying those concepts. We began working video into Web browsers in 1995. Now it's being used all over the Web." CAITY McPHERSON, the president of Bay Area Adult Sites, a coalition of 100 people who work in the sex-oriented Web site industry, created the sex site, Juicymango.com in 1997. Now she auditions strippers for Rouze.com, a Web site introduced this month that offers editorial material on subjects aimed at affluent men, like martinis, cigars and etiquette. It also offers erotic content, but its editors do not use traditional Internet pornography marketing strategies, Ms. McPherson said. "I suggested we use some synergy links to create partnerships with other sites and increase traffic," she said. "But the editors said, 'Why would we want to get rid of our traffic?' "They don't understand the sex sites are like a loop that generates more traffic, and the mainstream sites are like a rope where you just fall off when you exit. Playing by the mainstream rules means keeping your Web site an enclosed little world." "I live in Silicon Valley," she said, "and when I tell people at meetings I'm from the adult industry, everyone sort of gets all uptight, but afterward a few always give me a card and say, 'Please call me to talk about marketing strategies.' " Many experts agree that most mainstream sites will never be able to match the pure profit potential of sex sites, which have little overhead and an eager audience. "One thing that pornography has been more successful at is tapping into two revenue streams, advertising and selling subscriptions," Mr. Zinman said. "Only sites offering incredibly high-demand content can get both. Most nonadult sites have advertising, but few can sell subscriptions because you can get the content somewhere else." He added: "In the porn industry, you have a tremendous demand for the material product. Nonadult industry has to acquire the kind of information that consumers will want to pay for to make a profitable business model. Until then, profitable mainstream Web sites will continue to be an oxymoron."  Keeping It Out of Your House AFTER the United States Supreme Court overturned a 1997 Federal law that prohibited the dissemination of sexually explicit material over the Internet in a manner available to children, the market became flooded with software filters for blocking pornography from personal computers. Most Internet service providers and some Web browsers also offer optional built-in filter services for customers who want to censor Internet material. Here are some of the filters endorsed by the Federal Communications Commission:  AMERICA ONLINE -- (www.aol.com) offers as part of its membership fee optional parental controls that block E-mail messages from specific senders and confine access to certain sites. (800) 827-6364  CYBERSITTER -- (www.cybersitter .com) blocks sites the customer chooses and those from a list compiled and updated regularly by the company. $39.95 (800) 388-2761  CYBER PATROL -- (www.cyber patrol.com) selects objectionable sites and updates the list daily; software also filters sites with objectionable words or images. $29.95 (800) 828-2608  CYBERSNOOP -- (www.pearlsw .com) monitors sites visited. $49.95 (800) 832-7596  NET NANNY -- (www.netnanny.com) masks offensive words or shuts down browser that accesses banned sites. $39.95 (800) 340-7177  SURFWATCH -- (www.surfwatch .com) lists 25,000 banned sites. $49.95 (800) 458-6600 http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Jane Duvall with her husband, Jim, at their home in Bellingham, Wash. (John Stamets for The New York Times)

title: What's Your Bid on Peanut Butter? Groceries Join Big Items on a Name-Your-Price Web Site
body: Priceline.com Inc., an on-line bidding site for big-ticket purchases like airline tickets and automobiles, plans to begin offering consumers in the newyork area cut-rate prices on groceries like applesauce and cereal. In a deal announced yesterday, Priceline will license its trademark and software to Priceline.com Webhouse Club Inc., a new venture through which consumers can set the prices they are willing to pay for grocery store staples ranging from disposable razors to peanut butter. If participating supermarkets accept the prices, the purchases can be picked up at the stores with a shopping list reflecting the discounts. Consumers will print out the discount lists from their computers. Beginning Nov. 1, 600 supermarkets in newyork, New Jersey and Connecticut, including Food Emporium, A.&P. and D'Agostino, will begin taking part in the operation. Essentially, shoppers looking to shave costs from their grocery bills can log on to the Webhouse Club at Priceline.com and name their preferred price on a particular item. If the bid is accepted, the price is locked in and the cost of the item is charged to the customer's credit card. Members print out their private price lists and go to the store. "It's a whole new way to save money," said Walter D'Agostino, of D'Agostino supermarkets. Perhaps, but shoppers would be well advised not to count on buying a case of Coke for a buck or lobster tails for $1.99. Customers will receive up to 40 percent off regular store prices and half off on some goods. By offering a new way to save, Webhouse and its retail partners are taking aim at buy-in-bulk price clubs and on-line supermarket operators. Jon Otto, Webhouse's president and chief executive, said, "Unlike product-ordering Web sites, with their fixed prices, shipping fees and delayed delivery, we view America's neighborhood stores as a powerful and unmatched asset." Financial analysts said the Webhouse model might appeal to coupon clippers and on-line shopping aficionados but would not likely change the way most people shop for milk and bread. For one, they said they doubted that harried shoppers would take the time to point-and-click to bid on an entire shopping list to save 15 cents on a can of soup. What is more, many low-income consumers will be virtually excluded from the savings because getting the discounts requires a computer, an Internet account and a credit card. After 90 days, users will be charged $3 per month for the service. "I'm not overly excited about it," said Ray Dirks, an analyst with Security Capital Trading. "I really think the larger-price items are much more appropriate for something like this." But Priceline sees the expansion of its "name-your-price" concept to everyday, small-ticket items as a way to expand its Web-based business. "By initially allowing consumers to name their price for products in more than 140 frequently purchased grocery categories, and eventually expanding to a much wider variety of retail categories, the increased traffic to Priceline.com as a whole will help accelerate the growth of Priceline.com's airline, hotel and other businesses," said Jay S. Walker, founder and vice chairman of Priceline, which plans to expand the service nationally by next year. Priceline, based in Stamford, Conn., will also eventually receive fee-for-referral payments from stores. The goal, said Rakesh Sood, an analyst who follows the company for Goldman Sachs, is for consumers to become so familiar with clicking onto Priceline that they turn to the site for competitive prices on goods and services like rental cars and credit card deals. Retailers hope the concept will lure bargain hunters. "With the Webhouse Club, each of our customers can electronically tell us what they want to buy and the price they want to pay," said Christian Haub, A.&P.'s chief executive. http://www.nytimes.com

title: What Web Retailers Really Need Is a Whole Lot of Shelf Space
body: IN a clever advertising campaign promoting itself as "Earth's biggest bookstore," Amazon.com emissaries were portrayed earlier this year as searching for storage space in famously huge places like the Pyramids, the Taj Mahal and even the planet Mars. But about the same time, in the real world, the company was quietly settling into an anonymous-looking warehouse about 30 miles east of here. The 322,560-square-foot warehouse covers seven acres of former farm fields, an area larger than seven football fields. That is a pretty big building, but not in these parts. Here it is just one of dozens of similar bland, boxy buildings scattered among the sagebrush hills on the outskirts of a city more famous for glittering gambling halls. Hidden inside these otherwise unremarkable structures are the engines of a second economy for this region. In these high-technology warehouses, the virtual world of E-commerce is increasingly blending with the realities of commerce by any name: inventory, order fulfillment and delivery of products to customers. Here and across the country, dot-coms may see their shares soar, but some of the most mundane types of businesses are benefiting more tangibly, in a little-noticed ripple effect. For the warehouse industry, for instance, E-commerce is already causing significant changes, said J. Eric Peters, a supply chain analyst with Andersen Consulting. "And it's going to get a lot bigger." More than 80 percent of the nation's warehouses are wired with electronic management systems that keep track of products with bar codes and computerized databases, said Mr. Peters, who surveyed 200 warehouse managers last year. While only 22 percent of the warehouses were connected to the Web at the time, he said, that number is growing rapidly. Most of the nation's 2.5 billion square feet of warehouse space (enough to cover Manhattan nearly four times over) was set up to store cases and pallets of products for wholesalers and retailers. But E-commerce is pushing the warehouse industry to get wired to meet the growing demand for speedy delivery of small individual packages. And it is pushing on-line companies to master the back end of their businesses. These two trends meet in warehouses like those scattered near Reno. And inside these buildings, and in similar warehouses nationwide, experts say, some of the critical turf wars in E-commerce will be decided. "It's fairly easy to put up a pretty neat storefront on the Web," said Dale Rogers, a professor of supply chain management at the University of Nevada, Reno. "But you need a good supply chain behind the store. And that is difficult. Order fulfillment is where a lot of the battles are going to be fought in the future." Amazon.com moved into a building formerly owned by Stanley Works, a highly mechanized warehouse designed to supply retailers with packages of tools. But Amazon.com has had to reconfigure the inner workings of the building to handle the much more complex task of picking and packing products for individual customers. Books, CD's and videos are being shipped from the warehouse, and by the end of the year, 300 people will be working there, according to the company. But the company declined to allow a reporter inside the building. Although Amazon.com is moving aggressively to expand its distribution network, it has been uncharacteristically quiet about this more mundane side of its business strategy. When Amazon.com began in 1995, it had only 93,000 square feet of space for books at its headquarters in Seattle. In 1997, it leased a 202,000-square-foot warehouse in New Castle, Del. This year, it has expanded the back end of its operation almost tenfold, to 2.7 million square feet across the country, with two warehouses in Kentucky and one each in Kansas and Georgia. Amazon.com shares fell in August after the company announced that it was spending heavily on the distribution centers, further delaying the time when the company will make a profit. The company has not released any details about the cost of the warehouses, but its fixed assets rose to $156 million in June from $29.8 million at the end of 1998. According to some analysts, distribution was not part of Amazon.com's original business plan. But others say it is a logical and necessary step so that the company can compete effectively and continue to grow. "It's a similar strategy to how Wal-Mart expanded," said Mr. Rogers, who noted that many Amazon.com executives once worked for Wal-Mart. "They've got cash because of the company's gigantic market capitalization. And they believe they need a lot of facilities with a lot of inventory around the country. And not just to sell books. They're planning to be a big store." In many cases, experts say, the distinction between E-commerce and other kinds of commerce is getting harder to maintain as more companies conduct more of their business on line. Nowhere is that distinction being blurred more than inside a modern warehouse. Orders arrive by email or on Web pages and electronic bar code readers and radio transmitters are wired to a database that keeps track of the contents. There is an increasingly seamless interface between inventory and information. The Dell Computer Corporation, for instance, ships computer monitors to the West Coast from a warehouse near here. The computers themselves are built in Austin, Tex., and the two parts meet up on United Parcel Service delivery trucks on their way to customers in a dance choreographed by a Web-based computer tracking system. More than 500 companies use Reno as a distribution center, including Michelin North America, the parts division of General Motors, J. C. Penney, the winery Kendall-Jackson and the wholesale book distributor Baker & Taylor. Barnes & Noble is looking for a warehouse near Reno after deciding not to pursue a bid to acquire the book distributor Ingram. Reno has long been attractive as a distribution center because it is close to California and centrally located for shipments throughout the West. Space is cheap and plentiful. There is no inventory, individual or corporate income tax. And the railroad and Interstate 80 provide access. U.P.S. has a large shipping center here, a crucial ingredient for companies that ship small packages to individual customers, and the unitedstates Postal Service is planning to move a regional sorting center from Oakland, Calif., to the Reno-Tahoe International Airport. These factors have begun to attract more pure E-commerce to the area, too, like Testwave.com, which sells analytical instruments, and Igo.com, which sells batteries and other accessories for laptops, cellular phones and other tools for business travelers. Ken Hawk started Igo.com in 1991 when he was attending the Stanford Business School. The company, formerly known as 1-800-Batteries, grew so rapidly that Mr. Hawk found he had to move the business around the Silicon Valley nearly every year to find enough space. "After four moves, my C.F.O. and I said, 'Why are we in San Jose?' " Mr. Hawk said. "One of the great things about a dot-com is that it can be located anywhere." Mr. Hawk said he remembered the prediction of Faith Popcorn, the trend forecaster, that in the future people would live in places where they now take vacations, like nearby Lake Tahoe, and would go on vacation in places where they now work, like San Francisco or newyork. Mr. Hawk, who is an avid mountain biker, visited Lake Tahoe. He discovered that it got too much snow in the winter for reliable year-round shipping. But in Reno, at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, he found a place with enough space for his business to grow. Igo.com is now paying 60 cents a square foot here compared with $1.70 in San Jose, Mr. Hawk said, and it plans to add 40,000 square feet to the 18,500-square-foot-warehouse it leases. The company has grown to 111 employees from 24 since it moved here in June 1997, and it plans to hire 30 more workers over the next six months. With lower housing costs in the Reno area, Mr. Hawk said, most of his workers can afford to buy homes, something they could not do in Silicon Valley. Employee turnover is lower here, 1.5 percent a year, he said, compared with 30 percent to 50 percent in Silicon Valley. And Mr. Hawk can ride out the back door on his mountain bike into open space, one thing this area has in abundance. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Amazon.com's high-technology storage site, covering an area the size of seven football fields, is one of dozens of warehouses in Fernley, Nev., 30 miles east of Reno. (Andy Barron for The newyork Times)

title: A Web-Researched Ford in Microsoft's Future
body: A joint venture of the Microsoft Corporation with the Ford Motor Company, offering built-to-order automobiles via the World Wide Web, shows the potentially wrenching changes that electronic commerce is bringing in its wake. At a news conference here today, Microsoft and Ford executives took pains to argue that their venture -- allowing on-line customers to configure their own cars and obtain detailed information on product availability -- would not displace the traditional role of the car dealer. "This is not a world in which anyone is confused that the virtual world will replace the physical world," said Steven Ballmer, Microsoft's president. But he acknowledged that some car dealers were skeptical that the new partnership would continue to be a win-win situation for dealers as well as manufacturers. Indeed, several dealers said they believed that Ford was quietly trying to circumvent them, pre-empting their relationship with the consumer. "This is going to be a classic battle, but we won't back down," said Edwin J. Mullane, president of the Ford Dealers Alliance, a national organization representing 1,700 dealers, based in Hackensack, N.J. "We'll do everything we can to protect ourselves and the consumer," he said. "The consumer has to be serviced and taken care of. These guys at Microsoft don't even own a screwdriver." Other dealers, however, expressed optimism that there was at least as much potential for gain as risk in the rise of World Wide Web commerce. "I'm excited about linking up with Ford," said Peter Greiner, owner of Greiner Ford in Casper, Wyo. "If we give our customers the best Internet experience, they'll tell their friends." Under the plan outlined today, prospective buyers would enter data about their preferences on line and would be referred to dealers through whom to negotiate a price and take delivery. Some dealers are concerned that by providing more information about product availability, pricing and options, Ford may shift power from the dealer to the car shopper, effectively lowering profit margins. In its announcement today, Microsoft said Ford had made an undisclosed minority investment in Carpoint, the car-shopping service that is one of the most popular features of Microsoft's on-line service MSN. Separately, Microsoft said it had entered into an agreement with the American Honda Motor Company to license Microsoft's Dealerpoint technology, which is part of the Carpoint service. Dealerpoint is an on-line lead-management system to help dealers manage and respond to prospective Internet customers. Although the Honda agreement did not include an investment in Carpoint, Mr. Ballmer said Microsoft was actively seeking investments from other auto makers. He also said that Microsoft would at some point offer stock in Carpoint to the public, but that it had not decided on the size of the offering. The Ford-Microsoft venture on Carpoint, as it was described today, will directly link customers to Ford's manufacturing-system data base. That feature, which will be available on Carpoint beginning in the first quarter of 2000, will transform the automobile business, according to Jacques Nasser, Ford Motor Company's president and chief executive. "The impact is going to be huge," he said. "This is a different way of running our business." By making information on product availability easily accessible to customers, he went on, the service will put them in charge of the transaction, and will ultimately increase customer satisfaction. Ford and Microsoft executives also said consumer preference information that Ford can obtain through the service was a significant factor in its plans. Mr. Nasser said such information was vital for inventory and manufacturing, as well as design decisions, and could significantly reduce manufacturing costs. Mr. Ballmer said that Microsoft did not plan to sell data on individual customers' preferences, citing consumer privacy reasons, and that it planned to make its aggregate information available to Ford's competitors. But Microsoft's commitment to consumer privacy was challenged by at least one of the company's major on-line competitors. If Microsoft begins working with other car makers, "will Ford have access to purchase requests?" asked Mark Lorimer, president and chief executive of Autobytel, a leading Internet car site. "I don't think it's clear from what they said today." At the news conference, Mr. Ballmer said Carpoint now generates 140,000 referrals and $600 million in sales each month. Mr. Lorimer said Autobytel generates $1.7 billion in auto sales a month based on more than 200,000 referrals. http://www.nytimes.com

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Chevron and Phillips Discuss Joint Venture Chevron and Phillips Petroleum have discussed forming a joint venture in the petrochemical business, people close to both companies said, but they added that a merger of the companies was not imminent, despite a report in The Sunday Times of London that sent Phillips shares up $2.8125, to $56.5625. Analysts said that the recent recovery in crude oil prices meant oil companies were under less pressure to merge.  Page C2. Pressure on the Bank of Japan The Bank of Japan, which won independence last year, is under intense pressure from international investors to ease monetary policy to lift Japan's economy out of its decade-long slump. title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
No News Turns Into Bad News at Retailer
body: SOMETIMES the public shareholders are the last to learn the really important things about companies they own. Yesterday afternoon, the J. Jill Group, a catalogue and Internet retailer of women's fashions aimed at affluent 35- to 55-year-olds, announced that it would post a loss for the third quarter, which ends on Saturday. It is ending one of its two catalogues, formerly called Nicole Summers and lately called Nicole, only three months after announcing that it had repositioned the catalogue to aim for growth. Yesterday's announcement came after the company asked Nasdaq to halt trading, which it did at 2:07 P.M., with the share price down $4.50, or 40 percent, to $6.875. Trading resumed at 3:22 P.M., and the stock fell further, closing at $6.125. Just over a month ago, the shares were trading above $20. From then through yesterday, as the business was evidently deteriorating, the company made no annoucements. By the time it did talk, the stock had fallen by two-thirds. During the last couple of weeks, the share price had declined slowly, on gradually increasing volume. Then, yesterday before the announcement, the floodgates opened. By the time trading was halted, volume came to 3.6 million shares, more than the total traded over the preceding seven weeks and equal to more than a third of the total shares outstanding. It is not clear just how much of the bad news got out, or how it did. But the heavy volume and the rapid decline of the stock yesterday morning made it appear that something had leaked over the weekend. A company spokesman said that management would not discuss the stock price, and Gordon R. Cooke, the company's chief executive, did not return telephone calls. Mr. Cooke, who took over the company at the end of 1995, had developed a following on Wall Street as sales and profits grew rapidly and the company announced plans both to sell on the Internet and to open J. Jill stores in upscale malls. Yesterday it said that the Internet business, which began Sept. 1, was already accounting for 5 percent of sales and that plans for the stores were going well. But it also said that sales for the quarter would be about $46 million, roughly the same as in the quarter last year, and that the company expected to lose about 11 cents a share in the quarter, in contrast to a profit of 14 cents a year ago. While Mr. Cooke had been optimistic about both the Nicole catalogue and the J. Jill catalogue in an interview with Bloomberg News on July 15, in yesterday's announcement he was quoted as saying "the inevitable slowdown of J. Jill's rapid growth has happened sooner than we expected." The company blamed intensive competition and the "proliferation of E-commerce" for its problems. The Nicole catalogue was begun in mid-August to replace the former Nicole Summers catalogue. It was supposed to feature looser, less tailored clothing than Nicole Summers had emphasized. The fact it is being abandoned a month later presumably is an indication that reaction to it was far worse than expected. In the Bloomberg interview two months ago, Mr. Cooke had said that while both Nicole and J. Jill were aimed at women over 35, the former sold to women who read Vogue, while the latter was intended for those who read Martha Stewart. The real losers here are those who read the company's press releases and filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and assumed that if anything important was going on, they would be told.  Pay Attention To Those Tender Offers The pros on Wall Street who owned stock in Comsat, the satellite communications company, have made a lot of money at the expense of the amateurs. Lockheed Martin completed its purchase of 49 percent of Comsat on Saturday, paying an above-market price of $45.50 a share. If Lockheed buys the rest of the company -- which it may not be allowed to do -- it will pay considerably less for the remaining shares. Given that, it was in the interests of all shareholders to tender their shares into the Lockheed offer. Yet only about 90 percent of the shares were actually tendered, Lockheed announced over the weekend, and it will accept 54.26 percent of the shares tendered. Those who did not tender passed up a significant profit opportunity. While there is no way to know who they were precisely, you can be sure that the vast majority were individual investors who failed to understand what was going on. Many discount and Internet brokerage firms feel no obligation to offer advice when their customers are confronted with tender offers, and some investors may not have brokers at all. The result is that those who did tender -- including many professional traders and institutional investors -- are about $38 million richer than they would have been if all eligible shares had been tendered. That is money lost by the ones who did not tender. Yesterday, Comsat fell $5.56, to $30.44. If Lockheed is able to buy the rest of the shares, it will exchange one of its shares -- which closed yesterday at $33.875 -- for each remaining Comsat share. That purchase, however, is contingent on getting Congress to change the law to approve such a deal, and so far the House has refused to do so. Until it does, Comsat shares are likely to trade at a discount to Lockheed shares. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: "Reversal of Fortune" J. title: A Parent's View of the World Wide Web as It Reaches Adolescence - Correction Appended
body: Every young Internet millionaire owes a debt to Tim Berners-Lee, the creator of the World Wide Web. An Oxford-educated physicist, he stitched together the core software of the multimedia branch of the Internet while working in the shadow of the Swiss Alps at the CERN physics laboratory outside Geneva nearly a decade ago. Yet perhaps more important is what Mr. Berners-Lee did after he designed the Web. He has served as a kind of parental guardian of his creation, working tirelessly to insure that as much as possible the Web remains a public mass medium in cyberspace, an information thoroughfare that is open to all, Rolls Royces and Rollerbladers alike. That was his original vision for the Web -- a universal medium for sharing information based on freely available technology instead of being controlled by one or a few powerful companies. For the past five years, Mr. Berners-Lee, 44, has pursued that vision as the director of the World Wide Web Consortium, whose mission is to make sure that the fundamental software for identifying and sharing information on the Web is a public standard. Keeping the Web open, of course, has fueled its phenomenal growth, which in turn has created a much larger market for commercial exploitation. So it is one of the notable ironies of Net history: Because Mr. Berners-Lee chose not to cash in on his invention, he has helped expand the business opportunities for America Online, Amazon, Ebay, Yahoo and every eager start-up sprinting to join the dot.com gold rush. In a new book being shipped to bookstores this week, Mr. Berners-Lee expresses some irritation at being asked -- especially by incredulous Americans -- why he didn't go for the Internet gold. "What is maddening is the terrible notion that a person's value depends on how important and financially successful they are, and that that is measured in terms of money," he states in "Weaving the Web: The Original Design and Ultimate Destiny of the World Wide Web By Its Inventor" (Harper San Francisco). The book was written by Mr. Berners-Lee with Mark Fishetti, a freelance writer. "That suggests disrespect," Mr. Berners-Lee adds, "for the researchers across the globe developing ideas for the next leaps in science and technology." Still, Mr. Berners-Lee has no hair-shirt aversion for business. He writes that when leaving CERN, the European Laboratory for Particle Physics, in early 1994 he considered "starting a company with the working name of Websoft, to do much the same as Netscape," whose point-and-click browser software made the Web easily accessible. Yet that entrepreneurial flirtation was a brief one, and by his own account, it seems clear that Mr. Berners-Lee's instincts and abilities lay elsewhere. He is the son of two English mathematicians, Conway Berners-Lee and Mary Lee, who were computing pioneers in their own right, having worked on a team that designed one of the world's first commercial stored-program computers in the early 1950's. Indeed, in his book, Mr. Berners-Lee says the most tempting corporate option was to join "the research group of a large benevolent company." He did talk to several big companies about joining their research labs, but he eventually decided to go to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Laboratory for Computer Science and found the World Wide Web Consortium. "I wanted to see the Web proliferate, not sink my life's hours into worrying over a product release," Mr. Berners-Lee writes. At the consortium, he admits, he has restraints as well -- he must strive to be a neutral diplomat in standards debates among members like Microsoft, Sun Microsystems, I.B.M. and Oracle that are often at odds in the marketplace. Yet the consortium, Mr. Berners-Lee decided, was the right place for him. "I'd be free," he writes of his decision, "to really think about what was right for the world, as opposed to what would be best for one commercial interest." "Weaving the Web" is a book in two parts. The first is essentially a narrative of creation, while the second is Mr. Berners-Lee's view of the Web's future. His description of designing the Web underlines how much innovation is a step-by-step process, using the work of others and putting those building blocks together in new ways. In the case of the Web, the key ingredients were hypertext for linking text in a nonlinear format and the Internet. "I happened to come along with time, and the right interest and inclination, after hypertext and the Internet had come of age," Mr. Berners-Lee writes. "The task left to me was to marry them together." He came up with the software standards for addressing, linking and transferring multimedia documents over the Internet. They have the shorthand names that are second-nature to computer enthusiasts and even familiar to, if little understood by, millions of Web surfers: URL's (uniform resource locators), HTTP (hypertext transfer protocol) and HTML (hypertext mark-up language). If Mr. Berners-Lee seems matter-of-fact about his work, much of the computer science community was dismissive when they first saw it. "He took a very simple approach," Jim Gray, a leading computer scientist at Microsoft Research, said in an interview. "It is fair to say that everyone who saw it thought nothing of it. Very simple, very minimal, anyone could have done it. No big deal." "Well," Mr. Gray continued, "everyone was wrong and no one else did it -- Tim did it." Mr. Berners-Lee's breakthrough, apparently, is proof of the adage that genius is a fresh approach to the obvious. "I like that," Mr. Berners-Lee said last week in an interview. "The Web is obvious, after the fact." Critical to the creative process, in his view, is placing a good mind in an environment rich in the information that might be useful in solving a problem -- a "Web of information," he inevitably calls it. "Creativity is a Web-like process, it's nonlinear but not random either," he said. "It requires ideas just floating -- that is the state in which the mind can jiggle them into an insight." Mr. Berners-Lee believes that the next stage of the Web, if properly handled, holds the promise of greatly increasing the creative productivity of groups, corporations and of society in general. Whether that potential can be attained is an uncertainty that hinges, he insists, on the evolution of the new technical standards that the hundreds of members of the Web consortium are working to develop and refine. The Web's first stage, based on HTML, can be thought of as focused on addressing and presenting documents. The stage just beginning to unfold, based on XML (extensible mark-up language) and refinements like RDF (resource description framework), allows the data inside documents to be identified with programming "tags." Today, a user has to know or find the address of a Web document that contains information he or she wants. But increasingly, the Web should become far more "intelligent" as small programs sometimes called "logic engines" will be able to find the useful data on areas of intellectual inquiry -- finding some facet of Chaucer studies for Ph.D. research, for example, or corporate projects like mapping the relationships and dependencies among people, rivals and suppliers in an industry for competitive analysis. The next stage of Web technical standards essentially enables computers to talk to each other, so that they do routine and repetitive work involved in everything from homework to shopping. And that leaves people with more time and energy for doing the more creative tasks. The Web, in short, has the capacity to become a much more intelligent information infrastructure. "Now, we're writing documents that contain logic," Mr. Berners-Lee explained. "It's a huge step forward toward a semantic Web, which handles the meaning of data." Yet what Mr. Berners-Lee calls the "XML revolution," he writes, is "both a boon and a threat to the Web dream." The danger, he says, is a Balkanization of the Web -- if companies create their own XML tags that cannot be read by everyone else. If that were to happen, it would no longer be a universal medium of sharing information. The first line of defense against the threat, Mr. Berners-Lee says, is his consortium, as the guardian of the "technical integrity of the Web" -- keeping the standards open. Which is why, he says, he plans to stay at M.I.T. for the next several years. "It is so important that we get this right that I want to be there and throw my weight around," he said. His creation is still young. And Mr. Berners-Lee views it with a mixture of parental pride and concern, and he is not yet willing to let it go unsupervised. "I think of the Web as an adolescent," he said. "It has started realizing it has a new-found power. No one knows if it knows how to use it responsibly. And maturity is a long way off." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Business Day yesterday about Tim Berners-Lee, the creator of the World Wide Web, misspelled the surname of a freelance writer who collaborated with him on a new book. The writer is Mark Fischetti, not Fishetti. Correction-Date: September 21, 1999, Tuesday Graphic   Photos: Tim Berners-Lee, whose fresh approach to the obvious led to the World Wide Web. title:
Compressed Data;
'Digital Storage Lo cker' For Music Downloads - Correction Appended
body: It is an increasingly popular Internet activity: downloading, storing and playing digital music files on a computer or a portable player that can handle the MP3 digital music format. And it can be annoyingly difficult: Users often do not pay attention to where downloads land on their hard drives -- and since there is no industry-wide convention for naming music files, a song might arrive as a file called eleanorrigby.mp3 or, more blindly, 977X021.mp3. As a result, finding the downloaded tunes can be a scavenger hunt -- especially on Windows computers. Sensing a potential business opportunity, two executives with Internet start-up experience and venture capital, have set up a Silicon Valley company called Myplay. Its Web-based service, planned for a mid-October rollout, is meant to make it easier to download and organize music files by song title -- with artist and album also listed, if Myplay has the information in its data base. Each user's files would be kept in a personal "digital storage locker" on the Web. Other than offering a sample starter kit of some 100 licensed songs from an eclectic repertoire that includes Elvis Costello and George Gershwin, Myplay assumes that users will obtain their own music files out on the Internet. A user would have access to the storage locker from any computer connected to the Internet -- similar to the way Microsoft's Hotmail and other Web-based email services enable a person to check email from any computer, rather than being tied to a single desktop or laptop machine. Doug Camplejohn, the 34-year-old co-founder and chief executive of Myplay, is a former Apple Computer marketing executive. His cofounder, David Pakman, 30, is a former Apple colleague who was a business development executive at the on-line music distributor N2K, before it merged with CD Now earlier this year. The company, which is based in Redwood City, Calif., and whose financial backers include the Silicon Valley venture firms IVP and Interval Capital, plans to offer each customer a free storage locker that could hold 250 megabytes -- some five to six hours -- of music. While Myplay may eventually sell monthly subscriptions for additional storage space, the company's main revenue would come from advertising and from marketing pacts with music companies like Dreamworks Records, a unit of Dreamworks SKG, that has signed on as a charter advertiser. Adam Somers, a marketing executive with Dreamworks Records, said his company would offer individual tracks to Myplay customers, including one from the band Powerman 5000. People who downloaded the Powerman 5000 track might then receive promotional email about the band's albums, concerts and the like. "It's a way of finding out what people are listening to," Mr. Somers said. "It's another aspect of one-to-one marketing."
