In November, Arabella Churchill, Winston Churchill's granddaughter, is to have a face lift on celebritydoctor.com. (pg. 7)

title:
PERSONAL BUSINESS;
A Credit Card for Internet-Wary Shoppers
body: AIMING at consumers who want to shop on line but lack confidence in Internet security, American Express is starting to mail applications for the blue cards it is adding to its array of green, gold and platinum. Starting in November, in time for the holiday season, shoppers will be able to swipe American Express blue cards through readers they have plugged into their home computers. The cards contain a "smart" chip, the company says, that works in tandem with the customer's PIN number to prevent unauthorized use. Card readers will be supplied free through Jan. 31 to people who meet the credit qualifications. They will cost $25 thereafter. And just like other credit cards, the blue cards can be used in stores. At least one expert, Paul C. Kocher, president of Cryptography Research Inc. in San Francisco, is impressed. "It's a brilliant marketing approach" that marries the Internet and the credit card, he said, predicting that it would be "very successful." While Mr. Kocher contended that any encryption can be broken with enough effort, the new blue card will be more reliable and far less susceptible to fraudulent use than cards without the smart chip, he said.  Just in case, American Express will protect blue-card users against unauthorized charges, as well as damage or theft of their purchases and the no-return policies of some merchants. The blue cards were formally introduced on Sept. 8 but have not yet been widely marketed. They are intended to extend American Express's reach into the credit-card business, where its existing entry is the Optima card. The Optima card, only modestly successful, carries interest rates ranging from the prime rate plus 7.9 percent to the prime plus 9.9 percent. Neither the blue nor the Optima cards, unlike those of other colors, carries an annual fee. The blue card will have a six-month introductory period in which no interest will be charged on revolving balances. Then the fixed rates will be 9.99 percent for most customers and 12.99 or 15.99 for those who are less creditworthy. The company's traditional charge cards, as opposed to credit cards, require complete payment each month. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
YOUR HOME;
Selecting A Cybertech 'Bundler'
body: JUST a few years ago, newyork City residents who wanted local telephone service, cable TV or access to the Internet had fairly limited options. For local phone service, Nynex, now Bell Atlantic, was the only game in town. For cable TV, Time Warner Cable was the name found on most channel-selectors in Manhattan, Queens and Brooklyn. And for Internet access, the choices available to most residents were limited to the manufacturer, price and speed of their dial-up modem. Now, however, as the result of the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which encouraged competition among telecommunication service providers, residents have a broad array of options to choose from and can buy one or all of the services they need from one or more service providers. "Over the past few years, we've been bombarded by companies large and small proposing to deliver telephone, cable TV and high-speed Internet access to our buildings," said David Pian, director of technology and telecommunications for Rockrose Development, a Manhattan development and property management company. "And while there has been a weeding-out process over the past two years or so, there are a few companies out there that offer a wide range of choices to building owners and residents." Over the past year or so, for example, Dualstar Technologies Corporation, an information technology and telecommunications company based in Long Island City, Queens, has used its "Cyberbuilding" technology to provide various "bundles" of service to residents of multi-unit buildings in newyork City. In the Westbury House, a 38-unit condominium at 160 West 86th Street, between Columbus and Amsterdam Avenues, for example, the company provides local, regional and long distance telephone services, direct broadcast satellite television service and high-speed Internet access. Another major telecommunications provider in the newyork Area, RCN Corporation, based in Princeton, N.J., also provides multi-unit buildings with bundled telecommunications packages including local, regional and long distance telephone services, cable television programming and high-speed cable Internet service that can operate up to 50 times faster than systems using conventional dial-up modems. And just last Tuesday, Time Warner Cable of newyork City raised the ante in newyork City's cyberwars when it introduced Road Runner -- its own cable-based Internet access service that can provide equally swift connection speeds by using a cable modem hooked up to the company's existing coaxial cable network. Mr. Pian, of Rockrose Development, said that those who have the most to gain from the heating up of competition in the telecommunications industry are residents in multi-unit buildings. That is because in most cases, companies that provide "bundled services" are more likely to offer the best rates to buildings with large numbers of potential customers. "Selecting the right telecommunications provider is less about engineering and construction and more about choosing the best business partner," Mr. Pian said. While financial incentives for picking one service provider over another must always be considered, he said, a property owner -- or co-op or condominium board -- should not lose sight of the ultimate goal of ensuring that the occupants of the building have the ability to choose to the best service they can get at the lowest price possible. And that is only possible when an owner or board makes it possible for competition to exist in the building. "I'd say that three telecommunications providers is a nice round number for most buildings," Mr. Pian said, explaining that since most buildings in newyork City already have access to the services of Bell Atlantic and Time Warner, allowing one more provider into the building will stimulate the necessary competition. If the choice were up to Time Warner, however, the two service providers mentioned above would be all that is necessary. "The first advantage of our Road Runner system is that the building owner or board usually doesn't have to do anything," said Barry Rosenblum, president of Time Warner Cable. He explained that since the company's new high-speed Internet access system uses the same coaxial cable that carries its cable television programming, most buildings already have the necessary cable installed. "Except for the cable modem, no extra equipment is necessary," he said, adding that for customers who now have Time Warner's cable TV service, the additional charge for high-speed Internet access is $39.95 a month. That charge, he said, includes a $5 monthly rental fee for the cable modem and 24-hour-a-day connection to the Internet. The service is expected to be available this fall in parts of the Upper West Side, Upper East Side, eastern parts of Midtown in Manhattan, and Jackson Heights in Queens, and is expected to be available in all of Manhattan, Queens, Brooklyn and Staten Island in the spring of 2001. Another company that provides both television programming and high-speed Internet access in newyork City is Dualstar. "We are in the multi-unit dwelling business," said Land Grant, a spokesman for the company. "And we're focused on delivering telephone service, high-speed Internet service and direct broadcast satellite programming to residents of high-rise buildings in newyork City." Telephone service provided by the company, he said, would utilize AT&T Local Services. "Customers usually realize a discount of anywhere between 5 and 20 percent, depending on the services they require," he said. Mr. Grant said that the satellite television programming used in its system is provided by DirectTV, a direct satellite broadcasting company that provides subscribers with access to more than 185 channels as well as to the movies, sports packages and pay-per-view options. DirectTV packages start at $19.95, depending on the programming desired. Dualstar's high-speed Internet service, Mr. Grant said, starts at $38.95 per month, and allows subscribers to stay connected to the Internet "24 hours a day, 365 days a year." The Internet service, he said, is provided by using what is known as an "overlay technology." "That means that we can send a broad-band, high-speed digital signal over existing copper wiring in the building," he said, adding that the copper wire that carries the signal is usually the subscriber's existing telephone lines. "Overlay technology allows us to send both signals without one interfering with the other," he said. And while Dualstar's technology can provide Internet access at speeds of 1 megabit per second -- about 20 times faster than a dial-up modem, but slower than the speed possible with cable -- the speed is relatively constant. With cable modems, Mr. Grant said, the speed of the system can drop off as more people use the system. James Maiella, a spokesman for RCN, said that while that may be true for some systems that use cable modems, it is not true for all. "It depends on how you design your network," he said. He explained that when RCN wires a building for cable it limits the number of apartments to a specific fiber-optic connection so that no one cable circuit can become so overloaded as to cause a slowdown in the network. The cost for RCN's Internet service, he said, is $39.95 a month. Jeffrey Heidings, president of Siren Management, said that co-op and condominium boards that are contemplating allowing a new telecommunications provider into their building should keep some things in mind when negotiating a contract with the provider. For example, he said, some companies will agree to a "revenue sharing" arrangement with the property owner or co-op or condominium. "Some companies offer a flat amount per subscriber per year," Mr. Heidings said, adding that it was not uncommon for a board or building owner to receive $50 per subscriber. "Others offer a small percentage of the amount earned from subscriptions," he said. For simplicity's sake, he explained, most boards opt for the flat fee. Another thing to be aware of, he said, is the fact that in some contracts the company might reserve the right to use one building to "branch off" into other buildings. "If your building happens to be the one they're branching off from, that's probably going to cause a little more disruption than you might want," he said. And finally, Mr. Heidings said, with some contracts, the company reserves the right to automatically renew the contract on the same terms and conditions if the building owner or board does not specifically object. "Most of these contracts run for seven years or so," he said. "And I think that after seven years, you might want to be in a position to renegotiate the terms." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing. (Tom Bloom)

title: Big Internet Sites Joining Auction Network
body: Nearly 100 Internet sites, including three of the biggest -- Microsoft's MSN, Excite@Home and Lycos -- have agreed to share their auction listings so that an item put up for sale on one site will be available for bidding on all other sites. The move, which is to be announced today, is an effort to catch up with the huge popularity of Ebay, the dominant on-line auction site, which has more than three million items for sale at any one time, ranging from stuffed bears to minivans. The new auction network was established by Fairmarket, a small company in Woburn, Mass. Fairmarket initially created a service that let companies set up their own auctions, mainly as a way to sell discontinued items and products that have been returned. Its clients include CompUSA, New Line Cinema and CBS Sportsline's sporting-goods shop. These companies had used the site to sell their own merchandise, but they have now agreed to have all their products listed on general-purpose auction sites as well. America Online, the largest Internet service, does not run its own auctions. Ebay agreed to pay $75 million over four years to promote its auctions to America Online users. Yahoo, the second-biggest Internet service, has competed aggressively with Ebay by offering free auctions. Ebay charges a fee to list an item and then collects a percentage of the purchase price. Since Ebay experienced a series of computer blackouts in recent months, Yahoo's popularity has surged. It now lists 700,000 items. But the other popular Internet services have found it very difficult to make headway into Ebay's turf. Excite@Home, for example, has fewer than 20,000 items for sale on its free auction site -- a major incentive in its decision to merge those listings into the new broader network. "In auctions, scale is really valuable," said David Tse, a senior vice president at Excite. "If you put an item up for sale, you want the most potential bidders. If you are a buyer, you want to see the most products in the category you are interested in." The move represents the first entry into auctions by Microsoft, which has been rushing to make sure that its MSN Internet service matches all the features offered by competitors. In recent weeks, Microsoft has introduced an instant message software to match one of the most popular features of America Online, and a name-your-own-price travel service, modeled after the well-known offering of Priceline.com. While it is unclear how successful Microsoft will be in any of these areas, its entry into any market inevitably causes investors to raise concerns about the leaders of that market. In the first two days after Microsoft's travel service was announced, for example, Priceline's stock dropped nearly 20 percent. Ebay, which has a stock market value of $19 billion, did not respond to requests for comment on the new auction network. The third-biggest auction site is Amazon.com, the biggest on-line retailer. Though the company declines to say how many items it has for sale, Auctionwatch, a site that tracks auctions, estimates that Amazon lists between 100,000 and 200,000 items. In July, Lycos was the first big site to use the Fairmarket auction system, letting its users post items for sale and bid on items from all participating auctions. While Lycos had considered starting its own auctions or selling links to Ebay, as America Online has done, it decided that it "would take a long time to build, and going with a joint venture would give us more traction," said Jeffrey S. Bennett, the director of business development at Lycos. Fairmarket has also signed up Ticketmaster-Citysearch, which runs local auctions; Boston.com, a unit of The newyork Times Company, and Earthlink, the big Internet service provider. In all, these sites will contribute about 70,000 listings from the start to the Fairmarket network. Each member site will present the auctions in its own format and graphic design, so that shoppers will not know that the listings come from multiple sites. And each site will integrate the auctions with its other services. For example, Lycos users can have the auctions they are bidding on presented on their "My Lycos" start page alongside their chosen stock quotes and sports scores. At first, Lycos and Excite plan to offer auctions without any fees. Microsoft will not charge a listing fee but will impose a transaction fee of between 1.5 and to 5 percent, depending on the purchase price. Deanna Sanford, the lead product manager for MSN, said that Microsoft would be charging a transaction fee, even though others were not, because it expected such fees would become standard. Indeed, for Fairmarket to profit from the system, sellers must eventually charge such fees. Fairmarket is charging the sites about 1 percent of completed auctions. In addition, the site whose user buys an item also receives 1 percent of the purchase price from the site that posted the auction. But Fairmarket said it was waiving these fees for sites that offer free auctions. Mr. Bennett of Lycos said that even if competition prevented the company from imposing transaction fees, it could still profit by selling advertising on the auction pages. "We are in the business of aggregating an audience," he said. Analysts said it was not clear how much the Fairmarket venture could dent Ebay's market dominance. "For MSN and the others, it's a better starting point than if they did this on their own," said Fiona Swerdlow, an analyst with Jupiter Communications. "But Ebay is clearly out in front." But Mr. Bennett said that Lycos could still build a big business as newcomers come onto the Web with no loyalty to Ebay. "Hats off to Ebay, which has really benefited from its first-mover advantage," he said. "But the game is early, and there are a lot more folks to come in and be attracted to the auction space."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
China's Internet Providers Remain Bowed, Not Broken
body: In private they are puzzled and angry but in public, China's fledgling Internet companies have pasted on brave faces the last two days, ever since an important Government minister said that foreign shares in companies providing Internet content or services were illegal. No one quite believes that Wu Jichuan, the Minister of Information Industries, intends to force dissolution of the dozens of young, frontier companies that have attracted foreign funds from giants like Intel as well as from individuals and venture capital groups. Many of these companies also hope to make public stock offerings in the unitedstates. Foreigner ownership has never been allowed in Internet service providers, which connect users with the state-run gateways to the global Internet. But on the assumption that fortunes will follow the exponential growth of computer use here, tens of millions of dollars in outside money has rushed to companies developing Chinese-language electronic commerce and portals, or Web sites like Yahoo.com and Excite.com that serve as the front doors for users' Internet journeys. By Government estimates, widely considered to be low, China had more than 4 million Internet users as of June, with the numbers rising fast. Among the best known portals here are SINA.com and Sohu.com, and both have substantial foreign investment. Another pioneer, Sparkice I-Com, which runs Internet Cafis, an Internet access provider, has outside investors, too. The players in this risky field say they have cooperated with Government agencies to get where they are and profess surprise at what appears to be a sudden turn. Most of the affected companies said that the supposed ban on investment surely would not stick and, indeed, one ministry official hinted today that the rules might be eased in the future. Charles Zhang, the president of Sohu.com, which has investments from Intel, Dow Jones and other foreign companies as well as three professors at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said today that in building his company over the last three years he has worked closely with several Government agencies, including the Information Industries Ministry. Mr. Zhang declined to comment directly on the minister's remarks, only saying, "I think that venture-capital investment to develop high-tech industries is the path China is taking." Mr. Zhang held a previously scheduled news conference here today to announce his company's entry into E-commerce, a genuine frontier in a country where credit and debit cards are only starting to catch on. Appearing with him were officials of Intel China, which has provided capital for the project as well as the computer chips; Microsoft China, which provides the software, and Compaq Computer, which provides the hardware. But the sudden questions about legality hung over the meeting. At the news conference, James Jarrett, president of Intel China, said his company had invested in several Chinese Internet companies. He said he felt that, in the end, officials would realize that such investments contributed to China's progress. "Left unclarified," Mr. Jarrett said of the minister's statement, "this clearly would have a dampening effect on foreign investment in these sectors." Representatives of other investing companies went further in private, saying that a ban on foreign investment would be self-defeating for China because it would drive the same capital and energy to places like Taiwan and hongkong -- where companies could serve Chinese consumers from abroad. In an interview with Dow Jones Newswires today, an official of the Information Industries Ministry restated that outside investments in Internet companies were illegal. The ministry's position is that Internet content and services are covered by rules barring foreign ownership of telecommunications services -- rules that were written in 1993 and 1995, before the Internet was widely available in China. But the official, Wang Lijian, vice director of the ministry's news office, also said that the telecommunications rules would be revised later this year in a manner "beneficial for investment and development." Foreign entry into telecommunications services has been a prime topic in the Chinese-American negotiations over China's entry to the World Trade Organization. If those talks succeed, then outside investments in computer services are likely to be legalized in any case. Chinese and foreign businessmen here are speculating about Mr. Wu's reasons for raising the issue, which he first did in an interview Tuesday with the Financial Times. Some think it is a ploy to warn the unitedstates what could happen if China is denied entry to the World Trade Organization. Others think it is part of Mr. Wu's effort to solidify the powers of his recently formed super-ministry over the growing Internet sector. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Company Announces Appointments
body: The newyork Times Company has announced the appointment of two corporate executives. In addition, the company's Internet business unit has appointed a chief financial officer. James C. Lessersohn, formerly vice president for corporate planning, has been named vice president and treasurer of the company. Ann S. Kraus, formerly director of compensation, has been named vice president for compensation and benefits.  Ellen Taus, treasurer and vice president, will become chief financial officer of the Internet business unit, Times Company Digital. Mr. Lessersohn, 44, who succeeds Ms. Taus, joined the Times company as a project manager in 1987. He was named a vice president for corporate planning in 1997. Ms. Kraus, 49, joined the company as director of compensation in 1997. She was previously director for compensation of the Prudential Insurance Company. Ms. Taus, 41, joined the company as an assistant treasurer in 1996. She had previously worked for R. H. Macy, the American Museum of the Moving Image, TW Services and newyork and Foreign Securities. Times Company Digital operates nearly 50 Web sites, including the sites of The newyork Times and The Boston Globe, nytoday.com, winetoday.com and golfdigest.com. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Motorola Set To Acquire Cable Maker
body: Motorola Inc. confirmed today that it would acquire the General Instrument Corporation, a leading maker of cable set-top boxes, in a stock deal valued at nearly $11 billion. The move would make Motorola a key supplier of cable television equipment and allow the company to develop what it calls a "home hub" of products to offer broadband cable and Internet access to homes. The company says the deal gives it a passageway into the homes of millions of consumers and that it plans to develop new set-top boxes with cable modems that will enable consumers to surf the Web, make telephone calls, access email and even tune into interactive video and pay-per-view digital television. "This allows us to participate in the fastest-growing segment of the telecommunications industry," said Christopher B. Galvin, the chairman and chief executive of Motorola, which is based in Schaumburg, Ill. "There's an insatiable demand for bandwidth into the home." Edward Breen, the chairman and chief executive of General Instrument, of Horsham, Pa., which has the dominant position in set-top boxes, as well as a cable infrastructure, will head a new unit of Motorola that combines his company with Motorola's networking and Internet division to create a wired home that would offer everything from burglar alarms to high-definition TV. General Instrument had $2 billion in revenue last year. Motorola agreed to offer 0.575 of a share of its own stock for each share of General Instrument, which has 214 million shares outstanding. Based on today's closing price for Motorola, the deal would be valued about $10.7 billion. Shares of Motorola, which skidded on Monday on word of the deal, tumbled again today, losing $6.5625, to close at $86.625 in heavy trading. Shares of General Instrument also fell, closing at $47.27, down $3.23. Investors have not reacted enthusiastically partly because Motorola says the deal will dilute earnings in the first year before bolstering them in later years. But Wall Street analysts say the deal would give Motorola a dynamic new, high-growth component and fit nicely with its fast-growing cable modem division. "The potential of the combination is just huge," said Mona Eraiba, an analyst at Gruntal & Company. "It's going to open a huge market that is considerably bigger than the current market." She added, "Everything is going to converge in the set-top box." The entire cable television industry is consolidating and upgrading to offer high-speed Internet access, interactive video and additional channels. Big cable operators, like the AT&T Corporation, are spending billions of dollars to upgrade their cable offerings and buy set-top boxes. For Motorola, which has $29 billion in revenues and is rebounding from a sharp slump, the new division and emphasis on the Internet is expected to be a growth area that will complement its strong positions in semiconductors and cellular telephones. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: In the acquisition, Edward Breen, left, chairman of General Instruments, will head a new unit of Motorola. He listened to Motorola's chairman, Christopher B. Galvin, at a news conference in newyork yesterday. (Associated Press)

title:
NEWS WATCH;
A New Player Can Decipher MP3 Music Files on CD's
body: In an uncommon merger of competing technologies, Pine Technology, a company based in hongkong, says it has found a way to combine the best of MP3 music and CD players. The device, called a D' Music CD Player SM-200C, looks much like any other portable CD player and can play regular CD's. Its chief advantage, said Brian Hamilton, the vice president for sales and marketing at Pine Technology USA, is that the player can also read and decode music in the MP3 format, something regular CD players can't do. That means that rather than read MP3 music stored on chips (usually no more than a hour) in MP3 players, the D' Music CD player reads MP3 compressed music stored on compact disks, which can hold more than 100 songs and hours of music. The catch, and it may be considerable for many consumers, is getting the MP3 music onto to CD's. That requires another device, a CD writer, something that most computer owners must add to their personal computers. Nonetheless, Mr. Hamliton said the $299 player (three times the cost of a conventional CD player and about $100 more than most MP3 players) represented a significant step forward for Web-wired music lovers. "What we are seeing today is just the start of a lot of fantastic things to come in the next year or so," he said. The player will go on sale this fall.   MICHEL MARRIOTT http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: Panel Agrees on Overhaul of Internet Tax-Collecting Methods
body: Resisting political pressure from Congressional Republicans, a high-powered panel of executives and politicians voted yesterday to push ahead to develop a system that would make it easy and practical for Web-based businesses to collect state and local sales taxes on Internet commerce. The panel, the Advisory Commission on Electronic Commerce, is not yet ready to recommend whether taxes be collected at all on the Internet. But at the second meeting yesterday, in newyork, the members appeared to agree that the current quiltwork of levies and overlapping districts would need an overhaul before Internet merchants could ever be expected to collect the taxes. They voted to ask the states, which stand to lose revenues if their taxes are not applied to electronic commerce, to suggest ways to simplify the collection in cyberspace of the myriad taxes levied by more than 7,000 state and local governments in the unitedstates. "I'm proposing that we say to the states, 'You solve this problem,' " said Gov. Mike Leavitt of Utah. "The whole question is, can you technologically make a system like this work?" The proposal was adopted over the initial objections of the panel's chairman, Gov. James Gilmore of Virginia, and two tax opponents on the 19-member commission. And it came just a day after House Majority Leader Dick Armey and 34 colleagues sent the commission a letter expressing concern that the panel was focusing too much attention on how to tax the Net, rather then whether to tax it at all. Although the commission was appointed by Congress last year to make recommendations on tax policies for the digital age, Representative Armey reminded members that "only Congress can authorize one state to compel sellers in another state to collect Internet taxes." The letter described proposals to collect existing taxes as "new taxes." "This idea is not a popular one in Congress or among the American people," Mr. Armey's letter warned members. "You should also know that there are many members that will oppose any new taxes on the Internet." Governor Leavitt laid out his proposal after a morning of testimony about whether sales taxes should be applied to Internet commerce and whether the states could make their rates and collection structures simple enough that even small companies could accommodate the taxes without being unduly burderned. The panel hopes to hear proposals from the states and anyone else who cares to offer a solution at its next meeting, in San Francisco in December. Its report is due to Congress next spring. The commission adopted criteria that any Internet tax-collecting scheme must follow. Topping the list is simplicity: The plans should not call for any new taxes, they must remove excessive burdens from the sellers, they must not compromise the privacy of the buyer, they should acknowledge the sovereignty of states, they should treat buyers in all states the same, and they should eliminate multiple audits.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Red hot pace of Internet stock trading cools off, pulling high flying on-line brokers back to earth.
body: ALTHOUGH some stock market pundits are still worried about irrational exuberance, Bill Hatcher, a retiree who trades stocks and options on line, worries more about misplaced melancholia. "The sensation-mongers out there have scared everyone to death," says Mr. Hatcher, referring to the Zeitgeist of the on-line chat rooms he constantly monitors. "Whether it's Y2K, or inflation, you just don't see as many happy people out there trading now." It may just be the laws of gravity. But the outlook of individual investors has been taking a dive. And that is bad news for on-line brokerage firms, which have seen trading volumes ebb recently. If the trend holds, investors are on course to trade fewer shares on line this quarter than they did in the previous three months, making it the first such sustained decline in Internet trading volume for the nascent on-line brokerage industry. Summer is rarely a record-breaking time for stock trading. But trading volume -- on which on-line brokers depend mightily for revenues -- slumped more than just about anyone expected in July and August. September, at least so far, has not offered much relief. A few of the indicators: Charles Schwab, the largest on-line brokerage firm, reported yesterday that average daily revenue from trades by its customers dropped 14 percent from July to August, a figure some analysts viewed as a leading indicator for the industry. Credit Suisse First Boston noted that trading in a sample basket of high-flying Internet stocks was off 2 percent for the second quarter. And two brokerage analysts downgraded earnings estimates yesterday for the Knight/Trimark Group, the biggest market maker for shares traded on Nasdaq, including many big Internet stocks. Scott Appleby, an on-line brokerage industry analyst for BancBoston Robertson Stephens, reduced his estimates for Knight's earnings per share for the July-September quarter to 31 cents from 36 cents, or 14 percent. That is the second time in a month he has lowered his profit targets for Knight, whose revenues have skyrocketed in tandem with heavy trading in Internet stocks and individual investors' migration to on-line brokerage houses. In early August, he revised estimates for Knight downward from 40 cents. Shares of Knight fell $1 yesterday, or 3 percent, to $30.625. "It's an industrywide issue," Mr. Appleby said. "We expected a seasonal trough in the summer. But the volume has been unexpectedly poor." Few believe that America's love affair with on-line trading has faded. On the contrary, most analysts say that Internet brokerages have just begun to tap a huge pool of savings still stored in banks and in accounts with full-service brokers. Americans have 70 million brokerage accounts, but only 10 percent of them permit on-line trading. And as more people move their assets on line, taking a more active role in their investment decisions, trading volume tends to rise substantially. Moreover, the decline in trading in the third quarter comes after a nine-month growth frenzy in which Internet broker transactions doubled in size. By the end of June, they accounted for one in six stock trades made in America. That pace was not viewed as sustainable. Still, even a temporary trading slump could be hazardous to the on-line brokerage industry's health. Schwab, for example, derives almost half its total earnings from trading commissions, and most of its trades are now conducted on line. For smaller brokers -- there are three score of them competing for Internet investors now -- the dependence on trading commissions is far greater. All have seen sharp drops in their share prices. Schwab shares have fallen by half since April and closed yesterday at $36.4375, up 6.25 cents. E*Trade has tumbled 63 percent in the same period, closing yesterday at $23.5625, down 46.875 cents. What's more, many of the leading Internet brokers are geared for growth, not for a grinding battle for market share. E*Trade and Ameritrade, two of the best-known on-line brokers, are spending hundreds of millions of dollars to promote themselves, sacrificing earnings today for rapid growth tomorrow. Ameritrade said yesterday that it planned to spend $200 million over the next year on advertising, about as much as Mazda spent advertising cars and trucks last year. "E*Trade and Ameritrade depend on commission much more than Schwab," said L. Russell Keene, a brokerage analyst at Putnam, Lovell, de Guardiola & Thornton. He has a relatively bearish "hold" recommendation on both stocks. Most of the Internet brokerage firms will report third-quarter earnings in early October. Mr. Keene said he saw the first and second quarters of this year as exceptional. Internet investors, Internet stocks and Internet brokerage firms found themselves then in a virtuous circle. Investors opened new brokerage accounts and seized on high-flying Internet stocks, including the brokerage firms themselves, sending share prices skyward. "That really fueled an anomaly in trade volumes," Mr. Keene said. "If you ignore the first and second quarter and look at the trend, what we see this year is less worrying." He said stock trading volumes were still up over year-earlier periods, even though the increase was less robust than it was in the recent past: Third quarter commissions grew 40 percent in 1997 over 1996, 30 percent in 1998 over 1997 and seem likely to grow 20 percent in 1999 over 1998, he said. Other measures of on-line investment activity are also slowing, but not as much as trading commissions. Customers at Schwab, which reports certain operating statistics more regularly than most of its rivals, added $8 billion to the company's assets under supervision in August, allowing the firm to keep pace with expectations. Schwab also reported that it had 6.3 million customer accounts in August, up from 6.2 million in July and not far off analysts' predictions.. E*Trade and Ameritrade seemed to have slowed more, Mr. Keene said. He expects that Ameritrade will add about 50,000 new accounts for the quarter, down 50 percent from account growth in the second quarter. E*Trade, Mr. Keene estimates, will add about 200,000 accounts, well off its stellar performance in the second quarter, when 332,000 customers opened new accounts at that firm. "There are other indicators of a slowdown in the quarter," he said. "But it is by no means a terminal slowdown. The long-term trend is still healthy." But the summer swoon may give a clue as to how fickle retail investors are. They have fired the rise of Internet brokerage firms and then given them the shivers. "Just like we were seeing people act like cheerleaders for companies before, now you often see people just fan the fires of negativity," said Joe Andras, an electrical engineer in Laguna Beach, Calif., who manages his own stock portfolio and trades on line. "It can be frustrating, but it shows you that you have to look long term."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: U S West Reduces Internet Access Price
body: U S West Inc., which provides local telephone service in 14 western unitedstates states, said today that it was dropping the price of high-speed Internet access by a third to attract customers who now use slower connections. The new service, Megabit Select, costs $19.95 a month. It uses Digital Subscriber Line technology that increases the capacity of ordinary phone lines to provide on-line access about 5 to 10 times faster than conventional modems. Denver-based U S West has been the most aggressive local phone company in offering high-speed Internet access, signing up 70,000 customers, or 40 percent of the Digital Subscriber Line users in the nation. The company is moving to counter the threat of cable modems, which promise even faster Internet access, as well as unprecedented competition in its local-phone business. Megabit Select is available in almost all of the 40 cities where U S West already offers D.S.L., including Seattle, Denver, Minneapolis, Salt Lake City and Portland, Ore. Customers can use the service for a maximum of two hours at a time. In May, U S West cut the price for its cheapest digital service that offers unlimited use to $29.95 from $40. The new service still requires subscription to an Internet access service, such as U S West.net for $17.95, making the price of the package $37.90 a month. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Alcohol and Tobacco Sales Are Being Blocked by Ebay
body: The on-line auction site Ebay confirmed yesterday that it planned to prohibit the sale of alcohol and tobacco products on its service, asserting that the sales could subject some users to prosecution under a growing number of state regulations governing the sale of such products across state lines. Largely for the same reasons, the company decided in February 1999 to prohibit the sale of firearms on the site. The prohibition on sales of tobacco and alcohol, reported on Monday by Cnet.com, will begin on Oct. 13, company officials said yesterday. "Ebay users who believe they are paying attention to laws may be unknowingly nailed," said an Ebay spokesman, Kevin Pursglove. He said a handful of new state laws prohibit the sale of alcohol and tobacco products by unlicensed individuals. The laws have emerged in part in response to the Internet, which has made it easier for far-flung parties to engage in a transaction. Several bills have also been introduced in Congress that would limit or prohibit the sale of alcohol and tobacco products on the Internet. In fact, Ebay could be helping itself as well, as the state laws prohibiting sales conceivably could implicate the forum on which the sale was transacted. Mr. Pursglove said that fewer than 1 percent of the items sold -- or revenue accrued -- on Ebay came from alcohol or tobacco. In the last quarter, the company had sales of $622 million, he said. In an on-line chat session yesterday morning, several Ebay staff members discussed the reasoning behind the move with site members. Mr. Pursglove said the reaction was evenly split between supporters and critics. http://www.nytimes.com

title: CNBC Invests In Electronic Stock Trader
body: CNBC yesterday demonstrated the new willingness of media companies to move out of the meat-and-potatoes business of news and into the world of finance itself, taking a 12.4 percent equity stake in Archipelago, the third-largest electronic communications network for trading stocks. In making the cash investment in the network -- which amounted to close to $30 million, according to a person briefed on the deal -- the financial news cable channel, a unit of the General Electric Company, is lending its imprimatur to one of the contenders in the free-for-all among the nine electronic communications networks currently vying to dominate the new electronic marketplace for stock trading. Other investors in Archipelago include the E*Trade Group Inc., Goldman, Sachs, J. P. Morgan and Instinet, which is part of Reuters Group. Instinet itself, as the largest electronic communications network in the unitedstates, is also a competitor of Archipelago. Over the last few years, the emergence of the electronic communications network's has been a news event and an investment opportunity for media companies interested in electronic commerce. Most networks are registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as broker-dealers, although they function more like exchanges because they serve as electronic meeting places for other broker-dealers and thus facilitate the trades. In August, Archipelago applied to the Securities and Exchange Commission to be registered as a stock exchange, the Internet equivalent of the newyork Stock Exchange. CNBC is "just a great name -- that's a wonderful thing for us," said Gerald D. Putnam, the chief executive of Archipelago, which is currently the third-largest of the electronic communications networks, after Instinet and The Island ECN Inc., whose majority owner is the Internet broker Datek Online Holdings Corporation. Mr. Putnam said that he hoped the presence of two CNBC executives on Archipelago's board would help persuade the S.E.C. that his network was not designed simply to serve institutional investors to the detriment of individuals. "One of the things that is really important to us and really important to the S.E.C." in considering whether to register Archipelago as an exchange is that "we have representation of individual investors, not just big guys," Mr. Putnam said. CNBC, which for 10 years has covered financial news for lay audiences helps fill that need, he said. But the deal raised the issue of whether CNBC could provide arm's-length coverage of the emerging industry of networks when it has an investment stake in one of the major players. Even though other media companies have invested in electronic networks, they have been, at best, corporate cousins of news outlets. Dow Jones & Company, the corporate parent of The Wall Street Journal, has a stake in Optimark Technologies Inc. Bloomberg L.P. has one unit, Bloomberg News, that covers financial news and another, Tradebook, that functions like a network. Marshall Loeb, the former editor of Columbia Journalism Review, who is also a columnist for CBS Marketwatch, said, "This gets to the whole issue of covering yourself and as media companies grow bigger, they find themselves more and more in the position where they will be covering themselves and/or covering their competitors and this is invariably problematic." Mr. Loeb also said that, as the crowded field of electronic networks thins out, the winners are likely to be companies with the largest trading volume. So, the logic goes, the more often Island or Archipelago is mentioned in a financial news broadcast, the more likely the higher profile will give them a competition advantage. Bill Bolster, the president of CNBC, said that CNBC's journalists would give Archipelago no special treatment. "We've got to cover them all equally because our true point is to let everyone know what's going on everywhere," he said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Time Warner Offers Access To the Internet Via TV Cable
body: Seeking to capture a piece of the lucrative market in high-speed Internet services, Time Warner Cable announced yesterday that it is starting to give computer users in parts of Manhattan and Queens fast access to the Internet through the company's cable-television wires. The Time Warner connection is the first modem service using a television cable that will be widely available in Manhattan, said Gerri Warren-Merrick, a Time Warner spokeswoman. Although the number of potential customers is huge -- Time Warner serves more than a million customers in Manhattan, Queens, Staten Island and parts of Brooklyn -- hooking them up them has proven difficult. Time Warner Cable is completing a $400 million fiber-optic system, installed building by building in the sections of newyork City it serves, to make way for the new cable modem service, a project that is expected to be completed by the end of the year. "The challenge in newyork City is really to upgrade the system, and that is for the most part complete; it's 75 percent finished," said Barry Rosenblum, president of Time Warner Cable of newyork City. "We are scaling up to be able to connect 100 people a day at least, and we expect to be doing that out into the foreseeable future." Parts of the Upper West Side, Upper East Side and eastern parts of midtown as well as Jackson Heights, Queens, will be able to get cable modem service as soon as installation schedules permit, with the rest of Manhattan scheduled to receive service by the fall of 2000. The service would be available in the rest of the company's system by mid-2001. The high-speed modem service, known as Road Runner, costs $39.95 a month for Time Warner cable television subscribers and $59.95 a month for nonsubscribers. Installation is $99. Customers can use Road Runner as their Internet service provider or continue to use other providers. With a cable modem, a computer is always connected to the Internet.  Cable modems can receive data 50 times as fast as a modem using a standard telephone line. The Time Warner service will compete with Bell Atlantic, which began offering high-speed Internet access service in parts of Manhattan in July. Bell Atlantic plans to be able to serve 9 out of 10 households in the metropolitan area by the end of the year with digital subscriber lines, which also supply high-speed constant access to the Internet. The service costs between $40 and $90 a month. Time Warner already has 300,000 customers hooked up to Road Runner in upstate newyork, in parts of Ohio, Florida and Texas, and on the West Coast. The RCN Corporation, based in Princeton, N.J., which provides cable service to about 600 apartment buildings in Manhattan, also offers high-speed Internet access, said Jim Maiella, a company spokesman. The wait for faster access has been frustrating for some city dwellers, who have listened to their suburban friends brag about quick, 24-hour connections. "Before the service started, before we started to advertise, we had 8,000 reservations," said Joan Rasmussen, a Bell Atlantic spokeswoman. "newyork is potentially the most significant market for us." Mr. Rosenblum said the waiting list for Road Runner had several thousand names on it. He added that the company was encouraging people to sign up early for service, through the company's Web site, www.twcnyc.com. http://www.nytimes.com

title: 4 Leading Securities Firms Join Forces toBack Primex
body: The four largest securities firms in the unitedstates have joined forces to back Primex Trading, a novel electronic auction system for stocks, giving Primex a jump-start in the static-filled world of electronic trading. Citigroup's Salomon Smith Barney and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter yesterday said that they had joined three earlier backers, Goldman, Sachs & Company, Merrill Lynch & Company and Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities, as Primex's partners. Although several other new electronic trading networks have attracted investments from multiple banks and securities firms, support from the four leading Wall Street firms seems likely to secure Primex a substantial flow of trading orders from the moment it begins, probably next summer. Primex is aiming to be an electronic version of the newyork Stock Exchange. Participants will not only be able to buy and sell stocks at prevailing market prices, as they now do through many traditional and electronic exchanges, but also interact openly with one another -- in effect, bargain -- to find the best prices possible. "I think the fact four of the world's largest securities firms have backed this system suggests that it brings something new and unique to our ability to obtain the best execution for our customers," said Bill Hart, a managing director in equity trading at Salomon Smith Barney. Although the major Wall Street firms are key backers of the newyork Stock Exchange and Nasdaq, they have also taken stakes in a variety of new electronic trading networks that compete with traditional exchanges. Electronic networks have already stolen some of the business of matching buy and sell orders for stocks away from exchanges and the securities firms themselves. Exactly how electronic trading will eventually effect the marketplace is uncertain, and nearly all the players seem to be hedging their bets by investing in multiple alternatives. Peter B. Madoff, the manager and one of the founders of Primex, said the system differs from other trading networks in that it is open and interactive. In other words, it is intended to be a super exchange, giving users the ability to haggle for the best prices with other users on any other trading system. The idea is a good one, some analysts say, but the test will be whether it catches fire with investors. "Our ability to bring these five parties together is a significant statement," Mr. Madoff said. "They account for a significant portion of stock trading worldwide, and they share the same vision to create a new (stock trading) mechanism." Mr. Madoff said that Primex would welcome participation by the newyork Stock Exchange, which specializes in auction trading the old fashioned way, by open outcry. But there's little doubt that Primex will also compete with the stock exchange. People involved with Primex said that the participating Wall Street firms are likely to steer many stock transactions through Primex first.  For a small fee, Primex would then shop for the best prices available on all other participating exchanges, electronic networks or private broker-dealers. If floor traders on the newyork Stock Exchange turn out to be offering the best price, the order will end up there, but could otherwise be settled without ever crossing the exchange floor. "We having nothing to lose by going to Primex first," said an executive of a securities firm that has invested in Primex and who declined to be identified by name. "That's not really the case with some other electronic networks, because they will not be as broad." The firms involved with Primex declined to disclose details about the electronic network's ownership structure or the amounts of money they have invested. But one person involved said the four big Wall Street firms had equal stakes in the new venture, which was the brainchild of Peter and Bernard Madoff, two brothers who have been on the cutting edge of Wall Street stock trading for years. Start-up costs for electronic exchanges are not necessarily formidable. Merrill Lynch last week became the latest securities firm, after E*Trade, Goldman and J. P. Morgan, to buy a stake in Archipelago, one of the best financed of the new electronic networks. It paid about $30 million for a 14.3 percent stake, people close to the firm said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Trades Were Down Last Month
body: Stock trades made through Internet brokerage firms fell 2 percent in August, making it quite possible that on-line transactions will post their first quarterly decline, Credit Suisse First Boston said today. Fewer on-line trades were made in both July and August than in the corresponding months of the second quarter, indicating "a sequential decline in trading volumes" for the third quarter, an analyst, Jamie Earle, said. "On-line brokerages indicate they've already seen a pickup in trading volumes this month but are doubtful the increase will be enough to temper the softness" of July and August, she wrote. Internet brokers' transactions more than doubled in the nine months ended June 30, to almost one in six unitedstates stock trades, as investors bought shares of companies doing business on the Web. But trading has since slumped as Internet stocks lost favor. The Bloomberg unitedstates Internet Index has fallen 14 percent since July 1. Credit Suisse First Boston bases its statistics on spot checks with brokers and actual trading in 40 stocks that are actively bought and sold by on-line investors. The stocks include Verticalnet Inc., an operator of business-commerce Web sites; the software makers Broadvision Inc. and the Vignette Corporation, and the on-line brokers themselves. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
METRO NEWS BRIEFS: NEW YORK;
Serial Killer's Art Sales On Web Create Backlash
body: The State Department of Correctional Services yesterday temporarily revoked the arts and crafts privileges of a convicted serial killer whose artwork has been sold on the Internet auction site Ebay. The convicted man, Arthur Shawcross, 54, is serving 250 years to life in prison for killing 11 Rochester-area women, 9 of them prostitutes. He was convicted in 1991. Officials said Mr. Shawcross had been mailing drawings, oil paintings and portraits to dealers. His work would then show up on the Internet for public auction. In return, Mr. Shawcross would occasionally get gifts like clothes and shoes instead of cash, officials said. It is illegal for inmates to run any kind of business in prison, said Glenn S. Goord, the State Prisons Commissioner. Mr. Shawcross was charged with soliciting goods or services and selling personal articles without approval, Mr. Goord said. A disciplinary hearing was scheduled for Thursday. If convicted, Mr. Shawcross may be fined, lose various privileges or be transferred out of the Sullivan Correctional Facility in the Catskills. James Flateau, a spokesman for the Department of Correctional Services, said Ebay got in touch with the department after reading reports about Mr. Shawcross's sales. "They don't want their site to be misused either," he said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Starts The Recruiting For ItsNext War
body: The browser war may be a memory, but executives of the Microsoft Corporation conceded today that the company now faced an even greater challenge in the next phase of the Internet's evolution, as the role of traditional desktop software recedes and the power center of computing shifts from the operating system to the World Wide Web. Software is increasingly becoming a Web-based service whose main goal is to hasten the spread of electronic commerce over the Internet. At an event here to sketch out in broad strokes Microsoft's technical blueprint for Web software, the company's president, Steven Ballmer, gave his most candid appraisal to date of the hurdle his company faces. "We are at an inflection point," Mr. Ballmer said, adding that the Web strategy announced today was "as important if not more important" than plans the company detailed for the browser market in 1995. "We'll either come through this period with a strong following or we'll be in trouble," he said. Mr. Ballmer spoke at a conference that marks the start of a stepped-up drive by Microsoft to persuade software developers to use its technology for building Web-based applications and Internet-based commerce services. The company is positioning this shift as a way for personal computer software to embrace the Internet and is promoting its Windows DNA 2000 family of products. An initiative that includes several products scheduled to be introduced in the next 18 months, Windows DNA 2000 is being billed by Microsoft as a "comprehensive platform that enables the Web applications and services of tomorrow." But to date, those are only words -- and the notion of a single company establishing a software "platform," or standard, that becomes dominant will be difficult, if even possible, in the diverse world of the Internet. Microsoft, of course, controls the dominant software standard in the PC industry with its Windows operating system, which runs on 90 percent of PC's sold today. In the past, outside software developers had little choice but to write programs to run on Microsoft's technology. But basic Web technology standards are openly available and not controlled by any single company. So Microsoft has a much tougher job in trying to persuade developers to use its software for Web applications and E-commerce services. "It is a new world in a sense," said Tod Nielsen, a Microsoft vice president. "It used to be our sandbox." Microsoft executives also conceded that the company had not yet determined what its business model would be for making money as software moves from desktop products to Web-based services. "Don't know yet," Mr. Ballmer responded to a question on the subject. "But if you wait to have a business model in place, you'll be the last guy in the marketplace." Still, the broad outlines of Microsoft's strategy were presented today. For software programmers, Microsoft promises development tools and a full range of products to simplify the writing of Internet applications. The products start with Windows 2000, a major overhaul of the Windows NT operating system for corporate environments, which is expected to be shipped later this year. Windows 2000 is intended to help Microsoft compete against Sun Microsystems and I.B.M. in supplying the software to run the powerful computers that serve up E-commerce Web sites. The company also briefed developers on several other products, expected to be shipped by the middle of next year, including Microsoft Appcenter, software for running Web applications on centralized data centers, or "server farms." To create its Web platform, Microsoft is using an Internet standard known as Extensible Markup Language, or XML. XML opens the way to more automated intelligence in software by identifying, tagging and interpreting the kinds of data in, say, an email message or on a Web site. Microsoft showed today, for example, how an XML program could be added to calendar software so that it not only alerts the user of his anniversary, but also links to shopping software that includes his wife's gift preferences and favorite stores. XML is an open standard. But the Microsoft pitch is that such Web-based services will work best if developers use Microsoft software and tools. Its different software products, Microsoft says, will operate with rivals' software, but will work better the more Microsoft software is used. Still, some say, Microsoft's strategy amounts to an effort to control Internet standards. "The pure XML standard available to everyone is one thing, but if most people use Microsoft's XML implementations they become the baseline standard," said Jeffrey Tarter, editor of Softletter, an industry newsletter. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Dow Edges Ahead by 1.90; Technology Issues In Retreat
body: Stocks ended a lackluster session with mixed results yesterday as investors stepped back from Friday's rally in technology shares. The Dow Jones industrial average struggled to a slight gain, but most stocks ended lower as the dollar sank to a three-year low against the Japanese yen. After shifting in a narrow range for much of the session, the Dow rose 1.90 points, to 11,030.33. Broader stock gauges were lower. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index fell 7.53, or 0.5 percent, to 1,344.13, and the Nasdaq composite index fell 42.29, or 1.5 percent, to 2,844.77. Traders said investors, who sent the technology-dominated Nasdaq to a record of 2,887.06 on Friday, were ready to take profits yesterday. "This is a time of constant rotation between sectors," said Robert Freedman, the chief investment officer for the John Hancock Funds in Boston. "We move to a new high, then spend another week or so consolidating before it's another group's turn." Internet stocks had the steepest declines yesterday, as Yahoo lost 9 3/4, to 160 3/4, and Ebay fell 10 1/16, to 147 15/16. America Online fell 6 3/16, to 90 1/8. Traders attributed the drop to an article in Barron's magazine in which a short seller -- an investor who bets that the price of a stock will fall -- said America Online's stock price could be cut in half because of price competition. In a short sale, a trader sells borrowed shares on the expectation the price will fall before the stock has to be repurchased on the open market to replace the borrowed shares. 3Com rose 1 5/8, to 28 7/8, after saying it would spin off its Palm Computing unit, the maker of Palm electronic organizers. Stocks were also pressured by the latest slip in the value of the dollar. Signs of economic growth in Japan have strengthened the yen, pushing it to more than three-year highs against the dollar. A weaker dollar can hurt stocks in several ways. For one, it can entice foreign investors in unitedstates stocks to keep their money in investments in their own country. It also makes imported goods more expensive. Some analysts think higher prices of cars, electronics and other Japanese products could increase the chances that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates for a third time this year to keep inflation in check. Among Dow components, J. P. Morgan was the biggest decliner, shedding 3 1/4, to 124 13/16. Procter & Gamble fell 1 7/16, to 101 11/16, after announcing plans to form an Internet-based company to sell beauty products. Other consumer products companies, however, held up well. DuPont rose 2 3/4, to 68 1/2, and Eastman Kodak gained 2 7/8, to 75 15/16.  Treasury Prices Fall By Bloomberg News Bond prices fell yesterday on expectations that further losses in the dollar, already at a three-year low against the yen, will sap international demand for unitedstates fixed-income securities. "There's a perception problem" when the dollar falls against the yen, said Mike Faust, who manages $400 million in global bonds at Bailard, Biehl & Kaiser in San Francisco. The exchange rate is a "proxy for foreign demand" for Treasuries because Japan is the biggest foreign buyer of unitedstates Government bonds. The price of the benchmark 30-year bond fell 5/32, to 101 2/32. Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, rose to 6.05 percent from 6.04 percent on Friday. The dollar's decline against the yen the last three months has handed Japanese investors in Treasuries losses of 9 percent to 10 percent in yen terms, depending on the maturity of the security. unitedstates investors would have made 1.2 percent to 1.8 percent over the same period.
