title: Barnes & Noble to Phase Out Use of the Times List of Books
body: While on-line booksellers wage a fierce price war over newyork Times best sellers, Barnes & Noble Inc. is preparing to phase out its use of the newspaper's weekly list at its superstores. In place of the Times list of books, for which Barnes & Noble typically offers discounts, the bookseller intends to offer bargains based on the chain's own sales rankings. Executives at Barnes & Noble, the nation's leading bookstore chain, said they would begin shifting to the system in the coming weeks. They said they were making the change because their own sales rankings did not always match the Times best-seller lists. Barnesandnoble.com, the Web company that the chain spun off in a public stock offering in May, plans for now to continuing offering discounts based on the newyork Times best-seller lists, the Web company's spokesman, Gus Carlson, said. "We're looking at what they've done and we're looking at our own situation," Mr. Carlson said. "The best thing to say is that we're reviewing it." Since May, top on-line booksellers, including Barnesandnoble.com, Borders.com, which is part of Borders Group, and Amazon.com, have been engaged in a fierce competition to attract customers through 50 percent discounts on books from The Times best-seller lists. And Amazon.com, after a legal dispute with The Times, struck an agreement with the newspaper that allowed the bookseller to continue posting the lists on line. The Times had demanded that Amazon.com stop publishing the list on its site without a licensing arrangement. Back on terra firma, though, Barnes & Noble has decided that it does not need the list for its bricks-and-mortar superstores. "Frequently, there were titles that we went after -- for whatever reason -- that were selling like crazy, but were not on the newyork Times best-seller lists," said Alan Kahn, chief operating officer for Barnes & Noble. "The fact is that our list that we cut every weekend reflects more accurately what goes on in our stores," Mr. Kahn said. "Any retailer wants to sell more of what they're selling." For now, Barnes & Noble's top competitors said that they would continue to use the newspaper's lists as the basis for offering discounts. Bill Curry, a spokesman for Amazon.com, said that "we think it's a valuable way for customers to know the savings on best-selling books because it's such a well-known list." He predicted that Barnes & Noble's use of a different list would make it more difficult to compare prices against the promotions of other competitors. But Barnes & Noble executives note that many of the discounted books would probably appear on both lists. The chain will offer 30 percent discounts on its best-selling hard-cover titles and 20 percent reductions off its trade paperbacks. Borders, the second-largest bookstore chain, said it planned for now to continue using The newyork Times lists, although one executive indicated that his company was reviewing its options. At The Times, Nancy Nielsen, a spokeswoman for the newspaper, issued a brief statement about Barnes & Noble's action. The chain "has made a commercial decision, which is what it is in business to do," she said, adding that it is the newspaper's role to "review books and also report the most comprehensive and impartial sales data of all such lists." "Our list includes more than just one chain store," Ms. Nielsen said. "It includes several chain stores and independent booksellers, and thus, is a broader audience." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Bridging Two Worlds to Make On-Line Digital Music Profitable
body: An Internet start-up company plans to introduce a new Web site on Monday that is designed to bridge the competing worlds of on-line digital music and the traditional recording industry. Garageband.com will focus on the thousands of small and struggling musicians and groups in the unitedstates. Many have found it impossible to sign with a major recording studio but have also discovered that they cannot make a profit by giving their music away over the Internet. Founded by two Silicon Valley entrepreneurs, Tom Zito and Amanda Lathroum, with Jerry Harrison, a music producer who was a member of the rock group Talking Heads, the San Francisco-based company says it hopes to entice undiscovered musical groups with the promise of recording contracts and distribution agreements. At the same time, it plans the use digital audience polling as a way to improve the company's odds for releasing commercially successful CD's. Garageband.com is taking a new approach to the Internet MP3 phenomenon, which has frightened the nation's $13.5 billion recording industry with the specter of mass distribution of pirated music over the Internet. MP3 is an Internet standard for the digital distribution of music, and in the last two years it has spawned an explosion of Web sites, including MP3.com, Shoutcast.com and Broadcast.com, offering Web surfers access to music on their personal computers. But these sites do not offer pirated copies of commercial recordings. Instead, they aggregate the works of musicians who produce their own recordings and offer their music free to anyone who cares to download the MP3 files. And while some musicians use the sites to promote their CD's, the large majority do not have contracts with record labels. For all the interest and controversy the MP3 standard has created, it has yet to generate a viable business model for sustaining small and innovative musical groups, said Mr. Zito, Garageband.com's chairman and chief executive. "The MP3 advocates say record companies are toast," Mr. Zito said. "We believe record companies know a tremendous amount about marketing and promotion and getting music into the hands of consumers." Moreover, he argued, the value of all music downloaded over the Internet last year was less than $1 million, suggesting that a viable Internet music economy is a long way off. What is more, the exact shape of such an economy is still being determined as the recording industry and consumer electronics manufacturers struggle to agree on a format that will protect copyrighted music without alienating consumers. "The Internet offers recording artists the ability to reach fans directly in a way that has never been possible," said Roger McNamee, a managing director of Integral Capital Partners in Menlo Park, Calif. "Garageband has an interesting spin if they can figure out a way to scale it without becoming just like the record companies." The idea for the new company was formed last year when Mr. Zito visited Mr. Harrison's home and saw a large pile of demo recordings sitting on his floor. They had been sent by aspiring music groups hoping that he would help them produce a CD. "He asked me, 'Is there anything good there?,' Mr. Harrison recalled. "I responded, 'How would I ever know? I will never have time to listen to even a fraction of them.' " Mr. Zito approached Ms. Lathroum, who was then an executive and market researcher at the Netscape Communications Corporation, and asked if it would be possible to use the Internet to create an effective audience rating system for music. The resulting Web service will permit musicians to upload recordings that will be rated by music enthusiasts on the Web. By next year, Garageband.com plans to begin awarding a recording contract for the most popular music each month. "I would say that this is an Internet version of Dick Clark's "American Bandstand," but I'm pretty sure few people on the Net are old enough to remember American Bandstand," Mr. Zito said. Garageband.com is hoping to attract listeners who are willing to sample unknown recording artists by offering prizes like backstage passes to concerts and visits to recording studios. But the emphasis will be on the people who make the music. "We're creating an on-line community by musicians for musicians," said Mr. Zito. "Obviously, we believe the fans will come where the musicians are, because that's where they'll hear the best music." Currently, only about 600 of the 30,000 CD's published each year are profitable, Mr. Zito said. The promise of Garageband, he said is that by employing sound statistical techniques he hopes to get a reliable indicator of which recordings will be popular -- and profitable. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Amanda Lathroum, Tom Zito (standing, center) and Jerry Harrison (seated, center) listen to a rock band in a California studio. They founded Garageband.com to link the emerging on-line digital music industry with traditonal recording companies. (Peter DaSilva for The newyork Times)

title:
Compressed Data;
On-Line Radio Tries The All-Talk Format
body: An entrepreneur who made his name in rock radio almost 30 years ago is now trying his luck at Internet radio. Bob Meyrowitz, 56, whose DIR Broadcasting in the early 1970's created the syndicated radio series "King Biscuit Flower Hour," plans to start a radio network on the Internet this week. Recognizing that, so far, so-called streaming, or continuous, audio is not always of the highest fidelity on the Net, Mr. Meyrowitz plans an all-talk network, which he calls Eyada.com. Dave Herman, who was host of the morning show on the newyork rock station WNEW-FM for 26 years, is Eyada.com's program director. Initially, Eyada.com will offer one channel of programming about the entertainment industry, with 15 hours of programming each weekday and four hours each on Saturday and Sunday evenings. The lineup of hosts for the entertainment channel, which begins officially transmitting on Wednesday, includes Lionel, host of Court TV's "Snap Judgment"; Richard Johnson, editor of Page Six, the gossip page of The newyork Post; George Rush and Joanna Molloy, The newyork Daily News husband-and-wife gossip columnists, and Bob Berkowitz, the former host of Real Personal, a discontinued sex advice program on CNBC. Next month, Eyada.com plans to introduce an all-talk channel for sports, and it expects to add channels on teen-agers, women and business by the end of 2000, Mr. Meyrowitz said. He said he had raised just under $10 million from private investors and hoped to reach 20,000 listeners a day, ranging from age 20 to 40. The network intends to sell banner ads and audio commercials. Lisa Allen, a senior analyst for Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass., criticized Eyada.com's planned programming, which she said "is not uniquely suited to the new medium." She also predicted listeners would ignore the advertising. "If there's one thing that's clear, it's that Internet users do not like ads and avoid them," Ms. Allen said. "There's no reason to think they'll listen to radio ads on line." But Mark Mooradian, a senior analyst for Jupiter Communications in newyork, said that if the network could establish its brand, it might be able to create a niche for itself before the likes of Don Imus and Howard Stern hit cyberspace.  "They're not on line yet, but I promise you they will be in a year," Mr. Mooradian said. JANE L. LEVERE http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Bob Meyrowitz wants talk on line.

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Debate on Internet Taxes Takes Political Turn
body: Politics and business appear headed for a clash when an elite group of high-technology and government leaders appointed by Congress to draft sales tax policies for the Internet meets in newyork this week. At their first meeting this summer, in Williamsburg, Va., most in the group, the 19-member Advisory Commission on Electronic Commerce, seemed to agree that Internet sales should be subject to the same taxes levied on sales in the physical world. The key question, they said, was how to devise a more uniform tax rate or a system that made it easy for companies, whether big or small, to collect the taxes levied by more than 30,000 state and local jurisdictions. But the panel's chairman, Gov. James Gilmore of Virginia, a Republican with an aggressive antitax agenda, says he is not convinced Internet sales should be taxed. That view has triggered suspicions among some business members that their colleagues from the political arena may be inclined to stifle any solution that could be construed as a new tax levy. An aide to a high-technology representative on the commission, who asked not to be identified, said a workable solution was being circulated that called for businesses to collect sales taxes on Internet commerce if state and local governments agree to adopt a single tax rate for each state or commit to new technologies in the form of free, easy-to-use software to enable companies to calculate any tax rate. "Most of the commission members, plain as day, can see a deal right in front of them," said the aide. "But the commission staff is pushing it away." Governor Gilmore denies trying to stifle debate on any proposal and says he simply wants to insure that all sides get a fair hearing, including whether sales taxes even have a place on the Internet. "There are some folks who are in the commission and around the commission who do not believe that this is the issue," Mr. Gilmore said. "They assume already that taxes should apply to the Internet and electronic commerce, and they do not believe any discussion ought to be held about that." The commission was created last year as part of Federal legislation imposing a three-year moratorium on any new state or local taxes on Internet access or sales. Composed of eight business representatives, eight politicians from state and local governments and three members of the Clinton Administration, the panel was supposed to begin work in December. But that was delayed when groups representing state, county and city governments -- concerned about losing the tax revenues that pay for many crucial operations -- complained that Congressional leaders had appointed too many business representatives. Adjustments were made, and those same state and local groups expressed pleasant surprise when many of the key business members sided with them at the commission's first meeting. C. Michael Armstrong, chairman and chief executive of AT&T; Theodore Waitt, chairman and chief executive of Gateway, and David Pottruck, president of Charles Schwab, voiced support for taxing Internet commerce as long as a new, simpler and equitable system could be devised. Although state and local governments the last four decades have been unable to agree on a simple way to collect sales taxes from mail-order companies, some are optimistic that the threat of losing huge revenue opportunities from taxes on Internet sales might inspire a solution. "We recognize that the present system is a mess and needs to be addressed through simplicity and uniformity," said Neal Osten, director of the National Conference of State Legislatures' Commerce and Communications Committee. "We need to make it easier for companies to comply." The commission also contains strong tax opponents, however, like Grover Norquist, president of Americans for Tax Reform, who has proposed using the insurgence of the Internet as an opportunity to get rid of sales taxes. Whether or not the commission can reach a consensus and draft a comprehensive proposal for Congress by next year, Governor Gilmore says that at least it can clearly define the issues for Congress. In addition to sales tax, the group is expected to study international tax issues on the Internet and taxes on Internet access. He said the group hoped to have a final report to lawmakers next spring. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Gov. James Gilmore of Virginia heads the tax panel. (Peter DaSilva for The newyork Times)

title:
TECHNOLOGY: E-Commerce Report;
Afte r promising a revolution, two Web companies are making some progress attracting both buyers and sellers.
body: THE Internet is ground zero for outsized declarations from companies that promise to revolutionize, reinvent or obliterate parts of the retail industry with business plans unimaginable in pre-Web days. Earlier this year, two companies with similar business models, Mercata and Accompany, were started amid such fanfare, promising to revolutionize E-commerce by attracting groups of buyers interested in a certain product and extracting wholesale prices from manufacturers and distributors. As middlemen, the companies would exact a fee on each sale. In a win-win-win strategy, manufacturers would sell items in bulk, customers would get lower prices, and Mercata and Accompany would join the pantheon of E-commerce stars. But several months later, the revolution seems far off, with neither site having spent enough money on marketing to attract large numbers of users. There are some promising signs, however: More manufacturers are showing interest, giving the sites access to more brands, and the number of buyers seems to be increasing on both sites. And with more marketing money on the way, analysts say, the companies could start realizing their goals. In theory, the group-buying method, combining the aspects of an on-line auction and a low-risk opportunity to find inexpensive goods, seems well suited to the Internet. Typically, the sites offer goods for limited amounts of time and mark down the price as more people make offers. On a recent day, for example, Mercata offered a Ryobi drill at a starting price of $40. As more visitors bid, the price dropped. When the so-called power buy was finished four days later, 500 people had bought the drill for $34 -- well below the suggested retail price of $89. Even those who had bid higher got the $34 price, while those who had made lower offers clicked away empty-handed. Accompany, which sells more high-technology goods, uses a similar bidding method. Earlier this month, Accompany listed a Palm V organizer on its site for $350, a price comparable with those of lower-price on-line retailers. Once Accompany had more than 20 bids at that amount, the price dropped to $325, where it stayed until the bidding was closed two days later, with 75 buyers. Accompany negotiates with the manufacturers beforehand to determine a scale of prices based on the number of buyers interested. The risk for early buyers, of course, is that they will jump in at the higher price and risk having to pay it if no one else joins in. Conversely, if no one offers to buy the product at the initial price, the price never drops. "The issue is a cross between the prisoner's dilemma and the bystander effect," said Greg Kahn, chief executive of Webehavior, a research firm. "If they all cooperate, they will reap a greater benefit, but cooperation puts them at risk -- as in the prisoner's dilemma. That leads everyone to wait for someone else to jump in first -- which is the bystander effect." These group dynamics, he said, "can really only be eliminated by setting the initial price at or below the market price." Both companies seem poised to do that. Accompany can offer lower prices in part because it does not ship products; the manufacturers ship directly to buyers. Accompany charges suppliers between 2 and 8 percent of the sale for each bulk purchase. Mercata, which sells a wider range of goods, employs a hybrid approach. Some of its suppliers ship directly to customers, others through distributors. When necessary, Mercata accepts inventory from the manufacturer and ships through Hanover Direct, a subsidiary of Keystone Fulfillment. Mercata and Accompany both declined to disclose traffic or revenue figures, but executives from both companies said they remained optimistic. "So far, we've exceeded all expectations," said Tom Van Horn, Mercata's chief executive. The most promising statistic, he said, is the popularity of power buys, as their time-limited group offerings are known. "We've held power buys where our participants exceeded 1,000 people," he said. "When you go after a specific product in a limited window of time, that's a number that's very valuable to a manufacturer." He predicted between 10,000 and 20,000 buyers for some sales by year's end, based in part on his plans to spend $20 million to $30 million on marketing in the fourth quarter. Marc Johnson, an E-commerce analyst with Jupiter Communications, sees such marketing as imperative because "this is a situation where critical mass is absolutely crucial, so marketing and traffic is like oxygen." Marketing is getting more difficult and expensive, Mr. Johnson said, given the growing demand for prime advertising spots on portal sites like America Online and Yahoo. But the group-buying sites have something other on-line retailers lack: stickiness. As with auction sites, customers return to the Mercata and Accompany sites frequently to check on their purchases. Because portals need return customers to bolster their advertising revenue, they have been willing to view group-buying sites as partners rather than as tenants. Both companies have negotiated partnerships in which the bidding will occur on a portal site -- Mercata on Microsoft's MSN, Accompany on Excite -- and they say more such deals are coming. Another key to success is the participation of major brand-name manufacturers. Both companies report some hesitation by companies reluctant to do business over the Internet using a new retail approach. But executives from both companies said they had made significant progress in signing up suppliers. "In manufacturing circles, people discuss things," said Mr. Van Horn, of Mercata. "So signing Toshiba, RCA, Harman Kardon and Sharp helped us add Panasonic, Canon and Philips." Salim Teja, Accompany's co-founder and vice president for strategic development, also said "things are getting better" with manufacturers -- particularly those, like 3Com, that have significantly increased production on certain items and now want to avoid having excess inventory. "We're on everyone's radar screen now, which is what we wanted to do," Mr. Teja said. "Now that we have some momentum and customers, people are willing to take a step back and re-evaluate us." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The Web pages of Mercata, above, and Accompany, two companies that try to get lower prices for consumers by attracting large numbers of buyers to obtain discounts from manufacturers.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Internet Ventures Select Agencies
body: Three "dot-com" companies have named agencies for new accounts. Screaming Media in newyork, a Web content network, selected Mad Dogs and Englishmen in newyork as agency of record for on- and off-line advertising. Billings were estimated at $5 million to $7 million. The decision came after a review that had been called the "Chiathlon" after Jay Chiat, the former chairman and chief executive at Chiat/ Day who is interim chief executive at Screaming Media. The review included three other finalists: Digital Pulp in newyork, Eisnor Interactive in newyork and Mann Buckvic in Cincinnati. Roxy.com in Marlborough, Mass., an on-line electronics retailer, chose Gotham Inc. in newyork, part of the Interpublic Group of Companies. Billings were estimated at $12 million to $15 million. The decision came after a three-month review that had been narrowed to Gotham and two other finalists: CGN Marketing and Creative Services in Boston, part of Epsilon Data Management, and Hanft Byrne Raboy & Partners in newyork. And Real Media in newyork, an Internet marketing company, named Mezzina/Brown in newyork to handle off-line advertising. Billings were estimated at $2 million to $3 million. That decision came after a monthlong review that included three other newyork-based finalists: DeVito/ Verdi, Hanft Byrne and Stein Rogan & Partners. Real Media and its previous agency, M & C Saatchi in newyork, parted ways last year over what were described as creative differences. Lot 21 in San Francisco continues to handle the Real Media on-line account.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
BUSINESS: DIARY;
The Engine Can Search, But Can It Really Dance?
body: Alta Vista, the Internet search engine majority-owned by CMGI Inc., is running ads -- its first -- in magazines like Business Week. The ads feature a black-and-white photograph of an evocative scene -- a young girl at a ballet lesson, for example -- superimposed with intriguing queries in conversational English. Now, anyone who has used a search engine knows that phrasing a successful query is something of a black art, involving carefully chosen keywords, odd punctuation and Boolean operators in just the right places -- in other words, nothing like those in the ads. Can Alta Vista's giant servers really return a useful answer to the ad's query, "Are triple-turn fouettes considered neoclassical exaggeration?" Actually, no, and not just because accent marks are well nigh impossible to type into the search window on a Windows PC. (There is no such problem with a Macintosh; Alta Vista plans to add a Mac-like solution to its site this fall.) Searching without the accent found more than 1.8 million Web pages. The first one didn't answer the question but was at least on point: a dance school in Canada offered a Quicktime movie of a fouette and some notes about the turn's history. After that came scores of pages about poetry, sculpture, economics, typography, furniture; in short, none of the next 150, enough to weary the most intrepid Web surfer, had anything to do with ballet. "We didn't mean them to be taken literally," David Emanuel, a spokesman for Alta Vista, said of the ads' queries. "They are supposed to be provocative, to get people thinking about the Internet and what they might find." Since they are also starting to provoke puzzled calls, Mr. Emanuel said, the company is considering modifying its site to direct anyone who types in one of the ad queries to a screenful of searching tips.   PATRICK J. LYONS http://www.nytimes.com

title: By the Numbers: Redefining a Life of Nonstop Possibilities
body: IT looks like a top-heavy fraction whose value is a bit larger than Pi. But to trend watchers, the expression "24/7" has worked its way into the language as an abbreviation for a clock-defying world where financial markets run continually and news channels promise never-ending headlines (along with weather and traffic reports). Log on to Slate, Microsoft's on-line magazine, and you'll find a section called "24/seven" that contains columns and emails to the editor. Redbook magazine had "24/7" for quick recipes and life-style tips. United Airlines has used it in an advertisement. Figuring out how 24/7 became popular, though, is almost a 24/7 proposition in itself. "I'm not sure how it got into the vernacular," said Kurt Jenkins, a graphic designer who uses the Web address www.24-7.com. "It's a younger people's saying." (This from someone who is all of 29.) Chris Wilson, the entrepreneur who owns Mr. Jenkins's address and about 200 others containing alphanumeric variations on 24-7, agreed that it probably originated with people under 30. "It began as a kind of a Generation X term to describe the Internet," he said.  "We figured that a lot of older people had tried to capture this catch phrase with symbols and logos, but they missed it." In a world where speed counts, syllables are precious. "It's just too long to say '24 hours, 7 days a week,' so it was abbreviated," said Andrew Nelson of Britannica.com, the on-line arm of the venerable Encyclopaedia Britannica. "In the Web world, 24/7 is the shorthand for saying 'We're live all the time.' " Is it written 24/7 (with the numbers separated by a slash)? Or simply the consecutive digits 2, 4 and 7? " 24/ 7 is the way it should be written," Mr. Wilson said, "but on the Internet the only punctuation is a dash. I think a lot of people rushed to capture it and they missed the boat." The dash is crucial, he said. "You look at 247 and think, 'What's that?" A 7-Eleven doesn't say '711.' " Dictionaries have yet to take note of 24/7. Not even Microsoft's new Encarta, which has entries for "twenty questions" and "twenty-twenty," defines it. Neither does the monumental Random House Historical Dictionary of American Slang; its third volume, covering entries from P to Z, has yet to be completed. The project editor, Jesse Sheidlower, said recently that he had not reached the T's, but 24/7 was certain to be included. "The definition will probably be something very simple like 'constantly,' " he said. "It doesn't mean 24 hours a day, seven days a week. It refers to things that can't literally be 24 hours a day, seven days a week. We have an example like running the vacuum cleaner 24/7 for two days in a row." Not possible, he said. "If you had an example like 'He was happy 24/7' or 'He was stoned 24/7,' you'll never know if that's absolutely literal. It probably means 'most of the time.' " Not to terrified executives who dread having to deal with round-the-clock customer complaints. Kyle Shannon, a co-founder and chief creative officer of agency.com, a newyork Internet advertising agency, remembers a strategy session with one high-powered client a couple of years ago. "I was talking about the nature of the Internet and how it's this two-way thing, not just putting messages out but getting messages back," he said. "She went, 'Oh, my God.' She said, 'This Internet thing, it's like a 24/7 focus group.' " The sociologist Stephen Bertman maintains that the "social speedometer" has continued to climb in the 1990's. "We are now nearing a velocity called 'warp speed,' " he wrote in "Hyperculture: The Human Cost of Speed" (Praeger, 1998). "It is one that can, if we are not wise enough or strong enough, warp the fundamental nature of our lives." It may be too late. "Right now, 24/7 is defined as when people are sitting at a computer," Mr. Shannon said. "But the Palm VII and interactive television are coming. Right now the Internet is a place you log on to. It's going to become like a dial tone, all pervasive. That will be real 24/7." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
Foreign Affairs;
Honey, I Shrunk the World
body: There is a club here in Melbourne, the Kelvin Club, where they have a rule that really appeals to me: If you are at the bar and your cell phone goes off, you have to buy everyone in the bar a drink. The reason they need such a rule here is that Australia has become one of the most wired countries in the world, with both the Internet and cell phones. America is first in PC's per capita; Australia is second. America is fourth in Internet usage; Australia is sixth (Iceland is first!). The Premier of the Australian state of Victoria, Jeff Kennett, campaigned so heavily on the Internet that he is now best known to voters by his domain name, Jeff.com. The Internet has been adopted here with such zeal for a simple reason: Australia is a million miles from everywhere, and sparsely populated across a vast continent. The Internet can shrink that distance between Australia and the world, and between Aussies and Aussies, for almost no cost. "For years we have been praying for faster airplanes -- we thought that would be our salvation," says Annie Hayes, an Australian conference organizer. "With the Internet, we can be so much more in touch with the world now, without actually leaving here." Paul Gilding, the former head of Greenpeace, has an environmental consulting firm in Sydney: "Two years ago we thought we were going to have to leave Australia because you just couldn't operate a global business from here," he said. "Clients would say, 'We'd love to have you as advisers, but you can't service us from Australia.' Now we're not only advising DuPont in Delaware , but we're able to attract experts to come live in Sydney from all over the world because they feel they can have the best of our life style and be connected." Jim Bacon, the Premier of Tasmania, the remote island off Australia's south coast, has reached for the Web with gusto. And no wonder. Tasmania has long been known as either "the beginning of the end of the world" or "the gateway to Antarctica." Says Mr. Bacon: "Suddenly we are connected. We have a little resort on the coast of Tasmania called Killynaught Cottages. The owners were telling me the other day they are getting all sorts of bookings now over the Internet, and just got one from Saudi Arabia." Australians will often tell you that theirs has been a "derivative country." They would wait for things to be invented in the U.S. or U.K. and then adapt them. That may change, said Matthew Symons, director of Schoolsnet Australia. "The Internet got adopted here for education very early because we have all these far-flung schools where you had, say, one art teacher, working in total isolation -- so there was a real need to wire them all in. Once they were wired together, though, they started forming communities, and instead of looking for some American solution to their problems, they started sharing with one another and coming up with organic Australian solutions. It is a fascinating study in network effects." Three years ago, Pauline Hanson, a xenophobic, anti-globalization politician, gained popularity here. One way the Australian Government sought to combat her influence was by wiring the whole country. "Hanson gained popularity because rural Australia felt it was being left behind -- banks were closing, telephone boxes were being removed. Rural communities felt there was unequal access to the new economy," said Education Minister David Kemp. "So the Government decided in 1998 to include access to Internet technology in the basic service package offered to everyone by the state phone company. She was taking our supporters and this was one way for us to win them back." The only problem, of course, is that being wired is always a two-way street. The Australian mining company Western Minerals took advantage of the stock market's obsession with ".com" companies by abandoning the mining business and relisting itself on the stock exchange as a sex products store -- Adultshop.com, offering sexy lingerie. Years ago, the Australian Government set up an ethnic TV station called Imparja, to give a cultural voice to remote, outback Aboriginal communities. However, the station developed a taste for American sitcoms, particularly "Seinfeld." People from all over Australia -- including the Aborigines -- started watching it to soak up the worst of Americana rather than the best of the Aboriginal. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Group Puts Disaster Data on Internet
body: Environmental advocates have published new information on the Internet about the risks of chemical accidents, outflanking a new law that suppresses this kind of information on the ground that the details could help terrorists. The published information includes state-by-state summaries of "worst-case scenarios" presented by thousands of companies in the unitedstates to the Environmental Protection Agency, part of an effort to help government agencies and people who live near factories prepare for toxic catastrophes like explosions at chemical plants. Among the potential disasters that the hypothetical summaries describe are these: *A 90-ton rail car of chlorine at a chemical plant in Muscle Shoals, Ala., ruptures and sends a toxic cloud 14 miles. *In Wilmington, N.C., the consequences of a major accident at a sulfur products company are felt 25 miles away. *A one-ton container of chlorine leaks at a water plant in Bradenton, Fla., sending fumes into a nearby neighborhood and state park. The Environmental Protection Agency originally intended to put the entire document on line for the public to browse. But last month, Congress and President Clinton, presented with warnings by security specialists that electronic dissemination of the information could provide terrorists with a road map to sensitive domestic targets, enacted a law suspending release of the information for one year. Now, however, a public interest group has published state-by-state executive summaries of the accident scenarios, not suppressed under the new law, on its Web site, saying it wanted to give the public some sense of the risks posed by the sites as well as the information the Government chose not to disclose. "It shows the futility of trying to restrict public information," said Rick Blum, a spokesman for OMB Watch, one of the public interest groups that runs the Internet site at www.rtk.net. "In this information age," Mr. Blum said, "information is going to be used, it will be copied and it will be redistributed. You can't put the genie back in the bottle." The summaries of the risk management plans are not heavily detailed and do not include estimates of how many people live within reach of a plant accident site -- a number that some security experts said could be used by terrorists to rank targets by potential casualties. But the roughly 14,000 summaries do include brief descriptions of the consequences of major events at sites -- usually described as highly unlikely -- as well as more likely but less severe accident scenarios, some based on actual past mishaps. Advocates of releasing the information say the compilation of the summaries could show the public that the information was kept off the Internet more to avoid embarrassing chemical companies than to impede terrorists. They say that hundreds of accidents occur at plants each year, although the Federal Bureau of Investigation has acknowledged only a single thwarted act of sabotage, against a chemical plant in 1997. The summaries can be obtained from the E.P.A. but are not as easily accessible as the group has made them. "Keeping this information out of a national database has never been a serious barrier to terrorists," said Paul Orum, the Washington coordinator of the Working Group on Community Right-to-Know. "To actually combat terrorists, companies need to improve site security, harden facilities, add fail-safe equipment and, most fundamentally, reduce the hazard they knowingly bring to a community." Security officials who backed restricting the information said that publishing it would turn the Government into a clearinghouse for information that could threaten national security. Robert Burnham, chief of the F.B.I.'s domestic terrorism section, told Congress in May that the agency "has consistently maintained that the potential release of this worst-case-scenario data in an uncontrolled manner would provide targeting tools and new ideas for criminals and terrorists." Lawmakers agreed to suspend release of the information, and some expressed outrage that the E.P.A. had intended to make the data easily accessible under the Clean Air Act amendments of 1990. Representative Thomas J. Bliley Jr., the Virginia Republican who is chairman of the Commerce Committee, said in July that Congress "never imagined" that the information collected from chemical companies under that law would become "a worldwide electronic database, easily searchable from Boston to Baghdad, from Los Angeles to Libya." The new law exempts the information from the Freedom of Information Act for one year, allowing the Administration to devise a system for releasing the information while assessing "the increased risk of terrorist and other criminal activity" that could result from posting the information on the Internet. Congressional aides involved in drafting the legislation said they were not overly alarmed by the availability of the summary information on the Internet, noting it was not as detailed as the complete worst-case-scenario report. The text is often dense when describing the worst possible disaster at a plant, and it emphasizes the precautions sites take in handling hazardous materials. Referring to one scenario in which acetylene, ammonia and three other toxic substances are released at a chemicals plant in Gainesville, Fla., officials at the plant, Archimica Inc., emphasize in their summary that their "prevention program insures that our facility is operated under safe conditions and that any risk of a release is minimized." The plant does acknowledge three incidents in the last five years in which chemicals were released. The environmental advocacy groups hope to win more complete disclosure in the future, noting that publication of annual toxic release audits by the E.P.A. has led many companies to reduce their emissions. "This isn't going to help anyone create a problem," said Mr. Blum. "It is going to help communities make themselves safer." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Many Media Voices of a Few Merged Masters
body: IF the media and telecommunications giants have their way, decades' worth of Federal rules intended to guard the marketplace of ideas may soon fall, all in the name of the Internet. In the last few days, top executives from four of the information industries' largest corporations -- Viacom, CBS, AT&T and Mediaone Group -- have asked the Government to give them a break from tight restrictions intended to prevent cable and broadcast television from falling into too few hands. The theory behind the rules is that, in allocating a limited spectrum of communications frequencies, the Government must insure that there are enough different voices, opinions and news gatherers to keep its citizens informed. Never before has a corporate merger threatened to exceed the current limits on concentration of media ownership. But two of this year's biggest deals -- Viacom's planned acquisition of CBS, announced Tuesday, and AT&T's pending purchase of Mediaone -- cannot be completed without either changes in the rules or significant divestitures. Hoping to avoid selling assets that could be combined profitably, top executives of the companies told the Federal Communications Commission last week that the concentration rules are now archaic -- obsolete in an Internet world that unshackles producers of programming from old economic restraints and assures diverse voices and original content. "There is no question that that rule is no longer relevant in a broadband Internet world," Mel Karmazin, chairman and chief executive of CBS, said of the regulation that would force Viacom and CBS to sell some stations to stay within rules limiting a company to stations serving 35 percent of the nation's homes. A remarkably similar position was articulated to challenge the rules governing cable TV systems. To replace regulations left unenforced after an adverse court decision seven years ago, the F.C.C. had been prepared to issue new rules this week, but postponed them for at least a month after fierce lobbying from AT&T. "Very significantly, the market has changed," said James Cicconi, general counsel and head of government relations for AT&T, which with the Mediaone acquisition will become the nation's largest cable company. "The Government should now take a look at whether the original rationale of the rule is still valid -- namely, the ability to bottleneck programming." What is the answer? Has the Internet indeed promoted new and original voices to the point that traditional concerns about diversity of content can be abandoned? Or, despite the easy, low-cost access it provides to a cybermarketplace of ideas, is the Internet quickly being dominated by a handful of big corporations, just like television, radio, the movies and newspapers before it? Some critics are concerned that the arguments in favor of media mergers confuse content with delivery -- that while there are many new channels to deliver information, there is remarkably little original information being gathered or produced. At bottom, these analysts say, media companies are making claims for a diversity that simply doesn't exist. "The same big players are every bit as keen on swallowing the Internet as they have the traditional media," said Mark Crispin Miller, director of the Project on Media Ownership and a professor of media studies at newyork University. "The consensus is that the Internet is getting less diverse and more homogenized as it becomes more commercial." Certainly, trends in the older media are hardly reassuring for the Internet. The declining number of American newspapers is an old story. Where a half-century ago there were some 2,200 daily newspapers, there are now about 1,500; most cities have only one. Radio has fallen on even harder times. While it used to be that many stations in even midsized cities had their own reporters, that has become the rare exception.  Instead, most stations rely on the same handful of national and local news services. Metro Networks, a Houston-based company that supplies traffic, weather and sports reports to about 1,700 radio stations, has lately become a huge new presence in radio news, often supplying coverage to many stations in one market, sometimes with the same reporters appearing on several stations under different names to give the appearance of competing, exclusive reports. In newyork, for example, Metro works for 41 stations. While the number of television stations has grown sharply, from 96 in 1950 to 1,216 this year, studies show consistently that they give local news short shrift. "There is actually more local news than there used to be," said Janine Jaquet, research director for the Media Ownership Project. "The flip side is that a lot of this stuff is coming from fewer sources." Many stations rely heavily on wire-service offerings, syndicated features and the kind of crime and violence stories that they -- and their competitors -- can cover easily by listening to a police scanner. Other topics, however, may be neglected. "A principal accused of child abuse makes the news; general problems in education don't," said Paul Klite, executive director of the Rocky Mountain Media Watch, a Colorado organization that studies news content around the nation. The television industry points to cable as evidence that new media give rise to new sources of information. C-Span brings live Congressional proceedings into cable subscribers' living rooms, and three 24-hour news and information channels -- CNN, MSNBC and Fox News -- vie for viewers' attention. Moreover, cable systems in a growing number of cities and regions are now offering 24-hour local news channels that some analysts say are bringing original reporting to their areas. STILL, some of cable's early promises of diversity have gone largely unfulfilled. In exchange for their local monopolies, for example, many cable companies vowed to serve the public interest by devoting channels to civic-minded topics like local government, education and the arts. But in many cities, critics say, public access programming is mediocre at best. "The public access channels on cable are virtually entirely unused," said Lawrence Grossman, the former president of both NBC News and PBS, at a Fordham Law School symposium earlier this year on the impact of large media mergers. "The last I saw, 18 percent of public access education and government channels were being used. And when they are used, they are virtually unwatchable." Some viewers prefer a camera's unmediated broadcast of a city council meeting to a reporter's filtered account. But analysts say neither public access programming nor cable TV's heated chat-show debates substitute for original investigative reporting, or even the pedestrian but thorough coverage of public affairs once provided by local and national broadcasters. "What you've got is a huge diminution of the number of voices providing information that is necessary for an informed citizenship, and the Internet doesn't change that," said Andrew Jay Schwartzman, president of the Media Access Project, a Washington group that promotes diversity on the airwaves. "It certainly reduces the barriers to organizing and to discourse. That's important for democracy," Mr. Schwartzman said. "But it's no replacement for journalism and news gathering." By all accounts, the Internet was supposed to break the mold of the older technologies by offering a vast new array of voices and opinions. And indeed, a rich cast of original content of varying degrees of usefulness now flows from the Internet, from The Onion and Salon to Matt Drudge. But while experts are divided over what the Internet may look like in the future, many agree that the most popular Web sites -- all controlled by commercial interests -- are already beginning to look alike. "The notion that technology will create competition and new voices, and so we don't have to worry about these companies getting bigger, is false," said Robert W. McChesney, a professor of communications at the University of Illinois and author of a new book, "Rich Media, Poor Democracy" (University of Illinois Press). Mr. McChesney contends that powerful economic forces will inevitably lead to the domination of information on the Internet by today's media giants. First, he said, because they have the newsrooms and production studios, the big media companies already control the means of producing the Internet's content. Even wealthy companies like Microsoft, he noted, have found it difficult to compete. Second, Mr. McChesney said, established media companies already have both brand names to attract viewers and relationships with advertisers. Finally, it is the established companies, he said, not the start-ups, that have the wherewithal to invest in the Internet for the long term, swallowing heavy losses for a few years in the hope of gaining longer-term profits. IN any event, his research shows, about half of the venture capital provided to Internet start-ups is coming from established media companies. So they are likely, he said, to have a big interest in many of the new Internet companies that survive. Other experts are more optimistic, seeing the Internet as a powerful forum for diverse and informative voices. Andrew L. Shapiro, a senior adviser at the Markle Foundation, has written a book titled "The Control Revolution: How the Internet Is Putting Individuals in Charge and Changing the World We Know" (Century Foundation/Public Affairs). He points to what happened in December 1996 when Slobodan Milosevic, the Yugoslav leader, shut down an independent Belgrade radio station, Radio B92, which had regularly broadcast news of protests against his regime. The station rerouted its programming to the Internet, where it was available to computer users in Serbia and around the world. "That was an outstanding example of how human rights advocates can use the Internet in ways they could never use television or newspapers to get around a thug like Milosevic," Mr. Shapiro said. "It's certainly true that a lot of things that happened with cable, television, and radio -- that have led to the dumbing-down of content -- are now happening on the portal sites. But I'm still optimistic. A lot of it will take steering people to the appropriate content: away from the commercial portals to the more diverse sites." WHILE there will almost certainly be Congressional hearings on the Viacom-CBS merger, there has been far less hand-wringing among lawmakers about the recent information industry deals than there was even just a decade ago, when the trend of big media mergers began to take off. Paul Wellstone, the Minnesota Democrat who was the only Senator to openly criticize the Viacom-CBS deal for its possible effects on public discourse, said the politicians' silence was a clear reflection of both Washington and media economics. There is no lobby these days for media populism. "When you look at the mix of money and politics, it's all on one side," Mr. Wellstone said. "The political dialogue and political imagination is set within a narrow parameter." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Newsboys in 1908, preparing to peddle papers that have since folded: Newspaper, radio and television have come to be dominated by a handful of big corporations. (Corbis)(pg. 4); (Lisa Haney)(pg. 1)

title:
The Nation: Paradox of the Internet Era;
Behemoths in a Jack-Be-Nimble Economy
body: IN the modern Internet economy, the race of capitalism belongs to the fleet and nimble. The preferred organizational model, it seems, is the Silicon Valley start-up -- informal, entrepreneurial and youthful. "Three people, under 25, with a hot idea -- those are the companies we're backing," explained Ron Conway, who heads a start-up investment fund in Silicon Valley. Yet across much of the corporate America the ethos of "bigger is better" is flourishing -- and last week's announcement that Viacom Inc. agreed to buy the CBS Corporation for $37.3 billion is merely further confirmation of the recent trend. The five biggest merger deals ever came last year, when the total value of corporate acquisition activity reached a record $1.6 trillion, equal to 19 percent of the annual output of the economy. So far this year, reports Thomson Financial Securities Data, a research firm, the mergers total $1.06 trillion, only slightly behind the 1998 pace. Business deals on this scale have not occurred since the turn-of-the-century days of J. P. Morgan and John D. Rockefeller. The forces behind many of the big deals are rapid technological change, deregulation and freer trade, which make it more efficient to market products and manage operations globally. The booming stock markets have fueled the merger binge because most of the corporate purchases are made with shares instead of cash. Such mergers seem to pass the logic of a high-school economics course. They are intended to expand a network for the distribution of goods or services or consolidate overlapping networks. The goal is to more efficiently use a high-fixed-cost network -- whether that network distributes phone calls, banking services or gasoline. Yet the logic behind many deals is tricky to explain -- and ego, hubris and management fads are often part of the motivation. Over the years, research on mergers has found that many fail, as post-deal returns for shareholders often trail the market averages. Putting together two large organizations is a difficult management challenge, business analysts say, even when the two companies are a good fit strategically. "The companies are so large in most of these deals that they already have all the sins of bureaucracy," observed Rosabeth Moss Kanter, a professor at the Harvard business school. "Some of the merger activity we're seeing is defensive strategy in times of rapid technological change and uncertainty. It's an attitude that we'll link up with another company before someone else does." Merger deals are always oversold when they are announced. A helping of hyperbole is expected, but certain arguments are particularly suspect, business experts warn. Deals are often presented as a "merger of equals," an ego-stroking euphemism intended for the ears of the chief executive and staff of the acquired company. "The merger of equals is a myth," Ms. Kanter said. "Show me one." Another suspect assertion is that a big merger will result in the new economic math of synergy -- a term that first gained currency during the wave of conglomerate mergers in the 1960's, a business fad that in hindsight appears to have been folly. But today's executives still sometimes play the synergy card when justifying a deal, saying that "one plus one will equal three" or "two plus two will equal five." The hoped-for synergy rarely materializes. "Most of the time, it's two plus two equals three," said Michael Cusumano, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Sloan School of Management. The modern synergy strategy usually involves putting together two companies in related fields, and then trying to cross-promote the offerings of each. An example is Travelers Group's purchase last year of Citicorp for nearly $73 billion, assembling a financial services empire that includes insurance, commercial banking, investment banking and a stock broker. The "financial supermarket" is a catchy phrase, but it is not yet proved to be a winning business strategy, industry analysts say. A notable failure is Sears, Roebuck's venture into financial services, which it abandoned in the early 1990's. The big media mergers are partly inspired by visions of the payoff from combining related businesses. Michael Eisner talked a lot about synergy when Disney acquired Capital Cities/ABC in 1995. And the Viacom's planned purchase of CBS is similar. Both deals link entertainment studios with television networks for distributing that programming to the households of viewers. Yet the Disney-Capital Cities/ABC merger has proved to be a disappointment so far, most industry analysts agree, and the Viacom-CBS merger faces some of the same challenges. THE business strategy, it seems, runs counter to some basic free-market principles. Isn't the producer of entertainment programming better off having several networks bid for his programs? And isn't a television network better off being able to choose among competing suppliers of programs? Is becoming a much bigger corporation a stimulus to creativity -- vital to the entertainment business -- or a hindrance to it? "The challenge for the big combined media companies like Disney, Time Warner and now Viacom is how to make these very large corporations with complex sets of relationships work in ways that pay off," said David Nadler, chairman of the Delta Consulting Group Inc., a management consulting firm. "Just owning a bundle of different properties doesn't mean you get the profit-making synergies that executives talk about when they announce these mergers." BIG companies, to be sure, can succeed in being creative, even entrepreneurial, if organized and managed properly. The Microsoft Corporation, for example, has become a huge company, but it keeps its software programmers working in modular teams of three to eight people. Perhaps the leading big-company success story, though, is the revival of the International Business Machines Corporation under Louis V. Gerstner Jr. When he took over the stumbling computer maker in 1993, Mr. Gerstner was widely expected to turn the bigger-is-better rationale on its head, breaking up I.B.M. into a group of smaller companies, which, it was assumed, could better keep pace in fast-changing technology markets. Instead, Mr. Gerstner kept the company together. He decided I.B.M.'s huge investment in research and development was an underused asset that could be spread profitably across the company's many computer divisions. And he streamlined management, slashed bureaucracy and built up I.B.M.'s faster-growing services and software businesses. The results have been impressive, as profits and I.B.M.'s stock price have rebounded. The laudatory reviews extend well beyond Wall Street. The Washington Monthly recently published an article, "What Lou Gerstner Could Teach Bill Clinton: Lessons for Government from I.B.M.'s Dramatic Turnaround." Even those Silicon Valley start-ups, of course, are eager to get bigger, and the hopes of many involve mergers. Microsoft and America Online, for example, are frequent buyers of other companies. With the exception of America Online's multibillion-dollar purchase of Netscape last year, most of the Microsoft and America Online deals are smaller purchases, up to a few hundred million dollars, of promising start-ups that have begun to take off. The new economy may favor the nimble, but a paradox is clear. "The dream of those three-person Internet start-ups is to grow to a 100-person company and get bought out," observed Eric Greenberg, director of management studies at the American Management Association. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Making Deals" -- Top merger and acquisition deals of all time (all announced last year)  ACQUIRER: Exxon ACQUISITION: Mobil ANNOUNCED: Dec. 1, 1998 VALUE (billions of dollars): $86.4  ACQUIRER: Travelers Group ACQUISITION: Citicorp ANNOUNCED: April 6, 1998 VALUE (billions of dollars): 72.6  ACQUIRER: SBC Communications ACQUISITION: Ameritech ANNOUNCED: May 11, 1998 VALUE (billions of dollars): 72.4  ACQUIRER: Bell Atlantic ACQUISITION: GTE ANNOUNCED: July 28, 1998 VALUE (billions of dollars): 71.3  ACQUIRER: AT&T ACQUISITION: Tele-Communications Inc ANNOUNCED: June 24, 1998 VALUE (billions of dollars): 69.9  TOP DEALS SO FAR THIS YEAR  ACQUIRER: Vodafone Group* ACQUISITION: AirTouch Commun. title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
Car Rental, Greens Fees Add Up to Miles
body: Three airlines have recently formed alliances, and bonus miles are being awarded for booking airline tickets on the Internet. Northwest has two new car rental partners -- Avis and Hertz. Now, members of Worldperks can earn 50 miles a day for cars rented from Alamo, Avis, Budget, Dollar, Hertz and National. A flight is no longer necessary to earn the mileage with any of the Worldperks car-rental partners. TD Waterhouse Group, a discount brokerage firm, has launched a customer reward program in conjunction with American Airlines. Since Aug. 2, TD Waterhouse customers have received AAdvantage miles for depositing additional assets, maintaining minimum balances and adding to money-market positions. Troon Golf joined America West's frequent flier program in July. Members of Flightfund earn three miles for every dollar spent on greens fees, up to 500 miles a round. More than 30 Troon golf courses in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, South Carolina, Texas, Australia and Scotland are participating. To encourage the purchase of airline tickets on line, America West Airlines (www .americawest.com), American Airlines (www.aa.com), Delta Air Lines (www.delta-air.com), Northwest Airlines (www.nwa .com) and US Airways (www.usair.com) are offering participants in their frequent flier programs up to 1,000 extra miles for tickets purchased through their Web sites until the end of this year. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Andreessen Steps Down From AOL
body: Marc Andreessen, who became an icon of the Internet age as a co-founder of the Netscape Communications Corporation before it was acquired by America Online last year, is stepping down after seven months as America Online's chief technology officer, the company said yesterday. In his place, the company hired William J. Raduchel, the chief strategist of Sun Microsystems. The chief technology officer's job at America Online is not to run its vast computer network, but to plan a network of the future that will connect not only to computers but to telephones, televisions and all manner of new gadgets. Mr. Raduchel's background may fill the bill better than Mr. Andreessen's. He has been involved in Sun's Internet strategy and forging alliances with other big companies, including Fujitsu, Sony and more recently America Online. Moreover, Mr. Raduchel, a 53-year-old former Harvard professor and veteran technology executive, may be more suited to the ways of America Online, where executives tend to be in their late 30's and 40's, than the 28-year-old Mr. Andreessen, who was a student before forming Netscape. Of course, when Mr. Andreessen took the job at America Online in February, it was seen as a sign that the sprawling company in Dulles, Va., was reaching out to former Netscape employees and to Silicon Valley in general. As one of the inventors of the Internet browser at 23, Mr. Andreessen was the first of the young entrepreneurs who were changing the world -- and getting rich -- by building the Web. But Mr. Andreessen said he figured out that he would rather be investing in and working with start-ups rather than attending meetings about corporate strategy. "America Online's mission is to bring the Internet to everyone and to accomplish that mission is clearly a matter of size and scale," he said. "Start-ups have a different role. They are about breaking the rules and trying new things that might fail or might change the world." So, he has arranged a part-time position with America Online that will allow him to make personal investments in start-up companies as well as advising America Online about investing in or acquiring them. "I look at all the creativity in the start-up world and it's like white water rafting," Mr. Andreessen said. "You can't tell what's going on from the shore. You have to be in the middle of the rapids." Over the last year, Mr. Andreessen has made personal investments in Replay, a company that makes digital video recorders, and Accompany, an on-line store. But he says his new role will give him the time to serve on more boards and work more closely with companies. Another factor that was not endearing about his new job, Mr. Andreessen conceded, was that his English bulldogs could not take the Virginia heat, and he had to send them back to his home in Palo Alto, Calif. Mr. Andreessen was the last America Online employee among the small group of engineers from the University of Illinois who founded Netscape along with Jim Clark, the founder of Silicon Graphics. Indeed, of the top seven executives at Netscape at the time of the acquisition last November, only one is still working for the company full time. Barry Ariko, Netscape's chief operating officer, is the No. 2 executive in Iplanet, the joint venture between America Online and Sun to sell software that runs Web sites. Mr. Raduchel was one of the top four executives at Sun and has served over the last 10 years as its chief financial officer and its chief information officer. He said that like Mr. Andreessen, he has been considering investing in or working for start-ups. "I had already told Scott that I wanted to look at doing something different after 10 years on the inside as a staff guy," Mr. Raduchel said, referring to Scott McNealy, Sun's chairman, who was one of his economics students at Harvard. But then Steve Case, America Online's chairman, heard that Mr. Raduchel was considering leaving Sun and just two weeks ago called him to offer him Mr. Andreessen's job. "I wasn't planning to take another job like I had," Mr. Raduchel said. "But I realized I enjoy the leverage that big companies give me. You can paint on a three-by-five card in your house or you can paint on a billboard in Times Square. And that's what I'd rather do." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: America Online named William J. Raduchel of Sun Microsystems as its chief technology officer.

title:
Palo Alto Journal;
Hackers Enjoy One Last Meal From the Master of .com Cuisine
body: In the mid-1970's, the social nucleus of many of the men who were creating both the Internet and the personal computer industry was a hole-in-the-wall Sichuan Chinese restaurant across the street from Stanford University. Theirs was an informal network that included people like John McCarthy, a pioneer in artificial intelligence, and Whitfield Diffie, an inventor of modern cryptography, who was then a Stanford graduate student and carried custom chopsticks. Bill Gosper, a mathematician and legendary computer hacker, ate at the restaurant every evening for a decade. It has been a quarter-century since Louis Kao opened the restaurant, Hsi-Nan, and was discovered by a ragtag collection of computer hackers, hardware engineers and network designers. They came because Louie, as Mr. Kao is universally known to his devoted followers, was a master at preparing the perfect fare for hackers. Today more than 30 computer scientists, electrical engineers, programmers and mathematicians gathered to mark the retirement of the 59-year-old Mr. Kao and enjoy one final meal cooked by the chef whose restaurant was for a decade the soul of Silicon Valley. Over the years, it was a movable feast: Hsi-Nan had four locations before it finally closed in 1995. (Mr. Kao subsequently opened a pizza parlor.) And it was a striking contrast to the restaurants that are now exemplars of the valley -- places like Il Fornaio in Palo Alto or Bucks in Woodside. In Hsi-Nan's heyday, from 1974 to 1984, the talk there was not of Internet megadeals but of the visions of mostly young men who were passionate about the power of personal computing. It was a period characterized by a fervor for computing rather than by get-I.P.O.-quick Internet start-ups. Largely because of the affinity that hackers have typically had for spicy Sichuan cuisine, Hsi-Nan was a magnet that drew the nation's computer elite. "I still find myself lusting after Louie's crab with black bean sauce," said Mark Mannasse, a computer researcher at a Compaq Computer laboratory in Palo Alto. At the lunch today, at Mr. Kao's pizza parlor in Redwood City, where he prepared Chinese dishes for his guests, there was some debate about just what the connection between computer hacking and Chinese food actually is. Several people believed it was simply a consequence of the fact that Chinese restaurants are open late, matching the late-night culinary habits of hackers -- a group obsessed with completely understanding, exploring and controlling the computers they design, often working deep into the night. Others believed that the mysteries of a Chinese restaurant menu were akin to the complexities of a computer's instruction set, driving hackers to explore and experiment. "Chinese food was made for the hackers," said Steven Levy, author of the 1984 book "Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution." "They were open late at night," Mr. Levy said of Chinese restaurants, "and they had menus that were complex yet logical, so that the mysteries that most people never crack at a Chinese restaurant were a reward for a hacker." Mr. Kao had his own explanation. "These people appreciate what I do," he said. "They have taste buds for gourmet food." In any case, Mr. Mannasse said, such were the mystical powers of Mr. Kao's meals -- dishes like ant-climb-tree, eggplant in hot garlic sauce, orange peel chicken, pickled cucumber -- that they go a long way toward explaining the chemistry of Silicon Valley. One of Mr. Kao's dishes, made with zucchini, was so hot, Mr. Mannasse remembered, that it was referred to as "zukes and nukes." "You're eating spicy food, and you can't help but talk loudly," he said. "As a result, ideas were passed around, and that explains the valley." Jeff Rubin, a systems programmer at Stanford's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, even worked for Mr. Kao as a waiter in exchange for Chinese lessons. Which is why Mark Seiden, a veteran programmer, remembers one day when a manager of the laboratory came to lunch with a Digital Equipment salesman. At one point the two were arguing about a technical detail, and the manager called a halt to the debate. "There is no point in arguing," he said. "We can settle this very easily.  Let's ask the waiter." "Can you tell us about the cache on the KL 10?" the laboratory manager asked Mr. Rubin. "It's a 32K two-way set associative cache," he replied, and then walked away, leaving the salesman's mouth hanging open. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Louis Kao, who for years owned a restaurant that fed the biggest brains in Silicon Valley, preparing a lunch celebrating his retirement. (Peter DaSilva for The newyork Times)

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Nasdaq Hits New High as Computer Companies Rebound
body: The Nasdaq composite index soared to a record yesterday as investors snapped up shares of Internet companies and software makers. But the swing toward technology stocks came at the expense of industrial stocks, which finished mostly lower, sending the Dow Jones industrial average down. The Nasdaq index rose 35.04 points, to close at 2,887.06, easily surpassing its previous closing high of 2,864.48, on July 16. For the year, the Nasdaq has gained 31.7 percent. The Dow industrials, however, fell 50.97, to close at 11,028.43, after giving up a gain of 62 points. For the week, the Dow lost 50.02, or 0.5 percent, but it is still up 20.1 percent so far this year. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index rose 4, to 1,351.66. The Nasdaq's strength came from hefty gains by the on-line auction house Ebay, which rose 13 9/16, to 158, and the Internet search provider Yahoo, which rose 7 13/16, to 170 1/2. Software companies also gained ground, with Microsoft rising 15/16, to 95, and Oracle, a maker of business software, picking up 2 5/16, to 46 3/8. "Technology is back," said Arthur Hogan, chief market analyst at Jefferies & Company. "This is a group that had been battered in recent weeks, and it's nice to see money coming back into the group." Traders suggested that Thursday's unofficial test run for Year 2000 computer glitches may have eased concerns about computer-related companies. Some programmers had feared that the string of nines in Thursday's date, 9/9/99, would cause computer programs to fail. But with no major problems reported, programmers and Wall Street professionals alike gained confidence that Jan. 1, 2000, would pass without difficulty. Stocks also benefited from a relatively benign Government report on producer prices for August, which eased investor concerns about higher interest rates. The Labor Department said that rising energy costs pushed producer prices up a higher-than-expected five-tenths of a percent, but when the volatile energy and food categories were excluded, the index actually fell a tenth of a percent. Financial markets tend to set aside food and energy price changes and focus on the figure known as core inflation. The drop in the core rate last month was better than economists had expected. The markets have been uneasy lately because of concerns that the Federal Reserve, which has already raised interest rates twice this year, would push rates higher a third time because of the economy's strength. "This was pretty much the icing on the cake," said David Orr, chief economist at First Union Capital Markets Group in Charlotte, N.C. "The market is correct to now relax, at least temporarily." But while most stocks rose, the big industrial companies that dominate the Dow fell. Caterpillar tumbled 2, to 56 3/4, and Chevron, which rose throughout the week as crude oil prices improved, fell 1 5/8, to 95 15/16, as investors took profits. Maytag, the appliance maker, plunged 14 13/16, to 41 3/4, after saying its third-quarter earnings would miss Wall Street analysts' estimates because of weak sales for its lower-priced goods. Healthsouth, which runs rehabilitation centers, fell 2 3/16, to 5 11/16. The company, based in Birmingham, Ala., said late on Thursday that it would delay spinning off its in-patient hospitals and warned that its operating margins for the third and fourth quarters would fall below forecasts. Hon Industries of Muscatine, Iowa, an office furniture company, eased 1 9/16, to 22 9/16. The company warned that third-quarter earnings would be below Wall Street estimates, citing difficulties in hiring new employees. National Semiconductor gained 2 5/8, to 34 5/8, after reporting better-than-expected first-quarter earnings of $47.1 million, or 25 cents a share. Amplidyne, a maker of power amplifiers for wireless and satellite telecommunications based in Raritan, N.J., climbed 2 1/8, to 12 1/4, after introducing a set of products to offer high-speed wireless Internet access. Intuit, which makes Quicken and Turbotax software, gained 5 15/16, to 103, after announcing a 3-for-1 split. "Most of the market came through this week fairly unscathed," said Mr. Hogan of Jefferies & Company. "But until we hear from the Fed, there's still resistance against taking the entire market to new highs." The Russell 2000 index of smaller companies rose 3.42, to 441.19. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners 6 to 5 on the newyork Stock Exchange. Volume totaled 808.54 million shares. Overseas, Japan's Nikkei stock average rose 0.19 percent. European indexes were mixed, as Germany's DAX index rose 0.9 percent, Britain's FT-SE 100 fell 1.1 percent, and France's CAC-40 gained 0.6 percent. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average over the past year.
