title:
Need Asparagus? Just Click It.;
On-Line Grocers Take Aim At Established Supermarkets
body: Consumers these days think nothing of buying books or Barbies on line. But will they also E-shop for eggs? Webvan Group, based in the San Francisco area, is the latest to place a big bet that time-starved consumers will soon abandon shopping carts and checkout lanes for the convenience of having diapers, juice and lettuce delivered. The company, which has been filling orders only since May, is spending $1 billion to build automated warehouses in 26 markets and is planning a public offering of stock next month to raise as much as $345 million to finance even more growth. Peapod, Streamline.com Inc. and Shoplink Inc., among others, are also investing in systems and additional operations to take on the $450 billion brick-and-mortar supermarket industry. Within a few years, the companies say, consumers in virtually any metropolitan area will be able to buy food staples and household products by computer with the same quality and prices offered at Safeway or Kroger. Though analysts are skeptical, most predict that they will be profitable within two years. "The whole issue about whether this is a speculative business is waning," said John R. Icke, chairman and chief executive of Shoplink in Boston, which says it makes more than 2,300 deliveries a week, with an average order of $102. "I think we are just an indicator that if you get set up correctly to do this business, people will shop this way." But Shoplink and others face an uphill battle. The challenge will be to attract and retain enough repeat customers in a volume-driven business with razor-thin profit margins. It will take more than the ease of pointing and clicking to get consumers in the habit of ordering bread and milk on line. The companies must overcome die-hard shopping habits, often limited product selections and a preference among some people simply to squeeze their own melons. In addition, price is likely to be a factor for many budget-conscious consumers. On-line grocers say their real edge is offering consumers an easy way to scratch off one more tedious item from their weekly "to do" lists. Essentially, they say, they are selling convenience as much as canned goods. And, they add, they will become even more competitive with traditional grocers as they work the kinks out and market more aggressively to the public. Because on-line grocers often lack the buying power of Kroger, Safeway and other large chains, they cannot always match their prices or offer the same discount deals. Tack on delivery fees of as much as $30 a month or Federal Express shipping costs, and the final price for $100 of goods can be enough to keep many people from hitting the send key. Peapod (www.peapod.com) charges a variety of rates, from $5 for a single delivery in San Francisco to $19.95 for an unlimited number of $60-plus monthly deliveries in Chicago. Shoplink (www.shoplink.com) charges a monthly fee of $25 for a once-a-week delivery. Extra orders are $15. Shopping by computer works like this: after logging into the Web site, customers can browse the so-called aisles, identified by categories like general grocery, baby, health and beauty and snacks. But filling a shopping cart comes with hassles that can try the patience of even the most loyal E-customer. Want cereal? It is not as simple as grabbing it off a shelf. At Peapod, for instance, shoppers must click on "cereal and breakfast," but that does not immediately show, say, Grape Nuts. The menu then asks if shoppers want bagels, pancakes or all cereals and oatmeal. It goes on. From there, the shopper must decide between various options, like cold family cereal or children's cereal. Only then can they find the Grape Nuts or Cheerios. For anyone needing about 50 items, making out a shopping list can take as long as driving to the supermarket and going through the aisles. The companies note, though, that after the first purchase, customers can order from their original lists and revise them with relative ease. Another drawback is that the services are useless to poor or low-income consumers who lack credit cards and computers. And many consumers will need to be convinced that an order of produce will not mean getting stuck with bruised peaches and too-green bananas. Further, while some sites will deliver goods to locked boxes, which include freezers, in a customer's garage, others require the buyer to be home to receive the delivery. Still, as prices, distribution and consumer awareness improve, the on-line grocers bet that they can increasingly encroach on competitors who must factor store displays, checkout clerks and real estate for parking lots into their pricing structures. So far, though, the traditional supermarket chains, while watching the action carefully, have little to fear from their on-line rivals. Virtual supermarkets sold a measly $148 million worth of groceries, health and beauty aids and other household items last year, according to Jupiter Communications, which tracks electronic retailing. By 2002, Jupiter says, the figure is expected to soar to $3.5 billion, but even that would still represent less than 1 percent of overall supermarket sales. And few on-line operators have made money so far, though they make the typical Internet argument that building market share takes priority. The Kroger Company, for one, is not panicking. "Based on the numbers we've seen," said Gary Rhodes, a spokesman for the company, "we think it's still very, very small." But Kroger is still experimenting with various virtual models. "I think it boils down to cost and proving that you can deliver the right order to the right customer at the right time," Mr. Rhodes said. "There probably aren't too many retailers that can do all of that consistently and profitably at this point." Analysts agree, saying that the on-line end of the industry is essentially in a period of costly trial and error and that consumers may ultimately decide it is a silly idea. "Right now all of E-commerce is a loss-leader business," said Ken Cassar, an analyst with Jupiter's digital-commerce group. "The game today is acquire customers and lose as little money as possible." The risks have not stopped companies from rapidly expanding in hopes of persuading shoppers to defect from the neighborhood grocer. Streamline's revenues more than doubled in the latest quarter, to $3.63 million, but it lost $4 million, compared with $2.6 million a year earlier, in large part because of investment spending. Now the company, which raised $42 million in a public stock offering in June, is accelerating its national growth even more. Streamline's initial strategy was to operate in 7 to 10 markets by the end of 2001 and 13 markets by 2004, but the company has revised the plan to capture the momentum of greater-than-expected consumer demand and changing market conditions. The company, based in Westwood, Mass., now expects to be in 20 markets by 2004. Peapod, too, is ramping up. "Because of the competition in the category we do intend to speed up our plans and start growing again," said Andrew Parkinson, chief executive of Peapod, which is based in Skokie, Ill., and operates in eight markets, including Chicago, San Francisco and Long Island. "What that means is you'll see us go into multiple cities in 2000 and going forward." Like the other companies, though, Peapod has yet to turn a profit and is still working out the bugs. In its latest quarter, it had flat revenues of $17.5 million and a net loss of $4.9 million, compared with a loss of $4.5 million in the period a year earlier. The company now promises only next-day service, scrapping its effort to deliver groceries to customers within three hours. It has also switched to central distribution centers, no longer having drivers fill orders from existing supermarkets. And Peapod is continuing to tweak its product mix. Netgrocer, too, has struggled to perfect its methods and cost structure. In just four years in business, it has dismissed half its 70 workers, replaced its management team and scrapped a planned public stock offering. The company, which delivers nonperishable items -- from graham cracker pie crusts to pet flea collars -- via Federal Express, had 1998 revenues of about $3 million, but lost $17 million. But with more than $4 million in new, private financing, a leaner cost structure and a growing customer base, the company is now on solid footing, said Fred Horowitz, Netgrocer's president and chief executive, who noted that the average order price has risen to more than $60 from $49 in the last six months. "We're built for people who like to cheat in the express lane," Mr. Horowitz said. Losses per order have dropped to $1 from $4, and "our goal is that this business can be profitable in two years," Mr. Horowitz said from the company's cavernous distribution center in North Brunswick, N.J., where workers recently filled orders for everything from shampoo to pasta sauce. For all its ambition, though, Netgrocer's experience so far highlights the risky nature of a fledgling industry that, even if ultimately successful, is likely to produce its share of casualties, analysts said. Investors so far are not sold. Unlike many other highflying Internet stocks, shares of on-line grocers have languished. Peapod's shares, which began trading in June 1997 at $16, now trade for about $6. And Streamline's shares, which began trading this June at $10, have since slumped to about $7. "It's sort of an emerging business right now, and a couple of new players are trying to get at it, and no one yet appears to have the perfect model," said Ellen Baras, an analyst who follows the business for William Blair & Company. Webvan (www.webvan.com), for one, has had trouble sticking to its promise to fill orders in 30 minutes, and customers who order Coke sometimes wind up with Pepsi, analysts said. A Webvan spokesman said the company, whose founder, chairman and chief executive is Lewis Borders, co-founder of Borders Books, is in a "quiet period" because of its pending stock offering and could not comment. For these businesses, "there are a couple of things going on," said Ms. Baras of William Blair. "First of all, the business models are being refined and, two, a lot of customers are still getting used to the concept." Robert and Loida Brisbane of Long Island are sold on the idea. "Because we have a baby and both work and everything, it just happens to be more convenient than always having to go to the grocery store, so we thought we'd give it a try," said Mr. Brisbane, 37, a junior high school principal in Queens. "It makes my life a lot easier," agreed Mrs. Brisbane, 38, a police officer in Queens. In the three months the family has been using Peapod after learning about it from a television commercial, she said, it has freed up more time for "just hanging out and going out to dinner together." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Robert Brisbane, a junior high school principal, inspects a delivery from Peapod.com with his daughter Diamond. title: Betting the Farm On the Virtual Store - Correction Appended
body: FOR eight years, Fred Parks says, he sold all manner of antiques and collectibles, "everything but tube socks and T-shirts," from a series of stores in downtown Baltimore. About a year ago, he closed his latest store, but he didn't go out of business. He took his expertise in ceramics -- Art Nouveau, Art Deco and Arts and Crafts styles -- to Ebay, the largest of the on-line auction sites. Now working from home and a studio that he rents for $100 a month, he has lowered his expenses, he says, and increased his prices and profits. "If I opened a store, I might have 35 people on a good day," he said. "I get thousands in my virtual store." More and more people are making a living from on-line auctions, often closing their brick-and-mortar stores or quitting jobs to vend bric-a-brac electronically at auctions like the ones at Ebay (www.ebay .com), Amazon.com (www.amazon.com) and Yahoo (www.yahoo.com). According to a report issued in March by Forrester Research, a consulting company that tracks E-commerce, spending on auction sites will grow from $1 billion in 1998 to an estimated $2.3 billion this year. While none of the auction sites knows how many people have turned electronic auctions into full-time jobs, Ebay estimates that it has about 10,000 "power sellers," who sell merchandise for $2,000 to $25,000 or more each month. Mr. Parks said he had no regrets about going virtual. "I at this point have no interest in ever having a store again," he said. "Why would I?" Why? Well, there are the long hours at the computer, and the tedium of wrapping and sending countless packages. Sometimes the auction sites crash, suspending business for days and putting a crimp in the cash flow. And there are the prickly customers who think nothing of firing off rude email tirades. But for Mr. Parks and others, the increased profits and ability to open for business at any hour are ample compensation for the drawbacks of Web auctions. The Forrester Research study projects that by 2003, auction sites will account for $6.4 billion in spending. As more store owners get a taste of selling on line, more stores will close, analysts predict. Michael May, a digital commerce analyst for Jupiter Communications, a research firm in Boston, explained: "They are Main Street, mom-and-pop-type stores that realize they are selling a far greater percentage of their inventory through sites like Ebay, and they can't justify paying rent anymore." For instance, take Mike Baker, who had averaged $30,000 to $40,000 in revenue a year selling baseball cards and photographs from his store in Springdale, Ark. Now he makes bulk purchases of movie star photos and art prints to sell in on-line auctions, and he reports that his gross revenue is in six figures. Mr. Baker said he had been initially startled by the effectiveness of auction sales two years ago when he posted some Marilyn Monroe photos that were readily available from other sources. "If I got $6 back, I broke even; if I sold them for $12, I did good," he said. They sold for $36.10 each. (Mr. Baker has since self-published a book, "Strike it Rich on Ebay.") Or take Chris Gwynn, who quit his job as a marketing analyst with the Yankee Group in Boston to sell refrigerator magnets on line. He has now branched out to auctioning new action figures and has created his own site (actionfigureauctions.com) to sell them. Mr. Gwynn makes less money than he did as an analyst. "But within a year," he said, "I should be doing a lot better than I was." Auction sites have made it fairly simple for people to hang out a shingle because they require sellers to do little more than enter information in a series of text boxes. That has made it possible for even the computer-phobic to become involved in E-commerce. "I was scared of it and I thought I was too old to learn," said Claudia Bennett, an antiques dealer in Vernon, Tex. Ms. Bennett, who is 52, is now designing her own Web page, and she says she does not regret closing her 14,000-square-foot store or quitting her job at the post office to underwrite her antiques operation. "Now for the first time, I am making money at it," she said. While anyone can sell on line, not just anyone can make a living at it. "It's not as easy as saying, 'I am an E-merchant,' " said Mr. Parks, who bought a $1,200 digital camera, lights and a booth to make his ceramics and other wares look appealing on line. "A bad photograph will not make you money." Even though successful, full-time auction entrepreneurs set their own hours, they say the job is extremely demanding. One such Web merchant, Lisa Harrington, said she had owned a tropical fish store in Houston that went bankrupt. But six years after the bankruptcy, she was drawn into Ebay when she helped a friend who was struggling with an on-line business. She struck out on her own in June 1998, and in the year that followed, she said, she took in $250,000, selling everything from electronics to motorized self-scooping cat litter boxes. To generate that kind of income, Mrs. Harrington signs on at 8:30 A.M. on workdays and does not sign off until 2 A.M., taking only an hour on some days to watch a soap opera. She takes only Fridays and Mondays off. "They are dead," she said. On a typical workday, she handles about 600 email messages, monitors 20 auctions and packages about 20 items for shipping. She also has to scare up fresh stock over the phone and on line. Although customers pay for shipping fees -- and Mrs. Harrington confides that she sometimes makes a small profit on the shipping charges -- there are other costs that new sellers tend to overlook, like the fees charged by auction sites, usually a percentage of the selling price. Mrs. Harrington said that she paid an average of $2,000 a month to Ebay alone. She also uses sites like Utrade, Ubid, Haggle and 321Gone.  Mr. Baker also puts in long hours selling his celebrity photos and art prints. "I start at 6 every morning," he said. "I work until 6. Then I take a break. Then I go back up around 10." Alan Hunter, who auctions sports and political memorabilia on line, said he put in eight hours a day photographing items, writing descriptions, uploading information onto the day's auction sites, answering email and packing up items to bemailed out. "But that doesn't include the time you spend hunting this stuff up," he said. "The toughest part is that you have a commitment to it every single day." Those who are not willing to put in long hours may get involved in too few auctions to really make money. Even worse, they may be slow to respond to customers, which can result in the posting of complaints referred to as dreaded "negative feedback." When a transaction is completed, the seller and buyer can write a short message commenting on it. Such feedback is available for all to see, and it works as a self-policing mechanism, warning people away from buyers or sellers who other people think are dishonest. The problem for someone selling goods at a lot of auctions is that it is easy to accrue negative comments. The more customers a seller has, the greater the chances that some of them will be slow to pay or hard to satisfy. If a seller posts a complaint about a buyer, the buyer may retaliate. "And before you know it," Mr. Hunter said, "you have 20 negative feedbacks." The alternative is for a seller to grin and bear it when dealing with a testy buyer -- a frequent occurrence. Sellers often try to increase profits a few percentage points by avoiding auction site fees. For instance, there is no rule against a seller getting in touch with auction losers to make separate deals if the seller has multiple copies of an item. Arlen Miller, who quit his job at Planet Hollywood in Orlando two years ago to deal full time on line in Disney collectibles, said: "I'll look at Ebay stuff, and if I have the same item on my list, I'll go back when the auction is over. You can go in and look at all of the bidders. If it went for $50, and I have it for $30, I'll send a note." But Mr. Miller draws an ethical line. "I would never step on someone's toes by doing that before their auction is over." The auction game is outgrowing the boundaries of Ebay, Amazon and Yahoo. The Forrester study predicted that the future of on-line auctions would be in sales of new retail products sold by companies, often on their own sites, rather than by individuals. "Over time, consumers will prefer buying from businesses rather than individuals since businesses are more accountable and offer first-run merchandise," the report said. A check using Yahoo's search engine turned up a list of close to 200 auction sites, including head-to-head Ebay competitors as well as specialty sites like Justbeads.com, which auctions beads, and Floorspace.com, which auctions industrial machinery. Off-the-shelf auction software makes it possible for individuals and small businesses to set up their own auction sites. "Auction software costs about $5,000," said Mr. Gwynn, the refrigerator magnet magnate who sells his action figures on his own site. "The server is a few hundred dollars a month." Mr. Gwynn does not allow other people to sell on his site. If he had set up the site that way, he said, he would have been competing against Ebay; that, he added, would be a losing proposition. In an early test of his sales plan, Mr. Gwynn said, he auctioned 96 Austin Powers figures, which sell at retail for about $11, in a week. He sold many of them in the $20 range, and some for as much as $38. "They were popular that week, and they were hard to get," he said. Not all the figures have flown off the shelves. Mr. Gwynn has found it difficult to sell everything from Barbie to "Star Wars" figures on a single site. So he will soon specialize even more. He plans to set up auction sites that are organized to reflect the way collectors collect: by manufacturer. That will make it easier to reach collectors looking for specific toys through on-line bulletin boards and newsletters, he said. While the on-line auction entrepreneurs do a lot of selling, they do little buying on line. "I never have really been able to buy on Ebay to re-sell and make a profit on it," said Mr. Baker, the print seller. In fact, some sellers worry about what Ebay and other sites will mean for their sources for items, like garage sales, if everyone is selling everything, including the kitchen sink, on line. So far those fears have proved to be unfounded. The number of yard sales each weekend proves that people still need to clean out their attics -- and that most of them still do it the off-line way, especially if they don't own a digital camera.  Sales Strategies TOP sellers agree that the most important ingredient for success in on-line auctions is choosing the right words to describe the item up for bid. The trick is to include as many potential search words as possible in the limited space allowed for the title line of a listing. That way, when a prospective bidder searches for a particular item, there is a greater chance for a hit. "You take a Marlboro lighter," said Mike Baker, who sells movie star photos and art prints in on-line auctions. "If you write 'butane lighter, Marlboro Zippo style,' you've got four key words. A lot of people would put 'Great, beautiful, hard-to-find Marlboro lighter.' That way you have only two words." Spelling counts, too. Buyers who search for a product using the correctly spelled word will never find a listing with a misspelling. The result is fewer bids. In fact, clever buyers intentionally search using misspelled words to find the best deals. For instance, a search on Ebay for "beanie babies" produced 10,066 listings. But a search using the misspelling "beenie" returned only 10 listings, some ripe for the picking without any bids.   ROY FURCHGOTT http://www.nytimes.com Correction  A credit was omitted in Circuits yesterday for a picture of Fred Parks, a trader, with an article about on-line auctions. The photographer was Ann Grillo, for The New York Times. Correction-Date: September 10, 1999, Friday Graphic   Photos: NEW LINE OF WORK -- Chris Gwynn, a former marketing analyst, sells action figures on his own auction Web site. He said he expected to exceed his previous income within a year. (Michael Quan for The New York Times)(pg. G1); NEW LOCATION -- Fred Parks, a Baltimore auction trader, moved his business to the Web. title: Concerts to Introduce Humanitarian Web Site
body: Three all-star pop stadium concerts on Oct. 9 -- in New Jersey, England and Switzerland -- are to introduce Netaid.org, a Web site that seeks to end poverty by bringing together relief organizations with donors and volunteers. In a news conference yesterday, Bono of U2 described Netaid as "the Yellow Pages of aid in cyberspace." The concerts, produced by the people who assembled the Ethiopian famine-relief benefit Live Aid in the 1980's, are to take place at Giants Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J.; Wembley Stadium outside London, and the Palais des Nations in Geneva. At Giants Stadium, the performers are to include Puff Daddy, Celine Dion, Sting, the Algerian singer Cheb Mami, Mary J. Blige, Busta Rhymes, Jimmy Page of Led Zeppelin, Counting Crows, Jon Bon Jovi and the Italian rock singer Zucchero. Wyclef Jean of the Fugees and Bono are to perform a song they wrote in honor of Netaid, "New Day." Giants Stadium tickets go on sale tomorrow through Ticketmaster. At Wembley the lineup includes David Bowie, Bryan Adams, Bush, the Coors, George Michaels, Robbie Williams and the reunited Eurythymics. A private concert in Geneva, where many of the relief organizations have headquarters, is to feature Bryan Ferry, Des'ree and the Scottish group Texas. Jewel and Sheryl Crow have both agreed to perform, but their location has not been decided. The concerts are to be televised on VH1, MTV and, in Britain, on the BBC. Radio stations will carry the events to 60 countries, and there will be an Internet Webcast. The concerts are not primarily for fund-raising, although the immediate proceeds will be dedicated to aid refugees in Kosovo and for relief work in Africa. Donations from listeners will be directed to the Netaid Foundation, which will distribute contributions under the direction of the United Nations Development Program, its antipoverty agency. But the main purpose of the events is to draw worldwide attention to Netaid, a novel alliance of the United Nations, Internet entrepreneurs and musicians. "It's about a billion hits against poverty, and we want to punch that sucker out," Quincy Jones, the musician and producer, said at the news conference. Netaid will provide information and eventually direct connections for people working on projects as diverse as environmental problems, disaster relief or lobbying to cancel the international debts of the 52 poorest countries. "The idea is for it to become the largest portal and directory for antipoverty organizations in the world," said Bob Chlopak, a spokesman for Netaid. After the concerts, the site will be overseen by the United Nations Development Program. Cisco Systems, the networking company that has built the Web site and donated $10 million to the Netaid Foundation, announced that Netaid was 10 times larger than any other Web site. Kofi Annan, the Secretary General of the United Nations, appeared at the news conference. By satellite, President Clinton and Prime Minister Tony Blair of Britain activated the Web site in North America and Europe. Nelson Mandela, the former President of South Africa, also appeared by satellite. "As the Internet reaches more and more communities," Mr. Mandela said, "they will gain access to new information and resources they can use to uplift themselves." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Disney Names Head Of Internet Group
body: The Walt Disney Company named Steven Bornstein, president of its ABC Inc. unit, as head of Disney's Internet group today, and said that the veteran television executive would become president of the Web portal Go.com later this year. He was named chairman of the group, Buena Vista Internet Group, after the departure of Jake Winebaum, who left in June to join a venture that fosters Internet start-ups. Mr. Bornstein will also be named president of Go.com after Disney completes its previously announced merger with a search service, the Infoseek Corporation, at the end of 1999, and spins off its Internet assets into a new company, Go.com. Disney, which is based in Burbank, currently operates the Go Network portal with Infoseek, as well as Web sites like ESPN.com. "Steve joined ESPN when cable was a nascent industry -- much like the Internet today -- and was instrumental in building ESPN into the undisputed market leader," Michael Eisner, Disney's chairman, said. Mr. Bornstein began managing programming at the all-sports cable network just four months after it start in 1980, and 10 years later he was named chief executive of ESPN. He rose to become a corporate officer at Capital Cities/ABC and joined Disney when it bought Capital Cities in 1996. Last February, he was named president of ABC Inc. http://www.nytimes.com

Some Go on Line to Buy Furniture . . . And Some Get In Line
body: THEY'RE not just buying books anymore. Internet customers have quickly moved past life insurance and airplane tickets and are surfing for furniture: poufs and pillow-back sofas, writing desks and ergonomic office chairs. Lisa Marie Pagano, a Hollywood decorator, has E-shopped for high-profile clients, including Nicholas Cage, from newyork to Los Angeles. "When I go on the Web for a big-ticket item, it's a risky thing," she said. She can't just carry a lamp or an ottoman to a client's house to try it out, leaving a credit card behind at a shop. But she does turn to the Internet when she's stumped, say, by a star's request for three huge antler chandeliers for his screening room. ("They're very popular out here," she said.) At www.Widerview.com, a Northern California site, she found Paul Bunyan-size elk chandeliers and ordered $20,000 worth. "They came in crates that were as big as cars," she said. "I would have paid three times as much in Los Angeles." Furniture shopping on the Web is growing by the day, with manufacturers and electronic marketers offering speedier downloads, easier navigation and slicker sites. While some industry analysts doubt that surfers will spend $10,000 on a dining room sight unseen, others note that customers in stores are already making a giant leap of faith by leaving hefty deposits on furniture 12 weeks in advance. But there is no debate that the furniture business is making a bet on the Web. Witness the current ".com clutter." "Up until a few months ago, people had virtually no choices," said Michael May, a digital commerce analyst at Jupiter Communications, a new-media research company. What has limited the growth of furniture sales on line, he said, "is simply a lack of supply, not of demand." The good news -- and bad news -- is that more of everything is suddenly available. Hundreds of mom-and-pop digital retailers like Fred Friar, who sells handmade sassafras chairs from his West Virginia farm, now have the opportunity to be seen (in his case, at www.home.earthlink.net/ ffriar/). For the style-starved, there are small shops showing well-designed wares, classic and new. Big retailers like Crate and Barrel, Smith & Hawken and Restoration Hardware are testing the water with on-line stores; Ethan Allen is plunging in: the company, with sales of $762.2 million for the latest fiscal year, is to introduce a site in October offering 4,000 furniture choices. (A guide to sites is on page F5.) "With $300 million in venture capital being thrown at home-furnishing Web sites this year, something big is going to happen," said Brian Carroll, on-line editor for Furniture Today, a High Point, N.C., trade newspaper. "But who the winners and losers will be is unknown. The consumer will decide. She'll shop; we'll adapt." In contrast to the gender bias on the Web, in July of this year, almost as many women as men over age 18 visited the 21,000 Web sites studied by Media Metrix, which measures on-line shopping behavior. On the other hand, many Web retailers and analysts sense that men are more comfortable shopping for furniture on line than in a store. But just how much anyone is really spending remains unclear. Mr. Carroll estimated that of furniture-store sales for 1998, which totaled $45.3 billion, maybe 3 percent of sales were generated on line. "Manufacturers themselves don't know how the products are purchased, whether from a retailer or a site," Mr. Carroll said. (Internet stores have noticed that the peak hour for shopping in the Northeast is 11 A.M., with people apparently buying lamps and sofas from the office.) New Internet shoppers say they were first emboldened by small purchases at Amazon.com. Elizabeth Dettoni, who works for an on-line brokerage, took to the Internet to arrange much of her recent move from a 600-square-foot studio in Manhattan to a two-bedroom condo in Westchester County. Five days before her move, she spent about $800 on a mission-style armoire, bookshelves and a table from Sauder, at www.sauder.com. As promised, the furniture was delivered ready to assemble the day she moved in. And when she found a chipped part, the company replaced it and sent it to Ms. Dettoni's home via priority mail. "These people went the extra mile," she said. Ms. Pagano, the Hollywood decorator, also savors the convenience. She downloads images from Web sites and sends them via email to clients on movie sets, or they "conference shop" on line, linked by cell phones and laptops. "Instead of jaded people in Los Angeles or newyork showrooms, people with major attitudes, I deal with lovely, homespun people who are very happy to spend time with you," she said. Of course, traditional stores fear that their business will be destroyed by on-line transactions; having invested in display, advertising and sales help, they worry that shoppers will test-drive recliners in the stores, sample the store service and then use the Internet to find the best price. (Mr. Carroll, who has price-shopped himself, argues that "furniture on the Net is no different in price than it is in most stores, although the perception is that it is.") The field is so new, there is no reliable measurement of shoppers' habits yet, but the tea leaves read differently to Linda Lewi of Homeportfolio.com, an on-line clearing house for consumer information about high-end appliances and furniture. Based on a sampling of site visitors, she said, "Consumers are using the Internet for information and service, then turning to retailers to buy." For shoppers, the ultimate empowerment may come the day digital retailers end "showroom shutout," the decades-old "to the trade" system that has kept some haut designers behind closed showroom doors. Throwing down the gauntlet, Homeportfolio.com, has plans for a new digital shopping area in October featuring products of some companies that once sold only to architects and designers. Opening a Web site means there is no big-box store to rent or stock. For companies selling $2,800 Knoll sofas, circa 1965, from Antwerp, Belgium (at www.fiftie-fiftie.be), or $4,600 boardroom tables (from www.dwr .com, a site in San Francisco), it feels less like the grand opening of a retail store than an eerie new kind of fishing -- like rowing out onto a vast etherous pond, casting with a quiet plunk and waiting for a customer to bite. At 7 A.M. on July 12 from his office in San Francisco, Rob Forbes went fishing. His lure was www.dwr.com, otherwise known as Design Within Reach, a new home furnishings catalogue and Web site, both designed by Pentagram, the international design firm and a partner in the venture. Mr. Forbes, the former director of inventory management at Williams-Sonoma, did not anticipate catching much of anything the first day, though he advertised in Metropolis magazine and threw out some bait: photographs of hundreds of modern furnishings from classic to new designs, including the hot Cricket outdoor chair from Italy for $45. Lo, there was soon a frenzy of orders. "We were in battle mode," he said, recalling the 80 email messages and more than 200 phone calls the first day. One of the first customers was Ronald Fiore, who designs showrooms for Baker Furniture. He spotted a dining chair by Charles Eames for $140 and ordered two for his Greensboro, N.C., loft. They were delivered exactly when promised, the next week. "I thought it would be a deal where you'd have to buy a containerful from Italy to get that price," he said. H ERE are some tips for surfing for home-furnishings: * Anticipate slower downloads of pages at 11 in the morning (and again later in the evening, when the children are in bed). Many electronic retailers say these are peak shopping times. (Seema Williams, an electronic commerce analyst at Forrester, a digital-commerce research company in Cambridge, Mass., said, "Unless personal productivity figures suffer, employers seem to be tolerating it.") * Most sites offering furniture expect the customer to call their orders in by telephone. Note that many smaller sites do not have telephone service after business hours. * Try starting out from a search engine like www.altavista.com (searching for "furniture makers"). Altavista's searches are objective, not based on a site's popularity. If you're looking for something very specific -- say, antler chandeliers -- be prepared to dig. And to wait: you'll probably be going to smaller sites with pipsqueak servers. Once you're there, allow at least half an hour to download images. * A site operated by Furniture Today, an industry newsletter, at www.furnituretoday.com, offers a comprehensive list of manufacturers with Web sites. * Startup sites will often go the extra mile. They may negotiate on pricing, and many offer free shipping and free returns. Ask for a guaranteed delivery time. Sites also offer what they call "quick ship" items, manufactured and shipped within days of ordering. Most credit card fraud on the Web is by consumers taking advantage of retailers, not the other way around. The seller will verify your credit card information. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: OF MICE AND MERCHANDISE -- Design Within Reach sells Eames on its Web site. (Montage by Tony Cenicola and Shelley Camhi/The newyork Times)(pg. F1); GOING GLOBAL -- Rob Forbes, founder of Design Within Reach, left; antler chande liers, right, from Widerview.com were made in Colorado; below, Hugh Fogel of Unica holds a bowl designed in Belgium that can be ordered on his Web site. (Gretel Daugherty for The newyork Times; Tom Pidgeon for The newyork Times (left); Kim Steele for The newyork Times (above left))(pg. F4)

Home Furnishings, Modern and Classic, From the Internet - Correction Appended
body: TOUCHY-FEELY, persnickety and an Internet novice -- it would take a lot of handholding to get me to buy a sofa without first karate-chopping the pillows. Now, I'm at least tempted. In the last four weeks, I sampled about 80 home-furnishings sites, from Fred Friar's front-porch location to Homepoint.com, a megasite with the virtual heft of a Spiegel catalogue. To find furniture E-tailers, I usually started with the www.37.com search engine. I spoke with consumers who had shopped at many of the sites and questioned the sales staff as if I were a potential buyer. Generally, they were well informed and personable, and most important, low-key. There was no pressure to buy; in fact, many collegially shared information about other sites. (Engaging service must make up for the lack of an opportunity to actually bounce on the bedsprings.) At night on a home computer, surfing can be slow as molasses, and frustrating. One tip: Do something else while shopping. I took along a Nicholson Baker novel. There are half a dozen or so big players -- including Homepoint.com and Living.com. Personally, I found these new megasites overwhelming: they test the bounds of how much is too much. Mike West, the founder of Homepoint.com in Greenville, S.C., says his company offers "anything and everything from America's 3,700 furniture manufacturers." "For our customers, quality is not a driving force," he said. "We offer a tremendous selection and choice for customers who are concerned with 'Will it fit in my home?' " But a word of caution about some high-style sites, too. It seems 40's and 50's design is ubiquitous on the Web. At first it all looks kind of swanky, like an Austin Powers set, but after your umpteenth Eames "potato chip" chair, the look can be as cloying as an overdose of Pringles. Here is a guide to some of the better sites:  blindambition.com -- A leading site among the competitive miniblind suppliers on the Web; plug in window dimensions, and order wooden Venetian blinds, delivered in days at low prices (30 by 60 inches, $88). Almost everything is in stock.  bludot.com -- Hip storage from a small furniture design cooperative in Minnesota. The text can be too cute ("sawing logs" for a maple bed). But see Modulicious, the site's mix-and-match modular system made of maple veneer and painted steel, well priced at $399 to $899.  dwr.com -- Design Within Reach is a professional-looking, fast, concise site with modern classic pieces for home and office. Offers a huge inventory and quick delivery. Prices appear to be fair, often lower than you would find in a Manhattan store; there are discounts for large orders.  www.eckhart.nl -- This Rotterdam site offers a huge inventory from European furniture manufacturers. The problem is getting prices for some of the pieces. Try calling 011-31-10-414-1616 during business hours in the Netherlands (six hours ahead of newyork). There is warm customer service in English.  www.fiftie-fiftie.be -- A Belgian dealer in vintage furniture, objects and rare books. The site is in English, the prices in euros (about one to a dollar) or in Belgian francs (100 of them equals about $262). American collectors are heading here for the selection of midcentury furniture and objects from Europe and Japan.  formdecor.com -- This Los Angeles dealer of vintage furniture is favored by production designers and foreign collectors; a site for high-end collectibles like the rare Eames Greige Zenith Armshell, offered at $595. --  f-u-p.com -- A site based in Portland, Ore., with modernist classics; prices and shipping fees are high, but the look of the page is fashionable, and the product mix is intelligent.  georgesmith.com -- Very fine handmade English sofas and chairs from the company's newyork and Los Angeles showrooms, offered at 40 to 50 percent off; smart sales help.  hmhome.com -- A beautiful, efficient site, from the 75-year-old Herman Miller company, offers a professional room planner, but the site may ultimately alienate some franchisees: consumers can buy directly from the factory here, with a discount on seating and home-office products (but not on classic designs by Charles and Ray Eames, George Nelson and Isamu Noguchi). Some quick-ship items (click I Want It ) include the Aeron ergonomic office chair, $749 fully loaded, which undercuts some dealers' prices. The Web site's customer-service phone lines close maddeningly at 5 P.M. Eastern time. And the phone number is hard to find on the site. Here it is: (888) 520-7646.  www.industrial-home.com -- A homespun site that offers one-of-a-kind modern furniture and accessories for collectors. See the vintage 1960 Viscontea lamp by Achille Castiglioni for Flos, $650. A rare Alain Richard double-tiered buffet sold this week for $1,200.  marthastewart.com -- For those who can't get enough, Martha Stewart's Web site is appropriately pastel-colored; the ever-expanding inventory includes a creamy green hobnail glass table lamp for $68. noguchi.org -- A gentle, intelligent blockbuster and a real find: the Isamu Noguchi Foundation Web site is soft-sell, and the best source for the designer's Akari paper lamps -- you get thumbnails of all the styles, by type (floor, table), but you then have to call or send an email for prices. Sales benefit the foundation and its museum.  simplymodern.com -- A small, speedy site for desks, accessories and objects straight out of "The Jetsons." There's a nice Finnish plywood trash can for $42.  www.shakerworkshops.com -- A source long favored by European collectors, this Massachusetts maker of authentic Shaker furnishings has a site that offers settees, chairs, tables, dressers and beds, in kits or assembled. Skip the bric-a-brac and the Shaker recipe of the month, and move on to furniture. The kits make terrific family projects.  store.moma.org -- The Museum of Modern Art's collection is in many ways the definition of modern design, but the site can be surprisingly slow.  www.unicahome.com -- This is like going to Moss in Manhattan but without the erudite design pilgrims and jabbering tourists. This site, operated by a Birmingham, Mich., store, has a similar inventory but with better prices. Here you will find Philippe Starck office supplies, Droog laundry baskets and a $250 coat rack from Christophe Pillet. Verner Panton's Phantom chair is $250 at this site, which has nice links to other design sites.  widerview.com -- A reputable site for country and traditional styles, antler chandeliers, matelasse bedcovers, fair prices and warm, knowledgeable service. Urbane shoppers will have to dig a little to find the pearls: go to Urban Scapes, then to Take a Seat and to Mike Room Service. Keep clicking to view the collection of upholstered furniture. The best dining tables I've found for under $700 are at this site, too, but again it takes some persistence: start with the home page, go to Natural; then under Furniture, click on Antique, and keep clicking. You will find European farmhouse tables of recycled wax-finished pine; shipping is not free, but there is a $150 cap.  www.ziahouse.com -- A crisp, punchy Web site from a tiny Berkeley, Calif., store that has a tightly edited collection of modern furnishings. On the home page, click on Products. Objects here tend toward a "crafty" look, but there are plump sofas covered with colorful Tricia Guild fabrics, hard-to-find Santora Melone storage cabinets and a $1,000 Peter Sandback coffee table. There is no way to order except by calling the store's number, prominently displayed on every page.  MEGA-RETAILERS  www.furniture.com -- In July alone, 600,000 different visitors clicked on this huge site, according to Media Metrix. Based in Framingham, Mass., the site offers middle-of-the-road contemporary furniture and a room-planner tool. There's an on-line magazine with a story called "When His Meets Hers," a smart idea since Web sales are are almost evenly split between men and women.  www.goodhome.com -- A cooperative venture from Hearst, Mattel, Broderbund and the Thomas H. Lee Company (which built the Snapple brand), www.goodhome.com is expected to announce today that it is merging with another "not yet running" Web site, www.nhabit.com to form a mega-megasite called Goodhome. With $50 million in start-up money, the site, based in San Rafael, Calif., will go live on Sept. 21 and will offer 50 room scenes. "Every item of the room works together and is for purchase, including the fresh flowers," said Douglas Mack, the chief executive of Goodhome.  www.homepoint.com -- The mother ship of mass marketers, it has crisp, hyperactive pages. Featured recently was Fire-N-Ice, a $52 gooseneck desk lamp, but the site also sells chairs, beds, tables, you name it. Almost everything takes four to six weeks for delivery, but there is usually no charge for shipping.  www.living.com -- Can be slow to download, but there are 299 lamps, 213 sofas and lots more, from manufacturers like Natuzzi and Lane. Furniture from the site, which is based in Austin, Tex., may take from six to 12 weeks for delivery, and any purchase above $300 requires a 33 percent deposit. There's a nice $150 leather basket for fire logs. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  Because of an editing error, an article on Sept. 9 about new home-furnishings Web sites, including www.fiftie-fiftie.com, a Belgian Web site that gives prices in euros and francs, misstated the dollar valuation for 100 Belgian francs. It is $2.62, not $262. Correction-Date: September 16, 1999, Thursday Graphic   Photos: BEAUTY, EFFICIENCY AND COST -- The Herman Miller site has the Aeron chair, far left, for $749, fully loaded. CHAIRS WITHIN REACH -- The sleek Design Within Reach site offers one-click shopping.

title: Free College Notes on Web: Aid to Learning, or Laziness?
body: Students at Ohio State, Boston and Michigan State Universities, take heart: you may never have to take notes in a lecture again, nor will your counterparts on 59 other large campuses across the country. A new Internet venture called StudentU.com is hiring students this semester at 62 universities and paying them to take notes in as many as 50 core courses on each campus. The note takers post their jottings, within 24 hours, on a central Web site. Among the notes already listed are those taken on Tuesday in John Syer's course on world politics at California State University in Sacramento and on Aug. 24 in Robert G. Schwebach's lecture on financial markets at Colorado State. The service, which went on line yesterday, is free. And the correspondents, most hired through their fraternities and enrolled in the courses, are paid $300 a semester to open their notebooks to the world. The creator of the site, Oran Wolf, a 27-year-old graduate of the University of Texas, who hopes to earn a profit through advertisements, said he started the service to help students augment their own notes or to help them catch up after a sick day. But he conceded that his offerings could be abused by those with less legitimate excuses, like chronic oversleeping or lingering hangovers. "I definitely don't believe students should skip class," Mr. Wolf said yesterday from his Houston office, as he admitted that he, on occasion, had done just that. "It is important for them to attend the class, use this information as supplements to the course and if they do that, they are going to make A's." There is no shortage of critics who believe that the arrival of Mr. Wolf's venture -- along with other Web sites that sell sample term papers and synopses of great books -- signals nothing less than the erosion of liberal education, if not civilization. But Mark Edmundson, a professor of English at the University of Virginia, one of the institutions where Mr. Wolf has set up shop, believes that the problem lies more with universities -- and their reliance, often for financial reasons, on 300-student lecture courses -- than on those trying to beat the system. "There's something sleazy about students' taking notes and selling them on the Web," Professor Edmundson said. "But if you can buy the notes and satisfy the course requirements, maybe the course should have been distributed as a book, rather than having this charade of somebody standing up and going through a lecture that for all purposes doesn't change from year to year, and doesn't allow students the possibility of discussion." Peter Wood, a professor of anthropology and the associate provost at Boston University, which is also on Mr. Wolf's list, said the university might consider taking legal action once notes from the university appear on the site -- which, as of yesterday, they had not. "I, like thousands of faculty members, spent a great deal of time developing my courses within a specific intellectual context, a context that I control," he said. "For someone who is not educated in my field to offer what could be erroneous versions of that material, without my permission, strikes me as something which could potentially be illegal." Mr. Wolf, who likens his note takers to journalists protected by the First Amendment, said the seeds of his idea were first sown while he was studying economics at Austin, when he had occasionally taken advantage of a similar service there. For $30 per class, a private note-taking firm would arrange for him to get paper copies of any notes he had missed. After graduating in 1995 and moving to Houston, Mr. Wolf learned that the university there had no such service, and so he founded his own. Initially taking 10 hours of notes a day himself, he expanded his operation to include about 3,000 subscribers -- they too paid $30 for each class -- and about 40 note takers. Mr. Wolf said professors at the University of Houston were at first wary of helping him and his note takers gain access to classes, if they were not enrolled. But he said he won them over when they realized that attendance did not drop as a result. When Mr. Wolf discovered that such services were rare on other campuses, he said he decided to expand into a national operation. With an investment from Net Strategy, a Houston company that has nurtured other Web companies, and a rolling banner of advertisements that includes the Capital One Visa Platinum Card, Mr. Wolf began recruiting note takers at fraternities at 62 of the country's largest universities. He said he was not necessarily looking to hire top students. "Some of your best note takers aren't straight A students," he said. "They might have a kind of learning disability, a test anxiety, where they don't do well on tests. But they might take 15 pages of notes on a given lecture. What I look for is a dedicated student who attends class religiously." Among those who were tantalized by his offer to pay $300 per semester, plus $200 for every five note takers recruited, was Anje Castro, 22, a senior at California State University in Long Beach. "I thought that it was a really, really easy way to make money," said Ms. Castro, whose major is international business. "I have to go to class anyway." Ms. Castro was hired to provide notes on Prof. Wendell McCulloch's international law class, which she was already taking. So far, her correspondence has been brief, given that the class has met just once. "Already have homework," she wrote, on Aug. 31. "Bummer." Because he has assembled his operation so quickly, using students already in courses, Mr. Wolf said he would not be asking professors for permission to broadcast their notes. Thus many are likely to be as surprised as Professor Syer at Sacramento, who learned from a reporter yesterday that his introduction to the world's 10 largest countries had been reproduced by an anonymous note taker for all to see. "I'm going to get up there and take on the policies of the U.S. Government, the policies of the Indonesian Government, the policies of the Chinese Government," he said. "If I think this is something that is going to be quoted globally, it may change what I say." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Connects Inventors to Information (and One Another)
body: RODNEY LONG is an Alabama inventor who typically spends 16 hours a day on the Internet, logging on to things like inventor forums and an on-line patent database (www.patents.ibm.com /ibm.html) that has been sponsored by I.B.M. since 1997. Mr. Long, a former maintenance mechanic for U. S. Steel, has already seen one of his inventions go into production: a device that moves granulated materials like cement and sand more reliably through processing plants. That success has spurred him to keep tinkering, often with on-line help. "Without the Internet," he said recently, "I wouldn't have the other 27 inventions that I do." Another inventor who is fond of the Internet is Nancy Beaule of Lewiston, Me., the inventor of the Pie Saver. (It keeps pie edges from burning and can be seen at www.betabake.com.) She applied for a trademark more than a year ago, but had no idea where her application stood until she checked the Federal Patent and Trademark Office's Web site four months ago, and discovered, to her relief, that her trademark was pending. Lately, she has used the Internet to do patent searches. (The Pie Saver, by the way, is also available in supermarkets and at Yahoo's shopping site.) Inventors like Mr. Long and Ms. Beaule are flocking to the Net. To be sure, part of what they find there is silliness of the mad inventor variety. There are, for example, roughly a dozen Web sites that seem to exist solely to highlight kooky -- if not downright absurd -- inventions. But the silliness is vastly outweighed by Web sites that together offer a veritable dream shop for inventors. Inventors can find on-line support groups, chat rooms, message boards and patent and trademark databases. And the main goal of some sites is to alert inventors to those suspicious promotion and development companies that have long snookered inventors, especially beginners. One such company bilked Gary Kellmann out of $3,000 when he was 19 and was trying to sell his first invention, an alarm clock that could be turned off with a remote control. Mr. Kellmann of St. Charles, Mo., is now 30 and has four inventions on the market, including adhesive "belly buttons" that give a pierced look without the pain. But he wishes he had had access to the Internet information when he started out. He used to drive two hours at a stretch from Southeast Missouri State University in Cape Girardeau to downtown St. Louis to research patents. Basic patent searches can be done on line from the comfort of a computer chair, and pages of resources can be called up in less time than it takes to say Alexander Graham Bell. The Patent Office formally opened a full-text patent database on line in April. Because of the heft of the database, some inventors say it is best used for cursory searches, rather than the full-fledged ones that tend to be done by professional search firms. Still, the database contains text and images for more than two million patents, dating to 1976, and more than one million registered and pending trademarks, dating to 1870 (www.uspto.gov). Before the new database was rolled out, the Patent Office offered only abstracts of patents on line. For the complete text, inventors usually had to visit a Federal patent and trademark depository library, get access to a private -- and often expensive -- on-line service, or a professional search firm. Inventors can also find useful information at the sites for the National Inventors Hall of Fame (www.invent.org) and the United Inventors Association of the U.S.A. (www.uiausa.com). Both groups are revamping their Web sites. The association recently started offering an invention evaluation service through its Web site. The service costs $695, or about half of what an inventor might have to pay for working with, for example, a patent lawyer and a university evaluation service. But the Internet offers something that is perhaps as important as databases and services: the opportunity for inventors, who are often solitary figures, to connect to one another. Until recently, such connections were not easy to make. There were few support groups for inventors and many parts of the country still do not have them, said Carol Oldenburg, administrator for the United Inventors Association, a national group with some 3,000 members. Inventors often keep to themselves because they tend to be individualistic and "very paranoid," said Victor Lavrov, a mechanical engineer in Fullerton, Calif., who is also the founder of Inventnet, a popular Web site (www.inventnet.com). "Before the Internet, there was minimal communication among inventors," said Ronald J. Riley, an independent inventor who has a Web site for inventors (www.inventored.org) and posts an on-line listing of people and invention promotion firms that he contends offer questionable value to inventors (www.rjriley.com/site-index). Like other invention experts, Mr. Riley credits the Net with helping to persuade independent inventors, who include weekend hobbyists and downsized corporate researchers, to get involved with others. "Inventors are now talking more freely and sharing information," said Michael S. Neustel, a patent lawyer who opened a Web site in August 1998 under the banner of the National Inventor Fraud Center (www.inventorfraud.com). "Without the Internet," he added, "it would also be tough for consumer-minded organizations like ours to exist. It's just too time-consuming to contact inventors individually." Mr. Long, the inventor of the granulated material feeder, credits the fraud center with helping him avoid an invention promotion firm that has generated some complaints. The experience of Dr. Frank Evans shows what the Web can mean to small inventors. Dr. Evans, who is retired and lives in Baltimore, spent some eight years designing a portable wind-powered generator that can run a device like a small radio or television. In 1996, Dr. Evans posted his invention -- which catches the wind in cups shaped like Oriental soup spoons -- on a message board that is offered on line by the Inventors' Network of the Capital Area, a nonprofit association for inventors in Washington, Maryland and Virginia (inca.interspeed.net). Last December, Dr. Evans found someone to help him develop the machine: Fred Currence, a marine engineer who owns a prototype development shop and who just happens to live 20 blocks away.  Site-Seeing: Inventors  Here are a few of the sites inventors use on the Web:  THOMAS REGISTER OF AMERICAN MANUFACTURERS www.thomasregister.com This site, which is run by Thomas Publishing Company, lists some 156,914 manufacturers, as well as 135,415 brand names.  INVENTORS' ALLIANCE www.inventorsalliance.org This is a resource-studded Web site for an inventor's group that is based in the San Francisco Bay area.  PATENT CAFE www.patentcafe.com A site that is run by an inventor, Andy Gibbs. Inventors can get access to a number of resources and even order specialty coffee on line.  INVENTORS' DIGEST www.inventorsdigest.com This is the on-line version of the official magazine of the United Inventors Association and lists a number of resources, including timely news for inventors.  ABOUT.COM INVENTORS PAGE inventors.tqn.com About.com, formerly known as the Mining Company, offers on its Inventors page a number of links to services for inventors. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Gary Kellmann, above (Bill Stover for The newyork Times), wishes that he had had the Internet when he tried to sell his first invention, and Rodney Long, left (Melissa Springer for The newyork Times), finds it useful in his tinkering.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Business School Puts Courses In Hands of an On-Line Market
body: You have heard of on-line auctions for Beanie Babies, breakfasts with bigwigs and even spare kidneys. But what about bidding for seats in business school courses? Students at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School of Business are in the throes of such an auction this week. Students registering for elective courses log on to Wharton's course-auction Web site and bid on the ones they want. (Students sign up for core courses through the traditional registration system.) Each student starts with 5,000 points. An eager marketing major might place 2,000 points on a course offered by a popular marketing guru, for example, and bid 500 points each on four others. At the end of the day, computers run the numbers and match the highest bidders with the number of open seats. The seats are sold for the "clearing price," the highest losing bid. "It really puts you in charge," said Karin Magnuson, a second-year Wharton student. Other business schools have built similar systems. But Wharton's course auction adds a twist: The school runs 10 rounds of auctions each semester. After the second round, it allows students to "sell" courses as well as bid on them.  The result is a frenzy of speculation. After all, these are people who have come to business school to learn how to outsmart the markets or, at the very least, turn a quick buck. At semester's end, every student receives a replenishment of 1,000 points for each course completed. But students who want a bigger stash down the road buy courses with the intent of selling them at a higher price. Ms. Magnuson, for example, was selling a marketing course for 3,200 points on Wednesday. She insisted that she was not trying to exploit her classmates. "I'm just trying to prepare for next semester," she said. Anjani Jain, deputy vice-dean and director of the M.B.A. program, designed the auction almost three years ago. His plan was to mimic a free market. Students cannot buy multiple seats in one class, but they are allowed to purchase seats in an unlimited number of classes, in the same time slots if they want. Students cannot see minute-to-minute market data, however. They can only see what price the courses demanded in the last round, put in their bids for the current round and wait until the round ends to see whether they were outbid. "We want our students to be in the classroom instead of watching a ticker tape," Dr. Jain said. Still, many students spend much of their first few weeks watching -- and at times cursing -- the auction. Statistics from previous auctions show that by the sixth and seventh rounds, prices soar as students worry about missing out on the courses they want. Last spring, the average seat price climbed from 423 points in the first round to 1,090 points in the seventh. The bubble popped by the 10th round when the average seat price bottomed out at 172 points. Meanwhile, skilled bidders have not only learned about the vagaries of supply and demand, Dr. Jain said. They have first-hand experience of on-line auctions to take with them into the world of electronic commerce. "It has actually spawned some ideas," he said, "about Internet-based commerce using auctions."   LISA GUERNSEY http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Q & A;
AOL Options For Browsers
body: Q. I use America Online for my Internet service provider, but how would I install a Web browser other than the one from AOL?  A. If you have version 3.0 or later of AOL's software, you can run different Web browsers with it. With these later versions, you can run just about any Internet program from your AOL connection, including Telnet, F.T.P. (file transfer protocol, good for downloading files from remote servers) and Internet relay chat, or I.R.C. You can download a copy of Netscape's Communicator or a newer version of Microsoft's Internet Explorer browser using AOL. Windows users are advised to use the AOL keyword Netscape to get to the downloading area for Communicator and Browser for Internet Explorer. AOL advises Macintosh users to stroll through the Mac Orchard (www.macorchard.com), a Web site devoted to Apple-friendly Internet applications. AOL's on-line help area (keyword: Help) has more information about how to set each of these up. After you've installed the new browser software, sign on to AOL. If you are using Netscape, you will have to start it separately after you have connected to AOL, since it will not act as the default browser. Cnet, the technology news site, also keeps a helpful page devoted to Web browsing software and how to use it (home.cnet.com/category /0-3773.html).   J. D. BIERSDORFER  Circuits invites questions about computer-based technology, by mail to Questions, Circuits, The newyork Times, 229 West 43d Street, newyork, N.Y. 10036-3959 or by email to QandA@nytimes.com. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
STATE OF THE ART;
A Toy, Yes, But a PC At Heart
body: SEGA'S new Dreamcast video game console, which goes on sale in the unitedstates today, is the first of the next-generation home game machines to arrive on these shores. As a game machine its power is unrivaled, except by high-end personal computers costing more than 10 times as much, and it makes the graphics on the current market leader, the Sony Playstation, appear grainy and jerky. The Dreamcast is the closest thing to an arcade-quality game experience you can get at home. But the $199 Dreamcast is more than just a game console. Unlike earlier generations of game machines, which were closer to toys than to computers, the Dreamcast blurs the distinction between PC and game console. It has a 56K modem, for example, and it comes with software for connecting to the Internet for activities like email, Web browsing and chatting. Oddly, it comes from the box with Internet software but no complete games, which have to be purchased separately.  Game reviews, page 5 Some people say that inexpensive, Internet-enabled game consoles like the Dreamcast, along with its future rivals, the Sony Playstation II and Nintendo's Project Dolphin (also known as N2000), will become an alternative to PC's for millions of people who want to connect to the Net through TV screens. Of course, people who are already on the Net might be alarmed by the prospect of millions of Internet newbies whose common bond appears to be a love of Sonic the Hedgehog (Sega's most popular game character) and an ability to type with their thumbs. It would be a mistake, however, to dismiss these new game consoles as frivolous. While the Sega Dreamcast clearly has the pedigree of a game machine, it has the digital genetics of a computer. Besides the built-in modem, it has a powerful microprocessor, fancy 3-D graphics and audio chip sets, a special kind of CD-ROM drive that also plays audio compact disks, 26 megabytes of various kinds of system memory, and -- surprise -- even a custom version of Microsoft's Windows CE. All play and no work makes the Dreamcast a very dull toy. Windows CE makes the Dreamcast a very interesting device because it means that thousands of software developers could create applications for it if the Dreamcast gains a large enough following. The Dreamcast console has four high-speed ports on the front, and it comes with a single game controller that plugs into one of them. Other options for these ports include extra controllers, keyboards, steering wheels, force-feedback joysticks, microphones, guns and fishing reels that jerk in step with the action on screen and, down the road, digital cameras and other smart devices. For those who get excited about such things, the controller has a slot for an optional Tamagotchi-like smart-card device called a visual memory unit. A serial port on the back can work with a printer or a storage device like a Zip drive, although Sega would have been smarter to include a Universal Serial Bus, or U.S.B., port instead. The Dreamcast is built around a 128-bit microprocessor. The current market leaders for game consoles, the Sony Playstation and the Nintendo 64, use 64-bit processors. Basically, that means the 200-MHz Dreamcast chip can process twice the information its rivals can in any tick of the clock, enabling programmers to add sophisticated software features like the ability to recognize and exploit patterns in the user's playing style. In other words, the system can adapt to give the player a greater challenge over time, a trait shared by some newer PC games. Once upon a time, about five years ago, Sega sold more game machines than Sony and Nintendo combined. But for a number of reasons, few of them technical, Sega botched the introduction of its ill-fated Saturn system, Dreamcast's predecessor, allowing Sony and Nintendo to take over. Today Sega has less than a 2 percent share of the market, said Kelly Henry, an analyst with the International Data Corporation. Video game players appear willing to embrace whatever system gives them the most realistic thrills, and for the next year at least, that will be Dreamcast. Sega said more than 250,000 Dreamcast systems had been ordered in advance of today's nationwide rollout, and the company expects to sell 1 million systems by the end of this year. Even so, Sega has no illusions about toppling the market leaders. At best, the Dreamcast will keep Sega competitive for a while. It is no exaggeration to say that Dreamcast could be Sega's last chance to stay competitive with Sony, Nintendo and maybe even Microsoft, which has been exploring the idea of creating its own video console machine. (Microsoft is already one of the largest makers of computer games and game peripherals.) But if Sega has a year's head start on Sony and Nintendo in the 128-bit processor race, that also means that the Playstation II and Dolphin systems will be a year more advanced when they finally arrive in 2000. Sony has already demonstrated an Internet-enabled Playstation II prototype that is more powerful than Sega's Dreamcast while remaining backward-compatible with current Play station games. Nintendo's N2000 Dolphin system, like the Playstation II, will double as a DVD movie player. Sega says its Dreamcast system is designed to take advantage of new technologies that will be developed in the next year or two, but that may be whistling in the dark. A year from now, when Sony and Nintendo release their new systems, Dreamcast could be toast unless Sega can lock its customers into the Internet. The new Sega system has been transformed by the Internet. When attached to a phone line, the Dreamcast console can be used as an Internet terminal. Users can send and receive email, participate in chat groups or get game-playing tips on the Sega Dreamcast Online Gaming Network and browse the Web. Sega says Dreamcast users can connect through any Internet service provider, but it lists AT&T Worldnet as its preferred service and includes a Worldnet software disk. Basic AT&T service will cost $9.95 a month for 10 hours of Internet access, $19.95 for 150 hours of access and $21.95 a month for unlimited access. Those who sign up for either of the more expensive plans will get a free Dreamcast keyboard, for no-thumbs typing. One thing Dreamcast owners will not be able to do, however, is play games against one another over the Internet, a rather astonishing lapse in an otherwise impressive system. On-line games are one of the Internet's most popular activities. A Sega spokesman said the company would offer on-line competitive games in "the next 12 months or so." Until then, Dreamcast users can only taunt one another with email and chat. There's not much sport in that. At some point, however, the Dreamcast and its game-console rivals will emerge as network information devices, ready to slug it out with low-cost PC's, set-top boxes like Web TV, smart telephones and other information appliances. Let the games begin. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: FANTASY HARDWARE -- Sega's new Dreamcast console and controller. (pg. G3)  Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)(pg. G1)

title: Ford Loses Bid to Keep Documents Off Internet
body: Asserting that an Internet site has the same free-speech rights as newspapers and other traditional media, a Federal judge ruled here today that the Ford Motor Company could not stop the owner of the site from using information that he had gleaned from confidential Ford documents. Ford had requested a preliminary injunction barring Robert Lane, the owner of the Web site about the company, from using, copying or disclosing the documents, which Ford said contain trade secrets. But Judge Nancy G. Edmunds of Federal District Court ruled that free speech under the First Amendment took precedence over Ford's secrets. Newspapers and magazines have won cases over the years preventing corporations from exercising prior restraint on the publishing of information. Today's ruling adds to a small but growing collection of court rulings granting the same Constitutional protection to Web sites, said Mike Godwin, a lawyer specializing in free-speech issues on the Internet. "It's an important case because it further establishes the scope of First Amendment protections in cyberspace," Mr. Godwin said. The first cases involving prior restraint on the Internet were filed by the Church of Scientology in an effort to stop the electronic posting of church documents, Mr. Godwin said, adding that the church had prevailed in some cases and lost in others. Judge Edmunds couched her decision today in broad language, saying: "In the realm of law, we are only beginning to grapple with the impact of the communications revolution, and this case represents just one part of one skirmish -- a clash between our commitment to the freedom of speech and the press, and our dedication to the protection of commercial innovation and intellectual property. In this case, the battle is won by the First Amendment." Judge Edmunds did grant Ford a preliminary injunction barring Mr. Lane, a 32-year-old nursing student, from infringing on the company's copyrights. This might prevent Mr. Lane from posting Ford documents in their entirety on his Web site, as he had done until Ford sued him two weeks ago. But the copyright decision had little legal significance, several First Amendment lawyers said, because Mr. Lane's lawyer had already promised the court last week that his client would not post any more Ford documents on the site. Mr. Lane can write about the documents and quote them extensively without worrying about copyright issues, the lawyers added. Ford's lawsuit, accusing Mr. Lane of violating its trademarks, copyrights and trade secrets, is still pending and could result in financial damages against Mr. Lane. His lawyer, Mark Pickrell, also agreed in court last week that his client would tell Ford whatever he knew about who provided the documents. But Mr. Lane said in court he did not know who had mailed them to him or dropped them off at his home, so this agreement may not help Ford. Mr. Lane's site, which is called www.blueovalnews.com, is named for Ford's corporate logo, a blue oval with "Ford" inside. The site was started last year to provide news for Ford Mustang fans, but broadened this summer after Ford became critical of some of the news posted on it. Mr. Pickrell welcomed today's ruling as a victory for free speech. Ford said it was pleased that Mr. Lane's constitutional rights had been respected but also glad that its copyrights would be protected. Ford lawyers want to discuss the ruling with Mr. Pickrell, and have not yet decided whether to appeal, said Terry Bresnihan, a company spokesman. The case is particularly awkward for Ford because many of the secret documents say the company may someday be able to build automobiles, particularly sport utility vehicles, that emit less pollution and have better fuel efficiency than current models. Yet the company is lobbying against tighter emissions and fuel-economy regulations as unrealistic. The company builds the least polluting sports utility vehicles currently on the market, although not the most fuel-efficient. The Environmental Protection Agency has proposed new rules that would crack down on tailpipe emissions from sport utility vehicles in particular. Separately, the Senate is considering whether the Administration should be allowed to raise fuel-economy standards for sport utility vehicles, pickups and minivans. Mr. Bresnihan said today that the company had been frank in discussions with the Environmental Protection Agency about the feasibility of lower-emissions vehicles. Documents regarding fuel economy describe technologies that may not be feasible for technological and marketing reasons, he said. David Cohen, a spokesman for the environmental agency, declined to comment on the documents, but said, "We're convinced that the rules we've proposed and the final standard will be the toughest ever."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Lucent Introduces New Internet Voice Lines
body: Lucent Technologies Inc., a leading maker of telephone equipment, announced today a line of products that carry voice calls on high-speed Internet lines, eliminating the need for separate wires. The product, called Stinger, lets a phone company give voice calls on data lines higher priority than other information. The system is designed to insure the quality of the call is as good as on a regular voice network. Lucent's technology works with so-called digital subscriber lines. Those lines provide Internet access about 30 times faster than traditional dial-up modems and let phone companies combine several lines on one copper wire. By offering voice services over digital subscriber lines, phone companies can reduce the need for extra wiring for voice services. "What this is going to do is really allow (phone companies) to bring DSL to the masses," said Kevin Oye, Lucent's vice president of strategy and business development for data systems. Lucent shares rose $1.4375, to $67.50. The new product lets phone companies combine as many as 16 voice phone lines and Internet and data services on a single copper wire.
