Though data networks can carry more information than voice networks, equipment makers have had difficulty maintaining voice quality on data systems. Lucent's Stinger distinguishes voice from other information on the network with electronic tags, letting the network know to give voice calls priority. The technology could eventually be used to prioritize other information, such as offering first and second-class email, Lucent said. Lucent said about 20 customers were testing Stinger, which costs about $440 for each copper wire connected to it. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MAKING A MEDIA GIANT: THE MUSIC SCENE;
A New Force in Distributing Music Across the Internet
body: The proposed merger of Viacom Inc. and CBS would create a formidable force in the sale, distribution and promotion of music over the Internet, industry analysts said yesterday. The merger would marry Viacom's MTV Interactive, the parent of two popular Web sites, MTV.com and VH1.com, with the music properties of CBS, which include Country.com, one of the the most popular country-western music sites, and with 163 radio stations owned by CBS's Infinity Broadcasting subsidiary (though many of those are talk or news formats). For record companies, that translates into a union of two of the predominant sources of album promotion, namely, the powerful MTV brand and one of the nation's largest chains of radio stations, said Jordan E. Rohan, on-line media analyst at Wit Capital, an on-line investment bank in newyork. "If a company wants to promote, market and sell music on line, it needs to deal with the new Viacom," Mr. Rohan said. Mark Mooradian, an analyst with Jupiter Communications, a newyork-based market-research firm, said the merger could be a boon to the MTV brand in particular -- both on and off line. He said MTV's already tremendous influence over record companies could grow with access to CBS's television network, affiliate stations, radio presence and outdoor advertising. "MTV now has this unprecedented reach," he said. Nicholas Butterworth, president and chief executive of MTV Interactive, declined to comment on the potential benefits of the merger. However, at a news conference announcing the deal yesterday, the CBS chairman, Mel Karmazin, said the deal envisioned creating relationships between the CBS-owned country-western networks, CMT and TNN, and Viacom's MTV and VH1. In one aspect of music promotion, CBS thus far has been an Internet laggard: it has declined to make available over the Internet the audio from any of its 163 radio stations. It has stated repeatedly that it would not do so until it could find a profitable business model. Industry analysts said, however, that the merger offered some possible new business models given potential cross-marketing and sharing of content with the MTV brand. In fact, SonicNet.com, owned by Viacom, a music-news, information and technology company, assists radio stations in offering their programming over the Internet, in effect giving CBS strong in-house expertise. A CBS spokesman, Dana McClintock, said the day was drawing nearer when CBS would permit its stations to put its audio content on line. More generally, Viacom's chairman, Sumner M. Redstone, said he expected the new entity to be a formidable new media company. "We have 300 million worldwide households to drive traffic to all of our sites," he said, adding that while it was too early to give specifics, the company considered the Internet a strong part of the puzzle. "As we've already told the financial community, the Internet is not an add-on; it's a major giant new growth business." Mr. Mooradian said both companies have told Wall Street they intend to spin off parts of their Internet business in separate public offerings. During yesterday's news conference, Mr. Karmazin suggested those plans had not changed, alluding to Viacom's stated intention to spin off MTV Interactive in a public offering in the next year. The two companies own or have an interest in Web sites visited by millions of Internet users each month. According to Media Metrix, Viacom's sites, including the Nickelodeon sites, received 6.5 million unique visitors in July. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Mr. DeLay's New 'Killer' Tactic
body: With the House scheduled to vote on campaign finance reform this month, defenders of the corrupt status quo are up to some old tricks. The most pernicious is an attempt by Representative Tom DeLay, the Republican whip, to amend the Shays-Meehan soft-money ban by exempting certain political activities on the Internet from Federal election fund-raising laws. Mr. DeLay knows that his amendment has a certain superficial appeal for Internet users, many of whom reflexively oppose cyberspace infringements of any kind. But his approach would not simply gut Shays-Meehan. It would circumvent laws in existence for decades by opening new avenues for abuse. Repeating their performance of last year, Mr. DeLay and House Speaker Dennis Hastert know that they do not have the votes in the House to block a campaign cleanup. Scores of Republicans are prepared to join with nearly all the Democrats to pass the legislation, as they did before. So once again the opponents are throwing up several "killer amendments" that might undercut the legislation or force Democrats to vote against it. Mr. DeLay asserts that since "hate-mongers and pornographers" can freely use the Internet, campaign fund-raisers ought to be able to do so as well. But he is deliberately distorting the effects of the Shays-Meehan bill in order to scare people. Mr. DeLay charges that under both Shays-Meehan and existing law, "political discussion" through email and chat rooms would be "restricted and monitored" with requirements that anyone advocating a candidate's election disclose his or her identity. He contends that provisions under current law requiring that all campaign ads or brochures disclose the identity of the person paying for them would affect Internet users. But these disclosure requirements have not been interpreted as applying to the Internet or email, and the Shays-Meehan bill would not change that interpretation. In any case, the Federal Election Commission has begun studying the issue of how Federal campaign finance laws should apply to the Internet. That is the proper forum for addressing any potential problems. All these alleged concerns of Mr. DeLay are actually a smokescreen to weaken existing laws and introduce new channels for use of unlimited campaign funds. His amendment, for example, would allow corporations and unions to make campaign expenditures for ads on the Internet, which existing law forbids. It would also allow state political parties to circumvent existing limits on what they can spend for Presidential or Congressional candidates, as long as they spent the money on the Internet. House members should see Mr. DeLay's bill for what it is, a "killer amendment" that would turn the clock back. Other amendments to be offered by Republican foes of campaign reform are also designed to create mischief. Some would raise existing contribution limits, encourage special-interest money to flow to independent groups for use in campaign attack ads or place new restrictions on unions. Fortunately, House members are smart enough to see through these smokescreens. If they block these amendments, they can make campaign finance reform a reality at last. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Code-Cracking Project Shows Need for Stronger Locks
body: When an international team of researchers demonstrated recently that they could break the standard lock that protects financial transactions over the Internet, they sent a clear message to the E-commerce community: Now is the time to get stronger locks. The researchers showed only that locks of a certain strength, known as R.S.A. 512-bit encryption codes, could be broken. But it is precisely that code strength that is used for a number of the financial transactions with E-commerce sites on the Internet. The computing power used for the demonstration, while typically available only to governments or big corporations was insignificant compared with other code-cracking efforts, said Arjen Lenstra, one of the main researchers for the seven-month effort. Moore's Law, which says that computing power roughly doubles every 18 months, suggests that such power may someday be available to individuals. Even more important, improvements in the techniques used for factoring large numbers -- a process that enables R.S.A. codes to be cracked -- may reduce the computational resources required. "As soon as you break something then within a relatively short time, many people will be able to break it," said Mr. Lenstra, a computer scientist at Citigroup. "I have no doubt that within a few years it will be more or less a triviality." The Government has long restricted the export of strong encryption, citing concerns that it might be used to conceal messages or transactions by terrorists or drug traffickers. In the last year, because of market pressures, it has relaxed those standards somewhat for encryption products related to E-commerce, but the 512-bit standard remains prevalent among Web sites. "The level of security has been 512 for so long that it's still a part of the infrastructure," said David Wagner, a computer security researcher at the University of California at Berkeley. "It will be several years before this changes." The current export-control policy, which requires companies seeking to export encryption products to go through a one-time review, is so complex that many encryption experts, secure-software manufacturers, and Government officials interviewed for this article could not say how it applies to R.S.A. products. "The problem with the encryption policy is that the devil is in the details," said Roszel Thomsen, a lawyer specializing in export controls at Thomsen & Burke, a Washington law firm. "The policy has been drafted with a degree of ambiguity that is calculated to allow the regulators to make up their minds case by case." From the Government's perspective, "complicated is in the eye of the beholder," said William A. Reinsch, the Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration. "We're trying to pursue a balanced policy," he said. "I believe that the critics of our policy are those who do not believe that national security and law enforcement concerns are as important as we believe they are." Many security experts believe that encryption export standards have been tied to levels decipherable by the National Security Agency, whose research groups -- staffed with mathematicians -- devote enormous resources to code cracking. "Organizations could already be breaking E-commerce keys regularly, and just not telling anyone," said Bruce Schneier, chief technology officer of Counterpane Internet Security, a consulting company in San Jose, Calif. "I think there's a 100 percent chance the N.S.A. does this already; they would be remiss in their charter if they didn't." The researchers' actual feat was to factor a 155-digit number into its two component prime factors. The inherent difficulty of factoring, an immensely hard and time-consuming task for even the most powerful computers, provides the security for R.S.A. Factoring a certain large number associated with an R.S.A. key enables that key to be cracked. Named for its founders -- Ronald Rivest of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Adi Shamir of the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovoth, Israel, and Leonard Adleman of the University of Southern California -- R.S.A. is an example of what is known as an asymmetric or public-key system. Each merchant on the World Wide Web possesses a public R.S.A. key, which is listed in a public record, and a private key, which is known only to that merchant. When a message has been locked with a public key, only the private key can unlock it. This asymmetry of keys is essential for Internet transactions because unlike faster "symmetric key" methods of encryption, R.S.A. does not require that the sender and the receiver of an encrypted message meet to transfer a secret key. A secure Internet transaction, like a credit-card purchase, typically takes place in a protected tunnel temporarily established between a computer user's Web browser and an E-commerce site. This protected tunnel, designed by Netscape but now an Internet standard, is known as SSL, or Secure Socket Layer. Since R.S.A. encryption is very slow for long messages, the browser establishes the tunnel with a faster, symmetric key technique. But then the symmetric key must be securely transported to the E-commerce site. This transport depends on R.S.A. The transaction uses the strongest encryption that both the Web browser and the site support. To comply with the export controls, browsers come in both domestic and exportable versions. The exportable version, frequently shipped even with computers purchased in the unitedstates, is limited to 512-bit R.S.A. transactions except with certain authorized sites -- typically large banks or brokerage firms -- that have paid extra for stronger encryption capability. Government controls have been eased since January, enabling a larger class of sites to use 1,024-bit R.S.A. encryption -- considered secure by most experts -- in transactions with exportable browsers. But many restrictions still apply. The bigger problem, however, is that many Web sites are using 512-bit encryption for all their Web transactions, regardless of the type of browser. While new symmetric keys are generated for each individual transaction, the R.S.A. key for each individual site typically stays fixed for one year. This means that a time-consuming code-breaking effort has a huge payoff: Cracking a single R.S.A. key can potentially unlock a year's worth of transactions. "There is no legal reason that American companies should persist in using low-level encryption for their sites," Mr. Thomsen said, adding, "No one in their right minds should be using 512 today." And yet many major E-commerce sites, like Microsoft's and Gateway's on-line stores, still use 512-bit encryption for their Web transactions. While security software can be designed to allow easy upgrades to higher levels of encryption, the Government does not let manufacturers build this capability into their software, said Scott Schnell, senior vice president for marketing for R.S.A. Data Security and its parent, Security Dynamics Technologies. Thus, upgrading can be a costly process. Security Dynamics had $39 million in revenues from encryption software last year, accounting for 42 percent of the worldwide market, in addition to licensing the R.S.A. encryption algorithms to more than 500 other software makers. But Mr. Schnell said Federal export regulations had hurt R.S.A. severely in its sales abroad because "no one wants to buy weak encryption products." "I think we need a clear base line that makes 1,024 the standard for public key cryptography," he said. Even then, the pace at which cryptography standards will be broken may only increase. "In another 10 years, we can expect to make another jump of difficulty level," said Mr. Lenstra, the Citigroup computer scientist.  "It's always going to be a race." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Arjen Lenstra, a Citigroup computer scientist, worked on the encryption project. (Dith Pran/The newyork Times)  Chart: "A Weak Link in Internet Transactions" Commerce on the Internet requires a high-level of security. To provide that security, merchants and customers rely on a technology that uses a combination of two kinds of encryption keys to protect transactions. Here is how the system works and one way it is vulnerable.  1. Someone who wants to buy something over the Internet must fill out a form with personal information and provide a credit card number.  2. To protect the information, the form is encrypted. Because the file may contain a lot of data, the quickest way to encrypt it is to use a key, called a symmetric key, that is generated by the computer sending the file.  3. When a file has been encrypted using a symmetric key, anyone who obtains that key can open the file. To allow the merchant to open the data file, the symmetric key must be sent along with it.  4. To protect the symmetric key, it is encrypted using a public key published on the Internet by the merchant. The public key is usually part of the solution to a math problem.  5. When the encrypted files arrive, the merchant uses his private key, which contains the rest of the math problem's solution, to unlock the encrypted symmetric key and then uses that key to unlock the data file.  HOW THE SYSTEM IS VULNERABLE -- If the problem used to generate the public and private keys is not sufficiently difficult, it is possible to figure out the what the private key is using the published public key. Someone who did that could then intercept and open all files intended for the merchant. (pg. D2)

title: Internet Wars
body: With each new technological advance, the Internet beckons as a rich and competitive playing field for business, communication and entertainment. One of the most promising recent innovations is high-speed Internet access through upgraded cable television lines. Before long, these lines are expected to offer a nearly limitless variety of television programs, movies, music, face-to-face telephones, commercial transactions and other interactive services. But that lucrative prospect has produced a battle royal in cyberspace. It revolves around AT&T's acquisition of major cable systems as well as its big stake in Excite@Home, an Internet service provider that would give AT&T customers access to the World Wide Web. The fear is that by controlling both the cable and the avenue to the Internet, AT&T can dictate where users can go and what to buy. The alarms are understandable. America Online, with more than 18 million customers, has joined with other Internet companies and consumer groups to warn that they all could get shut out if AT&T gains an Internet stranglehold, or be forced to pay high fees to AT&T to reach potential customers. Similar concerns have been raised over Time Warner's plans for its cable lines. The critics want the Federal Communications Commission to require AT&T and Time Warner to grant equal access to America Online and other companies that provide Internet services. For now, the commission has demurred, and rightly so. As William Kennard, the F.C.C. chairman, has said, it seems premature to impose rules on cable Internet access to head off a problem that does not yet exist in a market that has not yet developed. The F.C.C. is also right to try to block localities from imposing restrictions. Whether consumers will have a choice other than cable monopolies like AT&T and Time Warner will depend on the emergence of other high-speed technologies. Local telephone companies have begun to upgrade their service with a technology known as digital subscriber lines, or D.S.L., which could compete with cable. They may not have acted so quickly if it were not for the threat of AT&T and Time Warner. Satellite and wireless communications might also provide consumers with another way to tap into the Internet. America Online points out that these alternatives to cable are only in formative stages. But the interest of consumers is served by letting all these technologies develop and taking regulatory action only if they fail to provide adequate competition. The Internet's future and its prosperity clearly depend on the principle of maintaining open access for all competitors. This principle has led the Justice Department to block Microsoft from using its operating system monopoly to force consumers to use its browser as the sole means to surf the Web. With 130 million users around the world, the Internet is driving a major part of the American economy. The question now becomes whether cable systems, which are inherently monopolistic enterprises that traditionally belong to the companies that built and paid for them, become so dominant that they will restrict consumer choices in getting news, watching programs or buying products. In monitoring AT&T and Time Warner as they venture more and more into cable Internet services, the F.C.C. should not let down its guard. Even though cable systems are not now regulated, as telephone lines are, the F.C.C. should insure competition and open access in the future. For now, it is best for the F.C.C. to wait and see how the new world unfolds before trying to set rigid rules for it. But if AT&T and Time Warner do not exercise some self-restraint and act like good citizens, allowing fair access for America Online and other Internet service providers with a legitimate service to offer, they will find themselves subjected to demands for regulation by the F.C.C. and local communities. It is in their interest to preserve the open spirit of the Internet. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Patents;
For people with only one telephone line, a way of routing incoming calls to a Web site.
body: FOR the last few years, telephone companies throughout the country have been busy adding new area codes to metropolitan regions to accommodate the rising demand for new phone numbers. In Seattle, where for decades one area code covered the area, there are now three. Callers in the two new areas must dial 10 digits for every call, and so must people in the city who phone the suburbs. Many of these new area-code calls are now billed as long-distance calls. It is a cumbersome solution to the threat of running out of phone numbers altogether, as more people demand separate lines for their telephones, faxes and modems. After all, you cannot receive calls if your line is tied up on the Internet. Now, three Swedish inventors have won a patent for an invention that aims to ease such congestion and perhaps eliminate the need for costly multiple lines. Their invention routes conventional telephone calls to a World Wide Web site that then notifies a user of an incoming phone call in much the same way that email systems report that a person has new mail. The three -- Anders Danne, Goran Bangge and Hans Hall -- have designed a system in which a window pops up on a computer screen to notify a user that a call is coming in over the telephone line; the window comes with buttons that the user can click on to answer the phone, ignore the call, put the caller on hold, take a message or redirect the call elsewhere. But first, potential users must subscribe to the system. Then, incoming calls are routed through a phone network where information about the person calling is deciphered from their phone number. That information might include the caller's name, a company name or an address. The network then determines whether the person being called is a paid-up subscriber. If so, software in the system activates a connection with a Web site and sends an alert message to the subscriber's personal computer. The window would also incorporate caller I.D. technology to include information about the caller so that anyone using his phone line to surf the Internet could decide whether or not to take the call without first logging off. The invention won patent number 5,946,381.  Death Is Transitory, But Software Is Eternal Move over, Ouija board. Making contact with the afterlife has gone digital. Lynn Svevad, an inventor in Holland, Mich., has patented a computer program called "Forever By My Side," and with it, anyone can hold a conversation with dead relatives or friends -- as long as they don't mind that the responses are prerecorded. Ms. Svevad has written software that lets the living call up images of the deceased, complete with voice and motion, using material that would have been collected while the person was still alive. Details like personality and mannerisms can be added. After that is complete, Ms. Svevad allows the living to choose from three levels of communication with the dead: basic, intermediate and advanced. Hoping to speak with your late great-grandma? First click on her downloaded image, then say "hi" into the computer microphone. The greeting is digitized, and the computer takes over, "relating said spoken electronic format to an appropriate response by said selected deceased relative or friend," Ms. Svevad explains in her patent. In other words, the computer picks great-grandma's response and the mannerism (a pinch on the cheek?) that it deems likely of her. Repeat Steps 1 through 4 over and over, and viola, you're talking to the dead. As a bonus, Ms. Svevad's software can also be programmed to remember special occasions. So even if great-grandma passed away years ago, she can still greet you on your birthday with cheery best wishes. Ms. Svevad received patent number 5,946,657. Patents may be viewed on the World Wide Web at www.uspto.gov or may be ordered through themail, by patent number, for $3 from the Patent and Trademark Office, Washington, D.C. 20231 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY: E-Commerce Report;
Some on-line retailers are finding that customer reviews of products can help build loyalty to a site -- and sales.
body: E-COMMERCE companies fill their sites with reviews of products they sell, reviews that are generally taken from marketers or magazines. But they know that consumers often give more credence to the opinions of "real people" -- friends or peers who buy similar products. The problem for Internet retailers is how to harness the opinions of those real people without letting the negative comments chase prospective buyers away. The solution, some E-commerce companies are finding, is to allow customers to have their say, and hope that it ultimately builds sales. "There is a role for this kind of voice on the Net," said Barry Parr, an analyst with the International Data Corporation, a research firm. "You need to wear your filters when you read them, but you can glean some really useful information." The practice of posting customer reviews started at Amazon.com, which began its reader reviews when it started its on-line bookstore in July 1995. In addition to including excerpts from published reviews, the site allowed readers to rate books on a five-star scale, and to post comments of their own. At the time, such reviews were a novelty because on-line stores generally relied on authoritative third parties, like professional book reviewers, to help readers decide what to buy. "When we introduced it, people asked, 'If your goal is to sell products, how can you allow it?' " said Paul Capelli, an Amazon spokesman. "But it's been a very effective tool to get attention and move product." For example, he said, a recent novel, "Lip Service" by M. J. Rose, failed to attract a publisher, but Ms. Rose published the book on her own and offered it for sale on Amazon. It was reviewed so favorably by Amazon users that it entered the site's Top 100 list. The author was then signed by Pocket Books, a unit of the Simon & Schuster division of Pearson P.L.C. When the book was re-released, it was among Amazon's top 5 best sellers during a recent week. "The customer reviews were driving her sales," Mr. Capelli said. The book's success is no longer limited to Amazon; it is now moving well on Barnesandnoble.com, where it ranks in the current top 100 sellers. Following Amazon's lead, other on-line retailers have instituted programs that allow buyers to rate products. For sellers of computers and other high-priced goods, posting customer reviews is an even greater departure from the retail norm, analysts and executives said, because many established sources offer advice on buying these products. Indeed, an entire publishing industry has been built on giving computer buyers authoritative advice. NECX Direct, an Internet computer and electronics retailer that began posting customer reviews of products two years ago, says such reviews augment buying guides from publishers. "This is a very potent motivator for helping people decide what to buy," said Keith Halloran, the company's director of marketing. "In the end, sales are made by the testimony of real users, not rebate offers or what PC Magazine says." Mr. Halloran said the site could afford to risk turning customers away from certain products because, like many other Internet retailers, NECX does not carry its own inventory. Rather, when a customer places an order, NECX has the product delivered directly from a distributor. So even if a customer is turned away from one product, he said, the company offers enough products in each category to make sales likely. "If the customers say, 'It's a bad product; you shouldn't buy it,' we don't lose because we don't hold anything in stock," he said. "So we print everything -- the good, the bad and the ugly." Provided it's not too ugly. Mr. Halloran said NECX edited customer reviews for profanity "or transparent efforts to discredit manufacturers," and also watched for obvious boosterism from manufacturers. "I'm sure that happens," he said, "but most reputable manufacturers refrain from it." Mr. Parr of the International Data Corporation said that even if such reviews failed to help sales, they could still serve an important purpose: increasing the reviewer's loyalty to the site. "People who are big contributors to reviews tend to have a sense of ownership," he said. "It gives them a sense of status in a place that really matters to them, and it's pretty hard to place a price tag on that." Notably, the trend toward using customer reviews is also being embraced by publishers that have built their businesses on offering objective, often lab-tested, reviews. Consumer Reports, published by Consumers Union, recently said it would publish reviews of E-commerce Web sites from Bizrate.com, a company that compiles customer feedback. And Cnet, an Internet company that publishes reviews of computer products, recently began posting readers' comments about products. Alice Hill, editorial director for Cnet, said that the decision was not easy: "It took some letting go of that attitude that you're the editor, saying, 'This is all you need to know.' " Ms. Hill said that the service, which allows readers to submit a "thumbs up" or "thumbs down" review alongside their comments, has even helped the site's professional reviewers, who test products in a laboratory environment. For instance, she said, Cnet editors recently confirmed a flaw in a digital camera's lens cover after customers pointed out the problem. "So this gives us a volume approach as well as a lab approach," she said. Though the number of sites offering customer reviews is growing, analysts said one important on-line type -- manufacturers that sell directly to consumers -- would not soon join the trend. "Companies are so protective of their brands and image, it would be hard to imagine any of them taking that kind of risk," Mr. Parr said, referring to companies like Nike and Compaq Computer. Among manufacturers that sell directly to consumers, Dell Computer comes the closest to offering customer reviews. In the Talk Forum section of its site, Dell lets readers post questions or speak their minds about products they have bought. Manish Mehta, senior manager for on-line support, said that the company edited only offensive, profane remarks. "The fact that you can absolutely slam Dell frees up people to be open," he said. Dell, Mr. Mehta said, would be reluctant to post reviews in areas of its site where shoppers are poised to buy. "Conversion is so critical in E-commerce," he said. "When you finally get customers to select a product, to introduce something that might cause them to abandon a purchase would not be a good thing." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: NECX Direct has let customers post their reviews on its World Wide Web site for about two years.

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
Click Here For Art
body: Founded nearly 20 years ago by Philippa de Menil and Heiner Friedrich, the Dia Center for the Arts had a mission from its inception to support art that might be too unorthodox for other arts organizations, including multimedia and electronic work. It is only a hop, skip and a jump from working with mixed media to the Web, which has similar conceptual, technical and esthetic problems. The Dia Center's Web site, started in 1995, has two purposes. One is to give information about the nonprofit arts center, whose main location is 548 West 22d Street in Chelsea. Visitors can find schedules for exhibitions, readings and forums, and photographs of past and current shows. The site is also an exhibition space for artists who work on the Web. "It's not a prerequisite to be familiar with technology," said Sara Tucker, the Dia Center's director of digital media, referring to the criteria for choosing artists for the site. "What has happened over time is that we've invited artists who didn't have experience with the medium. And using that approach, we've found that we've had surprising and interesting results." WHAT YOU SEE: A section called "Artists' Web Projects" features 11 works, including "The Thief" by Francis Alys, a loop of an ominous shadowy figure entering a window, which Ms. Tucker says is a metaphor for the anxiety that people have as they confront the windows of computers. There is also "Almost Home," a set of witty video diptychs, part Disney, part Salvador Dali, by Arturo Herrera, that evoke slot machines. (The prize is the waggish combinations a viewer can create, not a pocketful of nickels.) In "Between a Rock and a Hard Drive," Kristin Lucas's series of nearly 40 typewriter keyboards, surrounding images of waiting rooms, allows visitors to click on the keys and receive words, phrases and noises. If you don't get it at first, each artwork is accompanied by a lucid and illuminating introduction, usually by Dia's curator, Lynne Cooke. The Web site also offers contemporary poetry from its series of readings, which you can find under "Programs and Events." Audio recordings are available for the center's 1987-88 poetry season, whose participants included Seamus Heaney, John Ashbery, Amy Clampitt and Robert Hass. More readings are to be made available in the future. LINKS: To Stadium@Dia, a separate organization affiliated with the Dia Center that offers its own Web art projects. WHAT YOU GET: A periscopic look into exhibition spaces of the future. ERIC V. COPAGE  DIA CENTER FOR THE ARTS www.diacenter.org http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos.

title:
SENIORITY;
Grandma's Guide to the Web
body: FOR Betty Fox of Bayside, Queens, 1998 got off to a bad start. In February, Mrs. Fox, now 69, retired when her employer, a medical billing company, relocated. To help her avoid boredom, her older son, Marty, set her up with WebTV so she could surf the Internet on her television set. That led to more frustration for Mrs. Fox, who knew little about computers and nothing about the Web. Her first on-line visit was to search for a new recipe for peach pie. She typed "peaches" into a search engine and came up with 85,870 pages. That was fun, at least at first. "I felt like I had just won at bingo," she said. Her elation soon turned to disbelief, however, when she found that she had called up far more than she had bargained for, including pornographic sites involving women named Peaches. She also found sites having to do with peach wholesalers in South America. Then she decided to search for sites that would be of help to "seniors." The search engine turned up some useful sites, but also thousands of others, many involving high school and college seniors. Mrs. Fox, who has a penchant for alphabetized lists, was appalled at the disorder and imprecision of the on-line world. And she suspected that she was not the only older person struggling to cope with it. "I just knew there had to be a better way," she said. "Especially for people like me who didn't know Internet from schminternet. Everything seemed such a hodgepodge." So Mrs. Fox, a widow and grandmother, decided to take action. With the help of the son who had given her the WebTV and works in the technology field, she started her own site (www.grandmabetty.com) for people over 50. It went on line in September 1998 and contains original material plus hundred of links to other sites, all selected by Mrs. Fox based on what she thinks are its visitors' interests. To be sure, there are many commercial, nonprofit and Governmental Web sites for older people, run by entities as diverse as AARP (www.aarp.org) and Microsoft (www.microsoft.com/seniors). But for scope, ease of use and relevance, few sites can match grandmabetty.com. Not to mention orderliness and precision. The site can send you directly to the pie recipes, without the pornography. The home page displays a photograph of her holding her grandson, David, when he was a baby. Above it is a list of areas on the site, including "Ask Grandma," where people can send her email. Another, called Sponsors, invites ads for the site, but Mrs. Fox has since decided that she will not accept advertising; she wants her site -- essentially her hobby -- to be objective, although, of course, many links contain ads. She says she has turned down advertising for products like vitamins and promotions for sites selling Viagra. Most of the site's categories offer very good lists of links. Under investing, there are links to scores of sites, from American Express to Ziegler Thrift Trading, an on-line brokerage firm. Other categories include entertainment, government, health, travel, magazines, memorabilia, news and weather. There's even a way to find winning lottery numbers in the various states. "Government" will take you from the Administration on Aging all the way to the White House. Fred B. Chernow, 67, a retired school principal and author of "The Sharper Mind" (Prentice-Hall), a book about memory improvement, found the site while exploring the Web and likes it because it address common problems. "There are always suggestions for things to do," said Mr. Chernow, who lives in Westbury, N.Y. "It's a great antidote for loneliness." Mrs. Fox says her site has about 150 visitors a day, a small number compared with many popular sites but a sign of the Web's reach. She gets about 30 email messages a day and answers them all, but she won't give legal, medical or financial advice. She still manages grandmabetty.com from her Queens apartment, using her WebTV device, and would like to expand the site to include features like chat rooms. "But right now, I'm keeping it at a level I'm comfortable with," she said. "It's a starting point for seniors who want to go on line." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Betty Fox and her grandson, David, in 1991.

title: Intrusions on Electronic Privacy
body: In trying to prevent criminals from using new electronic technologies in illegal activities, the Clinton Administration has been deaf to the privacy concerns of law-abiding citizens. The Justice Department argues that electronic surveillance by the Government would hurt only those involved in crime, not the law-abiding citizen. But erosions of privacy affect all Americans. As more people use computers and new technology to communicate and conduct business, balancing the need to protect electronic privacy against law enforcement requirements is crucial. Two recent examples show the Administration's failure to achieve a good balance. The Justice Department has drafted legislation that would authorize Federal law enforcement officers, with court-approved warrants, to secretly enter a suspect's home or office to disable encryption programs on their personal computers or install devices that can allow investigators to read the encrypted text. The intent is to thwart the ability of criminals to conceal information. But the threat to civil liberties may become substantial as encryption on personal computers becomes common. Under current wiretap law, law enforcement agencies can seek court authorization to tap phone lines or to place hidden microphones in private buildings. More than 1,000 wiretaps are approved by courts annually, though requests for warrants to use hidden microphones are rare. Civil liberties groups are worried that surreptitious entry would become far more common if the disabling of encryption were to become standard practice whenever a suspect is thought to use a computer. Last week the Federal Communications Commission, at the urging of the Justice Department, adopted new rules making it easier for law enforcement agencies to monitor the movement of callers using cellular phones. The regulations require that phone companies be capable of providing general location information at the beginning and end of any cellular call under surveillance with a court order. Turning cell phones into tracking devices is an unwarranted expansion of surveillance power. The new requirements would also give government agents the ability, applying to both cell phones and ordinary phones, to continue monitoring conference calls even after the surveillance target drops off the call and allow them to determine whether a suspect is using features like call forwarding and call waiting. Each of these changes may appear limited in scope. But taken together, these policies unduly erode privacy protections in the electronic realm. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Auction for a Kidney Pops Up on Ebay's Site
body: Bidding for a human kidney, described on the Internet auction site Ebay as "fully functional," began at $25,000 and reached $5,750,100 before the company abruptly ended the auction yesterday afternoon. In the pantheon of bizarre items that Internet users offer for sale on Ebay -- host to about 2.6 million auctions a day -- human organs are forbidden. To buy or sell them is a felony under Federal law, and trading in illegal goods is a violation of Ebay's rules. A second kidney auction was posted yesterday afternoon starting at $4 million but had not received any bids, The Associated Press reported. Chances are the auction, and the second posting, were jokes. But whether or not the offers were real, the incidents underscore the ease with which the Internet enables transactions of any kind, regardless of social custom or law. "A market is just a buyer and a seller and the thing they're transacting, and the Internet allows anyone to meet up with anyone," said Kevin Werbach, managing editor of the technology industry newsletter Release 1.0. "If you could get something through a normal channel and there was sufficient supply, you probably wouldn't go to Ebay." Steve Westly, Ebay's vice president for marketing and business development, said yesterday that the company was working with law-enforcement officials to insure that no illegal transactions occurred. "Ebay has zero tolerance for illegal items on the site," Mr. Westly said. "We do not know whether this was a prank or real, but what people should know is we treat this very seriously." Earlier this year, after users had posted auctions for a missile, a rocket launcher and other military weapons, whose sale among civilians is generally illegal, Ebay, based in San Jose, Calif., banned the sale of guns and ammunition on the site. The company has no automatic screening mechanism for items that it deems unacceptable. The kidney seller, identified as "hchero" of Sunrise, Fla., put a $25,000 floor on the bidding when he made his offer, last week. "You can choose either kidney," he wrote in his description. "Buyer pays all transplant and medical costs. Of course only one for sale, as I need the other one to live. Serious bids only." The National Organ Transplant Act, enacted in 1984, makes the sale or purchase of human organs punishable by up to five years in prison or a $50,000 fine. And while the Internet can bring together invisible buyers and sellers in the ether, the actual transplant of an organ requires a real-world hospital and corporeal surgeons. "You can't do an organ transplant on the sly," said Henry Greely, a law professor at Stanford University who specializes in bioethics. "You need a host of professional intermediaries before this could happen." Still, if such a sale took place through an Internet site not based in the unitedstates, it might raise jurisdictional questions, Professor Greely added. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Names New Leaders For Troubled Net Business
body: Searching for a way to revive its beleaguered Internet business, the Microsoft Corporation named a new leadership team for its on-line group yesterday and indicated that it would emphasize its technology underpinnings and continue to move away from a media strategy. As anticipated, the company named Richard Belluzzo, a longtime Silicon Valley hardware executive, as the new head of its Consumer and Commerce Group. Mr. Belluzzo, who resigned last month as chairman and chief executive of Silicon Graphics Inc. after a failed turnaround effort at that struggling work station company, will report directly to Microsoft's president, Steven Ballmer, as group vice president for the company's Internet business. The two longtime employees who have been leading the group, Brad Chase and Jon DeVaan, have been promoted to the position of senior vice president, Mr. Ballmer said. Mr. Ballmer declined to give significant details about the company's strategy for catching America Online, the dominant Internet service provider, and AT&T, whose Internet business, Worldnet, is also larger than Microsoft's service, MSN. But he did give several hints about the direction the company would take. "We're going to focus on fewer things and do those things well," he said. "We're going to be unabashed about technology. We're not a media company although we will develop media style skills." Analysts said Mr. Ballmer had been focusing on technology and on controlling expenses to rein in the division's losses, estimated at $500 million to $700 million a year. "What really struck me today is when Steve said Microsoft was going to rely on its strength as a technology company," said David Readerman, a managing director at Thomas Weisel & Partners, a San Francisco investment firm. "The decision to bring Belluzzo was the defining element in that direction." For his part Mr. Belluzzo, who helped build Hewlett-Packard's laser printer business as a longtime executive there, said he would rely on his strengths in consumer businesses and his ability to master the Internet's "changing business models." In response to questions, Mr. Ballmer appeared to step toward closing the door on issuing a so-called tracking stock that would reflect the value of the company's Internet business, saying that although a final decision had not been made, there were no such plans. Mr. Ballmer also acknowledged that a string of security flaws that have plagued Microsoft in recent months -- including an episode this week in which instructions were spread on the Internet for breaking into accounts on its free email service, Hotmail -- had hurt the company's Internet brand. "It's never good when your products fail to to do what consumers want," he said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Click Here for the Ivory Tower
body: FOR almost as long as students have been going to college, educators have been trying to bring college home to them. More than 100 years ago at Cornell University, professors traveled to rural areas on horseback to teach farmers about the latest agricultural research. Correspondence courses have been available for decades, first through themail and then through television and video. But the development of the Internet has created new excitement around what has become known as distance learning. This summer a start-up company called Unext.com (www.unext.com), based in Deerfield, Ill., announced a venture that is one of the most ambitious yet: delivering executive training and, eventually, a full M.B.A. program over the Internet. This summer, Unext.com (pronounced you-next) christened its virtual school Cardean University after a Roman goddess, Cardea, who could "open what is shut and shut what is open," in the words of a company press release. The plan attracted attention not only because one of the initial investors was the former junk-bond king, Michael R. Milken, but because of the five prestigious institutions the company had brought on board -- the University of Chicago, Columbia University, Carnegie Mellon University, Stanford University and the London School of Economics and Political Science -- a veritable all-star team of elite universities. The plan is for Unext.com to produce, market and distribute the courses -- as well as hire a corps of employees to serve as mentors and email correspondents for Cardean's students. The universities will provide the curriculum and the impressive credentials, without risking their endowments on untried technology. Some of them have projected that their own campuses will each earn at least $20 million in royalties from Unext.com within five to eight years. "This is a way to embark on distance education by using what others bring to it," said John Preis, associate dean for finance and administration at Columbia University's School of Business. "We think this is a home run." Distance learning, it seems, has come of age. But has it? Since the dawn of the Web in the mid-1990's, the concept of earning degrees entirely on line has become a rallying point for university presidents, politicians and profit-seekers alike. Yet while millions of people are diving into on-line shopping malls and chat rooms, virtual universities have been something of a bust. "I think it's going to be the joke of the 21st century," said Carole S. Fungaroli, an adjunct professor in English at Georgetown University who is writing a book about the value of university degrees. "I don't see anything that these people are offering that you can't get better on campus." Western Governors University, a venture started by 17 states and Guam, opened its on-line doors to much fanfare last year but has enrolled only 120 students, far below its projections. California Virtual University, a project initiated by the California Board of Regents in 1997, folded this spring, citing financial problems. Many other virtual university projects have appeared to be nothing more than on-line catalogues of courses that can be taken for credit only by students who are already on campus. One place the distance education concept has been successful is Wall Street, where analysts' reports are thick with data on the rapidly growing adult-student market. The Apollo Group, the company that runs the University of Phoenix, an accredited institution that offers on-line degrees, has seen its stock soar more than 1,500 percent since 1994. Apollo, which also operates other educational programs, now has a market capitalization of $1.7 billion. Administrators at the universities that have signed up with Unext.com readily admit that the possibility of becoming part-owners of a publicly traded Internet company is a part of Unext.com's attraction. "I was less interested in the income stream than in the market capitalization of Unext.com," Meyer Feldberg, dean of the Columbia University School of Business, told The Wall Street Journal. "The huge upside essentially is the value of the equity in the I.P.O." There have been other concerns raised about Unext.com. The management of the company is made up of several Chicago professors, including John P. Gould, a former dean of the university's Graduate School of Business, and two Nobel laureates, Gary Becker and Merton H. Miller. Several other members of the Chicago faculty have publicly raised questions about conflicts of interest. Whose interests will be served, the company's or the institutions that need to protect their good names and academic integrity? The entrepreneur behind Unext.com is Andrew M. Rosenfield, a business consultant and University of Chicago alumnus who was running Lexecon, a company that employed many of the same people who are now involved in Unext.com. In the last decade, he has also served as a part-time law professor and trustee for the university, remaining immersed in the culture of an institution known not only for breeding free-market intellectuals but also for being strongly resistant to change. In the mid-1990's, Mr. Rosenfield started thinking about about creating an Internet-based education company that would be both a radical departure and a continuation of the values of his alma mater. He wanted to create an on-line environment that would be "the technological equivalent of the small break-out session or the evening at the coffee shop, where students really teach each other." He also wanted to reach students outside the unitedstates who wanted access to education delivered by American universities but who could not travel to get it. He mulled over the idea with Dr. Becker -- his former professor and now longtime friend, who had won his Nobel prize for his theories about human capital. The two brainstormed over lunch at the University of Chicago's faculty club and while watching Chicago Bulls games. The first investor for the company, which was founded in December 1997, was Knowledge Universe, a company owned in part by Mr. Milken. His involvement stirred gossip throughout the higher-education community last year, when Mr. Rosenfield started to shop his idea around to select universities. By the time Mr. Rosenfield signed up his first partner -- Columbia University, in March 1999 -- the contracts included the condition that Mr. Milken's investment would never exceed a 20 percent ownership stake and that he would have no voting rights. In the last four months, four more universities have signed on; the last was Carnegie Mellon, which struck a deal in July. Other universities, like Cornell, were approached by Unext.com to be pioneering members but declined. Cornell has already developed its own distance-education technology, said Jonathon D. Levy, executive director of Cornell's distance-education office. Critics say that the partnership could damage the universities' academic credibility. The quality associated with getting a degree from these schools cannot be replicated on the Internet, said John K. Wilson, an outspoken graduate student at the University of Chicago who has written columns accusing administrators of jumping in blindly with "dollar signs in their eyes." University administrators have responded vaguely to questions about how much the deals may be worth. Mr. Preis, at Columbia University, confirmed reports that his institution expected to make at least $20 million in five to eight years. Other university administrators said they expected the same return. But Unext.com would not confirm the $20 million figure. "That's the universities' expectation," said Edwin Eisendrath, the spokesman for Unext.com. Mr. Eisendrath added that not every university had signed the same deal. He would not elaborate. Within the business faculties themselves, the reaction to the announced deals has ranged from approval to confusion. Administrators at some of the participating schools have pleaded ignorance about exactly what the deal means and who will be affected. At the University of Chicago, a committee was formed to talk about Unext.com before the deal was signed, but at Columbia University, most professors had not heard of the proposal before they awoke to an announcement of the deal. In Carnegie Mellon's case, a Chicago public relations firm sent out an announcement about the university's involvement before the university's press office had a chance to see the release and fix a large error. The announcement said Carnegie Mellon would offer courses in E-commerce courses through Unext.com, but the dean of the Graduate School of Industrial Administration, Douglas M. Dunn, said it had no plans to do so. The university, Dr. Dunn said, is still negotiating over exactly which courses Carnegie Mellon will help create. Meanwhile, some professors are wondering what involvement with Unext.com will mean to their scholarly reputations, the coin of the realm in the academic world. Robert Connolly, a professor in the Kenan-Flagler Business School at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, has worked with another distance-education company, called University Access, to create several economics courses using the Web and videotape. The experience, he said, has improved his teaching skills but hurt his standing in his department. "I can't get people in my own school to talk to me about it," Mr. Connolly said. Colleagues who have been willing to acknowledge his distance-education work expect that his research -- a professor's ticket to tenure -- must be suffering, he said. "They look at it and say, 'If you are spending time on that, that takes time away from your research and publishing.' " The American Association of University Professors has also asked questions about teaching quality in distance education courses. Last spring, when an on-line university called Jones International University became the first completely Internet-based school to gain accreditation, the association wrote a letter of protest to the accrediting agency. The letter cited "major worries about the denigration of quality" that could come with on-line education. Most distance-education courses are not cheap either. The Caliber Learning Network, a company based in Baltimore, persuaded three universities -- the University of Pennsylvania, Johns Hopkins University and the University of Southern California -- to join it in offering business courses via satellite television and the Internet. Tuition is high; students who take the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton Direct program pay $2,500 each for six-week courses. Most of the students can afford to attend, said Alison Pierce, Wharton Direct's director, because they are already in upper-income brackets and the companies for which they work pick up most of the tab. While Unext.com expects to benefit from companies' tuition-reimbursement programs as well, it will offer lower tuition prices, Mr. Rosenfield said. The company has not yet set its prices, but the cost of an Internet-based education, he said, should not be more than that of attending schools in person. Still, critics ask, what will a degree from Cardean University be worth? Dr. Fungaroli has called such on-line programs "a new version of a trade school." And students who enroll in M.B.A. programs from Stanford or the University of Chicago, Mr. Wilson argued, are doing so to build networks of contacts. "There is a real question about whether the 'good old boys' network' can be created in the same way it is created in elite business schools," he said. But International Business Machines, Unext.Com's first customer, is willing to give the concept a try as a way to encourage their employees to learn without losing them to on-campus business schools. I.B.M. will offer its employees a finance course this year. It is also a partner in the Unext.com venture; the courses are being delivered through Lotus Learning Space, software developed by Lotus, an I.B.M. subsidiary. Mr. Rosenfield admits that Unext.com does not plan to offer a full M.B.A. on line for years. Until then, the company will focus on executive training. Unext.com is not being structured to attempt to compete with what universities are already offering on campus, Mr. Rosenfield said. In fact, Mr. Rosenfield himself calls on-campus education the best way to learn.  "For people who have the ability to attend facilities-based schools, we recommend it," he said. But, he asked, why not also attempt to create a worthwhile experience for people who cannot attend those schools? "They will not have direct interaction," he continued, "but what they will have is the wisdom of professors and pieces of their knowledge that are captured and scalable. And they will have supporting resources and mentors who are their guides." So would Mr. Rosenfield take these courses? "Absolutely," he said. "The days when you ended your education at college, or graduate school, are truly over." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Carole S. Fungaroli, who is writing a book on the value of college degrees, is a critic of virtual colleges. (Shana Raab for The New York Times)(pg. G9); ENTREPENEUR -- Andrew M. Rosenfield of Unext.com, an ambitious venture in Net-based teaching. (Todd Buchanan for The New York Times)(pg. G1)

title:
DOWNTIME;
Capturing Not-So-Still Life: Webcams in Many Flavors
body: SPAM decomposing on a plate, penguins falling on their faces and a cubicle dweller coping with day-to-day office life: Webcams have brought out an odd combination of the voyeur and exhibitionist. "Cam," like .com, has become a trendy technological suffix for sites like the Spam Cam (www.fright.com/spam/spamcam.html), the Penguincam (www.discovery.com/cams/penguin/penguinmain.html) and the Davecam (ranier.oact.hq.nasa.gov/staff/davecam.shtm). There is Kremlinkam, Fogcam, Trafficam. Animals, in particular, seem to draw large Internet audiences to sites like Puppy Cam, Catcam, Sharkcam. They are overshadowed only by webcams that cater to voyeurs, like the well-known Jennicam. Last year there was Monicacam, which surveyed the building office doors of Monica Lewinsky's lawyer. Prices for Webcams have become reasonable; rebates and discounts available for many models can bring the cost of Webcams down sharply from list prices. For less than $100 and a dial-up Internet connection, home computer users can set up their own cameras, hook them up to the World Wide Web and become one-person broadcast studios. Jennifer Ringley, of Jennicam fame, uses four Webcams for her broadcasts, including a Connectix Quickcam Pro, a model now sold under the Logitech name. That model was also featured in a pivotal scene in the recent movie "American Pie." More than 1,000 Webcams are sold each day, according to NPD Intelect, a market tracking firm in Port Washington, N.Y. All Webcams on the market can take single shots and can record digital video. Single shots can be used to update Web pages, can be sent via email to friends and relatives or can be manipulated in photo editing programs. Digital video feeds allow business executives and families to talk over the Internet, emulating the futuristic videophones in the "Jetsons" cartoons. Webcams with motion sensor capabilities have also found a niche as security devices for computers -- you leave it on and if someone moves nearby it captures the image. The market leader for home Webcams is Logitech, which has models compatible with Macs and personal computers. Other large manufacturers are Panasonic, Creative Labs, Intel and Kodak; all of them sell Webcams in the $80-to-$130 price range, mostly for PC's. The brand-name companies are popular because of their warranties and level of technical support, but low-cost cameras can also succeed. Ezonics has carved out a niche with its Ezcam, which costs less than $50 after a rebate. A Webcam consists of a digital camera and software, which are sold as a package. When selecting the camera, the most important things to consider are picture quality, the maneuverability of the camera (how well it pans or tilts) and the cost. In the last two years, Webcams have improved in quality while dropping in price. But home digital studios still have a long way to go; the quality of the pictures is far from that seen on television or in camcorder shots. Lighting in the Webcam world is seldom flattering, the pictures are jerky, and the resolution is poor. Nonetheless, users still find it a great novelty to see their own movements captured on computer monitors for the very first time. The installation of Webcams has been standardized. Almost all manufacturers sell PC models that feature Universal Serial Bus, or U.S.B., ports, and some still sell versions with parallel and serial port connections. Not too long ago, installing a Webcam meant digging into the innards of the computer to put in a video capture card. U.S.B. connections mean that users are ready to go after plugging in the camera and popping in a software CD -- barring any software glitches, which can be a nightmare to solve. Computers manufactured after 1996 probably have U.S.B. ports. For earlier models, U.S.B. cards can be purchased for $30 to $150 to plug into the PCI slot. (A computer that is too old for a PCI slot is probably not powerful enough to handle a Webcam's video feed.) The minimum system requirements are: Windows 95 or later, a Pentium 100-megahertz chip or faster and 16 megabytes of RAM and 10 megabytes of free hard-disk space. The main components of Webcams are analogous to those in the human eye. A Webcam has a lens; a sensor, which captures images like a retina, and a computer chip, which acts like a brain to translate the light patterns into data. Glass lenses generally produce better pictures than plastic ones. But glass lenses are also up to three times as expensive so the Webcams designed for home users tend to have plastic lenses. Two types of resolution are available for sensors. Common Interchange Format, or C.I.F., sensors cost a lot less than Video Graphics Array, or V.G.A., sensors but have only one-third the resolution. The greatest resolution for home Webcams is 640 by 480 pixels, the V.G.A. resolution. Any resolution higher than that has been augmented by software. V.G.A. Webcams have sold for $140 and up, but prices recently dipped below the $100 mark. Creative Labs recently came out with a V.G.A. Webcam III priced at $80. There are two competing technologies for image sensors: Complementary Metal Oxide Silicon, or C.M.O.S., and Charged-Coupled Devices, or C.C.D. While C.M.O.S. is less expensive, smaller and uses less power, it is not as efficient as C.C.D. in very low light. On the other hand, bright light causes C.C.D. sensors to produce a halo-like effect known as light bloom. But in most lighting situations, both types perform comparably. All cameras work best with soft diffused lighting hitting the face. An important, but not critical distinction between home Webcams is in how fast they can capture images. Webcams, like film, create moving images by capturing a succession of still images, or frames. The higher the number of frames per second, the higher the quality. The recommended minimum frame rate is 12 to 15 frames per second. A rate of 30 is good, and 40 will give very smooth quality. The maximum rate is usually possible for only the smallest picture sizes on the computer. As the size of the picture goes up, the frame speed goes down. For videoconferencing, however, the speed of the connection rather than the speed of the camera is usually the limiting factor. Some optional features to consider include shutter buttons, microphones and the length of the cord. Shutter buttons allow the user to snap pictures manually instead of having the software solely in charge. Built-in microphones are not vital because microphones and sound cards are often installed separately. In addition, the ideal position for microphones is not the same as the ideal position for cameras. Long cords give the user more freedom in deciding where to place a Webcam. The Kodak DVC323, for example, has a generous 10-foot cord. All Webcams come with basic photograph and video capturing software. The more expensive models come with high-end photo editing programs like Adobe Photodeluxe, a lower-end version of Adobe's well-known Photoshop software. Webcams intended for a more sophisticated audience also include videoconferencing software, like Microsoft's Netmeeting. Other popular programs allow for automatic Web page updating and security functions. Most software can be mixed and matched with different cameras, and many shareware programs are also available for downloading from the Web. Parents should be aware that the Net teleconferencing software has opened up a new level of prank calls. "The plain fact is that there are people who are very into being exhibitionist," said Jim Carlton, a senior brand manager for Creative Labs. "Every once in a while," he said, "people call up to show me their private bits." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo/Chart: Logictech Quickcam Home Price: $99.95 Maximum video resolution: 320 by 240 pixels Features: built-in microphone; low resolution; attaches to monitor with adhesive; can tilt and pan, but with limited range. title: Filling Up on Gas, and Web Ads
body: GAS pumps are no strangers to advertising. Their nozzle handles have long been adorned with junk food ads encased in clear plastic. And their sheet metal bases often serve as tiny billboards. So it should come as no surprise that an evolution in gasoline pump advertising will start making its way across the unitedstates this fall. The Internet-linked gasoline pump -- called, perhaps predictably, the Millennium Series by one maker -- will turn those pitches for salty foods and sugary drinks into multimedia extravaganzas of sorts. "If you look back at the history of the gasoline pump, you can see a clear development of their technology from purely dispensing gasoline to a number of other functions," said Douglas Pinner, the chairman and chief executive of the Tokheim Corporation, a gas pump maker in Fort Wayne, Ind. "At the same time you clearly see the advent of utilizing the dispenser as a marketing device." Tokheim's new Millennium pumps -- which BP Amoco will test this fall before a broad rollout next year -- will be stuffed with individual stripped-down computers and touch-screen controls. And much like computers in, say, a law office, the pumps will be connected into a local area network controlled by a more powerful central computer that will make the link to the Internet. Mr. Pinner said most customers visiting Tokheim's Web browsing pumps would see banner ads above the display's on-screen pump controls or around weather forecasts, traffic reports or local hotel lists if those options are selected. Ads will flood the pump's full screen only when customers press on banner ads promoting discount coupons for items in the station's convenience store. The coupons will be produced by an in-pump printer. The browser will work only while gasoline is being pumped and will not allow customers to check email or search for Web pages of their own choosing. Tokheim's basic technology, which it developed in conjunction with Radiant Systems Inc., a provider of computer systems and software for retailers in Alpharetta, Ga., is largely the same in concept as a system now being field-tested in Kitchener, Ontario, by the Time Line Media Corporation, a small software maker for the petroleum industry. At a Pioneer gasoline station currently testing a Time Line system that retrofits existing pumps, consumers are treated, or perhaps subjected, to full-motion video ads for things like cell phone service and a local theme park. Time Line also mixes news headlines, weather and traffic with the ads. Its president, John Lowndes, said he hoped to make its sponsors' messages appealing by using cameras to target specific ads to different vehicle types. Tokheim and Time Line vary when it comes to the issue of how much advertising motorists will tolerate as they fill their tanks. Mr. Pinner said the advertising on Tokheim pumps would be "very subtle" because Tokheim's research showed that customers did not want to be inundated with advertising. Mr. Lowndes said he hoped that pumps could also serve as electronic commerce sites for a variety of services, accepting, for example, orders for florists or payments for parking tickets. "I look at a gas station as a community access point." He acknowledged, however, that giving customers a reason to linger at do-everything pumps could lead to congestion and could ultimately undermine the station's ability to sell gasoline. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Time Line Media's system retrofits pumps to offer full-motion ads.

title: On the Money
body: To the Editor: I never imagined I would be quoting Bob Dylan's lyrics from "Positively 4th Street," "You say, 'How are you?' 'Good luck,' but you don't mean it." "Following the Money, Through the Web," (Aug. 26) revealed the mind-set of Congress and Washington, which is talking about disclosure but placing it in hard-to-find spots that politicians do not make it any easier to locate. Congressional efforts to keep the activities of the Federal Election Commission to a bare minimum reveal volumes about the ambivalence of informing the public. The Watergate scandals of 25 years ago created the legislation to make the flow of funds to campaigns more transparent. Fortunately the power of the Internet brings democracy and accountability much closer to the average citizen. Nevertheless, the distinct feeling I come away with is that Congress doesn't mean it. The current salvo for requests for information from citizens has been the response, "Go to our Web site." Regrettably there is little quality control on some of the Federal sites. It is reassuring that efforts from the private sector like Public Disclosure are putting this information at our fingertips. Ultimately we all lose. Congress should mean it and not be satisfied with simply putting the information on the Internet. As they used to say in the early days of computing, garbage in, garbage out.  STEVEN A. LUDSIN East Hampton, N.Y., Aug. 26, 1999  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
STATE OF THE ART;
Financial Software Slugfest
body: IN his stage play "Millennium Bug," Steven Tomlinson, an economist and performance artist, describes a new software package called Veritas 2000 that not only manages your personal finances, but also your soul. Veritas 2000 promises to lead consumers out of debt and into affluence, but it does so by tracking the user's spending and savings down to the most minute level, spewing alerts and threats if a penny is spent unnecessarily. Neither Quicken 2000 Deluxe ($59.95, or $39.95 for previous Quicken users) nor its archrival, Microsoft Money 2000 Deluxe ($44.95 until Nov. 30, $64.95 afterward), dare to intrude so deeply into personal spending habits. But they do take the idea of personal financial management to new levels, especially with the aid of the Internet. Both of these new programs jingle with features that help the user manage daily finances, plan and invest, prepare for taxes, do on-line banking, shop for insurance and even tap into financial information around the clock and around the world through affiliated Web sites. These Year 2000 deluxe versions use the Internet for everything from ferreting out information on investments to tracking down the best financing options for major purchases. In a sign of the times, both Quicken and Money provide detailed guidance on employee stock options. Quicken and Money have been slugging it out for years, and their epic rivalry is similar to that of baseball's Mark McGwire and Sammy Sosa. Both are in a league by themselves, and both continue to hit home runs at a hectic pace. Quicken scored with its checkbook interface, Money countered with its better on-line integration, Quicken took the lead with tax integration, Money fired back with better planning tools, Quicken added easier data entry, and so on. This year, both programs sport improved interfaces, and both programs are swinging for the virtual fences with their Internet links. There is not enough space here to list all of the features of the deluxe versions of both of these programs and their respective Web sites, www.quicken.com and www.moneycentral.com. The big news is that Microsoft has scrapped its former access fee of $9.95 a month for MSN Money Central, which is now free. Quicken.com remains free. Some of the other major features include the ability to track bank accounts and credit cards, balance multiple checkbooks, customize a budget, spew out endless graphs and charts in a pathetic effort to impress one's spouse, plan for retirement or college or other major events, grab current financial news and stock quotes off the Web, analyze thousands of stocks and mutual funds, track investment performance, pay bills on line, and even enter data without having to wait to load the actual program. Even so, users will probably spend 80 percent of their time just balancing their checkbooks. The fictitious Veritas 2000 program also bristles with features, but in the end they function mainly to highlight the risk that focusing too much on numbers and data can cause the user to overlook the more important things in life, like happiness. Both Intuit, the maker of Quicken, and Microsoft have tried to program a warmer and fuzzier feeling into the software. Both programs seem determined to help the user plan for future happiness, and both get fairly personal. Quicken will tell you how much your car is worth and will scour the Internet to tell you how much your neighbors paid for their houses. Money will help you find the best way to pay for your new refrigerator and will help you plan "what if" scenarios that include winning the lottery and getting hit by a bus. I'm surprised that neither program offered to lend me $20 until next Tuesday. In preparing for this version of its Money program, Microsoft determined that nearly two-thirds of all the families that owned a personal computer already had some sort of personal financial management software. That is not surprising, considering that many computer manufacturers sell PC's with such software already loaded (some include both Quicken and Money.) Even though the software is already installed, only half of the PC owners actually try the programs, Microsoft found, and of those, only a third used it on a continuing basis. One could make several inferences from these findings. One supposition is that most PC owners do not need financial software because they are natural wizards at managing their finances, using conventional analog techniques like checkbook registers and shoebox receipt bins. No, I didn't think so, either. More likely, they have watched their computers lose, mangle or hold their other data captive, and they would rather entrust their financial data to a hardened criminal than to a hard drive. Or they have come to believe that using a personal finance program is more trouble than it's worth. That may have been true when entering data into the older programs, but consumers now have the ability to transfer data directly into the program from their bank accounts, investment portfolios and credit card statements. Each program has relationships with more than 600 banks, and downloading bank statements sure beats plugging each check into the electronic register one at a time. If you are already using one program or the other, there are no features in the new versions that are so dazzling as to warrant switching. If you are using an ancient version of either program -- more than a few years old -- and are happy with it, you ought to upgrade anyway, if only to avoid any potential problems with Year 2000 compatibility. The 2000 versions of Money and Quicken are fully Year 2000-compliant. For people just starting out with a personal financial manager, Money 2000, with its impressive Setup Assistant, clean design and use of audio and video coaching, is the easier program to learn. Although I had better not explain why, I was grateful that the program offered to send me reminders by email when it comes time to pay bills and file my expense reports. Microsoft is offering a free 90-day trial of Money 2000 Deluxe. Information on the offer is available at www.microsoft.com/money. For Macintosh users the choice is easy, as Microsoft has no plans for a version of Money for Macs.
