Almost immediately, the two men decided to go into business together, according to the S.E.C.'s suit. From at least September 1998 until the Flores-Tabb meeting, Uniprime had issued a stream of news releases about its intention to acquire car dealerships and become one of the largest dealer chains in the country. Uniprime currently claims to own only a handful of dealerships in newyork and South Carolina. In May, Mr. Flores and Mr. Tabb formed a company, New Technologies, to promote Plasma Plus. Uniprime got a large stake in the company and Mr. Flores, who signed over Plasma Plus's patent rights to New Technologies, became New Technologies' president. Then the games began. Uniprime never released any meaningful financial reports, and, because it trades in the loosely regulated on-line world of small-stock bulletin boards, was not required to file extensive disclosure reports with the S.E.C. Its glowing news releases about the promises of Plasma Plus, though, were enough to stir up a frenzy among investors. On July 19, the day Mr. Funkhouser of the N.A.S.D. saw "Buy UPCA!" flash across his computer screen, Uniprime announced a "major breakthrough in the field of H.I.V. research." The release claimed that five AIDS patients in Spain had been successfully treated with Plasma Plus. The next day, Uniprime's shares jumped $3.25 to $5 as more than five million shares of the company were traded. Presto. Uniprime, with shares that were worth about 25 cents each in January, now had a market value of about $100 million. "Hallah! Hallah! Hallah! Shout it from the rooftops of the banks," read the July 20 posting of an apparent Uniprime investor, a "Mr. R," on Raging Bull, an Internet stock board. "Praise the money. From the church of the immaculate buck. Praise the money." Raging Bull is gossip central in the mania surrounding Uniprime. To date more than 10,000 messages have been posted about Uniprime on the site, making it one of the most talked about stocks on Raging Bull's message boards. Some investors were skeptical of Uniprime's claims from the beginning. On July 21, an investor with the screen name "Darking" took speculators to task in a message posted on Raging Bull. "Believing this is a cure for H.I.V. is like believing (on my say so) that I have a cure for aging," Darking wrote. "Not bloody likely." Even so, enough investors bought the hype to give Uniprime a valuation far out of proportion to its real financial prospects. According to the S.E.C.'s complaint, Mr. Flores had little in his background to suggest he had stumbled upon an AIDS cure. In 1983, the complaint says, Mr. Flores was convicted on a charge of conspiracy to commit murder "based upon his participation in the murder of a friend's parents in their Colorado house after they refused to hand over valuables to Flores and their son." Mr. Flores was sentenced to 25 years in prison, but was paroled in 1992. Moreover, Mr. Flores, who claims to be a native of Spain with unitedstates citizenship, went to great lengths to pad his resume, according to the S.E.C. He claimed to have spent 15 years in a laboratory outside Lisbon doing immunology research, an impossibility given the prison time Mr. Flores was serving. He also claimed to be an honors graduate of the University of Colorado and the University of Madrid. But the commission's complaint said he never attended the University of Colorado and had not graduated with honors from the University of Madrid. Claims of having successfully tested Plasma Plus on five patients were also dubious and a supposed agreement to do further research with an AIDS foundation in the Bahamas was a fabrication, the complaint said. Although the S.E.C. suspended trading in Uniprime's shares on July 22, some investors, either because they could not be convinced otherwise or because they were actively participating in pumping up the shares, refused to give up on Uniprime. "This investigation is not by the S.E.C.!" posted "Irvine" on Raging Bull on Aug. 16. "This is the gov. trying to suppress information to the public with pressure from the major drug companies." Small brokerages are often some of the most active participants in the trading that envelopes the free-wheeling world of stock bulletin boards. The bulk of the trading volume in Uniprime's shares passed through three small brokerage firms, Knight Securities Inc., the Wien Securities Corporation and Hill Thompson Magid & Company. Uniprime's shares, which resumed trading on Aug. 5, now trade at about 25 cents, beaten flat by last week's raids on the company by law enforcement officials. Perhaps one burned Uniprime investor, "Consolimd," in a message posted on Raging Bull on Aug. 14, best captured the current mood of Uniprime investors: "Aaaarrrrgggghhhh!" Meanwhile, the Postal Inspection Service has filed a criminal complaint against Mr. Flores and the S.E.C.'s investigation is continuing. While not new, the lesson of the Uniprime scandal is still valuable, regulators say. "It shows the perils of investing in companies that do not file disclosure documents with the S.E.C.; the only disclosure this company made was press releases," Andrew J. Geist, the S.E.C.'s associate regional director in newyork, said. "You wonder whether investors are looking at these companies with a critical eye." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY: E-COMMERCE;
Companies learn that selling merchandise on line can be surprisingly messy, especially those pesky returns.
body: LIFE was much easier for E-commerce companies when their primary focus was on acquiring customers. They could simply take the company public, spend huge sums on advertising then wait for the customers to show up. Things became messy when shoppers actually arrived. Suddenly, E-commerce executives realized that managing on-line sales could be as difficult as managing off-line merchandising. Merchandise returns, in particular, have been nettlesome for Internet stores, especially those without previous experience in catalogue or traditional retailing. Analysts and executives say E-commerce sites have not done enough to give customers the same confidence in their return policies as off-line merchants do and have been slow to devise effective systems for refunds and exchanges. In short, they say, if Internet retailers want to attract more return customers, they are going to have to deal better with returns by customers. "Handling returns is a complicated process that can't be standardized the same way as outbound shipments," said James Vogtle, an E-commerce research director with Boston Consulting Group. "And it's a process that's not getting the attention it needs." For every $100 in goods an E-commerce company ships, $5 worth is returned, according to a recent study by Boston Consulting in conjunction with Shop.org, an Internet retailing trade group. That 5 percent rate compares favorably with that of direct marketing companies, which have return rates of 5 to 7 percent, as well as traditional retailers, whose returns total 6 percent of sales, according to the National Retail Federation. But the comparison is also somewhat misleading because a large percentage of Internet commerce is made up of items like books and CD's, which have low return rates. The real problem is not the number of returns, but how those returns are being handled. Analysts and executives say customers are often subjected to poor customer service when trying to make returns, resulting in delayed exchanges or mishandled refunds. Because most sites require customers to pay for shipping items back to the retailer, the process can be costly, as well. These problems are reflected in two surveys conducted among more than 2,000 Internet users by Jupiter Communications, an Internet research firm. In one survey in which Internet shoppers ranked their top 12 sources of dissatisfaction with E-commerce sites the fifth-greatest concern was returning merchandise. In the other study, also conducted by Jupiter, 40 percent of those surveyed indicated they would buy more on line if they could return items easily. Not only have retailers been frequently caught off guard by the volume of orders received, but, says Ken Cassar, a Jupiter analyst, E-commerce sites often cede control of fulfilling orders -- as well as handling returns -- to outside companies. "When things do go wrong, a vast majority of the time it's because there's a gap in the seams between various parties," Mr. Cassar said. "The fewer times the baton is passed, the greater the chances are for success." Jonathan Morris, executive vice president of Bluefly, an on-line retailer of clothing and housewares, says the company sees a return rate for clothing "in the low 20 percent range" -- nearly 10 points below the catalogue rate for apparel. Bluefly, which uses a third-party to handle orders and returns, manages the return process in several steps. After a customer calls and indicates a problem, the item is shipped back at the company's expense, using a United Parcel Service packing slip included with each item delivered. The item is inspected when it arrives, and the customer's account is credited "within a week of them sending it," Mr. Morris said. The fulfillment center repackages and restocks items that are in perfect condition; imperfect items are either repaired or discarded. To insure that no orders are mishandled, Bluefly "is all over the fulfillment house," Mr. Morris said. "We manage them really closely," he said, "and treat them like they're virtual employees." Of returns in general, he added, "This is definitely the less-sexy side of the business, but it's as important -- if not more important -- than any other aspect." Andrew Brooks, chief executive of Furniture.com, an Internet-only retailer, said that because the cost of returned furniture -- and dissatisfied customers -- was so high, the company designed its Web site to insure that customers made the right choice. "The best way is to make the customer as educated as possible about what they're getting," Mr. Brooks said, adding that Furniture.com's return rate is materially lower than that of catalogue companies, though he would not disclose a specific rate. Furniture.com's Web site enables customers to view photos of an item from a number of angles and use a room-design option to see how it would fit with their current furniture. The company also allows customers to email or speak to design consultants and have fabric swatches sent to them free. Once the furniture is shipped, customers can hold the furniture for a week before returning it -- at no cost. The only catch: customers get a store credit, not a cash reimbursement. Clothing companies like Lands' End and Levi Strauss are also improving their sites with modeling technology that allows customers to indicate their physical dimensions and receive guidance on what size to order. But when it comes to accepting returns, perhaps the best option is one that remains unreachable for companies that operate only on line -- namely, physical stores. The Gap and Federated's Macy's, for instance, accept returns of merchandise at their stores even when items are purchased on line -- a policy that is not shared by many Internet retailers who have physical outlets. Angela Kapp, vice president for special markets and new media at Estee Lauder, which includes the Clinique Web site, agreed there was a benefit in allowing customers to return items to a physical store. She said Estee Lauder customers could do so as long as the department store in which the company's products were sold allowed it. But that option has limits, Ms. Kapp said. "What if you live 20 miles away, or you don't feel like going to the mall?" she asked. "Isn't that the reason why they got on line in the first place?" http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Gap accepts returns of Web purchases at stores.

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
First Out of the Starting Gate
body: Thanks to a combination of foresight, luck and good timing, Richard Forman has won the right to boast. His company, Register.com, is the first and most aggressive player in the game of breaking up the monopoly on Internet address registrations that a Virginia company, Network Solutions Inc., has enjoyed for six years. But the starting gate is still closed to the more than 250 companies expected eventually to compete in what is stacking up to be a risky venture even by Internet standards. One big unknown is how far registration fees will drop from the $70 Network Solutions charges for an initial two-year registration as more competitors enter the arena. An even bigger gamble is that key rules for the game remain unknown. Some of those rules will be decided this week when the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, or Icann, the nonprofit group charged with introducing competition into the business of registering names ending in the popular domains of .com, .net and .org, holds its fourth board meeting in Santiago, Chile. Icann is expected to approve a uniform dispute resolution policy that the companies will have to follow in cases of cybersquatting -- the practice of registering domain names just to hold them in hopes of making a profit -- and other tangles over trademark issues. The policy will play a large role in determining what legal liabilities the new competitors will ultimately face. Other important issues also remain the subject of protracted negotiations between Network Solutions, based in Herndon, Va., and the Department of Commerce, which chose Icann last year to run the Internet's addressing system and to establish the framework for introducing competition to Network Solutions' cash-cow monopoly. Those issues include contract terms for allowing competing companies to register addresses in the master data base of domains that Network Solutions will continue to administer -- including how much they will pay Network Solutions as a service fee for each name they register. Although the delays and uncertainties have a number of potential competitors in a holding pattern, they have provided an unexpected bonus for Register.com, which was one of five companies chosen in April to participate in a pilot round of competition with Network Solutions. Register.com, the first of the five to go live, won't say how many names it has already registered. But Mr. Forman, insists that the numbers are encouraging. "We are the second largest registrar in the world," he says with confidence. Register.com has competed aggressively with Network Solutions in what are expected to be important areas of the business -- like providing customer service and computer operations for running Web sites. Register.com has entered into partnerships with nearly 20 companies, including Staples and Mastercard, giving it a link on their Web sites and offering services related to building a Web site. It also has partnerships with 30 Internet service providers. But like the registration of domain names themselves, those are all areas where Network Solutions has had a head start. With the exclusive right since 1993 to register addresses that end in .com, .net and .org at $70 each, Network Solutions has reported snowballing profits for the last 11 quarters. Anticipating competition, it has spent much of the last two years building international partnerships and new services aimed at small businesses that want to build a Web presence. Network Solutions now has more than 500 employees and averages 400,000 new domain name registrations a month. Register.com, by contrast, has about 100 employees and a lot less cash. But Mr. Forman is confident that when the dust has settled, he'll be on top. "I spent a lot of money building these systems; I know how much they cost," he said. "You're going to see a lot of companies that just can't do the business." Paul Merenbloom, an Internet analyst with Prudential Securities, agrees in part with that assessment. "The potential here is for a very large industry," he said, "but it is likely to be controlled by -- or rather comprised of -- a few rather successful companies, some largely successful, a few moderately successful companies and a large number of nominally successful companies." He added: "I think Rich has positioned himself in the first heat, and, given the inevitable issues and delays, he and others in the first group have a natural time advantage. That's not to say that over time the playing field won't level. I think it will." But while those delays offer some advantages to the first five companies, they are also making it difficult for them and for other potential competitors to develop solid business plans and raise capital, Mr. Merenbloom said. "It's unclear what the requirements are to be successful -- other than quality service at a reasonable price," he said. "The real issue right now is that nobody wants to do the wrong thing." Complicating the picture are Internet giants like America Online, which is also participating in the pilot round of competition. Like the other bigger companies in that group -- France Telecom and Melbourne IT -- it has done little yet to kick off the business and has said even less about what its plans are or whether it will try to go head-to-head with Network Solutions. Ken Stubbs, chairman of the only nonprofit group participating in the test round of competition, the Internet Council of Registrars, said a lot of people were "waiting to see what comes out of these negotiations." "If you don't know how much money you are going to make next week, it's hard to sign a lease on a new apartment," Mr. Stubbs said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Richard Forman says his company, Register.com, is the second-largest registrar of Internet names in the world, but many crucial rules that will govern its competition with rivals have yet to be worked out. (Chester Higgins Jr./The newyork Times)

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Multimedia Transmissions Are Driving Internet Toward Gridlock
body: Like a nation's highway system, the Internet has traffic rules that prevent chaos and gridlock. But an increasingly popular type of multimedia traffic is turning out to be a cyber road hog that flouts the rules and creates traffic jams. This scofflaw traffic, known as streaming media, is widely hailed as the future of home entertainment, capable of eventually delivering high-quality audio and video programming over the Internet. Unfortunately, network experts warn, it may drive everyone else off the road. Streaming media is analogous to broadcast media in that the audio or video material is produced as soon as a computer receives the data over the Internet. The problem is that the streaming data does not respond to network congestion in the way other Internet traffic does. When a computer sending conventional data encounters congestion, it significantly slows its own transmission rate, but a computer sending streaming data will reduce the flow only slightly. So if streaming traffic competes with conventional traffic for the same congested strip of roadway, the streaming traffic, like some V.I.P. motorcade, just assumes the right of way and lets all other data traffic pile up. The difference, said Van Jacobson, chief scientist for Cisco Systems Inc., a leading maker of Internet traffic routers, is that conventional traffic "is polite; this stuff is impolite." "People writing software for that traffic -- they don't care," Mr. Jacobson said of streaming media. "In the long term, it's a problem." By its very nature, streaming media has to flow continuously to the user's computer, so it cannot follow the same traffic rules as conventional data. But even so, it is possible for packets of streaming data to interact civilly with other traffic on the Internet. The reason they do not, Mr. Jacobson said, is that streaming media providers have no incentive to comply with traffic rules. Today, he said, "if Real Networks is polite and Microsoft isn't, then Real looks crummy." Even elbowing all other data aside, today's streaming media produces a very low quality of entertainment most of the time. Much of that lack of quality today is due to slow modems at the user's end. In three to five years, when cable modems and souped-up digital telephone lines are expected to be common, most Internet users may be listening to live Webcasts or playing high-quality radio on their computers. In 10 years, movies and commercial television might very well be carried over Internet channels. This increasing demand will add vast amounts of streaming traffic to the Internet and could lead to what Mr. Jacobson calls "congestion collapse" -- the Internet equivalent of gridlock. Internet service providers are also concerned. Tony Blake, vice president for marketing and business development for AT&T Labs Research, calls the trend disturbing, adding, "What people are saying is, 'If my stuff gets through, that's all I care about.' " He said AT&T and other Internet service providers were pressuring the producers of streaming media to head off the problem before it grows out of control. Streaming media traffic is also of growing concern to the Internet Engineering Task Force, an industry group that is the closest thing the Internet has to a governing technical body. Mr. Jacobson, an active task force participant, said the group has not yet formally addressed the issue because "it's not big enough to kill the Net." Not yet anyway. But a number of Internet service providers are getting nervous. Mr. Jacobson said he would like to see streaming media use congestion controls that are compatible with those used for conventional data-packet traffic. Today, according to measurements by the National Laboratory for Applied Network Research at the University of California at San Diego, none of the existing streaming media providers are using such controls. Real Networks, the largest streaming media provider, declined to respond to the growing criticism, although a spokesman, Jay Wampold, said the company was trying to address congestion problems. Over the last year, he said, Real Networks had installed a network of computers for delivering the company's broadcasts that bypasses the Internet's main traffic routes. Kevin Unangst, lead product manager for Windows Media, the streaming media division at the Microsoft Corporation, said the company was working with network companies to route its streaming data around the Internet's main arteries. "We know bandwidth and optimizing bandwidth is a huge, huge issue," Mr. Unangst said, using an industry term for transmission capacity, "and we're covering all the bases." But Mr. Jacobson said that while actions like those taken by Real Networks and Microsoft might help, they would not resolve the problem. The bottlenecks are not on the main thoroughfares, he said, but on the side streets and access roads. "As you get out to the edge of network, closer to users, that's where the bandwidth gets limited," he said. While cable modems and digital subscriber lines will increase bandwidth to the home, a truly significant increase in Internet bandwidth would require ripping out 300 million copper wires and replacing them with fiber. "That's not going to happen fast," Mr. Jacobson said. The remedy, experts say, lies in providing incentives for streaming media providers to comply with traffic rules. With the proper incentive structure in place, streaming material from both Microsoft and Real Networks would look slightly worse than it does now, Mr. Jacobson said, but at least the competition for bandwidth would be fairer. As a standards-setting organization, the Internet Engineering Task Force does not have legal authority to force software developers to adopt congestion control measures. But standards, which enable all the computers linked to the Internet to talk to one another, can sometimes be used to discourage disruptive behavior. "It's the tragedy of the commons," said Sally Floyd, a researcher at the AT&T Center for Internet Research at the International Computer Science Institute in Berkeley, Calif. "Only with the right incentive structure, do the right things happen." The "tragedy of the commons" is an example from economic game theory. If a group of farmers must graze their cattle in the same small patch of grass, or commons, it is in the farmers' collective interest not to overgraze, lest all the grass die out and all the cows starve. The problem is that it is in each individual farmer's interest to act counter to the common good. Ordinary Internet traffic -- email and data transmissions to and from Web sites, for example -- follows a basic set of traffic laws known as the transmission control protocol, or T.C.P. Since the late 1980's, when rising Net traffic led to severe congestion problems, T.C.P. has included a congestion control mechanism that instructs a transmitting computer to slow down the data flow by half as soon as the data it is sending encounter congestion. Only when the congestion clears does the data speed up again. "What's interesting is that congestion itself is effectively the error signal that gives the sender the feedback to speed up or slow down," said Robert J. Berger, president of Internet Bandwidth Development, a consulting firm in Saratoga, Calif. "It means that there will almost always be at least a bit of congestion, but that's O.K." But it is not O.K. when traffic that conforms to T.C.P. runs into traffic that does not follow those same rules. When the point of congestion is reached, T.C.P. traffic cuts its sending rate in half. But streaming traffic just barrels through the stoplights. This in turn creates more congestion, which further slows the law-abiding traffic. Streaming media traffic "needs to back off," said Scott Shenker, head of the AT&T Center for Internet Research in Berkeley. "I think most researchers feel it's a flaw in the Internet architecture that there's no way to deal with this." Both Mr. Shenker and Mr. Jacobson believe the solution to the streaming media problem is to build incentives into the architecture to encourage good behavior. But they have very different ideas of what form those incentives should take. Mr. Shenker prefers to plant a mechanism within Internet routers that he calls "fair queuing," which would force packets sent from different sources to wait their turn to be sent. Mr. Jacobson's proposal, developed with Ms. Floyd in 1989 and only now being tested in Cisco routers, uses a kind of virtual penalty box. When the router experiences congestion, it takes a random sample of its traffic. If a certain host computer is overrepresented in that sample, its packets are placed at the end of the line. This creates the right incentive structure, he said, because the Internet service providers do not have to persuade Real Networks or any other company to obey the rules. Rather, he says, "The customers do, instead, because the quality" of their audio and video "gets really crummy." Fair queuing and penalty boxes rely on software fixes to change the incentives. Another approach, favored by many service providers, is to create economic incentives for fair sharing of the roadways. The basic idea is that heavy users should be paying for the extra bandwidth that they consume. This model, known as differential service, is already being deployed on the Internet. But there are many questions about how it should be adapted to streaming media -- most especially about who should pay. "The real puzzle about streaming media is who is going to make the money -- if we knew this, then we could answer a lot of the technical questions," said David Clark, a senior research scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Laboratory for Computer Science. Whatever solution is eventually adopted, the streaming media problem is certain to be resolved, these experts say. "An Internet that's growing and can handle streaming media is in everyone's interests," said Mr. Blake of AT&T Labs. "We poke each other with sharp sticks all the time, but slowly we move forward." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING;
Newspaper Stocks: An Internet Story
body: THE conventional wisdom of the new economy says newspapers ought to be on their last legs. In this view, it will not be long before the Internet eats the newspapers' lunch by siphoning off readers and advertising to Web sites. Until recently, that kind of thinking depressed share prices of the big publicly traded newspaper companies. In 1998, while the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index was rising 26.7 percent, the Bear Stearns Diversified Newspaper Index inched up just 1.5 percent, and the trend was little better in the first part of 1999. Not any more. Since April 1, newspaper stocks have surged 22 percent while the broader market has been bouncing up and down. And there may be more good news ahead for the sector, analysts say. William Drewry, an analyst at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, said the spurt is just the start of a long stretch of outperformance, as stock valuations catch up with important improvements in fundamentals. A new cadre of cost-conscious and shareholder-friendly managers has been slashing payrolls, shedding ancillary businesses, reducing debt and buying back stock, Mr. Drewry said. By his calculations, industry revenue is growing at 5 percent annually, bolstered by firm advertising prices, while costs apart from raw materials (mainly for labor) are growing only 3 to 3.5 percent a year. And with the often-volatile price of newsprint now low, he expects the industry to parlay its widening margins into double-digit earnings growth. Those factors make newspaper stocks attractive as a value investment, even after the recent run-up. But there may be a growth investment here, too: Largely unnoticed by the market, newspapers have invested aggressively in their supposed nemesis, the Internet, and are already generating impressive revenues on line. For example, the second-largest job recruitment Web site, CareerPath.com, is run by a consortium of newspaper companies. And newspapers control valuable Internet assets in their vast archives of articles and photographs, as well as data bases and reporting resources, said Steven Barlow, an analyst with Credit Suisse First Boston. Of course, moving on line means grappling with a host of nimble and aggressive new competitors for readership and ads. "The big question," Mr. Drewry said, "is not how big the Internet market becomes, but how much can newspapers capture." Kevin Gruneich, an analyst with Bear Stearns, said he thinks "the Internet fear factor" may wane in coming months. Mr. Gruneich, who began advising investors to shy away from newspaper stocks in early 1998, turned bullish in June on near-term prospects for several of them. A broad-based rebound in advertising and a sharp, 23 percent decline in newsprint costs since January prompted his change of heart, he said. Knight Ridder is an example of a company with an upside both on line and off, he said. Every decrease in newsprint prices bolsters its profits, he noted, while its Internet operations, principally the Realcities news, entertainment and commerce Web site, yield at least $30 million a year in revenue. He expects the stock to rise to $64 or $65 within a year, from $54 today. William Bird of Salomon Smith Barney is bullish on the Washington Post Company because of its combination of strong free cash flow and a history of using cash effectively for share repurchases and acquisitions.  The stock is also attractive, Mr. Bird said, because of its overfunded pension plan, its Internet assets and its Kaplan Education subsidiary. His 12-month price target for the stock is $675; it now trades at $556. Mr. Barlow of Credit Suisse First Boston said he thought newspaper-company profit margins would hold up relatively well, even if the economy slowed. His choices in the sector include the Gannett Company and the Tribune Company, which get one-third to one-half of their cash flow from broadcasting operations. He sees Gannett rising to $80 a share, from $68.9375 Friday, and Tribune to $100, from $94.75, within a year. Barbara Marcin of Gabelli Asset Management said she is keen on The newyork Times Company, because "the best way to invest in the Internet is through companies that sell their own products over the Web." She expects the company's Internet operations to expand the reach of its principal newspaper properties, The Times and The Boston Globe, and account for $4.50 of the $48 price she expects the stock to reach within a year; it closed at $37.4375 on Friday. The industry's price-to-earnings multiples, which ran at an average 40 percent premium to the broader market from 1988 to 1998, now lag behind the S. & P. 500. But bullish analysts like Mr. Drewry think the multiples will rise again as newspapers spin out their on-line businesses with their own stock listings. Mr. Drewry sees a precedent for newspapers in the shift in investor perception that turned cable stocks into highfliers. "Two or three years ago, cable companies were seen as losers in the next generation of communications," he noted. But partly because of Microsoft's investment in the Comcast Corporation in 1997, investors began looking at cable companies as attractive bets on the Internet infrastructure. Newspapers look ripe for a similar rethinking by investors, he said, even if Bill Gates doesn't buy one. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph plots Bear Stearns Diversified Newspaper index since April.

title:
LAW AND ORDER;
In New Jersey, Hate Groups Find Business Is Good
body: Hate is flowing like an underground river through America's communities, occasionally breaking the surface and splashing communities into consciousness. And New Jersey, it seems, is one of the headwaters for E-commerce in the hate trade. Music, books, posters, jewelry and videos preaching racism and intolerance are some of the exports for which the state is becoming increasingly well known. Four of the top hate bands recommended on such sites as Pillage and Plunder are based in Middlesex, and the New Jersey skinheads site is operated from Turnersville. Concern over the presence of hate groups has risen in recent weeks since Buford O. Furrow Jr., a white separatist from Washington State, opened fire on schoolchildren in a Jewish community center and killed a postal worker in Los Angeles. In New Jersey, several nationally known hate groups have established cells -- from Sussex and Passaic Counties, where the National Alliance and neo-Nazi groups have given speeches, to Gloucester County, where cornfields were cut with swastikas. In addition, law-enforcement officials say the Ku Klux Klan has been recruiting this summer in Ocean and Gloucester counties. "New Jersey has traditionally been a place for skinheads and the Klan," said Shai Goldstein, New Jersey regional director of the Anti Defamation League of B'nai B'rith. "These are subterranean groups that are secretive in terms of their membership, but at the same time they are out there giving their message." Deputy State Attorney General Robin Parker, bureau chief for New Jersey's bias crime office, said hate groups no longer needed to be rooted to a specific town, since the Internet provided an anonymous rallying place as well as a public platform for their views. "It lowers the barrier for access," Mr. Parker said. The bias-crime office now offers a one-hour class for teachers to help them convey to students of all ages the dangers of the Internet's hate community, which is constantly using such familiar avenues as cartoons and music to recruit members. "They dress it up as something very nice and very popular," Mr. Parker said. "Parents and teachers have to talk to kids so they don't get sucked in. That's where it starts for a lot of young people in the state. They are made comfortable and then they are easier to bring into these organizations." Indeed, Mr. Goldstein said: "There is a lot of activity here in E-commerce. New Jersey-based Web sites offer a variety of items from music calling for the deaths of people of certain races and religions, to neo-Nazi posters and videos. It's not trinkets, it's hate material." He offered the local example of a connection between possession of hate paraphernalia and acts such as those committed by Dennis Lurty, 27, of Burlington County, who was sentenced last month to seven years in prison on weapons charges. Mr. Lurty had a record of hate-related offenses, and when videotape of him firing weapons and making anti-racial and anti-Semitic remarks was obtained by the Attorney General's office, he was sentenced to jail for violating his probation. "Lurty was the head of the group White Victory and formerly of the Atlantic City skinheads," Mr. Goldstein said. "At his sentencing his father still didn't get it. He kept saying his son was just a redneck and that all the hate material he had was just memorabilia." Sites that are frequently accessed on the Web for such skinhead and neo-Nazi groups as the White Pride Network and United Skins offer items for sale through two main sources, both in New Jersey -- the Red, White and Blue and Micetrap. Red, White and Blue, also the name of a hate band, is situated in Matawan. Micetrap is the name listed on numerous reviews of hate music -- known as "white power music" or "Nazi ska" -- and endorsements for various hate sites. The post office box for Micetrap is in Turnersville and is held by James Delnegro, according to a person who asked not to be identified. A woman who answered the telephone at Mr. Delnegro's home said: "He works during the day, does his skinhead thing at night. Look on the computer for him, you know, Micetrap or whatever, or call back later." When asked in a telephone interview about his business and ties to the skinheads, Mr. Delnegro would only say, "The site's none of your damn business." In Turnersville, a community of 80,000 people, residents say hate is something that has been a part of their area for a long time. Lynn Bombaro who lives in neighboring Sicklerville and works in Turnersville, said it was a challenge raising her 14-year-old-son in an area where residents have fought school desegregation and where skinheads and the Klan are actively recruiting. "Just last week one of these groups put hate pamphlets in the pages of books in the library," Ms. Bombaro said. "There have been hate crimes from here to Vineland." Mr. Parker said placing pamphlets of any nature into books in a public or school library was against the law. "It is crossing the line on the First Amendment," he said. "These groups have also been known to add books to school libraries, books on hate." Mr. Parker is currently preparing for the case against seven men who, among other offenses, allegedly cut a swastika into a cornfield in Mansfield in Burlington County. The case is scheduled to be heard in Burlington County Court in October. "That is a case of seven people terrorizing the African-American population over a three-year period," he said. "Dead animals left on lawns, spotlights on homes in the middle of the night" while they shouted racial epithets. Mr. Parker said that while he did not think residents should be terrified by the existence of such groups, they should be concerned. "The ray of hope for our state is that it is so densely populated, which makes it harder for them to thrive," he said. "More rural areas can be a focus for Klan activity.' Mrs. Bombaro agreed and added: "They don't like the migrant workers. There is a large Mexican population that is constantly under assault here." Jim Leavy, pastor of the First Baptist Church of Turnersville, said he was saddened but not surprised by the existence of a group that traffics in hate based in his town. "There is a man down the street from the church who will not come to services here because it is integrated," Mr. Leavy said. "It's a shame that people think they have to feel that way. I would hope that people in our state would do all they can to help educate people and stop the spread of this hatred among us."  Spreading Hate In New Jersey  Following are hate groups with active memberships in New Jersey, according to the Southern Poverty Law Center, the Jewish Defense League and the state Attorney General's office. Day of the Rope, Berlin Knights of Freedom (Ku Klux Klan), Eatontown and Ocean City Hammerskin Nation, Harrison National Alliance (white separatists), Hewit New Jersey Skinheads, Turnersville United Skins/Pillage and Plunder, Middlesex http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Clockwise from top left, three groups with Internet links to New Jersey: White Pride Network offers items for sale through Micetrap in Turnersville; New Order Knights Ku Klux Klan welcomes visitors; and Plunder and Pillage have a Middlesex address.

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
Double Vision
body: The newyork Public Library has married an educational and entertainment tool of the turn of this century with one from the last one, in a new on-line digital collection of 19th-century stereographs. This summer the library completed a three-year project to digitize 12,000 stereographs, paired photographs that appear three-dimensional when viewed through a stereoscope. The images, all scenes from newyork, New Jersey and Connecticut, include 5,000 that show sites across newyork City from the Bronx Zoo to Coney Island. In some ways stereoscopic views were the Internet of their day, which lasted from the 1850's until World War I. At first they were an educational entertainment for the well-to-do, but after the Civil War their price gradually dropped and their popularity spread. Until newsreels eclipsed stereographs, people would spend hours gazing through stereoscopes at various images. Today, desktop computers, for all their power, cannot render the old stereographs into three dimensions. That still requires the special viewer, or a facility for crossing one's eyes just so. Julia Van Haaften, the library's curator of photographs, expects that relatively few people will hold stereoscopes to their computer screens. But she said many researchers would look at the collection for information on how people lived and what neighborhoods looked like. The new collection also resolves a conflict for the library: how to both preserve valuable materials and make them accessible to the public. Putting the images on line gives researchers worldwide access, but minimizes the need to physically handle the originals, Ms. Van Haaften said. "By putting them out on the Internet," she said, "they have gone from little precious objects to being available to every man once again." What You See: A search engine sends visitors to virtual bins of pictures of similar subjects. There, researchers can scan thumbnail images and look for the exact picture they want. The pictures show everything from stacked cannonballs in the Brooklyn Navy Yard to horses trotting down Broadway to Staten Island sunsets. Almost as interesting as the picture is the original text on the back of the cards. A scene of children playing in the surf at Rockaway Beach, for example, is accompanied by a description of the summer getaway: "Frail and Fantastic wooden pavilions for dancing, drinking beer, and eating clams abound, and prices are moderate. It is a place for common people." Links: For visitors who want the full effect, the Web site links to the San Diego Historical Society, which offers stereoscopes for $3. There are also links to the library's digital collection of 19th-century photographs of black Americans. What You Get: Access to an interesting collection of images of the way life used to be, and the chance to experience the entertainment of an earlier era.   JULIAN E. BARNES  THE newyork PUBLIC LIBRARY STEREOSCOPIC VIEWS digital.nypl.org/stereoviews http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
PERSONAL BUSINESS;
Pairinga Tax Break and Web Giving
body: SOME highly popular new Web sites have built impressive followings on a simple premise: If you stop at them before shopping on the Internet, some portion of what you spend will go to charity. As well intended as the pitch sounds, operators of the sites have conceded that consumers were probably not eligible for tax deductions on the money being diverted to the charitable groups. But one of the most popular of these sites, iGive.com, now says shoppers at its site may be able to take that deduction after all. The company sent email to its shoppers last week to alert them to the development. The company has petitioned the Internal Revenue Service for a private letter ruling that would confirm the propriety of its approach, but in the meantime it has received the approval of its tax lawyers at Hogan & Hartson in Washington. A private letter ruling, which could take as long as two years to secure, would give the company confidence that its shoppers' tax deductions would not be challenged, but it would not protect its competitors' patrons. The question of tax deductibility may be technical and, for some consumers, may involve such small sums that they will not bother with the paperwork. But given the rapid growth of these Web sites, the nickels and dimes can add up. For example, iGive, said its 68,000 members have raised $307,000 for charity in the nearly two years since the site's founding. And tax deductibility may broaden its appeal. Already, one competitor, Greatergood.com, has said that it, too, is looking at ways to offer a tax deduction. Right now, most of these shop-for-a-cause Web sites make their money from the commissions they collect from retailers in exchange for sending traffic their way. Shoppers then have the opportunity to name a charity, which typically receives a cut of that fee, but not always. The new approach at iGive.com is to give shoppers the option of keeping that cut for themselves, in the form of a rebate, or having it forwarded to the charity of their choice. Because the shopper can demand the cash, routing the money to a charity would be more likely to qualify as a tax-deductible gift for the shopper. "This money looks like any other money you give to your worthy cause," said the company's founder, Robert Grosshandler. He pointed to the letter from his tax lawyers saying the I.R.S. has once before permitted such an arrangement, by a credit card company that wanted to let customers divert part of their charge volume to charity. Even if iGive prevails with tax authorities, consumers may find it hard to count on the deduction. For starters, iGive allows consumers leeway to name just about any cause under the sun, and its devotees do. One beneficiary, for instance, is the Broken Nose Fund, a Portland, Me., cause that was not registered as a charity with regulators when it was started by a man who wanted to raise money for his third nose job. As long as no one was taking a tax deduction, it hardly mattered if some causes were not bona fide charities under section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code. But if consumers are claiming deductions based on their shopping habits on iGive, tax experts say they had better be sure to count only charities that qualify. MR. GROSSHANDLER, who says he is a big believer in personal responsibility, quarrels with the idea that his customers need a lot of hand-holding. "We are not in the business of vetting organizations for tax deductibility," he said. Another potential hitch to claiming the tax deduction would be if the cause never gets the money. Although shoppers at iGive have so far identified 5,300 causes to receive the $307,000 they have generated in commissions, iGive has only sent $240,000 worth of checks, to about 1,600 of these causes. In some cases, iGive cannot locate a cause named by its shoppers. What's more, every cause must raise at least $10 through the Web site before iGive issues a check. If shoppers do not spend much or choose a cause that is obscure, the charity may fail to meet iGive's minimum. The biggest question may simply be what happens if shoppers start to flock to the site more for the rebate than to lend a hand to charity. At least two other sites offering discounts, Ebates.com and Esumer.com, have staked out the rebate turf. So, while the tax strategy might work, it might also transform iGive from a high-minded bankroller of charities to just another E-commerce play. That might anger some retailers, who might not relish seeing their goods discounted without any of the image-polishing they now get by steering dollars to charity. Since iGive began offering the rebate last week, few people have chosen to take the money rather than give it to charity, according to Mr. Grosshandler. But he conceded that if people came to iGive not to give, but to receive, the site would have to rethink its mission. "If everyone chooses to get a check, the business model will not work," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: iGive.com says shoppers using its site can help charity and get some tax deductions.

title: Firm Ends Web Sales For 'Mein Kampf'
body: Bertelsmann, the German publishing giant, pulled "Mein Kampf" from its on-line bookstore, BOL, today after being accused of selling hate literature. BOL's German and Dutch services have never sold "Mein Kampf," an autobiographical manifesto that Hitler wrote in prison several years before he led the Nazi party to power in 1933. It is full of anti-Semitic tirades. But BOL said it would stop offering the book on its English and French services to prevent Germans from buying it anyway. Distributing unannotated hate literature is illegal in Germany, but not in Britain or France. The Simon Wiesenthal Center in Los Angeles had filed a complaint with the German Justice Ministry accusing Barnesandnoble.com, which is Bertelsmann's American on-line bookselling partner, and the rival bookseller Amazon.com of violating German law by selling such books to German customers. Because the Internet crosses national boundaries, BOL said, it chose to stop offering the book entirely.Bertelsmann had already recommended last week that Barnesandnoble.com, in which it owns a 40 percent interest, stop selling texts that could be considered hate literature in Germany. Amazon.com continues to offer an English version of "Mein Kampf" in all the countries to which it delivers but does not sell the book in German. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Compaq Computer Announces Net Deals
body: Aiming to increase its role in electronic commerce, the Compaq Computer Corporation announced alliances today with two companies controlled by CMGI Inc., an Internet venture company. Compaq, the world's leading maker of personal computers, said it had made an investment in Engage Technologies Inc., an Internet software company, and disclosed a marketing alliance with Ancestry.com Inc., a maker of World Wide Web research tools. The pacts came as Compaq and CMGI, the majority owner of both Ancestry.com and Engage, sealed a previous deal under which CMGI, which is based in Andover, Mass., is given an 83 percent stake in Compaq's Altavista search engine and Compaq becomes the largest outside shareholder of CMGI. Compaq plans to use Engage's technology to enhance its Internet marketing programs by plugging Engage products into its Web site, www.compaq.com. Engage, which went public in July, provides products and services that allow its corporate clients to create and use profiles of Web surfers to focus ads and content. In its alliance with Ancestry.com, an on-line resource for researching data about families, Compaq will become the premier PC vendor on the Myfamily.com and Ancestry.com Web sites and will help Ancestry.com broaden its member base through joint marketing programs. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Discloses More Flaws in Software
body: Three weeks after security holes were found in its Office 97 software, the Microsoft Corporation today acknowledged similar vulnerabilities in the recently released successor, Office 2000, and in other programs. The company said it had known for several weeks about the Office 2000 flaw, which could allow data, software or hardware to be damaged via email or commands sent from a malicious Web site. But it said it had chosen not to disclose the problem until a remedy was ready. The Office 2000 flaw is not identical to the one in Office 97 and cannot be exploited in precisely the same way. But as with the Office 97 flaw, an attack could be started using a software component called Jet to execute arbitrary commands hidden in an Office document. Separately, Microsoft acknowledged today that there was a bug in its new Internet chat software, "MSN Messenger," that would allow co-workers and others who had access to a person's computer to see a person's email password for the Microsoft's Web-based "Hotmail" service. It promised to fix the flaw by week's end. Microsoft security bulletins on the Office 97 flaw had explicitly said that Office 2000 users were not vulnerable. Microsoft said it had been concerned about publicizing a security hole that it could not yet plug. "Our policy is not to arm malicious coders until a solution is in place," said Andrew Dixon, group product manager for Office at Microsoft. "We wanted to make sure that the information is there before we announced the vulnerability." While the Jet component is most commonly associated with Office, it is also installed in conjunction with hundreds of other programs written by other companies for Microsoft operating systems, Mr. Dixon said. The repair, or patch, which Microsoft said would be released by Friday, is intended to protect users against vulnerabilities in Office 97, Office 2000 or other programs using the Jet component. Mr. Dixon said Microsoft would send a security bulletin disclosing the details of both problems to 1.5 million Office users as well as issuing articles with technical details of the problems. The security bulletin and patch will also be posted on the Web at http://officeupdate.microsoft.com. Juan Carlos Garcia Cuartango, an engineer in Spain, said he discovered both flaws late last month and immediately informed Microsoft. While Mr. Cuartango decided to post a notice about the Office 97 flaw to an Internet mailing list, he did not publicly disclose the Office 2000 flaw until today, and Microsoft then acknowledged it. "I decided to keep this confidential until the patch is published," he said today in an interview. The flaws are particularly dangerous because Microsoft's Web browser ordinarily "trusts" documents from Microsoft Office programs like Word or Excel and opens them without warning the user. Since the security flaws can be exploited from an Office document hidden in an email message, a user reading email on line can inadvertently unleash rogue programs or viruses. Two weeks ago, Microsoft addressed the problem by making available a tool that configures the browser to alert the user before opening such documents. It has taken the Office team several weeks to come up with a more fundamental solution because the company was concerned that non-Microsoft programs that use the Jet component might no longer work once the patch was installed. "We wanted to make sure it didn't produce incompatibilities," Mr. Dixon said. "We wanted to make sure it's rock solid before introducing it this week." The Jet component is represented by a Windows file named odbcjt32.dll. Since so many users are vulnerable, experts are advising Microsoft users to download the patch as soon as it is available and to exercise caution when opening unknown Word or Excel documents.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Another Twist in Skirmish Over Instant Messaging
body: In its latest tweak at America Online, the Microsoft Corporation announced today that it would release a computer protocol to enable subscribers of competing instant-messaging services to communicate with its own customers. Microsoft officials said the move was intended to pave the way for communication among subscribers of the handful of major companies offering instant messaging, a feature that allows computer users to contact one another instantaneously and chat on line. Thus far, users of instant-message services have been largely relegated to sending messages to users within their own service. In a pitched battle with America Online, which pioneered instant messaging, Microsoft has sought to deliver messages from its own subscribers to users of America Online's software without the company's permission. America Online, which says it has 43 million users of one form or another on its instant-messaging software, has accused Microsoft of hacking into its system to route messages to and from America Online customers. At least 14 times, America Online has changed its protocol -- the specifications that allow two software programs to communicate -- and each time Microsoft programmers have found a way around the barrier. Microsoft, which has amassed 1.5 million users of its instant-messaging software in less than a month of service, is not alone. Other instant-messaging competitors, including Tribal Voice, which has five million instant-messaging members, have said they also intend to link to users of America Online's software. In this respect, the latest twist in the skirmish underscores a larger issue: with 60 million to 100 million people estimated to use instant messaging, there is growing momentum among the competitors to create standards so their subscribers can communicate. "We're at a watershed," said Richard Dym, vice president for marketing for Tribal Voice, based in Scotts Valley, Calif. "In order for this form of communication to take the next step, to maybe even replace email, we need openness." Mr. Dym said the growing use of instant messaging had started momentum in the last year to create a standard protocol so competing services can exchange messages over the Internet. And he said Microsoft was adding to that momentum by putting its substantial resources and weight behind the standards quest. For its part, America Online said it, too, favored open standards permitting communication among users of different services. Tricia Primrose, an America Online spokeswoman, said the company had been working for several weeks with the Internet Engineering Task Force, which is overseeing the creation of standards for a protocol. Mr. Dym called it "a big-time irony" that Microsoft was releasing its instant-messaging protocol, since it has jealously guarded the source code for its operating systems and software programs. But Rob Bennett, vice president for marketing at MSN, Microsoft's on-line division, said the comparison was unfair. He said Microsoft's willingness to publish the protocol was consistent with a policy to make its software widely "interoperable." The Internet Engineering Task Force praised Microsoft. The move will help "in informing our development of robust, open protocols for Internet-wide interoperability in this area," wrote Vijay Saraswat and Dave Marvit, who are leading the standards committee. In another front in the instant-messaging battle, Microsoft officials said today that they had identified and reprimanded an employee who used a false identity to send a message discrediting America Online to a computer security expert. The employee sent a message under the name Phil Bucking of Bucking Consulting, but the security expert, Richard Smith, traced the message back to Microsoft. Today the company confirmed that the message had come from an employee, who had stepped forward to confess. Mr. Bennett declined to say what disciplinary action had been taken, but defended the employee as having tried to do the "right thing" by publicizing what Microsoft contends is a security flaw in America Online's system. "This is a case of good intentions and bad execution," he said. In the early 1990's, Microsoft dismissed an employee for anonymously posting criticisms of I.B.M.'s competing operating system on on-line bulletin boards.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
DOWNTIME;
New Ways to Play MP3 Music, Without Plugs or Speakers
body: WHEN the first portable MP3 player appeared on the market last year, it looked like some shrew-size mammal living in the shadows of the thundering dinosaurs of cassette and compact disk players: humble enough but poised to evolve into the planet's dominant species. Now other companies have joined Rioport, a new sudsidiary of Diamond Multimedia Systems, in the market for ultraportable, chip-based music players. They are cleverly designed, Walkman-like devices (mini-computers, really) that are the size of pagers, each one slightly different. They download music from a computer and store it on a RAM chip, which plays it back through headphones. This year Samsung released a series of players in Korea called the Yepp. Major consumer electronics companies like Casio and Thomson Multimedia are expected to develop players for the North American markets soon. "They are the hottest new thing in portable audio players," said Amy Hill, spokeswoman for the Consumer Electronics Manufacturers Association. "Every teen-ager I know wants one of these things, and older people do, too." Forrester Research, an Internet consulting firm, projects that sales of the players will reach about 1 million units by the end of this year and anticipates a surge to 32 million units by 2003. The rapidly increasing popularity of devices that can capture and replay music found on the Internet has often been described as nothing less than a revolution, driving a new kind of E-commerce as well as raising fears of copyright violation. Certainly there is enough music, some free and most a credit-card transaction away, available for on-line downloads. More is becoming available every day, much of it in the MP3 format. Music CD's can also be used to create MP3 files. But freeing listeners from the computer has long been considered vital if downloadable music is to be embraced by mainstream consumers. "The players are crucial as a way of getting the music off of the PC," said Joe Butt, director of consumer technology research at Forrester. "Sitting at your computer and listening to downloaded music was a big yawn." The chief advantage of hand-held MP3 players is that they do not depend on tape cassettes or whirling optical disks to play recorded music. They have no moving parts, making them extremely mobile, skip-resistant and gentle on batteries. And while improvements are certain to be made as these portable players evolve, the newest offerings are worth a close look. But they do have disadvantages. They are relatively expensive, with list prices from $169 to $299.95. Playback time is limited, usually no more than an hour. And the sound, while improving, still lacks the power and richness of music heard on most CD and minidisk players. Most of the players have limited storage; if the memory is full, users must erase what is stored there before they can add more music or other audio input. And to use these new machines, you must be able to link them to a computer. Computers get the music, or other recorded sounds like the spoken word, usually by downloading it in highly compressed, high-fidelity audio formats. Downloading music into the computer and transferring it to the player takes far more time and effort than popping a CD into a portable player. Just as important, users must know enough about computers to master software programs, usually on CD-ROM's included with the players, that permit the players and computers to communicate. Like the players themselves, some of the programs work better and more easily than others. The quality of the software can be just as important as the model of player. The Rio PMP500, expected to be on store shelves late this fall, is the only second-generation player on the market. It is a re-engineered update of last year's Rio PMP300 (the first MP3 player on the market) and at $269 costs about $100 more than its parent did when it went to market last November. The new Rio also has a 64-megabyte internal memory, twice as much as the old Rio. With an additional removable flash memory card, the memory can be expanded to 96 megabytes. A typical five-minute high-quality music selection takes about five megabytes of memory. In terms of design, the Rio 500's hardened plastic case appears more durable than its predecessor. Rioport has replaced the old Rio's confusing array of buttons, arranged in a circle, with a few well-placed, recessed buttons. The new player also features a slightly larger display screen that is backlit so that the helpful playback information, like the lengths and names of tracks, can be read in low light. A key feature, found only on the new Rio, is a speedy Universal Serial Bus line to transfer audio files from computers. The player's software comes in Mac and PC versions. And the player itself comes in three different finishes -- conservative silver, translucent teal and translucent purple. Like most of the players, the Rio 500 has a voice recorder and is capable of playing multiple audio formats like those used for Audible's books on tape. But while the new Rio is capable of playing at much higher volume than the old one, its overall sound still tends to be tinny. The Rave MP ($269) by Sensory Science is a distinctively hourglass-shaped MP3 player and voice recorder that has 64 megabytes of internal memory. Like the Rio 500, it has a slot for additional memory. Like the Rio 500, the Rave MP operates on a single AA battery and has a large LCD screen.. Unlike any other player on the market, the Rave doubles as a rudimentary personal digital assistant. It includes a clock and can store as many as 128,000 telephone numbers or more than 13,000 pages of text. Like most players, the Rave connects to computers by a cable plugged into the PC's printer port. Its software is hardly intuitive, but once it is mastered, converting compact disk music into MP3 files or downloading audio files from the Internet takes only a few minutes on a Pentium class computer with at least a 56K modem connection. Transferring the music takes about 30 to 40 seconds for a 5-minute selection. The Rave can be clunky to use, especially its horseshoe-shaped array of buttons. Some of its display icons and indicators for things like battery life and volume settings are too small to be of much real use. The overall sound is adequate and best when heard through Sennheiser MX4 Audiophile Earbuds that are packaged with some of the Rave players. (All the MP3 players come with some kind of headphones.) Half the size of a shirt pocket, the Nomad is Creative Labs' long-awaited entry into the portable media player arena. The machine has a retro-forward look, bearing a striking resemblance to the communicator device from the original "Star Trek" television series. The Nomad is finely engineered with a row of tiny buttons along its smooth sides. A liquid crystal screen the size of a quarter on the front smartly lets listeners know what tracks they are listening to by name and performer. But it is the sound that really sets the Nomad apart from the competition. Music heard on the player is rich, full and detailed. The Nomad is also distinctive in the way it links to the computer. It uses a docking station that connects by cable to the computer's printer port and doubles as a recharger for the two AAA nickel-metal hydride batteries the device uses. The software is fairly simple to use and works smoothly. Unfortunately, the Nomad comes with only 32 megabytes of internal memory. But it also comes with a 32-megabyte flash memory card for a total of 64 megabytes. Like most players it can record up to four hours of speech. Unlike most players, however, the Nomad has an FM radio tuner. I-Jam by I-Jam Multimedia, released last week and sold only on the Internet, is the newest of the MP3 players. Covered with rubberized skin that comes in 10 colors from dark gray to plumlike purple, it is also by far the smallest -- about three-quarters the size of a standard computer mouse. Yet despite its small size, it is capable of a big sound and has lots of features. It includes an FM tuner and treble and bass tone controls, and it is compatible with both PC's and Macs. It comes with 32 megabytes of storage, on two 16-megabyte Scandisk memory cards about the size of postage stamps. The I-Jam can hold only one card at a time, meaning that it gives only 16 minutes of playback of near CD-quality music. The I-Jam comes in a range of models, priced from $199 to $299.95. As with all the players, industry experts say, the price is certain to drop as more are sold and the cost of flash memory drops. "These kinds of electronics are deflationary," said Ms. Hill of the electronics manufacturers association. "As time goes on the players will offer more and better features for less money." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos/Chart  Rave MP Maker: Sensory Science Price: $269 Storage capacity: 64 megabytes on board, expandable to 96 MB for 96 minutes of near CD-quality music playback and more than four hours of voice recording with built-in microphone. Power: One AA alkaline battery. Computer connection: Cable to PC parallel port. Chief assets: Personal digital assistant features.  I-Jam Maker: I-Jam Multimedia Price: $199 to $299.95 Storage capacity: None on board, two 16-MB Multimedia cards for 16 minutes of near CD-quality music playback from each card. No voice recorder. Power: Two AAA alkaline batteries. Computer connection: Separate Multimedia card reader plugged by cable into PC parallel port. Chief assets: Small size, FM tuner, good sound.  Rio PMP500 Maker: Rioport Price: $269 Storage capacity: 64 megabytes on board, expandable to 96 megabytes for 96 minutes of near CD-quality music playback and more than four hours of voice recording with built-in microphone. Power: One AA alkaline battery. Computer connection: Universal Serial Bus cable to PC and Macintosh. Chief assets: PC and Mac compatible, large screen, ease of use.  Nomad Maker: Creative Labs Price: $169 to $249 Storage capacity: 32 megabytes on board and 32 MB on removable flash memory card for 64 minutes of near CD-quality music and four hours of voice recording with built-in microphone. Power: Two rechargeable AAA NiMH or alkaline batteries with an estimated playback time of five hours. Computer connection: Docking station plugged by cable to a PC parallel port. Chief assets: Excellent sound reproduction, FM radio tuner, ease of use.  Note: Items are shown slightly larger than actual size. (Tony Cenicola for The New York Times)

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Taking Internet Music To the Living Room
body: For those tired of listening to their MP3 collections through computer speakers or the headphones of a portable player, there is a way to transport the Internet music experience to the living room. Netdrives, in Ithaca, N.Y., has developed a compact disk player for home stereo systems that can play traditional CD's and disks recorded in the MP3 file compression format that is popular among Internet music aficionados. The company says the component, called the Brujo (pronounced BREW-hoe), is the first consumer MP3 player that is PC free, meaning that it never needs to be connected to a personal computer. Instead, song files are downloaded from the Internet, then transferred, or "burned," onto a standard recordable CD. "Because of the Brujo, MP3's are no longer limited to computer speakers," said Jennifer Wolfe, the president of Netdrives. The Brujo comes with a remote control. Unlike many commercial CD players, which can hold five or more CD's at once, the Brujo has only one disk tray. But because a standard CD can hold more than 11 hours of MP3 music files there should be no concern about disk swapping unless you are playing a regular CD. Of course, if you intend to make MP3 CDs, you will need a CD recording drive for your computer. So Netdrives sells a companion product called the Burner, a retransferable CD recorder that works with Macintosh and Wintel computers. The devices cost $300 each or $550 when bought together. They are available on the company's Web site at www.netdrives.com.TIM HILCHEY http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Cowboy Poets at Home on the Web
body: WHAT, you may ask, is cowboy poetry? Cowboy poetry is for people who define "deconstruction" as what you do when you break camp, but who find meter and mood and metaphor in the rough beauty of that camp. Cowboy poetry is for people who think The newyorker is someone to feel sorry for and The Paris Review is where The newyorkers go to watch fancy ladies dance the cancan. It is also for people who know better but do not care. It is for people who know that plain and straight does not mean stupid, would rather risk being trite than being untrue and agree with John Ford that if the West did not really happen that way, it should have. "Cowboy poetry is simple, it's to the point, it tells a story and is fun, or thoughtful, or even very sad (and we hope it rhymes)," Michael Schroll wrote by email. "There are a lot of cowboy poets out there, some say 100,000 of us (I wonder about those figures, though; anyone can call themselves a poet) all trying to tell their stories in a simple way that our friends can understand and appreciate." Here, from www.cowboypoems .com, is a tiny sample from Mr. Schroll, who bills himself as Wyoming's resident cowboy poet: The cowgirl looked into his eyes He took her breath away. She knew he rode for X BAR 9 Her words he couldn't say. The Cowboy Cattle-Log is a mix of Western music, literature, tourism and merchandise links based in Recluse, Wyo., including Dry Crik Press and Cattle Call Magazine (cattle-log .com) Cattle Call has a Featured Poet page. This is from "Fallin' Asleep" by Fred Engel: Late in the evenin', when the Sun's gone down, And I'm in my blankets, I've spread on the ground, My mind starts driftin' While lookin' up at the sky, And thoughts cross my mind, That make me wonder why. "I've for a long time written these little stories and these things that rhyme, and then I found out it was called cowboy poetry," Mr. Engel, a cattleman, said by telephone. He says of the poetry, "It's a genuine attempt to keep the undisputed symbol of the American West alive." Mr. Engel reads a poem each week on KPIG radio (107-oink-5 FM) in Freedom, Calif. He guesses that his poem "Attention Vegetarians" got the most response. In 1985, the first Elko, Nev., Cowboy Poetry Gathering was held at the Western Folklife Center. Its Web site, www.westfolk.org, highlights the 1999 gathering in January, with links, history and stories. Users with Real Player can listen to a lot of poetry. Similar gatherings, attracting big audiences, have spread to Alpine, Tex., Riverton, Wyo., Medora, N. D., and many other places. There is poetry about the buffalo soldiers and about rural women. (See Barney Nelson's speech at the Westfolk site on the need for poems "about the ten thousand antelope, wildflowers, redtails and dawns we saw while driving the kids to school.") And there are Irish cowboy poets, like John P. Doran, "the Celtic cowboy." His Web site combines poetry and his day job, outfitting wilderness trips in Washington State (www.cowboypoet.com). Mr. Doran grew up on a ranch in Twisp, Wash., and remembers asking his father if he could learn to play the bagpipes. "I don't see no reason; it's in your heritage," his father told him. He said cowboy poetry is "the same old Irish tradition of telling the story in verse." His personal totem is the coyote: High above the valley floor, where the rocks are sharp and bare, he sits back on his haunches and drinks in the cool night air. He sings a song of freedom, of the wilds and of the night and bestows his nocturnal hymns to a horse-thief moon so bright. Then it made me think that I was him upon that distant hill. For my spirit soared and my heart found peace just to know he's out there still. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: PRAIRIE POETRY -- Several Web sites feature the plain, simple, to-the-point, rhyming verse known as cowboy poetry. Some of the sites, including the Cowboy Cattle-Log, also offer music, travel information and merchandise.

title: AT&T's Planned Mediaone Deal Poses Testfor U.S. Cable Policy
body: As two Federal agencies review the AT&T Corporation's $58 billion bid to buy Mediaone Group, they face the central question of whether the combination is, in essence, too large to block. AT&T executives say the acquisition is needed to establish a cable network so vast and powerful that it will provide high-speed Internet service, cable TV and telephone service that can compete with the regional Bell companies. Those companies have so far kept newcomers from challenging them in their local phone markets. But three consumer groups said today that the cost of opening the local markets was not worth the price and urged the Government to kill the deal because it would permit AT&T to dominate both the cable television industry and the market for high-speed Internet service. In papers filed at the Federal Communications Commission and the Justice Department, the groups asserted that the proposed acquisition would violate a raft of antitrust and telecommunications rules intended to limit concentration of ownership in the cable and other industries. "Regulators should never accept a massive concentration in one market as a condition for increasing local competition in another," Mark N. Cooper, research director for the Consumer Federation of America, said. "This merger breaks all the rules." AT&T's deal for Mediaone, the fourth-largest cable operator, is quickly becoming an important new test case of antitrust policy. It has also prompted a re-examination of the current cable ownership rules, rules that have been suspended for seven years because of litigation between regulators and the industry. While AT&T has recently set out to have some of those rules rewritten, consumer groups maintain that the deal would enable AT&T to dominate two markets. "This merger will result in inflated cable and broadband Internet service prices for consumers and thwart the development of vibrant competition in these markets," the three groups -- Consumers Union, the Consumer Federation of America and the Media Access Project -- wrote in a letter to the Justice Department today. In response, AT&T executives reasserted the central argument they made in May when the deal was announced: By growing so quickly, the company will benefit millions of telephone customers nationwide by using the newly acquired cable lines to break into local telephone markets that have been dominated by a handful of Bell companies fiercely resistant to competition. "It's an extreme stretch to suggest that there's any antitrust issue here," said James W. Cicconi, general counsel and head of government relations at AT&T. "There is no competitor to the services we are offering that is being taken out here. Far from it: the whole purpose is to provide local competition." "We will be providing competition where it doesn't now exist," he said. Federal communications guidelines prohibit a single company from holding a 5 percent active interest or 10 percent passive interest in companies whose wires come close to 30 percent or more of the nation's homes. But seven years ago, a Federal judge threw out some of those rules in a case in which AT&T is not involved, and the F.C.C. voluntarily stayed the enforcement of those guidelines. That case is now on appeal, and agency officials say they are reviewing cable-ownership rules, a review they hope to complete before deciding about the AT&T deal. Consumer groups have contended that after the merger with Mediaone, AT&T's cable market penetration would reach 57 percent of the nation's households.
