Executives at AT&T, which completed its acquisition of Tele-Communications Inc., the No. 2 cable operator, earlier this year, have said they think the market penetration would not be anywhere near that level. But they have also told analysts they think it would be more than the 30 percent permitted under the rules that have been suspended. The company has asked the F.C.C. both to raise the 30 percent threshold and to change its ownership attribution rules so that a small ownership interest in a cable company would count less than it now does. At the Justice Department, Federal antitrust rules written during the Reagan and Bush Administrations generally make any proposed merger suspect if it increases an economic index used by the Government by 50 to 100 points. But an analysis by the three consumer groups says that the AT&T-Mediaone deal would raise the index, the Hirschman Herfindahl Index, in many markets by 700 to 3,000 points, even including proposed spinoffs that AT&T has already announced. "AT&T's proposed acquisition is a blatant blatant violation of our nation's antitrust laws and our nation's competition laws," said Gene Kimmelman, co-director of the Washington office of Consumers Union. Mr. Cicconi of AT&T disputed the consumer groups' figures. He also said they had distorted the true size of the market and failed to recognize that AT&T competes with other high-speed Internet services offered by the regional Bells and with satellite broadcasting companies. To block a merger on antitrust grounds, "one has to show that market power is being used to constrain competitors, which clearly is not the case here," Mr. Cicconi said.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Business Travel;
It's possible to track airlines flights on a nearly real-time basis through the Internet.
body: AS the number of airline delays in the unitedstates soars, travelers can go on line to track their flights or those of colleagues. Trip.com (www.trip.com) offers a Flighttracker service that lets travelers check the speed and altitude of a specific flight, the direction the aircraft is heading, and the flight's exact departure and arrival times. This information, which is provided by the Federal Aviation Administration and updated by Trip.com every seven seconds, is displayed either on a topographical map or in a text message. Trip.com also offers an email flight notification service, which automatically sends an email to as many as three people with the exact arrival time of a traveler's flight; before departing, travelers can request that this email be delivered. Both the tracking and email notification services are free. Dimensions International, a privately held software company based in Alexandria, Va., has developed an Internet-based software system called Flight Explorer that uses a topographical map to display all commercial flights in the unitedstates air system, plus select general aviation flights. The software can also track specific flights, and offers detailed air traffic control data as it tracks them. In addition, it can simultaneously display all the flights of one airline, or all flights departing from one city. Flight Explorer updates its information every 10 seconds, also using F.A.A. data. The software rents for $9.95 for 10 hours of use a month; additional hours are extra. Dimensions International's Web site is www.dimen-intl.com.  Hotel Update Several new or newly purchased hotels in newyork City are offering discounted rates through late summer or early fall. The new Bentley Hotel, a converted office building at 500 East 62d Street at York Avenue, is offering introductory rates through Sept. 6 of $125 a night for a standard room, $140 to $205 a night for a room with a king-size bed, and $325 for a suite. From Sept. 7 through Nov. 30, rates will range from $225 to $325. All rates include breakfast. The 197-room Bentley features telephones with voicemail and computer hookups, cable TV and CD players, and a roof-top restaurant with views of the East River. The hotel is owned by Amsterdam Hospitality Group, a privately held newyork hotel company. The new 92-suite Phillips Club, opening Sept. 1 at 155 West 66th Street, between Amsterdam Avenue and Broadway, is offering introductory rates of $270 for junior suites and $300 for one-bedroom suites through Oct. 31; rates will start at $400 on Nov. 1. Junior suites contain kitchenettes and separate sitting areas, while one-bedroom suites have full kitchens and living rooms. All suites contain dual-line phones with computer hookups, high-speed Internet access and fax machines with dedicated lines. Guests also have free use of the nearby Reebok Sports Club. The hotel is adjacent to 96 extended-stay apartments also operating under the Phillips Club name; all are owned by Millennium Partners, a newyork real estate developer. The former Ritz-Carlton Hotel, at 112 Central Park South between Sixth and Seventh Avenues, has been taken over by Bass Hotels and Resorts, and renamed the Central Park Inter-Continental newyork. The hotel is offering a weekday room rate of $199 a night through Sept. 12; from Sept. 13 through Dec. 31, rooms will start at $269 during the week. The hotel also has a special rate of $199 a night, good Thursdays through Sundays until Sept. 12, which includes 50 percent off all hotel services like food, parking and telephone charges. On Sept. 13, this weekend rate rise to $249, but will continue to include the 50 percent discount on services.  Airline Update AMR's American Airlines is introducing DVD video players for movies in first class on its Miami-Buenos Aires MD-11 service beginning Sept. 1. The devices will then be phased into first-class service on other international flights and eventually into business class on international and unitedstates transcontinental flights. Passengers will receive as many as 20 disks of popular films. UAL's United Airlines sent a letter apologizing for air traffic control delays to participants in its frequent-flier program who travel a minimum of 25,000 miles annually and who flew into, out of or through O'Hare International Airport in Chicago from April through early August. The carrier also is giving each of these travelers a bonus of 2,500 miles for inconvenience caused by the delays. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
When it comes to using the Internet to reach consumers, the operative word is 'potential.'
body: ADVERTISING on the Internet, like most uses of this new medium, is still in the early stages of a long and presumably fruitful evolution. In other words, it is long on potential but, so far, short on success stories. Part of the problem is that although the Internet has gathered a mainstream audience, many companies have yet to figure out how to use it effectively for advertising. As a result, they have been reluctant to pour money into Web ads: just 1 percent of the $200 billion spent on advertising last year was spent on line. According to a report to be released today, however, that figure is about to rise. Jupiter Communications, an Internet research firm, projects $11.5 billion in spending for on-line advertising in 2003, compared with $2.1 billion in 1998. Jupiter projects that in four years the Internet will rank fourth among advertising media in total ad spending, jumping ahead of cable television, magazines and yellow pages and vying with radio for the No. 3 spot behind broadcast television and newspapers. The report follows similar projections made last week by Forrester Research, an Internet consulting firm. The Jupiter report is based on projections of growth in both overall advertising spending and the on-line audience. And the company's research indicates that two crucial players in traditional advertising -- car makers and consumer goods manufacturers -- are finally warming up to the Internet. The report predicts that in 2003, automotive companies will devote 13 percent of their advertising budgets to the Internet, compared with 5 percent this year, and consumer goods makers like Procter & Gamble will spend 7 percent of their ad budgets on the Internet, compared with 2 percent this year. Jupiter predicts that the on-line audience in 2003 will be 64 million unitedstates households, compared with 38 million now. But according to Rich LeFurgy, chairman of the Internet Advertising Bureau, an industry trade group, expectations for higher Web spending also reflect fundamental shifts in the perception of the Internet as an advertising medium. "In 1995 and '96, advertisers were putting up sites for their products, and looking at it as a sales channel," Mr. LeFurgy said. "But that was confusing for advertisers who couldn't sell their products on line, like soft drink makers, so that was a dead end." Not only do consumer packaged goods companies lack the expertise -- and in some cases, the desire -- to sell directly to consumers over the Internet, but consumers would not be likely to go to Coke's on-line store, for example, to buy soda, he said. "These companies couldn't figure out why they should be advertising on line," Mr. LeFurgy said. More recently, however, companies have recognized the Web's potential for brand advertising, as opposed to direct sales. So instead of sending consumers to their own Web sites to buy goods, companies like Procter & Gamble are spending money on branding campaigns to build awareness. And through cooperative advertising efforts, they can send consumers to, say, an on-line grocery store where buyers can find their products alongside the products of the other cooperating marketers, Mr. LeFurgy said. As more companies migrate toward brand-based advertising, they are also looking less at the number of people who actually click on a Web ad, Mr. LeFurgy said. He said that a user's propensity to click on an ad is not necessarily the best way to gauge its effectiveness in building brand awareness. Marketing strategies must also change if companies are to succeed on line, said Patrick Keane, an analyst with Jupiter. The tendency of many companies to view their Web initiatives as somehow separate from their core businesses has helped perpetuate the theory that Internet advertising does not work, Mr. Keane said. When marketers do set aside money to advertise on line, he said, "their on-line campaigns too often look different and feel different from their off-line campaigns -- and that's just not an effective way to manage a campaign." He added: "Advertisers are going to realize that they have to integrate their campaigns across all media," instead of merely adding a Web site address to "a TV ad or whatever else they're doing." Furthermore, Mr. Keane said, "the fragmented nature of media consumption means marketers will need to hit consumers at multiple media points." Mr. LeFurgy also noted that an abundance of new Internet businesses rely on ad revenue. In recent months, Internet service providers and PC makers have used advertising revenue as a means to lower their prices, giving consumers the chance to get cheaper machines and Internet access if they agree to look at advertisements. Meanwhile, as Internet advertising builds momentum, spending on other media may suffer, Jupiter predicts. Mr. Keane said the Internet's anticipated cannibalism of other media is, in fact, taking place as people spend more time on line. Internet users spent an average of 7.1 hours a week on line in 1998, according to Jupiter, which predicts that will increase to 10.2 hours a week in 2003. "And they'll use other media less because there's only so much time in the day," Mr. Keane said. "People have been a little myopic about on-line advertising, just looking at the fact that the dollars are smaller," he added. "It's not about the numbers. It's about how the Internet is reinventing advertising."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Commerce Dept. Seeks to Close Government Information Service
body: For almost 50 years a small agency of the Commerce Department has done business in the resale of Government documents and reports. Now the department is proposing to shut down the service, saying it is no longer viable because of the wealth of free information on the Internet. The announcement of plans to close the agency, the National Technical Information Service, comes just three months after the Clinton Administration rejected its plan to begin a fee-based Internet search service designed to help people more easily find and buy the Government documents the agency sells. On the same day that the service, usgovsearch.com, was announced, the Administration halted it. And last Thursday, Commerce Secretary William M. Daley said he would ask Congress to close the service and transfer its extensive archives to the Library of Congress. "This way, the American people can find the documents they want via search engines that currently exist -- and the more powerful ones being created -- and download them for free," the statement from the Commerce Department said. "We will propose legislation to Congress next month to achieve these ends." Although the agency sells some of its reports for thousands of dollars each, the increased use of the Internet by Government agencies to make free documents available to the public has resulted in declining sales, Mr. Daley said. He pointed to a recent report from the Commerce Department, "The Emerging Digital Economy II," which is available free on the department's Web site but costs $27 if requested through the information agency. The decision was lauded by advocacy groups that have pushed the Government to post more reports and public information on line. "We think this is great news," said Ari Schwartz, a policy analyst at the Center for Democracy and Technology, a nonprofit organization based in Washington. "We think that this shows that the Commerce Department is really looking at the Internet and realizes what it can mean for public access to Government information." The agency has 250 employees, who Mr. Daley said would be put on a priority list for re-employment within the Government if Congress approves the plan to close the service. The agency was turned into a self-sustaining agency during the Reagan Administration, meaning it was charged with financing itself through its sales. Mr. Daley said the agency had not operated at a profit since 1993, and from 1995 to 1998 registered more than $5 million in operating losses. The plan for a fee-based Internet search service was intended as a joint venture with Northern Light Technology, an Internet database company in Cambridge, Mass., which was going to split the profits with the Commerce Department agency. It has since begun the service on its own. http://www.nytimes.com

title: MCI Net Snag Could Drive Small Providers Out of Business
body: The 10-day partial shutdown of MCI Worldcom's high-speed data network took a cataclysmic toll on dozens and possibly hundreds of small Internet service providers who were forced to close altogether last week. Some say they may go out of business as a result. These mom-and-pop players, along with more than a quarter of all Internet service providers nationally, rely on MCI to route subscribers onto the Internet. The network problem also took its toll on regional and national Internet service providers, including America Online, which said yesterday that two million subscribers from its combined America Online and Compuserve services may have been affected. But small service providers felt the biggest impact because unlike their larger counterparts they typically cannot afford a backup -- that is, a contract with a second major network company. So when MCI went down, they went down with it. "For our industry, this is a killer -- a company killer," said A. K. Jordan, president of Intellitech, a service provider in Highland Park, N.J., with about 500 dial-up customers. Mr. Jordan said that starting on Saturday, Aug. 7, the company's subscribers were no longer able to get access to the World Wide Web and were able to get email only from other Intellitech customers. He said he was told that MCI was assuring customers that the problem was a result of congestion and that the system would be up and running in two hours -- a message he passed along to subscribers who called to complain. "We came out looking like liars and incompetents," he said. When the situation did not improve, Mr. Jordan and his business partners took the extraordinary step of telephoning roughly one-quarter of their subscribers to explain the situation and to ask them not to quit the service. He said he now planned to give his customers a free month of access. His situation is not unique, according to DataXchange, a Washington-based company that buys Internet access wholesale from MCI and sells it to small providers, like Mr. Jordan's Intellitech. Mark Stutz, a spokesman for RMI.Net, the Denver parent of DataXchange, said that of the 150 small service providers to which it resells MCI services, 66 "lost their networks completely." Mr. Stutz estimated that because of those failures alone, some 250,000 subscribers lost Net access. He said that some of the providers said they had had so many subscriber cancellations they might go out of business. "It doesn't get any worse than this," Mr. Stutz said. "It's hard to imagine a worse-case scenario for our industry." An MCI Worldcom spokeswoman, Linda Laughlin, said the company would offer customers two free days of Internet access for each day they had been unable to use MCI's network to get access. Ms. Laughlin characterized the partial shutdown as an "unsatisfactory" performance and said MCI Worldcom expected it would take "several weeks" to regain the trust of its customers. Some industry analysts said MCI might be underestimating the public- relations toll. Jeanne M. Schaff, senior analyst with Forrester Research, a Cambridge, Mass.-based market research firm, speculated that "most" of the stranded Internet service providers would look to one of the other major Network providers for access to the Net. For now, though, MCI is the biggest player. According to a survey released in July from Cahners In-Stat, a San Jose, Calif., market research firm, MCI provides national backbone access to 40.9 percent of national service providers and to 23.6 percent of small and regional providers -- defined as those serving fewer than 25 area codes. Most, if not all, larger and regional providers rely on more than one company for backbone Net access. For example, Earthlink Network, a Pasadena, Calif.-based service with 1.4 million subscribers, employs MCI and six other backbone providers, including AT&T, I.B.M. and Sprint, and thus experienced only minor headaches last week, said Steve Dougherty, director of technology acquisition for Earthlink. He said the company simply rerouted traffic that would have gone over the MCI network to another provider. At America Online and its subsidiary Compuserve about 2 million of 20 million subscribers were vulnerable to the network failure over the weekend because the primary access numbers they use to dial into the Internet rely on the MCI backbone. In most of those instances, America Online urged customers to try a different access number; however, in the case of 50 communities, representing roughly 500,000 subscribers, there was no second access number available, the company said. For those customers, America Online created a toll-free number. However, some subscribers might not have been apprised of the change since they were unable to sign onto the Internet in the first place to receive an update.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Finalists Named For Internet Work
body: Three Internet-related companies in newyork have narrowed reviews on accounts. Newspage.com named four finalists in a review for its first off-line branding account, with billings estimated at $10 million to $15 million. They are Chadwick Communications in newyork; TFA/Leo Burnett Technology Group in Boston, part of the Leo Burnett Company, and Grey Advertising in newyork. In addition, Pro Media Inc. in Natick, Mass., will compete for the off-line media buying and promotion duties. Real Media Inc., an Internet marketing company, named four finalists in a review for its trade account, with billings estimated at $2 million to $3 million. Real Media and M& C Saatchi in newyork, hired in September, parted ways over what were described as creative differences. The finalists, all in newyork, are DeVito/Verdi, Hanft Byrne Raboy & Partners, Mezzina/Brown and Stein Rogan & Partners. A decision is expected by the end of August. Lot 21 in San Francisco remains the Real Media interactive agency. And the Gay Financial Network Inc., which operates a Web site, Gfn.com, aimed at gay men and lesbians, named three finalists in a review to find the first agency to handle its account, with billings estimated at almost $2 million. Matthew L. Papa, associate marketing manager at Gfn.com in newyork, identified the finalists, all in newyork, as: Interactive8, Mad Dogs and Englishmen and Prime Access. A decision is expected in a month, he said.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Welcome to College. Now Meet Our Sponsor. - Correction Appended
body: Starting today, when students at Appalachian State University check their email or course outlines on line, they will be looking at advertising from dozens of companies including Amazon.com, Dell Computer and an apartment-locator service called SpringStreet. Something similar will be happening soon at Villanova University, the University of Memphis, the University of Oregon, the University of Idaho and more than 500 other institutions that have signed up commercial companies to run campus Web sites and email services. "Christmas '98 was the first 'E-Christmas'; we think this is the first 'E-back-to-school,' " said Chad Muir, chief executive of Campus Pipeline, a company that says it has agreements to provide Web services to 420 colleges and universities, including Appalachian State, at little or no cost. While at many universities students continue to use Web pages that the universities have created and paid for themselves, at these 500 institutions advertisers will be paying the bills. And the placement of advertising on what some regard as the purest area of the Internet -- the educational domain -- has spurred a heated debate. The issue is what place advertising should have in the college environment, real or virtual, particularly in public institutions. Some educators are alarmed at what they see as a crass commercial intrusion, yet administrators and others say that faced with financial constraints, they have little choice. "There is no place for commercial advertisements within the precincts of any school that takes its educational mission seriously," said Scott Rice, an English professor at San Jose State University who is researching the effects of commercialization on education. Jeff Williams, director of information-technology services at Appalachian State, said he had heard such arguments. But that is not stopping Appalachian State -- a public institution in Boone, N.C. with 12,500 students -- from adopting the advertising model and avoiding the need to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars to create the Web sites on its own. "Some people will say that it's not ethical to advertise," Mr. Williams said. "Given our druthers, we'd rather not ourselves. But it's a pretty attractive model. We'll live with it." Mr. Williams has rolled out the program by instructing 2,500 first-year students at Appalachian State to log into the system this week. They will be among the first in the country to experience such advertising-based pages on a university Web site. Each page includes a square advertisement -- what the company likes to call a sponsorship -- in the top right-hand corner. A page labeled Campus Central has information about campus events as well as paid advertisements -- not labeled as such -- that link to businesses offering textbooks, financial aid information, educational testing services, auctions and housing. A Web Shopping section will provide additional links to on-line retailers. Campus Pipeline will also try to learn more about what is essentially a captive audience. When students first log into campus Web sites, they will be asked to fill out an optional form about their interests. If they do, they will receive product pitches in their email. Faculty members at Appalachian State are just learning of the deal -- and several are voicing concerns about both commercialization and student privacy. "We're throwing our freshmen to the wolves," said Andrew Koch, an associate professor of political science. "The university has become a shill for the corporate community." "This tells volumes," he continued, "about the university, its funding, and the business mindset that has taken over." But as campuses struggle with the costs of technology -- and the constant need to upgrade it -- such deals are becoming more and more attractive, administrators say. Creating an internal Web service, known as an intranet, that seamlessly pulls information from multiple data bases around campus could cost as much as $2 million for a midsize public university, if not more. Public universities, especially, are finding it difficult to pay such costs while many are facing tightening budgets. Campus Pipeline, a start-up company based in Salt Lake City, began approaching colleges late last year. It has investments from Sun Microsystems, Dell Computer and McKinsey & Company, among others, and says it intends to bring 100 of its 420 clients on line by the end of the fall term. In addition to advertising revenue, it plans to earn commissions on student purchases from Web sites to which it provides links. In addition to Campus Pipeline, at least one other company, called YouthStream, is offering similar services, and says it has signed up more than 100 colleges and universities. YouthStream, based in newyork City, has opened a site called MyBytes.Com, which provides students with on-line calendars, materials to supplement their classes, financial-aid information, and Web pages for courses if professors choose to use them. Each page includes an advertisement or a link to an electronic shopping area. Some students are expecting to be practically awash in promotions as soon as they log in to their college's Web site. "I don't see anything wrong with it, unless it gets out of hand," said Ken Greene, a junior at the University of Memphis. "That's all the Web is, is lots of advertising." But the concept is a striking departure for most institutions of higher education. Academia, after all, is where the Internet grew up, and for years, as the Web has become increasingly commercialized, colleges have kept their distance, priding themselves on creating an on-line presence that is free of promotion. This summer, however, colleges have been bombarded by pitches from companies that are eager to gain electronic access to the Internet-loving student market. Many are approaching athletic departments, hoping to strike deals to promote apparel or soft drinks on pages about sports teams. Policy makers at some colleges are even being approached by administrators on their own campuses who want to provide Web links to on-line stores like Amazon.com, so that the college can take in commissions. "The academy is not a billboard community," said Margaret A. Miller, president of the American Association for Higher Education. "But it is also the case that the academy is subject to the same economic strains as the rest of the world." The result, Dr. Miller said, is that the costs of technology create a "blurring line" on the issue. At Appalachian State, Mr. Williams said, "There is no way we could have done it ourselves." As one of Campus Pipeline's first colleges, Appalachian State has not yet had to pay anything for the services. Other colleges and universities may have to pay for installation, which could cost as much as $32,000, but that sum administrators say is still far less than the cost of designing and maintaining a system. Besides, Mr. Williams said, colleges like Appalachian State do not have much choice. Students now expect to be able to fill out financial-aid forms and register for classes on line. Colleges that do not offer such services may lose their ability to attract students. A similar approach was taken almost a decade ago by Channel One, a program started by the Whittle Communications company that supplied middle schools and high schools with television sets and paid for them with commercials. It is still derided by some educators as a means of pushing advertising in front of captive students. In this latest example, the executives of the Web-based companies see their approach as nothing more than a continuation of a trend that has already become a big part of higher education. Public and private universities of all sizes have already turned over dining services to Marriott, student unions to Taco Bell, copying centers to Kinkos. "Schools are increasingly getting out of specialized services that they would rather outsource," said Harlan Peltz, YouthStream's chief executive. Yet many educators say they want a line to be drawn, particularly when it comes to spaces -- on or off line -- where students are supposed to be learning and exploring. Thomas Ehrlich, a former president of Indiana University, said he was troubled by the idea of advertisements on sites where professors hold on-line office hours or post syllabuses. "I think that is much too intrusive," said Mr. Ehrlich, who is now a fellow at the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching. Other colleges with large endowments, like most Ivy League universities, have declined to have commercially sponsored Web sites. Many of them say that they have the resources to create on-line services like admissions and registration without outside help. That may lead students at less selective colleges to be exposed to a barrage of advertising, while students at elite colleges are insulated from it. "You create a different set of haves and have-nots, so to speak," said Jose-Marie Griffiths, chief information officer at the University of Michigan, where the idea of having commercially sponsored Web pages was rejected. For those that have signed up, protecting students' privacy has been a large concern. As Campus Pipeline and YouthStream collect information about students, university administrators say that they want to make sure that the information is not sold or traded to other companies. Susan Hilton, an assistant director in the computing center at the University of Oregon, said that her campus had been working with Campus Pipeline to whittle down the list of questions it asks students and to keep the information confidential. "That took a while to make that point," she said. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  A front-page article yesterday about universities that have signed up commercial companies to operate campus Web sites referred incorrectly to an agreement between the University of Oregon and one such company, Campus Pipeline. While the university has agreed to test Campus Pipeline's software with a small number of students, it has not contracted to adopt the software fully or have the company run the campus site. Correction-Date: August 18, 1999, Wednesday Graphic   Photo: An Appalachian State University Web page with advertising. Such ads have become a subject of dispute. (pg. A1)

title: A Big Step Toward Electronic City Services
body: An effort to fix newyork City's Year 2000 computer problems has yielded a technological bonus fit for the new millennium: a new high-speed network, installed this summer, that will eventually allow newyorkers to go on line with a computer to do just about anything now done by standing on line at a government office. Within the next five years, city officials hope, individuals and businesses will be able to use the Internet to pay parking fines or taxes, obtain copies of licenses and birth certificates, bid on municipal contracts, submit construction plans and apply for all manner of permits. The groundwork for all of this was laid in late June, when technicians shut down nine different computer systems that had controlled all of the city government's finance and accounting operations for more than 20 years. The hardware running the systems was antiquated, officials said; the software was almost certain to crash at the start of next year. A week later, the technicians brought on line a single, centralized financial management system running over a vast new telecommunications and computing network. That transition has caused its share of problems and complaints, including some late payments to vendors. Growing pains aside, city officials said, the network offers untold possibilities for speeding the delivery of services and information. "It's sort of like building roads before you know everything that is going to run over them," said Robert W. Townsend, the executive director of the city's Financial Information Services Agency, which has spent the last six weeks fine-tuning the network. The network will eventually connect internal city agency systems to the city's public Web site -- NYC Link. The Web site (www.ci.nyc.ny.us) has offered public access since July 1996 to an array of information about government services and events, the ability to obtain government forms and a way to register complaints or communicate with officials through email. But like other cities across the country, newyork has ambitious plans to expand its on-line services. The city is already working with I.B.M. to develop a one-stop, on-line city payment center, to be called NYCSERV. The center will allow users to pay bills from computers at home and work or at public libraries, and from kiosks in government buildings, said Avi Duvdevani, First Deputy Commissioner of the city's Department of Information Technology and Telecommunications. "If you owed a parking ticket," he said, "had tax bills, owed for Department of Health restaurant violations, because you happened to be a restaurateur, and also had a D.E.P. violation for filthying up the street, all those bills could be paid, not in one transaction, but under one umbrella session on the Web. And you could pick and choose which ones you want to pay." Not only will this be more convenient for constituents, officials said, but the city also eventually stands to save millions of dollars in overhead costs -- from paper forms and other supplies to staffing. City officials expect the demand for these electronic services to be huge. Pages on the existing Web site were viewed 17 million times over the last year. An exact measurement of the number of individuals who called up the site was not available. The new high-speed network is already serving its most basic purpose: running the city's new financial management system, which has completely updated the administering of the city's $38 billion annual budget. But with more than 4,000 users at 125 different city offices across all five boroughs, putting the system in place has not been easy. Payments to hundreds of city vendors, suppliers, contractors and others, involving virtually every city agency, have been delayed over the last six weeks because the new system performed slower than expected or because city workers were not familiar with the new technology. In some cases, nonprofit agencies that provide foster care and child welfare services under contracts with the city's Administration for Children's Services could not give foster parents their weekly stipends or caseworkers their paychecks. In other cases, contractors working for the city's Department of Design and Construction said they could not meet payrolls or pay for building supplies. There is now a backlog of about 180 payments, said Matthew G. Monahan, a spokesman for the agency. Workers from several departments have been temporarily transferred to help reduce the backlog, he said, and the agency expects to be caught up by Labor Day. The delayed payments, however, represent only a fraction of about 80,000 checks totaling about $6 billion that the system has processed successfully since going on line. And city officials say the deals and any other inevitable glitches are a small price to pay -- on top of the project's $157 million cost -- for a system that, in addition to all of its futuristic possibilities, is completely free of Year 2000 problems. City officials had long known that without the new system or a costly overhaul of the old ones, the city ran the risk of seeing all of its financial operations grind to a halt on Jan. 1. But while the Year 2000 problem has forced expensive overhauls throughout the world, it presented an opportunity in newyork City to replace systems entirely. The Year 2000, or Y2K, problem, stems from computer programming that customarily used two digits in dates to refer to the year. When presented with 00, many computers and programs cannot differentiate between 1900 and 2000. The city's systems had not been updated since 1977 and would have required complex debugging. Instead, the city decided to replace it all -- buying about 3,000 new I.B.M. desktop computers and developing the new financial management software to accomplish what the old systems used to do separately. The move also gives officials at the city's Office of Management and Budget and at the City Comptroller's office, who oversee the budget, swifter access to check on city spending. "To us, the biggest up-front advantage is getting over this Y2K hump," said Stuart Klein, the first deputy director in the Office of Management and Budget and one of the officials who has been overseeing the start-up of the new system. But replacing the system had a major side benefit, he said: a fast new network connecting all of the city's agencies. That network is what will make providing electronic government services possible in the future. The same wires that carry all of the city's financial information will also carry every other imaginable type of city data, from records of health and building code violations to birth and death certificates to license and permit applications. Some of this information is still passed between city agencies by interofficemail. With the ability to share all of this information electronically, the city has quickly set a course for greater automation. Instead of punching traditional timecards or signing a sheet, city employees soon will swipe an identification card or press a thumb to a scanner. Work hours will then be downloaded directly into the payroll system. The system, called Citytime, is just one way that the new network will modernize operations, officials said. The future, said Allan H. Dobrin, the Commissioner of Information Technology and Telecommunications, will be "more of an E-government, where people don't have to go as much to government offices but can access services on line." http://www.nytimes.com

Compressed Data;
New Way to Travel the Web While Leaving Few Footprints
body: Privada Inc. of San Jose, Calif., is betting that when typical consumers become aware of how exposed they are to invasions of privacy on the Internet, they will part with $5 a month for a cloak of anonymity. Depending on a user's computer setup and Internet service provider, a single visit to a Web site, for instance, can often reveal the Internet address assigned to the visitor's computer, the visitor's email address, the browser and operating system being used, and what plug-ins or Active-X controls have been installed. It can give away even more information if the user has not removed the unique serial numbers embedded in Microsoft's Windows 98 operating system and Intel's Pentium III microprocessor. Little wonder that a recent Harris poll for Business Week found that fears of losing privacy were the top reason people decided not to go on line and that among those who do, only 3 out of 10 give valid information when asked to register at a site. Privada plans to unveil a new service today, called Web Incognito, that lets users make all of their Internet activities -- email, on-line chats, Web browsing and even purchases -- completely anonymous. The service works by encrypting the data flowing out of a subscriber's computer and redirecting it to the Privada service after it leaves the Internet service provider. Web Incognito masks the data's origins and sends it on to its intended destination. Responses, like those from Web sites or email recipients, flow back to Privada, which passes them back to the subscriber. The service, which can be switched on and off, also stores the subscriber's "cookies," files that identify the user to Web sites, so it does not interfere with standard Web surfing. Web Incognito differs from other anonymity software in two important ways. It covers all Internet activity, not just Web browsing or email, for instance. And the identity it protects can be shared with police officers who have appropriate warrants. "Our service is for protecting the privacy of consumers, not for hiding criminals or criminal activities," said Barbara A. Bellissimo, Privada's chief executive. While she said the company expected to take some heat from privacy rights groups, she added, "We felt it would be irresponsible not to give law enforcement agencies the information if they have valid warrants." The free software and information about the subscription service are available at http://www.privada.net/.ROB FIXMER http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Privada offers a new anonymity service.

title:
E-Commerce Report;
Conventional retailers are integrating Web sites with stores, improving service in both arenas.
body: TRADITIONAL retailers have spent the last two years watching the Internet play havoc with their businesses. To divine the secrets of the new medium, they have been forced to study their virtual counterparts for clues on how to compete in this radically different arena. Many have sought the counsel of Internet consultants, while others have felt compelled to wade through stacks of dot-com and E-business books -- bought, no doubt, at Amazon.com. Now that some of the faster readers have finished studying, they seem poised to turn the tables on their Internet brethren. Retailers of the so-called bricks-and-mortar variety are plotting their revenge not simply by creating Web sites of their own, but by integrating their Internet operations into their physical stores. Executives say that by mingling the virtual and physical retail environments, they can better serve customers in both. There is, of course, a newly minted buzz phrase associated with this trend -- "clicks and mortar" -- but those in the industry say the transformation has been brewing for a while. "We've been dealing with a lot of companies almost paralyzed with fear about the Internet," said Melissa Bane, an E-commerce analyst with the Yankee Group, an Internet consulting firm. "Some of the smarter ones are starting to realize that it's their game to lose. They already have the customers, and now they can use the Internet in their stores as a tool to expand their share of customers." According to Activmedia Inc., an Internet research firm, 54 percent of companies with on-line and off-line sales operations now report substantial two-way interaction between the two divisions. Analysts and executives say most of that interaction focuses on such things as marketing campaigns, but the strategy is starting to move beyond simply printing the address of the company's Web site on its receipts and shopping bags. For example, Recreational Equipment Inc., an outdoor goods retailer, has placed Internet kiosks in 52 of its 53 stores and has integrated Web access into its cash registers, said Matt Hyde, vice president for on-line sales. The kiosks allow shoppers to look up detailed information on every product that Recreational Equipment carries, regardless of whether that particular item is available in the store. Blocking software bars users from going to sites other than the retailer's (www.rei.com) and its outlet site (www.rei-outlet.com). Meanwhile, cashiers can look up items on line through the Web-enabled registers. "It's just a quantum leap in terms of customer service," Mr. Hyde said. "Say I'm in our Wisconsin store, and I'm looking for a haul bag for a rock-climbing trip to Yosemite. I'm not going to find that in that store. Before, I'd stand in line at customer service, a rep would look it up, and I'd have to know exactly what I wanted for them to be able to help me because chances are they wouldn't be familiar with haul bags. Now, I can look that up with or without a salesperson, I can see pictures with all the product info, and I can buy it at the checkout counter and have it delivered." Anecdotal evidence suggests that Recreational Equipment was the first major retailer to put kiosks into its stores, starting in Seattle, in 1996. Such kiosks are quickly becoming standard fare, however. Companies like Sears, Gap, Compaq Computer and Borders Books, among others, have begun major efforts to give customers a virtual shopping option even as they browse the aisles. "I am sure that 10 years from now, every major retail company will have an Internet-enabled device in the store," said Rick Vanzura, president of Borders Online, who began the bookseller's campaign to install Internet kiosks in each of the company's 270 superstores. Mr. Vanzura, who recently left Borders to join a start-up company, said the Internet effort would cost Borders "in the eight figures," given the technology infrastructure it requires. In the coming months, he said, the store kiosks will allow customers to order not only any of the 700,000 titles in the Borders warehouses, but also out-of-print books, which will be printed and shipped to the customer's home. "It's certainly an expensive proposition," Mr. Vanzura said. "But I'm confident we'll see a return on that investment -- and it won't take decades." David S. Pottruck, co-chief executive of Charles Schwab, said the cost of integrating his company's Internet strategy with its off-line strategy had gone far beyond the price of Internet kiosks. Mr. Pottruck, who said he coined the phrase clicks and mortar in a recent speech, noted that when the company merged its on- and off-line divisions last year and lowered the charge for off-line clients from roughly $65 a trade to $30 (to match the on-line fee), it cost the company between $125 million and $150 million. Beyond that, he said, Schwab had to integrate on-line trading kiosks more fully into its 300 offices, train its advisers to serve customers both on line and off and bolster the company's customer service systems. But the move has clearly paid off, he said, given the company's leading position in the on-line trading category and its customer growth this year. And more changes will be in order, as customers become technically savvier, he predicts. "We won't need people to provide some of what's needed today, but it will open the door for people to provide new services that we don't have today," Mr. Pottruck said. "You might click on an icon on your computer and have someone appear immediately to help you." Outside of the realm of finance, he said, "traditional stores will need to use the Internet to create a richer shopping experience." "Supermarkets will have to provide a range of experiences -- cooking tips, recipes you can get at a kiosk -- instead of simply being places to pick up merchandise," he said. "Those days are gone." Ms. Bane, of the Yankee Group, said that once companies integrated the Internet into their point-of-sale systems, cashiers could conceivably access a customer's previous buying history during checkout and suggest other items to buy. Or, once shoppers returned home, they might find a coupon in their email from a store they recently visited. The store's knowledge of the customer's on- and off-line purchasing history is potent marketing material, she said, adding, "They can leverage the technology investments they've already made." The Gap, for one, has no immediate plans for such a comprehensive integration of its on- and off-line stores, Rebecca Weill, a company spokeswoman, said. But the company has created "Web lounges" at eight of its flagship stores, featuring black leather couches, chairs and computers framed with brushed metal casings. "They're always crowded," Ms. Weill said of the lounges. "Sometimes people even buy items from the kiosk instead of going through the store for them." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Shawn Melvin, a college student, searched for books on line at a Borders store in the World Trade Center. (Chang W. Lee/The newyork Times)

title:
MEDIA;
Book Industry Study Shows Sales Increased 4% Last Year
body: After struggling through a drought in the mid-1990's, when readers bought fewer copies of consumer books, the publishing industry posted gains of more than 4 percent last year and is poised for more modest increases despite the rapid emergence of on-line booksellers. In its annual snapshot of the word trade, the Book Industry Study Group issued cautious sales projections for the glamour side of trade publishing, which produces novels and nonfiction, and better prospects for college textbooks and business titles. The unit sales of adult trade books are projected to grow more than 2 percent annually through 2003 -- an indication that on-line sales are not expected to increase the market for popular books. "We don't see the total market expanding in any dramatic shape for five years," said Albert N. Greco, an associate professor of business at Fordham University who helped prepare the projections. "If you say 10 years, it might be even more modest," he continued. "I think people are reading less, and I just don't see that we're going to turn the corner and become a nation of readers." In 1998, the sales of adult hard-cover and trade paperback books -- the top moneymakers for trade publishers -- rose more than 4 percent from a year earlier, to 497 million copies. It was the second year of growth in unit sales after a two-period ending in 1996, when consumers cut back on their purchases. Children's books also made gains, emerging from a 1997 slump to sell more than 364 million copies in 1998 -- a gain of 6 percent but still less than 1996 sales levels. The study does not include figures for 1999, but several top publishers say they are experiencing a surge in sales that encompasses not only popular fare like "Hannibal" by Thomas Harris or the Harry Potter children's series by J. K. Rowling but also for histories like John Keegan's "The First World War." "We've seen a strong market since last summer: all publishing divisions, all formats, all categories," said Peter Olson, the chief executive of Random House, the Bertelsmann A.G. unit that is largest trade publisher in the unitedstates. Mr. Olson gave credit for some of the strength to on-line retailers that now account for roughly 4 to 5 percent of the company's sales. Mr. Olson said that the company's worldwide sales of $1.6 billion for the year ended in June had exceeded expectations. The North American side of the company -- in the unitedstates and Canada -- accounted for about 80 percent of all sales. "I think that the attention that Amazon.com and Barnesandnoble.com have generated has increased interest in books in general, and that has led to buying not just on line, but in stores," Mr. Olson said. An earlier industry study this year, which relied on consumer diaries of book purchases, found that Americans bought fewer copies of books in 1998. But the Book Industry Study Group speculates that the discrepancy may be because that study did not include acquisitions made by libraries. Though the industry study does not predict an expansion of the market because of on-line sales, its current sales figures indicate that electronic publishing and bookselling are reshaping the market in other ways. For example, the unit sales of books about science and technology declined from a peak of 80 million copies in 1995, falling 8 percent, to 74 million copies, last year. And those drops are expected to continue, the result of a shift to electronic publishing -- that is, distribution of books by disk, CD-ROM or over the Internet -- by technical publishers like Bertelsmann's Springer Verlag unit in newyork. In the last few weeks, Springer has transformed "Prokaryotes," a four-volume $2,000 set of books about bacteria, into an electronic version that will sell for less than half that price. Rudiger Gebauer, Springer's chief executive, said that no one was sure yet whether electronic publishing would expand the market. But he expected that the electronic versions would make such books accessible to many more people. "The libraries, in theory, keep information to everybody," he said. "but in reality it's only the people who go to the library. On-line publishing opens it up to virtually everybody." The Book Industry Study Group report also suggests that the Internet and on-line book sales may figure in the continuing fall-off in mail-order purchases, which has dropped 26 percent from a high of 105 million copies in 1993. But the Internet does not affect all categories. Religious books, for instance, are not sold in high volumes by electronic booksellers, but sales in that category continue to improve, rising almost 16 percent, to 170 million copies since 1993. And those numbers do not include sales figures from thriving fundamentalist Christian publishers. "You've got an aging population, and I think as people go on in life they turn to more spiritual matters," said Eric Major, director of the Doubleday religious division for Random House. "Oddly enough," he added, "we've seen a surge in books about the lives of saints or books about people's religious experiences. The great thing about this area of religion publishing is that it now includes business books, parenting books, dieting books and relationships books." The sales of business books and textbooks for college and elementary students also continue to grow. In 1998, the number of business books sold increased more than 12 percent from a year earlier with projections that this field will continue to thrive. At the university level sales grew more than 19 percent, to 176 million copies, between 1993 and 1998. But those trends have not necessarily raised sales by the 80 or so university presses in the unitedstates. The sales of university books grew by almost 4 percent to 18.5 million copies from a year earlier. And the report projects only modest increases for the next five years. "That's an indication of a mature market," said Peter J. Givler, executive director of the Association of American University Presses, a trade organization. "I think that it is very much a market in turmoil. The sales for university presses have been flat for a couple of years, and the presses are looking for new sources of revenues." Some university presses are starting to experiment by publishing electronic journals, he said, but to date it is unclear to the members whether on-line bookselling and electronic publishing will be a boon. "On-line bookselling has had this extraordinary growth," Mr. Givler said, "but nobody knows how that is going to play out. It seems that everybody thinks this is a logical way to purchase books and there ought to be some way to work it out, but we haven't found a way to do it." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "What People Are Reading" Mass market paperback sales peaked in 1995 but have been disappointing since then and are not expected to revive anytime soon. Trade book sales for adults and children, however, rose strongly in 1998 and are expected to grow over the next couple of years, as are sales in the professional and religious book categories. Figures are number of books sold each year.
