The case was settled on Monday with an agreement that Amazon.com would continue to list the best sellers only in alphabetical order and to publish the list only when it became available to the general public. To John H. Barton, a professor of law at Stanford University, the rush to claim ownership over databases is tantamount to a modern land grab, with dangers for endeavors that traditionally build on the work of others, like scientific research. "I have to say I'm sympathetic to the plight of a movie producer who sees the product distributed digitally without any payment," said Mr. Barton. "But we are reaching the point where we're creating serious complications for the kind of data flow you need for democracy and scientific inquiry to work. People are commercializing everything and selling it. I'm worried that we are going to patent facts." The proponents of stronger intellectual property rights have their own worries. Testifying before the House Judiciary Committee, Terry McDermott, the chief executive officer of the National Association of Realtors, argued that cyberpirates were stealing real estate multiple listings and threatening the very basis of his industry. Though the Internet has become the battleground, the fears of the realtors and others reach back to a Supreme Court decision in 1991 that had nothing to do with the Web. In Feist v. Rural Telephone, the Court ruled that the publisher of a regional telephone directory had the right to copy numbers from a local directory because he was in effect adding value to an existing body of fact. The decision challenged a venerable doctrine of copyright law, which held that the "sweat of the brow" expended in compiling a list, even if the information was in itself openly available, entitled it to protection. What's at stake, argues Jonathan Band, a lawyer who represents the Online Banking Association, is money. He said there are few cases in which companies have suffered seriously from pirates or scientific research has been stymied. The bottom line is that one of the oldest commodities, information, is suddenly in huge demand. "It's not the piracy, or the fear that we'll lose the incentive to invest in data," he said. "It's that those who have information can make a lot more money." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The way it was: A stock ticker in the mid-1930's after a heavy day of trading. (William M. Rittase)

title: AT THE MOVIES
body: Worldwide Web Of Intrigue In the spring of 1998 two Florida filmmakers, Eduardo Sanchez and Daniel Myrick, trained three unknown newyork actors to shoot film and videotape. They told the actors to go to Seneca Creek State Park in Maryland for several days with this rough idea: to scare themselves as much as possible and improvise a movie about searching for a monstrous woman called the Blair Witch. They gave the actors plenty of food and two hand-held 16-millimeter cameras. "We wanted it to look like a documentary because we had no money," Mr. Sanchez said. That has certainly changed. The two filmmakers and their partners are sharing in the profits of a box office bonanza, "The Blair Witch Project," that has startled Hollywood because it broke every possible rule. It had no stars, a tiny budget of $30,000 and an oddball story about three filmmakers who disappeared and left behind only their film. The movie has also startled the world of independent film because top executives at Miramax, Fine Line and other established companies either walked out in the middle of the movie's first screening at the Sundance Film Festival or rejected it out of hand as uncommercial. But Bill Block, a partner at Artisan Entertainment, a smaller independent company, saw the film at its first midnight screening at Sundance and pounced on it. And to the amazement of Mr. Block and his partners at Artisan, Amir Malin and Mark Curcio, "The Blair Witch Project" is nothing less than a phenomenon among moviegoers in the 18- to 30-year-old range. By this weekend its box office receipts will pass $100 million. Artisan expects that it could reach as much as $140 million, and the company is already planning a sequel. Then there are the expected huge sales from the the video, to be released on Halloween. (Abroad the film has so far opened only in France, where its box office revenue has been surprisingly modest.) The two filmmakers, and the three producers in Orlando, Fla., who were financially struggling last year, are expected to divide about $30 million. By all accounts what has made the film so successful is the Internet. Its Web site, www.blairwitch.com, blurred the line between reality and fiction. It displays "police reports" and newsreel-style interviews that make the movie seem real. Heated discussions have broken out on the Internet about whether the movie is fiction or a documentary. The reaction to the Web site has been powerful; there have been nearly 80 million "hits" on it. "There was a young Internet audience out there that hasn't been tapped," said Mr. Block, a former talent agent. "This movie converges with that audience. They've embraced it. All the kids have seen it on the Internet. In some ways it's the first Internet movie." Mr. Malin, who was one of the owners of October Films, said he hoped "Blair Witch 2" could be released as early as next summer. No one is quite sure what it will be about, but there is every possibility that more "lost" film will be found from the three main actors, Heather Donahue, Michael Williams and Joshua Leonard (above). "This taps into a niche the way 'Easy Rider' tapped into a niche in the 1960's," Mr. Malin said. "It taps into an audience that's been weaned on television and the Internet." Mr. Malin spoke over the telephone while on vacation in southern Tuscany. He can afford it now. "I had to escape 'Blair Witch' hysteria," he said happily.  'Pi' Plus One After four years at Harvard, Darren Aronofsky returned home to Coney Island not entirely sure what to do with his life. "I spent a year hanging out with my friends; most of them were either stockbrokers or drug dealers," he said. "Both weren't a good influence." So Mr. Aronofsky (above), who is now 30, decided to enroll at the American Film Institute to study directing. It took several years after graduating to scrape together $20,000 from friends to make his first feature. He did not seek money from his relatives. "I didn't want to bankrupt my family any more after college," he said. The feature, "Pi," was a strange and mesmerizing film about a man encumbered by severe headaches who immerses himself in Jewish mysticism, numerological theory and the stock market. Mr. Aronofsky won the director's award at the 1998 Sundance Film Festival for the movie, which was named one of the top 10 films of 1998 by several newspapers. The success of "Pi" could have guaranteed a Hollywood career for Mr. Aronofsky. But he is now completing another offbeat drama, although on a much larger scale. The movie, "Requiem for a Dream," based on a novel by Hubert Selby Jr., is what Mr. Aronofsky called a psychological horror film dealing with various addictions. "In show business, entertainment is the first rule, and I totally want to entertain people and make films that are exciting to watch," Mr. Aronofsky said. "But there's no reason you can't also explore new techniques in film language as well as new ideas that are not normal subject matter for most movies." In the film Ellen Burstyn plays a woman addicted first to candy and television who then turns her obsession to diet pills. Three other characters also "come face to face with their own worst nightmares," Mr. Aronofsky said. The cast includes Jared Leto, Jennifer Connelly, Marlon Wayans and Louise Lasser. The film is to be released next year by Artisan Entertainment. Mr. Aronofsky is also planning several other high-profile projects. One is "Proteus," a World War II science fiction thriller for Dimension Films, a division of Miramax. The other is based on the comic strip "Ronin," about a 13th-century samurai who is transported into Manhattan in the 21st century. "I call it a cyber-samurai movie," he said. Meanwhile he is busy in the editing room with "Requiem for a Dream," which was made mostly in -- where else? -- Coney Island. "Someone once told me you've got to make them cry, make them laugh or scare them," Mr. Aronofsky said.  "I'm hoping to do all three in this movie."  'Angel' Alumna Yes, there's life after "Charlie's Angels." Ask Cheryl Ladd. "I've done 35 television films and features and mini-series, and I haven't stopped working," said Ms. Ladd, who played Kris Munroe in the 1970's series. "But even now all people want to talk about is 'Charlie's Angels.' People are still so attached to those girls. It was such a phenomenon. There are still 'Charlie's Angels' fan clubs and newsletters. It's like Trekkies and 'Star Trek.' " Ms. Ladd, 48, is hardly complaining. She appears in a new film, "A Dog of Flanders," based on the children's book written in 1872. The tale of a young boy and his friendship with a remarkable dog, the book has been adapted for films three times: in 1924, when it was called "Boy of Flanders"; in 1935, and in 1959. The current version, directed and adapted by Kevin Brodie, will be released on Aug. 27. Ms. Ladd (above) said she had decided to appear in the movie for one reason. "I wanted my career to have one children's classic like this," she said. "I wanted to have my 'Old Yeller' or 'Pollyanna.' I wanted to make a movie that families can see forever." Ms. Ladd said "Charlie's Angels," which took her from obscurity to almost instant fame, had had a surprising impact on her career. "There are young directors who can't wait to meet me and put me in their films precisely because of 'Charlie's Angels,' " she said. "They grew up with the series. And there are older directors who won't let me walk past their door because of 'Charlie's Angels.' " "There is a stigma sometimes because of that particular show," Ms. Ladd acknowledged. "For some directors it's seen as a ball and chain. On the other hand it's given me a bit of a career." Over the last two decades Ms. Ladd has appeared in some surprisingly dark feature films. Last year she played opposite Ben Stiller in "Permanent Midnight," based on the turbulent life of a Hollywood writer and heroin addict. Ms. Ladd portrayed the star of a television series -- she was given a fictional name -- who helped the writer stay clean. Ms. Ladd lives near Santa Barbara with her husband, Brian Russell, a writer. She has a daughter and a stepdaughter, both actresses in their early 20's. "I tell them that the major pitfall is the amount of rejection and the out-and-out cruelty you have to take when you want to get work," she said. "Waiting two hours in a room with other actors to get two minutes to see if you're the person for the part. It's so hard on your psyche. You get hundreds of nos for one yes." She said it was certainly difficult for older actresses to find work in movies. But television, Ms. Ladd said, is less restrictive. "Television has been kind to all of us from 'Charlie's Angels,' " she said. "There are a lot of good roles for women." Nonetheless, she is still looking for the one film role that would take her career far beyond "Charlie's Angels." She said with a laugh, "I'm constantly looking for the Mrs. Robinson part." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos

title: Fight for Internet Access Creates Unusual Alliances
body: Unimaginable as it might have seemed a year ago, President Clinton's top private lawyer and the former senior aide to Kenneth W. Starr in the impeachment battle recently joined to argue on the same side of one of the biggest legal fights in years. The two men, David E. Kendall and Brett M. Kavanaugh, are but one example of the unusual alliances being forged in the dispute over which companies will end up dominating high-speed Internet service delivered through cable systems. Mr. Kendall, representing America Online, and Mr. Kavanaugh, whose firm represents G.T.E., are among a legion of advisers who are quickly finding business in the dispute, which has turned into the latest full employment act for lawyers and lobbyists here and in many cities around the nation. Their common adversary in the fight is AT&T, which is rapidly acquiring cable systems and offers high-speed Internet access over those lines exclusively through a company, Excite@Home, in which it owns a major stake. Led by America Online and G.T.E., a coalition of Internet service providers and other telephone companies have mounted a nationwide campaign to force AT&T to let cable customers use Internet providers other than Excite@Home without additional fees. The AT&T opponents have several business interests with billions of dollars in future revenues at stake. G.T.E. is developing a rival high-speed Internet service, and many smaller providers believe that if AT&T's system proves popular, they will be doomed if they are shut out. Some of the other telephone companies in the fray are either competitors of AT&T or are using the issue to press for greater deregulation and the ability to compete with the company's long-distance service. AT&T contends that it would have little incentive to upgrade its cable systems to provide high-speed Internet service if it must serve as a carrier for all providers and that in any case, comparable telephone- and satellite-based services will insure competition. While a precise figure on spending on the lawyers and lobbyists and for campaign contributions is not available, executives and lawyers involved in the case estimate that it is already in the tens of millions of dollars. "In a field where exaggeration is common, it is fair to say that this issue is regarded as the most important public policy question in telecommunications for the decade," said Andrew Jay Schwartzman, president of Media Access Project, which promotes consumer rights and diversity on the airwaves and has taken sides against AT&T. "In the near term," Mr. Schwartzman said, "there's billions of dollars in revenue at stake. Over the longer term, the outcome of this fight will play a large role in determining who will be the dominant telecommunications and Internet players for the next decade. As a consequence, the bedfellows are stranger than strange." When Mr. Kendall and Mr. Kavanaugh found themselves on the same side recently, for instance, "their eyes were like saucers," recalled William P. Barr, the general counsel at G.T.E. and a Attorney General in the Administration of President George Bush, who was in the same room with them. For their part, consumer groups have joined the anti-AT&T side but acknowledge that they are in an awkward position, allied with telephone companies that they have sharply criticized in the past. The consumer advocates have also criticized William E. Kennard, the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, after lobbying fiercely to get him appointed two years ago. Mr. Kennard has in essence sided with AT&T by formulating a policy that only the Federal Government, and not local authorities, has jurisdiction, but ruling out intervention for now. There have been high-stakes struggles over telecommunications policy in the past, but perhaps never one fought on so many fronts, including a number of localities where approval is needed -- and conditions on the Internet issue can be attached -- if AT&T is to assume the franchises of the cable companies it is acquiring. One reason cable has become a focus of the Internet battle is that it is expected to be a dominant source of high-speed service, at least in the near term. Today fewer than 1 million homes have such connections, offering speeds 10 to 80 times those of conventional phone lines. But by 2002 the number of high-speed customers is expected to reach 10 million to 16 million, industry analysts say, with 60 percent to 85 percent using cable connections. The current dispute is also notable because it involves a convergence of technology that has far outpaced laws, court opinions and regulatory decisions, all of which treat cable and telephones differently and, for better or worse, have said little explicitly about the Internet. On one front where AT&T's opponents have scored their biggest gains, the issue is heading to a Federal appeals court. It will hear oral arguments in October over a decision by Portland, Ore., to require AT&T to open its cable lines there to any Internet company on the same terms as Excite@Home. The dispute also is moving to a new group of cities that are considering whether to permit AT&T to acquire the cable franchises controlled by Media One. Among other places, new skirmishing is expected in the suburbs of Boston and in other parts of Massachusetts, where a drive to get the issue on a statewide ballot in 2000 began this week, as well as Minneapolis-St. Paul, Richmond and major parts of Florida. In Washington and cities around the nation, both sides have retained battalions of advocates. This week, for instance, the anti-AT&T forces announced that in addition to Mr. Kendall, they had retained Lloyd Cutler, the former White House counsel, and Bruce Ennis, a leading Washington lawyer. For its part, AT&T and the cable industry have retained many of Washington's lobbyists, including Vin Weber, the former Republican representative from Minnesota, and the lobbying firm founded by the late Dan Dutko, a major Democratic fund-raiser who died in an accident two weeks ago. More than 50 lobbyists for AT&T and the cable companies showed up at an organizational meeting last December. "A lot of people have told me that they owe me thank-you notes," said Gregory Simon, a former top aide to Vice President Gore, who is collaborating with Richard Bond, a former chairman of the Republican National Committee, in directing the anti-AT&T coalition. "They were retained just so I couldn't hire them. In Washington it took weeks to find somebody who was not lobbying for AT&T. I could not find three firms that had not been retained on this issue." Nonetheless, the regional Bell telephone companies have managed to retain some well-known Washington figures for the fight, including Haley Barbour, a former chairman of the Republican National Committee; Michael D. McCurry, the former White House press secretary; and Susan Molinari, the former Republican Congresswoman from Staten Island. They say that Congress and Federal regulators should eliminate restrictions on their clients to make it easier to offer high-speed Internet services to compete against AT&T. The experience in Florida is illustrative of the magnitude and fervor of the struggle. Local records show that AT&T and the cable companies have retained more than 40 lobbyists in the state. G.T.E. responded by persuading officials in Broward County to adopt an ordinance requiring AT&T to open its cable system to other Internet service providers -- and by agreeing to pay the county's legal costs if AT&T sued over the issue. AT&T lawyers say they are preparing to challenge G.T.E.'s legal assistance to the county. There have also been Potemkin-like efforts at local organizing, a process that is known by some consumer advocates as Astroturf campaigns, in contrast to grass roots. Contrived rallies were staged in front of San Francisco City Hall, for instance, and both sides have made extensive use of telephone banks to gin up support by asking loaded questions and making alarmist predictions. Executives and lobbyists from all sides are pouring campaign contributions into the coffers of the major Presidential contenders, although none of the candidates have stated a clear preference. (The issues have transcended party politics, although some of the major players have been identified with particular candidates. For example, James W. Cicconi, general counsel and head of government relations for AT&T and a former aide to President George Bush, was recently co-chairman of a fund-raiser in Washington for George W. Bush. George Vradenberg, the general counsel for America Online, is a top adviser and fund-raiser for John McCain. And Mr. Simon has been raising money for his former boss, Vice President Gore.) Lawyers on both sides say the candidates are not likely to take a position that could jeopardize more donations. While competing legislation over the issue was introduced in Congress in recent weeks, both sides acknowledge that there is nothing the lawmakers will likely do any time soon. As a result, the anti-AT&T forces have embarked on a strategy of trying to find support in states and municipalities, hoping the issue may then begin to resonate with more force in Washington. Despite the intensity of the fight, there is a widespread assumption that it will be settled either at the corporate bargaining table or by a Supreme Court decision, which could be years away. "Everybody's got a business motivation here and everybody likes cloaking their arguments in terms like open access," Mr. Cicconi said, "but what's really going on here is AOL has a business plan and wants the government to put its thumb on the scale to tip the balance in its favor." He said the opposition has been "going in at the local level and hiring as many people as possible who have connections with city commissioners and local officials." But consumer groups and AT&T's corporate rivals say the battle is as much over principle as it is over business. "I'm in awe of the magnitude and money involved," said Donna N. Lampert, who had to leave her law firm, which represents major cable companies, to continue her work for America Online. "But at its core this is really about an important principle. This involves a lot more than whose garage the Mercedes will be parked in, as the saying goes about big money cases. It involves who will control the Internet." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart/Map: "OVERVIEW: A Growing Battle Over Internet Access" Battles are being fought at the Federal, state and local levels to determine whether AT&T must offer competitors equal access to its cable customers in providing high-speed Internet service. Map highlights places where AT&T has prevailed, AT&T has failed and cities and states where lobbying battles are being waged.  Portland, Ore. -- Voted to deny the transfers of cable licenses unless AT&T treated all high-speed Internet providers equally. As a result, AT&T says it cannot develop high-speed service in the area. A Federal judge ruled against AT&T's court challenge two months ago; an appeal will be heard in October.  San Francisco -- Last month approved local cable licenses for AT&T but said it would revisit the issue this winter. Also agreed to support Portland in the lawsuit filed by AT&T and said that if Portland prevails on appeal, the decision would also be binding on AT&T in San Francisco.  Federal Government -- AT&T and the cable companies have so far tamped down opposition to limiting access and no bills are expected to be adopted soon. The Clinton Administration has taken no position; the Federal Communications Commission, while asserting that it has jurisdiction, has said no intervention is called for at this point, in essence siding with AT&T.  Broward County, Fla. -- Adopted an ordinance to require equal treatment of all Internet service providers by AT&T. The company has filed a lawsuit in Federal court to strike down the ordinance. (pg. A14)

title: Microsoft Says Worker Wrote Smear of Rival
body: The Microsoft Corporation acknowledged yesterday that one of its programmers apparently masqueraded as an independent computer consultant earlier this week in an effort to discredit America Online's tactics in the companies' quarrel over instant messaging. Microsoft had reason to be red-faced about the incident yesterday -- first, because the company was unable to identify the employee who forged an email message on Tuesday accusing America Online of irresponsible behavior, and second, because whoever did it sent the message to the one computer security expert who was most likely to trace it back to Microsoft. The ruse has added a bit of Spy vs. Spy melodrama to a bitter dispute over instant on-line messaging that America Online and Microsoft -- the world's two largest Internet service providers -- have been waging for several weeks. The dispute began last month when Microsoft introduced a clone of the AOL Instant Messenger program, which permits computer users to chat over the Internet with other computer users. Since Microsoft released its clone, the two companies have waged a public war of words while simultaneously carrying on a hacking cyberwar as America Online has tried to electronically lock Microsoft Messenger users out of its network and Microsoft has at least 13 times managed to find new backdoors. America Online executives say Microsoft is making illegal use of proprietary directory information that is essential to connect instant messenger users via the Internet. The Microsoft disinformation incident came to light on Wednesday when Richard Smith, the president of Phar Lap Software and a leading computer security expert, received an email message from someone identifying himself as Phil Bucking of Bucking Consulting. The author suggested that he was developing his own instant messaging program and was studying America Online's tactics in blocking Microsoft users. In his message, he asserted that America Online is using a programming error that has created a security flaw -- one not found in Microsoft's clone program -- to detect the Microsoft Messenger program. The author said he was writing Mr. Smith because Mr. Smith had "significant credibility with the press." "I think you would agree that this is a heinous and risky action," stated the electronic message, which was sent using a free Yahoo email account. "I am perfectly fine with AOL and MS fighting it out with standard software practices, but putting user security at risk is unacceptable. It is inconceivable that a company would even consider doing this." When Mr. Smith, who has criticized Microsoft's software development and privacy practices in the past, examined the message, he discovered that it had originated within Microsoft. "Microsoft is trying to use me as a pawn in their fight with AOL," he said. In a telephone interview today, Rob Bennett, the director of marketing for Microsoft's Internet service, MSN, confirmed that the author of the message was almost certainly a Microsoft employee, but he said the company had not yet discovered his or her identity. "I think it's somebody who got a little overpassionate but went about it the wrong way," Mr. Bennett said. Computer industry analysts said that the incident echoed a 1992 controversy in which Microsoft employees masqueraded as independent computer users and posted messages to public computer bulletin boards with opinions critical of I.B.M.'s OS/2 operating system, a product that competed with Microsoft's Windows. "This is par for the course for Microsoft marketing," said John C. Dvorak, a columnist for PC Magazine. "In the past we called them Microsoft munchkins. It was a scandal." Microsoft executives said there had been no Microsoft plan to play dirty tricks in its dispute with America Online. Mr. Bennett also said that members of Microsoft's software development team had told him they knew nothing about the incident. Mr. Bennett, however, insisted that the accusations made in the message were accurate and that America Online's programmers had been exploiting a security flaw in the AOL Instant Messenger software to identify Microsoft Messenger customers. He said that since the dispute began, , Microsoft had made 13 changes to its program to get around America Online's efforts to block users of Microsoft's clone. "It's unfortunate they're putting user security at risk," he said. An America Online executive disputed that there was any security issue involved and said the company would not acknowledge that its software contained a vulnerability known as a buffer-overflow error. "It's a fake issue by a fake consultant, " said Barry Schuller, director of interactive services at America Online. "Our whole approach is all about privacy and security for our members, and I think this is really embarrassing for Microsoft." A buffer overflow error is a type of programming defect that could permit an intruder to execute rogue programming instructions on a remote machine via a computer network. In some cases buffer overflow bugs can be exploited to crash remote programs while simultaneously executing illicit code. Microsoft said that in the case of AOL Instant Messenger, the buffer overflow error did not result in a program crash. But by running a program on its servers, America Online could exploit the bug by weeding out users whose software did not have the error and therefore had to be using the Microsoft clone. Mr. Smith acknowledged that the code Microsoft was questioning in America Online's program might not, in fact, be a bug. But if it was, he said, America Online's exploiting it to detect the Microsoft clone was risky from the standpoints of privacy and computer security. "Putting network backdoors in software products should be against the law," he said. "I don't like the idea at all of 'spyware.' " Microsoft posted a change to its program last night to work around the new America Online strategy, Mr. Bennett said. But he added that the workaround did not use a buffer overflow error. Separately, AOL and the Novell Corporation announced yesterday that Novell, a software provider in Provo, Utah, had licensed the AOL Instant Messenger software. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Clown Alleys Dot the Information Highway
body: IT'S summer: time to run away and be a clown. Or perhaps rent one, or pick up a few styling tips and a nose job? Step right up to the Internet and its clown alleys, the traditional name for the section off the midway that housed the clowns' dressing quarters. Ringling Brothers and Barnum & Bailey Circus has its own Web site, www.ringling.com, with an on-line Clown Alley for each of Ringling Brothers' two touring units. Between the lines of the clowns' capsule biographies there lurks an intensity of feeling that suggests that some of these people have clown blood. Thomas Wheaton's biography, for instance, notes that his great-grandparents were both Ringling Brothers performers: "his great-grandfather was an albino, billed as 'the Wild Man From Borneo,' while his great-grandmother was an acrobat." The Ringling Brothers pages are glitzy show biz. For a grittier look at clown life, a site by John Decker displays evocative pictures of the former clown tent at Clyde Beatty-Cole Brothers Circus (www.intac.com/jdeck/clown_alley/Cl.html). Inside the tent, photos show the clowns applying makeup, choosing costumes, lining up at the chow wagon and practicing their juggling as they wait for their cues. "The old-fashioned clown alley ended after the 1997 season," said Renee Storey, the circus's vice president for administration. The Clyde Beatty-Cole Brothers clowns now use a trailer and recreational vehicles, she said. The 11-year-old International Clown Hall of Fame and Research Center in Milwaukee (webdom.com/chof) is a major resource for students of the various styles of clowning and clowns of the past, including Roman and medieval forebears. "Most of the queries I receive pertain to clown history," Kathryn O'Dell, the center's executive director, wrote by email. "Many folks who contact me had a family member who was a clown and write me for assistance as they search their genealogy." From 1989 through 1998, 41 clowns have been inducted into the Hall of Fame. Its Web site includes posters of each year's inductees, as well as close-ups and biographies. Red Skelton and Emmett Kelly Sr. are among the charter members. Bob Keeshan, television's first Clarabelle and later its Captain Kangaroo, is there. So are Oleg Popov, the Russian clown; Max Patkin, the "Clown Prince of Baseball"; a number of television Bozos and many Ringling, Shrine Circus and foreign greats. There is a Clown Web Ring, www.cswnet.com/imaclown/ring.html, with 161 sites for individual clowns and organizations, chat rooms and tips on balloon tying, juggling and magic. A driving force among many clowns is religion, as a sample of site names on the Web ring makes clear: A Place for the Christian Clown, Powerhouse Youth Ministries With Brother BoBo, the Joybringers Web Pages, Clowns 4 Jesus and O. B. Joyfull. "Clowns in general are very giving, caring people," said Geoffrey L. (Hickory) Turner of Latham, N.Y., a computer programmer and consultant who founded Hickory's Clown Alley (www.webclowns.com/info_links.htm). "Many of them are involved in their church and, in their children's programs at church, incorporate their clown into that ministry. Also, there is a need to deliver the gospel in a new and fresh way -- clowning is one of those ways." Mr. Turner, 46, said via email that he became interested in clowning in 1991 after watching a worship service led by a clown troupe, the Joyful Joeys. "I was 'Boss Clown' for six years, touring throughout New Jersey and newyork, leading our unique brand of worship," he wrote. He started Hickory's Clown Alley in 1997, and it now receives 2,500 visits a month, along with email from around the world, a sort of clown cultural exchange. Mr. Turner said he adds about 15 clowns a month to his mailing list. Three types of clowning in particular are attracting new performers, Mr. Turner wrote, starting with church clowning. "In the early years of America, clowns would get on the stage and mime the scripture readings for those in the back who couldn't hear," he said. "This died away in the late 1800's but is now experiencing a well-received revival." Another popular specialty is hospital clowning: "Patch Adams is alive and well," Mr. Turner wrote. And recently, he added, there has been a flurry of activity in clowning for the deaf, through sign language and standard mime techniques. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The world of clowns is presented on the Ringling Brothers Web site.

title: How to Spend an Allowance Without Leaving Home
body: JORDAN RAY, age 10, faced a shopping dilemma. Too young to go to the toy store by himself, Jordan, of Brooklyn, had to pester his dad to drive him there whenever he wanted to check out a new video game. That proved to be just as painful for his father, Robert Ray. "When we went to the store, I would stand there, feeling like I was just a pay object," Mr. Ray said. "He'd pick out something, then I'd pay. He did not understand the concept of sales tax, or of cost. He only understood the concept of 'I'm getting something.' " All that changed in June, after Jordan finished the fifth grade. As a graduation gift, his grandmother set up a new kind of account to make it possible for Jordan to shop alone -- on the Internet. With a $50 credit in an on-line account, Jordan eagerly logged on. But as he tried to decide which video games to buy, he realized he had a new problem: shipping costs put him over budget. It took him a few weeks to figure out a solution: when he finally made his first purchase in July, he opted for less expensive items -- videotapes -- because then he could afford to pay the shipping costs. "I love it," Robert Ray said about his son's account. "Now he understands cost." (Of course, this being the Internet, Jordan still doesn't understand sales tax.) As Jordan agonized between choosing "Lady and the Tramp" or "The Parent Trap," he became a member of the newest group to be pursued by E-commerce entrepreneurs: children. Jupiter Communications, the Internet research firm, predicts that children ages 5 to 18 will spend $1.3 billion on line by 2002. Encouraged by such projections, a number of companies are rushing to introduce Web sites designed to encourage children like Jordan to buy from on-line retailers who sell items like clothing, toys and books, including J. Crew, Toys "R" Us, Kaybee Toy and Hobby Stores and Barnes & Noble. "This is a natural evolution, because today's kids are sophisticated and already are comfortable using the Internet for other things," said Anya Sacharow, an analyst at Jupiter Communications. "The main thing that was stopping them from buying on line was that they didn't have their own credit cards." At three new on-line shopping sites, they don't need their own credit cards -- they rely on their parents'. At Icanbuy, Rocket Cash and Doughnet, parents set up the children's accounts and either deposit a minimum amount (from $1 to $25, depending on the site) by charging it to a credit card or establish a credit line with a spending limit. Either way, children do not have to have direct access to their parents' credit card information to make purchases. "I don't think we'll ever replace the mall as a place where kids go to hang out with their friends, and I don't think we'll have tons of teen-agers sitting alone at home, shopping by themselves on line," said Carol Kruse, co-founder and vice president of marketing at Rocket Cash (www .rocketcash.com). "But we can offer really neat items and better convenience and sometimes better prices." But some psychologists and financial planners question whether it's a good idea to make it easier for today's children to spend money. "Parents feel guilty about their children, and they try to make it up to them by buying things," said Carol Seefeldt, a professor at the University of Maryland's Institute for Child Studies. "I see a lot of parents who do not want their children to ever delay gratification, but that's the wrong approach." In fact, Professor Seefeldt said, children who learn that they have to earn their rewards are more likely to achieve success both in academics and later in life. "Saving and investing gives kids an important sense of self-control over their lives," she said. "We want to teach them to take care of themselves rather than to expect people to take care of them." A generation or two ago, teaching a child to manage money wisely meant learning to save or invest, not spend. In those days, high-school students learned to budget and to balance a checkbook in required home economics classes. But today, those courses are often bypassed electives. "Parents are the ones who are teaching children how to spend, but very few are sitting down and teaching them formally how to balance a checkbook," said Dara Duguay, executive director of the Jumpstart Coalition, a nonprofit group in Washington that is working with Icanbuy (www.icanbuy.com) to expand an education section on its site. The proprietors of the on-line shopping sites aimed at children say they don't encourage kids to be spendthrifts. "The ability to shop is already there, in stores and malls and through catalogs," said Jeffrey Mason, president and chief executive of Rocket Cash. "All we want to do is offer the same convenience to kids who are shopping at a mall to shop on line. I don't think it's possible to really restrict shopping, other than to control their access to money." Where on-line sites have a practical appeal is in relatively remote, mall-deprived regions. For Anna Morton, a 14-year-old who lives in central Oregon in a small town called Sisters, the closest town with stores that appeal to her is 18 miles away. "She's very mature, literate and excited about the things that are out there, like books, CD's and software," said Anna's mother, Rebecca Morton. "But she couldn't get any of it. Now she puts her baby-sitting money or her allowance into her Rocket Cash account, and she has the opportunity to manage her own money and get what she wants." Anna has so far bought a sweater from J. Crew through her account. "I love it," she said, "because I can be independent and not have to talk to my parents all the time about what I want." At all three sites, children can keep track of how much money is in their accounts and track how much they have spent. If the money runs out, they may not buy anything else until a parent makes another deposit to the account or extends the credit line. "We want to teach kids to manage their money wisely, to know that they are going shopping with their own money and when it runs out, they can't spend any more," said Paul Herman, a co-founder of Icanbuy. Some parents agree that the accounts teach children fiscal discipline. Kelly Cirilli of Rensselaer, N.Y., said her 11-year-old daughter, Stephanie, saves up the money in her Icanbuy account instead of squandering it the way she used to. "Instead of bringing her out to shop all the time, where she wants to waste $10 on candy and junk and stuff like that," Ms. Cirilli said, "I put $25 into her account every two weeks and she's saving it because she wants a shirt that costs more than $40." To promote a more traditional form of money management, some on-line shopping sites offer or are planning to offer savings accounts. At Icanbuy, for instance, children can open a savings or checking account with an on-line bank insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. Account holders can watch interest accrue (2.57 percent on savings, 6 percent on checking). To close the account, a parent must mail a signed letter to the bank, which will in turn mail a check for the balance. Earlier this month, the Doughnet site (www.doughnet.com) added a feature to allow children to make payments from their accounts to the National Resource Defense Council or the Rain Forest Alliance. "Those sorts of things are useful because they have a big educational component for kids," said Don Blandin, president of the American Savings Education Council in Washington. "Kids use the Internet every day, and they're going to grow up managing their money over the Internet. It will be commonplace for this generation. I just would like to see more places on the Internet that focus on saving and investing." Although the majority of on-line shoppers under age 18 are not donating to charity or setting up on-line savings accounts, some are learning first-hand about saving money. Jordan Ray, for example, "even asked his grandmother to take him to rent the video games he was considering buying, so he could test them," his father said. "I don't want to waste money on something I don't really want or need," Jordan said, as if that were the most natural idea in the world.  Where to Shop and Save Learning to Budget and Spend on the Web The sites below offer on-line accounts that parents can set up for their children to shop with and, in some cases, to save with. To ease parents' concerns about privacy and safety, three of the four sites have created secure payment mechanisms. They all insure that under-age shoppers can spend their money only on merchandise from approved retailers.  ICANBUY: www.icanbuy.com Aimed at children aged 8 to 18, Icanbuy connects shoppers to 22 on-line vendors, including Etoys, CD Now and 999 Software. The site requires a minimum balance of $1; a parent deposits money into the account with a credit card. Children can then spend it without having access to a parent's credit card account information. Parents can set limits on the amounts of purchases. For birthdays and holidays, children can create a wish list of items that grandparents and others can check before buying a gift. Shoppers also can use money from their accounts to make donations to such charities as the Special Olympics or the World Wildlife Fund or to set up a savings account that earns 2.57 percent interest at Security First Network Bank, an FDIC-insured on-line bank that has its headquarters in Atlanta.  DOUGHNET: www.doughnet.com Started in June 1999 and aimed squarely at teen-agers, Doughnet connects shoppers to 31 on-line vendors, including Barnes & Noble, Toys "R" Us and Egghead Software. Instead of opening the account with a deposit, a parent uses a credit card to establish a credit line with a guaranteed minimum balance of $50. Whenever a shopper makes a purchase, Doughnet provides the merchant with the parent's account information and the parent's credit card is charged. Parents can limit the amount of purchases. Shoppers can also donate to such charities as the Natural Resource Defense Council and the Rainforest Alliance. The site plans to add F.D.I.C.-insured on-line banking.  ROCKET CASH: www.rocketcash.com This site is aimed at children aged 10 to 18 and offers connections to 38 vendors, including Amazon.com, Kaybee Toys and J. Crew. To establish an account, the site requires a minimum balance of $25; a parent deposits money into the account with a credit card. Then, children can spend it without having access to a parent's credit card account information. Parents can limit the times of day during which a child may make a purchase.  ALLOWANCENET: www.allowancenet.com This site for preteen-agers is scheduled to make its debut Sept. 13. With an emphasis on earning and saving, the site will collect no money from children or their parents. To open an account, a parent and child will choose from an on-line list of 112 chores, deciding which ones the child must perform to earn a weekly cash allowance (from the parents) or "diditz" credits from the site. Children will check off the chores as they perform them; at the end of each week they will print out a "bill" and present it to parents to be paid. The "diditz," meanwhile, will accumulate on the site and children will be able to spend the credits on merchandise provided by the sites' advertisers. According to Allowancenet officials, payment security measures are unnecessary because users of the site do not spend real money. As Allowancenet signs up more users and adds cash transactions, they added, it will begin encoding them. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Jordan Ray, 10, played a video game with his grandmother, Louise Ray.
