title: Internet Showing its Value In Remote Alaskan Villages
body: FROM this remote town about 30 miles north of the Arctic Circle, six doctors serve a dozen villages in an area the size of Indiana. With the help of the Internet, diagnosing health problems has become just a little easier. Janette Shackles, the medical director of the Maniilaq Health Center in Kotzebue, remembers phone calls before the advent of Internet-based images during which she played 20 questions with doctors' assistants in the villages. "I'd say, 'Where did this person get shot?' and they'd say, 'Back behind the school,' " she recalled. "The images really help a lot." Alaska, the state with more caribou than people, has widened its entrance ramp to the Internet. Until February 1999, one fiber-optic cable owned primarily by AT&T had served the entire state. "It was running with every photon burdened," said Ronald Duncan, president of General Communications in Anchorage. With two fiber-optic cables working and one more to follow soon, Alaska will be better connected than ever to the lower 48 states, with enough capacity to let every one of Alaska's 600,000 residents make a phone call at the same time. In Kotzebue, where the ocean freezes over in October or November, pricey phone calls and faxes that used to bounce -- slowly and shakily -- from tundra to satellite and back again are now local calls, using extra bandwidth from the new connections. Kotzebue residents also found it easier and quicker this year to join the nine million people who saw and heard live video and audio from the Iditarod dog sled race on Dogsled.com in March. "It has gone from being like the Long Island Expressway at rush hour to a major interstate across Nevada in the middle of the night," Mr. Duncan said. The fiber-optic advances will reach a population that is unusually sophisticated when it comes to the Net. Alaska has relatively young residents, as many older people retire to warmer climates. According to 1998 figures from Fort Nocs, an E-commerce company in Anchorage, 40 percent of the households in the lower 48 states have computers and about a quarter of them are on line, while 73 percent of Alaskans have computers and just over half of them are on line. Alaskan Internet service providers have complained about seasonal fluctuations, with use plummeting in the summer, when there are at least 36 days when the sun doesn't set, and rising steeply in the winter. "It's remote, and when it's really cold, there's not a lot to do, so a lot of people will jump on the Internet," said Ben Phillips, head of OTZ Telecommunications in Kotzebue, an Internet service provider for 150 to 200 people. Michael Hendrix works for the Northwest Arctic Borough School District, where every classroom has an Internet connection. His responsibilities include 1,500 users and 600 work stations that have been configured to protect the operating system from either inadvertent or malicious fiddling. "We make it so they can't get to where they can mess stuff up," he said of the teachers and students who use the system. If there's a problem with the system that could be fixed with just a few keystrokes, someone has to fly there to fix it. Of the region's 11 villages, the one nearest to Kotzebue is 60 miles away, and no roads connect them. But sometimes flying isn't an option, even with medical emergencies. Bad weather and high costs can maroon a patient in the villages. "In the past, we would take an X-ray of a person with a broken leg and send it by courier to Anchorage," said Eugene Smith, information manager for the Maniilaq Health Center. "There was a big delay in the process. There would be times when the bone would set before a diagnosis could be made. Now we digitize the film, and it's in Anchorage the same day." Ed Carns, a temporary doctor at the clinic, said he has never seen an emergency room in the lower 48 states that is as well wired as the one in Kotzebue. On his first night on call, a clinician from Point Hope phoned at 2 A.M. about a toddler who had possibly been sexually abused. The clinician sent along pictures of the girl, and Dr. Carns, though initially skeptical of the new technology, was able to determine that her injuries were not related to abuse. "I became a believer at that moment," he said. Telemedicine, made possible by the new lines, is also proving to be a money saver. "The typical medical paradigm is when in doubt, evacuate, but that can cost $25,000 a pop, for a jet to Anchorage and a small plane out of the village," Mr. Duncan said. The Internet can also help address one of the biggest problems for professionals in rural Alaska -- isolation. "If you're the only teacher in town, with no one to share issues with, or if you are a doctor trying to get continuing education, it's very, very difficult," Mr. Duncan said, pointing out the value of the camaraderie that can develop through email and training materials available on the Web. Of course, increased bandwidth from the new cables will enable Alaskans to use the Web for entertainment as well as research. So while John Clark, a student in Kotzebue, used the Internet to research the differences between tap water and filtered water for a class project, Gordon Foster, the system administrator at OTZ Telecommunications, uses it to play cribbage and hearts and to keep in near-daily touch with his father in Tennessee. At Surf City, an Internet cafe in Anchorage, Andrew Stevenson of Sydney, Australia, and his fiancee, Katherine Moore, stopped during their eight-month tour of Europe and the unitedstates to send email. They were pleased with the speed of the 10 computers there, especially after traveling in Eastern Europe. ("They had an Internet cafe, but no computers," Ms. Moore said.) The Internet has reached even the state's remote coastal villages, where a women's cooperative produces and sells knitted goods like scarves made from the soft underhairs of the Arctic musk ox. The co-op's three-year-old Web page (www.qiviut.com) accounts for about 1 percent of its business, including at least one order from Iraq, said Sigrun Robertson, executive director of the cooperative, which is called Oomingmak. The word that translates as "the hairy or bearded one." Karen R. Crane, the state's director of libraries, archives and museums, found how small the world could be when a patron at a library asked for information about Russian monasteries, a task that would have taken researchers weeks, she said, before the libraries came on line. "With the Internet, the citizen in rural Alaska can be as tied in to what's happening in the world as a person in Anchorage or newyork or Seattle or any place else," she said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: A Web site has helped the Oomingmak cooperative increase sales of products made by women in remote villages. (Chris Arend); (Bill Bacon)

title: Nebraska Students Getting a Look at the Innards of the Internet
body: THE cables, circuits and switches that make up the Internet are invisible to most people. But starting this fall, engineering students at the University of Nebraska at Omaha will get a firsthand look at exactly what route those Web pages and email messages travel before appearing on their computer screens. All they will have to do is look up. Above them, in classrooms and hallways, they will see dozens of shiny red cables snaking along thin, stainless steel tracks hanging from the ceiling. And if they walk past the glass walls of the wiring closets, they will see bundles of red cables hanging from black hooks, looking like giant rubbery -- and relatively untangled -- spaghetti. The exposed lines are not the result of a bungled floor plan or unfinished construction. They are there by design to show students how buildings are engineered in the Internet age. Other elements of the building -- including its ducts and plumbing -- are exposed as well. They are all part of the Peter Kiewit Institute of Information Science, Technology and Engineering, a $26.5 million structure that opened this summer. Peter Kiewit Sons, an Omaha engineering company, has donated millions of dollars to the institute. "We had a great desire to build something that wouldn't simply house programs," said Winnie L. Callahan, the institute's executive director. "The idea of a building as laboratory came immediately to mind." At the University of Colorado at Boulder, the Integrated Teaching and Learning Laboratory was built in 1997 using the same philosophy -- its structure is a teaching tool for engineering students -- but with less of an emphasis on cables and networks. And in recent decades, other buildings -- notably the Pompidou Center in Paris -- have been designed with the purpose of exposing their insides, often for esthetics more than education. The Kiewit institute carries the concept into an age in which Internet connections are considered to be nearly as important to the mechanics of a building as running water. Computer-engineering students, educators say, must have a hands-on understanding of how they work. "Books are nice, but all the technical information in the world doesn't give you the feel of a fiber-optics connection," said Bing Chen, co-chairman of the computers and electronics engineering program at the University of Nebraska at Omaha. "It doesn't give you the sense of how all the networks are really distributed in a building." The students will be expected to do more than simply look at the wiring, however. Professors at the institute say they will be giving students a chance to manipulate the networks, working from wiring closets and other areas where network traffic is routed. Dr. Chen said he planned to have students literally watch the electrical impulses flying over the wires using Hewlett-Packard analyzers that help managers monitor networks. "I like students to track it down, almost to the electron level," Dr. Chen said, referring to Internet traffic. "We aren't interested in black boxes, where it just goes out into the ether." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: EXPOSURE -- Paul Pokorny, system manager at the College of Engineering at the University of Nebraska, is framed by the switch that controls the connections among networks. The exposed lines are intended to show students how buildings are engineered in the Internet age. At right, the foyer has exposed steel girders. (Photographs by Jeff Beiermann for The newyork Times)

title:
NEWS WATCH;
On-Line Medical Information Does Poorly on Accuracy Exam
body: The growing field of on-line medical information was recently given an exam, and the results were not good. According to a study published this week in the journal Cancer, more than a third of the medical sites scrutinized had not been subjected to peer review. And at least 6 percent of them contained wrong information. Dr. J. Sybil Biermann, an orthopedic oncologist, and three colleagues at the University of Michigan conducted the study. They reviewed nearly 400 Web pages retrieved by four search engines after they searched variations of the words "Ewing sarcoma," a form of bone cancer that occurs in children and teen-agers. A few sites, for example, overstated or understated the survival rate among those with the disease, which experts estimate to be 70 percent to 75 percent. The researchers found that the site of Encyclopaedia Britannica said the mortality rate was 95 percent. Such information could lead a parent away from worthwhile therapy, Dr. Biermann wrote. "The devastating effect these postings would have on vulnerable patients is incalculable," she added. Tom Panelas, a spokesman for Encyclopaedia Britannica, said the company planned to fix the problem by posting a new article or deleting the passage about the mortality rate. He added that Britannica would update its entries on cancer this year. The Internet, Dr. Biermann said in an interview, is changing the dynamics of traditional medicine. "It used to be that the physicians deliver the information, the patient accepts it, and that is that," she said. Now, "in many cases physicians are not even the primary information provider." Dr. Biermann recommends that patients ask doctors for their interpretations of what shows up on line and that doctors refer patients to reputable, peer-reviewed sites. "Anybody can put information on the Internet about any medical condition," she said.   LISA GUERNSEY http://www.nytimes.com

title: Rescue Time at the Apollo: Time Warner to Control Board
body: State officials are working out final details of an arrangement that would give Time Warner a controlling role in rescuing Harlem's financially troubled Apollo Theater, officials and corporate executives said yesterday. The negotiations are also expected to resolve a lawsuit brought by the state accusing a six-member majority of the Apollo board of failing to collect millions of dollars owed the theater by Percy E. Sutton, a prominent businessman and former Manhattan Borough President. The settlement would require Mr. Sutton and his associates to repay $1 million to the theater, according to people involved in the negotiations. A company controlled by Mr. Sutton produces "It's Showtime at the Apollo," a weekly variety program for television. The agreement is expected to be presented to the Apollo's board at its meeting on Monday. The settlement would also include a financial contribution from Time Warner, estimated at $400,000 to $500,000. As part of the settlement, unitedstates Representative Charles B. Rangel, a powerful Harlem Democrat, would step down as chairman of the theater's nine-member board and would be replaced by the actor Ossie Davis, and Time Warner would add 10 people from the entertainment industry to the board, expanding it to 19 members, said Richard D. Parsons, the president of Time Warner. The theater, once Harlem's golden stage on 125th Street, is owned by the state but operated by the nonprofit Apollo Theater Foundation. The close involvement of Time Warner, the world's largest entertainment and media company, with revenues last year of nearly $27 billion, was supported by State Attorney General Eliot L. Spitzer as a way to bail out the long-deteriorating Apollo, where Duke Ellington, Ella Fitzgerald, Nat (King) Cole and other legends entertained. Charles A. Gargano, the chairman of the Empire State Development Corporation, the agency that owns the theater, said the state had approved Time Warner's plans to take control of the board and was eager for the rescue effort to begin. The suit's settlement has been stalled for weeks while lawyers for Mr. Rangel and Mr. Sutton negotiated with the State Attorney General's office over how to resolve the accusations made last November in a lawsuit filed by Attorney General Dennis C. Vacco. Mr. Rangel and five other board members were accused of failing to collect at least $4 million from Inner City Theater Group, a company controlled by Mr. Sutton, a close friend and longtime political ally of the Congressman. Mr. Rangel has repeatedly said he will not sign an agreement that did not exonerate him. He said yesterday that the precise wording was still being negotiated. "I don't need anybody to vouch for my honesty," said the Congressman, a 15-term House veteran and the senior Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee. Mr. Sutton, who became a defendant in the lawsuit last month at his own request, is also seeking language that would clear his name. "Percy Sutton has acted honorably at all times in his relationship with the Apollo Theater," said Peter Parcher, one of his lawyers, "and if there is a resolution, it will reflect that fact." The complaint said Mr. Sutton was required to give the theater 25 percent of his gross profits from the show, which would have amounted to $4 million over a five-year period. But Mr. Sutton and Mr. Rangel said the contract they signed included confusing language that had been misinterpreted and that the show had consistently lost money. In April, Mr. Spitzer, who replaced Mr. Vacco as Attorney General, came up with another figure, saying the theater was owed "well over one million." Mr. Spitzer said in a letter to the foundation's lawyers that this figure was derived from an audit commissioned by the theater. But lawyers for the foundation have said he misread the audit. Mr. Spitzer would not speak on the record about the proposed settlement yesterday. But lawyers working on the case said that an agreement was expected to be reached before Monday's meeting of the Apollo Theater Foundation board. The new members would be added at that meeting. Time Warner officials provided details of their role for the first time yesterday. The company's involvement is not a surprise. Mr. Rangel and Mr. Parsons, who have worked together on Harlem economic development issues, have said they have long wanted to bring Time Warner into the Apollo. In March, the company said it was eager to adopt the Apollo, but only if the allegations of wrongdoing had been cleared up. Outlining his company's plans yesterday, Mr. Parsons said George Wein, the jazz impresario who created the Newport Jazz Festival, and six other people, three of them officials of Time Warner, had agreed to join the board. The new board members will also include Val Azzoli, the co-chairman of Atlantic Records, a Time Warner subsidiary; Keith Clinkscale, the former chief executive of Vibe, a publication owned by Time Warner; Byron Lewis, the founder of Uniworld, an advertising and marketing agency aimed at African-American consumers, and Jonelle Procope-Terrell, a lawyer. Although Time Warner will control the board, Mr. Parsons denied that the company was taking over the theater. "It's definitely not a takeover," he said. "It's a partnership that we're forming between Time Warner and the Apollo Theater Foundation." Company officials said the entertainment company would not run the theater, and would not have the power to hire or fire its executives. Among the first issues facing the new board will be whether to approve or rebid a multiyear contract for Mr. Sutton's company to distribute "It's Showtime at the Apollo" for forthcoming television seasons. A rival distributor, Frank Mercado-Valdes, president of the African Heritage Network, whose charges of favoritism led to the state investigation last year, said yesterday that he had considered it futile to bid on a new contract under the existing board, but said he would like to do so now with a new board in charge. Time Warner's contribution will be part of a financial package that will include Mr. Sutton's settlement as well as some city, state and Federal government money and charitable donations. About $400,000 is expected to come from the Upper Manhattan Empowerment Zone. Mr. Parsons is the chairman of that program, which uses Federal, state and city money to stimulate economic development. Mr. Gargano said the Empire State Development Corporation had already agreed to give the theater $300,000, but the money was held up pending resolution of the lawsuit. Acknowledging that the sums were small, Mr. Parsons said his company would help start an endowment campaign to raise more money for the theater, which he described as a cornerstone for economic development in Harlem. "I don't think you can bring life back to Harlem without bringing life back to 125th Street," he said, "and you've got to start with the Apollo." Reviving the theater would also spur other development, including new restaurants. Under the proposed agreement, Mr. Sutton and some of his associates in the Apollo deal would be responsible for repaying the $1 million that Mr. Spitzer contended last April was due the Apollo foundation out of profits reaped by the distributors, according to an audit by the accounting firm KMPG. His predecessor, Mr. Vacco, had contended that as much as $4.4 million was owed to the foundation, but after reviewing the audit, Mr. Spitzer said that $1 million was a fairer figure. The initial dispute between the state and Mr. Sutton and Mr. Rangel centered on whether the percentage due the foundation was to come from net or gross profits. The foundation later sued its lawyers at White & Case, an action not affected by the proposed agreement. Some of the money going to the Apollo will be used to replace the theater's dilapidated marquee and broken-down seats and to create a souvenir shop, Mr. Parsons said. But he said that the theater was in "functionally sound shape" and needed to attract top performers and large audiences even more than it needed renovation. Most nights the fabled theater is dark. Mr. Parsons said the goal was to bring "interesting and inspired multidimensional programming" to the theater, perhaps by using it for a new television talk show starring the rap performer Queen Latifah, or for movie premieres or televised beauty pageants. Mr. Rangel said he was delighted that Time Warner was finally getting involved in the theater, but he emphasized that he, and not the Attorney General, should be given the credit for bringing in the company. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Percy E. Sutton in the newly renovated Apollo Theater in 1985. His company produces "It's Showtime at the Apollo," a weekly program. (John Sotomayor/The New York Times)(pg. B4)

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Internet Selloff Brings Nasdaq A Correction
body: The technology-laden Nasdaq market slumped for the fifth consecutive session yesterday as Internet stocks suffered another pummeling. The Nasdaq index fell 47.99 points, or 1.85 percent, to 2,540.00, and is now down 11.3 percent from its high of 2,864.48 on July 16. This means the market is experiencing a correction, which Wall Street defines as any decline of more than 10 percent; a drop of 20 percent is considered a bear market. Other market gauges also declined on light trading as investors continued to be concerned about the possibility of further increases in interest rates in advance of the scheduled release today and tomorrow of key reports on the economy. The Dow Jones industrial average slipped just 2.54 points, to 10,674.77. But the broader Standard & Poor's 500-stock index was down 16.85 points, or 1.27 percent, to 1,305.33. "People seem to have gotten scared and tired" in recent weeks, said George Cohen, a portfolio manager at Cohen, Klingenstein & Marks. Internet stocks, he contended, have been particularly vulnerable to this shift in sentiment because they were bid up to "absurdly" high levels. Also referring to the Internet sector, Scott Marcouiller, an analyst at A. G. Edwards, said: "They're not giving any sign of bottoming yet. Our recommendation is to avoid them." Amazon.com tumbled 6 7/16 a share yesterday, to 88 7/16; Ebay fell 8 5/8, to 75 3/4; CMGI declined 5 7/8, to 76, and Priceline.com dropped 6 13/16, to 66 1/4. "We've had a heck of a meltdown," said Fane Lozman, chairman of Scanshift, a Chicago research firm. "People have lost huge sums." Once again, stocks pushed higher early in the trading day, only to sag in the afternoon. Stocks in the morning were buoyed by a firming of the bond market after the Treasury said it would reduce the amount of bonds it auctions and use some of the budget surplus to buy back debt. The Dow jumped as much as 152 points, aided by Dow Chemical's planned acquisition of Union Carbide. Shares of Union Carbide rose 10 9/16, to 59 3/8. Financial and drug stocks helped drag the Dow lower, though. American Express and J. P. Morgan each slid 3 3/16 a share, American Express to 123 1/2, and Morgan to 124 1/8. Merck fell 2 1/2, to 64 1/2, and Johnson & Johnson slid 2 3/16, to 92. Bucking the trend were some companies whose products are considered to be tied closely to the economy. International Paper rose 2 15/16 a share, to 54 15/16, on talk of higher prices. But analysts expressed surprise at the strength of shares in such stalwarts as Alcoa, Exxon and Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing, which all rose more than a point. Despite the widespread distress elsewhere in the sector, an initial public offering by Internet Initiative Japan, which connects Japanese companies and consumers to the Internet, met an enthusiastic reception. Shares of the Tokyo-based company climbed 8 5/16, to 31 5/16. But at least two more initial public offerings were withdrawn, according to Thomson Financial Securities Data: Reynard Motorsport and Country Maid Financial. Also withdrawn this week were Mobilvest, Simtek, Spectrascience, Avado Brands and Travelscape.com. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average over the past year. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Co. Names Managers for Internet Unit
body: The newyork Times Company yesterday named a senior management team for its new Internet division, Times Company Digital. Martin A. Nisenholtz, the division's chief executive, announced the appointment of David A. Thurm, vice president for production at The newyork Times, as chief operating officer. Also named was Richard J. Meislin as editor in chief. Mr. Meislin was formerly editor in chief of the NYT Electronic Media Company, the precursor to Times Company Digital. Andres Rodriguez was named general manager of Abuzz, the company in Cambridge, Mass., that the Times Company bought three weeks ago. Abuzz's software culls information from various sources and connects people who have questions with people or places that have answers. Kenneth A. Richieri, formerly assistant general counsel of The Times, will become vice president and general counsel of the unit. Times Company Digital said it had reorganized its more than 50 sites into two categories: national, and regional and emerging. The leaders of each will carry the titles of group vice president and publisher. Cristian Edwards, will lead the national on-line sites, including The newyork Times on the Web, Wine Today and Golf Digest. Lincoln Millstein, will head the regional and emerging properties, which include Boston.com, newyork Today and the on-line sites of the Times Company's smaller newspapers and broadcast properties. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Travel Agents Express Anger On Internet-Only Plane Fares
body: Travel agents reacted with anger and disappointment yesterday to the latest airline offers of additional discounts on tickets booked over the carriers' World Wide Web sites. "No matter how the airlines dance around it, this is an attempt to put travel agents out of business," John Hawks, president of the Association of Retail Travel Agents in Lexington, Ky., said of the latest round of discount offers. Mr. Hawks added that he expected Congress to take a critical look at Internet-only fare offers when it returns to the topic of airline passenger rights, possibly later this year. The American Society of Travel Agents in Alexandria, Va., also opposes Internet-only fares. "All fares should be available to all travelers," said Dina Long, a spokeswoman for the association. Airlines say they are simply doing what every business tries to do -- lower costs. "We're not trying to put anybody out of business," said Dave Swierenga, the economist for the Air Transport Association, the industry trade group. "But now we have a new technology that bypasses a big part of the labor component of writing tickets, and obviously that's hard for agents to deal with. This is simply a rational business decision in a world that's changing, and travel agents need to recognize that the ticket-writing function can now be done more simply by technology." That new technology is, of course, the Internet, which allows passengers to buy tickets directly, without having to go through travel agents, who book about 80 percent of airline tickets, or reservations agents. Travel agents can match fares loaded into the computerized reservations systems as well as most fares posted on an airline's Web site, but special low fares for last-minute weekend travel are usually made available only to an airline's email subscribers, while other bargain fares are increasingly found only on the Web sites of airlines. Airlines offer Internet-only fares in hopes of persuading more passengers to book electronically because it saves the carriers money. "It costs Delta up to 400 percent more to book and deliver a ticket using the traditional processes," Vince Caminiti, a Delta executive, said in a speech to a business travel association in Minneapolis last month. The airline industry's ticket commission costs fell to $5.2 billion in 1998 from a high of $7.6 billion in 1993, mainly because in 1995 the carriers succeeded in scrapping the traditional 10 percent agent's commission and imposing a maximum $50 fee for each transaction. Over all, commission rates fell to 6.3 percent this June from 10 percent in June 1994. To help pick up the slack, travel agents have increased their sales of cruises and land excursions, package tours and hotel rooms. Many also charge customers a fee for such once-free services as rewriting tickets and planning itineraries. On Monday, Northwest Airlines reduced leisure fares by as much as 25 percent for travel between next month and December. Most other airlines quickly matched Northwest, including Delta Air Lines. Then on Tuesday, Delta offered an additional 10 percent off the sale fares for passengers who book their tickets on the Delta Web site. Other airlines matched those reductions as well.  Unlike an unsuccessful attempt by Delta last January to charge $2 for each round-trip flight not booked on its Internet site, this week's Internet moves appear likely to succeed. At least for now. "The airlines are very brave at doing such things when we're in a robust economy," Mr. Hawks said. "But if there's any business that's cyclical, it's airlines, and when the downturn comes, as it will, travel agents will remember how they were treated."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Web Sites for Class Reunions Strengthen Old School Ties
body: LIVING in London, Carolyn Band Mehta did not attend her 20th high school reunion in Newton, Mass. Surfing the Internet, though, she stumbled across her reunion Web site. It was almost as good as the real reunion -- in some ways, even better. "I loved it," said Ms. Mehta, who graduated in 1978 from Newton South High School, outside of Boston. "I made it a favorite site. I read every single entry. It was the perfect medium for a reunion." The Web site, www.nshs78.org, was set up by a classmate, Charles Strange, who runs a computer business. One day he received an email message from the reunion chairwoman, Lily Chou, who was doing an Internet search to turn up lost classmates. The two decided to create a Web site for the reunion. They put up a message board, a list of "lost people," a directory of email addresses and a link to the school newspaper. After the reunion, held last October, they added photographs, a post-party message board, and a transcript of the E-reunion -- a live chat session held during the reunion so that people there could communicate with those who couldn't make it. As it turned out, Mr. Strange was not able to go. But he was on his computer for more than five hours that evening, as the host for the E-reunion from his home in Tampa, Fla., while about a dozen people logged in from as far away as California to write things like, "Whatever happened to . . ." and "I always had a crush on . . ." Plenty of schools and colleges have Web sites, many of which include an alumni page or some basic information on upcoming reunions. Several sites purport to let people look up their classmates by state, city and high school, but these tend to come up practically empty. There are few of the less formal sites, like the Newton South site, but it may be that these slapdash, homegrown endeavors are the ones that strike the deepest chords. "Ours was completely accidental," said Mr. Strange. "Its success was not a function of anybody sitting around planning. It's not high gloss. There are no graphics on this thing. The pictures are non-professional. If you didn't go to Newton South, it's a meaningless site." Another site with a serendipitous origin was set up for the class of 1979 at Bryan Adams High School in Dallas, which held its 20th reunion in late June. A few years ago, Lorri Crossno Nevil, a Web designer, bumped into her class president, Bucky Eacret, at Six Flags Over Texas. They talked about the forthcoming reunion, and Ms. Nevil suggested hosting a Web site. It began as a message board and evolved into a planning tool. Finding missing classmates no longer necessitated hefty postage costs or long-distance phone calls to people's parents. Ms. Nevil had hoped to set up a Web cam to broadcast the reunion live over the Internet, but decided it was too technologically complex. "Maybe for the 25th," she said. The Bryan Adams site, at www.bryanadams-hs.org, includes a section for lost people, directions to the reunion hotel, a list of attendees, a way to send E-greetings to classmates, and a selection of 1970's background music. "May the force be with you," the home page intones. (Star Wars was hot at the time.) The reunion committee did most of its planning on line, with software to allow conferencing. "The meetings were really effective," said Camille Shipes Garner, the reunion's chairwoman. "You didn't have to pick a place and worry about a babysitter. It was a lot of 'Let me go and put my child to bed and I'll come back on line.' The meetings ended up going four or five hours, and people would just come in and out as they could." Ms. Garner herself took full advantage of the board. When she asked whether anyone could lend the reunion a karaoke machine, a classmate responded within hours, offering hers. At the reunion, the organizers collected up-to-date email addresses and took pictures with digital cameras. These are now up on the site, protected by a password. Nevil plans to add captions. Bryan Adams High School, like Newton South, ran an E-reunion. It had its share of technical problems. A router wasn't working. Somebody stepped on the phone line and disconnected it. People had been looking forward to typing to a classmate who lives in Africa but, because of electrical and time-zone problems, she never made it to the E-reunion. Still, Ms. Nevil received universal accolades for her effort. "About 20 people said to me if it hadn't been for the Web site, they probably wouldn't have come," she said. "They said, 'When I saw so-and-so was going to be there, I decided I was coming, too.' " But even as such Web sites foster more participation, they have the curious ability to let people partake of their reunion without actually going. "You can be a voyeur at your own reunion," said Ms. Mehta of Newton South. "A lot of people don't want anyone to know what they look like now. You can hear what other people are doing without letting them know what you are. You could never hide like that before." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: KEEPING IN TOUCH -- Lori Antoine Krone, left, Lorrie Crossno Nevil and Eric Lewis sent messages to absent classmates at the 20th reunion of Bryan Adams High School in Dallas. Below, Roger Hamm, left, Melinda Roberts, Stacy Sowers and Todd McQueen looked at old photographs. (Photographs by Mark Graham for The newyork Times)

title:
What I Did On My Summer Vacation;
Some Teen-Agers Parlayed Computer Skills Into Jobs With Signing Bonuses, Travel and Executive Perks - Correction Appended
body: WHEN 18-year-old Eamon Walsh and two of his high school friends get together, they chat about summer concerts, the heat and -- more often than not -- their marketing plan. Instead of rising at noon and heading to the pool, Mr. Walsh backs his car out of the driveway before 7 A.M., picks up his friends -- Tamara Metz, 18, and Thomas Purtell, 17 -- and heads to work at Evolve, an Internet company in Vienna, Va. Evolve hired the students to create a company to develop and sell a new piece of software that allows users in different locations to work on one document at the same time. Evolve is sending them to England for a week this month, all expenses paid, to learn from other companies. "We thought that was pretty cool," Ms. Metz said. Nice work, if you can get it. Yet, Mr. Walsh and his friends are hardly the only teen-agers with computer skills to take summer jobs that come with lavish perks and hourly wages well over the Federal minimum. All over the country, computer-savvy students in high school or their first few years of college are landing summer jobs that look a lot like professional, full-time employment. Some are making enough money to cover most of their tuition at private colleges. Others are receiving signing bonuses simply for accepting summer employment. "Increasingly, the pool of students that companies look at is creeping back, is becoming younger," said Mark Oldman, co-founder of Vaultreports.com, an on-line publisher of internship and job information. Companies are desperately seeking young people who know their way around computers, Mr. Oldman said, and they know they are missing out on talent if they focus only on college juniors and seniors. In some cases, the students receive job offers before they even start looking for them, receive raises before the summer is over and are asked to stay on part time throughout the fall and winter. Some are taking home more money than they know what to do with. "I'm mostly just sticking it in a mutual fund now," said Xan Charbonnet, 18, who has been working at Vtel, a digital video-conferencing company in Austin, Tex., for two summers now. Internships can pay anything from $4,000 to $10,000 for a summer. The phenomenon has emerged over the last few years, employers say, as Internet start-up companies have proliferated and established software and hardware companies have grown. Finding enough people to do the technical work has become a primary concern. "It doesn't matter if they have a high-school diploma or a college degree," said Raj Goel, chief technology officer at Brain Link, an Internet-service provider in Queens. "It just depends on whether they have the skill sets and the experience." If the students work out, many employers say, the risk of hiring such unproven workers can be well worth it. Teen-agers generally accept less pay than college juniors or seniors or graduates, yet are often able to do the same work. Besides, the 20-somethings with computer skills are often not available, employers say: they are either starting their own companies, looking for an equity stake or have priced themselves out of the market. By contrast, teen-agers are a bargain. Mr. Walsh's wage, $8 an hour, is at the low end for some summer positions. "We're not getting paid a lot of money because the company is helping us start up our company and letting us go with it," he said. "There's another high schooler here who makes $12 an hour doing HTML," the code behind Web pages. Some students have fared even better. When Brain Link, for example, hired Tugrul Galatali, a 1999 graduate of Stuyvesant High School in newyork, and Jason Lee, a Stuyvesant senior, it agreed to pay them enough to cover a substantial share of their first year's college tuition. For Mr. Galatali, the total will come to about $7,000 this summer. With the $10,000 scholarship that he has already won, his tuition at newyork University will just about be covered. Mr. Goel, his supervisor, said he is willing to offer good money for "true geeks" -- people who "breathe computers," rather than those who have decided to take a battery of college computer classes because they were told to do so. He is a fan, he said, of those who "haven't gotten their heads screwed up by useless classes in college." Microsoft is legendary among computer-programming interns for its pay. The company will not disclose how much it offers, but former interns report that pay ranges from $6,000 to $10,000 for the summer, depending on experience. Typically, potential interns are first interviewed on campus, then flown to Redmond, Wash. for follow-up discussions. They are encouraged to make the trip into a weekend getaway, with their rental car, meals and lodging covered. Once an intern is hired, the company helps pay for some housing and rental-car costs. "I live in a pretty privileged environment," said Nolan Myers, a Microsoft intern who is a junior at Harvard University. "This is pretty much standard for technical positions right now." For some teen-agers, the perks of a technology-related summer job can outweigh the pay. Henry Fabian, 16, and Shamarrah Broadus, 18, have their own offices with windows overlooking Wall Street. They work at Marketing Technologies Group, a small software-training company in Manhattan's so-called Silicon Alley. "My mother is amazed" said Mr. Fabian, a junior at Washington Irving High School in Manhattan, sounding pretty amazed himself. At Intel, the chip-maker based in Santa Clara, Calif., interns receive health insurance and vacation days. At Microsoft, interns rave about what one called Barbecues with Bill G. -- informal dinners at the sprawling, waterfront home of Bill Gates, Microsoft's founder. The other lure of the internships, of course, is real job experience. Unlike interns in other industries, who might spend their summers filling coffee urns, high-tech employees are expected to do more meaningful work, no matter what their age. For example, Alex Pakhomov, 17, is responsible for sales and marketing at Mondosoft, a newyork start-up company that develops search-engine technology. A month ago, Mr. Pakhomov was one of four Mondosoft representatives sitting around a conference table during a sales meeting with Random House, the publishing company. Sandy McCarron, director of on-line production for Random House, said she was hardly fazed by his presence. "Frankly, with all these young programmers we have here, I didn't even notice that he was an intern," Ms. McCarron said. Hiring teen-agers -- who, whatever their skills, cannot be expected to have fully matured -- for positions of responsibility does pose risks. At Barnes Wentworth, a network and engineering company in Manhattan, one teen-ager became more of an embarrassment than an asset after falling asleep during a meeting with a client. The client took a picture of the snoozing teen-ager, posted it on an internal Web site and then sent the student's supervisor a link to the site via email. Maia Aron, Barnes Wentworth's company's chief operating officer, dismissed him soon after. But even that experience has not kept Ms. Aron from hiring other young people. She gave a raise to another summer employee, Calvin Tan, 16, after finding out that the student she had fired easily got another job at a higher salary. "We were outraged," she said. "We asked Calvin, 'That kid is making more than you?' " Many of the students who get valuable internships have been the beneficiaries of advanced high-school programs or internship programs coordinated by industry associations. Mr. Walsh and his friends learned most of their software-programming skills at Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology in Fairfax, Va., and got their jobs with Evolve after winning a contest that the company sponsored last spring. Many students in newyork got their internships through the newyork New Media Association, a nonprofit group designed to provide professional services to local Internet companies. The group started its internship program last year, directing technologically proficient students to Silicon Alley companies. It has placed nearly 80 students this summer. One company that has taken advantage of the program is Doubleclick, an on-line advertising firm. "It is so incredibly competitive out there," said Laura Ianuly, Doubleclick's vice president of human resources. "People know they can walk across the street and get another job at the competition in an hour." Ms. Ianuly said she sees the company's interns as prospects for permanent employment -- and tries to make it worth their while to stay and then come back next year.  Many of Doubleclick's interns, who this year are all college students, get signing bonuses of $2,000 to cover relocation to newyork. And an additional bonus of several thousand dollars may land in their laps by the end of the summer. Many companies do not even wait until the next year: they ask the teen-agers to stay on through the fall and winter, working part-time after school. "The companies keep the kids, they don't want to get rid of them," said Ted Nellen, a teacher of a class called Cyber English at Murry Bergtraum High School in the Bronx. And then there are the rare stories of the teen-agers who, by summer's end, are offered lucrative full-time jobs without even setting foot in college. One such student is Ariye Shater, a graduate of the High School of Telecommunications, Arts and Technology, in Brooklyn. Mr. Shater was offered a full-time job at a company in Forest Hills, Media Linx, after working there last summer. At age 18, Mr. Shater said, he was offered a salary of more than $50,000 a year, if he would forgo college and stay on as a full-timer. "It was very tempting," Mr. Shater said. "My parents weren't happy about it." They were relieved, he said, when he chose to go to college at the State University of newyork at Stonybrook. He has continued to work for Media Linx part time, telecommuting from his dormitory room. At this point, many companies would happily settle for that. Even part-time high school students are in demand. Just a few weeks ago, Mr. Nellen, the Bronx high school teacher, said, he received an email request from an internship program. "We can't fill the spaces," the note said. "Do you have any other kids on your end?"  Finding a Job What It Takes Unlike many students who take other office internships, interns for computer companies should be ready for real work -- not just making photocopies. What else are high-tech recruiters looking for? SYSTEMS EXPERIENCE -- Knowing how to set up a computer or install software, employers say, can improve your chances of snagging a job. Many 17-year-old network managers got their start installing computers and networks at their high schools. PROGRAMMING -- Software programmers should know the C++ programming language. Being able to create applications using Java and PERL helps too. ANALYTICAL SKILLS -- These are the most critical, employers say, especially since some programming languages may become obsolete. Aaron Gavios, vice president for sales at Mondosoft, a software company, said he asked applicants how to tackle hypothetical business problems. THE INTERNET -- "Those students who are on the Internet all day, they are in tune," said Laura Ianuly, vice president of human resources for DoubleClick, an Internet advertising agency. And your mother said you were wasting time playing Doom. CONTACTS -- Sometimes, it isn't what you know. "I don't know how you can get these jobs if you don't know someone," said Bobby Impollonia, a 17-year-old programming intern at Goldman Sachs. Several interns suggest getting to know your high school computer-science teacher. THE RIGHT ATTITUDE -- As with any job, certain rules apply. "One student didn't show up for a week," said Raj Goel, chief technology officer at Brain Link, an Internet service provider. "She said it was too much work." Mr. Goel was happy to let her go.   LISA GUERNSEY http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Circuits yesterday about teen-agers' summer jobs misstated the location of Murry Bergtraum High School. It is in Manhattan, not the Bronx. A picture caption with the article misspelled the surname of one of the teen-agers. She is Tamara Metz, not Mett. Correction-Date: August 6, 1999, Friday Graphic   Photos: GAINFULLY EMPLOYED -- Shamarrah Broadus, 18, and Henry Fabian, 16, above, work at Marketing Technologies Group in Manhattan. At right, Tamara Mett, 18, left, Thomas Purtell, 17, and Eamon Walsh, 18, work at Evolve in Vienna, Va. (Ann Grillo for The newyork Times)(pg. G1); FAST TRACK -- Shamarrah Broadus, left, and Henry Fabian, have their own offices at Marketing Technologies Group. At right, Thomas Purtell, left, Tamara Metz and Eamon Walsh were hired by Evolve to create a company to market a new piece of software that lets users in different locations work on one document at the same time. title: House Approves a Bill to Restrict On-Line Sales of Liquor
body: The House today overwhelmingly passed a bill that would restrict on-line liquor sales, overriding objections from California lawmakers that the proposal favored liquor wholesalers over small wineries and breweries trying to broaden their reach through electronic commerce. The bill, which passed 310 to 112, would allow state attorneys general to go to Federal court to prosecute out-of-state companies that violate state restrictions on alcohol sales. Similar legislation has already passed the Senate, attached to an appropriation bill. Although the proposal was largely intended to reduce the availability of alcohol to minors shopping on line, the issue became much broader, pitting large liquor distributors that often have state-licensed monopolies against budding small businesses. Though the White House has generally opposed any new regulations on electronic commerce, it has not yet voiced an official position on the House or Senate bill. States can regulate the import and sale of liquor within their borders, and almost every state prohibits or limits the direct shipment of alcohol from out of state to residents or unlicensed sellers. But attorneys general have been reluctant to take action against growing mail-order and on-line sales because there was no effective way for them to prosecute out-of-state companies. Aggressively opposing the bill were representatives from California and other areas with wineries and breweries that are often unable to distribute their products through traditional wholesalers licensed by the states. There are more than 1,600 small wineries in the country, vying for limited shelf space in traditional retail outlets. Many of the vintners have gone on line. Prohibiting on-line sales "will restrict interstate commerce and limit consumers' choice around the country," said Representative Lois Capps, Democrat of California, who argued that the bill put unfair restrictions on "law-abiding citizens." "If this were a bill to cut down on underage drinking, I'd vote for it," Mrs. Capps said. "But it's not. It's an attack on our vintners." But Representative Joe Scarborough, Republican of Florida, who sponsored the bill, disputed that assertion, saying the proposal would affect only illegal sales. If that is the case, said Representative Zoe Lofgren, another California Democrat, the House should extend the same power to attorneys general trying to enforce their gun laws on out-of-state sellers. "If we're going to give attorney generals in our states the ability to protect citizens from a $20 bottle of cabernet, then they ought to be able to protect them equally from AK-47's, Tec-9's and other weapons of mass destruction," she said. Ms. Lofgren proposed two amendments to broaden the bill to gun sales, but both were ruled non germane. The House did approve an amendment by two Republicans, Representatives Robert W. Goodlatte of Virginia and Christopher Cox of California, specifying that the bill does not give states any authority to impose new or discriminatory taxes on Internet liquor sales.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Trading Is Mixed as Internet Shares Fall Sharply Again
body: Stock prices were mixed yesterday, but traders said investors remained extremely skittish about high valuations and the direction of interest rates. "Investors are very nervous right now, and rightly so," said Bill Allyn, head of listed trading at Jeffries & Company. "We have been talking about valuations for months, and now it is finally hitting home." Internet stocks, the epicenter of speculative activity for much of the year, took another hard hit. TheStreet.com's Internet index fell 20.96, or 3.9 percent, to 519.07, pulled down by stocks like America Online, Yahoo and CMGI. The index has fallen nearly 35 percent since it peaked on April 12. Interest rate worries pulled down the Nasdaq composite index, which fell for the fourth consecutive session. Big declines in Unum Provident, the insurance company, and Charles Schwab, the big discount brokerage house, dragged down the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index, and small stocks slumped. But the Dow Jones industrial average managed to move up, largely on strength in Hewlett-Packard and Procter & Gamble. "This is not just an isolated day," said Bob Gasser, head of unitedstates equity trading at J. P. Morgan Securities. "It is a lot tougher for the market to deal with rising interest rates than with good corporate earnings." Mr. Gasser and other analysts said the market was likely to remain in a highly unsettled state until at least Friday, when July employment data are scheduled to be released. The Federal Reserve Board, which meets Aug. 24 to debate whether it should raise short-term interest rates, is likely to pay close attention to that report. By the close, the Dow Jones industrial average had risen 31.35, or three-tenths of 1 percent, to 10,677.31. The Standard & Poor's 500 index closed at 1322.18, down 5.87, or four-tenths of 1 percent. The Nasdaq composite lost 35.64, or 1.4 percent, to 2587.99. And the Russell 2000 index of small-company stocks fell 6.35, or 1.4 percent, to 436.28. The pace of business quickened a bit from Monday but still remained fairly subdued. Trading volume on the newyork Stock Exchange was 734.9 million shares. On the Nasdaq stock market, just over a billion shares changed hands. Much of the action yesterday was focused on Internet stocks. Early in the day a number of Internet shares rallied on reports that Yahoo was in negotiations to buy Excite@Home. But those rumors were quashed by George Bell, Excite's president. Yahoo, which dipped lower on the initial reports, fell further later. The stock closed at 125 3/8, down 6 15/16. The stock has lost nearly half its market value since early April. Stocks of Internet brokerage firms, which have also been beaten up recently, were battered again after Bill Burnham, an Internet analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston, issued a report saying the companies might see their first-ever decline in trading volume, in the third quarter, because of weakness in the Internet stocks their companies favor. "To see growth in negative territory is significant, but not earth shattering," Mr. Burnham said. "I was surprised the stocks sold off as much as they did" after the report was released. Schwab, the largest on-line brokerage firm, fell 4 11/16, to 37 3/4. E*Trade Group fell 4 5/16, to 24 11/16; Knight/ Trimark Group lost 4 7/32, to 37 1/32, and Ameritrade Holding dropped 2 3/4, to 21 1/4. America Online, the world's largest Internet service, continued its slump, with the stock falling for the fourth session, shedding 4 1/16, to 88 13/16. Since April 6, when it peaked at 175 1/2, the stock has fallen nearly 50 percent. And CMGI, the Internet venture capital company, fell 6 7/16 yesterday, to 81 7/8. "The good news from this summer's selling of Internet shares is that the bears will be hard pressed to still call this a bubble market," said Thomas M. Galvin, chief investment officer at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "At this point, the easy money appears to have been made in Internet stocks." Pressure on these stocks extended to new issues. Four new Internet offerings were priced yesterday: 1-800-Flowers.com, Quotesmith.com, Bigstar Entertainment and Splitrock Services Inc. All closed below their initial offered price. Elsewhere, Unum Provident fell 15 5/16, or 30 percent, to 36 3/8, after the company, one of the nation's largest disability insurers, said that second-quarter earnings fell because of costs associated with the June merger that created it. Qualcomm was the biggest loser on the Nasdaq, falling 12 1/2, to 140. The stock slid after Motorola said it would make semiconductors for phones to compete with Qualcomm. Among Dow stocks, Johnson & Johnson gained 2 1/4, to 94 3/16 after an analyst at J. P. Morgan upgraded his recommendation on the stock to "buy." Proctor & Gamble gained 3 9/16, to 93 11/16. title: Scramble to Fix Computer Security Flaws
body: Three giants of the computer industry Microsoft, Hewlett-Packard and Compaq Computer -- found themselves scrambling today to address a rash of serious security vulnerabilities in software designed to interact with Microsoft's Internet Explorer Web browser. The flaws, first made public last week, are particularly insidious because they allow intruders to plant malicious programs on a computer merely by sending an email message or by luring a victim to a malicious Web page that automatically plants a file on the visitor's hard drive. In either case, the victim would receive no warning of a potential security violation because the flaws enable intruders to bypass the security controls of Internet Explorer and pass undetected through traps set by antivirus software. Tom Noonan, president of Internet Security Systems in Atlanta, said today that several of his client corporations had expressed concern that "now that this information is in the wild, their systems are exposed." "They worry that they are building their network on top of a vulnerable system," he said. Unlike the Melissa virus or the Explore.exe worm, programs that exploit these newly discovered security bugs do not require that the victim take any action; rather, such programs can be activated if a user merely reads a malicious piece of email while on line. As of this evening, there had been no reports of intruders having exploited the flaws, but Microsoft announced that the problems had prompted plans for a major change in the security design of its Windows operating system and the Internet Explorer browser that it recently integrated into Windows. Currently, if Internet Explorer encounters on-line documents created by one of the Microsoft Office suite of programs -- Word, Excel or Powerpoint -- it assumes that they are "safe" and loads them on the user's computer without warning. The problem is that these are very powerful documents capable of launching executable code, whether benign or malicious. Microsoft said future operating systems would not trust such documents. Andrew Dixon, the Microsoft Office product manager, said the company was developing an applet, or small Java program, that would issue a warning before opening Office documents. The immediate problem with Office is that Word or Excel documents can relay an arbitrary command to a computer through a flawed data-base component that shipped with all but the last boxes of Office 97. The Office team worked over the weekend to develop and test a solution to this, Mr. Dixon said. But by this evening they still did not feel confident enough to release a patch for the problem to the 50 million registered users of Office 97. When a patch is available, he said, it will be posted on the Web at http://officeupdate.microsoft.com/Articles /MDAC_typ.htm. In addition to the Office flaws, security holes were found last week in software shipped with Hewlett-Packard's Pavilion models and Compaq's Presarios. Both models were designed to offer customers remote support via the Internet, using Microsoft's browser. Both computer makers configured the browser to allow powerful little programs to run without warning the user. Unfortunately, these applets have the ability to run any other programs. Hewlett-Packard planned to have a patch available soon, said a company spokesman, Ray Aldrich. He said the fix would be posted on the Web at http://www.hp.com/support/ hppavilion.html. "We believe this problem is serious and should be immediately addressed," Mr. Aldrich said. "We do so much testing but sometimes we miss stuff." Hedy Baker, the public relations manager for Compaq's consumer product division, said the company planned to issue an advisory on Wednesday to Compaq support centers and expected to send out a software update to owners of the affected Presarios by the end of next week.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: A Showdown On Messaging May Unite Web Users
body: For more than a week, the Microsoft Corporation and America Online Inc. have engaged in a public spat over open access to the instant-message systems that have become increasingly popular on the Internet. Despite their rhetoric, though, neither company has much of a track record for making it easy for competitors to gain access to the markets that America Online and Microsoft hold dear. Microsoft, of course, stands accused by the Justice Department of unfairly using its control of the Windows operating system to stifle the market for Internet browser software from Netscape Communications -- a company that America Online now owns. And much of the appeal of America Online's service lies in its offering both content and features, like instant messages, that are not available to other Internet users. The current showdown between the two companies concerns America Online's refusal to let Microsoft, among others, link its on-line users to America Online's instant-messaging system -- a form of electronic mail that lets two people conduct a real-time conversation. Jealously as each may guard its own advantages, both Microsoft and America Online are quick to call for openness in any market in which they are behind. Thus, America Online has initiated a vast lobbying campaign calling for open access to offer Internet service through cable television systems, largely because it has been shut out by the AT&T Corporation and other operators. And it is no accident that Microsoft is taking the lead in talking about open standards in instant messaging, a service in which America Online has 80 million users. Until very recently Microsoft had no instant-messaging subscribers on its MSN on-line service. Unlike email, which can be exchanged by all Internet users regardless of the service they subscribe to, instant-message systems so far have been proprietary. Thus, users of Microsoft's new instant message system can communicate only with each other and not with the far larger number of instant messengers on America Online's networks. But Microsoft has found a backdoor to America Online's main instant-message system, setting off a heated debate that embroiled much of the Internet industry last week. And during the last two weeks, the two companies have played at least six rounds of hide and seek, as America Online blocked access to Microsoft, and Microsoft quickly found another way in. By last Friday, many observers were fed up with both sides. "It is unseemly for Microsoft to hijack their way into AOL's system," said Eric Schmitt, an analyst with Forrester Research. "But America Online should open the thing up." The history, culture and underlying technology of the Internet has pressed most proprietary systems to give way to open technical standards. And America Online acknowledges that it cannot fight these forces forever. "AOL realizes in the end this will all be open," said Paul W. Noglows, an analyst with the investment firm Hambrecht & Quist. "They just want to control how it becomes open." America Online's reluctance to embrace an open standard is certainly understandable, considering how much its instant-message system -- and the related "buddy list" technology that lets friends quickly determine if each other is on line -- have contributed to its rise as the most powerful company on the Internet. "It's an important reason you pay your $21.95 for AOL each month," Mr. Noglows said. But even three years ago, America Online acknowledged that it could not keep instant messages limited to its proprietary on-line service. So the company introduced AOL Instant Messenger, a program that anyone with an Internet account could download and use free to send instant messages to both America Online members and any other AOL Instant Messenger user. Instant Messenger enables America Online subscribers who use instant messages at home to also use them at work, even if their office computers do not use the America Online subscription service. But the product also allows people to drop the American Online subscription service entirely and still keep chatting with their friends. Despite the dropouts, America Online can theoretically still make money from Instant Messenger users, because the software has space for advertisements. But since people rarely click on those ads, the revenue is slim. Still, the company believes it will ultimately find ways to make money from a program that millions of people use for hours at a time. America Online was so enamored with instant messages that last year it bought Mirabilis, an Israeli company that makes ICQ, the second most popular instant-message system. ICQ is the classic Web business: it has grown purely by word of mouth to an audience of some 38 million users, but it still has no visible source of revenue. So far, America Online has not linked the two instant-message systems, largely because the hip, college-age ICQ audience does not care to associate with American Online users, who are mainly high-school students and their parents. Moreover, America Online has been wary of doing anything that would open up instant-message systems too quickly. Now that other companies -- not only Microsoft, but even more notably, Yahoo Inc. -- have created their own instant-message systems, there has been increasing demand to link all the systems together. In fact, an industry task force has been formed to develop a standard for such interconnection. America Online has long said that it would support such a standard, once it was developed. But it has done nothing to hasten the development of a consensus -- though, in hindsight, the company planted the seeds for its current crisis. First, America Online did nothing to prevent anyone from mimicking its software, as Microsoft has. Microsoft's own message program, by contrast, encrypts messages, so that no one can create backdoor links its system, as it has done to America Online's. America Online also published on its own Web page a method that people could use to write their own programs to exchange instant messages with users of the Instant Messenger system and to see which of their America Online buddies were on line. The company now says that this recipe was meant only for computer hobbyists and users of the Unix operating system. But on the Web page, America Online did not note any restrictions on the use of the system. And so several companies, including Yahoo and Prodigy Communications, used the information to create instant-message programs that linked to America Online's system. The systems from Yahoo, Prodigy and Microsoft came to light the week before last, and America Online blocked them all -- attracting the glare of publicity. Suddenly, the company's go-slow strategy no longer seemed feasible. America Online's well-oiled crisis-handling machine, led by the public-relations firm Robinson, Lerer & Montgomery, declared that the company would put the development of an instant-messaging standard "on a fast track." The company promised to work actively with the existing industry task force, and it convened its own parallel committee of top industry executives to help shape an instant-messaging standard. These moves, though, did little to appease Microsoft and the other companies. American Online's parallel committee, for example, represents companies like Sun Microsystems, Apple Computer and Real Networks, that are more notable for their longstanding grudges against Microsoft than their involvement in instant messaging. A group of eight other companies, led by Microsoft and Prodigy, wrote a letter to America Online's chairman, Stephen M. Case, arguing that the best thing he could do to further instant-message standards was to stop blocking their programs. "People are looking for a real gesture from AOL," said Brad Chase, one of the executives in charge of Microsoft's consumer and Internet division. "They should stop blocking users now." Microsoft and Prodigy say they will convene their own group to forge a standard at a meeting in newyork in September. With all the attention, an industrywide instant-messaging format is likely to be developed this year. And unless there is significant disagreement about how the standard operates, all the major players -- including America Online -- have now committed to linking their systems to it. That should mean, ultimately, that people will choose their instant message systems as they do email programs: on the basis of marketing, distribution and product features. Less clear is what will happen until a standard is adopted. Last week, America Online made overtures to several companies, including Prodigy, to begin discussions about linking to their message systems. But with all the bad blood, such deals may be hard to negotiate now, especially with Microsoft still intent on cracking America Online's system. Yet, however extreme Microsoft's approach -- and however unlikely an advocate of open systems the company may be -- the walls that divided instant-message users are tumbling down. "Microsoft's tactic worked," Mr. Schmitt said. "It was the fastest way to get AOL to move toward standards." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: America Online's AOL Instant Messenger had several backdoors that allowed competitors such as Microsoft and Yahoo to sneak in their own users. An industry task force has been formed to develop an open standard. (pg. C8)
