title:
COMPRESSED DATA;
Xerox Dusts Off Its Used Copiers
body: The Xerox Corporation is not satisfied with just being the world's biggest seller of new copiers. Now it is using warehouse sales and Internet auctions to attack the $1 billion-plus market for used copiers, as well. More is at stake than added revenue. While Xerox dominates the corporate market, it has never had more than a toehold among small businesses, the prime customers for used machines. "We want that segment of the market to see that Xerox has affordable options for them," said Andrei S. Hall, vice president for Xerox's nine-month-old Certified Pre-Owned Business Unit. More important, it wants those companies to think of Xerox when they can afford more. Xerox's research shows that one of every four small businesses buying a used copier is buying its first copier. If that copier is a Xerox, its next purchase might be an expensive Xerox digital copier. "There are more small businesses out there than large corporations, and they are the ones that are growing and hiring," Mr. Hall said. Mr. Hall's group has already trucked refurbished copiers to 40 cities, where it held two-day sales in rented hotel or showroom spaces. He insists he has not trucked unsold equipment away, and plans to hold at least 60 more such sales this year. In June, Xerox began selling used equipment on www.xerox.com, its Web site. In July, its lower-priced used equipment began appearing on two auction sites, www.ubid.com and www.onsale.com. Today, Xerox and Ubid Inc. will formally announce their alliance. "The warehouse sales just hit a few cities, but the Internet can help us reach people all over the U.S.," Mr. Hall said.   CLAUDIA H. DEUTSCH http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Digital Commerce;
The battle over instant messaging is another case of a company clinging to customers like flypaper.
body: THE keening outrage in the national news media last week over America Online's proprietary behavior toward its Instant Messaging customers strikes many longtime computer industry executives as just plain goofy. The immediate question is whether America Online has the right to enforce -- and by what means -- the network barriers that separate its 80 million Instant Messaging customers from (a) the clutches of its grasping competitors and (b) the rest of the instant-messaging world. But in fact, this is just business as usual. Examine the practices of any market leader and its products in the last 20 or 30 years -- I.B.M., Digital Equipment, Lotus Development, Microsoft -- and it is clear that America Online is simply acting out one of the most enduring concepts in the technology industry. Today's buzzword for the concept is "stickiness," a rather glib term for how a company gets and keeps customers in the notoriously slippery world of the Internet, where a Web site can be come-and-gone at the click of a mouse. "Sticky" has also long been the goal of vendors and service providers. Many have built their biggest successes upon enticing customers with sweet-smelling technical solutions that, once installed, make it extremely painful to switch to a competitor's product. This has been the dominant, albeit unheralded, business model of the computer and software industry since its inception. Back in the days of "big iron" mainframe computers and workstations, companies like the International Business Machines Corporation and the Digital Equipment Corporation were the biggest flypaper vendors in town, selling the computers, the operating systems and often the software, too. Their hegemony was broken by the personal computer -- and then stickiness between Windows and its applications catapulted Microsoft to its monopoly in the PC industry. That's because once buyers commit their customer data bases, corporate documents and financial data to an operating system and brand of application software, they are basically stuck. Anyone who has tried even to switch from one company's word processor to another's can imagine the exponential agony of trying to move an entire corporation from, say, Unix to Windows. But that is a classic sticky application, one that effectively "persuades" customers to stick around. First they are enticed by how convenient it is to use the product. Then they stay because it becomes so terribly inconvenient to leave. On the Internet, stickiness has more to do with collecting valuable personal information about consumers and holding their attention than with storing their data bits. Finding a way to create consumer stickiness is a high priority most particularly for portal sites -- Yahoo, At Home's Excite, Lycos, America Online, Microsoft's MSN -- and retailers like Amazon.com. Every day, it seems, these vendors hang a few more strips of flypaper: free email, custom news services, address books and directories, calendars and event planners, gift services, personal Web sites. Customers sign up and stick around, plugging in more and more personal and family and financial information as they return again and again. Companies like America Online and Microsoft are planning "digital wallet" services that will enable users to consolidate all their sign-in names and passwords. The sales pitch is convenience -- ostensibly consumers would not need to keep repeatedly re-entering the same personal information as they travel and shop the Web. But obviously such wallets are also powerful flypaper applications that, if successful, will tie up consumers' data with a single vendor that will process all their Internet purchases and activities. This type of "service" raises the collective eyebrow of those who remember the enormous power shift in the technology industry when the Internet's open protocols and the Web's freely available programming language, HTML, first loosened the hold that the flypaper vendors had on their customers. Of course, the goal of the free market economy is to whup all your competitors and become the de facto flypaper standard. And that is fine as far as it goes. But as the technology food chain has lengthened to include hundreds of millions of consumers, the concept of "sticky" versus "stuck" has taken on new cultural and economic portent. To be sure, America Online's competitors -- particularly Microsoft -- are acting purely in their own commercial interests. Microsoft, the great imposer of unilateral standards, provided the industry with a Fellini-esque moment last week when an executive was quoted as saying, "We should all just speak the same language," adding, "It shouldn't matter what software or phone you are using." Gaining access to America Online's Instant Message system, thus its customer data base, puts a crimp in the on-line giant's growing domination of cyberspace. But you can bet that if America Online's rivals succeed, they will scramble for a way to alter any new standard to their own ends, just as Microsoft unilaterally rewrote two key open Internet languages, Sun Microsystems' Java and Netscape's Javascript. In the short term, an open standard for instant-message applications has the potential to unstick consumers and reconnect them to the rest of the Internet. Which is why today, battles for dominance of the Internet are of great public interest. Everyone is watching, and millions more people have a stake in the outcome. As one entrepreneur said last week, "It's the users who are going to decide if they prefer to stay in a segregated community or talk to other communities." And that is the kind of sticky situation the industry may not have a strategy for. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title: Hewlett-Packard Sees Its Future as an E-Commerce Revolutionary
body: In the computer industry, power grows not from the barrel of a gun but from the interface of a protocol. And no one may be more aware of that right now than Rajiv Gupta, a 36-year-old Hewlett-Packard computer designer, who for years has seen how the Microsoft Corporation's control of a series of software protocols, or technical formats, has made Microsoft the dominant force in the computer industry. Mr. Gupta is now leading an ambitious Hewlett-Packard effort to establish a comparable edge in Internet-commerce technology with a set of programming protocols called E-Speak. The E-Speak initiative is perhaps the most crucial part of a sweeping makeover by Hewlett, which is intent on transforming itself from a stodgy maker of computers, printers and test equipment into a 21st-century Internet services company. So intent is the company that it is jettisoning its 60-year-old test-and-measurement equipment business and has just gone outside the computer industry to hire a new chief executive, Carleton S. Fiorina, from the telecommunications equipment company, Lucent Technologies. E-Speak, which Hewlett introduced last month, is a network-oriented programming language designed to let companies and individuals quickly put new Internet business ideas into action by easily translating them into software code. It is a measure of the company's commitment that it has put Mr. Gupta, one of its top hardware designers, in charge of this effort. "This will open a whole new service economy," he said. "You will have a business ecosystem that is created." Of course, if this effort sounds conceptually similar to the Java software initiative that Hewlett's chief rival, Sun Microsystems, began mounting several years ago, Mr. Gupta does not necessarily rebut the comparison. "We have nothing against the idea of standing on the shoulders of giants," he said, before adding whimsically, "or on the toes of dwarfs." In fact, E-Speak is the technical foundation for Hewlett's new E-Services business as it tries to catch up not only with Sun but with the International Business Machines Corporation; both rivals have used Java effectively to develop E-commerce offerings for corporate customers. And E-Speak is compatible with Java, as well as Jini, Sun's newest attempt to develop a networking system to automatically link together all kinds of computing devices. That said, the Hewlett business vision is a radical one, even by Internet standards: The company contends that E-Speak and E-Services will help usher in an information service economy that goes a step beyond that made possible by the first generation of Web protocols, known as HTML and HTTP. Those first protocols made possible electronic directories like Yahoo and E-commerce World Wide Web sites like Amazon.com. But HTML and HTTP alone are unable to support electronic bazaars that can allow for transactions between thousands of independent buyers and sellers, who may have had no prior contact and want to do business on a single, one-time basis. Consider the example of a person who speaks French and English and wants to set up a home business translating business letters in French into idiomatic English. In the E-Services model, all that our translator would need is a personal computer connected to the Internet. The E-Speak software would act as a broker for the translation service, matching buyer and seller in cyberspace and handling all of the underlying financial details of the service. If the E-Services model works, the boundaries of such a new electronic economy are extensive. Mr. Gupta concedes that there are already hundreds of different E-commerce business models based on the concept of acting as a broker between buyer and seller. But he insists that Hewlett's E-Services approach, based on E-Speak technology, will win because it offers a complete computing system intended to easily link different components of a business venture, rather than forcing the businesses to worry about the underlying technologies. "All of the Internet messiahs want to create commerce brokerages," he said. "Our vision starts where other visions end." The big question, of course, is whether the market will see what Mr. Gupta sees. This is not the first time Hewlett has tried to create a new computing paradigm. In 1990, the company rolled out Newwave, a system that worked on top of Microsoft's Windows and was intended to automate many of the basic tasks of using a personal computer. Newwave, though, was largely ignored in the marketplace. And this time around, Hewlett is facing a variety of competing technologies, each with a head start on E-Speak and each meant to bring similar capabilities to the Internet. One of them is Microsoft's Biztalk version of the XML extension of the HTML Web protocol. XML is an Internet protocol that is intended to make it easier to interconnect different kinds of business computing systems. Sun Microsystems has already incorporated XML into its Jini technology, which is still feeling its way in the marketplace. These efforts, like E-Speak, are meant to make it easier for to incorporate new business models into computer networks. "Can E-Speak whip Jini?" said Paul Saffo, a computer industry consultant at the Institute for the Future in Menlo Park, Calif. "It will be interesting to watch." But Mr. Gupta, at least, has no doubts about the world-altering potential of his system, which began as a so-called skunkworks, or secret, research project by three engineers at Hewlett-Packard Laboratories in 1991. Having grown up in a family of small-scale industrialists in Northern India, Mr. Gupta arrived in the unitedstates in 1984 to attend graduate school at the California Institute of Technology, in Pasadena. He recalls being more surprised by the similarities between Indian and American cultures than by the differences. "It was something of an anticlimax," he said. Though it was his first time outside of India, Mr. Gupta found it easy to adapt to life in California. "Unlike the books and movies, people were quite normal," he said. Mr. Gupta, who is married and has two children, lives in Los Altos Hills, near Palo Alto. If he succeeds, even by Silicon Valley standards Mr. Gupta will have proven to be something of a wunderkind. He came to Hewlett-Packard at age 28 in 1991, fresh out of graduate school as an expert in processor design and software compilers -- software that translates the programmer's instructions into machine code. Until three years ago, his principal role was as the technical lead designer for the joint Intel-Hewlett IA-64 microprocessor project -- the chip that became the Merced, on which the Intel Corporation is banking its post-Pentium future. The E-Speak software project was still only a sidelight. But when the IA-64 chip design left the lab to be turned over to a development team, Mr. Gupta shifted his full attention to pursuit of his E-Speak vision. And now, even if the IA-64 chip design ultimately becomes Intel's technical standard-bearer, Mr. Gupta contends that E-Speak has the potential to make a bigger impact. In the rapidly moving Internet economy Hewlett-Packard is staking its future on a huge gamble -- a vision of the business world transformed by Internet software, which is the same strategy being pursued by some formidable competitors. But Mr. Gupta contends that when E-Speak technology finds its way into the world it will have an impact that extends beyond business, helping recreate the genuine human communities that are so far largely missing on the Internet. Beyond today's chat rooms and email lists, he looks to build the Internet into every aspect of life through a software system that will interconnect computers, cell phones, pagers and whatever other digital gadgets may come along. "I'm very passionate about this," he said. "This will fundamentally change our lives." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Rajiv Gupta, who is leading Hewlett-Packard's effort in Internet software, helps his daughters, Veda, 3, at left, and Anya, 15 months, as they prepare for a frog race. (Andy Barron for The newyork Times)

title: Less Web Shopping Seen
body: The percentage of people with Internet access who are making purchases from Web sites declined slightly in the second quarter of 1999 after four sequential quarters of spectacular growth, according to Greenfield Online Inc. The study by Greenfield, a Westport, Conn., Internet marketing research firm, hints at the limits of market penetration of the medium as a shopping platform -- suggesting a ceiling that has been unknown until now. "This is the first indication of the size of the population that will use the Internet to shop," Rudy Nadilo, Greenfield's president and chief executive, said. Mushrooming E-commerce sales -- and visions of geometric growth into the future -- have fueled the recent boom of Internet stock valuations. Greenfield's study does not necessarily indicate that sales on the World Wide Web have stalled, since the total number of people with Web access continues to grow rapidly. And the finding that 71 percent of people on line bought at least once in the last three months is respectable, even if it stays at that level. From the first quarter of 1998 to the first quarter of this year, the percentage of people with on-line access who said they had bought something through a Web site rose to 74 percent from 47 percent, Greenfield said. But in the latest quarter, Greenfield found that the percentage had slipped to 71 percent. The findings were based on 2,598 respondents selected randomly from Greenfield's national pool of more than one million individuals who have volunteered to participate in on-line research.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MEDIA;
Cutting Through the On-Line Clutter
body: While most of his readers are still asleep, James Romenesko is up at 5 A.M. each weekday, furiously surfing the Web. He reads newspaper sites, magazine sites, gossip sites and alternative sites in search of stories that are appropriate for the two digests of Web links he publishes. For Mediagossip.com, Mr. Romenesko seeks news and criticism about the media and those who work in it. For The Obscure Store and Reading Room (www.obscurestore.com), he scours for stories that are more offbeat, like a recent piece about a batboy attacking a baseball team's mascot and another about the struggles of a Pee-Wee Herman impersonator. "He is absolutely the best for finding goofy stories," said Steve Knopper, himself a practitioner of the emerging specialty of Net scavenging. Mr. Knopper writes Yahoo Internet Life's Daily Net Buzz column (www.zdnet.com/yil/content/depts/ netbuzz), which also provides links to articles from a variety of news sources. Summaries of news predate the Internet, of course. But in the digital era, when virtually anyone with Net access can operate an electronic clipping service, the genre has spawned thousands of news hounds -- not to mention the news links on big portal sites like Yahoo and Excite. Yet, largely through grass-roots, word-of-mouse popularity, sites like Mr. Romenesko's are catching on with a discerning crowd -- including reporters and editors of many news organizations, who rely on the sites to help filter the welter of information on the Web. Such digests, whether compiled as a collection of links on a Web site or distributed by electronic mail, sift the on-line content of established media organizations like ABC News (abcnews.go.com), MSNBC (msnbc.com) and The newyork Times on the Web (nytimes.com), as well as alternative outlets like newyork Press (newyorkpress.com) and The Smoking Gun (thesmokinggun.com). Other examples of Net digests, with their own growing audiences, include Media Grok and Davenetics (www.davenetics.com). Many digests do not link to news sites like The Wall Street Journal Interactive Edition or TheStreet.com that charge readers a fee. And Mr. Romenesko even declines to include free sites that require readers to register, like The newyork Times Web site -- though he will sometimes cite some of the articles that appear on the Times's affiliated city guide, newyork Today (nytoday.com), which can be read without registering. A gatekeeper for gatekeepers, Mr. Romenesko said that, according to the traffic logs for his two sites, his "many thousands" of daily readers included regular visitors from National Public Radio, CNBC, Conde Nast, Hearst and numerous other media organizations. Like some of the other more popular Web news sifters, Mr. Romenesko is himself a professional journalist. But it is not until after updating both his sites with new links and images by about 8:30 A.M. each weekday that he heads off for work at The St. Paul Pioneer Press, where he covers the Internet. He receives no pay for the time he devotes to his own Web sites, though he does use them to link to items he is auctioning on Ebay, like old issues of Spy magazine. And recently he began running paid banner ads on the sites. Mainly, though, he operates the sites "for personal pleasure and not for great financial gain." "I've always been interested in D.I.Y. -- do it yourself -- movements and projects," Mr. Romenesko said. "And I see my work as an on-line D.I.Y. venture. While other sites brag about growth and expanding employee payrolls, I talk about staying a one-person operation." Another soloist is Mr. Knopper, who writes Daily Net Buzz from his home in Chicago. Daily Net Buzz includes breaking news, entertainment, sports, technology and quirky stories. "I'm always looking for stories that have a twist," Mr. Knopper said. Some of the other news digests focus on a specific industry or niche. Some readers say these compilations are changing the way people consume news in the digital age. For example, Erik Rydholm, chief operating officer and a founding partner of the Motley Fool financial site, said he was much less informed before he began reading Media Grok, a daily on-line newsletter published on the Web site of an International Data Group technology magazine, The Industry Standard (www.the standard.com/articles/mediagrok). Media Grok provides summaries of and links to media coverage of the Internet and technology. "Until this thing came out, I actually didn't keep up with the industry, because it was too much of a pain to go from site to site," Mr. Rydholm said. "Now I can do my competitive research, and it only takes me about 15 minutes a day." And in an industry where value is often measured by page views and unique users, the most popular digests play an important promotional role for the World Wide Web sites that they send readers to. In fact, many journalists now pitch their stories for inclusion in Mediagossip, Media Grok or other digests. "We're constantly getting email from people at media outlets," said Mark Glaser, one of four writers who compile Media Grok. "And we appreciate it. If people are pointing us to things, it makes our job easier." By the same token, Mr. Glaser said he had received email from reporters asking why their articles were neglected in favor of competitors'. James Poniewozik, the television critic for Time magazine, a former media critic for Salon and a regular reader of Mr. Romenesko's sites, noted that on-line journalism provided more immediate feedback than print journalism. "On line," he said, "you are, at least theoretically, constantly aware of the number of hits you're getting." Newsletters and Web sites that link to technology news are among the most popular. "What I find especially in the coverage of technology is that there is such a scrum of journalism today," said Scott Rosenberg, managing editor of Salon and a longtime technology reporter. "There is such a pile-on. It's almost impossible for a single human being to monitor it all." Mr. Rosenberg relies on about a dozen digests of links to technology coverage. These sites include Scripting News (www.scripting.com), which is published by Dave Winer, a software developer who has written for Hotwired. Dave Pell, managing director of Arba Seed Investment Group in San Francisco, publishes a free email newsletter called Davenetics. Each day, Mr. Pell summarizes and links to the latest technology stories, putting his own spin on the news through the headlines and summaries he writes. Mr. Pell started Davenetics in February with about 50 subscribers, after realizing that he often emailed his business associates several times a day about news stories he had found. Davenetics now has more than 1,500 subscribers, and Mr. Pell says most of his readers work for or invest in Internet companies. Mr. Pell, who has invested in companies including the on-line magazine Feed and the product information site Productopia, calls himself a "total content fanatic." And he says he is not alone. "If you look at the growth of E-commerce, it still doesn't come close to the people who are looking for information," Mr. Pell said. In contrast to independent newsletters like Davenetics, digests published by media outlets like The San Jose Mercury News or The Industry Standard publish links to their own stories as well as articles from their competitors. In that respect, the digests can serve as supplements to the originating publication -- or as substitutes. Media Grok's Mr. Glaser, for example, says that readers have told him that they read his site's news summaries instead of the actual articles he links to. Mr. Glaser, though, says he reads about 25 stories and skims another 10 or 15 each evening that he works on Media Grok, which he does from home. The Industry Standard says Media Grok, which is available by email and on the magazine's Web site, is read by about 100,000 people each day. "There are a lot of people who are reading it who are business people that are using it as a service to keep up with the news," Mr. Glaser said. "I didn't realize we would become a substitute for the news." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Dave Pell, managing director of a San Fransisco investment company, summarizes technology stories for more than 1,500 subscribers. (Thor Swift for The newyork Times)

title:
MEDIA TALK;
A Growing Internet Business Magazine Adds a Familiar Byline
body: If anyone in journalism has nine lives, James Fallows does. Mr. Fallows, a former editor of U.S. News and World Report, outspoken press critic, author of "Breaking the News: How the Media Undermine American Democracy" and -- most recently -- Microsoft consultant, will join The Industry Standard magazine as a columnist. Jonathan Weber, the editor in chief of the Standard, a weekly Internet-business magazine published by International Data Group, is expected to announce the appointment tomorrow. And Mr. Fallows will have plenty of company: within the last month, Mr. Weber has lured reporters and editors away from several news organizations, including Thomas Goetz from The Wall Street Journal, Kenneth Li from The newyork Daily News, and staff members from Inc. magazine, Wired and The San Jose Mercury News. And on Friday, Mr. Weber hired Amy Bernstein, the editorial director of Brill's Content magazine. He said the editorial staff, which last month had 27 members, would grow to 45 by the end of September. Mr. Weber said that he had begun to think of the San Francisco-based Standard as the Rolling Stone of the Internet business economy, and of Mr. Fallows as a columnist who will help attract a broader readership. "We are focused on the phenomenon of Internet business," Mr. Weber said. "But it is such a big and influential phenomenon with so many different dimensions that there's an enormous amount of interest from people who are not in the business." The Standard's unaudited circulation base is 115,000; by contrast, Wired's is 425,000. The Standard says its advertising pages grew 140 percent from June 1998 to June 1999, with gains averaging 30 percent every quarter since the magazine was founded in April 1998. Mr. Fallows said that in joining the staff, he was "trying to create some version of my pre-U.S. News life, which is writing books, magazine articles and writing a frequent column." He added: "My plan is basically to write about the outside world and the Internet. What should the outside world make of these castles being made of sand or of steel girders every day? How should people building these castles think of themselves historically and in the eyes of their citizens? Think of me as an interested amateur observer."   ALEX KUCZYNSKI http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: James Fallows will write for The Industry Standard magazine. (Associated Press)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Alta Vista Chooses Wieden & Kennedy
body: Alta Vista, the on-line search engine and new-media commerce site owned by the Compaq Computer Corporation, has awarded a new worldwide account to Wieden & Kennedy in Portland, Ore. Billings were estimated at $50 million to $60 million. The decision returns Wieden & Kennedy to the technology category six weeks after it lost assignments from the Microsoft Corporation. Charles Rashall, vice president for sales and marketing at Alta Vista, in Palo Alto, Calif., attributed the decision to the agency's "unique set of skills and good understanding both of technology and customer needs." The decision came after a two-month review, he added, declining to identify the other participants. The Portland headquarters of Wieden & Kennedy will be the lead office on the account, to be joined by a new office in Palo Alto. The agency's newyork office will handle broadcast media, and offices in Amsterdam, London and Tokyo will jointly handle international duties. The deal with Alta Vista came two days after Wieden & Kennedy lost the Miller Genuine Draft beer account, with billings estimated at $60 million, to the J. Walter Thompson Chicago unit of the J. Walter Thompson Company, part of WPP Group P.L.C. Miller is sold by the Miller Brewing Company unit of the Philip Morris Companies, which kept Wieden & Kennedy as the agency for Miller High Life.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Attention, Wannabe Gazillionaires;
A Company That Captures the Spirit of the Age
body: To: Potential Investors From: me@me.com Subject: Internet Start-up and Initial Public Offering It's not just young upstarts from Silicon Valley or Silicon Alley anymore. Even the old freight-delivery dowager U.P.S. is declaring itself an Internet player (it ships a lot of stuff bought on Web sites) and announcing that it is going public. The I.P.O. craze has reached the point that the stock exchanges themselves are hatching plans to sell shares. So I believe the time is right to take the Internet-I.P.O. phenomenon a pioneering step further, which I plan to do, with my new company, me.com. The company promises to be an extraordinary opportunity for a select group of investors, and I'm giving you a chance to be one of them. Since I am in the pre-I.P.O. stage, the exact details of my company are still a closely guarded secret. Good buzz, as we all know, can be worth billions in today's frenzied market. A careful blend of mystery and hype are key ingredients in the marketing plan of any good Internet start-up. As part of the comprehensive marketing strategy, I will also be shaving my head, piercing two or three body parts (as yet undisclosed), and lying shamelessly about my age. The company is positioned across three markets with explosive growth potential -- the Internet (see company name above), intellectual property (I have lots and lots of ideas) and the human genome project (hey, I have as many genes as anyone else). Yes, the company's losses are already mounting. But as we all know, in the Internet era there are no losses, only investments. In the hyperspeed land grab for mind share and market share in the New Economy, actually making money is a character weakness -- a sure sign of a worrisome lack of imagination in not being able to come up with more and more ways to spend money. The financially meek, after all, will not inherit the high-tech economy's Next Big Thing. Me.com has already attracted the financial backing of Dick Digit, the Internet visionary and co-founder of harebrained.com, a company I regard as nearly as path-breaking as my own. Dick, of course, is now a gazillionaire because harebrained.com was acquired only four months after it was founded for a stupifying sum by a major computer company desperate to jump on the Internet bandwagon. Which brings me to the company's long-term (a maximum of six months) strategy, which is founded upon two plans that are calculated to trigger results. Plan No. 1: Create some buzz and persuade Microsoft that America Online is anxious to buy me.com, which will prompt Microsoft to buy the company so that its archrival will not get it. Plan No. 2: Plan No. 1 in reverse. Convince America Online to snap up me.com to keep it out of Microsoft's clutches. Either way, me.com is a decided winner. Finally, I think I should say a bit about an aspect critical to business but regrettably neglected in most Internet start-ups -- management. The management structure and philosophy behind me.com is, I'm proud to say, one of its unique features. It is the ultimate "lean" company, quick and responsive, distinctively able to react faster than flamemail over a T3 line. Me.com has a totally flat organizational structure, no layers of bureaucratic flab bogging down the decision-making process. I am the chairman, chief executive officer, chief technology officer and sole employee of me.com. It's all me, just me.  Addendum: F.Y.I. The Net being the Net, if you actually go looking for www.me.com on the Web, as many of you wannabe gazillionaires will doubtless do, it will indeed take you some@me.com. Last week, Net surfers would find a page that was part of the corporate Web site for Job 1 Systems Inc. of Sunnyvale, Calif., a company that provides "financing and strategic services for start-ups." But Brian G. Job, a graduate of Stanford and the Harvard business school, said he had just sold off the Web address, or domain name, to an eager bidder. And like everything else on the Net, me.com is changing fast.   STEVE LOHR http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: 'Casino Mentality' Linked To Day Trading's Stresses
body: The pause in the relentless stream of stock tips scrolling up the screen in the Internet chat room called Daytraders was brief, and it was mechanically enforced. But after the shooting spree this week at two Atlanta firms that specialize in the rapid-fire buying and selling of stocks known as day trading, several hundred on-line investors observed a virtual moment of silence. "Violent acting-out is often associated with high levels of stress, and we cannot ignore the setting in which he chose to vent his rage," the chat room's manager, David Mason, told his assemblage on Friday, referring to Mark O. Barton, who killed nine people at the two trading sites before shooting himself. In cyberspace and in trading rooms, many of the nation's swelling ranks of day traders repudiated the notion that Mr. Barton's own day-trading activities contributed to the violent outburst. "This had nothing to do with day trading," said a middle-aged woman getting into a Mercedes convertible in the parking lot of the All-Tech Investment Group in Montvale, N.J., on Friday afternoon. "The guy was a nut," said the woman, who described herself as a day trader. But the incident -- along with the mediocre performance of the stock market in recent days -- has also prompted a smidgen of soul-searching among the amateur investors who use the instant availability of stock information via the Internet to buy and sell the same stocks within a single trading day for quick personal profit, or loss. "Day trading's stresses are not more or less than most jobs, but there are different kinds of stresses," wrote an investor who uses the name Eileen in the Daytraders chat room. "E.G., there is no security at all, and no regular paycheck." Those particular stresses, like coping with wild gains and losses from day to day, are unfamiliar to most Americans, who have begun to indulge in day trading by the thousands only in recent years. That is in part why All-Tech, where Mr. Barton once traded in the Atlanta office and where he opened fire last week, employs a psychologist as part of its training program for day traders. "We want to train people in what goes through your mind when you're trading," said Mark Shefts, president of All-Tech. "We want to help make people aware of what goes through your mind when you're making money and when you're losing money." It seems that being aware of what you are doing, however, does not always help you stop. A 31-year-old San Francisco lawyer said that in addition to borrowing as much as he was allowed against his stock portfolio, he had borrowed $20,000 from his credit card company and put the money directly into the market. As a result, at times he borrowed up to $40,000 to buy securities, mostly in Internet stocks. "During conference calls and drafting sessions, I would sneak out to check my portfolio," said the lawyer, who asked that his name not be used because he did not want his firm to know about his trading or his family to know about his debts. But, he said, he could not resist the potential payoff. "I was a gambler sitting at a table" in Las Vegas, he said. "My palms got sweaty thinking about how much money I could make." When the market soured, the lawyer said, he simply had to admit to himself, "Well, that was dumb." He then waited out the market until it rebounded, and paid off the interest on the money he borrowed to buy the securities in the first place. He remains heavily in debt. Still, while psychologists warn about the stress of living in a state of perpetual high risk and investment experts warn that long-term investing has proved far more profitable, most day traders blame the mechanics of the system for their heightened sense of anxiety. A telephone interview on Friday with a 37-year-old day trader in Port Aransas, Tex., was continually interrupted as he checked the status of the unfulfilled order he had placed minutes before with the on-line brokerage Charles Schwab. "They hold an order for up to eight minutes," fumed the investor, who said his account had dropped to $94,000 from $120,000 a month ago. "That's fine for some old guy who buys Pepsi one morning and sells it the next." But the delay foiled his ability to take advantage of an uptick of three-eighths in the stock price. "My order was at one-eighth and I would have sold at the half," he said. "I'd already be out with three or four hundred dollars in my pocket." The trader, who is known in on-line trading chat rooms as Captain Jack but did not want to see his real name in print, pays someone else to run his oil business so he can trade full time. Jokes about "going trader," replacing "going postal" as the term for seemingly random violent eruptions, circulated through day-trading discussion forums on Friday. Tom Gardner, co-founder of the Motley Fool, one of the oldest investment information sites on the Internet, said he thought there was a connection between Mr. Barton's trading and his rampage. "It's not fair to say that day trading caused this, but I do think there's a casino mentality to it that would tend to draw somebody who was very intense," Mr. Gardner said. "It makes sense that the outcome of that intense personality and intense failure would compound the likelihood of this kind of behavior." Mr. Gardner, an advocate of long-term investing, admonishes day traders to face the fact that their strategy is just "bad math." That may be true, but most day traders seem to agree with Jim Cox, a 20-year-old senior at the University of Connecticut who thinks it is possible to beat the numbers. "I've been in this chat room for a couple of years, and I've noticed all the nicknames change," said Mr. Cox, who frequents the Daytraders chat room. In less than a year, Mr. Cox said, he has made $190,000, sometimes borrowing as much as $100,000 against his account. "I'm assuming 80 percent of them fail. But you have to be smart. If I keep going the way I am, I can make $10,000 a week easy." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Many day traders, conceding that their job is stressful, blame the mechanics of the system for their anxiety. (G. Paul Burnett/The newyork Times)

title: email, E-Commerce And Now E-Buildings
body: IT hasn't become as routine as electricity, water and heat, but quietly and at an impressive pace information technologies -- especially new modes of electronic data transmission -- are joining established utilities as services that Manhattan apartment dwellers have come to expect. "We already take cable television, local telephone connections and long distance for granted," said Jonathan Rudes, the senior managing director of Newmark and Company Real Estate Inc., and a member of the Real Estate Technology Forum, which is helping the industry match information technologies and market demands. "We generally expect that we'll walk into our houses or apartments and, like lights and heat, those two services will be there on demand." Familiarity with other information-entertainment technologies, Mr. Rudes said, should breed expectations regarding their availability. He cited "smart" appliances operated by remote control and card- or thumb-reading security systems as future examples. With more people communicating by email and shopping by computer, he said, high-speed Internet access in Manhattan apartments is already starting to become commonplace. "Until you have high-speed Internet access at home, you don't realize how much you need it," said Ari Rubenstein, a commodities trader and adviser who, with his wife, Atoosa, rents a $3,300-a-month, 1,000-square-foot apartment in 180 Riverside Boulevard, a new Trump Place luxury building overlooking the Hudson at 68th Street. "Now, I wouldn't move into a building without it." Mrs. Rubenstein, the editor of CosmoGIRL!, a new magazine and web site for teen-agers, is equally enthusiastic about high-speed Internet access, and her cell phone -- both "time savers," she said, "when time is a precious commodity." Neither considered the building's offer of satellite or cable television (they opted for cable) an attraction, since they "don't watch and don't particularly care." But Mr. Rubenstein, in particular, was intrigued with the promise of the building's internal computerized information system, through which the concierge can track packages, make travel, restaurant or theater reservations and provide a range of interactive services, including teleconferencing, in which tenants are able to see and speak via computer with visitors at the front desk. The system also coordinates residents' maintenance and security/access requests. Colin Abernethy and his wife, Alexis, didn't concertedly search for a high-tech residence either. But after finding the new space they wanted at their price and location -- 1,700 square feet for under $700,000 in the Ice House at 27 North Moore Street in TriBeCa -- they discovered that they needed all the information services their condominium can provide: digital satellite television; cable, if they desired; a responsive local telephone service, including the possibility of telephoning internally -- and free of charge -- with other residents and building staff; a reliable and economic long-distance carrier of their choosing, and, yes, high-speed Internet access. "They may have started as amenities, but now they're necessities," said Mr. Abernethy, a former managing director at Bear Sterns who helped found Flextrader.com, a web site for retail investors, and plans to open a computer-equipped home office. Mrs. Abernethy, he explained, is the director of sales for Material Connexion, a materials resource library. She works at home, on her laptop, up to four hours a day. "I'm on line seven or eight hours," he said. "When it comes to processing information, wherever I am I need speed and choice." So does Simone Procas, a litigation associate at the law firm of Gibson Dunn & Crutcher L.L.P., who with Edward Ferguson, the head of newyork City's Trade Waste Commission, will be moving next year into a $635,000, 1,300 square foot condominium being built at 53 North Moore Street. "At work I go on line for legal information -- past cases, recent court decisions, The newyork Law Journal," Ms. Procas said. "If I can get that at home, great; it means I can come in less often on weekends." WAS it requisite to their apartment search? Not really, said Ms. Procas, whose priorities were location, space and price. "But it's nice to have the potential for several phone lines, cable television, the Internet, where I also shop for books, read breaking news and plan our vacations," she said. She could get used to these at-home services "very quickly," she said. That's what building owners and managers are banking on as they install the infrastructure for information technologies, particularly high-speed Internet access, in new construction as well as renovations. "They want to take advantage of having a captive consumer audience -- residents who will be in their buildings 12 to 24 hours a day and who will need services," said Christopher H. Martorella, the managing director of Boston Financial, a real estate investment firm. "Now, their audience is more technologically savvy; they probably use more technology on a daily basis, and feel more at ease. Owners and managers want to capture revenues from that." And they don't mind benefiting from the desire of service providers to get access to those tenants. The competition can be so intense that vendors will offer to discount or bundle services, waive installation charges and wire the building virtually free of charge. Some developers may arrange to collect a small fee for every resident who signs up for a particular service. Nancy Packes, the president of Feathered Nest, a Manhattan real estate brokerage, said that developers are giving increasing attention to the electronic sinews of their buildings, especially when their target groups of residents come from certain industries or professions. "Attracting these market segments," Ms. Packes said, "has made high-speed Internet access standard in the last year and a half. No new building has gone up without it." Pamela Liebman, the president of Corcoran Group Marketing, said developers are also recognizing that many residents today want to work out of their apartments. "And a number of those residents were spoiled in school and at the office, where they had available to them fast and sophisticated technologies," Ms. Liebman said. "No wonder they have certain expectations regarding services that should be available to them at home." Owners and developers of residential buildings, said Mr. Rudes of Newmark, are beginning to see information services as a point of competition. "It's starting with the technologies -- who can offer better reception or faster, cheaper speeds," he said. "Later, the competition may focus on content" -- who can provide better-quality, lower-cost information; who has the smarter, more thoroughly wired "information concierge." Landlords are also retrofitting older buildings with the new technologies. Herb Hauser, president and chief executive officer of Barnes Wentworth, a technology engineering company, said there are about 50 major retrofit projects around the city right now. "The whole retrofit market, and service industry, is likely to pick up," Mr. Hauser said, "once landlords and co-op boards discover how simple and inexpensive it can be -- $75,000 to $125,000 to bring fiber optics and broadband conductivity to a 110 to 125 unit apartment building. And you don't have to have a mess of wires or drill lots of holes in people's walls." Developers and owners of residential properties understand that these new technologies are like apartment balconies, Mr. Martorella said, noting, "Residents may not use them, but they like to know that they can walk outside if they want." Laughing ruefully at the analogy, Waiman Leung, a resident of the Ice House, agreed. Mr. Leung, an options trader, paid $550,000 for his 1,700-square-foot condominium. He loved the high, domed ceilings, the TriBeCa neighborhood, the space and the price, which he said was a lot less than what he had seen in SoHo. As for the building's high-tech options, he said, "The D.S.S, or direct satellite service television, was a big draw, because I love watching football, along with Bloomberg financial news and CNN. And the satellite dish on the building's roof means that I get games from across the country and great reception." Mr. Leung's home entertainment system attests to his infatuation. He hooked up the satellite video output connection in his bedroom to a Macintosh flat-panel monitor for what he considers to be "the best picture on the market," and the satellite audio output connection to a Bose system "to boost audio quality." He has a wide-screen, high-definition television in his living room, connected to six speakers for a surround-sound effect. WHAT of high-speed Internet access, which he relies on in the office and has yet to use at home? Mr. Leung said that neither he nor his friends have found the proffered combinations of price and speed -- that is, the money they must pay for the higher speeds they like -- to be irresistibly attractive. "So," he said, "we haven't signed up yet." But as with balconies, so with technology; Mr. Leung and his friends say they like the very notion of choice. "Developers, owners and managers may not fully understand the technologies," Mr. Hauser said, "but they know that they are important to residents and that residents want options. That gives the developers enormous power. In effect, the spaces in which people live may determine the shape of the information industry." The problems arise in the choices available. "It's as if it's 1900 and building owners wanted to install elevators," Mr. Hauser said. "If they went to Otis, they would get an elevator with an electric motor. If they went to another company, they'd get one driven by hydraulics. A third company sold steam-piston-driven products. There are many ways, technologically, to provide any one service, like television or high-speed Internet access, and every technology provider has a product and an agenda." And every product has its merits, drawbacks and risks, as members of the co-op board at 133 West 17th Street are discovering. Jack Piry, the co-op's vice president, described the situation this way: The turn-of-the-century building has 24 apartments ranging in size from about 1,300 square feet to more than 3,200 square feet. Maintenance starts at $869 and runs up to $1,575 a month. He said that one of the last apartments sold, a 2,000 square foot penthouse, went for approximately $700,000. The only electronic services this co-op has are telephones, from Bell Atlantic, and cable television, from Time Warner. "We don't have even the option of getting on line fast, if we wanted it in the future," said Mr. Piry, who works with computerized patient data for newyork Hospital. "The phone jacks are not always conveniently placed" (his is above the washer-dryer) "and as for cable television, the reception has not always been great, in part because of the wires." VISITORS to 133 West 17th Street cannot miss the wires -- like two giant vines dangling along either side of the building, with a loose-hanging high wire in between. In most newyork City buildings, cable television service comes in from the street to the basement, then courses up through the service hallways or stairwells, branching off on each floor to deliver the service to each apartment. In 133 West 17th Street, however, cable television is supplied through cables that run outside the building from a box on the roof, and then into the individual apartments. The cables are unsightly, and, exposed to the weather, they have been damaged periodically, producing "ghosts" of broadcast images on residents' television screens. "Many of us would like better-quality, cheaper cable," Mr. Piry said. "We'd like the opportunity for higher-speed computer use, and we'd certainly like fewer wires that are no longer exposed. Oh, and customer service for both telephone and cable has been an issue." Don Judd, a member of the building's co-op board, suggested alternatives: For the television service alone, they could try a satellite dish, assuming, that is, that a dish placed on the building's roof would be in the satellite's line of sight. Or they could try a fiber optics-based system, especially since, according to a company spokesman, RCN Corporation has been "building out" in newyork -- that is, installing and extending the reach of its own fiber-optics lines beneath the streets. "The good thing about using an RCN" or similar company, Mr. Judd said, "is that the cable service is cheaper and the one company could handle telephone local service, cable TV and, through a cable-modem arrangement, Internet access for each apartment -- and with minimal wires." But there are drawbacks, said Mr. Judd, who is responsible for the relationship between Lucent Technologies and Sun Microsystems worldwide. These include the lack of competition, which he believes generates more and better services at an improved price; the limitations of any cable-based technology -- that the more people using it simultaneously, the slower the operating speed, and the issue of what happens if someone wants to go back to Time Warner: Would they be charged an installation fee? "The bottom line for users," Mr. Hauser said, "is that they're at a stage when they can order 17 different kinds of spaghetti, but it's still spaghetti sitting there on their plate. Somebody has to take the bowl, untangle the mess and figure out which of the spaghetti is really gourmet pasta."  A Glossary of High-Tech Terms  Bandwidth: A measurement indicating the volume of information that can be transmitted over a network, usually expressed in megabits per second. The higher the bandwidth, the wider the information pipeline, the greater the flow of data. Even using the fastest modems currently available with phone lines, users can access the Internet over regular telephone wires at only 56 kilobits per second (that's 56,000 bits per second). By contrast, T-1 speeds can reach 1.544 megabits (1.544 million bits) per second, while digital subscriber lines (D.S.L.) can approach T-1 speeds. Bit: The smallest unit of computerized data. The word comes from collapsing binary digit. Bps: How fast data are being moved, expressed in bits per second. Byte: -- There are usually 8 bits to a byte, or a single character. Cable modem: A technology that uses a modem and coaxial cable to give computers speedy access to the Internet. The same coax may deliver your cable television service. Coaxial cable: Cable configured with an inner conductor and an outer shield positioned around a common axis. Dial-up connection: Accessing the Internet using a telephone and modem. Direct connection: High-speed access to the Internet; just turn on your computer (if it is suitably hooked up to a T-1, cable-modem or digital subscriber line) and you're in. D.S.L.: Digital subscriber line, a way of using electronics to move data at high speeds (at close to 1.54 megabits per second) over regular twisted-pair, copper phone wires. Fiber optics: A form of communications using light transmission through optical (glass) fibers. Intranet: The computer communications network internal to a building, company or organization. I.S.D.N.: Integrated Services Digital Network, a network of all-digital, high-bandwidth telephone lines that can simultaneously deliver audio signals, video signals and data. In other words, it's a way of moving more and different data over regular twisted-pair, copper phone lines at a brisk 128,000 bits -- that's 128 K -- per second. Very popular in the late 1980's and early 90's, it is much less popular now. L.A.N.: A system of connected computers within a building, an apartment, a house or other small area. Leased line: A telephone line rented for someone's use 24 hours a day, seven days a week. A T-1 is an example. Think of it as a private line. Modem: A device connected to the computer and to a telephone line or cable through which one computer can talk to other computers. T-1: The name given to a bandwidth or category of leased telephone lines that allow very rapid movement of data (1.544 megabits or 1,544,000 bits per second) over the Internet. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: A satellite dish along with an antenna for local broadcasts atop 27 North Moore Street in TriBeCa. The cable connects, in his laundry closet, to a communications hub, which connects to high-speed T-1 line in subcellar. title:
Ideas & Trends: The End of Writing;
Content Provided Below
body: MY friend the fiction writer is sensitive, so I asked the dreaded question directly. "How's the novel coming along?" "Very well, thanks," she answered. "I'm workshopping it right now." At this moment, individuals are workshopping short stories, novellas and plays. Others have screenplays or theater pieces in development. Still others engage in content creation. They create content, or provide it, for the Internet. Actively productive souls everywhere are developing scripts. Workshopping books. Providing content. Doesn't anyone write anymore? Not necessarily. Some pesky writing tasks have been eliminated, with the popularity of projects like the script-free MTV show "The Real World," which chronicles the daily taped lives of not entirely compatible roommates. Or the summer horror flick "The Blair Witch Project," where rather than writing dialogue in advance, the filmmakers sent the actors into the woods, intentionally frightened them for days on end, and then filmed them. What once had to be written can just be lived. But even when writing occurs, why is it no longer called writing? I started to wonder this back in the heady days of the Web entertainment boom, when I was hired to write a Web drama. At that point, the Microsoft Network was using the "television model" to try to conquer the Web. The "show" would "air" twice a week on an MSN "channel." I was the sole writer. Well, I was definitely sole. But the writer part became increasingly unclear. A few weeks into the assignment, MSN executives were starting to notice that the Web is like TV about as much as it's like a sliding door -- they both have a screen. They wanted to stop calling the episodes "episodes." The producer asked me what we should call them. "Stories?" I asked. "Chapters?" "Chapters!" said the producer. "Jenny Lyn, that's very 'print.' " She told me to stop being "so print." She said the suggestion was "very old media" of me. This was an insult. Old media, once a role model for new media, had become an evil twin as the new form struggled for its identity. And the words of old media had gone too. When the producer introduced me to the programming staff, I expected her to say I was the writer of the site. Instead she said: "This is Jenny Lyn. She's the creative on this project." Naturally I was flattered. I didn't have to worry about being creative. I was the creative. Creative, an adjective in my youth, was now a glamorous noun. But this new job title also betrayed an underlying suspicion by the producers that writers don't really do anything; they somehow simply are. CREATIVE had become a noun in the same alarming way "workshop" turned into a verb. Once, writers attended fiction workshops. Now, writers workshop fiction. The act of sharing the work with others has become part of its creation, and the sense of the individual starts to get lost. Once, writers escaped into the wilderness to cultivate their voices. Now, they gather together with each other or with development executives to hone their craft, make contacts, compare their voices, or make their voices sound more like one another. Meanwhile, the only people going into the wilderness are the terrified actors in "The Blair Witch Project" who aren't cultivating their voices but do scream a lot. In fact, the way that sensational events occur in book publishing is by avoiding cultivating those voices. Instant books bear the name of one writer but are actually divided up among different writers, all refraining from writing in their own style. That's how book-packaging houses -- the writing factories of the literary industrial revolution -- get them done so quickly. If a book is, say, about a timely vegetable scandal, one writer will be assigned the tomatoes, the next the carrots, and so forth. Such compartmentalization has occurred in the film and television industry for years, but has gotten more extreme with the growth of the sheer numbers of people on writing staffs, performing uncredited rewrites, or doing "polishes." Together, the publishing and film worlds will soon have a joint writing factory in the form of Tina Brown's media convergence empire, which will put non-fiction articles into "development" before they are even written. William Goldman, the screenwriter and author, has decided to expose the anguish of the development process in a new way. Last month, he offered studio chiefs a spec screenplay -- yes, a screenplay written for no pay by one of Hollywood's highest paid writers -- to studios. But there's a catch. The screenplay, "The Big A," is not finished. Any studio head who wants to read it must return a written response with comments. And Mr. Goldman plans to publish these comments, plus critiques from six screenwriters, along with the incomplete screenplay, in a forthcoming book. In Hollywood, the ultimate expression that film development has mechanized the writer's creative process is the screenwriting software that solves story structure problems and suggests plot twists. If it actually worked, perhaps writers could simply "program" or "input" instead of having to "write" in the future. The unspoken threat of the digital era is that it will chip away at the individual author's voice and intent, that content will become more and more automated and mass produced. THE heroes of the digital era will be those who restore individual voices. It seems remarkably fitting that it was Peter Norton who purchased the love letters of J. D. Salinger, the last guy to escape into the wilderness. Mr. Norton made his fortune inventing Norton Utilities, featuring the Norton Disk Doctor, a program that salvages the memories of crashed computers. With heart-warming functions like "UnErase," it is one of the few software innovations with a sense of justice. Mr. Norton demonstrated that sense of justice and respect for memory and author's intent when he purchased the letters for $156,500 and then offered to return them to Mr. Salinger. "He may want them returned," Mr. Norton said. "He may want me to destroy them. He may not care at all." He said he would leave it up to the writer. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: It's not writing. It's content creation, or workshopping, or . . . never mind. (The newyork Times)

title:
INVESTING;
In the Internet Gold Rush, Fund Customers Find a Research Treasure
body: CLICK on "buy." Click on "sell." Click on "payoff." The mutual fund industry has joined the rush to the Internet over the last two years -- and the move seems to be benefiting both the fund companies and many of their customers. Investors can buy funds on the sites of many no-load fund companies or through the sites of one of several brokerage firms that offer fund supermarkets. To avoid losing customers to on-line firms, many no-load fund groups, including the Vanguard Group, American Century Investments and T. Rowe Price Associates, have opened their own on-line brokerage firms, trading individual stocks and sometimes offering thousands of funds beyond their own. Such supermarkets will be the conduits for the bulk of all fund purchases by 2003, with most investors relying on fund company sites for information only, according to James Punishill, author of a report on Internet investing for Forrester Research, a consulting firm in Cambridge, Mass. By 2003, Forrester predicts, investors will hold $1.2 trillion in mutual fund assets in Internet-based accounts, up from an estimated $128 billion by the end of this year. The most noticeable change brought by the Internet, however, has been its capacity to deliver detailed research to virtually all investors, no matter how much they have to invest. Using that information -- which is often free -- investors can compare funds before making choices. Dozens of Web sites offer performance figures as well as portfolio tracking, so investors can monitor their holdings and the shifts in their asset mix of stocks, bonds and cash. "The self-directed investor has at their disposal what five years ago professional investors didn't even have at their disposal," said Cebra Graves, Internet strategist at Morningstar Inc., the financial publisher in Chicago. Morningstar's Web site lets investors compare funds and portfolio holdings at no charge (www.morningstar.net). For varying fees, investors can gain access to more detailed screens and data. Morningstar also supplies data to other companies like E*Trade, whose site provides free access to research and sorting tools using end-of-quarter data. The Mutual Fund Education Alliance, an association of no-load funds, offers a site at www.mfea.com with fund industry news, investment planning tools and links to fund company sites. Investors can register on the site to gain access to a personal portfolio tracker. In other words, the Internet lets investors get the information they need when they want it. "Inevitably, you didn't get the brochure at the right time and, inevitably, the information you need isn't in there," said Shelton S. Unger, head of on-line services at Vanguard. With the Internet, a great deal of information is available immediately, she added, and you "sort of find your own path." Vanguard recently updated an investment planning service to allow investors to prepare on line for retirement, college or other investment objectives. The service considers the user's risk tolerance and time horizon, among other factors. One bonus for the fund industry is that many investors who know the Internet are willing to receive routine information, like shareholder reports, on line instead of in themail. That can help keep down a fund's expenses. When an investor requests a prospectus over the phone, for example, Vanguard spends $10 to $12 to respond -- in labor costs for the phone representative and for printing and mailing. Internet use is climbing at Vanguard: 37 percent of all shareholders used the Web to get information or to make a transaction in the first quarter of 1999, up from 20 percent a year earlier, Ms. Unger said. The trend is evident elsewhere. At Charles Schwab & Company, 45 percent of all mutual fund transactions were on the Internet in mid-June, up from 25 percent a year ago and 16 percent at the beginning of 1998. "What we see is that the process of investing is easier, richer than it's ever been before," said Jeffrey M. Lyons, senior vice president for mutual funds marketing at Schwab. Instead of searching through magazine and newspaper articles for information and advice, investors can go on line to sort through thousands of funds and run through detailed asset allocation scenarios for growth or value investing as well as domestic or international choices. "Then, immediately, they click a button and invest in the fund," Mr. Lyons said. Schwab and other companies say the ease of Internet trading has not caused investors to flip rapidly in and out of funds. Schwab customers are charged a redemption fee if they sell shares within six months of purchase. Brian C. Murray, general manager for E*Trade's mutual fund group, which reserves the right to charge a fee for sales made within three months, said, "There appears to be an even stronger buy-and-hold ethic than I expected." The fund industry has also found the Internet to be useful for reaching retirement investors. The 401(k) Forum is an Internet-based retirement investment adviser hired by companies to offer personal 401(k) advice to their employees. Fidelity Investments, which already offers extensive Web-based services to its retirement plan participants, is now offering a service aimed at small businesses, "e401k," that is a 401(k) plan sold and maintained entirely over the Internet. Despite the success of the Internet as a means for research, the average investor remains a little reluctant to click and invest. That largely reflects how many people began using the Internet just last year, Forrester's Mr. Punishill said. In fact, most fund investors with Internet access visit fund company sites only for tasks like checking on a portfolio balance or downloading a prospectus, according to a survey taken last fall and published by American Century. Although 46 percent of Internet users with funds visited fund Web sites in 1998 -- up from 28 percent in 1996 -- only 9 percent bought or sold shares, up from 3 percent in 1996 but down from 11 percent in 1997, according to the survey. The main reason for their reluctance is the fear that the Internet is not a secure place to conduct business. Some 52 percent expressed concerns about making Internet fund transactions, though that share was down from 68 percent in 1996. PEOPLE who buy funds on the Internet are more likely to use fund supermarkets, where they can get consolidated statements and gain access to funds from other companies, Mr. Punishill said.  Although fund companies have been forming their own brokerage firms, virtually none of them -- with the exception of Fidelity and Vanguard -- will be able to compete effectively with the big discounters, he asserted. "Very few fund companies will have the resources or know-how to turn themselves from a mutual fund company into a brokerage firm," Mr. Punishill said. "They are different business models altogether." Some experts say the majority of investors are unlikely to ever use the Internet to buy or sell funds. Eli E. Neusner, a senior consultant at Spectrem Group, a financial services consulting firm, argues that as a percentage of mutual fund investors, those investing on line will peak in just a few years. Investors can be overwhelmed by the amount of information on a Web site, Mr. Neusner said, and often prefer to speak with an adviser for guidance, particularly when dealing with complicated issues like estate planning or saving for a child's college education. On the Internet, he said, "no one has found a thoroughly efficient way of walking an uncomfortable investor or even a moderately experienced investor through a financial strategy." But Mr. Graves at Morningstar predicted that on-line technology would evolve to the point that any client could use the Internet to talk with a financial adviser on line. Once that happens, he said, "the Internet is no longer a technology that favors one demographic over another." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Getting Wired" The Internet is having a growing impact on how investors buy, sell and research mutual funds. title:
INVESTING;
Media Companies Adding Web Cachet
body: INVESTORS in search of long-term growth in Internet companies may want to heed this adage: Brands rule. In some ways, that may seem a subversive notion these days. After all, scores of freshly minted dot-com stocks have climbed to dizzying valuations, and many Web-focused investors have bypassed the old-line media companies that control brand-name magazines, music, movies and other so-called content with Internet potential. But Wall Street is betting that the situation is about to change, as traditional media companies accelerate their efforts to gain on-line advertisers and audiences. Three companies leading the charge are Time Warner, Walt Disney and CBS. "We know the products that they offer, and we've come to expect a certain level of quality from them versus some newbie who comes out of nowhere and claims that on the Web they're the hottest thing," said Mark Hardie, a senior analyst with Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. And these companies can cross-promote their efforts, giving them a leg up on independent content providers. All three companies have announced deals in recent weeks that add to their Internet assets, but the moves have caused little stir in their stock prices. "I'd say that value is not being recognized in the marketplace right now." said Tom Barrett, an analyst with MFS Investment Management, a money manager in Boston. So investors who hope to gain from such stocks may have to think long-term. Tom Wolzein, an analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein in newyork, expects the percentage of cash flow that these companies derive from the Web, an amount now negligible, to climb into the double digits over the next four to five years as they expand their on-line businesses. Cash flow is a good benchmark for media company profitability. The on-line build-up is under way. Time Warner, for example, said on July 13 that it would merge Columbia House, the record club it owns with Sony, with the on-line music store CDnow. Time Warner will own 37 percent of the new company, which by the end of the year will offer music that can be downloaded directly from the Internet -- the hot new market for music. After the CDnow deal was announced, Mr. Wolzein raised his 12-month price target for Time Warner stock by 28 percent, to nearly $91 a share, citing the company's overall Internet profit potential. The shares closed Friday at $72. Assuming that the overall on-line advertising market continues to flourish, Mr. Wolzien projected that in 2001, Time Warner would have cash flow of $8.7 billion, of which 3 percent would be from Internet businesses. By 2004, he said, cash flow would reach $12 billion, with the Internet portion climbing to 11 percent of the total. Time Warner has also moved to correct one misstep. It is phasing out its Pathfinder site -- a platform for magazines including Time and Money. Users tended to skip its home page and go directly to the magazine Web sites. Instead, the company will focus on hub sites for target audiences, combining related magazines with links to the Web sites of other Time Warner properties, including WarnerBros.com and CNN.com. Disney's Internet business took a big leap last year, when the company bought about 42 percent of Infoseek, an on-line search service, and then created its own portal, the Go Network. Together, the destinations are the fifth-most-popular Web property, according to Media Metrix, an Internet research company in newyork. On July 12, the company announced plans to buy the rest of Infoseek and merge all of Disney's Internet holdings into a new company that it will control, Go.com. Shares in the new company will be offered publicly through a tracking stock -- meaning that the assets continue to be owned by Disney but that the share price effectively tracks the performance of those assets. Disney can use the tracking stock for acquisitions. Disney's stock has been struggling this year, in part because of falling merchandise sales. But Jill S. Krutick, an analyst at Salomon Smith Barney, expects the shares to rise from their current $27.4375 to the mid-$30's in the next year, partly because of Disney's Internet investments. Mr. Wolzien expects Disney's on-line business to account for 4 percent of $5.8 billion in cash flow in 2001, rising to 14 percent of $8.6 billion in cash flow in 2004. AT CBS, the strategy has been to tap into existing Web-based businesses. The company bought positions in several specialized Internet companies -- including Marketwatch.com, Sportsline USA, Medscape and Rx.com -- in exchange for millions of dollars' worth of promotion across its TV and radio properties. CBS is also reportedly developing a portal similar to the Go Network. Mr. Wolzien projected that CBS would report cash flow of $2.5 billion in 2001, 5 percent of which would be from on-line holdings, with cash flow rising to $4.1 billion in 2004, 10 percent of it from the Internet. James Marsh, an analyst at Prudential Securities, expects CBS shares to hit $51 in 12 months, up from $43.9375 on Friday. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo/Drawing: Time Warner, CBS and Disney are leaders in the charge by established media concerns to increase their Internet assets. title: Officials Struggle to Regulate On-Line Sale of Prescription Drugs
body: The Food and Drug Administration announced steps today to curb the illegitimate sale of prescription drugs over the Internet, while officials at another agency, the Federal Trade Commission, asked Congress to require electronic pharmacies to post detailed on-line information about their licenses and the doctors who write the prescriptions they fill. But the officials' pronouncements, made during a Congressional hearing to examine the burgeoning electronic drug trade, revealed as much about what the Government cannot do as what it can do. While the authorities say they may be able to rein in domestic companies marketing pills on line, they acknowledge that the bulk of the business is conducted overseas. "Ten years ago, it was hard for you to buy a foreign drug; you had to go to a foreign country," William K. Hubbard, associate commissioner for policy at the F.D.A., said in an interview. "Now the Internet makes it simple, and you can't do anything about these foreign sites because you don't have the reach to foreign countries." The growth of prescription drug sales in cyberspace has been troubling state and Federal officials for the last year, but no one agency has the authority to regulate it. Typically, medicine is prescribed by doctors, who are licensed by state medical boards, and is dispensed by pharmacies, also licensed by the states. But the explosion in electronic commerce, coupled with demand for the impotence pill Viagra and other new "life-style drugs," has turned the old system on its head. Now doctors are prescribing pills on line to patients they have never met, in states where they are not authorized to work. Pharmacies are shipping pills across state lines without the requisite licenses. Regulatory authorities have disciplined some doctors and pharmacies, but the work is slow and difficult because the ownership of Web sites is so hard to track. At the same time, no one knows how many electronic pharmacies exist. Representative Ron Klink, the Pennsylvania Democrat who pressed for today's hearing before the Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee of the House Commerce Committee, said that his staff had identified more than 200, but that there might be twice that many. Mr. Hubbard, of the F.D.A., said his agency would immediately begin trying to identify each site and learn where it is registered, so the authorities in those states could be alerted. Mr. Klink, meanwhile, said he intended to introduce legislation next week along the lines of the trade commission's proposal, which would require that any Web site selling medication state its name, address and telephone number, as well as the states in which the pharmacy and its cooperating doctors are licensed. The on-line pharmacy industry is already objecting to the bill. "All we are saying is that if you are selling a pharmaceutical product, just like your neighborhood pharmacy has to display their license, you have to display yours on your Web page," Mr. Klink said in an interview. "We are asking nothing more from the electronic commerce people than we are asking from anyone else who is in business." But William Razzouk, chief executive of PlanetRx.com, an on-line drugstore licensed to ship medicine to all 50 states, said he preferred a voluntary system set up by the National Boards of Pharmacy, a coalition of state licensing authorities. The coalition has begun registering on-line pharmacies, and accrediting them with its seal of approval. http://www.nytimes.com
