title: Security Flaws In Software Are Reported
body: Microsoft and Compaq Computer yesterday acknowledged several significant software security flaws that could enable intruders to gain access to the computers of millions of customers and to damage their data via email or through commands sent from a malicious Web site. Certain Hewlett-Packard computers are also said by one expert to be vulnerable, but a spokesman for the company said yesterday that the company would not confirm the security vulnerability. The vulnerabilities, which affect computers running Microsoft's Windows operating system and Internet Explorer browser in combination with other programs, are invisible to antivirus programs, illustrating the risks inherent in the growing complexity of today's personal computer software. Consumers who are at the greatest risk are those running programs shipped as part of Microsoft's Office 97 suite of programs and owners of some newer models of computers made by Compaq and Hewlett-Packard that automatically upgrade the manufacturers' own software over the Internet. A Microsoft official said yesterday that the company was creating a fix for the security holes and that it planned to issue a security bulletin on its Web site instructing people what precautions to take. "We take security issues very seriously," said Andrew Dixon, group product manager for Office at Microsoft. "Right now, we are working on testing a solution and steps for customers to take." The new flaws also raise troubling questions about Microsoft's decision to integrate its Explorer Web browser into the Windows operating system. That decision is a key issue in the company's antitrust battle with the Justice Department. Microsoft has passionately defended the browser integration, asserting that it offers significant consumer benefits. However, a number of computer security experts who are familiar with the newly discovered flaws said that by tightly integrating Web browsing software with its personal computer operating system, Microsoft had greatly complicated the challenge of insuring that Windows was secure. "A single operating system and single provider of tools dominates the market," said Doug Tygar, a professor of computer science at the University of California at Berkeley who specializes in computer security. "Because Microsoft is linking all these aspects of computing, all the walls that usually prevent such attacks aren't there." Reports of flaws were posted on NTbugtraq, a computer security mailing list, over the last two days. There is no evidence that the flaws have been exploited, according to the manufacturers involved. The flaws involve two separate interactions of programs with the Internet Explorer browser. The first involves a vulnerability in one version of a "dynamic link library," or dll file, that is part of Microsoft's Office 97 suite. The flaw is believed not to exist in the newly released version, Office 2000. The Office software component, known as Jet version 3.5, creates a security vulnerability because Microsoft has configured its Internet Explorer program to "trust" Office programs, including Word, Excel and Powerpoint. These programs can create documents that are themselves powerful programs and that can act as a Trojan Horse, carrying malicious code via a Web document into a personal computer. The Jet flaw was first reported by Juan Carlos G. Cuartango, a programmer who previously discovered several security holes in two browsers -- Microsoft's Internet Explorer and Netscape Navigator. Although the flawed version of Jet was replaced with a newer version in the last boxes of Office 97 shipped, the original still resides on the hard drives of millions of personal computers. The new flaw does not involve the small programs call "macros" that have caused Microsoft security headaches in the past. Rather, Jet sends queries to various data bases when the Office programs request data. The queries can be used to trigger low-level operating system commands -- including commands that erase files or entire hard drives. Because of the extensive integration between Office applications and Windows, such a query can be sent on behalf of a cell in a spreadsheet, a field in a word document or other portions of an Office application. What makes the new flaw especially serious is that antivirus software does not monitor such queries and therefore is not effective against an attack. Mr. Dixon of Microsoft said yesterday that the company was considering giving users a new alert mechanism that would warn them about data base queries before they were executed. The second security flaw has to do with the way software shipped with computers from Compaq and Hewlett-Packard -- and possibly other manufacturers -- is designed to interact with the Internet Explorer Web browser. The manufacturers' software, designed to work with the security controls in Internet Explorer 4.0, would enable an intruder to execute commands remotely. The Compaq security flaw appears particularly serious since it can be used to spread the flaws to other brands of computers. Compaq's Presario computers, which are consumer models, are shipped with a tiny Java program that has been "digitally signed" -- meaning it has been authenticated by Compaq. This program is designed to enable Compaq to update programs on a computer over the Internet or other computer network. But it also has the power to execute programs -- and can be directed to do so by a Web page. It can also be sent via email. While the existence of this program was posted to a European security mailing list a year ago, a recent bug that exacerbates the problem was discovered by Richard Smith, the president of Pharlap Software, in Cambridge, Mass. Mr. Smith said in an interview that he had discovered a security problem on Hewlett-Packard computers as well and had notified the company. The company declined to discuss the matter. Adding to the Compaq problem, Microsoft's integrated Web browser will run any program digitally signed by Compaq, in some cases without warning. While the vulnerable program will run without any warnings only on certain Compaq Presarios in their default configurations, it can also be sent to and temporarily stored on any computer running Windows 95, 98 or NT, according to Mr. Smith. In this case, the browser will open a box saying that the browser wants to run a program digitally signed by the Compaq Computer Corporation. If the user allows the program to run, it will execute commmands on the computer. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart/Diagram: "Holes in Computer Security" Two problems have been identified in Microsoft products that can allow files to bypass security features in the Windows operating system and its built-in Internet Explorer browser. In either case, mali-cious files, posing as files that have security clearance, could pass into a computer undetected and take control of it or destroy data.  SCREENING FILES -- Just as airline passengers pass through metal detectors at an airport, files arriving at a computer from the Internet have to pass through a detector in Windows that identifies suspicious files and warns the computer user.  ONE SECURITY BREACH -- Microsoft gave files created by several of its programs, including Word and Excel, unlimited clearance to bypass the Windows security checkpoint, much as a flight crew boards a plane without going through a metal detector.  A SECOND BREACH -- Similarly, several computer makers give their own software security clearance as a way to update their clients' computers via the Internet. Their files also bypass Windows security, much as airplane mechanics use side doors to get to the plane on the tarmac. (pg. C14)

title: Vendor of News From Afar Yields to Technology
body: It has survived almost everything newyork could throw at it: wars, blackouts, the Depression, the decline of Times Square and even its revival. But now Hotalings News Agency, the purveyor of newspapers and magazines from around the globe that has become a newyork City institution, is disappearing from the street. Yesterday, the Hotaling family closed the store it has run in Times Square since 1926, and retrenched to a kiosk inside the tourist information center on Broadway just north of 46th Street. The main culprit, according to the family, is the Internet. Newspapers across the country have put their news -- and worse, their help-wanted and real-estate ads -- on the World Wide Web. Foreign papers and magazines are also available on line. So many homesick immigrants from Damascus and heartsick newyorkers dreaming of a job in Des Moines no longer need to go to Hotalings to buy a newspaper. "We never had any competition; now the Internet is our competition," said Susan A. Carey, 53, who owns the business with her brother, Arthur G. Hotaling, 49. Their grandfather founded the business in 1905. The city's booming economy has only made things worse for the store, Mr. Hotaling said. A lot of his customers used to be "people who were looking to leave the city," he explained. "With the economy as strong as it is and newyork City being the place to live, they aren't leaving the city in droves the way they were." The problem began four or five years ago, said Marvin Cohn, who has worked at the store since 1985 (and first visited Hotalings as a customer in 1950). The San Jose Mercury News had always been popular with certain customers who Mr. Cohn speculates were looking for jobs in Silicon Valley. When the newspaper put up its Web site, these customers disappeared. That, he said, "was the beginning of the end." Today, the trade publication Editor & Publisher tracks 3,744 newspapers with Web sites, including almost 1,500 overseas papers. In the unitedstates and Canada, the number of daily and weekly newspapers available on line has more than doubled in the last two years, to 2,224, according to the company's 1999 yearbook. Hotalings tried to find ways to compete. It spruced up the store, which is on the south side of 42d street between Sixth Avenue and Broadway (it is now so attractive that CNN sometimes uses it as a set), and it expanded its selection of American magazines. But business did not pick up. Earlier this year, the store stopped staying open until 9 P.M. and started closing at 6. And it cut its staff from 22 employees to a dozen or so. Finally, Mr. Hotaling said, he decided to cut back the store's retail operation to the kiosk, which he had opened a year ago. The company's business of delivering out-of-town newspapers will move from the back of the store to a warehouse far west on 52d Street. "Everyone sounds like this is such a sad thing," he said. "I'm pretty -- depressed is not the word, but I was so stressed about what to do, and now that I've made the decision I'm very encouraged." To prepare, he began cutting back on the number of publications he carries -- though he still has daily and weekly papers from 225 cities around the unitedstates, and about 1,000 overseas publications, from the staid Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung to the racy Russian tabloid Speed, whose name is the only English word in its pages. The new newsstand will contain most of the overseas papers, Mr. Hotaling hopes. But the display space is limited, and browsing will be more difficult for impulse buyers drawn by headlines like "Gangsters drink human blood with champagne" (from the July 25 Sunday Herald of Jamaica). The customers are likely to be different, too. At the kiosk, the customers tend to be foreign tourists who buy European titles, said Gabriel Toussaint, who tends the counter. While American tourists come into the information center, they do not buy newspapers or magazines, he said. At the store, three-quarters of the customers were repeat visitors, Mr. Hotaling said. Which is not to say they were not a diverse group; Anderson Celius, who has worked at the store for a decade, has learned phrases in a half-dozen languages, most recently Russian. He worries about leaving 42d Street, "the heart of the world," as he called it, and said he finds the situation unfair. "When 42d Street was unclean, dirty, we were trying to keep it alive," Mr. Celius said. "Now that it's better, we're moving." There were some foreign tourists at the store yesterday, including one man from Monte Carlo complaining that he was stuck in the land of baseball when the European soccer season was about to begin. A little boy was looking for foreign publications for a school project, and a young woman was buying a stack of out-of-town newspapers for her boss. But most were immigrants in search of a taste of home, like Ismail Deakete, from the Ivory Coast, who imports African art and speaks little English. He said Hotalings was the only place he had been able to find the magazine Jeune Afrique, so "toujours I come in here." Then there are the real old-timers, like Joey Sasso, who has been coming to Hotalings since the store was located on 43d Street in the old newyork Times building. (That store closed in 1983.) Mr. Sasso, who will be 78 next month, buys Editor & Publisher every Friday to keep up with the media business, and out-of-town newspapers to find fodder for his freelance gossip column, which he pounds out on a typewriter. But even he is thinking of abandoning paper for computer bits and bytes, he said, adding, "I've got to get on the Internet, honey, that's the thing." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Arthur G. Hotaling has watched Hotalings News Agency struggle in competition against the Internet. (Chang W. Lee/The newyork Times)

title: Martha Stewart Selling Stake in Her Company
body: For those who wish they could be Martha Stewart, now at least they can own a piece of her company. Ms. Stewart, the doyenne of domestic details, plans to sell $100 million in stock in her company, Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia Inc., according to documents filed yesterday with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Investors will be able to buy stock in a company dominated by the monthly homemaking bible, Martha Stewart Living, but whose television, merchandising and Internet businesses are growing robustly. But even as Ms. Stewart sells a stake in her company, she is retaining control of an empire that had $180 million in revenue last year, slightly more than twice the sales it had two years earlier. The company had net profit of $23.8 million in 1998, up from $9.4 million in 1996. Though the company will issue class A shares, which will have one vote each, Ms. Stewart will own all the class B shares, which have 10 votes each. Still, the figures do not indicate how much of the company she will eventually own because they do not detail how many shares the company will have to sell to raise the $100 million. The document also says the company is reorganizing the ownership of the company. Of the proceeds raised in the offering, Ms. Stewart may spend up to $42 million to buy out the remaining 6.2 percent stake owned by Time Warner under the terms of an agreement reached in 1997. Time Warner had been an initial backer of Ms. Stewart's magazine, the basis of her empire, but Martha Stewart Living reportedly spent $75 million in 1997 to buy out most of the magazine operation. Ms. Stewart's company has also agreed to sell a 5 percent stake to Kleiner, Perkins, Caufield & Buyers, a venture capital firm in San Francisco, for $25 million. As part of that deal, Kleiner, Perkins will receive a warrant that it can exercise for $21 million, allowing the firm to buy into any Internet business set up by the company. That investment puts the total value of the company at slightly less than $500 million because Kleiner, Perkins is getting more than just the equity stake. Ms. Stewart has been expanding her company, particularly in merchandising, a move that bolsters her brand name and image and generates higher profit margins than the magazine operations. For example, publishing revenue of $127 million represented 70 percent of the company's $180 million in sales last year. A year earlier, publishing had represented about 81 percent of the company's $132 million in sales. Meanwhile, merchandising, which was 5.1 percent of 1997 sales, rose to 8.3 percent of sales last year. Internet business sales jumped to $14.7 million last year from $4.8 million in 1997, though the division is not yet profitable. Ms. Stewart has also been pushing ahead with television projects to exploit the brand name. The document also discloses that Ms. Stewart earned $5 million in salary and bonus last year. The company expects to be listed on the newyork Stock Exchange.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: PUBLIC LIVES
body: Reports of Death Are Exaggerated This is a case of a carefully orchestrated advertising and marketing campaign working too well. In the film "The Blair Witch Project," one of the sleepers of the summer, an actress named HEATHER DONAHUE plays a documentary filmmaker named Heather Donohue. The film's producers describe "The Blair Witch Project" as a "mockumentary," meaning that it mocks what they consider the pretentiousness of conventional documentaries. The film is scary stuff for some -- and apparently realistic. So is the Web site for "The Blair Witch Project" (www.blairwitch.com), which says that Heather and two other student filmmakers "disappeared in the woods near Burkittsville, Md., while shooting a documentary" in 1994. "A year later, their footage was found." Attention, casting directors: It was was Heather Donohue, fictional character, not Heather Donahue, actress, who disappeared. The Internet Movie Database (www.imdb.com), a frequently consulted resource for agents and directors, listed Ms. Donahue as "deceased" for several days this month. "That was the only point where I was, like, 'O.K., people, let's establish where the parameters of the film and the marketing could go,' " Ms. Donahue said. "One of the residual effects of the far-reaching and very effective marketing plan is somebody somewhere assumed it was real. Lots of people still think it's real, and now when you tell people it's not real, they think you're trying to trick them. It's this conspiracy-within-a-conspiracy thing that's happening."  And the Encore? ADAM SPIEL may be the luckiest man in New Jersey, or at least in Parsippany, where he works for a payroll administration company. Last year Mr. Spiel, 34, spent $50 on three raffle tickets at the Metro West Jewish Community Center in Whippany and wound up walking away with an orange Ford Explorer. A month ago, he won free front-row tickets to a Tom Petty concert from WAXQ-FM, the newyork radio station known as Q104, by being the first caller to give the correct date of Mr. Petty's birthday (Oct. 20). And he won the heart of the woman of his dreams by wooing her on the Internet, having met her at Match.com. That woman, ROBIN STEINBERG, 30, an account manager for CMP Media in Manhasset, N.Y., called Mr. Spiel on Monday to thank him for their first date without a modem -- dinner at a Long Island restaurant. She was not surprised by his response. "I was the 25th caller," he said. He explained how, after weeks of trying, he had got through to the Q104 morning show on Monday. The prize was two tickets to an invitation-only concert by PETE TOWNSHEND, the legendary guitarist and songwriter of the Who, at the Supper Club on West 47th Street. Mr. Spiel and Ms. Steinberg related this story between some passionate kisses in a corner banquette on Wednesday night. For their entertainment, Mr. Townshend, 54, who once hoped aloud to die before he got old, played the improbable role of lounge singer. He put down his electric guitar after the classics "Won't Get Fooled Again" and "Behind Blue Eyes" and put on glasses -- he had to read the sheet music -- to accompany himself on the piano for "Slit Skirts" and "Let My Love Open the Door," two songs from his solo albums. Mr. Townshend was joined for the second half of the 90-minute show by EDDIE VEDDER of Pearl Jam, who appears on the recording they were promoting, a concert in behalf of a Chicago orphanage. The album is scheduled to go on sale on Sept. 21. When the show was over, Mr. Spiel was pleased. Ms. Steinberg was already scheming, thinking of the next opportunity for him to use his luck to show his love. "Now he has to win tickets for Barry White and Earth, Wind and Fire for me," she said. JAMES BARRON with Jacques Steinberg http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: HEATHER DONAHUE; PETE TOWNSHEND

title: House Hearing Focuses On Vulgar Internet Names
body: A Congressional hearing called to examine intellectual-property and trademark issues on the Internet became sidetracked today by questions about who was responsible for a flurry of obscene addresses on the World Wide Web. The hearing by the Courts and Intellectual Property Subcommittee of the House Judiciary Committee brought together officials from the Commerce Department and Network Solutions, a government contractor in Herndon, Va., that had held a monopoly on registering Internet addresses ending in the domain names .com, .net and .org. Network Solutions has a policy against objectionable or vulgar names. But this spring, the Commerce Department had authorized five other companies to begin competing in the registration process on a trial basis. And Network Solutions, which continues to administer the system, decided not to impose its rules on the competitors. That decision had resulted in a rush of domain-name registrations using obscene or vulgar words. Representative Christopher B. Cannon, a Utah Republican, said the episode had raised concerns about the Commerce Department's ability "to oversee how this process should go forward and how well it works." Network Solutions said its decision had been made after conversations with the Commerce Department. The Commerce Department said it had discussed the matter with the company only after Network Solutions asked if it would object to the company's position of not censoring the new registrars. "If we had, that would have raised serious First Amendment questions," said Becky Burr, a senior Commerce Department official who is overseeing the shift in the administration of the Internet from government contractors to a new, international group, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, known as Icann. "We would prefer that there not be dirty words on the Internet," Ms. Burr said after the hearing. "But for the U.S. Government to be involved in that decision would raise serious constitutional questions." Ms. Burr was clearly frustrated by the focus on the issue during the hearing, which was called to explore questions like "cybersquatting," in which company names or other valuable words are registered as Internet addresses by someone other than the company and then resold. "Frankly, we have bigger fish to fry," Ms. Burr said in reference to a protracted stalemate with Network Solutions on the terms for opening its business to competition. The deadlock, on issues like the rights to the vast database of more than five million Internet addresses that the company has compiled, had delayed plans for introducing competition on a permanent basis. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
John Doe Need Not Apply
body: FIVE years ago in Australia, back when the World Wide Web had only a few strands, a computer consultant and grandfather in Melbourne named John Carter received a message on Fidonet, a public bulletin board, intended for a John Carter who lived in South Africa. As the Internet grew, the Australian John Carter searched for the South African John Carter and found a lot of other John Carters in the process, via search engines like whowhere.com and Internet Address Finder. So the John Carter home page, NetSmart John Carters (members .tripod.com/jcarter/jcwww.html), was born. Mr. Carter sent email messages to all the other John Carters he could find and posted links to their home pages, when available, on his site. He also presented some of the replies he received, which begin with salutations like "Hi John, What a great name you have!" and "By gorrah, annudder one!" There's a story from John Robert Carter, an Australian living in England, who visited a cafe there with the name "John R. Carter" printed in large letters out front. After a little discussion with the owner, he wrote, "it turned out that we were BOTH called John ROBERT Carter, and that his birthday was the same date as mine, and he was exactly 30 years older than me! Strangely, we didn't really get on. He overcharged me for my cup of tea. So what's in a name?" And John Carter of St. Petersburg, Fla., wrote: "In fact, at my job (semitechnical position at a mutual fund company), one of the corporate lawyers' name is John Carter. His secretary's name is Debbie Carter (no relation), and Debbie's husband's and son's names are both John Carter!" He tips his hat to Dr. John Carter, a character on the television show "E.R." The site is also peppered with mentions of "John Carter of Mars," the title of one Edgar Rice Burroughs novel and a character in several others. "There seems to be veritable plagues of me," wrote John Carter, the South African. "I know of John Carter the bishop, and a John M. Carter the physicist. (John Carter the physicist once caused my mother much alarm and despondency. The physicist and I both worked at the Nuclear Physics Research Unit at the University of the Witwatersrand at one time many years ago. One dark and stormy night I was working late when my mother phoned asking for me. She was vehemently told that I had gone off to New Zealand and wouldn't be back for quite a while.)" Via email, the original Mr. Carter said he was not aware of any other home pages for people with common names. A brief search for sites for the James Smiths, Mary Joneses, Bob Johnsons and Jose Rodriguezes of the world did not yield any similar pages. Their loss. But people with common names have formed clubs. "It was very gratifying at the time to receive responses from namesakes from all walks of life around the world," Mr. Carter, the Webmaster, wrote in an email message. "It made me realize just how much the Internet has shrunk the world." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A place for John Carters around the world to find one another.

title: Senior Microsoft Executive To Leave Management Job
body: Paul Maritz, a senior executive at the Microsoft Corporation, is returning to his roots as a programmer as part of the company's campaign to persuade software developers to continue to rely on its technology despite the rise of the Internet. In an internal email to colleagues on Tuesday, Mr. Maritz, a group vice president, said he was handing off most of his day-to-day management duties to work more closely with William H. Gates, the chairman, to help "set technical direction in the company" and "to educate myself on the details of technologies that I have not had the chance to be as 'hands on' as I would have liked over the last several years." Mr. Maritz said he intended to begin his technical-immersion project by "writing some" code using various Microsoft software tool kits including Visual Basic, Visual C++ and Visual J++, and move on to Microsoft's new programming projects. "So be warned," Mr. Maritz wrote to the other members of Microsoft's developers group. In the email, Mr. Maritz said he also planned to focus on promoting Microsoft's development tools within the software community. Mr. Maritz's hands-on push into the technology of development tools, colleagues say, comes as Microsoft is engaged in an effort to both simplify the process of software development and marry its Windows technology with the technology of the Internet. The rise of Internet-based computing poses a continuing challenge, which has been called the post PC era, to Microsoft. The challenge is not that personal computers might go away, or even decline in number, but that computing may no longer revolve so much around PC technology -- which Microsoft dominates with its industry-standard Windows operating system. Accordingly, Microsoft is trying to persuade outside developers to use its software tools instead of the tools of rivals like Sun Microsystems Inc. The goal is to position Microsoft's tools as the glue between PC and Internet technology. "Paul has the experience and respect, both inside and outside Microsoft, to push that initiative hard," one Microsoft engineer said. The Wall Street Journal reported yesterday that Mr. Maritz was passing off most of his daily management duties to David Vaskevitch, a vice president in the developers group. Like many senior Microsoft executives, Mr. Maritz, 44, who joined the company in 1986 from the Intel Corporation, is immensely wealthy from his Microsoft shares. In recent months, a number of other top company executives have taken leaves of absence or left the company. Mr. Maritz's move to relinquish most daily management duties raised the question of whether he, too, was about to step out. But in his email, he suggested that was not the case. His shift of assignments, he wrote, did not portend "some major change, or that I am about to leave the company."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
What's in a name? Well, no more TCI. After the acquisition, AT&T goes on a rebranding tear.
body: IF the Mercedes-Benz brand name can be affixed to a sport-utility vehicle, if the Heinz brand name can appear on mustard and if the Fritos brand name can be attached to chili, then why not use the AT&T brand name for cable television service? The AT&T Corporation is doing just that, announcing yesterday an ambitious "rebranding" program to change the name of all products and services offered by Tele-Communications Inc., which AT&T acquired in March for $59.4 billion. Beginning Tuesday, the TCI Cable name will disappear, to be replaced by the moniker AT&T Cable Services, part of a unit known as AT&T Broadband and Internet Services, as well as the AT&T blue-globe logo. The change, which will take about six months to complete, has a budget of $30 million just for the tangible elements, including $8 million for new signs, $6 million for new employee uniforms and $6 million to repaint 15,500 service trucks. The renaming will be extended beyond TCI Cable to include TCI Digital Cable, now AT&T Digital Cable, which provides features like an interactive on-screen guide and pay-per-view channels, and TCI@Home, now AT&T@Home, the high-speed Internet service provider. In addition, part of the $150 million that TCI Cable has spent annually on marketing will be devoted to pitches informing more than 10 million customers of more than 600 local cable systems that whatever was once TCI will henceforth be rebranded with the familiar AT&T name. "It's the largest brand transition in our company's history," Leo J. Hindery Jr., president and chief executive of the broadband unit in Englewood, Colo., said in a conference call news conference. The brand switcheroo is emblematic of efforts by AT&T to remake itself into a provider of myriad communications services in addition to its mainstay long-distance telephone operations. The goal is for AT&T to keep pace with the regional Bell operating companies like the Bell Atlantic Corporation and SBC Communications Inc., which may offer long-distance services in a year. With the takeover of TCI, and the pending purchase of Mediaone Group Inc. for $62.5 billion, AT&T, the nation's largest long-distance provider, will also become the largest cable TV company. AT&T is betting that the venerable AT&T brand name, freshened when the words "American Telephone & Telegraph" were eliminated in favor of the initials, will prove more appealing to consumers than the TCI or Mediaone brands. "AT&T is obviously very well-known to consumers for the long-distance business," said Doug Seserman, senior vice president for marketing at AT&T Broadband and Internet Services. "And prior to the spinoff of Lucent Technologies, AT&T was branded on other products like telephones and computers." Research among consumers found that "AT&T stands for trust, reliability, quality of service and good price value," he added. "And AT&T is also seen as the best brand to bring bundled services to homes, whether long distance, cable or Internet." While the puissance of the AT&T name may benefit the TCI operations, the rebranding is risky, too, because it has the potential to tarnish the luster of the AT&T image. "TCI is a typical cable company brand with a typical cable company image -- quite negative," said Clive Chajet, chairman of Chajet Consultancy L.L.C. in newyork, a brand and corporate identity consulting firm. "Those brands have never gained for themselves good reputations." Still, Mr. Chajet said he thought the rebranding was a shrewd move. "AT&T is a classic example of a great brand name -- as good as it gets," he said. "That certainly would benefit any communication service with the convergence of components like television, telephones and high-speed access to the Internet." And as for any dilution of the AT&T image by extending it beyond telephony, Mr. Chajet said that "years ago I was hired by AT&T to work on the AT&T Universal credit card, and when we asked consumers if the AT&T name would work on a credit card, they said absolutely." "If you are old enough to remember, the AT&T nickname was Ma Bell," he added, chuckling. "And who is more trusted than mother?" The initial advertising to promulgate word of the rebranding is being created by two agencies that had worked for TCI, Mr. Seserman said: Jordan McGrath Case & Partners/ Euro RSCG in newyork, part of the Euro RSCG Worldwide unit of Havas Advertising, and Thomas & Perkins in Denver. "We're working with our colleagues in Basking Ridge as to long-term plans for marketing communications," Mr. Seserman added, referring to the New Jersey village where AT&T has its headquarters. The two principal AT&T agencies -- Foote, Cone & Belding Worldwide in newyork, part of True North Communications, and Young & Rubicam Advertising in newyork -- are also working on assignments, he said. As for the Mediaone name, Mr. Hindery said that "we're fully intending" to rebrand it as AT&T Cable Services as soon as the deal closes, which he anticipated for sometime in the first quarter of 2000.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
The Times in Joint Internet News Operation
body: The newyork Times said yesterday that it was establishing a joint news operation with TheStreet.com, an on-line financial news service, as part of the Times's effort to expand and enhance its presence on the Internet. The newspaper said that the goal of the alliance was to help The Times provide regularly updated business news and analysis on its Web site and is one of several initiatives aimed at differentiating the Times's Internet offerings from those of its competitors. "We're not presuming that the stories are going to appear in our paper; their prime purpose is to serve the Web audience," Joseph Lelyveld, executive editor of The Times, said in a statement. "That said, we expect that many of the readers drawn to The Times by the upgraded spot business coverage on our Web site will gravitate to the newspaper itself for greater depth and analysis." The paper said that Jack Lynch, an assistant business editor with The Times, would help hire and oversee six reporters for TheStreet.com and would report to Mr. Lelyveld and Dave Kansas, TheStreet.com's editor in chief. In February, The newyork Times Company agreed to invest $15 million in cash and services for a minority stake in TheStreet.com, which made its initial public stock offering in May. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
A CONVERSATION WITH: JOHN MAEDA;
When M.I.T. Artist Shouts, His 'Painting' Listens
body: Within the art world, Prof. John Maeda, 32, is an anomaly -- a prize-winning graphic designer and kinetic artist with a fistful of engineering degrees from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. From his base in M.I.T.'s Media Laboratory, where he is the Sony Career Development Professor of Media Arts and Sciences and directs the Aesthetics and Computation Group, Professor Maeda uses the computer as a tool and medium to create art that can be produced only digitally and that has the specific look of the new technology. One of his best-known pieces is a drawing called "Time Paint," in which colors fly through space. Another piece, "The Reactive Square," is about squares that change shape when a viewer shouts at them. Professor Maeda's computer- generated art pieces have been shown at the Ginza Gallery in Tokyo and in that great digital art gallery -- the World Wide Web. We talk in his dark computer-filled Cambridge offices on an otherwise sunny summer day.  Q. Your last book, "Design By Numbers," (M.I.T. Press) is an art book that is also a manual for a new computer language that you invented to help artists understand the guts of computer design. Why create a whole new computer language?  A. Several reasons. I wanted to make a system that was free of charge. Second, all the programming languages are in English. Because this one is free and distributed on the Web, we are now offering it in French, Spanish and German. It will soon be in Korean and Japanese. The third reason was that programming languages are made for people to write programs -- big applications. For someone just starting out making art on their computers, they don't want this big Mack truck of a system. They just want a simple bicycle that they understand. So I designed the visual equivalent of a simple bicycle. Design by Numbers, D.B.N., was an attempt to demystify the technology behind computer art, to show how simple it is, and that people can do it. D.B.N. can run directly within any Java-enabled Web browser. The Web site address, by the way, is dbn.media.mit.edu.  Q. When you are creating your own computer art pieces, do you ever use prepackaged drawing programs like Adobe?  A. Oh, yes, all the time. There are all kinds of fine touches that prepackaged software makes easy. I could invent my own finishing system, but this is faster. Of course, the basic ideas, I create.  Q. Yet, I sense you're scornful of Adobe users?  A. The problem is that most people can't just "finish" things with it. They have to use it to start them, also. For much of recent history, people have created with brush, ink, paper -- the materials of art. Now that they have begun creating with software and computers, the styles that emerge are homogeneous because the software is universal. Without being able to know how to program, you can't break out of the technology -- just like if you don't know how to use brush and ink, you're limited. For most people, this really isn't a problem; they aren't necessarily looking for anything new. But for people who are seeking the next step, the prepackaged becomes an impossible barrier to break free from. I make everything I do. Many people are surprised that I don't have a programmer making things for me.  And others are surprised that I don't have an artist controlling me, telling me how to program. Because today, people don't realize that it is possible to think and create on the computer. Artists are used to thinking that programming is very hard -- impossible. And technologists are used to thinking that they can never become artists. Me, I just make things. It's just a natural flow of action and thought. If people see, "Oh, he does that," then maybe they'll think, "I can do it too."  Q. But lots of nonartists use computers for creating images . . .  A. They are using it as a tool, but not as a material. And to use it as a tool, you need to understand the medium, which means understanding the technology. Young people are changing this, because they have grown up with computers.  Q. If a conventional artist produces an object on a computer, does that automatically make it art?  A. It's art, but it's just a painting and no different than conventional art. It's not intrinsically different or superior just because it was created digitally and it's not digital art. Because digital art starts with an understanding and appreciation of the medium -- which, unfortunately, is today programming.  Q. When you were growing up in Seattle, what were your aspirations?  A. My aspirations were my father's -- and his were that all of us kids would go to either Harvard or M.I.T. He didn't know what or where they were. He was a cook and a tofu maker by trade. These were the only two schools he'd heard of. His were immigrants' dreams. Also, I was very good at math and at drawing and I had a teacher who said, "You should go to M.I.T. because it's a good place for math."  Q. Did the term artist ever come on your screen as a child?  A. Some of my teachers felt that I should become an artist, but my parents looked down upon this because they pictured me as poor. So I got to M.I.T. in 1984 -- a time when, all of a sudden, the computer had become visual. There was a great demand on the campus for people who could design icons, choose fonts. I worked at different places on campus doing this type of work and I thought I was so good at it. People used to tell me, "maybe you should be a graphic designer." I didn't know what that was. I only knew what engineers, tofu makers, and Japanese restaurant owners did. Then, I saw this book, "A Designer's Art," by Paul Rand and I was shocked. Paul Rand did the I.B.M., ABC, U.P.S. logos and I saw how exquisite his power over space was and I realized I wanted to do this. I told my father. He said, "No way.  You must be an engineer." So I went on and got my bachelor's and my master's in engineering, and once I did that, I told my father that I still wanted to be an artist and he said, "Now that you're a man, you can do what you want." So I thought the very place to go was the M.I.T. Media Lab and I joined the Ph.D. program here.  Q. Were you happy at the Media Lab?  A. Not happy, on two levels. The Media Lab was more a technology place than an art place and I was constantly reminded of that fact. I was fortunate to know Muriel Cooper, the design professor at the lab, and she gave me the best advice, which was, "Go away." So I went away. I went Tsukuba University, the great classic design school outside of Tokyo.  Q. What did studying in Japan teach you?  A. The most important thing was to not to be embarrassed about who I was. I had always been embarrassed about coming from a manual-labor family. In Japan, I was studying conventional art, and I used my hands all the time. That made me feel in touch with my human side, which I had lost when I came to M.I.T. I think the people who make things in Japan are kind of elevated. There are television shows there where cooks and noodle makers are shown as heroes. The ordinary, well done, is celebrated. So, once I realized that I came from a tradition that mattered to me, I gave up on technology and swore it off. Then, one day, my teacher at the art school asked, "John, what are planning on doing with your life?" I said, "Honor the classics, sir." He accused me of being the Japanese equivalent of a horse's rear end. "When you're young, you should do things that are new. When you're old you can always go back to the classics. They'll always be there," he said. From that point, I went back to technology and rediscovered everything. I became a sort of born- again technologist.  Q. Does the new technology mean the end of art as we know it?  A. Yes, it does. It represents a new dimension to the way art will be understood or perceived. It's a departure from appreciating a singular moment. What that means is . . . the reason why we can appreciate art is because most art has a single resting point: canvas. It's painted. It's dried. It aspires to be perfect. The medium of the computer is continually shifting. It can shift at will, in a microsecond. Or an hour. There's no limit on how it can be taught to change.  Q. In the 1960's, there was a kind of avant-garde-technoart movement that came out of Bell Labs. Do you like the abstract technoart of the 60's?  A. Definitely. Because they were pushing the limits of their medium.  They had a vision, but they didn't know how to make it succeed. I like a computer artist named Michael Noll, who was a Bell Labs scientist. He could make all these things, but he didn't know what they were and didn't know how to contextualize them. Karl Gerstner, whom I respect the most, was a visionary artist/designer, who foresaw the potential of computers, but didn't know how to realize them.  Q. Does this mean that the artists of the future will all be going to M.I.T.?  A. I think artists of the future will have to go to better art schools, which will teach them how to control technology instead of being controlled by it. M.I.T. is one option. One of the things that brought me back to M.I.T. was the idea that engineering will be the humanities of the 21st century. I believe there is room in this world for a humanist technologist. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Prof. John Maeda of the M.I.T. Media Laboratory combines the disciplines of art and science, using the computer as a tool for creating art. (Rick Friedman for The New York Times)

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Internet Stock Fever Spreads to Britain as Freeserve's Issue Surges
body: Freeserve P.L.C., the British upstart that radically changed Internet competition here by offering customers free access to the World Wide Web, transformed itself into a $3.3 billion company today by selling shares to the public. In the first initial public offering of a major European Internet company, Freeserve's shares rose 37 percent on the opening day of trading. Freeserve was the most heavily traded stock in London today, an indication that the euphoria over Internet public offerings, by now common in the unitedstates, had spilled over to Europe. Whether that euphoria will last over Freeserve was unclear. Its competitors have offered customer inducements to rival what Freeserve offers, and the company has lost money since its creation 10 months ago by Dixons Group P.L.C., Britain's top electronics retailer. Nonetheless, Freeserve is considered a pioneer in the rapidly expanding Internet market in Europe. It stunned competitors by quickly becoming Britain's most heavily used access provider with 1.3 million users, displacing AOL U.K., a venture of America Online and the German media giant Bertelsmann. Freeserve's main innovation is in luring customers by not charging them the monthly subscription fee for Internet access. Instead, it shares a percentage of the revenue generated by the cost of a user's telephone call with the phone company, which charges all calls by the minute. Freeserve also derives revenue from advertising and electronic commerce. By the market's close in London today, Freeserve shares had risen from their issue price of £1.50, or $2.39, to £2.055, making the company worth £2.07 billion, or $3.29 billion. Ninety-five million shares changed hands, representing nearly two-thirds of the offering. Freeserve's American depository receipts traded on the Nasdaq market in newyork rose similarly, to $32.125 from an offering price of $23.67. Each A.D.R. represents 10 common shares. Interest in the public offering had soared in the last week as investors sought 30 times the shares available. But analysts said the demand was at least partly a case of pure stock speculation, not necessarily any long-term bet on Freeserve's future. "Everyone's jumping in and jumping out. But that's the way it goes," said Miles Saltiel, an analyst with West LB Panmure Gordon. "It's less outrageous than it could have been." Freeserve plans to use the proceeds of the stock offering to invest heavily in marketing and additional content. Like many Internet companies, it has yet to turn a profit. Indeed, the company lost £1.04 million, or about $1.65 million, on revenue of £2.73 million from its September start through April. Even measured by the outsized valuations of Internet companies, many analysts seem to think that the company is overvalued. "The valuation of Freeserve looks quite high compared to many U.S.-based Internet companies like a Yahoo," said Peter Wyatt of Credit Lyonnais Securities here. "However, it's the only major Internet play in Europe, and it's got that Internet cachet." Mr. Wyatt said he was advising clients to sell shares in the company; he said Freeserve was worth about half its closing share price. Several free-subscription Internet service providers have intensified the competition for Freeserve in recent months including British Telecommunications P.L.C., Virgin Group and the Microsoft Network. It seems that almost any company tangentially connected to the Internet in Britain now offers a subscription-free service. Even the British soccer team Manchester United offers free Internet access. "The service is no longer unique," Mr. Saltiel noted. "It's going to be a struggle for them. It will be a battle of the deep pockets." In what may be the most telling sign yet that Freeserve's model has taken hold, AOL U.K. announced that it, too, would enter the competition next month with its own free-subscriber service, to be called Netscape Online. The move is a strategic about-face for the company, which has relied on subscription revenue; only two months ago it questioned the sustainability of a free-subscription business model. Adding to some confusion about Freeserve's business model is that deregulation among European telecommunications companies, and new pricing plans that may include all-you-can-eat American-style calling plans, could kill the very subscription-free model that Freeserve created. "The model is quite elegant and has been quite successful," said Noah Yasskin, an analyst at Jupiter Communications here. "But long term, the future is based on unlimited calling plans, so there is a real question about how they will respond." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A Freeserve compact disk, software for free subscription. (Reuters)

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
NTL to Buy Cable and Wireless Unit in $13 Billion Deal
body: NTL Inc.  moved to become the biggest cable-television company in Britain today with a $13 billion deal to buy the consumer divisions of Cable and Wireless Communications P.L.C. The proposed acquisition by NTL, a newyork-based telecommunications company founded six years ago, which operates mainly in Britain, received financial backing by France Telecom and increased speculation of further consolidation in the British communication services industry, where telephones, the Internet and television are converging. NTL would double its size to control about two-thirds of the British residential cable-television market with the acquisition, with a total of 2.8 million customers, vaulting from No. 3 to No. 1 over Cable and Wireless and Telewest P.L.C. Such a move had been anticipated since last week, when NTL signed an exclusive negotiating agreement with Cable and Wireless that blocked a rival offer from Telewest. Cable and Wireless had been trying to sell its residential cable unit for some time to focus on business services. Under the terms announced today, NTL will pay £6.3 billion ($10 billion) in cash and securities and assume £1.9 billion ($3 billion) in debt. France Telecom will invest $5.5 billion in NTL, increasing its stake in the company from 10 percent to 25 percent. Industry analysts said the acquisition would help NTL compete in the burgeoning high-speed Internet services business against British Telecommunications P.L.C. The acquisition would also strengthen NTL's position in the pay and interactive television field as it fends off British Sky Broadcasting Group P.L.C. "It's a really good move," said Sharon Armbrust, a senior analyst at Paul Kagan Associates, a media consulting firm in Carmel, Calif. She said NTL's managers "have really put themselves on solid financial ground with the investment by France Telecom." The deal is contingent upon the approval of the Bell Atlantic Corporation, which owns 18.5 percent of Cable and Wireless Communications. Bell Atlantic's board was expected to meet on Tuesday. Founded by two American money managers, Barclay Knapp and George Blumenthal, NTL began in 1993 as a spinoff of Cellular Communications Inc. Mr. Knapp, chief executive, and Mr. Blumenthal, chairman, sold Cellular Communications to Airtouch Communications Inc. for about $2 billion in 1996. NTL's shareholders include the Microsoft Corporation and the Comcast Corporation and funds managed by Goldman Sachs Group L.P. "The NTL guys are big salesmen," said Ms. Armbrust. "They don't stop here. It's a little like an Internet company. They get momentum by creating more momentum." NTL was one of the first companies to bundle telephone service, cable television and Internet access into a single service, much as AT&T is trying to do with its acquisition of TCI. "These guys are ahead of the U.S.," Ms. Armbrust said. The deal is also is a potential boon to France Telecom, which gets a piece of a major business outside its French domain. "It is a unique opportunity for France Telecom to participate in the development of innovative and convergent services combining telephony, digital TV and the Internet with one of the largest alternative telecom companies in the U.K.," Michel Bon, chairman and chief executive of France Telecom said in a statement. NTL, which is listed on the Nasdaq market, said it would seek a listing on the London Stock Exchange six months after the acquisition was completed. NTL shares rose 56.25 cents, to $99.8125 on Nasdaq. Cable and Wireless shares fell 2.6 percent, to 745.5 pence ($11.78). France Telecom shares rose 4.7 percent, to 69.55 euros ($74). http://www.nytimes.com

title: Judge Rules Internet Gambling Is Not Beyond Reach of State Authorities
body: In a case followed closely by law enforcement agencies across the country, a judge has ruled that newyork authorities were justified in freezing the assets of an Internet gambling company, even though the company's computers are based outside the unitedstates. In a decision disclosed yesterday, Justice Charles E. Ramos of State Supreme Court in Manhattan said that the newyork Attorney General's office, working with Federal authorities, was within its rights last year when it froze $800,000 in assets of World Interactive Gaming Corporation, an Internet gaming company that is based in Bohemia, N.Y., but has placed its computers in Antigua, a Caribbean island nation where casino gambling is legal. The $800,000 represented most of the company's assets. Justice Ramos cited the State Constitution, which bans gambling, as the basis for the Attorney General's authority and said the company's Web site created a "virtual casino within the user's computer terminal" in newyork State. "The act of entering the bet and transmitting the information from newyork via the Internet is adequate to constitute gambling activity within newyork State," Justice Ramos wrote in his ruling, which was dated last Thursday and disclosed yesterday by Eliot L. Spitzer, the State Attorney General. Government agencies have struggled with how to regulate commerce on the Internet. Internet gambling, in which wagers are placed by computer, is of special concern to Federal authorities because of its potential for fraud and abuse, and the Internet companies' seeming ability to defy Federal and state laws against gambling. Alan R. Kesner, chairman of an Internet gambling task force for the National Association of Attorneys General, which represents law enforcement officers in all 50 states, said, "What the judge was saying was that even though you are on the Internet, you are where you are. You are not magically transported to Antigua, where gambling is legal. You are still in newyork." Mr. Kesner likened Internet gambling to playing poker over the telephone. "You can't see the other guy's hand," he said. "He says he has four aces and he can prove it to you by sending you a printout." Anthony G. Colleluori, a lawyer for World Interactive Gaming, said the company planned to appeal Justice Ramos's ruling. Mr. Colleluori said that in a 1997 case begun by Mr. Spitzer's predecessor, Dennis C. Vacco, a state investigator opened a $200 account in a bank in Antigua. She downloaded software from World Interactive's Web site that allowed her to play blackjack, roulette and other casino games. The investigator typed in newyork State on her identification form. (The Web site is now inactive.) "The computer server rejects her," Mr. Colleluori said. "newyork does not permit gambling. She types in Nevada, where gambling is legal. The server lets her bet. She bets less than $20. She loses. The money leaves the bank in Antigua. The entire transaction took place where? We say Antigua." Anthony N. Cabot, a lawyer for Nevada casinos, said that the Minnesota Supreme Court last year upheld a consumer fraud action against an Internet gambling company and that this year Missouri sued an Idaho Indian tribe for putting its lottery on the Internet. Justice Ramos also ruled that World Interactive had violated state securities law by failing to register a sale of stock in the company that raised $1.8 million in capital for Jeffrey Burton, a 36-year-old stock promoter and president of World Interactive, and other company officials. "We failed to register once," Mr. Colleluori said. "We'll pay our fine and move on." World Interactive was the central target of a group of nearly 60 gaming companies singled out by Mr. Vacco, the Federal Trade Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and a Wall Street industry group, the North American Securities Administrators Association. Last August, the F.T.C. alleged in a complaint that World Interactive misled consumers in its stock offering by claiming it would "conservatively" earn $100 million in its first year. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Next Stage of the Cellular Tour;
As Europe Zooms Ahead, U.S. Fiddles With Formats - Correction Appended
body: After 24 years as lead singer for the Leningrad Cowboys, Finland's most popular home-grown rock band, Mato Valtonen figured it was time for something new. Noticing that Finnish teen-agers were perpetually tapping out messages on their cellular phones, Mr. Valtonen set up a business last year that transmits jokes and horoscopes for about 30 cents apiece. He was soon drawing thousands of requests a day so he added a half-dozen other quirky services, including a dictionary that translates words into 10 different languages and wireless chat rooms that attracted about 7,000 visitors on a recent Friday night. In the next few months, he plans to start what amounts to a wireless Internet site, using a new class of phones that have highly simplified Web browsers. Based on a slimmed-down, text-only Web format, the site will offer bus schedules, restaurant listings, stores and games. If all goes as he hopes, people will eventually make restaurant reservations and hair appointments -- and pay his company, Wapit Ltd., a few pennies every time they do it. "We just think up ideas and see whether they catch on," Mr. Valtonen said. "But I'm convinced that companies will see this as an important opportunity." Improbable as it may seem, Mr. Valtonen is part of a very serious rush across Europe into wireless data services that is keeping the Continent, along with Japan, well ahead of the slower-moving unitedstates. Teen-agers in Italy already use their cell phones to tap out millions of short messages every day. Germany's top-selling tabloid, Bild, offers scores of news and sports bulletins through short messages. Here in Finland, it is possible to tap out an order for a taxi or a take-out pizzas. And now, with the impending start of wireless Web transmission, European cellular carriers are gearing up for a huge increase in the speed and ease of transmitting wireless data. As a result, the gap could widen. Indeed, history may be repeating itself. In the early 1990's, European wireless companies jumped ahead of their American counterparts by adopting a single technical standard for digital cellular. As a result, digital phones with built-in paging and message functions arrived years earlier in Europe than in the unitedstates. They also worked anywhere in Europe, long before American phones worked throughout the unitedstates. "Europe has always been about one or two years ahead of the unitedstates in wireless technology, and they still are," said Herschel Shostek, an analyst in Wheaton, Md. Beginning this fall, cellular phone carriers from Scandinavia through Germany and down to Italy plan to start the text-only wireless Web sites for mobile phones. And next year, most European carriers plan to offer a technology called general packet radio service, or G.P.R.S., which will let people with newly equipped wireless phones send data fast enough to browse the Internet in full color. The new service is also designed to let customers stay connected all day long. Many companies plan to charge only for the data customers send or receive instead of for each minute they are connected. European governments are also setting the stage for even faster, "third generation" wireless networks. Most plan to hand out or auction off new radio licenses for so-called wideband networks that will be able to carry video conferences. Finland, where wireless phones now outnumber traditional ones, has already issued its new licenses; Germany, Britain and other European countries plan to do so next year. No one, however, is quite sure what kinds of features customers will actually want. And the third-generation systems will not be ready in Europe for at least two years, slightly behind Japan's timetable. unitedstates carriers are pushing wireless data as well. But Americans, who first got digital phones only a few years ago, have barely begun to use them for two-way data transfer and messaging. Just as the absence of a common standard delayed the ability of Americans to use their phones anywhere in the country, it is slowing down the rollout of more-advanced services. AT&T and other wireless carriers are pushing a third-generation technology called EDGE. Other big players, including Sprint and Bell Atlantic, are pushing a rival approach called wideband C.D.M.A., or code division multiple access. The conflicting standards "have slowed things down considerably," said Mark Lowenstein, an analyst at the Yankee Group, a research firm in Boston. "A lot of the technology is coming out of Silicon Valley, but in terms of actually using it, the early adopters are in Europe," Mr. Lowenstein said. "They have a much bigger base of digital users, they have one harmonious technology and particular countries are doing more to market new services." The unitedstates also faces a more difficult chore in getting from here to there. The American carriers do not have a middle-term technology comparable to G.P.R.S. in Europe, and the third-generation services are not expected to reach the market for a few years. Moreover, the Federal Communications Commission is insisting that carriers use existing radio frequencies, which are likely to become overloaded if customers transmit video and graphics on top of voice conversations. Paradoxically, much of the inspiration for new wireless data services comes straight from the unitedstates. Yahoo Inc. is setting up wireless Internet gateways in Germany. Phone.com, a small California company, developed the simplified browsers and servers -- known as wireless access protocol, or WAP -- that European wireless carriers are now embracing. Meanwhile, the Microsoft Corporation is locked in a fierce competition with a European consortium called Symbian over establishing a global standard for personal digital assistants -- hand-held devices -- that would use these wireless networks. Most of the big cell phone manufacturers are rolling out Web-ready phones designed for G.S.M., or global system for mobile communication, the dominant second-generation wireless standard in Europe. Nokia of Finland, which will probably be first to the market, plans to start selling its version in August. The Nokia phone is about the same size as an ordinary cell phone. It offers no graphics or pictures, but it has a small screen to display text. In Germany, Mannesmann A.G., the country's largest mobile phone operator, has signed contracts with the main television networks to deliver news, sports and weather over a wireless network. Handelsblatt, Germany's biggest financial newspaper, will provide business news and stock market information. Customers will also be able to reserve airline tickets with Lufthansa and train seats with Deutsche Bahn, the national railway. "We are not interested in niche markets," said Dirk Wierzbitzki, director of product marketing at Mannesmann's mobile telephone unit in Dusseldorf. "We see this as a mass-market business." An exuberant talker who sprinkles his sentences with American phrases like "killer app" and "Internet value chain," Mr. Wierzbitzki has reason to be bullish. Mannesmann customers already tap out 100 million messages a month, and the volume is climbing 20 percent a month. "Europe is definitely ahead" in the use of cell phones as an interactive device, said Fabiola Arredondo, managing director for Yahoo Europe, which recently teamed up with Mannesmann. For Mr. Wierzbitzki, the next big shift will come with the start of G.P.R.S. next year. The service, which will require new handsets, has a theoretical top speed of about 114,000 bits of data per second. Since the airwaves will inevitably be bogged down by congestion, the real speeds may be significantly slower. Even so, they would be far higher than those of Europe's current cell phones, which have a top speed of 9,600 bits per second -- the top speed of most American cell phones, too. But maybe more important is the way it will work. The system is designed to charge customers based on the amount of data transmitted rather than by the minute. That can be a a big change from customers who can pay $1 a minute during business hours. "Always connected, always on line -- that's our vision," Mr. Wierzbitzki said. Though Mannesmann has not yet announced a pricing plan, Mr. Wierzbitzki envisions deals along the lines of 10 megabytes for about $10. For an ordinary consumer using the wireless Web format, that would amount to almost unlimited browsing and E-mail for a month. But that is not the only point. The idea is sell "mobility services" -- traffic and shopping information, banking, full-time access to E-mail. "You need to forget about traditional Web surfing," said Ilkka Raiskinen, vice president for business development at Nokia Mobile Phones. "If you're walking around Helsinki, you don't want to browse the Web. You want to know where a restaurant is, where you can buy clothes and how do you get there." Mannesmann already has a separate subsidiary, Autocom, that provides navigation aids through wireless networks. Executives are now looking at services that would warn drivers about traffic jams and recommend other routes, as well as automatic S O S buttons that would call for help if an accident occurs. "There is a huge pent-up demand for data over wireless phones, but the barriers have always been reliability, speed and cost," said Anders Thulin, a consultant at McKinsey & Company in Stockholm. "All those barriers are reduced now." Even the most enthusiastic wireless bulls caution that the third-generation networks to deliver all of this fast and efficiently are still several years away. Though carriers have agreed on the design of the system, the advanced technology is by no means ready for prime time. Still, Mr. Raiskinen of Nokia predicted that at least 10 percent of wireless phones would be Internet-ready by the end of next year. He cautioned that speed itself would not usher in overnight change. "The success will be based more on content," he said. "It's not a revolution. This is very much about evolution." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Business Day on Tuesday about wireless data services in Europe misstated the position of two American companies on a proposed standard for new wireless technology. The companies, Sprint and Bell Atlantic, support a proposal called C.D.M.A. 2000, which would be compatible with a current technology known as C.D.M.A., for code division multiple access; they do not endorse wideband C.D.M.A., which is a rival proposal. Correction-Date: July 31, 1999, Saturday Graphic   Photo: Mato Valtonen saw his fellow Finns' penchant for sending messages on cell phones and founded a business sending jokes and horoscopes. Now he is planning to start a kind of Web site, for a new class of phones. (Soile Kallio/Lehtikuva, for The New York Times)(pg. C8)

title: PUBLIC LIVES
body: Housecleaning And History Cross CAROLE HALL says the timing was a coincidence -- her husband, LLOYD, was rushing to list their John F. Kennedy Jr. figurine on the Ebay on-line auction service before "Jeopardy!" came on at 7:30 P.M. on July 16. "We had no idea that 40 minutes later he was going to take off," said Mrs. Hall, who lives in Pawtucket, R.I. Nor did she have any idea that the figurine, which she bought for $1 at a yard sale several years ago, would go for $227.50. "I thought maybe I'd make $5," Mrs. Hall said, explaining that her only motive in selling the statuette was to clear some shelf space. "We have too much in my house," she said. "It looks like a gift shop." The first thing her husband did when he got up on the morning the Kennedy plane was reported missing was to log on to Ebay. "He said, 'John John's figurine is up to $90,' " Mrs. Hall recalled. "I said, 'It's more collectible than I thought.' But they have this little news thing that comes on the screen. He says, 'John John's plane is missing.' If I had known, I wouldn't have put it on. I wouldn't take advantage of a disaster like that." Ebay was flooded with Kennedy memorabilia last week, including dozens of copies of George magazine that were offered for $10 to $20. Not everything was selling, though. As of 5:30 P.M. yesterday, no one had bid on a pair of used airplane tickets. The seller wanted $4,850. "These two airline tickets were given to me personally and before leaving the plane by John F. Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette," the seller wrote. "They were sitting next to me the entire trip from Miami to newyork, a trip that I will remember forever." Nor had any would-be buyers met another seller's $10,000 opening bid for figurines of Mr. Kennedy and his sister, Caroline. The buyer of the Halls' figurine turned out to be LENNY VEGA, a hairdresser in Manhattan. "He's very special," Mr. Vega said of Mr. Kennedy. "I grew up watching him on television, but I never had the chance to see him."  Another Sale Of the Century "This is the last great amazing celebrity sale," NANCY VALENTINO declared yesterday. Ms. Valentino is a vice president at Christie's and the resident expert on Marilyn Monroe, whose belongings -- her stilleto-heeled shoes, her earrings, her Golden Globe Award, her piano, her inexplicably lopsided chandelier -- will be sold at auction on Oct. 27. Even the dress she wore when she sang "Happy Birthday, Mr. President" to John F. Kennedy at Madison Square Garden in 1962 will be on the block. Yesterday the dress was on display at Christie's, in Rockefeller Center, and VREDY LYTSMAN, a spokeswoman for Christie's, was saying that the auction house expected the sale price of the flesh-colored, full-length dress to be in "the high six figures." That would put the Monroe auction in the stratospheric range of other big-money celebrity sales -- the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis auction with the $574,500 humidor and the $442,500 rocking chair, the Diana auction with the $222,500 blue velvet dress, and the Duke and Duchess of Windsor auction with the $415,000 mahogany table, to name only three. A conversation with Ms. Valentino leaves no doubt that she believes Marilyn Monroe is worth it. "She's so present," Ms. Valentino said yesterday as camera crews zoomed in on the dress. "That's the phenomenal thing about her fame. She's so present." And what about the future? Well, Ms. Valentino said, "the century she was so identified with is coming to a close." JAMES BARRON http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: MARILYN MONROE; JOHN F. KENNEDY JR.

title: San Francisco Lets AT&T Bar Cable Access to Rivals
body: In the latest skirmish of what has become a national fight, the Board of Supervisors here declined tonight to compel AT&T to open its cable television system to competing providers of high-speed Internet access like America Online. The action, on a vote of 9 to 2, followed a day of last-minute negotiations between the supervisors and AT&T. San Francisco was the latest battleground in a lobbying effort -- at the Federal and local levels, in the courts and before regulatory agencies -- to determine who will provide high-speed Internet access over cable television lines and on what terms. Rivals like America Online and local telephone companies are making the case that high-speed Internet service should be more like long distance service and that the company providing the connection should not have a monopoly or undue advantage in providing service. Cable operators like AT&T contend that there will be little financial incentive for them to upgrade cable systems to provide Internet service if their systems merely become a gateway to other Internet service providers. Although AT&T prevailed here, the supervisors did require the company, as a condition of its assuming the cable franchises of Tele-Communications Inc., to upgrade its cable system to digital technology within four years. And the supervisors reserved the right to revisit the issue. Fewer than a million homes now have high-speed Internet service through their cable or telephone companies, typically at about $40 a month. But analysts estimate that the number will rise to 16 million by the end of 2002, with 80 percent of those connecting through cable. An AT&T spokesman, James R. Peterson, said it would cost $50 million to upgrade San Francisco's cable infrastructure to digital technology permitting high-speed Internet connections and other services. "We are very pleased to obtain the transfer of control without imposition of cable and bundling requirements," Scott Morris, AT&T's vice president for local government relations, said after tonight's vote. "We now have the opportunity to make the investments we want to make." On the local level, AT&T's purchase of the cable giant Tele-Communications Inc., has provided a strategic wedge for its opponents, who have sought to make the transfer of TCI's cable franchises to AT&T contingent on what they are calling "open access" to high-speed Internet connections. Their first victory came in December in Portland, Ore., which approved precisely such terms. In early June, a Federal judge in Portland upheld the move. The decision is to be considered by the unitedstates Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and is being watched closely, with AT&T contending that the Federal Government, not local governments, should regulate competition. Earlier this month, Broward County, Fla., voted to require AT&T and MediaOne to open their cable systems to competing providers. And last week, the National Association of Counties, meeting in St. Louis, passed a resolution backing the right of municipalities to require open access. Before its vote tonight, San Francisco's 11-member Board of Supervisors unanimously resolved to support open access in principle. The resolution, proposed by Supervisor Leslie Katz, requires the city to monitor open-access legislation and legal decisions around the country and then reconsider the matter in December; an open-access bill is pending in the California legislature. But Tom Ammiano, the president of the Board of Supervisors, was not satisfied. He called the board's ultimate action tonight "a lot of hocus-pocus and hooey," adding, "So much for open access." He predicted that the issue would ultimately be put to a local referendum. Katie Roper, executive director of the Bay Area Open Access Coalition, a group financed by GTE, Pacific Bell and other companies that want access to AT&T's lines, said the member companies fully intended to compensate AT&T for access to its cable lines. "We're not asking for free access," she said. Officials for Hands Off the Internet, a group financed by AT&T, among others, countered that AOL, GTE and other aspiring high-speed access providers were spending millions to develop their own technology and should not be allowed to piggyback on AT&T's investment. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Weakness in Technology Hurts Shares
body: Stocks moved broadly lower yesterday, led by big technology and Internet issues, as concerns about the sudden drop in the dollar and a possible future increase in interest rates provided an excuse to take profits. Selling was most pronounced on the Nasdaq stock market, where the composite index, which fell 6 percent last week after hitting a high on July 16, declined an additional 2.7 percent yesterday. Microsoft, Yahoo, Amazon.com and Cisco Systems were among the biggest decliners. The index was down 73.21 points, to 2,619.19. Despite the extended decline, the Nasdaq composite is still up more than 19 percent this year. "The Nasdaq is correcting for the excesses it recorded over the past month," said Bryan Piskorowski, market analyst at Prudential Securities. "All in all, the market is in pretty good shape, but it needs to take a pause." Peter J. Canelo, an investment strategist at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, suggested that technology stocks might fall out of favor for a while. "It has been my thesis that good second-quarter earnings would help technology stocks, but that after those numbers were reported worries about Y2K and the like would cause the market to rotate back to areas like energy, cyclical and financial services stocks," he said. He added, "The market needs a shift in leadership to keep advancing, and I think that will happen." Compared with the Nasdaq, the drop in other averages was more modest. The Dow Jones industrial average fell 47.80 points, or 0.4 percent, to 10,863.16. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index slipped 9.18 points, or 0.7 percent, to 1,347.76. The Russell 2000 index of small company stocks dropped 5.51 points, or 1.2 percent, to 442.87. Trading activity was unusually light, even for a summer Monday. On the newyork Stock Exchange, 616.2 million shares changed hands, the third-lowest total so far this year. America Online was the most active issue on the Big Board yesterday, slumping 7 13/16, to 100 1/8, on news that top executives at the on-line service company sold four million shares yesterday morning. Meanwhile, volume on the Nasdaq market was 837.4 million shares. "We are going to see this sort of trading pattern," said William Meehan, chief market analyst at Cantor Fitzgerald. "I think a lot of portfolio managers are taking profits and putting on longer-term hedges, particularly in technology stocks, which despite their terrific long-term prospects are very pricey right now." Christine A. Callies, chief investment strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, said in a research report released yesterday that stock prices could remain in an extended trading range for some time. "The risk-reward status of the S.& P. 500 at levels above 1,300 will remain poor for most of the second half," Ms. Callies wrote.
