"Investors should not chase rallies but should use trading bounces to rebalance portfolios and raise modest amounts of cash." High valuations and worries that the Federal Reserve Board might raise interest rates again took a toll on technology stocks. Microsoft fell 2 5/8, to 87 5/8. Hewlett-Packard lost 2 1/16, to 105 11/16; Cisco Systems fell 1 7/8, to 61 1/16, and Lucent Technologies shed 1/2, to 64 5/8. It was also a bad day for energy stocks. Chevrondropped 1 7/16, to 92 3/8. Royal Dutch Petroleum, which is in the S.& P. 500 index, fell 1 11/16, to 59 1/16. And BP Amoco lost 2 5/16, to 111 3/4. Some consumer-oriented stocks that have been battered in recent months did better yesterday. Playboy Loses Round Over Search Engine Ads
body: Giving a green light to a common but controversial Internet advertising practice, a Federal judge in California has refused a request by Playboy Enterprises to stop the Web search services Excite.com and Netscape.com from placing ads for pornography sites with the search results for the words "playboy" or "playmate." Declining Playboy's request for a preliminary injunction, Judge Alicemarie H. Stotler of the Federal District Court in Santa Ana, Calif., said Playboy was unlikely to succeed in a trial with its contention that Excite Inc. had violated trademark laws. Marissa Gluck, an analyst with the research firm of Jupiter Communications, said the decision was good news for search services, which she said derived 20 to 30 percent of their ad revenue from the sale of banner ads linked to keywords. In its lawsuit against Excite and America Online's Netscape Communications unit, which licenses Excite's search technology, Playboy had challenged this practice, known as banner ad keying, saying that it could divert customers looking for Playboy's site and also tarnish its reputation. In her opinion on June 24, Judge Stotler found that although Playboy held trademarks for Playboy and Playmate, it did not have a monopoly on the generic use of those words in English. For that reason and others, the court said, Playboy had not shown that Excite had made commercial use of Playboy's trademark, as would be necessary to justify a trademark infringement lawsuit. Judge Stotler also ruled that even if Excite had used Playboy's trademarks, that use would not have been improper because Playboy had offered no evidence that consumers would be confused about the relationship between Playboy and a banner ad for a pornography site. A lawyer for Playboy said the company would appeal the decision.   CARL S. KAPLAN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A Federal judge in California said placing ads with search results is permissible.

Youthful Leader For Internet Push
body: Though only 28, Seth Goldstein is an experienced member of newyork's Internet industry, having started the Site Specific ad agency in 1995. But recently, he has been the Inspector Gadget of Silicon Alley. It was after selling Site Specific in 1997 to what is now USWeb/CKS that Mr. Goldstein started a business called Root.net, which aimed to help digital road warriors assemble their portable arsenals. When that venture did not travel well, Mr. Goldstein became an entrepreneur in residence with Flatiron Partners, the Internet venture capital arm of Chase Manhattan. His mission has been to figure out how to make money from the emergence of gadgets -- other than PC's -- that may be connected to the Internet. "Everybody is talking about how people will access the Internet throughout the day, from the refrigerator in the morning telling them the weather to their car dashboard giving directions and playing music from MP3 files," he said. "But it's not clear how we're going to get there. And that uncertainty creates investment opportunity." Chase has agreed to put up as much as $50 million to back gizmo companies. And in seven months, Mr. Goldstein has managed to go through half that money by investing in a handful. Among them is Scout, a San Francisco company making a small device that would sell for less than $100 and would receive information broadcasts of information of interest to "urban youth." Another is Vertical One, an Atlanta maker of software to bring together balances from several banks; it would be used first on Web sites and later on wireless devices. Internet Appliance Network, a company that Mr. Goldstein created with backing from Russell I. Pillar, chief executive of Virgin Entertainment, is also in the group. It would offer on-line services based on small devices used only for email and Web surfing. Thinking Media is another of the companies. It is a newyork concern that makes a Java software program called Sonata that is used in on-line advertising and has applications in wireless devices. Kozmo.com is also getting an infusion from Flatiron. The increasingly popular newyork service employs an army of bicycle messengers and promises to deliver rental videocassettes and snacks to wired, sugar-starved couch potatoes within an hour of an order placed through its Web site. Mr. Goldstein helped secure backing for Kozmo by using a computer to summon a messenger to the Chase conference room where he was making the pitch. "A guy shows up with 15 pints of Ben & Jerry's within half an hour," he recalled. "That really greased the wheels."   SAUL HANSELL http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Seth Goldstein helps invest in Internet gadgets. (Jeffery A. Salter/The newyork Times)

title: I.B.M. Challenges EMC With New Data-Storage Line
body: I.B.M. is making a bid to regain its leadership position in the high-performance end of the data storage business today with the introduction of a new generation of big disk systems. The new product line, code-named Shark, arrives at a time when the demand for data storage is growing at a torrid pace because of the Internet, electronic commerce and data mining -- all of which require fast access to vast amounts of information. And the new storage line, analysts say, represents the International Business Machines Corporation's effort to challenge the current leader in high-end storage systems, the EMC Corporation. EMC may not be a household name, but it is one of the most striking success stories in high technology. By commercializing a flexible high-performance storage technology known as RAID (redundant array of independent disks), EMC grabbed the top spot in the lucrative market for large external storage systems away from I.B.M. Today, big Internet companies like America Online and many major corporations -- including those using I.B.M. mainframe computers -- employ EMC systems as their main data storehouses. EMC, based in Hopkinton, Mass., has grown to become a $4 billion-a-year company. Its stock has been the second-best performer among the Standard & Poor's 500 companies during the 1990's, trailing only Dell Computer. And its market capitalization exceeds that of such corporate stalwarts as General Motors and Boeing. The I.B.M. Enterprise Storage Server line, according to analysts who have been briefed in advance by the company, promises to be stiff competition for EMC both in terms of price and performance. "I.B.M.'s strategy is to try to come out with higher performance systems at significantly lower prices," said John McArthur, an analyst at the International Data Corporation, a research firm. The proof, analysts cautioned, will be in the marketplace as the big systems, which can cost $1 million or more, become generally available in September. "But this could be just what I.B.M. needs to be competitive with EMC," said James Porter, president of Disk/Trend Inc., a research firm. The new high-performance storage systems, I.B.M. said, have data-retrieval times that are far faster than rival products on the market. The company asserts that users can scale the systems from 420 gigabytes to 11 terabytes (enough to hold all the words in the Library of Congress). And I.B.M. says that its new line of storage products can be used with a variety of computer systems: I.B.M. 390 mainframes, Unix computers and machines running Microsoft's Windows NT operating systems. In an internal memo, James Vanderslice, senior vice president of I.B.M.'s technology group, called the new product "the biggest storage announcement" the company had made in the high-performance end of the market since the 1960's. In the memo to Louis V. Gerstner Jr., the chairman, and the rest of I.B.M.'s top management, Mr. Vanderslice described the new storage line as an Internet-related product that would allow Big Blue to deliver "the advanced functions our customers need to manage the explosion of data as they become e-businesses." Other computer makers have also recognized the importance of high-performance data storage products -- and the business opportunity in that market. Sun Microsystems Inc. and the Hewlett-Packard Company are entering the market, for example. "These companies feel they have to, because storage is becoming a central strategic product -- as important as the computer itself," observed Steven Milunovich, an analyst at Merrill Lynch & Company. "Data drives everything else in electronic commerce." The $14-billion market for sophisticated external storage systems increasingly spans a variety of computing platforms -- mainframes, machines running the Unix operating system and Windows NT servers. "This product hits the high-end of each of those market segments," observed Ronald Kilpatrick, the general manager of I.B.M.'s storage systems division. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MEDIA;
An Entrepreneurial Exception Rides The Internet in Japan
body: Masayoshi Son seems an unlikely deal maker in the bubbly and free-spirited world of the Internet. Short, boyish-looking and soft-spoken, Mr. Son -- while in Japan -- wears the Japanese business uniform of a white shirt and an immaculately pressed black suit. In public, he sometimes stands stiffly and smiles only slightly. He bows often to emphasize his humility. Moreover, he lives in Tokyo, the risk-averse capital of the world, where the Internet is still a foreign concept to many. But if there is such a thing as an Internet financial and media empire, Mr. Son's company, Softbank, may be it. Mr. Son, 41, and Softbank are already among the most powerful financial forces in cyberspace, controlling key stakes in 100 Internet information providers in the unitedstates and 20 such companies in Japan. The stakes in publicly held companies, worth $15 billion to $20 billion, are sprinkled widely. Softbank now owns 28 percent of Yahoo, and it has important stakes in Geocities, E-Loans, E*Trade, USWeb, Message Media, and TheStreet.com. And Softbank is intensifying its focus on the Internet with new deals all the time. Last Tuesday, for example, it agreed to pay $20 million for a 40 percent stake in Webhire, an on-line recruiting company. And Softbank may sell much of its 70 percent stake in Ziff-Davis, the publisher of such magazines as PC Week. "If you want a global player in the Internet, they are the player," said Jarett F. Wait, chief operating officer in Asia for Lehman Brothers, which recently released a 195-page report on the company. "There's nobody else that comes close." But while Mr. Son is Japan's leading entrepreneur, the oddity, and perhaps the reason, is that he is not ethnically Japanese. A Chinese-Korean, he grew up poor in southern Japan, closed off from normal avenues in Japan's corporate world because of discrimination against the Korean minority. Denied a chance to succeed at a leading company, he started Softbank and has become one of Japan's richest men. Softbank's aim is to become a global Internet "zaibatsu," a Japanese-style empire with investments in many linked companies. Softbank has begun Internet ventures through Yahoo in Germany, France and Britain; it has investment alliances with Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation in Europe, and a joint venture in South Korea. "For the next 10 years, we do nothing but Internet," Mr. Son said, speaking in English during an interview in his spacious office. "Because that's where the whole society is going to have a big revolution." Now, after building the foundations of his Internet kingdom in the unitedstates, Mr. Son is turning back to Japan -- one of the least entrepreneurial societies. Last month, he and Frank G. Zarb, chairman of the National Association of Securities Dealers, announced a plan to form a new trading exchange, a Japanese version of Nasdaq, that could become a center for electronic brokerage activity, electronic research and entrepreneurial ventures in Japan. Mr. Son will feed that entrepreneurial spirit with venture-capital funds that aim to pour $85 million into building Japanese start-ups and grooming hundreds of Softbank wannabes. On June 29 Mr. Son held a reception for 1,400 budding entrepreneurs. He spent the morning of July 5 with Prime Minister Keizo Obuchi and other Government officials to offer some ideas for reviving Japan's economy. The entry of Mr. Son, an entrepreneur from the Korean minority, into the Prime Minister's residence underscores the changing times in Japan. Yet he faces some enormous challenges. So far he has been a kind of venture capitalist, backing Internet enterprises early and riding on their success. But he does not manage or plan them. And the soaring value of Internet stocks has perhaps exaggerated his ability to pick individual winners. Mr. Son's appetite for expansion has often outstripped his financial ability. Even now, he often taps the bond markets, and is carrying about three times as much debt as equity. If there is a shake-out in the Internet, or if Internet stocks prove to be a bubble that pops, then Softbank may falter. Moreover, as Mr. Son ventures into relatively new territory -- like the stock exchange -- he is taking risks in areas in which he has no proved expertise. Still, no one seems eager to bet against him. And almost no one is better than he is at adjusting to a new situation; he sometimes comes across as a chameleon. He can backslap and talk in colloquial English with American investment bankers and then discuss the details of new computer chips with the techies. He can also turn somber and bow and speak in polite Japanese to melt into a Japanese business crowd. This knack for mixing comes from his personal background, which has haunted and helped him since his days growing up in a small town on the southern Japanese island of Kyushu. Mr. Son's grandparents came to Japan from Korea, where his family had lived for 21 generations after migrating from China. His father and other Koreans illegally built their houses on land owned by Japan National Railways, which led to a long-running conflict with the authorities. It was on that land that Mr. Son's father raised pigs and chickens and illicitly made sake. The home brew was apparently lucrative, for he became the first person in town to buy a car. When Mr. Son's family moved out of its Korean neighborhood so he could attend a better school, to try to melt into society the family took a Japanese last name, Yasumoto. "I was a good student, but in those days I had a darkness in my mind all the time," Mr. Son wrote in an essay in 1992. "It was because of my nationality. When I was with friends, I was very happy. When I came back home alone, I had the feeling that I was hiding something from my friends." He took on his real Korean-Chinese name, Son, when he went to the unitedstates at 16 to attend high school and then on to the University of California at Berkeley. It was his American experience, he says, that laid the groundwork for his career. "If I had stayed all the time in Japan," Mr. Son said, "I probably would have become much more conservative, just as other Japanese." One important element in the effort to change attitudes of young people will be to expand opportunities for them to finance their companies and to reward them with stock options -- and that is where the new stock exchange comes in. In February, Mr. Son met John L. Hilley, an aide to Mr. Zarb for the first time through a mutual friend. Over dinner at a French restaurant at the Royal Park Hotel, close to Softbank's offices, Mr. Hilley began pouring out his frustrations over trying to break into the Japanese market. He had been in meetings his whole trip and had received very little encouragement. "I said, 'Maybe we can help, maybe you went to the wrong place,' " Mr. Son recalled. He told Mr. Hilley, "You need someone who has the entrepreneurial spirit to make this happen." Mr. Son and Mr. Zarb then began talking about setting up a new exchange, an idea made possible by recent changes in the securities regulations under Japan's financial liberalization. The idea also dovetailed with Mr. Son's ambition to help shape electronic brokerage and the Internet in Japan. Even if this proposal fails and Mr. Son suffers a blow to his reputation, he still has his bet on the Internet. He says that as Internet technology evolves, the potential for returns from the information that travels on the network will be far greater than anything realized so far. "That's my fortune-telling, " he said. "I'm betting on that." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Masayoshi Son, without the usual black suit, in his office in Tokyo. (Stuart Isett/Sygma for The newyork Times)

title:
Patents;
An Internet entrepreneur finds a way for newsstand dealers to profit from subscription sales.
body: HE may have become a billionaire selling airline tickets on the Internet. But Jay Walker thinks he knows a better way to sell magazines at the newsstand, too. Mr. Walker, chairman and chief executive of Priceline.com, and a business partner have just received a patent for a new method of selling magazine subscriptions. It is the latest in a series of patents Mr. Walker has received in recent years for various business methods. Currently, buying a magazine at a newsstand means paying about three dollars a copy, or far more than the same issue would cost with a subscription. Publishers prefer subscriptions, which guarantee sales of multiple issues, and so they load magazines with subscription cards that promote reduced issue prices for a 12- or 24-month subscription. But newsstand owners and other retailers can hardly be blamed for not pointing out to customers that it would be cheaper to subscribe than to buy individual magazines from them. But what if publishers and magazine sellers could profit, while readers got a cheaper price for each issue? That is the idea behind a new method of magazine subscribing patented by Mr. Walker and his associate, Sanjay Jindal. People buy magazines off the rack for convenience, but also to read them in a timely fashion. So in spite of the cost being double or triple the subscription price, about a billion single-issue copies of magazines are sold each year. Many of those are impulse purchases. Subscribing may be cheaper, but it has disadvantages that discourage many readers. First-time subscribers may have to wait up to 12 weeks for a subscription to be processed, missing the issues that appear in the meantime. And people typically cannot pay cash for a magazine subscription; they have to mail in a check or submit a credit card number, or send a subscription card and then pay a bill. In their patent filing, Mr. Walker and Mr. Jindal also point out that readers have to pay full newsstand price for a magazine in order to get the subscription card in the first place. A reader's discounted rate applies only after the subscription begins. The patent describes a new method of subscribing to a magazine at a retail outlet. When a customer purchased the magazine, either he or the retailer would fill out a subscription card on the spot. Information about price, length of the subscription and mailing address would be entered into a point-of-sale terminal. The data would then be transmitted to a subscription fulfillment house for immediate processing. The retailer would receive a percentage of each subscription sold, and the reader would get the newsstand's current issue of the magazine at the subscription price. Mr. Walker and Mr. Jindal received patent 5,926,796. Mr. Walker, who lives in Ridgefield, Conn., has been granted more than a dozen patents in the last two years for methods of conducting business, including patents for awarding prepaid telephone time, for employment searches, for figuring foreign exchange insurance premiums, for post-paid traveler's checks, and even for a computer game and a method of playing lotteries. He shares the patents with other inventors, but they all belong to his company, Walker Asset Management L.P. Mr. Walker is perhaps best known, though, for a patent awarded last August for a method of buying and selling goods over the Internet. It is the method on which he had already based Priceline.com, a Web site that uses a "reverse auction" technique that enables consumers to name their own price for airline tickets -- which airlines can choose to accept or not. Mr. Walker, Bruce Schneier and James Jorasch won a patent for this kind of "buyer-driven commerce," and gained exclusive rights to that particular form of electronic sales. Priceline.com, which went public in April, had a stock-market value of about $11.6 billion, based on Friday's closing price of $81.1875 a share. That would make Mr. Walker's personal stake worth almost $5 billion, assuming he still has the 61.3 million shares reported in the prospectus last March.  Practice Deck For Blackjack Winning at blackjack depends largely on the luck of the draw -- or so it seems. Players hope to receive the right combination of randomly drawn cards the total of which will beat the total drawn by a casino dealer, without exceeding twenty-one. Alfred Smith believes that winning strategies for blackjack can be learned -- especially for players who know how to count the cards that have already been dealt. Toward that end, he's patented a blackjack practice deck of cards. "It is mathematically demonstrated that if you can count cards, you will beat the casino, which is why they kick you out if they catch you," Mr. Smith said. Card counting -- keeping track of what has been dealt and thus knowing what cards are left to play -- is not against the law, but casinos prohibit it and make great efforts to identify card counters. "They consider it cheating, but there is a lot of controversy about that, because it is you using your intelligence." Mr. Smith, a former restaurant owner who now lives in Florida and is marketing his blackjack practice deck through Web sites, catalogues and stores that cater to blackjack aficionados, has designed a deck that features two-card combinations of blackjack hands on each practice card. Players study the practice cards and memorize what strategy to use to respond to each possible combination. "There is something called basic strategy, which is derived by harnessing computers," Mr. Smith explained. "If you have no idea what cards have been played, what this gives you is the best expectation of playing every hand with the maximum opportunity to win or the minimum loss." But if a player does know what cards have been dealt -- if he is counting cards -- then he can use a different strategy for his next move. Mr. Smith continued: "There are many card counting systems out there. Whether you use basic strategy or a card-counting system, with my deck you can practice 'Do I know what to do with this combination?' What the cards do is take all of what you could refer to as the two-card decision totals and put them on one card." The two-card combinations appear on the practice cards as one card peeking above another, and they can be shuffled, dealt and read from either direction. "With the practice cards, I could do in 15 minutes what took me an hour when I was dealing hands to myself," he said. "I could review them on the bus to Atlantic City and get the numbers in my head. I went from $5 and $10 hands to $25 hands, and I feel comfortable playing $100 hands." Mr. Smith received patent 5,895,048. Patents may be viewed on the Web at www.uspto.gov or may be ordered through themail, by patent number, for $3 from the Patent and Trademark Office, Washington, D.C. 20231. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Jay Walker, chief executive of Priceline.com, has received patents on a variety of new business methods in recent years. (Associated Press)

title:
TECHNOLOGY: E-Commerce Report;
For local merchants interested in on-line sales, faith may be the biggest element of the business plan.
body: ONLIKE most people drawn to the siren song of Internet commerce, Phil Worley started a Web site last spring with a modest goal: bring in some additional sales for the small-town hardware business. No 50-page business plan. No venture capital. No initial public offering. After three months of advertising Weber grills on the site, operated by The Hartford Courant (www.courant.com), at prices lower than many competitors, his experience has not met even his humble expectations. In other words, he has not sold a thing on line. "I haven't seen much payback," said Mr. Worley, owner of Worley Ace Hardware in Canton, Conn., a town of about 8,000 that lies 14 miles west of Hartford. "But I feel like I need to be there, since so many in my industry are. I'm keeping the faith." For many people dipping their toes into E-commerce, the process requires an element of faith -- whether for consumers concerned about security, investors uncertain of their return or retailers with no idea how consumers' on-line behavior will evolve. But for local merchants who want to participate in the world's hottest industry, faith is perhaps the biggest component. It is not only that owners of small businesses often lack the time, expertise and marketing budgets to compete with bigger companies. It is not yet clear that people will look to local merchants when they surf the Net for bargains. Meanwhile, on-line city guides, which seek to aggregate local businesses for ads and transactions, are a fragmented bunch, with only experimental ideas on how to approach local markets. "It's not a pretty picture for local merchants right now," said Lisa Allen, an E-commerce analyst with Forrester Research, an Internet consulting firm. "First of all, a lot of what's sold on line are commodities, and you don't need to buy a book or CD from a local yokel store," she said. "But also, the national players have the deep pockets to create sites with the best user experience and market them. And the mom and pops don't have that." Ms. Allen said local merchants would attract $680 million in Internet sales this year, or 9 percent of the total $7.8 billion projected by Forrester. By 2003, Forrester expects local merchants to increase those sales to $6 billion, but that number will account for just 6 percent of the projected $108 billion in Web sales. In promoting the potential of local E-commerce, some executives point to the fact that people spend nearly 80 percent of their money within a 20-mile radius of their homes. But "interests, not geography, will be important on line," Ms. Allen said. "If you're a wine aficionado, you won't necessarily go to the local site," she added. There are, however, certain categories that show greater local potential on line -- including tickets, which Forrester anticipates will reap 43 percent of local Web sales, or $2.6 billion, by 2003. Such numbers bode well for Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch, which runs a network of city guides catering primarily to entertainment-minded consumers. Perhaps mindful of the limits of local E-commerce, many merchants use the Web for marketing rather than for completing transactions with customers. Here, businesses like employment agencies, realtors and car dealerships are among the biggest spenders, analysts and executives said. "More and more things in the real estate industry will be done on line, so I'd expect our ad budget to grow on line in the next couple of years," said Stat Geer, regional manager for the Chicago Title Insurance Company, which advertises on the Chicago Digital City site, operated by America Online in conjunction with The Chicago Tribune. Indeed, at least one study shows that local advertising on line is gaining momentum. According to a report last month by Kelsey Group and Constat Inc., the Web has surpassed direct mail as an ad medium for local businesses and is nearly equal to local spending on newspaper advertising. The report said that 17.2 percent of businesses involved in local commerce use the Web for advertising and promotion, versus 15.5 percent for direct mail, 18.7 percent for newspapers and 37.2 percent for Yellow Pages. On-line city guides like Digital City and Citysearch, as well as guides owned by newspapers (including The newyork Times, which publishes the newyork Today site), have until recently attracted advertisers using the same formula as any local media: provide local news and entertainment information, and sell ads surrounding that content. But with the E-commerce bandwagon picking up speed, more local merchants are demanding not only advertising opportunities, but sophisticated Web sites that enable them to sell goods within the city guide. "The bar is a lot higher now," said Charles Conn, chief executive of Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch. "When we used to sell sites in our city guides to merchants, they wanted four or five pages with pictures, maybe a menu if they were a restaurant. Now they want streaming audio, the recipe of the day, and merchants want the ability to transact." Mr. Conn, who said merchants pay between $100 and $700 a month for a site within a Citysearch guide, noted that consumers, too, will increasingly expect local merchants to offer more transaction capabilities. "I think because people have been trained by tools like Amazon and Ebay for buying on line, they'll look not only for fresh information from sites like ours, but transaction tools to help them get things done." That, of course, is the great hope of merchants like Mr. Worley, of Worley Ace Hardware, who pays $200 a month for his site. "As with so many people who are trying E-commerce, this is a large experiment for me," he said. "But I haven't really given this a lot of attention, since I have so much going on running the business. I suppose to do it right you have to do it big. And I haven't done that yet." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Worley Ace Hardware has sold nothing through its Web site, left. But Phil Worley, above left, says he will keep the site. (George Ruhe for The newyork Times)

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
For Zoe Baird, a New Opportunity for Public Service
body: The invitation was "the kind of thing that makes your eyes glaze over," as one attendee put it -- a meeting to discuss the dispensation of Internet addresses. But perhaps because they scented resources or perhaps because the summons came from Zoe Baird, representatives of several nonprofit groups gathered in Washington on Thursday to hear why they should care that the Internet's first governing body was being formed without their input. The gathering marked the beginning of a new crusade for Ms. Baird, President Clinton's onetime nominee for Attorney General, who has served as the president of the Markle Foundation the last year and a half. Though she has long advocated public representation in decisions about technology, Ms. Baird is now starting to act -- and to spend a lot of money in the process. Today, the newyork-based Markle Foundation will announce plans to give away $100 million -- more than half of its $187 million endowment -- over the next three to five years to carve out a place for the public good amid the frenzied commercialization of the Internet. The idea is to make a difference in areas from governmental policy to health care to children's media before it is too late. "We've concluded that this is a critical time to build things that benefit the public into the development of communications media," Ms. Baird said. "The forces that are driving the growth of all this won't do that. We have to consciously attend to making it happen." The move is significant both because of the scope of the spending and the singularity of the goal. Markle plans to give away its assets at least twice as fast as the 5 percent required by law. The average for the nation's foundations is only slightly more than the minimum. "They're eroding their assets, and they're doing it on purpose," said Sara Engelhardt, president of the Foundation Center, a newyork-based group that tracks foundation giving. "Their interest in technology has obviously led them to believe that this is a pivotal moment and spending now is as important as investing and having more money in the future." In another departure from conventional grant-giving, the donations will not be limited to nonprofit groups. Markle's first major commitment is to a joint venture with Oxygen Media, an Internet start-up working to develop women's programming across different media platforms. Markle and Oxygen will spend a combined $8.5 million the next three years to conduct research on the information needs of women. Markle has pledged an additional $1 million to finance programming based on the study's findings. Markle's new mission also reflects a turning point for Ms. Baird, who has kept a relatively low profile since 1993, when the Clinton Administration withdrew her nomination to serve as the nation's first female Attorney General. Ms. Baird faced a storm of criticism over having hired illegal immigrants to take care of her children and her failure to make Social Security payments for them. But she has not been resting. After returning to her job as corporate counsel for Aetna Inc., Ms. Baird spent a year at Yale Law School as a visiting scholar before joining Markle in January 1998. She has served for six years on the President's Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board, and sits on the boards of several nonprofit organizations. Despite all this involvement by Ms. Baird, some associates say they sensed that she was casting about for a more meaningful challenge. Jimmy Carter, who brought Ms. Baird into the White House as his associate counsel and whose Carter Center is now receiving a Markle grant, says he remembers seeing Ms. Baird at the Clinton inaugural gala shortly after her nomination was withdrawn. "She was sober and very disappointed but was determined to find another place to utilize her talents," Mr. Carter said. "I don't think she was ever quite satisfied with being a lawyer that would research land titles and things like that. I think she saw herself doing great things." Perhaps still bearing the scars of that intense public scrutiny, Ms. Baird, 47, was guarded and careful to be accompanied by Markle's public relations specialist in several interviews last week. On a hot afternoon, she wore a black suit and stockings, softened by a pink scarf loosely tied around her neck. She declined to say where she lives in Connecticut or much about her personal life. But once she started to speak about the urgency of the task at hand, it was hard to mistake the light in Ms. Baird's eyes for anything but passion for her cause. The foundation, which was established in 1927 by John Markle and Mary R. Markle, whose families made their fortunes in coal mining and finance, has a broad goal of promoting "the advancement and diffusion of knowledge" and the "general good of mankind." Over the years, its focus has ranged from medical research to the role of mass communications in a democratic society. The decision to dedicate Markle's resources to information technology -- the foundation is perhaps best known for seeding "Sesame Street" in its early days, and has tended to focus on more traditional media grants -- emerged from many months of consultation and research. At a time the Internet industry is almost entirely preoccupied with its own growth and the Clinton Administration has for the most part seen fit to leave well enough alone, "I was really struck by how little public discussion there is in the field," Ms. Baird said. "I think people need to see a way for themselves to be influential and to speak for the public interest, and I hope we can help them find paths to do that." To Stephen M. Case, chief executive of America Online, which is working with Markle for a second year on an effort to provide in-depth election information over the Internet, Ms. Baird's willingness to work with the for-profit sector will be key to determining Markle's effectiveness. "The notion of a private-public partnership is very critical," said Mr. Case, who invited Ms. Baird to speak at his home recently on the subject. "It's clear that Markle got it; they've recognized that the Internet is a social force, and they're figuring out where nonprofits, governments and companies can work together in new ways." Although Ms. Baird's business experience is rooted in bigger, more traditional companies, staff members say she is already beginning to run Markle more like an Internet company, distributing authority in a decentralized fashion among the 20-person staff. Still, it seems some of the attributes that qualified her to be nominated for Attorney General apply to her role as foundation president, too: "Being with her is part cross-examination, part enthusiasm and willingness to think outside the box," said Kim Spencer, executive director of Internews, a Markle grantee. He credits Ms. Baird with pushing his organization to come up with new ways of generating revenue. "But you can always see the lawyer in her." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: As president of the Markle Foundation, Zoe Baird has shifted its focus. (Andrea Mohin/The newyork Times)

title: Times Co. to Sell Services at Digital TV Center
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it would offer to sell the services of its digital operations center, now used by five of the company's eight television stations, to other stations nationwide beginning Jan. 1. The Digital Operating Center is a central master-control room in Norfolk, Va., from which a handful of people can control all of the Times Company's television stations, from Huntsville, Ala., to Des Moines. Elden A. Hale Jr., executive vice president of the Times Company's broadcast group, said the Digital Operating Center had allowed the company to cut its control room staffs by almost 50 percent. That has been made possible by the increasing automation of most functions that occur in a station's master control room. Traditionally, these rooms were where controllers switched cameras and program feeds or inserted commercials and station identification logos at the appropriate time. At most stations now, however, almost all of those functions are handled by computer, so controllers spend most of their time watching for problems. The Digital Operating Center, thought to be the first of its type, holds control facilities for all eight stations, and as few as two people can remotely control all eight -- though more people may be required during particularly intensive programming periods such as live shows, particularly sports events. The local stations also maintain the ability to take back control if they encounter problems or if they want to handle particularly difficult shows themselves, such as the local news. The main impetus for the Times Company project was the national transition to digital television, now under way, Mr. Hale said. Under Government rules, every TV station must begin broadcasting on its second, digital channel under a staggered timetable that ends in May 2003. To do that, most stations are building or planning to build a second control room for the digital channel. Sometime in the next decade or so, the analog channels that have long been in use will be taken off the air. At that time, the stations will need only one control room once again. Under the Times Company's system, both the analog and digital channels of a station can be controlled from the Digital Operating Center. The company has been phasing the system in for its stations since last December, and the remaining three stations will be ready by the end of the year. "The instant success and faster-than-projected assimilation of our own stations into the consolidated Digital Operating Center convinced us" to begin trying to sell the service to other stations, Mr. Hale said. Several other companies have already made inquiries and visited the Norfolk operation, Mr. Hale said, but no deals have been made. Some other station groups have centralized portions of their control operations, but none of these are as comprehensive as the Times Company's system, Mr. Hale said. The Times Company owns television stations in Norfolk, Va.; Memphis; Oklahoma City; Wilkes Barre-Scranton, Pa.; Huntsville, Des Moines; Moline, Ill., and Fort Smith, Ark. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
BUSINESS: DIARY;
Cashing I n on Geography
body: When China.com, the hongkong-based Internet company, went public two weeks ago and saw its market capitalization zoom to nearly $1 billion, eyes lit up at Mail.com in newyork. Mail.com's main business is providing email services, but it also happens to own the rights to a roster of easy-to-remember geographically based Internet domain names, like Asia.com, USA.com, Europe.com and India.com. So the company hired Salomon Smith Barney, the newyork investment bank, to help it find partners to develop them into information-based Web sites. "You've got to start with the domain name," said Gerald Gorman, the chief executive of Mail.com. "We're the only company in the world that has these beachfront properties." Those hot properties, now used only for email addresses, will probably not be sold outright, Mr. Gorman said. Instead, Mail.com wants to use them in joint ventures with Web site developers. "We're looking for a synergistic scenario where these become sites in their own right," he said. He cited as a model the relationships his company has with CNET and a General Electric unit, NBC, and a G.E. affiliate, Snap.com. Mail.com manages their email functions and gets a cut of ad revenue from the sites.   RICHARD TEITELBAUM http://www.nytimes.com

title:
LONG ISLAND JOURNAL;
Live on the Web, Glimpses of East Hampton
body: THIS is the summer of iHamptons.com," declared Steven Gaines. Mr. Gaines, the best-selling author of "Philistines at the Hedgerow: Passion and Property in the Hamptons," is the Hamptons insider of the moment, and although the comparison makes him cringe, the Liz Smith of the rolling dunes. His social chronicle, which came out last summer and was just released in paperback, boils down to, he said, "rich people behaving badly." And now, after taking the multitudes on a good read about them versus us, both now and then, and the shenanigans behind closed gates, Mr. Gaines has planted one video camera on Main Street in East Hampton and pointed another from the back of a friend's mansion at the town's swanky Main Beach, making this the season for all the world to watch just how the crowd east of the Shinnecock Canal actually behaves, live over the Internet. The candid camera setup is part of the Web site Mr. Gaines set up not long ago with Robert Florio, president of the Internet service provider Hamptons Online. Their intent is to virtually capture, brand and sell that beguiling Hamptons cachet without triggering yet another traffic jam. "You don't have to be here to be here," said Mr. Florio, who handles the technical end of the site. Browsers can shop at the local book emporium, Bookhampton, order daisies from Steven Spielberg's and Donna Karan's florist or buy Hamptons furniture from the chi-chi East End interior designer John Rogers. Or just read Mr. Gaines's daily gossip column, perhaps adding their own two cents' worth in a forum for more serious issues, like development, and whether or not the violinist Itzhak Perlman should be allowed to build a music school in a potato field. To hear Mr. Gaines tell it, to peek at the Hamptons through cyberspace instead of in person simply makes sense. "This is a way to promote and help the Hamptons, to bring money into the Hamptons without hurting it anymore," said Mr. Gaines, referring to the loss of open space and the influx of tourists. "Day trippers come out here and they expect to see Kim Basinger and Alec Baldwin walking on the street or Billy Joel in the local bar, and that doesn't happen," he said. Well, almost never. Gwyneth Paltrow, Steven Spielberg and Hugh Grant were all spotted on Hamptons sidewalks this month. "This is still a very closed society where people's social lives are spent in their homes behind the hedgerows," he said. "You very rarely see the celebrities out, maybe at a restaurant or two. Sure, Katie Couric has to go to the drugstore, so you might catch her at Rite Aid. The problem for day trippers is when you get there, there's no there there. There's nothing to do." The Hamptons, Mr. Gaines contended, are not Hollywood East and they are not tourist friendly. Each of the towns has two main streets. Reservations in restaurants are nearly impossible to obtain, and regulations about takeout food are strict. Parking at the beach is prohibited without a parking sticker. And there are hardly any restrooms or public facilities. "It's easier to buy a $12,000 watch than to get a Coca-Cola," he said. "You can tell in Southampton and East Hampton who the day trippers are. They are wearing undershirts and flipflops or athletic gear like bicycle pants and they are eating dripping ice cream cones on the street and they are terribly disappointed." It was quiet the other morning at Mr. Gaines's Wainscott home. The phone, which he said usually rings incessantly, was still. Even his old mutt, Robbie, didn't starting barking until several minutes after a visitor settled onto a leather couch in the high-ceiling living room overlooking the pool. The calm can be deceiving. Mr. Gaines, 51, the son of a Brooklyn schoolteacher and a bookkeeper for a children's clothing manufacturer, started spending most of his time in the Hamptons writing back in 1976. He gave up his Manhattan town house in in 1991, enjoys the small village atmosphere that pervades the Hamptons in winter, and has been plugged into the beguiling behind-the-hedgerow whirl since he co-founded the Hamptons Film Festival seven years ago with Toni Ross, a restaurateur and daughter of the late Time-Warner chief Steve Ross. Mr. Gaines claims his real friends are the caterers, the shopkeepers and the workmen, the year-rounders who hear all the stuff that's going on. "That's the thing about the Hamptons," Mr. Gaines said. "This is really a stage upon which you can invent yourself. You don't have to be a blueblood." He has written 10 books, including biographies of Calvin Klein and Halston. But he is not, Mr. Gaines insisted, on the big-celebrity circuit. "When I get invitations to these very glamorous dinner parties, I dread it," said Mr. Gaines, who nonetheless said he has plans for every night through the end of the year. "I always find an excuse. I'm very much a homebody and not crazy about going to all these events. For example, I didn't go to Puff Daddy's party. But my phone has rung off the hook from people who were there. I have every detail, including how low his pants were hanging." How low? "Low, I understand, in that kind of hip-hop home-boy fashion," he said. Mr. Gaines fell in love with the Hamptons the year he graduated from high school and visited a mother's helper in Westhampton Beach with some friends. Not knowing what to expect, nor the difference between East Hampton and Westhampton, he rented a white dinner jacket for the occasion and brought it along encased in plastic. The accommodations were so bad they slept in the car. The jacket stayed in the trunk. "It seemed like another world, it was so remote," he said. "The houses disappeared, people disappeared. It took a long time to get there back then, there were just fishing bait and tackle shanties and occasional duck farms. I felt that a curtain fell behind me and the horribleness of newyork City was masked, was gone. I felt a tremendous lightness and happiness coming out here." He still does. "Somehow when I go to newyork City, I have to come back here," he said. "It's not until I cross the Shinnecock Canal that I think like, ahhhh, that I kind of sigh." "It's one of the most beautiful places on earth," he said. "The natural beauty of the potato fields and the ocean to me is the equivalent of the Grand Canyon. The first time I saw those flat stretches of potato fields that rush right up to the ocean, it took my breath away in the same way." "The thing is nobody let them develop the North Rim of the Grand Canyon," he said, "but they let them develop the Hamptons to a point where they have almost obliterated the great beauty. Now mostly what's left is just a chic summer resort."  A Recipe Challenge Neither Bobby Flay, chef and owner of Manhattan's Mesa Grill and Bolo restaurants, nor Mario Batali, chef at Babbo and Po in Greenwich Village, has a restaurant in the Hamptons. But this is summer. So last Saturday night, Mr. Flay and Mr. Batali, who are also celebrity chefs on television's Food Network, were displaying their culinary talents in a recipe challenge on a stage at the East Hampton Airport. The cooks had 15 minutes to prepare a meal using surprise ingredients: three lamb chops, hazelnut biscotti, pine nuts, grape tomatoes, chili peppers and tennis racket-shaped pastas, along with pickings from a well-stocked kitchen. On each cooktop, a pot of water was already boiling. "I have two lives," said Mr. Flay, not referring to the city and the Hamptons, where he spends weekends grilling and playing golf. "I have my TV life. But 90 percent of the time, I'm in my restaurant. This is showtime." Mr. Flay, author of the cookbook "Boy Meets Grill," was accompanied by Laurent Gras of the Waldorf Astoria's Peacock Alley and a reporter who specializes in making reservations. The live version of the cable program "Ready . . . Set . . . Cook!" was part of a Global Tastings fund-raiser for East Hampton's cultural center, Guild Hall. More than 1,200 people paid $125 in advance, $150 at the door, to stand in long lines for samples of fire-roasted octopus, malty lagers, prawns, wine, lamb tenderloin, hoisin-marinated pork chops, chocolate-dipped strawberries, Evian water and hand massages. Mr. Flay dumped the pasta into the water. Mr. Gras diced up zucchini and scallions while supervising the reporter, who crushed biscotti and pignoli nuts, then dipped the chops in the mix for Mr. Flay to saute. Meanwhile, Mr. Batali, assisted by Charles Brucculeri, the chef at the Bryant Park Grill, caramelized onions and portobello mushrooms, encrusting their lamb chops with Captain Crunch cereal. While E. Clarke Reilly, an assistant editor from Newsday who likes to cook, was creating biscotti Napoleon, Sara Moulton, executive chef at Gourmet, gave a culinary-challenged reporter a quick lesson in whipping instant pudding. Add raspberries, blackberries, marshmallow fluff, crushed Oreos and whipped cream in a wine goblet for a parfait a la Fischler. The race was a draw. Nobody even tasted the results. Afterward, Mr. Batali said he was heading right back to Manhattan. He avoids the Hamptons in the summer. "It's hot and filled with mean newyorkers," he said. "There are 35,000 people and 6,000 seats. I like to go to restaurants out here, but you can't get reservations." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Steven Gaines, a best-selling author, has set up a Web site that allows an on-line visit to East Hampton. (Gordon M. Grant for The newyork Times)

title: Making Up Beds And Home Pages
body: THE precise number of the nation's bed-and-breakfasts is unknown, although it is often estimated that there may be as many as 25,000 of them. For their owners, often mom-and-pop entrepreneurs, the Internet has come as a godsend. A recent poll by the Professional Association of Innkeepers International (www .paii.org), the biggest professional association of bed-and-breakfasts, found that 22 percent of members' guests in 1998 made their bookings through the Internet, up from 6 percent just two years earlier. "We wouldn't have gotten through the winter without the Internet," said Bill Smollen, the president of the Bed-and-Breakfast Association of Mississippi, who with his wife, Shirley, owns and operates the 1902-08 Stained Glass Manor Oak Hall in Vicksburg. Their Web site (www.vickbnb.com) has averaged about 30 hits, or visits, a day since the beginning of the year, from which they average about one and a half daily bookings. They consider this percentage remarkable, especially since some of the visits are not to book a room, but instead are piggybacked from links devoted primarily to recipes, the Civil War and other topics that lead them to the Stained Glass Manor Web site. About 10 percent of their inquiries are from overseas, and this year they have had guests from, among other places, Switzerland, Australia, Brazil, New Zealand, Germany and hongkong. But for reasons Mr. Smollens has not quite figured out, their Web site received a single day high of 387 hits on Feb. 9 -- followed less than three weeks later by a record low of 19, also for reasons that escape him. Christy and Earl Collins, who for the past year have owned the six-room Village Inn Bed-and-Breakfast (www.villageinnbb.com) in Stone Mountain, Ga., are still amazed at the Internet's power to attract browsers and, eventually, guests. "We're getting over 1,000 hits a month," Mrs. Collins said, "and our occupancy has been going through the roof." The Internet, she added, has changed the business for good. "Before, you had to be listed in the guidebooks, and that took at least two years, and in some you had to pay to be in" she said. "Now you can get onto a Web site and be in business from Day 1." No one knows that better than Sandy Soule of Riverside, Conn., the author of seven books on bed-and-breakfasts, inns and small hotels. "The Internet has not only leveled the playing field and transformed the business," she said with a bittersweet laugh, "it has put an end to many guidebooks -- including mine." Now she is writing The Inn Traveler, a newsletter that will be published by bedand breakfast.com beginning in September (but not at first on the Web site). The Internet's pulling power is evident from coast to coast. In the seven months since the Artists' Inn Bed-and-Breakfast in South Pasadena, Calif., set up a Web site (www.artistsinns.com) to market its nine rooms and suites, bookings have soared. "I'm listed in a bunch of books and I've advertised in newspapers from San Diego to San Francisco, but now people contact me from Australia, France, Germany, England, New Zealand, Japan and all over," said Janet Marangi, who has owned the Artists' Inn for six years. What has especially surprised and elated Mrs. Marangi and others is the growing percentage of business travelers who stay with them during the work week. About 15 percent of the Artists' Inn's guests are business travelers, Mrs. Marangi said, and some weeks almost 25 percent. Mrs. Collins of the Village Inn said that business travelers represent about 10 percent of her guests, and that the percentage had at least doubled in the last six months. Bruce K. Hudson of Ellicott City, Md., a national sales manager for a company that makes microwave components, does his own Web research. While attending an industry show early in June in Atlanta, with some 45,000 others, he spent two nights at the Village Inn Bed-and-Breakfast in nearby Stone Mountain. "It has everything I need, especially peace and quiet," Mr. Hudson said. "Besides, I like to support mom-and-pop operations, because their whole stock in trade is friendliness and service." Of course, not every bed-and-breakfast experience is memorable. When Mark and Carla Frauenfelder of Los Angeles drove from Maine to North Carolina a few years ago, staying at B & B's along the way, they found most of them "wonderful," Mr. Frauenfelder said recently. Yet despite his familiarity with the Internet -- Mr. Frauenfelder writes the monthly "Living on Line" column for Playboy magazine -- one proved disappointing. "I was surprised," he said, "because on the Internet site, it looked more like a two-story farm, and had 'farm' in its name. But instead of an intimate, quiet place it turned out to be a two-story house filled with the Brady Bunch." Because the Web site displayed only line drawings of the property, not photographs that showed the interiors, he said, "we went more by name and location, and wound up making a mistake." These days, Mr. Frauenfelder said he would probably check with the dozen or so bulletin boards and handful of chat rooms devoted to bed-and-breakfasts. And he suggests never booking a B & B on line without first viewing somewhat detailed pictures of each room and, if possible, the grounds. While even detailed photographs can be touched up or out of date, many guests and operators of bed-and-breakfasts say that does not appear to happen often. On the contrary. "You can tell a lot from the little touches you see on the Internet," said Ms. Soule of The Inn Traveler, "and from viewing the pictures, you increase your odds of ending up in the right place. If it's a family trip, for instance, you don't want to stay where there are lots of antiques the children could knock over." Mr. Smollen in Vicksburg offered another reason for studying the pictures on the Internet: "Each B & B has a different personality," he said, "and each room is different." Each of his four rental rooms and the separate carriage house are pictured on the Stained Glass Manor Web site, along with room rates, directions and cancellation policy. Each room in the Artists' Inn in South Pasadena is decorated to resemble the work of Gauguin, Matisse, Degas or another renowned artist. Everyone contacted for this article recommended that prospective guests pick up the telephone after surfing the Internet and talk with the owners or managers of the property that interests them. "You can not only ask things that aren't on the Internet," Mr. Smollen said, "but a lot of times you get a sense just from talking with them if you're likely to enjoy their company." The biggest pitfall for Web surfers is that many sites, much like telephone directories, provide listings but not impartial assessments. The more candid sites acknowledge as much. For example, the well-regarded Bed-and-Breakfast Inns Online (www.bbonline.comreadme.html) in Madison, Tenn., asserts flatly that the home pages, listings, pictures and descriptions on its Web page "are paid advertisements provided by individual innkeepers, innkeepers associations and reservation services" and that the provider"assumes no responsibility for the accuracy of the information" or for "the operation of individual inns listed." Eric Goldreyer, founder and pres ident of bedandbreakfast.com in Golden, Colo., said there was no way to inspect the 27,000 properties worldwide (including fewer than 200 hotels and motels) on his site. But 6 of the site's 17 employees contact each property every six months to make sure that the telephone number, room rates and other information are up to date. And, Mr. Gold reyer said, the site will soon add a forum for guests to list their own recommendations and ratings about places they have stayed. Meanwhile, he said, one way to keep risk to a minimum is to ascertain whether a property belongs to a national, state or local association; such organizations usually inspect properties and monitor standards. (The Michigan association, for example, requires that members have insurance, keep records, provide guest comment cards, and adhere to existing safety and security standards.) These associations have Web sites, easily accessible, that list member establishments, and the sites of individual bed-and-breakfasts often indicate association membership. "Standards have beeen rising nationwide, especially fire and safety standards," said Pat Hardy, the co-executive director (along with Jo Ann M. Bell) of the Professional Association of Innkeepers International. "So now it's also not just whether there's a reading lamp in the room, but whether there are reading lamps on both sides of the bed."  Where to search and click Here are some Web sites with extensive listings of bed-and-breakfasts: Professional Association of Innkeepers International, www.paii.org, is the biggest association of bed-and-breakfasts. title:
The Way We Live Now: 7-25-99: The Ethicist;
I'm Not a Prude, but . . .
body: I am the father of two early-adolescent boys, who are both active Web surfers. I'm not a prude, but I think exposure to the more extreme sexual images available on line is not a good thing at their ages. I could retain a secret list of the Web sites they visit. But is that ethical? Is it equivalent to putting a hidden TV camera in their room (which I would consider a violation of their privacy), or is it an acceptable way for a parent to keep informed and be able to initiate discussion of this tricky topic?- William S. Kessler, Seattle. Your concern for your sons' well-being necessitates neither that you cast them adrift in a sea of disturbing pornography nor that you abandon your respect for their privacy and fill your house with hidden cameras, tiny microphones and cagey men in dark glasses who would make everyone uneasy at the dinner table. There's nothing wrong with being involved with what your kids see on line; it is deception that is unsettling. Just as you probably wouldn't sneak a look at their diaries to learn what they're writing, you shouldn't surreptitiously tap their computer to find out what they're reading. If you intend to retain a list of the sites they visit, tell them. That way, you can discuss those sites with them, just as you might discuss a book that you saw them reading around the house. But especially at this age, your boys may find any parental scrutiny -- even of the most innocuous activities -- embarrassing. The problem is balancing their right to free inquiry with your duty to shield them from truly disturbing images. And here the solution is not a technical fix but the more difficult task of teaching your kids a system of values. Part of that system reserves certain activities --drinking, driving, perusing pornography -- for adults. In any case, just as the boys can hide an ugly and upsetting magazine under the bed, they can browse on-line pornography with a friend's computer. But by creating a situation at home in which conversation is encouraged and privacy is respected, you have a better chance of helping them deal with the rough stuff. I bought airline tickets for a business trip, but at the last minute one of the players offered me a flight in his corporate jet. In the time I spent seated next to him, I wrapped up the deal. But now I have a nontransferable credit for a round-trip flight to Nowheresville, U.S.A., good for one year. I feel weird about billing my employer for the expense, given that I'll probably end up using the ticket for a vacation. Then again, I did have to lay out the cash way in advance, and I'm now constrained by the limitations of this credit. So who pays? Me? Or my employer? -- D.K., newyork City If the ticket is nonrefundable and buying it was a necessity of the job, you should unquestionably be reimbursed. After all, you bought it in good faith, you didn't know it would go unused and you can't return it. Just explain the situation to your boss. If she's smart, she'll be happy to give you the ticket as a reward for your ingenuity in closing that deal. One caution: Such resourcefulness can be taken too far. If, for instance, you'd paid for a hotel room and then spent a night of heretofore undreamed-of ecstasy closing the deal in the room of one of the players, your boss might reimburse you for your expense, but you'd face a whole other set of ethical problems. Do you have ethical queries that you need answered? Send them to ethicist@nytimes.com or The Ethicist, The newyork Times Magazine, 229 West 43d Street, newyork, N.Y. 10036. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Christoph Niemann)
