title: U.P.S. Going Public And Its Employees Hope for Windfall
body: Ever since two Seattle teen-agers started a telephone message service in 1907 that grew to become United Parcel Service of America Inc., the company, now the world's largest package delivery service, has been a rarity in corporate America. It is owned by its employees, and many spend their entire working lives there. The company's top 15 executives all began their careers sorting packages. Even more unusual, for 92 years U.P.S. has resisted the entreaties of investment bankers and remained private. But yesterday, in the latest sign that the siren song of Wall Street is too hard to resist in an age of instant riches and the Internet, U.P.S. said it would sell 10 percent of itself to the public later this year. The stock offering will very likely be one of the biggest in history, raising $3 billion to $5 billion. And in today's overheated stock market, analysts think U.P.S. shares will soar because of the company's link to the Internet -- as a prime deliverer of goods bought on line -- creating a windfall for tens of thousands of the company's managers, employees and retirees. That means that the local U.P.S. deliveryman in his chocolate brown uniform and matching truck could see his net worth soar. "For years that's the thing everybody has been hoping for," said Jason Vines, a driver who was picking up packages yesterday in Manhattan and received the news from the company through its cellular network. "Now it's going to happen." James P. Kelly, the chairman and chief executive of U.P.S., said the company, which estimates that it ships 6 percent of the nation's gross domestic product, had taken care to structure the deal so that it would preserve the company's culture. Though 10 percent of the company will be listed on the newyork Stock Exchange, 99 percent of the voting rights will remain with the current employees and managers. "In designing our plan," Mr. Kelly said, "we've insured that this fundamental element of our success will continue as an essential part of our future." But once its stock begins trading, U.P.S., which is based in Atlanta, will come under the kind of pressure for short-term profits felt by other large corporations. Though in the past it could invest in new technology or expansion in Europe without worrying about the effect on its stock price, that luxury might be lost. "This was an internally fed culture with an unusual sense of purpose," said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the president of the nonprofit Chief Executive Leadership Institute in Atlanta, who worked as a consultant to U.P.S. for 12 years. "There is a hometown flavor to them. It is very meritocratic." The formula has been a success. U.P.S. posted profit of $1.7 billion last year on sales of $24.8 billion, making it larger and more profitable than its rival, Fedex. Its 330,000 employees delivered more than 3 billion packages to 1.6 million customers in more than 200 countries. U.P.S. trucks and planes ply routes in virtually every corner of the world, making it one of the most recognizable brands. Mr. Kelly said that U.P.S. needed to issue stock to the public to maintain its competitiveness against rivals like the FDX Corporation, which owns Fedex; DHL and several increasingly aggressive foreign postal services that are also planning to issue stock soon. As the package delivery service has become global in recent years, U.P.S. has expanded into Europe, Asia and Latin America. It has also moved into the fast-growing logistics business, taking charge of the delivery of all parts and components for large manufacturers. U.P.S. has more than $3 billion in cash and can borrow billions more, but it does not have publicly traded stock to use as a currency for deals. "We think we need this flexibility," Mr. Kelly said, "to provide ourselves with another tool should we decide to do the kind of strategic acquisitions we are talking about." But analysts also said that it was becoming increasingly difficult for U.P.S. to continue to turn its back on the soaring values investors are giving an Internet-related company. Last year, FDX shares soared 47 percent after investors identified it as a so-called Internet play. U.P.S. executives think they have an even better story to tell. They point to a report by Zona Research of San Francisco that concluded that U.P.S. delivers 55 percent of all the goods bought on the Internet. While $80 billion worth of merchandise was bought on line last year, Forrester Research in Boston estimated that the figure will balloon to $3.2 trillion by 2003. That sort of talk should play well to investors when U.P.S. shares begin trading. "Their timing is excellent," said Edward M. Wolfe, an air freight and logistics analyst at Deutsche Bank Alex. Brown in newyork. There is also a strong reservoir of demand for U.P.S. stock from employees, their families and friends. The company now issues private stock to managers as part of their annual compensation and lets employees set aside part of their paychecks to buy shares. The U.P.S. board sets the price of the stock each quarter based on the company's performance and future prospects. But it retains the right to buy back shares when employees retire to reissue them to others. In the last 50 years, the shares have risen in value every quarter except one, in 1997, when they fell 25 cents after the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which represents 202,000 U.P.S. workers, struck the company. Yesterday, Chip Roth, a teamster spokesman, said the union was "analyzing the I.P.O. for its potential impact on employees." Mr. Sonnenfeld said, "U.P.S. family members and friends that have seen the performance of U.P.S. stock have always wished they could buy some." Still, in place of a stock known for stability, they will have shares subject to the wild swings of the overall stock market. Under the plan, U.P.S. will create two types of stock: A shares held by insiders and B shares held by the public. Each A share will have 10 votes compared with one for every B share. But instead of having to sell shares to the company, holders of A shares can convert them to B shares and sell them on the open market. Today its internal stock is priced at $47 a share, giving the company a value of about $26 billion. But most analysts think that figure is extremely conservative, based on the valuations given to FDX and others. Some said it could go as high as $50 billion, which would mean that the company would raise $5 billion. U.P.S. said it would use the cash to buy shares from employees who wish to sell. About 125,000 employees are shareholders. Still, no employee interviewed yesterday said he would sell. "It's a pot of gold for when I retire," said David Arroyo, 32, a driver who has worked at U.P.S. nine years and holds 500 shares. title: Finding the Unexpected on www.ididn'tknowthat.com
body: ONE of the great vacation pleasures is breaking away from the beaten path to find a lesser-known pleasure in an out-of-the-way spot, like coming across a quirky roadside market on a winding Kentucky byway. And one reward for digging your way past the Web's megamalls can be finding sites that tell you what you didn't realize you wanted to know, like the one listing the best roadside markets in Kentucky (www.kyfb.com/roadside.htm). The problem is, as summer wears on, who has time to scout the Internet? So, here's a shortcut, a handful of sites that may spark your interest. National Park Service Trails www.nps.gov/trails/ Some people like nothing better than lumbering into the wilderness on a whim, heading down a trail wherever it may lead. For the rest of us, there is the National Park Service's Web site. It indexes sites for scores of national parks, pointing you to pages on day hikes and backpacking, and giving information on changes in elevation, hiking times and levels of difficulty. A walk to "the Windows" at Arches National Park in Utah, for example, is considered an easy climb. A hike to Bighorn Gorge in Death Valley National Park in California and Nevada is strenuous, requiring scrambling around an eight-foot-high dry fall. Your feet will thank you for knowing the difference.  The Internet Guide to Outlet Shopping www.outletbound.com A vacation just wouldn't be a vacation without the thrill of buying brand names for less. If you are driving on your trip, chances are you will see billboards announcing outlet malls. This guide to outlets, however, does one better: it tells you which outlets are in which states, how many stores are at each location and which offer a free on-line brochure. You can also search by brand name or product.  unitedstates High Points Guide www.americasroof.com Roger Rowlett, a longtime hiker, and some fellow hikers have created a Web site dedicated to high-pointing -- the act of reaching the highest point within a geographic region. The home page offers a colorful map and chart of the highest points in each state, as well as rankings of the most difficult points. Mount McKinley in Alaska, not surprisingly, occupies the top slot for height and difficulty. But who knew that Florida's Britton Hill has the lowest high point (345 feet above sea level), and the least difficult climb? If you prefer to head down, not up, don't miss America's Basement: Guide to America's Lowest Points (www.americasroof.com/lowest.html). Lakes and rivers predominate.  Festival Finder www.festivalfinder.com Cajun zydeco. Reggae and world music. Classical or alternative rock. Whatever your musical tastes, you will probably find a festival to meet your fancy here. There are lists of events for the current month, and you can search by state, festival name and performer. The site indexes more than 1,200 concerts, including Blissfest, an annual weekend bash of ethnic acoustic music in Cross Village, Mich., population 500.  Storm Chaser Homepage www.stormchaser.niu.edu/chaser/chaser2.html "So, you want to be a storm chaser?" this site asks. Don't just jump in a truck and head for the whirling tunnels like the ill-fated amateurs in the movie "Twister." Come to this site and read about the anatomy of a thunderstorm or see the latest videos shot by storm chasers. Weather fanatics can also dip into daily (and sometimes hourly) graphs, satellite images and forecasts from the National Weather Service, the Weather Channel, NASA and more.  Yahoo!'s Golf Course Guide sports.yahoo.com/pga/golfcourses Golf sites abound on the Internet, but if you are looking for a simple list of golf courses by state and town, go to Yahoo! Instead of glossy resort photographs, Yahoo! offers a no-frills, alphabetical list containing the essentials (greens fees, how to get there) as well as data that can help you plan your outing. (Are metal spikes allowed?) The site is linked to Yahoo!'s weather pages, so if you call up a page about a course in Boise, Idaho, the site will deliver a page about the weather there. You will be so prepared that there can be only one excuse for coming in 20 strokes over par: your dog chewed your club handles.  New England Lighthouses, a Virtual Guide www.lighthouse.cc/ Beacons have a way of beckoning. Jeremy D'Entremont, a lighthouse enthusiast who runs a one-man company called Coastlore Productions in East Boston, Mass., has created an on-line guidebook to more than 70 lighthouses in New England, stocked with maps, photographs and historical information. Check out his index of lighthouses in the unitedstates that offer overnight accommodations (www.lighthouse.cc/links/ overnight.html). One lighthouse, in Isle au Haut, Me., is a bed and breakfast.  Road Trip 1999: Baseball Stadiums www.roadtrip99.com Countless baseball fanatics have harbored the fantasy of taking in a game at every Major League Baseball stadium in North America. Some actually do it. Rob, 21, is trying to fulfill the quest this summer, taking a 66-day car trip from San Francisco across the northern unitedstates, down the East Coast and back West. His site, with daily updates, offers information about each stadium, the team, scores and links to Yahoo!'s list of restaurants and hotels in each city. By mid-July, he had traveled 7,350 miles and watched 13 games.  Sacred Site Tourism www.luckymojo.com/sacredtourismlist.html Catherine Yronwode, this site's free-spirit author, defines sacred sites as natural and manmade places "ranging from Mayan ruins to Freemasonic lodges, from Australian Aboriginal bora rings to Neolithic megaliths, and from wayside shrines to the Virgin Mary to formal labyrinth gardens in Europe."  Yesterland, a Theme Park on the Web www.mcs.net/ werner/yester.html No time to travel to a theme park? Travel back in time instead. Werner W. Weiss, a Disneyland aficionado, has devoted Web pages to attractions that have been refurbished in the park or eliminated. Look at the pre-1978 Matterhorn, one of Disneyland's most popular roller coasters, which has undergone face lifts since it opened in 1959. Or step inside the Pirates Arcade Museum, which featured mechanical games in glossy cabinets. In today's Disneyland, the games have been replaced by a gift shop. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Lycos Is Starting an Internet Venture Fund
body: Lycos Inc., the Internet search site, plans to form a $70 million venture-capital fund to invest in start-up Internet companies that may provide content and services to its Web sites. Lycos said today that it would invest $10 million in Lycos Ventures L.P. Other investors include Mellon Ventures Inc. and the Vulcan Ventures firm of the Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen. The fund will focus on companies in electronic commerce, on-line media and the development of Internet technology, content or services. Lycos's Web properties include its search site, on-line phone book WhoWhere and Wired magazine's Wired News site. It has invested in other companies like the on-line investment bank Wit Capital Group Inc. and the on-line bookseller Amazon.com Inc. As it invested, Lycos found that many start-ups could benefit from small investments coupled with access to Lycos's distribution power. "Rather than having to own these companies, we can invest in them, nurture them and add their products to the network as it makes sense," Bo Peabody, vice president for network strategy at Lycos, said. Lycos may not offer distribution services to all the companies in which it invests, Mr. Peabody said. Lycos will also use the fund to locate targets for larger-scale investment. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
A Company Short on Buzz but Long on Results
body: Hoover's Inc. has seen its main business grow 145 percent a year since 1995 and has been around almost a decade. It has little debt and nearly turned a profit in the last quarter. And yet, it's an Internet stock. The company, which sells data on 14,000 public and private business and institutions, priced its shares at $14 apiece last night, at the high end of the expected range, raising more than $40 million in its initial public offering. While the offering did not generate the buzz that many Internet companies have lately, financial analysts say Hoover's may be around long after the highfliers fall back to earth. They note that along with a strong record producing Hoover's Handbook, a staple of libraries, and a CD-ROM, the company has moved aggressively to deliver information over the Internet. When the stock begins trading today, investors will have a chance to determine just how valuable that information is. "The enthusiasm for the stock is not the same tone" as some recent initial offerings, said John Fitzgibbon, a stock analyst at Redherring.com who says he uses Hoover's frequently. Shares of Gadzoox Networks Inc., for example, more than tripled yesterday in their first day of trading. Hoover's sold 3.25 million shares, giving the company a market value of $160 million. That valuation does not count 6.9 million more shares that can be issued through stock plans or warrants. The company, based in Austin, Tex., already had some weighty investors. Among its largest stockholders are Time Warner's Warner Books subsidiary, and a company backed by Michael R. Milken, the former Drexel Burnham Lambert junk-bond chief, which just bought a 9 percent stake for about $7.25 a share. Hoover's now gets more than 80 percent of its revenue from Hoover's Online, its Internet Web site (www.hoovers.com). The company estimated it had 30 million page views by two million different people in the first quarter of the year. Most of those used Hoover's free services. But the company says it has 29,000 individual subscribers and 1,300 more corporate and academic accounts. Prices range from $109.95 a year for individuals to $1,500 to $30,000 for institutions. Hoover's Internet sales soared to $7.7 million in the fiscal year ended March 31, nearly double the level of the previous year. Total sales were $9.2 million in the most recent fiscal year, with the balance coming from CD-ROM's and publications. Though Hoover's posted a $2.2 million net loss for the fiscal year, up from $1.8 million the year before, losses for the two most recent quarters narrowed. Not that valuation comparisons mean much for Internet stocks, but the company's numbers stack up well against those of some competitors. Marketwatch.com, which has a market value of $600 million, had sales of $7 million last year, but a $12.4 million loss. Hoover's plans to use $10 million from the offering for marketing purposes. The remaining $30 million will be used to expand its on-line products and for general corporate purposes. The marketing and on-line expenses will cause operating losses and negative cash flow "for the foreseeable future," the company said. Ken Fleming, an analyst with Renaissance Capital, a money manager in Greenwich, Conn., likes the company but notes that it will have to fight to get the attention of institutional buyers. "Lots of Web companies are coming public and competing for attention with other Web start-ups," Mr. Fleming said. "That's been the main concern about Internet I.P.O.'s; there are a lot of them, potentially too many." Despite the company's warnings about future losses, Hoover's would have turned a profit in the quarter ended in March if it had not expensed certain noncash stock compensation. The marketing campaign "more than likely means losses for the next few quarters," Mr. Fleming said. Knowledge Universe, whose primary investors include Mr. Milken; his brother, Lowell, and the Oracle Corporation's chief executive, Lawrence Ellison, has agreed to spend $2 million on Hoover's services along with taking a stake in the company. Geoffrey Moore, a senior vice president at Knowledge Universe, said, "We don't make short-term investments." Warner Books owns 22 percent of Hoover's, while Media General owns 19.7 percent. Directors and executives hold 11.1 percent. Insiders are generally prohibited by the lead underwriters, J. P. Morgan and Lehman Brothers, from selling their shares for 150 days. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: "On-Line Dependent" Hoover's gets much of it's revenue from Hoover's Online. title: There's Still Hope for Last-Minute Planners
body: UNEXPECTEDLY, you find that you can get away for a week or so in late summer or in early fall. But so late in the season, where can you go and what's the best way to get there? Where can you find transportation and rooms at reasonable prices and places that haven't nearly shut down because of foul weather or because they're not popular at that time of year? Ask a travel agent? That can be fruitful if you know one who is familiar with your tastes and is an expert on the places and activities that interest you. For example, if you're a wealthy outdoors-oriented client of Ray Kane, who runs Pisa Brothers Travel Service in newyork, he might send you skiing in Chile or fishing in a remote Alaskan bay. For a cost-conscious couple who are Francophiles, he suggests Paris in September, when there are wonderful values in air-hotel packages. Kay Brylawski of Flora Tours in Jenkintown, Pa., suggests that beach enthusiasts visit Aruba, which generally escapes the hurricane season that plagues other Caribbean isles. For fall foliage, she says popular tours often have late cancellations and smaller bus companies, operating from larger cities and selling through travel agents, often have last-minute room. In the West, Myrna Ross of World Travel Partners in Phoenix lists Hawaii, Disneyland (near Los Angeles) and Catalina Island off the Southern California coast among her choices. "You can fly from Phoenix to Los Angeles right now for $88 round trip," she said. "There's always somebody at Disneyland in September, although it's less crowded than in summer. And Catalina is very relaxing, with a broad range of hotels but no cars and no crime." These days, more vacationers are turning to cyberspace to do their own research if not complete travel planning. A good starting point on the Internet is the Great Outdoor Vacation Pages (www.gorp.com), where you can search by activity (camping, fishing), location (by state or country) or type of attraction (scenic drive, forest, beach, archeological site). Gorp will help plan a solo vacation as well as a group activity. The Internet abounds in sites that sell vacation packages. They brim with so-called hot deals, some enticing. Be aware, though, that these are probably distress merchandise -- tours that have failed to sell. Typically, such sites embrace only tour companies that pay to be listed. One that does better is the Online Vacation Mall (www.onlinevacationmall.com), which features packages from 13 major mass-market tour companies. Another exception is Vacation Packager (www. vacpac.com). It is run by the Official Tour Directory, the travel industry's most comprehensive listing of tour companies, covering more than 800 destinations and 300 vacation interests and activities. The site has links to state tourist offices and lists of toll-free telephone numbers of airlines, hotel chains, auto-rental companies and the like. Particularly useful for last-minute choices is TravelHUB (www.travelhub.com), a consolidated site for the package offerings of several hundred specialized travel agencies. An extensive directory of companies specializing in cruises can be found at dir.yahoo.com/Business-and-Economy/Companies/Travel/Cruises. For the Caribbean, late summer and fall are bargain times. Yes, it is hurricane season, but, Liane Beck of The Travel Company's Miami office noted: "The captain doesn't want to go through a hurricane any more than you do, and he's going to use his sophisticated navigational equipment to circumvent it." There are also late-summer deals for Alaska, she said. Sometimes, age can be a factor in planning a trip, at either end of the spectrum. Family Travel Times, a 15-year-old bimonthly newsletter devoted to travel with children, is developing www.familytraveltimes.com. The accent is on air-land packages, cruises and hotel specials. The catch: the best material is available only to newsletter subscribers for $39 a year. Probably the broadest selection of learning vacations for older travelers is from Elderhostel, the Boston-based nonprofit organization with one- and two-week residential study programs around the world. Many programs fill up quickly months ahead, but others always have vacancies. The problem for last-minute decision-makers is to find out which ones. One way is to call Elderhostel toll-free at (877) 426-8056. If you are specific -- asking, for example, about hiking in Montana or arts and crafts in West Virginia -- you should find vacancies. Obtain suggestions from the Web site, www.elderhostel.org, where you can do your booking. Once you have decided where you want to go, the next issue is getting there. If you are traveling by air, your search for the lowest fare can be trying. Many Web sites profess to help, sharing a small selection of data bases. But few can provide senior fares or accommodate the discount and companion-flies-free coupons that stuff your mail. Sometimes prices differ among sites, because one includes taxes in its fare quotations and another does not. Among the Web sites that can help is www.smarterliving.com, which will scan the Internet for the weekly specials of 20 airlines and email you free-of-charge about those originating in the cities of your choice. It also scans for Internet-only specials of car-rental companies and hotels. The new Farebeater feature at the discount site www.1travel.com promises to find the lowest fare on the days and routes you plan to fly. This can be useful for bookings too late to meet advance-purchase requirements for most discounts. For rental cars, the smartest advice for do-it-yourselfers is to phone your travel agent or the car company. Then you can compare, with a real person, the many discounts, free days and upgrades for which you may be eligible through club memberships or coupons. In popular areas at peak season, last-minute rooms can be hard to find. It is often easiest to look at weekend or weeklong packages that offer rooms alone, rooms plus meals or rooms, meals and transportation from and to home. If your destination is a large city in North America or Europe, a hotel consolidator, a company that contracts for large blocks of hotel rooms, can probably assist. It may not offer discounts at tight times, but it will have rooms at hotels that are otherwise sold out. You could try the Hotel Reservations Network (www.hoteldiscounts.com or, by phone, 800-715-7666); Quikbook (www.quikbook.com or 800-789-9887) or Travelscape.com (www.travelscape.com or 888-335-0101). When asked about availability in newyork for three days, Hotel Reservations Network produced 51 choices in Manhattan and five in the suburbs, from the modest to the Waldorf-Astoria. For smaller cities or regions, the local convention and visitors' bureau or chamber of commerce may be able to direct you to accommodations at popular times. You'll find listings and contact at dir.yahoo.com/Recreation/Travel/Convention-and-Visitors-Bureaus. Or you can, of course, try a hotel Web site, a toll-free phone number or a travel agency in person, by phone or on line. It may take digging and time, however, to find the best deal for when you want to go. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: If you're looking for winter in summer, there's skiing in the Chilean resort of Portillo. (Randy O'Rourke/The Stock Market); Convenient for Westerners on holiday, Catalina Island, off the coast of Southern California, has a broad range of hotels and no cars. (Michele Burgess/The Stock Market)

title: Microsoft Selling City Guides to Ticketmaster for $240 Million
body: The Microsoft Corporation agreed yesterday to sell its Sidewalk series of Internet city guides to a rival, Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch, in a stock deal worth $240 million. Microsoft confirmed that the deal, news of which had emerged during the weekend, would give it a 9 percent stake in Ticketmaster with the option to increase that eventually to 13 percent. Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch, which is controlled by USA Networks, will fold the Sidewalk sites into its network of Citysearch sites. As it retreats from the city-guide business, Microsoft will retain two components of Sidewalk -- its buying guides and searchable business directories -- and fold them into a new local service on its MSN network. Ticketmaster Online will provide much of the content for that as-yet-unnamed MSN service, including ticketing, personal dating services and arts and entertainment reviews, company officials said. Microsoft will also feature Ticketmaster's ticket-selling operation throughout the MSN network and on its WebTV service. "In one fell swoop, Citysearch got rid of a rival and gained a distribution partner," said Lisa Allen, an analyst with Forrester Research, an Internet consulting firm. "It gives Citysearch an immediate presence in some big markets, and it gives Microsoft a graceful exit from its city-guide strategy." Ticketmaster Online's chief executive, Charles Conn, said that the cross-marketing agreement included no restrictions, allowing Citysearch to continue providing content to MSN's rivals. Sidewalk and the Citysearch service, which both offer on-line information about local entertainment, news and shopping in dozens of cities, have been rivals since Sidewalk opened its first site in early 1997, months after Citysearch started its service. Microsoft initially hired experienced journalists to produce a kind of on-line magazine and event guide. But the company shifted Sidewalk from that emphasis as an anticipated boom in advertising from restaurants and theaters failed to materialize. Instead, it veered more toward electronic commerce and product information. Citysearch, though, has cashed in on arts and entertainment content by selling tickets and offering a dating section and local auctions. The deal, which is expected to close in the fall, will allow Citysearch to more than double the number of city sites it runs, from 33 to 77 worldwide. Citysearch, now the third-most- popular city guide network as measured by Media Metrix, a Internet research firm, would become the largest, attracting an estimated 7 million monthly visitors. Citysearch would reach nearly 11 percent of Internet users in the unitedstates each month. The Digital Cities service of America Online would remain in second place among city guides, with a 6.3 percent reach. newyork Today, owned by The newyork Times Company, competes with Sidewalk and Citysearch in the newyork market. Microsoft rarely sells businesses; moreover, the Sidewalk sale represents another step in the evolution of the company's Internet strategy away from entertainment and information. By selling Sidewalk, the company sheds an unprofitable division, while keeping components that bolster its inventory of E-commerce offerings. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Not All Hit It Rich in the Internet Gold Rush
body: As Barnesandnoble.com was preparing to go public in April, employees talked giddily about their future wealth. Having accepted stock options as a big chunk of their compensation -- a common practice among Internet ventures -- many of them dreamed that their shares would mimic those of companies like Theglobe.com, whose stock shot up 500 percent on the first day of trading. People were walking around with calculators trying to estimate what they would be worth and discussing plans to repay student loans or buy new apartments, one Barnesandnoble.com insider said. But after an early jump, the venture's stock actually dove beneath its initial offering price. Within a month of going public, half a dozen or so disillusioned employees had tendered their resignations. The stock has since bounced slightly above its initial price. Since the start of 1999, many an enterprising soul has founded an Internet company, offered stock, and created a fortune, sometimes achieving a billion-dollar stock market valuation seemingly overnight. As more than one cultural commentator has noted, envy is rife. Everyone from new college graduates to established professionals like Lou Dobbs, the CNN financial journalist who quit to run Space.com, seems to be hurrying to get a piece of the action. But like any gold rush, this one has a lot of seekers who never hit the mother lode. While statistics are not available for Web entrepreneurs who fail, the venture capitalists that finance such Internet start-up companies have a rule of thumb. For every 10 ventures that receive financing -- and there are plenty that do not -- 2 will be stock market successes, which means spectacular profits for early investors; 3 will be sold to other concerns, which translates into more modest profits, and the rest will fail. That means a lot of Internet entrepreneurs, their early investors and their employees end up disappointed. For Internet ventures that get far enough for stock offerings, the odds of making money are much better. Yet even those may not be able to sustain high prices long enough for people with options to cash out. Company officers are not allowed to sell their shares for several months after the offering, and stock options granted employees may not vest for years even if they can be exercised below current market price. Right now the market for Web stocks is sizzling. Of the 126 initial public offerings of Internet stocks priced this year, 73 are trading above the price they closed on their first day of trading, according to CommScan, a market research company in newyork. And after 30 days the stocks had gained an average of 126 percent. Still, 53 of the offerings have failed to live up to their fabulous first-day billings and 17 are below the initial offering price. Not getting really, really rich should not be news, but during these heady times it is, in fact, a violation of expectations. Clay Shirky, a professor of new media at Hunter College who admits to occasional bouts of jealousy about the new riches himself, argues that people both inside and outside the industry have developed a distorted view of how easy it is to get wealthy. Mr. Shirky, who, by his own admission, spends numerous hours talking to industry colleagues about the newest millionaires, said, "The perception that about one person in six gets lucky is a fiction." It cannot be more than one in a thousand of the many people who have worked for Web ventures, he said. For those left behind, even if they have achieved modest success, it can mean bitterness. What makes it even harder to take is the apparent randomness of success. After all, nearly all Internet companies are losing money. Paul Cohen started a Web site called Biztravel.com, for business people who are always on the road. Thinking he needed big backers and professional management to make the site into a booming business, in 1996 Mr. Cohen sold a majority stake for "less than a million" to a consortium that included the News Corporation, Intel, Informix, and Sir Bernard Ashley of Laura Ashley. The group then invested $20 million more, but in Mr. Cohen's view, it was not focused on exactly which market it was aiming at. The company has been through two chief executives since the acquisition and now the position is vacant. A Biztravel spokeswoman, Mimi Bloom, confirmed that "our investors are very open to the possibility of a sale," which is just what agitates Mr. Cohen. "The majority of the investors are going to lose their stake," predicted Mr. Cohen, who does not think the purchase price will equal their investments. "It could have been an I.P.O., a big one," he wistfully observes. Perhaps the new windfall has been toughest on the industry's pioneers, who simply arrived too soon. Howard Rheingold founded some of the Internet's best-known and most highly regarded ventures over the last two decades, including Electric Minds, an Internet meeting place, which Time magazine named one of the Top 10 Web sites in 1996. But all his businesses have since failed, and Mr. Rheingold, though comfortable, is hardly swimming in Internet money. "I've had to meditate on this a lot," he admitted. Not everyone is disconsolate, of course, but handling real-world bumps after harboring Trump-sized ambitions can be humbling. Juno Online Services Inc., a Web access and email service, went public at the end of May at $13 a share, and its stock almost immediately fell. The price went as low as $8.875 before rumors of a merger sent it to the mid-$20's, where it has stayed. "It is human nature to feel better when fortunes are doing better than poorly," concedes its president, Charles Ardai, who did not return calls until his stock was past the offering price. "But we make sure to remind people it is a volatile industry." One of the hardest lessons for would-be Midases to absorb has been the incredible arbitrariness of the stock market. These days, starry-eyed start-up owners are also discovering that some of the same forces that created blow-out Internet offerings, namely the good will of the market and day traders, can be very fickle indeed. If the market suddenly goes cold and a company has already set a date for going public, there is little it can do but pray. "Timing is everything," said David Cowan, a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, a Silicon Valley venture-capital firm. Mr. Cowan, who has backed some of the Internet's most successful sites, including Etoys, nevertheless recently watched as Flycast, an on-line advertising firm that he helped finance, got off to a disappointing start. "It is absolutely the case that an I.P.O.'s success has a lot more to do with the I.P.O. market than with the fundamentals of the business," he said. And when the market goes sour, even the most impressive gain can fade a bit. Two months ago, Dave Kansas, editor of Thestreet.com, was the talk of the Internet world. When Thestreet.com, in which The newyork Times Company has invested, went public in May, its price quickly surged from $18 to $60. Mr. Kansas found himself the subject of numerous articles that were amazed that a mere journalist could suddenly be worth as much as $9 million. As a company officer, however, Mr. Kansas is prohibited from cashing out until November. In the meantime, he has watched the value of his stock drop by half. "I joke with friends, 'Hey, I lost a million bucks last week, what did you do?' " Mr. Kansas can joke, of course, because he is still, on paper, worth millions, but for lower-level employees a leaking stock balloon can undermine dreams. Managers who count on stock as a motivator have had to learn to punt. Todd Krizelman, the 25-year-old co-chief executive and co-founder of Theglobe.com, watched his company's stock rocket from its offering price of $9 to almost $49 and then settle back to the high teens. On paper he is worth many millions, but his employees are working on much smaller paper gains. "It was great euphoria when we were going public; the fact that it had turned us around so quickly has been a challenge," he said. Mr. Krizelman says he does not want employees to be like day traders, checking the stock price 40 to 50 times a day. "Ninety-five percent of our employees have stock options," said Mr. Krizelman, who sold 5 percent of his holdings in the second quarter. "We tell them it is the right bet in the long run." Marie Toulantis, the chief financial officer for Barnesandnoble.com, also argues that most of her employees are too smart to focus on today's stock price. "I don't think it was anyone's major reason for leaving," she said of the staff departures. "Options can take four years to vest; it is not like cash today." Another Internet truism that entrepreneurs are coming to terms with is that even good ideas with lots of backing do not always flower into fortunes. Web Flow was one of the first software companies to offer "multiplatform" applications -- programs compatible with numerous computer types and operating systems -- making it an incredibly promising company in 1995. Bob Arasmith, its vice president for engineering, remembers that venture capitalists were vying to back them. "It was no effort to get millions," he said. The company raised $4 million in December 1995 and $10 million more six months later. But the marketplace did not take to the concept as quickly as the venture firms. By the spring of 1998, the company was out of business, and the board sold it back to its software developers for pennies on the dollar. Today, Mr. Arasmith is president of a company that makes a similar product and seems circumspect about the future. "We hope to be profitable, but I don't imagine that we will sell out for $100 million," he said, "and we don't walk around looking at Ferrari dealerships like we used to." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Todd Krizelman, 25, the co-chief executive and co-founder of Theglobe.com, is worth millions. title:
BOOKS OF THE TIMES;
Microsoft Capitalism As Mirror Of America
body: THE PLOT TO GET BILL GATES An Irreverent Investigation of the World's Richest Man . . . and the People Who Hate Him By Gary Rivlin 360 pages. Times Books. $25. It's safe to say that few among the public have ever heard of Tim Berners-Lee and that few newspapers and magazines have hailed him as a visionary. But Mr. Berners-Lee, a physicist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, created the World Wide Web. He did it to enable himself and his friends to share their research, not to make money, and that is just the point of "The Plot to Get Bill Gates," a spirited new book by Gary Rivlin. Mr. Rivlin has written an intimate history of the do-or-die competition that reigns in the lucrative, high-stakes world of computer technology, a history that centers on the amazing success of Mr. Gates and Microsoft, which he started with Paul Allen and has guided to fabulous wealth. Mr. Gates has been written about as much as any contemporary figure, and Mr. Rivlin covers some well-trodden ground. But he also casts a light not just on Mr. Gates but on the world that loves him and hates him and that has made him a celebrity even as it has essentially ignored people like Mr. Berners-Lee. "Today, the science and tech world's stars are entrepreneurs, fabulously well-to-do titans honored with sweet-smelling profiles everywhere from People to The newyorker," Mr. Rivlin writes. "Nowadays, it's as if a technical breakthrough isn't a breakthrough, at least in the realm of the popular press, until someone figures out how to shrink-wrap the idea and make truckloads of money off it." It is well known that Mr. Gates has made truckloads of money; his wealth has an almost Homeric quality. In 1997, when his net worth was one-third what it is today, his income amounted to $22,000 a minute. Mr. Rivlin tells the often unsavory story of how Mr. Gates acquired that money: generally not by producing a better product but by imitating his rivals' products and being better than they were at marketing and then destroying them in the ensuing competition. Mr. Rivlin writes some graphic passages about Mr. Gates as a kind of corporate predator, and his descriptions of the cult of Bill Gates that prevails at Microsoft have an anthropological ring. But at the heart of this narrative is the dark side of fabulous success. It is the fabulous envy that that success generates, the cult of hatred that Mr. Rivlin argues is behind the scheming and plotting to "get" Mr. Gates, scheming and plotting that, in Mr. Rivlin's description, have united Mr. Gates's main competitors with the unitedstates and other governments in what has now become a well publicized antitrust case. In other words, on the moral plain "The Plot to Get Bill Gates" is a complex tale, although it is handled surely by Mr. Rivlin, a reporter at Upside magazine and the author of two previous nonfiction books. If you want to dislike Mr. Gates, Mr. Rivlin gives you plenty of reasons to do so. But his ultimate point of view is that Mr. Gates has only been more conspicuously successful than almost all others in a cutthroat capitalist game that is as American as robber barons and price fixing. The very captains of industry who have become obsessed with toppling Mr. Gates from his pedestal, Mr. Rivlin shows, have done unto others more or less as Mr. Gates has done unto them. Mr. Rivlin's book in this sense is a kind of moral portrait of America today. We are a country that worships the entrepreneurial killer instinct even as it makes the collective flesh crawl. "Basically, all the big companies, all the companies that have won, are run by bloodthirsty killers," Mitchell Kertzman, the president of Sybase, a Silicon Valley software company, told Mr. Rivlin. But Mr. Rivlin's message goes further than that. "Even those who can't stand Microsoft's business practices and find its gluttonous eating habits revolting might wish they had invested $10,000 in Microsoft stock in 1986," he writes. If you had done so and held on to it, you'd have a holding worth more than $4.5 million now. Mr. Rivlin maintains his hard-headed point of view throughout his portrait of American capitalism at its most raw and rampant, but the argument does have some bugs in it. The implication is that the Government's antitrust suit against Microsoft stems more from a kind of generalized envy of Mr. Gates than from the law, but he gives rather short shrift to the legal case. Mr. Rivlin also asks whether Microsoft has really behaved differently from other corporate giants in trying to squeeze out the competition. He gives a couple of examples of other contemporary companies that have behaved ruthlessly toward their competitors, including rather small and seemingly harmless competitors; but his argument here is thin and far from authoritative. Mr. Rivlin sometimes seems caught uncertainly between two visions of the Gates phenomenon.  Mostly he seems to agree with Nathan Myhrvold, Microsoft's chief technology officer, who invented what he called Captain Ahab's Club. He holds that Mr. Gates has been turned by jealous competitors into a kind of Great White Whale, mercilessly hunted by demented Captain Ahabs. At other times Mr. Rivlin describes a kind of ruthlessness on Mr. Gates's part, an impulse to annihilate competitors, that subverts Mr. Myhrvold's comparison. Among the conclusions one draws from this book is that Mr. Gates defeated his business adversaries even though his products, like the cumbersome, crash-prone Windows operating system, were not as good as theirs. But throughout, Mr. Rivlin lays out all the information, not only about Mr. Gates and Microsoft but also about various other larger-than-life figures who inhabit the ultra-rich, ultra-ambitious world of the computer business. His description of the hate-Gates industry and his intimate glimpses into the personalities and practices of Silicon Valley are bright and readable pieces of urban sociology. Mr. Rivlin, in other words, has performed the not inconsiderable task of taking on an already overworked subject and saying something new not only about it but about what it reveals about the rest of us. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Gary Rivlin (Chris Duffey/Times Books)

title: Broadcom to Buy Hothaus For $280 Million in Stock
body: The Broadcom Corporation, a leading maker of high-speed communications semiconductors, agreed today to buy Hothaus Technologies Inc. for $280 million in stock, enhancing its position in the emerging market for phone calls using Internet technology. Broadcom will issue two million of its Class B shares for Hothaus, a closely held developer of software that enables communications over broad band networks. The transaction is expected to close in two months and begin contributing to Broadcom's earnings within 18 months. Broadcom, which is based in Irvine, said it would combine Hothaus software with its semiconductor designs to provide lower-cost transmission of voice and video over broadband networks, including cable-television systems. Cable operators, including the AT&T Corporation, are beginning to offer phone service over their cable lines in the hope of getting a piece of the $100 billion unitedstates local phone market. "It enhances Broadcom's position," said Patti Reali, a Data Quest Inc. analyst. "This is a long-term move to prepare for what is going to happen." Hothaus, which is based in Vancouver, British Columbia, specializes in so-called "digital signal processing" software used in Internet appliances, servers and phone and cable modems, many of which use Broadcom chips. Hothaus software handles such tasks as compressing voice signals, dividing those signals into packets and allowing the packets to pass over the Internet. Broadband hopes to take some of the software functions and include them into chips to offer customers a complete, low-cost system that will help speed deployment of Internet phone and other broadband services. "This is one of the most strategic acquisitions in the history of the company," said Henry Nicholas 3d, Broadcom president and chief executive. Hothaus's 70 employees will become part of Broadcom's cable business unit, and Ross Mitchell, the president and chief executive of Hothaus, will remain with the company. Broadcom will take an as-yet-announced charge in its fiscal third quarter to cover acquisition-related expenses. The acquisition is Broadcom's fourth this year, and like the others uses stock to add closely held companies. Broadcom's stock price has been among the best performers in the sector, rising 271 percent in the last 12 months. The earlier purchases involved issuing 6.36 million shares worth roughly $611.3 million when the transactions closed. Broadcom, which rose $1.3125, to $139.8125 on Friday, reports its earnings on Wednesday. http://www.nytimes.com

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Broadcom Plans to Acquire Hothaus for $280 Million Broadcom, a leading maker of high-speed communications semiconductors, has agreed to buy Hothaus Technologies for $280 million in stock. Broadcom will issue two million of its Class B shares for Hothaus, a closely held developer of software that enables communications over broadband networks. The acquisition will enhance Broadcom's position in the emerging market for phone calls using Internet technology.  Page C2. U S West Agrees to Qwest Merger The takeover battle for U S West and Frontier ended in a compromise Sunday as U S West accepted an unsolicited merger offer from Qwest Communications International and Global Crossing said it would stay with its merger partner Frontier.  The Metro Section.
