title:
JERSEY FOOTLIGHTS;
Check Your Tickets, or the Web
body: New Jersey theatergoers with access to the Internet have little excuse to be late at curtain time. Web sites of individual companies like Crossroads Theater (www.crossroadstheatre.com) and Paper Mill Playhouse (www.PaperMill.org) provide all the needed details, like what, when and how much. But web surfers may get a more comprehensive picture by entering the home pages of the New Jersey Theater Group (www.nj.com/njtheatre/) or www.NJTheater.com. The New Jersey Theater Group site, opened in 1996, provides schedules and descriptions of plays, directions to theaters and ticket prices. For actors, there is a list of scheduled auditions. The other site, www.NJTheater.com, was opened in 1997 by James M. Curran, a computer programmer and analyst. His site does not provide ticket information but lists all theaters in the state, not just the Theater Group's 20 members. It also provides cast lists and, in some cases, actors' biographies and photographs. Unlike most sites of its nature, it carries no advertisements and was not designed to make money. As Mr. Curran, who pays the few costs of maintaining it, explains, he started the site for three reasons: "to help the smaller theater companies; so I would know what's playing and, um, to meet actresses."   MATT MURO http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MUSIC;
The MP3 Revolution: Getting With It
body: JUST a year ago, writing an article about MP3 meant going into elaborate detail in defining the technology. At that time, the term -- shorthand for the 1992 formula used to compress audio into manageable, easy-to-share computer files -- had been mentioned in only four articles in this newspaper; since then, it has been mentioned in more than 85, becoming a part of the entertainment vocabulary almost as quickly as the name Lewinsky became part of the political one. But in the many media reports about the record industry's crackdown on the proliferation of illicit MP3's, the more copyright-friendly alternatives being developed behind closed doors and the many trumpeted agreements between recording labels, technology companies and Internet start-ups, what has been consistently overlooked -- even in the new MP3 issue of Wired magazine -- is the message of the medium. Not in the future, but now: most of the recent controversy about on-line music has been over how it is going to change the experience of selling and purchasing music, but much more interesting is the question of how it is changing our experience of listening to and handling the music. Listening to music on the Internet is not simply a novel alternative to CD players or a way to use the computer as a separate but equal stereo system. Nor is it an opportunity to level the playing field -- as utopians like to dream -- and allow all musicians, great and small, access to all listeners mainstream and marginal. It is a key to unlocking the restrictions that all audio storage media before them have posed to musicians and fans. The CD was a medium similar enough to a record that one could still call it an album without being corrected. But with the Internet, the idea of the album is dead. Nonetheless, the CD did wreak its own changes, and not just in the acoustic differences between analog and digital sound. Making an album no longer meant coming up with 45 minutes of music, conceptualized into two sets of five or so songs, each side self-sufficient enough to stand on its own. Instead, it meant coming up with 60 to 70-something minutes of songs, arranging them in a long ebb and flow and then maybe throwing on a few leftover scraps as bonuses at the end. Creating memorable artwork was no longer done in the painterly two-dimensional space of an album cover or a gatefold sleeve, but in the sculptural three-dimensional package and the choice of materials used. And listening was a completely new experience: no longer were we beholden to the flipping of sides every 22 minutes, but we could put five or a hundred CD's into a player and shuffle and rearrange the track order -- or just hit random and let the technology decide. As a musical format, the Internet is a much cooler medium. It enables users to have multiple sound systems, to watch visual displays synchronized to the music, to talk to other people listening to the same Internet radio station, to make compilations of favorite songs with a few mouse clicks, to email a song to a disk jockey to play, and to put a CD into a computer and, with the click of a button, access digital liner notes. The list could go on and on, and this is only the beginning of the medium's evolution. With those who originally created much of these capabilities falling prey to new industry regulations, lawsuits and takeovers, it may also be the medium's creative summit as well. With faster and better-sounding alternatives already available or in development, there is little doubt that MP3 -- developed by a multinational committee as an open standard free to anyone -- is a transitional format. But it is MP3 that has the versatility and added functions that make it more forward-looking than its more proprietary corporate rivals developed by Real Networks, Liquid Audio, Microsoft, AT&T and Lucent. Bypassing the financial implications, the biggest change on-line music distribution brings to those who make music is that it frees them from the constraints of a platter, disk or cassette that holds limited information and costs money and time to manufacture and ship. A new studio recording could be a 3-minute song or a 24-hour music cycle intended to accompany the listener throughout an entire day. The decisions made by bands in the on-line world no longer involve sequencing 70 minutes of songs, but determining at what rate new music should be released to fans and in what amount. This scenario is slightly futuristic, because the medium of the Internet won't change the message of the music until it becomes the dominant form of distributing music (or at least a new market on par with record stores). For now we will concentrate on the present, on the hunter-gatherer experience of using the Internet and computer as record store, record album and stereo. TO do this, it's best to walk you through the process. So, if you are reading this and you own a PC with a halfway decent Internet connection, follow the instructions below and within an hour or two you will have a completely free state-of-the-art Internet stereo system that might explain what an MP3 player's got that a CD player doesn't. To begin with, you need software to play MP3's on your PC. I'd suggest downloading two software players, Winamp (www.winamp.com) and Sonique (www.sonique.com). The Winamp is the most commonly used MP3 player, and many of the most interesting free MP3 programs on the Internet are only compatible with Winamp; Sonique is more self-contained, easier to operate and beautifully designed in adjustable sizes. Similar to a stereo, in addition to playing songs, both offer a wide-band graphic equalizer, the shuffle capabilities of a CD player, VU meters and spectrum analyzers, volume and balance controls, and, in the case of Sonique, pitch control so that you can change the speed of the song being played. Next, you'll want to download what are called skins and plug-ins, most of them created not by entrepreneurs but by random computer users as young as 11 years old. Skins are faceplates that cover your MP3 player like masks, creating a visual appearance of your choice. There are hundreds to choose from, and you can switch between them as often as you want: you can have a Star Wars MP3 player, a Britney Spears one, a wooden-looking stereo, a high-tech interface, or you can scan your favorite image, design a skin yourself and email it to Winamp or Sonique for other MP3 users to download. Plug-ins are more exciting supplemental programs, ways to personalize and soup up your MP3 player. The best of these allow you to operate your Winamp with a remote control, add effects like reverb to the music, search for and display song lyrics as you listen, or match the beats on two different MP3 files and mix them together like a D.J. Then there are the visual plug-ins, the Internet equivalent of cover art. These are programs in which waves, fractals, wallpaper patterns, animated characters and all kinds of images dance and morph on your computer screen in response to the rhythm, amplitude and frequencies of a song as it's being played. Once you have a fully loaded MP3 player brimming with skins and plug-ins, you'll need music. A number of search engines capable of scouring the Web for MP3 files have been built. These include mp3.lycos.com, www.audiofind.com, www.audioseek.com or the mega-search engine www.palavista.com, which tend not to differentiate between legitimate sites and fly-by-night pirates and thus often lead to dead ends. For beginners, it's better to start at www.scour.net or the newer www.listen.com, both of which have limited but very reliable archives of legal music. If you can't find what you're looking for at any of these sites, you can always go to the newsgroup alt.binaries.sounds.mp3.requests and post a message naming the album or song you're looking for and chances are someone will post it for you within a few days. Often an easier alternative to downloading music is streaming music, or listening to music live in real time. This is the province of Internet radio stations, which, in a medium as democratic as the Web, are about as numerous as Internet radio listeners. (All you have to do to start broadcasting is download a special Winamp plug-in from www.shoutcast.com). There are a number of good sites housing hundreds of radio stations, chief among them www.shoutcast.com and icecast.linuxpower.org. But to better appreciate the advantage Internet radio has over college radio stations, go to www.mp3spy.com and download the program MP3spy. Once loaded, MP3spy will arrange Internet radio stations by genre and let you know what song is playing, how many people are listening and the quality of the transmission. While listening, not only can you talk with other listeners and the D.J., but you can also send the disk jockey songs to play. To send your favorite songs to a D.J., you'll need the next component of your Internet stereo system: the "record" button, also known as the CD ripper, which enables you to turn CD's (or records or cassettes or random noise recorded into a microphone) into MP3 files. The best of these also serve as CD players and jukeboxes, searching the Web as soon as you insert a CD and letting you know the track sequence and recording notes. Though there are many of these programs, one favorite is Musicmatch 4.0 (at www.musicmatch.com). Most users prefer to make MP3 files from Real Audio's very quick, versatile and efficient Real Jukebox. But one problem with Real Audio software is that it is a bully, always trying to kick all other music software off your desktop and then pop up at the ready whenever your computer starts to do anything vaguely musical. So, with your MP3 player, your skins and plug-ins, your CD ripper and your Internet radio connections, what have you learned? Beside the fact that integrating the pieces of your MP3 software and developing a system for downloading music and maintaining a playlist can be a nuisance akin to finding the jewel boxes for the disks in a 100-CD changer, you've learned that there is a whole universe that already exists on line built around the MP3. It is not a world of pirated music, as the record industry would have you believe, but one in which you can choose and design the look and feel of your music player, the lengths and types of compilations you want to make for yourself, and the interactive visuals that accompany the sound. After all, the main difference between the MP3 and the CD is not that the music is on line instead of in stores, it's that the MP3 is not packaged, perfected and made easy to use by an industry before being given to consumers. The technology is open-ended and evolving, which means that the message is that the medium is putty and, for now, as a listener you can mold it in any way you want. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: At left, Rust Ghosts, a skin, or faceplate, that covers a MP3 player like a mask. Below, a windowed 3D Winamp plug-in, or supplemental program. (pg. 29); Mooamp, above, a skin used to cover an MP3 player; Sonique, right, a popular digital audio player, and, left, the Power Render Dancing Can, a visual plug-in, the Internet equivalent of album cover art. (pg. 30)

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: GREENWICH VILLAGE -- BUZZ;
Web Ropes in Horror Film's Fans
body: THE SETTING -- The midnight opening of "The Blair Witch Project" on Tuesday night attracted a line of fans stretching well around the corner of the Angelika Film Center. The low-budget horror film, made in eight days by five friends from the University of Central Florida, has been promoted heavily on the Internet for months. Tickets for the three late-night screenings were sold out days in advance, but that didn't stop the truly devoted, who began to line up for seats at 10 A.M. They wore "Blair Witch" T-shirts and clutched posters, some bragging that they had already seen bootleg tapes. The filmmakers mingled with the crowd. THE BUZZ -- Griselda Tomayo, 37, of the Upper West Side was among the first to arrive. Twelve hours later, she was still reveling at being first in line as she ate a chef's salad inside a tent, one of four donated by a sporting goods store. "I've seen the film already, but I really was dying to see everyone's reaction," she said. "I think it's the scariest movie I've seen since 'The Exorcist.' I was a Catholic schoolgirl at the time, and I had to sleep in my mother's bed because I was so afraid I was going to get possessed." Outside the tent, a small group of admirers gathered around Abby Marceluk, 24, of Philadelphia, and Eric Alan Ivins, 26, of Pompono Beach, Fla., the founders of "A and E's Blair Witch Project's Fanatics Guide" (tbwp.freeservers.com). "We fell in love because of this movie," Ms. Marceluk said. They met in a discussion room on the film's Web site (www.blairwitch.com) and plan to get married, she said. Mr. Ivins put a hand on her shoulder. "We were keeping in touch through the Web site, and we actually met in person at the Florida Film Festival, where they were screening the movie," he said. "It was love at first sight." Farther down the line, David Viola, a 22-year-old Upper West Sider, chatted with friends as he ate a prosciutto and mozzarella sandwich. "If it wasn't for the Web, this movie would be nothing," he said. His friends all nodded. Edie Nugent, 18, was in full agreement. She said she had been following the film on line for months. "Movie makers should take heed," she said. "It's not just net geeks on line." Ms. Nugent was wearing a "Hello, I'm Heather Donahue" name tag. "Heather's one of the stars," she explained, rolling her eyes after someone asked. Like nearly everyone in the crowd, she also wore a silver pin fashioned after the twig figures that play an important part in the movie. "I was here at 10 in the morning to show my support," she said. "These filmmakers cater to their fans, and because of it they have the most loyal fan pool I've ever seen. One of the producers actually got me sunblock today when I was waiting in line."   KIMBERLY STEVENS http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Some fans outside the Angelika made it a campout. (Frances Roberts for The newyork Times)

title:
THE RIGHT THING;
You've Got Mail. You're Being Watched.
body: "IT was tragic," recalled Mary Beth Heying, a principal at Edward Jones & Company, the brokerage firm in St. Louis. In April, an employee had complained to the human resources department after receiving an email containing inappropriate material, meaning off-color jokes, pornography and so on. "We investigated and found that a large number of associates were involved" in distributing such messages, Ms. Heying said. Depending on "the egregiousness of their involvement," she said, the company dismissed 19, warned 41 and allowed 1 to resign. The company has a "very clear" written policy on email, Ms. Heying said. Some 2,700 of its 17,000 employees have email or Internet access at work (none of the brokers do, because written communication is heavily regulated in the brokerage industry), and each of the 2,700 was given a copy of the policy when receiving email access, Ms. Heying said. An American Management Association survey this year found that 27 percent of companies do what Edward Jones does -- monitor internal email -- up from 20.2 percent in 1998. In the vast majority of cases, employees are informed of the surveillance. There is little dispute that companies have both the power and the legal right to monitor email sent on the company network on company time. But there are conflicting ethical imperatives at work when managers consider a monitoring policy: on the one hand, to avoid unwarranted intrusions into employees' privacy; on the other, to keep unchecked circulation of off-color jokes and other inappropriate material from creating a hostile atmosphere. Allan A. Kennedy, a management consultant and co-author of "The New Corporate Cultures" (Perseus, 1999), starts from the premise that "companies that monitor email traffic or use the power of modern technology to act as Big Brother to the employees are dehumanizing the work environment." Still, he sees a need for policing email, given how it can expose a company to litigation. He says the best approach is to let workers frame the policy. "An employee-based email monitoring system would not be as disrespectful," he said. "It would be from one employee to another, saying 'We don't want to work in an environment where this kind of thing goes on.' It'd be equivalent to the kind of natural monitoring that would have gone on around the water cooler." In reality, though, monitoring is rarely continuous; far more often it is used only when a company has someone or something to investigate -- when, as at Edward Jones, an employee complains about a particular message. Indeed, Laura P. Hartman, a professor of business ethics at the University of Wisconsin, thinks the threat of monitoring may be seen as a strong-enough deterrent that companies can spare themselves from much actual monitoring. Employers are naturally uneasy about unmasking inappropriate email and dismissing offenders. But invasion of privacy isn't the root of the unease; the distress of firing is. Most managers dread having to do something so painful to the person across the desk. "We have a zero tolerance policy with regard to inappropriate email, and people know that," Ms. Heying said. "Does that mean we didn't feel badly about 20 associates? Oh, by all means, we do." email takes companies into new ethical territory, as they struggle with controlling a technology so utterly different from other communications tools. Unlike a phone call or hallway conversation, email leaves an audit trail that can pinpoint the abuser. But unlike a paper memo, email moves at lightning speed, both in delivery and in composition, often with little reflection or second thought. It will probably be awhile before there is corporate consensus on the fairest balance between privacy and protection. Until then, the responsibility to do the right thing falls upon employees, who can use common sense as a guide. If an employee's passion for email privacy is born of a desire not to have the boss find out he's been placing bids all day for vintage comic books in an on-line auction, chances are he already knows he shouldn't be doing that at work. In this new high-technology world, a remarkably old-fashioned rule of thumb applies: Don't do what you wouldn't want to be caught doing. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Rose Cassano)

title: SBC-DirecTV Deal Is Set, Executives Say
body: Adding television to its portfolio of digital communications services, SBC Communications Inc., one of the nation's biggest local phone companies, has agreed to a wide-ranging marketing and distribution partnership with DirecTV Inc., the big satellite broadcaster, executives close to the deal said yesterday. The companies plan to announce the deal on Monday at the Satellite Broadcasting and Communications Association's convention in Las Vegas, Nev., the executives said. The deal with DirecTV would fill a big hole in SBC's product line and give SBC a much-needed weapon -- television -- as it gets ready to go head to head against the AT&T Corporation in a battle to offer consumers integrated packages of long-distance and local telephone, video and high-speed Internet services. AT&T has agreed to spend more than $90 billion to become the nation's No. 1 cable television company by acquiring Tele-Communications Inc. and Mediaone Group Inc. Cable systems already deliver television channels and sometimes Internet service, but AT&T wants to retool cable networks to also offer local phone service, breaking open the Baby Bells' de facto monopoly in residential markets. Faced with that threat, the Bells are scrambling to put together communications packages of their own. SBC, which does business as Southwestern Bell, Pacific Bell and Nevada Bell, has already said it wants to offer high-speed Internet service using normal phone lines to 8.1 million of its 18 million residential customers by the end of the year. Some analysts also expect SBC to win regulatory approval to sell long-distance phone service to its customers in Texas in the next six months. SBC and DirecTV declined to comment. Since 1994, DirecTV, which is part of the Hughes Electronics unit of the General Motors Corporation, has grown to become the nation's largest direct-broadcast satellite provider -- and by far the biggest competitor to cable services -- with more than seven million customers. Over the last few months, SBC has conducted negotiations with both DirecTV and its main rival, the Echostar Communications Corporation, which has about 2.5 million subscribers. But under its deal with DirecTV, SBC would not be allowed to pursue a second satellite partner for at least a few years. SBC will begin marketing DirecTV service to its customers in Arkansas, California, Kansas, Missouri, Nevada, Oklahoma and Texas this fall, executives close to the deal said. SBC owns the Southern New England Telecommunications Corporation, the dominant local phone company in Connecticut, and has a pending deal to acquire the Ameritech Corporation, the leading local phone company in the Midwest. But SBC has no firm plans to expand its DirecTV partnership into those regions because both Ameritech and Southern New England Telecommunications own cable television operations that compete against DirecTV, executives close to the deal said. In its core markets, however, SBC plans to offer the DirecTV service, traditional phone service, high-speed Internet access and perhaps wireless phone service on a single bill, the executives added. For communications companies, the power of such integrated packages comes in the opportunities to create promotions that span different products. SBC, for instance, could potentially offer free voicemail, call waiting and Caller ID to local phone customers who sign up for DirecTV. The satellite television service would carry the brand of both companies. Hughes also offers a satellite Internet service known as DirecPC, but that service did not appear to be part of the SBC deal. America Online Inc., the No. 1 Internet provider, has recently struck marketing deals of its own with both Hughes, for satellite delivery of the on-line service, and with SBC for high-speed delivery over digital subscriber lines. Bell Atlantic, SBC's main local phone rival, also has a marketing deal with DirecTV, but that agreement does not appear quite as wide-ranging as SBC's. Since striking its deal last year, Bell Atlantic has followed a relatively conservative timetable for introducing Bell Atlantic-DirecTV service; it is not yet available in newyork City, for instance. Bell Atlantic phone customers who sign up for the satellite television service receive separate bills for the two services, and Bell Atlantic and DirecTV do not yet offer significant cross-promotions. (A Bell Atlantic spokesman said yesterday that such promotions were on their way.) The recent deal is actually SBC's second go-round with DirecTV. In the fall of 1995, SBC conducted tests with DirecTV, but that initiative fell apart after AT&T acquired 2.5 percent of DirecTV the following January for $137.5 million. The chairman of Hughes Electronics, DirecTV's parent, at that time was C. Michael Armstrong. Shortly after Mr. Armstrong became chairman of AT&T in November 1997, AT&T sold its interest in DirecTV, opening the door to DirecTV's latest partnerships with the Bells. When AT&T sold its interest in DirecTV, AT&T said that consumers appeared to prefer to buy the satellite dish and converter needed for the DirecTV's service from consumer electronics retailers. Executives close to the SBC deal said SBC was considering a fairly radical promotion to deal with that concern: giving away DirecTV dishes.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: At Least Some Domain Names Draw Money at Net Auctions
body: CAN the unwieldy Internet domain name JewelersMallofAmerica.com really be worth the $2 million that its owner is asking for it on an Internet auction site? If so, the more straightforward ad.com would seem a bargain, with an asking price of only $500,000. And hispanics.com, which was bid up to only $5,100, is a gem. The rush to register Internet addresses a few years ago produced a horde of speculators eager to cash in on the appreciated -- or busted -- values of their virtual real estate. Thousands of Internet addresses are being offered for sale daily at auction sites like Ebay, Amazon.com and Yahoo. The most popular themes for sale involve the 2000 election, assorted body parts and the stock market. If auctions are the fairest way to assess market value, then most of the domains appear worthless -- attracting bids that fall short of the $70 initial registration fee required by Network Solutions, the Internet domain registration body that once had exclusive control over .com, .net and .org domains. JewelersMallofAmerica.com and ad.com did not receive any bids in their first four days of being listed on Ebay. In fact, a search of current and completed auctions revealed that more than 90 percent of domain names offered for sale on the sites receive no bids. Many names have awkward 'e' and 'i' prefixes like eBillionaires.com and iWimbledon .com, or are strung together by unappealing hyphens like cowboys-r-us .com. To attract bidders, some sellers suggest uses for their addresses. The owner of hillary2OOO.org, a name that uses capital 'o's in place of zeros, proposes a parody site of the First Lady's senatorial campaign. Some domain name sellers never intended to start Web businesses. Others had business plans that never got off the ground. In some cases, the Internet addresses became obsolete when the company's name changed. Todd Bernhard, the president of Internet Headquarters, registered memo.com in 1993 after he left Sun Microsystems to start a company called Memorandom. When the company changed its name to Internet Headquarters and its Internet address to hq.net, Mr. Bernhard found himself with a valuable piece of Internet real estate. "Ebay seemed like a good way to market our domain to a high-tech audience," Mr. Bernhard said. The domain name was recently bid up to $50,000 on Ebay. But he sold it later for an undisclosed amount. A popular way for owners to test the value of domain names is to put them on sale with high reserve prices that are not disclosed. If the test run is encouraging, owners will frequently offer the item for auction again. Rick Schwartz, a self-proclaimed virtual real estate developer who owns more than 3,000 names, browses auction sites daily, looking for good deals. In one day he bid on pennsylvania.com, dailystockpick .com, digitalnews.com and faithful .com. Before domain name auctions took off a few months ago, Mr. Schwartz searched registration databases and made offers to owners through email. Now, he says, the auctions have brought sellers out in the open. Among Mr. Schwartz's most valuable properties are porno.com and men.com, for which he paid $42,000 and $15,000, respectively, in 1997. He estimates that they are worth far more now and does not plan to sell any of his names soon. Mr. Schwartz said he had several million in annual revenue from advertising on his sites and other Web-related business. About 2,000 of his domain names have pornographic overtones. But he has a sentimental side, too. A few weeks ago, Mr. Schwartz bought hy.org on Ebay for $400 to set up a commemoration site for his late father, Hy, who died in 1997. Straightforward names are the most valuable, Mr. Schwartz said. "It should be easy to spell, easy to remember and have a direct association with product you are trying to sell," said Mr. Schwartz, who decided to forgo marshmallow.com because there is little money to be made with the confection. He said there was a definite premium for .com addresses, which are more popular. "If you buy a dot-net, it's almost spitting in the wind." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Fresh From Your Browser's Oven
body: YELL people that you're going to track their every move on a Web site, store that information in files and analyze it later, associating it with personal data they gave the site earlier, and the response might be, "Back off, Big Brother!" But that is not a paranoid vision of personal-data piracy. It's simply what happens when, as you browse the Web, you (or your browser, without your knowledge) accept a "cookie," a short bit of text that a Web site can store on a user's machine. In other words, it happens every day, millions and millions of times. The term cookie has been used by computer scientists for a long time, but its origin is murky. A Web site uses a cookie to recognize return visitors. It can be no more than 4,096 characters long, but it is often as short as 10 or 20 characters. Cookies can let users avoid tediously typing in their user names and passwords at sites that require them. (But you wouldn't want to let a cookie to keep track of your password for a site where someone could do real damage to your bank account, like at a stock trading site.) And cookies help shopping sites keep track of a limited amount of information, like the contents of a shopping basket or a mailing address. They are ubiquitous because they smooth the unending stream of transactions between Web browsers and Web servers that make up the constant electronic chatter of the Internet. When a user types in a Web address or clicks on a link, the Web browser -- like Netscape Navigator -- sends a request for the Web page to a Web server, another computer with specialized software that receives and processes requests for Web pages, graphics, sounds and other elements. If no cookie is involved, each request for a document or graphic is handled the same way each time. If a cookie is involved, the site knows you've been there before and may know your preferences. On a site that issues cookies, the software that handles requests from browsers for pages and images can issue a unique identifying number the first time a browser makes a request for pages. That identifying number is sent to the browser, which stores it as a cookie on the user's hard drive. The next time the user wants to go to the same site the browser sends the identifying number as part of the request. That helps the company that runs the Web server track the number of different visitors to its site. It also means that a record can be kept of all visits by that browser to the site. Cookies can be set to expire at a specific date and time. Virtually all major electronic commerce sites use cookies to send a browser a session identifier that allows a user to drop items in a shopping basket, browse other sites and return within hours or even days without losing any of those selections. It may sound spooky, but it's important to recognize cookies' limits. They are not active spying programs, just plain text. A cookie can't suck information from a user's machine and secretly transmit it to a Web server. Many discussions of cookies revolve around credit card numbers. Because of security concerns, these are rarely stored as cookies. A cookie might contain a credit card number, but only if the user provided it as part of a transaction and the Web site was irresponsible enough to send it back as a cookie. Any responsible site stores in a cookie only information, like a name and password, that a user knows is going into the cookie. And if a cookie is used by the Web site to call up a database file with personal information provided by the user, that information is stored at the Web site, not in the cookie. A user can control what information finds its way into cookies and decide whether to accept cookies in the first place. A browser delivers a cookie for only a particular site -- the site that initially sent the cookie to the browser. That keeps one site from raiding another site's cookies. The only information in a cookie is what the user provides. If you don't give information about yourself to a site by filling out a form or otherwise handing over personal details, that site has little or no way to connect you, as an individual, with your surfing expedition through its pages. This is not entirely foolproof because a Web surfer can pick up cookies without realizing it from some advertising companies and companies that sell demographic information. A company with a banner ad on a Web page might send an identifying cookie to your browser, and it would be able to track that browser if it called up pages at other Web sites carrying the company's ads. The advertiser could, through an agreement with a commercial site, also get a copy of personal information you gave to the shopping site when making a purchase and be able to associate that information with your browser. Netscape offers an option that allows a user to reject cookies sent from sites other than the one that's feeding out the current Web page. One way to deal with cookies is to say, "No, thanks, no dessert for me," when a server offers your browser a cookie. All the current versions of Web browsing software offer options in their security preferences, or in a specific cookie-setting panel, for automatically refusing all cookies or for accepting them on a case-by-case basis. (Internet Explorer for Macintosh is unique in offering the ability to accept all cookies from a given domain, like trustworthy.com.) Depending on the browser, you can more or less easily view cookies you have already stored and delete some or all of them. Personal security software, like WRQ's At Guard program, can also help provide a measure of cookie control. If you refuse to accept cookies, however, some sites won't let you in, others dump your shopping cart each time you leave the site, and still others behave erratically or forget your preferences. Privacy advocates are keeping a close eye on cookies. Many people and organizations, including the Federal Trade Commission, are voicing concerns about what Web sites might do with the personal information they collect through cookies or E-commerce transactions and are advocating that sites adopt privacy policies. A wise user will treat cookies with the care parents now exhibit over candy at Halloween. Verify first, and eat later. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: When a user connects to a Web site that uses cookies, short pieces of information that are stored on users' computers, a set of handoffs occurs between the user's browser and the Web server. The user types in a request for a Web page. Behind the scenes, the browser translates that into a format that the Web server can understand. The browser opens a connection to the Web server and sends as plain text the page request, as well as some information about itself (its platform, version, number and operating system).  1 -- Browser connects to Web site and sends this message: GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: www.nabiscorescipes.com:80 Referer: http://www.nabisco.com Browser: Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 4.01; Windows 98)  The Web server software usually runs on a computer more powerful than even a high-end home personal computer. A single machine might run software that handles requests for many Web sites. The server software packages its response with header infor-mation that helps the browser interpret the page. That includes language and page length in bytes. The server might also send a cookie.  2 -- Server sends response back to browser: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Tue, 13 Jul 1999 22:06:07 GMT Server: Apache/1.3.4 (Unix) Set-Cookie: visit=1102918597974995; path=/; expires=Wed, 14 Jul 1999 22:06:07 GMT Last-Modified: Tue, 06 Jul 1999 23:57:13 GMT Accept-Ranges: bytes Content-Length: 7790 Content-Type: text/html Web page follows here in HTML (Hypertext Markup Language)  Most browsers can be configured through their Options or Preferences settings to prompt a user to decide whether to accept a cookie. In this case, if the user clicks Decline, the cookie data are just discarded. If the user clicks Accept, the data are stored on the user's hard drive in a special cookie file or folder.  3 -- Browser elicits Decline or Accept options  If the cookie is accepted, the browser checks its cookie file on the next visit to the same Web site and discovers that it has a cookie stored for this site. The cookie is retrieved and inserted in the text that the browser sends to make the next file request.  4 -- Browser sends to Web site:  GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: www.nabiscorecipes.com:80 Cookie: visit=1102918597974995 Referer: http://www.nabisco.com Browser: Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 4.01; Windows 98)  The Web server receives the cookie and can then store it in a log file that keeps track of all the visits to a site. Or the server might associate that cookie with an active shopping session and retrieve a user's already selected items.  5 -- Web site processes cookie  Some sites, like Amazon.com, use cookies to greet users on their return by name. (But account information like a mailing address is typically protected by passwords at many sites.)

title:
NEWS WATCH;
A Man With a New Mission: A Computer in Every Kitchen
body: Computers may be proliferating throughout the house, but they have generally bypassed the kitchen. Bob Lampson wants to change that, and as the man who brought the Juiceman juicer and Breadman bread machine to countless kitchen counters (via countless infomercials), he may just be the fellow to do it. His company, CMI Worldwide of Seattle, has come up with the Advantage 2000. While the machine does not slice and dice, it lets the cook do a lot of things: watch a cooking show on TV or a CD-ROM video, browse for a favorite recipe on the Web or get that famous Neiman Marcus cookie recipe via email. The machine uses a non-Windows operating system, with a browser by Spyglass, and CMI Worldwide will provide Web access through its own portal for a monthly fee. The company is betting that people who spend a lot of time in the kitchen will be willing to pay extra for the convenience of sending email or searching the Web without having to go elsewhere in the house. The machine, which a company official said should be on the market this summer, will be available in two models. An under-the-cabinet version (pictured) with a fold-down screen will cost about $2,800. The plan is to market it mostly to builders who want to include it as a kitchen feature. A countertop model, priced at about $1,000, will be marketed to the public -- largely through infomercials, of course. HENRY FOUNTAIN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Free Service Is a Way to Keep Prying Eyes Off Your email
body: A new company in Palo Alto, Calif., has created a free email service to fend off the on-line equivalent of Dumpster divers -- people who root through mail servers to find messages that you sent days, weeks or even years ago. The company, Ziplip.com, says it will protect your email messages from snoops and delete all traces of the messages after they have been read by their intended recipients. To lock up messages that are sent over the Internet, the service scrambles the messages using 128-bit encryption -- the strongest encryption code that the unitedstates allows to be sent over the Internet. The company then applies an even stronger encryption code to the messages that are stored on Ziplip's computers. The service does not ask users to set up new email accounts, as does Hushmail.com, another snoop-resistant service that opened this summer. People who want to use Ziplip must go to the company's Web site at www.ziplip.com to type and send messages. They are required to provide the email address for the intended recipient but are not asked to fill in their email addresses or other information. Ziplip then sends a brief email message to the recipient that includes a Web link to the actual message on Ziplip.Com's Web site. Users are encouraged to use passwords to keep the messages even more private. "Technology is allowing someone to literally track every move we make," said Kon Leong, president and chief executive of the company. "I thought it was about time that technology was used to counter that trend." LISA GUERNSEY http://www.nytimes.com

title: Take These Jokes . . . Please
body: HOW many jokes has Gary Lewis sent by email in the last month? Like a lot of jokes that circulate on the Internet, it isn't even funny. Mr. Lewis, an architect who lives in Lake Mohegan, N.Y., is a human hub on what may be the Internet's most far-flung network: joke tellers and their electronically captive audiences. Mr. Lewis's modest goal is to put a little laughter into the lives of his 32 or so closest friends and acquaintances. Lately, however, some of his material hasn't been going over so well. "Some people have asked to be taken off the list," Mr. Lewis said ruefully. "You start seeing the same jokes over and over again. So I try to do the right thing and spend more time editing. But then you think, 'Is this really funny? Which joke is more appropriate for this particular person?' It's easier trying to design a very complicated building." As anyone with an email address knows, one of the most popular uses of the Internet has little to do with electronic commerce or real-time stock quotes. Jokes are often the first email new Internet subscribers receive and, in time, the most common. That's partly because they are so easy to tell. Forget the setup and timing -- just click on the Forward button on your email program and you're a regular comedian. Internet joke-telling is developing as an art unto itself, with its own customs, critics and avant-garde. One video clip on the email circuit shows an animated monkey in the passenger seat of a car boogeying to music from the radio, next to an apparently oblivious human driver. If that doesn't sound funny, take it from those who have their computers set to play it over and over -- it is. Even as new joke forms develop, a debate has broken out among some of the computer network's more sophisticated jesters over whether the Internet mode of distribution is destroying the age-old essence of humor, and, if so, what to do about it. At stake, some say gravely, is the future of the joke itself. "The volume diminishes the impact of a good joke," said Al Paster, 70, a retired computer programmer who frequently replies to Mr. Lewis's email jokes by correcting their punchlines. In a gesture toward quality control, Mr. Paster refuses to pass on E-jokes. "What really disturbs me is when the jokes I know -- and I know quite a few -- are changed for the worse," he said. "I predict the death of humor by the millennium." Others have noticed a pall settling over off-line humor as a result of the Internet's unparalleled capacity for joke propagation. "I'm going out to dinner tonight with people and normally any lull in the conversation I could fill in because I knew five new jokes," said David Perlmutter, a newyork lawyer who has 43 addresses on his joke list. "Now the only way they don't know those jokes is if they haven't read my email. It's socially depressing." On the other hand, more people are telling jokes than ever before. Take Peter Coan, a typically reserved architect in Ghent, N.Y., who stunned friends at a dinner party last month by telling a banjo joke he found on the Internet. (The difference between a banjo player and a Treasury note? Eventually a Treasury note matures and earns money.) "This is abnormal for me," acknowledged Mr. Coan, who took to the Internet in search of jokes shortly after his wife took up banjo playing. "I'm not that interested in jokes. I know two or three jokes and I can't even remember them. But these rang true." Certainly, the Internet allows for convenient sorting of jokes by category. There are Web sites featuring frog jokes, lawyer jokes, light bulb jokes, Microsoft jokes and, of course, Star Trek Lost Episodes. But by releasing the sender from the obligation of actually uttering the words, some humor experts say, the carbon-copy nature of the Internet zaps the hidden level of meaning that makes jokes funny. "Joke-telling allows us to get away with saying things that are taboo, impolite, politically incorrect," said Lawrence E. Mintz, director of the Art Kliner Center for Humor Studies at the University of Maryland. "Internet jokes lose that value because the teller doesn't have the personal commitment to the joke. People send whole strings of jokes that they have no commitment to." Dispatched along with the oral tradition are the tone of voice and overall delivery that are so often the key to getting laughs. The ability to scroll down to the punchline tends to undermine even the best setup. But Internet humorists may be injecting meaning into their material in new ways. Because of the concentric circles through cyberspace that most jokes seem destined to travel, a sense of community with strangers often develops among a given joke's thousands of recipients. And there is heightened competition to be the first to relay a good one -- a more difficult task when everyone is connected. "I sent a technology joke yesterday to a principal in a management consulting firm in Los Angeles," said a manager at a financial services firm who asked that his name be withheld because his company prohibits sending jokes over its email system. Later, the recipient got the same joke from Esther Dyson, the technology pundit. "Can you believe it?" he said. "I beat her." Since many companies have cracked down on the jokes stampeding through their corporate networks, sending them requires a dedication by employees to flout the rules or spend evenings at home giggling into the screen. "They don't want us doing this but I say, I'm doing it anyway," another surreptitious joker said, referring to his employer. "They can only control my life up to a point.' Standards are being raised, too, by the challenge of getting onto premier distribution lists. Joke mavens who take themselves seriously forward only a small portion of the jokes that reach their email In box. At rec.humor.funny, a venerable newsgroup devoted to jokes, fewer than 2 percent of submissions make the cut. "On average I accept one per day, and on a busy day I can receive as many as 100," said Jim Griffith, the moderator. "A lot of them are jokes we've seen before. And a lot of people aren't as funny as they think they are." For Andrew Gelb, a lawyer in Los Angeles who began receiving floods of jokes as soon as he got an Internet account last fall, email jokes offer a dimension others do not: headers that offer clues to their provenance. "I like to look at the long list in the message to see who else got the joke," Mr. Gelb said. "I get a kick out of how fast and how far these things travel.' A list of one-liners, for instance, reached Mr. Gelb recently from Carollee Krueger, a fellow wine aficionado in Santa Monica, Calif. Ms. Krueger received the joke from Mr. Lewis, the architect, who got it from Mark Paine, an I.B.M. consultant who lives in North Salem, N.Y. Mr. Paine received it from Tom Dietsche, a chemist at Dow Chemical in Midland, Mich., who got it from a colleague in another building, who got it from his brother David Czerepinski, a junior high school science teacher in Madison, Wis., who got it from Warren Avery, a computer salesman in Tempe, Ariz., who hit it off with Mr. Czerepinski last year at his wife's high school reunion and has been sending him jokes ever since. Unfortunately for the purposes of this exercise (or not), Mr. Avery had deleted his joke archive the day before he talked to a reporter and could not recall the joke in question. In earlier times, jokes were thought to spread as traveling salesmen pollinated their customers with one another's humor. Pre-Internet, the phone was the most efficient distribution tool, wielded with particular proficiency by Wall Street traders, who were credited, among other things, with some of the more tasteless attempts at humor that followed the explosion of the space shuttle Challenger. Now joke trackers say they see a growing body of original material from all types of individuals. And with each link in an email chain forwarding jokes to dozens of others, jokes flit across the world in a matter of hours. "It's like the Industrial Revolution of jokes," said Dave Barry, whose humor column for The Miami Herald is distributed widely on the Internet. "Instead of doing something useful with your day, you're probably reading a joke. And you've noticed that at the same time there's been this huge explosion of jokes going around, there's also been this huge surge in the economy." Whatever the impact on the gross national product, Barry Wellman, a sociologist at the University of Toronto, said Internet joke-sending played a role in maintaining relationships that might not otherwise be sustained. "Jokes are a way of reaffirming a connection with somebody," said Mr. Wellman, who has his own archive of 748 jokes and a list of more than 100 people to whom he sends good ones that roll in. "Before email, what did people do? They did nothing or they sent a Christmas letter. Jokes serve as a Christmas card, but they come much more often because it's really easy." Trea Graham, 57, could do without the weekly Christmas cards from her son, a naval engineer. A recent dispatch included some dog haiku that she thought was funny, but she said she would rather get email he had written himself. "If you asked him, 'Francis Spencer, are you contacting your mother a lot?' he would say yes because he's pushing a button and going 'Forward to Mom,' " Ms. Graham said. "Well, it's not the same thing." The same liberal forwarding attitude has caused other kinds of offense to be taken as well. "People feel free to be more edgy or sexist or racist because they feel less responsible for the joke," said Patrice Oppliger, a lecturer at Northeastern University who is studying joke-sending habits. "People who would never tell these jokes face to face send them out en masse." That's nothing a little technology can't solve. A Web site called Jester, for instance, uses "collaborative filtering" techniques to recommend jokes based on user ratings of a set of samples (shadow.ieor.berkeley.edu /humor). "Humor is a very difficult thing to characterize," said Ken Goldberg, who is one of the site's designers and an engineering professor at the University of California at Berkeley. "The computer treats all jokes as numbers." Of course, there has already been considerable evolution of the Internet joke form. One of the first computers to be connected to the nascent Internet in 1973 offered off-color limericks on request. Anyone who contributed three new ones received a copy of the entire database. Since then, the Internet has proved hospitable to more elaborate jokes. A longtime rule that mandates a punchline after 15 or 20 seconds, or you lose your audience, doesn't apply in a medium where jokes are meant to be read instead of heard. Long lists, like the Top 26 Children's Books Not Recommended by the National Library Association (No. 25: "The Little Engine That Could Becomes Intoxicated and Kills Civilians"), are thus more plentiful. Not surprisingly, technology jokes, particularly the Microsoft subgenre, have found an appreciative audience on the Internet. (Microsoft acquires the Vatican, Christmas, the year 1995, the rights to all further "Microsoft Acquires" announcements and so on.) "Not only do you have more people on line," said Mr. Griffith, the newsgroup moderator. "But you have more people who understand why Microsoft-bashing is funny." And jokes that might never find an audience off line have suddenly become worth telling on the Internet. One of Mr. Griffith's favorites involves the chemical cesium: "With the Internet there are enough people out there who appreciate cesium humor," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Gary Lewis, of Lake Mohegan, N.Y., sends jokes regularly to a list of 32 family members and friends. (Chris Maynard for The newyork Times)(pg. 1)  Drawing (James Yang)(pg. 8)

title:
The Once And Future Network;
Wiring the Home Has Made Big Strides, but Has Far to Go
body: IN the old days -- say, a couple of years ago -- home networks meant figuring out a way to use a personal computer and some simple X-10 modules to turn lamps on and off, control the sprinkler system and manage a simple home security system. That was before the availability of inexpensive PC's, the rise of the World Wide Web and the advent of high-speed connections to the Internet. Today, an estimated 15 million to 20 million American homes have more than one PC, and family members often find themselves vying with one another for access to the Internet from the den, the living room or the bedroom. The number of multiple-PC homes is expected to double in the next few years, the importance of the Internet for communications and commerce is expected to soar, and home networks are suddenly a practical necessity for many people, not just a project for electronic tinkerers. Large businesses typically attack the problem of networks by hiring full-time administrators to worry about wiring topologies and network protocols, but in households where even programming the VCR or getting Junior to take out the trash is an ordeal, hiring a network specialist is out of the question. Yet industry analysts say we are rapidly approaching the day when a much broader array of home devices will be sharing data, not just PC's and peripherals, but also television sets, stereo systems, smart land-line telephones, cellular phones, digital cameras and even kitchen appliances. A consumer might download music from the Internet through a computer and play it on a home stereo, for example, or play a DVD movie on the home-office computer but watch it on the big television set in the living room. In the home of the near future, if all goes as planned, someone might simply point a digital video camera at the television and the two devices would instantly recognize each other. A signal sent from the computer in the car could arm the home security system or turn down the thermostat. A computer in the master bedroom could display images beamed from the camera in the nursery or over the front door. In some of the more imaginative scenarios, the refrigerator could know it was low on milk and eggs and place an order with the local supermarket, and a microwave oven could check a database that listed the allergies or eating habits of family members and issue an alert if an unwanted ingredient was detected when a package's bar code was waved in front of it. All the clocks in the house would set themselves by linking to the PC in the den, which would set its own internal clock via the Internet, checking with an atomic clock in Colorado. The technology to create all such fancy networks exists today. But to many consumers, it may seem like a complex solution in search of a simple problem. Right now, according to surveys done by computer network companies, the main reason to build a home network is to share Internet access, whether through a conventional dial-up modem or, increasingly, through a high-speed cable or digital subscriber line (D.S.L.) modem. A network enables two or more computers to share the high-speed connection at the same time, so family members don't have to take turns. Setting up a network, at a typical cost of $50 to $100 for each connected computer, is often cheaper than buying a modem for each PC and getting a second or third phone line from the phone company. And once the household signs up for high-speed cable or D.S.L. access -- typically at a cost of $40 to $60 a month for the line, plus equipment and installation fees, plus additional monthly fees of $20 or more for the Internet service provider (unless the cable provider is also the I.S.P.) -- it is often cheaper to add a new PC to a network than it is to set up a separate high-speed connection for a new PC. The second most common reason to build a network, the surveys found, is to enable two or more family members to play multiplayer games together. Playing against the computer is increasingly passe; racing against Dad in a Formula One race or teaming up with little sister in a dogfight is the future of PC games. And playing games, by the way, is the second-fastest-growing use of home computers, after surfing the Internet. The traditional reasons for having a computer network in the office -- the need to share printers, files and applications -- are farther down the list for PC users at home. Home networks will become much more interesting and complex in the next few years with the growing deployment of new digital devices like television set-top boxes, smart telephones and wireless Web pads that connect to the Internet via radio waves. The trend is expected to accelerate as consumers begin buying digital entertainment, like music, videos and books, over the Net and downloading on one device -- probably a powerful PC acting as the household's Internet gateway -- then transferring the files to another device that can handle them better. That device might be a stereo with a better speaker system, a television with a larger screen or some sort of specialized digital device, like an electronic book that can be carried to the comfy couch in the living room. But not yet. Despite the recent arrival of a number of different home network kits that promise to simplify the task, setting up the connections isn't that much easier than it was when only hobbyists were doing it. The conventional way to build a PC network in offices, using a technology called Ethernet, is also popular in homes where PC users demand high-speed connections (10 million to 100 million bits per second) and have the technical determination to make Ethernet work. The most popular Ethernet kit for home networks, which involves stringing wires, is Linksys's Homelink, which connects two PC's for about $100. Although Ethernet has snaked into many homes, most consumers are not keen on do-it-yourself projects that involve boring holes in walls, stringing wires along the floor with duct tape or paying hundreds of dollars for custom installations. But under the battle cry of "no new wires," more than a dozen companies have come up with alternatives that connect PC's over the phone wiring a house already has. I've tried several of these, including the Intel Corporation's Anypoint Home Network kit ($189); a variation from Farallon Communications called Homeline ($139 to connect two computers), for the several million houses where Windows PC's and Apple Macintoshes co-exist, and one called Homefree from Diamond Multimedia Systems ($100). Unlike Ethernet systems, these new home network kits that connect through phone lines are intended to appeal to consumers who love the Internet but don't necessarily like computers. The kits are relatively easy to install and configure. The current phone line standard allows connection speeds of one million bits per second, much slower than Ethernet, but second-generation versions of the kits scheduled to arrive this fall are expected have a data transfer speed that is 10 times as fast. All of these kits use the home's existing telephone wiring to share data without interrupting normal phone service or high-speed D.S.L. Internet service. The computers share the same wires as the phones but operate at a different frequency that does not interfere with voice traffic. You need a phone jack near each computer, and users who have multiple phone lines must make sure that all the wall jacks in the network have the same phone number. Despite promises of simplicity, however, the phone line products have been known to cause even experienced network users to have conniptions. Computers are complex things, and getting them all to work in harmony is tricky. Sometimes the network stops working for no apparent reason: printers can stop printing, and laptop computers brought home from the office can cause configuration confusion. That's when cryptic error messages can make even the most patient person reach for the aspirin bottle. "There are definitely some kinks that need to be ironed out," said Michael Wolf, an industry analyst with the Cahners In-Stat Group of Phoenix, who noted that these first-generation network kits were still too hard for average consumers to use. "When you get beyond the techno-geeks, you have some problems." Not all computers are hostile in network environments. Network connectors and file-sharing software are standard equipment on Apple Macintosh computers, which makes home networks easy as long as all the computers are Macs. But 9 out of 10 computers sold today are not as network-friendly as the Macintosh. Companies like Intel and Microsoft, whose technologies form the basis of the most common home PC's today, acknowledge that home networks could be made simpler. They say they are working on next-generation products that will simplify the setup process and make home networks more reliable and easier to use. Microsoft, for example, plans to emphasize "universal plug and play" capabilities in its next version of Windows for consumers, and it is working with the 3Com Corporation to create a series of home network kits that will go on sale later this year. Compaq, the world's largest PC maker, plans to make home network technology a standard feature in its consumer PC's. Meanwhile, nearly every major PC maker, and many of the largest consumer electronics companies, have joined one or more working groups that are trying to establish common standards for networks that connect through phone lines, radio waves, infrared signals, home power lines and a variety of special wires. Mr. Wolf, of Cahners In-Stat, said he expected home phone-line systems to be the most common solution for home networks in the next few years, followed by wireless systems and systems that connect through electrical outlets. Networks that connect through a home's electrical wiring have appeal in residences where phone jacks may be scarce. They connect PC's to regular 110-volt wall outlets. One such kit is the $199 Intelogis Passport network. But power lines are finicky, and interference from refrigerator and air-conditioner power spikes can degrade the network's performance. Data moves at less than half the speed of the basic home phone line alternatives. A more appealing solution, especially for people who use portable computers and handheld information devices, is to bypass wires altogether by connecting devices with radio waves. Wireless network kits like Proxim's Symphony (which costs $199 for each laptop and $149 for each desktop) offer data transmission speeds that are comparable to the speeds of current phone-line systems, but wireless systems invariably cost much more than wired systems. A company called Sharewave has created wireless network technology that connects PC's and other devices at Ethernet speeds. Computer and consumer electronics products based on Sharewave technologies are expected to be in stores next year. Motorola has been demonstrating a wireless home-network hub that is expected to be on sale later this year. These are all solutions for retrofitting homes and apartments with computer network equipment. The ultimate and most expensive approach to building a home network is to buy a new house that has high-speed wiring already built into the walls. Many new subdivisions are being built with such wiring as a standard feature, and some analysts expect computer networks to be as common in new homes in the 21st century as plumbing and electricity. "We expect that in a few years, almost all new construction will include network cabling," said Michael Kwatinetz, a market analyst with Credit Suisse First Boston. Two new subdivisions in Houston, each with nearly 2,000 homes, have been built with I.B.M. Home Director network hubs built into closets or garages. At DC Ranch, a development outside of Scottsdale, Ariz., each of the 8,000 houses that have been built or are planned has high-speed connections in the walls. And each home is linked to the others and the world on a fiber-optic network that provides data services, digital television and digital phone service. A new development of 50,000 homes near Las Vegas, Nev., is to be built with internal networks as a standard amenity. Eventually, the most optimistic forecasters say, Internet access will be nearly as common as phone access in houses. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos (Photographs by Tony Cenicola for The New York Times)(pg. 7)  Chart: "The Family Circle"  For anyone who is ready to set up a home network, here are some of the products available.  CONNECTING VIA PHONE LINE  Intel Anypoint www.intel.com/anypoint/home.htm Cost and platform: $189 to connect two PC's; Windows only. Installation: Parallel-port version is easy; PCI version requires installing cards. Pros: Best out-of-box experience; parallel-port version does not require opening the computer. Cons: Software glitch required getting a patch from the Internet.  Farallon Homeline www.farallon.com/homenet Cost and platform: $139 to connect two computers; Macintoshes or PC's (but Mac-centric). Installation: PCI card installation required. Pros: Best system for connecting Macs and PC's. Cons: PCI cards? Sorry, that rules out iMacs.  Tut Systems Homerun www.tutsys.com Cost and platform: $199 to connect two computers; Windows only. Installation: Requires PCI card. Pros: Adds RJ-45 Ethernet ports as well as phone-line ports. Cons: Requires opening the computer; must have phone jacks nearby.  Diamond Multimedia Systems Homefree www.diamondmm.com/homefree Cost and platform: $100 to connect two Windows computers. A U.S.B. version for linking Macintoshes (including iMacs) and PC's is coming in August. Installation: Requires installing PCI cards. Pros. Low cost; phone line system. Cons: Unless the PC has Windows 98 2d Edition, the Mac must be the gateway computer on the network.  WIRELESS CONNECTIONS  Proxim Symphony www.proxim.com/symphony (2.4-gigahertz radio frequency system) Cost and platform: $199 per PC card for laptops, $149 for PCI card for desktops; Windows only. title:
THE POP LIFE;
On the Rise And on Line
body: In 1995 two Manhattan club owners started the Macintosh Music Festival to fill the summer gap left after the New Music Seminar -- a weeklong mix of panels, deal making and scores of alternative rock concerts -- collapsed under the weight of its debt. The new festival, the club owners said, would merge computer technology with live performance, posting 360-degree concert photos and written descriptions of shows on the Internet to become the first festival to take place simultaneously in clubs and on the Web. To many people at the time, the whole concept seemed like a lot of smoke blown around an attempt keep the clubs crowded and to sell more beer. But next week the annual event returns with a new name, the Digital Club Festival, and a victory smile. Not only has figuring out how to put a price tag on the connection between music and the Internet become a top priority of the record business, but just last month SFX (the company that turned the concert industry upside down by buying more than half of the country's concert promoters as well as many concert halls, ticket companies and tours) announced that it was beginning an Internet spending spree and had made a deal with Intel to cybercast 20 shows this summer. Suddenly the Digital Club Festival seems prescient. Last year, the festival says, 250,000 computer users watched live feeds of concerts on line; this year it expects more than half a million. There are three components to this year's festival, said Andrew Rasiej, a former owner of Irving Plaza who runs the Digital Club Network with Michael Dorf of the Knitting Factory. The first is the music: some 350 bands at 25 clubs over four nights, beginning on Tuesday, with live feeds available free on its Web site: www.digitalclubfest.com. Passes that allow access to all shows (space permitting) are available on line or from Ticketmaster for $50. Among the groups performing are Bush, Everlast, Live, Public Enemy, the Donnas, Spain, Will Oldham, Frank Black and Public Enemy. The second component is two days of lectures and panel discussions on technology and music, called Plug-In, at the Marriott Marquis Hotel. Beginning on Monday and open to 800 people for a prohibitive fee of $1,300 to $1,400, it includes many of the biggest executives in the record and technology industries, like Chris Blackwell of Palm Pictures, Danny Goldberg of Artemis Records, Strauss Zelnick of BMG and Rob Glaser of Real Networks. Many of these executives wouldn't even attend the festival in its first year, Mr. Rasiej said, noting that record companies can no longer afford to be seen standing on the sidelines of the Internet-music movement. Perhaps this is why musicians as well known as Wyclef Jean of the Fugees, Seal, Public Enemy and the Artist Formerly Known as Prince are performing on Monday night at an awards show for Web sites, the Yahoo! Internet Life Magazine On-Line Music Awards, at Studio 54. Finally, the week also sees the beginnings of Mr. Rasiej and Mr. Dorf's new company, the Digital Club Network, created with the belief that live concerts should not disappear into the ether when the show is over but should be archived and exploited like studio recordings. "What A&E and Bravo were to cable TV in 1985," Mr. Rasiej said, "we believe the Digital Club Network will be to broadband in the year 2005."  Going Commercial After nearly 13 years on public radio, "Rhythm Revue" is graduating to commercial radio. The show, a popular rhythm-and-blues flashback produced every Saturday by Felix Hernandez on WBGO in Newark (88.3 FM), will be heard on Jammin' 105 (WTJM, 105.1 FM in newyork) beginning on Saturday morning from 7 to 11. It will also be broadcast on Sunday nights from 6 to 10. The station, which changed its format from adult contemporary to rhythm-and-blues oldies in December, first approached Mr. Hernandez with the offer a month ago. He said it was a difficult decision to leave WBGO, but in the end the cons were outweighed by the pros, which included "reaching a wider audience and the high probability of syndicating the show." Despite concerned email from fans, Mr. Hernandez said that besides the insertion of commercials and extra hours, the show would not change, and that he would continue to choose the music.  Dead? No Prob! This week Private I/Mercury Records announced that it would be releasing the first of three recordings of Patsy Cline duets on Sept. 14. These aren't rarities rescued from the vault, but recent recordings, made 36 years after Ms. Cline's death. With the support of Ms. Cline's children and former husband, the producer Michael Blakey hired a scientist to help him remove sections of Cline's original vocals and then reconstructed the tracks, adding extra orchestration and the voices of Willie Nelson, Glenn Campbell, Waylon Jennings, Crystal Gayle, Bob Carlisle and others. This is not the first time music has been made using the voice of someone too dead to object. Recent years have seen similar albums or songs with John Lennon, Nat (King) Cole and the Mexican singer-songwriter Jose Alfredo Jimenez. But Mercury's confidence in the three separate Cline CD's points to a new genre that may be growing so popular that it will need its own section in record stores: "Rock-and-Roll Over in Your Grave." Perhaps sections of Jimi Hendrix's guitar solos can be replaced with riffs by some of today's fine young guitarists, like one of the guys from Korn. Janis Joplin's entire "Pearl" album could be remade as a duet with Britney Spears. And a supergroup called 27 Grave could be digitally created, featuring Hendrix, Joplin, Kurt Cobain, Jim Morrison and others who died at that age. And while we're at it, why not replace the trumpet in Miles Davis's "Kind of Blue" with belching sounds? Or has that already been done? http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Gavin Rossdale of Bush is taking part in the Digital Club Festival. (Associated Press)
