title: Dow Jones Quarterly Profit Tops Expectatio ns Again
body: Strong gains in advertising and low newsprint prices combined to propel Dow Jones & Company's second-quarter earnings above analysts' expectations. The company reported yesterday that its net income for the quarter reached $57.2 million, or 62 cents a diluted share, a penny above the consensus estimate reported by the First Call Corporation. It was the second consecutive quarter in which earnings exceeded expectations, and the strongest improvements came in the company's print publishing operations. Ad linage at The Wall Street Journal increased 6.9 percent in the second quarter over the corresponding period in 1998. But the improvement accelerated sharply in June, when advertising linage was up 19 percent over June 1998. Advertising revenue at all Dow Jones unitedstates publications grew 10 percent, pushing print publishing revenue up 6 percent, to $327 million. Over all, revenue rose 4.9 percent over the 1998 period, to $510.6 million. Operating income was $104.8 million, up 6.9 percent from the pro forma figure for the second quarter of 1998. At the company's Ottaway community newspapers division, operating income rose 47 percent, to 23.6 million, despite slight advertising losses, because of economies that pushed up that division's cash-flow margins to 33.1 percent, from 25.1 percent a year ago. "From an investor's point of view, it is sensational The Journal is doing as well as it is," said Lauren Rich Fine, an analyst with Merrill Lynch. "It is carrying the whole company." But she was more guarded about the prospects for the company's electronic publishing division, where operating income dropped 44.6 percent, to $10.2 million, despite a 1.4 percent rise in revenue, as the sales force was expanded to sell the Dow Jones news wires product overseas. "One of the reasons investors are interested in Dow Jones is the emerging electronic segment, and there are a lot of caveats," Ms. Fine said. In a report issued yesterday, she pointed out that The Wall Street Journal's Interactive edition continued to grow, with 306,000 subscribers to date, up from 223,000 a year ago; it brought in $7.9 million, up 46 percent. But the far larger newswire business, Ms. Fine wrote, "is relatively stagnant." The company reported total electronic revenue of $98.9 million for the quarter, up 1 percent from a year earlier; revenue from the news wires was $51.1 million, basically unchanged. http://www.nytimes.com

title: MCI Worldcom In Deal to Build Internet Access
body: MCI Worldcom Inc. made a big move into the consumer market for high-speed Internet access yesterday, announcing a partnership with Earthlink Network Inc. to sell retail services in as many as 25 markets by the end of the year. MCI Worldcom's Uunet operation, the No. 1 supplier of wholesale Internet access, has conducted high-speed tests with America Online Inc., the leading retail provider of Internet and other on-line services. But America Online has come to focus on the regional Bell local phone giants as partners for delivering high-speed Internet service to consumers. Earthlink, in contrast, wants to use Uunet's network to offer high-speed Internet links applying a technology called digital subscriber line, or D.S.L., in up to 25 markets by 2000, an Earthlink spokesman said. Earthlink, which plans to announce quarterly financial results today, is one of the nation's top five Internet providers, with about 1.2 million customers. D.S.L. lets consumers use standard phone wires to link to the Internet at speeds as much as 30 times as fast as what is possible with today's fastest dial-up modems. Deploying the technology, however, requires phone companies and communications carriers like Uunet to invest hundreds of dollars a customer for new equipment. Earthlink is testing a D.S.L. product in California using systems provided by the Pacific Bell unit of SBC Communications Inc. and is already offering D.S.L. service in Charlottesville, Va., through the Sprint Corporation's local phone operation. "Uunet's extensive national D.S.L. network will allow us to offer D.S.L. services to our members on a much broader scale than before," Jon Irwin, Earthlink's senior vice president for broadband services, said. Uunet also said yesterday that it had deployed D.S.L. systems in 1,000 central telephone switching centers around the nation. Those central offices are mostly controlled by the Bells and the GTE Corporation, but the Telecommunications Act of 1996 requires the local phone incumbents to allow other communications carriers to deploy equipment inside those offices. Each central office can provide high-speed Internet links to homes and businesses within a radius of about 3.5 miles.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Merrill Posts 23% Increase In Earnings
body: Merrill Lynch & Company, the nation's largest brokerage firm, posted robust second quarter earnings yesterday, even as the financial powerhouse struggles with infighting and tension in its upper ranks. Buoyed by a stock market that continued to produce gravity-defying gains last quarter, Merrill reported earnings of $673 million, or $1.57 a share, up 23 percent from the $549 million, or $1.31 a share, it earned in the corresponding period last year. Merrill's earnings easily topped analysts' expectations of $1.46 a share, according to consensus estimates compiled by the First Call Corporation. In trading yesterday on the newyork Stock Exchange, shares of Merrill rose $1.375, or about 1.8 percent, to $79.25. But Merrill's shares still trade well below their 52-week high of $109.125, and should the stock market slow or the economy enter a recession, Merrill's earnings could suffer. Indeed, Merrill may be vulnerable to a takeover later this year or next if its stock price weakens or if it is unable to successfully execute its plans to bolster its sales presence on the Internet. "I think Merrill is very well positioned for the global trends driving the industry today -- investment banking trends in Europe, strong trends in the U.S. that continue and Asia's longer-term prospects," said Richard Strauss, a securities industry analyst with Goldman, Sachs & Company. "But investors are also going to be keeping a close eye on its Internet strategy, and in the near term I think that expectation is just as important." The sharp reversal in Merrill's fortunes in the last year has produced a startling shift in how the once seemingly impregnable firm is perceived by many of its competitors and Wall Street. The firm's finances were hammered by last year's economic chaos overseas, and it was slower than firms like the Charles Schwab Corporation to embrace the enthusiasm for trading that is sweeping the Internet. On Monday, Merrill announced that Herbert M. Allison Jr., its president, resigned after being told he would not run the firm one day. Mr. Allison, a cool, detached figure who seemed oddly out of sync in Merrill's gregarious, hard-driving culture, had been at odds with Merrill's chief executive, David H. Komansky, for some time. Differences within the firm about how to respond to the growth of the Internet also added to managerial tensions. While the stock market seemed to react mildly to Mr. Allison's departure, there is still concern about the lack of a clear successor to Mr. Komansky and how quickly the company will put its house in order. "There's a sense around the Street that Merrill is adrift," said a senior executive at a rival firm. "I still marvel at where this company was two years ago and where they are today." Merrill counters that it is focused on achieving its financial goals and has managers in place who are up to the task of running the firm in an era of brutal competition and rapid change in the financial services industry. "We're very fortunate to have many talented executives in senior management and great bench strength," said Paul W. Critchlow, a Merrill spokesman. Nonetheless, some analysts yesterday questioned how deep Merrill's managerial bench truly is. Leading candidates to succeed Mr. Komansky include John L. Steffens, a vice chairman who heads on-line efforts and supervises the firm's army of retail brokers, and Jeffrey M. Peek, who oversees asset management. Beyond that, some say, the candidates are slim. Although attention has focused on Mr. Allison's shortcomings since his resignation was announced, Mr. Komansky has presided over a string of high-profile blunders or miscues in recent years. Those include the aggressive marketing of complex financial products known as derivatives to Orange County, Calif., which helped send the county into bankruptcy; a big expansion into emerging markets, which created financial headaches last year, and an unusually deep involvement in the near collapse of the Long-Term Capital Management hedge fund. Although Merrill also has had difficulties with its $5 billion acquisition of the British firm, Mercury Asset Management, which it acquired last year, Merrill said Mercury's funds were performing better and that it was "absolutely happy" with its returns on that investment. Merrill's earnings announcement yesterday disclosed smart gains in its overall asset-management business. Revenue from the business was up a record 7 percent from last year, to $1.16 billion, while total assets under management grew 5 percent, to $516 billion. Analysts were generally pleased with the results from asset management and other key units as well. "Trading was a bit lighter than I expected and investment banking a bit better," said Joan S. Solotar, an analyst at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "Over all, it was a solid quarter." In the period, Merrill's net revenue, which includes interest income less interest expense, rose 12 percent, to a record $5.4 billion. Commissions rose 8.8 percent, to $1.59 billion, and trading revenue jumped 7.6 percent, to $1.06 billion. Investment banking revenue totaled $908 million in the second quarter, up 1.1 percent from last year's booming quarter. Merrill said equity underwriting revenue was sharply higher from that of last year's second quarter, and nearly double the levels recorded in the first quarter of 1999. But underwriting fees in most debt categories declined in the second quarter, reflecting concerns about interest rates, the firm said. Analysts said they expected Merrill to post solid results for the third quarter. But uncertainty about the firm will probably emerge starting in December, when Merrill is scheduled to introduce new Internet-related products and trading accounts. "People are worried about the fourth quarter, when on-line trading and the retail products that come along with it will be rolled out," said Sallie Krawcheck, an analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein & Company. Other analysts shared Ms. Krawcheck's interest in how Merrill's Internet strategy will be deployed. "There is an inherent conflict with their brokers, which may be compounded by the fact that Launny Steffens will be running both the retail and Internet sides of the business," Ms. Solotar said. "I am hopeful management realizes it needs a cohesive Internet strategy and has a window of five months to put it together."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Motorola Rolls Itself Over;
After a Bad Year, Almost Everything Is Coming Up Rosy, and Wireless
body: A year ago, Motorola Inc. was faltering badly. Investors were dumping shares, complaining that the company had lost its way. It had missed a critical beat a few years earlier, betting on analog products when the world began craving all things digital. The company took a charge against earnings of $1.9 billion a year ago, but today it is on the rebound. Shares that were selling for $38 last October are going for nearly $100 -- a $30 billion leap in market value. The reason: a revamping that trimmed the work force and refocused the company's marketing of cellular telephones and semiconductors. In addition, demand has begun to revive in the critical Asia market, which slumped in 1998. Today, Motorola handily beat Wall Street projections by reporting earnings of $273 million, or 44 cents a share, for the second quarter of the year, up from $6 million, or 1 cent a share, a year ago. Analysts had estimated 41 cents a share. The announcement came after the close of trading. But ahead of the earnings release, shares of Motorola closed at $96.50, down $2.50, on the newyork Stock Exchange. Underlying Motorola's recent spate of good fortune is a less-well-known strategic shift, top executives say. The company plans to recast itself from a manufacturer of technology hardware to a software maker that is boldly vowing to bring the World Wide Web not only to cellular telephones and pagers but even to the automobile, which could soon be wired to download video games for backseat passengers. It is unclear whether Motorola's futuristic musings are just that, but the company has already invested billions of dollars and hired thousands of new software engineers. It also says it will equip every cellular telephone it makes next year with an Internet browser. "We are becoming much more of a software company," said Dennis A. Roberson, chief technology officer at Motorola. "It's a very significant break for us. There are more software capabilities in the devices we produce, and we're expanding into the Internet space." None of these ambitions would be possible, of course, without a recovery in the sale of cellular telephones and microchips, which account for about 68 percent of revenue. This year, the company is finally selling substantial numbers of digital cellular telephones, allowing Motorola to compete against Nokia of Finland and Ericsson of Sweden. Still, executives at company headquarters here in Schaumburg, a suburb of Chicago, are cautious about using the word "turnaround" just yet, and for good reason. Motorola faces some huge problems, ranging from a billion-dollar investment in a tottering satellite venture called Iridium to the challenge of regaining market share in the increasingly competitive market for wireless products and infrastructure. Although it is now making and selling digital products, for example, Motorola still does not have a digital telephone able to supply the One Rate plan at AT&T Wireless, one of the nation's largest wireless service providers. Motorola executives say such multiple-system phones should be ready later this year. Christopher B. Galvin, the 49-year-old chief executive, talks about creating a "new Motorola," a company in search of "breakaway opportunities." Doing so means fostering double-digit growth at a giant with $30 billion in revenue and more than 130,000 employees. Motorola is emphasizing software ventures, in part, to make the company more flexible and less capital intensive. Wall Street analysts have been almost universally optimistic about Motorola in the last year. But several analysts said the company still had to prove it could execute its plans. "They have been a well-regarded stock lately," Kenneth Leon, a wireless communications analyst at ABN Amro, said of Motorola. "But they have a growth rate in the low teens, and their competitors, like Lucent and Nokia, have growth rates in the 20's and 30's." Motorola says a corporate makeover is well under way. Some factories have been shuttered and their functions farmed out, and executives have been trying to do away with a "warring tribes" culture that pitted one division against another. Gone is the sense of invincibility that once pervaded the company, analysts say. "Motorola had an insular attitude," said Merle Gilmore, an executive vice president at the company. "We need to change that view. Things are happening too fast. Customer demands are too exacting. Now you need to be part of an overall echo system." The company found itself outside that echo system in recent years and did not adequately foresee technological changes and market trends. Motorola stumbled when the wireless industry began to shift from analog to digital technology. In 1994, it practically owned the cellular market, with a 60 percent share in the unitedstates. Nokia, which then had only 11 percent of the unitedstates market, is now the leader at about 34 percent, with Motorola second at about 31 percent, according to Herschel Shosteck Associates. Motorola executives saw the shift coming but did not expect it to come so swiftly, they now acknowledge. Motorola's problem was compounded by a rash of product delays, marketing miscues (Motorola's once trend-setting flip phones have recently been perceived as having lost their fashion edge) and repeated complaints that the company was using bully tactics with some of its customers. "They used to be very arrogant," said Phillip Redman, an analyst at the Yankee Group in Boston. "They used to push phones on people and say, 'If you want our phones, you have to buy so many.' " The company suffered huge losses in cellular handsets and infrastructure -- the bay stations and servers that make cellular calls possible. A $1.1 billion profit in 1997 became a loss of $1 billion in 1998. Motorola is trying to fix its cellular and chip divisions. In recent months, the company has sold off its low-end chip manufacturing business, laid off more than 17,000 employees and shifted more than 3,000 engineers to develop new digital handsets. "In handsets, Motorola is emerging as a winner again," said Matthew Hoffman, an analyst at Dataquest. "And the pie is growing 30 to 40 percent a year. There could be 200 million handsets sold this year. And that's good for Motorola." The company faces a fierce competition in cellular infrastructure from Ericsson, Nortel and Lucent Technologies. All three rivals possess a "switching technology" -- the costly and critical component that is at the hub of all telephone service. Motorola is the only major supplier of cellular service without an end-to-end solution. "They have a big challenge ahead on the infrastructure side," said Jane Zweig, an telecommunications analyst at Herschel Shosteck. Motorola's executives say, however, that they are working on a solution: a complex packet-switching technology that would shuttle voice, data and video from the Internet to wireless devices. To get there, Motorola has announced ambitious joint ventures with Cisco Systems Inc., a leader in networking, and with Sun Microsystems Inc., best known for its Java programming language and its Solaris operating system. Motorola and its partners are by no means alone. Lucent (which bought Ascend Communications) and Nortel (which acquired Bay Networks) are also working to develop wireless Internet access and what they call the "broadband living experience." But Motorola is betting that its approach will put it ahead of the pack, eliminating the need for circuit switching technology. The company is experimenting with microchips for everything from shoes, doorknobs, sofas and the family pet, chips that the company hopes will pervade an interactive society in which trillions of snippets of voice, data and video are beamed worldwide. Mr. Roberson, the chief technology officer at Motorola, foresees enormous opportunities as well as fun in the "trillion device problem" of linking everything up wirelessly. "Embedded processors of the world unite," he said with a smile. Motorola chips already power cellular phones, digital cameras and 3Com Palm Pilots, television sets, printers and microwaves. But in the company's view of the future, Motorola chips will also be the "digital DNA" inside a new breed of "smart" products. Motorola does not just want to make the chips. It wants to design and develop the software that runs them, and to work with customers to create new products. The company is developing myriad devices, from flat-panel displays and set-top boxes to a wireless biotechnology product that might someday take an individual's blood sample and instantly transmit it to doctors, or even offer a diagnosis using a genomics data base. For the short term, Motorola is trying to broaden its revenue sources. The company has a strong business in two-way radios (sold to governments and large industry), consumer-oriented walkie-talkies, called Talk About, and "smartcards," which can be used for security clearances, automated tellers, debit cards and other types of E-commerce. Its paging business is slumping, but Motorola is a leader in cable modems and chips supplied to networking companies like Cisco Systems. Motorola is also a leading supplier to the auto industry, selling global positioning satellite technology. A new division of the company is working on high-definition television and interactive television. One of the more troublesome projects, however, is the Motorola-led consortium called Iridium, a big satellite communications network that has been on the brink of bankruptcy in recent months. The network of 66 satellites, which offers telephone service anywhere in the world, has had a difficult time signing up subscribers and making loan payments, some of which are guaranteed by Motorola. Analysts worry that Motorola could be hurt by a mounting debt load. "Iridium is an exposure, and no one is happy with it," said Wojtek Uzdelewicz, an analyst at S. G. Cowen. "The biggest risk is that Iridium will stay afloat and Motorola will increase its financing, and then you'll have this sinkhole. The hope is that Motorola makes a decision very soon." Motorola is moving ahead with another satellite venture called Teledesic L.L.C., which would deliver voice, data and high-speed Internet access to hand-held devices. Other partners in the $9 billion effort include William H. Gates, the Microsoft chairman; Craig McCaw, the cellular telephone pioneer, and Boeing. Last week, Motorola won the contract to develop the satellites for a low-orbit system that is expected to be launched in 2004. Wall Street analysts say that if the satellite ventures work, Motorola's prospects will be enormous. Meantime, they are cheering Motorola's plan. "We like the story; we think the turnaround is for real," said Michael Ching, an analyst at Merrill Lynch & Company. "The challenge, of course, is execution. Now Motorola has to deliver the products on a timely basis." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Christopher Galvin, Motorola's chief, seeks "breakaway opportunities." (Michael L. title: Sony and Time Warner Make Music Deal
body: Joining the growing ranks of media companies with quasi-independent Internet units, Time Warner and Sony said yesterday that they would merge Columbia House, the music club they jointly own, with CDnow, the struggling on-line music store. The resulting company will focus on selling compact disks and video tapes from all labels and studios, although the emphasis will be on promoting Sony and Time Warner products. And by the end of the year, it will offer music that can be downloaded directly from the Internet, a market that many in the music industry have long feared but are now moving quickly to embrace. "The first business that will benefit the most from the Internet will be the revolution in music," Gerald Levin, the chairman of Time Warner, said. The new company, not yet named, will be publicly traded so that it can give employees stock options and use its shares as currency in acquisitions. CDnow's existing shareholders will have 26 percent of the new company. Time Warner and Sony get 37 percent each. Other big media companies are also rushing to create publicly traded Internet operations. On Monday, the Walt Disney Company said it had agreed to buy the 58 percent of the Infoseek Corporation it did not already own and would create a new class of stock tied to its on-line operations. And the NBC unit of the General Electric Company is creating a similar venture by merging its stake in Snap, a search service, with Xoom, a publicly traded on-line merchant. As in other industries, record labels are moving to sell directly to their customers on line at the risk of alienating their traditional retailers. In April, Bertelsmann and Universal Music, a unit of the Seagram Company, agreed to form their own Internet music store called Getmusic.com. CDnow has been struggling to increase sales and move toward profitability. Selling compact disks is a business with low profit margins, and CDnow has spent tens of millions of dollars on promotion -- as much as $70 to bring in each new customer. By contrast, within months after opening its own music store last year, Amazon.com surged past CDnow in sales by doing little more than promoting compact disks to its book buyers. Indeed, yesterday, CDnow officials told analysts that revenue in the second quarter would be about $35 million, less than expected and less even than the company's sales in the first quarter, a rare decline for an Internet company. Even a recent merger with its chief rival, N2K, has failed to reverse CDnow's fortunes. As a result, its share price has declined slightly over the last year as shares in other Internet companies have skyrocketed. Yesterday, the market reaction was no better. CDnow's shares fell $1.9375, to $20.3125. Analysts questioned whether the business formed from CDnow and Columbia House would be as attractive as an Internet company. Columbia House has revenue of $1.3 billion, but its sales have been declining because baby boomers have stopped buying compact disks to replace vinyl records. The combined companies will also have about $250 million in Internet sales this year. "I understand why CDnow wants to align with big record companies," said Derek Brown, an analyst with Volpe Brown Whelan & Company. "But I'm not sure what Columbia House record club brings to the party." The merger with Columbia House has been in the works for nearly a year. It was initially proposed by Nancy Peretsman, an investment banker with Allen & Company, in a discussion with Richard J. Bressler, then the chief financial officer of Time Warner. The companies agreed in principle to the deal early this year, but negotiations were protracted -- in part because CDnow was occupied with its own merger and with disputes among its executives, people close to the transaction said. Moreover, there were differences to work out between Time Warner and Sony. In addition, other companies, including BMG-Universal and Deutsche Telekom, expressed interest in CDnow, executives close to the negotiations said. The deal announced yesterday is a complex web of commitments. Sony and Time Warner will guarantee $200 million in existing CDnow debt and another $150 million in new debt. And they will promote CDnow on their existing Internet sites as well as on their album covers and broadcast networks and even through inserts in boxes of Sony electronics products. Some of this promotion will simply be given to CDnow. In other cases, the company will have the right to buy advertising at a discounted rate. The new company is expected to hire a chief executive from outside the company. Richard Wolter, the chairman of Columbia House, will run the record club. Jason Olim, the chief executive of CDnow, will run the on-line record store. And Jonathan V. Diamond, the chairman of CDnow, will leave the company. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Nobuyuki Idei, left, the chairman of Sony, and Gerald M. Levin, the chairman of Time Warner, talked yesterday before announcing a venture in Internet music sales with the Internet retailer CDnow. (Associated Press)

title: Amazon.com Gets Into Two New Businesses
body: Moving to position itself as the Internet's first true department store, Amazon.com plans to introduce two new divisions today, one for consumer electronics and another for toys. Amazon has grown from just an on-line bookseller into the largest Internet retailer by far, with more than 10 million customers. In addition to books, Amazon already operates sections for music and videos, as well as an auction site. Analysts estimate its sales will exceed $1.3 billion this year. Through a gifts section it introduced last year, Amazon has offered a handful of toys and electronics items. But now it will offer thousands of products in each category. So far, neither category has attracted many sales on the Internet. In 1999, on-line sales of toys will be $52 million, according to estimates by Jupiter Communications, the Internet research firm, and sales of electronics will be $78 million. By contrast, on-line book sales will be $1.1 billion. In toys, some prominent on-line merchants have already emerged. The leader is eToys, which went public earlier this year and has established a well-known brand. But its sales in the fiscal year ended March amounted to just $30 million. Toys "R" Us, the leading toy-store chain, has fumbled its first on-line efforts and is now working on a new initiative in conjunction with Silicon Valley venture capitalists. Kay-Bee Toys, the chain owned by the Consolidated Stores Corporation, bought Brainplay.com, a specialized Internet site. The electronics field is more fragmented, with a handful of start-ups, like 800.com, and electronics sections on larger sites, like the Cendant Corporation's Netmarket. One hurdle to on-line electronics sales has been that large manufacturers like Sony have not wanted many of their products sold on line. In part, this has been to protect their local dealers, but some manufacturers have been debating whether to open on-line stores of their own. Jeff Bezos, Amazon's chief executive, said that the company, which is based in Seattle, had secured access to a wide range of consumer electronics, but declined to say how many items Amazon would carry. Analysts said that the battle between Amazon and Etoys would be hard fought. "In terms of customer service, they are both singing from the same choir book," Mark Johnson, an analyst with Jupiter, said. "Amazon just has unbelievable scale and a much larger customer base." Of course, not so long ago skeptics were predicting that Amazon itself would wilt in competition with Barnes & Noble, the much larger bookseller. That did not happen, and Toby Lenk, chief executive of eToys, said his company could be the David to slay Amazon's Goliath. His company's strength, he said, was its specialization in goods for children. And eToys, which is based in Santa Monica, Calif., has initiated a pre-emptive strike, opening its own children's bookstore yesterday, with 85,000 titles. "The same rules don't apply when you sell things for kids than when you sell books," Mr. Lenk said. For example, Amazon offers a service that lets repeat customers buy items with a single click of the mouse, assuming they have already entered their shipping address and credit card information. Mr. Lenk said that eToys requires a password for customers to complete purchases to prevent kids from charging on their parents' accounts. Mr. Bezos argued that the one-click purchase system would be an important convenience for customers and would drive impulse purchases. Customers, he noted, have the option of disabling the feature. And, he said, since Amazon would store and ship all its products from its network of warehouses around the country, shoppers could combine books, toys and electronics in one order, saving on shipping costs. Much of Amazon's toy section emulates the look of eToys, with lots of information about toys and suggestions for children, broken out by age groups. Amazon said it was developing more reviews and other information content about its products. For example, it said it had hired Dr. Penelope Leach, the pediatrician and author of several books on child rearing, to recommend educational toys. Similarly, for the consumer electronics section, Amazon has hired editors to write buying guides and individual product reviews. "Over time, we will do a full Consumer Reports-level of testing," Mr. Bezos said. For now, Amazon does not accept money from electronics or toy makers to promote their products. Eventually, it will charge fees for prominent placement of positive reviews, as it does with books. But Mr. Bezos said that the opinion in the review would be independent of any fee paid by a manufacturer. And readers will be able to submit their own product reviews and ratings, as they do with books, he said. Mr. Bezos would not say how much Amazon thought these new departments would contribute to its sales. But he noted how quickly the company's past expansions had grown. "We launched music and four months later we were the leading seller of music on line," Mr. Bezos said. "And we became the No. 1 seller of videos in 45 days." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Gain for On-Line Industry on Privacy Issue
body: While finding that the on-line industry has a long way to go in protecting the privacy of consumers, the Federal Trade Commission has approved a report it requested recommending that Congress hold off on legislation to regulate how companies collect and use consumer data. The report, approved 3 to 1 by the commission, was a victory for industry groups that have been scrambling for the last year and half to avert privacy legislation. They have made a case for self-regulation, encouraging companies to declare policies that allow consumers to choose and control the information collected about them over the Internet. Christine Varney, a former Federal trade commissioner who is now a legal counsel to the Online Privacy Alliance, a group of Internet and technology companies that was formed a year ago when the commission threatened to seek legislation, said, "I think it does reflect that the industry has done an enormous amount of work over the last year and a half and we are on the right track." But privacy advocates insist that the latest surveys of the privacy practices of on-line marketers -- and the commission report itself -- prove self-regulation insufficient. "I think there is plenty of evidence that self-regulation has not worked," said Marc Rotenberg, executive director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a civil liberties advocacy group. "What these privacy policies are telling people is how much privacy they don't have. The consequence as a legal matter is expectations of privacy in the on-line world continues to decline." The report was not without criticism of the industry. It cites a recent survey by Georgetown University showing that while 66 percent of Web sites now post privacy policies -- up from 14 percent a year ago -- only 10 percent also follow the commission's criteria for protecting personal information, giving consumers choice and control over such information and a form of redress if it is misused. "The self-regulatory initiatives described above reflect industry leaders' substantial effort and commitment to fair information practices," the report states. But it goes on to say that "only a small minority of commercial Web sites have joined these programs to date." The report will be submitted on Tuesday at a hearing of the House Commerce subcommittee on telecommunications, trade and consumer protection, at which commissioners and others on both sides of the privacy issue are expected to testify. The ranking Democrat on the subcommittee, Representative Edward J. Markey of Massachusetts, says he intends to introduce an on-line privacy "bill of rights" to protect consumer control over personal data.  Today an aide to the Congressman, Colin Crowell, said the commission's report "doesn't make logical sense." Robert Pitofsky, chairman of the commission, denied the conclusions were in conflict. "Responsible elements of the Internet community have begun to do what they set out to do," he said. "On the other hand, just putting a notice on the Internet about a privacy policy is not all the protection that consumers deserve." In addition to Mr. Pitofsky, Commissioners Mozelle W. Thompson and Orson Swindle approved the report. Commissioner Sheila F. Anthony voted against it. Mr. Pitofsky said the commission would continue to monitor privacy. The report comes a year after the commission released the first survey on Web site privacy and won approval of legislation requiring Web sites that collect information from children to get parents' permission. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Globalization Widens Rich-Poor Gap, U.N. Report Says
body: Globalization is compounding the gap between rich and poor nations and intensifying American dominance of the world's economic and cultural markets, according to the latest human development report published today by the United Nations Development Program. The 262-page report, the 10th the program has issued, is the first to focus on the spread of the Internet and computer technology as well as the impact of globalization. It concludes that the so-called "rules of globalization" should be rewritten to save the 60 countries that are worse off they were in 1980 from falling even further behind. While short on specific proposals for making international markets work "for people rather than profits," the report recommends, as have previous versions, faster debt relief, redirection of aid to the poorest countries and a task force to review "global governance." It also endorses a tax of one American cent on lengthy emails to raise $70 billion a year that could be used to connect the world's Internetless. The report warns that the glaring, growing inequalities in the distribution of wealth pose a "dangerous polarization" between rich and poor countries. As in previous reports, it says little about what role the poorest nations themselves play in their predicament. It says little about the corruption and mismanagement of resources in many of the poorest countries that have discouraged foreign investment and squandered millions of dollars in foreign aid. The report highlights the dominant role of the unitedstates, and as a result, of English -- the language of choice for 80 percent of web sites -- in the new global telecommunications marketplace. It notes that 26 percent of Americans use the World Wide Web -- as opposed to 3 percent of Russians, 4 one-hundredths of 1 percent of the population of South Asia and 2-10ths of 1 percent for Arab states. And it says that the unitedstates has more computers than the rest of the world combined. It also notes that the annual sales of General Motors are larger than the gross domestic products of Thailand or Norway, and that Ford generates more income than Saudi Arabia. America and the other rich, industrialized nations hold 97 percent of all worldwide patents, it says. Moreover, the report says, the gap between globally well-connected and unconnected peoples is likely to grow even faster given the technology explosion. The number of Internet users today, 150 million, is expected to grow to 700 million by 2001. An American needs to save a month's salary to buy a computer; a Bangladeshi must save all his wages for eight years to do so. Richard Jolly, a British economist and the report's main author, said the report is neither anti-American nor anti-free market. "The report specifically endorses markets as the best guarantee of efficiency," Mr. Jolly said, "but not necessary of equity." America, he said, was among the first to appreciate the dangers of monopoly and, as such, to pass antitrust laws to dilute concentrations of economic power. The international community, he said, has yet to figure out how to deal with such global market concentrations. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Disney to Merge Internet Holdings With Infoseek
body: Eager to assume more direct control over the future of its assets on the Internet, the Walt Disney Company announced yesterday that it would create a single company combining its own Internet holdings with the Infoseek Corporation, the search service and portal. The new company, to be known as Go.com, will merge Disney.com, Disney's Club Blast, the Disney Store Online and other holdings with Infoseek, the company said. Disney already owns roughly 42 percent of Infoseek. The deal, which had been widely expected, is the company's attempt to create an entity whose stock will provide Disney with a currency for additional Internet acquisitions. It will also help attract Internet managers who expect part of their compensation to come in the form of stock options in an industry where share prices have soared over the last few years. Disney and Infoseek are already working closely together, but many in the industry view a dual management structure as unwieldy. The company clearly hopes that creating a more consolidated operation with its own shares will streamline both management and deal making. Once the deal is completed, Disney will own 72 percent of the new company, through a tracking stock, meaning that the assets continue to be owned by Disney but the share price effectively tracks the performance of those assets. Infoseek shareholders will own the balance, or 28 percent. Under terms of the agreement, Infoseek shareholders will get 1.15 shares of the new company for each Infoseek share. Aside from the stake owned by Disney, 35 million of Infoseek's 62 million shares, or about 57 percent, are held by others. Those will become 41 million shares in the new company, leaving roughly 145 million shares of the tracking stock outstanding. Though Disney did not provide much financial data yesterday, James Preissler, an analyst at Paine Webber who follows Infoseek, said, "If you are a believer in the synergy that Disney brings to the story, from both a content standpoint as well as a distribution standpoint, then the deal bolsters that strategy." On Wall Street the initial impulse when the deal was announced was to wonder whether it might fall apart if Infoseek shareholders believed they were not being paid enough. There was precedent for that concern since Lycos shareholders, angry that USA Networks Inc. was not paying enough of a premium for Lycos, blocked that merger earlier this year. Infoseek shareholders filed seven suits yesterday in Delaware Chancery Court over the buyout. Disney shares rose 18.75 cents yesterday to close at $27.8125, while Infoseek shares dropped $5.5625 to close at $45.9375. Still, Mr. Preissler said he thought the deal was likely to go ahead. "It fairly values all the assets that are contributed," he said. "The ratios for each company's assets make sense because the on-line assets from both companies are treated roughly the same and the Disney catalogue business is given a lower multiple, relative to the other two, as it should be." He added, "Moreover, everyone understood that Disney would push for a merger, and investors were not anticipating the same kind of takeout premium." Disney said the combined company was expected to have revenue of $350 million, of which $150 million would come from traditional sales from the Disney catalogue. The balance will come from Internet operations of the two companies, Disney said. A year ago, when the company made its initial investment in Infoseek, the Disney chairman, Michael D. Eisner, talked about the advantages of melding Infoseek's Internet capacities with Disney's marketing prowess. "When all the technology is out there, it is the entertainment value that attracts people," he said. Some critics wondered yesterday whether Disney, a mature media company, could work well with the faster-moving Internet operator. Disney's image, certain and safe, has no edge. John Tinker, who follows Disney for Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities, said he saw the deal as a creative venture for Disney. But he views the key challenge as Disney's ability to sublimate its traditional image within Go.com. "Disney has kind of an image of monitored, safe sex," he said. "On the Internet everyone wants freedom." Mr. Eisner said the company was well aware of that. "You don't want big corporate brother pushing you to a certain site," he said. Still, there are more subtle moves a marketing company might make, Mr. Eisner continued, such as using jokes on the Go.Com home page to liven it a bit and differentiate it from the competition. Several analysts said management would pose the most immediate problem. Jake Winebaum, the former chairman of Disney's Internet operations, left this year to start his own company, backed by Disney. Harry M. Motro, president and chief executive of Infoseek, is leaving the company once the deal is completed. Steve Wadsworth, president of Disney's Internet operations, is expected to take over. If so, he faces a variety of problems at Go.com. Infoseek stock has not done as well recently as those of its competitors, and though the Go.com assets' customer base has increased, it is not rising as fast as Yahoo's, for example. And the company failed to meet analysts' first-quarter estimates. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Michael D. Eisner, chairman of Disney, announcing the acquisition of Infoseek. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Th e organization that specializes in the business of doing good is doing well on the Internet.
body: THE Advertising Council, the nonprofit organization that produces and distributes public-service announcements, has risen in the last four months from 23d to 9th place in rankings of the most visible advertisers on the Internet, according to Nielsen/Net Ratings, an Internet measurement service. That is not because the council has increased its advertising budget. It has no such budget. As it does in other media, on the Internet the council relies on the benevolence of Web sites to run its advertisements in unsold space. As a result, banner advertisements that the council created on behalf of nonprofit groups on recycling, drunken driving, crime prevention and nearly 20 other public-service causes appeared 133 million times on the Web last month. Such messages reached 16.2 percent of all people who surf from home, according to Nielsen/Net Ratings. This puts the organization in the ranks of such other highly visible on-line advertisers as the Microsoft Corporation and Amazon.com. The council's increased visibility represents a gesture of good will on the part of Web publishers. But what does it say about the medium that so much advertising space is being given away? "It's another indication that there's a ton of unsold inventory on the Web, as if we needed any more," said Jim Nail, an analyst who covers Internet advertising for Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. Indeed, 40 percent to 70 percent of the ad space on even the most highly trafficked Web sites goes unsold, said Rich LeFurgy, chairman of the Internet Advertising Bureau, an industry trade organization. For what Mr. LeFurgy calls second- or third-tier sites, the proportion of unsold space is even higher. One explanation for the unsold space is that the Web offers practically infinite publishing opportunities. Thus it has exponentially more advertising capacity than do television, radio and print media, which have limited space and air time. Reluctant to have space allotted for advertising appear empty -- the digital equivalent of dead air time in broadcast media -- Web sites often plug in ads promoting their own services to take up the space. But a site can use just so many of those ads without looking tired. "So why not plug in some public service, be a good guy?" Mr. Nail suggested as the reason for the widespread use of the public-service banners. "When people see that, they say, 'Hey, this site is good.' " Besides perceiving that the Web site at hand has a social conscience, the public is also exposed to messages intended to improve society and public safety and to promote the nonprofit groups that advocate these causes. The spirit of mobilizing communities is what propelled the advertising industry to create the War Advertising Council 57 years ago. Then, the group's focus was to rally the nation in support of World War II. One of its first initiatives was a campaign featuring Rosie the Riveter, the character that motivated women to enter the work force during the war. Now, the organization is known as both the Advertising Council and the Ad Council. In 1997, the council added an on-line component to its public service campaigns. The banners are created by advertising agencies that volunteer staff time, and are available on the council's Web site (http:// www.adcouncil.org) to anyone who wishes to display them. Peggy Conlon, president of the Ad Council, likens the increasing use of council banners on line to the early days of television, when public-service commercials helped fill air time. "The more stations that went on the air, and the more hours they programmed, the more space there was to fill," she said. "We're being brought along on the Internet by the phenomenal growth of the industry." Over the years, the council has grown significantly: in 1998, the group received $1.2 billion in donated space from all media. Donated space on the Internet soared from $5 million in 1997, based on cost estimates given the council by the contributing sites, to $28 million in 1998. That makes the medium an even bigger supporter of public-service campaigns than newspapers, which contributed $21.2 million in space in 1998. Even so, the sacrifice is a bit different: Web publishers have a lot of unsold space to give away, while traditional media companies often donate space they could have used for paid advertising. Last year, the National Crime Prevention Council was the top-ranked media campaign for the Ad Council, receiving $128.1 million in donated media space. Jacqueline Aker, media director for the National Crime Prevention Council, said the Internet played an important role in helping her organization achieve its mission of educating the public about crime prevention, with 5,000 people a day visiting its Web site. An anti-crime campaign aimed at teen-agers has received what Ms. Aker described as exceptional placement on line because many teen-age-theme Web sites are wary of accepting excessive paid advertising. "Some sites like the Cartoon Network use our banners all the time," she said. "The creative makes a big difference, too. Our banners are really cool." They were fashioned by Saatchi & Saatchi, along with its interactive agency Darwin Digital, both of which are newyork units of Saatchi & Saatchi P.L.C. For all the good that such public-service advertisements do, some people still suggest that the incredible reach the Ad Council has achieved is a sign of a sluggish climate for advertisers on the Web. Wenda Millard, a council board member who is executive vice president of the on-line advertising network Doubleclick Inc., called that view cynical. "Not all inventory on the Internet is going to be valued by advertisers," she said. "Some of the top sites may be top sites based on traffic, but it might not all be desirable space. I think it's very natural that you'll have tons of open space. The barriers to entry for the Web are so phenomenally low that literally your grandmother can create a Web site." And if Grandma wants to put a public-service ad for the council-created character Smokey Bear on it, all the better. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Company Replaces Publisher at Boston Globe
body: The newyork Times Company announced today that one of its key executives had moved to Boston to succeed the publisher of The Boston Globe, a member of the family that had run that paper for 126 years. The new publisher, Richard H. Gilman, headed The Times's circulation department in newyork with the title of senior vice president for operations. He succeeds Benjamin B. Taylor, whose family sold The Globe five and a half years ago to The newyork Times Company, parent of the newspaper. In earlier assignments, Mr. Gilman, 48, was responsible for circulation, production and the development of operations like the new color printing plant at College Point, Queens. Mr. Taylor, 52, will remain chairman of the Globe Newspaper Company board. The directors of the Globe Company advise the management of The Globe newspaper. At meetings with top managers and the newsroom staff today, Mr. Gilman and Mr. Taylor did not specifically address questions about why the change was made, people at the meetings said. In an interview in his office today, Mr. Taylor said that the hardest question he was asked was why. "That's not an easy question to answer," he said. The shift in top management at The Globe was effective immediately. It came several months after Sunday circulation and the high-margin help-wanted advertising revenue began experiencing declines. It also came a year after newsroom turmoil surrounding the departure of two columnists: one who acknowledged fabricating material and another who was accused of plagiarism. In a statement today, Arthur Sulzberger Jr., chairman of the Times Company, said Mr. Taylor's "commitment to the newspaper, service to the community and dedication to quality journalism are unquestioned." In the same statement, Mr. Sulzberger said, "I know Rich Gilman will bring vision and leadership in the strongest traditions of The Globe and will be an outstanding publisher during a time of rapid change in the news industry." Mr. Gilman, joined The Times in 1983 and has held his current post since 1993. He earned an M.B.A. from the Harvard Business School and spent the first 10 years of his career as a reporter and editor at The Arizona Daily Star in Tucson. Sitting with Mr. Taylor in the publisher's office here, Mr. Gilman said that all decisions about The Globe's future would be generated locally. "Where we go from here -- all that needs to be developed in Boston," he said. In the newsroom, the prevailing reactions were surprise and sorrow. "I wasn't totally surprised that they would make a significant move, but I didn't expect Ben to be gone," said the newspaper's editor, Matthew V. Storin. Eileen McNamara, a columnist who has worked for The Globe about two decades, said: "It's an especially sad day to me when the man sitting in the front office is no longer connected to the city in the way the Taylor family always has been." The loss of local family control over community newspapers has been a trend in the industry for a generation or more, as large newspaper chains have bought out newspaper-owning families. When the Times Company bought The Globe in 1993, it agreed to make no management changes for five years -- a period that ended last year. Benjamin Taylor's cousin, William O. Taylor, was publisher at the time of the sale, and Arthur Sulzberger Jr.'s father, Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, was chairman and chief executive of the Times Company. This year, William O. Taylor announced he was retiring from the Times Company board. The issue of local control is felt particularly hard in this center of New England, a city whose prickly sense of self and pugnacious attitude toward newyork City are reflected in rivalries in spheres from sports to scholarship. Christopher Lydon, a former writer at both The Times and The Globe, who is now host of a radio program on WBUR-FM in Boston, said: "Boston is a franchise town now, as most American cities are. We don't own our own village conversation anymore. All the commercial media in Boston are owned or controlled by distant emperors." Wall Street's reaction to the management change was muted, if not negative. The Times Company stock closed at $38.75, down 93.75 cents, or 2.4 percent. Kevin R, Gruneich, a senior managing director at Bear, Stearns who follows the newspaper industry, described today's developments as "just an evolution in the relationship that the parent company has with The Boston Globe." He added: "I think that the integration of The Boston Globe into The newyork Times Company will be positive." In 1998, advertising revenues at The Globe rose to $449 million, an increase of just 1.8 percent from the previous year, while help-wanted advertising declined -- as it did in markets like Los Angeles, San Jose, Calif., and Dallas. In the same year, advertising revenue at The Times in newyork increased 7 percent. In the first quarter of 1999, advertising revenue at The Globe was down 2.5 percent from the previous year, while at The Times it was up 5.44 percent. One of the biggest concerns at The Globe in recent months has been the loss of Sunday circulation, which stands at 730,000. It declined 18,306, or 2.4 percent, between March 31, 1998, and March 31, 1999. Mr. Gilman said he planned no cutbacks in the news budget. "The Globe is a great newspaper, one of the best in America," he said. "The challenge for us is to find a way to preserve that." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Richard H. Gilman, right, a senior vice president at The newyork Times, is replacing Benjamin B. Taylor as publisher of The Boston Globe, which has been run by the Taylor family for more than a century. (John Blanding/The Boston Globe)

title:
Compressed Data;
E-Commerce Twist: Full-Service Shipping
body: Commercekey, an Internet start-up, has come up with a business plan with a new wrinkle in the crowded electronic commerce market. In addition to peddling software and transaction services to help businesses set up shop on the Web, the company, with roots in the Greek shipping industry, has its own world class fleet of cargo vessels standing by to deliver customers' merchandise around the world. The company, which is based in newyork and plans to announce itself later this week, is a joint venture between two Greek industrial giants, the Vardinoyannis Group of Companies and Leventis Group. Together, the two companies give Commercekey access to a huge fleet of freighters along with a network of climate-controlled warehouses throughout the world. Owning its own fleet of vessels could help Commercekey clear one of the big hurdles in electronic commerce: distribution. "We come from a tradition of merchants and bottlers," said Alkiviades David, president and chief executive of Commercekey, whose family has a major stake in Leventis. Vardinoyannis owns the biggest oil refinery in Greece, Motor Oil Hellas, along with numerous television stations, newspapers and Internet service providers. Leventis, meanwhile, is Greece's primary Coca-Cola distributor and also owns an Internet telecommunications network in Eastern Europe. Mr. David and Demosthenes N. Vardinoyannis, Commercekey's chairman, met while they were in high school in Switzerland many years ago. The idea for Commercekey grew, in part, out of a video conferencing venture Mr. David had started years ago; that technology has become a component of Commercekey's service offerings. Together the two companies have invested an initial $12.5 million in the unitedstates arm of Commercekey, and they plan to take the company public early next year.   LAURIE J. title:
TECHNOLOGY: E-Commerce Report;
As women start to use the Internet more for shopping, the prospects sharply improve for on-line retailers.
body: WHILE the E-commerce engine has been warming up in recent months, it remains fueled largely by the wallets of affluent men and computer geeks. That fuel, however, is about to receive a powerful additive: X chromosomes. Women are joining the Internet more quickly than ever, nearly erasing the gender gap among the medium's 92 million users. Perhaps more significant for the Internet economy, though, is the fact that the percentage of World Wide Web shoppers who are women has jumped the last 12 months, to 38 percent from 29 percent, according to a Commercenet/Nielsen Media Research study. Industry executives expect that presence to rise quickly in the next year, bringing with it opportunities in several categories and expanding E-commerce as a whole. "The early part of the E-commerce revolution was a revolution of rich white males," said Katherine Borsecnik, senior vice president for strategic business at America Online. "That's changing. And with 80 to 85 percent of household spending controlled by women, the total retail dollars involved in that change is very high." Of course, the immediate impact of that change will be felt in traditional female retail strongholds, said Fiona Swerdlow, an analyst with Jupiter Communications, the Internet research firm. Ms. Swerdlow forecasts that categories like apparel, health and beauty and toys will particularly benefit from a growing presence of women shoppers -- meaning sites like those for Gap, Lands' End, Estee Lauder's Clinique, eToys and Toys "R" Us should benefit. Not only will these categories benefit from first-time buyers, executives said, but they will also reap the fruits of higher spending from more experienced female Internet shoppers. Indeed, according to a survey by NFO Interactive conducted last week, women who shopped on the Internet in the last year said they planned to spend 20 percent more on line in the next year. The survey gathered responses from 880 unitedstates Internet users -- 437 of whom were women -- who said they had bought goods over the Web in the last 12 months. Travel and apparel are the most favored purchasing categories for female Internet shoppers, according to the survey. Women shoppers responding to the survey said they planned to spend, on average, $965 on travel and $783 on apparel on line, respectively, on those categories in the next year. The other on-line categories with the greatest growth potential among repeat buyers, according to NFO, include sports and fitness -- on which the women in the survey said they planned to spend an average of 71 percent more in the next 12 months than in the last. Others were food and drink (a projected spending rise of 27 percent), apparel and accessories (24 percent) and home and garden (13 percent). "I've always said the Internet would take off when women came on line, and it's true," said Marleen McDaniel, chief executive of Women.com, which offers information, shopping and advertising directed toward women. Women.com has catered to what Ms. McDaniel called characteristic shopping behavior among women -- in particular, a propensity to gather a great deal of information before making a purchase. "Women are avid consumers of information, and shopping is their passion," Ms. McDaniel said. Given that assumption, the site provides "tons of original content," she said, which women can use to make buying decisions. "We'll have an article on echinacea, within the subject of healing herbs," Ms. McDaniel said. "So we'll have a link next to it for colds, and what about echinacea makes it a remedy. Adjacent to that, we'll have an ad for a pharmacy that sells it. Then users can go to the community section of our site and ask a nutritionist, a woman doctor, when to take it. For advertisers, it's fantastic because you're catching a consumer right in flight." The payoff is apparent in the site's shopping figures, Ms. McDaniel said. According to @Plan, an Internet research firm, 51 percent of Women.com's audience had made purchases on the Internet in the last six months, more than 10 percentage points higher than the average for women on line. Retailers are also using gender-specific approaches to cash in on perceived differences in shopping behavior. "We do a lot of things to skew toward women," said Steve Hamlin, vice president of iQVC, which is the on-line arm of the Comcast Corporation's QVC home-shopping TV channel and whose clientele is 70 percent female. "Women enjoy the experience of shopping more than men, and are more willing to look at content and browse the site." For that reason, he said, areas of the site like the jewelry section and the wedding boutique include more editorial content and advisory features than, for instance, the area devoted to sporting goods. Mr. Hamlin also said that the site had seen a significant rise in computer electronics purchases by women since it began selling prebundled systems. "Women generally feel less confident when making these kinds of purchases," he said, "so they're more comfortable knowing that a certain scanner goes with a certain computer." Other sites take a more gender-neutral approach. Fingerhut, the Federated Department Stores subsidiary that wholly or partly owns several Web sites, including Andy's Garage and Mountainzone.com, "doesn't spend a lot of time looking at gender," said Andy Johnson, senior vice president for market development, even though 65 percent of Fingerhut's Internet shoppers are women. "We're trying to create processes to serve individual customers as much as they want, no matter their gender." Ms. Borsecnik, of America Online, takes a similar view. "A vast majority of what we do has nothing to do with gender," she said, noting that roughly 50 percent of the company's shoppers are women. "Our approach is more of a translation of what works off line to the on-line world." Because some retail categories that tend to attract women have not yet developed fully on line, the gender impact may not be felt immediately, Ms. Borsecnik noted. "Categories like house and garden hardly register among on-line shoppers, but off line, 25 to 30 percent of all purchases fall into that," she said. By contrast, Ms. Borsecnik said, music CD's account for 13 percent of all purchases made on America Online, while "music has to be less than 2 percent of off-line purchases." The growth in women shoppers may speed the maturation process for categories like house and garden, as companies rush to market -- once they know the dollars are there. At the same time, Ms. Borsecnik said, many merchants are already setting up shop in hopes that doing so will give a greater number of women reason to log on, ready to spend. "There's still an element," she said, "of 'build it and they will come.' title:
INVESTING;
Kaufmann's StarsTry To Regain the Heavens
body: SHAREHOLDERS of the Kaufmann Fund must wax nostalgic as they consider its recent performance and wonder if the fund's best days are behind it. Certainly, they remember years like 1991, when the fund returned 79 percent, outperforming its small-stock growth fund peers by 20 percentage points, on average. They remember when the stock-picking prowess of its managers, Hans Utsch and Lawrence Auriana, was so widely celebrated that their imprimatur could "make" a new issue. But they also remember January 1998, when the fund sold short Amazon.com. That decision, a bet that the stock's price would decline, cost the fund $85 million when the position was closed in January 1999. The miscalculation was all the more unnerving because it coincided with a slide in the fund's relative performance. Though investors may forgive management for underperforming the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index, since small-capitalization stocks have lagged behind larger stocks the last few years, they are no doubt frustrated by the fund's failure to capitalize on the surge in small stocks in the second quarter. While the average small-cap growth fund tracked by Morningstar Inc. gained 12.17 percent this year through June 30, the Kaufmann Fund declined 0.53 percent. That weakness dragged down the fund's three-year average annual return to 5.11 percent, little more than half the 9.39 percent average for its category. Mr. Auriana, 54, attributes the poor showing to a drift in the fund's investment style. In the aftermath of last summer's market turmoil, he said, "we got cautious." As such, the fund increased its investments in health care stocks last fall to 28 percent of the portfolio, versus an average weighting of 13.5 percent for small-cap growth stock funds, and pared back technology stocks to 15 percent, compared with the average of 29 percent. But the health care component of the Russell 2000 small-stock index fell 0.81 percent this year through June 30, while the technology sector forged ahead 17.92 percent. "We should have stayed true to our bottom-up style" of selecting stocks, Mr. Auriana said. The other problem, in Mr. Auriana's view, was the sharp rise in Internet stocks. Though Web stocks made up 9.3 percent of the Russell 2000 as of June 30, as calculated by Salomon Smith Barney, the fund owns none. But that, he said, "we don't regret one bit." He added, "We invest in profitable companies with clear business prospects." Still, he acknowledged, "shorting Internet stocks was wrong." But some believe that the fund's troubles go beyond style drift and Web-phobia. For one thing, said Michael Lipper, chairman of Lipper Inc., the fund research firm, the small-stock universe that Mr. Utsch, 62, and Mr. Auriana once mined so successfully is now filled with analysts, making it tougher for them to maintain an edge. And some critics contend that the pair allowed the fund to grow too large and unwieldy. Kaufmann's assets swelled from $40 million in 1990 to a peak of $6 billion in 1997, before shrinking to a still bulky $3.3 billion. "The last time Kaufmann ranked in the top 20 percent of its category was 1994," said Jeff McConnell, an analyst with Morningstar, when assets were $1.6 billion. To deploy all its money, Kaufmann has expanded the number of companies in which it invests and moved away from its micro-cap emphasis. The median market capitalization of stocks in the fund has grown to $1.96 billion -- almost six times the $327.7 million in 1994. Mr. Auriana says size has not weighed on the fund's performance. Stephen Savage, editor of The No-Load Fund Analyst, notes that Kaufmann's total expense ratio of 1.89 percent has cut into the fund's returns. "It wasn't an issue when the fund was doing well," he said. The average total expense ratio for small-cap funds tracked by Lipper Inc. is 1.418 percent. TO turn things around, Mr. Lipper thinks the fund needs to restructure its portfolio. Management could, for example, use losses to unlock long-term gains in some health care holdings, freeing money for more promising areas. In his view, "the fundamental issue is security selection." Cendant, Kaufmann's largest holding at 8 percent of assets, is a case in which stock selection has raised questions. Not only is Cendant a large-cap stock, but critics say that holding such a big position in the company means that Kaufmann has missed out on other opportunities.  Last year, Cendant's shares plummeted as low as $6.50 in the wake of an accounting scandal. But the fund bought more shares, reducing its average cost to less than $10 a share. Cendant has since recovered, closing Friday at $20.625. Mr. Auriana is comfortable with the stock, saying, "They have strong franchises, they generate lots of free cash flow, and the accounting problems are behind them." Moreover, he said, "in effect, we've taken Mr. Lipper's advice." The fund recently reduced health care to 17 percent of its assets by taking profits in long-time holdings like Steris and Cardinal Health. And it restored technology to 27 percent by, for example, increasing its position in Alpha Industries, a maker of integrated cellular-phone circuits. "We're comfortable with how the fund is positioned now," he said. The portfolio consists of profitable companies that he and Mr. Utsch believe are growing faster, and selling at cheaper price-earnings ratios, than the S.& P. 500. "We have a history of investing in good growth companies," Mr. Auriana said. "In no way have we altered our style." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Hans Utsch, left, and Lawrence Auriana plan adjustments, but no major change in investing philosophy, for the lagging Kaufmann Fund.
