title: Addition to Consumers' Arsenal: net Complaint Services for Hire
body: GIVEN the service economy's hire-someone-else mentality, which leads some people to pay others to walk the dog and tutor the children in baseball, it is no wonder that you can now hire Internet businesses to complain on your behalf. Sites like Complain.com and Fight Back promise to write letters, make phone calls and, if necessary, whine in exchange for a modest -- and sometimes not so modest -- fee. "A lot of people have tried to handle problems themselves, but they're frustrated and angry," said Bill Tran, president of Caveat Emptor (www.cemptor.com), which went on line in March. "They want to forget about it," Mr. Tran said. "That's when I jump in." One angry America Online customer, Elizabeth Huntington of Bradenton, Fla., failed to get an erroneous AOL charge canceled after three discussions with customer representatives over four weeks. "I don't think that business, especially AOL, takes me seriously," she said. She turned up Caveat Emptor (www.cemptor.com) by searching for "complaint" on the Web. A week after Caveat Emptor sent a letter, AOL returned $48 to Ms. Huntington, along with a refund for a $50 bank overdraft fee. "When they got the letter from me through Caveat, then they took me seriously," Miss Huntington said. She wouldn't have got her money back without Caveat Emptor, she said. Companies and clients say their specialized services are more effective than the efforts of a consumer working alone. "The reason the average person can't do this is that the average person does not have the kind of resources that we have," said David Horowitz, a consumer advocate who writes a "Fight Back" syndicated newspaper column and has a Web site at www.fightback.com. With Americans buying and spending more than ever, the inevitable result is more services, products and goods to complain about. In addition, customer satisfaction with technology products may be declining in the face of rising product quality, creating a rich customer base for the professional complainers. Some Web enterprises will complain for clients on a budget. The Consumer Complaint Resolution Company (www.complaintresolution .com) bills $29.95, or a 20 percent commission on the amount recovered. Fight Back will send out a letter personally signed by Mr. Horowitz for $25, a flat fee the company said covered administrative costs. Complain.com (www.complain.com) pleads a case for only $19.95. Caveat Emptor writes free complaint letters (but may start charging someday). A number of these sites, like Fight Back and Caveat Emptor, also have complaint bulletin boards for posting complaints publicly. The goal is to give companies and agencies an incentive to shape up. "This is a new way of handling it, where you can use the power of the Internet and the power of mass public exposure to resolve people's problems," Mr. Horowitz said. Specialized expertise can carry a hefty price tag. Gary and Sandy Rattigan of Somerville, Mass., started Complain to Us in 1997 (www .complaintous.com). They charge $50 per hour (and a 30 percent commission when larger sums are recovered). They say they have an overall success rate of about 80 percent. Ellen Phillips of Alexandria, Va., gave up teaching English in middle school last year to turn all her attention to her business, Ellen's Poison Pen (www.ellenspoisonpen.com). She recently raised her rates to $30 per 100 words and $65 per hour. Clients spend an average of $400 for her services. An Ellen's Poison Pen customer, Jamie Urick of Frankfort, Ill., explained, "If you have leg pain and you go to a physical therapist, you go to an expert -- it's the same thing." Mrs. Urick and her neighbors were frustrated that repeated pleas to state and county officials had resulted in no action against a noisy dirt bike track. Mrs. Phillips composed a biting letter whose recipients ranged from the county sheriff to the Governor of Illinois. The sheriff replied immediately. Even though the case cost the complainers $240 and may still end up in court, the residents said the sharp, professional tone of the letter was worth it. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Common Ground Elusive as Technology Have-Nots Meet Haves
body: FOR the average Internet user in the unitedstates, life is a never-ending stream of dilemmas: Upgrade now or later. Order I.S.D.N. or wait for cable modem service to arrive. Buy the Palm V organizer or go with the one that connects to the Web. Check email while on vacation or leave the laptop at home. But a conference held here in June underscored a very different reality: in many corners of the world, there are dozens of developing countries where widespread access to the Internet -- of any kind -- remains a distant possibility. While it is true that some of the earth's most remote places are now linked to the Net -- one recent addition is Bhutan, a small kingdom in the Himalayas, which inaugurated its first Internet link last month -- there are still no connections at all in Iraq, North Korea and a handful of African countries. In many countries that have Internet connections, Net access is concentrated in the largest cities and is prohibitively expensive when set against an individual's typical income. That expense largely restricts the use of the Internet to an elite, mostly made up of foreigners, government workers and business people. And in some cases, government censors put the Internet out of reach for most people in their countries. The conference here, called INET 99, was the annual meeting of the Internet Society, a nonprofit group that coordinates Internet-related projects around the world and has the motto "Internet Is for Everyone." Each year, the group holds a three-day conference; previous locations have included Prague, Montreal, Geneva and Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. This year, 1,600 network administrators, academics and business people gathered at the gleaming, cavernous San Jose Convention Center in the heart of Silicon Valley. That backdrop accentuated the fast-paced, high-risk, moneyed world of high technology, a world very far away from the everyday experiences of the people attending from developing nations. Many people at the conference, from places like Japan, Germany, Finland and the Netherlands, were sophisticated Internet users, concerned with cutting-edge technical issues. But many others were from countries where Internet connections are available to only a privileged few. "It created a sort of schizophrenia," said Will Foster, a research assistant at the University of Arizona in Tucson who attended the conference. "The presentations by Ebay and E*trade highlighted the tension between the go-go growth of Internet start-up companies in Silicon Valley and the realities of Internet connectivity in countries like Cameroon." Each year, a workshop is held for a week preceding the conference; this year, 143 people from 66 developing nations attended. It is aimed at sending participants home with additional technical and administrative skills for running networks. Those accepted for the workshop -- 570 people applied -- have basic technical skills. "They also have to have leverage within their organization, and the organization has to have leverage in the country -- for example, someone running networking for the major university in the country or within the P.T.T.," said George Sadowsky, the Internet Society's vice president for education, referring to the shorthand used for many countries' national telecommunications providers. The demographics of the workshop shift each year, as telecommunications needs change across the world. The first workshop, in 1993, had a large contingent of Eastern Europeans. This year, more than half of the participants were from Africa, which accounted for about 13 percent of the world's population but just 1 percent of the world's Internet users as of the end of March, according to data from Mike Jensen, a consultant with the Association for Progressive Communications, a nonprofit group based in Johannesburg. Excluding South Africa (where 1 in every 177 people uses the Internet), for every 4,123 Africans, there is just 1 person who uses the Internet, according to Mr. Jensen's figures. Wawa A. Ngenge, the national coordinator for the Sustainable Development Networking Program in Cameroon, said his country got its first Internet connection in 1997.  Internet service providers there pay the national phone company $3,000 per month for a 64-kilobits-per-second line, which is not much faster than the fastest dial-up modem; such slow speeds are common in developing countries and mean that I.S.P. customers must put up with very slow speeds. Just 15,000 people out of 15 million have Internet access, all of it concentrated in the capital, Yaounde. Using the Internet costs about $3 per hour in Cameroon, a country where the average civil servant makes about $200 a month, Dr. Ngenge said. One thing slowing the Internet's spread in developing countries is the fact that many governments there enjoy a telephone monopoly. Dr. Sadowsky said such governments feared that the Internet might reduce the revenue from international telephone calls and faxes. "Telecommunications rates are extraordinarily high," Dr. Sadowsky said. "In the worst case, the P.T.T. provides one-fifth of a country's G.N.P. Part of our work is in convincing countries that if you ignore the Internet, you'll keep your telephone revenues the same, but you'll pay in opportunity cost, in terms of economic and social development." Once the main conference began, those who had attended the workshop found little use for the general sessions, many of which focused on state-of-the-art wireless communications, E-commerce, venture capital and the development of Internet II. After a panelist at one session mentioned that 40 percent of all venture money was invested within a 40-mile radius of where he was sitting, a member of the audience asked about the prospects for venture capital investments in the developing world. "Remember, we're technology investors," the panelist answered politely. "They're so far away from us," Dr. Ngenge said of conference participants from wealthier countries. "We're worrying about two different sets of problems." One prominent set of problems is, of course, political. In Laos, for instance, the Communist government considers the Internet a destabilizing influence because of the free flow of information associated with the Web and keeps connections scarce, said Paula Uimonen, a Swedish researcher in Geneva who is studying the Internet in Laos and presented a paper at the conference. "It's obvious that it's a lack of political willingness," she said. In some countries, users who can connect to the Internet sometimes find that access to certain sites is blocked, according to Human Rights Watch. The group said that some Mideast countries, for example, blocked access to political sites under the guise of protecting users from pornography. Laos has had email since late 1994, Ms. Uimonen said, and got its first I.S.P. last year. There are 1,000 Internet users, most of whom are foreigners. There are two cybercafes in the capital, Vientiane, but Laotians are not allowed in. The connection of Myanmar, formerly Burma, to the Internet remains similarly tenuous. All modems must be registered with the government, which is run by the military, Dr. Sadowsky said. Neither Laos nor Myanmar had representatives at the conference. Immigration policies can make it hard for people to get to the conference. Two Cubans were invited to participate in the workshop, but one was not given a visa and because of that, the other stayed home. A person from Sudan was registered for the conference and had a visa but was detained by the Immigration and Naturalization Service in newyork, then sent back to Sudan. A 24-year-old network administrator from Hanoi named Tuan Bui Anh arrived in California without incident. He said Vietnam got its first Internet connection in late 1997. Before that, computer users could send email but could not go out on the Web. Net Nam, the main I.S.P., and four other service providers have connections concentrated in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City. E-commerce has yet to make an impression in places like Vietnam, where few people have credit cards. Following a keynote speech given by Meg Whitman, chief executive of the Ebay auction site, Mr. Tuan seemed a bit bewildered. "I think this is for the Americans only," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Students studying computers in Hanoi, Vietnam, in 1995. People in developing countries often find it hard to get Internet access. (Fuminori Sato/Impact Visuals)

title:
DOWNTIME;
World Wide Banks: On-Line Financial Choices Grow
body: JACK JACKSON can't remember the last time he wrote a check and hasn't spoken face to face with a bank teller in years. Mr. Jackson has handled his personal banking on line with Bank Boston since 1989, and he expanded to on-line banking for his public relations business three years ago. Although he experienced two instances of bank errors that cost him several hours on the phone with customer service, that has not deterred him from banking on line. "I think I've had to deal with the best and worst that it has to offer," Mr. Jackson said. "It's easy to set up and it can be incredibly convenient, but anyone who has really bad financial habits may find that their problems will be exacerbated when they go on line. It's definitely not for everyone." One big difference with many on-line banking accounts is that as soon as you direct the bank to send out a payment from your account, that money's gone. You can't mail out a $50 check and figure that you can get to the bank to deposit the money to cover the check before it's presented by the recipient's bank for payment. But one thing on-line customers gain is convenience -- the bank's always open for business. A few years ago, Mr. Jackson was unusual. Although some of the largest banks in the country, including Wells Fargo, Citibank and Chase Manhattan, have offered their customers on-line bill-payment options for nearly a decade, only during the last couple of years have customers really started to warm to the idea of clicking on the Send button at an on-line banking site. According to IDC, a market research firm in Framingham, Mass., the number of people in the unitedstates participating in at least one on-line banking function (like viewing deposits, transferring money between accounts and paying bills) rose to 12.4 million in 1999 from 1.4 million in 1996. IDC expects that number to rise to 18.7 million by the end of next year. Industry analysts cite the widespread availability of modem-equipped computers as one reason for the increase in on-line banking activity. They add that people are also finally starting to get comfortable with the notion that entering bank account information on line is no riskier than giving a credit card number over the phone. "On-line trading has really made people aware of how to bank on line," said Mitch Caplan, president of Telebank, a phone- and Internet-based bank. "The security issues aren't really there any more." But while on-line trading offers discount services, many banks charge more for on-line accounts. It has become much more convenient to pay bills and transfer money to other accounts via computer because many banks are moving their entire on-line consumer banking areas onto the Internet and off private networks, which required the customer to use communications software and a modem to dial directly into a company's computer system. To pay bills on line with Chase in 1994, for example, a customer had to call Chase's customer service and order software disks for logging onto a private network. Since Chase moved its on-line banking functions to the Internet last February, on-line customers have been able to gain access to their accounts from any PC with an Internet connection by going to the bank's Web site and punching in an identifying name and password. So what should you expect if you wean yourself from your checkbook? Setting up access to your bank account via the Internet is relatively simple. After securing your bank accounts with a customer ID and a password, you enter the account numbers and addresses of each company or person you pay regularly. As long as you can provide that information, you can send payments to large companies (like your cable and credit card companies) as well as to individuals, like your piano teacher. Some banks charge a monthly fee, usually $5 to $15, for unlimited bill payments, but many are providing Internet banking access and bill payments at no extra charge. The convenience of on-line banking has won some fans, like Lisa and Alex Giassa of Teaneck, N.J., who have had an on-line account since August 1998. "It's definitely a convenience thing for us," Ms. Giassa said. "If I know I have a bill due in a few days, I can go upstairs, pay it in a couple of minutes and not deal with any envelopes." But lest you think that the click of a Send button will instantaneously send off your son's college tuition payment on the day it is due, think again. Only about half of electronic payments are actually transmitted to recipients electronically. Many utility companies and merchants are not set up to receive electronic payments. Such companies are sent checks via regular mail -- an annoying lesson for those who don't make allowances for the delayed delivery and miss payment deadlines. And that delay brings up the question of the "float" and why there's more of a float in electronic banking. In banking terms, a float is the period between the time you issue a check and the time it becomes available to the recipient. If you issue a check to an out-of-state recipient, the money will not be credited to the account of that company or person for up to five business days after the check gets to the recipient's bank. A recipient in the same state gets access to the money in up to three business days after it is deposited, while someone with an account at the same bank will get the money within one business day. If you have a regular checking account and issue a check, the money won't be deducted until it is presented to your bank by the recipient's bank for payment. But for many electronic accounts, the bank automatically debits your on-line account soon after you hit the button to instruct the bank to issue a check out of your account. "The float is a big psychological issue for a lot of people," said Jim Bruene, editor of Online Banking Report, an industry newsletter. "The tighter someone's funds are, the more he or she relies on it. None of this is very meaningful when you're making 2 percent interest on cash balances." The fact that some organization -- sometimes a bank, sometimes a check-processing company -- is able to hang onto your money for the length of the float means that it can make money off your money, in very short-term investments. Even though a payment is taken out of an on-line account right away, that doesn't necessarily mean that the recipient of the money is paid quickly. For example, Philip Goodman, a film and video producer in Manhattan, paid a friend $25 out of his Chase Online checking account. His checking account was debited quickly, but the money did not show up in the recipient's account for three days, Mr. Goodman said. "They say it's electronic, but it's not," he complained. "They debit your account and then send a check. I can send a check!" Most on-line banks use third-party check consolidators like Checkfree to process the checks from on-line accounts, send them along and disburse the money. In those cases, the bank pays Checkfree the amount of the check, and Checkfree pays the company or person receiving the check. If the check recipient is set up to receive payments electronically, through a process known as electronic transfer, the payments move through an automated clearing-house system within 24 hours, said Matthew Lewis, a senior vice president at Checkfree. But if the recipient is not set up to receive payments electronically, Checkfreemails a check to the recipient's bank, where it is processed in a transaction that can take up to five business days if the payment crosses state lines. The Federal Reserve is not sure about on-line banking's effect on the float. "We've tried to do what we can to manage float, but whatever happens with the electronic technology is still an unknown at this point," said Doug Tillet, a spokesman for the newyork Federal Reserve Bank. Knowing that money is paid out of an account right away can help on-line customers if they want to make last-minute electronic payments, he added. If the recipient of a payment is set up to receive electronic transfers, most on-line banking customers can issue a payment at, say, 4:59 P.M. on the day the payment is due and won't have to allow for mail delivery times. According to Bank Rate Monitor, an on-line service that tracks interest rates for credit cards and personal loans offered by major banks, at least 215 of the 350 largest Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation-insured banks in the country offer the ability to pay bills electronically. But bill consolidators like Checkfree are also providing electronic payment services to nontraditional banks on the Internet, which means your choice of where on the Internet to pay your bills is becoming a lot broader. Internet-only banks can be a good choice for people who keep a lot of money in their checking accounts because they generally pay higher interest, but they also tend to charge higher fees for automated teller machines. Personal and business financial software like Quicken and Microsoft Money offer an electronic bill-paying option via Checkfree. Customers can also use such software, which gives a user an overall financial picture, with many types of on-line accounts. In addition to bill payments, Checkfree and other consolidators, like Transpoint and Cybercash, are also working with banks and other financial sites to bring your bills and account information to you on line. With its E-card, First U.S.A., a leading credit card issuer, offers customers on-line access to detailed information about their credit card purchases as well as the ability to pay their bills on line. Many banks are finding ways to let customers see their bills on line as a way of offering better service than the nontraditional banking competitors who are zeroing in on their business. A type of bill-presentment service was recently announced by Chase Manhattan Bank, First Union and Wells Fargo; they are forming a new company that will enable people and businesses to both receive and pay bills electronically. The company, called the Exchange, will serve as an electronic hub that will allow companies issuing bills to reach consumers through their financial institutions. Consumers will be able to log on to their on-line banking site and view lists of their outstanding bills, said Sharon Osberg, executive vice president for financial services at Wells Fargo. The three banks will have a customer base of 60 million and almost 60,000 corporations, said Wendy Grover, a spokeswoman for Wells Fargo. Ms. Osberg added that by the time the Exchange was fully up and running next year, all electronic payments would be settled on the day they were issued, effectively eliminating any float. But whether an electronic overdue notice will be easier to ignore than a piece of paper that says "account past due" in red letters on it remains to be seen.  Things to Bear in Mind  Here are some questions to ask yourself when you consider banking on line, along with some points to bear in mind if you decide to sign up:1  * Where do you pay your bills? If it's at home on the kitchen table, can you just as easily get to a computer? If you have computer access only at the office, you may not feel comfortable having bills scattered all over your desk.  * Are most of your bills to the same businesses or people every month? If so, banking on line would enable you to set up repeat payments that would automatically pay out on a particular day each month, saving you a lot of time. If you tend to do business with different people, stores and companies and you don't mind addressing envelopes, you might want hang on to your checkbook.  * Do you foresee paying bills and transferring funds on line? Or would you use the service primarily to check your balances? If the latter is true, your bank's automated phone service will give you the information much faster than you'll be able to retrieve it by going on line.  * When you sign up for an Internet checking or savings account, have your password mailed to you via regular mail, not E-mail. It's a good idea to have a hard copy of documentation on your accounts from the bank in case any discrepancies occur.  * If your bank switches from a private dial-up network to the Internet, download all your account balances and the account numbers of the people and businesses you pay regularly before you make the switch.  * If you regularly receive more than one bill from the same company (for example, cable bills for two different residences from the same cable service provider or two different phone bills from the same phone company), be sure to enter the number for each account on your recipient list in such a way that you'll be able to tell them apart. Otherwise, you might pay the wrong amounts to the wrong accounts -- mistakes that could take you hours to rectify.  * Avoid installing or downloading on-line banking software or setting up an on-line account outside normal business hours. Although some banks have technical support around the clock, most do not.  * You may want to wait a few weeks before downloading or installing upgraded software from your bank to avoid any early glitches. When you do download or install an upgrade, keep a backup of the program and your financial data on a storage disk or a separate computer. * Reconcile your accounts as frequently as you would with paper-based banking. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: AT THEIR FINGERTIPS -- Lisa and Alex Giassa, shown at home in Teaneck, N.J., are among many people signing up for on-line banking. (Norman Y. Lono for The newyork Times)

title: G.M. Internet Sales Hit Snag in Texas
body: The General Motors Corporation, the world's largest auto maker, has been denied a license to sell used cars directly to Houston customers through the Internet because Texas does not let manufacturers own or control dealerships. G.M.'s Driversite program was denied a license to transfer titles for used vehicles in a June 29 letter from the Texas motor vehicles division to Ross Hendrix, G.M.'s director of used-car retail operations. The denial was reported in Automotive News, a weekly trade publication. Some Houston-area dealers have resisted the test of the Driversite program, which would let customers buy three-year-old vehicles on the Internet and take delivery from two or three company-owned sites in Houston. The dealers were upset because commissions were not going to be paid to them during the test. G.M. was given 20 days from June 29 to request a hearing on the denial. It has not yet done so. The company leased and prepared a Houston site for Driversite and hoped to open it this month. G.M. has identified two other sites it expected to open this month or in early August. The Ford Motor Company, the No. 2 auto maker, is testing a program in four cities to sell returned lease cars to customers through the Internet. Customers pay $300 to order a vehicle, which is then delivered to a nearby dealership. The dealer completes the sale and gets a commission from Ford based on the purchase price, which is not negotiable. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Higher-Speed Lines Leave Door Ajar for Hackers
body: ABOUT two weeks after Frank Keeney was first connected to cable modem service in Pasadena, Calif., he discovered that along with the delights of a 24-hour connection and high-speed Internet access came the potential for big trouble. "I went to log in and found that someone had compromised my computer," he recalled. "When you log into a Linux system, it will normally show a short message stating the last time logged in and from where. Since I had not logged in for a week or so, I knew there was trouble. I checked to see if someone else was on line and, sure enough, he was on at the same time. "I tried to kill his log-in session, but it was too late. He had already issued the command to erase every file on the computer. I watched while he erased everything on my hard drive." Mr. Keeney's experience is not isolated, several computer security experts said. The shift from dial-up Internet connections to cable modems and D.S.L. (digital subscriber lines -- fast, constant links to the Net that use telephone lines) are making home computer users vulnerable to the types of attacks from hackers that in the past were almost exclusively a worry for corporations. "Most people aren't thinking at this level yet," said Christopher W. Klaus, chief technology officer for Internet Security Systems, an Atlanta-based maker of complex security analysis software used by large corporations. "Service providers are looking at trying to put as many people on the Internet as possible. The more security isn't brought up as an issue, the greater the problems." Cable modems and D.S.L. lines are presenting two new problems for ordinary residential users. The biggest source of trouble comes simply because these lines mean that users are constantly connected to the Net, so their computers are always potential targets of hackers.. The second problem has to do with the types of connections used by faster lines. Communications between computers on the Internet rely on a series of numbers known as I.P., or Internet protocol, addresses. For dial-up users, those addresses are constantly shifting, making them their computers elusive targets. While it can be a nuisance to dial in to reach the Net every time you want to check your email, the practice automatically provides its own measure of security. Unfortunately the protection afforded by the dial-up shell game largely or completely vanishes with cable modems or D.S.L. lines. Because their customers don't flit on and off the Net, many high speed service operators give them fixed I.P. addresses. While they may not be publicizing their new services' security problems with the vigor they bring to boasting about the more desirable features, cable modem and D.S.L. providers acknowledge that their residential customers are facing new kinds of security woes -- even if personal computers, of course, are less likely to be the targets of hackers than are corporate or government systems. "Where we are today, from a consumer standpoint, is where companies were back in the late 80's, when firewalls weren't a big issue," said Kevin McElearney, vice president of network support services at Road Runner, a cable modem partnership that includes Time Warner Entertainment, the Mediaone Group, Microsoft, Compaq and Advance/Newhouse. Residential customers using high-speed services, he said, "are in an environment where they have to realize that there are security issues." "Your risk is increased the longer you leave any computer connected," he said. "We're learning together in this new world of always being on line in the home," said Jeff Waldhuter, director of technology and engineering at Bell Atlantic Science and Technology Center, the research branch of the telephone company and D.S.L. service provider. "Now that we're getting on with these connections, we're learning that we have to add more security. We're growing up. These networks are going to be vulnerable." The move to the always-connected world seems to have come at a somewhat inopportune time. Internet Security Systems has been tracking a "dramatic increase" in the use of a hacking technique known variously as probing, sniffing or scanning, Mr. Klaus said. Probing software automatically scans computers connected to the Internet and evaluates the level of their security protection, looking for weak systems vulnerable to easy attack. "It's not uncommon to have someone twist the doorknob of your home computer," Mr. McElearney said. For probers, a typical home computer running Apple's Mac OS or Windows 95 or 98 without the maker's latest security updates or additional security software is the closest thing to an unlocked door they are likely to find. After his hard drive disaster, Mr. Keeney installed security software on his computer in Pasedena that tracks and records break-in attempts by probing software. He has found that unwanted visitors test his computer's security about twice a day. "Most computers on cable modems will be probed," he said. "If weaknesses are found, someone will exploit them." Unlike people who create and spread viruses or worms, probers don't need the computer's owner to advance their cause inadvertently by, say, opening a tainted email attachment. For them, an insecure system offers seemingly endless potential. Mr. Keeney's hard drive crash is an extreme example of what hackers can do once inside a computer. But others can cause just as much harm even though they come and go without leaving an immediate trace. Among other things, Mr. Sullivan said, once hackers gain entry they can extract credit card numbers from stored files, read email, copy files, send email over your name -- "in short, just about anything," he added. Most cable and D.S.L. modems also make it easier for hackers to go after specific computers. In dial-up systems, the addresses belong to the service provider's modems, rather than to its customers. When customers dial in for a connection, each one gets an I.P. address of the modem reached for that session; each modem is associated with a finite number of I.P. addresses. The next time the computer may well connect with another modem and get another address, particularly if the customer has a large service provider operating huge banks of modems. "To some extent that's security through obscurity," Mr. McElearney said. For cable-modem and D.S.L. customers, not only are their addresses fixed, they are also often easy to learn. The addresses appear in the headers (which usually aren't displayed) that travel with every email message or newsgroup posting customers send. Many service providers have begun to respond to the problem. Some, including Road Runner, are introducing a system that regularly rotates their customers' I.P. addresses. Addresses based on this system, however, may not change for several days and will still appear in the headers. Mr. Klaus is also distressed about one unintended side effect of the steep decline in computer prices. Inexpensive PC's increasingly mean that some families now own several computers, all of which can be serviced by a single high-speed line. To take advantage of that, some people are setting up mini-networks in their homes, with one computer acting as the go-between to the Internet for all the others. The proxy server software that makes that possible, however, often has very flawed security measures, Mr. Klaus said. To obscure their identities, sophisticated hackers will first log into a home network software before launching an attack against their ultimate target. Junk-mail spammers can resort to the same trick. In either case, the result can be highly embarrassing for the unsuspecting home network owner, who will appear to be the originator of the hacking or spam. Right now, there is not a straightforward answer to the question of how to guarantee security while enjoying high-speed Internet connections. For Larry Rogers, who tracks Internet security problems at Carnegie Mellon University's CERT Coordination Center, part of the solution is simply hard work. "People with these connections need to play systems administrator," he said. "It's a matter of vigilance." That vigilance can include something as simple as having Windows users make sure that Network Neighborhood -- a file-sharing system -- is turned off. Mr. Rogers also suggested steps like regularly downloading software security patches from Microsoft's Web site or modifying arcane portions of the operating system. Not surprisingly, these are just the kind of housekeeping tasks that many users somehow never get around to. Some software companies are offering their help. In May, Sybergen Networks (www.sygate.com), which mostly makes corporate security protection software, introduced a $29.95 software package for home users called Syshield. Similar products include Conseal Private Desktop by Signal 9 Solutions (www.signal9.com). Such software generally blocks the computer from receiving some types of data, limiting the paths in for hacker. Syshield can also be set up to in effect disconnect the computer from the Internet late at night. The ultimate protection is that now used by Mr. Keeney, who has become a computer-security consultant since his 1997 attack. He has copied, on a much smaller scale, the system used by most corporations. All his Internet business now runs on a network with a single computer operating as a firewall and using the Linux software system. Because it is difficult for hackers to get past the firewall computer in such set-ups, that computer acts as a sacrificial lamb of sorts. Mr. Keeney freely admits, however, that most home users are unlikely to adopt such a complex setup. If the speculation in the industry is correct, they may never have to. Many believe that "security appliances" -- extremely stripped-down computers with security software that sit between another computer and its Internet connection -- may eventually hit the consumer market. Such systems for business users are already available. Of course, another answer would simply be to put up with the slow speeds and petty annoyances of a dial-in modem. But for anyone but the more basic email user, Mr. Klaus does not think that is a great idea. "There are too many benefits that outweigh the security risks, provided you take precautions," he said. To prove his point, Mr. Klaus added that he was now shopping for cable modem service for his home. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: ONCE BURNED -- Frank Keeney has increased security on his computer system. (Edward Carreon for The New York Times)(pg. G1)  Diagram: "How Safe Are You?" How computer users connect to the Internet  DIAL-UP -- Computers use numerical I.P. addresses to communicate over the Internet. With dial-up service, an I.P. address is assigned each time the user dials in.  The next time, the user reaches a different modem and the address changes.  CABLE MODEM OR D.S.L. -- With new, higher-speed cable modems and D.S.L., many users get fixed I.P. addresses. Users often keep their computers connected to the Internet constantly, making them more vulnerable to hackers.  What the hacker tries to do Hackers use probing "sniffer" software that scans computers connected to the Internet, evaluates their security and attempts to attack weak systems. Hackers can also go after specific computers by obtaining the fixed I.P. addresses that are included in email or newsgroup postings by users of cable modems or D.S.L.  Beating back the hacker Among the steps users can take to frustrate hackers:  -- Downloading security patches or purchasing protection software.  -- In a home network, setting up one computer as a firewall, without valuable data, that hackers cannot get past. Inexpensive, stripped-down computers may eventually be available to do the same thing.  -- Disconnecting the computer from the Internet when not needed. Some software can be set up to do this automatically. (pg. G8)

title: NEWS WATCH
body: SUMMER BOOK CLUB -- Public libraries learned long ago that if you want to get children to read books over the summer, you probably need to dangle a prize before their eyes. Now a new Web site called Book Adventure has brought the same concept to the Internet. The site, www.bookadventure.com, offers prizes to children who earn points for successfully answering on-line questions about the books they have read. Points can be redeemed for prizes, like gift certificates to Barnesandnoble.com. "We want it to be self-motivating," said Brent McCallister, program director for the site, which is sponsored by the Sylvan Educational Foundation, a nonprofit organization based in Baltimore. "This is a great way to harness the power of the Web in a safe, educational way." BASEBALL ACTION -- Baseball fans who cannot tear themselves away from their computers can still catch each pitch and play of next Tuesday's All-Star Game as it happens by logging on to www.majorleaguebaseball.com and clicking on the Sportsline USA's Baseball Live feature. Baseball Live uses animated illustrations to add depth to coverage along with chat forums and troves of statistics. For fans abroad, it may be the best alternative to watching on TV. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Seek -- but on the Web, You Might Not Find
body: Search engines just cannot keep up with the Web. That is the finding of two scientists for the NEC Research Institute who have spent the past six months determining how many Web pages exist -- and how many are actually picked up by the likes of Alta Vista and Yahoo. Their results, which are published today in the journal Nature, paint a meager picture: Of 11 search engines studied, not one indexes more than 16 percent of the Web. Most cover less. "Search engines are increasingly falling behind in their efforts to index the Web," wrote Steve Lawrence and C. Lee Giles, the scientists who conducted the study. In a similar study two years ago, the researchers found that the largest coverage of a single search engine, Hotbot (www.hotbot.com), was 34 percent of the Web. The results of the current study, which are available at www.wwwmetrics.com, show that Northern Light (www.northernlight.com) has the largest coverage, with an index that contains 16 percent of Web pages that can be indexed. Lycos (www.lycos.com) and Euroseek (www.euroseek.net) appeared to have the least, covering only 2.5 percent and 2.2 percent, respectively. The study revealed more about the state of the Web, particularly about how much has become commercial: 83 percent of sites contain commercial content while only about 6 percent contain scientific and educational content. Only 1.5 percent have pornography, a figure that might surprise many Web surfers. The researchers also found that people who are searching for information that is less well known are probably missing out because some search engines use the popularity of Web pages to determine whether they should be indexed. To begin their research, Dr. Lawrence and Dr. Giles estimated the size of the Web. Their tally: 2.8 million sites and 800 million pages. They then used an automated program to plug 1,050 queries into each search engine and tabulate the results. The queries, which included phrases like "smart matter" and "rocchio algorithm," were obtained from a list of queries used by their fellow scientists at the NEC Research Institute. "These are not representative of general Web users," Dr. Lawrence acknowledged in an interview. "But the important issue here is that the search engines seem to be biased toward more well-known information." What's more, they are probably finding information that is out of date. Even the newest pages retrieved from the search engines were as many as eight months old, according to the researchers' data. For those seeking a way out, Dr. Lawrence suggested conducting a metasearch -- one that combines the results of several search engines. He hesitated to suggest specific names, but a search on the word metasearch in Hotbot turned up these: www.metacrawler.com, www .metasearch.com and www.dogpile.com. Of course, who knows what else might be out there?   LISA GUERNSEY http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Web Watching" Most search engines cover only a small percentage of the 800 million Web pages that are open to the public, according to the NEC Research Institute.
