Billings were estimated at $8 million to $10 million. Charles Gamble, president and chief operating officer at Digital Satellite in Dallas, said the decision came after a four-month review that had been narrowed to Richards and two other finalists he declined to identify. Richards will handle branding duties, and Click Here, its interactive division, will handle Web site design and on-line advertising duties. And Young Adult Professional Associates in Syracuse, which operates a Web-based community aimed at young professionals, awarded its new account to Moody Communications in newyork. Billings were estimated at $5 million.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: 3-Week Delay In Opening Up Internet Name Registration
body: The protracted effort to introduce competition into the lucrative business of registering Internet addresses has been delayed for at least three weeks because of escalating tensions among the Clinton Administration, its handpicked successor for running the global network and the Government contractor that has had a monopoly on the business. The delay is just the latest sign that the debate on the issue -- which has previously been confined largely to Internet insiders -- is quickly turning into a high-profile, high-stakes political game of chicken, the results of which could lead to a dangerous tug-of-war over what is essentially the Internet's telephone directory. The dispute centers on the move to break up Network Solutions Inc.'s hold on the business of registering the so-called domain names that people use as Internet addresses in the popular directories of .com, .net and .org. The company has had the exclusive worldwide right to assign Internet addresses that end in any of those three-letter suffixes since 1993. Last year, in what was to be the final step in a decadelong process transferring control of the Internet to the private sector, the Commerce Department created the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, or Icann, to oversee the network. Icann's charge was to open up the registration of Internet addresses to competition. But the creation of Icann and just about everything its interim board has proposed have stirred opposition and controversy. The latest delay comes on the heels of both a letter-writing campaign by Ralph Nader and tax watchdog groups and an inquiry from the chairman of the powerful House Commerce Committee, Representative Thomas J. Bliley Jr., questioning the actions and the authority of the Commerce Department and Icann. The potential fallout of the dispute threatens both the centralized structure of the Internet and the ability of Icann to carry out its task. "It's great political theater," Michael M. Roberts, the interim president of Icann, said of the intense lobbying from both sides that has moved both to Capitol Hill and high levels of the Clinton Administration. Mr. Roberts said discussions about the dispute and its potential effect on how the Internet operates have reached both the Pentagon and the President's Critical Infrastructure Assurance Office. Those questioning Icann say they are concerned that the interim board is overstepping its authority. They have seized on the board's refusal to hold open board meetings and its decision to impose a $1-a-year fee on every domain name registered. Representative Bliley, a Virginia Republican, sent blistering letters to the Commerce Secretary William M. Daley and Esther Dyson, the interim chairwoman of Icann, on Tuesday. That was the same day a special Congressional commission, headed by Gov. James Gilmore of Virginia, convened its first meeting on Internet tax policy in Williamsburg, Va. Mr. Bliley's accompanying news release offered a preview of the potential political fallout some fear could find its way into the campaigns against Vice President Al Gore, who has positioned himself as a champion of a tax-free, unregulated Internet. "Isn't this ironic," Mr. Bliley said, "just as Governor Gilmore is working hard with the Advisory Commission on Electronic Commerce to encourage the growth of electronic commerce, Icann is imposing a tax on the Internet behind closed doors." Mr. Bliley's letters ask for records and information about the process used to select Icann's interim board members and set its $5.9 million budget, as well any analysis of its legal authority to levy the $1 fee. The letters also seek information about statements Icann officials made threatening to terminate the authority of Network Solutions, a Virginia company, to register new Internet addresses during its last meeting, in Berlin. After that threat, Network Solutions began a full-scale lobbying effort in Washington, seeking an investigation of Icann. Icann, meanwhile, has accused the company of "funding and otherwise" fostering much of the criticism. Although Icann has since acknowledged that only the Commerce Department has the authority to cut off Network Solutions' right to register domain names, the company is also deadlocked with Commerce officials over crucial details for opening its registry to full-scale competition. One of five companies picked in April for the first round of competition with Network Solutions, Register.com, has been successfully registering names for several weeks. And Icann and the Commerce Department had hoped to open the system to more companies on Friday. Instead, they announced the three-week delay, and people close to the process said that they expected it to drag on even longer. Besides making sure that the technical bugs can be worked out to insure that the $20 million system that Network Solutions built will run smoothly when multiple competitors come on line, the two sides remain deadlocked on key issues that were supposed to have been ironed out months ago. The major question is who has rights to the Network Solutions data base that holds the information about who owns the more than five million registered domain names. They are also wrangling over how much the companies entering the business will have to pay Network Solutions to administer the central registry. Network Solutions also must reach an agreement on terms under which it will recognize Icann's authority. Network Solutions has refused to sign the contract Icann has developed, saying it is overly restrictive and gives Icann more power than the Administration intended when it drafted its plan for handing Internet oversight to the private, nonprofit body. Mr. Roberts, meanwhile, insists that if Network Solutions refuses to compromise, the Commerce Department and Icann could find another company to take over administration of .com., .net and .org. But that could not be done quickly or easily and would likely cause some disruptions for Internet users and electronic commerce. Such a scenario could also force a split in the root of the Internet, which is essentially the phone book of the Internet. Mr. Roberts said Icann was preparing to move the main root server for the network from Network Solutions' headquarters in Herndon, Va., to California. But unless Network Solutions agrees to hand over the corresponding data for that root, it might not immediately be able to find all of the names that Network Solutions has registered. That could create chaos on the Internet because computer users or their Internet service providers would have to know the so-called IP address of any site they wanted to visit or send email to, for example, 204.177.154.13 instead of www.amazon.com. Network Solutions, meanwhile, could continue running its own root server, meaning Internet service providers would have to either choose between the roots, set up their systems to recognize both or create their own roots. Becky Burr, a senior Commerce Department aide leading the negotiations, said she remained optimistic that the problems would be resolved without such drastic measures. "I believe that we'll get there," she said on Friday. "I believe it is in everybody's best interest not to swing threats around." Others are not so sure. A group of Internet technical experts has begun talking about what the Internet might look like without a central root system -- and without Icann. Karl Auerbach, a video network developer for Cisco Systems Inc. who has been involved in the Internet's engineering task force for years, says he does not think a split root would be such a bad thing. He said a split would essentially force Internet service providers to create a competing list of directories, much like telephone companies do. "What would result is that each of the root systems would try to be more inclusive than its neighbors, and the net result would be that they all end up being essentially the same as everybody," he said. "The number to Fred's Barber Shop would still be the number to Fred's Barber Shop." Such a system, he said, could also allow Internet service to cater to certain cultural or age groups, meaning they could set their directories to keep their customers Web browsers from reaching certain sites that they might find offensive. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Media Talk;
Report on Television,Rebuttal on the Web
body: The concept of letters to the editor has new meaning on the Internet, where email reactions can fly back and forth almost instantly. Now CBS News has added another twist, posting a lengthy list of objections from the subject of one of its investigative reports on Cbsnews.com, the news division's World Wide Web site. The aggrieved party, Charter Behavioral Health Systems, the nation's largest chain of psychiatric hospitals, was the subject of a "60 Minutes II" special report, by Ed Bradley, on abuses of children in some of the hospitals. The report ran on April 21 and was repeated on June 16, with CBS reporting that Charter had closed the North Carolina hospital that was prominently featured. But Charter, saying the report had several unfair or inaccurate elements, sent CBS a videotaped statement from its chief medical officer, Dr. Gary Henschen, and a lengthy document detailing those elements and asking CBS to correct its statements on the air. Instead, CBS News posted Charter's lengthy complaint on its Web site, adding its own rebuttals to each Charter point (www.cbs.com/flat/story_161689.html). "It's a very comprehensive response to their objections," said David Gelber, the producer of the investigative report on Charter. "We didn't feel any of their objections were valid. If we felt we had made a mistake, we would have addressed it in the broadcast." But Karen Jenkins, a spokeswoman for Charter, said the Web site had not displayed all the documentation Charter had sent to CBS, and she noted that the Web posting would not reach the great majority of people who saw the broadcast on television. "At least it allows the public to see there are two sides to the story," she said. "But we were disappointed that our response did not get on as part of the broadcast." In closing the June 16 program, Mr. Bradley told viewers about the Charter response and described how to find the CBS News Web site where they could read the accusations and rebuttals "exactly as they appear in our correspondence with Charter." Spokesmen for Abcnews.com and Msnbc.com said neither of those sites had been used for such exhaustive complaint and rebuttal. But they said that they did get plenty of email and that journalists responded to most of it -- making letters to the editor interactive. Merrill Brown, editor in chief of Msnbc.com, said most reporters' bylines were "hot," meaning a reader can click on a byline and send an email message to that reporter. "The response rate, especially of aggrieved parties, is incredibly fast," Mr. Brown said. "We've had cases where we posted a story at 7 P.M., and at 7:05, there's a response in my in box." "The mere fact of having hot bylines keeps our feet to the fire all the time," he said.   LAWRIE MIFFLIN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: CBS News put a reply on this site.

ELECTRONIC commerce companies have spent millions trying to make their sites more "personal," with technology that allows them to customize their product offerings to a particular shopper's needs, and software that automatically responds to customer inquiries by email. Now those sites are trying a novel approach to personalization: real people. Partly in response to the customer service blunders of last holiday season, and partly in anticipation of another Internet shopping blitz this winter, E-commerce sites are starting to use live chats and Internet telephony applications to answer questions, solve problems and, ideally, sell customers more things. In doing so, these sites are further crushing the myth that E-commerce companies can get by without investing in a real, live customer support team. "Many players are looking at this," said Judy Neuman, vice president for interactive media at Eddie Bauer, and the secretary of Shop.org, an industry trade group. "It will become the cost of entry going forward." In addition to Eddie Bauer, which is owned by Spiegel Inc., companies like 911Gifts.com, Etoys, CBS Sportsline, Furniture.com, Lands' End, Hewlett-Packard and 1-800-Flowers.com, among others, indicated they were implementing live customer service. In Eddie Bauer's case, Ms. Neuman said, customers will be able to click on a button and communicate with a customer service representative via a one-on-one, text-based chat. If that doesn't suffice, customers will be able to speak to a representative through their computer, using Internet telephony technology. "Especially as the Internet moves into the mainstream, consumers are looking for that comfort zone that ties into the world they're used to," said Chris McCann, senior vice president of 1-800-Flowers, which is implementing an Internet telephony package to provide customer service. "Once users get used to shopping on the site, they won't use it as much, but we like to think of these things as training wheels for new users." Ms. Neuman declined to name the customer service vendor Eddie Bauer will use or the cost of the system -- although she did say the cost was "substantial"and that the service would be available starting in October. To handle the rush of inquiries during the holidays, Ms. Neuman said the company would bolster its customer service staff from roughly 12 people to a maximum of 60. According to Ken Allard, an analyst with Jupiter Communications, companies that sell customer service applications have proliferated in recent months. Some, like Webline, offer a range of products, from software that sends out automated responses to email inquiries to Internet telephony packages and chat software. Webline's customers include Cisco Systems, Hewlett-Packard, Mortgage.com and GTE, among others, and its comprehensive customer service system costs roughly $1,500 per representative to implement. Other companies address only part of the customer service equation. For instance, Liveperson offers chat-based customer service for roughly $250 a month per representative; its system is utilized by CBS Sportsline's on-line golf store, among other sites. Meanwhile, Net2phone Inc., a unit of the IDT Corporation offers an Internet telephony-based customer support package, which is currently being tested by 1-800-Flowers. The system costs between $500 and $5,000 a year per representative, depending on the size of the customer service team. Industry analysts and executives said the trend toward improved customer service on line began with a chorus of complaints after last year's holiday shopping season, when many sites were caught off guard by the tremendous influx of shoppers. Those sites often failed to deliver products on time, then failed to respond promptly to customers' emails. Meanwhile, because many E-commerce companies were founded on the assumption that customer service should be fully automated, the sites frequently lacked phone-based support systems. In addition to losing repeat customers, executives say feeble customer service systems have resulted in customers not spending money in the first place. In the last six months, several studies have indicated that between 33 and 66 percent of customers bail out of transactions before they are completed. With more customer service options available to steer consumers through the purchase, executives hope to convert shoppers into buyers at a much higher rate. E-commerce sites also say the average amount of an order is typically higher when customer service representatives assist in sales because they can "upsell" additional items to potential customers. If that bears out, the cost of additional staffing suddenly looks like a bargain, according to Peter Baltaxe, president of 911Gifts.com. "Say a customer service rep converts five shoppers to a sale every hour through a chat," said Mr. Baltaxe, who plans to implement such a service in the coming months. "Assuming a $100 gross margin revenue, and the fact that we pay a customer service rep between $10 and $15 an hour, the return seems to be a no-brainer." Even with the more costly customer service packages, however, the payoff is fast, according to Lou Zambello, senior vice president for operations at Etoys. Mr. Zambello said the company planned to implement live customer service support, which will include both a chat component and an Internet telephony package. While declining to cite the company's planned customer service expenditure, he said a full suite of customer service applications could cost retailers "a few million, when all is said and done; but it will still pay for itself pretty quickly." Mr. Zambello added that Internet retailers can afford to pay for such services because they spend comparatively little on routine transactions, which are handled electronically. "It then makes sense to spend more on the tougher transactions, which are the ones where you'll win the most loyal customers," he said. As for the idea that live customer service represents an unexpected and unwanted addition to the E-commerce business model, Mr. Baltaxe of 911Gifts said the practice fitted a larger trend. "People look at Amazon buying warehouses and realize that it does make sense to have a warehouse, and that the low-overhead, virtual, personless business model doesn't really exist," he said. "It's the same with this. We still have to talk to customers. It's another piece of the model where people are starting to add more overhead costs. Internet businesses still have tremendous advantages, but I think it's turning out to be a little different than some people expected." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Agency Preview, a new Web site, nudges the old-fashioned account review into cyberreality.
body: A FRENCH company is bringing an Internet service to the unitedstates intended to assist in conducting account reviews on line, helping agencies hook up with advertisers and consultants seeking shops. Maydream S. A. is introducing a Web site named Agency Preview (www.adforum.com), a data base that will include information about subscribing agencies like credentials, client rosters, billings, specialty services and awards. The site will also offer samples of creative work that can include television commercials. Other companies have already been capitalizing on the benefits of interactivity for agency reviews by offering Web sites, including Business Partnering International in Richmond (www.agencyfinder.com) and Pile & Company in Boston (www.agencycompile.com). The role cyberspace is beginning to play in how agency searches are conducted is indicative of the ways the Internet is changing the way the advertising industry operates. "We're finally bringing the agency search process in line with the new technology," said Neil Kreisberg, executive vice president and group director at Grey Advertising in newyork, one of more than 30 American and European agencies taking part in the start-up of Agency Preview. "Given the technological revolution in most of what we're doing," he added, "the way the process is being run now is pretty archaic." Other examples of the transformative nature of the Internet for Madison Avenue include Web sites like www.adsgallery.com and www.portfolios.com from Warp 10 Technologies Inc. in San Francisco, which are meant to offer on-line showcases for the work of agencies, graphic and Web designers, copywriters, photographers and other creative talent, and on-line services for buying and selling advertising space and commercial time like Adauction.com in San Francisco and Adoutlet.com in Columbus, Ohio. One agency, Mann Bukvic Gatch Partners in Cincinnati, has even put up a Web site (www.yourpitch.com) to compete for an account placed in review by Screaming Media, a new media company in newyork. "The advertising world is becoming more and more reliant on global information," said Herve C. de Clerck, the founder and president of Maydream, who goes by the fanciful title of dream leader. "Our goal is to connect advertisers, consultants and agencies in an efficient manner, so that their new-business efforts can be maximized. "Advertisers don't want to waste time talking to agencies that aren't right for them," he added, "and agencies don't want to waste time chasing business they will ultimately not win. And consultants want to identify agencies they might have initially overlooked -- or that might have conflicts." There are 13 consultants, which help manage reviews, participating in Agency Preview. "I really believe it's a plus," said Leslie Winthrop, managing director at AAR/Bob Wolf Partners in newyork, a consultant that is part of the worldwide AAR consulting network. "To have more information that's more easily accessible is more cost efficient for the client," she added. "And we can spend more time with the agencies." Consultants will pay $9,500 a year to have full access to the Web site. Agencies will pay $2,000 a year to subscribe; in addition to the data they can put up, they can also provide hot links to their own Web sites, list email contact information and offer animated presentations. To oversee Agency Preview, Maydream, which is based in Boulogne, France, has opened an American unit, Maydream Inc., in Hoboken, N.J., where Rob Drasin is vice president for unitedstates marketing and sales. Now that's something you don't read every day, "Hoboken" and "France" in the same sentence. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
ECONOMIC VIEW;
States Chasing Sales Taxes Down the Internet Highway
body: IT is one of the more vexing economic issues of the Internet age: how to insure that state sales tax revenues are not eviscerated by the shift to on-line retailing, where borders are all but meaningless and sales tax collection is spotty at best. The question has riled both state and local governments, which fear that their tax bases will disappear down a phone line at 56 kilobits a second, and electronic retailers and Internet service providers, which fear that revenue-hungry governments will view electronic commerce as a cash cow to be milked every which way. The basic problem has been around as long as mail-order catalogues. When consumers order books, compact disks or flowers from an out-of-state retailer, they are technically liable to pay sales taxes. Companies, however, are bound to collect the taxes only from consumers in states where the company has a physical presence. Although some merchants collect the tax even where they are not required to do so, most do not. So for orders by mail, or phone -- or the Internet -- consumers can end up with a tax-free purchase. That reality has left traditional retailers complaining of a competitive disadvantage. And it has left state and local governments worried that technology is leaving tax policy far behind. Denied reliable sales taxes, they may have to look elsewhere for revenue, with unpredictable consequences. It is not too hard to come up with potential solutions. But don't look for them to be agreed upon and implemented quickly. Last week saw a flurry of attention to the issue, but no consensus on anything. The Clinton Administration issued a report on the "breathtaking" growth of electronic commerce and the technologies that make it possible, suggesting that the nation is only starting to get a handle on all the ways the Internet is changing the economy and necessitating adjustments to public policy. Some of the biggest names in business weighed in with a report about lost sales tax revenues that suggested the states have gotten themselves in a lather about nothing. And the Advisory Commission on Electronic Commerce, established last year by Congress to help sort out the taxation issue, held its first meeting and quickly got into a heated debate about . . . office space. The Administration's report, prepared by the Commerce Department, acknowledged that the Government was only starting to collect and analyze information looking specifically at the quantity and composition of electronic commerce. But while it cited only vague estimates of the size of that business -- between $7 billion and $15 billion last year, growing to as much as $80 billion in 2002 -- it included a set of examples that made clear how powerful a force electronic commerce has become: * The on-line sales of Dell Computer more than doubled last year, and by next year the company expects them to account for half its revenue. * Quicken Mortgage, an on-line mortgage provider from Intuit, arranged $400 million in loans in the first quarter of this year, a pace far ahead of the $600 million in all of 1998. * US-Style.com recently started a service allowing Japanese consumers to buy American goods through a Japanese-language Web site. The report said the service highlighted the global nature of electronic commerce and the potential for it to become a trade issue. BUT what has all that activity meant for sales tax collections? Not much, according to the study done by Ernst & Young for a coalition that included America Online, Cisco Systems, Microsoft, Time Warner and Wal-Mart. The study found that state and local governments lost $170 million in sales tax revenue last year because of Internet commerce, or one-tenth of 1 percent of total sales and use tax collections. "The 'revenue crisis' from Internet sales has not materialized," it concluded. "The Advisory Commission on Electronic Commerce, state and local government and Congress have time to carefully deliberate on the appropriate taxation of E-commerce." That is good news for the commission, which spent a portion of its first session last week debating whether its executive director had created a conflict of interest in accepting free office space from an electronics-industry lobbying group that employs her husband. (Like any good commission, it opted to study the matter further before making a decision.) There are technical and political hurdles to creating a system that would automatically add the appropriate sales tax to Internet purchases and funnel the revenue to the proper government. But none of them are insurmountable; the electronic payment systems used by the credit card companies and banks are the obvious model. The real problem is whether the commission, Congress and the Administration can work quickly enough to get ahead of the Internet wave, or whether public policy is doomed always to paddle in its wake. Given the libertarian ethos that has always pervaded cyberspace, perhaps the latter is just the outcome that the E-commerce industry and Internet users want. http://www.nytimes.com

title: In the Latest Fray Over Access to the Internet, Three Los Angeles Commissioners Resign
body: The struggle between the nation's cable television operators and Internet service providers over high-speed access to cyberspace has roiled city politics in Los Angeles, where three political appointees have resigned in a debate on policy over the issue. Los Angeles has become another battleground for control over "broadband" Internet access through cable modems that can offer service up to 100 times faster than a standard telephone line as cities, which regulate local cable franchises, have been forced to deal with the issue in the face of conflicting messages from the Federal Government. Cable companies, led by AT&T through its acquisition of Tele-Communications Inc., are increasingly offering high-speed Internet access, through service providers with which they are allied; rivals like America Online say the cable companies should be forced to allow consumers a choice of providers. The debate has split City Hall and brought about a rare public controversy. Mayor Richard J. Riordan gave his support to the cable companies, while a majority of his appointees on the Board of Information Technology Commissioners favored a policy requiring so-called open access for competitors. Rather than cast a vote against the Mayor, the three commissioners on the five-member board resigned last week, leaving the panel without a quorum. Now, as city leaders struggle with the question of corporate market share versus consumer interest, the way to create that policy has been delayed. "Usually, you don't see such clear disagreements between the Mayor and the commissions that are resolved with such public resignations," said Tracy Westen, a member of the commission during the Bradley administration who is creating an Internet platform called the Democracy Network to sponsor exchanges between political candidates and voters. "Typically they either go along or negotiate it out or resign more quietly, but this has sort of gained a life of its own." The issue has been no less controversial for other cities around the nation trying to figure out how, or whether, to step into the fray. Portland has required that cable companies let competitors use their broadband Internet access, a position upheld this month in a Federal District Court ruling. In San Francisco this week, city officials rejected a plan allowing cable companies to exclude competitors, and ordered a policy to allow competition. But William E. Kennard, the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, declared on June 16 that the issue should be regulated by Federal authorities and not left to the tens of thousands of local municipalities. It is a conflict that has also brought an aggressive lobbying campaign often unseen at the local level. In seeking approval of its franchise transfer to AT&T, TCI paid lobbying companies more than $130,000 to represent it, according to city records; America Online and AT&T have retained two firms each. City staff members trying to draft policy on the issue have received hundreds of documents. The issue has become a "full-employment act for lobbyists," said Mark Ridley-Thomas, a City Councilman whose technology committee has taken up the issue. Over the last several months, the Mayor and his senior staff members concluded that the city should not intervene right now, said Kelly Martin, the Mayor's chief of staff. The Mayor's office believes that the access should be regulated by the Federal Government, she said, and is concerned that requiring access could inhibit investment in the technology. A city report recommended a policy that allowed cable operators to exclude Internet companies from providing direct broadband service for the moment, but included "re-opener" clauses allowing the city to review the situation if the market became monopolized. The Board of Information Technology Commissioners was expected to vote on June 21 on a nonbinding recommendation to the City Council on the report. One commissioner who resigned, Robert Duggan, said he thought open access of some form was important and resented the pressure he said he felt to support the Mayor. " 'If you can't support it, you should go away quietly,' " he said he was told. " 'You work for the Mayor, he's appointed you, and you're going to embarrass him if you can't come out for the position. So if you can't support him, why don't you just resign?' " Ms. Martin said no pressure was exerted on the commissioners to change their position or resign. Mr. Ridley-Thomas said politics often involved maneuvering and dealing that the public never saw, but that the resignation of three commissioners put this dispute on another level. "I think it causes the usual behind-the-scenes machinations to be put on Front Street," he said. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING;
Trading In Bonds On Line, At Last
body: IT was a bold experiment in cyberspace finance, and at 11:30 one recent Tuesday morning, it was about to be tested in the real market. Robert A. Schoch, business manager of the Lancaster, Pa., school district, huddled around a computer screen with Louis J. Verdelli and other advisers here, waiting to see if anyone would bid over the Internet for $29.2 million of the district's bonds. Five minutes, then 10, went by without a bid. Mr. Schoch grew apprehensive. Then, just as the noon deadline for the auction was drawing near, the screen came alive. Offers appeared from as far away as Utah. At last Mr. Schoch allowed a smile to crease his poker face. The district's first Internet financing had succeeded. The Lancaster auction was one small part of an accelerating electronic revolution. The bond market -- both for new issues like Lancaster's and for trading in existing bonds -- is being dragged out of the dark ages of fragmentation and opaque pricing, and thrown into a fiercely competitive and still ill-defined future. "There's a thick veil of secrecy in the bond market," said Marilyn Cohen, president of Envision Capital Management, a fixed-income specialist in Los Angeles. "It's one of the last dinosaurs to fall." By replacing old bonds with new through the electronic auction, Lancaster will save $1.1 million, plugging an immediate budget hole and allowing the city, the thrifty heart of Amish country, to avoid raising taxes next year. Lancaster's advisers say the savings come from the bigger market created by the Internet, which drew distant underwriters who had rarely vied for Pennsylvania school bonds. "We think the impact of that is to lower their interest rates," said Mr. Verdelli, senior managing consultant at Public Financial Management, the adviser who arranged the bidding on a system run by a Pittsburgh-based creature of the Internet, MuniAuction. Click-of-the-mouse bidding on new issues is a striking leap forward from past practice in the bond industry. Like most issuers, both municipal and corporate, Lancaster used to negotiate bond deals with a single underwriter; in many places, bidders must still show up in person to drop a written bid into the equivalent of a ballot box. And the upheaval in the secondary markets, where dealers, brokers and investors trade bonds after they are issued, is bound to prove more profound. After all, some $350 billion of bonds and other debt securities are traded daily, 12 times the volume on the newyork Stock Exchange. Most stock trades are executed on exchange floors or through Nasdaq's electronic dealer network, and each trade's volume and price is immediately displayed to all. Not so with bonds, which change hands much as they have for most of the century, mainly through a patchwork of private channels. Bond trading on the newyork Stock Exchange is trivial, confined mainly to small lots. "If there was ever a market that needed liquidity and transparency, it's fixed income," said Douglas M. Atkin, president of Instinet. His firm, a unit of Reuters, operates the biggest private stock-trading service for institutions. And later this year, Instinet plans to start a dealer-to-dealer bond-trading service, initially for unitedstates Treasuries.  Unheard Upheaval While there are big changes under way in the bond business, they have attracted far less attention than the more advanced revolution in stocks, where instantaneously available prices have made possible a frenzy of speculative activity and driven even Merrill Lynch to announce a plan for cut-rate commissions. But the impact could be just as far-reaching. Already, spreads -- the difference between the prices at which professionals buy bonds and the prices at which they sell them -- are beginning to narrow, eating into bond dealers' profits. So, naturally, the dealers are trying to hold off the electronic tide. And brokers, the middlemen between investors and dealers, worry about survival in a world where investors have new power. Changes in how bonds trade are not always visible to ordinary investors, most of whom own bonds only through mutual funds. But ruptures in the system tend to echo loudly. An example was the virtual paralysis of the market for any bonds other than Treasuries in the latter part of 1998, when foreign turmoil touched off a ferocious flight to quality. The Federal Reserve found itself obliged to engineer a rescue of a big hedge fund that had bet disastrously on historic relationships among various types of bonds. Surging interest rates shook stock markets. But while prices of securities can move at the speed of light, market structures have been slow to change, and then only under duress, as when industrywide fixed commissions for stocks were abolished in 1975. Back then, Congress charged the Securities and Exchange Commission with overseeing the creation of integrated markets for both stocks and bonds. The bond part of the mandate has largely been ignored. But now the pace is picking up: Arthur Levitt, the chairman of the S.E.C., is pushing bond market openness. And this month, the House of Representatives overwhelmingly passed a bill that would direct the commission to adopt rules for collecting and publishing price, volume and other transaction data for corporate bonds, and to enforce the rules within a year. (The measure has no Senate counterpart yet.) Initially, modernizing bond markets will benefit mainly institutional investors, but consumers stand to gain indirectly through their stakes in mutual funds, pensions and retirement accounts. Taxpayers will gain in places like Lancaster that exploit the new systems. And within a few years, retail customers are very likely to be in possession of basic information about bonds like transaction charges and meaningful market prices. Until now, ignorance has cost them more than $20 billion a year, by one estimate. "The fixed-income investor is the odd-man out in the market," said Arthur F. Goat, a retiree in Short Hills, N.J. "You're flying blind." Dominated by the giant dealers who benefit most from the status quo, the Bond Market Association, the industry's chief trade group, has lobbied hard to slow and restrict the modernization process. The industry has pledged to improve transparency in the corporate bond markets, but says it is concerned that the costs involved might outweigh the benefits by impeding trading activity and harming market liquidity. But, prodded by regulators and some in Congress to fill the market's information vacuum, even the trade group sees the writing on the wall. "Electronic trading systems are rapidly becoming essential tools in the portfolio and trading operations of both sell-side and buy-side participants in the unitedstates fixed-income securities markets," the association's director of research, Andy Nybo, acknowledged in his survey of 1998 industry developments.  Buying Debt in the Dark As a result of the market's fragmentation, even professional investors face serious disadvantages in trading corporate and municipal bonds. To get a market price, they must conduct an unwieldy and imprecise shopping expedition among a dozen or more dealers, or rely on what one dealer tells them -- or, for less active issues, fall back on what may be little more than a wild guess. Individual investors, who hold only 5 percent of corporate but 30 percent of muni bonds, have even less clout. In municipal bonds, for example, the best an individual investor can do is to view the prior day's prices for 1,300 or so issues that may have traded, out of 1.4 million outstanding, on a Web site run by the bond association (www.bondmarkets.com). Some of those -- there is no telling which -- are dealer-to-dealer prices unavailable to ordinary investors. With comparison shopping so difficult, dealers can charge large markups, especially on lesser-quality bonds, and generally get the better of any bargain. Quoted prices can be all over the map. On Friday afternoon, for example, different dealers were offering Ford Motor Credit 5 3/4 percent notes due in February 2004 at anywhere from $95.472 (yielding 6.9 percent) to $96.034 (yielding 6.75 percent) per $100. "Price competition is at the heart of the free-market system," said Representative Michael Oxley, an Ohio Republican who heads a House subcommittee that held a hearing on bond trading last September. "And you can't have true competition if people have a hard time figuring out exactly what they're paying." That is a big reason the industry has dragged its feet: dealers' fear that the traditionally wide spreads in bond trading will shrink. "The people who are living off the spreads, their profits are going to come down," said Frank D. Korth, a portfolio manager at the National City Investment Management Company in Cleveland.  Squeezing Intermediaries Threatened, too, are the firms that advise issuers and underwrite bond issues. "The intermediaries are scared to death," said Myles Harrington, a founder of MuniAuction, the firm that owns the system used in the Lancaster auction. Last month, the company drew a $6 million investment from the Carlyle Group, a private Washington investment firm whose principals include former Treasury Secretary James Baker 3d and Frank Carlucci, a former Defense Secretary. As with Merrill Lynch's belated decision to embrace on-line stock trading, bond dealers are being forced to weigh what they would lose in narrower spreads against the risk of losing business to upstarts and the possibility that trading volume would rise if investors found the market less treacherous. An early effort to breach the wall was Capitalink, J. P. Morgan's 1989 venture into direct sales of corporate bonds to institutional investors, bypassing other financial institutions. Traditional bond market players howled. "The competitive threat Capitalink poses to our industry cannot be overemphasized," a Merrill Lynch official, Richard Fuscone, wrote in a memo quoted in a 1996 paper by Robert J. Kauffman of the University of Minnesota and Arthur R. Kennedy 3d of Morgan. After Merrill bought an entire issue of Deere & Company notes at a dog-in-the-manger price to pre-empt its trading on Capitalink, Morgan gave up. In the early 1990's, Larry E. Fondren, an entrepreneur who ran a sort of computer-dating service for insurance companies -- arranging joint ventures and advising on mergers and reinsurance -- tried his hand. He set up Intervest Financial Services, which allowed clients to trade anonymously with one another and with dealers, and tried to negotiate a deal to link it to computer terminals of Bloomberg L.P., then on 60,000 clients' desks. Mr. Fondren struck a deal in 1995, but Bloomberg pulled the plug after six months, partly relented, and then cut Intervest off for good in 1998, said Mr. Fondren, who has filed a breach-of-contract suit. In court papers, Mr. Fondren said Bloomberg told him it had acted at the insistence of bond dealers, because clients were getting too much price information. A spokesman for Bloomberg, which is partly owned by Merrill, said that Intervest was dropped because of low trading activity and that the allegations were groundless. Merrill itself has had a change of heart since it helped thwart Capitalink. "Ten years ago, we did not believe electronic distribution was in the best interests of clients or the industry," said Timothy Gilles, a Merrill spokesman. But the markets and technology have evolved, and Merrill now backs electronic trading, he said. In any event, the concept is back with a vengeance. The Bond Market Association says there are now more than two dozen electronic systems for marketing or trading bonds. At the start of 1998, there were 11. "It's a brave new world out there," said Edwin McGuinn, president of Limitrader Securities, one dealer that has hung out a cybershingle. Entrants in the electronic race include individual entrepreneurs, banks, securities dealers, bond brokers and information purveyors like Bloomberg and Reuters. Most focus on attracting institutional buyers of bonds, whose high volume they hope will make their systems viable. Just last week, a consortium of seven giant financial-services companies announced a new trading system for dealers, called Brokertec. So far, most of the electronic systems are bulletin boards for dealers to post offerings; final prices are set when trades are consummated by phone. In a few cases, buyers and sellers see prices on the screen at which they can count on executing a trade. Other systems bring dealers and institutions together for real-time trading or periodic order-matching sessions, with traders' anonymity a big selling point. Then there are the new-issue auction systems like MuniAuction, which make possible innovations like bidding on selected maturities out of a series that formerly had to be bought in its entirety Moreover, bidders see where their offers rank (though not their rivals' specific bids) and are free to raise their bids repeatedly, as some did in the Lancaster auction. In traditional auctions, bidders get just one shot. Lancaster's electronic auction of new bonds is one of about 200 such municipal borrowings since Muni Auction's first deal in late 1997. As for corporations, many now routinely market commercial paper -- short-term i.o.u.'s -- directly to investors, bypassing broker-dealers, and there are systems being developed for selling longer-term corporate debt this way. The Government's Treasury Direct program allows investors with as little as $1,000 to bid for new bills, notes and bonds.  A Certain Inevitability But while the old methods are crumbling, the process is likely to take several years -- and it may never make bonds as transparent as stocks. Micah S. Green, executive vice president of the Bond Market Association, told a House panel in March that he supported the goals of the proposed legislation. He said, too, that his group would soon add to its Web site the previous day's dealer-to-dealer prices for 100 or so of the most active investment-grade corporate bonds. (The new data are due to make their debut this week.) But he sought to persuade lawmakers that there were key differences in bond and stock markets. For instance, he said, most bonds do not trade actively: only 4 percent of about 400,000 corporate issues outstanding in 1996 traded even once that year. He also contended that too much transparency could increase volatility in thin markets. "Revealing prices and trading volumes instantaneously could hurt market liquidity," Mr. Green said, by, say, making it obvious when someone was trying to unwind a large position piecemeal. He asked Congress to choose evolutionary change, led by the private sector, over Government-mandated change. Whichever path is chosen, it is clear that the bond business is galloping toward an automated future with fewer intermediaries. Until recently, "if you wanted to sell a block of $10 million in municipal bonds, you'd call up 20 brokers and ask them to give you a bid," said Peter J. Allegrini, managing director of Prudential Investments, who runs a portfolio of high-yield municipals. "Today, you plug your bonds into the Bloomberg and press a couple of buttons, and the whole process is down to 15 minutes." In a few years, perhaps one-third of trades in Treasury debt will take place electronically, said F. James Claire, director of taxable fixed-income trading for a unit of First Union Bank in Charlotte, N.C. But if Mr. Claire's attitudes reflect those of many bond traders, electronic trading will develop more slowly in markets for corporate and tax-exempt bonds, where trading is thinner. There simply is no substitute in a decentralized market, he said, for communicating by voice with the other players. "You want to be able to talk to a guy and hear noise in the background; you need that color to hear what's going on," Mr. Claire said. "You're not going to get any color looking at the screen." Moreover, he said, screen updates sometimes lag when trading action heats up, and electronic screens do not leave behind as solid a transaction record as do telephone calls, which are routinely recorded. So, much of Mr. Levitt's lament about the least-liquid sectors of the bond market seems likely to linger. "The sad truth," he said, "is that investors in the corporate bond market do not enjoy the same access to information as a car buyer or a home buyer or, dare I say, a fruit buyer. And that's unacceptable." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Louis J. Verdelli, center, a financial adviser, showed Robert A. Schoch, left, the business manager of the public school district in Lancaster, Pa., the on-line system for selling $29.2 million of the district's bonds. (John Zeedick for The newyork Times)(pg. 10)  Chart: "Behind From the Start" When retail investors buy bonds directly, they pay high transaction costs, without the discount trading channels available for stocks. They also pay higher prices than institutions do for the same bonds, reducing their effective yield.  Example: Stocks vs. Bonds $25,000 Revlon stock 870 shares at $28.75 bought on the newyork Stock Exchange. The investor pays a commission on the trade. title:
JERSEY FOOTLIGHTS;
Hey, That's Not James Taylor
body: Would you like to view the schedule of concerts at the PNC Bank Arts Center in Holmdel? It must be on the Internet. Sure enough. A search comes up with pncbankartscenter.com. But the site isn't really the art center's, which is actually artscenter.com. And it provides more than a look at Brooks and Dunn in cowboy hats or even Cher in a skimpy outfit. Someone out there created the bogus address, which connects automatically to whitehouse.com, a pornography site (one that schoolchildren looking for information on the Clintons' residence regularly stumble across). And there may not be much the Arts Center can do about it. Dominic Roncace, general manager of the arts center, said he found out about the pornographic site a week ago and turned the matter over to the center's lawyers. "It is not uncommon for things like this to happen, but it is all so new that the law and the courts are just beginning to catch up," said Christopher Young, president of Cyveillance, an Alexandria, Va., company that searches the Internet to find infringements of this sort on behalf of clients. "In the case of a public entity, connection with a pornographic site can hurt their image. There are ways to find out who is doing it and you can ask them politely to stop."   KAREN DeMASTERS http://www.nytimes.com

title:
PRACTICAL TRAVELER;
Taking Children To Exotic Places
body: BEFORE I was married, in 1991, I traveled as much as I could in what was then called the Third World. My husband, Jinx, shared my fondness for these regions. We were determined that having children wouldn't slow us down, so after our first daughter, Allie, was born in 1992, we took a trial vacation to the Baja peninsula for a couple of weeks, albeit with a rented house as our base. When Allie was 18 months old, we departed for six months in Central America. Our second child, Katherine, was an infant when we took off for three years of combined work and vacation in Southeast Asia. Friends and relatives were worried: What would we do in a health emergency? Would they get enough nutritious food? Don't children need stability and a bed they can call their own? We had questions, too. I read and reread Lonely Planet's "Travel With Children," now in its third edition, by Maureen Wheeler, co-founder of the guidebook series with her husband, Tony. It answered many of my questions and offered crucial reassurance. These days, there is the Internet. Some Web sites I've found recently include www.havechildrenwilltravel .com, a newsletter available for $29 a year (four issues). Much of its coverage focuses on travel in the unitedstates and Europe, but it sometimes deals with destinations in the developing world. About.com, formerly miningco.com, has forums and chat rooms on traveling with children at www.travelwithkids.about.com. Another interesting Web site, www.familytravelforum.com, has forums as well as links to child-friendly destinations and books. We found that keeping the children happy was key. We didn't try to do major jungle treks or long expeditions to ruined cities. We went to the beach, a playground or pool. We ate outdoors when we could. One excursion a day was enough, usually in the morning. When we found a comfortable place, we stayed a while.  Directory of Doctors For peace of mind medically, we joined the International Association for Medical Assistance to Travelers, or I.A.M.A.T., a nonprofit organization that publishes a directory of participating doctors worldwide, all of whom speak English or French, have been trained in a Western medical institution and pledge to charge a fixed amount for a first visit; I used it a couple of times, with gratifying results. The organization (membership is by donation) also sells a freestanding mosquito net that I wish we'd had on our trips. The SFO Medical Service, a joint project of the University of California at San Francisco, San Francisco General Hospital and San Francisco International Airport, has a site on the Internet that covers some of the basics of traveling with children: itsa.ucsf.edu/sfomed. (Click on "Travel Medicine.") It also operates a clinic at the airport that provides health care and advice. We continued to pay our Blue Cross premiums, to get catastrophic coverage for expenses beyond $2,000 each. From previous travels in Asia, I knew that doctors there are pretty good at treating local maladies, if sometimes overly reliant on antibiotics, and that care is inexpensive by American standards. If anything major were to arise, we'd fly back to the unitedstates, or head to Singapore, which has the region's best hospitals and doctors. Before leaving, we had the usual vaccination updates, as well as gamma globulin, an infectious-hepatitis prophylactic, before our trip to Central America, and its recent successor, the hepatitis A vaccine, before leaving for Asia. We declined the rabies vaccine, though one doctor recommended it. Malaria prophylactics are a subject of some controversy; each family should decide what's right for them with their own doctors. Most urban and tourist centers in Asia are fairly safe from malaria, and doctors there tend to know how to deal with it if presented with an early enough case. To protect against mosquito bites, we covered as much of the body as possible between dusk and dawn, sleeping under mosquito netting and applying repellents, first a commercial one formulated for children then a one-to-three-parts mixture of citronella and coconut oils that we mixed ourselves and seemed to work just as well. Toward the end of our stay Jinx did get dengue fever, a serious disease carried by day-biting mosquitos; it cannot be prevented by vaccination or treated except symptomatically. Jinx got his dengue bite on a remote Thai island, but dengue fever is also on the rise in many cities. (He was very ill for about five days and got good care at a hospital in Chiang Mai, in northern Thailand.)  Sanitation Issues Sanitation was a prime concern, as most travelers' ailments in developing countries tend to be gastrointestinal. Breastfeeding an infant, if possible, is the easiest and healthiest way to feed a child. Well-known formula brands are easily bought -- but the headache of washing and sterilizing the bottles along with the questionable purity of even some of the bottled water makes it more chancy than breastfeeding. When my girls used bottles and cups, I washed them with tap water and soap, rinsed them with bottled water and, when possible, let them dry in the sun. Asian toilets tend to be a ceramic trough set in concrete, with foot treads on either side of the hole. A basin or tank of water nearby, with a little bucket, is used to flush. The basin water is used only for this purpose, and you avoid touching the bucket, except for the handle. Disposable diapers are widely available, although larger sizes can be hard to find. Quality varied; we'd save good ones we'd imported or bought in cities for nights or long bus trips, use cheap brands for short-term duty, and, if possible (at the beach, for instance), go without, as many Asian families did, keeping a close eye on the toddler and cleaning up when necessary. Diaper rash was a constant concern in the tropics; any skin lesion is an entry point for germs. A good diaper cream is essential, but even more so is antibacterial ointment. I applied it to any skin lesion, on adult or child, until healed. When the children had a stomach upset, we followed the same regime as for ourselves: bananas, plain rice with traces of ketchup or soy sauce and plenty of clear fluids. (We drank bottled water; if we ran out, in a pinch I would boil tap water.) We had come prepared with packages of hydrating solution, a powder of nutrients, salts and sugars that dissolves in water, but the children refused it -- too yucky. After visiting a small island in southern Thailand that had a water shortage, the girls came down with diarrhea and fever, Allie so seriously that we were ready to take her to a hospital when the illness subsided.  During that one awful night I was tortured with guilt; then I remembered that children in the unitedstates get ill, too. Another bit of hard-earned wisdom: Carry much less. On our first trip with Allie, to Central America, we took an enormous backpack stuffed with diapers, as well as a stroller, a portable crib and other paraphernalia. On our second trip, to Asia, we abandoned the crib, tried to get rooms with four beds and made little bunkers with pillows and bits of luggage that managed to contain a sleeping child fairly well. A good stroller, on the other hand, was crucial. It allowed us to take an occasional daylong expedition that might include a napping child and served as a high chair. I could loop bags over its handle, and the canopy blocked the tropical sun. You can buy children's clothing as you go -- it's very inexpensive, often well made and suited to the climate. Feeding the girls turned out to be less a problem than we'd feared. Packages of corn crisps, rice cakes and other munchies can be bought at every corner store and travel hub. At mealtime, our children tended to stick with favorites available on the travelers' circuit: pancakes, omelets, grilled cheese sandwiches and spaghetti with tomato sauce. They shunned vegetables, but familiar fruits -- bananas, peeled apples, oranges -- helped balance their diets. After a while, they discovered regional specialties: In Thailand, pad siew (rice noodles fried with egg, meat and soy sauce), chicken and cashews, and the noodle soup called kway tiao; In a pinch, they ate rice or noodles with ketchup or soy sauce -- not the most balanced meal, but sustaining enough, combined with the Western breakfasts of eggs and toast available almost everywhere, along with a daily children's multi-vitamin. It was sometimes very hard work, and occasionally Jinx and I wondered what we were doing. But a majority of the time, we had rewarding experiences: the day we witnessed the release of baby sea turtles from a Sri Lankan beach; the lakeside picnics, with barbecued chicken and sticky rice, in Chiang Mai; the horse-drawn buggy ride in Bombay. Despite our qualms, we all survived, happy and generally healthy, trusting our own common sense and the fates that seem to control everything in Asia anyway. The International Association for Medical Assistance to Travelers is at 417 Center Street, Lewiston, N.Y. 14092; (716) 754-4883; on the Internet www.sentex.net/iamat. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Leticia Plate)

title:
RIO TO NEW DELHI, BY DESKTOP: PARIS;
From the Louvre To the Sewers
body: France was slow to join the cyberworld, but all the basic information that a visitor to Paris needs can now be found on the Web. Paris Tourisme, at www.paris-tourisme .com, is a good place to start. A click on "Welcome" calls up an menu in English divided into nine chapters, among them: Museums, Hotels, City Tours, detailed maps of Paris and its suburbs; Paris Airports and Paris for Kids. Each chapter heading leads to a wide range of options. In the museums listing, for instance, there is lively information on no fewer than 42 museums. The Paris for Kids section includes attractions, parks and zoos, and even suggests where to find baby sitters at night. Under the heading Paris From A . . . to Z is a range of practical information like where to rent bicycles, how to find philatelists and which is the best flea market. This site offers a limited selection of hotels and has no information on restaurants, but it has a good search engine. The site promotes the Touringscope bus trips around Paris in addition to walking tours. The French Government sponsors two sites. The Paris Convention and Visitors Bureau site, www.paris-touristoffice.com, switches into English by clicking on a Union Jack. It offers 10 chapters, including some not listed by Paris Tourisme. Paris night life covers everything from cabarets and opera houses to jazz clubs and trendy cafes (it notes, for example, that Le Flore in St.-Germain-des-Pres is host to philosophical discussions in English at 7 P.M. on the first Wednesday of the month). The restaurants section even includes where to find dining spots with, say, terraces or views, while the hotel information offers a broad choice, from student hostels to luxury hotels (in picking a price range, be sure to use French francs). Although this site does not have a search function, it does offer links to other Paris Web sites. The French Tourist Office, www.fgtousa .org/regional/paris.htm, is another source of extensive information about Paris -- offering numerous links to other sites. An example: a click on general information leads to "wines," which in turn leads to tips on wine-tasting classes, including those that are held in English. The site even offers pen portraits of close to 100 famous French men and women. Some other useful Web sites are maintained by entities outside of France. The @Paris Traveler's Guide, at infocities.com, is lively, though I noticed its information about museums was limited. I enjoyed the Lonely Planet site, lonelyplanet.com/dest /eur/par.htm, if only because it starts with an introduction to French history and its recommended reading list ranges from Rousseau and Voltaire to Marguerite Duras and Michel Foucault. For the off-the-beaten-track visit, it even proposes the Paris sewers (I have been there: they are interesting and not too smelly). A site that seems particularly informative on hotels is www.france.com/travel /hotels. It is run by the French Hotel Reservation Center and covers just about everywhere -- Paris and throughout the country. Hotels can be chosen by district and by price, and there is a useful box indicating how convenient different parts of town are for getting to museums, shopping, businesses and the like. The information includes room prices as well as address, telephone and a photograph of each hotel. The site even offers to find hotels at the lowest possible rates. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawings (Bryan Leister)

title:
RIO TO NEW DELHI, BY DESKTOP: SYDNEY;
You Can Go Home Again, And to the Beaches
body: As a onetime resident of Sydney who sneaks back annually during the down-under summer, I found surfing the Web to explore my former city as a vacation place a revelation. On Yahoo's Sydney Web site, travel .yahoo.com/destinations (click on the Oceania heading or search for "Sydney"), I found solid, sometimes imaginative information, on sightseeing, restaurants, transportation, hotels and best of all, the beaches. The site opens with a refreshing essay by Mary Ann Harrell, a writer who once lived in the city and who describes how the place has changed. This is a fine mood-setting piece (originally printed in National Geographic Traveler). A travel advisory from Knoll Travel Watch reminds would-be visitors that Sydney is the host city for next summer's Olympic Games: in September and October 2000, the city will be packed. But the good news in the travel advisory is that street crime is not a serious problem, except for late at night in King's Cross, an area replete with strip joints and bars. The Where to Eat in Sydney guide on Yahoo, seemed accurate and up to date. I clicked on my old neighborhood in Lane Cove and found 28 restaurants -- 27 more than when I lived there -- including a Chinese takeout called Tow Yin. More seriously, the guide also mentioned Doyle's on the Beach, a wonderful seafood place on the harbor shore. A main course and appetizer (known as an entree in Australia) would cost the equivalent of about $26, it was reported, which sounds about right. At the top end of the scale, the guide listed Rockpool, perhaps Sydney's finest seafood restaurant, where main course and appetizer cost about $76. One of the weaker points of the site was the accommodations listing. There are links to the major hotels, but some don't give room rates. For example, the site for the Inter-Continental, a luxury hotel built atop a colonial structure, offers a photo of its building and panoramic harbor views, and gives the number of rooms -- 498 -- and suites, but you have to fill out a reservation form to get a rate. The hotel section does list less expensive choices, including bed-and-breakfasts and corporate apartments in Sydney and its suburbs. I was encouraged to see that the opera house, Sydney's principal venue for contemporary dance, concerts and opera, is described in all its glory. Ferry services on the harbor -- one of the city's strong points -- were all listed, with schedules. Perhaps most innovative for the visitor interested in the beach is www.realsurf.com. On the site's Northern Beaches Tour, I viewed a photo of the waves at North Palmy, the local jargon for North Palm Beach, one of my favorites. Larry's Report that day on realsurf.com said that "Palm Beach and the joey were the pick this morning, about a meter and glassy waves, the peaks shifting about." However bizarre that sounds ("barren joey" is local slang for the peninsula at Palm Beach), it is authentic Sydney beach talk, and a fair testament to the sense of variety of city life that a Web site can give. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
The Way We Live Now: 6-27-99: Word & Image;
Memoir of A Memoirist
body: There is life after a memoir, most immediately an education in the business of bookselling. Never mind the name of my book; this is not a sales pitch. It's a report on a writer's journey through the commercial jungle in which superstores daily devour independent family stores and the Web has now begun to chew up the chains. The publishers that feed these beasts are also in turmoil. Between the signing of a contract and receipt of a manuscript, they often change their stripes, names or bosses or, as in my case, find themselves swallowed by an alien conglomerate. In their enlarged state, publishing staffs remain an acquisitive breed but begin, as dinosaurs should, to display clear signs of paranoia. Nevertheless, I can testify that contrary to legend, publishers still employ fine editors. They are an overworked species, to be sure, for they no longer just polish prose. They must battle for attention to their books inside the corporate hierarchy and lobby the salesmen to feign enthusiasm for words they are unlikely ever to read. No matter how grand those words, the publishers pale if they approach 200,000 in number. That's when even the most condensed typeface propels a volume beyond 500 pages, consuming so much paper that it breaks the psychological list-price barrier. The optimal maximum price of a book these days is $30, or $29.95 to be precise. Though still less than half the price of an orchestra seat at a Broadway play, that is the number at which sellers perceive reader resistance, even if they then offer an array of fluctuating discounts. (The $30 translates into a truly jarring list of $42 Canadian!) Contrary to conventional economics, the greater the demand for a book the deeper the discount. That is because the predators in superstores and on the Web currently prefer to achieve market share rather than profit. The standard come-on at chains like Barnes & Noble or Borders is now "10 percent off." When they sense unusual public interest and order a huge stack of any book, the big stores will bargain down the wholesale price and offer 30 percent off list. And in their wild competition for market share on the Internet, Barnesandnoble.com and Amazon.com will virtually forgo all profit to offer best sellers at discounts of 40 or 50 percent, or even a losing 60. The superstores have lured readers as well as browsers away from their cozy independent shops. The emporia let you linger in comfort and finger a vast inventory, with coffee service to boot. Now the Internet, though less tactile, has proved itself even more economical and, since you can shop there at any hour in any dress, more convenient as well. In a mere five years, the chains and Web sites together have deprived the nation's independents of more than half their market share and driven hundreds out of business altogether. As my book appeared this spring, the American Booksellers Association offered obituaries of independents in Idaho, Illinois and Cape Cod. Even Just Books, a most imaginative store in Greenwich, Conn., which has survived by displaying me and other authors at televised community breakfasts, has nonetheless lost about 20 percent of its sales to the Web over the last 18 months. And Politics and Prose, a warm old shoe in Washington that was chosen "bookseller of the year" by Publishers Weekly for recruiting a dedicated staff, presenting authors nightly and giving discounts to its discussion groups, reports "intense competition from on-line" sellers. The shifting earth beneath the entire industry has an obvious effect on every book's life span. The initial print orders are dictated by the cold and continental calculation of the chains, no longer the educated and local literary taste of the independents. Since publishers already must take back more than 30 percent of the books they send out -- for full refunds -- they dare not trust their own judgment of a book's appeal. When this system fails to anticipate demand, the publishers expect modern printing technology to spit out more copies fast, but that often risks missing the opportunities created by good reviews, radio and television exposure and an author's traveling roadshow. Ah, the "author tour": if truth be told, it is itself a function of the print order. The more modest a publisher's expectation for a book, the smaller the budget for the writer's planes and hotels. Thus authors are urged to become paid lecturers, so that someone else will underwrite their incidental visits to bookstores and local broadcasters. It becomes mere coincidence when an author appears in places that harbor a special interest in his work. It seems an even greater coincidence if all the booksellers in his path are truly prepared to meet the demand his appearance may arouse. But why worry about maldistribution if readers can so easily order on the Web? Well, when a reprinting of my book was delayed for a week by a snag in printing its jacket, Amazon.com decided to post a message that my memoir would not be available "for 4-6 weeks." And Amazon is so magnificently automated, it took 10 days to reach a live person who knew how to erase that erroneous message. The chances are slight that my royalties will ever exceed the amount advanced to me when I delivered a finished manuscript 18 months ago. Yet I am happy to keep plugging for the publisher's account, for reasons best explained long ago by George Orwell: "1. Sheer egoism. Desire to seem clever, to be talked about, to be remembered after death. 2. Esthetic enthusiasm. Perception of beauty in . . . words and their right arrangement. 3. Historical impulse. Desire to see things as they are, to find out true facts and store them up for the use of posterity. 4. Political purpose. Desire to push the world in a certain direction, to alter other people's idea of the kind of society that they should strive after." I hated the long and lonely labor of writing. And I dreaded the commercial aftermath. Yet despite the chaos that attends a book's publication and promotion, I am driven now by an overriding emotion: I love to have written. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Internet's lure spurs a round of real and imagined deal making.
body: ON the Internet almost anything is possible. But that's the bad news, for both companies and investors, who must confront a menagerie of potential products and deals to find a few that someday just might pay off. The painful confusion can be seen in several of the rumored deals in the market this week. On Tuesday, Dan Dorfman writing on the Jagnotes.com Web site said that the Compaq Computer Corporation was interested in trading its Alta Vista Internet service for stock in CMGI, an Internet investment concern. (The companies confirmed those talks yesterday.) On Tuesday, someone using the name of Andy Nguyen posted a rumor on a Yahoo message board that Gateway Inc., the computer maker, would offer to buy Earthlink, a big Internet service provider, for $75 a share. (The companies decline to comment.) Through subsequent and circuitous events, the Earthlink rumors forced Mindspring, another Internet service provider, to publish a cryptic statement that it was in talks about possible "business combinations." It declined to elaborate. What all these possible deals have in common is that neither the personal computer companies nor the Internet concerns are really comfortable in their own businesses, and they are wondering of the grass is greener on the other side. Selling computers these days has all the security of cliff diving, as prices are falling as fast as an Acapulco diver. Compaq's inability to keep from very painful belly flops, quarter after quarter, was largely the reason that the board dismissed its chief executive, Eckhard Pfeiffer, two months ago. Seeking profits, both Compaq and Gateway, which is doing somewhat better as it uses the increasingly popular direct sales approach, have decided to try to funnel their customers to Internet services they control. That way they can earn monthly fees or at least advertising revenue. Gateway, in fact, has been able to attract 400,000 customers to its Gateway.net Internet service, although by offering one full year free, it's hardly a big money maker yet. Compaq's Internet activities revolved around Alta Vista, a popular search service that it acquired with the Digital Equipment Corporation last year. Compaq at first ignored Alta Vista. But earlier this year it decided to plump it up in preparation to sell a piece to the public. And it began its own Internet service that directs users to Alta Vista. The Internet companies, meanwhile, have been struggling with their own businesses. None of the Internet service providers has found a way to break out of the pack to compete with America Online, which continues to snare half the new on-line users. Providing Internet access is largely a commodity telecommunication service, much like long distance. As for the Internet portal businesses, the biggest, like Yahoo, may well attract a big- enough audience to profit from advertising, but it's still unclear how Alta Vista will survive. But it is certainly far from clear that computer makers and Internet companies should jump into each other's arms. Potential buyers, say, for Internet service providers include telecommunications companies that want to offer all-in-one packages, or a host of other technology businesses. Microsoft, for example, has been sniffing around looking to buy Internet service providers, a sharp reversal from its stance a year ago, when it was considering selling its MSN Internet access. Internet portals, like Alta Vista, because they can attract large amounts of traffic, could well be attractive for companies including media companies and on-line retailers. Compaq, according to people close to its executives' plans, appears to be intrigued by owning a smaller piece of a larger Internet effort. CMGI is a combination of a venture capital investment fund and an incubator that has started a number of successful Internet companies, including Lycos. A potential purchase of Alta Vista by CMGI has the financial advantage of being an exchange of one Internet stock for another. CMGI's stock, which closed at $96.50 yesterday, is trading at nearly two and a half times the value of its underlying holdings, according to Keith Benjamin, an analyst with BancBoston Robertson Stephens. That premium reflects the buoyant Internet market and investor confidence in the company's management team. The value also allows it to pay a reported $2 billion to $3 billion for Alta Vista, which no traditional media company could afford. By contrast, the same sort of analysis shows that a Gateway-Earthlink deal would be difficult, as Gateway suffers from a real world valuation of 27 times earnings. Earthlink, like most Internet companies, loses money. Walter Winnitzki, an analyst with Hambrecht & Quist, figures that buying Earthlink would cause substantial dilution to Gateway's earnings, something its management is loath to do. Gateway and Earthlink declined to comment on whether they have had any talks. But Garry Betty, Earthlink's chief executive, said in a telephone interview that the company did not want its main method of finding new customers to be through buyers of computers. "If that is all you had to rely on, it would be very risky," he said. Nor, Mr. Betty added, is the company focused on acquisitions. The intention, he said, is to grow through aggressive marketing for new subscribers, largely those who want to graduate from America Online. While the Yahoo posting about an Earthlink Gateway deal may have been nothing more than someone trying to hype a stock, it did have the unintended effect of prodding the cryptic admission of deal making by Mindspring. In response to the reports about Earthlink, one Mindspring executive told a reporter that the company was not in any merger talks. "That wasn't exactly true," said Charles Brewer, the company's chief executive, yesterday. "And the misinformation needed to be corrected." Mr. Brewer did say, without elaborating, that Internet service providers have the potential to become more profitable as they grow larger. Analysts say that Mindspring well could be trying to buy another Internet service provider, like Prodigy Communications. Or it could be considering bids from a telecommunications company, Microsoft or perhaps even a computer maker. On the Internet anything is possible.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Trade Agency Finds Web Slippery With Snake Oil
body: Snake oil salesmen have been around for ages. But they are proliferating in the electronic age, according to the Federal Trade Commission, which announced today that it had identified hundreds of Web sites promoting phony cures for 30 ailments, including AIDS, multiple sclerosis, liver disease and cancer.
