title: Ruling for Net Music Storage Device
body: In a major defeat for the recording industry, a Federal appeals court has ruled that a popular device used to download and store music from the Internet does not violate Federal anti-piracy laws. The unitedstates Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in San Francisco found that the Rio MP300, manufactured by Diamond Multimedia Systems Inc., did not qualify as a "digital audio recording device" and was not subject to the restrictions of the 1992 Audio Home Recording Act. The court found in a 3-to-0 vote that the Rio, a pager-sized device that can store CD-quality songs encoded in the so-called MP3 format, was not primarily a recorder and so was not subject to the 1992 act. The court's decision torpedoed a suit filed in October by the Recording Industry Association of America, which had aimed at the Rio and Internet MP3 music files as a major source of music piracy. MP3 is widely used by lesser-known artists to distribute their music, but the record industry fears the format will lead to rampant piracy in cyberspace, where files can be copied and sent rapidly. After a lower court rejected its request for a preliminary injunction barring sales of the Rio last fall, the industry association appealed. After the ruling, the association said in a statement, "We filed this lawsuit because unchecked piracy on the Internet threatens the development of a legitimate marketplace for on-line music, a marketplace that consumers want." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Sotheby's and Amazon.com Strike a Deal to Sell on Line
body: Five months after announcing a $25 million plan to begin its own on-line auction business, Sotheby's has entered into an alliance with Amazon.com to begin selling art and collectibles later this year. The arrangement, announced yesterday, combines Amazon's on-line expertise and broad customer reach with Sotheby's reputation as an authority in the business of selling fine and decorative arts. "We are bringing to the table technology, customer service and an introduction to 10 million people," said Jeffrey P. Bezos, the founder and chief executive of Amazon.com. "One of the biggest problems in the on-line auction business is the ability to authenticate what we sell, and that's something Sotheby's can help us do. There's no other partner out there that could help us build this." Amazon is also hoping to tap into Sotheby's large international data base of collectors. By working together, Sotheby's and Amazon are trying to strengthen their positions in the fast-growing and highly competitive field of on-line auctions. In January, Christie's, the Rockefeller Center auction house and Sotheby rival, announced that it, too, would start an on-line auction site, Christies.com. It will begin conducting on-line sales in September. Christie's, which is owned by Pinault-Printemps-Redoute of France, is said to be in negotiations with other on-line companies to form an alliance similar to that of Amazon-Sotheby's, but a spokeswoman at Christie's would say only that it was going ahead with its site as planned. In April, the auction site Ebay bought Butterfield & Butterfield, the San Francisco-based auctioneers, for $260 million. Ebay is also said to have discussed some kind of partnership with both Sotheby's and Christie's, but people close to both auction houses said those talks had ended. On a smaller scale, Artnet.com, a high-end portal devoted to selling artwork on line, went public in Germany last month. "We see the Sotheby's-Amazon deal not as art world news but as an attempt by Amazon to compete with Ebay," said Hans Neuendorf, chairman of Artnet. "For Sotheby's, it's a way to expand into low-priced collectibles." Mr. Bezos disagreed with those remarks. "That's not true," he said. "We're trying to create a whole new auction site, one that makes sense for valuable objects. The point is to break new ground selling fully authenticated, fully guaranteed objects on line using Sotheby's experts around the world and its network of more than 2,800 dealers." Under the agreement, Amazon will invest $35 million in the Manhattan auction house, or less than 2 percent of Sotheby's. It has agreed to buy one million shares of class A common stock at about $35 each and is buying a warrant for $10 million that entitles it to buy one million more shares of Sotheby's class A for $100 each. Shares of Sotheby's rose $4.125 yesterday, to $39.25, while Amazon.com rose $15.1875, to $111.6875. Three different auction sites will be available by clicking on Amazon.com or Sothebys.com. Amazon will keep its three-month-old amazon.com/auctions, which sells everything from washing machines to Andy Warhol paintings to a $75,000 space capsule. Anyone can buy and sell on this site, but Amazon will guarantee purchases only up to $250. A joint site, sothebys.amazon.com, will offer all areas of collectibles, from coins and jewelry to porcelains and Barbie dolls, but sellers will be only professional dealers and they will be responsible for guaranteeing the objects they sell. The third site, sothebys.com, will sell the more traditional auction-house fare, such as paintings, furniture and decorative objects. For this site, the seller, whether it is a dealer or Sotheby's, will guarantee all the property. "We haven't thought of these different sites as having different price points but rather each having different and special characters," said Diana D. Brooks, Sotheby's chief executive. "Now dealers from around the world will be able to offer their property to an unlimited number of potential bidders, and buyers will be able to participate in some of the most exciting on-line auctions." Participation will not simply be on line. In April, Amazon acquired Livebid.com, a provider of live auctions on the Internet. Mr. Bezos said it would begin broadcasting some of Sotheby's auctions. Bidders will be able to see the items on their computer screens, read the descriptions and bid while an auction takes place. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Diana D. Brooks, Sotheby's chief executive, and Jeffrey P. Bezos, the founder and chief executive of Amazon.com, announcing their companies' alliance at a news conference yesterday at Sotheby's. (Associated Press)

title: The Beat Goes on Line, and Sometimes It's Legal
body: IF there is a "Phantom Menace" of the Internet, it's MP3, the compression software that enables CD-quality music to be sent on line. Like the film, MP3 comes with a considerable amount of hyperbole, promise and, alas, science fiction. The fiction is a consequence of the buzz. MP3 is said to be so easy to use that many surfers assume that they can swiftly point, click and download, say, the entire Smashing Pumpkins catalogue. With all the talk about MP3 as the future of music on line, more and more people believe that MP3 is synonymous with on-line music. "The mass market has no clue what's behind MP3," said Mark Hardie, a senior analyst at Forrester Research, which recently issued a report on digital music distribution. "The format is meaningless to them. They just want the music." But just as Kleenex is only one brand of tissue, MP3 is only one form of on-line music. It is also technically tricky, legally sticky and essentially a work in progress. In other words, if you're having trouble getting started, don't worry -- it's not your fault. MP3 is one major step in the evolution of music on line, which began more than a decade ago. The simplest way to describe it is as a way of storing music in digital code. But it is by no means the first way or the last. Among the first, at least in terms of music on line, were WAV and .AU files. With the rise in the late 1980's of bulletin board services -- electronic message systems formed around common interests -- a subculture emerged of fans who swapped songs in one of those formats. But because of these formats' limited compression technology and the fact that early modems had bandwidth the size of a cocktail straw, a three-minute song could take hours to download at the common modem rate of 2,400 baud. In 1987, the Motion Picture Experts Group, or MPEG, of the International Organization for Standardization in Geneva began researching and developing a way to compress digital video -- in other words, to reduce the amount of code, and thus the amount of storage space, needed for a given image. The result, in 1992, was the MPEG format, which could also be applied to audio files. It reduced storage space without sacrificing CD-quality sound. MPEG-1 Layer 3, which would become known as MP3, was the most powerful version, capable of squeezing a song into one-twelfth the space that a WAV file would require. With the simultaneous increase in bandwidth to 14,400 Kbps and then 28,800 Kbps, and even faster speeds, the new compression technology meant that the same three-minute song that took hours to send as a WAV file could now be sent in minutes. Since MPEG was originally intended for digital video, it did not immediately catch on for music. Instead, Web surfers flocked to software like Real Networks' Real Player and Microsoft's Net Show, which allow them to "stream" audio quickly (to download songs or other sound in such a way that it can be played as it is being downloaded). Sitting at the keyboard, a user could listen to live concert Webcasts, radio and, yes, pirated recordings without lengthy downloading. But the compromises in sound quality helped create a demand for something that would provide CD-quality sound. It was not until the mid-90's that college students on high-speed networks began rallying around MP3, which is considerably more efficient at compressing the space needed for the digital code. With MP3, a dozen albums can be squeezed onto a single CD-ROM. Like many popular music trends, the grass-roots movement around MP3 soon caught the attention of entrepreneurs who were looking for a new market. It also caught the attention of record industry executives, who were rocked by the potential invasion of their market. MP3.com, a company based in San Diego, recently announced that it would file an initial public offering that could raise up to $115 million. Though the company's Web site (www.mp3.com) includes more than 56,000 songs from 11,000 artists, it is not the official source for MP3 -- there is no official source. MP3 songs exists everywhere. They can be found on pay-to-purchase sites like Emusic.com (www.emusic.com), which presents selections from a variety of independent record labels, and on pirate sites run by individuals who illegally post digital versions of copyright-protected music. Many search engines can find MP3 songs; 2look4 is devoted to MP3 searches, and Lycos has an MP3 search area. Olle Waltari, an 18-year-old student in Stockholm, created MP3Place (mp3place.net) to help surfers find the files. But times have changed. "MP3 might have lost a little of that 'underground feeling' that it had a year or two ago," he said via email. He said he was finding more legal MP3 sites and fewer illegal ones. Most major record labels have not made their artists' music available on MP3. Sites that offer music illegally are easy to find, but getting the songs is another story. Many record companies are issuing cease-and-desist letters to the creators of such sites or, often more effectively, threatening the I.S.P.'s that play host to the sites, which in turn threaten to pull the plug. The copyright issue is already fueling a new wave of digital compression wares. Despite the fuss, MP3 is a decade old -- eons in the high-tech universe. Many companies, as a result, are quickly developing and releasing compression alternatives. The Recording Industry Association of America (and the Fraunhofer Institute, the Geneva organization behind MP3) has been working to develop a Secure Digital Music Initiative, or SDMI, standard, which would include a way to handle artists' royalties. Whatever standard SDMI comes up with will probably work with various formats. The concern that is pushing the initiative to meet a June 30 deadline is not so much the playing of MP3 files on computers but a new generation of consumer devices in both portable and home stereo versions that will play electronically delivered music in one format or another. (The unitedstates Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled yesterday that one of these devices, a portable player of MP3 files called the Rio, was not illegal.) After meetings in Los Angeles, London and Tokyo, SDMI has agreed to the release of devices this year that can play unprotected MP3 files, with the understanding that manufacturers will switch to protected versions of all formats as soon as the SDMI specifications are ready. A number of formats are available. Liquid Audio's Liquid Music System encrypts music so that it cannot be illegally copied.  And Microsoft's MS Audio creates files half the size of MP3 and offers a royalties system. AT&T, one of the companies that worked with the Fraunhofer Institute on MP3, has its own system, called A2B. VQF, a new grass-roots program, is said to compress files three times as much as MP3, with even better quality. Even MP3 has its own successor, the higher-quality MP4. It is clearly still the Wild West for digital music on line, and MP3 is an old but still formidable gunfighter. Forrester Research predicts that SDMI will ultimately become accepted, whatever formats are used.. As for now, Mr. Hardie said: "This is just techies arguing tooth and nail about what's better. If you're still arguing over formats, then you're not ready for consumers."  Copyright Law Legal Pitfalls Are Easy to Find Along With Music THE heart of the MP3 controversy is the copyright issue. Because of the ease of moving digital files from CD to computer and from computer to computer, executives at major recording labels are concerned that their artists' music will be illegally copied. The Recording Industry Association of America tried unsuccessfully to prevent Diamond Multimedia from releasing the Rio, a portable MP3 player, because of the potential for piracy. (Diamond recently announced that it would include special encryption features to address the problem.) Some artists want to retain copyright themselves, deciding on their own whether to distribute music over the Net for a fee. The rapper Chuck D recently made his group Public Enemy's latest album, "There's a Poison Goin' On," available in its entirety before it was released on CD. The MP3 format is legal but can be used illegally. On sites like MP3.com, many unsigned artists have granted permission for surfers to download their songs, which is legal. But on sites where permission hasn't been granted, copying those songs is illegal. Prerecorded music -- a CD, for example -- can be copied to a tape cassette or to an MP3 format for personal use, to listen to on a computer or portable player. That copy cannot legally be given, traded or sold to anyone else.   DAVID KUSHNER http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: The singers Alanis Morissette, left, and Tori Amos will offer live performances on a Web site devoted to MP3 music. (Ebet Roberts; (Sara Krulwich/The New York Times)(pg. G7)  Diagram: "Squeezing Sound" Audio compression exploits the fact that human hearing is not perfect. For example, loud sounds can mask other sounds, making them inaudible to the human ear. This masking allows the amount of data to be reduced from the original signal without losing sound quality.  Digital audio, like that on CD's, uses only a fraction of the original file size when converted to the MP3 format so the files can easily be distributed over the Internet.  DIGITAL AUDIO SIGNAL Original digital signal has a high data rate, based on sampling the analog sound at many points.  FILTERING The signal is divided into several frequency bands.  COMPRESSION Masking caused by the loud sound allows parts of the signal to be represented with fewer bits, enabling compression.  (Source: Cambridge Research Laboratory, Compaq Computer Corporation)(pg. G7)  Chart/Drawing: "Web Music: Getting to MP3" While the music industry worries about how to make songs available on the Web without losing money, and some artists are turning to on-line music as a new channel to their fans, many computer users are left wondering where to find music on line and what to do when they find it. Here are some tips on music in the popular MP3 format, one of many formats that can be used for storing music digitally.  Finding MP3 audio:  Though sometimes elusive, MP3 audio is widely available on the Net. MP3.com (www.mp3.com) offers more than 10,000 pop, alternative, country, hip-hop and spoken-word tracks, mainly by lesser-known artists, though major stars like Tori Amos and Alanis Morissette will be offering live performances through the site. It also features instructions under the MP3 for Beginners banner. You can scour the Web, looking for an artist or song title, through MP3 search sites like 2look4 (www.2look4.com). Because of potential copyright violations, Top 40 tracks might prove difficult -- or impossible -- to find. Sites offering titles illegally require surfers to download directly from a server with a special password. As the Recording Industry Association of America pursues more bootleg sites, these pirate tracks are becoming increasingly elusive.  Playing MP3:  COMPUTER-BASED PLAYERS: To decode MP3 files, you need special software (a comprehensive list is available at www.mp3.com/software). MP3 players are widely available free (or for a small shareware fee) for downloading. For Windows, Winamp (www.winamp.com) and Musicmatch (www.musicmatch.com) are popular; Macintosh users can try Macamp (www.macamp.com). The new Real Player Plus G2 from Real Networks (www.real.com) supports MP3, as well as streaming Real Audio and Video.  PORTABLE PLAYERS: The so-called killer app for MP3 is special hardware that allows listeners to enjoy the music away from the computer. Priced at less than $200, the palm-size Diamond Rio has become the Walkman of MP3, playing about an hour's worth of music (www.diamondmm.com). Alternatives include the MPMan (www.eigerlabs.com/mpman/index.html) and the Nomad from Creative Labs (www.nomadworld.com/products/welcome.html). Players designed specifically for use in cars, like the Empeg Player (www.empeg.com), are beginning to hit the market as well.  Making MP3:  Programs like Musicmatch for Windows and Audiocatalyst (www.xingtech.com/mp3 /audiocatalyst) allow you to digitally extract and write audio tracks from compact disks to your hard drive, a process sometimes called ripping. With Musicmatch, for example, you simply insert a CD into your CD-ROM drive and click on Record on the Musicmatch player; a selected track will then be converted into MP3 within a few minutes. To record the MP3 track onto a CD, it must be first converted to a WAV file (using an encoder like Winamp), then burned onto a disk using a CD recorder device. To post the tracks on the Internet (which is illegal without copyright permission), it's just a matter of creating your own Web page or using a free service like MP3.com.  (Illustration by Gorka Sampedro for The New York Times)(pg. G7)

title: Battle Over Internet Names Escalates
body: In the latest sign of escalating tension between the Internet's new oversight board and Network Solutions Inc., the company that controls the distribution and registration of Internet addresses, the board's interim chairwoman said today that the company was fostering unfounded criticism of her group. The chairwoman, Esther Dyson, made her accusations in a letter in which she sought the help of the consumer advocate Ralph Nader in ending the company's control of the lucrative business of registering Internet addresses that end in .com, .net and .org. On behalf of her organization, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, or Icann, Ms. Dyson sent a letter responding to queries made last week by Mr. Nader and James Love, director of the Consumer Project on Technology. In their letter, sent Friday, the two men, responding to growing criticism of the interim board's activities, asked Ms. Dyson a series of fairly broad questions about Icann and the board, and how it sees its role in setting policy for the global network and in spending the $1 fee it has voted to impose on every Internet address, or domain name, registered. The board's third meeting last month, in Berlin, ignited intensified criticism from Network Solutions, based in Herndon, Va., and others that the nonprofit group was moving too fast on policy rather than focusing on creating the panels that will make policy recommendations and elect permanent board members.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Boom Mind-Set Deeply Etched in Chip Capital - Correction Appended
body: In Silicon Valley these are the days of miracles and wonder. In the midst of the longest sustained boom in the nation's high-technology heartland, there is a palpable air of unreality that has come to color the outlook of the computer engineers, venture capitalists and software hackers who make up the valley's rank and file. Wage rates in the region are about 60 percent above the national average and are growing far more quickly than average. Driven by the vast new wealth created by a wave of Internet-related start-up companies and the increasingly vast inflows of venture capital, good times have arrived in abundance and have stayed longer than ever before. The good times have led so many valley workers to sports car showrooms that Raymond Lane, the president of Oracle, the giant data base company, complained recently that he could not find the new Porsche he wanted in Northern California; one local dealership had a six-month waiting list. (He ordered one from a Southern California dealer through the Internet.) And in meetings at power breakfast spots here like Il Fornaio or Bucks in Woodside, executives shake their heads over stories such as the one about the home in a comfortable Palo Alto neighborhood that sold in April for $1 million more than the $2.4 million asking price. But indicators like those have in turn led to a growing sense of unease among many valley longtimers who oscillate between a faith in what has been called the "long boom" and the knowledge that each of the valley's booms in the last half-century has inevitably been followed by a bust. "The valley is now divided into two camps," said John Shoch, a partner at Alloy Ventures, a venture capital firm based in Palo Alto. "There are those people who are firmly inside a reality-distortion field and there are the rest of us who realize that this is going to end but who can't help going along for the ride." The talk at the restaurants and sports clubs is frequently of the power of "Yahoo dollars" or "Weimar currencies," the fruits of a stock market that seems to have a bottomless appetite for Internet start-ups. In fact, stock certificates have in many ways become the currency of the valley -- to such an extent that the Menlo Park Presbyterian Church receives more than 10 percent of its contributions in stock instead of money. And St. Joseph's, a Roman Catholic school in Atherton, devotes part of its endowment to its own venture capital fund. While the surging stock values have allowed companies to attract the best and brightest employees and acquire other companies, there is also a growing perception that the excesses of the boom may have permanently undermined the valley's traditional no-nonsense, engineering-driven culture. At the Palo Alto office of R. R. Donnelley, the printing company that publishes the documents known as red herrings that are a key part of the rite of going public, the valet parking, the pool table and the cigars in a thermidor occasion more than one raised eyebrow. And such is the cash rattling around that an editor at the high-speed Internet service At Home recently purchased a new $625,000 home on his debit card. Indeed, one consensus is that this unrivaled wealth creation has led to a stock market bubble that will certainly end, but nobody knows when or how. "There are some people who are making the case that the Internet has changed the law of physics," said Fred Hoar, a longtime Silicon Valley publicist. "But this is still a Newtonian world, and when you throw something up in this world, it's going to come down." One thing that has made this boom so unusual is that it has gone on for so long. It has been more than six years since the valley has seen tough times, a fact that has caused memories here to grow hazy and has led some longtimers here to look for ways to cling to a past that seems increasingly distant. Roger McNamee, a fund manager at Interval Partners in Menlo Park, has followed the valley's ups and downs since the beginning of the PC era. Now he points across a parking lot at his Toyota Camry, a modest car contrasting with the more typical turbo-charged luxury cars. He says he hangs onto the car as a touchstone to a world he is in danger of losing contact with. Economists and researchers who are trying to understand the apparent disappearance of the valley's decades-old boom-and-bust cycle point to the convergence of two separate trends that set the economy into a sustained period of overdrive. The semiconductor industry, long the bedrock of Silicon Valley, was just beginning to recover in 1993 when the demand for Internet communications gear started its rapid acceleration. Then in 1995 the Web economy kicked in, creating a remarkable business spiral. Yet, although there have been booms before, this one has altered the valley in ways that many of the region's longtimers regret. And not without reason: only 38.2 percent of the valley's homes, for example, are affordable to those making the median income, compared with 65 percent nationally, according to the National Association of Home Builders. "People who are inclined to make money fast are flocking here," said Garth Hardwood, an environmental researcher who grew up in Menlo Park but has moved to the coastal village of Pescadero to escape the valley scene. "It's hard to grasp what's going on -- it's so big and fast, and people are so aggressive." Even within the industries that gave Silicon Valley its name, some lament what the boom mind-set has done to the valley's entrepreneurial culture. "It is a corrosive effect on the valley parallel to Wall Street in the mid-1980's," said Eric Schmidt, who was the chief technology officer at Sun Microsystems before decamping to Utah two years ago as president and chief executive of Novell. "The level of expectation is well beyond the norm, even in Silicon Valley," he added. "People have very short attention spans when it comes to their careers. It is a youth phenomenon, a new generation of entrepreneurs who have not had to concentrate on building institutions that endure. Moreover, the venture industry has no longer had to build a long-term business. The corrosive effect is in creating a short-term versus long-term way of thinking." And the wild successes of Stanford students like Jerry Yang of Yahoo or Joe Kraus of Excite have now made it common for graduates to choose Silicon Valley start-ups first. "Today 75 percent of my students are joining emerging companies," said John Hennessey, the dean of the school of engineering at Stanford University. That is a sharp turn from the days when the normal career meant joining an established high-technology company like Hewlett-Packard. "You've got this funny psychology in which the reality and the unreality coexist," said Michael Borrus, a managing director at Petkovich & Partners, a San Francisco investment firm. "These kids really believe they're going to get wealthy and this youthful optimism is overriding the fact that maybe 9 out of 10 of them won't have an I.P.O. in their lifetime." It is, however, an economy in which several waves of new workers have never known anything but explosive growth. "In the semiconductor industry, we've known historically that every four years we get hit cross the lip," said Mr. Hoar, the publicist, who was an early employee at Fairchild Semiconductor, a pioneering chip maker. "There is one group that has seen it all and they have the scars. On the other hand you have this group that says, 'Every breath I take is golden.' " That latter view rankles some valley pioneers like Andrew Grove, a founder of Intel, and Steven P. Jobs, Apple Computer's co-founder. Mr. Grove said that only recently had he begun to hear the phrase "exit strategy" -- do we want to be acquired or aim to go public? -- which is now routinely part of the planning for start-up ventures that have yet to sell their first product. "This is not reality," Mr. Jobs said. When Apple started, he said, his role models were William Hewlett and David Packard, who set out to build an institution rather than an overnight gold mine. And ignoring that reality will ultimately bring its own reckoning, Mr. Hoar said. "There is one chapter that keeps repeating itself in this valley, and that's Chapter 11," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  A chart in Business Day on Wednesday showing economic trends in Santa Clara County, Calif., credited a data source incorrectly. It was the VentureOne Corporation, not Venture One Economics. title: F.C.C. Says It Should Regulate High-Speed Access to Internet
body: Anxious cable companies got a boost yesterday when the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, William E. Kennard, said his agency, not local governments, should regulate high-speed Internet access. Thus far, the F.C.C. and Congress have declined to regulate cable Internet services. Mr. Kennard, in a speech to the National Cable Television Association in Chicago, was responding to a Federal court ruling in Portland, Ore., two weeks ago affirming the authority of local governments to require the AT&T Corporation to allow competing Internet service providers onto the cable system it acquired in its purchase of Telecommunications Inc. this year. AT&T has said it will appeal the decision, but cable executives want assurance that if they spend billions upgrading their cable systems, they will be able to use their own high-speed Internet access providers. AT&T is a majority owner of the cable-Internet service Excite@Home, while Time Warner Inc. owns the Roadrunner cable modem service. America Online and other Internet service providers are lobbying the F.C.C. and local governments to force the cable companies to open their systems to them. Mr. Kennard said he was studying his options for getting involved in the Portland case. Cheryl Leanza, deputy director of Media Access Project, a nonprofit telecommunications law firm, said that generally courts had tended to defer to the F.C.C. in complex regulatory matters. The Portland case was widely followed because it set a precedent for how other local governments might behave. "What we have here is a power struggle that goes back to the Civil War," said Howard Anderson, president of the Yankee Group, a consulting firm. "It is a question of whether the Federal Government or the state government will have control. For the cable operators, it is not so much about money, as about power. What they want to do is to exclude the other Internet providers." News that the F.C.C. might intervene in the matter sent stocks of cable operators up yesterday. Time Warner shares rose $4.625 to close at $66.687, Comcast rose $1.93 to close at $32.875 and Adelphia jumped $6.875 to close at $62.875. Time Warner stock also benefited from its bid to focus attention on its Internet-related business. Yesterday it named Richard Bressler, who has been the company's chief financial officer since 1995, head of its new on-line unit, Time Warner Digital Media, which includes all the company's Internet presence, including electronic commerce. Time Warner's chairman, Gerald Levin, described the new entity as the company's "single most important growth area." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Gates Testifies, and the Republicans Seek to Forge Closer Links
body: Al Gore may not have invented the Internet, but he and President Clinton have honed their skills of extracting political contributions from Silicon Valley. Now, in a three-day "High Tech Summit" on Capitol Hill, Republicans are trying to show that they have the capacity to be even better friends of William H. Gates and his competitors. This morning, Mr. Gates -- his once-sharp barbs about Washington lawmakers replaced with such deferential comments as "you've raised an interesting issue, Senator" -- was filled with prognostications about how the Web, wireless networks and electronic commerce would turn "consumers into big winners." And the members of the Joint Economic Committee, led by Republicans, were so filled with praise for the Microsoft Corporation and its entrepreneurial ilk that they only once, and then only obliquely, raised the uncomfortable question of how antitrust laws were applied to the world's most powerful software company. Left unsaid, but understood, was that it is President Clinton's Justice Department that is pursuing Microsoft in court a few blocks away. Indeed, the subtext of the three days of hearings, which began with the Federal Reserve chairman, Alan Greenspan, and continued today with Mr. Gates's appearance, is that Republicans are eager to get the Government off the valley's back. Certainly, many in Silicon Valley would be happy to see Microsoft have its hand slapped by the Government. But that did not stop heads from nodding today when Mr. Gates talked about how keeping "a light hand" on the regulation of technology industries "is working very, very well." No sooner had he finished talking than the Senate voted to lighten the touch even more: Over the Administration's objections, it approved a bill that would limit the liability of high-technology companies for any damage from the Year 2000 computer bug. President Clinton has pledged to veto the legislation, a version of which has already been passed in the House, providing yet another wedge for Republicans who maintain that the White House is the valley's fair-weather friend. "There are two things going on here," a Republican member of the committee said after today's hearings, asking not to be further identified. "There are real issues we'll have to deal with," among them hearings on Internet privacy, data encryption and support for basic research. "And there are questions of political funding. Which of those goes first? That will depend on how cynical you are." Mr. Gates once reveled in an apolitical nature. Until a few years ago, Microsoft maintained only a small presence in Washington, eschewing professional lobbyists and suggesting that the importance of what happens in hearing rooms pales in comparison with what happens in software labs. Meanwhile, the Republican leadership, or at least those leaders without significant high-technology constituencies, largely ceded the territory to Mr. Clinton and Mr. Gore. But these days, they see an opportunity. Software makers are still haggling with the Administration, and Mr. Gore in particular, over rules limiting the export of programs that offer high-level encryption of data -- which American intelligence agencies fear will be exploited by potential enemies. And at today's hearings, William L. Larson, the president of Network Associates Inc., described how the company is about to lose "a seven-figure deal" to provide such software to Chrysler, after its new parent, DaimlerChrysler, insisted on purchasing programs that could be shipped around the world. The business is likely to go to a German competitor, Mr. Larson said. Others used the moment to lobby for an extension of the research and development tax break. Charles Vest, president of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, warned against "growing complacency" about American high-technology superiority, and noting that Federal funds for basic research and development were declining. He said that at this point "the unitedstates is living off of historical assets that are not being renewed." The Internet's origins lie in a system developed by the Pentagon and used for years, largely in obscurity, by academics. But the big draw today was Mr. Gates, who received the gentlest of handling all around. There were no tough questions about charges that have arisen during the antitrust trial. In fact, there were no tough questions at all -- either from the Senators or from students who were asking questions, via an Internet link, from university and high school projects that Microsoft is backing. While it was never discussed, the Republican-dominated panel was aware that Microsoft greatly increased its giving to political causes in the 1997 and 1998 election cycles, and the expectation is that the amounts could increase significantly for the Presidential election. The company and its employees gave about $1.3 million in unregulated "soft money" over the last two years, putting them among the top dozen or so in this category. It was listed as a "table sponsor" for the Republican Congressional Committee dinner last week. While tables sell for $25,000 -- relatively small stuff in the world of big contributors -- the move was viewed as a sign of things to come as Republicans seek to exploit Microsoft's unhappiness with its treatment by the Clinton Administration. Microsoft has increased its permanent lobbying staff in Washington and has also reached out to some of the capital's longtime consultants. Among the lobbyists under contract is the former chairman of the Republican National Committee, Haley Barbour. Roughly two-thirds of Microsoft's political spending already goes to Republicans, a figure that a senior employee at the company's Redmond, Wash., headquarters said "would probably come as a surprise to most Microsoft employees." Mr. Gates did everything he could today to steer clear of controversy. He talked about forthcoming inventions that would help members of Congress in their work, including new types of portable digital devices that would help them "access your own 'digital dashboard' " even when they are out of Washington. He banished from his vocabulary almost all his usual tech-speak, talking as if he was giving a speech to an interested but somewhat unsophisticated chamber of commerce. Invited to give his views on the state of American antitrust laws, he said that "the laws as they are currently written are fine." The implication he left is that they are being wrongly interpreted in Microsoft's case. But he dodged specific mention of the litigation, other than to say "things like integration of new features are one of the freedoms companies have" under those laws. Part of the Microsoft case hinges on the matter of whether the company is integrating its Internet browser into the Windows operating system in a way that undercuts the ability of competing browsers to operate. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: William H. Gates explaining a point yesterday to the Joint Economic Committee in Washington. (Justin Lane for The newyork Times)

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Another Company Takes the 'Hong Kong' Out of Its Name
body: Score another one for globalism over localism. hongkong's local telephone company, hongkong Telecommunications Ltd., said today that it would change its name to Cable and Wireless HKT to tighten ties with its London-based parent company, Cable and Wireless P.L.C. hongkong Telecom said the new name was intended to convey the company's broader ambitions as a supplier of Internet connections and electronic commerce, as well as traditional telephone services, throughout Asia. "We are rooted in hongkong and will continue to focus on hongkong with investment," said Linus Cheung, the chief executive of hongkong Telecom, at a news conference. But he added, "For the future performance of our company, we will have to move out of hongkong." To some people here, the move is more discouraging evidence that hongkong is losing its brand-name prestige as a commercial center. Last November, HSBC Holdings, the parent of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, announced plans to drop the "Hongkong" from the English name of its flagship bank in favor of the HSBC abbreviation. "Every time the hongkong name is removed from a major company, you reduce the publicity for hongkong," said Ian K. Perkin, the chief economist of the hongkong General Chamber of Commerce. "It downgrades the world's perception of hongkong, which is disappointing." Mr. Perkin also questioned hongkong Telecom's decision to tie its image to Cable and Wireless, a 127-year-old British company that cobbled together its global network by constructing telephone operations in onetime British colonies, from the Caribbean to India to hongkong. "Cable and Wireless is a company that followed the British Empire around the world," he said, "The name seems to be a throwback." To hongkong Telecom, however, the Cable and Wireless name symbolizes a thoroughly modern company no longer wholly dependent on either its home market or traditional voice communications. Its ventures outside hongkong include building the first fiber optic cable linking Chinese cities. hongkong Telecom's nonvoice services range from fax and data transmission to Internet access and interactive television. Voice communications generate only 40 percent of the company's profits, Mr. Cheung said, and that figure could fall to 25 percent in three years. "Our vision is to make hongkong the Internet hub and E-commerce center of Asia," Mr. Cheung said, noting that the company had spent $20 billion (hongkong), or $2.58 billion (unitedstates), to upgrade its networks here. Some analysts said the name change might have been dictated more by corporate imperatives in London. Although Cable and Wireless had one of the first genuinely global telecommunications networks, investors have not rewarded the company with a commensurate valuation in the stock market. "They weren't getting credit for it because most of the assets weren't named for Cable and Wireless," said Lloyd Fischer, a telecommunications analyst at Salomon Smith Barney in hongkong. Mr. Fischer predicted that the name change would have little effect in the home market because the company would not be changing its Chinese name, which translates as "hongkong Telecom." More than 95 percent of hongkong's residents are Chinese. HSBC also kept the Chinese name of the hongkong bank.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Sotheby's and Amazon Join On Internet Auction Site
body: Five months after Sotheby's announced a $25 million initiative to begin its own on-line auction business, it has entered into an alliance with Amazon.com. The two will begin selling art and collectibles later this year. The arrangement merges Amazon's on-line expertise and broad customer reach with Sotheby's reputation as an authority in the business of selling fine and decorative arts. "We are bringing to the table technology, customer service and an introduction to 10 million people," said Jeff Bezas, founder and chief executive officer of Amazon.com. "One of the biggest problems in the on-line auction business is the ability to authenticate what we sell and that's something Sotheby's can help us do. There's no other partner out there that could help us build this." Under the agreement, Amazon is making a $35 million investment in the Manhattan auction house. It has agreed to purchase one million shares of Class A common stock at about $35 a share. Amazon is also buying a warrant for $10 million that entitles it to purchase an additional one million shares of Sotheby's Class A stock at a price of $100 a share. Amazon's total investment is about $45 million. There will now be three different auction sites, all available by clicking on Amazon.com. Amazon will keep its three-month old auction business, which can be reached on its general Web site. Like a gigantic flea market, it sells everything from washing machines to Andy Warhol art to a $75,000 space capsule. Anyone, whether they be a dealer or a collector, can buy and sell on this site, but Amazon will only guarantee purchases of up to $250. Sothebys.amazon.com will offer all areas of collectibles from coins and jewelry to porcelains and Barbie dolls, but sellers will be only professional dealers and they will be responsible for guaranteeing the objects they sell. The third site, Sothebys.com, will sell the more traditional auction-house fare, such as paintings, furniture and decorative objects. For this site, the seller, whether it a dealer or Sotheby's, will also guarantee all the property. All three sites will be available by clicking on either Amazon.com or Sothebys.com. "We haven't thought of these different sites as having different price points but rather each having different and special characters," said Diana D. Brooks, Sotheby's chief executive.  "Now dealers from around the world will be able to offer their property to an unlimited number of potential bidders and buyers be able to participate in some of the most exciting on-line auctions." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
Dow Rises, but Nasdaq Is Pulled Down by Internet Sector
body: Stock prices were mixed and activity remained subdued yesterday as traders and investors delayed putting money to work before an important inflation report that is scheduled for release tomorrow. Long-term interest rates, which have risen sharply in recent weeks and put pressure on stocks, eased a bit yesterday. Still, the drop in rates did little to alter the consensus that the Federal Reserve will raise short-term interest rates to dampen growth when its policy makers meet later this month. Stocks that are sensitive to the business cycle, which do well in an expanding economy, helped to push the Dow Jones industrial average higher. But Internet stocks were crushed, pushed lower by negative developments affecting three of the group's most important companies -- America Online, Charles Schwab and Ebay -- as well as concerns about higher interest rates. "The big, high-cap stocks are the allure, and money is coming out of technology and Internet stocks and even some small stocks" to move into those companies, said Bill Allyn, head of listed trading at Jefferies & Company. For the most part, however, money was not going anywhere. For the sixth time in the last eight sessions, fewer than 700 million shares changed hands on the newyork Stock Exchange. At 832.2 million shares, volume on the Nasdaq market was a bit better but still well short of the one-billion-share trading sessions seen recently. Led by DuPont, General Electric and Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing, the Dow rose 72.82 points, or seven-tenths of a percent, to 10,563.33. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index was flat, rising 0.36 point, to 1,294.00. But the Nasdaq composite index, dragged down by the Internet sector, fell sharply. At the close, the Nasdaq was off 49.57 points, or 2.03 percent, to 2,398.31. Some traders and analysts said the market's tone might change after tomorrow's release of May consumer price data. The April numbers showed the biggest monthly increase in more than nine years. That report rattled financial markets and led to an ever-rising chorus that the Fed would move soon to raise interest rates. A report showing the April figures to be an aberration would be helpful but hardly conclusive, said Jeffrey Applegate, chief investment strategist at Lehman Brothers. "The stock market has priced itself for at least one Fed tightening, and if the Fed does go, it will have to position itself for another," Mr. Applegate said. "If the consumer price numbers look pretty benign, then the market might take comfort from that," he added. "But I suspect this is not something that will be sorted out with the next one or two data points. I don't think we are out of the woods yet. There are just too many crosscurrents." Analysts who follow Internet stocks have been saying for some time that the sector was particularly vulnerable. Still, yesterday's downdraft was particularly drastic. Concern about slowing subscription rates led to big declines in America Online. At the close, the stock was down 9, to 90 1/2. Ebay continued to suffer from a computer system failure last week, falling 29 7/8, or 18 percent, to 136. And Schwab was punished after it reported that its daily on-line trading volume fell 28 percent in May, compared with April activity. The stock closed at 83 15/16 a share, down 10 5/16. "Given the price-earnings ratios for companies like America Online and Schwab, there is not much room for error," said Michael Molnar, a managing director in retail sales and trading at Salomon Smith Barney. "These were material, fundamental events." Weakness in these issues also helped to drag down other Internet shares. Cisco Systems, a component of the S.& P. 500, fell 2 7/8 a share, to 107 13/16. Amazon.com shed 13 13/16, to 92. And Yahoo lost 16, to 119 1/4. For the Dow, DuPont gained 2 7/8, to 70 3/16. General Electric closed at 103 3/4, up 2 13/32. And Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing gained 3 5/16, to 89 1/4. Elsewhere, drug and medical service company shares slumped. Becton Dickinson, the nation's largest manufacturer of medical syringes, declined 8 3/4, to 30 5/16, after notifying Wall Street that earnings for the third quarter and the full year would fall short of expectations because of slower sales in Europe. Pfizer continued to drop, falling 2 3/8, to 95 1/8. And Warner-Lambert slipped 1/2, to 62 1/4. The price of the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose 25/32, to 88 15/32. Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, fell to 6.09 percent, from 6.16 percent on Friday. title: U.S. Drops a Joint Venture For InternetAccess to Its Data
body: The Commerce Department has officially pulled out of an Internet partnership with a private company after the project raised concerns about fee-based access to Government documents. The service, which was designed to let paying customers find Government information on the Internet quickly and easily, was officially started today, but as a strictly private venture. The Commerce Department's National Technical Information Service had planned to begin the service last month with the private company, Northern Light Technology, but the venture was held up after critics questioned whether it contradicted the Clinton Administration's pledge to make the Internet and Government information more accessible. So while top-level Commerce officials who had been unaware of the partnership investigated the matter, Northern Light began offering free trials of the search service. The lack of Government participation in the venture will not constrain what is offered through the service, since it searches publicly available data bases and no license is required. But the decision does mean a loss of potential revenue for the National Technical Information Service, a for-profit agency of the Commerce Department that was going to receive half the fees. Today Commerce officials said the department was officially out of the venture. And Northern Light, which built the service, announced a new pricing plan for the search engine, which enables Internet users to find information more easily in millions of Government Web pages, data bases and proprietary news articles and periodicals. The service makes it possible to search quickly for information on topics as general as "abortion" or "missile technology." "The positive feedback we have received has clearly demonstrated the need for this service and the value it offers to anyone wishing to gain easy, pinpoint access to the vast amounts of information produced by, for and about the U.S. Government," David Seuss, chief executive officer of Northern Light, said in a statement. The company also said it would make the service available free to schools and libraries, and it dropped its planned price for one-day access from $15 to $5. Monthly and yearly subscriptions for individuals will be $30 and $250, respectively. Prices for corporations and other groups will be based on the number of users. http://www.nytimes.com

A Bit of Flamboyance For an Internet Conference
body: What has Dennis Rodman got to do with the Internet industry? Until this week, almost nothing. But on Thursday, the flamboyant professional basketball star will take the microphone at the Web Attack Internet marketing conference in San Francisco. Michael Tchong, producer of the conference, said he hoped to get Mr. Rodman to talk about his coming electronic commerce venture, which Mr. Tchong stumbled upon in the course of a trademark search on the term Webzilla.com. The search turned up Mr. Rodman's venture, Rodzilla.com. The point of inviting Mr. Rodman to the conference, Mr. Tchong said, is to illustrate to Web marketers that they need to be outrageous to be heard above the noise.  "There's got to be hundreds of pro basketball players today, but ask anybody to name two and they'll say Michael Jordan and Dennis Rodman," Mr. Tchong said. "Now that's brand marketing." Mr. Rodman has not been asked by the conference organizers to make any prepared remarks. But he has been instructed on precisely what to wear. The contract for his appearance requires Mr. Rodman, who apart from his hair color is perhaps best known off the court for donning a wedding dress and other outrageous attire, to wear a T-shirt bearing the logo of Iconocast, the Web marketing consulting company that is sponsoring the conference.   LAURIE J. title:
