Now, he added, "the constituency is saying no. Instead of asking about the digital highway, the people here are asking about the potholes, the ditches and the U-turns."  Sparring in Cyberspace Strange things happen when people who live in cyberspace meet face to face. Consider the case of Frank E. Carey, a member of the Security and System Reliability Architecture Group at A.T.& T.'s Bell Laboratories in Holmdel, N.J. Mr. Carey's job is to prevent people from stealing phone company services. Mr. Carey's gray hair suggests that he is at least twice as old as most of the hackers and "phone phreaks" with whom he spars. "The kids are fun," he said. "I enjoy a little repartee with them." Mr. Carey appeared to be genuinely disappointed by the absence this year of Phiber Optik, a young hacker who is now in a Federal penitentiary. It was then that Mr. Carey spied Mr. Goldstein, who publishes a quarterly magazine called 2600 that contains news of the hacker community and handy technical tips. The magazine, Mr. Goldstein said, is published in Middle Island, L.I., and has a circulation of 20,000. "The vast majority are newsstand sales," Mr. Goldstein said. "The people who read it don't want to be on lists of any sort." "He complicates my life," Mr. Carey still smiling. "The phone companies complicate our lives," Mr. Goldstein shot back, his eyes narrowing under his headband. After the two cordial adversaries parted, Mr. Carey paused. "This is fun," he said. "Definitely weird, but it's fun." Graphic   Photo: Emmanuel Goldstein, left, editor of A Hacker Newsletter, speaking with Frank Carey of A. T.&T.'s Bell Labs at the annual Computers, Freedom and Privacy Conference this week in Chicago. (Steve Kagan for The newyork Times)

title: Computer Snoopers Imperil Pentagon Files, Experts Say
body: Armed with increasingly sophisticated snooping tools, unauthorized computer programmers operating both in the unitedstates and abroad have gained access to hundreds of sensitive but unclassified Government and military computer networks connected to the global network Internet, computer security experts said. "There is no information to indicate that command and control systems were affected by these intrusions," a spokeswoman for the Defense Information Systems Agency said Wednesday. Classified Government and military data, like those that control nuclear weapons, intelligence and other critical functions, are not connected to the Internet and are believed to be secure. But the agency acknowledged that the compromised computer systems include those used for ballistic weapons research, aircraft and ship design, military payroll, personnel records, procurement, modeling of battlefield environments, and computer security research. Information is placed on Internet computers to make it easier to be shared by authorized users both within an organization and in remote offices, say, between collaborating scientists at different Government research labs, or between the Pentagon and its military contractors. While most of the intruders appear to be hackers out for the computer equivalent of a joyride, Federal investigators say that some of the intruders have been able to take control of several military computer systems, which enabled them to steal, alter or erase computer records, even to shut the computer systems down. "The problem is a very significant one," said Michael Higgins, deputy director for information security at Defense Information Systems Agency's Center for Information Systems Security. He added, "Such intrusions are bound to continue because such information will be passed along to other intruders." The apparent ease with which hackers are entering military and Government systems suggests that similar if not greater intrusions are under way on corporate, academic and commercial networks connected to the Internet. It also raises troubling questions about privacy and data security. Several sources said it was likely that only a small percentage of intrusions, perhaps fewer than 5 percent, have been detected. Of those that have been discovered, some are using advanced data encryption techniques that prevent or hinder the military from discovering the nature of the data that are being stolen. "We've got real problems, and the problems have not been confined to Government and military sites," said Eugene Spafford, an associate professor of computer science at Purdue University who directs a national computer security program. In a private but unclassified briefing to a corporation recently, Mr. Higgins of the Defense Information Systems Agency told executives of a defense contractor that "major portions" of the Defense Department's unclassified networks had been penetrated by hackers, "adversely affecting D.O.D. military readiness." Mr. Higgins's remarks were initially reported in the newspaper Federal Computer Week and were confirmed by his office on Wednesday. The break-ins have increased significantly since February, when the Computer Emergency Response Team, a quasi-Government organization financed by the Defense Department and based at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, issued an alarm that unknown intruders were gathering tens of thousands of supposedly secret passwords that were being transmitted from computer to computer on the global Internet. Since then, security experts said, the number of captured passwords has probably exceeded a million.  'Probably No Secure Systems' Military investigators said "dozens of regional network service providers" -- the main Internet hubs that service the majority of American companies and individuals that use the Internet -- had been successfully attacked. "There are probably no secure systems on the Internet," said Peter G. Neumann, principal scientist at SRI International, a think tank in Menlo Park, Calif., formerly the Stanford Research Institute. "Some are just administered better than others and are harder to break into." There are an estimated 2.2 million "host" computers on the Internet, which is used by more than 20 million people. "I don't want to sound alarmist, but there is legitimate cause for concern," said Scott C. Charney, chief of the computer crime unit in the Justice Department's Criminal Division. "As we go toward greater connectivity, and as more information is stored on the networks, the risks go up proportionately."  'An Evil Web' Most of the attacks appear to use a "sniffer" program that is surreptitiously inserted into a computer. Each message passing through the computer on its way around the global network contains the sender's user identification, secret password and other information needed to gain access to the destination computer. The sniffer program captures virtually every authorized password and user ID passing through the computer -- sometimes thousands a day -- and stores them for retrieval later. Later, using the pilfered ID's and passwords, the hackers can easily gain access to Government, military, corporate and private computer systems, where they plant more sniffers. The vulnerabilities being exploited by sniffer programs were discovered last summer, but it was not until February that attacks became widespread enough to alarm Internet administrators. Since then, the attacks have outpaced the abilities of security experts to detect them. Also, many of the attackers are clever programmers who can effectively make their programs invisible. There are several security techniques that can block or discourage such attacks, but each requires making the networks less convenient for legitimate users. The cost to scan, repair and secure affected networks would vary from installation to installation, but would certainly be expensive, as would the installation of hardware and software mechanisms to prevent subsequent attacks. Such schemes often involve the use of specially secured computer "firewalls" as buffers between a local network and the Internet. Other techniques include sophisticated password authenication systems and strong data encryption, which is hindered by the Government's policies restricting widespread use of encryption algorithms. The easiest defense against the schemes is to change passwords frequently, security advisers said. However, some "Trojan horse" programs have been found that are programmed to detect attempts by users to change their passwords, and then automatically capture the new passwords, one investigator said. "It's an evil web that we've weaved here," said James V. Christy 2d, special agent and director of computer crime investigations for the Air Force Office of Special Investigations at Bolling Air Force Base in Washington, D.C. "You can have two completely secure sites, and they could be doing everything right, but if they're communicating and go through a system that isn't secure, they could be compromised."  Setting a Trap Earlier this year, Air Force investigators helped New Scotland Yard in England arrest a British computer programmer who was gathering data from the Rome Air Development Center at Griffith Air Force Base in upstate newyork. The investigators set a trap for the hackers and watched them operate on a Rome subnetwork for two weeks. "In the past when we went in in a case like this, it was like going in at night and turning on the light, and watching the roaches scatter," said Mr. Christy of the Air Force. "This time we basically went in at night without turning on the lights, and with night vision goggles. It was absolutely amazing where these guys went and what they were doing and what they had access to." "Besides compromising all our systems at Rome, they were going downstream and attacking contractors and other Federal agencies," Mr. Christy said. Mr. Christy said newer sniffers capture more than just the password and ID, including contents of messages and files. In some cases, the intruders are stealing so much data from Government and military computers that they inadvertently overload and crash the systems, he said.  The Heart of the Issue Paul Strassmann, a former principal assistant Secretary of Defense in charge of Pentagon information systems, said: "When you're talking about the national information highway, if you don't consider the security dimension you really don't have anything. From a political standpoint, the heart of the issue is security and privacy." Without a cohesive Government data security policy, Mr. Strassmann said, "We are exposing the world's first information-based society, with 50 percent of the world's computing power and 70 percent of its advanced software capability, to enormous dangers. This is the place where the first information Chernobyl will happen." Mr. Strassmann raised the specter of "information assassins," highly skilled programmers who work for foreign governments, rival corporations or organized crime, who exploit computer security weaknesses to manipulate the stock market, hide drug-money transactions, or destroy the data bases of financial institutions. Most critical financial and military computer systems employ stringent data security systems, including data encryption, sophisticated user authentication, electronic firewalls and physically locked doors to prevent unauthorized users from tapping into their systems. "Everyone is looking at the bright promise of the National Information Infrastructure and the Internet and connectivity as a whole, but they are not looking at the flip side, that there are people coming onto the net who don't have the same high ideals and goals, and who are willing to abuse the rights of others," said Mr. Spafford, the computer expert at Purdue. "I have likened it to selling swamp land in Florida for vacation homes. There are a couple of details they neglect to mention." Graphic   Diagram (pg. B10)

title: On the Information Highway, email Litter Problem Grows
body: Early one morning two weeks ago, Jason Lavoie, a network engineer for a company that provides Internet access in Maine, was rudely awakened by his beeper. There was trouble on the system that demanded immediate human intervention. Logging onto his computer to see what was wrong, Mr. Lavoie found hundreds of messages jamming his electronic mailbox -- complaints about a flood of commercial email that appeared, to the untrained eye, to be coming from his employer, Maine Internetworks Inc. Before Mr. Lavoie could figuratively pull the plug, thousands of unsolicited advertisements for a company called Master Graphics in Fallbrook, Calif., had come coursing through Maine Internetworks' computer system and were relayed to Internet users across the country -- who were now letting him know how they felt about it. It did not matter that Master Graphics was not a client of Maine Internetworks -- Mint.net, for short -- which has strict rules against sending unsolicited commercial email. The sender managed to hide his email address from potentially angry Internet users by routing themailing through Mint.net without permission or payment. Mr. Lavoie had to spend the rest of the day cleaning up the mess and plugging the security hole that allowed the computer to be infiltrated. "It costs us bandwidth and system resources, and it costs my time to respond to the complaints," Mr. Lavoie said. "What the sender really is doing is shifting the cost of junk email to the end user rather than to the person sending it." What happened to Mint.net occurs every day on the Internet. Junk email, called spam, has been a problem ever since the public began to join scientists and academics on the Internet several years ago. But what was a trickle has become a torrent. Several times a week, and often several times a day, Internet users log on to America Online, Compuserve, Netcom or one of the many smaller companies that provide gateways to cyberspace and find an increasing number of shrill promotions clogging their electronic mailboxes: "Make Big $$$ On Line -- Secret Revealed," "Stuff for FREE!" or "You Can Now Dramatically Increase Your Sexual Attractiveness!" While some Internet providers are trying to sue junk emailers for electronic trespassing, the legal system is scrambling to catch up to a problem rapidly becoming as obnoxious to many people as dinner-time telemarketing. Last week, two anti-spam bills were introduced in Congress, and the Federal Trade Commission will conduct a hearing on the problem next month. Wildcat entrepreneurs selling everything from software to sex have learned that it is so cheap to automatically crank out millions of messages that just a few sales can easily cover the cost. The irritation the mass mailings cause to everybody else is considered well worth the price -- especially with loads of new software making it easy for junk emailers to cover their tracks. Commercial mailers even spam the spammers. Last month, a mass emailing for a program called Stealth Mailer was sent by Fred@nowhere.com. "Send Your email Out, At Up to 250,000 + Messages/Hour," the ad promised. To help themailers escape detection, the program allows them to fake the return address and route the junk email through different servers. Internet service providers "will spin their wheels" trying to track down the culprit, Fred@nowhere.com boasted. "Last year at this time, I'd get maybe a few junk emails a week," said Scott Hazen Mueller, vice president of engineering for Whole Earth Networks, an Internet service provider in San Francisco. "Now I get 5 to 10 a day." Before Mr. Mueller tightened security, hit-and-run junk emailers were infiltrating themail server at Whole Earth Networks several times a week. The problem is figuring out where the spam comes from and to whom one can complain. Federal law makes it illegal for companies to send unsolicited business faxes, but there is no law preventing a junk emailer from writing the same unwanted message to millions of hard disks. Federal law also requires telephone marketers to stop calling people who complain about the intrusions, but complaints to junk emailers -- if they can be found -- are almost always ignored. In addition to disguising the source of their mailings by routing them through unsuspecting third parties, junk emailers commonly forge their electronic return addresses. The Master Graphics spam that jammed Mint.net's computer supposedly originated from an address in an Internet domain called Dcez.com, run by the DC Easy-Link Corporation in Alexandria, Va. But email to the address was automatically returned marked "User unknown." Anyone who wanted to complain directly to Master Graphics was confronted with another obstacle: The company has no listed phone number; only a street address was given for those who wanted to order the company's product, a digitized personal signature to use on computer-generated documents. An attempt to arrange an interview with Master Graphics' representatives by mail was unsuccessful. "You'd think that any business model that depends on alienating 99 percent of your target market would be guaranteed bankruptcy," said Stanton McCandlish of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a public policy group in San Francisco. "If you get this type of advertisement, the sender is either a scam artist or totally clueless. It's time for the free ride to end. Why should the whole network have to pay for you to send eight million emails for free?" Some service providers try to fight back by using filters to block mail from notorious spammers. But junk emailers just keep changing their Internet addresses, like mutating viruses eluding an immune system. And even blocking junk email is costly, eating up a large amount of a service provider's computer time. Sensing that stopping junk email has become a popular cause, Representative Chris Smith, Republican of New Jersey, introduced legislation last week that would broaden the law against junk faxes to include email. Another bill introduced by Senator Frank H. Murkowski, Republican of Alaska, would require junk email to be clearly labeled as an advertisement and include a real street address, email address, telephone number and valid routing information. Some Internet denizens fear Senator Murkowski's approach would legitimize junk email, and the idea of any kind of legislation runs contrary to some people's libertarian view of the Internet. "There is no way to legislate this problem away unless every single jurisdiction in the world adopts the same law," said Mr. McCandlish of the Electronic Frontier Foundation. But Mr. Mueller, who recently helped start a group called the Coalition Against Unsolicited Commercial email, said a country that became a haven for junk emailers could be threatened with the "Internet death penalty," having its connections to the unitedstates cut off. Marc Rotenberg, head of the Electronic Privacy and Information Center, a nonprofit group in Washington, said a ban on junk email might be unconstitutional. He thinks the flow could be stemmed by prohibiting the resale of email addresses. "You don't have many people sending junk email who are collecting the addresses themselves," he said. "They are buying them from a broker. That's an area that we think could be regulated." Some large Internet service providers, fearing Government regulation and realizing that fighting spam can be a selling point in a competitive market, are going after junk emailers in the courts. Earlier this month, Earthlink in Palo Alto, Calif., won an injunction against Cyber Promotions of Philadelphia, one of the biggest junk emailers. A Los Angeles Superior Court judge found that Cyber Promotions had trespassed upon Earthlink's electronic territory and prohibited the mass emailer from sending advertisements through Earthlink's computers without permission. Sanford Wallace, the president of Cyber Promotions, which has also been the target of legal action by the on-line services Compuserve and America Online, insists that he has done nothing illegal and that his company is providing small businesses with a valuable service. "email is a fraction of the cost of any other medium, and it goes at the speed of light," he said in an interview. Cyber Promotions and its Internet service provider, Apex Global Information Services, called Agis.net, in Dearborn, Mich. -- one of the few service providers that allow junk emailing -- have tried to fend off possible regulation and counter bad publicity by promising to develop a universal list of consumers who have asked not to receive junk email. And Cyber Promotions is collecting names -- 38,000 so far -- of people who have told the company they want to receive email advertisements. "That's Plan B," Mr. Wallace said. "When and if a law says we can't do Plan A -- sending unsolicited email -- then we will be prepared." But many Internet users, who feel violated when they find any kind of advertisement injected into their computers, are leery of such promises. Not all of them are willing to wait for a legal remedy or industry self-regulation. Earlier this month, a group of Internet users tried to crash Cyber Promotions' computers by sending a barrage of electronic messages. That assault was fended off, but the next day a more sophisticated hacker attack knocked the company off the Internet. Cyber Promotions was barely fazed. The next day it was back on line churning out millions of messages a day for its customers and selling software to help freelancers send junk email. One of the products, Webcollector, crawls through the World Wide Web and harvests email addresses. In the interest of diversification, the company also sells E-filter, which consumers can use to block Cyber Promotions' junk email from their computers. The offering for the software was sent by junk email. Graphic   Photo: Some of the junk mail that appeared recently on the screen of an America Online customer. For many email users, this volume of unwanted messages would represent a relatively light day of 'spamming.' (pg. 33)

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Chinese Books For Sale on Line
body: An Internet-based bookstore began operating today in Beijing, offering more than 160,000 Chinese titles, according to the Compaq Computer Corporation. Compaq, based in Houston, said the enterprise, known as Beijing Book Center Online and developed by Compaq China and the China Information Highway Corporation, was opened in Beijing by Compaq's president, Eckhard Pfeiffer, and the Vice Mayor of Beijing, Lin Wenyi. China Information Highway will handle technology deployment, systems integration and infrastructure. Compaq will provide servers, along with technical support. "E-commerce is the focus of the information industry and the star of 21st-century businesses," Mr. Lin said. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
GAME THEORY;
Seeing Dollar Signs in Sports Fans' Play
body: FOR years and years, investing was likened to sports because investing, like sports, generates statistics about winners and losers and because America is a sports culture that will make stadium analogies about anything. So Wall Street was a big high-stakes sporting event, and traders (the vast majority of them men, many former high school football captains) were gilded jocks. Then a funny thing happened. Geeks started making billions of dollars, and Wall Street investment firms started bragging about how many Ph.D.'s they had in their offices. Online investing became a mass mania, and regular people started reading charts and analysts' reports on their computers. As the stock market soared, we became enraptured with high-tech-start- up mythology. We became a stock-trading culture. So now sports are likened to investment opportunities. Witness Sportsdaq (www.sportsdaq.com), the product of a tiny startup called Sports Futures Inc. Sportsdaq is a fictional stock exchange where sports teams are tradable securities. Unlike most fantasy sports games, in which players put athletes into fictional teams whose performances correspond to the athletes' statistics, Sportsdaq is pure market psychology. The only real-world statistic in the system is the end result of the sports season: which team wins the championship. When the championship game is over, that team is worth 100. The rest are worth zero. Until then, Sportsdaq traders can use their initial budget of 100,000 Sportsdaq dollars to buy team stocks. Stock price is a direct reflection of shareholder confidence in a team's future performance. If the market thinks the Yankees team has a 10 percent chance of winning the pennant, its stock trades at 10. If traders decide a team is going to lose, they can place an order to sell it short. The market can buy as much stock as it wants -- the supply of securities is open-ended. But the combined team prices have to add up to 100. So Sportsdaq acts as a market maker, ensuring that the value of the index stays constant. The content is sports, but the experience is more akin to E*Trade. You make investments. You track them over time. But unlike E*Trade, where activities are extremely private, Sportsdaq is semipublic. You can compare your performance against other people's -- if you're a hotshot fictional day trader, you can be ranked (imagine a high-score board on E*Trade). Competition keeps people engaged -- it keeps their eyes open for new market opportunities. It also allows Sportsdaq to market sports that don't have a mainstream following in the unitedstates. "Let me give you this scenario," said Andrew Hoppin, 28, Sports Futures' chief executive. "I am a big baseball fan. I've spent all this time paying attention to baseball and investing in baseball. But I can't crack the top tier of traders in the game because they've found this great opportunity investing in cricket securities. If I find other people are beating me out in the game because they know about cricket and they're able to take advantage of cricket, that will incentivize this American baseball fan to go find out what cricket is all about." Conversely, a European Sportsdaq could give American sports leagues a chance to interest ardent cricketeers in the curious backwater pastime called baseball. Sportsdaq is in discussions with European new media companies and stateside leagues about a transcontinental exchange. Ultimately, Sportsdaq's real customers are the people selling sports, wherever they are: teams, broadcasters and merchandisers. From their perspective, the Web site is a giant focus group churning with useful information. Broadcasters have to decide which games to air in which local markets. Retailers have to decide which jerseys to stock in different parts of the country. The home team and the reigning champs are no-brainers. But what else do you put on the racks -- or the airwaves -- in Camden, Me., and Oak Ridge, Tenn.? Sportsdaq will feature advertising, collect e-commerce commissions and sell premium services. But fundamentally, Sports Futures is in the research business. "Even if we direct no revenues from the site itself, we think the information coming out of the market is going to be a significant enough revenue stream to drive the business," Mr. Hoppin said. "The leagues have a lot of interest in it because they want to understand the breakdown of the audience.  They want to know how to access different audiences that they haven't accessed before, and we have an opportunity, because it's a site where people keep coming back, to track that." The difference between Sportsdaq and most e-commerce sites is that it's not selling data that's invisible to the users. "We'll package data differently for third parties," Mr. Hoppin said. "But fundamentally, it's the same data you see on your screen: what do people think about the outcome of a sporting event." Meanwhile, Sportsdaq will offer different sets of detailed data to its traders as a premium service. "The software tools are going to enable people to do very detailed statistical analysis," Mr. Hoppin said. "We're going to be working with a partner in New Mexico who's developed models for casinos in Las Vegas that they use to set their odds for sports. We're going to be translating that into a form that we can use for our game, for people to be able to parse data from statistics from the real sports world in a format that's going to enable them to look at these issues in a quantitative fashion and make investment decisions." Somehow, it's appropriate that online trading research should be supplied by Las Vegas oddsmakers. In Las Vegas, as on Wall Street, some people hit the jackpot. Some people lose their shirts. But the house always wins. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: IN PLAY -- Sportsdaq fan-investors take the field while marketers fill the virtual stands.

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Competitors Don't Seem to Hurt Schwab
body: THE invasion of the full-service brokers does not seem to be slowing the Charles Schwab Corporation so far. Schwab, now the leading online brokerage firm, said yesterday that the first quarter in which it faced head-on competition from Merrill Lynch & Company and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter will be its most profitable quarter ever. The San Francisco-based Schwab expects to earn $162 million to $171 million, or 19 cents to 20 cents a share, in the quarter that ends tomorrow. That would be a penny or two a share more than any analyst surveyed by First Call/Thomson Financial had expected, and 2 to 3 cents a share higher than their average estimate of 17 cents a share. Schwab rose $5.8125, or 17 percent, yesterday to $39.75 in trading on the newyork Stock Exchange. "It's clear that no one is interrupting their momentum," said Richard Strauss, an analyst at Goldman, Sachs & Company, who has been recommending Schwab's stock to clients. Merrill Lynch and Morgan Stanley have taken dead aim at Schwab with recent introductions of online trading services for the same $29.95 commission that Schwab charges. Mr. Strauss said he does not think that those competitors pose immediate threats to Schwab's growth, though other analysts disagree. The brokerage firm's chief financial officer, Chris Dodds, attributed its better-than-expected performance to a surprisingly active stock market this quarter, especially in December, when some thought that trading would decrease as the end of the century approached. Guy Moszkowski, an analyst with Salomon Smith Barney, who is not recommending purchase of the Schwab stock, said that the brokerage firm's increases in commission revenue should not have come as a big surprise. "We know the Nasdaq has been going bananas," Mr. Moszkowski said. "And the newyork Stock Exchange has been no slouch either." Shares of several other online brokerage firms also jumped yesterday as investors recognized that robust trading should benefit all firms that derive much of their revenue from commissions. The E*Trade Group rose $2.375, to $28.125; the TD Waterhouse Group gained $1.8125, to $17.125, and Ameritrade Holdings closed up $2.25, to $22.75. Mr. Dodds said Schwab earned commissions in December on an average of 236,000 trades a day, its highest rate ever. About 80 percent of those trades were placed electronically, he said. "Coming into the Y2K situation, there was a little bit more uncertainty than normal," Mr. Dodds continued. But as the year drew near an end, it became clear that Schwab would again show a rate of growth in customer assets that its competitors and some analysts have called unsustainable. Schwab now holds more than $700 billion n customer assets, a gain exceeding 40 percent from the end of 1998, Mr. Dodds said. The company has opened more than 1.3 million accounts for the second straight year, giving it in excess of six million accounts held by about five million clients. It was gains like those for several consecutive years that caused traditional brokers like Merrill Lynch to take notice. The final slap came a year ago, when Schwab's stock market value surpassed that of Merrill Lynch. Increasingly, Schwab is considered a direct competitor to the biggest brokerage firms. After all, analysts say, each of them is trying to gather as many customers and investment assets as fast as it can. So far, Schwab has been doing that with a much lower cost structure than the traditional firms have. Unlike Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley and Salomon Smith Barney, a Citigroup unit, Schwab does not have an army of stockbrokers on its payroll. But it does have a network of 320 branches to support, a financial burden that pure online brokers like E*Trade do not have to shoulder. Schwab's combination of electronic technology and personal service has become the model for the financial services industry. But, some analysts wonder how Schwab will distinguish itself once that model is copied. "There have been some concerns about Schwab's ability, over the next year or so, to cope with some of the competitive responses that their success has generated," Mr. Moszkowski said. Still, he said he would not underestimate the ability of Schwab's management to continue to reinvent the firm's business model. "They have always figured out a path that has been successful," he said. He and other analysts said that even though they thought that Schwab would continue to grow, they questioned why investors placed a much higher value on the firm's shares than on those of Morgan Stanley or other successful securities firms. Shares of Schwab have been selling for as much as 50 times earnings, compared with a multiple of about 15 for some of its traditional competitors. "I have to believe that this is about as good as it gets" for Schwab and other brokerage firms that cater to individual, or retail, investors, said Steve Galbraith, an analyst with Sanford C. Bernstein & Company. "All the stars are clearly aligned right now in retail land." Individual investors came rushing back into the market in the last few months of this year, buying shares of mutual funds and bidding up prices of technology stocks. All the trading pushed the stock market indexes to record high after record high. The question, analysts say, is, what happens to shares of Schwab and other online brokers when the markets cool off? For their part, Mr. Dodds said, Schwab's managers are confident that "the things we have to offer investors are going to enable us to keep growing at this rate."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Practical Traveler;
Tighter Security For Web Buyers
body: THE Internet has been a boon for wired travelers with the patience and savvy to surf for good deals, but it can also leave unwary travelers in a highly precarious position. This year, for example, a technical administrator for an Internet service provider in Seattle discovered that hundreds of Web sites had left their customers' credit card information completely exposed to anyone with an Internet connection. Among those sites was a travel company that arranged trips to Cancun; so not only could thieves use the card but they could also find out a family's travel plans and visit the empty home while they were away. Executives of travel Web sites are quick to point out that no such thefts have been reported, but the mere threat continues to vex Internet users. Jupiter Communications, a newyork-based research firm, says that 17 percent of online shoppers surveyed are "extremely reluctant" to use credit cards online. But the situation is improving, as technology companies and travel sites continue to roll out features and policies meant to protect customers from fraud -- and as consumers become more accustomed to online buying. The most popular travel sites now give customers myriad ways to pay for tickets and secure reservations, while also paying the first $50 of any fraudulent misuse of credit cards (credit card issuers are liable for the rest). And every reputable online travel site features secure sockets layer (SSL) transactions, which encrypt credit card data while in transit, virtually guaranteeing safety. Safe 'Neighborhoods' "On the Internet you can't tell when you're in the bad part of town," said Terrell B. Jones, president of Travelocity (www.travelocity.com), which announced a merger with Preview Travel (www.previewtravel .com) in October. "Everything looks just about the same, so we have to convince people we're a safe place to do business. And that's especially true when you're selling a $280, nonrefundable electronic ticket. People don't want to make a mistake." Mr. Jones said that Travelocity saw a measurable difference in sales last year when it posted a notice telling consumers that they would not be liable for the first $50 of any credit card misuse, if the card issuer did not cover it. "We also told consumers they could call in their credit card numbers if they weren't comfortable giving them online," he said. In addition, the company allows consumers to mail or fax credit card numbers to secure reservations. "Somehow people think a fax is an unbreakable secure encryption system, which it isn't, but that's O.K., it's what they're comfortable with," he said, noting that about 50 people a day phone or fax their numbers. Analysts and executives say it is now common for the better-known travel sites to offer the option to phone or fax credit-card numbers. But most travel sites will not honor a personal check. Airlines cannot hold seats based on a personal check because it can take several days for bad checks to be reported, during which time the airlines cannot sell the seats to other buyers. "And they don't want a 7-year-old booking a flight on the Concorde, which happened once," Mr. Jones said. Travel sites are also sweetening the pot to encourage reluctant shoppers to part with their credit card numbers online, mostly because sites know how much cheaper it is to process a reservation online. Companies can pay $25 or more in overhead every time a customer service representative answers the phone. Thus the deluge of online travel incentives: the Hotel Reservation Network (www.hoteldiscount.com), a Dallas-based service that books hotel rooms nationwide, is offering rebates up to $50 this month for reservations made completely online; through April 30, United Airlines (www.ual.com) is giving 3,000 miles upon each customer's first online booking, plus the standard 1,000-mile bonus for each online purchase. Sites are offering other forms of encouragement as well -- most notably convenience. Online travel companies have made it easier than ever to complete transactions, in part because they now offer a degree of personalized service that's almost unsettling. For instance, Expedia (www.expedia.com), Travelocity's chief competitor, allows registered users to create a file of travel preferences for everyone in the family, including frequent flier numbers, seating and food preferences, disabilities and age (in case anyone qualifies for discounts). Expedia will also store a user's home airport the first time a trip is booked through the site, which, when combined with the travel preferences and credit card information stored by Expedia, can whisk users through a reservation in three to four clicks. Travelocity boasts the same capability, and both sites go to great lengths to assure that personal information will remain confidential. Travelers who are either too leery of storing personal information on multiple travel sites or don't want to spend the time typing it in are candidates to use an increasingly popular online technology called the "digital wallet." These wallets allow users to store their information either on their computer or on a secure Internet site, where it can be used to fill in forms with one click. Two of the more popular wallet devices are offered by eCode (www.ecode.com) and Gator (www.gator.com), each of which provide the service free. ECode, based in Santa Clara, Calif., stores a user's personal and credit card information -- as well as log-ins or passwords for sites requiring registration -- on the company's secure server. Whenever users confront a blank form on any site, they click a button and their relevant information is instantly sent -- encrypted -- to the site. Gator, which has compiled hundreds of thousands of users in a few months, stores your information on your computer. Frequent travelers must store it on laptops to use a digital wallet on the road. Downloading a Wallet With both Gator and eCode, users must spend a few minutes downloading the wallet software, which does not work with a Macintosh. Wallets only help fill out the transaction forms -- ticket returns or any other issues arising from the purchase must be handled directly with the merchant. And these wallets don't yet store the more-complete dossier of information that travel sites typically do. But that may change quickly, as technology improves. "Our vision is for Gator to evolve into a general purpose assistant," said Jeff McFadden, the company's chief executive. "So if you're on United Airlines' site looking to book a trip to Bermuda, Gator could recognize that and say 'Hey, would you like me to check all the rest of the airline sites for a better rate?' " Gator, based in San Mateo, Calif., was begun last year by Mr. McFadden and a team of entrepreneurs, who began offering the service to consumers in June. Since then, Mr. McFadden said, the company's electronic wallet has been downloaded by hundreds of thousands of people. ECode is used by more than 100,000 people, said Rohit Chandra, the company president, who founded the firm in 1997. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Robert Neubecker)

title:
WHAT'S NEXT;
New Ways of Securing Online Data
body: THE problem with passwords is that there are so many of them, a problem the computer industry is confronting with solutions that range from virtual key rings to smart cards that do all of the logging in for you. The basic solution is to store the passwords in a file called a key ring. This file is usually encrypted with a master password, ideally one that is easy to remember. Key rings have been used for many years, but lately researchers have concentrated on making them easier to use by integrating them with the many Web sites that require passwords. Researchers also are experimenting with putting more information into key rings and adding automated features that look up passwords. The latest version of the Mac OS comes with an integrated tool that unlocks the key ring with a spoken phrase. You can also encrypt the files on your Mac and store the password in the central key ring. In addition, researchers are re-examining how key rings protect passwords and other confidential data. Netscape's Web browser stores the email passwords of users in a primitive key ring. Last week, several code breakers at Reliable Software Technologies in Dulles, Va., announced that they had cracked the protection in a short time using pencil and paper. Gary McGraw, the chief technology officer at Reliable Software, which makes an extra effort to ensure that its software does not crash, emphasized the danger of poorly designed key rings. Most people use the same password for everything, Mr. McGraw said. "So you knock over someone's poorly protected machine at home, get their password and then use it to get into someone's corporate machine," he said. Or their bank account, or their Amazon account, or . . . the list goes on. One of the latest solutions to the problem is a tool called v-GO, from the newyork City based company Passlogix. The tool stores basic passwords for Web sites and mail servers using the common strategy of creating a central encrypted file. What is novel about the tool is its integration with Web browsers to keep track of what sites are visited and what user name and password are used at each one. The software matches the user name and password to the U.R.L. and automatically enters the proper data in the forms. Users can also include addresses and phone numbers if they wish. The tool also allows you to change your identity as you change sites, from "WB123" at one place to "Koosbane41" at another, for example. Marc Boroditsky, the chief executive of Passlogix, says that his company plans to integrate its key ring with public-key encryption technology. "In the future," Mr. Boroditsky said, "we want to handle on-line banking and medical records." In a public-key encryption system, a person has a public key and a private key. The public key scrambles a message and may be used by anyone, but the private key that is needed to unscramble the message must be kept secret by the person who holds it. The newer key rings promise to hold private keys and manage the construction of digital signatures that can be used to endorse transactions. These digital signatures are more secure than passwords because they change with each transaction. A doctor might request a copy of an X-ray or a diagnosis and use an online key ring to sign the request with a digital signature. Digital signatures are created by complex cryptographic codes and are designed to mimic pen-and-paper signatures. In this case, only someone with the password to the key ring can add a signature to a document. Banks and other institutions that depend upon pen-and-paper signatures hope to save time and money by recognizing digital signatures. Mr. Boroditsky also said that Passlogix is exploring ways of encouraging users to select passwords that are truly random, like the time of day, instead of words that might be susceptible to guessing, like a birth date, an address or the name of a child or a pet. In the long term, passwords will be stored on smart cards and other secure hardware. Mr. McGraw said that his company could have found the passwords stored by Netscape even if Netscape had used the most secure encryption available. PC software is inherently insecure because all parts of the computer are accessible. Donna Farmer, the president of the Smart Card Forum, says that the smart-card technology is being embraced by many companies that need secure and convenient protection that goes beyond passwords. "I think authentication and privacy are going to be the driver," Ms. Farmer said. Indeed, American Express has taken the lead in this area by introducing a new brand of credit card -- called Blue -- with an embedded smart card. The company hopes that its use of the smart card to do a better job of protecting against fraud will attract a significant portion of transactions made over the Internet. Confronted by a smart card, a potential thief cannot simply copy a name, credit card number and expiration date. The thief would have to copy the data stored inside the card -- a task that the smart card designers have tried to make impossible. Alan Gilstrap, a vice president at American Express, says that the Internet transactions are just the beginning. "There's a good deal of excess capacity on these cards," Mr. Gilstrap said. "There's a great potential to add new features after issuance. I can't steal the thunder from our marketing department, but the cardholder will be able to add new features that fits their lifestyles in the future." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing. (Mary Ann Smith)

title: Expedia Seeks To Dismiss Suit
body: Expedia Inc., the Internet travel arm of the Microsoft Corporation, said yesterday that it had sought to dismiss a patent infringement suit filed against it by the Internet buying service Priceline.com and questioned whether Priceline owned the patent at issue. An Expedia spokeswoman, Suzi LeVine, said her company had filed a legal response to Priceline.com's October patent lawsuit that questioned whether Priceline or its vice chairman, Jay Walker, owned the patent for an Internet-based hotel-price-matching system. Priceline began selling "name your own price" airline tickets over the Internet in April 1998. It has since expanded into home mortgages, hotel rooms and new cars. Priceline's original suit, which was filed in unitedstates District Court in Connecticut, had charged that Microsoft's conduct violated the state's Unfair Trade Practices Act. It asked the court to uphold the Priceline patent, block Microsoft from violating the patent and award unspecified damages. 'There's a real question about whether Jay Walker and Priceline are the rightful owners of the patent in question," Ms. LeVine said by phone after the filing of the dismissal motion, which she said was made in the same Connecticut court. "We believe the court should sort out who actually owns the disputed patent, if anyone, before it can try to determine whether anyone is infringing the patent," she said. A spokesman for Priceline said late Monday that he had not seen the Microsoft filing and would withhold comment until he had more details. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
OUTLOOK 2000: MARKETS & INVESTING;
Trading Will Evolve With or Without Wall Street
body: Late one evening, sometime early in the next century, you settle into your lumbar-support leather recliner and tell your wireless voice-activated computer to sign you on to eBay, where you enter the spirited bidding for an antique Nokia cellular telephone, a slightly foxed first edition of "Bridget Jones's Diary" -- and 10,000 shares of United Parcel Service. Far-fetched? Maybe. But electronic technology is having such an immediate impact on American financial markets that a team of analysts at Lehman Brothers recently suggested that the stock exchange of the future might evolve not from traditional institutions like the newyork Stock Exchange, but from e-commerce companies or Internet auction sites. To be sure, that is only one very long-term possibility, the analysts said. And the evolution might work in reverse -- with the Big Board transforming itself into a 24-hour Internet market that could challenge the auction sites of today. As that speculation suggests, Wall Street is approaching the new millennium the way superstitious pilots approach the Bermuda Triangle -- fearing the worst, hoping for the best but prepared for just about anything. "The market will be constantly remaking itself," predicted William C. Freund, director of the Pace University Center for the Study of Equity Markets in Manhattan and a former chief economist of the newyork Stock Exchange. "The model of today is a scene of creative destruction." Regulators have tried to create an environment that will foster greater innovation and competition in stock trading. A remarkably long-lived bull market has attracted millions of new investors. But the real engine driving market change today is computer technology: cheaper, faster computers connected by high-speed communications lines and guided by innovative software. This fast-forward evolution has given rise to a host of bargain-priced online brokerage services that, in turn, have produced an awesome increase in the amount of stock trading Americans do each day. Forrester Research estimates that the number of online brokerage accounts, which stood at roughly three million in August 1998, will reach 5.4 million by the end of this year and more than 20 million in the next four years. Further, trading volume on Nasdaq increased 28 percent annually between 1994 and 1998, on average, while the year-to-year increase on the Big Board during that period was 23 percent, Salomon Smith Barney reported recently. That compares with average annual growth rates of roughly 19 percent on Nasdaq and 13 percent on the Big Board between 1989 and 1993. But the same technology that has unleashed this tidal wave of fresh business has also helped Wall Street cope with that flood by fostering the birth of more than a dozen computerized trading networks, called electronic communications networks, or more often simply E.C.N.'s, where buy and sell orders can be matched in seconds. In recent months, some E.C.N.'s have started staying open for trading after the traditional stock exchanges have closed, making it even easier for investors to trade. Some E.C.N.'s now handle enough trading to pose a competitive threat to the Nasdaq market and, to a lesser extent, the newyork Stock Exchange. But those markets are not ceding their territory without a fight. Both Frank Zarb, the chief executive of the National Association of Securities Dealers, which operates the Nasdaq market, and Richard Grasso, the president of the newyork Stock Exchange, are working on plans to convert their markets into for-profit corporations. They argue that the new ownership structure would allow them to react more quickly and compete more effectively. And competition among the E.C.N.'s themselves is rising, prompting widespread predictions that only a few of the current crop will survive very long into the new century. "But it becomes very quickly clear that this is a business that requires scale and yet it's one in which very little distinguishes the different players -- in short, it's a commodity business," said Guy Moszkowski, a brokerage industry analyst with Salomon Smith Barney. Moreover, each E.C.N. further fragments the market when customers want the broadest, deepest market possible. "So they face an almost self-defeating business challenge," Mr. Moszkowski added. Yet, new competitors continue to arrive. By summer, Wall Street expects the debut of Primex, an E.C.N. that advertises itself as an "electronic auction market." Its hefty backers -- including Merrill Lynch & Company, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter and Salomon Smith Barney -- account for more than half the trading volume on the newyork Stock Exchange. Nor is the stock market the only place where the ground is shaking. The nation's major options exchanges -- the Chicago Board Options Exchange, the Chicago Board of Trade, the American Stock Exchange, the Philadelphia Stock Exchange and the Pacific Exchange -- are all facing increased electronic competition. The International Securities Exchange, an electronic options exchange based in Manhattan and sponsored by a group of large brokerage firms including E*Trade and Ameritrade, plans to open its virtual doors in March, if regulators agree. Another electronic rival, backed by the Chicago Stock Exchange and Goldman, Sachs & Company, is on the drawing board. Regulatory demands for greater public access to the prices at which bonds trade is also likely to push that traditional marketplace toward greater reliance on electronic trading, Mr. Moszkowski said. The deep, relatively homogeneous markets for Treasury debt will probably be the first to adopt electronic trading broadly, he said, but the corporate and municipal markets will not be far behind. More than a dozen bond trading systems are already operating or are expected to open in the next year or so. Though European and East Asian markets have been quicker to adopt electronic trading equipment, American markets remain in the forefront of these changes simply because this revolution is being driven largely by the demands of individual investors, who play a much larger role in the American marketplace than they do elsewhere. Indeed, individuals play a much greater role in American markets than they once did. From the cloudy vantage point of the mid-1970's, the American securities market seemed to be a purely institutional party, with big pension funds and mutual funds pumping in giant orders and elbowing aside the little guy. But last year and into the first half of this year, more than 51 percent of the Big Board's volume consisted of trades of fewer than 10,000 shares apiece. While some small orders are submitted by large index funds, which constantly adjust their portfolios to reflect the larger market, the growth in small orders also reflects a larger role by individuals, Mr. Moszkowski said. But as foreign markets catch up, American investors will no doubt push for cheap, fast access to them as well. That will add to the pressure on Wall Street and its regulators to find a way to develop a global electronic market that has adequate regulation, sufficient financial safeguards for all participants and ready access to accurate, comparable information from market to market. Already, this technological revolution has produced a long "to do" list for regulators. As the new year opens, they must wrestle not only with the competitive and regulatory issues surrounding E.C.N.'s and their traditional stock exchange rivals, but also with some important developments prompted by the new techology. Most are fairly technical, but one change that individual investors are sure to notice will be the conversion of stock quotes from the traditional fractions into less unwieldy dollars-and-cents prices, a change that is scheduled for next summer. Market experts like Professor Freund expect that this change will put additional pressure on Wall Street profits by reducing spreads, the difference between the prices at which a trader can buy and sell the same stock. Today, a market maker might buy a stock for $10 a share and sell it for $10 1/16 -- a difference of 6 1/4 cents. With decimal pricing, that gap could shrink to perhaps 5 cents, or even less. "The conversion can't compare with the Y2K problems, as a technological challenge; this is not like converting to the metric system," Professor Freund said. "But it will change the economics of market making. It will narrow the spreads, and that will put some market makers out of business." Indeed, for everyone on Wall Street, from the brokerage giants to the newest E.C.N.'s, competing effectively in the new century is going to mean finding the right balance between computers and human beings, according to Mr. Moszkowski, the securities analyst. "Anything that can be automated must be automated because of the competitive pressures to keep costs low," he said. The work left for human traders -- using their firms' capital to ease the handling of giant orders from big institutions that will have to pay handsomely for the service -- is going to require far more than routine skills as the difficulty of conducting these trades increases. "Institutional orders will need people much more skillful than ever before," Professor Freund said. "The seat-of-the-pants trader is not going to make it." Lee Korins, the chief executive of the Security Traders Association in Manhattan, acknowledged that technology was reshaping the life of his members in significant and unpredictable ways. But he cautioned against confusing technology as a means with technology as an end in itself. "Our markets work so well because we have risk takers in them, not because we have a particular technology," Mr. Korins said. "Electronic systems will do away with certain work experiences. But as long as we make sure the risk taker is included as we go forward, I don't have a big problem with these changes." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Cindee Sokal works as a day trader at the All-Tech Investment Group in Dallas. (Mark Perlstein for The newyork Times)  Chart: "Threats to Wall Street's Status Quo" The newyork Stock Exchange and Nasdaq are still the dominant stock markets with a history of handling large institutional orders...but smaller orders, many of them placed by individual traders through online accounts, now represent a larger share of trading...which has nourished the growth of new, faster and cheaper ways of trading.
