Terms were not disclosed. Tegic's software is licensed to 20 wireless-phone makers representing 90 percent of the world market, America Online said. America Online and Tegic plan to develop a version of America Online's Instant Messenger service to send messages from wireless telephones. The purchase will enhance America Online's strategy of providing its Internet services on a range of devices, including hand-held computers, cell phones and televisions. America Online, which is based in Dulles, Va., said on Monday that it would raise $1.25 billion in a convertible-note sale. Separately, America Online said its instant-messaging unit, ICQ, which stands for "I seek you," had signed agreements with companies like the auctioneer eBay Inc. and the American Greetings Corporation to advertise and sell products to ICQ's 50 million registered members. America Online bought ICQ when it acquired Mirabilis Ltd., an Israeli company, in June 1998 for $287 million. At that time, ICQ had 12 million registered users for the free service, which allows people to see if friends are logged on, then send messages that immediately appear on the other user's computer screen. America Online said today that ICQ had reached 50 million registered users. http://www.nytimes.com

title: A Stock-Network Deal Is Said to Be Stalled
body: The Softbank Corporation has been in negotiations to acquire a large stake in the Island E.C.N., a fast-growing electronic network for trading stocks, according to people who have been briefed on the talks. The company has made a multimillion-dollar offer to buy the stake from Datek Online Holdings Corporation, which owns the nation's fourth-largest online brokerage firm and about 85 percent of Island. The talks have broken down, however, and it is unclear whether the deal will take place. Officials at Softbank and Datek declined to comment. Executives briefed on the deal said Softbank, a Japanese investment company that owns large stakes in E*Trade and Yahoo, was expecting to bring those two companies in on the deal. Executives at Yahoo could not be reached for comment. And a spokesman for E*Trade said the company was not now in talks with Datek or Island. The people briefed on the talks said that there could still be an investment or a joint venture. But if a deal does occur, it would make Island, which is seeking regulatory approval to become a full-fledged stock exchange, the most formidable of a new breed of low-cost electronic trading systems that have emerged on Wall Street in the last few years. By matching buyers and sellers, electronic communication networks have helped bypass the middleman's role on Wall Street and squeezed profits. Known as E.C.N.'s, for electronic communications networks, the networks are putting increasing pressure on the nation's biggest brokerage firms and financial exchanges, which are racing to retool their organizations to compete with discount brokerage firms and electronic trading upstarts. People close to the talks said the Island deal was being brokered by the Softbank Corporation, which would like to control Island. Softbank has numerous joint ventures and is interested in online finance. For Datek, which plans to retain a big stake in Island, any deal would provide a windfall. It would also strengthen the Island trading system, which is drawing business away from the Nasdaq stock market and Instinet, an electronic trading system operated by Reuters. A deal would also strengthen Datek Online, the company's brokerage arm, which has been plagued by regulatory and criminal investigations over the last two years. Vulcan Ventures, the venture capital fund financed by Paul Allen, the Microsoft co-founder, decided in July not to proceed with a planned investment of $75 million to $100 million in Datek and Island partly because of concerns about various investigations. TD Waterhouse, another large online brokerage firm, also decided to pull out of a planned $25 million investment in Island in October because of concerns about governance and valuation. TA Associates, a venture capital firm, and Group Arnault N.V., invested $15 million apiece in Island E.C.N. in May. Since then, Jeffrey A. Citron, 29, has stepped down as chief executive of Datek, though he retains a significant stake in the company. Datek executives say that Mr. Citron stepped aside pending the conclusion of a number of investigations into the online brokerage firm, which was a pioneering day-trading firm in the 1980's and 1990's. The Manhattan district attorney, the Securities and Exchange Commission and at least one other law enforcement agency are investigating whether Datek took part in money-laundering activity or illegal trading practices as recently as 1998. The company was also sanctioned by the S.E.C. in May for filing false financial reports and illegally dipping into customer accounts. Executives of Datek Online say that in recent months they have been trying to remake the company, whose management has changed considerably over the last year. They insist that any improprieties occurred long ago, and largely in a day-trading unit that was spun off in 1998. The company has embarked on an $80 million television advertising campaign and has reported a sharp increase in trading volume in recent weeks. People close to the talks with the Softbank-led group say that Datek recently rejected an offer because it placed too low a value on Island and because it wanted guarantees that some additional stock orders would be directed to it, perhaps from E*Trade, the No.  2 online broker; Yahoo, the Internet portal with a popular financial site; or other partners. Others say that the deal broke down because, among other issues, it would have been difficult to spin Island off from Datek. In another hindrance to a deal, Datek executives are said to be concerned about possible conflicts arising from Softbank's many relationships. Softbank has joint ventures abroad with the Nasdaq stock market, which competes with Island. But one executive said that the companies had briefed the National Association of Securities Dealers, which operates the Nasdaq stock market, and few objections were raised. Electronic trading networks now account for more than 30 percent of all Nasdaq trading volume. Charles Schwab & Company, the nation's largest online brokerage firm, has a joint venture with FMR's Fidelity Investments and Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, which together own a large stake in Redibook, a relatively new electronic communications network. E*Trade and Instinet each have a stake in Archipelago, which has many investors among big brokerage firms, as well. Island is one of the strongest networks, with heavy trading in popular Internet stocks like Yahoo and Intel. On Monday, for instance, Island executed trades in nearly 200 million shares worth more than $8 billion. The Island system, which was created in 1996, remains popular among day traders and online traders who cite its fast executions.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
True North will acquire Stein Rogan, a shop that specializes in digital communications companies.
body: AN agency company that was early to explore cyberspace is expanding again in the fast-growing realm of digital communications, acquiring a newyork shop specializing in online and offline advertising for dot-coms. True North Communications in Chicago, the world's No. 7 agency company with estimated billings of $12 billion, is buying Stein Rogan & Partners in newyork, which has estimated capitalized billings of $75 million from clients like Apartment.com, Blackboard.com, Cars.com, Flycast, Mail.com and FasTV.com. Stein Rogan, with 70 employees, will operate as an autonomous unit of True North, which also owns traditional agencies like FCB Worldwide, Bozell and Temerlin McClain. The top managers of Stein Rogan, which also has a small office in Chicago, will continue leading the agency. They include Tom Stein, president, and Mark Rogan, executive vice president and creative director. The deal for Stein Rogan, which started in 1986 as Stein Kilpatrick & Rogan, is indicative of the intensification of efforts by Madison Avenue to meet the challenges posed as the Internet remakes advertising, marketing and the media, particularly in competing against upstart startups. Giants like True North, the Omnicom Group, the Interpublic Group of Companies and the WPP Group are responding with strategies that range from acquisitions to investments in independent new-media shops to opening digital units within their traditional agencies. "Omnicom probably has the largest list of dot-com clients," said Michael J. Russell, an analyst who follows the advertising industry for Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in newyork, "but Bozell has Datek and FCB has Amazon.com." Omnicom and True North lead among the biggest agency companies in estimated revenue to be derived from dot-coms in 2000, by Mr. Russell's estimates, at about 3 percent of the total, compared with about 1 percent for the others. The mad dash to capitalize on the dot-coms is not limited to agencies. For instance, NBC, part of General Electric, is combining several of its online operations with the portal Web site Snap.com and Xoom.com, an electronic commerce company. The combined company, named NBCi, began trading yesterday on the Nasdaq Stock Market. The True North cyberholdings include R/GA Interactive and 50 percent of Modem Media.Poppe Tyson, the digital agency that began as two interactive units of FCB and Bozell before being combined and eventually sold in an initial public offering. And DoubleClick, the giant Web ad network, started in 1995 as the Internet sales group of Poppe Tyson. "With the explosion of e-commerce companies seeking to brand themselves online and offline, it's obvious not every one is going to win," said David Bell, chairman and chief executive at True North. "Tom and Mark are experts in placing their chips on those that are." Mr. Bell discussed the acquisition in an interview yesterday; the formal announcement is to be made today. Terms of the deal are not being disclosed, though recently agency acquisitions are being made for prices equal to about one year's revenue. Stein Rogan's 1998 revenue was $12 million and its revenue for the first six months of 1999 was $11 million, according to estimates by IQ Interactive News, a weekly supplement to the trade publications Adweek, Brandweek and Mediaweek. The 1999 figure placed the agency 24th among the top 50 interactive agencies ranked by the supplement. "We're ready to move on to bigger and better things," said Mr. Stein, 43, "and True North is going to help us get there." "We'd started out as a general advertising agency but took those capabilities and focused ourselves in 1995 as 'the information agency, using interactive media as a marketing venue," he added. "We saw an opportunity that today involves building brands in the Internet space in entertainment, education, finance, e-business of all sorts." "And there's going to be a tremendous continuing intensity of activity in that space," Mr. Stein predicted. "There will be not just a lot of dot-com advertising on the Super Bowl, but all through the first quarter." "I'm exaggerating a little bit to say one or two business models come across our desks every day," he added, "and every one we see is ramping up for 2000." Mr. Rogan, 44, echoed his colleague's optimism, but noted that the growing popularity of the Internet brings more dot-com campaigns, which makes it increasingly difficult "to break through the clutter." "So what you do for dot-com brands has to be done a lot smarter," he added, "and in Internet time." As an example, he cited the work Stein Rogan has produced for Cars.com, an automotive Web site operated by Classified Ventures, a consortium of large newspaper companies. The campaign sought to balance the needs of car shoppers with the needs of car dealers, who are the site's primary revenue source. "We needed to build a value proposition for Cars.com with consumers," Mr. Stein said, "but at the same time not alienate dealers, who pay the freight." So rather than proceed with a campaign carrying the theme "Drive home a better deal," the Cars.com ads carry this theme: "Car shopping the way it should be. Simple." And the offline ads for Cars.com, on television and in newspapers, "have the look and feel of the Web site," Mr. Rogan said, by including "a lot of screen shots" and even "duplicating the browser frame" computer users see. "The creatives fight that," he added, "saying, 'People know they're going on the Web.' But there's nothing wrong with a product demonstration." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Campaigns are taking to the streets to raise awareness of companies' products and services.
body: THE battle among advertisers for eyeballs is not limited to the Internet. There is still warfare being waged street by street as more marketers -- including dozens of dot-coms -- turn to outdoor advertising to increase awareness of their products and services. The growing popularity of the outdoor medium, particularly in urban centers where consumers are concentrated, is underscored by two ad blitzes scheduled to begin tomorrow. One is for Powerstreet, the new brand for the online brokerage services of Fidelity Investments, and the other is for Moe Ginsburg, the venerable apparel retailer. Both are spending extensively in the next four to eight weeks to blanket cityscapes from subway platforms to telephone kiosks to bus shelters with pitches meant for mass consumption. In both instances, the goal is to cut through the clamorous clutter that bewitches, bothers and bewilders passers-by on crowded streets. But those who recall the Yogi Berra-ism about nobody going to a popular restaurant anymore because it's too crowded may wonder whether nobody will see the signs because there are so many of them. "I would agree that it's getting a little cluttered," said Steve Cone, president for corporate and retail marketing at Fidelity in Boston. "On the other hand, I've never seen Times Square busier, and Broadway is rocking and rolling." "We created Powerstreet to remind people that we are a major player in the online brokerage business," he added, and the "broad reach" that outdoor ads provide "is a critical part of an integrated media plan." His reference was to the television, radio and print campaign for Powerstreet -- formally known as Powerstreet Online Trading at Fidelity.com -- that continues as the outdoor advertising arrives in Boston, newyork and San Francisco. "You don't want the wallpaper effect," said Rob Hofferman, vice president and account director at Korey Kay & Partners in newyork, the Ginsburg agency. "You want something that could generate not only visibility but also impact." Korey Kay has arranged with Outdoor Systems, which sells ad space for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, to replace all the signs on the uptown and downtown sides of the N and R subway station at 23rd Street and Broadway in Manhattan with Ginsburg displays. The "brand station," as it is called, is intended to complement the "brand trains" sold by Outdoor Systems, limiting ads in subway cars to one or two advertisers. "Clutter is an issue," said Sheri Baron, president of Gotham Inc. in newyork, the Powerstreet agency, "but what this is about is presence and dominance." "In locations where people are out and about," she added, "there's no better way to own 'share of mind' than this use of outdoor." Gotham, part of the Interpublic Group of Companies, plans to virtually cover the five boroughs of newyork by peddling Powerstreet with pithy posters on 6,000 displays owned by TDI Worldwide. The signs are to be posted on buses, phone kiosks, commuter rail stations and walls. They will carry headlines like "Ask newyorkers for personal info, and they'll tell you where to go" and "newyorkers take everything personally. Why not online trading?" "It's newyork bravado," Don Allman, president at TDI, said, laughing, "newyork as the center of the universe." There will be similar displays, though not Big Apple-centric, on TDI ad space in Boston and at the Embarcadero station of Bay Area Rapid Transit in San Francisco. The newyork portion of the campaign is "the largest concentration in one market we've ever done," said Mr. Allman, whose company is the outdoor advertising unit of Infinity Broadcasting, majority owned by the CBS Corporation in newyork. "To some degree it's akin to a television roadblock," he added, using the term for a commercial that runs at the same time on numerous networks or stations so viewers perceive it to be inescapable. "In a word, it's going to be awesome." And it's also going to be, in three words, "the most expensive" campaign TDI has ever sold to a single advertiser in a single market, Mr. Allman said. Fidelity is estimated to be paying $2.5 million for ad space valued at about $5.5 million. The discount is part of a deal Fidelity signed under a program named CBS Plus that packages sponsorships among CBS media outlets. The total budget for the Powerstreet introduction is estimated at $50 million to $60 million. The budget for the brand station was estimated at $20,000 by Harve Ganz, manager for newyork transit at Outdoor Systems, which is coincidentally being acquired by Infinity. "For a long time, people have asked about buying a whole station, so this is an experiment," Mr. Ganz said. "The brand train was slow to take off, but once people started seeing it, it caught fire." Brand train advertisers include the Bronx Zoo, Kenneth Cole, newyork University, Procter & Gamble and Seagram. For the Ginsburg station, which a half million people are estimated to use each month, "it would be a lot cheaper and easier to run the same ad or two over and over," Mr. Hofferman said. "But to keep people involved and engaged, we're going to run every ad we've done" since landing the account in September. That amounts to 12 to 14 ads, which carry cheeky headlines like "You didn't spend two years at Wharton to get noticed for the latest trend in pleats" (for the retailer's traditionally styled suits) and "You're too sexy for glen plaid, too sexy for two buttons, too sexy to blend in" (for designer suits). Consumers concerned about ad clutter outdoors may want to hide indoors for the next month, especially if they traverse Times Square. To capitalize on the throngs expected to celebrate the arrival of 2000, gathering in front of sites including 1 Times Square and 2 Times Square -- where ad space is sold by Sherwood Outdoor -- marketers are rushing to affix additional signs to buildings. Among the newcomers to Times Square are De Beers, JVC and the World Wrestling Federation. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Fidelity Investments' outdoor advertising for Powerstreet, its online brokerage service.

title: Regulators See Need for Rules of the Roadfor Online Trading Firms
body: Online brokerage firms are the hot rods of Wall Street, providing fast and cheap access to stock market investors every trading day. Now, securities regulators want these firms to install seat belts. After months of inquiries into the practices of the nation's online brokerage firms, securities regulators in Washington and newyork issued weighty reports on the industry yesterday, identifying lapses in investor protection at many online operations and offering suggestions about how to correct them. The reports, issued by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the office of Eliot L. Spitzer, the newyork state attorney general, are an attempt by securities regulators to bring some order to the fractious online brokerage business, which has transformed the way investors buy and sell stocks. Until now, much of this change, driven by technological advancements, has been watched by regulators from the sidelines. Although neither of the reports recommended new rules for the online industry, they telegraph to the brokerage community a regulatory commitment to online investor protection. Laura Unger, the S.E.C. commissioner who wrote the report, said in a statement: "I think it may still be premature for extensive rulemaking in this area, but the report will allow the commission to focus upon and consider the most vital issues concerning online brokerage." By the second quarter of this year, investors had opened about 9.7 million online brokerage accounts, almost three times the number in force in 1997. Online trading volume has grown, the S.E.C. said, from fewer than 100,000 trades a day in mid-1996 to more than half a million now. This explosive growth, according to the regulators, has made the nation's stock market much more accessible to investors. But the popularity of online investing, Mr. Spitzer's report said, "also poses unique risks to the public, and presents tough challenges to regulators charged with ensuring the integrity of the trading environment." Mr. Spitzer's report, the result of nine months of inquiries into the practices of seven firms in five states, concluded that online brokerage firms hyped their technology and services, contending that they provide direct and immediate trade execution while playing down the risks of computer system breakdowns. For example, the report found that many firms do not update customer account information regularly enough to provide accurate readings on investors' margin accounts. That has allowed investors to buy stocks using money they thought was in the account when in fact they had none. In addition, Mr. Spitzer's investigators reported that online investors were able to buy stocks in their individual retirement accounts that exceeded the value of those accounts. Both of those findings gave substance to the fears of some market observers that online brokerage firms will do anything to keep investors trading. A top concern of the S.E.C. is that some online firms may try to escape their obligation to ensure that investments that their customers make are suitable for their circumstances. Suitability is a principal avenue of protection for investors under federal securities laws; almost one-third of the arbitration cases filed by investors with the National Association of Securities Dealers since 1995 involved investments said to have been unsuitable for the investors who bought them. In the past, some online firms have contended that because their customers make their own investment decisions, even if based on research taken from the Web site, the firm need not consider whether an investment is suitable to the investor. Glen Mathison, a spokesman for the Charles Schwab Corporation, said yesterday that the firm's executives were still digesting the regulators' reports and he could not comment on the specifics. But he said that existing regulation adequately covers suitability. "There's no need to separate out online investing for some sort of differentiated or specialized regulation," Mr. Mathison said. Nevertheless, the S.E.C.'s report identifies situations in which online firms would have to meet suitability requirements. For example, while an online firm that simply executes orders without providing any research would not need to examine its customers' trades for appropriateness, the report said that a firm that published research should believe that the information is plausible and that the recommended investments "may be appropriate for at least some of its customers." Lewis D. Lowenfels, a prominent securities lawyer at Tolins & Lowenfels and an expert on suitability, said: "Regulators have now begun to address in-depth problems that new technology is raising among investors. This is a sensible way to proceed. Any attempt to set rigid rules when the industry is in such a state of flux would be counterproductive." Without naming individual firms, both reports maintained that online brokerage firms needed to tone down their promises of instant market access and be more clear about the risks of system failures or delays. "Over the past few years, online trading has revolutionized the investment world," Mr. Spitzer said in a statement. "With this new technology comes the need for new 'rules of the road' for both investors and brokerage firms." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Point-and-click with a personal touch: Internet company offers customized computer cursors.
body: A SMALL Internet company is hoping that the adage about tall oaks growing from little acorns also applies to cyberspace, as it seeks big results from turning perhaps the tiniest place on a computer screen into advertising. The company is Comet Systems in newyork, which has developed a proprietary technology for commercializing cursors, the arrows that point and click their way through the Internet. On Web sites where marketers have bought ad space, computer users who have installed Comet software can be offered customized cursors. The Comet Cursors are colorful miniature billboards in fanciful shapes that can range from Pokemon characters and Energizer bunnies to telephone directories and "Star Trek" spaceships. They also come in generic forms with themes like pets, holidays and sports. The Comet efforts are indicative of the so-called rich media applications being introduced to increase interest in online pitches, particularly the banner ads that tend to be as dull as, well, arrow-shaped cursors. "The test of any rich-media product is how effective it is at getting more customers and creating more brand awareness," said Marissa Gouck, an analyst at Jupiter Communications in newyork. "The trick is to keep it something special," she added, "because often, the more ubiquitous it becomes, the less effective it becomes." Research by Millward Brown Interactive, a unit of the WPP Group, that was commissioned by Comet and sponsored in part by four large advertisers showed that differentiated cursors can significantly increase the ability of computer users to recall seeing ad banners and their desire to click through to read the ads. "It struck me that if the cursor could change contextually with each site you visit, the advertising impression would remain with you," said Jamie Rosen, recently promoted to chairman at Comet from president, "because it's a way of stamping a personality onto a site." Mr. Rosen founded the company in 1997 with Dean Margolis, the chief executive, who left during the summer, and Tom Schmitter, the chief technical officer. "Like any new technology, the problem with putting an image in the cursor space is one of education, getting people familiar and comfortable with it," said Ben Austin, marketing director at Comet. "But invariably, every time we show it to people, they become believers." The Comet technology is used on more than 55,000 Web sites, by the company's count, with licensees that include AT&T Worldnet; the Comedy Central cable network, jointly owned by Time Warner Inc. and Viacom Inc.; Mattel, and the Warner Brothers Online unit of Time Warner. Under an agreement signed last month with 24/7 Media in newyork, a product named the Cometized Banner, which automatically serves branded cursors when an ad banner is clicked through, will be delivered across the 24/7 ad network. Campaigns with commercialized cursors have appeared on Web sites operated by AltaVista, Lycos, theglobe.com and Yahoo, sponsored by marketers like BellSouth, Energizer and Toshiba. "We incorporated the Comet Cursor into our own site, Energizer .com," said Harriet Blickenstaff, a spokeswoman for the Eveready Battery Company in St. Louis, a division of Ralston Purina. "It captures the fun and surprise of the bunny." "In terms of driving people to the site, the results were inconclusive," she added. "But we would still deem it successful because it fits our strategy, our tone, our spirit." The arrival of advertising in yet another Internet space could generate a backlash among critics of the increasing commercialism of communications, who could complain, to paraphrase the outcries of the defeated villains in melodramatic old movies, "Cursors, foiled again!" But "the nice thing about the Comet Cursor is that the user has to make an active choice to get it," said Beth Suitt, advertising manager of BellSouth Intelliventures in Atlanta, referring to the need to download the software, known as a plug-in. "It's more of an opt-in experience instead of being put in your face without permission," she added. "That gives advertisers an opportunity to stick to users' minds without being intrusive." The plug-in aspect can be a minus as well as a plus if users are wary of the time it takes to download the Comet Cursor from sources like www.cometsystems.com and www.cometzone.com. "We pay for the sins of our predecessors," Mr. Rosen said, laughing, "when people see a download and think it's going to crash their computers." But Comet plugs the plug-in process as brief, lasting less than 10 seconds. (If you try it late on a Friday, when your computer is choking as colleagues file articles on deadlines for Saturday, Sunday and Monday, it may take five minutes.) So far, by Comet's estimate, 15 million computer users have downloaded the plug-in. "It's a neat little application that improves response rates for advertisers," said Will Margiloff, advertising sales director at theglobe.com in newyork, which has developed promotions with holiday themes using Comet Cursors. "We'll continue to use it with almost every promotion we do going forward." But can the commercialized cursor become more than just a promotional ploy? "There's definitely a gimmicky aspect to it," Ms. Gouck at Jupiter said. "The approach Comet has is pretty good, but technology can go only so far. "I've seen some great executions of the Comet Cursor and I've seen some awful ones," she added. "A lot depends on the creative capabilities of the advertiser." And Comet's technology initially proved more popular with individual home pages and small-business sites than with marketing giants. For example, none of the four large advertisers from the Comet survey have used the technology so far. "We were pleased with the results," said Gretchen Briscoe, a spokeswoman for one advertiser, Procter & Gamble in Cincinnati. "The cursor drove awareness and people remembered the brand, but we've got no plans going forward to use it." Let's hope P.& G. rethinks its reticence. Who wouldn't relish the chance to see a Comet Cursor shaped like a can of Comet cleanser? http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: New technology can turn cursors into miniature billboards. (Comet Systems)

title: Microsoft Drops Instant Message Fight With AOL
body: Microsoft has backed off in its battle with America Online over instant messages on the Internet, saying the latest version of its MSN Messenger service will not operate with AOL's Instant Messenger. Microsoft contends that America Online's latest attempt to block MSN Messenger from working with Instant Messenger involves "a very serious security bug" that could allow computer code to be run on a personal computer without the computer user's approval or knowledge. "To provide an update to MSN Messenger service that would continue to enable interoperability, Microsoft would need to put our own users at risk in a similar fashion," Yusuf Mehdi, director of marketing for Microsoft's Consumer and Commerce Group, said on Wednesday. Ann Brackbill, a spokeswoman for America Online, said, "We're glad they have decided to respect the security and privacy of our members and users." Concerning Microsoft's allegation of a security bug, she said: "We said four months ago that it was a fake issue, and it still is a fake issue today. We would never do anything to compromise the security of our users." Microsoft first released its Internet chat software in early August, challenging America Online's dominance of the market. One advantage that Microsoft promoted was the ability to work with America Online's software, allowing MSN customers to exchange instant messages with America Online users. America Online immediately complained that Microsoft engineers had hacked into its proprietary network and blocked Microsoft from linking to its software. Microsoft redesigned its chat software to bypass America Online's block, but was then stymied again and again as America Online continued to put up blocks. Mr. Mehdi denied Microsoft had "lost" the battle to America Online. "There are no winners," he said. "Consumers will win when an industrywide instant messaging standard is in place that ensures all users the ability to message with others regardless of which service they're using." As of last month, America Online had 45 million people signed up for the messenger service, while Microsoft said today that it had 4.5 million users. http://www.nytimes.com

title: 3 Big Airlines Join Others On Priceline
body: Priceline.com, the online company that lets consumers bid for everything from airline tickets to cars and groceries, has signed up three of the nation's top six airlines, in effect doubling the number of airline seats it can sell. By signing up the carriers -- No. 1 United Airlines, No. 2 American Airlines and No. 6 US Airways -- Priceline is now working with eight of the nine largest unitedstates carriers. Other carriers working with Priceline are America West, Delta, Continental, Northwest and T.W.A.; 20 foreign lines also participate. Airline tickets were the first merchandise Priceline sold when it began operations in April 1998. Prospective buyers submit an offer for a ticket online; if their price is accepted, they must purchase the ticket.  Buyers also must be flexible about their departure time, and be willing to make a connection en route. Those conditions have made Priceline's service far more practical for leisure travelers than for those flying on business. Although Priceline has insisted from the start that its ticket program would help airlines get rid of unsold seats, most major airlines resisted cooperating with the company, supposedly because they were unwilling to turn over control of their inventory to a third party. Initially, only T.W.A. and America West, among the smallest of the nation's major airlines, worked with Priceline. Then last summer, Delta joined up, and was followed by Northwest and Continental. Richard Braddock, chairman and chief executive of Priceline, said the decision by American, United and US Airways to join forces with the online company represented an endorsement of Priceline's success. According to Mr. Braddock, Priceline's weekly sales of airline tickets have increased tenfold since January; the company sold 5,000 tickets a week at the beginning of the year and now sells more than 50,000 a week. Mr. Braddock, who said Priceline's airline program generated 80 percent of the company's total revenues, also predicted the addition of the new airlines would create "dramatically better results" for the airline program. And he said the expanded airline program would lure more customers and create more opportunities to sell them Priceline's other services. Brian Harris, airline analyst for Salomon Smith Barney, said the decision by American, United and US Airways to participate proved that the company was "an important distribution channel." "In the past, airlines felt they could ignore it," he said, but that hurt them, and now they want in on it." As part of its agreements with the three airlines, Priceline has restructured warrant agreements with all its unitedstates airline participants to give them equity positions close to the size of their share of the domestic market. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING;
Latest Lure On the Web: Free Trades
body: THE price war among online brokerage firms has escalated so rapidly that the stock trade has gone from being a commodity to a come-on. As commissions for executing stock trades sank lower and lower, Wall Street experts said it was only a matter of time before somebody started giving away trades. Well, that time has come: the American Express Company on Monday began promoting an online brokerage service with commission-free stock purchases for anybody who deposits $25,000. That offer, which American Express officials say is not temporary, has caused a lot of head-shaking in an industry that already abounds in gimmickry. To entice investors, online brokers are tossing in everything from trips to Hawaii to $100 bills. "It's getting very messy," said Stephen D. McDonald, chief executive of TD Waterhouse Group, an online brokerage firm that charges $12 for some trades. "Next thing you know, we'll be giving away toasters." There are no small appliances on the immediate horizon. But the firms have started so many giveaways that even their executives have trouble keeping track of what is being dangled before investors' eyes. Last week, DLJdirect, the online brokerage arm of the investment bank Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, was using ads on financial Web sites, making two offers simultaneously to new account holders: investors who knew where to look could choose to accept a credit of $100 or six months of free Internet access, which would be paid in the form of a $120 credit. E*Trade Group went a little further this month when it started offering $150 to customers of a competitor, the Discover Brokerage Direct unit of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, for switching to E*Trade. That was double the offers of $75 that E*Trade and Discover had made for opening accounts. Ameritrade, an Omaha-based firm that charges $8 for some trades, is trumpeting an offer that may be worth more than those that E*Trade and DLJdirect have on the table. In exchange for opening a new account, customers can get two round-trip plane tickets to London, Mexico or Hawaii. The catch is that the tickets are free only after a customer pays for a nondiscounted, seven-night stay at certain hotels. "There's a lot of crazy things going on in terms of marketing and account acquisition," said James Marks, an analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston. Online brokerages are spending so much money on advertising and promotion for very similar services, he said, that they find themselves "in a position like American Express where you have to come up with almost a gimmick that isn't sustainable." Mr. Marks recently turned cautious on the stocks of some on-line brokers, including Ameritrade and E*Trade. Although he was an early proponent of heavy marketing spending, he now fears that some online brokers are spending far too much to acquire new accounts. This summer's slowdown in online account activity, he said, raised doubts about whether the online brokers could continue their growth pace. Shares of some of them, which ran up sharply in the first half of the year, are now about 50 percent off their highs, despite a rally on Friday. "The accounts that these guys really want are the investors that will take out margin loans," or borrow to buy stocks, Mr. Marks said. But advertising low-margin interest rates does not attract customers the way free trades or other promotions do, he said. AS cluttered as the landscape has become, American Express managed to steal the spotlight, if only briefly, by creating a new business model for the brokerage industry. While some of the biggest Wall Street firms are struggling to shift from commission-based models to fee-based models, American Express has decided to charge neither commissions nor fees. "We thought that this is kind of an interesting way we can differentiate ourselves," said Ruediger Adolf, a senior vice president at American Express. While Mr. Adolf prefers not to describe the free stock trades as a loss leader, American Express is giving away a service that costs it at least several dollars to provide. Mr. McDonald estimates that it costs the biggest and most efficient brokerage firms at least $8 to carry out a stock trade ordered electronically. The cost for firms that have to pay others to execute and process their trades could run as high as $25, he said. "We make money in other ways," Mr. Adolf said, referring to the interest that American Express earns on the cash in customers' accounts and on loans that customers take to buy stocks. "With traditional brokers, this would be a very, very dangerous game because you fundamentally are cannibalizing your main business." In other words, American Express has nothing to lose by giving away trades -- except money. Mr. Adolf declined to say how much American Express expected to lose on the commission-free trades, but on the whole, he said, "we think we absolutely can make money in this business." The company is not making all stock trades free. Customers with at least $100,000 in their accounts pay no commissions, but those with less than $25,000 in their accounts pay $14.95 a trade. For the people in between, American Express came up with an interesting twist: they can buy stocks without paying a commission, but must pay $14.95 each time they sell shares of a company. That move, unusual for a brokerage, comes directly out of the mutual fund playbook. Many fund companies let investors buy fund shares without a sales charge, but charge one when the shares are sold. A key component of the plan: Mr. Adolf said American Express did not want to attract the type of investor for whom free trades would be most appealing -- the hyperactive trader. What could sound better to somebody who spends his days buying and selling stocks than an account that charges no fee and no trading commissions? Instead, American Express, like some other financial services firms offering low-priced trades, preaches long-term investing. "We do not subscribe to very aggressive trading strategies, particularly day-trading," Mr. Adolf said. To head off a rush of day traders, American Express has put in a speed bump: Even those customers with $100,000 will have to pay $14.95 to sell a stock the same day they bought it. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Cartoon (Chris Murphy)

title: Merrill Lynch Has Trouble Processing Trading Orders
body: Just three weeks before its scheduled introduction of an advanced online stock-trading system, Merrill Lynch & Company is struggling to handle customers' trades the old-fashioned way. For about three hours yesterday, Merrill Lynch brokers could not process orders to buy or sell stocks of companies traded on the Nasdaq Stock Market during that exchange's busiest day ever. Brokers who entered customers' orders to buy or sell Nasdaq stocks near the 9:30 a.m. beginning of the trading day in newyork did not find out for two hours or more what prices their customers received. In some cases, brokers entered orders to sell stocks they thought they had bought at lower prices earlier in the day, only to find out later that they had unintentionally sold for less than they had paid. Some of Merrill's 14,000 brokers complained that the failure was the latest of several technical problems the firm has had as it prepares for the start of the new service, Merrill Lynch Direct, on Dec. 1. The new system, a radical departure for Merrill, the nation's biggest brokerage house, will allow investors to trade stocks electronically without the help of a broker for $29.95 a trade. On Monday, brokers reported that the computer workstations they use to place orders and monitor stock prices and customers' accounts suffered sporadic failures through most of the day. A Merrill spokeswoman disputed those reports and said the company was unaware of any systemwide problem on Monday. "I suspect you've had pretty significant diversion of resources" to ensure on-time introduction of online trading, said Steve Galbraith, an analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein & Company. Mr. Galbraith said that David Komansky, Merrill's chairman and chief executive, assured him last week that Merrill would meet the Dec. 1 deadline, although the system would remain a work in progress after that date. The spokeswoman attributed yesterday's problem to a "normal, scheduled, upgrade" of a mainframe computer. She said it was unrelated to any other technical problems and would have no effect on the firm's effort to introduce online trading. The spokeswoman said that the problem affected several thousand Nasdaq stock trades from about 9:30 a.m. until 12:30 p.m. Once the problem was cleared up, she said, all pending trades were executed. Customers unhappy about the prices they received for the stocks they bought or sold "absolutely" will get the prices they would have received without the delay, she said. That will be good news to one Merrill broker who watched in agony yesterday as an order to sell a Nasdaq stock lingered on his computer screen, flashing the word "sending" as the stock's price quickly retraced its morning rise. The stock already had risen more than $5, or 15 percent, since the broker placed an order to buy several hundred shares of it. Hoping to capture that profit, the broker entered an order to sell the shares he believed he had bought. He later learned that the shares had been bought for about $4 more than he expected and sold for about 25 cents less, turning an apparently profitable trade into a loser. That is the type of glitch more commonly associated with online trading operations, whose systems are more dependent on technology. The Charles Schwab Corporation, the leading electronic brokerage firm, has suffered through a variety of technical problems in the last few weeks, ranging from slowdowns of its order-taking system to a two-hour failure two weeks ago. "The reality is everybody's site crashes about once a week," Mr. Galbraith said of online brokerage firms. "That's actually one of the risks these traditional firms are taking in going on the Internet. When you have an outage now, it's really public. When Schwab crashes, it's all over the Internet." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
E-Commerce Report;
Web site publishers and advertising agencies square off on ownership of data on customers.
body: ON the Internet, where information is king, some of the most valuable information is data about user or customer behavior. Of this, one of the most closely followed measurements is so-called click data, which focuses on who has clicked on an advertising banner or some other particular link. Web site publishers, advertising agencies and companies that buy those ads have relied heavily on that data to build their businesses, and until now they have been generous about sharing it freely with each other. Now one of the Internet's biggest advertisers is raising the question of whether that data belongs to anyone but the advertisers, and the resulting debate could shape the future of the advertiser-publisher relationship. According to executives within the Internet advertising industry, I.B.M. is testing new techniques of serving its ads to Internet users in a way that prevents publishers from knowing who clicked on I.B.M. ads displayed on their Web sites. I.B.M., these executives say, may then withhold the click data from publishers unless they can be persuaded to do otherwise. An I.B.M. official declined to comment about the proposed policy, saying it was premature to speculate. Indeed, industry executives said the company had merely floated the idea of claiming ownership of click data. But the I.B.M. talk has brought the issue of data ownership to a head, and given new impetus to a debate that has loomed as one of the most important facing the industry. "This is just the tip of the iceberg; and the bottom of that iceberg is the issue of who owns the data," said Michael Donahue, executive vice president of the American Association of Advertising Agencies. "The ad agencies don't want to be cut out because they want access to that data. The advertisers say, 'It's my money, so it's my data,' and the publishers say, 'That ad is part of my site's content, so it's my data.' " The possibility of losing access to click data has sent a shiver up the spines of Web site publishers, who rely on these statistics to gauge the effectiveness of advertising and to gather information about the buying interests of their users. That data is tremendously valuable to publishers, who can command high advertising fees for showing, for example, a mortgage company's ad to someone who has recently clicked on an advertisement for a realtor. Publishers also fear that if I.B.M. assumes such a stance, other advertisers will follow suit. Beyond I.B.M.'s considerable spending power -- industry executives rank the company as one of the top three advertisers on the Internet -- it has been influential in shaping industry policies. I.B.M. spearheaded an effort earlier this year, for instance, to force Web site publishers to post privacy statements or lose the company's advertising. Internet advertising executives cite two potential justifications for withholding click data. For one thing, their traditional relationship with print publishers and television and radio networks suggests that the data belongs to advertisers. The ad buyers generally do not share the results of advertising campaigns with networks or print publishers when those media run so-called direct response advertisements -- for example, a commercial that invites viewers to call an "800" number to buy a product. Advertisers acknowledge that Internet publishers play a far more active role in bringing qualified buyers to their doorstep than other media. But they also make the point that the Internet ultimately resembles the direct response model, so they could be justified in handling the data in a similar manner. Of equal importance for some advertisers is the suspicion that publishers and other companies that deliver ads are not above selling click data to an advertiser's competitor. These companies espouse a so-called Chinese wall policy dictating, for instance, that publishers do not sell information about people who clicked on one car company's ad banner to another car company. But industry executives say that there are violations. "I don't think it's pervasive, but there are people doing it," said Kevin O'Connnor, chief executive of Doubleclick Inc., an Internet advertising network. "And advertisers want to put a stop to it." According to industry executives who spoke on condition of anonymity, I.B.M.'s new advertising approach enables it to deliver ads from its own server computers -- a departure from the norm, since advertisers generally rely on publishers or third-party advertising companies like Doubleclick and Flycast to deliver ads on their behalf. Moreover, the way the ads are coded prevents publishers from tracking who clicked on I.B.M.'s ad banners. Most other advertisers, of course, lack the technological wherewithal to deliver their own ads or to otherwise separate publishers from click data. But publishers fear other advertisers could eventually deliver their ads in a manner similar to I.B.M.'s new technique. Or, even if they lack the technical expertise to block access, advertisers might seek either to contractually prevent publishers from using that data or to force publishers to pay for it. Industry executives say that I.B.M. is sensitive to concerns about causing a ripple effect, having staked a good measure of its business future on the growth of the e-commerce industry. But as the company joins others in pouring millions of advertising dollars into the Internet economy -- and as the value of customer data continues to rise -- I.B.M. may decide that now is the time to establish a precedent on the matter. According to Vivienne Bechtold, director of interactive marketing for Procter & Gamble, the issue could force advertisers to re-evaluate the role of publishers in helping to build ad campaigns. Ms. Bechtold, who is also a member of a coalition of Internet advertising and publishing leaders known as the Future of Advertising Stakeholders, or FAST, stressed that Procter & Gamble had not determined its own position on the issue. "I can understand why I.B.M. would consider this stance," she said. "On the other hand, the dynamics of the Internet raise the question: If we share the data, would advertisers benefit more from that collective expertise than if we treated them in the traditional, customer-supplier way?" Ultimately, she said, "advertisers could adopt a hybrid approach, where we choose to share with some, while with others, we treat it in the traditional way." Other trends are complicating the matter, including the tendency of advertisers to establish so-called "pay for performance" deals with Web sites. In those agreements, a publisher's payment is often based on the percentage of users who click on ad banners, so advertisers would naturally disclose click data to publishers. Other advertising deals remain on a "CPM" model, whereby advertisers pay a set rate, typically in the $25 range, for every thousand banners shown on a site. But about half of Internet advertising deals are a combination of pay-for-performance and CPM, so disputes over who owns the data could quickly muddy the waters. Publishers, meanwhile, are using so-called "collaborative filtering" technology to aim ads at consumers on their sites -- and can offer even more precise targets when they know what ads their customers are clicking on. Indeed, according to Anil Singh, chief sales and marketing officer for Yahoo: "We can target clusters of our audience that have a higher propensity to click on certain types of offers. That's a great service for advertisers. If we were unable to collect data in that effort, it would hurt the services we could offer our clients." At the same time, a growing number of advertisers are choosing to deliver their ads through third-party servers like Doubleclick and Flycast, which also rely extensively on click data. Those companies have much at stake as well. "Are we willing to step back and not have access to the data?" asked Doubleclick's Mr. O'Connor. "I'm not so sure. It could very well not be a good thing for the advertisers." At the center of this issue is Rich LeFurgy, chairman of the Internet Advertising Bureau, an industry group that represents Internet publishers. Mr. LeFurgy, who is also the chairman of FAST, said the advertising bureau and I.B.M. were seeking common ground. "They understand our position, we understand theirs," he said. "But this is stuff that's not to be underestimated in terms of its importance and implications." Internet publishers, however, have little leverage in the debate, in the view of Jim Nail, an analyst with Forrester Research. "Advertisers are ultimately the source of all the money, so they hold the trump card in this," Mr. Nail said. "If they want to do it, they can." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Rich LeFurgy, left, the chairman of the Internet Advertising Bureau, an organization that represents publishers, discusses online direct marketing with Shane Moore of MyPoints.com, a shopping Web site. (Don Hogan Charles/The New York Times)

title: Internet Companies Set Policies to HelpProtect Consumer Privacy
body: To address online privacy concerns, a group of leading Internet advertising and data-profiling companies have agreed to adopt policies that allow consumers to find out what information is collected by the marketers and to turn off the data-gathering technology. The industry initiative is set to be announced on Monday at a public workshop about online profiling in Washington, which is being held by the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Commerce. The spread of Internet technology and its use by companies to identify personal patterns of online buying and behavior is a subject of increasing concern to privacy groups and the government. Profiling software can monitor every World Wide Web site that a computer user visits, every online advertisement she views, every mouse movement she makes. "This technology is something we haven't examined closely, yet it allows companies to collect great amounts of information without the slightest knowledge by consumers that it is being collected," said Robert Pitofsky, the F.T.C. chairman."It certainly strikes me as a troubling notion. And this surreptitious nature of the data collection makes this different from other privacy issues we've dealt with." The 10 companies involved in the self-regulatory effort are Internet "middlemen" businesses that place ads on Web sites and assemble demographic profiles for marketers and Web sites. Until now, most pressure for online privacy policies had been applied to the brand-name sites of the Internet like America Online, Microsoft's MSN, Yahoo and Amazon.com. "We are by and large invisible to consumers, so we do need to make an extra effort," said David Zinman, vice president of marketing for Adknowledge, a company controlled by CMGI that is in the group, which has been tentatively named the Network Advertising Initiative. Kevin Ryan, president of Doubleclick Inc., another member of the group, said, "We're doing this as one step toward the broader goal of making consumers feel comfortable on the Internet." The companies started working together on voluntary privacy-protection guidelines earlier this year after prodding from the F.T.C. and the Department of Commerce. The Clinton administration has generally adopted a self-regulatory approach to Internet privacy, though it did endorse online privacy legislation for children, which was passed last fall. The unitedstates policy of self-regulation has been a sticking point in long-running trade negotiations with Europe, which has adopted a data protection law. To try to settle the dispute, David L. Aaron, the undersecretary of commerce for international trade, and the European Union's top negotiator, John Mogg, met in Washington yesterday. Their discussions will continue today. The companies in the initiative plan to announce that they have agreed to clearly notify consumers of their data collection practices and allow them to "opt out" of the profiling technology. The companies are also working with Web sites and advertisers so that their privacy policies clearly state that they are using these Internet middleman services, known as infomediaries. In addition, the host sites and advertisers should have links to the profiling companies, making it easier for users to opt out. The companies in the initiative have pledged to have their privacy practices checked by independent Internet monitors including Trustee, BBB Online and Webtrust. The group is also setting up its own Web site, www.networkadvertising.org, where consumers can read about the practices of Internet advertising and profiling companies, and opt out if they choose. Besides Doubleclick and Adknowledge, the companies initially in the group are Netgravity, a unit of Doubleclick; Adsmart and Engage Technologies, which are also controlled by CMGI; Matchlogic, a unit of Excite@home; Flycast Communications; 24-7 Media; AdForce; and Real Media. At the profiling workshop, Doubleclick says it will clarify its position on how it plans to work with Abacus Direct, an information company whose database contains the catalog-buying habits of 88 million households. In June, when Doubleclick said it would buy Abacus for $1 billion in stock, privacy groups were very worried about how Doubleclick might merge the Abacus buying data with its online profiles. Mr. Ryan said that the Abacus catalog-buying data will not be linked to Doubleclick's online profiles without clearly notifying consumers and letting them opt out. Doubleclick has met with the F.T.C., Mr. Ryan said, to discuss how that notification and choice could be clearly presented to users so they do not have to be technically sophisticated to opt out. But no final arrangements, he added, can be made until the merger closes later this month. Many key issues about online profiling technology, privacy experts say, lie in the future as the software becomes increasingly powerful. The profiling companies note that their technology identifies a user's machine through an identifying software tag on its browser. But, they add, the profiling software does not track individual users by name. Privacy advocates say that the distinction between a person's machine and the person can be a fine line at best -- and a line quickly crossed if a person buys an item online with a credit card or registers by name at a Web site. "There are a lot of serious challenges to privacy raised by the activities of these companies, which people don't have knowledge or control of," said Deirdre Mulligan, staff counsel for the Center for Democracy and Technology. Evan Hendricks, editor of Privacy Times, said, "Putting up some principles does not represent a serious effort to protect Internet privacy."   http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Free Software Sounds Alerts On Sites' Use of Personal Data
body: Amazon.com may have attracted 13 million shoppers, but how many of them really know what the company plans to do with their personal information? That is the question asked by Enonymous.com, a new company that wants to give Web surfers a more complete picture of exactly how sites plan to use their names, email addresses and any other information they collect. The company, in San Diego, is distributing a free Internet utility called Enonymous Advisor. A computer equipped with the Advisor, which can be downloaded from www.enonymous.com, detects sites that request personal information. When a fill-in-the-blank form is opened on a user's Web browser, a window pops up with information about how the site rates on consumer privacy. The ratings are based on Enonymous's evaluation of the site's privacy policies. Amazon.com, Yahoo.com and Expedia.com are among about two dozen sites receiving one star each -- the lowest rank, which means that the site may share personal data without permission. The maximum rating is four stars. Paul Capelli, a spokesman for Amazon.com, said that the company was not very concerned about the rating. The company's privacy policy states that it "does not sell, trade, or rent your personal information to others." But the next sentence continues: "We may choose to do so in the future with trustworthy third parties, but you can tell us not to by sending a blank email message to never@amazon.com." "I think our policy is clearly defined," Mr. Capelli said, "and that our customers are comfortable with it." Enonymous.com awarded four stars to sites like Ebay.com, Aol.com and Hotmail.com, which share users' information only with their permission and will contact them, via email or otherwise, only with their permission. In the next year, the company plans to make money (instead of simply giving away software) by creating the online equivalent of anonymous post-office boxes for people who want to receive certain kinds of advertisements without giving out their email addresses. But in the meantime, said David Taylor, Enonymous's president and chief executive, "we're trying to define some new rules." LISA GUERNSEY http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Q & A;
Web Buying: Is It Safe?
body: Q. When you buy something online, how do they make sure credit card information is safe from computer hackers?  A. E-commerce Web sites usually use data encryption methods to ensure the safety of your financial information. When you type in your credit card number and hit the button to submit it to the company, the information is encrypted for travel across the Internet. Even if the number is intercepted, it will be scrambled and useless to most people. The site you were doing business with can decrypt the information with a special password once it arrives. There are a few ways to tell if a site is using a data encryption scheme. Many will post security notices on the home page, and your Web browser will often give you an alert message when you are entering a secure part of the site that is set up to protect your privacy. You may also notice that the U.R.L. of the page you are on begins with "https://" instead of the regular "http://" prefix. The "s" indicates that the site is using the Secure Sockets Layer protocol to encrypt your data. You may want to make sure your Web browsing software supports encryption -- most current ones do. Some browsers will display an icon of a closed padlock at the bottom of the window to indicate that the page is secure, and clicking on the lock will give you security information. J. D. BIERSDORFER  Circuits invites questions about computer-based technology, by mail to Questions, Circuits, The newyork Times, 229 West 43rd Street, newyork, N.Y. 10036-3959 or by email to QandA@nytimes.com. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Some Chinese Flexibility on Internet Seen
body: A high-ranking Chinese telecommunications official reiterated the ban on foreign investment in Internet projects today, but hinted that limited foreign participation might be possible in the future. "Our existing policy hasn't opened our telecommunications" market, said the official, Chang Xiaobing, a deputy director general at the Ministry of Information Industry. This means that foreign companies investing in Chinese Internet services or content providers now are doing so at their own risk, Mr. Chang said. "If you do that, you must be responsible for that," he told reporters at a two-day unitedstates-China telecommunications conference in San Francisco. Mr. Chang said that Internet interest is surging in China, with the number of users tripling to an estimated six million at the end of this year from two million in 1998. China's Internet service providers have long been restricted from foreign investment. But content providers such as portals sites, which offer online news, email and electronic commerce services, have fallen under a regulatory gray area, attracting millions in investment from such companies as Intel, I.B.M. and Yahoo. In September, Information Industry Minister Wu Jichuan adopted a tough line, telling reporters that foreign investment in Internet content providers had always been prohibited. The pronouncement sent chills through the industry, causing some foreign companies to redirect investments outside China or begin formulating new investment models. Many others, though, have clung to their investment plans, while some, including Yahoo, channeled money into Chinese Web sites even after Mr. Wu made his remarks. Chinese officials have said they would issue a clarification of the rules on Internet content providers by the end of the year. Today, Mr. Chang declined to provide details on the new rules or when they would be issued, but hinted that there would be room for foreign involvement. "In the future, if my government decides to open our telecommunications market," he said, "in my personal opinion I think maybe we first will open the value-added services market." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Schwab to Offer Rich Clients Access to P rivate Offerings
body: Now that anybody with an online trading account has a shot at those coveted first-time stock offerings, what do brokerage firms have left to offer exclusively to the rich? For the Charles Schwab Corporation, a firm once synonymous with discount investing, the answer is a chance to invest in companies before they sell stock to the masses. Schwab is teaming with OffRoad Capital, which connects wealthy clients with emerging companies. "You can't go to a cocktail party these days without hearing about private equity deals," said Susanne Lyons, enterprise president for Schwab Retail Client Services. "People are becoming emotionally involved with getting in on the ground floor." Schwab will offer clients who have more than $1 million invested with it free access to private stock offerings from OffRoad, which began operations in June and, like Schwab, is based in San Francisco. Federal securities laws limit participation in private stock offerings to investors with a net worth of at least $1 million because the deals are highly risky. The move is Schwab's latest attempt to cater to wealthy investors, who traditionally have been clients of brokerage firms like Merrill Lynch & Company and Goldman Sachs Group. Ms. Lyons said that Schwab had "tens of thousands" of customers with more than $1 million in their accounts. OffRoad has raised only $10 million in two offerings so far, said Stephen D. Pelletier, the company's chairman and chief executive. But he expects the pace to quicken now that it has formed an alliance with BancBoston Robertson Stephens, an investment bank known for financing emerging companies. Mr. Pelletier said he saw Schwab as an ideal partner because it "has aggregated more self-directed high-net-worth investors than anyone." OffRoad finds private companies seeking $3 million to $15 million in second-stage, or so-called mezzanine, financing. It screens these companies and electronically presents information about them to prospective investors. After reading about the companies and interviewing management -- either over the Internet or live in a San Francisco TV studio -- investors decide how many shares they want at the offering price. The minimum investment is $25,000; clients are not obligated to invest in any deals. OffRoad's "openness" fit with Schwab's business model, Ms. Lyons said. "It's online," she said. "It's immediate. It's very fair." Ms. Lyons said that the low cost of entry into OffRoad's deals was enticing because even wealthy investors are inclined to spread their bets. "Some of these companies will do well," she said. "Some won't." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Trying to Turn Stocks Into a National Pastime
body: Three years ago, corporate America thought that the mostly male audience watching the World Series aspired to drive Chevy pickup trucks, shave with Gillette's razors and drink Coors beer -- judging by the amount of money that was spent on expensive ad time to promote those brands. This year, General Motors still hopes World Series fans will buy trucks and Anheuser-Busch expects that they will quaff lots of Bud. But if ad spending in the series between the newyork Yankees and the Atlanta Braves is any indication, millions of baseball fans are mainly angst-ridden about which of the Internet brokerage firms they should use to trade stocks. On-line investment firms, many of which did not exist two years ago, have collectively bought more World Series ad time than any other industry, displacing even G.M., the marketing monolith of sports, according to people who placed the ads. During nearly every inning break and throughout the pregame shows, FMR's Fidelity is pitching its offerings against E*Trade or Merrill Lynch, with Datek and Ameritrade also vying for a slice of baseball fans' household income. The spending binge is part of the investment world's attempt to turn stock trading into a new national pastime, perhaps with room for baseball, too. The number of Americans who own stock has soared to just below half, according to a recent survey. The richest investors also seem to have developed a passion for talking and trading stocks and outsmarting the market -- turning investing itself into a sport, or, some critics say, a wager. "Stock trading for some people is a serious activity, and for some it's legal gambling," said Todd Gitlin, a professor of culture, journalism and sociology at newyork University. "These brokerage firms are the house." That house has gotten a little crowded. More and more investors are trading stocks on their own, but they are spoiled for choices about where to do so. About 130 Internet brokerage firms are competing for a universe of on-line traders that now numbers about 10 million. Large brokerage firms, many of which have never tried to sell their services during mass-market events like the World Series or the Super Bowl before, are trying to make sure they are not left behind. "Stock investing is more a part of the American mainstream than it's ever been," said Stephen Cone, head of consumer marketing at Fidelity Investments and one of this year's biggest World Series advertisers. "It's water-cooler conversation. We want to be heard along with everyone else." The on-line brokerage companies, and their off-line rivals, are in a vicious fight for market share that happens to have heated up this fall. Many of the large investment companies have in recent weeks announced that they will double or in some cases triple their ad spending to get their message out. They are collectively expected to devote $1.5 billion over the next year on marketing, more than companies spend to promote Coke, Pepsi, Miller Lite and Tylenol combined. None of the companies would say how much they are spending on the World Series alone. Baseball and NBC, the network owned by General Electric that is carrying the series, are the beneficiaries. Network executives have had their hands full placing all the ads in time slots that are not back to back. The idea of exclusivity -- sole sponsor of the pre-game show, for example -- has gone the way of full stock trading commissions. Even the newyork Stock Exchange sees sports and Wall Street as natural allies. The exchange, which is preparing to become a public company itself in the near future, has hired a bevy of high-price sports talent, including Sammy Sosa, the Chicago Cubs home-run slugger, to promote the theme that the Big Board is "at the center of the sports universe." The paradox is that baseball, compared with golf, tennis and even football, is everyman's sport. Its loyal fans are more ethnically diverse, more male and less likely to have a fat investment portfolio than those of other leading sports, advertisers say. Moreover, the stock market is not as red hot as it was early in the year, and on-line brokerage accounts are not growing as fast. So why the rush? E*Trade, one of the first Internet brokerage firms, made a splash by buying expensive air time on the World Series last year. Its account growth soared not long after. E*Trade has since increased its ad spending to $350 million for fiscal 2000 from $250 million the year before. The new level is roughly what Burger King spends to promote it brand name. Now, Charles Schwab, Ameritrade and some old-line brokerage firms, including Merrill Lynch and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, are trying to match E*Trade's marketing blitz. "Money is just flooding in as people want to build brand awareness," said Len Short, head of marketing for Schwab, which has bought some advertising slots from local stations during the World Series but is not a national sponsor. "Most of it, frankly, is uneconomical. Prime time does not give you bang for the buck. But with all the noise people are trying to create momentum." Fans are a little overwhelmed. On a television hanging from the ceiling at the Carriage House of Sports in Brooklyn, Penn and Teller, the celebrity magicians who promote Fidelity's on-line trading service, compete for attention with loud conversation and the clack of balls on the bar's pool table during Game 2. Adam Bertapelle, 25, is a devoted Yankees fan but no active trader. "I just blank it out," he said of the brokerage advertising. "I don't know anyone who has enough loose money lying around to bet on stocks." At Park Avenue Country Club, a Manhattan sports bar where an attendant stands guard in the marble restroom, the ads are closer to their target. Scott Kephart, 36, who works for a computer networking company, has an E*Trade account and trades stocks every week. "They are going after everyone with income. They're trying to say anyone can do it, just try," he said, just after a World Series commercial break featuring Merrill's pitch for its overhauled brokerage service. Owning stock is becoming a normal thing for the majority of Americans, said Mr. Gitlin, the newyork University professor. But the majority of people who hold stock, often in mutual funds, do not trade very often. He said he thought that the brokerage firms were capitalizing on broader stock ownership to inculcate a culture of trading. "If owning stock is normal, why can't trading be normal?" he said. He added, however, that the firms appeared to be fighting for a relatively small percentage of Americans who have enough money to invest significant amounts in relatively high-risk trading accounts. Whether the costly ads ever pay off in terms of new on-line trading accounts is questionable, many in the industry acknowledge. They consider World Series advertising to be brand promotion, not carefully focused marketing. And, with the tumult in the financial world resulting from the rise of the Internet, some of the advertisers are talking as much to Wall Street, and even to their own employees, as much as to potential customers. The subtext is that with all the change going on in the industry, they are here to stay. Merrill is an example. The largest traditional brokerage house, Merrill is simultaneously promoting its own new on-line offering and seeking to reassure customers, and its own brokers, that the old way of doing business with the company is not about to disappear. "This is the best place right now to put out a mass message, and that's important to us," said Charles V. Mangano, senior director for brand management at Merrill. "We are reinforcing the message with the press, our employees, the analysts who cover our company. They all watch the World Series." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A Merrill Lynch commercial features an employee reassuring a customer that things will stay the same, despite changes like on-line trading. (pg. C9)

title: In High Technology, the Grind Evolves
body: In May 1994, Jeff Treuhaft, 25, joined a little Silicon Valley start-up called Mosaic, later to be renamed the Netscape Communications Corporation. The pace was brutal -- 18 hours a day, seven days a week in the early months -- but the work was exhilarating. "The really tough part was that my son was 9 weeks old when I started at Netscape," he recalled. Five years later, Mr. Treuhaft has two more children and a tidy nest egg from the sale of Netscape this year to America Online. Like many former Netscape executives, he is stepping back from the front lines of the Internet business, working part time as an investor and adviser to a few start-ups. Suddenly, Mr. Treuhaft finds himself free to play with his children, feed them lunch, even tag along on a school field trip to the pumpkin patch down the road. "It seems mundane stuff," he said, "but when you finally get a chance to do it, you appreciate it." At Microsoft, Netscape's main rival in the infamous Internet browser battle, some have made similar personal choices. Brad Silverberg, a former senior vice president, took a sabbatical in the summer of 1997 to decompress after directing Microsoft's hurried march to catch up and then gain leadership in the Internet software business. He took a solo bicycle trip through the Canadian Rockies, spent time with his wife and two children and thought about all the personal things that had been shunted aside for work. "Time is the one thing you cannot get back," said Mr. Silverberg, 45, who now works part time as an investor and adviser to start-ups. The trade-off choices made in so many American households of personal life versus work, time versus money, are magnified in the Internet economy. The time pressure is so intense because a lead of just a few weeks or months over a rival can be a huge competitive advantage in the Internet land rush. And the financial rewards for the front-runners can be astronomical. Still, if the Internet is going to be a transforming technology, like electricity, it must spread throughout the economy and society, as it finds new uses and new customers.
