title: Morgan Stanley to Offer On-Line Trading toAll Its Customers
body: In old-line Wall Street's latest entry into the Internet stock-trading bazaar, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter is preparing to introduce an overhaul of its brokerage business and to offer all its clients the option of buying and selling stocks on line at discount prices. The plan, expected to be announced as early as this week, is similar to an offering put forward in June by Merrill Lynch & Company, the country's largest brokerage house. But Morgan Stanley hopes to ambush Merrill by giving all its customers an on-line trading option immediately, beating Merrill's planned start date by at least six weeks, people close to Morgan Stanley said. Morgan Stanley already operates Discover Brokerage Direct, an on-line discount broker. Its new plan envisions eliminating Discover as a separate unit and rolling it together with traditional brokerage services provided by Morgan Stanley's 11,000 full-service brokers. Renamed Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Online, the electronic service will be available either a la carte, for $29.95 a trade, or as part of a full-service brokerage account that carries an annual fee based on assets. The firm will also take a page from Charles Schwab, the leading on-line broker, by converting the 450 nationwide branch offices where its brokers work into walk-in retail centers. All its brokerage customers will be able to deposit checks, research stocks, get a consultation or meet with their broker, people close to Morgan Stanley said. A spokesman for the firm declined to comment on any aspect of the plan. "Morgan Stanley thinks it is really going to be a game of segmenting the market going forward," said Steve Galbraith, an analyst with Sanford C. Bernstein & Company, who said he had heard an outline of the planned overhaul. "They think you have to be able to cater to all segments of the wallet." The move marks a significant strategic shift by Morgan Stanley that carries several risks. By offering its full-service customers the option of trading on line for a fraction of the price they pay in commissions now, Morgan Stanley may suffer a sizable drop in the revenue it gets from commissions, at least in the short term. Discover brokerage clients will also be slapped with a rare price increase in the ultra-competitive on-line brokerage business, where Discover has already been losing market share. At $29.95, Morgan Stanley has set its new on-line commissions to match Schwab and Merrill, making that the high-end benchmark. Discover Brokerage Direct has been charging $14.95 for most stock trades, already higher than the $5 to $8 commissions of rock-bottom on-line discounters. People close to Morgan Stanley said that the firm expects Discover -- famous for its get-rich-instantly ads featuring a tow-truck driver who owns a tropical island and a schoolboy who flies his own helicopter -- to lose some of its on-line customers when it doubles the cost of trading. But they said many others would pay the higher commissions because Morgan Stanley will now offer them an enriched selection of its stock research and more access to initial public offerings of issues underwritten by its blue-chip investment bank. "They will pay more, but they will get more," one person close to the firm said. Morgan Stanley was the first traditional Wall Street firm to dip its toes in the waters of on-line retail stock trading when it bought Lombard Brokerage, a small San Francisco-based company, in 1996. But it held the operation at arm's length, naming it after its Discover credit card and never integrating it with the firm's much larger full-service operation. Though some Discover customers have had access to Morgan Stanley's highly valued stock research, for example, Morgan Stanley took its name off the research reports and made them available on line after a delay to avoid angering full-service brokers and customers. Morgan Stanley spent tens of millions of dollars promoting the Discover brokerage business on television, in print and on line in recent years. That investment seemed predicated in part on the belief that on-line stock trading was a separate subset of the brokerage business. Like Merrill Lynch, however, Morgan Stanley has found that on-line stock trading is more fundamental than that, forcing it to overhaul its operations sooner and more completely than its executives had envisioned only a year ago. People close to Morgan Stanley said that the firm was most worried about the rapid growth of Schwab, which combines inexpensive on-line trading with efficient call centers and help lines and has lured customers away from all the major brokerage firms. In some ways Morgan Stanley's overhaul is similar to one that Merrill announced June 1 and expects to finish introducing on Dec. 1. But Morgan Stanley is hoping to steal Merrill's thunder with its coming announcement because it thinks it can offer all its retail brokerage customers access to Discover's on-line trading platform immediately, while Merrill promoted its plan months before it had prepared the technology to offer the service. People close to Morgan Stanley also said that the firm expected its plan would cause less internal dissent than was the case at Merrill, where an unusually large number of brokers have defected to rivals since the firm announced its new on-line trading platform and pricing structure. The key, these people said, is that Morgan Stanley will offer a broad array of pricing options that gives brokers more discretion in how much they charge each customer. For an asset-based fee of at least $1,500 a year, Merrill Lynch is offering unlimited trading of stocks and bonds either through its brokers or on line. Merrill also said it would introduce an on-line trading service called Merrill Lynch Direct, with individual trades for $29.95. Some Merrill brokers have rebelled because the new pricing structure reduces how much they make from some of their accounts. Morgan Stanley has addressed that issue by allowing brokers to negotiate prices with customers who want some combination of self-directed on-line trading and help from a broker. Customers who want such a combination will be charged a percentage of the money they invest with the firm that ranges from less than a half-percent to 2 percent a year. The fees will vary based on the amount of assets and the discretion of the broker involved. Customers who want to trade online with little or no help from a broker will be charged $29.95 a trade. Full-service customers who do not want to trade on line will still have the option of paying higher commissions for broker-directed trading, as they have in the past. Morgan Stanley's announcement puts fresh pressure on other full-service brokerage houses to make on-line trading available to all customers who want it. But some rivals say they are not planning to offer deeply discounted stock trading. The Salomon Smith Barney unit of Citigroup, for example, is planning to introduce on-line trading by early next month. But the service will be offered only to customers in fee-based or traditional brokerage accounts, not at a discount. Another traditional brokerage firm, Paine Webber Group, is introducing an account that allows clients who invest at least $100,000 and pay an annual fee to make as many trades as they want, either on line or through their brokers. But Paine Webber has not set up a separate on-line-trading service. Paine Webber executives stressed that their new account, called Insight One, gave brokers more "flexibility" in pricing brokerage services than Merrill is allowing its brokers. Donald Marron, Paine Webber's chief executive, said the firm kept about $1 annually of every $100 invested with it, and he did not expect that ratio to decline because of the new account. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING: DIARY;
The March Continues Toward 24-Hour Trading
body: E*Trade Group, the on-line broker, plans to let its customers trade round the clock within the next two years. "We are working within the next 12 to 24 months for round-the-clock trading," said Christos M. Cotsakos, the chief executive. Mr. Cotsakos said E*Trade, which already offers after-hours trading, would expand its hours gradually. It is likely to introduce its new trading session two hours before the regular market opens at 9:30 A.M. Eastern time, he said. "It'll be sometime in the new year," he said. Since early September, E*Trade has offered after-hours trading between the regular market close of 4 P.M. and 6:30 P.M., routing orders through Instinet, an electronic stock matching system owned by Reuters Group. Mr. Cotsakos said E*Trade also planned to use a competing system, Archipelago, sometime in the new year, once the size of the after-hours trading volume justified such a move. Many on-line brokers have begun to offer after-hours trading through trading systems better known as electronic communications networks, or E.C.N.'s, a move that has forced the newyork Stock Exchange and Nasdaq, operated by the National Association of Securities Dealers, to consider expanding their hours. But the relatively small trading volume after the market close has raised doubts about its feasibility, let alone profitability. E*Trade, of Menlo Park, Calif., has a stake in Archipelago and is considering investing in one or more E.C.N.'s, according to Mr. Cotsakos. "We are looking at everything," he said, without elaborating. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MARKET INSIGHT;
Schwab Counters A Pincers Movement
body: THE Charles Schwab Corporation, a pioneer of discount stock brokerage and even cheaper on-line brokerage, is getting it from all sides these days. After staking out a position between low-cost electronic trading shops and traditional brokerage firms, Schwab finds that both ends are moving toward the middle: Deep discounters like E*Trade Group are adding services for investors, while full-service firms like Merrill Lynch are offering on-line trades at a discount. The brewing storm of competition has frightened investors out of Schwab's stock, which has fallen more than 60 percent from its high in April, to $28.4375 on Friday. In an interview last week, Richard K. Strauss, an analyst at Goldman Sachs Group, talked about Schwab's predicament, its prospects and why he thinks it will hit $50 within a year. Here are excerpts from the conversation:  Q. Why did Schwab go from being a darling to getting dumped so quickly?  A. Schwab's stock tends to go through a bad period once every couple of years. Typically, the cause is that Schwab is transforming itself, facing a new competitor or there's a slowdown that is either seasonal or cyclical. Those tend to be the things that change the fortunes of Schwab's stock. However, the company has an incredible track record of making those downdrafts into buying opportunities.  Q. Which of those usual suspects is the culprit holding down Schwab's stock this time around?  A. This right now is more of a seasonal slowdown. But it's also a smoke screen of sorts from other E-brokers who are talking about adding accounts but not talking about growing assets profitably.  Q. Those competitors certainly are talking -- and advertising -- plenty. Isn't Schwab going to have to match the huge ad budgets of these upstart firms?  A. If you look at E*Trade and Ameritrade combined, their marketing budget next year is going to be well over $500 million. That's more than double what Schwab will be spending. Schwab has over $600 billion in customer assets. E*Trade and Ameritrade combined have no more than $50 billion. The economics speak for themselves.  Q. But by doing all that advertising and price-cutting, aren't they putting pressure on Schwab's profit margins?  A. Not necessarily. Look at what Schwab has done in 1999. They have brought in $75 billion of net new money and their profit margin during that period has averaged close to 15 percent of revenue, which is the highest their margin has ever been. Of the $75 billion they've brought in, $25 billion came in this summer during a slowdown that really was a stealth bear market.  Q. How long can they keep up that pace of gathering assets in the face of increasing competition late in a long bull market?  A. Schwab's customer-asset base has gone from $7 billion to $600 billion in 12 years. There have been some pretty hairy markets during that time but Schwab has continued to take in assets during those periods of turmoil. The company's profits have been growing 35 to 40 percent a year. My growth projection for them now is 25 to 30 percent. Even with the seasonal slowdown this summer, their earnings should be up close to 60 percent this year. My forecast for their long-term growth is higher than it's ever been.  Q. Is the new money rolling into Schwab in bigger or smaller chunks?  A. The average new account they're bringing in starts out with $44,000 and that's 42 percent bigger than their new accounts were last year. The company's average account size now is about $100,000. That's the kind of account that a full-service broker like Merrill Lynch would be going after.  Q. Speaking of Merrill Lynch, that firm is about to offer on-line trades for $29.95 each, the same price Schwab charges. How much of a threat is that to Schwab?  A. Financial services is an incredibly fragmented industry. Merrill has $1.5 trillion of customer assets but that's only about 3 percent of the total investable assets in the U.S. The moves that Merrill is making have been painful for Merrill in the short term. But if anyone has the capital and the staying power to compete with Schwab, it's not the E-brokers, it's the full-service brokers. It will depend on how quickly they can get their cost structure down so they can continue to offer great service but at a better price.  Q. So Schwab is being smart in positioning itself as an alternative to the traditional brokers rather than competing against the little guys on price?  A. Schwab is competing with anyone who is trying to gather assets. In the asset-gathering world, it's getting more and more difficult to accumulate assets, in part because there are so many competitors and partly because more people are choosing to do it themselves. To a large degree, Schwab has enabled and empowered that trend. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Richard Strauss

title: Schwab Profit Rises; Trading Decreases
body: The Charles Schwab Corporation, the No. 1 unitedstates discount and Internet brokerage firm, said yesterday that its third-quarter profit rose 27 percent from the period a year earlier, but it processed fewer stock trades than earlier in 1999 because of unsettled financial markets. Schwab, a San Francisco-based broker with 6.3 million clients, earned $124.5 million, or 15 cents a diluted share, matching forecasts. That compared with $97.8 million, or 12 cents a share, in last year's third quarter, when financial-market turmoil battered profits at most unitedstates brokerage firms. Schwab's stock price gained $1.875 yesterday, closing at $29.9375 on the newyork Stock Exchange. The stock fell $3.6875, or 1.1.6 percent, ahead of the results on Wednesday and has lost more than half its value from a high of $77.50 in April. The latest results are a decline from Schwab's record first-half results. As well as having made fewer trades, it opened fewer accounts in the recent quarter than in the first two quarters of 1999. Compared with 1998, though, it showed gains in these two key measures of an on-line brokerage operation. Schwab processed 175,400 trades a day in the third quarter, up from 141,900 a year earlier but down from 200,000-plus a day in the first two quarters of the year. It opened 282,000 accounts, slightly up from 278,400 a year earlier but down sharply from 421,900 new accounts in the second quarter. http://www.nytimes.com

title: A Plan for Trading on Wireless Phones
body: An on-line brokerage firm, the Ameritrade Holding Corporation, and Sprint PCS Group, the nation's largest all-digital wireless telephone network, said today that they had forged an agreement that would enable their customers to trade on line over the wireless network of Sprint PCS, a unit of the Sprint Corporation. The agreement will also let customers of the companies get access to their investment accounts and receive stock information on the Sprint PCS Wireless Web. The two-way transaction service is the first of its kind through wireless phones and is expected to be available in late October. Customers of Sprint PCS, which is based in Kansas City, Mo., who have an Internet-ready Sprint PCS phone will be able to get access to their Ameritrade account at no extra charge as part of any Sprint PCS Wireless Web service plan -- starting at less than $10 a month when added to an existing voice plan of $29.99 and higher. Once an Ameritrade account is called over a Sprint PCS phone, all Ameritrade fees apply in the same manner as if a customer were using a desktop computer for standard on-line brokerage services -- now $8 for each stock-market order. Sprint PCS operates the largest 100 percent digital, 100 percent PCS nationwide wireless network, serving more than 4,000 communities. http://www.nytimes.com

title: TD Waterhouse Shifts Electronic Networks
body: The TD Waterhouse Group, which pulled out of a deal last week to invest $25 million in Island, an alternative stock-trading system, said this week that it would invest in Redibook, one of Island's rivals. John Chapel, president of Waterhouse's unitedstates brokerage operations, said that Waterhouse, the No. 3 Internet brokerage firm in the unitedstates, chose Redibook over Island because it was impressed with the caliber of the investors lined up behind the firm. Island and Redibook, computer systems that match up stock orders automatically and electronically, are known as electronic communications networks, or E.C.N.'s. In May, Waterhouse said it would pay $25 million for a 12.5 percent stake in Island, which is owned by Datek Online Holdings, the No. 4 Internet brokerage firm. Redibook attracted attention late in July, when it announced three new investors: the Charles Schwab Corporation, the Fidelity Investments unit of the FMR Corporation and Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. Waterhouse, a unit of the Toronto-Dominion Bank that trades separately, last week became the second investor to scrap a deal with Island, in part because executives clashed on the value of the 12.5 percent stake. Vulcan Ventures, which is led by a Microsoft co-founder, Paul Allen, withdrew from a planned $25 million investment in Island in June. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Business Travel;
On-line reservation systems appear poised to shake up the traditional travel agent business.
body: TO a visitor, Los Angeles can seem like Queens with dazzling sunlight -- a vast, bewildering, high-density commercial and residential expanse where navigation is aided by the fact that the buildings are low enough to allow you to spot the topographical landmarks and aim the car at least at a known point on the compass. That's the Los Angeles most tourists know, and finding a suitable hotel there is a cinch. But the Los Angeles where many business travelers end up -- downtown, off in the east-central part of the city -- is a very different place where giant glass skyscrapers cluster, as if for security, on high ground above a derelict business district that hasn't seen good times since Harlow was an ingenue. Here, the streets are dark and eerily empty at night and it's a long way to Beverly Hills or Westwood. As a consequence, choosing from among the many good downtown hotels becomes a little more personal, since you're more likely to be confined to quarters longer and dependent on the hotel's individual services and characteristics. To nut-shell the point, as they say on the other side of town: here you want to choose your hotel deliberately, and not on some vague recommendation from a travel agent. So in making arrangements for a business trip that required a four-night stay in downtown Los Angeles last week, I tried out Travelocity. That service is about to surpass Expedia from Microsoft's as the largest Internet travel-booking service after its parent, Sabre Group, completes plans to spin it off into a separate publicly traded company. Sabre is the reservation system controlled by AMR, which also owns American Airlines. The site (travelocity.com) was easy to use, if you paid attention. I was pretty specific about what I wanted for a stay during which both my wife and I would be conducting separate business. No convention hotels. No brassy 1,500-room joints with soaring atriums and splashing fountains. No venerable old hotels with elaborate public spaces downstairs and rooms upstairs that evoke the Y.M.C.A. Within 15 minutes on line at Travelocity, I had evaluated more than a dozen hotels and booked what turned out to be an excellent choice, the Wyndham Checkers, a small luxury hotel with gloriously quiet rooms, large marble bathrooms, impeccable service (you can specify which newspapers you want left at your door, if you don't choose to have the ubiquitous USA Today foisted on you first thing in the morning), and jiffy-fast valet parking. The on-line price: $209 a night, slightly below the rack rate and competitive with other quality hotels in the neighborhood. While booking it, I felt as if I was in control to a degree that I'd never been while selecting a hotel in an unfamiliar location. The Travelocity site provided accurate data and -- this is important, in the endless galaxy of Web travel hype coming from who knows where -- credible information, including customer evaluations from the trusted Zagat survey Could a travel agent have arranged the same thing to my specifications? Possibly, but only if I were a preferred customer deserving of a lot of time and attention. What does this say to the travel agent business? It says, stand by for heavy rolls, mates. After a fitful start, the on-line travel marketplace is finding firm footing as people become adept at using the Internet and as personal computers achieve greater household penetration. They're in 38.8 percent of unitedstates households this year, three times the figure of 1995, according to Forrester Research Inc. Consumer fears about on-line credit card security have been the biggest bugaboo for the rapidly expanding Internet travel industry, but this is changing. In surveys, Forrester Research found that 53 percent of on-line respondents last July said they felt secure using credit cards on the Internet, up from 15 percent in early 1998. Among those who don't use the Internet, however, there is overwhelming distrust of the idea of on-line credit card purchases. Industry officials believe that smart customers, including business travelers who book their own trips, will increasingly take their business to on-line booking sites. Within two years, the industry "will be generating about $20 billion in sales," said Phillip C. Wolf, president and chief executive of PhoCusWright, an on-line travel industry research company. Travel sites like Travelocity and Expedia that establish themselves as trusted brands will dominate this new market and furiously shake the foundations of the traditional travel agency business, industry experts believe. The competition could become fierce, too. Earlier this month, one of the most aggressive American retail giants said that it was developing its own on-line travel site for booking airline tickets, rental cars and hotels. Wal-Mart is the name. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
At their annual meeting, large-scale marketers became more familiar with all things E-business.
body: BEG your pardon, Irving Berlin. The contention of the closing general session of the 1999 annual conference of the Association of National Advertisers was that there's no business like E-business. E-business -- as in electronic commerce, interactive advertising, electronic retailing, the new media and on-line marketing -- was the sole focus of the concluding session of the conference yesterday at the Ritz-Carlton Hotel here. The session, lasting more than three and a half hours, was notable for two reasons. One was that, according to those attending who work for interactive advertising agencies, the audience of large national advertisers seemed completely comfortable with the technical terminology the speakers used, everything from "streaming media" and "channel conflict" to "data mining" and "first-mover advantage." The second was that the session included no sponsored segments, unlike the general sessions on Sunday and Monday. The sponsorships, bought by the Conde Nast Publications unit of Advance Publications, and five national radio networks, drew complaints from many attendees for huckster-like sales pitches from the stage. In fact, the media sponsorships -- unique among ad industry annual conferences -- were the inspiration for jokes during an awards dinner Monday night. "Here we are, sponsors," said Myer Berlow, president for interactive marketing at America Online Inc., whose company co-sponsored the awards with the trade publication Advertising Age, "and we don't have a commercial." "It was great to hear Rush Limbaugh talk about something he knew about," Mr. Berlow continued, referring to the talk show host's speech during the presentation sponsored by the radio networks, "his rate card." How E-business rates with advertisers proved to be compelling content at the closing general session, which had as its moderator a newly minted "E-trepreneur": Lou Dobbs, the former CNN business news anchor who is chairman and chief executive of a fledgling Web site company, Space.com. Mr. Dobbs should not worry about his enterprise, according to the opening speaker, Robert J. Herbold, executive vice president and chief operating officer of the Microsoft Corporation, because "aggressive newcomers have created the buzz" in E-business while "incumbency has never been worth less." One reason, Mr. Herbold said, is that the goal of many new E-commerce sites is "to 'clean up the value chain' and get it direct from the source to the consumer." He cited Proflowers.com, which ships products to customers not from florist shops but from growers. "The Web is a distribution system, a medium and a marketplace," Mr. Herbold said, adding that Internet advertising will "become absolutely gargantuan" and far more creative than it is now. For instance, he suggested that marketers selling packaged-goods products of "low interest" to consumers could "revisit the marketing of the 40's and 50's when brands were sponsors of something important to people" and "become sponsors of Web sites with information of value." Michael A. Beindorf, chief operating officer of Planetrx.com, an on-line drugstore, offered rules to "contend with the 'futurity' of what is already happening today" in E-business. While "brands continue to matter," Mr. Beindorf said, "you will have to move much faster" to "put a stake in the ground and create a positioning" that will differentiate brands from one another in the minds of computer users, a benefit he described as the "first-mover advantage." The ability to measure sales more quickly and more precisely with on-line advertising means that "marketers will become accountable for expenditures and results," Mr. Beindorf said, "maybe for the first time." Accountability was the subject of a panel on channel conflict, though not the kind facing viewers torn between watching "Will and Grace" or "Dharma and Greg." Rather, the term refers to the problems confronted by marketers whose products can be sold on line as well as by brick-and-mortar retailers, who may resent the powerful new competition. "For 95 percent of our products, it doesn't make sense" to sell "directly to the consumer," Vivienne Bechtold, interactive marketing director at the Procter & Gamble Company, said. "But certain products that go to specific targets, like Pampers Preemie and coffees, there's an opportunity to sell them maybe more effectively on line, maybe through a retailer." P.& G. is planning to start a Web site, Reflect.com, that will sell customized beauty products directly to consumers. "We'll be using on-line media and off-line media to drive on-line awareness" of the site, Ms. Bechtold said. At the First Union Corporation, which signed the millionth user of its financial Web site Oct. 1, "we're getting away from the mass-marketing mindset of 'one size fits all,' " said James J. Garrity, senior vice president for marketing. Instead, he said, the company is embracing "tailored solutions differentiating consumers based on who are our most loyal, profitable customers." And the Ford Motor Company is grappling with the "huge impact" of "disintermediaries," independent Web sites that act as sales channels for new and used vehicles, according to David G. Ropes, Ford's director for corporate advertising and integrated marketing. Ford is "spending $20 million in retraining our dealers," he said, "getting connected not only through their own Web sites but through the main company site." By the end of the year, he added, 85 percent of Ford's dealers will be on line. There was also business without an "E" prefix at the conference. The advertiser association formally mothballed a much-disputed proposal, made at the annual conference last year, to invite advertising agencies to join as members. The proposal drew castigation from officials of the agency trade group, the American Association of Advertising Agencies. John J. Sarsen Jr., president and chief executive of the advertiser association, and O. Burtch Drake, president and chief executive of the agency association, said separately that officials of both groups would meet sometime early next year to discuss cooperation on two long-divisive issues: How marketers review advertising accounts and the ways marketers compensate their agencies. "Everyone's happy with that," Mr. Drake said. And attendees breathed a loud sigh of relief as the conference, which began Saturday afternoon, ended last night. When the advertiser association held its annual conference here in October 1996, a rare Florida northeaster washed out all outdoor activities, confining attendees inside. This time, by contrast, the weather was as sunny as, well, the outlook for E-business. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Biggest Nasdaq Market Maker Says Its Income Will Trail Forecasts
body: The Knight/Trimark Group, the biggest Nasdaq market maker, said today that its third-quarter income would rise less than analysts had forecast because of fewer trades from Internet brokers, the company's main customers. Earnings will be 17 cents to 19 cents a diluted share, the company said, less than the 30 cents a share forecast by analysts. It earned 13 cents in the quarter a year earlier. Knight/Trimark gets about half its orders from the E*Trade Group, Ameritrade, the TD Waterhouse Group and other Internet brokers, whose trades fell 5 to 10 percent in the third quarter, the first such decline, according to Hambrecht & Quist. On-line investors traded less because of a slump in the Internet stocks they favor. "The first and second quarters were the high-water mark of the confluence of on-line trading and Internet stocks," said Kenneth Pasternak, Knight/Trimark's chief executive. "In the third quarter, we came down to levels that were sustainable. It was difficult to guide analysts down because you don't know when the bubble's burst until it already happened." Shares of Knight/Trimark, based here, fell $3.61 today, or 12 percent, to $26.375. They traded as low as $25, a seven-month low. The company first sold stock to the public in July 1998 at a price, adjusted for a 2-for-1 stock split in May, of $7.25 a share. The stock price reached its peak on May 11 at $81.625, the day before the split. Today, Mr. Pasternak, referring to "the bubble of the last few quarters that created unreasonable expectations" that revenue would double every year, said, "We're confident that we can continue to grow at 30 to 50 percent a year." Knight/Trimark says it expects its revenue for the third quarter to increase 49 percent, to about $138 million. That would still be down 38 percent, from $224 million in the second quarter. Trades executed in the third quarter rose 95 percent compared with those a year earlier, to 20.4 million. That was down from second-quarter trades of 21.5 million. http://www.nytimes.com

title: I.B.M. to Take Part in Alliance With Other Computer Giants To Better E-Commerce Security
body: I.B.M., the world's largest computer company, said today that it would become part of an industry alliance to create better security for electronic-commerce transactions. In addition to I.B.M., the Trusted Computing Platform Alliance includes the Compaq Computer Corporation, the Hewlett-Packard Company, the Microsoft Corporation and the Intel Corporation. The alliance's purpose is to develop a universal standard for equipment and software so that technology companies can make personal computers more secure, I.B.M. said. "It's good that there's that many vendors involved," said Roger Kay of the International Data Corporation. "The agreement favors the average PC user in terms of giving them control over distribution of their information and greater comfort in doing E-business." Business-to-business trade on the Internet is expected to increase to $1.3 trillion in 2003 from $43 billion last year, according to Forrester Research. Alliance members said the agreement makes sense as more consumers buy goods and services on the Internet. "We see E-business expanding, and PC's are a critical piece of that expansion," said Alan Hodel, a Compaq spokesman. "As PC's evolve, the standards for security need to evolve with them." PC users will benefit most directly from the alliance's efforts, Mr. Kay said. "This gives the user a greater degree of assurance that the transaction they were doing wasn't being snooped, and they'll be more comfortable moving their business to the Internet," he said. Mr. Kay predicts that other companies, like the Dell Computer Corporation, may join the alliance. "Dell sounded like they'd go along with it," he said. A spokesman for Dell, based in Round Rock, Tex., was not immediately available to comment. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Easing on Software Exports Has Limits
body: When the Clinton Administration recently announced plans to relax restrictions on exports of data-scrambling software, a key issue that escaped notice was that the new policies affect only shrink-wrapped software, not the original source code -- the lines of instructions that programmers actually write. When it comes to source code, the Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration, William A. Reinsch, said last week that, "nothing has changed." The exclusion of source code from the relaxed rules threatens to constrain software developed under the so-called open-source model, most notably the Linux operating system, an upstart competitor to Microsoft's Windows. Linux and other open-source programs are created by loose-knit coalitions of programmers around the world who exchange source codes. Many of these teams have developed unusually error-free software in part because access to the source code allows each programmer to find colleagues' mistakes, improve on a program's efficiency, offer fixes for bugs and add new features. Before software written in any of today's more sophisticated programming languages can run on a computer, it must be compiled, a process that translates the text of the source code into combinations of ones and zeros that can be understood by a microprocessor. Once a program is compiled, it is almost impossible to determine what the original source code was. Thus it cannot be adapted or modified by other programmers unless the source code itself is published. This happens to suit Government intelligence and law enforcement agencies, which worry that access to the source code for encryption and security software would enable terrorists, drug dealers and other criminals to devise secure communications networks that agents would not be able to monitor. Last May, Attorney General Janet Reno wrote to the German Justice Minister, Herta Daubler-Gmelin, asking for her help in writing new regulations to control the proliferation of the source code for encryption software that is distributed over the Internet. Paradoxically, the Government is increasingly turning to open-source software to build secure communications networks that protect Government secrets or citizens' privacy. Of particular note is a cousin of Linux known as OpenBSD, which is popular in Government agencies because its development team conducted unusually rigorous security audits to anticipate and plug holes that attackers might use to gain entry. While it might seem logical that the hidden code in compiled software would offer greater security than code anyone can read, many security experts argue that the opposite is true. Open source, they say, is ultimately more secure because the people writing security software know exactly how the systems they are protecting run. Theo de Raadt, the leader of the OpenBSD development team, said last week that his group's software had been bought by many Government laboratories and agencies. "I went down a list," he said, "and it includes hundreds of them." He refused to name the agencies but said it was fair to assume that the list included some of the Government's most security-conscious operations. OpenBSD is also used as the basis for many security applications. For example, Network Flight Recorder, based in Washington, makes a device that monitors activity on a network, watching for packets of data that suggest suspicious or forbidden activity. The problem is that by the Government's definitions, OpenBSD is foreign software. Mr. de Raadt lives in Calgary, Alberta, and he uses many Canadian programmers to add security enhancements. He said that the more liberal rules of the Canadian Government made it possible for his team to pursue absolute security without fear that the Government would regulate it. The OpenBSD CD-ROM bears a label boasting, "Made in Canada, Land of Free Cryptography." Yet the Internet and software development defy the notion of national boundaries. OpenBSD originated at the University of California at Berkeley (the BSD stands for Berkeley software distribution). Mr. de Raadt led the push to increase the security by adding software in Canada that could not be exported by developers in the unitedstates. Even so, several key security enhancements came from programmers in the unitedstates. For example, the Naval Research Lab in Virginia is using OpenBSD as a foundation of its new IPv6 project, an attempt to increase the security of both the Internet in general and the secure parts of the global network used by the military. No open-source development can be a made-in-America project. The Naval Research Lab's Web page thanks several Italians who contributed some of the source code that works with OpenBSD. Thus, the Navy's project is built with Italian enhancements to a Canadian product that was born in a unitedstates university. What is more, it is likely that the software contains pieces of code contributed by programmers in Finland, Germany, Eastern Europe, Russia, Australia, India, Mexico and other countries. Many security professionals argue that the nationality of a piece of source code is irrelevant, that what matters is achieving a blend of software produced by the best minds everywhere. Gregory Perry, the chief technology officer of Network Security Technology in Herndon, Va., says that OpenBSD is the most secure operating system in the world. He added that his company already used it for many projects and was exploring commercializing the system or selling expert support. The appeal is not only security but cost. Marcus Ranum, chief executive of Network Flight Recorder, said the OpenBSD operating system enabled his engineers to read the source code, check for bugs and build a very secure tool for detecting attackers. If the Attorney General succeeds in persuading the Europeans and Canadians to shut off the flow of open-source security software, he said, "I think it would be a tragedy." But if Ms. Reno should have her way, the software industry is developing end runs. The Administration, for example, has so far declined to regulate the international movement of source code if it is printed on paper, presumably out of concern that such regulation would violate the First Amendment. Thus, several companies are already shipping printouts of their code to Europe where it is scanned into computers. When asked about the policy's impact on the development of Linux, FreeBSD, and other open-source projects that serve the Government's own needs, Mr. Reinsch, the Commerce Under Secretary, said: "It's an important question which we need to study a lot more. We don't have all of the answers." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Theo de Raadt, the leader of the OpenBSD development team, with the group's open-source software on compact disk. (Todd Korol for The newyork Times)

title:
Merrill Lynch Catches the Spirit;
A Traditional Brokerage Firm Spouts the On-Line Gospel
body: Can you teach an old bull new tricks? Merrill Lynch & Company, the world's largest brokerage firm, is about to find out, as it introduces a set of on-line services intended to transform its buttoned-down brokerage business into a force in electronic commerce. The digital version of Merrill Lynch wants to sell not just stocks and bonds, but steaks and bonbons, too. In recent weeks, Merrill has added on-line shopping and auctions to its portfolio of World Wide Web sites and the firm's executives have started using cyberspeak to describe a grand plan that sounds more at home at Amazon.com than Charles Schwab, the leading on-line brokerage firm. Merrill Lynch wants to manage "the total financial relationship" with its customers, not just their investments, said John L. Steffens, a vice chairman who heads Merrill's brokerage business. If Mr. Steffens has his way, Merrill's clients will band together and use their enormous buying power to extract the best prices from hundreds of on-line merchants for everything from champagne to diamond rings to office supplies. They will pay for all those purchases with their Merrill Lynch Visa debit cards and receive rebates in the form of points they can apply toward other purchases, air travel or for discounts on brokerage services. "We began to think of our clients as a community and this is their community membership card," Mr. Steffens said, slipping his own Signature Visa card out of his wallet and flashing it. Merrill account holders will buy about $7 billion in goods and services with their Merrill Visa cards this year, Mr. Steffens said, adding that he believes that on-line sales could help raise that total to $100 billion annually within six years. All this E-commerce talk comes less than two months before Merrill is scheduled to begin its long-anticipated leap into low-cost on-line trading, a risky move down-market that has created friction within the ranks of its 14,800 brokers and worries among the firm's shareholders. Many fear that Merrill will cannibalize its existing business by offering trades for just $29.95, the same rate Schwab charges. Indeed, when Merrill announced its on-line initiatives June 1, its stock price dropped more than 10 percent, from $84 to $75.25, and has not recovered since. Merrill shares closed yesterday at $70. Preparing for a Dec. 1 kickoff, Merrill has teams of technology specialists at two sites in central New Jersey and another in Cambridge, Mass., tuning up and testing the on-line trading service, Merrill Lynch Direct. The new service will allow Merrill customers to set up on-line accounts, log in and trade stocks, bonds, mutual funds and, eventually, more exotic securities like stock options. In the current model, one screen has a column of buttons that users click for up-to-date summaries of all their accounts or to search across them for holdings of a particular stock. Add up all these changes and you get a big, blurry picture of what customers will get from Merrill in the future, observers say. "Is Merrill trying to become an electronic-commerce company or are they still a financial-services conglomerate with a hefty focus on brokerage?" asked Henry McVey, an analyst at Morgan Stanley, Dean Witter & Company. "That's unclear. To date, what we've seen is more of a shotgun approach to the Internet, including free research, E-shopping and on-line trading." Mr. Steffens, who is 57, replies that "I didn't have a change of heart" about incorporating new technology into Merrill's brokerage operation. But he clearly is reading from a different playbook this year than last, when he made a public remark he now regrets about how on-line trading could be "hazardous" to investors' financial health. That view was consistent with Merrill's frequent pronouncements that individual investors should stick to a disciplined investment strategy and not get caught up in the day-to-day market frenzy. But it was regarded as evidence that traditional brokerage firms were blind to the changing needs of investors, who have clearly embraced on-line trading. Now, Merrill is engaged in a difficult balancing act: The firm wants to be able to claim it offers everything an active trader needs -- while generally discouraging active trading. What Merrill wants from its customers is clear: more of their assets. The firm holds about $1.5 trillion of assets belonging to about five million clients. The assets at Merrill have grown more than 15 percent annually this decade, Mr. McVey said, but that growth rate pales when compared with Schwab's pace of almost 40 percent a year. Schwab, based in San Francisco, has been taking in more than $25 billion of new money from customers every three months and losing a lot less to traditional brokers than Merrill had once predicted. "There certainly has been some graduation process," said Guy Moszkowski, an analyst at Salomon Smith Barney. "But Schwab wants to hang onto those people. Now, Merrill's saying, 'We've got to have them in-house earlier.' " The typical Merrill customer has been getting younger and wealthier, just not fast enough for the firm's taste. Many baby boomers are comfortable enough with technology and distrustful enough of stockbrokers' motives to go it alone, or with only the occasional help from firms that do not have armies of commission-hungry brokers. Merrill is introducing a raft of new services to attract those investors. Easily the most important of those changes -- despite all the attention Merrill's decision to offer on-line trading has attracted -- is the current push to convert most clients to a fee-based account Merrill calls Unlimited Advantage. These account holders -- for a pre-set cut of their assets starting at $1,500 a year -- can have access to all of Merrill's on-line services, including research by the firm's own analysts and, soon, from the Standard & Poor's Corporation. Those customers will also be able to make as many trades as they want, either electronically or through a broker. Still, other aspects of Merrill's new strategy -- like the use of technology to expand the firm's base of institutional clients and a shift away from a reliance on commissions -- are more critical to its ability to compete as an independent firm amid a consolidating industry. Indeed, compared with those changes, one person close to Merrill's top management said, the impending rollout of on-line trading "is the biggest nonevent around." More than anything else Merrill is trying, the switch to fee-based accounts heralds a transformation in the relationship between the firm's brokers and their clients. For years, Merrill has pushed its brokers to shift more customers from paying commissions for every transaction to paying an annual fee based on a small percentage of total assets. Many brokers balked because they felt they had more control of their own earnings in a commission-based system. Less than 10 percent of Merrill clients' assets are in fee-based accounts. What were once mere encouragements are now turning into dire warnings. Merrill executives routinely refer to the impending extinction of brokers who do not adopt the new approach. They laud Unlimited Advantage for aligning the brokers' interests with those of their clients, and for removing much of a broker's incentive to induce clients to make excessive and unwanted trades, a practice known as churning. "There are a lot of clients who will actually look at this account as favorable because it minimizes the potential for churning," Mr. Moszkowski, the Salomon Smith Barney analyst, said. But it also takes away some motivation for brokers to interact with clients. Once a client's assets are in-house and producing a fee, the broker's attention naturally will turn to gathering more from someone else. Mr. Moszkowski predicted that many Merrill customers, contrary to brokers' fears, will end up paying more in fees than they previously paid in commissions. That is already happening, according to Mr. Steffens. On average, Merrill now keeps about 77 cents of every $100 invested at the firm. But 55 percent of the new accounts, he said, are producing a higher return for Merrill than that. The new accounts are an opportunity for Merrill to reverse a slide in the amount it makes on its accounts, Mr. Steffens said. To illustrate the firm's predicament, Mr. Steffens drew a large X on a napkin. The downward sloping line represented the decline of Merrill's cut of the assets from 1.5 percent in 1985 -- or $1.50 of every $100. The other line depicted the rapid growth in assets from $188 billion in 1985 to its current $1.5 trillion. "We have been in a price decline for years," he said. Brokers concerned about the firm's latest price cut, Mr. Steffens contended, should focus instead on helping Merrill continue to make it up on volume. One longtime Merrill broker said he was resigned to earning 30 percent less from clients with more than $1 million in their accounts. To make up the difference, he said, he would have to spend more time prospecting for new clients and less time cultivating existing ones. Some brokers are not so accepting, though. Merrill acknowledges that the changes have driven some brokers to join competing firms. And others are complaining about what they think is a too-aggressive swing the firm has made to compete with cut-rate competitors. But Merrill says it still is attracting more seasoned and productive brokers than it is losing. One of the twists to Merrill's new approach is that it goes much farther afield than Schwab has -- particularly in its embrace of E-commerce. Long seen as an innovator among leading brokerage firms, Schwab has no plan to branch out into electronic commerce beyond its core financial-services businesses, said Daniel Leemon, a vice president who maps strategy for Schwab. "What customers on the Web don't need these days is to be inundated with offers," Mr. Leemon said. "We think that begins to dilute what the brand means to people. I don't think anyone wants to come to Schwab for an auction of their Beanie Babies." But Merrill executives are resolute about the important role the firm can play in helping customers -- including about 450,000 small businesses -- manage their daily finances. Customers care as much about saving money on their regular purchases as earning money on their investments, said Randal Langdon, who oversees Merrill's E-commerce operations. Mr. Langdon, once a top Merrill broker, beamed like a new father as he demonstrated how Merrill's new shopping Web site could track down a copy of a Harry Potter children's book for just $2.99. "That's $20 retail," he said. Merrill is already arranging discounts for business owners on office supplies, and helping them auction excess inventory over the Internet. Mr. Steffens said Merrill will consider brokering group purchases of other things business owners need, like insurance. "What we're trying to do is basically build more complete banking capabilities, so they keep bigger balances with us," Mr. Steffens said. "This is not about selling books and airline tickets; it's about building relationships." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: John L. Steffens, a Merrill Lynch vice chairman, is overseeing its shift to a brokerage model heavy with on-line features. Last month, he spoke of the move at a technology conference in San Francisco. (Peter DaSilva/Jupiter Communications)  Chart/Graph: "Bull in a Cybershop" Merrill Lynch & Company, facing intense competition from on-line brokers, is adopting a wide-ranging strategy to attract more assets by offering not just financial services but also E-commerce services to its customers. title: Datek Online's Chief Agrees To Step Down
body: Under pressure from his own management team and a group of outside investors, Jeffrey A. Citron agreed to step down yesterday as chairman and chief executive of Datek Online Holdings and to relinquish any role in the company he helped fashion into a Wall Street powerhouse. Mr. Citron, who is 29, will still be the company's largest shareholder, but Datek executives said they hoped his departure would help end some of the questions about the company, which has become the subject of a growing number of criminal and regulatory inquiries. Indeed, law enforcement officials said yesterday that they were looking into Datek and Mr. Citron as part of an investigation of Robert E. Brennan, the penny-stock promoter who has been banned from the securities industry for life. Datek executives said they were unaware of any investigation into possible ties between Mr. Brennan and Datek and Mr. Citron but added that they were cooperating with several criminal and regulatory investigations. "There's no question we want to disassociate ourselves from the past," said Edward J. Nicoll, Datek's former president and chief operating officer who was named to replace Mr. Citron as chairman and chief executive. "The company's value has been diminished as a result of the investigations. But we want to do the right thing, ethically, morally and in every way." Datek, which grew from a small Brooklyn operation into the nation's fourth-largest on-line brokerage firm, is best known on Wall Street for creating an electronic trading market called Island ECN, which matches buyers and sellers of stocks without market makers. To help finance a plan to register Island as a stock exchange, the company, now based in Edison, N.J., has recently invited outsiders to invest, opening itself to more scrutiny. In recent years the company has been the subject of investigations by the Manhattan District Attorney, the unitedstates Attorney's office in Manhattan and the Securities and Exchange Commission, for a range of possible offenses, including participation in a money-laundering scheme, illegal trading activity and fraudulent accounting practices, people close to the investigations said. Partly because of concerns about those investigations, Vulcan Ventures, the venture capital firm financed by Paul Allen, the co-founder of Microsoft, decided in July to withdraw from a planned $300 million investment in Datek. Two other companies, TA Associates of Boston and Groupe Arnault of Paris, went ahead with investments totalling $195 million. Last year, Datek dropped a planned initial public offering of stock because of similar concerns, despite widespread enthusiasm about the company's prospects. Mr. Citron, who joined Datek when he was 17 and worked his way up from clerk to day trader to chief executive in 1997, was considered a technological and trading wizard. Mr. Nicoll said that Mr. Citron "literally changed the shape of Wall Street" by helping to build a small firm into a premiere on-line brokerage house in less than a decade. Bill Burnham, a general partner at Softbank Capital Partners and a former analyst, said that Datek under Mr. Citron's leadership broke new ground on Wall Street by introducing low-cost electronic trading, thus empowering individual investors. "He's an incredibly talented guy," Mr. Burnham said. "I think he just realized that the company would benefit if he stepped aside." Mr. Citron did not return calls for comment. In a statement the company released, Mr. Citron said he was "stepping aside to let this seasoned team of professional managers lead Datek Online as it begins on an important new phase in its development." The company said that Mr. Citron would "pursue other interests." But Mr. Nicoll said that Mr. Citron's decision to step down came after more than a month of meetings with his management team and with the consultation of several of the company's large investors. Prompted by an investigation by the unitedstates Attorney's office into trading activities at Datek, top executives at Datek also conducted an internal inquiry, according to people close to the company. Datek's review shed light on Mr. Citron's relationship with Raft Investments Inc., a firm that lent money to day traders and is under inquiry by the unitedstates Attorney's office, those people said, though they declined to elaborate on what the review found. After the company's review, Mr. Citron agreed to step down. Although Mr. Citron owns about 30 percent of Datek, the company said that he entered into an agreement to turn over all his voting and management rights to the company's board. According to the pact, Mr. Citron will have no role in the company for two years. After that time, it is unclear what roles he may resume. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Jeffrey A. Citron, Datek's chairman, last year at his home in Brielle, N.J. (Steven O. Boljonis for The newyork Times)

title:
STATE OF THE ART;
Another Makeover For AOL
body: AMERICA ONLINE, the world's largest Internet service, this week announced the worldwide debut of a new version of the basic software used by its 18 million subscribers. AOL customers do not need the new software, AOL Version 5.0, but it is actually a pleasant improvement over earlier versions. It maintains AOL's traditional emphasis on ease of use instead of jazzy, cutting-edge innovation, but it does add a handful of new features intended to appeal to a Norman Rockwell audience. The new features on the AOL welcoming screen include My Calendar and My Places (right below My Weather) and, inexplicably breaking syntax, You've Got Pictures. AOL has also made changes behind the screen. It has expanded both the number and length of the screen names available to subscribers, improved its search engine for finding information, not just within AOL but also on the wider World Wide Web, and bolstered the reliability of the service to reduce the number of busy signals and broken connections. Over all, with version 5.0 America Online has succeeded in its declared attempt to "make the connected experience even more central to members' everyday lives," assuming that your life was somehow incomplete without having access to an on-line picture album and a digital calendar, plus a witty new screen name. With its new My Calendar feature, in fact, AOL goes so far as to urge subscribers to "plan your life on line!" That is essentially the same vision described last month by the closest thing America Online has to a direct rival, the MSN.com on-line service from the Microsoft Corporation, which pithily calls its new vision the Everyday Web. AOL wants to be the window through which its customers get the most current news and weather, check up-to-the-minute stock prices and investment portfolios, share letters and pictures with Grandma, search for information, find out what time Sally has to be at soccer practice, go shopping on line, play games, check Billy's school lunch menu, set up a family Web site, make plans for weekend entertainment, pursue hobbies and trade gossip and jokes with friends. Of course, if you are doing all this at standard dial-up modem speeds, you probably don't have time left in the day to have much of a life. The agenda is ambitious, but AOL 5.0 manages to pull it off with a newly redesigned welcome screen that cleverly organizes all these activities, and more, into a relatively simple and orderly rectangle. My Calendar may turn out to be the most popular new feature. It is a server-based calendar, which means the calendar does not reside on the user's own computer but rather in a giant digital brain floating in a vat of goo at AOL's headquarters, with tentacles stretching out to any computing device it can reach. Well, perhaps that is overly dramatic, but you get the idea. What it means, really, is that AOL subscribers can check their personal calendars from any computer that has an Internet connection and a Web browser. It can be checked from home, from work and on the road. Later, when AOL figures out how to do it, the personal calendar will be available on non-computer devices, like smart digital phones, pocket-size organizers or even automobile dashboard screens. AOL asserts that it will use all its skills to protect this private information from computer criminals and snoops. But I would probably not make intimate or sensitive entries like, "Tuesday 3:30 P.M.: Drive gold bullion to the bank." Because the calendar is server-based, AOL can "push" local event information, like the weather report or local music and television listings, down to the subscriber's calendar. The information is based on the user's ZIP code. But even though it had already asked for my ZIP code, My Calendar still asked me to choose my personal weather and concert choices from a long list of cities. The only explanation I can think of is that people who enter a ZIP code for Buffalo, say, are graciously being offered a chance to pretend that they can order weather from San Diego. AOL is famous for its You've Got Mail alerts, and now, for better or worse, it has added You've Got Pictures. AOL, in partnership with Eastman Kodak and a joint AOL-Kodak venture called Picturevision, wants America to throw away its shoeboxes and store photographs instead in on-line digital photo albums. People with digital cameras can easily take advantage of this new service, but so can people with conventional film cameras. Thousands of drugstore and photo finishing centers around the country will soon offer customers the choice of getting pictures back as conventional prints, as digital pictures posted directly to a private photo album on AOL, or both. The owner then can discard bad shots, order special prints and copies of the good ones, send photos to friends and relatives, and -- this is the scary part -- set up slide shows of vacation photos to share with millions of unsuspecting viewers all over the world. The You've got Pictures feature in AOL 5.0 works only with newly developed pictures. AOL says future releases of the software will enable people to upload their existing digital pictures, either from digital cameras or from scanned prints. Then there is My Places, a corner of the welcome screen where the user can set up one-click access to five favorite on-line destinations. This is something of a dud for anyone even vaguely familiar with the concept of Web bookmarks because My Places allows links only to AOL's own content. It is like being offered trips to anywhere in the world, as long as you stay in Iowa. There are many delightful places in Iowa, of course. But still. And, as mentioned here last week, AOL has a new search engine that prowls not just AOL content, but also the entire Web. Other search engines cannot search AOL content because AOL blocks them. The new AOL 5.0 software is available for Windows computers only. AOL says a Macintosh version will be available "later." A preview version of the Windows software was made available late last month. The easiest way to get the software is to wait for AOL to carpet-bomb your neighborhood with free CD-ROM disks, as it is wont to do. Those in a bigger hurry can download it from the AOL.com Web site, but beware: The basic software is a 13-megabyte bolus that takes about 40 minutes to squeeze through a 56-kilobit modem. With a slower 28.8-kilobit modem, it takes 1 hour 20 minutes. America Online is also distributing a special version of AOL 5.0 that comes with -- surprise! -- a copy of Microsoft's Internet Explorer 5.0 Web software. That is surprising because AOL owns Netscape, Microsoft's bitter rival in the Web-browser category. The AOL 5.0 with Internet Explorer 5.0 browser combo weighs in at 25 MB, so double the downloading times given above. Either way, the software is free. The catch is that it costs $4.95 to $21.95 a month to use it, depending on how much time is spent on line. Of immediate concern to all those people who have been saddled with drab AOL screen names like Bill836283 (please do not try to send email to this address -- I made it up) is that AOL has now made screen names 16 characters long, instead of 10. That will enable Bill to change his screen name to something less common, like Bill836283652049, although I suspect that he is more likely to want to change it to something like BillThePresident. Also, AOL now allows seven screen names per account instead of five, which is welcome news to large families, and to small families where everyone wants to have multiple screen names. There are many valid reasons to have more than one screen name. A person may wish to have one screen name for a home-based business and a different one for personal use, for example. But this is AOL, after all, where a quick search of member profiles reveals that more than 100 subscribers answer to "sex moron." (AOL simply stopped counting at 100.) There is reason to suspect that other subscribers may simply need the extra screen names for their multiple personalities so they can participate in on-line chat sessions with themselves. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: America Express's Web Broker To Set Sights on Wealthy Clients
body: The American Express Company said yesterday that it would turn its flagging on-line brokerage business into a new Web broker with lower commissions and free stock trades for wealthy clients later this autumn. The new unit, American Express Brokerage, will charge customers $14.95 a trade for up to 3,000 shares on each order. For customers with more than $25,000 in their accounts, orders to buy will be free, and those with account balances of more than $100,000 will pay nothing to trade. All customers will pay 3 cents a share for orders of more than 3,000 shares. The new unit will offer more mutual funds, customer service and financial planning tools than Financial Direct, American Express's existing Web brokerage business. Company officials declined to pinpoint a starting date for the new unit, other than saying this autumn. The unit will be run by the American Express Financial Advisors division in Minneapolis. For customers with more than $100,000 in their accounts, the free stock trades will come with no strings attached, unlike the $1,500 annual fee that Merrill Lynch & Company will charge customers for free on-line trades. The company hopes, though, that these clients will bring in fee income when they turn to American Express's 9,300 financial planners for other advice, American Express executives said in a conference call. "We will revolutionize the industry; the game is going to change in a big way," said Doug Lennick, an American Express executive vice president. The company will not allow these wealthy customers to buy and sell the same shares on the same day because it does not want day traders as customers, company officials said. Shares of American Express rose $3.125 yesterday, to $140.6875, after gaining 4.7 percent on Monday. American Express, which has businesses ranging from charge cards, travelers checks and mutual funds, is among a number of full-service brokerage firms that are offering on-line trading in response to customer demand and the success of Web brokers. The company, whose financial planners have two million customers, is not worried that the revamped on-line brokerage operation will alienate its advisers, American Express executives said. Officials would not say how many customers the on-line business has, saying only that the company had "several hundred thousand" brokerage customers over all.  http://www.nytimes.com
