title: Schwab to Offer Customers After-Hours T rading Session
body: The crowd at the after-hours trading post continues to grow, with Charles Schwab & Company, the largest on-line broker, announcing yesterday that it will begin offering a late stock-trading session to its on-line retail and investment advisory customers in November. The session, which initially will run from 4:30 P.M. to 7 P.M. Eastern time, Monday through Friday, makes Schwab the latest and biggest of half a dozen or so on-line brokerage firms to offer late trading. "We felt we had to begin to offer this product now or risk having a competitive advantage taken away that is inherently ours," said Lon Gorman, a vice chairman of Schwab who oversees capital markets and trading. About one-third, or two million, of Schwab's customers live on the West Coast, where regular trading currently ends at 1 P.M. local time. Customers will be able to make late-session trades through Schwab's Web site in virtually any Nasdaq stock and in shares of companies that were listed on the newyork Stock Exchange after 1979. Those shares are not subject to the Big Board's Rule 390, which prohibits trading of some stocks away from the exchange. The late session will differ from normal trading in several respects, Mr. Gorman said. To protect investors against the relative illiquidity that will result from having fewer participants in the after-hours session than in daytime trading, Schwab will accept only limit orders, which specify the maximum price a buyer is willing to pay or the minimum that a seller will accept. Trades will be executed through the Redibook electronic communication network, the electronic trading system in which Schwab is a partner with Spear Leeds & Kellogg; Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, and Fidelity Investments. Last month, Redibook joined with several other electronic trading systems in an agreement to share price information during after-hours trading. That agreement, combined with the decision by Nasdaq and the newyork Stock Exchange last week to keep their price-reporting systems open until 6:30 P.M., gave Schwab the "sense of comfort" that an after-hours trading system could operate fairly, Mr. Gorman said. Other on-line brokerage firms that have recently announced plans for late trading include Morgan Stanley Dean Witter's Discover Brokerage, E-Trade Group and Datek Online. Charles R. Schwab, the firm's chairman and co-chief executive, said in an interview that the after-hours session is one of several planned steps that could pave the way for round-the-clock trading. Mr. Schwab said the firm was considering steps that would encourage more late trading, such as offering lower trading commissions or other incentives during late hours. Such a step is "a long way out there," he said. But, he added, "I feel very comfortable that we've developed a system with the order flow, liquidity and transparency that is needed." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Travelocity Makes a Deal To Dominate Web Market
body: Travelocity, the on-line travel service, said yesterday that it would acquire a smaller rival, Preview Travel, in a deal that will vault it past Microsoft's Expedia to be the largest travel site on the Web. Travelocity is part of the Sabre Group, the reservation system that is controlled by the AMR Corporation, American Airlines' parent. Because Preview Travel is a publicly traded company, the deal would allow Sabre to spin off Travelocity as a separate company without the expense of an initial public stock offering. Other corporations have started to merge their on-line operations with Internet start-ups to create publicly held units. Sony and Time Warner, for example, merged their Columbia House record club unit with CDNow, an on-line music store. And Disney is combining its Internet assets with Infoseek, a Web search service. "It's very hard to have a dot-com company, which is valued on a multiple of revenue, inside a traditional earnings-per-share company," said Terrell B. Jones, the president of Travelocity, who will be the chief executive of the combined company. "Every dollar you invest in Travelocity reduces Sabre's earnings." Travelocity and Preview said the deal would probably close early next year after expected shareholder and Government approval. Sabre will own 70 percent of the combined company, which will use the Travelocity name, and the existing holders of Preview stock will own 30 percent.  Before the deal was announced, Preview had a market capitalization of $243 million, giving the combined company a value of $810 million. The price of Preview's shares rose by 38 percent yesterday, to $24.3125. Preview, which was founded 15 years ago to create television programs about travel, became one of the earliest publicly traded e-commerce companies with an initial public offering in November 1997. Its stock price hit $39 in August 1998 but has languished ever since. In the second quarter of 1999, Travelocity sold $170 million worth of travel services and Preview sold $90 million. Preview's revenue from commissions and other sources in the second quarter was $7.3 million. "The story has been Travelocity and Expedia running neck and neck, with the other players falling further and further behind," said Philip Wolf, chief executive of Phocuswright, a consulting firm that specializes in on-line travel services. "The big guys have a new enhancement each week and the smaller players can't keep up." As Expedia and Travelocity won the bulk of the mainstream travel business -- airline, hotel and car reservations -- Preview increasingly focused on package tours and cruises. It also offers travel planning information and sells advertising space on those pages. Mr. Jones said Travelocity hoped to expand its package tour and cruise business and add advertising clients. It will keep offices in Fort Worth, Tex., Travelocity's headquarters, and in San Francisco, where Preview is based. James Hornthal, founder and chairman of Preview, will be the new company's vice chairman. No job was announced for Chris Clouser, who recently left Northwest Airlines to be Preview's chief executive. Travelocity and Preview also announced that they had extended Preview's agreement to be the exclusive travel agent on America Online for five years. They have also renewed Travelocity's similar deal with Yahoo, another Internet search service. America Online already owns about 5 percent of Preview, and Yahoo is expected to make a small investment in the new company when the merger is completed. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Recording Industry Escalates Crackdown on Digital Piracy
body: For years, frustrated record companies have watched helplessly as millions of illegally copied songs circulated on the Internet, but a crackdown on digital piracy that will have a wide-ranging impact on consumers is about to begin. In fact, the first elements are already in place. Few consumers are aware that Philips CD burners, the devices that record data or music on compact disks, have been adding a digital serial number to every CD the machines make to enable copyright owners to trace any recording to the machine that made it. "We don't encourage illegal behavior," said Marijke van Hooren, a spokeswoman for Royal Philips Electronics. "If there is illegal use, there's a way to find out more or less what's happening." She added, though, that Philips does not keep a registry associating serial numbers with owners. Whatever privacy questions the serial number may raise, it may ultimately prove to be the most benign of the music-protection systems about to land on store shelves. While record companies have given up on the millions of unprotected songs currently estimated to be circulating on the Internet, they plan to make the most desirable music available only in protected form. By Christmas, the major labels hope to make some of the most popular recordings available on line in formats protected by rights-management technologies from companies like the Microsoft Corporation, Liquid Audio and the Intertrust Corporation. But yet to be addressed, is the key issue of how to protect music on CD's from being ripped -- converted into computer files -- and illegally distributed on the Internet. While a final specification is yet to be determined, the Secure Digital Music Initiative, the recording industry's antipiracy effort backed by the consumer electronics and technology industries, has made some progress toward a standard for protecting newly issued CD's. Hardware that will support the future Secure Digital specifications is just now making its way into portable music players. Software will follow in the next 12 to 18 months when the rest of the specifications are determined. At that time, the major labels will quietly start issuing commercial CD's containing an electronic fingerprint that, in theory, will prevent the music from being illegally distributed. But it is not clear whether the Secure Digital technology will provide enough security to thwart the millions of teen-age and college-age pirates who routinely rip CD's and distribute the music to friends. What is more, the technology will most certainly embed data in each song that will allow only one computer or portable player to play it. Analysts say that fact is likely to make protection technologies so cumbersome that consumers will have a strong incentive to get around them. "Never before has such a burden of complexity been put on the consumer," said Richard Doherty, president of Envisioneering, a market research and technology firm that tracks the consumer electronics and computer industries. "This will be a real test of mettle." The key component of the Secure Digital technology is digital watermarking, embedding an electronic identification in CD's. While the consortium has not agreed on the final specification for protecting commercial CD's, the most promising approach involves using two types of digital watermarks -- fragile and robust -- on each CD. The robust watermark, supposedly tough to remove, will identify that the CD is new, protected music that can be played only on devices that are compliant with the Secure Digital Music Initiative. The purpose of the fragile watermark is to prevent music from being compressed by software that does not conform to the Secure Digital standard. If a CD is ripped and then illegally compressed for storage on a computer or portable player, the fragile watermark will be destroyed. Music that has the robust watermark but not the fragile watermark will not be playable on a Secure Digital-compliant player. In August, the consortium selected a watermarking technology developed by Aris Technologies for the robust watermark. This selection will likely provide a licensing fee bonanza for Aris, a privately held company based in Cambridge, Mass. The standard for the fragile watermark -- and thus the recipient of those licensing fees -- has not yet been announced. But watermarking technology has potential problems. No one has yet developed a way to insert a watermark that cannot be easily removed. Some Internet sites offer software capable of removing watermarks. Moreover, by design, the watermark must affect audible components of the digital signal, so that clumsy attempts to remove it will degrade the sound. Some critics say that for discerning listeners, the watermark itself might adversely affect the quality of the music. Joseph M. Winograd, chief technology officer of Aris acknowledged that watermarks could be removed. "I would say that no security is absolute," he said. "Our goal is to set the bar for circumvention as high as is practical and possible." As for fears about loss of sound quality, however, he said, "We can demonstrate that to the most adept and acute listeners of the recording industry, content with the watermark cannot be distinguished from content without it." The next generation of portable players of music recorded as MP3 files, the format most widely used on the Internet, are now just now hitting the market. Diamond Multimedia Systems's Rio 500 is among the first capable of detecting the robust watermark. When watermarked music starts to appear, these devices will prompt the user to upgrade to software that will play and copy the new music. This software, still in development, will not play music that contains the robust watermark but lacks the fragile one. Moreover, the software will only allow the user to make four copies of each song, including songs in MP3 format. And each copy will contain information that only allows it to be played on a single device or machine. Additional copies will require re ripping a CD or re-downloading music. That means that music downloaded with software that comes with a portable player will not play on a digital car stereo or PC. "This is something S.D.M.I. would like to consider," said Leonardo Chiariglione, the consortium's executive director. But based on the specifications under consideration, he conceded, consumers who are used to listening to digital music on any player will experience the inconvenience and expense of having to have a separate copy for every player they own. Another issue is that since any music downloaded from the Web or ripped from a CD is limited to a single player, an entire music collection can be destroyed if that computer's hard drive or portable player fails. Mr. Doherty says that when he asked recording industry executives about this issue they "just looked at the ceiling." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Several generations of Philips CD recorders have been adding a digital serial number to every CD made so the recordings can be traced.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
The On-Line Brokerage Battle
body: HEARD the pitch about dumping your full-service broker? Remember the ad about the stock-trading teen-ager with his own helicopter? Seen the television spot where the hunky stud muffin rubs the bunions of an older woman who is basking in her on-line investment wealth? If there is one thing the Internet has brought to every American, it is a blitz of advertising from brokerage firms eager to lure do-it-yourself types on line. But that marketing flurry, it seems, was just the preview. The real advertising battle is just starting. Over the next year, the top 10 on-line brokers have budgeted about $1.5 billion to fill airwaves, newspapers and magazines, billboards, other Web sites and email in-boxes with advertising, all preaching some version of the mantra that you can get rich faster if you take charge of your own investments. To put that in perspective, Ford Motor spent the same amount of money hawking cars and trucks last year. And Walt Disney and Coca-Cola combined do not flog themselves nearly as hard. The question is will all this marketing money pay off in the form of revenue-generating customers. On-line companies are already well known for putting promotion before profit. But the latest spending spree ups the ante considerably. Several of the leading on-line brokerages, including Ameritrade, TD Waterhouse and National Discount Brokers, are set to triple their ad spending the next year to compete better with E*Trade, the advertising king of the on-line financial services industry, according to advertising industry experts and the companies themselves. The on-line brokers are busily signing up celebrity representatives like the actress Geena Davis (TD Waterhouse), the self-parodying blond bombshell Anna Nichol Smith (E*Trade) and the teen-age Russian tennis star Anna Kournikova (Charles Schwab). They have already reserved air time for the World Series and next winter's Superbowl. And the cost is mounting: E*Trade now spends about half of its revenue on marketing, analysts say, while other brokerages are pouring the bulk of proceeds raised from initial public offerings into splash campaigns. All of this spending raises questions about a business that, so far, has been one of E-commerce's biggest success stories. Stock trading is still one of the best on-line businesses. People are flocking to it, talking about it and spending on it like never before. But the number of companies looking for a piece of the action -- and the ferocity with which they are fighting for it -- has made the economics look increasingly dismal. Some people within the industry now fear that it is on the verge of a vicious cycle of rising ad spending, sharper competition and slower growth -- even if the stock market remains robust enough that people are tempted to trade stocks as a hobby. "I don't think anyone expected that we would see the industry spending over a billion dollars on this market," said J. Peter Ricketts, Ameritrade's senior vice president for marketing and sales. "Not everyone can do well. Some will see diminishing returns." Ameritrade intends to be one of the winners. That is why the company announced earlier this month that, after reducing ad spending earlier this year to move toward profitability, it has now reversed course. The company has planned a yearlong advertising program it values at $200 million, roughly as much as Mazda spends annually to market vehicles and well over half of what Ameritrade is expected to receive in revenue this year. Ameritrade, the No. 6 on-line broker, is also a bellwether of another trend: the rising cost of attracting each now customer. For a time, on-line brokerages seemed to have it easy. For not much more than $100 in ad spending, they could attract a self-motivated trader who would buy and sell stocks and pay commissions at a pace that would return a profit to the brokerage firm in about a year. Better yet, traders, unlike book or computer shoppers, tend to be "sticky," to use E-commerce parlance; they remain loyal to an established relationship. But a combination of rising ad spending, slowing account growth and the proliferation of on-line brokerages -- there are perhaps 50 with national ambitions and solid financial backing, about 130 all together -- has pushed that cost way up. Ameritrade has warned analysts that it is currently spending about $500 for each new customer it signs up. The company hopes that figure will go down later this year, when it expects a rush of new on-line customers. E*Trade and National Discount Brokers also say they are now prepared to spend $400 to $500 to sign up each new customer, at least double what it was taking earlier this year. The costs include giveaways like the Sprint long-distance minutes, United Airlines frequent-flier miles and $75 in free trades that E*Trade is using as promotional incentives. "If they go over $500, the stock trading business stops making sense," said Bill Burnham, a venture capitalist at Softbank Partners and an expert on the on-line brokerage industry. But he observed that the brokerages are reluctant to slash ad spending now, fearing they will be left behind. "It's a war of attrition," he said. The war is much more typical of consumer products companies, like those selling soda, credit cards, or paper towels, than it is for Wall Street. Only a couple of years ago, $20 million was considered a sizable advertising campaign by Wall Street standards. E*Trade will not say exactly how much it plans to spend on advertising this year. But industry executives say it has committed to spend about $300 million. That would be more than Merrill Lynch, Paine Webber and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter combined, according to estimates of brokerage firm marketing budgets compiled by Bear, Stearns, the investment bank. The comparison is all the more significant given that Merrill Lynch, which plans to offer $29.95 on-line trading later this year, and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, which owns the Discover brokerage, have their own on-line offerings to promote. E*Trade was also the big spender among the on-line brokerages last year (and the second-biggest marketer among on-line companies over all, after Amazon.com). The campaign was widely considered a raging success. The research firm International Data Corporation found that consumers named E*Trade as the dominant on-line broker, even though its 14 percent market share of Internet trading volume is second to Charles Schwab's 25 percent share, says Paul Johnson, an on-line brokerage analyst at International Data. The advertising also made E*Trade the fastest-growing on-line broker as measured by number of new accounts; E*Trade now has an estimated 1.25 million active accounts. The firm broke new ground among brokerage firms by advertising its services during prime time -- on "Ally McBeal" and "E.R.," for instance, and buying six slots during last winter's Superbowl, the most expensive television time available. It used to be that Wall Street ads appeared only during Sunday morning talk shows and featured narrators intoning about the solidity of a company in a deep baritone, while a camera panned a rock in the sea. E*Trade, in contrast, introduced ads that aimed to be young and hip, and occasionally hilarious. Its early ads poked fun at hidebound full-service brokers, including a spot that showed a hapless broker waking at dawn to prepare for another day of fruitless cold calling. Now the emphasis is more on empowering investors than dumping brokers. One new spot shows an on-line trader watching a preview for a new movie starring Anna Nichole Smith. He declares it the worst movie ever, then dumps stock in "Trimount" the Hollywood company that produced it. The point, says Jerry Gramaglia, E*Trade's marketing chief, is that investors can take charge and act immediately to get financial results. That ad, along with others that include the rich woman and her young man and another depicting a hermit who gets investment advice from the stuffed moose head and woodchuck in his cabin, have garnered enough attention that E*Trade has every intention of keeping its marketing budget "north of our rivals," Mr. Gramaglia said. He acknowledged that at $400 to $500 the cost of attracting new customers could become prohibitive for the on-line brokers. But he said E*Trade had also diversified the products its offers to include on-line banking, bonds, mortgages and mutual funds, making the old stock-trading business model an anachronism. He also predicted that those who worry too much about average costs per customer might regret it. "You can drown in a river that averages three feet," he said. "This is about creating the dominant on-line financial brand." Most of E*Trade's competitors are trying to catch up to its marketing lead -- what people in the ad industry refer to as "share of voice." Charles Schwab, which has seen its market share slip somewhat in recent months, looks set to challenge E*Trade ad dollar for ad dollar over the next year. "There are some markets where we double our spending and still lose share of voice to them," Len Short, Schwab's executive vice president for advertising, said. "We are not going to be the leader if we underspend the competition." Mr. Short, who like Mr. Gramaglia is a veteran of long-distance telephone advertising wars in the early 1990's, estimates that it requires about $300 million a year in spending, sustained for many years, to build and maintain a brand as a household name. Schwab's latest ads have picked up E*Trade's light-hearted tone. In one ad, Ann Kournikova, the teen-age tennis wonder, lectures fellow players about "asset allocation." Mr. Short said the spots aim for a slightly different crowd than the E*Trade ads. Schwab, seeking to highlight its large call-in centers and bricks and mortar offices, boasts about it ability to educate investors and, if necessary, hold their hands while they learn to trade. None of the other Internet brokerages seems likely to match the marketing spending of E*Trade and Schwab. But Ameritrade promises to come close with its $200 million campaign. Its television spots feature Stuart, a freakishly red-haired teen-ager with a Mohawk haircut and muttonchops who taunts his girlfriend's stockbroker father with his passion for on-line trading. "Believe in yourself" is the theme. Not long ago, such promises to lift ad spending might have generated positive buzz for the on-line brokerages among investors. The potential for the companies to capture first-time stock traders was considered so great that deficit spending on ads helped pump share prices into the stratosphere. Most on-line brokerage stocks are in fact still up for the year, but many are down close to 60 percent from their April highs. And Wall Street seems less impressed with the marketing promises now. Richard H. Repetto, an on-line brokerage analyst at Lehman Brothers, rocked the industry recently when he downgraded his recommendations on both E*Trade and Ameritrade to "outperform" from "buy." He cited the increased ad budgets and higher cost of luring new customers as early warning signs of a battle among brokers for new clients that could end up eating away at the business. "It's not crazy to go after new customers aggressively, given the long-term potential," Mr. Repetto said. "But you have to consider the increased cost of getting more customers and what you have to do to keep them. There comes a time when there has to be a shakeout." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: An ad for on-line stock trading depict types like Stuart, top, Ameritrade's red-haired iconoclast and, above, E*Trade's "sugar mama" and her younger friend. title: Who's on First at Excite@Home, Anyway?
body: The board of the Excite@Home Corporation yesterday canceled a meeting set for Monday to vote on splitting the company's Excite Web portal from the At Home cable modem venture, apparently because Cox Communications Inc., one of the venture's big shareholders, threatened to veto the plan, an executive close to Excite@Home said yesterday. It has been clear since the summer that the AT&T Corporation, the biggest shareholder in Excite@Home, does not believe that Excite and At Home belong together and that AT&T has been considering a deal to give America Online Inc. enhanced access to AT&T's widespread cable television systems. Capping a bizarre series of corporate statements that have roiled Excite@Home's stock, AT&T appeared to reiterate that stance yesterday, but only after a senior AT&T executive and Excite@Home's president appeared to deny it. There was much speculation on Wednesday that the companies were near a deal under which Excite@Home would be split, with America Online acquiring Excite and AT&T retaining At Home. AT&T would then make a deal to give America Online more access to its cable systems to provide high-speed Internet access. On Wednesday, that scenario propelled shares of Excite@Home up by as much as $9.125, to $47.50, in Nasdaq trading before closing at $43.4375, up $5.0625. On Wednesday night, while not appearing to deny that AT&T was in favor of a split between Excite and At Home, Leo J. Hindery Jr., chief executive of AT&T's cable operation, did deny that AT&T was negotiating to sell its stake in Excite@Home outright to America Online. "Absolutely not," Mr. Hindery told Reuters. "There have been no discussions under way whatsoever." Confusion over the nature of any deal, coupled with Mr. Hindery's strong language, sent Excite@Home's shares down at the opening of the market yesterday. Then, George Bell, Excite@Home's president, was reported by Bloomberg News to have said yesterday at a conference: "Is Excite in play? No." By the end of the trading day, Excite@Home's stock had lost $2, closing at $41.4375. But after the market closed, AT&T issued an official statement that appeared to contradict Mr. Hindery and Mr. Bell, in spirit if not in letter. "We have periodically explored, and we continue to explore, many alternatives with respect to our Internet strategy and our ownership interest in Excite@Home," the statement said, adding that no firm decisions had been made. "The alternatives include internal options as well as discussions with third parties." Through all of the confusion, what emerged was that AT&T in fact continues to consider a side deal with America Online, perhaps to the detriment of Excite@Home, and that AT&T's sophisticated communications operation, wary of misleading investors, could not abide what could be considered blanket denials by Mr. Bell and Mr. Hindery. Cox and Excite@Home declined to comment. AT&T refused to elaborate on the statement.    http://www.nytimes.com

title: For Internet Dating Site, a Seamy Surprise - Correction Appended
body: SUSAN BERGIN, the creator of an on-line matchmaking service, recently used the Alta Vista search engine to determine how easy it was to find her Web site, called singleswithscruples.com. After typing "singles with scruples" into the search box, Ms. Bergin was glad to see her site come up first on the list of results. But when she scrolled down the list, Ms. Bergin noticed that one of the other results posted appeared to be a repeat listing of her site. The title line, "Singles with Scruples Dating, Friendship and Matchmaker Services," as well as the descriptive sentence beneath it, were identical, word for word. Only the Internet address was different. When Ms. Bergin clicked on the listing and saw what looked to be an on-line dating site called Net Encounters, she grew more and more annoyed that someone had used her domain name to attract Web surfers to another dating site. But when she clicked on the site's Links icon and saw links to pornographic photos, she was horrified. "It was a pornography site disguised as a dating site, and anyone looking for my site with a search engine could have come across it," Ms. Bergin said. "Needless to say, I was upset." Ms. Bergin's experience is similar in many ways to those of other Web site owners affected by a large-scale fraud, described by the Federal Trade Commission last weekas involving a Portuguese hacker and an Australian pornography company. In both cases, so-called metatags -- key words and other indexing code -- were cloned from other Web sites and used to direct Web surfers to pornographic material. In the case involving the Portuguese hacker, the trade commission said that up to 25 million Web pages might have been affected. The owners of two other on-line dating services, www.lovecity.com and togethernj.com, reported seeing cloned descriptions of their sites attached to the Net Encounters site in searches conducted on Alta Vista. In all three instances, the unsuspecting visitor to Net Encounters is led to believe that it is a dating site and is asked to submit personal information under the guise of submitting a free personal advertisement, which the hacker can use for future solicitation. The registered owner of the Net Encounters site is in Britain. "It's a big problem for us, and it leaves a bad taste for anyone who deals with it," said Rob Piccola, president of Love City. "We've built up a brand awareness over the past four years, but now we have customers asking us if we're running pornography sites." In the case described last week, a Federal judge ordered many of the sites run by the Australian company and the hacker off the Web, and Australian authorities said they were considering civil or criminal charges against the company. The hacker cannot be located. Owners of legitimate Web sites who want to take action themselves can sue under the Federal Trade Commission Act, which prohibits unfair or deceptive practices involving commerce. "The F.T.C. Act gives us a broad authority to make sure these advertisements aren't misleading," said Dean Forbes, a staff attorney at the commission. But like Ms. Bergin, whose business generates no income yet, many site owners do not have the money to enter a protracted legal battle. Ms.  Bergin said she had asked Alta Vista to remove the Net Encounters listing but that it still appeared when she searched for her site. "To a small business, it's a pain in the neck that's not easily disposed of," said Marc Brown, a lawyer who sent a letter to the registered owner of the Web address for Net Encounters on Ms. Bergin's behalf. Mr. Brown added that when the cloning involved a hacker in another country, the challenge of enforcing F.T.C.  regulations was greatly compounded. "This seems to be a case where private enforcement by lawsuits will not work as well as public enforcement by the Government, or in some cases, two governments working together," said Tim Stanley, chief executive of Findlaw.com, a legal site based in Mountain View, Calif. Representatives at Network Solutions, the leading Internet domain registry, as well as at Alta Vista, say they have limited ability to oversee the conduct of Web site owners. "It's partly a balancing act between the majority of people who are honest and who want to get on the Internet fast, and waiting for the F.T.C. to produce regulations that will protect domain names and content," said Nancy Huddleston, a spokeswoman for Network Solutions, which receives close to 13,000 domain name applications per day. "As the Internet grows, the problem will grow proportionately with it." David Emanuel, a spokesman for Alta Vista, said that the first recourse for the owner of a purloined site should be to get in contact with the apparent perpetrator directly. "It puts the search engines in a difficult position because we can't legislate," he said. "We add 600,000 site submissions a week, and as people become more crafty and learn how to do it, it's very difficult for us to weed this type of infringement out." Mr. Emanuel said that the company did have an active team dedicated to spotting clones and that it was working on a proprietary technology that would recognize multiple key words to weed out duplicate pages. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Circuits last Thursday about the diversion of Web surfers to pornographic sites while they are looking for legitimate sites misidentified the Federal statute that covers individual suits over deceptive business practices. A person can sue under the Lanham Act, which, among other things, deals with unfair competition, not the Federal Trade Commission Act. Correction-Date: October 7, 1999, Thursday Graphic   Photo: People seeking this singles site were misdirected to a pornographic one.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
America Online Enters Hong Kong With Eye on Mainland
body: Stephen M. Case has planted his flag in hongkong, but his gaze is fixed on the Chinese mainland. Mr. Case, the founder and chairman of America Online Inc., was here this week to introduce his company's newest Internet service, AOL hongkong. The service -- a partnership with a highflying local Internet provider, the China.com Corporation -- will offer the usual menu of AOL services, plus a dollop of home-grown features like Cantonese pop music, Chinese cooking tips and horse-racing forums. But Internet analysts said AOL hongkong is most intriguing as a starting point for future expansion into China. With an on-line market that is projected to quadruple from 3.8 million users this year to 16.1 million in 2003, China beckons Internet providers the way it used to attract detergent makers. "AOL is definitely a force to be reckoned with," said Hanson Cheah, executive director of Asia Tech Ventures, a venture capital firm here that specializes in Internet companies. "They can use their marketing prowess and brand name to blanket the market. But China presents big challenges." In an interview, Mr. Case acknowledged that hongkong was "a logical staging area for China." But he added: "First things first. We want to launch hongkong, and then we'll see what happens." Mr. Case may be wise to temper his ambitions. Beijing recently alarmed foreign investors when a top official seemed to slam the door on foreign investment in Internet companies. The official, Wu Jichuan, the Information Industry Minister, later softened his tone, saying: "We will open these areas sooner or later. The question is, we have to have the proper rules in place." Beijing's mixed signals have left foreigners scratching their heads. Shares of China-related companies like China.com have taken a drubbing. But Yahoo, the Internet portal service, recently went ahead with plans for a venture with Founder, a Beijing electronics company. Mr. Case said he planned to meet with Mr. Wu in Beijing on Thursday and hoped to get a better understanding of the Government's position. "I think this is being debated within the Chinese Government as well," Mr. Case said. "I have little doubt that when the dust settles, the Chinese will embrace foreign investment in the Internet." Analysts here generally share his optimism. They note that Mr. Wu is being pulled by competing interests: telecommunications executives, who want to retain monopoly control of China's network, and technology executives, who want to open the network to stimulate equipment sales. Beijing is also torn between wanting to harness the power of the Internet and wanting to restrict potentially provocative information about issues like Tibet and Taiwan. Despite all this, China's President, Jiang Zemin, has said that he wants the Internet to become an engine of economic growth. "Clearly, there is going to be resistance to pure, unfettered access," said Duncan Clark, a partner at BDA China, an Internet consulting firm in Beijing. "But China knows that it needs to develop the Internet." China's ambivalence may be dispelled later this year when Beijing is expected to issue new rules governing foreign investment in the Internet. The current ban derives from a 1993 law that prohibits foreign companies from owning or managing telephone networks in the country. If China did open up its market, America Online would have a well-connected partner in China.com. Among the company's original investors is Xinhua, the official Chinese news agency. Xinhua still owns a 13.6 percent stake. America Online bought 10 percent of China.com for $25 million in June and has an option to increase its holdings to 25 percent. At a news conference to introduce AOL hongkong, Mr. Case emphasized the strong local flavor of its programming. In addition to local pop stars and stock quotations, the service will offer Chinese-language news from Sing Tao, a hongkong newspaper, and email in Chinese and English. Peter Yip, the chief executive of China.com, said hongkong was an impressive Internet market on its own. He said the territory would have 940,000 on-line users by the end of the year and 1.6 million by 2001. Currently, the market is dominated by the local phone company, Cable and Wireless HKT. Mr. Yip said his company and America Online hoped to turn hongkong into both a regional Internet hub and a gateway to China. Lest there be any doubt about their good intentions, he added: "They're opening their markets at a Chinese pace. We have to be sensitive to the pace of reform in China."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
America Online Unit to Reduce Subscription Costs in Britain
body: Hoping to stem its market slide in Britain, America Online said today that it would lower the monthly cost of subscribing to its service here. AOL will charge users one British penny a minute, or 1.65 cents, in addition to the monthly subscription fee of 9.99 pounds , or $16.45, making it more competitive with Freeserve P.L.C., the British market leader, which requires only the cost of a local phone call to connect to the Internet. The move surprised some analysts because AOL U.K. had introduced Netscape Online, a subscription-free service similar to Freeserve, with considerable fanfare only a month ago. AOL U.K. is a unit of AOL Europe, which in turn is a joint venture between America Online and the German media conglomerate Bertelsmann. In contrast to the unitedstates, where Internet access over a telephone line is relatively inexpensive, access in Britain and most of Continental Europe can seem prohibitive. Users pay by the minute for local phone calls, in addition to the charge levied by the Internet access provider. In Britain, the cost can be high as 6.6 cents a minute during peak hours, and range downward to 1.65 cents a minute at night or on weekends. As a result, Internet services like Freeserve and its imitators have emerged, luring customers by not charging a monthly subscription fee for Internet access. These subscription-free services make money by sharing a percentage of the revenue generated by the cost of the user's phone call with the telephone company. AOL U.K. users spend an average of 17 minutes a day on line while users of America Online in the unitedstates spend an hour a day on line. Now, AOL hopes to increase its share of business by keeping its metered charges on a par with those of its free-subscription competitors. "If you make it cheap enough to use it all the time, people will use it all the time," said Robert W. Pittman, the president of America Online, in a telephone interview. Some analysts said the new pricing system could cannibalize subscribers from America Online's new sister brand, Netscape Online. Bruce Kasrel of Forrester Research said, "It undermines Netscape Online, but they are willing to put Netscape Online on the chopping block if it means all of the subscription-free services are on the block with it." AOL has traditionally relied on the monthly subscription model, which tends to provide significantly higher profit margins than the free-subscription model. As well as getting a part of local phone charges, the free services depend on revenue from advertising and electronic commerce. Mr. Pittman maintained that America Online would not encroach on Netscape Online's customers because, he said, the two brands appealed to different segments of the market. Netscape Online, he said, is for the budget user, while AOL's proprietary content appeals to families. Some analysts speculated that the move to what AOL U.K. labeled "off-peak all the time" would result in a surge of new subscribers that might overwhelm the company's network, much as happened in the unitedstates in late 1996 and early 1997, when the parent America Online introduced flat-rate pricing. But Mr. Pittman said, "I hope we've learned from our mistakes." Noah Yasskin, an analyst at Jupiter Communications here, predicted that as phone companies like British Telecommunications moved toward flat-rate pricing for local calls, the war between free-subscription Internet services and subscription-based services would blur. Freeserve said today that it would offer 10 free hours of Internet access a month during off-peak hours if users placed a certain total of calls with its partner, Energis P.L.C. Freeserve is expected to announce its first-quarter financial results on Tuesday, and analysts expect its growth to have slowed as a result of increased competition. http://www.nytimes.com

title: As America Online's No. 2 Brand These Days, Compuserve Is Being Rejuvenated
body: In a conglomerate-driven world, investors expect big companies to own more than one brand. Viacom operates MTV and VH1. Coca-Cola sells Diet Coke and Tab. The question is whether this business model can work in the still-forming and highly volatile market of Internet service providers. The first such attempt in this industry -- America Online's ownership of its former rival, Compuserve -- suggests that the answer is yes, even if serious challenges remain in keeping the new brand profitable. America Online said last week that so far in its fiscal first quarter, which will end on Thursday, the long-struggling Compuserve added 300,000 subscribers. Although the company declines to give a total subscribership, industry estimates now place the figure at 2.3 million -- which would still be well below Compuserve's peak of 3.6 million in 1995. On the surface, there is an easy explanation for the recent upswing: since the quarter began, Compuserve has offered cash rebates to new subscribers who buy certain brands of computers and agree to sign up for three years of Internet access at $21.95 a month. The rebates notwithstanding, AOL executives consider the surge in Compuserve subscriptions a sign of healthy growth in a cutthroat industry, and a measure of redemption. When the company acquired Compuserve in 1997, it predicted the dawning of a multiple-brand era in the Internet access market, a view that industry analysts doubted would be fulfilled so soon. America Online's premise is that the Internet access market will fragment into different consumer tiers -- budget or "value" tiers; premium tiers, and various other levels in between. The company considers the America Online brand a premium service, for which subscribers pay $21.95 a month, without rebates, for fare including 19 separate topic "channels," 15,000 chat rooms and a wildly popular instant-messaging capability. The company considers Compuserve, which these days is a glorified Internet access provider offering a smattering of content and chat, a "value" brand. "It's like Hertz and Budget," said Audrey Weil, a senior vice president of AOL and general manager of Compuserve. "Hertz is the largest and most dominant," Ms. Weil said, "but Budget has a brand name you've heard of and that is a good alternative in the value space." The analogy extends only so far, of course: Hertz does not own Budget, and in some places, their rental rates are similar. America Online's reasoning differs from the conventional wisdom about the market for Internet service providers. Until very recently, many industry executives and analysts predicted that providing Internet access service was a business that would go the way of utilities; as with electricity, consumers would care little who provided access so long as the electrons flowed. But America Online executives have taken a different view, especially the company's president and chief operating officer, Robert W. Pittman. Formerly president of MTV Networks, Mr. Pittman oversaw development of the VH1 brand in 1985 (which at the time he said he envisioned as MTV for "old folks, dullard, the not so hip") and he is a flag-waver for the many-brand business model. So is Steve Case, America Online's chairman, who in an interview cited its acquisitions of Netscape and the instant-messaging service ICQ. "We've migrated into being a multibrand company," Mr. Case said. But whether the Compuserve brand specifically will thrive remains in question. Before the recent rash of Compuserve subscriptions, membership had been languishing since America Online's 1997 deal to acquire Compuserve, which had suffered a long decline under the ownership of H & R Block. Elsewhere, though, the Internet access market has been booming -- led by America Online's own flagship service, which has grown to more than 18 million from 11 million since the company bought Compuserve. Not long after the purchase, America Online laid off 500 Compuserve employees and began to shift back-room and technology operations from Compuserve headquarters in Columbus, Ohio, to the parent company's home in Reston, Va. America Online says that by sharing such costs, it was immediately able to turn Compuserve profitable, although it has declined to give specific figures. And yet, the first real subscriber growth by Compuserve under its new ownership has come only since America Online began offering the rebates -- $400 with the purchase of certain computers, if a subscriber signs up for three years of Compuserve, and $100 with PC purchases if the customer agrees to a one-year subscription. The viability of this business model has been questioned by competitors and some analysts. "A $400 rebate up front is uneconomical; they're not going to make any money," said Charles Betty, president and chief executive of Earthlink, which agreed last week to a merger with Mindspring that would form the nation's second-largest Internet service provider after America Online. Certainly, the rebate offer of $400 a customer -- which does not include Compuserve's marketing costs -- exceeds the $180 to $200 that Mr. Betty said Earthlink pays to gain a new subscriber. But Mr. Pittman, while declining to give specific figures, said Compuserve can operate in the black under the rebate arrangement because of its technology-sharing relationship with America Online. "We are going after the price buyer," Mr. Pittman said, adding that Compuserve would accept lower profit margins than AOL. "We will live with the smallest margin we can live with," he said. There are other outstanding questions. A survey this month by J. D. Power & Associates of customer satisfaction among seven top Internet service providers found that Compuserve ranked second from the bottom and America Online ranked dead last, according to Peter Dresch, director of media relations for J. D. Power in Agoura Hills, Calif. The others, in descending rank of satisfaction, were Mindspring, Earthlink, AT&T Worldnet, Microsoft MSN and Prodigy. In the case of Compuserve, customers ranked the service as below average in four of the survey's categories: cost and billing, email services, navigation and ease of use. Ms. Weil, of Compuserve, said she expected consumer responses to improve with time. America Online challenged the survey, asserting that it included few users of the latest version of Compuserve -- Compuserve 2000, which was introduced in February. The J. D. Power survey was conducted starting in July, but the bulk of Compuserve 2000 users, AOL said, were added after the survey was conducted. Two decades old, Compuserve was among the first big-name on-line communities, and it was originally populated with technology-savvy, business-oriented subscribers for whom Compuserve was both a community and a research tool. It was also among the first services to substantially expand overseas, but its growth languished as the emergence of the Internet spelled the end of proprietary on-line communities built on the old Compuserve model. The new crowd of price-oriented users is a different breed. America Online maintains an existing hourly pricing plan for what it calls the "classic" Compuserve clientele, versus people who opt for the Compuserve 2000 service to which the rebates apply. At the time of America Online's acquisition of Compuserve, there was much gnashing of teeth by old-guard users about the arrival of the newbies. But such tensions seem to have passed, said Mike Bayer, who has been a Compuserve member since 1981 and a volunteer system operator for Compuserve since 1984 and is now an on-line forum leader. The company declines to say how many current customers are holdovers from the old days, but Mr. Bayer estimates that it is about one-third of the total. There is still a question about whether Compuserve's success might be a burden to America Online, if the popularity of the rebates could cannibalize the premium brand, said Scott E. Reamer, director of Internet research for S. G. Cowen, the newyork-based brokerage firm. Mr. Reamer said investors would want to watch the next several quarters carefully to see if America Online could continue its own impressive growth while Compuserve grows, too. But right now, he said, the Compuserve acquisition is starting to look good for America Online. "No one really expected much from Compuserve when AOL bought it," he said. "They've turned it around." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Robert W. Pittman, America Online's president, with Audrey Weil, general manager of Compuserve unit, at map showing AOL locations. (Marty Katz for The newyork Times)

title:
PERSONAL BUSINESS;
The On-Line Trader Is Becoming the New Big Man on Campus
body: SHORTLY before 9 A.M. on Sept. 17, an alarm sounded on Derek O'Banion's personal computer -- the signal that Vitria Technology, an Internet business software developer, had begun its first day of trading on Nasdaq. Vitria, offered at $18, soared to $45 but quickly dipped. Mr. O'Banion pounced, buying 200 shares at $43.375, watching them rise to $46, and then selling when they slipped to $45.50. Ten minutes and a $425 profit later, he was back in bed for another half-hour of sleep before his 10 A.M. introductory fiction-writing class. With the school year in full swing, Mr. O'Banion, a senior at the University of Puget Sound in Tacoma, Wash., is one of thousands of college students who fit on-line stock trading into already busy schedules of lectures, exams and keg parties. Younger versions of the office workers who sneak in trades while the boss isn't looking, more students are checking prices and shifting their portfolios between, and sometimes during, classes. "I don't expect it to conflict, but if it does, once in a while I can miss a class," said Mr. O'Banion, 21, a computer science major. "It's not like I haven't done that before." Most undergraduates grew up with personal computers and saw the stock market soar throughout their teen-age years. And they have easy access to financial news and research in their dormitories, fraternity and sorority houses and campus computer rooms. Many students appear to be taking a relatively safe approach to on-line investing. Mustafa Gultekin, a finance professor at the University of North Carolina, said that of about 70 students in the undergraduate investing club last year, only two were day-trading. "That's a sure way to lose money," he tells students. Indeed, last month, the North American Securities Administrators Association reported that 70 percent of day traders lose money. GOMEZ ADVISORS, a research firm in Lincoln, Mass., that follows the on-line brokerage industry, said a July survey of on-line traders showed that about 548,000, or nearly 11 percent of the nation's 5.12 million on-line traders, were 25 or younger. While the firm could not say how many of those under-25 traders were students, it reported that nearly 5 percent, or about 25,000, were placing orders from schools, mostly universities. About 61 percent, or 305,000, were placing orders from home, a number that could also include some students. Gomez found that, like their older counterparts, nearly half of the younger on-line traders had long-term, or at least 10-year, investing strategies. But nearly 23 percent of them invested on line primarily for fun or challenge, compared with 13 percent of their elders. Mr. O'Banion is more active than most students, making as many as 20 trades daily since he opened an on-line account last spring with MB Trading of El Segundo, Calif., using $10,000 he inherited. While his portfolio has grown about 40 percent, he has lost and recouped thousands of dollars along the way, he said. He has cut down on his trading since spending $1,000 in commissions shortly after he started, even with discounts for frequent traders. For Mr. O'Banion, the thrill of the moment and the dream of great riches are why he continues to day-trade -- and why he focuses on initial public offerings of Internet stocks.  "When you get into an I.P.O., your heart starts racing, because you could make or lose a lot of money real fast," he said, shortly after making his Vitria Technology trades. Because he concentrates on the first few hours of trading, beginning at 6:30 A.M. on the West Coast, Mr. O'Banion said investing does not usually cut into class or study time. Other students spend more time following the market than trading in it. Rodger Bucchianeri and Jeffrey Monat, 21-year-old seniors and roommates at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, opened on-line accounts two years ago. They watch CNBC and get stock quotations from Bloomberg terminals in campus buildings. Mr. Bucchianeri also carries a pager that displays stock prices and news, which he monitors during his classes. Louis Cohen, a senior business major at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, has made three or four trades a week since opening his on-line account with E*Trade at the beginning of this year. His portfolio started with stock in blue-chip companies like Philip Morris and Merck that he received as gifts from his parents and grandparents, beginning in first or second grade. He now has $15,000 to $20,000 in the market, mostly in long-term holdings, but with $2,000 to $3,000 allocated to making short-term moves. Mr. Cohen, 21, consults with Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity brothers who are also interested in stocks, and he is in close touch with his older brother, Lawrence, a day trader in Forest Hills, Queens. "If he sees something I should look into, he'll send me an instant message, and I'll do the same with him," Mr. Cohen said. FOR many student investors, managing an on-line portfolio is training for a career on Wall Street or in the broader business world. Mr. Bucchianeri, who has already done internships with Paine Webber, J. P. Morgan and Bear, Stearns, regards his early start in investing as a chance to take risks that he might shun later. As he put it, "I can afford to lose it all, so I'm looking for the high gains." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Derek O'Banion, a student at the University of Puget Sound, trades stocks on line from his dormitory. (Daniel Sheehan for The newyork Times)

title:
STRATEGIES;
Of Overconfidence And the On-Line Trader
body: "DON'T confuse brains with a bull market." While no investor should forget that market truth, anyone who is tempted to start trading stocks on line should pay special heed. New research has concluded that on-line investors are particularly prone to giving their own brains all the credit for their short-term success and discounting the role of luck. And all too often, such conceit leads to self-destructive behavior. The research, by Brad M. Barber and Terrance Odean, associate and assistant finance professors, respectively, at the Graduate School of Management at the University of California at Davis, focused on trading by more than 1,600 individual investors from 1991 through 1996 at a large discount brokerage firm; at some point during those years, the investors switched from trading by phone to trading on line. (Because the firm, which the professors declined to identify, was a discount brokerage house, the investors were never receiving brokers' advice.) Over all, the professors found that the fortunes of the investors took a turn for the worse once they moved on line. Before the switch, these investors turned in stellar performances, beating the market by an average of more than two percentage points a year. Such performance not only put them ahead of the vast majority of individual investors, but it was also enough to beat more than 90 percent of mutual fund managers. Yet after the switch, the investors lagged behind the market by more than three percentage points a year, on average -- a significant reversal of more than five percentage points. Intuitively, the downturn might not look that surprising, since we generally expect several fat years to be followed by lean ones. But that doesn't explain the returns of these investors: Speaking strictly statistically, an investor's performance in any given year is totally unrelated to that of the previous year, just as the fifth flip of a coin has a 50-50 chance of coming up tails, even after four consecutive heads. SO what happened to these investors? The professors dug deeply and came up with several findings. They observed, for example, that not only did the turnover rates rise sharply for these investors' portfolios, to 96 percent a year from 74 percent, but that these investors also became twice as speculative in their trading. The professors devised a particularly creative way to measure that speculation. They defined speculative trading very narrowly, as any sale of an entire position in a stock at a profit, followed by a new purchase of any other stock within three weeks. In that way, the professors virtually eliminated trades for which the investors' motives might have been other than speculative -- like tax-loss selling or raising cash. Of course, these investors could justify their new on-line hyperactivity if their replacement stocks performed better than their old ones, as they generally did before the switch. In fact, during those early years, the investors looked like geniuses: Their replacement stocks outperformed the stocks they sold at an annualized rate of more than four percentage points. After the switch, however, the investors started looking like Wrong-Way Corrigans: Their sold stocks outperformed their eventual replacements at an annualized rate of more than five percentage points. In other words, once they went on line, these investors would have been a lot better off had they resisted the temptation to sell their original stocks. The professors' conclusion strikes me as quite fair: Over all, these investors never had genuine ability, but merely experienced a run of luck before switching to on-line trading. Confusing the bull market with brains, they became overconfident, trading much more often and more speculatively than they did before -- to their own detriment. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Bolder, but Wiser?" The behavior of investors changes as they go on line, according to a study of customers of a discount brokerage firm. After moving on line, their portfolio turnover rate rose, as did their percentage of speculative trades. Data are from a study of more than 1,600 investors from 1991 to 1996.  Turnover rate Before trading on line: 74% After trading on line: 96%  Speculative trades as a percentage of total Before: 16% After: 30%  (Source: On-Line Investors: Do the Slow Die First? by Brad M. Barber and Terrance Odean)

title: 2 Providers Of Net Access Set to Merge
body: Earthlink Network Inc. and Mindspring Enterprises Inc., two pioneers in the business of selling Internet access, announced a merger agreement yesterday, with hopes of more effectively challenging America Online. The merger, a $1.7 billion stock swap, creates a company with 2.8 million subscribers. It will be named Earthlink but will operate out of Atlanta, Mindspring's home. Earthlink is now based in Pasadena, Calif. The combined entity would leapfrog Internet services from AT&T and Microsoft to become the clear but distant second-place service provider in the unitedstates behind America Online, which has 18 million subscribers. "We're able to aspire to something that is more exciting than we could in the past," said Charles Brewer, who started Mindspring out of his apartment in 1994 and saw it grow into one of the top five Internet service providers in the country. "Our goal is to be No. 1 in the world," added Mr. Brewer, who will become chairman of the new company. The merger of two companies that symbolized success for the small Internet service provider underscores what some industry observers see as inevitable consolidation in the Internet access market. Yet, the number of small Internet service providers continues to grow, now standing at more than 5,000 in the unitedstates and Canada, and entrepreneurs are pursuing alternatives to the subscription-fee business model. Netzero, for example, is a growing advertising-based service that is free to consumers. The industry is also being changed by high-speed, or broadband, access with digital subscriber lines and cable modems. Such access threatens the dominance of the traditional dial-up service provider, while Earthlink, Mindspring and America Online are forming partnerships to offer these broadband technologies. But the real competition among service providers today is to add subscribers, and Earthlink and Mindspring insisted that their merger would allow them to do that more efficiently. The companies said they planned to merge back-office operations and to redirect some of the savings to marketing. "We're both spending a tremendous amount toward accelerated growth," said Charles Betty, EarthLink's president and chief executive who will be chief executive of the combined company. "We stepped back and said 'Wow, we should be doing this together.' " Earthlink projected adding 230,000 subscribers in the third quarter, while Mindspring will add roughly 80,000 new subscribers. As of March, each company had 1.1 million subscribers, according to Jupiter Communications, a newyork-based market research firm. For the second quarter, Mindspring reported revenue of $86 million and operating losses of $12.7 million, while Earthlink reported revenue of $78 million and operating losses of $28.5 million. The new company will trade under the Earthlink stock symbol, ELNK, on Nasdaq. Mindspring shareholders will receive one share of the new company for each share they hold, while Earthlink shareholders will receive 1.615 shares. Mr. Betty said the company would have a combined $500 million in cash to seed the marketing effort. He said the deal should be completed by the first quarter of 2000. Earthlink shares fell $1.125, to $42.375, on the Nasdaq stock market. Mindspring shares dropped $5.50, to $27.375.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
S.E.C. Chief Wants One Site For Posting All Stock Prices
body: The chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission proposed a system yesterday for displaying electronically all orders to buy and sell unitedstates stocks and called such a central posting essential to preserve the integrity of the nation's stock markets. Arthur Levitt, the S.E.C. chairman, outlined his general vision for the financial markets yesterday after months of wrenching changes in how stocks are traded. New electronic trading systems have emerged, on-line trading by individuals has exploded, trading by small investors has begun to occur outside the exchanges' hours of operation and the exchanges themselves have proposed becoming publicly traded for-profit companies. Mr. Levitt seems most concerned that if trading continues to migrate to the new electronic market systems, investors may not get the best prices. Information about orders and transactions across the entire market are not now available in any one place. Technology, he said, allows the creation of a central system in which investors will be fully informed about prices everywhere, from the newyork Stock Exchange, the Nasdaq market, the American Stock Exchange and the new systems. He stressed that he was asking for the development of a technology that would allow all orders to be shown to investors, not an institution or a place where all orders would be executed. In this way, competition would continue, along with innovation and pressure to keep costs low. "The beauty of this is technology has taken us to the point where we may be able to enjoy the benefits of competition while getting the benefits of centrality," Mr. Levitt said. Speaking at Columbia Law School, Mr. Levitt also said he was intrigued by the possibility of creating a single, self-regulatory organization to oversee the markets but suggested that each exchange continue its own surveillance. The exchanges now have self-regulating units, but those units could be compromised or at least conflicted if the exchanges become public companies with an obligation to provide the highest return to shareholders. In other areas, he was most concerned about fairness. He urged the elimination of a rule by the newyork Stock Exchange that prohibits the trading of certain stocks by exchange members anywhere other than on the exchange floor. Fees charged to outside participants by the new electronic stock networks, he said, should also be eliminated.  And the options exchanges, which have been effective monopolies for decades, must open their doors to true competition, he said. "I recognize the industry's inherent resistance to change," Mr. Levitt said in an interview before the speech. "But I'm willing to fight very hard to move in the direction of change rather than being a custodian." Frank Zarb, the chairman of the National Association of Securities Dealers, the parent of the Nasdaq market, applauded Mr. Levitt. "I think he's saying to us, 'You guys get this stuff fixed or we're going to have to see that it gets fixed,' " Mr. Zarb said. "It's a good clear menu of the major issues facing the industry -- a call for bold change when bold change is required." Mr. Levitt said his ideas were a result of yearlong deliberations with the S.E.C. staff and conversations with market participants. The proposals will result in stock markets that are more open, accessible and fair to all investors, he said. But given that so much about Wall Street remains hidebound even as great change has rocked the industry, the proposals will displease many in the business, both new and established. The organization that appears to have the most to lose under the proposals is the newyork Stock Exchange, though its chairman said yesterday that the exchange was prepared to reinvent itself with the times. Mr. Levitt, 68, who has been the nation's chief securities regulator since 1993, this month became the longest-serving chairman in the commission's history. With the speech, he sought to position himself as the chairman who seized technological advancements as a way to level the playing field for investors and market participants of all types. Mr. Levitt couched his speech by asking many questions. This will surely disappoint market players who were looking for answers from the nation's top regulator and a clearer regulatory blueprint, though initial reaction to the speech yesterday was strongly positive. Jack Brennan, chief executive of the Vanguard Group, the mutual fund giant, said, "While innovation is a great thing, you always want to know that the innovation taking place is happening with integrity." Mr. Levitt made clear that he was not giving the securities industry its marching orders. Rather he was trying to shape the dialogue that must occur before changes can be made. "I want to see the natural genius of the marketplace give vent to a better, cheaper, more protected market," he said. Because commission approval is necessary for market participants that want to expand their businesses, however, Mr. Levitt's opinion is critical for firms and exchanges that want to move quickly to form alliances, make deals or extend their hours without losing business to more nimble competitors. The stock markets are undergoing rapid change and appear on the verge of even more competition, with demand growing for instant access. While innovations like new electronic markets, extended trading hours and on-line trading have helped drive some investors' costs down, there is a potential downside. Individuals buying and selling stocks may not be getting the best prices on their trades because the various marketplaces are not connected. In some cases, an order placed in one venue may be completed there even though a better price may be available elsewhere. And though some electronic networks already offer trading into the evening, there are relatively few orders, meaning investors cannot be assured of getting as good a price as they would in a bigger pool of orders. With his proposal for a centralized system for stock market information, Mr. Levitt is treading on turf explored by another S.E.C. chairman, Harold M. Williams, in the late 1970's. Back then, the commission set out to help the securities industry create a national market system through a central book of orders to buy and sell stocks. But the powerful Wall Street brokerage firms and exchanges blocked the plan and it quietly died. Luckily for Mr. Levitt, Wall Street may not be as opposed to the proposal this time around. One reason is that technology has advanced sufficiently since the 1970's that such a system could easily be created. Moreover, many of the established brokerage firms own parts of the new trading networks, giving them a foot in the old and the new camps. Bernard L. Madoff, principal of Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities, a market-making firm that stands to lose from one of Mr. Levitt's proposals, sounded sanguine yesterday. "A central limit-order book -- that's something we have to see more of what it would look like," he said. "It's been something that has been talked about for a very long time. It's been difficult to achieve because of turf wars but probably if it ever has a chance of happening it would have a better chance today." Mr. Zarb said the securities dealers group would soon be filing with regulators its plans for a central order book that has many of the characteristics described by Mr. Levitt. "What we're going to be filing with the S.E.C. this week or next has all the tools," Mr. Zarb said. Previous efforts to create such a book failed to win broad member support, because some big dealers worried that by running such a centralized order book, the group would be competing with them. Mr. Levitt's idea for a single self-regulatory organization to police the investment arena is not exactly new. What was new in his speech was his suggestion that the crucial duty of market surveillance would remain local and performed at each exchange, close to the operations. The S.E.C. chairman said that plans by both the Big Board and the Nasdaq to issue shares in their organizations to the public could not be pursued until well-researched plans for spinning off both exchanges' regulatory arms were provided to the commission. "We must be certain that their plan to create a separation is sufficiently definite," Mr. Levitt said in an interview yesterday. "There can be no backing away from it. There won't be any game playing." Some market experts had hoped that a single independent regulator would be a condition of any conversion by the exchanges to public companies, but Mr. Levitt stopped short of insisting on that. Even the tradition-bound newyork Stock Exchange took Mr. Levitt's calls for change in stride. A central order book appears to be a problem for the exchange since it would include those stocks whose executions are now handled exclusively by specialists on its floor. Mr. Levitt's call for the elimination of a rule by the exchange that bars members from trading listed shares off the floor, known as Rule 390, would bring more competition for the exchange's specialists as well. Nevertheless, Richard A. Grasso, chairman of the exchange, said his organization was up to the challenge. "Change driven by customer patterns and by technological advancement necessitates reinvention," he said in an interview. "Those that reinvent themselves will succeed beyond their wildest expectations. We have always been successful at reinventing ourselves." The S.E.C. chairman expressed interest in opening options trading to increased competition as well. The established exchanges, including the Chicago Board Options Exchange and the American Stock Exchange, have had a virtual monopoly on the options they traded. Under a gentleman's agreement, they did not trade each other's offerings. But they are now beginning to trade each other's options and feeling the heat from an electronic trading system, the International Securities Exchange in newyork, which expects to begin trading options in March. Mr. Levitt pointed out that the prospect of a new entrant has fostered some nascent competition among the established options exchanges. The S.E.C. studied four actively traded options and found that competition has reduced the effective costs of buying and selling them by a range of 22 percent to 44 percent. Interestingly, the new electronic communication networks, such as the Island E.C.N., that have brought much of the recent upheaval to Wall Street also stand to lose if Mr. Levitt succeeds in eliminating the fees they charge. Douglas M. Atkin, chief executive of Instinet, the oldest, most established electronic trading network, was enthusiastic about Mr. Levitt's ideas, even though his company reaps fees. "If you get to an efficient market structure, a pure central limit order book," Mr. Atkin said, "then there's no need for E.C.N. fees." Presumably, the networks would get more business if quotes were more widely disseminated and could alter their business model in other ways to remain profitable. The electronic networks, however, will benefit from other ideas floated by Mr. Levitt, such as the creation of a centralized order book and the elimination of the rule restricting trading in certain Big Board stocks. Harold S. Bradley, senior vice president and portfolio manager at American Century Investment Management in Kansas City, Mo., said he was struck by how open the commission seemed to the young firms. "It's mind-blowing how realistic their thinking is about the evolution and change in the marketplace," he said. "This is an exciting and visionary statement from an agency that has traditionally protected the monopoly players." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Key Issues" Arthur Levitt, chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, identified several areas of the financial markets as ripe for change. Here are his suggestions and who the likely winners and losers would be if the proposals were adopted.  CENTRAL BOOK OF ORDERS Calls on market participants to study the possibility of a central system to display all orders for stocks in the unitedstates. This would give investors much more information on the current market in each stock and the amount of interest in it, and enable them to track trades. WINNERS -- Investors LOSERS -- newyork Stock Exchange; Nasdaq market makers and American Stock Exchange  OPTIONS MARKETS Calls for the options markets to be linked, so that investors can be assured of seeing all the prices available from many dealers. Some market centers must also increase their capacity. Finally, more competition must be encouraged. WINNERS -- International Securities Exchange, a new electronic marketplace for options; investors, as competition results in lower prices and better execution if all prices are quoted in a central system LOSERS -- Chicago Board Options Exchange; Pacific Exchange; Philadelphia Stock Exchange and American Stock Exchange  E.C.N. FEES Calls for an end to the fees charged by electronic communication networks to outsiders trading on the networks. Nasdaq market makers do not charge such fees. WINNERS -- Market makers and investors LOSERS -- Electronic communication networks like Instinet, Island E.C.N., Archipelago and others  newyork STOCK EXCHANGE RULE 390 Calls for an end to Rule 390, which prohibits members of the exchange from dealing in certain listed securities off an exchange, say on Instinet. WINNERS -- Electronic communication networks, Nasdaq market makers and the National Association of Securities Dealers, the parent of Nasdaq LOSERS -- newyork Stock Exchange; Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities, a firm that trades both N.Y.S.E. and Nasdaq stocks and would see increased competition. (pg. C8)

title: Realnetworks, Realjukebox and Finally, It Seems, Real Money
body: Realjukebox is starting to earn some real money for its developer, Realnetworks Inc. Realnetworks, a Seattle company that makes software for sending audio and video over the Internet, will announce a series of alliances on Thursday with companies that will sell products or provide information to users of Realjukebox, a software product that allows people to copy, store and play music from compact disks on their personal computers. Checkout.com, the new Internet entertainment Web site co-founded by the Hollywood talent manager Michael Ovitz, will become the exclusive on-line vendor of compact disks and provider of entertainment information for users of Realjukebox. Another company, 800.com, will be the exclusive seller of electronic products, while MP3.com will provide music that users of Realjukebox can download free. Terms of the deals are not being disclosed. But industry executives said that Checkout.com would pay Realnetworks at least $8 million; the two other deals are somewhat smaller.
