Together the deals would represent a nice lift for Realnetworks, which had revenue in its latest quarter of $28 million and a net loss of $270,000. "Realnetworks is getting to a new level of scale in terms of the impact we have and our ability to derive economic benefit from it," said Rob Glaser, the company's chairman and chief executive. He said income from the agreements would be spread over several quarters. Realjukebox, which can be downloaded free over the Internet, has gained 10 million users since its introduction in May. The software allows users to store music from compact disks on their hard drives, to download music from the Web and to play back the music on their personal computers or download it to new portable digital music players. That large base of users is what made it attractive to Checkout.com, a new entertainment service that hopes the deal will drive users to its Web site as it fights to distinguish itself from numerous other on-line music vendors. "It's not like we're just throwing some ad banners out there," said Richard Wolpert, Checkout.com's acting chief executive. Checkout.com, a privately held company based in Beverly Hills, Calif., bills itself as an entertainment portal, providing information like biographies and concert reviews, in addition to selling compact disks. Its other big backer is Ronald W. Burkle, a billionaire supermarket entrepreneur. Mr. Ovitz and Mr. Burkle have purchased several Internet companies to augment their fledgling Internet empire. Realnetworks is also announcing a deal with Sony Music to allow consumers who play a forthcoming album by Rage Against the Machine on their computers using Realjukebox to download an unreleased track of the band's live performance at Woodstock this summer. Realjukebox users will also be able to preview three tracks from the record about a month before its scheduled release in early November. The announcements come as Realnetworks begins shipping the final version of Realjukebox. The 10 million downloaded until now have been beta versions.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Beanie Baby Scams And Identity Thefts
body: THE world's flea markets, souks and bazaars have always been magnets for the criminally minded, from mountebanks and snake-oil salesmen to plain old-fashioned pickpockets. It should be no surprise, then, to learn that the global marketplace that has sprung up on the World Wide Web has drawn its share of crooks. By all objective measures, the rise of E-commerce has seen an accompanying rise in E-crime. Swindlers pose as merchants, taking people's money without ever sending along the wares. Then there are the technologically adept thieves, who have discovered on-line auction sites as a relatively safe and efficient way to fence their stolen goods. Most feared of all, perhaps, are the dreaded hackers who trespass in other people's networks, sometimes to vandalize, sometimes to steal data and, on occasion, to commit an especially pernicious crime that the authorities have started to call "identity theft": taking people's log-in names, passwords and credit card numbers to assume their identities and buy merchandise. None of this means that buying goods on the Internet has to be inherently dangerous. But if people want to avoid being cheated, law-enforcement officials and security experts caution, they must learn to recognize and avoid the risks of on-line shopping. Some of the best advice can seem counterintuitive. Consider the use of credit cards. One common fear expressed by people who may window-shop, but not buy, on the Internet is that it is risky to use credit cards on line. They worry that if they send their credit card information into cyberspace, it might be hijacked. But many law-enforcement officials and computer-security experts recommend that consumers use credit cards for on-line purchases as a precaution in the event they unwittingly do business with a bogus entity. They note that most fraudulent payments to on-line con artists are made by check or money order; some people even send cash. By using a credit card, they say, consumers can dispute fraudulent charges before they pay their bills. And in the unlikely event that a hacker steals a credit card number, Federal law limits liability to $50. So where, in the new and ever-changing world of E-commerce, does the danger lie? On-line auctions are among the riskiest forums, law-enforcement officials and outside monitors say. The Internet Fraud Watch, a monitoring group set up by the National Consumers League, reports that 68 percent of all the Internet-related fraud complaints it received in 1998 concerned auction sites. During the first six months of 1999, the group received 5,287 auction complaints, surpassing the 5,236 it received in all of 1998. The problem with on-line auctions is that their great advantage from a bargain hunter's perspective -- no middlemen -- is also their great disadvantage when it comes to security. So buyers must trust sellers to deliver what they promise. Needless to say, some sellers prove less than trustworthy. And they laugh all the way to the bank. "HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA," read a message that was posted on the Web in December 1996 by a man who California authorities now think used on-line auctions to defraud Beanie Baby fanatics out of thousands of dollars by pretending to sell stuffed animals that were never delivered. "All you people are really quite ridiculous. You make a deal via email, never see the person, never speak with the person and then get upset when you get ripped off. You must be a bunch of morons." The post ended, "I really hope, for my sake, that you all disregard the posting and continue as usual." The Beanie Baby scams continued until July, when the authorities arrested the man they say is responsible: James R. Denlinger Jr., 29, of San Jose, Calif., who was charged with computer fraud and conducting a false auction. He has pleaded not guilty. A closer look at his case, detailed by court records and the authorities, highlights some of the possible perils of on-line auctions. HE offered Beanie Babies on several small auction Web sites. Although he always listed his mailing address as a suite or an office room number, detectives say, he actually used private post-office boxes that he rented for short periods to collect the money. He always asked for checks or money orders. "He had a fleet of names, like Tom Richard and Ian Oerlin, that he would ask people to write checks or money orders to," said Detective Mike Hopkins, an investigator with the Sonoma County Sheriff's Department, who worked on the case. "But with a few strokes of the pen, Tom Richard could become James Richard Denlinger. And Ian Oerlin could become James Denlinger." On-line auction houses have taken steps to combat fraud. They recommend obtaining working phone numbers and verifying the physical addresses of sellers, possibly through on-line directories. Many auction houses advertise escrow services, which, for a small fee, will hold payments until the deal goes through to everyone's satisfaction. Several on-line auction houses offer services for person-to-person credit card payments. Some, like Ebay, offer insurance. And many have forums where customers can rate sellers. The only problem with that last safeguard is that many unscrupulous sellers rate themselves by disguising their email addresses and giving rave reviews. James Denlinger did, officials said. Quite a few thieves have looked at on-line auction sites and seen the perfect virtual fence, the way to sell their stolen property. Two men were arrested in newyork City in August on charges of trying to sell stolen cartoon art -- fittingly, an animation frame from Dr. Seuss's "How the Grinch Stole Christmas" -- on Ebay for $1,500. The winning bid was placed by an undercover detective, and the men were promptly arrested. IN Clearwater, Fla., a computer repairman was arrested in July after an undercover detective posed as a thief to sell the man stolen VCR's and then bought the VCR's back from him through an on-line auction site. "It's the perfect venue to commit crimes," said the detective, Javier Rosas of the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office. "Why go to a store where someone can recognize you or there might be a videotape to record you?" But the biggest fear of all, most law-enforcement officials and security experts agree, is identity theft. While an individual's liability is limited to $50 for lost or stolen credit cards, the aggravation and time it takes to repair damaged credit histories makes it nettlesome. Still, it is not necessarily a risk that Web shoppers run. The larger, more established sites use sophisticated encryption technology to protect their customers' credit card information. And while no encryption is impossible to crack, security experts say, it is so difficult and time consuming that it would hardly be worthwhile for a hacker to try to break into an individual email in transit just to get one card number. Most hackers would rather break into a corporate Web site to steal an entire database of credit card numbers. David Truog, an analyst with Forrester Research, a consulting firm in Cambridge, Mass., points out that it is easier for a waiter to steal a credit card number in a restaurant or for cellular-phone hackers to steal credit card numbers by eavesdropping on phone calls when people order from catalogues. When it comes to crime in the E-commerce arena, he said, "there's a legitimate reason for fear and trembling, but it should be the companies who are fearful because consumers are very well protected." And Dorothy E. Denning, a professor of computer science at Georgetown University who catalogued computer crimes in terrifying detail in her recent book "Information Warfare and Security," (Addison-Wesley), said that nothing in her research had dissuaded her from buying books on line. STILL, there are occasional horror stories. Recently, agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation worked on a case in newyork that they dubbed the Keystroke Snoopers. It involved a ring of people who used email to send a so-called Trojan horse, a disguised, malevolent computer program opened as an attachment, to thousands of people. This particular program captured all the keystrokes made by the people who received it. So the ringmasters were able to figure out the credit card numbers of people who ordered goods on line because they received a verbatim record of everything they typed on their keyboards before the card numbers were encrypted. The ring was made up of youngsters. "They made some purchases, but they seemed mostly interested in using the credit card numbers for pranks," said Edward M. Stroz, the special agent in charge of the computer unit in the F.B.I.'s newyork office. "One sent something like 16 dozen roses to somebody; another sent someone eight refrigerators." But law-enforcement agencies worldwide are gearing up to fight computer crime used for more malevolent purposes. In newyork City, Lieut. Christopher Malinowski pounds a cyberspace beat for the police. "Mostly, we find people are essentially doing the same old scams with new technology," he said. That is why the F.B.I. trains agents to handle garden-variety frauds perpetrated on computers, saving its computer experts for crimes unique to computers, like hackers who steal data. It is an ever-evolving field: new laws had to be drafted when investigators found in 1996 that they could not prosecute someone who stole data and emailed it across state lines under a statute prohibiting the interstate transportation of stolen property, because the electronic data were not considered "tangible." More laws are on the drawing board. "I constantly challenge myself to make sure I'm using the right analogy," Mr. Stroz said. "We're seeing new kinds of crimes, and if you start off with the wrong analogy, you can really get boxed into the wrong way of thinking about a problem."  'Buyer Beware' Goes for Web Shopping, Too  PAY BY CREDIT CARD -- If you don't get the merchandise, you can challenge the charge with the credit card company. Don't deal with cash-only sellers.  ENCRYPT, ENCRYPT, ENCRYPT -- Don't give your credit card number on line unless the latest security protocols are in place and you trust the company in question.  CHECK YOUR STATEMENTS -- Always review your credit card statements for billing errors or unauthorized purchases. correct problems immediately.  DO BUSINESS WITH COMPANIES YOU TRUST -- Only deal with companies you know and find to be reliable. Be sure you know what the company is and where it is.  PRINT OUT THE OFFER -- This way, you will have documentation if you need it.  WHEN IN DOUBT, CHECK IT OUT -- Ask the Better Business Bureau about the company's complaint record. However, fraudulent companies often come and go quickly, so the absence of a complaint record is no guarantee that a company is legitimate.  FOR AUCTIONS, TRY ESCROW -- For a fee, you can send payments to an escrow service, which will hold the money until everyone is satisfied with the sale.  KNOW WHOM YOU'RE DEALING WITH -- If you can't verify a seller's identity and figure out his or her real address and telephone number, don't do business.  FOR MORE INFORMATION -- Check for more tips at the Internet Fraud Watch Web site at www.fraud.org/ internet/inttip/inttip.htm, or the Federal Trade Commission's site, www.ftc.gov/bcp/menu-internet.htm. MICHAEL COOPER http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (David G. Klein)

title: Converting email From Spam to Steak
body: HANS PETER BRONDMO is building an Internet company squarely astride the most bitter cultural divide in the on-line world -- the war over privacy and email spam. There is possibly no more bitter issue for most Net-smart computer users and Web surfers than the tidal wave of digital junk mail -- known as spam -- that has accompanied the explosion of electronic commerce. When coupled with the tendency of every Web business to deploy data-mining software to chart each mouse click a visitor to a Web site makes, the Internet has increasingly become a battleground between digital-age marketeers and consumers. The email war and the ethical issues that commercial email raises hinge on the issue of "opt in," the use of a check box or other device to permit a computer user to decide whether to receive electronic mail and on what subjects. For example, a customer may want to be alerted to new books and compact disks by favorite authors and musicians or may want timely customer service information on an electronic device that he or she has bought. The new power and precision made possible by these Internet software technologies carry the potential for great abuses. "The important thing is whether or not it is genuinely opt in," said Tara Lemmey, the president of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit foundation here that focuses on civil liberties in cyberspace. "Then companies can get around spam and other issues as well." But it is just as easy to lose a potential customer when using commercial email incorrectly, Internet marketing experts say. "You can do great damage to your brand quite quickly," said Preston Dodd, an Internet analyst at Jupiter Communications, a market research company in newyork, "because your customer can respond to you almost instantly with a message like, 'Stop sending me these emails you blankety-blank.' " So Mr. Brondmo, who was born in Norway and graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Media Laboratory, is carefully picking his way through a potential minefield with Post Communications, the business he established in 1996 in a converted brewery in San Francisco's multimedia gulch. Today, Post provides clients with customized marketing programs based on software tools that blend traditional database marketing with email focused on specific consumers. Many Internet marketers are confident that email will transform the traditional direct-mail world, which came of age in the era of mainframe computers. Today's paper-based direct mail is based on information drawn from customer lists and demographic data. However, the precision and timeliness of mail-based direct marketing pale compared with the new world of on-line commerce. "In this business we get 90 percent of all of our responses in 48 hours compared to direct marketing, which takes six weeks," Mr. Brondmo said. Moreover, he argued, in building a relationship with a customer a company creates a much more powerful and receptive market. Selling to a new customer is 5 to 10 times more expensive than selling to an existing one, he said. That is because the marketing costs incurred in attracting new customers are extremely high compared with the cost of simply notifying existing customers that a new version of a product or a peripheral add-in is available. Mr. Brondmo contends that it is possible to stand the old $160 billion direct-mail marketing world on its head by honoring the Internet's cultural values of privacy and user control while using powerful server computers to identify specific customer preferences. "I don't believe there is a single customer in the world who wants a marketing relationship with a company," he said. "Customers want a service relationship." That subtle shift is one that has not caught on yet among direct marketers, who still use costly "campaigns" that send unsolicited mailings to millions of people. The direct-mail world has traditionally counted on the statistical assurance that it will obtain a 1 percent or 2 percent return from each mailing campaign. But in the digital world, where such campaigns are reviled as spam, there is an explosion of start-up companies creating a thriving industry variously known as digital direct marketing, on-line direct marketing or electronic direct marketing. In addition to Post, there is a variety of service providers and software application companies, like Digital Impact, Messagemedia, Media Synergy, Flycast, Connectify, Kana Communications and others, all trying to help companies build electronic relationships with customers. Many Internet commerce experts think that digital direct marketing is the future of electronic commerce on a much larger scale and that it will soon begin to displace other types of Internet advertising like banner advertisements. "The pace at which this thing is moving is remarkably fast," said Marc Singer, the author of "Net Worth" (Harvard Business School Press) and a co-leader of McKinsey & Company's Continuous Relationship Marketing business here. The reason, he said, is that electronic direct marketing is much more profitable than other on-line advertising strategies. He estimated that marketers who used banner ads spend as much as $1,500 a customer. In contrast, the per-customer cost of electronic mail marketing may be as low as $50 to $100. For Post's first client, the Palm Computing unit of the 3Com Corporation, the makers of the Pilot hand-held computer, email substantially changed the company's relationship with its customers by giving it more control. "When I saw what Post was doing, I remember coming back and telling my colleagues, 'I've seen the future of direct marketing,' " said Andrea Butter, who was then the marketing director for Palm's consumer business. With Post, Palm Computing, based in Santa Clara, Calif., created an email service program for its customers, asking whether they wished to receive occasional electronic messages about their Palm Pilots. Customers instructed the company on its Web page about the kind of communications that they wanted and how frequently they wanted email sent. The program was an instant success. The company had already compiled a large database of email addresses of its customers and 25 percent of them responded that they were interested in receiving email tips and marketing information. For Ms. Butter, the new program, which Palm named In-Sync, provided a clear way to save on staying in touch with her customers and to provide her with an avenue to advertise in a way in which the customers felt they were being served. "It turns the world upside down," she said. "A normal ad in a magazine is completely self-serving. As a marketer you have to realize that unless you can add value, the customer is likely to ignore you." Mr. Brondmo, who began his career as a software developer and has worked at Apple Computer and the video editing company Avid, among other enterprises, contends that the most important aspect of the new technology is that Post can transform a marketing relationship into a service relationship. Post's service can generate as many as 300,000 email messages an hour for a client, with far more individualized content than is possible in the off-line world. He says that if a company uses email effectively, it will have the opposite effect of spam. "The best possible email marketing campaign would be one where when the customer hasn't heard from you by midweek, he'll send you email asking why," he said. Post clients, like Music Boulevard and Harlequin Publishing, use the service to alert their customers to titles of interest. Wegmans, an East Coast supermarket chain and a Post client, is experimenting with shopping lists and recipes to build customer loyalty. For Ms. Lemmey of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, the intimate relationship that Internet marketers dream of raises other potential concerns that have not been addressed. WHILE there has been much glowing talk about the ability to determine user preference, so much so that it has been established as the Holy Grail of Internet marketing, there may be an unforeseen dark side, she said. "There is a fine line between targeting and redlining," she said. "What if an insurance company or an H.M.O. knows that you're reading about cancer or Alzheimer's disease on line? They may decide not to issue you an insurance policy or provide health care." She acknowledged that she did not know of such cases, but added that the discussion over the meaning of opt in was only beginning for the fledgling on-line direct marketing industry. "Just because someone says it's O.K. to use my personal information to target me doesn't say for how long," she said. Mr. Brondmo acknowledges that in the Internet world the values of the old direct-mail industry no longer apply. He says that if that new technology is to gain the confidence of the Internet generation, the companies will need to rethink their outlook. "I tell them, 'Ask not what you want to know about your customer, but rather what your customer wants to know about you," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Hans Peter Brondmo, the founder of Post Communications, and Cheryl Vedoe, the chief executive, hope to make consumers happy to see email. (Thor Swift for The newyork Times)

title: On-Line Trading Changes Landscape for Old-Line Brokerage Firms
body: LAST year, John (Launny) Steffens, the vice chairman of Merrill Lynch & Company, gave a speech at a computer trade show, warning of the financial risks of zealously trading stocks over the Internet. In March, he started doing it himself. Using the Internet meant he could place orders on weekends and when his financial consultant, as stockbrokers are known at Merrill Lynch, was out of town. "It was easier for me to do it and more convenient," he said in a recent interview at his office on the 32d floor of the World Financial Center. If anyone doubted the shift toward Internet investing, the trend became clear on June 1, when the nation's largest investment house, Merrill Lynch, announced that it was joining the Internet revolution. The firm said it would begin selling stocks on line for $29.95 a trade on Dec. 1, placing it in direct competition with discount firms like the Charles Schwab Corporation, which already offers Internet trading for that price. With Merrill Lynch lowering its drawbridge to accept cheap Internet trades, pressure mounts for other full-service brokerage firms to do the same. If they follow Merrill Lynch's lead, it will mean a move away from the tradition of brokers who advise and steer investors to stocks -- in return for a commission -- toward a world where consumers go on line to research, then buy, their own stocks. The question for consumers will be figuring out whether Internet trading is right for them and finding the cheapest, most reliable place to do it. The question for Merrill Lynch -- and by extension, the financial services industry -- is how it is going to pay for its gigantic infrastructure of brokers, sales staff and analysts if all the consumer cares about is finding a cheap and mechanically reliable place to trade. Already, on-line trading accounts for 37 percent of all retail trades, according to U.S. Bancorp Piper Jaffray, an investment firm. That percentage is expected to grow. A recent study by Gomez Advisors, a company that advises E-commerce companies, and Harris Interactive, an Internet market research company, found that 16 million more investors are likely candidates for on-line trading. But these rising numbers have been accompanied by costly glitches. One company's stock soared 38,000 percent after on-line investors bought it by mistake, using the wrong ticker symbol, Arthur Levitt, the chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, said in a May speech before the National Press Club. He also spoke of a woman who tried to buy $18,000 worth of stock but ended up owing more than $250,000 after the stock's price soared and her cancel orders didn't go through. Consumers need to be educated to prevent such gaffes, Mr. Levitt said. Investors must understand basics such as how to place a "limit" order, setting the maximum price they will pay for a rising stock, he said. And they need to factor in phone lines that can clog and systems that become overwhelmed, causing time lags in placing and canceling orders. The National Association of Securities Dealers, which operates the Nasdaq stock market, sent notices to member brokerage firms earlier this year with advice on how to educate consumers and on ways to design Internet systems to head off problems. But the bottom line is that those who buy on the Internet assume more responsibility for their investing behavior. COMMISSIONED stockbrokers were never objective advisers, said David S. Pottruck, president and co-chief executive of Charles Schwab, the discount brokerage firm, which has never used brokers to recommend stocks. They stood to gain financially by pushing stocks and investment products with large commissions, he said. But at least stockbrokers were trained on investments and worked under regulations requiring that they recommend only those stocks suitable to the client. Reputable brokers advised the unsophisticated against risky and expensive behavior, like rapid trading in and out of stocks. Investors who come up with their own stock picks must determine themselves whether a particular stock fits their financial goals and weigh the tax consequences of a trade. A way to alert buyers when they order a particularly inappropriate stock over the Internet may be developed, Mr. Litan said, but it is unlikely that an Internet brokerage firm would be required to refuse the order. The July shootings in Atlanta, where a day trader killed nine people at two brokerage offices after losing more than $100,000 in 15 days of trading, increased public awareness of the dangers of that particular form of investing. But people buying stocks from the comfort of home rather than at a day-trading office can also make big mistakes. Bill Bunke, 37, of Manhattan Beach, Calif., said he gave up his pool-maintenance business to trade stocks on line. In 18 months, Mr. Bunke said, he lost $25,000 of a $70,000 inheritance. "It was only $8 a trade, and by nature I like to gamble and it looked so easy to me," he said. "There were times I bought shares of a stock I'd never heard of before. I really got addicted." But others have taken a more deliberate approach and done well. Andrew Lohmann, a 36-year-old graduate student in Claremont, Calif., has never bought stocks any way but by using his computer. Since 1995, he has turned the $4,000 he decided he could afford to lose into $50,000 by buying stocks like Schwab and America Online. Robert Litan, who buys stocks over the Internet for some of the same reasons more than five million other Americans do, said, "It's so easy." He began investing on line in 1998, four years after investors first bypassed stockbrokers with the click of a mouse. But Mr. Litan is not just another guy in search of cheap Internet brokerage commissions, which average less than $16 a trade, a fraction of what a full-service broker would charge. As director of economic studies at the Brookings Institution, a research group in Washington, he knows that dangers lurk for naive Internet investors -- not to mention for the nation's 607,000 brokers, many of whom he thinks will soon be forced out of the job. Pouring a large chunk of one's savings into individual stocks isn't a good idea for the average investor, Mr. Litan said. Most people would be better off in mutual funds, managed by professionals, he said, rather than trying to decipher the analysts' reports increasingly offered by on-line brokers. But the real risk, Mr. Litan said, is to the livelihoods of brokers, who on average earned $168,726 in 1998, according to the Securities Industry Association. Some investors, particularly wealthy ones, will always be willing to pay to be coddled by a hands-on broker, he said. But "for the mass market, the traditional broker will become irrelevant," he predicted. Why pay high commissions for a broker's advice when most of them can't beat the market anyway? he asked. Merrill Lynch executives announced their move onto the Internet after traveling to Silicon Valley and Austin, Tex., early this year, where they heard from customers clamoring for on-line investing. At the same time, the company rolled out a second program it hopes will skim off investors who want access to Internet investing but are willing to pay for more personalized service. For a fee starting at $1,500 and increasing with the size of the account, Merrill will provide unlimited trading over the Internet or with a broker, as well as advice on stocks and financial planning tools. That program began July 1. Both programs come with checking accounts and debit cards. Merrill Lynch says it will continue to offer traditional, commission-based broker trades, with customers paying $35 to $105 in commissions for up to 100 shares, depending on the stock's price. "Some clients like the traditional relationship," said Susan Thomson, a Merrill Lynch spokeswoman. Investors with at least $50,000 to invest can also opt for professional money managers. Merrill Lynch executives stress that the change simply means its brokers will focus more on fee-based financial consulting and less on pushing stocks for a commission. Full-service brokerage firms have been moving in that direction for years, said Samuel Hayes, professor of finance at the Harvard Business School. Some brokers will continue to act like salesmen, he said, drawing in customers they then direct to the firms' fee-based investment products -- mutual funds, trusts and money managers. Merrill Lynch has stressed financial planning in training its brokers over the last decade, Miss Thomson said. Its certified financial management program, begun in 1980, was enhanced last year, she said. Whether consumers accustomed to thinking of brokers as salesmen will start seeing them as objective financial consultants remains in question, Mr. Litan said. "It wouldn't surprise me if the effort fails." BUT Mr. Steffens -- who got his start at the firm in its broker training program 36 years ago, and whose son, Andrew, is a Merrill Lynch broker in North Carolina -- predicts the ranks of Merrill's 15,000 "financial consultants" will grow, not diminish. "I would like to have 17,000 to 18,000 five years from now," he said. Still, even Merrill Lynch recognizes its brokers probably will be earning less, at least initially -- up to 18 percent less, by in-house estimates, Miss Thomson said. The firm has agreed to make up the difference for the next two years. In a West Coast office, a new Merrill Lynch broker said the firm's shift away from commissioned brokers toward fee-based financial consulting comes as no surprise. In-house, he said, old-style stockbrokers are viewed as dinosaurs. "And they went belly up and legs up." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: John Steffens thinks on-line trading will mean more jobs but lower salaries for brokers. (Merrill Lynch)

title: On Many Travel Web Sites, a Limited View of the Beaten Path
body: AMID great fanfare, 9,800 independent travel agencies joined together earlier this year to set up a new Internet site called Vacation.com. They billed it as "the leading source of active, fun vacations on the Web." Users presumably could find whatever vacation opportunities they might crave. Several months later, its cruise offerings included many familiar names. But 11 major lines -- Princess, Cunard, Silversea, Radisson Seven Seas and Disney among them -- were conspicuously absent. If you wanted to sail the Mexican Riviera on a Princess love boat or sail northern Europe in acclaimed Silversea luxury, you would be wasting your time at Vacation.com. A search of the same site for golf resorts in the unitedstates, another category, produced 58 vacation packages, mostly at chain hotels. Fifty-three were marketed by the same tour company, Delta Dream Vacations, which is hardly alone in the field. As for skiing, all the site's resorts were in the Rocky Mountains; none were in the Northeast or overseas. For Colorado, there were 22 skiing choices, 21 of them Delta Dream Vacations packages. Such experiences illustrate a big problem consumers face when dealing with travel marketing in cyberspace: many sites are more promotional than informational. They cover companies or resorts that pay in some way to be included or that let them provide the material. Sometimes they allow both, which means that the lists are often limited and not objective. Nevertheless, the sites draw hordes of consumers, whether or not it's profitable business. Record sales are reported monthly, and predictions for the next few years are huge. Considerable sales attention and advertising have focused on Priceline.com (www.priceline .com), a reverse auction in which the buyer names the price he is willing to pay for an airline ticket or a hotel room, and Priceline shops it among suppliers. If a ticket or a room meets that price, the buyer wins and is committed to accept the deal. (Priceline obtains a credit card number in advance.) If the price is not met, the buyer owes nothing but does not have another free chance to bid. The company says that sales have been strong. Spot checks of consumers have indicated mixed results. Some said they received good deals, but others complained about having to accept flights at odd hours from alternate airports, with connections to boot. Meanwhile, many travel sites look great but are thin or lopsided in content. Other sites try hard to be comprehensive, informative and fair, but cannot feature every name or place in the industry. Consider Restaurant Row (www.restaurantrow.com), based in suburban newyork. It calls itself "the world's largest dining guide," covering more than 100,000 restaurants in 47 countries. It recently listed 1,433 restaurants in newyork City and a surprising 1,007 in Philadelphia. (That city's nationally acclaimed Le Bec-Fin was missing, however, although Restaurant Row did include Le Bec Fin in Rio de Janeiro.) To add restaurants -- the site's advertised goal is 400,000 by the millennium -- it seeks "volunteer recruiters" to entice restaurateurs to submit prices, hours, menus, photographs and reviews. The recruiter who signs up the most restaurants in one month receives $100. At the same time, the dining public is asked to rate the listed restaurants on line. With two reviews, the "21" Club in Manhattan is rated an overall 4.0. (The site doesn't say 4.0 out of what.) "The food may not be the best, but this place is not famous for nothing," an anonymous reviewer wrote. Through so-called strategic partnerships, a mainstay of electronic commerce, many other sites tap into the Restaurant Row database. So, if you're looking for restaurant suggestions from the sites of CBS News, Nation's Restaurant News or the 1010 WINS radio station, you have tapped into Restaurant Row, although sometimes they offer other restaurant databases as well. Partnerships, licensing agreements and advertising are largely what keep travel E-commerce going. With airlines cutting back on commissions and promoting their own Web sites, on-line agencies like Travelocity (www.travelocity.com), Expedia (www. expedia.com) and Preview Travel (www.previewtravel.com) are hurting, even though they report soaring sales. They say that they don't mind if people are site-seeing, as long as they visit often, which impresses advertisers and partners. There are several important ramifications in the crush to market travel on line. One is that too many companies do essentially the same thing -- dozens, maybe hundreds offer help in planning vacations. A recent test of a dozen sites promising the lowest air fares took 2 hours and 17 minutes to browse and turned up few significant differences. Meanwhile, the same material can appear on many, many sites. For example, the Hotel Reservations Network (www.hoteldiscounts.com) says it has partnerships with 500 other sites, which means that you can delve into its database through Expedia, Travelocity and Preview Travel sites, to name just three, as well as through its own network. When I searched Travelocity for a double room at the Sheraton newyork for Aug. 24, I was quoted a price of $279 a night. In a Travelocity section linked to the Hotel Reservations Network, I was quoted $199.95 for the same thing. The two partners weren't fully integrated; I had to search one and then the other, although I had reached both through Travelocity. This presents a challenge to the prospective traveler. Just about anything you may want to know about travel is somewhere; your task is to determine how to find the sites most suitable for you and try to navigate them. When several sites share the same database, what the public sees can sometimes vary sharply from one to another. Microsoft's Expedia and the Web site of Continental Airlines (www.flycontinental.com) share the same flight-booking system. But if you request information about fares and schedules between Philadelphia and Denver, for example, Expedia will produce a large range on several airlines. Continental, however, will offer only its own flights, even if they are less convenient and more expensive than Expedia's. In time, the challenge to consumers' tolerance will doubtless diminish. Weaker sites will drop out as they realize how elusive Internet profits can be. For the present, though, three principles are important for the consumer: define as specifically as possible what you are looking for; become familiar with sites that you trust so that you learn their strong points and weaknesses and how to navigate them best, and use those same sites whenever you pursue a travel interest. I learned to rely on Zagat (www.zagat .com) for restaurant recommendations in metropolitan areas of the unitedstates and in some cities abroad. The site covers a range of prices and tastes, with capsule reviews and ratings drawn from hundreds, sometimes thousands, of readers' dining experiences. In cities not covered by Zagat, I search the Web for the place I'm going to and see what it produces. A search of Yahoo (www.yahoo.com) for restaurants in Mumbai (formerly called Bombay), India, led me to the "Guide to Bombay Restaurants" (theory.tifr.res.in/bombay/disclaim.html), compiled by Sourendu Gupta and two of his colleagues in the department of theoretical physics at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research. Mr. Gupta, who says he eats out twice a month, was tired "of half-baked restaurant reviews in the city newspapers." He may not be a professional gourmet, but his comments sound authentic to a former newyork Times correspondent who lived in India many years ago. Throughout the Internet, much attention is focused on security, as it should be. In travel, as elsewhere, a major deterrent to buying on line is unease about providing credit card data and other personal information. I have used my Visa card to buy airline tickets and book hotels on line, and I have never been burned. To promote security, or at least a facade of it, travel sites are increasingly requiring visitors to register a user name and password. Security experts recommend that passwords be combinations of letters and numbers, like XV78cT9q, and be changed periodically. And, of course, we're told not to use the same password at more than one site. Registration is typically free, but that's not much help when you are expected to remember or to keep a handy record of two dozen or more user ID's and 28 passwords. All said, here are some travel sites that are particularly helpful: *Smarterliving (www. smarterliving.com). A multipurpose site that shines with free E-mail service that alerts users to the weekly airline discount specials from airports of their choice. *1Travel.com (www.1travel .com). An on-line agency focusing on discounted travel arrangements. Its exceptional features are a highly informative section written by Terry Trippler, an air-fare specialist, who explains complicated airline rules, and an "airline savings tool kit" with valuable suggestions on how to save money. *Great Outdoor Recreation Pages (www.gorp.com). A large directory of international outdoor travel programs. Little is missing. *Travel section of About.com (home.about.com/travel). A comprehensive set of guided links to an enormous variety of travel-related topics. *Skymall Newsroom (www.skymalltravel.com/ newsroom). A compendium of travel news from a variety of sources, including The Associated Press, CNN, USA Today, Reuters and The Wall Street Journal.  Rules of the Road for On-Line Vacation Planning NAVIGATING cyberspace to get the most out of travel planning can be tricky, time consuming and frustrating. But diligence and patience can pay off if you follow a few rules: BE SPECIFIC When searching the Internet for, say, fall foliage trips, pick a search engine -- www.yahoo.com, www. altavista.com or www.hotbot.com, for example -- and search for terms like "fall foliage" and "Vermont" and perhaps "restaurants" and "bed and breakfasts" as well.  LOOK CLOSELY -- When a site is appealing, sample it for the amount and variety of choices and quality of descriptive material. Who supplied the material? Sometimes the site will tell you; sometimes you can guess or can't tell. If there is no information about the company or the people who run the site, be careful. Would you buy a car from a classified advertisement without first seeing the car or its owner?  VISIT OFTEN -- When a site satisfies you, get to know it well by using it repeatedly, assuming your travels warrant it. You will quickly learn what the site can and cannot offer, plus you will discover searching tricks that save time.  KEEP NAMES NEARBY -- If you must register to use a site, carefully record your user name and password and keep the record near your computer.  KEEP RECORDS -- Keep careful records of any travel transactions, and back up important information that you have downloaded into your computer.  ASK FOR HELP -- With commercial sites, don't hesitate to E-mail customer support if you have problems, but be patient about waiting for a reply.   PAUL GRIMES http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Leann Johnson)

title:
PERSONAL FAVORITES;
CARTER BREY, Principal Cellist, New York Philharmonic
body: Frank Music Company (www.frankmusiccompany.com) -- The Frank Music Company is to newyork City musicians what the Louisville Slugger Company is to baseball players. Life would be conceivable without it, but why bother? The fact that Heidi, the proprietress beloved by thousands, now has her catalogue on line has done nothing to diminish the low-tech charm of this quirkiest and most complete of sheet music sources. 1-800-Flowers (www.saflowers.com) -- This should be a required bookmark for guys. You're out of town, you've settled back with "The Terminator 3" and room service and you just remembered with a start that tomorrow is your anniversary? No problem. Plug in your laptop, navigate over to this site and order a dozen red big ones to be delivered tomorrow morning. You're golden. Travelocity (www.travelocity.com) -- I find this site indispensable for planning itineraries and purchasing tickets when I can't get my travel agent on the phone instantly, which is usually. Air travel, hotels, it's all at your fingertips with a free registration. You can tap into their database and view information organized, for example, by schedule, price and carrier. BMT Micro (www.bmtmicro.com) -- A wonderful shareware site for users of Windows, OS/2 and Linux. Very well organized. No penguin mascots. I run OS/2 and Linux on my laptop and am probably the world's only principal cellist able to write a shell script to run on a Unix machine. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: Speed It Up, Webmaster, We're Losing Billions Every Second!
body: PETER GRANOFF knows how important it is to be slow. He is in a business where for centuries patience has not just been a virtue but also a necessity. He sells wine. The best wine can take years to make; even the very cheapest still must sit in its bottle for several months. "There's little way to speed that up," said Bill Newlands, Mr. Granoff's colleague. Indeed, Mr. Granoff said, "The whole point of wine is to slow life down. It has to do with community, with family, with friends, with relaxation over meals, with conversation. These are the ways in which we maintain our sanity." But Mr. Granoff sells wine over the Internet. He is a proprietor of a five-year-old company that last week changed its name to Wine.com (www.wine.com) but as Virtual Vineyards (www.virtualvineyard.com) was one of the earliest E-commerce sites -- "We were one of the first half-dozen sites to process credit cards over the Web," he said -- and one that is now faced with several new competitors. And so he would kill to save a second. "Site speed is of paramount importance," said Mr. Granoff, a master sommelier who suddenly sounds exactly like any of the hundreds of thousands of Web entrepreneurs. "We're constantly looking for ways in which we can leverage the technology. It's a never-ending process. Any E-commerce company worth its dot-com is engaged in a similar endeavor." That is why his company has hired Keynote, the first of a growing number of "Web-performance measurement companies," whose mission is to help get Web sites up to speed. "We really can't afford to be oblivious to this issue," Mr. Granoff said. Call it speed anxiety. Over the last year, an entire industry has sprouted up to measure, assess and suggest ways to improve "ease of navigation" and Web page design and to help avoid system crashes, which brought unwelcome headlines recently to Amazon.com and Ebay. On the Web right now, "performance" is almost entirely synonymous with speed -- the time it takes a customer to download the first page of a site, to link to another page or to buy something. Speed is so important for on-line brokers, whose livelihood depends on making many transactions throughout the day, that the Government may hold hearings on it; the General Accounting Office is researching on-line trading delays. The need is even more obvious for corporations whose reputation is based on the promise of speed, like Federal Express and United Parcel Service. All of these subscribe to Web-performance companies. It would be hard to find an E-commerce site that feels exempt from the pressure to go faster, whether it sells wine, art or long, leisurely novels. Art.com uses Service Metrics, another measurement company, and Amazon.com subscribes to Keynote, as does its main competitor in on-line book sales, Barnesandnoble.com, which also uses Gifwizard, Website Garage and Webcriteria. "Consumers are busy; they don't have time to wait 30 seconds to load," said Niel Robertson, a founder of Service Metrics, based in Boulder, Colo. "The idea is to get in and get out, to do it quickly. Companies live and die by this rule." Alistair Williamson, a founder of Webcriteria in Portland, Ore., added, "Even if your network is performing flawlessly, a speed bump -- a page that takes twice as long as a previous page -- could drive customers away." Umang Gupta, the head of Keynote, based in San Mateo, Calif., likes to say that "on the Internet, your competitor is just a click away." "If you go to Amazon.com or Barnesandnoble, there's not much difference in selection, in the look and feel of the pages," Mr. Gupta said. "You won't be able to tell the difference at 10 brokerage sites. The difference usually comes down to speed -- the speed of downloading or the speed of delivery." The Web-performance industry is not subtle about tapping into speed anxiety, speed envy and speed greed. Keynote commissioned Zona Research to conduct a study this year into "the economic impact of unacceptable download times." Titled "The Need for Speed," the report concludes: "On the Internet, the need for speed is a fact of life. In almost every way imaginable, speed rules." THE report cites the "eight-second rule," an unsubstantiated but widely held belief that customers will abandon their efforts to enter a Web site if download time exceeds eight seconds. It estimates that Internet companies in the unitedstates lose more than $4 billion each year from purchases that are not made because customers found Web sites too slow. It's easy to see E-commerce companies painting this in the starkest terms: an extra second costs $4 billion. Service Metrics has taken a more direct line of attack, monitoring the performance of specific companies within a particular industry during their most crucial periods. It looked at the performance between April 1 and April 15 of nine commercial sites designed to help with the preparation of income taxes: Yahoo Tax Center was the fastest, at an average of 1.65 seconds to download the first page; 1040.com was the slowest, at 13.97 seconds, and Quicken Tax Center's was in the middle, at 6.54 seconds. The report did not say which site was the most helpful, clear or accurate, or the most likely to prompt a tax audit. For Mother's Day, Service Metrics determined that the download time for FTD Flowers was on average two-thirds of a second faster than 1-800-Flowers. Victoria's Secret had the fastest average download time (2.81 seconds) and Hallmark the slowest (7.26 seconds). Godiva Chocolates was in the middle, at 3.37 seconds. Whether or not these marketing maneuvers have been effective -- out of the hundreds of thousands of E-commerce sites, Keynote claims only 1,500 subscribers -- it would be unfair to call them scare tactics. "The Webmasters are already scared," Mr. Gupta said. "It's important to be fast, and we're certainly investing in the site to make it run faster," said Dean DeBiase, the chief executive officer of Autoweb, which, along with Autobytel and Autoconnect, is one of the top car-buying Web sites. "Everyone has to do that." It's true that getting to a home page is slower than turning on the TV set, and buying something over the Web can be slower than buying it by telephone. It's also true that the numbers performance companies cite, like 7.26 seconds, assume optimum conditions for the user -- high-speed T-1 connections, for example, rather than regular phone hook-ups, which are two to three times slower. But it's still quicker, and for many people, more convenient, to go on line than to travel to an auto showroom or a local liquor store. So there is more going on than simply an objective measurement of time. Internet users have become rewired for speed. "When you talk about the Internet consumers," Mr. DeBiase said, "a bunch of words come to mind, and they all seem to start with I: 'impatient,' 'insistent,' 'informed.' " Speed is big these days. It's been the subject of an essay in Harper's Magazine, the topic of the first of Ted Koppel's "Brave New World" television programs and the focus of a new book, "Faster" by James Gleick (Pantheon Books), which ranges from MTV to microwaves to "multitasking," from instant polling to Type-A personalities, from fast forward to "speed" (amphetamines). Even the Metropolitan Transportation Authority in newyork City is getting into the act, issuing a recent report that buses in Manhattan travel on average an alarmingly inadequate 6 miles an hour compared with 16 miles an hour clocked by buses in other cities. HAS the Internet helped inspire all this, or simply reflected it? "It's a little of both," said Mr. Gupta of Keynote, who immigrated at 21 from India, where he grew up with neither a television nor a telephone. "There's a natural tendency for Americans to get things done fast, and they're willing to embrace new technology that makes it possible. Mr. Granoff notes that the Internet consumer's expectation of speed extends beyond download or transaction time to all aspects of the business, including inquiries by email. "I've had customers chew me out for not getting back to them within a few hours," he said. Wine.com likes to emphasize the convenience, friendliness and education it offers on-line customers, a gambit that seems common among E-commerce companies but may be particularly important to a company whose product is alcohol, given the tangle of state laws -- which may soon be exacerbated by pending Federal legislation -- that slows down distribution and delivery time. But if Mr. Granoff sees seven essential characteristics of a good wine, from intensity and sweetness to "complexity," Cyrus Khoshnevisan, his Webmaster, sees but three essential characteristics of a good wine-selling Web site, or of any Web site: "Can the users find what they want? Is it easy to understand? Is it fast?" Mr. Khoshnevisan's job focuses on the answer to the last question, and he uses Keynote to help him monitor the performance of the site, which is far more complicated than the average user might realize. Wine.com has two rooms full of about 20 powerful computer servers that run the site. Keeping a site up to speed is not just a matter of buying the latest and most powerful computers, though that certainly helps. It means maintaining a balance between the requirements of an alluring design and the restrictions of a limited bandwidth. A little cartoon of a popping champagne cork, Mr. Granoff said, is not worth waiting the extra time it would take to download it. It also means trying to anticipate slowdowns in the system caused by constant hazards like a malfunctioning computer in the network, overloaded traffic (illustrated famously by the release of the Starr Report on the Web) or something as mundane as a street repair crew accidentally cutting a fiber-optic line. Webmasters try to limit the damage by working on their connections, in several senses of the word. They often place their servers in different places across the country and use more than one Internet service provider to diminish the potential effect of any single glitch. They also chat up their service providers -- what is called "relationship management" -- so that when there is a problem, they are more likely to get action to put together the most efficient routing. Such networking requires data: the more specific information they have, the more the Webmasters know what to ask for. Keynote and Service Metrics are the only performance companies that have physically put computers in cities worldwide to measure the time it takes to download a page in each place, a service for which companies are paying anywhere from $700 to more than $1 million a year, depending on both the number of pages and the number of cities measured. Mr. Khoshnevisan checks not only the time for his Web site in 10 cities, but he also compares it with the Keynote Business 40 Internet Performance index, which Keynote compares to the Dow Jones industrial average. THE number indicates the average time over a business week it takes Internet users in 25 cities to get to the home page of 40 specific companies, chosen to be "a cross-section of the Web universe," said Dan Todd, who manages the index. This year, the weekly index, which is based on calculations every 15 minutes, has fluctuated between 8 and 5.5 seconds, providing a benchmark of comparison for other companies. This came in handy one day a few months ago, when Mr. Khoshnevisan noticed the data on his Web site indicated an alarming average of 15 seconds to download in Chicago. Because he saw that the average time in newyork was a normal 6 seconds and that the Keynote 40 was also at about 6 seconds, he knew it was not a systemwide problem. He contacted his Internet service provider and they pinpointed a single malfunctioning computer in the network, which they were able to bypass. Chicago download time was back down to 6 seconds within an hour. Another billion dollars in sales had not been sacrificed. The Webmaster might even have reached for a glass of wine, except that he doesn't drink. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Wine.com's Webmaster, Cyrus Khoshnevisan, left, and its master sommelier, Peter Granoff. title: What's Your Bid on Peanut Butter? Groceries Join Big Items on a Name-Your-Price Web Site
body: Priceline.com Inc., an on-line bidding site for big-ticket purchases like airline tickets and automobiles, plans to begin offering consumers in the newyork area cut-rate prices on groceries like applesauce and cereal. In a deal announced yesterday, Priceline will license its trademark and software to Priceline.com Webhouse Club Inc., a new venture through which consumers can set the prices they are willing to pay for grocery store staples ranging from disposable razors to peanut butter. If participating supermarkets accept the prices, the purchases can be picked up at the stores with a shopping list reflecting the discounts. Consumers will print out the discount lists from their computers. Beginning Nov. 1, 600 supermarkets in newyork, New Jersey and Connecticut, including Food Emporium, A.&P. and D'Agostino, will begin taking part in the operation. Essentially, shoppers looking to shave costs from their grocery bills can log on to the Webhouse Club at Priceline.com and name their preferred price on a particular item. If the bid is accepted, the price is locked in and the cost of the item is charged to the customer's credit card. Members print out their private price lists and go to the store. "It's a whole new way to save money," said Walter D'Agostino, of D'Agostino supermarkets. Perhaps, but shoppers would be well advised not to count on buying a case of Coke for a buck or lobster tails for $1.99. Customers will receive up to 40 percent off regular store prices and half off on some goods. By offering a new way to save, Webhouse and its retail partners are taking aim at buy-in-bulk price clubs and on-line supermarket operators. Jon Otto, Webhouse's president and chief executive, said, "Unlike product-ordering Web sites, with their fixed prices, shipping fees and delayed delivery, we view America's neighborhood stores as a powerful and unmatched asset." Financial analysts said the Webhouse model might appeal to coupon clippers and on-line shopping aficionados but would not likely change the way most people shop for milk and bread. For one, they said they doubted that harried shoppers would take the time to point-and-click to bid on an entire shopping list to save 15 cents on a can of soup. What is more, many low-income consumers will be virtually excluded from the savings because getting the discounts requires a computer, an Internet account and a credit card. After 90 days, users will be charged $3 per month for the service. "I'm not overly excited about it," said Ray Dirks, an analyst with Security Capital Trading. "I really think the larger-price items are much more appropriate for something like this." But Priceline sees the expansion of its "name-your-price" concept to everyday, small-ticket items as a way to expand its Web-based business. "By initially allowing consumers to name their price for products in more than 140 frequently purchased grocery categories, and eventually expanding to a much wider variety of retail categories, the increased traffic to Priceline.com as a whole will help accelerate the growth of Priceline.com's airline, hotel and other businesses," said Jay S. Walker, founder and vice chairman of Priceline, which plans to expand the service nationally by next year. Priceline, based in Stamford, Conn., will also eventually receive fee-for-referral payments from stores. The goal, said Rakesh Sood, an analyst who follows the company for Goldman Sachs, is for consumers to become so familiar with clicking onto Priceline that they turn to the site for competitive prices on goods and services like rental cars and credit card deals. Retailers hope the concept will lure bargain hunters. "With the Webhouse Club, each of our customers can electronically tell us what they want to buy and the price they want to pay," said Christian Haub, A.&P.'s chief executive. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
'Digital Storage Lo cker' For Music Downloads - Correction Appended
body: It is an increasingly popular Internet activity: downloading, storing and playing digital music files on a computer or a portable player that can handle the MP3 digital music format. And it can be annoyingly difficult: Users often do not pay attention to where downloads land on their hard drives -- and since there is no industry-wide convention for naming music files, a song might arrive as a file called eleanorrigby.mp3 or, more blindly, 977X021.mp3. As a result, finding the downloaded tunes can be a scavenger hunt -- especially on Windows computers. Sensing a potential business opportunity, two executives with Internet start-up experience and venture capital, have set up a Silicon Valley company called Myplay. Its Web-based service, planned for a mid-October rollout, is meant to make it easier to download and organize music files by song title -- with artist and album also listed, if Myplay has the information in its data base. Each user's files would be kept in a personal "digital storage locker" on the Web. Other than offering a sample starter kit of some 100 licensed songs from an eclectic repertoire that includes Elvis Costello and George Gershwin, Myplay assumes that users will obtain their own music files out on the Internet. A user would have access to the storage locker from any computer connected to the Internet -- similar to the way Microsoft's Hotmail and other Web-based email services enable a person to check email from any computer, rather than being tied to a single desktop or laptop machine. Doug Camplejohn, the 34-year-old co-founder and chief executive of Myplay, is a former Apple Computer marketing executive. His cofounder, David Pakman, 30, is a former Apple colleague who was a business development executive at the on-line music distributor N2K, before it merged with CD Now earlier this year. The company, which is based in Redwood City, Calif., and whose financial backers include the Silicon Valley venture firms IVP and Interval Capital, plans to offer each customer a free storage locker that could hold 250 megabytes -- some five to six hours -- of music. While Myplay may eventually sell monthly subscriptions for additional storage space, the company's main revenue would come from advertising and from marketing pacts with music companies like Dreamworks Records, a unit of Dreamworks SKG, that has signed on as a charter advertiser. Adam Somers, a marketing executive with Dreamworks Records, said his company would offer individual tracks to Myplay customers, including one from the band Powerman 5000. People who downloaded the Powerman 5000 track might then receive promotional email about the band's albums, concerts and the like. "It's a way of finding out what people are listening to," Mr. Somers said. "It's another aspect of one-to-one marketing." TIM RACE http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in the Compressed Data column of Business Day on Monday about the formation of an on-line music company, Myplay, misstated the name of a venture capital firm that is backing it. The firm is Integral Capital Partners, not Interval Capital. Correction-Date: September 22, 1999, Wednesday Graphic   Photo: Myplay aims to simplify handling of MP3 music files.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: E-COMMERCE REPORT;
A ne w piece of hardware could help Internet merchants cut fraud-associated costs, if it catches on among consumers.
body: CREDIT card companies love the Internet, since they pocket a share of most E-commerce transactions. But like everything in the world of revolving credit, that love has limits. Stolen cards used to make purchases on line, in particular, cost credit card issuers millions each year -- pushing the price of doing business on the Web higher for banks, merchants and, ultimately, users. So even as the major credit card companies and the banks that issue those cards explore ways to build Internet market share, they are also looking for ways to limit fraud. The recent introduction of the American Express blue card, which comes with an embedded computer chip, is an example of both efforts. Since the card's chip can access a user's personal information, it will eliminate the hassle of typing in that data in every Web purchase -- and, American Express hopes, encourage people to use its card. At the same time, proponents say, the chip limits fraud by guaranteeing the shopper's identity and, they add, offering greater protection of the buyer's information during the transaction. The key to these features is a piece of computer hardware that, until now, has been foreign to the desktop: a credit card reading device. Starting in November, blue card owners will be able to obtain such a device, which they will be able to plug into their PC's, enabling them to swipe the card at home much like a sales clerk would at a retail store. Other credit card issuers are exploring similar technologies. One company that makes a card-reading device for personal computers, UTM Systems (www.utmsystems.com), recently announced that four major unitedstates banks affiliated with both Visa and Mastercard International will begin distributing its system free to consumers before the end of the year. UTM's founder and chief executive, Robert Lee, declined to name the banks, but said they served "well over 10 million customers." The device, which costs the card issuers $6 a unit, is simple. When a user is ready to make an on-line purchase, the credit or debit card is placed in the UTM card reader, which is inserted into a floppy disk drive. A small window then appears on screen, asks for a personal identification number and sends the encrypted information to the retail site. When the transaction is complete, the window disappears. David Robertson, president of the Nilson Report, a credit card industry newsletter, predicted that credit card companies would be aggressive in spreading such technologies. "American Express is the first, but you'll see everyone start to do this by the end of the first quarter of next year," he said. "It's inevitable." From the standpoint of fraud prevention, card issuers have great incentive to promote the devices, he said. Issuers lose roughly 8 cents for every $100 in on-line sales to fraudulent card use -- "slightly higher than the market at large, but it's growing," Mr. Robertson said. "The industry has been fabulously successful at pushing fraud down in general," he added. "But that just highlights the liability associated with the Internet." Which is not to say that Visa, American Express and Mastercard are stepping lightly into the electronic frontier. Each has begun major Internet-related advertising efforts, of which Visa's is the most aggressive. According to the Nilson Report, 59 percent of Internet credit card purchases are made with Visa, 28 percent with Mastercard and 12 percent with American Express. Off line, Visa has a 51 percent share, compared with 25 percent for Mastercard and 17 percent for American Express. In part, the success of PC-based credit card readers hinges on how insecure consumers feel about credit card transactions on the Web. While such devices in fact provide users more security than some other Internet transactions, surveys indicate that consumers are less concerned about entering their credit card data on line than they used to be. One recent survey by Navidec, a consulting firm, indicated that 21 percent of Internet users worry about credit card security during transactions, about half the number that expressed such concern in 1997. However, Paul Hughes, an analyst with the Yankee Group consulting firm, says that new Internet users might warm to these devices, given the trepidation with which many still approach on-line shopping in general. "That said, the credit card companies are going to have to do some creative marketing to drive these into the hands of consumers," he said. At least one on-line merchant is leery of such creativity. "If credit card companies say that only with this device is a transaction secure during transmission, that would be a disservice to E-commerce as a whole," said Peter Baltaxe, senior vice president of 911Gifts.com. "I don't know of a single documented case of a credit card number being taken in transit." If credit card companies succeed in spreading the gospel of card-reading devices without scaring consumers, it could help the cause of E-commerce merchants, who have gone to great lengths to reduce fraud in recent years. Internet retailers have cut the rate of fraud from as much as 15 percent of on-line transactions earlier in the 1990's to roughly 2 percent today, but given the difficulty of achieving a profit on line, that figure still rankles executives. More important, however, is the premium Web merchants pay in credit card transaction fees because of the higher risk of fraud associated with on-line purchases. The biggest Internet-only retailers can negotiate transaction fees of roughly 2 percent, which are competitive with off-line retailers, but most E-commerce sites pay at least 1 percentage point more -- often 3.5 percent. Such purchases -- so-called "card not present" transactions in industry parlance -- are deemed riskier because the retailer cannot physically match the credit card with the buyer. Card-reading devices would presumably solve that problem, since they insure the identity of card holders by requiring them to enter a personal identification number. "Would we like to have fees reduced, seeing that we're always dealing with the card-not-present issue?" said Elaine Rubin, chairman of Shop.org, an electronic-commerce trade group. "Clearly we'd love that. Is that going to happen? It's too early to tell." Both American Express and Visa representatives agreed. "We would have to look at the entire value proposition" before reviewing on-line merchants' transaction fees, said Michael Biendorff, who heads Visa's recently formed Evisa unit. "Right now, it would be premature to speculate." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: UTM Systems has announced deals with four major banks affiliated with Visa and Mastercard International to distribute UTM's PC credit-card reading device.

title:
PERSONAL BUSINESS;
A Credit Card for Internet-Wary Shoppers
body: AIMING at consumers who want to shop on line but lack confidence in Internet security, American Express is starting to mail applications for the blue cards it is adding to its array of green, gold and platinum. Starting in November, in time for the holiday season, shoppers will be able to swipe American Express blue cards through readers they have plugged into their home computers. The cards contain a "smart" chip, the company says, that works in tandem with the customer's PIN number to prevent unauthorized use. Card readers will be supplied free through Jan. 31 to people who meet the credit qualifications. They will cost $25 thereafter. And just like other credit cards, the blue cards can be used in stores. At least one expert, Paul C. Kocher, president of Cryptography Research Inc. in San Francisco, is impressed. "It's a brilliant marketing approach" that marries the Internet and the credit card, he said, predicting that it would be "very successful." While Mr. Kocher contended that any encryption can be broken with enough effort, the new blue card will be more reliable and far less susceptible to fraudulent use than cards without the smart chip, he said.  Just in case, American Express will protect blue-card users against unauthorized charges, as well as damage or theft of their purchases and the no-return policies of some merchants. The blue cards were formally introduced on Sept. 8 but have not yet been widely marketed. They are intended to extend American Express's reach into the credit-card business, where its existing entry is the Optima card. The Optima card, only modestly successful, carries interest rates ranging from the prime rate plus 7.9 percent to the prime plus 9.9 percent. Neither the blue nor the Optima cards, unlike those of other colors, carries an annual fee. The blue card will have a six-month introductory period in which no interest will be charged on revolving balances. Then the fixed rates will be 9.99 percent for most customers and 12.99 or 15.99 for those who are less creditworthy. The company's traditional charge cards, as opposed to credit cards, require complete payment each month. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Red hot pace of Internet stock trading cools off, pulling high flying on-line brokers back to earth.
body: ALTHOUGH some stock market pundits are still worried about irrational exuberance, Bill Hatcher, a retiree who trades stocks and options on line, worries more about misplaced melancholia. "The sensation-mongers out there have scared everyone to death," says Mr. Hatcher, referring to the Zeitgeist of the on-line chat rooms he constantly monitors. "Whether it's Y2K, or inflation, you just don't see as many happy people out there trading now." It may just be the laws of gravity. But the outlook of individual investors has been taking a dive. And that is bad news for on-line brokerage firms, which have seen trading volumes ebb recently. If the trend holds, investors are on course to trade fewer shares on line this quarter than they did in the previous three months, making it the first such sustained decline in Internet trading volume for the nascent on-line brokerage industry. Summer is rarely a record-breaking time for stock trading. But trading volume -- on which on-line brokers depend mightily for revenues -- slumped more than just about anyone expected in July and August. September, at least so far, has not offered much relief. A few of the indicators: Charles Schwab, the largest on-line brokerage firm, reported yesterday that average daily revenue from trades by its customers dropped 14 percent from July to August, a figure some analysts viewed as a leading indicator for the industry. Credit Suisse First Boston noted that trading in a sample basket of high-flying Internet stocks was off 2 percent for the second quarter. And two brokerage analysts downgraded earnings estimates yesterday for the Knight/Trimark Group, the biggest market maker for shares traded on Nasdaq, including many big Internet stocks. Scott Appleby, an on-line brokerage industry analyst for BancBoston Robertson Stephens, reduced his estimates for Knight's earnings per share for the July-September quarter to 31 cents from 36 cents, or 14 percent. That is the second time in a month he has lowered his profit targets for Knight, whose revenues have skyrocketed in tandem with heavy trading in Internet stocks and individual investors' migration to on-line brokerage houses. In early August, he revised estimates for Knight downward from 40 cents. Shares of Knight fell $1 yesterday, or 3 percent, to $30.625. "It's an industrywide issue," Mr. Appleby said. "We expected a seasonal trough in the summer. But the volume has been unexpectedly poor." Few believe that America's love affair with on-line trading has faded. On the contrary, most analysts say that Internet brokerages have just begun to tap a huge pool of savings still stored in banks and in accounts with full-service brokers. Americans have 70 million brokerage accounts, but only 10 percent of them permit on-line trading. And as more people move their assets on line, taking a more active role in their investment decisions, trading volume tends to rise substantially. Moreover, the decline in trading in the third quarter comes after a nine-month growth frenzy in which Internet broker transactions doubled in size. By the end of June, they accounted for one in six stock trades made in America. That pace was not viewed as sustainable. Still, even a temporary trading slump could be hazardous to the on-line brokerage industry's health. Schwab, for example, derives almost half its total earnings from trading commissions, and most of its trades are now conducted on line. For smaller brokers -- there are three score of them competing for Internet investors now -- the dependence on trading commissions is far greater. All have seen sharp drops in their share prices. Schwab shares have fallen by half since April and closed yesterday at $36.4375, up 6.25 cents. E*Trade has tumbled 63 percent in the same period, closing yesterday at $23.5625, down 46.875 cents. What's more, many of the leading Internet brokers are geared for growth, not for a grinding battle for market share. E*Trade and Ameritrade, two of the best-known on-line brokers, are spending hundreds of millions of dollars to promote themselves, sacrificing earnings today for rapid growth tomorrow. Ameritrade said yesterday that it planned to spend $200 million over the next year on advertising, about as much as Mazda spent advertising cars and trucks last year. "E*Trade and Ameritrade depend on commission much more than Schwab," said L. Russell Keene, a brokerage analyst at Putnam, Lovell, de Guardiola & Thornton. He has a relatively bearish "hold" recommendation on both stocks. Most of the Internet brokerage firms will report third-quarter earnings in early October. Mr. Keene said he saw the first and second quarters of this year as exceptional. Internet investors, Internet stocks and Internet brokerage firms found themselves then in a virtuous circle. Investors opened new brokerage accounts and seized on high-flying Internet stocks, including the brokerage firms themselves, sending share prices skyward. "That really fueled an anomaly in trade volumes," Mr. Keene said. "If you ignore the first and second quarter and look at the trend, what we see this year is less worrying." He said stock trading volumes were still up over year-earlier periods, even though the increase was less robust than it was in the recent past: Third quarter commissions grew 40 percent in 1997 over 1996, 30 percent in 1998 over 1997 and seem likely to grow 20 percent in 1999 over 1998, he said.
