body: As part of an investigation into the practices of on-line brokerage firms and day-trading houses, the Securities and Exchange Commission is examining whether the firms and their customers abide by the regulations governing the selling of stocks short, a bet that prices will fall. One former day trader who has told his story to regulators said that the firm he was associated with used a system to circumvent short-selling rules and estimated that illegal short sales accounted for as much as 30 percent of the sales at one office while he was a customer. Regulators are stepping up their scrutiny of on-line brokerage firms as the number of investors making computerized trades at home or in day-trading rooms is exploding. The number of on-line brokerage firms stood at 140 in June, up from 100 six months earlier. The number of on-line brokerage accounts is expected to reach 10.5 million by the end of 1999, up from 7.1 million in 1998, according to Gomez Advisors, a research firm specializing in electronic commerce. Regulators have grown increasingly concerned that some on-line firms are not fully enforcing securities regulations. How firms enforce the rules that apply to investors who sell stocks short is of concern to the S.E.C. and is one of the issues the commission is questioning on-line brokerage firms about, Chris Ullman, an S.E.C. spokesman, said. Selling a stock short is a relatively sophisticated technique that enables an investor who is pessimistic about a company's prospects to profit from a decline in its shares. A short-seller essentially sells stock he does not own, hoping to buy it back later at a lower price. If the stock rises instead, the investor will have to pay more to buy it back than he received when he sold it, creating a loss in his account. The business of selling stocks short is more highly regulated than the outright buying -- known as going long a stock -- or selling of shares held by a customer in his or her account. That is because in the years surrounding the Crash of 1929, groups of short-sellers were found to have harmed investors by forcing down the prices of certain stocks by the sheer force of excessive and unrelenting selling. To rid the markets of such manipulations, regulators devised a rule that investors can sell short only if a stock's last trade was at the same price or higher than the previous trade. Regulators also require that investors who sell shares they do not own must first arrange to borrow the shares so that they can be delivered to the person buying them. This is supposed to prevent the sales of many more shares of a stock than are available for trading, a technique known as naked shorting. If an investor is unable to borrow a stock, he is not supposed to be able to sell it short. Muriel F. Siebert, chairman of the Siebert Financial Corporation, a well-known discount brokerage firm, said that her firm's computer system automatically alerted a manager if a customer tried to sell a stock that was not held in the account. The manager then tries to find shares to borrow. If successful, the trade is done; if unsuccessful, the short sale is not executed. An article in The Wall Street Journal earlier this month reported that some investors were selling short shares of initial public offerings of stock, even though those shares are not typically available to be borrowed. But professional traders say that naked shorting extends well beyond shares in I.P.O.'s. These people suspect that the rapid-fire trading that is common among day traders does not leave a firm enough time to ascertain that a stock can be borrowed before the trade is executed. These traders also suggest that some firms flout the uptick rule and allow their customers to sell stocks they do not own even when the stocks are declining in price. These fears are confirmed by the experience of John H. Skiersch, 33, a performance artist in Chicago who lost more than $200,000 day trading stocks in 1997 and 1998. Mr. Skiersch described how one of the two firms he traded with allowed its customers to circumvent short-sale rules. Upon opening an account at the firm, which Mr. Skiersch declined to identify, customers were asked to pay $100 to have a corporation set up with its own taxpayer identification number. Then the firm created an account for the entity that was linked to the customer's regular account. Fictitious stockholdings were then placed in the corporate account. In Mr. Skiersch's case, his "corporate" account held $200,000 to $250,000 worth of stocks for which he had never paid a cent. The fake holdings included 500 shares each of Intel, Dell Computer, Cisco Systems and other stocks that a customer might want to sell short. "They manufactured these positions," Mr. Skiersch said. "The software was then tricked into believing that you were long the positions so you could initiate sales without ever owning the stock. I believe it was intentionally premeditated to violate the essence of the short sale rules." Mr. Skiersch estimated that up to 30 percent of all the sales executed in that office of the day-trading firm violated short-sale rules. "When regulators were in the office one day, the whole office was instructed not to sell on any downticks that day," he recalled. Mr. Skiersch does not know if the questionable practices are still taking place at the firm, but he has since talked to the S.E.C., the National Association of Securities Dealers and the Illinois state securities regulator. Day-trading firms may try to skirt requirements by allowing a customer to short a stock as long as someone else in the day-trading room owns the shares in question. Day traders might also sell stocks short without borrowing them during market hours as long as they close out their short position before the end of the day. Regulators say both practices are against the rules. Some short-sellers and other traders have argued that the rules are outmoded and should be changed. Several longtime Wall Street traders said that one sign of illegal short selling is when the daily trading volume in a stock far exceeds the number of shares available to the public, which is known as the float. One trader pointed to the recent trading in Grand Toys International, the Canadian distributor of the wildly popular Pokemon and Furby toys, as an example. The company has a little more than 1.5 million shares available to public investors, but on Wednesday, almost 20 million shares, or 13.3 times the public float, changed hands. Even if only 10 percent of those trades were short sales, they would have exceeded the public float by half a million shares.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS;
New Trading After Hours Is a Success, Two Firms Say
body: In a small corner of Wall Street, people have been talking about this for years: Why not offer individual investors a way to buy and sell stocks after the 4 P.M. closing bell at the newyork Stock Exchange? Institutional traders have long been able to trade overnight for their biggest and wealthiest clients, often reacting to late news like a company's earnings release. Last night, many small investors got their first shot at the after-hours market through two on-line brokerage firms -- Discover Brokerage and Dreyfus Brokerage Services -- which opened their electronic doors to eager investors between 6 and 8 Eastern daylight time. Just about 60,000 shares -- or 142 orders -- were executed last night, a pittance when compared with the nearly 1.8 billion shares that were traded during the day on the major exchanges. The companies involved said they did not expect an explosive start. But it was the first time small investors had the chance to buy 200 of the most active Big Board and Nasdaq stocks so late in the day through a new electronic trading format. About 1,200 orders were entered, but only a small number were matched and executed. (The most active stock was the Microsoft Corporation, which traded 5,500 shares, followed by America Online.) The firms say they just wanted an orderly beginning to what they hope will become a pioneering effort to bring round-the-clock trading to the masses. "I'm happy to tell you the launch was successful," Michael O. Sanderson, the chief executive at Marketxt Inc., the electronic trading system that created the after-hours forum, said during a conference call at 7:20 P.M. "The system is working as planned." The new format meant reopening the markets after a two-hour close. (The delay is intended to give investors time to digest late-breaking news and events.) It could serve as a preview of what is to come when the nation's largest stock exchanges begin offering after-hours trading on a huge scale next year.  Experts warn that investors face greater risks in after-hours trading, largely because the systems are untested and not as active. Regulators want the big exchanges to move toward extended hours with caution. But officials at Discover Brokerage, a unit of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, and at Dreyfus Brokerage Services, a unit of Mellon Bank, say they are working hard to educate and protect smaller investors. Only the most active stocks are traded, for example, and investors must use limit orders, which means a trade at the investor's specified price. Executives at Discover Brokerage, which ranks ninth among on-line brokers in average daily trades, say they chose not to heavily publicize the first day of after-hours trading. Other on-line brokers are entering the market. Last week, E*Trade Group teamed with Instinet, the electronic trading unit owned by Reuters Group P.L.C., to provide after-hours trading beginning in September. Just days later, the Chicago Stock Exchange said it would enter the after-hours market in October. Datek Online Holdings, which owns Island, an electronic trading system, was the first to offer after-hours trading to its customers in Nasdaq stocks between 4 P.M. and 5:15 P.M. The service, which began earlier this month, is now commission-free, and tens of thousands of customers have signed up, said Robert O. Bethge, a spokesman. Datek says that on an average day about 600 trades are executed in its after-hours market. Customer demand for after-hours trading clearly exists. One clue is that at Discover Brokerage, up to 40 percent of the firm's on-line orders are placed at a time when the markets are closed. Wall Street analysts say other on-line brokerage firms are recording similar numbers. Whether or not large numbers of individual investors are demanding the right to trade in the late hours, a growing number of on-line brokers and Wall Street trading houses are scrambling to forge new alliances and develop the electronic means to offer such a system. They are racing ahead of Wall Street's biggest brokerage houses, and even the major stock exchanges with the small players on Wall Street saying they are providing what the small players on Main Street want: equality with their larger brethren, who can trade anytime. "Philosophically it's unfair and suspicious," said Jim Laird, an electronic-commerce analyst at Yankee Group in Boston. "Financial firms have risked talking out of both sides of their mouth, so there's been an inherent contradiction." Part of the after-hours movement can be attributed to heightened competition among on-line brokers trying to stand out and offer new services while investors are riding a record-breaking bull market. In recent months, Charles Schwab & Company, E*Trade and Fidelity Brokerage have been making aggressive moves to attract more "active investors," a growing and highly profitable segment of the market. "They all want the guys who trade 100 times a year," said James Punishill, an analyst at Forrester Research. For that reason, on-line brokerage firms are installing faster software, arranging better access to the markets and coordinating initial public offerings. Technology is also being developed for wireless trading from mobile hand-held devices. The firms can now begin to assess the true demand for these services. "The question becomes how many people are going to show up," said Larry Connors, a co-founder of Tradehard.com, an on-line service for professional traders and fledgling day traders. "I think it'll take some time before we know. We think there's a market for this kind of thing." Thomas J. O'Connell, the president and chief operating officer at Discover Brokerage in San Francisco, said he was pleased with the start. Though he said he could not give out exact numbers, about a third of the orders entered into the system were executed in the first hour of trading last night, and the volume was about 1 percent of what the firm does on a typical day. "The genie's out of the bottle," he said. "It's like having one of the first Netscape browsers. You know it's going to be big." http://www.nytimes.com

title: You've Got Romance! Seeking Love on Line
body: TOM BUCKLEY didn't have much use for a dating service, or so he thought. "I didn't need to pay a company to help set me up to get a date, a girlfriend, a fiancee, a wife," said Mr. Buckley, 30, a steel broker in Portland, Ore., who plays rugby in his spare time. But after a lonely Thanksgiving dinner where he was the only single adult at the family dinner table, Mr. Buckley signed up for a free week on Match.com. What ensued on the matchmaking service was an email romance with Terri Muir, a schoolteacher on Vancouver Island in British Columbia. "Anybody who knew us would never have thought we would have gone down that road," Mr. Buckley said in a telephone interview. "My rugby mates would roll in their graves." Reflecting on the couple's instant attraction, he said, "email made it easier to communicate because neither one of us was the type to walk up to someone in the gym or a bar and say, 'You're the fuel to my fire.' " Mr. Buckley said email had enabled him to be more honest because he knew that if he wasn't, he would eventually get caught. Thirteen months after their first feverish exchanges, Mr. Buckley and Ms. Muir lied to their family and friends and sneaked away to Vancouver to meet for the first time. At their wedding one year later, at a winery in Oregon, they finally told the tale of how they had met to their 100 guests. More and more single people, used to finding everything else on the Internet, are using it to search for love. More than 2,500 Web sites for adults are now devoted to matchmaking, said Daniel Bender, founder of Cupid's Network (www.cupidnet.com), an Internet portal for personals sites that went on line in 1995 listing only a handful. At a time when many people are staying single longer, busy professionals barely have time to squeeze in workouts and rules about sexual misconduct pose barriers to romance in the workplace, the Internet can be a fast and efficient way for single people to find each other, the creators of these services say. Many singles say they post their ads on a lark, expecting little. They take advantage of free trial memberships, yet concede that despite their doubts, they wonder "what if." Will Knedlik, a lawyer in Kirkland, Wash., who specializes in suing traditional dating services for fraud, is optimistic about the potential for the Internet to accomplish successful matchmaking. "The Internet is changing the landscape and process of the personals," Mr. Knedlik said. The print personals don't work very well and the expense is very high, he added. "With the Internet, the cost is so much less and the transaction time is shorter." One thing the Web has to distinguish it from more traditional personal advertisements is the size of the dating pool. John Spottiswoode, president of Match.com (who, incidentally, met his wife in junior high school), said his company registered its two-millionth subscriber in August. This year, the company was acquired for about $50 million by Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch, which also purchased the Internet's other largest personals matchmaking service, One and Only (www.oneandonly .com). The two companies will eventually be merged to chase after the 66 million single people in the country today who are not only looking for love, but tickets to concerts, said Charles Conn, chief executive of Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch. Another of the Internet's large dating services, American Singles, (www.as.org), is a not-yet-for-profit-but-soon-to-be-acquired company that has been on line since Valentine's Day 1994. It says it has 125,000 active members. All these sites and more are also linked through Cupid Network, which Mr. Bender, 38, started in 1995. (He met his wife through a personals page on Prodigy nine years ago, and he also runs American Singles.) At first, Mr. Bender said, Cupid Network listed only a handful of sites. Today, the 2,500 linked sites are broken down by region, religion, race, sexual preferences and even values, as evidenced by a site called Singles With Scruples (www.singleswithscruples .com), a free service that says it caters to singles with "character, integrity and service to others." "Single people tell us that their No. 1 challenge is access to finding other single people," said Trish McDermott, the Online Dating Coach for Match.com. She said she spent most days counseling the company's clients through email. With many services, users fill out questionnaires that combine fill-in-the-blank descriptions with short essays. Mate-seekers not only describe themselves in exacting detail, but also choose -- frequently down to hair color -- what features they most desire in a soul mate. Many sites encourage users to submit photographs, and some offer audio samplings. The services use software to sort and match preferences of the sort commonly expressed in personal ads: for nonsmokers, blonds, lovers of cabernet, for example, or for bald but vigorous men who like parasailing, Wagner and long walks in the country. Those seeking a mate submit their forms with their preferences, then receive a list of matches, which includes brief profiles and anonymous email addresses set up and run through the on-line dating service. After a free weeklong trial, many services charge $10 to $20 monthly. Some services are always free. On Match.com, users can hide their profiles while doing their searching or hang out their personal shingles to attract potential dates. After scanning the list of matches, a date-seeker sends an email message to someone the sender thinks might be a dream date and hopes that the message will be answered with alacrity. "There's a full world of people on the Internet instead of the few faces you see at work," said Julie Warren, 25, a consultant in Falls Church, Va., who met her fiance, Scott Mastbrook, on American Singles, after he posted an ad looking for someone to show him around Phoenix when he was traveling there on business. Ms. Warren was working in Phoenix at the time and had met other men through the service. Ms. Warren said she had felt unencumbered by the usual stigma associated with searching for love in the personals. "I've met a lot of neat people just talking in chat rooms," she said, adding that using the service to find dates seemed natural to her. Relationships that begin on line may have a better chance of succeeding because they start from the inside, from communication, and work their way out, said Dr. Andrea Baker, an associate professor of sociology at Ohio University-Lancaster who studies successful on-line romances. "For many people, this does seem to work well in the sense of focusing more on the thought processes and common interests before they have appearance to distract them from how they feel about the person," Dr. Baker said. But a romance cannot continue solely on line forever. And, if a suitor has built an email house of cards, it will tumble. That's what Dr. Maryanne Shiozawa, 26, a chiropractor in Manhattan, discovered when she finally dated a man she had met through an on-line dating service, one of two services that she had signed up with. "This person lied straight out, he wasn't as tall as he described, he wasn't in as good shape as he claimed to be, he was just painting a picture to impress me," she said.  After their date, Dr. Shiozawa sent her date a Dear John email. Still, she continues to meet men from from personals on line, she said, because she hates the bar scene and feels safe meeting men in cyberspace. For Robert Spradling, the house of cards fell apart later than the first face-to-face meeting, and at great personal cost. He had struck up an on-line romance with a Ukrainian woman whom he had met on American Singles. The woman immediately asked him for money to pay the agency she was using to translate and send her romantic emails back to him. There are many such agencies in the former Soviet Union, Mr. Spradling said. Next she told Mr. Spradling she wanted to start her own matchmaking agency. Mr. Spradling, 42, an employee in the development office at Morehead State University in Kentucky, footed the bill for that, too. After sending her about $8,000, Mr. Spradling asked her to marry him, via email. She said yes and invited him to Kiev. "When you meet somebody and you think you're in love, you never see any faults," said Mr. Spradling, who said the couple had made wedding plans when he was visiting. After his return to the United States, Mr. Spradling never heard from her again. He's sworn off finding love through the Internet for now. "If I paid twice as much, it would still be worth what I learned," Mr. Spradling said. "I caution a lot of guys to be careful and keep their head and learn a lot about who they're dating on line." Still, the Web can work like a fairy tale for some people. When Diana Hathaway first spotted Greg Timmons, he was playing guitar in a swing band at an outdoor concert in San Luis Obispo, Calif. She called her sister by cell phone from the concert to tell her about the cute guitarist. They planned to see the band play again at a local club the following week so Ms. Hathaway, 39 and recently divorced, could meet him. But she never put her plan into action. A month later, Ms. Hathaway posted a personal ad on Match.com, saying she was thinking of moving to a new town for a fresh start. One email response she received read, "Before you go, there's a gentleman you might want to meet." Eight quick email notes later, the gentleman invited her to a local club to see his swing band. Ms. Hathaway went, and there was that cute guitarist, Mr. Timmons. Less than nine months later, they were married. For Christmas, Ms. Hathaway filled a binder with the 339 email messages the couple exchanged while they were courting and labeled it "We've Got Mail."  Rules for Romance Keeping Safety in Mind While Finding a Date FINDING a soul mate on the Internet can be as random an experience as bumping into that person in the supermarket. To try to beat the odds, start with a service that has lots of members. Or go to one that a specific target audience. Many people try both, like placing different sorts of bets on a roulette wheel. Conde Nast runs a free service, www.swoon.com/go/personals, which it says has 125,000 active members. The site's irreverent tone asks users to fill in profiles featuring a "sin index," which is the standard drug, cigarette and alcohol-use questions found on many of the services, and to catalogue their pop culture favorites. The service at www.2ofakind.com has 150 categories users fill out to start their matches. A free trial is offered, then the cost jumps to $1 for each match. There is live chat on www.hugkiss .com, a page featuring virtual animated hugs and kisses to use to seal email after an on-line romance has sparked. The site includes a column, "Ask a Mom," offering advice on all matters of love. If romance blossoms on line and you arrange a face-to-face encounter, take precautions. Experts advise that first dates be held in public, preferably in daytime. Park your car close to the meeting place. Tell a friend where you are going and when to expect you back. Despite the flurry of excitement you may feel if you think you've found your soul mate, there is always the possibility that your date can become "the date from hell." More likely, though, if you don't hit it off, it will simply be chalked up as a bad date.   BONNIE ROTHMAN MORRIS http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: TIME FOR A CONFESSION -- At their wedding in Turner, Ore., Tom Buckley and Terri Muir announced to their guests that they had met through an on-line matchmaking service. (Shane Young for The New York Times)(pg. G1); Diana Hathaway Timmons, above (Kim Kulish for The New York Times), of Los Osos, Calif., holds a scrapbook documenting her email courtship with her husband, Greg. Dr. Maryane Shiozawa of Manhattan said she had learned on a first date that a man seh had found on a matchmaking site had "lied straight out." (James Estrin/The New York Times)(pg. G7)

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
America Online Offers Free Internet Use in Britain
body: America Online Inc. introduced its own free Internet service in Britain today, with the goal of overtaking the growing crowd of competitors that already offer customers access to the World Wide Web at no charge. The new service, known as Netscape Online, is managed by AOL Europe, a joint venture of America Online and Bertelsmann A.G., the large German media conglomerate. First announced last month, Netscape Online represents a strategic about-face for America Online, which had historically relied on monthly subscriptions and only three months ago questioned whether Britain's free-subscription businesses could be sustained. The introduction of Netscape Online comes at a precarious time for America Online in Britain, where its formerly large share of the market has eroded. A main reason is the subscription-free newcomer Freeserve P.L.C., which was created last September by Dixons Group P.L.C., a British retailing chain, and in three months surpassed America Online as Britain's most-used Internet service provider. Freeserve sold shares of itself to the public a month ago in a bid to gain financing for further expansion. By using the Netscape brand for the new service, America Online hopes to differentiate it and not cannibalize its content-rich subscription services like AOL U.K. and Compuserve. It is not only going after Freeserve but the hundreds of other Internet service providers that have sprung up around Britain. Today, America Online took out full-page advertisements in almost all of Britain's national newspapers for its new service with a headline that read: "Beware part-time Internet providers -- the N is nigh." Unlike the Internet service business in the unitedstates, where access over a telephone line is relatively inexpensive, access in Britain and in most parts of Europe can be quite expensive for users because they must pay by the minute for local phone calls, in addition to the charge levied by the Internet access provider. As a result, subscription-free Internet services have emerged, luring customers by not charging them the monthly subscription fee for Internet access. Instead, the services share a percentage of the revenue generated by the cost of a user's telephone call with the phone company, which charges all calls by the minute. A subscription-free service also derives revenue from advertising and electronic commerce. Analysts called America Online's move a short-term solution to a significantly longer-term problem, notably how America Online can make money and how it can keep its higher-margin businesses from losing customers to the subscription-free service. "It doesn't answer the question of how AOL competes internationally," said Evan Neufeld, vice president and director for international research at Jupiter Communications in London. "I don't buy it as a long-term strategy to move the customers upstream to their subscription services." It remains unclear whether subscription-free Internet services are a passing fancy or are here to stay. As telephone companies consider flat-rate pricing and upgrade their systems for faster and more sophisticated connections, "Netscape Online could be like the flavor of the day," Mr. Neufeld said. "Maybe we'll all be talking about these wacky companies offering free Internet access five years from now," he said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Privacy Questions Raised in Cases Of Syphilis Linked to Chat Room
body: In what health officials believe is the first time a disease cluster has been traced to cyberspace, the department of public health here has tracked an outbreak of syphilis cases to an America Online chat room. Officials from the San Francisco Department of Public Health said six men who had contracted syphilis in the last three months have traced their last sexual encounters to partners they met through a chat room created by an America Online member, San Francisco Men 4 Men (SFM4M). The case is a new development for public health officials who traditionally define an affected group by the members' physical proximity or relation and poses a question for the electronic age: when does the right to on-line privacy yield to public health issues? Some of the men who were infected with syphilis know their multiple partners only by their computer nicknames, or "handles." While such anonymity could be an obstacle to public health officials in other cases, say among people who met in a bar, in this case, America Online knows the participants' real names but would not divulge them. So the only way to contact the scores of sex partners the syphilis-infected men met on line has been through email and postings in the chat room itself. Although the number of men known to be infected so far is small and their infections were identified early and are fully treatable, they represent a sizable number of the 17 syphilis cases reported in San Francisco this year, and the cluster has provided a frightening glimpse of a potentially larger public health risk, as more and more people use computers to find sex partners, officials said. Besides the six men who met partners through the America Online chat room, which is open only to its subscribers, a seventh local man who contracted syphilis since June said he met his sex partners through an Internet relay chat room, known as an I.R.C. Together, the seven men have identified 99 sex partners in the last three months -- one man had 47 partners -- and five of the seven men have H.I.V., the virus that causes AIDS, health officials said. At a time when both syphilis and AIDS cases are at an all-time low in San Francisco, as in the rest of the country, officials are now worried that these seven syphilis cases may indicate a new venue has been created for unsafe sex. The core group of individuals using cyberspace to meet multiple, anonymous sex partners is the same as that which would use bathhouses or highway rest stops or other pick-up venues to engage in unsafe, potentially dangerous sex, said Dr. Jeffrey Klausner, the director of the sexually transmitted disease unit at the public health department. Not only did five of the infected men expose numerous partners to H.I.V., but because syphilis causes open sores that increase the vulnerability to H.I.V., their partners are at greater risk of contracting the virus, Dr. Klausner said. "We've discovered that the Internet chat room is becoming an important sexual network," he said, "and one that poses particular challenges for us." Once the health department traced the cluster of syphilis cases to the chat room, Dr. Klausner said he called America Online to find out how the department could contact all the exposed sex partners, as well as those men who might have contact with the exposed men. America Online does not give out the names of subscribers as a matter of policy, unless presented with a court order or in the event of special cases like a physical threat, said Rich Damato, a spokesman. Asked whether the syphilis cluster constituted a physical threat, he said, "I would not want in this case to speculate what would constitute a physical threat." Dr. Klausner said that the health department considered trying to subpoena the names of the chat room subscribers, but "there wasn't a large enough public health risk to warrant that." Instead, in a move applauded by Internet privacy advocates, America Online put the health department in touch with Planet Out, a worldwide on-line service in San Francisco for homosexuals. Tom Rielly, chairman of Planet Out said that the service used email, volunteers and its own Web site (www.planetout.com) to get the word out in the last two weeks to the chat room users who would be more likely to read mail from the service than from other sources. "What we did first was send a letter out to the chat room names the health department obtained from the men who were infected," Mr. Rielly said. Then, he said, Planet Out posted instant messages to people who were in the chat rooms. It also trained 60 volunteers to visit the chat rooms and talk to people there, and posted information on its Web site. Of the 99 men who were directly exposed to syphilis, 33 have been tested. Dr. Klausner estimated that another third had contacted their own doctors, while the remaining still do not know that they were exposed. Deirdre Mulligan, staff counsel for the Center for Democracy and Technology, a policy organization in Washington that advocates protecting privacy rights in the cyber age, commended the health department and Planet Out for how they handled the situation. By contacting people on line, the agency has a chance to reach not just infected participants, but also those who may be at risk, she said. "They're saying, 'Look, be careful,' " Ms. Mulligan said. "They're potentially reaching a much broader audience." Tim Westmoreland, a senior policy fellow and public health expert at Georgetown University Law School, also applauded the effort. "I've never heard of a case like this -- ever," he said. One sticking point, he said, is that the health department cannot be certain that infected participants will return to the chat rooms. But on the whole, he said, warning people in chat rooms is an easier way of contacting people and more efficient than traditional door-to-door methods. "This is a new way of defining the community," he said. "It's not defined by physical geography, but by the use of cyberspace." (A spokeswoman for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in Atlanta said that she had never heard of another cluster traced to cyberspace, but could not be certain that one exists but was not reported.) There are thousands of chat rooms based in San Francisco alone, encompassing a broad range of subjects and sexual interests. Mr. Rielly said about 100 to 1,000 of the chat rooms are geared to gay men and lesbians. Only perhaps six or seven of those chat rooms are expressly for people who want to meet sex partners, he added. Dr. Klausner of the health department said that since Planet Out began its outreach, the number of men seeking testing at the department's sex clinics had nearly doubled. But in a SFM4M chat this afternoon, several participants rejected the notion that the syphilis cluster is anything to worry about. One man, who identified himself as a doctor, said incorrectly that the cluster represented a total of seven cases in San Francisco in seven months, rather than just over two months. Another said that "sex is dangerous no matter how you cut it."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS;
Two Firms Plan to OfferLate Trading
body: Two more on-line brokerage firms have struck an agreement to offer customers after-hours stock trades, beginning this evening. Discover Brokerage, the on-line unit of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company, and Dreyfus Brokerage Services, a division of Mellon Bank, plan to begin allowing small investors to trade in some of the most active Nasdaq and newyork Stock Exchange issues tonight from 6 P.M. to 8 P.M. The result will be an evening session after the major exchanges close at 4 P.M. Discover, which ranks ninth in average daily trades among on-line brokers, and Dreyfus, a much smaller player, will use MarketXT, formerly known as Eclipse Trading, a new after-hours electronic trading network backed by Morgan Stanley and several large trading firms. There has been a flurry of activity in recent weeks among on-line brokerage firms and electronic trading networks, which say they are paving the way for 24-hour electronic stock trading and aiming to offer small investors all the advantages and conveniences that institutions have long enjoyed, such as trading on news announced after the markets close. Last Friday, the Chicago Stock Exchange said it would offer after-hours trading to smaller investors in October, making it the first exchange to do so. E*Trade Group, the giant on-line brokerage firm, and Instinet, the electronic trading network owned by the Reuters Group, said days earlier that they would join forces in September to offer trading from 4 P.M. to 6:30 P.M.; Datek Online Holdings already offers trading in Nasdaq stocks from the close until 5:15 P.M. The brokerage firms say small investors are eager to trade cheaply and conveniently over the Internet. Some live on the West Coast -- where the newyork markets close at 1 P.M. local time -- and others simply prefer the convenience of trading from home, after the markets close. So while the major stock exchanges -- the Nasdaq Stock Market and the newyork Stock Exchange -- are contemplating an evening session, a number of alliances are being formed among on-line brokerage firms and so-called electronic communications networks, or E.C.N.'s, which are low-cost computerized trading systems, which are fast winning acceptance as efficient ways to sort and match orders. Experts says it is unclear whether several after-hours systems acting independently of one another will attract enough orders for customers to get good prices and whether there is truly sufficient demand for such service. In the Discover and Dreyfus alliance, customers will have their Internet trades directed to MarketXT, an electronic system that will be supported by market makers at Morgan Stanley; Herzog Heine Geduld, and Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities, creating a kind of hybrid stock exchange with both electronic and human components. This evening, MarketXT will have its first trial, said Michael O. Sanderson, chief executive at MarketXT Inc., which is based in newyork. "We'll have three market makers generating live quotes," he said. Investors will be able to trade in the 200 stocks that make up the Standard & Poor's 100 and the Nasdaq 100 -- among the most popular issues available, Monday through Thursday. Thomas J. O'Connell, the president and chief operating officer of Discover, which is based in San Francisco, said the system would only accept limit orders, meaning an order to buy 100 shares of Microsoft must be accompanied by a price. "This won't be dominated by hedge funds or institutional traders," Mr. O'Connell said. "This was totally developed and conceived with the individual investor in mind." Executives at Discover, one of the nation's fastest-growing on-line brokers, say that there has long been a need for after-hours trading. For more than a year, 25 to 40 percent of the brokerage firm's on-line orders have been placed after the markets close, they say. Those orders sat and waited in an electronic queue until the opening bell at 9:30 A.M. the next day. Now, investors will be able to ask that their trades be executed well past dinner time. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MARKET WATCH;
Chopping Downa Limb Before Investors Fall Off
body: NEWS from the market stratosphere: The Charles Schwab Corporation, the nation's largest discount and on-line brokerage firm, is steadily reducing the number of stocks it allows its customers to buy using borrowed money. More than 1,000 stocks are now off limits for Schwab customers wishing to invest on margin. Expanding the list appears to be a way for Schwab to protect itself against a plunge in prices that might leave it holding the bag if the value of customers' shares falls below the balances in their accounts. One customer says Schwab employees told him the move was related to the firm's concerns about the level of stock prices. Daniel D. Hubbard, director of corporate communications at Schwab, confirmed that the list of such stocks has expanded lately but would not say how quickly or reveal which companies are on it. Like many brokerage firms, Schwab has limited the amount of money its customers can borrow to buy Internet shares, but most of these stocks can still be bought on margin. Most of the banned companies are thinly traded over-the-counter stocks, Mr. Hubbard said: "What we are trying to provide to the customer is a sense of the volatile nature of securities markets in general and margin investing." David Eidelman, a money manager at Eidelman, Finger & Harris in St. Louis who is a Schwab customer, says the firm expressed additional concerns when he called after having been notified that securities he had bought on margin could no longer be bought that way. Two Schwab employees, he said, told him that the switch was motivated in part by fears held by the firm's risk committee that the stock market would be increasingly volatile in coming months and that share prices were vulnerable. Schwab told him it was trying to protect itself and its customers. Mr. Hubbard denied that Schwab is concerned about the broad market, saying that any action by the firm was a result of liquidity concerns. "Say there's a stock that trades 1,000 shares a day," Mr. Hubbard explained. "Say a customer owns that stock on margin and the price goes down. Say the customer doesn't come up with the required cash, and we have to sell the stock. That's going to drive down the price." But Mr. Eidelman pointed out that two of his holdings that were scratched from the list -- Travis Boats & Motors Inc. and National City Bancorporation -- trade fairly actively. In recent weeks, Schwab also informed him that he could no longer borrow to buy shares of American Bancorporation (Ohio).  All three stocks can still be bought on margin at six other firms Mr. Eidelman polled. The fact that some of the stocks Schwab is eliminating from its list of marginable securities are neither excessively volatile nor overpriced glamour issues indicates that the firm may be concerned about more than a few Internet fliers. Schwab is not alone in its concerns over vast numbers of investors trading stocks on borrowed funds. Margin debt at the newyork Stock Exchange stands at $176.9 billion, a record that doesn't count investors who have borrowed on credit cards to buy stocks. By reducing the number of stocks that its customers can buy on margin, Schwab is giving up real money. Interest on customers' borrowings is a big percentage of Schwab's net interest revenue, which totaled $475.6 million last year, or 17 percent of all revenues. "I've never seen anything like this," Mr. Eidelman said. "I can see why Amazon.com, because of its volatility, is not marginable. Or if trading is halted in a stock. But never to take a nice, solid, stable company and say it's not marginable." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the newyork Stock Exchange's margin debt since 1991.

title: Chicago Exchange Sets an After-Hour Plan
body: The Chicago Stock Exchange, the nation's third-largest stock market, said today that its board had approved a plan to offer after-hours trading to both institutional and individual investors starting in October -- the first exchange to do so. The move creates yet another forum for investors eager to trade after the 4 P.M. close at the major stock exchanges and holds out the eventual prospect of around-the-clock trading. "Now that investing has become a national pastime, it has become clear that after-hours trading is here for good," said Richard K. Strauss, an analyst at Goldman Sachs & Company. "So everyone's scrambling to be a first mover." On Tuesday, E*Trade Group, the big on-line broker, said it was joining Instinet, the Reuters Group unit that is one of the largest electronic trading networks, to offer after-hours trading to smaller investors between 4 P.M. and 6:30 P.M. And earlier this month, the Datek Online Holdings Corporation began offering its on-line investors after-hours trading via a unit called Island E.C.N. -- for electronic communications network -- between 4 P.M. and 5:15 P.M. Analysts say a movement is clearly afoot to create a global 24-hour stock-trading network using the Internet and the kind of low-cost electronic trading networks that are shaking up Wall Street. Even so, the leading markets have been moving cautiously. The newyork Stock Exchange, the world's largest stock market, and the Nasdaq market, home to many popular technology issues, are also considering offering after-hours trading. While they study the move, which is also being monitored by regulators, new rivals say they will fill the vacuum to offer trading in Big Board and Nasdaq stocks. "We believe this is a subject that has legs, and it's our responsibility to be responsive to our customers," said Robert H. Forney, the chief executive of the Chicago Stock Exchange. "We think this will promote competition and give investors the benefit of that competition." A spokesman for the newyork Stock Exchange reiterated today that the Big Board is studying the issue of after-hours trading under the supervision of the Securities and Exchange Commission. The National Assocation of Securities Dealers, which operates Nasdaq, has considered closing the market at its regular time, 4 P.M., then reopening at 5 P.M. for an evening session. That plan may have to be rethought if competing electronic networks trade during that hour. A Nasdaq spokesman declined comment today. According to its plan, the Chicago Stock Exchange -- which operates a highly automated auction-style forum -- will offer its more than 150 member brokerage firms after-hours trading in some of the nation's best-known Big Board and Nasdaq stocks between 4 P.M. and 6:30 P.M. Eastern standard time. Officials at the Chicago exchange said that their electronic trading system would let almost any brokerage firm or on-line broker tap into its after-hours market to trade, by limit order only, in the stocks that make up the Standard & Poor's 100-stock index, the Nasdaq 100-stock index and other very active stocks, including such big names as McDonald's, AT&T, Microsoft and Intel. A limit order is at a specific price, instead of an open order to buy or sell at the current market price. The Chicago exchange now offers a half-hour of trading after the closing bell but mainly for institutional investors. The new system will greatly expand the hours and try to tap the lucrative retail market that fast-growing on-line brokerage firms are poised to dominate. The Chicago exchange is going head-to-head with Island and Instinet as well as trying to get a jump on other exchanges, which face the same competition. Lisa Cervenka, a spokeswoman for the Chicago exchange -- which trades about 50 million shares a day -- said it had a low-cost electronic trading system that executes trades automatically. The system, she added, is expected to be accessible over the Internet to hundreds of brokerage firms by October. What all the after-hours trading systems seek is liquidity -- enough order flow to make profits and create active and efficient marketplaces. Island, for example, depends on Datek clients and other brokers with access to the Island system for trading in Nasdaq stocks. Instinet will bring together more than a million E*Trade customers with institutional orders for mostly Nasdaq issues and some Big Board ones. And Chicago officials say they will have a mix of Big Board and Nasdaq orders at prices competitive with the electronic communications networks.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Schwab to Offer Wireless Trading Servic e
body: The Charles Schwab Corporation, the largest unitedstates discount and Internet brokerage house, said today that it would start a wireless trading service to let customers use pagers, mobile phones and hand-held computers to trade stocks. With the new service, Schwab will go up against such rivals as Discover Brokerage, a unit of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company, and the brokerage arm of the mutual fund company Fidelity Investments, which already offer such trading. Schwab, based in San Francisco, said it planned to offer the service by year's end to "active" customers who trade more than 48 times a year. Tracey Gordon, a Schwab spokeswoman, did not say what features would be offered or how much it would cost, saying only the service would be "very competitive." Schwab said it was in a partnership with Aether Technologies, a closely held provider of wireless products and services, to develop the new service. Aether is also Discover's partner in its wireless trading and information service. Wireless fees at other brokerage firms range from $30 to $69 a month, and wireless devices cost up to several hundred dollars, so the service is expected to appeal mainly to traders with hefty portfolios. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Another Twist in Skirmish Over Instant Messaging
body: In its latest tweak at America Online, the Microsoft Corporation announced today that it would release a computer protocol to enable subscribers of competing instant-messaging services to communicate with its own customers. Microsoft officials said the move was intended to pave the way for communication among subscribers of the handful of major companies offering instant messaging, a feature that allows computer users to contact one another instantaneously and chat on line. Thus far, users of instant-message services have been largely relegated to sending messages to users within their own service. In a pitched battle with America Online, which pioneered instant messaging, Microsoft has sought to deliver messages from its own subscribers to users of America Online's software without the company's permission. America Online, which says it has 43 million users of one form or another on its instant-messaging software, has accused Microsoft of hacking into its system to route messages to and from America Online customers. At least 14 times, America Online has changed its protocol -- the specifications that allow two software programs to communicate -- and each time Microsoft programmers have found a way around the barrier. Microsoft, which has amassed 1.5 million users of its instant-messaging software in less than a month of service, is not alone. Other instant-messaging competitors, including Tribal Voice, which has five million instant-messaging members, have said they also intend to link to users of America Online's software. In this respect, the latest twist in the skirmish underscores a larger issue: with 60 million to 100 million people estimated to use instant messaging, there is growing momentum among the competitors to create standards so their subscribers can communicate. "We're at a watershed," said Richard Dym, vice president for marketing for Tribal Voice, based in Scotts Valley, Calif. "In order for this form of communication to take the next step, to maybe even replace email, we need openness." Mr. Dym said the growing use of instant messaging had started momentum in the last year to create a standard protocol so competing services can exchange messages over the Internet. And he said Microsoft was adding to that momentum by putting its substantial resources and weight behind the standards quest. For its part, America Online said it, too, favored open standards permitting communication among users of different services. Tricia Primrose, an America Online spokeswoman, said the company had been working for several weeks with the Internet Engineering Task Force, which is overseeing the creation of standards for a protocol. Mr. Dym called it "a big-time irony" that Microsoft was releasing its instant-messaging protocol, since it has jealously guarded the source code for its operating systems and software programs. But Rob Bennett, vice president for marketing at MSN, Microsoft's on-line division, said the comparison was unfair. He said Microsoft's willingness to publish the protocol was consistent with a policy to make its software widely "interoperable." The Internet Engineering Task Force praised Microsoft. The move will help "in informing our development of robust, open protocols for Internet-wide interoperability in this area," wrote Vijay Saraswat and Dave Marvit, who are leading the standards committee. In another front in the instant-messaging battle, Microsoft officials said today that they had identified and reprimanded an employee who used a false identity to send a message discrediting America Online to a computer security expert. The employee sent a message under the name Phil Bucking of Bucking Consulting, but the security expert, Richard Smith, traced the message back to Microsoft. Today the company confirmed that the message had come from an employee, who had stepped forward to confess. Mr. Bennett declined to say what disciplinary action had been taken, but defended the employee as having tried to do the "right thing" by publicizing what Microsoft contends is a security flaw in America Online's system. "This is a case of good intentions and bad execution," he said. In the early 1990's, Microsoft dismissed an employee for anonymously posting criticisms of I.B.M.'s competing operating system on on-line bulletin boards.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Cell Phones Are No. 1 With Business Travelers
body: Modern travelers will use cell phones in the car, on the street and even while standing beside another telephone. That is one of the conclusions of a new survey of the technological habits of 1,000 business travelers conducted by the research firm Greenfield Online. A cellular telephone is the No. 1 piece of electronic gear carried by travelers, with 7 out of 10 travelers surveyed toting one. The vast majority, 94 percent, of those who carry cell phones use them in cars. Nearly two-thirds, however, said they make calls while walking. Half of those surveyed make calls on their cell phones from offices, hotels and airports while traveling, although wired phones are plentiful. Margot Turk, Greenfield's director of NetReach Services, said respondents were not asked why they make cell phone calls from places where other phones are available. "We think that it's convenience. If you use your cellular phone, you don't need to worry about the 15-digit calling card number. You don't need to wait in line for a pay phone," Ms. Turk said. Only about half of the business travelers surveyed carry laptop computers on business trips, a figure that surprised Rudy Nadilo, Greenfield's chief executive. "Obviously, email still has a ways to go in being the mainstream business communications tool," Mr. Nadilo said. Only about 36 percent of the respondents own pagers. Hand-held PC/personal digital assistants have not reached high levels of usage among business travelers. Only 1 in 10 surveyed take such a device on trips. However, among those who own such devices, 92 percent take them on trips. And the survey found that the most popular device was the Palm Connected Organizer, owned by 77 percent of those surveyed who owned a hand-held PC.   STEPHEN C. MILLER   http://www.nytimes.com

title: E*Trade Joins Push to Extend Trading Hours - Correction Appended
body: The E*Trade Group, the big on-line brokerage firm, and Instinet, a stock trading network that serves institutional investors, said yesterday that they would team up to offer small investors the opportunity to trade stocks after the major exchanges close for the day. The announcement shows that individual investors, long shut out of the trading arena after the 4 P.M. closing bell, are demanding more service and getting it from technology-knowledgable trading networks. Until now, after-hours stock trading has been monopolized by institutional investors and Wall Street brokerage firms buying and selling stocks on late-breaking news or early-morning tips. The surge in on-line investing and the development of electronic trading networks has given smaller investors the power to ask for greater access to the stock market and for tools to imitate the professionals, who are predicting the emergence of a global marketplace for stocks that never shuts down. "This is just another signpost on the way" to round-the-clock trading, said Henry M. McVeigh, an analyst who covers on-line trading at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter. "A growing number of retail investors prefer to enter their buy and sell orders after the closing bell." The newyork Stock Exchange and the National Association of Securities Dealers, which operates the Nasdaq stock market, have talked about offering trading in an evening session in the next year, but want to wait at least until they have put Year 2000 computer problems behind them. But while the exchanges study the issue, electronic trading is shaking up the establishment and pitting traditional brokerage firms and stock exchanges against discount on-line brokers and low-cost computerized trading networks. E*Trade is not the first, but it is the biggest firm to extend the trading day. Just weeks ago, Datek Online Holdings began offering a similar Internet service. E*Trade and Datek Online are moving swiftly to make available a service that they say will "change the rules" and "empower the individual investor." E*Trade and Instinet, a unit of Reuters Group P.L.C., say that beginning in September they will offer on-line trading in newyork Stock Exchange and Nasdaq stocks between 4 P.M. and 6:30 P.M., creating an after-hours market that serves both institutional clients and retail investors. It is the first time retail investors will get direct access to Instinet, which has served institutional clients since 1969. Eventually, the service's hours could be extended. Although it is unclear how much demand there is among small investors for after-hours trading, executives at E*Trade and Instinet say that customers have been calling for extended trading hours for some time and so they decided to allow it as an experiment. "What our customers want is access to opportunity and a level playing field with larger institutional investors," said Christos M. Cotsakos, chairman and chief executive at E*Trade, which is based in Menlo Park, Calif. "It's all part of democratizing personal investing." Earlier this month, Datek Online began offering a trading forum from 4 P.M. to 5:15 P.M. through its electronic trading network, the Island E.C.N., and says more than 50,000 accounts have signed up for the service, which is free from commissions through the end of the month. "We're very excited about the start," said Robert O. Bethge, a spokesman for Datek, which is based in Edison, N.J. "We're just keeping the store open for an extra hour and a half." There are, to be sure, a number of hurdles. Light trading activity could mean more drastic swings in stock prices, and not all stocks may be available for trading. The Island system at Datek is used only for Nasdaq stocks, while Instinet's system handles Big Board stocks as well, though not all of them. Regulators have cautioned the major stock exchanges to move warily on after-hours trading formats and to take into account that smaller investors may not be adequately informed about the risks. Others are worried about bad executions, or pricing problems on transactions, in a system that works on auto-pilot. Wall Street analysts, however, see round-the-clock trading as inevitable, and already there are signs of a mad dash. Discover Brokerage, the on-line division of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, has already announced plans for extended hours, and so has Wit Capital, which plans to team up with America Online. A number of other small electronic communications networks, or E.C.N.'s, are also planning after-hours trading. And Wall Street brokerage firms and other trading and software firms are scrambling to form alliances to compete in the new electronic trading marketplace. "Everybody and their grandmother are investing in E.C.N.'s," said James Punishill, an on-line trading analyst at Forrester Research. "The only one delaying this is Nasdaq and the Big Board, who don't know what to do about this." One institution that is moving aggressively is Instinet. It faces stiff competition from fast-growing Island, which is popular among day traders for its fast executions and its dominance of Internet stocks. Instinet has begun a big advertising campaign, acquired a stake in another E.C.N., Archipelago L.L.C., and held talks with at least one major day-trading firm about acquiring new software to reach the retail investor market. In reaching an exclusive deal with E*Trade through the end of the year, Instinet signaled it would plow ahead with its stated ambition to enter the fast-growing retail marketplace. Douglas M. Atkin, chief executive at Instinet, said yesterday that retail investors have been asking for access. He also said many retail trades coming through E*Trade may match up with small institutional orders that are often sliced up into smaller pieces by Instinet clients. The next step? Datek already says it has plans to offer its customers trading before the opening bell at 9:30 A.M. And Mr. Punishill at Forrester says other on-line brokers will come forward soon. In six months, everybody will be in this, he says. After-hours trading is going to go universal. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Business Day yesterday about the teaming of E*Trade Group, the on-line brokerage firm, and Instinet, a stock trading network, to offer after-hours trading to small investors misspelled the surname of an analyst who covers on-line trading at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter. He is Henry M. McVey, not McVeigh. Correction-Date: August 19, 1999, Thursday Graphic   Photo: Christos M. Cotsakos, head of E*Trade, said customers wanted extended hours. (Ann Dowie)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
When it comes to using the Internet to reach consumers, the operative word is 'potential.'
body: ADVERTISING on the Internet, like most uses of this new medium, is still in the early stages of a long and presumably fruitful evolution. In other words, it is long on potential but, so far, short on success stories. Part of the problem is that although the Internet has gathered a mainstream audience, many companies have yet to figure out how to use it effectively for advertising. As a result, they have been reluctant to pour money into Web ads: just 1 percent of the $200 billion spent on advertising last year was spent on line. According to a report to be released today, however, that figure is about to rise. Jupiter Communications, an Internet research firm, projects $11.5 billion in spending for on-line advertising in 2003, compared with $2.1 billion in 1998. Jupiter projects that in four years the Internet will rank fourth among advertising media in total ad spending, jumping ahead of cable television, magazines and yellow pages and vying with radio for the No. 3 spot behind broadcast television and newspapers. The report follows similar projections made last week by Forrester Research, an Internet consulting firm. The Jupiter report is based on projections of growth in both overall advertising spending and the on-line audience. And the company's research indicates that two crucial players in traditional advertising -- car makers and consumer goods manufacturers -- are finally warming up to the Internet. The report predicts that in 2003, automotive companies will devote 13 percent of their advertising budgets to the Internet, compared with 5 percent this year, and consumer goods makers like Procter & Gamble will spend 7 percent of their ad budgets on the Internet, compared with 2 percent this year. Jupiter predicts that the on-line audience in 2003 will be 64 million unitedstates households, compared with 38 million now. But according to Rich LeFurgy, chairman of the Internet Advertising Bureau, an industry trade group, expectations for higher Web spending also reflect fundamental shifts in the perception of the Internet as an advertising medium. "In 1995 and '96, advertisers were putting up sites for their products, and looking at it as a sales channel," Mr. LeFurgy said. "But that was confusing for advertisers who couldn't sell their products on line, like soft drink makers, so that was a dead end." Not only do consumer packaged goods companies lack the expertise -- and in some cases, the desire -- to sell directly to consumers over the Internet, but consumers would not be likely to go to Coke's on-line store, for example, to buy soda, he said. "These companies couldn't figure out why they should be advertising on line," Mr. LeFurgy said. More recently, however, companies have recognized the Web's potential for brand advertising, as opposed to direct sales. So instead of sending consumers to their own Web sites to buy goods, companies like Procter & Gamble are spending money on branding campaigns to build awareness. And through cooperative advertising efforts, they can send consumers to, say, an on-line grocery store where buyers can find their products alongside the products of the other cooperating marketers, Mr. LeFurgy said. As more companies migrate toward brand-based advertising, they are also looking less at the number of people who actually click on a Web ad, Mr. LeFurgy said. He said that a user's propensity to click on an ad is not necessarily the best way to gauge its effectiveness in building brand awareness. Marketing strategies must also change if companies are to succeed on line, said Patrick Keane, an analyst with Jupiter. The tendency of many companies to view their Web initiatives as somehow separate from their core businesses has helped perpetuate the theory that Internet advertising does not work, Mr. Keane said. When marketers do set aside money to advertise on line, he said, "their on-line campaigns too often look different and feel different from their off-line campaigns -- and that's just not an effective way to manage a campaign." He added: "Advertisers are going to realize that they have to integrate their campaigns across all media," instead of merely adding a Web site address to "a TV ad or whatever else they're doing." Furthermore, Mr. Keane said, "the fragmented nature of media consumption means marketers will need to hit consumers at multiple media points." Mr. LeFurgy also noted that an abundance of new Internet businesses rely on ad revenue. In recent months, Internet service providers and PC makers have used advertising revenue as a means to lower their prices, giving consumers the chance to get cheaper machines and Internet access if they agree to look at advertisements. Meanwhile, as Internet advertising builds momentum, spending on other media may suffer, Jupiter predicts. Mr. Keane said the Internet's anticipated cannibalism of other media is, in fact, taking place as people spend more time on line. Internet users spent an average of 7.1 hours a week on line in 1998, according to Jupiter, which predicts that will increase to 10.2 hours a week in 2003. "And they'll use other media less because there's only so much time in the day," Mr. Keane said. "People have been a little myopic about on-line advertising, just looking at the fact that the dollars are smaller," he added. "It's not about the numbers. It's about how the Internet is reinventing advertising."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: MCI Net Snag Could Drive Small Providers Out of Business
body: The 10-day partial shutdown of MCI Worldcom's high-speed data network took a cataclysmic toll on dozens and possibly hundreds of small Internet service providers who were forced to close altogether last week. Some say they may go out of business as a result. These mom-and-pop players, along with more than a quarter of all Internet service providers nationally, rely on MCI to route subscribers onto the Internet. The network problem also took its toll on regional and national Internet service providers, including America Online, which said yesterday that two million subscribers from its combined America Online and Compuserve services may have been affected. But small service providers felt the biggest impact because unlike their larger counterparts they typically cannot afford a backup -- that is, a contract with a second major network company. So when MCI went down, they went down with it. "For our industry, this is a killer -- a company killer," said A. K. Jordan, president of Intellitech, a service provider in Highland Park, N.J., with about 500 dial-up customers. Mr. Jordan said that starting on Saturday, Aug. 7, the company's subscribers were no longer able to get access to the World Wide Web and were able to get email only from other Intellitech customers. He said he was told that MCI was assuring customers that the problem was a result of congestion and that the system would be up and running in two hours -- a message he passed along to subscribers who called to complain. "We came out looking like liars and incompetents," he said. When the situation did not improve, Mr. Jordan and his business partners took the extraordinary step of telephoning roughly one-quarter of their subscribers to explain the situation and to ask them not to quit the service. He said he now planned to give his customers a free month of access. His situation is not unique, according to DataXchange, a Washington-based company that buys Internet access wholesale from MCI and sells it to small providers, like Mr. Jordan's Intellitech. Mark Stutz, a spokesman for RMI.Net, the Denver parent of DataXchange, said that of the 150 small service providers to which it resells MCI services, 66 "lost their networks completely." Mr. Stutz estimated that because of those failures alone, some 250,000 subscribers lost Net access. He said that some of the providers said they had had so many subscriber cancellations they might go out of business. "It doesn't get any worse than this," Mr. Stutz said. "It's hard to imagine a worse-case scenario for our industry." An MCI Worldcom spokeswoman, Linda Laughlin, said the company would offer customers two free days of Internet access for each day they had been unable to use MCI's network to get access. Ms. Laughlin characterized the partial shutdown as an "unsatisfactory" performance and said MCI Worldcom expected it would take "several weeks" to regain the trust of its customers. Some industry analysts said MCI might be underestimating the public- relations toll. Jeanne M. Schaff, senior analyst with Forrester Research, a Cambridge, Mass.-based market research firm, speculated that "most" of the stranded Internet service providers would look to one of the other major Network providers for access to the Net. For now, though, MCI is the biggest player. According to a survey released in July from Cahners In-Stat, a San Jose, Calif., market research firm, MCI provides national backbone access to 40.9 percent of national service providers and to 23.6 percent of small and regional providers -- defined as those serving fewer than 25 area codes. Most, if not all, larger and regional providers rely on more than one company for backbone Net access. For example, Earthlink Network, a Pasadena, Calif.-based service with 1.4 million subscribers, employs MCI and six other backbone providers, including AT&T, I.B.M. and Sprint, and thus experienced only minor headaches last week, said Steve Dougherty, director of technology acquisition for Earthlink. He said the company simply rerouted traffic that would have gone over the MCI network to another provider. At America Online and its subsidiary Compuserve about 2 million of 20 million subscribers were vulnerable to the network failure over the weekend because the primary access numbers they use to dial into the Internet rely on the MCI backbone. In most of those instances, America Online urged customers to try a different access number; however, in the case of 50 communities, representing roughly 500,000 subscribers, there was no second access number available, the company said. For those customers, America Online created a toll-free number. However, some subscribers might not have been apprised of the change since they were unable to sign onto the Internet in the first place to receive an update.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Small Internet Providers Survive Among the Giants
body: America Online is the undisputed king of Internet service providers, having added 5.1 million members the last year alone, for a total of more than 17 million subscribers. But its growth rate masks a remarkable trend: the company's share of the Internet-access market is no longer growing as it once was and may, in fact, be declining. The market for Internet service providers, or I.S.P.'s, rather than consolidating around America Online, Microsoft and telephone companies like AT&T as many industry observers had predicted, remains a diverse industry with wide open possibilities for competitors, including mom-and-pop operations. America Online's monthly subscription plan, meanwhile, is now just one of many business models for Internet access, and new models seem to pop up weekly. Free access, often supported by advertising, has taken root in Europe and is spreading to the unitedstates. And hardware manufacturers are teaming with service providers to offer a range of discounted plans. There is no doubt that America Online remains the leader of the pack. The nearest competitors, Worldnet from AT&T and MSN from Microsoft, have fewer than two million members each. But research firms generally agree that America Online's market share is not growing the way it has in recent years. One sign of the wide open nature of the Internet access market is the beleaguered state of MSN. Its membership numbers are flat, and Microsoft acknowledges that it is losing market share, although it declined to release exact numbers. The company plans to bolster its marketing budget and make a run at big growth later this summer, said William R. Diefenbach, group product manager for MSN Internet access. The persistent -- and, in some circles, unexpected -- growth of small local Internet service providers continues to make for a complex market. Boardwatch Magazine, a widely circulated trade journal, reports that its directory of Internet service providers in Canada, the unitedstates and the Caribbean grew 36 percent between last October and July, to 6,511 from 4,800. Greg Tally, editor of the directory, said the increase was partly the result of existing service providers' registering with the directory for the first time, but he added that many were new. "There still are plenty of up-and-coming I.S.P.'s," he said. "It's still exploding." Most service providers are relatively small, serving several hundred dial-up customers, Mr. Tally said. Boardwatch reports that of the service providers in its directory today, 5,895 offer local access numbers in fewer than 25 area codes, whereas only 616 are available in more than 25 area codes, meaning they are accessible on a regional or national basis. Those numbers may be misleading because some small Internet service providers primarily serve local businesses rather than dial-up customers like the average Web surfer. But both Mr. Tally and MSN's Mr. Diefenbach said the small providers remained a powerful force in the dial-up market. "We have seen, in aggregate, the smaller and local and regional I.S.P.'s gaining share," Mr. Diefenbach said. Access Internet Communications Inc., a small service provider with several thousand customers in Cupertino, Calif., says it has seen its dial-up subscriber base grow by 25 percent a year. James Thomatos, the company's vice president of sales and marketing, said the demand for access was so great that there were plenty of new customers to be shared among Internet service providers. But he said small service providers were also attracting customers because they offered more personalized service than the big services. "When you call here, someone answers the phone," he said. "Have you ever tried to do business with the phone company? It's not the easiest thing to do." Further complicating the market are efforts to offer free Internet access, a concept already popular in Europe and making its first major wave in the unitedstates with a company called Netzero Inc. In the last six months, Netzero, based in West Lake Village, Calif., has grown faster than any other service provider in the country, with the exception of America Online. Last October it had 100,000 subscribers. It now claims 1.3 million. "We add one every 13 seconds," said Mark R. Goldston, the company's chairman and chief executive. Netzero plans to make money by showing special ads in a box that is always present on its subscribers' screens. Netzero filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on July 14 for an initial public offering of stock, which is likely to take place before the end of the year. Alta Vista, a search engine and portal owned by Compaq Computer, last Thursday began offering free, ad-supported Internet service. The company will use the service to drive traffic to its Web sites, increasing advertising income. Even Microsoft has recently talked about offering cheap or free access, but it has not disclosed solid plans. Industry analysts, some of whom have expressed skepticism about the idea of free access in the past, say the idea's time may have come. "The price is going toward zero," said Drew P. Ianni, an analyst for Jupiter Communications, a newyork-based market research firm. A handful of businesses are offering free computers as an enticement to sign subscribers up for Internet service, but this model is unproven. In a variation on this theme, the Microworkz.com Corporation is selling a computer for $299 with a year of free Internet access included. After its partnership with Earthlink Network Inc. fell apart amid an exchange of lawsuits earlier this month, Microworkz teamed up with AT&T to provide the Internet access part of the deal. Mr. Ianni says that consolidation is imminent and that AT&T, America Online or MSN will begin to snap up large Internet service providers like Earthlink and Mindspring Enterprises Inc. "We're in the lull before a firestorm of acquisitions," he said. Market research firms cannot agree on whether the market share of industry leaders is dipping, rising slightly or holding steady. One firm, Cahners In-Stat Group, reported this month that America Online's market share dipped over the last year to 21.5 percent from 24.3 percent. It estimated the total number of Internet accounts in the unitedstates at 66 million. IDC, another market research firm, estimates that America Online's market share has dropped to 39.3 percent from 42.1 percent in the last year, and that MSN dropped to 4 percent from 5.9 percent. It puts the size of the Internet access market at just 37 million accounts. Barry Schuler, president of America Online's interactive services group, said its "market share has been steady." He argued that it was a testimony to the on-line service's strength that no other major Internet service provider had broken out of the pack to even claim a strong second place. Mr. Schuler added that America Online, which charges $22 a month for unlimited access, does not feel threatened by the free services. He said he did not believe they could attract enough advertising to make the business profitable.
