Surveys show that names of loved ones, birth dates and sports teams are the most frequently used passwords, while hacker folklore says some of the most popular individual passwords are sex, love, god, password, secret and qwerty. A good password, security experts say, must balance between being intuitive enough to remember and being too difficult to guess. Passwords should be at least six characters long and consist of a mixture of upper- and lower-case letters, numbers and non-alphanumeric characters. Here are some strategies for creating memorable but not easily guessed passwords: * Take two short words, capitalize one or more letters, and run them together with punctuation marks or numbers in between. * Choose a line or two from a favorite song or poem and use the first letter of each word. * Create words that mimic easily remembered sounds. * Use letter combinations based on shapes on the keyboard, like spirals or zig-zags. * Use at least two passwords for Web sites and networks: a complicated, relatively obscure password for opening more important accounts and a less difficult password for tasks like common Web site registrations. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Circuits on Thursday about problems with computer passwords misstated the name of the company at which Alessandro Piol is a managing director. It is Invesco Private Capital, not Investco Private Capital. Correction-Date: August 7, 1999, Saturday Graphic   Photos: Ron Dilley, a network administrator at Applied Digital Access near San Diego, with passwords on a computer screen. Mr. Dilley has 129 passwords to remember. (Robert Burroughs for The newyork Times)(pg. G1); LOCKED OUT -- Forgotten passwords are no minor inconvenience. They add up to millions of dollars annually in help-desk costs and lost productivity. (pg. G8)

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Trading Is Mixed as Internet Shares Fall Sharply Again
body: Stock prices were mixed yesterday, but traders said investors remained extremely skittish about high valuations and the direction of interest rates. "Investors are very nervous right now, and rightly so," said Bill Allyn, head of listed trading at Jeffries & Company. "We have been talking about valuations for months, and now it is finally hitting home." Internet stocks, the epicenter of speculative activity for much of the year, took another hard hit. TheStreet.com's Internet index fell 20.96, or 3.9 percent, to 519.07, pulled down by stocks like America Online, Yahoo and CMGI. The index has fallen nearly 35 percent since it peaked on April 12. Interest rate worries pulled down the Nasdaq composite index, which fell for the fourth consecutive session. Big declines in Unum Provident, the insurance company, and Charles Schwab, the big discount brokerage house, dragged down the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index, and small stocks slumped. But the Dow Jones industrial average managed to move up, largely on strength in Hewlett-Packard and Procter & Gamble. "This is not just an isolated day," said Bob Gasser, head of unitedstates equity trading at J. P. Morgan Securities. "It is a lot tougher for the market to deal with rising interest rates than with good corporate earnings." Mr. Gasser and other analysts said the market was likely to remain in a highly unsettled state until at least Friday, when July employment data are scheduled to be released. The Federal Reserve Board, which meets Aug. 24 to debate whether it should raise short-term interest rates, is likely to pay close attention to that report. By the close, the Dow Jones industrial average had risen 31.35, or three-tenths of 1 percent, to 10,677.31. The Standard & Poor's 500 index closed at 1322.18, down 5.87, or four-tenths of 1 percent. The Nasdaq composite lost 35.64, or 1.4 percent, to 2587.99. And the Russell 2000 index of small-company stocks fell 6.35, or 1.4 percent, to 436.28. The pace of business quickened a bit from Monday but still remained fairly subdued. Trading volume on the newyork Stock Exchange was 734.9 million shares. On the Nasdaq stock market, just over a billion shares changed hands. Much of the action yesterday was focused on Internet stocks. Early in the day a number of Internet shares rallied on reports that Yahoo was in negotiations to buy Excite@Home. But those rumors were quashed by George Bell, Excite's president. Yahoo, which dipped lower on the initial reports, fell further later. The stock closed at 125 3/8, down 6 15/16. The stock has lost nearly half its market value since early April. Stocks of Internet brokerage firms, which have also been beaten up recently, were battered again after Bill Burnham, an Internet analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston, issued a report saying the companies might see their first-ever decline in trading volume, in the third quarter, because of weakness in the Internet stocks their companies favor. "To see growth in negative territory is significant, but not earth shattering," Mr. Burnham said. "I was surprised the stocks sold off as much as they did" after the report was released. Schwab, the largest on-line brokerage firm, fell 4 11/16, to 37 3/4. E*Trade Group fell 4 5/16, to 24 11/16; Knight/ Trimark Group lost 4 7/32, to 37 1/32, and Ameritrade Holding dropped 2 3/4, to 21 1/4. America Online, the world's largest Internet service, continued its slump, with the stock falling for the fourth session, shedding 4 1/16, to 88 13/16. Since April 6, when it peaked at 175 1/2, the stock has fallen nearly 50 percent. And CMGI, the Internet venture capital company, fell 6 7/16 yesterday, to 81 7/8. "The good news from this summer's selling of Internet shares is that the bears will be hard pressed to still call this a bubble market," said Thomas M. Galvin, chief investment officer at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "At this point, the easy money appears to have been made in Internet stocks." Pressure on these stocks extended to new issues. Four new Internet offerings were priced yesterday: 1-800-Flowers.com, Quotesmith.com, Bigstar Entertainment and Splitrock Services Inc. All closed below their initial offered price. Elsewhere, Unum Provident fell 15 5/16, or 30 percent, to 36 3/8, after the company, one of the nation's largest disability insurers, said that second-quarter earnings fell because of costs associated with the June merger that created it. Qualcomm was the biggest loser on the Nasdaq, falling 12 1/2, to 140. The stock slid after Motorola said it would make semiconductors for phones to compete with Qualcomm. Among Dow stocks, Johnson & Johnson gained 2 1/4, to 94 3/16 after an analyst at J. P. Morgan upgraded his recommendation on the stock to "buy." Proctor & Gamble gained 3 9/16, to 93 11/16. And Hewlett-Packard rose 3 3/4, to 108 1/2. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average over the past year. title: House Cuts Could Force S.E.C. Layoffs
body: At a time when record numbers of Americans are investing their money and their trust in the stock and bond markets, a House panel has recommended a budget for the nation's top securities regulator next year that would require it to cut its work force by 10 percent. Under terms approved by the House Appropriations Committee last week, funds for the Securities and Exchange Commission in the year 2000 would be $324 million, 7.6 percent below the $351 million the commission says it needs to maintain current staffing and activities. The House is expected to vote on the measure this week. A diminished S.E.C. budget is the result of stringent caps placed on discretionary Congressional spending in the 1997 budget agreement. "Every bill that we have with the exception of defense is at or below last year's levels," said Elizabeth Morra, communications director for the House Appropriations Committee. "It's not a question of whether we wanted to fund them. It's a question of not having enough funds to go around." At $324 million, the House's recommended budget for the S.E.C. is well below the $370.8 million approved for the commission by the Senate in June. At the time, Senator Judd Gregg of New Hampshire, chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, said additional money was needed for the S.E.C. to combat swindlers on the Internet. Differences between the levels approved by the Senate and the House will have be reconciled in a House-Senate conference committee this fall. While maintaining its current level of staffing and operations would require a budget of $351 million, the S.E.C. says cracking down on the increasingly sophisticated securities frauds that many investors are falling victim to requires even more money. "We were expecting and need a large increase to keep up with the Internet, additional litigation support and more staffing," said James M. McConnell, executive director of the S.E.C. In addition to laying off 10 percent of its staff, the commission said the House's recommended budget would jeopardize the S.E.C.'s ability to bring new fraud cases. Also at risk would be its monitoring of new market developments such as the anticipated moves by the newyork Stock Exchange and the National Association of Securities Dealers to become for-profit, privately held exchanges. Scrutiny of day trading firms, on-line brokerage houses and the flock of new, privately run electronic exchanges would be hindered as well, a spokesman for the S.E.C. said. Richard H. Walker, director of enforcement at the S.E.C., said the House's budget "would cause very serious consequences for all investors but especially for small investors." He added, "Any substantive reduction in the enforcement budget would embolden fraudsters to expand their illegal activities." The bull market in stocks combined with the sweeping transformation that electronic trading has brought to the markets has already strained S.E.C. resources. Corporations registered a record $2.55 trillion in securities with the commission in 1998, up 77 percent from the amount filed in 1997. And the total average trading volume of all on-line brokers was approximately 340,000 trades a day in late 1998, a more than threefold increase over electronic trading volume in early 1997. The commission also said that it had brought nearly 100 Internet-related enforcement actions since 1995 and that it received 200 to 300 email messages each day, many related to possible frauds conducted on the Internet. The number of complaints from investors about on-line brokerage services received by the S.E.C. increased sixfold from fiscal 1997 through the first six months of this year. The S.E.C. more than pays its freight through fees that it levies on issuers of securities and on market participants. Thanks to the robust stock market, the Congressional Budget Office projects that next year the commission will collect $501 million in fees that will then go into the so-called appropriations pot from which Congress finances the S.E.C. and other agencies. Those fees would exceed the House's financing level for the S.E.C. by $177 million. In a letter to Representative Harold Rogers of Kentucky, chairman of the House Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, State and the Judiciary, which parcels out money to the S.E.C., Arthur Levitt, chairman of the commission, wrote: "On-line trading now accounts for approximately one-third of all retail stock trades. Increasing our staff to maintain and enhance Internet surveillance, conduct investigations and prosecute violations of Internet fraud is absolutely essential to our efforts to effectively protect investors."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: A Showdown On Messaging May Unite Web Users
body: For more than a week, the Microsoft Corporation and America Online Inc. have engaged in a public spat over open access to the instant-message systems that have become increasingly popular on the Internet. Despite their rhetoric, though, neither company has much of a track record for making it easy for competitors to gain access to the markets that America Online and Microsoft hold dear. Microsoft, of course, stands accused by the Justice Department of unfairly using its control of the Windows operating system to stifle the market for Internet browser software from Netscape Communications -- a company that America Online now owns. And much of the appeal of America Online's service lies in its offering both content and features, like instant messages, that are not available to other Internet users. The current showdown between the two companies concerns America Online's refusal to let Microsoft, among others, link its on-line users to America Online's instant-messaging system -- a form of electronic mail that lets two people conduct a real-time conversation. Jealously as each may guard its own advantages, both Microsoft and America Online are quick to call for openness in any market in which they are behind. Thus, America Online has initiated a vast lobbying campaign calling for open access to offer Internet service through cable television systems, largely because it has been shut out by the AT&T Corporation and other operators. And it is no accident that Microsoft is taking the lead in talking about open standards in instant messaging, a service in which America Online has 80 million users. Until very recently Microsoft had no instant-messaging subscribers on its MSN on-line service. Unlike email, which can be exchanged by all Internet users regardless of the service they subscribe to, instant-message systems so far have been proprietary. Thus, users of Microsoft's new instant message system can communicate only with each other and not with the far larger number of instant messengers on America Online's networks. But Microsoft has found a backdoor to America Online's main instant-message system, setting off a heated debate that embroiled much of the Internet industry last week. And during the last two weeks, the two companies have played at least six rounds of hide and seek, as America Online blocked access to Microsoft, and Microsoft quickly found another way in. By last Friday, many observers were fed up with both sides. "It is unseemly for Microsoft to hijack their way into AOL's system," said Eric Schmitt, an analyst with Forrester Research. "But America Online should open the thing up." The history, culture and underlying technology of the Internet has pressed most proprietary systems to give way to open technical standards. And America Online acknowledges that it cannot fight these forces forever. "AOL realizes in the end this will all be open," said Paul W. Noglows, an analyst with the investment firm Hambrecht & Quist. "They just want to control how it becomes open." America Online's reluctance to embrace an open standard is certainly understandable, considering how much its instant-message system -- and the related "buddy list" technology that lets friends quickly determine if each other is on line -- have contributed to its rise as the most powerful company on the Internet. "It's an important reason you pay your $21.95 for AOL each month," Mr. Noglows said. But even three years ago, America Online acknowledged that it could not keep instant messages limited to its proprietary on-line service. So the company introduced AOL Instant Messenger, a program that anyone with an Internet account could download and use free to send instant messages to both America Online members and any other AOL Instant Messenger user. Instant Messenger enables America Online subscribers who use instant messages at home to also use them at work, even if their office computers do not use the America Online subscription service. But the product also allows people to drop the American Online subscription service entirely and still keep chatting with their friends. Despite the dropouts, America Online can theoretically still make money from Instant Messenger users, because the software has space for advertisements. But since people rarely click on those ads, the revenue is slim. Still, the company believes it will ultimately find ways to make money from a program that millions of people use for hours at a time. America Online was so enamored with instant messages that last year it bought Mirabilis, an Israeli company that makes ICQ, the second most popular instant-message system. ICQ is the classic Web business: it has grown purely by word of mouth to an audience of some 38 million users, but it still has no visible source of revenue. So far, America Online has not linked the two instant-message systems, largely because the hip, college-age ICQ audience does not care to associate with American Online users, who are mainly high-school students and their parents. Moreover, America Online has been wary of doing anything that would open up instant-message systems too quickly. Now that other companies -- not only Microsoft, but even more notably, Yahoo Inc. -- have created their own instant-message systems, there has been increasing demand to link all the systems together. In fact, an industry task force has been formed to develop a standard for such interconnection. America Online has long said that it would support such a standard, once it was developed. But it has done nothing to hasten the development of a consensus -- though, in hindsight, the company planted the seeds for its current crisis. First, America Online did nothing to prevent anyone from mimicking its software, as Microsoft has. Microsoft's own message program, by contrast, encrypts messages, so that no one can create backdoor links its system, as it has done to America Online's. America Online also published on its own Web page a method that people could use to write their own programs to exchange instant messages with users of the Instant Messenger system and to see which of their America Online buddies were on line. The company now says that this recipe was meant only for computer hobbyists and users of the Unix operating system. But on the Web page, America Online did not note any restrictions on the use of the system. And so several companies, including Yahoo and Prodigy Communications, used the information to create instant-message programs that linked to America Online's system. The systems from Yahoo, Prodigy and Microsoft came to light the week before last, and America Online blocked them all -- attracting the glare of publicity. Suddenly, the company's go-slow strategy no longer seemed feasible. America Online's well-oiled crisis-handling machine, led by the public-relations firm Robinson, Lerer & Montgomery, declared that the company would put the development of an instant-messaging standard "on a fast track." The company promised to work actively with the existing industry task force, and it convened its own parallel committee of top industry executives to help shape an instant-messaging standard. These moves, though, did little to appease Microsoft and the other companies. American Online's parallel committee, for example, represents companies like Sun Microsystems, Apple Computer and Real Networks, that are more notable for their longstanding grudges against Microsoft than their involvement in instant messaging. A group of eight other companies, led by Microsoft and Prodigy, wrote a letter to America Online's chairman, Stephen M. Case, arguing that the best thing he could do to further instant-message standards was to stop blocking their programs. "People are looking for a real gesture from AOL," said Brad Chase, one of the executives in charge of Microsoft's consumer and Internet division. "They should stop blocking users now." Microsoft and Prodigy say they will convene their own group to forge a standard at a meeting in newyork in September. With all the attention, an industrywide instant-messaging format is likely to be developed this year. And unless there is significant disagreement about how the standard operates, all the major players -- including America Online -- have now committed to linking their systems to it. That should mean, ultimately, that people will choose their instant message systems as they do email programs: on the basis of marketing, distribution and product features. Less clear is what will happen until a standard is adopted. Last week, America Online made overtures to several companies, including Prodigy, to begin discussions about linking to their message systems. But with all the bad blood, such deals may be hard to negotiate now, especially with Microsoft still intent on cracking America Online's system. Yet, however extreme Microsoft's approach -- and however unlikely an advocate of open systems the company may be -- the walls that divided instant-message users are tumbling down. "Microsoft's tactic worked," Mr. Schmitt said. "It was the fastest way to get AOL to move toward standards." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: America Online's AOL Instant Messenger had several backdoors that allowed competitors such as Microsoft and Yahoo to sneak in their own users. An industry task force has been formed to develop an open standard. (pg. C8)

title:
Digital Commerce;
The battle over instant messaging is another case of a company clinging to customers like flypaper.
body: THE keening outrage in the national news media last week over America Online's proprietary behavior toward its Instant Messaging customers strikes many longtime computer industry executives as just plain goofy. The immediate question is whether America Online has the right to enforce -- and by what means -- the network barriers that separate its 80 million Instant Messaging customers from (a) the clutches of its grasping competitors and (b) the rest of the instant-messaging world. But in fact, this is just business as usual. Examine the practices of any market leader and its products in the last 20 or 30 years -- I.B.M., Digital Equipment, Lotus Development, Microsoft -- and it is clear that America Online is simply acting out one of the most enduring concepts in the technology industry. Today's buzzword for the concept is "stickiness," a rather glib term for how a company gets and keeps customers in the notoriously slippery world of the Internet, where a Web site can be come-and-gone at the click of a mouse. "Sticky" has also long been the goal of vendors and service providers. Many have built their biggest successes upon enticing customers with sweet-smelling technical solutions that, once installed, make it extremely painful to switch to a competitor's product. This has been the dominant, albeit unheralded, business model of the computer and software industry since its inception. Back in the days of "big iron" mainframe computers and workstations, companies like the International Business Machines Corporation and the Digital Equipment Corporation were the biggest flypaper vendors in town, selling the computers, the operating systems and often the software, too. Their hegemony was broken by the personal computer -- and then stickiness between Windows and its applications catapulted Microsoft to its monopoly in the PC industry. That's because once buyers commit their customer data bases, corporate documents and financial data to an operating system and brand of application software, they are basically stuck. Anyone who has tried even to switch from one company's word processor to another's can imagine the exponential agony of trying to move an entire corporation from, say, Unix to Windows. But that is a classic sticky application, one that effectively "persuades" customers to stick around. First they are enticed by how convenient it is to use the product. Then they stay because it becomes so terribly inconvenient to leave. On the Internet, stickiness has more to do with collecting valuable personal information about consumers and holding their attention than with storing their data bits. Finding a way to create consumer stickiness is a high priority most particularly for portal sites -- Yahoo, At Home's Excite, Lycos, America Online, Microsoft's MSN -- and retailers like Amazon.com. Every day, it seems, these vendors hang a few more strips of flypaper: free email, custom news services, address books and directories, calendars and event planners, gift services, personal Web sites. Customers sign up and stick around, plugging in more and more personal and family and financial information as they return again and again. Companies like America Online and Microsoft are planning "digital wallet" services that will enable users to consolidate all their sign-in names and passwords. The sales pitch is convenience -- ostensibly consumers would not need to keep repeatedly re-entering the same personal information as they travel and shop the Web. But obviously such wallets are also powerful flypaper applications that, if successful, will tie up consumers' data with a single vendor that will process all their Internet purchases and activities. This type of "service" raises the collective eyebrow of those who remember the enormous power shift in the technology industry when the Internet's open protocols and the Web's freely available programming language, HTML, first loosened the hold that the flypaper vendors had on their customers. Of course, the goal of the free market economy is to whup all your competitors and become the de facto flypaper standard. And that is fine as far as it goes. But as the technology food chain has lengthened to include hundreds of millions of consumers, the concept of "sticky" versus "stuck" has taken on new cultural and economic portent. To be sure, America Online's competitors -- particularly Microsoft -- are acting purely in their own commercial interests. Microsoft, the great imposer of unilateral standards, provided the industry with a Fellini-esque moment last week when an executive was quoted as saying, "We should all just speak the same language," adding, "It shouldn't matter what software or phone you are using." Gaining access to America Online's Instant Message system, thus its customer data base, puts a crimp in the on-line giant's growing domination of cyberspace. But you can bet that if America Online's rivals succeed, they will scramble for a way to alter any new standard to their own ends, just as Microsoft unilaterally rewrote two key open Internet languages, Sun Microsystems' Java and Netscape's Javascript. In the short term, an open standard for instant-message applications has the potential to unstick consumers and reconnect them to the rest of the Internet. Which is why today, battles for dominance of the Internet are of great public interest. Everyone is watching, and millions more people have a stake in the outcome. As one entrepreneur said last week, "It's the users who are going to decide if they prefer to stay in a segregated community or talk to other communities." And that is the kind of sticky situation the industry may not have a strategy for. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title: Less Web Shopping Seen
body: The percentage of people with Internet access who are making purchases from Web sites declined slightly in the second quarter of 1999 after four sequential quarters of spectacular growth, according to Greenfield Online Inc. The study by Greenfield, a Westport, Conn., Internet marketing research firm, hints at the limits of market penetration of the medium as a shopping platform -- suggesting a ceiling that has been unknown until now. "This is the first indication of the size of the population that will use the Internet to shop," Rudy Nadilo, Greenfield's president and chief executive, said. Mushrooming E-commerce sales -- and visions of geometric growth into the future -- have fueled the recent boom of Internet stock valuations. Greenfield's study does not necessarily indicate that sales on the World Wide Web have stalled, since the total number of people with Web access continues to grow rapidly. And the finding that 71 percent of people on line bought at least once in the last three months is respectable, even if it stays at that level. From the first quarter of 1998 to the first quarter of this year, the percentage of people with on-line access who said they had bought something through a Web site rose to 74 percent from 47 percent, Greenfield said. But in the latest quarter, Greenfield found that the percentage had slipped to 71 percent. The findings were based on 2,598 respondents selected randomly from Greenfield's national pool of more than one million individuals who have volunteered to participate in on-line research.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING;
In the Internet Gold Rush, Fund Customers Find a Research Treasure
body: CLICK on "buy." Click on "sell." Click on "payoff." The mutual fund industry has joined the rush to the Internet over the last two years -- and the move seems to be benefiting both the fund companies and many of their customers. Investors can buy funds on the sites of many no-load fund companies or through the sites of one of several brokerage firms that offer fund supermarkets. To avoid losing customers to on-line firms, many no-load fund groups, including the Vanguard Group, American Century Investments and T. Rowe Price Associates, have opened their own on-line brokerage firms, trading individual stocks and sometimes offering thousands of funds beyond their own. Such supermarkets will be the conduits for the bulk of all fund purchases by 2003, with most investors relying on fund company sites for information only, according to James Punishill, author of a report on Internet investing for Forrester Research, a consulting firm in Cambridge, Mass. By 2003, Forrester predicts, investors will hold $1.2 trillion in mutual fund assets in Internet-based accounts, up from an estimated $128 billion by the end of this year. The most noticeable change brought by the Internet, however, has been its capacity to deliver detailed research to virtually all investors, no matter how much they have to invest. Using that information -- which is often free -- investors can compare funds before making choices. Dozens of Web sites offer performance figures as well as portfolio tracking, so investors can monitor their holdings and the shifts in their asset mix of stocks, bonds and cash. "The self-directed investor has at their disposal what five years ago professional investors didn't even have at their disposal," said Cebra Graves, Internet strategist at Morningstar Inc., the financial publisher in Chicago. Morningstar's Web site lets investors compare funds and portfolio holdings at no charge (www.morningstar.net). For varying fees, investors can gain access to more detailed screens and data. Morningstar also supplies data to other companies like E*Trade, whose site provides free access to research and sorting tools using end-of-quarter data. The Mutual Fund Education Alliance, an association of no-load funds, offers a site at www.mfea.com with fund industry news, investment planning tools and links to fund company sites. Investors can register on the site to gain access to a personal portfolio tracker. In other words, the Internet lets investors get the information they need when they want it. "Inevitably, you didn't get the brochure at the right time and, inevitably, the information you need isn't in there," said Shelton S. Unger, head of on-line services at Vanguard. With the Internet, a great deal of information is available immediately, she added, and you "sort of find your own path." Vanguard recently updated an investment planning service to allow investors to prepare on line for retirement, college or other investment objectives. The service considers the user's risk tolerance and time horizon, among other factors. One bonus for the fund industry is that many investors who know the Internet are willing to receive routine information, like shareholder reports, on line instead of in themail. That can help keep down a fund's expenses. When an investor requests a prospectus over the phone, for example, Vanguard spends $10 to $12 to respond -- in labor costs for the phone representative and for printing and mailing. Internet use is climbing at Vanguard: 37 percent of all shareholders used the Web to get information or to make a transaction in the first quarter of 1999, up from 20 percent a year earlier, Ms. Unger said. The trend is evident elsewhere. At Charles Schwab & Company, 45 percent of all mutual fund transactions were on the Internet in mid-June, up from 25 percent a year ago and 16 percent at the beginning of 1998. "What we see is that the process of investing is easier, richer than it's ever been before," said Jeffrey M. Lyons, senior vice president for mutual funds marketing at Schwab. Instead of searching through magazine and newspaper articles for information and advice, investors can go on line to sort through thousands of funds and run through detailed asset allocation scenarios for growth or value investing as well as domestic or international choices. "Then, immediately, they click a button and invest in the fund," Mr. Lyons said. Schwab and other companies say the ease of Internet trading has not caused investors to flip rapidly in and out of funds. Schwab customers are charged a redemption fee if they sell shares within six months of purchase. Brian C. Murray, general manager for E*Trade's mutual fund group, which reserves the right to charge a fee for sales made within three months, said, "There appears to be an even stronger buy-and-hold ethic than I expected." The fund industry has also found the Internet to be useful for reaching retirement investors. The 401(k) Forum is an Internet-based retirement investment adviser hired by companies to offer personal 401(k) advice to their employees. Fidelity Investments, which already offers extensive Web-based services to its retirement plan participants, is now offering a service aimed at small businesses, "e401k," that is a 401(k) plan sold and maintained entirely over the Internet. Despite the success of the Internet as a means for research, the average investor remains a little reluctant to click and invest. That largely reflects how many people began using the Internet just last year, Forrester's Mr. Punishill said. In fact, most fund investors with Internet access visit fund company sites only for tasks like checking on a portfolio balance or downloading a prospectus, according to a survey taken last fall and published by American Century. Although 46 percent of Internet users with funds visited fund Web sites in 1998 -- up from 28 percent in 1996 -- only 9 percent bought or sold shares, up from 3 percent in 1996 but down from 11 percent in 1997, according to the survey. The main reason for their reluctance is the fear that the Internet is not a secure place to conduct business. Some 52 percent expressed concerns about making Internet fund transactions, though that share was down from 68 percent in 1996. PEOPLE who buy funds on the Internet are more likely to use fund supermarkets, where they can get consolidated statements and gain access to funds from other companies, Mr. Punishill said.  Although fund companies have been forming their own brokerage firms, virtually none of them -- with the exception of Fidelity and Vanguard -- will be able to compete effectively with the big discounters, he asserted. "Very few fund companies will have the resources or know-how to turn themselves from a mutual fund company into a brokerage firm," Mr. Punishill said. "They are different business models altogether." Some experts say the majority of investors are unlikely to ever use the Internet to buy or sell funds. Eli E. Neusner, a senior consultant at Spectrem Group, a financial services consulting firm, argues that as a percentage of mutual fund investors, those investing on line will peak in just a few years. Investors can be overwhelmed by the amount of information on a Web site, Mr. Neusner said, and often prefer to speak with an adviser for guidance, particularly when dealing with complicated issues like estate planning or saving for a child's college education. On the Internet, he said, "no one has found a thoroughly efficient way of walking an uncomfortable investor or even a moderately experienced investor through a financial strategy." But Mr. Graves at Morningstar predicted that on-line technology would evolve to the point that any client could use the Internet to talk with a financial adviser on line. Once that happens, he said, "the Internet is no longer a technology that favors one demographic over another." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Getting Wired" The Internet is having a growing impact on how investors buy, sell and research mutual funds. title: Archipelago Sells a Stake To Instinet
body: In the latest round of a building competition between established stock markets and a group of upstart electronic competitors, Archipelago Holdings L.L.C., a leading electronic network for trading Nasdaq stocks, said yesterday that a rival, Instinet, had agreed to buy a 16.4 percent stake in it. Archipelago also said it would seek approval in a few days from the Securities and Exchange Commission to become a self-regulated, for-profit exchange and was considering an initial public offering. Archipelago's bid for exchange status comes after Island E.C.N., a competing trading system that is a subsidiary of Datek Online Holdings, recently announced a similar move. Others may follow. Instinet, a subsidiary of Reuters Group P.L.C. and the world's largest private stock-trading service for institutions, is also the oldest electronic communications network for trading stocks. But it has no desire to become an exchange. It joins a list of big-name investors in Archipelago, a company formed two years ago by Gerald D. Putnam, a former stock broker, and partners from Townsend Analytics, a Chicago software firm. Since it was founded, J. P. Morgan & Company, E*Trade Group and Goldman Sachs Group have all bought stakes. Archipelago refused to disclose what Instinet paid for its stake. But in January, Goldman Sachs and E*Trade each paid $25 million for a 24.5 percent stake. Subsequent additions of J. P. Morgan, the American Century Companies, a mutual fund company in which Morgan has a 45 percent stake, and now Instinet has diluted the ownership percentages. Each major partner now owns a stake of 16.4 percent. Douglas M. Atkin, the president and chief executive of Instinet, said talks about a possible stake had been taking place for six to nine months. Still, yesterday's announcement is the latest in a flurry of recent developments in a rapidly evolving web of trading systems that are vying to compete with the newyork Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq market operated by the National Association of Securities Dealers. Last week, three on-line brokers -- Charles Schwab, the FMR Corporation's Fidelity Investments arm and Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette's DLJ Direct unit -- said they were joining with Spear, Leeds & Kellogg, a stock-trading firm, to build a new electronic communications network, or E.C.N., as they are called. In response, the Big Board and Nasdaq said they were considering plans to convert from nonprofit institutions to for-profit corporations. "There is a lot of positioning going on, but there is a long way to go," said Dan Burke, an analyst at Gomez Advisors, an on-line and electronic-commerce research firm based in Concord, Mass. It costs about half as much to execute a trade through an electronic network as through an established exchange, and the growth of such systems has led several top Wall Street firms to invest in them, Mr. Burke said. Still, he noted, "there is a lot of stock trading infrastructure that is in place. Getting rid of that will not happen tomorrow." In a conference call with reporters, Mr. Putnam from Archipelago said he expected to receive a S.E.C. ruling on setting up an exchange in 9 to 18 months. "The regulatory structure challenges don't seem to be onerous," he said. "An all-electronic stock exchange is a reality; it's going to happen. We would like to trade newyork Stock Exchange-listed stocks as well as Nasdaq listings and compete on an all-electronic basis." Archipelago, which handles about a 2 percent share of the Nasdaq trading market, is a small competitor with Instinet, which accounts for about 15 percent of Nasdaq's overall daily volume. Still, Mr. Atkin of Instinet said that in the greater scheme of things, he did not consider Archipelago a competitor at all. "We didn't buy into what Archipelago is now, but what it wants to be, which is a for-profit exchange," he said. "In the medium term, that is not the area of the financial services industry we want to play in. We are striving to be a global brokerage firm. I think those strategic differences make this a complementary relationship." Mr. Putnam said that, as an electronic stock exchange, Archipelago could "very easily" operate 24 hours a day. "It would be a natural for us to go in that direction," he said. On matters of self-regulation, Mr. Putnam said Archipelago would be responsible for issues like market surveillance. But he said other functions might be delegated to an outside party if a single regulatory body for all markets emerged. Nine electronic networks now trade stocks, but that number is sure to dwindle, Mr. Atkin said. "When all is said and done, I think the E.C.N.'s will be a footnote," he said. "There does need to be a common operating platform for trading all of these stocks. The issue is, who is going to put the model in place? "Archipelago has an excellent chance of being one of the few winners in this space," he continued. "But if Nasdaq or the newyork Stock Exchange went public, it would be consistent for Instinet to own a stake in marketplaces where our clients are trading substantial amounts of liquidity."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Positions Harden in Instant-Message Fight
body: Hostilities continued yesterday in the bitter debate about whether Microsoft should be able to link into America Online's popular instant message system, with Microsoft rebuffing America Online's invitation to discuss a possible deal. The dispute broke out last week when the Microsoft Corporation introduced new software that lets users send instant messages both to users of Microsoft's Hotmail service and to users of the America Online service as well as others who use the AOL Instant Messenger, or AIM, software. America Online said that Microsoft was acting like a hacker, connecting to its system without authorization. In subsequent days, Microsoft has issued several new versions of its software as America Online has cut off each preceding version. On Friday, America Online sent a letter to Microsoft, demanding that Microsoft stop using its system but inviting the company to negotiate some sort of message exchange. In a written response yesterday, Brad Chase, a vice president of Microsoft, asserted that Microsoft had done nothing wrong. "There has been and is no unauthorized use or access of AOL's services or products," Mr. Chase wrote. "Nor has Microsoft violated the privacy or security of any AIM users." The letter had no direct response to America Online's invitation to discuss an accord. Rather, Mr. Chase called on America Online to stop its efforts to block Microsoft's software. America Online's reaction was quick and stern. "It's clear from reading their letter that America Online and Microsoft still have significant disagreements on privacy and security," said Kenneth Lerer, a principal with Robinson, Lerer & Montgomery, America Online's public relations firm. As for Microsoft's reaction to America Online's invitation, Mr. Lerer said "their silence speaks for itself." Rob Bennet, a product manager in Microsoft's consumer and commerce business, said that America Online was not in fact amenable to discussions. "Their letter was not a negotiation but a club," Mr. Bennet said. He said that Microsoft wanted to work for an open standard through an industry consortium rather than to negotiate a bilateral deal with America Online. Mr. Lerer said that America Online believes instant messaging will ultimately be open, so that users of any instant message software will be able to communicate with users of any other program. Each system is now in effect a closed universe. Internet industry executives, however, said they saw no indication that America Online is moving to open its base of 40 million instant message users to other companies. Last week, America Online cut off systems from Prodigy and Yahoo that had also found a way to link to its system. Those companies say that America Online has made no efforts to indicate the terms on which it would allow access. Until now, America Online has not been active in the industry task force that has been trying to write open standards for instant messages, said Vijay Saraswat, a researcher for AT&T Labs and the co-chairman of the task force. Microsoft has been active in the task force and has proposed a standard. But Mr. Saraswat said that Microsoft has yet to show a commitment to those standards. "America Online is not alone," he said. "Microsoft is not following a public protocol, even though they had proposed one."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:

title:
Compressed Data;
Playboy Loses Round Over Search Engine Ads
body: Giving a green light to a common but controversial Internet advertising practice, a Federal judge in California has refused a request by Playboy Enterprises to stop the Web search services Excite.com and Netscape.com from placing ads for pornography sites with the search results for the words "playboy" or "playmate." Declining Playboy's request for a preliminary injunction, Judge Alicemarie H. Stotler of the Federal District Court in Santa Ana, Calif., said Playboy was unlikely to succeed in a trial with its contention that Excite Inc. had violated trademark laws. Marissa Gluck, an analyst with the research firm of Jupiter Communications, said the decision was good news for search services, which she said derived 20 to 30 percent of their ad revenue from the sale of banner ads linked to keywords. In its lawsuit against Excite and America Online's Netscape Communications unit, which licenses Excite's search technology, Playboy had challenged this practice, known as banner ad keying, saying that it could divert customers looking for Playboy's site and also tarnish its reputation. In her opinion on June 24, Judge Stotler found that although Playboy held trademarks for Playboy and Playmate, it did not have a monopoly on the generic use of those words in English. For that reason and others, the court said, Playboy had not shown that Excite had made commercial use of Playboy's trademark, as would be necessary to justify a trademark infringement lawsuit. Judge Stotler also ruled that even if Excite had used Playboy's trademarks, that use would not have been improper because Playboy had offered no evidence that consumers would be confused about the relationship between Playboy and a banner ad for a pornography site. A lawyer for Playboy said the company would appeal the decision.   CARL S. KAPLAN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A Federal judge in California said placing ads with search results is permissible.

title:
Patents;
An Internet entrepreneur finds a way for newsstand dealers to profit from subscription sales.
body: HE may have become a billionaire selling airline tickets on the Internet. But Jay Walker thinks he knows a better way to sell magazines at the newsstand, too. Mr. Walker, chairman and chief executive of Priceline.com, and a business partner have just received a patent for a new method of selling magazine subscriptions. It is the latest in a series of patents Mr. Walker has received in recent years for various business methods. Currently, buying a magazine at a newsstand means paying about three dollars a copy, or far more than the same issue would cost with a subscription. Publishers prefer subscriptions, which guarantee sales of multiple issues, and so they load magazines with subscription cards that promote reduced issue prices for a 12- or 24-month subscription. But newsstand owners and other retailers can hardly be blamed for not pointing out to customers that it would be cheaper to subscribe than to buy individual magazines from them. But what if publishers and magazine sellers could profit, while readers got a cheaper price for each issue? That is the idea behind a new method of magazine subscribing patented by Mr. Walker and his associate, Sanjay Jindal. People buy magazines off the rack for convenience, but also to read them in a timely fashion. So in spite of the cost being double or triple the subscription price, about a billion single-issue copies of magazines are sold each year. Many of those are impulse purchases. Subscribing may be cheaper, but it has disadvantages that discourage many readers. First-time subscribers may have to wait up to 12 weeks for a subscription to be processed, missing the issues that appear in the meantime. And people typically cannot pay cash for a magazine subscription; they have to mail in a check or submit a credit card number, or send a subscription card and then pay a bill. In their patent filing, Mr. Walker and Mr. Jindal also point out that readers have to pay full newsstand price for a magazine in order to get the subscription card in the first place. A reader's discounted rate applies only after the subscription begins. The patent describes a new method of subscribing to a magazine at a retail outlet. When a customer purchased the magazine, either he or the retailer would fill out a subscription card on the spot. Information about price, length of the subscription and mailing address would be entered into a point-of-sale terminal. The data would then be transmitted to a subscription fulfillment house for immediate processing. The retailer would receive a percentage of each subscription sold, and the reader would get the newsstand's current issue of the magazine at the subscription price. Mr. Walker and Mr. Jindal received patent 5,926,796. Mr. Walker, who lives in Ridgefield, Conn., has been granted more than a dozen patents in the last two years for methods of conducting business, including patents for awarding prepaid telephone time, for employment searches, for figuring foreign exchange insurance premiums, for post-paid traveler's checks, and even for a computer game and a method of playing lotteries. He shares the patents with other inventors, but they all belong to his company, Walker Asset Management L.P. Mr. Walker is perhaps best known, though, for a patent awarded last August for a method of buying and selling goods over the Internet. It is the method on which he had already based Priceline.com, a Web site that uses a "reverse auction" technique that enables consumers to name their own price for airline tickets -- which airlines can choose to accept or not. Mr. Walker, Bruce Schneier and James Jorasch won a patent for this kind of "buyer-driven commerce," and gained exclusive rights to that particular form of electronic sales. Priceline.com, which went public in April, had a stock-market value of about $11.6 billion, based on Friday's closing price of $81.1875 a share. That would make Mr. Walker's personal stake worth almost $5 billion, assuming he still has the 61.3 million shares reported in the prospectus last March.  Practice Deck For Blackjack Winning at blackjack depends largely on the luck of the draw -- or so it seems. Players hope to receive the right combination of randomly drawn cards the total of which will beat the total drawn by a casino dealer, without exceeding twenty-one. Alfred Smith believes that winning strategies for blackjack can be learned -- especially for players who know how to count the cards that have already been dealt. Toward that end, he's patented a blackjack practice deck of cards. "It is mathematically demonstrated that if you can count cards, you will beat the casino, which is why they kick you out if they catch you," Mr. Smith said. Card counting -- keeping track of what has been dealt and thus knowing what cards are left to play -- is not against the law, but casinos prohibit it and make great efforts to identify card counters. "They consider it cheating, but there is a lot of controversy about that, because it is you using your intelligence." Mr. Smith, a former restaurant owner who now lives in Florida and is marketing his blackjack practice deck through Web sites, catalogues and stores that cater to blackjack aficionados, has designed a deck that features two-card combinations of blackjack hands on each practice card. Players study the practice cards and memorize what strategy to use to respond to each possible combination. "There is something called basic strategy, which is derived by harnessing computers," Mr. Smith explained. "If you have no idea what cards have been played, what this gives you is the best expectation of playing every hand with the maximum opportunity to win or the minimum loss." But if a player does know what cards have been dealt -- if he is counting cards -- then he can use a different strategy for his next move. Mr. Smith continued: "There are many card counting systems out there. Whether you use basic strategy or a card-counting system, with my deck you can practice 'Do I know what to do with this combination?' What the cards do is take all of what you could refer to as the two-card decision totals and put them on one card." The two-card combinations appear on the practice cards as one card peeking above another, and they can be shuffled, dealt and read from either direction. "With the practice cards, I could do in 15 minutes what took me an hour when I was dealing hands to myself," he said. "I could review them on the bus to Atlantic City and get the numbers in my head. I went from $5 and $10 hands to $25 hands, and I feel comfortable playing $100 hands." Mr. Smith received patent 5,895,048. Patents may be viewed on the Web at www.uspto.gov or may be ordered through themail, by patent number, for $3 from the Patent and Trademark Office, Washington, D.C. 20231. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Jay Walker, chief executive of Priceline.com, has received patents on a variety of new business methods in recent years. (Associated Press)

title: Security Flaw Is Discovered In Several Unix Programs
body: A leading computer security group is reporting a significant rise in potentially dangerous attacks that exploit security holes in programs shipped with the Unix operating system. Unix is the most common operating system for servers, the powerful computers that control the flow of data over large networks, including the Internet. "We've seen a good number of reports related to thousands of different machines on scores of different sites," said Shawn Hernan, a member of the Computer Emergency Response Team, or CERT, at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. "This is not like the Melissa virus, but it's a fairly significant event in Internet security." The Melissa program infected about 19 percent of the nation's large corporations in March. The full extent of the damage might not yet be evident -- and may not be for some time -- because the attacks, when successful, give those cracking into a network what is known as "root access," basically complete control over the server. This enables the crackers, as such intruders are known, not only to wreak immediate havoc with networks but to plant small, hard-to-trace programs that can be set off later. Mr. Hernan said a wide range of organizations, from small companies to universities and large corporations, reported being attacked last week, but, citing CERT policy, he declined to name specific companies or organizations. In some cases, crackers had removed or destroyed fundamental computer programs and pieces of the computers' operating system. Bob Todd, a network engineer for an Internet security company, said a client he would describe only as a "large state or Federal agency" had been attacked multiple times both from within the unitedstates and abroad. He said he had heard that at least half a dozen other government agencies had also been hit. While the attacks did some mischief, like altering Web pages, Mr. Todd said he had not seen any serious damage so far. Mr. Todd's company, the Advanced Research Corporation in Vienna, Va., was apparently the first to report the attacks in a posting on Bugtraq, an Internet security mailing list. Later, explicit instructions for exploiting the newest of the security holes were also posted to Bugtraq; Mr. Todd said his company was not responsible for that posting. The attacks primarily exploit software that manages an appointment calendar program that is shipped with Unix operating systems from makers of powerful servers, including Sun Microsystems Inc. and the Hewlett-Packard Company. Sun has already released a patch for the problem, and Hewlett-Packard plans to do so soon, according to CERT. In addition to the calendar program, the crackers are also exploiting two previously identified Unix flaws. They appear to be using an automated software script that tries to exploit each security hole in turn, Mr. Hernan said. He based that conclusion on having found similar entries in the log files that servers keep of each transaction on a network and on seeing identical pernicious files on the attacked computers. Patches for the previously identified bugs have been available for some time, but many system administrators have not applied them. "System administrators don't apply patches as quickly as we'd like," Mr. Hernan said. "They have their own priorities." Patching the security holes after an attack cannot repair any damage already done. Of special concern with these attacks is that it is very difficult to determine what has been done since these bugs give the intruder complete control over the affected machine, Mr. Hernan said. Beyond immediate damage, crackers exploiting these bugs have installed so-called Trojan horse programs that obscure their activity and can set off malignant processes at a later date, the CERT report said. Intruders have also created additional routes into the affected networks and installed "sniffer" programs capable of intercepting email and passwords. The safest response to such an attack is to erase the hard drive, reinstall the operating system and software and then restore the data from back-ups that predate the attack -- a very time consuming process. The calendar bug involves what is known as a "buffer overflow" vulnerability, one of the most common types of software security holes. The attacker pretends to make an entry in the calendar, but the "entry" is really a carefully designed chunk of information that is too large to fit the storage space the program allots for the entry. The overflow spilling out into the computer's main memory consists of software code that can do any number of things but usually grants the cracker root access. A university system administrator who asked not to be identified said his network had been attacked, but he said there had been little damage since this particular cracker's clumsy execution caught the attention of system personnel. He said he suspected that the intruder might have been using an attack recipe obtained from someone else. "There's a large cracker community out there, and they talk to each other," he said. "These people waste an enormous amount of resources." http://www.nytimes.com
