title: Potential Rival Remains Wary of Microsoft's Power
body: As Stephen M. Case, chief executive of America Online, contemplated making the biggest deal of his career -- the purchase of Netscape Communications -- he stopped for a moment last fall to ponder whether his company could finally afford to dump Microsoft. Two years earlier, America Online executives were thinking they had no choice but to use the Microsoft Corporation's browser instead of Netscape's as the default for their millions of customers. Microsoft had made an offer they could not refuse -- a high-profile spot on the Windows desktop. But by last fall, America Online, the world's largest Internet service provider, was a powerful force with 16 million members. And soon it would actually own Netscape. So Mr. Case, in an email to other executives at his company, suggested, "Maybe we can get comfortable with putting our support behind Netscape so they really have browser share momentum." "Specifically," he added, "if we push share to Netscape, can Microsoft really pull us out of Windows 98 (legally, as well as would it be palatable given current antitrust attention)." The response was swift. Less than 20 minutes later, Robert W. Pittman, the company's president, replied: "I do think Microsoft is too strong to throw them out of the tent. They can hurt us if they think they have no other option." Unquestionably, America Online is now an industry powerhouse. But documents and testimony offered last week at Microsoft's antitrust trial during an appearance of David M. Colburn, an America Online senior vice president, disclosed that the company's leaders still feel constrained, even threatened, by Microsoft -- chastened, perhaps, by Netscape's experience. When Microsoft made Netscape an enemy, it used every resource to turn the rest of the industry against the company. The campaign was remarkably successful. Now, as America Online prepares to branch out in new directions under a campaign with the slogan "AOL Anywhere," the documents show that the company is still looking over its shoulder, wary of stirring Microsoft's wrath. Most of the documents were brought to the trial by Microsoft. The company was trying to show that America Online had the resources to become a serious challenger, undercutting the Government's contention that Microsoft holds an unstoppable monopoly. But many of the documents cut both ways, for they also showed that with all its hard-won power, America Online repeatedly pulled back from any new business venture that would upset Microsoft. "To manage reality, we need to continue working with Microsoft wherever we can," Kathy Bushkin, an America Online corporate communications executive, wrote last November in an internal document titled "Microsoft Relationship." The documents describe a plan to work with Sun to build a personal computer that used no Microsoft software, thus "breaking the deadly embrace with Microsoft" in the words of a Sun executive. (On the stand, Mr. Colburn pointedly disavowed the "deadly embrace" language, noting that Sun holds a special animosity toward Microsoft.) But America Online's intention was different. While the company was working with Sun on that project, "we are also developing Apollo for the desktop version NT," Ms. Bushkin wrote, using the company's code name for itself. This, she explained, "shows our agnostic approach to operating systems." Similarly, her memo, like others, noted that as America Online ventured into other new businesses with Sun -- designing telephones and television set-top boxes to run the on-line service -- the company was also working on other versions "for Windows CE, to insure that Apollo TV and Apollo phone work on that platform as well." In a note to Ms. Bushkin about a news release last November announcing the Netscape deal, Mr. Case summarized America Online's strategy this way: "The logical way to go is to assure Microsoft and investors that we will continue to be bundled with Windows and continue to attempt detente." While making the Netscape deal, Mr. Case said, America Online ought to give Microsoft "a bearhug." The investment bankers whom America Online hired to analyze the acquisition and suggest future directions repeatedly urged moving aggressively against Microsoft by using the Netscape browser. "Extend the browser to be a more comprehensive desktop application, bundling communications and productivity applications to absorb more share of computing time, with the goal of becoming the users' de facto environment," one analysis advised. Microsoft executives predict that sooner or later, America Online really will take them on. The on-line service is laying low now, the company says, so as not to give Microsoft ammunition to use in the antitrust trial. But in another memo, an America Online executive noted that no one ever comes out ahead in a war with Microsoft. So, as Mr. Pittman put it in his note to Mr. Case: "I think we need to stay in business with them, create a need for them to need us. And then leave ourselves the flexibility to always accommodate them to a certain extent." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Ruling for Net Music Storage Device
body: In a major defeat for the recording industry, a Federal appeals court has ruled that a popular device used to download and store music from the Internet does not violate Federal anti-piracy laws. The unitedstates Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in San Francisco found that the Rio MP300, manufactured by Diamond Multimedia Systems Inc., did not qualify as a "digital audio recording device" and was not subject to the restrictions of the 1992 Audio Home Recording Act. The court found in a 3-to-0 vote that the Rio, a pager-sized device that can store CD-quality songs encoded in the so-called MP3 format, was not primarily a recorder and so was not subject to the 1992 act. The court's decision torpedoed a suit filed in October by the Recording Industry Association of America, which had aimed at the Rio and Internet MP3 music files as a major source of music piracy. MP3 is widely used by lesser-known artists to distribute their music, but the record industry fears the format will lead to rampant piracy in cyberspace, where files can be copied and sent rapidly. After a lower court rejected its request for a preliminary injunction barring sales of the Rio last fall, the industry association appealed. After the ruling, the association said in a statement, "We filed this lawsuit because unchecked piracy on the Internet threatens the development of a legitimate marketplace for on-line music, a marketplace that consumers want." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Witness Keeps People Off Edgesof Their Seats
body: The Microsoft Corporation put its most important rebuttal witness in the Government's antitrust trial on the stand today, a senior executive from America Online, and set out to prove that the on-line service had deceived the judge about its plans to compete with Microsoft. But the effort proved to be a bust in terms of how it played in court. By midafternoon, the halting, tedious examination of David M. Colburn, a senior vice president of America Online, had put several people in the courtroom to sleep. Finally Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson called Microsoft's lawyer, John Warden, up to the bench and told him he was not getting much if anything out of the questions or the documents Mr. Warden was offering as evidence. Judge Jackson urged Mr. Warden to hurry up and finish. For weeks, Microsoft's lawyers have been saying they would base a good part of their rebuttal case around their allegation that Mr. Colburn did not tell the complete truth when he testified as a Government witness in October. Specifically, they said, America Online's plan to purchase the Netscape Communications Corporation was well under way at the time of Mr. Colburn's earlier testimony, and planning documents showed that America Online intended to mount a strong challenge to Microsoft, though Mr. Colburn made no mention of that in his original testimony. The strategy apeared to be two-fold. Microsoft would challenge "the completeness and candor of prior testimony," the company said in a court filing -- raising credibility issues, just as the Government's lead trial lawyer, David Boies, had done with many of Microsoft's witnesses. The second part of the stategy would be to show that America Online, through its purchase of Netscape, intended to mount a strong competitive challenge to Microsoft, undercutting the Government's assertion that Microsoft holds an unassailable monopoly. But Mr. Colburn did not cooperate. Today Mr. Warden offered as evidence presumably the best selections from the trove of documents Microsoft subpoenaed from America Online, Netscape and Sun Microsystems, a partner in the deal. Mr. Colburn recognized few of them, however, and quarreled with Mr. Warden's interpretation of almost every one. Judge Jackson showed little interest. "I'll admit it," he said with a shake of the hand about one America Online document offered as evidence. "I don't know what's probative in it; I really don't. Without some testimony to give it substance, I don't know what it means." Earlier, Mr. Warden had displayed documents showing that America Online planned to work with Sun to build a personal computer that used no Microsoft software, thus "breaking the deadly embrace with Microsoft" in the words of a Sun executive. But Mr. Colburn said the plan went nowhere. It was, he said, intended to create lower-price personal computers, so more people could afford to join the service. But while the planning was under way, computer prices fell sharply, "so the talks are largely dead." The documents Mr. Warden presented did show that America Online executives, including the chief executive, Stephen M. Case, were concerned about Microsoft. In one, Mr. Case wrote, "Our relationship with Microsoft is strained and will get much worse no matter how we play it." He then wondered what would happen if his company stopped distributing Microsoft's Web browser to its 16 million subscribers and replaced it with Netscape's browser. But for all the discussion, Mr. Colburn and many of the documents said, America Online finally decided to keep the relationship with Microsoft just as it had been -- and to continue using Internet Explorer. The company renewed its contract with Microsoft in January. Outside the courtroom, a Microsoft lawyer gamely asserted that Mr. Colburn's statements would be useful in later written pleadings, Judge Jackson's lack of interest today notwithstanding. By shortly after noon today Judge Jackson's attention was clearly flagging as Mr. Warden began another series of questions without looking up at the judge. A lawyer at Microsoft's table quickly sent Mr. Warden a note, and as soon as Mr. Warden read it, he called for a lunch break. The judge readily agreed. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
A Bit of Flamboyance For an Internet Conference
body: What has Dennis Rodman got to do with the Internet industry? Until this week, almost nothing. But on Thursday, the flamboyant professional basketball star will take the microphone at the Web Attack Internet marketing conference in San Francisco. Michael Tchong, producer of the conference, said he hoped to get Mr. Rodman to talk about his coming electronic commerce venture, which Mr. Tchong stumbled upon in the course of a trademark search on the term Webzilla.com. The search turned up Mr. Rodman's venture, Rodzilla.com. The point of inviting Mr. Rodman to the conference, Mr. Tchong said, is to illustrate to Web marketers that they need to be outrageous to be heard above the noise.  "There's got to be hundreds of pro basketball players today, but ask anybody to name two and they'll say Michael Jordan and Dennis Rodman," Mr. Tchong said. "Now that's brand marketing." Mr. Rodman has not been asked by the conference organizers to make any prepared remarks. But he has been instructed on precisely what to wear. The contract for his appearance requires Mr. Rodman, who apart from his hair color is perhaps best known off the court for donning a wedding dress and other outrageous attire, to wear a T-shirt bearing the logo of Iconocast, the Web marketing consulting company that is sponsoring the conference.   LAURIE J. FLYNN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Dennis Rodman, who made a 1996 promotional appearance in a wedding dress, has a marketing tip: Outrageousness sells. (AP)

title: Developing a Repetition-Free Language forWeb Transactions
body: Aiming to make shopping on the Web easier, a consortium of credit card companies, Internet merchants and developers of on-line payment technologies plans to announce today that its members have agreed to develop a standard for executing electronic commerce transactions. The standard, known as electronic commerce modeling language, will eventually enable consumers to buy from multiple Web sites without re-entering data like a name, shipping address or credit card number. The coding of so-called electronic wallet software will store such customer information on a secure server and is intended to pass the data to different merchants' Web sites with fewer problems. "This is an important first step," Ken Cassar, digital commerce analyst for the Internet research firm Jupiter Communications, said. "A lot more needs to be done, but the parties who've joined in are pretty much the ones you'd want." Until now, electronic wallet technologies have faltered because the coding used by merchants to format checkout pages has varied widely. For instance, the code used to indicate a consumer's credit card number could begin with "CC#" in some cases, and "CN" in others. The wallets were sometimes unable to recognize the variations, and thus could not work with many sites. As a result, consumers have generally ignored the wallet companies. That situation will change, according to the electronic commerce consortium, which includes America Online, Microsoft, Dell Computer, Compaq Computer, Visa USA, I.B.M., Sun Microsystems, Mastercard International and American Express, as well as a host of Internet merchants and electronic wallet providers. Once merchants can essentially speak the same language, wallet companies will be able to offer consumers the prospect of one-click checkout across many sites. Such a feature could increase Internet sales substantially, since customers often bail out of transactions rather than go through several time-consuming steps to complete a purchase. In February, a report by Jupiter found that 27 percent of on-line buyers abandoned their orders before check-out for that reason. "This will be particularly important for attracting new customers," said John Pettitt, chief technology officer for Beyond.com, a software retailer. "Every time you ask a customer to do something, you risk losing them." Mr. Pettitt said Beyond.com offered one-click checkout to America Online customers who had signed up for its Quick Checkout electronic wallet, and he said the feature had "been very successful for us." Aside from that, however, he said Beyond.com had declined to do business with other companies that offer electronic wallets, like Cybercash and Transactor Networks, "because they don't have a critical mass of users." One reason for that lack of critical mass is that consumers see little reason to sign up with an electronic wallet company that does not have a large number of merchant partners. According to Mr. Cassar of Jupiter, electronic wallet companies have made little headway until now in part because they have had to persuade retailers to format their sites to conform to their particular wallet technology. The hope has been to sign up enough retailers to become the de facto standard and thereby consolidate the market. "But instead they've Balkanized the market," Mr. Cassar said. At stake for wallet companies is not only the potential to charge a fee for each transaction processed, but also the opportunity to gather valuable consumer data. "If I've got a wallet company and I build a list of 100,000 names and addresses of people who've bought from Barnesandnoble.com, that's pretty valuable," Mr. Cassar said. While the electronic commerce consortium's agreement on how to define data overcomes one hurdle in the effort to spread the use of electronic wallets, the use of consumer data represents a far more thorny issue. The wallet companies say they will protect consumers' privacy. But there are others who might object to such gathering of information. "If I'm a merchant who competes with Barnesandnoble.com, I'm not going to be happy about a wallet company selling that information to a competitor," Mr. Cassar said. Since credit card companies already sell lists along those lines, he added, they will probably resist any efforts on the part of wallet companies to compete on that front, as could portals like America Online, which can use such information to deliver more advertisements to highly specific audiences. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Encryption Products Found To Grow in Foreign Markets
body: Commercial data-scrambling technology that is made outside the unitedstates has become significantly more available in the last 18 months, according to researchers at George Washington University. The researchers' report, which is to be presented today in testimony before the Senate Commerce Committee, is part of a growing body of evidence suggesting that the Government's efforts to restrict the spread of "strong encryption" technology for secret electronic communications have largely failed. "The Government must acknowledge that there are foreign products, and it must concede that they are of comparable quality to U.S. technology," said Bruce Heiman, legislative counsel for Americans for Computer Privacy, the Washington-based computer industry lobbying group that financed the study. The Government has long imposed export curbs on encryption technologies, invoking national security and crime prevention concerns. Officials have argued that scrambled messages would improve the ability of terrorists and other criminals to organize and plan illegal operations. The new data, though, indicate that 805 encryption products are now available in 35 countries outside the unitedstates -- a 22 percent increase since December 1997. Moreover, 167 products are based on encryption algorithms considered too strong to be cracked by even the most powerful computers. "In addition to the absolute increase in the number of products, we've also found that six new countries have companies that are now selling encryption technology," said Lance Hoffman, director of the Cyberspace Policy Institute at George Washington University. He pointed to companies like Cybernetica in Estonia that use the unitedstates export restrictions as a marketing tool. "Cybernetica advertises: 'Strong crypto. Long keys. No export restrictions,' " he said. The report also asserts that the unitedstates has lost its monopoly on the basic mathematical technologies underlying data encryption. For example, of the 15 algorithms now being considered by the National Institute of Standards for a new American encryption standard, 10 have been developed outside the unitedstates. The report does not offer evidence of actual use of encryption systems abroad. But Mr. Hoffman said researchers had compiled material suggesting that the most powerful encryption software was now readily accessible internationally. "I'm holding in my hands a computer magazine we found on a French newsstand," he said in a phone interview yesterday. The publication, Magazine Dot Net, contained a CD-ROM with encryption programs including Pretty Good Privacy and a program called Scramdisk that features advanced encryption algorithms like DES, Triple DES, Blowfish and Idea -- any of which would present formidable challenges to code breakers in the Federal Government. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
A Hitch to Marital Web Bliss;
Excite@Home Is Often at Odds With Its Cable Parents
body: It is early in the honeymoon for the At Home Corporation, a provider of fast Internet access through cable lines, and Excite Inc., the country's second-largest Internet portal, which it just bought for $6.7 billion. But Excite may already feel like the bride who finds that her in-laws are bent on undermining the marriage. Executives at several of the big cable companies that control the newly combined company are now dropping loud hints that they think the deal, which they approved, was a mistake -- most notably, Leo J. Hindery Jr., who runs the cable operations for AT&T, owner of 58 percent of the voting shares of what is now called Excite@Home. Mr. Hindery has publicly questioned whether At Home should be so closely tied to a single source of news, email and other services. That has been the strategy long articulated by Thomas A. Jermoluk, formerly head of At Home and now chief executive of Excite@Home. His plan is to use fast Internet access to steer users directly to pages run by Excite, replicating the all-in-one power of America Online Inc. It is a big challenge to take on America Online, which adds some 600,000 paying customers a month and is planning its own high-speed service, through telephone wires. But the Internet world is changing, with far faster networks soon to be hooked up to computers, televisions and all manner of devices. And with a potential of 65 million homes served by its cable systems, 26 million current users of Excite and a market value of $18 billion, Excite@Home has as good a chance as any company to be a contender in this new market. It does, that is, so long as everybody in the family gets along. "The biggest threat to At Home now is themselves," said Abhi Chaki, head of broadband consulting at Jupiter Communications, a market research firm in newyork. "There may well be an implosion." Indeed, since At Home was born in 1995, its cable parents -- primarily AT&T, the Comcast Corporation and Cox Communications -- have done as much to stunt its growth as to nurture it. They have, for one thing, been slow to add the capability to handle two-way data traffic. So At Home, which once promised to have a million subscribers in its first year, will not reach that milestone until the end of this year, giving phone companies and satellite providers the chance to develop rival high-speed technology. The cable companies gave At Home the right to block any other provider from using their systems to offer high-speed Internet access, but that block ends in 2002. In addition, Excite@Home may be a pawn in its own parents' bickering. Looking at its board, it is no wonder one cable executive called it "the Falcon Crest of Silicon Valley." The core is L. John Doerr, the venture capital impresario at Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers, and John C. Malone, who as chairman of Tele-Communications Inc. agreed to back Mr. Doerr's plan for high-speed service. Also on the board is C. Michael Armstrong, chairman of AT&T, which recently bought TCI, and Brian L. Roberts, president of Comcast, which AT&T just outbid in the takeover battle for another cable company, Mediaone. So far, despite the public griping, Mr. Jermoluk, known as T. J., has been able to get the board to back his plan, negotiating deals with 21 cable companies to offer its high-speed service. "I've been really impressed with the force of will that T. J. has to pull this strange collection of bedfellows into a common team," said Geoffrey Y. Yang, a venture capitalist with Institutional Venture Partners in Menlo Park, Calif., who served on Excite's board. "When you talk to the guys who work at At Home, there is almost a cult of T. J. To them, he's larger than life." Now Mr. Jermoluk has to bridge an entirely different culture gap. For as much as the cable companies see At Home as their prodigal son hot rodding around Silicon Valley dreaming of being in show business, to Excite it is a timid Mama's boy. "The cable companies, while entrepreneurial, are not necessarily moving at Web pace," Mr. Yang said. Of more concern to At Home's owners is the World Wide Web credo that a company must dominate a market or die. At Home, typically, wants every advantage and is trying to lock cable systems into exclusive deals and funnel users into services on which it controls the advertising. The cable companies are used to cozier competition, with system operators owning pieces of many programming channels. And they are more used to operating under the watchful eyes of regulators. "Left to its own devices, At Home would go and play things up that have a negative effect on cable," said one At Home board member. Since the cable companies are spending $5 billion to $10 billion to upgrade their systems to handle two-way data, they insist that At Home not appear so monopolistic as to invite new Government regulation. That is what America Online has been asking for as it complains bitterly to Washington that the cable systems will not let it buy broadband access wholesale, bypassing At Home's service. Mr. Hindery has told cable executives that on AT&T's systems, the country's No. 1 portal, Yahoo, will get equal placement to Excite. And last week a Federal court upheld a rule by Portland, Ore., requiring AT&T's cable system to offer access to other Internet services. Mr. Jermoluk is quick to point out that At Home users can go anywhere on the Web. But he says it is essential that the first screen customers see, with links to news, email, shopping and so on, be Excite's. At Home figures it will only break even from its 35 percent of the monthly fees for its Internet service. (The cable operators keep the rest of the fee, now about $40.) So advertising must provide the profit. "We think that over time, the revenue from transporting data will continue to fall," Mr. Jermoluk said. "That's why in our long-term business model, half our revenue comes from the media side." Some analysts disagree, saying the transporting of data -- which happens to be what AT&T and At Home's other parents do for a living -- can be profitable. "Internet access is going to be a commodity," said Mr. Chaki of Jupiter. "But there are still going to be people who make a lot of money on access. And their whole subscription model is muddled because they have this media play through Excite." If the board did not agree, though, why did it approve the Excite deal? Excite had decided to sell itself because its stock market value was too low to make big acquisitions, and it feared that it would fall further behind Yahoo. Ultimately, At Home's board decided it, too, could best protect its investment by growing. "Frankly, Excite isn't Yahoo and At Home isn't AOL," one board member said. "So it was a logical pooling of resources." Excite may not quite be Yahoo, but it has come a long way since it was founded by a group of Stanford University graduate students in 1995.  Running a marathon at the pace of a sprint, Excite transformed a tiny search engine into a vast portal, a collection of services from stock quotes to shopping. "There was never enough time," said George Bell, Excite's chief executive, who is now president of the combined company. "You worked. It got dark. You woke up. Someone handed you a piece of pizza and it started all over again." Excite's breakneck style is far different from the more measured pace of At Home, which has taken years to prepare for a battle that could play out over a decade. It's no surprise, then, that the two chief executives could hardly be more different. Mr. Jermoluk, a windswept blond from Hawaii, is an ambitious Silicon Valley engineering executive, known for his laid-back style and wild office parties. Mr. Bell, a sober, dark-haired newyork publishing executive, is just as ambitious, but is known for hands-on control and long hours. And while Mr. Jermoluk is always the engineer, Mr. Bell has far more of a media perspective. "T. J. will come in, and if he's feeling particularly perky, he'll ask about whether we should use an interrupt model or a polling model to get data from the cable modems," said Adam Grosser, the head of engineering. "George wants to know about page views and advertising revenue." Both executives say that for it to work, the merger must not hinder Excite's ability to keep up with the other portals. So far, the combination seems smooth, aided by the coincidence that the two companies occupy adjacent office buildings here on the northern edge of Silicon Valley. And since there is little overlap in their operations, there have been no layoffs. While it was Mr. Jermoluk who offered the No. 2 spot to Mr. Bell, several board members were pleased, hoping Mr. Bell's reputation for detail would help compensate for some gaps in service quality they attribute to Mr. Jermoluk. They also seemed reassured to have a talented backup to Mr. Jermoluk, who, with stock options worth more than $400 million, may not have a strong incentive to stay on indefinitely. Mr. Jermoluk says he will stay, though, and there is certainly no shortage of things that he and Mr. Bell say they plan to do. Excite, for example, will be reformatted to serve users equally well at slow and fast speeds, offering those on the faster broadband connections more video and graphics. Excite's vast marketing data base will also be expanded to incorporate data from cable set-top boxes, which are really minicomputers. That way people who watch the Food Channel, for example, will see ads for frying pans when they later surf the Web. And any Excite user in an At Home service area will get a barrage of offers for high-speed access. The company also has to complete development of its interactive television service, another project Mr. Jermoluk persuaded a skeptical board to back. He wants to offer news, shopping and Internet surfing on TV screens, somewhat the way the Microsoft Corporation's WebTV does. (AT&T is the only cable company interested so far.) There is some deal making to do over Road Runner, the rival cable Internet service started by Time Warner and Mediaone. Mr. Jermoluk has long wanted to buy Road Runner, and some deal is more likely now that AT&T is buying Mediaone, and Microsoft, which owns 10 percent of Road Runner, has invested in AT&T. But some executives at Time Warner and some of At Home's owners wonder whether the industry would not be better off with two competing services. Even without those deals, Excite@Home will have to complete its $500 million nationwide backbone network to link the cable system so it can handle all the customers Mr. Jermoluk is expecting. By 2002, he wants 10 million to 15 million subscribers to the Internet service and 40 million to 50 million people using its interactive television service. It is no accident that Mr. Jermoluk is tuning his plans to 2002 -- the year the exclusive contracts end and cable operators can sell access to America Online, Road Runner or anyone else. By that point, Mr. Jermoluk says, Excite's service will be so popular that the cable systems will want to offer it. "Our job is to be a strong enough and powerful enough brand, like MTV and ESPN, that the cable systems will want to keep working with us," he said. And ultimately, Mr. Jermoluk said, Excite@Home has a measure of protection from too much interference from its meddlesome parents because they own so much of its stock. "If we are a valuable property for them," he said, "why would they go a different way and throw away their equity value?" http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: George Bell, left, president of Excite@Home, and Thomas A. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Account Decisions By On-Line Services
body: Three on-line services have made decisions involving accounts. Firstsource.com in Santa Ana, Calif., an Internet-based computer product retailer that is part of En Pointe Technologies, named D'Arcy Masius Benton & Bowles Los Angeles, a unit of MacManus Group, as the first agency to handle its account. Billings were estimated at $20 million. The decision came after a two-month review that had been narrowed to D.M.B.& B. and three other finalists: Cole & Weber in Seattle, part of the Ogilvy & Mather Worldwide unit of WPP Group P.L.C.; Rieches Baird in Irvine, Calif., and TFA/Leo Burnett Technology Group in Chicago, a unit of the Leo Burnett Company. Altavista.com, the search engine owned by the Compaq Computer Corporation, is conducting a closed review for its first advertising campaign. Though billings were not disclosed, the bigger search engines spend tens of millions of dollars annually on brand advertising. Charles Rashall, vice president for marketing and advertising sales at Alta Vista in Palo Alto, Calif., said about six agencies, which he declined to identify, would participate, adding that he expected a decision in four to six weeks. The agency has to be "capable of reinforcing our brand leadership position," Mr. Rashall said. And Accutrade, an on-line brokerage firm owned by the Ameritrade Holding Corporation, awarded its account to Romann Group in newyork. Billings on the account, which had been at Doremus & Company in newyork, part of Omnicom Group, were estimated at $5 million to $10 million. Peter Ricketts, president at Accutrade in Omaha, said that the decision came after a monthlong review in which Doremus did not take part. The review was narrowed to Romann and a second agency, which he declined to identify. Accutrade was "looking for an agency with on-line discount brokerage experience," Mr. Ricketts said. Romann had handled the account of DLJ Direct, the Internet-based brokerage subsidiary of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, part of AXA's Equitable Companies. That account, with billings estimated at $30 million, was shifted in November to Kirshenbaum Bond & Partners in newyork.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MARKET INSIGHT;
Handicapping Wall Street As Old Line Goes on Line
body: IN hindsight, rather than extolling the Internet, maybe securities firms should have advised customers to stay away. Now the retail brokerage business, which generated about $12.8 billion in commissions in 1997, is getting a comeuppance because of low-cost, on-line trading. The latest -- and biggest -- blow to the primacy of flesh-and-blood brokers came last week, when Merrill Lynch said that by December it would offer on-line trading for as little as $29.95 a trade. Of course, that could generate huge savings for its five million customers. Less obvious, however, is how Merrill will recoup the big chunk of change it will lose. The market has apparently decided that there is no positive answer to that question, and most brokerage stocks have moved sharply lower since Merrill made its move. Sallie Krawcheck, an analyst who follows Wall Street firms for Sanford C. Bernstein & Company, talked last week about Merrill's announcement. Here are some excerpts.  Q. Just how big a deal is Merrill's move?  A. It is hard to overstate the significance of this. It is a sea change in the retail brokerage business. Managements at all of these firms are going to have to craft responses to what Merrill has just announced in very short order. The traditional businesses of firms like Merrill, Dean Witter and Smith Barney have never experienced pricing pressure, and now they are. And we are not talking about taking prices down by 20 percent, but by 90 percent. For some time, we had been forecasting that the retail business would contract by 5 percent a year going forward, as the traditional business became outdated. This is like death by fire.  Q. Aside from the cost issue, why have so many people apparently turned away from full-service brokers?  A. Retail brokers have done a poor job of attracting the next generation of investors. If full-service retail brokers don't get clients early, they generally don't get them at all, because those who need brokers have not gone to full-service brokers, but a whole set of different financial intermediaries. The typical client of a retail broker is in his or her mid-60's. So the image of a traditional broker in the industry has evolved to something like a Cadillac, or the last car you drive before you die.  Q. A number of on-line trading firms have run advertisements belittling the advice retail brokers offer. Is it realistic to think that investors can do everything on their own?  A. Over the last few years, there has been a lot of bickering between brokers and the Internet. But all of these things can co-exist. There is no reason advice can't be delivered electronically. And the value of advice, given the massive amount of information available to everyone now, is, if anything, even greater than previously.  Q. Based on the recent movement in the stocks, investors seem to agree with you that the Merrill announcement is a seismic event. But is it fair to assume that retail is equally important to all these firms?  A. The market does an extremely poor job in discriminating among the companies. Momentum is the biggest driver for the group. We estimate that for Merrill, retail brokerage accounts for about 25 percent of its quarterly earnings. The stock has fallen about 14 percent in a week. At Paine Webber, the same number is about 50 percent. Its stock is down by about 11 percent.  Q. The threat of on-line trading isn't the only reason these stocks are down, is it?  A. In addition to the Internet fears, we have fears of Fed tightening and concerns about Y2K. Of the three, the Fed will probably impact the group the least. When the Fed fine-tuned monetary policy in 1997, it was a tremendous opportunity to buy the group. Despite these worries, right now the businesses for these firms are in good shape. All of the stocks are telling us earnings are not going to be good, but equity underwriting is on a path to be up 25 percent over the first quarter. Trading volumes remain robust, both in fixed income and, to a lesser extent, in equity. And Asia and Europe are real bright spots for these firms.  Q. So which stocks do you like?  A. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter is down 22 percent from its highs and has taken a greater hit relative to its retail earnings than Merrill has. It appears the market has again forgotten the real underlying earnings power this company has displayed. For clients who want exposure to financial service stocks, we think this is a real core holding. Bear Stearns is also off 27 percent, but should it be taking a hit? They are primarily a clearinghouse, and the stock is perennially cheap. At the moment, it is trading at less than nine times next year's earnings. It just doesn't get any respect. For long-term investors with a bullish long-term view on the international aspects of the business, we like Goldman Sachs, though the stock appears fairly valued. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Krawcheck

title:
MARKET WATCH;
Call Off the Death Watch for Brokers
body: IS the full-service stockbroker going the way of the dodo bird? Merrill Lynch's announcement on Tuesday that it would capitulate to the on-line trading frenzy by offering do-it-yourself investors $29.95 Internet trades later this year looked to some people like the beginning of the end of the tradition that Merrill represents. Any corporate announcement that reverses decades of business practice and entrenched philosophy, as this one did, is breathtaking. Sure enough, investors knocked down brokerage stocks on the news. Fears that Merrill's embrace of on-line trading and its deep-discounted commissions would hammer profits drove the American Stock Exchange's Securities Broker/Dealer index down 5.4 percent the day the news broke. The index ended the week down 8.3 percent. Investors are right to be concerned about profitability at brokerage firms. The $29.95 trades to be offered by Merrill Lynch are well below the firm's current commission schedule and no doubt the first salvo in what may devolve into a nasty price war. Net profit margins at brokerage firms -- currently around 6 percent, according to the Value Line Investment Survey -- will be much lower in the years ahead. But any celebration of the death of the full-service broker is premature. Although the number of old-fashioned brokers will surely dwindle, and those left will have thinner wallets, many will survive, even thrive. The practice of buying and selling stocks with the help of a human being is not going to be supplanted by the click of a mouse just yet. This is certain, however: Brokers who do not provide value to their customers are an endangered species. "The lay-up business -- sell 1,000 shares of a $50 stock for a $500 commission -- is going away," said Shad Rowe, who runs Greenbrier Partners, a money-management firm in Dallas. "People don't have to pay for no-brainer trades anymore. But brokers who can truly represent their customers? Their value goes up." On-line investing has a lot going for it. The beauty of the Internet, of course, is that it often eliminates the middleman and thereby cuts costs for consumers. It also allows Americans to pursue one of their quintessential delights: the do-it-yourself gig. Buying and selling stocks on line has the added appeal of providing investors with the sense that they are in the midst of a high-stakes game. Indeed, these people may not want a broker to interject herself between them and the action because that dilutes the rush. After all, people who frequent the craps tables in Las Vegas don't usually ask others to throw the dice for them. It could be that the world of investors is in the process of dividing into those who want help and those who don't. Still, the trial and error that usually surrounds any do-it-yourself effort will prove much more painful in investing than it would in, say, plumbing or wallpapering. It's much harder to fix an investment that went awry than to have a professional come in and correct a mangled drain pipe or rehang some paper. An argument can also be made that now, more than ever, investors need help sorting through the cacophony emitted by CNBC, Internet investing chat rooms and the growing number of publications devoted to financial issues. Furthermore, with American families more time-starved than ever before, it seems strange that the interest in do-it-yourself investing should surge just now. Much of the investor enthusiasm for on-line trading is a result of the lengthy bull market. When stocks are going up, it's easy to have success in the market as a do-it-yourselfer. On-line trading aficionados have not yet had to endure a bear market. "As soon as the market starts requiring that people spend a lot more time watching over their investments rather than just looking at the paper and seeing that their Internet stock went up, people will have to work on figuring out why a stock's not working," said Seth Novatt, managing director at CIBC Oppenheimer in newyork. "There are many people who won't want to spend the time doing it." One of the reasons that investing on one's own is alluring, of course, is that many investors have been burned by full-service brokers. But all brokers are not the smirking pickpockets that on-line brokers' advertisements portray. Many are honest and hard-working, and bring years of experience and professionalism to bear on their clients' behalf. (Full disclosure: From 1981 to 1984, this columnist was a stockbroker at Dean Witter Reynolds in newyork.) "The truth of the matter is, people want advice from experienced people who have been in the business," said David Eidelman, a money manager at Eidelman, Finger & Harris in St. Louis. "A broker may call me up and say, 'Did you notice this stock has been slipping?' or point out something I didn't think of. The extra commission I pay that broker is more than made up by the service he provides." Money managers say that a full-service broker must perform many duties if he wants to earn higher commission rates. Here is a list of what the pros say investors have a right to expect: * Honesty. * Perspective. An alert broker cannot help but learn from the market, a school of hard knocks to be sure. Sharing these lessons with clients can help them from having to learn the hard way on their own. * Discipline. A good broker helps assess the risk in an investment, playing the devil's advocate on a stock that may look attractive or a bond with an alluringly high yield. * Expert editing. A professional broker will help delete stocks that look shaky or inappropriate from a portfolio and will keep a client diversified. * Error protection. A computer will not keep clients from making dumb mistakes -- buying a stock that was supposed to be sold, for example. A trustworthy broker will, and will also keep customers from making trades with costly tax consequences. * Superior execution of trades. A good broker will work a customer's Nasdaq or option trade, for example, squeezing between bid and asked prices or watching for other ways to save an investor one-eighth or one-quarter of a point. * Grading of a firm's research analysts. An honest broker will give her customers the benefit of her experience, separating the amateurs from the pros. * Independent research. A hard-working broker will check out rumors or tips, using bona fide sources of information that are relatively independent. * Good investment ideas that are off the beaten track. Of course, if the broker provides all of these services but consistently loses money for his clients, he should be fired. Making money is the goal, after all. A result of Merrill's on-line initiative will certainly be an increased focus among the customers of full-service firms on the costs levied and the benefits provided by their brokers. This is a good thing. If brokers don't perform, they will be bounced, either by their clients or by their firms. No matter how painful it is in the near term, survival of the fittest is long overdue on Wall Street. "Brokers are going to have to adjust their philosophy as well as their commissions," said Rod Fadem, a broker at Oppenheimer & Company, in Clayton, Mo., who has been in the business since 1960. "The philosophy must be 'everything for the customer first.' Investors need to have someone on their side." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Wiring Wall Street" Last week, Merrill Lynch shook the brokerage world by announcing a major push into on-line trading. title: Paine Webber Says It Will Offer On-Line Trading
body: Paine Webber Group Inc. the fifth-largest unitedstates broker, said yesterday that it would offer on-line trading in the third quarter, joining other Wall Street firms in their entry into the growing but fiercely competitive Internet market. Mark B. Sutton, president of the firm's private client group, which caters to wealthy investors, said a group of its clients was already trading stocks under a pilot program. Mr. Sutton spoke at a press briefing held two days after Merrill Lynch & Company said it would start offering on-line trading in July. Merrill's announcement was seen as increasing the pressure on other traditional brokers to follow suit despite fears that on-line trading will cut into the brokerage commissions earned by their brokers for executing trades. Share prices in traditional brokerage firms have fallen along with the broader market this week. Paine Webber recovered a bit yesterday, rising 93.75 cents, to $42.75, while Merrill slipped 75 cents, to $69.9375. On-line brokerage firms like the Charles Schwab Corporation and E*Trade Group Inc. have thrived on the explosion in on-line trading. Schwab's stock soared to record highs in April, giving the company a market capitalization exceeding Merrill's, before declining somewhat amid a loss of investor enthusiasm for Internet companies. Marten Hoekstra, director of marketing for Paine Webber, said at yesterday's briefing that the firm would not offer on-line trading as a single service, but as part of a package. "We are going to combine on-line services with advice," he said, arguing that the firm was simply meeting the demands of its clients, many of whom have portfolios worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. Mr. Hoekstra said Paine Webber would not join the price war waged by discount brokers, some of which execute trades for less than $10. Mr. Sutton said the pilot program had two packages. One offered on-line trading, financial advice and other services for up to 2 percent of the client's assets. The other package charged a flat $1,200 fee for a limited number of trades and a couple of consultations a year, among other things. But he said the fee structure was not yet set. Mr. Sutton said Paine Webber had not lost client funds despite its late start in on-line trading. http://www.nytimes.com

title: In Spanish and Portuguese, Web Growth Spurt
body: IN January, Anna Spinello, a clothing designer in Buenos Aires, set up a Web site to help boost sales of her spring line. By clicking on a little flag, a viewer can see the site in English, Spanish or Portuguese. "Considering we haven't publicized it, we've had an amazing response," said her son Francesco Spinello, 42, who manages the small, family-run business (www.annaspinello.com) that sells to boutiques in Argentina, Chile, Uruguay and Brazil. "We've made a lot of contacts that should pay off with the next collection." The Spinellos are part of a wave of Latin Americans who have recently discovered the Web. Lagging perhaps two years behind the unitedstates, Japan and Western Europe in its development, the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking Internet market is one of the fastest-growing in the world and has emerged as the latest battleground for viewers among such Internet titans as America Online and Yahoo. "This is the year the scales are tipping," said Heather Killen, the vice president of Yahoo International, who oversaw the start-up of a Spanish version of the Yahoo portal (espanol.yahoo.com) in June 1998. "The shape of the Internet is no longer a comet with the U.S. as the head and this thin trail behind." Latin American governments, aware of the need to promote local Internet access and business so that more precious dollars do not flow overseas, are also beginning to look at ways to encourage more people to get on line. The governments of Argentina and Chile, for example, have mandated that privately held phone companies charge half price for local Internet access phone calls. Recent privatization of the state-run phone company in Brazil, which is the only Portuguese-speaking country in Latin America, is expected to lead to reduced phone charges and better infrastructure and service in that country, the most populous in the region, accounting for roughly half the Internet users. "If they don't allow citizens on line, they realize their country is going to be at a significant disadvantage in the future," said Annika Alford, chief Latin American Internet analyst for IDC, a market research company in Framingham, Mass. Among the Internet's contributions to Latin America will be allowing the Spinellos and other merchants to expand their reach across borders. "The Internet is an extraordinary medium to improve communication and exchange among different cultures and languages," Mr. Spinello said. "In Brazil, for example, we have few clients now but there is great potential for growth." Internet companies in the unitedstates, faced with slowing growth at home, are looking for expansion through service in languages other than English. This year, for the first time, there will be more people gaining access to the Web from outside the unitedstates than from within, many of them preferring to do so in their native tongue. The Spanish-speaking population in the unitedstates also holds growth potential for Internet companies. Luis Hernandez, an 18-year-old bilingual senior at Hollywood High School in Los Angeles, uses the Internet to search for information about his favorite Latin bands and to chat with childhood friends living in Mexico as well as other Spanish speakers using one of America Online's Hispanic chat rooms. The Spanish language "is easier for me to write in -- I'm faster," he said, adding: "It's our culture. We understand ourselves." As they rush to sign up Spanish-language consumers, Internet giants in this country face stiff competition from both Latin American media companies and existing Spanish-language portals -- the industry term for a site that is both a primary destination and a gateway to the Internet at large -- based in the unitedstates. Of these portals, Starmedia Network (starmedia .com), which saw its stock nearly double on the first day of trading in its initial public offering last week, has grabbed much of the attention for its Spanish-Portuguese site. But other ventures are vying for the same users, and the last few weeks have seen a flurry of announcements of new sites in the Spanish-language Internet sector. Among the competitors are Que Pasa (quepasa .com), a Spanish-English site, and Yupi (yupi.com), which recently acquired Ciudad Futura, a Spanish-language on-line entertainment site (www.ciudadfutura.com), and says it is the front-runner with more than 5.7 million users and 80 million page views per month from both the Yupi and Ciudad Futura sites. Starmedia lays claim to 60 million page views per month and 2.4 million users. Bloomberg recently announced that it would soon open a bilingual personal finance site for Hispanics in the unitedstates (www.negociosbloomberg.com). Just how many Hispanic Internet users there are is the subject of some debate. The number of users of the Internet at large -- or of a specific site -- is hard to measure, in part because of differences in the methods of measurement in the fast-changing world of electronic media. While operators of Web sites typically keep detailed logs of user traffic, there is no generally accepted industry auditing process for those data. And outside companies that try to compile Web usage data, a la television's Nielsen ratings, must extrapolate from audience samples that are widely thought to undercount Internet use from work and ignore or undercount Internet use from overseas. Companies like Starmedia, lumping together Hispanics in this country, Portuguese-speaking Brazil, the countries of Spanish-speaking Latin America, Spain and Portugal, come up with a figure of about 20 million users worldwide, two-thirds of them in Latin America. IDC, which takes a slightly more conservative approach, based on its figures showing that there is an installed PC base in Latin America of nearly 16 million computers and an Internet penetration rate of 20 percent, estimates that by the end of 1999 there will be 7 million Latin Americans on line. At an annual growth rate of 32 percent over the next five years, IDC predicts that number will grow to 19 million on line by the year 2003. Hispanics in the unitedstates are another large and growing market for Spanish-language sites. Data from Nielsen Net Ratings, which monitors Web traffic, indicate that about 5 million of the 30 million Hispanics in the unitedstates are on line. A study by Forrester Research, however, put the figure closer to 10 million. A focus group study by Yahoo indicated that 70 percent of American Hispanics preferred to get at least some of their content in Spanish. That would suggest that there might be as many as seven million Hispanics in this country surfing Spanish-language sites. Yupi, with headquarters in Miami Beach and offices in seven Latin American countries, estimates that 20 percent of its traffic comes from American users. While Hispanics in this country may be an important sector of the Spanish-language audience, the big growth in the user base is expected to come from Latin America, particularly Brazil, with a population of 160 million. Pedro Rosa, 33, a writer and translator in Rio de Janeiro, said he downloaded software and regularly communicated via email with other writers in the unitedstates and elsewhere. He also conducts much of his research on line, sometimes using the Brazilian search engine Cade (cade.com.br), sometimes an English or French one. "It gives me access to a lot of dictionaries and translating tools," said Mr. Rosa, who has also taken screen-writing courses over the Web through a company called Online Learning, based in Los Angeles. Already the Web is breaking down national barriers. On Starmedia's bulletin boards and classified pages, for example, people from many Latin American countries post notices side by side or banter in chat rooms. Some speak of the Internet as having achieved a "virtual regionalization." Winning over locals like Mr. Rosa may prove a challenge for unitedstates companies moving into an increasingly crowded market. Already there are in the neighborhood of 450 Internet service providers in Brazil, 240 in Mexico and 170 in Argentina, according to numbers from America Online's Latin American unit, as well as long-established major destinations, many of them sponsored by Latin American media giants like TV Globo (globo.com.br) and Grupo Folha (uol.com.br) in Brazil and Grupo Clarin (clarin.com.ar) in Argentina. A common strategy is to find local partners who can help pave the way in a market where personal relationships are key to business success. "You can't sit in a city on another continent and say, 'Right, I'm going to launch something in Chile,' " said Phil Ingram, marketing manager of Orientation.com, which is based in New York and is creating a network of country portals. "You have to have local contacts who can build bridges." Orientation.com plans to carve a niche for itself by focusing on some of the smaller, overlooked countries -- Colombia, Costa Rica, Chile -- with a network appealing to business travelers, offering a currency converter, weather forecasts and trade show information in English and Spanish. America Online has formed a 50-50 partnership with the Cisneros Group, a major entertainment and telecommunications force in Latin America that is based in Venezuela. And last month, the two partners hired Charles Herington as president and chief executive of AOL Latin America, which will first tackle the Brazilian market and later Argentina. Mr. Herington previously helped Taco Bell and Pizza Hut spread their franchises in South America. Marketing Internet services, however, will prove more complicated than selling fast food. Sites must be locally tailored. Jack Davies, president of AOL International, promised that Brazilians will not find themselves force-fed a service planned for North Americans, but will instead find a product reconceived for their needs. "It's going to be very bright, very alive, very colorful, more so than corresponding AOL.com's because of the festive nature of Brazil," Mr. Davies said. Though features like chat, email and up-to-the-second news have proved enormously popular in Latin America, as they have elsewhere in the world, electronic commerce, including sales of books, CD's, computer equipment and clothing, may catch on more slowly because of cultural and logistical differences. Brazil, for example, does not have the unitedstates' extensive tradition in mail-order catalog buying on which to build an electronic commerce market. "We Brazilians like to see the thing, touch it, like to be sure we're going to have something," said Mr. Rosa, who once ordered books from Amazon.com but had to wait seven weeks for them to arrive and vows never to buy on line again. Further slowing the expansion of the Internet user base in Latin America has been the regional economic crisis. The number of Internet users in the region more than doubled from 1997 to 1998; the 1999 growth appears to be only half as fast, IDC said. Mr. Herington at AOL, among others, said that the Internet itself might provide the solution by improving communication and distribution channels. Adding to the obstacles for Latin American Web surfers are underdeveloped telephone systems, the relatively high cost of Internet access and the fact that many phone companies in Latin America charge by the minute for local calls. Mr. Rosa, who estimates he spends an average of 60 hours a month on line, pays the equivalent of $20 a month to his Internet service provider for unlimited access, but local toll charges add another $40 to his monthly phone bill. "How many people can afford this?" Mr. Rosa said of his fellow Brazilians. "Most people don't have enough money to afford a computer. The base isn't going to expand unless we do all sorts of socioeconomic development." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: The Internet market of Spanish and Portuguese speakers is one of the fastest-growing in the world. Luis Hernandez of Los Angeles uses the Internet to chat with friends living in Mexico. (Chris Pizzello for The New York Times)(pg. G8); NEW TO THE WEB -- Anna Spinello, a clothing designer in Buenos Aires, and her son Francesco recently put their family-run business on line. (Horacio Paone for The New York Times)(pg. G1)

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
Shares Slip but Rebound; Nasdaq Up, Other Gauges Flat
body: Stocks slumped in early trading yesterday but rebounded somewhat after bargain hunters stepped in to scoop up shares of Internet and other high-technology issues. By the close, the Nasdaq composite index had reversed course and posted a solid gain, but the other main gauges were flat. Once again, concern about higher interest rates dominated trading, analysts said. A report showing that sales of new homes surged unexpectedly in April was the latest in a series of reports suggesting that the economy continues to grow at an unsustainably fast pace and that the Fed will most likely raise rates. "Interest rate fears are the big problem," said Kenneth Ducey, director of trading at BT Brokerage, a unit of Bankers Trust. "People are very nervous" that the Fed or the fixed-income market may tighten credit. A key report on the nation's employment situation is set to be released tomorrow. However, Alan Greenspan, the Fed chairman, said nothing bearing on rates in a lunchtime appearance in Boston, and the markets seemed to take that as a cue to rally. One exception was brokerage stocks, which continued to reel from Merrill Lynch's announcement of a new on-line trading service. Merrill finished down 4 9/16, to 70 11/16, after two analysts cut earnings estimates for next year. Nasdaq, which is dominated by computer and other high-technology issues, finished with a gain of 20.38 points, or eight-tenths of a percent, to 2,432.41. At its low, just after noon, the loss was more than 47 points. The Dow Jones industrial average, meanwhile, ended 18.37 points lower, or two-tenths of a percent, to 10,577.89, after being down nearly 132 points before the comeback. Eighteen of its 30 components lost ground while 12, mostly cyclical issues, rose. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index rose 0.55 point, to 1,294.81, but advancing stocks barely surpassed declining ones, 243 to 241, with 16 unchanged. Despite the recent wide swings, the Chicago Board Options Exchange's volatility index has been remarkably subdued, according to Lawrence D. Cavanagh, an options strategist at Value Line. With a decline of 1.69 points yesterday, the index stands at 26.23, far below this year's high approaching 35 in mid-January. "Option premiums have not jumped the way they usually do" when the investment tide turns, Mr. Cavanagh said. "A lot of people are not terribly worried." Stocks fell in six of the preceding eight sessions, pulling the Dow 4.6 percent below its record 11,107.19 on May 13. "What the market continues to do is unwind the real economic fear of last year, which motivated investors to own the safest vehicles in each asset class," Greg Smith, chief investment strategist at Prudential Securities, told clients yesterday. For stocks, this was the large-capitalization growth stocks, which are unlikely to "return to the growth rates they had previously shown." Still, inflation fears should ease and June should prove "pretty good for both stocks and bonds," Mr. Smith predicted. Some of yesterday's biggest gyrations were in Ameritrade, the on-line broker, which closed with a gain of 5 7/8, to 85 5/8, after trading as low as 73 and as high as 91 5/8. On April 14, the shares were worth more than twice as much, peaking at 188 3/8. Charles Schwab, the nation's biggest on-line broker, slumped as low as 91 1/4 yesterday before finishing at 96 1/8, down 3 3/8. After trading as low as 151 1/2, Ebay rallied to close up 2 5/16, to 168 13/16, while Amazon.com recovered from a low of 97 1/8 and finished up 6 5/16, to 112 1/8. J. P. Morgan lost 2 5/8, to 130 7/8, the biggest drag on the Dow, while I.B.M. had the most positive impact, rising 1 3/4, to 113 3/4. American Home Products, which tumbled on Tuesday after announcing an earnings shortfall, recovered 1 13/16, to 53 13/16.  Treasury Prices Flat By Reuters Another wave of strong economic data jolted Treasuries yesterday, although the losses were contained by the notion the market has cheapened enough to entice buyers. Early in the day, Treasury yields rose to their highest levels in at least a year after the Commerce Department reported a 9.2 percent rise in new single-family home sales in April to a 978,000-unit annual rate. That topped the 890,000 rate the market had expected. The price of the 30-year Treasury bond was unchanged at 90 22/32. The bond's yield fell to 5.92 percent, from 5.94 percent on Tuesday. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average, since May 1998.
