title: Trying to Move On-Line Radio Beyond a Niche
body: Until recently, it might have been fair to enlist the cliche "those crazy kids" to describe people who listened to radio on the Internet. But a series of announcements last week signals that the demographic profile of on-line listeners is expanding beyond 20-somethings to include the corporate set. Last Monday, Yahoo started a Web radio service called Yahoo Radio (http://radio.yahoo.com/), comprising 10 audio channels that visitors can listen to using software called the Realplayer G2 from Real Networks. The audio programming for Yahoo's service is provided by Spinner.com, a San Francisco company that announced plans last week to go public in September. Separately last week, Looksmart, another search engine, announced plans to produce an on-line talk show devoted to Internet topics. Behind the scenes, these deals underscore the growth of a multilayered industry with players convinced that the PC will be the radio tuner for the next generation. The entrepreneurs driving the convergence of radio and the Internet say that listeners will flock to specialized audio programming delivered over the PC, sponsored by advertising aimed at individual listeners. But the emergence of the technology poses a question for the industry: Is the business proposition sound, or is it more white noise about the Internet? Spinner.com illustrates one example of the type of business model these companies are relying upon. The company, founded in 1996 as TheDJ.com, offers 175,000 songs on 120 channels; the fare includes punk, funk, gospel, gumbo, surf and swing. Visitors to the site download a player called Spinner Plus, which enables them to listen to the channels. Like traditional radio stations, Spinner.com and its competitors license the songs at a per-play fee from music industry groups like the American Society of Composers, Artists and Performers. Spinner.com makes its money by several means: displaying banner ads on the site; embedding audio commercials within the programming -- 90 seconds each hour -- and by taking a cut of transactions when visitors buy music at the site. The company also displays banner ads on the audio player, but because listeners can minimize the image of the player, they might not see those commercials, the company acknowledges. Still, Josh M. Felser, president of Spinner.com, said that the site's traffic was growing 25 percent a month and that Spinner.com had 1.3 million unique listeners last month. People who register to use the site's audio player must divulge their sex, age and some musical interests, allowing the company to give highly targeted information to advertisers. "We do what radio does, only better," Mr. Felser said. "It's going to take time for ad buyers to wake up to our capabilities." That sentiment and the Spinner.com business model are copied by several competitors, including Rolling Stone Radio, a partnership between the on-line music hub Tunes.com and Real Networks. Another competitor, Imagine Radio, which was acquired in February by the MTV Networks unit of Viacom, creates individually customized radio stations. Visitors to the site can choose the genre of music they want to hear and indicate which artists they would like to hear more or less often. These Internet companies are vying for consumer attention with some 1,600 traditional radio stations that have made their programming available over the Internet. Greg Verdino, vice president of Arbitron New Media, which studies radio listening patterns, said more than 3,500 radio stations were still not on line. But he said they had better start thinking about it, citing studies showing that people who listen to radio on the Net listen to less radio on traditional stations. "It's potentially" a threat, he said. "It's also potentially an opportunity." A study released in April by Arbitron New Media found the portion of Internet users who had listened to radio on line more than doubled in the previous six months to 13 percent from 6 percent. "It's going to be huge," said Rotem Perelmuter, former chief executive of Imagine Radio and now vice president for strategy at MTV, referring to on-line-only radio content. "The operating profits from radio are $6 billion," he said. "We're going to take a big chunk of that." Not everyone is so optimistic, at least in the short term. Some industry analysts say that despite the recent growth, most radio listeners will not regularly turn to their PC's for listening. Skeptics point out that the audiences even for the most popular on-line radio hubs remain in the low tens of thousands of visitors daily. "A radio advertising executive is going to look at that traffic and go, 'Come on, I can't sell advertising on that,' " said Mark Hardie, a senior analyst with Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. Mr. Hardie thinks on-line radio will remain a niche market. Patrick H. Keane, an analyst for Jupiter Communications, a market research firm in newyork, is less pessimistic. Mr. Keane said a new category of at-work radio listener was emerging. He said he thought there was a growing market for on-line audio programmers to reach into offices where employees may listen while they work. "You're definitely looking at a niche audience, but I'm firmly convinced it's going to grow," Mr. Keane said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The on-screen control panel for Spinner.com's Spinner Plus software.

title: What This Has Been All About.com
body: It was a few days before Miningco.com was scheduled to go public in March. Scott Kurnit, the company's founder and chief executive, called its lawyer to ask whether there was any law that prevented a company, on the day it goes public, from changing its name. Not exactly, the lawyer said -- but if he was going to do that, Mr. Kurnit should alert Bear, Stearns, the investment bank managing the offering. "Bear, Stearns would freak and make me pull the offering," Mr. Kurnit said recently, explaining why he did not go ahead. Indeed, it was only yesterday that Mr. Kurnit told his bankers that as of this morning Miningco.com was to become About.com. Mr. Kurnit says the new name better expresses the nature of the service, a collection of 600 sites on various topics, each run by a specialist. His newyork company hopes to compete with big sites like Yahoo by being more selective and having more of its own content. It may come as no surprise, however, to the bankers and others that something has been up at Miningco.com. The company is behind an elaborate $15 million teaser promotional campaign over the last two weeks that spread the question "Hello, is anybody out there?" in advertisements, in anonymous email messages, and through such tactics as holding up signs with the slogan behind the set of the "Today" show. The tease seems to have attracted some attention. "Hello, is anybody wondering about those mystery ads?" wrote The Wall Street Journal in a short item in its advertising column that quoted advertising industry executives speculating that Miningco.com was behind the campaign. The whole affair shows how the fast-moving Internet and the even faster-moving market for Internet stocks have warped the traditions that companies have followed for generations. Not too long ago, for example, it would have been considered bad form, at the least, to change the name and key elements of a company's strategy six weeks after raising $75 million from investors. Not everyone is so sure. Analysts were split when told of the name change late Friday by a reporter. "This is all about brand," said Paul W. Noglows, an analyst at Hambrecht & Quist, noting that at least some of the success of Yahoo, for example, has been its lively name. "But at the end of the day, Miningco is taking a risk, given the success it has achieved to date. It remains to be seen whether About.com will be worth the effort." Andrea Williams, an analyst with Volpe Brown Whelan, one of the underwriters of Miningco.com, was more positive. "The old name was fine," she said. "In fact, I liked it more than some people. But About is simple and easier to remember." A bigger question, of course, is whether the name change, and all the capital that the company is using to promote it, can blast Miningco.com from the middle of the pack. Media Metrix, the Web audience- measurement company, said Miningco.com was the 24th-most-visited site in March, just ahead of the Weather Channel, owned by Landmark Communications, with 5.8 million users. So far the company's sale of advertising -- its principal hope for making money -- has been modest, with $3.7 million in sales for 1998. Mr. Kurnit says another use for the money from the offering is to hire more sales representatives. Beyond cosmetics, Mr. Kurnit says the name change is the centerpiece of a strategy that will pit About.com more directly against the big portal sites like Yahoo, Lycos and America Online's service. The company lost that battle once already. At first, the company was positioned as a human alternative to what were then known as search engines that simply found Web pages with words that matched whatever a user typed in. Its approach was to hire part-timers it called guides to create a handmade lists of the best sites in their specialties. The name, at first the Mining Company, evoked images of the guides panning for gold amid the dross of the net. Miningco.com attracted a certain following, but it hardly kept pace with the portal sites, which have added a wide range of services, from email to stock quotes. Mr. Kurnit said the company would use some of the capital it raised to add features to match the offerings of the portals. As for revenue, the site's new design gives a large portion of each screen over to links to various shopping sites, which all pay the company a commission on sales. Moreover, the new name helps highlight some of the differentiating features that the service has developed over the last few years in addition to its Web directory. The guides write articles on their subject areas, now amounting to the largest collection of original content of any Web site, Mr. Kurnit says. And they run chat rooms and message boards on related topics. Mr. Kurnit says that each guide's site -- now called About Fly Fishing, About Anesthesiology, and so on -- is positioned as a center of information on its topic. So why didn't he change the name before he went public? That is what Audionet did, becoming Broadcast.com on the eve of its public offering. And Dejanews, a site that searches Internet news groups, has just redubbed itself Deja.com in an effort to broaden its scope in preparation for a stock offering. Mr. Kurnit said he did not think he could afford the advertising campaign that was necessary to change names until it became clear the stock market was so hot that Miningco.com could raise twice as much money as it had originally proposed. But if the company delayed its offering to alert investors to the name change, the froth on the market could subside and Miningco.com could lose its windfall. Even now, he is not sure of the reaction. "I think the stock will go up by $20 or down by $20 -- I'm not sure which," he said. "But we're not going to be a $20 billion company digging up the gems of the Web." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Miningco.com is behind the elaborate publicity campaign asking "Hello, is anybody out there?" to promote its name change. (James Estrin/The newyork Times)(pg. C1); The Internet company formerly known as Miningco.com projecting its teaser message on Broadway side of the Flatiron Building in Manhattan. (Frances Roberts for The newyork Times)(pg. C2)

title: New Breeds of Investors, All Beguiled by the Web
body: THERE is a myth that most of the people trading on the Internet are like Spyridon Ganas. Since opening an account with E*Trade on his 18th birthday in January, Mr. Ganas has taken to Web trading with a vengeance, betting not just on volatile technology stocks, but on the even more volatile options on technology stocks. A long-term investment is one he holds for more than a day or two. "I'm part of the Internet generation," said Mr. Ganas, a high school senior in Shrewsbury, Mass., "and it was more natural for me to use the Internet for investing." Looking at the madcap market these days, especially the gyrations in shares of technology and Internet companies, it is natural to wonder whether the dominant investor is in fact some sort of recent Nintendo graduate who has wired his joystick right into his brokerage account. But the phenomenon is far broader than the day traders who have made on-line investing almost a full-time pursuit. The number of households with people trading on the Internet has nearly tripled, to 6.3 million in the last 16 months, according to NFO Worldwide, a research firm based in Greenwich, Conn., that regularly surveys on-line investors and other Internet users. An even more impressive number of households -- 20 million -- tap into the Internet for investment news, quotes and ideas, NFO surveys have found. To understand more about who is using the Internet for investing and how it is changing what they do with their money, Money & Business asked NFO to assemble focus groups of active on-line traders, occasional on-line traders and the larger group of investors who glean information from the Web but do not trade on line. Fittingly, the discussions occurred not in person but in a special chat room on the Internet, where the 35 participants could read and respond to questions posed by a reporter as well as the answers they typed in. While these people represented a wide range of ages, incomes, investment philosophies and behaviors, a common thread emerged: The Internet has bolstered their confidence about investing and emboldened them to take greater risks. "I feel a little more daring, now that I'm a better-educated investor," wrote Dorothy Brown, 52, of Morgantown, W. Va. She had mainly favored bond investments, but she shifted funds into stocks after trying trading at Charles Schwab's Web site. In the focus groups as well as in follow-up interviews, the participants said they felt increasingly secure about their investment decisions as they used the Internet to monitor their portfolios, follow news about their holdings and track the comments of other investors. Those who trade on line said they felt empowered by the minute-to-minute control that Internet investing allows -- and liberated from the intermediaries who have guided them in the past, like stockbrokers and mutual fund companies. "With on-line trading, the easy access to the market is driving people to trade more, driving their confidence level up, raising their risk tolerance," said Lee Smith, a vice president in NFO's Internet research division. "They are holding stocks for a shorter period of time and holding stocks more than mutual funds." If the trends hold, they will begin to alter the composition of America's retirement nest egg and the landscape of financing available to American businesses. They already have Wall Street in a tizzy, as traditional brokerage firms and stock markets confront upstarts and a few established players that have been quicker to latch onto new trading technologies. Even longtime professional traders now face a powerful new market mover. "In the market's run from 3,000 to 8,000, a lot of the upward movement had to do with the fact that people were invested in mutual funds and were not apt to sell very quickly," said Charles Geisst, a finance professor at Manhattan College in the Bronx. "It's no coincidence that in the last year and a half, as Internet trading has become more common, the market has become more volatile." Only after a number of years -- including a couple of serious bear markets -- will it be clear whether the newfound confidence and self-reliance of so many on-line investors is justified. What is already clear is that a big and growing group of Americans are engaged in a high-stakes experiment to see whether they have been prudent in betting their future on stocks they trade themselves.  Just Made to Trade Perhaps the Internet's most significant impact on investing -- evident in the fast growth of on-line trading volume and the increasing volatility in the markets -- is how it emboldens many investors to trade stocks more often. NFO's surveys have found that among investors who have been trading on line for less than a year, 16 percent are what it calls heavy traders, those who say they have conducted more than 10 trades in the last six months. But of Web investors who have had on-line accounts for more than a year, 30 percent are heavy traders. That's not only because active traders were first to jump on line. An NFO survey found that only 13 percent of investors who started trading in 1997 were heavy traders back then. Many of the focus group participants said that their experiences matched the surveys' findings about the seductions of the Web. "I trade more often, because it is easier and can be done 24 hours a day," wrote James Moyer, 45, of Elma, N.Y. "If a stock is moving -- up or down -- I am aware of it on a daily basis, and can sooner decide it is time to buy or sell. I don't have to fumble through a newspaper or an end-of-month report from my account." Many said they were trading more often because they were using the Internet -- often at their jobs -- to watch prices throughout the day. That offers the temptation to pounce the moment they see reasons to hop in or out of a stock, though even some who do so are ambivalent about the merits of such trading. "I do trade more than when a trade cost more than $8," said Treg Owings, 41, of Madras, Ore., who said he checked his portfolio often during the day. "You might trade something because it looks like it is dropping, and the next minute it is up $5. The cost of trading with a broker might discourage in-and-out trading and might save some people money in the long run."  Goodbye, Middle Guy Many people are relying less and less on traditional sources of guidance, like brokers and mutual funds, as they actively trade stocks in their Internet accounts. "I do not miss the frustration of the broker trying to sell you something," said Bev Waldrip, a retired customer service representative for BellSouth who lives in Blairsville, Ga. "They do not understand the word 'no.' " Indeed, NFO, whose research clients are mainly financial services concerns, is finding that Web trading is becoming much more of a threat to the big, full-service brokerage firms like Merrill Lynch and Paine Webber, which often charge commissions 10 times higher than those at the on-line firms but provide access to a broker for advice. "It used to be that the bulk of on-line investors came from the discount brokers, because they are more comfortable making independent decisions," Mr. Smith of NFO said. "Now, transfers from full service are starting to grow as people realize that all the information they see on line makes them less dependent on their brokers." Similarly, the infatuation with on-line stock trading threatens to halt the two-decade-long shift of investment assets out of individual securities and into mutual funds. "I would rather manage my own 'fund,' " said Thomas Holycross, 68, of White Lake, Mich., who opened an account 10 years ago with what is now DLJ Direct, the discount unit of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. Charley Kashou of Mequon, Wis., says he is putting less into mutual funds now. "I've been doing too well in stocks to put it in funds," he said.  The Research Tool One of the most striking aspects of the focus groups was how important the Internet has become even to investors who have never placed a trade on line. "The Internet is speeeeeeeeeeeeeed," wrote Leo Lomasney, 62, a longtime investor from Rochester, N.H., who said he was too lazy to learn how to trade on line. "The Internet has allowed us poor people access to the information that the brokers used to own," he added, explaining that he uses several Internet sites to get investment ideas. Jerry White, 52, a semiretired engineering executive in Ferndale, Calif., checks the value of his portfolio on line every day, reads investing news on the Web and occasionally ventures onto message boards to see what others are saying. He is trading more often, he said, because the Internet gives him more ideas. Still, he feels more comfortable trading through the Morgan Stanley Dean Witter broker who has an office near his home and with whom he can compare notes. "I'm making faster choices," Mr. White said. "I'm still not sure they are better choices."  Navigating the Chats The many message boards and chat rooms where users share ideas about investments with one another are, of course, the most controversial sources of investing information on the Web. The Securities and Exchange Commission has highlighted these sites as fertile breeding grounds for fraud. And a substantial number of Web investors simply have no use for stock tips from strangers. "I don't use the message boards or chat rooms -- they are too large and time-consuming for my needs," said Mr. Moyer of Elma, N.Y. "I know what I'm looking for and go to more reliable sources than what an anonymous Net user has to say." Mr. Ganis, the youngest participant in any of the focus groups, takes an even more cynical view. "Message boards can't be trusted," he said, "but they're useful if you want to hype a stock you just bought." By contrast, Ms. Waldrip, the former BellSouth employee, who is 57, said she had had good luck with on-line investment tips. Someone she met in a chat room on America Online suggested buying the stock of Home Depot, an investment with which she has been happy. While several people in the focus groups reported bad experiences with tips on line, many said the message boards still had allure. "I lost a lot when I was new to them; I believed people," said Mr. Kashou, the Wisconsin investor. Yet even though the boards are populated by "a lot of hypesters," he added, he continues to read them, because "occasionally I find a good idea." Besides, many investors said, traditional sources of investing information just seem anachronistic in the Internet era. "If I read the paper, the opportunities to strike are already gone," said Thomas Fitzgerald, 33, of King of Prussia, Pa. "It is always old news after you have been on the Net."  Pluses and Minuses As people become comfortable using the Internet for investing information, the principal lure to leap into trading on line is the very low commissions of the on-line brokers. But the focus group participants said that as they experimented with on-line trading, what they liked best was the sense of control it gave them. "Price is a big factor, but that alone wouldn't do it," said Mary Hill, 49, of Salinas, Calif. "On-line trading is easy, always available, and I don't have to listen to someone try to tell me what they think," she said. Most of the focus group participants were satisfied with their on-line trading experiences, though a few complained of being stymied by the occasional computer glitches that have kept big on-line brokers like Charles Schwab and E*Trade from processing orders. "I've had trouble getting on a couple times," said Wendall Sherk, 34, of Florissant, Mo. "But brokers don't answer their phones at bad times, too, so that's no different." Jennifer Crissey, 32, of Milford, Pa., was not so sanguine. "I have had problems with orders not going through or the Web site being down with Schwab," she said. "This has prompted me to switch many of my accounts" to another on-line broker. NFO's surveys have found that about 22 percent of on-line investors have switched their Internet broker at least once. But most have moved for lower prices or better investing features, with only 14 percent of the switchers citing complaints about service or computer problems. Still, highly publicized computer glitches at most of the major on-line brokers have discouraged some people from trying on-line trading. Mike Carlson, 48, of Aurora, Colo., said that his family had been planning to move some mutual funds to an on-line brokerage account, but that the recent problems at on-line trading sites "caused us to back off."  Doing Well, for Now Presumably, the best measure of the value of any investing tool is how well a portfolio performs. Many focus group participants said they thought that going on line had made them more successful investors, though some had lingering doubts. Robert Grisinger, 47, of Junction City, Kan., said his return has been higher, "but that could be because it seems the market is booming and hasn't taken a good crash lately." Another reason that on-line investors cite for their having done well is their eager buying of the stock of Internet companies -- the hottest, if the most volatile, sector of the market recently. "I am taking advantage of the Internet explosion," said Mr. Fitzgerald of King of Prussia. "It's a wild ride, but returns are big if you play it right." Professional traders have long observed that a large part of the activity in Internet stocks comes from small orders entered through on-line brokers. And a Gallup survey for Paine Webber earlier this year showed that 44 percent of on-line traders have invested in Internet stocks, compared with 15 percent of investors over all. Still, a lot of participants said the Internet stock ride was just too wild for their tastes. "I braved into Internet stocks about a year ago, bought Lycos and sold it four days later at a $500 profit," recalled Mr. Moyer, the New Yorker. "The reward was great, but the trauma was awful. I haven't bought an Internet stock since." Even among more active traders, there is a widespread feeling that the wave of Internet investing will soon crest. "I think on-line trading has spurred part of the new high record prices and is spurring them on," Mr. Moyer said. "If the market takes a downturn, it may be a really big one, as people won't ride out the storm." Indeed, like investors through the ages, the Internet traders are more concerned about how other investors will behave than about their own investing. "It is like driving," said Mr. Owings, the Oregon investor, who is proud of his purchase of technology stocks like Dell Computer and Ebay. "You have to worry about the other guy." Another focus group member, Dean Coston, 75, who was deputy under secretary of Health, Education and Welfare in the 1960's and is now retired, pointed the finger at the generation of beginning investors. "The thing that concerns me is all the younger investors who have never experienced anything but a rising market," said Mr. Coston, of Falls Church, Va. "They don't know that what goes up will come down. It will be terrible for them." But to Spyridon Ganas, the high school senior who trades options in technology stocks on line, the beauty of the Internet is that it lets him take advantage of what he considers the folly of his elders. "The baby boomers think the stocks are worth it," he said. "So I might as well ride the wave."  The Many Faces of Internet Investing Who is using the Web to trade stocks or research investments? The stereotype -- a manic young daytrader -- is only a piece of the picture.  Bev Waldrip, 59 PERSONAL -- Retired customer service officer for BellSouth. She lives in Blairsville, Ga. INVESTING EXPERIENCE -- After they retired, her husband started buying and selling horses, while she took an equal amount of money to invest in stocks. At first, she used a full-service broker nearby. When her son bought her a computer, she dived into the Internet and opened an account with an online broker. TRADING STYLE -- "I like placing the order and checking late at night to see if one went through," she said. "I can go outside and work in the yard and make money with my stock act at the same time." Another attraction: "If I made a little error, no one would know it." LESSON LEARNED -- "Last year, we didn't make much. We were trading too much. My son was helping me, and if we didn't make money on a stock in a day or two we'd sell it and buy something else." This year, she is trading a little less and her portfolio is doing better.  Terry Sneed, 43 PERSONAL -- Theatrical director, based in Chattanooga, Tenn. INVESTING EXPERIENCE -- Invests through a stock broker and companies' dividend reinvestment plans. Has never traded online, but uses the Internet to monitor his portfolio and get investing ideas. TRADING STYLE -- Keeps his broker so he can get a second opinion on investments, but he is willing to make his own stock picks. "The Internet helped me decide to buy Yahoo on the first day of its IPO. My broker tried to talk me out of it, but I had used it and recognized it as a dynamic company. Now my broker thinks I'm a guru." LESSON LEARNED -- "I had signed up for someone who sent stock tips by e-mail. I followed them and they seemed good, so I bought a company that sounded like it was on the cutting edge. I lost 88 percent."  Spyridon Ganas, 18 PERSONAL -- High school student in Shrewsbury, Mass. He plans to study business at Babson College in the fall. INVESTING EXPERIENCE -- Got interested in the markets watching the "Nightly Business Report" as he worked in the kitchen of his family's pizzeria. title:
Q & A;
The Privacy Keys: How They Guard Secrets
body: Q. How does the PGP encryption software work?  A. Pretty Good Privacy, or PGP, is a freeware program that runs on most platforms and lets you encrypt, or secretly encode, computer files. It is one of the most popular methods for encrypting messages moving across the Internet to deter snoopers. Readers need the proper key, or decryption tool, to decipher the text. PGP works with what is called public key cryptography. Each PGP user has a public key, which is made available without any attempt at hiding it. Someone who wants to send you an encrypted message uses your public key to put the message into code, and that puts the message into a form that can be deciphered only by someone with a second key -- your private key, which you do not share with anyone. To send a reply, you use the recipient's public key to put the message into code, and the recipient's private key is used to decode it. A good beginner's guide to the program (along with links to download sites for PGP) is at www.arc.unm.edu/drosoff/pgp/pgp.html. PGP, which was invented by Philip R. Zimmermann, proved to be so effective an encryption method that the Federal Government filed a lawsuit (which it later dropped) against the program's creator because the freely available technology could be used to code messages sent by enemies of the unitedstates.  Q. What exactly does it mean when something is called digital? I hear the term constantly, but I'm not sure what it means.  A. Along with a wealth of new technology that is becoming commonplace in the home, the computer revolution has also introduced new terms into common usage. Just as the ubiquitous prefix cyber (from the Greek word kybernan, meaning to steer or govern) has become increasingly attached to various aspects of on-line life -- cybershopping, cyberchatting and so on -- the term digital has also been popping up more. Computers are considered digital systems because at the simplest level, they can distinguish between only two values: 1 or 0, on or off. All computer data must be encoded in digital form as a string of 1's and 0's. Casually speaking, the word digital has also generally come to identify things related to computers. When you hear cameras or video cameras being called digital, it means that the data produced by these devices are in a digital format. The opposite of digital is analog. In an analog system, you aren't limited to recording your data as either a 1 or a 0. All values can be expressed in a continuous way, and all points between 1 and 0. A popular analogy to illustrate the point is based on clocks. On a digital clock, each value, like 11:21, is very specifically expressed. But on an old-fashioned analog clock, with big and little hands, the hands move continuously around the clock face, covering all points in between. J. D. title: 2 Internet Trading Networks in New Alliances
body: The landscape of the stock-trading business continued to shift yesterday, with both Instinet, the dominant private trading system, and its scrappy rival, Island ECN Inc., announcing potentially important alliances with other players. Instinet, which is a unit of Reuters Group P.L.C., is paying $20 million for an 11.4 percent stake in W. R. Hambrecht & Company, the brainchild of the Silicon Valley financier William R. Hambrecht. Hambrecht operates the OpenIP0 system, an on-line auction-based system for underwriting initial public stock offerings. Trading in initial public offerings has become a sore topic among on-line investors. Almost weekly, small investors who cannot have their orders filled watch in frustration as an initial offering, initially priced in the teens for the few institutions able to buy, soars. Douglas M. Atkin, Instinet's chief executive, said the current situation hurt both the companies and the individual investors. If a stock is priced at $19 and the first trade is at $30, "that is money that's coming out of the company's coffers and being given to a few big institutions," he said. In his view, Hambrecht's auction system is fairer to individual investors and allows the company to keep more of the money investors are willing to pay for its shares. Mr. Atkin said Instinet would soon develop links to allow its institutional members to submit their orders to Hambrecht's auctions directly over Instinet. In addition, the two companies are negotiating a joint venture that would allow Instinet to export the initial-public-offering auction service to Europe and Asia. For Island, the news yesterday was that Waterhouse Investor Services Inc., a subsidiary of Toronto-Dominion Bank and a substantial discount brokerage firm here and in Canada, would buy a 12.5 percent stake in Island for $25 million. An agreement in principle has been reached, and final papers should be signed in the next two months, the companies said. Executives at Island, a subsidiary of the Datek Online Holdings Corporation, said the fresh capital would help Island build the infrastructure it would need if it were granted stock-exchange status by the Securities and Exchange Commission. At present, Island runs a distant second to Instinet in the proliferating field of electronic communication networks, or E.C.N.'s, the computerized systems that match buy and sell orders that brokers submit for their customers.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: America Online Challenges Microsoft's WebTV
body: Only weeks after completing the purchase of the Netscape Communications Corporation -- the Microsoft Corporation's archrival in Web browsing software -- America Online Inc. announced yesterday that it would take on Microsoft in delivering the Internet over television sets. The new product, to be known as AOL TV, will compete directly with Microsoft's WebTV, which already has about 800,000 users. AOL TV will be built around four partnerships announced yesterday, including a deal with the Hughes Electronics Corporation, a General Motors subsidiary, to deliver high-speed access to America Online and the Internet via home satellite dishes. The deals reinforce a growing rivalry between America Online and Microsoft, which announced last week that it had invested $5 billion in the AT&T Corporation to prepare for the convergence of telecommunications and computing. That convergence, which will among other things bring high-speed Internet access into homes over television cable systems, poses a huge threat to America Online and other Internet service providers. America Online, which was built around dial-up modem technology, stands to lose many of its 17 million subscribers if they find speed more alluring than the comfort of America Online's content, design and features. In addition to deals America Online announced earlier for local phone companies to provide high-speed access to its members, two partnerships announced yesterday -- with Hughes Network Systems and DirecTV, both subsidiaries of Hughes Electronics -- pave the way for America Online to be packaged with DirecTV, the most widely used home-based satellite television system, with seven million users. America Online also announced partnerships with Royal Philips Electronics N.V. to create a set-top box for sending and delivering material from the World Wide Web over telephone lines and other cables. The box will be powered by the National Semiconductor Corporation's GX processor, a computer on a single chip. That represents a major break for National, which announced last week that it was abandoning its financially disastrous Cyrix line of processors, which compete with the Intel Corporation's Pentium line. In yet another snub of Microsoft, America Online announced it was working with Network Computer Inc., a subsidiary of the Oracle Corporation, to develop an operating system for AOL TV. Network Computer already builds set-top box operating systems in Europe and Asia to compete against WebTV. Its alignment with America Online will "add momentum to a competitor to Microsoft," Van L. Baker, the director of consumer market research for Dataquest, a market research firm based in San Jose, Calif., said. "This clearly reinforces the rivalry between AOL and Microsoft." Yesterday's announcement helped lift the entire technology sector, and all participants in the deal enjoyed gains. America Online jumped $13.125, to close at $141.4375, a gain of more than 10 percent. Hughes Electronics rose $2 to close at $60.625, while National Semiconductor closed at $20.1875, up 56.25 cents. Philips Electronics gained $1.1875 to close at $90.625. Microsoft rose 18.75 cents, to $79.875. Mr. Baker said the success of AOL TV would depend on what type of content the company planned to deliver over television sets. He said WebTV had learned that its customers were not very enthusiastic about surfing the Web. As a result, the company is now emphasizing content that enhances the television experience, such as highlighting Web pages associated with a given television program. Along those lines, Barry M. Schuler, the president of America Online's interactive services group, said his company did not plan to simply stream the service's existing content onto television, but to create "an entirely different service" that would emphasize combining television and the Internet. For example, users could chat with other viewers of the same program or could visit Web sites associated with a program or could shop for, say, a compact disk while watching MTV. He said the company planned to have a service available sometime next year but had not yet made a decision on pricing. Microsoft purchased WebTV in August 1997 for $425 million. It offers two pricing options, a standard service for $24.95 a month and a slimmed-down version for $19.95. Mr. Schuler said America Online planned to make more announcements in the coming weeks regarding other providers of set-top boxes and about partners who would provide technologies to deliver America Online over hand-held devices, pagers and cellular telephones. Mr. Schuler said AOL TV would be marketed primarily to the company's existing subscribers. He said members used the service 55 minutes a day on average and were likely to be interested in moving the experience to the television. As to whether America Online and Microsoft will end up competing or cooperating in the set-top box space, Mr. Schuler said he was "anxiously awaiting" word about whether Microsoft would be interested in providing AOL TV over WebTV or through the five million set-top boxes it will be producing for AT&T. William B. Keating, general manager of the platform division for WebTV, said: "I don't have a position on that. It's a complicated question. I'm sure if we entered into discussions, we'd be happy to talk with them."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Toys 'R' Us, Fidelity Choose Agencies
body: Two big advertisers -- Toys "R" Us and Fidelity Investments -- made decisions yesterday involving accounts, each with billings estimated at $50 million. Toys "R" Us, the struggling toy retailer, named the Leo Burnett Company in Chicago and the Burnett media agency, Starcom Media Services, to handle the creative and media portions of its account. "We want to gain back the dominance this company has enjoyed with kids and their families," said Warren Kornblum, who recently became chief marketing officer at Toys "R" Us in Paramus, N.J. "We felt Burnett understood where we want to go with the brand." The creative duties had been handled by the Kaplan Thaler Group in newyork and the media duties by Quantum Media International in newyork, owned by Bohbot Entertainment and Media Inc. Both initially took part in separate creative and media reviews that began in February, but were eliminated when the reviews were narrowed in March. The finalists for the creative duties were Burnett, Deutsch Inc. in newyork and the Southfield, Mich., office of Doner. The finalists for the media duties were Starcom, the Media Edge unit of Young & Rubicam Inc. in newyork and Western Initiative Media in Los Angeles, a unit of the Interpublic Group of Companies. Fidelity, part of the FMR Corporation, expanded its agency roster by adding Gotham Inc. in newyork, a unit of Interpublic, to handle campaigns for its retail brokerage operations, including on-line trading. Some retail brokerage ads had been created by an in-house team and some by an Interpublic sibling of Gotham's, Hill, Holliday, Connors, Cosmopulos in Boston, which continues to handle corporate advertising, retirement and retail mutual fund campaigns for Fidelity. Most of Gotham's duties are new, reflecting efforts by Fidelity to be more aggressive about Internet investors. Debra McConnell, a spokeswoman for Fidelity in Boston, said the decision came after a review that had been narrowed to Gotham; Hill, Holliday, and two other finalists: Grey Advertising in newyork and Martin/Williams Advertising in Minneapolis, a unit of Omnicom Group. The decision returns Gotham to the brokerage category two months after losing the account of the E*Trade Group Inc. in Palo Alto, Calif., an Internet brokerage firm, to Goodby, Silverstein & Partners in San Francisco, also a unit of Omnicom.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Presses Rival on Details of aDeal
body: A lawyer for Microsoft tried to make the case today that America Online planned to use "all of its marketing muscle" to promote its newly acquired product, the Netscape Navigator Web browser. But an America Online executive disputed that, saying the company thought "the browser business is dead." The back and forth came this morning as Microsoft took the deposition of Barry Schuler, the president for interactive services at America Online, in preparation for the resumption of the antitrust trial late this month. Microsoft plans to make the case that America Online's purchase of Netscape Communications for $10 million this year seriously undermines the Government's argument that Microsoft is a monopolist with no serious competition. If America Online stepped up Netscape's competition with Microsoft's browser, that could seem to support this assertion. Quoting company documents obtained by subpoena, the Microsoft lawyer, Steven Holley, noted that one America Online executive proposed in December to increase the marketing of Netscape's browser -- perhaps, Mr. Holley said, even using direct mail to send millions of copies of the software, as America Online has done with its own software. Mr. Schuler said the executive's suggestion was just an opinion, not company policy, adding that America Online was "not actually considering" direct-mail marketing. In some cases it was hard to know which of Mr. Holley's assertions came from America Online documents that Microsoft had obtained and which might have been his own suggestions because America Online tried to insist that every document be marked as confidential -- even newspaper clippings and news releases. Mr. Holley managed to persuade the America Online lawyer to take the confidential markings off the newspaper clippings. Mr. Schuler insisted that America Online had little interest in Netscape's browser. The company was much more interested in Netscape's Internet portal business, he said. The browser business was decimated, he said, by Microsoft's decision to bundle a competing browser with the Windows operating system. Mr. Holley spent most of the morning questioning Mr. Schuler about the timing of America Online's decisions in the Netscape deal. He pressed Mr. Schuler to acknowledge that an America Online lawyer had informed David Boies, the lead Justice Department lawyer, about the company's proposed acquisition of Netscape in early October, before the trial began, but kept it secret from the Government and the judge. Mark Murray, a Microsoft spokesman, said, "If that was the case, it would cast the testimony of Netscape and AOL witnesses in a very different light." Microsoft plans to call David Colburn, a senior America Online executive, as a hostile witness to question him about earlier testimony and how it related to the acquisition plans. But Mr. Schuler said George Vradenburg, a senior company lawyer, had simply told Mr. Boies on Oct. 3 that America Online and Netscape were in "a very preliminary conversation of a sensitive nature about a potential commercial relationship." Mr. Vradenburg and Mr. Boies are former law partners, and Mr. Boies was preparing to take a deposition from Mr. Colburn that day. America Online said Mr. Vradenburg wanted to make sure Mr. Boies did not stumble into that confidential area. This Oct. 3 discussion is central to Microsoft's assertion that America Online, Netscape and the Government plotted, in essence, to keep the proposed deal from Microsoft and the judge until the other companies' witnesses had testified. A senior Justice Department official said Mr. Boies and Government lawyers had taken Mr. Vradenburg's imprecise remark on Oct. 3 to mean that America Online was considering using Netscape in its on-line service, adding, "for the life of me I don't quite understand the relevance." But Mr. Murray added, "These issues will be a significant part of our rebuttal case." A Government lawyer, Philip R. Malone, asked Mr. Schuler if America Online and Netscape had "delayed or postponed" their acquisition agreement "because of any concern about the impact it might have on the trial." "No, we did not," Mr. Schuler said. http://www.nytimes.com
