title: Levitt Strongly Critical of Methods of On-Line Brokers
body: Maybe some tow-truck drivers do own islands that they bought with profits from trading stocks on line. But Arthur Levitt, the chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, said today that he thought brokerage industry advertisements focusing on the get-rich aspect of on-line investing were doing more harm than good for both Wall Street and the public. In a stinging rebuke to the companies that have aggressively promoted such "grandiose and unrealistic expectations," Mr. Levitt said that even ads intending to offer a tongue-in-cheek look at the potential rewards of on-line investing trivialized what to most Americans is an important, and often confusing, responsibility. Mr. Levitt also admonished individual investors to better educate themselves about on-line trading and whether it was appropriate for them. But to a greater extent than before, he focused the spotlight on whether brokerage firms were being honest in portraying the potential risks and rewards of on-line trading. Mr. Levitt, who made his remarks in a speech at the National Press Club, also called on brokerage firms to strengthen their disclosure of the risks of trading stocks over the Internet. And he disclosed that the commission, which plans to double the number of agents policing the Internet for investment fraud, was preparing a new round of enforcement actions against firms that had misused the Internet. The S.E.C. and the National Association of Securities Dealers, which governs securities firms, are about two-thirds of the way through a sweep of on-line brokerage and day-trading firms to assess their compliance with regulations. So far, the results of those examinations give Mr. Levitt cause to worry. "Based on our initial findings, I sent a letter this morning to all of the on-line brokerage firms asking them to improve the quality of their disclosure to investors," he said. Over all, Mr. Levitt said, he does not think new regulations are necessary to oversee on-line investment. "Yet there may come a time when the S.E.C. sees a need for new approaches to better meet the imperatives of the Internet," he added. Mr. Levitt also made clear that he was bothered by commercials that imply that teen-agers who trade on line can afford their own helicopters. "I don't accept the notion that tongue-in-cheek is all there is to it," Mr. Levitt said. Without mentioning the firm, Mr. Levitt cited a well-known ad for Morgan Stanley Dean Witter's Discover on-line brokerage unit, which portrays a tow truck driver who bought an island with his trading profits as one that "trivializes a process that is so crucial and so important." Mr. Levitt acknowledged that the S.E.C. does not directly regulate brokerage advertising, which is instead the purview of the regulatory unit of the N.A.S.D. "But nobody is going to stop me from giving my own feelings to you about advertising that may be cute but is ultimately demeaning," he said. Mr. Levitt announced that he had asked that the N.A.S.D. conduct a round-table discussion with brokerage firms and advertising professionals to help improve fairness in advertising. Mary Schapiro, president of the N.A.S.D. regulatory unit, said today that she, too, was concerned about the tenor of recent on-line brokerage ads. "They have failed to be truly balanced in disclosing the risks as well as the benfits" of on-line trading, she said. One willing participant in the organization's round-table discussion, tentatively scheduled for mid-June, is Discover Brokerage Direct, the Morgan Stanley Dean Witter unit that ran the ads that drew Mr. Levitt's ire. Wesley McDade, a spokesman for the brokerage unit, said the firm "would welcome the opportunity to participate." Mr. Levitt also announced the formation of an advisory group to help the commission examine issues specific to on-line trading. And to better enforce the rules in a rapidly changing industry, the S.E.C. would double, to 250 lawyers, the number of people the comission has working to uncover investment fraud on the Internet. The commission has already asked for an $11 million increase in its budget for the 2000 fiscal year to expand its efforts to combat Internet fraud, he said. Today, the White House said it would ask Congress to approve an additional $5.5 million for that purpose. The S.E.C. is also working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation on a project called "Operation Investnet," to address fraud on the Internet. But it is the brokerage firms themselves that might have the greatest effect on investors but that are not doing what they should to educate their customers, Mr. Levitt said. While most on-line brokerage firms address the different types of orders for trades that investors can enter into the system, "fewer firms discuss how market volatility and the use of margin can affect on-line investors, and almost none talk about the risks or what to do in the event of system capacity and outage problems," Mr. Levitt said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: List of Final Witnesses Released in Microsoft Trial - Correction Appended
body: The Microsoft Corporation and the Government both released the names today of the final witnesses each intends to call when the antitrust trial resumes later this month. The list indicates that the Government hopes to shore up its case, while Microsoft's goal, at least in part, is to change the subject of discussion to one that might make the Government's case seem irrelevant. The most surprising announcement came from Microsoft. The company is summoning David Colburn -- a senior executive for America Online and an important Government witness earlier in the trial -- to testify as a hostile witness in the final, rebuttal stage of testimony. Mr. Colburn will be questioned about "the completeness and candor of prior testimony," Microsoft said, and as part of the company's effort to argue that America Online's purchase of the Netscape Communications Corporation undermines the Government's case. "Our rebuttal witnesses will show that the $10 billion merger of AOL and Netscape completely undercuts the Government's case" by showing that "competition and innovation are stronger than ever in the software industry," said William H. Neukom, Microsoft's senior vice president for law and corporate affairs. Microsoft will also call Gordon Eubanks, the former chairman of the Symantec Corporation, maker of the Norton Utilities programs for Windows, and Richard Schmalensee, an economist and dean of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Sloan School of Management. Mr. Schmalensee was Microsoft's economic witness earlier in the trial. The Justice Department is also recalling its chief economic witness, Franklin M. Fisher, another M.I.T. economist. It will also recall Edward Felten, the Princeton University computer scientist who served as a Government witness earlier in the trial, and Gary Norris, an International Business Machines Corporation executive who was for several years director of I.B.M.'s software strategy division. Government officials said they were confident of their case and hoped their rebuttal witnesses would shore up areas of weakness exposed during the earlier part of the trial. One witness, Mr. Felten, is being called in part to rebut any technical statements Microsoft might make that Government lawyers find questionable. He and his staff found several of the technical flaws in Microsoft's demonstration tapes played in court earlier. The overarching goal, Government officials said, is to keep the strong legal advantage they believe they have already gained. A senior I.B.M. executive, John Soyring, has already testified for the Government, and there is some overlap between the areas he discussed and the ones Justice Department lawyers intend to raise with Mr. Norris. But they also intend to question him about Microsoft's efforts to stop I.B.M. from offering software on its computers made by Microsoft's competitors, according to a filing with the court. With its witnesses, Microsoft wants to open up new areas of evidence. A filing with the court shows that the company wants to use Mr. Colburn to help make the case that Netscape, America Online and the Government plotted, in effect, to hide for two months the developing deal between Netscape and America Online because they were afraid news of it would hurt the Government's case. A Justice Department official called that "a desperate attempt to distract attention from Microsoft's illegal behavior. "Nothing about the transaction has any relevance to the case," the official added, "and nothing about it will break Microsft's stranglehold on the operating system market." Mr. Eubanks, now the head of Oblix, a business-directory software manufacturer, led Symantec during the years when the company sold utilities that Microsoft later incorporated into the Windows operating system. But Microsoft wants to show that Symantec then came up with new ideas, like antivirus software, to replace the lost business and continued to prosper. Microsoft describes Mr. Eubanks as a friend and competitor. In a filing with the court today, Microsoft said Mr. Eubanks would testify about "the rapid pace of change in the software business, and the inability of anyone to predict the directions in which computer and communication technology would evolve over the last 10 years," and "the expansion of the concept of an operating system through the addition of new features and functions." In a recent interview, Mr. Eubanks said, "Microsoft has done some bad things," but added that the company and its chairman, William H. Gates 3d, had been victims of the American tendency to tear down those who are too successful. Both Mr. Fisher and Mr. Schmalensee will have to repair damage they did to Government and Microsoft cases during earlier cross-examination. Mr. Fisher said he did not think Microsoft's behavior had harmed consumers, a statement he later tried to modify. And Mr. Schmalensee was shown to have offered opinions in previous years that were opposite the ones he was espousing in court, leading Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson to question his credibility. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Business Day on Tuesday about the lists of witnesses in the Microsoft antitrust trial referred incorrectly to comments by Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson about the earlier testimony of a witness, Richard Schmalensee of the Sloan School of Management at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The judge questioned an apparent contradiction in Mr. Schmalensee's testimony; he did not question his overall credibility. Correction-Date: May 7, 1999, Friday

title:
METRO NEWS BRIEFS: NEW JERSEY;
Lawmaker Proposes Bills Regulating the Internet
body: In an attempt to regulate the Internet in New Jersey, a legislator yesterday proposed bills that would require "junk" email messages to be labeled as advertising and require software to warn Internet users that their identities can be traced. Assemblywoman Barbara Buono, Democrat of Metuchen, said she had introduced the package of six bills after a report last June from the Federal Trade Commission found that the Internet was under-regulated. For example, she said, while 85 percent of Web sites collect data about users, only 14 percent tell users that personal information may be reused. Unlike a California state law with similar intent, the bills are intended to avoid violating interstate commerce protections by applying only to junk email, often called spam, originating in New Jersey, and to software sold within the state. If the law passes, violators would face $500 fines for a first offense and $1,000 fines for subsequent ones. David Rocah, staff attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey, said his group is most concerned about the bill that would require email advertisements to be labeled. "When the Government forces me to apply a label to my speech that I don't want to apply to it, that violates the Constitution," he said.   http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Agroup cites some progress in convincing companies to peddle their goods on the Internet.
body: TO address the nagging issue of how to make Internet advertising more effective and profitable, a group of advertisers and Web publishers formed an organization called FAST, or the Future of Advertising Stakeholders, last August. But during a trade show on Internet advertising being held here this week, FAST's chairman, Richard A. LeFurgy, joked that maybe the group should change its name. "How about 'not-so FAST,' " Mr. LeFurgy said yesterday. Meeting during the @d:tech conference on Internet advertising and marketing, FAST members said yesterday that while they had made progress in the last nine months, much work remained to convince companies to spend their advertising dollars on line. The mixed sentiment is reflected in two studies released to coincide with the conference. The good news for advocates of on-line advertising comes from the Internet Advertising Bureau, an on-line advertising association also led by Mr. LeFurgy. The bureau reported that Internet advertising revenues hit $1.92 billion in 1998, more than double the $907 million spent in 1997, surpassing the $1.58 billion spent on outdoor advertising in 1998. Mr. LeFurgy called that a significant benchmark. The study also found that the types of products and services advertised on line were becoming more diverse. During the fourth quarter, noncomputer retail advertising represented 29 percent of Internet advertising, compared with 20 percent for computer-related advertising. Mr. LeFurgy said that demonstrated that Internet advertising was no longer merely the realm of the technology set. Yet a study to be released this morning by the Association of National Advertisers has found evidence that mainstream advertisers continue to feel uncertain about the medium. The association's study, which mostly focused on the advertising patterns of the 500 largest industrial companies, concluded that the percentage of companies it surveyed that advertised on line had decreased to 61 percent during 1998 from 68 percent the year before. Those that do advertise on the Internet are spending less than they did a year ago, the study found -- $649,000 in 1998 versus $714,000 the year before. The figures were based on reports from 121 member companies, although a handful of the companies surveyed in 1998 differed from those that participated in 1997, thus making the year-to-year comparisons inexact, said Robin Webster, the association's senior vice president. Still, Ms. Webster said, the study clearly showed that major corporations remained skeptical of how to put a value on on-line advertising. "They're still not comfortable with it," she said. Specifically, 68 percent of companies surveyed said that a "key barrier" to advertising on line was that they did not yet know how to measure their return on investment -- in other words, whether the ad dollars they spend bring in new consumers or revenue. Advertisers want proof that the ads they pay for wind up on consumer monitors, not downloaded halfway, or never seen at all, Ms. Webster said. "In print you have a tear sheet, on TV you get a report that the commercial ran," she said. "This medium has not been able to do that yet." At the same time, she said the association's study found major corporations were increasingly comfortable with the Internet in general. She said that in 1998, not one company reported it had limited Internet advertising because senior management did not "appreciate the value of the Internet." In 1997, 33 percent of companies surveyed gave that response. Ms. Webster was quick to praise FAST, of which she is one of 750 members, for being the "best vehicle" for helping create standards for Internet advertising and measuring the effectiveness of on-line ads. The organization has recently published guidelines for Internet advertisers and publishers on three topics: how to protect consumer privacy, how to create standard sizes and placement for advertisements and how to measure how many people view an ad. The hope is that the guidelines will become de facto standards, much the way print and television have accepted standards. "We've made tremendous progress in the last eight months," Mr. LeFurgy said. "We've taken on issues of breadth and depth." Vivienne Bechtold, director of interactive marketing for Procter & Gamble, which helped form FAST and is one of the nation's largest advertisers, said the prognosis was improving for Internet advertising. She said P.& G. now advertised 30 brands on line -- including Crest, Tide and Cover Girl -- three times more than it did a year ago. She attributed some of the increased comfort to the work of FAST. "Considering it's a totally volunteer organization with no resources, it's made some really great progress," she said. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY: E-Commerce Report;
On-line security isn't expensive. But by ignoring it, many sites are risking customers and Government intervention.
body: TO placate those who worry about how secure it is to shop on line, companies typically proffer the idea that buying on the Internet is no more risky than giving a credit card to a waiter in a restaurant. Given recent reports of E-commerce security lapses, that analogy may be giving waiters a bad name. Analysts and executives agree that a vast majority of E-commerce sites are secure, but some say the trend may actually be heading in the opposite direction. Many companies so fear being overtaken by a competitor who got to the Web first -- of "getting Amazoned," in the industry vernacular -- that they rush past security issues in their zeal to establish a Web site. Some companies lack the technical knowledge to use security safeguards; others say they cannot afford security products and advice. And there are those who simply do not consider it a priority. "I wish I had a dollar for every one of my clients that said, 'I don't care if the transaction is really secure; I just need my customers to think it is,' " said Larry Erlich, partner at Domainregistry.com, a Philadelphia company that registers Internet addresses and provides Web consulting services. In the case of one recently disclosed security problem, though, the issue seems to have been not a lack of concern by the Internet retailers but a limited technical knowledge. Two weeks ago, a Seattle Internet service provider, Blarg Online, reported that several software products that were used to create the "shopping cart" technology employed by some Web retailers could leave credit card numbers and other personal data exposed on a company's server, if the software was improperly installed. Those wishing to get at that information simply needed to type a few words and numbers into a search engine like Alta Vista, and they would have been able to get access to a compromised site's data files. The makers of the software say they have addressed the problem, but industry experts said problems involving other software and other Web sites could follow closely behind. One reason, said David Taylor, a vice president at the Gartner Group, a Stamford, Conn., research firm, is that many Internet companies have realized the value in collecting and selling customer data, "and in their quest for that data, people are being less than judicious about how they gather that information." Even the leading Internet companies are not immune to security problems. Earlier this month, for example, Yahoo acknowledged that customer data of one of its merchants had been exposed to the public. In that incident, customers of Vitanet, a retailer of nutritional products, had their addresses, order information and partial credit card numbers posted on a demonstration site that Yahoo had set up for study by would-be Web merchants. Only after being alerted to the security lapse several weeks later did Yahoo correct the problem, which it attributed to a software bug. Despite that stumble by Yahoo, many experts say that those most vulnerable to security flaws are small and medium-size sites. First, smaller operations often lack the money to hire security auditors -- which can cost $15,000 or more for a one-week sweep of a site -- and they generally lack the internal expertise to perform such audits themselves. Second, because they typically operate with a lean technical staff, such sites tend to rely on one software vendor for security needs. In fact, it requires more than one type of software to secure a site, security experts say. Still, some consultants say it is really not very expensive to provide at least a basic level of security. "If you're going ballistic with security, you could spend a lot of money," said Mamoon Yunus, a regional manager for i.Informix, the E-commerce division of the computer services company Informix. But otherwise, he said, "it needn't cost a lot." For instance, software designed to encrypt customer information as it travels to the seller, such as that sold by Verisign, costs $350 a year. And through companies like Cybercash, E-commerce sites can get credit card encryption and processing services set up for roughly $400, plus a fee of 20 to 25 cents a transaction. And for as little as $30 a month, smaller merchants can get secure on-line storefronts through companies like Cybercash and Internet providers. "Basically, there's no reason to have a security problem, except for a failure to do the homework," said Steven Kramer, president of the Picture Palace, an on-line retailer of rare and unusual movie videos. Those who run E-commerce sites say there is one additional issue deterring elaborate security systems: the customer's desire to move quickly through a transaction. For increased security, customers would have to go through multiple layers of registration and identity verification before buying, and many would bristle at the inconvenience, said Steven Rabin, chief technologist for Interworld, which develops sites for a number of large retailers. But Mr. Taylor, of Gartner Group, said that if reports of security breakdowns continued, E-commerce companies could be under increased pressure to regulate themselves if they do not want the Government to intervene. Mr. Taylor said more E-commerce sites should follow the lead of Gateway, the computer seller . In its privacy and security statement, Gateway asserts that "none of the tens of thousands of people who have made purchases through Gateway's Web site using SSL" -- secure sockets layer technology -- "have reported fraudulent use of their credit card as a result of their on-line order." When asked if, in the event of a security breakdown, Gateway would post information about it and the company's response, Chuck Geiger, Gateway's vice president for E-commerce, said: "It's a good idea, but I'd have to consult with our legal and public relations folks. But in terms of full disclosure and being honest, it makes sense." Mr. Taylor said that getting the entire industry to follow Gateway's example could be difficult, though. "The minute these companies start talking about security, they run the risk of bringing the party to a halt," he said. "But this is something the Government could impose, because it wouldn't be expensive for a merchant to do." The E-Commerce Report appears on alternate Mondays in Business Day, and every Monday in the Technology section of The newyork Times on the Web: www.nytimes.com/tech. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title: Israeli Scientist Reports Discovery of Advance in Code Breaking
body: An Israeli computer scientist is expected to shake up the world of cryptography this week when he introduces a design for a device that could quickly unscramble computer-generated codes that until now have been considered secure enough for financial and government communications. In a paper to be presented Tuesday in Prague, the computer scientist, Adi Shamir, one of the world's foremost cryptographers, will describe a machine, not yet built, that could vastly improve the ability of code breakers to decipher codes thought to be unbreakable in practical terms. They are used to protect everything from financial transactions on the Internet to account balances stored in so-called smart cards. Mr. Shamir's idea would combine existing technology into a special computer that could be built for a reasonable cost, said several experts who have seen the paper. It is scheduled to be presented at an annual meeting of the International Association for Cryptographic Research, which begins on Monday. The name of Mr. Shamir, a computer scientist at Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovoth, Israel, is the "S" in R. S. A., the encryption design that has become the international standard for secure transmissions. He is a co-inventor of R.S.A. -- with Ronald Rivest of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Leonard Adleman of the University of Southern California. R.S.A. is known as public-key cryptography. In this system, a person has a public key and a private key. The public key is used to scramble a message and may be used by anyone, so it can, even should, be made public. But the private key that is needed to unscramble the message must be kept secret by the person who holds it. R.S.A., like many public-key systems, is based on the fact that it is immensely difficult and time-consuming for even the most powerful computers to factor large numbers. But Mr. Shamir's machine would make factoring numbers as long as about 150 digits much easier, thus making it much simpler to reveal messages scrambled with public-key encryption methods. A number of advances in factoring have been made in the last five years. But most of them are the result of applying brute force to the problem. When R.S.A. was created in 1977, Mr. Shamir and his colleagues challenged anyone to break the code. Employing 1970's technology, they said, a cryptographer would need 40 quadrillion years to factor a public key, and they predicted that even with anticipated advances in computer science and mathematics, no one would be able to break the code until well into the next century. In fact, a message the trio had encoded with a 129-digit key successfully withstood attack for only 17 years. It was factored by an international team of researchers in 1994. Using Mr. Shamir's machine, cracking the 140-digit number would be reduced to the difficulty of cracking a key about 80 digits long -- relatively easy by today's standards. Researchers said that if his machine worked it would mean that cryptographic systems with keys of 512 bits or less -- that is, keys less than about 150 digits long -- would be vulnerable in the future, an exposure that would have seemed unthinkable only five years ago. The longer 1,024-bit keys that are available today would not be vulnerable at present. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Two May Aid Comcast Bid For Mediaone
body: Disturbed by the AT&T Corporation's cable television ambitions, America Online Inc. and the Microsoft Corporation may back the Comcast Corporation in its fight against AT&T to acquire Mediaone Group Inc., the big cable television carrier. Mediaone said yesterday that America Online, the No. 1 Internet service provider, and Microsoft, the No. 1 maker of personal computer software, had entered into confidentiality agreements with it. That would give the two titans of cyberspace access to Mediaone's secret internal financial information as part of due diligence in deciding whether to assist Comcast. Comcast held preliminary discussions with America Online and Microsoft early in the week, but the talks have since become more serious, executives close to the negotiations said. The executives added that Paul Allen, who was a founder of Microsoft but left that company in 1983, is among the other parties who have expressed interest in joining Comcast. Comcast, one of the nation's biggest cable operators, needs help because its agreement to acquire Mediaone for $53 billion in stock is in serious jeopardy. Last week, AT&T tried to break up that deal with its own unsolicited offer to acquire Mediaone for $58 billion in stock and cash. AT&T wants to build on its recent acquisition of Tele-Communications Inc., the No.  2 cable television provider, by acquiring Mediaone so it can offer consumers across the unitedstates integrated packages of television, telephone service and high-speed Internet access over cable lines. If AT&T, already the nation's biggest phone company, was to succeed in acquiring Mediaone, it could end up with cable links to as many as 60 percent of the nation's homes. That prospect is especially worrisome to America Online, which has already emerged as a critic of AT&T, if not an "avowed enemy," as one executive close to the web of negotiations put it. The reason is that cable television carriers, unlike local phone companies, are not obligated to open their networks to outsiders (except local broadcast television stations). What this means is that as AT&T begins to deliver high-speed Internet access to millions of homes using cable systems, the company is under no obligation to let America Online offer service to those customers. America Online and other Internet companies are trying to persuade Congress and regulators in Washington to change the rules, but that initiative is not moving quickly. For now, AT&T is winning the battle of influence at the Federal Communications Commission by saying that it will not spend the billions needed to upgrade cable systems to deliver advanced services if it then has to share those systems with others. Moreover, AT&T is promising to use the upgraded cable networks to deliver not just Internet service, but local telephone competition as well. So for America Online, the reasons to help Comcast fight AT&T are clear. If a combined America Online-Comcast succeeds in acquiring Mediaone, America Online will get a guaranteed channel for selling its services to consumers over cable modems. (Even if America Online does not end up participating in a bid for Mediaone, it will still get high-speed links to millions of homes through its deals with local Bell phone companies.) The problem for America Online may be that Comcast needs cash. While Comcast's standing offer for Mediaone is all stock, AT&T has offered most of an AT&T share plus almost $31 in cash for each share of Mediaone. And in the largest syndicated financing to date, managed by Goldman, Sachs & Company and Chase Manhattan Bank, AT&T has already lined up $30 billion in commitments from lenders to back up its offer. Comcast does not have that kind of financial firepower, and America Online may not either. At the end of the last quarter, America Online had only $1.8 billion in cash on hand. Even if it could raise a few billion more, it would still not be in AT&T's league. One obvious solution for America Online would be to use its stock, which has given the company a market value of about $130 billion. But Mediaone's shareholders may have qualms about taking America Online shares, which trade at about 400 times estimated earnings. Valuations of that nature may not be sustainable, especially if America Online becomes part owner of a cable company, since cable companies are generally valued much more conservatively. In addition, accepting a bundle of America Online and Comcast shares would not be wholly tax-free for Mediaone's shareholders -- although taking a mix of cash and AT&T stock would not be wholly tax-free either. In some ways, Microsoft's position is the opposite of America Online's. Microsoft has almost $22 billion in cash on hand, but does not seem to have an obvious strategic reason to go to war against AT&T. Microsoft would like to sell software for high-speed Internet connections, but Microsoft and AT&T could find many mutually profitable ways to work together. Microsoft has invested $1 billion in Comcast, but that alone would not seem reason enough to make a strategic enemy of AT&T. Mr. Allen may be the most intriguing candidate for Comcast. He has already invested heavily in the cable television industry, and he may not care about working with AT&T in the future. Under its original deal with Comcast, Mediaone has until Wednesday to accept another offer. The company is almost sure to accept AT&T's offer, if only in the hope (or knowledge) that Comcast and whatever friends it is able to enlist will be able to respond with a higher one. Mediaone's board is set to meet this weekend but could very well wait until the last minute to accept AT&T's offer. That is because once Mediaone formally accepts, Comcast will have only five days to respond. Mediaone might want to wait in order to give Comcast more time to prepare its second offer. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Questions Delay in Announcement of a Merger Last Year
body: A lawyer for the Microsoft Corporation tried today to show that the Netscape Communications Corporation and America Online delayed the announcement of their merger for several weeks last fall, apparently because they feared that earlier disclosure of it might hurt the Government's antitrust case against Microsoft. In an attempt to suggest a plot between the two companies and the Government to keep their intentions from Microsoft's legal team, the lawyer, Michael Lacovara, questioned Peter Currie, a senior vice president for Netscape, for more than two hours. The deposition was the first of several that will be taken to prepare rebuttal arguments for the trial, which is in recess. All but about 10 minutes of the deposition was taken in public, as the result of a suit filed by 13 news organizations, including The newyork Times, under a 1913 law intended to make antitrust cases subject to public scrutiny. During the final few minutes of the deposition, the lawyers discussed what they described as confidential business information, and the public was asked to leave the room. But during the public portion, a small gathering of reporters and other onlookers at a Washington hotel watched as Mr. Currie, in response to questions from Mr. Lacovara, said discussions of the deal between the two companies were quite active last August and September, "but then they went into hiatus for weeks and weeks -- until mid-November." Finally on Nov. 23, America Online announced that it was buying Netscape for $4.2 billion, while also forming an alliance with Sun Microsystems. In his questions, Mr. Lacovara said nothing about why he thought the "hiatus" had occurred. But Microsoft is basing the major portion of its rebuttal case on the thesis that the Netscape-America Online deal changes the competitive landscape of the software industry, seriously undermining the Government's charge that Microsoft is a bullying monopolist with the power to cow the computer industry. In support of that notion, Mr. Lacovara quoted from an underwriters' report on the proposed deal presented to the Netscape board last fall, which called the acquisition "an industry-defining transaction." Mr. Currie scoffed at that, saying, "It sounds like the kind of thing they might have said." Microsoft and Government lawyers both completed presenting their principal cases at the end of Feburary, when the antitrust trial went into recess. It is currently expected to resume in late May, when both sides offer three rebuttal witnesses. During the earlier part of the trial, in October, James Barksdale, Netscape's former chairman, and David Colburn, a senior America Online executive, testified for the Government. This was during the hiatus in the merger talks. At the time of their testimony, no hint of the discussions came out in court. Presumably, had Microsoft known of the proposed deal, the company could have made the argument earlier that it undermined the Government's case and could have questioned executives of the two companies about it. Mr. Currie said he heard no significant discussions within Netscape last fall about how the proposed deal might affect the antitrust trial. "There was a very brief discussion -- will this have an impact," he said. "But mainly we were looking at the business issues. There were only a very few people at Netscape worrying about the trial. And remember, at that time we had no deal." Mr. Lacovara also suggested that Netscape informed the Justice Department about the proposed deal in September. Today, David Boies, the Government's lead lawyer in the case, said the Government was not informed until mid-November. But Microsoft has subpoenaed thousands of pages of documents from Netscape, and Mr. Lacovara said, "I would not ask a question like that unless I had a good faith basis for believing it is true." Asked what the September revelation would prove even if true, Mr. Lacovara said only, "Let us shake the case out, and then we'll tell you." After the deposition had ended, Mr. Boies called the Netscape-America Online issue "a sideshow." Mr. Colburn of America Online testified last October that his company had ended its relationship with Netscape and had chosen Microsoft's Internet Explorer as the default browser for its service because Microsoft had promised America Online a prominent advertisement in all copies of Windows. Microsoft argued in court that America Online had chosen Internet Explorer because it was technically superior; it offered specific features that Microsoft valued that Netscape could not match. Microsoft also argued that Netscape never did produce a version of its browser including those features. But Mr. Currie said Netscape's main interaction with America Online in September and October was Netscape's effort to persuade America Online to adopt a new version of the Netscape browser that did include the specific features the company wanted. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Peter Currie is a senior vice president for Netscape. (Associated Press)(pg. C4)

title: America Online Reports That Net Tripled
body: Continuing its vigorous growth, America Online Inc. reported profits of $420 million for the first three months of the year, a figure that included a number of one-time items. Excluding the special items, the company earned $117 million in the quarter, up 200 percent from the comparable period a year earlier. That comes to 11 cents a share, 20 percent higher than the 9 cents analysts had estimated. The special items included a one-time pretax gain of $567 million from the sale of shares in Excite Inc. And the company took a charge of $103 million related to its acquisition of Netscape Communications, which was completed in March. Its flagship on-line service added 1.8 million subscribers in the three months, bringing the total to 16.9 million. The service continued to occupy more of members' time, with the average account in use 55 minutes a day, up from 46 minutes a year earlier. "Both membership and advertising revenue was higher than I expected," said Stephen M. Case, the company's chairman. The winter months are always strong for the company as people who receive computers for Christmas sign up for the service. Still, membership is accelerating, Mr. Case said, adding, "More and more people can afford PC's as the prices come down." Advertising and payment from companies doing business on America Online's services increased 119 percent, to $210 million. The company released its earnings report after the close of the market. The shares had dropped $9 during the day to close at $153. In after-hours trading, the shares rose as high as $157. Analysts noted that for the first time in recent years, America Online's advertising revenue grew faster than that of Yahoo Inc., the largest advertising-supported Web service. America Online dominates the market for home users, while services like Yahoo are used mostly by people in offices. "If you want nighttime coverage for your message, AOL is your only choice," said Brian C. Oakes, an analyst with Lehman Brothers. "If you want to reach people in the daytime at their businesses, you can choose from a lot of portals." Alan M. Braverman, an analyst with Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities, said America Online had a backlog of $1.3 billion in advertising sold for future periods. "That comes out to $133 million a quarter for the next two and a quarter years," he said. "That means that they essentially have half their nut covered already." Over all, analysts said, the company is showing increasingly strong financial performance. Its gross profit margin, Mr. Oakes said, rose from 38 percent in the last quarter of 1998 to 41 percent in the most recent quarter. "They had a big kick in revenue and they are running their network more efficiently," he said. Over all, the company reported revenue of $1.3 billion, up 66 percent from a year ago. The bulk of that was $869 million in subscription fees, which increased 50 percent. Mr. Case said that the company's Compuserve service had begun to show a small increase in its base of two million subscribers after years of steady declines. Still, the company has yet to come up with a marketing message for a major promotion for the service, he said. Mr. Case declined to comment on reports that America Online is considering backing the Comcast Corporation's battle with AT&T to buy Mediaone Group, the cable company. But he indicated that America Online wanted access to cable systems in order to offer high-speed access to homes. "We want to do things that support our strategy of building a more ubiquitous medium," Mr. Case said, adding that the company had the ability to make another big acquisition, even as it incorporates Netscape. "We have the management bandwidth, but we will only do things if they make sense." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Metro Business;
ABC to Leave Web Site
body: Walt Disney Company's ABC television network said it would not renew a contract that put its on-line sports and entertainment news on the Web site of America Online, the No. 1 Internet service provider. ABC, which has provided sports and entertainment news and information to AOL's sites since 1994, is to quit doing so by the end of the week. ABC removed its national news content from AOL in January, after AOL replaced it with news from rival CBS. ABC declined to say what portion of its Web site users came from the links to AOL, which has more than 17 million subscribers. The end of the alliance with AOL comes as Disney focuses on building its Go Network of Web sites, which it runs with Infoseek Corporation. AOL also has grown closer to CBS through agreements to promote each other's services. "We had a really long, productive relationship with America Online," an ABC spokeswoman, Michelle Bergman, said. "In the five years since our relationship started, the landscape of our business has changed dramatically." ABC declined to disclose financial terms of its contract with AOL, and AOL officials were not immediately available to comment. Some of the ABC content was exclusive to AOL. For example, the network ran a site called Kidzine for children, and supported many of its sports broadcasts with content exclusive to AOL.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Foreign Affairs;
Judgment Not Included
body: Articles about the shootings at Columbine High School contained two sets of initials you don't often see together: N.R.A. and AOL. That the N.R.A., the National Rifle Association, should feel guilty about the Columbine massacres goes without saying. The idea that two high school kids were able to amass an arsenal that included an Intratec fingerprint-resistant, high-volume assault weapon; a Hi-Point 9-millimeter carbine; a sawed-off pump-action shotgun, and a sawed-off double-barreled shotgun should make anyone who opposes gun control ashamed. But what about AOL, America Online, the Internet provider that housed the warped Web site of Eric Harris, one of the presumed student gunmen? According to The Times's reporting, the AOL Web postings attributed to Mr. Harris included instructions on how to build pipe bombs ("shrapnel is very important"), an illustration of a creature toting a shotgun and a knife while standing on a pile of skulls, and the song lyrics: "What I don't do I don't like. What I don't like I waste." Should we be as worried about the Internet as the Intratec? The short answer is no. AOL is not the equivalent of the N.R.A. -- but that doesn't quite end the matter. Here's why: Assault weapons have only one purpose, and that is to kill other human beings. The Internet, alas, is everything and its opposite. It can be an incredible knowledge tool and an incredible microphone for hate. It can be a place where grieving Columbine students can come together to comfort one another and a place where a student outcast can nurse his grievances, research his revenge and find encouragement from neo-Nazis. But precisely because the Internet is such a neutral, free, open and unregulated technology it means that we are all connected, but no one is in charge. The Internet is democracy, but with no constitution. It is Orwellian in the way it can connect us all, but with no Big Brother watching over us all. And therefore personal judgment and responsibility are critical when using this technology. The only filter is the one you bring in your own head or your own heart, and since kids often lack the judgment microchip, it is even more critical that parents and educators provide it. Fortunately, some of those closest to this technology get it the best. After Columbine I called Steve Case, the C.E.O. of America Online. I expected to hear him say: "AOL has nothing to do with this story. Goodbye." But he was clearly wrestling with it. "I share the outrage that everyone feels about this incident," said Mr. Case, "and to the extent that there is an Internet connection -- finding information about bomb-making or whatever -- it is alarming and troubling. This is especially hard for me because I have spent most of my life building a medium that I want to be used for the better. But the Internet empowers people in ways that were not possible with television or newspapers. With these broadcast-type media there was a producer or an editor making decisions for the audience -- deciding what they should see or hear. That simplified things, and it also deprived the audience of the full range of choices." The Internet changes that by giving people unlimited choices and unlimited power to make them. "When they have more choices," Mr. Case argued, "they have more responsibility to show good judgment. We can't unilaterally impose that judgment, and we shouldn't try. But we can try to offer certain tools like technological filters, and educate parents about them and encourage them to take some responsibility here. The same attention that parents should pay to what their kids watch on television, or how they use the telephone, has to be paid with the Internet, only more so, because this is an interactive technology with no editor. Instead of us trying to be the all-powerful censor, we are trying to encourage parents to take control of the dashboard. Technology can be a useful tool, but it can't be a replacement for caring, involved parents." To put it another way, if we are all connected and no one is in charge in cyberspace, then cultivating citizens in the schoolyard or the backyard becomes that much more important. The more the Internet makes us all broadcasters, all researchers, all consumers and, alas, all potential bomb makers, the more critical it is that our teachers, parents and communities are still making us all citizens. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Web-Page Distribution System Could Unclog Internet Traffic Jams
body: Tax time was crunch time for the World Wide Web site of Intuit Inc., the supplier of personal finance software. Traffic shot up to as much as 20 times its levels the rest of year, as customers downloaded the latest revisions to Intuit's Turbotax tax preparation program. But unlike tax seasons past, this time Intuit had the help of Sandpiper Networks Inc., a start-up company that has developed a way to speed the delivery of information on the Web. "Customers got it faster than they would have with us," said Rick Parkinson, director of the planning and delivery group at Intuit. Sandpiper and a rival start-up company, Akamai Technologies Inc., are pioneering a way to distribute material over the Internet that avoids much of the congestion that can turn the World Wide Web into the World Wide Wait. And the companies are starting to be noticed. This week, Sandpiper is expected to announce that America Online, the largest provider of Internet access, has made a small investment in the company and will incorporate Sandpiper's technology into its network. The Inktomi Corporation, a supplier of Internet software is expected to invest in the start-up company along with two Sandpiper customers -- the Times Mirror Corporation and NBC. Sandpiper is raising a total of $21.5 million in this, its second round of raising venture capital, with each of the corporate partners believed to be putting in $2 million to $3 million and the rest coming from venture capitalists. Akamai, meanwhile, recently scored a coup of its own, hiring as its president and chief executive George H. Conrades, formerly president of the GTE Corporation's BBN unit and before that a top executive at I.B.M. As more corporations turn to the Web for marketing and sales, long waits on the Internet are becoming bad for business. And while the companies can improve service somewhat by buying more powerful computers for their Web sites, they have less control over the network traffic jams that can develop between their sites and the users. "Since nobody controls the Internet, how do you insure quality of service?" said Scott Yara, vice president for marketing at Sandpiper, which is based in Westlake Village, Calif., outside of Los Angeles. The answer proposed by both Sandpiper and Akamai is to distribute the contents of a Web site to server computers dispersed throughout the Internet, so that information does not always have to wend its way through the network from a single site. "The whole name of the game here is to push content to the edge of the Internet, very, very close to the end user," said David Goodtree, vice president for marketing at Akamai, which is based in Cambridge, Mass. One use of such a service would be to help with big Web events that could bring the Internet to its knees. The Los Angeles Times, owned by Times Mirror, used Sandpiper to help cope with the on-line demand for the Starr Report last year and for the newspaper's coverage of the Academy Awards in March. But Sandpiper and Akamai contend, and some analysts agree, that distribution of Web content will eventually be a full-time necessity, as Internet traffic continues to grow. "The demand is so high and straightforward," said Ted Julian, an analyst with Forrester Research, a market research firm in Cambridge. A somewhat similar technique, known as caching, is already in use. If, for example, an Internet service provider in Los Angeles finds heavy demand among its customers for a Web page based in newyork, it will create a local copy of the page in Los Angeles. But the actual producer of the Web page in newyork has no control over this cache, and thus no way of preventing the information on it from becoming outdated. Moreover, the producer of the Web page usually does not know how many visits or "hits" the copy on the cache receives. Both Sandpiper and Akamai sell their service directly to the Web content providers, automatically distributing the content to servers, updating the material as necessary and keeping track of the number of visitors. Sandpiper was founded three years ago by David Farber and Andrew D. Swart, software experts who had worked for Interactive Systems, a Unix company. Leo S. Spiegel, whom they recruited to be president, started a computer company while still in college. That company, LAN Systems, was sold to the Intel Corporation and R. R. Donnelly & Sons. Akamai, which says its name means "intelligent, clever and cool" in Hawaiian, grew out of a math class at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Tim Berners-Lee, the M.I.T. researcher known as the father of the Web, suggested to Tom Leighton, a professor of applied mathematics, that "load balancing" on the Internet would be a good problem for his class to tackle. The classwork led to algorithms that are used by Akamai, which was founded by Professor Leighton and a graduate student, Danny Lewin. Akamai, which is only now beginning commercial service, says that customers for its trial service included 5 of the 10 most popular Web sites. But Mr. Goodtree would not identify any of them. Akamai seems to have a more sophisticated approach, but Sandpiper has the advantage of being first, said Peter Christy, principal at Collaborative Research, a market research firm in Los Altos, Calif. Akamai also has deployed 400 servers, compared with only 32 for Sandpiper. "We could handle the load today of 15 Yahoos and the top 20 Web sites combined," Mr. Goodtree said. But the deal with America Online and Inktomi could help change that. Inktomi already provides more than 300 cache servers to America Online, and Sandpiper will now be able to use those, as well as Inktomi servers in other networks. "It really expands our footprint," Mr. Spiegel said of Sandpiper (which calls its service Footprint). The biggest challenge for the companies, though, might not be each other but new entrants expected in the market. Mr. Julian of Forrester said these could include big computer service providers like I.B.M. and Electronic Data Systems as well as companies like Exodus Communications that provide computer sites used to host Web pages. Even Intel announced last week that it would enter the business of providing servers to host Web pages. But some of these companies might decide to ally themselves with Sandpiper or Akamai rather than compete with them. Another challenge could be persuading companies to entrust distribution of Web pages to outsiders. Mr. Parkinson of Intuit, for instance, said it made sense to use Sandpiper to save Intuit from having to invest in enough capacity to handle the rare peak demand. But at times of normal demand, Intuit prefers to run its Web site by itself, to guard its competitive information. "You give up a little bit of control every time you give something to someone else," he said. Lemont Southworth, technology manager for latimes.com, said another problem was that Sandpiper's system cannot handle the individually customized advertisements that many Web sites offer. Another possible threat is that if technologies like high-speed cable modems and optical fiber can sufficiently reduce congestion, there would be less need to store Web pages close to users. But both companies insist that cable modems, by increasing the flow of information between users' computers and Internet sites, will only increase the strain on Web site providers, much as widening freeway on-ramps can worsen congestion on the freeway itself. So content will still need to be dispersed. "I really believe it's the next evolution of the Internet," Mr. Spiegel said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Leo S. Spiegel was recruited to head Sandpiper Networks, a Web services provider. (Ed Carreon for The newyork Times)

title: U.S. Cracking Down on Internet's Information Brokers
body: The Federal Government today began cracking down on the deceptive practices of a proliferating number of private investigators who advertise on the Internet that they can inexpensively provide confidential details about bank accounts and telephone records. In the first civil case of its kind, lawyers at the Federal Trade Commission accused a Colorado couple of violating the law by posing as bank customers to trick banks into providing confidential information. The couple, James and Regana Rapp, had advertised on their Web site that their company, Touch Tone Information Inc., could obtain bank records, unpublished telephone numbers and financial assets. Government officials said Touch Tone Information, one of scores of investigative agencies that glean confidential information under false pretenses, had employees make hundreds of telephone calls in which they claimed to be either a bank customer or relative. The Federal Trade Commission Act makes it illegal to use such deceptive trade practices. Mr. Rapp acknowledged in an interview today that he and his employees had tricked many banks and other institutions into providing confidential information. Touch Tone's Internet site advertised that for $100 it could obtain information within 10 days about a bank account -- $200 for a stock account. It also said it could obtain telephone toll records and unlisted numbers and addresses. Mr. Rapp said that as a result of the lawsuit, he had removed his Web site and would stop the practice of posing as a customer of the institution that he was trying to get information from. He said the trade commission's action would curtail only a small part of his investigations business and complained that it would only hurt victims -- clients like mothers seeking payments from dead-beat fathers and government agencies that he said had employed him to track down assets. "If you're a dead-beat dad or a neglected spouse," Mr. Rapp said, "you don't have to worry anymore." Commercial Web sites run by private investigators have flourished in recent years, advertising the ability to find a wide array of public and confidential information -- like telephone records and credit and bank accounts -- for lawyers, spurned spouses and burned business partners. Some of the information they sell is available in public records, but other information can only be obtained by deception or bribery, privacy experts say. Although law-enforcement officials in some states like Connecticut and Massachusetts have prosecuted investigators who illegally obtain information by pretending to be either a bank customer or relative, the Federal Government has moved more slowly. Many privacy experts say that as long as law firms and big businesses are largely insulated from Government prosecution because the laws are narrowly written, the deceptive practices of investigators like the Rapps will never be curtailed. "The F.T.C. cannot stop this practice because there is a lot of value for this data, and people will continue to pay for it," said Evan Hendricks, editor of Privacy Times, a Washington newsletter that covers privacy issues. But officials at the Federal Trade Commission said the case was filed as a warning to both the information brokerage industry and the bigger fish, the firms that retain the investigators. "We want to send a message to others that this kind of deception and invasion of privacy is unacceptable," said Robert Pitofsky, chairman of the commission. Today's lawsuit is part of a broader policy agenda promoted by Mr. Pitofsky to address privacy issues and the Internet. Earlier this week, the commission announced a proposal for new rules intended to protect the privacy interests of children on the Internet by generally requiring operators of Web sites to obtain parental consent before soliciting information from children under 13. The agency has asked Congress for the authority to seek civil penalties against brokers who obtain sensitive financial information about individuals under false pretenses. In its case brought today, the agency sought forfeiture of Touch Tone's profits and an injunction against any future deceptive practices by the company. Representative Jim Leach, the Iowa Republican who heads the House banking committee, recently introduced legislation that would make it a crime to knowingly deceive a financial information to obtain confidential information. But the proposal would also raise the burden of proof for civil cases, which has created some concern at the Federal Trade Commission. Officials at the Justice Department have said they believe they implicitly have authority to make criminal cases under Federal wire fraud laws. Still, the laws on the issue are far from clear. Orson Swindle, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, dissented from the agency's decision to file a lawsuit against Touch Tone on the ground that he did not think the Federal Trade Commission Act or the agency's guidelines on the law prohibited the Rapps' conduct. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Robert Pitofsky, chairman of the Federal Trade Commission. (Associated Press)

title: America Online to Compete in Assigning Internet Domains
body: America Online, the world's largest on-line service, was one of five companies chosen today to compete with Network Solutions Inc., which currently enjoys a Government-backed monopoly in the lucrative business of assigning the Internet addresses known as domains. The surprising choice of America Online introduced a seemingly formidable competitor to the business of assigning Internet addresses -- and prompted questions about whether smaller companies would ever compete effectively. "It's unfortunate," said David J. Farber, a professor of computer science at the University of Pennsylvania and a board member of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, an Internet civil liberties group. "I think it was a good opportunity to spread the wealth. Now you get AOL against N.S.I., and they can have a ball." The stock of Network Solutions, which had lost half its value over the last few weeks, surged today, closing at $92, up $32, or 53 percent, from Tuesday. America Online climbed to $142.75, up $14.0625. The other four companies selected in this first round -- the competition will open to many more companies this summer -- were Register.com, a comparatively small, newyork-based domain name reseller; a subsidiary of France Telecom; Melbourne IT of Australia, and the Internet Council of Registrars, an international consortium that helped lead the movement to break Network Solutions' monopoly. The selections were the first major action taken by the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, or Icann, the nonprofit corporation established last year by the Clinton Administration to move management of the Internet from government to the private sector. Since 1993, Network Solutions has had an exclusive right to assign companies and individuals Internet addresses in the so-called top-level domains -- those ending in the suffixes .com, .net and .org. Icann's interim chairman, Esther Dyson, today characterized the move as "a major milestone" in bringing "Internet users the benefits of real competition." But just how much competition the companies will offer Network Solutions remains to be seen, since the companies must pay Network Solutions a $9-a-year fee for each name they add to the central registry, the data base of Internet addresses that Network Solutions will continue to own. They will also have to pay a $10,000 fee to help cover the costs of the software developed by Network Solutions to let others add addresses to the registry. In the seven years since it was granted an exclusive Government contract to build the data base and registry system, Network Solutions has transformed itself into a Fortune 500 company, offering a variety of registration services and establishing partnerships around the world. "The economic reality is that Network Solutions has all the market movement in its favor," said Keith Benjamin, an Internet analyst with BancBoston Robertson Stephens in San Francisco, "and there's nothing Icann or the Government can do to really unseat Network Solutions." He added, "They have a crucial relationship with essentially every Internet service provider on the planet." As for America Online, which has 17 million members, Mr. Benjamin said: "This is a business that AOL is not going to be easily suited for. They cater to a consumer market, so it is a little confusing why AOL is doing this." In addition to selecting the five initial companies, Icann announced that 29 applicants, including AT&T, had met its accreditation criteria and were expected to be certified to compete when the system is opened to unlimited competition this summer. A spokesman for Network Solutions, Christopher Clough, called competition "good for everyone," but added: "Obviously, we have a head start. We have the most established company. We have the world's leading experts on the domain-name system." Referring to the fees that competitors will pay for access to the registry, he noted that Network Solutions was not only "taking on five new competitors but five new customers." Bill Burrington, vice president for policy at America Online, said his company saw an opportunity to create a "value-added service." But he emphasized that "it's too early to say how the process will play out." "This is all new," he said. "We are doing this on the fly -- in Internet time," Mr. Burrington said. "We don't know where this is all going." http://www.nytimes.com

title: More Problems For Schwab Site
body: Customers of the Charles Schwab Corporation were unable to place stock trades yesterday morning through the Internet broker's Web site. It was the sixth time that has happened this year. Schwab's Web site, which processed a record 160,000 trades a day in the first quarter, failed for 15 minutes starting around 11 A.M., a spokeswoman, Tracey Gordon, said. Customers may have experienced "periods of slowness" for an hour thereafter, she added. A recent string of short service interruptions was caused by Schwab's attempts to increase its Web site's capacity by adding another mainframe computer. Schwab recently said that it would spend heavily this year on its Web side and other technology. Schwab's competitors have also suffered shutdowns and glitches, notably the No. 3 Internet brokerage firm E*Trade Group Inc. The problems have frustrated on-line investors, spurred lawsuits and caused state regulators to begin an inquiry into the on-line brokerage industry. Schwab, which has 2.5 million on-line accounts, last week reported a record $142.9 million profit in the first quarter, more than double the $68 million profit in the quarter a year ago. The failure did not hurt Schwab's stock, which gained $8.25 yesterday, closing at $115. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
A Program That Can Remove Advertising on Internet Pages
body: A German electronics company is tackling those banner advertisements with a product that strips most advertising off Web pages. Web Washer was developed by engineers at Siemens A. G. who wanted to get rid of advertising they thought was obtrusive. During testing on the company's intranet, they discovered that it also reduced the time pages took to load in a browser. The software sits on a user's computer and waits for a user to click on a link. Web Washer looks at all the pieces of what is being requested and if anything looks as if it might be an ad, the program will toss out that part of the request. Roland Cuny, the Siemens engineer who came up with the idea for Web Washer, said the program could filter out "any kind of undesired information, like over-designed background images on Internet-intranet pages, ad banners, graphics, frames, Java scripts, Java applets and pop-up windows" and could be tuned by the user to be more -- or less -- restrictive. The program is free for personal use and is available at the www.siemens.de/servers/ wwash/wwash_us/buy.htm site. Current versions run only on Windows 95 and 98 and NT, though Mr. Cuny said Macintosh and Linux versions were in the works.   STEVEN E. BRIER http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
STOCK MARKET HITAS INVESTORS FLEE TECHNOLOGY AREA
body: In a stunning reversal, investors piled out of technology stocks and other market darlings yesterday, pummeling the very shares that propelled the broad market averages to records last week. After rising 271.8 points, or 2.6 percent, during the morning, the Dow Jones industrial average ran out of steam shortly after noon and ended the day down 53.36 points, or a half-percent, at 10,440.53. The Nasdaq market started the day in negative territory and never climbed out as investors fled the computer, Internet and telecommunications stocks they had been favoring. Amazon.com lost 16 percent, Dell Computer declined 7.3 percent, and Microsoft fell 6.5 percent. The Nasdaq composite index, home to most of the nation's technology companies, fell 138.43 points, or about 5.6 percent, to close at 2,345.61. That was the composite's second- biggest fall in points but only its seventh in percentage terms. Its largest point decline took place on Aug. 31, at the height of the Russian economic crisis. Volume on the newyork Stock Exchange exceeded 1.21 billion shares, the second-heaviest trading day in the exchange's history. Nasdaq trading volume was also brisk, at 1.198 billion shares. Early in the day, investors took refuge in stocks whose fortunes closely track the performance of the economy, but even those shares began to sputter at the close. "This kind of a sharp and dramatic reversal is not just business as usual," said Byron R. Wien, unitedstates investment strategist at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter. "There's a message here. The message is everything finally began to sell off from sheer exhaustion." Though oil prices rose in the morning, traders said this alone was not enough to kill the rally in the Dow. The shift away from the glamour stocks of technology, health care, Internet and telecommunications companies began last week and it simply gained momentum. The Standard & Poor's/Barra Growth stock index -- a collection of companies with high growth rates and lofty stock valuations -- has fallen 10 percent in the last five trading sessions. Some of the biggest losers yesterday were stocks that had previously seemed to levitate. Even after yesterday's collapse, these shares are trading at high prices based on their earnings and are well above their lows. America Online, for example, fell 23 7/8 a share, to 115 7/8. That is down more than 30 percent from its high of April 6, but the shares are now where they were just about a month ago. Likewise, the Charles Schwab Corporation, a brokerage concern that is a favorite Internet play because of its on-line trading services, closed down 32 percent from its high of one week ago. Still, it is up 81 percent since the start of the year. Reflecting the damage done to Internet stocks, the American Stock Exchange's Internet index is down 18 percent from its high set last Tuesday. Proving once again that the market's leadership can change on a dime, investors last week began to realize that excessive valuations in stocks posed more risk than they could comfortably accept. Rather than flee stocks entirely, they shifted to shares of some companies that had been left for dead. Previously unglamorous companies such as Allied Signal,, Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing and Smurfit-Stone Container registered impressive gains. "Investors had the idea that it's a new economy and a new stock market and that meant you don't have to worry about the old rules of diversification and quality," said Alan F. Skrainka, chief market strageist at Edward Jones in St. Louis. No longer. The move away from growth stocks with high valuations and into companies that are viewed as cheaper began last week. Market strategists pointed to two events that gave investors pause. The first was the European Central Bank's move on April 8 to cut interest rates, a signal that policy makers are committed to keeping the world on a path to economic growth by jumpstarting Europe's economies. When economic growth around the world is scarce, as it has been recently, investors retreat to stocks they know can produce good earnings in spite of any malaise -- these are shares with hefty and reliable profits, so-called growth stocks. Indeed, these investors are willing to pay premiums for these profits. But when growth is plentiful, a broader group of companies benefits and investors can find improving profits in less expensive stocks. The second scare for growth-stock investors came last Monday when Compaq Computer warned that its quarterly earnings would be half what analysts had been expecting. This reminded traders that technology, for all its promise, can also disappoint. Adding to investor concern about growth stocks in general, and technology stocks in particular, was the news on Friday that Robert Stansky, the manager of Fidelity Investments' Magellan fund, had sold large positions in many hot technology stocks that had been among his biggest holdings. Mr. Stansky moved into "value stocks," more mundane shares that were trading at lower premiums to their earnings growth rates. Traders noted yesterday that there were so few buyers for many falling stocks that sellers could get out only if they accepted prices well below the prevailing market. Some fell sharply even though relatively few shares exchanged hands. Companies waiting in the wings to offer their shares to the public for the first time were likely losers in yesterday's market decline as well. Three Internet concerns, Net Perceptions Inc., Proxicom Inc. and Launch Media Inc., had planned initial public offerings this week. Until investors become more hospitable to companies like these, such offerings are likely to remain on hold. Strategists pointed to the effect that hordes of rapid-fire day traders -- many of whom are relative newcomers to stocks and have yet to experience a severe, protracted decline in stock prices -- could have on the market. In recent months, these traders have created momentum and profits as they piled into stocks. If they are now piling out, they may create tidal waves of selling. "This is a case where a lot of these stocks have some unreasonable gains," said Laszlo Birinyi, who heads his own stock research firm in Greenwich, Conn. "Now people are starting to lock in the gains when they can. As these stocks decline from their highs, the movement feeds on itself." Longtime traders worry that a flood of calls from brokerage firms will go out to stock investors on Tuesday for more funds to prop up diminished portfolios that they have borrowed against to buy more stocks. Customers must meet these requests, known as margin calls, with fresh money or with cash raised by selling stocks. If shares are sold, the market decline could accelerate. A spokeswoman for Ameritrade, a large discount brokerage firm, said that it had slightly higher margin calls than normal, adding that it had no discernible problems with trading. She also said that the brokerage firm had previously imposed higher borrowing limits, presumably lessening the number of margin calls that would go out to customers. Of course, investors could jump back into their former stock darlings if they judge the selling to be overdone. Such a strategy has served them well in the last five years and was especially shrewd when the market rebounded from its correction in October. Microsoft, for example announces its earnings today. Investors may like what they see and bid the stock back up again. Still, Mr. Wien of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter said that the unitedstates stock market remains overvalued and that the broad market averages will experience a correction, defined by traders as a decline of 20 percent. "What you're seeing is a resolution of excessive valuation in the market. I expect the indexes to decline further, but I don't think we're in a bear market."  Treasury Prices Rise (By Bloomberg News) Bond prices snapped a four-session slide and posted their best day since April 8 as stocks fell, increasing the appeal of less risky Treasury securities. The price of the 30-year benchmark bond rose 2 8/32 , to 96 8/32 . Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, fell to 5.51 percent from 5.57 percent on Friday. Yields on two-year notes, the most actively traded Treasuries and among those considered the safest, fell 6 basis points, to 4.93 percent. title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ONLINE;
When Latin Pride Took to the Streets
body: The Young Lords Party fought hard for the empowerment of poor Hispanic people back in the 60's and 70's. The group, formed in Chicago, gained particular fame when the newyork branch, begun in 1969, engaged the city's hospital, sanitation and prison systems in a series of bold street actions. But when James Freedman, a high school student in Puerto Rico, and a classmate, Gabriel Espinosa, were researching the Young Lords for a high school history paper, they found almost nothing on the Web. So two years ago, Mr. Freedman, who is Puerto Rican and is now a student at the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta, decided to construct a Web site about the group's newyork activities. "I put it up to have information out there," Mr. Freedman said. The students found few useful books, with the exception of one 1971 volume, "Palante, Siempre Palante!," by Michael Abramson and others. (The title, which is the same as the Web site's, means, "Forward, Always Forward.") Most of the information on the site, and all the photographs, come from the Abramson book, which is cited on the home page. Another important source for the site is a 1996 Public Broadcasting System documentary about the Young Lords that was produced by Iris Morales. Mr. Freedman describes himself as a math-science type who researched the Young Lords only because they appeared on a list of suggested paper topics. Conversations with two history teachers intensified his interest. Mr. Freedman particularly enjoyed reading about the Young Lords' 1970 takeover of Lincoln Hospital in the Bronx to demand better medical care. "I kind of admired that," Mr. Freedman said. WHAT YOU SEE -- The pictures of dashing young activists in berets and sunglasses, against the background of a Puerto Rican flag or the logo of the Young Lords Party, seem ripe for Hollywood. One page, "The Flight," is a capsule history of Puerto Rican immigration to newyork, including information about where the community settled in Brooklyn (around Columbia and DeGraw Streets in what is now known as Cobble Hill) and a mention of Mayor Robert F. Wagner's visit to the island in the 50's, when he invited all able-bodied Puerto Ricans to come work in the city. Another page, "Prisons," recalls the Young Lords' protests against conditions in the Tombs and the 1971 riots at Attica. According to a page titled "The Beginnings," the Young Lords used to sweep the garbage of the South Bronx into the streets so that the Sanitation Department, which the group said was neglecting the area, would have to pick it up. LINKS -- No serviceable ones. WHAT YOU GET -- The electronic preservation of a neglected chapter in newyork history.   MARCIA BIEDERMAN  PALANTE, SIEMPRE PALANTE! http://netdial.caribe.net/dfreedma/Ylord.html http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo.

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY: CYBERSCOUT;
GOING, GOING . . . BIDDING FOR BARGAINS
body: On-line auctions are a growing segment of the Web. A pioneer, Ebay, started in 1995 and now lists a couple of hundred thousand items every day; Amazon.com, which began life as a bookseller, recently cobbled on an auction subsection. With these merchandise auctions, the Web site acts as a go-between for individuals selling and individuals buying. Sites that offer travel include Onsale; Adventurebid, which, as its name implies, specializes in such excursions as white-water rafting, ballooning and climbing; Bid4vacations, with cruises, skiing and ranches that take guests; Luxurylink, with high-priced hotels and other destinations; Goinggoinggone, a potpourri, and others.
