title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Sony to Propose a Method For Protecting Digital Music
body: Responding to the growing threat of digital music piracy via the Internet, the Sony Corporation plans to propose a new copy protection method today designed to enable the recording industry to sell music safely, both on line and on digital formats like CD's and audio DVD's. The proposal is the first such method to be submitted to an industry standards group, the Secure Digital Music Initiative, which was established last month by the Recording Industry Association of America The new method consists of two separate copy protection systems, Magicgate and OpenMG, both of which require special hardware systems for scrambling music files before they are sold and unscrambling them for listeners. Magicgate will embed a special chip in each recorder and playback device. OpenMG, which is intended for personal computers and related devices, will require that consumers purchase a hardware device known as a dongle, which will attach to a personal computer's serial port. The dongle will insure that an encrypted music file be copied by an approved digital recording device before it can be played. Sony said it had also developed a third copy-protection system known as Super Magicgate, which is intended to be a long-term solution to the business problems presented by copy-protection methods. Such an approach might permit a consumer to listen to an unlimited amount of music for a single subscription fee. A spokeswomen for the recording institute said yesterday that the standards group planned to meet tomorrow in Hollywood and that 90 companies had expressed an interest in joining the initiative. She said the group expected other proposals besides the Sony plan. The recording industry has been reeling in recent months as consumers have begun routinely using a technology known as MP3 to share digital, compressed music files that can be played on a personal computer or recorded as CD's. Last year the institute unsuccessfully sued Diamond Multimedia after it introduced a tiny portable player known as the Rio that permits a computer user to get an MP3 file from the Internet and then listen to it anywhere. And many consumer electronics industry analysts believe that the emergence of the Internet and inexpensive digital copying systems presents a profound threat to the existing system of music distribution on compact disks. Already, a number of musicians have begun to break ranks with the studios and are distributing their music directly via the Internet. "There is a tsunami headed toward the recording industry," said Rick Doherty, the president of Envisioneering, a consulting firm for the industry in Seaford, N.Y. He said the danger facing the industry is that it was attempting to make it more complicated for consumers to listen to music at the very time that the Internet was dramatically lowering the barriers to digital music. "This is a marvelous reflection of everything that is good about the Internet, and the world is voting with its keyboards," he said. Although the industry may succeed in erecting technical copyright barriers around music recorded in studios, Mr. Doherty said that it would face a growing challenge from musicians who retain control over their live performances. In addition to the standards group, five record companies announced on Feb. 8 that they were joining I.B.M. to conduct a market trial of a system that permits distribution of full-length, CD-quality recordings to consumers in an encrypted format. The music companies included BMG, EMI, Sony Music, Universal Music and Warner Music.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Official Concedes That He Erred in Testimony
body: The Government's lead lawyer accused a Microsoft executive of making up evidence at the antitrust trial today, and, after presenting the witness with his own email contradicting his statements, forced him to correct his testimony. The courtroom incident focused on a matter of timing: when the executive, Daniel Rosen, had known that a software rival was making an Internet browser to run on the Microsoft Windows 95 operating system. On its own, it is not a central element in the Government's case against the Microsoft Corporation. But the episode is part of the Government's persistent effort to undermine the credibility of Microsoft witnesses. For Microsoft, the credibility issue has become enough of a problem that Federal District Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson joked that Microsoft's lawyer was embarking on a "heroic endeavor" when he began questioning Mr. Rosen this morning. It was the second day that David Boies, the Justice Department's lead trial lawyer, and Mr. Rosen had clashed concerning the software giant's intentions and actions at a key meeting with a competitor in 1995. The session is a key chapter in the Government case against Microsoft, and the court's determination of exactly what happened at the meeting could affect the outcome of the case. Microsoft insists that the session with executives of the Netscape Communications Corporation was a routine business meeting intended to find "common ground" on which the two companies could cooperate concerning Internet software. Mr. Rosen is the executive who led the Microsoft team at that meeting. The Government contends that Microsoft threatened Netscape at the meeting and made an illegal offer to divide up the Internet browser market -- a deal that Netscape says it refused. Both sides have made their arguments in court this week with piles of email and harsh words. When Mr. Rosen was dismissed at midday, it was clear that executives of Netscape and Microsoft left the 1995 meeting with very different views of what had happened. The real fireworks today came after Mr. Rosen said that he did not regard Netscape as a rival in June 1995 and that one of his goals was to "encourage them to write a good browser for Windows 95" -- the Microsoft operating system introduced in August 1995. Far from encouraging Netscape, however, the Government contends that Microsoft tried to persuade Netscape to cede the Windows 95 browser market to it, even though Netscape had long planned to produce a Windows 95 browser. Mr. Boies asked Mr. Rosen when he had first obtained an advance copy of Netscape's browser for Windows 95. Mr. Rosen said it was not until after the June 21 meeting. Mr. Boies then presented an email dated May 11, 1995, that Mr. Rosen wrote to another Microsoft executive. It included the notation "Can i borrow/copy the Netscape Win 95 new client they gave us?" The "client" refers to the new Netscape browser. But Mr. Rosen replied that he never got the test version, which he said did not work properly. Mr. Boies responded: "You don't remember that, do you? You're just making that up right now." Mr. Rosen said, "No, I remember it." "You're sure it was May and not April?" Mr. Boies asked. Mr. Rosen answered, "Yes." With that, Mr. Boies introduced an email from Mr. Rosen to another Microsoft executive on April 27 that said: "Do you remember who took the Netscape win 95 browser they gave us during our last meeting? I'd like to get a copy." Confronted with his own email, Mr. Rosen paused, then said, "I stand corrected." Afterward, on the courthouse steps, Mr. Boies said that the testimony raised questions about Mr. Rosen's credibility and memory. "He was saying that he was trying to encourage Netscape to produce a browser at the June meeting," Mr. Boies said. "In fact, Netscape had already done it and he had it." The Government presented notes taken by Marc Andreessen, a founder of Netscape, at the June 21 meeting, in which he wrote that Microsoft's proposals amounted to a "threat that Microsoft will own the Windows 95 client market and that Netscape should stay away." The Government also introduced as evidence an email written on June 22, 1995, by David Kaiser, an executive at America Online, to another executive of the on-line service, recounting a conversation he had with Mr. Andreessen. Mr. Andreessen, Mr. Kaiser wrote, told him that at the meeting the previous day, Microsoft offered Netscape a deal: Microsoft would invest in Netscape, take a seat on the board, and Netscape would agree not to compete with Microsoft head-on. If Netscape accepted, Mr. Kaiser wrote that Mr. Andreessen had told him, it would become "Microsoft's special partner." If Netscape rejected the deal, Mr. Kaiser said in the email, "Microsoft would crush them." But Microsoft also introduced documents that supported its version of the June 21 meeting. An email written on June 22 by Richard Wolf, a Microsoft executive who attended the meeting, said he did "not think that they have the intention of competing with us in defining a platform," for underlying Internet software that Microsoft planned to include in Windows 95. Still, Mr. Wolf added, that "does not mean they will drop a broad-based client," meaning a browser. After the testimony, William H. Neukom, Microsoft's senior vice president for law and corporate affairs, said: "The record is quite clear. There was no effort by Microsoft to dissuade Netscape from creating a browser for Windows 95. It did and its browser was quite popular."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Goldman, Sachs is a latecomer to selling stocks on the Internet, which may end up an advantage.
body: AS every Wall Street firm struggles to figure out how to play the Internet, an advantage may lie with those that, like a fresh recruit to a midnight poker game, have yet to put their chips on the table. Unlike its chief rivals, Goldman, Sachs & Company has never been a retail brokerage firm, meaning that it does not have an army of brokers selling stock to the public. Only a year ago, Goldman was seen as lagging so far behind Morgan Stanley Dean Witter and Merrill Lynch in the lucrative retail business that it risked becoming a niche player in financial markets. The Internet could change all that. Goldman is now actively studying ways to become a retail broker using the Internet, people close to the firm said. One way would be to work out a joint venture with an on-line brokerage firm, possibly FMR's Fidelity Investments, Charles Schwab, or E*Trade. Another way would be to create its own on-line brokerage offering. But the people close to the firm dismissed as highly unlikely the possibility that Goldman would buy E*Trade or another publicly traded on-line leader, saying that sky-high stock market valuations of Internet companies rule out a purchase of that kind. The strategy discussions are taking place as Goldman itself prepares to go public, reviving a plan that was shelved last September amid world financial market turmoil. Unless the unitedstates stock market undergoes a serious correction, Goldman will likely issue shares as early as late April, people at Goldman said. Going public and developing a strategy for the Internet are seen as separate but related activities, Goldman executives said. One said the firm intended to have a clear Internet strategy in place when it begins marketing shares to investors, especially given the intense enthusiasm displayed by investors for Internet-related stocks in recent weeks. Also, Goldman could use its stock as a currency to make acquisitions or enter alliances after going public. "Investors are going to ask about the Internet," said one person familiar with Goldman's strategy discussions. "You can't hem and haw and say you're thinking about it. They will want to know exactly what you're doing and you want to be able to tell them." Goldman is not the first Wall Street firm to take the Internet seriously. Morgan Stanley, Merrill Lynch and Paine Webber, three leading brokerage firms with big retail operations, have all offered some Internet services for their customers. But Goldman's situation is intriguing to many in the industry precisely because the firm does not have a major retail operation -- and can thus change its strategy and enter a new business without spending heavily to build up a traditional network of retail brokers. In fact, several Goldman executives spoke with evident relish about the delicate task facing Merrill Lynch and Morgan Stanley. Those two rivals must balance the interests of their thousands of retail brokers, most of them paid through commissions earned when they trade stocks for their clients, with the growing promise of Internet trading that largely eliminates the role of the traditional broker. Goldman calls this a "channel conflict," and says it provides firms without a significant number of retail brokers a chance to challenge established competitors. "Warfare used to be who had the biggest infantry," said the person familiar with Goldman's strategy talks."You had to feed and clothe those guys and they died for you on the front lines. Now you don't need to be in the infantry business at all. We have smart bombs." Leslie Tortora, Goldman's head of global technology, and Larry Buchalter, managing director in the firm's fixed-income division, are heading a new committee to study the matter. The committee met for the first time only a week ago and it seems unlikely to reach a recommendation immediately, people close to the situation said. The existence of the committee was first reported by The Wall Street Journal. Goldman has already dipped its toes in Internet waters. It has reserved blocks of shares of companies it underwrites for distribution to retail investors through E*Trade, a leader among the dozens of existing on-line trading firms. Both Goldman and E*Trade are also partners in an electronic stock trading network called Archipelago. E*Trade's share price rose $8.4375, or 20 percent, to $48.5625, in trading yesterday on speculation that it would seal a fresh alliance with Goldman. But while people close to Goldman do not rule out new links to E*Trade, based in Palo Alto, Calif., they played down their relationship with the company. E*Trade has overemphasized ties with Goldman in news releases, one Goldman executive said. The executive said that such releases might have given the impression that Goldman had chosen E*Trade as its main on-line partner, an impression he said was inaccurate. On the contrary, Goldman is still debating how best to deploy one of its potential on-line aces: its stock research. Goldman has talked with both Fidelity and Schwab as well as E*Trade about distributing Goldman research.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MARKET WATCH;
A Tale of Two Markets, And Only One Safeguard
body: IT has become fashionable for investors to think they no longer need brokers to help them with their investments. A computer, a modem and an on-line account, so the thinking goes, are all you need to make a fortune in stocks. Never mind that a big part of an honest broker's job is keeping customers away from investment mistakes, a task that not even the smartest machine can do. The fact is, today's electronic access to stocks requires of on-line investors a heightened responsibility for their own actions. Few investors may yet realize just what this responsibility involves. Investors may not know, for example, that if their on-line trading firm is a member of the National Association of Securities Dealers and problems crop up in their accounts, they may be left holding the bag. Some 100 brokerage firms offer on-line trading services. Those that are members of the newyork Stock Exchange abide by its rules; firms that belong to the N.A.S.D. follow its regulations. A little-known but crucial difference between the two sets of rules leaves investors who use N.A.S.D. brokers more vulnerable. The difference involves "suitability," a pillar of the securities laws. The newyork Stock Exchange essentially requires its members to make sure that an investment is suited to a client's needs and circumstances before making the sale, even if the transaction was the investor's idea, not the broker's. By contrast, if a customer trading through an N.A.S.D. firm buys a stock that has not been recommended by the broker, the firm is under no obligation to evaluate whether the investment is appropriate. Although this difference has existed for years, the recent popularity of on-line trading makes it a deeper concern. A customer of an N.A.S.D. member firm who trades his way into huge losses from an inappropriately risky investment cannot sue the firm to recover on suitability grounds unless the firm recommended the investment. (Clouding the issue is the fact that many on-line firms offer research reports that make recommendations.) The N.A.S.D. rule creates a major gap in investor protection, said Lewis D. Lowenfels, an expert in securities law at Tolins & Lowenfels, a law firm in newyork. Much of the nation's on-line trading is done at N.A.S.D. firms. Of the top 15 on-line brokerage firms in the unitedstates, according to Gomez Advisors Inc., eight are members of the N.A.S.D. These include the giants Ameritrade, E*Trade, Datek and Suretrade. "Suitability is one of the main avenues of protection under Federal securities laws for investors," Mr. Lowenfels said. Indeed, the issue of suitability looms large among investors unhappy with their brokers' performances. According to the N.A.S.D., an average of 29 percent of arbitration cases filed with it each year since 1995 involved investments alleged to have been unsuitable for the customer who bought them. The N.A.S.D. says it is re-examining its rule, given the recent surge in on-line trading. "The technology offered by these firms is very enticing," Mr. Lowenfels said. "With that enticement, shouldn't their responsibilities rise to what the newyork Stock Exchange requires?" http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Big Difference" The chart shows the membership numbers in the National Association of Securities Dealers compared with the newyork Stock Exchange, since 1995

title:
PRELUDES;
When a Buddy Makes It Big
body: STEVEN ALDRICH and Kent Kille have been good friends since junior high. They lived on the same street in Chapel Hill, N.C., played basketball after school and attended the University of North Carolina together. They're both 29, married and hard-working. But there's one glaring disparity: Mr. Aldrich is worth about $10 million, and Mr. Kille, well, isn't. Mr. Aldrich was the co-founder of an on-line brokerage site that was sold to Intuit in 1996; he now is president of Intuit Insurance Services. Mr. Kille teaches political science at the College of Wooster in Ohio and is working toward a Ph.D. at Ohio State. Although the two are still close, keeping in touch through email, holiday cards and occasional visits, Mr. Kille sometimes wonders if he went wrong somewhere. "At Christmas, I was with Steven and two other friends, one of whom gave up academia to go into business, and I thought, 'Did I make the right decision?' " said Mr. Kille (pronounced KILL-ee), who lives in a two-bedroom apartment in Wooster. Their contrasting stories are hardly unique, especially in a world where more and more 20-somethings seem to be founding technology companies and selling them for rich sums. According to the Census Bureau, the median annual income of 25- to 34-year-olds was $21,821 as of last March -- and some, burdened with debt, have negative net worth. But Jeff Skoll, 33, a founder of Ebay, the on-line auction service in California's Silicon Valley, has already piled up $10.2 million in stock. Or how about Todd Krizelman and Stephan Paternot, co-chief executives of Theglobe.com, a shopping, news and business information site that went public in November? By the end of the company's first day of trading, they were each worth about $50 million. Not bad for a couple of 25-year-olds from Cornell. Yet these young impresarios say they aren't all that different from you and me. Unlike many of their counterparts in the entertainment industry, who live in Beverly Hills castles and travel with entourages, they are almost apologetic about their wealth. Some of them say they have no time to spend their cash. And if they did, what would they buy? "Most of us in the Valley work so darn hard," Mr. Skoll said. "It's not like we have much of a chance to slow down and appreciate the finer things." Like houses. Mr. Skoll still shares a home in Los Altos, Calif., with four roommates. Though Mr. Aldrich lives in a town house overlooking the Potomac River in Alexandria, Va. -- "we're the youngest in our neighborhood by about 30 years" -- he carries a mortgage and drives a beat-up 1992 Toyota Camry. Mr. Krizelman and Mr. Paternot breeze into their office in jeans and Theglobe.com T-shirts, "partly for brand-building, but also because that's who we are," Mr. Krizelman said. They are also quick to point out that they know about suffering. They started their company in a fraternity house, paid employees in pizza, nearly flunked out of school and had no social life to speak of. When they moved to Manhattan in 1996, they rented tiny apartments -- 280 square feet in Mr. Paternot's case. Three years and many dollars later, they say that only the sizes of their offices and apartments have changed. Otherwise, their wealth is on paper. "All our money's tied up in stocks -- we can't sell it, we're not planning to buy boats," Mr. Krizelman said. If anything, he said, his wealth has a greater effect on others than on him. "The irony is that the people around you change," he said. "Not our good friends -- most have become lawyers or bankers and are earning significant cash -- but people who were never friends and now want to be. You're sensitive that people might pay attention to you because of the company, and you look for people who don't have any interest in that." As for Mr. Aldrich, his money lets him and his wife, Allison, indulge in some dreams. "My wife went to school to get her master's in art history, which is something she wouldn't have been able to do without the financial wherewithal," he said. BUT Mr. Aldrich sees Mr. Kille and his wife, Nicola, as proof that wealth is not essential for personal fulfillment. "They're really happy," he said. "It's not an issue of sitting around saying, 'We've done well and you haven't.' " Mr. Aldrich often picks up the check when he dines with Mr. Kille, but it's not expected. Mr. Kille said Mr. Aldrich comes across as a regular guy with a large piggy bank. "I'm happy for him," Mr. Kille said. "He's worked hard, and it's not like he's Leonardo DiCaprio. I don't think Steven's going to be on the front page of the National Enquirer or Teen Beat any time soon." Still, Mr. Kille said, he's not opposed to earning a few extra bucks himself. "I love teaching and interacting with my students," he said. "But if someone wanted to pay me a couple hundred thousand dollars to do it, that would be fine." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Rose Cassano)

title: Microsoft Trial Explores an Odd Alliance
body: A senior executive of the Microsoft Corporation reported in Federal court today that America Online had, at least for now, renewed its contract to equip its users with Microsoft's Internet browser -- even though it is buying Netscape Communications, Microsoft's main competitor in the browser field. The executive, Brad Chase, quickly added that he believed America Online would abandon Microsoft soon enough, dealing a serious blow to Microsoft's effort to make its browser, Internet Explorer, the industry standard. Finishing three days of testimony in the Federal antitrust trial against his company, Mr. Chase said he believed that America Online had chosen to stick with Microsoft for the time being in part for political reasons -- because the company wanted to influence the outcome of the antitrust case. "If they switched to Netscape, our market share would drop to 30 percent," Mr. Chase said. That would make Internet Explorer, Microsoft's browser, the underdog and "would be inconsistent with AOL's desire to support the Government in this case." America Online signed an agreement with Microsoft in 1996 to use Internet Explorer as the default browser for its subscribers. Since those subscribers now number more than 16 million, about 40 percent of the computer users equipped with Internet Explorer are using it in conjunction with America Online. The motivation for the agreement is a subject of hot dispute at the trial. The Government and a senior America Online executive who testified as a Government witness say the company chose Microsoft, and agreed to limit its members' use of Netscape, because Microsoft dangled irresistible bait: promotion of America Online's service on every personal computer running the Windows operating system. Microsoft argued again today that America Online actually chose Internet Explorer over Netscape because it was a better product. The Microsoft-America Online contract expired Jan. 1. But even with the renewal, Mr. Chase testified he believed an eventual switch of browsers was "inevitable." In Securities and Exchange Commission documents that Microsoft submitted as evidence, America Online declared it would create a new browser, working with Sun Microsystems, to compete with Microsoft -- and to use with the America Online service. Mr. Chase ended his testimony at midday, and John T. Rose, a senior vice president for Compaq Computer, took the stand. David Boies, the lead Government attorney, first used Mr. Rose to bolster the Government's assertion that Microsoft is a legal monopoly under antitrust law -- a finding that must be made if most of the Government's other charges are to stick. Questioning from Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson helped Mr. Boies by leading to the central issue of whether Microsoft could raise prices with impunity, a hallmark of the monopolist. The judge asked Mr. Rose, "Is it fair to say there is no commercially viable alternative to the Windows operating system?" "That is correct, Your Honor," Mr. Rose said. Mr. Boies asked him whether it was true that Compaq had not even considered looking for another operating system to replace Windows after Microsoft imposed a steep price increase for Windows last year. "That is correct," Mr. Rose said. Then Mr. Boies began a challenge of the central tenet of Mr. Rose's testimony, which continues Thursday. In his written, direct testimony, Mr. Rose took issue with a Government accusation: that Microsoft threatened in 1996 to cancel Compaq's license to sell Windows with its computers when Compaq began loading Netscape on its machines. Mr. Rose said the real problem was that Compaq had separately signed a contract with America Online at about the same time, requiring Compaq to replace the Internet Explorer and Microsoft Network icons in Windows with an America Online icon. But Mr. Rose said the people who signed that contract did not realize that Compaq had agreed in a telephone call with Microsoft executives a few days earlier not to tamper with those icons. Mr. Rose said that "there was simply a communication breakdown" at Compaq, and some of the documents Microsoft submitted with his testimony support his story indirectly. But Mr. Boies showed that some people involved in the first agreement, with Microsoft, were also involved in the second one, with America Online, and he said that it was odd that they did not know of this conflict.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: A Government Attack on Multiple Fronts
body: At the Microsoft trial today, a Government attorney attacked the testimony of the company's senior marketing executive on multiple fronts, and at times the witness's explanations seemed to cause even the judge to question his credibility. During his two days on the witness stand, Brad Chase, a Microsoft vice president, tried to hammer home one central point: Microsoft's decision to bundle a Web browser with the Windows operating system was not anti-competitive because alternative browsers are easily available. As a result, he argued, if Microsoft's browser, Internet Explorer, is gaining market share, that is only because it is a superior product. This afternoon, David Boies, the Government's lead trial lawyer, introduced a document from Microsoft files prepared last May. Titled "Internet Explorer Marketing Review," it was loaded with statistics, analyses and marketing assessments. Mr. Boies pointed to one conclusion: Most people who switched to Internet Explorer did so because "it came with my computer," suggesting that the browser was gaining ground largely because it was bundled with Windows. Asked about that, Mr. Chase explained that the 20-page strategy assessment "was done by a summer intern" and had no standing within the company. "Do you know where a supposed summer intern got all this information?" Mr. Boies asked, his voice laced with incredulity. Mr. Chase said he did not, prompting Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson to observe that the study appeared to be in the form of a slide show for a meeting, and he asked, "Do summer interns do slide presentations at Microsoft?" Mr. Chase said it was possible that an intern prepared the show and never presented it. Earlier in the day, Mr. Boies continued to challenge a videotape Mr. Chase played last Thursday that purported to show how easy it was to download Netscape Navigator, the principal competition to Internet Explorer from the Netscape Communications Corporation. Mr. Boies began the attack last Thursday, noting that the difficult and time consuming parts of downloading and installing Navigator had been edited out. Mr. Boies tried to show his own demonstration tape on Thursday to counter Microsoft's. But under the rules of the trial, he had to allow Microsoft 72 hours to examine it. When Mr. Boies finally played his tape today, he managed to force Mr. Chase to acknowledge that some answers he had given Judge Jackson on Thursday had been incorrect. Specifically, Mr. Chase had told the judge that an America Online customer downloading Netscape from the service would see a simple, self-explanatory series of screens that makes the process easy. The tape Mr. Boies played today showed that the process was considerably more complicated. Judge Jackson asked several questions along the way indicating that he was confused. Later, Mr. Boies tried to deflate Mr. Chase's assertion that Internet Explorer had won the majority of critical product reviews in the last two years. Among other things, he showed the results of a Microsoft tracking poll of professional Web developers, who concluded in the fall of 1997 that "Netscape is still perceived as having the best browser." Mr. Chase offered the view that these developers used Netscape primarily to check their Web sites to assure that they worked well with Netscape. The judge seemed puzzled by that explanation and asked, "Is this just speculation, or do you know that for a fact?" Mr. Chase said several Web developers had told him that. At midday, Mr. Boies offered what he thought would be an explosive new document, one that a Government official called "a naked attempt at market division." The document did appear to be just that, but it was so old that Microsoft's lawyer appeared successful in convincing the judge that it was irrelevant. The document, an email message to Microsoft's chairman, William H. Gates, Mr. Chase and others, was dated March 1990 and was written by Mike Slade, a Microsoft executive who had just returned from a meeting with the leaders of Intuit, manufacturers of Quicken, the popular accounting software. "I made a fairly surprising proposal to them," he wrote. "Usually we can topple anyone," but "we'd rather not compete with you. So how about this?" Then he suggested that Intuit write software for Apple computers and others running DOS but leave the new market for Windows computers to Microsoft. He said Intuit's leaders seemed receptive, and "if they were listening carefully, this could have been interpreted as a chance to avoid competition with us." The proposal is quite similar to one that the Government charges Microsoft made to Netscape several years later, an accusation that Microsoft denies. Mr. Boies said he was offering this memo, despite its age, "because this is something that shows a pattern of anticompetitive behavior." But Mr. Chase said he had no recollection of the document or events surrounding it. And eventually the judge told Mr. Boies to move on to another subject. After Mr. Chase completed his testimony this evening, William Neukom, Microsoft's senior vice president for law and corporate affairs, asserted that he "hasn't been moved an inch off of the central point of his testimony." On Wednesday, John T. Rose, a senior vice president for the Compaq Computer Corporation, takes the stand. In his direct written testimony made public today he said he believed that most consumers wanted a computer "with broad functionality that is simple and easy to use right out of the box." He endorsed the idea of giving them a Web browser but added, "It is irrelevant to users whether the feature is incorporated in application or operating-system software." Mr. Rose also took issue with the Government's accusation that Microsoft threatened in 1996 to cancel Compaq's license to sell Windows with its computers when Microsoft learned that Compaq was also loading Netscape on its machines. Mr. Rose said the real problem was that Compaq was deleting some on-screen icons, including one for Internet Explorer, that Microsoft had pre-loaded. This was done, he added, as the result of an agreement with America Online. When Compaq restored the icons, Mr. Rose said, Microsoft withdrew its threat.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NOTEBOOK;
On-Line Research Papers
body: For undergraduate scientists, getting their research into a national academic journal is usually a far-away goal that involves a Ph.D. But now they have an Internet publication just for them. The National Journal for Young Investigators put out its first on-line issue in December, selecting eight undergraduate research papers from 96 submissions. It intends to have three issues a year, with the next set for June. It also has links to student internship opportunities and science news. The journal is run, and the articles peer-reviewed, by 35 student editors in various colleges, aided by their faculty advisers. It has a $150,000 budget and is supported in part by the National Science Foundation, the private Burroughs Wellcome Fund, Duke University and Swarthmore College, with a lot of advice from editors at Science magazine. The address is: www.jyi.org Some of the published papers were senior science theses, "and those are usually very high-quality," said Andrew Medina-Marino, a Swarthmore senior who has taken the year off to run the journal in Washington. A major goal, he said, is to give researchers and editors undergraduate experience in the publication process, like how to review a paper and deal with ethical questions. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
Several Lawsuits Challenge Internet Ads
body: A recent round of lawsuits, including one from Playboy Enterprises, threatens to challenge some fundamental assumptions of Internet advertising. Playboy, no stranger to the courts when it comes to protecting its famous brand, is suing Netscape Communications and Excite in an effort to keep banner ads for pornographic, non-Playboy sites from appearing when Web surfers use either Netscape or Excite to look for material with the key words "playboy" or "playmate." Searching for Playboy magazine on Excite, for example, summons a come-hither ad from Tease.com. Just a few weeks before, Estee Lauder filed a similar lawsuit against Excite, accusing the search service of trademark infringement, "bait and switch" false advertising and unfair competition. A search for Estee Lauder on Excite, or on Excite's associated search provider, Web Crawler, brings up an ad for the Fragrance Counter -- a retailer that Estee Lauder says is not an authorized seller of Estee Lauder products. The Fragrance Counter is also named in the Estee Lauder suit. Selling advertisers access to so-called key words, so that their banner ads appear near certain search results based on the key words -- such as a competitor's brand name -- is widespread in the Internet business. Typing in "Amazon" on the Lycos search engine, for instance, may elicit an ad for the bookseller Amazon.com's chief rival, Barnes & Noble. Searching for a pair of Levi's jeans with Netscape may bring up an ad for the Gap. (To find out just how widely their names are being used in keyword purchases, companies often use a free service called Bannerstake -- www.namestake.com -- to display ads associated with their names.) Currently, ad sales based on key words account for roughly a quarter of the advertising revenue generated by portal and search sites like Excite -- a category of Web sites that together generated more than $450 million from advertising, according to Jupiter Communications. If Playboy and Estee Lauder prevail in court, the rules of Internet advertising would need to be substantially rewritten. "At the end of the day, the search engines are selling advertising against a trademarked name and making a profit on it," said Drew Ianni, a Jupiter analyst. "Any change would have an impact on the bottom line."   LAURIE J. FLYNN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: Nasdaq Revives Proposal to Test Trading Halts
body: With continued volatility in Internet stocks, Nasdaq regulators are now moving to temporarily halt trading of the most wildly unstable shares. Frank G. Zarb, chairman of Nasdaq's parent, the National Association of Securities Dealers, has asked the association's board to consider testing trading halts for one year. A proposal to institute the use of trading halts was rejected just two weeks ago by a Nasdaq committee of market makers and brokerage firm officials that had studied the issue as a possible remedy to large daily price swings in Internet-related shares. But in the wake of recent warnings about on-line trading by the Securities and Exchange Commission's chairman, Arthur Levitt, and the disclosure by the newyork State Attorney General, Eliot L. Spitzer, that he would investigate the Internet trading industry, Mr. Zarb will now ask the association board to consider allowing halts. Association officials said the plan, which would also require S.E.C. approval, would allow Nasdaq to halt trading in a stock immediately "when there appears to be significant corporate news or when a company's security is experiencing extraordinary volatility, either of which is impacting the fairness and orderliness of the market." The enormous level of recent trading activity, Mr. Zarb said in a statement, has created "new issues of volatility and trading practices, issues that must be addressed by the exchanges and member firms to preserve the fairness of the market for investors." Advocates say that trading halts have worked at the newyork Stock Exchange and that they would stem the sharpest price moves of Internet-related stocks. But opponents contend that halts could increase volatility by causing investors to rush to make trades before a halt. A key issue that has not been resolved is what specific criteria Nasdaq officials would use before halting trading in a stock, said Bernard L. Madoff, a leading Nasdaq market maker and head of the Securities Industry Association trading committee. "It's something long overdue, and I think it would be a sensible way to deal with some of the volatility occurring in the marketplace," said Mr. Madoff, who expects that officials of both the association and the S.E.C. will approve trading halts. While the idea has been dismissed before, he said, "I think the circumstances in the marketplace today are such that there is so much volatility, and so many small public orders coming in, that it makes more sense." http://www.nytimes.com

title: State Bills Take Aim At 'Spam'
body: AS lawmakers around the country discover that their constituents are concerned about Internet issues, bills to regulate or outlaw junk email are popping up in state legislatures. Three states already have laws on the books, and four more are considering them. Advocates of the laws say they are glad that states are interested in shielding consumers and Internet service providers from the scourge of junk email, known as spam. But they worry that a patchwork of different state laws could hamper legitimate on-line marketing. "We would prefer a single good Federal law, but if we can't find a Federal solution, we're going to have to work state by state," said John Mozena, a board member of the Coalition Against Unsolicited Commercial email. "We don't want to make it difficult for people to do authentic business on line. We just want them to be paying their own freight." In the last Congress, a coalition-backed proposal to extend to email an existing law banning junk faxes made little headway. A weaker measure, favored by the Direct Marketers Association, would have required that junk email be labeled as advertising and that recipients be given an easy way to get off mailing lists; it passed in the Senate but stalled in the House. The email coalition and the marketers' group said in December that they had tentatively agreed on a joint proposal, but Mr. Mozena said last week that he was not sure it would be made final. A bill in Texas appears to be the broadest a state has yet considered; it would outlaw any unsolicited advertisement that imposes a cost or charge on the recipient, addressing one of the main complaints about junk email, that recipients cannot avoid paying for connection time to receive it. Bills in Washington and Maryland would protect Internet service providers by making it illegal to violate providers' rules against spam. A Virginia bill would outlaw use of forged headers to obscure junk email's true origin. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Big Investors in E*Trade Sold Stakes Before System Problems - Correction Appended
body: Several major investors in the E*Trade Group, the on-line brokerage firm whose trading system failed for several hours during parts of three trading days last week, sold big chunks of stock just before the problems occurred. The two largest individual shareholders in E*Trade, which is based in Palo Alto, Calif., and its second-largest institutional shareholder all sold large blocks. But the company's biggest investor, the Softbank Corporation, a Japanese software company, did not sell any shares. Shares of E*Trade soared from $5 on Oct. 8 to $66.4375 on Feb. 1, but fell sharply after clients could not execute trades on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. E*Trade shares closed yesterday at $42.75, up $2.5625. General Atlantic Partners, a Greenwich, Conn., venture capital fund, and an affiliate, GAP Coinvestment, sold 4.2 million shares, or about 48 percent of their holdings, according to Lisa Nash, an E*Trade Group vice president. The sales were registered before the problems and were to have taken place Feb. 2 and Feb. 3. The sales were dictated by the fund's "very strict investment policy discipline," Ms. Nash said. Tom Murphy, a General Atlantic spokesman, declined comment. Christos M. Cotsakos, the chairman and chief executive of General Atlantic, has the second-largest individual stake; he and his family sold 370,000 shares, lowering their stake to 2.6 percent, from 2.9 percent. "This was part of a planned portfolio diversification strategy," Ms. Nash said. "It was planned, and largely executed, at the beginning of last week" during a brief window when insiders are allowed to sell shares. "There were absolutely no changes in the planned sales because of the outages." William A. Porter, E*Trade's founder, sold 200,000 shares in a family trust, reducing his stake to 4.3 million shares, Ms. Nash said, while Debra J. Chrapaty, the chief information officer, sold 50,000 of her 833,000 shares. E*Trade's problems have raised questions about the vulnerability of investors who execute trades in volatile stocks. Eliot L. Spitzer, the newyork Attorney General, said last week that he would investigate the Internet trading industry after his office received dozens of complaints about delayed orders and unavailable trading systems.   http://www.nytimes.com Correction  Because of an editing error, an article in Business Day yesterday about the sale of large amounts of E*Trade Group stock by several big investors misidentified one seller's employer. Christos M. Cotsakos is chairman and chief executive of E*Trade, not of General Atlantic Partners. Correction-Date: February 12, 1999, Friday

title: Sun-America Online Terms Disclosed
body: Sun Microsystems Inc., one of the biggest makers of computers that run Internet sites, will pay America Online Inc. a minimum of about $1.28 billion over three years as part of their agreement to sell the Netscape Communications Corporation's software. Sun agreed to help America Online sell Netscape's Internet software in November, when America Online agreed last year to acquire Netscape, the dominant maker of browser software, for $4.3 billion. America Online in turn agreed to buy about $500 million of Sun's computers over four years. In a regulatory filing on Tuesday, Sun disclosed that it guaranteed America Online revenue of $975 million from sales of Netscape products over three years. It also agreed to pay in the same period annual marketing fees of $10 million and a total of $278.5 million in licensing fees. Sun said that the agreement would make it a bigger player in the market for computers and software that run the Internet and other, smaller computer networks. America Online and Sun together have products that serve a wide range of markets, from the individual user looking at the Web on a personal computer to corporations setting up Web sites. America Online agreed to pay Sun $5 million a quarter for licenses on Sun products that are part of the agreement, plus $1 million a month for technical support of some products. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Schwab Lands Feet First on Net;
Broker Leap-Frogs Rivals to Front of On-Line Trading
body: There are many brand-name banks and brokerage houses battling on the front lines of American investing. Only one of them, the Charles Schwab Corporation, has made peace with the Internet. Schwab, the quarter-century-old discount broker that has long cast itself as a Wall Street outsider, has converted most of its brokerage business to the Internet with an ease few analysts predicted. Moreover, it has quickly come to dominate the booming business of trading stocks on line. Its giant computing center in Phoenix handles almost a third of all Internet trading -- meaning that one in 20 stock trades in America passes through the Schwab system. All this has come while its rivals struggle with the new medium. Merrill Lynch & Company, the country's biggest retail broker, will begin a limited on-line trading service soon, but like other full-service firms has been slow to embrace the Internet. E*Trade, a leading on-line competitor, has suffered a streak of embarrassing trading shutdowns. Nearly all other Internet stock-trading companies talk of "earnings before marketing expenses" instead of profits. Schwab stands practically alone: It has made the wrenching transition -- and made money from it, too. But even as it becomes known as the Houdini of finance for its ability to squeeze profits out of difficult situations, it is undertaking an even trickier make-over. Schwab is trying to convert itself into a full-service brokerage firm for the Internet age. The idea is to use the Web to challenge -- more directly than ever before -- the retail arms of Merrill, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company, Citigroup's Salomon Smith Barney and others. It plans to offer more advice, research, analytics and even hand-holding to customers. Schwab is also fighting to distinguish itself from well-financed on-line trading competitors like E*Trade, Ameritrade and Waterhouse Securities that are clawing at its on-line dominance and offering lower prices. The transition will be closely watched by Schwab's competitors. All are trying to figure out how Americans will invest early in the next century, what role the Internet will play and how investment advice will be distributed. Schwab intends to hog the middle of the road, somewhere between Merrill on the full-service side and E*Trade on the discount side. But it will need sharp elbows to keep that space for itself. "Our mission now is to create a new model of a full service brokerage firm," said David S. Pottruck, Schwab's co-chief executive. "We are not a discount firm anymore." But Mr. Pottruck was careful to distinguish his vision from that of the existing full-service brokerage firms. "I mean a new kind of full-service firm," he said. "Not the kind that sells its own load funds and gives brokers free trips to Hawaii." Mr. Pottruck is a burly native of Levittown, N.Y., who wrestled and played football at the University of Pennsylvania. He had a brief stint on Wall Street before joining Schwab 15 years ago. Promoted to share the executive reins with the chairman, Charles R. Schwab, a year ago, he has made his message resonate: Schwab intends to go after the big Wall Street firms, which control much more of America's investment money than discount firms do, and it will use the Internet as its weapon. A visit to the company's San Francisco headquarters is like dropping in on a West Coast consultants' convention. The dress is Gap casual, the carpets are earth tone and the fixtures gray stone -- no marble or mahogany. And the nouns are all semiotic: segmentation, alignment, high-tech, high-touch and empowerment. But the mission is in many ways the logical extension of the idea that first prompted Mr. Schwab, the 61-year-old founder, to pioneer discount brokerages in the 1970's: distrust of Wall Street. Schwab began as a refuge for investors who felt they were burned by brokers who got commissions each time a stock was bought or sold. Schwab did trades for less and paid its brokers in salary and bonus, not commissions. Now, it is starting to give its customers many of the tools full-service brokers and professional money managers have at their disposal, but for a fraction of the cost. Using the Web, Schwab thinks it can make the desktops of its 2.2 million on-line customers resemble a broker's. Its site has industry research from Standard & Poor's, insider-trading reports from Vickers, live interviews with chief executives from Briefing.com, stock research from Credit Suisse First Boston and Hambrecht & Quist and a proprietary stock screening service that can pinpoint equities that meet an investor's customized criteria. Many are free, though investors with less than $100,000 in assets pay fees for research and some other services. Schwab is also working out the kinks in an email service that it says will make "warm calls" and "hot calls" to existing clients, as opposed to cold-call solicitations. The automated system is designed to monitor clients' portfolios and give them an electronic heads-up if the price moves up or down significantly or if a new equity or mutual fund comes closer than an existing holding to meeting investment goals. email is also seen as a way of knitting together the old and the new Schwabs. The old Schwab has 275 branch offices, places where customers still go to conduct transactions or open accounts. The new Schwab plans to expand those centers and build at least 200 new ones to form what Mr. Pottruck calls the "social fabric" of investing. They will hold seminars and training sessions. A client who sets up a child's trust, say, might get an email invitation to a live discussion on custody accounts and estate planning. "The way Barnes & Noble should compete with Amazon.com is not to offer books at lower prices but to create links between on-line and local services," Mr. Pottruck said. "How do you tie the two together and build relationships? That's the next phase on the Internet business." Schwab is also moving the line in the sand between itself and Wall Street investment banks, which typically work for companies that sell stock as well as customers who trade shares. That is a role that Schwab has often criticized as leading to conflicts of interest. Schwab still does not underwrite securities on its own, avoiding becoming investment bankers for companies. But it has agreed to join investment banks that act as lead underwriters in offering Schwab customers a chance to buy new issues, recognizing that it cannot compete across the board with the big brokerages without giving customers access to some hot initial public offerings. For the first time late last year, Schwab's name appeared on the cover of a prospectus for an initial offering. The company joined Hambrecht & Quist -- it has also reached stock distribution agreements with J. P. Morgan and First Boston -- to find buyers for the public offering of the Select Comfort Corporation, a Minneapolis-based maker of air-mattresses. Not a sexy high-technology issue, but Schwab added a dollop of data base marketing: It was able to find 250,000 of its clients who own a mattress from the company. Many were eager buyers of the shares. But perhaps the biggest initiative is its "signature services." The plan is to retain more wealthy customers, especially those who park more than $500,000 in assets. Many will get a team of perhaps eight designated consultants to help manage their portfolios. And though the company does not plan to advertise it, the wealthiest, if they choose, will be able to have a single broker monitor their investments. Much of this high-end push is part of Schwab's unstated goal to remove Merrill from atop the hierarchy of retail investing. Schwab acknowledges that the people it loses to full-service firms tend to be the wealthiest clients who say that they have graduated from Schwab's do-it-yourself ethic to a full-service broker. Part of the answer is Schwab's network of fee-based investment advisers. Through these 400 advisers so far, the firm refers customers who do not want to manage their own money to professionals who invest for them through Schwab. But for those who do not want to rely on advisers, Schwab's latest initiative is to convince wealthy customers that they can control their own money and get the help they need. "We want our customers to feel we can help them to trade out of a 20,000-share position without losing a point," Mr. Pottruck said, referring to the difficulty clients have making large trades electronically at predictable prices. "We will offer everything Merrill does and many things you can never get at Merrill." Merrill, whose nearly $1.5 trillion in customer assets is about triple what clients invest through Schwab, intends to be a major player on line as well as in its traditional business, said Jim Wiggins, a spokesman. "We have over 400,000 clients with $300 billion in household assets who already use Merrill on line to actively manage their accounts, and we are just scratching the surface," Mr. Wiggins said. "Anyone who thinks that Merrill Lynch won't be using the Internet to magnify the value we deliver to clients is making a major miscalculation." In fact, Schwab still often acts like an underdog, perhaps because some of its good fortune could easily be short lived. Schwab will surely face more competition from full-service firms in coming months, even though many of them face pressures from their brokers not to lure clients on line. Moreover, 20 or so low-cost on-line trading companies are nipping at Schwab's heels. Julio Gomez of Gomez Advisors, an Internet consultancy that rates on-line trading firms, ranks Schwab's Web service as No. 8 out of 20, in part because its $29.95 fee for each trade is at the top end of an industry where $8 trades are no longer unusual. E*Trade; DLJ Direct, a unit of the investment bank Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette, and Morgan Stanley's Discover Brokerage, among others, also offer some research. Schwab's 28 percent share of the on-line trading business is slipping, Mr. Gomez said. But Mr. Gomez also points out that Schwab is perhaps the only on-line broker to have grown out of its capacity problems. It can now handle 88,000 on-line customers at one time. E*Trade, by contrast, had three days within the last week when its trading system crashed, and Ameritrade had a costly shutdown early this week. Schwab, unlike its cut-price competitors, also has healthy profits to sustain marketing campaigns and capacity upgrades. But perhaps the sharpest arrow in Schwab's quiver is its willingness to cannibalize its business if it sees the market is changing direction. Take its transition to the Internet. Early last year Schwab stopped discriminating against on-line traders and gave them access to all services that its higher-paying clients had, even while lowering the cost of on-line trades. Mr. Pottruck estimated that pretax earnings would take a $150 million hit. In fact, Schwab's Internet integration did dampen earnings early last year because of reduced trading commissions and technical glitches. But by year-end, surging volume was more than compensating for declining commissions. And in a tough year for Wall Street, Schwab's revenues jumped 20 percent, and its net profits rose 30 percent, to nearly $350 million. Those numbers have made Schwab the envy of Wall Street, where the San Francisco firm was not long ago dismissed as a self-righteous pipsqueak. "Chairman Greenspan said buying Internet stocks is like a lottery ticket," said Michael Freudenstein, a finance industry analyst with J. P. Morgan, referring to the Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan. "Well, this is a lottery ticket with an earnings stream attached." Asked what some executives at the blue-chip investment bank Goldman, Sachs & Company were pondering when they debated strategy recently, a banker there answered with one word: Schwab. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Schwab's Web site can handle 88,000 customers at a time. Charles R. Schwab, left, and his co-chief executive, David S. Pottruck, are challenging bigger firms on line. (L. Lauterborn/Schwab)  Graphs: "Pumping Up the Volume" While many brokers have been slow to embrace on-line trading, Charles Schwab has shifted much of its business to the Internet with more success than predicted.  The graph shows that the revenue per trade may be lower . . . and Schwab's Average Commission since 1997  Another graph shows . . . but more people are trading on line, and what the Internet trades as a share of all trades at Schwab since 1997  A third graph shows . . . contributing to strong profit growth. And the growth of Schwab's Net Income since 1997. (Source: Charles Schwab)

title:
THE MARKETS;
N.A.S.D. Chief CautionsFirms About Internet Trading Risks
body: The head of the parent organization of the Nasdaq stock market says that the frenzy for trading stocks over the Internet may be creating an increasingly risky environment for investors, which could undermine the public's confidence in financial markets and perhaps even create greater regulatory scrutiny of brokerage firms. Frank G. Zarb, chairman of the National Association of Securities Dealers, which oversees Nasdaq and regulates its member firms, said last week in a letter to the chief executives of the organization's more than 5,000 members that the "frenetic" activity in the marketplace this year was posing greater problems for the industry. He suggested that the turbulence could have a "lasting impact on self-regulation." Mr. Zarb's letter came amid growing concern that the explosive growth of on-line trading in volatile Internet and high-technology stocks was creating a risky and unhealthy environment for small investors who regulators say may be naively trying to trade their way to fast riches. The Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulates the nation's financial markets, says it has been flooded with complaints about poor service and execution of on-line trades in recent weeks. The Attorney General of newyork, Eliot L. Spitzer, said last week that he would investigate the Internet trading industry. And two weeks ago, Arthur Levitt, the chairman of the S.E.C., cautioned investors to approach on-line investing with greater care. In the letter, which was issued last Thursday but posted on the N.A.S.D.'s Web site yesterday, Mr. Zarb said he was also responding to a growing number of complaints from investors about poor service and the execution of on-line trades. He said he was also concerned about customers' borrowing to trade in risky stocks, about advertisements and promotions' creating "unrealistic expectations" about making money trading on line as well as promises of instantaneous access to the market, even during volatile times. Mr. Zarb also said that some brokerage firms, including day-trading firms that house and train traders to speculate aggressively in the hopes of making a quick profit, were inappropriately extending credit to traders, pooling customer money and lending it to traders to use to try to make larger profits. Whether a speculative day trader or an on-line trader who may, for example, trade actively from home, Mr. Zarb suggested that member firms become more scrupulous in dealing with the problems arising from on-line trading. "Today's conditions suggest an increased responsibility for regulators -- for us and for state and Federal authorities -- to be extra vigilant," he wrote. "But nothing can help more than investor education." Officials at some of the largest on-line brokerage firms said that they were well aware of Mr. Zarb's concerns but that they were not trying to seduce investors into risky trading. "We are very concerned about acting responsibly," said Lisa Nash, a spokeswoman for E*Trade, which had technical problems last week that left many investors unable to trade. "We let our customers know about the risks and rewards of investing on line. We think they understand that risks have always existed before there was an Internet and after." Some day-trading officials, however, are disturbed by all the scrutiny being directed at day traders and the suggestions that day traders are creating volatile and risky markets. "They need a scapegoat," said Harvey I. Houtkin, president of All-Tech Investment Group in Montvale, N.J., a company that trains and houses day traders. "Why is this happening? Because the big boys are losing a lot of money to electronic trading." He added, "The real problem is with on-line brokers who can't execute trades, not with direct-access traders."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Auction System Set For Pricing Stock Offerings
body: William R. Hambrecht, the longtime Silicon Valley investment banker, plans to introduce a system for underwriting initial public stock offerings through the Internet. While other firms have given on-line investors an opportunity to get in on the ground floor of new stock offerings, Mr. Hambrecht's approach would have a new wrinkle: through an on-line auction. The new approach is to be announced today by W. R. Hambrecht & Company, the investment banking boutique he started last year after leaving Hambrecht & Quist, which he co-founded in 1968. His new firm intends to cater to the current fashion among small technology companies of selling stock to the public on line. E*Trade, the on-line broker, recently took a partial interest in a new on-line investment bank, E*Offering, that is backed by another Silicon Valley banker, Sanford Robinson. Wit Capital, currently the leader in offering new shares via the Internet, has participated in several dozen initial stock offerings by big Wall Street houses, making a portion of the shares available to investors on line before public trading begins. And Wit has attracted competition from a number of other firms including Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette and Charles Schwab. But Mr. Hambrecht wants his system to be more than an adjunct to traditional new offerings, in which the initial price is set by a big brokerage firm and most shares are allocated to its favorite customers. Mr. Hambrecht intends for the price and allocation of shares to be set completely on line through what is called a Dutch auction. Potential investors in a planned stock would log into the firm's system and indicate the highest price they would be willing to pay for a given number of shares. The offering is set at the highest price at which there is enough demand to sell all the shares. Anyone who bid at that price or higher is allocated shares at that price. Everyone else is out of luck. The first market test of the system would be with an offering for Ravenswood Winery, the Sonoma County, Calif., maker of a well-regarded zinfandel. Ravenswood, which filed its offering with the Securities and Exchange Commission last Friday, hopes to raise about $11 million. Compared with a traditional offering, this approach would probably mean higher prices when going public and, therefore, more money for the company issuing the shares. Mr. Hambrecht also contends that the approach will mean less frenzied trading by investors in search of a quick buck. "We want to put the issuer together with the people who want to own the stock for the long term," he said. Mr. Hambrecht plans to charge the companies issuing stock a fee of 4 percent of the capital raised, compared with 7 percent charged by a typical Wall Street underwriter.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
PERSONAL BUSINESS;
Electronic Middleman for Mortgages
body: NEVER before had William Ikley enjoyed much leverage when applying for a loan, especially a mortgage. But this time, Mr. Ikley, 36, a butcher who lives in Eldersburg, Md., had a firm deal just one business day after logging on to the Priceline.com Web site. And he, not a lender, was in charge. "It's been a real easy experience," he said. "There wasn't any pressure, doing it from home." In fact, he applied while in his pajamas. And he expects to have a check in hand tomorrow, 10 days after initiating the name-your-price mortgage. Priceline.com made its name by letting consumers offer bids on airline tickets -- then hotels and, in newyork City, cars. The vendors can then accept or reject the offers.  Now the company has extended this method for more complex transactions: mortgages. The new program might not be such a smooth process for everyone. Mr. Ikley needed only a small second mortgage, a $5,000, five-year home equity loan. He was knowledgeable enough to do without the guidance provided by mortgage brokers, who stand to lose business to this potentially less expensive electronic middleman. And as Mr. Ikley learned, Priceline's lenders are not exactly giving money away. He will be paying 8.17 percent rather than the 6.9 percent he had optimistically proposed. Still, his transaction represents another stage in the evolution of what Priceline calls buyer-driven commerce, which harnesses the Internet's speed and vast scope. The Tower Group, a consulting firm in Needham, Mass., estimates that by 2001, 10 percent of first mortgages in a $1 trillion-a-year market will involve the Internet. Many Web sites and institutions already match borrowers and lenders, but Priceline's is the first program that lets the consumer initiate the terms. "We put the customer more in control," said Richard S. Braddock, a former senior executive at Citicorp who is now chairman of Priceline. THE mortgage process, conducted in partnership with Lendingtree, an on-line loan originator, is fairly straightforward. A loan seeker can apply to finance a particular house, condominium or co-op or to qualify before choosing a property. The borrower visits www.priceline.com and specifies a type of financing (like 15- or 30-year, fixed rate or adjustable), an interest rate, points and a desired closing date. A monthly payment may also be proposed. The applicant also supplies income and other information that a lender can use to evaluate creditworthiness. A $200 deposit is charged to a credit card. Any response from among Lendingtree's 15 lenders, including the Dime Savings Bank of newyork, Greenpoint Financial and the Money Store, must arrive within two business days. If a lender accepts, the deal is struck and the deposit is applied to the usual fees, like the appraisal. Or the lenders can submit counteroffers. If the borrower rejects them, the application dies and the $200 charge is erased. The charge is not refunded if the customer walks away from an accepted bid. Unlike Priceline's other businesses, its mortgage service relies on applicants who have already done enough homework to know what they want and what terms they can reasonably expect. At Priceline.com, borrowers cannot browse through an array of rates and terms without risking a commitment. "It doesn't really allow for shopping," said James P. Punishill, an analyst at Forrester Research of Cambridge, Mass. Other on-line services -- Web sites of individual lenders or the dozens of so-called aggregators like E-Loan or Quicken or Lendingtree itself -- do allow borrowers to survey the financial landscape. Armed with information, though, Priceline customers will gain great flexibility, according to Theodore Iacobuzio of the Tower Group. They will probably save money, too, unless they can strike a deal with, for example, a local bank that throws in a free checking account or other services. Brokers, for their part, are taking this new mortgage-market refinement in stride, said A. W. Pickel 3d of Lenexa, Kan., co-chairman of the technology panel of the National Association of Mortgage Brokers. "There's definitely a place for it," he said, but he contended that he and his colleagues, many of whom have Web sites of their own, would not suffer much, because consumers need the hand-holding that brokers provide. Priceline is not as free of added costs as borrowers might think, Mr. Pickel said, because lenders must add to their rates or points the fees they pay to Priceline but which the service does not disclose. Mortgage brokers collect fees in similar ways. Though Mr. Iacobuzio thinks the on-line mortgage business has "a very big future," he said it would be many years before paperwork disappears and transactions can be conducted electronically end to end. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: William Ikley, above, at work at Giant Food in Laurel, Md., obtained a home equity loan by way of Priceline's new Web site, left. He offered to pay 6.9 percent interest; one business day later, he had a deal at 8.17 percent. (Marty Katz for The newyork Times)
