title: MCI Worldcom to Start Internet Service
body: MCI Worldcom Inc., the No. 2 unitedstates long-distance company, confirmed yesterday that it would start a new Internet access service using information and content from America Online's Compuserve unit. The new service allows MCI Worldcom to re-enter the consumer Internet business that the MCI Communications Corporation exited last year. MCI sold its Internet operations to gain regulatory approval for its $40 billion acquisition by Worldcom Inc. last September. The new MCI Worldcom Internet service is available to MCI Worldcom long-distance subscribers for $16.95 a month for the first 150 hours of local access. MCI Worldcom will send customers one bill for the long-distance and Internet services. Customers using just the Internet service will pay $19.95 a month. Compuserve will provide MCI Worldcom's service with access to news, weather, favorite links and Instant messenger, a pop-up window that allows on-line users to chat with one another. MCI Worldcom dissolved a previous alliance with the Internet search engine Yahoo when MCI sold off its Internet business to Britain's Cable and Wireless for $1.75 billion and closed its merger with Worldcom. MCI Worldcom said it did not anticipate any regulatory problems with the new service. It noted that its relationship with Compuserve was not exclusive. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
System C rash Doesn't Hurt E*Trade Stock
body: Internet stock traders are known, with some justification, as a hair-trigger lot, bidding up the shares of companies on the slightest hint of good news and dropping them with scorn at the first dimming of otherwise glowing prospects. So why wouldn't E-vestors be bailing out of E*Trade Group after two days in which the on-line broker's trading system was down for hours at a time? If that wasn't enough, Eliot L. Spitzer, the Attorney General of newyork, said yesterday that he would investigate the Internet trading industry after his office received complaints about delayed orders and unavailable trading systems. Yet E*Trade's stock hardly flinched. Sure, it fell $1.75 a share yesterday, to $53.50. But given the usual volatility of Internet companies, that is essentially unchanged. And that still leaves E*Trade's market value of $6 billion higher than more established, and decidedly more profitable, firms like Paine Webber,Bear, Stearns and Lehman Brothers. Investors -- a good number of whom use E*Trade and its on-line rivals -- have apparently concluded that the company's problems and the cloud of complaints above the entire industry will not ultimately rain on the parade of on-line investing. "Every other big broker in the space has also had problems and system outages," said Stephen C. Franco, an analyst with Piper Jaffray. "Investors accept that the brokers use cutting-edge technology that doesn't always work perfectly." Mr. Franco released a report yesterday that indicated the number of on-line brokerage accounts last year doubled to 7.3 million, with total assets of $420 billion. This growth has hardly slowed, even at brokers that have had well-publicized system failures. Mr. Franco said, for example, that Ameritrade was forced in the fourth quarter to pay $3.1 million to compensate customers whose orders were mishandled. Even so, only 3 percent of its clients closed their accounts during the quarter, he said. "It is so difficult to move a brokerage account that people rarely do it," he said. Of course, the usual crop of lawyers sprouted yesterday, threatening to file class-action suits to recover the losses E*Trade customers say they incurred from the unavailability of service. Legal experts, however, said that winning such cases would be difficult, either as class actions or as individual suits. "We can't hold people liable for every honest mistake," said Lewis Lowenfels, an expert in securities fraud with Tolins & Lowenfels in newyork. To win a case, he said, an investor would have to prove a broker with a system problem committed the financial equivalent of malpractice. A more difficult challenge for on-line brokerage firms is posed by investors who placed orders to buy initial public offerings that were first priced at, say, less than $20 a share, then filled at closer to $100 a share. Technically, the law provides little protection for investors who place market orders, which are filled at the best available price, rather than limit orders, which specify a maximum share price. Mr. Lowenfels, though, said some brokers might be vulnerable to complaints they violated rules requiring them to make sure investments are suitable for their customers. If a broker knew that a customer who placed an order to buy 1,000 shares of a stock at $20 would not have the resources to buy the stock if the best available price was $100 but executed the trade anyway, that client might have a case, he said. Maryann A. Waryjas, a lawyer with Jenner & Block in Chicago, argues that such laws have not been adjusted to take into account brokers that are machines, not people. "Historically, your broker would call you back and tell you the I.P.O. had gone way up and that you couldn't get it for the offering price," she said. "The technology has gotten ahead of the rules." As for E*Trade, its contract with its customers states that the company, which is based in Palo Alto, Calif., is not liable for system problems. But Lisa Nash, an E*Trade spokeswoman, said that it would still compensate customers who had legitimate claims that they were harmed. "Rather than hiding behind what the legal agreement says, we will try to do what is right," she said. "We have a virtual brand. If people don't trust us, it weakens the power of the brand." She declined to say how much the company expected to pay in compensation, but she said that fewer than 10,000 customers were affected. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Investors seem to have shrugged off bad news concerning E*Trade, an on-line brokerage firm whose corporate offices are in Palo Alto, Calif. (Associated Press)(pg. C7)

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Drop in Computer Issues Hammers Nasdaq for 83.34 Fall
body: Computer-related shares fell sharply yesterday, dragging the Nasdaq composite index down 3.3 percent, its biggest loss in more than five months, as Merrill Lynch cut its estimate on Intel's profits for 1999. The skid in high-technology stocks reverberated elsewhere, but less severely, in a session also marked by frantic activity in the stocks of on-line brokerage houses amid temporary shutdowns for a second day in the processing system at E*Trade, the No. 3 Internet broker. The Nasdaq composite fell 83.34 points, its third-biggest point drop ever, to 2,410.07. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index fell 23.58, or 1.85 percent, to 1,248.49. The Dow Jones industrial average held up relatively better and even nosed briefly into positive ground in the afternoon before slipping 62.31, nearly 0.7 percent, to 9,304.50. One measure of the wild swings in technology shares was Siebert Financial, a minor player in the on-line brokerage industry, which soared as high as 70 5/8 from Wednesday's close of 49 1/2 and then dived after the Attorney General of newyork said he was investigating the ability of on-line brokers to process large numbers of trades. The stock ended with a loss of 6 1/4 at 43 1/4. Other factors weighed on the market as well. Saying stocks had simply become too expensive, Douglas R. Cliggott, the top unitedstates equity strategist at J. P. Morgan Securities, recommended lowering holdings in stocks to 50 percent from 60 percent, putting 25 percent in cash and keeping bonds at 25 percent. "Based on current 30-year Treasury yields and our guess at first-quarter corporate earnings, the S.& P. 500 is now 16 percent rich relative to our fair value measure," Mr. Cliggott said. To justify today's prices, he added, profits would have to rise 12 percent this year and bond yields would need to drift back toward 5 percent. He said such an outcome was not very likely. Considerable money was also shifting yesterday from technology and other highflying issues into economically sensitive areas like the paper industry. Union Camp rose 3 7/16 , to 67 5/8; Georgia-Pacific was up 3 3/16 , to 69 15/16 , and International Paper, the second-best performer among the Dow industrials, climbed 2 5/8, to 44 3/16 . The best performer was another such stock, Alcoa, which jumped 3 5/8, to 86 11/16 . "You see profit taking in the recently strong tech stocks, and some money flowing into cyclicals," said Robert H. Stovall, president of Stovall/21st Advisers. Microsoft was the biggest drag on the S.& P. 500, falling 7 3/4, to 159 1/16 . Intel was right behind, falling 8 9/16 , to 130 1/8; followed by Lucent Technologies, down 7 1/8, to 102 7/8; Cisco Systems, off 5 7/8, to 105 1/4; General Electric, down 2 3/4, to 100 1/8, and Dell Computer, off 5 1/2, to 102 3/8. Internet shares other than brokers were also pummeled, with Ebay slumping 39 1/4, to to 239; Yahoo falling 2 11/16 , to 337, and Amazon.com declining 7 3/4, to 118. "It was a pretty bleak day," said Neil T. Eigen, a managing director at J.& W. Seligman. "A lot of these Internet stocks have paused." Advanced Micro Devices, Intel's biggest rival in chips, announced that it might report an operating loss for the first quarter after having been expected by Wall Street to earn 13 cents a diluted share. Trading was halted, and the stock fell 2 1/16 , to 18 7/8. The biggest drag on the Dow, accounting for almost 40 percent of its decline, was I.B.M., which fell 5 11/16 , to 169 9/16 . AT&T lost 3 9/16 , to 91 7/16 , and J. P. Morgan fell 3 3/8, to 100 7/8. Morgan was one of several weak bank issues. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average, since Jan. 1998. title: AT&T Finds Internet and a Crowd of Critics
body: As the AT&T Corporation aggressively enters the cable business, with plans to offer high-speed Internet connections to millions of American homes, a growing group of rivals and consumer groups has begun a nationwide lobbying effort to force the telephone giant to open its system to Internet competitors. The fight pits AT&T, which has struck cable deals in recent months that will give it access to nearly half of the nation's homes, against a coalition led by America Online, the world's largest internet service provider, with 15 million customers. It has also drawn a large group of companies that are the Internet gateways for millions of Americans, as well as some prominent former Washington officials who are now lobbyists working for the telephone industry, the cable industry and the Internet service providers. "This is the biggest issue in the whole technology communications realm," said Charles M. Brewer, chairman and chief executive of Mindspring Enterprises Inc., an Internet service provider with about 340,000 subscribers that joined with America Online, U S West, MCI Worldcom and others today in formally unveiling their anti-AT&T coalition, called Open Net. AT&T is expected to receive approval from Federal regulators as early as this month to complete its $31.8 billion acquisition of Tele-Communications Inc., the second-largest cable company, with 14 million subscribers. By providing high-speed Internet service over cable systems on a broad scale, AT&T will be able to offer millions of consumers the ability to navigate through the World Wide Web at speeds up to 100 times faster than the typical connection through ordinary telephone lines. But there is a catch. AT&T intends to require that any customer who subscribes to its high-speed cable modem service must also pay the monthly fee of $40 or so for Internet access provided by the At Home Corporation, of which AT&T will be the largest shareholder when it completes its acquisition of TCI. That has prompted protests by other Internet providers that fear they may be frozen out and complain that AT&T will control the computer standards on the Internet for video, audio and other transmissions. Both sides say the outcome of the battle -- which is just beginning before regulators and Congress here, and in courts and municipalities around the nation -- may determine whether the Internet will continue to be a free-wheeling technology or will be dominated by a handful of large corporate interests. And both say the fight will determine which companies survive the shakeout of the industry and which profit the most as the Internet matures. "The Internet would not be happening but for the fact that consumers can now choose their service provider in an unimpeded way," Mr. Brewer said. "If we had to rely on the owners of the last mile of transmission, it's unquestionable that the Internet would not have developed as it has." Executives at AT&T and the cable companies respond that America Online and other competitors are trying to muscle in and make use of technological improvements to the cable systems that are requiring investments of billions of dollars. Executives at AT&T and the cable companies say there will be plenty of other providers of high-speed access to the Internet, such as digital telephone technology and satellites. Moreover, they say, customers will still be able to make use of America Online and other Internet providers -- though they will still have to pay the At Home fee. The AT&T and cable executives contend that revenues from At Home will help to defray the huge capital costs associated with upgrading the cable system and that the cable companies did not undertake such an investment simply to provide what they call a "dumb pipeline" for competitors to take advantage of. "There's a certain arrogance to their position, which confuses what's good for AOL with what's good for the Internet," said James W. Cicconi, general counsel and head of government relations at AT&T. "It's certainly disingenuous and borders on hypocrisy to say for years that the government should stay out of regulating the Internet and then suddenly invite the government in when their business interests change. This is just a very big competitive player trying to disadvantage a smaller player that came up with a better idea." Earlier this week, AT&T reached an agreement with Time Warner for access to 12 million of that company's customers to provide local phone service through cable lines. While AT&T executives indicated that they did not anticipate competing with Time Warner's own high-speed Internet service, rivals questioned whether the agreement could ultimately lead toward AT&T's offering some kind of service over Time Warner's cables. While scores of companies are trying to develop higher-speed Internet service through telephones and satellites, some experts say cable modems ultimately hold the greatest promise of making the World Wide Web much faster, and therefore much more attractive to computer users and businesses. At least 350,000 homes -- some estimates run as high as 700,000 -- have some kind of high-speed Internet service, according to a study released today by the Federal Communications Commission. But analysts such as Forrester Research Inc. estimate that by the end of 2002, 16 million American households will have high-speed computer connections to the Internet, and nearly 80 percent of those will be through cable-based providers like At Home and its top competitor, Road Runner, a unit of Time Warner. Although some analysts and executives involved in the fight believe the regulatory war is simply a sideshow to a possible commercial settlement, both AT&T and America Online are prepared to spend millions of dollars for lobbying and legal expenses and have retained some of the biggest lobbying and press relations firms in Washington and around the nation. The fight is being waged on four fronts: in Congress, at the Federal Communications Commission, before local cable regulators in cities around the country, and in the Federal courts. Consumer groups have lined up with America Online, contending that AT&T and the cable companies are trying to control the content of what passes through their wires, just as they tried to control what programs appeared on their channels before that practice was prohibited by an act of Congress. "They are doing what Microsoft is accused of doing: building a system where they say you can't separate the transmission from the actual content," said Gene Kimmelman, co-director of the Washington office of Consumers Union, referring to the Government's antitrust suit filed against the software company. "They're saying if you want AOL, we'll let you have it but you have to pay At Home first. This is precisely what telephone companies can't do. The request from our side is let's open up access to cable wire the same way we require them to open up for programming." In recent days, the Federal Communications Commission has declined to step into the fight, but has said it will watch the situation closely. Officials there say they do not want to do anything that might impede the progress of upgrading the cable lines. But cable regulators in a growing number of cities, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle, have held hearings and vowed to consider the issue as franchise licenses are renewed this year. And one city, Portland, Ore., has blocked AT&T's cable venture from moving in without first opening its proposed new broadband pipeline to rival gateways like America Online. The move by the city's cable regulators recently prompted AT&T to file a lawsuit in Federal court there.  Local Phone Alternative WASHINGTON, Feb. 3 (Bloomberg News) -- MCI Worldcom Inc., the No. 2 long-distance phone company in the unitedstates, will immediately begin offering local phone service to residents in newyork State by leasing the Bell Atlantic Corporation's local phone network. MCI Worldcom will offer flat-rate pricing for a local phone line at about 5 percent below Bell Atlantic's service. In the newyork City metropolitan area and surrounding counties, it will also offer customers a basic local phone line and 100 phone calls a month for about $14.99 a month. MCI Worldcom has offered local service to residential customers in some markets, including newyork City, by leasing the complete phone service of the regional phone companies at a discount and reselling it. It discontinued that resale service last year, saying the discounts given by the regional carriers to rivals were not steep enough to be able to make a profit. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Free email Site Cuts Back On Services for Some Users
body: Juno, a newyork company that pioneered the concept of free email, recently announced that thousands of its users would be able to check their email only once a day. The reason, the company said, is that those users live in regions of the country where telecommunications costs are more expensive. Users affected by the change who still want to check email more often must pay $2.95 a month. Charles Ardai, the company's president, said that "fewer than 1 percent" of the company's 6.5 million subscribers were affected. But he was less than reassuring when asked whether he might expand the geographic area falling under the once-a-day for checking email. "I have no opinion about that," he said. While the Juno service is free, users view banner advertisements that appear at the top of messages. The idea of advertising-supported email, and the related concept of advertising-supported Internet access, have attracted many entrepreneurs. But analysts contend that the business model presents difficulties because millions must be spent on marketing and technology to build a subscriber base to attract ads. Mr. Ardai wrote to the subscribers affected by the latest Juno limitation and suggested his motive was not profits, but keeping the service widely available. He asked those subscribers who could afford it to pay $2.95 a month to upgrade their service so they would be helping to subsidize the accounts of members who cannot afford service. "You will be helping us to move closer to this important goal," he wrote, of providing "free email services to all Americans." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Vast Riches and Rude Vagaries of Internet Trading
body: There is perhaps one good thing to say about the exuberant frenzy in Internet stocks: It is opening up the Silicon riches beyond the young boys' club that has hoarded them until now. The latest Internet billionaire, for example, is not some lucky Stanford graduate student or nocturnal Seattle programmer barely past shaving age. Yesterday's billion-dollar lottery ticket was in the hands of Muriel Siebert, a veteran of breaking through glass ceilings for four decades. Mickey Siebert, as she is known to those old enough to remember when electronic trading meant calling your broker on the telephone, caused quite a few waves in 1967 as the first woman to buy a seat on the newyork Stock Exchange. Later, she was the first woman banking superintendent of newyork State. Yesterday, the shares of the Siebert Financial Corporation, the holding company for Ms. Siebert's brokerage firm, soared $23.50, or 90.4 percent, to $49.50. A week ago, the shares traded at $11. The stock's ascent places Ms. Siebert's paper wealth slightly over $1 billion. Siebert Financial has benefited from investors' fascination with on-line trading, which has turned out to be the hottest business on the Internet. In the fourth quarter of 1998, one in every seven stock trades in this country was entered over the Internet, according to Bill Burnham, electronic commerce analyst and trading guru at Credit Suisse First Boston. And in January, he estimates, on-line volume rose by a third. As a result, the shares of any company that offers stock trading on a World Wide Web site has been surging. Even shares of JB Oxford Holdings, a Beverly Hills brokerage firm being investigated on charges of market manipulation, rose 153 percent yesterday, to $12. Never mind that the electronic trading business is hardly easy. The E*Trade Group, despite a $100 million investment in technology, suffered significant system problems yesterday and was unable to accept trades in two periods during the day. Analysts say E*Trade will suffer no long-term damage from the incidents because most of the other on-line firms have also had occasional computer glitches. "It's like handing out speeding tickets at the Indy 500," Mr. Burnham said. "You can pull over whoever you want to." In this fast field, Siebert Financial had been something of an also-ran. The brokerage firm has offered on-line trading for the last several years. But Mr. Burnham says it is a minor player in this market, with no more than a few thousand on-line trades a day. Moreover, the firm hardly has a blue-chip pedigree. It went public in 1996, not through a traditional offering, but by buying a defunct Brooklyn furniture company, a tactic looked down upon by Wall Street. But that hasn't stopped stock traders from seizing on Siebert as potentially a cheaper way to bet on electronic brokerage than by buying the expensive leaders: E*Trade, Ameritrade and Charles Schwab. It's not that many people actually believe that Siebert will be the next E*Trade, but that enough people are willing to bet that someone else will think so. "There is a group of marauding traders who are doing this with their eyes wide open," Mr. Burnham said. "There is talk in the chat rooms; then there is takeover speculation, and finally the stock starts to move, bringing in the momentum players." But there are only 710,000 shares of Siebert Financial that the public can trade, as Ms. Siebert owns 92 percent of the company. Since 10.4 million shares of Siebert Financial traded on the Nasdaq stock market yesterday, the average share changed hands seven times during the day. (Nasdaq counts each trade twice.) What that means, of course, is that the real price of Siebert Financial, should Ms. Siebert choose to sell it, will likely be far less than the value ascribed to it by the market yesterday. "I have no intention of selling any of my stock," Ms. Siebert said in a terse telephone interview. "We've been in business for a long time." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: "Two Faces On Line" Internet trading has helped Siebert Financial, but technical problems that shut down E*Trade for parts of yesterday, gave the stock a hit. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
After the frenzy of Super Sunday, account activity takes center stage again.
body: NOW that Super Bowl XXXIII has gone the way of its XXXII predecessors, Madison Avenue is making its annual turn from funny animals, glitzy special effects and bosomy models to the nuts and bolts of the business: account activity. In the wake of Super Sunday, there have been developments affecting accounts with billings estimated at more than $375 million involving advertisers from the Internet and the breakfast table to Wall Street and the pantry. E*Trade Group Inc., an Internet brokerage firm, is conducting a so-called creative shootout for its traditional advertising account, with billings estimated at $100 million. Executives at E*Trade, which operates a stock-trading Web site at www.etrade.com, have asked the incumbent agency, Gotham in newyork, to offer campaign ideas along with Goodby, Silverstein & Partners in San Francisco, a unit of Omnicom Group that was represented on the Super Bowl with the "really big bag" spot for Cracker Jack and the commercials for Anheuser-Busch about a swamp shootout between the Budweiser frogs and Louie the lizard. Michael Sievert, vice president for marketing at E*Trade in Palo Alto, Calif., confirmed reports of the review this week in the trade publications Advertising Age and Adweek. He said that E*Trade wanted to explore what new perspectives Goodby, Silverstein might bring to the business. The on-line portion of the account remains at Modem Media.Poppe Tyson in Westport, Conn., a unit of True North Communications. F. Stone Roberts, co-chairman and chief executive at Gotham, a unit of the Interpublic Group of Companies, said that he had not yet decided whether his agency would take part in the shootout. "We may end up standing behind the work we have produced," he added. "I have a high degree of confidence what we've done has been incredibly effective." The current campaign for E*Trade carries the theme "Someday, we'll all invest this way." Gotham has handled the traditional, or off-line, part of the E*Trade account for two years. The on-line brokerage industry has become increasingly competitive; at least two E*Trade rivals have recently changed agencies. A more familiar investment name, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company, completed a review for its consolidated media account, with billings estimated at $200 million, by naming Starcom Media Services in Chicago for media buying. Leigh Pierce, a spokeswoman for Morgan Stanley in newyork, described the consolidation as "a cost-saving measure." She declined to identify the other participants in the review; Advertising Age reported that Starcom, a unit of the Leo Burnett Company, was selected in a shootout with Optimum Media in newyork, part of the DDB Needham Worldwide unit of Omnicom. The Morgan Stanley media duties had been divided among agencies including Starcom, DDB Needham and Black Rocket in San Francisco, for Discover Brokerage Direct. The Starcom gain was the most recent in a series that has brought in accounts with billings estimated at more than $500 million from advertisers like the Budget Rent-a-Car Corporation, the Ralston Purina Company and the Sara Lee Corporation. Speaking of Burnett, the agency landed additional assignments from a longtime client, the Kellogg Company, which shifted two products there from another roster agency, J. Walter Thompson USA in newyork, owned by WPP Group P.L.C. Anthony T. Hebron, a spokesman for Kellogg in Battle Creek, Mich., confirmed a report in Advertising Age that the company had reassigned some brands but declined to discuss them. However, advertising executives close to Kellogg's agency relations identified them as Honey Crunch Corn Flakes and an undisclosed new product, which join brands at Burnett like Corn Flakes and Special K. Thompson continues handling brands like Raisin Bran and the new Country Inn Specialties line. Though Bob Jeffrey, president at Thompson newyork, declined to discuss the changes, referring inquiries to Kellogg, he did acknowledge that the agency had named "a new core team" for the Kellogg account in North America as part of plans to "make sure we have the right resources for every client." John Clinton, chairman at Thompson Canada in Toronto, was named to the additional duties of running the Kellogg North American business, Mr. Jeffrey said, along with Kay Allison, as head strategic planner, and Alan Platt, as creative director. Norman A. MacMaster will continue as executive vice president and global business director for the Kellogg account, Mr. Jeffrey said. As Thompson lost business from one client, the agency gained assignments from another, the Coty unit of Joh. A. Benckiser G.m.b.H., which named the Thompson London office to introduce its Rimmel brand of cosmetics in 27 countries this year. The worldwide advertising and marketing budget for the year was estimated at more than $40 million. Rimmel, described as Britain's top-selling cosmetics line, has been handled by Thompson offices in that country and five other markets: Eastern Europe, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Scandinavia. Finally, the Clorox Company in Oakland, Calif., named roster agencies to handle products added to its lineup with the acquisition of the First Brands Corporation, completed last week. Under its previous ownership, First Brands in June awarded those assignments, with billings estimated at $30 million to $40 million, to McCann-Erickson Worldwide Advertising in newyork, part of the McCann-Erickson World Group unit of Interpublic. DDB Needham San Francisco, which handles bleaches, household cleaning products and Armor All automotive products for Clorox, adds the STP automotive products line and the Glad line of plastic bags, wraps and containers. The San Francisco office of Young & Rubicam Advertising, which handles Clorox brands in categories like charcoal, cat litter and water filtration, adds the Jonny Cat and Scoop Away cat litter brands and Hearthlogg fire logs and starters. There were also assignments covering all the former First Brands brands. The duties for campaigns aimed at Spanish-speaking consumers were awarded to Bravo Group in San Francisco, a unit of Y.& R. Media planning duties were assigned to Diamond Communications in San Francisco, a joint venture of DDB Needham and Clorox. And media buying was dispatched to the Media Edge in newyork, a unit of Y.& R. All the Clorox changes are effective on May 1 -- only 274 days to Super Bowl XXXIV on Jan. 30, 2000.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: America Online to Buy Moviefone for $388 Million in Stock
body: Mr. Moviefone is hooking up with the "You've got mail" man. America Online said yesterday that it had agreed to buy Moviefone Inc. for stock valued at $388 million, linking two companies notable for their sonorous spokesmen. Moviefone provides movie show times and sells tickets through the 777-FILM telephone service and the Moviefone.com Internet site. Most of its $20 million in annual revenue represents advertising from movie studios promoting films. But about 20 percent of its sales come from commissions on tickets purchased through the service. The deal is the latest in an aggressive expansion effort by America Online, which has agreed to buy a range of Internet-related companies, most recently the Netscape Communications Corporation. Yet the Moviefone acquisition is a departure of sorts for America Online, which has mainly served as an advertising medium for other companies that do business on line. "This is the first time that America Online has bought something that can be considered a commerce company," said Keith Benjamin, a BancBoston Robertson Stephens analyst. Barry Schuler, president of America Online's flagship service, said the company wanted to make acquisitions in areas in which electronic commerce would be important. "We really like businesses where the on-line medium will transform them in the future," he said. "And we think that movies are sort of thing that people will be doing on line more and more." America Online said it would promote Moviefone prominently on its various on-line services, especially Digital Cities, its network of local guides. The Moviefone.com site will be expanded to include more information about films, creating more positions for advertising. America Online, which is based in Dulles, Va., also wants to expand the service to offer ticketing for live events as well as movies. "We think that electronic ticketing has a lot of upside and is at its very early stages," Mr. Schuler said. That would open another front of competition with Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch Inc., the company that recently combined operations of the nation's leading live-event ticketing service with a local-information Internet service. The company is controlled by USA Networks Inc. Separately, Mr. Schuler said America Online saw an opportunity to use Moviefone's phone line and links to theaters as a way to promote the America Online brand. The service will be renamed AOL Moviefone. Moviefone, which is based in newyork, sells tickets for about 4,000 of the nation's 27,000 movie screens, though it represents about 60 percent of the screens in the five biggest markets: newyork, Los Angeles, Boston, Chicago and San Francisco. In newyork, it has a reciprocal promotion arrangement with The newyork Times, among others. The Times offers Moviefone promotional advertising space in return for its sponsorship mention on Moviefone's recorded message. Andrew Jarecki, Moviefone's chief executive, said he had been looking to sell the business to an Internet company for several months. "I've always thought that the Internet would be an important part of our business, but I've been surprised by how tremendously fast it has grown," he said, adding that 25 percent of the three million Moviefone users each week already use the company's World Wide Web site rather than its phone service. Moviefone shares trade on the Nasdaq market, but the Jarecki family controls 73 percent of the company's equity and 92 percent of its votes. For the quarter ended Sept. 30, 1998, the company showed a loss of $920,000 on revenue of $5.5 million. The deal values Moviefone at $29.25 a share. With rumors of a deal swirling yesterday, the company's shares closed up $1.50, to $26.50, after trading as high as $33. America Online's shares fell $4.5625, to $171.1875, on the newyork Stock Exchange. "You will see even more consolidation like this," said David Readerman, an analyst with Thomas Weisel Partners in San Francisco. "The leaders want to bulk up so the strong will get stronger." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Patents;
A dangerous monopoly? Paying computer users to read Internet ads and then storing their data.
body: THE basic premise of Cybergold, an electronic commerce company in Berkeley, Calif., is that the best way to get consumers to read Internet advertisements is to pay them to do so. It finds advertisers willing to pay people who sign up at its World Wide Web site (www.cybergold.com) and look at the ads; then it compensates consumers who demonstrate in some way that they have read an ad by crediting an account in the consumer's name. Amounts range from 50 cents for downloading America Online software to $100 for referring a new paid-up subscriber to the At Home Internet service. Once enough money accumulates in a consumer's account, it can be put in a bank account by direct deposit, used to pay credit card bills or sent to a favorite charity. Cybergold recently received its second patent covering the concept of offering incentives to people to pay attention to ads. But the company's patents cover two other intriguing approaches to advertising in cyberspace. The first is a way for consumers to store direct-marketing information about themselves on their computers -- like their income bracket, ZIP code, hobbies and profession -- so they can be compensated every time they decide to release such information to advertisers. "The notion here is that the information about you belongs to you and doesn't belong to anybody else," Mr. Goldhaber said. "And you can decide when you release it and whether you want to be paid for it globally or on an ad hoc basis." The patents also cover a way of turning conventional advertising-based publishing on its head. In Mr. Goldhaber's patented Internet publishing system, which he said the company planned to introduce in coming months, on-line authors or other creators of on-line content would not paid a set fee by a publisher. Instead, they would receive a tiny commission from each new reader, who in turn has been paid to read an accompanying advertisement. Cybergold would act as a clearinghouse for these transactions, effectively cutting out the role of a publisher. "First you get paid to see the ads and then you use that to pay for the content," he said. "You change the flow of money. But you don't change the basic setup, which is that advertising supports publishing." Mr. Goldhaber contends that these are concepts that empower individuals who want to self-publish or consumers who want to compensated for their time. But he and Gary Fitts, co-founder of Cybergold, are coming under fire for having patented these ways of doing business. Jamie Love, director of the Consumer Project on Technology in Washington, said he would press Congress to conduct hearings on Cybergold's patents as well as other so-called business-methods patents. Mr. Love said he disagreed with the idea that Cybergold's system was novel enough to be patented, contending that he had written articles on a similar concept back in the 1980's. "And I didn't consider myself the inventor then," he said. "This is typical of the poor quality of review they give at the Patent and Trademark Office for this sort of thing." Mr. Love described as "dangerous" the legal monopoly that these patents provide, arguing that politicians would likely use such cash incentives to get potential voters to read their material on line. "Suppose one candidate in a given campaign were the only one to be given a license to the patent," he said. "He would be the only one who could disseminate information this way." Mr. Goldhaber conceded that politicians would probably use the system, noting that while it is illegal to buy votes, it is not illegal to pay voters to read political tracts. "Instead of offering a drink down at the bar for coming to a rally," he said, "you can offer a buck and let them go down to the bar and buy their own drink." But he argued that Mr. Love's concerns were unfounded. "The Internet is not just about hackers anymore," he said. "It's about real business. If patents are valid in other arenas, they ought to be valid on the Internet as well. People who globally criticize patents on the Internet are just wrong." Cybergold most recently received patent 5,855,008.  Angry Internet Jousting Over Simulated Warfare Computer programmers were busy spewing vitriol last week on Slashdot, an Internet site (www.slashdot.org) that proclaims itself as specializing in "news for nerds," over another Internet patent. The patent, assigned to Rtime, of Seattle, covers certain aspects of playing three-dimensional games on the Internet. One aspect is a type of real-time data filtering that insures that only relevant data is distributed to participants. Another is a global time base that keeps different users synchronized within milliseconds. "Any time you have two or more people distributed across the Internet that want to act in real time, you have to resolve slow performance issues," said Chip Overstreet, chief executive of Rtime, a company with eight full-time employees. Mr. Overstreet said the technology was developed by programmers who helped build the unitedstates military's Simnet, a virtual-reality system used to train soldiers for combat. Some of those weighing in on Slashdot wondered whether Rtime would try to extract a licensing fee each time someone tried to play private sessions of Doom or Quake or other three-dimensional games over the Internet. Mr. Overstreet declined to comment specifically on the remarks made on Slashdot. Michael Snoswell, a founder of Cyberterm, a software company in Adelaide, Australia, was one of those who derided the patent on Slashdot. But after reading the patent carefully, he said in a telephone interview, he was less concerned. "The animosity over this patent arose because it was seen as cornering the market," he said. "Initially, when you read the patent you think it covers everything. But then when you read the fine print, it looks a lot more narrow. It's not going to become a generic solution over time. It wouldn't surprise me that this will fit a niche market. But eventually that niche market will get smaller and smaller as other technologies crowd it out of the market." Patent 5,841,980 was granted to Rolland M. Waters and John Allred and was assigned to Rtime. Patents are available by number for $3 from the Patent and Trademark Office, Washington, D.C. 20231. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Small On-Line Brokers Raise Share of Trades
body: In a new world order that is melding Wall Street and Silicon Valley, the business of buying and selling stocks for smaller investors is being shaped as much by lesser-known on-line brokerage firms as it is by the big brand-name firms. While Charles Schwab & Company and E*Trade have established themselves as the most recognizable on-line names, the fastest-growing firms are Waterhouse Securities, a discount broker turned on-line provider that does relatively little advertising, and Datek Online, a broker that caters to what some in the business call "hyperactive traders." And that, analysts say, is another hint that when it comes to the retail market -- that is, smaller investors -- the shape of things to come may be trickling up from below. "All the big Wall Street firms are looking at how these companies are shaping on-line trading," said Bernard L. Madoff, a member of the Securities Industry Association, which represents many of the big investment houses. "Nobody at this point can or should ignore it; it's not a passing fancy." So while on-line trading grew by a record 34 percent in the fourth quarter, according to a study by Credit Suisse First Boston, a number of large banks and Wall Street firms have been trying to find ways to buy into that success. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter is tapping into the market through its on-line subsidiary, Discover Brokerage; Merrill Lynch is planning its own on-line operation, though not so geared toward active trading, and Goldman, Sachs & Company and E*Trade recently joined forces to invest $50 million in Archipelago, a computerized system that electronically matches stock trades. The system is not unlike Island E.C.N., an electronic communication network developed by Datek. Trading volume in Island -- which some call an electronic stock exchange -- has been explosive in the last year. It is many times larger than Archipelago, analysts say, and according to the Nasdaq stock market, it is the leading trader in such stocks as Yahoo and Amazon.com. "All this Internet technology has been developed on the edge of the market, and now it's moving to the core," said Bill Burnham, an analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston. Indeed, officials at Datek say that Island, which gets much of its business from active day traders, or speculators, now accounts for about 10 percent of all Nasdaq volume. Datek says it is gaining on Instinet, the electronic system owned by Reuters, which matches institutional trades. "If we're not really ahead of them, we're in striking distance," said Robert Bethge, a spokesman for Datek. Instinet officials, however, say that there are numerous complications in counting stock trades. A spokesman, Terry Mulry, also says that Instinet's market share in Nasdaq has remained consistent over the last few years. But no one doubts that Island has become a force in the industry, one big enough to attract the interest of E*Trade, which officials close to the company say was at one time in talks to either shuttle its trades through Datek's system or acquire the system. Because of the tremendous success of on-line brokerage firms, shares of Schwab, E*Trade and Ameritrade have been soaring in recent months. And last week, the Toronto-Dominion Bank, which owns Waterhouse Securities, said that it would consider spinning off a portion of the brokerage firm to the public. A sticking point with the smaller on-line brokerage firms, though, is that many on Wall Street are wary of linking up with a firm whose fortunes are tied too heavily to speculative, volatile trading in Internet stocks, in which companies like Datek specialize. Even on-line brokers like E*Trade are moving toward more mainstream customers whose trading activity may be more steady and less volatile. "It's not uncommon for day traders to trade 60 times a day," said Mr. Madoff, who also operates Bernard L. Madoff Securities, a market-making firm. "This is not investing; it's a casino mentality. Very few Wall Street firms want to be involved in on-line day trading. There's a lot of risk involved." Datek has another problem. Last May, the Manhattan District Attorney's office said it was investigating whether Datek had taken part in a money-laundering operation as well as other possibly fraudulent activity related to a day-trading subsidiary that had been spun off a little earlier. Datek officials have denied any wrongdoing and called such accusations "baseless and defamatory." Analysts say that smaller companies like Datek have been leading the push toward faster, more efficient trading technologies. Datek is now considering registering Island as an independent stock exchange with the Securities and Exchange Commission. If the S.E.C. approves this, some analysts say, Island could further reduce transaction costs and possibly even generate stock-quotation revenue that now goes to the Nasdaq market. Joseph Ricketts, president of Ameritrade, which is one of the largest on-line brokers, says his firm is also considering linking up with an electronic communication network, or E.C.N. "If you register as a stock exchange, you can charge for quotes," Mr. Ricketts said. "The Nasdaq and the newyork Stock Exchange make hundreds of millions of dollars selling quotes. That money doesn't belong to the exchanges; it belongs to the customers. One way we can get it back is through an E.C.N." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "On Line, No Shortage of Brokers" The on-line brokerage industry, which now handles about one in seven stock trades, is becoming more competitive, with some upstarts, like Datek and Waterhouse, beginning to challenge more-established firms, like Schwab and E*Trade. title:
TECHNOLOGY;
The Privacy Group ThatTook On Intel
body: Their small office is tucked away in Washington's eclectic Eastern Market area, bordering the seedier side of Capitol Hill. The hours are long, the pay low and the benefits modest. With an annual budget of just $250,000 to cover salaries for three full-time lawyers and three half-time helpers, they don't even have a fax line. Yet with just the touch of the button, employees of the Electronic Privacy Information Center can reach more than 10,000 people, an international audience that is educated and technologically savvy. Perhaps that is why executives from the Intel Corporation, facing a boycott from the privacy center over an identification feature in Intel's new computer chip, traveled across the country on Thursday to meet with the center's lawyers, Marc Rotenberg, Dave Banisar and David L. Sobel, aggressive advocates for protecting privacy and civil rights in the digital age. "We don't have fancy K Street offices," Mr. Banisar said, referring to the capital street that is home to many lobbyists. "We don't have fancy K Street salaries." "But," Mr. Rotenberg said, "we know how to use the Web. And on the Web, this stuff really spreads like wildfire." Indeed, just hours after the privacy center and two other groups, Junkbusters and the Electronic Frontier Foundation, announced their planned boycott of Intel, the world's largest computer chip maker, the company reversed a plan to activate an identifying signature in its soon-to-be-released Pentium III chip. Privacy advocates say the feature, intended to enhance the security of electronic commerce and safeguard against software piracy, would make it easy for on-line marketers, even governments, to track people on the Internet. Although questions were being raised by more groups than just the privacy center, the boycott did play an important role in Intel's decision to review its plans for the Pentium III, an Intel spokesman, Tom Waldrop, said. "I think it is safe to say that the concerns were heightened greatly by the three privacy groups' issuing the threat of the boycott, but those concerns were not new," Mr. Waldrop said. "We had heard them from others, just not as strong." Founded in 1994, the Electronic Privacy Information Center is one of several on-line civil liberties groups that are playing an increasingly visible role in the shaping of policy for the digital age. It has often focused on the Government, earning a pit-bull reputation in fights with the Clinton Administration over export controls on computer security technology, or encryption, and the Administration's refusal to pass Internet privacy laws. But it also has no hesitation about going after the high-technology companies that are its allies on other issues. And the privacy center has been quite successful defending the Internet user. Mr. Sobel, a 45-year-old Miami native, played an important role in two disputes with America Online, one a successful challenge to the company's plan to sell customer information to marketers, the other a high-profile lawsuit over the company's release of personal information on a gay sailor that resulted in his discharge. America Online has since vowed to keep such personal information about its customers private. Mr. Rotenberg, a 38-year-old Boston native, is credited by some with starting the digital age privacy movement in 1991 with a campaign that forced Lotus to abandon plans for releasing a CD-ROM for marketers with personal information gathered by Equifax Inc., one of the nation's largest credit bureaus. Mr. Banisar, a 32-year-old native of Baltimore, has dedicated a lot of his time recently to studying international encryption laws, writing reports challenging the Administration's claims that its desire to control the technology is a position supported by a majority of countries. The group has used the Freedom of Information Act to monitor the Government's actions, and has been the first to disclose, among other things, the Federal Bureau of Investigation's desire to redesign the telephone system to ease wiretapping. "I think EPIC right now is sort of the pre-eminent privacy advocacy group in the unitedstates," said Joel Reidenberg, a professor at Fordham University Law School in newyork and an expert on international privacy laws. "Marc Rotenberg has really taken the lead on privacy issues in pushing American public policy toward strong, fair information practices." Lance J. Hoffman, a computer science professor who heads the Cyberspace Policy Institute at George Washington University in Washington, called the group "the closest thing to a sort of consumer ombudsman for privacy that we have in cyberspace." Even Ira C. Magaziner, who as President Clinton's top Internet adviser often drew EPIC's harshest criticisms, said the group played an important role in tough policy decisions. "I think that as an advocacy group it is their role to be a kind of burr in the saddle of policy makers," he said. "And in a sense it is not always their job to be completely reasonable. It is their job to make noise and get press attention. And I think they do that very effectively." Mr. Rotenberg, Mr. Sobel and Mr. Banisar formed the privacy center after working together in the Washington office of the Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility. Much of their financing comes from the Fund for Constitutional Government, a nonprofit organization dedicated to protecting civil liberties. They also receive money from other organizations and, occasionally, companies. The privacy center has perhaps been most visible in the encryption debate. It has also strongly opposed the Administration's continued call for self-regulation of the privacy practices of on-line marketers, pushing instead for laws to protect consumers. It has joined the American Civil Liberties Union and other groups in their fights against on-line censorship, and has worked with Congress on privacy issues involving automated health care records, Social Security and copyright and data base protections. And the list keeps growing. "This is the environmental issue of the 21st century," Mr. Banisar said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Marc Rotenberg, from left, Dave Banisar and David L. Sobel of the Electronic Privacy Information Center oppose plans to include identification features in a computer chip. (Marty Katz for The newyork Times)

title: Worries About Big Brother at America Online - Correction Appended
body: Like the divided generations of Irish before them, the two opposing camps of contributors to America Online's discussion group on Ireland rarely agree on anything. But when the world's leading on-line service suspended their contentious electronic debate last month, participants on both sides were united in their dismay. "Don't stop just to appease the AOL Thought Police," one proponent of a united Ireland wrote to the Unionist contingent. "I'd much rather have someone vehemently disagree with me than know that anyone has been silenced!" America Online reopened its Irish Heritage discussion after a 17-day "cooling off" period, and if there was a strangely muted quality to the contributions at first, things are mostly back to normal. The politics folder, which now bears the slogan "a place for cordial political debate in the spirit of harmony," has spawned more than 12,000 of the usual postings regarding British treason and Sinn Fein terrorism since the beginning of the year. But the episode has fed a growing discomfort with the social and political power America Online has come to wield by dint of its surging popularity and its unusual purview over individual communication. And it underscores the challenges the company may face as it seeks to maintain both civil discourse and satisfied customers while presiding over 180,000 continuing conversations on topics from the teen-age idols 'N Sync to Presidential impeachment. Balancing free expression with civility has always been a struggle for America Online and other electronic publishers that provide areas where people can voice their opinions by typing them into the ether. But it is America Online's scope combined with its editorial control that some critics say is cause for concern. With 15 million subscribers, America Online is now the gateway to cyberspace for more Americans than the next 15 largest Internet service providers combined, according to a report released last week by the International Data Corporation, a market research firm. This week, announcing strong earnings, the company said 1.6 million accounts were added in the last three months of 1998 alone. But some members have begun to chafe at its definition of civility, or at least the way it seems sometimes arbitrarily applied. And some civil liberties advocates say the service deserves closer scrutiny as a new breed of institution that governs speech and yet is immune from First Amendment claims. A flurry of recent clashes in discussion areas ranging from race relations to fiction writing have served to heighten concerns over the company's more subtle methods of monitoring the discussions on its message boards -- on-line discussions that subscribers can follow and contribute to over time, as distinct from the simultaneous and sometimes chaotic (but also monitored) exchanges in "chat rooms." In particular, some subscribers cite the on-line service's practice of deleting message board postings without explanation and of attaching the equivalent of demerit marks to the accounts of individuals deemed to have offended another subscriber.  Who Decides What's Offensive? "The question is, who gets to decide what's 'offensive?' " says Renee Rosenblum-Lowden of Riegelsville, Pa., who recalls being cited for a violation for posting a message in a debate on abortion advising an opponent, "If you can't stand the heat get out of the kitchen." Under America Online's contract, referred to among members as TOS, for "terms of service," all subscribers promise not to "harass, threaten, embarrass, or do anything else to another member that is unwanted." Often transgressions are reported to America Online by other discussion group participants, whose identities are not released to those accused. According to the company's subscriber contract, three such violations may result in the suspension or termination of an account. Ms. Rosenblum-Lowden -- whose screen name is now "Prejteach 2" because her "Prejteach" account was closed -- says she and a group who take part in discussions on the Women in Action board have been picked as targets for complaints by those who disagree with their liberal views. "Unlike a court of law, you don't face your accusers," she said. "That gives people free rein." America Online officials concede that judging what is unduly offensive in often-complex political disputes or long-running personal battles can be tricky, especially given the volume and range of messages. That is why the company has enlisted nearly 14,000 volunteers to patrol the boards, and employs a group of about 100 known as the Community Action Team to determine when a comment crosses the line. In intervening in conversations between its users, America Online says its objective is to maintain a sense of community. Although legal liability for libelous statements appearing on its boards was once more of a concern, a provision of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 essentially grants on-line services immunity from prosecution over such matters, characterizing them as a "common carrier" like a telephone company -- simply a means by which information is transmitted, with no responsibility for the information itself. Most terms-of-service violations are handled case by case. In an extreme case like the Irish board, where dozens of violations were being reported every day by the most active participants, the company said there were enough profane and offensive postings that it became necessary to shut down the whole discussion. The discussion archives, which sometimes remain on the service for several years, were wiped clean during the weeks that the board was shut down, so no trace remains. "There's a certain amount of judgment required in situations on whether something is particularly harassing or threatening of other members," said Katherine Boursecnik, America Online's vice president for network programming. "That's where things get the most difficult. We train people to be agnostic about the specific content and to look more at things like tone: Is it threatening, harassing, profane, vulgar?" But given the well-documented tendency of normally sober citizens to act out on line, the problems of privacy protection and threats to minors -- as well as Congressional efforts to regulate on-line speech -- Ms. Boursecnik said the company's supervisory policies were necessary to provide the open atmosphere its customers wanted. "We are a service that prides ourselves on having a wide-ranging appeal to a wide range of individuals," she added. "But at the same time we're also a family service."  For Some, Control Is Seen as a Virtue Indeed, for many subscribers, America Online's virtue is its controlled environment. A members-only on-line service distinct from the unfettered Internet, America Online has achieved market dominance by promoting itself as a place where families and first-time Internet users can feel comfortable. While members can venture out into the World Wide Web and other parts of the Internet from the on-line service, many seldom do, preferring America Online's relative safety and familiarity. The service is far from the only Internet discussion area to enforce its own standards of acceptable speech. Popular Web destinations like the search and directory site Yahoo, discussion-oriented sites like Theglobe.com, and sites operated by traditional publishers (including The newyork Times) reserve the right to remove postings on the message boards they provide to Internet users. And those who find America Online's terms unacceptable can always go to another on-line service, or to the Internet's entirely unmonitored forums called news groups. But America Online's extraordinary market dominance, critics argue, makes it the only place in practical terms for a growing number of people to speak their mind in cyberspace. Many Internet users find the unmoderated news groups too technically complex to use and too overrun with advertising to be productive for discussion. Since it serves as an Internet service provider, America Online has a far more potent enforcement mechanism for its rules than most other discussion areas on the Web. Since subscribers pay a monthly fee with a credit card, the company can bar individuals from logging on -- thereby denying them, among other things, access to E-mail. "America Online is the operating system of the Internet," said Andrew L. Shapiro, the First Amendment fellow at the Brennan Center for Justice at newyork University Law School, comparing the service to the Microsoft Corporation's Windows operating system, which runs on 90 percent of the world's personal computers. "We've moved distressingly close to the model that the Internet was supposed to replace, which is a couple of big companies having a disproportionate amount of control over the information market," Mr. Shapiro added. "A good argument can be made that AOL needs to take on more responsibility for protecting free speech, whether courts require it or consumers simply demand it." Although some subscribers, like John Navin, 38, of Mount Lake Terrace, Wash., said he had dropped his America Online account to protest the Irish board shutdown, others dissatisfied with its interventions remain with the service out of choice, habit or necessity.  Going Elsewhere Is Not an Option When Sheila Fahey found the Irish discussion shuttered last month, for example, she and others tried to migrate their discussion to a site on the World Wide Web called Ireland Uncensored. But she found the forum confusing and too difficult to follow. Instead, she says she and several other Irish nationalists now screen each other's postings before making them public to vet them for possible terms-of-service violations. "We've all learned not to use first-person pronouns," said Ms. Fahey, 41, a paralegal in Chicago. "If an English teacher looked at some of our postings, they are so passive-language-filled they'd have a cow." (When the discussion was reopened, the monitor posted a message pleading for harmony: "We encourage you to make this a more amiable place where any person, regardless of faction, can openly discuss political issues and current events.") For Robin Olderman, 54, a high school English teacher in Houston, it means putting up with what she describes as feeling like a kid in a playground whose friends go running to the teacher. "I take issue with the way the rules are enforced arbitrarily," said Ms. Olderman, who is currently operating under a "mutual nonharassment notice" from America Online explaining that she and another subscriber are never to speak to each other via the service again. Perhaps more disturbing to some subscribers is the removal of postings from message boards. On the Writers Club board, which like many areas of America Online is administered by a separate company that contracts with the service, more than a dozen of the most active participants over the last several years recently left en masse after the board monitors began removing their postings and reporting terms-of-service violations more frequently to the Community Action Team. The writers now congregate on a board called "Sanctuary" in the American Civil Liberties Union area on America Online, where the terms-of-service rules do not apply. On the race relations message board, Jay Lutsky, 31, of Edison, N.J., said he compared an active participant who accused everyone on the board of being his enemy to Robespierre, the French Jacobin leader responsible for the revolution's Reign of Terror. It was removed by monitors after the other participant said it was slander. "I said it was opinion; I'm entitled," Mr. Lutsky, a teacher, said. "I understand AOL is a large private corporation, and I guess it's technically their property, but I don't think it should be allowed to interfere with the First Amendment rights of people." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  A front-page article on Jan. 31 about America Online's role in monitoring individual communication misspelled the surname of the company's vice president for network programming. She is Katherine Borsecnick, not Boursecnik. Correction-Date: February 12, 1999, Friday Graphic   Photo: Renee Rosenblum-Lowden and her husband, Michael, in Riegelsville, Pa. title: Inflated Stocks Cushion Pitfalls Of Net Mergers
body: A handful of leading companies will come to dominate cyberspace. That snippet of rhetoric has become all the analytical underpinning there is to justify the unprecedented stock market values of the prominent Internet companies like Yahoo, America Online and Amazon.com. On the face of it, that well could be true. On the other hand, the Internet may make it easier for new competitors to constantly challenge the leaders. Yet one of the byproducts of the irrational exuberance in Internet stock prices is that the prophesied greatness of certain companies becomes self-fulfilling. Their huge market values allow them to grow by acquisitions. Look at the $3.6 billion purchase announced yesterday by the investors' darling Internet site, Yahoo, of Geocities, the leading creator of electronic communities organized around people's hobbies, passions and peccadilloes. Geocities is, in fact, an extreme example of the sort of tantalizing potential implicit in many Internet companies. It is the fifth- most-trafficked Web site, on which 3.5 million people have created home pages that were viewed 53 million times a day in December. Geocities has the right to put advertising on or next to all of those pages, but in all of 1998, its revenues totaled a meager $18.4 million. (Profits? Nah. It lost $19.8 million last year, double the loss of a year before.) Those modest (to be generous) fundamentals did not stop investors from valuing Geocities at $2.2 billion on Wednesday, before the acquisition was announced. With that price tag, Geocities was essentially too expensive for any company, no matter how big, for which traditional rules of finance applied. But Yahoo, which has a market value of $38 billion, an infinite multiple of its just more than break-even earnings, was easily able to exchange its shares for those of Geocities without breaking a sweat. Indeed, Yahoo's offer of stock worth $113.66 for each Geocities share, was a 52 percent premium over the company's share price Wednesday. Nonetheless, because Yahoo's value is so high -- and the price it paid represents only about 10 percent of its shares -- Yahoo is telling investors that the deal will have no effect on its per-share earnings after it closes in the second quarter. Indeed Yahoo is promising that it can turn around Geocities and make it add to earnings next year. As is usual with Internet stocks, investors leaped at any sign of motion. Yahoo's stock surged by $31.875, to $367.75. Normally, companies' stocks fall when they announce expensive acquisitions. Thus the market is in many ways encouraging the big companies like Yahoo to buy up other Internet companies. The same economics has been behind the other Net deals recently, including the purchase of Excite by At Home and of Netscape by America Online. And many analysts expect Amazon to make some big acquisitions, as well. But while the mystical multiplication of the stock market limits Yahoo's risk from buying Geocities, the potential rewards from turning the site's huge audience into profits will come much harder. "Yahoo's plans to seek incremental revenue from Geocities are difficult to see," said Brian C. Oakes, an analyst at Lehman Brothers. "If I have a Web page that says I love the newyork Jets, who will want to advertise there if they don't control the content?" Yahoo does have a bigger advertising sales staff than Geocities does and has technical resources that can cut that company's costs. Moreover, Jeff Mallett, Yahoo's president, says the company sees two areas beyond advertising on the home pages for growth at Geocities. First, it hopes that people who publish home pages will include links to related stores on their pages. For example, a page on cooking would have a link to a kitchen supply site, which in turn would pay a commission on any sales that would be split by Yahoo and the creator of the site. In addition, Yahoo sees Geocities as a great source of information about the interests of both the creators of the home pages and the people who look at them. It hopes to use this information to expand the profiles it is creating about people's interests -- profiles it uses to send people electronic mail with advertising customized to their particular interests. Yet whether or not Geocities ever produces much in incremental profits for Yahoo, the acquisition may well pay for itself simply by bolstering Yahoo's perceived "leadership" in the market. Most important, Geocities will substantially strengthen Yahoo's position in the highly watched Media Metrix rating of how many people visit a Web site at least once in a month, a measure they call reach. Yahoo's sites now rank third, reaching 48.2 percent of the Internet audience. All of America Online's properties combined reach 54.5 percent of the audience, while Microsoft's sites reach 48.4 percent. Geocities, by itself, reaches 33.4 percent of Web users. Though Yahoo's reach has mostly been flat, Lycos, another Internet service known as a portal because it is a gateway to other on-line services, has been climbing the rating charts. The main reason is that it has been buying up other sites including many of the community sites that compete with Geocities. All of the Lycos sites in December had a reach of 46.5 percent of the audience. Even amid constant speculation that Lycos will soon be acquired, it is worth $5.3 billion, a huge number but a small fraction of the value of Yahoo. Many Lycos investors, as well as its management, were hoping that if it were able to surge past Yahoo, it might well gain some of the market value accorded to leaders. "You can never have too much cash or too much reach," said Chris A. Kitze, the chairman of Xoom.com, a community site that competes with Geocities. No such luck, Lycos. With Geocities, Yahoo says its reach will increase to 58 percent of the Web audience, an undisputed top position, for now. And that will allow the magic multiplication of Internet stock values to keep working and let the company make even more acquisitions, just maybe allowing it to fulfill the prophecies of its cyber-dominance. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "The New Cybermath" The substantial value placed on Internet companies by investors --despite the scarcity of profits in the industry -- has fueled a spate of mergers among the most popular sites. Yesterday, Yahoo agreed to buy Geocities for $3.6 billion. Last week, At Home agreed to pay $6.7 billion for Excite. And late last year, America Online agreed to pay $4.2 billion for Netscape.
