title: America Online's Profit Rises Significantly
body: America Online continued to show vigorous growth and improving profitability in the latest quarter, earning $122 million on sales of $960 million, the company said yesterday. That profit included $33 million in tax breaks carried forward from the company's earlier losses. Excluding those benefits, America Online would have earned $88 million, or 17 cents a diluted share, in the quarter ended Dec. 31, up 349 percent from $19.6 million, or 4 cents a share, in the period a year earlier. That exceeded the 14 cents a share that analysts have been forecasting. Revenue was up 62 percent from $592 million. America Online continues to maintain the lion's share of the market for Internet access in homes and small business. In the quarter, the company's fiscal second quarter, America Online increased its subscriptions by 1.6 million, to 15.1 million. Advertising continued to be increasingly important to the company, although monthly subscription fees are still its biggest source of revenue. Subscription revenue in the latest quarter was $779 million, up 61 percent. Advertising revenue was $126 million, up 133 percent. Advertising represented $4.25 a subscriber a month, a sharp increase from $3.10 a month a year earlier. Shares of America Online rose $10.50, to $165.50. The company also announced a 2-for-1 stock split. http://www.nytimes.com

title: As On-Line Trading Increases, So Do Complaints
body: One of the millions of small investors who have recently flocked to cyberspace placed an order through his on-line brokerage account for a hot new Internet stock, Theglobe.com, thinking it would cost between $15 and $25 a share. His order was filled for 2,300 shares, at a price of $90 a share and a bill of $207,000 -- nearly $150,000 more than he expected. Another investor placed an order on his personal computer to sell 30 shares of a different company, never got an electronic confirmation, and so placed the sell order again, winding up selling 60 shares, twice the amount of shares he had held. A third investor tried to cancel an order to buy 45 shares of a stock and received an acknowledgement that his cancellation order had been received. But the sale went through anyway, and the investor wound up purchasing the stock. The three are among hundreds of investors who have recently complained to the Securities and Exchange Commission, which reported today that the record amount of on-line trading -- now 25 percent of all retail trading and growing fast -- has also brought a record number of complaints. Most commonly, investors report sharp discrepancies between the prices they see on their PC screens and the prices they wind up paying. As of Sept. 30, the number of complaints had risen 330 percent from the previous year, to 1,114. In more recent weeks, with new issues of volatile Internet and technology stocks coming to market at prices that are seducing new investors into trying to get rich quick, S.E.C. officials report that the complaints are coming in faster than they can be processed. The growing problems prompted Arthur Levitt, the S.E.C. chairman, to caution small investors who have swarmed onto the Internet to approach on-line investing with care. In addition to keeping the fundamentals of investing in mind, he said, investors should take such precautions as placing limits on the prices of buy and sell orders to avoid the recurring kinds of problems that are plaguing the emerging group of small traders called cybervestors. "Investors need to remember the investment basics, and not allow the ease and speed with which they trade to lull them either into a false sense of security or encourage them to trade too quickly or too often," Mr. Levitt said. "Some of the issues raised specifically relate to on-line trading, others are generic to all investing. The majority of them can be addressed through better education and investors insuring that they have done their homework." By the end of this year, 10 million brokerage accounts are expected to be able to trade on the Internet, nearly twice the number now. The stunning growth of on-line trading has already transformed Wall Street, sharply cutting commission costs, increasing the speed of trading and making stock trading more accessible than ever before. But like the proliferation of sport utility vehicles, the explosion of on-line trading has prompted a certain complacency that can be dangerous. The flood of complaints hitting both the securities firms and regulatory agencies comes in large part from angry investors who had mistakenly thought that the ability to trade almost instantaneously through their PC's put them on an equal footing with seasoned Wall Street traders. Yet in part the problems being encountered demonstrate that technological advances in PC's and the Internet trail the advances made at the stock exchanges. For example, the stock price that consumers see on their screens may bear no resemblance to the actual real-time price at the exchange -- particularly when the stock is volatile or during periods of heavy volume. Those lags have become common with hot new Internet issues, whose prices can soar or plummet in a matter of seconds. Mr. Levitt said in an interview today that some problems were rooted in investor misunderstandings about the new technology. Other problems have been caused by the growing number of neophyte traders, many caught in the speculative fever of recent months. Through the new technology they are able to buy and sell in an instant, without any understanding of the risks associated with such highfliers. The more than 100 brokerage companies now on the Internet have taken different approaches to resolving client complaints. In certain circumstances some companies have been willing to undo the trades, but standards vary greatly from firm to firm and are highly dependent upon the specific circumstances -- and status of the client. And the wave of filings at the regulatory agencies demonstrates that in many cases the companies are not reimbursing customers. Instead, to reduce the problems and also try to insulate themselves from possible liability, many brokerage firms post warnings about trading problems on their World Wide Web sites that may be caused by stock volatility and high volume. Those statements were posted even before the National Association of Securities Dealers issued a notice on Tuesday recommending that the firms begin to educate investors and tell them of possible delays and other potential problems. Mr. Levitt warned small investors that since the stock prices they see on their computer screens may not necessarily reflect the real-time market prices, they should consider the advantages of placing orders that limit the price for a trade to be executed. He also cautioned investors not to forsake the basic principles of investing and understand that as much as the new technology has provided important benefits it can also have shortcomings. Nancy M. Smith, director of investor education at the S.E.C., said that the most common complaints concerned investors who bought securities at prices significantly higher than the prices on their screens. Other complaints, she said, came from investors who had moved with a few mouse clicks into securities that, upon reflection, they should never have been purchased. Still others thought they had canceled purchases before those orders had been executed, only to learn they had not.  Investor Rules of Thumb, and Mouse  The National Association of Securities Dealers offers some basic warning flags for investors when they open an account with an on-line brokerage firm:  DELAYS -- High trading volumes can delay the execution of an order, which may mean that a stock's price is significantly different than when the order was placed. Clients should ask their firms how orders are handled, particularly in a volatile market.  TYPES OF ORDERS -- Clients should seek an explanation of the difference between market and limit orders. A market order is done by a brokerage firm regardless of a stock's price. Limit orders are executed only at a specified price or better.  ACCESS -- Clients may have difficulty gaining access to their accounts in periods of heavy Internet traffic and may have difficulty reaching their broker on the phone in periods of high volume. They should ask for an explanation of their firms' procedures for responding to these access issues. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Auctioneer Facing Fraud Inquiry
body: Ebay Inc., the Internet auctioneer, is under investigation by the newyork City Department of Consumer Affairs over users' complaints about fraud. Ebay, which does not sell any merchandise itself, runs on-line auctions and makes money by charging listing fees and taking a cut of each sale. The newyork agency has not concluded whether Ebay could be held legally liable for the actions of people who use its service to buy and sell collectibles and other items. The agency is investigating complaints from consumers who contend they were cheated through person-to-person on-line auctions. The department declined to comment on the types of fraud or the number of cases. "It has always been Ebay's practice to offer to fully cooperate with any investigation involving improper items on the site," Ebay said in a statement, while adding that the newyork agency had not contacted the company before the investigation was reported earlier today in The newyork Post. Shares of Ebay gained $20.75, or 11 percent, to $217.50, after a study from researcher Jupiter Communications said on-line auctions would sell $3.2 billion worth of merchandise a year by 2002 as the number of consumers bidding on-line surges more than sixfold. The company says that it receives an average of 27 complaints about fraud for every 1 million auctions. It conducted about 9.5 million auctions in the third quarter. Ebay said on Jan. 15 that it would offer its users free insurance for purchases between $25 and $200 and a user-identification system to increase confidence in security of its on-line trading network. http://www.nytimes.com

title: On-Line Trading Woes Ruffle All Sides in Deals
body: Many small investors are becoming frustrated with the limitations of stock trading over the Internet, even as they continue to pour money into the on-line brokerage firms that now account for one of every four retail stock trades. But the same trading frenzy that is causing headaches for them is also causing trouble for market makers -- the professional trading firms that match buyers with sellers or take the other side of trades themselves -- forcing them to change their procedures to keep up. Some have quit trading the most popular stocks of on-line investors or shut their automatic trading systems, delaying orders by up to 20 minutes. Meanwhile on-line brokerage firms are continuing to have problems like Web pages that are slow to load, servers that conk out and some trades that fail to be executed. Trying to cope with the turmoil, some brokerage firms like Waterhouse Securities Inc. are requiring on-line investors to make trades in the most volatile stocks by talking to a broker instead of using a computer. Many firms, including the Charles Schwab Corporation, the on-line trading leader, have limited or eliminated the ability of customers to own some of their stock through margin loans. And others are scaling back the aggressive advertising that industry analysts say has contributed to the Internet logjam. Still, investors and some industry officials worry that a big market tumble could completely freeze out on-line traders. "If on normal days this doesn't work at all, that's a bad enough problem, but whenever there is a big downdraft on the market, a lot of people are going to be shut out," said Steve Salgo, a computer programmer in Plano, Tex., who trades stock options from his home. He said he has changed on-line brokers eight times in hopes of improving performance, but things only got worse during the last few weeks. "Most of the time there is a slow response. And then sometimes there is no response." But Bernard L. Madoff, whose firm Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities is one of the largest market makers, said, "This thing is not going to stop until people start losing money. I've never seen this type of mania, people trading 100 and 200 shares without any regard to fundamentals." Attempting to address the extreme volatility in some stocks and initial public offerings, a special Nasdaq committee of market makers, brokerage firms and other industry officials will meet again today to discuss whether to recommend any trading-rule changes to the Securities and Exchange Commission. Already, the group has suggested extending the time market makers have to post prices before an initial public offering begins trading, but the S.E.C. has not acted on the recommendation. Other ideas under discussion include allowing Nasdaq officials to temporarily halt trading in extremely volatile stocks and requiring retail customers buying shares immediately following an initial public offering to place limit orders that guarantee they will not be filled at a price far higher than they expected to pay, according to a person involved in the discussions. Analysts predict investors will see more Internet delays this week, even though popular high-flying stocks with on-line traders like Amazon.com Inc. and Yahoo Inc. have now fallen more than 30 percent from their highs two weeks ago. But some industry officials say the stunning rise in on-line trading volume this year has begun to level off. Still, "I think it's going to take a slowdown in the market in combination with more infrastructure spending to turn this around; that will take months," said John Robb, co-founder of Gomez Advisors Inc., an Internet consulting firm in Concord, Mass. He said on-line brokerage firms' failure rates -- the number of times Web pages failed to load -- rose 63 percent in the first week of January, compared with the average rate during the third quarter of 1998, and he said the situation has not improved since. At Waterhouse, Web trading went down for about 35 minutes on Tuesday and another few minutes Wednesday, said John Chapel, the company's president. For the time being, the firm has cut back advertising and prohibited trading in 10 stocks through its Web site, including Amazon.com and Yahoo. The firm has eliminated margin borrowing for the same 10 stocks, meaning customers who call Waterhouse to place a trade in those stocks must cover the entire price of their purchase with money in their accounts. The temporary measures will be reversed when "the frothiness lifts," Mr. Chapel said. The number of on-line trades has held steady at Discover Brokerage Direct after jumping more than 20 percent at the beginning of the year, said Tom O'Connell, executive vice president. "We are looking at this as our new level," he said. The firm, a unit of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company, has eliminated all margin lending on 16 stocks, up from just two issues six weeks ago. The problems have spilled over to Nasdaq market makers, and at one point at least 16 had stopped trading Amazon.com, Mr. Madoff said. Many that continue to trade the most volatile stocks have removed them from their automated trade systems and are executing them by hand, causing trades that normally take 2 to 20 seconds to take up to 20 minutes, he said. His firm has temporarily stopped trading Yahoo, Amazon.com and the Infoseek Corporation, though it is still averaging about 125,000 trades a day in other issues. While the most extreme volatility may have abated somewhat, industry analysts expect on-line trading growth to continue to surge throughout the year. On-line trades now account for 25 percent to 30 percent of all retail stock trades, double their market share a year ago, according to Gomez Advisors. The firm expects the number of on-line brokerage accounts to top 10 million by the end of the year, up from 6.8 million at the end of 1998.  http://www.nytimes.com

body: TODAY, I am opening the doors to what we call the New Jersey Virtual University. This initiative provides an on-line index of distance learning courses offered by colleges and universities across the state. And it invests $500,000 to help faculty members learn how to best incorporate this technology into their curriculum. . . . "Log on to njvu.org and discover that you can earn a master's in engineering on line at the New Jersey Institute of Technology. Or get an associate's degree at Atlantic County Community College. . . . The Virtual University will put New Jersey at the forefront of distance education." Governor Whitman State of the State Address  F.A.Q. ABOUT N.J.V.U. Frequently asked questions about the New Jersey Virtual University: Q.  Isn't the phrase "the forefront of distance education" a mixed metaphor? A.  Well, yes. Q.  And isn't this "virtual university" stuff just a lot of feel-good rhetoric to make New Jersey sound technologically trendy, and wouldn't the $500,000 be better spent on problems in the real-life university world, like deteriorating buildings, high tuition and the fact that the state has almost no big-time collegiate sports teams? A.  Well, you could say . . . Wait a minute; the idea of these F.A.Q.'s is to ask specific informational questions, not sweeping philosophical ones. Q.  Oh, sorry. So, does N.J.V.U. have fraternities and sororities? A.  You bet! You've heard of chat rooms? Well check out our Frat Room, where you can hang out with cyberbrothers and sisters and learn cool frat lingo like "keg stand," "ice luge" and, of course, "expulsion." But you can't join a V.U. frat or sorority until you complete the Self-Hazing Program. Q.  I'm really good at Myst(R). Am I eligible for an N.C.A.A. athletic scholarship? A.  Not yet, but V.U. is considering suing under Title IX to get gamers the same recognition that women's sports now get. We are committed to providing cyberstudents with the illusion that they are getting a well-rounded education; calling computer gaming a sport is a big part of that. Q.  When I take a virtual course, will I be dealing with an actual university professor? In fact, will I be dealing with a person at all? Or will I be getting graded by some computer that will just randomly sprinkle pre determined comments into my assignments, with no human being there to notice whether the comments make sense or even whether the computer gets one of those glitches that makes it spit out gibberish? A.  Ha! That's a good one! Let's put *// a gooD %one. Let's put it this way: You have the same chance of encountering an actual professor at N.J.V.U. as %0wd Princeton. Q.  Speaking of Princeton, does V.U. have any fun and wholesome events akin to Princeton's Nude Olympics, in which sophomores run naked across campus while onlookers grope and otherwise abuse them? A.  Although we know it must be gratifying for parents to be paying $30,500 a year so that their disrobed children can be gawked at, we prefer to preserve at least some dignity in the higher-education arena. title: Earnings for Donaldson, Lufkin Slid 32% in the Fourth Quarter
body: Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Inc., the eighth-biggest unitedstates securities firm by capital, said yesterday that its fourth-quarter earnings declined 32 percent as revenue from trading tumbled. The firm said net income for the quarter ended Dec. 31 fell to $68.7 million, or 47 cents a diluted share, compared with $101.4 million, or 77 cents a share, in the quarter a year earlier. The results matched analyst estimates. The company also said yesterday that it would decide this quarter whether to spin off all or part of its on-line brokerage unit, DLJ Direct. Spinning off the on-line unit "is something we are looking into," Joe Roby, the company's chief executive, said in an interview. "We are aware of the market value of some of DLJ Direct's competitors." For the quarter ended Dec. 31, the company, which is 74 percent owned by the Equitable Companies, a unit of the French insurer Axa S.A., said that its trading revenue fell 78 percent, to $6.92 million. A global market decline in September and October, set off by Russia's default and currency devaluation in August, hurt trading at most brokerage firms. The company also lost $7.2 million on investments in its merchant-banking business in the quarter, compared with a $44.6 million gain a year earlier. That drop "reflects the impact of a regular quarterly mark-to-market valuation of the portfolio," it said. "DLJ did not sell any substantial portfolio assets during the quarter." Revenue from underwriting securities rose 11 percent, to $282.5 million. Fees from investment banking rose 28 percent, to $300.6 million. Commissions rose 24 percent, to $228.9 million. The firm was the No. 1 underwriter of high-yield bonds in the quarter, according to the Securities Data Corporation. Shares of Donaldson fell $4.9375, to $47.3125, yesterday on the newyork Stock Exchange.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Patents;
It may be 'big, really big,' but an on-line airline ticket discounter is also being challenged.
body: A WASHINGTON patent lawyer is challenging a fundamental patent issued last summer to Priceline.com Inc. The lawyer, Thomas Woolston, contends that he filed for a patent about 16 months before Priceline applied for its patent in September 1996 covering an on-line auction system that allows consumers to bid for items like airline tickets over the Internet. Mr. Woolston's patent, which was issued in December, in part covers a computerized marketplace that enables "the purchaser to speculate on the price of collectibles in an electronic market for used goods while assuring the safe and trusted physical possession of a good." Indeed, Mr. Woolston, a baseball fan, first thought of his invention as a way to buy and sell baseball cards over the Internet. Although that is very different from the business that Priceline conducts -- it advertises widely, with the actor William Shatner concluding "I told you Priceline was going to be big, really big" -- Mr. Woolston contends that his patent covers the buyer-driven auction model of doing business on the Internet. His start-up venture, Mercexchange, is at this point little more than a company name and a board in search of venture capital. "We're defining our markets right now," Mr. Woolston said. Priceline.com operates a system under which users go to an Internet site and name the price they are willing to pay for airline tickets, hotel rooms or other items. Priceline then tries to find an airline or other company willing to accept that price. Jay S. Walker, vice chairman and founder of Priceline, dismissed Mr. Woolston's challenge. "When you have a landmark patent, you have to expect, as we did, that all kinds of people are going to come out of the woodwork to claim that the Patent Office made a mistake, and that they really invented it first," he said. "Our patent is no exception." Mr. Woolston said that he discussed working with Priceline.com to develop the auction technology but that the talks failed because the company "expressed no serious interest in cooperation." Mr. Woolston has requested that the Patent Office conduct a proceeding known as an interference. It could be months before the agency decides whether to initiate such a review, which could then take several years. Normally, such disputes over issued patents must be fought out in the courts. But for technical reasons, Mr. Woolston is able to challenge the Priceline patent through the Patent Office -- a far less costly way to challenge a patent. Mr. Walker said it was "not inconceivable" that the Patent Office would grant the interference, but expressed confidence that the patent given to Priceline.com would survive such scrutiny. Priceline was assigned patent 5,794,207. Mr. Woolston received patent 5,845,265.  Truth in Labeling, With a View to Safety Frank C. Sadlo, a substitute high school teacher in Louisville, Ky., received a patent last week for what he contends is a way to encourage the practice of safe sex. Mr. Sadlo's idea? Sell condoms that fit to size. "If you walk by the condom rack at the drugstore, you'll see that there are just two sizes -- regular and medium," Mr. Sadlo said. Class A condoms are 7.1 inches in length, according to Mr. Sadlo, while class B condoms are 6.3 inches. "But medical research of the male anatomy shows that the length of an erect penis ranges from about 3.5 inches to 13 inches," he said. "Clearly, one size cannot fit all." Further, Mr. Sadlo said, 15 percent of men are unable to use the latex condoms on the market because their circumference is too small for the condoms to stay put. "There are a lot of people that the condoms just aren't going to fit," he said. "For lots of men it's too long, so there's an unrolled portion at the base which can have a tourniquet effect and restrict neurological and vascular functioning. And if it's not long enough, it's going to have a tendency to pull off or break." Mr. Sadlo has patented a system of selling condoms that vary in length and width. Men could pick up a measuring strip at the drugstore and then take their measurement at home in privacy, he said. When they returned to the store, they would consult a coded chart for the appropriate size. The chart would be similar to, but a bit more complicated than the weight-and-height charts that women consult when they buy pantyhose at a store. But Mr. Sadlo said the size of the condom would not be evident on the package. "It would be coded, so you would pick out say, a J-M," Mr. Sadlo said. "The actual condom package would not indicate any length on it." Mr. Sadlo said he hoped to license his invention. "It can be a real funny subject," he said. "But it can help save a lot of lives because it will be a lot more reliable and comfortable, so a lot more people will be willing to wear them." Mr. Sadlo received patent 5,857,466.  A Trapdoor of Sorts For Discarded Cutlery It can cost a cafeteria thousands of dollars a year to replace flatware that has accidentally been thrown away. Richard E. Edwards has come up with a solution: a trash can with an electronic metal detector. The can described in his patent features a chute at the top. If garbage passing through the chute contains a fork or a knife or a spoon, an alarm sounds and a spring-loaded door closes the base of the chute. Once the metal has been retrieved, the chute opens again. Mr. Edwards, of Long Beach, Calif., received patent 5,797,497. Patents are available by number for $3 from the Patent and Trademark Office, Washington, D.C. 20231. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Ebay to Offer Free Insurance and ID System
body: Ebay Inc., the Internet auctioneer, said today that it would offer free insurance and a user-identification system to increase users' confidence in the security of its on-line trading network. Ebay, which holds auctions for small businesses and individuals, said it would begin in March to provide users with insurance through Lloyd's of London for transactions from $25 to $200. The company has asked Equifax Inc., the largest unitedstates consumer-credit reporting service, to start a verified-user program in March in which consumers can register their Social Security number, driver's license number and date of birth for $5. Equifax will verify the data by comparing it with information from other sources and award users with a special icon appearing next to their name on the Ebay site. Details of the plan were first reported in The Wall Street Journal today. The cost of the free insurance program should not affect profit margins at Ebay, the company said, adding that it would not see gains from the verified-user program because it would offer it at cost. Ebay said it averaged about 27 complaints of fraud for every million auctions, or about 257 total complaints in the third quarter, when it had about 9.5 million auctions. The National Consumers League's Internet Fraud Watch has noted that person-to-person auctions account for the greatest incidence of fraud on line, with buyers sending money but failing to receive the merchandise. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Delta Sets a Fee for Not Using Its Web Site
body: Starting this week, there are two new classes for Delta Air Lines passengers: wired and unwired. Citing the rising cost of conventional booking methods, Delta is imposing a surcharge -- $1 one way, $2 round trip -- on domestic tickets purchased anywhere but on the airline's own Internet site. No other airline has yet followed suit, though United Airlines, a subsidiary of the UAL Corporation, said yesterday that it was studying such a move. While travel agents acknowledge that the surcharge will not fall on them directly, they contend that the airline's long-range strategy is to further weaken travel agents, whose commissions have been sharply cut by the carriers since 1995, by weaning customers away altogether. "Here the airlines are making more money than they've ever made," said Diane Hanmer, the owner of Diane's Travel in Bartlesville, Okla., "and they're penalizing the people who can't afford a computer and the older generation, who aren't real familiar with using it." Delta declined yesterday to discuss the surcharge policy, though it said that slightly less than 2 percent of its ticketing is now done through its Web site (www.deltaairlines.com). United (www.ual.com) said its Web site's share of its bookings was 1.5 percent, while American Airlines (www.aa.com), a unit of the AMR Corporation, said its Internet bookings were just under 2 percent and growing by 25 percent a year. Over all, Jupiter Communications, a market research firm in newyork, has forecast that air travel bookings through the Internet will grow to 8 percent ($7 billion) in 2002, from 2 percent in 1998. And as the electronic share of bookings grows, many agents and travel industry officials say the major airlines are determined not to yield that business to such Internet travel agencies as Expedia, Preview Travel, Travelocity and Internet Travel Network, whose sale of airline tickets is increasing steadily. The Microsoft Corporation, for example, said last week that its MSN Expedia service (on MSN.com) posted sales of $250 million last year -- mostly airline tickets -- a 150 percent increase over 1997. While that is minuscule compared with the airline industry's $79.45 billion in revenues in 1997, the last year for which figures are available, the Internet agencies' sales are expected to continue growing. "Airlines have been cutting commissions to travel agents for years, long before on-line travel came on the scene," Suzi LeVine, a product manager at MSN Expedia, said. "This is another step in that direction and ultimately against customers' ability to gain access to a broad set of choices." The airline industry has consistently denied any such intent. The two-tier Delta policy is reminiscent of Citibank's policy in the early 1980's, in the early days of the automated teller machine, of requiring a $5,000 minimum balance for customers at some branches to be served by human tellers. At the same time, it follows a trend in other services -- notably stock trading -- in which on-line customers are offered lower rates. At the Satellite Airlines Center on East 59th Street in Manhattan yesterday, Dr. Wilbur Bowne, who was booking a Delta flight to a meeting in New Orleans, called the surcharge "unfair to the customer." But he also said that in the future he would use the Internet. Ken Ward, a travel agent in Atlanta, Delta's corporate backyard, said: "I've been surprised by the groundswell of resentment toward Delta. Two dollars for a round trip isn't much, but to a lot of customers it's a lot like creeping taxes." In Delta's message to travel agents on Monday, advising them of its new policy, effective immediately, the company said its cost of distributing tickets had increased more than 280 percent since 1990, to more than $1 billion in the fiscal year 1998, while revenue had grown just 50 percent over that same period. Moreover, it added, three of the four computer reservation systems used by most airlines and travel agents had already announced fare increases effective early this year. It said it would not apply the surcharge to tickets from its Web site because it was the least expensive way of issuing tickets. The expense of traditional ticketing has led the airlines in recent years to encourage another electronic innovation, the paperless ticket. But all tickets purchased through Delta's Web site, whether traditional or paperless, will be exempt from its new surcharge. The Travel Industry Association of America said that the number of people who booked airline, hotel and rental car reservations on the Internet increased 24 percent last year to 6.7 million, from 5.4 million in 1997.  With sales of $816 million, according to Jupiter, travel is the second-largest on-line industry, trailing only PC hardware and software sales ($836 million). While slow to merchandise their own Web sites, airlines are going all-out now to reap its presumptive riches. In the last two years they have been adding not just bargain fares available only on their Web sites, but discounts for hotels and rental cars. They often give bonus frequent-flier miles to customers who book on their Web site and frequent fliers can pay for certain bargain flights for a nominal fee plus frequent-flier miles. Thus Continental Airlines recently posted round-trip flights between Houston and Newark and between Seattle and newyork for $29 plus 17,500 miles. Many who book on airline Internet sites appear to be younger passengers who have flown only infrequently in the past, the airlines say, and have rarely if ever dealt with a travel agent. United said that 81 percent of its sales last year came through travel agents. Nevertheless, travel agents contend that booking directly with airline Web sites will ultimately hurt consumers. "They will inevitably pay more," said Joe Galloway, the president of the American Society of Travel Agents, "since they won't have the comparative fare and schedule options -- provided by travel agents -- that can help them save hundreds of dollars, as shown by every independent study."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Seeking Speed, America Online Joins Forces With Bell Atlantic
body: In a move to compete with high-speed cable-modem services, America Online and Bell Atlantic yesterday announced a joint marketing effort to sell high-speed Internet access to America Online's customers. The alliance marks a significant step in America Online's effort to retain its leadership as a "portal," or entry point, to the Internet in a market increasingly moving toward high-speed Internet access. The cable-modem business currently has only about 500,000 customers nationwide but is expected to more than double this year. That presents a threat to local telephone companies and to portals, which make their money primarily by selling advertising on sites that millions of Internet users pass through daily. Of the top portals -- which include Yahoo, Netcenter and Go -- America Online, with 15 million members, is the largest. The cable modem business is dominated by At Home and Roadrunner, which are portals as well as technologies for accessing the Internet over TV cables. While America Online and other portals can be used over cable modems, they are not users' first stop in cyberspace. At the same time, local phone companies are eager to compete with cable companies by offering asymmetrical digital subscriber line, or A.D.S.L., technology over existing phone lines. A.D.S.L. service does not require customers to dial in, and connection speeds are about 20 times faster than standard modems. "This deal is part of our plan to beat cable modems," said Amy McIntosh, president of consumer data services for Bell Atlantic. America Online said many of its members in Bell Atlantic's East Coast territory would be able to purchase the service this summer for an extra $20 a month, bringing the total cost to $40 a month. That is in line with the $40 a month charged by cable modem services but about $20 less than Bell Atlantic charges for full Internet service over A.D.S.L. America Online members who have cable modems pay $10 a month, about half the fees charged dial-up members. America Online's president, Robert W. Pittman, said: "Some of our customers are interested in speed, and we want to provide it for them in a package that makes sense." Bell Atlantic said that close to 7.5 million customers would be able to get A.D.S.L. by the end of 1999. "Most people who want high-speed Internet are going to look first to their Internet service provider, not the local cable provider or phone company," Andy Fuertes, a senior analyst at Allied Business Intelligence, a research firm, said yesterday. "So having someone like AOL involved who is more savvy about marketing to the consumer is a big plus." America Online shares fell $7.875 to $145.75 yesterday, while Bell Atlantic rose $1.1875, to $54.9375. http://www.nytimes.com

title: E*Trade Investment Bank Sets Underwritings on Internet
body: E*Trade Group Inc. said today that it was starting an investment bank to raise money for companies by selling stocks and bonds over the Internet, challenging traditional securities firms as it did when it began selling stocks on line. The new bank will underwrite stock sales for companies, raising $25 million to $50 million and charging its clients 30 percent less than investment banks typically demand. E*Trade, the No. 2 on-line broker after the Charles Schwab Corporation, will own 28 percent of the company. A group including the investment bankers Sanford Robertson and Walter Cruttenden 3d will own the rest. E*Trade, based in Palo Alto, is trying to do to underwriters what it has already done to brokers: get their business by taking advantage of the Internet to reduce costs. E*Trade's new venture, called E*Offering, focuses on underwriting because it is "one of the last bastions" of inefficiency in the securities industry, said Kathy Levinson, president of E*Trade's brokerage business. Securities firms often charge fees totaling 7 percent of the amount they raise and sell most of the shares to favored institutional clients. The new company plans to keep 4.5 percent and sell half the shares to retail investors. E*Offering will be led by Mr. Cruttenden, the former chief executive of Cruttenden Roth Inc. in Irvine, Calif. Mr. Robertson, who founded Robertson, Stephens & Company in San Francisco in 1978, will be a board member. He left the investment bank after it was sold to the BankBoston Corporation last year.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
Shares End Mixed as Nasdaq Rallies but Blue Chips Falter
body: Stocks ended mixed yesterday, with many issues pulling back after last week's rally to record highs raised investors' concerns that the market was getting too expensive. The Intel Corporation was among the prominent exceptions, rallying on expectations that its earnings, which are scheduled for release today, will exceed forecasts. "Shares rose too far too fast in a remarkable week in the market," said Franklin Morton, research chief at Ariel Capital Management in Chicago, which oversees about $3 billion. A week into the year, the Nasdaq composite index is already up 7.3 percent, the Dow Jones industrial average is up 4.1 percent, and the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index is up 2.3 percent. Yesterday, the Dow average closed down 23.43 points, or nearly a quarter of 1 percent, to 9,619.89, though it rebounded from a deficit earlier in the session that reached 111 points. The S.& P. index declined 11.21 points, or about nine-tenths of 1 percent, to 1,263.88. Intel helped the Nasdaq set a closing high for a seventh consecutive session. The index jumped 40.18 points, or 1.7 percent, to 2,384.59. Declining issues outpaced advancers, 1,970 to 1,118, on the newyork Stock Exchange; trading volume was 818.1 million shares. The S.& P. telephone index led the decline in the S.& P. 500, retreating 4 percent after a 5.3 percent gain in four days. BellSouth lost 3 1/16 a share, to 47 7/16; SBC Communications dropped 2 9/16, to 55 1/8, and Bell Atlantic fell 1 11/16, to 54 15/16. Intel climbed 10 1/16 a share, to set a closing high of 139 3/4. After a surge in computer-buying during the holiday season, Intel, the world's biggest manufacturer of computer chips, is expected to report earnings of $1.07 a share, up from 96 cents a year earlier, based on the average estimate of analysts polled by the First Call Corporation. That would surpass Intel's own optimistic forecasts. Internet shares surged, led by issues like E*Trade Group, an on-line brokerage firm, which jumped 20 7/8, to 88 1/2, after posting a smaller-than-expected loss for its first quarter. Campbell Soup fell 6 7/8, to 45 3/8, its biggest decline since 1980, after the company, world's largest maker of soup, said fiscal year 1999 earnings would probably fall short of analyst expectations, as the company cuts costs and reduces shipments of condensed soup in the unitedstates. Pharmaceutical shares, among the top performers last year, fell for a third consecutive session. Pfizer Inc. declined 4 1/2 a share, to 117 3/4; Schering-Plough lost 2 1/8, to 52 3/4. Ascend Communications Inc., a telecommunications equipment maker, gained 5 1/4, to 761 1/16, on speculation that Lucent Technologies, the world's biggest telephone-equipment maker, offered to buy it for more than $16 billion. Lucent and Ascend officials declined to comment. Lucent shares fell 2 5/16, to 112 15/16. General Motors rallied 6, to 86 1/16, after David Bradley, an analyst at J. P. Morgan, raised his 1999 earnings estimate for the auto maker to $8.75 a share, from $8.40. Individual and institutional investors have been betting in recent days that G.M.'s earnings prospects would rise. Some investors interpreted the G.M. rally and Friday's stronger-than-expected employment report from the Labor Department as signs that the economy remains buoyant. They are concerned, though, that the Federal Reserve -- which helped contribute to the market's strength by lowering benchmark borrowing costs three times starting Sept. 29 -- may be through cutting rates. "If interest rates have bottomed, or if we get an uptick in rates, that's it for the market," said Frank Curzio, president of FXC Investment Group in Queens. Concern that Brazil's debt and currency problems will crimp economic and corporate-profit growth in the unitedstates also weighed on stocks. Brazil's Bovespa index fell 5.6 percent, as a call by the second-most- populous state in Brazil to withhold debt payments to the Federal Government prompted investors to pull money out of the country. That raised concern that Brazil might eventually default on its foreign debt, causing shock waves in the unitedstates similar to those set off by Russia's default in August.  Bond Prices Fall By The Associated Press Bond prices slipped yesterday as the dollar fell further against the Japanese yen, making Treasuries less attractive to international investors. The price of the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 1 8/32, to a price of 98 22/32. Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from price, rose to 5.30 percent, from 5.27 percent on Friday. Bond prices were hurt partly by the continued decline of the dollar against the yen. The dollar fell to a 28-month low against the yen yesterday, extending a slump from last summer's highs despite continued strength in the American economy. title: Microsoft Presses Its View About Rivals' 3-Way Deal
body: In its antitrust trial today, the Microsoft Corporation made its most concerted effort yet to convince a Federal judge that the recently announced deal that brings together three of its rivals -- America Online Inc., the Netscape Communications Corporation and Sun Microsystems Inc. -- seriously weakens the Government's case. In a three-way deal announced in late November, America Online agreed to buy Netscape for $4.2 billion and made a side agreement to buy and jointly develop technology with Sun. Last month, Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson, who will decide the outcome of this nonjury trial, expressed the view that the deal "might be a very significant change in the playing field as far as this industry is concerned." During today's cross-examination of the Government's last witness, Franklin M. Fisher, an economist, Microsoft's legal team presented as evidence comments made by executives of the three companies who characterized the deal as sure to strengthen their competitive muscle in software used to browse the World Wide Web, in electronic commerce and in Internet technology -- all areas of head-to-head competition with Microsoft. A Microsoft lawyer, Michael Lacovara, repeatedly tried to get Mr. Fisher to concede that the triumvirate of rivals with ambitious plans for the future did indeed pose a genuine threat to Microsoft's dominance in the personal computer software business. At times, Mr. Fisher would give an inch or two, saying, for example, that moves planned by the three companies were a "hopeful sign" that they might some day be a counterweight to Microsoft. But each time he was challenged, Mr. Fisher returned to his view that Microsoft has a monopoly in the personal computer operating system market with its Windows family of products and that it has illegally used its market power to defend that monopoly. "None of this," Mr. Fisher replied at one point, "affects my conclusions." Mr. Lacovara prodded Mr. Fisher repeatedly to admit that the emerging technology championed by the group -- the combination of Sun's Java software, an Internet programming language, and Netscape's Web browser -- could pose a serious challenge to Microsoft in the long run. Mr. Fisher allowed that it was difficult to predict what might happen. Yet any such challenge will not come soon, he said, adding, "I don't think it will happen at all if Microsoft is permitted to go on as it has." Microsoft insists that the America Online-Netscape-Sun deal fundamentally changes the competitive landscape and undermines a linchpin claim in the Government's case: that Microsoft has a resilient monopoly. "This deal was the shot heard around the world, in the industry, by the public and in this courthouse," said William H. Neukom, the Microsoft senior vice president for law and corporate affairs. Today, Judge Jackson gave another signal that he is weighing the impact of the three-company deal on the case. He interrupted the cross-examination of Mr. Fisher to directly ask his opinion about a column this morning on the Op-Ed page of The Washington Post by David Ignatius, based largely on an interview with Stephen M. Case, the chairman of America Online. In it, Mr. Ignatius quotes Mr. Case as saying that the deal is not intended to mount a challenge to Microsoft's mainstay, the Windows operating system, which controls the basic operations of more than 90 percent of personal computers sold today. "AOL's merger with Netscape has no bearing on the Microsoft case, as nothing we're doing is competitive with Windows," Mr. Case was quoted as saying. "We have no flight of fancy that we can dent in any way, shape or form what is a monopoly in the operating system business." After reading the quotations, Judge Jackson asked Mr. Fisher if he agreed with that view of the deal. "I certainly do," Mr. Fisher replied. Judge Jackson then asked lawyers for both Microsoft and the Justice Department whether they planned to call Mr. Case as a witness. Another America Online executive, David M. Colburn, has already appeared as a witness for the Government. Mr. Case is not on the 12-person witness lists for either side, but he could be called as one of the two additional witnesses allowed to each side after Microsoft presents its defense, which is expected to begin early next week. Both Microsoft and the Government told the judge that they would wait until Microsoft had presented its defense, expected to last six to eight weeks, before naming their two so-called redirect witnesses. Later, on the courthouse steps, David Boies, the lead trial lawyer for the Justice Department, made no commitment, but he said Mr. Case would be a "useful witness" for the Government. "He's very knowledgeable," Mr. Boies said, "and Microsoft is pinning a lot of hopes on the effect of that merger." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Irish Debate Forums Are Reined In by AOL
body: America Online has decided that subscribers who favor or oppose Irish nationalism can continue their heated disagreements in AOL's on-line forums, but they're going to have to be more cordial about it. On Dec. 11, AOL, the world's largest on-line provider, pulled the plug on 23 Irish Heritage discussion forums. AOL said it had done so because the political debates had included too many personal attacks and "vulgarity and profanity," which violated AOL's terms of service. Last week, AOL reopened the discussion groups after "cleaning them up," said a spokesman, Jim Whitney. In a note to visitors to the discussion groups, AOL stated, "We encourage you to make this a more amiable place where any person, regardless of faction, can openly discuss political issues and current events." "We encourage and remind you to debate issues only and not resort to personal attacks or member harassment," the note continued. Some Irish nationalists who favor Irish rule for Northern Ireland dispute AOL's account. On The Irish People Web site (inac.org/IrishPeople /top/121998/121998aol.html), critics contend that AOL is seeking to silence outspoken Irish nationalists to make the service more appealing in Britain, where AOL is trying to build membership. Mr. Whitney denied that AOL's actions were motivated by that. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
On-Line Giant May Link To CBS News
body: CBS News will announce a deal with America Online Inc. later this week to become the exclusive broadcast news provider for the on-line service, executives involved in the agreement said yesterday. The deal lacks only some final details, the executives said. When completed, it will mean that CBS will replace ABC News as the provider of news in text, video and audio on America Online. For CBS, the move to American Online has the potential to jump-start what has been a lackluster presence on the Web. By wide consensus, CBS News has lagged far behind the other news networks in terms of what it has offered to users of the Internet. For America Online, a deal is likely to mean a more favorable financial arrangement than the service had with ABC, one executive said. The exact terms of the deal were not available yesterday, but one executive involved in the negotiations said that it would be along the lines of "promotion for promotion." The deal was reported in the Hollywood Reporter yesterday. Executives from CBS, America Online and ABC, declined to comment on the record. An America Online spokeswoman, Wendy Goldberg, labeled it "a rumor and we don't comment on rumors." Gil Schwartz, the chief spokesman for CBS, said, "We don't have anything to announce." Michelle Bergmann, a spokeswoman for the ABC News on-line service, said, "It's our standing policy not to comment on contractual arrangements." The America Online contract is known to be near an end. An executive involved in the CBS deal said it would include America Online's affiliated services, AOL.com and Compuserve. That will give CBS access to America Online's 15 million subscribers, by far the biggest number on the Internet. The Internet services of the other network news organizations have been far ahead of CBS. CNN's Web site and MSNBC.com, which NBC operates with the Microsoft Corporation, are among the most heavily trafficked sites on the Web. Recently, CBS had been in talks with CNN about a merger of news-gathering resources. That arrangement might have required CBS to pay for access to CNN's news material. The CBS chairman, Mel Karmazin, said in December that he was looking instead for a way to generate revenue from CBS's news product. CBS does have a promotion-for-pay arrangement with the on-line services that use its Sportsline and Market Watch products. And CBS had already established a relationship with America Online last fall in a promotion campaign for its new fall prime-time entertainment lineup. That promotion was regarded as highly successful by CBS executives. An executive involved in the America Online-CBS negotiations said that American Online was also concerned with competitive Internet moves being made by the Walt Disney Company, the parent of ABC, which recently started an Internet portal, the Go Network. http://www.nytimes.com

title: E*Trade Cut Option Price Just Before Stock Surged
body: E*Trade Group Inc., the No. 2 on-line broker, reduced the exercise price on employee stock options two weeks after its stock traded at a 21-month low and began a three-month surge that increased its price sixfold. On Oct. 22, the company told employees they could trade in options carrying higher exercise prices for new ones at that day's closing price of $17, according to the company's annual report, filed this week with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company said options covering almost 3.5 million shares have since been "regranted" under the program. E*Trade rose to a record $60.125 a share on Tuesday from an intraday low of $10 on Oct. 8. On Wednesday, the stock fell $9.3125, or 15 percent, to $50.8125, after dropping as low as $48. Employees who took advantage of the lower-priced options had total paper gains of $117.7 million at Wednesday's close. More than two-thirds of E*Trade's 700 employees are eligible for stock options, which vest at a rate of 25 percent a year. Employees who traded in their old options "start from ground zero, as if it was day one of the vesting period," said a company spokeswoman, Lisa Nash. "This decision was certainly not taken lightly." The company did not specify the exercise price on options that were traded in by employees. According to its January 1998 proxy statement, the company's president, Christos Cotsakos, and four other senior executives received about 550,000 options at an average exercise price of $27.42 in July and August 1997. Companies with volatile stocks should not reprice options when their share prices dip, said Graef Crystal, an executive compensation consultant. Doing so, he said, creates "a virtual money machine, an antigravity device." On Oct. 8, two weeks before the options-adjustment program was instituted, shares of E*Trade and other on-line brokers, like the Charles Schwab Corporation and the Ameritrade Holding Corporation, closed at 52-week lows on concerns that the bull market in stocks would end because of economic crises in Russia, Japan and emerging markets. Before Wednesday's decline, E*Trade shares rose for eight straight days on optimism about the company's financial results for the current quarter. Industry executives and analysts say on-line brokers' trading volume rose by more than one-third, largely because of heavy activity in Internet stocks. In its annual report filing, the company, based in Palo Alto, also disclosed that it had invested $2 million in KAP Group, a company led by the founder and chairman of E*Trade, William Porter. That company is trying to establish an on-line options exchange. E*Trade invested another $15.3 million for a less than 20 percent stake in Critical Path, a provider of email software to large Web sites. E*Trade Group owns 42 percent of E*Trade Japan, its joint on-line trading venture with the Softbank Corporation, after making an $8 million investment, according to the filing. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
Dow Retreats for First Time in Nine Trading Days
body: The stock market ended lower yesterday for the first time in nine trading days, weakened by investors who sold to secure some profits from a 1998 rally that accelerated at year-end. Merck & Company, up 40 percent for the year; Lucent Technologies Inc., up 172 percent, and the Microsoft Corporation, up 115 percent, led the decline. "Stocks have moved up so dramatically that money's being taken off the table," said James Margard, chief equity strategist at Rainier Investment Management in Seattle, which manages $5 billion. "Investors have recognized that some large stocks may be overvalued." The Dow Jones industrial average fell 46.34 points, to 9,274.64, after having gained 530 points since Dec. 16. The Standard & Poor's 500 index declined 9.88 points, to 1,231.93. The Nasdaq composite index dropped 14.82 points, to 2,166.95. Advancing issues slightly outpaced those declining on the newyork Stock Exchange. With one day left in 1998, the S.& P. 500 index has soared 27 percent for the year, on track for an record fourth consecutive year of gains exceeding 20 percent. The Nasdaq composite index is up about 38 percent, and the Nasdaq 100, an index of the market's largest shares, is up 83 percent, the best year in its 14-year history. "The market's had a tremendous run," said Peter Coolidge, senior equity trader at Brean Murray & Company, a newyork brokerage firm. "There's no catalyst pushing us higher." With many investors and traders on vacation for the year-end holidays, trading has been light this week. Monday and Tuesday's levels were about 20 percent below last week's, and 604.92 million shares changed hands yesterday, compared with a three-month average of 726 million shares. Merck fell 2 1/4, to 148 13/16 ; Lucent dropped 3 7/16 m to 108 5/8m and Microsoft fell 1 1/2m to 139. Internet shares fell after posting spectacular gains in recent days on optimism that commerce conducted on the World Wide Web will boom. Charles Schwab, the No. 1 on-line broker, fell 3 1/16 to 56 3/8. Earlier this week, Schwab's stock market value surpassed that of Merrill Lynch & Company, the largest brokerage firm. Now, Schwab's market capitalization is down to $22 billion, below Merrill's market capitalization of $24 billion. Ubid Inc., an on-line auctioneer, fell 24 1/2, to 119; Skymall Inc. fell 13, to 27 3/4, and America Online Inc. dropped 7 1/16 , to 147 9/16 . The Internet directory company Yahoo fell 25 3/8, to 244 5/8. Genesis Direct Inc. soared 2 13/16 , to 9 7/8, after themail-order catalogue company said it would sell some merchandise through Excite Inc., the second-biggest Internet directory. Genesis was the second-most active stock. Amoco fell 3 1/4, to 54 3/4, and British Petroleum's American depository receipts fell 6 3/4 , to 83 3/16 , as B.P. received unitedstates approval to acquire Amoco. Amoco ceased to be a member of the S.& P, 500 index as of today so money managers who mimic the index must sell the stock. Most strategists are still confident about the outlook for stock markets.  Laszlo Birinyi, president of Birinyi Associates Inc., said he expects the Dow average to reach 12,000 by the end of 1999. Mr. Birinyi studies "money flow," which examines the number of shares traded every time a stock goes up or down, and is considered a gauge of the conviction behind the price move. Mr. Birinyi said in an interview that money flow analysis indicates that International Business Machines, Ford Motor and America Online are likely to rally in 1999. Investors reduced the amount of money they added to equity mutual funds by 28 percent this year, and almost tripled their purchases of bond funds. Still, in the week ended Monday they added $3.16 billion more to stock funds than they redeemed, according to Trimtabs.com, a research firm. By any measure, the bull market in stocks is still under way. The Wilshire 5000 index, the broadest indicator, is up 22 percent for the year.  Still, small and mid-capitalization shares continue to lag. The benchmark Russell 2000 index is off 6 percent this year, after being down as much as 31 percent. In the bond market yesterday, Treasuries rose for the third consecutive day, reflecting investor expectations that inflation will remain low next year. The 30-year bond rose 6/32 , to 102 18/32 . Its yield, which falls when the price rises, declined to 5.08 percent from 5.09. Two-year notes rallied amid optimism generated by stronger-than-expected demand at the Tuesday auction. The yield on the new note fell to 4.53 percent, down 16 basis points from the auction rate. With one day left in 1998, 30-year Treasury bonds have handed investors returns of 18.7 percent, when price gains and reinvested dividends are taken into account. That is the best result since 1995, when long-term Treasuries returned 34.7 percent. Volume yesterday was 25 percent below the average for a Wednesday in the last month, according to Govpx Inc., a bond pricing service. About $37 billion of Treasury bills, notes and bonds traded through most of the major brokers by 3 P.M. newyork time. Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average, since Dec. 1997. title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Schwab, for Now, Bests Merrill on Strength of On-Line Trading
body: As recently as a few weeks ago, it seemed like America's corporate giants need not worry too much about the Internet. After all, if upstart companies that specialize in on-line commerce were ever to realize investors' much-hyped expectations for future profits, Fortune 500 members could always just buy them. Not anymore. The recent explosion in share prices of companies linked to the on-line world has been so spectacular that their market value is rapidly eclipsing that of more established competitors, even when the on-line companies still lag far behind in terms of profits and revenues. Yesterday, the Internet passed another such milestone, this time shaking some core assumptions in the finance industry. The market value of the Charles Schwab Corporation, the discount broker based in San Francisco, reached $25.5 billion. That puts it in the No. 2 position, ahead by a nose of the industry standard-bearer and Wall Street heavyweight, Merrill Lynch & Company, which investors now say is worth $25.4 billion. Market value can change drastically day to day, and investors still value one big investment bank, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company, above Schwab. But Schwab's helicopter-like ascent is unheard-of in speed, analysts said, and perhaps in its challenge to the way Wall Street treats the on-line craze. Consider that just two weeks ago, the market was awash with unconfirmed rumors that Merrill might consider buying Schwab to give it a presence on line, a possibility that now seems far-fetched given the huge increase in Schwab's stock price. "Merrill has to be concerned about this," said Richard Strauss, a securities industry analyst for Goldman, Sachs. "There is significant value in Merrill for many reasons. But the Internet is clearly something that they have to make a top priority." Schwab has been swept up in the Internet stock frenzy, which has inflated the share prices of some new on-line companies well beyond competitors that trail them in selling goods electronically. America Online, perhaps the best-known Internet entertainment and commerce company, recently surpassed Disney in market value. Amazon.com has a market value well above the combined value of two leading book-selling rivals, Barnes & Noble and Borders. Investors value Ebay, the new Internet auction company, at more than five times Sotheby's, the old-world benchmark. Schwab's rise is attributable to the fact that, unlike Merrill and other rivals in the finance industry, it has transformed itself from a traditional retail broker, albeit one that specialized in discounted fees, into a company that does most of its business on line. Merrill, meanwhile, has delayed plans to offer a limited on-line trading service to some customers until early next year. Morgan Stanley and Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, Wall Street houses that like Merrill have a more diverse array of businesses than Schwab, have substantial on-line operations. But only a small part of their revenue is Internet-related. Schwab, moreover, dodged a bullet from rivals like E*Trade Group Inc. and the Ameritrade Holding Corporation, services that focus exclusively on cut-rate, on-line stock trading. Even as on-line trading has soared as a percentage of total stock trading, Schwab has maintained its market share of 30 percent, analysts said. The company has watched the revenue it derives from each trade it handles slide as investors switch to less expensive trading through its Web site. As recently as late last year, it earned $63 on every trade it handled, and now that average has fallen to $53. But a sharp increase in the quantity of trades has more than made up for that loss, and profits are rising at a rapid clip. "Schwab did a great job turning the Internet to its advantage when it could easily have become a victim," Bill Burnham, an on-line commerce analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston, said. "Now, any fears that they will be superceded by the Internet have subsided. They are the leader." Many analysts warn that the lopsided valuations placed on companies with the suffix ".com" has the classic symptoms of a financial bubble and will probably prove fleeting. Some say the same about Schwab's sudden rise, and indeed its valuation by some traditional measures seems extraordinary. Schwab, whose shares closed yesterday at $63.625, up $3.25, now trades at 65 times its projected profits next year, a ratio more familiar to the speculative Internet world than the brokerage community. Merrill, which closed yesterday at $70.75, down $1.0625, trades at 16 times its forward earnings. Merrill manages $1.4 trillion in client assets, three times what Schwab manages. Merrill's revenues in the last year totaled $17.5 billion, seven times Schwab's. "It just does not make that much sense for Schwab. These lofty multiples get applied to Internet companies that are not mature and are thought to have an enormous growth path ahead of them," said Guy Moszkowski, a brokerage stock analyst at Salomon Smith Barney. "I don't see how you apply that kind of thinking to Schwab. It has been around for 25 years and has a more mature business." Likewise, officials at Merrill say they are not about to overhaul their strategy because of daily changes in stock prices. "We have a long-term strategy that is global, that has been very successful in growing clients' assets, revenues and market share," Jim Wiggins, a Merrill spokesman, said. "We are sticking to it." Even if Merrill chose to do so, it might have a hard time mimicking Schwab's heavy Internet focus. Schwab has always sought to provide brokerage services at a low cost. That makes the company more vulnerable to competition from purely Internet companies than full-service brokers like Merrill, which compete on providing advice and financial planning services to customers. Moreover, Merrill has a network of 14,000 brokers who would probably resist any move by Merrill management to shift a large proportion of the firm's business on line. "Just from a structural position, it's incredibly difficult for Merrill to rush into the Internet business," Mr. Burnham said. "They would have a huge political issue." title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Another Big Day for Issues Connected to the Internet
body: Stocks were mixed yesterday as the growing use of the World Wide Web for shopping and stock trading lifted such Internet retailers as Skymall and sent Charles Schwab, the No. 1 on-line brokerage firm, past Merrill Lynch in market value. Traditional retailers, like Wal-Mart Stores and Sears, Roebuck, fell. Electronic commerce "is a legitimate avenue of growth for many companies," said Trent May, manager of the $1.2 billion Invesco Growth Fund. Mr. May has 3 percent of his fund -- which has returned 41 percent this year -- invested in America Online. The Nasdaq index, which is heavily weighted toward technology stocks, rose 17.27 points, or eight-tenths of a percent, to 2,180.30, its fourth record in six sessions. The Dow Jones industrial average rose 8.76 points, to 9,226.75, for its seventh straight advance, matching the longest string of gains this year. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index fell eight-tenths of a point, or less than one-tenth of a percent, to 1,225.49. About eight stocks fell for every seven that rose on the newyork Stock Exchange. Stocks pared gains with an hour left in the trading session amid selling by "momentum" investors -- professionals and individuals who chase rising stocks looking for short-term gains. "There is a lot of fear surrounding Internet stocks and what will happen when the market comes back to reality," said Tim Ghriskey, a senior portfolio manager at the Dreyfus Corporation, which oversees $95 billion. A little more than 531 million shares changed hands on the Big Board, well below the daily average of 729 million shares for the last three months. Trading is expected to be slower than usual all week, as it typically is in the week between Christmas and New Year's. That could mean stocks will move erratically as the year-end maneuvering of money managers has a disproportionate effect. Skymall, the nation's largest in-flight catalogue retailer, soared 23, to 35 9/16, after doubling on Thursday and was the most active stock in unitedstates trading. The company estimated that its Internet sales rose sevenfold in 1998 as more people shopped on line. Schwab rose 3 1/4, to 63 5/8. The company now has a market value of $25.5 billion, more than the $25.1 billion for Merrill Lynch, the biggest unitedstates securities firm by number of brokers. Merrill fell 1 1/16, to 70 3/4. "A lot of people did their Christmas shopping on line this year," said Ryan Crane, who follows Internet stocks for AIM Advisors Inc., which oversees $100 billion and owns CDW Computer Centers, an on-line computer seller, and Infospace.com, an Internet directory. "Those same Internet-savvy people that are shopping on line are probably the ones that are buying these stocks." Traditional retailers declined. Wal-Mart slumped 1 1/4, to 79 7/8. Sears fell 7/8, to 41, May Department Stores dropped 5/8, to 60 1/16, and J. C. Penney lost 1 1/16, to 47 5/8. Professional investors began cutting the amount of money they put into general retail stocks like Wal-Mart in late November, according to money-flow statistics from Bloomberg Analytics. The money-flow data measure the amount of money institutional investors put into a stock each time the price rises compared with the amount they take out when it falls. Of the 20 most active stocks yesterday, 18 benefit directly or indirectly from the Internet's growth. Active Apparel Group soared 10 1/4, to 11 1/2, after the sportswear maker said it created a Web site to sell its clothes, marketed under the brand names Everlast, Converse All Star and MTV's the Grind. The company's market value surged to $29 million yesterday from $3.1 million. E*Trade Group climbed 11 3/4, to 56 3/4, after the No. 2 on-line broker said its new Web site had signed up more than 500,000 members since September, when E*Trade began a $100 million marketing campaign to add new accounts. Amazon.com, the on-line retailer, jumped 27 1/8, to 351 15/16. America Online, the No. 1 on-line service, jumped 20 5/8, to 157 1/4, and Yahoo gained 28 3/8, to 275 1/2. Netscape, the Internet software company, rose 9 1/2, to 68 3/16. The surge in Internet stocks for months has been driven by individual investors, who have been "day trading" -- buying shares in the hopes of selling them minutes or hours later at a profit. With many professionals out of the office this week, the effect of individuals will be even more pronounced, analysts say. "All these Internet stocks are going to run this week," said Bill Burnham, electronic commerce analyst with Credit Suisse First Boston. "There are no institutions in the market, they're all on vacation, and all these people sitting at home after having their turkey dinner are going to move the stocks."
