title:
Business Travel;
An Internet buying service is planning to book hotel rooms for guests at prices they propose.
body: PRICELINE.COM, the Internet buying service that tries to book flights for travelers at prices they propose, is planning to do the same thing with hotels starting next month. According to Jay Walker, vice chairman of the company, rooms will be offered by late October at more than 1,000 hotels in 26 cities nationwide, including Dallas, Houston, newyork, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Chicago, Denver, Seattle, Boston and Washington. The company hopes to add more unitedstates cities later this year and international destinations next year. Mr. Walker would not name the participating hotels but said all would be major chain properties. The process will be similar to the way Priceline books airline seats. Using the company's World Wide Web site (www.priceline.com), travelers will select a city and a geographical zone within it, travel dates, the amount of money they are willing to pay and a minimum category of hotel desired. The categories, from two star to five star, will be described on the site. The company's computer will scan its data base in an attempt to find a hotel that will accept the named price; the request will be accepted or rejected within an hour. Travelers are guaranteed the minimum category of room chosen; in turn they must take the hotel assigned. They will not know the specific hotel (or its location, except for the broad geographical zone) until the reservations are confirmed and paid for, Mr. Walker said. Reservations will be accepted up to a year in advance but no later than 48 hours ahead. There will be no fee to consumers. Priceline, based in Stamford, Conn., has sold more than 60,000 economy-class airline seats, most of them domestic, since it introduced that service in April, according to Mr. Walker. Critics have asserted that most major domestic airlines do not participate in the program; Brian Ek, a company spokesman, responded, "We're offering tickets through major airlines, but we cannot say what they are." Passengers must be willing to travel anytime between 6 A.M. and 10 P.M. and make one stopover; they cannot choose their airline, and they earn no frequent-flier points. Priceline, which recently added a car-buying service in the newyork area, received a patent last month for its method and use of "buyer driven commerce."  New Swiss Airline A new airline, Swiss World Airways, began service earlier this month between Newark and Geneva, with flights every day except Wednesday. The president and chief executive of the company is Peter A. Leishman, who formerly helped found two British low-fare start-ups, Debonair and Easyjet. The Geneva-based airline received approval from the Department of Transportation only a few days before it started flying, according to Mr. Leishman, and is only now getting its flights into the computer reservations systems used by travel agents. Swiss World Airways' Boeing 767 -- the airline currently has just one jet, which it leases -- seats 159 passengers in three classes. One-way unrestricted fares range from $167 to $530 in economy class, $667 to $1,000 in business class and $1,267 to $2,000 in first class. The carrier offers a few unconventional twists. Food service consists of mostly cold choices to avoid reheating, with only one hot entree cooked on board. Travelers flying on discount fares pay for food, drinks and headsets; full-fare travelers get them free. The frequent-flier program consists of instant lottery-style tickets offering a gift or a premium that applies to the next flight. The airline hopes to add a second flight to Geneva from newyork in November, via Basel, and service from Dulles International Airport or Baltimore-Washington International Airport next spring. The toll-free worldwide reservations number is (011-800-11) 767-767.  Shuttle's New Boston Home The US Airways Shuttle is scheduled to move on Sunday from Terminal A at Logan International Airport in Boston to the newly renovated Terminal B. The new shuttle gates will be 10, 12 and 13 at the end of the concourse. Counters for ticketing and check-in will be next to the security checkpoint at the entrance to the main concourse and at the gates. The shuttle offers 17 daily round-trip flights between Logan and La Guardia Airport in newyork, as well as 15 daily flights between Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport and La Guardia.  Train to the Plane A rail link from Copenhagen International Airport to the Central Railway Station downtown opened Sunday. The seven-mile trip takes 11 minutes and costs $2.60, compared with a taxi fare of around $20. The train terminal is underneath the airport's departure and arrival halls.  Hotel Update Two new hotels on the hip side are scheduled to open tomorrow, one in Chicago and one in Denver. The House of Blues Hotel, a Loews Hotel, at the Marina City riverfront complex in Chicago, is the first in a series planned by House of Blues Hospitality. The 367 guest rooms will offer in-room faxes, CD players, videocassette recorders, voicemail and two-line phones, as well as direct Internet access via TV sets. Meetings and other events can be arranged in the House of Blues Music Hall and Restaurant next door; the complex also has a 36-lane bowling center and a health club. In downtown Denver, the 189-room Hotel Monaco is situated at 1717 Champa Street in two renovated adjoining buildings, the 1917 Railway Exchange Building and the 1937 Art Moderne Title Building. Rooms will have CD players and two-line phones with data ports for computers. The hotel is part of the Kimpton Hotel and Restaurant Group.

title:
THE MARKETS: MARKET PLACE -- COMPANY REPORTS;
S.E.C. Crackdown on Technology Write-Offs
body: It is upgrade time at America Online. Never mind the noise about its new 4.0 browser software version. The Securities and Exchange Commission has ordered the on-line service, and the rest of the technology industry, to improve the way they account for mergers and acquisitions. The issue is how technology companies have seized on a footnote in the accounting rules related to research expenses to write off most of the purchase price of companies as soon as they acquire them. This prevents a continuing drag on profits that would result from writing off the purchase price over several years. The S.E.C.'s move comes as it is cracking down on a number of accounting practices it finds abusive. In comments at newyork University, Arthur Levitt, the chairman of the commission, said his staff would immediately increase its scrutiny of companies that use certain aggressive accounting techniques to inflate their quarterly earnings. In choosing to make an example of America Online, the biggest Internet company, the commission took the extreme step of blocking it from publishing its fiscal fourth-quarter earnings for nearly two months. America Online finally reached an agreement with the S.E.C. and published its earnings yesterday. It wrote off $70.5 million related to research at two companies it acquired, representing 22 percent of the $316 million it had paid for them. Previously the company had said it planned to write off a vast majority of the purchase price, though it gave no specific figures. Separately, Lynn E. Turner, the S.E.C.'s chief accountant, called on the accounting industry to tighten its rules related to writing off the cost of research. In a letter to the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants, he said that a study by the S.E.C. had found "significant problems in the recognition and valuation" of the research write-offs. The letter outlined a proposed standard for such write-offs that is much stricter than accountants have been using. And the commission threatened to make companies take the embarrassing step of restating published earnings in cases where it deemed their research write-offs to be "materially misleading." Analysts said that the change could inhibit acquisitions, especially by smaller technology companies. "It has more significance for other companies besides AOL," said Keith Benjamin, an analyst at BancBoston Robertson Stephens. "You will see more young Internet companies forced to take lower write-offs." America Online is less affected, he said, because it has become big enough to absorb the additional charges. At issue is how companies account for the value of "in-process research and development" -- research that has yet to be turned into a marketable product -- at companies they buy. In an acquisition, companies estimate the value of all of the assets they are buying, both tangible ones like buildings and intangible assets like brand names and customer lists. If the purchase price is higher than the value of all of these assets -- and it usually is -- the remainder is added to an item known as good will. Companies are forced to write off the value of all of these assets over a period of from 3 to 40 years, depending on the useful life of the asset. The one exception is in-process research, which is written off immediately. Since technology companies are especially interested in showing investors accelerating earnings growth, many have started attributing the bulk of their acquisition costs to in-process research. The S.E.C. letter listed a number of what it described as "abuses" in this practice. In one case, for example, a company that the commission did not name wrote off nearly all the purchase price of an acquisition as in-process research, even though the target company had not spent a significant amount of money on research or development. "If a company didn't spend significant amounts on R&D, it would raise questions in my mind," said Baruch Lev, a professor of accounting at newyork University. He conducted a study of 400 acquisitions, mostly of technology companies, and found that the buyers wrote off 75 percent of the purchase price as in-process research. America Online said that it would not be deterred from buying more companies because of the change in rules. "When we look at acquisitions we will look for those that have the right strategic value and the right economic value," said J. Michael Kelly, the company's chief financial officer. Because the allowed write-off was less than analysts had expected, America Online posted an unexpected profit for its fourth quarter. It earned $7.1 million, or 3 cents a fully diluted share. That compares with a loss of $11.8 million, or 6 cents a fully diluted share, a year earlier. America Online said it would write off the rest of the cost of its acquisitions over 5 to 10 years. That will mean a deduction of between $25 million and $50 million a year from its reported profits. The company told analysts yesterday that its core business continued to do better than expected and that as a result, it predicted it would meet their previous earnings estimates. Shares of America Online increased $2.375 each yesterday, to $117.125. Jonathan Cohen, an analyst with Merrill Lynch, said that the market was not concerned with the deductions from profits. "Reported earnings is one small piece of a larger picture at technology companies that includes revenue growth, market position, audience size and brand equity," he said. Yet even if investors are ignoring the good will charges now, Jack Ciesielski, a money manager and the publisher of the Analyst's Accounting Observer, argues that it provides a useful reminder of how much companies are spending on acquisitions, especially if the good times end. "If there is a big blob of good will and they aren't earning a return on it, investors can see it and start asking questions," Mr. Ciesielski said. "If you have an immediate write-off, the trail is destroyed." Graphic   Table: "America Online Inc. The period also included a $17.7 million charge for the settlement of litigation. c-Included charges of $80.2 million for acquired research and development, restructuring charges of $33.8 million, and settlement charges of $16.6 million. d-Net loss, which included a contract termination charge of $24.5 million for quarter and year. title:
Compressed Data;
Real Networks in Pact With America Online
body: It seemed a risky step when Rob Glaser, chairman of Real Networks Inc., appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee in July, joining a chorus of Microsoft bashers. He complained that some of the Microsoft Corporation's latest software refused to work properly with his company's so-called streaming programs, which deliver audio and video over the Internet. Mr. Glaser is no garden-variety Microsoft adversary. He is himself a former Microsoft executive, and Microsoft holds a 10 percent stake in his fast-growing Seattle company. Yet his public dispute with Microsoft has certainly not hurt Mr. Glaser's business so far. There are no signs of retaliation from his giant neighbor, former employer and investor in Redmond, Wash. Meanwhile, people in increasing numbers -- now more than 30 million -- are using his software. And today, Real Networks plans to announce that America Online Inc., the on-line leader, has chosen its technology as the main way for users to play streaming media on the new version of the service, AOL 4.0. That word comes as America Online begins its own marketing drive today for AOL 4.0 -- not only an upgrade for its 13 million current subscribers, but also an effort to lure the millions of other people who will be sent America Online disks in themail. The America Online agreement is a marketing coup for Real Networks. "It is piggybacking on AOL's powerful distribution network," said Jae Kim of Paul Kagan & Associates, a research firm. The Internet, in Mr. Glaser's view, is on its way to becoming a mainstream mass medium for receiving the recorded voice and television-style videos. Already, 85 percent of the Web sites that offer streaming media make use of the technology from Real Networks. And if anything, he says, the spat with Microsoft over his Senate testimony seemed to help, with the volume of daily downloads from the company's site (www.real.com) rising by nearly 20 percent immediately afterwards. "People heard and read about streaming media," Mr. Glaser said, "and wanted to see what all the hubbub was about."   STEVE LOHR Graphic   Photo: Detail from Real Networks site.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
AOL 4.0 (and Lots of It) All on CD-ROM
body: America Online, the world's largest Internet and on-line service provider, wants to get its software into the computers of as many consumers as possible, and in trying to do so it has sometimes been accused of carpet-bombing the country with millions of 3.5-inch diskettes. No longer. Starting next week, AOL will begin precision-bombing the country with millions of CD-ROM disks containing version 4.0 of the AOL software. As in the past, consumers will find disks stuffed into mailboxes, cereal boxes, newspaper wrappers, airline snack packs and magazine inserts, and perhaps even stuffed in packages of frozen steaks. They will be distributed at banks, gas stations, shopping malls "and anywhere consumers go," a company spokeswoman said. Although finding an AOL diskette stuffed into a package of frozen steaks might lead one to suspect otherwise, the AOL spokeswoman insisted that the company has a methodical distribution strategy for the CD-ROM's. (It tested the diskettes to make sure they could withstand freezing.) Version 4.0, which was introduced in July, is widely regarded as a welcome update to AOL's software. But really, how many AOL CD-ROM disks does one need? Besides making handy drink coasters, the diskettes can also be disposed of by surreptitiously dropping them into children's candy bags on Halloween.   PETER H. LEWIS

title: Happy Birthday, Your Team Won, Your Stock Crashed - Correction Appended
body: WEEKDAY mornings for Jessica Nierenberg, a 23-year-old research manager at a market research company in San Francisco, usually begin with a dash to her neighborhood bus stop for a 30-minute ride to her office in the city's financial district downtown. By 8:30 she is at her desk, pouring herself a bowl of breakfast cereal and firing up her computer for a glimpse at what the planet has wrought while she slept. What greets her on her computer's screen is selected and displayed by My Yahoo, a free service by Yahoo, the giant Internet information company based in Santa Clara, Calif. My Yahoo shows Ms. Nierenberg how many email messages she has waiting to be read and a sampling of news headlines -- she can decide to call up any of the articles on domestic, political and international news for a more detailed look. Weather forecasts for her area and for Boston, her hometown, are parked in a corner of the screen. That wake-up dose of Internet offerings is, more or less, created specifically for Ms. Nierenberg, who, while computer savvy, doesn't consider herself a computer nerd (she does not have a computer at home, for instance). What she gets is a tailor-made collection of information that she has informed Yahoo she wants to get regularly. "It definitely saves me time," said Ms. Nierenberg, whose work requires her to be on a computer for at least eight hours a day. "It's nice to be able to push one button whenever I log on and to get all of this." The process that delivers all of that daily digital data to her and millions more is called personalization, the newest wave washing over the ever-changing shores of the Internet. After years of shaky starts, personalization promises to re-emphasize the personal in personal computing. Without a "personalized page," as she likes to call it, Ms. Nierenberg would have to resort to laboriously searching the Internet herself, plowing through more than 650,000 sites on the Web alone. One of the chief ideas driving personalization, many Internet experts say, is that the Internet, a victim of its own success, has become too voluminous for most people to handle comfortably and efficiently. If you're not using personalization, said Joe Kraus, senior vice president and co-founder of Excite, "you are not taking advantage of the medium." The thinking behind personalization goes something like this: What if your computer "knew" you, had a reasonable sense of your on-line interests and preferences and could respond to them? Forcing the computer to conform to your information needs rather than forcing you to conform to the computer's requirements is a step, many agree, toward realizing the vision that Nicholas P. Negroponte, director of the Media Laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, calls "the daily me." Services like My Yahoo, My Excite and even the set-top Web cruiser My Web TV (like other personalized features offered by America Online and the Microsoft Network, it is part of a service that requires a monthly fee) are increasingly fetching the kinds of content that their users say they want: specific types of news, weather forecasts, sports scores and schedules, stock quotations, horoscopes, television schedules, movie show times and state lottery results, for example. Many of these services also feature lists of users' favorite Web sites, chat rooms and message boards, along with daily health tips, travel alerts and on-line reminders of occasions like anniversaries and birthdays of relatives and friends. "It is empowering," said Steve Boxer, a computer consultant who owns Pachyderm Consulting in Brooklyn, speaking of his experience with personalization. "It really molds your computer to your interests." The first personalization service from a major on-line company was the Microsoft Network, or MSN. When it began in the fall of 1995, it offered users a relatively primitive capacity to customize the kinds of information they received. In January the following year, Excite created My Excite, which was followed that summer by My Yahoo. In July, Netscape, the leading Internet browser company, started offering My Netscape. While America Online offers its members very limited personalization with My AOL, a company spokesman said AOL will begin a much more fully featured service called My News in the next few weeks.. Competition among the companies offering personalization is intense, resembling at times the browser wars between Netscape and Microsoft. Refinements by one are often followed quickly by similar refinements by the others. Representatives of the personalization services refused to disclose just how many dollars each company has poured into creating and continually tweaking its service. But Mr. Kraus did say that his company, Excite, had spent a "significant investment in terms of manpower, money, hardware and engineering time" in creating its version of personalization, called My Excite. Nor will the companies reveal the number of subscribers for each service. "It has exceeded some expectations," said Henry Sohn, a senior producer for personalization for Yahoo. "Part of that is due to the overall growth in the Internet with each quarter. But it is clear that personalization services are really popular." THE promise of personalization had been on the lips of computer visionaries for years, even while the Internet struggled to find its identity. In the mid-1990's, software makers began selling off-the-shelf products like Pointcast Network that automatically log on to the Net, download categories of information broadly defined by users and then log off. These products, known as "push" technologies, began falling out of favor because they tended to be resource hogs and to deposit overwhelming amounts of information on computer hard drives. As many began to complain that push information was not selective enough, some users started looking for something that could pull from the Internet more specific information that matched their interests. "Back then, people didn't know what they wanted, so they wanted things pushed at them," said Rob Bernstein, a senior editor at Yahoo Internet Life, a monthly magazine about Net use. "The Net pretty much rejected that idea. Pull it down. That is the idea of personalization." But the idea of personalization, some experts acknowledged, has been difficult to sell. Part of the problem, said David Sze, vice president for network programming and content at Excite, is that personalization is hard to describe. The concept, he noted, tends to "come off very soft, vague." Using personalization is hardly automatic. First, you must register for it. (Many of the companies offering personalization, including Excite, Yahoo and MSN, have been trying to entice potential users by including very visible links from their popular home pages to their personalization pages.) Registration also means filling out an on-line questionnaire that can take anywhere from a few minutes to a half-hour to complete. (My Excite goes another step, giving brief descriptions of why it requests certain information. It says, for example, "Your birth date is used to provide your horoscope.") Designers of personalization services noted that the more information users provided about themselves, the more personalized the service would be. The My Yahoo form is much more tedious when it asks users to choose the information they want and how it is to be displayed. Each user enters preferences for a front page and pages for subjects like health, entertainment, business, chat and message boards. Each subject page has a dozen slots, and each slot holds a pull-down menu offering 36 choices of content, like sports scoreboards, information about vitamins and herbs, and news headlines. A user may choose one menu item for each slot. Each selection leads to that categories of information being displayed and updated whenever the personalized pages are viewed. My Yahoo goes even further, pressing for even more detail about a user's "specific interests." The categories there, like news, life styles, music and shopping, are more finely tuned. The answers may very well determine whether the Epicurious Web site for fine cooking appears on your finished page rather than Gamespot, which is popular among computer twitch gamers. "It helps us in a number of ways to offer a service that users find more relevant," Mr. Sohn at Yahoo said of the questionnaire. Once the services have an idea of what users want, they extract the information from various sources. To do that, they use relationships with news operations and other partners as well as their own powerful search engines. In most cases, as with My Yahoo, My Excite and My Netscape, the information is stored in central databases. When someone goes on line and types in a user name and a password, a cookie -- an identifying tag stored on the user's computer -- tells the personalization service who is requesting information. Based on what is in the cookie (for My Netscape it is a 16-digit number) the information is unlocked from the database and sent in a fraction of a second to the user. Most of the services regularly update their information and use both machines and people to match the right streams of information with the right users, personalization managers say. Just how these services actually work depends on closely held proprietary technologies, but many personalization operators agree that the services have been made possible by advances in database hardware and software in the last several years, by high-speed user-indentification systems and by the capacity to generate pages on the fly over the Internet. "Making it easy for people is our overarching design point," said Eckart Walther, product manager for My Netscape. "It makes information come to you rather than you going to the information." Nathan Beckord, a 26-year-old research associate for an investment bank in San Francisco, uses My Yahoo to check his stock portfolio and to glance at news about his investments. "For each portfolio, I have it customized to display what I want, quote the volume, and below that it shows the news," he said. Mr. Beckord also has the service set up as his default page, so it is the first thing he sees when he goes on line at work or at home. Users like Mr. Beckord are very useful to Internet companies, which is why the companies invested in personalization. The detailed information users give them about exactly what they want to see on line serves as a kind of survey. The information helps personalization managers decide what kinds of content to add, maintain or remove from their offerings. More important, many of the same managers said, the information makes it possible to match the advertising to users' interests and needs. Much as sporting goods manufacturers know that they have a better chance of reaching their market by advertising on ESPN, the national cable sports network, rather than with general-interest programs, advertisers are looking for much of the same result by having their advertisements sent over the Internet to people whose declared interests identify them as likely customers, explained Mr. Sze, of Excite. Mr. Sohn, of Yahoo, offered an example. "If we know someone is not interested in travel," he said, "then we are not likely to display an ad from an airline or travel agency." And the better his company is able to aim advertising, he added, the more it can charge for that advertising. But Mr. Sze said the use of personalization as an effective advertising tool had just begun. "The true value of this is not being realized the way it is going to be," said Mr. Sze, adding that on a scale of 1 to 10, personalization's use of advertising was in the 3-to-5 range. But, he said, Excite is preparing to step up its use of targeted advertising on the Internet. Mr. Walther also noted that personalization made good business sense because it was a way to capture more users, people who are approaching the Internet differently from their early-adopter predecessors. "We are seeing a lot more practical use of the Web," he said. "A lot of people don't go on the Web to just have fun." He said people tended to care more about how much time they were on the Internet and how much they accomplished. Personalization, he said, especially speaks to such users. And, added Mr. Boxer, the New York computer consultant, many new Internet users start with personalization services and keep returning to those companies. "Everyone has to start someplace," he said, "and the people who control the starting place hold some very valuable real estate." Because personalization requires the user to give a series of very specific preferences, there are growing concerns about what companies will do with all this new information. Mr. Sohn and other personalization service operators said the industry followed strict guidelines to protect users' privacy. Many of the companies' policies regarding privacy are clearly stated on line and linked to the questionnaires. "We care very deeply about privacy," Mr. Sohn said. "We go overboard to make users aware that we don't sell usage information to anyone." Another objection to the current personalization services is that they simply do not go far enough. Walter Bender, associate director of the M.I.T. Media Lab, said he would like to see additional levels of integration between, for example, on-line information and personal on-line calendars. The result, he said, would be more sophisticated services that would not only deliver tailored content but would also match that information with what a user was actually doing. You're taking a business trip to the Caribbean? Your computer would start delivering news, weather and travel information about the Caribbean as your departure date approached. Nonetheless, many Internet experts say, personalization is expected to be the buzz on the Internet for years to come, as it is tweaked and refined along the way. "It's not going to go away," Mr. Sze predicted. It is simply a matter of Internet destiny, others say. "This is the only medium," Mr. Kraus said, "that is inherently personalizable." Correction  An article in Circuits on Thursday about Web personalization services referred incorrectly to the one offered by the Excite search engine. Excite offers its personalization service on its home page (www.excite.com), not as a service called My Excite. The service began in January 1996 as Personal Excite, not as My Excite. In April 1997 it was renamed My Excite, but it is no longer called that. Correction-Date: September 21, 1998, Monday Graphic   Photo: HIS WAY-- Steve Boxer of Brooklyn is among the users of Web personalization services. (Andrea Mohin/The New York Times)(pg. G8)

title: Netscape and Qwest Plan To Announce Web Alliance
body: Forming perhaps the deepest alliance yet between a big Internet content provider and a long-distance company, the Netscape Communications Corporation and Qwest Communications International Inc. plan to announce a far-reaching strategic alliance today. The deal will link Netscape, a company whose browser software for navigating the World Wide Web made it synonymous with the Internet, to Qwest, a well-financed start-up that is building one of the most advanced fiber optic communications networks. The intent of the venture, to be known as Netscape Contact, is to enable consumers to manage voicemail, email and fax communications through a single site on the Web. Under intense competitive pressure from the Microsoft Corporation, which distributes its Web browsing software free, Netscape recently moved away from selling consumer software. It has instead focused on building its Netcenter Web site into an aggregation of information and communications services that generates revenue through advertising and direct sales. The Qwest deal will allow Netscape to broaden its Web offerings while also helping to insulate Netcenter from Internet traffic jams. For Qwest, securing an alliance with Netscape could prove a marketing coup. Along with IXC Communications Inc., the Williams Companies and Level 3 Communications Inc., Qwest is among a new breed of long-distance carriers that are building national networks based on Internet technology rather than on traditional phone technology. "This is a great distribution channel said Joseph P. Nacchio, Qwest's chief executive. "The Netcenter customers are more educated, more computer-centric and higher spenders." Mr. Nacchio said he expected the venture to generate between $150 million and $175 million in revenue over the next 18 months. Qwest will pay Netscape for the right to share the branding on Netscape Contact. In return, Netscape will pay Qwest for access to its network. In the end, Netscape expects to make about $25 million net over three years on the deal. Netscape now mainly employs the Sprint Corporation and the MCI Communications Corporation to provide Netcenter with high-speed, high-capacity access to the Internet. Those relationships are not endangered by Netscape's deal with Qwest, Mr. Homer said. Netscape will use Qwest's network for additional capacity, he said. Over the summer, Netscape added a search engine and email to its Web site in an effort to compete against so-called Internet portal companies like Yahoo and Excite. Working with Qwest, Netscape intends to begin selling long-distance phone service for 9 cents a minute any time of the day and to offer an integrated "in box" for voicemail, faxes and email. On Monday, Qwest announced that it had agreed to buy a rival Internet service provider, the Icon CMT Corporation, in an all-stock transaction valued at $185 million to attract corporate customers to its new super-fast Internet access. As Qwest expands into the Internet service market, it intends to sell Netscape software. Some of Netcenter's main competitors, including Yahoo, Infoseek, Lycos and Excite, have already made deals with long-distance phone companies. None of those agreements, however, appear as ambitious as Netscape's pact with Qwest.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
A former television executive enters a deal to provide content for Web-faring women.
body: IN a bow to advertisers marketing products to women, America Online said yesterday that it had agreed to sell three of its women-oriented services to a new venture formed by Geraldine B. Laybourne, the former head of cable television operations for the Walt Disney Company and ABC, who will develop them for the on-line service's new Women's Channel. Ms. Laybourne, long considered one of the most successful women in the television industry, left Disney/ ABC in May to form Oxygen Media, a company devoted to creating programs for women and children, both on line and on television. Before joining Disney/ABC, she built up Nickelodeon, the children's cable network. The terms of the deal were not disclosed. But a person close to both companies said that America Online would retain an equity stake of about 10 percent in Oxygen and would receive millions of dollars in cash. In return, Oxygen will get three content services: Electra, a service aimed at women; Moms Online, which is for parents, and Thrive, a service devoted to health issues. Under terms of the deal, these sites will be displayed prominently on America Online's new Women's Channel and other places on its service and on its World Wide Web site, AOL.com. Thrive was part owned by Time Warner Inc., but America Online bought out that stake before selling the service to Oxygen. Similarly, Moms Online had several other investors, which Oxygen bought out. The deal attests to the growing importance of women to on-line marketers. According to America Online, about 51 percent of its 13 million users are women, up from only 16 percent in 1994. "The traditional media have missed the boat with modern women," Ms. Laybourne said. "There is nothing that serves women the way ESPN serves men or Nickelodeon serves kids. We want to create a brand on both television and the Internet that brings humor and playfulness and a voice that makes a women say, 'You really understand me.' " Oxygen and the other women's services hope they can sell ads to makers of the sort of package goods that have typically been promoted on soap operas and other women-oriented television programming. America Online, for example, has an extensive deal to develop new forms of advertising for Unilever, the maker of Wisk detergent and Lipton tea. Some of the Unilever ads are expected to be placed on the services being sold to Oxygen. "Eighty five percent of purchases are made by women," Ms. Laybourne said. "We can be a real facilitator of commerce." The move also represents yet another flip-flop for America Online on the question of whether it wants to create its own programming or rely on outside companies for what the Internet industry calls "content." Initially, America Online was dependent on outside publishers for content. Then it began taking partial stakes in content companies, including iVillage Inc., another service aimed at women. About a year ago, it began to bring some content more directly under its control. It created Electra as its own women's area, competing directly with iVillage. One reason for the latest about-face is a longstanding professional relationship between Robert W. Pittman, the president of America Online, and Ms. Laybourne. Having hired Ms. Laybourne 20 years ago when he was an executive of MTV Networks, which started Nickelodeon, Mr. Pittman called her the day her resignation from Disney/ABC was announced to explore potential deals. Moreover, America Online has now decided it wants to pull back from operating its own content areas, in part because it has discovered that it can exact multimillion-dollar payments from content companies to display their services prominently to its members. As a result, the service would rather offer a menu of a handful of featured content areas in each topic. "Our audience tells us they want us to do the hard work of finding the best content on line and putting a context around it," said Barry Schuler, president of America Online's interactive services unit. "We need to own the top level, but when it comes down to the hard-core editorial stuff, we think that's a game of consolidation and critical mass, and we don't need to own all of that." While America Online now calls Oxygen the "centerpiece" of its Women's Channel, the company also has relationships with most of the other players in programming for women. It is the largest shareholder of iVillage, with a stake of just under 20 percent. And its service also has links to Women.com Networks, the Hearst Corporation's Homearts service and the on-line complements of the Oprah and Rosie O'Donnell talk shows. "Competition is healthy for the marketplace," Mr. Schuler said. "Our audience wins when there is more than one strong player out there." Candice Carpenter, the chief executive of iVillage, agreed. "It's crazy to think that what may be the biggest category on line will only have one player," she said of women's programming. "I'd rather have a few good competitors who will develop the space intelligently and aggressively." Ms. Carpenter denied industry reports that the relationship between iVillage and America Online had become strained. "AOL has been fabulous," she said. "They called me the day that this deal was discussed the first time. And I've signed a lot of big deals with AOL's competitors, and they have given me no flak for it." Moreover, she added, "We were offered Electra and Moms Online, and we turned them down." At this stage, it is hard to discern much difference between the strategies of the two companies. Ms. Carpenter said that iVillage was designed to have more places for advertising than the existing Electra and Moms Online services. And iVillage is less interested than Oxygen in pursuing television programming, she said. Ms. Laybourne said the deal with America Online would be the first of many partnerships Oxygen would forge with big media and on-line companies. In the coming months, she said, she will decide whether to create television programs for an existing network or make the high-stakes bet on forming a new cable network. Oxygen is also already selling sponsorships to companies that seek to sell goods to women.

title:
Media Talk;
Internet Magazine Obtains Prime Spot at America Online
body: A deal by the Internet magazine Salon to become an "anchor tenant" on America Online highlights some noteworthy developments both at the on-line publication and on the World Wide Web. People close to the deal, announced last week, say it will cost Salon (www.salonmagazine.com) less than $500,000 a year. Andrew Ross, Salon's vice president, said Salon would pay America Online "considerably less" than some other anchor tenants -- who are guaranteed a prominent position on one or more of America Online's 19 primary channels -- though he declined to specify the size of the payment. Started in 1995 by David Talbot, a former editor of The San Francisco Examiner, Salon has broken out of the pack of Web 'zines by mixing a breaking-news sensibility with the off-beat style of an alternative magazine. America Online's willingness to sign Salon as an anchor tenant -- particularly if the deal was cut rate -- is a clear sign of the magazine's increasing acceptance in the mainstream. As an anchor tenant on America Online's Lifestyle and Influence channels it joins the likes of Time magazine and E! Entertainment, adding what Chris Marentis, vice president for interactive marketing at America Online, called an "irreverent attitude" to the mix. The deal says something, too, about how Salon perceives its own status. Executives say Salon, which was born on a shoestring budget and nurtured by word of mouth, must now start spending to move its distribution to the next level. Salon says it already receives 12 million hits a month, or 600,000 singular visitors, but America Online offers access to 13 million fresh eyeballs. Salon's America Online deal might well be paving the way for a bigger stage as well: Wall Street. Mr. Ross confirmed that Salon was at least considering the possibility of taking itself public. He said investors might be interested in Salon if "we can show we have a proper business and get steady returns."   MATT RICHTEL Graphic   Photo: Detail from Salon, an on-line magazine.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Three Marketers Select Agencies
body: Three marketers have made decisions on their accounts. Cars.com, an Internet automotive data base service, named Stein Rogan & Partners in newyork as the first agency to handle its on-line and traditional advertising account. Billings were estimated at $26 million for 18 months. Cars.com, a unit of Classified Ventures L.L.C. in Chicago, made the decision without a formal review. Weight Watchers International, a unit of the H. J. Heinz Company in Woodbury, N.Y., named Seiden Group in newyork to handle the account of its weight-loss centers, which Seiden had handled on a project basis. Billings were estimated at $25 million. Lowe & Partners/ SMS in newyork, which once handled those duties, continues to handle media planning and buying; Lowe is part of the Lowe Group unit of the Interpublic Group of Companies. And the Texas Department of Economic Development in Austin selected McCann-Erickson Southwest in Houston to handle its Texas tourism account, which had been handled by GSD&M in Austin for more than a decade. Billings for the five-year contract were estimated at $12 million a year. The decision came after a two-month review that had been narrowed to McCann Southwest, which is part of the McCann-Erickson Worldwide Advertising unit of Interpublic, and GSD&M, a unit of Omnicom Group.

title:
THE MARKETS IN TURMOIL: THE INTERNET;
Have Laptop, Will Track Each Blip in the Market
body: LIKE many other investors, Allen Page, 31, a packaging salesman in Pasadena, Calif., had a bad week last week. But if not for his cellular phone, his laptop, his Internet account and his pager-like device that receives stock prices, it could have been worse. Wielding his portable electronic arsenal, Mr. Page was able to limit the damage by exercising options on beaten-down stocks, sometimes trading from the shoulder of the freeway between sales calls with his laptop plugged into his cell phone. Mr. Page is part of a rapidly swelling contingent of investors who keep an open line to their financial position as they go about their daily lives. He is in a position to know: "Sixty percent of my customers are hooked up on the Internet, and I can walk in the office and ask them the price of a stock and they'll tell me what it is," he said. "It's scary. It wasn't like that a year and a half ago." Most investors who track the movements of their stocks on the Internet -- about three million now have on-line brokerage accounts -- are enthusiastic about the virtues of expanded access to information. But in a time of market volatility, some on-line investors warn that such close contact with the ups and downs of a portfolio can have an emotional effect that is not always beneficial to strategic reasoning. Investors who are on line trade more often than those who are not, for example. According to E-Trade, the on-line brokerage firm, its customers average 25 trades a year, far more than the typical customer of a full-commission brokerage firm, who trades once or twice a year, or customers of a discount brokerage firm who trade four to six times a year. Part of the reason is that on-line brokerage firms typically charge much lower commissions than traditional ones, a feature that would naturally attract more active traders. But even for investors who trade through human brokers, monitoring a stock in real time on line can induce decisions more hasty than wise. "There's just something about watching it live, where you feel an immediacy and an urgency to do something, more than if you came home at the end of the day and looked at it in the paper," said Jeffrey S. Mitchell, 38, who has lost money by not waiting an extra hour to see what happened to a stock. Mr. Mitchell, of Westport, Conn., runs a software company and calls his broker when he sees opportunities on line. IN addition to hair-trigger trading, the Internet offers investors another double-edged sword: on-line discussion groups. Many "tips" posted on line have been exposed as erroneous or even fraudulent. But there is a subtler danger: the psychological attachment, or aversion, an investor can develop for a stock that is the subject of debate on financial World Wide Web sites like Silicon Investor or The Motley Fool. Posting a comment about a stock puts personal credibility and pride on the line, not just money. "When you buy a stock and talk about it on Silicon Investor, it becomes more than just a stock," Mr. Mitchell said. "You become polarized on the Internet, and then you feel, by selling or shorting, you are giving in to the dark side." Still, Mr. Mitchell and others said they found that on-line discussions bolstered their confidence about investment choices. And soaking in the rhythm of the market through cyberspace clearly gives individual investors new ways to participate directly in the market. Kathy Levinson, the president of E-Trade, attributed some of the intraday volatility seen in the market early last week to the ability of on-line investors to react swiftly to the market's gyrations. "Now that consumers can get information so readily, they can take advantage of a downward movement and buy into it, or an upward movement and sell into it," Ms. Levinson said. "There's more confidence and comfort when you can see your stock and watch it move." Tom Gardner, co-founder of the Motley Fool, one of the oldest investment sites on the Internet, said that the more information individual investors had access to, the better off they were, even if they lost some money along the way. "People can misuse their freedom," Mr. Gardner said. "But the long-term benefit of knowing this stuff, having information, being able to ask questions far outweighs the effect of a person who sees they're down 12 percent and makes a foolish decision." On-line investors appear to be climbing a learning curve. Dr. Jacob Snyder, 39, who lives in Kotzebue, Alaska, said his strategy had evolved since he opened an on-line brokerage account with Charles Schwab three years ago and began participating in discussion groups on Silicon Investor. It seems that no one in his town of 2,000 was interested in talking with him face to face about the merits of Intel or Applied Materials. "At the end of last year I discovered that I had a lot of short-term gains and short-term losses that exactly balanced out," Dr. Snyder said. "I decided I was acting too quickly. So I've forced myself to slow down." Still, last Monday, as he listened to the news of the market slide while traveling to visit his brother on Washington's Olympic Peninsula, Dr. Snyder was eager to log on to a computer. "I had bought myself a bunch of shorts to hedge my position," he said, meaning that he had protected himself against falling prices by selling borrowed shares of some stocks. "So as soon as I arrived, I signed on." He then took advantage of the market's dive to close his position profitably.
