title: Filters Let Users Screen Out On-Line Advertising
body: FOR every problem, there is an equal and opposite invention. First there was dirt, then vacuum cleaners. Next there were television commercials, followed quickly by the remote control, for whizzing past them. In October 1994, Hotwired, a portal site, introduced the Web's first advertisements, and less than a year later, Web Filter emerged as the first software to keep ads from loading on Web pages. A handful of such filters are available now, many for free, some for sale, with more being introduced all the time. They range from Intermute (www.intermute.com), a virtual mute button that removes soundtracks, pop-up frames and automatic refresh features, to a "decaf" filter to avoid Java script (muffin. doit.org) to @Guard (www.atguard. com), a new $29.95 utility from WRQ that includes a personal firewall. Each day several hundred people download a filter from Junkbusters .com, a crusader in the battle against unsolicited information, including junk snail mail. The site includes links to other filters as well, including a link to Web Free (www.falken. net/webfree), for Mac users. But Internet advertisers are far from rolling up their banners and finding a different medium. "We think Web ad filters aren't necessary," said Lyn Chitow Oakes vice president of marketing at Flycast Communications, an Internet advertising network. "Web advertising is not very intrusive, it doesn't stop you from getting to the information you want, and it doesn't break up programming at all." Her company's ads are designed to load faster than the underlying content. Internet service providers are likewise unfazed. "There are filters out there so somebody could record a TV show and skip the commercials, but not many people do that," said Myer Berlow, senior vice president for interactive marketing at America Online. Besides, he said, AOL users spend much of their time in chat rooms, using email or visiting content areas, where they are not bombarded with ads. Many filters work by serving as a proxy, an intermediary between the browser and the user, refusing ads and filtering out cookies, the small files that allow servers watch where a user browses. A filtered Web page shows little broken window icons where the ads would be. About 1 percent of Internet users filter ads, according to Junkbusters, and many others simply direct their browsers to refuse all images. The user can instruct Junkbuster's filter, the Internet Junkbuster, by customizing a list of ad sources to be ignored. Such lists of sources are available on line for downloading. "It's really an extremely minimal product," said Jason Catlett, head of the Junkbusters Corporation, and it uses only 200 kilobytes of disk space. The programs help speed Web surfing by reducing the loading time of each page, and they cut down on the distraction of animated ads, some that come with soundtracks. A more important reason to filter ads, Mr. Catlett said, is that each time a person clicks on a Web page, the ad company can learn about what he or she finds interesting, by which links or ads are visited. "A lot of people don't mind the ads themselves -- it's the surveillance behind them they dislike," Mr. Catlett said. But inertia keeps many people from filtering out their ads. "I really, really dislike animations blinking at me," said John Chapin, a software design professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. "But if I were to take a step back, advertising revenues support a lot of the 'free' sites I like to look at." Mr. Catlett said many people are afraid to download a piece of software. "It still is a step that requires some small amount of technical confidence," he said. "And in our experience, many people do not mind the ads. If you search on a search engine, the ads seem to speak directly to what you're searching for. Search engines sell the keywords that people are searching for." While some companies look at ways to get around such filters, many believe that if someone goes to the trouble of filtering ads, there is no use antagonizing them, especially when there are so many other potential customers to reach. Mr. Catlett said he believed that most surfers would continue reading and visiting banner ads. "They never knew a time when there were no ads on the Web," he said.

title: America Online Grows Despite Increasing Fees
body: Showing that a 10 percent price increase hardly dented its rapid growth, America Online said its operating earnings totaled $57.3 million for the quarter that ended June 30, a tenfold increase over the same period a year earlier. That represents operating income of 23 cents a share, exceeding the 19 cents that analysts estimated. In a rare move, however, the company said it could not publish its net earnings pending an agreement with the Securities and Exchange Commission over several special charges. America Online said that it expected to write off most of the $287 million it paid to acquire Mirabilis, an Internet chat service, and the $29 million it paid for Net Channel, the maker of a device to connect televisions to the Internet. Companies generally like to take the highest possible one-time write-offs in connection with acquisitions to reduce the ongoing drag on future earnings from the required accounting adjustments. America Online also expects to write off about half of the $35 million cost of settling a class action. Steve Case, America Online's chairman, said that whatever the S.E.C. decided, the company would meet its earnings forecasts for the coming year. And in any case, he said, the operating results for the last quarter would not change as a result of the negotiations with the S.E.C. Over all, the company continued to show very strong momentum in nearly every aspect of its business. Although America Online raised the price of its unlimited dial-up service from $19.95 to $21.95 a month on April 1, its subscriber base increased by a net of 665,000 during the quarter, to 12.5 million. "My prediction was that we would see no member growth," Mr. Case said. "Despite a price increase and reduced marketing expenditures, we continue to have a great relationship with the mass market." Nonetheless, the pace of subscriber growth has slowed to 5.7 percent during the most recent quarter, compared with a 7.5 percent increase in the corresponding period in 1997. In the quarter, America Online also significantly pared promotional spending, to 12 percent of revenues, compared with 21 percent a year earlier. The company said its marketing expenses would increase, however, as it began to promote its new software version 4.0. Over all, revenues increased by 67 ,percent to $792 million. Of that, the company took in $83 million from advertising and other deals with on-line merchants, an increase of 87 percent from a year earlier. Indeed, the company said it had a backlog of $510 million in commitments for on-line advertising. Mr. Case said that as a result of huge layoffs in the Compuserve subsidiary, that division was close to breaking even. Compuserve will test various marketing approaches for the rest of this year, he said, predicting that it would not realize net earnings until more aggressive promotions begin next year. America Online's stock fell $5.0625, to $110.9375 in trading on the newyork Stock Exchange before the preliminary earnings were announced. In after-hours trading, the shares jumped $7.8125, to $118.75.

title: Deal to Create The Largest Interactive Ad Agency
body: In a combination that will create the largest agency devoted to creating advertising on the Internet, Agency.com has agreed to buy Eagle River Interactive. This deal, which is expected to be announced today, is the latest in a mad game of Pac Man, in which the dozens of small agencies founded by young entrepreneurs are racing to gobble each other up. Behind the scenes in many of these transactions is the Omnicom Group, the huge advertising agency holding company, which has taken stakes in several of the most prominent start-up interactive agencies. Omnicom owns 40 percent of Agency.com, which is based in newyork, and all of Eagle River Interactive, based in Chicago. The terms of the deal have not been disclosed, but Omnicom's stake in Agency.com will increase to just under half as a result of the deal, said Chan Suh, Agency.com's chief executive. In recent months, Agency.com has also bought Online Magic, Spiral Media, Ketchum Interactive and Interactive Solutions. The later two were also owned by Omnicom. Interactive agencies provide a range of services, including helping companies set up their own sites on the World Wide Web and placing "banner" advertisements on other sites to bring in traffic. While this business incorporates the sort of writing and design skills used by conventional advertising agencies, much of the work of the interactive shops more closely resembles such detailed computer programming typically provided by technology companies. "An interactive company is one part creativity, one part technology and one part business strategy," said Felice Kincannon, who looks after Omnicom's interactive holdings through a unit called Communicade. Indeed, technology companies have been expanding into this field. Both the International Business Machines Corporation and the Electronic Data Services Corporation have set up big interactive design departments as an adjunct to their business of building elaborate Internet sites for companies. And two of the most aggressive acquirers of interactive agencies -- U S Web in Santa Clara, Calif., and iXL in Atlanta -- have been buying both technology and design companies. Still, the conventional advertising companies have the greatest ties to the existing Interactive agencies, with True North Communications, Grey Advertising and the Interpublic Group all owning stakes in at least one of the top 15 agencies. Omnicom, however, has been the most aggressive, with stakes in 4 of the top 15 ranked by Adweek magazine, including Agency.com, now tied with iXL for first place; Think New Ideas, the fifth-ranked agency; Organic Online, No. 7, and Eagle River, No. 14. In total, its six agencies have 1,500 employees and revenues of $180 million. That represents about one third of what Jupiter Communications estimates is a $500 million market this year. "Instead of picking one horse to ride, Omnicom has spread its bets and has watched how the race turned out," said Seth Alpert, a senior adviser to Ad Media Partners, a newyork investment bank that specializes in media companies. "So far, they have done a pretty good job. As it has with conventional advertising agencies, Omnicom has been able to buy into the younger interactive agencies by offering to act as the friendly, but unintrusive, big brother. "They are not backseat drivers," Mr. Suh said, adding that Agency.com had few client referrals from other Omnicom agencies. But it has been able to ask executives of the holding company questions from time to time. "It's like having your own consulting company on call," he said. Yet Omnicom has subtly encouraged the strongest of its flock to absorb the laggards. In February, it flew the top executives of all of its interactive companies for a retreat in Miami. While Omnicom did not play explicit matchmaker, the flirtation was as heavy as on a college spring break. "It was a courting thing," said Kevin Rowe, the chief executive of Eagle River. After a first date of a joint project for Compaq Computer, Eagle River and Agency.com decided to get hitched. As a result of the combination, Agency.com will have 575 employees in 10 offices and 1998 revenues of about $80 million. Founded in 1995, Agency.com's largest clients include British Airways, GTE and Metropolitan Life. Eagle River, a descendant of a company that placed billboards on Colorado ski slopes, serves clients that include Sprint and Disneyland Paris. Many advertising industry executives expect that Agency.com is trying to grow quickly in preparation for an initial public offering. Mr. Suh declined to comment on any potential offering. Yet others wonder whether many of these young companies are expanding faster than they can handle. "I get worried for a company like Agency.com," said Gene DeRose, the president of Jupiter Communications. "I think they have to be careful about how they integrate their acquisitions." Mr. DeRose pointed to the example of CKS Group, one of the first publicly held interactive agencies, which has found melding its many acquisitions harder than it expected. CKS's stock trades at less than half of its 52-week high of $64.25, reached last September; the shares closed at $19.3125 Friday, off 12.5 cents, in Nasdaq trading. Others point out that the acquisition prices for interactive agencies is vastly higher than for conventional ad agencies, which typically are sold for about the total of their annual revenues. The high water mark for pricing was recently set by ICC Technologies, a Hatboro, Pa., maker of humidity control systems, which recently moved onto the Internet by buying Rare Medium, a small newyork agency for $45 million, more than 11 times its revenues. Many other more traditional buyers are turning up their noses at those prices. "We recently met with a foreign agency who said they were looking for an Interactive shop in this country," Mr. Alpert of Ad Media Partners said. "We told them they would have to pay four or five times revenue, and they were aghast and went home."

title: Senate Panel Would Reduce Tax Moratorium onInternet
body: A proposed six-year moratorium on taxes in cyberspace would be reduced to only two years under the version of the Internet Tax Freedom Act approved by the Senate Finance Committee. The committee also voted last week to force states and local governments that tax Internet access to end these taxes, but left untouched claims for millions of dollars in taxes that America Online did not collect from customers and may now have to pay at its own expense. The Finance Committee's version of the bill differs significantly from those passed by the House and by the Senate Commerce Committee. The House version calls for a three-year moratorium, while the Senate Commerce Committee's version would keep the six-year moratorium. Both the House and the Senate Commerce Committee versions would block states from citing the presence of computer servers to establish a company's physical presence within a state. The Senate Finance Committee's version is silent on this issue. Until most of these and other differences are worked out, the bill is unlikely to reach the Senate floor for a vote. The Senate is in recess until the end of the month. The Internet Tax Freedom Coalition, the leading electronic commerce group lobbying to make cyberspace free of taxes and tariffs, contends that confusion about taxes is hampering the growth of commerce in cyberspace. That argument was rejected by Senator John H. Chafee, Republican of Rhode Island, and Senator Bob Kerrey, Democrat of Nebraska, both members of the Finance Committee. Senator Chafee, citing testimony by America Online that electronic commerce will grow to $20 billion by 2000, said a two-year moratorium was enough to determine how to tax cyberspace transactions properly. Senator Kerrey dismissed the arguments of industry lobbyists that taxes are crippling electronic commerce. "This is no infant industry in swaddling clothes," he said, citing 30 percent growth a month in retail sales on the Internet. "Wall Street can't throw money at Internet companies fast enough." The 19-to-1 vote by the Senate Finance Committee to approve its version of the bill came last Tuesday, the same day that the Commerce Department issued a report showing a growing disparity in access to the Internet among various income groups. People making more than $75,000 a year are seven times as likely to have access to the Internet as those making $15,000 to $20,000 a year and more than twice as likely as those making $35,000 to $50,000. The concept of making the Internet a tax-free zone was criticized by Michael Maserov, a senior policy analyst with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. "This is just one more tax break for the affluent at the expense of the poor," he said. The Senate Finance Committee rejected, on a 10-to-10 tie vote, a proposal by Senator Kent Conrad, Democrat of North Dakota, that would have allowed states that tax Internet access and data sold over the Internet to continue those levies. Senator Conrad, who was formerly his state's elected tax commissioner, said he saw no compelling reason for the Federal Government to interfere with state tax policies. The "ability of states or local governments to collect tax" on transactions before July 29 would not be affected by the Senate Finance Committee's version of the bill, according to the committee's chairman, Senator William V. Roth Jr., Republican of Delaware. That provision is a serious setback for America Online, the nation's largest Internet service provider, which collects sales taxes on behalf of foreign governments but has refused to collect the same taxes when they are required by the states and local governments.

title:
SPENDING IT: FOCUS ON AIR TRAVEL;
Name That Fare! (And Other On-Line Challenges for Travelers)
body: JUST because August is around the corner and you still haven't planned your summer vacation, don't despair. The Internet can help book a quick -- even bargain-priced -- getaway. Priceline.com has generated a big buzz since its start-up in April, when it kicked off a multimillion-dollar advertising campaign, promoting a "name your own price" service for buying discounted plane tickets. Priceline's on-line auction, though, is only one of the most recent additions to the Internet's fare deals. Depending on how nimble a traveler you are -- and how much inconvenience you can endure -- various travel opportunities are only a click away. Each week, the World Wide Web sites of individual airlines post deeply discounted fares for travel that weekend. Other sites gather and update information on inexpensive fares from several sources. Still, Priceline has made a sizable impression in a relatively short time. Jay Walker, chairman of the company, based in Stamford, Conn., said it had already sold 40,000 tickets, generating revenues of more than $10 million. Though Priceline has satisfied some customers, its lengthy list of requirements has frustrated others. And most major domestic airlines do not cooperate with the service, since they promote their own specials on line to fill their empty seats; this limits Priceline's offerings. To use the service, customers make a ticket request on its Web site, saying where and when they want to travel and how much they are willing to pay. (Travelers without Internet access can bid by phone.) If a bid is much lower than published fares, it will be rejected. To determine a reasonable price, customers should research the standard range of fares on the desired route. Once a bid is submitted, Priceline sorts through the airline seats at its disposal. It says it can notify customers within an hour whether a bid for a domestic flight has been accepted or rejected -- 24 hours for international flights. In submitting bids, customers also provide their credit card information. If a bid is accepted, a ticket is automatically issued and the credit card is billed; if the bid is rejected, travelers can submit other bids using different airports or different dates, but cannot re-bid with higher amounts using the same itinerary. There are other restrictions: tickets are not refundable or exchangeable and are not eligible for frequent-flier miles. Priceline's services are free for travelers using electronic tickets, which are generally available only on domestic flights; if travelers require a paper ticket, they pay a $12.50 overnight delivery fee. And those are just the rules for getting tickets. The flights themselves may challenge an individual's notion of ease and comfort. Travelers must be willing to leave anytime between 6 A.M. and 10 P.M. on their selected date if flying domestically, or any time if flying overseas. Flights may also require a stop or a connection en route. A potentially bigger obstacle is that the auction site seems to have the cooperation of only a few domestic airlines. Eight of the 10 major unitedstates airlines -- Alaska, American, Continental, Delta, Northwest, Southwest, United and U S Airways -- say they have chosen not to work with Priceline. The other two -- America West and Trans World Airlines -- declined to comment, though industry executives say they do work with the service. That is not to say you can't get tickets on the major carriers through Priceline's auctions. As a licensed travel agency, the company offers discounted seats on major airlines through the Worldspan computerized reservations system and its inventory; Priceline also sometimes resells the wholesale seats offered by consolidators. Mr. Walker, though, said that less than 5 percent of the tickets Priceline sells are through Worldspan or consolidators. Mr. Walker declined to identify which major unitedstates carriers worked with his company, saying only that a total of 15 unitedstates and international airlines are offering Priceline seats to sell. The limits on inventory can stymie bidders, as Michael Spohn, a 21-year-old student at the University of Missouri, has discovered. Since late May, Mr. Spohn, an intern in the retail advertising department of The Des Moines Register, has placed bids with Priceline nine times to fly from Omaha, Des Moines or Cedar Rapids, Iowa, to his hometown, St. Louis. Each time, he said, he has bid three or four days before he wanted to travel and set a price $10 to $15 above the lowest available published advance-purchase fare; in his research, he also found that seats were still available on these routes. Yet each bid was rejected; he suspects that Priceline simply had no seats to sell on those routes. "I don't understand why they can't do it," he said, "especially if you offer bids above the airlines' lowest fare." Mr. Walker said Priceline could not offer seats in all markets, acknowledging that it had "no lift in small cities that have no lift." "You need to be willing to drive to a bigger city," he said. Priceline has its fans, including George Miller, 54, artistic director of the Theater Outlet in Allentown, Pa. Several weeks ago, Mr. Miller bought two roundtrip tickets, at $550 each, to fly on Aer Lingus from Newark to Dublin for his honeymoon, which is to begin today. The lowest published fare offered by the airline for the same date was $598. Mr. Miller said he found Priceline to be "very prompt and very courteous." Ashita Patel, 34, a pharmacist from Edison, N.J., is also happy: Earlier this month, she bought four roundtrip tickets, at $300 each, for her family to fly on United from Newark to London for a September wedding. United's lowest published fare for that time was $788. (Prices do not include tax.) She said she was "shocked that they could do it so fast. It only took 12 hours." OTHER Web sites also offer deeply discounted tickets; in some cases, they can arrange for cheap hotel rooms and car rentals, too. Most major unitedstates airlines offer special weekly Internet fares, usually for travel that weekend; prices are much lower than their cheapest advance-purchase fares. The drawback, of course, is that destinations are limited: You have to go where they want to take you. On-line travel agencies including Preview Travel, Expedia and Travelocity have special features that help track low fares. Preview offers low fares and announcements of airlines' latest specials. Expedia, owned by Microsoft, and Travelocity, controlled by AMR, the parent of American Airlines, send regular email to travelers listing the lowest published fares on the routes of their choice. Travelocity also posts a list of each day's lowest fares. Cheaptickets.com, a consolidator based in Honolulu, sells published and unpublished discount fares for flights on domestic and foreign airlines; Michael J. Hartley, its president, said it obtains the unpublished discounts from established carriers. Travelers must provide credit-card information before they can conduct a fare search; requests result in a choice of 25 fares, which the customer can accept or decline. Another site, Bestfares.com, based in Dallas, has sections with general access to rate information and others only for subscribers, who pay $60 a year to get more detailed travel data and more deals. A site operated by 1travel.com, a Zionsville, Pa., travel agency, provides another path to discounts. It publishes all airlines' weekly Web specials and will send email lists of them, customized to the traveler's requirements. It also provides data on deeply discounted international tickets sold by several large consolidators. Graphic   Photo: Michael Spohn, an intern at The Des Moines Register, has had no success with Priceline.com, an on-line service that lets users bid for air fares. He says it has rejected each of his nine bids for a ticket to St. Louis. (Steve Pope for The newyork Times)  Chart: "Wings on the Web" The Internet has become one of the best places to find discounted airfares, with travel agencies and the airlines themselves competing on line to deliver cheap tickets. title:
An Expert at Trades;
N.A.S.D. Chief Makes Bold Moves as Markets Combine
body: Frank G. Zarb is standing in his office, wielding his signature prop, a Louisville Slugger embossed with his name, and he's grinning one of his signature giant-killer grins. Mr. Zarb is not a home-run hitter like Ken Griffey Jr. or Mark McGwire, but in his own way the 63-year-old chairman of the National Association of Securities Dealers, the parent company of the Nasdaq stock market, has been slugging them out of the park this year and shaking up the financial markets in the process. Earlier this year, Mr. Zarb reached deals to fold the American Stock Exchange and the Philadelphia Stock Exchange into the N.A.S.D. as companion exchanges to Nasdaq. And now he is thinking of going abroad, discussing an alliance with the Deutsche Borse in Frankfurt. Since arriving at the N.A.S.D. early last year as a kind of Mr. Fix-it, Mr. Zarb has been a man in perpetual motion, racing around the globe promoting a new Nasdaq, the "Next Nasdaq," as one slogan says. The bold moves are aimed at creating what Mr. Zarb calls a "market of markets," a global financial network that will pose an even greater challenge to Nasdaq's chief rival, the richer and more prestigious newyork Stock Exchange. Bold as they are, though, the moves are just Mr. Zarb's attempt to ride a larger wave of change, one that is transforming trading worldwide. At a time when investors are increasingly turning to Internet trading and other low-fee electronic formats, pressure has been building on traditional exchanges not only to keep pace with technology but also to sharply lower costs. "It's time to challenge the status quo," Mr. Zarb, a longtime Wall Street player, said in a recent interview in his office at the headquarters of the N.A.S.D. here. "I came to a very early conclusion that the velocity of change was going to be upon us and that we had to do something." Looming over Mr. Zarb and his counterparts at other exchanges is the most sweeping makeover of financial markets in the last quarter- century, experts say. By the millennium, the result could be the initial stages of a global electronic marketplace. Not since "May Day" 1975, when the era of fixed commissions came to an end in the unitedstates, has the structure of financial markets been put through such a flurry of activity. The changes include a worldwide push toward consolidation. Overseas, the London, Frankfurt and Paris stock exchanges plan to form alliances aimed at creating a Pan-European exchange. Early in July, the Chicago Board of Trade and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange agreed to combine back-office operations. On Thursday, the Chicago Board Options Exchange and the Pacific Exchange announced a merger. "Most people don't understand that we're in the beginning of a revolutionary change in the U.S. market structure," said Douglas Atkin, who heads the international unit of Instinet, an electronic trading network owned by Reuters. "This is making the whole process from mutual fund management to settlement more efficient." The driving forces behind all this change are technology and globalization. Computers and software are lowering costs and making trades faster and more efficient. And in a mature bull market, financial exchanges -- like the big companies they list -- are looking for global growth. To the average American investor, the changes mean that buying shares of Coca-Cola, Microsoft or even Deutsche Telekom could be much easier and cheaper in the coming years. Global 24-hour trading is not far off, and dabbling in bonds, options and futures could come at the click of a mouse. There are those who worry that the melding of exchanges could result in monopolistic tendencies and that regulatory and accounting issues will cloud a global financial network. Still, industry executives see the rapid pace of change lowering costs, driving a global surge in the sale of stocks and other financial products. Mr. Zarb did not ignite the change, of course; he merely seized upon it. But perhaps more than any other market leader, he says he is willing to ride the frenzy to transform Nasdaq into a truly electronic marketplace with links to other exchanges. Mr. Zarb is neither a commanding speaker nor a visionary, but colleagues say he has a fiery temperament and knows how to usher in change. And that is what is necessary for Nasdaq, which has been promising to revolutionize Wall Street since the early 1970's, when it arrived as an automated quotation system for the over-the-counter market. Even though it has landed high-technology giants like Intel and Microsoft, Nasdaq's image has been tarnished by a history of lax regulatory practices and a price-fixing scandal among its dealers that arose a few years ago. One of Mr. Zarb's tasks is to change that image. Already, he says, the N.A.S.D. has tightened regulations, offered individuals better access to the market and laid the foundation for a group of financial exchanges that provide both auction trading, in which agents for buyers and sellers meet directly on crowded floors, and electronic systems that link dealers around the world. Nasdaq is even testing direct Internet trades. The Big Board's answer? A big marketing effort to sustain its status as the premier marketplace, home to perennial all-stars like General Electric and AT&T. Its slogan is "The world puts its stock in us." And, for the most part, it does. Richard Grasso, chairman of the newyork Stock Exchange, has brought in dozens of major foreign listings in the last few years. And while the Big Board has not struck a deal with another large exchange and its leaders disagree over whether technology will lead to the demise of its trading floor, Mr. Grasso does not ignore the pressures. "This is the beauty of the American market landscape," he said. "You have alternatives, and that heightens our competitive focus." Mr. Zarb is determined to be more than an alternative. He wants to establish Nasdaq as a superior model to the auction system. And he knows something about overcoming adversity. He grew up in Brooklyn, the son of a refrigerator repairman, and studied nights to earn an M.B.A. at Hofstra University. Before long, he found himself at the investment firm of Cogan, Berlind, Weill & Levitt, in the company of Sanford I. Weill, now the chief executive of Travelers Group, and Arthur Levitt Jr., now chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission. He left in the 1970's for a stint in the Labor Department under President Richard M. Nixon and became "energy czar" under President Gerald R. Ford after the Arab oil embargo. But he has always come back to Wall Street, where he has made a fortune. In 1987, Mr. Weill asked Mr. Zarb to take over the "beleaguered Smith Barney," as he says it was known. He managed to raise its profile and its profitability. He also ran Alexander & Alexander Services, an insurance broker, in the 1990's. And then came the offer to head the N.A.S.D. When Mr. Zarb arrived, Wall Street firms were pressing the exchanges to lower their costs because of the boom in Internet trading and the growth of alternative trading systems, such as the Electronic Communications Networks, an S.E.C.-approved system that matches buyers and sellers. But the new competitive arena was international. "In Europe, there's a huge competitive race between the Big Board and the Nasdaq," said William C. Freund, an economics professor at Pace University. "Daimler-Benz, for instance, recognized you need a presence in the U.S. because if you're going to buy a company here, the currency is no longer cash, it's stock," he said. Daimler was the first German stock to list itself directly on the newyork Stock Exchange. For Nasdaq, the proposed marketing and listings alliance with the Deutsche Borse is one path to international glory. Nasdaq has also started a marketing campaign in Europe and continues to promote itself as a model for younger, growth-oriented exchanges like Easdaq, a kind of European Nasdaq, and Ausdaq in Australia. Meanwhile, Europe is awash in speculation about other alliances. And there is talk, both in the unitedstates and in Europe, about a global system that could offer unified trading in the world's 1,000 largest companies. In this new world, however, competitive concerns are not limited to stock exchanges. The Chicago Board of Trade, the world's largest futures exchange, faces a challenge from Cantor Fitzgerald, a Wall Street brokerage firm that has teamed up with the newyork Board of Trade to start an electronic futures exchange that promises to be cheaper. The Chicago exchange, which maintains a huge trading floor, plans to counter with its own electronic system, even though many members are reluctant to undermine their frenzied, face-to-face call-and-answer system. "The competitive landscape is rapidly changing," Patrick Arbor, chairman of the Chicago exchange, said in a report in June. "And the rabbit that dawdles in complacency may indeed find itself losing the race to the perceived turtle." Alfred R. Berkeley 3d, the president of Nasdaq and the man who heads Mr. Zarb's lineup against the Big Board, does not intend to dawdle. His vision is of a Nasdaq that will be linked to exchanges around the world as well as to private trading systems like Optimark, a new automated trading method that could eliminate layers of brokers and middlemen. The Big Board, however, has not exactly embraced the electronic revolution. Technology, yes; electronic trading, no. The face-to-face auction system, Mr. Grasso says, is simply the best and most efficient model, and there are no plans to change that. "You never say never," Mr. Grasso said, "but I've yet to see a technology replicate it." At the heart of the debate over the future of exchanges is just what they will look like. Some may resemble Nasdaq, which operates a huge computer center in Trumbull, Conn., with chilled rooms populated by mainframe computers and blinking screens but few people. For the Big Board, it will remain a cacophonous floor of traders and brokers, augmented by sophisticated technology. William R. Harts, vice chairman of the Philadelphia Stock Exchange, says that there will always be a need for an exchange-like entity, if only to fulfill a regulatory function. "But the writing on the wall may mean an exchange is not a physical floor," he said. "All these exchanges are not merging for the fun of it -- they're merging because at some point the physical floors become less important." Yet even as many Wall Street participants are skeptical about whether computers can replace the human touch, in Europe, Australia, Canada and even in the unitedstates, technology appears to be winning the battle. And Mr. Zarb is betting in that direction, even while hedging with auction trading on the American Exchange. "Everything's going to be linked," he said. "Everything's going to be connected." And in the center of things, Mr. Zarb said with that same long-ball hitter's look in his eye, will be Nasdaq. Graphic   Photo: Frank G. Zarb was hired to bring some firepower to the N.A.S.D. title: From a Broker, Concern About On-Line Trading
body: On-line trading can be hazardous to your wallet. That was the cautionary conclusion of John L. Steffens, vice chairman of Merrill Lynch & Company, in a speech at the Spotlight conference, an annual gathering of computer industry executives and entrepreneurs held here this week. Mr. Steffens said that the ease and convenience of Internet-based trading was seducing people into buying and selling stocks more often than they should. So-called E-traders, he said, tend to trade three to four times more often than people who buy and sell shares through traditional brokerage firms. And E-traders pay a price for that haste and frequency. Mr. Steffens cited a study by economists at the University of California at Davis that looked at the trading habits of 60,000 households from 1991 to 1996. According to the study, the most active traders had a rate of return of 10 percent per year, compared with a 15 percent return for those who traded least often. "People are killing themselves by trading too much -- there's no question," said Terry Odean, an assistant professor of finance at the university and one of the study's authors. According to Mr. Steffens, 25 to 30 percent of retail stock trades are done electronically, and the median age of an on-line trader is about 36. Mr. Steffens, 57, is of the old school of stock market investing, which is guided by a principle of long-term stock holdings. When held for years, not months or weeks, stocks gain value, he said, and serious investors recognize that. Most of the 200 or so people in the audience were in their 30's and early 40's, and their livelihood depends on promoting the benefits of the Internet. Some two-thirds of those said they traded stocks on line. "The question is, are you interested in fun and games or investing?" Mr. Steffens said in an interview. "The two are very different." Mr. Steffens added that on-line trading had also caused increased volatility in the stock markets because of the ease with which it is done. And he agreed with an audience member that on-line trading could become the "Las Vegas of the next century." There are several firms that offer no-frills electronic trading. But while Merrill Lynch uses the Net to give clients instant access to research and other information, it does not yet offer on-line stock trading, though it plans to do so for some customers by the end of the year. Whether Mr. Steffens convinced his audience was unclear. He did, however, make some kind of impression. When a conference official polled the audience before Mr. Steffens's presentation, most people said they considered the Internet as more of an opportunity for Merrill Lynch than a threat. Thirty minutes later, when the same question was posed again after Mr. Steffens's remarks, most people in the audience decided that the on-line world was a threat to the brokerage firm. David Braunschvig, a managing director at Lazard Freres & Company, who attended the conference, said of the opinion swing: "It's not that they were more bearish on Merrill, but they realized the complexity of the whole landscape. It was the first time they started thinking of the relative merits of, and challenges for, an established brand coming into the on-line arena."

title: Internet Brokers Chart the European Investor
body: Alan English has an addiction, and he's not ashamed to discuss it. "I log on every day, sometimes from the office, in the morning and in the evening," Mr. English, a 51-year old computer consultant, said like a boy taken with a new toy. "Some days I don't trade; some days I trade four or five times a day." "At the end of the day, the cost of a trade and the spread on shares can be quite significant," Mr. English said, still hooked a year and a half after he began shopping for stocks over the Internet. Mr. English is one of a growing number of Europeans with on-line investment fever. After years of relying on elaborate social security systems, Europeans are being urged by their governments to take a greater hand in planning their financial futures. The result is a stock market boom. And as surfing the World Wide Web gains popularity, more and more Europeans are logging on to shop for financial products, retrieving detailed financial information and buying and selling shares. True, compared with the unitedstates, where about 20 percent of all stock trades are now entered over the Internet, the movement is in its infancy. But as the trend gathers force, American Internet brokers have begun moving into Britain and are increasingly setting eyes on the Continent. Their arrival poses a challenge for the few and fledgling European on-line trading companies -- whose ambitions are for the moment limited to individual national markets, in contrast to the global strivings of their American competitors. Thus, experts expect the arrival of the Americans to accelerate big changes in the securities business that are already under way as Europe forges itself into a single market. Nowhere is the trend more apparent than here in Britain. In April, Charles Schwab started an on-line trading service, and in June, the E-Trade Group, based in Palo Alto, Calif., announced a joint venture with a British partner, as well as licensing agreements in Germany. Other Internet brokers, like Ameritrade and DLJ Direct, part of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, are studying moves to catch up. American brokers, under competitive pressure at home that is reducing profit margins, are being drawn to the lucrative potential of Europe, where the idea of a discount broker is still novel, said Stephen Eckett, author of "Investing Online," a leading guide to Internet investment. Though Europeans can already use American on-line brokers to buy shares in the unitedstates, the Americans do not actively promote this business for fear of rankling European securities regulators. Thus, at the start, the American on-line brokers operating in Europe, like Schwab, are offering their customers the chance to trade only on individual national exchanges. The long-range goal, however, is to gradually expand the system into a truly global marketplace where investors in any country will be able to trade shares freely across national boundaries. For while European Internet use still lags behind that in the unitedstates, it is expected to burgeon in the next several years. In Britain, for example, more than 12 million people, or about 20 percent of the population, are expected to be using the Internet by 2001, sharply higher than the 5.5 million at the end of 1997, according to the market analysts IDC Research. That compares with a projection of 40 percent in the unitedstates by 2001. On a recent trip here, Mr. English, who lives in the northern city of Sheffield, met with dozens of amateur Internet traders -- ranging in age from the 20's to the 70's -- to forge plans for Web investor clubs throughout Britain and to gain readers and contributors to a weekly magazine that he and fellow private investors post on the Web (www.angelfire.com/al/bbbugle). In Europe, unlike the unitedstates, banks provide both banking and full brokerage services. As a result, many people turn to their banks or the banks' brokerage affiliates to trade securities. For European banks and brokers, the results of the American invasion will be to accelerate the spread of electronic financial services that is already well under way, and presumably to bring prices down. In Finland, 420,000 customers of Merita Bank, more than a quarter of its client base, bank on line, including trading stocks by computer. In Sweden, SE Banken operates a thriving on-line banking and brokerage business, and one of the largest brokers, DT Securities, lets customers trade on the fully electronic Stockholm exchange through an on-line subsidiary called Nord Net. In Germany, banks including Deutsche Bank and Dresdner Bank operate all-electronic banks, and the main activity is stock brokerage. In France, Groupe Wargny, whose brokerage arm is 19 percent owned by Dresdner, has established a strong presence with its Telebourse on-line trading system. Moreover, the European single currency, which is to gradually replace national currencies beginning on Jan. 1, 1999, is expected to foster the spread of stock trading across national borders. For instance, the stock exchanges in Frankfurt and London recently announced that they would merge and invited other European exchanges to join. The American on-line brokers, despite their aggressive plans, will not have it easy. Computer penetration of European households lags behind that in the unitedstates, and those that do have computers often do not use the Web -- in part because many Internet programs are in English, rather than other European languages. But price is a factor, too, as the cost of Internet access in Europe averages about $85 for 20 hours -- about four times that in the unitedstates -- according to a recent study of electronic commerce by the business information group Phillips Tarifica. To build a European business, the American brokers are applying formulas that often correspond to those that worked at home. Schwab, for example, built a beachhead in Britain, first by acquiring Sharelink Investment Services, one of the largest British discount brokers, in 1995 and earlier this year introducing on-line brokerage services like it has in the unitedstates. But Schwab also offers full-service brokerage services, and an interactive phone system like its Telebroker service in the unitedstates. Next, Schwab wants to encourage customers in Britain and the unitedstates to trade across the Atlantic by enabling them to buy and sell shares on both countries' stock exchanges -- which requires payment and clearing arrangements and regulatory approval in newyork and London. "Once we have the Web architecture," said Guy Knight, the spokesman for Charles Schwab Europe, "we will have the capacity to release that across Europe." Other American companies, like E-Trade, are signing up local partners, and licensing their systems to spread the risks. This spring, E-Trade announced a joint venture in Britain and licensing deals for Germany and central Europe. Those moves followed the start of operations in Canada and Australia, and go hand in hand with expansion into Asian countries like Japan. "We are moving parallel on a number of markets," said Judy Balint, E-Trade's head of global marketing. Such aggressive expansion has European stock market regulators off balance. With most brokers still aiming for customers in their individual countries, regulatory systems have yet to be tested. E-Trade began advertising its services in Britain even before forming a joint venture there, but was restrained by British stock exchange regulators. Beyond that, differences between European governments and Washington on how to protect consumer privacy have led to a clash over computer browsing technologies that threatens to slow the evolution of the Internet into a global supermarket for electronic commerce, including securities trading. Web browser software like the Netscape Navigator and the Microsoft Internet Explorer, which are among the most commonly used in Europe, do not comply with European privacy guidelines. They are seen as too easily enabling businesses to collect information about Web surfers without their permission. In the meantime, European banks and brokers are not waiting for governments to protect their business. In Britain, Barclays P.L.C., one of the largest banks with 2,500 branches throughout the country, will be the first to fight off the competition when it introduces its on-line brokerage service in September, complete with financial information and a real-time share trading service. Phillip Bungey, head of research and development at Barclays Stockbrokers, said the system would quote prices to customers, who would then have 15 seconds to respond. Barclays will let customers trade shares in about 2,000 companies on the London Stock Exchange and the Alternative Investment Market, a small-company market. In the future, he said, Barclays wants to enable its customers to trade electronically on unitedstates markets, like Nasdaq, though clearing and settlement problems remain to be settled. Justin Urquhart Stewart, the director of corporate development at Barclays Stockbrokers, said brand loyalty could give domestic European brokers a leg up on the American competition. "We control 15 to 20 percent of the British market" for stock trading, he said. He cited the example of the insurance industry, which was shaken in recent years when retailers like supermarkets began selling insurance policies, only to see customers return en masse to name-brand insurers like Prudential. "Name brands are important to people," he said. Increasingly, too, American on-line brokers may be squeezed by the very revolution they have helped start. Mr. Eckett, the author of "Investing Online," predicts a "major collapse" of commission fees. He said that in the unitedstates, commissions on Internet trades had dipped as low as $5 a transaction since Web trading began about four years ago. "The same will happen in Europe," he predicted, as consumers surf the Internet in search of cheaper financial services. Yet some experts are betting that the change in European investors' habits will ultimately play into the hands of the American on-line brokers and their global investing approach. In the old days in Britain, said Julian Costley, chief executive of Electronic Share Information Ltd., the financial information company that E-Trade chose for its British partner, "the idea of the stockbroker was slightly feared and respected." But he predicted that Europeans would increasingly come to regard stockbrokers the same way that many of them do bank tellers -- as irrelevant holdovers from an earlier, pre-electronic era. "There are now longer queues at the A.T.M. than inside at the teller," he said, "and hundreds of thousands of investors are out there, playing into the hands of stateless companies, global companies, with no brand baggage." title:
INVESTING IT;
At Schwab, a Big Web Shift
body: THE longtime traditional discount broker Charles Schwab & Company is morphing into a haven for Web mavens. The quarter that ended in June marked the first in which more than half of Schwab's total customer trading volume -- 52 percent -- was done on line. From a consumer investment powerhouse built on a foundation of branches and telephone centers, Schwab, the nation's largest discount broker, now trades more than $2 billion in securities weekly over the Internet. With its huge customer base and marketing might, Schwab established itself as the dominant electronic broker in the first quarter of the year, handling 32 percent of the country's on-line trades, according to Piper Jaffray. That was almost three times more than the second-ranking broker, E-Trade Group. Schwab's transformation had a rocky reception on Wall Street earlier this year. The company's stock lost almost a quarter of its value from December to May, as declining commissions from Internet trading began to concern investors. Schwab charges customers as much as $75 or $100 or more to buy or sell securities through traditional channels. Over the Internet, it collects a flat $29.95 fee for each stock trade order up to 1,000 shares. In the last three weeks, though, Schwab's shares jumped 24 percent, as higher volume began to offset lower commissions, and the company got caught up in Wall Street's enthusiasm for Internet stocks. Schwab shares closed up $4.4375, at $41.25, on Friday. The company's second-quarter earnings, reported on Thursday, rose 19 percent, to $76.3 million, because of the surge in on-line trading. That amounted to 28 cents a diluted share, in line with analysts' estimates. The changes at Schwab were built of necessity. Squeezed on one side by full-service brokers and on the other by deep-discount brokers that charge as little as $5 a trade, the firm needed a way to lower its commissions while maintaining its lofty profit margins. "Over all, they're faring very well in what is clearly a tough competitive environment," said Michael Sears, a Lehman Brothers analyst. Schwab handled an average of 127,400 securities and mutual fund trades a day in the three months ended in June, up 22 percent in 18 months. During the period, Schwab's daily average of computer trades shot up 94 percent, to 66,000.

title:
Foreign Affairs;
The Mouse That Roars: A Global Tale
body: So I was talking on the phone to my mother out in Minnesota the other day, and she sounded upset. What's wrong, mom? I asked. "Well," she said, "I've been playing bridge on the Internet with three Frenchmen and they keep speaking French to each other and I can't understand them." When I chuckled at the thought of my card-shark mom playing bridge with three Frenchmen on the net, she took a little umbrage. "Don't laugh," she said. "I was playing bridge with someone in Siberia the other day." There are those who argue that the Internet and globalization are overrated, and there are those who argue that they are underrated. I think Bill Gates has this one right: In the short run they're probably overrated, but in the long run, their impact on our lives and nations is vastly underrated. Herewith a few random conversations from a recent trip to Italy, Albania, India, Jordan and Israel. At a conference in Italy, I run into John Wall, president of Nasdaq International, the stock exchange. He tells me 20 percent of all Nasdaq's business now comes from individuals sitting at home and trading stocks and bonds via the Internet through small brokerage web sites. "And Merrill Lynch and the other big boys aren't even in this business yet," says Mr. Wall. "Once they get into it, we anticipate that 70 percent of our trades will be over the Internet." To better empower Internet investors, Nasdaq has created a Web site where you can get the latest S.E.C. filing of any Nasdaq-listed company, its latest quarterly earnings report, or the consensus opinion about its stock from the top Wall Street analysts. This will empower individual investors, as never before, to sit at home and move their money around, rewarding solidly performing companies and countries and punishing the weak -- with the click of a mouse. John Burns, the newyork Times New Delhi bureau chief, tells me a delightful story about his 70-year-old Indian cook. Although John has four different satellite dishes on his rooftop ("I'm practically running an uplink station," he says), he still couldn't get the World Cup matches off Indian TV. When he was complaining about this over breakfast, his cook invited John to come over to his house next door. When they entered, John found the cook's illiterate wife watching the BBC. "I said, What's she doing? She doesn't even speak English." The cook answered: "She's learning." The cook explained that a friend of his had started a "private" cable system and strung cable into his house along the local telephone poles -- for $3.75 a month. "Then he hands me the television remote," says John, "and with increasing astonishment I start at channel 1 and click all the way to channel 27. He had television stations from China, Pakistan, Australia, Italy, France. With all my satellite dishes, I had only 14 channels." I'm having a chat in Amman with Jordan's top newspaper columnist, Rami Khouri. I ask him what's the talk of Amman, and he says, "Amman was just added to CNN's worldwide weather highlights." This means Amman has arrived in some way, he explains. It means someone at CNN thinks Amman is now important enough for tourists and business execs to need to know its weather. In Milan I meet Jules Kroll, who heads a leading global corporate investigative firm. He tells me his team has just cracked the case of a 14-year-old from Sweden who was using the Internet to threaten to blow up a U.S. consumer products company in San Francisco, whose products the youth objected to. The company thought it was an idle threat until the youth said he would bring down part of the company's computer system -- and did. I am interviewing I. K. Gujral, India's 78-year-old former Prime Minister, about how globalization is affecting his country's culture. "My granddaughter is 4," he says. "She is always talking about bubble gum, not Indian food, or she says, 'I don't like Pepsi, I like Coke.' She even speaks English more often than Hindi. I asked her one day why she doesn't speak to me in Hindi, and then she went to her mother and asked: 'Doesn't grandfather speak English?' The other day my granddaughter said she wanted pizza. So her grandmother said that she would make her a pizza. My granddaughter said, 'No, no, I want Pizza Hut.' " Thomas Wolfe said, "You can't go home again." He was wrong. In the era of the Internet and globalization, in the era of cultural homogeneity and universal connectivity, you won't be able to leave home again.

title: U.S. Data Code Is Unscrambled In 56 Hours
body: In a 1990's variant of a John Henry-style competition between man and machine, researchers using a homemade supercomputer have cracked the Government's standard data-scrambling code in record time -- and have done it by outcalculating a team that had harnessed thousands of computers, including some of the world's most powerful. That breakthrough, in a contest sponsored by a Silicon Valley computer-security software company, is being hailed by critics of unitedstates export policy for data-scrambling technology as proof that a well-heeled group of terrorists or other criminals could easily break the code used by many banks, financial institutions and even Government agencies. The Government has long sought to keep the most powerful scrambling, or encryption, software out of the hands of foreign computer users by setting limits on the strength of such software that can be licensed for export. Critics of that policy have argued that not only is more powerful encryption technology already available from foreign producers, but also that the Government-approved version is too weak to truly protect legitimate business users. The code was cracked by a small team that spent less than $250,000. The type of encryption that was broken, known as D.E.S., for Data Encryption Standard, has traditionally been used by banks and other financial institutions for protecting the transmission of funds and other transactions requiring high security. It has also been used in certain instances by the unitedstates military. The form of D.E.S. that was broken uses a 56-bit key, far more secure than the 40-bit keys that the Government allows to be freely exported. A bit is a value that represents either a 1 or a zero. As the keys become longer, breaking the encryption method becomes exponentially more difficult. Because of concerns about security, however, many business users are increasingly employing a more robust form, called Triple D.E.S., in which the length of the digital key that unlocks the scrambled data is only three times as large but exponentially more secure. Triple D.E.S. has never been broken. "This is more evidence that the Government's crypto policy has been overtaken by technology," said Marc Rotenberg, director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a privacy-rights group in Washington. "It's about time to end the limits on strong encryption techniques." The winners of the $10,000 prize -- given by the contest's sponsor, RSA Data Security Inc. -- were John Gilmore, a computer privacy and civilliberties activist, and Paul Kocher, a 25-year old cryptographer who has gained notoriety in recent years for clever attacks on security systems, including those designed to protect smart cards and Internet software. Mr. Gilmore and Mr. Kocher were able to unscramble the key to unlock and read a single block of scrambled data in 56 hours. Their homemade machine beat a network of almost 20,000 computers, ranging from desktop PC's to multimillion-dollar supercomputers working cooperatively in a method known as distributed processing. Under almost all encryption methods, each message is scrambled in a different way. Thus, breaking the key to the contest message created by RSA Data Security did not give them access to other messages scrambled with D.E.S. The Government has long asserted that it would not be possible for a terrorist or other criminal group to design and make a computer capable of cracking D.E.S. To prove that building a supercomputer would be within the means of many sinister groups, Mr. Gilmore assembled his computer for $250,000 from thousands of customized chips capable of testing more than 90 billion different keys each second. "The real news here is how long the Government has been denying that these machines were possible," said Bruce Schneier, a cryptography consultant and president of Counterpane Systems in Minneapolis. The effort was financed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a San Francisco-based civil liberties and privacy organization that has sparred with Government and industry over the impact of new technologies on traditional civil liberties. Mr. Gilmore, who was a co-founder of the foundation and who for years has been active in promoting privacy and civil liberties issues on the Internet, was the first employee of Sun Microsystems Inc., a computer company founded in 1984. In recent years he has been an outspoken advocate for traditional privacy rights in cyberspace, which he believes are threatened by the potential for Government abuse of new technologies. The computer was designed by Mr. Gilmore and Mr. Kocher, who assembled a team of about a dozen computer researchers to build the machine from more than 1,000 chips, each designed to test millions of the mathematical keys that can unlock a scrambled message. The chips and the circuit boards on which they were mounted -- 27 boards each holding 64 chips -- were installed in several old Sun computer chassis. The boards were linked by a cable to a standard personal computer that controlled the entire process. In recent years the growing power of personal computers and the ability to hook inexpensive computers together has made cracking D.E.S. far less daunting to organizations with limited resources. In 1997, RSA Data Security Inc., a Silicon Valley software company, offered a prize to the first person or organization that successfully cracked a D.E.S. scrambled message. The prize was claimed within five months by a a group of researchers using a loosely connected collection of computers scattered around the Internet. In early 1998, the prize was claimed in 39 days. Mr. Gilmore named his custom chip Deep Crack, a tongue-in-cheek allusion to I.B.M.'s chess-playing Deep Blue. Each Deep Crack chip has a collection of 21 special search units capable of performing a D.E.S. encryption on a character millions of times a second. On Wednesday evening, after checking billions of keys, the computer was able to determine that the message that had been hidden by the RSA judges was: "It's time for those 128- , 192- , and 256-bit keys." To unscramble the message, it had to try 17,902,806,669,197,312 keys, or about 25 percent of all the possible combinations. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
A Marketing Pact; A Strategy Pact
body: Two sets of companies announced agreements yesterday without disclosing their terms. Quantum Leap Communications, part of Leap Group in Chicago, signed an Internet marketing agreement with Broadvision Inc. in Redwood City, Calif. Broadvision makes software that enables businesses to build custom Internet sites for electronic commerce, customer service and delivery of interactive content. The two companies will jointly sell Web-based marketing and commerce software, using Broadvision applications and content from Quantum Leap. After the agreement was announced, Leap shares more than doubled in price, closing on Nasdaq at $7, up $3.78125. And two design firms -- Deskey Associates in newyork and Raymond Loewy International Ltd. in London -- have formed a strategic alliance. The alliance is meant to promote Loewy's expansion in the unitedstates and provides Deskey with broader access to clients in Asia, Europe and the Middle East. The companies will serve worldwide clients together and market their combined resources as well as work independently on existing assignments. Deskey works for clients like Black & Decker, I.B.M., Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble, while Loewy works for clients like Barilla, Exxon and Nestle.

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Some Clouds Dim a Star of On-Line Trading
body: Datek Online, one of the nation's fastest-growing on-line brokerage firms, has postponed an initial public offering of stock because of widening investigations into its trading practices, according to bankers who were briefed on the deal. The firm has won praise in recent years from Wall Street and Federal regulators for its innovative technology, including a flourishing electronic stock exchange, the Island E.C.N. But in May, Datek's practices came under question after the office of the Manhattan District Attorney, Robert M. Morgenthau, said it was investigating whether Datek had participated in a money-laundering operation. And now, the Securities and Exchange Commission appears to be going beyond an initial investigation into offshore transactions involving Datek and looking into whether the firm offered customers guaranteed stock returns, a practice that could run afoul of S.E.C. antifraud provisions. The agency is also investigating whether Datek encouraged illegal trading practices by some of the more than 200 day traders on its desks in the 1990's, according to people who said they were interviewed by the S.E.C. two weeks ago. The investigations could be a big setback for the company, now the fifth-largest online brokerage firm, with 95,000 customers and $2 billion in assets under its watch. Datek, whose on-line unit is not a target of any investigation, has won high ratings from publications like Barron's and Smart Money in the last year. It is unclear exactly which parts of the once-sprawling company are being investigated, but the inquiries cover activities as recent as 1997, when Datek had both trading and on-line units, according to those who have been interviewed by law enforcement officials. Datek, which is based in Iselin, N.J., said in a statement yesterday that it "does not comment on its capital-raising or financing activities," such as a public stock offering, or on press reports about investigations. The company has in recent months distanced itself from its old trading unit, which was spun off in March to Heartland Securities, a money management firm. Still, in the statement yesterday, Datek denied guaranteeing stock returns to its customers or engaging in illegal trading activity. In recent months, law enforcement officials say that two investigations into possible stock manipulation and fraudulent offshore deals intersected and that Datek's activities were found at the crossroads. One of those cases, they said, involved A. R. Baron & Company, a brokerage firm, now defunct, whose top executives pleaded guilty or were convicted in the last year of defrauding investors in the early 1990's. Although the details are sketchy, officials in one investigation are looking into whether Datek and at least one person in the A. R. Baron case were involved in manipulating the stocks of companies that sold unregistered shares to overseas investors in Regulation S offerings, which have been the subject of numerous investigations in recent years by the S.E.C. and the Manhattan District Attorney. In a separate investigation, the S.E.C. filed suit three months ago against Sheldon Maschler, who once headed Datek's trading operation. The suit contended that he took part in a scheme to manipulate the shares of the Alter Sales Company, an auto company based in Miami. Datek was not named in the suit. The agency has also been investigating whether Datek manipulated shares of the Fortune Petroleum Company in conjunction with a Regulation S stock offering, according to people interviewed by the S.E.C. Wall Street stock analysts say that Datek continues to tighten its controls under the leadership of Jeffrey A. Citron, the 27-year-old chairman and chief executive. Datek, they say, is hoping that its profitable on-line operation can survive, and indeed thrive, unscathed by the investigations, making a public offering possible at a much later date. "It's an attractive company in an attractive market," said James Marks, an on-line analyst at CS First Boston, which has held discussions with Datek about a public offering. "But these issues under investigation have to be resolved for a successful I.P.O." Two weeks ago, investigators from the S.E.C. met or spoke with several former traders about trading practices at Datek, and several months ago traders told officials from the District Attorney's office that for several years Datek's trading operation had orally guaranteed customers a return of 16 percent. The firm, they said, encouraged traders to sign up relatives and friends to invest large sums of money to bolster trading commissions. "We knew some shady dealings were going on," said Dale A. Tucker, a trader who recently left the firm to go to graduate school. "We didn't understand the accounts up there, but I think a lot of people didn't care because we were making a lot of money." Datek, which was founded in 1970, began as a small brokerage firm serving customers in Brooklyn. In the mid-1980's, it opened a Manhattan branch. Mr. Citron, who was hired as a clerk just after graduating from high school, helped transform the small firm, which had trading profits of $2 million in 1991, to one with profits of more than $94 million in 1996. The company used computers to exploit the Nasdaq stock market's small-order execution system, and its people became known on Wall Street as "SOES bandits." In 1996, Datek moved into on-line trading, and quickly established itself as a leader there, winning acclaim for its $9.99 trading fees and its fast executions. When profits in that area soared, Mr. Maschler -- who Datek says is no longer an employee -- led the push for an initial public offering, according to his associates. Wall Street analysts have been enthusiastic about the company's prospects and some expected Datek to raise $150 million in an offering this year. Piper Jaffray was one of the investment houses prepared to take Datek public, according to analysts, before the investigations tabled those plans.
