title:
Compressed Data;
Priceline Expands Into Automobiles
body: Will car dealers be more willing than airlines to leap at dollars dangled under their noses? That's the question facing Priceline, an Internet service that is meant to let consumers buy things by making "reasonable offers" that sellers can choose whether to accept. Priceline's first service, for air tickets, met a chilly response from airlines, which do not want to undercut their high last-minute fares for business travelers by letting customers propose their own discounted offers. Only a few domestic airlines have agreed to participate, and so Priceline can fill only about a quarter of customer offers, which must be within 15 percent of the lowest published fare. But today Priceline plans to introduce a car-buying service with fewer restrictions than its airline service, and it may have a better chance of acceptance among the many highly competitive car dealers. In essence, consumers log onto Priceline.com and specify the models of car they are looking for along with the options and colors they would accept, and the price they will pay. These offers are sent by fax to every car dealer within the region specified by the buyer. The first dealer to call and accept the bid sells the car. Dealers can also submit a counteroffer. In existing on-line car buying services, like Autoweb, Carpoint and Autobytel, customers enter the car they want. Then, typically, one dealer calls them back to name a price and try to close a deal. "The best thing about our service is that you never talk to a car salesman," said Jay Walker, Priceline's chairman. "You show up with your check and you drive the car home."   SAUL HANSELL Graphic   Photo.

title:
FRUGAL TRAVELER;
Seattle: Latte for a Little
body: TO twist the words of Will Rogers, Seattle never met a fad it didn't like. From the early gold-rushers who put the city on the map to the coffee-swilling entrepreneurs who made $2 java a national obsession, the denizens of the city by the sound have always had a keen sense of what was hot -- and profitable. While most of the world was flying by propellers, in Seattle, Boeing began making jets. And when rock and roll was fading, Seattle spawned grunge. This knack for trendsetting has made it a favorite of the young and restless. I, meanwhile, have always been a little behind the curve, a man who invested in an electric typewriter just about the time that personal computers -- another Seattle specialty -- began popping up on desktops. So, in the hope of gleaning a sense of the future from this forward-looking burg, I traveled to Seattle for four days in early June, just a few weeks after the blossoming of the city's rhododendrons, and just about when its notoriously wet weather starts to give way to more temperate conditions. I knew that such a short-term search for the Zeitgeist would probably be futile, but I also suspected I would have a good time looking. I was late in getting a ticket, of course, and lost out on the cheaper 14-day advance fares. I checked airline consolidators, who acquire tickets in bulk and sell them at cut-rate prices; they were offering fares in the $450 range, tax included. I wanted something cheaper. In the spirit of Seattle's favorite son, Bill Gates, I took to the Internet, checking a service called Priceline (priceline.com), where you name the price you wish to pay and then wait to see if an airline will match your bid. The process is advertised as taking an hour and a credit card; I had both. My first offer was $300, leaving within a week from any newyork City airport and agreeing to one stopover each way. I typed in my dates, my email address, and my credit card number and sure enough, an hour later, the computer responded: No dice. I plowed through the application again, this time bidding $320. "Sorry," read the reply. I had just about resigned myself to the consolidator ticket, but decided to move up my trip by a couple of days and try $350. Bingo: A $350 round trip, tax included, on America West, with a stopover in Phoenix. My Rough Guide to the unitedstates told me that accommodations in downtown Seattle generally were either snazzy or sleazy; decent midrange lodgings were usually outside the city center. I turned again to the Web, searching seattle.yahoo.com, and found an ad for the Seattle Inn, "the preferred economy inn of downtown Seattle." The site showed inviting pictures of an indoor pool and the Space Needle -- the symbol of the 1962 world's fair -- hovering just above the hotel's roof. The price: $60 for a single, with an additional 10 percent off for reserving by email. The final logistical detail was a car. A representative at America West suggested Avis, which set me up with a terrific springtime deal: $99 for five days and unlimited mileage. Mind you, after a 10-hour journey to Seattle via Arizona, I was in no mood to drive. And the dusk and fog looming over the city made my first impressions fairly grim. The Kingdome, the city's aging stadium, sat hulking and gray to the left, while in the distance, the Space Needle seemed almost limp in the damp air, with two of its three legs wrapped in billowy pink construction netting. (Depression threatened. Ah, where is Frasier Crane when you need him?) My spirits lifted when I got to the hotel, which had a motor lodge feel but a very friendly staff. My room was small and the towels even smaller, but it was clean, comfortable and equipped with cable. I thought about a swim; in that weather, however, the last thing I wanted to do was get wet. I awoke to a sunny day and a view of the Needle, with its U.F.O.-shaped pinnacle nicely framed against a blue sky. Seattle rises on a series of lush hills with saltwater Puget Sound to the west and the freshwater Lake Washington to the east. This sloped, spindly topography creates one of the city's ironies: While individual areas are pedestrian friendly, you almost always must drive to get to the place where you can walk. (Interstate 5 separates the east and west parts of the city, while a finger of Lake Washington separates north and south.) The isolated pockets have fostered a mix of distinct neighborhoods, from the sedate elegance of Queen Anne, north of downtown, to the taste treats in the gritty International District, where Thai and Chinese food are plentiful. My personal favorite was Capitol Hill, on the city's eastern slopes, home of some of Seattle's most quirky restaurants and bars as well as a large gay and student community. I spent almost all of my second day there, on Broadway, and ate at two of the city's nicest cheap dining spots, the Broadway New American Grill and Cafe Septieme. But my first day was spent downtown, where, still groggy, the first goal of the first day was to sample that dark, steamy and decidedly peppy local beverage. I quickly happened on one of many branches of a place called (what else?) Seattle's Best Coffee, on Second Avenue. The store offered all sorts of exotic variations, from the high-caffeine coffee coffee milkshake to something called an Oregon Chai Tea Latte; I chose a simple tumbler of house blend ($1.45). My haze lifted. The first brush with a possible fad came right around the corner at the Three Dog Bakery, a new store catering to the untapped market for pastries, cakes and other delectables aimed at an exclusively canine clientele. Though the dog biscotti looked appetizing, I refrained and moved on to more human delights at the Pike Place Market. The turn-of-the-century downtown marketplace was almost demolished in 1971, during one of Seattle's numerous fits of reinvention. Instead, civic leaders undertook a classy refurbishment, complete with red brick streets and flower-lined alleys.  Its dozens of stands sell the best of the region's natural bounty, including just-caught Dungeness crabs, as well as pungent displays of cut roses and freshly baked bread. "Fish up!" shouted a wisecracking salesman at Pike Place Fish Company, throwing a giant slab of fish about 10 feet to a waiting comrade. "Get 'em while they're frish." I also found a tourist-information stand offering free maps and weekly guides -- and, at noon daily, half-price same-day tickets on anything from opera to cruises. One of the best deals at the market is the Three Girls Bakery, a luncheon that is usually packed and dates back to 1912. Ihad an enormous sourdough and pastrami sandwich ($4.25), and trundled down through the market's four stories of shops toward the harbor. While the waterfront primarily comprises kitsch shops and fish-and-chip stands, two diversions lured me in. The first was the Seattle Aquarium, where I bought a City Pass ($23.75), which equates to half-price admission to six different Seattle attractions. The aquarium's collection was modest, but swarmed by children. I was especially entranced by the clouds of freshly hatched salmon, all swimming in perfect rows in a circular tank. The exhibits, strangely enough, piqued my appetite. I headed to Ivar's Acres of Clams, a Seattle institution founded by Ivar Haglund, an eccentric old entrepreneur whose motto was "Keep Clam!" Between the market's fish staff and Mr. Haglund's wit, I determined that bad puns must be an occupational hazard for Northwestern fish merchants. I ordered a four-piece meal of fish and chips ($4.95) and watched the locals feed the gulls. "Sea gull lovers are welcome," reads a quote from Mr. Haglund, who died in 1985. "Please do not feed the pigeons." A TROLLEY runs the length of the waterfront, but I walked inland a bit to Pioneer Square, a tree-lined promenade and the jumping-off point for a past generation of treasure seekers. I stopped into the Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park museum (free), which gives a fine overview of the continent's last great gold rush. It began just over 100 years ago when the S.S. Portland docked in Seattle with two tons of nuggets. The rush petered out a few years later, but the crush of would-be millionaires buying supplies in Seattle for the trip north pulled the little lumber town into the 20th century. As the crowds streamed south toward the Kingdome for a Seattle Mariners game, I moved north up First Avenue against the current (just like a good salmon). First Avenue, downtown's main drag, is eclectic, reflecting both the progressive present and frontier past. Chic boutiques and the Seattle Art Museum (a City Pass locale) sit side by side with gun shops and X-rated movie houses. Darkness was falling as I followed First Avenue uptown, stumbling into Belltown, an emergent district on the northern fringe of downtown. I counted six trendy-looking restaurants on a single block, complete with $14 entrees and skinnier-than-thou waitresses. I moved a little farther north to the Belltown Pub, a handsome bistro featuring two dozen local microbrews and $7 burgers. I chose a pint of something called Mac and Jack's African Amber and a cheeseburger. I finished the night at the Crocodile Cafe, a bar-cum-club-cum-greasy spoon where local grunge legends Nirvana and Pearl Jam used to play. Decorated with giant papier-mache reptiles, the Crocodile had four bands on tap for $6. I listened intently, half expecting to hear The Next Big Thing. As it turned out, the first entertainer that night had been imported from Australia. Stomach filled, feet tired, ears sated, I retired. I drove up to Capitol Hill on Saturday, catching the breakfast buffet ($7.95) at the Broadway New American Grill, a sunny, stylish diner with sidewalk tables and a collection of Miro-inspired sculpture. From there, I walked up Broadway, enjoying the colorful tile fringe on the sidewalk and the flowering dogwood and dahlias. With Seattle University to the south and the University of Washington to the north, Capitol Hill is awash with young artists and music stores and coffeehouses that cater to them. One exemplar is Habitat Espresso, a petition-laden nonprofit enterprise on Broadway with weekly readings of plays, screenplays and poetry. I was a little intimidated by the T-shirt worn by the tattooed counterman: "Sit. Consume. Die." But the coffee was good and strong. The remainder of the day was spent the hilltop views in nearby Volunteer Park (where I saw an exhibit at the Seattle Asian Art Museum), the park's Conservatory (where I wandered hothouse rooms full of flora, also gratis), and the Japanese Garden at Washington Park Arboretum. (Did I mention that the coffee was strong?) After a quick portobello mushroom sandwich ($7) at Cafe Septieme, I bopped along with the bustle of Broadway, cutting along side streets and finally ending up in the Baltic Room, a 1930's style speak-easy with nightly jazz, a $3 cover and a clientele that likes to dress with an eye toward the Jazz Age. I settled in sleepily at the lovely Gaslight Inn, a restored Victorian bed-and-breakfast with a sun-drenched deck and a small outdoor pool. My single room with four-poster bed and a shared bath was $73 a night, tax included. Sunday was a consummate Seattle day: rainy. I took shelter in the city's museums, and used the City Pass to hit the Museum of Flight's fantastic aeronautic displays, the kid-oriented Pacific Science Center (who knew I would weigh 410 pounds on Jupiter?) and, of course, the 605-foot Space Needle, from which I saw the ghostly pink-tinted peak of Mount Rainier hovering on the southern horizon. Having been landbound my first three days, I made water sports the goal of my last. My plan for the evening included oysters ($9.25 for six at the grand old McCormick and Schmick's) and fish (an indulgent $16 halibut dish at Flying Fish). But my first stop was the ferry to Bainbridge Island ($3.60 round trip), a large suburb eight miles across Puget Sound. The sun had burned through the morning clouds, and bright white streaks flashed across the sound's deep water. Sailboats glided by; I settled back for the ride. As the modern skyline shrunk in the distance, I looked around. Most of my fellow passengers were smiling, eyes closed, faces warmed by the sun. For such renowned trendsetters, Seattle's citizenry seemed positively content in the face of the next millennium. Then again, I thought, maybe they're just thinking of what they are going to do next.  The bottom line Including meals, room and car rental, I spent an average of $110 a day in four days in Seattle. Two good investments were "Seattle Best Places," by Nancy Leson and Stephanie Irving, (Sasquatch Books, $16.95), and a City Pass ($23.75), which offers admission to six Seattle attractions: the Space Needle, Pacific Science Center, Woodland Park Zoo, Seattle Aquarium, Seattle Art Museum and Museum of Flight. I bought my plane ticket, $350 round trip, two days in advance through Priceline (www.priceline.com). During the current high season, 14-day advance-purchase fares on most major airlines should be in the $400 range.  What to Do The Seattle Asian Art Museum, 1400 East Prospect Street in Volunteer Park, has a lovely exhibit of artifacts from India, China, Japan and Korea. Suggested donation is $6, $4 for students. Open 10 A.M. to 5 P.M. Tuesday through Sunday, until 9 P.M. on Thursday; closed most Mondays. (206) 654-3100. Free on the first Thursday of every month. The nearby Conservatory is open 10 A.M. to 7 P.M. daily; free. The Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park, 117 South Main Street, is open 9 A.M. to 5 P.M. daily; free. (206) 553-7220. A trip to Bainbridge Island on Washington State Ferries cost $3.60 round trip. Boats leave regularly from Pier 52; (206) 464-6400. The six City Pass attractions are the Seattle Aquarium, Pier 59, (206) 386-4320; the Pacific Science Center, Seattle Center, (206) 443-2880; the Space Needle, also at the Center, (206) 443-2100; Woodland Park Zoo, (206) 684-4800; the Museum of Flight, 9404 East Marginal Way, (206) 764-5720; and the Seattle Art Museum, 100 University Street, (206) 654-3100. The art museum is closed most Mondays; the rest are open daily.  Where to Stay The Seattle Inn, 225 Aurora Avenue North near downtown, has 150 rooms, an indoor pool, a hot tub and parking. Double rates with breakfast range from $73 to $93. Reservations: (800) 255-7932, fax (206) 728-7666. The Gaslight Inn, 1727 15th Avenue, is a refurbished Victorian on Capitol Hill with 16 rooms, most with private bath. Doubles: $68 to $158. Continental breakfast included and served in a charming dining room. Reservations: (206) 325-3654, fax (206) 328-4803. The College Inn, 4000 University Way Northeast, across from the University of Washington, has 27 simple and affordable rooms, from $45 to $83. All have shared bath. Call (206) 633-4441, fax (206) 547-1335.  Where to Eat Three Girls Bakery, 1514 Pike Place in the Market, (206) 622-1045. Ivar's Acres of Clams, Pier 54, (206) 624-6852. Mama's Mexican Kitchen, 2234 Second Avenue, (206) 728-6262, offers huge plates of burritos, tacos and enchiladas, most for $6 to $10. The Belltown Pub, 2322 First Avenue, (206) 728-4311, offers straightforward American cuisine with entrees from $8 to $14. Broadway New American Grill, 314 Broadway East, (206) 328-7000, has a hearty $7.95 weekend buffet from 8 A.M. to 1 P.M. Cafe Septieme, 214 Broadway East, (206) 860-8858, has entrees for $6.50 to $15, with cheaper sandwiches. McCormick and Schmick's, 1103 First Avenue, (206) 623-5500, has a $1.95 bar menu from 3 to 6 P.M. and after 10 P.M. Flying Fish, 2234 First Avenue, (206) 728-8595, is a pretty (if expensive) seafood spot in Belltown. Entrees are $13 to $19. The Crocodile Cafe, 2200 Second Avenue in Belltown, features local bands, a diner-style restaurant and separate bar. Cover charges range from $6 to $10. (206) 448-2114. Garage, 1130 Broadway, is a stylish billiard hall in a converted building along a street once lined with auto-repair places. It has 18 pool tables, a bar and a restaurant. A 10-inch pizza is $7.50 and a Hefeweizen, a local microbrew, is $3.25. Sidewalk seating. (206) 322-2296. The Baltic Room, 1207 Pine Street, has live jazz Tuesday to Sunday nights. Admission is usually free Sunday through Thursday, with $3 cover Friday and Saturdays, though prices can go higher. (206) 625-4444. title: Teen-Ager Admits Using Virus To Steal Computer Passwords
body: A teen-age computer hacker pleaded guilty in Manhattan Federal Court yesterday to stealing more than 500 passwords from America Online users last year. Prosecutors said that the teen-ager, referred to in court papers as John Doe, had obtained the passwords by sending email messages to America Online subscribers from February through April. When the clients clicked on an attachment included with the message, a computer virus known as a Trojan horse, because it cloaks its true purpose, was activated and secretly recorded the users' keystrokes, including their passwords, said Mary Jo White, the unitedstates Attorney for the Southern District of newyork. The passwords were then forwarded by the virus program to an email account that the teen-ager held under a false identity on Juno, a Manhattan-based Internet service provider. It did not appear that the teen-ager was able to, or attempted to, profit from his work. Credit card numbers were not taken, and thus no merchandise was purchased with them over the Internet, said Tricia Primrose, a spokeswoman for America Online. The teen-ager was charged with unlawful interception of electronic communication, a felony, but because of his age he pleaded guilty to an act of juvenile delinquency. Normally, the sentence for that crime is six months' probation, according to prosecutors. Lawyers with the unitedstates Attorney's office declined to discuss the specifics of the case, citing confidentiality. They did say, however, that the boy had obtained the computer program used to get the passwords through a person he had met on line. The teen-ager's lawyer declined to comment. An investigator, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said that the teen-ager had been caught by the Federal authorities with the help of Juno, which alerted the authorities when the teen-ager called into his account. The call was subsequently traced.

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
The battle for Internet supremacy is shifting to the companies that sell the connections to users.
body: WHEN America Online rebuffed AT&T's merger flirtations last month, it could hardly have known that the long-distance giant would soon marry what may be the on-line service's most potent long-term enemy: the At Home Corporation. At Home, in which AT&T will get a 42 percent interest as part of its $31.8 billion acquisition bid for Tele-Communications Inc. last week, markets a high-speed Internet service over cable television wires. It is hardly a force today, with only about 100,000 subscribers. America Online says it has 12 million customers, more than half of the homes in the unitedstates that have on-line access. Still, a new front is opening in the Internet wars with the development of so-called broadband services like At Home that offer transmission speeds 20 to 100 times as fast as traditional modems. That is fast enough to offer rich graphics, live video feeds and an end to the finger-tapping delays that most on-line users endure today. Right now, the most visible battles in the broadband world are among various technology providers -- for example, between cable-modem systems and a new standard of high-speed Internet access over telephone wires called digital subscriber lines. And the cable industry itself is divided: one group backs At Home, and another supports Time Warner's cable-modem service, Road Runner. But a much more intense clash is brewing over whether access to broadband lines will be open to America Online or any other on-line service or will be closed to all content except that chosen by the system operator, just as cable systems now choose which channels to carry. Not surprisingly, both At Home and Road Runner want to use their wires to promote their own on-line news, information and entertainment. Why does this matter? For the same reason that media giants like the Walt Disney Company and General Electric's NBC have been buying Internet directory services: It is clear that whoever controls the front door that people use to start their Internet surfing -- a "portal" in industry jargon -- will control the biggest share of advertising and shopping revenues. And whoever sells the connection to the Internet, as America Online and At Home both do, controls the portal. Just hours after the AT&T-TCI deal was announced, America Online's chairman, Steve Case, issued a statement challenging At Home's exclusive deal to provide high-speed programming over TCI's cables and challenging AT&T to let his service offer high-speed cable-modem access under its own brand. This did not sit well with At Home. "The thought that AT&T or TCI will become a dumb pipe and turn over the portal service to AOL is just ridiculous," Thomas Jermoluk, At Home's chairman, said in an interview last week. "AOL is paranoid about keeping exclusive control of the portal. But in the new broadband world, the facilities provider wants to participate in the revenue stream when users see ads and buy things." The stakes are compounded for At Home, which has a minority of its shares trading publicly. The company's stock has soared to a value of $4.2 billion despite huge losses because of the perceived potential of its exclusive contracts with TCI and other cable systems. To be sure, even if At Home controls the first screen its users see, any At Home user with only a modest technical ability could use the cable modem to gain access to America Online or any other Internet service at high speeds. That is no different than the ability of a current America Online user to jump right to Yahoo or any other Internet site. But experience shows that most people use whatever pops up on the first screen they see. At Home, however, does not want simply to depend on inertia. It has been developing attractive content that takes advantage of its service's speed. Its news and information screens, for example, have much bigger, brighter color graphics than other Web-based services. And it offers a wide range of short video clips from sources like CNN. Mr. Jermoluk says that one measure of the allure of these flashy offerings is that half of At Home's first customers were America Online members and that most of them dropped the on-line service once they got used to the cable offering. America Online, he said, will have to give up its dream of being the exclusive portal in a broadband world. "We have the access to the home," he said. "If AOL wants to get there with broadband, they will have to work with us." Robert Pittman, America Online's president, insists that despite the protests over the current cable lockout, he is not worried. "Broadband is just not ready for prime time," Mr. Pittman said. As much as consumers may want faster access, broadband will not take off, he said, until its price comes down from the current $40 a month and customers can hook themselves up easily without technicians visiting their homes, as the current technology requires. More important, Mr. Pittman argues that for the foreseeable future, the most likely customer for broadband services is someone who is already on line at slower speeds. Thus, America Online offers the biggest pool of broadband prospects in the world. So the cable companies and the phone companies will all eventually trip over themselves to cut deals with the on-line service. "Since we have so many subscribers," he said, "we have big buying power already." Moreover, Mr. Pittman argues that AT&T's strategy of selling telephone, cable and Internet services in one package will ultimately prove ineffective. "They talk about bundling, but what's missing is someone to sell the bundle," he said. "The only thing TCI can sell is cable TV. AT&T has 80 million customers, but it was only able to get one million customers for Worldnet," the Internet service AT&T introduced two years ago. He said that America Online has fared better on AT&T's turf, selling long-distance telephone service since last year through a carrier called Tel-Save Holdings. "We have an interactive relationship with our consumers," he added, "so when we started offering long distance we converted one million lines in six months." Graphic   Drawing. (Tom Bloom)

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Web Surf With Disney
body: Disney Online, a three-year-old unit intent on bringing all the fluff and pink that is Disney to cyberspace, yesterday opened Disney's Internet Guide, a Web search and directory site for children and families. Dubbed Dig (www.dig.com), the new site is designed to compete with Yahooligans, Yahoo's popular kids' directory. And in a sign that the company is wasting no time capitalizing on its new partnership with Infoseek, the site will also soon serve as the kids' directory on Infoseek. Like Yahooligans, Dig contains eight wholesome categories, like Animals and the Outdoors, Stories and Comics, Games and Toys, and Arts and Entertainment. Each of the Dig categories, which, according to the company, "collectively represent what Disney Online considers to be the best of the Web for kids and families," have been picked by Dig team members and will be reviewed every few days. "It really comes back to our overall Disney Online mission, to provide a gateway to the Internet," said the president of Disney Online, Richard Wolpert. Mr. Wolpert said Disney Online had been working on development of the new site for a year. Disney Online has lagged behind its competition. According to a rankings list maintained by Media Metrix, Disney Online barely registers among the top 20 Web sites. The new partnership with Infoseek, in which Disney acquired a 43 percent stake in Infoseek, is expected to help, but analysts are skeptical of Disney's overall prospects of displacing others as a so-called portal site -- the Web site Internet users see when they first log on. "If you're using Yahoo now, particularly if you're an adult, there's no way you're going to switch to Infoseek and Disney, not in this life," said Keith Benjamin, an Internet analyst with BancAmerica Robertson Stephens. A link to the new site will also be available on the Disney home page (www.disney.com). Dig is Disney's fourth Web site. In addition to Disney.com, the company maintains Family.com and Disney's Blast Online, a paid subscription service for children.

title: Disney Joins Rush to Build Web Gateways
body: The Walt Disney Company joined the nation's biggest media and technology companies yesterday with its own effort to control where people go in cyberspace. Disney announced a complex deal valued at about $900 million in which it will buy 43 percent of Infoseek, a service that helps guide users on the World Wide Web. Disney and the other companies are following a trail blazed by America Online and Yahoo, which are rushing to construct gateways to the Internet, known as "portals," that are the starting points for most people as they look for news, entertainment and other features. With more users than any other sites on the Internet, these services are the most attractive to on-line advertisers. The announcement capped two weeks of fevered developments across the media and technology industries. Last week, the NBC unit of the General Electric Company struck a deal to take control of Snap, an upstart on-line directory service created by Cnet, for up to $65 million in cash and more than $100 million in free television promotions. On Monday, it was reported that the AT&T Corporation had been negotiating to acquire America Online. On Tuesday, the Microsoft Corporation opened a public test of its new portal, known as Start, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of the year. In the meantime, the Netscape Communications Corporation is busy shifting its focus from making browsers to operating its own portal, and media giants like Time Warner and the News Corporation are looking to build or buy similar services. While there are tens of thousands of commercial Web sites, most of the attention is focused on the handful that help users find the information they are looking for. Because most people use these sites to start their treks through cyberspace, they are far and away the most popular places on the Internet. As a result, they have attracted the lion's share of advertising and investor interest. America Online, which a year and a half ago was drowning in busy signals and irate customers, has rebounded into the powerhouse of cyberspace with 12 million paying customers, a market value of $20.3 billion and the self-assurance to rebuff AT&T's takeover offer last month. Yahoo, the largest of the free, advertiser-supported portal services, attracts more than 70 million users worldwide every month and has a value of about $6 billion despite barely breaking even. As these sites grow rapidly in market value and viewership -- if not profits -- many companies are deciding that they need to buy one quickly, despite the high prices, before they become unaffordable. More than one media giant has expressed regret for not having bought America Online when it was cheaper. "The media companies are starting to wake up and realize that the Internet has the reach of a mass medium," said Jonathan Nelson, chief executive of Organic, one of the largest on-line advertising agencies. Moreover, as television, telephones and computers converge into one integrated network of communications and entertainment, companies of all sorts see portals as a possible key to their future strategy. The power to funnel users to certain advertisers and content sites is worth millions of dollars in revenue. "The search engines have become to the Internet what Windows is to the computer desktop," said Alec L. Ellison, a managing director of Broadview Associates, a technology investment banking firm. Disney's intention is to create a new Internet service that combines Infoseek with its existing offerings, which include Web sites for ABC television, ABC News, the ESPN sports network, Disney's movies and a site of original Disney entertainment for children. "There is no site that has both the breadth of Infoseek's search and directory service and the depth of Disney's news, sports, entertainment and family content," said Jake Winebaum, chairman of Disney's Buena Vista Internet Group. Disney, like many other media companies, has been talking to several portal services over the last year. A few months ago, it was close to buying a part of Excite, the No. 2 portal service, but the deal fell apart over the price, investment bankers said. With the stock of the search services trading at stratospheric prices, big companies have been loath to buy them either with cash or their own, more conventionally valued shares. Disney then turned to Infoseek, completing the deal yesterday morning after negotiating all night. That deal gets around the problem of Infoseek's high stock price by trading some of its own Internet ventures -- at the high value such companies carry -- for shares in Infoseek. Specifically, Disney will receive 43 percent of Infoseek in return for $70 million in cash and relinquishing ownership of Starwave, a company that creates elaborate Web sites. Starwave's biggest venture is the sports site it operates on behalf of ESPN. Disney bought Starwave in several phases over the last year from Paul Allen, the co-founder of Microsoft. Keith Benjamin, an analyst for BancAmerica Robertson Stephens, estimated that Disney paid about $400 million for Starwave and that it would be worth about $800 million if it were an independent company. Yesterday's announcement represented something of an about-face for Disney. When it bought full control of Starwave two months ago, it announced plans to integrate the technology company, based in Seattle, with its own Internet operations in Burbank, Calif. Now, all of Starwave will become part of Infoseek, which is based in Sunnyvale, Calif. Disney also agreed to lend Infoseek up to $139 million over the next five years in return for the option to bring its ownership to 50.1 percent. Disney, however, will get back most of the cash it is spending, as Infoseek has agreed to buy $165 million in advertising from Disney over the next three years. That money will buy both television advertising on ABC and promotion at other Disney operations, like the Internet pavilion at Disney World. "It's a great deal for Disney, but not as good a deal for Infoseek," said Mr. Benjamin, the analyst. Infoseek should have started turning a profit this year, Mr. Benjamin said, but now the added expense of buying all that promotion from Disney will keep it from breaking even until 2001. "It's probably the best they could get, because without Disney, Infoseek would languish in fourth or fifth place," he said. NBC's deal to buy a stake in Snap was much more favorable to the shareholders of Cnet, Mr. Benjamin said. In particular, it will provide more than $100 million in free television advertising. NBC, however, has much more limited ambitions for Snap, a service with well-regarded technology but few users. The television network hopes that heavy TV promotions will turn Snap into a popular, stand-alone service. NBC's other Internet activities, especially its MSNBC news service, operated with Microsoft, will remain separate. Disney, by contrast, is looking to merge its properties into a unified service that will have more of a cohesive feel, similar to America Online. Right now, America Online charges users $22 a month for both access to the Internet and its own content. Portal services like Infoseek and Snap have been free to users. But Mr. Winebaum of Disney said the company hoped to come up with extra services for which users would pay fees. Disney's ESPN site earns half its revenue, for example, from add-on services like fantasy sports leagues. Even as the big media companies are buying existing portal sites, many other companies are jockeying for position to earn money as Internet gateways. Smaller sites that began offering specialized services are trying to emulate the look and features of sites like Yahoo. And the big technology companies have their own portal ambitions. The most feared is Microsoft's Start, because it will be the first page seen by users of the Internet Explorer browser software that is now part of the Windows operating system. Meanwhile, Netscape, whose software business has been devastated by Microsoft, has been trying to turn its often-visited but dreary home page into a service with as much news and information as the other portals. And Compaq Computer is even trying to turn its products into portals by installing several buttons on its computer keyboards that direct users to certain Web sites. Analysts said that all these moves represented the massing of forces for what will shape up to be a long and brutal war over which two or three portal services will become dominant. With the stakes in the on-line world far lower a few years ago, America Online spent a $1 billion on television advertising and distribution of sign-up disks to surge past its rivals, Prodigy and Compuserve. "This time," Mr. Benjamin said, "it will be much more expensive for someone else to catch up." title: America Online Announces It Will Remain Independent
body: Cooling off merger discussions with the AT&T Corporation, America Online Inc., the nation's largest cyberspace company, said yesterday that it would remain independent. America Online has been in preliminary talks about a potential acquisition by AT&T, the nation's No. 1 long-distance company, for several weeks, according to people close to the discussions. But yesterday America Online's top executives said they had no intention of selling the company. "We are committed to remaining an independent company, as that is the best course for our customers, shareholders and employees," Stephen M. Case, the company's chairman, and Robert W. Pittman, its president, said in an email message to employees. "We continue to be eager to establish alliances with a wide range of telecommunications, media and technology companies." One person close to the companies said that while Mr. Case appeared to oppose the idea of a merger, Mr. Pittman was willing to consider such a move. The conversations between the two companies were described by one person involved in the talks as "fluid." The person said that several issues needed to be worked out before any deal could be announced. In particular, the two companies were discussing the fate of Tel-Save Holdings Inc., a small independent long-distance company that owns the exclusive right to market long-distance service on America Online. In acquiring America Online, AT&T would presumably want to use the on-line service to sell long-distance service. But there remain questions about whether AT&T would agree to acquire Tel-Save for a price above its $1.1 billion market value, in addition to agreeing to acquire America Online. One indication that the talks had not progressed far enough to include a concrete offer was that Mr. Case did not discuss details of the merger discussions with America Online's board members until The Financial Times reported yesterday that America Online had rejected an offer from AT&T, said a person close to America Online. Still, people close to AT&T said that C. Michael Armstrong, AT&T's chairman, had meetings with top executives at America Online's headquarters in Dulles, Va., during the week of May 17. Perhaps as telling as the talks themselves is what they reveal about the direction that Mr. Armstrong wants to take AT&T. Seeking to jump-start AT&T's entry into local phone markets, Mr. Armstrong helped engineer AT&T's $11.3 billion acquisition of Teleport Communications Group, Inc., a leading competitive local phone provider, in January. But that deal was mostly speculative; it may be years before AT&T offers local phone service to millions of consumers. Acquiring America Online would be another bid for the future, but it would have an immediate impact on AT&T's growth prospects and on the structure of the telecommunications industry. AT&T has built a sizable business providing Internet access to consumers, serving 1.1 million customers. America Online has about 12 million customers and enjoys a brand that consumers associate with cyberspace, rather than with monthly long-distance bills. But in addition to the Tel-Save question, any deal between AT&T and America Online would face serious hurdles of finance and corporate politics as well as potential personality clashes. One problem for AT&T could be financial, though that does not seem to have deterred Mr. Armstrong. As the most widely held stock in the nation, AT&T is mainly valued based on its ability to deliver steady earnings growth. But America Online's shares trade at almost 10 times the multiple of estimated earnings for this year than do AT&T's. That means that if AT&T acquired America Online using stock, all the new shares would massively dilute AT&T's future per-share profits. AT&T could use cash, but that would require servicing a huge amount of debt. America Online has a market value of about $20.3 billion. More personally, Mr. Case recently joined the board of Worldcom Inc., the No. 4 long-distance company, which has agreed to acquire the MCI Communications Corporation, AT&T's archrival. Mr. Case joined Worldcom's board after America Online agreed last year to sell its data communications network to Worldcom in a complex three-way transaction in which Worldcom also acquired the network of Compuserve, another big on-line service, while America Online took over Compuserve's customers. America Online is now one of Worldcom's biggest customers. Presumably, one of the financial rationales behind AT&T's seeking to acquire America Online is that some of America Online's traffic could be moved to AT&T's network, saving costs. It is unclear, however, if the arrangements between America Online and Worldcom would allow that.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Guide to Entertainment Opens on the Internet Today
body: Entering a market crowded with some of the biggest companies in cyberspace, The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it would introduce an Internet service about entertainment, restaurants and shopping in newyork City and its suburbs. The site, called newyork Today, will be available, starting today, at www.nytoday.com. The service will compete with newyork Sidewalk from Microsoft, Digital Cities newyork from America Online and Citysearch newyork from Citysearch, a privately held company. All the companies are seeking a share of the rich market for local advertising, which includes classified advertising, yellow pages listings, outdoor, broadcast and print ads. "Local advertising is the biggest and most profitable market for advertising," said Brian C. Oakes, an analyst with Lehman Brothers who follows newspapers and Internet companies. "It is critically important for newspapers to win the local market, both in print and on line." Newspapers may have an edge over technology companies because of their history and reputation in the cities they serve, analysts said. "One of the problems for all these local arts and entertainment sites is that they all look the same," said Patrick Keane, an analyst with Jupiter Communications, a newyork research firm. "The Times has an established brand, while the others have to build theirs from scratch." Daniel J. Donaghy, the general manager of newyork Today, said that he hoped that the breadth of the news and reviews about newyork events written for The newyork Times would distinguish the site from the competition. But Mr. Donaghy said the company expected that the most important advantage would be technology that allowed each user to customize the service to see both information and advertising related to the user's own interests. The site is designed to look like an appointment calendar, with weather forecasts, arts events and other information listed by date. In one unusual feature, advertisers can have their sales and other promotional events mixed in with the arts and entertainment listings. Users can see a list of these sales and, if they choose, have sales for categories of their choice displayed when they first enter the site. In addition to the calendar listings, newyork Today has a number of other close links between advertising and the site's editorial content. For example, a user who searches the classified advertising listings of The Times for, say, condominiums in Greenwich Village will also see advertisements offering listings of the same type of property from several real estate brokers. That advertising will be marked as such and displayed in red type, while editorial content will be in blue type. Martin A. Nisenholtz, the president of The newyork Times Electronic Media Company, said that such links were a service to users in the long tradition of publishing. "People often buy the newspaper as much to read the ads as to read the news," he said.

title: Critics Contend U.S. Policy On the Internet Has 2 Big Flaws
body: Nearly one year after President Clinton disclosed a list of ambitious goals to foster the commercial growth of the Internet, critics say that the Administration's contradictory policies on data encryption and its slow progress on privacy controls have left the nation's nascent electronic commerce industry adrift on a rudderless ship. And critics contend that two major issues seem particularly in disarray -- a policy for protecting consumer privacy on line, and an export policy on data-scrambling, or encryption, technology. "The whole area of E-commerce is going to come unglued unless we solve the crypto policy, unless we resolve the privacy issue," said David Farber, a professor of computer science at the University of Pennsylvania and a board member of the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Because electronic commerce -- buying and selling products and services on line -- is widely considered the engine that promises to drive commercial activity in the next decade, the stalemates on those two key points have overshadowed an otherwise productive year for the Administration on information-technology issues. Mr. Clinton's senior adviser on Internet issues, Ira Magaziner, in an interview last week declared success in meeting most of the one-year goals that he had set in drafting the President's framework for a tax-free, self-regulated digital marketplace. Most important, he said, the Administration made considerable progress on international accords to keep Internet commerce duty free. Mr. Magaziner also noted that pending legislation would put a moratorium on domestic Internet taxes; that a framework had been developed for making the issuing of Internet addresses a self-governing and competitive system and that Congress was close to putting into effect a treaty to protect digital copyrights in cyberspace. In the private sector, companies and Internet consortiums have developed a variety of filtering products and rating systems to give parents options for controlling where their children can venture on the Net. Those efforts have so far averted new attempts at Government controls over Internet content. "If you had asked me a year ago would we be as far as we are, I would have been cautious about it," Mr. Magaziner said. "I think we have made tremendous progress." Yet, two weeks shy of the White House's own July 1 deadline for initiating an effective code of conduct to protect consumer privacy on line, the Administration is scrambling to address a report issued last week by the Federal Trade Commission. That report, the culmination of more than 10 months of hearings and investigations, paints a dismal picture of the industry's efforts to police itself on privacy issues. It proposes that legislation be enacted to protect children on line -- not just from the usual suspects like pedophiles, but from predatory marketers who gather information about children and their families with no apparent regard for privacy rights. Industry groups generally praise the Administration for staying true to its vow to let the private sector lead. With a little more time, they say, they will have the proper controls in place. But privacy advocates and academic observers say that the Administration has been inconsistent and passive. Worse, they say, it has failed to provide the kind of leadership that would force the private sector into the kinds of cross-industry agreements needed to make self-regulation work. About the only thing everyone, including Mr. Magaziner, agrees on is that the Administration has made no progress in resolving its most glaring policy contradiction: its continued support for Government regulation of encryption technology. Bowing to law enforcement concerns about terrorists and drug cartels using strong data-scrambling technology to conceal their crimes, the Administration has refused to let American companies freely export strong encryption. But the same kinds of computer security that the Federal Bureau of Investigation and other police agencies insist on controlling are exactly the kinds of security that must be in place before credit card and other sensitive transactions can be considered safe from hackers and on-line thieves. "E-commerce cannot succeed without strong encryption to protect people on the Internet," said Robert Holleyman, president of the Business Software Alliance, an industry association whose members include the Microsoft Corporation, the Netscape Communications Corporation, Novell, Sun Microsystems and the nation's other top software developers. In a sign of just how crucial encryption policy is to the computer industry, Microsoft's chairman, William H. Gates, and his top rivals put aside their differences last week and traveled to Washington for a closed-door meeting with Attorney General Janet Reno and the F.B.I. director, Louis Freeh. "It is fair to say this is one area where our policies are not consistent with the rest of the approach, and the reasons are because of the concerns of law enforcement," Mr. Magaziner said. As for privacy, Mr. Magaziner said it was too soon to call self-regulation a failure. Many in the on-line business world agree. "People have to understand that this is a fairly new phenomenon," said Harris Miller, president of the Information Technology Association of America, a trade group. "The technology is still being developed to give people the confidence that their privacy is being protected." What is more, says Henry H. Perritt Jr., dean of the Chicago-Kent College of Law at the Illinois Institute of Technology and president of the Center for Information Law and Policy, if progress on self-regulation is slow, it is the Administration that is to blame. Lending a sense of urgency to that perception is the fact that in October, strong privacy protections take effect in European Union nations and those measures could have a serious impact on American companies doing business overseas. Mr. Magaziner has been globe-trotting for the last few weeks trying to dissuade other nations from following the European model, assuring them that self-regulation will work. An industry-Administration summit meeting to help draft privacy guidelines has been in the planning stages for months. Final dates, June 23 and 24, were set the day that the trade commission issued its dismal findings about children's privacy on line. Graphic   Chart: "A 13-Step Internet Program" Here is an overview and status report on the Administration's proposals and goals for promoting electronic commerce, which were spelled out last July.  ONE YEAR GOALS  Develop rules and solutions for protecting privacy on the Internet -- A Federal Trade Commission report found that private industry efforts have been inadequate. The Commerce Department will hold a conference this month on the subject, just days before a progress report is due.  Secure international agreements to keep the Internet tax-free -- Japan has signed an agreement and it has general support worldwide. The World Trade Organization recently adopted a one-year ban on tariffs on information sold on line.  Reach agreement with state and local governments to keep the Internet tax-free -- Legislation is pending to create a three-year moratorium on taxes on Internet access, on-line services and information traveling across the Internet, at least until a study on taxing electronic commerce can be done.  Ratify World Intellectual Properties Organization treaty on digital copyrights -- The Senate has ratified the treaty. Legislation to put the treaty into effect has passed the Senate and is pending in the House of Representatives.  Make control of Internet domains private and competitive -- Currently, domain names are assigned by Network Solutions Inc. under a Government-sponsored monopoly. The Administration has released a plan for handing governance over to a nonprofit corporation, but the international community still has to reach agreement on who will be on the board.  Develop rules for authenticating electronic transactions -- International discussions are continuing and legislation is pending to adopt a uniform national standard.  Develop Internet rating and filtering systems that can screen content deemed unsuitable for children -- Several technologies are being developed, but their effectiveness is debatable. Legislation is pending to require schools that receive Federal Internet funds to install software to screen content.  Get more involved in electronic commerce -- The Administration wants to expand its GSA Advantage on-line shopping service.  LONGER-TERM GOALS  Create international standards for Internet security -- The Administration remains deadlocked with private industry over controls for encryption technology.  Create a seamless environment for electronic commerce worldwide and insure access for all -- International discussions are continuing.  Update U.S. patent policy to meet the needs of the electronic age and seek worldwide agreements to protect patents -- Work is underway.  Promote private sector development of electronic technical standards and oppose efforts by other Governments to impose standards -- International discussions are continuing.  Monitor developments in electronic payment systems and oppose imposition of restrictions -- Work is underway. (pg. D7)

title: Sailor Victorious in Gay Case of On-Line Privacy - Correction Appended
body: In a victory for gay rights, with implications for the millions of people who use computer on-line services, both the Navy and America Online have reached settlements with a highly decorated sailor who was investigated by the Navy after he posted a message in which he described himself as "gay." Under the Navy agreement, the 36-year-old sailor, Master Chief Petty Officer Timothy R. McVeigh, will retire from the military with full benefits and with tens of thousands of dollars to pay his legal fees. The Navy had originally sought to discharge Mr. McVeigh without any benefits, despite 18 years of unblemished service, after he posted a note on the on-line service in which he identified himself as "Tim," whose marital status was "gay" and whose email address was "Boysrch." The Navy's settlement with Mr. McVeigh, who is no relation to the man convicted of bombing the Federal Building in Oklahoma City, is expected to be announced on Friday. In a separate settlement, America Online, the nation's largest on-line computer service, with 12 million users, has apologized to Mr. McVeigh for violating his privacy and has agreed to pay him damages. The company acknowledged that it had confirmed to a Navy investigator that Mr. McVeigh was "Tim." Under the settlement, both sides agreed not to reveal the amount of money paid to Mr. McVeigh by America Online. As a result of the case, the company has also announced new policies intended to guarantee the privacy of its users. The policies will require that all of the company's nearly 5,000 customer-service representatives be provided with special "scenario training" to insure that they do not give out private information about users without the user's consent or without a court order. The company has also rewritten its privacy policy to make it far clearer, and has made the new policy available on line to all users. "I'm happy that this case has been resolved on my terms," Mr. McVeigh said in a telephone interview today from his home in Honolulu. "I think that all sailors can take comfort from this. I hope it sends a message that the rules and regulations that are in place need to be followed by the military." The Navy said it would withhold comment on the settlement until the terms were made public. Mr. McVeigh, who normally would not have been eligible for retirement for another two years, said he felt some sadness in leaving the Navy. "It's a job that I've been doing for 18 years, that I'm good at, that I like, but I'm ready to move on to bigger and better things," he said. "I think this opens a much broader opportunity for me." Mr. McVeigh's lawyer, Christopher Wolf of Washington, said the settlement with the Navy was a very significant victory. "It shows what we alleged at the outset, that Mr. McVeigh's electronic privacy rights and his rights under the military's 'don't ask, don't tell' policy were seriously violated by the Navy," Mr. Wolf said. "It is the first time, as far as I'm aware, that the Navy has let stand a court decision that it has broken the law in this area. Obviously it has a precedent that can be relied on in the future." Last January, Judge Stanley Sporkin of Federal District Court in Washington ordered the Navy to halt its efforts to dismiss Mr. McVeigh and ruled that the Navy's investigation into his sexual orientation was a clear violation of the military's five-year-old "don't ask, don't tell" policy. The policy was intended to allow gay service members to remain in the military so long as they were discreet about their private lives. Judge Sporkin also appeared to side with lawyers who suggested that the Navy and America Online had violated a 1986 Federal law that bars computer service companies from releasing confidential information about customers without the person's permission or a court order. Mr. Wolf said that under the settlement with the Navy, the Defense Department would not appeal the judge's ruling. The case dates to September, when Mr. McVeigh sent an email message to the wife of a fellow crewman aboard the nuclear-powered submarine Chicago about a Christmas toy drive for the crew's children. Navy officials said the woman was disturbed by the return address on his email -- "Boysrch," which apparently referred to "boy search" -- and she consulted the customer profile listed under the return address on America Online. The profile identified the user as Tim of Honolulu, whose hobbies included "collecting pictures of other young studs." The information was passed on to a Navy investigator, who contacted America Online. Without identifying his ties to the Navy, the investigator asked for the full name of Tim. America Online acknowledged this year that a customer-service representative had violated the company's in-house rules and confirmed to the investigator that Tim was Master Chief Petty Officer McVeigh. In interviews, Mr. McVeigh, who was described in recent performance evaluations as "an outstanding role model" and "the embodiment of Navy core values," has declined to discuss his sexual orientation, saying it was irrelevant to a case that should be focused instead on the possibility of misconduct by the Navy. A spokeswoman for America Online, Tricia Primrose, said the settlement between the company and Mr. McVeigh was reached several months ago but was not announced at the time. "In our review of the situation, we recognized that we had made a mistake as a result of human error, and that we absolutely regretted it," Ms. Primrose said. "We've taken responsibility for this action and satisfactorally resolved it with Mr. McVeigh." As a result of the case, she said, America Online will require all of its customer-service representatives to undergo "scenario training, in which we give them examples of the ways in which they could be misled" into turning over confidential information to unauthorized callers. The representatives, she said, will also be required to read and sign a copy of the company's privacy policy every six months, with the understanding that violations of the policy "will be sanctioned all the way up to and including termination." She said the company had also recently rewritten its privacy policy to make it clearer, and had made it available on line. "We wanted to make this easier to read, written in plain English," she said. "It was a big overhaul to make this document understandable to us mere mortals." The policy opens with a statement that America Online is "committed to protecting your personal privacy" and that "we understand that for you to take full advantage of the benefits of this interactive medium, we must do everything we can to insure that your privacy is secure." Correction  An article on Friday reported settlements by the Navy and America Online with a highly decorated sailor who was investigated by the Navy after he posted a computer message, under an anonymous email address, in which he described himself as gay. America Online, which divulged the sailor's real name to the Navy, agreed to pay him damages for violating his privacy. Under the Navy's part of the agreement, the 36-year-old sailor will retire with full benefits and with tens of thousands of dollars to pay his legal fees. The first paragraph of the article described the settlements as a "victory for gay rights." That phrase was supplied in editing. It failed to take the Navy's view into account. And it did not reflect any opinion expressed by the sailor, Master Chief Petty Officer Timothy R. McVeigh, whose lawyer has commented only on the privacy aspects of the episode. The Navy, which withheld comment at the time, now says the settlement was in no way a victory for gay rights, since the service was achieving at least part of what it wanted: the departure of Mr. McVeigh, because of what appeared to be a declaration of homosexuality. Correction-Date: June 17, 1998, Wednesday Graphic   Photo: Timothy R. McVeigh will retire from the Navy with full benefits as a result of a gay-rights victory. (Associated Press)(pg. A14)

title: America Online to Buy Internet Chat Service for $287 Million
body: With all the frenzy over the Internet, entrepreneurs have been able to create and sell companies for huge sums without ever earning a dime. But in what may be a record of financial weightlessness, America Online said yesterday that it would pay at least $287 million for a company that has never taken in a penny in revenue and has no plans to start charging money. What the company, an Israeli concern called Mirabilis Ltd., does have is users, 12 million of them who spend an average of more than an hour a day on its Internet chat service. Ultimately, America Online hopes to put advertising on the chat service and sell its members products and services. "When you talk about making money on the Internet, no one is doing more than America Online," said Robert W. Pittman, the company's president. He compared the Internet today to the early days of cable television. MTV, which Mr. Pittman helped start, took in only $500,000 in revenue its first year. Mirabilis is highly regarded among savvy Internet users for its chat service, known as ICQ (shorthand for "I seek you"), which enables them to detect when fellow users are on line and to communicate instantly with them. With no promotion other than word of mouth, it has already achieved something of a cult status, growing at more than 50,000 subscribers a day. ICQ is attractive to America Online because it appeals to a much younger and more technologically sophisticated audience than the mainstream America Online brand. "If this were 1980, think underground album-oriented rock radio," Mr. Pittman said. Moreover, he said, ICQ users spend an average of 75 minutes a day on the service, compared with fewer than 10 minutes a day for highly touted search and directory services such as Yahoo and Lycos. Many Internet stock analysts praised the deal as an inexpensive way for America Online to increase its customer relationships. The company's shares rose $1.50 yesterday, to $84.75. But there is some skepticism that chat services, no matter how popular, will turn into big money makers. "email, chat and instant messaging are not good advertising platforms," said Bo Peabody, the chief executive of Tripod, an on-line community service recently bought by Lycos. "When you chat, you look at what you are writing, not what other people are writing," he said. Moreover, advertisers worry that their advertisements will be associated with content that they do not control and may be embarrassing. As a result, chat services that do take ads receive the lowest rates of any type of Internet service. That has not stopped other companies from buying similar services. Most notably, Microsoft paid a reported $400 million for Hotmail, which offers free email services. (Unlike ICQ, Hotmail had started to sell advertisements.) Mirabilis also helps America Online's efforts to expand overseas. About 40 percent of ICQ's members are in the unitedstates, 40 percent are in Europe and the rest are spread elsewhere. Mirabilis was founded two years ago by four Israelis in their early 20's. With a few million dollars in backing from local investors, it has built one of the most popular services on the Internet. Yossi Vardi, the Mirabilis chairman, said the company had been in discussions with a number of suitors since last August. But they were initially put off by the price the company wanted. "People were quite amazed with our growth and it took them a while to come to grips with that," he said. America Online agreed to pay $287 million in cash up front and up to $120 million in additional payments starting in 2001, depending on the performance of Mirabilis, which will continue to be run as a separate subsidiary in Tel Aviv. America Online's own Internet chat service, AOL Instant Messenger, will continue to be a separate product mainly to allow Internet users to communicate with those on America Online's service. America Online will also provide some technical support to Mirabilis. Mr. Peabody of Tripod said that since America Online now controlled the two largest chat services it should embrace an open standard that would allow the user of any chat service to send an instant message to a user of a competing service, much as electronic mail works now. "Now that AOL has a monopoly on the instant messenger space, I'm hopeful they will open the market to everyone," he said. Tripod hopes to offer its own message service and such a standard would help it break into the existing market. Tricia Primrose, a spokeswoman for America Online, said that there were no standards for instant messages now, but that "historically AOL supports open standards that gain critical mass and acceptance by consumers."

title: F.T.C. to Call for Laws to Protect Children on Line
body: Amid mounting public concern about the abuse of personal data in an increasingly digital world, the Federal Trade Commission is expected to censure the Internet industry today in a report to Congress for doing virtually nothing to insure adequate consumer privacy protection on line. In a departure from the Clinton Administration's hands-off approach to the Internet, the agency will call for legislation that would require sites on the World Wide Web to obtain parental consent before collecting personal information from children, according to the report. The commission said it would make recommendations on privacy for other Web users this summer. "Children are told by parents not to talk to strangers whom they meet on the street, but they are given a contrary message by Web sites that encourage them to interact with strangers in their homes via the Web," the report says. Representative Edward J. Markey, Democrat of Massachusetts and the ranking minority member of the House telecommunications subcommittee, said, "This is a historic benchmark that changes forever the discussion of the protections which children need in a cyberera." In a study of 1,400 Web sites in March, the commission found that 85 percent collect personal information but only 14 percent provide any notice about what they do with the data. Only 2 percent provide such notice with a comprehensive privacy policy, the report said. "Those numbers are frightening," Mr. Markey said. "If privacy protections are not built into Internet commerce, then a vast majority of Americans will never trust the Internet." Although few had seen the long-anticipated report yesterday, news leaks about it added fuel to a heated debate among industry leaders and privacy advocates about how to address privacy concerns. Several companies and trade groups rushed to blunt the effect of the report with announcements of new policies. Technology trade groups representing more than 10,000 companies sent President Clinton a letter asking for a chance to allow self-regulation to work. And the Direct Marketing Association touted its own study, which showed that 70 percent of the top 100 children's Web sites publish a privacy policy. The group, which has lobbied against legislation, said late yesterday that it had adopted a new policy to seek parental consent for on-line marketing involving children younger than 13. "This is business stepping up to the plate, moving in the direction that it needs to, and that is how self-regulation works," said Connie Heatley, senior vice president of the association. For many companies trying to do business on the Internet, the entire promise of the medium rests on the ease with which it allows the collection of information for focusing advertising and marketing. Based on forms that consumers fill out when they first visit a site, or on simply tracking which areas of a site they visit most frequently, Web site owners can, for example, determine which advertisements to show them. "If it's not customized and personalized, it might as well be television," said David Card, a senior analyst at Jupiter Communications, an on-line consulting operation in newyork. "I'm nervous that we'll get stuck with a law that would eliminate the technical ability to do that." Still, consumers have continually expressed fears about what happens to information that they provide in cyberspace. Anxiety about the use of of medical and financial information on line is one of the top reasons people do not use the Internet, according to several recent polls. And some companies have decided that electronic commerce would be more helped than hurt by ending such practices. America Online, which has been much criticized for privacy lapses, said yesterday that it would not use the information that it gathered about what members did on line for any marketing purposes. "This can be extremely valuable information in the marketplace," said Jill Lesser, the on-line service's deputy director for law and public policy. "The ability to target consumers is extremely valuable. But you have to strike a balance." Ms. Lesser added: "It's hard to fault the F.T.C. for calling a spade a spade. Hopefully this will be a catalyst for companies to look at privacy protection as a business imperative." But Government action is needed, privacy advocates said, because children have never been more more vulnerable to commercial exploitation. "We're creating a new children's culture, and if we don't set ground rules for how that's done, we could see a whole set of very egregious, manipulative practices that could do a lot of harm to kids," said Kathryn C. Montgomery, president of the Center for Media Education, a child advocacy group. The problem with many sites aimed at children is that they make divulging information seem like a game, Ms. Montgomery said. For example, the Popsicle Web site, published by the Good Humor-Breyers Ice Cream unit of Unilever, asks children to choose whether they want to be commanders or passengers. Just one catch: Commanders have to fill out their age, sex, favorite TV show and favorite popsicle before blasting off. And in case anyone was inclined to just go along for the ride, the passenger option cautions: "Sure, you can ride in the big stuffed chair, but you'll miss out on the chance to win free Popsicles. Plus it's really cold in outer space without a Spaceship. Why not be a commander?" Popsicle's privacy policy says that it does not release the data it gathers to third parties.
