title: The Hum of Search Engines Is Music to Netscape's Ears
body: The search is on for search engines. A number of companies -- including Netscape Communications and some big traditional media players -- are looking to build or buy their own Internet search services. These services, initially meant only to help Internet users find information from among the millions of pages of on-line material, have now become the primary gateway to cyberspace for many people. Netscape is in the midst of high-stakes negotiations to choose a company to provide the central search function for its ambitious new Internet site. The second tier of search businesses, including Lycos, Infoseek and the Snap service of Cnet, are actively negotiating with Netscape, people involved in the negotiations say. The two larger search services -- Yahoo and Excite -- have talked to Netscape, too, but are said to be less interested. Netscape's hunt for a deal is only one part of its plan to expand its World Wide Web site, called Netcenter, into a full source of communication, information and shopping, to compete with America Online and Yahoo. Now that it is giving away its browser, the company hopes advertising will become a major source of revenue. Last week, for instance, it announced an agreement to offer electronic-mail services. Existing search companies worry about Netscape as a potentially powerful new competitor, simply because millions of people already use Netscape's Web browser software. "They will take market share from all the players," said Steven T. Kirsch, the chairman of Infoseek. "We're not afraid of competition, but that's bad for our business." A deal with Netscape may help a company jump ahead of its competitors. The chairman of Cnet, Halsey Minor, said his company would consider selling a piece of Snap, a service modeled on Yahoo, to Netscape or to a big media company to bring in traffic. "There are a lot of options for us to partner with people who can help us build a brand," he said. Yet it is unclear whether Netscape is interested in building any brand but its own. Mike Homer, general manager of its new Web site division, says Netscape wants a search company to provide it with the information to offer a search service along with a directory of the Internet, similar to the yellow pages, under the Netscape brand name. Netscape had hoped to have a deal set a few weeks ago, but has not reached an agreement, people involved in the talks said. It has asked for large cash payments and stock in the search company, which would earn money from selling advertising. Many companies see such terms as too steep a price for a deal that might last only two or three years. "Would you give away 20 percent of your company for a two-year deal?," a top executive of one search engine company asked. "After that, where do you go?" Mr. Kirsch of Infoseek acknowledged that reaching a deal might be difficult. "We're interested in a deal that expands our reach, if we can do something that makes sense for both parties," he said. "But my past experience with Netscape has led me to believe they are very aggressive negotiators." Mr. Homer said Netscape was also negotiating for sources of other content, like stock quotations and computer industry news. Search services have evolved into popular gateways through which people venture onto the Internet. That makes advertisers interested in these services, which have also collected substantial revenue by selling links to other sites, like those selling books or music. Moreover, these sites have been using their popularity to expand into other services, like email, news chat groups and other activities that keep viewers lingering longer and looking at more advertising. Excitement about the search companies has driven their stock prices to spectacular heights. Yahoo, which is barely profitable, has a market value of more than $5 billion. And competitors are lining up. Microsoft is creating Start.com, a jumping-off point to the Internet that will feed people to Microsoft Web sites. And investment bankers report that many big traditional media companies are considering buying search sites, too, so they are not left out of what could be the next big type of media property. Many Internet experts, however, predict an ultimate shakeout. "There will be three -- four, max -- global, comprehensive Web on-line services," said Jeffrey Mallett, the chief operating officer of Yahoo. He argues that Netscape is not in a position to be one of them. "Netscape's brand conjures up software and browsers, not an on-line service." Mr. Homer of Netscape says it is precisely the company's software that will give it an advantage on line. For example, a prominent link on the Netscape browser (marked "search") now funnels Netscape users to one of several search engines, which pay the company for the traffic. After Netscape reaches its deal, that link will increasingly point users to its own service.

title: America Online Libel Suit Dismissed
body: In a decision that was heartening for Internet access providers, a Federal judge today dismissed a libel suit brought against America Online by a high-ranking aide to President Clinton. But the judge let stand a similar suit against Matt Drudge, the cyberspace gossip commentator. The judge, Paul L. Friedman of Federal District Court here, said that he was reluctant to dismiss the suit brought by Sidney Blumenthal against America Online but that the clear intent of Congress -- to protect Internet service providers from liability for material disseminated by them but created by others -- left him no choice. But in allowing the suit against Mr. Drudge to stand, the judge called the commentator "simply a purveyor of gossip" who had no right to the libel protections enjoyed by legitimate journalists. Judge Friedman's ruling, in a suit filed after Mr. Drudge reported old rumors of domestic trouble between Mr. Blumenthal and his wife, Jacqueline, is hardly the last word. The case is almost certain to be appealed to the unitedstates Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, and perhaps to the Supreme Court, which may be called upon to further refine how the First Amendment squares with news gathering and dissemination in the world of computers. The principals reacted to the ruling with caution, with the notable exception of Mr. Drudge. The Blumenthals' lawyer, Jo Bennett Marsh of Baltimore, said his clients were "elated by the court's recognition that Drudge is in no way 'a reporter, a journalist, or a news gatherer,' but is 'simply a purveyor of gossip,' who must answer for his defamation of the Blumenthals." Ms. Marsh said they would seek on appeal to have America Online reinstated as a defendant. George Vradenburg, the general counsel for America Online, said the ruling was consistent with Congress's intent to encourage diversity on the Internet, and with previous court decisions. Mr. Drudge's lawyer, Manuel Klausner of Los Angeles, said he would appeal. "We feel we have a strong case," Mr. Klausner said, adding that the judge had "inaccurately characterized what Mr. Drudge does with 'The Drudge Report.' " Mr. Drudge said by telephone from Los Angeles: "I'm going on the record. I'm not a journalist. I'm a kangaroo! I'll see Mr. Blumenthal in court." What Mr. Drudge does -- news, gossip or both -- has been heatedly debated in recent weeks. On the one hand, he has had some success in breaking news about the President's supposed involvement with other women. On the other hand, critics in the more traditional news organizations complain that he puts rumors and innuendo on his Web site without checking first. Last August, just as Mr. Blumenthal was starting work at the White House, Mr. Drudge publicized what he has since acknowledged as "reports on an old rumor" about troubles in the Blumenthal household. The next day, he ran a retraction and apology on his web site and in The Washington Post. But the Blumenthals were not satisfied and seek $30 million in damages. In dismissing the claim against America Online, Judge Friedman cited language from the Communications Decency Act passed by Congress in 1996 to prohibit the transmission of indecent material over computer networks. The act was overturned by the Supreme Court last year on free speech grounds, but Judge Friedman found its language regarding protection of Internet providers to be applicable, although he did so reluctantly. Because America Online has the right to exercise editorial control, the judge wrote, "it would seem only fair to hold A.O.L. to the liability standards applied to a publisher or, at least, like a bookstore owner or library, to the liability standards applied to a distributor. But Congress has made a different policy choice."

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
CYBERSCOUT
body: ON-LINE AIR FARES Name Your Price www.priceline.com It remains to be seen how it works out, but Priceline looks like a good idea for a traveler's Web site. You enter the price you are willing to pay for an airline ticket, and if an airline has an empty seat for which it would rather get something than nothing, Priceline lets you know. In more detail, you request a round-trip ticket for a particular destination, with a specific range of dates and the price you will pay. If one of the participating airlines accepts your offer, you hear back by email within an hour, or you can call Priceline's toll-free number. Electronic tickets are sent at no charge; real tickets are delivered by Federal Express or Express Mail for $12.50. For practical purposes, the restrictions mean the clientele will be largely vacation travelers: tickets, which are neither changeable nor refundable, must be round-trip coach; there is no choice of departure times or airlines, and frequent-flier miles are not given. Flights must start in the unitedstates or Puerto Rico. On the other hand, there are no blackout dates or advance-purchase rules. The participating airlines are American, America West, Continental, Delta, Northwest, T.W.A., United and U.S. Airways, or their affiliates, as well as most major international airlines. The selling of airline tickets on Priceline started April 6. The company plans to extend the concept to automobile loans and home mortgages later in the year. Priceline, which is based in Stamford, Conn., is a new privately held company. The site can handle more than 100,000 hits a minute, the company says. More than 620,000 individuals tried Priceline on opening day, Andrea Butler, vice president of public relations, said. Business was "steady and increasing all week," she added. "Every 25 seconds every 24 hours someone gave a guaranteed credit card request for a ticket." How many people actually got tickets? "We're keeping that close to the vest," she said. The Web site is clean and uncluttered. A tour, if you need it, leads you through the steps to navigate Priceline, starting with the cities you want to travel between, the price you want to pay and finally typing in a credit-card number. People who are wary about sending a card number through cyberspace can telephone a toll-free number. Of course, airline tickets have been available on the Web for some time, and all the airlines named above have Web sites. On them you'll find far more choices of departure times, class of service and the use of frequent-flier and other discount opportunities. A couple of airlines have held on-line auctions for tickets. But Priceline is the only site I know of that intends to do business by allowing you to name your price for a plane ticket.  BUSINESS BOOKSTORE For Globe-Trotters www.landseer.com/market/books.html Let's not forget the business traveler. Landseer's Business Traveler Bookstore opened a Web site last month. When I checked it recently, 14 titles were featured, from "Dun & Bradstreet's Guide to Doing Business Around the World" to "How to Negotiate Anything With Anyone, Anywhere Around the World." I clicked on one, "Kiss, Bow or Shake Hands: How to Do Business in 60 Countries," and got a summary of the book, which covers "the protocols of appointments, business entertaining, greetings, forms of address, gestures, dress and gifts." There were also authors' names and the price as well as a button to click to add the book to your shopping list. It was a familiar scenario, since Landseer is part of amazon.com, the Web bookstore. So while you're there, you can order a couple of romance novels to take on the trip.   L. R. SHANNON Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Tolls Are Increasing For Web On-Ramps
body: after several years of sharply declining prices, connecting to the Internet is getting more expensive again. Last week, America Online, the world's largest Internet service provider, raised its prices by 10 percent for its most active customers, those who formerly paid $19.95 for unlimited access to the Net. The new rate is $21.95 a month. WebTV Networks, a Microsoft subsidiary, announced a 25 percent increase in monthly fees for its WebTV Plus service, effective June 1. The new fee for the premium service will be $24.95 a month. The previous rate, $19.95, will still be offered for a lower level of service that will be called WebTV Classic. Starting next month, AT&T Worldnet Services will redefine "unlimited access" as 150 hours a month. Customers who use more than 150 hours a month will be billed a surcharge of 99 cents for each additional hour. The new fees will affect only the most active users, those who spend an average of nearly five hours on line a day. Earlier, AT&T had considered and rejected a plan to place a three-hour time limit on all on-line sessions to keep some customers from hogging an access port all day. These pricing changes may be the first steps toward tiered pricing and services for the Internet, where customers who use the Internet the most will pay the most. America Online and AT&T Worldnet were the first major services to offer unlimited access for $19.95 a month, and their retreat is significant. Some Internet service providers have explored the idea of charging customers a premium for guaranteed access, free of the busy signals and congestion that have plagued some customers with unlimited-access plans. Others have explored variable pricing, where one hourly rate would apply during peak hours and another during off-peak hours. But not every Internet user will be asked to pay more. Some, in fact, will pay less. AT&T customers who chose the limited-access plan, $9.95 a month for 10 hours with a $2.50 per hour surcharge for additional hours, are getting a price break. Beginning May 1, the surcharge is being reduced to 99 cents. AT&T also promised to install more modems and phone lines to reduce congestion in its busiest markets. And AOL announced that it was beginning trials of a new high-speed Internet service, called a Digital Subscriber Line, in five cities this year. The DSL service would offer connection speeds many times faster than today's fastest dial-up modems for a monthly fee of $49.95 plus a onetime setup fee of $150. The service has been awaited eagerly by Internet users frustrated by long waits for downloading software, video and graphic images, and World Wide Web pages. The initial trials will take place in Birmingham, Ala.; Redmond, Wash.; Phoenix; San Francisco, and the Washington suburbs. GTE Internetworking will provide the service. The $49.95 monthly fee includes access to AOL. While $50 a month for Internet access may seem high to those now paying $20 for conventional modem access, it is less than a third of the cost charged by phone companies for DSL access in many areas of the country.

title: Yahoo's First-Quarter Earnings Exceed Expectations of Analysts
body: Yahoo Inc., the Internet directory service, reported first-quarter earnings today that exceeded Wall Street analysts' expectations. Yahoo said traffic on its World Wide Web pages had increased by nearly 50 percent since the fourth quarter of 1997. Yahoo has become one of the few profitable Internet companies by turning its well-known brand name and popular services into a lure for advertisers. From a simple directory born in a Stanford University dormitory room, Yahoo, based in Santa Clara, Calif., has branched out to offer electronic commerce, financial services and telecommunications. Shares of Yahoo rose $4, or 4.3 percent, today, to $97.25, in Nasdaq trading. Yahoo shares fell along with other Internet issues Tuesday, amid concern that the stocks' prices had risen too high in the last few weeks. Yahoo shares are up 45 percent this year and up nearly sixfold from their 52-week low of $16.62. For the quarter ended March 31, Yahoo earned $4.3 million, or 8 cents a fully diluted share, compared with a loss of $740,000 in the quarter a year earlier. Revenue tripled, to $30.2 million. Analysts had expected Yahoo to report earnings of 4 cents a share, according to First Call, an investment research company. Yahoo said that traffic on the Yahoo global network of sites increased to an average of 95 million page views a day last month, compared with an average of 65 million page views a day in December. A page view is defined as one electronic page of information displayed in response to a user request. Yahoo said it continued to have the largest audience of any Web site or on-line service, with more than 30 million adult users in the unitedstates in March. It also said it had more than 12 million registered users, reflecting the number of people who have submitted personal data for Yahoo's registration process to get access to special services.

title: Anger Over Bank Merger Spills Onto Web
body: The joke tellers said that UBS stood for "Unemployed Before Summer" and that Union Bank of Switzerland might as well be the Titanic. But the sarcasm about the proposed merger of the company and the Swiss Bank Corporation was not just limited to conversations in corporate hallways. A Web site critical of the proposed merger reflected the depths of Union Bank employees' resentment about the prospect of dismissals in one of the biggest banking mergers in history. But this time, unlike other mergers where emotions run high among employees, the authors vented their anger in public. The Web site, housed on America Online, vanished over the weekend after an article about it was distributed on Friday by Bloomberg News. But Swiss Bank took some lumps, too. "What's SBC stand for?" one joke read referring to the Stamford, Conn., offices of SBC Warburg Dillon Read, Swiss Bank's unitedstates investment banking unit. "Severance Beats Connecticut." The Web site included a mock newspaper front page, complete with headlines and a picture of the Titanic, according to the Bloomberg News report. There was a section for job hunters, a place to post email and a list of things to do in Stamford, a suburban community not well known for its hip nightspots. The $25 billion union between the two companies was never billed as a marriage of equals. Swiss Bank is, in effect, the acquirer, and the combined companies expect to eliminate 13,000 jobs worldwide. Defections at the unitedstates investment banking units were expected because of the overlap between the companies' operations. But many employees at UBS Securities in newyork, the Union Bank unit, were not waiting for dismissal notices. On Monday, for instance, 23 bankers from UBS Securities left for Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. Among them was Richard Barrett, the former managing director of UBS's financial institutions group. The same day, Furman Selz hired David MacCallum, UBS's global head of the life sciences group. Last Friday, Salomon Smith Barney hired three former UBS energy specialists. And several equity traders are expected to join Lazard Freres & Company this month. Industry watchers say the relationship between the unitedstates arms of the Swiss rivals has been unusually testy compared with other recent mergers, including those of Salomon Smith Barney and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter. "This one gets the soap opera, bang-for-the-buck award," said one stock analyst who has heard complaints from friends at UBS. "Instead of seeing individuals leaving, you are seeing whole departments." Andrea de Cholnoky, head of the global securities and wholesale banking practice at Spencer Stuart, said, "What we see as recruiters is a ton of people calling us up scrambling to find jobs." Tricia Primrose, a spokeswoman for America Online, confirmed that the Web site was shut down, but not by America Online. "It was taken down by the account," she said. Ms. Primrose, citing privacy concerns, would not identify the authors or confirm whether they were employees of either of the companies. She said America Online had received no complaints about the site. "Anybody has a right to create what they want," she said. In a statement, UBS said the Web site reflected "unproductive comments of a few disgruntled employees." It went on to say, "We do not know the source of the Web site, the reason it was created or why it was shut down." An official from SBC said the company had no comment. One of the main reasons UBS Securities' employees are upset is the lack of information about the merger from management. One investment banker, who recently landed a job at another firm and asked not to be identified, said he first heard about the merger not from his UBS bosses but from a friend at SBC a few days before the announcement. Another investment banker who left and also asked not to be identified, said he met an SBC executive in mid-December who told him he would be assigned a new job in the company by month's end. But the banker said he did not hear from the executive until the end of February, after he learned most of the top jobs would be filled by SBC professionals. "And they were trying to keep me," he said. "What about the people they didn't like?" Mitchell Lee Marks, a consultant in San Francisco who advises chief executives on how to handle the cultural aspects of combining companies, said poor communication between management and employees was all too common in most mergers. "The irony here is executives will spend a lot of money on investment bankers and lawyers to advise them on a merger but not spend a lot of money integrating the companies," he said. "The first thing I tell executives is know what you are going to do." That is especially important now that disgruntled employees have easy access to a worldwide audience over the Internet and are eager to voice their complaints. Samuel Hayes, a professor of investment banking at the Harvard Business School, said, "This could well be the beginning of a new chapter in employees' capacity to express their views about how they don't like their companies being merged."

title:
Hackers' Bazaar;
On-Line Auction Services Put Haggling Back Into Sales
body: You can usually haggle over the price of a car, or cut a better deal for that rowing machine at a garage sale. But an airline ticket? Imagine walking up to an airline counter, flashing a wad of bills and offering $300 for a ticket to Florida when the lowest available fare is $400. The ticket agent would probably call security. Yet that, in essence, is what consumers will be able to do with an Internet service scheduled to be introduced on Monday. Fares are already all over the map, of course -- but they are dictated by the airlines. Now, though, five of the eight top domestic airlines and several big foreign carriers have agreed to respond electronically to bids for round-trip tickets made by consumers over the Internet, according to Priceline, the company establishing the system. While the tickets have significant restrictions meant to weed out business travelers, industry consultants expect leisure travelers to be able to use the system to buy tickets at well below listed fares, sometimes without advance purchase restrictions. Over the next year, Priceline executives say they plan to extend the concept to the purchase of cars, to interest on home mortgages and even to charges for international phone calls. Technology, in short, is bringing commerce back to the bazaar. Ever since the railroad and the Montgomery Ward catalogue extended the reach of big businesses from coast to coast, companies have largely sold their products at fixed prices. But now more and more goods and services are being sold through auctions or other forms of electronic negotiation. With some 150 World Wide Web sites running auctions of various sorts, the Internet is already loaded with the sort of haggling never seen at the local mall. The acknowledged leader of on-line bidding is Onsale, a Menlo Park, Calif., company that takes bids from 10,000 people a day for surplus computer and electronic goods. And EBay of San Jose, Calif., offers electronic classified advertising in which individuals can auction off their own property. (It has fostered a thriving market in Beanie Babies.) All manner of specialized auctions have popped up, from Bearauction, which sells teddy bears, to Guitarauction, which sells guitars. Businesses, too, are starting to use Internet auctions to buy everything from office equipment to electric power. "The idea that there are fixed prices you have to accept is not actually ingrained in human nature," said Stuart Feldman, director of the Institute for Advanced Commerce at I.B.M.'s labs in Hawthorne, N.Y. Retailers, he said, have imposed fixed prices because they have not been able to bargain individually from the home office with far-flung customers. Nor have they been willing to delegate sales clerks with the authority to set prices in the field. "Now, the Internet allows communication at no cost and infinite speed," Mr. Feldman said. "And you can program computers with rules for what deals they can and can't make, instead of trusting a $5-an-hour clerk." The result, marketing experts say, is likely to be higher prices for goods that are more in demand and more bargains for consumers willing to buy things that are off the beaten path. "If you put out a catalogue with prices good for 90 days," Mr. Feldman said, "some stuff doesn't sell because you priced it too high, while some things fly out the door because you priced it too low." Of course, to judge by the reputation of car buying, the one market in which negotiation has long been common, many American consumers do not like to haggle. But the Internet is radically changing the automobile market, too -- not to eliminate bargaining but to give it clear rules, much the way trading on a stock exchange is regulated to insure that the transaction is fair to both buyers and sellers. And some experts assert that on-line auctions appeal to a certain type of consumer who sees them as a multiplayer computer game in which real dollars are at stake. "Onsale is the perfect shopping experience for men," said Vernon Keenan, an electronic commerce analyst with Zona Research. "Not only do you find a bargain, you have to hunt it and kill it before you take it home." Even before the Internet, computerization began allowing companies to replace fixed prices with prices based on a computerized assessment of supply, demand and type of customer. A prime example can be seen at a rental car counter, where each customer seemingly pays a different rate depending on corporate discount, club affiliation or myriad other deals. Now these systems are evolving into two-way bargaining. Many credit card and long-distance telephone companies, for instance, will cut prices for customers who call and ask for lower rates. The people who really want discounts get them, while everyone else pays full price. The Internet offers a way to connect these central computers, which make ever-finer pricing distinctions, with a mass of customers. "We are moving to an age where businesses will quote a different price to every customer for every product every day," said Jerry Kaplan, chief executive of Onsale. Companies are especially attracted to the Internet as a way to clear out inventory that is either old or, like the unsold plane ticket, will have its value vanish. It is a low-cost way to reach lots of potential customers, yet it is not as public as traditional advertising. That is why big airlines have taken to selling last-minute tickets through email lists and have agreed to participate in the new Priceline auction. "It's plenty easy to fill your airplanes by offering discounts," said Donald S. Garvett, a vice president of SH & E, an airline consulting firm that has done work for Priceline. "But you cannibalize your business with people who would be willing to pay higher fares. Priceline lets you find new demand." On Priceline's Internet site, users enter the price they want to offer to travel to a specified destination on a given date. They agree to accept a ticket on any major airline, anytime of the day, with up to one stopover. The tickets are not refundable and do not earn frequent-flier miles. These restrictions are expected to scare off most business travelers. The offers will be matched against minimum prices that airlines have submitted to Priceline's computers. If any airline is willing to sell the ticket at the offered price, the user's credit card will be automatically charged. These restrictions are so tough, critics say, that Priceline may have a hard time finding customers. "This doesn't seem to be what works for the mainstream consumer, said Kenneth J. Orton, chief executive of Preview Travel, one of the leading Internet-only travel agencies. "People will pay more to fly a nonstop on a major airline rather than changing planes and using a second-tier carrier." He also pointed out that the airlines are operating at the highest capacity in years and thus do not have many surplus seats. Jay Walker, a Connecticut entrepreneur who founded Priceline, said the airlines had committed to providing 100,000 seats a day to the system. By the end of the year, he said he expects Priceline to be able to sell 1,000 to 3,000 tickets a day. But he said participating airlines would not allow their names to be disclosed, just as name-brand manufacturers do not talk about how they liquidate excess stock. "Go to Ralph Lauren and say, 'Where can I buy your clothes?' " Mr. Walker said. "He will say Bloomingdale's and my own stores sell my clothes at great prices. Ask if you can get them at the outlets in Secaucus, N.J. He'll say maybe once in a while." Mr. Walker acknowledges that secrets are hard to keep on the Internet. "There will be all sorts news groups that talk about who is selling tickets on Priceline and at what prices," he said. The airlines did force Priceline to modify its proposed system to give consumers less bargaining room. At first, Mr. Walker proposed allowing customers whose initial offers were too low to raise their bid twice to find a price the airlines would accept. But "the airlines said they were not interested in being pinged every $5 to find our real demand," Mr. Walker said. If consumers offers are turned down, not because the price they offered was too low but because there were no tickets available on the dates they requested, Priceline may give them the opportunity to change the dates and try again. Moreover, as the Priceline system is extended into cars and other markets, it is likely to allow more back-and-forth bidding. One vision of the future of commerce can be seen here in the narrow computer room of Onsale in "going, going, gone" time, the hour between noon and 1 P.M. when most of its 24-hour auctions close. A dozen computer monitors set up on card tables flash as the final bids zip in from all over the world. On a given day, more than 100,000 people will scan Onsale's 1,000 auctions, and between 10,000 and 20,000 of them will submit bids. On one recent afternoon, there was heated bidding to buy 15 long-discontinued personal computers, available without disk drives. With minutes to go before the hammer falls, "RM" from Indiana raised his bid from $249 to $259. He posted a message that all the other bidders could see: "Last time," he wrote hopefully. Indeed, he was the last. Onsale's computers closed the auction and started charging the winner's credit cards and sending them email to say they had won. Meanwhile, another computer, sitting under the card table, prepared new Web pages for the next day's auctions. Mr. Kaplan, Onsale's chief executive, scanned the monitors and tallied up how many Internet users were lingering on the Web site in anticipation of new goods. "There are 500 people outside the doors waiting to get in," he said excitedly. If companies like Onsale and Priceline take hold, though, there could be millions outside those electronic doors. title:
LIBRARY/MAPS;
Planners Ease Travel, but Would Jack Kerouac Have Used One?
body: AAA MAP 'N' GO 3.0 (DeLorme; $39.95; Windows 95 and 3.1.)  TRIP PLANNER 98 Version 6.0 (Microsoft Expedia; $39.95; Windows 95.)  TRIPMAKER DELUXE 1998 (Rand McNally; $44.95; Windows 95 and NT.) REMEMBER those automobile-club travel packets that ended up on the floor with empty coffee cups and chip bags during your childhood family vacations? Well, you can create the same kind of printout with a CD-ROM trip planner but design it to your specifications. AAA Map 'n' Go by DeLorme, Trip Planner 98 by Microsoft Expedia and Tripmaker Deluxe 1998 by Rand McNally can each plot routes to the places you specify, and each offers listings for lodging, restaurants and attractions. They also make use of multimedia features that paper maps will never have. Microsoft's Trip Planner 98 has several 360-degree moving images of tourist sights, including a breathtaking view of the 18th-century houses preserved on Philadelphia's Society Hill. Tripmaker Deluxe has video tours of popular destinations like the Everglades in South Florida, replete with pelicans and alligators. So much for deciding where to go. To see how to get there, you use a trip planner to design your trip. Among the three evaluated here, Tripmaker Deluxe offers the most options. For example, you live in Chicago and you want to visit the Cable Car Museum in San Francisco. First, you fill out a driver profile, settings for how fast you want to drive (say, 75 miles per hour on highways, if you're willing to risk a ticket), when you want to be in the car (between 10 A.M. and 3 P.M.) and how often to stop and stretch your legs (20 minutes every 4 hours). There are also provisions for choosing the quickest, shortest or most scenic route and for setting a daily budget. Then you enter some sightseeing stops to make along the way, perhaps at the Dinosaur National Monument in Colorado, Lassen Volcanic National Park in central Northern California and the Monterey Bay Aquarium south of San Francisco, and you specify how much time you plan to spend visiting each place. After several seconds of calculations, Tripmaker Deluxe produces a 9-day trip, with 2,914 miles driven in 44 hours and 18 minutes behind the wheel. But it tells you it will cost $1,721, which is $521 over budget. So make some minor adjustments: You spend five hours at Lassen instead of the whole day, start an hour earlier every other morning and drive only the quickest route instead of the scenic roads for parts of the journey.  Tripmaker Deluxe says that trip will take only seven days; with the money saved on lodging and food, the overrun is only $166. AAA Map 'n' Go and Trip Planner 98 feature most of the trip-planning options in Tripmaker Deluxe. In fact, when this particular Chicago-to-San Francisco trip is plotted along the quickest route, using the same driving speeds, all three software planners fall within 3 hours and 105 total miles of one another. What tips the scale in favor of Tripmaker Deluxe is that its multiple options encourage would-be travelers to ponder, weigh and juggle the many details of a long road trip before they pack up the kids and turn the key in the ignition. title: Powerful New Encryption Standard Delayed by a Weakness
body: A Government standards group has delayed the adoption of a new data scrambling standard for protecting the world's most sensitive financial transactions, including most banks' electronic funds transfers, after the discovery by two computer scientists of a weakness that could allow the code to be cracked. The flaw was discovered by Eli Biham, a well-known cryptographer at the Technion research institution in Israel, and by Lars Knudsen at the University of Bergen in Norway. A paper detailing their discovery is to be presented at a technical conference in May. In their paper, which is available on the Technion Web site, Mr. Biham and Mr. Knudsen report that an ultra-strong version of the unitedstates Data Encryption Standard known as Triple D.E.S. can under certain circumstances be reduced in strength so that it is no more robust than the current encryption algorithm, which financial institutions have widely used as a security mechanism for several decades. Computer security experts are eager to replace the current code because it has become vulnerable to new code-cracking techniques. When the code was developed, its designers had predicted that if it could be broken it would take hundreds of years, requiring constant trial-and-error calculations by the world's fastest supercomputers. But the code was publicly broken for the first time last year by a loosely organized group of computer users just to show that it could be done. Thousands of members of the group volunteered the use of their own computers, ranging from desktop PC's to supercomputers, whose processors were combined over the Internet to attack the problem over a five-month period with an approach known as massively distributed computing. In distributed computing, each computer tests just a few of a vast array of possible keys, or numbers, to break the code. The strength of most modern encryption systems is determined by the length of the numerical key that is used to encrypt the information. While the proposed new standard uses a key the same length as the current key -- 56 bits -- it encrypts the message three times with three different keys. For each key, there are several possible ways of encrypting the data, known as modes. Mr. Biham and Mr. Knudsen said the flaw appeared in a single mode of the Triple D.E.S. proposal, which is before a subcommittee of the American National Standards Institute. The scientists stressed in an interview that their paper, which also proposes several modifications to strengthen the standard, described only a theoretical weakness and not a practical means of breaking the Triple D.E.S. But they suggested that the weakness was cause for concern. As a result of the distribution of the paper within the subcommittee, it decided to drop the vulnerable mode of the proposed standard, said the chairman, Blake Greenlee. "My hat's off to Eli; he did a nice job," Mr. Greenlee said. The subcommittee that is evaluating the standards is known as X9.F1, and it oversees the development of new cryptographic tools. The subcommittee is now awaiting final approval of its revised standard by the entire committee, he said. Once the committee gives its approval, there is a 60-day public comment period before the new standard takes effect. The Triple D.E.S. is intended to serve as a stopgap measure while the National Institute for Standards and Technology completes work on a still more secure design known as the Advanced Encryption Standard, or A.E.S. Competing proposals for that system, which is intended to protect computer data transmissions well into the next century, will be submitted this summer. The A.E.S. will have key lengths of 128, 192 and 256 bits, as compared with the current 56-bit length of D.E.S., placing it safely beyond the reach of the most powerful computers now anticipated for the future. The original D.E.S. key is a secret number that is used to perform a series of mathematical scrambling operations on a message or on other computer data. When the scrambled message is received, the same secret key is used to reverse the process and unscramble the data. The current D.E.S. is based on research that was originally done at the International Business Machines Corporation's Thomas J. Watson Research Laboratory in the 1970's as part of a project code-named "Lucifer." It was adopted as a national standard in 1977.

title: Biggest Sender Of Junk Mail On Internet Agrees to Stop
body: In a consent decree that represents a turning point in the escalating war against Internet junk email, or "spam," the company most responsible for stuffing millions of email boxes with unsolicited advertisements has agreed to pay $2 million to settle the last of several lawsuits brought against it by Internet service providers. The judgment against Cyber Promotions Inc. in Los Angeles County Superior Court in effect banishes the company from cyberspace at a time when the cottage industry it helped to spawn and vigorously championed is under sustained attack by legislators and computer software engineers alike. Under the terms of the agreement, the chief executive of Cyber Promotions, Sanford Wallace, will be held personally liable for $1 million if he or any company affiliated with him emails unsolicited advertisements to the customers of Earthlink Network Inc., one of the nation's biggest Internet service providers. Mr. Wallace, who once gleefully embraced his Internet nickname "Spamford" and brashly defended his right to flood the Internet with junk mail, also agreed to write a letter of apology to Earthlink subscribers "for any inconvenience" he may have caused. The draft letter, included in court documents distributed on Friday by Earthlink, says that his company's legal battles have "put Cyber out of the spamming business." "The most important benefit of this judgment is the message we've sent to spammers that illegally tap our resources and clog up the Internet with this trash -- we won't stand for it," said Garry Betty, chief executive of Earthlink, which is based in Pasadena, Calif. "On top of that, now they'll pay a very real penalty." Mr. Wallace, who negotiated the settlement himself, could not be reached for comment. Mr. Wallace is far from the only spammer on the Internet. The ability to send millions of email messages for the price of an Internet account has give rise to a whole industry of electronic hawkers. But Mr. Wallace was among the first and was considered particularly pernicious because he developed and sold programs like "Cyber Bomber" that enabled others to follow more easily in his digital footsteps. More recently, he ceased sending spam himself and sought to build a business as a conduit for other spammers who are typically cut off by their Internet providers as soon as their activities are discovered. Earthlink and virtually every other company that sells Internet access have fielded thousands of customer complaints over the last year about unwelcome email clogging mailboxes with material about get-rich-quick schemes and pornographic Web sites. Such advertising is estimated to account for about 10 percent of all email worldwide and is blamed for slowing other traffic over the global computer network. While the Internet companies most affected by the surge in junk mail pursue its purveyors in court, software programmers are developing technical ways to block bulk email and legislators are writing laws that aim to protect consumers from what is sometimes seen as an invasion of privacy. Last week, Washington became the first state to enact an anti-spamming law. The measure makes it illegal for junk emailers to forge return addresses or misrepresent the point of origin of a message, a common tactic used to circumvent the restrictions Internet service providers place on the distribution of bulk email. On Tuesday, California lawmakers will hold the first hearing on a bill that seeks to keep Internet users from receiving unsolicited commercial email. And several anti-spam bills are pending in Congress. Bulk emailers contend that they are simply pursuing a business opportunity, that many email recipients are glad to be informed of their products and that their right to free speech would be violated by such measures. In the Earthlink case, the court prohibited Cyber Promotions from sending junk email to Earthlink customers based on the same anti-trespass laws that prevent somebody from cutting across a front yard. The case was the last of several judgments against Cyber Promotions, which is based in Dresher, Pa., and has been inactive for several months since its Internet provider refused to continue to provide a connection to the network.The ruling makes it unlikely that it will resume operations. "This is the nail in the coffin that put Cyber Promotions out of business," said Pete Wellborn, a lawyer who argued the case for Earthlink. "But Sanford Wallace is very much an entrepreneurial figure. I would not be surprised to see him back on the Internet in one form or another."

title:
USER'S GUIDE;
Interview With the Spammer
body: IF YOU think the junk email clogging your In box is causing you problems, try being the poor spammer. That's the person we should really feel sorry for. At least that is what Patrick Tuminaro Jr. told me on the phone the other day after I finally tracked him down in Lancaster, Calif., to tell him to stop sending junk email that promised to make me rich if I invested $34.95 in an Internet marketing guide. "People who get the email, a lot of them are crazies," Mr. Tuminaro said. "You wouldn't believe it. "There's a guy out there who said he's going to come over here and kill my parents," he said. "This is a legitimate business. We're not breaking the law." Umm, I feel your pain, Mr. Tuminaro, but while we're talking here, could you just take a second to remove my name from your mailing list? "Another thing," Mr. Tuminaro said. "Our company, Alpha Online, we've been in business for six or eight months. "You know how long that is in the bulk-mail industry? The average life is three weeks before they pull the phone lines. But I was up front with my carrier. I went through a lot of trouble." I went through a lot of trouble, too, to hunt down Mr. Tuminaro. But it was worth it because I learned how to fight back. After years of resignedly hitting the delete key on increasing amounts of spam, I must say it feels good to stand tall and proclaim: I do not care how much you send, I will defeat green eggs and spam! Perhaps you would like to join me. Even if you are a passive resister, there are plenty of ways to fight spam without getting in contact with the spammer directly. An informed look at any piece of junk mail will reveal who the spammer's on-line service provider is, enabling you to complain via email. Lots of providers are unaware of the spammers in their midst and are only too happy to squelch them. Here is how to track spam. First, look at the return address at the very top -- in the header -- of the offending message. (For more information on decoding email, see the article above.) On that first line, you will see two pieces of critical information: the domain name of the computer that sent the spam and the computer-specific Internet Protocol number assigned by the nonprofit Internet Assigned Number Authority. In the spam I received from Mr. Tuminaro, for instance, the domain name was given as sparrow.mooncrater.net and the I.P. address was 209.84.113.35. While it is fairly easy to fake the text-based domain name, the I.P. number is usually reliable. That is because your own provider automatically added it to the header after making a note of what computer sent it. "Your I.S.P.'s mail server knows exactly where it came from," said Steve Blighty, a hardware engineer in Boston who is the author of sleuthing software called Sam Spade. Armed with an I.P. number, you can use a number of tools. For Windows 95 and NT users, I recommend Sam Spade, which will perform a number of neat tricks. It is a sophisticated set of tools, so give yourself some time to play around with it (www.blighty.com/products/spade). If you do not have a Windows machine, or if you want an easier place to fight back, you can use a Web version of Sam Spade (www.blighty. com/spam/spade.html). Using Sam Spade, you can find out who owns a domain name. You can learn which provider is responsible for assigning a particular I.P. number and generally find an email address to send complaints to. The software automates the process of selecting and searching through one of the many "whois" servers, whose databases cover specific geographic territories around the world. With Sam Spade, you also can do a "trace route," which will generate a list of all the computers that a piece of spam passed through as it wended its way across the Internet. "A trace route can tell you who's immediately upstream of the spammer, and now you have another place to complain," said Mr. Blighty, who decided to write Sam Spade after he got sick of seeing his favorite Usenet newsgroup overrun by spam. "You start to become knowledgeable about which bits of the Net are likely to be most responsive to complaints," he explained. In the end, I used a more prosaic approach to find Mr. Tuminaro. The spam I received suggested that if I wanted to remove my name from futuremailing lists, I should send a request to a computer at aoci.com. I looked up the computer's registration at www.internic.net/wp/ whois.html and found Mr. Tuminaro's name, address and phone number. He said that he sent out as many as four million pieces of junk email a week on behalf of clients willing to pay as little as $20 for the one-time privilege of piggybacking on top of his superfast, T-1 connection to the Net. "So you're running a spam nest!" I said. "No, I'm a bulk-mail specialist," he replied. Sparrow.mooncrater.net was just one of Mr. Tuminaro's bulk-mail customers. "He's not a client anymore," Mr. Tuminaro said. Why not? I asked. "He's, uh, in transit." But Mr. Tuminaro has plenty of other customers. He said that bulk mail on the Internet was much more cost-effective than paper mail. "I don't have to pay for paper or stamps," he explained. "I just take a list of 150,000 names, and it takes my server about 20 minutes to send it all out." Bulk-mail customers pay as little as $20 to send spam to 20,000 email addresses. "You only have to sell $20 to break even," he said. "You can't beat that." Just watch me. Graphic   Photo (Margaret Riegel)

title: Export Laws Challenged by Sale Of Encryption Software Abroad
body: An American maker of data-scrambling software said today that it would circumvent unitedstates export policies by allowing its Dutch subsidiary to begin selling an international version of Pretty Good Privacy, a strong encryption program that does not provide a back door for law enforcement surveillance. Because the company, Network Associates, is the nation's largest independent maker of computer security software, its action could have a serious effect on unitedstates export policies on software. Network Associates' decision to sell a program specifically prohibited by the Commerce Department comes at a time when the Clinton Administration is already fighting Congressional attempts to end export controls on encryption software for fear that such restrictions will hurt the ability of American industry to compete internationally. "This is the biggest challenge yet to the U.S. policy," Ted Julian, an analyst at the Forrester Group in Cambridge, Mass., said. "It potentially has a tremendous consumer base." The battle over data scrambling -- software that hides everything from love letters to passwords to credit card numbers from prying eyes -- has become a bitter struggle in recent years between the American software industry and privacy advocates on one side and national security and law enforcement officials on the other. The Clinton Administration, in the name of fighting crime and terrorism, has been trying to force the industry to build back doors into encryption software to make it possible for law enforcement officials to secretly decode private messages. Opponents argue that the keys to the proposed back doors could be too easily stolen, compromising not only privacy but also the security of credit card numbers and other highly personal information. The Government does not restrict powerful encryption software domestically but, with very few exceptions, it limits export licenses to codes that can be easily cracked. Earlier this week, Justice Department officials testified before Congress that they had no plans to introduce domestic controls on strong encryption technology. Government officials said yesterday that they had not yet determined whether Network Associates would be violating unitedstates laws in selling P.G.P internationally. "We'll be looking at this very closely," William A. Reinsch, the Under Secretary for export administration, said. "The question of whether or not this product is based on legal or illegal export of U.S. technology is a question to be investigated. If the Government determines that it was illegal, then we'll take appropriate action." In part, that decision will hinge on whether the entire software package was developed independently from the unitedstates company, Mr. Reinsch said. Network Associates executives said that in developing the international version of P.G.P. they took care not to violate unitedstates laws. The international version was developed by Network Associates in Europe in partnership with a small group of cryptographers at Cnlab Software in Switzerland. Network Associates said that the international version would be marketed by its European subsidiary, Networks Associates International B.V., based in the Netherlands. "We're not sure what the impact of this will be," Peter Watkins, general manager of the company's Net Tools Secure Division, said. "This is the first time that a U.S. company has taken this approach, but there are no prohibitions against this." While unitedstates laws restrict the export of strong encryption products, there are no restrictions on exporting the text of the original source code. This loophole allows programmers in other countries to translate the source code into new software programs. P.G.P was written in the early 1990's by a privacy activist and computer programmer, Philip Zimmerman, and was freely distributed in the unitedstates. Mr. Zimmerman also made his source code available internationally in text form. As a result, versions of the program have long been widely available in many countries. Network Associates' executives said they had met with Commerce Department officials earlier this year to explain their plan but the department had not responded. Mr. Reinsch said that his staff had been briefed by the company. Richard Hornstein, vice president of legal affairs for Network Associates, said the Justice Department was notified because "we wanted to make sure they felt comfortable about this, but there was no way the Commerce Department should have a role." Network Associates is not the first unitedstates company to attempt to use an international partnership to circumvent export restrictions. Currently C2net Software Inc., an Oakland, Calif., security software concern, sells an international version of its Web server which has powerful, built-in cryptography. The company said that the international version of the product was developed overseas independently from the unitedstates product. Sun Microsystems has run into Government opposition to a similar project which was based on a cooperative development project with Elvis+, a company formed by scientists from the former Soviet space program.

title:
User's Guide;
Hunting the Elusive Spammer
body: APPARENTLY no one informed the sparrow.mooncrater.net postmaster that there are only two kinds of "personal" email I really like to get: a short note from my literary agent promising to send a check right away or a quick line from my husband announcing his intent to come home early to cook dinner. Try as I might, I just could not fit the junk email I got the other day from sparrow.mooncrater.net into one of those categories: "Subject: A Personal Message . . . Find out the secrets that some of the wealthiest Internet marketers are using to propel their sales through the cyberspace roof." This particular bit of spam went on (and on and on) about how I could become fabulously rich if I were the kind of person willing to pay $34.95 for an Internet marketing guide. But I am not that sort of person. In fact, I would happily settle for a lean-to on the sand in Acapulco and a job selling ice-cream cones to tourists if I never had to endure spam again. Spam is a betrayal of all that mail once stood for. Remember when you were a kid and your mom said there was mail for you, and that meant your favorite aunt had written you a letter and maybe enclosed a pressed violet she had picked from her yard? Now, that was mail. There once was a quiet satisfaction in knowing that someone out there had something personal and interesting to say to you. When I got old enough to read Jane Austen, I discovered that in early-19th-century England, themail carrier came to your house repeatedly in a single day. And he delivered gossipy messages from friends or invitations to dinner at the vicarage. Sealed with wax. Of course, paper mail lost its allure long ago. As an adult, I accepted the fact that most of what the unitedstates Postal Service delivers to me consists of unwanted bills, garbage from my Congressman and glossy catalogues with a vaguely Southwestern theme. I was willing to put up with that when I still had my email to look forward to. But the on-line world has gradually gone dark in the past couple of years as direct mailers have capitalized on the Internet's growing population, clogging all our in boxes. Junk email is worse than junk paper mail for a very simple reason: the recipient bears a portion of the cost. No matter how trivial the charge, there is a philosophical issue here. When spammers complain that attempts to curb their behavior violate their right to free speech, I respond, Say whatever you want, as long as I do not have to pay a single penny for it. For me, it was time to take a stand. Maybe I could just phone a spammer to explain my position? If I told that touching story about my aunt and the dead violet, the postmaster at sparrow.mooncrater.net might have an epiphany about the sanctity of email. Of course, first I had to find the culprit. I tried to reply, but my email bounced. Then I looked up the computer's registration at www.internic. net/wp/whois.html, but the phone number on the form had been disconnected. This task should become easier over the next few months, as the computers that route email over the Internet begin to use new tools to prevent spammers from faking return addresses, available on the latest version of the popular Sendmail mail-delivery program. But in the meantime, the spammers have the upper hand. I figured I needed help from an experienced spam fighter, so I called Matt Korn. As America Online's senior vice president in charge of network operations, he has to sort 26 million email messages a day, culling them for spam. Although spam is a universal problem for on-line services, America Online's huge population has made it a particularly ripe target. In fact, spammers unleash software programs that interrogate AOL's system to collect lists of screen names, Mr. Korn said. Customers can protect themselves by not publishing their names in the member directory. "I recommended, for instance, that my own kids not publish their names in the directory," Mr. Korn said. America Online estimates that on a given day, as much as 30 percent of the email that arrives from the Internet consists of spam -- clogging computers, annoying customers and prompting Mr. Korn to assign an anti-spam team to stanch the flow. "It's my No. 1 challenge," Mr. Korn said. For now, America Online uses software filters to block email that originates from addresses of known spammers and also tells customers how to restrict incoming mail to a list of approved addresses (for help, type keyword junk mail). Doesn't the phrase "restrict incoming mail" say something sad about the state of the Internet? In less than a decade, we have managed to discover the most revolutionary communications medium of the century, populate it, commercialize it -- and rob it of much of its ability to convey useful information. You need not be on America Online to use common sense when confronting spam. Don't be fooled by email that claims you can get your name removed from futuremailing lists by sending a reply message to a specific address. "In general, they actually use this as a validation attempt, to get a new list of email addresses that are active," Mr. Korn said. I knew my attempt to track down the spammer was probably drawing more attention to my own email address. But I could not stop myself. I found out that the address to which one could mail $34.95 belonged to a rent-a-mailbox outfit in Fort Collins, Colo. A woman named Cindy answered the phone there, at Mailboxes Etc., and confirmed that the spammer was a customer. "But I can't give you any more information," she said. "It would violate the customer's privacy." Next: Interview with the spammer.  email address: Slatalla@nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Margaret Riegel)

title: Internet Is Expanding Arms Race With Junk email
body: The Internet's most popular software for routing and delivering email on the Internet is being armed with a powerful set of tools to fight the unsolicited junk electronic mail known as spam, which is increasingly bedeviling cyberspace. The war over spam has pitted computer users, privacy-rights advocates and Internet service providers against companies like Cyber Promotions and Quantum Communications, which fire off millions of advertisements each day in the form of email messages. Not only are most spam messages unwelcome, but their sheer volume -- now estimated to account for about 10 percent of all email worldwide -- frequently clogs the electronic pipes through which all data on the global computer network must pass, slowing the entire system. Now, Sendmail, the electronic post office used on about 75 percent of the computers that route email messages to their proper recipients on the Internet, is being fitted for battle with the spammers. On Tuesday, Sendmail's author, Eric Allman, is to announce the addition of anti-spam tools to version 8.9 of the software as part of his plan to create a company that will continue to develop new features for the free version of the program and sell software and support services to business users. Mr. Allman created Sendmail while he was working as a Unix programmer at the University of California at Berkeley in 1981 and made it freely available to the thousands of administrators and computer researchers who have built and maintain the Internet. In recent years, the program, which has been developed based on the Internet's tradition of cooperation, has been used by spammers to stuff themailboxes of Internet users with messages promoting get-rich-quick schemes, weight-loss plans and advertisements for pornography, among other unwanted come-ons. The new version of Sendmail includes a variety of anti-spam features, including the ability to reject mail from known spam addresses and a mechanism that will force spammers to disclose their real Internet addresses. Today most spammers hide their email addresses to make it more difficult for irate computer users to retaliate. Version 8.9 also offers the ability to check automatically a continuosly changing list of spammer's addresses called the Realtime Blackhole List and to reject messages coming from such addresses before they are stored on themail computer's hard drive. Internet experts said that by arming administrators with these new anti-spam weapons, Mr. Allman's software would make the first serious dent in the rising deluge of junk email. The problem is becoming serious for some of the nation's largest Internet service providers. For example, officials at UUNET, the big Internet provider that is now part of Worldcom Inc., said that at the end of 1998 they had seen their mail volume double, and they estimated that at certain times, as much as 50 percent of that traffic was spam. "It's a real war," said Kyle Jones, a senior systems analyst at UUNET. While he asserted that the systems engineers who maintain the Internet were slowly gaining the upper hand against the spammers, he also said that progress was being made at the expense of the openness and sharing that marked the early days of the Internet. Deploying the new version of Sendmail to Internet service providers will mean that the companies that suffer the burden of unwillingly carrying the most spam will be able to modify their systems to fight back quickly. "Spam is an arms race," Mr. Allman said. "When we get better, they get better." On the other hand, he added, many spammers are using inexpensive, off-the-shelf programs and lack the technical skill to circumvent Sendmail's new spam blockers. Randall Winchester, a computer systems administrator at the University of Maryland at College Park who helped Mr. Allman test the new tools, called them a real big victory. "As more people use this version, it will make a huge difference," Mr. Winchester said. His records show that the new software frequently deflects thousands of email messages an hour from the university's more than 40,000 student email accounts. Mr. Allman said that it generally takes about a year for his entire customer base to adopt each new version of his software. But as major Internet service providers begin to deploy the new technology, he said, it will be increasingly difficult for commercial spammers to avoid detection. Spammers are also under attack in Federal and state legislatures and in the courts, where major Internet service providers like America Online are suing them for harassing customers and stealing resources. On Tuesday, Mr. Allman is to announced plans to start a company, Sendmail Inc., to continue development of both the free version of the program and a new commercial product line. The company, to be based in Emeryville, Calif., has $1.25 million in initial capital from investors including the co-founders of Sun Microsystems, Andreas Bechtolscheim and William Joy. Currently Sendmail's only significant competition is the Microsoft Corporation, which offers a similar program that handles electronic post office functions for corporate computer sites. Microsoft currently has only a 1.3 percent market share, said Greg Olson, Sendmail's chief executive. Graphic   Chart: "Screening for Spam" Programmers and computer system administrators have tried many strategies to automatically filter out spam -- unsolicited junk email -- from other electronic messages. Here are four of the measures that will be built in to the latest version of Sendmail, the delivery program most widely used on Internet servers.  AN END TO PROMISCUOUS RELAY-- Larger servers are usually set up to help smaller servers and individual computers by doing most of the work of routing email for them in a process called relay. Right now most servers will relay for any computer that asks them to, making big computers at major companies and universities unwitting accomplices in spreading spam. The new software will turn down relay requests unless they come from users or servers approved by the system administrator.  MOST-WANTED LIST -- New versions of Sendmail will instruct servers to reject automatically messages sent by sources appearing on a widely circulated list of known spam originators.  REALITY CHECK -- Spammers often put a fictitious return address on their messages, partly to slip past filters like the most wanted listand partly to duck replies. The new version of Sendmail will look up return addresses on an Internet registry and will only deliver mail if the domain name in the return address is registered.  VERIFYING THE SENDER -- Sendmail will also send a short verifying query back to the sending host for every message and wait for an answer before making delivery. This will slow down legitimate email sent in small batches only trivially but may swamp the servers of those who send large batches of mail -- legitimate bulk mailers as well as spammers -- with tens of thousands of queries. The hope is that the cost of the powerful servers needed to cope with such a flood of queries will deter spammers more than legitimate bulk mailers.(pg. D6)

title:
Taking In the Sites;
Tuning Into the Music of Developing Nations
body: Once upon a time, before the Internet had pictures and was all the rage, Quincy Jones, the music impresario, sat with William H. Gates, the computer magnate, at a technology conference, talking about the future. The year was 1992, and the conversation was a melding of the two titans' respective passions: the preservation of musical cultures and the nascent on-line universe that would become cyberspace. It took six years to realize a complete fusion of the vision that emerged that night. On Wednesday, Mr. Jones will introduce Qradio, a venture that marries the Internet to his advocacy of the rich, varied and largely unknown music of developing nations. "Web radio," a technology that transmits audio programming to Internet-connected personal computers, offers the potential to reach a wide audience at a fraction of the cost of traditional broadcasting. "It's a different sort of landscape, a 21st-century language," Mr. Jones said of the Internet. But while his site is devoted to music, unlike broadcast radio, it is not limited to sound. Rather, it is a multimedia product of which actual radio is only a part. Though it is being formally introduced this week, Qradio began in February with an initial focus on South Africa. It offers a data base of South African musicians, including biographies, discographies and sample clips, a multimedia history of musical evolution in the region and continuous feeds of three of the South African Broadcasting Corporation's 16 radio stations. Qradio, which was started with $5 million in private investments, plans to sell advertising, but it hopes to derive revenue from the sale of CD's and audio tapes marketed by means of on-line music samples. Mr. Jones and his partners in the venture say they hope eventually to broaden the site to embrace music from other parts of Africa, as well as from the Americas. Ultimately, it could serve as a medium for breeding new species of music, but for now, Mr. Jones suggests that the goal is to build bridges between cultures and technological classes. "Here we are, entering the next century," he said. "That number with three zeroes behind it is very heavy. It's ironic -- here we are dealing with the Internet and some of these people in South Africa don't have electricity." Adam Clayton Powell 3d, a lifelong friend and former employee of Mr. Jones, said the seed that germinated into Qradio was a 1991 trip that the two of them took to South Africa just as that nation's legacy of apartheid was collapsing. At the time, Mr. Powell said, the two men discussed the feasibility of a cable channel to promote the various indigenous musical cultures of the region, but the costs for such a venture were prohibitive. Even then, Mr. Powell said, the notion of using on-line technologies as a delivery mechanism piqued Mr. Jones's interest. "We have got to come back," to South Africa, Mr. Powell, now the vice president for technology and programs of the Freedom Forum in Arlington, Va., recalls his friend saying. It would take the development of the World Wide Web and the technology known as streaming audio before the possibility of on-line radio transmission would be realized. But the technology alone cannot insure that anyone will be listening, and industry analysts question whether a medium born in the 1920's will ever find an acceptable fit in the medium of the millennium. "To put radio on the Internet is not what it's all about," said Alan Brody, an independent media analyst in Scarsdale, N.Y. "It's like using TV to broadcast shipbuilding information. It's a cute idea but that's not where the future is. The future is in personalizing what we hear on the radio." Mr. Powell disagreed. Now that virtually all new personal computers are equipped with audio capability, more people than ever will use the Web as a platform for radio-like programming. "Radio is the most ubiquitous medium we have," Mr. Powell said. "It's a form familiar to us as a species. We have a long tradition of oral history, and this fits that tradition." What is more, Qradio starts at a time when music is among the few real success stories in the on-line marketing efforts lumped together under the term electronic commerce. At-Plan, a marketing research firm, says its latest data show that CD's and tapes are the fifth- most-popular product sold on the Web, bought by 1.3 million people in the last quarter of 1997 and that more than 12 million people visit music-oriented Web sites in a typical 30-day period. The question with Qradio, as it is with many new on-line ventures, is whether enough visitors will frequent and shop at a niche Web site to make it financially viable. Distinguishing oneself in new media, experts in on-line broadcasting say, demands a delicate balancing act -- a product that is narrowly focused enough that an audience cannot get it elsewhere yet of broad enough appeal to support advertising and direct on-line sales. Many other players in the medium are embracing a more horizontal strategy. The print publishing group Imagine Media of Brisbane, Calif., which specializes in computer-oriented magazines, last week started a new Internet service called Imagine Radio, a group of 20 original radio stations created just for the Web. Audio Net, a Dallas-based company that has been in the streaming audio business for two and a half years, offers 260 radio and television stations from around the country, plus some 400 special events each day. "When you're in your car you've got 30 radio stations," said Audio Net's president, Mark Cuban. "On TV, there are 20 to 100 stations. On the Net, you have millions. That's why the economics of the stand-alone radio doesn't work. It's expensive to be successful. It's really easy to get in the door. It's difficult to make money." Vern Fotheringham, a founding partner of Qradio, said: "The more people who denigrate Internet opportunities, the better I like it. It means there are fewer people out there trying to build fallow content. We're about marrying the capture of content while everyone is looking at it as a substandard, living today but prospering in the future. But after 50 years in the music business, Mr. Jones says that what is most important is encouraging the development of a medium that speaks to people across cultures and economic levels. "It's very important that the urban voice gets in there," he said. "You know -- a PC in every pot."
