title: With Goto.com's Search Engine, the Highest Bidder Shall Be Ranked First
body: In the world of Internet search services, finding just the right business model is proving as elusive as finding an entirely relevant list of search results. But the effort can be seen on the Web sites of all the industry's most familiar names. Yahoo, the biggest of the dozens of sites devoted to navigating the Web, is looking more like a commercial on-line service every day, with "channels" that organize information into categories. Likewise, Excite and Lycos have also added chat rooms, electronic mail and a wide range of original content like news, financial services, shopping and local entertainment guides. And earlier this month, Infoseek announced its entry into electronic commerce, adding travel-booking and home-buying services. "The function of searching has become a commodity," said Alan Braverman, Internet analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston. "So search engine companies are making a transition into Internet media companies." And as they do, consumers are changing the way they use them. Search engines were originally developed to help Internet users find what they were looking for among the millions of pages on the World Wide Web, and as such they were judged solely by how well -- and how quickly -- they matched key words to results. Today, however, searching is only one small reason people go to sites like Yahoo, Lycos, Infoseek and Excite. On Yahoo, for example, only one out of three users goes there to search, said Jerry Yang, co-founder of the company, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif. The rest of the time, they go there to use other Yahoo features like email or chat services or Yahoo Finance, which has become one of the most popular financial sites on the Web. "We certainly are becoming more on-line service-like," he said. "But that doesn't make our navigation service any less important." It does, however, mean visitors to sites like Yahoo and Excite tend to stay longer -- and potentially do more -- than if the site offered only searching. And that has translated into more advertising. Last year, Yahoo was the top ad-supported Web site for the second consecutive year, generating $53.2 million in advertising, according to the Electronic Advertising and Marketplace Report. That is up 180 percent from $19.0 million in 1996. Excite ranked second of all Web sites, generating $40.2 million in advertising in 1997. Despite a huge growth in advertising, profits have been elusive for all but Yahoo and Lycos, which had its first profitable quarter in 1997. Infoseek stumbled as it struggled with management changes, and has since refocused itself toward consumers rather than businesses. Excite lost money last year, though analysts appear bullish on its prospects. But while Yahoo and others are trying to turn their sites into destinations in themselves, an ambitious start-up is taking an entirely different approach. Goto.com, a spinoff of Idealab, a self-described business incubator based in Los Angeles, says it will focus entirely on searching and on making money by encouraging Web sites to pay for more prominent placement in the search results. Rather than ranking search results according to where and how often certain key words appear, as conventional search engines do, Goto.com actually ranks results according to how much sites are willing to pay. The service posts the per-word pricing in an open auction, allowing Web sites to continually bid for higher placement on a given topic. Goto.com then requests that visitors vote on the quality and relevance of search results -- information that is later used to improve future searches. Bill Gross, president of Idealab, said an important difference between his approach and that of other search sites was that Goto.com was not trying to become a media company. "They make money when you stay -- I make money when you leave," Mr. Gross said, comparing his service to the Yellow Pages. "We're changing the alignment of the proposition. We really are a true search engine." By letting a combination of market forces and user feedback determine the results of searches, Goto.com will actually provide better results, he said. "We're not letting a blind algorithm decide," Mr. Gross said. Mr. Gross said the Web had simply become too large for the conventional search approach of matching key words. But, his critics say, a true search engine is exactly what Goto.com is not. Its "pay for placement" approach leads to skewed results, they argue, particularly when the information being sought is not readily available on a commercial site. Yet Mr. Gross insists that nonprofit groups, universities and even medical organizations will find it in their interests to pay for placement. "There's almost always a way that someone will make money by having you come to a site," he said. "Even if it's philanthropic, it wants your attention." And if some sites do not care to pay, they will still appear in the search result -- at the bottom of the list of paid sites. That way, at least, users will know where to find the smallest sites, rather than having them mixed in with larger, typically commercial sites. Perhaps one reason for industry skepticism is that "pay for placement" has already been tested. Two years ago, the Open Text Corporation, then a search service, allowed advertisers to pay for premium placement in search results. But the practice was quickly abandoned when consumers complained. "We got a pretty strong emotional response," said Abe Kleinfield, a vice president at Open Text, based in Waterloo, Ontario. "People thought it was immoral." But the difference in approach is important: Open Text did not tell users that it was allowing companies to pay for higher placement; Goto.com is open about the practice. But regardless of the approach, Goto.com may not succeed simply because it is so late to the market, analysts say. "I wouldn't be bullish on any newcomer," Mr. Braverman said. Success today comes from branding and distribution, and Yahoo and a few others are going to be tough competitors on both counts. "The main reason people go to Yahoo is habit," he said. Rather than embrace new entries, he said, the market is likely to favor more consolidation. Mr. Gross is confident that his strategy will work. "What these guys have is traffic, but they don't have a good business model," he said. title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
A Voice for the Irish
body: No shamrocks or leprechauns here. "Traditional musicians and their year-round fans view St. Patrick's Day in the same jaundiced light that seasoned drinkers see New Year's Eve: it's amateur night," said Don Meade in his column On the Fiddle, a regular feature of a Web site called Irish Voice Online. Music events on "Paddy's Day," he continues, "tend to attract a lot of once-a-year, 'Kiss-me-I'm-Irish' types who can't tell a hornpipe from a gaspipe." Behold Ireland for the Irish (and the Irish in America). Mr. Meade, who is Irish-American, also writes for the Manhattan weekly newspaper Irish Voice. It was founded some 10 years ago as a forum for Irish immigrants, who were flocking, legally and illegally, to the Northeast when Ireland's economy took a nasty spill in the 1980's. A rudimentary version of the paper went up on the Web in summer 1996. The latest site, with many of the articles in the newsstand version, went up last August. "We are still writing for the Irish newly arrived," said Darina Molloy, 27, a former reporter for The Connaught Telepgraph in County mayo who came to newyork in 1994. Besides writing and reporting for the Irish Voice, she also organizes stories for the Web. "But we've also tride to expand the audience to Irish-Americans and to anyone interested in Ireland and Irish affairs," she said. The number of visitors to the site, while still small, is growing quickly. Weekly hits, or page views, are averaging 3,000, up from 800 hits a week last fall. The Irish Voice says the newspaper's circulation is 65,000. WHAT YOU SEE Irish Voice Online covers news about the Republic of Ireland, Northern Ireland and Irish communities in America, especially those in the newyork region. An article on Feb. 11 by Ms. Molloy, for example, reported that recent Irish immigrants were returning to a newyork institution where their numbers had been dwindling: the newyork City Police Department. An article on March 4 bearing the headline " 'I Owe Nothing,' Says gertie Byrne," brings readers up to date on a complex lawsuit pitting two Irishmen in County Mayo against an Irish-American woman in newyork over a festival held at Yonkers Raceway in 1994. OUTSIDE LINKS Scores, including news groups and chat rooms in Scottish Gaelic, Irish Gaelic and Manx, a nearly extinct language spoken on the Isle of Man. WHAT YOU GET A work in progress. Ms. Molloy says the newspaper's first priority is to establish digital archives so more than one issue at a time can be displayed on the Web. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
News on the Web by Time and Saatchi offers a way to change on-line banners instantly.
body: AN innovative effort to make banner ads more closely resemble the constantly changing content of the World Wide Web sites on which they appear -- and thereby increase their appeal -- is scheduled to be introduced today by cyberspace divisions of two media and agency giants. Time Inc. New Media in newyork, part of Time Warner Inc., and its on-line digital marketing agency, Darwin Digital in newyork -- part of the Saatchi & Saatchi Visions unit of Saatchi & Saatchi P.L.C. -- have joined forces to offer what is being called N.O.W., for News on the Web. N.O.W. provides the ability to instantly change the headlines and text of banner ads across all the Web sites on which they are displayed to deliver timely messages. The idea behind those newsy nudges is to take advantage of the immediacy of the Internet and thus heighten the interest of computer users in clicking on the ad banners. While banners are the simplest and most prevalent form of on-line advertising, critics decry their generally static nature, the lengthy lead time usually required to change their content and the frequently low rate of follow-up or "click-through." The anti-banner forces advocate alternatives like email or so-called push technology for sales pitches. "The Web is by nature instantaneous," Hala Makowska, vice president for brand development at Time Inc. New Media, said in an interview last week during which she offered a preview of the changes. "So we thought, 'Why can't we create a banner that lets people know the news instantaneously?' " "We've seen this incredible phenomenon of people turning to the Web when breaking news happens," she added, "such as Princess Diana's death and the stock market's wild fluctuations. This is an opportunity to really deliver the message that we are real-time publishers." Here is how N.O.W. is meant to work. Say someone is using the Internet search engine Yahoo and a banner ad for the Money magazine Web site -- operated by Time Inc. New Media -- pops up. The banner reads: "Money.com. Our archives alone could make you rich." Suddenly, that generic message is displaced by these words, which in an attention-getting device appear at the bottom of the banner, then float to the top: "Money.com News N.O.W. Stock market crashes, falls 500 points." The hope of Time Inc. New Media and Darwin Digital is that only investors with the long-term time frame of a geological era would not find that news bulletin a compelling enough reason to click on the banner and be linked to the Money Web site. "Right now the entire process of advertising on line is very off line," said Daniel Reznick, chief technology officer at Darwin Digital, which developed the N.O.W. banner. Currently, it can typically take four days to two weeks to revise or replace the content of banner ads. "Though we're not saying banners are the answer," he added, "they definitely are a viable sales tool." Darwin Digital is using a customized Java technology -- the programming language of Sun Microsystems Inc. -- to build the N.O.W. banners; Mr. Reznick declined to discuss details because, he said, they were proprietary. The headline delivery service will be operated by editors at each of four Web sites that are to offer the new banners initially; in addition to Money (www.money.com), they are the sites of Fortune (www.fortune.com), People (www.people.com) and Time magazines (www.time.com). Access to those sites is also available through Pathfinder (www.pathfinder.com), the Time Inc. New Media network that includes on-line versions of Entertainment Weekly, Life, Sports Illustrated and Teen People magazines. There are about 22.8 million page views a week for Pathfinder, said Graham Cannon, communications director at Time Inc. New Media. The N.O.W. banners are to appear at first on Pathfinder and on two of the dozen or so Web sites on which Time Inc. New Media advertises through Darwin Digital. Besides Yahoo (www.yahoo.com), the other is the Lycos Internet search engine (www.lycos.com). Time Inc. New Media and Darwin Digital are already "working on a lot of interesting applications for the banners" apart from disseminating news, Mr. Reznick said. For example, "you could have real-time sports scores," he added, "or play-by-play while a game is on." Other potential uses include alerting consumers to limited-time or time-sensitive offers like sales, rebates, coupons and "bogos" (buy one, get one free).

title:
SPENDING IT;
The Newest Phone War
body: CONSUMERS looking for the cheapest long-distance telephone rates need only log onto the Internet, the newest arena of intense competition, where companies are offering special prices from 5 to 10 cents a minute. This week, the AT&T Corporation is expected to start offering its Internet customers long-distance calls at just 9 cents a minute, matching new rates introduced recently by MCI Communications. Both giants are scrambling to respond to the initiative of a little player that had a big idea: Tel-Save Holdings, a long-distance provider in New Hope, Pa., that caters primarily to small and medium-sized businesses. Since Dec. 18, it has contracted with America Online to offer the 9-cent-a-minute rate to the on-line service's 11 million subscribers. With promotions on its main screen and in full-page newspaper ads, America Online has signed up almost 400,000 customers so far, and expects to have a million by the end of June. Many industry experts call such programs the start of a revolution that will lower all long-distance rates, a result of making a connection in consumers' minds between the Internet and phone service. Eventually, the experts say, the Internet will become a major transmission vehicle for the calls themselves and the line will blur between telephone and Internet. "It's going to change the industry," said Jeffrey Kagan, a telecommunications consultant and author of "Winning Communications Strategies" (Aegis Publishing Group). The new rates are just the beginning, he said, adding, "The question is: How low can they go?" A long-distance company can offer a lower rate to Internet customers because the company saves money. The customers enter their own billing data when they sign up, and in most cases must pay with a credit card, receiving their bills through their computers. For the companies, that means no paper bills and no postage costs, while the reliance on credit cards also reduces the companies' exposure to bad debt. Not all the long-distance carriers are joining the Internet price war. The Sprint Corporation, which offered the first 10-cent-a-minute plan, does not offer Internet customers a better rate. "We think it's restrictive to say one kind of customer can get one kind of rate and another customer can get another kind of rate," said Robin Pence, a spokeswoman for Sprint. She also criticized the Internet-based marketing plans because they usually provide customer service only on line. Still, many telecommunications executives and analysts say that this is only the beginning of a shift toward new kinds of communication via the Internet. The current Internet plans offer new rates for long-distance calls carried by traditional phone lines, but AT&T plans to start a cheaper service in May that will carry long-distance calls over an Internet-style network. That service, called AT&T World Net Voice, will start in three cities, still to be announced, and expand to 16 by the end of the year. AT&T will charge 7.5 to 9 cents a minute for calls using Internet protocol. Internet protocol, or Internet telephony, as it is also known, uses a regular phone. But a separate transmission switch digitizes and compresses the caller's voice into packets of data that are moved through the Internet and reassembled at the phone on the other end. "From AT&T's point of view, Internet protocol is critical to our future success and growth," said Daniel H. Schulman, a vice president at AT&T's World Net Service. "In fact, we think the Internet protocol is to the communications industry what the personal computer was to the computing industry; it's that fundamental a change." The technology, though, which is just two years old, is still slow and cumbersome. Many people who use Internet protocol for long-distance calls report frustrating time lags between the speaker and the listener. AT&T says it has reduced the delays, but callers must still dial a local access number, wait for a prompt, enter an authorization code and then dial the number they want. But with improvements in quality in the next five years, the Internet telephony business is expected to grow from less than $1 billion a year today to $24 billion -- about 17 percent of the projected unitedstates long-distance market, according to the International Data Corporation. About 25 million American homes are connected to the Internet. And their occupants tend to be more affluent and make more long-distance calls. In a survey last year, International Data found that in homes with a personal computer connected to the Internet, the average respondent was 41 years old, had a household income of $70,400 a year and spent an average of $58 a month on long-distance calls. Among households without a computer, the average respondent was 47 years old, had a household income of $38,700 and spent an average of $30.50 a month on long-distance calls. While it may make good business sense for long-distance carriers to focus on the most profitable market segment, some consumer advocates are not impressed. "What we've constantly seen here is benefits for volume users at the high end of the market, while rates have actually risen for consumers at the low end of the market, unless government has intervened to put a lid on rates, or forced them down," said Gene Kimmelman, co-director for Consumers Union. But Mr. Kagan, the telecommunications consultant, predicted that as Internet telephony improved, it would push down all long-distance rates. "Within a year's time, we're going to see traditional long distance down to the 5-cent mark," he said. As the long-distance industry changes, the line separating telephone and Internet services may start to break down. Customers might buy telephones with a screen, for example, and dial into the Internet to place a call. Long-distance companies may start focusing on other, more profitable businesses, like cellular phone service, pagers, call forwarding and electronic mail. "Long-distance companies will still make plenty of money, but they will make it from these higher-margin services," Mr. Kagan said. title:
Business Travel;
A Web site allows travelers to create an interactive guide based on data from Fodor's.
body: REVIEW TRAVEL INC., whose World Wide Web site has traditionally focused on vacationers, is now wooing business travelers. It is currently the only business travel Web site that allows users to create an interactive guide to destinations based on data from Fodor's Travel Publications' Gold Guide series of books. The Preview site (www.previewtravel.com) is aiming its Business Travel Center at owners of small businesses in a move it hopes will ultimately generate more bookings. Owners of small businesses and people with home offices currently account for 30 percent of the site's almost three million registered users, while the rest are leisure travelers. The Business Travel Center has a news wire that carries a constant stream of information on travel specials. The center also allows users to select hotels and restaurants based on Fodor's data, as well as personal criteria. Users can then create their own mini-guides to any of 87 different destinations covered by the Fodor's data; these guides can then be printed and taken along. Preview also can book air, hotel or car rental reservations. According to Ron Pernick, a Preview spokesman, the site can sell the special rates featured on the travel news wire, based on availability, as well as other deals Preview arranges with travel suppliers. In recent months, Preview has promoted special discounts from AMR's American Airlines, Continental Airlines, Hilton Hotels, Republic Industries' Alamo Rent-A-Car and Avis Rent-A-Car, among others. Preview, which went public last November, operates a ticketing service for America Online, which has held a minority stake in Preview since 1995. The company has no current plans to operate its Business Travel Center on America Online, Mr. Pernick said. Preview had sales of $80.4 million last year, up from $20.3 million in 1996.  Regency Renovation The Regency Hotel in newyork, the flagship property of Loews Hotels, is undergoing a $25 million renovation, its first in 10 years. The hotel's restaurant and all guest rooms are being redecorated, using deep-toned silk and velvet fabrics, mahogany and leather. Six new one-bedroom suites, each with two full bathrooms, will be created from 12 smaller guest rooms, bringing the total number of suites up to 91. Work on the hotel -- on Park Avenue at 61st Street -- is scheduled to be completed by mid-October.  Survival Guide June Langhoff, a freelance writer from Pacifica, Calif., who specializes in high-tech issues, is the author of a new book, "The Business Traveler's Survival Guide" (Aegis Publishing Group, Newport, R.I., $9.95). Designed to take some of the mystique out of getting connected on the road, the book is full of handy tips on tools (wired and wireless) for travelers, on working abroad, and on keeping equipment secure. There are also some real-life business travel horror stories -- such as the lawyer who was charged $300 to receive a 60-page fax at a newyork hotel.

title: Threat to Corporate Computers Is Often the Enemy Within
body: The computer supervisor at a Midwestern engine manufacturing company approached his bosses earlier this month and made them an offer they could not refuse. Either they gave him a big raise immediately and agreed to a list of other job demands, or he would shut the company down, according to Erik Thompson, a computer security consultant who was called in to help the company after the incident. The employee, Mr. Thompson said, got his raise, and yet another company discovered what thousands of businesses have learned the hard way in recent years: Despite justifiable fears about rogue programmers attacking an organization's information systems over the Internet, the greatest threat to a company's data security probably works just down the hall. "Nobody wants to think that the guy I work with may be a bad guy, my worst nightmare," said Charisse Castagnoli of Internet Security Services Inc., a consulting company that is based in Atlanta. "If you look at the statistics, though, about 70 percent to 80 percent of security breaches are internal." According to an informal survey conducted by the Computer Security Institute, an association of corporate data security officers, for the Federal Bureau of Investigation's International Computer Crime Squad, computer attacks by insiders were more common last year than external Internet-based attacks. More than 87 percent of the corporate, financial, government and university information security managers polled by the survey said disgruntled employees were the most likely cause of data security incidents, ranging from sabotage, fraud and theft of proprietary information to unauthorized snooping in a colleague's email or the storing of digital pornography on a company computer. Several different dynamics are increasing the risk of insider fraud or sabotage, security officials said. Companies increasingly are relying on outside contractors for technical work, and giving those outsiders insider privileges, in part because of a shortage of programmers made worse by the work needed to fix year 2000 programming flaws. "The Y2K problem is causing a lack of programmers, and people are hiring anybody," said Michael Zboray, a vice president at the Gartner Group in Stamford, Conn., using the industry's acronym for the year 2000 problem. "Companies are now doing Y2K development offshore," he said, "sending work to Russia and India, and they haven't a clue as to what's coming back. They don't do background checks. What we're hearing is an undercurrent of back doors being programmed in." According to the Computer Security Institute, companies employ on average one computer security administrator for every 1,000 users of the computer system. The budget for computer security, traditionally 1 percent to 3 percent of the total information technology budgets for many corporations, is expected to rise to 3 percent to 5 percent this year, the institute said. But, as with the case of the automotive engine manufacturer, most companies are fearful of adverse publicity and never report internal security breaches, even the most severe ones, to law enforcement agencies, security analysts contend. "Most firms would rather go public with the news that their chief executive officer was an active alcoholic than the news that there was an insider security problem," said William J. Malik, a vice president and research director for the Gartner Group. One notable exception occurred earlier this month when a former computer network administrator for a Government subcontractor was arraigned in Federal court in New Jersey, charged with having destroyed critical company data in 1996 using a software "logic bomb" that detonated three weeks after he was dismissed from his job. The logic bomb erased all of the engineering programs and files at Omega Engineering Inc. of Bridgeport, N.J. Backup tapes were stolen as well, and losses from the sabotage could eventually cost the company more than $10 million, unitedstates Secret Service investigators said. Speaking to a data security conference last month, Dan Nielsen, a special agent with the F.B.I.'s newly renamed National Infrastructure Protection Agency, said insider attacks are rarely reported, and thus the agency has no reliable estimate of the losses sustained. But the tally for the relatively few attacks that were reported in 1996 was $100 million, according to the Computer Security Institute/F.B.I. survey. Early responses from the 1997 year-end survey indicate a 30 percent rise in reported losses in the last 12 months, said Richard Power, president of the Computer Security Institute. And it appears that the percentage of companies reporting computer security incidents in 1997 will also rise sharply, to more than 60 percent, he said. Half of the 563 information security professionals responding to the 1996 survey said their organizations had sustained the unauthorized use of systems last year, and among those, insider attacks were reported to be more common than external attacks. The 249 organizations that were able to quantify the losses from all computer attacks reported losses totaling $100 million. The Computer Security Institute is now compiling results from the 1997 survey. Instead of going to the legal authorities, victims of inside attacks typically go to the technical authorities. There is a growing industry of computer security consultants and disaster recovery experts. Mr. Thompson, the computer security consultant who was called in last week to help rescue the engine manufacturer, said of the employee: "He was the only one who could run the software that made the manufacturing hardware work. They couldn't fire him, because firing him shuts down the assembly line, and by the time they get someone else in there to replace him they are out of business." Legends abound in the computer world about programmers and system administrators who booby-trap the systems they create, using such potential software weapons as logic bombs, back doors and encryption as leverage in case they are dismissed or not paid. "It's very common," Mr. Thompson said. "We deal with three or four cases of disgruntled employees a day, typically encrypted files. Word processing files, spreadsheets, accounting, payroll, engineering diagrams, it depends on what's critical to the business." Encryption, formerly the province of military and government spies, has now become a tool embedded into standard commercial software. It allows files to be scrambled so that only the person with the proper password can unlock and read the file. It is common for employees to encrypt a file and forget the password, but some employees encrypt files for malicious reasons. "Lawyers are the worst," Mr. Thompson added, saying that they were prone to anger their secretaries. "The secretary is the one who runs the business. She encrypts the case files, and says, 'To hell with you, I'm not going to give you the passwords.' The lawyer has to be in court the next day. It happens several times a week." If a disgruntled employee is a potential nightmare, the mother of all nightmares is a disgruntled system administrator, or sysad. The sysad typically has access not only to sensitive company files, but also to the security systems that guard them from unauthorized users within and outside the company. "The most powerful person in your company is the sysad," said Peter Shipley of Berkeley, Calif., one of the country's top computer security experts. But he said that the system administrators are often underpaid and underappreciated. "The attitude is, if things are working flawlessly, you're obviously not doing any work, and if things are failing, obviously you're not doing your job. Unfortunately that's the way it works," Mr. Shipley said. To be sure, tens of thousands of system administrators around the country have a reverential attitude toward protecting the data in their care, and so far only a relative handful have used their power to intimidate or gain revenge on a company. But security analysts say any organization that gives one person control over critical "choke points," like computer networks, is making a grave mistake. Katherine Fithen, manager of operations for the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT), a quasi-governmental agency in Pittsburgh that is responsible for tracking and responding to security violations at networked computer sites, said her group seldom hears from companies whose systems have been attacked from within. But, she added, CERT has received several queries recently from companies that were about to dismiss their system administrators, asking how they can protect themselves, just in case. "The sysadmin knows the inside of the system, knows how the networks are configured, how the trust mechanisms between machines work, and they have the best understanding of how to do damage," she said. Last year, companies in the unitedstates spent hundreds of millions of dollars buying and installing network security tools, including network firewalls, which are combinations of computer hardware and software intended to keep unauthorized visitors from penetrating a company's internal network and gaining access to sensitive information. But if the attacker already has authorization, Mr. Shipley noted, even perfectly functioning firewalls can fail to protect a system. Companies that install the computer equivalent of thick steel doors to keep out intruders may have only screen doors internally, he said. And programmers often know how to tunnel through the firewall, creating fictitious user accounts, or leaving open a "back door" into the system to allow outside access. "It starts innocently enough," said Ms. Castagnoli of Internet Security. "You're going to work from home, you're an administrator, you need remote access. Where it goes over the line is when people start putting in protections for themselves, to cover their tracks. Then there's the what-if scenario: 'If something happens to me, I'm going to get back at them.' Now we're in the category of revenge." "There was a relatively recent case on Wall Street, where a sysad at one of the financial houses was fired," she said. "He had remote home access, and came back in from home and deleted a number of sensitive files." And last month, the complete payroll data base of Pixar Inc., a computer firm best known for its work in creating special effects for movies, was distributed to all employees via an email message purportedly sent by the company's chairman, Steve Jobs. Mr. Jobs denied sending the list, and company officials said they suspected that a disgruntled employee was responsible. Last April, a temporary employee from Queens was charged with breaking into the computer system of Forbes Inc., the publisher of Forbes magazine, and causing a system crash that left hundreds of employees unable to use their computers and cost the company more than $100,000. While incidents of both internal and external computer crimes are on the rise, some see a positive sign in the fact that more cases of computer attacks are being reported. "The growing acceptance that there is a widespread problem has probably led other people to go ahead and admit to incidents," Mr. Power of the Computer Security Institute said. And the F.B.I. said more companies are coming forward to share information about internal security problems.

title:
INVESTING IT;
On-Line Trade Fees Falling Off the Screen
body: THERE is no end in sight to the price war among on-line discount brokers. The average commission for the 10 leading on-line brokerage firms had dropped from nearly $53 in early 1996 to about $32 in the middle of last year -- about a 40 percent decline. But by late 1997 it had tumbled further, to about $16, according to researchers at Piper Jaffray. Some brokers have even pushed on-line commissions into the single digits; Ameritrade and Suretrade, for example, have a basic rate of about $8. So, jittery investors may ask: Are these prices as good as they seem? Is the execution good? Are there hidden costs? Interviews with experts -- including those who say they look out for the average investor -- indicate that these offers are, for the most part, a very good deal. "This is only benefiting the individual investor," said Andre Scheluchin, an editor of the Discount Brokerage Survey, published by Mercer Inc. in newyork. "If an individual investor is trying to save some money, on-line trading is where to do it." One reason for those savings stems from a shift in a basic industry pattern. Since the mid-90's, many discount brokers have moved to flat fees from a system in which prices varied by transaction size. This change means the new bargain-basement commissions apply to many investors and many trades. Another plus: there are not many special or hidden charges. "The prices you see quoted are the prices you get," said Bill Burnham, an analyst who covers the on-line brokerage industry for Piper Jaffray. And even when there are special charges, only rarely do the total commissions leap far above the advertised offer. For instance, Ameritrade, like many other on-line discounters, offers its $8 deal for "market" trades -- those executed at whatever the current market price is. The company charges more for "limit" orders, in which the investor sets a ceiling or floor on the price he will accept. But even with the extra fee, a limit order costs only about $13 at Ameritrade. A new on-line survey by the American Association of Individual Investors, based in Chicago, found that people were pleased with the quality of on-line trades, too. Less than 5 percent of the 350 people surveyed were dissatisfied with the price they received or the speed of the execution. Of course, "You're not going to get hand-holding or proprietary research" from the discounters, Mr. Burnham said. But, price war or no price war, the industry has never been known for such services; they have mostly been the province of full-service brokers. (Nevertheless, a growing number of on-line brokers are offering lots of tools for the do-it-yourself investor, from news to real-time stock quotations to 24-hour access to trading information. Even sophisticated research tools, like stock charts and earnings reports, are available.) The Internet's capacity as an efficient trading mechanism has made it the center of discounters' price rivalry. In 1996, there were about 20 on-line brokerage firms, according to Computerized Investing, a publication of the investors' association. But the count has risen to 52 this year and further intensified the price competition, particularly given the bull market and the growing use of the Internet. Indeed, there were close to three million on-line brokerage accounts in 1997, according to Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. And the company's analysts expect that number to top 14 million by 2002. Despite the galloping popularity of on-line trading, falling prices have raised some concerns. When the stock market plunged in October, for example, a number of on-line outfits had trouble executing trades and handling the flood of calls and activity. While the companies and several analysts say that many of those problems have been fixed, investors may still worry -- particularly since the new bare-bones prices and pell-mell growth may not give all these brokerage firms big financial cushions or support staffs. "At some new firms, applications are being lost, and people are not picking up the phones," said Alex Stein, a principal at Gomez Advisors, which tracks on-line investing. "If you're charging $7 a trade, you might not be staffing your customer service." And investors should realize that the new low prices, although of wide reach, do not apply to all trades. For example, Schwab Online, which charges $29.95 for on-line trades, charges $144 for non-Internet ones. There are other restrictions on these bargain prices. While E-Trade charges a flat rate of $14.95, for example, there is an extra $5 due if the stocks to be bought or sold trade on Nasdaq. And DLJ Direct, which charges $20 a trade for the first 1,000 shares, adds an extra fee of 3 cents for every share thereafter, up to 5,000 shares. Moreover, while most analysts and advisers applaud the drop in trading costs, some worry that it may lead individual investors to discard the standard long-term "buy and hold" strategy in favor of a riskier, active-trading approach. "Now, for just $8, you say, 'Well, if I'm wrong, I'll just buy it back,' " said David L. Brown, chief executive of Telescan, which offers on-line resources to investors. "There's probably that tendency to jump in and jump out because it's so cheap." (Source: Piper Jaffray Equity Research)

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
For Daisy Fuentes Fans and 'PR Food' Lovers
body: There are about 29 million Hispanic Americans, and surveys show that more than 80 percent of Hispanic American adults have access to computers at home or at work. But while few Web sites cater to this audience, the goal of Latina Magazine Online is to establish an on-line community for everyone interested in Latino culture. Christy Haubegger, the founder and publisher of Latina, a magazine for Hispanic American women that is based in newyork, said the Web site, like the magazine, is intended for Americans as opposed to recent immigrants, who tend to be more interested in the music and pop culture of Latin America. "We're more likely to cover Daisy Fuentes," a former MTV host, "than we are Thalia," a leading singer and soap-opera star in Mexico, Ms. Haubegger, 29, said. The editors of Latina are experimenting with the site, which was started in May 1997. With the help of newyork Online, a Brooklyn-based Web site designer that specializes in sites aimed at black and Hispanic people, a new version of Latina Magazine Online is set to appear this Friday, the third version in nine months. The current version, with little promotion, has attracted 40,000 to 70,000 hits, or page views, a week.  WHAT YOU SEE -- The current version of the site, begun in August, has a search engine for Latino-related Web sites as well as message boards, which the last version did not have. Ms. Haubegger said Latina Magazine Online was trying to reach viewers who may not be interested in the print magazine. "A lot of men may not be comfortable reading this on the bus," said Ms. Haubegger, holding up the March issue with headlines like "Fashions for el y ella." But, she said, men may read the message board. Some messages posted on the board are poignant. On Jan. 29 someone named "Xernna" wrote: "I am of Puerto Rican as well as Cherokee descent and because of this, I have been rejected by the Spanish communities in my area. I want to know if anyone has experienced anything similar." (Three people replied.) Other postings are heartfelt in a different way. "STcinnamon" asked on Jan. 17, "Does anyone know of a Puerto Rican community or restaurant in either Houston or Dallas? I'm craving PR food!" The revamped Web site will feature articles especially for the on-line magazine, said Alejandro Santandrea, 23, Latina's Web site coordinator. Not only will there be gossip and entertainment items about Latina entertainers like Jennifer Lopez, but also news briefs on issues of interest to Hispanic people. Performers and other artists may also be brought in for scheduled "live chats," an extension of one of Latina magazine's most popular features "El Papi Chulo," a look at favorite male stars. The Spanish phrase "translates, sort of, to 'the cutest mack daddy,' " Ms.Haubegger said.  LINKS -- Some, mainly those contained in archived articles.  WHAT YOU GET -- A work in progress for a group just beginning to find its way onto the Web.  Latina Magazine Online http://www.latina.com/ Graphic   Photo

title: Bloomberg to Supply AOL With On-Line Business Data
body: Bloomberg L.P. will announce today that it has signed on as America Online's featured provider of business information, giving another vote of confidence to on-line consumer markets that have yet to show a profit. The position at America Online was vacated at year's end by Dow Jones after a contract dispute. In a sign of how on-line business strategies are changing, America Online paid Dow Jones for its business information; Bloomberg is reportedly paying America Online an undisclosed sum to be a featured part of the on-line service, which claims 11 million subscribers and is based in Dulles, Va. Financial news and information will begin appearing on America Online later this week. Terms of the partnership were not disclosed, but America Online typically charges millions of dollars for "anchor tenancies," deals that feature news or entertainment services on its opening screen. For example, Intuit, a maker of tax and financial software, paid America Online $16 million up front this month and is guaranteeing a total of $30 million over the next three years for an anchor tenancy. "A few years ago, you wouldn't think of Bloomberg content as something that would appeal to the kind of market we have," Barry Schuler, America Online's president of interactive services, said. Today, however, the market for personal finance information is booming. America Online reports that its users look up 60 million stock quotes each day and track six million portfolios, a growth of 70 percent in the last year. In addition, America Online's position as the largest Internet service provider -- it delivers an estimated 56 percent of all Internet users -- proved irresistible to Bloomberg, which is looking to broaden its consumer reach. "The bottom line is there's a large interest in financial and business news," said Michael Bloomberg, the former Salomon Brothers trader who parlayed a $10 million buyout in 1981 into the upstart financial news business that bears his name. It now employs 700 reporters in 80 bureaus worldwide and includes a news service, radio and television networks and book publishing. Its core business, however, remains the Bloomberg terminal, a proprietary news box that delivers immediate stock quotations and analysis to the desks of 90,000 financial professionals who pay $1,200 a month. Of the $1.3 billion in reported revenue for the privately held company, 99 percent comes from the terminal service, a spokeswoman said. Mr. Bloomberg said the America Online deal would not "cannibalize" the professional part of his business, because it would not include the analysis and deep financial data available to terminal subscribers. Despite a dearth of revenue in the consumer portion of his business, Mr. Bloomberg has continued to make deals to provide on-line news and information. In the last six weeks alone, he has announced agreements with CNet, an Internet news service, and its fledgling on-line service, Snap; with the Women's Wire service on the World Wide Web, and with the cable-modem Internet service At-Home. Bloomberg's two-year-old Web site says it delivers 17 million page views a month. "We think it will be lucrative for us," he said, "because if we can deliver for advertisers the eyeballs and minds that they're trying to have pay attention to their message, AOL will make some money and the customers will be well served." In a report to be released tomorrow, the on-line analysis group At-Plan says that its survey of 40,000 Internet users in the last quarter of 1997 showed 12.1 million were actively using on-line finance sites. The survey also showed that sales of stocks and mutual funds on line grew 291 percent in the last nine months. "This is the future of investing," said Mark Wright, the chief executive of At-Plan, which is based in Stamford, Conn. "A vast new industry is being created overnight. If you look at the profile of the typical user, you can see why the Bloombergs of the world have such great interest.  Our research found that 8.4 million Internet users have self-directed portfolios of over $100,000." Bloomberg is not the only provider of professional financial information that is gambling on the consumer market. Edgar Online, for example, provides Securities and Exchange Commission filings on its Web site and to a variety of other Web resources, including Yahoo. "It's an interesting bridge between two very different organizations," said an Edgar spokesman, Jay Sears. "It shows the incredible demand for financial information from a mass market that didn't exist until a few years ago. Bloomberg is high end, and on the other end, there's AOL. It's a very interesting match. It'll be interesting to see how they do. The devil's in the details."

title: America Online Settlement Cleared
body: A judge in Chicago approved a settlement today in a class-action lawsuit filed by subscribers who had trouble signing on to America Online Inc. last year. The lawsuit was filed after the company, based in Dulles, Va., was besieged by complaints from subscribers who found they had trouble linking to the company's network after it switched to a flat monthly fee in late 1996, leading to a surge in use. The settlement provides refunds based on the plan a subscriber used and the amount of time spent using the network. Judge Stephen Schiller of Cook County Circuit Court approved the settlement. In a 10-page opinion, Judge Schiller wrote that as of November, America Online had testified that it had received 128,479 claims related to the proposed settlement and only 250 objections. Some lawyers had argued the that accord would benefit only a small number of the estimated eight million class members. Judge Schiller said in his ruling that the plaintiffs might have had trouble proving damages because the average America Online subscriber increased usage to 14 hours a month from seven hours after the change in pricing and the company had informed subscribers about an expected surge in demand for access to the service. The company has not specified the cost of resolving the nationwide class action, though it did say last April that it thought a $24 million charge it took against earnings would cover refunds and credits for all subscribers. America Online previously reached an agreement of voluntary compliance with 45 state attorneys general in the matter. That agreement was incorporated in the court settlement.

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
For Children, an Olympic Computer Event
body: When Elina Teplinsky, an 11th grader at Polytechnic Preparatory Country Day School in Brooklyn, watched the opening ceremonies of the Winter Olympics last week, she noticed an odd detail. Instead of releasing doves near the Olympic torches, as is the tradition, the International Olympic Committee released biodegradable, dove-shaped balloons. Her curiosity piqued, Miss Teplinsky, a 16-year-old resident of Bensonhurst, did some research and shared her findings on the Internet. "The balloon dove idea came to life for reasons of safety and in deference to animal lovers," she wrote, "after some doves were roasted to death by the Olympic flames" during the Seoul games of 1988. As part of a school project devised by Poly Prep, which is in Bay Ridge, and Alfred Doyle, the head of the school's computer department who also works with the Public Broadcasting Service, Poly Prep students are filing stories about the Winter Olympics in Nagano, Japan until its close on Feb. 22. They are also editing similar contributions by students from around the nation and the world. The stories are displayed, with the help of WNET-TV in newyork, on "Cyber School," a PBS Web site. Unlike similar sites, like that of Scholastic magazine, Poly Prep is perhaps the only site put together by students and teachers themselves.  WHAT YOU SEE -- The commentary ranges from the surprisingly polished to the unrestrained. Eric Shoikhetman, a 16-year-old 10th grader at Poly Prep, wrote that one of the odd consequences of the Olympic hockey competition is that teammates from National Hockey League clubs who will represent their respective countries will end up on opposing teams. "For example," he wrote, "instead of the Rangers' Wayne Gretzky passing the puck to Brian Leetch in the slot for a power play goal, the Great One will have to maneuver his way around Leetch in his attempts to score." Students in Japan were surprisingly blunt. Tomoaki N, a 16-year-old student from Hyougo, wrote: "I was surprised to watch the opening ceremony. Because it reminds us of old Japanese culture, which we can seldom find these days. However, in fact not many Japanese people are interested in this Olympic. I think we ought to be proud of this festival in Japan." title: America Online to Raise Fee For Unlimited Use to $21.95
body: In a major defection from the standard monthly price of $19.95 for Internet access, America Online, whose 11 million members make up more than half the home Internet market in the unitedstates, announced yesterday that it was increasing its charge for unlimited access to $21.95. America Online introduced its $19.95 flat-rate plan at the end of 1996. It announced its new pricing at the same time that it disclosed a broad management reorganization that elevated Robert W. Pittman, currently the president of America Online's network division, to the newly created position of president and chief operation officer of the entire company. In a separate announcement, the company said it was laying off half the remaining employees of Compuserve, the onetime rival that it purchased last week. Mr. Pittman, the founder of MTV, joined America Online in 1996 and was widely credited with curing the busy signals that had earned the service the nickname America Onhold and with increasing the company's profitability. America Online's shares surged $11.9375 yesterday to an all-time high of $110.4375 on the announcement. It is scheduled to release its earnings after the market's close today. "The Internet industry needs to raise prices," said Michael Parekh, an analyst at Goldman, Sachs. "None of the 4,000 Internet service providers that want to grow their subscriber base can make money at $19.95." Stephen M. Case, America Online's chairman, said the price increase was not expected to add to the company's profits this year. "The primary reason is to absorb higher network costs and to fund innovations like new content," he said of the price increase. International Business Machines recently replaced the unlimited pricing plan for its Global Network service with 100 hours a month for $19.95 and an additional fee for more time on line. Telephone companies, on the other hand, have been lowering prices. Bell Atlantic is offering unlimited Internet access at $17.95 a month, and MCI Communications recently dropped its rate to $14.95 a month. Mr. Pittman said yesterday in a telephone interview that the price increase might slow the company's rapid growth by prompting some customers to cancel their memberships. But he predicted that it would be "a one-time blip" and that "we will go right back to the growth curve, albeit more slowly." Customers, he said, would still be willing to pay extra for America Online's content, service and reputation. America Online also offers a plan that costs $4.95 a month for the first three hours and $2.50 an hour after that. Three-quarters of its customers, however, are on the unlimited plan. The company announced that it would lay off 500 of the 1,000 employees of Compuserve, mostly from customer service, which will be contracted to outside companies. In addition, the company said it would halt development of a planned new service that would have offered Compuserve's on-line forums on a wide range of topics to users of the Internet's World Wide Web. Instead, America Online said it would concentrate on improving the main service, which has more than two million paying customers. As for the appointment of Mr. Pittman as the No. 2 executive in the company, Paul W. Noglows, an analyst with Hambrecht and Quist, said: "This is a real positive for AOL. He has the energy to build the AOL brand going forward." As expected, the heretofore independent America Online Studios division run by Ted Leonsis, who was once America Online's president, will be folded into Mr. Pittman's oversight, and its advertising and marketing functions will be combined with a unified, companywide sales operation.

title: U.S. Losing Battle on Control Of Data Encryption, Study Says
body: The Clinton Administration is losing its battle to increase international controls over how reliably computer data can be scrambled to insure privacy, according to a report scheduled to be released Monday by an independent research group. The Administration has been lobbying members of the European Union and other industrialized nations to back its efforts to place controls on "strong encryption," a technology for scrambling data so effectively that the code cannot be broken and the content cannot be deciphered without a digital key. Data encrypting is used increasingly to protect the privacy of financial transactions, medical records and business communications. The Administration wants the ability to descramble all encrypted messages to keep tabs on criminals. In a report scheduled to be released Monday, the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a Washington-based research group, says that its survey of 243 governments showed that the unitedstates is virtually the only democratic, industrialized nation seeking domestic regulation of strong encryption. That finding directly contradicts the Clinton Administration's assertion in Congressional hearings that it has the support of most nations on this issue. David Sobel, who directed the study by the research group for the Global Internet Liberty Campaign, a civil liberties advocacy group, said of the Administration: "They make the claim that other countries are accepting the U.S. position on this, then in an attempt to make that a reality, our Government launched a worldwide lobbying campaign on encryption policy." William A. Reinsch, the Under Secretary for export administration in the unitedstates Commerce Department, denied that the study contradicted the Administration's assertions. "All the Administration has ever said is that there are more countries that go farther than we do," Mr. Reinsch said. "The study confirms that."

title: A Reorganization Is Expected at America Online
body: Just a year and half after creating a division to nurture on-line programming, America Online is preparing to dismantle the unit in a management reorganization that would shift both the company's focus and executive power, people close to the company said yesterday. The reorganization, which is expected to be announced next week, would consolidate the power of Robert W. Pittman, who runs the company's other main division, AOL Networks, which operated the company's core on-line services. He would also oversee the development of new on-line content, an area that is now overseen by the president of the AOL Studios division, Ted Leonsis. Mr. Pittman, the founder of the MTV cable network, is widely credited with giving discipline to the on-line service, improving its customer service and focusing it more on the bottom line. An America Online spokeswoman said yesterday that the company would not confirm the reorganization. The changes would represent a sharp about-face for America Online, which in recent weeks had been negotiating to sell a controlling interest in AOL Studios to Bertelsmann A.G., the German media conglomerate, and Madison Dearborn Partners, a Chicago venture capital firm, for $200 million. The sale would have removed the money-losing studio division from America Online's financial statements, raising its profitability. Executives of Bertelsmann and Madison Dearborn could not be reached for comment yesterday. The deal was scuttled because the Securities and Exchange Commission ruled that it would restrict America Online from making acquisitions using its stock, people close to the company said. With its stock price triple what it was a year ago, the company has been planning acquisitions. Moreover, America Online decided that it was more important to keep full ownership of its creative operations and indeed to bind them more tightly into its business. Mr. Leonsis, a flamboyant entrepreneur, has reported directly to Stephen M. Case, the company's chairman. He is now expected to report to Mr. Pittman, although his exact role is still being decided. Mr. Leonsis would still oversee the development of new content for the service as well as for Compuserve, a competing on-line service that America Online recently purchased. AOL Studios has developed a number of sites, both for America Online and for the World Wide Web. These include Entertainment Asylum, which covers Hollywood; Electra, a women's interest site, and Digital Cities, which provides entertainment and shopping guides for 32 cities. The studios unit also oversees what remains of Greenhouse, an earlier effort to nurture small-content partners by making minority investments in their ventures. The moves reflect the company's rapid evolution. Only a year ago, America Online made headlines when many of its customers got busy signals when they tried to sign on and later when its electronic mail service failed several times. But those problems hardly hurt it in the marketplace. In the last year, it has added nearly 5 million members, more than all its competitors combined. It now has more than 11 million paying customers. And in September, it agreed to buy Compuserve and to sell its data network to Worldcom, giving it $225 million in sorely needed cash. Now America Online is trying to profit from its huge audience by selling advertising and by selling products on line. Analysts say that as these arrangements begin to bring in cash, the company has less need to sell a piece of its studio division. At the same time, merging the studios back into the network division would create a unified advertising sales operation. Until now, the network division and each of the units within studios had separate advertising sales staffs competing with each other. Although none of the studio units has really started to make money, analysts say that in the on-line world, as in television and other media, building an entertainment brand can take years of investment. Analysts praised the company's apparent intention not to pull back from this effort. "Given that their business is going so well, generating a lot of free cash, why do they need to sell a piece of the business that could be one of the keys to their future?" said Brian C. Oakes, an analyst with Lehman Brothers. "Why should they trade short-term cash for the potential to build the next Disney?"

title: Feeling Abandoned By America Online
body: In December, Hecklers Online, a publisher of humor and games, sent a holiday greeting card promoting the redesign of its site on America Online. The card's punch line: "All you have to do is find it." This jab at the on-line service that gave Hecklers its start in the summer of 1995 was one of the milder manifestations of a growing frustration among America Online's small content partners. They were favored children in the company's early days, when keeping subscribers on line was the way to make money. But in the year-old era of flat pricing, advertising revenues are far more crucial to earnings than revenue from customers who linger on line. The shifting business model has brought substantive changes in America Online's relationship with its small partners. In a redesign of the service last fall, America Online buried its partners' brands under subheadings known as channels. "We went from having a button right on the screen to now, we're virtually nowhere," said Mike Ragsdale, a founder of Hecklers, which is based in Tuscaloosa, Ala. At one time, the partners said, they were each guaranteed that their sites would be featured on America Online's opening screen for at least 15 minutes a day. Now visitors who are looking for the site have trouble finding it. In addition, in the last year, Greenhouse, the division formed in 1994 to incubate services like Hecklers, or Motley Fool, the popular, irreverent site for investors, has shifted gears. Instead of creating partnership deals with start-ups and joint ventures with large media companies, America Online Studios is creating new offerings in house. America Online is also expanding its World Wide Web offerings. Studios have produced fare like the just-introduced Digital Cities and Electra, a site dedicated to women. The idea is to create content for a mass audience rather than for niche markets. "We've moved away from making minority investments in companies," said Anne Bentley, a spokeswoman for Greenhouse."Our strategy is to launch wholly owned networks. Our new mission reflects our belief that there is limited shelf space on line or on the Internet and that in order to compete in the content business, we needed to launch categories that target large consumer segments, not niche plays" That is a natural progression for the industry as it becomes a mass medium, industry analysts said. The weeding out of partners, through attrition and expired contracts, has reduced the number of America Online partners from 400 to 300 in the last year. "We want our partners to be successful," said Barry Schuler, America Online Networks' president of creative development. "But guess what? We can't guarantee that. Just like in television with the new fall season, there's going to be one success for every eight failures." Two years ago, Mr. Schuler said, America Online paid everyone to create content. Now, he said, the "frothy investment days are over." "We've made a billion-dollar investment in building our market -- a very big distribution channel," he continued. "We have over 50 percent market share. Our business model won't work without there being lots of successful partners." With joint ventures like the health-focused Thrive With Time and internally grown fare like Digital Cities, America Online pays less attention to some of its own investments. Hecklers and 24 other mini-publishing operations -- called content developers in the world of on-line services -- started through America Online's Greenhouse program, which offered new companies seed capital of $100,000 to $500,000 in exchange for 20 percent equity. Begun in 1994, when America Online had fewer than one million members and was dwarfed by its rivals Compuserve, with 2.4 million subscribers, and Prodigy, with 1.2 million members, Greenhouse was created to nurture innovative ideas from people not working for established media companies. The deals and nature of the products varied widely, from Motley Fool, perhaps the best-known Greenhouse offering, to the gay and lesbian offering, Planet Out. The company financed these special-interest areas at a time when it was an upstart service eager to differentiate itself from other established on-line services. Today, the premise on which those deals were based no longer exists. With flat-fee pricing, the time a member spends on line represents a net cost to America Online for system overhead. And advertising rates are based on how many times an ad is viewed, so fast turnover in the company's own content areas is more profitable than are long visits to its partners' sites. The shift began in December 1996, when America Online instituted a flat monthly fee to compete with Internet service providers that had begun offering unlimited access for $19.95 a month. The service quickly turned to other revenue sources like advertising and electronic commerce. But advertising for its partners' products proved harder to sell than advertising for its own material. As the service began to compete with its partners for ad sales, it began, not surprisingly, to give more prominence to the material it developed. "There's competition between us and AOL in terms of selling advertising, and there's competition between us and sister sites like Parent Soup," said Rob DeBaun, a founder of Moms On-Line, a Greenhouse partner based in Port Townsend, Wash. "It's a bit of a Darwinian rat race, with not enough advertising dollars to go around." Now, partners are caught in a quandary: Even as the likelihood of their snaring a slice of America Online's traffic deteriorates, they need the on-line service for its electronic publishing tools, and its audience. Carol Fitzgerald, the co-creator of the Book Report, one of the last start-ups to receive Greenhouse capital, said, "The reason we were on AOL exclusively all this time, the really good thing, is we got great promotion." Her business partner, Jesse Kornbluth, was hired as America Online's editorial director last June.  Now he is building a site on the Web, like some of the other Greenhouse partners. But they all insist that they need to keep their presence on America Online. "It has definitely made us appreciate and perhaps focus more on our Web site to make ourselves as independent as possible of AOL," Mr. DeBaun said. "You don't know what's going to happen. A year from now, they might charge us for carriage. "Two years ago, they were more concerned about us publishing on the Microsoft Network or Compuserve.  Now, they've become the 800-pound gorilla of on-line services, they're mostly competing with the Web." Graphic   Chart: "Finding Hecklers" Before AOL redesigned its service last fall, Hecklers, a publisher of humor and games, could count on being an option on AOL's opening screen for at least a small part of each day. Now, to get to Hecklers screen, users must first click on the channelsbutton and then choose the entertainment channel. On the next screen, the user must click on the "word of mouth" button. The link to Hecklers is in a pull-down menu on the "word of mouth" screen. Selecting "Hecklers" takes the user there.

title:
SPRING AND SUMMER CRUISES;
Finding a berth or joining a debate on line
body: On a chilly Sunday night in January, the Cruise Cafe -- the chat room of America Online's Cruise Critic site -- was buzzing, a silent babble of tales from distant lands. Debates raged: Dawn Princess or Majesty of the Seas? St. Croix or Tortola? Sea Bands or ginger capsules? Besides chat, Cruise Critic contains plenty of exhaustive and sometimes unflattering ship reviews by the site's editor, Anne Campbell, who not only has been on more than 60 sea voyages but also has twice sat through the movie "Titanic." America Online was a good first port of call, but I wanted to see what was available in the more turbulent waters of the Internet. Since cruise lines traditionally rely on travel agents to handle their marketing and sales, it's no surprise that the lines' Web sites are often little more than electronic brochures, with information on ships, itineraries, and photographs of people in the grip of an unremitting pursuit of fun. Most don't even take reservations. The site with the most bells and whistles is the new Disney Cruise Line (www. disney.com/disneycruise). I waited eight minutes to download a tiny, 12-second video clip of Mickey Mouse cavorting on deck. The cruise line sites do give you a feel for the different vessels available, from the huge, ritzy, Vegas-at-sea behemoths all the way down to tiny, intimate river barges, as well as the different types of cruises. There are now themed cruises for Elvis fans, bird-watchers, gay men and women, singles, photographers, wine tasters, golfers and nudists (take plenty of S.P.F. 30). The most comprehensive place for travelers' feedback on specific cruises now seems to be Cruise Opinion (www.cruiseopinion.com). Recent cruise passengers are asked to write comments on their experiences, good and bad, and to numerically rate their ships on 42 criteria. When I checked in, there were 928 such reviews on file. For briefer, pithy snippets of information, I liked the searchable Fielding's Cruisefinder (fieldingtravel.com), an electronic version of its guidebook. The unattractive-but-useful Getcruising site (www.getcruising.com) has a Cruise Selector. I clicked on "winter," "South America" and "exploration and culture"; three suitable cruises -- and some less-than-perfect matches -- were found. You can also compare statistical information for more than 100 ships here. The cheapest of those for which prices were given was the Seawind Crown of Premier Cruises (where the "average per day" cost was listed as $95 per person); the ship shown as having the largest number of cabins was the Carnival Destiny of Carnival Cruise Lines, with 1,321. If you're worried about hygiene, you can check the ships' "Green Sheet" scores from their mandatory twice-yearly sanitation inspections at the Centers for Disease Control site (www.cdc.gov). Celebrity Cruises' Galaxy had the highest scores last year: 99 and 100 percent. Anything above 85 percent is deemed acceptable by the C.D.C. When you are finally ready to make a booking, there are any number of Web sites that will take your reservation over the Internet. If you prefer to lay out all that money the old-fashioned way, in person, you can find a searchable data base of cruise-specific travel agents at the Cruise Lines International Association's site (www.cruising.org). I did a search that revealed nine such agents in my ZIP code. Back at the Cruise Cafe on a Wednesday night at 10, Anne Campbell was making her weekly live appearance to take questions. While 47 cruise hounds discussed various ships as though they were personal friends ("Has anybody seen Elation?"), the problems of finding an ATM in the Caribbean and the shots you need for Djibouti, I tossed out this iceberg: "What's the attraction of a great big floating hotel?" Ms. Campbell's was the most eloquent reply: "Relaxing, being able to do anything you want, stay in bed, sit in the sun, eat eat eat. And the outside world never intrudes."
