title: On-Line Service Accuses Navy of Deception in Inquiry About Sailor
body: America Online today accused the Navy of deception after an internal investigation showed that the computer service company had violated its own rules and disclosed confidential information to the Navy that identified a 36-year-old sailor as homosexual. The sailor, Senior Chief Petty Officer Timothy R. McVeigh, is facing dismissal from the Navy for homosexuality. He has sued the Pentagon to block the dismissal, charging that the Navy violated Federal privacy laws in obtaining information about him from America Online. In a statement, America Online, which has 11 million subscribers and is the nation's largest on-line service, said it believed that the Navy "deliberately ignored both Federal law and well-established procedures for handling inquiries about A.O.L. members." The computer services company, whose headquarters are in Dulles, Va., said one of its customer-service representatives did provide information about Chief Petty Officer McVeigh to a Navy investigator who "did not identify himself properly and did not reveal the true purpose of his call." The petty officer is no relation to the man convicted of the Oklahoma City bombing. In its statement, America Online said the actions of the customer-service representative violated the company's own rules on confidentiality. "This clearly should not have happened, and we regret it," the statement said. "This is a case of human error under very unusual circumstances. We want our members to know that their privacy is of paramount importance." In a separate statement today, the Navy defended its handling of the case and said investigators had enough evidence to identify Chief Petty Officer McVeigh as homosexual "without further information" from America Online. "There were no intentional violations of any Federal laws or regulation by Department of Navy personnel," the statement said. Asked if there might have been an unintentional violation of Federal privacy laws, a Navy spokesman declined comment. The move to dismiss Chief Petty Officer McVeigh, a highly decorated crew chief aboard the nuclear-powered submarine Chicago whose home port is Honolulu, came after the Navy linked him to a customer profile posted on America Online for "Tim" from "Honolulu, Hawaii," who listed his marital status as "gay" and whose email address was "Boysrch," which presumably referred to "boy search." A Navy investigator has acknowledged that he called America Online without identifying his connection to the military and asked for the full name of "Tim," and that America Online readily confirmed that the customer was Timothy R. McVeigh of Honolulu. "The investigator misled our representative into confirming information the Navy already possessed about Senior Chief McVeigh, both by failing to disclose his identity and purpose and by portraying himself as a friend or acquaintance of Senior Chief McVeigh's," America Online said. Lawyers who specialize in privacy issues say that both the Navy and America Online may have violated the Electronic Communications Privacy Act of 1986, which bars the release of customer information by computer-service companies without a subpoena, a court order or the consent of the customer, none of which the Navy had. David L. Sobel of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a privacy rights group, said the case "cuts to the heart of the issue of on-line privacy -- so much of the allure of the Internet has been based on the option to exercise anonymity." Christopher Wolf, a Washington lawyer for Chief Petty Officer McVeigh, said that as a result of America Online's acknowledgment today, "it is clear that what they did was improper and probably illegal." Mr. Wolf said the petty officer had not ruled out a lawsuit against the computer services company. "I know he's very disturbed that his confidentiality has been breached," the lawyer said. "But for the disclosure by A.O.L., there would not have been this action by the Navy to try to force him out of the service."

title: Sailor Fighting Discharge Over Policy on Gays Wins a Reprieve
body: A sailor who is challenging his discharge from the Navy for violating the military's policy toward homosexuality received a last-minute reprieve yesterday after filing a lawsuit against the Secretaries of Defense and the Navy. The Senior Chief Petty Officer, Timothy R. McVeigh, who is based in Honolulu and is no relation to the convicted Oklahoma City bomber, was to be discharged at midnight, Hawaii time. Navy officials this week found Mr. McVeigh guilty of violating the "don't ask, don't tell" policy, which allowed homosexual men and women to serve in the military if they kept their sexual orientation to themselves. In response to a lawsuit by Mr. McVeigh, Government lawyers have delayed the discharge until Wednesday to allow time for a judge to review his claims. Mr. McVeigh, a decorated submarine crew chief, maintained that the only evidence against him was information obtained by the Government from the on-line service America Online, in violation of the Electronic Communications Privacy Act. Mr. McVeigh's lawyers also claimed that proper military procedures were not followed in the investigation. On Sept. 12, Mr. McVeigh, who was described in his most recent performance review as an "outstanding role model," was removed from his job and told he was being investigated on charges of homosexual conduct. Mr. McVeigh later learned that the basis for the investigation was an America Online member profile, which had been obtained by a civilian involved with his submarine unit after she and Mr. McVeigh exchanged email in August about a charity toy effort. In the profile, the word "gay" was listed under marital status. Privacy advocates said the case had broad implications for defining the military's "don't ask, don't tell" policy, as well as for electronic privacy rights for all individuals. "This case is likely to define the bounds of Government investigations on the Internet," said David Sobel of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a privacy rights group based in Washington.

title:
Business Travel;
PC Magazine's advice: Don't trade your travel agent for a World Wide Web site just yet.
body: MANY of the World Wide Web's top sites for business, as well as leisure, travel have been rated by PC Magazine, and found wanting. Warning readers not to give up their "old, reliable" travel agent, the magazine survey says: "The sites are useful and interesting, but a traditional travel agent handles most arrangements more efficiently. Also, an agent won't forget you after finding you a fare. If a lower fare comes along two minutes after you book yours, no travel web site has any means of letting you know as a travel agent can." The most favorably rated of the 15 sites surveyed was that of Biztravel.com (www.biztravel.com). PC Magazine commended it for the detailed profile it allows users to create, its management of frequent-travel programs and its "clear and helpful" format. Here are the magazine's observations on other sites related to business travel: *American Express Travel (www.americanexpress.com/travel) is "good for the traveler without a lot of special needs," but lacks extras like Biztravel.com's ability to book flights using frequent-flier miles. The magazine points out that travelers buying tickets through American Express can pick them up at an American Express agency, or have them delivered free of charge. *CNN Interactive's Travel Guide (www.cnn.com/TRAVEL) is "useful for any business traveler" with its "easy-to-use reservations system, an effective low-fare tracking system and the valuable CNN on-line guidebook." Another feature PC Magazine likes is the site's ability to monitor low fares. *Flifo (www.flifo.com) is "a good place" for frequent travelers "to learn about where they're going and to set up a well-organized, detailed itinerary." Ticketing services -- for electronic ticket processing or tickets by mail, with free delivery -- are also noteworthy, according to the article. *Internet Travel Network (www.itn.net) is praised for performing "most of the basics for a business traveler" and for allowing a user to sign up with a local travel agency. Shortcomings the magazine sees include storage of only four frequent-flier program numbers and no storage of car or hotel program data. *Microsoft Expedia.com (www.expedia.com) is "very efficient for that quick business jaunt to Cincinnati" but is marred by design flaws. The article says that Hotel Pinpointer, a feature enabling users to instantly view a hotel's location on a map, is "unparalleled," but the fare-tracking service is "the most Spartan of any site." *The Trip.com (www.thetrip.com) "handles the basics of booking a trip well." The magazine likes the site's email fare service and its flight-tracking capability, but calls some of its destination information "a bit stale." *Travelocity (www.travelocity.com) is praised for a "user-friendly design, superb customer support and excellent knack for finding low fares." Minuses are an "inflexible" fare-watching feature and cryptic jargon that describes hotels and flights, according to the magazine. *Travel Web (www.travelweb.com) offers "an excellent level of detail in searching for and booking a hotel," the article states, but goes on to say that "in other areas you'll find other sites more useful." The survey appears in the Jan. 6 issue of PC Magazine.  Airline Update Next month, Lufthansa will introduce a $150 million upgrade of its long-haul first-class and business-class service, in an effort to catch up with trans-Atlantic competitors. Both classes will feature seats with more leg room, as well as improved food service and amenities. Business-class travelers flying on Air Canada to London's Heathrow Airport are now eligible for spa service at the nearby Radisson Edwardian Hotel. Northwest Airlines and KLM Royal Dutch Airlines said all of their flights would be smoke-free starting with the spring 1998 schedule, except for intercontinental flights to and from Japan.  Hotel Update Leading Hotels of the World, the reservations organization that represents more than 300 luxury hotels, has begun a guest recognition program. Travelers can participate in the program only if they are nominated by a hotel general manager. According to Deborah Yager, director of strategic marketing and sales, guests who qualify would be those who regularly stay at a specific hotel, or who stay in a suite when they travel. Whenever they make a reservation at one of the hotels, program participants will receive a room upgrade if available; early check-in and late checkout privileges, and gifts like a bathrobe or chocolates.  Additional benefits include a quarterly newsletter and use of a special concierge desk. Ms. Yager said Leading Hotels planned to nominate fewer than 100,000 guests for the program, for which there is no charge.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Interactive Agencies Are Set to Merge - Correction Appended
body: Three newyork companies specializing in interactive advertising sales are merging with the help of institutional investors to create one of the biggest companies in the field. Petry Interactive Inc., Katz Millennium Marketing and Interactive Imaginations Inc. plan to combine early next month to form a company with a sales staff of 40 in seven cities, representing 3,400 World Wide Web sites for advertising sales, sponsorships and other marketing initiatives. Each of the companies will own 25 percent of the new company, which has not yet been named. The remaining 25 percent will be owned by the investors, who will put $10 million into the new company; they include the Travelers Insurance Company unit of Travelers Group, Big Flower Holdings Inc. and the Prospect Street NYC Discovery Fund. David Moore, 45, chief executive of Petry Interactive, will be chief executive of the merged company. Jay Friesel, 48, president and chief executive of Katz Millennium Marketing, will be executive vice president for sales and administration of the merged company. And Michael Paolucci, 27, chief executive of Interactive Imaginations, will join the merged company as a consultant and board member, focusing on new ventures.  Correction  An entry in the Addenda listing of Business Day on Dec. 22 about a planned merger of interactive advertising companies included one such company erroneously. Katz Millennium Marketing will not be among the companies combining to form 24/7 Media. The president and chief executive of Katz Millennium, Jay Friesel, is leaving to join 24/7 Media as executive vice president for sales and administration; Katz Millennium remains part of the Katz Dimension unit of Katz Media Group. Correction-Date: January 6, 1998, Tuesday

title: Guidelines Don't End Debate on Internet Privacy
body: In agreeing to let private information brokers and credit reporting companies be governed by voluntary privacy protection guidelines, the Federal Trade Commission is betting that companies that maintain vast computerized dossiers on people and businesses can police themselves in the face of ever more powerful information technologies. Many civil libertarians insist that the F.T.C.'s bet is a high-stakes gamble with the privacy rights of all Americans. The agreement sets in motion the first meaningful trial of the Clinton Administration's privacy policy, the stated goal of which is to protect individual privacy in the Internet age without resorting to new laws and regulations. Indeed, the agreement clearly defines the two camps -- corporate America and privacy rights groups -- that are struggling for ascendancy in a networked world in which corporations increasingly rely on consumer data bases for myriad aspects of their business. The data companies are in effect saying that they can be trusted to act responsibly and to police their own ranks. Known variously as "individual reference services" or "look-up services," businesses like Lexis-Nexis, Equifax and Information America gather and sell many types of very private data, including credit and financial histories and medical records. Such information is widely used by banks, mortgage companies, insurance companies, law enforcement officials, direct marketers and others. While the new guidelines will permit consumers to "opt out" of these commercial databases in some cases, they do not offer individuals any new access to information about themselves held in the computers of look-up services. The agreement does not offer average people an easy way to check what personal information about them is being sold or to find out who is getting it, nor are people given a means to contest its accuracy. Privacy groups argue that the new guidelines are insufficient, especially because they offer no remedies for people who believe they have been harmed by the dissemination of information in commercial data bases. The guidelines are the data industry's response to the public outcry that erupted last year after it became known that a major data provider, Lexis-Nexis, was making Social Security information available to the general public via the Internet. Under the new guidelines, data companies will hide certain kinds of information from the public while continuing to make the information available to qualified customers, including law enforcement agencies and private investigators. "There will be no Social Security information or birth dates available over the Internet," said Tim Davies, chief operating officer of National Information Services at Lexis-Nexis, a division of Reed Elsevier. Mr. Davies acknowledged that the agreement also clearly defined the difference between the unitedstates Government and European governments with regard to privacy protection. The Clinton Administration is now in the midst of a debate with the European Union over a strict new privacy directive scheduled to go into effect next year across Europe. Europe is set to enforce a strict Data Protection Directive that would cut off the flow of commercial data to nations whose privacy protections are deemed inadequate. The unitedstates has few individual privacy laws, but the Clinton Administration and unitedstates data brokers are trying to persuade the Europeans that industry agreements like the one announced yesterday meet the standards of the directive. The F.T.C.'s chairman, Robert Pitofsky, says that laws may not be necessary. While acknowledging his disappointment that the industry group has refused to give consumers access to information about themselves, he argues that voluntary restraints should be given a substantial test before new laws are enacted. "This is an impressive step in the direction of self-regulation," Mr. Pitofsky said. "The history of self-regulation is you start here and then see where you go in the future." He acknowledged that previous attempts at self-regulation by this industry had fallen short, but he said the willingness of the 14 participating companies -- which constitute about 90 percent of the information broker industry -- to submit to third-party audits had created a more rigorous safeguard. The data provided by information brokers has become a flash point, in part, because of the potential for such companies to facilitate credit card fraud and the theft of personal identity. For example, someone with access to another person's Social Security number may be able to use that number to obtain other data, including information about assets and professional licenses, said an F.T.C. report to Congress that accompanied yesterday's agreement. Mr. Davies said that there was little evidence linking identity theft to the look-up services. But the F.T.C. report noted that a recent investigation by the Federal Reserve Board had concluded that "fraud related to identity theft appears to be a growing risk for consumers and financial institutions, and the relatively easy access to personal information may expand the risk." Privacy advocates also said the agreement could represent a step backward for civil liberties because it gives law enforcement agencies access to vast data bases. Traditionally, the government and courts have placed strict limits on the ease with which police officials can collect certain types of information on citizens without subpoenas. Now those safeguards could be eroding, privacy advocates say, as more and more information is centralized in vast computer databases. "This stands the Fourth Amendment on its head," Marc Rotenberg, director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a Washington D.C. privacy rights group, said of the Constitution's ban on unreasonable searches. "This is like giving law enforcement copies of the telephone book but telling individuals that they have to request specific listings."

title: News-Ad Issues Arise in New Media
body: Scrambling to make huge investments in the Internet pay off, some of the biggest news organizations have begun linking advertisements to news on their World Wide Web sites more closely than in the mainstream print or broadcast media. In recent weeks, CNN and MSNBC have both started running advertisements for the on-line store of Barnes & Noble. The ads offer to sell books tied directly to the topic of the news stories they abut. For example, with a recent CNN article on the killings in a Kentucky high school there was a button promising a link to books on teen-age violence. The news sites collect a commission for each book sold from these ads. The publishers and advertisers say they are trying to exploit the interactive nature of the medium, offering readers a new dimension in easy and relevant shopping. But others, even in the advertising business, worry that as the interests of the publishers and advertisers become more intertwined, the independence of news reporting could be compromised. "The pressure for ad dollars is so great that some Web sites would do anything to bring in the money," said David J. Moore, chairman of Petry Interactive, a company that sells Internet advertising. "I'm a guy who likes to make money, but to the extent that publishers start to mix advertising and editorial, they risk losing the confidence of the consumer." The deals have been sought by Internet publishers who are frustrated by the limitations of simply selling advertisements and increasingly looking to earn commissions from sales made through their sites or fees for passing on the names of people who are interested in a product. These arrangements also play into the needs of cash-hungry on-line merchants -- and skeptical producers of mainstream brands -- who want to pay for ads only when they produce results. "Transaction-driven stuff will account for the lion's share of advertising revenue," said William Doyle, an on-line advertising analyst with Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. "Right now, this is a great medium for direct marketers and not so great for brand builders, in terms of cost efficiency." Because the Internet is in its commercial infancy, advertisers and publishers are inventing a new set of rules, one that is very different from those in print or broadcast news. For example, CNN's travel articles all have links to an on-line travel agency, run by the Internet Travel Network, under the CNN brand. And at the ends of book reviews on The newyork Times on the Web are links that readers can use to buy the books directly from Barnes & Noble. Publishers plan sports stories paired with buttons selling team jerseys; compact disks and tickets are for sale with the entertainment news, and coverage of technology trends is accompanied by links to stores selling the latest gadgets. Yet the ability to create customized advertising for Internet news articles creates added challenges in the already difficult relationship between news and advertising. Most newspapers and magazines allow advertisers to determine the general placement of ads, say in the sports or business section. And television stations get some of the profits from the sales generated by those late-night ads for miracle knives. But never before have publications had such a direct interest in sales tied to their news reports. Indeed, to help Barnes & Noble devise a list of recommended books, CNN, a unit of Time Warner Inc., sends the bookseller a daily schedule of the top news items on its Web sites, something TV networks ordinarily would not disclose to advertisers. "Instead of saying the lines are getting blurry, say we are creating a new paradigm that is not editorial and not advertising," said Susan Boster, the director of marketing for Barnes & Noble's Web site. "It is a service offered to consumers." Beyond simply buying advertising space, the bookseller sees itself as a partner with the various news and information sites. "Since they get a percentage of each sale, they are encouraged to change their offerings to increase sales," Ms. Boster said. She said that the publishers are given instant access to data about what titles are selling well on other sites so they, too, can include links to the hot books. With the links just a few months old, Ms. Boster says, it is too soon to say how well they are doing. Not every publisher is enamored with these arrangements. Some do not want their profits to depend on their advertisers' prices or the quality of the service. While some sites, like the Web search engines, mingle book sales links with other offerings, some more traditional news organizations have taken pains to segregate them. For example, on the General Electric cable unit, MSNBC, the list of books to buy is identified with the word "advertisement." And officials of CNN's Web sites insist that the links do not compromise its editorial independence. "CNN takes its journalism very seriously," said Richy Glassberg, general manager of advertising sales for CNN's Web sites. "The advertisers have nothing to do with the content." Still, Merrill Brown, the top editor of MSNBC, acknowledged that tension had already arisen from the news site's coverage of on-line bookselling. It dealt with the conflicts by removing the Barnes & Noble advertisements from those articles. Mr. Brown said that while it was easier to prevent such overt biases as treating advertisers in a more favorable light, editors were still being drawn into discussions of the commercial aspects of their publications far more so than in more established media. "The pressure is not how we cover the news," he said. "The pressure is enormous to make advertising and sponsorships that make sense."

title: New Security System for Internet Purchases Has Its Doubters
body: After two years of development and dozens of trials around the world, the credit card industry is readying an elaborate system meant to improve the security of making purchases over the Internet. The system, called Secure Electronic Transaction, is to be introduced early next year and promises to make it harder for someone to steal a credit card number sent over the Internet. It will also make it easier for shoppers to verify that the on-line merchants they are dealing with are legitimate and for the merchants to authenticate the identity of the shoppers. Yet, after the system's proponents, including perhaps a dozen financial and software firms, have invested tens of millions of dollars in its development, they are finding there is a growing backlash among bankers and companies doing business on the Internet. The system, which is often called by the acronym SET, is too slow, too expensive and far too cumbersome for shoppers to use, the critics say. "SET is not a panacea and it ain't cheap," said Allan A. Weinberg, senior vice president of the First Data Corporation, the country's largest credit card processor, which handles such big Internet merchants as the Dell Computer Corporation and Amazon.com Inc., the on-line bookstore. "If you want to sell more sweaters or greeting cards on the Internet today, you are just not going to get a return from your SET investment." First Data is grudgingly building the capability to accept SET transactions because some of its clients have asked it to do so, Mr. Weinberg said. But he predicted that two years from now, a "relatively small" portion of Internet transactions would use SET. The controversy is yet another reminder that electronic commerce, like the rest of the Internet, has flourished on simple technology developed in small steps by millions of users, rather than by complex systems designed over years by committees of experts. And it highlights how problems that seem insurmountable -- such as consumers' fear of using cards on the Internet -- can vanish in months, potentially rendering research into solutions an expensive exercise in futility. "Last year, we did a survey and three-quarters of our customers said credit card security was an issue," said Chris McCann, senior vice president of 1-800-Flowers, which does 10 percent of its business on line. "Today less than one-third see it as an issue." What's more, the added security of SET is hardly needed when fraud on the Internet is minuscule and existing browsers already have more than adequate ability to prevent hackers from eavesdropping. "Credit card shopping on the Internet is going like gangbusters today," said Cliff Conneighton, chief executive of the Internet Commerce Services Corporation, which runs shopping sites on the World Wide Web for the Panasonic Consumer Electronics Corporation and Random House Inc. "The fear of shopping is diminishing rapidly. It's always good to have truth on your side, and the truth is that it's not very risky." Credit card companies argue that the reason they are pushing SET now is precisely to stay ahead of the criminals who will eventually find ways to exploit the weaknesses of the current system. "As a bank, we just can't say, 'Let's chose the option that is less secure,' " said Gary S. Roboff, senior vice president of the Chase Manhattan Bank, which is testing SET with Wal-Mart Stores Inc. "The reason SET will happen is that it's truly in everyone's best interest to make it happen," he said. "Consumers will have a degree of security they can't have any other way, and the merchants will have lower fraud losses." Yet in return, it is much more complicated for a shopper to use SET than the security automatically built into today's browsers. First, a customer must get a special program, known as an electronic wallet, which works in conjunction with Internet browser software. The Netscape Communications Corporation and the Microsoft Corporation include such electronic wallets in their latest browsers, but credit card companies plan to offer their own versions. Any SET wallet will be able to handle five different credit card accounts; debit cards will be added in a future release. Before going shopping, consumers will need an electronic certificate -- effectively a digital identification card -- associated with each credit card. They will either receive this on a disk or by downloading it from their card company's Web site. To shop, users would do as they do today, browsing a store's Web site and selecting items to purchase. At the end of a shopping spree, the user would press an on-screen button to pay using SET, automatically starting the wallet program. The shopper would select which credit card to use, and the wallet would transmit the card number, purchase details, and the unique identifying information in the certificate to the merchant's Web site, in an encrypted form. What happens when the transaction reaches the merchant is how SET differs from the current browser systems. The credit card number itself is passed while still encrypted right to the processing bank. That means that a sophisticated electronic thief tapping into the system, or a crooked employee snooping in the system, will not find any valid card numbers. (This is one of the biggest risks of the current system.) Moreover, by validating the electronic certificate, the merchant can be much more certain of the cardholder's identity. That means that someone who steals a credit card from someone's wallet cannot use it to make purchases on the Internet. Similarly, the shopper's wallet software will examine the digital certificate of the merchant, automatically providing a warning if the merchant is not authorized to accept credit cards. "SET gives people the confidence to shop with people they don't know," argued Steve Herz, senior vice president of Visa International Inc. Merchants have often been the victims of what little fraud there has been on the Internet. Yet even the merchants that have been most hurt by this fraud say that SET is not the solution to their problems. "It's not clear to me that SET is compelling enough for either consumers or merchants to go out and use it," said William S. McKiernan, chief executive of Cybersource, which runs an on-line software store that had huge losses from fake credit cards. The biggest issue, he said, is what will encourage consumers to get wallet software and then download the required certificate. At first, only the largest banks will be set up to issue the certificates at all, meaning that millions of people will not be able to use SET even if they want to. The big banks may be wary of pushing SET too hard, because it will cost an estimated $3 to $5 a customer for them to sign people up for SET.  Companies like the GTE Corporation are hoping to charge the banks as much as $1 each just for the digital certificates. Most card companies are expected to absorb these costs, although some may pass them on to their cardholders. Similarly, the banks that provide credit card processing services to merchants will have to spend as much as $1 million each to set up the software they need to process SET transactions. And all that money gets a system that many people who have used it say is hardly ready for prime time. "It's so slow it will lead to the electronic equivalent of arterial sclerosis," said Mr. Roboff. In Chase's tests, SET transactions take 30 to 40 seconds. "If you have millions of people out there trying to use it, it will collapse under its own weight." The delays arise from the time it takes to encrypt the information. Moreover, the resulting information transmissions are many times longer than those that are not encrypted. Even more troublesome, the SET standard published by Mastercard International Inc. and Visa is so loose that versions of SET software written by different companies are not compatible with each other, forcing two of the biggest companies looking to cash in on the SET software market, I.B.M. and the Verifone Inc. unit of the Hewlett-Packard Company, to announce that they would work together to create a true standard within the SET standard. The card companies say they are working to speed up SET software and resolve the compatibility issue. The bigger question is whether they will provide tangible incentives for merchants to use it. "To get the merchants on board, the card associations have to put their money where their mouths are," said Karen Epper, an analyst at Forrester Research. Visa has decided to change its price structure in ways that are likely to reduce the fee merchants pay for SET transactions by 3 cents to 5 cents, but this is hardly enough encouragement, analysts said. Possibly more significant, Visa has said merchants will have less liability for fraud in transactions using SET than with other Internet transactions. Yet even if merchants do want to encourage SET, experts say they would be crazy to turn away paying customers who do not use it. And as a result, it may do little to halt the sort of fraud it was meant to prevent. "SET will not have 100 percent market share for a long period of time," Mr. Weinberg of First Data said. "You'll just move the crooks over to non-SET transactions." Graphic   Chart: "Price of Added Security" Credit card and technology companies have developed a software system called Secure Electronic Transaction (SET) to prevent fraud in on-line shopping. However, this added security is expensive and cumbersome.  Benefits  Software distributed to a consumer by a bank or software company encrypts the consumer's card number so it cannot be stolen. Merchant can verify the cardholder's identity. Consumer can verify that merchant is legitimate.  Drawbacks  Encryption is slow. Transactions can take up to 30 seconds. It is complicated for cardholder to get set up with essentials. System is expensive for cardholder's bank to set up. Various versions of SET software from different vendors are not compatible. (pg. D6)

title:
Updates/Media and Technology;
America Online Wins Round in Lawsuit Over Connection Delays
body: America Online has won a temporary reprieve from some of the legal trouble connected with the company's inability to provide enough Internet communication lines to deal with a huge increase in business. Appellate justices reversed the Texas class-action status of the lawsuit against America Online on Friday, ruling that the company did not receive proper notification of claims against it from customers. The suit was returned to state district court for further action. The company must first receive the standard 60-day notice of intent to file a suit under the state's Deceptive Trade Practices Act, the judges ruled. Then further consideration of a new class-action status can occur. The lawyer for the on-line service, James Tancula, said that voluntary agreements to compensate consumers for the earlier problems have made the suit unnecessary. A settlement is pending in a national class-action suit in Chicago. But Jim H. Pearson, a lawyer in Houston, said the ruling could jeopardize legitimate claims of an estimated 500,000 Texans. They were among the America Online customers who contracted for flat-fee Internet access at $19.95 monthly, only to discover that the company could not provide adequate service.

title: 2 On-Line Ad Firms Announce a Merger
body: Two privately held providers of Internet on-line advertising management software and services said today that they had agreed to merge to become what they say will be the largest and most comprehensive company in the industry. The two Palo Alto companies, Click Over Inc. and Focalink Communications Inc., combine the backing of two prominent Silicon Valley venture capital firms. Click Over is financed by Kleiner, Perkins, Caufield & Byers, and Focalink is backed by the Mayfield Fund. Representatives of both companies said the companies planned a new round of financing soon. Collectively, the two companies have more than 200 on-line advertising customers using their services to plan and buy advertising, to manage sites and analyze interactive marketing data from the Internet. The companies have competed head to head in certain niches against other start-ups, but hope that by combining forces they can attract more business. The market for Web advertising is still in its infancy. Cowles/Simbanet, a research firm, estimated that Web advertising jumped 27 percent in the third quarter, to $169.8 million, while spending in the first nine months of 1997 was $387 million, topping 1996 levels. Executives of the companies said they expect to close the deal in December. Financial details were not disclosed. The combined company will employ 50 people.

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
CYBERSCOUT
body: TRACKING DOWN THE BEST FARES www.bestfares.com www.yahoo.com In the old days, two or three years ago, airline fares could change in a few weeks, or even in a few days, in response to competitors' changes. Now, thanks to the World Wide Web, they can change in minutes, and often only on the Web. The deals circulate largely by word of mouth, or word of email, and are very difficult to find. It is also hard to know where to start. I started with www.bestfares.com, an electronic offshoot of Best Fares magazine, a 15-year-old print publication with a circulation of about 59,000. The on-line edition, which counted more than 475,000 visitors last month, includes late-breaking news and Internet-only deals. Its sections are Newsdesk, with fare deals "that may only last for a few hours"; Hidden Travel Deals, the "top 25 hottest hidden travel deals"; Frequent Flyer; Scam Watch, information on "travel scams and bogus advertising"; Bargain Alley, "deep discounts on airlines, hotels, cars, cruises, leisure travel, seniors and more," and Other Good Stuff, with information on hotel discounts, weather, currency exchange, an ATM locator (with the Visa logo), ski reports and more. Of these sections, Newsdesk, Scam Watch and Other Good Stuff are accessible at no charge. To enter the other sections, you must be a subscriber to Best Fares magazine, which naturally you can become on line. Newsdesk offers both national and international fares and other travel news; the list changes rapidly. Recent examples include flights from Detroit to six cities in Mexico for $206 round trip; newyork to Cozumel, $374 round trip, and Quito, Ecuador, for as low as $378 round trip. The section highlighted a one-way one-person fare from Chicago to Indianapolis for $22 for the Thanksgiving holiday, perhaps the least expensive air fare anywhere. The deal, Best Fares said, was valid Nov. 23, 24, 27 and 28, and people 62 and older could take a companion of any age for an additional $19.79. Southwest, United, Delta and American Trans Air were said to be offering this fare. Once you find an appealing deal, it is up to you to get the tickets through the airline, a travel agent or otherwise. Best Fares offers information, not bookings. If I had started instead with Yahoo, www.yahoo.com, which a lot more people know about than Best Fares, I also would have done fairly well. That Internet directory service has a travel component connected with the independent Travelocity service, where I searched for a one-way flight from Chicago to Indianapolis (a distance of about 170 miles) on Nov. 23. There were three at $41 the day I checked it, the same day that Best Fares was reporting the $22 fare. Less than a week later, there were three $26 flights. With Travelocity, you can book the flight on line and receive tickets either electronically or by mail.  CHECKING OUT AIRLINE SITES www.ata.com www.delta-air.com www.ual.com The three airline sites I tried were less useful. The American Trans Air site, www.ata.com, requires calling an 800 number to book the flights. You can sign up and request that special fares be emailed to you each week. Delta Air Lines, at www.delta-air.com, works sporadically, but occasionally reveals special discounts. I was unable to unearth any fare information at all from the United Airlines site, www.ual.com. Maybe they were having a bad week.   L. R. SHANNON Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: A Lawyer Minus the Briefcase
body: Artificial intelligence, or computer-based reasoning and problem solving, has, after years of hype and disappointments, begun to come of age in a few fields marked by clear rules and precise terms. It has been used to help doctors diagnose diseases; it has been used to beat the chess champion of the world. But another goal in artificial intelligence research has proved more elusive. For more than 25 years, experts in artificial intelligence in the unitedstates and Western Europe have tried to figure out how to teach computers to think as lawyers do. Lawyers who have followed the efforts have been skeptical, doubting whether computers could perform legal reasoning. But next month, their skepticism will be tested by the Virtual Patent Advisor, a new software product designed to identify and help avoid patent conflicts. In December, the General Electric Company's GE Power Systems unit, based in Schenectady, N.Y., plans to introduce the system, the first in a series of virtual legal advisers intended to prevent and help solve corporate legal problems. The result of research by the Jnana Technologies Corporation, the Virtual Patent Advisor aims to help identify patent infringement problems. The system, which can run on a desktop computer and can use the Internet, questions an engineer to define the structure and purpose of an invention idea and then searches data bases and compares design features with existing patents. It can then create lists of potentially conflicting patents, apply rules of patent law to the facts it has gathered and generate reports to the company's lawyers. Ideally, the engineer, apprised of potential conflicts, could alter the design or turn to the company to find some other solution. Robert C. Lampe Jr., a senior patent lawyer at GE Power Systems, said he expected the product would reduce to less than an hour a process that now takes as long as a week. "It's a tremendous productivity tool," he said. Computers have long been used to conduct key-word searches in legal research and to prepare tax forms and wills. But David R. Johnson, chairman of Counsel Connect and co-director of the Cyberspace Law Institute, said the virtual advisers would go well beyond this, bringing together case-based and rule-based reasoning capacities and the ability to draw on multiple data bases. At least one doubter was intrigued by the idea. "It sounds like it would make legal practice more fun -- get rid of the drudgery," said Ronald Dworkin, a professor of law and philosophy at newyork University and a professor of jurisprudence at Oxford University. "But I guess what I'd insist on is that this is all limited by the fact that the law is essentially imaginative and interpretive," he added. These qualities, he said, "can't be programmed, no matter how sophisticated the programming techniques." Wendy Gordon, a law professor at Boston University, said she was concerned that a computer, unlike a human, could not perceive voice quality, facial expressions and other cues that signal confusion or ambiguity. And Robert C. Sheehan, executive partner at Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, said, "The most advanced cutting edge of the law is always where you're able to take a set of facts and come up with a novel idea." Software, he said, "won't be creative." But those who work in artificial intelligence say that to the extent that law relies upon tightly woven arguments, supporting precedent and well-defined rules, it can be a perfect template for artificial intelligence. That is because the fields best suited for artificial intelligence are the highly mathematical ones that have "very little subjectivity in them, like chess," said Edwina L. Rissland, professor of computer science at the University of Massachusetts at Amherst and president of the International Association for Artificial Intelligence and the Law. The fields that lend themselves least to artificial intelligence, she added, are those "in which it's very hard to pin down the meanings of the words." "Probably much harder than law," she added, "would be things like politics and further still would be something like psychiatry." Professor Rissland said that research into the use of artificial intelligence in legal contexts had divided into two general categories. In the first, rule-based reasoning, the computer uses if-then statements to move from facts to conclusions or from possible conclusions to supporting facts. In the second, case-based reasoning, experience from previous, analogous cases is applied to solve new problems. Professor Rissland, in more than a decade of research, pioneered computerized case-based reasoning and constructed a system that meshed the two forms of reasoning. Frederic W. Parnon, a lawyer, ran across Professor Rissland's work in 1995 when he decided to devise software systems that could perform legal functions. He later founded Jnana, which developed the Virtual Patent Advisor. Professor Rissland has served as an adviser and occasional consultant on Jnana's virtual advisers, though she has no financial stake in the project. After spending two years creating the underlying technology for the systems, Jnana approached large corporations and asked them to support development of applications addressing specific legal concerns in exchange for favorable licensing terms. In trying to identify a prospective client for a new technological product, Mr. Parnon said, "You have to get this confluence of someone who's enlightened, who has a business problem to solve; then there's a fit." G.E. was the first large company to sign on. Several other companies are considering participation in other adviser systems. Mr. Parnon said that a telecommunications company, which he would not identify, was working with Jnana to develop a system to advise managers about human resources. A major legal research company, he said, is interested in software that will query legal researchers about facts, search data bases and send researchers to the appropriate areas of the law. Mr. Parnon declined to provide details of the development costs or licensing terms. But companies that have not participated in development would pay for the software at an annual cost equivalent to the salary of a junior lawyer. But even artificial intelligence experts acknowledge its inherent weakness. "It's hard for a good lawyer to come up with novel, inventive arguments," Professor Rissland said, "and it will be even harder for a machine to do so -- probably." title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
A campaign draws attention to the accountability factor in measuring visits to Web sites.
body: REMEMBER when commercials for Winston cigarettes proclaimed, "It's what's up front that counts?" Now the Audit Bureau of Circulations, in the first campaign in its 83-year history, is urging advertisers and agencies to demand what counts up front. The campaign, which begins appearing in trade publications this week, is sponsored by A.B.C. Interactive, a year-old unit of the bureau that is devoted to auditing visits to World Wide Web sites that carry advertising. Print and Web-site banner pitches, created by Slack Barshinger & Partners in Chicago, declare that A.B.C. Interactive is "bringing true accountability to the Web" through "independent, third-party" audits likened to the bureau's verification of the circulations of newspapers and magazines. The start of the campaign is one of several developments in interactive advertising scheduled for this week. Others include the acquisition of BBG New Media, a Boston new-media agency, by Think New Ideas Inc., a national new-media shop affiliated with Omnicom Group; the introduction of an email ad service by Moviefone Inc., offering studios a chance to tell moviegoers about coming films, and a new on-line public service ad initiative by the Advertising Council and the Internet Advertising Bureau. The A.B.C. Interactive campaign is indicative of the increased attention being paid to Web site audits as ad spending in cyberspace increases. A.B.C. Interactive has grown to 92 clients like Conde Nast Publications, part of Advance Publications; The Detroit News, owned by the Gannett Company; the Hachette Filipacchi Magazines unit of Lagardere Group and Yahoo Inc. Still, "the requirement for Web site audits is not where we'd like it to be at this time," said Mike Lavery, president and managing director of the bureau in Schaumburg, Ill. One reason for that, he added, was that "people are trying the Web, exploring how it best works for them, so the demand for accountability is not where it is in traditional media." The campaign acknowledges those issues. One print ad, for instance, carries this headline: "Your Web site ads should be creative. Web site numbers shouldn't." "As the Web evolves into a real medium," said Gary Slack, managing director at Slack Barshinger, data "will need to be down to earth; it's time to be accountable." "One goal of the campaign," he added, "is to get more content providers to prepare for the demand for audits from advertisers and agencies that will be there in the future, to anticipate the questions they'll ask when you walk into their office." The campaign, with a yearlong budget of almost $250,000, will appear in trade publications like Advertising Age, Adweek, Brandweek, Marketing Magazine, Mediaweek and Webweek as well as on the Web sites of some of those titles. Buying Web ads will also be the subject of a panel discussion at the bureau's 83d annual conference and meeting, which runs Wednesday through Friday at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel. Turning to the other interactive activities, the acquisition of BBG New Media, to be announced today, calls for that agency to become the Boston outpost of Think New Ideas, which now has offices in Atlanta, Los Angeles, newyork and Seattle. All employees and accounts of BBG, which include the Fidelity Investments unit of the FMR Corporation and the I.B.M. Corporation, will be absorbed by Think New Ideas. Joe Nicholson, 38, chief executive of BBG, and Dan McCartney, 38, president, will become managing directors at Think New Ideas. Think New Ideas will acquire all outstanding stock in BBG -- to be renamed Think Boston -- for 303,334 shares of Think New Ideas stock, worth almost $3.4 million at the close of trading last week; $175,000 in cash, and additional shares of Think New Ideas based on how Think Boston performs in the next two years. Think New Ideas is part of Communicade, a division that manages Omnicom's interests in six interactive shops; Omnicom owns 19 percent of Think New Ideas. The Moviefone email ads, also to be announced today, are an example of a push service, or customized direct marketing, on the Internet. The service, called Moviemail, will promote four to six films through the end of the year; the first is "The Jackal," to be released on Friday by the Universal Pictures unit of the Seagram Company. Moviefone will provide studios with the email addresses of users of Movielink, the Moviefone Web site (www.movielink.com), who have registered for Moviemail by identifying categories of films they like. Moviemail will match those preferences with coming releases and send emails about the film, related promotions, locations of nearby theaters and opening-day showtimes. Moviemail will be sent free to computer users; more than 100,000 have already registered, said Matt Blumberg, general manager of Movielink in newyork. The studios will pay fees on a per-user basis, he added, comparable to the fees charged for the Moviefone telephone service and the Movielink Web site, which run about $150 for every 1,000 people. Other studios signed so far, Mr. Blumberg said, include the Columbia and Tristar units of the Sony Corporation and the New Line Cinema and Warner Brothers units of Time Warrner Inc. As for the public service on-line ad initiative, details are to be announced on Wednesday by the Ad Council, the nonprofit organization that coordinates pro bono campaigns for the agency and media industries, and the Internet Ad Bureau, an industry association with more than 200 members. The initiative, named the Online Public Service Network, will seek to automate delivery of pro bono banner ads so the council can become one of the largest advertisers on the Internet. The banners will offer links to Web sites of council causes like the Coalition for America's Children (www.kidscampaign.org) and the use of safety belts (www.nhtsa.dot.gov). The network's goal is an estimated $15 million in donated ad space annually. New media will be asked to donate 5 percent of their ad inventory to the council's public service announcements. The initiative will supplement pro bono efforts by Internet companies like Double Click Inc., which donates banner space on the more than 70 Web sites for which it sells advertising.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
A Clinton adviser argues the economic case for self-regulation of sales pitches in cyberspace.
body: THE Clinton Administration's point person on Internet issues is lobbying Madison Avenue to help insure that a policy providing for the self-regulation of cyberspace -- including sales pitches aimed at children -- withstands strong, sustained challenges. "What you are doing is essential to the success of the Administration's strategy," Ira C. Magaziner, senior adviser to President Clinton for policy development, said yesterday at a conference about youngsters and on-line advertising. "The tremendous economic benefits of the Internet will not work if we don't get efficient industry self-regulation on issues like privacy and content, especially in the children's area." "If you fail, we will have to go the legislative route," he added. "That gets caught up in the political process and will be less rational and efficient." About 100 people heard Mr. Magaziner as he gave the keynote address at the conference, held at the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan. The conference was sponsored by the Children's Advertising Review Unit, an organization that is part of the longtime voluntary self-regulatory process of adjudicating advertising disputes. In April, the children's unit issued voluntary guidelines on Internet marketing to junior consumers. That has become a contentious topic, with parents complaining about what they perceive as disingenuous appeals to their sons and daughters for data in exchange for trinkets or email signed by cartoon characters. The guidelines include recommendations that advertisers disclose why they are requesting information from children and what will be done with it. Three months after the guidelines were issued, President Clinton disclosed his worldwide economic commerce strategy, which was based on a position paper from a task force headed by Mr. Magaziner. The position paper was surprising for its forthright advocacy of self-regulation instead of governmental intervention, primarily because Mr. Magaziner was the architect of the Clinton health care plan, which failed after being criticized for relying too heavily on regulatory bureaucracy. One reason that cyberspace warrants a laissez-faire approach, Mr. Magaziner said, is that "interactivity gives you the unique ability to empower people, parents, schools and libraries to protect themselves." Mr. Magaziner acknowledged that there had been protests about the new policy. "People say: 'You're just being a shill. You're leaving the Internet open to let industry do all this terrible marketing to children,' " he said. " 'How can you do that, particularly as Democrats?' " "People get afraid of change," he said, "afraid of something their kids understand better than them." But, Mr. Magaziner asserted, he is responding to a larger, more damaging fear, which has hampered the growth of "the new digital economy": the fear that "governments would step in and overregulate, overtax and overcensor the Internet and strangle development." Electronic commerce will be "the engine of growth for the world economy and the U.S. econony in the next quarter-century," he added, saying, "If we get in and regulate it, we'll just mess it up." Those who want to police on-line content should "look to the private sector for the means," Mr. Magaziner said, perhaps in the form of "brand-name filters," software developed by organizations like the Children's Television Workshop or the Christian Coalition. He added that it was "essential that children's privacy be protected and children not be exploited, that information is not gained from children without parental permission." Asked by a member of the audience if that was a "practical impossibility," he replied: "When a C.E.O. really wants to do something, then it gets done. What we are saying to C.E.O.'s is that if you think the Internet will be a business opportunity, make this a priority." The Children's Advertising Review Unit is administered by the National Advertising Review Council, formed by the Council of Better Business Bureaus and three organizations: the American Advertising Federation, the American Association of Advertising Agencies and the Association of National Advertisers. On-line ads for children "offer some exciting opportunities for creativity and innovation," said Walter J. O'Brien, president of the review council and vice president of the Better Business Bureaus, but the "consequences of even a small misstep can be significant." "Are we up to the challenge Ira issued today?" he asked. "I think we are, but if we aren't, we'll get beaten down" by Government regulation. Mr. O'Brien said he would pursue a request from Mr. Magaziner that the children's unit ask the European Union to follow the American de minimis approach to Internet regulation, rather than adopt Government strictures. Elizabeth Lascoutx, vice president and director for the children's unit, said the voluntary guidelines had worked well since April, adding that "we're working on about 30" questions about on-line children's ads. "The real challenge," Ms. Lascoutx said, "is that a lot of Web publishers and developers don't come out of advertising. Though they're responsive when we get to them, they don't have any background on self-regulation." Jeffrey Perlman, senior vice president for government affairs at the American Advertising Federation, said he saw a similar problem in dealing with World Wide Web sites put up by fans or entrepreneurs who advertise, promote or sell popular toys and collectibles. "They're people who don't intend to do anything wrong," he said, "but they don't know what to do."

title: Delays, Glitches, Unanswered Calls, but Nothing Like 1987
body: On the first day in history that the newyork Stock Exchange handled more than one billion shares, small investors bumped up against agonizing delays in getting through to their brokers. But it sure beat banging their heads against the unbreachable wall of silence that greeted desperate sellers in the crash of 1987. The difference was that, this time, brokerage firms were better prepared for the onslaught of orders. More people were ready to man more phones, and on-line systems that did not exist a decade ago processed a huge number of trades. But 1.2 billion shares is a lot -- and glitches abounded. "I've been waiting for this moment to do some bargain buying, and I wasn't able to," said Matthew Barlow, an investor in newyork. He was unable to connect to his Internet trading account with Fidelity Investments. The phone line to reach a broker was busy, and even the touch-tone trading system crashed, he said. "I was so frustrated I left work and went to the Fidelity investor center on Park Avenue and they said they couldn't help me because they couldn't get through either," he said. Investors throughout the country had similar experiences. Telephone lines at big discount brokerage firms were backed up, especially at the beginning of the day. At Charles Schwab & Company, customers who could get through on the telephone spent as much as 25 minutes on hold. Other customers simply heard busy signals. Over all, Schwab handled 300,000 trades and another 1.2 million inquiries. Fidelity answered a record 700,000 calls on Monday and more than that yesterday, shifting hundreds of employees from other duties to handle the crush. Last night, for the second straight night, however, Fidelity was unable to calculate closing prices for many of its stock funds by the deadline required to include them in newspaper tables. A Fidelity spokesman attributed the problem to the heavy trading and large movements in the prices of many securities. Stockbrokers took longer to deal with clients' calls because their firm's computers were bogged down. Smith Barney even turned off its system for nearly half an hour in the middle of the day to switch to a system that could handle higher volume. And the Internet trading systems, which have promised investors more immediacy and control, rebuffed some orders with cryptic messages like "server not available." On-line brokerage offerings from Charles Schwab, Fidelity Investments, E*Trade Group and Ameritrade all said they suffered from at least some delays yesterday. The heavy volume overwhelmed a Nasdaq computer system at 3:17 P.M., and from then until the close Nasdaq work stations -- the machines brokers use -- did not show correct last-sale prices for Nasdaq stocks, although such information was available on other machines. But none of those services calculate Nasdaq index figures on their own, relying instead on the Nasdaq computer that was overwhelmed. It was more than two hours after the market closed before Nasdaq was able to calculate the levels of its indexes. The final figure showed the Nasdaq composite up 67.93, to 1,603.02. "Nasdaq got backed up with orders," said Timothy McCarthy, president of Charles Schwab. "We had delays in getting our orders back." He said that generally the newyork Stock Exchange was able to keep up with the record volume. Other brokerage firms said, however, that while exchange trades were executed on time, there were delays of up to an hour in getting confirmations. Despite the delays, the executives of many brokerage firms expressed satisfaction that investors fared better yesterday than they did in 1987, when trading was backed up for hours and unanswered telephones were even far more prevalent. "If it wasn't for all the technology, there is no way we could have handled all the volume we did," Mr. McCarthy said. Schwab, for example, now handles half its transactions using computers or touch-tone phones, systems that were not available 10 years ago. Even though some customers complained that they could not log into on-line trading systems, other brokerage firms also expressed satisfaction that they handled as much volume as they did. "It's been awesome," said Kathy Evinson, president of E*Trade Group, which handled more than 40,000 trades Tuesday, nearly double its usual volume. "By 10:30 we executed 8,000 trades, close to our normal volume for the day," said Joseph A. Konen, president of Ameritrade Holding Corporation, an Omaha discount brokerage company. Ms. Evinson of E*Trade said that many of the problems that its customers experienced could be traced to the precarious nature of the Internet. One customer suffered delays because his Internet service provider sent his trades through 18 different networks before they reached E*Trade's computers.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: ON THE NET;
Many users of commercial on-line services are getting a steady diet of 'spam.'
body: Make Money Fast By Sending Unsolicited Commercial Advertisements on the Internet! Explore Your Sexual Fantasies, Wearing Only a Credit Card! Learn How YOU Can Make $$$ Running Pyramid Schemes Via email! Such is the tenor -- or nearly so -- of millions of unsolicited, commercial email messages sent each day to the electronic mailboxes of Internet and on-line service subscribers. Computer users, especially those on popular services like America Online, complain that junk email has overtaken their systems. Internet service providers confirm that the problem is getting worse, with the volume of unsolicited commercial email, especially the indiscriminate, automated bulk mailings known on the Internet as "spam," growing at an exponential rate. "At the time the Federal Trade Commission held its workshop on unsolicited commercial email in June, I was receiving three or so unwanted messages a day," said Deirdre Mulligan, staff counsel for the Center for Democracy and Technology, a public interest group in Washington. "Now, I'm getting 15 to 20 a day, and I'm not even on AOL." George Vradenburg, vice president and general counsel at America Online, said that on some days, as much as 30 percent of the eight million to nine million email messages arriving at America Online from the Internet were spam. Last Friday, the company filed suit against Prime Data Systems of Bowling Green, Ky., which it said not only spams but also sells software tools that permit others to send millions of unsolicited messages a day. Aside from annoying many people, the real problems with spam, some Internet experts say, involve the traffic jams and computer crashes it can cause. The problem has grown so acute that even some of the most vociferous opponents of Government regulation of the Internet are now hoping for legislative relief. Four bills intended to ban or regulate junk email have been introduced in Congress in the last six months. Among the states, more than a dozen bills, including one in the newyork Senate, have been offered. And the Federal Trade Commission and has commissioned a study of possible solutions. Some Internet service providers have begun to refuse to relay messages originating from certain computers known to be heavy extruders of spam. But the tactic threatens to alter the very nature of the Internet, which grew into a powerful communications medium on the fundamental premise of computers on the network freely handling and forwarding one another's messages. "That's what the Internet is all about -- using other people's services," said Peter Kennedy, a First Amendment and Internet specialist at George, Donaldson & Ford, a law firm in Austin, Tex., that is representing plaintiffs in a lawsuit against an alleged spammer in California. "That's where the tension arises. The Texas case, which goes to trial next month, sheds behind-the-scenes light on spam. According to the lawsuit, Craig Nowak, a student in San Diego, used one of the automated spamming software programs now widely available on line to send out thousands of random email solicitations offering "Free Grant Money." For a $19.95 "application fee," the suit said, Mr. Nowak offered to match customers with private foundations that make cash grants. What the customers received was a form letter and a photocopied list of foundations. Because people change email addresses often, bulk email lists have a high percentage of invalid addresses. When a message is sent to an invalid address, it is "bounced" back to the machine that sent it. Spammers do not want to deal with the return of thousands of invalid messages, so they typically forge a return email address. According to the lawsuit, Mr. Nowak forged -- apparently at random -- a return address using the Internet domain "flowers.com." It was a bad choice. The flowers.com domain is owned by Tracy LaQuey Parker of Austin, whose 1992 book "The Internet Companion" was one of the first popular guides to the Internet. On April Fool's Day, allegedly after one of Mr. Nowak's mailings, a deluge of bounced messages and complaints to flowers.com overwhelmed the computers of Mr. Parker's Internet host, Zilker Internet Park. Smoot Carl-Mitchell, Zilker's president at the time, said he was forced to shut down Zilker's systems for half a day, blocking all email for more than 1,000 customers. It took him a week to patch the system and fully recover, Mr. Carl-Mitchell said. He joined Ms. Parker, her business partners and two Texas Internet associations in filing the lawsuit, which asks for unspecified damages for electronic trespass and harmful entry by computer. Mr. Nowak's telephone went unanswered last week, when calls were placed seeking comment. Then there is Sanford Wallace, the self-proclaimed "King of Spam" whose Cyber Promotions Inc., based in Dresher, Pa., generated millions of unsolicited messages a day -- until he was summarily cut off from the Internet late last week by the lone remaining service that provided a pipeline for his bulk-mail customers. Apex Global Internet Systems of Dearborn, Mich., had suspended Mr. Wallace's operations for three weeks last month before a district court judge ordered Apex to restore service to Cyber Promotions through Oct. 16. "They pulled the plug at midnight" on the 17th, Mr. Wallace snarled last Friday. Having been booted by Apex, Compuserve and America Online, among others, Mr. Wallace said he was now plotting with several large spam factories, including Quantum Communications of New Hampshire, to get financing to create their own Internet backbone service. If they are successful, this spam cartel would create a haven for bulk mailers and insure a steady, uninterruptible flow of spam to millions of Internet users. "It would be much more difficult to oust us from cyberspace because we would be part of the infrastructure," Mr. Wallace said. Graphic   Drawing. (Randy Jones)

title:
The Ultimate Obsession;
What Will People Pay to Enter His World?
body: Entering the three-story foyer of Richard Garriot's hilltop estate is a short trip into another dimension. The high walls are covered with crossbows and other menacing medieval weapons, overhead is an imposing astronomical observatory. At eye level, there is a bullet hole in the staircase. But then, none of this is unexpected, for inside the insular computing gaming world Mr. Garriot, the creator of the popular 18-year-old Ultima series of Dungeons and Dragons-style computer games, has a reputation for building elaborate and compelling fantasy worlds. Now, with a new game on the market, he is poised to benefit from both the rise of the Internet and the rapid growth in popularity of multiplayer personal computer games. He is, in fact, quickly becoming the George Lucas of a business that is capturing an increasingly mainstream following. And, like some Hollywood figures, he is also attracting unwanted attention from everyone from conservative religious groups that believe his fantasy world to be a form of Satanism to obsessive fans, one of whom made his way into Mr, Garriot's Gothic foyer in the middle of the night not long ago, dodging into a side room to hide when Mr. Garriot fired his Uzi submachine gun at the staircase (hence the bullet hole). At the age of 36, Mr. Garriot finds himself in the midst of two trends that are changing the world of entertainment -- and that investors in companies like Electronic Arts, which publishes his work, hope will raise the value of their holdings. On one hand, he is in a business whose audiences are still growing, while those of broadcast television and the movies, are beginning to thin. On the other, the semi-solitary computer games, even highly successful ones like Myst and its successor, Riven, are beginning to find their popularity equaled or overtaken by multiplayer on-line games. This month, Mr. Garriot, who is the son of an astronaut and an artist and who wrote his first computer game when he was 15, has embarked on his boldest experiment yet in creating a world that blends fantasy computer games, the Internet and a mass audience. In three weeks, he has sold nearly 40,000 units of Ultima Online, currently the world's largest multiplayer game, which sells for $64.95. And as many as 9,000 players were recorded playing the game simultaneously on some evenings. Ultima Online, the ninth in a series of the computer adventures designed by Mr. Garriot stretching back to 1979, has almost instantaneously become what the company contends is the world's largest multiplayer computer game. Set in the fictional kingdom of Britannia, the game lures thousands of computer players to wander its cities, forests and seas simultaneously. It is an immense virtual play world, which would require 38,000 computer monitors stacked together to view simultaneously -- an expanse the size of a football field. Electronic Arts, the San Mateo, Calif., computer game company that acquired Origin Systems for $30 million in 1992, said last week that the game had quickly become its fastest-selling computer game ever. The company shipped 50,000 copies to unitedstates software retail stores at the end of September. It plans to ship 65,000 more copies next month. "This is a harbinger of things to come," said Nicholas Donatiello Jr., president of Odyssey L.P. in San Francisco. There are certainly still skeptics, who argue that the computer game business will remain child's play, but the numbers so far paint a promising picture. The combined sales of video games, computer games and arcades are forecast by the Interactive Digital Software Association to reach $5.3 billion in 1997, compared with about $5 billion for Hollywood's box office movie revenues. More important, the early success of Ultima is being taken as a sign in the computer game industry that the Internet is arriving as a standard feature built in to all computer games. The newest Ultima is representative of a dramatic shift in the computer gaming world where a still mostly male audience that once pitted its skills solely against software now finds it is immersed in a universe that science fiction writer William Gibson once referred to as a "collective hallucination." For the thousands of computer gamers who have for years followed the serial-style computer disk adventures that Mr. Garriot has designed, Ultima Online has become an overnight phenomenon. The game now has 38,000 registered users who have signed up to pay $9.95 a month. More startling, the game's average individual playing time has so far been six hours a day. And the percentage of registered users playing at any one time has averaged 25 to 30 percent -- far higher than usual. "For the people it appeals to, this is an incredibly immersive experience," said Larry Marcus, a consumer electronics industry analyst at BT Alex. Brown in San Francisco. For those like Mr. Garriot who are designing this new entertainment medium, there are still many unknowns. Although entertainment is universally viewed as the Next Big Thing on the Internet, no one is certain yet of the formula for success. Game developers acknowledge that there is a great deal of consumer resistance to paying an hourly fee for playing. Other major competitors in the on-line gaming world have taken different approaches. The Microsoft Corporation and Mpath Interactive, one of a number of start-up companies offering Internet gaming, each maintain a free area alongside an enhanced service for which they charge $29.95 a year. Total Entertainment Network, a San Francisco-based start-up game site, recently lowered its monthly flat fee from $29.95 to $19.95. On the other hand, 3DO, which helped pioneer commercial role-playing games with Meridian 59, recently changed its pricing from $9.95 a month to $2.49 daily. Electronic Arts, the nation's largest software game company, with 1996 revenue of $661.9 million and stock trading in the low 30's, acknowledges that it is cautiously watching Ultima Online for an indication of what might be possible in the Internet gaming world. Electronic Arts has set up powerful server computers made by Sun Microsystems, which host the game environment at six locations around the unitedstates, offering different "worlds" for computer gamers to travel in. Electronic Arts executives said the company was scrambling to set up more host computers even as it was trying to guess what the total number of users would eventually be. Spurred to date mostly by word-of-mouth inside the computer gaming community, Ultima Online is well regarded by industry analysts. "What's needed is these large-scale experiments," David Cole, at DFC Intelligence in San Diego, said. "If it's a success, it's great; if not, it's an R and D expense." Mr. Marcus said: "It's true that the best-selling PC game this Christmas will be Riven and it will be single player. But the No. 2 game will be Quake II and it will offer an Internet play feature." He added that multiplayer games were quickly becoming the standard for all top-selling games. For Mr. Garriot, who plays the role of an imaginary ruler, Lord British, in his games, Ultima Online is an avenue to extend an interactive storytelling medium he began perfecting as a high school student in Houston when he convinced his teachers to give him a foreign language credit for studying the BASIC computer language. The son of the physicist and astronaut Owen Garriot, who flew aboard Columbia in 1983, he went to his mother Helen, who is divorced and now works as a public-school art teacher in Enid, Okla., and asked her how to draw perspective for his games. He got help from his father in understanding the math underlying the perspective in drawing so that he could build it into the programming instructions for his games. In an era of Dungeons and Dragons-style board games, Mr. Garriot's first commercial game, "Akalabeth," became an instant hit in the fledgling software game business. At the age of 18, with the help of a California software company, he sold 35,000 copies of the game, earning $150,000 before he had completed his first year at the University of Texas. In 1983, Mr. Garriot started Origin Systems with his brother Robert, who had earned a master's in business administration from the Sloan School of Management at Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Perhaps better than any other computer game, the Ultima series has managed to embody the story-telling qualities that are the goal of the new computerized medium that is neither book nor movie. His first games had a simple theme that he now describes as, " 'You're the hero, now go kill the bad guys.' It was a poor concept and it's a boring story." Clad in jeans and sporting a long thin pony tail with a beeper and cell phone clipped to his belt, Mr. Garriot displayed a bulky sheaf of letters he said are representative of the thousands he has received from Ultima players, and in some cases their parents over the years. With Ultima IV, he changed his thrust and added social commentary to the plot, making a goal of the game achieving "the eight virtues of the avatar." The game quickly became a hit, selling more than 100,000 copies in 1984. Since then he has continued his experiments with different social themes in the games. With the first multiplayer version of the Ultima series, Mr. Garriot acknowledges that he has added an unpredictable element to his fantasy -- other human beings.
