title: $1.3 Billion McAfee Deal To Flesh Out Software Line
body: McAfee Associates Inc., continuing its aggressive drive to become a powerhouse in computer networking software, said today that it had agreed to buy the Network General Corporation for $1.3 billion in stock. The combined company, to be called Network Associates Inc., would be the 10th-largest software vendor and would offer almost every software product needed to keep corporate computer networks free of viruses and intrusion by hackers. In the last four years, McAfee has used acquisitions to grow from a publisher of cheap antivirus software to one of the biggest suppliers of sophisticated network management and security products. "They've had an unbelievable knack for timely, synergistic, high-yield acquisitions," said John Powers, an analyst at the BancAmerica Robertson Stephens investment bank in San Francisco. "I'm pretty enthusiastic about this deal." Under the terms of the transaction, McAfee would offer 0.4167 of a share, worth about $27.66, for each share of Network General. In Nasdaq trading today, shares of McAfee gained $2, to $66.375, while Network General's stock was up $2.50, to $23.375. McAfee, based in Santa Clara, Calif., said that it did not expect the acquisition to dilute its earnings and that it expected savings in operation costs, but did not specify them. Executives of McAfee said it was too early to tell whether jobs would be cut. The companies have few products that overlap. McAfee specializes in antivirus, network security and help-desk programs, while Network General, based in Menlo Park, Calif., specializes in diagnostic and performance-monitoring products. Executives said the combined product line would make it easier for technicians on help desks to manage huge networks running on the Microsoft Corporation's Windows NT networking software. "Network Associates has two emerging business opportunities, the Windows NT help-desk space and network security solutions," said William L. Larson, McAfee's chief executive. "We have a strong wind in our sales in this marketplace." Mr. Larson said that based on the surging popularity of Windows NT and the need for management tools, his company's revenue could rise between 30 percent and 40 percent for the next few years. Their combined net income for the most recent fiscal years would have been $130 million on revenue of $612 million. Mr. Larson will be chief executive and chairman of the new company. Leslie G. Denend, chief executive of Network General, will be president.

title:
Business Travel;
A special cell phone lets users far away tap into data from their own PC's and the Internet.
body: A NEW cellular phone service introduced by the Wireless Services division of AT&T this week offers access to a broad spectrum of information to help travelers. Called Pocketnet, the service gives users remote wireless access to selected data from their own personal computers and from more than 20 providers of Internet content. The cost is $29.99 a month, plus standard cellular voice service fees and activation charges. Users will also need a special cellular telephone made by Mitsubishi or Samsung; the phones have a list price of $299. Providers of travel-related Internet content that are working with Pocketnet include Accuweather, American Weather Concepts, Biztravel.com, Festivals.com, Internet Restaurant Guide, Mapquest, the Trip.com, Travelocity and Weather Underground. Each is offering data from its Web site that it regards as most useful to business travelers; Travelocity, for example, is featuring airline schedules of all carriers listed in the Sabre reservations system, as well as arrival and departure and gate information for 10 unitedstates and overseas airlines. Other participating content providers specialize in business, sports and general news. AT&T is selling Pocketnet service in 22 cellular markets nationwide, including Dallas, Miami, newyork and San Francisco; subscribers can use it in about 70 of the top 100 unitedstates cellular markets. It is not yet available in several cities, including Atlanta and Los Angeles.  Rewards at Shangri-La Shangri-La Hotels and Resorts, which owns and manages 35 hotels and resorts in Asia, is rolling out its first loyalty program. Called Golden Circle, the program has three levels of participation, with the top two levels requiring 10 and 25 annual stays, respectively. All participants stay on designated floors and have special check-in and checkout procedures. The amenities include continental breakfasts; fresh fruit; newspapers; free stays by spouses, and credits in frequent-flier programs, which vary according to level of participation. Second-tier members receive other benefits, including 6 P.M. check-out; guaranteed room availability for reservations made 72 hours in advance, and refreshments upon arrival, like milk and cookies, beer or chocolate. Top-tier members are also eligible for 8 A.M. check-in; a free suite upgrade, if available, and wine or champagne. Robert Hutchinson, Shangri-La's senior vice president of marketing, said the company had delayed starting a loyalty program until it had upgraded its reservations system so that it could track guests' personal preferences. Guests at Shangri-La through the end of this year will receive a membership application on arrival. Open enrollment via a direct-mail campaign will begin in January.  Airline Update For a few weeks, participants in T.W.A.'s frequent-flier program will receive two miles for each dollar spent using an American Express card to buy full-fare coach, business or first-class tickets on the airline. In effect from next Wednesday through Nov. 15, the promotion coincides with T.W.A.'s entry into the American Express Membership Rewards loyalty program. U S Airways now permits users of Priority Travel Works, its personal on-line reservation service, to redeem frequent-flier miles on line for travel in the continental unitedstates. Air New Zealand has introduced in-flight amenity kits for passengers in the business and first-class sectons. The kits provide several aromatherapy products, including five gels, an eye compress and a facial spray mist. United Airlines, part of the UAL Corporation, is now offering electronic ticketing on all of its nonstop flights between the unitedstates and London. Tickets can be bought directly from the airline or from a unitedstates-based travel agency.  Check-in, security and customs procedures are the same as for passengers with paper tickets. Holders of electronic tickets must check in with their passport and ticket receipt and with the credit card used to purchase the ticket, if it was booked by phone with the airline. United is also issuing duplicate receipts and itineraries, if desired, as well as a copy of the Warsaw Convention articles that govern international travel, information that normally appears on paper tickets.

title: America Online Turns to TV as a Model
body: Starting next week, America Online will begin overhauling its service in an effort to attract another two million to three million subscribers during the next year. The ambitious growth plan is intended to strengthen America Online's role as the main gateway to cyberspace for the nation's households, enabling the company to charge more for advertising and on-line banners with links to other Web sites. The changes in America Online are being announced today, and the on-line service's nine million current subscribers will notice the difference beginning next Monday, as new features are introduced gradually. The revised service will include a streamlined group of more prominently displayed "channels," each based on subjects of interest like sports, workplace and families and life styles. In addition, the featured offerings on America Online will be revised six times a day, adopting television-style programming categories like "good morning," "prime time" and "late night." The specially promoted offerings will be displayed on AOL Today, a kind of front page for the service. The drift toward a television model, analysts say, is a clear sign of the influence of Robert W. Pittman, the 42-year-old former MTV chief, who joined America Online nearly a year ago. He is president and chief executive of the company's main division, America Online Networks, which runs the on-line service. To grow further, America Online must lure newcomers, many of whom do not yet have personal computers at home. "The company now has to go after the real mass-market, couch-potato crowd," noted Brian Oakes, an analyst at Lehman Brothers. "So Pittman is making America Online more and more like a TV network." As a media executive, Mr. Pittman helped create the MTV and VH1 cable television channels. Later, he ran Six Flags amusement parks for Time Warner Inc., which eventually sold the business, and then became chief executive of the Century 21 Real Estate Corporation. All of his experience, Mr. Pittman says, is as a consumer marketer. And the early lesson to be taken from the nascent field of information and entertainment in cyberspace, he adds, is that it is a consumer-brand and media business, not a technology business. When Mr. Pittman came to America Online a year ago, he recalled, industry analysts were saying that the on-line service was in trouble. A key reason, they said, was that America Online's subscribers would increasingly graduate to more sophisticated Internet service providers to get direct access to the World Wide Web. "The so-called industry experts were absolutely wrong," Mr. Pittman said last Friday during an interview at the company's headquarters in Dulles, Va. "What is and will continue to drive this industry is simplicity, not complexity. What's wrong with on line? It's still too complex." The redesigned America Online, he notes, is based on extensive consumer research, much of it culled from the comments and complaints fielded by America Online's 5,000 customer service representatives. The No. 1 reason subscribers cancel their accounts, Mr. Pittman said, is that "they can't figure it out." With its simplified channel orientation, the redesign is intended to increase use by making the system easier to navigate. Each of the channels will also have a first screen, or front page, featuring current stories. On the lower left of the screen will be space for four banners, or links to related new-media Web sites. America Online is selling those placements as prime real estate in cyberspace, especially since 55 percent of all time spent on line or on the Web by households is by America Online subscribers. Customers will be able to use the new channel format starting next week. Later, they will be able to download an upgraded version of the service's underlying software, called AOL 4.0, which will include a tighter integration of the on-line service with the Internet. For example, in a box near the top of the screen, a user can insert either an America Online keyword or a Web address and the software will find it. The software rollout will come more gradually, extending into spring of next year in some regional markets. The phased introduction is a lesson learned from its traffic jams earlier this year, resulting in complaints and lawsuits, after the company moved to flat-rate pricing of $19.95 a month. "After those problems, one thing we learned is don't do anything significant all at once," Mr. Pittman said.

title:
Updates/Media and Technology;
Software to Track Business Prospects By Web Visits
body: One of the biggest fetters on the growth of advertising on the World Wide Web has been advertisers' uncertainty about how many people are actually seeing the banners and other visual gadgets they are spending to promote. Many Internet service providers and big organizations that provide access to cyberspace make copies of popular Web pages, like Yahoo (http://www.yahoo.com), for instance, and serve them up to their users instead of having them clog the Internet with repeated requests for the same material. The problem is that to the administrators of the Web page, the copying seems to be a single visit when the page may eventually be seen by thousands of people. That practice, known as caching, has disturbed advertisers and people who sell advertising on line because they have little way of knowing what they are getting (or selling) for their money. This week, a small company called Matchlogic Inc. (http://www.matchlogic.com) plans to introduce software that it says will solve the problem, allowing accurate counts of how many people see a Web ad. The software has the backing of a giant advertiser, General Motors, and of the Audit Bureau of Circulations, which certifies the reliability of circulation figures of printed publications and now of Web sites. "We went in and did a review of their technology and after agreeing that their technology did what they were claiming it did, we are now in the process of setting up to audit it," said Dick Bennett, the bureau's senior vice president for audit services. Philip Guarascio, vice president and general manager for marketing and advertising of General Motors' North American operations, said, "This technology is going to give us what we think is the most accurate headcount, and that will let us evaluate our current and future investments more accurately."   SETH SCHIESEL

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
New in ad sales cyberspace, the Softbank Network will cover topics from sports to travel.
body: A LEADING Internet advertising sales agent will offer another way to buy sales pitches in cyberspace. Softbank Interactive Marketing is scheduled to introduce today the Softbank Network, which will peddle advertising space on smaller, specialized Web sites grouped by content topics like sports and travel. The Softbank Network is meant to complement the company's Foundation Buy, which for more than a year has handled ad sales for big, popular sites with content of more general interest, including those operated by Fox News, Lycos, Netscape, Playboy and TV Guide. "We've been focused on one main product line, the Foundation Buy, representing on an exclusive basis large branded Web sites," said Caroline Vanderlip, chief executive of Softbank Interactive Marketing in newyork. "The Softbank Network becomes a second major line that aggregates advertising inventory from a variety of sites." The Softbank startup is indicative of the changes that are rapidly remaking the interactive ad field. Industry analysts have been predicting the rise of additional ad sales networks so advertisers can more easily reach computer users and so smaller sites can attract sufficient ad revenue to remain competitive with giant rivals. "These are sites that because of their size can't afford a sales infrastructure," Ms. Vanderlip said, adding: "We're not talking about Ma's Home Page. They're solid editorial environments with terrific content. By banding together, they can maximize revenue opportunities." The Softbank Network will become the ad sales representative for 30 Web sites with 45 million impressions or page views a month, a figure that Ms. Vanderlip predicted would reach 100 million a month by the start of 1998. By comparison, the 12 sites represented by the Foundation Buy now have 1.2 billion impressions or page views a month. "You can buy ad space on ZD Net, with 60 million impressions a month," said Ms. Vanderlip, referring to a technology site (www.zdnet.com) available through the Foundation Buy. "Or you could buy the technology portfolio of the Softbank Network, which includes sites strong in technology -- though not necessarily with the same brand awareness -- that together have eight million impressions a month." In addition to technology, sports and travel, the other portfolios or content groups are: arts and entertainment, college, finance and investing and games. Advertisers can also buy the entire network. "The Softbank Network creates a turnkey method for advertisers to reach their core audiences across many sites," said Doug Wintz, vice president for network development at Softbank Interactive Marketing. Among those sites are: Electric Library, a research site (www.electriclibrary.com); Fastweb, a scholarship data base search engine for college-bound students (www.fastweb.com); Games Mania, where computer games can be played (www.gamesmania.com), and PC Quote, for investors (www.pcquote.com). And the Softbank Network offers what Mary Winston, vice president for advertising operations, described as "certain targeting capabilities, by day of week, time of day, continent, country, state or operating system; someone can make sure an ad is delivered only to those with Macintosh computers at home." In selling ad space grouped by content, the Softbank Network follows in the cybersteps of Double Click, an interactive ad network based in newyork that offers categories like business, news, search engines and sports. "It was the recognition that in some cases advertisers were asking for more targeted editorial content," Ms. Vanderlip said. For the sites represented by the Softbank Network, Softbank Interactive Marketing will charge 40 percent commissions, compared with 15 to 30 percent commissions for sites on the Foundation Buy. That reflects the additional services the company will provide the smaller sites, which larger sites handle in-house; those include auditing, billing and inventory management. The Softbank Network will be sold by the 50 employees of Softbank Interactive Marketing, based in offices in 12 cities in America, Australia and Europe in addition to the company's newyork headquarters. Softbank Interactive Marketing was formed in April 1996 by the Ziff-Davis Publishing Company, Interactive Marketing Inc. and Network 1.0. Softbank Holdings Inc., part of the Softbank Corporation of Japan, is the majority investor in Softbank Interactive Marketing.

title: What's Left for AOL?
body: America Online's acquisition of Compuserve's customer base is a smart strategic move because it allows America Online to expand its reach while eliminating its chief rival. But the deal, which also includes the sale of America Online's transmission network, doesn't address looming hurdles. The most serious of these may be potential competition from bare-bones email and Internet service providers. Buying Compuserve's on-line service from the long-distance phone company Worldcom will raise America Online's subscriber base to 11.6 million from 9 million. Though America Online says it plans to keep the two services separate for now, the company clearly expects advertisers to notice its combined numbers. Its closest rival, the Microsoft Network, has 2.3 million subscribers. The big question is whether America Online will be able to hold on to its subscribers over the long haul. In effect, America Online acts as a middleman between the World Wide Web and the operating system, or desktop, on a personal computer. That's appealing for some people, especially those who are new to the Internet. But as more people become familiar with navigating the World Wide Web, they may not feel they need America Online to organize what's out there for them. Moreover, they may choose to avoid the advertising they get on America Online, a barrage that is sure to increase, by signing up with a local basic Internet access provider instead. America Online now gets 15 percent of its revenue from advertising and commerce -- on-line hawking. Over the next few years, it wants to raise that share to 50 percent. But computer users who just want to check their email may decide that they're just not going to wait for another advertisement to download. America Online maintains that what distinguishes it from other providers is that it offers exclusive content -- like on-line bookstores, magazines and financial advisers -- as well as a place to hang out. Some subscribers do sign on for those services. And by selling off its transmission network, America Online is sending a message that its main business will be media and entertainment, rather than telecommunications. But the fun house of novelties under the America Online tent -- the chat rooms, the treasure hunts, the celebrity "appearances" -- won't keep many of us. My computer-savvy friends laugh at me when I give them my America Online email address -- or when I call them an hour after sending mail to find out whether they've received it. America Online isn't the only on-line service that has had a problem with slow email. But it does seem to bear the brunt of people's frustrations, perhaps because it has more subscribers than anyone else. Of the monthly $20 that America Online charges subscribers for unlimited use, a couple of dollars is enough to cover the company's telecommunications expenses. This suggests there is potential for a price war for basic email and Internet service. The Baby Bells and long-distance giants, like AT&T and MCI, have only dabbled in offering email accounts. But when the time is right, they may try to crash America Online's party. Then there is the potential competition from a whole new category of information appliances. Low-cost Web phones and network computers, like WebTV, include their own on-line services. If, as some expect, people lease these devices directly from telecommunications companies, they'll be bypassing America Online. The lesson? In high technology, no company is big enough to rest.

title:
Market Place;
Latest Cyberdeal Seems to Have Room for Two Winners
body: Follow the money in yesterday's big Internet deal -- an intricate transaction involving Worldcom, Compuserve and America Online -- and it seems that the real value lies in the dull plumbing of cyberspace, not the glamour of new media. Worldcom Inc., the nation's fourth-largest long-distance phone company, agreed to pay about $1.2 billion in stock for the Compuserve Corporation. It will keep the under-the-hood side of Compuserve's business, managing data networks and providing data services for big corporate clients. In the next step of the deal, Worldcom will sell Compuserve's well-known but struggling on-line service to America Online for the equivalent of $250 million. In short, the plumbing of Compuserve, which is controlled by H & R Block, is worth nearly $1 billion, while its on-line service amounts to pocket change by comparison. Shares of Worldcom rose sharply yesterday, up $2.25, to $33.75, and were the most actively traded, with nearly 14.6 million changing hands. But if Worldcom jumped, then America Online shares soared, closing up $6.125, to $76.0625. The enthusiasm was not only because America Online had cut a good deal, but also because the acquisition should help it further a strategy of becoming a genuine media company -- and one able to draw more revenue from advertising and electronic commerce like on-line shopping. Advertising and commerce now account for about 15 percent of America Online's revenues -- up from next to nothing a couple of years ago -- with the rest coming from monthly subscription fees. The company wants to see the advertising and marketing revenues rise sharply in the coming years, toward the level of 50 percent. The key to attracting advertising dollars is building an audience on the scale provided by mainstream media. And America Online certainly appears well on its way. Today, it is by far the largest on-line service, with 9 million subscribers. By purchasing Compuserve, the second-largest on-line service, America Online, which is based in Dulles, Va., would add 2.6 million more subscribers worldwide. That would lengthen America Online's already yawning lead over its nearest remaining rival, the Microsoft Network, which has 2.3 million subscribers. "The next stage of the Internet economy is that the media companies will start to make money, not just the infrastructure suppliers as has been the case until now," said Kate Delhagen, an analyst at Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. "America Online is taking a leading role in that development, and acquiring Compuserve is a big step ahead," Ms. Delhagen said. "You assemble an audience of more than 10 million subscribers, and Madison Avenue has to pay attention." In the deal, America Online is increasing its focus as a media company not only by adding subscribers, but also by selling its ANS Communications unit to Worldcom. Less than three years ago, America Online bought ANS, once the Internet's network backbone and run by the National Science Foundation. America Online paid $35 million for ANS, seeking greater vertical integration and less dependence on major telecommunications companies. Today, the ANS investment seems to have been a particularly shrewd one for America Online, and one that points to the rising value of high-speed digital communications gear that keeps the Internet running. For ANS, Worldcom will give America Online Compuserve's on-line service and a cash payment of $175 million, putting a value on ANS of about $425 million. To be sure, America Online invested in ANS and Worldcom will assume $150 million in ANS lease obligations, which are the equivalent of debt. Still, the ANS investment has been a big winner for America Online, perhaps providing more profit in the last few years than the company's basic business. Yet Wall Street is evaluating America Online far less by its near-term profits than by its progress in assembling a working business model for the hybrid media, called interactive services, that combine communication, entertainment, information and on-line shopping. The company's market valuation -- or total market capitalization -- rose sharply yesterday to more than $7.4 billion. But Stephen M. Case, America Online's chairman, noted yesterday that it would be years before cyberspace was considered a mass medium. In the unitedstates, the on-line population has more than doubled in two years but still represents fewer than 20 percent of all households. "Today's deal really is a step toward the promise of a connected society," he said. "But there is still a lot of work to be done to make interactive services a mass-market media." The deal, executives said, is expected to take three to six months to be completed. It is subject to approval by the shareholders of the respective companies and will also be subject to review by the Justice Department's antitrust division as well as the European Commission, since both America Online and Compuserve have hundreds of thousands of subscribers in Europe. Mr. Case said he expected no challenge on antitrust grounds because the Internet business was still so young and relatively easy to enter. The list of current and prospective rivals, he said, includes Microsoft, Walt Disney, Time Warner and AT&T. "It's a pretty daunting list of potential competitors," he said. title: Worldcom To Acquire Compuserve
body: Worldcom Inc. will acquire the Compuserve Corporation for nearly $1.2 billion in stock, and then sell the struggling on-line company's subscription service to America Online in a complex three-way deal, according to executives close to two of the three companies involved. The three-company deal, approved last night by all parties, is expected to be announced as early as this morning. Under the terms of the deal, Worldcom, the nation's fourth-largest long- distance phone company, would keep the high-speed telecommunications lines and Internet gateways of Compuserve, which is largely owned by H & R Block. Compuserve's global computer network would enlarge the size and reach of Worldcom's Internet services unit, Uunet Technologies. Worldcom will also be able to add to its computer network as a result of the planned transaction with America Online Inc., the country's largest on-line service. To gain Compuserve's 2.6 million subscribers worldwide, American Online is to sell its Internet telecommunications unit, ANS, to Worldcom. In return, America Online will receive not only Compuserve's on-line service but also about $175 million in cash from Worldcom, according to a person close to the negotiations. The deal also calls for Worldcom and America Online to enter into a closer, large supplier-major customer relationship. As part of the deal, for example, America Online, which is based in Vienna, Va., is to gain access to an additional 100,000 modems from Uunet to insure that it is not again afflicted with network traffic jams as it continues to expand. Early this year, after the demand for its service surged when it introduced flat-rate monthly pricing, America Online was forced to grant credits to angry customers who could not connect to the dial-up service. Neither Worldcom nor America Online would comment on the transaction last night. H & R Block could not immediately be reached for comment. For America Online, acquiring the Compuserve subscribers would lengthen its already considerable lead among the major on-line services. At the end of June, according to Electronic Information Report, a trade newsletter, America Online had 8.6 million subscribers. And after Compuserve, America Online's nearest rival was the Microsoft Network with 2.3 million subscribers. Last week, America Online reported that it had surpassed 9 million subscribers. The deal -- which is now worth roughly $13 a share for Compuserve stockholders -- would be especially useful to America Online in its efforts to expand abroad. The company began an overseas marketing drive in earnest only about two years ago in a joint venture with Bertelsmann A.G., the big German publishing company. Since then, the 50-50 venture called AOL Europe has attracted 650,000 subscribers. Compuserve, by contrast, has traditionally been strong in Europe. Of its 2.6 million subscribers, more than 850,000 are in Europe. Combining America Online and Compuserve's European business should make it the largest European on-line service. Given the fresh surge in European subscribers, Bertelsmann has agreed to pay America Online $75 million to remain a 50 percent partner in AOL Europe, according to a person familiar with those discussions. And America Online and Bertelsmann have agreed to invest $25 million each to expand further in Europe. H & R Block, the tax-preparation firm based in Kansas City, Mo., that owns 80 percent of Compuserve, has been talking to prospective buyers of its faltering on-line service for months. Once an industry leader, Compuserve has suffered from the rapid ascent of America Online and competition from the Internet. But Compuserve's telecommunications structure and subscriber base remain attractive assets. And for America Online, which is mainly a consumer service, the strong position that Compuserve has among business customers is attractive as a way to expand quickly into another segment of the on-line services business. Stephen M. Case, chief executive of America Online, began talking seriously to H & R Block executives about acquiring Compuserve in the spring. And discussions have continued on and off since. Other suitors have been involved, as well. Besides Worldcom, the newyork investment firm of Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe has been in discussions with H & R Block. Late last week, the leveraged-buyout firm was close to a deal that would have given it a controlling interest in Compuserve with H & R Block retaining a minority stake, The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday. Of the Welsh, Carson deal, a person close to the talks said, "They just got outbid."

title: Mellon Bank Agrees to Buy Pacific, a Discount Broker
body: The Mellon Bank Corporation said yesterday that it would buy Pacific Brokerage Services Inc., a discount broker with a strong presence on the Internet, for an undisclosed amount in cash. The addition of Pacific would give Mellon a network to sell stocks, bonds and other investments. Pacific, which has 100,000 customers nationwide, would become part of Mellon's securities and asset management unit, the Dreyfus Corporation. The companies declined to disclose terms of the transaction, which was reported yesterday in The Los Angeles Times. But Brock Vandervliet, an analyst at Keefe, Bruyette & Woods, estimated that Mellon would pay less than $60 million, or about 12.2 times Pacific's earnings. "The pricing looks really good," Mr. Vandervliet said. "Strategically, it's an excellent move and a low-cost way to get into an area they needed to be in." With Dreyfus, Mellon has the largest mutual fund business among American banks and extensive brokerage services. However, it lacks Internet trading technology in its brokerage operations, a feature that is in high demand as more investors choose to order their own trades using personal computers. Mellon continues to seek out small acquisitions that add financial products to its arsenal, as opposed to buying other banks. This year the bank acquired Buck Consultants Inc., a firm that advises companies on benefits plans, and First Business Bank, a Los Angeles bank catering to companies in California. The closely held Pacific will keep its name, 130 employees and Los Angeles headquarters. Mellon, which is based in Pittsburgh, expects to complete the transaction in the fourth quarter. Mellon would be able to save money by clearing Dreyfus Investment Services transactions through Pacific instead of through a third party. Pacific will add $25 million to $30 million to Mellon's revenue. Mellon shares rose 12.5 cents, to $47.625 yesterday on the newyork Stock Exchange.

title: NEW YORKERS & CO.
body: A Patina of Privilege At a New Club in Chelsea Philip Crampton, the owner of Dusk of London, a new lounge on 24th Street between Avenue of the Americas and Seventh Avenue, has modeled it after the ritziest gentlemen's clubs of London. Mr. Crampton, who was born and raised in Nottingham, England, has strived to conjure up an impression of exclusiveness without the stuffiness of many British clubs. With its imported 45-foot-long bar, forest green walls and copper-tiled ceiling, the lounge affects an air of privilege and wealth. It offers a variety of beers, wines and cognacs ranging in price from $4.50 to $30, and appetizers including caviar ( $50 for 50 grams) and smoked salmon ($12). Patrons may or may not be amused by what must be among the most unique restrooms in the city. There are one-way mirrors in the bathrooms that look out over the bar. A Magazine-Styled Web Site For Surfing the Bronx Barbara Tallerman is in touch with the 21st century and in love with the Bronx. After a trial run late last year, Ms. Tallerman, who has called the borough home for the past seven years, recently started the Bronx Mall, (www.bronxmall.com), a sprawling, snappy and intricate web site. With scores of attractions and options, the web site covers all regions of the borough. Among the features are news and events, a chat room for borough residents, both current and former, information about cultural events and neighborhood issues and access to the menus of some restaurants. Ms. Tallerman charges $125 for three months of on-line advertisements. Advertisers can design their own pages or have on-line ads created for them.  Brews On Tap Again At Bohemian Hall in Astoria Three years ago financial problems forced Bohemian Hall, operated by the Bohemian Citizens' Benevolent Society, in Astoria, Queens, to close its beer garden. But last May the hall, which once served as a meeting place for local Czech and Slovak families, reopened the garden, at 29-19 24th Avenue. Customers can again enjoy authentic Czech beer in the outside picnic area. The refurbished hall will also contain an art gallery featuring Czech and Slovak art that is scheduled to open in late September. Prices in the beer garden start at $3.50 for tap brews. The garden is open on weekdays, 5 P.M. to 10 P.M., and from noon to 10 P.M. on weekends. Because it is closed at times for private parties, calling ahead is recommended, at (718) 274-4925.

title:
COMPANY REPORTS;
America Online Reports Operating Profit in Quarter
body: Exploiting its growing bases of customers and advertising, America Online Inc. announced earnings from operations for its fourth quarter yesterday that slightly exceeded analysts' expectations. But the company, the nation's largest on-line service provider, also said it had posted a net loss for the quarter and had restated its financial results for previous quarters after the staff of the Securities and Exchange Commission questioned the company's accounting procedures. Coming after the company took a $385 million charge against its earnings last November to change a previously disputed accounting policy, the announcement raised eyebrows and concerns across Wall Street. "The perception is bad," Alan M. Braverman, an analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston, said. "This has happened a lot of times to A.O.L., and investors could take that negatively. People are going to say, 'What's going on?' and 'Not this again.' " Discounting special charges, the company earned $10.9 million, or 9 cents a share, compared with $16.1 million, or 14 cents a share, in the comparable period last year. Analysts polled by First Call had predicted earnings of 7 cents a share. The service added about 600,000 new members in the quarter that ended on June 30, bringing its total to about 8.6 million. America Online tried to keep its membership steady at about eight million during the early part of the year when it could not supply the "all you can eat" access it had promised its customers and when dozens of state attorneys general had threatened to sue the company for deceptive advertising. But the company felt comfortable signing on new members after a $350 million network upgrade and the addition of about 150,000 new modems since January, bringing its total of modems to about 350,000. Revenue from sources other than subscribers, mostly advertising and marketing, almost tripled, growing to $90.1 million, from $31.3 million in the quarter a year earlier. "Over all, operationally we did very well," Stephen M. Case, America Online's chairman, said in a telephone interview. "We laid out a strategy in the fall called the new A.O.L. and there are a number of components to that and we have been filling that strategy." In its announcement about its accounting procedures, the company said the S.E.C. staff had taken issue with some practices over the second and third quarters of its fiscal year. After restating its prior earnings and shifting some costs to the fourth quarter, the company said, it posted a net loss for the latest quarter of $11.8 million, or 12 cents a share, on sales of $475.7 million. The quarterly revenue was up 42.2 percent from $334.5 million in the 1996 period. The company announced the results after major financial markets closed. Its shares closed at $71.50 yesterday, up 87.5 cents. During its second quarter, America Online took a $25.7 million charge to cover the projected cost of getting out of deals it had made with some of its information providers. But the S.E.C. staff suggested that the company move the charge to the fourth quarter, because the fourth quarter was when the separation agreements were actually signed, Lennert J. Leader, America Online's chief financial officer, said in a conference call with analysts. In its third quarter, which ended in March, the company had recorded about $12 million of a $100 million marketing contract with Tel-Save Holdings Inc., a long-distance telephone company. But after consultations with the S.E.C.'s staff, the company decided to spread about $7 million of that $12 million over the 40-month life of the contract. "I wouldn't call them disputes," Mr. Case said of his company's dealings with the S.E.C. "I would call them discussions. They are trying to understand this new world we work in. They probably have not seen deals like ours with Tel-Save before." The company had reported a profit of $2.6 million, or 2 cents a share, for the third quarter. The company revised those results to a loss of $4.7 million, or 5 cents a share. Rejiggering the Tel-Save contract mattered less to the company's bottom line than moving the settlement payments, but analysts said the Tel-Save adjustment looked worse because many of them said three months ago that the company was acting aggressively in recording revenue from the Tel-Save contract. For its fiscal year, the company reported a loss of $499.3 million, or $5.22 a share, on revenue of $1.69 billion, compared with a profit in the 1996 fiscal year of $29.8 million, or 28 cents a share, on revenue of $1.09 billion. Much of the loss, analysts said, resulted from a shift in the company's accounting policies last year when it began counting marketing costs as current expenses rather than spreading those charges across many quarters. And some were not very concerned about the latest S.E.C.-influenced changes. "A year ago, everyone was terrified that someone would put America Online out of business," Keith E. Benjamin, an analyst for Robertson, Stephens, said. "Now most of the competitive concern seems behind the company. Now the question is how much money they can make." title: On-Line Ad Spending Rising, Report Says
body: Advertisers aggressively increased their spending in cyberspace during the first half of the year. Advertising revenue on the World Wide Web reached $217.3 million through the first six months of 1997, according to Cowles/Simba Information, a unit of Cowles Business Media. That is more than triple the $61 million that the company reported was spent in the first six months of 1996. Electronic Advertising and Marketplace Report, a newsletter published by Cowles/Simba, reported its latest findings last week. Quarter-to-quarter growth was strong, as the on-line market grew 58.7 percent, to $133.3 million, in the second quarter of the year, up $84.0 million from the first quarter of 1997. According to the report, the industry is on pace to reach $446.0 million in Web advertising this year. Some of those numbers are seemingly more conservative than other reports. While Jupiter Communications has yet to release its numbers for the second quarter of 1997, its previous statistics have been higher than Cowles's. According to Jupiter, first-quarter Web advertising revenue reached $110 million; Cowles/ Simba reported revenues were $84 million for the same time period. The report was compiled by tracking 17 popular advertiser-supported Web sites.

title: Web Advertising Beyond Banners
body: As Internet users cruise around the World Wide Web, advertisments of all types line the roadside -- ads that are the functional equivalent of storefronts, with the merchants eager to lure people in to sample their goods. But luring is harder in a world without window displays. Advertisers started out in 1994 using simple banner ads, like roadside billboards. But advertisers were not totally satisfied with the banner and began looking for other models. "They haven't figured what ad form will be most effective and what should be in the ad," said Bill Doyle, senior analyst at Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. "So advertisers are playing with all the levers right now." And what have they found so far? Animated type, animated images, interactive trivia, banners that scroll along with news headlines in on-screen tickers, five-second pop-up windows and more. Last year, advertisers, particularly technology and business and financial services companies, spent $301 million advertising on the Internet, according to Marc Johnson, an on-line advertising analyst at Jupiter Communications in newyork. In the first quarter of 1997 alone, $133 million was spent, he said. title: America Online Backs Off Plan To Give Out Phone Numbers
body: Responding yesterday to consumer outrage and mounting concerns about privacy in cyberspace, America Online, the largest on-line service provider, abandoned its plans to begin providing lists of its customers' telephone numbers to telemarketers and other direct-sales peddlers. The reversal came less than 24 hours after the plans became widely known through news accounts and on-line postings. America Online drew immediate fire from politicians and privacy-rights groups for the telemarketing venture, in part because the company for years had assured subscribers that it would not release their phone numbers and other personal information to outside parties. Because America Online's eight million subscribers are already besieged by "junk" electronic mail, customers bemoaned the prospect of some of those same advertisers, or different ones, ringing the phone at home. "That's the most obnoxious form of solicitation," said Camilla M. Herlevich, an environmental lawyer in Wilmington, N.C., an America Online subscriber. "They always call at dinner time. We call it the arsenic hour." But the controversy goes beyond telephone numbers -- and transcends America Online, for that matter. For consumer-privacy advocates, the case illustrates the need for increased Government oversight of the buying and selling of the copious consumer information gathered in the course of everyday commerce. Savvy companies already mine the trove of available credit card information to find buying patterns that might lead to one more sale. But with the advent of cyberspace commerce, marketers are able to track their quarry even more easily -- tracking each click of the mouse, in some cases, as a user surfs the World Wide Web. So far, such efforts typically can identify no more than a user's computer, and not the identity of the individual operating the PC. Experts predict, however, that personal identification will eventually be possible, making privacy difficult to protect -- whatever the stated policies of companies collecting such data. Like magazines and other businesses with valuable subscription lists, America Online has already been selling lists of its subscribers' names and addresses. But those lists do not include the corresponding email addresses or customer phone numbers. A few weeks ago, however, America Online quietly proposed changing its longstanding policy to begin selling its telephone lists. Privacy advocates said that adding phone numbers to the mix would allow marketers to cross-tabulate with additional sorts of information that people might not be aware they were exposing by simply signing up to an on-line service. "The phone number is used as an identifier the way that the Social Security number is," said Evan Hendricks, the editor of Privacy Times, a privacy-rights newsletter. "They can use the phone number to look up the name and address and then you can find out about their house and how many kids they have." Telemarketers and other direct-sales organization have resisted Government regulation by agreeing to self-imposed privacy-protection guidelines that typically include provisions allowing consumers to request that their personal data not be sold to third parties. But the America Online episode is certain to raise new questions about whether the industry can continue to police itself. "It's unbelievable really, that AOL would be cashing in for profit by selling the personal privacy of their users," said Representative Bruce F. Vento, Democrat of Minnesota, who has introduced a bill to regulate the use of consumer information on line. "It just boggles the mind that they would do it quite this boldly." America Online would not reveal how many of its members called, faxed or sent electronic mail to the company to vent their displeasure. America Online executives insisted that they did not intend to "rent" the phone numbers. Instead, they said, American Online would provide the numbers to companies only as one part of an overall marketing deal. "The only calls we intended for you to receive would have been from AOL and a limited number of quality-controlled AOL partners," said Stephen M. Case, the company's chief executive, in a letter to subscribers yesterday. Those partners would have included Tel-Save Inc., a discount long-distance telephone company that reached a $100 million marketing pact with America Online in February, and CUC International Inc., a telemarketing giant that made a $50 million deal with America Online last month. America Online officials said yesterday that those pacts were broad based and would not be affected by scrapping the plan to share telephone lists. "We said, 'It's so insignificant, just drop it,' " said Robert W. Pittman, chief executive of America Online's operating subsidiary. "For it to get this blown out of proportion says we really screwed up the communication. "At the end of the day we didn't want to soil our reputation or confuse our members." The members were certainly confused, or at least angry. Internet bulletin boards were ablaze with irate missives about the company, some of them profane. Many of the complaints stemmed from the fact that America Online had tucked its only notice of the proposed policy shift in an obscure corner of the service. The notice had been posted on July 1, but did not come to widespread attention until Tuesday. "Unless you stumbled across it you wouldn't know unless you saw it on the evening news," said David Cassel, a freelance writer in Berkeley, Calif., who runs an Internet mailing list about America Online that has 12,000 subscribers. "People thought it was exploitative, deceptive and intrusive. People were outraged." The Federal Trade Commission has been investigating marketing practices in cyberspace since last summer, most recently holding a series of four "workshops" with industry groups last month. Yesterday, noting that credit card companies often pitch services to their customers based on analysis of spending patterns, Commissioner Christine Varney said: "The difference in perception is that people believe that AOL knows a whole lot more about them or has the capacity to know a whole lot about them than American Express does. Presumably they can see where you go, what you do, where your email comes from, who you're sending it to." Earlier this month the commission's staff sketched the outlines of a regulatory structure for Internet advertising when it determined that a World Wide Web site called KidsCom had probably engaged in deceptive practices when it collected personal information from children and used the data for marketing purposes without the consent of parents. But the commission has not issued any regulations on Internet marketing aimed at adults, and is still leaning toward allowing the industry to police itself. "It's about creating a dialogue with industry, and this marketplace is not going to work unless consumers have confidence in it," said Victoria Streitfeld, a commission spokeswoman. "The real effort has been to really not have Government come down on this emerging technology but to raise the issue."

title: $99 Companion Ticket for Delta Web Users
body: Delta Air Lines said today that it was offering a $99 companion fare to customers who booked tickets through the Internet, effective immediately. The Atlanta-based airline said the discount rate was an attempt to increase use of its on-line ticketing service, which started in December. Delta already offers 500 free miles to members of its Skymiles frequent- flier club who buy tickets on the World Wide Web. Any customer using the service to book a domestic round-trip flight will receive a voucher for the next purchase, allowing a second person to fly for $99. On-line ticketing is available at http://www.delta-air.com. Last week, Delta introduced electronic ticketing through its Web site, an alternative to getting a paper ticket in themail. Skymiles members using the on-line service and who opt for an electronic ticket will get 500 free miles, the company said. The $99 companion fare is available until Aug. 21 and is valid for travel to all 50 states, Delta said. The offers extend to customers buying Delta tickets through Travelocity, the Web site of Sabre Group Holdings Inc. Travelocity lets Web users book airline tickets, hotel rooms and rental cars worldwide. Its Web site is http://www.travelocity.com.

title: An On-Line Game Shift Stirs Protest
body: A group of subscribers to America Online has begun an on-line protest against the pricing practices and content changes of the service's lineup of games. The protest -- in the form of hundreds of electronic-mail messages to the company's chief executive, Steve Case -- were prompted by America Online's announcement that it would offer a premium-priced tier for its on-line games. In anticipation of the changes, which are to begin July 19, America Online, the nation's largest on-line consumer service, has dropped three popular role-playing games to make room for the new premium games. Company officials said that the games were removed because of "outdated technology." The premium games service, which will cost $1.99 an hour in addition to the flat rate of $19.95 a month, is produced by Worldplay Entertainment, formerly Imagination Network, a subsidiary of America Online. Worldplay also plans to offer a similarly priced on-line game service to clients of AT&T Worldnet Service and Earthlink Network. The Microsoft Corporation introduced a similar pay-to-play pricing plan for its Internet Gaming Zone earlier this month. Analysts say the move is necessary to find a new revenue stream. "This is essential for the continuous growth of the on-line world," said Adam Schoenfeld, a senior analyst for Jupiter Communications. "Flat-rate pricing can only be considered for access only." Internet users have historically been reluctant to pay for premium on-line services, though "there are indications that people are willing to pay for games," he said. America Online denied that its new pricing plan might be the start of a shift from the $19.95 flat-rate pricing it introduced six months ago. "We are absolutely behind flat-rate pricing," said Barry Schuler, president of creative development for AOL Network. "There is nothing on the horizon."

title:
Die, Vile Orc! Never, Puny Human!;
Is There Real Gold in On-Line Fantasy Games?
body: Regent Lord Anduin Lothar's loyal liege, Lord P, sat in his windowless bedroom in downtown Manhattan at 1:42 last Thursday morning, readying his righteous troops for an assault on the village of evil orcs just across the Eastern canal. "Ah, now it gets nasty," he said, loading inch-high wizards and knights onto a transport ship. "He's going to get hurt now." Lord P, a.k.a. Phillip A. Tavel, a normally affable 26-year-old student at Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law, looked up from the flickering computer screen in his walk-up apartment. "You can kind of get wrapped into things like this," he said, turning back to the images generated by the computer game Warcraft II: Tide of Darkness. "You can definitely get lost in this game -- look up and a few hours have gone by. And that can be nice. If the game is going to be an escape for you, that's the way to go." On the other side of the game board and in Oakland, Calif., the orc leader, Prouve, a.k.a. Alan Green, a 39-year-old designer of furniture and data bases, mustered his ogres and catapults to defend against Lord P's invasion. Internet entrepreneurs, venture capitalists and corporate giants alike are fervently trying to figure out how to make money off of people like Prouve and Lord P -- the hundreds of thousands of well educated, technically savvy, bewilderingly intense men (mostly) who spend hour upon week locked in various sorts of virtual combat. On top of the millions paid for software, gamers spent anywhere from $51 million to $90 million last year to shoot, build, score and dismember in cyberspace, according to analysts, who expect the number to top $1 billion by 2002. Anytime anyone projects a tenfold increase in a market in less than five years, eyebrows arch -- especially when the market is built on toys. But more than one analyst is bullish on the prospects of a business catering to men and women who can seem obsessed with fantasy combat. "On-line gaming is going to be the dominant form of gaming around the middle of the next decade," said Johnny L. Wilson, who has followed the industry since 1981, currently as editor in chief of Computer Gaming World magazine, the leading computer game publication. "Bragging rights are extremely important to gamers," he said. "We like to do a post-mortem, talk about what we did right, what we did wrong. There's not a lot of bragging in saying, 'I beat the computer.' But if I beat you, that's an entirely different experience and then the bragging builds its own community." But while almost everyone involved in the industry seems convinced that on-line gaming is about to become a big business -- perhaps even bigger than the roughly $1 billion cyberpornography industry -- few of them are at all sure where the money will come from, whether from long-term subscriptions, per-minute charges, advertisers or even monetary transactions within games. "This is the proverbial industry in search of a revenue model," said Mark Mooradian, an analyst for Jupiter Communications, a research firm in newyork City. "How do you support your network costs while attracting a mass number of users? Nobody's profitable at this point." There are three basic ways to make money in the computer gaming business: charge for a box of software, charge for time spent gaming on line or charge for both. That there are a large number of users ready to be attracted is an article of faith in the industry, if only because the mundane technical barriers to playing on line these days are often too daunting for the average computer user. As playing games over the Internet becomes easier, the argument goes, it will also become more popular. Quake, for instance, one of the hottest games, has sold about 600,000 copies, according to its publisher, id Software Inc., based in Mesquite, Tex. Quake players, fueled by adrenaline, generally stalk their opponents through dungeon-like environments and try to kill them with high-powered weapons. But despite the appeal of hunting real people, Forrester Research, a consulting firm in Cambridge, Mass., estimates that only 15 percent of Quake owners play the game in cyberspace. "There's a learning curve associated with getting on line with your game and it's just not that easy to do yet," said Seema Chowdhury, an analyst at Forrester. "But most people who play on line love it." Just ask Dennis Fong, known on line as Thresh. The 20-year-old undergraduate at the University of California at Berkeley took home $5,000, a souped-up computer and a red Ferrari 328 GTS convertible last month for winning a Quake contest in Atlanta called Red Annihilation that confirmed him as the best in the world. "People are a lot smarter and quicker than the computer," Mr. Fong said. "When you really get into it you turn the lights down and when someone jumps out at you, you can actually fall out of your seat. I've done that. It gets pretty intense." Few on-line game players do as well as Mr. Fong in the virtual arena. And few on-line game companies do as well as Mr. Fong in the ledger book. But at least the players are in it for fun. James Juliano, a 24-year-old asbestos remover in Queens, has spent more than 300 hours on a service called the Total Entertainment Network over the last two months, most of it in an adventure game called Dark Sun Online. Mr. Juliano pays $19.95 a month for unlimited access to the site, where he guides his hybrid, elf-human alter ego, Zyto, through various adventures with dozens of others around the world who are playing simultaneously. Mr. Juliano is the model customer for the "pay as you go" revenue model; Mr. Tavel for the sell-the-box model. Mr. Tavel paid for both the Warcraft software (which cost $45) and for time spent with on-line opponents (for which he paid Engage Games Online $2.50 an hour) -- until recently. Not long ago, Mr. Tavel, who is also a clerk for newyork State Supreme Court Justice Walter Tolub, discovered that he could troll for Warcraft partners on his own in Internet Relay Chat. Relay chat, or I.R.C., as it is called, is a way of linking computers on the Internet into "chat rooms" where many people can converse, or type, at once. Mr. Tavel and Mr. Green found each other on an I.R.C. "channel" called #macwarcraft, named for the game and Apple Computer Inc.'s Macintosh computer. At 12:30 last Thursday morning, dozens of people were doing the same. So, Mr. Tavel said he would not be paying fees very often anymore to any of the dozen or so companies that connect Internet gamers to one another for per-hour or per-month charges. He also will not be using America Online, which recently modified its "all you can eat" $19.95 monthly pricing plan to add per-hour surcharges for on-line games. "The fact that I.R.C. is free is a lot nicer," he said. "The value of it is that it should be free. You've got the software. You just want someone to play against." The hundreds of companies that make their money selling copies of the games by mail-order and in stores are picking up on that sentiment. Trying to drive sales of their products in an increasingly competitive market, they are investing hundreds of thousands of dollars in free on-line play areas for their products. Connecting as Mr. Tavel and Mr. Green did requires some technical sophistication, and game executives are aiming at the mass market. "It's like saying I'm going to have a party at my house and whoever wants to show up can come and you don't need an invitation," said Todd S. Hollenshead, chief executive of id, which also runs Quakeworld, a directory of free outside computers that are hosting multi-player Quake matches at any given moment. Blizzard Entertainment, an Irvine, Calif., division of Davidson & Associates Inc. that invented Warcraft, created an area on the World Wide Web called Battle.net to support a more recent game called Diablo. Davidson is owned by CUC International. The Microsoft Corporation is employing a similar approach in parts of its game site on the Microsoft Network and over the Web and Activision Inc., a leading game company, is developing a free area of its own for a strategy game due in the fall called Dark Reign. Recognizing that most popular off-the-shelf computer games will soon have free, relatively easy to use Web sites for encouraging on-line play, the market in "pay for play" games on line is shifting to huge games that exist only in cyberspace. Called "persistent environment" games, they might resemble Dark Sun Online, only bigger, with thousands of players in one continental-size virtual environment. Such games are being developed by gaming sites like T.E.N. and Mpath Interactive as well as by companies including Microsoft, the Origin division of Electronic Arts Inc. and the Sony Corporation. Those companies are trying to improve on current "massively multiplayer" games from the Kesmai Corporation, a unit of Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation, but mostly they seem to be taking their cues from the venerable elder statesmen of Internet gaming, the text-based games called M.U.D.'s, or Multi-User Domains, in which play is determined by typed-in commands, like "kill dragon." Almost all M.U.D.'s are free, and they remain popular with gamers who prefer to let their imagination do some of the work as they interact with dozens of other people in worlds shaped by the players themselves. "We basically have a much richer story line behind what players are doing," said Michael D. Denison, who helps run Darker Realms, one of the largest M.U.D.'s on the Internet. "It's more like the author writing the game rather than having the graphics drive the players around." "We have had five different couples who met on the M.U.D. who got married in real life, and there are four D.R. babies," he added. "Not many graphical games can say that." Graphic   Photos: From Law Student . . . to Field Marshal -- Phil Tavel, 26, spends his days studying law at Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law in newyork. After a long day of writing and memorization, Mr. Tavel likes to relax by dispatching footmen, like the figure above, archers and griffins to repel the marauding forces of the orcish invaders in an Internet game called Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness. (Linda Rozier for The newyork Times); From Craftsman . . . to Chieftain -- Alan Green, 39, is a designer of furniture and computer data bases in Oakland, Calif. Having honed his Warcraft strategies against automated opponents, he is now venturing onto the Internet in search of greater challenge. Last Thursday morning, however, his orcish legions, like the figure at right, were defeated by the noble forces of Mr. Tavel. (Ann Dowie for The newyork Times)

title: Bertelsmann Mum on Compuserve Rumor
body: Bertelsmann A.G. declined to comment today on a report that it was joining with America Online Inc. to acquire Compuserve Inc., its nearest rival in on-line computer services. Bertelsmann, the German media giant, would, according to a report today in The Wall Street Journal, provide the cash for America Online to sweeten its latest offer to H & R Block Inc., the Kansas City financial services company that owns just under 80 percent of Compuserve. H & R Block had reportedly objected to cash-short America Online's April bid to complete the deal in a stock swap valued at about $1 billion. Compuserve has been losing money and subscribers for more than a year, but it is a powerhouse in the commercial Internet sector with more than 1,200 business customers and the owner of a highly rated computer network. In addition, although America Online has 8.5 million users to about 3 million for Compuserve, America Online trails Compuserve in developing overseas markets and could become a much more formidable global competitor if a merger were completed. Bertelsmann is already linked to America Online, which is based in Dulles, Va. The privately held publishing and entertainment giant owns 5 percent of America Online's stock, operates America Online's service in Germany and puts America Online software on music CD's. America Online spokesmen and executives could not be reach for comment. There was no indication of how much cash Bertelsmann might provide or that a richer bid had actually been made to Block or Compuserve, which is based in Columbus, Ohio. "Our response is the same as it has been for the last several months," said Linda McDougall, a Block spokeswoman. "We are talking to a number of companies about Compuserve's future." Block originally set out to dispose of Compuserve by selling part of its holdings in a public offering and then spinning off the rest to Block shareholders after a market value had been established in open trading. But shortly after Compuserve's highly successful initial public offering in April 1996 at $30 a share, competition in the on-line market exploded, profits evaporated and the share price plunged. The price fell as low at $8.625 on Oct. 23 and closed at $10.75 on Thursday. Block put the spinoff plans on hold late last summer, telling shareholders the divestiture would be completed once Compuserve was "stabilized." So far, that goal has been elusive. Compuserve lost $119.8 million on revenues of $841.9 million in the fiscal year ended April 30 and is expected to be in the red for at least the first half of the current year. In February, when Robert Massey, Compuserve's chief executive, resigned, and Block decided not to appoint a permanent replacement, analysts said it was a clear signal that Block would like to sell Compuserve. Analysts say that American Online is only one of several possible suitors that might put a higher value on Compuserve than investors see for it as a stand-alone company. "It would also be a good strategic fit for Microsoft," said Alexander Paris Jr., an analyst at Barrington Research in Chicago, noting that a merger would push Microsoft's on-line customer base to more than five million. AT&T, MCI Communications and several of the Baby Bells are other potential suitors, Mr. Paris said.

title: Digital 'Watermarks' Assert Internet Copyright - Correction Appended
body: Playboy magazine, which has been plagued by on-line piracy of its pictures of scantily clad and nude women, is planning to announce today that it will place a digital "watermark" on its images in its most aggressive move yet to stop copyright infringement. The watermark technology, which was developed by the Digimark Corporation, will enable Playboy to encode ownership information into the photograph and will also let the magazine track unauthorized copies of its images on the Internet. "We saw our copyright being infringed all over the place," said Eileen Kent, vice president of new media for Playboy Enterprises Inc., which owns Playboy. "This technology may be the solution." The ease with which would-be thieves on the Internet can copy images from a World Wide Web site has put Playboy in a precarious position. The magazine has a free Web site where users can view a select number of its pictures and it also has plans to start a subscription Web site, which will offer more photographs, later this month. But users of the services can easily download the pictures and just as easily post them to their own Web sites. "That's exactly what we hope watermarking our images will prevent," Ms. Kent said. In April, Federal marshals and Playboy took action against Five Senses Productions in San Diego, which was accused of illegally publishing Playboy's images on the Internet. Previous attempts to add identification to images involved placing a string of code on the top of an image file, often referred to as "header information," but this code could easily be removed. Digimark, which is based in Portland, Ore., developed a digital watermark that encodes information about the owner of the image within the pixels of the photograph. Invisible to the eye, the digital watermark is essentially a pattern of pixels that have been changed by modifying the brightness levels of certain pixels in the detailed areas of the picture to remain inconspicuous. "Whenever a digitally watermarked image is downloaded from the Internet and opened in an image editing software program like Adobe Photoshop, the program will automatically identify the image as watermarked," J. Scott Carr, director of business development for Digimark, said. The watermark embedding and identification software, which is included without charge in 90 percent of new image editing software programs like Photoshop and Corel Draw, then displays a screen allowing the viewer to find out information about the image's copyright restrictions and information about licensing the image from its owner. Even if the user disregards the copyright information and edits the picture by cropping the image or making other modifications, the watermark remains intact, Mr. Carr said. Playboy will also employ Digimark's Markspider, a service that scours the Internet for images that contain the watermark. The Markspider service is scheduled to deliver its first report listing the digitally watermarked images it has found to Digimark clients in late July. "The worm is very appealing," Ms. Kent said, referring to the Markspider service. "We try to see who's doing what, where and when to our stuff." Digimark charges $500 to $5,000 for the watermarking and tracking service, depending on the volume of images watermarked. PBS recently began using the technology on its Web site to watermark 150 images that are part of a three-part series, American Visions, that runs as a companion to the television series. Ms. Kent said that Playboy is also exploring the idea of encoding the printed images that appear in the magazine. If printed at a high enough resolution, the watermark is readable if scanned into a computer. "We have to see if there is any degradation in the picture quality," she said. Intellectual property lawyers say such technology should make theft accusations easier to prove. "It lets you demonstrate infringement," Anthony Lupo, a lawyer in Washington who specializes in Internet law, said. "By having a copyright registered prior to infringement, you're entitled to statutory damages and attorney's fees," he said, eliminating the costly burden of prosecuting the case. Correction  An article in Business Day yesterday about technology that places a digital "watermark" on images to stop copyright infringement misspelled the name of the company that developed the technology. It is the Digimarc Corporation of Portland, Ore., not Digimark. Correction-Date: July 1, 1997, Tuesday

title: New Service Skims 150 Newspapers for Its Users
body: In the spring of 1995, a partnership of large newspaper companies formed the New Century Network to bring the country's dailies into the age of the Internet. Then they sat down to figure out what that meant. Starting today, after a couple of false starts when the project was quickly overtaken by the speed of Web development among papers, the network is disclosing the result: a service called Newsworks, which offers a daily report on the important news of each day compiled and assembled by Newsworks editors in Manhattan. Newsworks includes links to about 150 individual newspaper sites on the World Wide Web. Plenty of existing Web sites offer links to newspapers, John Papanek, Newsworks' editor in chief, acknowledged. But he said on Newsworks (http://www.newsworks.com) the information is sifted and organized into categories by New Century editors and then linked, with headlines, to member Web sites. "Everything that's news in any town in America originates in a newspaper," said Mr. Papanek, the former editor of Sports Illustrated, "but a huge percentage of it goes to waste because 99 percent of the rest of the country never gets to see it." New Century's executives predict that the editorial packaging, along with a one-stop Internet advertising service shared by the affiliated papers, will give its venture enough appeal to break into a Web news market dominated by about 30 sites such as those run by Yahoo, Netscape, Microsoft and a dozen big papers. These sites have about 80 percent of the advertising revenue on the Internet, according to Jupiter Communications, a research and consulting firm. Jupiter estimated that $300 million was spent on Web advertising last year, although other analysts say that figure is too high. But Steve Mitra, a senior analyst at Jupiter, said he was skeptical whether New Century would be successful. "It's one more stage of recycling the same old news," Mr. Mitra said. "You already have The L.A. Times and The Washington Post picking what they think are the best stories and laying them out on their site. So do we need another layer of editors doing our picking for us?" The newspaper companies that own New Century are Advance Publications Inc., Cox Enterprises Inc., the Gannett Company, the Hearst Corporation, Knight-Ridder Inc., The newyork Times Company, Times-Mirror Inc., the Tribune Company and The Washington Post Company, which among them publish about 225 dailies, not all of which are part of the network. The newyork Times, for example, has withheld its site from the network. Originally, New Century was founded as a technical aid and support group to help newspapers move quickly onto the Internet. But in the meantime, many papers flew onto the Web with their own sites. "So by the end of '95 we had shifted gears to build a network company," said Lee deBoer, New Century's chief executive. Bill Bass, a senior analyst with Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass., said that New Century had come up with an appealing role for a newspaper Web site consortium, but he predicted that there could be friction among the members. After all, each time an editor sends a reader to a member's site for a story, that member will capture a visitor impression, or "eyeball," helping it support higher advertising rates. "The reality is that their editorial abilities are going to be one-third of the skill set and two-thirds is going to be in diplomacy, because the minute The Washington Post story gets bumped for some story from Raleigh, The Post is going to go through the roof," Mr. Bass said.

title: Two Days That Shaped the Law
body: Busily clearing out its backlog on the final two days of its term, the Supreme Court decided four significant cases Thursday and yesterday. The decisions included a stirring rejection of Congress's clumsy attempt to censor the Internet, a predictable but by no means absolute affirmation of a state's right to ban physician-assisted suicide, and a ruling on the new Presidential line item veto that pretty much avoided the issue. In its final hours of business, it elevated the power of the states in the Federal system on a critical question involving the Brady Handgun Control Law, shortchanging not only the law but federalism itself. The Brady Law. Reinforcing its now-familiar hostility to the legitimate authority of the Federal Government, the Court struck down a key provision of the Brady law yesterday. The bitterly divided 5-to-4 decision, written for the majority by Justice Antonin Scalia, served up a cockeyed version of constitutional history and the Founders' vision of a strong central government to annul the law's requirement that local law enforcement officials conduct background checks on prospective gun purchasers. "Such commands," said Justice Scalia, "are fundamentally incompatible with our constitutional system of dual sovereignty." That is an excessively cramped view, as Justice John Paul Stevens noted in a powerful dissent joined by Justices David Souter, Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer. Moreover, it is clearly out of proportion to the "trivial burden" the Brady law actually imposed on state and local government to help address what Congress correctly called a nationwide "epidemic of gun violence." Justice Stevens noted further that the notion that Congress may impose an "affirmative obligation" on "state and local governments as well as ordinary citizens" has strong historical roots. It is firmly supported, he said, "by the text of the Constitution, the early history of the nation, decisions of this Court, and a correct understanding of the basic structure of the Federal Government." There may not be much that Congress can do to correct the Rehnquist Court's misguided vision of the state-Federal relationship. But it can insure the integrity of the Brady law by passing legislation that puts the burden on gun dealers for getting checks done. A new Federal checking system is already in the works and will eventually replace the system the Court has just outlawed. But in the interim, Congress must put another in place. Internet Censorship. The Court demonstrated a laudable passion for the First Amendment in a strong decision declaring unconstitutional a Congressional abomination called the Communications Decency Act of 1996. The act made it a crime to knowingly send or display "indecent" material over the Internet, where children can see it. The Court's forceful extension of free speech principles into cyberspace is sure to be remembered as one of the positive landmarks of the 1996-97 term. While the Court sympathized with the law's goal of protecting children from indecency, it correctly recognized that the "wholly unprecedented" breadth of the law threatened to suppress far too much speech among adults and even between parents and children.
