"The interest in encouraging freedom of expression in a democratic society outweighs any theoretical but unproven benefit of censorship," Justice Stevens declared in an opinion that wisely granted the Internet the highest level of First Amendment protection, similar to that accorded books and newspapers, rather than the narrower protections granted radio and television. In colorful prose, Justice Stevens described the Internet as the "town crier" of the modern age, expanding the reach of the soapbox orator and today's electronic pamphleteers. As such, his decision was both a ringing affirmation of the Internet's capacity to contribute to free expression and democracy, and a powerful rebuke to the censors in Congress and to President Clinton, who signed and defended the act. Assisted Suicide. For many Americans, the decision holding the most drama was the Court's ruling on physician-assisted suicide. This page had urged the Court to use the two cases before it to recognize the profound personal liberty interest that lies at the controversy's core and to deliver a ruling vindicating the right of suffering, terminally ill patients to die with dignity, in full control of their final moments. Ideally, the ruling would also have imposed upon states a duty to craft safeguards to prevent abuse. The Court did not do anything of the sort. As expected, the justices handed down a pair of unanimous decisions rejecting the constitutional challenges to laws in newyork State and the state of Washington that contain general bans on physician-assisted suicide, making it a crime. This is not a Court prone to taking an expansive view of due process or equal protection. In mitigation, the Court indicated that the question was still to some degree an open one, suggesting it was at least sensitive to the prospect that the laws could impose an intolerable burden on mentally competent, terminally ill individuals approaching death. "Throughout the nation, Americans are engaged in earnest and profound debate about the morality, legality, and practicality of physician-assisted suicide," said Chief Justice Rehnquist. The Court's approach "permits this debate to continue, as it should in a democratic society." One positive result of that debate has been to force the medical profession to concede that the inadequate help it now offers patients trying to cope with pain and depression at the end of their lives is not adequate. The Court has now spoken, but as the justices themselves acknowledged, this is unlikely to be its last word. Line Item Veto. The Court actually ducked this one. A Federal district court ruled in April that the President's new power to cancel individual sections of appropriations bills he had already signed into law plainly violated the constitutional separation of powers. The district court was right. But instead of ruling on the merits, the Supreme Court dismissed the case with the unconvincing argument that the injury to Congress was "abstract," and therefore that members of Congress lacked standing to bring the suit. The effect of this dodge was to reinstate the statute until the outcome of what is sure to be another challenge once the veto is actually used.

title:
Taking In the Sites;
Nerds Inc. Turns Typos Into On-Line Advertising
body: "Tommy if you don't learn how to spell you are not going to get anywhere. . . ." At the risk of making Mom really mad by contradicting her in public, it must be reported that poor spellers and bad typists can get somewhere, thanks to a new friend on the Internet. If you are in the habit of typing Internet addresses and you happen to type www.micorsoft.com instead of www.microsoft.com, you will get to Microsoft's site but it will be courtesy of typo.net. Typo.net, a subsidiary of Nerds Inc., is run by the company's two principal operators, Robert Hoffer, its chief executive, and Timothy L. Kay, the chief scientist. @evil-empire.com alter ego free. Mr. Hoffer said he has had a few takers for the gratis identities. The typo.net idea grew out of the brainstorming sessions that the two held to come up with new domain names for identity.net. Mr. Kay wrote an algorithm to generate the misspellings and a program to automate registering them. Mr. Hoffer and Mr. Kay then convinced Jason Brandt, account director and senior vice president of Rapp Collins newyork, an advertising agency owned by Omnicom Group, that their service could be valuable to some of his clients. As a result, the reckless surfer who types micorsoft.com will connect to a Web page that is programmed to splash a 15-second full-screen advertisement in the browser window before referring him to Microsoft's Web site. "We hope that we are doing both the clients and the URL a service by providing a redirect to their service," Mr. Hoffer said. "We don't believe there should be room in the minds of the consumers about where they are supposed to be going." To that end, the typo.net intercept page will begin with a line identifying itself and stating its purpose. By the time the Web surfer has read the legend and seen the advertisement, he or she will be ushered along to the site that Mr. Kay believes was intended to be the destination in the first place. Experienced Web surfers tend to tune out banner ads on Web pages the way that television viewers tune out commercials. But when you expect to see links to software patches and downloads, sports scores or an on-line newspaper, (nhtimes.com is one of their holdings) and instead there is a bottle of pop or a colorful candy lozenge coming at you, you tend to take notice. Mr. Hoffer promises not to take advantage of the mistakes of viewers for longer than the 15-second delay that he will promise his sponsors.  "Typo.net is designed not to be a destination site," Mr. Hoffer said.  "Our attitude about it is simple. We don't want this to become onerous for the consumer." Mr. Kay notes that typo.net will process a "typo" in about half the time that a browser would take to inform you of your error; you will not have to decipher a cryptic DNS (domain name server) error message, or take any other corrective action to get to your destination. While some may see typo.net as Web pirates -- ambushing the careless on the Internet -- Mr. Hoffer speaks of his service as a win-win proposition. This is a healthy stance to take considering the potential for litigation with registered names like dinsey.com, hahoo.com, amaxon.com and sprotsline.com. "There is clearly not a domain name problem, strictly speaking," said Peter Jaszi, professor of law at the Washington College of Law at American University. "The rules that govern this are private administrative schemes, applicable only to name as a precise format. The question is whether or not it's trademark infringement." Michael Levy, the president and chief executive of Sportsline.com., said: "I just have to hope that anyone coming to our site knows how to type. There are a lot of games; I wish they didn't take place but it's a lot of work to try and do anything about it." Typo.net holds the rights to two variations of the spelling of his popular URL, www.sportsline.com. Others may not be as reticent. "We deal with this domain name stuff all the time and it comes up in different permutations and flavors," said Scott Behm, a trademark lawyer for Microsoft. While he indicated that Microsoft would not hesitate to protect its customers from "confusion," he said the company would not necessarily turn to litigation. John Dreyer, the vice president for corporate communications at the Walt Disney Company, seemed largely unconcerned about yet another pilot fish feeding on the scraps of his company's site. "It sounds like a clever idea," he said, "and it may teach all of us to be better typists." Still, it remains to be seen whether any company will actually consider legal action against typo.net. "One of the things we are supposed to like in this country is imagination and free enterprise," said Pam Samuelson, a professor of law at the University of California at Berkeley School of Law. "It does a service to everyone; why not just have a sense of humor about it?" Graphic   Chart: "WHERE TO GO"  IDENTITY.NET http://www.identity.net  TYPO.NET http://www.typo.net/typo

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Interpublic invests in an Internet provider aimed at 'the transition generation' of young adults.
body: THE Interpublic Group of Companies is expanding its presence in the realm of on-line advertising by investing in Tripod Inc., an innovative interactive marketing and media company that focuses primarily on consumers in their 20's. Interpublic, the world's third-largest agency company, is spending about $2.5 million for an estimated 10 percent stake in Tripod, a five-year-old enterprise based in Williamstown, Mass. Tripod's operations include a Web site, at www://tripod.com; a magazine, Tools for Life, distributed with the Prentice Hall textbooks sold on campuses by Viacom Inc., and Student Advantage, a card offering discounts on goods and services in travel, entertainment and other fields. The operations all specialize in what Tripod describes on its home page as "the transition generation, young adults who are moving from college to the workplace." The investment by Interpublic, which owns giant agency networks like McCann-Erickson Worldwide and Lowe Group, is part of a $10 million infusion of additional financing for Tripod from investors that also include the Rho Management Company, a venture capital firm, and Cowen & Company, an investment bank that helped bring Interpublic and Tripod to each other's attention. The deal is emblematic of how the huge agency companies that dominate Madison Avenue are staking claims in cyberspace through investments in independent companies as well as by supporting internal start-ups. That strategy offers as many risks as it does rewards. For instance, although Interpublic has profited handsomely from an investment in CKS Group, a joint venture with the Infusion Com Corporation that was formed in November went sour as Infusion Com filed for Federal bankruptcy protection four months later. "You can't bat 1.000," said Barry R. Linsky, senior vice president for planning and business development at Interpublic in newyork. "It's learning on the fly, like shooting at a moving target," he added. "The trick is to manage your exposure and therefore your risk." Mr. Linsky discussed the Tripod agreement -- the first giving Interpublic a stake in what is known as an Internet content provider -- in a telephone interview yesterday. Details of the deal are scheduled to be announced today. "We're looking for opportunities where we can be a strategic investor, not a passive investor," he said, "and for ventures that will enable us to pass insights to our agencies and our clients." Interpublic executives began meeting with Tripod managers around Labor Day last year, Mr. Linsky recalled. "The more we understood what they were doing," he said, "the greater appreciation we had for what they were about: building an interactive destination with an orientation for a young audience, the so-called Generation X that's important to a lot of advertisers but not easy to reach." Those consumers, at the heart of the 18-to-34-year-old demographic segment, are among the most desirable because they are acquisitive and in the embryonic stages of forming brand preferences. The Tripod Web site is divided into content sections that bear headings like "Work and Money," "Living and Travel," "TriTeca" and "Daily Scoop." Among Tripod's service offerings are resume writing, job hunting and helping younger computer users create home pages. "People in this generation are living in a fundamentally different reality than people 10 or 15 years ago," said Bo Peabody, 26, chief executive of Tripod. "It's a much scarier, less secure environment in which mutual funds and condoms are as important as music and sports. "When they now come out of college, it's an entrepreneurial, do-it-yourself culture," he added. "You have to be savvy, and a little bit cagey, about your life. And they see the Web, with its 'infotainment' and 'edutainment,' becoming a medium with which to solve their problems." Tripod's advertisers include the AT& T Worldnet Service of the AT& T Corporation, Amtrak, the Chase Manhattan Corporation, the Fidelity mutual funds sold by the FMR Corporation, the Ford Motor Company, Mastercard, Northwest Airlines, the Sony Corporation and Visa. "We obviously think Interpublic can be a big help to us in the advertising community," Mr. Peabody said. "One of our mantras is 'Know what you don't know,' " he added. "While we may know the audience, and the technology to build communities on line, we may not know some of the relationship-building that goes on in an industry like that." Mr. Peabody founded Tripod along with Brett Hershey, a classmate of his at Williams College, and Richard Sabot, an economics professor there. Tripod now has 40 employees: 36 in Williamstown and 4 in newyork. The $10 million from the investors including Interpublic compares with the "almost exactly $4 million we've spent up until now," Mr. Peabody said, from investors like New Enterprises Associates, a leading venture capital firm. Mr. Peabody predicted that Tripod would become profitable in the first quarter of 1998. Gil Fuchsberg, director for new media and technologies at Interpublic, will become one of five members of the Tripod board.

title: Industry Group to Offer Standards for Privacy on Internet
body: In the face of growing concerns about privacy in cyberspace, a group of about 40 companies will propose standards this week intended to enable computer users to control what personal information is obtained when they visit Internet sites and how that information is used, as well as avoid unwanted junk email. The industry initiative, led by the Netscape Communications Corporation, an Internet software maker, is an attempt to cope with privacy issues that threaten to slow the growth of Internet commerce and lead to Government regulation. Americans are far more concerned about privacy on the Internet than they are about personal and financial information they give out over the telephone and through themail, according to a recent survey conducted by the Boston Consulting Group. Forty-one percent of the 9,300 people who responded to the on-line survey said they left Web sites rather than provide such registration information as their names, phone numbers and email addresses, while another 27 percent said they gave false information. The Boston Consulting report also estimated that as much as $6 billion in additional electronic commerce would be transacted by 2000 if consumers' concerns about privacy on the Internet were addressed. The industry proposal, called the Open Profiling Standard, is partly an attempt to address those qualms. But the move is also an effort to convince the Government that regulation is not needed because industry can provide consumers with the tools necessary to protect their privacy. The industry argued against Government controls last summer in voluntary hearings before the Federal Trade Commission. The commission's stance has been that privacy in cyberspace is a crucial consumer protection issue, but that the industry should be given a chance to show it can deal with the problem. Since the 1996 hearings, the commercialization of the Internet has steadily grown -- and done so without guidelines for the behavior of companies or on-line entrepreneurs. One annoying byproduct of that evolution is the recent surge in the volume of electronic junk mail, pitching products and get-rich schemes, whose promoters can often easily find email addresses from on-line services or on-line merchants. But Internet privacy concerns run far deeper than the nuisance of junk email. A person surfing the Internet leaves a digital trail, with each mouse click, allowing Web site operators to closely monitor a person's movements through cyberspace, preferences and interests. It permits marketers to personalize on-line products and services, enabling them to offer consumers more tailored information, entertainment and goods. But Internet technology also has the capacity for abuse, especially if detailed information about a person collected at one Web site is passed on to other companies without the person's consent. How well the industry is moving to address these kinds of privacy issues will be the subject of four days of public hearings to be held by the Federal Trade Commission starting June 10. After the hearings, the commission will submit a report to Congress in the fall on how well the private-sector initiatives are working. The commission will recommend what role, if any, the Government should play in protecting privacy on the Internet. Government officials and industry analysts who are aware of this week's proposal say it seems to be a significant step, though much will depend how it is put into effect. "This is important," Christine A. Varney, an F.T.C. commissioner, said. "The technology tools and standards are essential to protecting privacy in cyberspace. They are a necessary, but not a sufficient answer to the problem." The proposal's backers acknowledge that the initiative -- a set of technical standards and principles of practice -- is mainly a framework for addressing privacy issues. But they say it can put useful tools in the hands of both the public and the industry. "We're trying to make it easier for users to manage their personal information on the Internet -- who gets it, why and for what purposes," said Martin Haeberli, director of technology at Netscape. "The principle of informed consent is what the proposal embraces." The proposal was drafted mainly by a handful of Internet software companies like Netscape, Firefly and Verisign. But it also has the support of leading technology companies like I.B.M. and Sun Microsystems, media businesses like Knight-Ridder and The newyork Times Company, and advertising firms like J. Walter Thompson and Organic Online. Support, Mr. Haeberli says, has also come from technology policy organizations like the Electronic Frontier Foundation and the Center for Democracy and Technology. The standard proposal will be presented to the Worldwide Web Consortium, the main arbiter of industrywide standards for Internet software. Using the profile standard, a person would fill out a form including basic descriptive information like name, address, zip code and email, as well as extra information if one chooses to enter it -- age, marital status and hobbies. Beyond the standard, other industry groups, like Etrust Inc., a nonprofit company, are being set up to verify and enforce privacy standards. One significant Internet software company was not included in this week's proposal, the Microsoft Corporation, which is Netscape's main rival. Vying for leadership in standards setting is part of the competition between the two companies. Standards can divide the industry, but analysts do not think the privacy proposal will. It does not involve proprietary software from which Netscape and its partners stand to gain directly, they say. "This is intended to advance on-line commerce, but it is not a standard that will affect the landscape of the Internet software industry," said Eric Brown, a senior analyst at Forrester Research Inc. in Cambridge, Mass. "Netscape gets to make the announcement, so they may score some marketing points. But that's about the only advantage they get from this."

title: Study Sees Holes in Internet Security Plan
body: A panel of computer scientists said yesterday that the Government's plans for unlocking data-scrambling software to pursue criminals and terrorists on the Internet could actually increase security risks and raise the costs of on-line commerce. The researchers, in a study coordinated by the Center for Democracy and Technology, a nonprofit policy group in Washington, examined the technical challenges of the Government's Internet security proposal. The plan would permit American computer companies to export powerful data-scrambling software, but only if they established a system that would enable the keys to the code to be obtained by law enforcement officials with a court warrant. The plan calls for these software "keys" -- lengthy numeric codes -- to be held not by a Federal agency but by third-party companies. To get the keys, law enforcement officials or intelligence agencies would have to obtain legal authorization. The plan to use third-party key holders was advanced last fall by the Clinton Administration. It was made in response to concerns by civil liberties groups, including the center for democracy, that warned that letting a Federal agency hold the keys would make it too easy for the Government to monitor the communications of private citizens and in response to complaints by software companies that it would hurt sales. But the 11 computer scientists -- experts in the use of software that encrypts, or scrambles, data -- concluded that the Government's so-called key-recovery plan, however well intentioned, would introduce its own set of risks and costs. "A key-recovery system is going to be extraordinarily hard to design and build economically, safely and reliably," said Matt Blaze, a research scientist at AT&T. Another computer scientist in the group, Peter Neumann of SRI International, a research center in Menlo Park, Calif., said that having a key-recovery system in computing was similar to having a skeleton key to one's house as well as a personal key. The all-purpose skeleton key, it turns out, is easy to copy. "So the existence of skeleton keys or trap doors, as the Government is proposing, is inherently risky," Mr. Neumann said. Jerry Berman, executive director of the Center for Democracy and Technology, said: "Key recovery may be a nice idea, but it doesn't compute yet. The technical issues are the Achilles' heel of key recovery, and they need to be debated." William A. Reinsch, Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration, said the center's study seemed to assume a vast, centralized system that was not what the Administration intended. Besides, Mr. Reinsch said, a number of private companies as well as the Government are pushing for key-recovery software, and the expense will not be prohibitive. Companies, he noted, want to be able to tap into communications for such purposes as thwarting industrial espionage. Giving the Government access to the keys to pursue criminals, Mr. Reinsch said, will require the additional step of a court warrant. "But it won't require building a separate infrastructure for the Government's key-recovery plan," he said. Still, the Administration's plan faces fierce political opposition domestically and skepticism by some foreign governments. Last week, the House Judiciary Committee unanimously passed a bill that would relax export controls on data-scrambling software and permit companies and individuals to use any encryption programs they choose. Abroad, Germany said it would not do anything to regulate data-scrambling software for at least two years, while waiting to see how Internet markets developed. The unitedstates cannot "force its policy down the throats of other countries," said Peter Harter, global public policy counsel for the Netscape Communications Corporation.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
West Publishing Loses a Decision On Copyright
body: In a decision that experts said would drive down the price of legal research, a Federal judge has stripped away much of the copyright protection claimed by West Publishing, the nation's dominant publisher of court cases, for its law books. For 124 years, West Publishing's books containing major court decisions have been the standard in every court and law firm in the nation and its method of identifying cases has been the standard for citations in decisions and legal briefs. The law books, and in recent years their electronic versions, became so valuable that last June the Thomson Corporation paid $3.4 billion for the company. But the ruling, by Judge John S. Martin Jr. of the Federal District Court in Manhattan, means that rival publishers can electronically scan the decisions in West law books into their computers and then issue them in books, on line and in CD-ROMs. Under the ruling, only West's headnotes and other added material are protected. The judge said on Monday that West Publishing had no copyright protection to the actual decisions by the unitedstates Supreme Court and Federal Appeals Court that are reprinted in its law books. The 13-page decision follows up on a ruling by the judge in December, when he granted summary judgment against West in a case brought by Mathew Bender & Company, a unit of the Times Mirror Company. The judge said then that West's system for citing cases was not protected by copyright. Judge Martin said on Monday that the changes that West Publishing made in the court decisions were "trivial" and "mechanical." He noted that West corrects spelling and obvious factual errors, sometimes after consulting with the judge who wrote an opinion. "The most significant additions that West makes to the opinions that it reports," Judge Martin wrote, are to add citations to the same case in each of the various law books it publishes. Thomson said yesterday that it would appeal. Michael S. Harris, Thomson's general counsel, said that West had never claimed a copyright to the actual court decisions, only to its published versions of them with the changes that its staff makes. Thomson officials said that they were confident both that the decision would be overturned and that their dominance in the lucrative field of legal research would be unaffected. Several copyright and electronic publishing experts, though, said they expected new competition to emerge that would erode West Publishing's profit margins. "You are about to see the price of legal research spiral downward," said Joe Action, owner of Versus Law Publishing, a seller of specialty legal research data bases in Bellevue, Wash. "West's monopoly pricing is finished." Carl J. Hartmann 3rd, a lawyer for Hyperlaw, a small newyork legal publisher that was the second plaintiff in the case, called the decision significant because "West's power is based on its central positioning in the legal industry through its control of legal material, citations and a large volume of other stuff and now a judge has ended that control." Peter Jaszi, a professor at American University law school who specializes in copyright issues, said that if the decision was upheld it would "reduce the strength of West Publishing's claims to exclusivity and make it easier for competitors to enter the market, which will bring prices down." West has long courted judges. For example, it sent Supreme Court justices and other judges, The Minneapolis Star Tribune reported in 1995, on all-expense-paid trips to Caribbean resorts and gambling casinos. Judge Martin's ruling relied in part on a 1991 Supreme Court ruling that held that listings in telephone directory white pages cannot be protected by copyright and that purely factual material is not protected by copyright. Andrew L. Deutsch, a partner in Piper & Marbury in newyork who specializes in such issues, said that "the decision confirms what most lawyers who knew about the case thought about West's claims."

title: I.B.M. Researchers Develop A New Encryption Formula
body: I.B.M. plans to announce today that two of its researchers have come up with a new computer encryption formula that they say is nearly impossible to crack. The International Business Machines Corporation said that the breakthrough was still a long way from being employed outside the lab and that it did nothing to resolve the running dispute between the computer industry and the Federal Government over whether law enforcement agencies should be given access to encrypted communications. But it could ultimately help reduce the vulnerability of so-called public-key encryption, which is the favored security method used to safeguard commerce and privacy on the Internet. "They've made a big advance," said Joan Feigenbaum, a researcher at AT&T Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., who is familiar with the work of the two computer scientists who developed the system, Miklos Ajtai and Cynthia Dwork of I.B.M.'s Almaden Research Center in San Jose, Calif. "Scientifically, this is a big step in the right direction." But Bruce Schneier, a computer security consultant in Minneapolis and author of a standard textbook on cryptography, dismissed the news. "Theoretically it is important, but as a security breakthrough there is nothing new," he said. In public-key encryption, the sender of an electronic communication uses software that automatically scrambles the information by incorporating a publicly known numerical key. Decoding the scrambled transmission requires a private key, a number supposedly known only by the recipient. The security of the system depends, among other things, on how difficult it is for an electronic eavesdropper to crack the code using a powerful computer. If some of the codes that are generated by the system are difficult to break but others are easy, the system is inherently weak. I.B.M. said that its new system was the first to generate hundreds of codes at random, each of which is as difficult to crack as the hardest instance of the underlying mathematical problem. The system is based on a problem that has defied solution by mathematicians for 150 years, I.B.M. said. Mr. Schneier said that the cryptographic formulas now in use were already robust enough. The bigger challenge, he said, is creating security systems in the real world that are not vulnerable to hackers. "Cryptography is a lot more than math," he said.

title: America Online Posts Surprising Earnings
body: America Online Inc. said yesterday that it had returned to profitability in its third quarter after six months of heavy losses. The results surprised Wall Street analysts, who had predicted another loss for the nation's largest on-line service provider. America Online's advertising revenue surged while marketing costs were forced lower as part of a legal settlement with state attorneys general that forced the company to cut back its advertising. As a result, the company earned $2.6 million, or 2 cents a share, on revenue of $456.2 million, for the quarter, which ended on March 31. Analysts polled by First Call had expected a loss of 7 cents a share. The modest earnings were a retreat from the $15.1 million profit the company posted in its third quarter a year ago, but marked a significant improvement from more recent results. Over the previous two quarters, the company had posted a combined loss of $508.5 million. "I think we have turned the corner as relates to returning to profitability and we anticipate seeing progress in the future quarters," Stephen M. Case, America Online's chairman, said. "The progress we saw this quarter provides greater confidence in the soundness of our strategy." A cornerstone of that strategy was repositioning America Online as a media company along the lines of a magazine or newspaper, one that sells its product for about what it costs to make and hopes to make most of its profits from advertising. In February the company signed up its largest marketing client, Tel-Save Holdings Inc., a long-distance telephone operator. Tel-Save, which buys long-distance time in bulk and resells it at a profit, paid America Online what amounted to a $100 million advance. America Online booked about $12 million of that fee this past quarter, helping overall advertising and transaction revenue jump more than threefold to $60.7 million. Following the media-company model and forced to compete against companies that offer low-cost connections directly to the Internet, America Online abolished most per-hour charges in December. In their place, it established an "all you can eat" plan, offering unlimited access to the service for $19.95 a month. Users flocked to the service, but America Online's infrastructure could not handle the demand. Prodded by users, attorneys general from 36 states negotiated an agreement with America Online that required the company to offer refunds to many subscribers and to drastically curtail its advertising. So the company's marketing costs fell by almost 40 percent, from $146.8 million in the quarter that ended in December to $89.5 million in the most recent quarter. Mr. Case said the company intended to reduce marketing costs all along. Some analysts questioned whether America Online could sustain its profitability, noting declining gross profit margins and the artificially low marketing expenses. But others were ebullient. "They can turn on the engines now," said Alan M. Braverman, an analyst with Credit Suisse First Boston. "They've just scratched the surface with advertising and electronic commerce. I think the earnings are very sustainable." America Online did not announce the earnings until after financial markets closed. But shares of America Online began to rise almost immediately after the newyork Stock Exchange opened yesterday, finishing the day at $51.50, up $4.25. Before the markets opened, Hambrecht & Quist, a West Coast brokerage firm, announced that it had initiated coverage of America Online with a "buy" rating. Hambrecht & Quist's chief executive, Daniel H. Case 3d, is a brother of Mr. Case, the America Online chairman. The analyst who wrote the positive report said that the family connection had no bearing on his analysis.

title: 3 On-Line Services in Accord on Abusive-Billing Complaints
body: In another blow to the mixed reputation of computer on-line services, three of the nation's biggest providers have entered into a settlement with the Federal Trade Commission over complaints of abusive billing and marketing practices. America Online Inc.; Compuserve Inc., a unit of H & R Block Inc., and the Prodigy Services Corporation, a unit of International Wireless Inc., while admitting no violations of Federal law, have agreed to disclose more fully the terms of their so-called free trial offers and to make it easier for consumers to cancel the services. The three services also promised to end the practice of automatically debiting customers' checking accounts for the cost of monthly service without obtaining advance approval. In addition, America Online, the largest service, must establish a consumer education program about the use of electronic payment systems, which many on-line services use to bill their customers directly. America Online must distribute at least 50,000 brochures warning consumers about the dangers of automatic debit payment programs and their right to contest disputed charges. Spokesmen for each of the three companies said they had long ago ceased most of the practices addressed in the F.T.C. settlement, but today's action formally requires the on-line services to avoid such policies permanently. The F.T.C. voted 5 to 0 to approve the settlement, which carries no fines and does not require the companies to pay any refunds. But the settlement further tarnishes the image of the new industry that offers consumers and businesses a telephonic doorway to cyberspace. Internet access -- now offered by more than 1,000 companies, has been marred by service blackouts, slow data transmission, unexpectedly high costs and questionable sales practices by some providers. The F.T.C. sought the settlement after receiving thousands of consumer complaints. David Medine, a senior staff attorney in the agency's bureau of consumer protection, said that the Government did not seek financial penalties because the companies had already created refund programs for disgruntled customers. Mr. Medine also said that it was virtually impossible to calculate potential overcharges for the three companies' 12 million customers. He said that the F.T.C.'s goal was to stop deceptive practices and to require much more extensive disclosure of the terms of on-line service contracts. "The focus here was to get the whole industry on board with a set of acceptable practices, because this is a new industry and it was important to get in relatively early to set the ground rules for the future," Mr. Medine said. He added that the on-line services could continue to offer free or low-cost introductory offers. "But they must clearly, conspicuously and unavoidably tell you what you must do to cancel," Mr. Medine said. Kate Delhagen, senior analyst at Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass., said that the settlement would alter the industry's marketing practices only modestly, but for the better. "This move is about full disclosure," Ms. Delhagen said. "It's good for consumers, and absolutely essential as the on-line market begins to sprawl into mainstream America." Tricia Primrose, spokeswoman for America Online, said that the company had reached an agreement with the F.T.C. last fall on some of these issues. She said that the standards for billing, disclosure and marketing in the settlement announced today should be applied industrywide. "Ultimately, that's in the best interest of consumers," she said. America Online earlier this year stopped another billing practice challenged by the F.T.C. The company had added 15 seconds automatically to every Internet connection and rounded up all usage to the next minute. Thus, a 2-minute-and-46-second call, with the 15 seconds tacked on, becomes a 3-minute-1-second call, which is rounded up and billed as 4 minutes of usage. Ms. Primrose said all calls are now billed for their exact duration. Compuserve, in a statement, said that it had not violated any law and asserted that the F.T.C.'s concerns with Compuserve "were minor compared to other industry players." A company spokesman, Steve Conway, said the company was already complying with most of the provisions of the settlement. "We're happy to take the extra steps at this point," Mr. Conway said, "and we're also glad we had a voice in helping define the regulations." Mike Darcy, director of public relations at Prodigy, said that the company had already "changed our ways." "We've been in compliance with these conditions since October 1995," Mr. Darcy said. "We see little financial downside to the business. This is much less costly than litigation." America Online, based in Dulles, Va., has eight million subscribers. Compuserve, based in Columbus, Ohio, has about three million customers, while Prodigy, of White Plains, has one million subscribers.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
As the main character in 'Ellen' comes out, some companies see an opportunity; others steer clear.
body: THE commercials on tonight's controversial episode of "Ellen," in which Ellen DeGeneres's character announces on the ABC comedy that she is a lesbian, are very likely to get as much attention as the show's story line. Many viewers will no doubt forgo the trips to the refrigerator between scenes to find out which advertisers chose to ignore pressure to pull ads because of the controversial content, perhaps even sensing an opportunity to cash in on the episode's expected ratings rise. ABC will not disclose which advertisers have opted to sit this one out, and only the Chrysler Corporation has acknowledged doing so, saying its policy was to stay away from controversial programs in general.  On the other hand, some advertisers that have bought air time are creating commercials to introduce during the show. For instance, an on-line brokerage service -- the E-Trade Group of Palo Alto, Calif. -- is advertising on "Ellen" for the first time with commercials it created to run in newyork and San Francisco. "What will the ratings be for this show?" an announcer asks in the spot created by Gotham Inc. in newyork, a unit of the Interpublic Group of Companies. "How will it affect the network's stock?" The announcer then goes on to promote E-Trade. "We thought because the show has been getting so much attention that it was a great opportunity to reach our audience," said Rebecca Patton, a senior vice president at E-Trade Group. "We really appeal to people who think for themselves," Ms. Patton said, adding that the commercial was created in part to reach gay consumers who most likely will watch the show. She added, however, that the ad would be updated to run on other programs. "It's a very safe business decision to pull out of the show because of the controversy associated with it," she said. "I'm sure many companies have other ways to get to their target market, and they are trying to be safe." Indeed, Megan Giles, a spokeswoman for Chrysler, said, "We don't think it is a smart business decision to be advertising in an environment that is so polarized." The auto maker has not decided whether it will show commercials on "Ellen" during the rest of the season. Many other advertisers have been less forthcoming than Chrysler in discussing the situation. More than 130 companies sometimes advertise on the show, according to Competitive Media Reporting. Several of them merely said in response to inquiries that they were not scheduled to appear this week. Among them were the McDonald's Corporation, the Coca-Cola Company, the J. C. Penney Company, Domino's Pizza, the Ford Motor Company and General Motors. As for Chrylser, Ms. Giles said: "It is not a content issue at all. We don't want to sit in judgment of what a TV show is doing about sexual preference. It's a business decision about trying to stay out of the fray. The environment around this is so angry we feel we lose no matter what we do." In contrast, Volkswagen of America Inc., which has advertised on "Ellen" for two years, is introducing a humorous commercial during tonight's episode. The spot, created by Arnold Communications of Boston, depicts two young men with nothing to do but drive a Volkswagen. "Volkswagen respects the differing opinions people have about the subject matter," said Tony Fouladpour, a company spokesman. He added that the auto maker, a unit of Volkswagen A.G. of Germany, did not withdraw advertising from shows because of controversial subject matters. "The Volkswagen ad on this episode is not really about sexuality, nor does it endorse a particular life style," Mr. Fouladpour said. "It's about advertising our products to a target audience of drivers, which matches the viewers of 'Ellen' and which would include many different life styles." Pundits on both sides of the "Ellen" debate say the issue is whether advertisers are being responsible by distancing themselves from the coming-out episode or are perpetuating a homophobic attitude and risking alienating gay shoppers who, like everyone else, consume sodas and fast food, use toothpaste and deodorant and buy jeans and athletic shoes. "I think the one thing being lost here over all is that everybody is always saying they are looking for a desirable demographic, and we have good research that shows this is a desirable demographic," said Dave Mulryan, president of Mulryan/ Nash, an ad agency in newyork that specializes in the gay and lesbian market. He noted that according to statistics his firm gathered from research conducted with the Simmons Market Research Bureau, 45 percent of gay and lesbian consumers who tune in to ABC television programs have an annual household income of more than $60,000, and 90 percent of them say they buy products advertised to the gay community. "Here you have a group of loyal people that are watching," Mr. Mulryan said. "Companies should be saying right now that six months from now no one is really going to remember who didn't advertise, but they are going to remember who did." Yet groups that have rallied companies to pull their ads take a different view. The American Family Association, a conservative watchdog group, contends that consumers who share the group's view that the show is providing a one-sided view of "homosexuality as a normal, natural, alternative life style" can make their objections known to advertisers at the checkout counter. "The only option, one that is as American as apple pie, is to ask advertisers not to support programming that viewers feel is objectionable and to let them know that if they do, viewers will vote with their wallets the next time they are in the grocery store," said Ed Vitagliano, a spokesman for the group and editor of its magazine. That view may have had an effect on who is advertising on "Ellen," but it has also helped to generate publicity for the episode, which is expected to increase the show's ratings. Indeed, it allowed ABC to charge a premium of more than $300,000 for a 30-second spot, a network executive said. Advertising agency media buyers put the typical cost for a 30-second commercial on the show at $150,000 to $220,000, depending on the number of episodes for which time is bought and the show's ratings for a given period. ABC confirmed that it had sold out of air time for tonight's episode but declined to disclose how much the network charged. "We don't discuss our advertising at all," said Janice Gretemeyer, vice president of media relations for the network. As for whether longtime advertisers are likely to keep their commercials off the air beyond the current episode, agency media buyers say that remains to be seen. "The critical issue will be the ongoing tone of the show," said Ellen Oppenheim, senior vice president and media director at Foote, Cone, & Belding. "The advertisers who do elect to pull ads from a show do so because of concerns with their constituency, and that is something they will continue to be sensitive to." Yet Alan Jurmain, executive vice president and media director of Lowe & Partners/SMS in newyork, said: "I would suspect they will come back rather quickly. There might be a phobia connected with being associated with the coming-out episode, but I think there is also a passion for being connected with a show that has had higher than average ratings." In general, "media firsts get a lot of attention," added Mr. Jurmain, whose agency is part of the Interpublic Group of Companies. "This is the first official coming out of a sitcom character, so obviously, given the sociological concerns of this country and the issues that we wrestle with that are top shelf, sexuality is right up there," he said. "In that regard, this is a bit of broadcasting history."

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
America Online and TBWA Part Ways
body: TBWA Chiat/Day in newyork said yesterday that it had resigned as the lead agency for the creative portion of the America Online account, after almost two years. The decision came after America Online has fielded out several assignments to other agencies this year. Billings were estimated at more than $30 million. "We've decided to resign the account because the nature of our relationship has changed into something less than a full marketing partnership," said Mary Maroun, managing director of the newyork office of TBWA Chiat/Day, a unit of Omnicom Group. She added, "It's awkward when your client tells you they want to go shopping. It doesn't inspire you to invest time and energy in a relationship when they tell you they want to cheat on you." Ms. Maroun was referring to America Online's recent decision to assign Gotham Inc. in newyork, a unit of the Interpublic Group of Companies, the responsibilities to create America Online's next image campaign, which is scheduled to begin this spring. In January, America Online also moved its media buying account to Western International Media in Los Angeles, also owned by Interpublic, from TBWA Chiat/Day. Wendy Goldberg, a spokeswoman for America Online in Dulles, Va., said that the company did not plan to place the account in any formal review. "We are always looking for the best creative," she said.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: ON THE NET;
Who uses the Internet and how? We'll get back to you on that if someone figures it out.
body: THE World Wide Web has been hailed as the king of all interactive media, where publishers can learn everything there is to know about their audiences because surfers vote with every mouse click. But more than two years after the Web burst into the limelight as the next great commercial medium, it is remarkable how little is still known about who is using it and how. It is not as if the scores of Netrepreneurs with dollar signs in their eyes haven't made such knowledge a priority. Measuring Web use is the key factor in establishing the Internet as a viable advertising medium, which is where the money is -- or, rather, isn't in the case of the Web. Dozens of companies are now competing to become to the Web what A. C. Nielsen and its ratings are to television. (Nielsen itself, of course, is one of them.) Which is part of the problem. There are so many competing companies pushing different approaches that many advertisers are holding back until there is a standard way to compare how effective their ads are on various Web sites. Several well-meaning industry groups have been started, like the Internet Advertising Bureau and the Coalition for Advertising-Supported Information and Entertainment, and everyone seems to agree that an accurate and reliable standard is needed. But beyond recognizing that truism, there has not been much progress. The industry can't even agree on how much money has been spent on Web advertising. Estimates of last year's ad spending range so widely -- between $130 million and $301 million by five different market research companies -- as to be meaningless. But tracking advertising is really only one of the advantages to be had from measuring Web use. Even sites that do not accept advertising can benefit from learning more about the experience of those who visit. In retailing, this is called the art of merchandising. The best merchants not only try to make their shops as inviting as possible, they keep track of what sells and put it out front. And they lay out their floor plans to create a sense of flow that makes it as easy as possible for customers to move fluidly from one department to the next -- rather than head for the exit. But most Web sites still operate on the principle: If we build it, they will come. These sites, whether proferring information or pitching products, are like cut-rate discount stores where mounds of merchandise are piled on tables. The most hardy shoppers eager for a bargain may sift through the piles until they come across the gem they were seeking. But the rest of us who have little time or patience simply give up and walk out. This may be changing, as a few of the more enlightened Web publishers are beginning to realize the importance of improving the user experience. "Our producers want to know what is bringing eyeballs to the site," said Kevin Dando, manager of education communications for PBS Online. "How long they are spending on the site, if they are coming in, sampling something, and leaving quickly." Perhaps the best indicator that "usage analysis," as it is known in the industry, is becoming a hot niche is that the Microsoft Corporation has taken an interest. Last month, Microsoft announced that it had bought Interse Corporation, the leading maker of Web measurement software. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, though Government filings show that Terry Myerson, Interse's president and chief executive, alone received about $16.5 million worth of Microsoft stock as part of the sale. "We think usage analysis is a fundamental requirement of a site administration," said Russ Stockdale, group product manager of Microsoft's personal and business systems division. "Here you have an interactive medium. It is only natural to understand how your customers are interacting with it. We think it is a category that is here to stay." Interse competes with products from the Net.Genesis Corporation and Accrue Software Inc., among others. Each company's software produces myriad statistics, such as who visits a site, where they are coming from, how long it takes them to access specific pages and where they go when they leave. Phil Gibson, director of interactive marketing at National Semiconductor, is an enthusiastic proponent of such software. He credited use of some of these site analysis tools with helping National tailor its site to the needs of the tens of thousands of outside design engineers who visit it each week to learn detailed specifications about any one of the company's 27,000 parts. National does not accept advertising on its site. Its goal is to get visitors the information they need as quickly as possible. By carefully tracking where users went on the site, Mr. Gibson said that its administrators were able to reduce the average number of pages served to each visitor to just under three from seven. "The faster we can satisfy their need and get them back to work the better," Mr. Gibson said. "That builds the brand in their mind. They know that they can get the information in a snap whenever they need it." And after further analysis showed that a large portion of the visitors were coming from overseas, the site was organized around icons to accommodate non-English speakers. As a result of these changes and others, traffic has surged. The site was also chosen as a finalist in last year's National Information Infrastructure Awards. Mr. Stockdale of Microsoft believes that the need for site administrators to close the "feedback loop" will only grow as Web sites move away from simply dishing out static information and become more dynamic. Operators of corporate intranets, as internal Web sites are called, will want to know where their employees are going and what they are looking at so that they can tailor the content accordingly, Mr. Stockdale added. But let's not get ahead of ourselves. Such tracking will no doubt be a marvel. But for now, just getting administrators to check such basics as the number of error messages their sites are sending back to would-be visitors each day -- and correcting the problem -- would go a long way toward enhancing most people's Web-surfing experience. After all, without an audience, there's nothing to measure. Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title: On-Line Stocks Fall as Reports of Deal Persist
body: The shares of America Online Inc. and Compuserve Inc. fell sharply in heavy trading yesterday as both companies declined to confirm reports that America Online, the country's largest on-line service provider, was negotiating to buy Compuserve, its biggest rival. Shares of America Online fell $4.125, to $44.25, on the newyork Stock Exchange, while those of Compuserve closed at $12, down $1.625, in Nasdaq trading. The prospect of such a deal has divided analysts and investors between those who believe Compuserve's network resources are too valuable for America Online to pass up and those who worry about the impact of an acquisition on America Online's short-term earnings. Compuserve, the nation's second-largest on-line provider, which is controlled by the H & R Block Company, said last week that it was in talks to be acquired. But the identity of the suitor has not been disclosed. Speculation that America Online was the bidder, previously fueled by a report in The Washington Post, was revived yesterday when The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed sources, reported that the two companies were hammering out a $1.2 billion deal. While most analysts agreed that H & R Block, based in Kansas City, Mo., should sell its 80 percent stake in Compuserve to focus on its core business of retail tax preparation, analysts and investors are sharply divided on whether acquiring Compuserve would make sense for America Online, based in Dulles, Va. So the continuing reports of such a deal, coupled with both companies' steadfast refusal to comment publicly, seemed to push shares down in two ways. Those who bought the shares in the last week in anticipation of a takeover premium may be worried that a deal is bogging down, while those who worry about a merger's diluting America Online's earnings may be running for cover. Also, news yesterday that the Microsoft Corporation was planning to spend $425 million to buy WebTV Networks Inc., which makes devices that allow people to gain access to the Internet on their televisions, may have depressed America Online's stock amid fears that the company's customer base could soon come under renewed attack. H & R Block has been trying to get rid of Compuserve, which it bought in 1980, since last year, when it became clear that the growing popularity of the Internet was a major threat to proprietary on-line services like Compuserve and America Online. America Online has continued to garner subscribers, pushing its current total to about eight million, by fine-tuning an easy-to-use computer interface that appeals to families. Compuserve briefly tried to compete in that market last year with a service called Wow, but shut it down after only seven months to focus on business customers. Because corporate users spend the most time on line during the day, and families are more frequently in cyberspace at night, Compuserve and America Online could make more efficient use of their networks as one company, some analysts said. Buying Compuserve would also give America Online entree into Europe, where Compuserve is the market leader. And access to Compuserve's banks of modems in the unitedstates could help America Online relieve the network congestion that has plagued the service since December, when it introduced a popular plan that offered unlimited use for $19.95 a month. "Fundamentally, long term, I believe it would be a positive," Keith E. Benjamin, an analyst for Robertson Stephens in San Francisco, said. "They have been sorely in need of capacity." But while owning Compuserve is one thing, buying it is quite another, analysts pointed out. Estimates of Compuserve's worth range from about $1 billion to about twice that. America Online ended last year with only $111 million in cash on hand. The company lost $129 million on operations in the quarter that ended last December, so borrowing money for an acquisition could be difficult. "They can't service debt," said David M. Simons, a managing director at Digital Video Investments, an institutional research firm in newyork. "Debt is not an option." So America Online is apparently only left with the option of issuing new shares and distributing them to Compuserve's shareholders -- mainly H & R Block. But that route, which could require America Online to increase the number of shares outstanding by as much as 30 percent, would dilute the value of the existing shares. It would take time to integrate Compuserve's operations into those of America Online, analysts said. Only then, as profits increased, would per-share earnings return to pre-acquisition levels. "They had better find costs to take out which are greater than the dilutive impact of the shares being issued to make the proposed transaction palatable to shareholders," said Charles Federman, chairman of Broadview Associates, a merger-and-acquisition adviser for the information technology sector. An acquisition that diluted the profits of the acquiring company might have been easier for a technology concern in the past. These days, however, high-technology investors are looking for growing profit, not just growing revenue. And the implications for mergers that do not appear to provide that promise in the near future can be severe. Shares of the Rational Software Corporation fell 42 percent yesterday on fears that its plan, announced yesterday, to buy the Pure Atria Corporation, a rival software company, would reduce per-share earnings. Pure Atria's shares fell by a comparable amount. And shares of Ascend Communications Inc. remained about 10 percent lower than their price at the end of last month, when the company announced a plan to acquire the Cascade Communications Corporation. As for America Online, Mr. Benjamin said: "I wonder if the stock will tolerate any dilution to earnings. I wonder if they can get a deal done. My best guess remains that it doesn't happen."

title: Now That You're on Line, Check for the Bottom Line
body: After months of frustrating busy signals, Susan Markicz, a photographer in the Bronx, thought she had solved her problems connecting to America Online in February when her teen-age son said that schoolmates had told him about a toll-free number that gave users quick access to the on-line service. Using the "800" number, she believed, would give her the best of all possible worlds: America Online service for a flat rate of $19.95 a month -- and freedom from busy signals. "It was like hitting the lottery," she said. Not quite. Last Saturday, Ms. Markicz's family received a $541.65 bill from America Online for service in February. Hundreds of subscribers -- the company will not give exact figures -- have complained about unexpected charges, and in newyork State, the Attorney General's office is looking into the situation. Had Ms. Markicz found out about the toll-free number directly from America Online, she might have been spared the surprise. Those seeking information about the toll-free service from the company are informed they will be subject to a surcharge. That charge, the company tells those who read through several computer screens of information, is 10 cents a minute, or $6 an hour. But subscribers have been passing the numbers to one another in offices and schoolyards and even America Online's chat rooms. Users who switched to the toll-free lines without consulting the company were not informed of the surcharge. Often, as the toll-free numbers were passed from hand to hand and keyboard to keyboard, the crucial information about the extra charges was not. Also, thousands of personal computers shipped by Packard Bell NEC Inc. this winter included flawed America Online software that routed users to the toll-free numbers automatically, without any warning about the surcharges, according to representatives of both companies. These customers, however, are receiving refunds. Others, like Ms. Markicz, may not be so lucky. And some subscribers who had authorized the company to withdraw their monthly charges directly from a checking account have found those accounts depleted. "We are extremely concerned," said Marc E. Carey, a spokesman for Attorney General Dennis C. Vacco, "and we have ongoing discussions with AOL about this." It was unclear whether other states were engaged in similar discussions. The complaints are the latest in a series of difficulties that the company and the on-line industry in general have had in managing the entry of millions of people into cyberspace. Lawsuits and bitterness have become fixtures as once-entrepreneurial companies struggle to keep up with the explosive growth. Asked about the problem this week, America Online said it had received about 600 complaints a month since last fall. The company has about eight million subscribers. Analysts estimated that the company operated about 300,000 phone lines. America Online would not say how many of those lines are connected through the toll-free numbers. But Mr. Carey of the Attorney General's office said use of the toll-free lines appeared to grow this winter, when local access numbers were clogged by new subscribers attracted to the $19.95 plan, which began in December. In February the company added a second toll-free line, (888) 245-0113, to complement (800) 716-0023, which has been in service since July 1995, said Tricia Primrose, an America Online spokeswoman. Compuserve, the No. 2 on-line service company, with about 2.9 million customers, also offers a nationwide toll-free access number that costs users $6 an hour. The Prodigy on-line service, which has about a million users, charges customers 8 cents a minute, or $4.80 an hour, to use its toll-free line. This is not the first time state attorneys general have investigated America Online. In January the company reached a settlement with attorneys general from 36 states who had threatened to sue the company, complaining that customers were not getting the "unlimited access" they had paid for. Under the terms of that settlement, America Online agreed to pay refunds and offer free access to users who had been unable to gain access to the system in December and January. Yesterday, America Online settled a class-action lawsuit filed in Illinois. That settlement requires the company to extend refunds to customers who encountered similar access problems in February and March. Since January, the company has almost doubled the capacity of its network. In big cities, though, busy signals are still common during peak evening hours. The Packard Bell problem apparently caught America Online by surprise. Christine M. Shipman, a waitress in Lake Buena Vista, Fla., said she bought a Packard Bell computer at an Orlando Officemax store in late January. "I signed up with AOL and the next month I went in to check my billing and they had taken almost $600 out of my checking account directly," she said. "I panicked because that was my rent money. I was floored." The America Online spokeswoman, said: "Packard Bell erroneously set it to default to the 1-800 number. So when you were signing on to AOL it didn't give you a choice." But Sheri A. Benninghoven, a spokeswoman for Packard Bell, said the two companies were still trying to determine how the flawed software found its way to consumers. All of the affected Packard Bell customers will receive refunds, Ms. Primrose said, though she would not disclose how the two companies are dividing the cost. The second group of surprised subscribers might not be so fortunate. "We couldn't get on line using the local number," said Nadine Goldman, a prekindergarten teacher at a public school in the South Bronx. "Then my son said, 'Look, I got an '800' number.' He said he got it in an AOL chat room. So we started using it in early February. "Then I got my credit card bill, and it said I owed $536.05. I was hysterical." Ms. Primrose said America Online was dispensing refunds on a "case-by-case basis." "When they haven't seen it and weren't aware of the surcharge, we're working with them on refunds," she said. Some subscribers were dismayed that their children were able to switch a computer to one of the toll-free lines without adult approval. Theresa A. Abdelaziz's family received a $136 charge after Ms. Abdelaziz's 15-year-old son changed his computer's access number to a toll-free line. She said she had received an unequivocal response when she called the company for a refund.  "They denied it," the Bronx resident said. "They said they don't have that policy. They said that they would not allow any refunds or amnesty or credits or anything like that."

title: Compuserve Concedes It's in Acquisition Talks
body: The Compuserve Corporation, the struggling provider of the second-largest computer on-line service, acknowledged yesterday that the takeover reports swirling around the company were at least partly true, saying in a statement that it was in talks to be acquired. But Compuserve and H& R Block, which owns 80 percent of the on-line provider, declined to disclose the suitor's identity or any other details of the negotiations. The two companies released the statement after several reports that America Online Inc., the biggest on-line service, was preparing to make a bid for Compuserve. The shares of Compuserve, which trade separately, closed yesterday at $12.625 on Nasdaq, up $1.625 for the day and up $3.625, or 40 percent, from the opening price on Monday, when a small Wall Street newsletter first publicized talk of a possible bid by America Online. Shares of H& R Block closed at $31.50, up 87.5 cents, in trading on the newyork Stock Exchange, where America Online shares fell $1.125, to $44.625. Compuserve, based in Columbus, Ohio, had earlier refused to confirm any discussions, but The Washington Post, citing unnamed informants, reported yesterday that America Online was considering a buyout of Compuserve. America Online has refused to comment all week. Analysts said that selling Compuserve would make sense for H& R Block. "The quicker they get rid of Compuserve, the better," said Paul A. Mackey of Dean Witter, who has followed H& R Block since 1972, adding that Compuserve should fetch about $1.5 billion. "They clearly don't belong together." Martin Romm of Credit Suisse First Boston, said: "It makes sense for H& R Block, because as Compuserve has become a much more complex company, it's gotten further and further away from the H& R Block core business. To get Compuserve to the next level, they were going to have to make a substantial investment." And Block, whose core business is retail tax preparation, was not willing to make the investment. That company, which is based in Kansas City, Mo., bought Compuserve in 1980, and has been trying to shed it since last year. Block offered 20 percent of Compuserve to the public last April at an initial price of $30 a share. Since, then Compuserve's stock has lost about 60 percent of its value. Block intended to spin off the remaining 80 percent of Compuserve to its shareholders last September, but canceled that offering because Compuserve was performing poorly against competition from America Online and from services that provide direct access to the Internet. Compuserve, one of the first companies to bring cyberspace to the living room, now has 2.9 million subscribers, while America Online has 8 million. "The short answer for what caused Compuserve's demise is AOL," said Adam Schoenfeld, an analyst for Jupiter Communications, a cyberspace research firm in newyork. "AOL marketed Compuserve into the ground, and then Compuserve's response was way too little, way too late." Compuserve's response to America Online's family-oriented marketing was a family service of its own, called Wow. But Wow never caught on, and Compuserve shut it down in January, just seven months after its introduction. Mr. Schoenfeld and other analysts said America Online was the most likely suitor for Compuserve. Compuserve has many more subscribers overseas than America Online has, and buying the smaller company could give America Online a jump-start abroad. Acquiring Compuserve's extensive network of computers and modems could also help America Online mollify its many customers who have been stymied by busy signals when trying to dial into the service. But analysts pointed out that America Online had only $111 million in cash on hand at the end of last year, which could make a deal difficult. Its stock is also down 34 percent this year, which would make a stock deal less attractive to H& R Block.

title: Internet Encryption Company to Acquire Zoomit
body: Pretty Good Privacy Inc., a privately held data encryption company based in San Mateo, Calif., will announce today that it plans to acquire the Zoomit Corporation of Toronto, which is also privately held. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. Pretty Good Privacy said the acquisition would enable it to take its PGP encryption technology, which is primarily used by individuals over the Internet, into corporate network installations. Zoomit's core product is a so-called meta directory, which links the directories of an enterprise's various networks, providing a centralized repository for computer addresses and passwords. Integrating PGP with Zoomit's meta directory will provide a centralized system, or server, for managing encryption codes, known as keys. "We were looking for a key server and ended up with Zoomit, which produced a key server and much more," Tom Steding, Pretty Good Privacy's president and chief executive, said in a telephone interview. The product, he said, "allows people to put a key server into their existing system without building yet another directory." The combined company will ship a key server by the end of the second quarter, he said. Pretty Good Privacy was founded a year ago to apply commercially the technology of that name developed by Philip R. Zimmerman, who is now the company's chairman and chief technology officer. Originally distributed free over the Internet beginning in 1991, PGP Mail allows electronic mail users to encrypt, create digital signatures, verify and decrypt messages safely and easily. PGP is based on a class of technologies known as public-key encryption that is designed to protect electronic transactions by scrambling data so they can be read only by people with the keys to the code.

title:
INVESTING IT;
Some Investors Just Won't Deal Without the Net
body: BRUCE BENNETT would rather spend his money on fishing equipment than on commissions for his stock trades. That's why Mr. Bennett, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Mississippi, has used three different brokerage firms in the last year. Interestingly, those three firms share another trait besides cheap deals: they all offer trading over the Internet. That is no surprise. The Internet is the speediest part of the fast-growing area of on-line trading. Investors can trade on line through a company's proprietary software, through commercial on-line services or directly on the Internet. But while only 5 of the 12 on-line traders, or 42 percent, offered Internet access in 1995, 25 of the 33 on-line traders this year, or 76 percent, are offering Internet service, according to the American Association of Individual Investors, which conducts this annual survey. "All the growth in on-line investing is over the Internet," said Andre Scheluchin, managing editor at Mercer Inc., which also tracks this data. When financial-services firms decide to start offering on-line trading, the Internet is more and more often their choice. Consider full-service brokers. Merrill Lynch recently announced it would begin offering Internet trading to qualifying customers in January 1998, and in December Dean Witter purchased Lombard Institutional Brokerage, which does about half of its trading on the Internet. Mutual funds, which often offer prospectuses and applications on the Internet, are also edging into trading. The Scudder, Fidelity, Strong and American Century fund families now allow exchanges, redemptions or both over the Internet. And the last two also allow the purchase of additional shares on the Internet, if the fund is linked to the customer's bank account. It is not surprising that bargain-seekers like Mr. Bennett have flocked to this system. The average minimum on-line trading commission has fallen from $35.33 in 1996 to $34.48 this year, and some trades -- particularly the Internet ones -- go for as little as $9 or less. "As more and more brokerages go on line and offer Internet trading, the competition for who can offer the lowest fees is heating up immensely," said Kenneth J. Michal, an analyst with the American Association of Individual Investors. Another reason for the low prices is low overhead, said Julio Gomez, an analyst at Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. "It costs brokerages very little, if anything, to offer trades via the Internet," he said. But investors must realize that these bargain deals sometimes come with conditions and hefty side charges. That is to be expected; discount brokers, the biggest presence in on-line trading so far, often use this approach in their off-line business, too. "What's happening right now with the price wars," Mr. Gomez said, "is that these firms are simply giving customers what they want -- cheap trades -- and extracting their pound of flesh elsewhere." Scottsdale Online, for example, charges a flat fee of $9 a trade. To get that price, however, investors must keep a $10,000 account minimum; otherwise, they must pony up $19 a transaction. Investexpress On-Line charges $13.95 a trade, but the trade must be for at least 500 shares, with a minimum share price of $3. Some firms charge execution fees on each trade. At Computel that fee is $2.50; Net Investor charges $2.75. "Investors should always call and ask about extra charges -- processing fees, handling fees, sometimes they're called different things," Mr. Scheluchin said. "All firms put it in their literature, but sometimes it's hard to find." Optional services can be steeply priced, too; Datek Online, for instance, charges $50 to mail stock certificates. Large fees for inactive accounts -- Net Investor charges $50 -- are often levied on investors who fail to generate a minimum dollar amount of commissions within a certain period. And limit orders, through which investors set a price limit on a stock sale or purchase, can cost extra. A regular trade at Lombard and E-Trade costs $14.95, for instance, but limit orders are $19.95. Individual retirement accounts can be hit with high special fees as well. Some researchers think cheap, no-frills trading -- with or without hefty side charges -- may not be what many investors want. "What we're seeing is that most people want a higher level of service than deep-discount brokerages offer when it comes to on-line investing," Mr. Gomez said. "Though deep discounters will continue to exist, firms that offer more services and broker support will become the on-line brokerages of choice." And they will thrive even if they charge more for trades, he said. Among such firms, Mr. Gomez said, are American Express Financial Direct and e.Schwab, which charge $31.95 and $29.95, respectively, for trades of up to 1,000 shares. title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Clear Channel in Deal To Buy Billboard Company Clear Channel Communications, a big broadcaster, agreed to buy Eller Media, a closely held billboard advertising company, for $1.15 billion in cash and stock. The transaction, which analysts said had been rumored for weeks, was announced after the stock market closed. Earlier, shares of Clear Channel rose 5.4 percent. [Page D3.]  Retail Results Above Forecasts Several retailers announced earnings that were generally higher than expected, though forecasts had been lowered during the holiday shopping season. The stocks of many retailers, including Wal-Mart, whose earnings rose modestly, were sharply higher. [D3.] The retailers' strong performances helped lift stock prices over all, with the Dow industrials gaining 30.01 points, to 7,038.21. [D8.]  A Big Potential Competitor to Cable Rupert Murdoch's agreement to invest $1 billion in a new satellite television service startled cable and satellite companies around the country. The new service could be a full-fledged competitor to cable.
