title: Internet Advertising Growing Slowly
body: Reality check for the World Wide Web: Who is going to pay for it? With consumers proving resistant to register for let alone subscribe to services they are used to getting free, Web publishers, content providers and search engines have been looking for advertising revenue as they continue to burn start-up and promotional money at a furious pace. And while advertising on the Web grew in 1996, to a range of $200 million or more from $55 million in 1995, much of that spending came from within the industry itself -- that is, from technology companies advertising themselves on the sites of other technology companies. For example, Netscape Communications is both a leading advertiser and a leading site on the Web. All told, Web- or computer-related companies accounted for more than 50 percent of all Web site ad spending in 1996, according to Jupiter Communications, a research and consulting firm focusing on the Internet and other on-line services. That makes it difficult to calculate bottom-line spending totals or to decipher who is really making money, Internet industry analysts say. They say too much is being expected too soon from a new medium, especially one whose audience size is still difficult to determine. "These are very, very primitive beginnings," said David Carlick, executive vice president of Poppe Tyson, an advertising agency owned by Bozell, Jacobs, Kenyon & Eckhardt that specializes in interactive marketing. "But in time, the advertisers will follow the eyeballs." One big advertiser, however, describes its Web spending as very modest. "Our interest would increase when there are more sophisticated ways to measure its effectiveness as a marketing tool," said Kari Bjorhus, a spokeswoman for the Coca-Cola Company. Another large advertiser, the Procter & Gamble Company, considers its interactive efforts strictly experimental. The company is appearing on Web sites that include Yahoo, the search engine, and the magazines Elle and Road and Track. "We are truly, truly in a research and development phase," said Kristen Hall, a P.& G. spokeswoman."We're learning what works, what doesn't, how to measure it. We don't know yet." She would not say how much the company was spending. While the $275 million spent in 1996 seems considerable, it was an insignificant portion of the estimated $173 billion spent on advertising in the unitedstates last year. It brings to mind George Orwell's image of trying to weigh a flea on scales designed for an elephant. "It's below rounding," said Rich LeFurgy, vice president of advertising and marketing at the Starwave Corporation, an Internet publisher based in Seattle. Allen Banks, executive vice president at Saatchi & Saatchi Advertising, owned by Cordiant P.L.C., identified the main advertisers besides technology companies as financial service companies and the entertainment and auto industries. There are few ads for consumer goods. "I think there are some real expectations for the first time," said John Nardone, director of media and research services at Modem Media, an interactive agency owned by True North Communications. "Nineteen ninety-six was an exciting year, but there were no expectations. In 1997, we'll be seeing people using the Web as a true part of their media mix." But even optimistic projections estimate ad spending on the Web at around $5 billion by 2000, or only 2 percent of estimated total American advertising spending. So is anyone making money? The most successful sites have been the search engines like Yahoo, which reported earnings of $91,000 on sales of $8.6 million for the fourth quarter, becoming one of the few Web-related companies to report a profit. "We were very surprised by the fourth quarter," said Jerry Yang, a founder of Yahoo. Search engines like Yahoo, Lycos and Excite are popular with advertisers because they act as hubs through which consumers move out onto the Web. "People come to us as a starting point," Mr. Yang said, so "we have had the first shot at being profitable." He said advertisers on Yahoo included financial service and travel companies, auto makers and packaged goods companies like General Mills and Procter & Gamble. The leading site among advertisers, according to Jupiter Communications, is Netscape because of the popularity of its widely used Web browser. Many sites that provide specialized information also rank high among advertisers. Among the leaders in advertising revenue, according to Jupiter, are sites like ZD Net by Softbank's Ziff-Davis, CNET and Time Warner Inc.'s Pathfinder, all of which appear to attract a significant number of regular readers. The amount of time people are spending on the Web has increased 50 percent during the last 12 months, according to George Ryan, chief technology analyst at PC Meter, a market research company. Mr. Ryan said that the average Web user tended to resemble personal computer owners in general: college educated, high income and mostly male. This may account for the prevalence of technology, auto and financial services advertising on the Web. Advertisers are still looking for much more precise data on Web sites. "The three problems that are giving advertisers pause are audience measurement, creative limitations and audience size," said Peter Storck, senior analyst at Jupiter. "Advertisers want accountability," he said. "They want to know what their dollar gets them." Mr. Nardone said Modem Media had conducted studies that found on-line ads had changed consumers' perceptions. But hard data on the effectiveness of Web sites remain elusive. "There is no third-party measurement yet that's credible, no consistency in the way sites report data and no confirmation of data," he said. Indeed, the industry has only just started setting measurement standards with the Internet Advertising Bureau, a trade group, suggesting sizes for ads. Since Web sites are a very new medium for advertisers, it is difficult to judge their prospects for success. "Everyone wanted a payback in Year One," Mr. LeFurgy of Starwave said. "It's just unrealistic." A new magazine can take years to get out of the red. Time Warner's Entertainment Weekly, for example, turned a profit for the first time last year, seven years after it was introduced. Moreover, Web sites still have technical hurdles to overcome, especially in the speed that they transmit data, before they attract big audiences. "The Web is just getting bogged down," said Rick Markovitz, general manager, Interactive BBDO North America. Other agree. "Until it gets to the point where moving from site to site is like changing channels on TV, a critical mass of consumers will be loath to spend a lot of time on line," said Bill Bass, senior analyst at Forrester Research in Boston. Still, Mr. Bass remains optimistic. "Advertisers will spend as audience grows," he said. "Kellogg and Reebok are going to spend on on-line advertising to the degree that their customers are on line." He estimated that about 16 percent of households are currently on line, with 36 percent expected by 2000. And, since the Web is a new medium, analysts say that whole new forms of advertising, as yet unthought of, could become popular. "By 1999, there will be enough advertising on the Internet that this becomes a profitable business," Mr. Bass said. "A handful will make it a bit sooner." title:
Market Place;
America Online's Strategy Raises Eyebrows
body: America Online Inc. has long divided Wall Street into two sharply defined camps. To its supporters, the on-line service is a pioneer in a new medium, well on its way to building the first mass-market brand name in cyberspace. To its detractors, America Online is simply an aggressive marketer with mounting losses. America Online's executives have replied to critics by asserting that near-term losses were not losses at all but astute investments -- the necessary cost of attracting a big audience on line. Build the audience, they assured investors, and the profits will follow before long. But since the company reported its quarterly results last Thursday, analysts have raised new questions about how costly America Online's business strategy is proving to be, whether the company has the cash to execute its plans, and how long it will take for the company to show steady profits. In the December quarter, America Online reported strong growth in revenue to $409 million, but also a sizable loss of $155 million, both essentially in line with Wall Street expectations. What has concerned some analysts, though, are other financial measures -- especially the health of the company's balance sheet. America Online has absorbed big losses in the last six months. As a result, the shareholders' equity -- assets minus liabilities -- fell to $38.8 million by the December quarter, from $512.5 million in June. Analysts have also raised questions whether America Online is facing a cash squeeze. In particular, they point to a sharp jump in its current liabilities. Those liabilities, falling due within a year, include the costs of laying off workers, shutting offices, scrapping outdated marketing materials, and credits and refunds to customers, as part of a recent settlement with states representing subscribers who have been unable to connect to America Online's service. Today, the company's current liabilities dwarf its cash, accounts receivable and other current assets. "The key issue for America Online is cash flow," said David Simons, managing director of Digital Video Investments, a newyork research adviser to institutional investors. "America Online is running out of cash." Another worrisome sign, some analysts say, is the fall in gross profit margins during the December quarter, to 40 percent from 46 percent in the September quarter. That slippage is significant, they add, because America Online has changed its accounting and adopted a flat-price policy for unlimited service as part of an overhaul in its business plan. The changes are largely responsible for the losses the company, based in Dulles, Va., has taken in the last six months. It is a growth plan that calls for America Online to rely less on subscriber fees and increasingly on revenue from advertising and electronic commerce. Part of the rationale for the new plan is that on-line access is fast becoming a low-margin commodity business, given added competition from Internet service providers and phone companies like AT&T. By contrast, the ad and electronic commerce field is expected to yield higher profit margins. Judging from the December quarter, at least, the transition to higher-margin business has not yet begun. These trends have apparently caused even some of America Online's Wall Street loyalists to have qualms. On Friday, Mary Meeker of Morgan Stanley & Company cut her rating on America Online from "strong buy" to "outperform." In a research note to clients, Ms. Meeker wrote: "AOL is a company with a split personality -- it always does good stuff and bad stuff." She added: "The good news: Our instincts tell us that AOL is on the cusp of breaking out with a profitable business model (after years of building) and that the stock price (after a lapse or two) should continue its recent steady climb. The bad news: The numbers tell us we are wrong." Jonathan Cohen of Smith Barney, who also lowered his rating on America Online on Friday, said he did so because it looked as if the company's transition to higher-margin fields was going to take some time before it translated into improving margins for the company as a whole. For their part, America Online executives reply that the company's transition is going smoothly. They say that the big losses recently, and the impact on America Online's balance sheet, are mainly a one-time housecleaning as part of its new business plan rather than evidence of a frightening trend. "On the surface, it is worrying," Lennert Leader, America Online's chief financial officer, said. "But if you drill down, it's not." The big increase in liabilities, Mr. Leader explained, is mainly charges related to the corporate overhaul. And another addition to liabilities, he added, results from all the people who took up the company's offer in December to prepay for a year's worth of service at a discounted monthly rate. In accounting terms, the undelivered service is a liability. The drop in gross margins in the December quarter, Mr. Leader said, was in part caused by an unexpectedly large number of new customers signing up. In December, when America Online's flat-price plan began, the company had expected to sign up 800,000 new customers. In fact, he said, 1.2 million subscribers were added. The free-trial time and technical support given to new customers drives up costs, depressing margins, Mr. Leader said. In the current quarter, America Online will "likely show a loss," Mr. Leader said. But the loss will result mainly from the $10 million to $15 million the company will spend to add 50,000 modems to its network, through lease arrangements, to increase its capacity. Still, the company said it should generate positive cash flow in the current quarter. Stephen M. Case, the chairman of America Online, said the company was not suffering a cash squeeze and was not considering a debt or equity offering to raise money. "Capital is not a constraint in building our business or executing our business plan," he said. Yesterday, the American Online enthusiasts carried the day on Wall Street. The company's shares closed up $3.375, at $37.125. That price, though, is still $1 a share below its closing price last Thursday -- America Online reported its quarterly results after the markets closed that day. Graphic   Graph: "Battered Balance Sheet" America Online, reeling from a history of operating losses and more recent problems, assures investors that it is fine, pointing to the cash assets on its balance sheet. But the last six months of 1996 saw its immediate debts rise sharply, which the money on hand to pay the bills barely budged. title:
Market Place;
A corner turns for Yahoo and other Internet search concerns.
body: THANKS to those clown-size fish in the company's TV ads, or the hillbilly yodel in the radio spots, even investors who have never surfed cyberspace have likely heard of Yahoo -- a leader in the market for services that help users search for information on the World Wide Web. Following the example of McDonald's and other consumer-product marketers, Yahoo, like its closest competitors, Lycos, Excite and Infoseek, has been building brand awareness through sizable television and radio advertising campaigns. And Yahoo, the first of these four publicly held search companies to post a profit, appears to be the most aggressive brand builder so far. It plans to spend between $10 million and $15 million on ads this year; that included a spot during last month's Super Bowl. In all, the campaign is a significant outlay for a company with less than $9 million in sales in its most recent quarter. But a recent run-up in Yahoo's stock price indicates that Wall Street supports the brand-building strategy. Yahoo's main service, free to users and supported by on-line advertising, is a navigation and search engine, which finds material on the Web based on key words or phrases that the computer user types in. Because most Web surfers employ a search tool on almost every visit, having one of the best-known brand names can certainly stimulate traffic -- and ad sales. By some analyst estimates, Yahoo leads the pack in selling Web advertising. According to the Electronic Advertising & Marketplace Report, an industry newsletter, Yahoo ended 1996 with $19 million in ad revenue; its nearest rivals, Infoseek and Excite, respectively generated an estimated $14.1 million and $13.5 million. Yesterday, Yahoo's stock closed at $29.125 a share, up nearly 75 percent from its price as recently as Jan. 2. The stock has yet to climb back to the share price of $43 it achieved on its first day of trading last April, on an offering originally priced at $13 a share. But investors have reason for optimism. Last month, the company reported earnings of $91,000 on sales of $8.6 million for the fourth quarter, making it the first publicly traded search-engine company to break into the black. The company also said that the number of advertisers on Yahoo's Web sites had risen to 550, from 340 in the third quarter. That news, and positive forecasts for Web advertising generally, recently led several analysts to upgrade their recommendations for the stock. Yahoo has made solid gains, but investing in Internet companies is still not for the skittish. For one thing, searching for material on the Web through key words or phrases -- which is the basic method for Yahoo and its rivals -- remains a far too random exercise for serious research.  Most people browsing the Web -- whatever search service they use -- too often find themselves adrift in a sea of irrelevant information. That may help explain why Yahoo, in courting the consumer, is expanding beyond searches to develop new Web sites for specific demographic groups and is striking deals with big-name information and entertainment providers. Late last month, for example, the company started a site for women, providing a gender-specific guide to entertainment, events, health resources and information sources on the Web.  Next month, the company plans to start a life-style and entertainment site for twenty-somethings that it has created in partnership with MTV. These creations extend a long list of sites that include Yahooligans, for children, and regional sites like Yahoo Boston and Yahoo Japan. Alan M. Braverman, a Credit Suisse First Boston analyst, said that Yahoo was best positioned to take advantage of the huge growth in Web advertising expected in the next few years. "What creates the winner on the Internet is brand, distribution and content -- and not necessarily technology," he said. "Of the public companies, Yahoo is going to be a clear leader." For advertisers, the lure of Yahoo is the target audiences defined by its demographically or geographically focused sites. "What they want to be to the Internet is similar to a broadcast model," said Paul Noglows, an analyst at Hambrecht & Quist in San Francisco, who recently raised his recommendation on Yahoo to a "strong buy" from a "buy" and increased the 1997 earnings estimate from a loss of 14 cents a share to a profit of 4 cents. "They want to provide content that advertisers know will attract specific viewers." Like Yahoo, Excite wants to provide a broad consumer service and extend its brand through a range of ancillary sites, such as a guide to chat groups on the Web and a guide to news. Excite not only directs users to Web sites but reviews and ranks the sites, too. And Excite has broad distribution, thanks to an exclusive arrangement providing Web-navigation technology to America Online -- a relationship enhanced by Excite's recent acquisition of the Web Crawler search engine from America Online. In turn, America Online received a 20 percent stake in Excite. Excite's revenue is surging: $6.5 million in the fourth quarter, compared with $574,000 in the period a year earlier. Still, the company lost $12.7 million for the quarter, or $1.06 a share. Excite shares closed yesterday at $15.0625, down $1.9375. While Yahoo and Excite embrace the consumer market, Infoseek has abandoned it, choosing to aim for serious researchers and business clients by concentrating on development of a fast and efficient search technology. In late January, Infoseek's shares reached a recent high of $10.75, but then gave up ground after the company reported 62 percent revenue growth -- middling, by Internet standards -- to $6.1 million for the fourth quarter. The loss of $4 million, or 15 cents a share, was a penny a share higher than the $3.7 million loss it posted in the quarter the previous year. Yesterday, the company's shares slipped 25 cents, to $9. Among the search companies, Lycos is perhaps taking the most singular approach. Rather than compete solely on advertising sales, the company has expanded its business by licensing its search technology to other Web developers -- including many leading Internet access providers. Already, licensing fees account for about 14 percent of the company's revenue. For the first quarter, which ended Oct. 31, the company had sales of $3.7 million. Lycos shares closed yesterday at $17.75, down 87.5 cents each. For all the investor interest in Web searchers, the biggest question may not be which companies take the market lead, but just how far -- technologically -- the whole field still has to go. "Without search engines, there's no way the Internet growth that has occurred could have happened," Mr. Braverman said. "But do search engines really work? The answer is 'No.' In my mind, we are at the point of the $300 calculator that subtracts and multiplies."

title: Data Service's Users Not Told Of Other Lines
body: While thousands of frustrated America Online subscribers tried in vain to dial into the service through its clogged electronic doorways during the last few weeks, the company made little or no effort to let people know that they could use older entryways where the crowds were smaller. Most customers would notice little difference between the older telephone lines connecting to America Online Inc., the country's No. 1 on-line service provider, and the newer ones whose use the service encourages. But which lines consumers use makes a difference to the company, since it must pay fees to outside carriers if subscribers use their lines instead of America Online's own network. It could also add to the burden on America Online's computer system when subscribers use the outside lines. It is unclear how many phone lines independent of America Online's own telephone network are available in major metropolitan areas around the country and how much time subscribers might have saved if they had used them more often. Many of the access lines operated by other companies for America Online are older and can transfer data at half the rate of more modern lines. The Sprint Corporation runs a nationwide network of telephone lines known as Sprintnet that America Online subscribers could use to dial into the service. Some subscribers, who joined the service more than a few months ago, still use Sprintnet numbers to dial into America Online. But when new customers set up their software, or when veteran subscribers request a new list of access numbers, the service provides them only its current list. In major metropolitan areas, the current lists include few, if any, of the still-active Sprintnet numbers. "It's a combination of the speed of the modems, the amount they are busy during prime time, the quality of Sprintnet's network," said David A. Gang, America Online's senior vice president for product marketing. "I do not think it would help the customers to have the Sprintnet numbers on the list." Until 1995 almost all of America Online's incoming calls were delivered over networks belonging to other companies. But over the last two years, America Online has been building its own network of modems and telephone lines to reduce the charges that it must pay to other carriers. The company says that about 80 percent of its traffic now flows over what it calls AOLnet. The company has not yet extended AOLnet across the country, and still relies on Sprintnet for coverage in some rural areas. The company does volunteer Sprintnet access numbers in areas where AOLnet does not exist. But America Online volunteers no information about the usable Sprintnet numbers in area codes that cover cities like Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, Denver, Detroit, Houston, Los Angeles, Miami, newyork, Philadelphia, San Francisco, Seattle and Washington. In newyork City, for instance, a Sprintnet telephone number is (212) 206-0256. But when America Online customers use the keyword "access" to pull up a list of potential access numbers for the 212 area code, that number does not appear. "It would cost them a little bit, but it would seem to me that it would make sense to pay Sprint something to keep people happy," said William B. Haynes, president of a small computer consulting company in Charlotte, N.C. "People expect to be able to get their email. People expect to be able to get their stock quotes. I think there's a real responsibility that comes with that. If they have the opportunity to save some of that grief for people, they should. "Now with Charlotte so overloaded, why in the world aren't the Sprint numbers there in that listing?" Mr. Gang said that the company could reintroduce Sprintnet numbers to its listings, but added, "I do not see that happening in any major metropolitan areas any time soon." "It is obviously more efficient and more cost-effective to our shareholders to build our own network," he said. "We've got the best-quality network available." Neither company would disclose what it costs America Online to receive customer calls through Sprintnet. "It cuts into their margins," said David Readerman, an analyst at Montgomery Securities in San Francisco, "but they're not losing money on those calls." America Online recently reached a settlement with attorneys general from 36 states who had threatened to sue the company for deceptive business practices. In early December America Online began to promote an all-you-can-eat pricing plan that offered users "unlimited" access to the service for $19.95 a month. But the company underestimated demand and the AOLnet modems quickly became clogged, preventing many customers from using the system as often as they liked. "I've given all my clients the Sprintnet number and they're getting on line with no problems," Mr. Haynes said. Customers who dial (800) 473-7983 can find a Sprintnet telephone number in their area. Sprintnet usually offers speeds up to 14.4 kilobits per second.

title: On-Line Service Adds Modems And Posts Loss
body: America Online Inc. said yesterday that it would add 50,000 more computer modems to its on-line service, giving its frustrated customers more gateways to get through to the dial-up service. The extra modems will increase America Online's daily capacity by 60 percent, two months ahead of its previously announced timetable. Stephen M. Case, America Online's chairman, said that the new modems, leased from other companies, should "significantly cut down" on the recent problems experienced by thousands of the company's subscribers. Often, America Online customers have gotten only busy signals recently when trying to get connected to the service. The company, based in Dulles, Va., announced its accelerated plan for easing its service problems as it reported financial results for the quarter ended Dec. 31. The fast-growing on-line service reported that its revenue had risen 64 percent compared with the year-earlier quarter, to $409.4 million. But America Online's bid for growth has once again proved to be costly. The company posted a quarterly loss of $154.8 million, or $1.64 a share. The loss comes after a quarter, ended in October, when the company lost $353.7 million, or $3.80 a share. In the latest quarter, the loss was mainly attributed to one-time charges for operations and closed offices, employees laid off and outdated marketing materials. Excluding the nonrecurring charges, the company still lost money for the quarter. The level of the loss was essentially in line with analyst expectations, and not a surprise. America Online posted its results after the stock market closed yesterday. During the day's trading session, the company's stock price closed unchanged at $38.125 a share. America Online, company executives say, has begun a transition in its business. As part of its campaign for growth, America Online is offering all-you-can-use pricing to increase its subscriber rolls, and trying to garner more revenue from advertising and electronic commerce. Indeed, advertising and commerce revenues rose 67 percent to $40 million from the October quarter. "Our business model is on track," Mr. Case said. "And we are making every effort to increase our capacity so that we can handle the phenomenal surge in demand for AOL we've seen in the last few months." The increased demand -- and America Online's inability to cope -- has prompted a wave of consumer complaints and states threatening lawsuits. In response, America Online agreed last week to offer subscribers credits and cash rebates. The company said yesterday that it estimated the cost of credits and rebates to subscribers at $24 million -- a charge against earnings included in the quarter's $154.8 million loss. The service breakdown at America Online started in December, when it switched to a policy of charging a flat price of $19.95 a month for unlimited use. Before, the company had mainly charged subscribers on an hourly basis, in addition to a minimum fee for use of as many as five hours a month. America Online's accelerated program to let more subscribers connect to its network is a temporary fix. It is leasing modem time from other companies, while it continues to add capacity to its own network. As part of its agreement with these outside suppliers, America Online agreed not to name them, Mr. Case said in an interview. For the rest of the year, analysts will be looking closely at the impact, if any, of America Online's service problems on its business plan. It now has roughly 8 million subscribers, far more than any other on-line service. But as part of last week's agreement with 36 state attorneys general, America Online agreed to suspend marketing activities until it can give its current subscribers prompt access to its network. Yet the company's plan for sharply increasing its advertising revenue was based on continuing growth in its membership, to 10 million by later this year. "Whether the advertising and electronic commerce revenues will continue to grow despite the service disruptions is certainly in question," said David Readerman, an analyst for Montgomery Securities in San Francisco. In fact, America Online suffered a brief service lapse on Wednesday, as many customers were unable to get onto the service for a couple of hours in the evening. The company said that the brief breakdown came as it was making a routine upgrade of the software in its network. Graphic   Table: "America Online Inc. title: With America Online Demand Come New Rules of Supply
body: When America Online Inc. began its all-you-can-eat pricing policy in December, the company was making a number of risky bets at once -- not only with its own business, but also with the cyberspace fortunes of the 300 companies, large and small, that supply everything from news to fashion tips on the big on-line service. Clearly, America Online lost its bet that it could handle the added traffic generated by its flat-rate program. Last week, faced with the threat of lawsuits by regulators from several states, the company was forced to offer credits and rebates to angry subscribers. In the last two months, subscribers have often heard only busy signals when trying to get onto the dial-up service. The company is investing heavily to add high-capacity data lines and modems to ease the congestion, but solving the problem will probably take months. The flat-pricing strategy -- $19.95 a month for unlimited use -- also means a wrenching transition for the businesses that supply information, entertainment and special-interest forums on America Online. Many of these on-line producers, known in the trade as "content providers," report that since America Online went to a flat rate, the traffic on their sites has at least doubled. But for these independent contractors, the sharp increase in usage is no longer the windfall that it would have been a few months earlier. Before, when America Online was priced by the hour, the content suppliers received a share -- typically 10 percent or 15 percent -- of the revenue earned as subscribers lingered on their sites. The more people tapped into a given site, and the longer they lingered, the more money the content supplier collected. With flat pricing, the usage fees collected by content providers are now capped, just as they are for America Online itself. The usage revenue-sharing deals that America Online strikes with its suppliers are private contracts, and the terms vary. Yet at the annual conference for its content partners in Phoenix in early December, America Online executives had a clear message: Usage fees will fall under flat pricing, so to survive, content producers must get new revenue from advertising and on-line commerce. In a bid for growth, America Online, which is based in Dulles, Va., is limiting its revenue from connection fees paid by subscribers and hoping to more than make up the shortfall from advertising. Today, advertising represents only about 10 percent of the company's revenue, and analysts say that America Online wants to lift that to 30 percent in a year or so. "As a business," said Greg Wester, an analyst for the Yankee Group, "America Online will live or die based on advertising revenues from here on." So will America Online's content suppliers. The shift, analysts say, means a winnowing out of the least commercial sites on America Online -- services without the kind of narrowly focused business tie-ins that advertisers and marketers look for in their on-line sales efforts. America Online executives frequently compare the state of the on-line business to that of cable television in its early days. In the 1970's, they note, cable entrepreneurs at first thought they could support the business by subscription fees, but later moved to a mixed model of monthly fees and advertising. "Our business is going through exactly the same transition now," said Barry Schuler, America Online's president for creative development. With its television-style evolution as a business, analysts predict, America Online is moving toward a "top 100" approach in its dealings with the producers supplying the information, entertainment and forums on its service. (The newyork Times provides an on-line version of its daily newspaper, called @times, for America Online.) Mr. Schuler declined to discuss specific numbers. But he did say he expected that there would be a "general consolidation" in the number of content sites, both on on-line services and on the World Wide Web. Many of America Online's most popular content suppliers also have a presence on separate Web sites. They are trying to build their own brand names, outside the embrace of America Online, so that their fortunes are not totally tied to those of the big on-line service. Motley Fool, a popular on-line investment advisory service, is one example. It began on America Online in August 1994, and added a Web site in January 1996. From a staff of 3 people, the Motley Fool has grown to 45 full-time employees and 120 part-timers. Traffic on the Motley Fool site on America Online has doubled since flat pricing began in December, to about 300,000 households a month. The new policy changes the relationship between America Online and content producers, both forcing them to be more self-reliant and enabling them to be more independent. "It has a much more stand-alone feel to it now," said Tom Gardner, the 28-year-old co-founder of Motley Fool. Content producers, Mr. Gardner said, will look to America Online to provide the best network, easiest access and best interface in cyberspace. If it lags in those areas, he added, "I think information providers will be much more willing to look around at other service providers." The increase in the use of America Online because of flat pricing has already benefited the advertisers on the Knot, a site for people planning weddings. By January, traffic to the Knot had doubled from two months earlier, to 125,000 visitors a month, said Rob Fassino, a partner at Element Studios Inc., which produces the site. As a result, Mr. Fassino said, the number of people requesting information on line from Celebrity Cruises, an advertiser on the Knot, had doubled to 2,200 in the last three weeks, and about 3,500 on-line browsers had requested an entertainment guide offered by Reunite Wines, another advertiser on the site. Nancy Evans is the president of Ivillage, which produces two popular sites on America Online, and she also anticipates a rise in use. One site is for parents, called "Parent Soup"; the other, called "About Work," offers job advice. Both are also on the Web. Last week, Ms. Evans was in the midst of doubling her advertising staff to 10 people from 5. The hiring, she noted, was planned before the recent surge in America Online traffic, but anything that builds audiences will help bring in advertising. "America Online's move is the beginning of the answer to how you build a mass market and make money in cyberspace," Ms. Evans said. Like other on-line producers, she said that America Online subscribers might be angry with the company for congestion on the network. But once connected, they do not seem to vent their wrath in the chat areas. "People are happy to get to us," Ms. Evans said.

title: Getting Past the Busy Signal
body: The attorneys general of 36 states may be satisfied with the settlement they reached with America Online, but customers who have met with busy signals for weeks will be less convinced that the problem of network congestion has been solved. The on-line jam-up started in early December when America Online began offering a new pricing plan in which subscribers get unlimited use of the service for a flat $19.95 per month. Previously, the company charged customers a low monthly fee plus additional charges for each hour spent on line, a system that led customers to moderate their use of the service. The new policy created more demand for on-line time than the company had anticipated. The attorneys general contended that America Online had engaged in a deceptive business practice by advertising unlimited access and then failing to provide enough open lines to deliver it. The settlement plan would give customers a month of free service or a refund of up to $39.90 for the months of December and January. America Online will suspend its advertising beginning this month, and include in future advertisements a disclaimer on potential access problems. The company will also make it easier to cancel the service. The plan compensates some customers, primarily the lightest users, for their inconvenience but it will not necessarily solve the capacity problem. America Online is pursuing an aggressive strategy to expand its subscriber base, which has just passed eight million, so as to better attract advertising. To ease congestion, the company says it will hold its current size for the next few months, but it is committed to expanding its customer base to 10 million by the end of the year. The surest way to reach that goal is to resume aggressive marketing efforts. The company says it will spend $350 million this year to add phone lines and more modems to meet on-line demands. But steady investment in hardware may still be outpaced by rapid growth in subscriber numbers. In a business where survival depends on market share, there will always be the temptation to sell services well before the system's capacity expands. Policing the unrealistic promises of on-line services may become routine work for attorneys general. For consumers, that busy signal to the Internet may just become a fact of cyberlife.

title: On-Line Ire Is Not Pacified By Agreement
body: One day after the nation's largest provider of cyberspace services, America Online Inc., agreed to pay millions of dollars to compensate subscribers for two months of network congestion, many customers refused to be mollified yesterday, saying that the refunds could hardly make up for their lost business and time. Some customers said that America Online added insult to injury by inadequately staffing the telephone lines it set up to handle refund requests, leading to confusing journeys through touch-tone telephone systems and long waits on hold. And others said that America Online's policy of giving the largest refunds, about $40, to the smallest users was unfair to those who had suffered the most. "I think it's a great public relations move," said Conan S. Cocallas of Fairfield, Calif., who blames a recent inability to get through to the service for costing his small computer-parts supply company a $3,000 order. "But there is really no way to compensate for time lost. For people whose businesses rely on it, there's no way to say, 'We're going to give you back all that time you wasted listening to busy signals in front of your computer.' I just want it fixed." But Stephen M. Case, the chairman of America Online, said: "The feedback I got today from members was favorable. People wanted to know what steps we were going to take to satisfy our customers and we told them." Even some of the most critical customers said they would stick with the service until the network logjam had been cleared. The company has promised to spend $350 million to increase capacity and has said the problems will be resolved by June. America Online, which is based in Dulles, Va., and surpassed eight million subscribers last week, reached the pact with the attorneys general of 36 states on Wednesday after the prosecutors threatened to sue the company for deceptive business practices. Moving away from charging users for each hour spent on line, the company began offering -- and aggressively promoting -- a new price plan early last month that promised unlimited access to the service for $19.95 a month. But the company seemed to underestimate both existing users' appetite for on-line time and the number of new customers the offer would attract -- 1.4 million since last October. By the middle of last month, many America Online subscribers faced interminable busy signals whenever they tried to dial into the service with their computer modems. America Online still offers hourly rates, but the company said a vast majority of its customers now subscribed to the unlimited-use plan. Under the agreement the attorneys general will not file lawsuits against America Online. In exchange, the company will give subscribers who request it compensation ranging from a full, $19.95 refund for customers who used the service for less than two hours during either December or January to a 25 percent, $5 rebate for users who spent between 8 and 15 hours in either month on line. The company has said that the settlement will cost less than $50 million. Customers who spent more than 15 hours on America Online in either December or January are not eligible for a refund for that month, though all customers can choose to receive a free month of service if they write to an address in Utah. That satisfied the attorneys general but was an affront to some America Online subscribers. "Nonsense. Total nonsense," said Peter J. Magliarditi, describing the deal. Mr. Magliarditi, an independent researcher in Lewiston, N.Y., is seeking class-action status in Federal District Court in Buffalo along with 100 other America Online customers for a lawsuit against the company for breach of warranty. "They are punishing the people who tried the hardest to get on line by giving them no refund," he said. But Mr. Case defended the refund plan as fair. "The sense was that for someone who used 100 hours in a month, a refund was less appropriate than for someone who used 10 minutes in a month," he said. "The principle that has been guiding our thinking all along was that we've spent a decade building this brand and we want to do everything necessary to protect it and enhance it." That thinking appeared to please investors -- shares of America Online closed up 62.5 cents, at $37.875, on the newyork Stock Exchange, after a big increase on Wednesday -- but did not go over well with Roberta Rosenfield, a retired schoolteacher in Nanuet, N.Y., who has subscribed to America Online for two years. "I called the number they gave and held on for 40 minutes," she said. "It's a mess. During those 40 minutes they repeated a list of 15 other numbers to call for this or that. I tried one or two but didn't get anywhere. "We just want to get our money back."

title: REFUNDS PLANNED BY AMERICA ONLINE IN NETWORK JAM
body: America Online Inc., the fast-growing company that has ushered nearly eight million Americans into cyberspace, agreed yesterday to give millions of dollars of credits and refunds as compensation for network traffic jams that had been frustrating its customers since December. The humbling announcement by America Online came in response to threats of lawsuits by dozens of states and an angry outcry from many subscribers, who have often received nothing but busy signals lately when trying to get onto the dial-up service. The congestion began early last month after America Online, in an ambitious bid for further growth, started to charge customers a flat $19.95 monthly fee for unlimited use. Previously, the company had charged a much lower fee but began billing by the hour after the customer exceeded a monthly limit -- five hours, in most cases. Until yesterday, America Online had sought to address the consumer complaints by announcing plans to expand the capacity of its network and then, under mounting pressure, to consider credits or refunds only on a case-by-case basis. But the position of several state attorneys general was that America Online's aggressive marketing campaign, combined with the frequent failure to supply the advertised new service, amounted to a deceptive business practice. Generally, the agreement calls for America Online to issue refunds or credit toward future service, as the customer chooses, to cover network problems during December and January. Under of the agreement, customers can either receive credit for a free month of service or qualify for cash rebates up to $39.90. The state officials portrayed yesterday's blanket settlement as a milestone in extending consumer protection into the increasingly popular frontiers of the information age. "Cyberspace is a new and exciting place to acquire information," said Jim Ryan, the Illinois Attorney General who coordinated the states' campaign to settle with America Online. "But we must remain vigilant to make sure that consumers have the same protections there as they do in more traditional venues." Three dozen states joined yesterday's announced agreement. But the attorneys general and America Online executives said the pact would cover all America Online subscribers nationwide. Dennis C. Vacco, the newyork Attorney General, pronounced the agreement "wholly satisfactory" and added that it "should put an end to the misleading marketing campaign that America Online waged to attract subscribers." The pact also requires America Online to temporarily curb its advertising for the $19.95 service, and to make any ads "clearly and conspicuously" state that customers may encounter delays when going on line. Yesterday's agreement covers the problems encountered by America Online subscribers in December and January. The attorneys general said they would continue to monitor America Online and the rest of the on-line industry, especially marketing practices. America Online contends that yesterday's agreement should calm its customers as it spends $350 million through the first half of this year to add more phone lines and powerful modems, thus enabling subscribers to get on the service when they want. And Wall Street greeted the announcement as a step to put America Online's recent troubles behind it. America Online shares rose $2 yesterday to close at $37.25 a share. "We accept 100 percent responsibility for these problems," said Stephen M. Case, the chairman of America Online. "But the reason we have these problems is that the demand is so great. It reflects the surging interest in using interactive services and the Internet as more people rely on them in a more fundamental way, as they become part of everyday life." The financial impact on America Online is uncertain because it remains to be seen how many customers will take advantage of the agreement. But most analysts doubted that the total cost would be more than $25 million. Since the credits and refunds do require subscribers to write or call the company, not all of them are expected to take advantage of the agreement. And the larger impact could be that America Online's aggressive marketing campaign of television advertising and mailing start-up disks to millions of households has stirred interest that for now can be satisfied only by its rivals. Already, some disgruntled America Online subscribers are defecting to other services. Competitors like Microsoft Network, Compuserve, Prodigy and AT&T Worldnet have all reported unsually high rates of new subscribers signing on in recent weeks, partly because of America Online's highly publicized troubles. "For a while at least, America Online is handing a tremendous advantage to other services," said Mark Mooradian, an analyst at Jupiter Communications, a research firm in newyork. And Compuserve went so far as to run a last-minute advertisement during the Super Bowl last Sunday to try to capitalize on America Online's problems. The ad showed a black screen accompanied by the sounds of a computer dialing unsuccessfully to try to make a modem connection to an unnamed on-line service. Later, came silence and the printed words on screen: "Looking for dependable Internet access? Compuserve. Get on with it." But how much rivals may gain and America Online will suffer is as yet unclear. The company, based in Dulles, Va., has a huge lead on its competitors, with 7.5 million subscribers in the unitedstates at the end of last year. The second-ranked on-line service is Compuserve with 2.1 million subscribers in America, Jupiter Communications estimated; followed by Microsoft Network with 1.4 million, Prodigy with 1 million and AT&T Worldnet with 650,000. America Online's fastest-rising rival is the Microsoft Network, which began in August 1995. And after a tentative start to its marketing efforts, Mr. Mooradian of Jupiter said, the big software maker's service is in the midst of a $100 million marketing campaign to gain ground on America Online. America Online's headlong bid for growth is part of a strategy to attain that most elusive of goals in cyberspace -- a profitable business. The company's formula for business success is to cut costs, attract more customers and then attract advertisers. Today, only about 10 percent of America Online's revenues come from on-line advertising for everything from books to clothes to travel. The company's goal, analysts say, is to lift that to 30 percent or more. To do that, America Online believes it needs to build television-sized audiences, and company executives often compare themselves to a cable television network. Yet today, only about 15 million American households, or 15 percent, are connected to any on-line service or Internet access supplier. By 2000, the number is expected to rise rapidly to 43 million, estimates the Yankee Group, a research firm in Boston. "America Online is going to keep trying to build its audience, first and foremost, even if it means taking hits like this," said Greg Wester, an analyst for the Yankee Group. "For them, the game is not to win and be loved today, but to survive and be dominant in the year 2000 when 43 million households are in cyberspace." That certainly seems to be the approach taken by Mr. Case, America Online's chairman. As part of its agreement, the company has agreed to hold subscribers at eight million for a while and stop advertising in February while it expands capacity. But Mr. Case said yesterday that the company's previously stated goal of having 10 million members by the end of this year had not been abandoned. And, he added, he had no real regrets about offering a flat fee of $19.95 for unlimited use to attract newcomers to cyberspace. "When the dust settles," Mr. Case said. "I believe America Online will be recognized as a service that can handle millions of people and that millions of people want to use. And pricing for unlimited use is part of reaching a mainstream audience." title: New York Warning to America Online
body: Attorney General Dennis C. Vacco threatened today to sue America Online, the nation's largest on-line service, if the company did not relieve the congestion that has produced busy signals for members when they try to dial into the service. The on-line service has been inundated with complaints from customers around the country since America Online began offering computer users unlimited Internet access for $19.95 a month in December. America Online has acknowledged the problems and pledged to add capacity and provide better access in the near future. But last week, customers filed lawsuits in several states, including newyork, accusing the company of selling a service that it could not provide. Today, Mr. Vacco sent a written notice to America Online, which is based in Dulles, Va., warning that if negotiations to correct the problem broke down between his office and the company, he would file a civil lawsuit charging it with consumer fraud. "AOL jumped out of the gate in December with a new pricing plan offering unlimited access for $19.95 a month," Mr. Vacco said. "Unfortunately for the company, and even more unfortunately for its customers, it lacked the technological capacity to handle all the traffic that this new offer triggered."

title:
MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
An interactive advertising network is offering tutorials to plug the potential of cyberpitches.
body: ARE you ready for classes in interactive advertising from A for Apple to Z for Ziff-Davis? Those lessons for marketers and agencies, which began last week, are not being taught by a beloved pedagogue like Mr. Microchips. Nor are they to be found on a Web site like http://www.welcomebackkotter.edu. Rather, the tutorials are in the form of a campaign for Double Click, an interactive advertising network based in newyork with sales offices in cities including Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles and Toronto. The effort to promote the perceived potential of cyberpitches is being created by Digital Pulp, a small agency in newyork, and carries the theme "Building one-to-one relationships millions at a time." Double Click plans to spend slightly more than $2 million through 1997 on the campaign, which will include print advertisements, direct mail and of course appeals on its own Web site (http://www.doubleclick.com). "We want to be a catalyst, if you will, for the industry to grow and realize its potential," said Lee Nadler, marketing director at Double Click. "We recognize the need to bring in the big advertisers and the big money," he added, "and that's going to take some time. Yes, we're selling now, but we're also educating for tomorrow's dollars." Recent setbacks in the interactive realm are "getting everyone terribly confused," Mr. Nadler said, like the abrupt shutdowns of what had been promising electronic publishing ventures and disputes over measuring Web site traffic. "The promise of the Internet has led to a rush to put up sites," he added, "perhaps before they had a purpose. People need to know how to harness this." Mr. Nadler, who has also worked for Kirshenbaum Bond & Partners in newyork and the on-line service Prodigy, said: "Door-to-door sales was the most effective marketing tool because you got to know the customer. You built a relationship, a dialogue. Now the Web has that same power and same efficiency, but some people feel they're coming in halfway through." The first ad in the Double Click series makes that same comparison to how Fuller brushes and vacuum cleaners were peddled: "An introduction is made, interaction begins, questions are asked and answered, products are sold." The ad goes on to present tips on how to get the proverbial foot in the door, suggesting for instance that the creative content of interactive advertising "be tested before you spend big money on placements." The campaign deliberately eschews explanations of how interactive technology works, said Steven Sacks, president and creative director at Digital Pulp, because it was more important to "educate people on how this medium works and give them tools to take advantage of it." Double Click was formed in March by the merger of a unit of Poppe Tyson, owned by Bozell, Jacobs, Kenyon & Eckhardt, with what was the Internet Advertising Network. Double Click offers advertisers the ability to buy space on almost 70 sites in content categories like business, entertainment, news, search engines and sports, offering "affinity groups" of consumers interested in those areas. Among the sites Double Click represents are one devoted to the comic strip "Dilbert" (http://www.united media.com/comics/dilbert/), USA Today Online (http://www.usato day.com) and the Internet Address Finder (http://www.iaf.net). Double Click had hoped to have 100 sites in its network by the end of 1996, but Mr. Nadler said that goal would now be met "in the next few months." He attributed the delay to "strict criteria" that required sites be "well backed." Double Click also customizes banners and other interactive ads through a technology named Dart, for Dynamic Advertising Reporting and Targeting. "Dart allows us to recognize users when they come to a site on our network," Mr. Nadler said. "The advertiser tells us who the target audience is; for example, college students in California. We recognize those individuals and show them the message, within 15 milliseconds." Perhaps a sequel to the hit film "Jerry Maguire" will feature a zealous advertising agent who shouts, "Show me the message!"

title: America Online Moves to Placate Its Angry Users
body: With its network and the patience of its customers strained to the breaking point, America Online announced a series of new initiatives yesterday to try to relieve the congestion that has led to at least four class-action lawsuits and thousands of complaints from frustrated consumers. The on-line service has been flooded with complaints from people around the country who have been unable to dial into the service since it began offering unlimited use for $19.95 a month in December. To help ease the strain, the company announced that it would suspend its television advertising campaign, spend an additional $100 million to expand the capacity of its network, and add more telephone representatives to field calls from angry customers. But even these measures will not relieve the company's clogged modems until the spring at the earliest, said Bob Pittman, the president and chief executive of AOL Networks, the America Online unit that runs the on-line service. "It will be the end of spring before we are where we want to be," he added. "Some cities will feel it sooner because this is about going from town to town putting more modems in." The company has even resorted to a novel approach to solving the capacity constraints: asking customers not to use the service. In a letter posted to subscribers yesterday, Steve Case, the chairman and chief executive of America Online Inc., said that many users were so worried about not being able to get on the network that they were simply staying on all the time. "While that's understandable at one level," Mr. Case wrote. "It is obviously problematic at another." Mr. Pittman said the company had anticipated some increased use after the new pricing plan was introduced but the jump has been greater than expected. In December its customers logged a record 102 million hours on line, up from 45 million hours in September. The average America Online member now spends 32 minutes a day on line, up from 14 minutes in September. But judging from the number of complaints, one might conclude the average America Online subscriber spends more time trying unsuccessfully to dial on. Since the beginning of the year, a petition has been passed by email collecting scores of names. Its plea is simple: "We the users of AOL demand a dependable service." "For the last month, it has been almost impossible to get connected after about 3 or 4 o'clock in the afternoon," said Judith Handelman, a writer and editor in Scarsdale, N.Y. "I wrote to them and I got this long letter full of clap-trap." Many customers use the service as part of their businesses, making the difficulty of gaining access to email even more critical but also making it harder to quit the service. "I'd like to switch but I've got my AOL address on my business card," said Jean Wyman, an entrepreneur who lives in Los Angeles. The company said yesterday that it was aware of four class-action suits that have been filed against the service in California, Illinois, New Jersey and newyork. The newyork suit accuses America Online of breach of contract, deceptive practices, deceptive advertising and unjust enrichment. "If they didn't think that with eight million subscribers they didn't feel that they would have a tremendous burst of usage, then they are incredibly naive -- and I don't think they are that," said Edward Labaton, a partner with Goodkind Labaton Rudoff & Sucharow in Manhattan, which filed a class-action suit on behalf of four America Online members. Attorneys general in several states, including newyork and Wisconsin, are also alarmed by the complaints. Last month, America Online reached an agreement with 19 states promising to clarify its new pricing plan and offer refunds to consumers who ask to switch back to their old plan before April. "We're taking very close look at it," said Marc Carey, a spokesman for the newyork Attorney General, Dennis Vacco. Despite the many complaints, America Online said that it was still growing, with a net gain of 1.2 million subscribers in the quarter ending Dec. 31 for a total of more than 8 million. December was the service's best month ever, with 500,000 new subscribers. A spokesman said that the company would not say how many customers it has been losing in recent weeks. Under its new plan, it will increase its spending on system capacity to $350 million from $250 million. Next month, it said it would break ground on a data center in Reston, Va. The service currently has more than 200,000 modems in cities around the country for subscribers to dial up. It promised to increase that number by 75 percent, allowing an additional six million sessions a day. In addition, the company said it would hire 600 more customer support representatives for a total of more than 4,500. It will also suspend its television advertisements and stop distributing its ubiquitous floppy disks offering a free trial in areas where access has been a problem. The management, which has been denying the problem for weeks, has also become more humble. "Am I bloody?" Mr. Pittman, the company executive, asked. "Yes. Do my eyes have circles under them? Yes."

title:
Taking In the Sites;
How to Keep Your Privacy: Battle Lines Get Clearer
body: Whether sending email to a sweetheart, buying books on line or browsing for something your mother would rather not know about, privacy and anonymity are rarely guaranteed on the Internet. Between the logging done by corporate computer departments, Internet service providers, marketing mavens and the just plain curious, plenty of people are keeping track of the comings and goings on the Net. Last week, Representative Bruce Vento, a Minnesota Democrat, introduced the Consumer Internet Privacy Protection Act of 1997, intended to keep subscriber information from being misused by on-line service providers. But even if it is enacted, this measure will not help if your boss notices your browser has been going places it should not. To protect that email, head over to P.G.P., the home of Pretty Good Privacy. P.G.P. is a free product that can secure the contents of your email from hackers. It is so secure that it is classified as a munition by the Government and exporting it causes problems. Phil Zimmerman, the author of P.G.P., was investigated by the Government for three years for possibly violating munitions export laws after he posted the program on the Internet. The Government finally sent him a written note saying it had decided not to prosecute him. Other encryption programs are readily available on the Internet, and they are a hot button for the Clinton Administration and F.B.I., among others, because the good ones make email and files impossible to read. The Administration's stance was probably most clearly stated in a July statement to the Senate on the effect of encryption by Louis J. Freeh, the F.B.I. director. The Administration has floated several proposals, notably the Clipper chip and key escrow encryption, that give Government officials a way to unlock files. Law enforcement and national security officials say they need to be able to unlock files to protect against lawbreakers. The Clinton Administration has recently revised the encryption exportation policy, transferring oversight to the Commerce Department. The new policy is not listed on the Commerce Department's Web site, but the Internet Privacy Coalition has the executive order posted, along with reports on other privacy-related issues. The coalition promotes privacy and security on the Internet through the use of encryption and the relaxation of export controls on cryptography, so its offerings may sound a little one-sided. The encryption policy is a hot button for sites dedicated to privacy issues, too. The people at the Electronic Privacy Information Center cover encryption as part of the privacy issue and have a collection of articles, press releases and links that make for interesting reading. There is a site in the Netherlands that discusses remailers, security issues and other ways to remain anonymous for email and newsgroups. To keep from leaving footprints while browsing, try the Anonymizer. It appears to slow down your browsing somewhat, but the sites you visit should see the Anonymizer's address instead of yours. title:
Taking In the Sites;
Scout Getaway Options Or Feed Your Daydreams
body: Hoping to escape the winter by getting away to a dreamy island -- Jamaica, let's say? There are many ways to use the World Wide Web to find the attractions there that will make a trip stand out. Start with general travel banks, whether reliable names from print like Fodor's and Conde Nast Traveler, or Web resources like Time Warner's Pathfinder. Also, search engines like Yahoo have special travel categories. Then check out a promotional group like the local chamber of commerce or government tourist board. There are also interactive companies springing up -- like Preview Travel Inc., which offers tourist information and ways to book air tickets and package tours, and Travelocity, a reservations service -- that are full of information whether you are going to the islands or Vail, Colo. All told, these resources and some skillful searching can help you plan out the fine details of a winter vacation, be it in the sun or snow. In the case of a Jamaican getaway, you can learn about package deals, tucked-away inns, golf courses, scuba outfitters and nightclubs in Montego Bay, known locally as Mo' Bay. A search at Yahoo leads to a deep-sea fishing charter company, whose ship, the No Problem, goes out in search of yellowfin tuna, and to the Sandals resort chain, which lists its room rates and shows a photo of the pool. The Jamaica Tourist Board describes Montego Bay's white sand Cornwall Beach and bamboo rafts that float down the Martha Brae River. It also lists air and cruise lines that travel to the island and gives practical driving information. Fodor's offers a trip planner customized by such things as restaurant price range, along with things Jamaican not to be missed like jerk chicken and Red Stripe beer. Preview Travel is handy for printing out a page or two when you are deciding what to pack. Its site even links to a weather forecast, which on recent checking showed a steady 86 degrees in Jamaica for days to come.  Preview's backers include America Online and U S West. Travelocity, a reservations service backed by the Sabre air reservations services and Worldview Systems, an on-line publisher, describes how to take a side trip to Cuba, 90 miles away, and explains that reggae is now influenced by American rap. If you have frequent-flier mileage, you might also check out your airline, which probably offers package deals. The wealth of information on the Web does not mean you will not also want a trusty print guidebook. A guidebook typically starts with general information and histories and leads to particular activities. Which is good if you are sorting out which island to visit, then which beach, and then which sport you'll take up; or, in a Web sense, for figuring out what to search for. Also, a good book conveys an author's point of view, and ranks attractions -- far different from looking at the fulsome Web page published by a golf course or resort. Jonathan Runge's book "The Insider's Guide to the Caribbean," for example, candidly criticizes "all-inclusive" resorts -- where rooms, meals, drinks and tips are included in one price -- as "adult summer camps," and notes of Negril beach on Jamaica, "A very good mood prevails here, probably because everyone is so high." That is a perspective not readily obtainable from official promotion boards. Pathfinder, however, includes some frank and welcome advice when it says that tourists to Jamaica "should be aware that they'll certainly be exposed to the poverty, are likely to be offered drugs, and may find themselves (especially women travelers) receiving unwanted attention from con artists and others who prey on tourists." And for those essential instructions on how to make a pina colada, a site, strangely situated at the University of Michigan, tells the whole story, all the way back to the drink's invention by a bartender in Puerto Rico in 1957.
