title: Dean Witter To Purchase A Discounter
body: Dean Witter, Discover & Company said yesterday that it had agreed to buy Lombard Institutional Brokerage Inc., a discount securities firm that offers trading over the Internet and by toll-free telephone number. The terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. The parent of Dean Witter Reynolds Inc., the nation's third-largest brokerage firm in the number of brokers, is buying Lombard at a time when the electronic brokerage industry is growing rapidly, prompting full-service firms like Merrill Lynch & Company to offer trading through new electronic channels. The acquisition of Lombard "is consistent with what Dean Witter has been saying it was going to do in terms of adding distribution channels," said Michael Freudenstein, an analyst with J. P. Morgan & Company, who follows brokerage firms. "Lombard is an excellent vehicle for asset-gathering. It brings in a very different customer" than Dean Witter, he said. In another move to make its services more available, Dean Witter announced earlier this year that the Banc One Corporation would sell its investment products. Dean Witter, which has more than 8,000 brokers, also said that V. Eric Roach would remain Lombard's chief executive. Electronic brokerage tends to be a low-margin business, with Lombard advertising that it charges less than $15 a trade. Still, analysts said, full-service brokers can benefit from adding such businesses because they provide access to customers they may not have otherwise. Those customers may eventually want the research a traditional broker offers. "With the acquisition of Lombard, we expand our potential customer base," Philip J. Purcell, chairman and chief executive of Dean Witter, said in a statement. Lombard has 45,000 accounts and about $30 million in annual revenue, according to The San Francisco Chronicle. The four-year old company focuses on baby boomers, some of whom are considered comfortable making their own investment decisions. Shares of Dean Witter rose 50 cents yesterday, to $67.50.

title:
December 15-21;
Traffic Backs Up on the Internet
body: It sounded highly reasonable: with Internet use taking off, America Online would simplify things. Instead of convoluted formulas for charging users depending on how long they stayed on line, it would charge a flat $19.95 monthly fee. Clean and simple. Little did it know, though, what demand lurked among the masses huddled over their glowing screens. When the new price went into effect on Dec.. 1, America Online members took to it like desert travelers to a pub ladling out free beer. Phone lines clogged, many angry users could not get on, busy signals abounded. America Online expected that some people would "surf the net" a bit longer now that it's free. But they are only part of the problem. Others, once they get an A.O.L. connection, just hang onto it. Why face busy signals the next time? So they take a walk, go to work, go to sleep -- all the while keeping a phone line tied up. Defending against this, on-line companies automatically disconnect users if they detect no activity for a few minutes. But that approach grossly underestimates the digital ingenuity running wild in the land: programs have appeared -- with names like Keep Alive and Rascal -- to enable users to fool the company networks and hang onto that coveted phone link. And those programs are on the Internet.   HUBERT B. HERRING Graphic   Drawing. (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
Advertising;
A shot at getting the big spenders to invest in the commercial potential of the Internet.
body: THE big question on the collective mind of the on-line advertising community as the year comes to a close is: When are the big consumer products companies going to begin advertising seriously on the Internet? John L. Mezzina and Jordan Stanley, two advertising industry veterans, believe they have found a way to lure the big brands onto the Internet's World Wide Web. And if that were not ambitious enough, they also believe that they can get the Internet's famously tight-fisted denizens used to the idea of paying for stuff on the Web, while at the same time helping to transform Internet access into a free commodity. The means by which they hope to achieve all this is a new loyalty program they are introducing today called Free Ride. Computer users can earn points by buying brand-name products, or by looking at on-line advertisements. Once 1,000 points are amassed, those computer users earn a free month of Internet access from participating access providers. The program tries to allay the suspicions that many large advertisers have about who, if anyone, is paying attention to on-line ads. Rather than fool around with unproved measures, the companies that participate in Free Ride pay only when consumers actually buy their products and send in the bar code from the package in pre-paid envelopes. With that pitch, Mr. Mezzina and Mr. Stanley have managed to attract a roster of well-known consumer brands, including Nabisco's Oreo cookies, Duracell batteries, Kodak cameras and I.B.M. computers. "This whole program is designed to bring the consumer closer to the brand," said Mr. Stanley, who spent 17 years at Young & Rubicam before joining Mr. Mezzina at his company, Mezzina/Brown Inc., three years ago. "Everything has been for free on the Web," added Mr. Mezzina, who was vice president and group creative director at Young & Rubicam before forming Mezzina/Brown in 1991. "So this helps get consumers used to the idea of paying," even if someone else, namely the consumer product company, is footing the bill. Free Ride is by no means the only loyalty program being cooked up for the Web. Cybergold, a start-up in Berkeley, Calif., plans to start offering people the chance to earn cash by reading Internet ads early next year, the same time Free Ride plans to begin awarding its points. "We believe that the scarce resource in today's market is attention," said Victor Imbimbo, Cybergold's executive vice president of marketing and sales. But some analysts have questioned whether Cybergold's offer will attract the type of customers advertisers are looking for since anyone with idle time can simply click through ads and rack up points. Free Ride doesn't have that problem, because it gets paid only when consumers actually buy the products featured on its web site (http://www.freeride.com). But its challenge is to see whether consumers are enthusiastic enough about earning free Internet access to bother to clip bar codes and mail them in. "That is a recipe that consumers have shown they are not as high on as programs in which the consumer doesn't have to do anything extraordinary to get the benefit," like airline frequent-flier programs, Max Goldberg, chairman and president of the Promotion Marketing Association of America, said. Another stumbling block may be that Free Ride has only signed up two relatively unknown Internet service providers -- Earthlink and Infinet -- as initial participants in the program. Those who get their Internet access from one of the dozens of other providers will get no benefit by participating in Free Ride unless they are willing to switch to the participating providers. But Mr. Mezzina and Mr. Stanley do not see these as big obstacles. They are confident that they will sign up more access providers because Free Ride will prove to be popular. About 70,000 people signed up for the offer during a three-month test of the concept earlier this year, even though there was no reward. Half of those people spent 45 minutes at the site filling out a survey. "When I was in the packaged-good business, I couldn't get people to spend five minutes filling out a survey," Mr. Stanley said. The two men expect 15 to 20 percent of visitors to the site to sign up when the program goes live. They also have grand plans to turn Free Ride points into "the currency of the Internet" by expanding the reward from just free Internet access to premium services, like pay-per-view events, and other consumer products, like flowers. "Having redeemable points will be a very good thing," said Peter Storck, group director of on-line advertising at Jupiter Communications, a research firm in newyork. "Lots of us will be buying lots of stuff on the Internet." Bill Lawliss, vice president and general manager of the Prince Sports Group, a unit of Benetton based in Bordentown, N.J., is enthusiastic about the racquet maker's participation in Free Ride, which will be its first foray into Web advertising. "This gives us a tremendous vehicle to advertise our product on the Internet, and the cost comes to us only when someone buys something," he said.

title: Schwab to Allow Foreigners To Trade Securities on Line
body: Giving a new meaning to the term global investing, Charles Schwab & Company, the country's largest discount stockbroker, said yesterday that it would start allowing foreign investors to buy and sell domestic stocks and bonds through its site on the Internet's World Wide Web next week. The move could give a large lift to on-line securities trading, which has been gathering momentum since a handful of companies began allowing customers to trade on the Internet earlier this year. Schwab estimates that 28 percent of its total trades are now placed on line. But the bulk of those orders come via Schwab's proprietary on-line software; the company said that only 100,000 of its nearly 4 million customers used its Internet site to trade. Since the company started Internet trading for its domestic customers in May, many foreign customers have expressed interest. "Our goal is to fill the investment information gap that exists for our overseas clients," Gloria Lau, senior vice president of Schwab International, said. Currently, foreign investors get in touch with Schwab brokers, or use the company's automated telephone service. Using the Internet, they can more easily keep track of their trades, check the prices of securities and have ready access to their account statements. While Schwab may be the largest broker to offer Internet trading to foreigners, it is not the first. E*Trade, which helped pioneer securities trading on the Internet, has accepted foreign customers since it opened for business on the World Wide Web last February. About 3 percent of E*Trade's 100,000 accounts are from overseas, said Kate Connelly, a company spokeswoman. Schwab has been experimenting with foreign customers in recent weeks and has executed trades from accounts as far away as Bangladesh, Ecuador and Taiwan. The service is the same as the one provided to domestic customers except that foreigners are not permitted to buy domestic mutual funds because of Federal regulations. Many countries have strict regulations determining which foreign firms can trade securities on their soil. Schwab hopes to avoid confrontations with foreign governments by keeping a low profile.

title:
Let the Cyberinvestor Beware;
A Tale of Stock Promotion, Regulation and the Internet
body: Peter A. Usinger was incensed. He was using the Internet, as he often does, to check up on a little company he had bought stock in called Omnigene Diagnostics Inc. But when Mr. Usinger, a Rochester business consultant, reached the company's site on the World Wide Web, he did not find the usual information about its patented test to diagnose gum disease. Instead, he read that the company was in default on the license agreement that lets it use the patent -- the company's main asset. Mr. Usinger fired off an angry electronic message to the Web site manager, who had put up the information. Mr. Usinger correctly suspected the site manager was embroiled in a dispute with the company. "If you are not able to substantiate your claims and we have to take a financial loss," Mr. Usinger wrote, "we will notify our lawyers." The manager, Robert Gibson, shot back his own email, with enough details to convince Mr. Usinger. And that was the beginning of the end of a high-technology hype that had turned Omnigene Diagnostics stock from a dud into a high flier almost overnight. Within two weeks, the Securities and Exchange Commission halted trading in the stock and announced its action on America Online, the agency's first such use of an electronic bulletin board. With the expiration last night of the trading suspension, the cyberspace drama resumes today. If the stock follows the usual pattern, it could well fall back to earth with a thud. The Omnigene Diagnostics story shows the effects Internet technology is having, for good and bad, on investors and investing. Reams of information are available -- but truthfulness and accuracy can be almost impossible to judge. Amateur investors find their way to obscure securities and mingle on line with both stock promoters trying to drive prices up and short-sellers trying to drive prices down. But the tale also illustrates the changes occurring in the still-young world of Internet investing. Securities regulators are becoming more aggressive about on-line stock fraud; at the same time, individual investors like Mr. Usinger are becoming warier and starting to use the power of the Internet to protect themselves. "A lot has changed -- dramatically -- in the last six months," said John Stark, a lawyer for the S.E.C. who specializes in Internet fraud. "There was a real culture of trust and benevolence; now people are becoming more skeptical." And not a moment too soon. On-line investing is growing by leaps and bounds; with that growth has come a corresponding rise in scams, including manipulation of small stocks with few shares outstanding. "It's a growth industry," said William R. McLucas, the S.E.C.'s director of enforcement. Regulators are investigating several suspected "pump and dumps," in which the Internet is used to stir up investor enthusiasm and inflate prices. The perpetrators, who usually own shares they acquired for little or no money, sell them into the rising market. When the scam falls apart, legitimate investors are left holding the worthless shares. To be sure, such schemes have flourished for decades without the Internet. And the Omnigene Diagnostics story includes some traditional elements of stock hype, including the use of a radio talk-show host, who was paid with stock to promote the company. But the Internet was integral to the rise and fall of Omnigene Diagnostics, which is based in West Palm Beach, Fla. The stock was touted on electronic bulletin boards; clues about the company's problems first appeared on its site on the World Wide Web; the details were fleshed out using email, which was also employed to alert regulators, and the company's management took to the Net to defend itself before the S.E.C. stepped in on line.  An Internet Chorus of Praise When Omnigene Diagnostics first showed up on Internet bulletin boards in early October, virtually identical messages praising the company appeared on different boards, signed with different names. These messages said the company had no competition, had already racked up sales of $400,000, would have revenues of more than $2 million next year and had only 450,000 tradable shares. Urging readers to call the company's "800" number for more information, the messages concluded, "This could be your stock buy of the year . . . Take a look NOW." By then, the share price of Omnigene Diagnostics, known as "Oh My God" because of its ticker symbol of OMGD, had already jumped from $1, where it traded over the counter -- very occasionally -- in July, to about $4. But as the Internet messages flew, so did the price, topping $6.50 by mid-November. Even early on there were voices of caution. "Oh no, not another FL company," wrote someone on America Online's Investor Network. "I have heard that a lot of scams originate out of Florida." Other writers noted that the company did not seem to have filed documents with the S.E.C., and was not traded on an exchange. But naysayers were quickly shouted down by writers who accused them of trying to profit from a drop in the stock price. The boosters hinted of a deal with Procter & Gamble, and cheered each day's rising price with such lines as "I'm going to ride this train to the gold mine. Toooot!! TOOOOT!!" Meanwhile, the Internet was helping to bring together two men with a rather different view of Omnigene Diagnostics: Robert Gibson, a computer programmer in Florida, and Peter H. Mahler, president of the company's former parent, Omnigene Inc. of Cambridge, Mass. With sales at its diagnostics unit declining, Omnigene Inc. sold the unit in May 1995 to the American Biodental Corporation of Boca Raton, Fla., which makes dental implants. Though its testing operations continued in Cambridge, Omnigene Diagnostics was to be run from Florida.  A Spinoff's Growing Troubles But almost from the beginning, things went wrong, Mr. Mahler said. Omnigene Diagnostics quickly fell behind on its rent and royalty payments to its former parent. Most of its staff quit, and Mr. Mahler's company went to court to evict its one-time subsidiary. Though the company dropped the suit after receiving a payment, Omnigene Diagnostics still owes it money, Mr. Mahler said. Even worse, people were confusing Omnigene Inc. with Omnigene Diagnostics and its troubles; another spinoff, Omnigene Bioproducts, mistakenly had its credit shut off, Mr. Mahler said, adding, "It's an awful situation." But the final straw for Mr. Mahler may have been Omnigene Diagnostics' Web site, which had the address www.omnigene.com. The site was operated by Mr. Gibson, the computer programmer, whose main business includes running Web sites for legal process servers. Last year, at an Office Depot store in West Palm Beach, Mr. Gibson bumped into an old acquaintance, Dominic Scacci, and eventually agreed to do some programming for businesses Mr. Scacci was involved with, which included Omnigene Diagnostics. In fact, Mr. Gibson said, he ended up sharing an office with Mr. Scacci, who used his phones, computers and copier. But like Mr. Mahler, to whom he had spoken about Omnigene Diagnostics' computer system, Mr. Gibson said he was having trouble getting paid. The company did not seem to have nearly as much business as Mr. Scacci said. And earlier this fall, Mr. Gibson began to have suspicions about what Mr. Scacci was up to. "The company was always short of money, and suddenly Dominic drives up in a new car," Mr. Gibson recalled. He also found a list, left in his computer by Mr. Scacci, that indicated the company had been issuing hundreds of thousands of free shares to Mr. Scacci's other companies, his friends and family, Mr. Gibson said. "It started to smell," he said, so he called the S.E.C. Shares also went to Jerome Wenger, host of "The Next Superstock," a program that is heard on radio stations around the country, including WEVD in newyork. In an interview, Mr. Wenger said that he had received the stock for serving as a consultant to bring the company to investors' attention, and that he disclosed such arrangements to his listeners.  A Heated Debate In Cyberspace On Oct. 31, Mr. Mahler sent an email to Mr. Gibson complaining that the Web site's address infringed his trademark and saying that unless the site was removed immediately, "legal action will result." Instead, on Nov. 3, Mr. Gibson changed the first page of the site to the message that so irked Mr. Usinger, the Rochester investor. (Mr. Gibson also took his equipment out of the office he had shared with Mr. Scacci.) Which brings the story back to the angry email sent by Mr. Usinger, who had bought several hundred shares of Omnigene Diagnostics in October. After Mr. Gibson replied to his message, Mr. Usinger said, "all the little tricks you see in shells and scams started surfacing like little bubbles." So he decided to send some information to the S.E.C.'s on-line complaint division. He also decided to sell his stock, at a nice profit. As Mr. Usinger and a few other investors began posting their information on the bulletin boards, a free-for-all broke out in cyberspace. Some people scolded Mr. Usinger for trying to make people panic and sell their shares, and bulls and bears got into on-line shouting matches. Messages signed by Mr. Scacci appeared, saying that Mr. Gibson owed him money and had encoded the company's computer data. "He demanded $10,000 to give us the key," read one such message posted on Nov. 7 on a bulletin board on the Silicon Investor Web site. "I refused. This is when he decided to proceed to send falsehoods out over the Internet." As for the default on the patent license, a message on America Online signed Scacci6733 said that Omnigene Diagnostics "owns the patent purchased from Omnigene Inc. It's as simple as that." But there were a number of things Mr. Scacci did not tell people in his messages. A former stockbroker with a history of regulatory run-ins, Mr. Scacci has filed for personal bankruptcy protection twice, according to regulatory records. Mr. Scacci was the agent for something called the Austria International Fund, which was based in the Bahamas, according to documents filed with the S.E.C. by American Biodental. These filings say that it was really the fund, not American Biodental, that spent $189,000 to buy Omnigene Diagnostics. Omnigene Diagnostics was spun off in January, shortly before American Biodental filed for bankruptcy protection. But American Biodental's shareholders never received any OMGD shares, said Ingo K. Kozak, a director of American Biodental, which has changed its name to Biolok International Inc. Mr. Scacci said in a brief interview last week that on the advice of his lawyers he could not answer questions about the Omnigene situation. But he said his previous regulatory difficulties were basically problems with record-keeping. And he denied being the agent for the Austria International Fund.  A Posting of Import By the S.E.C. On Nov. 20, the S.E.C. said it was suspending trading in Omnigene Diagnostics' shares for 10 business days, the maximum allowed. The reason: questions about the company's "alleged ownership and other rights as to certain patents and trademarks, ODI's sales, past and projected, ODI's operations and facilities, and the number of freely traded shares." The S.E.C. posted a notice of the halt on America Online's bulletin board because "it looks like one of the vehicles people were using to disseminate a substantial amount of hype" about the company, said Mr. McLucas, the enforcement chief, adding that he expects the agency to make similar electronic announcements in the future. Whether the S.E.C. will go after anyone it believes has hyped the stock electronically is unknown; the commission never comments on current investigations. The company's fate will become clearer today, when trading can resume -- which will occur only if brokerage firms are confident they have enough information to make bids on the stock. In the past, stocks in which trading has been suspended have tended to plunge when it resumes. Mr. Gibson is still unhappy about his run-in with Omnigene Diagnostics and the investors who excoriated him on line. But, he said, "the good news is that this stuff can come to the surface quicker because of the open lines of communication" that the Internet allows. As for Mr. Usinger, he said that his Omnigene experiences have made him a more cautious investor. And that despite the abuse he received from some on-line critics, he does not regret having shared his discoveries about the company with his fellow Internet investors, some of whom also got their money out before trading was halted. "I thought everyone should know this," he said. "It's the difference between having something more before Christmas and having nothing." Graphic   Photo: Peter A. Usinger, an investor in Omnigene Diagnostics, first sensed something was amiss at the company when he read some information on its Web site. He then used the Internet to notify the S.E.C. and warn other investors. (Michael J. Okoniewski for The newyork Times)  Chart: "On-Line Hype Leads to a Halt" In the high-speed, high-technology world of cyberspace, on-line enthusiasm for a stock - whether from legitimate investors or stock promoters - can quickly send share prices soaring. But recently, the Internet has become integral to bringing some hypes to a halt. And for the first time, the Securities and Exchange Commission has posted a notice on an electronic bulletin board, announcing last month that it was suspending trading in the stock of an obscure company called Omnigene Diagnostics. (The suspension expired at midnight.) Chart lists excerpts from messages about the company that were posted on America Online bulletin board during October and November.

title:
Advertising;
Banner Ads On Internet Attract Users
body: One particularly popular activity in the realm of interactive media, apart from downloading photographs of Teri Hatcher, has been banner-bashing. Banners -- the tiny display advertisements that are the cyberspace equivalent of billboards -- have been roundly condemned as boring and ineffective because of their size and usually prosaic nature. But a new study from Hotwired, the Internet media service of Wired Ventures Inc., concludes that banner advertising perhaps ought not to be considered the Rodney Dangerfield of interactive advertising. The study by Millward Brown International, a marketing research company owned by the WPP Group, found that banners influence the attitudes of computer users because they make measurable advertising impressions, which can help build the brands being advertised. The efficacy of banners is only one of many issues concerning advertisers as they become further involved in -- and spend more on -- interactive media. For instance, a two-day conference sponsored by Jupiter Communications, which begins this morning at the Crowne Plaza Hotel at 48th Street and Broadway in Manhattan, includes panels on selling ad space profitably, measuring on-line audiences accurately and producing ads creatively. Banners will get attention, too, in a panel that will explore just how valuable they are. According to the Hotwired advertising effectiveness study, banners are not unlike television and radio commercials in their ability to stimulate awareness of and affinity for a brand, as well as purchase intent, though the reaction is somewhat more passive than that elicited by a television spot. And the impact of a banner may be restrained by any negative predisposition toward a brand on the part of the consumer exposed to it. The benefits of banners are evident, the study says, even if computer users ignore entreaties to "click here" and read additional material to which the banner may be linked. That is significant because some advertisers, like the Procter & Gamble Company, are basing their payments for interactive ads only on click-through rates. "A lot of the comments maligning banners come from anecdotal evidence," said Rex Briggs, research director at Hotwired in San Francisco, whose department collaborated with Millward Brown in designing the study. "There's such a focus on click-through because it's easy to measure and you know something has happened," he added, while "a banner represents a really small chunk of computer-screen real estate, so it's hard to imagine it's going to have an impact. And many have struggled with banners because it's a different form of communication." Mr. Briggs and Nigel Hollis, the director of group research and development at Millward Brown in Fairfield, Conn., offered a preview of the Hotwired study in telephone interviews last week. "There's a big debate in the on-line industry over whether these little banners have any value over and above the direct-marketing applications" of the click-throughs that may occur, Mr. Hollis said. "And the industry in general may be getting a little tired of them." "But people are staring at a fairly confined space and actively looking at something of interest," he added. "The banners have their attention, so if there's any relevance, they will affect the way people think." As for skepticism about the results of the study, given that Hotwired obviously has a stake in persuading advertisers that banners can be beautiful, Mr. Hollis said: "A big, well-established brand will not see as much incremental response to its banners. There is a limit to how far advertising at heavy rates can drive response." The study was conducted between Sept. 9 and Sept. 16, among 1,232 people on the World Wide Web site of the Hotwired Network (http:// www.hotwired.com). Some saw one of three test ads in the designated ad space on the site's home page, while others saw a control ad instead. One test ad was for a brand that had never been advertised on the Web, the Dockers khaki pants sold by Levi Strauss & Company. The second was for a company with an extensive presence in cyberspace, the AT&T Corporation, but for a product, the AT&T Worldnet Internet service, that had not been advertised on the Web to that point. And the third was for a company omnipresent among the digerati, the Microsoft Corporation, promoting the Microsoft Internet Explorer 3.0 Web browser. The survey results showed, for example, that in terms of consumer loyalty -- measuring the likelihood that a consumer would buy a product on the next so-called purchase occasion -- the impact of the banner exposure ranged from a 5 percent increase for Microsoft Internet Explorer to more than 50 percent for Dockers khakis and AT&T Worldnet. Of those who saw the Dockers khakis banner, 14 percent said they would buy that brand "for a purpose that other competing brands don't fulfill," compared with 5 percent of those in the control group who agreed with that remark. Asked if AT&T Worldnet would be a "good Internet service provider," 43 percent of those exposed to that banner agreed, compared with 31 percent among the control group. And in regard to Microsoft Internet Explorer, awareness of that product among those who saw that banner was 15 percent higher than for those in the control group. Though banners can be "a wonderful tool for marketers," Mr. Briggs said, "they don't preclude that there may be better ways to build brands and drive sales." Mr. Hollis recommended that marketers "make sure they focus on creating presence" in cyberspace in ways besides banners, like "prominent places on the Web." As a result of the study, Hotwired and Millward Brown have formed a pilot service to pretest banners. title: New Flat Rate Creates Surge In Use of America Online
body: Computer users eager to take advantage of America Online Inc.'s new flat-rate pricing plan overwhelmed the system yesterday, causing widespread busy signals across the nation as subscribers tried in vain to dial into the on-line service's computers. America Online, the country's largest on-line service with 7 million subscribers, instituted the new plan on Sunday -- which includes use of proprietary information services and unlimited Internet access -- and immediately began experiencing a surge in usage, a company spokesman said. Before Sunday, America Online had charged its users $9.95 a month for five hours of access, with additional hours billed at $2.95 each. "The numbers are off the charts," said David Gang, vice president of product marketing for America Online. He said that the company recorded eight million individual sign-on sessions on Sunday, the most ever. It was, in other words, as if each of the company's seven million subscribers logged on Sunday at least once -- and then some. Indeed, the enthusiasm yesterday seemed to extend to Wall Street, where the company's stock rose $4.625 a share on the newyork Stock Exchange, to $39.875. While the system overloads on Sunday and yesterday indicated that the new flat rate of $19.95 a month was popular, it was not popular with everyone. The attorneys general of 18 states, concerned that the company was automatically switching all its customers to the pricing plan -- which nearly doubles the basic rate -- had asked America Online to modify its procedure for enacting the new plan. Yesterday, an America Online spokesman said that the company, which is based in Dulles, Va., had reached an agreement with one of the states, Washington. "The agreement involved putting up a pop-up screen that essentially forces people to choose whether to accept the standard pricing of $19.95 a month or to choose alternatives," Michael Gross, the spokesman, said. "We will also take additional steps to inform users, including information on line, running advertising, and sending postcards to all our customers." Mr. Gang said that the company was confident it would reach an accord with the 17 other states and avoid any legal sanctions. Current subscribers who signed up for America Online before Sunday have the option of retaining their $9.95 monthly limited-access plans, Mr. Gross said. And any existing members who signed up for the $19.95 monthly plan have three months to change their minds. Anyone who has or will become members since Sunday, though, will be urged to accept the $19.95 fee schedule. Despite the usage surge for the first two days of the new rate, analysts said that the shift was a gamble for the company. While some frequent users will welcome the flat-fee pricing -- especially those who use it more than 10 hours a month -- a significant percentage of American Online customers typically have not used even the five hours of time available to them, and thus may not benefit from the new plan. The company has not disclosed its projections on how the new plan will increase revenues, but any gains from the higher monthly fees are expected to help America Online's bottom line. The company said last month that it had yet to make a profit, choosing instead to build its subscriber base and profits later through higher advertising and transaction fees. Analysts have said for months that if America Online were to continue to succeed, it had to match the flat-rate pricing plans of rivals like the AT&T Corporation, Compuserve Inc., the Microsoft Network, and scores of smaller, independent Internet-service providers. Mr. Gang said that America Online began bracing for the expected usage surge in September, when company officials decided to abandon the hourly pricing scheme. The company added 12,000 new modems last month, along with more phone lines and brawnier computer servers for such popular on-line services as electronic mail, chat and World Wide Web publishing. "We are expecting to spend $250 million between now and the end of June to continue to expand system capacity and add customer support," he said. Even so, Mr. Gang said, the company expects sporadic system slowdowns and access problems at peak times for at least the next month. "We're going into territory that nobody on the face of the planet has ever been before," he said.

title:
Taking In the Sites;
Web Offers an Outlet For Charitable Impulses
body: The spirit -- and reality -- of giving has a strong presence on the World Wide Web this holiday season. "The Internet is a perfect medium for nonprofits," said Robbin Zeff, author of the "Nonprofit Guide to the Internet." "Web sites allow nonprofits to give out sophisticated information in an easily accessible manner, and these groups are exploiting it." Private foundations are also getting into the act, putting up Web sites that enable grant seekers to learn about grant makers. The Philanthropy Journal Online is a good starting point. The site's index of nonprofit organizations is a comprehensive list of hypertext links to the Web sites for a number of nonprofit organizations. The Foundation Center site furnishes detailed information on the fund-raising process. It has a guide to writing proposals, a glossary of philanthropic terms and on-line grant application forms. Prospect research is the term used for finding possible financing, and two in-depth resources for the field are the Internet Prospector and the Prospect Research Page run by David Lamb, a fund-raiser at the University of Washington. Businesses interested in corporate giving can visit the site of the Council on Foundations, whose 1,300 members give over $6 billion in charitable grants every year. It has information on starting a foundation. The Ford Foundation, the world's largest private grant-making organization, will have its debut on the Web tomorrow. Its site will include detailed information for grant seekers. Corporate and foundation philanthropy attracts a lot of publicity, but the bulk of charitable gifts are made by individual donors. Last year individuals gave more than $116 billion to charity, while foundations and corporations gave an estimated $18 billion combined. For individuals, there are several sites that will try to make you feel good even as they relieve you of your money. Before you get caught up in the spirit of giving, it is worth learning as much as possible about charities. The National Charities Information Bureau is one of several sites that helps consumers identify worthwhile causes. It has a "tips for givers" section, as well as a rating system for more than 300 charities and their compliance with the bureau's "standards in philanthropy," which include, for example, an organization's use of funds. The Internet Nonprofit Center offers an interactive "nonprofit locator" service that searches more than a million tax-exempt groups in the unitedstates. Punch in keywords and a particular state and you will get back a detailed list of groups that match your specifications. While many sites are little more than electronic brochures for the charities, others use the Web in interesting ways to encourage giving. Operation Smile, a group in Norfolk, Va., that sponsors surgery for children around the world with facial deformities, has a site that not only provides comprehensive information, but also features movie clips that show before-and-after photos of patients. Some organizations combine celebrity appeals with multimedia tools to enliven their sites. City Harvest, a newyork-based agency that collects unused food from restaurants and supermarkets, uses a video clip featuring the actress Susan Sarandon asking for contributions. The site of San Francisco-based Coral Forest, an organization that works to protect coral reefs around the world, has teachers' guides, sounds of a coral reef, a map showing threatened areas and, in a surprising connection, links to Grateful Dead sites. (The group's guitarist, Bob Weir, is the brother of Coral Forest's executive director, Wendy Weir.) The National Black United Fund, based in Newark, is one of the groups whose site enables donors to find information about minority charities. The American Lung Association, which runs a successful old-media campaign through its annual Christmas Seals program, has moved to the world of new media this year. You can send, via the Web, Christmas, Hanukkah and Kwanza seals, as well as download a holiday screen saver. Many people who make contributions, of course, are doing so with an eye toward April 15, so it is worth making sure that the donations qualify for tax deductions. The Better Business Bureau runs a Philanthropic Advisory Service that has tips on tax deductions for charitable contributions. And there is always the Internal Revenue Service site. And there are other ways than donating money to help a charity. The Give Five site has tips for volunteer work. title: Excite's Stock Soars on Deal With America Online
body: Excite Inc. agreed yesterday to make its directory the exclusive tool used to search the Internet on America Online Inc. The announcement sent Excite's shares up 61 percent. Excite will buy America Online's Webcrawler Internet directory for about two million shares -- valued at $19.8 million at yesterday's closing price -- and replace it by moving its own directory onto the No. 1 on-line service. Internet directories are used to look up information on the global computer network. Excite's service will appear under the name AOL Search Powered by Excite. The move raises America Online's stake in Excite, based in Mountain View, Calif., to 20 percent from 12 percent and gives the company a seat on Excite's board. America Online, based in Dulles, Va., acquired Webcrawler for $1 million in June 1995, the company's chief executive, Stephen M. Case, said. Excite's exclusive agreement provides exposure to America Online's seven million customers. In exchange, America Online will sell advertising and get a majority of revenue from ads that appear on Excite's service on America Online. "This validates the search engines as a platform for advertising," said Jamie Kiggen, an analyst with Cowen & Company. Excite shares surged $3.75, to $9.875, in Nasdaq trading. Shares of America Online rose $1.625, to $32.75. Shares of other Internet search services also rose, on speculation that they could be takeover candidates. Yahoo Inc. rose $1.50, to $19.125, while Lycos Inc. rose 87.5 cents, to $11.50. Excite's purchase and distribution agreements will increase the number of people who use the service and give the company the second-largest reach on the Internet behind Netscape Communications Inc., Excite said, citing September survey results from PC-Meter, an Internet measurement service. Excite will continue to offer Webcrawler as a separate service on the Internet because of its brand name, said George Bell, Excite's president and chief executive. Excite's other acquisitions include the privately held McKinley Group Inc. and its Magellan Internet directory, and City.Net local guides. The agreement begins in two months and runs for two years.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
The Interpublic Group is linking up with an Internet broadcaster in a new media expansion.
body: THE Interpublic Group of Companies is expanding its interests in new media by going into the interactive advertising business with a client of one of its agencies. Interpublic, the world's third-largest agency company, with billings of $16.1 billion, is forming a joint venture with the Ifusion Com Corporation, which is developing a so-called Internet broadcasting system named Arrive. Terms of the deal with Ifusion, which is a client of the Interpublic agency Gotham Inc., were not disclosed. The purpose of Arrive, which is scheduled to begin a rollout in January, is to deliver customized information -- including advertising -- directly to computer users, relieving them of the need to search through the overwhelming amounts of data available on the Internet. Ifusion (http://www.ifusion.com) joins companies like Pointcast Inc., Backweb Technologies and Intermind in producing "push delivery" systems that are being likened to broadcast television channels. Interpublic has been exploring the realm of cybercommunications in two ways. One is by helping to finance and support the in-house efforts by the agencies it owns, which besides Gotham include Ammirati Puris Lintas, Lowe Group and McCann-Erickson Worldwide. The other is by investing in independent companies like CKS Group, in which Interpublic owns a minority interest. "We've been championing our agencies' development of their own skills," Barry R. Linsky, senior vice president for planning and business development at Interpublic in newyork, said yesterday, "and looking beyond that, where appropriate, by taking a stake in companies specializing in this arena. "We see a value in being involved in several platforms," he added, "in order to maximize our learning." Interpublic and Ifusion, which has been working with Gotham since February, will each own 50 percent of the company, to be called Really Perceptive Interactive Advertising L.L.C. It will start with about 10 employees at an office in newyork; its mission is to develop interactive advertising that is more precisely aimed at specific consumers as well as more compelling than present offerings like banners -- those signs adorning Web sites urging viewers to "click here." "Banners are boring," said Martin J. Smith, 53, vice chairman of Gotham in newyork, who will also serve as president of Really Perceptive, "and don't offer high enough value to advertisers." "This is all about content," he added. "We're hoping to create advertising that really gets people involved with the products." As an example, Mr. Smith cited an interactive game on the Arrive system that Ifusion is demonstrating this week at Comdex, the big computer trade show in Las Vegas, Nev. The game, with an ice hockey motif, advertises the Mennen Speed Stick deodorant brand marketed by the Colgate-Palmolive Company. "It's really fun to play, and it's addictive," Michael Recanati, chief executive at Ifusion in newyork, said in a telephone interview from Comdex. "And that's the point of an interactive ad: the more time you spend on the screen, the more time you spend with the product." Gotham has billings of $250 million from clients that include, in addition to Ifusion, the Bristol-Myers Squibb Company, the Dial Corporation and Maybelline Inc. Soon after Ifusion executives began working with Gotham executives, Mr. Recanati said, it became apparent "very early on that they really understood" what Ifusion was seeking to accomplish. "They've been so instrumental in developing the idea" of Arrive, he added, "we felt we needed to bring in" Interpublic as a partner. "Interpublic is a large company," Mr. Recanati said, "and we were somewhat concerned we would not be able to get through all the layers. But they've responded extraordinarily well." Executives from both Interpublic and Ifusion will serve on the board of Really Perceptive. Ifusion, founded last year, has offices in San Francisco and Vienna, Va., in addition to its headquarters in newyork. The company has announced agreements with eight "content providers" for Arrive, Mr. Recanati said, that include CNNFN, the cable television network owned by Time Warner Inc.; Golfweb, a golf Web site (http://www.golfweb.com); the Showtime Networks of Viacom Inc.; USA Today, published by the Gannett Company; the Weather Channel, the cable network owned by Landmark Communications, and Yahoo Inc., which operates an Internet search engine (http://www.yahoo.com). USA Today is also a client of Gotham. By coincidence, Ifusion and Really Perceptive are in the same Manhattan office building that once housed the newyork office of Chiat/Day, now the TBWA Chiat/Day unit of Omnicom Group. "I was just in Jay Chiat's kitchen the other day," Mr. Smith said, laughing.

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
CYBERSCOUT
body: BILL GATES EXPRESS Microsoft Expedia http://expedia.msn.com/ Microsoft's Expedia is a slick, easy-to-use travel service. That the leading maker of software for personal computers has produced an accessible Web site shouldn't come as a surprise, but Microsoft has stumbled in the past. Expedia is at least as simple to operate as the handful of other cybertravel services I have dipped into, but, since no one knows how many agencies are on line, it would be unfair to call it the best. It would also be premature: the service is less than a month old. There are five major sections: Travel Agent, where flight, hotel and auto reservations can be found and made; Travel Central, a library of guidebooks; Connections, where travelers exchange information; News Point, late-breaking news, weather and exchange rates, and Mungo Park, for virtual adventure travel, the safest kind. All this is free, except for what you or your company or school pays for an Internet connection. Expedia is also available on the Microsoft Network, its own on-line service. The Microsoft "campus" is in Redmond, Wash., so I decided to take a virtual vacation in the Seattle area. I signed in and filled out a form on the screen: name, email address, member i.d., password, country (only the unitedstates at this time). Then, with a cheery "Welcome Larry Shannon," Expedia said that its "wizards are ready to find the flights, rental cars and hotel rooms that are perfect for you." Wizards are the helpful aides in such software as Microsoft Windows 95 and Microsoft Publisher. And they are certainly smart. Next, I went into the Travel Agent Flight Wizard. The defaults are round trip and coach class, which would be fine for most travelers. (One way or multiple destinations, and business class or first class are options.) There were many options for airlines and other preferences. The most sensible, such as lowest price, were what you got unless you specified otherwise. Under Expedia's simple interface is Worldspan, a computerized reservation service used by professional travel agents. But you don't have to know, for instance, that Newark is EWR; the software knows. Then I was given a choice of flights, and picked the least expensive one. I then went into the Travel Agent Car Wizard, and was offered class of car (economy, for me) from one of nine rental car companies. Again, the defaults made sense. Unless you specify otherwise, you are directed to rental agencies at the airport you will arrive at and depart from. In the Travel Agent Hotel Wizard, you can select chains, price ranges and amenities (nonsmoking, swimming pool and such) and whether the hotel is in town, near the airport or near a local attraction. For many of the hotels, a mouse click brings up a map of the area with the hotel highlighted, and photographs and descriptions of the establishment. All of this is exceptionally fast for the Web, although it may slow down when it draws more users. As always on the Web, this is not objective information. It is supplied by the individual companies. You can book all these things on line or call a toll-free number. Microsoft makes a point that it uses leading-edge electronic security to protect credit card numbers and other personal information. I also dipped into the sequence World Guide-North America-unitedstates for background information about Seattle. There were 20 sites in the unitedstates listed alphabetically from Anchorage to Washington, D.C., but not Washington state. There were also options for Background, six categories including geography, and arts and culture, and Travel Essentials, eight categories such as food and drink and money and measurements. These are not especially helpful when you are traveling in your own country, but invaluable for foreign trips. According to Microsoft, the World Guide contains information on more than 50 countries and 200 cities, with 150 maps and 4,000 pictures. There were nine forums for exchanging messages, divided into geographic areas and such themes as family. In the North American forum there were about 30 messages. They ran from exchanges about the Grand Canyon and Disneyland to a request for information on finding a good bed and breakfast in newyork. Microsoft became a travel agency to start Expedia. Earlier this year, the software company applied for membership in the American Society of Travel Agents, and even hung out a sign to submit a photograph of it with the application. If the software business goes bad, Bill Gates has something to fall back on.   L. R. SHANNON Graphic   Drawing

title:
COMPANY REPORTS;
Big On-Line Company Has Quarter Loss
body: America Online Inc., in the midst of a broad revamping brought on by increasing pressure from other Internet companies, said yesterday that its revenue growth was strong in its most recent financial quarter. But the company said that a one-time charge related to a change in its accounting practices resulted in a loss of $353.7 million, or $3.80 a share. Without the write-off, the company said, it would have reported a profit of $19 million for the quarter, or 17 cents a share. Those results, released after the close of Wall Street trading yesterday, were ahead of analysts' expectations of 15 cents a share, according to First Call. In after-hours trading, shares of America Online rose 50 cents from the close of $24. In the past, America Online, based in Vienna, Va., has amortized the cost of attracting new subscribers over a 24-month period. As of Oct. 1, it has adopted the more conventional practice of writing off expenses in the period they were incurred. In announcing the accounting change last month, America Online said it would take a one-time pretax charge of $358 million against the quarter to account for all the costs that were amortized in previous quarters. The charge effectively wipes out any profits America Online has reported in the past. "On the accounting basis they are now on, they have never made a profit," said Ulric Weil, an analyst for Friedman, Billings, Ramsey & Company. "They are a start-up that has increased its subscriber base by leaps and bounds, but they have never made any money. And we're not likely to see any profits until the June quarter next year." Founded in 1985, America Online has grown rapidly to become the world's largest Internet access and on-line information company, with 6.9 million subscribers worldwide, easily outdistancing rivals including Compuserve, Prodigy and the Microsoft Network. Five years ago, it had fewer than 150,000 subscribers. It added 275,000 new subscribers last month alone, and 400,000 for the quarter as a whole. "I think the important point here is that we have not operated this company for purposes of earnings," said Lennert Leader, America Online's chief financial officer. "We felt it was way too myopic. We would be missing a lot of opportunity by focusing on earnings instead of our huge opportunity to build market share." America Online said it spent $130 million in the latest quarter to acquire those 400,000 subscribers. As with all on-line service companies, America Online has suffered from heavy defections among its new subscribers, a phenomenon known as churn. Yesterday, America Online said its customer retention rate had improved substantially in the last six months. It also said the average amount of time those customers spent on line rose, to an average of nearly seven hours a month. The company late last month announced a pricing structure that included an option of $19.95 a month for unlimited Internet access. Company executives acknowledged yesterday that the new plan, set to take effect next month, will be less profitable than the earlier, hourly pricing plan. But the company said that it expected to offset the decline in profits from hourly connection charges by offering new premium services and by generating new income from electronic commerce. Meanwhile, America Online's battle with bulk mail companies continued yesterday. Cyber Promotions Inc., a company that had sent hundreds of thousands of unsolicited electronic mail marketing pitches to America Online subscribers each week until America Online kicked them off the system last month, sued America Online again in Federal court on antitrust grounds. Earlier this week, a Federal judge had rejected Cyber Promotions' assertion that America Online had violated its constitutional right to free speech. Graphic   Table: "America Online Inc. title:
Business Travel;
Cathay Pacific and Swissair plan to test an airborne A.T.M. that will exchange currencies.
body: DESPITE the space squeeze aloft, cabins on international flights may soon have in-flight A.T.M.-type machines that dispense foreign currencies at exchange rates comparable to those in airports. Next spring, Cathay Pacific and Swissair will try out a small 150-pound model, developed by Aero-Design Technology and stocked with currencies by a yet unnamed banking partner. Called ATM Plus, the machine dispenses the currency of a flight's destination in two paper and two coin denominations. The A.T.M. knows the next destination through a link with the plane's flight management system, which helps keep a plane on track to a destination. On a flight to London, for example, a traveler could insert a $100 bill, as well as a debit or credit car, and obtain pounds but not, say, yen for a later stopover in Tokyo. ATM Plus can also dispense stored-value cards, more often called smart cards -- a feature that could work neatly with Swissair's new at-your-seat gambling system available on non-unitedstates flights. "There are certain passengers who would like to gamble," said Ravi Patel, Aero-Design's chief operating officer, "but are reluctant to use corporate credit cards or simply don't want others to know they're gambling." The smart cards keep track of wins and losses.  Booking on the Net Right now, fewer than 1 percent of corporate and other travelers use the Internet to book trips. But with Microsoft's new World Wide Web site called Expedia, which opened for business yesterday, the Internet may rapidly become more popular with travelers who not only want to book electronically but also seek up-to-the-minute information on fares. The site (www.expedia.com) is short on destination details. But if a traveler chooses three frequently visited city pairs, Expedia will email the lowest fares each week. To log onto Expedia, a user needs to provide only his or her name and email address. Once booked, tickets can be paid for on line by credit card, and there is a toll-free number for questions or problems. Tickets can be received in themail or picked up at an airport.  Beating the Plane Europe's expanding network of high-speed trains is making inter-city commutes a lot easier for business travelers, particularly with so many flight delays and traffic jams plaguing European cities. The two-year-old Eurostar expresses, heavily used by corporate travelers, have already captured about 40 percent of the London-Paris air shuttle market, according to Rail Europe, with some executives making a same-day round trip to either capital just for a meeting and lunch. Now, at the Paris end, time-saving rail routes are bypassing the city -- with streamlined connections at Charles de Gaulle Airport -- and fanning out in almost all directions. On the new Thalys line to the north, high-speed TGV trains -- sporting red and gray colors, push-button reclining seats and phone service -- are cutting travel time between Paris and Brussels to two hours from three. The trains go on to Antwerp and Liege, in Belgium, and Amsterdam (including Schiphol Airport), Rotterdam and The Hague, in the Netherlands. Heading south from Paris, the TGV's race at speeds topping 175 miles an hour to such French business centers as Lyons and Toulouse, beating planes downtown to downtown on distances of 300 miles or less. Occasionally, the trains do slow down when rolling along older unimproved routes, just as Eurostars brake for Britain's limited-speed track in East Anglia. Last month TGV's began clipping about 60 to 90 minutes off the roughly seven-hour runs from Paris to Milan, Italy's trade show center, and Turin, home to Fiat, the Italian auto giant. That makes the rail trip only two hours longer, downtown to downtown, than flying. And Italy's ETR 460 trains are slicing an hour off the Lyons-Milan run. Travelers can call (800) 387-6782 for Eurostar's new schedules and fares, or consult Rail Europe's World Wide Web site (www.raileurope.com).

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
TV Screen Opens Onto Internet
body: MICROSOFT recently demonstrated a redesigned version of its Microsoft Network (MSN) on-line information service, one that transforms the computer network into something strikingly like a television network. At about the same time, WebTV Networks redesigned my television screen to resemble an Internet computer more closely, including a World Wide Web browser, full Internet access and electronic mail. WebTV is the Internet without a personal computer, using a regular television set and a phone line. So, the PC is becoming more like a TV, and the TV is becoming more like a PC. These two developments are the clearest signs yet that digital convergence is no longer merely a media industry buzzphrase, but rather a description of a tectonic shift in our information environment. If the early success of WebTV is any indication, the epicenter of this upheaval may be gradually shifting toward the living room, and away from the office. The redesigned MSN service is scheduled to be deployed next month and will be discussed more fully in this column then. WebTV recently made its debut in consumer electronic stores. Early reports suggest it is gaining an enthusiastic reception from people who are looking for a simple, easy and relatively inexpensive way to investigate the Internet and the World Wide Web, without having to mess with a technologically daunting personal computer. WebTV has two major components. One is a $300 piece of equipment, smaller and slimmer than a video cassette recorder, which attaches to almost any television set. The other is an Internet connection service that costs $19.95 a month for unlimited access. The system also requires a standard phone line. The WebTV units now in the stores carry the Sony and Philips Magnavox brand names. I tested a prototype unit built by WebTV Networks Inc., the fledgling company in Palo Alto, Calif., that invented it. The first-generation WebTV system I tested is not going to steal my affections away from my personal computer. But as with many people who have a dominant geek gene masking a recessive couch potato gene, there were moments when I could envision watching the World Series from the couch and using WebTV's nifty remote control to zip over to the Web to check out the comparative stats of the Atlanta Braves and my beloved Yankees. If my old TV set had the picture-in-picture feature, WebTV would allow me to watch the game in a window on screen while surfing the net on the bigger picture. Or, we could be watching "The X-Files," for example, and be reminded that it has been ages since we've heard from odd Uncle Fudd. A press on the remote, a slight reach for the optional wireless keyboard (a $70 option), and we could be typing electronic mail to him. Electronic mail is emerging as the most popular application on the Internet, but email is still primarily an office-based service. Fewer than one-third of all households in the unitedstates have a personal computer. A vast majority of American households have telephones and televisions, however. Through Web TV, those that also have a valid credit card and a desire to get wired can be sending and receiving email in just a few minutes. For years, computer companies have been trying to figure out ways to transform a $2,000 computer into a crummy TV with a dinky, jerky picture and lousy sound. Now, WebTV and others have decided it makes more sense to integrate an inexpensive RISC computer chip and modem into a television set, transforming it into a better-than-average Internet box. (WebTV's 33.6-kilobit modem, coupled with some clever programming, actually made the Web a little zippier on my TV than on my modem-equipped PC.) At least for now, my personal computer is far better equipped than the WebTV device to take advantage of the many evolving technologies of the Internet. It is also much better suited for word processing, calculating spreadsheets, maintaining data bases and keeping a calendar, among other PC tasks. The WebTV box I tested had no provision for a printer (WebTV says a printer port will be added early next year) and, even though the box is designed to accept as many as seven peripheral devices, I seriously doubt that an inveterate couch potato would have the technical starch to add and configure a CD-ROM drive or a hard disk. The WebTV box comes with a Smart Card slot that may be useful some day for electronic shopping and home banking, but survey after survey finds those activities at the bottom of the list when on-line users are asked what they most want to do on the Internet Still, the WebTV system is very well thought out, and contains many technical flourishes that will impress Internet veterans. Text and graphics on TV screen were surprisingly good. The setup was easy and not nearly as tedious or complex as setting up a PC, finding and communicating with an Internet access provider, configuring a browser and other computer-based travails. In summary, I would be happy to find a WebTV unit under my Christmas tree, but probably not this year. The technology is not quite ready for prime time. It shows so much promise, however, that I will be watching eagerly to see what Sony, Philips Magnavox and other licensees do with their second and third-generation models. More information about WebTV is available from WebTV Networks Inc. at (800) 469-3288, or on the Web at http://www.webtv.net. Graphic   Drawing

title:
Market Place;
New modem plans by U.S. Robotics entice Wall Street.
body: THE Internet has the modem industry whistling. Millions of consumers are buying modems to connect their personal computers to the Internet and the World Wide Web, and to on-line information services like America Online and Compuserve. Millions more are expected to upgrade their older, slower modems to take advantage of new Internet multimedia applications, which include fancy animations, stereo sound, video clips and electronic mail with voice and video messages. As a result, modems have become a $3 billion industry, one that is growing this year an estimated 30 percent to 40 percent. The U.S. Robotics Corporation of Skokie, Ill., the modem industry leader with about 40 percent of the consumer market and 50 percent of the commercial-systems market, said last week that it had developed a new generation of analog modems capable of downloading information from the Internet at nearly twice the rate of today's fastest conventional modems. The new modems, which U.S. Robotics calls "x2" are expected to be available in February. They will enable users to receive data from the Internet at speeds as high as 56 kilobits a second (roughly 56,000 bits), compared with the 28.8 kilobits or 33.6 kilobits for the most common models sold today. The x2 analog modems achieve their faster speed because their technology lets them take advantage of the higher-quality digital switches and phone lines now in widespread use by phone companies and Internet service providers. Other modem and modem component makers have already signaled their intention to move to 56-kilobit technology. Rockwell International's semiconductor division, which makes the digital signal processing chip sets used by many modem makers, was the first to announce plans for 56-kilobit units last month. Motorola and Lucent Technologies also chimed in with their own 56-kilobit announcements. Including U.S. Robotics, each of the four companies has its own proprietary -- and incompatible -- method for achieving the higher downloading speeds. But while virtually all the top modem companies announced plans to deliver 56-kilobit modems or chip sets by next summer, the announcement by U.S. Robotics was the one that, at least initially, started Wall Street's wires humming. Unlike its three rivals, U.S. Robotics derives almost all of its revenue from modems. U.S. Robotics' stock price has resembled a sound wave this year, bottoming at $32.50 a share in January, soaring to $105.50 in May, falling once again to the upper $40's as recently as August and creeping up in recent weeks as rumors of the 56-kilobit modem announcement began spreading. On Tuesday, the stock soared more than $9 during the day, trading as high as $79, after the company said it would make a breakthrough announcement the following day. And, indeed, the next day it traded at more than $82 before the announcement was made. Perhaps following a "buy on the rumor, sell on the fact" tendency, U.S. Robotics shares have slipped since the announcement, ending last week at $73.375, down $2.625 Friday in Nasdaq trading. Jim McIlree, an analyst with Southcoast Capital in Austin, Tex., said that the retreat could at least be explained in part by disappointment that U.S. Robotics will not have the x2 technology available in time for the holiday season. He said the company was also vague on its pricing. But he said he remained strongly bullish on the stock. Nor did the post-announcement stock pullback discourage Steven D. Levy, an analyst with Oppenheimer & Company in newyork. "I'm still looking for a target price of 100 by the end of the year," Mr. Levy said. Mr. McIlree concurred. The analysts said that there were many reasons to be sanguine. U.S. Robotics was not first to announce a 56-kilobit modem, but it outlined a timetable that could make it first to market with real products. More significant, U.S. Robotics said that most leading Internet-access, on-line service and phone companies had endorsed its technology -- including America Online, Compuserve, Prodigy and I.B.M. Global Network. The modem company also said it would license its x2 technology to Texas Instruments, which makes the digital-signal processing chips used in U.S. Robotics modems, and collect royalties on the sales to other modem makers. Finally, U.S. Robotics said any of its modems sold since August could be upgraded to x2 speeds with a simple software upgrade when the code becomes available in January. The aggressive moves suggest that the U.S. Robotics version of the 56-kilobit modem will be in widespread use before any rivals. "U.S. Robotics is likely to have a six-month window of opportunity before alternative 56-kilobit solutions are available," said Rakesh Sood, an analyst at Hambrecht & Quist in San Francisco. Mr. Sood is forecasting earnings of $3.23 a share in 1997, on revenue of $3.081 billion, in contrast to his 1996 estimates of $2.33 and revenue of $1.966 billion. There are risks. U.S. Robotics has announced its intent to sell its modems before the International Telecommunications Union, the official standards-setting body, sanctions 56-kilobit technology. An I.T.U. standards decision is not expected until early 1998, though a North American standard may be reached next year. Until the standards are resolved, the 56-kilobit modems will not work at optimum speed -- or, in some cases, will not work at all -- unless the consumer's modem uses the same data sequencing code as the Internet service provider's brand of modem.

title:
Taking In the Sites;
Lights, Camera, Surf for Film Buffs
body: "Hey! I'm walkin' here!" Ratso Rizzo (Dustin Hoffman) yells at the heavy newyork traffic in "Midnight Cowboy." For harried pedestrians that's a quote worth recalling -- and, in fact, it was recently recalled in theater 6L at the Film Scouts site on the Internet. A fount of information about the movies, Film Scouts posted a tutorial on city mores and street talk as part of its coverage of the newyork Film Festival this month. "To the true newyorker, a street is merely that part of the sidewalk on which cars are permitted," it noted. While every Hollywood film studio has razzle-dazzle World Wide Web pages promoting its wares, more discerning Web-surfing film lovers can find reviews, interviews, movie clips and stills, archives of facts and trivia, previews and trailers, news from film festivals, Hollywood buzz and celebrity gossip, as well as chat-room discussions among fans and film makers at Film.com, Film Scouts and Hollywood Online. But the more interesting sites have their specialties. For instance, Film Scouts, which Netscape and Yahoo rank among the best of hundreds of movie sites on the Web, is noted for its festival coverage. Movie Critic, another site, matches films with viewer preferences. Movie Sounds specializes in audio clips from soundtracks. Film 100 profiles the 100 most influential people in film history. Esoterica abounds on a multitude of subjects. Texas films, Japanese movie ticket stubs and cheesecake from the 1950's all have their sites. On Early Motion Pictures 1897-1916, a site put up by the Library of Congress, one can download "The Last Days of President McKinley" and "Early Films of San Francisco." Scores of other sites serve as centers of instruction and information for independent film makers, meeting places for fans of actors, directors and genres -- from Mandarin to military aviation, to mention two of the 70 sites listed by Yahoo -- or practically any other enthusiasm, no matter how arcane. Looming over all of them is the Internet Movie Database, the London-based behemoth of film sites with more than a million entries on 81,000 films. "Actually it could be 250,000 titles if you include Indian film," said Col Needham, who began Internet Movie Database in 1990 as a discussion group of film buffs. These days it adds 40,000 pieces of information a week gathered from fans and other sources and screened by editors in several countries. With 300,000 cross-referenced entries on actors, directors and just about everybody who had anything to do with practically every movie, the site has become a major link for most other sites on the net. In the unitedstates alone, Internet Movie Database gets 1.2 million hits a day. For all their archives, though, movies sites are meant to entertain. Founded in 1994 by Mayra Langdon Riesman, a newyork film producer, Film Scouts made a name for itself with its fast-moving, virtually live multicasts from film festivals, especially Cannes and Sundance. Guided by the on-site characters Jerry the usher and Tom the projectionist, the Film Scouts visitor moves about the site's 24 "theaters." Seven of these feature reviews and clips from new releases. Others have interviews with film people from Robert Altman and James Ivory to Liv Tyler and Gerard Depardieu, a reference library and other features. If you get lost, just yell for Jerry.
