title:
LOOKING GLASS;
Games Wooing an Internet Audience
body: No one has as yet made a profit marrying multiplayer games to Prince Internet or built a business model with which to make money happily ever after. "There is no evidence of any single model working," said Steven L. Eskenazi, a new media analyst for Alex. Brown & Sons. "But over time there will be." The dozens of businesses trying to profit from Internet games must meet their players' expectations while accepting -- or overcoming -- the restictions of slow modems and connections littered with email. Racing in the fast lane are companies like Total Entertainment Network and Mpath Interactive. These "channels" deliver games with complex video components by reserving a line on the Internet for game commands. The result is that lag times between, say, the moment a shot is fired and when the opponent perceives the blow are short enough to play such "twitch games." Moving with the flow of traffic is America Online. For AOL, games are another way to keep its broad audience on-line a little longer. But the games share the same network space as a piece of electronic mail, and the lag times restrict the type of games possible. 'It makes a lot more sense in the short term to invest in the [game] software rather than trying to change the medium," said Lawrence Schick, general manager of AOL Games. With Jupiter Communications estimating that people will pump $1.6 billion into on-line games by the year 2000, the only model that might not make sense is avoiding the Internet altogether. Here are some game strategies.   KRIS GOODFELLOW Graphic   Chart lists gaming companies and their strategies.

title: AT&T Moves to Expand Its Role on Internet
body: The AT&T Corporation stepped up its efforts to become a major player on the Internet yesterday, offering secure transactions for consumers and easy-to-use tools for businesses marketing products on the World Wide Web. AT&T offered a suite of products for Internet commerce, most significantly a promise to cover any losses consumers suffer on unauthorized transactions. The growth of Internet business has been retarded by consumer worries about security. AT&T also addressed another concern of Internet users: the difficulty of learning new technology. AT&T disclosed a "turnkey" solution to maintain Web sites for business, requiring no technical knowledge on the part of users. Robert Allen, AT&T's chairman, said that the products would make doing business on the Internet as easy as dialing an "800" toll-free telephone number. The nation's biggest long-distance phone company said it would offer a service to allow businesses to build and maintain sites on the Internet's World Wide Web as well as provide ways to attract customers to the site. Mr. Allen said the company's new service would attract customers and "turn browsers into buyers." Under its program, AT&T said it would guarantee secure Internet transactions for Web shoppers who join the company's free Secure Buyer's program and charge their Internet purchases to their AT&T Universal credit cards. The company said that regardless of which Internet access provider consumers used, Web shoppers would not have to pay for purchases by unauthorized users. AT&T itself offers Internet access through its Worldnet service.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
An Internet newcomer is making money by selling moving ads as part of screen savers.
body: ADVERTISING in cyberspace has not been a lucrative venture for many. But one Internet company thinks it has hit upon a formula that could work. Pointcast Inc., a new company based in Cupertino, Calif., has begun what it calls "Internet broadcasting," delivering customized news, weather forecasts, stock quotes, sports scores -- and yes, even advertising -- directly into computers using an Internet connection. After just three months on line, its site is already challenging the Netscape Communications Corporation and Yahoo Inc. as one of the biggest earners of advertising dollars on the Web. In fact, the site's prospects were so highly regarded that within months of its start in May, the company raised $36 million from outside investors, including the Compaq Computer Corporation, the Gannett Company and Knight-Ridder Inc. "Pointcast is probably the most closely watched application in cyberspace," said Adam Schoenfeld, an analyst at Jupiter Communications Inc. in newyork. People are watching Pointcast because of its novel application called "off-line delivery," a technology that periodically logs onto the Internet and retrieves only the information that users have selected and stores it on the Pointcast "channel viewer," which also acts as a screen saver program. Analysts say it's the difference between going down to a newsstand and having a newspaper thrown onto the front lawn. The news and information is provided by Reuters, Accu Weather and Time-Warner, with CNN, The newyork Times and several Knight-Ridder newspapers coming soon. "From the very beginning, we approached this with the promise not that it delivers traffic but that it delivers a message to a demographic that is hard to reach," said Anna Zornosa, vice president of sales at Pointcast. "We approached people and said, 'We're going to get you into an environment that you haven't been able to get into.' " Thus far, Pointcast claims about 500,000 regular subscribers (a million people have registered by downloading the software free over the Internet at www.pointcast.com). In addition to the news content, viewers see a rotation of animated, 30-second "commercials" on a frame in the upper right-hand corner of the screen, a new advertising tool that executives contend is a compelling alternative to the static banner ads that now dominate the Web. "With banners, you're talking about very flat messages," Ms. Zornosa said. "If you want to tell a consumer your mint is best, you can't do that in a static banner. Contrast that with a 30-second animated commercial." Although Pointcast's "smart ads" are not full-motion video, they do run up to 10 frames a second, giving the ads a near-television effect. And because they are downloaded directly into a hard drive, they will also run when a computer is off-line or in the screen saver mode. Pointcast has about 50 commercials available and says it expects its fourth-quarter advertising revenue to top $3 million. That would make Pointcast one of the top ad-supported sites in cyberspace, according to Adspend, a web-tracking service owned by Jupiter Communications. Netscape tops the list with $9 million in the first half of the year. Pointcast has successfully lured large consumer-oriented brands into advertising in cyberspace, such as Avis, Fidelity, General Motors, Johnston & Murphy shoes and Nationsbank. "We're bringing new players to the Web," Ms. Zornosa said, noting that about 25 companies have agreed to pay the standard rate of $100,000 to advertise on Pointcast in the fourth quarter. For that money, advertisers are guaranteed 20 million "impressions," or viewings, a month. Each time a 30-second spot plays, it registers in the user's computer. When the user logs back on to Pointcast, that information is delivered to the company. Pointcast says the data will be verified by the Audit Bureau of Circulation. Meanwhile, Pointcast is beginning to face competition from companies including Freeloader Inc. in Washington, and V-Cast Inc. in newyork. Yesterday, Berkeley Systems Inc., known for its After Dark screen saver program, introduced a news and information station in the form of a screen saver, with news and features provided by, among others, USA Today, The Wall Street Journal and Sports Illustrated. Bill Bass, an analyst at Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass., said the Microsoft Corporation, the "Magilla Gorilla" in the field, was already working on a customized application called Active Desktop, which will be built right into the Windows operating system. "The problem is the more compelling your work, the more interested Microsoft is in doing something similar," Mr. Schoenfeld at Jupiter Communications said. But, he added, "Pointcast got out first and got out best, and that cannot be negated."

title: An On-Line Service Planning Expansion
body: City Search Inc., which produces community-based on-line information services for the World Wide Web, plans to announce today that it has placed management teams in Austin, Tex., and Salt Lake City in preparation for starting local services in those cities by the end of the year. City Search is also announcing that a new version of City Search/ Metrobeat in newyork City will begin by the end of the month, to give users more capabilities for personalizing the on-line guide to newyork activities. In July, City Search, based in Pasadena, Calif., acquired Metrobeat, the publisher of one of Manhattan's most popular city guides on the Web. "We're accelerating into new markets and establishing our local management teams ahead of schedule," said Charles Conn, president and chief executive of City Search. The company, which intends to assemble a national collection of local Web sites in the nation's largest markets, hopes to be set up in 30 cities by the end of next year. City Search started its local on-line service in the Raleigh, Durham, and Chapel Hill area of North Carolina in May and has added Pasadena, newyork and San Francisco. City Search is a privately held company financed by Goldman, Sachs, AT&T Ventures and private investors.

title: More Users Now Taking Direct Route to the Internet, a Survey Finds
body: A new survey of home computer users has found that for the first time, more people are gaining access to the Internet through direct Internet service providers than through commercial on-line services like America Online or Compuserve, still substantially owned by H & R Block Inc.. But the survey also found that most consumers are not very impressed with the on-line experience. The findings of the semiannual Homefront survey by Odyssey Inc. of San Francisco represented a significant shift from just six months ago, and appeared to reflect both the growing popularity of Internet-access services like Netcom and AT&T Worldnet, and a growing disenchantment with the proprietary information services. It found that 48 percent of all households connected to the Internet used an Internet service provider, compared with 35 percent who used a commercial on-line service. Six months ago, 54 percent of households with Internet access used a commercial on-line service, as against 30 percent for the Internet providers. Nicholas Donatiello, president of Odyssey, a San Francisco-based market research firm, said the numbers did not add up to 100 percent since many people did not know the name of their service provider. Underscoring the report, Pacific Bell Internet Services, a Pacific Telesis unit, said on Friday that it had signed up more than 51,000 subscribers in the first 90 days it offered Internet connections in California, making it one of the fastest growing of the Internet service providers. "There are now lots of places to get information, and lots of ways to get onto the Internet," Mr. Donatiello said. "Commercial on-line services are going to have to sell themselves in a different way than they have been selling themselves. They need to explain what value they bring in addition to access to the Internet and the World Wide Web." Unlike the service providers, who typically offer home computer users access to the Internet but little else, the commercial on-line services create a self-contained world of services and features available only to paying members. These companies, of which America Online is the largest, offer Internet access as a supplement to their own proprietary content: features like chat rooms, forums on everything from investing to astrology to AIDS, airline schedules and stock quotes. But on-line bulletin boards can be reached directly through an Internet service provider and can also advise, inform and support people. And World Wide Web sites offer a panoply of choices, many unavailable through on-line services. The new survey appears to mirror recent reports of troubles throughout the consumer on-line service industry. While America Online continues to grow, despite highly publicized breakdowns and disputes over its billing practices, other on-line services report stagnant or declining membership. In the last year, Apple Computer pulled the plug on its eWorld on-line service, and AT&T did the same with its Interchange service. The News Corporation abandoned Delphi Internet Services, and I.B.M. and Sears, Roebuck abandoned their 10-year, billion-dollar joint investment in Prodigy. Even Microsoft, whose MSN Network was initially regarded as America Online's biggest challenger, gave up on the consumer model and rebuilt the system from the electrons up as an Internet service. In the meantime, virtually all the national and regional telephone companies have started, or are preparing to start, Internet access services aimed at consumers. AT&T now trails only Netcom On-Line Communications Services of San Jose, Calif., in residential Internet customers. While home Internet users may not always know the path by which they get on line, they do know that they are not highly impressed once they get there, Mr. Donatiello said. No on-line service received a positive rating from a majority of users when they were asked to rate their experiences, the study found. The Internet and the World Wide Web scored best though just 40 percent of consumers rated them "very good." That was still higher than the leading on-line service, America Online, with 29 percent approval. America Online, with 6.5 million subscribers, is the only commercial on-line service that has managed to increase its market share consistently. By contrast, there are now several thousand Internet service providers in the unitedstates, led by Netcom, with 8 percent of its market, and AT&T Worldnet Services, with 7 percent. Both offer flat-rate pricing for virtually unlimited access to the Internet, as distinct from the hourly fees typically charged by the commercial on-line services companies. "On-line services are not going to be able to resist for long that kind of flat-rate pricing model," Mr. Donatiello said. The survey data indicated that 14 percent of all households in the unitedstates now have access to the Internet or to an on-line service. Over all, 36 percent of all households have a personal computer of some sort, which means that on-line households are still a minority even among PC households. Among households that have an on-line connection, electronic mail emerged in the survey as the most popular application, followed by research, and news and information-gathering, Mr. Donatiello said. Entertainment was fourth. The least popular applications named by consumers, according to the survey, were home banking, on-line shopping and making hotel and airline reservations -- applications that many companies view as necessary for the broad success of electronic commerce. "This is not good news for on-line services," Mr. Donatiello said. "We know that entertainment is the 6,000-pound gorilla that will get people at home to use on-line services. Information is just a little chihuahua. It will be harder for the on-line services to increase their penetration into households if people view them as substitutes for fax machines and the postal service." The Odyssey survey also concluded that while Microsoft was gaining awareness from home Internet users for its Internet Explorer software for browsing the World Wide Web, the Netscape Communications Corporation's Navigator software continued to dominate. "Of those who use the World Wide Web at home, 54 percent use Navigator while 6 percent use Microsoft Explorer," Mr. Donatiello said. The remaining 40 percent either did not know what browser they used or used one of the dozen or so less-known browsers. But while Microsoft Explorer has not yet become the browser of choice for many people, computer operators are still very aware that it is out there: almost as many knew about it as knew about Netscape's Navigator.

title:
Market Place;
America Online, now on the Big Board, has big plans.
body: AFTER watching its stock price drop by about 60 percent since May, America Online Inc. did something about it yesterday. It moved from the Nasdaq market to the newyork Stock Exchange. Things went well for America Online on its first day of trading on the Big Board, with its shares closing at $29, up $2. The shift to the newyork exchange is part of a fine-tuning of the company's strategy. Stephen M. Case, the 37-year-old chairman, who is not a man given to understatement, proclaimed the adjustments amounted to nothing less than "the new AOL." What is new is a big marketing push and some new plans for generating money from sources other than monthly subscriber fees, which represent more than 90 percent of America Online's revenues. The new marketing drive includes sending out videotapes to the service's six million subscribers, extolling the virtues of staying with America Online. That is important since its "churn rate," or the percentage of new subscribers who begin paying after a free trial period but cancel within a year, is 35 percent or more, said Gary Arlen, president of Arlen Communications Inc., a research firm. High churn rates have made growth more difficult and more costly for America Online lately. In a telephone news conference yesterday, Mr. Case conceded that the company had to improve its rate of retention. "We've kind of dropped the ball with new members," he said. To help, the company has increased its national service staff to 3,000 people, to help subscribers with problems. Some analysts believe overly ambitious growth is to blame for America Online's recent problems with spotty customer service, irritating delays experienced by subscribers trying to get connected and even a blackout on Aug. 7, when the service shut down for most of the day. Nonsense, is the reply from Mr. Case. His plan calls for even faster growth, trying to reach 10 million subscribers within a year. Besides the video-mailing to existing customers, America Online will begin a major new television advertising campaign next month. The company is not saying how much themailing and advertising campaign will cost, but analysts estimate the price tag at $100 million or more. The marketing drive is the latest move in America Online's mission, which Mr. Case describes as "bringing the on-line experience to a mass consumer audience." Critics who say the Internet poses a threat to a traditional on-line service, like America Online, he dismisses as technology elitists who are blind to the needs of the "mainstream novice audience." Only about 15 percent of American households are connected to on-line services or the Internet, and Mr. Case wants to change that. No one has doubted America Online's ability to generate growth, with revenues running at the rate of $1 billion a year. But critics say the cost of that growth has been too high. In fact, they say, if the company did not capitalize much of its marketing costs -- putting them on the balance sheet to stretch out the impact on profits -- it would have no earnings. Nor, they add, does America Online's business model seem to hold out any prospect for sizable profits, ever. Yesterday, Mr. Case conceded that its main source of revenue, monthly subscriber payments, was not where America Online would make money. Instead, the profits will come from advertising, fees from on-line commerce and even setting up private "intranets," he said. America Online executives said they signed up $27 million in new advertising contracts in the last 45 days. Most of the advertising, they said, comes not from computer companies and other marketers of technology but from consumer companies including Reebok, Citibank and Starbucks. The company views setting up private networks, which use America Online's software and telecommunications links, as a promising new business. Already, it is setting up a special-purpose private network connecting Hewlett-Packard with retail store managers handling its computers and printers, and an America Online intranet at the Harvard Business School allows professors to post information that students can use in their case studies. Over the next few years, advertising, on line merchandising and private networks, Mr. Case said, could account for hundreds of millions of dollars in high-profit business. In the future, he said, most of the company's revenues will continue to be from subscriber fees. "But most, if not all, of our profits will come from these new revenue streams," he said.

title: America Online Attempts to Regain Its Footing
body: America Online Inc. is to begin a new campaign today to attract subscribers in an effort to regain its waning momentum. While the company is still the largest commercial on-line service in the world, with 6.2 million subscribers, America Online has been undergoing many pressures in recent months, most notably the service failure that kept it unavailable to subscribers for almost 19 hours in August. The on-line service is also feeling pressure from the Internet, as many subscribers leave for direct Internet access, where rapid innovation is taking place. Meanwhile, America Online, which is based in Vienna, Va., is attracting new subscribers at a slower rate than in the past. "They have taken a lot of hits," said Emily Green, an analyst at Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. "They have had a need to buff up their image and to make sure people are aware that they want to stay out ahead of the competition." Steve Case, the chairman and chief executive of America Online, is to hold a conference call with reporters today, in which he is expected to discuss a new business model. A key element is a new version of its service software, Version 3.0, which was introduced during the summer. The new version has 22 categories, or areas, almost twice the prior version. The company plans to send electronic mail to members with tips on using the service. One big focus for Mr. Case is to keep the "churn rate" at bay, analysts said, referring to the rate at which customers join the service briefly, only to leave it. America Online is starting several programs intended to help keep its users interested in remaining on the service. Instead of mailing out floppy disks of its software, for example, America Online will be sending out video tapes to new members, to help them learn about the service. The company also plans a new advertising campaign in October, to run during prime-time television.

title: America Online Blocks 'Junk' email Aimed At Users
body: Responding to a torrent of complaints from subscribers who say electronic junk mail is clogging their computer in-boxes, America Online took the unusual step yesterday of blocking all incoming messages from five Internet sites that it said were responsible for sending millions of unsolicited commercial messages over computer networks each week. David W. Phillips, associate general counsel for America Online, said the five Internet sites -- three of which are associated with a marketing company in Philadelphia called Cyber Promotions Inc. -- were responsible for sending as many as 700,000 unsolicited commercial messages each day to the private electronic mailboxes of more than a million America Online subscribers. "We are worried that the quality of the user experience is deteriorating as a result of these junk emailings," Mr. Phillips said. While the other two big on-line providers, the Compuserve Corporation and Prodigy Inc., have quietly taken comparable steps in the past, America Online's announcement of a crackdown on junk email is the most sweeping and public acknowledgment yet of a problem that has affected all commercial on-line information services -- and the Internet itself -- since 1994, when millions of consumers began using the global computer network, and large numbers of commercial users went on line to pursue them. Known in Internet argot as "spamming," the practice of sending unsolicited advertisements and solicitations over computer networks is roughly analogous to plastering promotional fliers on automobile windshields in parking lots. It is the technological heir to bulk marketing, including postal mail, boiler-room phone operations and junk faxes. But while earlier episodes of Internet spamming have been met with the on-line world's version of vigilante justice -- sometimes including blacklisting, angry email counterattacks known as "flaming" or even software email bombs that clog the senders' systems -- the emergence of the Internet as a potentially lucrative marketing vehicle has moved the battles into the courts. America Online said it had been asking Cyber Promotions for several months to stop its bulk mailings and had begun returning hundreds of thousands of undeliverable messages to Cyber Promotions' Internet service providers. In some cases, the service providers dropped Cyber Promotions as a customer. In response, Cyber Promotions sued America Online, contending that the world's largest commercial on-line service had interfered in its business. Just last Friday, Cyber Promotions sought to stave off America Online's blockade by seeking a preliminary injunction in Federal District Court in Philadelphia. The court has not responded. Cyber Promotions' messages are sent on behalf of hundreds of small businesses that pay Cyber Promotions to send out bulk email over several networks. Sanford A. Wallace, president of Cyber Promotions, accused America Online yesterday of censorship and hypocrisy, citing America Online's practice of sending unsolicited commercial pitches to its own subscribers. When subscribers log on to America Online, they invariably get one or more marketing pitches from the network operator, promoting special rate plans, on-line guidebooks and other merchandise. "Maybe one of the reasons for their action is that AOL sees us as a competitive threat," Mr. Wallace said. "Unlike the pop-up screens that AOL forces all its members to see before they can get into their accounts, we're a little more responsible in our position." Mr. Phillips of America Online rejected the argument, calling it "an apples-and-oranges comparison." He said, however, that America Online would soon provide members with software that would enable them to block annoying solicitations, whether they come from America Online or any other source. Until then, Mr. Phillips conceded yesterday, America Online's plan to block all messages originating from the five Internet addresses, or domains, was not perfect -- and would not block unsolicited email from other addresses that America Online has not yet taken action against. It is relatively simple and inexpensive for companies to open new Internet domains, which would allow them to circumvent most blocking mechanisms. Moreover, any blocking of a domain would indiscriminately block any personal or other noncommercial messages that might come from that domain. But the scope of the spamming problem has become so severe that radical steps were required, Mr. Phillips said. For example, he said, one of the banned domains, netfree.com, distributes software that allows users to automatically "harvest" user names from America Online for the purpose of setting up bulk email lists. Another of the banned domains, honeys.com, sent mass emailings to America Online users, advertising a service that allows subscribers to see live video images of Las Vegas strippers over the network. The domains related to Cyber Promotions affected by the blockade are cyberpromo.com, answerme.com and servint.com. Reed Caldwell, the system administrator for Servint Inc. of McLean, Va., one of the five banned Internet domains and the company that provides Internet access for Cyber Promotions, said he was never contacted by America Online before it blocked all messages to and from his service yesterday. Mr. Caldwell said Servint itself had never sent unsolicited email, and said it was not his company's policy to interfere in the legal activities of his clients. Mr. Caldwell said he would have been willing to discuss the issue with America Online, which is nearby in Dulles, Va. "But if their definition of dealing with it is for us to cancel any of our clients they don't like, we can't do that," he said. America Online said it blocked the sites only after repeated requests to stop the mass mailings were refused or ignored by the operators of the five sites.

title:
Few Terms of Endearment;
The Fine Print in Cyberspace
body: THE Internet may be the forum of the future, but for millions of users it is no Hyde Park soapbox. Speech is regulated, not free, under the terms of contracts that people agree to when they gain access to the Internet through such services as American Online, AT&T Worldnet, Compuserve and the Microsoft Network. The fine print makes these companies the sole judges of what can and cannot be emailed, posted or transmitted. Sometimes the limits are bizarre. AT&T Worldnet bans disclosure of "personal matters," which could make a lot of email and chat room chatter not just pointless but prohibited. America Online, which is the biggest Internet access provider and which also offers chat rooms and instant messaging between members, warns that it may terminate members if they "transmit any unlawful, harmful, threatening, abusive, harassing, defamatory, vulgar, obscene, hateful, racially, ethnically or otherwise objectionable content." You also may not use the service to "harass, threaten, embarrass or cause distress, unwanted attention or discomfort upon another Member or user of AOL or other person or entity," or "post or transmit sexually explicit images or other content which is deemed by AOL Inc. to be offensive." Users were perhaps unimpressed last week, if not underwhelmed, when the system crashed and stranded them without service, regardless of caveats. Compuserve bans speech that "violates or infringes upon the rights of any others or which would be abusive, profane or offensive to an average person." But even if you never offend anyone, Compuserve "reserves the right in its sole discretion to edit or delete any information, software or other content appearing on the Service, regardless of whether it violates applicable standards for content." AT&T Worldnet emphasizes in its contract that "AT&T cannot and does not screen content provided by Members to the Service. Notwithstanding the foregoing, AT&T reserves the right to monitor content on the Service and to remove content which AT&T, in its sole discretion, determines to be harmful, offensive, or otherwise in violation of these Operating Policies." The contract says this policy "avoids the harm that can result from disseminating statements that are false, malicious, violative of the rights of others, or otherwise harmful." That policy contrasts sharply with AT&T's attitude about what you say over its long distance telephone lines. AT&T says it never monitors telephone calls (though it helps authorities with court orders to tap lines) and it does not regulate in any way what people say on the telephone. The Microsoft Network warns customers who violate its limitations on speech or "download a file that you know (or reasonably should know) cannot be legally distributed via MSN" that "your failure to observe any of the foregoing limitations may result in civil or criminal liability, as well as termination of your membership." People who like their speech unfettered can still find their way onto the Internet through some smaller access providers, like The Little Garden Net in San Francisco, which "exercises no control whatsoever over the content of the information passing through TLGnet." "You are free to communicate commercial, noncommercial, personal, questionable, obnoxious, annoying, or any other kind of information, misinformation, or disinformation through our service," the contract continues. "You are fully responsible for the privacy of, content of, and liability for your own communications."

title:
COMPANY REPORTS;
Human Error And Software Created Data Network Glitch
body: Software bugs and human error combined to create the huge system failure that blacked out America Online for nearly 19 hours on Wednesday, the company said yesterday. It called the failure a "a coincidental series of sequential events that will most likely never occur again." America Online provided details on the outage as it reported earnings for the fourth quarter that exceeded the estimates of securities analysts, but revenue that fell short, and it said that subscriber growth had slowed when compared with that in the third quarter. Shares of America Online declined 4.3 percent in Nasdaq trading yesterday, closing at $33.375, down $1.50. Yesterday's closing price was less than half the 52-week high of $71 -- a drop in the company's market capitalization of $3.27 billion. America Online said the problem on Wednesday had occurred as the company went off line at 4 A.M., Eastern time, to replace high-capacity switches within the local area network in the data centers that run the service. While the system was down, a subsidiary that provides network access, A.N.S., erroneously reconfigured the routing information that it sends to America Online. Because the network was down, its normal diagnostic systems could not detect the error. When engineers tried to bring the system back up, it did not work properly, a problem they assumed was a result of a flaw in the switch installation. They spent most of the day working through that process, to no avail, only to learn of the erroneous message from the subsidiary late in the afternoon. It was not the end of the trouble. "At the end of all this, we discovered a bug in the operating system of the routers that was exercised by this particular routing, and we were working with the vendor on that," said Matthew Korn, America Online's vice president for operations. Mr. Korn declined to name the vendor of the routing software. "This was our problem and we take responsibility for it," he said. "Our debugging tools and network-management tools were unable to take over and diagnose the problem." Despite the lengthy failure, users said that the day without America Online had represented more an inconvenience than a serious problem, and that they would probably remain with the service. The network's content providers, who lost revenue while the system was down, for the most part chalked it up to the inevitable vagaries of computer technology. "America Online has some special features which I like," said Fran Dym, a customer who is an independent public relations agent in newyork. "What this reinforces is the importance of having two Internet providers. There are just too many sites I rely on; I felt denuded yesterday." Most content providers took a stoic approach. "I'm in the technology business and things break," said David Ellington, founder and president of NetNoir, an African-American information service on A.O.L. "It was one day, and I'm sure A.O.L. has figured out a backup," he said. "They never want this to happen again." Ken Orton, president of Preview Travel in San Francisco, which provides ticketing on line through the network, said the outage meant that his business had to close. When the system came back up, "the buyers came back with a vengeance so we were able to recapture about 20 percent of what we lost. This morning, we are running at double normal volume, so my guess is we will make up most of it." America Online said it would compensate its subscribers with one day of free service, which it estimated would cost it about $3 million. "The disruption caused by the temporary unavailability of A.O.L. illustrates more clearly than ever before how important A.O.L. has become in the daily lives of our members," Steve Case, the network's chairman and chief executive, said. title: Data Network Fails, Vexing Small Business
body: In the most extensive network blackout yet in cyberspace, America Online, the nation's largest operator of an on-line computer network, was out of action yesterday, leaving its six million subscribers, including many small businesses and home-office workers, without electronic mail and other key communications services. The network outage, which occurred during the faulty installation of new system software beginning at 4 A.M., Eastern daylight time yesterday, also caused America Online's dozens of information publishers -- like the investment-advice service Motley Fool and the popular Health Respons Ability forum -- to lose many thousands of dollars in access fees or advertising revenues. And for the individuals and small-business users rendered digitally incommunicado yesterday, the blackout underscored how increasingly important email has become to modern commerce. "It brings you back to the days when there was no Internet," said Lynn Morgen, a founder and partner in Morgen Walke Associates Inc., a 120-employee investor-relations and communications agency in Manhattan. The company was unable to exchange email yesterday with its clients, or send electronic documents to its Paris office. "We can fax and retype documents," Ms. Morgen said, "but it certainly isn't as efficient." Network crashes are not uncommon in the on-line world. But for America Online, which casts itself as the user-friendliest service and which has blanketed the nation with its software diskettes -- even distributing them in the in-flight snack bags of some airlines -- yesterday's crash, which lasted until about 10:45 p.m., was an embarrassment. "This is a great way to burn customer loyalty," said Gary Arlen, president of Arlen Communications, a market research firm in Reston, Va. "Once you build a customer base of six million people, including folks who rely on you to do business, you can't knock out the network for the better part of a day." America Online said its service went down during a regularly scheduled maintenance update and software installation. Users who tried to log on throughout the day were greeted by text messages like the following: "The service is temporarily unavailable. Please try again in 15 minutes.  Thank you for calling." Steve Case, the chairman and chief executive of America Online, which is based in Vienna, Va., said last evening that the problem involved network routing software. He said the company would credit each subscriber's account for the lost day. "The real concern is we have six million members who rely on us, and we've let them down," Mr. Case said. To be sure, losing access to an on-line service is not yet tantamount, say, to doing without telephone service. And an estimated 15 percent to 20 percent of America Online subscribers have more than one on-line account, meaning that they could easily switch to another service yesterday. Moreover, larger business customers increasingly get their email and on-line access these days either through specialized Internet service providers or through their own corporate Internet host computers. So big companies for which electronic commerce is vital were unaffected by the America Online outage. What is more, many on-line information providers that distribute material via America Online -- including The newyork Times -- also operate their own sites on the Internet's World Wide Web and so were able to reach their audiences that way. But the investor-advice service Motley Fool, for example, operates its Web site through America Online and so was doubly doomed yesterday. Motley Fool receives about a third of its revenue -- or about $5,000 a day -- from the hourly use fees America Online charges subscribers. "I've come to expect that from time to time computers break down," said David Gardner, co-founder with his brother, Tom, of Motley Fool. "As it is, we announced today sort of a holiday," Mr. Gardner said. "But if it goes on more than a day, I'll be very upset." Ms. Morgen of Morgen Walke said her company frequently used America Online to tap into financial discussions -- or "chat rooms" -- on the Internet to keep tabs of industry scuttlebutt. Yesterday, her firm was receiving telephone calls that one of its clients was the subject of an on-line discussion in which the client was falsely rumored to be considering a merger with another company -- a rumor that she said could do untold damage to the client unless it was shot down. But without America Online, Morgen Walke was unable to go on line and rebut the rumor. "We have no way to access it or to respond to it," Ms. Morgen said. America Online has been the default choice for many small businesses and independent contractors without corporate connections, or without the patience of technical savvy to deal with the arcana of direct Internet access. "Without knowing it, a lot of consumers have developed real dependence on America Online, and maybe it doesn't become clear until the system goes down hard," said Jerry Michalski, editor of Release 1.0, an industry newsletter. "In one sense, it shows the value they derive from A.O.L., but it also makes A.O.L. look real bad." Analysts said the failure had to be particularly vexing to America Online because it came as the company is trying to diversify into additional services, such as on-line brokerage services, home banking and corporate on-line conferences -- all of which require reliable 24-hour availability. Some analysts said America Online had always paid more attention to marketing, attracting and retaining subscribers than it had to maintenance of its computer systems. As a business strategy, they said, America Online may have pursued the right course, because it has continued to grow even as rivals like Compuserve and Prodigy have weakened, but it is now vulnerable to failures of this sort. "They've done a good job of managing explosive growth over the last two years, and you can't expect them to be perfect," said Adam Schoenfeld, an analyst with Jupiter Communications. "But an outage of this duration is just disastrous," he said. In Nasdaq trading yesterday, America Online's stock fell early in the day to a low of $32.25 a share, but recovered to closed at $34.875, up 62.5 cents. Analysts said that periodic system failures, awkward user interfaces and other vagaries of the early on-line services were permissible when they had the market to themselves and when most users were computer hobbyists. But as the blossoming of the World Wide Web makes the global Internet increasingly accessible to anyone with a personal computer and a modem, services like America Online have to scramble just to stay in the game. "This is not cyberspace in trouble, this is one more death rattle from the old order," said Paul Saffo, director of the Institute for the Future, an industry research group based in Menlo Park, Calif. "America Online will likely survive, but its survival is tied to its ability to reinvent itself." It may be too late, in the case of Fran Dym, an American Online customer who is an independent public relations consultant in newyork. She lamented yesterday that she had been unable to receive important business documents and email she was expecting, to track her financial investments or to read the handful of newsletters that are sent to her email address daily. "What I'm going to do is find an Internet provider," Ms. Dym said. "This has taught me. And it'll probably be cheaper than America Online anyway." title: American Express and Microsoft to Create On-Line Travel Service
body: The American Express Company and the Microsoft Corporation announced yesterday that they would create an on-line service enabling business travelers to book air, hotel and rental car reservations with their personal computers. "Giving PC users real-time access to constantly changing information, in a marketplace like travel, delivers on the promise of the Internet," said William H. Gates, chief executive of Microsoft. While that promise is still in its early stages, a number of competitors are also expected to offer on-line booking sometime soon. The new Microsoft-American Express system will be able to operate through intranets, or internal booking networks, and will allow companies to capture travel data to insure compliance with corporate travel policy. Corporate America spends about $145 billion annually on travel-related expenses, which are typically a company's third-largest controllable expense, the two companies said in a statement. The new service will allow companies to list in the system the discounted rates they have negotiated with airlines, hotels and car rental companies. Financial terms were not disclosed, but American Express said it would have a two-year exclusive license to the jointly developed product. The system will undergo tests soon and is expected to be in full operation during the first half of next year. "This agreement with Microsoft represents an important step forward in launching the next generation of travel services," said Harvey Golub, the chief executive of American Express. The company is the biggest travel agency network in the world, with over $15.1 billion in travel sales last year, while Microsoft dominates personal computer software. While the new venture could presage bad news for travel agents -- especially the independent agencies outside the American Express network -- Dick Knodt, executive director of the American Society of Travel Agents, said that would not happen in the short term, and probably not in the long term either. "Everything their system can deliver is already in existence," he said, "but right now it is mostly in the computerized reservations systems that are owned by the airlines. So we see the threat to the airlines, not to travel agents." Mr. Knodt also said that other companies were working on similar products that they would soon offer to travel agents. These include the Internet Travel Network as well as Travelocity, a unit of the Sabre Group, which is owned by by the AMR Corporation, the parent of American Airlines, and the Worldview Systems Corporation. "Their customers will use the information to compare airline and hotel prices," Mr. Knodt said, "then most of them will still book through their agents."

title:
Patents;
The owner of a direct-mail company creates a system to send electronic ads to specific viewers.
body: AN increasing number of patents are being issued to inventors to protect innovations in information and entertainment technology, especially the emerging methods of exploiting the Internet. In one case, the owner of a newyork City direct-mail company, Carles Inc., has won a patent for a system aimed at distributing television commercials over a network so that each one is tailored to people in individual homes. The system is similar to those used by newspapers and magazines, which have long tailored advertising to specific reader groups, inserting flyers or printing ads that will appear in editions that go to areas with specific zip codes. The inventor, John Carles, says his system covers any closed network, like cable television systems, direct-broadcast satellite and even the Internet. "If someone uses the Internet to demographically select people by using an algorithm, then they're using the method in this patent," Mr. Carles contended. Mr. Carles's invention would enable advertisers to aim specific commercials at individual households. That, in turn, would let television networks or cable companies adjust their advertising fees according to the perceived audience value of the people in the target house. "If you're at General Motors and you have many different automobiles, you can bring each to a different target market group," Mr. Carles said. G.M. could buy commercial time during the broadcast of a movie, for example. "Instead of the commercial going out to everyone watching the movie," he said, "five messages would go out, each one targeted to a specific group." Thus, young families might see an ad for a sport utility vehicle. Single people might receive a commercial about sports cars or compacts and older viewers might watch an ad for luxury sedans. Using demographic, life style and census information available from private data bases, Mr. Carles's system first creates a profile of individual households. "Once you have a statistically significant sample of known users of a product or service," he explained, "you can create a statistical model that says these are the variables that identify these people. "Once you have that model, you can run it against a large data base of 85 million households, and pull out all the households that have these variables and rank them," he said. Each household in an area would be given a rating based on their potential to buy specific products and services. "An advertiser could say 'I want to buy the top 20 to 30 percent of this group, 20 percent of the next, and 20 percent of the next, and so on,' and run as many commercials as possible within one spot," Mr. Carles said. He said advertisers would find this kind of marketing necessary as cable channels increase in number and compete for viewers. The system would be able to communicate with televisions through addressable set-top boxes. Those are cable or satellite switching boxes with computer chips that allow them to receive coded messages. Thousands are already installed across the country. Mr. Carles, who received patent 5,515,098, said he hoped a cable company would license his invention and help him establish a company to bring his technology to market. Live (Well, Almost) On the Internet Last month, the founder of a small Texas sports entertainment company received a patent for a method of presenting live events on the Internet, via wireless services and on interactive television. David Barstow is the founder and president of Instant Sports Inc., an Austin, Tex., company that runs a sports site on the World Wide Web (http://www.instantsports.com). He also holds a Ph.D. in artificial intelligence from Stanford, but perhaps more important, is a devotee of baseball. In the 1980's, he began designing ways to enjoy baseball games via computer. Early on he compiled an index of 78 possible baseball plays that is now a central element in his patented method of displaying live events via computer. As a game unfolds, each play is entered into a computer using one of the 78 terms in a domain-specific language. "The way it works is at its heart is a discreet-event simulator that creates a dynamic data base with a lot of information about the game that is going on," Mr. Barstow said. "The discreet-event simulator is driven by the raw data coming from the site of the game, in cryptic shorthand about baseball." The simulator provides a graphic of a baseball field, with "stick figure players in the outfield and at bat," he said. It takes one to two minutes to feed data about a play to the simulator. "The raw data comes from the ballpark, drives the simulator, and from the simulator, we provide information to the fans on their own machines," he added. "We send an encoded command to fans' machines." His patent, he says, covers "the use of a domain-specific language to drive a simulation and to use that to provide real-time coverage of events. The patent covers a variety of different sporting events, not just baseball," Mr. Barstow said. "And it is broad enough to cover other live events, like traffic reporting." The invention, which is already in use on the Instant Sports Web site, received patent 5,526,479. From Your Pocket, Heat Relief People who go to live baseball games this summer may find themselves waving programs in front of their faces to cool off. But 20,000 people at next month's U.S. Open tennis tournament will be handed free fans that are the size and shape of a credit card. "There hasn't been a change in fan design since the 1930's," said Peter Geise of Areco North America, the Woburn, Mass., company that holds a patent for a fan named Breezer Fan Cards. Mr. Geise believed that people would carry fans if they were small and slim enough to be slipped into a shirt pocket or wallet. And that meant space on the fans could be sold to advertisers. The fans being given away at the tennis tournament will promote Heineken beer. A Fan Card fan slides out one end of a credit card-sized envelope and unfolds into a shape that looks like a snow shovel. Tabs on the fan wings are inserted into the sides of the envelope, which serves as a handle, to make the fan stable and secure. The fan is laminated, and when waved, moves volumes of air. It received patent 5,387,084. Patents are available by number for $3 from the Patent and Trademark Office, Washington, D.C. 20231.

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
CYBERSCOUT
body: HEALTH CAUTIONS . . . Shoreland's Travel Health Online http://www.tripprep.com Before journeying abroad, it is a good idea to worry about your health, and health information is widely available on the World Wide Web. Shoreland, in Milwaukee, has provided data since 1986 for doctors and other professionals who advise travelers. Last month, it opened a free Web site accessible to the public. The site provides information about 220 countries in four main categories: country profiles, including climate and topography; general travel health concerns; preventive medications and vaccines, and travel illness summaries. The pages move along briskly, partly because Shoreland has avoided the usual raft of graphic images. According to Steven Denny, a vice president of Shoreland, its information is gathered from a variety of sources, including the unitedstates Department of State, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the World Health Organization and a selection of medical literature. Since I had just returned from Quebec, I chose Canada, from country profiles -- not much of a health challenge. The State Department summary on Canada, a subcategory, would have been helpful had I been planning a trip to Toronto, which "has the highest pollen count of any North American city and hay fever sufferers should avoid it during the six-week peak season." It would have been more helpful if it had said which six weeks were peak. The only mention of Quebec was: "The prevailing language in Quebec province is French rather than English as in most of Canada. However, even in Quebec, English is spoken at most hotels and many tourist facilities." That, I suppose, is health information if an English-speaking visitor is concerned about a French-speaking doctor. There was no mention of the major health problem I encountered, Quebeckers' tendency to flavor everything with maple syrup. Still, Shoreland is not responsible for information from the State Department, and it is handy to have it available, with much else, in one place. Had I been researching Chad or China, to stick with countries beginning with the letter C, I would have been cautioned to "drink only bottled beverages (including water) or beverages made with boiled water." And, for China, I would also have been warned not to pet that passing pup, because "rabid dogs present a problem."  . . . AND MORE HEALTH CAUTIONS Centers for Disease Control and Prevention http://www.cdc.gov/ This site is not for the sensitive or the hypochondriacal. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in Atlanta, is a subsidiary of the unitedstates Department of Health and Human Services, and the information is reliable and detailed. Calling up the C.D.C. site brings a menu of 10 sections. Skipping quickly over the morbidity and mortality weekly report and other nontravel sections, I selected "travelers' health." Here was reference material on International Travel, Geographic Health Recommendations and Disease Outbreaks. Geographic health recommendations brought up 16 regions; North America was not among them. So I went to Central Africa, for Chad. Although the countries are listed, you go to a general regional section, because, as the C.D.C. points out, "diseases are not restricted to cleanly defined geographical areas, i.e. mosquitoes can fly over city or country borders." The section is divided into diseases transmitted by insects, through food and water, through intimate contact with people and other diseases. Within each section are subsections for each disease (malaria, AIDS), with descriptions, risks and preventive measures.  SHOPPING FOR BOOKS Adventurous Traveler Bookstore http://www.AdventurousTraveler.com Enough caution. Let's have an adventure. The Adventurous Travel Bookstore, in Williston, Vt., has been selling books through the Web since January 1995, an amazingly early date. Three thousand books for hikers, kayakers and other hardy travelers are listed, as well as maps, CD-ROM's and screen savers. The site is easy to use, albeit slow. You can search for books a number of ways. I entered "Canada," and soon had a long list. Finding "Hiking in Quebec," I clicked and got a succinct, positive description of the book. I clicked on "order form," and one appeared. Enter a credit card number and the deal is done, or you can order by phone or fax. You can even order the paper catalogue on line, but why would you want to do that?   L.R. SHANNON

title:
MUTUAL FUNDS QUARTERLY REPORT;
Fund Investing on the Net: Beyond Window Shopping
body: MIX Internet hype with mutual-fund frenzy and what do you get? Junk mail -- lots and lots of junk mail. Fancy cyber junk mail, to be sure, posted on the World Wide Web by scads of mutual fund companies as well as entrepreneurs trying to tap into both crazes. But for the most part, the contents of these electronic Web pages have not differed much from the multicolored marketing materials that fund companies send through the (non-E) mail. So while there has been plenty for mutual fund investors to read on the Net, there has been very little for them to do -- until now. This summer, financial Web sites are blossoming with interactive activities ranging from the practical, like on-line trading, to the educational, like work sheets, to the amusing, like trading contests. And while "brochure-ware" remains the norm, technology gurus predict fund investors will increasingly be able to act on the Internet. Companies that sponsor Web sites "realize there has to be more than information; you have to be able to do something with it," said David E. Weisman, director for money and technology strategies at Forrester Research Inc. in Cambridge, Mass. Fund investors have long been active on the Net, first by trading information in news groups. But since 1994, fund companies have been jumping in. Many started by providing marketing material through Galt Technologies' Networth, a sort of virtual financial mall (http://www.galt.com). Today, more than 70 concerns post material through Networth, and some bigger companies that sell directly to the public -- including Fidelity Investments, Vanguard and T. Rowe Price -- now have elaborate Web sites (http://www.fid-inv.com; http://www.vanguard.com; http://www.troweprice.com). Downloading prospectuses used to be the most exciting Net activity, and it remains a popular feature at Networth, where investors retrieve several thousand a day, said Robert O. Frasca, a founder of Galt, which has been bought by Intuit, the financial software company. But Galt has steadily improved its interactive features, including a program to help users pick funds. Tracking funds' performance is also a hot activity on the Web, both at Networth and on individual companies' pages. And a new company, Fundscape, offers investors free software that allows them to track and analyze their fund investments (http:// www.fundscape.com). Tracking is one thing; trading, another. The biggest hurdle for Internet trading has been security, of both information and money. Until fund companies and brokerage firms are satisfied the problem has been solved, you may be able to move money around on the Net but you will probably not be able to cash out of your funds altogether. Investors have been able to trade stocks over the Internet for months, but setting up a service to do the same for mutual funds has proved more complicated, said Barry Boyte, vice president of Jack White & Company, the San Diego discount brokerage firm. The hurdles, he said, included different regulations, different settlement systems and quirks like multiple classes of shares in the same fund. Nevertheless, Jack White is now opening its mutual-fund trading service to new customers (http://pawws.com/jwc). (Though the firm began the service in March, it originally promoted fund trading only to a small group of existing clients.) The bad news, for Internet addicts, is that they must send paper copies of their account applications to the firm; Federal regulators require it. The good news is that Internet traders get a 10 percent discount on the commission White charges. And within a week or two, the Charles Schwab Corporation will also start trading funds on the Net through its e.Schwab service (http://www.eschwab.com). About 550 funds can be traded without a transaction fee; the costs of trading the 600 other funds carried by Schwab will be the same whether customers place orders electronically or by phone. Fidelity hopes to start a fund-trading service later this year. Fund companies that sell directly to investors are also trying to give their customers account information on line, and even to allow them to move money among funds. For example, T. Rowe Price already has such a system available over a modem and plans to move it to the Net once it is comfortable that investor information is secure. In the meantime, the big no-load sites are trying to "go interactive" by sponsoring work sheets, contests and quizzes. Scudder's new site, for example, has work sheets on asset allocation, retirement planning and tuition planning, while Vanguard offers a retirement calculator and a quiz intended to test your fund knowledge. Contests are popular with investors, and sometimes educational. For example, a group of chatters on the mutual funds bulletin board sponsored by Brill Editorial Services (http://www.brill.com) started a contest in May to see whose mock portfolio performs best over three months. The winner will get bragging rights, but most contests have more tangible prizes. Gabelli Funds is sponsoring a stock-picking contest (http://www.gabelli.com) whose winner will get shares in Gabelli Global Multimedia Trust. But to enter, users are asked to fill out a questionnaire, as are entrants in Fidelity's trivia and "Guess the Dow" contests. Which brings up an important point: these folks are not adding interactive features just for the fun of it. Sometimes the information you give the companies can be used to generate leads for their sales forces. And it turns out that, without some activity to engage in, Internet users seldom return to a Web site. (Who reads a promotional flyer more than once -- if that?) That fact lies behind what its sponsor hopes will be the splashiest new fund site on the Web: the Fantasy Funds Challenge. Beginning later this month, a tiny brokerage firm in Dallas called 1-800-Mutuals plans to sponsor a trading contest in which participants will create a hypothetical portfolio from a selected group of funds; after 10 months, the monthly winners from each state will compete for a $1 million jackpot. The brokerage firm hopes that the contest (on http://www.1800mutuals.com) will be so successful that funds will pay to be included on the select list, though so far it has been a hard sell, said Richard Sapio, president and founder of the firm. But he is confident that the contest will generate positive publicity for his company, which basically sells a wrap account. (It selects certain funds for you and charges you 1 percent a year on top of the funds' fees.) Mr. Sapio's contestants will, in fact, be betting on his firm's success: He plans to pay the jackpot in installments over 20 years from the cash he hopes his company will generate. Whether investors will still be as crazy about mutual funds or the Internet in two decades is anybody's guess.
