(Source: "Who is the Online Investor," Galt Technologies and the Center for Strategy Research)

title: Suits Accord By America Online Set
body: America Online Inc. will give away millions of hours of on-line time to some subscribers to settle a series of lawsuits, lawyers involved in the litigation said yesterday. The agreement is intended to settle 11 class-action suits against America Online on allegations of improper billing practices. Max W. Berger of newyork and other lawyers representing America Online customers said that the settlement had received preliminary approval by the Superior Court in San Francisco. Final approval, the lawyers said, is expected after America Online customers are notified and a public hearing is held in San Francisco. Customers of America Online between July 15, 1991, and March 31, 1996, may be eligible to receive some free on-line time or cash compensation. But, Mr. Berger said, it will be mainly heavy users of the service during that time who will benefit. Anyone using America Online for five hours or less pays the monthly minimum charge of $9.95. Only customers charged more than the minimum amount, Mr. Berger explained, qualify as members of the "overcharged" class. Industry analysts estimate that 60 percent of America Online's five million subscribers use the service for less than five hours a month. Under the settlement, all members of the affected class who are America Online subscribers when the free time is given out will receive one free hour of on-line time. In addition, subscribers who paid the company more than $300 during the time covered by the settlement will receive additional free time. Former subscribers who paid at least $300 in the settlement period will be eligible for cash compensation. But the total payout by America Online as part of the cash settlement process will not exceed $500,000. The litigation covered a number of practices by America Online. But the plaintiffs' lawyers said the core of their case was the practice of adding 15 seconds to customers' on-line time for the purposes of billing, and also rounding up to the next minute. For example, Mr. Berger said, 46 seconds of time spent connected to the service would be a minute and one second, after adding the 15 seconds. Then, he added, the minute and one second would be rounded up to two minutes. "A company can charge whatever it wants," Mr. Berger said. "But the heart of our case was that there was insufficient disclosure."

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Mirror in Two Deals To Bolster Legal Publisher
body: The Times Mirror Company said yesterday that it would trade its higher-education publishing division to the McGraw-Hill Companies in exchange for Shepard's, McGraw-Hill's influential legal research and annotation subsidiary. In addition, Times Mirror said it would form a venture with Reed Elsevier P.L.C., the British-Dutch company that owns the Lexis-Nexis electronic information retrieval service, to own and operate Shepard's. The deals are expected to make McGraw-Hill the world's largest educational publisher and to strengthen both Lexis-Nexis and Times Mirror's legal publishing unit in the face of increasingly tough competition. Times Mirror said in March that it was looking to sell its Higher Education Group, which the company's chairman, Mark H. Willes, asserted was not strong enough on a stand-alone basis to fit his goal of focusing on core Times Mirror businesses. The group publishes numerous prominent titles in business management and the hard sciences, fields in which McGraw-Hill sees rich prospects for growth in Eastern Europe and in developing nations. McGraw-Hill's divestiture of Shepard's took on added urgency with the completion last month of an acquisition by the Thomson Corporation of West Publishing, both heavyweights in legal publishing and citation services. This merger left Shepard's, despite its profitability and its prominence as a search tool, more exposed in a field now dominated by the Thomson-West combination and by the Lexis system. The Thomson-West merger "was like a Pavlovian gong to which we were all but compelled to respond," Joseph L. Dionne, the chairman and chief executive of McGraw-Hill, said yesterday. With its deal, Mr. Dionne said, McGraw-Hill was leaving a field in which it had become a small player to become the world's largest educational publisher. The Times Mirror Higher Education Group comprises five imprints: Richard D. Irwin, Wm. C. Brown, Brown & Benchmark, Irwin Professional Publishing and Mosby College, the nursing-program publisher. The trade included "additional undisclosed consideration," to be paid by Times Mirror, which Mr. Dionne said would include some cash but no stock. Shepard's, in Colorado Springs, reported earnings before taxes and interest of $40.7 million last year, on sales of $86.3 million. Times Mirror and Reed Elsevier said yesterday that they would form a 50-50 partnership to operate Shepard's in what is expected to be the first step in a broader alliance between Matthew Bender & Company, Times Mirror's legal-publishing unit, and Lexis-Nexis. The companies said this deal might involve yet another swap of assets or a straight purchase. "We need to see whether they have any properties they might put in," Mr. Willes said yesterday. "We don't need cash, they don't need cash, and since we are forming up this joint venture, we need to have a whole series of conversations with them." Mr. Willes said Times Mirror and Reed Elsevier hope to merge elements of each branch's strengths, such as publishing parts of the vast Lexis-Nexis library of full-text legal decisions and case law through Matthew Bender's CD-ROM publishing division. The value of the Shepard's partnership will have to be determined by an outside appraiser for tax purposes, Mr. Willes added. Each element of the three-way deal must pass antitrust scrutiny as well.

title:
Market Place;
The Growth, and Pain, of America Online
body: America Online, one of the big success stories in cyberspace, has certainly suffered some embarrassing setbacks lately. But are these growing pains or signs of a troubled company? Since early in May, the stock price of the on-line service has fallen nearly 40 percent. Insiders have been selling shares at a brisk pace. The Federal Trade Commission and several state attorneys general are investigating accusations that America Online Inc. is overcharging customers. Then, the company, based in Vienna, Va., told securities analysts late Monday that its new president and chief operating officer, William J. Razzouk, recruited just four months ago from the Federal Express Corporation, was leaving. The puzzling explanation for Mr. Razzouk's sudden resignation, supplied in a press release issued at 2 A.M. yesterday, was that "the prospect of relocating his family to the Washington, D.C., area was a significant factor in his decision." Mr. Razzouk could not be reached for comment yesterday. But presumably, Mr. Razzouk and his family understood that becoming president at America Online would entail a move from FedEx's base in Memphis when he took the job in February. In an interview yesterday, Steve Case, the 37-year-old chairman of America Online, insisted that Mr. Razzouk's resignation was not related to differences between the two men over the company's strategy or management practices. Yet while portraying the move as one mutually agreed upon, Mr. Case left little doubt that the decision was in good part his own. America Online, he says, is undergoing a critical transition. Next week, the company begins a policy of discount pricing for heavy users. And it is beginning an overhaul of the service -- with a new look, some new features and faster access to the World Wide Web -- that Mr. Case describes as a "relaunch of A.O.L." The upgraded service is available to the company's six million subscribers, and will be pushed hard in a marketing drive this fall. For these next few months, Mr. Case said he wanted to oversee the transition himself, acting as a chief operating officer, the position Mr. Razzouk briefly held. "The more I got involved, the more I realized I should be involved," he said. Of Mr. Razzouk's resignation, he explained, "It was a decision I had to make, and it was a decision he had to make." Few companies are the subject of such vigorous debate on Wall Street as America Online. It has, in essence, become the focus of a larger debate about how to blend marketing and fast-changing technology to build a consumer business in cyberspace. As such, its stock has attracted a larger crowd of short-sellers betting against it than any other issue on the Nasdaq market. It also has an enthusiastic following among securities analysts, underwriters and investors, who have benefited considerably from their America Online holdings: $1,000 invested in its shares in June 1994 would be worth $4,700 today. Yesterday, America Online shares closed at $42.50, up 37.5 cents -- a steep drop from $70 early in May. Skeptics question whether the company can maintain its subscriber and revenue growth as the Internet becomes easier to use and more on-line media are on the World Wide Web. Computer users, they say, will buy low-cost access to the Internet through AT&T and other companies and tap into the Web directly -- no longer needing America Online's comparatively costly service. Since about 90 percent of America Online's revenue comes from fees charged subscribers for time spent on line, the transition to the Internet poses a threat to its business. "Growth is starting to hit the wall for America Online," said Greg Wester, director of Internet research at the Yankee Group in Boston. "To keep growing, they are going to have to make entry into the on-line market a lot easier and less expensive." At present, the service charges subscribers $9.95 a month for up to five hours and $2.95 for each additional hour. Starting next week, it will give frequent users the cheaper alternative of paying $20 a month for up to 20 hours. This effort to hold onto its heavy users could trim America Online's revenue. Mr. Case says that those who believe the Internet will be America Online's death knell are technology purists who fail to grasp that most consumers still want on-line access and services provided by a single company. And the slowdown in new-subscriber marketing, he adds, is only a summertime pause before its upgraded service is ready in the fall. Company executives say it is cooperating with Government investigations into its billing practices and plans to settle a class-action suit on the issue within weeks. They say the insider sales of 1.6 million shares since last November, according to CDA/Investnet, which tracks insider filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, are somewhat higher than in the past but not an indication of a lack of confidence in the company's prospects. Mr. Case, who sold 500,000 shares since November, said he did so in part to help pay for a divorce settlement, but that 85 percent of his net worth was still in company stock and options. And he said America Online's recent setbacks could be put behind it fairly quickly. Within a year or 18 months, he expects the company to have 10 million subscribers. "All we can do now is stand up and deliver," Mr. Case said. Graphic   Graph: "A Cyberslump" shows daily stock closing prices for America Online from Jan. to June. (Source: Datastream)

title: Former Chief of Lotus Joins On-Line Venture With AT&T
body: After struggling unsuccessfully to produce new on-line information services aimed at businesses, AT&T said yesterday that it would turn the task over to Jim P. Manzi, the former chief executive of the Lotus Development Corporation. He had left that company last fall to join Industry.Net, which specializes in matching buyers and sellers of industrial equipment on the Internet. Mr. Manzi agreed to become chairman, president and chief executive of Nets Inc., a company formed by the combination of Industry.Net and the AT&T Corporation's New Media Services unit. AT&T will become a minority owner of the new company, which will be privately held, as Industry.Net now is. Both companies declined to provide financial details about the deal, but an AT&T spokesman said that AT&T would invest some cash in the company, which begins operation next Monday. Yesterday's announcement was the latest in a series of shifts in AT&T's on-line strategy. In January, the company announced that it was abandoning the proprietary service called Interchange, which it had bought from Ziff-Davis for a reported $50 million in 1994, to move to the World Wide Web, which has many more potential customers. Last week, it introduced the Web version of the AT&T Business Network, an on-line service for business people that had little success on Interchange. That service will continue as part of Nets Inc. AT&T is also trying to sell the Imagination Network, an on-line game service that has also proved a failure. It still has a unit called AT&T Personal Online Services, which is developing products for consumers. "AT&T is still looking for a way out of that mess," said Gary Arlen, president of Arlen Communications in Bethesda, Md., referring to its on-line efforts. "They keep stumbling around." But John Petrillo, AT&T's executive vice president of strategy and new service innovation, said that Interchange had actually cost less than $50 million and that the company's efforts had provided useful lessons, namely that the company does not want to be in the business of publishing original on-line information. "You won't find AT&T developing a content business for itself," he said.  "That is not our strength." Instead, the company has turned to Mr. Manzi, who left Lotus three months after it was bought by I.B.M. Mr. Manzi subsequently invested an undisclosed amount in Industry.Net, which is in Pittsburgh, and makes money by bringing together about 4,500 suppliers of industrial products with 200,000 prospective buyers. He was named president and chief executive of the company and set up an office near his home in Cambridge, Mass., where Nets Inc. will have its headquarters. Michael E. Kolowich, president of AT&T New Media Services, will join the company as vice president of business operations. He worked for Mr. Manzi at Lotus in the mid-1980's. Nets Inc. will be licensed to use the AT&T brand name and will establish a sales link with AT&T Worldnet Service, the company's fast-growing Internet access service.

title: Virtual University Will Offer Authentic Degrees by email
body: Without so much as a ritual shovel to break the ground or a granite slab to mark the spot, the governors of 10 Western states today laid an intangible cornerstone for a new "virtual university" that they promised would soon allow students to take courses by computer and earn degrees on line. At a meeting here, the governors pledged to raise the money and lower the bureaucratic barriers to the plan, which has been more than a year in the making. While details are still uncertain, the governors say the first students will be working in electronic classrooms next year. Although there are already many examples of students learning at long distances from their teachers and colleagues, ranging from courses taught by mail or on television to those using the Internet, the Western Governors' University is the most ambitious yet. The university would be an accredited regional institution, in the form of an independent nonprofit corporation, with power to grant certificates of proficiency that would be recognized by employers, course credits that would be recognized by traditional colleges and universities and full degrees. At first, credentials would be offered in a limited number of specialties, but they could eventually be earned across the full spectrum of disciplines and at every level of accomplishment. "This is not a replacement for the existing system of higher education," said Gov. Michael O. Leavitt of Utah, who, along with Gov. Roy Romer of Colorado, has led the effort. "It is a new element. It is a supplement. It is a way of creating new choices and new opportunities. But while this is not a replacement, it is an important part of a quality education for everyone. Because this is the way the world is going to work in the future." Terry Hartle, vice president of the American Council on Education, an association representing 1,800 colleges and universities, said the governors were being driven largely by a rising population and an expected boom in enrollment in their region, which they could not realistically hope to meet by adding to traditional colleges and universities. "Technology is already having a profound effect on all sorts of education," Mr. Hartle said. "The question is whether you can deliver quality higher education on a massive scale using existing technology. High quality higher education is hard enough to do when you have people on campuses and in classrooms. Whether or not you can do it successfully at distances and at a large scale we do not know. " The governors envision a university in which teachers and students will obtain reading materials not just from libraries, but also from databases; where term papers will be handed in by email, and where classes will meet in on-line collaborative sessions, perhaps using video and voice links as well as keyboards. The governors say the whole arrangement will not only spread opportunities across the region's vast distances, but will also make education cheaper. At the same time, the university would be integrated with traditional educational settings -- libraries, high schools, community colleges and state university systems, along with training programs in the private sector and even county agriculture extension agents. Neither the teachers nor the students would need to be in the Western states, but the agreement of so many states -- and of their education communities -- to support the project would add to its credibility, the governors say. The main questions center on whether an education obtained at a keyboard and a cathode ray tube can be as good as one earned amid the ivied halls, sporting fields, and laboratories of the traditional system. Other difficult questions are where the money will come from, whether the on-line university will compete for students and resources with traditional schools, and how a corps of teachers skilled in the new communications technologies can be recruited and trained. Another question is whether electronic learning will deliver education to the disadvantaged, or whether the differences between computer haves and have-nots will only widen an education gap when computer skills are a prerequisite for schooling. The governors' agreement called for each of the states to contribute $100,000 to continue the planning process. The full start-up costs have been estimated at $6 million to $10 million. Conspicuous by its lack of involvement is California, whose population, economy and university system dwarf those of the other Western states and which has not been as active as the others in the early planning. Among the existing models of nontraditional schools that suggest the direction the governors' university could take are the Maricopa Community Colleges, a consortium in Arizona that is about to offer an associate of arts degree entirely over the Internet. At a more experimental level, there are virtual-reality campuses on the Internet like Diversity University and Athena University, which are trying out novel educational programs of their own. But enthusiasts say that what is available now is just a rough prototype of what visionaries in the field say is coming. At a practical level, businesses are interested in employees with programming skills and the ability to run computer networks, subjects natural to learn on line. Several big computer companies are supporting the governors, as is Simon & Schuster, the big educational publisher. The planning documents for the venture are available on the World Wide Web, at: http://www.westgov.org/smart/ vu/vu.html.

title: When On-Line Service Cannot Be Counted On
body: Blame sunspots or planetary alignment, computer gremlins or human error. More than a million computer network users suffered interrupted or erratic Internet and on-line service connections last week because of a variety of planned and unplanned service shutdowns. Because of a single bad line in a computer program, Netcom On-Line Communications Inc. had to shut down its entire national system for 12 hours on Wednesday, affecting more than 400,000 Internet users, most of them businesses. The Microsoft Corporation shut down its entire network Sunday for as long as 10 hours as part of a long-scheduled upgrade of the system's backup power supply. But after US West, which was to install the system, said on Thursday that itwas not ready, Microsoft decided to use the scheduled shutdown to do additional system upgrades. The company will have to take its 1 million subscribers off line again in the fall. The electronic mail system of America Online, the largest on-line service with more than 6 million subscribers, was knocked out for an hour Wednesday afternoon when a planned system software upgrade backfired. Meanwhile, the AT&T Corporation, which entered the consumer Internet market earlier this year, announced that it would shut down its system for as long as 8 hours every week for maintenance, affecting more than 100,000 Internet customers. System failures and software bugs are hardly new for the Internet. But the scope of the problems and maintenance announcements last week surprised many observers, as well as the companies involved. "Can you imagine the outcry if AT&T took down the phone system for 8 hours a week?" said Dennis Moore, vice president of marketing at the Oracle Corporation, a software data base company that provides services to banks, stock exchanges and other customers who do not like technical surprises. Part of the strain on the systems comes from the constant surge of new Internet and on-line service users, thought to be at least 10,000 a day in the unitedstates alone. Part comes from the rapid pace of technological change in Internet hardware and software technologies. And part comes from the chaotic nature of the unregulated Internet itself. Unlike the telephone system, which has relatively few service providers and a technical infrastructure that has been tightly regulated for decades, the Internet has thousands of independent service providers, many of them in business only a few years. To compete, they change software and hardware frequently. Technical standards are in flux, whipsawed by the intense competition among companies like Microsoft, Netscape, Sun and Oracle. Whatever the causes, the conflict of rising consumer expectations and increasing system crashes are likely to cause a shift in the way Internet services are marketed. "In the next year, competition between providers is going to be based more on reliability than on price," said Tom Evslin, an AT&T vice president who heads AT&T Worldnet Services. "As users make the Internet a part of their daily lives and businesses, it will be very important that it be available and reliable all the time. Quality will be one of the key areas of the competition." Mr. Evslin said AT&T decided to announce the scheduled weekly shutdowns, which occur from 3 A.M. to 7 A.M. Eastern time on Tuesdays and Thursdays, as a way to insure reliable operations at all other times. He said the service does not always go down for the full eight hours, and he noted that as a result of the down time, the service has not had any unscheduled outages. AT&T's entry into the Internet service business rocked the industry. The telephone giant already has 90 million long-distance customers, and in promoting its Internet service, AT&T trumpeted its reputation of reliability in the phone business. A spokeswoman for America Online said overall system reliability has improved significantly since 1994, when hordes of new users overwhelmed the service's network capacity, causing widespread shutdowns and slowdowns. The company also has periodic scheduled shutdowns for system maintenance. Although Mr. Moore asserted that Oracle's own internal network of 23,000 users was 100 percent reliable, others suggested that fail-safe Internet service for most consumers may not soon be ready. Even installing new technologies to provide improved reliability and backup capacity is a nightmare for global Internet providers like Microsoft, 40 percent of whose users are in Europe and Asia. Taking the system down after midnight in Redmond, Wash., for example, will knock out users in London, Tokyo and Sydney. Sara Fitzgerald, a spokeswoman for the Interactive Services Association, whose members come from the telecommunications, on-line and Internet industries, said that rapid subscriber growth, technological upheaval, global network expansion and traditional storm-related summer power problems would likely continue to put stress on networks. "When computers and software and hardware are involved, these these things can happen," Ms. Fitzgerald said. "As the population of users grows to include people who are less technically oriented, there may be less understanding of the problems of keeping systems up. It will take time for everyone to learn more about what is reasonable and what is satisfactory." The programmer whose botched line of code caused hundreds of Netcom engineers to work all night tracing the bug is still employed. "He feels bad enough already," said David Garrison, president of Netcom in Santa Clara, Calif. "We are on the learning edge of this new technology, doing it on a scale never done before. Part of that is trying the best you can, but recognizing that there are going to be mistakes made."

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
West Publishing Purchase By Thomson Is Approved - Correction Appended
body:
The Justice Department gave conditional approval yesterday to the Thomson Corporation's $3.4 billion purchase of the West Publishing Company, but it insisted that Thomson sell 58 legal publications valued at about $275 million and license certain services to competitors. Without the divestitures, the Justice Department's antitrust division said, the acquisition would have stifled competition in several states for the lucrative business of on-line legal research. W. Michael Brown, the chief executive of Thomson, said his company accepted the provisions and summed up the process as "a fair but exhausting review." The antitrust review had been joined by seven states, including newyork, Connecticut and California. They had objected that a combination of Thomson and West, two of the biggest legal publishing powers, would reduce bidding for distribution of each state's legal records while raising costs to consumers. Though all legal records are public documents, states earn income by auctioning electronic versions of their court proceedings to publishers like Thomson and West, which then plug in electronic links to footnotes, page references and cross references for customers. The other states that took part in the settlement were Illinois, Massachusetts, Washington and Wisconsin. "This settlement is a victory for all of us," said Anne K. Bingaman, Assistant Attorney General for the Antitrust Division. "Competition in the legal publishing industry helps keep costs low, improves product quality and increases innovation." To carry out the agreement, the Justice Department will simultaneously file an antitrust suit against the proposed merger and a consent decree outlining the divestitures. The proceedings will take place in Federal District Court in Washington. The 58 publications to be sold are owned by West and were deemed to overlap with services already provided by Thomson. Most are devoted to state legal proceedings and include a legal citation program and several state and Federal research guides. Most of the publications exist only in electronic form. The consent decree allows California, Washington and Wisconsin to reopen bidding on state court reports now contracted to Thomson. Thomson also agreed to license West's proprietary page reference system, Star Pagination, to competing services. That is an important concession, because the system amounts to a kind of research language that law librarians and researchers have learned and that they are unlikely to voluntarily give up for a competing one. The services to be sold account for about 4 percent of West's legal publishing income and are within the range of concessions that Thomson expected to make, Mr. Brown said. Thomson, which is based in Toronto but also has a headquarters in Stamford, Conn., owns research services like the Lawyers Cooperative Publishing Company and Clark Boardman Callahan through a subsidiary, Thomson Legal Publishing. It had sales from legal research services of $368 million last year. West Publishing is a closely held company -- it has only 200 shareholders -- based in Eagan, Minn. It is best known for its Westlaw research service and had $700 million in revenue from legal-affairs publishing last year, according to the Justice Department. The approval of the purchase is a partial setback for Lexis-Nexis Inc., the legal and current-affairs research service owned by Reed Elsevier P.L.C. of London, which is a major competitor of Thomson's. But under the terms announced yesterday, Thomson agreed to extend for five years Lexis-Nexis's license to three nonlegal data bases owned by Thomson. Analysts praised Thomson for its acquisition of West when the purchase was announced in February, even though the transaction is mostly financed by debt, which will be a drag on Thomson's earnings for the next few years. Because each company brings strengths that the other lacks, however, analysts were confident that the venture would be profitable, and Mr. Brown has said that the cost of the purchase will be paid off in about a decade. The move is also Thomson's most expensive step so far away from its traditional role as a newspaper publisher, a shaky business these days, and toward the more dependable cash flows of electronic research publishing. Thomson has sold numerous small newspapers in recent years, and today it derives a declining portion of its revenue from printed publications. The company, whose revenue was $7.25 billion in 1995, operates primarily in the unitedstates, Britain and Canada. Jamie Love of the Center for Study of Responsive Law, an organization founded by Ralph Nader, said the proposed settlement was a good one. "The Justice Department's agreement is not a trivial accomplishment," he said. "It really preserves competition in the market." The article also misidentified the publications' medium. They are on CD-ROM's and in books, not in electronic form only. Correction  An article on the Media Business page on June 20 about a conditional approval of the Thomson Corporation's purchase of the West Publishing Company misstated the ownership of 58 legal publications that the Justice Department has required to be sold. Thirty-six of the publications are owned by Thomson; not all 58 are owned by West.
Correction-Date: July 13, 1996, Saturday

title:
TAKING IN THE SITES;
The ABC's of Buying Foreign Stocks
body: Despite the incessant talk of a global economy, individuals who want to invest overseas might find that foreign stock exchanges seem very far away indeed. While it has always been easy for American investors to act on a hunch that the Boeing Company stock was going to go into the stratosphere, trying to do the same with a company like British Aerospace P.L.C. has proven to be both difficult and expensive. The only affordable options usually were either to buy foreign companies that list their shares on American exchanges or entrust American mutual funds to do the international stock-picking. By and large that remains true. Costs are too high and regulations too complex for most individuals to invest directly in foreign stocks. But now, thanks to the World Wide Web, this is beginning to change. Want to buy shares of Whitbread P.L.C., British Aerospace or Scottish Hydroelectric? The Electronic Share Information Ltd.'s Web site now lets customers to trade those shares directly over the Internet, just like many electronic brokerages do with American stocks. There is also more information available for free, as foreign exchanges try to attract global investors and overseas brokers seek to lure potential clients. Electronic Share Information, which is based in Cambridge, England, is one of many sites to offer free stock quotes. Most of the free quotes are between 15 and 60 minutes old, however -- real-time quotes generally cost money. Companies also charge for flashier features, such as the Electronic Share Information's ability to provide automatic electronic-mail notification if a certain stock's price rises or falls by some set amount. (The full-feature package costs about $30 a month.) While on-line trading has started to catch on in the larger, mainly European equity markets, investors seeking to put their money elsewhere must continue to follow the traditional route of buying the American-listed shares of foreign companies or investing in mutual funds. The bulk of international stock-related Web sites are still limited to simply providing information on either stock exchanges or individual companies. One of the better offerings is the Asiaone site, which provides information on the Singapore and Kuala Lumpur stock exchanges. The site gives users stock quotes and can be customized so that investors can quickly check up on the stocks in their portfolios, much like the fancier American sites, and all for free. For developing economies especially, the Internet holds the promise of attracting extra capital by reducing the hassle and lack of information that typically make investors shun these stocks. But for now, the sites are mainly sources of information, which itself can be a valuable commodity. Unfortunately, most stock exchange home pages, especially the smaller ones, are reminiscent of the soporific sites many American corporations have put up on the Web: lots of promotion, not much practical information. Another shortcoming of almost all foreign stock-exchange sites is the dearth of information about specific regulations and tax laws that govern foreign purchases of stock. Certain countries still have limits on what industries foreigners can invest in and how quickly dividends and capital gains can be repatriated. And finally, there is little discussion of currency risk, one of the biggest threats facing investors overseas. Finding specific stock exchange home pages is fairly simple using the standard Internet search engines. Alternatively, there are a number of indexes of stock exchange home pages and, to a lesser degree, companies that offer stock-related data and services. Three of the best are Yahoo, The Syndicate and the International Internet Business List. title: Identity Crisis: When a Criminal's Got Your Number
body: THE first that Verna Willis knew about her new Macy's charge account was when the dunning notices started arriving. Someone pretending to be Ms. Willis, a nurse in Brooklyn, had opened the account in her name and was charging up a storm on one of her Visa cards as well. The problems started when Ms. Willis lost her pocketbook, which contained, of course, a wealth of personal information, including her hospital I.D. card with her Social Security number. Even though she canceled the Visa account right away, someone was able to get hold of the replacement card and activate it using information about her.    Feeling Helpless "It's making me go crazy," she said, "because I feel so completely helpless." More and more people have that helpless feeling when they discover that a criminal has assumed their identity; what is often called "true identity fraud" is among the fastest-growing types of financial crime. It often begins with a stolen Social Security number. This, the closest thing to a universal identifier that Americans have, is used by banks and other companies as a method of identification, even though the numbers are widely available from public sources. It can be used to unearth other, even more private tidbits, which are also stored and traded among myriad computer databases. The vast Lexis-Nexis on-line information service recently offered a "locater" service that allowed users to look up a person's Social Security number and mother's maiden name. Lexis-Nexis canceled the service last week after a wave of complaints, but similar services continue to sell personal information over the Internet. Such trade in information is legal, and regulation of it difficult, perhaps even more so since a Federal appeals court ruling last week struck down restrictions and defended the "chaos and cacophony of the unfettered speech" on the new medium. The information can be stolen, too -- sometimes by hackers but more often, experts say, by people with legitimate access to personal data. In one alarming example, Federal prosecutors charged a caseworker at the newyork City Human Resources Administration with persuading 10 people in the Social Security Administration to give him personal information from the files of 11,000 people. This was used to activate credit cards stolen from themail and to open accounts in the victims' names. And if the Social Security Administration is vulnerable, despite its rigorous security measures, then creditors and hospitals and retailers -- even, say, the video store that keeps customers' credit card numbers -- are surely permeable. Social Security numbers themselves create a special vulnerability. Many companies, ranging from credit card issuers to MCI's 800-music-now record sales service, use Social Security numbers as if they were secret passwords, to enable financial transactions.    Chances for Mischief Yet Social Security numbers are hardly secret. They are on many college and employee I.D. cards, hospital tags and even driver's licenses in more than 30 states. This brings myriad opportunities for mischief: * A Texas woman was charged with receiving tax refunds by filing for returns with Social Security numbers taken from publicly available death certificates. * One David Campbell, in Watsontown, Pa., has been charged with running up $30,000 in debt by pretending to be another David Campbell, from nearby Williamsport, who happened to be born on the same day, by using the victim's Social Security number. * A gang in Los Angeles used stolen Social Security numbers to pass the credit check needed to rent apartments used as mail drops in a forged-check scheme. Still, Congress is considering bills to set up several wide-ranging new computer databases tied to Social Security numbers. One, the immigration bill, would authorize a test of a telephone system to verify new employees' legal working status. The welfare reform bill would use them to locate parents who are behind on child support. Social Security numbers were first issued, in 1935, simply to track earnings and pension benefits. Since this is the only system that assigns a unique number to nearly every legal resident in the country, it was immediately attractive for both business and government record-keeping. Congress first allowed the Internal Revenue Service to use the numbers to track income and tax payments in 1962. Next came welfare programs, military I.D. cards and immigration papers. Each time, the Social Security Administration said it isn't suited to run a comprehensive identification system. Still, Americans do need to prove they are who they say they are in order to do business or claim government benefits. Rather than a government identity number, some say the private sector can play a role. Hugh Gibbons, a professor at the Franklin Pierce Law Center in Concord, N.H., has proposed creating a class of super-charged notaries called oath helpers to identify people.  And America Online plans to issue "digital signatures" for use in purchasing on the Internet. Emerging technology offers other potential solutions. Credit card fraud has fallen sharply in France since the cards were embedded with microchips that store the customer's personal identification number. And the dream of many security experts is using biometrics, technology that can identify people from some unique physical trait. Already, California and newyork are using electronic fingerprint scans to catch people who apply for welfare under several names. Walt Disney World scans the hands of its season pass holders. And a Princeton company called Sensar is building an automated teller machine that scans the user's iris rather than using a card. Yet until these high-tech systems are in place, and their Orwellian implications are dealt with, more people will find, as Verna Willis did, that someone else is running around pretending to be them.  Keeping Identity Thieves at Bay IDENTITY fraud can be as exasperating as it is disturbing, often requiring days of letter writing and phone calls to disentangle an impostor's acts from your own. Still, in most cases you won't be held accountable for fraudulent transactions. Federal law limits the liability of credit-card holders to $50 for unauthorized purchases, and most banks don't even impose that charge. With automated teller machine cards, the limit is $500, and with checks the law is less clear on consumer protection. Many victims of identity fraud say law-enforcement officials consider their cases too minor for much attention, and there are few other resources to turn to for help. There is also distressingly little a person can do to keep from being victimized by such crimes. There are simply too many sources of personal information that can be used by criminals -- from public records to lost wallets to files kept by hospitals and employers. And there are too many ways for criminals to take advantage of this knowledge. But there are several steps you can take to keep identity thieves at bay and make sure your numbers stay as private as possible: Keep an eye out for missing mail. One of the most common criminal tactics is to file a change of address form with the post office for an unsuspecting victim. That way it will take longer to discover fraudulent credit-card charges or illicitly opened new accounts. Check your credit file every year or two to make sure no one is borrowing money in your name. TRW, one of the big three credit-reporting bureaus, will give you one copy of your report free each year (call 1-800-682-7654 for information). The others -- Equifax (1-800-685-1111) and Trans Union (1-800-916-8800) -- charge $8 for each report. Reveal as little personal information as necessary. Federal and local government agencies are authorized to demand your Social Security number, for example, for tax returns, benefit programs and drivers' licenses, among other things. But a few states that put Social Security numbers on drivers' licenses give residents the option of using different numbers. Some colleges that use Social Security numbers on identification cards also allow students to ask for different numbers. Consumers are not legally required to reveal their Social Security numbers to private organizations, but a company can refuse to do business with anyone who doesn't provide the information it wants. Thus, one must trust a bank with all sorts of private information in order to get a loan, but it may not be worth giving the same data to a video rental store.   SAUL HANSELL

title: Freewheeling Net Meets Free Market
body: LAST year was the year when nearly a thousand newspapers, magazines and new-media start-ups rushed to the Internet. This year, as the bills pile up, the same gang is puzzling over how to get these electronic ventures to pay their own way. So far, they are going about it with the old-fashioned methods, trying to lure advertisers and subscribers. The Wall Street Journal, The newyork Times and Time Warner have announced plans to charge for some or all of their Internet offerings starting this summer. It is not surprising that Internet publishing, a field open to giant media conglomerates and small entrepreneurs alike, is becoming more commercial. But it does sharply contradict the predictions of many technology mavens. Just a year or so ago, they said the Internet, with its academic roots, was a distinctive culture -- freewheeling, democratic and deeply anti-commercial. Advertising anathema to the Internet ethos, they said, and people would never pay for online material. None of the old commercial rules was supposed to apply. Guess again.    The Tricks of the Trade Now that the Internet's World Wide Web -- a multimedia blend of text, graphics, video and audio -- has become more accessible, it has become more commercial. And online publishers are trying all the tricks in the book -- from free trial periods to pay-per-view services -- to make a buck, or at least break even. At the start of 1995, there were only 100 newspapers online, but now there are 1,100, according to statistics compiled by Editor & Publisher and Planetary News, a consultancy specializing in electronic publishing. But "only the strongest are going to survive," said Steve Outing, president of Planetary News in Boulder, Colo. To make Internet publishing profitable the advertising market will have to take off. Last year, when advertising on Web sites was new, it totalled $43 million. That compares with $32 billion in television advertising, $22.5 billion in newspapers and magazines, $1.9 billion for radio. Predictions are that advertising will pick up and that sooner or later there will be a shakeout, as many publishers learn that they cannot attract enough advertising to support their Web sites. But advertising is only part of it. Electronic publishers are also angling to make readers pay for the information they use. That option becomes more realistic as programmers develop encryption to protect credit card transactions on the Internet. So far, the few online publishers who are charging readers, or plan to, are electronic-media units of respected magazines and newspapers or new ventures focusing on special-interest subjects like sports or politics. For instance, ESPNET Sportszone, a sports Web site jointly created by ESPN and the Starwave Corporation, has persuaded thousands of subscribers to part with $4.95 a month. ESPNET Sportzone is using the most common approach to coax money from readers. It is relying on a variation of the cable television model -- to have free-viewing areas and then to offer premium features that cost money. For newspapers online, a premium service might be a news report, sent daily by email, tailored to a subscriber's subject preferences. This summer, for instance, The newyork Times and Time Warner intend to offer personalized electronic reports, following the lead of The San Jose Mercury News's Newshound service. Another premium Internet service planned by major newspapers is electronic access to their archive of articles, charging a dollar or two per article. But a couple of online publications are going further. They let the customers try the product until they are hooked, and then charge them. One such publication is The Wall Street Journal's Interactive Edition. After an initial sampling period, which ends Aug. 31, the online Journal will cost $49 a year, or $29 for subscribers to the paper's print edition. Microsoft's Slate, the publication headed by Michael Kinsley, The New Republic's former editor, is using a similar technique. It is scheduled to begin publication in the next few weeks. There will be a sample period of a month or so, then a subscription fee.    Deep Pockets, Deep Hopes Microsoft clearly has not only deep pockets but also deep hopes. Inside Building No. 25 on Microsoft's corporate campus in Redmond, Wash., the news room for the Microsoft Network, its Web-based service, is bustling with newly hired editors and reporters. Microsoft is betting that it can outlast most of its competitors. "The investment issue is who blinks when, as new media evolves to become a business," said Laura Jennings, vice president of the Microsoft Network. Online publishers know they need a good lure. For some, that means putting out something readers can't get elsewhere, for others it means putting out some freebies. "With so may new people coming onto the Internet all the time, we think you have to offer a lot of content for free, letting people wander onto your front porch and then charge them if they want to get into the house," explained Rich LeFurgy, Starwave's vice president of advertising and product marketing. What is at stake is the growing on-line audience. Last year there were 8.4 million American households online. That number is expected to increase to 35 million by the year 2000, estimates Jupiter Communications, a research firm in newyork. Not all publications will thrive. Forecasts of future riches are little comfort, for instance, to Dale Dougherty, publisher of Web Review, a respected weekly Web magazine dealing with Internet culture and technology. It had a full-time staff of 12 people and advertising revenues of $10,000 a month -- a pittance compared to its costs. So last month, Mr. Dougherty warned readers that Web Review would shut down unless 5,000 people would pay $19.95 for a six-month subscription. To date, only 1,000 readers have said they would be willing to pay that much. "If the rules of the media game on the Web are that you have to spend a lot of money and not get much back," Mr. Dougherty said, "then this isn't much of a business yet."

title: Voluntary Rules Are Proposed For the Privacy of Internet Users
body: The on-line and direct marketing industries today proposed voluntary guidelines intended to protect Internet users against unauthorized collection of personal information. But the proposal, made at a Federal Trade Commission hearing on personal privacy in the information age, drew fire from civil liberties groups and others concerned over privacy issues. They argued that self-policing by the industry would not restrain on-line abuses that they said already range from surreptitious monitoring of activities on the Internet to the illegal sale of personal credit histories over the Internet. Critics said a rapidly evolving technology and abuses by those preying on unsuspecting Internet users would soon lead to calls for Government regulation of individual privacy on the Internet. "Today business is saying that they are opting for voluntary compliance," Robert Ellis Smith, editor of The Privacy Journal. "Five years from now they will be back here begging for regulation." The Interactive Services Association, which represents large on-line information services, and the Direct Marketing Association proposed draft guidelines they said would limit unsolicited marketing and electronic mail. The guidelines also cover marketing to children over interactive electronic services. "Self-regulation does work," said Robert Sherman, general counsel for the Direct Marketing Association. Yet he also acknowledged that no protection system would be perfect. "Law enforcement is not perfect, and there will always be bad actors," he said. Under the proposed guidelines put forward today, the two trade associations said that on-line solicitations to news groups, bulletin boards and chat rooms should conform with the stated policies of such forums. They also said that on-line solicitations should be clearly identified and should disclose the identity of marketers. The guidelines also said the marketing industries should give consumers a method to opt out if they did not want to receive the solicitations. Several public policy representatives said they hoped the marketplace would provide solutions to some of the privacy issues, foreseeing a time when Internet service providers would compete to offer customers privacy features. "We want a healthy competition where AT&T and MCI battle over who will protect our privacy best," said Alan Westin, a legal scholar who is an expert on privacy issues.

title: Pacific Telesis Will Offer Internet Services
body: The Pacific Telesis Group became the first regional Bell company to offer Internet services to its telephone customers yesterday, aiming for the California market in which an estimated half of the nation's Internet users live. "The phones are, as they say, ringing off the hook," said Mark W. Fisher, vice president of marketing for Pacific Bell Internet Services, the Pacific Telesis subsidiary that was formed last July to tap into California's large population of Internet users. According to market surveys, some 11 percent of all households in the state are connected to some sort of on-line service. But that means that California is also home to the country's largest concentration of on-line service providers, and Pacific Bell's competition is expected to be formidable. "The regional Bells have not developed the muscles that allow them to play in this highly fragmented environment," said Nick Donatiello, president of Odyssey L.P., a market research company in San Francisco. Mr. Donatiello said that while Pacific Bell had a potentially large opportunity to add new sources of revenue from on-line services, it was also exposing itself to substantial risk by competing in a complex new industry against a wide array of older, more established companies. In addition to such large providers as Netcom On-Line Communications Inc. of San Jose, Calif., which already has more than 400,000 customers, Pacific Bell will also have to compete with commercial on-line information services like America Online and H & R Block's Compuserve, with the Microsoft Network, with dozens of smaller Internet companies, with cable television companies, and with MCI Communications, Sprint and AT&T. Still, investors also apparently consider the Pacific Telesis Pacific Bell unit a formidable new competitor to Netcom, whose shares plunged on yesterday's news. Netcom's stock ended the day at $35.25, down $4.25 in Nasdaq trading. Shares of Pacific Telesis edged down 12.5 cents to close at $33.875 on the newyork Stock Exchange. AT&T, with 90 million long-distance customers, loudly proclaimed its intent to dominate the industry when it announced its Internet service in February. But AT&T was clearly unprepared for the task, and has been able to offer service to only about 25 percent of the 600,000 people who have signed up. Like AT&T before it, Pacific Bell announced a partnership with America Online that would give its customers reduced-rate access to the world's largest on-line information service. America Online's stock was buoyed by yesterday's announcement, rising $2.75 a share to close at $54 in Nasdaq trading. Also like AT&T, Pacific Bell promised yesterday to deliver low-cost, high-speed Internet access without busy signals or other service problems. But Pacific Bell is seeking to weed out the many computer novices who were lured by AT&T's offer of five hours of free Internet access a month -- users who then clogged AT&T's technical support lines with basic computer questions that AT&T was unprepared to answer. AT&T customers who take the option of five free hours are charged hourly rates thereafter, or they can opt for a monthly charge of $19.95 for unlimited Internet usage. Pacific Bell set its prices to attract the most active, and presumably most experienced, Internet users. Pacific Bell is offering a plan of $14.95 a month for 20 hours of Internet access, with additional hours costing 50 cents each up to a total maximum monthly bill of $19.95. The base price for service is $9.95 a month for 10 hours. Mr. Fisher said said all customers who called requesting service would be sent the necessary computer diskettes immediately.

title: Move to the Web Is in the Works For Compuserve
body: Deciding to flow with the relentless tide of the Internet rather than fight it, Compuserve Inc. is expected to announce today that it is rebuilding its entire on-line service on the standards of the World Wide Web, people briefed by the company said yesterday. Compuserve's decision to embrace the open standards of the Web follows similar moves by the Prodigy Services Company, the Microsoft Network and AT&T's Interchange Online Network, all of which started as closed, proprietary services. But Compuserve, the world's second-largest consumer on-line service, with more than four million subscribers worldwide, is by far the largest network to acknowledge that it cannot compete against the rapidly growing Web. "This leaves America Online as the last bastion of the proprietary world," said Gregory Wester, research director for the Yankee Group of Boston. "But even A.O.L. will back away from its proprietary software at some point. It's just a matter of time." American Online Inc., the No. 1 service, in the past expressed confidence that its proprietary model would continue to be attractive. At the same time, the company has become one of the largest Internet service providers, offering its six million customers access to the World Wide Web. "Over time, all on-line services will become Internet services," said Mary Modahl, a senior analyst with Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. "We expect A.O.L. to be last because they have the strongest position in the flood, and they'll hold out longer." Compuserve, a unit of H & R Block, was the first on-line service to use the proprietary software model, which requires subscribers to use special software and network access points provided by the service. It also requires that information providers use custom software tools to prepare information to be displayed on the network. According to people briefed by Compuserve in advance of today's announcement, Compuserve has begun rewriting its existing services in the hypertext markup language, H.T.M.L., the industry standard of the World Wide Web. Allen Weiner, an analyst with Dataquest in San Jose, Calif., said the H.T.M.L. model was attractive to information publishers because it allowed them potentially to reach millions of customers without having to write a different version of the same material for each on-line service. "In the past, content developers were forced to decide whether to develop for the Compuserve standard, for example, or for the World Wide Web standard, and now there's just one," Mr. Weiner said. The Web is also appealing to subscribers because it offers more advanced features than any proprietary on-line service can provide. Hundreds of companies worldwide are developing such Web-based features as audio, video, interactive chat sessions, multiplayer games and secure electronic commerce. Compuserve will continue to support existing versions of the DOS, Windows and Macintosh software used to gain access to the Compuserve Information Service and Wow on-line businesses, the people briefed by the company said. But beginning this summer, the company will distribute new software that more fully integrates access to the World Wide Web. Compuserve declined to comment on its plans.

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
CYBERSCOUT
body: OLYMPICS ON LINE  Atlanta Games http://www.atlantagames.com People planning to go to Atlanta for the Summer Games can dip into Atlanta Games for timely information about sports and cultural events and information about the city. Even those not planning to attend will find much of interest in this Web site, a product of the Interactive Studio at The Atlanta Journal-Constitution. There are pages on the games themselves, and on housing, Atlanta in particular and the South in general, food, transportation, night life and "Hey Atlanta," where "pen" pals are available. Selecting the night life category, I was asked to type in a key word. I typed "jazz," and in a moment had a list of 18 places. I selected Bourbon Street Cabaret and was presented with a short paragraph of information about the establishment -- its address and phone number, the days and hours at which a group was playing and a "no cover" note. The Interactive Studio has a staff of 35 preparing the information. When the games begin in July, the Web site will draw on the reporting of some 300 journalists covering the events for The Atlanta Journal-Constitution and other Cox newspapers.  ONE-STOP SHOPPING  Travelocity http://www.travelocity.com Travelocity, on the World Wide Web, bills itself as a "one-stop travel site," and to a large extent it succeeds, although it is so big, perhaps the largest of the newer such sites, that you will never explore it all. Its 200,000 pages combine the data bases of Sabre Interactive, the owner of the Sabre computer network, which provides travel agents with schedules, reservations capability and other information for airlines, hotels and auto rental companies, and that of Worldview Systems Corporation, a publisher of interactive and on-line destination information. Here, you will find Travel Reservations, a section of airline schedules, availability information and fares, with the ability to make reservations and buy tickets on line; Destinations and Interests, a guide to thousands of places around the world; Chats and Forums, where you can "talk" to experts and fellow travelers, and Merchandise, where such travel-related items as luggage and videos can be purchased by credit card. Of course, it takes time at the computer to arrange for time away from it. Like most Web sites, Travelocity leads users through many steps to get to the information they want. For instance, to get the names, addresses and phone and fax numbers of three hotels in Samos, Greece -- and that was all the information there was on those establishments -- I went through the following steps: First, I selected the Places to Go icon, which divides the world into 10 regions. One region, Europe, offered a list of 39 countries or regions, from Andorra to Wales, with the number of entries in each country in parentheses after the name. I picked Greece, with 646 entries, then chose Samos from a huge list of Greek destinations. That led to Lodging, and on to Hotels, also with three entries (there are many B & B's on the island, none of which are listed). For the three -- Aegeon Hotel, Astra Apartments, Doryssa Bay Hotel -- clicking on the Astra brought up the address and phone and fax numbers. Travelocity can certainly replace a travel agent, but only for people who are willing to navigate its vast spaces on their own.  DIRECTIONS  Route 66 Available from Route 66 Inc., (408) 446-0660 You don't have to go on line to figure out which way to aim your wheels for a vacation or business trip. Route 66 will plan your route, by car or bicycle, on a Windows or Macintosh computer. The program calculates the shortest, quickest or least expensive route from one place to another and shows the results in a description that can be viewed on screen, printed out or both. Printouts will be of most use for a driving trip, but some people may prefer to put the program on a portable computer they take with them in case they need to work out an alternative route. Speed, fuel prices and fuel consumption can also be entered and the description will take account of them. There are five menus (with a bunch of submenus) and 15 icons across the top of the screen. I managed to find the New Route capability within the Itinerary menus. I selected the fastest route by car from the New Jersey town I live in to Quebec City, a trip I plan to make this summer. A detailed itinerary appeared, divided under the headings Location, Indication, Direction, Time, Distance and Cost. For instance, after driving west northwest on State Highway 208 for 11 miles, I was instructed to turn onto U.S. 202 at Oakland, N.J., and head northeast. The suggested route was certainly a reasonable one, although it might differ in small details from one you worked out yourself. I had to scroll down the screen five times to read the entire set of directions. The map is too small and lacking in detail to be of much use, although if you don't know that both New Jersey and Quebec are in the Northeast it may be of some help. The basic Route 66 program, covering North America, costs $79.95, from Route 66 Inc., 7216 Coronado Drive, San Jose, Calif. 95129; (408) 446-0660, fax (408) 446-2342.  There are also 10 supplementary disks, which require the basic program, covering Europe, for $35 each.   L. R. SHANNON

title: New Nintendo Game Faces Internet Challengers
body: Nintendo of America, the longtime leader in the video-game market, gave its first unitedstates preview today of its flashy next-generation game machine, which it is hoping will revitalize the slowing video game industry this Christmas. But the new Nintendo machine, which will be more than a year behind schedule when it reaches the market in September, may be arriving at a time when much of the action is heading away from stand-alone video devices and toward PC games played by groups of contestants over computer networks. Nintendo made its announcement here the day before the opening of the digital entertainment industry's trade show, where the pervasive impact of the Internet is expected to draw most of the attention. A race is underway to develop "cyberspace arenas" enabling personal computer users to play multiplayer games over the Internet. The digital entertainment industry is hoping that by breaking down the boundaries of computer gaming and making it possible for people separated by thousands of miles to compete in activities ranging from flight simulators to sports like football and baseball, they will find a way to move the Internet beyond a medium for information retrieval and electronic mail. "If we build it they will come," said Kristen Asleson, vice president of marketing for Mpath Interactive, one of two heavily financed start-up companies now preparing to deploy services as early as this summer that will permit thousands or even millions of computer users to electronically locate opponents in a variety of games including some of the currently most popular computer games such as Command and Control and Warpath II. Stand-alone machines like Nintendo's new 64-bit player, which process information 64 bits at a time (compared with 16 bits for current Nintendo devices), can offer speed and performance that most network-PC games cannot yet approach. But faster computers, and network improvements, are expected eventually to close that gap. And many industry analysts contend that the social dynamics of multiplayer gaming, in which each personal computer user sits at his or her machine and is connected via modem to the Internet, will make such games preferable to one or two players sitting in front of a single television set playing Nintendo, Sega or other conventional video games. Moreover, the most enthusiastic analysts predict that multiplayer gaming will be the application that finally transforms the Internet into a major entertainment medium rivaling television and cinema. Companies like Mpath Interactive, based in Cupertino, Calif., and its most direct competitor, the San Francisco-based Total Entertainment Network, or Ten, have developed special server computers intended to insure adequate speed and performance for games played on the Internet. Both companies are now in final testing and will begin commercial operation of their on-line game services during the summer. Both Ten and Mpath have struck partnerships with Internet service providers and are hoping to build businesses that are based both on consumer and advertising revenue. "The people who are investing money in building the Internet have realized that gaming is a critical application," said Jack Heistand, chief executive officer of Ten. He said that the company will have invested more than $17 million when it starts operation later this year. Mr. Heistand said that in the testing phase of the Ten service it was easy to see how game playing is already competing directly with television viewing in the evenings. He said his computer operators could see use fall off when popular television series like "E.R." and "Seinfeld" were broadcast. But immediately afterward, users reconnected to the game service, Mr. Heistand said. In addition to Ten and Mpath, America Online is preparing to introduce its own multiplayer gaming service. The America Online game is based on a flight simulator game called Air Warrior, which had previously been available only on the low-membership Genie on-line service that General Electric sold earlier this year. In light of such activity, Howard Lincoln, chief executive of Nintendo of America, acknowledged today that his company was preparing to respond to the growing impact of the Internet. "Like everyone else in the Industry we have an Internet strategy, but we can't say what it will be yet," he said today. Nintendo's principal competitor, Sega of America, earlier this year said it was refocusing its strategy by setting up a new Silicon Valley based company to develop games for personal computers and the Internet. Among those trying out the game yesterday were Isaac Marshall, left, and Henry Sterchi. (Associated Press)

title:
COMPANY REPORTS;
America Online Profits Up But Stock Falls 10 Percent
body: America Online Inc. announced yesterday a continued surge in revenues, a rise in membership to nearly six million subscribers, and a new partnership to expand the on-line service into Japan. But even though America Online's third-quarter earnings exceeded Wall Street's expectations, investors drove down the company's stock by 10 percent in what analysts said was a combination of profit taking and concerns over a new pricing plan for the service's heaviest users. The new pricing option, 20 hours of connection time a month for $19.95, would represent lower prices for the relatively few customers who log on for more than 9 hours a month. Consumers can also choose the current pricing plan, $9.95 a month for five hours on line, with additional hours priced at $2.95 each. "Any time you change the pricing model, it creates a level of uncertainty and makes people nervous, especially after the run this stock has had over the past few months," said Jamie Kiggen, a managing director at Bear, Stearns in newyork. "I think we're just seeing some profit taking. The company is still demonstrating enormous momentum." The shares fell $7.25 yesterday, to $62.75, in Nasdaq trading. In the latest quarter, which ended March 31, America Online had net income of $15.127 million, or 14 cents a share, compared with a net loss of $3.296 million, or 5 cents a share, a year ago. Wall Street had expected earnings of 13 cents a share, according to a survey of analysts by the First Call Corporation. The latest figures included a special charge of $850,000 for the company's acquisition of Johnson-Grace Inc. in January, and good will amortization costs of $1.85 million, which reduced earnings a penny a share. America Online added an average of more than 300,000 new users a month during the quarter, widening its lead as the largest on-line service. The company, based in Vienna, Va., said revenues grew 186 percent, to $312.3 million, compared with $109.1 million in the corresponding quarter a year earlier. The company had revenues of $225 million in the three months ended Dec. 31, 1995, its previous high. America Online's growth was in sharp contrast to the plight of the Prodigy Services Company, which is being sold by its joint owners, Sears, Roebuck & Co. and International Business Machines. A management group led by Prodigy's president, Edward Bennett, is expected to buy the company in the next week for a price thought to be between $100 million and $250 million. That price is far below the estimated $600 million each that I.B.M. and Sears have invested. The identity of Mr. Bennett's financial backers remained unknown, although sources in the company said the partners did not include any telephone companies. Prodigy officials in White Plains declined to comment. Once one of the leaders in the on-line industry, and the first major service to embrace the Internet, Prodigy has been losing money and subscribers even while its rivals are surging. Prodigy, which used to report having more than two million users, is now believed to have about a million customers, making it fourth in the industry behind America Online, H & R Block's Compuserve Inc., and the Microsoft Corporation's Microsoft Network. "Prodigy is still stumbling around," Stephen M. Case, the America Online chief executive, said in a telephone conference call from Japan, where he announced a new joint venture called AOL Japan. America Online's partners in the Japanese venture are Mitsui & Company Ltd., an international trading company that will own 40 percent of AOL Japan, and Nihon Keizai Shimbun Inc., Japan's largest financial news publisher, which has a 10 percent stake. Mitsui also said it would buy a stake in America Online worth 3 billion yen, or $28 million. While American Online plans a push in the Japanese and European markets in the coming year, Mr. Case said it would be less aggressive in recruiting new members in the unitedstates. The summer months are traditionally a slow period for on-line services, he said, and the company will use the period to test new network capacity, to expand customer service systems, and to prepare for a major fall marketing campaign linked to an overhaul of the system's software. America Online has been working on the new software with Microsoft and the Netscape Communications Corporation. However, Mr. Case said the summer slowdown would not substantially affect the company's goal of reaching 10 million subscribers in the next 12 to 18 months, a figure that analysts said was achievable. However, getting new customers and keeping them are separate issues, Mr. Case acknowledged. The new pricing plan, the new software and the emphasis on customer service are all intended to reduce the company's relatively high rate of turnover, or churn, which Mr. Case said was about 29 percent.
