title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
On-Line Service Blocks Access To Topics Called Pornographic
body: In the most far-reaching example yet of Internet censorship, Compuserve Inc. has blocked access by its subscribers in the unitedstates and around the world to more than 200 sexually explicit computer discussion groups and picture data bases, after a federal prosecutor in Munich said the material violated German pornography laws. The action, which Compuserve described as a temporary move while it studies its legal options, underscores the extent to which diverse national, cultural and political values are coming into conflict with the essentially borderless technology of the global Internet computer network. In the unitedstates, Congress is considering legislation that would try to outlaw "indecent" material on the Internet, and free-speech advocates who oppose the legislation have argued that American law cannot hold sway over an international technology. Compuserve's move, in which German law is determining what material Americans cannot see, seems certain to add fuel to that debate. "This just shows how cyberspace doesn't belong to a single country," said Esther Dyson, chairman of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a computer privacy and free-speech public policy group based in San Francisco. "If you have laws in one nation it affects other nations as well." Compuserve, which is a unit of H & R Block and has headquarters in Columbus, Ohio, provides on-line information services, electronic mail and Internet access to more than four million subscribers in 140 countries. Company officials said yesterday that they had to block all subscribers' access to the Internet material in question because they do not yet have the technology to tailor Compuserve's on-line content to a single country. But William Giles, a company spokesman, said Compuserve was investigating ways to help tailor its information service to individual national laws. "We do business in hundreds of countries," Mr. Giles said. "It's a huge global market and in order to play in each country we have to play by their rules." A type of software filter that would let parents and other individual users screen access to material they might find offensive is supposed to become available on Compuserve within a month. But company executives conceded yesterday that such a solution might not meet the concerns of the German officials. Compuserve is the second-largest on-line company in the unitedstates, after America Online Inc. But it has a much larger overseas presence than America Online and is apparently the leading provider of Internet access service in Germany, which like most other foreign countries has lagged behind the unitedstates in adoption of Internet technology by consumers. America Online is expected to expand its presence in Europe, however, now that two large German corporations, Bertelsmann A. G. and Deutsche Telekom A. G. have each purchased a 5 percent stake in the company. Deutsche Telekom already has a dominant on-line business in Germany, called T-Online, with almost 900,000 subscribers, but it is a business-oriented service. The discussion groups blocked by Compuserve are among the more than 17,000 electronic conference groups that are part of an anarchic and freewheeling international computer conferencing system known as the Usenet, which is distributed via the Internet. The Usenet conference system carries discussion groups on almost every imaginable topic that are displayed in bulletin-board fashion on a computer screen, permitting computer users to post comments in certain categories and view what others have posted. In recent years, computer technology has evolved in such a way that it is now possible to send digitized images and even video clips as files made up of long strings of software code. Special software can then be used to convert the documents into images that can be viewed on a personal computer. In many of the groups hundreds of computer users post comments of a sexual nature. Of the more than 200 groups that Compuserve has banned, most are identified by the prefix "alt.sex" and range from the broadly commercial -- alt.sex.erotica.marketplace -- to the specific, like alt.binaries.pictures.erotica.fetish.feet. A number of the discussion groups are devoted to pedophilia or bestiality. The list of sites was presented late last week by prosecutors in Munich to Felix Somm, manager of Compuserve's German operations. While German authorities contend that the list violates the country's pornography and child-protection laws, critics of Compuserve's action -- some of whom posted complaints at the Usenet group alt.online-service.compuserve -- noted that some of the banned Usenet areas include discussion groups devoted to topics like homosexuality that were not necessarily pornographic or a threat to children. Ms. Dyson, of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, said that while many members of Congress might support placing restrictions on sexually oriented Internet material, Germany's new efforts at censorship raised thornier free-speech issues. "The American Government has to understand that while they may only want to outlaw indecency, the Germans could outlaw English on the Internet," she said. A spokeswoman at the German Embassy in Washington said that the embassy had telephoned the German Government in Bonn for more information on the situation but did not yet have a response. Whether it will be possible to impose a ban on any kind of on-line information is a question that has been hotly debated in the computer industry. While Compuserve has removed the specified Usenet groups from its own service offerings, it is still possible for a German personal computer user to use the Compuserve software to connect to the Internet's vast World Wide Web and read and view the sexually explicit material at thousands of other computer sites around the globe. The World Wide Web, a newer and much more diverse multimedia technology than Usenet, is designed to make it easy to hop from computer site to computer site on the Internet with a click of a mouse. Rather than try to impose global bans, many American computer executives say that the best solution to the problem of pornography on the Internet is to employ special filtering software that systematically maps out specific addresses that contain certain kinds of content. The software, which is being developed by companies like Surfwatch Inc. of Los Altos, Calif., can be run either on the user's personal computer or by the Internet service provider. When a user tries to retrieve a document from a restricted site, the software blocks the access. "In the future, every Internet operator will be subject to local laws," said Eric Schmidt, chief technology officer for Sun Microsystems Inc., a Mountain View, Calif., computer maker. "And software will be developed to provide the appropriate local censorship."

title: WHO NEEDS AMERICA ONLINE?
body: Ah, doughnuts, breakfast of champions!" Ted Leonsis exclaimed as he entered a conference room one morning in March and spotted a tray of standard-issue pastries. Leonsis is not a small man, so his quip drew a laugh. It also reassured his associates, who remembered how little pleasure Leonsis had found in his last meeting in this room. A month earlier, two Californians traveled to America Online headquarters in Vienna, Va., to present a proposal for an on-line site dedicated to surfing, the real kind, done in water. Assuming that the members of America Online's staff would be corporate types, the two Californians, Mark Bertignoli and Bob Wolfe, wore newly purchased suits and ties. Their presentation was equally buttoned up. Ten minutes in, Leonsis had heard enough. He turned to a colleague and fumed, "These are the [expletive] surfers?" and started reading his mail. Bertignoli and Wolfe took the hint. Now, for their second-chance presentation, they strolled in wearing caps, sunglasses, Hawaiian shirts, shorts and sandals. Bertignoli's first words were, "We're back, bitchin' and bad." Before he outlined his plans for Surf Net, he gave Leonsis a T-shirt from a cult film called "Surf Nazis Must Die." Only when he had done everything but ride a wave did he segue into cyber-speak: "Check this -- we can literally beam out from the beach. We can have live chat with near-video on demand, using a 540c laptop, a PC/MIA pocket insert and a 14.4 modem connected to a cell phone. And we can upload pictures in two minutes to a folder on a Web site." "What ABC did at the Super Bowl," said Randy Dean, head of America Online's sports department. "And then there's the interactive stuff," Bertignoli said. "We'll have trivia contests, a fantasy league, pictures of the surf injury of the month." The Californians showed off their graphics, then were ushered outside to await the verdict. "A fairly small market," a skeptic noted. "No," Leonsis said. "This isn't about surfers. It's about surf, sharks and sex -- and by sex I mean healthy bodies, pretty people, California. You saw that 30-foot wave, you took a deep breath. But you didn't really want to be there. That's the beauty of this: it's not just surfing for surfers, it's also for wannabes." The debate was brief. Bertignoli and Wolfe returned. But before Dan Krifcher, manager of an America Online division called Greenhouse, welcomed them to the service, Leonsis had two more questions. "You full time?" "You bet." "Profit or not?" "Megaprofit." Leonsis nodded. "Profit is cool." COOL" IS THE HIGHEST ACCOLADE IN the Leonsis lexicon, and he has conferred it on more than two dozen presentations this year. As a result, the Greenhouse -- a unit of America Online that the 38-year-old Leonsis formed in summer 1994 to attract fresh ideas from nontraditional sources -- has introduced an array of disparate talents. There's a writer who bills himself as a 60-second novelist, a site for people of color, a Health Zone, an astrology service, a cyber free-for-all called Hecklers Online and, with midsummer fanfare, Surf Net. Leonsis, who is president of America Online Services Corporation and its chief programmer, promises much more. "Between January and June of 1996, we'll launch 70 Greenhouse sites, which is equal to all the deals we signed last year," he says. "I can't think of a movie studio that productive." America Online can afford it. The company has grown from 300,000 subscribers in 1993 to more than 4 million today, with 250,000 members joining each month, making it the most popular on-line service in the country. As a result, the company has been a favorite of investors, who have driven up the stock price more than 2,800 percent since 1992. The Greenhouse signings are, nevertheless, necessary -- even crucial -- to America Online's future. Despite its current dominance, the company is vulnerable, and not just to its direct competitors, an increasingly aggressive Compuserve, a revived Prodigy, the yet-to-be-announced News Corporation-MCI Online Ventures service and the enormously endowed Microsoft Network. According to conventional wisdom, the only significant destination in cyber-space is the World Wide Web; by this argument, all commercial services are doomed to be nothing more than Internet-access providers. "We see a lot of talent entering the field on the Web without the blessing of the branded services," says Edward Bennett, president of Prodigy. "And where human attention goes, advertisers will follow." Some commercial services have already positioned themselves as Internet navigators. Leonsis calls them "Johnny-come-lattes" and scoffs at the conventional wisdom. "They all say, 'Content is king,' " he says. "But how can you argue that when there are 200,000 Web sites? The more that's out there, the better it will be for a service with strong programming." In other words, with such a huge and bewildering proliferation of sites, users will want a central starting place. So the challenge for Leonsis is to develop compelling content that is available only on America Online. Here he has a competitive advantage: he is the first on-line executive who can make a sizable investment in talent. On most networks -- including America Online in pre-Greenhouse days -- the economics of cyber-space are attractive to only the on-line service. Typically, these services charge customers a monthly fee that covers the first 10 hours of use. Their profit lies in signing up a great many customers, and then enticing them to stay on line for more than the basic 10 hours. For the independent creators of programming, however, the reward is minuscule: 20 percent of the revenue they generate. In the first wave of on-line growth, services tended to form alliances with established media companies (@times, the on-line version of The newyork Times, for instance, has been on America Online since June 1994) and to encourage user-generated content -- "chat rooms" and bulletin boards. As services began to look alike, however, it seemed that the key to growth was original programming. The Greenhouse is the first to recognize that quality programming costs money. And so, in exchange for 20 percent of the equity, America Online invests between $100,000 and $500,000 in its partners' sites. It's no wonder, then, that two months after America Online announced the Greenhouse, it had 2,000 applications. Suddenly, every service created its own version of the Greenhouse or found a reason not to need one (see box) or attacked America Online. Leonsis, who was mostly unknown outside the new media universe just a year ago, loves the attention and the competition. Now he is in a position roughly equivalent to head of programming at a television network or production chief at a movie studio; he finds it an apt comparison when it's suggested that he might become the Brandon Tartikoff of cyber-space. TED LEONSIS HAS NEVER HAD A PROBLEM with high visibility. On the rare occasion in his bachelor days when he was dateless, he tended to join paired-off friends at restaurants carrying a bust of Elvis Presley and announcing to the hostess, "Table for eight -- and the King doesn't like to be kept waiting." But his taste for the dramatic obscures the fact that Leonsis is a passionate student of "new media." An only child, Leonsis grew up in Brooklyn and Boston; he went to Georgetown University planning to become a teacher. He worked as a writer at Wang, where he learned to love computers. At 25, he started his first company by turning a data base about software products into a publishing enterprise. It's not surprising, therefore, that when Leonsis became a co-founder of Redgate Communications in 1985, at 28, he positioned it as "a new life form," not as an advertising agency. "At Wang, the basic premise was that you could take a keystroke and digitize it," he explains. "Bill Gates went a step further. He understood that once you digitize information, you change its DNA. Gates saw that anything could be software. So in '84 and '85, no matter what meeting I was in, I felt something cataclysmic was happening, that dogs would sleep with cats and the sun would set in the East." Which led Leonsis to experiment. At Redgate, he produced the first multimedia CD-ROM. He started six personal computer magazines and was the co-author of three books. He created an all-digital multimedia service and a CD-ROM shopping program. "Every other word out of Ted's mouth was 'digital,' " recalls Bob Nicholson, a former Air Force public-affairs officer (and a 20-year veteran of the Internet and its progenitor, Darpanet) who has worked with Leonsis since 1986. By 1994, the little agency in Vero Beach, Fla., that specialized in digitizing and redirecting information had seven offices, a staff of 120 and billings of $70 million a year. Leonsis didn't see that his future was on line. But Steve Case, chairman of America Online, had noticed that Leonsis' ability to bring buyers and sellers together through personalized digital technology was on a parallel track with his company's efforts to create an electronic marketplace. He arranged a breakfast with Leonsis; after a 90-minute conversation, he proposed that America Online buy Redgate. "Ted was coy," Case says, "but I knew he was mesmerized by the opportunity to play on a bigger stage." Leonsis quickly developed a strategy for the next stage of America Online's growth. "People work and come home, but they also need a third place -- the gym, a bar, whatever," he says. "When they push away from the dinner table, that third place is reading or talking or TV. Right now, online is in about 10 percent of American homes. If it's going to grow, it's got to attract the big audience, which, as a reflex, settles in front of the television set at 9 P.M. every Thursday. In that sense, my real competition isn't Bill Gates, it's 'Seinfeld.' " But in August 1994, when Leonsis joined America Online and logged onto the network in search of talent he could throw against "Seinfeld," he had trouble finding any great sites. On other networks he found the same numbing sameness. He thought he knew why: on-line services built their business on the wrong model. "Instead of developing original programming, we forged alliances with big media companies," he says. "But many of our partners look at online as an ancillary delivery system, a place to slap electronic versions of newspapers and magazines and press releases onto a medium that seems small and not terribly important to them. There's too much: online, not cable TV, is the medium with 500 channels, and it's ugly. We're all pretty pathetic." But amid the dross, Leonsis found the Motley Fool, a stock advisory site on America Online developed by Tom and David Gardner, two brothers in their 20's. The Gardners had the finest education offered by New England prep schools and elite colleges and then found they were allergic to conventional employment. They were equally dismayed by professional stock pickers, who as a group underperform against the Dow Jones average. If Wall Street was populated by "the wise," they reasoned, they would do better to embrace Fooldom. Using $50,000 of their own money, they bought stock, went on line and began comparing notes with their fellow amateurs. They were an immediate hit, both in the market, where they were outperforming the Dow by 22 percent, and on line, where they were on their way to converting 5,000 initial customer entries a month into 300,000 a month. "Two kids became our No. 1 personal-finance providers -- two kids!" Leonsis says. "Why? Because they tapped into the DNA of our community." Surely there must be others who could dispense knowledge and create a comfortable environment that allowed subscribers to become collaborators. A few weeks later, Leonsis and his colleagues brainstormed their way to a possible solution: a division that would transform the ultimate cyber-experts, the users, into content providers. Some Greenhouse content is quite high-minded. When its Afrocentric site, Net Noir, made its debut in July, its first guest was President Jean-Bertrand Aristide of Haiti. The Health Zone's fitness programming includes an interactive food diary that describes the caloric, fat and nutrient content of users' diets with just a few keystrokes. And on the Better Health and Medicine Forum -- founded by Elin Silveous and her husband, Dr. Allen Douma, soon after her multiple sclerosis was diagnosed -- there are 240 support groups and bulletin boards with 1,500 topics. Most initial Greenhouse investments, however, go to those who see themselves primarily as entertainers. Dan Hurley is a journalist who started writing "novels while you wait" on a Chicago street corner more than a decade ago and has since produced 17,254 "one minute" novels. He now conducts an on-line forum in which he interviews a member and then produces an instant story. Eugenie Diserio introduced herself to Leonsis by sending him some hostile E-mail ("I'm having trouble logging on. Did everyone in the world buy modems last Christmas? Is America Online going to be like Power Rangers?") and soon found herself starting Astronet, an interactive astrology service. It is Hecklers Online, though, that best expresses Leonsis' view that the ideal content provider is a party host, not a monologuist. Hecklers is a site where guests are regularly roasted and audience members are invited to ask impertinent questions. "Sean Michael and Scott Davis and I are old friends from high school who spent a lot of detention time together," says Mike Ragsdale, one of the site's three founders. "One night we were sitting around drinking beer and we decided to have some fun on line, so we went into a chat room and asked, 'What is a jihad?' Someone answered, 'A holy war.' We typed back, 'Isn't that an oxymoron?' Then a bunch of us would jump into a chat room and harass the people there until we'd be the only ones in 'Gay Cops in Houston.' " Surfers, the terminally ill, diet specialists, hecklers -- this is a ragtag band of talent. Isn't online supposed to be cutting edge, geared to the young and hip? "When I first got here, I thought we should be the MTV of the 90's," Leonsis says. "But it wasn't an accurate analogy. As I double-clicked into our community, I saw it was the American Association of Retired People, Christianity Today, military people, pet lovers -- a real Norman Rockwell picture of America. Face it, when you go to a cocktail party and America Online diskettes are being used as coasters, you know you've become mainstream." AS IF PROGRAMMING America Online, continuing as president of Redgate, running America Online's new Internet connection and being a husband and a father of two weren't enough, Leonsis has taken on another role: point man in the propaganda war against the Microsoft Network. Leonsis understood from the beginning that the on-line world has the potential to become significant to more than Wall Street and the current 11 million American users. And so, shortly after he arrived at America Online, he gave a five-minute talk on the subject. "This is the most important battle in the fight to stop Gates," he said. "Operating systems are episodic -- you buy them once every few years. But online is ongoing. It's bigger than computers -- it's about operating your life." The bottom line: beat Gates before Gates beats America Online. So he set the Greenhouse in motion. That zeal was not enough to keep NBC from moving its on-line site to the Microsoft Network. This defection from America Online was widely noticed, not least because it caused America Online stock to lose 6 points in two days. Leonsis, predictably, played this as a signal that the Microsoft Network would feature banal programming from brand names. "We told NBC: 'We need to do original programming with you, not just run promotional material as news. We paid you $1 million a year. We'll give you $1.5 million if you deliver original material.' The word is that Microsoft offered NBC $4 million. If so, it says they'll have every brand in there. It will be hard for a network that broad to have a point of view." Martin Yudkovitz, president of NBC Interactive Media, laughed at that analysis. "If Ted wasn't interested in NBC, he did a magnificent job at hiding it," he says. The Microsoft retort is even stronger. "We didn't pay tons of money to recycle NBC's old content," says Bill Miller, director of marketing for the Microsoft Network. "Microsoft as a shark buying everything -- that's wrong. If we wanted to do that, we would have announced 15 deals with names you've heard of." Miller contends that it's Microsoft, not America Online, that's friendlier to the unknown content provider. "Greenhouse is a great program, and I wish I'd thought of it -- though I'm not sure I couldn't have," he says. "But if you're not a winner in the Greenhouse competition, it's hard, if not impossible, to get onto America Online." More recently, Time magazine moved from America Online to Compuserve. Once again, Leonsis put great spin on what looked like a defection. "We have five Greenhouse areas that have been performing as well as Time," he explains. "If we didn't spend that money on Time, we realized we could spawn a dozen Greenhouse deals that might also perform at that level -- and we'd have equity in them. That was very compelling to us." As with NBC, memories differ. "What Compuserve is offering isn't just money," says Barrett Seaman, special-projects editor for Time. "You hit 'News' on Compuserve, and you'll get Time -- we'll be their gateway to the news. If we had gotten that kind of exposure on America Online, we might still be there." (As America Online users well know, The newyork Times icon is almost always on the service's welcome screen, giving it a visibility that makes it unequaled as a news site on that network.) At this point, even an observer who enjoys cyber-tennis might have trouble deciding whom to believe. But that's an old-media preoccupation. This is nothing less than media war, conducted by media via media, in which all victories are measured by points of market share. All that seems clear -- for the moment, anyway -- is that the service that wins the first scrimmages will be the one that creates the first generation of on-line celebrities. Here, at least, America Online has the advantage. As Leonsis likes to point out, the leaders in radio didn't flourish in the early days of television, and the leaders in the television business did not spawn the lucrative cable business. Rather, the pathfinders tend to come from young, small, aggressive companies with no legacy of success -- and that, Leonsis says with satisfaction, means America Online, not Microsoft. So he takes pleasure in telling the story of Brian Henley, the creator of a golf site called I Golf: when Henley was named a Greenhouse partner, he not only quit his regular job, he also convinced the Callaway Corporation, a maker of golf clubs with no history of interest in online, to pay $250,000 to sponsor his site for one year. Leonsis is delighted that the Motley Fools have, with Greenhouse financing, moved out of their one-room office, hired a staff and opened three new sites, including an entertainment review that they've called, inevitably, Follywood. And he cackles when he considers that customers spent 80,000 hours at Hecklers Online in its first month. But these, Leonsis knows, are the good times. "The Microsoft launch was true to form," he says. "The expectation their public relations machine creates is very hard to meet -- this was a software upgrade, after all, not an AIDS vaccine. But it's an awesome company, and they will figure it out. The challenge for America Online is to get as big as we can as fast as we can. That means more families, more minorities, more women coming to America Online. And it means getting ready for the backlash against the Internet, when the venture capitalists get burned and customers get lost and the magazines start running articles titled 'Whither the Web?' " All that pressure drives Leonsis in one direction: to sign more talent. "But I know if we open 40 new areas, 10 will be home runs, 10 will be good, 10 will be like everyone else's -- and we'll be embarrassed by the last 10." Leonsis leans back in his swivel chair. "And when that happens," he says, sounding very much like a network programming czar, "I'm going to have to start canceling shows."  THE COMPETITION  AMERICA ONLINE'S Greenhouse has not gone unnoticed by the competition. The other commercial services have cultivated new talent or, more commonly, asserted that talent development is nothing new.  Compuserve With 3.9 million subscribers, Compuserve is the second-largest on-line service, but it has been marketed so casually that it sometimes seems invisible. This year it woke up, announcing that next spring it will unveil a streamlined network -- Project Wow! -- for newcomers to on-line services and invest in Entertainment Drive (E Drive), which has been drawing an estimated 600,000 Compuserve users. But Compuserve doesn't usually invest in unknowns. "We get 150 inquiries a week from people who want to go on line," says Kevin Knott, vice president of product marketing. "Only a few can make it. We'll help anyone get up on the Internet, but we're very particular what we put on our service. It's very difficult and expensive to establish a new brand."  Prodigy Prodigy, with two million members, was the first service to reach out to a family audience. Since Edward Bennett took over as president in May, Prodigy has made it a priority to broaden its audience by developing talent, producing a remarkable number of new Internet sites that can be accessed only through Prodigy: 150 in the past 60 days. "Our aim is to give people information they can use," Bennett says. "We have sites about AIDS, computer-generated music, even one run by adopted children for adopted children." The secret of Prodigy's speed and scope is that it hires people to develop its sites in-house. "This way, we own 100 percent of our new areas," Bennett notes. "We found that classic information providers wanted too big a cut. They think their content is their brand. They don't understand the medium."  Microsoft The Microsoft Network, with 600,000 subscribers, made its debut in August with enormous fanfare and modest content. "We cast a broad net and made deals with more than 200 independent contract providers from companies valued at less than $10 million," reports Bill Miller, MSN's director of marketing. "These are people who, almost completely, found us." MSN is primarily an Internet-access link, not a commercial on-line service. "On-line services have said, 'We'll create the world and give you everything you could want,' " Miller explains. "We believe the Internet is too vibrant and strong to limit our customers to Microsoft, so we see our role as helping our users make sense of the Internet. We will invest in good ideas and good people, but the majority of people who look to us for funding will wind up on the Internet, where the barrier to entry is fairly small. We tell them, 'Do a great job on the Net and we'll promote you to MSN.' " Microsoft does occasionally skip this intermediate stage, however -- most recently when it hired Michael Kinsley, of "Crossfire," to start an on-line magazine.  News Corporation-MCI On-Line Ventures In the summer, Rupert Murdoch's Delphi service (100,000 subscribers) was on the verge of a major face lift. Delphi built a 200-desk, state-of-the-art newsroom, held endless meetings with print journalists and announced a contest to name the service. Then News Corporation and MCI announced a joint on-line venture, and two staffs and many ideas had to be integrated. Five months later, the electronic newsroom already seems like an artifact; according to the latest strategy, journalists will be hired, but more to provide content for traditional on-line categories than to create original content for an on-line newspaper. This approach, sources at News Corporation-MCI suggest, will be matched by a unique on-line environment. Despite the delay, Anthea Disney, former editor of TV Guide and now editor in chief of this new venture, sounds confident of eventual success. "I had no interest in trading 30 million readers a week for a rate base of 100,000," she says. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
For interactive advertising, 1995 has proved to be a breakthrough year. Now comes the shakeout.
body: INTERACTIVE advertising, finishing an ebullient, even euphoric, year punctuated by gains and breakthroughs, faces a shakeout in 1996 that will confront the nascent field with its first significant challenge. That prediction was offered yesterday at a daylong conference, "Spotlight on Interactive Advertising '95," for which the Advertising Club of newyork played host and Newsweek magazine, a unit of the Washington Post Company, served as a sponsor. The conference, which club officials anticipate will become an annual event, drew more than 500 attendees to the Plaza Hotel in snowy, blustery weather. Other issues addressed at the conference included the perils, if any, posed by the blurring of lines between editorial content and advertising in interactive media like World Wide Web sites. The event also featured displays and exhibits from 10 interactive agencies deemed "best of the year" by the trade publication Adweek. The prediction about looming problems came from Scott Kurnit, president and chief executive of the venture recently formed by the MCI Communications Corporation and the News Corporation that combines the Internet operations of both. Even though "there will be some new companies" emerging in 1996, Mr. Kurnit said, "there's no question this business will have a shakeout" after what had been "a year of enthusiasm and discovery." The primary reason, he added, was that "the realities will change" because the interactive realm is becoming so crowded. "Some will be better than others, rising to the top and capturing people's imagination," Mr. Kurnit said. "Some will be dormant. And some will go out of business." For instance, he said, "an entrepreneur might want to give real-time stock quotes on the Internet that aren't delayed 15 minutes, only to learn that some florist has a real-time stock crawl on his Web site, offering program content as the underpinning to an ad so that while you're there you'll buy flowers." "But," he added, "when we see every neighborhood florist on the Internet, what happens?" Another perspective on the issue was provided by Kelly Anthony Rodriques, chief executive at the Novo Media Group, a San Francisco company that was one of the Adweek honorees. "We try to have a very distinct point of view on our Web sites and CD-ROM's," he said, "that tells people 'here's what's sponsored and here's what's not.' " Joe Carter, the editor at the Novo Media office in Rowayton, Conn., demonstrated "Living Home," which has sponsors like the American Express Company and Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A. "There are very discrete areas on-screen," he said, pointing. "Here's the editorial zone; here's the advertising zone." However, G. M. O'Connell, a partner at Modem Media in Westport, Conn., which was also honored by Adweek, said he believed the blurring line was "an issue you face in every medium." "I don't think it's any worse here than what you see in children's television programming," he added, "where you wonder 'is it a show or is it a cereal?' At least you don't have that problem yet on the Internet." Mr. O'Connell said he was more concerned with "how you intersect someone's travel on the Web with your specific advertising message or get them involved within the context of your brand." He added, "Whether your home page looks like advertising or not, I think most people know." Kathleen L. Biro, president at the Strategic Interactive Group in Boston, a unit of Bronner Slosberg Humphrey that was also an Adweek honoree, agreed. "With traditional advertising, the customer is passive and bombarded with messages," she said. "Here's he's got to seek them out. And to have him seek them out, you've got to provide 'value added' content." For instance, she and two colleagues -- Ruben Pinchanski, vice president and new media development director, and Robert Cosinuke, vice president and marketing director -- demonstrated a Web site for L. L. Bean that seemed to offer as much information about national parks as it did about Bean merchandise. Not every moment of the conference was spent pondering weighty issues, of course. On Ramp, a newyork company also saluted by Adweek, drew visitors to its display with a cheeky Web site about "Melrose Place," the Fox nighttime soap (http://melroseplace.com). Though the stormy weather did not seem to affect turnout, it made an impact on many of the earnest young executives stationed at exhibits by offering them a plausible excuse to explain away slow computer connections, an affliction that might well be the technological bugaboo of the 1990's. "It's a little slow right now because it's cold by the door," one man reassured a visitor to his booth. Adweek also honored these companies: Avalanche Systems in newyork; the CKS Group in Cupertino, Calif.; Jupiter Communications in newyork; Open Market Inc. in Cambridge, Mass.; Organic Online in San Francisco, and poppe.com in Mountain View, Calif., the interactive unit of Poppe Tyson, which is owned by Bozell, Jacobs, Kenyon & Eckhardt.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: DIGITAL COMMERCE;
The prospect of Internet censorship raises troubling issues for business. - Correction Appended
body: FREE-SPEECH activists and Netizens took to the streets and to their keyboards last week, condemning as unconstitutional the new measures for censoring the Internet that are being considered by Congress. But while most of the outcry has raised valid concerns about the First Amendment and civil liberties, little of the discussion has focused on how censorship could cripple much of the Internet's commercial potential. The restrictions, part of the communications legislation being completed by a House-Senate conference committee, would make it illegal to use computer networks to transmit or store "indecent" material. Proponents said the bill would protect children using computer networks. If the provisions become law, any user or provider of network services or information who is convicted of violating it would face a possible sentence of two years in jail and fines of as much as $100,000. The legislation is expected to include, with some exceptions, private electronic mail, data stored on Internet servers and World Wide Web sites, and information transmitted by commercial on-line services and Internet-access providers. What is particularly worrisome is that the legislation could create restrictions on free speech that are as sweeping as they are vague. Indecency is a broad legal category that has been used to ban some foul language and sexually explicit material on radio and television broadcasts during periods when young listeners and viewers were likely to be exposed to them. But "indecent" has been also been used successfully by various groups to ban books like J. D. Salinger's novel "Catcher in the Rye" from high-school libraries, and to curtail the distribution of safe-sex educational materials to minors. In the context of the Internet, even nonpornographic material accessible and legal in other media would be off limits. And Internet entrepreneurs might not be aware of transgressions until the decency police knocked at their doors. "The real danger is to the smaller companies, the new World Wide Web providers and people who want to put up content on the Internet," said Donna Hoffman, a Vanderbilt University business professor who specializes in electronic commerce. "With the Web creating a new wave in commercial activity," she said, "we're expecting a boom in content providers who are starting to say, 'People are on the Net. Let's put stuff up and make money at it.' "But this legislation scares them," she added. "They're saying, 'I could go to jail if someone thinks it's indecent and I don't even know what words I'm allowed to use.' " Though Net censorship might pose the greatest threat to small companies unable to afford big fines or costly court cases, large companies also expect to feel the chill. Scott Kurnit, president and chief executive of MCI/News Corporation Internet Ventures, said: "We are at less risk than the entrepreneurs, because as a large company we have the resources to screen what we pass through the network. But we don't believe that's what the Internet is about. "And such a law would significantly diminish what we could offer -- it would be a very small version, sanitized for a lowest-common-denominator audience. You couldn't even call it the Internet anymore. I'm not sure that product would be interesting enough to consumers that anyone would buy it." A restricted Internet would become unmarketable because, like a telephone network, it becomes more valuable as more information is made available on it. Now, anyone with an Internet account can use a connected computer to find information about subjects from nuclear fission to dog grooming and to link up with millions of people around the world. The vast range of topics and opinions exchanged on the Net are both its attraction and its raison d'etre. Katherine Fulton, president of the Institute for Alternative Journalism and former editor of The Independent, a newspaper based in Durham, N.C., said, "If Jesse Helms had been able to stop me from publishing things he deemed indecent, we couldn't have published an independent alternative newsweekly." Senator Jesse A. Helms is the well-known conservative Republican from North Carolina. "This proposal will have more than a chilling effect," Ms. Fulton said. "It may well mean a cold death for everyone except very rich and very cautious media companies." The Internet is a powerful example of free speech and the free market in action; it is curious that the Net has alarmed the lawmakers of a nation founded on those principles. Those who condemn the proposed Internet censorship measure do acknowledge the existence of a problem: the need to protect children from pornography and anything else a parent deems harmful. But when it comes to Internet technology, "most of these laws are advanced by people who don't 'get it,' " said William Randolph Hearst 3d, the venture capitalist who is acting chief executive of the Internet start-up company @Home and the former publisher of The San Francisco Examiner. If the Internet is to become a true consumer technology that is welcomed into the home, Mr. Hearst said, parents should use technology to filter out offending material. But making censorship the filter would signal a fundamental change in the role that the Government plays in regulating communications. Mr. Hearst said, "I'd hate to see Government succeed in doing in the interactive space what they've failed or chosen not to do in traditional publishing and broadcasting, which is to set moral standards by regulation rather than by individual choice." Correction  A picture caption in Business Day yesterday with the Technology column, about possible censorship on the Internet, misstated the date of a rally in San Francisco to protest proposed Internet restrictions in the Federal telecommunications bill. It was Thursday, not Saturday. Correction-Date: December 19, 1995, Tuesday Graphic   Photo: Demonstrators in San Francisco Saturday protested Internet restrictions attached to a telecommunications bill Congress is considering. (Marc Geller for The newyork Times)

title: Telecommunications Giants Join Internet Security Quest
body: For all the commercial promise of computer networks, some big drawbacks remain. Companies have spent billions on private data networks in recent years, but these were mainly in-house conduits. And the Internet, while widely accessible, is still regarded as unreliable and not secure enough to conduct essential corporate business. In recent months, I.B.M.'s Lotus unit has been quietly working with a group led by the world's big telecommunications companies -- the AT&T Corporation, the Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation, Deutsche Telekom and others -- to try to combine the advantages of private networks with the Internet. The consortium seeks to establish a layer of software and hardware standards that would effectively rest atop the Internet. Their goal is to make the Internet more secure, reliable and easy to use, while opening private data networks so that, for example, customers and suppliers in an industry can share work and documents as freely as they want. In short, the consortium members said, computer networks should work like the telephone system does today, easily and globally, with no need for operating manuals or arcane computer commands. "The objective is to have the data-network equivalent of the universal dial tone," said L. Scott Perry, an AT&T vice president working on the consortium effort. The group, called the Multimedia Services Affiliate Forum, plans to become incorporated as a not-for-profit organization in newyork in mid-January. At that time, it also plans to announce its management structure, and possibly adopt a less ungainly name, Mr. Perry said. The consortium started meeting last summer, and had seven core members: AT&T, Deutsche Telekom, Lotus, Novell Inc., NTT, the Telstra Corporation of Australia, and Unisource, a joint venture of four European phone companies. To broaden support, the group held private meetings at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel from Dec. 6 through Dec. 9, and invited computer hardware and software suppliers, as well as telecommunications companies. The newyork sessions were attended by 24 phone carriers and 14 computer companies, including Intel, the Microsoft Corporation, Sun Microsystems Inc. and the Hewlett-Packard Company. Roughly three-fourths of the attending companies have said they plan to join the group. For the phone companies, the appeal of such a group is clear-cut. They are making huge investments so that their trunk lines and switches can handle so-called broad-band data networks, which can carry voice, video and text. They see common standards as a catalyst for increased data traffic, and thus more revenue. Analysts also noted that the phone companies want to be more than mere pipelines for data. The companies, analysts said, are experts in billing, maintenance and service. In data networks, as in telephone networks, they seek to be paid for those services -- and leading the standard-setting drive could help them achieve that. "This effort is very significant," said David Marshak, a vice president for the Patricia Seybold Group Inc., a research firm. "But the big question is whether this initiative is the one that companies rally around to set standards." Microsoft has been planning to set up its own group to establish data communications standards, tentatively called the Windows Open Internet Forum. Phone company executives hope Microsoft can be persuaded to join their effort instead.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Adding to the annual spectacle, NBC and the N.F.L. take the Super Bowl to cyberspace.
body: THE hoopla and hyperbole surrounding the Super Bowl are extending into cyberspace. NBC, which will broadcast the Super Bowl XXX on Jan. 28, and the National Football League are teaming for an interactive, multimedia Super Sunday project that is the largest for any sporting event, they say, obeying an immutable law since Super Bowl I that superlatives must be invoked in connection with the game. "We already own the eyeballs on the television screen," said Ann Kirschner, vice president for programming and media development at the league's N.F.L. Enterprises unit in newyork. "We want to make sure we own the eyeballs on the computer screen." The project includes a site on the World Wide Web sponsored by the N.F.L. and NBC, which is owned by the General Electric Company; a Super Bowl XXX curtain-raiser with broadcast and on-line elements under a common title, "Behind the Scenes," and a live on-line broadcast of the game from Sun Devil Stadium in Tempe, Ariz. The Web site (at http://www.superbowl.com) is scheduled to operate from Dec. 27 through Feb. 4 and will be separate from existing sites operated independently by the network and the league. NBC and the N.F.L. are also breaking ground by offering advertisers joint multimedia sponsorships of the project. There is commercial time available during "Behind the Scenes: Super Bowl XXX," an hourlong NBC special on Jan. 27, as well as interactive advertisements on the Web site. "This is the beginning of a number of interactive events accompanying major sporting events, including the Olympics," said Andy Batkin, chairman and chief executive of Interactive Media Inc. in Hermosa Beach, Calif. A division of his company, Interactive Media Sales, is selling the advertising on the Web site, and another, the Interactive Marketing Agency, develops interactive marketing strategies and media services for the N.F.L. And guess which marketer will be the title sponsor of the Web site and will participate in related programs? Why, it's the Microsoft Corporation, which has been cooperating with NBC on everything from development of an all-news cable channel, announced last week, to the marketing blitz for the Windows 95 operating system, with roles for NBC stars like Jay Leno and Matthew Perry. The relationship appears to be so intimate that William H. Gates, the Microsoft chairman, and Robert C. Wright, the NBC president, might as well join the cast of "Friends." Actually, this time the Microsoft-NBC tie "is a total coincidence," said Steve Guggenheimer, a product manager at Microsoft in Redmond, Wash., because it was NBC's turn to broadcast the Super Bowl in 1996. Microsoft "is always excited about opportunities to show the richness of the Internet to a whole new audience," he said. "What better event than the Super Bowl for doing that?" In addition to title sponsorship of the Web site, Mr. Guggenheimer said, Microsoft will help develop, produce and manage its content and infrastructure. And the fans in Sun Devil Stadium will find with their seat cushions free CD-ROM's that include Internet Explorer, the Microsoft Web browser. Microsoft's sponsorship role gives it category exclusivity, said Jonathan Miller, senior vice president of NBC Sports in newyork, meaning the network will not sell commercial time during the Jan. 27 special to other computer marketers. "We want at most five or six advertisers to buy the nine minutes of time, and already some have stepped up," he said. They include the M&M/Mars unit of Mars Inc., the Procter & Gamble Company and the Prudential Insurance Company of America. Mr. Miller declined to discuss rates, saying most sales would be part of packages. The special will recount the two weeks leading to Super Bowl XXX "in documentary style," Mr. Miller said, from "flights on team planes" to "rehearsals for the halftime show" to "how Wilson makes the footballs." Mr. Batkin said that after Microsoft's ad purchase, for an undisclosed price, remaining Web site sponsorships include a home-page promotion for $150,000, "offering everyone who clicks on a chance to enter a sweepstakes and win a trip to the Pro Bowl," and 10-second "real audio" commercials priced "at a premium to radio" spots. Some ad rates were set using a per-page-view standard common in interactive advertising. In this instance, the rate is $100,000, or 4 cents for each of the 2.5 million page views anticipated. Advertisers expecting less traffic can gamble, Mr. Batkin said, by agreeing to pay 4 cents for each view, rather than a flat rate of $100,000. If they are unlucky, he added, "we've set a ceiling of $150,000." Can all these interactive events be squeezed onto an already overcrowded Super Bowl schedule? "We have not yet seen any saturation point for fan interest," Ms. Kirschner said. "The Internet is ideally suited for the information they're thirsty for." Mr. Miller said: "You can't avoid the Super Bowl. At least, we hope not."

title: Secure Digital Transactions Just Got a Little Less Secure
body: The discovery of a vulnerability has shaken the computer security world's faith in the safe use of the data-security technologies on which most current and planned electronic banking, shopping and "digital cash" systems are based. The vulnerability has been found in a class of technologies known as public-key encryption -- designed to protect electronic transactions by scrambling data so they can be read only by people with the proper mathematical keys to the code. The flaw was identified by Paul C. Kocher, a 22-year-old researcher, who demonstrated in a paper a way that an electronic eavesdropper who is able to monitor the repeated process of unscrambling incoming messages could figure out the private key. It can be done, he says, by keeping track of the length of time, down to the microsecond, it takes to unscramble each message. The feat would be analogous to a burglar surreptitiously observing people in an office building as they punched in the security code of a door with a push-button combination lock. Even if the burglar could not see which buttons were being pushed, if he observed thousands of entries and timed each with a stopwatch, he might eventually be able to winnow down the possible number of combinations that could be entered within that precise time span. In theory, the burglar could then work through this list of possible combinations until he found the one that opened the door. Mr. Kocher's paper describes a type of attack -- not yet seen outside the lab -- in which a criminal using a PC could figure out the mathematical keys in minutes. Doing so might enable a network snooper to steal a consumer's computer banking deposit, siphon off a credit card number, read personal medical records or otherwise pilfer private data supposedly protected by the security technology. "If you're using an on-line system that is not explicitly guarding against this attack, you're going to be vulnerable," said Matt Blaze, a scientist at AT&T's Bell Laboratories who has studied Mr. Kocher's paper. Mr. Blaze is a well-known researcher in the field of codes and code breaking. Public-key encryption had been assumed to be so difficult to crack that only the brute force of a supercomputer could do it, and even then only if months -- or even years -- were devoted to the task. So highly has the Federal Government respected the technology's shielding power that its export is tightly controlled, for fear that the coding technique would enable foreign enemies and terrorists to conspire with impunity via computer. The newly discovered vulnerability does not affect various forms of private encryption technology between individuals or institutions communicating only with parties known to them, like the encrypted electronic funds transfers that banks perform with one another over secure computer networks. Rather, it is the electronic systems for use by members of the public that are the focus of the research paper, written by Mr. Kocher (pronounced KOTCH-er), who recently graduated from Stanford University with a degree in biology. Mr. Kocher's evidence suggests that while the basic coding technology in public-key systems still appears to be secure, those who install or use it without recognizing the newly disclosed, remarkably subtle vulnerability will put themselves or their customers at risk. Experts who have read the paper disagree over the likelihood of anyone's successfully mounting the type of attack Mr. Kocher describes. Nevertheless, his discovery of a chink in the best armor yet devised for digital commerce has presented scientists with the most sobering evidence so far that perfect security may be no more possible to achieve in the electronic realm than in the physical world of bank robberies and muggings at A.T.M. machines. "Kocher's paper is extremely important, and it will have enormous practical impact," Mr. Blaze said. "Everyone who is building systems in this category will have to re-evaluate their vulnerability." Everyone, in this case, is a broad group that includes anyone using, or planning to use, public-key encryption -- a technology designed to allow secure, private electronic interactions between and among members of the public. That includes most on-line shopping and consumer banking systems now in use or announced, as well as smart-card systems, like one planned by the unitedstates Postal Service, in which a digitally encoded credit-card-size device would hold electronic cash. It also includes various forms of "digital signature" systems, like one developed for civilian use within the Federal Government, intended to let recipients check the authenticity of documents sent over computer networks. "Many of the security systems that I am examining are good enough to keep out casual snoopers," said Mr. Kocher, who has worked as a security consultant for a broad range of influential software companies, including Microsoft, Netscape Communications and RSA Data Security, a provider of commercial public-key encryption software. "But they're failing catastrophically when it comes to protecting data against determined attacks." James Bidzos, chief executive of RSA Data, said he considered the danger cited by Mr. Kocher as more theoretical than real, but added: "We've never claimed that all this stuff is totally secure; the question is how much does it cost to attack it. It's important to remember that people can't become complacent." In public-key systems, the sender of an electronic communication uses software that automatically scrambles the information by encoding it through use of a publicly known numerical key. Decoding the scrambled transmission requires a private key, a number supposedly known only by the merchant's computer. Without this key, no outsider can unscramble the incoming messages. Breaking a public-key encryption code is not easy to do, Mr. Kocher acknowledges, and would require sophisticated knowledge by the criminal of how fast the software algorithms, or mathematical formulas, are calculated by a particular computer. Yet it can be done, he has concluded, and many experts say he is right. "Once you read his paper, you say, 'Oh yes, this is obvious,' " said Bruce Schneier, author of "Applied Cryptography," a textbook in the field. Security experts say the vulnerability can be corrected. One solution might be padding the elapsed time of the unscrambling process with random steps to make it difficult to determine how much time the real computation actually requires. But for systems already in operation, taking the precaution would require revisions whose cost and effort may be difficult to predict. "Among the people I'm working with about this," Mr. Kocher said, "there are lot of people who are panicking -- particularly for systems that cannot be changed easily." For future installations, designing safeguards against the vulnerability would be relatively easy, Ronald Rivest said. Mr. Rivest is one of the creators of RSA, a widely used standard for public-key cryptography, which he developed along with two other computer scientists, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adelman (the name RSA is based on the initial letters of their three surnames). He played down the impact of Mr. Kocher's findings. "This is an interesting kind of attack," Mr. Rivest said. "But it's not easy to mount." But any vulnerability undermines the security of an encryption system once it becomes known, cautioned Martin Hellman, a researcher at Stanford University and one of the developers of the first public-key encryption system in 1976. "In probably 99 percent of the cases this won't be a threat," Mr. Hellman said. "But if we don't protect against these rare cases, then the whole field of computer security will get a bad name." Netscape Communications, whose future depends on the public's faith in the security of on-line transactions, is so intent on ferreting out flaws that it recently offered to pay a $1,000 bounty to anyone finding a new security problem. On Friday evening, Netscape announced its first list of bounty winners, which included Mr. Kocher. The company has already modified a security component of its technology, known as the Secure Sockets Layer, to prevent the type of attack that Mr. Kocher first demonstrated at a university seminar on Nov. 29. title: BILL WOULD CURB ON-LINE OBSCENITY
body: A House-Senate conference committee agreed in principle today on tough new prohibitions against transmitting obscenity and "indecent" material over computer networks, rejecting a compromise offered by moderate Republicans and the on-line computer industry. Members stopped short of voting on the exact language of the bill. But in a key development, House members of the conference committee voted 17-to-16 for a measure that would impose fines of up to $100,000 and prison terms of up to five years for people who make "indecent" material available to minors. The vote means that the House and Senate both support similar prohibitions, the first that would ever be imposed on communications in cyberspace. The move was immediately denounced by a wide range of civil rights groups, who said the measure would violate constitutional rights to free speech and vowed to challenge it in court. It was also a blow to on-line services and information providers, many of which worry about being embroiled in legal battles over foul language and even for discussions about subjects like AIDS. On-line information services, including America Online and many newspapers, last week endorsed a compromise that would have restricted material deemed "harmful to minors." That phrase, advocated today by Representative Rick White, Republican of Washington, would have been tailored to explicit and graphic sexual material. With today's decisions, House and Senate leaders are rushing to pass the entire telecommunications bill by yearend, though many big issues are unresolved. The White House today refused to comment on the vote. In the past, Administration officials raised concerns about the tougher proposals, but they avoided entering the fight. President Clinton has threatened to veto the bill on other issues, like provisions to expand the number of the television and radio stations a company can own. But today's vote marked a victory by "family values" Republicans led by Representative Henry J. Hyde of Illinois and a defeat for more libertarian Republicans, including Speaker Newt Gingrich. Earlier this year, Mr. Gingrich criticized the Senate's position as "very badly thought out and not very productive." But today, Republicans who were clearly opposed to tough restrictions succumbed quietly to Mr. Hyde and conservative groups like the Christian Coalition. A handful of liberal Democrats sided with Mr. Hyde as well, including Representative Patricia Schroeder of Colorado. The key decision today was to push ahead with restrictions against providing "indecent" material to people under the age of 18. "Indecency" remains a vague legal concept that falls short of explicit or graphic sexual material but covers four-letter words and sexual material deemed to be "patently offensive" by local community standards. Opponents of this restriction argued that the indecency standard is too vague to be constitutional and has been applied only to television and radio broadcasting. The standard has not been used to regulate printed publications, and the new bill raises the incongruous possibility that newspapers would be able to print a word like "penis" on paper but not in their on-line editions distributed over the Internet. But Mr. Hyde ruled the day. "The reality is that parents do not watch their children 24 hours a day," he said during the conference committee meeting today. "This is not the time for weak solutions." In taking the harder line, the House members essentially embraced the Senate bill. The author of the Senate's restrictions, Jim Exon, Democrat of Nebraska, and other conservative lawmakers were jubilant after today's vote. "Now we have a framework for a final agreement that accomplishes what we set out to do," he said. Lawmakers who supported softer regulations were glum. "I'm disappointed," said Mr. White, arguing that his proposed alternative to an indecency standard was more clearly Constitutional. And he warned that no bill will block all pornography over the Internet, because users can retrieve material from outside the unitedstates as easily as they can from a library in the same city. Separately, the conference committee agreed to include a Senate provision in the final bill that would require television manufacturers to include a computer chip in all new sets that would allow parents to block out violent programming. Some Republicans thought the provision was too intrusive but bowed to popular support for it. But the real issue today was pornography on the Internet, and criticism of the pending legislation came fast and furious The American Civil Liberties Union immediately announced that it would challenge the bill in court if it becomes law, saying it violates First Amendment rights to free speech. Barry Ek, a spokesman for Prodigy Services, said the bill could embroil his company in a tangle of disputes over words as innocuous as "breast." "The indecency standard is very problematic," said Mr. Ek. "No one knows what it means. It's overbroad and it will be challenged in the courts for years. In our view, it is a giant step backward." Because the Supreme Court has defined "indecency" for broadcasters largely in terms of the famous "seven dirty words" listed by comedian George Carlin, the new bill would require scores of on-line bulletin boards and forums to change the way they do business. Brock Meeks, editor of a CyberWires Dispatch, a publication on the Internet devoted to communication and technology policy, liberally spices his commentaries with savage profanity. "I'd end up with $100,000 fine, absolutely," Mr. Meeks said today.  "It's a travesty when the Congress of the unitedstates is essentially putting handcuffs on me and treating the Constitution of the unitedstates like a rough draft." In deference to on-line services and other electronic publishers, both bills protect companies from penalties if they make "good-faith" efforts to keep indecent material out of the hands of minors.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Germans Join America Online In Europe Deal
body: Two of Germany's largest media groups and the country's biggest telecommunications company said today that they would join forces with America Online Inc. to offer Europe-wide interactive communications networks. The agreement in principle signed by the publishers Bertelsmann A.G. and Axel Springer Verlag A.G., and the German telephone giant Deutsche Telekom A.G., creates the largest and most financially powerful support group for any computer on-line service to date. And, at least on paper, it makes America Online the dominant force in Europe's fast-developing interactive market. The deal is aimed in part at preventing the Microsoft Corporation from gaining domination of the European on-line business through its new Microsoft Network. Bertelsmann has held a 5 percent stake in America Online since March, when the companies joined to begin a European on-line service. The companies are preparing to introduce the service next month in Germany and early next year in France and Britain. Today, Deutsche Telekom announced its intention to buy its own 5 percent stake in America Online. Springer, which publishes the huge German newspaper Bild Zeitung and other publications, said it would be a leading provider of content to the service. "This is very big news in the on-line industry, especially with the entrance of Deutsche Telekom," said Peter Krasilovsky, a senior analyst at the media consulting firm of Arlen Communications Inc. in Bethesda, Md. "We are in the stage where everything is very confused but everyone is forming these kinds of strategic alliances to make sure they are future players." America Online, based in Vienna, Va., is the world's largest on-line service, with more than four million subscribers, almost all in the unitedstates. Compuserve, a unit of H & R Block Inc., is the second-largest on-line company, with 3.8 million customers, and Prodigy, which is owned by I.B.M. and Sears, Roebuck & Company, is third, with more than 1.2 million subscribers. An estimated 11 million customers worldwide subscribe to a commercial on-line service, a number that is expected to explode in the next five years. In 1995 alone, the on-line business is expected to grow 30 percent in revenue, to $1.4 billion. During the last few months, Europe has become the fiercest battleground in the competition for dominance. Analysts said the announcement was yet another blow to the fledgling Europe Online S.A., based in Luxembourg, which is seeking to create the only all-European on-line service. In recent weeks, the service has had a spate of bad news, as one of its major investors, Pearson P.L.C. of Britain, reduced its holdings, and another, Matra Hachette of France, pulled out of the venture. And Axel Springer, which had been considering making a major investment, dropped out when it was not able to exercise enough control over the board of directors. The alliance among Deutsche Telekom, Bertelsmann and Axel Springer also creates stiff competition for Compuserve's European operation, which has about 200,000 subscribers so far, mainly in Britain. But officials of the three companies said today that they were not really concerned about Europe Online or Compuserve. Instead, they repeatedly said Microsoft was the competitor they feared most and was the reason they were bringing together so much muscle. Microsoft is offering its on-line service as part of its new Windows 95 operating system, and is giving access to the Internet and a variety of private services. Since the introduction of Windows 95 in August, the Microsoft Network has attracted more than 500,000 on-line customers. Because sales of Windows 95 are thought to be lower than expected in Europe, however, Microsoft's on-line service is starting out here with a relatively small presence. Mr. Krasilovsky estimated that fewer than 75,000 European customers were currently using the service. Still, the specter of Microsoft hangs heavily over European on-line efforts. "Look at everything they have done," said an executive of one of the companies announcing the alliance today. "They have dominated everything they have entered. We just have to stop that from happening here." While analysts were interested that Springer and Bertelsmann -- longtime rivals in the Germany publishing industry -- had teamed up in the America Online venture, the entrance of Deutsche Telekom was by far the most significant part of the deal. Deutsche Telekom already has a dominant on-line business in Germany, called T-Online, with almost 900,000 subscribers. These subscribers, however, tend to be mostly business customers using the system for business applications, like electronic banking and on-line reservations services for the German railroad and airline systems. AOL Germany, which is operated by Bertelsmann, provides more home consumer and entertainment services, including Internet access, chat forums, news headlines and home shopping. Analysts said the synergies could be enormous, with Deutsche Telekom providing America Online with low-cost telecommunications access throughout Germany, and America Online giving Deutsche Telekom global reach in a business that is predicted to be worth $20 billion in five years in Europe alone. America Online officials said discussion was under way about whether Deutsche Telekom would get a seat on its board in exchange for the 5 percent investment. Bertelsmann has effectively given Deutsche Telecom an option that Bertelsmann acquired earlier in the year after making its initial 5 percent investment in America Online to purchase another 5 percent stake. Though the size of Deutsche Telekom's investment was not disclosed, it would total at least $130 million based on the stock market value of America Online. Linking the players even more closely together, the Bertelsmann-America Online venture will buy one-third interest in T-Online. Ulrich Lissek, a spokesman for Deutsche Telekom, said there were no plans to merge the European on-line operations of the three companies. "We just have an agreement to go ahead, and now we have to work out the details," he said. Officials at all the companies stressed that the alliance would have to be approved by anti-cartel authorities in Bonn and at the European Union's headquarters in Brussels.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: Advertising;
On-line services are venturing into unexplored territory as they try to establish their brand names.
body: LIKE branding a steer, a branding campaign in advertising seeks to separate the advertised product or service from the herd. But are America Online's new television commercials outstanding or simply egregious? Consider this ad: As the spooky and majestic theme music from the film "2001: A Space Odyssey" grows louder in the background, a monkey's paw is seen pushing a computer mouse. The paw double-clicks on icons and the computer screen sputters and shifts. Does this mean the killer ape from "2001" has traded in his bone for a killer application? The camera then pulls back to reveal a different kind of primate, a nerd in a short-sleeved shirt brandishing an enormous, hairy glove. Then he smiles goofily and says, "Boy, that would have been even easier without the monkey glove!" However the viewer reacts to the campaign, developed by TBWA Chiat/Day of newyork, it is the most eye-catching effort in the still-nascent business of marketing computer on-line services. America Online of Vienna, Va., and its rivals, Compuserve of Columbus, Ohio, and Prodigy of White Plains, provide a combination citizens' band radio, public library and sewing bee, conducted round-the-clock on sophisticated computer networks. In the increasingly competitive marketplace for such services, one of the last concerns of these companies has been advertising. Subscribers walked in off the street, signing on faster than companies' computer networks could handle the load. A busy telephone signal often greeted new subscribers trying to use these services. Now, however, growth has slowed for Prodigy, owned by Sears, Roebuck & Company, and Compuserve, a unit of H& R Block Inc., while America Online's explosive expansion continues. Today, Prodigy's subscribers number 1.4 million, up about 8 percent from November 1994, while Compuserve's numbers are up 53 percent, to 2.2 million, according to Jupiter Communications, a consulting firm. By contrast, America Online has tripled to 4 million from 1.35 million a year ago. "We've never done a branding campaign before," said Theodore J. Leonsis, president of America Online Services Inc. "We wanted something that would be in-your-face and get us noticed, so we turned to Chiat/ Day because they walked the walk and talked the talk of cyberspace. We wanted to show diversity and humanity and fun." The campaign developed by TBWA Chiat/Day, famed for such campaigns as the Energizer battery bunny, is an often puzzling potpourri of 22 television commercials, each lasting 15 seconds. In one ad, a human caricature of a gap-toothed hillbilly is telling his daughter that he is in a computer "chat room" talking to a "fella" in distant Washington who is "pro-Nafta," as the North American Free Trade Agreement is known. Then, off screen, the sound of a shotgun, blowing away the computer screen, is heard. In a third spot, the camera pans across a huge office full of cubicles, where a white-shirted office worker is staring intently at his computer screen. "Your boss will think you're working," says an off-screen announcer. But the office worker says, "Thanks to America Online, I'm really just goofing off." America Online's rivals have taken different approaches. Prodigy's agency, Cliff Freeman & Partners in newyork, developed an ad campaign around computer bulletin boards that cleverly demonstrates the often-baffling cornucopia of information on computer networks. A fisherman wanders through a desert, a stock exchange and an opera, when all of a sudden a street bus named "Fly Fishing" comes into view. It's filled with happy fishermen and symbolizes Prodigy's "interest group" bulletin boards. Compuserve's agency, Martin/ Williams of Minneapolis, seeks to emphasize Compuserve's long-standing strength -- hundreds of data services that are more professional and business-oriented than those of Prodigy and America Online. The agency declined to discuss the television campaign, which it calls "Deeper Answers." TBWA Chiat/Day also refused to return repeated phone calls seeking comment on the advertising campaign it developed. Neither it nor America Online would detail the spending on the campaign. David Hoffman, who heads the Hoffman Group, a Woodside, Calif., consulting firm whose clients include AT&T and Motorola, said on-line services and their advertising are in unexplored territory. "By the nature of computer on-line services, it is elitist advertising placed in mass-market media like television," Mr. Hoffman said. Only 32 percent of American homes have computers, only 21 percent also have modems, and of these only 15 percent use on-line services. Therefore, Mr. Hoffman said, America Online is trying to appeal to only 6 percent of the potential national audience when it advertises on such shows as NBC's "Seinfeld." Especially with spots like "the monkey glove," America Online is in danger of alienating this audience, which might be difficult to motivate. "You have to know the joke to get the joke," Mr. Hoffman said. Gene De Rose, president of Jupiter Communications, the newyork consulting firm, disagrees. He said America Online, Prodigy and Compuserve were not competing against each other but against the Internet, which has a much more irreverent, free-form style. All three on-line companies have to struggle to avoid looking like the Reader's Digest, compared with Wired magazine. "AOL's being irreverent about themselves," Mr. De Rose said, "without necessarily talking down to their actual or potential audience."

title: Intuit Joins America Online To Create Banking Services
body: Intuit Inc. and America Online Inc. said yesterday that they would work together to develop electronic banking services for America Online's four million customers next year. The alliance brings together the maker of Quicken, the most popular personal finance program for personal computers, and America Online, the largest and fastest-growing consumer on-line information service. Terms were not disclosed, but both sides described the financial details as insignificant. As described by the two companies, Intuit will develop extensions to America Online's basic software that will give America Online users point-and-click access to their checking, savings, credit card, money market fund and brokerage records. The users will be able to pay bills and transfer funds electronically. Missing from the announcement was a list of the financial institutions that would agree to provide services to their customers over America Online. However, Scott Cook, Intuit's chairman, said he expects that most, if not all, of the financial institutions that have alliances with Intuit will open "virtual branches" on America Online next year. Those partners include American Express, Chemical Bank, Chase Manhattan Bank, H. F. Ahmanson & Company's Home Savings of America, Sun Trust Banks, the Travelers's Smith Barney, Texas Commerce Bank, Union Illinois Company's Union Bank and Wells Fargo Bank. Special software is expected to be incorporated into America Online's basic control software. A version for Windows is planned for the first half of 1996, with a Macintosh version expected at the end of the year. The America Online subscribers will not need to own Quicken. Steve Case, chairman of the on-line network, which is based in Vienna, Va., said there would be no charge to use the electronic banking features beyond basic America Online connection rates. America Online now charges $9.95 a month for up to 10 hours of connection time, with an hourly surcharge thereafter. However, the participating banks are expected to charge customers a fee, either monthly or per transaction, to use the electronic services.
