America Online is counting on banking and bill-paying services to create customer loyalty in an industry that is notoriously fickle. One recent study of on-line services calculated that as many as 45 percent of subscribers leave a service in a given year to try another. "Once people build a habit, they are less likely to switch services," Mr. Case observed. Both companies stressed that their alliance was not exclusive, and that they were free to work with other partners to develop electronic banking services. Intuit has developed a wide range of financial information services on the Internet's World Wide Web, and a subsidiary, Intuit Services Inc. of Chicago, handles electronic transactions for banks, brokerages and personal computer programs, including Microsoft Money, a Quicken competitor. The alliance between Intuit and America Online is likely to strain the once-close relationship Intuit had with the Microsoft Corporation, which has a competing on-line service, the Microsoft Network. Earlier this year, Microsoft called off a proposed $1.2 billion merger with Intuit after the Justice Department raised antitrust concerns. Shares of Intuit Inc. fell 75 cents yesterday to $82.25. America Online, the largest short-selling position on the American Stock Exchange, fell slightly more than $1, to slightly more than $80.50, in Nasdaq trading.  Apple Buys an Interest WASHINGTON, Nov. 13 (By Bloomberg Business News) -- Apple Computer Inc. has exercised a warrant to buy 5.1 percent of America Online Inc. for a fraction of the $161.5 million market value, according to a Government filing made today. The warrant to buy two million common shares was exercised on Nov. 9, according to a document filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Apple acquired option contracts last February, giving it the right to buy the shares for $12.5 million. America Online's stock has more than doubled since February. Apple recently said it would scrap its own on-line service and turn it into an Internet-based service.

title: Sega's Opening Move in Multiplayer Games
body: Sega Enterprises Ltd., one of the world's two leading video game makers, plans to announce on Monday that it is creating an independent software company to develop multiplayer games for personal computers and Sega video game machines. The new computer games would be accessible over the Internet and could be joined simultaneously by players at sites all over the country or, in some cases, the world. Analysts believe that multiplayer gaming is poised to become the fastest- growing segment of a $4.4 billion unitedstates video game industry. The video game industry has been dominated by two Japanese manufacturers, Nintendo and Sega, who won it away from the Atari Corporation in the mid-1980's by producing more appealing games. Sega's chairman, Isao Okawa, said he wanted to put the new company -- to be called Sega Soft -- in California to take advantage of what he perceived as this country's more entrepreneurial business climate. Sega is allying itself with Accel Partners, a venture capital firm in San Francisco, to tap into Silicon Valley's ability to quickly create companies that are more adroit at taking advantage of new markets than their larger competitors. As if to underscore his preference for the unitedstates, Mr. Okawa, who, at least in Japanese terms, is a brash and unconventional businessman, said that he planned to move to the San Francisco Bay area himself. His decision to use the Internet and the World Wide Web as both the way to sell the new breed of computer games and the way to play them provides yet more evidence that the Internet is rewriting the rules in every corner of the computer industry. Mr. Okawa, who is also the head of the CSK Corporation, the largest independent software development company in Japan, said on Friday that he had decided to adopt the Internet strategy after listening to discussions at a symposium he sponsors each year on information technology at a Northern California resort he owns. "I have come to realize that we are entering a time for the U.S. to lead the world into a new era of technology," he said. "Creative thinking is the key to the future, and the critical mass of creativity is here in Silicon Valley." Sega Soft, which will be independent from Sega and will have outside venture and corporate investors when it begins operations in December with a staff of 250, is planning to develop a new class of games that would permit people to compete interactively on their computer or game machine screens, even though they may be separated by thousands of miles. It will be run by Nobee Mii, a former I.B.M. executive who is credited with leading the development of that company's notebook computer business. Mr. Mii left the International Business Machines Corporation three months ago to join Accel Partners. Sega Soft, Mr. Mii said, has been set up as an independent start-up company, and not a division of Sega, so that it can attract software and game designers who would share in an initial public stock offering, if there is one. The new venture comes as the video game industry is entering a perilous transition period. All of the major players, including Sega, Nintendo, Atari, 3DO and a new entry, the Sony Corporation, are focusing on the next generation of 32- and 64-bit game machines, and industry analysts believe that there will be a shakeout because the market will not support all of the competing platforms. This is not the first attempt to create new technology initiatives in Silicon Valley by creating alliances between Japanese consumer electronic companies and new technology start-up ventures. Trip Hawkins, a longtime personal computer and software game executive, started the 3DO Company with the support of Japanese companies like the Matsushita Corporation, and General Magic was created by a small group of Apple Computer developers with backing from Sony and others. A number of companies are already rushing to use the Internet to support multiplayer gaming. Games such as Doom, a popular adventure game that involves shooting at enemies controlled by players at remote computers, was first distributed as a free preview edition over the Internet. Game players could play the first several levels before deciding to buy the more elaborate commercial version. Tom Kalinske, president and chief executive of Sega of America, who will share the title of chief executive of Sega Soft with Mr. Mii, said the new company was just beginning to explore the kinds of games that might be successful on the Internet. He said he could conceive of a multiplayer flight simulator game in which players might be charged for software permitting them to "fly" more powerful jet fighters, giving them an edge over their rivals. Mr. Kalinske said that Sega was planning to use Sun Microsystems' Java programming language to develop its new games. Java, the language Sun has indicated it will use on the Internet and the World Wide Web, is designed to permit programs to safely move from computer to computer without the danger of spreading viruses and other security threats. The Sega executives acknowledged that the success of the venture would be determined by their ability to quickly develop "hit" titles, much like the movie business. "This is going to pivot on good game play," said John Shoch, a partner at the Asset Management Corporation, a venture capital firm in Palo Alto, Calif. "There are bunch of very high profile games that just went splat." The Accel executives said that compared with some Japanese executives who weigh strategic decisions for a long time, Mr. Okawa had moved quickly to adopt the new Internet strategy. "He decided to do this after one meeting with us," said Joseph Schoendorf, a venture capitalist and a partner at Accel.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
6 Newspapers Put Help-Wanted Ads on Line
body: Six of the country's largest newspapers said yesterday that they had begun a job-listings service on the Internet that provides access to their combined help-wanted advertising. The newspapers are The Boston Globe, The Chicago Tribune, The Los Angeles Times, The newyork Times, The San Jose Mercury News and The Washington Post. The new service began providing electronic access yesterday to the help-wanted advertisements printed in the six newspapers. Executives at the papers said the service, called CareerPath.com (http://www.careerpath.com), would eventually be expanded to carry classified advertising purchased to appear exclusively on the Internet. They also said they planned to add other services to allow advertisers and job seekers to search electronic listings to match candidates with jobs. Some analysts said the move by the newspapers was largely defensive, because it is widely believed that on-line advertising will ultimately pose a broad challenge to newspaper classified advertising. By trying to establish an early presence in this expanding market, the analysts said, the newspapers hope to preserve their classified-advertising revenue, which is estimated to make up about 35 percent of the total revenue from printed advertising in newspapers. Miles Groves, the chief economist of the Newspaper Association of America, said the venture showed that newspapers were trying to keep control of their classified ad business. "The reality is if we're not there doing it, somebody else will be," he said. John Morton, a newspaper analyst, said electronic delivery of classified advertising was untested as an important source of revenue. He added that the move by the six papers had the potential to be significant financially but "whether it's going to be a plus or a minus remains to be seen." Among other concerns, analysts say newspapers' electronic advertising could eventually compete against the papers' own print advertising. There have been efforts for years to create national on-line businesses based on help-wanted advertising, but some of the early efforts have failed. Many newspapers, employment agencies, universities and corporations already list job openings on the Internet and on-line services. Timothy J. Landon, a vice president of The Chicago Tribune, said the newspapers did not expect substantial revenue for the first six months to a year. But, he said, "we expect significant revenues" after that. Executives of the newspapers said they were working to expand the service to many newspapers beyond the initial six. Each paper will set its own fees for the electronic advertising. Initially, the advertisements in most of the participating newspapers will be reproduced electronically at no extra charge. But analysts expect the papers will eventually charge advertisers additional fees for electronic distribution. Executives of the papers said that in addition to job listings, they planned to introduce a resume data base and a feature that would alert employers to applicants fitting certain profiles and applicants to specific job openings. Some of those services could be offered as premium services with special charges to employers or job applicants, or to both. The Chicago Tribune currently charges advertisers an additional fee of $1 a line for electronic distribution on a local electronic job listing run by the newspaper. Tribune executives said they would keep that charge in place but would add the advertisements to the new national service without another fee. Executives at The Washington Post said they expected to add additional fees for electronic distribution in January. The newyork Times's Sunday classified advertising is currently available on America Online. The paper had previously announced plans to place its help-wanted advertising on the Internet.

title: Easing Limits on Legal Publishing
body: Lawyers everywhere would love to pull court opinions into their computers free -- or at least for a lot less than the two big commercial legal-research services charge. And increasingly, that's possible. But it's not easy, at least while a dispute in the legal publishing industry frustrates competition from smaller publishers. While law librarians struggle to organize court opinions gathered electronically and put them on the Internet, scores of small publishers are marketing data bases and CD-ROM's that offer legal reference materials. The West Publishing Company, which has dominated the print market in these materials for decades, estimates the number of these publishers at nearly 200, up from 65 in 1992. "The vast majority are in the CD-ROM market and I'd expect that to grow at a brisk pace," said Joe Acton of Timeline Publishing in Bellevue, Wash., which runs a data base of court decisions. Timeline's data base, available for $6.25 to $10 an hour, includes decisions from the Supreme Court, Federal appeals courts and other courts in about 40 states. It also offers some statutes, court rulings and Federal agency rules. Mr. Acton said he expected to open a site on the Internet's World Wide Web this month. But for now, Timeline and nearly every other electronic publisher are vastly outgunned by West Publishing's Westlaw on-line service and by Lexis, the first legal publishing company to go electronic. The problem: West has made copyright claims on its case-citation system, which directs readers to specific cases and is recognized by most courts. West's on-line citation numbers refer to its volumes, which for decades have included all Federal and most state court decisions. Lexis, which is owned by Reed-Elsevier, can use those citation numbers under a licensing agreement with West. But a small CD-ROM publisher cannot afford that. And small publishers have shied away from using West's citation system, uncertain about what is permissible and worried about being sued. As a result, Mr. Acton said, most lawyers use the more familiar and comprehensive Lexis or Westlaw research services, which can cost more than $200 an hour. "There's a premium associated with information that's public domain," he said. "Small firms don't have the resources and they can't compete." Alan D. Sugarman, a CD-ROM publisher in Manhattan, said, "West always takes the position that it's, quote, 'available,' " to lawyers because they can look up cases in books in a law library. "But it's not 'available,' even in Manhattan," he added. "A lot of my customers are people in remote areas, where the only library is the county law library and it closes at 5 o'clock." Mr. Sugarman's company, Hyperlaw Inc., issues a CD-ROM, updated quarterly, that costs $450 a year for sole practitioners and $650 a year for larger firms. It contains Federal statutes, Supreme Court opinions going back to 1990 and appellate court opinions dating to 1993. West has generally won disputes in courts and legislatures. Mr. Sugarman has joined a large publisher, Matthew Bender, in challenging West's copyright claim in Federal court. But for the most part the small publishers have sought to bypass Westlaw and Lexis and persuade the courts to accept an alternative citation system that would be universal and not copyrightable. The publishers are also lobbying the courts to make opinions more accessible on line. Supreme Court decisions are available on the Internet, and all Federal appellate decisions can be retrieved for 75 cents a minute from electronic bulletin boards set up by the courts, but only three of the 94 Federal district courts release decisions on line. Eleanor J. Lewis, executive director of the American Association of Legal Publishers, a trade group, said that all district court opinions were stored electronically and could be released to electronic bulletin boards. "It's insane not to send district court opinions out electronically because they're already sitting there," she said. "Hundreds of agencies are putting stuff on the Internet for free every day, but the courts are not. They're not interested." Mr. Sugarman said: "It's almost a moral issue. The courts have two jobs: to issue the opinions -- to make law, in other words -- and to disseminate their opinions. They've abdicated their responsibilities." Most judges think otherwise. David A. Sellers, a spokesman for the Administrative Office of the unitedstates Courts, points out that the judiciary has a home page on the World Wide Web with instructions for access to the appeals courts' bulletin boards. For the district courts to do the same "would be a huge project," he said, because putting so many courts on line would be very expensive. Meanwhile, several law schools are collecting appellate opinions and putting them on the Internet. Some circuit courts have also waived the 75-cents-a-minute fee charged for the Federal Government's electronic distribution system. Henry H. Perritt Jr., a law professor at Villanova University who has led the effort to get on-line access to court opinions, said recent Supreme Court opinions, most of the circuit courts' opinions and material from many Federal agencies were available through the law schools' Internet links. But Mr. Perritt conceded, happily, that organizing information and devising research systems was a job for publishers and that Westlaw and Lexis were especially good at it. "Both do superb jobs," he said, adding that they are powerful and have well-designed search engines. "Nobody else in the world has anything remotely like this, and I doubt that what we're doing will ever be as good as high-end commercial publishers." Graphic   Photo: Alan D. Sugarman's Manhattan company Hyperlaw publishes legal material quarterly on CD-ROM's. (Chang W. Lee for The newyork Times)  Graph: "More Appeals, More Decisions, More Paper" shows the number of pages printed in the West Publishing's Federal Reporter series from '65 to '94 (Source: West Publishing)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
A report lays down guidelines for any attempt to measure the efficiency of interactive ads.
body: IN the constantly changing world of interactive advertising, "hits" are flops. That's an important conclusion of a report examining one of the most closely watched and contentious subjects confronting advertisers, agencies and researchers today: assuring accurate and comprehensive measurement of consumer exposure to advertisements that appear in interactive media like World Wide Web sites and on-line services. The report, "Guiding Principles of Interactive Media Audience Measurement," was presented yesterday at a news conference in midtown Manhattan by the Coalition for Advertising Supported Information and Entertainment, or Casie. That organization was formed last year by the Association of National Advertisers and the American Association of Advertising Agencies after marketing giants like the Procter & Gamble Company warned Madison Avenue to accelerate efforts to understand and use interactive media. Judy E. Black, who oversaw the report, said, "For the new media to succeed, they must offer the advertising industry acceptable measures of the advertising opportunities they deliver and a means to measure them against comparative alternatives." The relative lack of such assurances is a big reason why advertising remains a minor revenue source for most interactive media. Described as a working paper, the report declares that hits -- a measure of the gross number of requests for information or files from a specific Web site -- are "the least desirable level at which to measure cyberspace media." The reason, the report said, is that hits, which are a popular form of measurement among interactive-media companies, represent "a rubber yardstick" that inflates use by registering usage regardless of whether material is actually reviewed. " 'Hits' implies that the user has been exposed to the deeper material, which may never have been selected for display on the screen," the report found. Instead, the report recommended, interactive media ought to adopt methods equivalent to those used by conventional media, which tally user information in more familiar -- and more accurately measurable -- areas like demographics. Casie has the support of the Advertising Research Foundation, the venerable organization in newyork that helped set standards for measuring print and broadcast media. "We're building upon earlier work for earlier media," said Ms. Black, senior partner for new-media technologies and director for interactive development at the Bozell Inc. unit of Bozell, Jacobs, Kenyon & Eckhardt in newyork. Ms. Black heads one of four Casie subcommittees. Because marketers abhor a vacuum as much as nature does, more than a dozen companies, including the A. C. Nielsen unit of the Dun & Bradstreet Corporation, have offered methods to measure ads in cyberspace. "Our interactive media research committee will be looking at what all the companies do," Michael J. Naples, president of the Advertising Research Foundation, said, "but the industry will decide which measurements it will embrace and not embrace." "We can't have five different measurement systems out there," Ms. Black said, because it is vital to "compare apples with apples and oranges with oranges." But Casie, she added, would not "adopt any one system." Or as O. Burtch Drake, president and chief executive of the agency association, put it, "The market will decide who wins." The report also discussed these aspects of interactive media: Third party measurement and auditing. Like Ross Perot, the report favors third parties, in this instance "objective third-party research suppliers" that would measure audiences rather than relying on data from the media being measured. Comparability. Audience estimates "covering a particular interactive vehicle," according to the report, ought to be "directly comparable to estimates covering another interactive vehicle within the same interactive medium." John J. Sarsen Jr., president and chief executive of the advertisers association, said another goal was to develop data that facilitate "comparing interactive media versus other media." Privacy. "Every effort should be made to maintain consumers' privacy," the report urges, adding that identities of computer users "must not be revealed by audience measurement providers." The report will serve as the basis for further discussion, Ms. Black said, and will be refined and recast as interactive marketing matures.

title: Microsoft-Visa On-Line Plan Draws the Ire of Competitors
body: Microsoft and Visa International proposed an industry software standard for on-line payments and financial transactions yesterday, but opposition from key companies could lead to a standards war that impedes the rollout of electronic commerce over the Internet. The standard, which is based on Visa's current credit-card transaction technology used in thousands of stores, restaurants and other establishments around the world, is intended to guarantee the security and privacy of payments and purchases made via computer networks. Such security, intended to prevent thieves from intercepting credit card data sent electronically or from siphoning off electronic transfers of money, is widely seen as a necessary prerequisite to development of a true Internet economy. But critics of the Microsoft-Visa proposal said that instead of an "open" technical standard that would be freely available for use by any company, the partners were attempting to promote technology that would make the rest of the on-line world beholden to Microsoft and Visa. Although the two companies say they will freely distribute the software specifications, critics contend that the underlying programming code -- a necessary component for creating actual products -- will not be available except through licenses from Visa or Microsoft. "We feel that this standard won't be adopted broadly," said Mike Homer, a vice president at Netscape Communications Inc., a leading player in the emerging world of on-line commerce. "Microsoft is negotiating terms with individual vendors and that is totally unacceptable on the Internet, or to banks and merchants and software developers." The International Business Machines Corporation also objected, saying that the Microsoft-Visa approach could lead to a welter of competing technologies for electronic commerce that might make it difficult for merchants to serve all customers. "This needs to be in the hands of a neutral third party," said Bob Howe, I.B.M.'s general manager for banking, finance and securities. "An open standard will foster growth and increase competition. If we have multiple standards, added costs will inevitably be passed on to the consumer." Yesterday's announcement also revealed a deepening rift between Visa and the other leading credit-card provider, Mastercard International, which last summer had announced an alliance with Visa, in which the two would develop a common payment system for on-line purchases. Mastercard officials said yesterday that they had not gone along with Visa and Microsoft because they did not feel the technical specifications had been sufficiently developed, and they criticized Visa's go-it-alone stance. "It is contrary to our June 23 announcement with Visa that we would develop a single, open industry specification," Mastercard said in a news release. Yet Mastercard, too, has been pursuing a divergent path. Even while conducting joint development work with Visa, Mastercard has also been developing a competing on-line payment system. Mastercard has been developing that separate system, called Secure Courier and intended for on-line credit-card, debit-card and other types of financial transactions with Netscape, the leading publisher of software for "browsing" the Internet's World Wide Web, and with the Intuit Corporation, the leader in personal computer financial software. The partners say they intend to promote Secure Courier as an industry standard by making all the software code freely available to any company that wants to adopt it. A Microsoft official defended yesterday's announcement, saying that someone needed to take the lead in getting a security standard out in the marketplace and to avoid confusing consumers with competing approaches. "Both Microsoft and Visa recognize that both consumers and merchants would like a system that is endorsed by all major brands," said Tom Johnston, a Microsoft product manager. "If we confuse the consumer, or make it difficult for her to make purchases, then she won't shop." To be sure, Microsoft and Visa do have some influential industry supporters, including the Internet Shopping Network, one of the current leaders in on-line retailing; RSA Data Security Inc., whose data-scrambling technology provides the privacy component of the Microsoft-Visa system, and Spyglass Inc., which distributes Web-browser software that competes with Netscape. The Microsoft-Visa standard, called Secure Transaction Technology, or S.T.T., would provide specifications for software that would be designed to run on both the merchant's and the customer's computers and permit the secure and private exchange of financial information. It is based on a type of data-scrambling technology called public key cryptography that permits two parties that have not previously exchanged information to conduct a secret data conversation. The consumer impact of this intramural spat is hard to gauge. Today, when a customer pays by credit card at a store or restaurant, the point-of-sale terminal the merchant uses to electronically approve the transaction is communicating over separate dial-up networks, depending on whether the card is from Visa, Mastercard or some other credit provider. But the consumer is probably oblivious to the dueling networks operating behind the scenes, because the same credit-card terminal works with all the various networks. And yet, in the future, if incompatible technologies force merchants in the on-line world to choose between payment -- or take on the expense of adopting several systems -- consumers may find themselves with limited choices for making payments. Meanwhile, in the shorter term, some analysts say, the lack of an industry-standard transaction technology could significantly slow the advance of electronic commerce. "In the short run, it's very confusing," said Iang Jeon, an analyst at Forrester Research, a computer industry consulting firm in Cambridge, Mass.

title: Who Uses Internet? 5.8 Million Are Said to Be Linked in U.S.
body: Measuring the Internet population is a daunting challenge given the amorphous nature of cyberspace, with its lack of borders and its culture of anonymity. The latest attempt comes from O'Reilly & Associates, a publisher of computer books and Internet software, in a report to be published today. And the results look conservative: 5.8 million American adults are connected directly to the Internet. Another 3.9 million American adults use only commercial on-line services, like America Online, Compuserve and Prodigy. Estimates of Internet use worldwide have often ranged to more than 30 million, with the unitedstates representing perhaps half of the total. "We've tried to discern the real size of the Net, and we think we've got more reliable data than others," said Dick Peck, the vice president of business development for O'Reilly, which is based in Sebastopol, Calif. The method used for the O'Reilly survey, conducted with Trish Information Services, a market research firm, involved random telephone calls to 200,000 households from May to August. Of those, nearly 30,000 answered and agreed to be interviewed briefly. And of the respondents, the researchers conducted more in-depth interviews with Internet users in more than 1,100 households, and another 500 households that used commercial on-line services only. The O'Reilly firm believes its method of calculating the Internet population is more accurate than previous methods, which tended to rely on polling self-selecting groups of Internet users or estimated the number of users connected to host computers. Internet experts said that the O'Reilly survey would probably supply valuable information from the Internet and on-line households its researchers interviewed in depth. But they questioned how precise the survey was in calculating the size of the Internet population in the unitedstates. "Just because they made a lot of calls doesn't mean they have used a reliable methodology," said Donna Hoffman, an associate professor at Vanderbilt University's graduate management school. The O'Reilly research found that 67 percent of those with direct Internet access are male and over half are between the ages of 18 and 34. Their median household income was between $50,000 and $75,000, and nearly half work in organizations with more than 1,000 employees. Outside the educational field, the most frequent job occupations were sales, at 19 percent, followed by engineering, at 15 percent.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: ON THE NET;
The F.B.I. sting operation on child pornography raises questions about encryption.
body: FEDERAL agents swooped down on more than 125 homes and offices across the unitedstates on Sept. 13, seizing computers and diskettes from people suspected of trafficking in child pornography over the America Online network. But to date, the number of arrests in the sting operation remains at 15. More arrests are expected, but why haven't more occurred? Last week, Louis J. Freeh, the director of the F.B.I., offered an oblique explanation for the seemingly low initial success rate. At least some of the suspected child pornographers had used data encryption software, Mr. Freeh said Thursday in remarks at an International Cryptography Institute conference in Washington. In other words, they had scrambled their computer files so that only someone with the password -- or with proper code-breaking skills -- could view the contents. Mr. Freeh wisely did not say whether the F.B.I. agents were able to decipher the encrypted files seized in the investigation. It would be foolhardy, from a law-enforcement perspective, to tip one's hand. If the head of the F.B.I. acknowledged that his agency was powerless to crack a cryptography program like Pretty Good Privacy, the stampede for that software on the Internet would make the run on Windows 95 look puny. From a political perspective, Mr. Freeh's coyness is shrewd as well. By making even a subtle suggestion that some child pornographers may walk free because of unbreakable cryptography, he gains more leverage in seeking Government-mandated controls over the use of encryption technology. Mr. Freeh said that encryption was a "public safety" issue, and he said law-enforcement agencies around the world "will not tolerate" the use of private data encryption to impede investigations. He said encryption had also been encountered in the Philippines in a plot to blow up an American jet and to assassinate Pope John Paul II. (In that case, at least, one can presume the code was cracked.) It seems worthwhile to point out that even if the suspects in the child pornography sting, called Operation Innocent Images, used cryptography, that did not provide evidence that they were doing something illegal. Our legal system is predicated on the belief that one is innocent unless proved guilty, and there is no exception clause for technology. "Fortunately we are not yet at the point where the mere use of encryption overcomes the presumption of innocence," said David Sobel, staff counsel for the Electronic Privacy Information Center in Washington. Another point to remember is that the F.B.I. identified more than 100 suspects, and gathered sufficient information to warrant raids, using existing laws and enforcement techniques. On the other hand, there is no denying that child pornographers use data encryption to keep co-workers, family members and police from discovering their secrets. "We are involved in a couple of jobs every week resolving some kind of a child pornography investigation," said Eric K. Thompson, president of Access Data Inc. of Orem, Utah, a private company that specializes in cracking encrypted files for corporations and Government agencies. The Government's elite code-breakers at the National Security Administration are prohibited by law from using their talents against American citizens. The F.B.I. has its own code-cracking experts, but it routinely calls on independent experts like Access Data to help on some cases. After eight years of breaking into encrypted files, ranging from situations involving secretaries who simply forgot their passwords for important memos to cases involving corporate computer systems that were encrypted by disgruntled employees, Mr. Thompson has concluded: "Basically, the criminal element is becoming more computer literate, and they are discovering encryption. Files are becoming more difficult to break." Dorothy Denning, an expert in cryptography and a professor of computer science at Georgetown University in Washington, said she recognized the importance of encryption for businesses seeking to protect information. At the same time, she said, she also recognized the problems that law-enforcement agencies face because of cryptography. "So many people had been saying people in law enforcement weren't having this problem, and I didn't believe that," Dr. Denning said. So in May, she said, she spent two days calling sources at law-enforcement organizations. "I came up with over 20 cases -- child pornography, terrorism, murder, embezzlement, fraud, tax protesters, export violations -- and, in some cases, they were able to crack it, and others they couldn't," she said. What can be done? The Administration's plan is to seek voluntary compliance with a "key escrow" plan, which would enable citizens to use strong, private cryptography as long as a copy of the software "key" were made available to law enforcement officials. Last week, Mr. Freeh stressed that he preferred a voluntary approach. But "if consensus is impossible" on the encryption issue, he said, the F.B.I. might consider other approaches. The debate is certain to heat up as more information about Operation Innocent Images becomes known. There are no comforting answers, only an echo of advice from a time predating the Internet: There is no solution. Seek it wisely. Graphic   Drawing.

title: Company Says Electronic Mail Was Opened to Find Pornography
body: Responding to court orders related to a nationwide crackdown on the electronic transmission of child pornography, the America Online information service gave law enforcement agents access to the private electronic mailboxes of an unknown number of its subscribers, company officials confirmed yesterday. By reading and tracing electronic mail messages as they coursed through the America Online system, agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation were able to identify several thousand users of the service who viewed digitized images of children in sexual poses. They were also able to follow the electronic trail of messages beyond America Online identifying many more computer users nationwide who stored and traded pedophilic material, people familiar with the investigation said. America Online, which is based in Vienna, Va., is the nation's largest on-line information service, with 3.5 million subscribers. At least a dozen people suspected of being among the most active traders of child pornography on the computer network were arrested on Wednesday as part of the investigation, and the inquiry is continuing. The Justice Department indicated Wednesday that many more arrests were planned, but it released no new information yesterday. At least some of the arrests resulted from undercover operations conducted on America Online in the past year by law enforcement agents pretending to be boys and girls, court records say. In one case, an adult investigator posing as a teen-age girl on an America Online public forum invited a Las Vegas, Nev., man to cross state lines to have sex. He was arrested when he arrived at a motel suggested by the "girl." In other cases, an America Online spokeswoman said yesterday, concerned subscribers got in touch with either the F.B.I. or network administrators to complain about lewd pictures arriving unsolicited in their electronic mailboxes. Copies of the objectionable images were then provided to the F.B.I. by America Online, and the agency obtained court orders to search themailboxes of the senders, said the spokeswoman, Pam McGraw. Depending on the volume of mail a person receives, electronic mail messages can remain in an electronic mailbox for days or weeks, until they are deleted or displaced by newer messages. Because electronic mail has a life of days or weeks, can be traced and can be easily copied without alerting the owner, reading themailboxes was particularly effective. Ms. McGraw strongly denied yesterday that digital images of child pornography existed in any public areas of the service. It was unclear yesterday how much information about America Online subscribers is kept as a routine part of operating the electronic network and how much private information was provided to law enforcement officials. On many computer networks, administrators are able to automatically keep track of all actions undertaken by individual users, from the moment they log on to the system to the moment they sign off. Such records reveal much more personal information than the records a telephone company routinely keeps on each customer's phone calls. Ms. McGraw said America Online kept records of only the basic information needed to bill the subscriber, including the user's name, address, credit card information and time spent on line in each session. The company also keeps aggregate data of the total time spent by all users each day in specific areas of the service. In the F.B.I.'s announcement of a series of raids and arrests on Wednesday, it said it had concentrated its four-year investigation on America Online because of complaints of child pornography circulating there. Representatives of Compuserve Inc. and the Prodigy Services Company, the second- and third-largest on-line services, respectively, said they had not heard from the F.B.I. or any other other law enforcement agency about any investigation of child pornographers and pedophiles. While applauding the arrests, representatives of the other on-line services said they feared that the crackdown could have a negative impact on the on-line services industry, which serves more than eight million Americans. "There are a whole lot of hysterical stories going around that leave potential on-line customers with the impression there is nothing but pornography out there," said a Compuserve spokesman, R. Pierce Reid. The arrests are occurring just as Congress is preparing to debate several legislative proposals to place restrictions on the Internet and commercial on-line services in an attempt to stanch the flow of child pornography. Jerry Berman, executive director of the Center for Democracy and Technology, a public policy lobbying group, said, "We think this investigation establishes what we've been saying all along: that the existing laws work, that the industry will cooperate with law enforcement, and there is no need for flawed legislation that violates Constitutional rights."

title: Electronic Meeting Places Include Some Dark Alleys
body: If America Online took physical form as a city, it would be one of the largest metropolitan areas in the unitedstates, with 3.5 million residents. Like any big city, America Online has scores of public parks and theaters, thousands of bars and cafes, and -- as the Justice Department crackdown on child pornography made clear yesterday -- some dark alleys and back rooms where a few unsavory characters conduct illicit business. The same laws exist that make it illegal to prey on children in the physical world apply in cyberspace. And just as they do in real cities, crimes against children occur nonetheless, usually out of sight. Since 1991, agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation have been looking into the use of electronic mail to transmit digital images of child pornography among a relatively small number of America Online subscribers. There have been several arrests since then, although the dozen arrests made yesterday appeared to be the largest nationwide crackdown to date on electronic child pornography. For those unfamiliar with electronic networks, it can be unclear how people can exchange obscene or illegal images without detection. On computer networks, all information -- from simple text notes to pictures and sound clips -- is transmitted in the form of computer file made up of strings of 1's and 0's. Without actually opening the files and viewing them on a computer screen, it is impossible to determine whether the stream of digital bits holds a copy of the First Amendment, a letter or a picture of a 10-year-old engaged in a sex act. Under the Electronic Communications Privacy Act of 1986, Congress made it illegal for operators of computer networks like America Online, which is by far the nation's largest network, are prohibited from reading or monitoring private electronic mail messages sent over the systems without a search warrant or equivalent legal authority. The electronic privacy laws prevent network operators from secretly reading themail of their subscribers, but they also enable child pornographers to trade illegal images on a public network. In contrast to the privacy of electronic mail, America Online and other popular computer services, including Compuserve Inc. and the Prodigy Services Company, routinely monitor messages posted to public spaces on their systems, including electronic discussion forums and "chat rooms." Law-enforcement officials, private individuals, ordinary subscribers and representatives of the on-line services routinely visit and monitor the activity of these public areas, especially those that cater to younger members. Typically, any member discovered posting public messages of a suggestive or abusive nature, or soliciting or offering obscene images, is kicked off the system by having the account revoked. In more serious incidents involving clearly pornographic images the network could contact law-enforcement officials. Because of its privacy, electronic mail is a more popular way to exchange pornographic material on commercial on-line services. The only way the authorities find out about violations of the guidelines is if a member contacts the on-line service or a law-enforcement agency. But the question remains, how do people who share a common interest in child pornography meet on-line in the first place?  Often it is in areas of the network, "chat rooms" where two or more members can exchange typewritten messages as quickly as if they were sitting at keyboards on opposite sides of a desk. Their messages are posted publicly, for anyone to see. Using code words that signify child pornography, the two or more members then connect and arrange to exchange private messages. They drop off to chat privately, using a form of instant electronic mail, and send the images to one another's private electronic mailboxes. Occasionally they send an image to the wrong electronic address, and the surprised recipient typically notifies the authorities, or, as is increasingly the case, the soliciting member turns out to be a law-enforcement agent pretending to be a pornographer. Representatives of the on-line services said they notified law-enforcement agencies as soon as it became clear that illegal acts were occurring on the networks. All said they cooperated fully with the legal authorities in the case of subpoenas. As for solicitation of minors for sex, most cases appear to originate in chat rooms, where adults can masquerade as children, and where unsupervised children often conduct conversations with strangers. Once contact is established, the discussions typically move to private channels, the dark alleys of cyberspace.

title: Use of Computer Network For Child Sex Sets Off Raids
body: The Justice Department today announced a dozen arrests in a two-year investigation into the use of America Online, the country's largest computer network, to distribute child pornography and to lure minors into sex. The searches of 125 homes and offices around the country represented the largest investigation by Federal agents into the misuse of a nationwide computer network, in which information is exchanged between computers. Justice Department officials said the cities in which the searches took place included newyork, Newark, Dallas and Miami, and added that many more arrests were expected. "We are not going to permit exciting new technology to be misused to exploit and injure children," Attorney General Janet Reno said today in announcing the arrests. The culmination of the inquiry by the Federl Bureau of Investigation comes at a time when the agency has needed some favorable attention to offset a string of incidents that have cast it in a negative light. Its officials have come under fire for their role in the siege at Waco, Tex., the standoff with a white separatist in Idaho and, most recently, over an attempt to cover up aspects in the Idaho incident. The bureau said in the course of the investigation it collected pornographic evidence involving mostly victims of ages 2 to 13 who were pictured either nude or engaged in actual or simulated sexual acts. The Justice Department said the investigation began in 1991 and accelerated in 1993 after the abduction of a 10-year-old boy from his neighborhood in Brentwood, Md., a suburb of Washington. The boy, George Stanley Burdynski, has not been found. During that investigation, the Federal and state authorities focused on two suspects believed to have exploited juveniles in the Mid-Atlantic States, officials said. The investigation of them unearthed evidence that adults and minors were regularly using computers, linked through America Online and similar services, to transmit explicit images of juveniles. In addition, adults were using the service to seek out minors for sexual encounters. As a result of the Burdynski inquiry, agents in the Baltimore office of the F.B.I. and state authorities in Florida set up an undercover operation. Several of the arrests today resulted from agents' posing as minors and being recruited for sexual liaisons by adults using computer bulletin boards. The investigation focused on users of America Online because it had been used by the suspects in the Burdynski case and had been the subject of complaints, the Justice Department said. It added that the F.B.I. found that similar activities took place on several other on-line services in varying degrees. In a statement today, America Online, a service based in Vienna, Va., with 3.5 million subscribers, said it fully cooperated with the Federal investigators. The company said that conversations between people using its service were private, but that it did not knowingly tolerate the use its network for any illegal activities. A Justice Department official said the company itself was not a subject of the investigation. The F.B.I. said in a statement that the investigation had demonstrated how child pornographers were increasingly using computer networks. "The utilization of on-line services or bulletin board systems is rapidly becoming one of the most prevalent techniques for individuals to share pornographic pictures of minors, as well as to identify and recruit children into sexually illicit relationships," the agency said. It is a violation of Federal law to create, possess or disseminate child pornography, and those convicted of such a crime face up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine. Lawmakers have debated whether to restrict the use of computer networks. Today, a bill making it illegal to use computers to produce child pornography was introduced by Senator Orrin G. Hatch, the Utah Republican who heads the Judiciary Committee. The bill would expand the definition of child pornography to include any photograph, film, videotape or computer image produced by any means, including electronically by computer, if it depicts or appears to depict a minor engaging in sexually explicit conduct. "Today, visual depictions of children engaging in any imaginable form of sexual conduct can be produced entirely by computer, without using children, thereby placing such depictions outside the scope of Federal law," Mr. Hatch said in a statement. The Senate has passed a bill to outlaw pornography on the Internet computer network. The abduction of the Burdynski boy touched off an intense investigation that eventually faded from public attention. But the family kept up the search, and after more than a year two men, James A. Kowalski and Stephen Leak, were charged with molesting boys in the Burdynskis' neighborhood. Mr. Kowalski pleaded guilty to sexually abusing two of the boy's friends. Mr. Leak was found guilty of molesting another of the boy's friends. Neither man has been charged in the disappearance of the Burdynski youth.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: ON THE NET;
Privacy for computers? Clinton sets the stage for a debate on data encryption.
body: IN terms of its ability to raise the nation's blood pressure, the debate over data encryption has not yet reached the same levels as gun control. But last week the Clinton Administration appeared to set the stage for an equally divisive debate over the degree to which businesses and individuals have the right to keep secrets when using telephones, computers and other forms of electronic communications. In two days of public hearings last week in Gaithersburg, Md., home of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the Administration introduced its long-awaited proposals to relax restrictions on the export of cryptographic software. The Administration drew a line in the virtual sands of cyberspace, signaling that it is willing to permitAmericans to put stronger cryptographic locks on their electronic data only if a spare key to those locks is made available on demand to law-enforcement agencies. There looms the conflict. Although the debate is about export controls, the "export" issue is irrelevant in today's era of global electronic networks. Placing a common privacy program on an Internet computer in Austin, Tex., is effectively no different from sending a shrink-wrapped copy of the program to Moscow. The real issue is how much privacy the Government is willing to allow its own citizens, and the latest word from the Clinton Administration is that the right to electronic privacy, like the right to bear arms, is not absolute. Cryptography is the science of secret writing. In this digital era, it applies not just to notes, but also to telephone calls, money transfers, bank and credit card records, electronic mail, faxes and other computer files. The Clinton Administration's goal is to allow Americans to use the strongest possible cryptographic technology, while at the same time preserving the ability of law-enforcement agencies to perform court-authorized wiretaps as part of the effort to catch drug dealers, terrorists, child pornographers and other miscreants. In other words, it favors strong cryptography, but not too strong. The strength of cryptographic software is measured by the length of the software key necessary to encode and decode a message. The longer the key, the harder it is for an unauthorized user to decipher the message. In recent years, the Government has generally permitted Americans to export cryptographic software with key lengths up to 40 bits. Experts say that 40-bit keys are secure from casual snooping, but will fall quickly to a determined codebreaker. Last week, after more than a year of intense analysis, the Government introduced what it said was the best possible compromise. Under the new policy, companies can export encryption algorithms using 64-bit keys, which are much more secure, but only if spare keys are given to "escrow agents" who would make them available to law- enforcement agents under standard legal procedures, similar to legal wiretaps authorized by a judge. Otherwise, the 40-bit limit continues to apply. Such a "key escrow" scheme is anathema to many privacy advocates who fear Government abuses. The Government first proposed a key escrow system with its so-called Clipper Chip, a technology that failed to win acceptance even as a voluntary standard. The new scheme is somewhat more palatable than Clipper. Key escrow is still unpopular with American computer and software companies, which say it prevents them from competing against foreign companies that have no similar constraints, and with many multinational corporations, which say it prevents them from working with foreign companies that do not especially care for the idea of Uncle Sam holding the keys to their data banks. "If this was intended to be any sort of compromise, I don't think it achieved its end," said Whitfield Diffie, a Sun Microsystems engineer who attended the meetings. "I didn't see anybody who was enthusiastic." Raymond G. Kammer, deputy director of N.I.S.T., suggested that the hearings last week were intended to elicit public comment, and that the Administration's final position on cryptographic policy were still under analysis. But the emergence of key escrow issues at the N.I.S.T. proceedings suggests that key escrow is emerging as a nonnegotiable demand by some factions of the Clinton Administration, especially the Justice Department and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, led by Louis Freeh. "If this fails," said a figure familiar with the Administration's thinking on the proposed change in cryptographic policy, "it's going to lead to a very divisive debate. And the irony, for libertarians who oppose key escrow, is that if it fails, I am convinced that Louis Freeh cannot be true to his job without proposing domestic controls on data encryption." "He's not going to give up without a fight, and neither is the Justice Department," said the figure, who spoke on the condition he not be identified. Others say they do not think the Clinton Administration has yet arrived at a concrete position, even after more than a year of study and debate. "I don't think it's a final offer," said John Gilmore, an engineer at Cygnus Support, a computer company in Mountain View, Calif. "It looks to me like a weak strawman, a first offer, a proposal to dance." The question is whether American citizens and businesses have the patience to wait for the music to start. And the issue may be moot, anyway, because the Internet is no more controlled by the unitedstates than is the United Nations. "The Internet Architecture Board has specifically decided to ignore export controls in designing the security infrastructure for the next generation of Internet protocols," Mr. Gilmore said. "The Internet of 1998 will provide automatic, secure, and fully private communication, without key escrow, internationally." In other words, the Internet community is already planning to jump over the new line in the sand drawn last week by the Administration. Cryptogrophy that is stronger than the Government's proposed system will be built into the Internet by a dozen countries, and American companies and individuals would be foolish not to use it. At that point, millions of Americans will come into direct conflict with Government policy, and the popular gun-control bumper sticker may be replaced by one that says, "If cryptography is outlawed, only outlaws will have cryptography."

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
New Alliances For On-Line Work
body: Four interactive alliances have been announced. The SFM Media Corporation in newyork, the media buying service, has formed a joint venture with Digital Brands Inc. in newyork, a developer of digital and interactive technologies, to be known as SFM/Digital Brands. George Asposporos, 38, president of Digital, will head the joint venture as president and will oversee interactive initiatives for SFM clients like American Isuzu Motors and the MCI Communications Corporation. Nielsen Media Research in newyork, owned by the Dun & Bradstreet Corporation, and the Internet Profiles Corporation in San Francisco, which provides services for World Wide Web sites, have teamed to introduce measurement and evaluation services for the Internet. They plan to market two services of Internet Profiles, which is known as I/Pro. The services, I/Count and I/ Audit, will be marketed as Nielsen I/ Pro I/Count and Nielsen I/Pro I/ Audit. Also, Muzak in Seattle and Coupons Online in newyork have formed a joint venture that includes the marketing of interactive coupons and promotional programs for retailers. Muzak has also been granted an option to acquire an undisclosed stake in Coupons Online. And Targetbase Marketing in Irving, Tex., a direct marketing division of the M/A/R/C Group, has teamed up with Big Hand Inc., an interactive multimedia developer in Dallas, to create interactive media programs for clients of both companies. The companies plan their initial joint offerings to be marketing programs using new media like interactive kiosks and World Wide Web sites.

title:
PRACTICAL TRAVELER;
Booking a Trip On the Internet
body: JUST a few months ago it was all but impossible for do-it-yourself travelers to make reservations on the Internet, or even find any meaningful information beyond an 800 telephone number to call. Over the summer, however, some of the functions of travel agents' computerized reservations systems have been popping up on service providers' World Wide Web sites. The Web, a method of cruising the Internet that relies on slick graphics and text rather than arcane computer language, hides the plethora of mind-numbing commands used in travel industry computers. Travelers can now fiddle with reservations for hours -- as long as they don't mind dealing with the few dozen companies that accept on-line reservations. (The difficulty of insuring credit-card security has so far limited their numbers.) Even campsites in South Africa can be reserved on the Web. Although the vast majority of travel industry Web sites still display little more than copies of pamphlets, change is fast approaching. Travel agencies have long handled inquiries via the international collection of networks and communications systems that forms the Internet, but until recently there was no direct access to reservation computers from the Web. Service providers -- airlines, hotels, car-rental agencies and the like -- largely ceded booking operations on the Internet to retail travel agents, some of whom maintain elaborate Web sites that act as brochures, travel posters and electronic newsletters.  Access Widens Fast modems and, significantly, high-speed office and university computer networks have given millions of computer owners access to businesses that own Web sites. Even subscribers to such traditional on-line services as Prodigy and America Online now have access to the Web through personal computers. Companies familiar to business travelers are risking the open waters of a direct connection to the Web, trying to gauge the right mixture of style, substance and security. Hotels and rental-car agencies took the earliest steps, partly because security concerns restricted airlines' abilities to process credit-card information over the wide-open spaces of the Internet. Reservation systems, notably American Airlines' Saabre, have been popular features of such services as Prodigy and America Online for several years. The ability to offer sophisticated software and the relative privacy of on-line services, which require a password for access, allowed reservation systems to flourish in safety. The Web, however, is terra incognita and the airlines, especially, are proceeding cautiously. They will be competing with hundreds of companies in the travel industry that have found the Web an affordable alternative to sponsoring on-line services.  Checking Airlines Of the 30 or so airlines with Web pages, Southwest Airlines and American Airlines offered the most extensive sites recently, although Qantas's effort, brimming with cute pictures of cuddly koalas, may be the most charming. None offered reservations, although Southwest and American have posted their schedules on line and are reported to be working on reservations systems. Nonetheless, several other sites allow Web surfers to make reservations directly, bypassing travel agents. Typical in a recent electronic tour was the Web site belonging to Holiday Inns: Simple-to-follow pages led through a series of maps and questionnaires until a destination was selected. Hotel choice was based on a combination of nearby highways, tourist attractions or cities; the resulting list of properties contained just about all of the information needed to make a decision, including rates. Confirming a reservation involved clicking on a button and answering a few questions. At Alamo, renting a car was almost as simple, but descriptions of rental locations were, at best, terse. Chicago, for example, had three Alamo rental locations but none listed for O'Hare Airport. It turns out that the Franklin Park office serves O'Hare, the world's busiest airport. A novice traveler would never know. Hilton Hotels, whose Web site was among the easiest to use, provided exterior pictures of its hotels and an easy method of sorting through the tangle of pages. Users could skip directly to an item of interest by entering a word or phrase. Entering a telephone area code, such as 312 for Chicago, yielded a list of all hotels within the area. Hilton eschewed the lengthy reservation-questionnaire approach favored by Holiday Inns. Instead, its page provided a blank box to be filled with the name of any Hilton, a much faster process if the traveler already has a destination in mind. Holiday Inns' more structured approach is best for travelers who need help winnowing out unsuitable hotels. Even among the sites that don't accept on-line reservations, page complexity is rapidly growing beyond electronic handouts. Club Med constructed a series of inviting pages that included sound and clips of television commercials, which, although of limited usefulness, signaled a shift to something other than pictures of Speedo-clad couples frolicking in azure seas. Other sites are following suit, and it may not be long before travelers will be able to take video guided tours before booking. Truly helpful visual aids can be infuriatingly scarce. Holiday Inns provided an exhaustive table of distances to nearby attractions, but said that the London Mayfair Holiday Inn, at 3 Berkeley Street, was two miles from the Tower of London and 25 miles from Tower Bridge and the River Thames -- odd, since the Tower of London sits on the bank of the Thames near Tower Bridge. Hotel Discounters, a Bermuda-based booking agent, instead decided to post simple maps of London on its site, making it clear at a glance exactly what's in the neighborhood of each hotel.  Making Reservations Some companies accept reservations on the Web but don't have true on-line reservation systems. Most travel agencies and resorts fall into this category since they lack the complicated interfaces needed to link the Internet with their existing computer reservation systems. At Walt Disney World's colorful site, a "reservation request" form provided enough details so that an agent could phone back to complete the deal. The Web is an ideal place for resorts such as Walt Disney World, where myriad hotel options and seasonal promotions can cause traditional printed brochures to balloon in size. By contrast, Web sites can be updated in minutes. In a similar vein was the site operated by the South African National Parks Board, whose properties include Kruger National Park and its renowned bushveld campgrounds. Reservations for all of Kruger's campsites could be made on a single Web page, making it easy to arrange stops at different campgrounds on consecutive nights. Payment by credit card, however, was to be faxed separately, a concession to the lack of security on the Web. More services are planned for the Web. Trade groups such as the National Tour Association are setting up cooperative Web sites, giving travelers a single place to see hundreds of companies at a glance. Major credit-card companies are working on a unified method of handling payments over the Web, which would remove a major barrier to booking trips. More airlines are also testing Web sites. Nonetheless, making complicated travel arrangements on the Web may well be impossible for some time. The sheer complexity of wading through hundreds of Web pages is daunting, even without the problem of forwarding credit-card information. Here are some tips for making travel plans on the Internet a bit easier: *Avoid making last-minute reservations on the Internet. The vagaries of Internet email may result in a reservation arriving late or not at all. Routine maintenance may also prevent you from using a Web site for several hours. *Never transmit credit-card information over the Web unless encryption, which scrambles data, is available. Never provide your card number in response to an email request. If a payment problem arises, offer to telephone or fax the information. *Make a note of 800 telephone numbers and follow up all reservations with a phone call or separate email message, even if you receive a confirmation number. *Travel-related Web sites tend to have large graphics that can be excruciatingly slow to appear during peak periods, so avoid using the Web during business hours or early evenings. For highest Web speed, use a fast modem such as those rated for 28,800 or 14,400 bits per second. *Use the latest version of your Web browser software. Most sites that accept travel reservations have been recently started or updated, which means that they may expect you to use encryption, on-line forms and other advanced graphics. *Make printouts of all Web reservations and read the fine print. Travelers may not realize that they are looking at an overseas Web site and may find their legal rights limited by local laws. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
America Online Says It's Fighting Hacker Problem
body: America Online Inc., the largest on-line service in the nation, said yesterday that it was fighting computer hackers causing problems on its service, but it would not say whether its network had been breached. The San Francisco Chronicle reported yesterday that hackers had tampered with America Online's business and customer files and created a security breach that could affect the accounts of subscribers. A spokeswoman for America Online declined to discuss details in the report but said the on-line service was continuing to change its system software to combat a hackers program called AOHell. "From time to time, we've encountered problems as it relates to AOHell," a spokeswoman, Pam McGraw, said when asked to comment on the article. "We're not going to provide details." The Chronicle, citing "sources associated with the company," said the hackers appeared to have obtained access to a variety of files, including the personal files of Stephen M. Case, the president and chief executive of America Online. To sign up for America Online, subscribers must submit a credit-card number, which can be used for on-line purchases of products. The article said it was unclear whether the hackers could retrieve card information. America Online's stock was up $1.125 yesterday, to $71, on Nasdaq.

title: New York Democrats Offer On-Line Information Service
body: Even as they acknowledged daunting problems, newyork State's Democratic leaders told a gathering of loyalists today that the state party was in better shape than should be expected, given the licking it took in the 1994 elections. Though the mood on this first day of a two-day meeting of the state Democratic Committee was not all glum, the phrase "cautious optimism" seemed as far as most people wanted to go in describing the party's near-term future. Time and again, speakers talked of the "adversity" they faced in this period of Republican dominance, of the party's $400,000 debt and of the need to unify their divided ranks. "I don't think I need to tell anyone here today that the Democratic Party is in trouble," said State Comptroller H. Carl McCall. "We cannot afford divisive primaries that force Democratic nominees to limp to Election Day." To highlight its efforts to rebuild a grass-roots political network, the state committee unveiled an on-line information service that will allow computer users to tap into a vast array of information produced by the party about Democratic candidates and their adversaries. They said it was the most extensive on-line service provided by any state political party. Party leaders called the new service a keystone of the Democrats' efforts to move into the 21st century, even as they presented it to a cadre of long-time party officials, many of whom seemed dazzled and a bit confused by the world of computers, not to mention the Internet. The meeting was held in Syracuse partly to demonstrate the Democrats' concern about voters from north of newyork City, who overwhelmingly supported Gov. George E. Pataki last year. But the session was poorly attended by downstate representatives. Not even the county chairmen from Nassau, Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island showed up. Using money provided by the Democratic National Committee, the state party announced today that it had hired Patrick K. Schaefer as the party's executive director. A lawyer from Great Neck, L.I., Mr. Schaefer was deputy finance director for Karen Burstein's 1994 campaign for state Attorney General. Available on the World Wide Web starting next week, when the email address will be released, the state party's new on-line service will provide biographies, speeches, news releases and photographs of some 2,000 Democratic officials across the state, from President Clinton to congressmen to the local town assessor.

title: Planet Out: 'Gay Global Village' of Cyberspace
body: Planet Out, a new electronic media company that will make its debut on the Microsoft Network later this week, is seeking to become the "gay global village" of cyberspace. If it is successful -- and some of the most influential names in Hollywood, Silicon Valley, the on-line networks and the gay communities are offering their support to make sure it is -- Planet Out may also become a model for the type of highly focused marketing that other businesses, like magazine publishing, have found more and more successful. But in cyberspace, there are no printing costs and deadlines are measured in minutes. Words and images can be delivered faster and in greater quantities. Encouraged by a recent survey by Out magazine that indicates lesbians and gay men are far more likely than the general population to use personal computers, modems and on-line services at home, Planet Out also intends to extend its reach to America Online, the Internet's World Wide Web and other international networks. "Traditional mass media is very cost-intensive," said Tom Rielly, a high-technology industry marketing executive who is president and principal financial backer of Planet Out. "Gays and lesbians don't have a high level of ownership of mainstream media properties. The Internet is the first medium where we can have equal footing with the big players." Planet Out has received commitments from virtually all of the leading gay organizations to provide information on the new service, including the Human Rights Campaign Fund; the National Gay and Lesbian Task Force; Parents and Friends of Lesbians and Gays; the Gay and Lesbian Victory Fund; Digital Queers and the Gay and Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation. Planet Out's Microsoft Network service is being designed by Clement Mok Designs, based in San Francisco, which also designed the Microsoft Network, owned by the Microsoft Corporation. The World Wide Web version is being designed by Internet Media Services, based in Palo Alto, Calif., which created the Web sites for such companies as Sun Microsystems Inc., Adobe Systems and Harvard University. The Creative Artists Agency of Beverly Hills, Calif., has agreed to help Planet Out develop other entertainment projects. Besides being a potentially powerful global marketing force, some gay groups see Planet Out as a gathering point for millions of lesbians, gay men, bisexuals, transvestites and others who may be reluctant to associate openly in public. Hugh Dubberly, creative director at the Netscape Communications Corporation, said meeting and chatting electronically with gay men and lesbians on America Online gave him the courage to discuss his homosexuality publicly. "It's something that would have been unthinkable for me even a year or two ago," said Mr. Dubberly, who is 37, and a former head of design at Apple Computer Inc. "If I had relied on more traditional ways of meeting people, like going to bars, or going to meetings of various organizations, or picking up gay publications, it never would have happened." There are no undisputed measures of the gay market but "the gay community has always been one of the most active groups on line," said Russell Siegelman, general manager of the Microsoft Network. In an average month earlier this year, 40,000 individuals spent a total of more than 100,000 hours connected to the Gay and Lesbian Community Forum on America Online Inc., the first major service to create a forum just for lesbians and gay men. Ted Leonsis, senior vice president of America Online, said in a telephone interview that his company was providing some of the start-up costs for Planet Out by giving it cash advances against future royalties. Analysts said it was unclear whether Planet Out would be successful, but it would provide some insights into the emerging area of digital commerce. "There are lots of ideas about how to profit from the Internet and on-line services, and Planet Out's idea of marketing to a specific community is one worth trying," said Daniel B. Baker, president of Quotient Research Inc. of newyork, a company that helps mainstream businesses reach the gay community for advertising and marketing. Planet Out's services include arts and entertainment, news, "chat rooms" with personal advertisements, celebrity interviews, human rights action alerts, surveys, travel tips and health forums. Mr. Rielly acknowledged that the current regulatory climate in Washington, where members of Congress are seeking to restrict sexual content on the Internet, was a matter of concern. But he said personal ads on the network and chat sessions would be "PG- and R-rated, not X-rated." "We're not going to back down on controversial things," he said.
