title: Steve Case At a Crossroad
body: Steve Case knows from painful experience how quickly technology markets can shift, destroying a once-promising business. In 1983, Mr. Case left a good marketing job at Pepsico Inc. to try to cash in on the latest trend in consumer technology, the Atari video game. So he joined a fledgling company that was starting an on-line service for users of the popular Atari computer-game machines. Mr. Case points from his spacious office in suburban Virginia to a red-brick building nearby, the former home of the long-forgotten Control Video Corporation. "I arrived there just in time for the death of the video game business," he recalled. Things have improved immeasurably for him since then. Mr. Case, 36, is president and chief executive of America Online Inc., the nation's leading on-line computer service, which offers everything from email to magazines to hundreds of forums for interest groups, from golfers to gay men and lesbians. In 1995, the number of America Online members paying monthly fees has more than doubled, to 3.3 million, and the company's stock price has surged. Mr. Case has been called the "Bill Paley of cyberspace," a pioneer in the new medium of on-line services, just as the former CBS chairman led the way in television. These days, Mr. Case finds himself getting dinner invitations from Alvin Toffler, the "third wave" futurist, and requests from the Gap to appear in one of its ads for khakis. (He did.) Yet Mr. Case and his company now find themselves facing challenges as never before. Once, the attacks on the company came mainly on the cultural front, from an elitist Internet community contemptuous of America Online and its members for being technologically lowbrow. Today, as the frontrunner in the on-line industry, America Online must fend off threats to its fast-growing business -- from the rapid growth of the Internet, powerful new corporate rivals, even experts questioning its accounting. On Aug. 24, the Microsoft Corporation will enter the on-line business with the access software for Microsoft Network mounted on the company's next-generation operating system, Windows 95. No one knows how quickly -- or how successfully -- Microsoft's on-line business will grow, but estimates put it at up to nine million subscribers in the first year, well ahead of America Online. The Justice Department is investigating whether Microsoft's use of Windows as a marketing tool for Microsoft Network gives the company an unfair advantage in the young but fast-growing on-line business. No industry executive has prodded Justice more forcefully or more publicly to stop Microsoft than Mr. Case. Last week, the Justice Department announced that it was still investigating Microsoft, but that it would take no action before the Microsoft Network starts up, if at all. America Online even has a designated "Microsoft watcher," Scott Geltz, a 28-year-old staff member with an M.B.A. from Georgetown and an animus for the Redmond, Wash., software giant. Above the desk in his tiny office is a picture of William H. Gates, the Microsoft chairman. Beneath the picture, in large block letters, are these words: "THE ENEMY." Mr. Case said: "Fear of Microsoft has helped this company enormously. Despite all our growth and the rise in our stock price, no one here is congratulating themselves. We're totally focused on the future." America Online's future will be filled with increased competition -- and not just from Microsoft. Powerhouses from telecommunications, like AT&T and MCI, have recently entered the on-line business. America Online's traditional rivals like Compuserve, a unit of H & R Block Inc., and Prodigy Services, a joint venture of I.B.M. and Sears, Roebuck, have given their services face lifts or new management or both. The other big threat to America Online comes from the popularization of the Internet, the global computer network. Once the bailiwick of researchers, the Internet is increasingly accessible to consumers equipped with more powerful computers, modems and specialized browsing software like that offered by the Netscape Communications Corporation, whose initial sale of shares set records last week. As the Internet becomes easier to use, it appears to pose a threat to on-line services like America Online, whose appeal to many subscribers has been as a hand-holding middleman making 'Net technology less forbidding. Doubts about America Online's ability to withstand the pressure in an emerging field of fast-changing technology are the reason that while the company's stock is a highflier, it has also attracted droves of short-sellers, who are betting that its share price will fall. Questions have also been raised about the accounting used to show earnings at America Online. Abraham J. Briloff, emeritus professor of accounting at the City University of newyork, presented a paper on Friday at an American Accounting Association conference in which he called the company's accounting practices "in-your-face arrogance." In his paper, Mr. Briloff scrutinized America Online's financial statements during the nine months ended last March, when the company had rapid growth in membership and made a series of acquisitions. Among the practices Mr. Briloff questioned were the company's accounting for acquisition costs and the deferral of marketing expenses to bring in new members, which increases reported earnings in the near term. In an interview, Mr. Briloff said his paper was not meant to suggest that America Online did anything illegal or in violation of accounting rules, but to show the leeway companies have in accounting for certain transactions. (Deferring subscription marketing costs, for example, is routine in the magazine business and Compuserve recently decided to defer some marketing costs.) Yet Mr. Briloff said that by applying more rigorous accounting assumptions, America Online's results would be break-even. "Push the pencil a little more," he said, "and it comes out negative." "But," Mr. Briloff added, "it doesn't really matter to the stock price of a company like America Online. Investors are buying a concept. They don't care about earnings." In many ways, Mr. Briloff is right. Last Thursday, America Online reported its results for its fiscal fourth quarter, which ended on June 30. The earnings, at 13 cents a share, were slightly below Wall Street's expectations. Yet the company's share price jumped $5.25 a share, to $65.25, another new high for the stock. (On Friday, the share price declined $2.875, to $62.375.) Investors seemed to focus on stronger-than-expected revenues, at $152 million, up more than threefold from the year-earlier quarter. The average subscriber was spending more time on line, at 6.5 hours a month, up 30 percent from the year earlier, generating more revenue. Jim Callinan, a portfolio manager for Putnam Investments in Boston, a large America Online shareholder, explained that he focused on subscriber growth and revenues per subscriber, not earnings. Building the first mass-market brand in cyberspace is Mr. Case's mission. He speaks of amassing a global audience of "tens of millions of members" over the next several years, with the key being "communities of people communicating with each other." To go abroad, the company formed a $100 million joint venture last February with Bertelsmann, the German media giant. To pull America Online into the Internet world, the company has spent more than $150 million in the last year on acquisitions including Advanced Network and Services Inc., which has maintained much of the Internet backbone for the National Science Foundation. The company also recently purchased Global Network Navigator. G.N.N. has a popular site on the Internet's World Wide Web that serves as a directory to other Web sites, where graphics as well as text are displayed. America Online's strategy for the Internet is twofold. First, it is integrating access smoothly into its current on-line service. Second, it will begin a separate service later this month for more sophisticated computer users who want direct access to the Internet, which will compete with access providers like Netcom and PSI. But wherever it goes, America Online's focus is on fostering interest-based communities on line. The company has many suppliers from the world of traditional media, including ABC, CBS, The Atlantic Monthly, Wired, The newyork Times and many others. But the service's members spend 60 percent of their time communicating with one another. "This medium is about participation, and not just a place to find information and download bits," said Kathy Ryan, a vice president. The same mantra is heard throughout America Online's brick-and-mirror-glass headquarters. These communities will increasingly be linked to content created for the on-line environment, which the company wants to foster with start-up capital in its new Greenhouse project for on-line entrepreneurs. That is what America Online understands and that should be its lasting competitive advantage, insists Theodore Leonsis, senior vice president. "This is new medium, not a technology or software business," said Mr. Leonsis, who predicts that the on-line business will be "Microsoft's Vietnam." For Mr. Case, a founder in 1985 of Quantum Computer Services Inc., later renamed America Online, these are challenging times. But he sounds confident that America Online will prove its detractors and short-sellers to be wrong. "The investment debate," he said, "comes down to two different views of the future." "One view," Mr. Case explained, "is that we're a leader in an exciting new field, and we could become another Wal-Mart, Home Depot or even a Microsoft. The other is that we're a very fragile franchise about to be battered by competition from Microsoft and the Internet. We'll see." Graphic   Photo: Steve Case, president of America Online. title: MCI and News Corporation Seen in an On-line Venture
body: The MCI Communications Corporation and Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation are expected to announce the creation of a new Internet-based on-line information service today, deepening an alliance the two companies formed in May. The new service, which is expected to replace the News Corporation's Delphi Internet Services, will enter the fiercely competitive on-line market this fall with a range of offerings including multimedia entertainment, custom electronic newspapers, communications services and home shopping, a person familiar with the companies' plans said last night. The joint venture by MCI and the News Corporation will compete not only with the existing leaders of the domestic on-line market -- America Online Inc., H & R Block Inc.'s Compuserve and Prodigy Services, a venture of I.B.M. and Sears, Roebuck & Company -- but also with the Microsoft Network and a new Internet service that is expected to be introduced next week by the AT&T Corporation. Analysts said the proposed joint venture would be a logical result of several actions taken by both companies since MCI invested $2 billion in the News Corporation in May. "To be successful in the on-line business, you need to offer Internet access, which is what MCI brings, and you need to have content and strong brand names, which is what Murdoch has," said Gregory Wester, a computer industry analyst with the Yankee Group in Boston. Before it invested in the News Corporation, MCI already had a robust technical structure and a global network in place, but it had little in the way of information or services to put on the network. Earlier this year, MCI hired Scott Kurnit, a vice president at Prodigy, to help develop an on-line strategy. Mr. Kurnit is expected to be named head of the new network venture today. The News Corporation, meanwhile, is a publishing and broadcasting giant whose properties include Fox Broadcasting, 20th Century Fox, TV Guide magazine, the publisher Harpercollins and newspapers like The Times of London and The newyork Post. But its Delphi Internet Services has been languishing as a distant fourth behind America Online, Compuserve and Prodigy. Delphi, which the News Corporation acquired in 1993, was one of the first on-line services to recognize the importance of the Internet, but was never able to capitalize on its head start. Plagued by staff turnovers and technical miscues, Delphi repeatedly had to postpone plans to revitalize its service. The latest such overhaul was announced for September. In June, Mr. Murdoch moved Delphi's headquarters to newyork from Cambridge, Mass., and hired Anthea Disney, editor in chief of TV Guide, as creative director for the development of new Delphi services. Delphi has an estimated 160,000 subscribers. In contrast, America Online has an estimated three million customers, followed by Compuserve with 2.4 million and Prodigy with about 1.9 million customers. Microsoft plans to offer its on-line service as part of its updated operating system, Windows 95, but will limit the number of users at first.

title:
MEDIA: MAGAZINES;
Old distinctions blur. Advertising on line now involves audience consent.
body: IN the beginning, magazine publishers viewed on-line publishing as a dubious experiment that was simply an electronic extension of their publications. The formula was fairly simple: recycle the content, add some related information, set up a way for readers to make comments, and put it all on line. That was last year. A sea change in attitudes has taken place, as was evident last week at a conference on new media in newyork sponsored by the Magazine Publishers of America. Companies like Time Inc., Ziff-Davis Publishing and Conde Nast, a unit of Advance Publications, are now all on the Internet's popular World Wide Web, to which several million people have access. What publishers have come to realize is that on-line publishing is not just another version of print but indeed a new medium -- one that requires new business models, new sets of rules, even new definitions of old concerns like how to distinguish advertising from editorial material. What is really making the publishers sit up and take notice is that an increasing number of advertisers are creating their own sites on the Web, among them Alamo Rent-A-Car, Best Western, Federal Express, Goodyear, I.B.M., Kodak, MCI, Pizza Hut and Sony. Bruce Judson, general manager of Time Inc. New Media, a unit of Time Warner, says he thinks this growth in on-line advertising is just the beginning because it is now possible to develop a high-quality site on the Internet for less than $75,000 and the technology for developing such a site has become increasingly simple. "With the Web audience hitting critical mass, we are about to witness a creative explosion in the area of on-line advertising and marketing," Mr. Judson said. "Access to the World Wide Web will soon be as easy and commonplace as dialing a specific telephone number." Advertising, of course, is the bread and butter of the magazine industry. But if advertisers are going to set up their own on-line sites, what effect will that have on magazines? First, don't discount print as a place to promote these on-line sites for advertisers. Marketers are taking out ads in magazines to do just that. Advertisers are also paying to have their logos displayed in on-line magazines. These are clearly marked as advertisements, but they aren't ads in the traditional sense. Real ads on the Internet have to be specifically requested by the user. An automobile magazine, for instance, might display the names of three car companies. An interested browser simply points the mouse to a name and clicks. This brings up information, including pictures, about the company's cars. So publishers are trying to figure out how to convince advertisers that on-line magazines can deliver the desired customers. But counting the number of people who view these on-line sites is a tricky business. In print it is easy: publishers tally the number of magazines they sell, send their figures to the Audit Bureau of Circulations for review and then set advertising rates based on their circulation. Things are much more complicated on line. It is fairly simple to monitor the number of times a magazine site is called up, but virtually impossible to determine how many different people are using it. Is a site that is called up 12 times seen by 12 different people or the same person 12 times? The kind of demographic information that advertisers need is also scarce. Some Web sites have gathered such data about their consumers, but usually with the assurance that it will be kept confidential. Last week the Magazine Publishers of America issued a set of guidelines for developing a fair and accurate system for measuring Internet use. They called for a common set of standards and definitions that would also apply to on-line newspapers and television, and said a third party should audit and validate numbers. "This is clearly an evolving media and the way of measuring it is evolving," said Mr. Judson, who is the head of the magazine publishers' task force on Internet measurement. "This entire world is today in an experimental phase." Most on-line magazines are careful to make a clear distinction between editorial and advertising material. But what about Web sites sponsored by marketers? Esther Dyson, president of Edventure Holdings, a computer industry publisher, says that many of these advertiser-sponsored Web sites are offering interesting material and that they are beginning to compete with on-line magazines. Reebok International, for instance, has a Web site that runs profiles of winners of Reebok's annual human rights awards, like the 12-year old Pakistani who worked in a rug factory and became a campaigner for children's rights. Then there is a section called Sole Difference that lists volunteer opportunities around the country. There are also bulletin boards and chat sessions with coaches and athletes, but in all this there is a noticeable absence of the hard sell. "What they are doing is not selling shoes, but a notion, a life style, a bit of counterculture," Ms. Dyson said. "You post a passionate note on the Reebok bulletin board about an experience in the mountains. You say you were wearing Reebok sneaks. And maybe you were and maybe you weren't. The customer doesn't care who is sponsoring this." Many editors disagree, maintaining that consumers want independent information. They say that advertiser-sponsored material is the equivalent of advertorials in magazines and that consumers can tell the difference. "What I am saying is that these are the challenges and the dynamics," Ms. Dyson said. "The world just becomes a much messier place to negotiate."

title: Cyberspace-Rights Group Heads West
body: The Internet backlash is in full swing. The Senate has passed a bill that restricts free speech on computer networks. The White House and several foreign governments are restricting the use of private data encryption software. The Federal Bureau of Investigation wants increased capabilities to conduct telephone and computer network wiretaps. And in the midst of this, the Electronic Frontier Foundation, one of the first civil liberties groups created to influence public policy on issues related to cyberspace, is closing its Washington office and moving to San Francisco. The advocacy group characterizes the move as a logical, evolutionary step for a maturing organization, especially for one whose constituency has no geographical boundaries. Foundation officials also talk privately about a desire to escape "the corrupting influence" of Washington. But others say the move illuminates the financial travails and political feuds among the handful of public interest groups that specialize in cyberspace issues. The foundation has been plagued by staff turnovers and budget constraints for the last year, a critical period in which millions of Americans, and millions more abroad, have connected their computers to form a global network whose estimated population exceeds that of many countries. "In the end, our heart wasn't in Washington," said Esther Dyson, who was named chairman of the foundation as part of the transition, replacing Mitchell D. Kapor. "Our soul was in California, the center of net awareness. I think we can do more good by getting people in California to pay more attention to the issues." Yet the move suggests that the foundation, arguably the best known advocacy group for cyberspace, will have less of a presence during Congressional debates on such issues as computer pornography, free speech and privacy. "I don't know how to change policy made in Washington without being here," said Jerry Berman, a former director of the foundation and now head of the Center for Democracy and Technology. Mr. Berman founded the center after he was forced to resign from the Electronic Frontier Foundation last December in the wake of his support for the digital telephony bill that was approved by Congress. The bill, which requires telecommunications companies to design their systems to make law- enforcement wiretaps easier, was hotly opposed by many of the foundation's members. Several key policy analysts at the foundation quit along with Mr. Berman and formed the Center for Democracy and Technology. Rival groups snipe that much of the center's financing comes from large telecommunications companies, including AT&T and MCI, creating potential conflicts of interest. The Electronic Frontier Foundation was formed in Cambridge, Mass., five years ago by Mr. Kapor and John Perry Barlow, a Montana cattle rancher, state Republican Party official and occasional lyricist for the Grateful Dead. The two came together over concerns about law- enforcement crackdowns on computer "hackers" and their fears of abuse of computer users' rights. As the goals of the foundation expanded, it hired Mr. Berman, who had been the chief Congressional liaison for the American Civil Liberties Union. "Basically Jerry led the move to Washington from Boston, and his departure was the beginning of our departure from Washington," Ms. Dyson said. But she played down the apparent tension between the two organizations. "Frankly, Jerry is doing a very good job at what he is doing," Ms. Dyson said. "We have the same goals, but we are using different tactics." Ms. Dyson also conceded that a goal is to get wealthy businesses and individuals in California's Silicon Valley to pay more than attention to the causes of cyberspace. Most of the initial financing for the foundation came from a personal donation by Mr. Kapor, the founder of the Lotus Development Corporation. Most of the financing now comes from computer corporations, especially those in Silicon Valley. Ms. Dyson said rumors that the foundation had been unable to meet payrolls were untrue. She said, however, that staff reductions would be made as part of the move to California. Representatives of other cyberspace advocacy groups said financing was a constant problem. "We've found that the net community, while open to the message, is not particularly open with the pocketbook," said an official with another advocacy group, who asked that he not be identified.

title:
All the Comforts of Manhattan;
Why Rough It in the Hamptons? Goodies Are Delivered
body: The Lexington Avenue butcher shop's missive to its Upper East Side clientele was as pointed as its knives. Can summer in the Hamptons be savored without hung pheasant or designer chicken, liberated from cages and nurtured in the sweet air of Pennsylvania Dutch country? "We have been informed by many of our valued customers on how 'difficult' it is to purchase quality meats and poultry at the East End while away from Albert & Sons during the summer months," wrote the proprietors, Robert and James Moffa. Poultry lovers, fret no more. For a purchase of at least $100, the Moffas will happily provide chicken-to-pot delivery service from Manhattan to their customers' summer homes on the wind-scrubbed beaches of the Hamptons, almost 100 miles away. There goes the neighborhood. More and more Manhattan merchants are willing -- for a fee -- to treat the Long Island Expressway like a short subway line to Fifth Avenue, as long as they reach their prized and pampered clientele. Their basic pitch is this: don't leave home without it (Manhattan). Planning a Hamptons dinner party now requires no more effort than strolling out to the doorstep, where Manhattan merchants are eager to deliver table linens and dishwasher-safe wine glasses, shell steak and a good bottle of Lafite-Rothschild. Summer in the Hamptons traditionally was the period squeezed between Memorial Day and Labor Day, but the season has gradually expanded from Easter to Thanksgiving, an unsettling trend for Manhattan merchants who rely on their trade to newyorkers with second homes in the Hamptons. Aided by fax machines, computer modems and overnight delivery services, many summer residents are becoming "semi-commuters" who have taken to heart the words of the 19th century poet John Howard Payne, whose homage to "Home Sweet Home" was inspired by a rough-shingled saltbox house that still stands in East Hampton. Typically, the commuters spend four-day weekends in the Hamptons and the rest of the week in Manhattan. "Manhattan businesses are faced with the problem that the world is not in Manhattan in the summer, it's in the Hamptons, and basically they see their business drop like a stone," said Jerry Della Femina, the Manhattan advertising executive who also owns Jerry & David's Red Horse Market in East Hampton. He added, "If someone said, 'I want you to get all the affluent, influential newyorkers and then go to one spot and wait for us,' the fact is that they all go to the Hamptons." Given this view, it's not surprising that Mr. Della Femina advertises his celebrity newyork customers far more than the Long Island potatoes at his market: "See a big-deal ad guy groveling for customers. Catch Mort Zuckerman pushing a shopping cart. Stand on long lines next to minor celebrities. It's summer in the Hamptons." Peter Meltzer, a wine writer and publisher of the "Passport to newyork Restaurants," who divides his life between the Upper East Side and the Hamptons, said, that "For many, the Hamptons is an extension of Manhattan culture." "It's no surprise that people seek the same creature comforts," he said. "I think it's boring, and I try to seek out the contrast. I don't want to replicate Third Avenue on Main Street." If there is a border to this virtual community, it is bounded by the Long Island Expressway, the Long Island Rail Road and the Hamptons Jitney, which cossets its Manhattan customers with airline-style beverage service and a courtesy rule that limits cellular phone conversations to three minutes. Eight months ago, those borders were stretched into cyberspace with the advent of Hamptons Online, a computer bulletin board and self-styled "virtual beach" that offers customers computer access to most local Hamptons newspapers along with classified advertisements and restaurant reviews. More than 20 percent of the 750 subscribers are from Manhattan, said Robert Florio, the founder of the service. "I think we're seeing people stay longer because they've been liberated from their 9-to-5 jobs because of technology," said Tom Neely, president of the Southampton Chamber of Commerce. "You can do pretty much the same here as you can in Manhattan with faxes and computers." Even newyork charities have trailed their supporters to the Hamptons. The AIDS Resource Center on Seventh Avenue in Manhattan opened the Welcome AIDS Thrift Shop on Main Street in Southampton two years ago. Many of the initial donations came from Manhattan, and in turn the store raises money to support a temporary housing program in newyork for women and children suffering from AIDS. "We have a great number of people who come to the East End who are involved in arts and theater, and we knew we would have support," said Marie C. Bernard, a director of the store, who noted the lengthening of the summer season. Watching that trend, the owners of the Lexington Avenue butcher shop decided to launch their delivery service to eastern Long Island. Last summer the business at Albert & Sons dropped more than 60 percent while many of shop's customers were vacationing in Europe and the Hamptons, said James Moffa, the president of the company. He noted his customers' complaints about the difficulties of finding specific types of poultry in the Hamptons: pheasant, hung for at least 12 days, or Bell & Evans free-range chicken from Pennsylvania. He sent out letters announcing his service. Last week, the company prepared for its first run, but not enough orders came in to fill a truck with meat. Still, they tried to satisfy two orders from the Hamptons; the meat made it there by Federal Express. The pages of Dan's Papers, a free weekly newspaper in the Hamptons, is thick with the advertisements of newyork City businesses reaching out to the Hamptons. Some promote architectural services and professional family portraits. Others offer singles introductions and the Hamptons Mobile massage ("Two Hands, Four Wheels"). Sherry-Lehmann, an Upper East Side Manhattan wine shop on Madison Avenue, was touting its blue-ribbon delivery service with a full-page ad, "America's Best Wine Shop Goes to the Hamptons!" The company's chairman, Michael Aaron, is even more effusive about the service, which his father started in the 1950's when his family used to vacation on Fire Island. The store's trucks deliver wine to the Hamptons weekly for minimum orders of $175. Particularly popular this year, he said, are requests for the store's Sherry-Lehmann wine glasses and cases of Boyer Brut Blanc de Blancs, a sparkling wine. "This year our growth has been explosive," Mr. Aaron said. "We had small growth since the beginning of the 90's because of the recession, but we're up over 45 percent in the deliveries." Local merchants in the Hamptons have watched this flurry of activity with some skepticism. They point out the hazards of seasonal business and the failure of the Sfuzzi Italian restaurants in Manhattan to try hard enough to cater to the Southampton locals during the slow winter seasons. "I think their expectations were a little high," said Lee Walter, who divides his life between his home in East Hampton and his work promoting classical music concerts in Manhattan. "They have to be able to appeal to the local people. They're not going to spend a lot of money to have a couple of lettuce leaves on their plate." After Sfuzzi left, another group of newyorkers moved into the old dance hall that was popular in the 1940's and changed its name back to the original, Bowden Square. This roulette of newyorkers doesn't seem to faze the merchants who have lived in the Hamptons through seasons of winter and summer. They have also watched with satisfaction as the flow of business has reversed directions, from the Hamptons to Manhattan. Sonny Mattera, a butcher with silver hair and a pencil perpetually jammed behind his ear, shut down his 30-year-old shop in Queens to move to the Hamptons seven years ago. Sonny's Meat Market of Astoria, Queens, became the Village Shoppe of East Quogue. And the shop has thrived, he said, because he has stocked quality meats like pheasant and Bell & Evans chicken. Naturally, he announces, The Village Shoppe delivers to Manhattan. Graphic   Photo: James Maffa at the butcher's table at the Upper East Side shop Albert & Sons, which is pursuing the summer trade. (Frances Roberts for The newyork Times)

title: Internet Obscenity Bill Is Indeed Constitutional
body: To the Editor: Re "Censorship on the Internet" (editorial, June 22): Again you join critics of the communications decency amendment, who know no bounds in their use of misinformation about this constitutional and needed legislation. They will do anything to defend the status quo on the Internet with its obscenity, pornography, pedophilia and human-animal sexual debasement, all easily accessible, even to children. We would not have a pristine Internet even if the Exon-Coats measure were signed into law. Nothing in the legislation applies to constitutionally protected speech between consenting adults. Indecent communications must be conducted in a place inaccessible to children. Parents, schools and responsible industry must still be involved to make the Internet safer. But wringing one's hands while refusing to do anything to protect children and families is not responsible. We have addressed the constitutional questions by incorporating court-tested concepts in place for years for similar infractions by telephone or mail. The amendment would serve as a deterrent to those profiteers who post obscene pictures and indecent material at places on the Internet where children are free to roam. Most responsible businesses, universities and information providers will find reasonable, effective means to restrict child access to inappropriate material. The law will work, but it will not be foolproof. While speed limits don't eliminate all speeders on asphalt highways, they make them safer to travel. Why not have some common-sense rules of the road for the information superhighway?  JIM EXON U.S. Senator from Nebraska Washington, June 26, 1995

title: New Editor Is Appointed For Delphi
body: In a clear signal that he intends to compete vigorously in the increasingly competitive on-line information industry, Rupert Murdoch yesterday appointed Anthea Disney, editor in chief of TV Guide, to be the top editor at the News Corporation's Delphi Internet Services. Ms. Disney's appointment is the latest of several bold moves intended to revitalize Delphi, which languishes far behind such rivals as America Online, Compuserve and Prodigy, and which faces formidable and imminent competition from the Microsoft Network and AT&T's Interchange service. Compuserve is owned by H & R Block; Prodigy is a venture between I.B.M. and Sears, Roebuck & Company. "The appointment recognizes that the on-line universe is moving from a narrow, specialized group of users to a mass medium in terms of demographics, taste and appeal," said Scott Donaton, executive editor for interactive and new media for Advertising Age, the weekly trade magazine published in newyork. "Anthea Disney is the right person to tap that market." Ms. Disney, who is 48, is credited with transforming TV Guide into the magazine world's top producer of advertising revenue by bolstering its television listings with news and entertainment articles that appeal to a broad audience. Her task as editor in chief at Delphi will be to create a distinctive personality for the on-line service, which to date has been little more than an Internet service provider, and to covert the contents of Mr. Murdoch's publishing and television properties into the interactive, digital medium of computer services. The News Corporation owns -- besides TV Guide --Fox Broadcasting, 20th Century Fox, HarperCollins Publishers and Times Newspapers Ltd., among other properties. "We have some really stylish products, and we need to find a way to retain their character and style, and we need to define what is going to be the Delphi style," Ms. Disney said. Before joining TV Guide, Ms. Disney was executive producer of Fox Television's "A Current Affair" and editor in chief of Self magazine. She has also held senior editorial positions at US magazine and The Daily News. A native of Surrey, England, she began her career as a reporter and later foreign correspondent for The Daily Mail, a London newspaper. The announcement yesterday did not name a successor to Ms. Disney at TV Guide. Ms. Disney said a new editor would be named in a few days. Barry Golson, a potential successor, was named editor in chief of TV Guide Online on Tuesday. Mr. Murdoch, chairman of the News Corporation, moved Delphi's headquarters to newyork City from Cambridge, Mass., earlier this year and received a $2 billion cash infusion from MCI Communications in return for an agreement to provide information and services for MCI's own Internet ventures. Delphi also licensed the popular software Netscape Navigator to allow its customers to browse the Internet's World Wide Web services. Delphi is at least a year behind schedule in developing a new technical infrastructure for its service, and has suffered from several high-level executive defections. Alan E. Baratz, a former I.B.M. executive who joined Delphi as chief executive 10 months ago, said yesterday that the new user software, technical infrastructure and content services would finally be ready this fall. In recent months, Delphi has also hired new senior executives from AT&T, Prodigy, American Online and Microsoft.

title: An Early Flood Of Users Is Seen For Microsoft's On-Line Service
body: How popular will the Microsoft Corporation's new on-line service be? That is a question Microsoft's rivals, the Justice Department and many others are asking these days. To help find an answer, the Government has looked to a small private firm in Atlanta, Pipeline Communications Inc. The business experience of Pipeline, which provides customer registration services for computer companies, suggests that nine million people will have tried the new service, Microsoft Network, by the end of this year -- just four months after its scheduled introduction on Aug. 24. The projection is scary for today's big on-line services. The leading service in the unitedstates is America Online, with more than 2.9 million subscribers, according to Jupiter Communications, a research firm. Compuserve ranks second with 2 million subscribers, followed by Prodigy with 1.7 million. The Justice Department is investigating Microsoft's marketing of the Microsoft Network, and specifically the company's plan to place the access software for the service on its new operating system, Windows 95. Competitors say the marketing arrangement, called bundling, will allow Microsoft to use its dominant position in operating-system software to grab an unfair advantage in the fast-growing market for on-line services. Microsoft says such claims are nonsense. It accuses its rivals of running to Washington to restrain the company in a business it has not yet entered. Besides, Microsoft says, no one will be compelled to subscribe to its on-line service. Subscribers will be required to sign up and pay monthly fees as they do for rival on-line services. Still, in trying to determine whether Microsoft's marketing tactics will give the company a big edge in the on-line business, the Justice Department wants estimates of how quickly Microsoft Network is likely to grow. It asked for market projections in civil subpoenas issued to Microsoft and its on-line suppliers last week. Why does it matter? "If Microsoft Network has four million subscribers in two years, that's competition," said Gary Reback, a lawyer in Palo Alto, Calif., who represents many Microsoft competitors. "If it has 40 million in two years, that's devastating to competition." Enter Pipeline Communications, a two-year-old company that supplies customer registration services for computer hardware and software companies like Compaq, I.B.M., Lotus Development and Symantec. Traditionally, this customer registration was done by hand, with the customer filling out and mailing a postcard-sized form. Now, with 85 percent of personal computers shipped with modems, companies can request this information electronically with software that dials a toll-free telephone number. Pipeline Communications supplies the registration software to companies, collects the customer data in Atlanta and sends it along to the companies. In the electronic registration process, some computer companies offer trial subscriptions to on-line services like America Online to thank customers for supplying information about themselves, said Matt Thompson, president of Pipeline. Pipeline has found that about half of all customers decide to register. Of that number, 60 percent choose to accept the trial memberships for on-line services. Put another way, 30 percent of all customers respond to electronic offers for on-line services. "What we do is a pretty good analogy to what the Justice Department is looking into at Microsoft," Mr. Thompson said. Dataquest, a research firm, estimates that Windows 95 will sell 30 million copies in the first four months after its introduction in August. All the copies will have the access software for Microsoft Network, and 30 percent of 30 million is 9 million -- with many millions more in 1996, since sales of Windows 95 are expected to climb steadily. But people will most likely cancel in droves if, after sampling Microsoft Network, they decide it is an inferior on-line service. And even if the Government accepts the growth rate suggested by the Pipeline numbers, is that a violation of antitrust law? That is a question the Justice Department must answer.

title: A New Standard Is Proposed For Electronic Verification
body: A diverse group of companies, all seeking a missing component for doing business on the Internet, has rallied around a common system for verifying the trustworthiness of electronic messages and documents in cyberspace. The proposed standard, called Digital ID, is being promoted by Verisign Inc., a Silicon Valley company that made its debut on Thursday. The company is a spinoff from RSA Data Security Inc. of Redwood City, Calif., which has been offering similar services to companies for several years. The strong showing of computer industry support for Verisign and its Digital ID service effectively ratifies RSA's service and is likely to significantly accelerate the growth of digital commerce on the Internet. It also creates a private-sector alternative to the Government's own electronic verification effort, called D.S.S., for Digital Signature Standard. The Clinton Administration requires Government agencies to use D.S.S. for secure electronic transactions, and has been exploring the possibility of establishing the Postal Service as a central clearing house for digital signatures. Such a system would be needed for electronic voting, for example. Ameritech, Apple Computer, Mitsubishi, Netscape Communications and Visa International are among the investors who contributed a total of at least $5 million to finance Verisign. Besides the investors, who also include Bessemer Venture Partners, Fischer International Systems, Security Dynamics Technologies and RSA, other prominent companies endorsing the Digital ID service include Intel, Microsoft, Sun Microsystems, Lotus Development, which is being acquired by I.B.M., Commercenet, Cybercash, Dun & Bradstreet, Premenos, and National Semiconductor. The Verisign Digital ID technology will be embedded in a variety of software products -- including, apparently, all of the major operating systems for personal computers, and popular Internet server computers -- and will act as a link to Verisign's authenticating service. Using the system, electronic documents, financial transactions and electronic mail transmitted over computer networks can be placed in the equivalent of tamper-proof envelopes sealed with a digital fingerprint. The messages typically would be made private, and theoretically unreadable by unauthorized recipients, through the use of an established technology called public-private key data encryption. A sender of a message obtains the recipient's openly available public key and uses it to encrypt, or scramble, the message, which can then be decrypted only by the recipient's corresponding private key. Based on the trust given it by its supporters, Verisign would act as an independent clearing house for digital "certificates" of identity, vouching that the public key actually belongs to the person or company whose name appears on it, and that the contents of the message have not been tampered with. The Government's alternative, D.S.S., is also effective in certifying messages, but it has no component for privacy. Nor does it have the widespread distribution or broad industry support that Verisign announced on Thursday. "We put our faith behind the D.S.S. standard and we will be relying on it," said Edward A. Roback, a computer specialist at the National Institute of Standards and Technology in Gaithersburg, Md. "Others are free to make their own decisions."

title: Censorship on the Internet
body: On its way to passing a major telecommunications bill, the Senate has adopted an intolerably restrictive amendment called the Communications Decency Act. Fortunately, its flaws are recognized by no less a power in the House of Representatives than Speaker Newt Gingrich, who signals the need for a more serious, sophisticated way to deal with a complicated problem. That problem, as Mr. Gingrich said the other evening on his cable television program, is "How do you maintain the right of free speech for adults while also protecting children in a medium which is available to both?" Senator Jim Exon of Nebraska, the principal sponsor, either ignores or cannot grasp the important question framed by Mr. Gingrich. The Senator advertises his measure as a weapon in the struggle against obscenity and indecency on the electronic highway. As a ban on obscenity, it is superfluous. As a ban on indecency, it is unconstitutional. The bill makes it a crime, punishable by two years in prison and a $100,000 fine, to transmit or receive pornography on the Internet. This is redundant because Federal law already prohibits pornography by electronic communication. The same penalties apply to "indecent" material accessible to people under 18. The problem is not just that "indecency" is an impossibly broad category to define. The prohibition also violates the First Amendment rights of adults by limiting what they may say to each other by computer to material suitable for children. The Supreme Court has long distinguished between obscene, hard-core explicit sex material, which has no constitutional protection, and the merely indecent, sexually oriented and suggestive material that may be prohibited for minors. Even when protecting minors, however, the Court has clearly said that the law must use the least restrictive means available, not blanket censorship that prevents communication between consenting adults of materials that some might deem indecent. Senator Patrick Leahy of Vermont has a sensible alternative that would allow parents themselves to protect their children. He urges a quick Justice Department study of how to apply developments in computer software to let households, not Federal censors, control what electronic messages reach minors. Such an approach is gaining serious attention. Just last week three software makers proposed the creation of a voluntary rating system similar to movie ratings and demonstrated how new equipment may let parents screen out material according to the ratings. But the Senate, voting 84 to 16 for the new censorship law, chose not to have hearings on the potential of the new technology. During floor debate Senator Exon invited colleagues to inspect his special "blue book" of obscene communications on the Internet. All who looked deplored the graphic spectacle, but since it already was illegal and subject to prosecution it had no bearing on the bill's ban on indecency. The decency provision, part of a major telecommunications bill, deserves oblivion. We hope Speaker Gingrich will lead the House in rejecting this blunderbuss censorship measure and searching for something better.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: Advertising;
Hotwired gets Nielsen to rate its cyberspace auditing to help advertisers feel comfortable.
body: THERE were several developments late last week in the realms of interactive advertising, marketing and publishing. One involved the step of a leading electronic publication to address a closely watched issue in cyberspace: how to figure audience size. Hotwired, which has been called the most ambitious effort to develop a commercial media service in cyberspace, has reached agreement with the Nielsen Media Research unit of the Dun & Bradstreet Corporation for Nielsen to evaluate the audience measurement systems and methodologies being used by Hotwired and to perform regular reviews of that audience data. "It's not that any advertiser said, 'These numbers are fishy,' " said Rick Boyce, vice president and advertising director of Hotwired, owned by Wired Ventures in San Francisco, which also publishes Wired magazine. "The bottom line is to make advertisers as comfortable as possible," he added. "What Nielsen brings is a third-party, outside, disinterested perspective." Hotwired, which began to be delivered on the World Wide Web in October, offers a smorgasbord of text, photographs, video, sound and discussion groups. Hotwired has sold 14 of 16 advertising availabilities, Mr. Boyce said, to marketers, including AT& T, Coors, I.B.M., MCI Communications, Sprint and Volvo. The electronic address for Hotwired is http://www.hotwired.com/ for those with access to Internet. The auditing issue is important because advertisers and agencies are seeking standardized, reliable figures to measure actual use of interactive advertising and thereby determine whether ad rates being charged by the fledgling Internet media are bargains, fair value or exorbitant. "As people are trying to understand this medium, the media-buying community is looking for common measurements," Mr. Boyce said, "and analog analogies to help them make their decisions," like broadcast media ratings or print media audience measurements. "It's what Knight-Ridder calls 'a bridge of familiarity,' " he added. "If that doesn't exist, people disconnect; they feel there's not enough stable footing to make the crossing." The Audit Bureau of Circulations in Schaumburg, Ill., which audits media including magazines, newspapers and CD-ROM's, and Next Century Media in New Paltz, N.Y., a research company developing measurement systems for interactive media, are jointly recommending a four-point program for standards. The points include a recommendation for "census-based measurements" -- that is, complete audience counts -- rather than measurements based on samples of computer users. And they are also appealing for common counting standards for "click streams" -- usage information derived from the button pushes made on PC keyboards and remote control changers -- to insure comparability of counts across media and markets. Woolward & Partners, an agency in San Francisco that specializes in high-tech accounts and coined the term screen-agers to refer to young computer users, has completed a study of the Web as an advertising medium. "If you're advertising on the Web," Ed Gotfredson, media director, said, "you're probably paying about 40 times the C.P.M. of the equivalent print vehicle," using the shorthand term for cost per thousand readers. And the numbers being generated to measure usage, he added, "have no media relevance." "This does not mean, however, to cancel your company's Web efforts," Mr. Gotfredson said. "It is a matter of efficiently promoting your Web site/product so your return on investment is maximized." Just as interactive magazines compete against print magazines, so too are on-line research systems looking for acceptance from marketers that typically conduct research among consumers in personal interviews like focus groups. CLT Research Associates, a market research company in newyork, is introducing Opinionator, an on-line system for interactive dialogue with, and gathering data from, consumers. "We're not saying it replaces focus groups," David Pring, executive vice president of CLT, said . "It's a different dynamic." "We can get people on line from anywhere in the country, indeed the world, in a matter of hours," he added, and the system enables marketers to "build up a relationship" with consumers because responses can be tracked over time. One client of CLT that has used Opinionator is the American Express Company, Mr. Pring said. Finally, 01 Media in newyork is planning to introduce in November CD-ROM Advisor in print, disk and on-line formats, which will offer reviews and ratings of CD-ROM titles from consumers. 01 Media is being formed in association with Universal Media Inc., the publisher of magazines like Travel Agent and Unique Homes. "Unlike books, music and videos, with CD-ROM's there's no browsing mechanism, no demos," said Steve Rosenfield, president of 01 Media and publisher of CD-ROM Advisor, who is a former business development director of the Ziff-Davis Publishing Company. "People are buying blind," he said, "relying on the product packaging and advertising." Could that mean anyone relying on packages and ads for information is a cyberspace cadet?

title: Service Adds Another Portal To the Internet
body: America Online Inc., the country's fastest-growing consumer on-line information service, said yesterday that it would create a separate business to offer Internet access to computer users. To get the new Internet business off to a quick start, the company agreed to pay $11 million for Global Network Navigator, one of the most popular information sites on the Internet's World Wide Web. America Online already offers Internet access as one part of the on-line services it offers to an estimated 2.5 million subscribers. But to reach a broader audience of computer users who may not be interested in hobby forums, chat groups and other of its own information services, America Online and its rivals are creating separate Internet access businesses. "It's a little bit like why General Motors makes pickup trucks as well as Chevys, or why American Express offers gold cards as well as Optima cards," said Gary Arlen, president of Arlen Research of Bethesda, Md. "It gets them into different wallets." America Online said yesterday that it would acquire Global Network Navigator from O'Reilly & Associates Inc. of Sebastopol, Calif., a publisher of technical books, for $9 million in stock and $2 million in cash. G.N.N. is in effect an electronic publishing company, read by thousands of subscribers each month. America Online also said it had purchased rights to Webcrawler, a popular search tool that makes it easier to find information on the World Wide Web, the most popular service on the Internet. The announcements are the latest confirmation of a blurring line between consumer networks and Internet service providers, who are racing to create friendlier systems to attract the consumer market. "All roads are leading to the same place," said Steve Harmon, a media analyst with Paul Kagen Associates of Carmel, Calif. Mr. Harmon said that by making five major acquisitions in the last six months, America Online appeared to believe that it was easier to buy access into the Internet than to risk developing services and technologies on its own. America Online's main rivals, Compuserve Inc. and the Prodigy Services Company, disclosed their separate Internet service plans last year. But America Online, which has grown rapidly through aggressive marketing and by offering customers easy access to the on-line world, appears to have found a kindred spirit in the Internet world in the form of Global Network Navigator. G.N.N. was the first major electronic publishing site on the Internet's World Wide Web, offering more than a dozen "magazines," or subject areas, ranging from personal finance information to offbeat travel news. It organizes and catalogues the information for its readers in an easily navigated system. "G.N.N. is one of the strongest searching and directory companies in the world of the Web," said Adam Schoenfeld, vice president of Jupiter Communications Inc. of newyork. He noted that G.N.N. recorded more than 2 million "hits," or requests for information, from Web users in December. G.N.N. says it has more than 400,000 regular viewers, of whom 180,000 are registered electronic subscribers. There is currently no extra charge to read information published on the G.N.N. site, and the electronic publications are supported by on-line advertising. Lisa Gansky, who will become vice president and general manager of G.N.N. programming for America Online if the deal goes through, said the site would at least initially remain free and open to all Internet users.

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
Plodding Genie Plays Catch-Up
body: WAY back in 1985, when General Electric's Genie network made its debut, consumer on-line information services were fairly crude, unfriendly systems. Typically they offered low-speed, high-cost access to a closed network of proprietary information. They required the user to learn confusing keyboard commands to navigate text-only menus that were displayed in the narrow, 40-character lines designed to be seen on the dumb data terminals that predated the age of personal computers. A lot has changed in the last decade, of course. Today, someone signing up for a commercial on-line information service can expect point-and-click command systems, colorful graphics, simple sound and video, and access to the Internet, including the World Wide Web. So it was a something of a shock recently to dial into Genie -- one of the country's first and largest consumer information networks -- and be hurled back into the text-based, command-line world of yesteryear. But there it was, in a black-and-white flashback: a 40-character menu offering to let me connect at speeds of 300 bits to 2,400 bits per second. (In contrast, Prodigy is beginning to offer 28,800 bits per second, with speeds rising to 64,000 bits per second later this year.) If I wanted to really feel the electrons blowing in my face, I could pay an extra $2 an hour for a top speed of 9,600 bits per second. (Genie says it will drop the surcharge in August.) Genie does offer a couple of graphical front-ends -- basically, software that hides Genie's true appearance behind a skin-deep mask -- for Windows and Macintosh users. The front-ends can be obtained by calling Genie Client Services, (800) 638-9636. The software works only at 2,400 bits a second or slower, however. And once past the opening screens, Genie users are usually tossed back into the text-only service. There is still magic at 2,400 bits per second, at least for anyone who is new to cyberspace. But in contrast to its younger competitors, this Genie appears to have been stuck in its lamp for the last 10 years. General Electric Information Services of Rockville, Md., which operates Genie, promises that the service will get a complete face lift and technical overhaul in the fourth quarter of this year. The overhaul, they say, will make Genie a modern, compelling choice for the millions of people who are connecting their personal computers to cyberspace. But not everyone is convinced that Genie can survive as anything more than a niche service for people who like to play games over computer networks, Genie's strong point. The most damning vote of no confidence came this month when the NBC television network, which like Genie is owned by General Electric, announced a partnership with the Microsoft Network. The Microsoft Network does not have any paying customers yet, but NBC obviously thinks it is a better choice for the future than its own corporate cousin. Genie tried to smile despite the slap. "We don't want to dwell on the ones that got away," said Doug Wolford, a spokesman for Genie. "We've got some wins, too. The American Kidney Fund just signed with us, and they have 40,000 members." It is unclear whether the kidney association, which will post information on kidney ailments and treatments on Genie, will have the same attraction as NBC might have had. "I'm not surprised that NBC would go with a service more friendly to graphics and video," said Lorraine Sileo, who tracks the on-line industry for Simba Information of Wilton, Conn. The Microsoft Network is also getting advance praise from game developers, who say Microsoft's Windows-and-Internet system will be ideally suited to the new generation of interactive games that are now Genie's forte. But the Microsoft Network, like Genie's next-generation system, is not expected to be in operation until the end of the year. Meanwhile, the games on Genie are very interesting. In games like Cyberstrike and Battletech, users anywhere on the Genie network can play against other users. Such competition adds a compelling dimension to gaming, because unlike a human-versus-computer matchup, which can be mastered fairly quickly by a determined player, the human-versus-human contests are different every time. There are other networks that specialize in games, including the Sierra Network and TEN, the Entertainment Network. But Genie contends that it is a better value because, besides games, it offers a wide range on information and services on hobbies, investments, computers and software, news and so on. Once again, however, Genie is under pressure on pricing. Subscribers pay $8.95 a month, which includes four hours of non-prime-time access. (Prime time is defined by Genie as 8 A.M. to 6 P.M., Monday through Friday.) Additional hours are $3, and if one connects during prime time, a surcharge kicks in. Those trying to lessen the sting of high fees by connecting at the faster 9,600-baud rate will get stuck with yet another surcharge. Genie's pricing reflects its corporate heritage, Ms. Sileo said. "The whole idea when they started in 1985 was to make use of unused time on the G.E. information service network, in the hours when business people weren't on the network," she explained. To keep the system from getting clogged when the big-buck customers wanted to use it, Genie made it unattractive for the average consumer. It now appears that Genie wants to make itself attractive as a consumer service. But it may have waited too long. Too many other networks are better, cheaper and faster. Graphic   Drawing

title: In Search of Nielsens for the Internet
body: Like many companies still unsure whether the Internet is a business fad or the face of the future, the Chrysler Corporation recently took a leap of faith into on-line advertising. The auto maker purchased ads at several locations on the World Wide Web, the Internet's multimedia service. Chrysler has also created a kind of electronic brochure on the Web, including a virtual showroom of hot-concept cars, a look at safety systems and the standard lineup of Dodges and Jeeps. The challenge now is to figure out if anyone cares out there in Modem Land. Chrysler's predicament is shared by the tens of thousands of businesses that have begun running interactive ads on the Web, including Coors Brewing, MCA Records, a unit of the Matsushita Electric Industrial Company and MCI Communications. Right now, there is no reliable way of knowing how many people are interacting with these ads. Television has its A. C. Nielsen ratings, which tell advertisers how many sets are tuned in when their ads run. Radio has the Arbitron ratings. And magazines and newspapers have independent auditing agencies that verify circulation. Such audience measurements are the basis for the ad rates set by broadcasters and publishers. And the same data, in turn, enable marketers to gauge how well their ad dollars are being spent. For advertisers pumping their money into cyberspace, however, there are no Nielsens -- not yet, at least. That may soon change. In the last few months, a handful of ambitious software start-up companies have announced techniques for measuring the audience for Internet ads. Earlier this month, A. C. Nielsen, a subsidiary of Dun & Bradstreet, said it planned to enter the game, probably in a venture with one of these software start-up concerns. Arbitron, a unit of the Ceridian Corporation, has also expressed interest. Some of the start-ups, including Digital Planet and the Internet Profiles Corporation -- I/Pro, for short -- recently started performing their monitoring services for a few Internet advertisers. And while it is too early to predict whether either of these, or any other services, might become the industry standard, advertisers are eager for some sort of standard to emerge. Otherwise they must continue to rely on guesswork and trust. "Today, you come up with a number that seems reasonable and then keep raising the price as long as people are willing to pay it," said David Carlick, senior vice president of Poppy Tyson Advertising, one of two agencies enlisted by Chrysler to create its on-line campaign. More advertisers appear ready to start spending at least part of their budgets on interactive ads. Jupiter Communications, a market-research company in newyork, said the target audience was the nearly 4.6 million people with the Internet access and software allowing them to visit the World Wide Web, an area of the Internet where text can be mingled with photographs, film clips and sound. The Web allows browsers to move easily between sites by selecting highlighted elements. Jupiter forecasts that the number of Web users will more than double by 1997. John A. Dimling, president of Nielsen Media Research, predicts that the Web will be generating "hundreds of millions" a year in advertising sales by the end of the decade -- still tiny compared with the $125 billion a year now being spent for all media in the unitedstates, but money worth keeping tabs on. Chrysler, which so far is restricting its Web site to pictures and text (the address is http://www.chryslercorp.com), is also paying undisclosed amounts for ads in two other electronic sites on the Web. One is Time Warner's Pathfinder site (http://www.pathfinder.com); the other is Wired magazine's HotWired (http:www.hotwired.com). Internet advertisers are eager for data that would show the most effective sites on the Web. What is ultimately needed, said J. R. Julow, director of marketing operations at Chrysler, is a system that measures not only the effectiveness of one Internet ad over another, but one that can compare the effectiveness of Internet advertising with that of ads placed on television or in newspapers. Besides I/Pro, which is based in San Francisco, and Digital Data of Los Angeles, analysts say the companies that may provide the answer include Logical Design Solutions of Murray Hill, N.J., and a joint venture of the Delahaye Group of Portsmouth, N.H., and Internet Media Services of Palo Alto, Calif. Monitoring overall use of the World Wide Web is easy, since the network servers automatically create a log of network activity. But in most cases, this data is limited to tracking the number of times a single file on a Web site is called up. The big task for the new Web-monitoring services is analyzing the raw traffic statistics and turning them into useful marketing data, like determining how many times the same people viewed an ad, how long they lingered and what route they took to get there. Advertisers might also want to know what Web site they visited next, to determine where else it might pay to advertise to reach similar types of people. Initially, these emerging systems will provide only basic data, most often just the name of network servers, the universities, companies or commercial Internet providers who connect an individual computer to the Internet. Even in cases where more individual information can be ascertained through users' electronic registration forms, Internet publishers say their concern for consumer privacy would prevent them from disclosing the users' identities or other personal information. But as people routinely make purchases over the network, more specific consumer information is likely to be collected -- just as credit-card companies compile huge data bases on the spending habits of those who use their cards. That might make the I/Pro's and Digital Planets serve more as data-base builders than census takers, Adam Schoenfeld, a vice president at Jupiter Communications, says. "There's better tracking of new media than traditional media already, because everybody leaves fingerprints, showing where they were and where they went next," he said. Graphic   Diagram: "Advertising On Line" The Chrysler Corporation has placed ads at World Wide Web sites run by Wired magazine, top, and Time Warner, middle. By clicking on either ad, a computer user is transferred to Chrysler's onw site, bottom, where information about new cars and trucks can be found.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Judge Allows Libel Lawsuit Against Prodigy to Proceed
body: In a ruling that could change the nature of on-line information services, a newyork judge cleared the way yesterday for a $200 million libel lawsuit against the Prodigy Services Company when he ruled that the popular on-line network was a publisher, and not just a passive distributor of information. The ruling by Justice Stuart L. Ain of State Supreme Court in Mineola, L.I., rejects the argument by Prodigy, a joint venture of I.B.M. and Sears, Roebuck & Company, that it is not a publisher and thus cannot be held liable for comments posted electronically by its users. The decision by Justice Ain came in response to a motion filed by Stratton Oakmont Inc., a Long Island securities investment firm that sued Prodigy in January for libel and defamation. The suit arose from a series of messages posted on Prodigy's "Money Talk" electronic bulletin board in October by an unknown Prodigy user. The messages portrayed Stratton Oakmont, which specialized in penny-stock issues, and its president, Daniel Porush, as criminals and characterized the firm's dealings as fraud. Stratton Oakmont has been investigated by the Securities and Exchange Commission for reported irregularities and securities violations. In his decision, Justice Ain drew a distinction between Prodigy -- which uses human monitors and automated systems to remove objectionable material posted to its network -- and other information services that merely act as conduits for unfiltered information, much as a bookstore or library distributes information but does not publish it. "We disagree with the findings and we are currently looking at options," Brian R. Ek, a spokesman for Prodigy, said from its headquarters in White Plains. But no decision had been made yesterday on whether to challenge the judge's ruling. Meanwhile, the ruling clears the way for the lawsuit to proceed more swiftly. Prodigy has contended that although it had once advertised itself as a "family-oriented" service and screened all new messages posted to its bulletin boards, it stopped prescreening messages more than a year before the "Money Talk" messages were posted in October. The judge also held that Charles Epstein of Chicago, who managed the "Money Talk" forum as a subcontractor to Prodigy, was acting as an agent of Prodigy. Stratton Oakmont contends that Prodigy is responsible for Mr. Epstein's failure to remove the postings promptly. The decision, if upheld, could put the commercial on-line services in direct conflict with proposed "decency in communications" legislation now pending in Congress and several state legislatures. A bill proposed by Senator James Exon, a Nebraska Democrat, would hold providers of Internet, bulletin board and commercial information services liable for the content of information posted by users. A. Michael Froomkin, assistant professor of law at the University of Miami, said it appeared that Justice Ain's ruling was compatible with libel law as it pertains to traditional print media, because the question was whether Prodigy had knowledge of the information it presented to its subscribers. "If this decision is upheld, and if the Exon amendment is held to be constitutional, then it would put on-line services in a terrible position," Mr. Froomkin said. "They would have to monitor in order to satisfy the Exon censorship requirements, and by doing so they would incur tremendous potential liability." Ellen Kirsh, general counsel for America Online Inc., a Prodigy rival, said she hoped that on-line services would not be forced to choose between monitoring bulletin boards and assuming liability for users' messages.

title: Microsoft and NBC in Multimedia Alliance
body: The Microsoft Corporation and NBC announced an alliance yesterday to produce an array of multimedia products and services. But the details were so fuzzy that some industry analysts said the announcement was the digital-age equivalent of agreeing to be friends. William H. Gates, the chairman of Microsoft, and Robert C. Wright, the president of NBC, said in a conference call with reporters that the companies would jointly develop CD-ROM's, interactive television services and products for Microsoft's new on-line service, the Microsoft Network. "I'm a big believer that the interactive world can be very complementary with the broadcast world," Mr. Gates said. But unlike the MCI Communications Corporation, which recently agreed to invest up to $2 billion in Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation -- in part for access to its programming -- Mr. Gates said Microsoft would not pay NBC up front for access to NBC services like its coverage of the Summer Olympics or the Presidential election next year. "None of the discussions with NBC have, in any way, involved investing in all or part of NBC," he said. Mr. Gates and Mr. Wright would also not say how NBC and Microsoft planned to divide revenue from new CD-ROM's or services on the Microsoft Network. And Mr. Wright said the deal did not address how network personalities like Tom Brokaw would be compensated for multimedia products that draw on their talents. All told, said George Colony, the president of Forrester Research, a market research firm in Cambridge, Mass., "this is a very fancy way to say 'we're going to put our content on the Microsoft Network.' " With digital technology opening vast but uncharted new markets, Mr. Colony said, entertainment, technology and telecommunications companies are racing to forge alliances without worrying too much about the details. "A lot of this is hedging bets," he said. For all its fuzziness, yesterday's news had a measurable negative impact on two other commercial on-line services -- Prodigy and America Online -- that now carry material from NBC. Mr. Wright said NBC would phase out its involvement with both services, though the network would continue to maintain a site on the Internet's World Wide Web service. America Online stock fell $3.125 to close at $38.625 on unusually heavy Nasdaq volume of almost 3.9 million shares. The stock had been down as much as $7.25 during the afternoon. Shares of Prodigy's two owners, I.B.M. and Sears, Roebuck & Company, also slipped, although only slightly. Microsoft jumped $3.5625, to $84.875, as Wall Street reacted to the deal and to assurances by Mr. Gates that the company intended to ship Windows 95, its next generation of operating software, on schedule this August. But the deal had little effect on the shares of NBC's owner, the General Electric Company, which fell 75 cents, to $56.875. Although the Microsoft Network does not yet have a single subscriber, industry experts say it will be an instant heavyweight among on-line services because it will be rolled out with Windows 95. Users of the new software will be able to sign on to the service at the touch of a button -- giving it a big edge over services like America Online, the largest on-line service. Mr. Colony estimated that the Microsoft Network would sign up 2.5 million subscribers within three years, as many as America On-Line has now. Thomas S. Rogers, the president of NBC Cable, who oversees the network's multimedia ventures, said, "When you use the reach of a broadcast network in television and the reach of Microsoft on the PC, it's a great combination." Partly because of the lack of cash passing hands, NBC executives were quick to draw a distinction between this alliance and the one between MCI and the News Corporation. MCI paid up, they said, because it needs Mr. Murdoch's programming to fill its communications pipeline. "We're really two companies that are in the software business," Mr. Wright said of NBC and Microsoft. For example, he said NBC could harness Microsoft's expertise in CD-ROM's to bolster its efforts in this area. To date, NBC has produced only one CD-ROM title: a personal finance guide called "Your Portfolio." Mr. Wright said NBC would draw on Microsoft's expertise -- even borrowing the company's employees -- to create many more titles. Some industry experts questioned the value of the alliance with Microsoft, because NBC's service will still be available to America Online and Prodigy subscribers who browse the World Wide Web. But Martin Yudkovitz, the senior vice president of NBC Multimedia, said the Web site would not include the "coolest" features of NBC's on-line offering. The alliance also raises questions about Genie, an on-line service owned by General Electric. Mr. Wright said NBC would continue to promote its programs on Genie, which has 200,000 subscribers. But he said the Microsoft service was "a much larger undertaking" than Genie. For his part, Mr. Gates said the Microsoft Network would be open to services from NBC's network rivals, CBS, ABC and Fox. And he said the NBC deal would not conflict with a separate interactive partnership between Microsoft and Dreamworks, the entertainment company started by Jeffrey Katzenberg, Steven Spielberg and David Geffen.

title:
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY;
The Times Is Joining New On-Line Service
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it was joining with eight other large newspaper companies to create a national on-line information service on the Internet's World Wide Web. The service, called New Century Network, will enable personal computer users to call up news articles and other information, including job advertisements, from participating newspapers. It is expected to be in operation later this year. The service was disclosed in an announcement on April 19 but did not mention the Times Company's participation. At that time, Nancy Nielsen, a company spokeswoman, said the Times Company preferred to develop its own Internet opportunities. She said yesterday: "The original announcement was made before we had a chance to thoroughly review the proposal. Once we did, we thought it was a good fit for the company." Peter M. Winter, interim chief executive of New Century, said he wanted to get at least 75 newspapers to join the service within two years. The Times will be one of the first newspapers offered on the service. In time, he said, groups of papers will be able to offer specialized information packages that could also carry advertising. New Century Network is a joint venture of Advance Publications Inc., the Cox Newspapers Inc. unit of Cox Enterprises, the Gannett Company, the Hearst Corporation, Knight-Ridder Inc., the Times Mirror Company, the Tribune Company and the Washington Post Company as well as the Times Company. Together, these companies own more than 200 daily newspapers.

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
Safe, Friendly, Small Neighborhood
body: APPLE COMPUTER INC.'S Eworld on-line information service, the latest stop on our tour of cyberspace communities, will celebrate its first anniversary this summer by adding Internet access and some multimedia features. With the forthcoming Internet links, Eworld stands the best chance of any of the second-tier networks of joining the leaders of the consumer on-line industry. Or, it may instead become a good example of a popular niche network, one that has a distinct personality and a valuable set of features that appeal to a loyal but limited community of users. The first year has been a struggle for Eworld, with numerous growing pains.
