Despite its handicaps -- it is not available to users of Windows-based computers, and it does not yet have Internet links beyond electronic mail -- Eworld has done surprisingly well. It has attracted an audience of about 80,000 Apple Macintosh users, making it the fifth-largest commercial service, behind Compuserve, America Online, Prodigy and Delphi; it is roughly the same size as General Electric's Genie on-line service. When it brings the approximately 60,000 Applelink users into the fold later this year, Eworld could swell to become the fourth-largest consumer network. For consumers, Eworld has all the charms and frustrations of a small town. It is just off the information superhighway, making it hard to reach for some visitors, and once they get there, there is not always a lot to do. I was invited to visit a regularly scheduled discussion forum on Eworld recently and was confronted with a blank screen, the on-line equivalent of walking into a deserted auditorium. After a few moments, the moderator greeted me rather forlornly, by my screen name. I tried not to slam the door on my way out. The bigger electronic communities rarely have such voids, and they offer more services, richer information pools and fancier features. On the other hand, big crowds and bustle are not always good. Eworld appears to deserve its reputation as a kinder, gentler on-line community, one where women and children can feel safe on the virtual streets and where newcomers are almost always greeted pleasantly, not with the abuse and insults common on other services. The service has the cyberspace equivalent of constables on duty around the clock. Boors, bullies and sexual predators are bounced quickly. Users are not permitted to be completely anonymous. Eworld is also developing several interesting services specifically for children, both for fun and for education. "Right now, I think Eworld would be a good choice for women who wanted to go on line, in terms of ease of use, friendliness, its policy on screen names, and other stuff," said Mary C. Doyle, a senior analyst for Link Resources, a research company in newyork. From a purely subjective perspective, the level of discourse on Eworld's forums appears much higher than on America Online, for example. For better or worse, Eworld is invariably compared with America Online, with which it shares core technology. (One can expect Eworld's World Wide Web and Internet features to be similar to those of America Online's Macintosh features.) "Eworld is America Online with nicer artwork, no content and no users," said Adam Schoenfeld, vice president of Jupiter Communications Inc., a market research firm in newyork. By limiting itself to the Macintosh community, Eworld makes itself unavailable to 90 percent of the world's personal computing audience. The limited audience also discourages many potential information publishers, who are reluctant to invest in a service that faces withering competition from the Big Three (America Online, Compuserve and Prodigy); from Internet service providers like the Well, the Pipeline and Netcom, and from a formidable array of newcomers including the Microsoft Network and AT&T's Interchange. "They're facing a real uphill struggle against some of the better-funded services," Mr. Schoenfeld said. "It's a crowded field now, and they need to get that Windows interface up and running quickly." Peter H. Friedman, vice president and general manager of Apple Online Services, said the Windows version would be released in 1995, but he declined to be more specific. Apple has named Lawrence G. Tesler, the computer company's chief scientist, to be Eworld's chief technology officer. Plans for Eworld include such innovations as intelligent "agents" that will filter and sort a user's electronic mail and a text-to-speech technology that will use the Mac's built-in sound capabilities to read the contents of chat forums, using an array of voices. The Eworld service costs $8.95 a month for four hours of connection time and $2.95 for each additional hour on line. Although rates have come down significantly since the service made its debut, they are still higher than those recently announced by rivals. Prodigy, for example, offers a plan that reduces on-line costs to about $1 an hour. While Compuserve, America Online, the Microsoft Network and other competitors are aggressively entering the international market, Eworld charges its foreign customers $9.95 an hour. It is not likely to spread far at those rates. Eworld is a division of Apple Computer Inc. of Cupertino, Calif. Macintosh users can use Eworld for technical support, with answers delivered electronically within 24 hours. Eworld software is included with all new Macintosh computers sold in the unitedstates and Canada and is also available free by calling (800) 775-4556. Next: Netcom. Graphic   Drawing

title: Chief of Prodigy Services Is Planning to Step Down
body: The Prodigy Services Company, a leading provider of computer on-line information services, said yesterday that its president and chief executive, Ross Glatzer, would retire on Monday. He is the second senior executive to leave the company in two months. Prodigy, which is jointly owned by I.B.M. and Sears, Roebuck & Company named Edward A. Bennett, a former executive with Viacom Inc., to be president and chief executive. Mr. Glatzer, who is 48, said he approached I.B.M. and Sears about retiring last year, but held off while the search for a successor was conducted. The departure of Mr. Glatzer, who joined Prodigy in 1986, follows that of Scott Kurnit, the executive vice president and second-in-command, who left in March to join the new on-line services division of the MCI Communications Corporation. The change in command also comes shortly after Prodigy announced its first profitable quarter after 10 years in business, and as the on-line services market is about to become vastly more competitive. The introduction of new services later this year by the Microsoft Corporation and the AT&T Corporation, as well as the growing popularity of the global Internet web of computer networks, will only increase pressure on Prodigy and its two leading rivals, Compuserve, a unit of H & R Block, and America Online Inc. Mr. Glatzer said yesterday that he was leaving to spend more time with his family. "Sometimes in your lifetime, you get an opportunity you want to take advantage of," he said. But people close to the company, who spoke on condition of anonymity, suggested that his departure might have been the result of a management shakeout, and some analysts have continued to speculate that Sears and I.B.M. may try to sell Prodigy or try to involve additional partners. Mr. Bennett, who is also 48, said in a telephone interview that he relished the challenge of the new job. "I look at this industry as being like the early days of cable," he said, calling that period "a wild and woolly time, a new technology offering a lot of choices and room for everybody." "Everyone said there would be few winners and a lot of losers," he said, "but the fact is a lot of people made a lot of money. This is a great opportunity to be a leader." Most recently, Mr. Bennett has worked on new ventures with Norman Lear, the television producer.  Before that, he was president and chief executive of the VH1 music channel for MTV Networks, a unit of Viacom. At Viacom, he also oversaw the start of Ha! the TV Comedy Network, which later became part of Comedy Central, a joint venture of Viacom and Time Warner Inc. Peter Krasilovsky, an analyst with Arlen Communications Inc. in Bethesda, Md., said Mr. Bennett had made his mark as a turnaround artist with both VH1 and Ha!. "If you believe the next war in on-line services is for content, then Ed Bennett is a fine choice" to run Prodigy, Mr. Krasilovsky said. "He is a smooth politician with strong contacts in the entertainment industry and he should work well with I.B.M. and Sears." A user of on-line services himself, Mr. Bennett said he was aware that Prodigy had suffered from a look and corporate image that seemed to trail those of its rivals. "I like to make things attractive; I'm a makeover artist," he said. "This is an industry that needs to constantly reinvent itself." Prodigy recently became the first of the major on-line services to provide direct access to the World Wide Web, the multimedia portion of the Internet, though both Compuserve and America Online will offer similar services soon. Prodigy executives say they will soon offer an improved user interface, the screen of commands and icons used in navigating the service. Graphic   Photo: Edward A. Bennett, a former Viacom executive, was named yesterday as the new president and chief executive of the Prodigy Services Company. He will replace Ross Glatzer, who is retiring. (Susan Harris for The newyork Times)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: Advertising;
The Internet is being used because, as an executive says, everyone wants a connection to what's new.
body: WHEN G. M. O'Connell, a partner in Modem Media in Westport, Conn., a leading agency in interactive advertising, was asked recently about the appropriateness of marketing in cyberspace, he responded frankly. While Modem has shepherded advertisers like the AT& T Corporation, the Adolph Coors Company and the J. C. Penney Company onto the worldwide computer network known as the Internet, he told newyork Newsday, it probably wouldn't make sense for a company selling a product like toothpaste. So guess who's on line promoting a toll-free telephone number to call for free samples? An offer that drew so many calls that initial volume exceeded capacity? Why, SmithKline Beecham Consumer Healthcare, introducing a toothpaste called Aquafresh Whitening. Mr. O'Connell, in an interview Friday, laughed ruefully. "I plan on being right about 5 percent of the time," he said. "This is pretty indicative of the fact everybody wants to try this," he continued. "Companies want to be associated with change, with what's new. There's an aspirational image to technology right now." Indeed, marketers developing interactive initiatives are generating the cyberspace equivalents of many traditional advertising methods and tools, in much the same way that the infant medium of television mirrored such features found in radio as national networks and sponsored programs. There are Internet infomercials, for instance, being introduced by Williams Television Time in Santa Monica, Calif. And the Advertising Council, the agency industry's public service organization, and Zing Systems L.P. in Englewood, Colo., are expected to announce, perhaps as soon as this week, plans for public service announcements on the Internet. There are also ambitious efforts to develop measurements for interactive media that advertisers and agencies would use in the same manner as television and radio ratings. One research service, the Interactive Information Index, a venture of companies including ASI Market Research in newyork, has already signed a contract with General Motors. A second service, seeking to offer a ratings system for the World Wide Web, the multimedia portion of the Internet, was announced last week. For now, SmithKline Beecham is using a low-tech method to track its foray into cyberspace with Aquafresh Whitening, a higher-priced variety of its Aquafresh line of toothpastes that contains a special whitening ingredient. As callers to the toll-free number give their names and addresses to receive free 4.3-ounce tubes of the brand, they can identify how they learned of the offer. Through last Monday, 1,338 of 1,772 callers identified how they had seen the number; of them, 59.1 percent indicated they had seen the number on the Internet on a Usenet newsgroup, or bulletin board, that offers consumers "free stuff." The Internet marketing of Aquafresh Whitening is meant to supplement a large conventional broadcast and print ad campaign by Grey Advertising in newyork, the Aquafresh agency, said Gillian Hamburger, an account executive at the Ketchum Public Relations unit of Ketchum Communications in Pittsburgh. The Internet idea was Ketchum's, which posted the one-paragraph sample offer on the Usenet newsgroup late last month. Scott Martin, associate brand manager for Aquafresh at SmithKline Beecham in Pittsburgh, said he was skeptical of Ketchum's proposal at first. He recalled: "I thought, 'You want to do what? Well, this is kind of strange. What would we be getting out of it?' But it's turned out to make sense and be a good fit for us." The primary reason, he added, was that Aquafresh Whitening is new and "people on the Internet are probably more likely to try new products because people who use computers may be more willing to look at new things." Mr. O'Connell of Modem agreed. "It's a great case of electronic grass-roots marketing," he said. "I tip my hat to them." As for the World Wide Web ratings service, called the Digital Planet Netcount, it was introduced Thursday by the Digital Planet Corporation in Culver City, Calif. The goal is to provide advertisers on the Web with verified, quantitative data on Internet usage by consumers on computers. Two agencies -- the J. Walter Thompson Company, a unit of the WPP Group, and Young & Rubicam Inc. -- are participating in a test of the Netcount system. Advertiser participants include AT& T; the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer and United Artists film studios, owned by Credit Lyonnais; MCA Inc., a unit of the Matsushita Electric Industrial Company, and the Nutrasweet Company, part of the Monsanto Company. Now that toothpaste marketing has entered cyberspace, what's next? Perhaps Bucky Beaver, the Ipana toothpaste pitchbeast of the 1950's, will come back on a screen saver.

title:
FUNDS WATCH;
Expanding On-Line Services
body: MORE mutual funds are offering on-line investor services for everything from education to account information to interviews with fund managers. Vanguard Online, available through America Online (keyword: Vanguard), offers a four-step course on creating a diversified portfolio. Investors can also retrieve prospectuses, get account information or share ideas with other investors on message boards. The Montgomery funds joined the Internet's Networth investor service (http://www.xperts.montgomery.com/ 1) with a "Meet the Experts" program, a weekly commentary by fund managers based on investors' questions with the broadest appeal. The Fidelity Investments on-line service can be found on the Internet's World Wide Web (http://www.fid-inv.com). Among other things, investors can use an asset allocation worksheet, review fund performance and other data, order prospectuses or retrieve a demonstration copy of Fidelity Online Xpress, which can be used to place orders for stocks, options and mutual funds, get price quotes and account balances.  Recovery Expected In Real Estate Funds Real estate funds have fallen more than 3 percent so far this year, while domestic stock funds have risen nearly 9 percent. But coming off an incredible December, the moves do not necessarily indicate a long-term trend. "We expected some retracing early in the year because of December," said Susan Belden, senior editor of the No-Load Fund Analyst, a San Francisco newsletter. The outlook for the real estate funds is good, she said. The improvement in the real estate market merits higher valuations for the funds' investments, and cash flow and dividend yields are strong. While only five funds specialized in real estate in 1990, with a total of $80 million in assets, there are now 22 funds with more than $1.5 billion under management, said A. Jason Windawi, an analyst with Morningstar, the mutual funds tracking service in Chicago. Unlike health care, environmental and Latin American funds, which are fads based on industries or regions peripheral to the world economy, funds devoted to real estate allow investors to participate in one of the world's biggest classes of assets, commercial real estate, he said. For the most part, the funds buy real estate investment trusts, which trade like stocks and own a stake in properties. Ms. Belden's favorites include Cohen & Steers Realty Shares in newyork; CGM Realty and Fidelity Real Estate in Boston, and PRA Real Estate Securities in Chicago.  Emerging Markets Despite the drubbing that the emerging markets have taken lately, many fund groups say the long-term outlook is strong for people willing to take the bumps along the way. Warburg Pincus Emerging Markets, which carries no sales charge, will be co-managed by Richard H. King, manager of the top-performing Warburg Pincus International Equity, and Nicholas P. W. Horsley, the associate manager. Calvert New Africa, with a sales charge of 2.5 percent and a redemption fee of 2 percent for shares held for less than two years, will be managed by New Africa Advisers and will seek opportunities on the Johannesburg stock exchange and other African markets. Smith Barney Emerging Markets Portfolio, with a sales charge of 5 percent, can invest in equities in Eastern Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America. title: Privacy, Business and the Internet
body: Computer programs that protect data from eavesdroppers and thieves are eroding the Government's ability to look in on electronic mail and computer data transmitted over the telephone lines. The encryption programs allow callers to scramble information so that only the recipients can decode it. The programs are legally available for use in this country. But fear that criminals or spies will use encryption to hide crimes has driven the Government to classify the programs as "weapons" and restrict their export. The attempt to block exports is destined to fail; computer software can be sent anywhere in the world via phone lines, and foreign companies already sell encryption systems of their own. The chief victims of the export ban are American computer companies that are placed at a competitive disadvantage abroad, where finicky consumers reject American products in favor of foreign-made products with encryption systems built in. Any restriction on encryption systems inevitably interferes with the privacy rights of individuals and corporations. Encryption programs are like the envelopes that letters aremailed in -- they guarantee that a message will reach its destination without being read by eavesdroppers. Absent truly compelling reasons, people are entitled to private conversations, whether those conversations are conducted across town or across the globe. Misguided or not, the law has teeth. Ask Philip Zimmermann, creator of a popular encryption program called Pretty Good Privacy, or P.G.P. Mr. Zimmermann is currently the subject of a grand jury investigation, under suspicion of distributing P.G.P. abroad. He admits circulating the program free of charge in America but denies exporting it. But someone placed a copy of P.G.P. on the Internet, allowing users abroad to copy it. The program has become exceedingly popular worldwide. It is available on computers from Tokyo to London, and sold in a commercial version by a company that pays Mr. Zimmermann royalties. For two years, the unitedstates Attorney's office in San Jose, Calif., has been investigating Mr. Zimmermann for a possible violation of Federal export controls on munitions. A Federal grand jury will soon decide whether to indict him on charges that could result in five years' imprisonment and a $1 million fine. Government is right to worry about keeping pace with electronic criminals. But citizens should not generally be forced to surrender privacy just to make law enforcement easier. That is especially true in this case because it is doubtful that encryption software can be successfully blockaded.

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
Shootout at the On-Line Corral
body: WHEN the smoke cleared, Prodigy stood over its two main rivals in a "shootout" among on-line information services held last week at the Internet World trade show in San Jose, Calif. Compuserve finished second, and America Online, the fastest-growing service, brought up the rear in the contest, which was organized by Internet World magazine to determine which of the major information services gave consumers the best access to the global web of computer networks known as the Internet. In theory, Prodigy earned bragging rights as the provider of the best balance of pricing and features for users who want simple Internet access. In practice, the value of its victory was diminished because some of its rivals were not invited, and others, including Delphi Internet Services, simply chickened out. Even so, the results of the shootout are enlightening for the thousands of people who are shopping for Internet and on-line connections every day. The Information & Interactive Services Report, a newsletter published by Business Research Publications of Washington, says more than 10,000 people are signing up for on-line information services each day. At the end of March the consumer services had 7.3 million subscribers, up 47 percent in a year. They live in 5.9 million households, a discrepancy explained by the fact that many people sign up for more than one service, often tempted by free or low-cost trial memberships. "If the pattern holds, and there's no reason to believe it won't, we'll break the 10 million mark before the end of the year," said Rod Kuckro, the newsletter's editor. Eventually consumers will tire of maintaining multiple, redundant accounts. But choosing the service that offers the best balance of price and performance can be difficult, as the shootout revealed. Delphi and Genie -- the fourth and sixth largest on-line services, respectively, after Compuserve, America Online and Prodigy -- declined invitations to compete. Given their lack of modern, graphical software, they would have fared poorly. Apple's Eworld network, the fifth-largest on-line service and our next stop on a tour of on-line services, was not invited because it does not offer Internet services beyond electronic mail, said Andrew Kantor, associate editor of Internet World. Neither were AT&T's Interchange or the Microsoft Network, two prototype services that are likely to become major contenders later this year. Final scores, calculated by awarding points for good features and subtracting points for annoying ones, were Prodigy, 58.8 points; Compuserve, 26, and America Online, 10.2. "Prodigy won as much because of what the others lacked as for what they offered," said Mr. Kantor. "But to be fair, Prodigy offered all the required features decently." For example, Mr. Kantor said, "Compuserve got hit hard early on because of their poor email, and the fact that they charge per message after a certain number" of messages. Also, Compuserve still limits some users to access speeds of 9,600 bits a second, while the others offer 14,400-bit-per-second connections nationwide. The company plans to offer faster access speeds later this year. "AOL lost major points because of their lack of a Web browser, their inability to quote original articles in Usenet News, and because they are the most expensive service," Mr. Kantor said. America Online is expected to offer access to the World Wide Web before summer. Both Prodigy and Compuserve reduced their prices just before the shootout. Prodigy's new pricing plan reduces Internet access to about $1 an hour for some users. Delphi, which says it has more than 100,000 users, was the first commercial on-line service to embrace the Internet but now risks being the last to exploit it. "The timing was horrible," said a spokeswoman for Delphi, which is in the middle of a significant restructuring. As the fourth-largest service, Delphi was to have been this week's stop on the on-line tour, but its new software and services, originally scheduled for late last year, will not be ready until later this year. Delphi's absence from the shootout was unfortunate for it, as it appears that the Big Three are taking an insurmountable lead. A detailed review of Delphi will have to wait until later, along with any possible recommendation. As it stands today, Delphi is a poor choice for new users hoping to tap into the Internet. Even so, Rupert Murdoch, the Australian businessman whose News Corporation acquired Delphi a couple of years ago, said recently that he was committed to making Delphi the world's largest and best on-line service. A Delphi spokeswoman said, "We have two major goals: to bring the Internet to the broadest base of consumers possible, and to focus on becoming the premier publisher of content created exclusively for new media." Delphi has been promising its customers a complete overhaul since last year, but it erred seriously by moving first toward a proprietary system, instead of one using open, standard Internet technology now used by millions. Since recognizing its error, Delphi has been working strenuously to keep from losing more ground. It has licensed the popular Netscape browser technology from Netscape Communications Inc. of Mountain View, Calif., and will soon announce more of its open Internet strategy. Mr. Murdoch also plans to use the other units of his media empire, including the Fox television network, to create new features specifically for this new medium. For example, it might have a Simpsons feature -- Bart and Homer, not O.J. and company -- created especially for it. Delphi's pricing is $10 a month, which includes four hours of Internet access time. Each additional hour is $4. For heavier users, Delphi has a 20/20 plan -- $20 a month including 20 hours of connected time, with extra hours billed at $1.80. Graphic   Drawing

title: Rock Star's Forum Grows Too Raucous For On-Line Service
body: Fans of Courtney Love, the grunge-rock singer, were too rowdy for America Online, which deleted their forum after they repeatedly broke the computer network's rules. On Saturday, America Online suspended the Hole forum, a computer message board named for Ms. Love's band, because of numerous violations of the network's terms of service, including a death threat, USA Today reported today. A spokeswoman for America Online, Margaret Ryan, said she could not provide details of the threat or identify the computer user who made it. She told the newspaper that the person's membership had been terminated. Ms. Ryan said she believed it was the first time a message board had been closed down at America Online, which is based in Vienna, Va. "It's generally not our policy to do that," she told USA Today. America Online, which has hundreds of forums and more than two million subscribers, prohibits profanity and racial, ethnic, religious and sexual slurs, not to mention criminal activity. The Hole forum, in the service's "alternative rock topics" area, contained numerous messages about Ms. Love's relationship with her late husband, the rock singer Kurt Cobain, who committed suicide a year ago Saturday. Ms. Love has responded to some of the messages using on-line pseudonyms, said Jim Merlis, a spokesman for Geffen Records, Ms. Love's label. Messages left today at the office of Ms. Love's publicist in Los Angeles and her spokeswoman in newyork City were not immediately returned. In January the computer service removed users who had sent child pornography over the network. The computer service stressed then that it did not monitor private electronic mail sent over the network but did follow up on users' complaints about offensive material.

title:
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY;
Software Author Focus of U.S. Inquiry
body: Phil Zimmermann, the creator of a popular encryption-software program called Phil's Pretty Good Privacy, hardly appears to be a threat to national security. Soft-spoken, slightly rumpled and almost always smiling, the 41-year-old computer security consultant from Boulder, Colo., hardens only when he contemplates what might happen to his family if he is sent to prison. It is not idle speculation. For two years, the unitedstates Attorney's office in San Jose, Calif., has been investigating Mr. Zimmermann for a possible violation of Federal export controls on munitions. The supposed crime: placing a copy of his data-encryption program, widely known as P.G.P., on a computer connected to the global web of computers known as the Internet. A Federal grand jury is expected to decide in a few weeks whether to indict him on charges that could send him to prison for up to five years, if he is convicted, and result in $1 million of fines. Mr. Zimmermann proudly acknowledged writing the program, which other experts say is so good that for all practical purposes it is unbreakable. If someone scrambles a computer file or electronic mail message using P.G.P., it cannot be deciphered without the proper software key, or without million-dollar computers using weeks of brute force to break the code. Conventional law-enforcement wiretaps would be rendered useless -- which is precisely the Government's fear. But Mr. Zimmermann denied that he personally released the program into the Internet. He said he gave a copy of the program to a friend in Colorado several years ago. Before long, the program had spread to hundreds of computers overseas. It is now a de facto international standard, easily available on computers from Tokyo to London, and sold in a commercial version known as Viacrypt PGP by a division of Lemcom Systems Inc., which pays royalties to Mr. Zimmermann. If Mr. Zimmermann is indicted, his advocates and critics agree, it will lead to a major test of the First Amendment's role in the era of electronic speech, of the principles of privacy and of the role of the Government in regulating the borderless realm of cyberspace. To win, legal experts say, the Government may have to make the novel argument that the Internet is, in effect, a foreign country, and that placing a file on a computer in Colorado is equivalent to smuggling it out of the country. "The political drive I have for working on this technology is my concern about the power relationship between the Government and its people," Mr. Zimmermann said. "My own personal experience with this case has not renewed my faith in the notion that the Government will not abuse its power." Graphic   Photo: Philip Zimmermann, who wrote a leading encryption program, is being investigated by the U.S. Attorney's office in San Jose, Calif. (George Olson for The newyork Times)

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
New Wrinkles at the On-Line Big 3
body: PERSONAL computer users who have hesitated to go onto the Internet will soon have the Internet coming to them. Each of the major consumer on-line information services, including America Online, Prodigy and Compuserve, is racing to meld its system with the global Internet. The Big Three services will soon be joined by the Microsoft Network and AT&T's Interchange, two new and powerful rivals with Internet aspirations. At the same time, some of the leading Internet access companies, including Netcom Inc. and Performance Systems International, are creating consumer versions of their business-oriented Internet services. The terrain of cyberspace is in upheaval, and anyone going on line in the next year is likely to be dabbling at the edge of the Internet pool, if not falling into the deep end. Things are moving so quickly that even as this column begins the second leg of the on-line information tour -- visiting Delphi Internet Services and the "beta" versions of the Microsoft Network, Interchange and other services -- it is already time for updates on the three previous stops, Compuserve, Prodigy and America Online. "It's very difficult now to rank who's ahead" in the race to the Internet, said Peter Krasilovsky, senior analyst with Arlen Communications Inc. in Bethesda, Md., a market research company that tracks the on-line services. "People will have access to all areas of the Internet from all three services," he said. Mr. Krasilovsky noted that all three services bill customers at an hourly rate, which may not be attractive to current Internet users who prefer a flat monthly fee. If customers are as enamored of the Internet as everyone seems to expect, if they become what Mr. Krasilovsky calls "infomaniacs," "we may see a lot of defections to full-time Internet providers who offer flat-rate services," he said. The transformation of the consumer on-line services accelerated last week when H&R Block, which owns the Compuserve Information Service, purchased Spry Inc., the largest purveyor of Internet software and consulting services. Spry is highly regarded for its "Internet in a Box" software and for its "Air" series of Internet tools, including Air Mosaic, a program that allows users to browse the Internet hypertext service known as the World Wide Web. Compuserve already offers some Internet services, including electronic mail, Usenet news groups and file transfer protocol (f.t.p.), plus forums intended to aid Internet newcomers. With Spry in the mix, one can assume there will be a new one-click icon on the Compuserve screen that will send the user into the Web. Neither Compuserve nor Spry would comment on pricing for Internet services, saying only that numbers would be revealed later this month. Compuserve is currently the most expensive of the Big Three. Compuserve is more than just the Compuserve Information Service, however. The company owns one of the largest computer networks in the world, with more than 400 "pops," or dial-in points of presence, around the globe. It plans to sell high-speed Internet access independent of its consumer information service, offering customers two options for swimming in cyberspace: the shallow end, through Compuserve, or the deep end, as a traditional Internet service provider. It is unclear whether there will be a "gateway" that makes entering Compuserve from the Internet as easy as making a foray into the Internet from within Compuserve. The bad news for Macintosh users is that Spry has no Mac products. In January, Prodigy became the first of the Big Three to offer its users access to the World Wide Web, which is rapidly becoming the most popular destination in cyberspace. Already, the company says, 400,000 Prodigy subscribers (Windows users only) are tapping into the Web. Prodigy has an impressive Web browser, and it does some nice technical tricks that make Web browsing fairly zippy even on 9,600-baud modems. Prodigy is also testing higher-speed access, including options for 28,800-baud modems. The big news is that Prodigy is preparing for a complete overhaul of its system "in the first half of the year," a spokeswoman said. The new design, called P2, abandons Prodigy's proprietary software and adopts the World Wide Web coding scheme known as H.T.M.L., for hyper text markup language. It offers a cleaner and more usable screen design and more closely resembles the Windows look and feel. "Beta" testing for the Windows version of P2 begins later this month, while Macintosh users, still unable to use Prodigy's Web browser, will have to wait until late summer. Prodigy is also preparing to introduce multimedia mail, which will enable users to imbed pictures and sound in their electronic mail messages. America Online, the fastest-growing commercial service, already has the most extensive Internet services of the Big Three and plans to add World Wide Web access in 30 to 60 days. "Beta" testing of the Windows version begins later this month, with Macintosh trailing by a few weeks, a company spokeswoman said. America Online has also been on an acquisition binge, buying Booklink Technologies and Advanced Network Services, providing it with new software for Web browsing and a more reliable network infrastructure with the promise of high-speed access. The company's Internet Services division will also allow America Online to offer direct Internet service independent of the consumer information service; no prices, dates or other details have been disclosed. title:
The Executive Computer;
Software That Pits Alarmists Against Devil's Advocates
body: IMAGINE a security system for your home that would electronically scan your property and alert you to any chinks in the armor that might make you a target for burglars and vandals -- a broken window latch, maybe, or door left ajar. Now, what if the same system could canvass every house in the neighborhood? Would you want your neighborhoods to have it? The burglars and vandals? All of a sudden, you don't feel quite so private or safe. The equivalent of this open-sesame scenario is about to play out on the Internet, the global network connecting 30 million people and tens of thousands of network host computers. During the first week of April, Dan Farmer, an expert in data security at Silicon Graphics Inc., plans to release a software program intended to help network administrators around the world sniff out the holes in their own networks. But the program, which carries the name Satan, will enable anyone to identify weaknesses in just about any network connected to the Internet -- with or without the permission of that network's administrator. Satan's imminent arrival has grabbed the attention of the data-security establishment. Some experts are worried that the program will be used by computer hackers to gain unauthorized access to networks at large companies, government agencies and even military installations. SRI Inc., the prestigious technology think tank in Menlo Park, Calif., has tested the program and published a report warning of its potential harm. "It's so easy and simple to use that it's going to end up in the hands of malicious hackers who will use it without knowing its full impact," said Donn Parker, the SRI researcher who heads the organization's International Information Integrity Institute. "It discovers vulnerabilities for which we have no solutions." And the issue has heated up the long-simmering debate about whether freedom to distribute software could be considered a constitutionally protected right. Mr. Farmer, who co-wrote Satan with the Dutch researcher Wietse Venoma, says his intent was to help network administrators plug security holes before outsiders discover them. Over all, it will make networks more secure, not less, he argues. But he also readily admits that Satan, which will be freely available over the Internet, could empower a new generation of computer hackers and lead to a outbreak of break-ins. "Some people will be harmed by it, but mostly it will be helpful," said Mr. Farmer, who named the software Security Administrator Tool for Analyzing Networks, knowing full-well that the acronym would send chills up the spines of his detractors. He contends that the fears are misplaced. Satan, "gives you a look at networks that wasn't available before," he said. "You're going to learn more about your system and provide better security." Many network administrators will very likely agree. In fact, for those managing security on multiple host computers, Satan could be a guardian angel. Ernest Charles, a senior manager of information auditing and security at the accounting firm Ernst & Young, said the company plans to evaluate the program, and may put it to use. "From what I know, Satan looks like a promising tool," Mr. Charles said. "To date, there is no single tool that does this." Today there are dozens of programs on the market to help network administrators insure the security of their organizations' data, but most of them are costly and cumbersome to use. Satan is neither. According to people who've seen early versions, its graphical user interface makes it exceptionally easy to operate. Suddenly, cracking a computer's security won't require special technical skills, but simply the will to do it. The program uses a version of the easy-to-use Mosaic interface developed for scanning the Internet's World Wide Web service. Satan can automatically scan and analyze any network that the user has identified. What really sets Satan apart from other analysis tools is its ability to scan hundreds, even thousands, of host computers, and then divide them into classes according to their type and vulnerability. Security experts say Satan is the first heavy-duty tool available for performing such widespread scans. Most programs today are only able to evaluate the security of a single host computer. Several years ago, Mr. Farmer developed a program, known as COPS, that scans a company's network looking for password security hazards. That software, whose name stands for Computer Oracle and Password System, has an enormous following among network administrators; several copy-cat programs have since been released. Like Satan, COPS is available for free, even though most other types of computer-security programs are commercials products, often costing thousands of dollars. But this time, some of Mr. Farmer's critics think that he should be prevented from distributing Satan, or that its distribution should at least be carefully monitored. And the SRI report recommends that, at a minimum, network administrators build secure network "firewalls" to protect themselves from intrusion via the Internet, or install a type of software known as a TCP/IP wrapper to protect individual host computers. "We're warning people to get ready for an onslaught of people using this tool to attack," Mr. Parker, an author of the SRI report, said. As for the distribution of Satan and other security tools like it, Mr. Parker would like to see such software continue to carry a steep price tag and be treated as proprietary, commercial software that is illegal to copy. He argues that the high price of most of the security software now on the market has successfully kept them in the hands of technical professionals with legitimate reasons for using them. Another possible approach is to screen prospective buyers of such programs, as Bell Communications Research, the Baby Bells' R&D organization, does when distributing its Pingware security scanning program. Bellcore won't sell it unless the buyer can demonstrate a legitimate need for it. But Mr. Farmer is an advocate of the unharnessed flow of information, and that includes software code. He says he is unwilling to put any controls on the distribution of Satan, despite its critics. "It's virtually certain people will use it for harm, and that's regrettable," Mr. Farmer said. "But you can't pick and choose who you're going to give something to. You're setting up knowledge as something you have to have certain credentials in order to have, and that's wrong." Mr. Farmer spent several years developing Satan in his San Francisco apartment at night while he was working for Sun Microsystems Inc. during the day. Earlier in his career he worked for the Computer Emergency Response Team, the quasi-government agency at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. Today, Mr. Farmer's business card describes him as the "data security czar" at Silicon Graphics, the workstation maker in Mountain View, Calif. The company declines to comment on Satan, other than to emphasize it was an independent project by Mr. Farmer, who wrote it at home on his own time. But whatever the concerns of the data security establishment, it may be too late. Mr. Farmer said Kevin D. Mitnick, the computer hacker arrested last month and accused of a rash of Internet break-ins, had stolen a copy of Satan, entering Mr. Farmer's computer through his account on the Well, an Internet services provider based in Sausalito, Calif. He said he had no way of knowing whether Mr. Mitnick might have shared copies over the Internet, and if so, with whom. Mr. Farmer himself has also distributed several copies for testing. And since he has taken no pains to control its redistribution, it's impossible to tell how many copies are already out there. Just be sure to lock your doors. Graphic   Drawing

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
An On-Line Deal for Bertelsmann
body: Bertelsmann A.G. said today that it was forming a joint venture with America Online Inc. to offer on-line computer services in Europe. Bertelsmann, Germany's largest media company, plans to invest $100 million in the venture, which will be offered first in Germany, France and Britain later this year. The company will also pay $50 million for 5 percent of America Online, with an option to raise its stake to 10 percent. The announcement set off a rally in shares of America Online. The stock rose $11.25 a share today, or nearly 16 percent, to $82.25, in heavy Nasdaq trading. Both companies said it was important to claim a stake in the fledgling European market, where far fewer users of personal computer dial up on-line services than in the unitedstates. The European market could grow to $3 billion in just five years, industry experts said. The 50-50 venture gives Bertelsmann access to technology it needs to join the race for multimedia services that link computer, media and telecommunications. America Online gains a partner with vast film, television and publishing assets. Bertelsmann's holdings include Bantam Doubleday Dell Publishing Group, RCA Records, Arista Records and a magazine unit, Gruner & Jahr USA Publishing. The venture is the latest set up to compete with Compuserve Inc., a unit of H & R Block Inc., which is the biggest on-line network in Europe with more than 200,000 users. A powerful group of European investors, including the media groups Burda G.m.b.H. of Germany, Matra-Hachette S.A. of France and Pearson P.L.C. of Britain, has teamed up to start Europe Online. But a Bertelsmann official said the venture's chief competition would be the Microsoft Corporation, which is expected to introduce later this year an on-line network to which access can be made through the newest version of the company's Windows software. "Everyone in the industry is looking for an alternative to Microsoft," said Thomas Middelhoff, the Bertelsmann board member in charge of the on-line business. "We don't want to leave the future to Microsoft." Under the deal announced today, Bertelsmann will gain a seat on the board of America Online, which is based in Vienna, Va. Steve Case, president of America Online, said that his company had "no specific plans to spend the $50 million" being invested in the company by Bertelsmann. "We do believe that having additional capital will position us strategically to either acquire companies for cash instead of stock or to make investments in companies," he said. Mr. Middelhoff of Bertelsmann said his company was talking to the phone giants Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom about cooperating with their on-line services, Telekom Online and Minitel, to win access more quickly to homes in Europe. title: Discussion of the O. J. Simpson Murder Trial Is On-Line as Well as on the Air
body: Hard to believe, but there are some people who cannot get enough information about the O. J. Simpson murder trial from newspapers, magazines, television, books and radio. The Internet and other computer-based on-line information services are emerging as global repositories of trial news and trivia: *What was the name of Nicole's dog? (No, not Plaintive Wail or Bloody Paws, but Kato, after O. J.'s house guest, Kato Kaelin. The dog now lives on the Simpson compound and has been renamed Satchmo.) *Is there a conspiracy in the news media to frame O. J.? *Does CNN offer gavel-to-gavel television coverage of the trial for a businessman traveling in Europe? ("What's with you?" an unsympathtic reader responded. "C'mon, get a life!") *And why, hawk-eyed Internet users asked, did Judge Lance A. Ito suddenly stop using a Toshiba laptop computer and switch to an I.B.M. Thinkpad? Is he using it to tap into the Internet to get information about the trial? Thousands of people are doing just that. Scores of O. J.-related data bases, interactive discussion forums and electronic mail lists have opened in cyberspace since last June, when Mr. Simpson was charged with killing his former wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald L. Goldman. Commentators in the news media have already dubbed the Simpson case "The Trial of the Century." But judging from the role of information technology in these proceedings -- not only in the courtroom, with its giant Sony video monitor and laptop computers, but in millions of homes and offices from Toledo to Taiwan -- the Simpson case might be more accurately described as the first trial of the digital century. In fact, the technological devices loom so large in the courtroom that Judge Ito's office has received complaints that the trial is providing free promotions for Sony, Toshiba and I.B.M. Since then some of the equipment has been altered to make the brand names less prominent. The interactive nature of the Internet and other computer networks allows people around the globe to retrieve hourly news feeds, follow daily court transcripts, dissect the American legal system, study and debate the finer points of DNA analysis and propose and attack various theories about the crime. "Several people conducted their own ice cream melting experiments, because of the information that partly melted Ben & Jerry's ice cream was found at Nicole's condominium," said C. J. Morris of Thousand Oaks, Calif., a regular participant in an electronic forum that logs more han 200 messages a day. "And these experiments were done precisely and scientifically, right down to using the same type of container and the same flavor of ice cream that Nicole allegedly bought on the night of the murders." Unfortunately for Mr. Simpson, these virtual jurors and judges appear to have already reached their verdicts, posted as collections of on-line comments with subject lines like "Guilty as Sin," which is next to one called "Guilty But Will Walk on a Technicality." Far fewer are the subject lines that suggest Mr. Simpson is not guilty, like "Planting the Glove" and "Another Setup Theory." O. J. headlines and "chat" areas are available on most of the major commercial on-line services. Compuserve advises its 2.6 million subscribers that "if you can't arrange your schedule to watch all the trial coverage, we'll have daily updates." Prodigy, with 1.2 million subscribers, already has 20,000 O.J.-related messages in its data base. On America On-line, with 1.5 million subscribers, an O. J. forum in the "Court TV" section is abuzz with armchair analysts. Anyone with access to a personal computer, a modem and a telephone line can be a Robert Shapiro, a Marcia Clark, a Lance Ito, or a Geraldo. "We are as up to date as the lawyers themselves are," said Jack Walraven, who distributes court transcripts and other Simpson-related data to a global audience from his Internet computer in Victoria, B.C. "Because we have access to all the information, it makes for intelligent discussions." Well, sometimes. When the defense said it would produce a witness who would testify that she saw four men near the scene of the crime, a Seattle woman who subscribes to the America On-line forum was quick to note: "This woman who turns up to testify to seeing FOUR MEN -- coincidence that it sounds just like FUHR-MAN?" She seemed to be suggesting a conspiracy theory involving the defense and the prosecution, which has scheduled as a witness a Los Angeles police detective, Mark Fuhrman. The defense calls Mr. Fuhrman a racist and has suggested he may have planted a bloody glove at Mr. Simpson's Brentwood estate. With the click of a computer mouse, one can gain access to complete collections of Simpson jokes and lawyer jokes, not to mention Simpson cartoons and doctored photographs of dubious taste. No one even remotely associated with the trial escapes electronic scrutiny. Debating the trial in cyberspace has become so popular that people even log on to the O. J. forums to express their contempt for people who log on to the O. J. forums. "This is ridicously to spend this much time and $ on someone is totally guilty in some way if not at all," one person messaged. Reflecting the egalitarianism of the net, the message drew praise, scorn and a note earnestly criticizing the writer's syntax and spelling. On Compuserve each Sunday, subscribers can pose questions about the case directly to legal experts. Rather than rely on conventional news organizations for information and analysis, the computer networks allow anyone to be a reporter, commentator or publisher. "I started hunting all over the Internet for the grand jury transcript," Mr. Walraven said. When he finally found an electronic copy, "I figured, it doesn't cost anything to post it on the Internet, so why not make it available to everyone? It was basically an act of good will." It was not Mr. Walraven's only act of good will. Last month, he harnessed the Internet for British Columbia's large Japanese community to help reunite nearly 30 families and friends separated by the Kobe earthquake. But he is less known for that act of cyber-heroism than he is for the O. J. archives. Mr. Walraven said more than 10,000 people, mainly from North America but also from Asia and Europe, have retrieved files from his Simpson data base, and there are at least a dozen similar sites on the global computer web. "I am currently in France for the next several months and am upset that I will not be able to see the live broadcast," G. Eckl wrote to the O. J. discussion group on Usenet, requesting information on where to get court transcripts. "Try ftp site islandnet.com/Jack Walraven/OJ-stuff," responded Alice J. Murphy of Fairbanks, Alaska. Asked by electronic mail why she spent so much time in the O. J. forums, she responded in similar fashion. "The best way to get at the truth is to read the official court transcripts on the net, including the grand jury testimony, the preliminary hearing, the judge's rulings and the actual trial testimony," wrote Ms. Murphy, a Brooklyn native who now lists Internet surfing as her favorite sport. "Of course, one of the reasons I have time to do this is because there isn't that much to do up here in the winter." The O. J. mania in cyberspace has also been fueled by Internet's World Wide Web, which allows advanced Internet users to navigate easily through text files, photographs, sound files and even video clips. One area on the web, as it is called, allows visitors to view, over and over, a video clip of Mr. Simpson pleading not guilty at his arraignment. Time Inc. offers "O. J. Central" on the Web, complete with diagrams of the crime scene, photographs of the principal participants and articles extracted from Time, People and Vibe magazines, Mr. Simpson's book "I Want to Tell You," the Court TV network and NBC News. Walter Isaacson, Time Warner's editor of new media, said the web site that includes "O. J. Central" was "getting up to a million hits a week," a hit being an instance when someone taps into the service. Graphic   Photo: Computer services have offered data bases on the O. J. Simpson trial.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
Prodigy Sees Quick Growth From Internet Web Service
body: The Prodigy Services Company, struggling to regain ground it has lost in the consumer on-line information industry, said yesterday that the addition of a new Internet feature had led to phenomenal growth in the last two weeks. The company said that more than 100,000 Prodigy customers, many of them new subscribers, signed up for special software that lets them connect to the Internet's World Wide Web since the company began offering it on Jan. 17, and that the sign-up rate was continuing at 12,000 a day. Prodigy has an estimated 1.2 million users. The company, however, declined to be specific on how many of the Web users were existing Prodigy customers and how many were new to the service. The World Wide Web is the fastest-growing service on the global maze of computer networks known as the Internet. It allows even casual computer users to explore and use the Internet's vast information resources using point-and-click computer commands. Until Prodigy began its Web service two weeks ago, however, access to the Web required users to have better-than-average technical proficiency and special types of Internet connections. Compuserve and America Online, Prodigy's two main rivals, are expected to offer World Wide Web services later this year. "It makes sense that Prodigy would attract a lot of customers, because right now they have no competition," said Lorraine Sileo, an analyst with Simba Information Inc. of Wilton, Conn. "But obviously they will be copied, and at that point the loyalty of their subscribers is going to be tested." Nate Zelnick, associate editor of Information & Interactive Services Report, a newsletter based in Washington, agreed that Prodigy would be hard pressed to sustain its growth when Compuserve, America Online and other rivals, including the Microsoft Corporation, added Web services later this year. But Mr. Zelnick said Prodigy was preparing to completely rebuild its system this year, based on Internet standards. "They have some very interesting stuff coming up in P-2," Mr. Zelnick said, referring to the second-generation Prodigy software now scheduled for delivery within six months. "This is a good way to keep them competitive." According to Simba Information, Compuserve, a division of H & R Block, was the largest consumer information service at the end of 1994, with 2.66 million subscribers. Next was America Online, with 1.5 million, followed by Prodigy, with 1.2 million. But Prodigy experienced "very little if any growth in 1994," Ms. Sileo said, while America Online nearly tripled in size in the same period. She said Prodigy was promoting itself as a family-oriented service, while most new computers were being sold to a younger audience. Prodigy is owned in partnership by the International Business Machines Corporation and Sears, Roebuck & Company. Though it had an estimated $200 million in revenue in 1994, according to Simba Information, it has yet to make a profit.

title:
BUSINESS TECHNOLOGY;
Prodigy Leads Its Peers Onto the World Wide Web
body: The wired world is going wild over the World Wide Web. The Prodigy on-line information service yesterday became the first consumer computer network to open its electronic portals to the popular Internet service known as the World Wide Web. The Web allows even computer novices to easily search the global Internet network for text, pictures -- and, in some cases, sounds -- and analysts say it is rapidly emerging as the point-and-click prototype for the information superhighway. Prodigy's move follows an announcement last week that the Microsoft Corporation would include an optional connection to the Web in future products, including its Windows operating system that is used in tens of millions of personal computers. Prodigy's rivals, including Compuserve Inc. and America Online Inc., have also disclosed plans to offer Web access to their millions of subscribers in coming months. The expected rush of consumers to the World Wide Web could turn the global computer network into a truly mass medium. And the willingness of formerly tightly controlled commercial networks like Prodigy to open their doors to the Web marks a fundamental shift in the structure and strategy of on-line information industry, which last year generated nearly $13 billion in revenue. In the future, big private network operators like Prodigy and Compuserve are less likely to compete chiefly on the strength of the specialized software, electronic publications and information services found only on their networks; instead, such companies will need to recast themselves as open gateways to publicly accessible information. The endorsement of the Web by the commercial services is also likely to accelerate the rush of businesses hoping to conduct electronic commerce there, lured by the prospects of millions of potential new customers. So far, more than 1,700 businesses have set up shop in cyberspace with so-called Web sites. And new ones are opening daily -- including Fisher Scientific International's chemicals catalogue and Joan & Annie's Brownies, which when went on the Web this week. Compared with past ways of sharing information over the Internet, the Web uses less intimidating technology and provides greater security for conducting financial transactions electronically. Estimates of the number of Web users today range from one million to three million. But Prodigy, Microsoft and other consumer servicers are expected to introduce millions of new users to the Web. Clifford R. Kurtzman, president of the Tenagra Corporation in Nassau Bay, Tex., which helps businesses and organizations get established on the Web, said yesterday that Prodigy and other consumer systems "will tend to bring more of the home-shopping crowd into the Internet, where typically the major users have been businesses, universities and large organizations." "And as they come, I expect more businesses will come to take advantage of the opportunity to sell goods and services to them," Mr. Kurtzman added in telephone interview yesterday. Melissa Sommers, a potential client who was sitting in Mr. Kurtzman's office yesterday, said she was interested in selling contact lenses and other vision aids on the Web. Ms. Sommers, an optometrist who operates a shop called the NASA Vision Center in Webster, Tex., said she does not use a personal computer -- "That's what my kids do" -- and that the idea for her to place a catalogue on the Web first arose in a casual conversation last week with an architect interested in the Web. "Then a patient came into my office this week, and he was involved in this kind of thing, and we got to talking, and that's why I'm here," Ms. Sommers said. "It looks like a good business opportunity." Mr. Kurtzman said that Prodigy's move to the Web yesterday was "necessary for their continued survival," and would prevent -- for the time being, at least -- the erosion of their base of subscribers and advertisers. More and more commercial customers like Ms. Sommers, he said, are likely to bypass networks like Prodigy's and set up shop directly on the Web through increasingly inexpensive Internet access providers. In a report issued to its clients last week, Forrester Research Inc. of Cambridge, Mass., concluded that by 1998 the World Wide Web would have more 11.2 million users while all the commercial on-line services combined would have only 9.6 million users. "Once getting on the Web is easy and reliable for the consumer, there will be no going back to America Online or Prodigy," said Mary Modahl of Forrester. "The best content, the most people and the lowest prices will all be on the Net." A Prodigy spokesman said the Web access was something that the company had been planning for some time -- not as a defensive move but as an added service to the company's estimated two million users. But Shikhar Ghosh, chief executive of Open Market Inc. of Cambridge, Mass., one of many new companies that provide businesses with the tools and services needed to conduct electronic commerce, said Prodigy's endorsement of the World Wide Web -- as well as the endorsement by Microsoft and others -- was an affirmation that the on-line world had changed irrevocably. "The difference," Mr. Ghosh said, "is that historically people who control the access have controlled the content, whether it's on-line services, newspapers or libraries. Where we're going is that access and content are being separated, very much like the Internet model." While the Web was created in 1989 as a way for scientists to share information around the globe, it did not really catch the public's attention until 1993, when software that simplified commands for navigating the Internet became widely available. The key to the Web is hyper-linking, a technology that permits a publisher to create links among related documents, regardless of where on the computer network they physically reside. For example, someone reading a Web article on travel might click on a highlighted phrase referring to the South Pole, and be automatically connected to a computer in New Zealand that offers products and services to arctic travelers. As with the Internet itself, it is difficult to ascertain how many people regularly use the World Wide Web today. Most estimates are based on the number of "web browser" programs that have been distributed to allow people to take advantage of the graphical nature of the system. Spyglass Technologies Inc. of Naperville, Ill., has issued more than 20 million licenses for its Mosaic browsing software, and that was before it signed an agreement earlier this month to provide Microsoft with a Mosaic-based web browser for every copy of its next version of Windows -- Windows 95 -- due out later this year. "Our estimate of the Web is on the order of a million," said Matthew K. Gray, chief technologist of the Net Genesis Corporation, a consulting company in Cambridge, Mass., that provides services for World Wide Web access providers. Mr. Gray said he based his estimate on the volume of "hits," or requests for information, on his Web server computers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The rate of hits on popular servers is certain to increase with the newcomers. Some longtime Web users say the Internet can easily absorb the increase in traffic, even though there may be isolated problems of overloading. "The screaming hordes don't matter on the Web," said Mike Walsh, a principal of Internet Info, a market research and consulting firm in Falls Church, Va. "It's like all of a sudden having more viewers on a television broadcast station. It doesn't matter to the mechanism."
