(Sources: Merit Network Services; Open Market)

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
Microsoft's Next Move Is On Line
body: The Microsoft Corporation, in a move certain to accelerate the already dizzying growth of the Internet and on-line information services, disclosed plans yesterday to become one of the world's largest commercial providers of access to the global Internet computer network. In remarks scheduled to be delivered last night at a software industry conference in Seattle, William H. Gates, chairman and chief executive of the Redmond, Wash., software company, outlined plans to offer full access to the global computer network through the Microsoft Network on-line information service it plans to start up later this year. Until yesterday, Microsoft had not disclosed the extent to which it would link its network to the Internet. Microsoft already provides the software that controls the basic operations of tens of millions of personal computers. The company's entrance onto the Internet could help stimulate a mass market for the on-line sale of goods and services -- a market that thousands of companies are already trying to create by setting up shop in cyberspace. The move would also place heavy competitive pressure on the current leading providers of on-line networks and Internet access -- companies like Compuserve, Prodigy Services, America Online and Netcom Online Communications Services. "They have fired a salvo at the on-line information services and at the Internet service providers as well," said Allen Weiner, principal analysts for on-line strategies at Dataquest, a market research firm in San Jose, Calif. "They are going to force everyone to look at their strategies." Microsoft's planned high-speed information service with direct links to the Internet will be built and maintained by Uunet Technologies Inc. of Falls Church, Va., a leading commercial Internet service. Microsoft said yesterday it had paid an undisclosed sum for a minority stake in Uunet, which is privately held. Officials at Uunet said they would undertake a rapid expansion of their existing network to accommodate what analysts said could be millions of new Internet users brought into cyberspace by Microsoft. Microsoft also said yesterday that it had paid an undisclosed sum to license rights to two software products -- NCSA Mosaic and Spyglass Enhanced Mosaic -- to include in future versions of its Windows PC software, as well as in other unspecified Microsoft products. Mosaic, originally developed at the University of Illinois National Center for Supercomputer Applications, is a so-called Web browser that lets users search for and manipulate information in the subset of the Internet known as the World Wide Web. Thousands of companies have already established a presence on the World Wide Web, lured by the prospect of secure commercial transactions in a format that even novice computer users can quickly understand. Microsoft's explicit endorsement of the Web with yesterday's announcements -- and its promise to make Web access as simple as a click of a computer mouse -- could persuade thousands of more businesses to enter what they may have perceived as an arcane and technologically daunting marketplace. If the technologies described by Mr. Gates are put in place as planned before the end of the year, users of any personal computer equipped with a modem and future versions of Microsoft's Windows operating system will be able to dial into the Microsoft Network with a local phone call and, from there, to move seamlessly into the Internet at the click of a button. Conversely, any current Internet users could easily enter the Microsoft Network. Microsoft said in November that it planned to offer its network as a vehicle for businesses to sell goods and services to millions of computer users. Microsoft would take a percentage of the revenue generated by the businesses, and charge a monthly fee to consumers. The company has struck alliances with several banking and financial services companies, including Visa International, in advance of the introduction. Unlike current on-line information services such as Compuserve and Prodigy that use telephone company networks to offer limited access to the Internet, Uunet will provide the Microsoft Network with high-speed, dedicated circuits that are more than twice as fast. Microsoft's selection of Uunet as its network builder meant it passed over other Internet-access providers like Netcom Online of San Jose, Performance Systems International of Herndon, Va., and the telecommunications companies Sprint and MCI Communications. "I'm sure our competitors are not happy," said John Sidgmore, chief executive of Uunet. But he added that Microsoft's decision to plunge directly into the Internet would eventually benefit even his rivals by validating the Internet as a medium for digital commerce. "It's going to enable new classes of applications and users who were unaware, or unable, to get to the Internet before," he said. Windows is now installed on a majority of all new personal computers. By building an optional one-button connection to the Internet through its own on-line information service, Microsoft will be able to reach potential customers much more easily than any other Internet provider. Microsoft expects its next version of Windows, called Windows 95, to sell as many as 20 million copies in 1995, though its introduction is now delayed until August. The Microsoft Network will become operational at the same time. The first versions of the Microsoft Network and Windows 95 will not include Mosaic or full Internet access, said Bill Miller, director of marketing for Microsoft's network information services division. Initially they will include only Internet electronic mail and news services. But Mr. Miller said that access to the World Wide Web would be added before the end of the year.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
Prodigy Cuts Work Force As Part of Broad Revamping
body: The Prodigy Services Company, one of the country's largest on-line computer information services, dismissed an estimated 100 employees yesterday, or nearly 15 percent of its total work force. The company, which is based in White Plains, said the staff reduction included some senior officials and was part of a broad revaming prompted by both technical and strategic changes in the on-line industry. "Prodigy was built to be an end-to-end, do-it-all-ourselves service, and through advances in technology we can now farm things out," said Scott Kurnit, Prodigy's executive vice president. "As a result, we need fewer people." The company, which says it has more than two million subscribers, has announced plans to link its service more tightly with the global Internet, a worldwide network of several million computers that contains vastly more information than Prodigy alone can generate. Also, Prodigy recently formed a separate division to offer access to the Internet independent of its consumer information system. A key to the change is the emergence of standard production tools that unlike the proprietary tools used by Prodigy in the past, allow businesses and individuals to easily create information for Prodigy or the Internet without Prodigy's involvement. By adopting an Internet-standard production tool known as the Hyper Text Markup Language, Prodigy is opening its network to the rapid creation of new services, including news, sports and financial services. "It's so much easier to produce, and thus it's easier to do deals, and to have third parties develop content for us," Mr. Kurnit said. Prodigy, formed in the mid-1980's as a joint project of the International Business Machines Corporation and Sears, Roebuck & Company, has yet to report a profit. It has also added new subscribers at a slower rate than its two main rivals in the $500 million consumer information industry, H & R Block's Compuserve Inc. and America Online Inc.

title:
WEDDINGS;
Hilary Gleekman, William Greenberg
body: Dr. Hilary Amy Gleekman, an internist in the division of infectious diseases at Montefiore Medical Center in the Bronx, was married last evening to Dr. William Jay Greenberg, a founder and an owner of Physicians' Online Inc., a medical-information computer service in Tarrytown, N.Y. Rabbi Haskel Lookstein officiated at Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun in Manhattan. Dr. Gleekman-Greenberg, 31, is also a clinical instructor at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in the Bronx and is an actress. She graduated magna cum laude from Wellesley College, where she was elected to Phi Beta Kappa, and received her M.D. degree from Mount Sinai School of Medicine. She is a daughter of Barbara and Dr. Wallace J. Gleekman of Newton, Mass. Her father teaches chemistry at Brookline (Mass.) High School. Her mother is a reference librarian at the Waltham (Mass.) Public Library. Dr. Greenberg, 33, graduated magna cum laude from Tufts University and received his M.D. degree from newyork Medical College. He is the son of Marilyn and Allen Greenberg of newyork. His mother is an owner of Luisant, a cosmetics-brush manufacturer in newyork. His father is a partner in Graubard, Mollen, Horowitz, Pomeranz & Shapiro, a newyork law firm.

title: Libel Suit Against Prodigy Tests On-Line Speech Limits - Correction Appended
body: The Prodigy Services Company, operator of one of the country's largest on-line information services, has agreed to help track down a computer user who posted an electronic message accusing a Long Island investment bank of fraud and other criminal activity. Prodigy's move, agreed to late Monday in State Supreme Court in Nassau County, comes in response to a $100 million lawsuit charging libel and negligence by Prodigy and a subscriber, David Lusby of Key West, Fla. The suit seeks $100 million more in punitive damages. Through his lawyer, Mr. Lusby asserted that his Prodigy account was inactive and that someone else must have been using it without his authorization. Questions of defamation, slander and libel on the Internet web of computer networks have been gathering momentum, and the Prodigy case is not the first of its kind. But because of its size and the prominence of its litigants, the case seems certain to focus the attention of lawyers and legal scholars in an area where there is little case law to offer guidance. "This is a brand new area of law and technology, and the key issue is what standard a publisher of an electronic bulletin-board system is going to be held to," said Jacob H. Zamansky of the Manhattan firm of Finkelstein, Bruckman, Wohl, Most & Rothman. "You can disparage someone and libel them instantly in front of one and a half million people without anyone having the opportunity to take the message out or screen it." Mr. Zamansky is representing the investment firm Stratton Oakmont of Lake Success, L.I., and its president, Daniel M. Porush, which filed the suit last week. On-line computer services connected to the Internet, though now used by millions of people worldwide, are still relatively new. Because the networks combine the immediacy of the telephone with the persistence and potential reach of print, they tend to blur longstanding distinctions of libel, slander and legal jurisdiction. "Libel seems to be emerging as a locus of dispute on the Internet," said Margaret Chon of Syracuse University law school. "It's just the push of a button, and people sometimes don't stop to think about the consequences of doing that." Of the handful of resolved libel cases arising from electronic postings in recent years, the most widely cited is Cubby vs. Compuserve. In that case, filed against the service owned by H & R Block Inc., a Federal judge ruled in 1991 that Compuserve could not be held accountable for messages posted on its system any more than a bookstore owner could be held liable for the contents of a book he sells. Other rulings have said that telephone companies cannot be held responsible for the content of conversations they carry. "Prodigy is a very open network, very similar to a telephone network," said Carol Wallace, a spokeswoman for Prodigy. But Prodigy, unlike Compuserve and the phone companies, has long maintained the right to screen messages for content, primarily for vulgarity. "We have a machine that scans for unacceptable words" in each of the approximately 75,000 new messages posted to the system every day, Ms. Wallace said. Still, she noted that subscribers who enter the Money Talk bulletin board area, where the disputed message was posted, are directed to an opening message that says in part, "Prodigy does not verify, endorse or otherwise vouch for the contents of any note and cannot be held responsible in any way for information contained in any such note." The message that prompted the lawsuit first appeared on Oct. 22 or Oct. 23 on the Money Talk bulletin board, where subscribers post public comments on financial issues. "The end of Stratton Oakmont will finally come this week," read the message, bearing Mr. Lusby's name and identification code. "This brokerage firm headed by president and soon to be proven criminal -- Daniel Porrush [sic] -- will close this week." The message went on to assert that Stratton Oakmont had managed an initial public stock offering in a company, the Solomon-Page Group Ltd., which the day after the offering on Oct. 21 disclosed it had lost its major customer and source of 40 percent of its revenue for the previous three years. "This is fraud, fraud, fraud and criminal!!!!!!!" the message asserted. Stratton Oakmont says that nothing fraudulent or otherwise criminal occurred. Timothy J. Koenig, a Key West, Fla., lawyer representing Mr. Lusby, said yesterday in a telephone interview that his client was a former employee of the Prodigy Services Company and had not used the Prodigy account in some time. He said it was not the first time Mr. Lusby's account had been used to post offensive messages on the network. In the newyork hearing before Justice Stuart Ain on Monday, Prodigy agreed to remove any message concerning Stratton Oakmont or Solomon Page from its system, to screen all messages to the Money Talk bulletin board for three months and to block any messages about the companies, to track down the person responsible for posting the offending message, and to provide the court with a detailed explanation of how messages to the system are posted, screened and monitored. Correction  An article in Business Day on Wednesday about a libel lawsuit filed against the Prodigy Services Company by the investment firm of Stratton Oakmont misstated one term of an agreement reached by Prodigy at a newyork State court hearing. Prodigy agreed to tell the court whether it has the ability to screen and block messages posted on an electronic bulletin board. It has not agreed to block any messages. Correction-Date: November 19, 1994, Saturday

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
A Cyberspace Atlas: America Online
body: AMERICA ONLINE, the second stop on our virtual tour of cyberspace, is the most ambitious and aggressive of the popular online information services. It is impressive and infuriating in nearly equal measures. Point: America Online Inc. of Vienna, Va., has been advertising itself for some time as "America's most popular Internet service provider," when technically it had about as much to do with providing Internet services as does my Aunt Tootie. Such arrogance has contributed to America Online's reputation as America's Least Popular Service on the Internet. In some corners of the Internet, the letters "aol" in someone's electronic mail address are as damning as the scarlet "A" on Hester Prynne's dress. Counterpoint: AOL last week revealed plans to become a true Internet service provider and to offer its 1.25 million users the most impressive array of Internet services of any commercial online service. If the company delivers on its promises, AOL could in fact become a standard-setter for easy Internet access. Point: In my experience, America Online has been the least reliable of the Big Three services (Compuserve and Prodigy are the others) in terms of busy signals and system crashes, and it appears to be beset by the problems of overloaded resources as it adds 100,000 new users a month. Despite such strains, it just sent out more than a million free-trial-subscription diskettes to potential new customers. How bad has it been? At one point last winter I decided to cancel my subscription, but could not get through to anyone either by computer or phone to do so. Counterpoint: I am glad I did not cancel at the time, because the system is getting better. Nobody offers an easier-to-use system, and ease of use is vitally important to the millions of computer owners who are thinking about exploring the online information universe. One can argue that America Online is growing faster than the other services because it does a better job of giving customers what they want. What do they want? A relatively simple, inexpensive service that provides lots of interesting content and access to lots of free software, apparently. America Online makes it easy to get started. The software (for DOS, Windows or Macintosh computers) is available free by calling (800) 827-6364. It includes 10 hours of free connection time. The current pricing structure gets fairly steep for people who plan to use the system to its full extent. After the trial period, the base rate is $9.95 a month, which includes five hours of connection time. Additional hours are $3.50 each. The hourly rate will decline to $2.95 beginning Jan. 1. There are a couple of exorbitant extra charges on themail side: $2.50 a letter for sending a printed message to Aunt Tootie or others who do not have an electronic mail account, and $2 a page for sending messages to a facsimile machine. Other than that, America Online is one of the better bargains among the online services. It offers thousands of free software programs and perhaps the easiest system anywhere for downloading them (transferring them from America Online's computers to your computer). Remember, though, that you usually pay for connection time while downloading the software, and at America Online's anemic top speed of 9,600 bits per second, a big file can take many minutes, or even hours, to capture. The service offers access to a wide assortment of technical support and computer product data bases, and its selection of articles from affiliated publications (including a limited selection from The newyork Times) is impressive. Many people are fond of America Online's "chat" forums, where users can type messages back and forth. Some discussion groups are interesting, but, as any experienced cybernaut can attest, most are banal. Fortunately, America Online makes it easy to point-and-click oneself out of tedious groups and situations. AOL recently updated its opening screens, giving them a more colorful, more intuitive command structure. Once connected, the user is greeted by a voice that says, "Welcome." If there is electronic mail waiting, it adds, "You've got mail." The "spotlight" page that greets the user is well done, with six one-button shortcuts into the system: to electronic mail, to the top news story of the day, to the main menu and to a selection of other services a user might otherwise not know about. A visitor on Veteran's Day, for example, was offered a way to send messages of appreciation to soldiers; a chance to review rankings of more than 700 mutual funds, and an opportunity to discuss science-related toys for the holidays, The main menu screen has boxes representing 14 different services that can be reached at the click of a mouse, including the day's news, personal finance, entertainment, education, computing, sports, "kids only," online shopping and "the Internet connection." The Internet connection is what separates AOL from its rival services today. While most online services now allow users to send and receive electronic mail over the Internet, America Online also offers Gopher, WAIS and Usenet news groups. Gopher and WAIS are two ways to search for information on the vast Internet, while Usenet is a popular collection of about 6,000 different discussion groups that is most commonly reached through the Internet. By the standards of the Unix tribe and other indigenous inhabitants of the Internet -- the native population before the arrival of the great masses -- the current America Online Internet tools are weak. For internet neophytes, however, they are easy to use. More information about the service is available from America Online Inc. of Vienna, Va.; phone (703) 448-8700 or (800) 827-6364. title: Microsoft Seen Disclosing On-Line Network Plan
body: The Microsoft Corporation, seeking to extend its domination beyond the software industry into the realm of interactive services, is expected to outline its plans today for an ambitious on-line information service called the Microsoft Network. Analysts say the network, which has been known by its code name, Marvel, could become a leader in the $13 billion on-line services industry almost as soon as it goes on line in the middle of next year. "It's going to be a juggernaut by this time a year from now," said Jesse Berst, editorial director of the newsletter Windows Watcher. Microsoft plans to announce the service at the Comdex fall computer trade show, which begins today in Las Vegas, Nev. The keys to its strategy, according to people who have been briefed, are lowering the initial cost and complexity for consumers to use on-line services, giving businesses a greater financial incentive to offer goods and services electronically and offering technology superior to that used by other on-line services. For consumers, the Microsoft Network is expected to have a low monthly fee for basic services -- perhaps $5 a month -- with extra charges for specific uses, like $1.25 a day for detailed baseball box scores or a similar fee for selected stock quotes. Current consumer services typically charge $9.95 a month for five hours of connection time, plus $3 or more an hour for additional hours. Unlike other commercial plans that charge businesses a relatively high initial fee to develop and offer their services on line, Microsoft would provide simple and inexpensive software tools to help companies develop services on the Microsoft Network. The network would place relatively few restrictions on the types of services that could be offered, making it easier for companies to advertise on line, for example. Microsoft would take a percentage of the business generated through advertising or on-line sales. "It will be less than 50 percent, but substantially more than 5 percent," an executive familiar with Microsoft's plans said. In contrast, the leading consumer services now pay information providers an average of 10 percent to 20 percent of the connection time charges incurred by the consumers using those services. Eventually, another executive familiar with Microsoft's plans said, the company would like to eliminate all time-based fees and let customers pay only for the services they use, regardless of the time used. Industry executives who have seen prototype versions of the Microsoft Network said it appeared similar to existing on-line services, including those of Compuserve, Prodigy and America Online. But Microsoft has outlined ambitious plans to expand the service rapidly. The network will initially focus on electronic mail, news information data bases, personal finance and entertainment. A person close to Microsoft said the company intended to add an array of other services, including full access to the millions of computers on the global Internet. Eventually, the Microsoft Network will also be offered on interactive cable television and high-speed telephone networks. Microsoft has little experience in on-line services but so thoroughly dominates the personal computer software industry that any strategic moves it makes into other areas are viewed as having the potential to influence markets. "They have an opportunity to change the rules, and they're certainly going to," said Kathey Hale, senior analyst for on-line information services at Dataquest, a market research firm in San Jose, Calif. As word leaked out late last week of Microsoft's planned announcement today, shares of America Online Inc. plunged more than 10 percent. The stock recovered somewhat on Friday, rising $1.75, to $66.75. In a telephone conference with financial analysts and reporters last week, the president and chief executive of America Online, Stephen M. Case, took the unusual step of disparaging Microsoft's on-line strategy even before it was announced. "Our research has shown that very few people choose those kinds of premium or pay-per-view pricing plans," he said. Microsoft has been maneuvering to create foundations for the network for some time. In recent months it has agreed to acquire several companies that make software useful for displaying and manipulating information electronically, including Intuit Inc., maker of the popular Quicken personal financial software. Microsoft also announced alliances with several regional banks and with Visa International, which may eventually permit secure credit card and banking transactions over the Microsoft Network. The network will be closely linked with Microsoft's forthcoming Windows 95 operating system for PC's. Initially, only Windows 95 users will be able to use the network. The operating system contains several advanced technical features, people familiar with the software said, including the ability to perform more than one operation at a time, transfer and link information in one application to another automatically and reach the on-line service through an office computer network. The only other consumer service expected to offer similar capabilities is Interchange, a prototype system developed by Ziff-Davis Interactive of Cambridge, Mass. The company is for sale, and a list of potential buyers is said to include AT&T, which recently started its own on-line service for mobile executives. An industry executive familiar with Microsoft's plans said the company expected to sell 30 million to 40 million copies of Windows 95 in the 12 months after its introduction next May or June. Everyone with Windows 95 will be given a chance to subscribe to the service simply by clicking on one or two buttons and entering a credit card number, the executive said. Even if only 10 percent of Windows 95 users subscribe, the Microsoft Network will vault into the top tier of consumer information services, along with H& R Block's Compuserve, the Prodigy joint venture of I.B.M. and Sears, Roebuck & Company, and America Online. Compuserve and Prodigy each have about two million users and America Online has about a million. "A year from now it will be interesting to see whether the overall on-line audience has increased or whether Microsoft takes customers away from A.O.L., Prodigy and Compuserve, which are all vulnerable," said Gary H. Arlen, president of Arlen Communications Inc., a research company in Bethesda, Md.

title: America Online Buys 2 Internet Companies
body: America Online Inc., facing a challenge from the Microsoft Corporation in the market for on-line computer services, said yesterday that it had acquired two small Internet service companies for a total of more than $34 million in stock. The companies acquired by America Online, Navisoft Inc. and Booklink Technologies Inc., would become the core of America Online's recently formed Internet Services Company. The companies, which are start-ups that have generated no revenue to date, make software that allow businesses and consumers to more easily use the Internet, especially the rapidly growing area known as the World Wide Web. Some of the software would be incorporated into America Online's own consumer software, allowing the company's 1.2 million on-line services customers to gain access to the World Wide Web, which is increasingly being used by businesses to market goods and services to computer users. The acquired software would also be used as a cornerstone for a new on-line service that would focus on business applications for the Internet. "It's a brilliant move on A.O.L.'s part," said Mary Modahl, senior analyst at Forrester research Inc. of Cambridge, Mass. "Consumers are not going to buy more than one information service. They will go to the place that has the widest door to what's available in the on-line universe. By adding Web access, America Online will have the widest open door." "It's an aggressive move to counter what A.O.L. sees as a looming threat from Microsoft and is clearly timed to blunt the impact of Microsoft's announcement of Marvel next week," said Adam Schoenfeld, news director of Jupiter Research Inc. of newyork. Marvel is the code name for the rival on-line information service that Microsoft is planning to introduce next year along with its next generation of the Windows operating system. America Online's stock has been pummeled in the last two days, losing about 10 percent of its value, in reaction to investor fears about the competitive impact of Microsoft's Marvel. Yesterday, America Online's shares dropped $3, to $63.25, in Nasdaq trading. On Tuesday, the shares fell $6.75. In acquiring Booklink Technologies of Wilmington, Mass., for $30 million in stock, America Online would gain control of prototype software called Internetworks, which is scheduled to be formally introduced next week at the Comdex computer trade show in Las Vegas. Advance copies of Internetworks have been praised by some testers as superior to existing programs for browsing the World Wide Web, including Mosaic and its variations. Besides Web access, the software includes a full range of Internet services, including access to electronic mail, discussion groups and a variety of file searching and transfer tools. It is said to work especially well with the common computer modems and telephone lines used by consumers. Booklinks is a wholly owned subsidiary of CMG Information Services. In the second facet of the deal, America Online would acquire Navisoft for 65,000 shares of stock, which at current levels would be valued at slightly more than $4 million. Navisoft's president, David C. Cole, a venture capitalist who was formerly president of the Ashton-Tate Company and Ziff Communications, is to become president of America Online's Internet Services Company, the company said.

title: Interest Seen In Another Ziff Holding
body: The $1.4 billion sale of the Ziff-Davis Publishing Company to Forstmann Little & Company yesterday still leaves three of the Ziff family's operations on the block, including the much-anticipated Interchange Online Network, an electronic publishing system. Interchange, scheduled to begin final testing next week with more than 12,000 users nationwide, has been characterized as a new type of on-line information network whose technological capabilities go beyond those of America Online, Compuserve and Prodigy. Unlike those older services, Interchange was designed to take advantage of powerful, multimedia computers now available at relatively low cost. "There is interest from technology companies, publishing companies and from communications companies," said Michael Kolowich, president of Interchange, when asked to comment on potential buyers. Bidding closed at 5 P.M. on Interchange and the other properties, and bidders were not identified. "It's natural that the universe of interested buyers would be broader for Interchange than for the publishing company," Mr. Kolowich said, in part because of the lower price for the smaller companies and because so many companies were seeking a way to distribute information products and services electronically. Because the buyer of Interchange would automatically get an advanced publishing system and a stable of known information providers, interest is expected to be especially keen from older on-line services that have struggled to update their aging systems. Potential bidders whose names have surfaced include H & R Block Inc., which operates the Compuserve network, and Knight-Ridder Inc., which has been seeking to expand its electronic publishing. One rumor circulating last night involved Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation, whose Delphi Internet Services Inc. is in the same neighborhood in Cambridge, Mass., as Interchange and is most in need of a quick facelift. In preparation for the expected sale, Ziff executives forged a 10-year agreement that would link Interchange with the electronic content of Ziff's many computer magazines, developed by the Ziff-Davis Interactive division being sold to Forstmann Little. The remaining divisions, which could be sold individually or together, include the Ziff-Davis Exposition and Conference Company and the Information Access Company, both of Foster City, Calif.

title:
A Dispute About Disks;
U.S. Tries to Keep Secrets That Aren't Any More
body: The cold war is over but the Government has drawn a new line in the sand to control military exports: Technological information can be sent abroad if it is found in a book, but not if it is on a computer disk. In an action that illustrates the difficulty of preserving the nation's military export controls in the information age, the State Department has denied the request of a California engineer to export a computer disk that has samples of some powerful and widely used software encoding formulas. The request to the State Department's International Traffic in Arms Regulations Office was made this summer by Philip R. Karn Jr., a San Diego telecommunications engineer who filed it as a challenge to the regulations. Mr. Karn argued that the restrictions were meaningless because the same information could be obtained in standard cryptographic textbooks, which could be sent overseas without export controls and then used by simply typing or scanning the data into a computer. The same software is already freely available on computer networks around the world. The disk in question is a companion product to a popular textbook on coding techniques entitled "Applied Cryptography," written by Bruce Schneier, a computer scientist in Oak Park, Ill. The data on the disk are exactly the same as information in an appendix to Mr. Schneier's book. The information, known as source code, lists instructions that can be converted by a computer program to produce powerful cryptographic software programs that protect electronic communications. Source code on the disk includes instructions for the national coding standard known as the Data Encryption Standard, or D.E.S., and Pretty Good Privacy, or P.G.P., a popular program by Philip Zimmermann, a software developer in Boulder, Colo. The skirmish between Mr. Karn and the Government is the latest in a string of battles between the National Security Agency, the nation's electronic spying arm, and computer companies and privacy advocates. The agency has tried to restrict the export of most advanced commercial cryptographic hardware and software because it complicates its mission: eavesdropping on electronic communications around the world. Last year the Government opened an investigation into Mr. Zimmermann's activities after the Customs Department determined that copies of his program had been sent out of the country on the Internet, the global web of computer networks. The inquiry is still pending. "Does the State Department really think that foreigners can't type?" Mr. Schneier asked. "Or did the international scanner lobby get to them?"

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
Prodigy Developing a Service for Internet
body: Following the lead of its main rivals in the on-line information services industry, the Prodigy Services Company is developing a business information and product marketing service for the Internet global web of computer networks, company officials said yesterday. Prodigy also plans to give its nearly two million subscribers access to the thousands of often raucous bulletin boards known as Usenet, and to create special services of interest to business executives. These will be available beginning Oct. 10, a company spokesman said. Unlike subscription-based commercial computer networks like Prodigy, the Internet is a loose affiliation of government, university and corporate computer networks on which much information is available free once someone gets access through an Internet host computer. For commercial services like Prodigy, there are business opportunities in giving customers access to the Internet and in setting up sites or "nodes" on the Internet for use by businesses that want to offer product information, provide services and let customers shop electronically. Dozens of private companies have sprung up in recent months to set up such sites. The Internet strategy is "central to where we see our business going," said William C. Day, Internet product manager for Prodigy, which is based in White Plains and is a partnership of the International Business Machines Corporation and Sears, Roebuck & Company. "It's about time," said Jayne Levin, editor of The Internet Letter, a newsletter published by Net Week Inc. of Washington. "If they do it right they could really expand their market share. But there's already a lot of competition and the competition is very savvy and very good." Prodigy's main rival, Compuserve, a division of H & R Block, announced in August that it was forming a subsidiary to help businesses develop content for the Internet. A smaller competitor, America Online of Vienna, Va., which has about a million subscribers, also offers access to Usenet on the Internet and formed four new divisions earlier this month to explore new network services. Mr. Day of Prodigy said the company's new Internet site would be aimed at a "business, professional, male" audience, unlike the Prodigy Information Service's focus on family-oriented information. "It won't be called Prodigy, but it will be from Prodigy the company," he said. Mr. Day said Prodigy would work with Advantis, a subsidiary of I.B.M., to develop Internet access software for personal computers that used the Microsoft Windows and Apple Macintosh operating systems. Advantis is also developing software to ease Internet access for Prodigy customers with PC's based on I.B.M.'s own OS/2 operating system. The expansion of Prodigy's core information services network into the Usenet poses potential problems for the family-oriented service, company officials acknowledged. The Usenet, which most users currently reach through the Internet, consists of thousands of specialized "news groups" in which people with a common interest can exchange messages. Although most discussion groups carried by Usenet are benign, hundreds are devoted to sex-related topics, including pornographic pictures. And even on news groups devoted to such nominally inoffensive topics as cats and gardens, vulgar and abusive messages are common. Prodigy officials said they would give customers unrestricted access to Usenet and not try to regulate the content of the news groups reachable through the Prodigy system. But the company plans a new security system intended to let parents block Usenet access for their children and to verify a user's identity. The fee for using the Usenet groups, as well as a new service that allows thousands of computer users to "chat" by exchanging typed messages in real time, will be $3.60 an hour in addition to the basic Prodigy service charge of $14.95 a month, company officials said. Prodigy is also expected to announce today that it will begin letting customers connect to the service at higher speeds with no extra charge.

title: Mead Stock Falls on Report
body: Shares of the Mead Corporation fell yesterday after a report indicated that initial bids for its on-line information service were slightly lower than some analysts had expected. Several publishing companies, including the Times Mirror Company, the Thomson Corporation and Reed Elsevier P.L.C., have submitted preliminary bids of as much as $1 billion for Mead's on-line service, The Wall Street Journal reported yesterday. Final bids are expected before the end of the month. "We would be surprised if the properties did not fetch more," said Lawrence Ross, first vice president of Paine Webber Inc. in newyork. Paine Webber expects the final price to be $1.4 billion to $2 billion, he said. Shares of Mead fell 87.5 cents, to $49.875, on the newyork Stock Exchange. A spokeswoman for Mead , which is based in Dayton, Ohio, declined to comment on the report, other than to reaffirm that the company was on track to sell the unit before the end of the year. Representatives of the publishing companies cited in the article also declined to comment. Mead's Lexis service stores and distributes legal documents and information electronically to thousands of clients. The Nexis service contains archives of articles from thousands of publications, including The newyork Times.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
A Secret Computer Code Is Out
body: In an act of business espionage whose impact is not yet clear, someone has anonymously circulated the underlying software formula of one of the most popular coding systems used for protecting information sent over computer networks. The formula, which has been a closely guarded trade secret, belongs to RSA Data Security Inc. a small, privately held software company in Redwood City, Calif., that sells encryption software to the nation's largest computer and software companies, including Apple Computer, I.B.M., Lotus Development, Microsoft and Sun Microsystems. In recent days, one or more people have anonymously posted the formula on electronic bulletin boards on computer networks around the world. Although disclosure of the formula does not necessarily allow eavesdroppers to intercept and unscramble coded messages sent with the RSA encryption software, widespread dissemination could compromise the long-term effectiveness of the system, software experts said. And the disclosure does throw into question a two-year-old agreement in which the Government has allowed computer and software companies to export products incorporating the RSA system. Also unclear is the financial impact that disclosure of the formula will have on RSA, the leading maker of encryption software, with revenues estimated at $5 million to $10 million a year. Executives from RSA said in a statement released today: "RSA considers this misappropriation to be most serious. Not only is this act a violation of the law, but its publication is a gross abuse of the Internet." The Internet is the global web of computer networks on which the formula has been circulated. The formula, which is known as RC4, has become the de facto coding standard for many popular software programs including Microsoft Windows, Apple's Macintosh operating system and Lotus Notes. It is also the only software-based formula that the National Security Agency, the Government's electronic spy agency, will permit to be easily exported under an agreement the agency reached two years ago with the Software Publishers Association, an industry trade association. RSA Data Security executives said today that it was possible that public disclosure of the formula could compromise the agreement between the N.S.A. and the software industry. "I have been told it was part of this deal that RC4 be kept confidential," Jim Bidzos, president of RSA, said in an interview today. "We've kept up our end of the bargain. What's the worst that could happen? N.S.A. could say it's no longer exportable; that's entirely possible." The export issue may become moot. For one thing, the version of RC4 that the N.S.A. allows to be exported is a watered-down form of the software used in the unitedstates. And an official at the Software Publishers Association said that since the agreement was struck with the agency two years ago, much of the overseas market for encryption software has been overtaken by foreign companies using a coding formula known as the Data Encryption Standard, or D.E.S. D.E.S., which was invented at I.B.M. in the early 1970's and subsequently developed by the National Security Agency, is subject to tight export restrictions by the unitedstates Government. But Douglas Miller, the Software Publishers Association's manager of governmental affairs, said that his group had nonetheless identified at least 166 foreign-made software products that use the D.E.S. standard. The RC4 formula was first circulated on Tuesday to a specialized computer network mailing list of computer researchers who oppose the Government's stringent controls on data encryption technology. Themailing list, which has thousands of computer users around the world, is known as Cypherpunks, and themailings usually consist of highly technical discussions of data encryption. The message on Tuesday was sent from a computer in the Netherlands running a program known as an anonymous remailer. Such software permits computer users to send messages so that they are routed anonymously, leaving little or no evidence for tracing the message back to the original sender. Although motives for the disclosure of the formula remain unclear, there has been a bitter controversy between computer users on the Cypherpunks mailing list and executives at RSA Data Security. The company now holds several important patents that cover a technology known as public key cryptography, which permits individuals who have never met to easily send and receive secret messages. Members of the Cypherpunks group have contended that the RSA Data Security patents constitute a monopoly that is hindering the widespread use of data encryption software. Some members of the Cypherpunks have said they plan to take apart the RC4 formula to create their own version, which would not be controlled by RSA Data Security. RSA Data Security officials said they were conducting an investigation of this week's disclosure and would consider legal action against those who published the formula, if the person or people could be identified.

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
2 Companies Advance On-Line Shopping
body: The electronic home shopping mall came closer to reality yesterday as two of the biggest names in television retailing and computer networking stepped up their plans to sell goods in cyberspace. Home Shopping Network Inc., the nation's premier television retailer, said it had bought the on-line Internet Shopping Network. The amount was not disclosed. Also, America Online Inc., the fastest-growing consumer long-distance computer network, made its first foray into the lucrative commercial marketplace by setting up new divisions for advertising and shopping. The announcements follow recent statements by QVC Network Inc. that it plans to offer an on-line shopping service. "It's inevitable the way things are going," Steve Tomlin, vice president of interactive technology at QVC, said. "The problem is that not many people buy over the computer. Somebody's got to figure out a formula." The Home Shopping deal could transform the Internet Shopping Network from a narrowly based computer products retailer into a computerized shopping mall. "Today, the Internet, with its estimated 25 million users, presents us with the opportunity to expand our retailing expertise from television into this important venue," Home Shopping's president and chief executive, Gerald Hogan, said. Home Shopping plans to encourage major retailers to set up "stores" on the on-line service. Internet Shopping Network, which now only shows product descriptions, will soon provide still and, eventually, moving pictures of the items. Home Shopping's new on-line merchandising subsidiary, HSN Interactive, Inc., will first add consumer electronics and college textbooks and become a full-scale electronic mall by the fall of 1995, Peter Kern, senior vice president of Home Shopping, said. The unit will also help major retailers put their mail-order catalogues into a digital format and make them available on other on-line services such as Prodigy and Compuserve, he said. "In the long-term it's very smart," said an analyst, Peter Siris at UBS.  "At some point it will be a really big business." America Online said it had formed four new divisions as part of a strategy to tap emerging market opportunities. One unit, the AOL Services Company, will develop new revenue streams from interactive advertising. Another division, the Internet Services Company, aims to become a leader in the emerging global Internet market, with an initial focus on Japan and Europe. AOL International will move into new markets, while AOL Technologies will extend and leverage core technologies and operations resources. Home Shopping stock closed 62.5 cents higher at $12.50 on the newyork Stock Exchange. America Online rose $3.50, to $81, on Nasdaq.

title:
Method and Madness;
Little Brother
body: Not so long ago, high technology was seen as the likely handmaiden of totalitarian government, with surveillance systems and central computers tracking every citizen from cradle to grave. By a strange turn of events, what is now in progress is the very opposite of that nightmare. So many powerful technologies are streaming into private hands that Government is struggling to protect even the bare minimum of its legitimate domains. Once only governments could launch photo-reconnaissance satellites; now the C.I.A. is anxiously trying to curb commercial systems that can discern objects as small as a yard across, high enough resolution to interest generals as much as geologists. A fleet of navigational satellites designed to give military commanders their exact position anywhere in the world is now in essence available to anyone; the Pentagon has let the public listen in on a degraded signal, but commercial vendors with clever algorithms can restore it to near-military accuracy. The computers that tie together the Government's information systems have become increasingly porous. The better their security systems, the more tempting the challenge. Earlier this year the Pentagon discovered that a coterie of computer hackers had penetrated large parts of its sensitive though unclassified computer network and had even taken control of several military computers. Think tanks and academics have warned for years, quite erroneously, that terrorists would avail themselves of nuclear, chemical or biological weapons; it hasn't happened, because none of these items are easy to use and simpler means have always been available. But the samples of stolen Russian uranium and plutonium that have recently been captured in Germany are a clear warning that this blithe era of security may now be over. The samples seem to have come from reactor fuel and laboratories, not nuclear warheads. But that is small comfort, especially in view of new calculations that only one kilogram (2.2 pounds) of plutonium is needed to make a bomb, not eight kilograms as was generally assumed. And the smugglers caught by the German police were hawking four kilograms for a mere $250 million. PERHAPS THE MOST SURPRISING democratization of high technology is that of cryptography, once an elite art of those who guarded Government's most precious secrets. The first serious challenge to the National Security Agency's ability to crack almost everyone else's ciphers came from an ingenious coding approach created in academe in the mid-1970's and known as the public key cryptosystem. The commercial sponsor sold the program to American companies but was not allowed to export it. Then in 1991, a Colorado computer expert, Philip R. Zimmermann, produced a program apparently based on this system, which he named Pretty Good Privacy. A copy of Pretty Good Privacy found its way onto the Internet, free to takers from all countries, and all of a sudden Government-class security became available to everyone. Zimmermann's next project is to develop a pretty secure citizen's phone that scrambles conversations. At this point, of course, it's possible to wonder if the humiliation of Big Brother isn't being taken beyond reasonable limits. Some Government monopolies are not so bad: the use of force, for one. If you believe the F.B.I. is bugging your conversations, you'll want to see Zimmermann in the inventors' hall of fame; if terrorism and organized crime seem the more immediate threats, the universal right to absolute privacy looks less compelling. Is it possible for the state to get too weak in relation to its possible adversaries? That's the last thought that occurs to Americans across a wide spectrum of opinion, from free market economists to civil libertarians. From a variety of motives, they persistently call for governmental power to be curbed. The present headlong democratization of high technology is the flower of a decade of economic deregulation, and of the fading influence of military procurement as a driver of technical progress. The state is so familiar a political structure that its endurance is hard to doubt. For economists and political analysts, it is the only unit of account. Yet in his recent book, "The Transformation of War," the noted military historian Martin van Creveld argues that since modern states are no longer able to fight each other for fear of nuclear war, conventional warfare, too, has become outmoded. Since the purpose of states (at least in the view of military historians) is to fight each other, states that cannot do so must sooner or later yield to organizations that will, like sects, tribes or cults. "In North America and Western Europe, future war-making entities will probably resemble the Assassins, the group which . . . terrorized the medieval Middle East for two centuries," van Creveld predicts. Regular armed forces, as has happened in Lebanon, will degenerate into police forces or mere armed gangs; the day of the condottieri will return. Van Creveld is not the only analyst to fear for the state. From quite different reasoning, the political scientist Samuel P. Huntington argued in a widely read essay in Foreign Affairs last year that world politics would be shaped in future by clashes between cultures and religions. As the West loses its military and economic predominance, the counterresponse from the rest of the world will be couched in religious and cultural terms: "The fault lines between civilizations will be the battle lines of the future," he wrote. Even without fully embracing these forecasts of the state's eclipse, it's hard to ignore such recent incidents as the bombing of the World Trade Center or the car bombings of Jewish organizations in Buenos Aires and London. Terrorists with secure phones, satellite maps, accurate positioning and a sophisticated understanding of modern communications systems could bring down not just a few buildings but large sections of a modern economy. Big Brother is dead. The only serious likelihood of his resurrection lies in reaction to the chaos and disintegration that an era of Little Brothers might bring. Graphic   Drawing

title:
BUSINESS TECHNOLOGY;
America Online Says Users Of Service Exceed 1 Million
body: America Online Inc. of Vienna, Va., asserting that it is the country's fastest-growing consumer on-line information service, said yesterday that it had surpassed the 1 million subscriber level. The company reported 900,000 members just one month ago, and 800,000 in May. "It's 1 million down, 97 to go," said Steve Case, the company's 35-year-old president and chief executive, referring to the estimated 98 million American households. America Online yesterday also reported an alliance with Simon & Schuster, one of the world's largest publishers of educational materials, to form an interactive computer service called College Online. College Online would seek to become a commercial alternative to the global Internet, which now provides communication links for students, teachers, libraries and other educational resources on college campuses worldwide. In crossing the 1 million subscriber threshold, America Online has narrowed the gap between it and the two largest consumer on-line services, Compuserve Inc., a division of H&R Block, and the Prodigy Services Company, a joint effort of the International Business Machines Corporation and Sears, Roebuck & Company. Perhaps more significant, analysts said, was that America Online's subscriber number appears to be growing 28 percent a quarter, more than double Compuserve's rate and more than three times Prodigy's rate. On the other hand, critics have questioned whether America Online's network infrastructure can sustain such hyper growth. They cite slow system performance and frequent busy signals that have earned the service the nickname "America On Hold." Compuserve, which claims to have 2.2 million paying subscribers, is believed to be the largest consumer service, followed by Prodigy, which also claims 2.2 million users but counts multiple users per paying account. Analysts estimate that Prodigy has between 1 million and 1.3 million paying customers. Prodigy, meanwhile, announced yesterday that it had formed a marketing alliance with the CBS broadcasting network in which the partners will barter advertising space on each other's systems. CBS will use Prodigy to offer interactive entertainment features, including offering some Prodigy users the ability to view, on their computer screens, short preview clips from CBS's fall television lineup. Rod W. Kuckro, editor of the Washington, D.C., newsletter Information & Interactive Services Report, said the "Big Five" on-line consumer services -- Compuserve, Prodigy, America Online, the News Corporation's Delphi Internet Services and GE Information Services Company's Genie -- accounted for 85 percent of the 5.28 million paying customers of consumer on-line services in July. Delphi officials declined to divulge the service's subscriber base or rate of growth, but a spokeswoman said "we are number four" on the list. The spokeswoman said Delphi's rate of growth was comparable to America Online's. A Compuserve spokeswoman said her service was adding 60,000 to 80,000 customers a month. Genie, fifth on the list with an estimated 100,000 users, asserts that it has a 50 percent annual growth rate. (Source: America Online); "Top Five Services" shows the leading consumer-oriented on-line services, as of July 1994. (Source: Information & Interactive Services Report)

title: Attention Shoppers: Internet Is Open
body: At noon yesterday, Phil Brandenberger of Philadelphia went shopping for a compact audio disk, paid for it with his credit card and made history. Moments later, the champagne corks were popping in a small two-story frame house in Nashua, N.H. There, a team of young cyberspace entrepreneurs celebrated what was apparently the first retail transaction on the Internet using a readily available version of powerful data encryption software designed to guarantee privacy. Experts have long seen such iron-clad security as a necessary first step before commercial transactions can become common on the Internet, the global computer network. From his work station in Philadelphia, Mr. Brandenburger logged onto the computer in Nashua, and used a secret code to send his Visa credit card number to pay $12.48, plus shipping costs, for the compact disk "Ten Summoners' Tales" by the rock musician Sting. "Even if the N.S.A. was listening in, they couldn't get his credit card number," said Daniel M. Kohn, the 21-year-old chief executive of the Net Market Company of Nashua, N.H., a new venture that is the equivalent of a shopping mall in cyberspace. Mr. Kohn was referring to the National Security Agency, the arm of the Pentagon that develops and breaks the complex algorithms that are used to keep the most secret electronic secrets secret. Even bigger organizations working on rival systems yesterday called the achievement by the tiny Net Market a welcome first step. "It's really clear that most companies want the security prior to doing major commitments to significant electronic commerce on the Internet," said Cathy Medich, executive director of Commercenet, a Government and industry organization based in Menlo Park, Calif., that hopes to establish standards for commercial transactions on the Internet and other networks. The idea is to make such data communications immune to wiretaps, electronic eavesdropping and theft by scrambling the transmissions with a secret code -- a security technique known as data encryption. While Commercenet and other organizations have been working to develop a standard for the automated data encryption of commercial transactions, the small band of recent college graduates who formed the Net Market Company in New Hampshire appear to be the first to implement such technology successfully. Tests of Commercenet's encryption system, which is based on algorithms -- mathematical formulas -- developed by RSA Data Security Inc. of Redwood City, Calif., are expected to begin this fall. Commercenet hopes to create an easy-to-use industry standard for protecting Internet transactions. For now, Net Market's approach is available to the limited number of computer users who have work stations running the Unix software operating system and a sophisticated Internet navigational program called X-Mosaic. The data encryption program is called PGP, for Pretty Good Privacy, which is based on the same RSA algorithms used by Commercenet. PGP is available free, but it requires technical expertise to download it from the Internet. But within a few months commercial versions of PGP are expected to be available for personal computers using the Windows and Macintosh operating systems, which comprise the vast majority of computers in North America.  Security Breaches Reported The widespread adoption of standard data encryption tools cannot come too quickly for many Internet entrepreneurs, who hope to foster new levels of commerce on the rapidly growing network. Alarmed by increasing reports of security breaches on the Internet, many people and businesses are reluctant to transmit sensitive information, including credit cards numbers, sales information or private electronic mail messages, on the network. But the use of standard data encryption software, which scrambles messages so they can be read only by someone with the proper software "key," has been hindered by a combination of Government regulations and software patent disputes. Experts say the PGP encryption software used by Net Market is at least as robust as the so-called Clipper encryption technology that the Clinton Administration has been pushing as a national standard. But unlike the Clipper system, the software keys for opening and reading PGP-encrypted documents is not controlled by the Government. A version of PGP for individuals is available free through the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, but users must retrieve it from an M.I.T. computer through the Internet. Organizations wanting to use PGP for commercial purposes must obtain it on the Internet from a company in Phoenix called Viacrypt, a maker of computer security software and hardware tools. Prices for PGP begin at $100 a copy.  A Browsing Feature One achievement of the young programmers at Net Market was to incorporate PGP into X-Mosaic, the software that many Internet users rely on for browsing through the global network. X-Mosaic is a software tool that allows the users of Unix computers to browse a service of the Internet called the World Wide Web, where companies can post the electronic equivalent of a glossy color brochure with supporting sales or marketing documents. In the case of Noteworthy Music, the record retailer that leases a "store front" in Net Market's Internet computer, a shopper can look at color pictures of CD album covers. Mr. Kohn, a 1994 honors graduate in economics from Swarthmore College, came up with the idea for Net Market during his junior year abroad, at the London School of Economics. There, he persuaded an American classmate, Roger Lee, to join his venture. Mr. Lee, who graduated from Yale this past spring with a degree in political science, is president of the company. For technical expertise, they recruited two other partners from Swarthmore, Guy H. T. Haskin and Eiji Hirai. The four men live upstairs in the house in Nashua, commuting downstairs each morning to run the business. Because of the pressures of running the system and debugging the software, they rarely venture outside, even though they have a backyard swimming pool. "We don't get much sun," Mr. Kohn said, "but we're down to a case of Coke a day."  'An Important Step' Although Net Market has been selling various products like CD's, flowers and books for several months on behalf of various merchants, yesterday was the first time they had offered digitally secure transactions. "I think it's an important step in pioneering this work, but later on we'll probably see more exciting things in the way of digital cash," said Philip R. Zimmermann, a computer security consultant in Boulder, Colo., who created the PGP program. Digital cash, Mr. Zimmermann explained, is "a combination of cryptographic protocols that behave the way real dollars behave but are untraceable." In other words, they are packets of worth that have value in cyberspace, the same way dollars have value in the real world, except that they have the properties of anonymity, privacy and untraceability. Many details remain to be worked out, Mr. Zimmermann said. For now, Mr. Brandenberger, despite his historic transaction yesterday, will be paying with plain old dollars, when he gets his credit card bill. And sometime today, the Sting CD will arrive by fairly conventional means -- shipped FedEx from the Noteworthy Music warehouse in Nashua.
