Kohn, foreground, worked at the company's office in Nashua, N.H., yesterday. Behind him, from left, were the president, Roger Lee; program developer, Mark Birmingham; senior program developer, Guy H. T. Haskin, and chief information officer, Eiji Hirai. (MacArther S. McBurney for The newyork Times)

title: Wiretap Access Bill Is Ready
body: Telephone and cable television companies would have to modify their networks to make it easier for law-enforcement agencies to conduct wiretaps and trace messages, under legislation expected to be introduced in the House and Senate on Tuesday. The bill, long sought by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and backed by the Clinton Administration, promises $500 million in Federal money to help communications companies pay for the development and installation of the necessary software. It would also reimburse the companies for future costs related to retaining law officers' ability to conduct court-authorized wiretaps and trace calls -- tasks that require new methods as more and more communications are transmitted in the digital pulses of computer code.  Frenzy of Discussions Though a proposal was first put forth by the Bush Administration and later refined by the Clinton White House, its final form was not settled until late last week. A frenzy of last-minute consultations, spurred by White House and F.B.I. pressure to move the bill to Congress, resulted in agreements between the F.B.I., telephone companies and civil libertarians. Although Congress is hurrying to finish work on health care legislation and a crime bill, sponsors of the wiretapping legislation hope it can move quickly through the House and Senate after the Labor Day recess because much negotiation and deal-making have already taken place. "We'll deal with this promptly after the recess and get it to the floor by mid-September," said one of its sponsors, Representative Don Edwards, Democrat of California, chairman of the House Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights. The legislation is separate from a sweeping Congressional effort to overhaul the telecommunications market, a move that would let cable and telephone companies compete head to head and enable local phone companies to enter the long-distance market. A version of the telecommunications competition bill easily passed in the House earlier this summer but has become bogged down in the Senate.  No Stand by Cable Industry Cable industry executives said they had been too preoccupied with the telecommunications bill to take a position on the wiretapping legislation. Telephone industry officials said they would wait to comment on the wiretapping bills until after they had been introduced. One sticking point in the new wiretapping bills had been whether the rules would cover commercial computer network services, like America Online and Compuserve, through which an increasing amount of public communications now takes place. As drafted, the legislation would not require such network operators to provide special access for law-enforcement agencies -- although law-enforcement officials could seek a court warrant to examine billing records and other auditing information in an effort to determine who had been communicating with whom. The burden would be on the police or F.B.I. to convince a judge that such material was necessary for conducting a particular investigation. "This is a key part of the package that makes it, if not palatable, at least in the ballpark of acceptability for us," said Jerry Berman, policy director of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit Washington privacy-rights group that had opposed many of the broader powers in the Bush and early Clinton versions of the bill. The new legislation confines surveillance to public communications networks, excluding private corporate telephone and computer networks. Conventional cable television service, delivering information and entertainment into homes, would not fall under the legislation. But the legislation would embrace the two-way communications systems through which cable operators intend to offer telephone and computer communications. "Right now, cable television is on the verge of being covered," Mr. Berman said. "If they start to provide telephone services or become an Internet provider then they'll be covered as a telecommunications carrier."  A Top F.B.I. Priority The F.B.I. has made the wiretapping bills its highest legislative priority in recent years. And while all the parties generally agreed that wiretaps can be a necessary tool for police and Federal investigators in fighting crime and terrorism, various groups raised different concerns. Privacy groups had fought to restrict the monitoring powers contained in the bills. The communications industry, meanwhile, had balked at the cost of updating their networks and complained that the F.B.I. had not demonstrated that its investigators were being deterred by the increasing use of digitally transmitted communications. "I'm not a great fan of wiretapping," said Mr. Edwards, who is a former F.B.I. agent and is viewed by many as a sort of civil-rights sentry over the bureau. "But it's legal and we have to take care of it. We've worked with the F.B.I. and the Department of Justice, and they represent the Administration. I don't think there will be objections except perhaps from purists who don't like the idea of Government listening in on conversations." Under current law, the police or F.B.I. need only a court subpoena to obtain a customer's billing records from the phone company. But with on-line service providers, that information generally contains few details other than the billing address.  Worry About Monitoring Privacy-rights groups, however, had worried that the legislation would enable law enforcement officials to monitor all billing data attached to telephone, cable and computer communications. With the advent of two-way cable television and the growth of on-line services, such information in the future could paint increasingly detailed portraits of private lives -- including information like credit card and banking transactions, political preferences, social contacts and even what sorts of movies people watch. In drafting the legislation to sharply limit the ability of law enforcement officials to gather such information, privacy groups credit the bill's sponsors, Mr. Edwards and Senator Patrick J. Leahy, the Vermont Democrat who is chairman of the Senate Subcommittee on Technology and Laws. The Clinton Administration has supported efforts to preserve the eavesdropping capabilities of the F.B.I., which contends that advanced communications technology has made it harder and harder to monitor and trace even simple phone conversations. Earlier this year, the bureau's director, Louis J. Freeh, said Americans would simply have to give up a degree of privacy in exchange for the eavesdropping tools needed to fight crime. Older analog telephone networks send voices as electronic patterns that mimic natural sound waves. But now, thousands of phone calls sent in a format represented by the ones and zeros of computer code can intermingle at once on a telephone circuit. The F.B.I. says that often it cannot separate individual calls from the thousands of conversations. Under the legislation, telephone and other communications companies would have four years to install the new hardware and software that would enable law enforcement officials to sort out such conversations.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: Advertising;
From an executive at Ogilvy & Mather, some guidelines for tasteful advertising on the Internet.
body: EARLIER this year, when an tiny immigration law firm in Phoenix flooded the Internet with advertisements for its services, outraged Internet users responded by "flaming" -- sending the firm electronic hatemail -- and various other forms of hackers' revenge. Martin Nisenholtz, an executive with Ogilvy & Mather, had another idea: He wrote a list of six guidelines for advertising on the Internet, the global web of computer networks. Mr. Nisenholtz's proposed rules of conduct had less to do with the reactions to unsolicited commercial messages than with the need to create a suitable climate on the Internet for responsible marketing. As the Internet evolves from a Government-subsidized computer link for academics and scientists to a quasi-commercial global communications web now used by an estimated 25 million people, Internet advertising is both a means to finance the system's infrastructure and a powerful marketing tool. Advertising became inevitable after 1991, "when the Internet was opened for commercial traffic, when it became clear that the Government would not continue to finance its infrastructure," said Mr. Nisenholtz, senior vice president of Ogilvy & Mather Direct, a subsidiary of Ogilvy & Mather Worldwide. "Almost regardless of what happens, the genie is out of the bottle." Some Internet purists will never be comfortable with any commercial activity in cyberspace. But, Mr. Nisenholtz argued, others will accept or even welcome advertising if it is done properly. Mr. Nisenholtz's proposed guidelines were published last month in the newsletter Technology & Media, and subsequently in Advertising Age. Adherence to the rules would be a clear break with the anarchic conditions that allowed a two-member law firm to irritate millions of net users with unsolicited ads. These are some of the proposals of the six guidelines: *Don't send intrusive messages. No one should receive a commercial message he or she hasn't either asked to receive, or doesn't want to receive. For example, if a user requests information from companies selling ski equipment, companies within this category should be able to send information. But it should be forbidden to add the user's name to a mailing list to which she or he has not subscribed. *Don't sell consumer data without the express permission of the user. Unlike some commercial services, likemail-order catalogues, where users generally understand that their names will be sold to other businesses, Internet data should remain the user's private property. *Advertising should appear only in designated news groups and list servers. The most objectionable advertising on the Internet is unrelated commercial postings to news groups and conferences, which are usually cross-posted to hundreds of groups. Those who post off-topic commercial solicitations should be warned once by the news group or conference administrator, then filtered at the source from further postings. *Conduct promotions and direct selling only under full disclosure. Marketers should be free to offer promotions on the network. But users should be given an opportunity to review the rules, guidelines and parameters of an offer before they commit to responding. *Conduct research only with the consumer's informed consent. Marketers should be able to conduct consumer research so long as respondents are made fully aware of the consequences of answering the research questionnaire. *Never use Internet communications software to conceal functions. Marketers should never use communications software to surreptitiously gather data from unsuspecting users, such as scanning their hard disks for data without permission. "These really were meant as a kind of first step, a kind of stake in the ground for the marketing community to start to understand what the issues are," Mr. Nisenholtz said. The guidelines seek "a middle ground between being completely noncommercial and a complete free-for-all," he added. So far, Mr. Nisenholtz said he had received little feedback on his proposed guidelines, though Ogilvy & Mather has several clients that want to advertise on the Internet. Perhaps not surprisingly, the guidelines are viewed favorably by entrepreneurs seeking to create commercial venues on the Internet. "These are the most fascinating, in-tune set of principles, both with the culture of the Internet and with the whole notion of on-line business," said Chris Locke, president of the Mecklerweb Corporation in Westport, Conn. It is a subsidiary of the Mecklermedia Corporation, a publishing and trade-show company that has a commercial domain on the Internet. "There's this concern among the existing Internet community that business involvement means here comes the Philistines," he added. "But if we don't have business involvement, I don't think we'll have an Internet." Not everyone is so impressed with Mr. Nisenholtz's efforts. "These guidelines don't really prevent you from doing anything," said Michael Godwin, general counsel for the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a lobbying group in Washington. "But in a sense, no set of rules is going to be enforceable because the Net is not hierarchically organized. There's no one to police it. What you do know is if you cross the line, you'll generate far more bad publicity." Mr. Nisenholtz said the guidelines were intended to respect the difference between the Internet and commercial on-line services like Compuserve, Prodigy and America Online. These have operated primarily on a pay-per-use basis, like telephone services, with the exception of Prodigy, on which advertising shares each screen with other information. There is limited advertising on the other services, but it is typically segregated to on-line "malls," where it can be easily avoided. "In a commercial service like Prodigy or America Online, the user should understand that he's involved in a primarily commercial activity, and make a decision to accept or reject that service," Mr. Nisenholtz said. "You can't do that with the Internet because there's only one Internet. So you've got to set up some boundaries."

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
A Nice, Pretty, Quiet Online Neighborhood
body: APPLE COMPUTER INC.'s new online information service, called E-World for Macintosh, is the prettiest and friendliest town in cyberspace. The service, which Apple is promoting with each new Macintosh computer it sells, has cute little buildings, including an entertainment center, a post office, a computer center, a school, a marketplace, a community center, a corporate skyscraper and a newsstand. While other online services are about as easy to navigate as the newyork City subway system, E-World's pathways are logically laid out. And the little cartoon people who inhabit E-World are cute, too, with Easter egg-colored smocks and little feet. But there are empty spaces where their faces ought to be, and that pretty much sums up the problems with E-World in general. And oh yes, there is the "No Windows users allowed" problem. E-World does not plan to open its borders to users of the more popular Microsoft operating system until sometime in 1995. By that time, incidentally, Microsoft is expected to have its own online service, code-named Marvel. E-world is Apple's answer to Prodigy, Compuserve and America Online, the Big Three among consumer information services that can be reached from home with a personal computer, a modem, a phone line and a credit card. Once the user is connected to these services, a world of opportunities opens. One can send and receive electronic mail across the global expanse of the Internet, chat with strangers, get the latest headlines and sports scores, check stock quotes, shop for merchandise, grab free software and sift through libraries of articles. These are all useful and enjoyable services. But the Big Three offer greater depth in each of these areas than E-World does. A new citizen of E-World trying to research a vacation in Montana the other day could find only a handful of newspaper clippings, and the travel "chat" areas were deserted. Also, one of the great attractions of cyberspace is the ability to prowl around the Internet, a global information bazaar that is to E-World what Baghdad is to Bedford Falls. E-World has no Internet connections beyond mail at this point. To be fair, E-World is brand new and will no doubt add new features and services daily. Things will get livelier day by day. Many of the areas now under construction will be completed by the end of the year. In the meantime, there are just two major reasons to recommend E-World over other general interest services at this time: *Cheap mail. Unlike Compuserve, Prodigy or other services, there is no surcharge for incoming or outgoing electronic mail, even across the global Internet. Mail is one of most compelling services in cyberspace, offering virtually instant delivery without the bother of envelopes and stamps. Also, an E-World mail address has greater cachet on the Internet than do addresses from America Online, Prodigy or Delphi, which are often considered the wrong side of the tracks among snooty Internauts. Perhaps that is because it is so new. *Outstanding resources for Macintosh technical support. Apple has long had a network called Applelink for communications among Apple dealers and developers and paparazzi, a link that is being transferred to E-World. Dozens of Macintosh software and peripheral developers maintain forums on Applelink where users can get product information and ask questions of technical support personnel. Apple's ulterior motive, of course, is to offload much of its technical support burden from humans and telephones onto less expensive hard disks and global computer networks. It is hard to begrudge Apple this benefit, though, because while the customer has to pay to connect to E-World's technical support, the convenience of one-stop shopping for hardware and software solutions is worth it. It costs a minimum of $8.95 a month to visit E-World, a fee that includes two hours of evening and weekend connection time. The third and subsequent hours cost $4.95 on evenings and weekends and a whopping $7.90 from 6 A.M. to 6 P.M., local time, during the week. The blow is softened somewhat by the 9,600-baud access rate, which means one can grab files quickly. The software needed to connect to E-World is available to Macintosh users without charge by calling (800) 775-4556. Graphic   Drawing

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Capital Cities' On-Line Plan
body: Capital Cities/ABC Inc. said yesterday that it would provide interactive news, sports and soap opera updates to subscribers of the computer service offered by America Online Inc. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. The Capital Cities/ABC divisions involved include ABC News, ABC Sports, ABC Daytime, "Good Morning America," ABC Radio Networks, Audience Information, Corporate Initiatives and several of the company's publishing groups. Each division of Capital Cities/ABC plans to offer its own service aimed at different audiences. The interactive service is scheduled to begin in the fall. Its services would include an ABC News wire service, plus information from ABC News programs, as well as forum discussions. ABC Sports would offer interactive sports polls and trivia games. ABC also plans to provide story updates, story-line information and chats with stars and staff members from the soap operas "All My Children," "General Hospital," "Loving," "One Life to Live" and the newest talk show, "Mike & Maty." ABC Radio Networks will offer interactive forum discussions about top news and issues. Additional services planned include interactive bulletin boards, audience contests, polls, entertainment forums and celebrity biographies. America Online, based in Vienna, Va., has more than 900,000 subscribers and offers a variety of services, including electronic mail, computing support, interactive magazines and newspapers and on-line classes, as well as access to services of the Internet.

title:
BUSINESS TECHNOLOGY;
New Service Is Planned For On-Line Marketing
body: The Mecklermedia Corporation, a publishing and trade-show company, will announce on Wednesday the formation of Mecklerweb, an on-line service intended as a cross between an information center and a computerized shopping mall that many industry executives believe is an emerging electronic model for advertising, marketing and commerce in the information age. The venture by Mecklermedia, of Westport, Conn., is one of a growing number of commercial efforts being unveiled for the Internet, a global collection of computer networks connecting more than two million computers and about 20 million people. The service, which will begin in September includes more than 40 companies in a range of industries including the computer maker Digital Equipment, the computer-services company E.D.S., the advertising agency Ogilvy & Mather, and the publisher McGraw-Hill. The Mecklerweb will charge companies $25,000 annually to present information that potential customers can retrieve over the Internet at no charge from specialized server computers to be managed by Digital Equipment in Palo Alto, Calif.  Electronic Browsing Once connected they will be able to browse through electronic catalogs, reports, brochures and advertisements or communicate directly with the companies via electronic mail. For new services like the Mecklerweb, the challenge is to sell the concept to corporate customers. "This is Zen meets the on-line world," said Gerald Michalski, managing editor of Release 1.0, an industry newsletter. "There is a big melding and bumping going on of the traditional Madison Avenue view of the world and this cooperative 'lets build it together' ethos of the Internet." Initially the new service will not permit electronic transactions, although companies should be able to make direct sales over the network by early next year, said Chris Locke, president of the Mecklerweb Corporation, a subsidiary of Mecklermedia and the developer of the new service. The on-line purchase of goods and services will be based on software now being developed by Enterprise Integration Technologies Inc. of Palo Alto, Calif. "All of our partners see us having the potential to funnel business to them," Mr. Locke said. "We give the largest corporations an easy way to dip their toe into the Internet. Mr. Michalski said that in contrast to the traditional approach of advertisers forcing their information on a captive audience, the Internet model gives computer users a choice of whether to view commercials. Whether this new approach will survive the turbulent growth of the Internet is open to question.  Organized Into Regions In the Mecklerweb system, which people on the Internet will need to seek out to use, the service will be organized by regions covering such topics as law, manufacturing, medicine, arts, technology, education and the environment. "People will go into regions and get focused marketing information," Mr. Locke said. "We're trying to prove the Internet is a viable on-line marketing vehicle compared to the existing on-line services." The rapid emergence of the Internet as a commercial medium has surprised many large corporations that have been betting on future commercial networks controlled by cable and telephone companies. Mr. Locke said that these multi-billion dollar companies had been slow to begin building such commercial systems and unwilling to invest in risky new ventures. In contrast, he said, Mecklerweb will offer a quick way to test a promising technology on an open network not under the control of one or two large players. "Why wait for Bell Atlantic or Bill Gates to do this?" he said. "We're fast, cheap and out of control."

title: Mead to Sell Its Data Base Unit
body: At a time when communications and entertainment giants are eager to enter the electronic information business, the largest provider of on-line information services plans to drop out to concentrate on making paper. The Mead Corporation said yesterday that it would sell its Mead Data Central unit, which provides computer access to data bases that include Lexis, used by lawyers and legal scholars, and Nexis, which contains articles from a long list of newspapers, magazines and other periodicals. While profitable, Mead Data Central constitutes only 12 percent of Mead's operations, the bulk of which comprise paper products, wood pulp and lumber. Steven Mason, Mead's chairman, said the sale, which analysts estimated could fetch more than $750 million, would give the company the option of buying back stock, paying down debt, making other acquisitions or improving productivity at its paper mills.   'Tremendous Opportunity' "This is a time of tremendous opportunity for Mead in the forest products industry," Mr. Mason said. Some paper industry analysts applauded the announcement, saying that the information services had never been a good fit for Mead, which bought the unit for $6 million in 1968. "This is pretty far afield for paper makers," said Tore Stole, an analyst who follows forest products for the investment firm A. G. Edwards. "Management came through the paper ranks and they believe that Mead stock trades in accordance with the paper industry and that it is not getting full valuation for Mead Data Central." Mead's stock rose $1.25 yesterday to close at $44.50 a share on the newyork Stock Exchange. But some information-industry analysts questioned the wisdom of Mead's intended move. "Just as the the future is arriving in on line, Mead is selling it off," said Paul Saffo, a director at Institute for the Future, a management consulting firm in Menlo Park, Calif. And Gary Arlen of Arlen Communications in Bethesda, Md., a research company following the information services business, said it was "odd to see someone who has a brand-name awareness walk away from the business." Mead Data Central had earnings of $50 million in 1993 on revenue of $551 million. The company does not break out separate results for Lexis and Nexis. Jed Laird, who follows on-line services for Veronis Suhler & Company, media investment bankers in newyork, estimated that the unit was worth close to $1.5 billion. He said companies that might be interested in bidding could include Dun & Bradstreet, International Thomson of Canada and Reed Elsevier, a British publisher. He also said that Mead Data Central might prove an attractive property for one of the regional Bell phone companies. Mead Data Central's competitors include Knight Ridder Inc., which owns the Dialog information service used mainly by corporate librarians, and Dow Jones & Company, which operates the Dow Jones News Retrieval collection of financial news and information services. A Knight Ridder spokesman said that his company would look at Mead Data Central. A Dow Jones spokesman declined to comment. Jeffrey Pemberton, who heads Online Inc., a publisher of magazines for professional on-line users, said he did not expect Mead Data Central to fetch more than about $750 million because the market today was far more competitive than it used to be, with a far less certain future. Lexis, for example, has faced increasing competition in recent years from West Publishing's West Law on-line service, and Nexis faces increasing competition from a variety of electronic data-base services. One of its data bases is The newyork Times, which Mead Data Central holds exclusive rights to distribute electronically after the first 24 hours of each issue's publication. Last year The Times struck a deal with Dow Jones to make the daily contents of The Times available on Dow Jones News Retrieval for only 24 hours before shifting them to Nexis for distribution. It is unclear whether a sale of Mead Data Central would affect its exclusive rights to electronic archival distribution of The Times. Neither Mead nor The newyork Times Company would comment yesterday. John Reidy, an analyst who follows The newyork Times for Smith Barney Shearson, said yesterday that an end to Mead Data Central's exclusivity "would be terrific for The Times because of the potentially new larger demand for such a unique data base." title: America Online Signs Deal
body: America Online Inc. said today that it had signed a merger agreement with the Redgate Communications Corporation in a move aimed at increasing the number of media through which America Online can offer its computer-based services. Redgate, a closely held company, will receive 444,184 shares, or 6.2 percent, of America Online common stock for all of Redgate's common and preferred stock and warrants. Another 103,383 shares will be reserved for Redgate employee options that are being assumed by America Online. America Online's president and chief executive. Steve Case, said the merger of Redgate with an America Online subsidiary would combine his company's "on-line expertise and reach with Redgate's skills in multimedia and interactive marketing." Redgate, based in Vero Beach, Fla., offers multimedia content data bases, delivering the information through CD-ROM, cable, broadband, demand fax and private satellite networks. Its sales were about $13 million in 1993. America Online, based here, has more than 700,000 subscribers to a variety of on-line services, like electronic mail, stock quotes, conferencing, magazine and newspaper libraries and on-line classes. America Online, founded in 1985, had sales of $40 million in 1993.

title: Arizona Lawyers Form Company for Internet Advertising
body: In a move that is certain to increase the turmoil on global computer networks, two Arizona lawyers said yesterday that they had formed a company with the goal of making commercial advertising pervasive on the Internet. In doing so, they shunned a plan, announced earlier this week by two other companies, to create specific advertising zones on Usenet News, a popular network that is connected to the Internet, a global web of computer networks. The advertising zones, which would require advertisers to pay a fee to place their messages on the network, would theoretically allow the estimated 20 million Internet users to choose to view ads. The new advertising company, called Cybersell, was started by Laurence A. Canter and Martha S. Siegel, husband-and-wife partners in the immigration law firm of Canter & Siegel in Phoenix.  Focus of Criticism Mr. Canter and Ms. Siegel have been the focus of intense criticism on several computer networks since April 12, when they posted an advertisement offering their legal services on thousands of Usenet bulletin boards, called news groups, without regard for the interests of the specific news groups. The first product Cybersell will advertise throughout the Internet is "a health product, super-oxygenated water," Ms. Siegel said yesterday. "You drink it, and the fact that it has additional oxygen gives you additional energy and promotes the healing process," she claimed, adding that the ads would be ready "within days, certainly within two weeks." The Usenet is one of the largest networks within the Internet, read by an estimated 10 million people. Most of the computers comprising the Internet and Usenet networks are privately owned.  Violation of Tradition The act, while not illegal, violated long-held traditions against random placement of any type of messages on news groups. Such scatter-shot messaging is known as "spamming." Each Usenet participant pays, either directly or indirectly, for the data he or she receives. In contrast, the cost to spam an advertisement in thousands of news groups, where it is potentially read by hundreds of thousands of computer users, is typically less than $50. The first advertisement spamming by Mr. Canter and Ms. Siegel resulted in tens of thousands of complaints -- even death threats -- from Usenet readers. Electronic vandals jammed the law firm's telephone, facsimile and computer systems for days. But Ms. Siegel said the law firm made so much money from its ad -- offering, for $95 per person, to help foreign nationals fill out free applications for unitedstates Government "green card" work permits -- that it decided to continue with the ads.  An Alternative Proposal In response to the outcry, the Internet Company of Cambridge, Mass., and the Electronic Newsstand of Washington, both of which provide Internet services, announced that they would create "an acceptable channel" on Usenet where companies could place commercial advertising, product information, promotional offers and price lists. "Unsolicited advertising on the global Internet is as acceptable as junk fax is in the real world," said Robert Raisch, president of the Internet Company and chairman of the Electronic Newsstand, a joint venture of the Internet Company and the New Republic magazine. The Electronic Newsstand hopes to become a main distributor of books and magazines on the Internet. The advertising channels would be grouped under a broad "market" directory on Usenet, with many subdirectories created for different products and services. Mr. Raisch said companies that advertised on the market news groups would pay the Internet Company a fee to do so, and that 25 percent of the fees would be set aside to subsidize Internet services for all users.  Veterans Cite Other Ads Some network veterans said advertising was already accepted on the Internet, as long as it was done in accord with the wishes of the Internet community. "There are plenty of existing groups that have appeared spontaneously and organically," said Edward Vielmetti, vice president of MSEN, Inc., an Internet service provider in Ann Arbor, Mich. "They appear around existing discussion groups with a ready audience. That appears to work phenomenally well." In an interview yesterday, however, Ms. Siegel rejected the idea of special advertising zones, and said Cybersell would post its messages to all Internet users. "I think it's too limiting," she said of the advertising zone proposal. "Advertising has to take its place on the Internet, just as it has in other media -- newspapers, TV and radio." "What these people are planning to do is relegate ads to some sort of black hole off in a corner," she said.

title:
BUSINESS TECHNOLOGY;
What Price Data? A New Fee Plan - Correction Appended
body: How should information be priced in the information age? That is the central riddle of the digital revolution. Proposing an answer, Dialog Information Systems Inc., one of the largest publishers of electronic data bases for corporate librarians, will announce a new fee structure on Wednesday that departs from current industry pricing. Prices that corporate clients pay to download documents like business directories and scientific abstracts from Dialog's electronic libraries will now be based on the number of authorized users of the documents. Currently, corporate and professional customers of Dialog and competing services like Mead Data Central's Lexis-Nexis data bases, pay monthly subscriber rates and on-line search fees that often total tens of thousand dollars a year. But industry pricing has generally assumed that only the person conducting an on-line search of the data base would read the documents retrieved. Not only is there usually no pricing provision for sharing the information with co-workers, but also doing so may be a copyright violation. Now, Dialog means to sell clients the right to share the documents retrieved electronically. While some industry experts call the plan unworkable because it will be difficult to enforce, others see it as an understandable effort by Dialog to insure a revenue stream from the deluge of information it pumps through its computer networks. And clients may benefit, too, some experts say. "It's risky, but they've got no choice," Barbara Quint, editor of Searcher, a magazine for professional data base users, said. "They charge an awful lot of money for data which you are inhibited from using in any meaningful way." Dialog, a Palo Alto, Calif., subsidiary of Knight-Ridder whose electronic search service includes 450 data bases, said it would announce the new service here Wednesday at a conference for its subscribers. Some customers have been using the service on a trial basis since early March. Industry experts said the move went a long way toward addressing the central paradox of such data base services. For publishers of corporate and professional information like Standard & Poor's corporate register, computer networks represent a vast business opportunity -- and an enormous threat. Electronic distribution can disseminate these pubishers' information quickly and broadly to a clientele they might never otherwise reach. But that ease and breadth can make it virtually impossible to keep track of who is reading the material and to charge them a fee. Some big publishers of financial data bases available via Dialog -- including Dun & Bradstreet, the Information Access Company and American Business Information -- have agreed to the new Dialog policy. The possibility of losing control of the product "has been out there a long time," said Linnea J. Christiani, senior manager of licensing and distribution for Information Access of Foster City, Calif., which acts as a broker between Dialog and data base publishers. "At least this way we're getting paid." But notable holdouts to Dialog's new plan include the Institute for Scientific Information, the Gale Research Company, University Microfilms International and Psychinfo.  A Dissenter's Reasoning The agreement would give Dialog too much power over redistribution and reprint rights, said Dennis B. Auld, director of Psychinfo, a data base sponsored by the American Psychological Association in Washington. "I don't want any vendor having the say-so over my data," he said. Nancy E. Honig, who is associate general counsel of Dialog and has overseen the development of the new service, conceded that data base publishers might be worried about whether the new dissemination policy would devalue their commodity as copies of their documents disappear into the ether of computer networks. Indeed, she said Dialog itself was "of two camps" about whether the new service was a good idea. She estimates, however, that Dialog and its publishers are losing millions of dollars a year on electronic copies. Ms. Quint, the Searcher editor, said some publishers "are nervous about somebody taking their data once and then using it a zillion times." "The carrot Dialog is dangling," she said, "is that the producers will see the extra money, and that there's a lot of money to be made."  Keystrokes for email By adding a few keystrokes at the end of their search, Dialog searchers, many of whom are corporate librarians, will be able to send hundreds of copies of an article through a company's electronic mail system. Or they will be able to store an archival copy of the document, which employees can read from their own computers. Besides the fee for retrieving the document, additional fees will be levied depending on how many people will be able to use it. With a $2 document, for example, it would cost $6 for up to 25 people to have access to the document through the corporate archive. The client would pay $8 for permission to send electronic copies directly to 25 people. Previously, under the copyright laws, a searcher would have had to go to the publisher of the document to get permission to redistribute it. "Let's say we've got a librarian at Procter & Gamble, and part of her job is to identify resources on soap flakes," Ms. Honig said. The librarian might set up her Dialog account to be regularly alerted to new articles about soap flakes, which she would reprint in a monthly newsletter for 1,000 company employees. "Until now, that's been impossible to do without violating copyright law," Ms. Honig said. "She would have had to call every information provider and get permission from each one, and they all would have had different requirements." Dialog's main competitor, Mead Data Central, which is based in Dayton, Ohio. said it had no plans to offer a similar service. "Right now, mass distribution like that is not a priority for us," a spokesman, Anthony A. Sprauve, said. "Our emphasis is more on the individual end-user." Although the two companies increasingly overlap in the data bases they supply, Mead in its Lexis-Nexis service has traditionally specialized in full-text retrieval of newspapers, newsletters, public records and legal documents -- information more likely to be retrieved directly by individuals conducting their own on-line searches. Dialog has traditionally specialized in business directories and scientific bibliographies and abstracts -- data more likely to be searched by a corporate or professional librarian for co-workers. But Ms. Quint, the Searcher editor, argued that Mead could not long avoid the copyright issue. Some people doubt that such a payment system, which will operate on the honor system, can work. "We're talking about something you can reproduce infinitely with no cost to yourself," John Perry Barlow, vice chairman of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit group devoted to computer network issues. "The only thing restraining you is your conscience." John S. Rosenberg, the head of Online Resources, Inc., a research firm in Falls Church, Va., that specializes in data base searches and is a big Dialog customer, commended Dialog's new policy but said it could prove costly for the scrupulous. "There's going to be a fairly direct price increase for people who are honest," he said. "In the past it was so hard to get permission to do it, you just did it and didn't worry about it." But Ms. Quint maintained that because Dialog was for professionals, unlike consumer-oriented on-line services like Compuserve and Prodigy, compliance with the new fee structure might be strong. "They're institutional creatures," she said of the professional searchers. "They're not going to do anything illegal." She added that the system would allow them to avoid potentially expensive copyright litigation like that experienced recently by Texaco Inc. A large group of scientific publishers recently won a copyright infringement case against Texaco, which they said had routinely photocopied articles illegally. Texaco is appealing the case. Moreover, Ms. Honig also implied that Dialog intended to wield a big stick. "We're not going to be out there policing, but if it comes to our attention that a customer is abrogating copyright law, we're going to take action," she said. Theoretically, it could involve a lawsuit. "Of course," she added, "we would feel terrible about suing a customer. It would have to be an egregious case." Correction  An article in Business Day on Wednesday about the new pricing policy of an on-line computer service misstated the company's name. It is Dialog Information Services Inc., not Dialog Information Systems. Correction-Date: April 9, 1994, Saturday Graphic   Photo: Dialog Information Systems Inc. is to announce a new fee structure based on the number of people who are authorized to view an electronic document or to receive their own electronic copies. Nancy E. Honig, associate general counsel of Dialog, has overseen the development of the new service. (George Olson for The New York Times)  Chart: "Data by the Dollar" shows the fees of Dialog Information Systems on the number of people within a corporation who are authorized to download documents from Dialog. title: Test for Data Base Services
body: The Prodigy Services Company and America Online Inc., two large computer data base services, will compete for the endorsement of the American Federation of Teachers, a labor union with 835,000 members. The Washington-based teachers' union said it would encourage its members to subscribe to one or both of the services, which will offer discounts to teachers participating in the program. After a year, union members will be asked to grade the service they selected and the winning service will be endorsed by the union. The union will set up special forums for teachers on the winning service and will encourage all its members to sign up with that service. Prodigy, based in White Plains, has more than two million subscribers while America Online, based in Vienna, Va., has more than 600,000. Both provide access to electronic mail services, news and reference and software libraries through modem-equipped personal computers. Both will set up special chat lines for teachers to discuss union and classroom issues. Charges for access to Prodigy and America Online vary depending on the hours of use, but monthly bills average about $20. The discount to teachers will save them "several dollars a month," a union spokesman said.

title: I.R.S. Tries On-Line Tax Filing
body: In a test that glimpses the potential of the emerging national information network, the Internal Revenue Service said yesterday that taxpayers in nine states would be able to file their 1993 Federal tax returns by personal computer over telephone lines. The test program, which involves Midwestern and Southwestern states, is the latest attempt by the I.R.S. to streamline the tax process and reduce the amount of paper it handles. In another experiment this year, more than 300,000 single taxpayers in seven test states have already filed Forms 1040 EZ by entering the data on the keypads of their touch-tone telephones, the I.R.S. reported. There are several advantages to electronic filing. The I.R.S. said that taxpayers due refunds would get them in no more than three weeks, or even sooner if they choose to have them deposited directly into their bank accounts. Typically refunds take four to eight weeks for returns filed by mail.  Accuracy an Advantage Accuracy is another advantage. Returns that are received on paper must be keyed into mainframe computers at the I.R.S. by human typists, which often results in errors, an I.R.S. spokesman acknowledged. Electronic returns do not require retyping, so there is "virtually no chance" for transcription errors, he said. Taxpayers who file electronically will receive a confirmation by return electronic mail that their forms have been received, or a notice that more documentation is required. The new electronic filing systems do not entirely eliminate the need for paperwork. Taxpayers still must provide their legal signatures on a paper Form 8453 OL (the OL stands for On Line) and include paper copies of W-2 forms and supporting documentation. Computer experts said the technology needed to create and authenticate electronic signatures may not be widely available for several years.  Data Security at Issue Representatives of both the I.R.S. and the Compuserve Information Service, which will be used to transmit the returns, said their systems were secure from data eavesdropping. However, computer security experts said that the transmission of tax returns over public networks raised concerns about privacy and data security. "There isn't a chance in hell that I'd file my tax return over Compuserve or any other network," said Winn Schwartau, a computer security consultant in Seminole, Fla. "It sure looks like a lot of plain text traveling around." Plain text refers to computer data that have not been encrypted, or scrambled, to prevent unauthorized reading. In recent months, the security systems of thousands of computers on the global network known as the Internet have been penetrated by data thieves who have captured unencrypted messages. There is no evidence that Compuserve, which is owned by the commercial tax preparation company H & R Block, or Internal Revenue Service computer systems were affected by the widespread break-ins on the Internet.  Forms Can Be Retrieved In the program displayed yesterday, Compuserve subscribers are able to retrieve official I.R.S. documents and forms, research tax questions, purchase tax preparation software and have it delivered electronically, ask questions of tax experts, compare notes with other taxpayers, and, for taxpayers in the nine test states, file their own returns over the Compuserve network. The states are Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas and Wisconsin. The returns will be sent first to Compuserve's mainframe computers in Columbus, Ohio, then to a commercial tax company in Rome, Ga., and finally to the I.R.S.'s electronic forms center in Austin, Tex. Compuserve's estimated 1.7 million subscribers pay a minimum monthly fee of $8.95 for access to basic services and additional fees, ranging up to $9.60 an hour, based on the amount of time connected to special services. Within that cost, subscribers -- even those who choose not to file electronically -- can retrieve official I.R.S. forms and publications, which they can print out.  Software for Sale Taxpayers can also use the Compuserve system to buy the tax preparation software needed to use the filing system. The popular programs, Taxcut, Turbotax and Macintax, each cost $39.95. There is an additional fee of $14.95 for taxpayers to file their Federal tax returns using the Taxcut program, and $19.95 to file using Turbotax or Macintax. In comparison, H & R Block estimates that the average fee for tax preparation and filing in one of its walk-in offices is about $50. A less sophisticated form of electronic filing has been available in previous years, but only through I.R.A.-authorized tax preparation services and other commercial intermediaries. People who prepared their own return could take paper copies or a computer disk to the centers for transmission. The I.R.S. expects more than 10 million returns to be filed through these indirect services this year. The use of electronic mail systems to send sensitive information, including tax returns and medical data, raised concerns among privacy advocates. "Once you realize the increasing sensitivity of the information we send electronically, the importance of encryption increases," said David L. Sobel, legal counsel to an organization called Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility. Mr. Sobel said the new I.R.S.-Compuserve agreement was likely to focus attention on the Clinton Administration's efforts to establish a nationwide data encryption standard based on computer chip called Clipper. Computer and civil rights organizations oppose it because the Government holds the key to open and read any Clipper-encrypted message.

title:
Technology;
How to Keep Bandits from 'Snarfing' Your Passwords
body: WHEN the alarm finally went off 10 days ago, electronic bandits on the global web of computer networks known as the Internet had already made off with thousands of user passwords, the supposedly secret codes that act as keys to public and private computer networks around the world. No one knows how many passwords were stolen after the break-ins started last summer, but officials at the Government-sponsored Computer Emergency Response Team say tens of thousands of computers around the world have been put at risk of being attacked by the intruders, not just on the Internet but on any computer network attached to it. "A network of computers, especially one as extensive as the Internet, is not as secure as a stand-alone computer," said Michael DeFazio, executive vice president and general manager of the Unix Systems Group subsidiary of Novell Inc., one of the leading network software companies.  "With a stand-alone computer you can limit access in physical ways, putting it in a locked room guarded by people with guns, if you want. You can't do that on a global network." But there are technologies that can greatly reduce, if not eliminate, the types of break-ins that have occurred on the Internet in recent months, security advisers say. Data encryption, one-time password generators, "fire- walls" and a user-authentification system called Kerberos are all cited as effective ways to decrease the risk of password theft. Last week, a Mountain View, Calif., computer company posted its version of the Kerberos program on an Internet "server" computer, making it available without charge to any American or Canadian network that wants it. The company, Cygnus Support, hopes to recoup its investment by selling support services to companies that use the program. Used alone or in combination, Kerberos and the other techniques make it harder to steal passwords, or can render them useless if they fall into the wrong hands or can virtually eliminate their use on the network. Security experts say that once a break-in is discovered it is relatively simple to expunge password-grabbers from affected computers. At that point, it's a matter of changing passwords and patching the hole in network security that allowed the intruders to enter the system. But those steps alone are not enough to reduce the risk of damage from such password pilfering in the future, the experts say. For example, one small company that was an early victim of the Internet bandits cleaned its system and ordered everyone to change passwords. A short time later, technicians discovered that the intruders had planted another hidden program that was designed to recognize the "change password" request and steal the new one. Passwords are "the biggest single source of security problems on any networked environment, not just the Internet," said William Yundt, a director of Barrnet in Stanford, Calif., one of the first commercial Internet service networks to be attacked in the latest wave of break-ins. Here are some proposed solutions:   Data Encryption Data encryption is the high-tech equivalent of the secret decoder rings one used to find in cereal boxes. It is used primarily to hide the contents of sensitive information files, such as those containing financial data, medical records and classified material. A data file or password is scrambled using a special "key," or set of instructions, and it is difficult to unscramble unless the recipient has the same key. Encryption works well between two people who arrange ahead of time to use a common key, but it becomes cumbersome on an open network where there are millions of users and thousands of different types of computers. So the Government and various groups are proposing an encryption standard for use throughout the network. In fact, a strenuous debate is under way over which data encryption standard to support. The Clinton Administration wants one called Clipper, which is technically sophisticated but has a "trap door" designed into it that the Government contends it needs for national security and law-enforcement purposes. Groups concerned about potential invasion of privacy oppose the Clipper standard, arguing that the Government would hold the key needed to read everyone's electronic mail.  One-Time Password Generators Hardware solutions include electronic "tokens" that generate new passwords every minute. There are also "challenge response" systems that require a user to provide a unique code generated by a device similar to a pocket calculator. The advantage is that such systems generate one-time-only passwords that change every 60 seconds or so, and thus become invalid at the end of the user's session. The drawbacks, which must be weighed against potential benefits, are that such systems add complexity and cost. The password generators typically cost $35 to $100 or more depending on features, and some sort of synchronized password-authentification software is required on the "host" computer. The most popular such device in use today is the Secur ID, made by Security Dynamics Inc. of Cambridge, Mass.  Firewalls For higher levels of security, some organizations install "firewalls," typically a highly secure computer that acts as a buffer between the Internet and all the other computers within a company. The firewall system is effective because it presents only a single point of attack to be monitored and defended. Many companies place their firewall computers in a physically secure room. Firewalls are not widely used because the firewall barrier works both ways, limiting access to the outside world while blocking intruders from coming inside.  Kerberos Several computer security experts cited the Kerberos system as the most effective way to prevent passwords from being "snarfed" by network eavesdroppers (to use the digerati's term of art for snatching passwords). The Kerberos architecture eliminates the need for clear, unencrypted text passwords to be passed over the network. The process, described in the accompanying chart, appears complex, experts concede. But so does the inside of a door lock, and people still lock their doors. In practice, using Kerberos adds a single step to the computer network log-on process, and it insures much greater security. Will the Internet, or other networks, ever be completely secure? "It's a difficult thing to accomplish," said Mr. Yundt, who supervises the networks at Stanford University. "You can create an effective technology, but to embed it in every platform and application, in a way that it is globally used, takes a matter of years."    SOME PASSWORD DO'S -- AND DON'TS PASSWORDS are effective only to the extent that they remain secret. And security experts say they rarely stay secret for long, because most people fail to heed sensible password rules. The rules apply not only to passwords used on computer networks, but also to those used with most other networked systems, like the personal identification numbers used with automatic teller machines and the calling-card numbers used for charging long-distance phone calls. Here are ways to avoid being "snarfed": 1. Don't choose words that can be found in a dictionary, English or otherwise. Computer crackers often use "brute force," employing automated programs that test every word at lightning speed. 2. If possible, use at least eight characters. The longer the password, the harder it is to guess. 3. Use a mix of letters and numbers, and include special characters if possible. On systems that are "case sensitive," mix upper and lower case letters. The password "K2jw&#69" is harder to guess than "loverboy." 4. Don't use obvious, guessable passwords. License plate numbers, birth dates, Social Security numbers, pet names, sports teams and other familiar terms may be easy to remember, but they are also easy to guess. 5. It may seem obvious, but don't write your password anywhere people can find it. Don't keep it in your wallet or purse with your bank card, or in the desk drawer next to your computer. 6. Change passwords frequently, the more often the better. The best systems require a new password each time a user signs on. 7. Watch out for people looking over your shoulder. Professionals use telescopes in airports and near public phones. 8. Never "lend" your password to someone else, for any reason. 9. Never tell your password to anyone over the phone. Thieves posing as computer administrators say it's surprising how many people are willing to divulge their passwords to strangers. 10. Report any unusual "log on" experiences immediately to the system administrator. If you feel your password may have been compromised, tell the administrator right away. PETER H. LEWIS    A PASSWORD PILGRIM'S PROGRESS The Kerberos system uses multiple "keys" to protect computer networks on the Internet without exposing users' passwords to possible interception. Here's how it can work:  Step 1 Our hero -- call him Pete -- contacts the Acme network service company and gets a special password called a "secret key."  Step 2 Later, when he wants to use Acme as a gateway to the Internet, Pete sends a message to Acme's authentication computer.  Step 3 The computer sends Pete an encrypted response -- an electronic package of information that can be read only with Pete's "secret key."  Step 4 The response contains a temporary key good for this session only and an encrypted ticket that will expire if he doesn't use it soon.  Step 5 Pete sends two things back to the Acme computer: the ticket, as evidence that Pete is Pete, and an encrypted message coded with the temporary key, as further evidence that Pete is indeed Pete.  Step 6 Our hero receives a second encrypted ticket and decodes it with his temporary key.  Step 7 And here's the ticket! Pete sends it over the Internet to, say, NASA's computer data base of satellite maps, requesting access. The NASA computer queries Acme to verify that Pete has a valid ticket. Acme confirms that Pete is authorized to use the network, and NASA opens its gates. At no time does Pete's "secret key" go over the network to risk interception.

body: The security software supplier VeriSign Inc. agreed yesterday to acquire two companies, a provider of digital identification software and a Web-based electronic payment system, in stock deals valued in excess of $1.2 billion. VeriSign, based in Mountain View, Calif., said it had agreed to purchase Signio, the electronic-payments company, of Redwood Shores, Calif., for 5.6 million shares of common stock, worth $728 million based on Friday's closing price. It also agreed to acquire Thawte Consulting, a closely held provider of digital certificate software based in South Africa, for $575 million in VeriSign stock. Shares of VeriSign rose $19.8125 each, to $150.125 yesterday. http://www.nytimes.com

title: 3Com Up on Plan To Spin Off Palm
body: Shares of the 3Com Corporation rose as much as 16 percent today after its Palm Inc. unit, the maker of electronic organizers, filed for an initial public offering and said that Nokia, Motorola and America Online would buy shares. 3Com rose $5.8125, or about 13 percent, to $50.625 in heavy trading. The shares touched $52.1875, their highest since October 1997. The rest of Palm will be spun off to 3Com shareholders six months after the initial offering, which will be for less than 20 percent of the company. Nokia, Motorola and America Online agreed to invest as much as $225 million in private placements, giving them as much as 4.5 percent of Palm's capital stock.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: IN MY … HUTCH: DAN SCHULMAN
body: AS president and chief operating officer of Priceline.com, the online company that lets consumers bid for airline tickets, cars and other items, Dan Schulman keeps some symbolic mementos in the tall hutch behind his office desk. Perched two shelves above his Silicon Graphics flat-screen computer is a gargoyle with a computer on its lap. It helps chase away "evil technology spirits," he says. The hutch also houses a chain of carabiners, used to secure ropes during mountain climbing. "I used those when I climbed Mont Blanc," in the Alps, said Mr. Schulman, who joined Priceline in June from AT&T, where he was president of its $22 billion consumer long-distance division. "Any mountain climbing is just the thrill of accomplishing things that you actually can't imagine you could do." Elsewhere, knickknacks celebrate jumps in the share price of Priceline.com. Nearby are photographs of his two children, Molly, 5, and Jake, 4. "There is such a thing as Internet time, and it can be all-consuming," Mr. Schulman said. The family pictures, he added, "remind me that there is balance."   ROBYN MEREDITH http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Dan Schulman; GARGOYLE: "To ward off any evil technology spirits. It was given to me when I came here by a friend by AT&T. So far very successful, that gargoyle."; PRICELINE.COM BASEBALL HAT: De rigueur for many of the company's young workers. "I'm 41 and I'm one of the oldest ones here.": CARABINERS: "Once you come down off the mountain you can't believe you were up there." (Janet Durrans for The newyork Times)

title:
PRIVATE SECTOR;
Anyone Can Whistle?
body: Being worth more than $5 billion, as Charles Schwab is, means never whistling off-key. Mr. Schwab appears in a television commercial for his brokerage firm's new high-speed trading system. The rock anthem "Born to Be Wild" blares as Mr. Schwab trades behind closed doors. Then he strolls out of his office, whistling this Steppenwolf tune. But Mr. Schwab acknowledged last week -- in an interview to promote WebShops, his firm's program of seminars that teach on-line investing -- that his effort had to be electronically tuned and enhanced for the soundtrack. Though he put his lips together and blew, he explained, "it just wasn't loud enough."   PATRICK McGEEHAN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Charles Schwab

title:

BROADBASE TO BUY MAKER OF ONLINE MARKETING SOFTWARE
body: Broadbase Software Inc., a maker of software for integrating and analyzing customer data, said yesterday that it agreed to buy Rubric Inc. for $331.2 million in stock to acquire software for automating online marketing. Broadbase will issue about 3.6 million common shares to the stockholders of closely held Rubric. Shares of Broadbase fell $3.4375, to $92. The announcement was made after the close of trading in the unitedstates.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:

BEA SYSTEMS SAYS IXL ENTERPRISES WILL USE ITS SOFTWARE
body: Shares of BEA Systems Inc. rose as much as 16 percent after the company said its electronic-commerce software would be used by iXL Enterprises, which advises companies on Internet marketing and strategy. BEA Systems climbed $9.25, to $124.50, on the Nasdaq in heavy trading. Shares of iXL, which is in Atlanta, rose $1, to $38.75. http://www.nytimes.com

Y. & R. Starts A Multimedia Agency
body: Young & Rubicam Inc. has opened an agency in newyork named Y.& .R. 2.1, aimed at integrating online and traditional marketing services. The agency is starting with about 30 employees and five clients that Y.& R. declined to identify. Plans call for offices to be opened next year in Europe and Latin America. title: America Online Deal With Intuit
body: America Online Inc., the top Internet service provider, and Intuit Inc., the maker of the popular Quicken financial software, said yesterday that they would provide an online bill-paying service to AOL's more than 19 million subscribers. Terms of the five-year agreement were not disclosed. Intuit will be the exclusive provider of bill tracking and payment services for America Online's flagship service and the AOL.com World Wide Web site, starting early next year. America Online is offering the service as the number of households using the Internet to pay bills is expected to increase tenfold to 18 million by 2003. About 55 percent of consumers who use the Internet said they would be interested in paying bills online, according to a study from Roper Starch Worldwide and America Online. Intuit and America Online will let utilities, credit card companies and other billing companies present bills online to their customers using encryption technology. The service will also be available to users of America Online's CompuServe service. America Online has not determined yet whether a fee will be charged. Intuit is the top maker of personal-finance software. http://www.nytimes.com

LYCOS IN AGREEMENT TOBUY INTERNET GAMES COMPANY
body: Lycos Inc., an Internet portal company, said yesterday that it had agreed to buy Gamesville.com, a Boston-based Internet games company, for $207 million in stock. Gamesville.com's Web site specializes in "massively multiplayer" real-time games including Bingo Zone, Quick-Draw Poker and PopQuiz. The company says that its Web site has 2.2 million registered users, and that the total is growing by 10,000 a day. The company's stock rose $3.75 yesterday, to $59.75, in Nasdaq trading. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Priceline Will Add Phone Calls to Its Menu
body: Priceline.com said today that it would soon add long-distance telephone calls to its plane ticket, hotel room, car and mortgage services. Beginning in the first quarter of 2000, unitedstates consumers will be able to name a price for domestic and international calls from their home phones, the company said. The first carrier to sign up was Net2Phone Inc., though Priceline said it expected several others by the time the service started. Priceline, which began with airline seats in April 1998, has been adding products over the last year or so to increase revenue. Customers logging onto its World Wide Web site will submit a price they are willing to pay for long-distance service. Their offer will be evaluated based on carrier network capacity. If the price is accepted, Priceline will buy the call from the long-distance carrier, earning a spread between what it paid and the customer's offer. http://www.nytimes.com

body: Nasdaq plans to set up on-line trading from its Web site for small investors, according to Frank Zarb, chairman of the company's parent, the National Association of Securities Dealers. Speaking at the Japan Society in newyork last week, Mr. Zarb said Nasdaq had plans to allow on-line trading from its Web site for any person wishing to make a trade, so long as he or she was already set up and registered with an N.A.S.D. broker. Nasdaq's Web site, www.nasdaq.com, is heavily trafficked, getting about 23.5 million visits a day just for stock quotes. Because all users would already have registered accounts, brokers would be able to monitor the "suitability" of the investments, make sure traders had enough credit to cover their transactions and handle clearing and settlement. body: America Online Inc. said yesterday that its board had declared a two-for-one stock split, the seventh split in seven years. The concern, the world's largest Internet services company, said the more than two million individual AOL holders of the more than 1.1 billion shares outstanding would receive one additional share for every share they own on Nov. 8. title: IN MY… TRAVEL BAG: BARRY SALZMAN
body: Business travel can wreak havoc on a travel bag, says Barry Salzman, president for the international division of DoubleClick, the Internet advertising sales company based in newyork. His Tumi leather bag becomes scuffed during his frequent trips around the world to meet with clients and colleagues. The road is no kinder to the body, Mr. Salzman said, which is why he packs a supply of powdered protein drinks and a jump rope to exercise in hotel rooms at night. "You'll be happy to know that I don't use it on the plane," he said. But what really adds weight to Mr. Salzman's briefcase are office supplies. He carries business files, a Fujitsu laptop computer, two cell phones, two modems and a Palm Pilot. The load sometimes gets lighter as a trip progresses. Mr. Salzman carries a supply of mints, pens and press kits that he distributes at business meetings and to people he meets while traveling. "It's great to leave something behind," he said. "There is always an opportunity for me to be in sales mode. You never know who you'll be sitting next to in an airplane."   VERNE KOPYTOFF http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Shows what is inside the travel bag: PHOTOGRAPHS OF FRIENDS: "A collection of fun times to remind myself that there is more than life on the road."; PALM PILOT: Programmed with 1,527 phone numbers and lists of gyms, florists and favorite restaurants around the world.; FOREIGN CURRENCY: Includes money from 15 countries "I don't change money back, I just hang onto it in an envelope. I'm in and out of the airport."; ADAPTERS: For telephone and electrical outlets in every country he visits.; PROTEIN DRINKS: In flavors of chocolate, chocolate deluxe and vanilla cream. (Nancy Siesel/The newyork Times)

title:
INVESTING: DIARY;
Where On-Line Traders Find Satisfaction
body: Who's happiest with their E-broker? On-line brokerage customers of Fidelity Investments, according to a new survey by Spectrem Group and NFO Interactive, two market research firms. The study, conducted in June, polled 857 on-line investors. It first asked investors what they considered the most important attributes of their E-brokers' Web sites. If the answer was, say, speed of execution, the survey then asked them how satisfied they were on that count. In the No. 2 spot was TD Waterhouse, followed by Charles Schwab and DLJ Direct, according to the study. What were investors' top priorities? In order of importance, the respondents were most concerned that E-brokers keep their personal and portfolio data secure, offer uninterrupted access, have credibility, offer value and execute orders speedily.   RICHARD TEITELBAUM http://www.nytimes.com

title: Volatility and S.E.C.
body: To the Editor: Your Oct. 19 Business Day article on stock-market volatility omitted a culprit: regulatory reform. The Securities and Exchange Commission's policy of continuous electronic transparency put individuals on an equal footing with Wall Street professionals but also disrupted stable price formation. With on-line investors driving price, big dealers and institutions, which used to find where supply and demand really met, are being driven off the "level playing field." Imagine how unstable our political system would be with continuous voting by electronic polls that constantly recalculated the "consensus." The S.E.C. policy invites day traders to try "pump and dump" manipulations from Internet chat rooms, causing volatility and enforcement headaches. STEVE WUNSCH Pres., Arizona Stock Exchange newyork, Oct. 20, 1999 http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Schwab Web Site Goes Down Yet Again
<DTL >SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 22
body: The Charles Schwab Corporation's Web trading site failed today for almost two hours, the third disruption in three days, because of an unspecified software problem, the company, the largest Internet brokerage firm, said. The site began operating on a backup system around 11:20 A.M., said Greg Gable, a company spokesman. The site and automated touch-tone telephone trading were sporadically inaccessible to clients starting shortly after midnight and completely down after 9:30 A.M., he said. "The cause of the problem was some system software, and we're actively working with the vendor," he said, declining to further identify the problem. On Wednesday, the trading area of the site was down for more than two hours, and on Thursday, it failed for almost an hour. Schwab has now had 11 failures in 1999. It suffered seven in the first four months of the year amid a two-thirds increase in customer trades. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Escaping From Web Traps
body: To the Editor: While surfing your Internet site, I read the article about traps for Web surfers, describing several practices for leading the unsuspecting browser to advertisements, including "duplicitous banner advertisements that can be designed by graphics professionals to resemble ominous computer messages" -- banners that have been formatted to look like warning boxes but that contain embedded links to connect the viewer to another site. The insinuation that these practices are underhanded aside, I suppose that even The newyork Times must use all possible tools to fill its coffers: The advertising banner at the bottom of the page was a Windowslike alert box reading "Warning: Your tank is on empty."  REBECCA SIMONS newyork City, Oct. 7, 1999   http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Sued By Priceline
body: Priceline.com, which lets consumers bid on the Internet for plane tickets and hotel rooms, said today that it had filed a suit against the Microsoft Corporation, contending that Microsoft's new hotel service violates a Priceline patent. Priceline.com, based in Stamford, said it filed the suit in Federal District Court in Connecticut against Microsoft and its Expedia.com Web site. Last month, Microsoft began a service on Expedia that lets consumers name their price for hotel rooms. The suit also says that Microsoft violated the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act. Priceline.com said it provided Microsoft with confidential information about its business while the two companies discussed a possible joint venture earlier this year. Priceline.com has three patents for its "name your own price" business, and 17 more are pending. The shares of Priceline.com fell $3.6875, to $72.25; those of Microsoft fell $1.50, to $91.0625. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
COMPANY NEWS;
24/7 MEDIA SHARES RISE ON SPECULATION OF TAKEOVER
body: Shares of 24/7 Media Inc. rose 17 percent amid speculation that the Internet advertising company was in talks to be acquired by a larger rival, Doubleclick Inc. The newyork-based company's shares rose $6.875, to $47.375. Doubleclick rose $4.75 a share, to $136.625. In July, Doubleclick's chairman, Kevin J. O'Connor, said the company was seeking to buy more Internet advertising companies to expand ad sales that were now on more than 1,300 Web sites. 24/7 would be a good fit because it would add 150 Web sites to broaden Doubleclick's customer base and fend off rivals. Doubleclick is in talks to buy 24/7 Media for about $1.5 billion, the Silicon Alley Reporter Web site said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: 2 More Firms Will Expand Trading Hours
body: DLJ Direct Inc. and the brokerage unit of Fidelity Investments said yesterday that they would offer up to four hours of extra stock trading daily within the next month, becoming the latest on-line brokers to extend the trading day. DLJ Direct, the on-line brokerage unit of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Inc., will offer early-morning and evening stock trading sessions in late October. The morning session is expected to run from 8 to 9:15 A.M., with evening trading from 4:15 to 7 P.M. Clients will be able to enter limit orders for selected securities and all Nasdaq national and small-cap issues. Fidelity's Powerstreet on-line trading unit will offer trading from 4:30 to 8 P.M. Customers will be able to place limit orders for Nasdaq securities and a limited number of listed securities. DLJ Direct and Fidelity, which is owned by the FMR Corporation, will offer the trading through Redibook, an electronic communications network in which they hold stakes. http://www.nytimes.com

title: AOL Lets Lycos Use Its Messaging Feature
body: America Online Inc., the leading Internet service provider, will provide its instant messenger feature to users of the Lycos World Wide Web site, allowing Lycos customers to trade private messages with AOL subscribers. The new service, which will carry the Lycos and America Online brands, will be available in December to registered users of Lycos, the No. 3 Internet directory. Terms of the agreement were not disclosed. The agreement comes as AOL battles with Microsoft, Yahoo and other on-line services concerning access to the users of its instant messaging technology. AOL has blocked users of Microsoft's messaging software from connecting with its subscribers, seeking payment for access first. For Lycos, which is based in Waltham, Mass., the alliance may help it expand its user base; it hopes to draw more visitors to its sites to add revenue and compete better with Yahoo, the No. 1 Internet directory. The company has created other Web sites for children, including Webmonkey, which teaches them how to build a Web page. There are 45 million registered users of AOL's instant messenger worldwide. Lycos has 32 million registered users. http://www.nytimes.com

body: CMGI Inc. agreed yesterday to buy the Flycast Communications Corporation, an Internet advertising agency, for about $690 million in stock, CGMI's third acquisition of an advertising company in two weeks as it takes on the on-line marketing leader Doubleclick Inc. CMGI, an Internet venture capital company, will exchange 0.4738 share, worth $47.53, for each Flycast share.
