title: Stocks Drive a Rush to Riches In Manhattan's Silicon Alley - Correction Appended
body: There was something about the wave of unrepentant jubilance sweeping through iVillage's downtown Manhattan offices the day the three-and-a-half-year-old Internet company went public that made Susan Weaver uneasy. As employees who had been allowed to buy stock for as little as $6 per share watched it climb to $103 in its first afternoon of public trading, Ms. Weaver -- at 46, an elder in a company whose average hire is 31 -- addressed a cigar-wielding group gathered in the hall at iVillage, a provider of on-line information and discussion forums for women. "I just want everyone to realize this is Disneyland," she remembers saying that day in March. Ms. Weaver, iVillage's vice president for programming and a former NBC producer, later explained: "I didn't want them to feel that they were entitled to what was happening to them. This doesn't happen all the time." That is, it didn't used to. Particularly not in newyork, where the cluster of new-media companies known as Silicon Alley has always been viewed by its Western namesake as an also-ran in innovation and wealth creation. But since March, with Wall Street valuing infant Internet companies that have never made a profit in the same range as car makers and airlines, Silicon Alley has witnessed initial public offerings at the rate of one a week. And as investor fervor for Internet companies threatens to fade, the sprint for I.P.O.'s, as the offerings are known, has only picked up speed. Even as Internet stocks faltered last week -- iVillage, for example, lost almost 10 percent of its value in one day -- three newyork-based companies launched themselves on the public market to a respectable reception. And shares of StarMedia Networks, the most highly anticipated of last week's offerings, closed 74 percent above its initial offering price of $15 per share on Wednesday, its first day of trading. "It's unbelievable, it's surreal -- it's good, I guess, would be the sound bite," said Fernando Espuelas, 32, who three years ago created StarMedia, which provides Internet access in Latin America. The I.P.O., he said, has made him worth $162 million on paper. "Wow, that's the first time I've said it out loud. It's kind of weird." The Internet boom has created as many as a thousand paper millionaires among the founders and executives of Silicon Alley companies, said Uri Kaufthal, the president of AST StockPlan, which administers the stock benefit packages for several of them. Many junior employees among Silicon Alley's more than 100,000 workers -- at companies ranging from financial information services to Web site developers -- have collected enough to pay off student loans or consider buying an apartment. In a city where the well-worn paths to success have led through the trading floor or the ranks of large media corporations, the emergence of sudden Internet-bred wealth holds out the promise of much quicker rewards. It is exposing newyorkers to the Silicon Valley culture of entrepreneurial risk. And it is prompting resentment, envy and a scramble to be a part of it. "All of us had friends on Wall Street who always made so damn much money," said Sunny Bates, an executive recruiter for newyork-based Internet companies. "Now you can make a lot of money and you don't have to be an investment banker. Everybody wants to get on the train." Still, Silicon Alley is not embracing the I.P.O. life style without a healthy dose of apprehension. For one thing, the seeming arbitrariness of who is getting rich can be disconcerting, even for those who are now buying BMW's. Those at start-ups that have yet to issue a prospectus wonder whether their chance will come before it is too late. Workers in the Internet divisions of traditional media companies yearn for their operations to be spun off and taken public. Meanwhile, veterans of other industries worry that a generation is emerging with the expectation that working late nights for a couple of years at the right company should make them set for retirement. And among some early denizens of the Alley, many of whom started out with the conviction that technology could democratize society and create new modes of expression, there is a sense of loss as talk turns from changing the world to when their options vest. "There used to be a sense that we were on the cusp of a significant change that was at once economic and cultural," said Jason Chervokas, the editor of @NewYork, an industry newsletter that was recently bought by MecklerMedia. "But the original idea, which was, hey, let's build a medium with a new hip, gender-neutral image, has fallen by the wayside, and I regret that, I really do. The sense that you're allowed to experiment has been replaced by pressure for quarterly results." For Alley veterans and newcomers alike, it can be hard getting used to running into 20-year-old millionaires at parties in downtown lofts. "Being around this kind of gargantuan 'monetizing' day in, day out -- it warps your mind," Marisa Bowe, the editor of the on-line magazine Word, wrote in a recent essay in The newyork Observer about watching her Silicon Alley friends cash in. "Just a few years ago, we were dance or literature majors, actors with day jobs. Now we live in a strange world where it seems as if every 10th person has won the lottery."  A Fast Ride On the Money Wave But for bystanders, the logic of I.P.O. winnings is somehow harder to swallow than the luck of the lottery.  Paul Debraccio, who spent 15 years selling advertising at the magazine publisher Conde Nast before doing the same at a lower salary for an Internet company, Tripod Inc., says some of his former colleagues have a hard time understanding how he has come to be bidding on real estate in the Hamptons this spring. "The average person just can't conceive that in two or three years you can become a millionaire without having started your own company," said Mr. Debraccio, whose options in Tripod were converted to stock worth over $1.5 million when the company was sold to newyork-based Lycos Inc. last year. "At Conde Nast, the most you could make is $500,000 a year, and that's if you were a publisher." Mr. Debraccio is now the senior vice president for advertising at Uproar, an Internet games company in newyork that trades on the Vienna exchange but may soon offer shares in the unitedstates. As is typical for Internet company employees, he accepted a lower salary in exchange for stock options. "Part of it is about riding the money wave," he said.  "This is probably going to turn out good as well." Dave Kansas, the editor of the on-line financial news service TheStreet.com, is less sanguine about his paper wealth, which hovers around $9 million and has in recent days served as a somewhat obsessive topic of conversation in The Wall Street Journal's newsroom, where he used to be a reporter. (On May 11, the day his company went public, Mr. Kansas received several email messages from former colleagues along these lines: "Dave, I was just going to lunch, but I'm a little short today. Do you think . . .") "I've sacrificed a lot over the last three years," said Mr. Kansas, 32. "Can I value it at $9 million? I don't know." Indeed, even the biggest evangelists of the Internet wealth culture wax insecure about its scale -- and its future. That is in part because Federal regulations require that institutional investors and senior executives hold onto their stock for six months after the initial public offering. (Junior employees are not subject to those restrictions.) Moreover, stock options that are granted to employees typically vest over a four-year period, so just how rich somebody is depends on how many options they actually own and whether the stock price holds up until they can exercise them. "It's Monopoly money -- I don't count it," said Fred Wilson, a co-founder of Flatiron Partners, the newyork venture capital firm that has financed several of the most successful Internet companies to go public lately, including TheStreet.com, theglobe.com and StarMedia. "You can watch your value go up and down millions a day and you can't do anything about it. It's surreal." The giddy tone at many of the city's cyber-celebrations and the frequency with which new-media employees check the company stock price underscores the anxiety that their net worth is housed within a speculative bubble that is destined to pop. It is a fear that plagues the industry well beyond newyork. "Historically, to make a gazillion dollars in the computer business you had to have a good product, and there was pretty clear evidence about what made it good -- i.e., people bought it," said Jonathan Weber, the editor of the Industry Standard, a trade publication that follows the Internet economy. "The Internet boom and the I.P.O. phenomenon is so speculative that what separates certain companies from the pack is not always that obvious."  Finding Rewards In a Different Risk Still, many who have benefited even modestly from the boom remember when their friends and families scoffed at their choice to forsake more traditional careers for this strange thing known as the Internet. They do not quite see why the risk of their own opportunities should be deemed less worthy of reward than the risks, say, that investment bankers take with other people's money. For instance, Kate Hanley's starting salary at iVillage in 1996 was $15,000 less than the book editing job she was offered at Fairchild Communications. But as one of the first 30 employees of the company, she was granted 333 stock options at $6 per share. (iVillage's shares closed Friday at $47.875 -- less than half the price attained on the day it went public but still a healthy premium for Ms. Hanley's options, three-quarters of which have vested. She has not cashed them in.) Ms. Hanley was also given "friends and family" options, which allow employees and others designated by the management team to buy stock at the initial offering price. The proceeds from that stock, which Ms. Hanley bought at $24 and sold at the opening price of $95, netting her about $25,000, served as a down payment for the Chelsea apartment that she moved into this month. "People act as though I found this money in a bag on the street," said Ms. Hanley, 29, a producer for iVillage's computing site. "It's like, where were you when I was working for the last three years till 9 or 10 at night and on weekends?" For Ms. Hanley's friend Annie Rhodes, 28, who works at ToggleThis, another Internet company three blocks away, the iVillage public offering was bittersweet. "When they went public, I was sort of kicking myself,"' said Ms. Rhodes, who left iVillage two years ago and missed out on cashing in. "But it's also exciting. Until you know people who have hit it big with options, it doesn't really seem real. Now it seems like, God, it's not a joke. This could happen to us." Filled with that sense of promise, business school students who used to head straight to the finance courses that would get them to Goldman Sachs are packing into the electronic commerce class at Columbia and oversubscribing the entrepreneurial course at newyork University. Those with M.B.A.'s are not the only ones to be drawn by the prospect of entrepreneurial freedom and fabulous wealth. Ken Perlin, a professor of computer science and the director of the Media Research Laboratory at newyork University, said the Internet boom had changed the orientation of his students, particularly since Yahoo bought Webcal, the Web calendar that one of the laboratory students developed, for $12 million in stock last July. "Young people in this field think they should be millionaires, and that's a new phenomenon," Professor Perlin said. "The concern is that it's deceptive. I know a number of students who tried to make a go of it and it didn't work." But if there is angst or self-loathing among some of those who have tried their hand in Silicon Alley, Jeff Dachis, a co-founder of Razorfish, an Internet services company that went public April 27, does not share it. "I don't want to be lumped in with the hucksters of the world, because we have the real deal," said Mr. Dachis, 32, who bought a BMW 5-series as an I.P.O. gift to himself. "I feel completely and utterly entitled to whatever success comes our way. Not everybody's good, not everybody has the winning idea, not every idea deserves to be funded or to be public. I'm sorry, but there are sheep and there are shepherds, and I fancy myself to be the latter." Andrew Zolli, the vice president of the interactive division of the advertising firm Siegal & Gale, said he spent a week of sleepless nights pondering his past and future after watching friends and former colleagues at Razorfish make millions this month. Finally, though, he came to peace. "I love my job, and ultimately I believe this is still the most important medium of the next half century, and our ultimate judge is not the size of our bank accounts," said Mr. Zolli, 28. "When this insanity passes, what will matter is who had the really good ideas and good work. I really believe that." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  A front-page article on Monday about the flurry of initial public offerings among new-media companies based in newyork misstated the reason senior executives are often unable to sell their stock for several months after the start of trading. The practice is dictated by contracts between the companies and their underwriters, not by Federal regulations. The article also misidentified the headquarters of Lycos Inc., an Internet company. Although it has a sales and marketing office in Manhattan, it is based in Waltham, Mass. The article also misspelled the name of a strategic-communications firm. It is Siegel & Gale, not Siegal. Correction-Date: June 3, 1999, Thursday Graphic   Photos: Kate Hanley -- Producer at iVillage "People act as though I found this money in a bag on the street." (Ruby Washington/The newyork Times); Andrew Zolli -- Vice President at Siegal & Gale "Our ultimate judge is not the size of our bank accounts." (Marilynn K. Yee/The newyork Times)(pg. B6)

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Surfing to Soothe a Savage Breast
body: The Comcast Corporation, a cable giant with diverse holdings that include stakes in the television and on-line versions of the QVC shopping channel and E Entertainment Television, has added a more highbrow investment to its portfolio: Culturefinder.com. Culturefinder is a Web site that lists arts events and sells tickets to exhibits, operas, symphonies, dance and theatrical performances around the unitedstates. For Julian A. Brodsky, vice chairman of Comcast and chairman of the six-month-old fund, Comcast Interactive Capital Group, that announced the $3.75 million investment two weeks ago, the move was part of his company's effort to "leverage our involvement with the Internet and create an investment hedge against the changing relative values of content, commerce and distribution." For Eugene Carr, the founder and chief executive of Culturefinder.com, the investment by Comcast, which is based in Philadelphia, represented even more: further validation of a business that has enabled Mr. Carr to combine his entrepreneurial impulses with a lifelong affinity for the performing arts. Mr. Carr, a cellist who studied at the Juilliard School of Music while still in high school, earned an M.B.A. at Columbia University. He was the executive director of the newyork-based American Symphony Orchestra when he started Culturefinder.com in 1995. "I perceived that the Internet would be big and so would massive sites that collected around specific interests," he said in an interview in Culturefinder's crowded offices, which are situated, appropriately, near Carnegie Hall. "I knew that someone would do an arts site, and I thought it would be an incredible opportunity to do it myself." After polling administrators of 50 arts groups to see if they would support a site that listed their programs, Mr. Carr invested $50,000 of his own to start Culturefinder.com. He also got $300,000 from America Online to participate in its Greenhouse project -- an effort, since dropped, that backed content providers in their infancy. Some other Web publishers, like the Sidewalk operation of the Microsoft Corporation, list concerts and other performance arts. And some, like Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch Inc., sell tickets. But Culturefinder.com is the only national on-line directory of arts events and seller of electronic tickets for more than 2,200 organizations in some 1,300 cities. The institutions, which vary from the New Century Chamber Orchestra in Mill Valley, Calif., to the newyork Philharmonic, do not pay Culturefinder to be included in the listings. Instead, much of Culturefinder's revenue comes from the fees -- ranging from $2 to $4.50 -- it charges for each ticket sold. "Organizations like Ticketmaster Online compete with Culturefinder only on high-profile events," said James McQuivey, senior analyst for Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. "Focusing on art and culture gives Culturefinder an extra market Ticketmaster is not in." In partnerships with the on-line retailers Amazon.com, CD Now, Image Exchange and Reel, Culturefinder also peddles compact disks, arts posters and videos. For patrons who might want to venture far afield in search of a good scherzo, it has an alliance with Microsoft's Expedia on-line travel agency. The site also offers various articles, program notes and primers about the arts aimed at its estimated 250,000 different visitors each month, an audience that surveys indicate is two-thirds female, largely urban, highly educated and, on average, 36 years old. That gives Culturefinder a desirable demographic for its on-line advertisers, the largest of which is the Baldwin Piano and Organ Company. Mr. Carr and his staff of 14 "bring passion, experience and an intense focus on arts consumers and arts organizations," said Mr. Brodsky, the Comcast executive. "This, combined with superb technology and the dramatically quick adoption of E-commerce among upscale consumers, bodes well for Culturefinder's future." To stimulate sales, Culturefinder.com recently reached ticket sales-referral agreements with three other Web sites: the search portal Lycos.com, America Online's city guide service Digitalcity.com, and Ovationtv.com, the site of the arts-oriented cable television network. As a privately held company, Culturefinder.com does not report its financial results. But Mr. Carr said he expected revenue this year of about $1.5 million and a loss that he declined to quantify. He predicted that the company would become profitable as soon as 2001. He estimates that institutions in the unitedstates like those represented by Culturefinder sell close to $3 billion worth of tickets annually. But he said those organizations typically sell only 70 percent of their available tickets -- representing an opportunity for companies like his to help fill lots of empty seats. Besides America Online and Comcast, a number of prominent individual investors have put a total of $1.75 million in Mr. Carr's venture. They include Arthur Zankel, a partner in First Manhattan, a newyork-based investment advisory firm, and a member of the board of Carnegie Hall; Robert H. Lessin, whose privately held Wit Capital Group specializes in Internet-related investments; Thomas G. Stemberg, chairman and chief executive of Staples Inc.; Stuart G. Moldaw, chairman of Gymboree, and David Horowitz, former chief executive and president of MTV Network. "I gave him money for the American Symphony Orchestra and had a high opinion of what he accomplished with it," Mr. Zankel said. "I have great admiration for Gene's marketing skills and imagination, and I haven't been disappointed." David Kitto, director of marketing and ticket operations for Carnegie Hall, said Culturefinder could help arts organizations of all sizes expand their audiences, whether or not the arts groups have their own Web sites. "All of us are looking for ways to connect with the audience," Mr. Kitto said. "Culturefinder is not competing with us; they're providing an alternate means to purchase tickets." In Mr. Kitto's view, the biggest challenge Culturefinder now faces is creating identity and brand awareness. "They need to work to become the place arts consumers go to to find out about ticket availability," he said. For his part, Mr. Carr wants Culturefinder.com to expand to include arts listings outside the unitedstates. And to generate new commission income, he intends to begin offering special tour packages late this year, like an individually tailored Broadway weekend in newyork with hotel accommodations, theater tickets, meals and museum admissions. Unlike many Internet start-ups at this stage of business, Culturefinder is not now destined to be sold or to issue stock in an initial public offering, Mr. Carr said, though he does not rule this out in the longer term. "We've been very focused on raising the venture capital round," he said, referring to the Comcast infusion.  "At the appropriate moment, to raise additional funds, every financing option will be considered -- including an I.P.O." Mainly, the Comcast money will help Culturefinder promote its brand more actively, Mr. Carr said. "I'm trying to be Mr. Arts in cyberspace," he added, "to be front and center so when opportunities present themselves, I'm first in line." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Jack Manning/The newyork Times)

title:
INVESTING: DIARY;
No RushTo Upgrade Internet Stocks
body: It's been a black spring for Internet stocks, with the Bloomberg Internet Index falling 26.5 percent since its high on April 13. But are Wall Street analysts slapping "buy" signs on the reduced-price merchandise? Not especially, according to the First Call Corporation of Boston, which tracks analysts' recommendations. Last Thursday, First Call looked at the changes in analysts' recommendations for 10 large Internet stocks since April 13. They found that of the 19 changes since then, 9 have been positive and 10 negative. "Despite these stocks' being down, analysts don't appear to be ready to pull the trigger and get more aggressive on these stocks," said Chuck Hill, the director of research at First Call. "And that's probably because they're already quite bullish on these stocks to begin with." The 10 stocks First Call examined were Amazon.com, America Online, Mindspring, Lycos, Excite, Yahoo, Ebay, At Home, CMGI and Doubleclick. According to Mr. Hill, the 10 stocks now carry an average recommendation of 1.6, on a scale of 1 to 5, with 1 representing a "strong buy" and 5 a "strong sell." On April 13, the average consensus recommendation on the 10 Internet stocks was 1.7. (By contrast, he said, the average consensus recommendation for stocks in the Standard & Poor's 500 is 2.2.) Zacks.com, a Chicago research firm, said the "strong buys" that analysts have on the Internet stocks it tracks have remained flat since the end of March at about 37 percent of total Internet stock recommendations.   SANA SIWOLOP http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MARKET WATCH;
Pop! Goes the Bubble
body: HAS E-phoria ended? Highflying Internet stocks look mighty weak. Even on Friday, when other Nasdaq stocks were strong, many Internet shares couldn't muster their typical big moves up. As the week ended, shares of Internet concerns were well off their mid-April peaks. The Interactive Week index of 50 stocks is down 17 percent from its highs, while Thestreet.com index of 20 Net companies has fallen 26 percent since April 12. Battered E-investors are wondering whether the recent action is simply a pause in an upward trend or the beginning of the end of a glorious ride in these stocks. While no one is certain, there is a host of reasons why the downturn may continue. Broadly speaking, investing in Internet shares has changed. And investors who don't realize that are vulnerable. The factors working against these stocks are both macro and micro. One of the big-picture problems is rising interest rates -- bad for almost all equities, but especially damaging to stocks of Internet companies, which rely heavily on debt to finance their money-losing operations. As interest rates rise, these companies' debt costs do, too. Recent figures on Web use are also worrisome. Merrill Lynch's estimates of the total number of Internet users declined from 61.6 million in March to 61.1 million in April. While Merrill's resident Internet bull, Henry Blodget, cautions that one month may not make a trend, he points out that April's drop was only the second such decline in the last 12 months. Perhaps more significant than either interest rates or Web use, however, is the shift in supply and demand that has changed the way these shares trade. Simply put, there are many more E-sellers than there were before -- a change, almost imperceptible, that is weighing on many Internet stocks today. Start with the throngs of companies taking their shares to market. According to Commscan L.L.C., an investment banking research company in newyork, there have been 69 initial public offerings of Internet-related shares so far this year. During all of 1998, there were only 42 such offerings. And while E-commerce companies accounted for 11.5 percent of all new issues last year, excluding closed-end funds and American depository receipts, Internet I.P.O.'s have accounted for 44 percent of new stock issues in 1999. Also adding to supply is the fact that as newly public Internet concerns age, more stock hits the market from executives and insiders. These individuals are generally prohibited from selling any shares until several months after the I.P.O.'s. Even as extra Internet shares flood the market, demand is drying up. One measure: The money going into Internet-related mutual funds has dropped from $470 million in the week ended April 14 to $34 million last week. Complicating matters is a small-picture issue: a dearth of natural buyers -- the short-sellers -- waiting to step in even if these stocks keep falling. Investors willing to risk their money selling stocks short must buy them back later to close their positions. As a result, short-sellers represent future buyers. But since so many who bought this way lost their shirts betting against Internet stocks, few remain standing or solvent. At the height of the craze, Internet buyers were many while the sellers were few. Now the tables have turned. Ah, well. It was fun while it lasted. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph "No to the Net," plots daily closes since February, 1999 for the Interactive Week Internet Index.

title:
PERSONAL BUSINESS;
FrontDesk? Send Up A Computer
body: WE may know how much to slip the bellhop for dragging the bags upstairs, but the modern hotel evokes a new question: How much do you tip him for tech support? Consider Alex Peshev. He showed up at my room about 9 P.M. toting his wireless headset (used for communicating with the front desk) and found me muttering expletives as I struggled to work the television-based email. "I can trouble-shoot almost anything," Mr. Peshev said patiently. No surprise. He has a bachelor's degree in computer science and spends his days as a network administrator, which apparently will be a job requirement for the hotel worker of the 21st century. Welcome to a night's stay at the W Hotel, a stylish new 31-story hotel in downtown San Francisco that is your home office away from home. Like dozens of hotels trumpeting themselves as high tech, it offers Internet access, in-room computers and a wireless keyboard to send email via TV, and thus reinforces the tension that computer and Internet users feel every day: Sometimes technology is a panacea, and sometimes a real pain. The science-fiction-like amenities at the W were fine on the surface, but they required elbow grease, too. The radio crackled with static at first, Web access through the television was fuzzy, and the wireless telephone signals crossed when I tried to call the front desk. I wound up having an interesting conversation with a Norwegian fellow named Andre in room 1415. "Who is this?" he asked. "Well, who is this?" I responded cleverly. It turns out that Andre Backen is a computer game maker from Oslo and an Internet aficionado. It took him a half-hour to figure out the Internet access in his room. I should have sent Mr. Peshev, but he was probably busy upgrading the Unix computer in baggage storage. THEN again, the W had just opened, and at least it's trying, although in that regard it is not alone. Across the country, hotels are slowly adding technological amenities -- making data ports a default setting, offering a fax machine in every room, assuring that high-speed Internet access is as pertinent as a pillow mint. After all, what good is fresh breath if you can't email home about it? "We've come a long way from when there was a telephone by the side of the bed and maybe 'Magic Fingers' where you put 25 cents in and get a little shake," said John A. Marks, president and chief executive of the San Francisco Convention and Visitors Bureau. The conversation waxed philosophical. I mourned the fact that hotels no longer seemed a haven for business travelers but rather an enabler for the workaholic. Should a night's stay at a hotel really have to involve user manuals? Mr. Marks countered that hotels are justifiably responding to market demand. He argued that travelers -- particularly executives -- cannot afford to fall behind. Maybe not, but they will in most places. Big chains like Hyatt, Marriott, Wyndham and Hilton are just dipping their toes into technology with pilot projects: computers in some rooms or high-speed Internet access at one or two hotels like the Hyatt San Jose. The stumbling block is cost. Jonathan M. Tisch, president and chief executive of Loews Hotels, said it could cost several hundred thousand dollars just to add high-speed access lines to a single hotel. As for the W, owned by Starwood Hotels and Resorts Worldwide, the gadgets offered a marked upgrade over a traditional business night's stay -- once they were up and running. The $199 room included a CD player (with remote control and a selection of CD's delivered from the front desk), a VCR (movies cost $10), Compaq computer (I had to order it specially) and a Hewlett-Packard color printer/fax/copier (in 15 percent of the rooms). Had I been so inclined, I could have started an E-commerce business, filed for an initial public offering, then retired rich in time for cocktail hour. Among other features of the W was a sensor that detected if I was in the room. Hotel employees carry a device that looks like a garage-door opener. When pointed at a door, it indicates if the room is occupied, so an employee knows whether to enter. At one point, I was immersed in a moment of pure gadget bliss: I was listening to a Dave Matthews CD on the stereo, using the TV to switch back and forth between the newyork Knicks game and surfing the Net, and sipping a Heineken from the minibar. Like I'm not executive material. But the biggest asset of the place was its employees (and that isn't the beer talking), about a half-dozen of whom stopped by during the evening to make sure everything worked smoothly. I promise you, if Mother Teresa had a degree in engineering she couldn't have been as helpful. At one point, two employees came by just to refresh my towel supply and offer me a fortune cookie -- which required no tech support to open. IN the end, the high-tech hotel was a net plus, even if it does have some electronic bugs to work out. That was something that even Mr. Peshev, the bellhop/computer scientist, conceded. For example, he hates to wear his wireless headset to communicate with the front desk, because the ear piece is too small. "The first night my ear hurt so much, I couldn't even sleep," he said. "Sometimes," he added, "technology can be more of a headache than a help." He sounded tense. I tipped him $5. But maybe what he really needed was a quarter for the Magic Fingers. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: The W Hotel in San Francisco offers all the high-technology comforts of home, like email and fax machines, but glitches can crop up. The author, top, phones for help in operating television-based Web access in his room. V. Calamur, bottom right, arrived from the front desk to provide technical support for the room's wireless keyboard. (Darcy Padilla for The newyork Times)

title: New Security Fears As Hackers Disrupt 2 Federal Web Sites
body: An enduring cat-and-mouse game between Federal agents and computer hackers took a novel twist this week as the hackers turned on their pursuers, disrupting the Web sites of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the unitedstates Senate and forcing them to shut down. Both the Web sites, which remained closed through today, serve public relations functions, so no classified, confidential or personal material was compromised. But as the latest in a series of attacks against Government Web sites, including that of the White House, the new disruptions underscored the concerns of Government investigators that computer systems in many Federal agencies are too vulnerable to manipulation from the outside. "This is a critical risk," said Jack L. Brock Jr., an official at the General Accounting Office, the investigative arm of Congress, who has studied computer systems throughout the Federal Government. "We found that most agencies have weak computer security systems in place. This is a serious problem, governmentwide." In many cases, the hacking proves to be more annoying than compromising. This week, for example, vandals succeeded only in overloading the F.B.I. Web site with requests for electronic information and in posting inappropriate pictures and text on the Senate home page. The authorities said the hackers were retaliating for Federal agents' raids this week against computer hackers in several states. As a result of the attacks, both sites were almost immediately shut down as Government officials investigated how the breaches occurred. But as General Accounting Office investigators found by testing Government computer systems in recent years, including those of the Defense Department and the State Department, hackers can easily do more serious damage. In a recent investigation of one of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's 10 field centers, investigators reported to Congress that they "successfully penetrated several mission-critical systems," including one that calculated positioning data for earth-orbiting spacecraft and another that processed data from the spacecraft. The report concluded, "We could have disrupted NASA's ongoing command-and-control operations and stolen, modified or destroyed system software and data." The Clinton Administration has taken steps to combat threats to the nation's civilian and military computer systems, including a directive issued last May that ordered all major departments to develop a plan to protect their own computer systems. In January, President Clinton proposed spending $1.46 billion to develop a "cyber corps" of computer security experts to deal with the same issues. The proposals stand a good chance of passage on Capitol Hill, where Republican lawmakers have been pressing for Federal counterterrorism programs. But Mr. Brock said that while Government agencies had been responding quickly to specific problems, like those encountered this week by the F.B.I. and the Senate, managers had been slower to impose long-term solutions that would deny unauthorized access to their computer systems from people outside -- as well as inside -- the agencies. These managers, he said, "need to assess risks, the kind of information they have, how valuable it is and what they are doing to protect it." The incidents this week reflected a new aspect of the hacking wars: the tenacity of a group of cybervandals who are taunting the investigators trying to track them down. "This is the on-line version of a tantrum," said John Vranesevich, founder of AntiOnline, a Web site that educates the public about computer security issues. "It's like a parent with a rebellious 16-year-old old who sneaks out of the house, gets punished and sneaks out again. It's a constant back and forth." Officials at both the F.B.I. and the Senate said they did not know when the sites would be reopened. Bill Carter, an F.B.I. spokesman, said the bureau shut down its Web site Wednesday night before the hackers could penetrate so-called fire walls that protect sensitive information. Hackers made deeper inroads into the Senate computer system on Thursday, leaving an obscene message that said the intrusion was in response to the F.B.I. raids. Sherry Little, a spokeswoman for the office of the Senate sergeant-at-arms, which operates the Senate Web site, said unauthorized pictures and text appeared on Thursday evening, a major surprise to Senate computer experts. "We had the very latest protective software installed and updated as recently as two weeks ago," Ms. Little said. The Senate Web site provides general information on individual members, bills before Congress and historical information. The F.B.I. site contains news releases, crime statistics and general information, including the F.B.I.'s list of the 10 most wanted fugitives. Several F.B.I. agents declined to discuss bureau activity that might have precipitated the vandalism. But Mr. Vranesevich said that his organization, which closely monitors hacking and communicates with hackers through their computer names, has heard from at least six hackers in four states -- newyork, New Jersey, Texas and Washington -- who said they had been raided this week by Federal agents investigating their activities. Mr. Vranesevich said the attempts to penetrate the F.B.I. Web site were led by a hacker known as "Israeli Ghost" and came in retaliation for those raids and for the grand jury indictment earlier this month of Eric Burns, a 19-year-old northern Virginia man known by his Internet name, Zyklon. Mr. Burns was indicted on three counts of "computer intrusion" for breaking into computers operated by the unitedstates Information Agency and two companies. Federal authorities said he is also believed to be a member of a group that vandalized the White House public Web site last Sunday. Susan Lloyd, an F.B.I. spokeswoman in Washington, said Mr. Burns is scheduled to be arraigned next month in Alexandria, Va. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
The Crowds of Internet Investors Begin to Thin
body: How much more do Internet stocks have to fall before many investors lose interest? Not much, according to the latest mutual fund data. Perhaps convinced that buying on the dips would always pay off, investors kept pouring money into Internet stock funds in April and May, even as Internet stocks fell about 30 percent from their peak early last month. But that pace slowed sharply last week, as Internet funds pulled in just $34 million in new money. They had swallowed an average of more than $200 million a week, for a total of $1.3 billion, since the sector's high in early April. In all categories, stock funds drew $25.5 billion in new money in April -- usually a strong month because of contributions to Individual Retirement Accounts -- according to data released yesterday by the Investment Company Institute, the fund industry trade group. But overall fund sales have slowed considerably this month, according to fund company officials. In fact, Trimtabs.com Investment Research estimates that investors have actually pulled more than $3 billion out of stock funds since the market turned down on May 14. New investment in mutual funds has generally slowed somewhat from the torrid pace of recent years -- in part because of the increase in on-line trading of individual stocks. Now the very funds that invest in the most popular stocks of on-line traders may be losing some of their luster. Internet-stock funds took in $470 million in net new deposits in the week ended April 14 -- the same week Internet stocks peaked -- more than 10 times the $34 million recorded in the week ended Wednesday, according to AMG Data Services, an Arcata, Calif., research firm. "It's drying up rapidly due to the volatile market, and more specifically, this week's negative market action," said Robert Adler, AMG's president. Because so much money has piled into the funds in recent months, many people now have paper losses, even though the funds still boast some of the top performances of the year. In some cases, shareholders face hefty redemption charges if they sell, encouraging them to hold on for a comeback. "I am a little bit surprised the flows haven't turned negative already. It seems like an awful lot of hot money," said Scott Cooley, an analyst at Morningstar Inc., the fund researchers in Chicago. "I've got to think a lot of people haven't made a lot of money. People have definitely missed the bulk of the gains." Few Internet-stock fund shareholders have invested a big part of their wealth in these funds, one reason why more investors aren't pulling out, said David Kugler, president of the Monument Funds Group, which runs the Monument Internet Fund. "The average sophisticated investor says, 'I understand the power of the Internet, and I want to put a little money in this thing, but I don't want to have a coronary when we suffer tough times,' " he said. In contrast, investors began pulling money from stock funds almost immediately after the stock market began sliding from its peak on May 13. About $3.5 billion has fled stock funds in the last two weeks, according to Trimtabs.com, which tracks fund sales from Santa Rosa, Calif. "It hasn't been panicky selling," said Carl Wittnebert, director of research at Trimtabs. "It's just been persistent." For May, new sales are estimated at $9.7 billion, according to the firm. A handful of fund companies continue to get the lion's share of sales. More than half of net new fund investments last month went to Vanguard Group, Janus Capital and Fidelity Investments, according to the Financial Research Corporation, a Boston firm. All three fund groups said sales for May are decent but have eased from the I.R.A. spurt in April. Stock funds at Fidelity, owned by the FMR Corporation, have had net sales of $2.7 billion so far this month, and with three days to go will almost surely finish down from the $4.4 billion in sales last month. At Janus, a unit of Kansas City Southern Industries, stock funds have $3 billion in net sales for May, down from $4.8 billion in April. And Vanguard, whose index funds have made it the best-selling group this year, reported $3.2 billion in stock fund sales, down from $5.2 billion last month.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: With Later Hours, Later News Coverage - Correction Appended
body: Yesterday's decision by the board that governs the Nasdaq stock market to add an evening trading session puts new pressure on newspapers, wire services and television networks already competing to get the latest market information to their readers and viewers. Yet Nasdaq's plan to continue using the traditional 4 P.M. closing time for the day's prices could make the potential production headaches for newspapers less severe than they had feared. They had faced the prospect of having to update stock listings after 10 P.M. to reflect the late trading. The Associated Press, which provides stock listings to 900 newspapers, will update them with the evening results as fast as possible, said Randy Picht, business editor at the A.P. CNBC, part of NBC and its parent General Electric Company, and CNNfn, the business-news cable network owned by Time Warner, said they would continue to cover the markets whenever they are trading. But the later hours give CNBC a potentially costly problem. Between 8 and 10 P.M. on weeknights, the network has two programs -- "Hardball with Chris Matthews" and "Rivera Live" -- that earn higher Nielsen ratings and more advertising revenue than its daytime business coverage does. CNBC could run a crawl with the ticker figures along the bottom of the screen during those programs, or move the programs to new time slots, and executives there said that no decision had been made. "It's going to be a real sea change in financial news on television," said David Borman, executive vice president of CNNfn, which carries business news from 6 A.M. until midnight. He said the network would probably have to add reporters to cover business stories that break in the evening. Newspapers, too, may face that need. For example, companies inclined to release certain information only after the market closes may now release it at 10 P.M., rather than 4 P.M. Nancy Nielsen, a spokeswoman for The newyork Times Company, said: "As we learn more about the securities exchanges' plans, The Times will decide on the best way of supplementing the traditional tables, consistent with still providing prompt delivery of the newspaper to subscribers." "In whatever we do," she added, "we will also look for ways to make use of The newyork Times on the Web to update our financial market coverage." Both Richard J. Tofel, a spokesman for The Wall Street Journal, a unit of Dow Jones & Company, and Jim Henderson, deputy managing editor for the Money section of the Gannett Company's USA Today, said editors were waiting to see what final plans the exchanges developed before making decisions. Mr. Borman of CNNfn said he thought that the era of 24-hour trading was fast approaching. After-hour mechanisms like Strike "are filling the gaps, which are already getting smaller," he said. "Down the road, the markets will fill in all the gaps. I wouldn't be surprised by spring to see a morning session popping up. It's fascinating to see the competition going on, and the questions it raises, and we have a great front-row seat."  http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Business Day yesterday about the reaction of newspapers and television networks to the Nasdaq decision to add an evening trading session misspelled the name of the executive vice president of CNNfn. He is David Bohrman, not Borman. Correction-Date: May 29, 1999, Saturday

title: Coming Era of High-Speed Net Access Is Here and Now on College Campuses
body: EVERY time Barry Mason, a sophomore at Columbia University, logged on to the Internet in his dormitory room this past year, he experienced what most home users still consider a luxury of the future: a high-speed Internet connection. Now that he is at home, in Elizabeth City, N.J., for summer break and dealing with his parents' dial-up modem, Mr. Mason is realizing how nice it is to have a connection that is, in theory, almost 200 times as fast. "When I go home," Mr. Mason said, "I really miss it." Thousands of other privileged college students are very likely to be having the same thoughts this summer. While most home users are still waiting for broadband access to the Internet through high-speed cable or phone lines, students in university dormitories are already living in the future, and their experiences offer a glimpse of the benefits and problems that may lie ahead for much of the rest of society. While they are at school, many students have in their rooms high-speed access that is always on. At Columbia and scores of other colleges across the country, dormitories are directly wired to the Internet with Ethernet connections, high-speed wires that connect to the campus's main Internet hub at about 10 megabits per second. "Where else are you going to find an 18-year-old with a 10-megabit Ethernet connection?" said Vace Kundakci, deputy vice president of Columbia University's academic information systems. "Nowhere else but on college campuses." People who work at companies with high-speed connections have already had a taste of life with streaming multimedia and millisecond downloading times. But few of them have that access 24 hours a day, in their bedrooms as well. And of course, employers can be intrusive about how you spend your time at work. Students, on the other hand, are encouraged to experiment, play and learn on line whenever they want. A result, many students concede, is almost complete reliance on the Internet for information and correspondence. "If I were to suddenly lose my Internet connection, I probably would not be able to communicate," said Noemi Millan, a freshman at Princeton University. If students suddenly discovered that their Internet access had been taken away, she added, "there would probably be a riot." Ms. Millan said she went on line to post information, images and poetry on her home page, to read email, to stay on top of class deadlines, to download entertaining animated programs and to "find little factoids instead of schlepping all the way to the library." A few weeks ago, she placed her order for Mother's Day flowers on line instead of getting on the phone. Fiona Smith, a senior at Columbia, calls the Internet a "huge part" of her college education. "I shop on Ebay and do research on technology companies," said Ms. Smith, who is hoping to get a job with a company that will provide her email access and a fast Internet connection. "Maybe 30 percent of my Internet use is for studying," she said, "but this year it was higher -- maybe 50 percent -- because of a business-school project." Like many students, Ms. Smith said she got her news on line instead of on paper. Many students say they and their peers ignore printed classified advertisements when searching for jobs. When some students at Georgetown University were asked recently whether they would go to a conventional newspaper to search the classified advertisements, a few looked at one another as if they had never heard of the concept. With on-line searching available, they had not even considered it. The speed of broadband access has also rendered the Internet a major entertainment source. "Whenever we want to let our minds disappear, we find cool things to do on the Internet," said Rich Allan, a Princeton University freshman. That includes gaining access to games, videos and music. Trading MP3 music files is a popular pastime for college students. Free MP3's, which are compressed digital music files, can be retrieved legally on the Web from places like the mp3.com site. But in many cases, students make MP3 copies of CD's they already own, storing them on their computers or within personal files they keep on their college's network. They make copies of the files to trade with friends, or they play the recordings straight from their friends' computers. "It's a commonly held belief that it's O.K. to do it, and so everybody does it," said Fared Adib, a senior at the University of Missouri at Kansas City. But if the music is copyrighted -- and much of it is -- trade associations do not think that trading files without permission is O.K. at all. The Recording Industry Association of America is lobbying for the adoption of technology that would thwart illegal copying. The group has also started an education campaign for college students, called Sound Byting, to warn them about copyright violations. College administrators acknowledge that copyright infringement is an unfortunate byproduct of the quick downloading privilege that comes with fast Internet connections. "Schools are seeing the problems that accompany speed and ease," said Virginia Rezmierski, director of the office of policy development and education at the University of Michigan. "People are copying these things without thinking that this is someone's intellectual property." Jose-Marie Griffiths, chief information officer at Michigan, said she worried about what might happen if people outside college campuses got the same high-speed access without being educated about what could be copied legally and what couldn't. At that point, Ms. Griffiths said, "others might do more damage, trading for commercial purposes rather than just playing around." But Ms. Griffiths and Ms. Rezmierski both stressed that high-speed access had also generated many educational benefits. Faculty members, as well as students, are able to collaborate more easily than ever before, by running large computational programs on line, teleconferencing over the Web or working on projects that require people to download large files routinely. Easy and constant Net access has also improved students' interaction with the library, said Christine Haile, associate provost for technology services for the State University of newyork. She said that SUNY's libraries had found that electronic access to the library's card catalogue had led to increased use of the library's printed resources. "It's not reducing library business or traffic," Ms. Haile said. "In fact, it increases circulation." But libraries outside college campuses might still want to take note of another trend that has accompanied the installment of broadband access in S.U.N.Y.'s residence halls. When asked which students used more, access from dormitory rooms or elsewhere to the on-line databases provided by the university's library or the actual libraries standing on campus, Ms. Haile replied, "There is no question that students are using on-line access to the library more." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos (Jack Manning/The newyork Times; Frances Roberts for The newyork Times)

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
U.S.-EuropeanUnion Talks On Privacy Are Sputtering
body: After months of negotiations that had appeared headed for success, the unitedstates and the European Union have veered away from each other in a dispute over privacy protection that could disrupt trans-Atlantic electronic commerce. European authorities continue to insist that the unitedstates fails to provide enough consumer protection from companies that collect and often re-sell personal information. The issue is important because the European Union issued a directive last year that in theory prohibits companies from transmitting personal information to countries that do not offer "adequate" privacy protection. No one has tried to enforce the prohibition yet, and several European countries have not even passed national laws to carry it out. But the issue has alarmed many companies, because the directive applies to activities as varied as airline reservations, banking and on-line shopping. American officials, led by the Commerce Department, have been trying to persuade European officials to accept a system under which American companies would adopt a code of good behavior and be allowed to regulate themselves. Until recently, both sides seemed intent on reaching a compromise in time for a meeting of President Clinton and European leaders in Cologne on June 21. But as the negotiators prepare for a key meeting in Brussels on Friday, officials on both sides say the discussions have bogged down. If they fail to reach agreement on Friday, their chances of doing so before the meeting are low. "We are right back to the old story that they want us to invent a regime that looks like theirs," said David L. Aaron, Undersecretary of Commerce for International Trade, in a telephone interview. "Well, we aren't going to do that." Publicly, European officials say they remain open to a compromise in the next few weeks. "I can tell you there are problems, but the gap is consistently narrowing," said John Mogg, the European Commission's director general for financial services and the top European negotiator. In the last few days, experts on both sides have become skeptical about a deal. While American officials complain that Europe is trying to impose "data czars" on the unitedstates, European officials charge that American proposals would water down their protections to the point of meaninglessness. "Americans still have the illusion that they can change the directive, but they can't," said Spiros Simitis, a law professor at Johann Wolfgang Goethe University in Frankfurt and an adviser to the European Commission, the executive arm of the European Union, on the privacy directive. At the heart of the dispute are deep differences about the need for governments to protect privacy, particularly when it comes to the use of personal information as a marketing tool. The European Union's directive requires that companies that collect personal information, whether through routine business transactions or through tracking the sites a person visits on the Internet, must fully disclose what they will do with the information and give people a chance to say no. It also requires that companies give people access to data files about them and give them the right to correct errors. In principle, American officials say they agree completely. But they also argue that any system needs to be flexible, and they have adamantly rejected demands to set up quasi-public enforcement authorities. The American proposals call for giving companies "safe harbor" from the directive if they publicly embrace the European principles themselves. Companies could join self-regulatory associations, like the Better Business Bureau, or simply make formal public commitments to the principles on their own. The two sides are also squabbling over how much time companies should have in order to comply with the European rules. The unitedstates is pushing for about two years, and the European Union wants to offer only six months.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Price Flights for Internet Shares Are Less Dizzying
body: Stocks generally rebounded yesterday from a four-session losing streak, but not all Internet stocks caught the wave. In fact, three Internet issues fell below their offering price during their first day of trading, and two others posted gains that were handsome -- but remained less spectacular than those of their peers in recent months. The automatic doubling or tripling of a new Internet stock is history, investors seemed to say as they made clear distinctions among the various offerings. The shares of Ziplink Inc. and Juno Online Services finished at less than their initial offering prices, and those of Edgar Online gained mere pennies. Meanwhile, underwriters of an upcoming deal, for Private Business Inc., responded to the softening market by cutting the price and reducing the number of shares to be issued. "I can't recall an Internet I.P.O. that fell below its offering price on the day of offering," said Neil Barsky, co-founder of Midtown Research Group, a hedge fund that specializes in these issues. Noting that Internet stocks generally are down sharply from their highs, Mr. Barsky predicted that the tailspin would worsen. Still, he said, using the argot of earthquakes, "I don't think this is the Big One." Pessimism also emerged from Morgan Stanley, Dean Witter, whose highly regarded Internet analyst, Mary Meeker, told the firm's brokers and strategists that Internet stock prices, already down 46 percent from their highs of last year, could well skid 20 percent more. "It isn't uncommon at this time of year for prices of technology stocks to contract when catalysts are insufficient," the firm stated in summarizing her comments. "Also, as the number of Internet initial public offerings has increased sharply, it seems the deal quality has declined markedly and we wouldn't be surprised to see investor resistance." Market demand was underwhelming for Ziplink, a company in Lowell, Mass., that is a provider of wholesale Internet access services. It sold 3.5 million shares at $14, but the stock closed at $12.375 after trading as low as $9.75. Another laggard was Juno Online, which provides free electronic mail and is controlled by David E. Shaw, a hedge fund manager. It was priced at $13 and sank to $11.625. Edgar Online of Norwalk, Conn., whose business is helping investors extract information from documents filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, offered 3.6 million shares at $9.50. After opening at $8.75 and trading as low as $8.50, Edgar edged up to close at $9.5625. Though Internet euphoria has waned a bit for much of the year, it is only this month that Internet-sector initial public offerings as a group have failed to double from their offering prices. Through Tuesday, according to a tabulation by Thomson Financial Securities Data, 22 deals in May averaged first-day gains of 79 percent, slightly more than half the March gain and less than a third of the gains of a much less active January. The Thomson figures also show that price increases for new shares after four weeks of trading shrank in April to only about a quarter as great as the performance of other new shares at the peak in February. Still, some analysts remain bullish, at least on the higher-quality companies that will be the sector's survivors. For one thing, they noted a pattern in which these stocks have suffered immediately after the earnings season ends -- that is, the middle month of a given quarter. "Without any news there isn't any catalyst for these stocks to go up," said Keith Benjamin, an analyst at BancBoston Robertson Stephens in San Francisco. He added that "anybody who wasn't expecting this wasn't paying attention." Too many companies don't deserve their high valuations, Mr. Benjamin said, and too many others are going public these days. But he argued that the sector's recovery is only a few weeks away -- when the focus moves to second-quarter earnings, which, he said, will once again surpass expectations. "The fundamentals are fantastic" for the more established companies, Mr. Benjamin said. Henry Blodget, an analyst at Merrill Lynch & Company, contended in a report on Tuesday that most of the recent weakness is little more than the usual seasonal trading pattern. He also pointed to issues affecting the sector's leaders -- cable access for America Online; the integration of acquisitions at Yahoo, and the slower revenue growth and increased investment at Amazon.com. "We still expect to see at least a modest rally in the sector in June," Mr. Blodget said. "We do not expect the leading stocks to hit new highs, but we believe they will trade higher than current levels." In fact, Internet stocks picked up steam as yesterday wore on. America Online finished up $5.3125 a share, to $120.3125; Yahoo up $13.9375, to $140.875, and Amazon up $9.375, to $120.9375. An initial public offering that sold at a hefty premium was DLJ Direct, a stock that will track the performance of the on-line brokerage division of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. After 16 million shares had been marketed at $20, the stock began trading yesterday at $26.625 and climbed to $30 at the close. The other was Starmedia Network, which operates across Latin America. Its 7 million shares were offered at $15 and closed at $26.0625. "I.P.O.'s are as a rule driven by fits of euphoria and fits of depression," Mr. Barsky of Midtown Research said. "The Internet sector is that times 10." But it's a world of infinite possibilities, he added, one that unlike, say, biotechnology, can be experienced directly by ordinary people. "The investor," he said, "is the consumer." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Even as some Internet issues had weak first trading days yesterday, these traders in DLJ Direct -- Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette's on-line unit -- found interest strong. title: Universal Music and BMG Form Team for WebVenture
body: The frantic push by record companies to sell copyrighted music over the Internet is making for a kind of technological polygamy. In the latest example, two music industry titans, Universal Music and BMG Entertainment, said yesterday that they would team up with the AT&T Corporation and Matsushita Electric Industrial Company of Japan, to create technology to sell, store and distribute music over the Internet. Since both Universal and BMG had already announced similar initiatives with other companies, the deal underscored the desperation of the major record labels to establish a foothold in electronic commerce -- even if it means pursuing multiple solutions simultaneously and forging uneasy alliances with their own competitors and with competing technology companies. Universal, the largest record company, is already committed to an alliance announced earlier this month with Intertrust Technologies Corporation of Sunnyvale, Calif., to create a secure digital music technology -- that is, a way of delivering music to consumers on line while at the same time protecting copyrighted recordings from electronic piracy. Universal, a unit of the Seagram Company, and BMG, which is the music division of Bertelsmann A.G., are also part of the Madison Project, an initiative sponsored by the International Business Machines Corporation, to distribute music on line. Some record companies are parts of larger conglomerates yet find themselves aligning with manufacturers and developers that compete with the technology arms of their mother corporations. For example, Sony Music's own Magicgate software is designed to deliver music in a secure format, but Sony Music is also part of the Madison project, and has signed an agreement to use Microsoft's MS Audio 4.0 technology to distribute music on line. After long ignoring the Internet, the recording industry is now frantically seeking to establish a consumer alternative to MP3, the technology that has become the de facto standard for distributing music on line. The record companies dread MP3, which compresses digital sound into relatively small files that can be easily sent over the Internet with no way for the record labels to trace the distribution or prevent near CD-quality recordings. The major labels fear that they are already losing millions of dollars annually in revenues to MP3 recordings traded freely on line. In their search for a standard that will enable secure sales of music delivered on line, the record companies are "casting their lots with a lot of players," said Mark Mooradian, senior analyst with Jupiter Communications, a newyork-based research firm. Even so, Mr. Mooradian said they were dealing from a position of strength. The rush of deals, he said, demonstrated the power of the record labels ultimately to determine what standard will be used, and thus to dictate terms to technology companies, which are all vying to establish their protection schemes as the industry standard. For example, in attempting to analyze the apparently conflicting deals announced by Universal, Mr. Mooradian said: "When I talked to AT&T, they said, 'Intertrust is out and we're in.' Universal said, 'No, no, no, they're not out.' " Intertust declined comment yesterday. For their part, the record labels said they had no intention of signing exclusive agreements with individual technology partners. Larry Kenswil, president of electronic commerce and advanced technology for Universal Music, called the present scramble "the Wild West" and said his company intended to embrace whatever technology "people want to buy." Universal, he said, does not necessarily favor any single solution from AT&T or Intertrust; both technologies could wind up being part of a group of solutions eventually embraced by Universal Music. Fred R. Ehrlich, Sony Music's senior vice president for new technology, said of his company's tango with multiple partners: "Sony Music has made no exclusive relationships. I won't be surprised if record companies make many, if not multiple, alliances." Technology companies do not seem surprised or disturbed by the fact they are being courted by the already betrothed. Ronald J. Brachman, research vice president at AT&T Labs, said not just record labels but hardware and software developers were engaged in this evolving form of corporate polygamy, often referred to as "coopetition." All this is taking place against the backdrop of an international rush by an ad-hoc recording industry committee, the Secure Digital Music Initiative, to negotiate an industry standard by June from among the conflicting priorities of record labels and the makers of consumer music devices.    http://www.nytimes.com

title:
WHAT'S NEXT;
Squeezing 80 'Cups' of Data Into 1 Cup
body: AFTER recent crashes knocked out America Online and parts of AT&T, there were widespread fears that ever-spiraling Internet use would create network gridlock in the unitedstates. Aside from some glitches, that hasn't happened. But the salvation of communications networks has come from the world of theoretical physics and high-level optics rather than electronics. Through an alchemy of sorts called multiplexing -- its even more cumbersome name is dense wave division multiplexing -- telephone companies and Internet service providers can increase capacity quickly while cutting costs at the same time. The secret ingredient is light. And the harnessing of the photons of light for such purposes, a field called photonics, may eventually change the way computers operate, increasing their capacity as well. "Without fiber optics and this method of increasing capacity, there would be no World Wide Web," said Dr. Erich Ippen, a professor of electrical engineering, computer science and physics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. "It just enables everything. There's really a photonics revolution coming." The concept behind multiplexing is both old and relatively simple -- it is based on new ways to use fiber optic cables. The first fiber optic systems, the backbone of both the Internet and long distance telephone networks, sent only a single stream of laser-generated light pulses down each thin strand of glass fiber. Each cable typically carries 96 to 150 strands. With that much capacity, the only problem phone companies had at first was filling their systems. But the popularity of the Web soon eliminated that worry and left the companies looking for even greater capacity. To find that capacity, engineers turned to a well-known concept from radio and television broadcast technology, the fact that a single strand of fiber can simultaneously carry a number of different streams, or channels, of information. The trick is that each data stream must be sent on a different frequency -- in the case of laser light, that means color. For fiber optics systems, hundreds of different streams of messages can be transmitted at once along each of the strands in a cable. Unlike electrons, the subatomic particles that make all things electronic possible, photons are packets of light energy. "You can take a closet and fill it with electrons because they are particles," said Kathy Szelag, vice president for marketing at the Lucent Technologies Optical Networking Group. "But if you pump photons into that same closet, it will never be too full of light. There is no physical limit." In addition to Lucent, photonics multiplexing systems are made by Nortel Networks, Pirelli Cables and Systems, and Ciena. Like many elegant theories, however, multiplexing was a strategy that had to overcome a significant problem to be practical: as photons zip along their cross-country travels, they begin to scatter and slow. So it became necessary to amplify the signal in fiber optic lines. Early fiber optic systems used a complex patchwork in which the signal was converted from light to electricity, augmented electronically and then changed back into light. The process was awkward and reduced the system's maximum speed. Electronic amplification also made running multiple frequencies, or channels, too expensive and too complex. Each channel in a single strand of a fiber optic cable would require its own electronic amplifier every 25 miles or so, at a cost of about $75,000 each. Since there are more than 100 channels per strand in the most advanced cables, stringing more fiber optic cable remained a cheaper way to increase network capacity. A technological breakthrough, optical amplifiers, changed all that in the mid-1990's, about the time the Internet began making huge demands on networks. Optical amplifiers used newly developed lasers to excite the photons as they passed along. Not only are they neater in operation, but a single optical amplifier can excite a number of different channels at once, and the resulting signals it produces travel farther than ones that are amplified electronically. Suddenly, it was cheaper to change how signals were sent than to lay more fiber optic cable. For AT&T, which installed its first photonic multiplexing system in 1995, the optical amplifiers were an answer to prayers. AT&T expects the demand on its network to increase by 500 percent in the next five years -- with nearly all of that increase coming from Internet traffic. "Thank goodness this technology is growing rapidly," said Dr. George Gawrys, the planning manager for AT&T's transportation network division. "The alternative would have been awful." Not only does multiplexing allow networks to expand without adding an inch of new fiber optic cable, but it also saves money, allowing further price cuts for long distance telephone and Internet connections. Mrs. Szelag, at Lucent, estimated that the cost of adding capacity using multiplexing was about one-fifth the cost of laying more cables. The first system AT&T bought ran eight channels of light per strand -- all of it invisible to the human eye. The most advanced systems currently sold by Lucent offer 80 channels per strand of fiber, which allows each strand to carry 400 billion bits of information per second. So each strand is capable of moving five million simultaneous phone calls, or the contents of 600 CD-ROM's, every second, according to Lucent. Impressive as all that may be, Mrs. Szelag said that optical networking was at roughly the same stage of development as electronics was when the first Hewlett-Packard calculator came out. "Our job now is to make photons as important to the 21st century as electrons were to the 20th," she said. The photonics industry still has one major problem to overcome. Multiplexing is useful now for only extremely high-capacity lines traveling long distances because it has no effective system for switching or routing data and telephone calls. In a variation of the old amplifier problem, all that takes place within specialized computers after the photons are converted to electrons. Some very small-scale photonic switches have been developed using "micro-mirrors" that are controlled by electronic-based computers, and optical switching has been shown to work on a laboratory scale. But the industry's long-term dream is to create networks that can be all optical. Recently, an Israeli company, Trellis Photonics, began work on an optical switch based on crystals. NASA and a Massachusetts company, Optron Systems, are working on similar technology. If such research leads to successful optical switches and routers, that would be a major step toward optical computers, which could operate, in theory, at very high speeds. Many problems have to be overcome to get there. One of the most significant problems is the fact that there is no photon storage device to serve the function of a hard drive or floppy disk. Optical computing, if it proves feasible, would be such a dramatic change in technology that some people even use fanciful descriptions to get across the point that its final form might go far beyond the familiar. Ms. Szelag said the ethereal nature of photons could mean an odd computer indeed, leading to thoughts of "a computer with nothing inside it." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Illustration (Mary Ann Smith)
