title: Click Here
body: CRYPTONOMICON By Neal Stephenson. 918 pp. newyork: Avon Books. $27.50. Even if you haven't read "Gravity's Rainbow," Thomas Pynchon's absurdist, 10-ton World War II epic, you know how it begins: "A screaming comes across the sky." Less famous -- except to a geeky substratum of Pynchon obsessives -- is a line that arrives a few paragraphs later, as an Allied officer watches a V-2 rocket arc its way toward his position in London. Scanning the sky, the officer thinks to himself, "Incoming mail." Incoming mail! To some Pynchon fanatics, this line doesn't merely anticipate America Online's omnipresent jingle ("You've Got Mail!") -- it's one of many hints, packed into the DNA of "Gravity's Rainbow," that the secretive author was hip to the notion of cyberspace before almost anyone else. Sound dubious? A little. But as the World Wide Web increases its hold on the popular imagination, the search for literary antecedents has become in some circles as feverish as any day-trader's hunt for hot Internet stocks. Neal Stephenson came along a little late in the game to be considered one of the Web's genuine prophets. His first novel, a spiky academic satire called "The Big U," was published in 1984 -- the same year William Gibson, in "Neuromancer," coined the term "cyberspace." Stephenson didn't plant both feet in science fiction until 1992, when his novel "Snow Crash" -- a swashbuckling fantasy that largely takes place in a virtual world called the Metaverse -- became an instant, and deserved, cyberpunk classic. "Snow Crash" remains the freshest and most fully realized exploration of the hacker mythology. Set in a futuristic southern California, the novel rolls out a society in ruins. Citizens live in heavily fortified "Burbclaves," pizza delivery services are run with military precision by a high-tech Cosa Nostra, and the Library of Congress (now comprising digital information uploaded by swarms of freelance Matt Drudge types) has merged with the C.I.A. and "kicked out a big fat stock offering." In reality, Stephenson's hero delivers pizza. In the Metaverse, he's a warrior on a mission to squelch a deadly computer virus. Sounds perfectly preposterous -- and it is. But Stephenson, a former code writer, has such a crackling high style and a feel for how computers actually function that he yanks you right along. Despite all the high-tech frippery, there's something old-fashioned about Stephenson's work. He cares as much about telling good stories as he does about farming out cool ideas. There's a strong whiff of moralism in his books, too. The bad guys in his fiction -- that is, anyone who stands in a well-intentioned hacker's way -- meet bad ends. In "Snow Crash," one nasty character tries to rape a young woman, only to find out she's installed an intrauterine device called a "dentata." Stephenson's antiquated commitment to narrative, his Dickensian brio, is part of what makes his gargantuan new novel, "Cryptonomicon," distinct from the other outsize slabs of post-modern fiction we've seen recently -- David Foster Wallace's "Infinite Jest," Don DeLillo's "Underworld," Thomas Pynchon's "Mason & Dixon." For all the pleasures scattered throughout those books, they're dry, somewhat forbidding epics that beckon industrious graduate students while checking the riffraff at the door. "Cryptonomicon," on the other hand, is a wet epic -- as eager to please as a young-adult novel, it wants to blow your mind while keeping you well fed and happy. For the most part, it succeeds. It's brain candy for bitheads. "Cryptonomicon" could have easily been titled "Incoming Mail." It's a sprawling, picaresque novel about code making and code breaking, set both during World War II, when the Allies were struggling to break the Nazis' fabled Enigma code, and during the present day, when a pair of entrepreneurial hackers are trying to create a "data haven" in the Philippines -- a place where encrypted data (and an encrypted electronic currency) can be kept from the prying eyes of Big Brother. It is, at heart, a book about people who want to read one another's mail. "Cryptonomicon" is so crammed with incident -- there are dozens of major characters, multiple plots and subplots, at least three borderline-sentimental love stories and discursive ruminations on everything from Bach's organ music and Internet start-ups to the best way to eat Cap'n Crunch cereal -- that it defies tidy summary. Suffice it to say that some early scenes are set at Princeton University in the 1940's, where an awkward young mathematical genius named Lawrence Pritchard Waterhouse befriends the computer pioneer Alan Turing. (Turing's interest in Waterhouse goes beyond their bicycle rides and theoretical discussions; he makes "an outlandish proposal to Lawrence involving penises. It required a great deal of methodical explanation, which Alan delivered with lots of blushing and stuttering.") When war breaks out, Turing is dispatched to Bletchley Park in Britain, where he helps break Enigma. Waterhouse is ultimately assigned to a top-secret outfit called Detachment 2702, led by a gung-ho marine named Bobby Shaftoe, whose mission it is to prevent the Nazis from discovering that their code has been cracked wide open. Stephenson cheerfully stretches historical plausibility -- there are some absurdly heroic (if electrifying) battle scenes, hilarious cameos by Ronald Reagan and Douglas MacArthur, and shadowy conspiracies involving U-boat captains and fallen priests -- but plays the mathematics of code breaking straight. We witness, in detail, Turing's early attempts to create a bare-bones computer that will help decode Nazi messages, and are plunged into the organized chaos at Bletchley Park, where "demure girls, obediently shuffling reams of gibberish through their machines, shift after shift, day after day, have killed more men than Napoleon." Stephenson is even better at climbing inside the minds of his mathematical Wunderkinder. When Waterhouse goes for a walk on a deserted beach, for example, he can't help thinking that the ocean is a beehive of encoded information: "The ocean is a Turing machine, the sand its tape; the water reads the marks in the sand and sometimes erases them and sometimes carves new ones with tiny currents that are themselves a response to the marks." Stephenson intercuts these wartime scenes with chapters about Waterhouse's grandson, Randy, who works for a start-up company called Epiphyte that plans not only to create a data haven but also to use a cache of gold buried by the Japanese Army during World War II to back an electronic currency protected by state-of-the-art encryption. These chapters are the book's shaggiest and most winsome, if only because Stephenson is so plugged into Randy's hacker sensibilities. As he skims along, Stephenson riffs on everything from Wired magazine -- here called Turing, with the motto "So Hip, We're Stupid!" -- and Microsoft's legal team's "state-of-the-art hellhounds" to pretentious cultural-theory academics and Silicon Valley's interest in cryogenics. (Some hackers here wear bracelets offering a $100,000 reward to medics who freeze their dead bodies.) That "Cryptonomicon" contains the greatest hacking scene ever put to paper, performed by Randy while under surveillance in a Philippine prison, should further endear this novel to computer freaks on both coasts. I expect to see, for the next decade or so, dogeared copies of this novel rattling around on the floorboards of the Toyotas (or, increasingly, Range Rovers) that fill Silicon Valley parking lots. Should anyone else bother with it? My answer is a guarded yes. Stephenson could have easily cut this novel by a third, and it's terrifying that he imagines this 900-plus-page monster to be the "first volume" in an even longer saga. Worse, he strains too hard at reconciling the book's multiple plot strands. We can understand the subtle links between World War II code breaking and today's politicized encryption battles -- and the spiritual links between cryptographers in the 1940's and hackers in the 1990's -- without the nonsense about secret gold deposits and coded messages that filter down (improbably) through generations. Stephenson, I suspect, simply can't help himself; he's having too good a time to ever consider applying the brakes. A yea-saying comic book for the next millennium, "Cryptonomicon" is as fascinating, and as frustrating, as a string of partly decrypted code. Behind the pixilated swagger of Stephenson's prose, you catch frequent glimpses of the genuinely first-rate novel this might have been. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Alex Ostroy)

title:
INVESTING: DIARY;
The Internet, the S.E.C. And Stock Giveaways
body: The Securities and Exchange Commission may be trying hard to keep up with what is happening on the Internet. But the Internet seems to be falling behind on what is happening at the S.E.C. That, at least, is the view of Stephen J. Schulte, a securities lawyer at Schulte Roth & Zabel in newyork who specializes in Internet issues. As evidence, Mr. Schulte points to the continuing proliferation of "free stock" programs on the Net despite clear S.E.C. warnings that such giveaways risk running afoul of Federal securities laws. Since April 1998, when Travelzoo.com offered free shares to people who registered on its Web site, stock giveaways have become the rage. There is even a Web site (www.che.wsu.edu/fountain /contents/stock1.htm) devoted to tracking the other Web sites offering free stock. Giveaways have been the subject of S.E.C. attention since at least the 1970's. Consumers getting such shares usually run no risks. But the companies issuing them are not so lucky. In its older cases, the commission's legal staff has determined that securities offered in exchange for something of value must be registered, unless the company fits within certain limited exceptions. In recent months, the S.E.C. has issued "no action" letters advising several young Internet businesses that shares offered to those who visit their Web sites are not really "free," as that term is defined in Federal securities laws. Some of those companies have put their offers on hold while their lawyers negotiate. If the commission's advice wasn't clear enough, Mr. Schulte said, a senior S.E.C. staff member told a conference in late February "that 'free' stock is a misnomer" because "registration with a Web site provides value to the site's owner and therefore, involves consideration." Thus, Mr. Schulte added, the S.E.C. staff "has sent a clear message" that unregistered stock giveaways are probably a no-no. "However, this may be a case of message sent, but not received," Mr. Schulte said. True, he acknowledged, some companies say they have suspended their programs "pending S.E.C. clarification." But he added, "What further clarification do they need?" DIANA B. HENRIQUES http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Stephen Schulte

title:
INVESTING;
Where Strategy Means Keeping Up With the Kids
body: JOHN CABELL Jr. likes to tag along when his 14-year-old daughter, Elizabeth, heads to the mall. That is because Mr. Cabell, as co-manager of the $930 million USAA Aggressive Growth fund, is hungry for insight into what the under-21 crowd is buying. Between 3 and 4 percent of the fund's portfolio is invested in companies that focus on Generation Y -- which by its broadest definition encompasses 60 million Americans ages 4 to 21. It is an attractive group: Teenage Research Unlimited of Northbrook, Ill., estimates that the 31 million Americans between 12 and 19 spent $141 billion last year, up from $122 billion in 1997. And the teen-age population is expected to peak at 35 million in 2010. But because teen-agers are fickle, Gen Y companies can falter quickly, and investors can be left reeling. "This is such a niche and it's so volatile that it makes Internet companies look like I.B.M.," said Mr. Cabell, who is 45. Wall Street is the follower here, he added, and "it's the kids who are setting the trends." A one-time Wall Street darling, the retailer Gadzooks Inc. of Carrollton, Tex., is a case in point. Its stock price fell more than 80 percent from a 52-week high of $29.25 last June, as teen-agers shunned the private-label clothes it was introducing. The shares have only begun to recover, and are now trading at $9.625. Two other fashion victims were Pacific Sunwear, a beach-oriented company in Anaheim, Calif., and Hot Topic of Pomona, Calif., which cultivates a bad-boy image. Their stocks fell 55.3 percent and 61.5 percent, respectively, in the fourth quarter amid disappointing results. Analysts say the culprit in both cases was teen-agers' changing tastes: Young buyers were cool to Sunwear's wide-leg jeans and Hot Topic's gift offerings. Nearly a dozen public companies -- most of them retailers -- focus on Gen Y. Others, notably Skechers USA, a shoe retailer with a streetwise urban look, and Limited Too, a subsidiary of The Limited, are expected to go public this summer.  Gen Y retailers tend to operate in malls, sell products over the Internet and market to both boys and girls. Even when Gen Y companies don't make fashion missteps, they can experience the volatility characteristic of Internet marketers. The stock of Delia's of newyork, a clothing retailer that controls 95 percent of Iturf, an on-line sibling, climbed nearly tenfold between October and April in anticipation of Iturf's initial offering, hitting a high of $40. But since then, Delia's has tumbled more than 50 percent. (Iturf closed at $66 on its first day of trading on April 9, up from the initial price of $22. It now trades at $25.50.) Still, "there's significant money to be made from this demographic segment," said Joe Grillo, an analyst at BT Alex Brown in San Francisco. The trick for investors is to figure out which Gen Y companies have management that understands fashion and reacts quickly to change. Pacific Sunwear was able to turn around quickly, offering a Hawaiian look that has become popular. The stock now trades at $38.625, more than triple its December low of $12. "This is a very nimble, very flexible company," said Janet Kloppenburg, an analyst with BancBoston Robertson Stephens, who says the stock could hit $46 in 12 months. She also says Hot Topic has already put its line of gift products in order; traditional retailers might have taken eight months to do so. The stock closed on Friday at $25.0625, more than double its 52-week low of $9.875. She says it could hit $33 in 12 months. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Sheree Boyd)

title:
MARKET WATCH;
A Slap on the Cyberwrist
body: ARTHUR LEVITT has talked plenty tough about policing the Internet. As chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, Mr. Levitt is the nation's top investment cop. He has often warned about the dangers of on-line trading and prodded investors to make sure they know what they are buying. He has cautioned on-line brokerage firms against promoting themselves as a means to get rich quickly and urged them to better explain to their customers the risks and costs of trading through the new medium of the Internet. And he has cracked down on Internet investment fraud, dispatching his new cyberforce of Internet regulators against stock touts and illegal securities offerings. All of which is swell. But when Mr. Levitt had a chance last week to show that the S.E.C. will do much more than jawbone on-line brokerage firms that put the larger investing public at risk, he pulled up short. The S.E.C. accused Datek Online Brokerage Services, one of the fastest-growing on-line brokers, of dipping into customer funds to meet its own financial obligations, a violation of Federal securities laws. Datek did it not once but 12 times in the spring of 1998, the S.E.C. said. In addition to not having the required reserves on hand, the agency said, Datek filed a false report of its capital position with the commission. But Datek got barely a slap on its cyber- wrist. In one of those peculiar lawyerly agreements to dispose of the charges against it, Datek admitted nothing but agreed not to do it in the future. The brokerage firm will hire a consultant to make sure that it follows the rules that it may or may not have violated. And the firm agreed to pay a $50,000 fine. That is roughly the amount of trading commissions that Datek earns in the first half-hour of trading each day. And it is minuscule compared with the $50 million that Datek, the fourth-largest on-line broker, will spend this year to promote its services. Datek and other on-line brokerage firms are at the epicenter of a tectonic shift in the nation's securities markets. Island ECN, a Datek affiliate, has filed for permission to become the nation's newest stock exchange. Island and numerous other computerized trading systems have attracted thousands of new investors eager to flex their newly empowered status in the financial markets. That raises questions about whether the regulatory systems built to police an old way of doing business are adequate in a new world. The S.E.C. has already begun to look at whether on-line brokerage and day-trading firms are doing everything they should to protect customers, such as making sure their trades are being executed at the best possible prices. But part of policing is penalizing wrongdoing. Richard Walker, the S.E.C. enforcement chief, says the treatment of Datek was harsher than that in previous, similar cases. And he contrasts Datek's actions, which he said were unintentional and caused no customers to lose money, with cases in which frauds set out to use the Internet to steal money from investors. Certainly the latter such cases are worth prosecuting, but they are the equivalent of sweeping three-card monte dealers off the streets. Victims often ignore very visible warning signs, like something-for-nothing promises, out of greed. The victims of a brokerage firm that is dipping into customer funds, however, cannot possibly know what is going on. They need the S.E.C. to police the market's infrastructure with more than a popgun. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Guilty Plea in Bloomberg Fraud Case
body: A former employee of Bloomberg L.P., who hired construction contractors for the media company's office in Princeton, N.J., pleaded guilty yesterday for his role in a scheme to defraud Bloomberg of more than $1.5 million. Joseph Menno of Langhorne, Pa., pleaded guilty in Federal court in Manhattan to conspiracy and mail-fraud charges related to the scheme, which took place between July 1993 and November 1997. In addition to hiring construction and maintenance contractors, Mr. Menno was also responsible for approving Bloomberg's payments for their services. Prosecutors charged that Mr. Menno and his brother owned Remington Professional Services, a Bloomberg contractor. Mr. Menno did not tell Bloomberg about his ownership of Remington and steered millions of dollars of Bloomberg's contracting work to his firm. Remington hired subcontractors to perform that work and submitted bills to Bloomberg for contracting work that far exceeded the amounts the subcontractors had charged. Mr. Menno used his position at Bloomberg, the financial news and data provider, to approve Remington's inflated bills. Remington then paid off subcontractors with the fees from Bloomberg and retained a balance of more than $1.5 million for itself. As part of the scheme, Mr. Menno and his brother arranged for William Kramer, who previously pleaded guilty in the scheme, to pose as president of Remington and submit the bills to Bloomberg. For this role, Mr. Kramer received about 15 percent of Remington's profits. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Medical Records Company Announces Spreeof Deals
body: The Healtheon Corporation, a rapidly growing Silicon Valley start-up with big ideas for changing the health care system, said yesterday that it would buy WebMD Inc., a seven-month-old Internet company, in a stock deal valued at $7.85 billion. Healtheon is also allying itself with some of technology's best-known names, selling $250 million of its high-flying stock to the Microsoft Corporation and $110 million to other backers including the Intel Corporation and Excite Inc., the Internet portal company. Microsoft, which will have a stake of more than 10 percent in the combined company, Healtheon/WebMD, also pledged $100 million in advertising, which would be added to $40 million already committed for advertising by the DuPont Company. It is Microsoft's first big foray into Internet health care. The new company said it would also have promotional and other tie-ins with an array of media companies including CNN, MSNBC and the Westwood One radio chain and Internet companies like MSN and Lycos. Healtheon, which went public at $8 a share in February, reached a high of $114 yesterday before closing at $100.625, up $20.375. When it comes to buying other companies, "their stock is free money," said Linda Killian, a portfolio manager with the Renaissance IPO Fund. Although they have relatively few customers, and no profits, a common Internet predicament, Healtheon and WebMD have sweeping aspirations. Healtheon, which has been growing through acquisitions, offers electronic processing of health care claims and on-line registration for health plans. It also links doctors over the Internet with hospitals, pharmacies, laboratories and insurance companies. WebMD, a privately held company based in Atlanta, specializes in Internet support groups in which consumers can learn about health care subjects like nutrition and cancer, as well as physicians' services. Together, the companies hope to sell electronic products to hundreds of thousands of doctors whom they covet as gatekeepers to $800 million in annual health care spending. The doctors could also become a lucrative audience for drug company advertising and other medical marketers. The ultimate goal would be to link all types of customers and providers of health care, using the Internet as an end run around the many obstacles to communication between thousands of computer systems. "We want to bring the advantages of the Internet to health care, an industry that has been slow to adopt new technology," said James H. Clark, the co-founder of Netscape who also co-founded Healtheon in 1996 in Santa Clara, Calif. But for just that reason, some analysts questioned whether Healtheon and WebMD could ever herd thousands of notoriously independent-minded doctors into its system. "Health care is such a cottage industry and it is so hard to link all the doctors," said James Hudak, a managing partner of Andersen Consulting. "Health is fundamentally different than securities trading or auctioning on the Internet, like Ebay," he added. "Health is not a commodity." As for quality and accuracy, he said, "you have to know, is the information you are getting correct or is it coming from some cyberquack?" Privacy of medical records of patients is another sensitive issue. Jeffrey Arnold, chief executive of WebMD, said that personal information about consumers would not be sold without their consent. The WebMD Web site says that data about consumers will be sold only in broad aggregate form, for example as percentages. W. Michael Long, chief executive of Healtheon, said the company ruled out selling personal data to pharmaceutical companies or anybody else. As for protecting the data from unauthorized intruders, Mr. Long said that "security of the data has been a prime focus of our engineering over the last three years," from encryption into secure codes to storage on data bases. "We have been a market leader in demonstrating that the Internet can be as secure an environment as any," he said. Mr. Arnold of WebMD declined to disclose his company's finances. He changed the subject to $500 million in commitments, including an additional $150 million from Microsoft, which he said had been promised by companies that would subsidize doctors who would be recruited to use the company's Web sites. That $500 million would provide free introductory access to 180,000 doctors for five years. There are 5,000 doctors now using the system and 49,000 more whose fees have already been paid by sponsoring organizations like health systems. Healtheon/WebMD hopes to have positive cash flow by the end of next year. But before it can make a profit, it faces several years of charging off good will that it acquired in its chain of mergers and acquisitions. Healtheon and Mede America, another merger in process, have combined annual cash flow of about $130 million. Healtheon processes electronic claims for the United Healthcare Corporation, which has an 11 percent ownership stake in Healtheon through a business developed by United and later acquired by Healtheon. The Cigna Corporation also buys claims processing services. Healtheon also provides on-line enrollment services for a few thousand members of health plans served by Blue Shield of California. And Healtheon processes lab test orders for SmithKline Beecham Clinical laboratories, which is being purchased by Quest Diagnostics Inc. In the merger, 1.815 Healtheon shares will be exchanged for each WebMD share, so that existing shareholders of each company will have about 50 percent of the new company.    http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
MTV Is Buying TwoServices From TCI Music
body: Just weeks before it is to unveil a new on-line music venture, MTV Networks announced yesterday that it was acquiring music services on the Internet and on cable television. MTV, a division of Viacom, will acquire Sonicnet, one of the first Internet sites dedicated to music, and the Box, a pay-per-view cable television music service. In exchange, MTV will give a 10 percent stake in its on-line service to the owner of the two properties, TCI Music, a company based in newyork that provides audio and video music through cable, satellite and the Internet. Tom Freston, chairman of MTV Networks, said the on-line music division would be spun off as a separate publicly traded company in the next 9 to 15 months. TCI Music, a division of Liberty Media Group of Englewood, Colo., also announced that it would change its name to Liberty Digital. Liberty Media, a cable television programming distributor, is part of the huge cable company TCI, which was bought by the AT&T Corporation, although Liberty Media continues to operate independently. In a phone interview, Mr. Freston called the on-line music business "ripe for consolidation" as the major music labels seek ways to distribute music on the Internet. On-line commerce will be an important piece of MTV Networks' new on-line music venture, which is to be started next month. In addition, Mr. Freston said there were plans to create an interactive television channel selling tickets, music and other merchandise. "Our strategy is anyone who can drive traffic is going to be in a position to sell a lot of merchandise, a lot of tickets," he said. MTV's flagship music channel is available on television in 300 million homes around the world, and Mr. Freston said an expanded on-line presence was a logical next step. He spoke by telephone from Singapore, where MTV will start a Web site for the Asian market today. Industry analysts said traditional media companies were realizing the power television has to send viewers to the on-line medium, as well as the power of the Internet to extend what they can offer viewers in the finite time permitted by television. "On line can support strategies in ways broadcast can't," said Mark Hardie, a senior analyst for Forrester Research of Cambridge, Mass. "You don't have the air time for all you're trying to air." An on-line presence allows television programmers to direct viewers to their computers for additional services, particularly electronic commerce and eventually, as higher-speed connections become more widely available, music videos.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Ovitz Helps FormOn-Line Entertainment Venture
body: Michael Ovitz, the talent manager once known as the most powerful man in Hollywood, is trying to extend his reach into cyberspace. Mr. Ovitz is an investor in and co-founder of Checkout.com, a company that will offer information about entertainment and also sell compact disks, videos and games through a Web site of the same name. The other major investor, it was announced today, is the Yucaipa Companies, the group run by Ronald W. Burkle, the billionaire supermarket magnate. Last year, Mr. Burkle orchestrated the sale of Fred Meyer Inc., which he controlled, to the Kroger Company, thereby becoming the largest shareholder of the nation's largest supermarket chain. The Checkout Web site is being developed by Richard Wolpert, the head of Yucaipa's Internet ventures and also a partner in the new company. He was formerly the president of Disney Online. "I think the Internet is the greatest thing that ever happened to the entertainment industry, to the artistic community," Mr. Ovitz said, explaining that artists can now present their material directly to the public. Checkout's site, which is expected to be in operation this summer, will not immediately offer consumers the ability to download music, games or video, though that will come, Mr. Ovitz and Mr. Wolpert said. They described their site as a Web portal for entertainment. Type in a request, say, for the actor Jim Carrey, and a Web page about Mr. Carrey will be created with information about him, offers for videos of his movies and links to other sites. Mr. Ovitz and Mr. Wolpert said they would start other Internet ventures. They declined to discuss how much each partner had invested. Mr. Ovitz, the co-founder of the Creative Artists Agency, is trying to resurrect his career after being ousted from the No. 2 position at the Walt Disney Company in 1996, more than $100 million richer from a severance payment but without a position of power. Since then he has made an ill-founded investment in Livent Inc., the troubled Broadway production company, and has tried to bring a National Football League team back to Los Angeles. He also started a new talent management company, Artists Management Group, which promptly got into a bitter feud with his old agency. Mr. Ovitz said the new Internet company would not discriminate in favor of the performers he represents.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: America Online to Revise Shopping Service
body: America Online Inc. said yesterday that it would introduce a redesigned on-line shopping service this summer to capitalize on its momentum as a destination for electronic commerce among consumers. America Online, the No. 1 supplier of consumer Internet services, said its subscribers spent more than $1.8 billion shopping during the quarter that ended in March, marking the company's growing role as an E-commerce destination, and supplementing its basic Internet access service. The $1.8 billion compared with spending of $1.6 billion spent in the previous quarter, which benefited from the 1998 holiday sales season and is considered by many analysts to have marked on-line shopping's coming of age. In a bid to transform window shoppers into repeat buyers, America Online, based in Dulles, Va., said its revised service would include new personalization features that allow consumers to customize their on-line shopping at retailers operating on AOL's Internet services. The new version of its existing shopping channel will have enhanced product search tools, a faster checkout system and a merchant quality-assurance system for consumers, the company said. The new service will also offer a more sophisticated merchandising strategy for America Online's partners to drive sales of retailers' goods and services, the company said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: A World Of Choices To Plug In To the Net - Correction Appended
body: CONSIDER the Internet service provider. Depending on your on-line habits, it can be the home of your familial interactions, the envelope for your business memorandums, the conduit of your deepest desires. It can get about as much intimate use as the lenses of your glasses or the pages of a journal. It is the choice of a way to view Web pages and to send email, and as such it should not be approached without proper introspection and circumspection. Or should it? For many Internet users, new and seasoned, that choice depends on what start-up disk appears in a mailbox or cereal box on any given day, which provider an employer chooses or which program for an Internet service provider, commonly called an I.S.P., shows up on a new desktop computer. "Based on the correspondence we've received, and its emotional content, choosing an I.S.P. seems to rank somewhere between selecting a long-distance phone service and choosing a caterer for a bar mitzvah," Dr. Dawn McGatney, a Maryland pediatrician and Webmaster, said via email. Dr. McGatney runs a site called Compleat Guide to an I.S.P. You'll Enjoy Using (dogwolf.seagull .net/isp.html). "But we hear from many folks who are now on their fifth or higher I.S.P.," she added. "Once you switch one to two times, it's obviously easier. There is a bit of fear of the unknown here." Millions of people have decided they would rather switch providers than fight suboptimal service. As of January, 36.7 percent of home Internet users had changed their I.S.P.'s at some point and lived to tell about it, according to the Strategis Group, a Washington-based research company that studies patterns in telecommunications use. It's not an easy decision, but taking that step can be liberating, people who love their new Internet services say. The scope of the choice is formidable, with 4,500 Internet services available across the country. According to Forrester Research, America Online has 39.4 percent of all home accounts (with Compuserve, which AOL owns, the total is 41.9 percent); AOL's 17 million subscribers worldwide are a group larger than the combined daily circulation of the top 20 daily newspapers. Other large services, like AT&T, Earthlink, MSN and Prodigy, collectively share 15.3 percent of the market, while small I.S.P.'s -- those with less than 2 percent of the market, like Sprint, Erols and the local Bell telephone companies -- serve 41.3 percent. Internet services compete fiercely for new Internet users and for people who have been on line for years. AOL is the 800-pound gorilla in the middle of the information superhighway and the new user's magnet. Its simple-to-install software and ubiquitous distribution are the keys to its success. Andrew Shepherd, a Forrester Research analyst, said that as of January, AOL had captured 54 percent of all users who had been on line for less than six months and half of all users who had been on line for less than a year. It has also garnered its share of criticism, as have other large and small I.S.P.'s, for slow service, busy signals, the prevalence of spam and concerns about members' privacy. But Kathy McKiernan, an AOL spokeswoman, said that the company was experiencing its fastest growth and lowest turnover rate ever. Another service provider, Earthlink Network, based in Pasadena, Calif., is competing for customers by, among other things, marketing its Get Out of AOL Free plan and offering promotions like a free month of service or free setup. Earthlink can transfer Favorite Places Web sites from AOL to a new browser and will send email to everyone in a new customer's electronic address book to notify them of the change of address. Taking cues from AOL, Earthlink has created easy-to-use software that features a friendly on-screen guide, named Lisa.  "She'll say: 'Hi, welcome to Earthlink. I'll walk you through step by step. Click here,' but you can also shut her up," said a company spokeswoman, Kirsten Kappos. Other Internet providers, particularly smaller ones, win new subscribers in more personal ways. Paul Budlong of Seattle, for example, chose his small I.S.P., based in Seattle, after receiving email from someone who used it. "I liked the name," he said of Drizzle.com, and found it appropriate to local weather conditions. He switched from a provider in Portland, Ore., to Drizzle, which serves the Puget Sound region. He was frustrated by his old service's busy signals (it could take up to 20 attempts to get through) and "complete technomorons at tech support who were incapable of speaking plain English." He found the smaller local provider to be more helpful. "They email back, they call back, they explain things in simple terms, they're friendly, on the ball and very patient," said Mr. Budlong, who has an old 386 computer with software that could best be described as quaint. The support staff even downloaded a huge program for him that would have taken him hours to do on line. "I went downtown, knocked on the door, and they didn't even charge me for the disks," he said. "It was very cool." But the smaller I.S.P.'s are particularly vulnerable to mergers and acquisitions, so they are less likely to remain stable. People who find an I.S.P. they like might hesitate to rave about it because that might encourage others to join, leading to busy signals all over again. "I had a friend who wouldn't tell anybody when he'd find an I.S.P. he liked," said David Cassel, editor of the AOL Watch newsletter, which is distributed to an email list of 42,000 readers. "You really want a small service no one has ever heard about." The search for the perfect fit can be traumatic. While any other company that hung up on customers several times a day could expect a quick pink slip, an I.S.P. is harder to dump. Switching providers could mean forfeiting prepaid Internet service, spending hours rejiggering modem strings and software interfaces, losing old email messages and printing new business cards and resumes with the new email address. "The No. 1 reason that folks stick with an I.S.P. that they hate -- and they can get truly emotional on the subject -- is that they've prepaid a year or two in advance and stand to lose hundreds of dollars by leaving," Dr. McGatney said. "The trick here is always to read the I.S.P.'s terms of service before subscribing. Be sure that the I.S.P. offers a prorated refund for those who cancel early. The No. 2 reason would be the pain of notifying all your friends that you have a new email address, though many I.S.P.'s will forward your email forever at no charge." Mail sent to a closed AOL account, she said, bounces back with a note that themail could not be delivered. Jason Catlett, president of the Junkbusters Corporation, an on-line privacy advocacy group in Green Brook, N.J., said switching often required reconfiguring the user's computer. "That's probably a traumatic experience for many people," he said. Chris Sherman, a Web search guide at the Mining Company site, said some Internet patterns were hard to break. His parents started out with AOL and resisted a move to Mindspring, he said. "Even though Mindspring is so easy, they were comfortable with AOL," he said. "It's an inertia issue more than a branding issue." When choosing a provider, a computer user should decide whether one goal is to get broad-bandwidth Internet access, which allows Internet connections at speeds faster than the current standard consumer maximum, 56 kilobits per second on a conventional telephone line. These faster access routes to the Internet have many advantages: they can be open as long as the computer is on, there is no waiting for dial tones, and there is little waiting for Web sites to load. Internet service through a cable TV provider, which is available in some places, can typically download one megabyte of data in less than 8 seconds, compared with digital subscriber lines, or D.S.L. lines, at 15 seconds or a fast telephone modem, operating at 56K, at two and a half minutes. (Actual speeds can vary.) Cable Internet service connects a house through cable television wires, with, in most cases, the cable company acting as the Internet provider. D.S.L. connects a computer to the Net through existing phone lines but the computer must be within limited a distance -- a few miles -- of a phone company switching center. "You can pretty much count on the fact that the larger I.S.P.'s are in heavy-duty competition to roll out high-speed access," Mr. Sherman said. "The question is just when." Cable companies can now reach only about 23 million households. Their Internet service costs about $40 per month, said David Eiswert at the Strategis Group. D.S.L. lines are available to about six million households for about $50 a month, compared with a cost of about $20 a month for traditional dial-up services. "That's in some ways going to be one of the things that allows dial-up I.S.P.'s to really fight off cable in the short term," said Mr. Shepherd, of Forrester Research.  "They're providing service at half the cost." Some people decide not to pay for any I.S.P. and rely on free Web services instead. "People can take half-steps -- get a Geocities Web page and Juno email account and access the Web through a machine at work or the local public library if they don't want dial-up service," said Mr. Cassel, of AOL Watch. Juno, Hotmail and Alta Vista mail are examples of free email services that a user can log onto from a computer at a public library or Internet cafe. Free Web pages are available at sites like Geocities and Tripod. Many Web surfers, however, want Web access from home. Some choose their I.S.P.'s based on particular needs -- a frequent traveler might want to have access to the Internet service while overseas, for example, or a biology buff might need a large space on the Web to post a special page on the naked mole rat. Other customers choose a service like AOL because it provides something like a roped-off section of the larger Internet for children. There can be advantages in switching providers. "Changing your email address periodically and auto-notifying the sender to the old address with a message is a great way to get off of every spam list in the world," Dr. McGatney said. "Each time we've moved, our junk mail dropped to zero for the next several months."  Choices and Defaults  Don Ho Entertainer (through his Internet director, Christopher Soares). "We picked a local service provider based on price, service, tech support, dial-ups and personalized service, not necessarily in that order, mind you. We were with a local company. One of the partners, whom we started with, split and formed his own I.S.P. called Maikai.net (www.maikai.net). So now we're with them. Because I know the service will remain excellent! We've found that the larger I.S.P.'s are of little or no help when they're done setting you up with a D.N.S."  Linus Torvalds Creator of the Linux operating system. "I've never had to choose; I've always gotten a free Internet connection through my work (or my studies back when I was at the university)."  Jason Catlett President of Junkbusters, an on-line privacy advocacy group. "At the time I started using ISDN, Eclipse Internet was the only I.S.P. with ISDN-capable modems in my local calling area. Now many others do, but I haven't bothered to shop around. Also, I like the fact that they're comparatively small because of the rumors that some of the big national I.S.P.'s are considering deals where they sell details of their customers' surfing activities to advertisers."  Isabel Wang Co-founder of I.S.P.-Check, which helps users find Internet service providers and Web page hosts. "I was with Bell Atlantic for a long time. They claim they support 56K, but I was always connecting at 28, and there were busy signals on weekends and evenings. I'd get kicked off every five minutes. I switched to Starpower, which is good. It was really easy. Most I.S.P.'s can set you up the same day or the same minute when they have you on the phone."  Pattiann Rogers Poet, whose ninth book, "The Dream of the Marsh Wren, Writing as Reciprocal Creation," will be out in June. "There was an article in a computer magazine that gave Mindspring a very high rating. I couldn't always make connections reliably on Compuserve so I switched to Mindspring because of its rating and because I wanted service for a Web site. I've been with Mindspring several years now and am satisfied."  Talking Points Questions to Ask Before Buying Internet Service  Whether you are finding your very first Internet service provider or looking for the perfect one after seven false starts, choosing an I.S.P. is challenging. Here are some questions to ask when shopping around:  HOW COMMITTED DO I HAVE TO BE? -- Extra points go to providers offering trial memberships. Beware of those that tie you down to years of service if you want a good rate. Find out if you can get money back if you switch later.  CAN I GET CONNECTED? -- Try dialing the phone numbers of a prospective I.S.P. during peak times and make sure you hear a modem screech (good) instead of a busy signal (very bad). Ask about the service's user-to-modem ratio, and find out if there are any guarantees about how easy it will be to connect to the Web.  WILL MY I.S.P. KEEP UP WITH TECHNOLOGY? -- Find out if your prospective provider plans to offer broad-band technology like D.S.L. for speedier access to the Internet. If you are particularly fond of playing games, shopping or trading stock on line, make sure that the service has sufficient bandwidth to accommodate those activities easily. Talk to customer service or sales representatives to see if the provider has partners for D.S.L. service in your area or plans such partnerships. Or find out whether you could continue with the provider if you got a cable Internet connection; some I.S.P.'s offer discounts for people gaining access to the Net through cable modems.  IS THE PRICE RIGHT? -- If you don't choose unlimited access, make sure you can afford the often-steep hourly rates if you exceed your monthly minimum. You should find out if the provider has hefty setup fees.  IS THERE FREE, 24-HOUR TECH SUPPORT? -- You will most likely need it. To check out customer satisfaction with a provider, talk to other people who use it. If you can't find someone off line, try searching newsgroups on line for comments from the Web world at large.  IS ACCESS AVAILABLE ON THE ROAD? -- If you need access while traveling, your provider should have a wide range of local numbers in the areas you tend to visit or offer 800 numbers. If you decide on cable or D.S.L. service, make sure that you can connect in other cities through your provider when you are limited to a phone line on the road. With Web TV, you need a box unit to get on line from the road.  WILL I HAVE PRIVACY ON THIS I.S.P.? -- You should ask if the I.S.P. will sell your name to marketers or bombard you with spam. It is also wise to find out if you can post what you want on your Web page, including commercial material, if applicable. They say that breaking up is hard to do, but there are ways to soften the separation anxiety when changing I.S.P.'s. "Don't get wedded to your I.S.P.," said Jason Catlett, president of the Junkbusters Corporation, an advocate of on-line privacy. "They should be a commodity service, and you should be able to switch easily if they raise prices or start invading your privacy." Mr. Catlett noted that email tended to tie people to their I.S.P.'s. He suggested breaking that link by using an email forwarding service (like Pobox.com, Ziplink or a college alumni group that offers lifetime email addresses). That way you can keep one email address, regardless of how many times you change providers.   TINA KELLEY http://www.nytimes.com Correction  A table in Circuits on Thursday comparing Internet service providers referred incorrectly to one service, Erol's. The RCN Corporation acquired Erol's last year and now serves Boston, Philadelphia, New Jersey, Delaware, Rhode Island, Virginia, Maryland, New Hampshire, New York and Connecticut as RCN.com; the service does not operate under the name Erol's in those areas. title: Citizens' Electronic Inquiries Get Governments' Attention
body: GOODBYE, phone-menu torment. Adios, disembodied operators taking calls in the order received. A revolution in customer service is emerging on the government pages of the Web. Those daunting Web sites containing volumes of government data, images and icons are moving beyond the standard fare of search engines, links, forms that can be downloaded and the like. Now government officials actually accept questions via email. And, more important, they send answers. Looking for information on a rare disease? The unitedstates Department of Health and Human Services (www.hhs.gov) invites inquiries through its healthfinder .gov, which the site calls "a free gateway to reliable consumer health and human services information." Wondering whether a neighbor's drainage will affect your drinking water? The Environmental Protection Agency (www.epa .gov) has two dozen librarians fielding as many as 1,500 such email questions each month, with a typical response time of fewer than five days. Tax policy questions? The Internal Revenue Service (www.irs.gov) awaits your email. What about gulf war illnesses or military base closings? The Department of Veterans Affairs (www.va.gov) and even the Pentagon, with its chock-full site at www .defenselink.mil, are churning out email replies. "Agencies are learning how to use this tool to answer questions and to provide information," said Greg Woods, an Education Department official who is chairman of the Government Information Technology Services Board, part of Vice President Al Gore's initiative on reinventing Government. With an estimated 6,000 home pages just for Federal agencies, and countless others for state and local governments, the potential for email assistance is vast. Of course, most sites have search engines that can be used to zero in on information. But for some people, search engines are not the best option -- search terms may be hard to divine, or the results may be hard to interpret. So some consumers wanting information are finding that, though it may take a day or it may take weeks, specialists from the government are, in some cases, able to give direct answers to inquiries, point out material already on their sites or refer questioners to other government resources. When Lee Bergamini's mother-in-law was moving to Connecticut from Florida, he needed to notify Federal pension officials who deposit her benefit check in her bank. Mr. Bergamini found the Federal Technology Service's site at www.usgold.gov, which is in the process of publishing on-line directories of all Federal agencies and workers. He found the email address of Jack Finley, director for electronic messaging at Federal Technology Service. Mr. Finley was able to furnish Mr. Bergamini with the Pension Benefit Guarantee Corporation's phone number and mailing and on-line addresses. Susan Glickman, a Florida political consultant, got stuck when looking for a comprehensivemailing list of state legislators. She fired off an email message to the Florida Legislature's site (www.leg.state .fl.us), which sent her precise instructions on how to find and download it. Robert Bickner of Madison, Wis., and Linda Powell of Wilmington, Del., both researching family history, sent email inquiries to the National Archives and Records Administration (www.nara.gov) and received replies telling them how to get the records they sought. The National Archives agency expects that half of its queries from the public will be by email or fax by 2007, said Jennifer Nelson, the Webmaster for the agency. Mr. Bickner, a professor at the University of Wisconsin at Madison, said: "With very little effort, I got the records I have been looking for. I was so impressed that I sent a message back and said, 'Thank you for putting this very user-friendly feeling on things.' " Ms. Powell, a bookkeeper, said: "The best part is you're not on hold for half an hour. You send it and it's done." But before everyone stampedes the government sites, there is something of a catch with the email approach: the agencies' policies are inconsistent and clearly evolving. Some agencies would rather you called their toll-free numbers, or wrote to them, or searched the Web site yourself before sending any email queries. Yes, many post an email address, but some make it a challenge to find it on their sites. For instance, the "contact information" button on the Occupational Safety and Health Administration home page (www .osha.gov) leads to a directive to use the phone, not email, to reach the agency in emergencies and to call regional offices for policy or regulatory questions. Some hunting turns up a "suggestion box" page that solicits comments or ideas but bars inquiries about policy or regulatory issues. "The ideal Web site is to answer as many questions as possible, so the last option is to send an email which requires a person to intervene and answer a question," said Rich Kellet, division director for Emerging Information Technology Policies at the General Services Administration. "email is a difficult issue because of the volume and the potential for huge volume. So agencies are still working on how to answer those issues." In another development related to government information on line, the Government's National Technical Information Service and Northern Light Technology announced a fee-based search engine for Federal Government Internet sites and documents on Monday. But the Commerce Department has had second thoughts and has decided to make the service available without a fee, at least until there is a decision on whether charging fees for cross-agency search services would conflict with the Clinton Administration's policy on unrestricted access to Government information. Still, many government agencies are independently struggling with ways to provide information and assistance for free, officials said. Henry Lai, director of General Services' Center for Emerging Technologies, which oversees the agency's site at info.gov, said his staff generally directed people to the agency's information specialists who answer a toll-free number at the Federal Information Center. "We don't encourage people to send email," Mr. Lai said. Many agencies, including the Social Security Administration (www.ssa.gov), use a "feedback" link. But Social Security's site specifies that feedback means comments about the Web site, not requests for information. The agency fields 70 million telephone calls a year on its 24-hour toll-free lines. Even so, the agency manages to respond to 55,000 email messages a year, officials say, and its newyork regional home page, for one, does invite email questions. Over at the notoriously sluggish Immigration and Naturalization Service, there is a reason why the site www.ins.usdoj.gov contains no email addresses. Greg Gagne, a spokesman for the agency, said incoming messages "would be astonishing because of the huge demand" on a site visited by 430,000 users a month. "What may seem quite simple is quite often not so simple, and it takes an extraordinary amount of work to answer," Mr. Gagne said. Even so, the agency plans to revamp its Web site and include email capability by the end of the year, he said. The welcome mat is already out at the Internal Revenue Service, where chatty language and animated cartoon figures throughout the site are chipping away at the agency's stodgy image. At www.irs.gov, the agency promises: "We'll help you cut through the clutter. Now just tell us what else you need." Its email flow has grown to a projected 300,000 questions this year from 13,000 in 1996, said Dave Medeck, national director of the telephone operations division. Two hundred revenue agents and audit staff members answer the email, handling general policy questions but not individual tax cases, Mr. Medeck said. The mere fact of a personal reply is satisfaction for some who send email queries, and actually getting solutions can be empowering. Linda Scott-Aughtry contacted a Social Security branch in Baltimore by email and was able to resolve a months-old delay in payment of her benefits. "I quit school when I was in 10th grade," Ms. Scott-Aughtry said. "I've been working ever since. For me to go into the computer and accomplish that, it really made me feel great."  The On-Line Data Trail Coming Across Agencies With Facts to Share and Pleasant Manners IT was like having a personal government staff. I needed some research on past Presidential Cabinets. I could have plowed through library books, but I knew the National Archives and Records Administration would have my answer in its millions of pages of documents. I logged on to www.nara.gov. My information wasn't there, but an email address was. I sent off my query, and 12 days later I received the precise information, complete with citations and details, in an email message that was as chipper as a happy-face sticker. This was the most gratifying use of my tax dollars since the Park Service began building bike paths. So when tax season came along, I visited the Internal Revenue Service on line (www.irs.gov). My email query requested the agency's standard for reimbursable mileage costs, and back came the reply: 31 cents per mile. It was a softball, but I was still impressed that I got a reply in less than two days. Perhaps most impressive was my on-line encounter with the California Environmental Protection Agency (www .calepa.ca.gov). I wanted to know whether the air quality was improving in parts of my home state. The agency replied to my query in three days, stating that my message had been forwarded to the Air Resources Board. The same day, the ombudsman's office of the Air Resources Board came through with several Web addresses for air quality information. The specialist who wrote to me, Jon Pederson, also offered to mail an article on "clean air pockets" from The Los Angeles Times. The article arrived a few days later. Another delightful experience. But at some point, even email information seekers must do a little work. Asking the Census Bureau (www.census .gov) for specific economic information a while back brought an email response a month later listing several Census reports that I could order for $10 to $150 apiece. Then I'd have to search the pages myself for my data. I passed on the offer. RITA BEAMISH http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Robert Bickner received on-line help in genealogy research, and Linda Scott-Aughtry resolved a delay in Social Security benefits. (Andy Manis for The newyork Times; Sal DiMarco Jr. for The newyork Times)

title: Election Panel May Yield on Internet Giving
body: Responding to burgeoning political activity on the Internet, the Federal Election Commission is expected on Thursday to bring Presidential fund-raising into the age of electronic commerce. The commission is very likely to change its rules to allow political contributions by credit card to qualify for Federal matching campaign funds, two commission members said in interviews. Most of the Presidential contenders in 2000 have their own Web sites, and many are using the Internet to solicit campaign contributions paid by credit card. But so far, the commission has allowed matching money only for donations by check or other "written instruments" because of concerns over fraud. In March, the Democratic candidate Bill Bradley asked the commission to expand the matching funds, which come from checkoffs on taxpayers' returns, to on-line credit card contributions. In a letter to the commission, Robert Bauer, the Bradley campaign's general counsel, argued that on-line donations "broaden the base of financial support for Presidential campaigns and encourage renewed public confidence in American democracy." The Bradley campaign started its Web site on Dec. 4 and a campaign spokesman said it had received $30,000 in on-line pledges and had enlisted nearly 15,000 volunteers. The campaign has hired its own Internet consultant, Lynn Reed. The first $250 of each individual contribution to Presidential candidates is matched with taxpayers' money as long as candidates adhere to the Federal spending limits. In 2000, candidates who abide by the spending ceiling of about $40 million in the primary will be eligible for up to $16.8 million in matching Federal money. Some commission officials have been concerned that credit card donations do not have the same level of documentation or security as checks, the two commissioners said, but these reservations gave way to a desire to encourage Internet political activity. "Generally speaking, I don't think we ought to put barriers in the way of the use of the Internet for political contributions unless there's a compelling reason to do so," said David Mason, a Republican who serves on the six-member commission, which is evenly divided along party lines. Karl Sandstrom, a Democratic commissioner, said "advances in technology" had made on-line credit-card transactions secure enough to satisfy the agency's concerns. The expected approval of matching funds for on-line credit card donations is being watched by the Presidential candidates. "2000 will be a groundbreaking year for Internet campaigning," said Juleanna Glover, press secretary for Steve Forbes, a Republican candidate. "The Internet will be to the 2000 election what television was to the Nixon-Kennedy election." Ms. Glover said the Forbes campaign, which has had more than 400,000 visitors to its Web site, had relied heavily on the Internet to recruit volunteers and for small donations. Mr. Forbes does not plan to apply for Federal matching funds so he will not be affected by the commission's decision. The commission plans to review an array of Internet issues, the two commissioners said, but decided to act first on the matching-funds question because of the greater urgency. Other areas under review are how and whether to value as political contributions the Web sites operated by individuals that carry a candidate's messages and Web links that connect voters from one Web site to a candidate's site. Mr. Bauer said it would be impractical for the commission to try to broadly police the Internet. "It's the frontier, the political equivalent of the Wild West," he said. "The commission ought to stand back and learn a little more about what this medium looks like before it begins to introduce new restrictions and create broad policies." Most campaigns update their Web sites daily and include video snippets and text of the candidates' speeches and other political news. Elizabeth Dole's site also offers revolving snapshots, including one from her wedding day, as well as a memorial to Leader, the Dole dog who died on Feb. 28. The Dole campaign says it has enlisted over 5,000 volunteers on its Web site and taken in over $50,000 in pledges. Other candidates are also raising money on the Web, although it is still a small fraction of their fund-raising over all. The Gore campaign, which has raised more than $9 million, has drawn $17,000 in on-line pledges. http://www.nytimes.com

title: New Palm Pilot Links to Internet Wirelessly
body: Untethering the Internet from desktop computers, the 3Com Corporation intends on Monday to introduce the first version of its popular Palm Pilot hand-held computer that can tap into cyberspace using wireless links. The introduction of the unit, the Palm VII, could become a milestone in the evolution of the Internet, allowing users to link easily from cars or beaches. Though the Microsoft Corporation, Psion of Britain and other companies are trying to develop software to link wireless phones to the World Wide Web, the Palm Pilot has already come to dominate the hand-held computer market in the unitedstates and enjoys a passionately loyal base of customers. The introduction of the Palm VII will also bolster aspirations by the BellSouth Corporation to remain at the forefront of wireless communications. The Palm VII uses BellSouth's wireless data network, which covers most big cities in the nation. Though the new Palm Pilot does not provide phone calls, some communications analysts and executives believe that will not prove a huge hindrance. Most wireless phones that include data services do not allow the user to talk and gain access to the Internet at the same time, because the screen is pressed against the user's cheek during a phone call. 3Com intends to make the new product, which will have a list price of $599, available first in newyork, New Jersey and Connecticut. But people who buy the Palm VII in those areas will be able to use it around the nation. "There is now a seamless network," said Janet Boudris, senior vice president for strategic marketing for BellSouth's wireless data unit. "So if you get on a plane in newyork and get off in L.A., the service will work seamlessly." The Palm VII uses a technology known as Web clipping, which reformats Web pages to fit the Palm Pilot's screen. Among the operations that have signed up to provide content to the new units are Espn.com, for sports scores and information; Moviefone.com, film schedules and reservations; United Parcel Service, package tracking, and E-Trade, stock quotes. 3Com initially wants to charge $9.99 a month for a basic package of services, though a full complement could increase that to $24.99 a month or higher. Different price plans would also include different numbers of wireless transactions. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
A Consultant Reports a Flaw In Ebay's Web Site Security
body: Nothing lasts for long on Ebay, the popular on-line auction house, except, apparently, potential security flaws. Tom Cervenka, a consultant in Edmonton, Alberta, recently found a bug that can redirect personal information -- including passwords -- from the Ebay site (www.ebay.com) to his own computer. But the company has not remedied the security gap. Mr. Cervenka found that by inserting bits of the programming language Javascript into a description of an item for auction, he could surreptitiously get the screen name and Ebay password for the bidders on that item. "When I saw the site, I just decided to try a couple things that are common, wide-open, potential security holes, and I was surprised that everything I tried seemed to work," said Mr. Cervenka, a member of Because We Can (www.because-we-can.com), an informal organization of people with an interest in security. With an Ebay screen name and password, an intruder could place unauthorized bids and start bogus auctions while impersonating an unsuspecting victim. Similar security problems could exist with on-line email systems and chat sites, Mr. Cervenka said, where the user has the ability to modify a Web site. When Mr. Cervenka sent Ebay email about the security problem, he said he received only a form letter in return. "We are certainly aware of the fact that if you use the Javascript, that what he described can indeed occur," said Kevin Pursglove, a spokesman for Ebay. He also said that the company intended to continue allowing the use of Javascript because many people use it to enhance graphics in their descriptions of auction items. Referring to Mr. Cervenka, he said, "We do know that if someone uses the script the way the gentleman suggests, and there were any intrusion to an account, we have the ability to identify the violator of that within an hour's time and move promptly to suspend them from Ebay." No such suspensions have occurred, he said, adding that bidders' credit-card information remains inaccessible.   TINA KELLEY http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Got a Computer? Help Find E.T.'s Home by Calling From Yours
body: There's something irresistible about the idea that anyone with a PC and a connection to the Internet could discover evidence of extraterrestrial intelligence. The SETI@home program, run by the University of California at Berkeley, is part of a worldwide effort known as Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence, or SETI. SETI@home collects and analyzes data from the giant 1,000-foot-diameter radio telescope at the Arecibo Ionospheric Observatory in Puerto Rico. Earlier this week, the project's Web site (setiathome.ssl.berkeley.edu) began distributing software that will enable home-computer users to help the scientists crunch their numbers. The site was quickly overloaded with requests. So far, the number of downloads has risen to 200,000. "Conservatively the total number of users will be half a million," said David Anderson, a computer scientist and director of SETI@home. When SETI scientists around the country lost their Congressional financing in 1993, they were forced to seek new sources for the tremendous amount of computing power required to analyze data taken from the sky. In 1996, David Gedye, a former Berkeley computer science student, had the idea of giving hundreds of thousands of Internet users a discrete piece of the sky to analyze on their PC's. The result is a giant experiment in distributed computing. "We've been using a whole bank of computers at night but had never thought about harnessing the power of the Internet," said Dan Werthimer, the project scientist and a research physicist at the Space Sciences Laboratory at Berkeley. The software functions as a screen saver, analyzing the data only when the computer is idle. Once the chunk of data has been analyzed, a process that could take several days, it is returned to Berkeley in exchange for another slice of the sky. And, said Mr. Werthimer, if your screen saver finds alien life, "of course you'll become quite famous." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: SETI@home can use your computer to find space aliens.

title:
Q & A;
Clearing Your Computer's Deck
body: Q. I've been trying to run Scan Disk on my C drive, but this message appears: "Scan disk has restarted 10 times because Windows or another program has been writing to this drive. Quitting some running programs may enable Scan Disk to finish sooner." I have no other programs running and have even disabled the virus scan. What's wrong?  A. There are a few troubleshooting things to try when you get this particular message in Windows 95 or 98. First, press Control, Alt and Delete simultaneously to call up the Close Program dialog box. If there are any programs on the list except for Explorer and Systray, close them with the End Task button; do not close Explorer and Systray. And make sure your screen saver is set to None. To do this, right-click on the desktop area and select Properties from the menu. Click on the Screen Saver tab, pick None from the pop-up list and click OK. Try running Scan Disk again. If you still get the error message, restart the computer in Safe Mode to disable temporarily any device drivers that might be interfering. If you're using Windows 95, press the F8 key when you see the "Starting Windows 95" message and pick Safe Mode from the menu. If you use Windows 98, hold down the Control key as the machine reboots and pick Safe Mode from the Startup menu. If Scan Disk still won't run after that, restart the computer in MS-DOS mode from the Shut Down menu. At the DOS prompt line, type scandisk and press Enter.  Q. How much Web server space does an average person need to make a Web site?  A. That depends on what the person wants to put on that Web site. Web pages consist of files stored on a Web server. If the site is to consist of just a few pages of text and small images, for a personal family history page or a home-business advertisement, for example, you could probably get by with just a few megabytes of storage space. Many Internet service providers offer their users about two megabytes or more of free space on their servers for personal Web pages. You usually won't get your own domain name for the site with a basic setup through your I.S.P. If you have grand designs for a site with all the latest technology, like video and audio clips, animation, tons of images and interactive material, you'll need more server space to accommodate the larger files. Your provider may also limit the number of hits your page can get per month. If you have bigger things in mind, you should try to rent server space from a Web host company. Most of them have pricing plans that will allow for more server space, traffic and even a domain name of your choice for your site. To search for an appropriate Web host, try looking at the Yellow Pages section of the Ultimate Web Host List (webhostlist .internetlist.com). The Directory (thedirectory.org) also offers a state-by-state list of I.S.P.'s and Web hosts. J. D. BIERSDORFER  Circuits invites questions about computer-based technology, by postal mail to Questions, Circuits, The newyork Times, 229 West 43d Street, newyork, N.Y. 10036-3959 or by email to QandA@nytimes.com. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Mobilizing on Line for Gun Control
body: PETITIONS that circulate on the Internet are an iffy proposition. Many of them, no matter how lofty the cause, smack of spam. Understandably, people often ignore them. But a citizens' advocacy group, Move On (www.moveon.org), which last year circulated an on-line petition calling for Congress to "censure President Clinton and move on," is distinguishing itself as a model for on-line plebiscites. Move On said it had gathered 500,000 electronic signatures during the Clinton impeachment last year. In an ancillary campaign called We Will Remember, the group said it had received pledges amounting to $13 million and 700,000 volunteer hours for year 2000 political campaigns. In the wake of the school shootings in Littleton, Colo., last month, Move On turned its attention to gun control. So far, the group, based in Berkeley, Calif., said its Gun Safety First campaign had gathered more than 70,000 signatures on an Internet-based petition urging Congress to "accept its proper role in regulating firearms." And last week, as the Senate debated a bill intended to reduce crime among juveniles, printouts of the petition signatures gathered so far were delivered by hand truck to the offices of the Senate majority leader, Trent Lott of Mississippi, and the minority leader, Tom Daschle of South Dakota. Move On said that more than 100,000 individual email messages had been sent, through the site, to senators across the nation. Joan Blades, a co-founder of Move On, said the group's goal was to see that legislation would "include some common-sense measures to make it more difficult for children to gain access to weapons." Ms. Blades and Wes Boyd, who helped to start Move On, are the flying toasters people. To be more precise, they founded Berkeley Systems, which created After Dark, the popular screen-saver program known for winged appliances. After selling Berkeley Systems two years ago, Ms. Blades and Mr. Boyd began developing educational software from their home in Berkeley. When talk of impeachment started in earnest last year, Ms. Blades and Mr. Boyd started the Moveon.org Web site, for $89. Whether the group will be able to duplicate the momentum it achieved with the censure initiative is uncertain. "My gut tells me it's not necessarily true that the things that bring one constituency together would sustain it on other issues," said Jonah Seiger, co-founder and principal of Mindshare Internet Campaigns, a consulting company based in Washington. "The half-million people who signed up to support the position articulated in the Move On impeachment campaign may not necessarily share the same view on gun control." Ms. Blades expressed the opposite belief. "Our intent with Moveon.org was to give voice to the majority opinion outside the Beltway that it was time to censure and return our Government's focus to important national and international issues," she said. "I think this discrepancy between what is going on inside the Beltway and public opinion outside the Beltway is the key similarity with the Gun Safety First petition." Still, just how effective any on-line political effort can be is difficult to gauge. "The effectiveness is minimal, at best, until we're able to legalize initiatives on line," said Fred Kimball, president of Kimball Petition Management, a political consulting firm in Westlake Village, Calif., referring to recent efforts in California to make on-line signatures valid in ballot initiatives. Mr. Seiger is more sanguine. "What Move On showed from the beginning is the way the Net is truly changing the political process," he said. Ms. Blades said she and Mr. Boyd were looking into other areas that might lend themselves to on-line activism, like environmental issues. "Our intention is just to allow people to become involved, become a five-minute activist if you want to," she said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Some Abandon Water Cooler For Internet Stock Trading
body: In Florida, a young dentist tracks stocks between patients, sometimes even between an X-ray and a filling. In Washington State, a freight-company manager logs on to a financial Web site for four to six hours of his workday. A designer at a California architectural firm gets so absorbed in the market that his productivity falls 25 percent. The long bull market and cascading advances in technology have combined to drive capitalism's main numbers game into the heart of the American workplace, with millions of wage earners, managers and entrepreneurs obsessing about Wall Street. Their obsession, in fact, far eclipses the speculative 1920's, when elevator operators and bootblacks were a chief source of what passed for information. "Two years ago I would have never thought I'd be into doing this," said the dentist, Norma Victores, 30, of Hialeah, Fla., who follows the market on the Internet and has bought part of her portfolio of 21 stocks and mutual funds on line. "I used to think it was just for the big-timers." While much of the early concern about workday Internet abuse focused on pornography, the lure of the stock market has overtaken it, some specialists said. The Internet is making a lot of information available to small investors that was once accessible only to professionals. "That's where employees are really wasting their time," said Jonathan Penn, an analyst at Giga Information Group, a firm that advises companies on information technology. "I'd definitely put that first," he added, ahead of sports, personal email, chat rooms and pornography. The flick-of-the-finger ease with which office workers and others can research, monitor and trade stocks -- often able to return instantly to their assigned tasks -- is a growing concern for employers. Most of the people willing to discuss the issue were self-employed or worked for small companies where Internet abuses could be dealt with amicably. Larger corporations, while acknowledging the potential for abuse, generally denied that employees were using company time to trade stocks. Some devotees in the workplace said the activity could be addictive, but most simply found it a practical method for earning extra income. So far, the Government has not been able to measure any economic effect. Michael Harper, the acting associate commissioner for productivity and technology at the Bureau of Labor Statistics, suggested that the time spent by workers on the stock market was not unlike water-cooler discussion of football or movies and might even be a partial substitute for it. "We don't know whether they would be working or doing something else" if there was less absorption in the market, Mr. Harper said. But according to Media Metrix Inc., a newyork company that meters Internet use much the way Nielsen Media Research does television, 22.8 million Americans used Web sites on company time in March.
