title:
Compressed Data;
Lessons in Not Blocking The Ads That Feed You
body: Real Networks is trying to dodge a bullet, one that is headed straight for its own foot. The software company, which is based in Seattle, produces so-called streaming media technology that can be downloaded free from the Web and enables personal computers to receive live audio and video feeds on the Web. But Real Networks has also been selling another company's program, called At Guard, that enables PC users to block out Internet advertising. And that doesn't sit well with Real Networks' paying customers -- operators of Web sites that employ Real Networks technology and that in many cases depend on advertising for their revenue. After Real Networks sent email a few weeks ago to tens of thousands of people offering At Guard for half the usual $29.99 price, some Web developers fired off email of their own to Real Networks and engaged in heated debates on industry bulletin boards. Some have threatened boycotts or even defections to other brands of streaming media, like Apple's or Microsoft's. Real Networks got the message. Last week, the company decided it would stop selling At Guard altogether after June 15, Steve Haworth, a spokesman, said. Ad-blocking software like At Guard is intended to speed Web viewing by stopping graphics-laden ads from downloading to a user's PC. But many of Real Network's customers contend that widespread use of ad-blocking software could seriously hurt their industry. Web viewers need to accept advertising if they want free programming, said Scott Mathias, managing editor at ITVWorld.com, a producer of on-line programming. "If ad blocking is freely available," he said, "how will everyone's needs be met?" Although ad-blocking software has been available for several years, it has been slow to catch on. But Anne Marshall, a product marketing manager at WRQ, the Indianapolis company that produces At Guard, said the Real Networks promotion had been generating strong sales for her company. Ms. Marshall said that regardless of what Real Networks had decided, At Guard is a product that "puts choice back in the hands of Internet users."   LAURIE J. FLYNN http://www.nytimes.com

title:
E-Commerce Report;
An idea that seems to benefit almost everyone is catching more interest: bill delivery and payment in cyberspace.
body: SEEING opportunity in every crevice of the economy, a growing number of Internet commerce companies now want to serve as the bearers of bad news -- in this case, delivering bills on line. And the idea seems to be catching on, with some of the nation's biggest billers adopting on-line systems and one of the Internet's most popular Web sites expected to offer similar billing services by the end of the summer. The plan is simple. A company sends email to customers, notifying them to check a Web site for new bills. Or, alternately, customers simply know to check the site at regular intervals. In either case, the billing agent charges merchants a small fee while allowing them to save the $3 or so that it typically costs to print and mail a paper bill. Customers pay their bills on line without incurring postage or check-processing fees. And banks save on processing costs, because there is no paper to push. One key to the success of this approach, analysts and executives say, is to aggregate the billers on a single site to make bill delivery and payment as quick and painless as possible for consumers. Unless enough large billers are willing to move to on-line billing, though, the practice appears to have little chance of proliferating. Among the companies competing to bring more billers on line are the Checkfree Corporation, the industry leader so far, and Transpoint, a joint venture of Microsoft, First Data and Citigroup. As billing agents, Checkfree and Transpoint work with companies like BellSouth and Consolidated Edison to deliver their bills on line and with banks to work out the on-line payment process. Transpoint and Checkfree are racing to create partnerships with the biggest billers, such as electric utilities, credit card companies and mortgage lenders. Checkfree's early lead in the field comes in part from its having started sooner, in early 1997; the company says it has signed up many of the nation's top billers, including GTE, Chase Credit Card and MCI Worldcom. Both Checkfree and Transpoint are also signing partnerships with banks, so that a customer can visit his or her own bank's Web site and view and pay the bills of every company signed up by either billing agent. Since banks have offered various types of proprietary on-line bill-payment services for years, consumers can be expected to gravitate first toward bank Web sites to view and pay their bills. But stiff competition for the banks is on the way from portal Web sites, the gateways to the Internet that are visited by millions of Internet users each month. Though no portal deals have been made public, analysts say Checkfree and Yahoo have reached an agreement for Yahoo visitors to receive and pay the bills issued by each of Checkfree's merchant partners. (Yahoo and Checkfree declined to comment on the deal.) "This technology is unbelievably sticky," Robert Sterling, a Jupiter Communications analyst, said, using industry jargon for features that keep viewers coming back to a particular site. Customers who pay bills on one site will not only return out of habit, Mr. Sterling said, but will be reluctant to learn another site's system. With tens of billions of bills mailed in the unitedstates each year, at least millions of repeat site visits could be at stake. "This is potentially a King Midas technology," Mr. Sterling said. But if on-line bill delivery can save customers time, save merchants and banks money and provide Web sites with guaranteed visitors, why are fewer than 1 percent of the nation's merchants offering the service? "It's a chicken-or-egg problem," said Lewis Levin, chief executive of Transpoint. "Billers have been saying that they'd do something like this if there were billions of customers who were dying to get their bills on the Internet. Customers say they'd love to get their bills on the Internet if only billers would deliver them. I think the billers have finally realized they're the chickens and they have to invest in order to get this started." The investment, however, is significant. It costs an average of $150,000 to build a Web site with the technology to present bills to customers and accept payments on line, executives from Transpoint and Checkfree said. Both companies provide the software that enables consumers to view and pay their bills on line, and they charge merchants roughly the price of a stamp for each bill processed. For AT&T, one of the nation's biggest billers, such an investment was well worth the price, said Daniel H. Schulman, executive vice president for consumer markets. AT&T introduced its on-line billing service in March 1998, using a system designed in- house, Mr. Schulman said. Hoping to gain broader exposure for this service, AT&T is now negotiating to have its bills offered through Checkfree, too. Mr. Schulman said the company had been aggressively promoting the service. He would not disclose the number of customers using the system, "but we do well over a couple hundred million dollars in electronic billing per year," which he said could save up to 60 percent of the cost of paper bills. The system, at www.att.com, also enables customers to apply on line for on-the-spot credit for disputed long-distance charges and to learn about special pricing plans. "We could see if someone is making a slew of international calls," Mr. Schulman said, "and we could offer them a plan for that when they're paying at our site." Among other things, the on-line billing service makes it easier for customers to obtain a wealth of information about their accounts -- such as the name of each person called rather than just the phone number. In addition, customers who set up an on-line billing account receive a discounted long-distance rate of 9 cents a minute, with no monthly fee, as compared with 10 cents a minute and a $4.95 monthly fee for AT&T's "One Rate Plus" calling plan. Banks are also offering incentives for consumers to pay their bills on line. The Union Bank of California, for example, offers free banking and checking for a year when customers join its on-line program. Analysts and executives say that creating such consumer inducements is crucial to the success of on-line bill delivery. "Billers save money, but there aren't really enough incentives yet for consumers," said Ullas Naik, senior vice president for research at FAC Equities/First Albany, an investment banking firm. "Only when they offer those incentives will we see a broad-based migration." Mr. Naik suggested one such incentive: "Take a buck off each bill if you receive and pay it on line. That could save you $10 a month." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title: Real Networks Plans Deal for Internet Search
body: In a deal that will aim advertising at the growing millions who listen to music and watch video on the Internet, Real Networks Inc., a multimedia software maker, and Snap.com, an Internet hub, plan to announce on Monday that they are starting a search engine that will find content on the Web. The companies said the search engine would be embedded in copies of Real Player G2, a free program from Real Networks that enables people to listen to music and watch video over the Internet. Users of the Real Player program will be able to search the Internet for music, other audio or video files that can be played using the software. The catch is that when users begin the process, they will be taken to a Web site (http://real.snap.com), sponsored by both Real Networks and Snap.com, that will display advertising while the search is under way. Snap.com, an Internet portal site owned jointly by CNET and NBC, will provide the search engine technology behind the site. Real Networks says that about 60 million people have downloaded the Real Player software, but that only 30 million have the latest version, which is the Real Player G2. To use the search engine, they must download an enhancement to the G2 player. Jay J. Wampold, a spokesman for Real Networks, said he expected huge traffic for the search engine. "The uptake on this will be very quick," he said. The announcement comes a week after NBC Internet and Snap.com announced that they would team with Xoom.com, a direct-marketing company, to start a publicly traded company called NBCi. That deal is unrelated to the one involving Real Networks, which is not taking part in the NBCi project, the companies said. As part of the search engine announcement, Real Networks said it would provide the new site with its Real Guide directory service, which provides links to sites with real audio and video programming. Some 400,000 Web pages have such programming, with 85 percent of them featuring content in a format that can be listened to or viewed using Real Player; other competing formats include ASF from Microsoft. Snap and Real Networks said that they were also planning to start a multimedia search site for people who have high-speed access to the Internet. The site (http://speed.snap.com) will include richer graphics and the ability to download audio and video at faster speeds. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Start-Up Leads Phone Cause in Battle for Internet Access
body: Michael W. Malaga, chairman of Northpoint Communications Group Inc., stood at a whiteboard in his office here and explained how his newly public company planned to change the Internet business. Northpoint builds high-speed data networks using normal phone lines -- an approach that could render the networks of most current Internet service providers obsolete. He drew a box on his improvised map of the Bay area. "So I.S.P.'s have these big modems pools in every city," Mr. Malaga said, referring to the conventional Internet service providers, "and these access points for dedicated services like T-1 lines," he continued, drawing another box. "And then they aggregate the traffic somewhere else to transport to another city," he added, drawing a third box and connecting them all with lines. After pausing, the 34-year-old executive erased the entire schematic with three swift strokes. "In the future," he said, "they won't have to do any of this. We will allow I.S.P.'s to become sales and marketing companies." The question is whether by "allow" he really means "force." Although it had revenue last year of only about $1 million, Northpoint, which raised $360 million in an initial public stock offering on Nasdaq on May 5, now has a stock market value of about $5 billion. The company is perhaps the most advanced of a small cadre of aggressive new players that are building high-speed Internet networks based on a technology called digital subscriber line, or D.S.L. It is a technology that, if widely embraced by computer users, could do away with the dial-up modem access offered by the leading Internet service providers, like the network-access portion of America Online's business or Internet access provided by companies like Mindspring Enterprises. Indeed, D.S.L. is shaping up as the telephone network's main weapon against the cable television industry's mounting campaign to offer high-speed Internet access. That is why the Baby Bell local telephone companies themselves are taking a hard look at D.S.L. But so far, the smaller and nimbler D.S.L. upstarts like Northpoint are the ones having more success turning the technical concept into commercial reality. As it turns out, if the Internet service providers really are fated to obsolescence, they may be planting the seeds of their own destruction: for those companies are Northpoint's main customers. Northpoint uses advanced D.S.L. technology from Copper Mountain Networks Inc., which itself went public on Thursday, raising $84 million and achieving a stock market value of $1.5 billion. The technology, which combines software and hardware, enables Northpoint to build networks that can deliver up to 1.5 million bits of information a second -- or about 30 times as much Internet data over a normal phone line as is possible with a conventional 56,000-bit-a-second modem. Rather than sell the use of those lines directly to customers, Northpoint strikes deals with Internet service providers to use its systems to resell the high-speed data service to small and medium-sized business users and residential consumers. Until now, computer users seeking high-speed access through the telephone network have typically used a special kind of circuit called a T-1 line. T-1 can deliver 1.5 million bits of information a second, but it might cost the user $800 or more a month. A comparable system based on Northpoint's D.S.L. network might cost the user as little as $350. As a result, an Internet service provider can resell Northpoint's D.S.L. lines more economically than providing its own T-1 lines or leasing such lines from a telephone company. But the fundamental rules of communications economics mean that the success of Northpoint and its initial D.S.L. competitors, Covad Communications Group Inc. and Rhythms Netconnections Inc., may very well spell the end of broad profitability for traditional Internet providers. But Northpoint cannot afford to be greedily gleeful about this prospect. For if the Baby Bell local phone titans also expand into D.S.L., those same economic rules could endanger the long-term success of Northpoint and the other D.S.L. upstarts. An essential economic characteristic of the communications industry is that communications networks cost a lot to build but, once built, relatively little to operate. While it may cost billions to build a fiber optic link from newyork to Los Angeles, for instance, it costs only pennies, if that, to transmit a call using that network. As a result, the companies that control the assets -- the optical fiber, the switches, the advanced gear for transmitting data from one point to another -- control the pricing for communications services. These companies also reap most of the profits. It is very difficult to generate long-term success in the communications business by leasing communications capacity from others. The quest to control physical communications assets, and thus to control one's own costs and increase profitability, is the basic rationale behind many of the billion-dollar deals that have become so routine in the telecommunicatons business. And that is why Northpoint's business model may look so attractive to investors but also so potentially dangerous for Internet providers. For everyday Internet providers, squeezed between America Online's marketing juggernaut in the consumer market and the power of international giants in the big-business segment, Northpoint offers a compelling proposition. Northpoint can build the D.S.L. network, operate it and maintain it. That frees Internet providers to concentrate on finding customers, operating email and World Wide Web server computers, selling the service at a markup and answering the phone when something goes wrong. By using Northpoint, even the smallest Internet provider gets access to a high-speed data system more advanced than just about anything America Online is using -- and competitive with the cable modems that are beginning to sprout around the nation. But in one sense a deal with Northpoint is a Faustian bargain. The sacrifice is profit margin, because Northpoint controls the asset. An example illustrates the case: Northpoint generally sells a 160-kilobit line to an Internet provider for $75 a month. Flashcom, which is based in Westminster, Calif., and is one of Northpoint's biggest customers, sells that same line to end users for $79.95 a month. With discounts for buying in bulk, Flashcom is probably paying less than $75 -- but not much less. Because Northpoint controls the asset, Northpoint controls most of the profits. AT&T is pursuing much the same strategy, but using cable television systems, rather than traditional phone lines. When America Online and other Internet providers complain that AT&T will not have to offer the use of its cable systems to other Internet providers, what they really fear is the prospect that AT&T will sell access to those systems at prices that keep the bulk of the profits for itself. For Northpoint, the potential pitfall in its business plan is that the very economic forces that could let it absorb most of the profits from traditional Internet providers could eventually undermine its own profitability. Northpoint, after all, has to lease the actual copper phone lines to its customers from the Baby Bell phone giants (though at rates that are highly regulated). The company connects to those circuits by installing its own network equipment inside the Bell companies' central switching offices. And Northpoint buys this equipment from Copper Mountain and hires Lucent Technologies Inc. to actually install it. Moreover, Northpoint deals with the end-user customers only through its I.S.P. resellers. Given all this, what -- if anything -- is Northpoint's long-term asset? "The asset is really in the co-location," Mr. Malaga said, referring to the deals Northpoint has struck to place equipment inside the Bells' central offices. Indeed, Northpoint has hundreds of such deals, each of which can take months to negotiate. That has given Northpoint a head start on many of its potential rivals. But in the long run, the Bells are compelled by regulation to offer co-location to just about any company that asks for it. What that means is that Northpoint might well end up being more valuable as an acquisition target for a bigger company -- a Bell, say -- looking to make a quick D.S.L. splash. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Michael W. Malaga, chairman of Northpoint Communications Group, a San Francisco-based company that builds high-speed Internet networks. (Darcy Padilla for The newyork Times)(pg. C4)

title: Trying to Move On-Line Radio Beyond a Niche
body: Until recently, it might have been fair to enlist the cliche "those crazy kids" to describe people who listened to radio on the Internet. But a series of announcements last week signals that the demographic profile of on-line listeners is expanding beyond 20-somethings to include the corporate set. Last Monday, Yahoo started a Web radio service called Yahoo Radio (http://radio.yahoo.com/), comprising 10 audio channels that visitors can listen to using software called the Realplayer G2 from Real Networks. The audio programming for Yahoo's service is provided by Spinner.com, a San Francisco company that announced plans last week to go public in September. Separately last week, Looksmart, another search engine, announced plans to produce an on-line talk show devoted to Internet topics. Behind the scenes, these deals underscore the growth of a multilayered industry with players convinced that the PC will be the radio tuner for the next generation. The entrepreneurs driving the convergence of radio and the Internet say that listeners will flock to specialized audio programming delivered over the PC, sponsored by advertising aimed at individual listeners. But the emergence of the technology poses a question for the industry: Is the business proposition sound, or is it more white noise about the Internet? Spinner.com illustrates one example of the type of business model these companies are relying upon. The company, founded in 1996 as TheDJ.com, offers 175,000 songs on 120 channels; the fare includes punk, funk, gospel, gumbo, surf and swing. Visitors to the site download a player called Spinner Plus, which enables them to listen to the channels. Like traditional radio stations, Spinner.com and its competitors license the songs at a per-play fee from music industry groups like the American Society of Composers, Artists and Performers. Spinner.com makes its money by several means: displaying banner ads on the site; embedding audio commercials within the programming -- 90 seconds each hour -- and by taking a cut of transactions when visitors buy music at the site. The company also displays banner ads on the audio player, but because listeners can minimize the image of the player, they might not see those commercials, the company acknowledges. Still, Josh M. Felser, president of Spinner.com, said that the site's traffic was growing 25 percent a month and that Spinner.com had 1.3 million unique listeners last month. People who register to use the site's audio player must divulge their sex, age and some musical interests, allowing the company to give highly targeted information to advertisers. "We do what radio does, only better," Mr. Felser said. "It's going to take time for ad buyers to wake up to our capabilities." That sentiment and the Spinner.com business model are copied by several competitors, including Rolling Stone Radio, a partnership between the on-line music hub Tunes.com and Real Networks. Another competitor, Imagine Radio, which was acquired in February by the MTV Networks unit of Viacom, creates individually customized radio stations. Visitors to the site can choose the genre of music they want to hear and indicate which artists they would like to hear more or less often. These Internet companies are vying for consumer attention with some 1,600 traditional radio stations that have made their programming available over the Internet. Greg Verdino, vice president of Arbitron New Media, which studies radio listening patterns, said more than 3,500 radio stations were still not on line. But he said they had better start thinking about it, citing studies showing that people who listen to radio on the Net listen to less radio on traditional stations. "It's potentially" a threat, he said. "It's also potentially an opportunity." A study released in April by Arbitron New Media found the portion of Internet users who had listened to radio on line more than doubled in the previous six months to 13 percent from 6 percent. "It's going to be huge," said Rotem Perelmuter, former chief executive of Imagine Radio and now vice president for strategy at MTV, referring to on-line-only radio content. "The operating profits from radio are $6 billion," he said. "We're going to take a big chunk of that." Not everyone is so optimistic, at least in the short term. Some industry analysts say that despite the recent growth, most radio listeners will not regularly turn to their PC's for listening. Skeptics point out that the audiences even for the most popular on-line radio hubs remain in the low tens of thousands of visitors daily. "A radio advertising executive is going to look at that traffic and go, 'Come on, I can't sell advertising on that,' " said Mark Hardie, a senior analyst with Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. Mr. Hardie thinks on-line radio will remain a niche market. Patrick H. Keane, an analyst for Jupiter Communications, a market research firm in newyork, is less pessimistic. Mr. Keane said a new category of at-work radio listener was emerging. He said he thought there was a growing market for on-line audio programmers to reach into offices where employees may listen while they work. "You're definitely looking at a niche audience, but I'm firmly convinced it's going to grow," Mr. Keane said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The on-screen control panel for Spinner.com's Spinner Plus software.

title: U.S. to Offer Search Service That Links Its On-Line Sites
body: The Federal Government plans to put a World Wide Web service into operation today that is designed as a quick and easy way to find Government documents and resources on line. But the service will not be free, stirring criticism that the Clinton Administration has forgotten its promise to make the Internet and Government data more accessible to everyone. The new service, usgovsearch.com, will link together thousands of previously discrete Federal Web sites and provide cross- references for more than 3.8 million individual Government and military Web pages. For the first time, it will be possible to perform searches for topics as general as "missile technology" or "judicial branch" and compile results from any or all of the discrete data bases. The intended benefits include a new, easier way to search through the voluminous materials in the Commerce Department's National Technical Information Service, a trove that is generally considered one of the world's most valuable collections of scientific, engineering, technical and business reports. Until now, individual Federal Web sites have been freely accessible. That will not change. But people reaching and using those sites via the new search service will need to pay a $30 monthly subscription fee or $15 for a one-day pass. And those amounts do not include any additional fees -- with or without the new service -- that the Government charges for some documents. But Gary Bachula, Under Secretary of Commerce for Technology, defended the fees for use of usgovsearch.com as necessary to insure that the service pays for itself. "Govsearch is a breakthrough in the reinvention of government that Vice President Gore is continually trying to achieve," Mr. Bachula said. As to criticism that the Government is charging new fees for access to documents that already have been assembled at the taxpayers' expense, he noted that any material that is currently free on individual Web sites will continue to be so. "People still have the choice to get the information without this service," Mr. Bachula said. "But we believe a number of professionals, individuals, librarians, are going to find this to be invaluable. It helps you find what you need for a fee that's fair." Still, some public advocacy groups, who contend that even many existing fees for Government documents are too high, say that the Administration's information policy is heading in the wrong direction. "Does this mean Government is moving increasingly to a model of a pay service on the Internet for Government documents?" asked Gary Ruskin of the Congressional Accountability Project. The nonprofit group has been pushing to make court decisions and working drafts of Government documents like legislative amendments available more quickly and freely on line so that the public can be more informed about the government process. "You hear Clinton and Gore speechify until the cows come home about the Internet," Mr. Ruskin said. "But they do almost nothing to harness the Internet to serve democracy and help ordinary citizens to carry out their civic responsibility." Usgovsearch.com was developed by the Commerce Department's National Technical Information Service, or N.T.I.S., in partnership with a Cambridge, Mass., company, Northern Light Technology, which already operates a data base service that compiles 5,400 magazines, journals and news services. These Northern Light offerings will also be accessible through usgovsearch.com. James Love, director of the Consumer Project on Technology, derided the new service as "corporate welfare," calling it a "typical example of all these problems in N.T.I.S. that have never been solved by the Clinton Administration." During the Reagan Administration, the information service -- valued then and now as a crown-jewel information depository -- was revamped to become a self-financing resource. As a result, the agency charges fees for access to most of its research. Some materials are available for a nominal fee, like the "1998 Tax Products CD-ROM, IRS Publication 1796," for $13 plus a $5 handling fee. But others, like the "Davis-Bacon Wage Determination Database" are priced at thousands of dollars. In addition to reports, the agency offers resources like the World News Connection, an on-line news service that summarizes, in English, stories from local newspapers around the world and can cost $12,000 a year. "This is a wonderful national treasure," Mr. Love said of the N.T.I.S. "But who gets access? Do you think students get access to this?" Mr. Bachula, the Commerce Under Secretary, said the service was merely doing its federally mandated job and trying to make its services more valuable to those paying for them. Susan Stearns, director of enterprise marketing for Northern Light, said the new service was intended to enable individuals and others to find more easily the information they need on the Internet and in Government data bases without having to hire a professional researcher. "Traditionally, it has been very difficult to easily gain access to Government Web pages and information," Ms. Stearns said. "It's not that it doesn't exist or is completely inaccessible, but because it's difficult to locate using traditional search engines," she said, adding that Government Web pages are usually not linked to other sites on the Web. "They're kind of hanging out there on their own." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
BUSINESS: DIARY;
ComparingOld and New In Electronic Publishing
body: Exercises in valuing Internet-based businesses by traditional means can end in snapped pencils and thrown-up hands. New companies, new business models, no profits, no track record, no equivalent firm for comparison: the litany usually leads back to "it's worth whatever people will pay for it." But not every Internet company is operating in uncharted terrain. The Net stock enthusiasts who greeted its offering last week may not like being told so, but TheStreet.com is in just about the same business as Dow Jones & Company, or at least its electronic-publishing wing. Consider that each operates a financial-information Web site with original journalistic content; each site generates revenue by selling advertising and charging users a subscription fee for access to the best stuff. So, stacked up against Dow Jones and its electronic publishing operation (which also includes the Dow Jones Newswires and some other data services), how does TheStreet.com (in which The newyork Times Company owns a minority stake) compare? Here is a look. One curious lesson in these figures for potential acquirers: Taken just as an Internet play, the whole of Dow Jones is more attractively priced -- and you get The Wall Street Journal for free.   PATRICK J. title: CYBERSCOUT
body: It's no strain to arrange a demanding excursion on the Web. Just go to your search engine and type in a key word like "kayak" or "climb" and follow the trail. When I typed "backpacking" into Yahoo's travel subsection, 16 sites were listed, "kayak" brought 7, and "climb" 171. There are scores of such sites, and following are examples of what you'll find. PLANNING A HIKE www.nehikingholidays.com New England Hiking Holidays offers trips along trails of a range of difficulty; at night, you relax in an inn. Despite the service's name, the hikes are not limited to New England. There are also offerings in the American South, Southwest, Hawaii, Canada and Europe. The site is clean and easy to navigate. Among the treks offered this year are a five-day $1,065 hike ($1,125 in fall) in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, where Clare and Kurt Grabher, who operate New England Hiking Holidays, live; five days in the Shenandoahs, also $1,065, and a week on the southwest coast of Ireland (Counties Clare and Kerry), at $1,935. The prices are complete, including lodging and food, taxes and tips, although you do have to get to the place on your own. The day begins around 9 A.M., with a trip either on foot or by van to the start of the trail, and ends back in the inn in mid to late afternoon. Lunch is taken on the trail at a picturesque spot or in a pub or roadside inn.  There are two guides with the group to accommodate both people who want to stroll and those who want a strenuous hike.  RIVER ADVENTURES www.riversearch.com More than 30 whitewater outfitters from 10 countries are gathered together on Riversearch. Canoeists, rafters and kayakers point to an area on a list, click and view a map on screen; listed alongside are the names of Riversearch members who operate on that river. Most of the rivers are in North America, but a few others are in Costa Rica, Peru and Ecuador, Chile, South Africa, Australia, Fiji and China. I clicked on the Great Bend of the Yangtze River and was connected to an outfitter, Earth River in upstate newyork, that features two weeks on the Yangtze for $3,600. Whatever you click on, you ultimately find yourself at the outfitter's Web sites, some neat and some not so, with a range of offerings there.  FIRST-HAND ACCOUNT www.geocities.com/TheTropics/8168/travel.html In addition to commercial sites, you can find home pages with personal comments on the kind of activity you're researching by using the same method: type in the search term and hope for the best. I lucked into the Worldly Backpacking Page, a free home page on the Geocities service, where the proprietor, identified only as Eric, gives details and snapshots of his own travels, offers numerous tips and includes links to such related sites as youth hostels and places to make reservations. For novice backpackers there's a checklist on how to prepare for the first trip, as if you wouldn't have thought to check your finances or make an itinerary, and guides to costs. A main point of backpacking is that it is an inexpensive way to travel. How inexpensive? "I figure that it'll cost about $650 to $950 for every two weeks that you travel in Europe," Eric says, adding that the unitedstates should be "much cheaper" and Asia -- well, it's a big place and he doesn't much get into it. Geocities, like other such services, lets individuals construct their own home pages, in all their amateurish glory, for no charge, although you do have to put up with an advertisement.   L. R. SHANNON http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg

title:
INVESTING;
Putting On A Happier Profit Face
body: SHAREHOLDERS of Go2Net Inc., a network of Web sites that includes the Silicon Investor bulletin boards, the Metacrawler search service and the Haggle auction site, might have thought they were imagining things when they saw the company's most recent earnings announcement. "Go2Net Reports Profitable Second Quarter," the headline announced, while a second line touted "Pro Forma Net Income of $.07 Per Share." A profitable Internet company? Hardly. Only well into the April 21 news release would a reader find that Go2Net actually lost $52 million, or $4.07 a diluted share, in its second quarter, which ended March 31. And only after reading far, far down does one come across an astounding disclaimer about the financial statements: "They do not purport to be financial statements prepared in accordance with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles." Financial analysts and investors say they have never seen anything like what Go2Net and other Internet companies are doing: being as loose with their financial reporting as some investors are about buying the stocks. "I call them I.A.A.P. -- Inter-nut Accepted Accounting Principles," said Michael Murphy, an investor in Half Moon Bay, Calif., who specializes in technology companies and, with his Overpriced Stock Service publication, in shorting stocks, or betting that their prices will decline. "It's an attempt to go around traditional accounting standards with the hope that everyone buys into it," Mr. Murphy said. "And the investment banks that forecast earnings buy into it, because they are not going to kill the golden goose." Russell C. Horowitz, chief executive of Go2Net, said the company "is following standard protocols for reporting, both for Internet companies and for other industries." In addition, he said, "the Wall Street analysts do their models this way. In the absence of that, I think people would have an unbelievably hard time understanding what is going on under the hood." What the companies are doing is not illegal, as long as they use standard accounting in their reports to the Securities and Exchange Commission. Indeed, Wall Street has long looked differently at the financial results of cable television, cellular phone and outdoor advertising companies. Those companies, which must make huge infrastructure investments, also incur big expenses to deduct the deteriorating value of their assets from revenues. To clear the picture, analysts examine earnings before deducting those charges. Internet companies, however, rarely have those fixed investments. Their amortization charges usually are writing off high-priced acquisitions of other Internet companies. "I think that is a good way of looking at it in most cases," said Henry Blodget, who follows Internet companies at Merrill Lynch. "But in some, it is being abused." Consider Excite Inc., which operates a popular Web portal. Its news release on April 15, announcing first-quarter earnings, reported that "on a pro forma basis," the company earned a net profit of $2.5 million, or 4 cents a share. Pro forma results usually are reported to show the results of a company's continiung business, independent of some major event like a merger or divestiture. But in Excite's case, the pro forma results excluded $7.5 million of costs related to its joint marketing venture with Netscape Communications, as well as acquisition-related expenses of $2.4 million. As Excite noted in its release, on the basis of Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, or G.A.A.P., the company lost $7.4 million in the quarter, or 14 cents a share. "Basically, Excite reported earnings before marketing expenses," Mr. Blodget said. Excite declined to comment on Friday. Jack T. Ciesielski, publisher of the Analyst's Accounting Observer, an accounting research newsletter in Baltimore, put the broader issue this way: "Now companies seem to use 'pro forma' as meaning 'without the things that we don't like.' " Mr. Murphy said Cnet Inc., which operates several Internet news and entertainment sites, topped its April 21 first-quarter earnings announcement with the headline, "Proforma EPS Equals $0.09." The pro forma number excludes the expenses related to Cnet's recent acquisition of Winfiles.com -- a recurring item, because it will be stretched over several years -- and the one-time gain on a sale of stock. Doog Woodrum, chief financial officer for CNET, said, "I think we report earnings in a way that we hope provides investors with the best way to analyze our company." The pro forma numbers that some companies announce in their news releases do not show up in their reports to the S.E.C. Go2Net's most recent quarterly report did not include any mention of the 7 cents a share that the company put in the headline of its news release. "That's because the 10-Q is filed in accordance with S.E.C. guidelines, which require G.A.A.P. accounting," Mr. Horowitz said. Or, as Mr. Ciesielski, the accounting expert, noted, while regulatory filings must follow precise accounting rules, "press releases are still essentially free speech." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Ray Sherman)  Chart: "Reconciling Differences" Internet companies are trumpeting pro forma earnings, which focus on their current businesses but can ignore unpleasant accounting realities. Below are per-share returns for three companies for the quarter ended March 31.  Pro forma vs. Actual +7 cents -- -$4.07 +4 cents -- -14 cents +9 cents -- +8 cents*  *Excludes $0.53 one-time gain on the sale of an investment. (Source: Company reports)

title:
MARKET WATCH;
Big Blue, a Cup of Joe And a Little Perspective
body: EVERYBODY snickered last July when the Zapata Corporation, an obscure over-the-counter purveyor of fish byproducts, said that it was morphing into an Internet company. But when its stock more than doubled on the news, the snickerers went silent. If the gambit could propel shares of an unknown like Zapata, why not those of more established companies? Last week, the "Internet, c'est moi" strategy went big league. On Wednesday, shares in Starbucks, the trendy coffee emporium, hit a 52-week high when Scott Waltman, a Merrill Lynch analyst, reported that the company would announce an Internet strategy in June. Then, on Thursday, I.B.M.'s shares rocketed $20.50, or 9.1 percent, after the company's chairman, Louis V. Gerstner Jr., told analysts that a quarter of I.B.M.'s sales came from Internet-related businesses. So a murmur of the "I" word added $19 billion to I.B.M.'s market value and $420 million to Starbucks'. The gains proved evanescent -- I.B.M. shares lost $5.7 billion of the gain on Friday and Starbucks' value fell about $216 million by the end of the week -- but wealth was created nevertheless. Investors can be forgiven for embracing the Internet, because it is, indeed, changing the way things work. But people rushing to whatever.com are forgetting a cardinal rule of investing: Making money from world-changing events is tricky at best. Warren E. Buffett pointed this out on May 3 at Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting. In the question-and-answer period, he noted that two industries born in the 20th century had changed the course of history -- airlines and autos. But while they are wonderful businesses, Mr. Buffett said, they have proven to be lousy investments. Even as I.B.M. and Starbucks were enriching shareholders by laying claims to Internet status, news from the Web was not all upbeat. New issues of Internet stocks were mixed. A hot number was TheStreet.com (in which The newyork Times Company owns a minority stake), issued Tuesday at $19 a share. It closed the day at $60, but fell off to $46.25 on Friday. Cooler heads prevailed in two Wednesday offerings. Careerbuilder Inc., an on-line job recruiter, went public at $13 and closed the week at $14.25, up 9.6 percent from the offering. That was a modest showing for an Internet stock. And Biznessonline.com, a company that designs Web sites and offers Internet access, went public at $10, ran up to $17.875 but closed on Friday at $11.25. Last week also included the results of a Securities and Exchange Commission crackdown on Internet fraud. Regulators filed charges against 8 companies and 18 individuals, and warned that the S.E.C.'s "cyberforce" would bring more cases. Would-be Net fraudsters might want to reconsider their plans over a strong cup of Starbucks coffee. Back at the cafe, it is intriguing to note that even as Starbucks was planning its Internet foray, insiders at the company were busy selling shares. Through April, according to First Call, insiders sold 1.44 million shares; in all of 1998 they sold 2.4 million. A Starbucks spokesman said that diversification was behind the insider stampede, not skepticism about the Web strategy. "Most of our executives have a large part of their net worth tied to Starbucks," said the spokesman, Alan Gulick. But the selling does make for a murky brew. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: "Two Strong Jolts" The graph shows how $1,000 invested in I.B.M. and Starbucks would have grown last week

title: New Breeds of Investors, All Beguiled by the Web
body: THERE is a myth that most of the people trading on the Internet are like Spyridon Ganas. Since opening an account with E*Trade on his 18th birthday in January, Mr. Ganas has taken to Web trading with a vengeance, betting not just on volatile technology stocks, but on the even more volatile options on technology stocks. A long-term investment is one he holds for more than a day or two. "I'm part of the Internet generation," said Mr. Ganas, a high school senior in Shrewsbury, Mass., "and it was more natural for me to use the Internet for investing." Looking at the madcap market these days, especially the gyrations in shares of technology and Internet companies, it is natural to wonder whether the dominant investor is in fact some sort of recent Nintendo graduate who has wired his joystick right into his brokerage account. But the phenomenon is far broader than the day traders who have made on-line investing almost a full-time pursuit. The number of households with people trading on the Internet has nearly tripled, to 6.3 million in the last 16 months, according to NFO Worldwide, a research firm based in Greenwich, Conn., that regularly surveys on-line investors and other Internet users. An even more impressive number of households -- 20 million -- tap into the Internet for investment news, quotes and ideas, NFO surveys have found. To understand more about who is using the Internet for investing and how it is changing what they do with their money, Money & Business asked NFO to assemble focus groups of active on-line traders, occasional on-line traders and the larger group of investors who glean information from the Web but do not trade on line. Fittingly, the discussions occurred not in person but in a special chat room on the Internet, where the 35 participants could read and respond to questions posed by a reporter as well as the answers they typed in. While these people represented a wide range of ages, incomes, investment philosophies and behaviors, a common thread emerged: The Internet has bolstered their confidence about investing and emboldened them to take greater risks. "I feel a little more daring, now that I'm a better-educated investor," wrote Dorothy Brown, 52, of Morgantown, W. Va. She had mainly favored bond investments, but she shifted funds into stocks after trying trading at Charles Schwab's Web site. In the focus groups as well as in follow-up interviews, the participants said they felt increasingly secure about their investment decisions as they used the Internet to monitor their portfolios, follow news about their holdings and track the comments of other investors. Those who trade on line said they felt empowered by the minute-to-minute control that Internet investing allows -- and liberated from the intermediaries who have guided them in the past, like stockbrokers and mutual fund companies. "With on-line trading, the easy access to the market is driving people to trade more, driving their confidence level up, raising their risk tolerance," said Lee Smith, a vice president in NFO's Internet research division. "They are holding stocks for a shorter period of time and holding stocks more than mutual funds." If the trends hold, they will begin to alter the composition of America's retirement nest egg and the landscape of financing available to American businesses. They already have Wall Street in a tizzy, as traditional brokerage firms and stock markets confront upstarts and a few established players that have been quicker to latch onto new trading technologies. Even longtime professional traders now face a powerful new market mover. "In the market's run from 3,000 to 8,000, a lot of the upward movement had to do with the fact that people were invested in mutual funds and were not apt to sell very quickly," said Charles Geisst, a finance professor at Manhattan College in the Bronx. "It's no coincidence that in the last year and a half, as Internet trading has become more common, the market has become more volatile." Only after a number of years -- including a couple of serious bear markets -- will it be clear whether the newfound confidence and self-reliance of so many on-line investors is justified. What is already clear is that a big and growing group of Americans are engaged in a high-stakes experiment to see whether they have been prudent in betting their future on stocks they trade themselves.  Just Made to Trade Perhaps the Internet's most significant impact on investing -- evident in the fast growth of on-line trading volume and the increasing volatility in the markets -- is how it emboldens many investors to trade stocks more often. NFO's surveys have found that among investors who have been trading on line for less than a year, 16 percent are what it calls heavy traders, those who say they have conducted more than 10 trades in the last six months. But of Web investors who have had on-line accounts for more than a year, 30 percent are heavy traders. That's not only because active traders were first to jump on line. An NFO survey found that only 13 percent of investors who started trading in 1997 were heavy traders back then. Many of the focus group participants said that their experiences matched the surveys' findings about the seductions of the Web. "I trade more often, because it is easier and can be done 24 hours a day," wrote James Moyer, 45, of Elma, N.Y. "If a stock is moving -- up or down -- I am aware of it on a daily basis, and can sooner decide it is time to buy or sell. I don't have to fumble through a newspaper or an end-of-month report from my account." Many said they were trading more often because they were using the Internet -- often at their jobs -- to watch prices throughout the day. That offers the temptation to pounce the moment they see reasons to hop in or out of a stock, though even some who do so are ambivalent about the merits of such trading. "I do trade more than when a trade cost more than $8," said Treg Owings, 41, of Madras, Ore., who said he checked his portfolio often during the day. "You might trade something because it looks like it is dropping, and the next minute it is up $5. The cost of trading with a broker might discourage in-and-out trading and might save some people money in the long run."  Goodbye, Middle Guy Many people are relying less and less on traditional sources of guidance, like brokers and mutual funds, as they actively trade stocks in their Internet accounts. "I do not miss the frustration of the broker trying to sell you something," said Bev Waldrip, a retired customer service representative for BellSouth who lives in Blairsville, Ga. "They do not understand the word 'no.' " Indeed, NFO, whose research clients are mainly financial services concerns, is finding that Web trading is becoming much more of a threat to the big, full-service brokerage firms like Merrill Lynch and Paine Webber, which often charge commissions 10 times higher than those at the on-line firms but provide access to a broker for advice. "It used to be that the bulk of on-line investors came from the discount brokers, because they are more comfortable making independent decisions," Mr. Smith of NFO said. "Now, transfers from full service are starting to grow as people realize that all the information they see on line makes them less dependent on their brokers." Similarly, the infatuation with on-line stock trading threatens to halt the two-decade-long shift of investment assets out of individual securities and into mutual funds. "I would rather manage my own 'fund,' " said Thomas Holycross, 68, of White Lake, Mich., who opened an account 10 years ago with what is now DLJ Direct, the discount unit of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. Charley Kashou of Mequon, Wis., says he is putting less into mutual funds now. "I've been doing too well in stocks to put it in funds," he said.  The Research Tool One of the most striking aspects of the focus groups was how important the Internet has become even to investors who have never placed a trade on line. "The Internet is speeeeeeeeeeeeeed," wrote Leo Lomasney, 62, a longtime investor from Rochester, N.H., who said he was too lazy to learn how to trade on line. "The Internet has allowed us poor people access to the information that the brokers used to own," he added, explaining that he uses several Internet sites to get investment ideas. Jerry White, 52, a semiretired engineering executive in Ferndale, Calif., checks the value of his portfolio on line every day, reads investing news on the Web and occasionally ventures onto message boards to see what others are saying. He is trading more often, he said, because the Internet gives him more ideas. Still, he feels more comfortable trading through the Morgan Stanley Dean Witter broker who has an office near his home and with whom he can compare notes. "I'm making faster choices," Mr. White said. "I'm still not sure they are better choices."  Navigating the Chats The many message boards and chat rooms where users share ideas about investments with one another are, of course, the most controversial sources of investing information on the Web. The Securities and Exchange Commission has highlighted these sites as fertile breeding grounds for fraud. And a substantial number of Web investors simply have no use for stock tips from strangers. "I don't use the message boards or chat rooms -- they are too large and time-consuming for my needs," said Mr. Moyer of Elma, N.Y. "I know what I'm looking for and go to more reliable sources than what an anonymous Net user has to say." Mr. Ganis, the youngest participant in any of the focus groups, takes an even more cynical view. "Message boards can't be trusted," he said, "but they're useful if you want to hype a stock you just bought." By contrast, Ms. Waldrip, the former BellSouth employee, who is 57, said she had had good luck with on-line investment tips. Someone she met in a chat room on America Online suggested buying the stock of Home Depot, an investment with which she has been happy. While several people in the focus groups reported bad experiences with tips on line, many said the message boards still had allure. "I lost a lot when I was new to them; I believed people," said Mr. Kashou, the Wisconsin investor. Yet even though the boards are populated by "a lot of hypesters," he added, he continues to read them, because "occasionally I find a good idea." Besides, many investors said, traditional sources of investing information just seem anachronistic in the Internet era. "If I read the paper, the opportunities to strike are already gone," said Thomas Fitzgerald, 33, of King of Prussia, Pa. "It is always old news after you have been on the Net."  Pluses and Minuses As people become comfortable using the Internet for investing information, the principal lure to leap into trading on line is the very low commissions of the on-line brokers. But the focus group participants said that as they experimented with on-line trading, what they liked best was the sense of control it gave them. "Price is a big factor, but that alone wouldn't do it," said Mary Hill, 49, of Salinas, Calif. "On-line trading is easy, always available, and I don't have to listen to someone try to tell me what they think," she said. Most of the focus group participants were satisfied with their on-line trading experiences, though a few complained of being stymied by the occasional computer glitches that have kept big on-line brokers like Charles Schwab and E*Trade from processing orders. "I've had trouble getting on a couple times," said Wendall Sherk, 34, of Florissant, Mo. "But brokers don't answer their phones at bad times, too, so that's no different." Jennifer Crissey, 32, of Milford, Pa., was not so sanguine. "I have had problems with orders not going through or the Web site being down with Schwab," she said. "This has prompted me to switch many of my accounts" to another on-line broker. NFO's surveys have found that about 22 percent of on-line investors have switched their Internet broker at least once. But most have moved for lower prices or better investing features, with only 14 percent of the switchers citing complaints about service or computer problems. Still, highly publicized computer glitches at most of the major on-line brokers have discouraged some people from trying on-line trading. Mike Carlson, 48, of Aurora, Colo., said that his family had been planning to move some mutual funds to an on-line brokerage account, but that the recent problems at on-line trading sites "caused us to back off."  Doing Well, for Now Presumably, the best measure of the value of any investing tool is how well a portfolio performs. Many focus group participants said they thought that going on line had made them more successful investors, though some had lingering doubts. Robert Grisinger, 47, of Junction City, Kan., said his return has been higher, "but that could be because it seems the market is booming and hasn't taken a good crash lately." Another reason that on-line investors cite for their having done well is their eager buying of the stock of Internet companies -- the hottest, if the most volatile, sector of the market recently. "I am taking advantage of the Internet explosion," said Mr. Fitzgerald of King of Prussia. "It's a wild ride, but returns are big if you play it right." Professional traders have long observed that a large part of the activity in Internet stocks comes from small orders entered through on-line brokers. And a Gallup survey for Paine Webber earlier this year showed that 44 percent of on-line traders have invested in Internet stocks, compared with 15 percent of investors over all. Still, a lot of participants said the Internet stock ride was just too wild for their tastes. "I braved into Internet stocks about a year ago, bought Lycos and sold it four days later at a $500 profit," recalled Mr. Moyer, the New Yorker. "The reward was great, but the trauma was awful. I haven't bought an Internet stock since." Even among more active traders, there is a widespread feeling that the wave of Internet investing will soon crest. "I think on-line trading has spurred part of the new high record prices and is spurring them on," Mr. Moyer said. "If the market takes a downturn, it may be a really big one, as people won't ride out the storm." Indeed, like investors through the ages, the Internet traders are more concerned about how other investors will behave than about their own investing. "It is like driving," said Mr. Owings, the Oregon investor, who is proud of his purchase of technology stocks like Dell Computer and Ebay. "You have to worry about the other guy." Another focus group member, Dean Coston, 75, who was deputy under secretary of Health, Education and Welfare in the 1960's and is now retired, pointed the finger at the generation of beginning investors. "The thing that concerns me is all the younger investors who have never experienced anything but a rising market," said Mr. Coston, of Falls Church, Va. "They don't know that what goes up will come down. It will be terrible for them." But to Spyridon Ganas, the high school senior who trades options in technology stocks on line, the beauty of the Internet is that it lets him take advantage of what he considers the folly of his elders. "The baby boomers think the stocks are worth it," he said. "So I might as well ride the wave."  The Many Faces of Internet Investing Who is using the Web to trade stocks or research investments? The stereotype -- a manic young daytrader -- is only a piece of the picture.  Bev Waldrip, 59 PERSONAL -- Retired customer service officer for BellSouth. She lives in Blairsville, Ga. INVESTING EXPERIENCE -- After they retired, her husband started buying and selling horses, while she took an equal amount of money to invest in stocks. At first, she used a full-service broker nearby. When her son bought her a computer, she dived into the Internet and opened an account with an online broker. TRADING STYLE -- "I like placing the order and checking late at night to see if one went through," she said. "I can go outside and work in the yard and make money with my stock act at the same time." Another attraction: "If I made a little error, no one would know it." LESSON LEARNED -- "Last year, we didn't make much. We were trading too much. My son was helping me, and if we didn't make money on a stock in a day or two we'd sell it and buy something else." This year, she is trading a little less and her portfolio is doing better.  Terry Sneed, 43 PERSONAL -- Theatrical director, based in Chattanooga, Tenn. INVESTING EXPERIENCE -- Invests through a stock broker and companies' dividend reinvestment plans. Has never traded online, but uses the Internet to monitor his portfolio and get investing ideas. TRADING STYLE -- Keeps his broker so he can get a second opinion on investments, but he is willing to make his own stock picks. "The Internet helped me decide to buy Yahoo on the first day of its IPO. My broker tried to talk me out of it, but I had used it and recognized it as a dynamic company. Now my broker thinks I'm a guru." LESSON LEARNED -- "I had signed up for someone who sent stock tips by e-mail. I followed them and they seemed good, so I bought a company that sounded like it was on the cutting edge. I lost 88 percent."  Spyridon Ganas, 18 PERSONAL -- High school student in Shrewsbury, Mass. He plans to study business at Babson College in the fall. INVESTING EXPERIENCE -- Got interested in the markets watching the "Nightly Business Report" as he worked in the kitchen of his family's pizzeria. Learned to trade by playing a fantasy investing game offered by E*Trade. When he turned 18 in January, he put $1,000 into an E*Trade account. title:
The Nation: AT&T's Merger Deals;
Hold on. Maybe We'll Connect You.
body: THE antitrust authorities barely whimpered last month when AT&T, the nation's largest long-distance company, acquired Tele-Communications Inc., the second-largest cable company. The deal advanced AT&T's audacious plan to feed phone calls and Internet data over the same wire that carries video channels -- offering customers a svelte package of every electronic service they can imagine. And this month AT&T moved to buy another large cable company, Mediaone, and to bring Microsoft into its cable and Internet operations. C. Michael Armstrong, the chairman of AT&T, predicts little regulatory interference. And who knows? He may be right. Fifteen years after the Government split AT&T into pieces -- and even as it is asking the courts to break Microsoft's stranglehold over personal computing -- these two giants nevertheless are rushing to dominate phone, cable and Internet service. Has antitrust regulation been futile? Consumer advocates think so. Others point out that existing antitrust standards are not well-suited to handle telecommunications mergers. In such deals, higher prices, the ordinary province of antitrust enforcement, aren't as big a problem as the threat to diverse expression and sources of information. So regulators have to learn to deal with decisions that could concentrate control over the entertainment and information pouring into the home. And right now they are groping for answers. Already critics are pressing them to act against AT&T. Gene Kimmelman, the consumer advocate at Consumers Union, says, "Regulatory cowardice could turn AT&T into a behemoth that dictates what we see on the Web and watch on television." AT&T seeks to control cable systems that serve between 25 and 40 percent of the nation's cable customers, and to own minority interests in systems that serve another 20 percent. Mr. Kimmelman says no cable network could expect to thrive if it couldn't buy its way into AT&T's systems. Andrew J. Schwartzman, president of the Media Access Project, another advocacy group, worries that AT&T could wall itself off from competition by refusing to sell popular cable offerings that it controls to satellite services, or by refusing to carry programming owned by competitors. Kevin Werbach, managing editor of Release 1.0, a technology magazine, points to a graver threat. "The plan threatens to give AT&T excessive control over the future high-speed Internet," he says. Under AT&T's cable contracts, customers would be required to connect to the Internet using AT&T's online service, At Home, if they want high-speed connections.  Customers who prefer to use the content offered by America Online or some other service would be forced to pay more money and suffer inferior service. This, says Mr. Werbach, "threatens the crowning feature of the Internet, an open network that allows anyone to do business with anyone else without interference." FINALLY, there is the looming presence of Microsoft. It will write the software that provides electronic services for some of AT&T's customers. And that could give Microsoft the toehold it needs to dominate the cable world, much as it does the world of personal computing. But others say the doomsayers are missing the larger picture. Its complexities make it difficult for regulators to figure out how to act, or even whether to act. John Rose of McKinsey & Company, a consulting firm, says AT&T's plan would be "a transforming event," giving customers the option to drop the local phone company. Besides, Mr. Rose says, "once AT&T upgrades its cable service to provide snazzy digital features, so too will all the other cable companies." In other words, there would be greater competition and improved service. Steven Sunshine, a former anti-trust official at the Department of Justice, points out that the antitrust authorities have been right to proceed cautiously because the AT&T cable purchases do not violate the antitrust laws in any simple way. They replaced one cable monopolist, TCI or Mediaone, with another, AT&T. Jim Cicconi, general counsel of AT&T, says the critics see threats of dominance where there are none. AT&T would own and operate systems serving only about 25 percent of the market, he says -- far short of a stranglehold. And, he argues, AT&T will face competition from the regional phone companies and satellite services that will make it "impossible for any one company to control programming." So is AT&T destined to bring a fabulous array of inexpensive electronic services? Or is AT&T about to squash competition in video programming and crush some of the voices that communicate over the Internet? The simple answer is that no one knows. It is unclear, for example, whether the phone companies have a technology that can provide comparable Internet service or whether satellite services will ever reach beyond a small, wealthy niche. In this environment of daunting uncertainty and real or imagined threats to free expression, there are two options: watchful waiting and preventive detention. Robert Litan of the Brookings Institution, and once an antitrust official in the Justice Department, preaches watchful waiting. "Premature reaction by regulators could needlessly stunt innovation," he says, so the smart strategy is to wait, watch and pounce when something goes wrong. Messrs. Kimmelman and Schwartzman counsel preventive detention: Block AT&T's purchase of Mediaone. Waiting to react would give AT&T time to design its cable systems in ways that would make it virtually impossible to pry them open to competition in the future. MR. SUNSHINE preaches a middle ground. "There are many steps that regulators can take short of stopping a merger outright," he says.  They could insist that AT&T open up its cable wires to America Online and other Internet services if technically possible. Or regulators might insist that cable operators lease their popular networks for a fee to satellite services and other potential competitors. But Mr. Sunshine offers a more challenging point. "The antitrust laws protect a company's right to bring forth new technologies unless there is solid evidence of a threat to competition," he says. That is the right standard for guaranteeing low prices for shoelaces, cameras and other ordinary consumer goods. But it may be the wrong standard, he says, when issues other than economic efficiency are at stake. The law gives the Federal Communications Commission the right to hold up mergers to protect the public interest even in those cases where the Justice Department decides there are no serious antitrust problems. With the AT&T-Mediaone merger pending, the commission does not have much time to figure out how to factor the information needs of a democracy into its decision. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A 1965 TV-phone convergence. AT&T has other plans today. (The newyork Times)

title: Britain Fails to Stop Web Sites That List Spies
body: Despite efforts to stop the duplication on the Internet of a list of people identified as British spies, the names have been posted to other sites on the World Wide Web, British officials said today. The British Foreign Office said that even though the original list of more than 100 people identified by the site as British spies had been deleted from the Web, "mirror" sites duplicating the list had appeared. "The information can be accessed," a Foreign Office spokesman said. "To an extent, the cat is out of the bag." The Government said the "balance of probabilities" indicated that Richard Tomlinson, a former British agent living in Switzerland, had released the original list on a site based in the unitedstates. Foreign Secretary Robin Cook has described Mr. Tomlinson as a man who nursed a "deep-seated and irrational grievance" against his previous employers. Although not all the names on the list were connected with the Secret Intelligence Service, known as M.I.6, Mr. Cook said publication was potentially dangerous to people who had worked in the service. Mr. Tomlinson denies posting the list. "It does all point to me very strongly because I did threaten to do it," he told BBC-TV today. "I did have an Internet site, but I didn't actually put the names on the site." The police confirmed that they were investigating the release of the names -- said to include a Cambridge University academic described as a recruiter for M.I.6 and the son of a former Cabinet minister -- as a breach of the Official Secrets Act, Reuters reported. Once a page has appeared on the Internet, it is easy for another user to copy it and post the contents, a process known as mirroring. Mr. Tomlinson, 35, was dismissed from the security service in 1995. He was jailed for six months in Britain in late 1997 after he showed the synopsis of a book on his career to an Australian publisher. During his four years as an agent, he served in Moscow and Bosnia. British Government lawyers had previously obtained an injunction to shut down a Web site Mr. Tomlinson had set up in Switzerland, charging that he had threatened to publish the locations of M.I.6 offices around the world and a detailed list of officers. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
CRISIS IN THE BALKANS;
Yugoslavia Fears Loss of Its email
body: Internet users rushed to send last-minute email messages at a downtown Internet cafe today, after word circulated that the unitedstates was going to cut off Yugoslavia from the World Wide Web. "There was a rush here, and many people heard it was going to be shut down," said Borivoj Ivanovic, 23, a Web master at the Multimedia Center Maverick cafe. The loss of access is just a threat. But Internet providers here said they worry that a partial shutdown of the Internet -- the lone means of communication for many in Serbia -- is imminent. Behind the fears is an Executive Order by President Clinton that took effect on May 1, updating a 1998 order to prevent American companies from dealing in goods, services and technology with Yugoslavia. The effects have been almost immediate for companies like Informatika, an Internet provider and a software and hardware supplier in Belgrade. Its general manager said he had been notified by some American companies that he can no longer receive their services. The Administration denied trying to cut the flow of information to Yugoslavia and said it would not try to limit Internet access there. The National Security Council has said information services are generally exempt from embargoes, but electronic commerce is not. The Internet performs both functions. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Healtheon Is Expected to Join Forces WithInternet Provider - Correction Appended
body: The Healtheon Corporation, the Santa Clara, Calif., medical record-keeping Web site started by the founder of the Netscape Communications Corporation, Jim Clark, is expected to announce Monday that it is merging with WebMD, a privately held Internet provider of medical information. The deal is expected to be valued at more than $3.5 billion, with WebMD shareholders receiving Healtheon shares. The boards of both companies are expected to meet this weekend to approve the transaction. Mr. Clark, chairman of Healtheon, would be the chairman of the new company, which is expected to have headquarters in Atlanta, where WebMD is based. The chairman of WebMD, Jeffrey Arnold, would be chief executive of the new company and Healtheon's chief executive, W. Michael Long, would be chief operating officer. As with any negotiations, the talks could falter at the last minute. A spokesman for WebMD declined to comment on a possible deal. Healtheon executives did not return telephone calls seeking comment. Shares of Healtheon spiked yesterday, up $10 on reports of a possible deal, to close at $57 a share. Healtheon was started in 1995 by Mr. Clark and David Schell, a Harvard-educated doctor who was also a partner at the venture capital firm of Kleiner Perkins. The merger would give Healtheon access to more consumers. It currently focuses mainly on doctors, hospitals, insurers and other institutions. Healtheon has been an active acquirer, having bought ActaMed, an electronic data concern, in 1998, and Metis, a Web site developer of Internet-based health care information services, also in 1998. Healtheon called off a planned initial public offering last July, citing the temperamental market for Internet stocks then. The company went public earlier this year. WebMD was set to go public itself, but last week filed a statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission canceling its $55 million public offering. The company began in October 1998, but was earlier named Endeavor Technologies. It was founded by Mr. Arnold, an Atlanta native, who in 1994 -- when he was 24 years old -- started Quality Diagnostic Services, which describes itself as a cardiac arrhythmia monitoring company, with his wife, Meg. Mr. Arnold holds a Bachelor of Arts degree in communications from the University of Georgia. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Business Day on May 15 about a merger of the Healtheon Corporation and WebMD misspelled the name of a Healtheon founder. He is Dr. David Schnell, not Schell. Correction-Date: June 7, 1999, Monday

title: Internet Access for Schools
body: In its start-up year, the e-rate program created by Congress as part of the 1996 Telecommunications Act has helped tens of thousands of rural and low-income communities connect to the Internet. Given the growing needs, Federal Communications Commission chairman William Kennard has properly recommended that the program -- which subsidizes telecommunications services and Internet hook-ups for schools and libraries -- be financed at the maximum authorized level of $2.25 billion for the coming year. The commission is expected to vote on the plan this month. The e-rate subsidy provides a 20 to 90 percent discount on telecommunications services to schools and libraries depending on community poverty levels. The funds pay for telephone and Internet fees and wiring of classrooms, but may not be used to pay for computers, software or teacher training. newyork State received $164 million in e-rate subsidies this year, with about half of that flowing to newyork City schools, which are in desperate need of technological improvements. Despite strong support from schools and educators, the e-rate program has been politically vulnerable from the start. It is financed mostly by fees from long-distance phone companies as part of the bargain under the 1996 act. But the industry has complained loudly about the costs ever since. Under heavy pressure from lawmakers, the F.C.C. scaled down the program initially, awarding only $1.7 billion in the first 18 months, even though demand was much higher. More than 32,000 applications requesting $2.4 billion in subsidies have been submitted for the coming year. But Republicans in Congress are pushing to restructure and reduce the program. Senator Conrad Burns introduced legislation this week that would cut the program to roughly $1.9 billion a year for five years, to be financed by part of the current 3 percent Federal excise tax on phone service instead of the current e-rate fees. The rest of the excise tax would be eliminated. After five years, the aid would be financed through annual appropriations, and would be capped at $500 million a year. Their proposal would destabilize a program that works, and, worse, cut assistance even as telecommunications become increasingly important in education. http://www.nytimes.com
