title:
TV Notes;
Arnett's New Job
body: Just three weeks after his official departure from CNN, Peter Arnett has found a new home for his international reporting, though it's not on television. It is on the Internet. Mr. Arnett, who gained fame as CNN's reporter on the spot during the air raids on Baghdad during the gulf war, signed an agreement yesterday with a newly launched Web site called ForeignTV.com, which calls itself an Internet broadcaster specializing in foreign news. Mr. Arnett has signed on to conduct a series of interviews with world leaders for the service as well as to serve as an adviser to the service in creating news bureaus in various locations. CNN settled Mr. Arnett's contract after effectively removing him from the air in the wake of the scandal that became know as Tailwind, after a report alleging that nerve gas was used by unitedstates military forces in Vietnam. The report by CNN was carried on its news magazine program "Newsstand." Mr Arnett was the correspondent for the report, which CNN eventually retracted and apologized for showing. Mr. Arnett's agent, Richard Liebner, said that he was still seeking a traditional broadcast news position for Mr. Arnett but that this seemed an ideal way for him to re-establish some of his foreign reporting credentials. "This seemed to me like something that will allow Peter to travel," Mr. Liebner said, "to keep up his contacts, and get him cooking again."   BILL CARTER http://www.nytimes.com

title: Candidates Falling Into the Open Arms Of High Technology
body: Vice President Al Gore makes a point in his Seattle visits of stopping at Internet companies like Amazon.com, the on-line commerce pioneer. Other Presidential hopefuls, including Senator John McCain, Representative John R. Kasich and former Senator Bill Bradley, have recently toured Microsoft's campus here. So far Gov. George W. Bush of Texas has not come near either Seattle or Silicon Valley in Northern California. But that did not stop a group of high-technology executives from taking out a newspaper advertisement in The San Jose Mercury News last month, calling Mr. Bush one of the "visionary leaders who understand the New Economy" and urging him to run for President. The dance is on between Presidential candidates and high-technology executives, who were once regarded as bit players in campaign finance and whose industry in turn prided itself on its libertarian streak and almost dismissive attitude toward whatever was happening in Washington, D.C. Facing a host of tax and regulatory issues, and with the landmark Microsoft antitrust case serving as a powerful reminder that Federal officials can still sway the competitive landscape, many industry executives are clearly deciding that it pays to have friends in the White House and Capitol. Mr. Gore, who has long sought to position himself as the Administration's champion of computer technology and the Internet, has extensive contacts in the industry and pulled in roughly $400,000 last month at a Silicon Valley fund-raiser given by John Doerr, a founder of Technology Network, widely known as Technet, the prime lobbying and fund-raising organization of the industry. But Mr. Gore's competitor for the Democratic nomination, Mr. Bradley, who spent a year as a visiting professor at Stanford University in which he nursed his own Silicon Valley contacts, has also done well, taking in about $1 million at a large San Francisco fund-raiser last month that was well-populated with industry executives. And Governor Bush, though pledged to stay in Texas until the end of the legislative session this spring, is planning big fund-raisers for San Francisco and Palo Alto in early summer. Among those who signed the recent pro-Bush newspaper advertisement, which praised the Republican Mr. Bush for "creating an environment that stresses personal responsibility over government intervention, and innovation over regulation," were James Barksdale, founder of Netscape; Bob Herbold, chief operating officer of the Microsoft Corporation; Jeff Henley, chief financial officer of the Oracle Corporation, and Steve Behm, a vice president of Cisco Systems. It is still early in the campaign cycle, but it is already certain that computer-industry donations will be a bigger factor in the 2000 elections than they have previously been. "Unless high-tech people unplug their telephones, sign off email and leave the country in the next 18 months, they're going to give more than they've ever given before," said Larry Makinson, executive director of the Center for Responsive Politics, a nonpartisan group that tracks campaign finances. "They're certainly being hit up like never before." Contributions to 1998 Congressional campaigns from the high-tech industry totaled about $8.1 million, more than twice as much as the total in the 1994 campaigns. Even as industry contributions will continue to grow in 2000, they will probably still be well below the dollars spent by other industries, like energy and banking, that have had large lobbying and campaign-donation operations in place for a long time. Microsoft, whose total campaign contributions in 1998, $1 million, were more than triple its 1996 contributions, according to the Center for Responsive Politics, is planning to have a major presence in the 2000 campaign. (The contributions include individual giving by company employees, political action committee donations and so-called soft money, which is given to the political parties rather than the candidates.) A Microsoft spokesman, Greg Shaw, said the company acknowledged it was "a little slow in recognizing the importance of being a more visible and more active participant in Washington," but was now intent on "sharing its views and experience" with policy leaders there. For the Presidential aspirants, the booming industry is not just an obvious source of money. It is also the creator of technology that they are intent on understanding, since it could be vital to their campaigns. The number of American households with Internet access has doubled to nearly 44 million since the last Presidential election, according to Forrester Research Inc., a company that monitors technology trends. Candidates are already trying to use the World Wide Web to attract voters, with sites that offer video clips, questionnaires and invitations for visitors to "get involved" by volunteering to work for the campaign, donating money or at least signing up for regular email updates. For the high-technology executives, there is a growing array of reasons to want good friends in Congress or the White House. They have already won legislation creating a moratorium on taxes for Internet commerce, special visas for skilled foreign workers and an extension of tax credits for research and development, though they have had only minor success so far in measures to limit lawsuits for problems related to the year 2000 computer glitch. Still, while the more established interests in the relatively young computer industry, like Microsoft and America Online, are getting increasingly involved in the political process, many newer Internet companies and their top executives do not show significant signs of doing so, even as their stock prices have climbed so high that their market value has eclipsed that of huge companies in other industries. "When you're Amazon.com," said Wade Randlett, Democratic political director of Technet, the industry group, "you're a new company and you're trying to grow at 50 percent a quarter and your competitors are trying to kill you -- that just doesn't allow you to devote a lot of time to anything else." A spokesman for Amazon.com, Bill Curry, said the company had recently designated a person on the legal staff to monitor public-policy issues related to the Internet, and was evaluating whether the company needed to do a better job of establishing contact with public officials. "We want to avoid the mistake of being so focused on building a business that some day we find out we need relationships in Washington and we don't have any," Mr. Curry said. Calculating the precise impact the high-technology industry is having on the 2000 campaign is difficult. The most recent filings with the Federal Election Commission, for instance, show contributions by individuals through March 31 and do not reflect big fund-raisers held by both Mr. Gore and Mr. Bradley in the San Francisco Bay Area last month. The commission reports show Mr. Gore with about $83,000 in direct contributions from executives at high-technology companies, but they do not show the roughly $400,000 he pulled in at the fund-raiser given by Mr. Doerr, a leading industry venture capitalist. Many computer companies, which had little presence in Washington in the past, have set up political action committees for corporate giving that are expected to make major contributions to candidates or the national parties as the campaign heats up. Moreover, while many computer companies applaud the Federal lawsuit against Microsoft, in which a ruling is expected this summer, and thus may have a reason to reward Mr. Gore, the case is also a reminder that the Government has the potential to wield enormous power in shaping the industry, all the more reason for computer executives to take an interest in campaigns. The Microsoft antitrust battle is an obvious reason for anyone in the industry to pay more attention to Washington, even as the company says the case does not belong in a Federal courtroom. "A few of our competitors decided that Washington, D.C., was a place where they could out-compete us on issues that in our view would have been better resolved in the marketplace," said Mr. Shaw, the Microsoft spokesman. As Microsoft has become far more active in both making campaign contributions and deploying lobbyists, and tried to fend off a lawsuit pushed by a Democratic Administration, there is no question that the Republican Party has benefited. About two-thirds of the company's total contributions last year went to Republicans. In 1992, just 20 percent of them did. And Republican Presidential candidates, including Senator McCain of Arizona and Representative Kasich of Ohio, have traveled to Microsoft recently to meet with top officials. Microsoft executives said that the company was "steadfastly bipartisan" and that increases on the Republican side were attributable to the party's having taken control of Congress in 1994. Across the industry in general, many executives are not particularly partisan, meaning that either party could make inroads. "More than anything else, Silicon Valley is on the 50-yard-line of the political spectrum," Mr. Randlett of Technet said. "It's strongly free-market, free trade, pro-economic growth. And it's pro-choice, pro-public education and pro-environment, with the same if not greater fervor than the belief in free-market philosophy. Whichever candidate is most centrist is going to do best here." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: President Clinton and John Doerr, a founder of Technology Network, in September at a Democratic fund-raising dinner in San Jose, Calif. (Associated Press)(pg. A20)

title: Hospitals Reaching New Patients On Line
body: As the Internet grows, so does the amount of health information available on line. But the sheer volume of information available on the Web does not equal a speedy, or accurate, search. To give order to the chaos of the Web, a handful of health care organizations have put their imprimaturs on information-rich Web sites accessible to anyone with a modem. While many medical centers use Web sites to advertise practical information like hours, resources and the latest research, others consider themselves full-fledged digital publishers, in the business of educating patients as much as promoting themselves. The growing interest in acquiring medical information has fueled the idea, said Ann Metzger, a spokeswoman for the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (www.upmc.edu), which offers information about the university's medical specialties like gene therapy, stroke treatment and minimally invasive surgery. "We recognize that many people increasingly want information when they want it," Ms. Metzger said. "The Web is the ultimate expression of that." To keep up with the demand, the hospital now spends less time and money on printed brochures in favor of making more educational materials available on line. The Mayo Clinic has long provided books, newsletters, and recently, CD-ROM's of health information. Now, it also maintains a Web site (www.mayohealth.org), with a dozen full-time editorial workers who publish medical news daily. Each story is reviewed by at least three physicians, said Dr. Brooks Edwards, the medical editor for the site. It also gives access to medical expertise to people who live far from the clinic. In a busy month, doctors at the Mayo Clinic see 40,000 patients, Dr. Edwards said. But a busy month on the Internet brings 1.5 million visitors. Other on-line health centers report a wide geographic reach. The University of Iowa Medical Center said only 10 percent of the visitors to its Virtual Hospital Web site (www.vh.org) are from the state. Twenty percent are from outside the country. The Virtual Hospital contains digital versions of hundreds of medical textbooks and research reports, said Dr. Michael D'Alessandro, a co-founder and its director. In essence, it opens the bookshelves of the staff to the world. Making such data available introduces a new dimension to medicine. In an age of easily accessible medical information, the sight of patients in hospitals and doctors' waiting rooms clutching printouts of information mined from various Web sites is common. Armed with knowledge, patients are also filled with questions. "The Web breaks down barriers," Dr. D'Alessandro said. "It becomes more of a partnership or collaboration." But, he added, doctors who do not understand the on-line medium sometimes become frustrated.  To address that frustration, some hospitals have initiated training programs to teach health care workers about the Web and the vast information and misinformation available on it. But even with an abundance of information, the Web should supplement, not replace, advice and diagnosis from a physician, Dr. Edwards said. As medical knowledge expands, so do Web sites. Ms. Metzger of the Pittsburgh medical center said her hospital's site was a "work in progress that would never be completed." "People expect deeper information, the most current information," she said. "And that gives organizations like mine a responsibility to put up the most comprehensive information we can." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Volumes of material are available on health care organizations' Web sites, like this one from the Mayo Clinic.

title: Microsoft Is Acquiring 4% Stake in Nextel
body: Demonstrating that its ambitions are not tethered to the wired world, the Microsoft Corporation said yesterday that it had agreed to pay $600 million in cash for about 4 percent of Nextel Communications Inc., a big national provider of wireless communications. Yesterday's deal appeared to be Microsoft's biggest move yet into the fast-growing wireless communications market. As part of the deal, Microsoft, the No. 1 personal computer software company, will help Nextel deliver data services, including electronic mail and date books to wireless phones. In return, Nextel will use software developed by Microsoft as a framework for delivering an even broader range of Internet-based services to its wireless users. Coming less than a week after Microsoft announced a $5 billion pact with the AT&T Corporation to use Microsoft software in some of AT&T's cable television systems, yesterday's deal highlighted Microsoft's hunger to expand beyond the PC industry. Even as AT&T moves to use cable systems to deliver integrated packages of voice, video and data communications, new technologies are facilitating the delivery of services more advanced than phone calls and without wires. Microsoft wants to move its Windows operating system into both environments and into others. "Microsoft and Nextel will deliver the next generation of wireless services to enable people everywhere to stay in touch with the information they need, regardless of location," William H. Gates, Microsoft's chairman, said in a prepared statement. Mike Ozburn, general manager of Nextel's on-line unit, said in an interview, "Whereas yesterday, if you walked away from your PC, you would have no ability to touch the power of the Internet. When we launch Nextel Online, wherever you are, you will be able to access those Internet tools." Nextel's network, which uses wireless frequencies that were once used largely for dispatching trucks, covers about 70 percent of the unitedstates population. But Nextel plans to offer the service in only six, undisclosed markets this year. Using phones made by Motorola Inc., one of Nextel's primary backers, the company plans to offer the new services throughout its system next year. For Nextel, yesterday's deal came less than a week after it emerged from abortive talks to be acquired by MCI Worldcom Inc., the No. 2 long-distance carrier, which does not have a significant wireless operation. Those two companies walked away from weeks of negotiations after MCI refused to pay Nextel what it wanted. Nextel's discussions with Microsoft, however, had been developing for at least that long. Some executives in the wireless phone business and on Wall Street speculated yesterday that Nextel's growing confidence that it would get a cash infusion from Microsoft stiffened the company's backbone in its talks with MCI. Nextel is growing fast, but is not generating free cash flow because it must record large interest charges on its almost $10 billion in debt and because it is spending about $1.9 billion a year to expand its network. Seeking to refinance some of its own debt and perhaps to improve its cash position, Nextel is planning a new $1.2 billion bond offering, according to some executives on Wall Street. Nextel declined to comment on its financing plans. The convergence of the telecommunications and computing worlds took yet another step yesterday as Lucent Technologies Inc., North America's biggest maker of telephone equipment, announced that it had developed a new technology that could reduce from five to one the number of microchips needed in a phone that uses Internet technology. The Lucent technology could make Internet phones cheaper and easier to manufacture. http://www.nytimes.com

title: TV-Net Deals: One May Flop, The Other Flies
body: Just as one betrothal of a television network and an Internet company was on the verge of breaking off yesterday, another engagement was being announced. The proposed combination of some assets of USA Networks, the family of cable networks, with Lycos, the Internet portal, is about to be abandoned, people close to the negotiations said. Meanwhile, NBC said yesterday that it had agreed to merge some of its Internet assets with Xoom, a publicly traded electronic community that emphasizes direct marketing. The combined entity, worth $3.9 billion based on Xoom's market value, will operate under the name Snap.com and would be the seventh-most-visited site on the Internet. The driving force behind both developments is the stock market, which values Internet businesses far more than enterprises in any other industry. USA ran afoul of investors because it proposed combining Lycos, a pure Internet company, with USA's Home Shopping Network and Ticketmaster units, along with their associated Web sites. Never mind that the company would have had revenue of $1.5 billion -- 30 times that of Lycos alone. Lycos's stock fell on the news of the deal last February. And CMGI, the largest holder of Lycos stock, said it would vote against the acquisition. In recent weeks, executives of both Lycos and USA concluded that it was far from certain that a majority of shareholders would vote for the deal, people close to the deal said. They added that since USA was not willing to raise its bid, the two companies would agree to go their separate ways. "Lycos and USA just couldn't sell the deal to the Street, no matter how they repackaged it," said one executive with knowledge of the transaction. The deal's imminent demise was first reported yesterday by The Wall Street Journal. NBC's deal, meanwhile, is specifically designed to create a company exclusively involved in the Internet. It will operate under the name NBC Internet, or NBCi. NBC hopes that the shares of NBCi, independent of the network's parent, the General Electric Company, will ascend to the lofty levels of other big Internet portals. If so, it will be able to trade those shares in acquiring other Internet companies at prices that would be unthinkable if G.E. actually had to pay cash. Investors were as favorable to the NBC deal as they were scornful of the USA-Lycos transaction. News of the potential demise of the deal with USA bolstered Lycos shares by $15.75, to $105.25. In contrast, shares of Xoom jumped by $6.75, to $81.86 yesterday. "NBC has a lot of marquee value and the power to promote Internet properties," said Alan M. Braverman, an analyst with Nationsbanc Montgomery securities. "Xoom will help them capitalize on what they have. But it's not enough." Mr. Braverman said that NBCi would need to use its new public stock as currency in acquisitions to get a bigger audience. Indeed, he said that a newly single Lycos could make an attractive partner. "NBC would have loved to do a deal with Lycos before," he said. "Maybe they can again." Tom Rogers, the president of NBC cable, declined to say if NBC would be interested in a deal with Lycos. But he said the company's top goal in planning future acquisitions would be to build a service for people with high-speed Internet connections. NBC will contribute to NBCi its interest in Snap, the Internet portal that it bought a portion of from CNet last year. It will also contribute NBC.Com, the site that carries information about its television shows; NBC Interactive Neighborhood, a site that links NBC's affiliates; Videoseeker, a site that plays video clips over the Internet, and 10 percent of CNBC.Com, a personal finance site scheduled to begin in June. NBC will also contribute $370 million in cash, payable over four years, in the form of the note. In return, NBC will control 49.9 percent of the new company. By keeping its ownership below 50 percent, the losses of the company do not have to be incorporated into General Electric's income statement. NBC has the right to convert the note into an additional 3 percent stake in NBCi, which would presumably be useful were the company ever to make a profit. The current holders of Xoom shares will receive a 34 percent stake in the new company. And CNet will end up with a 13 percent stake. NBC will not include the MSNBC cable and Internet news service in the new company. MSNBC is a joint venture with the Microsoft Corporation, and its Internet site is filled with links to Microsoft's MSN portal, a direct competitor to Snap. The deal shows just how far Internet valuations have risen since last June, when NBC announced its investment in Snap. NBC agreed to pay $5.9 million for 19.9 percent of Snap and has a three-year option to buy a further 40.1 percent of the service for $32 million. Yesterday, NBC executives said that Snap was valued in the deal as equal to Xoom, which has a market value of $1.3 billion, giving NBC a paper return of 2,000 percent. Part of that return is a result of the sharp increase in audience Snap has experienced, in part because of the promotion it receives on NBC. In March, it was the 11th-most-popular site, visited at least once by 15.8 percent of the Internet users. Xoom was the 12th-most-popular site, reaching 15.7 percent of the audience. The combination would be the seventh-most-visited site, reaching 29 percent of the audience. Xoom was started by Chris Kitze, a 39-year-old entrepreneur who has started and sold four companies so far. On the surface, Xoom resembles other Internet communities like Geocities, which agreed to be bought by Yahoo, in that it offers free home pages, message boards, chat rooms and so on. But Xoom was built from the ground up to be a direct marketing vehicle, gathering data about its users' interests in order to sell them merchandise. Xoom members are regularly barraged with email offering electronics items like scanners. Xoom's direct marketing focus is very much in keeping with NBC's broader strategy. The network has been emphasizing programming in which it can sell related merchandise, as it did selling compact disks and videos related to its miniseries "The 60's." NBC also invested in Value Vision, a small cable shopping channel. NBC said that Robert Wright, NBC's president, would be chairman of NBCi's board. Mr. Kitze would be its president and chief executive. Halsey Minor, CNet's chairman who has also been the acting chief executive of Snap, would have no role in the new company. Similarly, Laurent Massa, Xoom's president and chief executive, will leave the company. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Extending Their Reach" Traditional media providers are vying for the attention of Internet users. title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Microsoft Looks to Nortel In Early Test for Network To expand the capacity of its internal data network, Microsoft has turned, at least tentatively, to Nortel Networks of Canada. The two companies plan to announce today that Microsoft has agreed to try a new Nortel optical networking technology. Microsoft, which does not plan to revamp its network until early next year, wants to take the next six months or so to determine which communications equipment makers will get the bulk of its business. But the Microsoft trial is a big vote of confidence in the optical networking group at Nortel.  Page C10. title:
Compressed Data;
Turning 'Sticky Traffic' Into Advertising Dollars
body: To ask Tom Phillips, the chief executive of Deja News, to describe the makeover he has given his business is to get a primer on Internet buzzwords. "This is the datafication of shared knowledge," Mr. Phillips said last week, as he prepared for a marketing campaign to be announced today. "This is the cross between Web as utility and Web as community." How does that translate for a service that since 1995 has been trying to make newsgroups simple to use? There will, Mr. Phillips said, be less emphasis on that -- the new name will be simply Deja -- and more of a focus on polls, charts and the ranking of products and ideas. Newsgroups, the on-line equivalent of kaffeeklatsches, generate repeat visitors, a coveted commodity known as "sticky traffic." Deja News attracted six million page views a day, but, Mr. Phillips admitted, was "not killer" in terms of generating revenue. Mr. Phillips, a co-founder of Spy magazine, said he expected Internet users to turn to Deja for information about people, activities and things. The idea is to become a sort of populist Consumer Reports. As evidence that people will be eager to participate, Mr. Phillips pointed to polls that he conducted at the Web sites of ABC News and ESPN. "They were the most popular thing we did there," he said. Equally important, Mr. Phillips expects to attract more advertisers eager to reach a certain group of consumers. "This is a big, broad idea," he said. Lisa Allen, an analyst with Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass., said: "Sticky's great, but revenue's even better. They've recognized, as have some others, that the lines between content and commerce are blurring. I hate to say they had no choice, but could they keep creating content that wasn't paying for itself?"   LISA NAPOLI http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Tom Phillips is remaking Deja News. (Fred R. Conrad/The newyork Times)

title:
Defining the On-Line Chief;
Ebay's Meg Whitman Explores Management, Web Style
body: In a Valley of unexpected millionaires, Meg Whitman is the unlikeliest of billionaires. Ms. Whitman recalls the day in November 1997 that a headhunter urged her to leave her comfortable job promoting Teletubbies at Hasbro Inc. The proposition: to head up a no-name Silicon Valley start-up that needed a chief executive. Her answer was "no." Like legions of graduates coming out of elite business schools in the late 1970's, Ms. Whitman had taken her Harvard M.B.A. and slipped quietly into a successful career at a blue-chip consulting firm. She later moved to corporate America, happy to work for the likes of Disney and Stride Rite. So it would take more than Internet stock options in a company she had never heard of for Ms. Whitman to give up the peaceful life she enjoyed with her husband and two sons in Boston. That was until Ms. Whitman visited the cramped San Jose, Calif., offices of Ebay Inc., the person-to-person Web auction community that was already attracting a following so devout it bordered on the cultish. After a few days of being wooed by venture capitalists and hearing the testimonials of users so addicted they slipped out of business meetings to monitor their auctions, Ms. Whitman was hooked. "I thought something was very right here," she said. "They had touched a consumer nerve." Ms. Whitman's "no" became "yes." And 14 months ago, she packed up her family and moved to California to begin preparing Ebay for the initial public stock offering that the company's founder, Pierre M. Omidyar, was already mulling. Since its $735 million offering last September, the company's market capitalization has blossomed to $22.1 billion -- the stock price skyrocketing 1,019 percent. And the 42-year-old Ms. Whitman, along with a cadre of early investors, has become very rich -- at least on paper. But more to the point, she is also one of the new generation of Internet executives who is bringing conventional corporate bona fides and consumer- product-style marketing to the Web. In the process, executives like Ms. Whitman are changing the way Web companies are run -- even as they develop a new management style suited to this emergent medium. With no technology background to speak of, Ms. Whitman leaves the heavy lifting to the tech experts. But what she does seem to have are many of the skills that may be necessary if Ebay is to prove itself more than a hot stock or consumer fad and become an established brand. In some ways, executives like Ms. Whitman are becoming to technology what Ray Kroc, the founder of McDonald's, was to fast food and consumer culture in the early 1960's. In those days, an executive did not need to understand the chemistry of ground beef to deliver a hamburger people wanted. Likewise, today's Internet executives do not have to be computer geniuses, but seasoned brand managers who immerse themselves in the culture they are trying to foster on line. Robert Kagle, a partner at the venture firm Benchmark Capital, an early Ebay investor that hired Ms. Whitman, may put it best: "I was looking for a brand builder to help make Ebay a household name. Understanding technology was not the central ingredient. You have to get the emotional component of the customer experience in your gut." Certainly, the Ebay brand is becoming synonymous with Ms. Whitman, something she is not entirely comfortable with. A man moving furniture at Ebay's headquarters last week pointed at her, a spark of recognition lighting up his face. "There she is," he shouted. "My wife said she's seen you on TV. Maybe 10 times. You're real popular." Ms. Whitman smiled and waved at the man. But the grin faded as she turned away. "That's what I hate," she said. "I even have the furniture man noticing me." The attention is not all that surprising, though. Ms. Whitman campaigns for Ebay as fervently as any candidate on the trail. In recent weeks she attended a press conference with the Governor of Utah; spoke to reporters at the National Press Club in Washington, where she also met with Congressional leaders to discuss on-line privacy, and was interviewed for a handful of coming profiles. "Personally, I don't care," she said, commenting on the media swirl. "But it is the right thing to do for Ebay." Ms. Whitman never planned on a Web career. After a summer selling advertising for her college magazine at Princeton University, she switched from pre-med studies and graduated with an economics degree in 1977. She got her M.B.A. from Harvard Business School two years later, and briefly worked at Procter & Gamble before moving to San Francisco in 1981 with her husband, Griffith R. Harsh 4th, who landed a neurosurgery residency at the University of California at San Francisco. There, she was hired by the consulting firm Bain & Company, where she worked for eight years. But the demands of her husband's career (they moved to Boston in 1992 when he became director of the brain tumor program at Massachusetts General Hospital) and the fact that headhunters called every time a new job emerged, led to a number of jobs at several companies. It was her two years as chief executive of Florists' Transworld Delivery in Michigan, though, that proved her biggest disappointment. Ms. Whitman had been hired by the florist-owned member association in 1995 -- better known as F.T.D. -- to help smooth its transition to a privately held company. But several key members opposed the idea, quick decisions were politically impossible and competition was eroding market share. Conceding defeat, Ms. Whitman quit in 1997, moved briefly to Hasbro and the next year found herself at Ebay. As if to test the new chief's technical mettle, Ebay's Web site crashed during her first day on the job, crippling trading for eight hours. "The No. 1 job at Ebay is keeping the site up," she said, so she assembled a team of senior managers to assess the site's reliability. As a result, Ebay added enough backup software and computer servers to increase trading capacity. But intermittent problems have persisted, and Ms. Whitman has not hesitated to tap powerful Silicon Valley connections to help her. "Last January, we were having short outages -- 10 to 15 minutes," she recalled. "It made everyone here crazy." So she called Scott G. McNealy, chairman of Sun Microsystems Inc., whom she has known for a decade. "I said, 'Scott, I need a nanny for this system until the baby gets better.' " Now Sun technicians are on call 24 hours. But the baby can still be fussy; just last Monday, trading was interrupted for four hours because of a computer glitch. Much of Ms. Whitman's job is understanding who uses the auction service. About a year ago, Ms. Whitman set up a consumer insight and analysis group to find out. In contrast to the situation at traditional retailers, she said, "there is no one between us and the consumer." So twice monthly Ebay posts customer surveys on the site. Among the suggestions that were adopted is "Ebay Life," a newsletter full of feel-good stories -- like the woman who collects wedding cake decorations, 50 of which she found on Ebay, or the stay-at-home mother who is an avid Ebay trader at night. Ebay, at times, can come off as a bit homespun, but that does not concern Ms. Whitman. "I didn't create this culture, but I want to maintain it," she said. Mr. Kagle can attest to that. It was he who prodded her to set up a feature that customers had been requesting: notification by email whenever favorite items are up for bid. And everyone is a source of feedback. Even the architects who redesigned their headquarters were asked to buy something and report back to Ms. Whitman. Three times a week, Ms. Whitman meets with staff members to review what other auction sites have that Ebay does not. Ebay's recent $260 million acquisition of the auction house Butterfield & Butterfield was spurred, in part, by the threat of competition, she said. And Ebay is rushing to expand into untapped regional as well as foreign markets. Whatever the sense of urgency that drives her, Ms. Whitman displays a calming, down-to-earth veneer -- perhaps a result of her upbringing as the youngest of three children in the comfortably affluent village of Cold Spring Harbor on Long Island's North Shore. Her father was a businessman, her mother a full-time homemaker with a sense of adventure. Ms. Whitman recalls the summer she was 6 years old when her mother, the three Whitman children and a family friend with five children of her own, embarked on a three-month camping trip across Canada to Alaska. Driving for long stretches in a camper with canvas bunks in the back, the children would sometimes get antsy and start to squabble. So Ms. Whitman's mother came up with an unusual solution to tire them out. She would stop the camper, order the children out on the deserted Alaskan highway and let them run ahead, creeping behind in the camper until they were weary. More than once, a passing trucker would stop to ask if something was wrong. "You could always hear the hiss of the air brakes," Ms. Whitman recalled. "We finally put up a sign on the back of the camper that said, 'We're O.K.' " And one year, during the family's annual Christmas camping trip on the island of St. John in the Virgin Islands, her parents were too late to make a reservation at the usual campground. Undaunted, the family bivouacked in a toolshed. That willingness to make do may help explain why Ms. Whitman was willing recently to move with her husband and children into a subdivision in Menlo Park that the locals refer to as "Woodside training houses," because executives there typically aspire eventually to the exclusive homes in that nearby town. "We didn't want to buy a statement house," she said (although not buying a statement house is a statement in itself). They do plan to move once they have finished remodeling a 3,800-square-foot home they bought in well-heeled Atherton. Working for Ebay will be her last job, Ms. Whitman said. Her stock options -- worth about $1.3 billion as of Friday's closing price -- vest over four years, and she plans to stay at the company at least five years. But by then, if she has not delivered, her options could be worth significantly less or, depending on the capriciousness of the market, nothing at all. For it is not yet certain whether the new brand-conscious executive is indeed the blueprint for the future, or simply an expensive experiment in Internet management. Yahoo and Amazon.com are already fast on the heels of Ebay hoping to grab the company's loyal customers for their own. And more are sure to come. "There is this constant roar," Ms. Whitman said. "The challenge is to reorganize your business every three months." And being on the run makes missteps inevitable. "You will be wrong sometimes," she said. "That is just going to happen." But uncertainty is a condition with which Ms. Whitman, and any investors in Internet stocks, for that matter, must learn to live with. "She has done a great job so far with the stock," said Alberto Vilar, president of Amerindo Investment Advisors, and one of Ebay's largest shareholders. "Anyone who wants to pick her off as a second-rate manager is barking up the wrong tree." But though a fan of Ms. Whitman, Mr. Vilar sounded the kind of warning that is an implicit part of being one of today's new Web chiefs: "Her board and shareholders are going to lynch her if she doesn't execute." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Meg Whitman of Ebay rushes out of a Salt Lake City hotel on the way to a news conference with the Governor of Utah. (George Frey for The New York Times)(pg. C1); Meg Whitman, with Matthew Bannick, left, the vice president for customer support, and Lynn Hrdin, the director of customer support, reads an account of Ebay in a local newspaper during a trip to Utah. (George Frey for The New York Times)(pg. C8)  Chart/Photos: "Whitman Sampler" On Ebay's Web site, individuals auction off the sublime, the ridiculous and rarities in between.  Human Bean Figurine, Minimum bid: $5.00 Flash Gordon Signal Pistol, Minimum bid: $2,655 1950's Lamp, Minimum bid: $18.01 Mobil Lubrite Metal Oil Can, Minimum bid: $9.99 Diamond and Emerald Ring, Minimum bid: $2,450 1985 Porsche Carrera Targa, Minimum bid: $13,100 Hummel Figurine, Minimum bid: $20.00 Burris 10x Pistol Scope, Minimum bid: $155  Chart: "Management.com"  With corporate bona fides that include a Harvard M.B.A. and executive stints at established consumer-product companies like Disney and Hasbro, Meg Whitman is bringing conventional management experience to Ebay. But as Ms. Whitman has found, running a Web company requires adapting some of the established methods to the emergent corporate management style:  THE OLD WAY * Decisions must be made in a matter of months. * The focus is on selling consumer products. * The chief executive monitors the company image. * The chief uses a hands-off management style. * Company strategy sessions might be held once or twice a year.  THE WEB WAY * Decisions must be made in a matter of days -- or even hours. * The focus is on selling consumers an experience. * The chief executive micro-manages the company image. * The chief uses a more approachable management style. * Strategy sessions might be needed several times a week. (pg. C8)

title:
TECHNOLOGY: Digital Commerce;
A marketer says a simple step would help companies ease consumer anxiety about on-line privacy: being upfront.
body: EVERY consumer study on the subject of on-line privacy has been unequivocal: people fear being bled by data vampires on the Internet. But consider this gnawing contradiction: If consumers are so fearful of their privacy, why did more than a million people reveal virtually everything personal, short of their DNA sequences, in hopes of getting free computers and Internet access? The answer is more subtle than the polar arguments of either free-market or privacy advocates. Free PC, a hatchling from the Idealab technology incubator in Pasadena, Calif., announced earlier this year that it would give away PC's and network access to 10,000 households between April and June. To be considered, applicants agreed to accept continuous on-screen advertising. They also had to complete an exquisitely detailed personal survey so that if they were chosen, Free PC could create their household's custom advertising profile. On the face of it, collecting personal information solely to deliver custom advertising sounds like the epitome of what most would call data abuse. But what Free PC has started, albeit clumsily, appears to be precisely the model for handling personal data that privacy advocates have been championing for years. And if it succeeds, it may also signal a death rattle for today's multibillion-dollar industry for personal data. "First of all, no one really cares about privacy; they care about being surprised," said Seth Godin, an on-line marketer whose book "Permission Marketing," was just published by Simon & Schuster (www.permission.com). People claim to cherish their privacy, he said, but "your credit card company already knows everything about you -- when you're having an affair or trouble at work, when you're seeing a bankruptcy counselor -- and this doesn't bother anyone." What does bother people, Mr. Godin contends, is when the possessors of such personal information do something unexpected with it. Say, when email in-boxes suddenly start filling with pitches for cable descramblers or Viagra-by-mail ads. Or when, the day after closing the deal on a new home, unsolicited letters from mortgage insurance and interior design companies start arriving. In fact, despite their deep distrust of most companies that collect data on the Web, a majority of consumers say they are interested in providing personal data to marketers -- under the right circumstances. A recent Vanderbilt University analysis of consumer responses, "Building Consumer Trust in Online Environments: The Case for Information Privacy" (www2000.ogsm .vanderbilt.edu/papers.html), reported that more than 72 percent of Web users would relinquish their data if they were assured of "a cooperative relationship built on trust" -- specifically, if the sites would provide statements about how the data were going to be used. In Mr. Godin's lexicon, that cooperation is the essence of permission marketing, which has three basic components: it is anticipated, it is personal and it is relevant. For example, one successful permission-style on-line promotion, for H & R Block, started with banner ads that said, "Click here if you want H & R Block to pay your taxes next year." Those who responded, Mr. Godin said, were obviously interested in both the subject -- taxes -- and the prize. Then the respondents were asked whether they would participate in an eight-week email contest. The incentive was that H & R Block would pay the winner's taxes for a year. The campaign's response rate was a remarkable 35 percent, Mr. Godin said. Before being acquired by Yahoo several months ago, Mr. Godin's company, Yoyodyne, created and ran 150 of these permission-style promotions. He says that the typical response rate for them has been 10 to 20 percent, compared with about 2 percent for traditional direct-marketing techniques. So why haven't more companies embraced the permission model? "Direct marketers are scared," Mr. Godin said. "The key to their multibillion-dollar industry is the buying, renting and selling of mailing lists. Permission marketers know that selling your list guarantees it becomes worthless." And though permission is Free PC's marketing model, Bill Gross, the company's founder, says he has been shocked by the vehemence with which privacy advocates have attacked him. "The issue is not privacy," Mr. Gross said. "It's disclosure." Free PC never made any bones about what it would do with the data, Mr. Gross said. It has also agreed to protect information about its customers rigorously. The privacy policy on Free PC's Web says: "Rest assured that we will never give out your personal information to anyone. No one, including our advertisers, will be able to identify you individually. And we will never sell, trade or give away your information." In an interview, Mr. Gross described even more fastidious protections: customer data will be used only within Free PC and not by any other company affiliated with Idealab.  "We've even said that our agreement with you is transferable to any potential acquirer of the company," he said, "so we can't sell the company to anyone who would potentially change our privacy policy." Neither of these important provisos, however, is stated on the company's site (www.free-pc.com), nor does it state whether advertising partners must match its stringent privacy rules. And Mr. Grossmight also want to state the company's intentions for the data submitted by the million-plus applicants who will not receive free PC's. (He has not decided, he said.) Another good idea might be to tell people whether accepting a free PC means that they subject themselves to a lifetime of email, or whether Free PC will expunge them from the company's data base if they decide they no longer want the service. These questions are too serious to leave unanswered. But despite -- or maybe even because of -- the controversy that Free PC has generated, the company may have finally forced open the door to a marketing model that puts control of personal information in the hands of consumers, and even gives them something in return. "If I go to a consumer and say, 'I'll pay for your attention,' that is so much more interesting than an advertiser who can interrupt your life without you getting any benefit out of it," Mr. Godin said of Free PC's strategy. "People calling you at home during dinner, you can't stop. Billboards on the highway, you can't stop. But if you don't like their deal, you can stop." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Joining Together to Win at E-Commerce - Correction Appended
body: Some of the nation's biggest sporting goods retailers are banding together to back a single company that will run Internet stores for all of them. It is a novel plan fraught with potential conflicts. But the retailers hope that by joining forces with some of their traditional rivals, they will be able to block any of the Internet-only sporting goods companies, now small, from growing to dominate all of them. Like retailers in many industries, the sporting goods chains have watched with trepidation as Amazon.com captured most of the on-line book business and Etoys quickly became the biggest Internet toy store. And it is hardly consolation, for any but the biggest retailer, that Barnes & Noble and Toys "R" Us are spending tens of millions of dollars each to try to replicate their physical-world leadership in cyberspace. These fears led the Athlete's Foot, a national chain of footwear stores, and three regional sporting goods chains -- Jumbo Sports, MC Sports and Sports Chalet -- to join the venture. It is being organized by Global Sports, until now a dealer in surplus shoes. Global will design and run separate Internet sites for each of the retailers taking part. But they will use common software, inventory and shipping operations. "This allows us to enter E-commerce without having to build the back room and all the infrastructure we need," said Robert J. Corliss, the chief executive of the Athlete's Foot. "We're confident that Global will be able to pull this thing off better and in a more timely fashion than if we tried to do it ourselves." Few industries have undertaken such joint efforts. One related approach, however, is being tried by the Wine and Spirits Wholesalers of America. That trade group recently endorsed a plan in which orders that are placed on a site called Wineshipper.com will be routed to a network of local liquor stores. So far sporting goods have sold modestly on line, and the biggest players have been chains that already havemail order operations -- including REI and Venator, the nation's largest sporting goods retailer, which owns the Eastbay mail order concern. "Global's idea levels the playing field a little bit for those who aren't set up to run a business like this," said John Horan, the publisher of Sporting Goods Intelligence, a newsletter. But there are many competitors looming, from manufacturers like Nike, which will open a big Internet store in June, to Internet-only stores like Fogdog. The Global deal is the brainchild of Michael Rubin, the 25-year-old entrepreneurial prodigy who founded Global Sports. Mr. Rubin started selling skis in his parents' suburban Philadelphia basement at the age of 13, with $2,500 from bar mitzvah gifts. By 16 he had a chain of ski-gear stores. At 18, he switched to buying up surplus goods and selling them to retailers. And in recent years, he started selling shoes, buying up the ailing Ryka and Apex brands. Mr. Rubin was bitten by the Internet bug last fall after seeing stocks of other companies shoot up when they announced Internet moves. He considered opening his own on-line store to sell the close-out shoes. But he was put off by the business model, pioneered by Amazon.com, in which companies plan to lose a lot of money for years as they build their brands. So he concocted this hybrid. "We looked at what was really good about the Web-centric retailers -- they can act quickly, they can raise unlimited capital, they can use their stock as compensation and they are not measured on traditional measures like earnings," Mr. Rubin said. "And we wanted to combine that with what the traditional retailers had: brands, customers and relationships with vendors so they can get the best prices and the best products." Global will put up all the capital, pay all the expenses and take all the risk of owning inventory. It will also have the potential to earn nearly all the profits from the business, if there are any. It will pay what is in effect a royalty to each store -- something less than 10 percent of sales under its brand. Instead of expensive Internet advertising deals, Global will rely mainly on its partners for promotion. "Every retailer who works with us is obligated to put the Web site address in every ad, on every billboard, shopping bag even every register receipt," said Michael Golden, the head of Global's Internet effort. Global hopes to start the sites for these four retailers and possibly others this October. To prepare for a surge of investor interest, Global moved its stock to the Nasdaq market last week. Its share price has quadrupled since the beginning of the year, most likely because word of its Internet plans has leaked out. An unusual aspect of this arrangement is that Global will operate several sites that will appear to consumers to be direct competitors of each other. Mr. Golden said that Global would have separate teams of people to design and operate each store's site. Indeed, the same pair of running shoes could well have a slightly different price on each of the sites, because Global intends that the site it runs for each retailer will match the prices that the chain has in its stores. There is very little price competition in the sporting goods business, however, because the big manufacturers discourage deep discounting. Still, the prospect of joining a group with some of its biggest rivals has so far kept Modell's Sporting Goods, the newyork area chain, from joining Global's group. "I wonder when they are working on six or eight accounts, who will get top priority," said Mitchell Modell, the president. Still, Mr. Modell said he was intrigued by the arrangement and might yet join. "There are very few ways to get involved in the Internet where you are guaranteed a return on your investment," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Business Day on May 10 about an electronic commerce venture backed by several sporting goods retailers misstated the name of a comparable Internet site supported by wine and spirits wholesalers. It is wineshopper.com, not wineshipper.com.
