title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
As Jay Chiat auditions shops for his new company's account, his old agency doesn't have the inside track.
body: A CO-FOUNDER of one of America's best-known agencies now wants to hire an agency. And it's not likely to be the agency he once headed. Jay Chiat, who had been chairman and chief executive at Chiat/Day, the agency known for campaigns for advertisers like Apple Computer, Energizer and Nissan, is seeking a shop to handle the account of Screaming Media (www.screamingmedia.net), a newyork company in which he holds a minority stake and is temporarily acting as chief executive. Screaming Media, formerly named Interactive Connection, is in a business known as content streaming, collecting and distributing to Web sites news articles on topics such as technology, health and business. The content is meant as an incentive for computer users to visit the sites more frequently and spend more time once they are there. Mr. Chiat is not automatically awarding the assignment, with billings estimated at $3 million to $5 million, to his former agency, now named TBWA/Chiat/Day, without a review. Rather, he plans to hold what could be called an on-line audition. "We're going to do our agency search on the Internet," Mr. Chiat, 67, said last week in an interview. "Agencies can go to our Web site and send us email on why they think they should be our agency," he added. "And they can put the pitch up on the Web." "If they present a compelling story," he added, "we'll hire them." Asked if TBWA/Chiat/Day would participate in the "Chiathon" -- the nickname for the review coined by Jim Pavoldi, a salesman at Screaming Media -- Mr. Chiat replied, "They're certainly invited." "I have total respect for the agency," he said. "They're a great agency. But I want to see if agencies out there understand what we're trying to do." Mr. Chiat said that he would "probably be a minor part of the decision-making" because of his former ties to TBWA/Chiat/Day. Whether Mr. Chiat is involved or not, TBWA/Chiat/Day is bowing out of the review gracefully. "Jay and I had dinner the other night," said Bob Kuperman, president and chief executive for the Americas at TBWA Worldwide in newyork. "And I told him he'd be the worst client in the world." "I lived with the guy for 10 years," Mr. Kuperman said, laughing. "I have to have him as a client now?" Mr. Chiat co-founded Chiat/Day in 1968 with Guy Day, as they merged Faust/Day with Jay Chiat & Associates in Los Angeles. Chiat/Day's bold risk-taking for accounts like Apple (the "1984" commercial) and Energizer (E. B. the battery bunny) earned the agency a reputation for creative prowess. Mr. Chiat left Chiat/Day after it was sold to Omnicom Group in 1995 and merged with the domestic operations of TBWA International to form the TBWA/Chiat/Day unit of TBWA Worldwide. Mr. Chiat has been serving as a consultant to Omnicom as he is paid out his share of the purchase price for Chiat/Day over several years. A campaign for Screaming Media would have two purposes, said Alan S. Ellman, 36, president, who joined Mr. Chiat for the interview. One would be to attract additional Web sites as clients as well as additional sources of news articles for the content the company provides. The other would be to promote a feature now being tested that Mr. Ellman termed "contextual commerce," which "utilizes interest in editorial to sell product." Mr. Chiat explained: "We have software programs that allow us to embed applets in editorial. So you can click on a word and a window comes up with an on-site link." For instance, a computer user reading a book review could click on the title or the author's name, bringing up a Web site like Barnesandnoble.com where the book could be ordered. "The Web sites split the revenue with us," Mr. Chiat said, "and the content provider." These programs are currently being tested. Mr. Chiat and Mr. Ellman acknowledged that contextual commerce could elicit objections from those perceiving it as another way the Internet blurs the lines between editorial and commercial content. "We'll have to do it with some kind of sensitivity," Mr. Chiat said. "We don't want to turn the editorial into a throwaway shopping paper." In addition to searching for an agency, Screaming Media is also seeking a chief executive to replace Mr. Chiat, who has been handling those duties temporarily. "I went to the Steve Jobs interim- C.E.O. school of management," Mr. Chiat said, smiling, referring to Steven P. Jobs, the interim chief executive at Apple. Mr. Chiat and Mr. Ellman listed other investors in Screaming Media as Regis McKenna, president of McKenna Group, a management consulting firm in Palo Alto, Calif.; Kevin O'Connor, chairman and chief executive at Double Click in newyork, and James D. Robinson 3d, the former chairman and chief executive of the American Express Company. Mr. Chiat also has other Internet interests. He is a member of the board of Cybergold Inc. in Berkeley, Calif., and an investor in Passlogix Inc. in newyork and Softcom Video in Iselin, N.J. Comparing his experiences on Madison Avenue and in cyberspace, Mr. Chiat declared that the on-line realm "moves at a factor at least 10 times faster than an agency." "If you have a short attention span like I do," he added, "it's perfect." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Jay Chiat, former chairman and chief executive of Chiat/Day, is now temporary chief executive of Screaming Media, an Internet company. (Rebecca Cooney for The newyork Times)

title: U S West Planning to Offer Web-Linked Screen Phones
body: The U S West Corporation intends to announce today that it will introduce a phone developed by Alcatel of France that includes a color screen, pop-out keyboard and one-touch access to the World Wide Web. U S West, the smallest of the Baby Bell regional telephone companies, appears to be the first local phone giant planning for wide use of such a device in the unitedstates. It intends to make the new phone, which could cost as much as $400, available in the third quarter throughout its service region in the western part of the nation. "This is the Internet for the rest of us," Solomon Trujillo, U S West's chief executive, said in a prepared statement. "Today, half of all Americans still aren't on the Internet because it's either too complicated or too expensive. With these new phones, we're going to blow open the Internet revolution to everybody by moving email and Web access to something people are already comfortable with -- the telephone." According to U S West, users will be able to configure the new phone to reach any Internet service provider from any normal telephone line. The phone will include computer chips and software to allow users to navigate the Web by touching Web links on the screen, rather than by using a mouse, the company said. U S West said it would not cost any more to use the new phone than it would to make a conventional call. Cidco Inc. of Morgan Hill, Calif., a leading maker of caller ID equipment, is among a handful of other companies that have developed a "smart phone." But while Cidco's unit includes email, it does not include full-fledged Web access. U S West said the new phone could support simultaneous Web sessions and normal phone calls only if the customer uses an advanced telephone technology called a digital subscriber line. On normal lines, the new phone will be able to support normal calls or Web browsing, but not both at the same time. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING: AT THE GATE;
Before Salon's Offering, Some Negative Reviews
body: IT is one thing for investors to bet their money on an initial public offering of an Internet company with a speculative but potentially lucrative business model. But analysts say next month's planned offering of Salon Internet seems to go several steps further, asking investors to put money into a flawed business model that happens to operate on line. Since 1995, Salon has operated as an Internet opinion magazine. (Think The Village Voice without the classifieds.) Contributors include Garrison Keillor and Camille Paglia. Yet analysts say that the business falls short on a number of fronts -- and that they are just plain confused about some numbers in the prospectus. Salon, for example, said it had about 1.2 million Internet visitors in March of this year, a healthy increase from 790,000 in March 1998. The numbers sound impressive. But Media Metrix, a company that measures Web traffic, isn't sure what the numbers refer to. It counted 521,000 Salon visitors in March 1999. According to Doug McFarland, senior vice president of Media Metrix, Salon's larger traffic numbers may take international users into account. But it is also likely, he said, that Salon, like many other Internet companies, is counting the total number of server hits that its sites receive, rather than individual users. Salon, based in San Francisco, declined to comment, because the company has entered the quiet period after the registration of its offering. But on April 28, Kaitlin Quistgaard, an associate editor at Salon, wrote an article on the site that took issue with Media Metrix's methodology for measuring traffic. Another worry is Salon's short roster of paying users in its Salon Member program, which furnishes members with email and discounts on Salon merchandise. It costs as little as $20 a year, yet had only about 1,050 members as of March. "Salon doesn't present a compelling traffic story," said Patrick Keane, an analyst at Jupiter Communications, a consulting firm. Salon is trying to attract more paying members. In March, it bought the Well, a virtual community that at the time had 7,000 paying members, for an undisclosed amount. In early April, Salon announced that it planned to add more news to its own site. But Neil Barsky, co-founder of the Midtown Research Group, which tracks initial offerings, said Salon's "huge" amount of content, and its move to provide more news, makes for a high-cost business model. The issue of advertising raises a flag, too. During the nine months ended Dec. 31, so-called barter transactions, in which it swaps free ads with other companies, accounted for $307,000, or 15 percent, of Salon's $2.1 million in revenues. The offering is expected to be priced at $10.50 to $13.50 a share. With 10.73 million shares outstanding, that would give Salon a market value of $113 million to $145 million. The company, which will officially change its name to Salon.com, plans to sell 2.5 million shares. Like most Internet companies, Salon loses money. But analysts are concerned that its expenses are so much greater than revenue. For the nine months ended Dec. 31, Salon lost $4.3 million on revenue of $2.1 million, versus a loss of $2.9 million on revenue of $689,000 for the comparable 1997 period. Of course, many investors want quick profits on new Internet stocks, selling them shortly after the offerings. But Salon is going public via an on-line process introduced recently by W. R. Hambrecht & Company, a San Francisco brokerage firm. Hambrecht conducts so-called Dutch auctions, in which the price is set at the highest possible level that allows all shares to be sold. So Salon's stock probably won't get the initial pop in price that many other Internet stocks have enjoyed. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos

title:
MARKET INSIGHT;
Is Midnight Near at the Technology Ball?
body: NO party lasts a lifetime, but since early November investors in technology shares of a variety of stripes have been in full boogie mode. From a 52-week low on Nov. 6 until April 9, its most recent peak, Morgan Stanley's High-Tech 35 Index gained more than 64 percent; many Internet stocks performed far better. The index has since cooled a bit, as money has moved into more staid -- and cheaper -- cyclicals. Still, through Friday, the index remained 47 percent above its November low. And Morgan Stanley's on-line brokerage unit is still running television ads of adolescents with their own helicopters and tow-truck operators who own islands. Or is it countries? The ads don't seem to be aimed at those who buy stocks for the dividend checks. Charles A. Morris, who has managed the $5.8 billion T. Rowe Price Science and Technology fund since 1991, took some time last week to talk about the sector and the possibility of a tech wreck. Q. People have been talking about a major correction in technology for some time. Is what we are seeing now the start of that, or is it the beginning of something else? A.  I don't think the rotation we are seeing indicates an end to the technology cycle, because technology reinvents itself every decade. During the 1980's, it was automation of the back office and deployment of mainframe and minicomputers. In the 1990's, it has been personal computers and cellular. Now, the industry is reinventing itself to Internet-work computing. Since these things tend to run in 10-year waves, arguably this particular cycle is just beginning. The real question is what happens over the very near term, because we have come a little too far, too fast. Technology funds are about 100 percent off the lows established last fall. Over the last 12 to 15 years it hasn't gotten much better than that without a correction of around 15 percent. That thins out the herd and sets the stage for the next leg up. In addition, tech stocks tend to do better in the fall and winter months than they do between April Fool's Day and Halloween. And Y2K is another complicating factor, because it may lead to a slowdown in spending in summer and early fall. Lastly, you have to look at some of the froth in the market, most specifically in the Internet sector. So all of that has to give you pause over the next three to six months. Q. What about Internet stocks? Aren't they likely be the hardest hit in the sector? A. You are already seeing signs that the Internet market is starting to tire. Amazon.com made a series of announcements recently that three months ago would have sent its stock up 30 percent. This time, the stock fell. You have seen some initial public offerings that have been mediocre performers. Indeed, Comps.com, which was priced on Tuesday, finished below the offering price when it traded on Wednesday. If you can get a meaningful correction of 30 percent to 50 percent across the Internet space, the market capitalization of these stocks will start to represent economic reality and encourage institutional ownership. Over the next three years, the median return for the Internet group is going to be negative. But a small minority of those stocks will put up terrific valuations that make today's valuations look low. Q. What is a realistic way to value Internet companies that have no earnings? A.  Wall Street has everyone fixated on a ratio of price to revenues. We didn't like that, and for the last six weeks we have been using what we think is a more practical valuation method, which starts with the multiple of revenues relative to a company's market capitalization. Once you get that number, then divide it by the target net margin a company aspires to in the future. This method allows you to compare stocks within the Internet stocks as well as to more traditional companies. Q. How much of an individual's portfolio should be invested in technology over all? A. People should have anywhere from 5 percent to 15 percent of their financial assets in this class. The more money they have to lose, the greater the percentage can be. Q. Have you been raising cash in anticipation of a blowoff? A.  Typically, between 3 percent and 7 percent of our fund's assets are in cash. Right now we are on the high side. Q. Which stocks do you like? A. We run a fairly balanced portfolio by sector. Five sectors comprise 80 percent of the fund's assets: software, communications equipment and services, hardware, semiconductors and information services. Our three largest positions are PSInet, a business Internet service provider, America Online and Softbank, which I think of as a closed-end mutual fund for Internet holdings. Our favorite holds include MCI Worldcom, Airtouch Communications, Xilinx, Adobe Systems, Ascend and Cisco. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Charles Morris

title:
MARKET WATCH;
An Internet Pl ay for Widows and Orphans
body: AT&T'S transformation from telecommunications dinosaur to technology-stock dynamo may have been clinched this week with the company's $58 billion deal to buy Mediaone Group, one of the nation's biggest cable television operators. The deal, combined with the recent purchase of Tele-Communications Inc., means that AT&T will become the largest cable company in the unitedstates, with 16 million customers and networks reaching more than 26 million homes. Mediaone is the latest in a spate of acquisitions -- $124 billion worth -- made by C. Michael Armstrong since he took the top job at AT&T 18 months ago. The deal maker has morphed the 114-year-old behemoth into the kind of hot technology concern favored by day traders on the Internet. Widows and orphans, say hello to the Motley Fool. The vision that Mr. Armstrong, 60, has for his company is vast. "The new AT&T is a global communications company that can satisfy customers end to end with any service, anywhere," he said in an interview Friday. Can he really provide local and long-distance phone service, wireless communications, Internet access and cable TV service to consumers around the world? Taking a vision this large and turning it into reality will take years, of course. The technical challenges are daunting. But while at AT&T, Mr. Armstrong has turned skeptics into believers by making good on all that he has promised so far. Revenue growth and earnings targets have been met. The $1.6 billion he vowed to cut from expenses in two years vanished in one. And the 15,000 jobs he planned to cut over 24 months became 20,000 jobs eliminated in 12. In the meantime, AT&T, unlike technology upstarts, had $53 billion in revenues last year, $6.4 billion in earnings and -- what's this? -- a dividend. At Friday's close of $60.4375, the stock yielded 1.46 percent. Dave Powers, senior technology analyst at Edward Jones in St. Louis, said AT&T was well positioned to capitalize on the need for increased network capacity, known as bandwidth, to reduce data bottlenecks. "Before, people looked at AT&T and saw the bulk of their revenues came from consumer long distance, a business under attack," Mr. Powers said. "And AT&T equipment had fallen behind the technology curve. But now the focus is going from consumer long distance to a company offering these broadband pipes, a much more exciting player." Mr. Armstrong, 60, is rooted in technology. He spent 31 years at I.B.M., starting in 1961, and managed research and development of Big Blue's communications systems and personal computers from 1981 to 1987, years of much turmoil in the PC business. He was running I.B.M. Latin America when he left in 1992. AT&T's chief also knows how to refashion a company under siege. From 1992 to 1997, he was chairman of General Motors' Hughes Electronics division, a defense contractor he dragged into the commercial satellite business when the cold war ended. G.M.'s Class H shares more than quadrupled during Mr. Armstrong's tenure. But his biggest act yet may be turning stodgy AT&T into a top-performing technology stock that even a conservative investor can love. The stock has risen almost 20 percent so far this year. But at 28 times trailing earnings, it is downright cheap for an Internet play. Especially one that has real assets, a healthy balance sheet and, perhaps best of all, management over the age of consent. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks monthly closes of AT&T stock since 1982.

title:
Q&A/Linda C. Fentiman;
Call to Monitor Long-Distance Health Care
body: TELE-MEDICINE is a field where law and ethics are lagging far behind what is going on, said Linda C. Fentiman, director of the Health Law and Policy Program at Pace University School of Law in White Plains. It is a trend that not only has the potential to expand access dramatically to quality health care, she said, but also to make it more impersonal, to reduce health-care costs -- or even increase them -- and to destroy a patient's right to privacy. And, she asks, Who should be regulating such practitioners? Tele-medicine is medicine at a distance. It may mean a local doctor consults a colleague at a teaching hospital by means of a teleconference, and perhaps the patient's X-rays are shared by modem and other high-tech equipment. It also encompasses tele-pharmacy, where medicines are sold on the Internet, and tele-health, where health information, not all of it reliable, is shared on Internet home pages. Ms. Fentiman, who lives in Manhattan, was a criminal defense lawyer in California in the 1970's. She was drawn to health law after representing clients who used mental-state defenses, and that interest spilled over to the bio-ethics law field and then the business aspects of health care law. Here are excerpts from a recent conversation with her: Q. What is the negative side of tele-medicine? A. There are several negatives and a lot of uncertainty. The real potential negative is that it may change the physician-patient relationship. Now, even in the managed-care era, we are accustomed to having a physician whom we consult on a regular basis, who knows us. With tele-medicine we're more likely to have a more complicated relationship with both our local physician and another physician at a distant location. There are questions about what are the ethical obligations the tele-physician owes a distant patient. There may be concern about patient privacy and confidentiality. When a patient is in a physician's office, she knows that the physician is examining her, but there is no one else there to see her. If it's a tele-mediated consultation, then not only will a physician and other health-care professionals at a distance "see" her but so also may technical people, video support people. So she may not be aware how much her personal privacy might be compromised. And there is the possibility that lots of her data may be sent over the Internet in order to do an effective tele-diagnosis. Q. What are the issues involved in the purchase of prescription drugs on the Internet? A. People have long been able to mail away a prescription to sort of a wholesaler and get their drugs in that way, and no one saw any problems. Now, there is no reason your local doctor couldn't order a prescription and you could order it over the Internet. The interesting new thing is how many of these Internet pharmacies have pharmacists who are answering questions as well as filling orders that are placed over the Internet. Virtually every state, including newyork, requires that a pharmacist be licensed in the state in which he is prescribing medication. There seems to be a potential problem if a pharmacist in, say, Chicago is answering questions for a patient in newyork and if that pharmacist is not licensed to practice pharmacy in newyork. So there are questions about whether the newyork oversight board can effectively limit or regulate or scrutinize what the tele-pharmacist is doing and is he or she practicing pharmacy in newyork without a license? Q. The answer is unclear at this time? A. Right. It hasn't been litigated. The on-line pharmacist has only been on line for under six months. Q. What do you think of reports of doctors on the Internet prescribing without face-to-face consultation? A. That seems very scary. Clearly, that physician doesn't have any personal observation of the patient, and the heart of the physician-patient relationship is face-to-face contact -- looking and touching. And also being able to pick up nuances in how a patient is telling about his symptoms. All that is missed when practicing via the Internet. There is a trade-off, perhaps, in the traditional tele-medicine setting between intimate contact and observation with a more accurate diagnosis. What you're getting through tele-medicine is often a high-tech second opinion. Often that is worthwhile for a patient who can't come to a major academic setting -- either it's too far or too expensive or the patient can't take time off from work. That patient can save a great deal of resources by having a tele-medicine consultation, but then the patient is relying on his local physician to fill in the gaps, to consult with the tele-doctor. Q. For decades there have been people who looked to other countries for certain drugs they could not obtain here. Doesn't the Internet pull those barriers down further? A. Yes, and that can be the plus of tele-medicine -- that it helps pull down barriers to access and quality of health care. And it puts the patient potentially more in charge of his own medicine treatment. But at the same time we don't have the paternalistic state medical board or paternalistic Food and Drug Administration protecting the patient from his own folly. The Food and Drug Administration has erred on the side of patient protection, generally speaking, screening out drugs if it's not absolutely certain that they're safe and effective. Now sometimes that is bad because patients sometimes don't get access to drugs that other countries think are effective. But sometimes it is good. The F.D.A. prevented the use of thalidomide in this country precisely because there was a very zealous F.D.A. scientist who said, "I see this causes birth defects in armadillos, and I'm not going to let it in this country." It was available in other countries. So the Internet makes medicine much harder to control. One of the issues is: if a person, say, in newyork was practicing tele-medicine on a patient in California, whose laws would govern? Q. Where do you see this going in the way of regulation? A. Different states, through their legislatures, have adopted varying approaches. California is very liberal in allowing it as long as the patient signs an informed consent form that says, I know I'm being diagnosed via tele-medicine. Georgia and Oklahoma, for example, have taken very protective stances. In Georgia you cannot practice tele-medicine in most cases unless you're doing it for free or you're doing it through the University of Georgia. newyork's position is that you can't practice tele-medicine on a patient in newyork unless you're licensed to practice medicine in newyork. And a lot of it is kind of turf protection. Now the interesting thing about this is: generally, medicine in the unitedstates has become much more national, so every physician in the unitedstates goes to a medical school approved by the A.M.A. Data about malpractice and other negative information about a physician goes to the national health care practitioner data bank. It is kind of ironic that at a time that we're recognizing that medicine is national in scope, states are digging in their heels and saying, Only our doctors within our borders can treat our patients. It's really an economic issue rather than a patient-protection issue. Q. How is the Federal Government supposed to deal with the confidentiality issues? A. Congress is required by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, which it passed, to act by this August to issue national confidentiality regulations. So far, there has been no action. But what has also happened is that newyork did a big study of patient confidentiality issues and decided that it would wait until after the Federal Government acted. So right now the law is very outdated because it assumes that all these medical records are on paper. The ongoing debate is: how protective should we be? Q. This is quite an emerging field, isn't it, where law and ethics are not resolved at all? A. Right. It has the promise to improve the quality of care, but if private insurers and Medicare and Medicaid won't pay for these services, then that becomes an issue. And if it becomes the norm that you always have to have a high-tech second opinion, that will drive up the cost of health care. And there is another area, the question of tele-health -- people who get information over the Internet. This affects the whole patient-physician relationship. It used to be patients relied on physicians to give them information -- now you have patients who can surf the net. But there is no control on the Internet in terms of the accuracy of information. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Linda C. Fentiman, head of Health Law and Policy Program at Pace University School of Law in White Plains. (Chris Maynard for The newyork Times)

title: School Districts Merge Studies and Technology
body: AMID the clutter of paintbrushes, chisels and lumps of clay in Jayne Karlin's classroom at Byram Hills High School here, there was something else that did not quite fit in: a computer, whose screen held moving images of camels against a backdrop of Egyptian pyramids and tombs. Its presence was just as important for Ms. Karlin's students' recent project on Egyptian burial jars as the clay or paint used in ceramics and sculpture class. As part of the school district's combining technology with curriculum, students in Ms. Karlin's class used a software program called Web Quest to research ancient Egypt, develop a design for their projects and answer questions. "The idea was to give them more of a research base before a production base," Ms. Karlin said. "I'm not a tech-y person, but with this program, students have to really research each site." Even as the Federal Government has begun a substantial program to link all schools to the Internet and many districts have begun to make investments in computer hardware and software, some educators, parents and taxpayers remain concerned about the role technology should play in the classroom. With yearly spending of $5 billion nationally on school computers, the application of computers in the classroom has come under increasing scrutiny, on issues ranging from its impact on the posture and physical health of children to the potential dangers and benefits of searching the Internet. Computers sometimes seem to drive the lesson plans, instead of being a tool that teachers could use in a lesson, both supporters and skeptics say. "The integration of new technology into the schools has been slower than we thought," said Jack Goodman, publisher of Net Guider, a Mount Kisco-based company, which produces software using the Internet with lesson plans in specific subject areas. "It's still dominated by a game-oriented mentality, but we are seeing more districts using computers as an educational tool, not just as a computer." A study released in February from the CEO Forum in Education and Technology -- a Washington-based coalition of business leaders that seeks to help students meet higher education standards -- reported that the number of public schools with Internet access had risen to 78 percent from 35 percent between 1994 and 1997. What had not increased, however, was teacher training -- at least one-third of the schools surveyed did not have the equipment or programs to provide appropriate training. Depending on the district, and in many cases depending on the teacher, computers can be used to underscore a science lesson or perform an experiment or re-create a medieval village or give drills in math and vocabulary. "We're not finding systemic application of the technology," said Peter Reilly, director of education technology for the Lower Hudson Regional Information Center in Elmsford. The center is a nonprofit consortium, which helps schools use technology. "Districts have been spotty. In the past, we saw lots of word processing and writing. Now we're seeing more actual publishing and research on the Internet." Some districts, like Byram Hills, have been on the leading edge with moving technology from a goal in itself to a educational tool. In Pelham, foreign language students use video equipment in language labs to practice their listening and speaking skills. Science students, from elementary grades through high school, use software programs that enable them to do experiments like testing the half-life of a radioactive substance. Computers have transformed technological projects. Students can work with software programs to solve problems that would previously have been handled with wrenches or hammers. In Elmsford, students can borrow laptop computers the same way they borrow library books, and at Westlake High School in Thornwood, high school students have conducted video conferences with their counterparts in Vienna and Florence. Insuring that all teachers in a district are comfortable with incorporating technology into their lesson plans is the next step in the technology initiative, many educators say. "Technology can profoundly change how children learn in the classroom," said Dudley Hare, executive director of the Westchester Education Coalition, a nonprofit organization based at Manhattanville College in Purchase. "We are seeing the next application of computers in the classroom, where the computer is now a vehicle, or tool, to answer a focus question." Districts that have succeeded in making the shift have spent money and time to prepare their teachers. "One of the problems for schools was that previously students were using the computers to give back facts and information," said Jackie Taylor, Assistant Superintendent for the Byram Hills School District, which started the Web Quest initiative last September. She continued: "The kinds of projects Web Quest inspires minimize the retelling of facts and require students to be active learners. Technology has to be imbedded in the curriculum. We want them to use the Internet effectively. The idea is for them to have a task that puts them in the role of having to accomplish something in the world." At Byram Hills High School, a group of students in a science class produced a Web Quest project on the solar system and planets. In a social studies class, the teacher, Steven Garcia, had developed a Web Quest project designed to teach students about the structure of daily life in a medieval village. For one sophomore, David Berke, who conceded that he had been nervous about computers in his freshman year, using Web Quest turned out to be an exciting experience. "Last year, all I did was memorize," David said. "This year was the first time I really was able to use computers. I can go on the Internet and apply what I learned." Even as districts like Byram Hills try to use technology to the students' advantage, concern remains about the growing technology gap between affluent districts and districts that have yet to use computers in the classroom. "There are inequities that exist among schools in the county," said Dr. Hare, whose organization recently sponsored a conference that dealt, in part, with how teachers could help their students produce academically sound projects. "In one district, you can have multiple machines, an integrated curriculum and well-trained teachers. Step across a district line, and you have schools with only one or two computers in an entire building, where students don't have access to the Internet." Ideally, computers would be a nearly invisible tool. "When I send people to look at sites, I want them to see where technology is part of the infrastructure instead of where technology smacks you in the face," Mr. Reilly said. "It should be a place where technology stands out by blending in."  Computers Change School Libraries CHAPPAQUA School libraries have undergone a metamorphosis from sleepy reference rooms to 2lst-century media centers where a district's technology program rises or falls on the library staff. "Informational literacy is the new hot item," said Linda Chapman, a library media specialist from the Somers Central School District. "Before, library skills were confined to the four walls of the library and were isolated skills in an independent curriculum. The problem now is that there is too much information. Now we teach information skills that integrate content and skills in collaboration with the classroom teacher." Of course, the school library still has books and story times, but now the library media specialist is responsible for managing electronic information, steering children to Web sites and showing teachers and students how to conduct an Internet search. At a recent conference on literacy and testing standards at Reader's Digest world headquarters here, the role of the media center was seen as critical. "The challenge is how to teach children to manage information," said Joanne Scolaro, a library media specialist for the Chappaqua school district. "The skills students need are different to function in the next century. The library is now the place where students are equal." One of the most important functions a library media specialist can perform is helping teachers refine research projects to focus on a manageable problem. Guidance on accessing the Internet and where to search are also part of the specialist's new role. Knowing when to use books and other traditional resources or the Internet is another aspect of their role. "We don't want to hear, 'My topic is," Ms. Chapman said. "We need to hear, 'My research question is.' "   MERRI ROSENBERG http://www.nytimes.com

title:
STYLE OVER SUBSTANCE;
To the Flea Market in Pajamas on Ebay
body: AMONG my friends, Ebay is hotter than Britney Spears. On-line bidding on everything from lady-head planters to Batman bubble bath bottles has become a daily ritual for us at home, at work, even at the gym. One pal, who doesn't own a personal computer but does have the East Village's largest collection of poodle bric-a-brac, bids on ceramic pooches and velvet dog paintings while sweating on the treadmill. His health club has a Web TV setup in its cardiovascular workout area. He and his wallet are thinner than ever. Internet shopping for canine kitsch has not entirely replaced his flea market habit, or mine. But the convenience of virtual browsing on Ebay -- the on-line auction servicethat is a national swap meet for 6.5 million users -- has become a shared obsession for our little clique. Why traipse to 26th Street at the crack of 9 every Sunday morning when you can hunt for junk in your pajamas any night of the week and still sleep in? Besides, the pickings are better in cyberspace than in the flower district. In the last six months, I have successfully bid on four superhero drinking glasses from Pizza Hut from 1976, a footed tiki bowl from a defunct Polynesian restaurant in Las Vegas, a vase shaped like Barbie, a set of 90 "Munsters" trading cards, six Archie comics jelly glasses with Sabrina's head embossed on the bottom, a glossy of Gypsy Rose Lee on "The Mike Douglas Show" and a copy of Phyllis Diller's last book (which at $11.50, including shipping, seemed like a real steal). It would have taken years to find such a diverse haul in person. Every time an Ebay-brokered shipment arrives in a recycled Kool-Aid carton or one of post office issue, I open it with the enthusiasm of a 6-year-old. My domestic accomplice, a clutter-hating proponent of financial responsibility, says: "Save the box. We're going to have to live in it someday." But I can't stop, even if I may soon need a warehouse. No pastime gives me greater pleasure than giving a good home to a Supergirl glass that was sitting in someone's basement in Kissimmee, Fla. for the last 20 years. Of course, Ebay is not limited to the ephemera my friends and I treasure. You can bid on vintage clothes, art, even real estate. But Ebay's true flavor comes from offerings more kitschy than vintage Chanel -- a rare pickle jar that sold for $44,000 in March is more quintessentially Ebay than a cashmere sweater that went for $220. The on-line auction house may not specialize in "junque," but it does sell a lot of it. Recent statistics estimate that Ebay users exchanged more than $500 million of merchandise last year and that fully one in 20 packages sent between private individuals via the post office is a purchase made on Ebay. That's a lot of tchotchkes changing hands. Even those of us whose idea of heaven is spending 10 hours trudging through 1,600 booths at an Atlantic City collectibles show are sometimes surprised by the things people collect. USA Weekend, a Sunday magazine insert to many newspapers, reported recently that Glenn Wright, a building contractor from Bothell, Wash., will make seven figures on Ebay this year selling a stash of antique fruit crate labels that he and a partner amassed. They called him the "fruit label millionaire." Last month, a 13-year-old boy from Haddonfield, N.J., spent like one. He bid away $3.2 million of his parents' money on such objects as a $1.2 million medical center in Jacksonville, Fla.; a van Gogh sketch, a 1971 Corvette convertible and a $400,000 bedroom suite that belonged to Canada's first Prime Minister, Sir John A. Macdonald. There were no poodle plates on his list, but my friends could relate. We've all overspent in a heated moment, bidding more than we should in the final minutes of an auction for lilac Fiestaware or a mint, box-fresh Hall China gold-dot casserole. Unlike our spending sprees, however, the New Jersey boy's bids were suspended. "We're not rolling in bucks," his mother told The Newark Star-Ledger last month. "I don't know if he decided it was a game." Actually, that's exactly what Ebay is. Navigating through the now-familiar Web site is like poking through the stalls of any flea market in search of that one item that will complete a collection or start a new one. My new Holy Grail is a set of "Hollywood Squares" collectors plates from the 1970's. A friend has one, but I want them all. I check in every day to see if someone is selling Rose Marie. As auctions progress, it's exciting to see how much people are willing to spend for such articles -- not to mention how they'll splurge on the type of toys their mothers gave away when they left for college in 1974 -- and to note which postings go ignored. It's interesting, too, to see which brand-new items become instant collectibles. Beanbags shaped like characters from the 60's Christmas special "Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer," for instance, which were sold at CVS stores last December to nostalgic baby boomers for about $5 each, are already commanding much higher prices. There is comfort in knowing that someone else is willing to pay 20 bucks for a stuffed Abominable Snowman. At a cocktail party I attended two weeks ago, a young computer-savvy man told me that in the last month he'd earned enough money selling on Ebay to buy a DVD player. His take was hundreds, not the millions of the fruit-label guy, but it was a start. He sold the T-shirts, snow globes and photographs that press agents had sent him over the years to promote new movies or television shows, things that had filled his cubicle at work and would most likely have ended up in the trash should he ever change jobs. "People will buy anything," he said. Having just spent $10 on a copy of the Totie Fields mashed-potato-diet book, who was I to argue? http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Lisa Haney)

title: Agreement Reached on Internet Privacy
body: In its second Internet-privacy enforcement action, the Federal Trade Commission said today that a multibillion-dollar investment company had agreed to change the way its World Wide Web site treated information it gathered from children and teen-agers. The commission announced a settlement with Liberty Financial Companies of Boston, whose Young Investor Web site has advertised itself as "a place to learn about money and maybe even earn some, too." The F.T.C. said Liberty Financial had not kept its promise that all data collected from users would be kept "totally anonymous." The company, whose survey asked Web site users about their weekly allowances, whether their parents were saving for their college education and other financial matters, actually used the information to identify specific individuals, the Government alleged. The company also failed to keep promises to send email newsletters and to award prizes in contests designed to appeal to children, the Government said. Robert Pitofsky, the trade commission's chairman, said Liberty Financial had agreed to post a more detailed privacy notice on its Web site and to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting personal identifying information from children. Hal Thayer, a spokesman for the company, which manages assets worth $61 billion, said today that Liberty Financial had kept the information it gleaned from children "confidential," if not strictly anonymous, and had never misused it. "Liberty Financial supports completely the F.T.C. policy to protect the privacy of children," Mr. Thayer said. Last August, in the Government's first Internet-privacy enforcement, the trade commission reached a settlement with Geocities, an organization based in California that offers members their own Web pages, email addresses and information of topics of interest to them. The trade commission said Geocities had lied when it told more than two million subscribers, both adults and children, that it would not disclose personal information it collected. In fact, the commission said, the information was used by advertisers. Geocities did not admit wrongdoing.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Stalking That Rare Recording
body: Take pity on the next generation of music fiends, for they may not know the pleasure of loitering in little record stores. People in their 20's, 30's and 40's, less and less guilty about shopping on the Internet, are regularly denying themselves the chance to go into a record shop and just look. In their defense, they complain that the clerks don't know the stock or know too much and beam out rays of fringe-scholar intimidation. Or buyers talk about what a waste of time it has become to go to a real store, although some of the bigger virtual record shops on line say they've got stock when they don't and end up sending out records six months later or not at all. As a suburban teen-ager within bus distance of newyork, I did a lot of growing up on my trips in the early 80's to specialist record stores, looking for funk, jazz, rock and punk. I discovered new neighborhoods, learned how to hold my own with older people, discovered places to eat and figured out whom I didn't want to talk to. I realize now with a sense of alarm what I might have lost if I had had access to the Internet with its current level of sophistication. I also contracted a mild form of the itch that still strikes when I see some long-coveted record or CD: the sensory love of the object. There's something about record stores, as kiosks of information, as places where you can learn about style, slang, art and sound, that I will never want to reject, no matter how much I struggle against the idea that records, as opposed to performance, can properly teach you about music. But there's still a place for independent, specialist record stores in newyork, despite the increasing availability of almost anything on line and the increasing dominance of chain stores like Tower, HMV and Virgin. Sometimes the ethnic and social profile of a neighborhood supports a store; sometimes a store presents a certain style so well and completely that one wouldn't want to go anywhere else to find it. Sometimes it's just a heady pit stop, the equivalent of a barbershop or cafe. Sometimes the stores become the origin of the music, not just the middlemen, as more record shops move into distributing hard-to-find records or just setting up their own record label. Each one of those CD's sent around the world is publicity for the store, and they're cheaper when you buy them at the source. I recently spent several pleasant days around the city revisiting some independent record stores, retailers of mostly new records. These stores have survived the dark days through specialization and fearsome knowledge of their own product. Almost all the stores below serve customers by mail order; some are getting a leg up on their competition by establishing Web sites.  African Music To walk into Roger Francis's AFRICAN RECORD CENTER is to experience that rare feeling of knowing that you did, in fact, get there before some other people. You can't believe you're seeing these racks full of pasteboard-cover LP's. Mr. Francis, a Brooklynite, has owned the African Record Center in East Flatbush since 1968, and from the beginning made trips to Africa to import the music. He started the Makossa label, which he runs out of the back room; his was the first place where records by Manu Dibango, Fela Kuti, Franco and others could be found in newyork. He has also organized American tours for some African artists. "We introduced African music to the unitedstates," said Mr. Francis, not quite suppressing a grin. "I will make that statement humbly but boastfully at the same time." He still keeps racks full of Nigerian, Ghanaian, Ethiopian, Cameroonian, Zairian, Haitian and Cuban LP's as well as CD's. Zouk music, from Martinique, is his bread and butter these days. Mr. Francis's brother Rudy runs the Yoruba Book Center, two blocks away, which specializes in books of the black diaspora. Its wares include the entire catalogue of the local Athelia Henrietta Press, which publishes books on Yoruban religion and culture. The bookshop also sells hard-to-find LP's of African and Haitian music, and its biggest sellers are cassettes of Yoruban religious music. The best seller at African Record Center is "Soukous Vibrations, Vol. 5" (Afro-Rhythms). I bought Lafayette Afro Rock Band's "Voodounon" (Editions Makossa), an LP, for $10.  Latin Music A chain store has moved in one block away from BATE, one of the city's oldest Latin-music stores, on Delancey Street on the Lower East Side. It makes Anna and Dominick Torres, owners of 31-year-old Bate, a little worried, as does the changing profile of the neighborhood; it's no longer the Latin stronghold it used to be. But Bate has something that many chains don't: back-catalogue items. In the rear of the store -- it's really two stores in one, with a separate counter for the rhythm-and-blues and hip-hop section -- the racks are deep with Fania, Harlequin and Tumbao, the collector labels of salsa. It's one of the few places in the city with a decent supply of Cuban music. In 1962, six years before the Torreses started Bate, Cristina Barreiro's father, Alfonso Rubio, opened CASA LATINA, a Latin-music record store on East 116th Street in East Harlem. Rubio, who died in 1978, was an Argentine tailor who fled Buenos Aires with his family when President Juan Peron decided to widen Avenida de Mayo and gave merchants 24 hours to vacate. "In '62, when my mother died," Ms. Barreiro said, "he wanted me to have a place that I could go to after school. So I used to leave school and come to the store." Ms. Barreiro has been working at the store since 1966; she now runs the place with her husband, Vicente.  The long, deep store, full of CD's, books, videos and percussion instruments, is becoming a city landmark. With the recent closing of the Record Mart in Times Square, Bate and Casa Latina are the best-stocked Latin music stores in the city; they're also places where you can sing a fragment of a song you've heard on the radio, and the owners will decipher and name it for you. "Vicente's a walking computer," Ms. Barreiro said. "Other stores used to call Casa Latina when a customer didn't know what he was looking for, and Vicente would help out. But he had to stop doing that. Now he just tells them that we have it." Casa Latina also sells congas, bongos, guiros and shekeres, as well as concert videos and books on salsa and Afro-Cuban music. At Casa Latina the best seller is Tito Rojas's "Alegria y Penas" (MP/Sony). I bought El Gran Combo's "Pasaporte Musical" (Combo) for $13.99.  Rock and the Fringe ROCKIT SCIENTIST in Greenwich Village feels familiar, like the one-stop shops that flourished in the 80's: small and narrow, a one-man operation, with tightly pruned sections that try to represent every strand of Western world hipsterism since 1955 or so. John Kioussis, a former manager of Venus Records, presides here, wedged between a cash register and turntable up front, offering advice and filling the room with loud music. Every good record store is for snobs, but the genre pool in Rockit Scientist tends toward the open-minded. Mr. Kioussis is especially good on 60's rock and soul, with respectable sections of reggae and jazz. OTHER MUSIC in the East Village, many times bigger, gets deeply into the outsider niche; anything nontraditional has rack space here. It's startling to find the shop so full of people late on a Sunday, milling around the brightly lighted store looking for fringe culture. This shop was founded a little more than three years ago by former clerks from the music section at Kim's Video on Bleecker Street, and since then the staff has grown to 20 from 3. The store now sells tickets to concerts around town, and the sections, like the store's habitues, keep dividing further and further into specifics. What was once "electronic music" now has separate sections for German minimalists and Vienna composers; what was once called "decadanse" now has separate sections for Japanese, French and Italian pop. (This is where you find retro flavors like the old records by Lucio Battisti, Nico and Francoise Hardy.) The store is the only place to find a three-CD set by the Dutch electronic composer Dick Raiijmakers; most of the records of the late-60's Brazilian Tropicalia movement, or the beautifully packaged "Tarot" album by the German musician Walter Wegmuller. One of the success stories of alternative culture in newyork, the shop presents the corners exceedingly well and doesn't bother at all with the mainstream. The best seller at Other Music is Tom Waits's new album, "Mule Variations" (Epitath). I bought Oval's "Szenario" (Tokuma), an import CD, for $22.99.  Reggae "When I was growing up, everyone wanted to be in a band," said Ira Heaps, the proprietor of the reggae record shop JAMMYLAND in the East Village. "Now everyone wants to be a D.J." So he changed his shop, which had been open since 1993, accordingly. Then, around 1996 he noticed that dub music -- extended remixes of reggae songs with deep echo and tape-edit experimentation -- had taken on a different meaning, bridging with the new electronic music. So he began to specialize in dub and stock as much vinyl as CD's; he may soon be the manufacturer and distributor of the vinyl albums from Blood and Fire, the English dub label. Jammyland, narrow, plentiful and homey -- there's an exposed kitchen in the back -- carries a small amount of African music and electronic dance music. But what makes it special is its supply of records on labels like Justice League, Reggae Retro and Clocktower, which aren't available at chains. The best seller is Augustus Pablo's "This is Augustus Pablo" (Above Rock Music/Jammyland). I bought that CD for $11.99.  Hip-Hop There are two D.J. booths at BEAT STREET in downtown Brooklyn, and three full-time D.J.'s, all continually pumping out loud hip-hop and reggae beats through enormous speakers. Amazingly, they don't quite clash; the downstairs space is that wide and deep. And students of rhythm are always standing around the booths. Beat Street is hip-hop central; this is where D.J.'s shop and where they can walk out with stacks of old breakbeat records as well as what's just hit the street. This is also where you find a full complement of kung fu videos, the new Missy Elliott single or a copy of Herman Kelly's "Dance to the Drummer's Beat," which is to an old-school hip-hop D.J. set what tomatoes are to chili. The best seller is Nas's "I Am . . ." (Columbia). I bought ESG's, "Come Away With ESG" (99), an LP, for $10.99.  Arabic Raymond Rashid inherited his record-and-video store, RASHID'S in Cobble Hill, Brooklyn, from his father, Albert, a Lebanese businessman who made soundtrack records from popular Arabic films and worked as an agent in the unitedstates for the Egyptian singer Mohammed Abdel Wahab. The family opened up shop in the mid-1960's and established, as Mr. Rashid likes to say, the largest collection of Arabic records in the world. Rashid's is a distributor as well, responsible for most of the Arabic CD's that end up in the chain stores; it's the place to seek out first for CD's by popular singers like Amr Diab or a collection of CD's by the singer Ahmed Adawiia, which were banned in Egypt because of risque lyrics. In a black velvet case, the store sells a 72-CD boxed set ($795) of the later work of Oum Kalsoum, "the daughter of the Nile," who may be Egypt's most popular musician of the century. The best seller is Ragheb Aleme's "Alby Eshekha" (Ahmed Moussa & Company). I bought Ahmad Fathi's "Ya Bou Zaid" (Al Jazira), a CD, for $14.98.  World Music The term "world music" is mostly a construction of record companies and music critics, but it's been a powerful enough presence for the last decade that several shops have sprung up to serve its culturally curious customers. Most of the business of world music was started by and continues to be run by Africanists, and it follows that the two world-music shops in Manhattan are particularly strong on African music. MULTI KULTI in Greenwich Village looks like a clubhouse or a cafe; back issues of Rhythm Music magazine are stacked in a bin for perusal, and books at the counter help customers navigate their way through the music of Trinidad, Cuba or Portugal. Some sections are catchalls. "Jewish music" extends from North Africa to Spain, and "drums" collects heavily percussive music from around the world. STERN'S MUSIC -- a shop, a record distributor and a record label -- originated in 1983 in the back of an electronics store in London; the newyork outpost opened last year in TriBeCa, and it's a little more academic than Multi Kulti. But the great thing about both stores is how easily a customer can hear the music. Both have chairs and listening stations; Multi Kulti keeps its merchandise unwrapped in the back, and Stern's will unwrap anything you want to hear. At Stern's the best seller is "The Music in My Head" (Stern's Africa). I bought "Prince Nico and L'African Fiesta Sukisa" (Sonodisc), a CD, for $14.78. title: CONCERNS RAISED AS AT&T PURSUES A NEW FOOTHOLD - Correction Appended
body: A whirlwind of deals surrounding the AT&T Corporation's cable television ambitions raised concerns in Washington and in many high-technology quarters yesterday about the prospects for competition in the fast-growing communications industry. Having cleared the way to become the nation's biggest cable television company by acquiring Mediaone Group Inc., AT&T yesterday also moved to the brink of a partnership with the Microsoft Corporation, the software giant, to increase Microsoft's role as a supplier to AT&T's cable systems. With its cable and possible Microsoft deals, AT&T -- which two years ago seemed a crippled giant losing ground to smaller, more nimble competitors -- is poised to once again stand astride the communications world. For Microsoft, a strong relationship with AT&T could become the company's most important vehicle for expanding beyond desktop computers into a new world in which millions of consumers use seamless bundles of phone, TV and high-speed Internet services. But for regulators and competitors in industries ranging from computers to telephones to Internet access, a partnership between AT&T and Microsoft, which is still being negotiated, could appear as frightening as it is formidable. AT&T's expansion into cable TV so quickly and broadly -- starting with a deal last year to acquire Tele-Communications Inc., then the No. 2 cable company behind Time Warner Inc. -- raised concerns on its own. On Tuesday, AT&T opened a path to acquire Mediaone, the No. 4 cable company, for $58 billion by persuading the Comcast Corporation to withdraw its earlier bid for Mediaone. Comcast, which will take over some AT&T cable systems, also agreed to offer phone service over its cable lines in league with AT&T, the nation's biggest long-distance carrier. Microsoft had earlier considered joining Comcast to fight against AT&T, but decided instead to seek a partnership with AT&T to use Microsoft's Windows operating system in some of AT&T's cable-based communications systems. The Senate antitrust subcommittee said yesterday that it would hold hearings into the competitive impact of AT&T's looming acquisition of Mediaone. AT&T wants to use cable systems to offer integrated bundles of telephone, television and high-speed Internet service to millions of consumers. The subcommittee's leadership said that AT&T's expansion into the cable business could speed the advent of local telephone competition, but added that AT&T's deal making might slow competition in video services. "This deal will likely increase AT&T's ability to provide competitive local phone service to residential customers, which we certainly support," Senator Michael DeWine, Republican of Ohio, the subcommittee's chairman, and Senator Herb Kohl, Democrat of Wisconsin, the ranking minority member, said in a statement. "But the jury is still out on how it will affect the cable/video market and we need to closely examine all of the competitive aspects of the deal." What clearly emerges from the blur of billion-dollar dealings is a sense that AT&T is assembling the pieces to create a profile of dominance in the communications landscape unmatched by any company since the old American Telephone and Telegraph broke up under Government pressure in 1984. Many analysts described AT&T's flurry of deals as good for all the companies involved, and the market supported that notion. AT&T's shares rose $5.375 yesterday, to $56.9375; Comcast shares gained $9.1875, to $73.3125, and Microsoft shares rose $1.0625, to $79.125. Mediaone's shares fell by 75 cents, to $76.875, perhaps on disappointment that an extended bidding war for the company now seems highly unlikely. In some ways, a resurgent AT&T could become a major force in promoting competition. With its cable lines into millions of homes, AT&T has now become the biggest threat to the regional Bells' dominance in local consumer phone service. In fact, AT&T's deal with Comcast, like an existing deal with Time Warner, is focused solely on telephone service. No other long-distance giant has assembled a full-fledged plan to offer local phone service to residential consumers nationwide, but AT&T has made offering local service in competition with the Bells a cornerstone of its strategy. But because AT&T is moving so fast to gain links to unitedstates homes, and because of its legacy as the nation's telephone monopoly, any strategic relationship it forges with Microsoft is bound to raise eyebrows. "AT&T is putting together a cable monopoly that is beyond the wildest dreams of John Malone," said Gregory C. Simon, co-director of the Open Net Coalition, a lobbying group that includes many of AT&T's competitors -- including America Online and Mindspring in Internet service and MCI Worldcom in long distance. Mr. Malone was the freewheeling chairman of TCI before its sale to AT&T. "And now that they have cornered the network," Mr. Simon, a former domestic policy adviser to Vice President Al Gore, said, "they are putting the network under lock and key by putting Microsoft technology inside the set-top box." Microsoft dominates the market for personal computer operating software. But its main objective in dealing with AT&T was to obtain assured access for its software and Internet commerce businesses -- preferred access, if possible -- to the fast-growing high-speed data network that AT&T is assembling. Under the terms of the deal being negotiated between AT&T and Microsoft, Microsoft is to invest about $5 billion in AT&T, perhaps in exchange for some sort of preferred stock in AT&T, according to executives close to the talks. AT&T would also agree to use Microsoft's software in its integrated packages of voice, video and data service. AT&T is adamant that Microsoft will not get an exclusive arrangement to supply its Windows CE software on the set-top boxes of AT&T's expanded network. But Microsoft is negotiating hard to get AT&T to allow Windows CE to be introduced in at least one large cable market as an early proving ground for Microsoft's set-top box technology, according to the people close to the talks. For Microsoft, a $5 billion investment is a fairly conservative hedge against the uncertain future represented by "broadband networks," in which households are continuously connected to high-speed data lines. These broadband networks -- whether built by cable companies, regional phone companies or wireless operators -- are expected to stream video, audio and text into people's homes, everything from movies-on-demand to electronic mail. And users are expected to tap into this rich flow of information and entertainment using various equipment, from Internet-enabled televisions to hand-held devices. The vision is of a world of many diverse information appliances -- and all of them will need software. Microsoft wants to compete in that market against traditional makers of cable television equipment, including the General Instrument Corporation and Scientific-Atlanta Inc. Before being acquired by AT&T, TCI had agreed to use Java software from Sun Microsystems Inc. in its advanced set-top boxes. Executives close to the negotiations said that agreement would not be affected by any AT&T deal with Microsoft. To bring the nation to this broadband future, the cable industry -- including AT&T -- is locked in battle against the Baby Bells, the GTE Corporation and the rest of the local phone industry. As that inter-industry fight intensifies, and as AT&T becomes a unifying force in the cable business, some of the rivalries that had traditionally divided cable operators may soon disappear. In acquiring Mediaone, AT&T will also get Mediaone's 25.5 percent stake in some of Time Warner's cable systems, its HBO network and its Warner Brothers film studio. Time Warner, which has bickered incessantly with Mediaone on a number of issues involving those businesses, sat on the sidelines as Comcast and AT&T jockeyed for Mediaone, rooting simply for a deal to occur. Even though AT&T would supplant Time Warner as the biggest cable system, Time Warner benefits by eliminating Mediaone's influence over its cable and movie units. "I am pleased with the outcome and pleased with the role Brian Roberts played in bringing the companies together with a solution that benefits the cable industry," Gerald Levin, Time Warner's chairman, said in a statement, referring to Comcast's president. Indeed, Time Warner is likely to look to create accords with AT&T on several fronts, media executives said. It hopes to buy complete control back of HBO and Warner Brothers. In return, it will likely look for ways for Road Runner -- a high-speed Internet service in which it holds an 36 percent stake -- to cooperate with At Home, a comparable service in which AT&T is a big shareholder. The services could be merged outright. Or they could be linked more closely using compatible technology. Toward this end, Time Warner is likely to complete an already planned venture to offer local phone service through its cable systems in cooperation with AT&T. Enactment of that deal, first announced in February, had been delayed by Mediaone, executives said. As AT&T moves into the high-speed Internet business through cable acquisitions, the biggest player in the Internet market -- America Online -- is not part of AT&T's party. Instead, America Online plans to offer high-speed services employing a technology that uses phone lines rather than cable wires. It already has pacts with Bell Atlantic and SBC Communications and is courting other local phone companies. America Online is eager to have access to cable systems as well, and considered backing Comcast in an effort to outbid AT&T for Mediaone. Ultimately, though, it decided the prospect was an expensive way to get into a business that is growing much more slowly than its own.
