title: Intel Planning Big Move Into Internet Services
body: The Intel Corporation, the leading maker of microchips, said yesterday that it was planning a big move into the Internet services business by building and running data centers around the world. The move is a striking departure for the big microprocessor producer, known for pumping out millions of silicon Pentium chips that serve as the electronic brains of most personal computers. Analysts say the Intel announcement reflects just how far the company is willing to go in seeking new ways to grow as it recognizes the Internet as both a challenge and an opportunity. "This is a stretch, but you have to give Intel's management credit for recognizing that the world is rapidly changing around them and trying to do something about it," said Drew Peck, a managing director of S. G. Cowen & Company, a securities firm. Sprawling installations filled with powerful small computers, known as server farms, are used to handle electronic commerce and host the World Wide Web sites for other companies. Intel presented its plans for the data farms at a meeting with securities analysts yesterday in newyork. Though Intel's profits have held up well so far, many analysts believe that the rise of the Internet will inevitably erode its margins. Consumers are increasingly expected to use simpler, lower-cost devices -- from hand-held machines to television set-top boxes -- to gain access to the Internet. The proliferation of these so-called Internet appliances, they note, will not replace personal computers by any means. But the Internet will fuel more diverse computing technologies and other access devices. This in turn will undermine the profits of the technology standard-bearers in the PC-centric era, that is, Intel and the Microsoft Corporation, whose Windows operating system runs most PC's. "Intel has to look for other opportunities for future growth and server farms could be a reasonably good hybrid," Mr. Peck said. Other analysts are quite skeptical. They say Intel is a late entrant into the fast-growing market for server farms, trailing established computer services powerhouses like the International Business Machines Corporation and Web hosting specialists like Exodus Communications Inc. These analysts also doubt that Intel's skills as a chip maker give it any edge in running huge data centers. "This is not a business for Intel to be in," said Howard Anderson, managing director of the Yankee Group, a research company in Boston. Intel insists that the server-farm plan fits neatly with its long-term strategy. "We want to be the building block supplier to the Internet economy," said Craig R. Barrett, the president of Intel. "And as part of that plan, we are going to make substantial investments to set up server farms around the world." Intel already has a pilot operation in Santa Clara, Calif., equipped with a few hundred server computers, powered by Intel microprocessors. By the third quarter of this year, Intel intends to have its first data center with more than 2,000 Intel-based PC servers running, catering to customers including Excite, the Web directory service. Soon after, the company plans to begin a network of data centers worldwide to host Web sites and handle electronic commerce for businesses. These huge computer farms, Intel says, are expected to cost more than $100 million each and be crammed with more than 5,000 servers. Intel views the server farms as "bit factories," said Gerry Parker, an executive vice president. The expertise the company has developed in planning, building and managing chip factories, he said, should translate well. "A lot of the same skills are involved," he said.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Bankers, Too, Chart Internet's Stratosphere
body: The quickest way for a chief executive to bolster his company's stock price, it appears, is to announce a connection to the Internet. In recent weeks, the banking industry has become accustomed to such announcements -- and with the associated stock-trading frenzy. The stocks of little-known regional financial companies like Florida Banks Inc. of Jacksonville, First Sierra Financial Inc. of Houston and the Patriot Bank of Pottstown, Pa., have jumped as much as 300 percent in a single day after the companies publicized their intentions to provide banking services over the Internet. Investors who bought in before the announcements are mostly sitting on paper profits. Among the buyers have been executives and directors of Florida Banks, First Sierra and Patriot Bank who purchased shares in the four to six weeks before each company announced its Internet plans. The executives say that while they are enthusiastic about the Internet plans, their recent stock purchases were not timed to take advantage of an Internet premium. And few, if any, of the insiders have cashed in so far by selling stock. In buying shares shortly before announcing their Internet ventures, however, the executives raise questions that are relevant to a large number of companies today. At a time when any corporate press release with the the word "Internet" in it seems to move stock prices, corporate America might need to take a broader view of what is considered material information to investors. The Securities and Exchange Commission defines materiality as anything a typical investor would need to know to make an informed decision. Securities laws prohibit people who are in a position of fiduciary responsibility and who have access to material, nonpublic information from trading on that knowledge. But it is not at all clear whether the executives in these instances ran afoul of those rules. In a legal sense, materiality cannot be judged solely by whether an announcement causes a stock price to move. Investors, it seems, have quite another view. The enthusiasm for Internet banking can be linked directly to the stock performance of Net.Bank Inc. and the Telebanc Financial Corporation. These two companies, which say they do all their business in cyberspace without the burden of brick-and-mortar branches, have captured the fancy of investors largely because they have already demonstrated the ability to generate profits. Telebanc, for example, is expected this year to earn $2.6 million, or 15 cents a share, double its profit last year. Those earnings would be even higher without a huge advertising budget intended to attract customers, said Henry Blodget, who tracks the company for Merrill Lynch and is recommending its shares. Mr. Blodget says the attraction of Internet-based banks is that they are not limited to serving customers in areas where the bank has branches. Like other Internet service businesses, the banks aim to pass the savings along in the form of higher interest rates on deposits. The public has enthusiastically responded to the stocks, if not the on-line bank accounts, pushing Telebanc shares up to $104.50 from $34 at the beginning of the year and less than $8 last October. Similarly, Net.Bank shares closed yesterday at $182.4375, up more than 500 percent since the beginning of the year. It is not surprising, then, that investors seem to have jumped on any bank's decision to reach out over the Internet. On April 13, when Florida Banks announced that it would begin offering Internet banking services in the third quarter, its shares soared from about $8, where they had been trading for most of the previous year, to as high as $37.75, closing at $31.25. They have since declined, closing yesterday at $11.8125, 47 percent higher than before the Internet announcement. Just three weeks before the announcement, four insiders bought 9,000 shares of Florida Banks at about $7 each. The purchases, totaling $63,500, increased each person's holdings by 1 percent to 20 percent. Though the purchases were relatively small in terms of the company's $63 million market value, they accounted for as much as half of the trading in the stock March 22-24. Should the insiders have been allowed to buy stock when an announcement about their companies' Internet plans was looming? T. Edwin Stinson, the chief financial officer of Florida Banks, who was one of four officials who bought shares, said the news was important but not entirely new. Florida Banks' plan for Internet banking was outlined in the company's prospectus for its initial public offering last July, he said. "We were extremely surprised by the reaction" of the stock, Mr. Stinson said. The main reason the company issued the press release, he said, was because it had signed a final agreement with a service provider that would allow the formal startup of the Internet service, and it wanted to get the news out before discussing it at an investment conference that week. Florida Banks also draws a strong distinction between its strategy and Telebanc's. "We don't want to service commercial customers that are not in the geographic markets that we are in," Mr. Stinson said. "We didn't imply that we are trying to be an Internet bank." The stock purchases were made "because the stock was trading below book value," Mr. Stinson said, referring to the net value of the company's assets and liabilities. Some of the company's directors had been lamenting that the shares seemed appreciably cheap, and "none of us benefited at all" since none of the shares have been sold, he added. Several weeks before First Sierra Financial, an equipment-leasing company, announced that it would establish "the first Internet-based business-to-business bank," its chief executive and a director bought 50,000 and 29,600 shares, respectively, at about $9 each. The purchases each represented about a day's average volume in the shares, which trade on Nasdaq. After the announcement on April 14, First Sierra's shares jumped as high as $30 and have since settled at $14.50. Thomas J. Depping, the chief executive, points out that the company's share price had started to move up after First Sierra reported strong first-quarter earnings. "I've been consistently buying shares since November," shortly after their price fell to $9 from $33 amid a downdraft in speciality finance shares, Mr. Depping said. A large block of stock became available in mid-March, prompting his decision to buy more, he said. The decision "really had very little to do with the fact that we were working on an Internet bank," he added. Joni S. Naugle, chief operating officer of Patriot Bank, said she, too, was surprised at the market reaction to Patriot's April 12 introduction of "Virtual Access Internet Banking" service. The company's shares, which had traded around $9.50 for two weeks, jumped as high as $18.75 on the news. Roughly a month before the announcement, Ms. Naugle and another company executive bought 1,000 shares each, while a director bought 7,400. Each paid about $10 a share. "The purchases were not related at all" to the announcement, Ms. Naugle said. "Insiders have been buying because the stock is on sale," trading roughly at book value, and they did not sell shares when the price jumped. Since then, the price has returned to its previous level, closing yesterday at $10. That is probably because once investors read Patriot's press release closely, they might have noticed that while Patriot was adding Internet banking services -- including the ability to transfer funds and pay bills on line -- it was not becoming an Internet bank. Similar services have been offered by big financial institutions like Citibank for more than a decade. But to date, only a small portion of Citibank's customers use the service regularly. The lesson for investors, of course, is that not all Internet connections are equal.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: U.S. Cracking Down on Internet's Information Brokers
body: The Federal Government today began cracking down on the deceptive practices of a proliferating number of private investigators who advertise on the Internet that they can inexpensively provide confidential details about bank accounts and telephone records. In the first civil case of its kind, lawyers at the Federal Trade Commission accused a Colorado couple of violating the law by posing as bank customers to trick banks into providing confidential information. The couple, James and Regana Rapp, had advertised on their Web site that their company, Touch Tone Information Inc., could obtain bank records, unpublished telephone numbers and financial assets. Government officials said Touch Tone Information, one of scores of investigative agencies that glean confidential information under false pretenses, had employees make hundreds of telephone calls in which they claimed to be either a bank customer or relative. The Federal Trade Commission Act makes it illegal to use such deceptive trade practices. Mr. Rapp acknowledged in an interview today that he and his employees had tricked many banks and other institutions into providing confidential information. Touch Tone's Internet site advertised that for $100 it could obtain information within 10 days about a bank account -- $200 for a stock account. It also said it could obtain telephone toll records and unlisted numbers and addresses. Mr. Rapp said that as a result of the lawsuit, he had removed his Web site and would stop the practice of posing as a customer of the institution that he was trying to get information from. He said the trade commission's action would curtail only a small part of his investigations business and complained that it would only hurt victims -- clients like mothers seeking payments from dead-beat fathers and government agencies that he said had employed him to track down assets. "If you're a dead-beat dad or a neglected spouse," Mr. Rapp said, "you don't have to worry anymore." Commercial Web sites run by private investigators have flourished in recent years, advertising the ability to find a wide array of public and confidential information -- like telephone records and credit and bank accounts -- for lawyers, spurned spouses and burned business partners. Some of the information they sell is available in public records, but other information can only be obtained by deception or bribery, privacy experts say. Although law-enforcement officials in some states like Connecticut and Massachusetts have prosecuted investigators who illegally obtain information by pretending to be either a bank customer or relative, the Federal Government has moved more slowly. Many privacy experts say that as long as law firms and big businesses are largely insulated from Government prosecution because the laws are narrowly written, the deceptive practices of investigators like the Rapps will never be curtailed. "The F.T.C. cannot stop this practice because there is a lot of value for this data, and people will continue to pay for it," said Evan Hendricks, editor of Privacy Times, a Washington newsletter that covers privacy issues. But officials at the Federal Trade Commission said the case was filed as a warning to both the information brokerage industry and the bigger fish, the firms that retain the investigators. "We want to send a message to others that this kind of deception and invasion of privacy is unacceptable," said Robert Pitofsky, chairman of the commission. Today's lawsuit is part of a broader policy agenda promoted by Mr. Pitofsky to address privacy issues and the Internet. Earlier this week, the commission announced a proposal for new rules intended to protect the privacy interests of children on the Internet by generally requiring operators of Web sites to obtain parental consent before soliciting information from children under 13. The agency has asked Congress for the authority to seek civil penalties against brokers who obtain sensitive financial information about individuals under false pretenses. In its case brought today, the agency sought forfeiture of Touch Tone's profits and an injunction against any future deceptive practices by the company. Representative Jim Leach, the Iowa Republican who heads the House banking committee, recently introduced legislation that would make it a crime to knowingly deceive a financial information to obtain confidential information. But the proposal would also raise the burden of proof for civil cases, which has created some concern at the Federal Trade Commission. Officials at the Justice Department have said they believe they implicitly have authority to make criminal cases under Federal wire fraud laws. Still, the laws on the issue are far from clear. Orson Swindle, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, dissented from the agency's decision to file a lawsuit against Touch Tone on the ground that he did not think the Federal Trade Commission Act or the agency's guidelines on the law prohibited the Rapps' conduct. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Robert Pitofsky, chairman of the Federal Trade Commission. (Associated Press)

title: America Online to Compete in Assigning Internet Domains
body: America Online, the world's largest on-line service, was one of five companies chosen today to compete with Network Solutions Inc., which currently enjoys a Government-backed monopoly in the lucrative business of assigning the Internet addresses known as domains. The surprising choice of America Online introduced a seemingly formidable competitor to the business of assigning Internet addresses -- and prompted questions about whether smaller companies would ever compete effectively. "It's unfortunate," said David J. Farber, a professor of computer science at the University of Pennsylvania and a board member of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, an Internet civil liberties group. "I think it was a good opportunity to spread the wealth. Now you get AOL against N.S.I., and they can have a ball." The stock of Network Solutions, which had lost half its value over the last few weeks, surged today, closing at $92, up $32, or 53 percent, from Tuesday. America Online climbed to $142.75, up $14.0625. The other four companies selected in this first round -- the competition will open to many more companies this summer -- were Register.com, a comparatively small, newyork-based domain name reseller; a subsidiary of France Telecom; Melbourne IT of Australia, and the Internet Council of Registrars, an international consortium that helped lead the movement to break Network Solutions' monopoly. The selections were the first major action taken by the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, or Icann, the nonprofit corporation established last year by the Clinton Administration to move management of the Internet from government to the private sector. Since 1993, Network Solutions has had an exclusive right to assign companies and individuals Internet addresses in the so-called top-level domains -- those ending in the suffixes .com, .net and .org. Icann's interim chairman, Esther Dyson, today characterized the move as "a major milestone" in bringing "Internet users the benefits of real competition." But just how much competition the companies will offer Network Solutions remains to be seen, since the companies must pay Network Solutions a $9-a-year fee for each name they add to the central registry, the data base of Internet addresses that Network Solutions will continue to own. They will also have to pay a $10,000 fee to help cover the costs of the software developed by Network Solutions to let others add addresses to the registry. In the seven years since it was granted an exclusive Government contract to build the data base and registry system, Network Solutions has transformed itself into a Fortune 500 company, offering a variety of registration services and establishing partnerships around the world. "The economic reality is that Network Solutions has all the market movement in its favor," said Keith Benjamin, an Internet analyst with BancBoston Robertson Stephens in San Francisco, "and there's nothing Icann or the Government can do to really unseat Network Solutions." He added, "They have a crucial relationship with essentially every Internet service provider on the planet." As for America Online, which has 17 million members, Mr. Benjamin said: "This is a business that AOL is not going to be easily suited for. They cater to a consumer market, so it is a little confusing why AOL is doing this." In addition to selecting the five initial companies, Icann announced that 29 applicants, including AT&T, had met its accreditation criteria and were expected to be certified to compete when the system is opened to unlimited competition this summer. A spokesman for Network Solutions, Christopher Clough, called competition "good for everyone," but added: "Obviously, we have a head start. We have the most established company. We have the world's leading experts on the domain-name system." Referring to the fees that competitors will pay for access to the registry, he noted that Network Solutions was not only "taking on five new competitors but five new customers." Bill Burrington, vice president for policy at America Online, said his company saw an opportunity to create a "value-added service." But he emphasized that "it's too early to say how the process will play out." "This is all new," he said. "We are doing this on the fly -- in Internet time," Mr. Burrington said. "We don't know where this is all going." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Footlights
body: NEWS  The Hard Way Everybody knows that if you don't practice, you don't get to Carnegie Hall. But Christopher Plummer is going to make it anyway. There was a time when he wanted to be a pianist, but he gave it up because, he says, it was "too much work." Instead he achieved fame as an actor, winning a Tony Award ("Barrymore") and appearing everywhere from Broadway to London's West End. So it is as an actor he will make his Carnegie Hall debut on Saturday night, portraying Shakespeare's characters when Neville Marriner leads the Academy of St. Martin-in-the-Fields in Mendelssohn's "Incidental Music to a Midsummer Night's Dream." L'Affaire Woody In a quiet exercise of diplomacy involving Woody Allen and the French Ambassador to the unitedstates, Francois Bujon de l'Estang, the honor of France has been upheld, and an honor officially bestowed upon the man whose art ranges from the feuilleton and the play to the cinema. At long last, Mr. Allen has been presented with the medal attesting to his appointment as a Commander in the Order of Arts and Letters, the highest award given by France's Ministry of Culture. For those who came late to this contretemps, Mr. Allen, to his surprise, learned from an article in The newyork Times last year that he had been named a commander on March 31, 1989. But for some reason the tangible evidence of the accolade had never been presented. Last month, after an exchange of correspondence, Mr. Bujon and Mr. Allen met at Mr. Allen's Manhattan apartment, and after what diplomatic sources described as a congenial and warm meeting, the deed was done.  Net Game Once upon a time, scholars determined to compare the many versions of early Shakespearean texts had to travel from library to library or trust the accuracy of recently published versions. But now the University of Pennsylvania is making available on the Internet the scanned texts of early Renaissance works from its library special collections. These include comparative versions of "King Lear," "Romeo and Juliet" and "Hamlet." The address of the Internet site, called "English Renaissance in Context," is www.library.upenn.edu/etext/.  Paging the Doctor She says you can call her Dr. Betty now. That's Betty as in Betty Comden and Adolph Green, the Broadway lyricists and librettists who gave the world hits like "Bells Are Ringing." It seems that Ms. Comden and Mr. Green journeyed out to Bloomington, Ind., for a tribute to Leonard Bernstein and came back with honorary doctor of music degrees from the Indiana University School of Music. Myles Brand, the president of the university, said, "The artistic contributions by Betty Comden and Adolph Green to American music theater distinguish them as leaders in their field."   LAWRENCE VAN GELDER http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos

title: I.B.M. Reports A 42% Rise In Its Profit
body: In another sign of continued health for high-technology makers, the International Business Machines Corporation reported first-quarter earnings yesterday that were well in excess of analysts' estimates. I.B.M. said its results were led by strong sales of services and software, which accounted for 60 percent of gross profit. Shares of I.B.M., which reported its results after the end of regular trading, closed at $171.875, up $2.125, on the newyork Stock Exchange. But I.B.M. soared in after-hours trading, gaining more than $17 to $189.375. Analysts said that I.B.M.'s results, coupled with the Microsoft Corporation's strong performance on Tuesday, should counter the gloomy outlook painted for technology makers this quarter after the Compaq Computer Corporation predicted, and delivered, half the earnings forecast and the Intel Corporation reported sales growth that was less than expected. "This is just what the tech doctor ordered," said John B. Jones Jr., an analyst with Salomon Smith Barney. I.B.M.'s service business, intellectual property and distribution put it in a different class than Compaq, he said. "Compaq has many of the same pieces, but not the same quality," Mr. Jones said. "Compaq addresses the world from a PC-centric standpoint. I.B.M. addresses it from a customer-service standpoint." Though some analysts said I.B.M.'s better-than-expected results reflected the company's ability to manage expectations, they also pointed to a growing division between leaders and laggards in the technology industries. I.B.M. has been able to position traditional strengths in data base management software and large servers as essential tools for electronic commerce. The company's huge consulting practice is also riding the Internet wave as customers rush to offer good and services on the World Wide Web. Other computer companies that have established a strong Internet identity, like Apple Computer and Sun Microsystems, also reported stronger-than-expected results this quarter. Sun's shares have fallen, however, after the company warned that sales might slow in the second half of the year if companies defer technology purchases because of Year 2000 concerns. That same warning was issued in an extremely strong earnings report on Tuesday by Microsoft, and its stock also closed down slightly yesterday. For the quarter, I.B.M. reported earnings of roughly $1.47 billion, or $1.55 a diluted share, up nearly 42 percent from $1.04 billion, or $1.06 a share, in the comparable period a year earlier. Revenue rose 17 percent, to $8.58 billion, from $7.32 billion in the first quarter of 1998. Per-share figures reflect a decrease in the average number of shares outstanding, to 911.9 million compared with 950.2 million in the first quarter of 1998. I.B.M. spent approximately $2.1 billion on share repurchases in the first quarter, up from $1.6 billion in the final quarter of 1998. Analysts expected I.B.M. to earn $1.41 a share, according to First Call, which tracks such estimates. It was the 12th consecutive quarter in which I.B.M. has exceeded estimates. "We started 1999 with a strong quarter," Louis V. Gerstner Jr., I.B.M.'s chairman and chief executive, said in a statement. "We saw a significant improvement in our business in Asia, and we also had double-digit revenue growth in Europe and the Americas. Services is clearly the largest and fastest-growing portion of the information technology industry, and we continue to extend our leadership position each quarter." I.B.M. said sales in the Americas increased 13 percent, to $8.8 billion; in Europe, the Middle East and Africa by 20 percent, to $6.3 billion; and in the Asia-Pacific region, 20 percent, to $3.5 billion. Hardware sales were up 17 percent, services were up 19 percent, and software up 10 percent. The company said it signed $9.8 billion in services contracts in the first quarter and concluded the quarter with a total services contract backlog around $55 billion. In a telephone conference call with securities analysts, Douglas Maine, I.B.M.'s chief financial officer, said that personal computer sales were up 50 percent, a "significant improvement." However, I.B.M. continues to lose money on PC sales, which contributed to an overall decline in the company's gross profit margin. In response to analysts' questions about slowing growth for information technology in the second half of the year, possibly due to Year 2000 issues, Mr. Maine said he did not see that. "There's an absence of anything we're hearing from customers that suggests a slowdown," he said, adding that "the I.T. sector in 1999 will continue to be the key driver" of worldwide growth in economic output. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
LIBRARY/SITES FOR NEW PARENTS;
Dr. Spock Yields to the World Wide Web
body: WHAT'S a new parent to do?  Dr. Spock has been knocked off his pedestal by pans of his real-life fathering. Dr. T. Berry Brazelton, as dear to many parents' hearts as was Dr. Spock, is locked in battle with his fellow best-selling child-raising author, John Rosemond, over toilet training, of all things. And from somewhere in your apartment rises a wail that, with luck, might belong to a rousing velociraptor -- but is more likely coming from the lungs of a far fiercer creature: your baby. As the icons of child rearing fall by the wayside or into professional squabbles, where can a new parent (the "desperate" goes without saying) still find authoritative, unimpeachable advice on everything from bed-wetting to bedlam? The Web, of course. No, seriously. Granted, as has often been noted, digging out reliable information from the Internet is a little iffier than hitting the advice section of a bookstore, thumbing through hand-me-down books or asking a relative who has actually done this before. There is, after all, some fairly strange stuff sitting on all those servers out there. When your 4-month-old suddenly refuses to take her bottle, you don't want your search engine to send you to some site revealing that a guerrilla team of highly trained babies knocked Flight 800 out of the sky with a barrage of diaper bombs. But there are a host of Web sites with sound information intended for new parents, from those still cooing at fuzzy-gazed newborns to those who spend the day coaxing toddlers off the bookshelves. Of course, how a new parent would find the time to spend on the Internet is a little hard to figure. Most sites offer a range of advice on topics like baby names, feeding, child-development milestones and sleep habits. As far as this goes, they don't offer much advantage over a book. But Web sites, with their ability to be quickly updated, allow parents to keep abreast of breaking news on the baby front, including new health studies, the latest thinking on various child-rearing issues and product warnings about child accessories like cribs and car seats. And of course, the sites allow new parents (and veterans) to exchange tips -- or just gripe -- on bulletin boards and in chat rooms. Some sites also allow you to customize their home pages to your needs, if you are willing to part with a fair amount of personal information. All that can be fairly reassuring stuff to a new parent struggling to get his or her bearings. The slew of ads peppering the more successful Web sites also offer their own peculiar form of reassurance. On those days when you feel convinced that no parent could be less competent than you, hop on line and take heart: you are no loser. On the contrary, you are suddenly very popular. You have just gone from being a consumer to a superconsumer (not to mention being the owner-operator of someone who soon will be fueling the economy with his own purchases), and a lot of big companies want you to know just how much they care. All of which suggests that new parents searching for help on line should exercise caution. The baby-advice sites offer especially good examples of the challenge of evaluating information on the Web. In this case, on the well-established sites, it is often not so much a question of assessing the trustworthiness of the information as trying to figure out if you are reading an objective piece of advice or a skillfully devised ad. Sometimes it is hard even to figure out who is running a site. That said, with a little common sense, most parents will be able to find something of value on the Web. They can even find information from some child-raising authors who first made their name in books. Dr. Benajamin Spock, who died last year, did some writing for the Web site Parenttime.com, and material from him can still be found there (if only he had thought to prepare a defense of his personal life, criticized in a biography that appeared after his death). Dr. Brazelton appears, among other places, on Babycenter.com, where (sponsored by a popular disposable diaper) he espouses his view that parents should not rush to toilet-train their children. Mr. Rosemond, a conservative who argues for early training (and criticizes Dr. Brazelton for accepting diaper-industry money), has his own site (www.rosemond.com). Still, with all the sites out there, none reviewed here seemed able to answer a basic question: Why do parents need a Web site to figure out babies, when babies seem to figure out their parents just fine on their own?  Site-Seeing: Finding Advice  Here are some other Web sites of interest to new parents:  PARENTHUB.COM: www.parenthub.com The site evaluates other child-rearing sites and lists links, stores, groups and companies.  KIDSHEALTH.ORG: www.kidshealth.org An award-winning site covering a wide range of physical and emotional health information concerning children.  BABIESONLINE.COM: www.babiesonline.com Links to sites and free services, including electronic birth announcements and email greetings.  MOJO'S MUSICAL MOUSEUM: www.kididdles.com/mouseum/index.html At 2 A.M., you're trying to sing baby back to sleep. Lost in the haze is the verse after "mockingbird." The lyrics section of this site is for you. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Mark Gamba/The Stock Market)

title:
LIBRARY/SITES FOR NEW PARENTS;
PARENT SOUP
body: www.parentsoup.com ONE of the most popular parent sites on the Web, Parent Soup offers an imaginative mix of ideas and activities. But despite the staff members' chipper personal descriptions of themselves, meant to give the site a homey feel, it is a highly commercial enterprise. That is hardly surprising, given that it is run by iVillage.com, the No. 1 on-line network of sites designed for women. Parent Soup is attractive and very well designed. For newcomers, there is a useful tour of what is being offered. Everything is polished, the writing is perky. So what if the overall tone often smacks of insincerity, as if it had been produced by a roomful of copy writers? For example, in describing the site's various "communities" -- sections tailored to the needs of parents of babies, toddlers, school-age children and so on -- the tour notes that each one has a "leader." "If you hang around in the chat areas or discussion groups," it says, "you'll probably get to know these special folks. And if you do, tell 'em to try eating a doughnut for a change and breathing some fresh air -- we lose more talented producers to starvation and oxygen deprivation." Visitors to the site are greeted with a series of links to other parts of Parent Soup and a Today in the Soup feature that can include everything from timely articles -- as in Babycenter, there was one on traveling with children -- to breaking news of interest to parents. It can sometimes make for an odd mix. Recently, the "hot topic" was "Crisis in Kosovo," and under it a link to an iVillage site of family horoscopes. The Kosovo feature was not a bad idea: Children upset by images of refugees, the site suggested, should be given concrete ways to help, like fund drives. There were links and phone numbers for a variety of aid groups. Like most of the other sites, Parentsoup.com has experts ready to provide a range of advice on medical issues, problems (like bed-wetting) and discipline. It all seemed useful enough, if similar to what is on the other sites (not to mention in the popular child-raising books). http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: More Problems For Schwab Site
body: Customers of the Charles Schwab Corporation were unable to place stock trades yesterday morning through the Internet broker's Web site. It was the sixth time that has happened this year. Schwab's Web site, which processed a record 160,000 trades a day in the first quarter, failed for 15 minutes starting around 11 A.M., a spokeswoman, Tracey Gordon, said. Customers may have experienced "periods of slowness" for an hour thereafter, she added. A recent string of short service interruptions was caused by Schwab's attempts to increase its Web site's capacity by adding another mainframe computer. Schwab recently said that it would spend heavily this year on its Web side and other technology. Schwab's competitors have also suffered shutdowns and glitches, notably the No. 3 Internet brokerage firm E*Trade Group Inc. The problems have frustrated on-line investors, spurred lawsuits and caused state regulators to begin an inquiry into the on-line brokerage industry. Schwab, which has 2.5 million on-line accounts, last week reported a record $142.9 million profit in the first quarter, more than double the $68 million profit in the quarter a year ago. The failure did not hurt Schwab's stock, which gained $8.25 yesterday, closing at $115. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
A Program That Can Remove Advertising on Internet Pages
body: A German electronics company is tackling those banner advertisements with a product that strips most advertising off Web pages. Web Washer was developed by engineers at Siemens A. G. who wanted to get rid of advertising they thought was obtrusive. During testing on the company's intranet, they discovered that it also reduced the time pages took to load in a browser. The software sits on a user's computer and waits for a user to click on a link. Web Washer looks at all the pieces of what is being requested and if anything looks as if it might be an ad, the program will toss out that part of the request. Roland Cuny, the Siemens engineer who came up with the idea for Web Washer, said the program could filter out "any kind of undesired information, like over-designed background images on Internet-intranet pages, ad banners, graphics, frames, Java scripts, Java applets and pop-up windows" and could be tuned by the user to be more -- or less -- restrictive. The program is free for personal use and is available at the www.siemens.de/servers/ wwash/wwash_us/buy.htm site. Current versions run only on Windows 95 and 98 and NT, though Mr. Cuny said Macintosh and Linux versions were in the works.   STEVEN E. BRIER http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Q & A;
Downloading More Speed For a Modem
body: Q.  I read that I can upgrade the speed of my modem by downloading software from the Web. How does this work?  A.  What you are referring to is sometimes called a firmware or flash upgrade. If the software is compatible with your modem, you can indeed increase the speed of the device without buying a new one. The modem's firmware, which is a combination of hardware and software, controls its operation. The software is written into the read-only memory (ROM), and it works with the memory chip in the hardware. For their firmware, some modem makers use "flash ROM," which can be erased and reprogrammed with new data. If you are thinking about using a flash upgrade, you should call your modem manufacturer or visit the company's Web site for more information and to make sure you can actually upgrade your model. Most sites offer specific instructions on how to proceed, as well as the necessary software available for downloading. You can damage your modem if you don't install the upgrade properly, so read the information carefully. At members.home.net/v90/modemhelp .htm, you'll find a helpful list of manufacturers' Web sites. Be sure to check with your Internet service provider to make sure that it can handle the faster connection.   J. D. BIERSDORFER http://www.nytimes.com

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Where Better to Find Out About Spiders Than on the Web?
body: SPIDERS belong on the Web, and not just to make a bad pun. They are interesting, colorful and far more useful than harmful to humans. Unfortunately, Internet menus are cluttered with listings for "Web spiders," a term for wide-ranging search programs. In the past year, the American Museum of Natural History in newyork has greatly expanded its on-line offerings, especially in conjunction with its new Hall of Biodiversity. In cooperation with Discovery Channel Online, the museum has created a spider page that focuses on a recent expedition to Western Australia (www.discovery.com/exp/spiders /spiders.html). In Spider Fact of the Day, one can find tidbits like E. B. White's inspiration for his immortal Charlotte -- Araneus cavaticus, the orb-weaving barn spider. The site mentions an estimate by William Bristowe, a British arachnologist, that the total weight of insects devoured each year by British spiders is greater than the weight of all British subjects. (The site does not say whether British cooking reduces the human biomass.) In Your Own Backyard describes and illustrates spider families. Name That Spider prints some of the 4,000 contest letters children wrote about spiders. The winner, Jeremy Falling of Manchester, N.H., is having a spider named after him. Up Close lets viewers identify magnified spider parts. There are comments on what the world would be like without spiders (overrun with insects and disease and devoid of most plants we eat). For students wishing harder science, the museum describes the Australian mission (research.amnh.org /entomology/spiders). Dr. Kefyn M. Catley, a native of Wales who helped create the on-line spider pages, is a former professional flutist who changed his career to zoology. In a recent interview at the museum, he recalled the boyhood bug stage he never outgrew, looking under the eaves long ago and wondering how a spider could build her web at night, and why she did not get stuck herself. "They're not a hard sell," Dr. Catley said of spiders. "Everybody on this planet has at least one story to tell." They do get bad press, he admitted. "People have this vision about how spiders went out to wreak havoc on mankind." Actually, he said, you are 11 times more likely to be killed by a bee or wasp, and 20 times more likely to die from lightning. Spiders are at least 360 million years old and are the dominant predators on Earth, he said. "People should think of them not just as allies, but as absolutely necessary," he said. The American Tarantula Society (torgo.cnchost.com/ats), in Carlsbad, N.M., calls itself the largest arachnid society in the world, and it offers one-stop surfing for students, teachers, breeders, collectors and lovers of T-shirts with larger-than-life tarantulas on them. The society holds an annual conference in June and publishes an arachnid magazine, Forum, six times a year. (Forum's letters page is called the Eggsac.) On-line articles include "How Bad Information Invades Kids' Books," in which the author laments the "icky spider mindset" in children's literature. Through the society, one can buy Texas tan and other tarantulas. The on-line shop sells books including "The Tarantula Keeper's Guide." The conditions needed to keep one species alive will often kill another species, the experts warn. "I feel that the Internet has been responsible for a flurry of interest in tarantulas as pets," Doug Martin, Webmaster of the society's page, wrote by email. "People from across the world are able to sell, breed and trade spiders as never before. This has resulted in a vast number of species being available to the public as opposed to one or two when I started out in the hobby." Mr. Martin's own site, Doug's Tarantula Page (www.geocities.com /Petsburgh/Farm/3173) is oriented toward the novice keeper. One link is to a bulletin board for buyers and sellers, a kind of arachnid stock exchange. But before even thinking about it, Mr. Martin cautioned, buy a book on responsible pet-keeping, check with an experienced owner and learn about state and postal regulations. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos (John Lemker/Animals Animals)

title: 'Sesame Street' Site: Serious Child's Play
body: THE office of Children's Television Workshop Online in Manhattan is a preschooler's decorating dream, with a wall-size blackboard, armchairs that fairly beg for someone to curl up and tell a story and a mesmerizing carpet of crayon-bright red, blue and orange that could have been designed by a "Romper Room" Martha Stewart. The only thing missing is . . . children. But maybe not. Most of the staff members who designed and created the new Web site (www.ctw.org) for the Children's Television Workshop, the creator of "Sesame Street," look too young to even have children themselves. But they have valuable firsthand experience: they are, after all, members of the first generation of children who grew up with Muppets. Tina Sharkey, the group's vice president and general manager, certainly fits that description, and she was described by her former boss, Candice Carpenter, a founder of the Internet company iVillage, as "more like a kid than any other adult I know." Ms. Sharkey, who is 34, said the "Sesame Street" show "invented one of the most important movements of the 20th century, empowering families to get involved with their kids' learning." Ms. Sharkey acknowledges watching "Sesame Street" still. "I was on the treadmill one morning last season, watching an episode about Slimey the Worm, who wanted to go into outer space," she said. "There was Tony Bennett, standing on a rooftop singing, 'Slimey to the Moon,' and all of a sudden, I started sobbing. It was amazing." The task that faced Ms. Sharkey and her team of 30 producers, designers and marketers at Children's Television Workshop Online in 1997 was to recreate on the Web the enormously familiar and comforting blend of education and entertainment that "Sesame Street" pioneered on television nearly three decades earlier. "We had to take what we as a company understand about a 6-year-old's mind-set and then apply it to the Web," Ms. Sharkey said. In some ways, "Sesame Street's" status as a pop-culture icon, as the veritable gold standard of children's programming, made the on-line team's job more complicated. They had to compete with a legend. The producers of "Sesame Street" understood kids and they understood television. But did they understand the Internet? In addition, the Web site for the company, which is nonprofit, had to define itself in relation to such well-entrenched commercial destinations as Disney Online's www.disney.com and the www.nick.com site of the Nickelodeon cable network. In February, Nickelodeon announced its plan to create a free on-line service for kids, tentatively named Project Nozzle. Scheduled to begin on Sept. 1 and backed by on-air promotions from Nickelodeon worth $100 million, the project is widely viewed as the network's attempt to "basically own the children's TV space on line," said Patrick Keane, a senior analyst at Jupiter Communications, a Web research firm. When Ms. Sharkey arrived at Children's Television Workshop's on-line division in July 1997, the Web site consisted of some material recycled from a previous on-line venture and a television schedule. The first step was to appeal to the Children's Television Workshop's core audience: families. One insight of the original designers of "Sesame Street" was that children would watch educational programs more readily if their parents watched, too, which is one reason the television series has always featured pop cultural references and celebrities and sophisticated humor. Web site staff members knew that a receptive family audience was already on line. A recent study from the Find/SVP and Grunwald Associates research firms showed that 67 percent of parents who own computers log on with their children. "We needed to build on the idea that we are the only company in the world who has this rite-of-passage relationship with kids and parents," Ms. Sharkey said. That meant creating a site that encouraged a preschooler to sit on a parent's lap and engage in collaborative mouse-clicking adventures -- what Web producers began to call "lapware." For the site's home page, "we had to think about the way kids play, how they like to have everything spread out all around them and then they want to choose one thing to do," said Paul Marcum, the on-line group's executive producer. The result was a menu that is as brightly colored as the office carpet and that offers users many options with names like Sesame Street Central, Preschool Playground and Activity Time. Realizing that children like to master tasks, the team designed interactive games.  In a counting game that features the popular Muppet called Grover as a farmer, children who match numbers hidden in his harvested vegetables are rewarded with a Tinkerbell-like jingling sound. A mismatch prompts the computer to emit a noise more reminiscent of a Bronx cheer. Another Children's Television Workshop staple has been storytelling. "When you're reading a book, the interaction might consist of turning a page," said Karen Kane, the team's director of programming. "But we created branching stories on line so children can control the plot, depending on what they click on." In a story about Telly the Muppet going into outer space, for example, a child can drag objects into the story to change the action. Dragging a moon into the story screen sets the scene at night; if a sun is dragged instead, the story's action occurs during the day. The activity is especially compelling for small children, who love repetition, because they can return to the story to change its plot numerous times. The redesigned site, called the CTW Family Workshop, went on line in September 1998, aimed squarely at families with preschoolers. True to the "Sesame Street" formula, the site also offers material for parents, including Internet technical advice explained in plain English and an easily downloadable program that lets a user tickle Elmo by clicking on a mouse. The flavor is unmistakably "Sesame Street." And Elmo is adorable. "I like the craft activities they have on the site -- I print them out, and we do them later," said Sandy Homan, a mother of two in Mount Laurel, N.J. Her 6-year-old son, Spencer, is a big fan of the "Sesame Street" television show and visits the Web site every day. "I think what he likes about going to the site on line is that he feels like he's a part of it," she added. "He can actively do things there, instead of just passively sitting, watching television." The designers have taken pains to make the site distinct from its commercial counterparts. For instance, the Muppet characters star in interactive games, but they are not promoted directly as products, the way commercial sites market their popular characters. The site has a store created by eToys that sells more than 250 products licensed by "Sesame Street," but the merchandise offers are not as prominent or intrusive as those on commercial sites. But unlike the television program, the Web site does carry advertising. There are no advertisements on content aimed directly at preschoolers, however, and advertisements aimed at older children are clearly labeled. Some people concerned with children's media issues say the limits are not enough. "I don't think children are a proper target for commercial speech," said Peggy Charren, a visiting scholar at Harvard University's Graduate School of Education and a leading lobbyist on such issues. "Ads tell children they need something they may not be able to afford when in reality, they probably don't need it." Gary E. Knell, executive vice president for operations at the Children's Television Workshop, responded that the Web site followed the same guidelines the organization had always followed on not interrupting content aimed at preschoolers with advertising. "We need something to be self-supporting," he said. "We don't want the on-line site to bleed the whole organization into oblivion. As with every not-for-profit venture, this one has to raise the money to support its content." In January, the Family Workshop site added content aimed at an elementary-school audience, older than the "Sesame Street" crowd. The site's new Kid City lets children 6 to 12 years old create their own home pages and collect and trade on-line stickers. So far, Family Workshop draws considerably fewer visitors than commercial sites. Certainly, the number of unique visitors to Disney Online's sites (4.6 million in February) and Nickelodeon Online's sites (nearly 1.5 million in February) continues to dwarf the number of visitors to the Children's Television Workshop's on-line venture (in February, 300,000), according to Media Metrix, a company that measures Web traffic. To broaden its on-line audience, Children's Television Workshop has struck a deal that allows it to distribute its content through the Excite search engine, in its Lifestyle category, and through Excite's Web Crawler search engine, under its Kids and Family heading. Since January, a version of the Children's Television Workshop's Family Workshop with exclusive interactive storytelling content has been available on America Online's proprietary service. "It was enormously important to us to get their content, not only because 53 percent of AOL households have children but because kids are coming on line at younger and younger ages," said Regina Lewis, an America Online spokeswoman. In the future, the site will probably be gently tweaked, rather than redesigned, to accommodate what is learned from research about how families use the Internet. In a recent research project, Sholly Fisch, vice president for program research at Children's Television Workshop and a former Marvel Comics writer, went into a handful of homes of computer users to observe how families navigate the Television Workshop site. "I found out it's not a linear experience for them at all, it's a family thing, with kids getting up from the computer to get snacks, an older brother coming in in the middle of a session, the phone ringing," Mr. Fisch said. "Now we have to go back and think about how to use that information to make the site work even better." All the tinkering in the world will probably not vault the site past larger commercial sites. But there are few sites on the Web that offer as much of a refuge from commercial pressure as the Children's Television Workshop site, much as "Sesame Street" on public television has offered a refuge from commercialism. And that's fine with Ms. Sharkey. "We're never going to be as big," she said, "and we're never going to have the reach or the resources. But you know what? We have something special."  Web Sites Appealing to Children  NICKELODEON ONLINE -- Includes www.nick.com, www.nickjr.com and others. * Number of unique visitors in February: 1.47 million. * Number of visitors ages 2 to 11: 337,000. * Content: Information on Nickelodeon television shows, interactive games, preschool content and a parents' forum. * Privacy policy: Does not collect personal information from visitors. * Advertising policy: On www.nickjr.com, ads appear only in areas for parents. On other Nickelodeon sites, if a user clicks on an ad that leads to an advertiser's Web site, a page warns that the user is leaving Nickelodeon.  DISNEY ONLINE -- Includes www.disney.com, www.family.com and Disney foreign language sites. * Number of unique visitors in February: 4.6 million. * Number of visitors 2 to 11: 392,000. * Content: For children, information and games based on Disney characters and properties; for adults, information about shopping and Disney vacation travel plans. * Privacy policy: Collects personal information during contest or sweepstakes registration, subscription registration and on-line shopping. * Advertising policy: Restricts many types of ads and clearly labels ads.  PBS ONLINE -- Includes www.pbs.org. * Number of unique visitors in February: 1.9 million. * Number of visitors 2 to 11: 170,000. * Content: Information on public television characters, educational games and links to affiliate sites. * Privacy policy: No child's personal information is ever posted or shared with a third party without parental consent. * Advertising policy: No ads appear on the site.  CHILDREN'S TELEVISION WORKSHOP ONLINE -- Includes www.ctw.org, www.stickerworld.org, www.sesamestreet.com and www.kidcity.org. * Number of unique visitors in February: 300,000. * Number of visitors aged 2-11: 45,000. * Content: For preschoolers, older kids and parents.. * Privacy policy: No personal information collected from children younger than 13 without parental consent. No personal information is shared with third parties. * Advertising policy: No ads appear on pages with content aimed at preschoolers. All ads are clearly identified. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Tina Sharkey of Children's Television Network Online, with friends from "Sesame Street."

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Dow Jones Annual Meeting Used as Forum for a Protest
body: Spearheaded by two Wall Street Journal reporters who just won the Pulitzer Prize, about 100 employees told the annual stockholders meeting of Dow Jones & Company yesterday that proposed cuts in pension benefits for more than half of the company's 8,300 employees are sapping loyalty and could provoke a strike. Bob Davis, the White House reporter of one of the two top-selling newspapers in the country, told the gathering on the 106th floor of the World Trade Center that he wanted "to alert the Dow Jones shareholders to the anger and resentment in the newsroom over management's decision to slash our retirement benefits." Mr. Davis, one of a six-member team that won the 1999 Pulitzer Prize for international reporting last week, added, "I believe workers would rather strike than accept management's terms." Through January, Dow Jones each year has paid 15 percent of the salaries of vested employees into a retirement account. But shortly after this year's contribution was deposited, Peter R. Kann, the chairman and chief executive of the company, said that the 15 percent payments -- technically designated as profit sharing -- could not be sustained when the company's profits had lagged for several years running. At the moment, the company is negotiating a new pension arrangement with the Independent Association of Publishers' Employees. The union numbers 2,400 Dow Jones employees among its members and, since January 1997, has been an affiliate of the Communications Workers of America. The initial Dow Jones proposal, according to both the union and company executives, would provide employees with a 5 percent benefit from company funds. In addition, employees could contribute up to 6 percent of their salaries toward a pension, with the company matching 50 percent of the employees' contribution. That proposal, last year, would have cost the company $21 million, as opposed to the $40 million it actually paid to about 5,500 company employees. Mr. Davis's allusion to a strike was not echoed by any of the negotiators for the union; indeed, as long as the contract remains in effect, employees are barred from such an action. Dow Jones's annual meeting has not been devoid of protests before, but participants in yesterday's protest said it was unusual for prominent Journal reporters to take the lead in such an action. Mr. Kann's opening speech to shareholders alluded to the complaints even before they were made. Looking out at dozens of his employees sitting among the audience of investors, he said, "The company is determined to make sure that the compensation packages we offer employees remain fully competitive." The company's opening offer, he said, "would already equate with what our competitors do, on average." Steve Liesman, another reporter on the Pulitzer-Prize winning international reporting team, followed Mr. Davis to the microphone and predicted there would be a potential loss of shareholder value if journalists brought less commitment to their work. "You can't punch it into a spreadsheet," he said, "but it's there." In response, Mr. Kann said, "I do understand the depth of feeling on this," although he added, "I do not think this is a productive forum for negotiating this issue." The poor performance of the company's market information business, Telerate, depressed earnings for several years before Dow Jones sold Telerate to Bridge Information Systems. Dow Jones had a net loss of $802 million in 1997 and net income of just $8.4 million in 1998. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Browser Foes Drop Enmity to Run Start-Up Together
body: For the last few years, Hadi Partovi has been a front-line warrior in the "browser war" -- the blood feud between Microsoft and Netscape in the market for Internet browsing software, the focus of the Government's sweeping antitrust case against Microsoft. As the lead product manager for the Microsoft Corporation's Internet Explorer, Mr. Partovi, in a flourish of competitive zeal, once led a group that loaded a giant script "E" -- for Explorer -- on a truck and drove to Mountain View, Calif., where they plopped it on the front lawn of the Netscape Communications Corporation's campus. When a videotape demonstration that Microsoft presented two months ago at its antitrust trial proved embarrassing, he was summoned overnight to set things right. Mr. Partovi, a 26-year-old Harvard graduate, speaks movingly of his emotional bond to Microsoft and its people. But this week, having just left Microsoft, he is joining a Silicon Valley software start-up founded by a pair of his former enemies from Netscape, Michael McCue and Angus Davis, and backed by Jim Clark, the co-founder of Netscape. The move, uniting onetime adversaries, seems a sure sign that the browser war is over. Microsoft and Netscape still compete in the browser market, of course. But it is no longer seen as the arena of excitement, corporate life-and-death rivalry and cutting-edge innovation that lures the young, entrepreneurial talent that keeps the frontiers of the software business moving ahead at a dizzying pace. To the youthful entrepreneurs at Tellme Networks Inc., the browser business is suddenly a backwater. They speak of it as "mature" -- no compliment in Silicon Valley, whose business culture is dedicated to pursuing the technologically new and hot, the Next Big Thing. "Browsers are an evolutionary business now," said Mr. Davis, a former browser product manager at Netscape. "What you want to do is walk into a space and make a revolutionary change." Mr. Davis speaks with the wisdom of 21 years. He joined Netscape at 18, becoming its youngest employee. For Mr. McCue, 31, Tellme Networks is the second start-up. He joined Netscape in early 1996, when it bought his small company, Paper Software Inc., for an estimated $20 million. At Netscape, he was vice president for technology. They are part of a growing number of former employees who have left Netscape, mostly to form start ups. In Silicon Valley, they are known as Netscapees, and their numbers are likely to increase now that the purchase of Netscape by America Online Inc. is complete. Among others, Tellme has signed up John Giannandrea, a senior programmer at Netscape, who led efforts to put Java, an Internet programming language of Sun Microsystems, into the Netscape browser. Mr. McCue, who left Netscape in December, said that the purchase by America Online was not really the reason he departed, but a further prod to take the entrepreneurial path again. Just what slice of the Internet software business Tellme is aiming at is a closely held secret. "All I can say is that we're not going after some niche market," Mr. McCue said. "We want to use Internet technology to revolutionize an industry again." Venture capitalists and industry executives believe that Tellme intends to use some combination of natural-language and speech-recognition technology to give users a simpler way to find information on the World Wide Web or retrieve it from a computer, probably with a telephone. The industry experts base their speculation on the name of the company, the backgrounds of its founders and recent technology trends. The industry experts say the goal is to allow people to speak a simple question or command -- such as "What is the weather forecast for San Francisco today?" or "Send me my email" -- and receive replies by either voice or email. "Natural language technology is at the very forefront of commercialization now," said Richard Shaffer, a principal of Technologic Partners. "But a lot of companies are working on it, so if that's where Tellme is going, it will find a lot of competition." Whatever the business plan, it proved alluring to Mr. Partovi. By leaving Microsoft, he walked away from unexercised stock options worth "millions," he says. To try to keep him, Mr. Partovi says, Steven Ballmer, the Microsoft president, offered him a corporate staff position working directly for him -- a chance that would be regarded as a career-boosting prize at Microsoft. "Talking to Steve Ballmer was the hardest thing about leaving," Mr. Partovi observed. Yet Mr. Partovi, too, had decided to leave the big-company environment and join a start-up. He looked at a dozen companies, he said, but found Tellme the most promising. Mr. McCue knew Mr. Partovi well from the browser wars and, he said, wanted him on his side in the new venture. Is there any residual hard feeling from the days of bare-knuckle competition -- including some Microsoft tactics that the Government has called illegal -- when the browser war was at its height? Hardly, says Mr. McCue, who looks back at the Microsoft-Netscape confrontation as a pragmatic capitalist, not as a lawyer. "It was mainly a lot of heavy-duty, good clean competition," he said. "We viewed that experience as an asset in recruiting Hadi." Mr. Partovi offered his own retrospective olive branch. "There was nothing really personal about the browser wars," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Co-founders of the Tellme Networks in a jovial mood outside their temporary offices in Palo Alto, Calif. title: U.S. Urges New Rules to Guard Privacy of Children on Internet
body: The Federal Government proposed new rules today to protect the privacy interests of children on the Internet. The rules, prepared by the Federal Trade Commission, would require commercial Web sites to get parental consent before seeking information from children under 13. It would also require the sites to post notifications about what they do with any information obtained from children. The proposal comes after a new law expanding the agency's authority on privacy issues. That legislation moved through Congress quickly last fall after studies by the Government and experts showed that the vast majority of Web sites collect personal information from consumers and children and that very few companies provide notice about what they do with such information. "Kids are a particularly vulnerable audience," said Robert Pitofsky, chairman of the Federal Trade Commission. "You mix the invasions of privacy with kids and you have a particularly combustible mix." Web sites that ask children to provide personal information about themselves and their families have proliferated in recent years. Sometimes the sites offer prizes in exchange for information. Children who want to win a Nintendo Game Boy from the Blue Bunny ice cream trucks can register at www.bombpop.com by supplying their name, address, age, email address and favorite kind of ice cream. The Web site does not say what it does with the information. At another site, run by the Liberty Fund, a large asset manager in Boston, children are asked questions about their family's finances, including whether their parents use mutual funds or brokers, whether the children have received bonds or stocks as gifts, and what the family does with its money. The site, www.younginvestor.com, says the surveys are "completely anonymous" but it also uses "cookies," which are programs that track a user's comings and goings at a particular site. A study by the Federal Trade Commission concluded last June that 89 percent of children's sites surveyed collected personal information from children and that few of the sites had tried to provide for meaningful parental involvement in the process. The study found that only 23 percent of the sites even tell children to seek parental permission before providing personal information, 7 percent say they will notify parents of their information practices, and fewer than 10 percent provide for parental control over either the collection or use of the information gleaned from their children. After that study, Congress passed a law last October proposed by the Federal Trade Commission that gave it wide authority to adopt new rules that would protect the privacy interests of children and their families. If, as expected, the proposed rules are approved this year by the commission's four members, compliance would provide a "safe harbor" from Government lawsuits for improper trade practices. The proposal applies to any commercial Web sites directed to, or that knowingly collect information from, children under 13 years of age. It would require companies to obtain "verifiable parental consent" through various means. Web sites can provide a consent form that would be signed by the parents and returned by postal mail or facsimile, take credit card numbers from parents, offer a toll-free number that parents could call, or accept email accompanied by a unique "digital signature" that demonstrates that the email was not sent by the child. Privacy experts have warned that standard email is not sufficient because children can easily send what appears to be their parents' consent. "Generally, the proposal looks pretty good," said Katharina Kopp, a senior policy analyst at the Center for Media Education, a Washington research and advocacy group that has pushed for the rules. "But the F.T.C. could have given stricter guidance that email, by itself, does not work to provide verifiable parental consent." But industry lobbyists have argued in favor of a wide latitude in developing mechanisms to get parental consent. "We believe there should be broad flexibility," said Jerry Cerasale, a lobbyist for the Direct Marketing Association, which represents 4,600 companies that use the Internet, telephones and mail to sell products. Some privacy experts said the rules would be hollow without a vigorous enforcement program in which the Federal Trade Commission would audit a sample of companies to assure that they are getting adequate consent and following their own privacy guidelines. "The most important piece of this policy will be whether the F.T.C. verifies what the companies are actually doing," said Jason Catlett, president of the Junkbusters Corporation, which promotes consumer protection on the Internet. Mr. Pitofsky, the commission chairman, suggested that the agency would be vigorous in enforcing any rules that are ultimately adopted. "Unless there's a monitoring mechanism to see what people do when they say they are abiding by the rules," he said, "the rules are an empty gesture."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Apple Media Software Challenges 2 Rivals
body: In a direct challenge to both the Microsoft Corporation and Real Networks Inc., Apple Computer today introduced a new version of its Quicktime multimedia software designed to permit computer users to receive video and audio programming over the Internet. The distribution of multimedia material is emerging as one of the hottest businesses on the Internet. Last week in Hollywood, Microsoft announced its own technology in the field, known as MS Audio 4.0, and the International Business Machines Corporation and Sony Inc. announced an agreement to make their competing systems compatible with each other. All three companies, plus a handful of other developers, large and small, are vying to produce the technology that will ultimately be adopted as the standard by the recording industry. That industry is deeply concerned about the rapid growth of a vibrant cottage industry around the MP3 audio standard, a format for storing audio files. Because MP3 has no built-in copyright protection schemes, the recording industry views it as a serious threat; hundreds of thousands of MP3 users are already exchanging music over the Internet without paying musicians or record companies. Multimedia programs -- incorporating audio, video, and computer graphics -- can be played on computers in two basic ways: streaming media, which delivers the program as the user watches or listens, and downloaded media, which is delivered in its entirety to the user's hard drive and then viewed or heard. Programming can originate from television or radio broadcasts or from recorded music. Until now, the battle over the market for Internet viewing of multimedia presentations has largely been between Microsoft, which has built many of the most popular formats into its Windows Media Player, and Real Networks, maker of the Realplayer streaming software. However, analysts said today that Apple's strategy would probably make it a three-way race. In addition to announcing an initial public test, or beta, for Quicktime 4, Apple said it would offer software that would make it possible for server computers using its Mac OS X operating system to distribute multimedia content over the Internet. They said the server software would support a streaming technology that has been defined as a standard by an Internet engineering task force backed by many companies. Separately, at the National Association of Broadcasters meeting in Las Vegas, Apple executives said today that its new server software would have the support of several key hardware manufacturers, including Cisco Systems, I.B.M., Silicon Graphics Inc. and Sun Microsystems. The result will be relatively inexpensive server computers that will allow independent artists or small businesses to offer programming to large audiences over the Internet. Industry analysts said today that Apple should have a significant advantage in the market for Internet multimedia software since much of the multimedia material already offered on line was originally created in the Quicktime format. "It depends on the media," said Andrew Gore, editor in chief of Macworld magazine. "For movies, they have a tremendous advantage. However, for live video, Microsoft has made a significant inroad." Apple officials said today that the company's strategy was different from those of both Real Networks, which charges a licensing fee for its server software, and Microsoft, which offers its server technology only on the proprietary Windows NT operating system. Because Apple is releasing the source code for its server software, it will be simple for organizations that want to transmit multimedia material to adapt their own systems. Phil Schiller, Apple's vice president for worldwide marketing, said the company would make an effort to insure that the new Quicktime software incorporates a wide variety of different media formats known as "codecs" (for compression-decompression), bodies of software coding that transform audio and video programming into digital format for transmission and translate it back on the user's computer. "We support more codecs than anyone in the world," Mr. Schiller said. Indeed, in recent months the competition in the streaming media market has shifted to a battle to demonstrate the highest quality in codecs. While it is hard to tell the differences when one is using a modem that delivers speeds of 56,000 bits a second, Mr. Schiller said, the rapid shift among consumers to high-speed cable modems and digital subscriber lines is making distinctions more apparent. The Quicktime 4 viewer can be downloaded free by both Windows and Macintosh users from Apple's Web site. A $29.95 version lets users create and edit digital content. And separately, Apple said today that it had begun shipping professional video authoring software. http://www.nytimes.com
