title: Candidates Set For Internet Registry Work
body: The first five companies to compete with Network Solutions Inc. in the business of registering Internet addresses will be selected this week, even though the Government has not yet made final the terms under which the company will open its data base. The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, the nonprofit corporation established last year by the Commerce Department to take over administration of the Internet, has scheduled a briefing for Wednesday at which it will name the five applicants to begin the initial test round of competition with Network Solutions. That company has had an exclusive Government contract for registering names in the Internet's top-level domains like .com, .net and .org since 1993. The Internet Corporation declined to say how many companies had applied for the competition, which it expects to start by the end of the month. It hopes to open the process to an unlimited number of companies worldwide by the summer. Complicating the process has been the lack of an agreement between Network Solutions of Herndon, Va., and the Commerce Department on the terms under which the company will let rivals into its registry. With the explosive growth of the Internet, Network Solutions has moved from an obscure Government contractor to a Fortune 500 company. That has created a tough situation for the Clinton Administration, which is trying to balance the interests of the monopoly it created with those of the Internet community. The sticking points concern which data and equipment in the domain-name registry built by Network Solutions is public and which is the company's property. Because Network Solutions created the domain-name registration system under an exclusive Government contract, everything from the software it developed to worldwide data bases of Internet address holders is in question. The two sides must also agree on how much new registrars will pay Network Solutions for the transition. The company has proposed that they pay $10,000 to help offset the cost of the software it has developed for the shared registration system. It is also negotiating how much companies will pay it as a fee for maintaining the registry. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Compaq Computer Ousts Chief Executive
body: The Compaq Computer Corporation, the world's largest personal computer maker, ousted its president and chief executive, Eckhard Pfeiffer, yesterday in a dramatic boardroom coup that reflects just how much the Internet is shaking up the computer industry. The forced resignation of the 57-year-old Mr. Pfeiffer, a leading figure in the personal computer industry, came as a surprise, especially the timing of the move. Compaq had just hosted hundreds of its leading corporate customers at a conference, where Mr. Pfeiffer confidently detailed the company's plans for the future. And on Thursday, Compaq will hold its yearly shareholders meeting on its corporate campus in Houston, where the featured speaker was to have been Mr. Pfeiffer. But with increasing urgency in recent days -- as Compaq warned that its first-quarter profits would be half of Wall Street's expectations and the company's stock price kept falling -- the longtime Compaq chairman, Benjamin M. Rosen, led the call for Mr. Pfeiffer's resignation. After consulting with the other Compaq directors, Mr. Rosen met with Mr. Pfeiffer over the weekend and told him the board agreed that he should resign, according to a person close to the board. "It wasn't a request on Ben's part," the person said. Mr. Rosen said yesterday that Compaq's problems were not fundamental strategic errors, but mainly that "we're not executing as well as we should have." Asked about specific areas for improvement, Mr. Rosen replied, "The Internet opportunity for Compaq is incredible." He noted that Compaq, especially after its $8.7 billion purchase of the Digital Equipment Corporation last year, had everything from its own Internet search engine, Alta Vista, to large server computers for hosting Internet services and electronic commerce. "We have it all, but some of our competitors have done a better job of positioning themselves and exploiting that opportunity," Mr. Rosen said. I.B.M. and Sun Microsystems have succeeded in casting themselves as suppliers of Internet hardware and services, for example, while Dell Computer has positioned itself as the personal computer maker whose direct sales model lends itself most naturally to marketing on the Internet. In a brief statement announcing Mr. Pfeiffer's resignation, Mr. Rosen suggested that the accelerating change brought about by the Internet had overtaken Compaq's management, led by Mr. Pfeiffer. "As a company engaged in transforming its industry for the Internet era," Mr. Rosen said, "we must have the organizational flexibility necessary to move at Internet speed." Earl Mason, Compaq's chief financial officer, also submitted his resignation yesterday. He had previously been offered the job of chief executive of a company outside the personal computer industry, an offer Mr. Mason informed the Compaq board he planned to accept. His departure, Compaq said, was not related to Mr. Pfeiffer's resignation. "It was just an unfortunate coincidence of timing," Mr. Rosen explained. Mr. Pfeiffer could not be reached for comment. But in a brief statement, he said, "Compaq has come a long way since I joined the company in 1983," adding that "under Ben's guidance, I know this company will realize its potential." A search will begin immediately, Mr. Rosen said, for Mr. Pfeiffer's replacement. But in the meantime, Compaq will be headed by Mr. Rosen and two other directors, who will form a three-person office of the chief executive. The two are Frank P. Doyle, 67, a retired executive vice president of the General Electric Company; and Robert Ted Enloe 3d, 60, a private investor. All three men will move to Houston to oversee the company, until a successor to Mr. Pfieffer is in place. This is the second time Mr. Rosen, 65, has engineered the ouster of a Compaq chief executive. In 1991, he saw off Joseph R. Canion, an engineer who had helped design Compaq's first machine on a restaurant place mat. Mr. Canion had led the rise of Compaq, founded in 1983 and backed by Mr. Rosen's venture capital fund, Sevin Rosen. It thrived in the early years mainly by offering customers more powerful computers than its main rival, the International Business Machines Corporation, for about the same price. But Compaq proved ill-suited for responding to the severe price-cutting that developed in the early 1990's. So Mr. Rosen led the boardroom revolt that pushed Mr. Canion out in October 1991. In his place, the board installed Mr. Pfeiffer, a German native who rose through the company's international operations and was a fierce advocate of low-cost, efficient production. "In 1991, we were just a PC company," Mr. Rosen said. "Now we're a broad information technology company." Moving quickly to replace a chief executive is made easier at Compaq by the board structure that Mr. Rosen insisted on when the company was founded. The chairman and chief executive roles are split, with Mr. Rosen serving as a chairman who is not part of the management staff. In addition, the board is nearly all outside directors. Mr. Pfeiffer was the only member of Compaq's day-to-day management team on the board. The remaining 11 are Mr. Rosen and 10 outside directors. "It's Ben's board, and the man really behind Compaq has always been Ben Rosen," Richard Shaffer, a principal at the research firm Technologic Partners, said. "With this move, it certainly seems that Ben Rosen is rethinking the Compaq business model once again." Compaq profits have been squeezed recently by a combination of forces, including an eroding share of the fast-growing and lucrative business of PC servers, the large computers that serve as hubs of corporate networks and World Wide Web sites, analysts say. Other near-term problems, they say, are accelerated price-cutting on desktop PC's and the difficulty integrating Digital Equipment into Compaq. Ten days ago, Compaq warned that its profits for the first quarter would be about $250 million instead of the Wall Street consensus estimate of $540 million. Compaq's stock price closed on Friday at $23.625, representing a 44 percent decline so far this year. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The Internet revolution caught up with Eckhard Pfeiffer yesterday.

body: The Wizard of Menlo Park may no longer be with us, but that isn't stopping Thomas A. Edison from selling Web servers. Lloyd E. Kruckeberg, a devout fan of the inventor since childhood, was looking for a name last year for his new E-commerce company when he discovered that Thomas A. Edison had been abandoned as a company name nearly 50 years ago. Mr. Kruckeberg secured trademark rights to the name and to use of the inventor's signature as the Web company's logo, along with rights to an Edison image that adorns the company's press releases and Web site. The current Thomas A. Edison Inc. may not be inventing anything as world-changing as the light bulb, but that hasn't impeded the company's copy writers. "Get ready," reads a pitch on the company's Web site, "because at Thomas A. Edison Incorporated, we're here to revolutionize your life, again." The company and its 70 employees are based in Amarillo, Tex. Its first product is a $10,000 software and computer combination to help small companies do business on the Web. But while the E-commerce company may have succeeded in securing rights to Mr. Edison's name, likeness and signature, it hit a snag with the Internet domain. The Web address www.thomasedison.com was already owned by the Brockton (Mass.) Historical Society, which maintains an on-line museum devoted to the inventor. Thomas A. title: Despite a Passion for the Net, Many On-LineVolunteers Want Pay
body: David Mann has played piano and written arrangements for Frank Sinatra, serenaded President Truman on his yacht and written popular music like the song "In the Wee Small Hours of the Morning." More recently, from his home in Kinnelon, N.J., he sits at a different keyboard, talking about classical music with the members of a chat room on America Online. By his estimate, he puts in at least five hours a week as a volunteer, moderating a weekly chat session, answering email and filling out an on-line report about his duties. In exchange, he and more than 10,000 other people who perform similar tasks for the on-line service get a free account and the designation "community leader." What they do not get is a paycheck, which is fine with Mr. Mann. "I am not too concerned with being remunerated, since my purpose was to fulfill an obligation to my art -- my Muse, as it were. I merely believe that I owe it to the cause of good music to steer less knowledgeable people in the right direction," said Mr. Mann, 82, in an email interview. "I deem it not only an obligation for me to do so, but a privilege." While Mr. Mann considers his role a privilege, some former volunteers for America Online view it as work and have filed complaints with the Labor Department. They say volunteers at the company are treated like employees and perform functions that are integral to the on-line service's mission and should be paid. In asking the Labor Department to investigate their claims, they have raised two decidedly Internet-age questions: When does taking part in and enjoying a community transcend hobby status and become work? And what does an Internet company owe to the people who give it life, not to mention high valuations on the stock market? While the Labor Department will not comment on the complaints against America Online or any action it is taking, the industry and the volunteers themselves are looking on with interest. If the department does find America Online in violation of laws like the Federal Fair Labor Standards Act, it could change the on-line landscape, since America Online is not the only company that relies on the passions and goodwill of people like Mr. Mann. Dozens of other Internet businesses, including Prodigy Communications, iVillage and Geocities, are built on the foundation of a virtual community, where volunteer participants establish, lead and police discussion areas. In turn, the businesses proudly boast about the number of members who take part in their communities, and trade on those numbers to attract advertisers and make multimillion-dollar business deals. Without their contributions, company executives acknowledge that their services would be virtual ghost towns. "They're the core foundation of our business," said Bruce Zanca, a spokesman for Geocities, a Web community where he says four million people have built free home pages. Mr. Zanca said 1,800 volunteers contributed their time to the management of the on-line community, hosting chat rooms and enforcing community standards, among other tasks. In exchange, they get Geo-Points they can use to buy products and services on Geocities. "The monetary exchange probably wouldn't be an inducement," Mr. Zanca said. "These people are the cyber equivalent of scout leaders and P.T.A. members and the Rotary and Kiwanis Clubs. Why do people participate in these programs? It's the same reason I coach Little League on Saturday mornings. It's something people do for their own personal reasons." The local Little League is a different proposition, however, than Geocities, a publicly traded company with 300 paid employees that was bought in January by Yahoo in a stock deal worth about $3.6 billion. The notion of volunteering for a for-profit corporation is an unusual one, so there is little precedent by which to judge these relationships. But one question the Labor Department might be asking as it looks into the complaints about American Online is whether the volunteer force is providing a service that the company would have to pay for if volunteers did not exist, said Jeffrey Chamberlain, an employment lawyer based in Albany. "It's the difference between volunteering at I.B.M. to assemble computers and volunteering at the I.B.M. soup kitchen," Mr. Chamberlain said. "The difference between doing good and making computers is relatively conceptually easy to understand." In the digital age, the lines between volunteering and working without pay are less clear. Many of the people who volunteer on line say they do the work for personal reasons -- not for the corporation. Terri Bass spends, by her estimation, 20 to 30 hours a week in her home in Middleton, Wis., as a supervisor in the pet care forum on America Online. She says she loves her virtual, unpaid job: hosting chat sessions, checking bulletin boards for inappropriate comments, responding to email from those who visit the area. Sure, she said, she would like to be paid. "Who wouldn't love that?" she said. But even without financial compensation, she derives great satisfaction from her work. "We are a close-knit family here," she said. "Most of my best friends are here." It may seem peculiar to the uninitiated that so many people would give so much time, without financial compensation, to a company with $2.6 billion in revenue last year and a stock market valuation of $130 billion. Perhaps even more peculiar is the notion that volunteers would be so personally invested in the work they do. But it is a phenomenon that is part of an on-line tradition. "Like sex, it looks funny from the outside," said Howard Rheingold, author of the book "The Virtual Community" (Addison-Wesley, 1993). "Any virtual community that works, works because people put in some time." But in exchange, he said, what the members of virtual communities need and want is respect. Many Internet businesses, in the frenzied rush to capitalize on industry buzzwords, have used the word "community" in their marketing, but not necessarily in deed. Mr. Rheingold said he suspected this was the case with the management at America Online. Scott Kurnit, founder of the Mining Company, a guide to the Internet, chose a different strategy to compensate the people who manage various topics within the company's directory, like "pregnancy" or "Southern food." Mr. Kurnit said he knew when he started the company that he would need a large group of guides to fulfill his promise of a "human-powered" search engine, but that the economics of hiring a large staff were unrealistic for a start-up operation. Instead, he pays the guides a combination of a monthly stipend and a cut of the net revenues generated by advertising on their sections. Mr. Kurnit says the guides, who now number 692, earn between $500 and $11,000 a month, depending on the popularity of the section. In addition, he said, he issued 200,000 shares of stock to the guides, which is now worth a total of about $10 million. (The company went public last month, making Mr. Kurnit, on paper, worth more than $50 million.) In exchange, the guides sign over the rights to the sites they create, and agree not to work for other on-line services in a similar capacity. While for guides who have less trafficked sites, the compensation might not equal a living wage, Mr. Kurnit feels his program offers a fair reward, and that the company benefits more than it would if he relied on volunteers. "My view is entrepreneurs are the best workers -- they work tirelessly," Mr. Kurnit said. "Volunteers are unreliable, and have an expectation that you owe them something." However, Mr. Zanca of Geocities disagrees that the quality of work he gets from his volunteers is less than if he were to pay them. He also said he was not concerned that the Labor Department inquiry might affect the way his company is structured. "We think the Net has a new dynamic," he said, "and in new dynamics, laws and regulations need to be re-evaluated." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: David Mann, a songwriter and pianist, is a volunteer for America Online. (George M. Gutierrez for The newyork Times)

title: Paging Allies Focus Strategy On the Internet
body: Threatened by the specter of irrelevance in an era of near-ubiquitous cellular phones and email, most of the nation's largest paging companies have formed an alliance to deploy inexpensive hand-held computers that use a new two-way wireless technology developed by Motorola Inc. The companies intend to announce the alliance today at the Comdex technology conference in Chicago. With the explosion in use of wireless telephones, the paging business has come under intense pressure in recent years. Some 73 million people in the unitedstates now use wireless phones, compared with only about 56 million who use pagers. What is more, the increasing use of wireless phones has forced paging companies to slash prices. It is big news these days when a paging carrier makes money. And as communications equipment makers begin incorporating email and in some cases rudimentary World Wide Web browsers into wireless phones, paging companies face an even greater threat. The new alliance may be the paging industry's best-coordinated and most comprehensive response. The group is in talks with the Microsoft Corporation and the 3Com Corporation about incorporating the new Motorola technology into hand-held computers that use Microsoft's Windows CE and 3Com's Palm operating systems. The paging alliance is based on a simple concept: most wireless phones that include Web services do not allow talking and surfing at the same time. When the user is talking, the screen is generally pressed against the person's cheek, making it impossible to, say, negotiate a meeting time while actually looking at one's schedule. The paging companies want to sell small units that are separate from a phone but that could include a small keyboard, email, a date book and address book and that would have a battery life measured in weeks instead of days or hours. "Our vision of the future is that most people will carry two wireless devices," said John D. Beletic, chairman of the new alliance and chairman of Pagemart Wireless Inc., one of the largest paging companies. "One is going to be a telephone, and the characteristics of the telephone are that they are going to get smaller and smaller and smaller." He added: "But when you use this phone maybe you wanted to set up a lunch with me, and while you're talking to me you may be wanting to look at your calendar. Or I'm giving you important information and you want to enter that into a data device. And these devices won't be optimized for voice. They will have calendar, memos, directory, text messaging, and from a wireless standpoint it will be optimized to penetrate into buildings and will be optimized to work for weeks on a couple of double-A batteries." In fact, such devices already exist. The American Mobile Satellite Corporation and the BellSouth Corporation's wireless data unit offer advanced two-way paging services using small units made by Research in Motion Ltd. of Canada, based partly on technology from Ericsson of Sweden. Skytel Communications Inc., one of the paging carriers in the new alliance, already offers two-way service using units from Motorola and Glenayre Technologies Inc. "We believe we have the best performance from a network standpoint," John Kampfe, a spokesman for the BellSouth wireless data operation, said. "The latency of messages is in seconds rather than minutes, which allows people to chat from their devices." But current two-way pagers generally do not offer true nationwide coverage, since most reach only big cities. Nor do they use popular operating systems, though the upcoming Palm VII organizer will use the BellSouth network. The new alliance wants to offer service nationwide and to incorporate the new Motorola technology, known as Reflex, in the Windows CE and Palm operating systems and in devices that use Sun Microsystems Inc.'s Java programming language. "Paging has really had to in many ways redefine itself as an extension of the desktop computer as opposed to a cheaper method of staying in touch," said Jeanine M. Oburchay, a wireless analyst for Bear, Stearns.  "The advanced networks we're seeing built out now are the paging industry's way of redefining itself into a remote messaging industry or remote email industry." Mr. Beletic said Pagemart, which is based in Dallas, spent about $310 million to upgrade its network for the new devices. He wants to begin offering advanced two-way services later this year and wants to persuade makers of standard hand-held computers to incorporate the new wireless technology by early next year. Under license from Motorola, Glenayre, of Charlotte, N.C., is also developing chips for the new technology, which based loosely on the programming language of the Internet. Glenayre's products could help draw in developers wary of relying on a single vendor, analysts say. The paging carriers participating in the alliance are Airtouch, Arch Communications, Conxus, Metrocall, Mobilecomm, Pagemart, Pagenet, Skytel and TSR Wireless. The only major paging carrier that had not yet signed on as of Friday was Ameritech's paging unit. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY: E-Commerce Report;
As on-line auctions move into pricier mechandise, escrow services offer those about to be scammed a little safety.
body: INTERNET auctions are promoted for their ability to rid the world of middlemen and let buyers and sellers strike deals in free-market harmony. But as auction sites look to cash in on the trend by selling more costly goods, this Internet utopia is coming under threat. Higher prices can mean lower levels of trust. That is why, in recent months, Internet escrow services have gained a following in person-to-person selling circles. These services, in which a third party holds the money until both buyer and seller are satisfied with the transaction, can reduce the risk of fraud, bounced checks or goods that fall short of expectations. Internet executives and analysts say a vast majority of business is still conducted without such services, but that could change quickly, as Beanie Babies and baseball cards are eclipsed on the auction block by Bordeaux and BMW's. The services work as their off-line counterparts do: The parties strike an agreement, the buyer pays the sale price -- plus a fee, which is typically 5 percent -- to the escrow service, and when the buyer accepts the item, the escrow service transfers the money to the seller. Though some on-line auction companies, such as Auction Universe and Edeal, provide their own escrow services for customers, others, like Amazon.com, Ebay and Yahoo Auctions, offer the services of third-party escrow providers, often in exchange for a percentage of the escrow fee. Notably, the escrow services collect the fee even when a transaction falls through, as was the case with Heather Krolak, a 24-year-old photographer and artist from Brooklyn, who entered into an agreement to buy a Patrick Nagel painting on Ebay in early February for $1,500. "I was skeptical," Ms. Krolak said, noting that works by Nagel, a nationally known artist in the 1970's and 80's, typically command much higher prices. "It seemed like a little too good of a deal." Because the seller was in Spring Valley, Calif., Ms. Krolak asked him to conduct the transaction through I-Escrow, one of the two leading on-line escrow providers. (Tradesafe, I-Escrow's chief competitor, is also available on Ebay. Both sites are also available on Amazon's auction channel.) Ms. Krolak and the seller clicked onto I-Escrow's site and registered, creating a secure page in which they could further negotiate the length of the inspection period and other terms of the deal. Ms. Krolak argued for a one-week inspection period, while the seller wanted to allow only one day. The seller also informed Ms. Krolak that the artist's signature was slightly off, but that he had a letter from the artist's brother verifying the painting's authenticity. "I thought that was a little odd," Ms. Krolak said, "so I stuck to the one-week inspection period." Upon receiving the painting, Ms. Krolak had it inspected by two experts, who declared that it was not a Nagel. She sent it back, forfeiting the $120 escrow fee. "I was disappointed, and I lost the fee," she said. "But it was worth it because I would have lost a lot more if I hadn't used it." Would she bid on expensive artwork again? "You have to be careful -- especially with art," she said. "But sure I would." This is just the kind of testimonial that Internet auction sites are hoping for, since Web auctioneers are intent on pushing the average sale price for an item beyond the current $45 level so they can collect fatter commissions. That means that consumers can expect to see more so-called special event auctions, like a recent Ansel Adams auction on Auction Universe, and more specialized auction sites where rare items are offered. (Auction Universe is a division of Classified Ventures.com, which is partly owned by The newyork Times Company.) "With more auction sites that are specific to collectors, we could see an enormous growth in the need for escrow services," said Sue Rothberg, a senior analyst with Gomez Advisers, an electronic commerce research firm in Concord, Mass. "When you're talking about things like antique Shaker furniture, those people are serious shoppers who don't want to mess around." Ms. Rothberg said that in a recent survey, she found that just 4 of the top 15 Internet auction sites offered some form of escrow service. "But that will blossom, I'm certain," she said. According to Ken Pereira, Tradesafe's chief executive, less than 1 percent of auction transactions use escrow, although he expects such use to exceed 4 percent by year's end. In the future, Mr. Pereira said, "we don't see it going much beyond 10 percent," because he expects that most auctioned goods will still have relatively low prices. But operators of escrow services see ample opportunity to profit. Edeal, a Toronto-based auctioneer that offers customers an escrow option, is one such example. "If we start doing large volumes of deals, there's constant cash in trust for us. It's not our money, obviously, but you could have a period of a week where there's $10 million in trust. We could invest it in an extremely secure Treasury bill, for example, and roll it over at, say, 5 percent." The company is "still figuring out the legalities of it," said Leon Kuperman, chief technology officer for Edeal. "But we know there's some potential there." But some other auction sites avoid this approach. "We're licensed in California, so we have to put the money in a noninterest-bearing trust," said Sanjay Bajaj, vice president for marketing and business development at I-Escrow. "But we make our money on fees. We don't want any incentive to delay payment to sellers." Mr. Bajaj said the number of registered I-Escrow users had grown to 50,000 from 5,000 in the last five months, but "you'd be surprised at how many people still don't know about these services." One reason, perhaps, is that escrow services generally do not receive prominent placement on auction sites. On Ebay, for instance, information about the service's escrow providers is located two pages within sections titled Safe Harbor and After the Auction. Escrow information may gain prominence as the value of auctioned goods rises, though -- and in response to mounting concerns about auction-related fraud. Noting that the National Consumers League had seen a 600 percent increase in on-line fraud reports since 1997, Zona Research warned in a recent report that "if the on-line auction community does not take steps to limit fraud then it could face serious problems, including government intervention." Given a choice between government intervention and a free-market solution, auction providers may quickly see the virtue of promoting escrow services front and center on the user's screen -- representing one small victory for Internet middlemen. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Illustration (Tom Bloom)

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Privacy on Internet Poses Legal Puzzle
body: Each time a revolutionary new technology has arrived, the governments of the day have been leery of its capacity for mischief and criminality. Centuries ago, there were calls for giving the authorities the power of prior restraint lest the printing press become an instrument of sedition and slander. Later, there were qualms about selling automobiles to the public because crooks could use them to escape the police. As the designated representative of this rich and checkered tradition, Philip Reitinger, a prosecutor for the Justice Department, knew he faced a tough crowd last Tuesday in Cambridge, Mass. He was speaking at a conference to mark the 35th anniversary of the founding of the Laboratory for Computer Science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a gathering of technology's true believers. Mr. Reitinger, square-jawed and pin-striped, opened with a bit of dry humor, laced with sarcasm. "It may come as a shock to many of you, but people commit crimes on the Internet," he said. So began a spirited discussion and debate on a seemingly narrow subject, "Should the Laboratory for Computer Science Anonymous Remailer Be Shut Down?" But the discussion focused on some of the broadest social and legal issues involving the Internet: identity, privacy, anonymity and free speech. Mr. Reitinger's opposite number on the panel was Nadine Strossen, a professor at the newyork Law School and president of the American Civil Liberties Union. They were joined by Frans Kaashoek, an associate professor at M.I.T., who has been in charge of the anonymous remailer since it began operating in 1996. An anonymous remailer, a type of data-network relay, is essentially a technological buffer, offering confidentiality to its users. It can be used to mask the origin of a piece of email or the computer from which a person is browsing the World Wide Web. It does this by stripping off the identifying information on an email, for example, and substituting an anonymous code number or term. Sophisticated remailers, like the one at M.I.T., also route messages through many different relay computers around the world, leaving no record of the path an anonymous message traveled after leaving the remailer. But computer experts have occasionally tracked messages from remailers, either because a person used an anonymity service incorrectly or because of security flaws in a remailer. There are about 40 anonymous remail services worldwide. They are used by, among others, dissidents and human rights representatives in nations with repressive governments, whistle-blowers in companies or government agencies, minority groups fearing discrimination and people simply wishing to avoid the bulk email advertising that marketers increasingly send over the Net. In Kosovo, some people with on-line connections have started using anonymous remail services to try to maintain confidential communications and avoid detection by the Serbian military. But anonymous remail services, Federal prosecutors say, are also used by child pornographers, extortionists, software pirates and drug dealers. Though not illegal, remailers are often viewed with suspicion by law enforcement agencies. They occupy a gray area in cyberspace, and Mr. Kaashoek good-naturedly underscored that fact by wearing a black ski mask for much of the panel discussion. After his opening, Mr. Reitinger turned to his theme. "Anonymity has a down side to it," he said. "It's hard to put a pseudonym in jail. There are not a lot of indictments that say, unitedstates of America versus John Doe. If people are truly anonymous, there can be no law enforcement." Mr. Reitinger and Ms. Strossen have debated these issues in the past, so their early exchanges had the practiced rhythms of old sparring partners. Her opening salvo: "We've got to make sure that freedom of speech, freedom of the press and privacy are as protected in cyberspace as they are in the rest of life. Certain individual rights cannot be sacrificed because of the panic and fears of abuse of a new technology, or because it creates problems for law enforcement." Mr. Reitinger, a senior counsel in the Justice Department's computer crime and intellectual property division, agreed that the Internet had made his life more difficult. Trying to trace a path of criminal communications often involves working with authorities in 8 to 20 nations, he observed. Anonymous remailers can make that tracing far more difficult, if not impossible. Mr. Kaashoek said M.I.T. had received several subpoenas from state and Federal authorities since the university's remailer was set up in 1996. M.I.T., he said, has answered the subpoenas but he noted that typically the tracking information it can offer involves only one leg of a many-legged path of communication. "If a person is using our system correctly," Mr. Kaashoek said, "law enforcement isn't going to find that information very useful." As a medium, the Internet does seem unique in the way that it magnifies the issues of privacy and anonymity. "The problem is that this technology is just so darned powerful," said Paul Saffo, a director of the Institute for the Future. "It makes it easy to be anonymous, but it can also make it far easier to track people down and invade their privacy." Mr. Saffo did not attend the debate, but both Ms. Strossen and Mr. Reitinger addressed the point that Internet technology has raised the stakes on matters of privacy. Both agreed that the technology poses difficult challenges, though they approached the subject from understandably different vantage points. Ms. Strossen said she was "very concerned" that new software technology allows corporations or governments to track a person's every mouse click and to assemble vast digital dossiers on individuals. "It can include all your personal financial transactions and your medical records," she observed. "I don't think our laws adequately protect individual privacy anymore. The technologies of anonymity and cryptography may be the only way to protect privacy." To which Mr. Reitinger replied: "I think we are perilously close to a lose-lose situation in which citizens have lost their privacy to commercial interests and criminals have easy access to absolute anonymity. That's not a world we want." There was scattered clapping for various remarks made during the debate, but that comment from Mr. Reitinger was greeted with sustained applause. Sophisticated criminals, of course, will always have access to the latest technology, whether cars or software. Nodding to that reality, Mr. Reitinger told the audience of computer scientists, "I'm just asking that you help law enforcement to capture the stupid criminals." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Prof. Frans Kaashoek of M.I.T., wearing a mask to underscore concerns about anonymous remailers, joined Philip Reitinger and Nadine Strossen. (Ed Quinn for The newyork Times)  Chart: "Internet Stealth" People use anonymous remailers to send email messages, trying to mask the identity of the original sender. There are about 40 remailers around the world.  1. Messages can be sent to the anonymous remailer by anyone, from anywhere. Some remailers assign I.D. number to users, a list of which is kept by the remailer administrator.  2. A remailer receives an incoming message, automatically strips off all traces of the sender's identity and then forwards the message -- to a single electronic mail box, or to thousands of addresses or to other remailers.  3. Because the messages are remailed in a random sequence different from the order in which they arrive, people who may be monitoring the remailers cannot match the outgoing messages with the incoming messages to identify who sent which message.  (Source: William Stallings, author of "Protect Your Privacy: A Guide for PGP Users")

title:
The Net's Real Business Happens .Com to.Com;
A Market That Dwarfs Retail E-Sales
body: Each month, Patricia Ruszkay, a purchasing agent for BOC Gases, a global distributor of industrial gases with American headquarters in Murray Hill, N.J., pulls a chair up to a computer, logs on to the Internet, and looks for a bargain. In this case, the bargain involves not only the price of the product, but an entire cost-saving process set in motion when the on-screen "order" button is clicked. Nearly 7,000 miles away from New Jersey, in a Japanese gas processing plant, a BOC supplier receives the million-dollar order for tungsten hexafluoride, a highly toxic gas used in semiconductor manufacturing, among other purposes. And within minutes, some 2,500 miles miles from Murray Hill, a BOC distribution center in San Diego receives electronic notice from Japan that the shipment is on the way. No multilingual phone calls or faxes required. No written purchase orders, invoices or shipping notices to lose. And, because the entire process takes place on the World Wide Web, there are no extra charges for handling the order over a special long-distance data network -- which until a few years ago would have been the only way to conduct business electronically. BOC makes some $20 million worth of purchases from the Japanese supplier a year, and BOC officials say the Internet will save the company several hundred thousand dollars annually. There may be more headlines about retailers selling books and compact disks on line, or consumers Web-auctioning the contents of their attics to one another. But in terms of dollars and impact, the real electronic-commerce action these days is the business-to-business transactions quietly taking place among companies like BOC and its suppliers and customers. In 1998, American companies had $43 billion worth of sales to one another over the Internet, five times the consumer retail total, according to Forrester Research, a market research firm in Cambridge, Mass. Within four years, Forrester says business-to-business sales on line will reach $1.3 trillion, or 9.4 percent of corporate America's purchases. Another research firm, the Aberdeen Group, is even more exuberant in its calculations of business-to-business E-commerce, estimating that the market may now be 10 or more times larger than the on-line consumer arena, and hold at that level. Word early this year of strong on-line Christmas sales "put visions of sugar plum fairies into people's heads," said David Alschuler, a vice president at Aberdeen, which is based in Boston. "But the fact is, business on the Internet is cutting significant costs out of the supply chain, with better procurement and resource planning," Mr. Alschuler said. In the long run, "that will have a far bigger impact than what you buy from Amazon.com," he added. While computer companies like Cisco Systems and Dell Computer have been the notable leaders in business-to-business E-commerce organizations in other lines of business have also joined the parade. Harley-Davidson, Mobil Oil and Los Angeles County are among the disparate cases cited by Alyse Terhune, an analyst with the Gartner Group, a research firm in Stamford, Conn., as evidence that business-to-business E-commerce "is absolutely proliferating beyond the high-tech companies now, into just about everything." Mobil, for instance, recently implemented an Internet ordering system for its roughly 300 lubricant distributors, saving the company $100,000 a year in ordering costs, and cutting the error rate for such orders from 30 percent to virtually none, Ms. Terhune said. Certainly, E-commerce has brought fundamental change to businesses like BOC Gases. Its British parent, the BOC Group, has been pushing for on-line supplier and customer transactions throughout its multinational operations, which include a wide variety of warehousing, distribution and cargo-handling services. And the benefits transcend mere back-office efficiency. Alex Cahill, a BOC purchasing manager in Murray Hill, cites the example of tungsten hexafluoride. The company sells the gas in six-foot steel cylinders that are worth $10,000 each when filled, making for an unwieldy, expensive inventory. "In previous years, our stock has been bloated to accommodate for miscommunication, upturn in demand, returns or problems with quality," Mr. Cahill said. "So it was typical to have three months of inventory in the system -- which could be between 50 and 60 cylinders, with a bunch en route." The primary reason for such "blind stocking," as Mr. Cahill put it, was the inefficiency of the order fulfillment process. "We have quite a lot of people interested in each purchase order," he said. "All that communication was handled through faxes, emails or the phone, one on one -- which is great until someone goes on vacation or sick leave, or they leave the office for a few hours, or transcribe something incorrectly." Under the system, which the San Diego site put in place in March 1998, BOC negotiates a bulk purchase with suppliers for a year's worth of gas, and posts the information on a restricted-access Web site. This site, or "extranet," is accessible only to select BOC suppliers and customers, and to BOC employees like Ms. Ruszkay who place orders by choosing from an on-line catalogue of gases that has been screened for price and selection, based on the bulk purchase agreement. As the order progresses through delivery, both the supplier and BOC will update the Internet order page, noting the shipping dates, quantity, and shipping method. This gives key personnel instant access to the order's status, which cuts down the need for correspondence, slashes the amount of time spent processing purchase orders and greatly reduces the opportunities for human error. Perhaps more significantly, Mr. Cahill said the system's precision had enabled the company to reduce substantially the number of filled cylinders it keeps in stock, saving his division "several hundred thousand" dollars in annual inventory costs. Fulton Wilcox, BOC's director of technical business development, conceded that the estimated $60 million worth of business the company transacted last year on the Internet represents but a tiny portion of BOC's annual revenue of $1.2 billion. But because the buyers using the system tend to be the biggest and most valued of BOC Gases' customers, dollar volumes tell only part of the story, he said. "Even if we had the hard numbers of exactly how much in sales we do on the Internet," Mr. Wilcox said, "it's still chump change compared to what it's doing to deepen the customer relationship and reduce the overall cost of ownership." He was referring to the costs a customer incurs not only in buying gas from BOC, but in storing and tracking it. That seems to be the case with the military contractor Raytheon Systems, one of BOC's key customers. In 1997 BOC approached what was then the Hughes Aircraft Company (Raytheon merged with Hughes later that year) and offered to put its catalog of gases on an extranet and let the company order around the clock, if necessary. The customer accepted, and now orders as many as 30 cylinders of gases each week for its El Segundo, Calif., plant, for use in research and development. Despite such headway, there are speed limits on the growth of corporate E-commerce. While the overall size of the business-to-business market dwarfs the consumer market, the rate of E-commerce adoption among corporations has been -- and will continue to be -- much slower, says Chris Davis, a vice president CSC Inc., an information technology consulting concern. "The business-to-business space is just a lot more complex," Mr. Davis said. "And organizations don't always behave like consumers." With layers of bureaucracy to navigate, and with procurement and sales methods ingrained in the corporate culture, he said, those who champion E-commerce within corporations must be prepared to move slowly. Indeed, "the sun and the moon and the stars have to line up to make this work," said Mr. Wilcox, of BOC. "We're so intertwined with a customer and their processes, we can't just do things suddenly without re-engineering the whole process. That's why business-to-business E-commerce will have a more organic growth than the flash growth on the retail side." And unlike consumer-oriented E-commerce, there are no ready-made software programs sophisticated enough to quickly apply to most business situations. Analysts and industry executives note that the requisite business-to-business software tends to be expensive -- often more than $1 million for the initial software license, from vendors like Ariba Technologies Inc. and Spaceworks Inc. And making the system fit the specific needs of a particular company, not to mention keeping it in tune, typically requires an internal support staff as well as continued consultation with the software vendor. "For every dollar that businesses will spend on the packaged application, they'll spend $5 to $50 on system development and integration," said Ms. Terhune, the Gartner Group analyst. BOC was pulled into E-commerce by a longtime customer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, which has been buying gases from the company since 1989 for use in science experiments and other purposes. Four years ago, seeing the Internet's potential for more efficient business practices, M.I.T. persuaded BOC and another of the university's big vendors, Office Depot, to offer their products for sale in virtual catalogues. Like BOC, Office Depot gave it a try, liked what it saw and has since become an E-commerce evangelist. BOC hired I.B.M. in early 1996 to custom-design its extranet. But the system also includes a large amount of software written by BOC's own engineers, which helped keep the initial outlay below $1 million, according to Mr. Wilcox, who said annual maintenance now ran around $150,000. Beyond money, though, companies embarking on E-commerce must also become accustomed to doling out ample portions of trust. BOC, for example, gives its suppliers unprecedented access to its own inventory data, in order to keep its stockpiles replenished. And BOC customers like M.I.T. give BOC access to their cost accounting systems, to avoid having to re-enter data as an order works its way through the process. Such trust is a departure from traditional business practices, Mr. Wilcox conceded. "But somebody's got to be willing to do something a little differently for this to work." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A parts-order page from Harley-Davidson's H-D Net, the E-commerce network through which the company communicates with dealers. (pg. C6)  Chart/Photos: "Order It, Truck It, Use It" Even when buyer and seller are near each other, as are a Raytheon SYstems site and a BOC Gases distribution center outside Los Angeles, Internet commerce can streamline transactions  1. At Raytheon, in El Segundo, Calif., Kerri Wilkerson, an environmental researcher, uses her company's custom page on the BOC Gases on-line catalogue to reorder argon gas, which she needs for a piece of laboratory equipment.  2. At BOC Gases, in City of Industry, Calif., Sheri Dahlgren, the site services manager, is able to track the status of customer orders like Ms. Wilkerson's.  3. After a Raytheon order arrives electronically at the BOC Gases warehouse, drivers like Gary Corriston load their trucks as specified in the digital bill of lading.  4. At Raytheon, it is the job of a BOC employee, Daniel Mata, to manage the customer's inventory of gases.  5. As Mr. Mata completes Ms. Wilkerson's order, he uses a scanner to record the delivery - data that will be uploaded to BOC's on-line ordering system.  6. In the lab, Ms. Wilkerson measures water samples to be tested by the machine in front of her -- a plasma emissions spectrometer, which uses argon gas to detect metals in water.

title: A Surge in On-Line Ticket Sales, Too
body: FIRST books and music, now event tickets: Another area of electronic commerce is far exceeding expectations. In a preview of its first-quarter results, Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch said last week that it sold nearly $60 million in tickets over the Internet in the quarter, more than tripling the sales in the corresponding quarter a year earlier. Perhaps more important, on-line sales in March accounted for nearly 10 percent of total ticket sales for the Ticketmaster Corporation, the nation's dominant ticket seller. Analysts were not expecting the on-line share to be that high any time before 2000. "I wouldn't be surprised now if we saw that number reach 50 percent within three years, which could have dramatically positive implications for our forward estimates" for the on-line company, said Keith Benjamin, an Internet analyst for BancBoston Robertson Stephens. Tickets are a natural product for on-line sales because of the inconvenience of buying them in person at the box office, Mr. Benjamin said. "My thesis has been pretty simplistic: I hate waiting in line," he said. Charles Conn, chief executive of Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch, said 5.8 percent of visitors to the Ticketmaster Web site in the first quarter bought tickets. This so-called "conversion rate" is much higher than the average for Web commerce sites, which Mr. Conn said was about 2.7 percent. Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch was formed last year when USA Networks bought Citysearch and divided Ticketmaster Inc., which it already owned, into two subsidiaries, Ticketmaster Online and Ticketmaster Group Inc. It then combined Citysearch and the on-line half of Ticketmaster into a new company and sold stock in the new entity to the public in December. Mr. Conn attributed the strong on-line ticket sales to improved site design and the proliferation of Citysearch sites; the number has grown by five in the last two months, to 23. Citysearch's city guide sites include links to the Ticketmaster site from event listings. "And the growth in E-commerce around the holidays helped us enormously, because a whole generation of people got comfortable buying on line," he said. Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch will release its complete first-quarter results at the end of the month. The early numbers are surprising, said Ron Rappaport, an analyst with Zona Research, an Internet research firm in Redwood City, Calif. "Stories like this are a testament to the fact that consumers are approaching the Internet as a viable medium for transacting, rather than information hunting," he said. "This can also be reflective of the aptitude of the company," Mr. Rappaport said. "When you embed Ticketmaster into Citysearch, you're collapsing Web real estate, so there's a convenience factor that's realized." Ticketmaster Online's competitors have engaged in a flurry of mergers recently. In January, Tickets.com merged with Advantix, which itself had recently acquired Protix. Earlier this month, the combined company said it would acquire both Tickets Live and Ticket Stop. But analysts said the competition lags far behind Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch because its sibling, Ticketmaster Group, controls off-site ticket sales for about 80 percent of the country's theaters, concert halls, arenas and clubs. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
ECONOMIC VIEW;
Is Mr. Gates Pouring Fuel On His Rivals' Fire?
body: THE worthies of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology had just finished thanking William H. Gates profusely for paying for a planned new computer science building with a handwritten personal check for $20 million. No sooner had Mr. Gates walked out the door last week than a procession of leading researchers at the university's renowned Laboratory for Computer Science sketched out projects and visions of the technological future that all headed in one direction: away from the personal computer. In a talk called "The Post PC Internet," David Clark, an M.I.T. computer scientist, described a world in which the personal computer is less important because everything -- TV, wristwatch, eyeglasses, toaster -- has a computer-on-a-chip and "everything is going to be connected to the Internet." For example, a watch face might temporarily become a tiny screen displaying your appointments for the day, information sent wirelessly to the watch from its storage folder on the Internet. "The future of computing is inevitably heterogeneous," Mr. Clark asserted. "Get used to it." He means technologically heterogeneous, not ruled, as PC's are, by a dominant technology standard like Microsoft's Windows operating system. Shrink-wrapped software will go the way of the buggy whip, according to the M.I.T. computer experts. Consumers will be given computers -- "information appliances" in the new world -- free, or more accurately, bundled into a monthly service charge, on the model of cellular phones. Much of corporate computing, predicts Hal Abelson, an M.I.T. professor, will shift to the service model as well. The large computer installations at companies that run their own Web sites will be replaced by centralized hosting services. The analogy is with electricity: in the 19th century, factories had their own generators, but with the rise of electric utilities, manufacturers left power generation to the specialists. Mr. Abelson expects that even storage of corporate data, from procurement orders to customer records, will be handled by outside service suppliers. "You'll see the market for disks being replaced by storage services," he said. Mr. Clark summarized with this forecast: "What does the future look like? Well, it's a network full of services." So is Mr. Gates supporting a computer lab dedicated to the destruction of Microsoft's world? After all, many of the pronouncements heard last week at the conference marking the 35th anniversary of the M.I.T. computer lab -- an incubator for pioneering work ranging from word processing and spreadsheet software to PC networking and email -- sound strikingly like the marketing slogans of Microsoft's rivals. The network is king? The mantra of Sun Microsystems is "The network is the computer." Big iron at the hub of hosting operations and Internet services as the business of the future? Key chapters in the I.B.M. playbook of Louis V. Gerstner Jr. Microsoft, of course, resists the notion of the post-PC era. An unrivaled marketer, Microsoft knows the opinion-shaping power of a deftly phrased concept, and buying patterns tend to follow ideas. But mostly, the company seems to object to the term post-PC; failing to counterattack when the demise of your lifeblood business is heralded would be a strategic mistake. BUT Microsoft itself is moving toward the future foreseen at M.I.T. Steven Ballmer, Microsoft's president, described a reorganization last month as the "renewal of our vision" to put a "PC on every desk and in every home." But now, Mr. Ballmer says: "We want to extend that notion. While the PC will stay central, we realize there is demand for computing on non-PC devices." Translation: The only religion at Microsoft is winning. And the Windows CE operating system is its bid to get its software into these non-PC devices. If the lucrative commodity of the future is Internet services sold by subscription, that is fine with Mr. Gates. He just calls it by a different name: software. In a question-and-answer session in Technology Review with Michael Dertouzos, director of the M.I.T. computer lab, Mr. Gates said, "Software will evolve into even more of a service business than it already is, and in the long term there will probably be a move toward a subscription-style model." The stakes are high in the future shape of the information economy, and not just for Microsoft. That makes some people suspicious that Mr. Gates is trying to buy the future, by using big donations to computer science departments at M.I.T., Stanford, Harvard and Cambridge to bend academic research in Microsoft-friendly directions. But Mr. Dertouzos, at least, has demonstrated independence of mind. He was briefly on the list of witnesses Microsoft planned to call in its antitrust trial, but according to colleagues, he agreed to testify as an expert witness on one condition: no coaching from the Microsoft legal staff. He was soon dropped as a witness when his deposition testimony did not echo Microsoft's defense. A towering man, Mr. Dertouzos issues an emphatic declaration of academic independence. "Nobody has bought me yet," he said, "and I'll cripple anyone who claims they have." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INVESTING: DIARY;
So Are They Shopping Until Their Shares Drop?
body: Internet companies went on a buying spree in the first quarter of 1999, using the sky-high valuations of their shares to buy up other companies -- almost all of them Internet-related, too -- at a record pace. According to Thomson Financial Securities Data, Internet concerns announced acquisitions worth $12.29 billion in the quarter -- more than in all of last year, when their purchases of companies came to $8.61 billion. Among the biggest deals last quarter were the At Home Corporation's plan to acquire Excite Inc. for $5.95 billion in stock and Yahoo's agreement to buy Geocities for $4.66 billion in stock. "The trend we're seeing is one of high- multiple companies buying other high- multiple companies," said Thomas Burnett, director of Merger Insight, a research firm in newyork, adding that almost all the deals were for stock. Mr. Burnett said that while the on-line acquirers so far had gone after their own kind, that was likely to change. "The idea would be to use your high-multiple stock to buy a real company," he said. He speculated that an Internet service provider like America Online would find it increasingly attractive to buy or team up with a non-Internet media company like CBS Inc. "They've got to leverage their 16 million customers," he said, referring to America Online. Other targets for Internet companies may be savings institutions or banks, which could provide on-line financial services, Mr. Burnett added.   RICHARD TEITELBAUM http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks value and number of acquisitions by Internet companies since January, 1998. (Source: Thorman Financial Securities Data)

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY: CYBERSCOUT;
GOING, GOING . . . BIDDING FOR BARGAINS
body: On-line auctions are a growing segment of the Web. A pioneer, Ebay, started in 1995 and now lists a couple of hundred thousand items every day; Amazon.com, which began life as a bookseller, recently cobbled on an auction subsection. With these merchandise auctions, the Web site acts as a go-between for individuals selling and individuals buying. Sites that offer travel include Onsale; Adventurebid, which, as its name implies, specializes in such excursions as white-water rafting, ballooning and climbing; Bid4vacations, with cruises, skiing and ranches that take guests; Luxurylink, with high-priced hotels and other destinations; Goinggoinggone, a potpourri, and others. The better-known Priceline is not a true auction site; you offer a price for an airline ticket or hotel room, and if a company accepts it, it lets Priceline know. By and large, in travel sites you are dealing with established companies, not individuals, which can increase confidence. Still, flexible travel plans are usually essential. Most of my auction experience comes from comic strips, where an unconscious twitch or sniffle raises your bid for an antique whatzit by thousands of dollars. But a two-night stay for two people at a five-star European hotel seemed too good not to try for, at least at first glance. And since the auction was on the Web, I could scratch an itch without inadvertently bidding. The site holding out this temptation was Onsale, www.onsale.com, which sells thousands of things outright, computer products in particular, as well as sports and fitness gear and home and office stuff, and has added auctions to the mix. The At Auction travel section offers many deals. Cruises are a major ingredient, and 10 were listed -- Scandinavian, Aegean and Tahitian among them -- and five other travel offers were highlighted. I clicked on one that said "2-Night Stay for Two/Five-Star Hotels/ Europe/Bids Start at $9." I found that there were a total of four five-star hotels available in four different cities; that the ostensible list price for the accommodations was $650, and that the current bids were in the $49 to $109 range (bidding starts at $9, but goes up only in $10 increments). Five high bidders were listed by initials and hometowns: A. G. of Newport Beach, Calif., had offered $109. The four hotels were in Ankara, Turkey; Goteborg, Sweden; Luxembourg and Stockholm, cities not at the top of most people's choice of destinations, and the rooms were "based on availability." Onsale went on: "The Five-Star Hotels are part of a well-known international chain, but since Onsale is offering such an incredible deal to its customers, we can't use the name!" Well, O.K., I guess. In the detailed rundowns on each of the otherwise unidentified hotels, it turned out that the hotel in Goteborg is less than 13 miles from the airport and the one in Stockholm is 22 miles from the airport, but the place in Ankara is "just minutes" from the airport and the one in Luxembourg is in the airport. Flexibility is essential: the trip must be made before July 31. "You will receive an email within four business days requesting your top three date choices and your destination," Onsale says. "Confirmation will be given within four days." Even though you don't know the name or location of the hotel you are bidding for a room in, you can't do it anonymously yourself. You must register with Onsale, giving your name and address, day and evening phone numbers, fax number, email address and credit-card information, concocting a user name and password. Trying to be a little less ambitious, I also dipped into a two-night cruise from newyork to nowhere in an outside stateroom, the "best available at time of booking," aboard Premier Cruise's Seabreeze, with an official price of $1,156. Bids ranged from $359 to $369. Down in the fine print it was noted that a "port charge of $89.50 per person will be charged in addition to the winning bid price," a substantial fraction if the $369 bid wins.   L. R. SHANNON http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
About New York;
Air and Light: Helping a City Keep Its Soul
body: FRED KENT walked toward Seventh Avenue along West 43d Street, pausing in mid-stride to enjoy -- nothing. He beheld the intersection's southwest corner, where a building had been razed months earlier to create -- for now -- an open space. Mr. Kent could see the tip of the Empire State Building looming elegantly beyond. Standing on 43d Street, he could actually get an unusual panoramic view of the buildings and billboards. Better yet, he could feel the space. "It changes everything, doesn't it?" he said. "It doesn't get any better than this." Right on both counts. The space on the corner is as temporary as it is serendipitous. Bulldozers and dump trucks are already rumbling into it, as the foundation is laid for a new office building for Reuters. The tower will join another building across the street for Conde Nast magazines. This will attract thousands of office workers to the area, who will have to cram themselves into the throngs of tourists who have descended upon the sanitized Times Square. The construction and crowds bode well for the economy, but those developments worry Mr. Kent. He is the president of the Project for Public Spaces, a newyork group that designs urban oases in parks, waterfronts and squares. Often, creating people-friendly areas means making them pedestrian-friendly. He thinks that notion has been lost in the remade Times Square. As a result, even the unexpected open space on 43d Street seems out of place. "Seeing this is like, God, we need light and air," he said. "We have it here, but we don't even plan to use it. Everything is so damn crowded, you feed suddenly awkward, and you can't enjoy the openness you feel when a building is taken out. If the street is not changed to compensate for the excessive density, it's going to lose its allure. The street has been transformed, but it has not changed to handle all the pedestrians." Taking his cue from planners in Zurich and Copenhagen, Mr. Kent suggested reducing the traffic flowing through Times Square. Right now, cars are almost always stacked up at a choke point near 46th Street, as the eight lanes of Broadway and Seventh Avenue feed into five lanes. Traffic usually eases after the cars pass through the choke point. Mr. Kent suggested moving the point further north, which he said would open up more space around the pedestrian islands that include the always packed TKTS booth. Choke point is a fitting term for the crushing experience that would make any sane person want to strangle the urban designers who dreamed up the current layout. Like many of his fellow newyorkers intent on dodging the tourists, watch sellers and turbaned preachers on the sidewalk, Mr. Kent walked in the street, close to the gutter. On one pedestrian island, several dozen teen-agers posed for a class picture. He walked past them, cutting diagonally across the street, where he caught the attention of a police officer. "Don't let him go that way," one officer yelled to his partner as he tried to wave Mr. Kent back to the crosswalk. "The sidewalk's open." Maybe in some parallel universe. The one Mr. Kent tried to walk on was filled with teeny-boppers shouting up to their idols in the MTV studios. Not an inch was open. The street, in contrast, had few cars and lots of open space. "THERE is just too much excess capacity in the roadway here," Mr. Kent said. "If we moved up the choke point, we could double the size of the islands and widen the sidewalk. It doesn't take a genius. If you look at this now, you know there's something wrong with this picture. Traffic engineers don't think about it. They think about moving cars through a given space. But is the role of the city to absorb more automobiles, or to create wonderful public spaces?" Weed out the traffic, widen the walkways and the square will be there. He is trying just that in Astor Place, where he has been enlisted by administrators at Cooper Union to revamp the public spaces around the college. Some streets may be closed, others might be redrawn to accommodate shoppers, markets and restaurants. He is even talking about expanding the small park just south of the college. "When you put a park in a square, that's exciting," Mr. Kent said. "You have quiet open space and active green space." Then a space has a special place. "It goes to here," Mr. Kent said, pointing to his heart. "You're talking about soul. Does place have a soul?" http://www.nytimes.com

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Dow Jones Industrials Rise To Fifth Consecutive High The Dow Jones industrial average rose to a fifth consecutive record as Eastman Kodak soared on unexpectedly strong earnings. But computer stocks extended their weeklong slide, leaving major indexes mixed. The Dow gained 31.17 points, to 10,493.89. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index slipped 3.86 points, to 1,319, and the Nasdaq composite index slumped 37.73 points, or 1.5 percent, to 2,484.04.  Page C3.  Kodak Earnings and Sales Increase First-quarter profits at Eastman Kodak, excluding one-time charges, rose 9.3 percent, to $259 million, or 80 cents a diluted share. Sales rose 6.5 percent, to $3.1 billion. The news sent shares of Kodak soaring $6.4375, or 9.67 percent, to $73.  C2.  Output Increased Slightly in March Output at the nation's factories, mines and utilities rose one-tenth of 1 percent in March despite a decline in production at automobile plants. In a separate report, the Commerce Department said housing construction fell 1.3 percent in March, dropping to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.77 million units.  C3.  I.R.S. Caterpillar Net Surpasses Revisions Caterpillar, which had sounded an earnings warning last month, posted a decline in quarterly profit that was smaller than analysts' latest forecasts. Estimated Loss at Nissan Grows Yoshikazu Hanawa, the president of Nissan Motor, reported a revised estimate of fiscal year losses at the auto maker that were more than three times as bad as the company had anticipated.
