title:
PERSONAL BUSINESS: DIARY;
Flocking to the I.R.S. Site
body: The Internal Revenue Service has been reaching out to taxpayers on the Internet since 1996, and this year, taxpayers are reaching back in record numbers. From Jan. 1 through last Sunday, the I.R.S. Web site was visited 573.6 million times, up from 231 million during the same period a year ago. The site, called The Digital Daily, covers topics like regulations, deadlines and electronic filing of tax returns (www.irs.ustreas.gov/prod/cover.html). But the centerpieces of the site are the forms and publications to download and use, said Jerry Conway, the senior technology adviser for the Digital Daily. Mr. Conway said the family of 1040 forms is the most popular part of the site, followed by publications about new provisions like benefits for higher education and the child tax credit. Among new features in The Digital Daily are a W-4 form calculator for figuring how much tax to have withheld from paychecks, a section for owners of small businesses and an education section that helps teachers orient students in grades 8 to 12 to the inevitability of taxes -- something for which many are not prepared. "They work for three hours at $7 per hour and expect a check for $21," Mr. Conway said. "Taxes are a culture shock for them."   SHELLY FREIERMAN http://www.nytimes.com

title: Settling the Microsoft Case
body: After a decidedly uneven presentation of its case in court, Microsoft has come forward with a proposal to settle the antitrust suit it has been challenging since last year. The word from the Justice Department and some of the 19 state attorneys general prosecuting the case is that Microsoft's initial offer does not address their concerns about what they regard as anticompetitive conduct by the company. But the department and the attorneys general are right to pursue a possible settlement with Microsoft. A negotiated agreement, if done right, would be preferable to years of litigation, appeals and uncertainty for businesses and consumers in the fast-changing computer and software industry. Any resolution of the antitrust suit, whether negotiated or ordered by the courts, would have to remedy the problems defined cogently by the Justice Department. Microsoft has been clearly shown to exercise monopoly power in operating-systems software for personal computers in ways that coerce competitors and clients, depriving consumers of choices. The initial focus of the suit was the contention that Microsoft, by tying its operating system to its Internet Explorer browser, was muscling aside the rival browser made by Netscape. During the trial, the prosecution expanded its attack to include charges of strong-arm tactics against computer makers, software rivals and others. In offering to settle, Microsoft has put forth a document suggesting that it would consider changes in its restrictive contracts with Internet companies and computer makers, including possible limits on its ability to customize the opening screen of Windows. But before accepting such promises, the Justice Department would have to be satisfied that Microsoft had truly changed its ways. The best mechanism to guarantee this might be an agreement on new rules for pricing and other incentives to insure freedom of choice by the company's rivals and consumers. If a set of adequate ground rules cannot be agreed upon, the company may find itself faced with demands for an outright breakup. Microsoft and the Justice Department tried to reach a settlement before the trial began last October. They are silent now about their talks, which may be a healthy sign. Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson of unitedstates District Court has called for the trial to resume in May, but talks could continue even after that date. The company should be commended for at least raising the possibility of a settlement. Its behavior contrasts with that of Senator Slade Gorton, a Republican from Washington, the company's home state. Mr. Gorton has turned into a Microsoft cheerleader, and clumsily tried to cut off antitrust appropriations for the Justice Department. He also belittled Judge Jackson in a recent visit with employees at the company's headquarters in Redmond. Microsoft immediately disassociated itself from those comments, a recognition that serious discussion of the issues is better than name-calling. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
The Nation;
When Privacy Is More Perilous Than the Lack of It
body: HIDDEN in the Microsoft Word document that carried the Melissa virus around the world last week was a seemingly innocuous serial number that helped Federal agents identify the computer responsible for the program. The incident dramatically illustrated technology's growing power for promoting both good and evil. The serial number itself -- known in computer parlance as a global unique identifier -- lies at the heart of a continuing controversy over tradeoffs between individual privacy rights and the common good. The dispute involving the Microsoft numbering system came just weeks after the company's partner, the Intel Corporation, announced that it was building serial numbers into each copy of its newest microprocessor, the Pentium III. The announcement touched off protests from privacy activists, who argue that such numbering spells the end of anonymity in cyberspace.  But computer engineers say that as computer networks become pervasive, similar numbering schemes are necessary for the networks themselves and for the functioning of increasingly sophisticated software systems. In response, privacy rights experts say that society has always found ways to balance its needs with the right to individual privacy. Published telephone numbers, for example, were later offset by the option of unlisted numbers. Today the Web has seen an explosion of ambitious marketing organizations that have used the infrastructure in unforeseen ways to build remarkably invasive profiles of Internet surfers. By combining vast data bases with data-mining software to form something resembling a vast vacuum cleaner, these new automated systems are rapidly tracking as well as predicting human behavior. What advertisers have been doing on a mass scale for decades is now done one on one. "The No. 1 threat today to privacy is not Big Brother, it's big bucks," said Amitai Etzioni, a social scientist at George Washington University, who is the author of the newly published "Limits of Privacy" (Basic Books). The invasiveness of such Internet data miners is balanced by the power of the technology to help track criminals, as Richard Smith showed last week by helping to identify the New Jersey man who was arrested and charged with spreading the Melissa virus. Last month Mr. Smith, who is president of Phar Lap Software in Cambridge, Mass., publicized the existence of the serial number in Microsoft's Office documents. He raised ethical questions about the company's intention in automatically recording such numbers in its data base. After his announcement, Microsoft immediately said it would stop the practice and erase the numbers -- which it said were being collected in error -- from its data base. Last week the company issued a software utility program enabling computer users to delete the numbers from their documents. Mr. Smith, a computer hacker in the constructive sense of the word and an amateur sleuth, was able to compare the document's number with those in other documents posted on the Web. His research paid off quickly when late Thursday state and Federal officials arrested David L. Smith, a 30-year-old software programmer who lives in Aberdeen, N.J. Mr. Smith was charged with three second-degree offenses, including interference with a public service and conspiracy, together carrying a maximum penalty of 40 years in prison and $480,000 in fines. Mr. Smith's name had appeared in one of the documents found on a Web site maintained by a virus author who called himself VicodinES. Electronic identity is both useful and increasingly necessary in cyberspace, say technologists. "I think the psychology surrounding this debate is very interesting," said Jim Waldo, a Sun Microsystems software engineer, who helped design an early predecessor to Microsoft's software numbering system. "People want anonymity, but at the same time they want to track everyone else." THE technology tradeoffs won't necessarily become simpler as technology becomes more sophisticated. For example, the Federal Communications Commission has mandated that the nation's cellular phones be able to provide location information to within 400 feet by 2001. Because most 911 calls are now made from mobile phones, such information is vital for emergency response teams. Privacy activists, however, are concerned that such information will be misused by law enforcement. There is a simple solution, they argue. "The general approach is to collect the minimum of personally identifiable information possible and to explore new techniques that permit authentication without identification," said Marc Rotenberg, the director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center. Privacy rights must be balanced against the common good, says Mr. Etzioni, who worries about the growing computing powers of Internet marketing companies. "Their data bases have more information about people than the Stasi secret police ever had about the East Germans," he said. At the same time, he says, the dangers of allowing criminals and terrorists access to unbreakable encryption software are particularly high. The answer lies in striking a balance. "The Internet is becoming a world city," he said. "Everything happens in it from commerce to crime. To leave the role of Government out is foolish." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: Virus Suspect Meant No Harm, Lawyer Says
body: A lawyer for the man accused of creating the Melissa virus, which infected thousands of computers and overloaded email systems worldwide as it spread, said his client never intended to do anything wrong. Authorities said the suspect, David L. Smith, a 30-year-old computer programmer, created the virus in his Aberdeen apartment, and may have named it for a topless dancer in Florida, where he used to live. His lawyer, Steven Altman of New Brunswick, N.J., said Mr. Smith would plead not guilty. "The computer world is a world where people do things, experimental things, just about every day," Mr. Altman said today, refusing to discuss the virus further. "Nothing he did, or intended to do, had a premeditated or wrongful intent." He said his client had been wrongfully portrayed as a dangerous, computer-hacking recluse. Mr. Smith was arrested on Thursday night at his brother's house in Eatontown, N.J. He faces charges that include interruption of public communications, conspiracy and theft of computer service -- charges that carry a maximum penalty of 40 years in prison and a $480,000 fine. Mr. Smith was released on $100,000 bail Friday morning. While the world learned of his arrest, Mr. Smith spent most of the day sleeping, his lawyer said. "He's very upset, scared and nervous. This has been a horrible ordeal," Mr. Altman said. "They went in there as gangbusters -- local authorities, State Police, the F.B.I. -- Ted Bundy, that's what they treated him like." In a telephone interview from Vermont, where he was spending the weekend, Mr. Altman said he spoke briefly to Mr. Smith and to Mr. Smith's mother on Friday. Mr. Altman said he had not seen the charges filed against Mr. Smith. Mr. Smith was tracked down with the help of America Online technicians. Investigators determined that the first copy of the Melissa virus originated from Monmouth Internet Corporation, based in Red Bank, N.J. Investigators from the state's four-year-old computer crimes task force determined that the telephone line used to send the first copy of the virus was wired into Mr. Smith's apartment, the New Jersey Attorney General, Peter G. Verniero, said. Mark R. Stevens, operations manager for Monmouth Internet, confirmed the company had provided New Jersey investigators with records of Internet use on March 26. That was the day the bothersome virus first appeared and spread around the world like a malicious chain letter. It came disguised as an "important message" from a friend or colleague and caused affected computers to fire off 50 infected messages, slowing email systems to a crawl. Apparently frightened when the F.B.I. posted a warning about Melissa last week, Mr. Smith threw his computer equipment into one of the trash bins at his apartment complex, investigators said. Mr. Smith worked as an on-site consultant, or a troubleshooter, for A.T.&T. Labs in Florham Park, N.J., employed by Iselin-based CGS Computer Associates, an A.T.&T. spokesman said today. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Columbia University Explores How to Profit From Educational Offerings on the Internet
body: Joining the race to the Internet and its riches, Columbia University has formed a company and hopes to make a profit by providing courses, research and other university material on line. Columbia officials said yesterday that while they did not yet have a specific blueprint, they hoped to devise a program that differs from more traditional on-line education programs that offer courses or degrees. They said they had incorporated the new subsidiary, Morningside Ventures Inc., about 10 days ago, and named Ann Kirschner, a former National Football League executive with a background in new technology, to run it. Although Columbia has not lined up specific programs to offer through Morningside Ventures, , Michael Crow, the university's executive vice provost, offered as an example the kind of multifaceted product he has in mind for people interested in the weather: "We could have available the latest lectures on the subject, real-time analysis of the latest research being done, maybe a three-day course on interannual and seasonal forecasting, or the chance to sit in on Prof. Mark Cane's great lecture on the historical evolution of long-range forecasting." Many colleges and universities are putting courses on the Web, and some have even begun to offer degrees that can be earned without setting foot on campus. But only recently have they begun to think of creating profit-making subsidiaries that can tap capital markets to help pay for the high cost of ambitious Internet programs. newyork University formed such a company last fall to handle Internet offerings that it expects to sell to companies and other users, and many other universities are weighing commercial ventures. In a sign of investor interest in on-line learning, Columbia's own business school has agreed to provide courses and other material to Unext.com, an Internet start-up company, in return for royalties that can be exchanged for a share of the company. The business school's agreement is separate from Morningside Ventures. When a report about the business school's partnership with Unext.com appeared yesterday in The Wall Street Journal, more than a dozen venture capitalists called Columbia to inquire about it, Dr. Crow said. He said Columbia was not sure yet how big its new company might grow, but that it wanted the option of tapping capital markets or developing alliances with other businesses. He said Columbia also felt the need for a company that could compete with the wealthy companies that are now flocking to higher education. "University education is undergoing a fundamental transformation," Dr. Crow said. "We needed an organizational entity that would allow us to interact rapidly." He added that Columbia was eager to let the business world know of its intentions quickly, because business developments related to the Internet occur so fast. Columbia is taking the new venture seriously. It has already spent several million dollars to develop ideas, Dr. Crow said, and expects to spend several million more. "But if it took $50 or $100 million to build the kind of interactive learning space we're talking about, it is not probable that we would take that kind of money away from our existing operations," he added. "We would look for risk capital to do that." Columbia has already brought in two executives to develop the new company: Ms. Kirschner, who was vice president of interactive programming and development for the N. F. L. and had been associated with two other digital start-ups before that, and Vikram Nagrani, a former principal at Morgan Stanley who is now Morningside Venture's chief operating officer. Although the new company had not been disclosed on campus in advance of yesterday's public announcement, some faculty members who participated in discussions about Columbia's digital future expressed excitement. Nicholas Turro, a chemistry professor who has lectured to industry figures, said he has already talked with Ms. Kirschner about how he might be able to put that course on line. "What excites me," he said, is that people at the new company will "do the work of putting it on line," while he can concentrate on his own work. Ms. Kirschner said the aim was to do for learning what Amazon.com has done for books. "Amazon.com creates a community of readers and a thirst for books, and then, by George, a way to buy those books," she said. "We want to create a community of learners." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Man Is Charged In the Creation Of email Virus
body: After a global search for the author of the fastest-spreading computer virus in history, investigators in New Jersey arrested a 30-year-old software programmer on Thursday night and charged him with writing and sending out the now-famous Melissa virus. The programmer, David L. Smith, 30, was taken into custody after F.B.I. agents and officials from America Online helped investigators from the New Jersey Attorney General's office home in on the Internet access provider that was apparently first used to send the virus, which has now infected more than 100,000 computers worldwide. Investigators from the Attorney General's Computer Analysis and Technology Unit then spent three days sorting through records of thousands of customers' files and electronic transmissions from the provider, Monmouth Internet Corp. of Red Bank, N.J., and determined that the telephone line used to send the first copy of the Melissa virus was wired into Mr. Smith's apartment in Aberdeen Township, according to the New Jersey Attorney General, Peter G. Verniero. A law enforcement official who spoke on the condition of anonymity said that the authorities had seized Mr. Smith's computer and other records. Since March 26, when it was first uploaded to the Internet Newsgroup alt.sex from a stolen America Online account, the Melissa virus has spread like a malignant chain-letter, invading a computer users' email programs and sending itself on to as many as 50 correspondents in the users' email address books. By replicating and sending itself so rapidly, the virus clogged and in some cases incapacitated computer networks at about 300 corporations, experts said. Although Melissa was not as destructive as other viruses that can destroy files or corrupt hard drives, technology experts say it is an ominous threat to Internet commerce because it used a new, and particularly efficient, method of transmission to replicate at an extraordinarily rapid rate. "It's possible that in the near future, viruses could spread around the globe in a matter of an hour or two, and if it's a destructive virus, do incredible amounts of damage," said Steve R. White, senior manager of anti-virus research at I.B.M.'s Watson Research Center in Hawthorne, N.Y. "It's going to demand an entire new way of combating them, new approaches and new technologies." Law enforcement officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity said that Mr. Smith had apparently named the virus after a topless dancer in Florida. They said he was a programmer for a software company that writes code for A.T.&T., but they would not identify the company. Neighbors and acquaintances described him as a prototypical computer zealot, a man who lived with two cats and whose social life seemed to revolve around the Internet. Ann Trautmann, who lives one floor below Mr. Smith in the Ken Garden apartment complex in Aberdeen, said he rarely ventured out of his apartment or spoke to neighbors. "He was a very solitary person; he was a quiet neighbor," said Ms. Trautmann, a quality assurance specialist at a software company. "I'd hear his modem go off once in a while." The only person at the Ken Garden apartment complex yesterday who could recall conversing with Mr. Smith was a technician from the Cablevision company, who three weeks ago asked him if he would like cable television installed in his home. "This fellow said, 'No, I'm always on my computer,' " said the technician, who identified himself only as John. "And this struck me as, not odd, but a bit out of the ordinary." Mr. Smith, who was arrested at his brother's apartment in Eatontown, N.J., was charged with interruption of public communication, theft of computer services and wrongful access to computer systems. He was released on $100,000 bail. Distributing a computer virus is also a Federal crime, but Mr. Verniero said he doubted Federal charges would be necessary because the New Jersey statutes provided for a possible $480,000 fine and a maximum prison sentence of 40 years. "If he's convicted, he will do hard time," Mr. Verniero said. Although Mr. Smith was also charged with conspiracy to interrupt public communication, Mr. Verniero would not say whether officials were looking for other suspects. Some private anti-virus experts said the so-called "digital fingerprints" on the code embedded in the virus indicated there were at least two programmers involved. The Melissa virus was embedded into an email attachment, and designed to exploit a feature of the Microsoft Outlook email program, so that each time the infected document was opened, it automatically sent itself out to as many as 50 other people. Technology experts fear that other high-tech saboteurs may use similar techniques, known as worm programs, to transmit more harmful viruses in the future, at speeds which far outpace the current ability to prevent, detect or disable them. America Online, which was exploring whether one of its own accounts had been used to launch the virus, tipped off New Jersey officials that the virus may have originated from a specific Internet protocol address, which is a number that identifies a given computer's Internet address, at a New Jersey Internet provider, said Mr. Verniero. Mark R. Stevens, operations manager for Monmouth Internet, said the company provided New Jersey investigators with a list of names of 12 of its customers who on March 26 used that specific address to send and receive information to the Internet. Among the customers was David L. Smith, whose email address was Dlsmith@monmouth.com, and who later canceled his account, Mr. Stevens said. The State Police then tracked down the possible suspects by using "good old-fashioned detective work," said Mr. Verniero, who was joined at the news conference by Gov. Christine Todd Whitman. Both Mr. Verniero and Mrs. Whitman seemed to go to great lengths to praise the work of the State Police, which has been the target of widespread criticism in recent months over allegations of racial bias. As F.B.I. officials, computer industry analysts and New Jersey authorities yesterday tried to assess the damage caused by the virus and plot strategies for preventing future outbreaks, there was still widespread confusion about whether Mr. Smith was actually VicodinES, a shadowy virus author whose style and past activities led virus experts this week to identify him as a possible source of the Melissa episode. At Mr. Verniero's news conference today, New Jersey law enforcement officials said they believed that Mr. Smith had combined several viruses, including one created by VicodinES. "He is not Vicodin," said Paul M. Loriquet, a spokesman for Mr. Verniero. "He is not the Vicodin guy." But Richard Smith, an independent Cambridge, Mass., software developer and computer sleuth who on Monday alerted F.B.I. officials to the fact that Mr. Smith's name appeared in documents found on a Florida-based Web site, said today he still believed that Mr. Smith and VicodinES were the same person. He noted that in early postings VicodinES said he was in Florida, and that authorities said David Smith had moved to New Jersey from Florida. In addition, he said he had found David Smith's name in the documents posted on the VicodinES Web site as far back as last July. One document written about viruses by VicodinES and signed "peace, VIC" on July 5, 1998, contained a notation that listed David Smith as the most recent author, said Richard Smith. According to a report by The Associated Press, David Smith grew up in Matawan but lived in several cities in Florida in the early 1990's, including Winter Park, Orlando, Tallahassee and Fort Lauderdale. In 1996, The Associated Press said, he filed for bankruptcy in Fort Lauderdale, listing $23,860 in credit card debt. Stuart Lipson, a Miami attorney who represented Mr. Smith in the bankruptcy case, called him a "good-looking, pleasant, regular guy." He told The Associated Press that Mr. Smith moved back to New Jersey to live with his parents after filing for Chapter 7 protection. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: David L. Smith is accused of starting a virus that spread worldwide. (Associated Press)(pg. B6)  Map of New Jersey shows location of Aberdeen: The launching of the virus was traced to Aberdeen Township.(pg. B6)

title:
National News Briefs;
U.S. Appeals Ruling On Internet Pornography
body: The Justice Department today filed an appeal of a judge's ruling that blocked enforcement of a Federal Internet pornography law. Government lawyers had until today to decide whether to appeal a preliminary injunction barring enforcement of the law, the Child Online Protection Act. The injunction was granted here on Feb. 1 by Judge Lowell A. Reed of Federal District Court. The measure, signed into law by President Clinton last year, would require commercial Web sites to collect a credit card number or some other access code as proof of age before allowing Internet users to view on-line material deemed harmful to minors. First-time violators would face criminal penalties of six months in jail and $50,000 in fines. Repeat violators would face an additional $50,000 a day in fines. The law also provides for civil penalties of up to $50,000 a day. The case will be considered by a three-judge panel of the unitedstates Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, said a Justice Department spokeswoman, Chris Watney. The department has argued that the law is a sensible way to keep Internet pornography away from children. But the American Civil Liberties Union contends that the measure violates free speech guarantees. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Deal Makes Yahoo a Multimedia Service
body: Yahoo Inc. confirmed yesterday that it would buy Broadcast.com Inc., the Web's No. 1 audio-video provider, in a deal valued at $5.7 billion that positions it for the rapid shift to high-speed, multimedia Internet services. The acquisition of the Dallas-based company gives Yahoo the programming power to fight rivals as they switch their networks from pages of static text to services incorporating video and sound. "Through this acquisition we get to combine Broadcast.com's growing base of rich media content with Yahoo's distribution platform," Tim Koogle, Yahoo's chief executive, said in a conference call to analysts. "Our users expect richer and richer medium content. This acquisition allows us to add truly unique and differentiated services." Dawn Simon, an analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman, said the rush to broadband or high-speed Internet access was driving companies like Yahoo and its rivals America Online and Lycos to multimedia services.  "Yahoo has to satisfy its audience with new and original content; that's where Broadcast.com comes in," she said. Terms of the deal call for Yahoo, based in Santa Clara, Calif., to trade stock worth $130 for each Broadcast.com share in a pooling-of-interests transaction that Yahoo expects to close in the third quarter of this year. Yahoo says the deal is also aimed at creating television-style commercials on the Internet. Yahoo closed at $179.75, up $11.375, yesterday; Broadcast.com rose $11.8125, to $130.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Senator Eases Opposition to Encryption Software Exports
body: In a surprising about-face, Senator John McCain said this week that he was abandoning his support for the Clinton Administration's policy requiring that law enforcement agencies be given keys enabling them to unlock scrambled data. The switch by Senator McCain, the Arizona Republican who heads the Commerce Committee, is almost certain to stand the Government's encryption policy on its head, killing both the Administration's demands for so-called key-recovery systems for police agencies and its restrictions on what kinds of encryption products unitedstates software developers can export. Senator McCain announced this week that he would join Senators Conrad Burns, Patrick J. Leahy and Ron Wyden in sponsoring a bill that would replace the Administration's current prohibitions on the export of powerful encryption with a review process that would give the software and computer industries a strong voice in what technologies could be shipped overseas. Key-recovery systems are being pushed by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the National Security Agency and other Federal law enforcement agencies, which argue that advances in encryption technology will make it increasingly difficult for the police and intelligence agents to monitor the computer communications of suspected terrorists and other criminals. Right now, that concern is focused mainly on email and other digital documents sent over the Internet. But increasingly, telecommunications of all kinds, including simple telephone calls, will use Internet technologies, making traditional wiretaps all but impossible without keys to unscramble conversations. The unitedstates software industry has argued that the restrictions put American companies at a disadvantage for no good reason, since any criminal who wanted to scramble data could simply use an advanced encryption product produced in a foreign country. Privacy advocates oppose the Government's policy, arguing that only strong encryption can guarantee personal privacy in cyberspace. The Administration declined to comment yesterday on the proposed bill, which has not yet been filed, until a copy was available. The about-face for Senator McCain, who is widely believed to be testing the waters for a Presidential bid, is significant in that it brings together Senate leaders who last session sponsored opposing bills on the subject. Senators Burns, a Montana Republican; Leahy, a Vermont Democrat, and Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, have staunchly opposed key-recovery programs. Senator McCain, on the other hand, last session sponsored a bill with Senator Bob Kerrey, a Nebraska Democrat, that would have required key recovery on all federally financed computer systems. Senator McCain's office said the legislation would be filed when Congress returns on April 12 from a two-week spring recess. David Crane, an aide to Senator McCain on the Commerce Committee, said the Senator hoped to move the bill to the floor quickly after that. While the McCain proposal does not go as far as a House bill that would lift all export controls on encryption, the computer industry and privacy advocates cautiously applauded it as having the potential to break a years-long deadlock with the White House over encryption policy. "I think on balance, it is a very encouraging development," said David Sobel of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, which has staunchly opposed key-recovery programs as an intrusion on the privacy of computer users. Mr. Sobel said he was pleasantly surprised by Senator McCain's shift in position. "The only thing I can speculate on is that his Presidential ambition has made him more sensitive to the business concerns," he said. Others said they saw the shift as simply a broader recognition in Congress of the need for change. Robert Holleyman, president of the Business Software Alliance, said it was "becoming increasingly clear that the number of policy makers who support modernizing export control policy for encryption products is growing, not shrinking." The strength of encryption software is measured in the number of bits -- ones or zeroes -- that make up the "key" used to scramble the data. As the keys become longer, breaking the encryption becomes exponentially more difficult. Currently, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Export Administration, which oversees the Administration's encryption policies, requires that makers of data-scrambling products stronger than 56 bits show that they are developing key recovery systems that would give law enforcement agencies easy back door access to scrambled data. Although in the last year the Administration has eased those requirements for some industries, primarily financial services, many common software products cannot be exported. Mr. Crane said the proposed legislation would replace the Administration's current licensing process with a review board tilted in industry's favor and would lift all restrictions on exporting encryption under 64 bits to friendly nations. The review board could grant exceptions for nonmilitary products stronger than 64 bits if they were "generally and publicly available," Mr. Crane said. The President would ultimately have the authority to override any exemptions granted by the board, citing national security. Unlike the House bill, there is no provision that would make it illegal to use encryption while committing a crime.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Optimism Over the Internet's Growth Leads Shares Higher
body: Stocks rose yesterday as Yahoo's acquisition of Broadcast.com raised expectations for consolidation in the on-line industry and lifted prices for SBC Communications and other telephone companies on optimism that the Internet's growth will increase demand for data transmission. "People say the Internet is one of the best inventions since the Industrial Revolution," said Robert Bloom, the chief executive at Friends Ivory & Sime, which manages $4 billion. "As long as the I.P.O.'s with the dot-coms after their names keep going up, this thing will continue." The Dow Jones industrial average gained 46.35, or 0.5 percent, yesterday, closing at 9,832.51 after being little changed for much of the day. The rise late in the session came from computer-guided buy programs, said Birinyi Associates, a research firm in Greenwich, Conn. The Standard & Poor's 500 index rose 7.35, to 1,293.72, and the Nasdaq Composite index, which is packed with Internet stocks, climbed 31.97, or 1.3 percent, to 2,493.37. Advancers and decliners were about evenly matched on the newyork Stock Exchange. The Dow, after closing above the 10,000 milestone for the first time Monday, added just 9.99 points for the week. Stock markets are closed today in observance of Good Friday. The Nasdaq Composite index rose 3.1 percent, its biggest weekly gain since the end of January. The S.& P. 500 gained 0.9 percent. Volume yesterday was lighter than usual, with some investors out for Passover. Some 705.7 million shares changed hands on the Big Board. "A lot of people are pulling back from the marketplace, because they're worried about Kosovo," said Ken Ducey, the chief trader at BT Brokerage, a unit of Bankers Trust. "We have a three-day weekend coming up, and anything could happen over there." Yahoo and Broadcast.com rose after Yahoo agreed to buy Broadcast.com for $5.7 billion, fueling speculation of more Internet combinations. Broadcast.com rose 11 13/16 , to 130, and Yahoo advanced 11 3/8, to 179 3/4. Following their lead, Intervu, which helps corporate Web sites transmit video and audio events, soared 15 1/8, to 59 1/2. Realnetworks, which makes software that lets users send and receive sound and video over the Internet, rose 35 11/16 , to 157 7/8. "There are going to be plenty more Internet tie-ups," said Benoit Flamant, who manages $330 million as chief executive of IT Asset Management in Paris. "The priority for Yahoo and others is not profits but to grab subscribers and market share." America Online rose 3, to 150, and was the most active stock in unitedstates trading. Since joining the S.& P. 500 just three months ago, America Online has become the 12th-most-valuable stock in the index. It is still the index's only Internet company. Telephone stocks gained, leading the S.& P. 500's advancers, after Blake Bath, an analyst at Lehman Brothers, said strong growth in the data business would compensate for competitive pricing and regulatory uncertainty. He raised his rating on SBC to buy from neutral. SBC rose 2 9/16 , to 49 3/4; Ameritech rose 2 5/8, to 60 1/4, and BellSouth rose 1 3/16 . to 41 1/4. American Express rose 3 1/4, to 121, contributing most to the Dow's advance, after Athina Meehan, a Morgan Stanley Dean Witter analyst, said earnings at the world's biggest charge card issuer would rise as it issued more cards overseas.  Treasuries Are Lower The prices of Treasury securities fell yesterday after several economic reports heightened concern that inflation could become a problem. The 30-year bond fell 2 2/32 , to 93 31/32 . Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, rose to 5.67 percent, from 5.62 percent on Wednesday. The drop was largely the result of the report by the National Association of Purchasing Management, whose index of manufacturing activity climbed in March. Its index of prices, a gauge of inflationary pressures, also rose. Additionally, the Commerce Department reported that Americans' personal incomes and personal spending rose in February, and the Labor Department said first-time applications for state unemployment benefits fell last week. Because the observance of Passover and Holy Week is this week, yesterday's session was shortened. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
New methods of agency payments drive a stake through the heart of the old 15% commission.
body: THE 15 percent commission on media spending that clients pay advertising agencies as their fee was once standard in the advertising business. Now it is about as dead as the three-martini lunch. Corporate America is turning away from billings-based commissions in large numbers, and many now routinely look at a wide range of new formulas that can be custom- tailored for a client's needs. The new methods of agency payments may include anything from straight hourly fees for labor to performance incentive fees to fixed retainers, or a variety of combinations. Driving the changes are two key factors: belt-tightening clients who began cutting commissions more than a decade ago, and vast changes in how ad agencies reach consumers that go way beyond network TV advertising. The commission formula tends to encourage costly media buys and has been criticized for overlooking important emerging mediums such as the Internet. Together it amounts to a sea change in how agencies are paid, which is underscored by the fact that giants like Young & Rubicam and DDB Needham Worldwide, a unit of Omnicom Group, now oppose the structure that once made Madison Avenue very profitable. The nation's top two advertisers, the General Motors Corporation and Procter & Gamble, are both moving away from billings-based compensation plans. G.M. spent $3.09 billion in advertising and promotion in 1997, and P.& G. spent $2.74 billion, according to Advertising Age, the industry trade publication. Procter & Gamble now pays media commissions but will soon change that. In July, the company will institute a series of tests around the globe that will determine how "to link financial rewards of our agencies to increased sales revenue" at P.& G., said Gretchen Briscoe, a P.& G. spokeswoman. "The traditional commission does not reward increased sales or development of holistic marketing plans," Ms. Briscoe said. "We want a system that's media neutral." G.M. has been using a variety of compensation programs over the last decade, ranging from traditional commissions to straight fees to performance incentives. The auto giant is now working toward "a performance-based fee compensation" system with agencies "where we don't already have one," said Philip Guarascio, G.M.'s vice president for advertising and corporate marketing. One key advantage to performance fees is that they encourage agencies to think about how to promote as broadly as possible, utilizing every marketing resource available from web site design to Internet marketing, Mr. Guarascio said. It also requires the discipline to set and later evaluate very specific goals that keep both the agency and the client on target. "It's not just about doing the work, it's about how well the work is done -- that's what accountability is about," Mr. Guarascio said. In 1997, only 35 percent of advertisers paid their agencies based on media commissions, down from 61 percent three years earlier, according to a study by the Association of National Advertisers Inc., a newyork-based trade group. Meantime, the study showed just 9 percent of respondents paid agencies 15 percent. Though that would seemingly be bad news for ad agencies, especially the giants that routinely handle accounts that spend $50 million in media and more (translation: $7.5 million in commissions), DDB Needham says the opposite is the case: the changes are not happening fast enough. Keith Reinhard, DDB Needham's chairman and chief executive officer, said the old system undervalues an agency by paying a flat rate that is not based on merit. "It's ludicrous because it doesn't talk about quality," Mr. Reinhard said. "If we're going to be brand architects and strategists, we have to figure out a way to get paid for our thinking." The commission system was developed in the last century as a way to attract agents to place ads in newspapers, said Robert Lundin of Jones-Lundin, the Chicago-based consultancy that conducted the trade group study. The 15 percent figure was "picked out of a hat" and never well loved among clients, Mr. Lundin said. But it was not until the mid-1980's that cost-conscious clients began reducing commissions en masse, creating something of a panic in the industry. The cuts "tapped into a pent-up anger clients had about paying 15 percent, whether an agency performed or not," said Edward H. Vick, Young & Rubicam's chief operating officer. In classic Madison Avenue fashion, agencies have since turned clients' lemons into lemonade, by coming up with new formulas that can earn an agency even more than a 15 percent commission, said Mr. Lundin. Last year, DDB Needham made some $6 million in additional compensation beyond its base fees for reaching client objectives, Mr. Reinhard said. Meantime, the 15 percent commission's demise has actually benefited some small agencies because commissions on small media budgets often do not adequately pay agencies for their work. "The amount of work you do for a client with a $4 million or $5 million budget is very often the same amount as the client with the $10 million or $15 million budget," said Adam Stagliano, president of Weiss Stagliano Inc., a newyork shop with about $100 million in billings. Sometimes that means more than a 15 percent commission. Ciociola & Company, a $50 million shop also in the city, often takes a guaranteed fee with a provision to take the greater of either fees or media commission, Mel Ciociola, the agency's chairman, said. "Flexibility is the watchword," he said. While labor-based compensation agreements now outpace billings-based payments, according to the trade group study, more than 30 percent of advertisers now also include some type of incentive compensation agreement that ties bonus money to the agency's performance. Young & Rubicam said the performance might be based on increased sales, or on other qualitative research measures such as brand preference or consumer awareness. "Incentive compensation says that we'll take less up front and if we're successful, we have an opportunity to make a lot more money," Mr. Vick said. "We're saying we're willing to put a large part of our profit at risk." On the downside, linking advertising to sales revenue can be risky because often problems beyond the scope of advertising cause a brand to fail, such as the wrong price point or poor distribution. Mr. Lundin, whose company conducted the trade group study, said that this problem may soon be solved because a more exact formula to measure the success of advertising has been defined in the academic world, and he expects it will be adopted by business in the future. Still, until then, incentives tied to sales remain a risk -- though some agencies consider it worth it. "Our clients take those risks every day," Mr. Reinhardt said, "so why shouldn't we?"   http://www.nytimes.com

title: U.S. Agents Seeking Clues To Who Made email Virus
body: Federal agents hunting for the author of the Melissa computer virus obtained a court order yesterday seeking background information from America Online, one day after seizing a computer from a Florida Internet access provider that may hold clues to the origin of the virus. The Melissa virus, which emerged last Friday, can spread exponentially because it automatically sends itself from one recipient's email account to as many as 50 others. It has spread more quickly than any other computer mutation in history, infecting more than 100,000 computers in five days, computer security experts have said. The search for the creator of the virus has focused on a small group of virus writers who use monikers including VicodinES and ALT-F11. Those nicknames have been associated with key aspects of the release of the virus and with virus-creation. The Web page for VicodinES promoted the ability of its author as a "noted virus researcher" and cited several viruses he had created. It was published on a computer kept at Access Orlando, a small Internet service provider in Orlando, Fla. The computer, or Web server, held a loose collection of sites called SourceofKaos, which included dozens of other sites of virus writers and virus collectors. Access Orlando does not own the computer, but leases space to its owner, Roger Sibert, for $150 a month. On Wednesday, agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation asked Access Orlando to remove the server for the Internet as a way to preserve any evidence of Melissa's origin it might hold, said Ron Spohn, projects manager for Access Orlando. Mr. Spohn said he acceded to the request after the bureau showed him documentation that it was illegal to tamper with data that might be used in a criminal investigation. Mr. Spohn said the F.B.I. later confiscated the computer. "They were going to look for clues on the actual machine itself," he said, referring to digital evidence preserved in the computer's logs that could be traced to VicodinES. Mr. Sibert, the operator of the SourceofKaos sites, said he did not personally know VicodinES but had exchanged email messages with him in the past. Mr. Sibert said that he allowed people with unpopular views to use his Web server to post sites on the Internet and that many of the roughly 80 sites belonged to virus writers or virus collectors. The F.B.I. declined to comment on Access Orlando or on any other aspect of the investigation, except to confirm that it was conducting one. America Online said yesterday that it had received a court order regarding the Melissa virus from a Federal law-enforcement agency, but declined to specify the information sought by the court order. "Our policy is to cooperate when presented with a formal request," said Wendy Goldberg, an AOL spokeswoman. The F.B.I. declined to confirm that it was the agency that had obtained the court order. Computer security experts searching for VicodinES said it appeared that he used an AOL account last Friday morning in first posting the virus to the Internet. The AOL account belongs to a civil engineer in Seattle, Scott A. Steinmetz, who said his account had apparently been broken into to post the virus. Mr. Steinmetz, 36, said he was not the subject of an F.B.I. investigation."It sounds like somebody took my password and has been trashing me on the Internet and has also created a notorious computer virus," he said. Since his account was identified as a possible source of the virus, "every hacker in the world has sent me an email," Mr. Steinmetz said. "Some of them congratulated me and some of them had nastier things to say." He said he was "stockpiling" the messages for investigators if they want them. Officials from Global Connection, an Internet provider in Kingsport, Tenn., said they also received a call from the F.B.I. on Thursday in connection with the Melissa investigation. Global Connection was host of the Web site of Codebreakers.org, a group that includes some virus writers and to which VicodinES apparently once belonged. Alex Potts, sales and marketing manager for Global Connection, said the company had already decided to disconnect the Web page from the Internet on Tuesday to "err on the side of caution." Mr. Potts said the company had read news reports and received emails that connected the site to the Melissa virus.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: $5.6 Billion Deal by Yahoo Reported Set
body: Yahoo is expected to announce today that it has agreed to buy Broadcast.com in a stock swap valued at $5.6 billion, executives close to the talks said yesterday. The boards of both companies met yesterday and approved the deal, which had been rumored for some time, the executives said. Broadcast.com shareholders are expected to receive 0.77 share of Yahoo for each of their shares, which values the deal at about $130 a share, analysts said. Yesterday, shares of Broadcast.com rose $4.8125, to $118.1875. In after-hours trading, the company's shares rose an additional $6.8125, to $125. Representatives for both companies did not return calls for comment yesterday. But an analysts' meeting to discuss the acquisition is scheduled for this morning. Mark Cuban, the chairman and president of Broadcast.com, and Todd R. Wagner, the chief executive, are expected to remain at the combined company. Shares of Broadcast.com, which sends audio and video over the Internet, jumped by $31 two weeks ago after Business Week reported that it was in talks with Yahoo. Shares of Yahoo fell $3.9375 yesterday, to $168.375. The deal is another move by Yahoo to take advantage of its $34 billion stock market value by using its shares to pay for acquisitions. In January, Yahoo agreed to exchange stock, now worth $3.7 billion, for Geocities, a service on which three million people publish Internet home pages. While $5.6 billion is an astounding price for a company as small as Broadcast.com, analysts said that Yahoo was almost compelled to make such expensive purchases. "Yahoo won't be able to sustain its extraordinary valuation unless they make acquisitions like Geocities and Broadcast.com that help them capture more of their users' time," said Keith Benjamin, an analyst with BancBoston Robertson Stephens. "If they don't buy, their market value will lose $5 billion over time," he said. Broadcast.com runs a vast site with all sorts of audio and video programming that can be seen or heard over the Internet. But with the current level of technology, the sound has much more static than a radio station and the pictures are small and flicker like a dim candle. Two-thirds of the company's revenue come from corporations, which hire it to operate conference calls and investor meetings over the Internet. The remainder of its revenue, and the vast bulk of its traffic, comes from advertising and product sales on programs that range from foreign news broadcasts to high school sports. The company lost $16.4 million last year on sales of $22.3 million. Yahoo's acquisitions have been meant to broaden its audience so that it could maintain its position as the second most popular collection of services in cyberspace after America Online. Yahoo, once simply a directory of other Web sites, has refashioned itself as a broad portal, or gateway, to a wide range of services from stock quotes to electronic mail and now to television and radio programming. Broadcast.com was visited by 8.9 million Internet users in February, according to Media Metrix, an audience measurement firm. Yahoo and Geocities reached 36.9 million users. But nearly all of the Broadcast.com users already visit Yahoo's sites, so the combination only gives Yahoo one million new users, not enough to overtake America Online, which recently bought the Netscape Communications Corporation. In addition to sheer reach, the deal has the potential to help Yahoo move from the current state of the Internet -- which mainly involves sending static pages of information over relatively slow modems -- to the expected world of broadband services, in which audio and video programming can be delivered over cable television systems or much faster modems that use telephone wires. In anticipation of the shift to broadband services, Excite, one of Yahoo's chief rivals, agreed to be bought by the At Home Corporation, the leading provider of broadband programming through cable systems. Similarly, Lycos another Internet portal is combining with the Home Shopping network and other assets owned by USA Networks in a complex deal. "It makes sense for the most heavily trafficked site on the Web to acquire the largest provider of streaming audio and video on the Web" said Paul Noglows, an analyst with Hambrecht & Quist. "With the advent of broadband, Internet sites will come to closely resemble broadcast networks," he said. All of this merger activity is being fueled by the unprecedented rise in Internet stock prices. Investors are bidding up the stocks of companies -- no matter how young, unprofitable or implausible -- to prices that defy even the most optimistic valuations. For example, on its second day of trading yesterday after its initial offering, Priceline.com, an Internet service that sells discount airline tickets, rose in value to $11.7 billion, more than any airline in the world. And yesterday, Ziff Davis sold 14 percent of its on-line subsidiary ZDNet. By the end of the day, ZDNet's stock market value was $2.6 billion, more than the $2.2 billion value of the parent. The only justification for this would be that Ziff Davis's print publications -- including PC Magazine, one of the most profitable publications in the world -- in fact have a negative value. With values like these, Internet companies simply cannot be bought by established companies where stocks are valued on profits, not promise. Thus Broadcast.com is out of reach for such logical buyers as CBS or Walt Disney. But it is an easy bite for Yahoo, which can simply exchange its highly valued stock for that of Broadcast.com.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Cable and Wireless Sues MCI Worldcom
body: Cable and Wireless P.L.C. sued MCI Worldcom Inc. yesterday, contending that the long-distance company violated the terms of an agreement to sell its Internet business. The MCI Communications Corporation sold its Internet assets last September to Cable and Wireless for $1.75 billion to gain regulatory approval for its $40 billion acquisition by Worldcom Inc. In the lawsuit, Cable and Wireless contends the combined MCI Worldcom failed to effectively transfer MCI's Internet customers, hindered Cable and Wireless's ability to operate the Internet business and picked former MCI Internet customers as targets for marketing promotions. Cable and Wireless contends it has lost Internet customers and revenue and marketing opportunities. Cable and Wireless said it also incurred significant recruiting costs to fill positions that MCI Worldcom failed to transfer. The company said it had to divert staff from other areas of its business to fill the gap. MCI Worldcom, based in Jackson, Miss., said it could not comment on pending litigation. The lawsuit, filed in Federal court in Delaware, seeks unspecified damages and other relief. MCI agreed last year to divest itself of its Internet business to calm regulators' concerns that the combined MCI Worldcom would dominate the Internet market. Under the terms of that agreement, MCI sold its wholesale Internet business, which connected 1,300 smaller service providers to the Internet, and its retail business with 250,000 consumer and 60,000 business customers. MCI also agreed to transfer 1,000 employees to Cable and Wireless and said it would not try to woo back any customers for up to two years. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
CRISIS IN THE BALKANS;
Serbs' Revenge: NATO Web Site Zapped
body: In an electronic assault on NATO's presence in cyberspace, computer users in Serbia managed to temporarily disable the alliance's site on the World Wide Web last weekend and cause intermittent outages over the last few days, NATO officials said Wednesday. Paul Magis, NATO's web master, said computer hackers bombarded the site in what is known as a "ping attack," which twists a protocol that Internet computers use to query one another into a weapon that overloads a server with more queries than it can handle simultaneously. As a result, anyone trying to retrieve information from the NATO site was blocked from doing so all day Saturday, and parts of Monday and Tuesday. To guard against such attacks, NATO officials said they have added an additional server and a filter to block out all "ping" queries. The site has been flooded with thousands of email messages a day, some of which were designed to overload NATO's computer, and some of which contained files with viruses. But the attachments containing the viruses were not opened and did not enter the computer system, Mr. Magis said. The NATO site, which includes press releases and transcripts of speeches by NATO officials, serves as a public relations tool for the alliance. In the week since NATO began attacks on Yugoslavia, the number of pages requested by Internet users has jumped to 90,000 a day from an average of 30,000 previously, Mr. Magis said. The most popular items are the video footage of NATO air strikes taken from the fighter planes. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
DOWNTIME;
Turning Coupon Users From Clippers Into Clickers - Correction Appended
body: THE shoppers weren't the problem. Three years ago, the marketing company Supermarkets Online decided to test the idea of offering grocery coupons over the Internet. The company created a Web site offering coupons that consumers could print out and redeem at their favorite supermarkets. "Consumers liked it immediately," said David Rochon, president and chief executive of Supermarkets Online, "even though they had to print out the coupons, even though they had to cut them out afterward so they looked like normal coupons, even though we only had a half-dozen or so offers a week on the service. They let us know right away that they wanted even more." The problem was with the manufacturers. "Our version was not acceptable to the manufacturers who offer coupons because of all the potential of fraud, the worry that nothing would prevent people from counterfeiting unlimited amounts of coupons," Mr. Rochon recalled. "We realized then that if manufacturers weren't willing, there wouldn't be an on-line service." That was just the first of the many hurdles purveyors of on-line coupons have faced. Clearly, there was a market. American shoppers are predisposed to using coupons to save money -- four out of five shoppers used coupons in 1997, redeeming more than $3 billion worth of the offers, according to industry studies. To compete with traditional coupons, E-coupon companies have struggled to come up with a secure, well-targeted way to turn those coupon consumers from clippers to clickers. For its coupons, Supermarkets Online created a new system that calls for consumers to print out a shopping list of discounted products. Emblazoned with a special bar code, the shopping list can be scanned at checkout at 9,300 participating stores nationwide to total a shopper's savings and then issue a credit, in the form of "Web bucks," that can be redeemed to pay for subsequent purchases. "By the time we officially launched the site in January 1998, we had the solution in place, and that was the breakthrough," Mr. Rochon said. Since then, the number of offers on the site (www.valupage.com) has increased to about 50 a week; the number of coupon shoppers visiting the site has also gone up significantly, from 20,000 a month in January 1998 to more than three million last month. For shoppers, on-line coupons offer a major advantage: customization. Instead of picking through a random selection of coupons that arrive in themail or tucked into the daily newspaper, shoppers can fill out on-line questionnaires specifying their interests, ZIP codes and shopping habits and then receive email with relevant offers on a regular basis. The mechanics differ slightly from site to site. At some sites, consumers can print out paper coupons, redeemable at brick-and-mortar stores. In other cases, the coupons can be redeemed electronically at on-line stores. And, as is the case with Valupage.com, a shopper who redeems the site's offers earns "Web bucks" that can be used like cash. In recent months, the variety of on-line coupons -- offering discounts that range from 50 cents off a package of Huggies diaper wipes to $500 off a General Motors vehicle -- has proliferated with the introduction of numerous on-line sites. Rather than relying on determined shoppers to hunt down their coupon Web sites, many companies have struck deals that will distribute their coupons on popular portal sites and on-line services. "This is just the first step in the evolution of on-line coupons because there's an enormous opportunity here," said James McQuivey, a senior analyst in on-line retail strategies at Forrester Research. "In the next two to three years, companies will figure out how to get coupons more and more easily to consumers." Starting this month, for example, America Online's customers will find Supermarkets Online's grocery offers distributed on an AOL food channel. The on-line offers from Emaginet.com, which specializes in so-called E-centives that can be redeemed on line, appear on the on-line site of the newspaper USA Today, in the Marketplace section. Val-Pak Coupons Online, which specializes in offering shoppers coupons for such local products and services as pizza and dry cleaning, struck a deal last month to team up with Yahoo to distribute its coupons to the 50 million users of the popular portal site. Val-Pak will eventually be able to send customized coupons to Yahoo's registered users to offer them products available in their communities. "It is a good fit because the portal sites know exactly where their users are registered," said Todd Leiser, vice president of Internet technology at Cox Target Media, which owns Val-Pak. Another on-line coupon company, Coolsavings.com, last month announced a deal with General Growth Properties, the nation's second-largest regional mall company, to offer on-line coupons that can be redeemed at local malls around the country. In fact, on-line coupon companies envision a time in the not-too-distant future when they will be able to deliver a customized package of offers and information based on a shopper's past habits. "We won't even need to know your name, just where you live geographically and what you like to buy," Mr. Rochon said. "It will go beyond mere coupons. "If you buy a lot of Oreos, maybe you'll get a coupon for a new kind of cookie that tastes similar. It could expand far beyond grocery savings. Maybe you'll get a package of coupons in your email for savings at your favorite hardware store, gas station, even the shoe repair." Until that day, however, finding on-line coupons remains a hit-and-miss proposition. Surfing the Web looking for the perfect coupon is enormously time-consuming: compiling the list that appears on this page took four hours. A more useful approach for the shopper: limit the hunt to a trusted site or two, then get regular updates on weekly offers. Better yet, find a site that sends email updates directly to you. Because this is a relatively new industry, it pays to call ahead to the retailer to confirm that the coupons will be honored. And as with all coupons, check the expiration date before you print them out: many on-line coupons are good for only a week. "It's early in the life cycle of on-line coupons," said Ken Cassar, an analyst at Jupiter Communications. "Going to the next level, where they are really convenient and easy to use, might be a bit of a stretch. But it's going to happen." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Circuits on Thursday about on-line coupons used an obsolete name for a company that offers E-centives, redeemable on line. While it used to be called Emaginet, its name is now E-centives Inc. Correction-Date: April 3, 1999, Saturday Graphic   Photo: CHECKING OUT -- On-line coupon sites have made new alliances and expanded their offerings in their efforts to draw a larger share of shoppers who now use only coupons clipped from newspapers and fliers. (Gabe Palmer/The Stock Market)  Chart: "Picking Up Pennies and Dollars on Line" Here is a sample of Web coupons compiled from on-line coupon sites and manufacturers' sites and by searching for coupons at a number of search engines. Coupon sites usually require some form of registration. The simplest ask only for the user's home ZIP code and then make available a list of locally offered coupons, which can often be printed out. Other sites require a ZIP code and an email address, which could make you a target for advertisements, and some ask for more detailed information, like your sex. All of the local coupons listed here are for the 11743 ZIP code, in Huntington, N.Y. The www.valupage.com site allows a shopper to specify a particular supermarket in the area.
