title: Microsoft Judge Sets Date In May for Trial to Resume
body: The presiding judge in the Microsoft antitrust trial today tentatively set May 10 as the date for the trial to resume and laid out a longer timetable for additional testimony, oral arguments and written submissions, virtually insuring that the trial will not end much before 2000. That is a far cry from the fast-track trial originally anticipated. When the Justice Department filed the landmark antitrust suit last May, Government lawyers and the judge, Thomas Penfield Jackson of unitedstates District Court, said that because the issues were urgent, the trial would proceed quickly. "I am prepared to devote the month of September to this trial," the judge said then. He was talking about September 1998. But the trial did not get started until the end of October, and first stage, cross-examination of each side's witnesses, took more than four months -- far longer than anyone had expected. Microsoft generally spend four or five days cross-examining each of the Government's 12 witnesses. The protracted trial insures that the Government will fail to achieve its pre-eminent goal in filing the suit last May 19 -- to stop the bundling of a Web browser with Microsoft's new operating system, Windows 98, which had not yet been released. In fact, last spring, responding to Microsoft's request that the start of the trial be postponed until January 1999, Judge Jackson said: "By the time you propose to be ready, 16 to 18 million horses will already be out of the barn, and that's too late." The "horses" to which he referred were copies of Windows 98, which went on sale last June. But by the end of this year, Windows 98 will be near the end of its lifespan; the next version, Windows 2000, is scheduled to be released early next year. Already, tens of millions of personal computers have Microsoft's Web browser, Internet Explorer, installed by default. Antitrust experts say now that if Microsoft loses, the Government will ask for remedies that would set broader rules for the future rather than attempting to mediate current behavior. "This industry moves too fast," a senior Government official involved in the case said today. "Just look at what has happened already during the course of this trial. This argues for broader remedies." While the trial was under way, America Online agreed to buy Microsoft's major competitor in the browser market, the Netscape Communications Corporation, and begin cooperating with Sun Microsystems on new Web browsers and related technology. Executives from those three companies testified against Microsoft at the trial, and Microsoft argued that the new alliances evinced strong competition in the industry, making the antitrust suit unnecessary -- a point of view the Government disputes. And last summer, a Federal appeals court ruled in Microsoft's favor in a related, earlier case, saying the company had the right to bundle its browser with Windows if the combination benefitted consumers. After that, the focus of the Government's case seemed to shift to emphasize issues like Microsoft's contracts with computer makers and Internet service providers. It remains possible that the two sides will settle the case in the next few weeks, eliminating any need for further trial proceedings. They held two hours of talks at the Justice Department Tuesday evening and plan to meet again -- though officials decline to say where or when. Tuesday evening's session was described as cordial but inconclusive. During the scheduling hearing in court today, neither Judge Jackson nor the litigants made any mention of the talks. Outside the courtroom afterward, representatives of Microsoft, the Justice Department and the 19 states that joined in the suit stood before reporters to say that none of them would discuss the settlement talks while they were under way. "If there are going to be productive settlement discussions, they must not take place publicly," said David Boies, the Government's lead trial lawyer, who took part in Tuesday's session. Government officials and Microsoft executives all seemed to be viewing the talks seriously today. Last week, Justice Department lawyers were dismissive of Microsoft's approach for settlement discussions, calling it nothing more than a public relations maneuver. The May 10 date for resumption of the trial is tentative because Judge Jackson is hearing another trial now and said he was not sure when it would end. When the Microsoft trial does resume, each side will present three rebuttal witnesses, and each witness is expected to spend about one week on the stand. After that, in roughly 30-day intervals, the litigants each file findings of fact. They both offer oral arguments. After an expected summer vacation, the judge will issue his own findings of fact. After that, the litigants file conclusions of law. Finally, late this year -- or possibly early next year -- the judge will issue his ruling. If Microsoft is found guilty, a separate proceeding will most likely be scheduled to consider what remedy will be applied.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Banned Belgrade Station Turns to the Internet
body: As part of a clampdown on news organizations last week, the Serbian police raided the offices of Radio B92, the single independent radio station in Belgrade, and pulled the plug on its transmitter. Unfortunately for the police, they had no way to pull the plug on the Internet, where the radio station continues to put out its reports. On March 24, the police told the station that its broadcasts were violating transmission laws and arrested the station's editor in chief, Veran Matic. He was released eight hours later. Ari Schwartz, a policy analyst for the Center for Democracy and Technology in Washington, said Mr. Matic had then begun uploading reports onto the Internet, where they can be read on a Web site, www.opennet.org. The station also maintains the www.helpb92.xs4all.nl Web site, and the British Broadcasting Corporation downloads the content and broadcasts it back into the Balkans by radio. According to the Center for Democracy and Technology, B92 broadcasts music and news that is not officially sanctioned. In recent years, the station has been shut down several times by the Serbian police. Until its broadcasts were banned, most listeners in the unitedstates faced a language barrier -- except for a five-minute English program every morning, B92 broadcast in Serbo-Croatian. But since the ban, the Opennet Web site has carried an English translation of its news, while the Helpb92 site contains some material in English. Mr. Schwartz said the experience of B92 showed that governments could not easily stop the flow of information in the Internet age. "In today's day and age, it is much more difficult to censor," he said. "Governments have to learn new ways of openness." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Fun for Pranksters
body: YOU'D think pranksters would be at their wits' end. Real-life headlines -- President's DNA tested in sex scandal, Baltimore Orioles play baseball in Cuba -- seem stranger than fiction, defying anyone to come up with an eye-catching practical joke on April Fool's Day. You'd be wrong. Thanks to various Web sites and software programs, it is easier than ever to fool and be fooled. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology has a 120-year tradition of students' playing benign engineering pranks. A year ago today, students hacked the front page of the M.I.T. home page and replaced it with one that announced "Disney to Acquire M.I.T. for $6.9 Billion." So proud are students of their handiwork that they have archived examples of their famous on-line and off-line pranks, including the Disney one, at the M.I.T. Hack Gallery (hacks .mit.edu/Hacks). Jeffrey Schiller, M.I.T.'s computer network manager, said his team was ready to defend itself against any similar efforts this year. "We are always vigilant," he said, "so my bigger concern is, how funny will it be?" Mr. Schiller said that he discovered last year's Disney hack within three minutes, but left it up for the day because "it was hilarious." A good starting point for exploring Internet-based pranks is April Fools on the Net , run by David Barberi of 2meta Consulting, in West Chester, Pa (www.2meta.com/april-fools). It serves as an archive of various fake email messages and other pranks. Among the classics in the Top 20 Fools section: the "Internet Cleaning" hoax of 1997, which warned that the entire Internet needed to be shut down on April 1 that year. That one encouraged people to turn off their computers and servers and disconnect their Internet connections so that "Internet-crawling robots" could remove "electronic flotsam and jetsam" to create a "better-working and faster" Internet. "Avoid wearing nylon (or other dielectric fiber) undergarments because of the possibility of electrical discharge," the message warned helpfully. And of course it urged Internet users to post the message prominently and to pass it to others. These hoaxes "thrive on the newbies," said Rob Rosenberger, a security expert who documents hoaxes and debunks phony virus warnings on his site (kumite.com/myths). "One of the first things any new user invariably gets is a hoax of some kind that he or she then forwards to everyone they know," he said. Intelligent, educated users who throw away chain letters received via the Postal Service seem keen on forwarding the most outrageous fake email about Internet "tolls," or "Walt Disney Jr." giving free Disney World passes to a lucky few thousand people who add their names to an email list. "The technology makes it so much easier to send messages that no one thinks before hitting the Send button," Mr. Rosenberger said. "They think they can change the world with a few clicks of the mouse." There is a strong distinction, of course, between the April Fool's tradition of jokestering on the Web and the malicious hoaxes meant to inflict harm on individual or networked computers. For those wanting to go beyond jokes and fashion for a more sophisticated and personal spoof, there is April Fools.com, which promises: "We don't want to fool you. We want to help you fool someone else." Most of the pranks can be played free (aprilfools.infospace.com). Another repository of shenanigans is The Free Site. Some of the tricks there, like programs that simulate an accidental erasure of every file on a hard drive, complete with realistic messages and sound effects, are on the cruel side (www.thefreesite.com /aprilfools .htm). Tricksters who are looking for something tamer can try the April Fool's electronic greetings at the Hallmark Cards site (www .hallmarkconnections.com/SID =ff13164a3/cardshtml). If you do get an email today that seems too good, too bad or too amazing to be true, it probably is. If you harbor suspicions, visit Hoax Kill (www.hoaxkill.com), which tracks urban legends, bogus virus warnings and other pranks and offers help "to actively combat them." Be careful out there today. You've been warned. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The M.I.T. home page, as altered by April Fool's hackers last year.

title:
THE MARKETS;
Investors Stick to Big Names in Quarter
body: In its final sprint to the 10,000 mark, a peak once scarcely imagined, the Dow Jones industrial average showed that stock market investors intensified what had already seemed an inexhaustible preference for the biggest and best. "It was all the big names -- the big caps," said Alfred E. Goldman, chief market strategist at A. G. Edwards in St. Louis, in reviewing the first three months of 1999 yesterday, as managers finished dressing their portfolios for client inspection. "We're in a very selective market, so the deal is, you've got to buy the big-name stocks." Yesterday's action, however, was not entirely a matter of professionals adding recent winners and shedding losers, since the market suffered a late sinking spell that pushed the Dow 127.1 points lower to pare its gain for the quarter to 6.6 percent. The Standard & Poor's 500, also dominated by large companies, lost a proportionally similar amount to finish the quarter ahead by 4.6 percent. It was the first time since the final quarter of 1996 that the Dow beat the S.& P., and it did so despite a 35 percent skid by Philip Morris Companies. Much of that slide came this week after an Oregon jury ordered the company to pay $81 million in damages to the family of a Marlboro smoker who died of cancer. By contrast, Standard & Poor's indexes of medium-sized and small companies slumped 7 percent and 9 percent, respectively. "You still have the large-capitalization, global growth companies leading the market and still have the narrowness that prevailed last year," said Timothy E. O'Grady, senior portfolio manager for First Capital Group in Morristown, N.J. Software, computer and many other high-technology companies also sparkled, with Microsoft rising 29 percent, to finish at $89.625, where its total value surpassed $450 billion, 25 percent more than the No. 2 General Electric. The Nasdaq market, which is heavily weighted with technology, spurted 12 percent over the winter, with CMGI, which develops and operates Internet and direct marketing companies, soaring 244 percent to finish at $183.0625. Amazon.com, the Internet bookseller, jumped 61 percent, to $172.1875, to surpass the price of Yahoo, the leading Internet search directory, at $168.375, up 42 percent for the quarter. Joining the high-technology winners were brokerage houses, airlines and various retailers, beneficiaries of continued avid consumer spending that itself is partly fueled by rising stock prices. Citigroup posted the biggest gain among Dow stocks -- although it was not the biggest contributor to the average's 605-point gain -- as it climbed 29 percent, to $63.875, more than double its low of last October when foreign economic turmoil was its most intense. Charles Schwab & Company and Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette paced a giant run-up in brokerage firm stocks, which were badly battered last year. Each of them rebounded 70 percent during the latest quarter. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter climbed 41 percent, Lehman Brothers and Merrill Lynch & Company by about one-third and Bear, Stearns & Company by 25 percent. Airlines, aided by low fuel prices, as well as free-spending travelers, were led by Delta and Southwest, each up 33 percent, and UAL, which rose 30 percent. AMR, which experienced a 10-day sickout by its pilots, and U S Airways, however, edged lower. Among retailers, Consolidated Stores, up 50 percent, and Dollar General, up 44 percent, posted some of the biggest gains. Wal-Mart Stores Inc., the No. 1 retailer, gained 13 percent to push its market capitalization -- what it would theoretically cost to buy every share -- above the $200 billion level. Drug stocks were mixed, with American Home Products 16 percent higher, Pfizer up 11 percent and Merck up 9 percent. Abbott, Bristol-Myers and Eli Lilly all lost between 4 and 5 percent, while Warner-Lambert, maker of the controversial diabetes drug Rezulin, lost 12 percent. Utilities weakened as interest rates crept higher, with the S. & P. utility index falling 10 percent. Nonetheless, there was little sign of faster inflation, and precious metals turned in another poor performance, with the Philadelphia gold and silver index slipping 8 percent. Looking ahead, the Dow after millenary milestones has advanced in the following quarter on two of every three occasions, and has also done better than other market indexes. Its biggest rise was 12.5 percent after the average hit 6,000 in late 1996, according to LIM Research.com. The biggest loss was 1.2 percent in the quarter following the Dow's July 1997 surge to 8,000. The research company also noted that the Russell 2000 underperformed the general market in the quarter following seven of the last eight 1,000-point milestones. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Stock Leaders and Laggards In the First Quarter" lists common stocks with the largest gains and declines in percentage terms in the first quarter of 1999. (Source: Associated Press)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
I.B.M. vows to pull ads from Web sites that lack clear policies on protecting consumer privacy.
body: SAYING it hoped to ward off Government regulation and increase consumer confidence in electronic commerce, the International Business Machines Corporation, the second-biggest advertiser on the Internet, said yesterday that it would pull its ads from Web sites that lacked clear privacy policies. In a letter sent to 350 Web sites it advertises with in the unitedstates and Canada, I.B.M. said that as of June 1 it would advertise only on sites that posted such policies. The announcement, thought to be the first by a unitedstates company, comes as the Federal Trade Commission, Congress and the European Union are closely monitoring the effectiveness of efforts by on-line businesses to police themselves on the issue of buying and selling personal data they gather. I.B.M. said its own recent survey had found that only 30 percent of the 800 sites worldwide from which it buys ads had privacy policies posted. "It was a little to our surprise, frankly, that so many sites didn't have privacy policies," said Abby Kohnstamm, I.B.M.'s senior vice president for marketing. Ms. Kohnstamm and Chris Caine, vice president for governmental programs, cited three factors behind the decision announced yesterday: I.B.M.'s own history of protecting consumer privacy, research showing that consumer concerns about privacy are inhibiting the growth of electronic commerce, and the need for the industry to prove that it can regulate itself. "Market-led policies need market leaders," Mr. Caine said. Robert Pitofsky, the trade commission chairman, who last year told Internet companies to make fundamental improvements in protecting consumer privacy or face tough new regulations, said he was encouraged by the announcement. "I think it is a good move," Mr. Pitofsky said. "I'm not sure whether it will catch on or not, but I think it is important that a company with the stature and prestige of I.B.M. take the first step. Time will tell if others see it in their best interest." Even privacy advocates who view industry self-regulation as ineffective and unenforceable called the I.B.M. move a positive step in pushing companies to tell consumers what type of personal information they collect and how it is used. "It is exquisitely timed," said Jason Catlett, president of the Junkbusters Corporation, which promotes consumer protection on line. "I don't think it's going to have an enormous effect," he added, but "I still feel I have to applaud I.B.M. because their heart is in the right place." Mr. Catlett, saying that I.B.M. had a good history of protecting privacy, also pointed out that the company had avoided negative publicity like that recently faced by the Microsoft Corporation and the Intel Corporation for embedding in their products identifying numbers that could allow marketers and others to track computer users' movements through cyberspace. All three companies are members of the Online Privacy Alliance, which was formed last year to push companies to address privacy concerns after a survey by the F.T.C. found only 14 percent of Web sites had clear privacy policies posted. Microsoft, the No. 1 advertiser on the Internet, applauded the move by I.B.M. and said it would watch its effects closely. "Because privacy is very important to us, we are always considering all ways in which we can encourage privacy protections," said Tom Pilla, a Microsoft spokesman. "We don't have any immediate plans to follow suit." Although I.B.M. will not dictate standards for what privacy policies on Web sites should be, it does refer Web publishers to the Online Privacy Alliance, which has a list of recommended practices that are based on principles recommended by the F.T.C. last year. The debate over the issue has reached a critical point as the F.T.C. nears a decision on whether a report to Congress due this spring will recommend the passage of new laws to protect on-line privacy. A group of business interests, in conjunction with the F.T.C. and Georgetown University, recently completed a follow-up to the F.T.C. survey last year of on-line privacy practices. The results of that study, which have not been released, are expected to be a determining factor in the agency's decision. Mr. Pitofsky told Congress last year that he would push for regulation if significant improvement was not found. He said yesterday that progress was being made, but he acknowledged, "I just don't know how much, and I hear radically different versions from differing groups." He also emphasized that the report to Congress would look at more than just the numbers. "You want to know what kind of policy" that Web sites "are putting up there," he said. Some key points, he said, are whether the policies are clear and whether they explain that consumers have a choice in how the information they supply is used. Indeed, I.B.M. cited the new survey in the letter that its on-line advertising agency, Ogilvy One Worldwide, a newyork unit of WPP Group P.L.C., sent out yesterday morning. "We believe that this presents a very timely opportunity for the private sector to continue to take the initiative in posting and following privacy policies," the letter said in reference to the survey. "While the appropriate privacy statement will vary from site to site, we strongly encourage Web site owners to employ industry best privacy practices." I.B.M. said it spent about $45 million on on-line advertising last year, or 7 percent of its worldwide media budget. That is expected to increase to $60 million, or 10 percent of its budget, this year.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Business Travel;
Priceline.com Stock Zooms In Offering
body: Priceline.com, the Web site that hired William Shatner of "Star Trek" as its pitchman, saw its stock price fly off to a distant galaxy in its first day of trading yesterday. Priceline's shares jumped from an offering price of $16 a share on the Nasdaq market to a high of $85 before settling at $69, a more than fourfold increase. That gives Priceline, which lets consumers bid on airline tickets, cars and other items, a market value of $9.8 billion, the highest first-day value ever achieved by an Internet company. Priceline, which lost $114 million last year selling $35 million worth of airline tickets, is now worth more than the United Airlines, Continental Airlines and Northwest Airlines combined. That value is all the more astounding because Priceline has only been in business for 11 months. That did not stop Morgan Stanley, the lead underwriter, from doubling the proposed price, to give the company a value of $2.3 billion in the offering of 10 million shares. The stock market has accorded Jay S. Walker, Priceline's founder, paper wealth of $4.3 billion. Mr. Walker's previous claim to fame was that he started Newsub services, which sells magazine subscriptions in credit card bills. The offering comes amid a buying frenzy in the shares of nearly any company involved in the Internet. "It doesn't matter what these companies do or how they are priced," said David Simons, who runs Digital Video Investments, an advisory service. "Each new Internet I.P.O. is nothing more than red meat to the mad dogs." But a number of analysts praised the company for its sales method. Priceline calls itself a "demand collection system" in which customers name the price they want to pay for a trip, or a certain model car, and so on. If Priceline can find someone willing to sell at the specified price, the customer is committed to buy. "We like Priceline's business model," said Peony Kao, an analyst with Renaissance Capital. "It can be expanded from airline tickets to loans, cars and a lot of other things." Ms. Kao said she was impressed with Priceline's growth, with revenues expected to increase fivefold this year to $175 million. "The company has a lot of potential," she said, "but whether it's worth $10 billion remains to be seen." Like most Internet companies, Priceline has spent far more on building its systems and marketing than it has generated in revenue. But the nature of its business adds a number of unusual risks. Its biggest constraint has been the unwillingness of most major airlines to undercut their existing prices by selling through Priceline. Priceline had tried to make the restrictions for buying tickets so onerous that it would not attract any high-margin business travelers. For example, buyers have to be willing to fly at any time on the travel day they specify, on any airline, and to accept at least one change of planes. Even so, only Trans World Airlines and America West sold tickets through the service at first. Last fall, Northwest and Delta Air Lines agreed to participate. But in order to induce Delta to join, Priceline granted it warrants to buy 18.9 million shares of the company's stock, a stake worth $1.3 billion yesterday, or 13 percent of Delta's $10 billion market value. Even with the addition of these airlines, Priceline was only able to sell about 25 percent of what it termed "reasonable bids," which it defines as those no more than 30 percent less than the lowest fare for a particular route. And to satisfy even that many customers, the company has had to sell many of its tickets for prices below what it pays the airlines. The company hopes to make up some of those losses selling credit cards and other products to people while they are bidding. The company's prospectus indicates that even these moves may not be enough to make money. "We are unlikely to make significant profits unless we make new or complementary products and services and a broader range of existing products and services available through the Priceline service," the company wrote. A number of other people have found near instant paper wealth as a result of the Priceline offering. Richard S. Braddock, the former president of Citicorp, who became Priceline's chief executive last August, now owns shares worth $980 million. General Atlantic Partners, a venture capital firm in Greenwich, Conn., saw its $28 million investment turn into a stake worth $1.8 billion. Nicholas J. Nicholas Jr. the former co-chief executive of Time Warner, owns stock worth $264 million.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
CRISIS IN THE BALKANS: IN BELGRADE;
Even Milosevic Foes Criticize Western Media
body: Frustrated by the war propaganda that passes for news here, a small but significant minority of Serbs spend long hours every day watching satellite television, exchanging email and surfing the Internet. But few find the Western version wholly convincing. They say that NATO's media manipulation is simply more subtle than Belgrade's official blunderbuss, that Serbian interests in Kosovo are ignored or trivialized and that Serbs are being demonized to justify the bombing. Vesna Kostic, an economic journalist and an open opponent of the Yugoslav President, Slobodan Milosevic, spends several hours a day watching Sky News, BBC televsion news and CNN, listening to the banned Belgrade independent radio station, B-92, on satellite, exchanging email around the world and reading Western newspapers on the Web, through her two Internet providers. One of them is offering free use of the Internet during the war, and Mrs. Kostic fears that the Milosevic Government will find some way to shut the providers down. Still, she says, "the West is not pushing a campaign against just Milosevic anymore, but against the entire Serb people," and she is offended by the content and the tone. "I know the West is more reliable, but it's not wholly reliable -- that I also know," she said. "It's better than our stupid propaganda, but it's obvious the West is also conducting a propaganda war, a public relations war, and it knows how to do it very well." Reliable information is scarce, she said. "You can't know what's true. How many planes have been shot down? Is Fehmi Agani dead or alive?" she said, referring to the moderate Albanian professor and negotiator who NATO says was killed by Serbs in Kosovo. Mrs. Kostic was arrested by Mr. Milosevic's Serbian government in 1994 and sentenced to three months in jail, which was reduced to a year's probation. "I know the Serb police are terrible," she said. "I'm frightened of them. But it's not only Albanian human rights at stake, it's mine as well. Milosevic is already moving against the independent press and the opposition. This bombing will mean keeping that creature in power another 100 years and destroying the opposition." Asked if she believes Western accusations of Serbian atrocities in Kosovo, she sighed. "I do believe Serb forces are pushing out Albanians," she said. "I hope they are not slaughtering civilians, but I do believe they are intimidating them to go out. I don't approve of it, but I understand it. When you're in a war, you can't afford to have people shoot you in the back." To watch the Western news stations, she said, "You wouldn't know that there is an Albanian army fighting against the Serbs," a reference to the guerrillas of the Kosovo Liberation Army. "I know it's terrible now," she said, "but Milosevic didn't create Kosovo. He made it worse, but the riots started in 1981. The Albanians had a state within a state already, but they wanted more. Now the West is fighting for their independence while claiming that Serbia will keep sovereignty. It's the hypocrisy I hate." Dusan, 21, a student of electrical engineering in Novi Sad, northwest of Belgrade, spends hours on the Internet, exchanging information with friends about what sites are hit by the bombs, tracking down rumors and monitoring Western media. He is a pro-democracy demonstrator, a member of Otpor, the Student Resistance Movement. He was reached by telephone after he attached it to an email message, but fearing mobilization into the army, he insisted that his surname not be used. "I'm against Milosevic, and I don't think I'm a victim of propaganda by either side," he said. "I watch and read our media and the international media, including The newyork Times and The Washington Post, and I'm in touch with students all over the world." But Dusan complains that Serbs are being demonized and that the world talks of Nazis now to justify an act of aggression on a sovereign country fighting an insurgency. "NATO says this is the worst humanitarian crisis in Europe since World War II," he said, "but three years ago a half-million Serbs were cleared out of Krajina. But it wasn't in the interests of the U.S. to put Croatia down, so there was less information and no outrage. "I understand NATO must justify its actions, but the bombing of Yugoslavia is wrong. I know Slobodan Milosevic is doing bad things, and lots and lots of people in Serbia hate Milosevic. But there are also a lot of innocent people here, and now his regime is stronger than ever. Horrible things are happening, but horrible things have happened all through the Balkans." Radio 021, the only independent media outlet in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city, was also shut down. "Everything will be shut down, and then what?" Dusan asked. "It will be another 20 years before democracy comes here, and there's a bigger humanitarian crisis than before." Vuk Micovic, like Dusan, is a student leader who published his phone number on the Internet. Students use the World Wide Web and email almost exclusively to exchange information, he said. "Most of the authorities don't even know what email is," he said. "During the student protests our Web page was popular, and the police broke in and said, 'Where is that Internet?' as if they could confiscate it." Mr. Micovic, 23, uses the Yugoslav Internet service provider EUnet and a university provider called Afrodite. In Novi Sad, he said, it can take four hours to get a connection. No one knows how many people in Yugoslavia use the Internet or email. A study financed by the unitedstates Agency for International Development suggested that perhaps 50,000 in this country used email; Belgrade alone has nearly two million people. A spokesman for EUnet, who would not give his name, said that his company and the various other providers had about 60,000 subscribers in Yugoslavia, and that at least 100,000 people used email. They include the Serbian Orthodox Church, which has sent email to contacts around the world. An impassioned recent message from the Rev. Sava Janjic of the Decani Monastery, for example, appealed for an end to NATO bombing, which, it said, "will only make things worse." Many more Serbs have access to satellite receivers that enable them to watch Western television, including German and Italian channels. But Mr. Micovic, too, finds his access to information no easy guide to reality. "Either way I go, I stand to lose," he said. "Supporting the bombing is stupid, because it makes everything worse. Most people in the West don't understand the mentality that exists here. The bombing has weakened any chance to turn Serbia into a democratic country. "For a long time here we have been trying to build connections between students and other groups, and we were making some progress, but after the bombing it's largely destroyed. Milosevic now has the power to do what he pleases, and some of my friends have already been drafted." Even a professional television journalist here, who spoke on condition of anonymity, says no one can believe in the state media, which cycle rumors and propaganda in a crude way. "We joke that if so many NATO planes have been shot down," he said, "their pilots must already speak Serbian and are hiding in a village tending the cows, because no one can find them." He watches a lot of Western television and surfs the Internet for six or seven hours a day, he said. "But there is a lot of nonsense there, too. On CNN they said that 8,000 to 12,000 Albanian refugees were crossing the border every hour," he said, laughing. "First, it's impossible to know. But in 10 hours that's 100,000 people, and in four days that's a million people. And in seven days, all of Kosovo is empty." But does he believe that Serbian forces are committing atrocities in Kosovo? He sighed. "I think they do it," he said. "I think they'll do whatever is necessary to stay in power, and they try to destroy the K.L.A. and expel as many people as possible." But in the end, he said, the point is not the percentage of Serbs who live in Kosovo. "What's important is that for centuries Kosovo was part of the Serbian state. And if we say that now Serbia will give it up and be smaller, fine, but we must agree to do it. NATO has put the whole region on the edge of a real eruption." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A policeman watched yesterday in Belgrade as a resident of the city smashed the glass doors of the German Embassy. German fighter jets have taken part in the NATO air campaign against Yugoslavia. (Associated Press)

title:
GIVE AND TAKE: When Charity Begins on Line;
Pitfalls for Internet Shoppers With Charitable Bent
body: As Americans become increasingly comfortable shopping on line, it is a pitch many succumb to: Buy an Elmo toy or a Stephen King novel through a given Web site, and part of the purchase price will go to the charity of your choice. "I already like to shop on line," said Sissy Brunk, who patronizes iGive.com, one of at least a half-dozen sites making this pitch. "It makes you feel good that while you are shopping, a little bit goes to a worthy cause." She is convinced she is helping a children's charity she admires. Like credit cards that promise to give a sliver of whatever amount is charged to a favorite cause, these shop-for-a-cause Web sites are a new twist in Internet commerce, seeking to appeal to Americans' charitable side. Most have started in just the last few months. They claim together to have raised hundreds of thousands of dollars for groups from the Humane Society to Hands on San Francisco, a volunteer group. While that sum is modest, many charities think this is just the beginning. "We consider it an enormously important area for fund-raising," said Wayne Pacelle, a senior vice president for the Humane Society. But once you buy Elmo on line, it is impossible to know, in every case, what happens to the few dollars you thought were speeding their way to a good cause. Though many charities are getting checks directly from the sites, money may not end up in the charities' hands as fast as you imagined -- if at all. Amounts collected may fall below some level that the retailer or Web site has set before it will send a check. Money may not be credited to the charity because of computer glitches. Or shoppers may fail to follow cumbersome instructions. Here are some of the pitfalls: *iGive.com prides itself on letting shoppers name any cause they fancy, and since the site was born in November 1997, shoppers have suggested more than 4,300 of them. But in interviews, the site's founder said that shoppers' purchases had not resulted in enough money for iGive to issue checks to more than half of those causes. iGive requires at least $10 to be collected in a charity's behalf from retailers, but it has not verified half of those that meet that threshold. The upshot is that fewer than a quarter of the causes have been paid or can expect checks soon. iGive, which said that it had written checks for $200,000 of the $300,000 already collected for charity, said it would do its best to make sure every charity got its money. *CharityWeb.com says it divides any money that has been raised to 20 causes that have "peace, life and love" in common unless shoppers email other instructions. Those 20 include a Stanford University day care center, where the site's founders, a 1996 Stanford M.B.A. and his wife, send one of their children. The day care center is one of only two causes that have received money, only a couple of hundred dollars, so far. The founder, Kurt Hansen, said that he included the center because he was on its board but that the site was largely made up of causes he had no connection with. *One site that seemed full of promise only weeks ago, CharityMall.com, says it has temporarily shut down. Another, SocialGoods.com, has been absorbed by a rival, 4charity.com. These disruptions raise questions as to what will happen to money already promised. Some charities say they do not want to participate, and some object to how their names are sometimes being used. The American Red Cross, for instance, agreed last year to conduct pilot programs with three new Web sites -- Shop2Give.com, 4charity.com and Toysrweb.com -- but recently decided to bow out after the programs failed to generate the desired financial results. Until told by a reporter, the Red Cross was unaware that it was also listed on two other sites, iGive.com and MyCause.com. The appearance on other sites "dilutes the brand, and it can be very confusing," said Bill Blaul, a Red Cross spokesman. He said the group would probably ask the Web sites to remove the organization.  From the Promise Of the Internet To the entrepreneurs behind the Web sites, these hiccups are just growing pains. The sites promise a stream of revenue from shoppers' purchases to charities. Typically, the money the sites say will go to charity comes from commissions they earn from on-line retailers like Amazon.com and J. Crew in exchange for referring customers. Most Web sites keep part of the commission, but those that send it all to charity can still make money by selling advertising and product placement, finding corporate sponsors or hawking information about shoppers' habits to market researchers. Many sites promise not to disclose personal information without permission, though it is too early to know whether they keep their word. Just as it is transforming other aspects of everyday life, the Internet holds huge potential for charities. Nonprofit groups can use it to reach donors as never before, sending them email about initiatives, creating forums where donors can meet and inviting donations at a fraction of the cost of mass mailings. Proponents of these shopping sites say they, too, are helping reinvent charity. "We have become part of the fabric of a large number of nonprofits," said Robert Grosshandler, who founded iGive after selling his software company. iGive, 18 months old, appears to be the oldest site, and perhaps the largest, claiming 44,000 registered shoppers doing what it calls "Technogiving." The sites' popularity is growing as charities tell donors to check them out, as shoppers tell other shoppers and as people surf the Internet. "The Internet is a great medium for this kind of giving," said Fiona Swerdlow, an analyst for Jupiter Communications, a research firm in newyork. "It should be something that appeals to a lot of consumers." Not to mention charities. "This kind of thing helps a lot," said Lenna Silberman Scott, a spokeswoman for Families of Spinal Muscular Atrophy in Libertyville, Ill., which said the $600 it had received out of $1,300 promised from iGive would help finance research and provide wheelchairs and other medical equipment to families in need. The shop-for-a-cause sites are quick to promote their lofty role. But they are all very much for-profit businesses, although two that send all of the commissions to charity say they are seeking nonprofit status. Some were created by successful entrepreneurs, some by freshly minted business school graduates. They tend to be mom-and-pop operations with little venture capital or corporate backing. And as private businesses, they divulge almost nothing about how well they do. "There are significant differences," said William P. Massey, president of the National Charities Information Bureau, a newyork group that monitors charities and says shoppers can stumble unless they understand how sites work. It is far from clear what rules, if any, apply. The sites, technically affiliates of the retailers, which play no significant role in their activities, do not consider themselves fund-raisers or solicitors, governed by state laws.  None appear to be posting bonds or otherwise insuring that money collected is not diverted. Two already appear to be having difficulty. CharityMall.com, the one that has gone dark, is run by two brothers, both electricians. The site hopes to convert itself to nonprofit status to make itself more attractive to sponsors. It is the only site whose retailers had agreed to pay charities directly, so the money raised so far is not at risk, one brother said. Another, SocialGoods.com, created by two 1998 Harvard M.B.A.'s, has been absorbed by 4charity.com., a rival started by a 1998 Stanford M.B.A. SocialGoods.com's founder, William Morrison, said causes would get any money they were promised. The growth of such sites represents "the beginning of the problem," said Michael DeLucia, director of charitable trusts for New Hampshire and president of the National Association of State Charity Officials.  Too Little Information And Too Much Choice So what are consumers to do? With hundreds of thousands of charities -- many with similar-sounding names -- pleading for help the old-fashioned way in mass mailings and cold calls, giving money away is already tougher than it should be. Confusion over how electronic transactions work, how much actually goes to charity and who, if anyone, might claim a tax deduction, is not helping. An answer to even the simplest question -- which site delivers the most to charity? -- is not obvious. Buying an item from most sites yields only half as much for a worthy cause as buying the same item from 4Charity.com or from CharityMall.com, if it re-emerges. 4Charity, which is seeking nonprofit status, can funnel all money it receives from retailers to the charities because it relies heavily on volunteers and plans to pay its bills by selling information about collective shopping habits to companies, according to Scott Dunlap, its founder. Oddly, sites like Shop2Give.com and MyCause.com, which offer shoppers hundreds of thousands of charities to choose from, raise some of the thorniest issues. The sheer number of choices makes it harder for any one charity to meet a site's minimum threshold. And consumers may have trouble picking and choosing, given what's presented. iGive alone lists 46 causes devoted to the welfare of ferrets. Interested in finding a worthy cancer cause? iGive provides 35 choices, ranging from three chapters of the American Cancer Society in Texas, to Cancer Care of Ridgewood, N.J., to Cancer Caring Center in Pittsburgh, to the Cancer Curing Society in Bonita, Calif. Thus some consumer advocates say Web sites with fewer choices might have more appeal. 4charity enlists the cooperation of the 25 charities it highlights, while Greatergood has signed contracts with all 14 of its charities. So, though consumers may not get as much latitude, there is some accountability. With more than 4,000 causes to keep tabs on, Mr. Grosshandler of iGive says he counts on shoppers to inspect his work. The site provides each shopper with a detailed accounting of how much the causes selected by that shopper have "earned." The shopper is then free to call on the charity to make sure a check was received. "We think we have a million auditors," Mr. Grosshandler said. But whether charities can or want to handle inquiries concerning trivial sums is another matter. "The site is abrogating its responsibility" in expecting consumers to question the charities, said Mr. Blaul of the Red Cross. The Web sites also leave the impression that the process is as quick as a mouse click. Greatergood.com, for instance, asserts, "At least 5 percent of whatever you spend will go to the not-for-profit you choose, automatically. It's that easy!" If only it were. Most retailers make the sites generate a certain amount in referral commissions. J. Crew, for example, typically requires a site to earn $250 in commissions before it writes a check. Thus, a site entitled to a 5 percent commission would have to generate $5,000 in sales -- perhaps 150 polo shirts -- before it could expect payment. Moreover, because the sites often set their own commission thresholds, starting at $10, any one charity has to inspire shoppers to buy the equivalent of six or seven polo shirts -- or even a dozen -- before it sees a dime. Hands on San Francisco, for example, has been told that it is entitled to more than $100 through 4Charity but must be patient; the site makes payments only four times a year. The group is also waiting for a check from iGive, a delay chalked up to a clerical error. Tracking money given to a certain charity is not always easy. During the holidays, one retailer, Cyberian Outpost, had computer problems and for several weeks lost information about which commissions were owed to which causes. Though the retailer said it had paid the sites what it estimated it owed them in total commissions, sites like Shop2Give and 4Charity had no way of knowing how much they owed various causes unless shoppers got in touch with them to reconstruct their purchases. Some sites also require shoppers to take multiple steps to insure that their cause gets credit. iGive requires an electronic proof of purchase by way of email, but the site says 10 percent of shoppers never send it. "We consider that 10 percent a failure," Mr. Grosshandler said, adding that those funds still go to some charity. Other sites dance around facts consumers might want to know, particularly those that might remind shoppers that the sites have mercenary motives and might dip into any money they receive from retailers to pay their own bills. MyCause tells visitors that it is "sustained by an additional commission paid by our affiliate retailers," implying that its fees are not coming at the charities' expense. Shop2Give used to imply that retailers called all the shots. The site told shoppers that it allowed the retailer "to decide the amount to be donated." Some big merchants like J. Crew say they did weigh in, but in at least one case involving a major retailer, Shop2Give had more influence than that. "We would have no voice in what an affiliate partner does with the revenue stream," said Ben Boyd, a spokesman for Barnesandnoble.com, a Shop2Give retailer. The site is "mischaracterizing our commission as a pledged donation." After being made aware of the conflicting accounts, Shop2Give said it was changing its language. "Shop2Give then determines how much of this total commission will go to a nonprofit organization," the site now tells shoppers. Consumers can also be forgiven for thinking they are eligible for a tax deduction. They are not. Yet only two sites, MyCause and Shop2Give, make that clear. And Shop2Give even tells shoppers not to lose hope -- it is "actively working on finding a solution that can accommodate tax benefits." It is hard to see how. Whatever money goes to charity is a result of the site's diverting some, or all, of what it gets from the retailer.  Legal Loopholes And Regulators' Fears The biggest fear of state regulators and charity watchdogs is that many sites are accountable to no one. Only a few, Greatergood, Shop2Give and 4Charity, say they have registered under state law to do cause-related marketing. Other sites like iGive and MyCause say the existing laws do not apply to their activities. State laws might come into play when sites raise money without the charities' cooperation. When the American Camping Association, for example, found itself listed on MyCause.com, it requested information about the site's activities, to no avail. Though the group has not asked to have its name removed, "we feel very removed from it," said Bob Shultz, the director of development. Another educational charity, which demanded anonymity, sought to remove itself from iGive, only to be told that it had no say in the matter. iGive shoppers decide which causes to include. Use of a charity's name without its approval may violate laws in many states. In Pennsylvania, no one can solicit on behalf of a charity without its consent, said Karl Emerson, director of the Pennsylvania Bureau of Charitable Organizations. For every bona fide charity that participates over its objections, regulators also worry that imposters could seek out listings and bombard shoppers with email, imploring them to make the imposters the beneficiary. Greatergood.com, one of the more stringent sites, requires charities to be on the list the Internal Revenue Service keeps of nonprofit organizations that qualify for tax-deductible gifts. Other sites say they make case-by-case determinations, while iGive merely requires causes to affirm they are nonprofits and engage in good works. Some causes like the Broken Nose Fund in Portland, Me., have neither applied to the I.R.S. for permission to accept tax-deductible donations nor registered with charity regulators in their home states. "I am not registered because I am trying to make money for myself, because I need surgery," said Ashley Lenartson, who is looking to raise $15,000 to fix his own nose for the third time. iGive's Mr. Grosshandler acknowledges that some groups on its site are not bona fide charities and says the site's job is not to play Big Brother. "I am sure there is a brother Bob in the 4,300 charities," he said, referring to the possibility that someone may have registered a cause close to home. "If he's their favorite worthy cause, it's great." Therein lies the dilemma. If these Web sites survive, they will come to resemble electronic shopping malls with as much to show for themselves as the credit card companies that pioneered the help-a-favorite-cause pitch. Nearly 6 percent of the $596 billion in Visa and Mastercard volume last year went to cards that diverted a fraction of purchases to worthy causes, according to the Nilson Report, an industry newsletter in Oxnard, Calif. But there are key differences. Credit card issuers are often well-established companies that have earned consumers' trust. They enter contracts with every charity they represent. And though Internet companies often fall between regulatory cracks, banking has always been well monitored. The future of these shop-for-a-cause sites depends a lot on what results they deliver for charities and consumers. What worries Mr. Dunlap, the founder of 4charity.com, is that some sites -- ones that mislead consumers or alienate charities -- "will ruin it for the rest of us." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "A Guide to the Sites" These shop-for-a-cause Web sites raise money for charities by collecting commissions from retailers for referring customers to them. While one site says it gives all of the commission to charity, others keep a portion. Here is how they compare.  WEB ADDRESS: www.4charity.com FOUNDERS: Stanford M.B.A. in Mountain View, Calif. Staffed by volunteers. It recently absorbed the operations of Socialgoods.com, a rival site created by two Harvard M.B.A.'s. NO. OF RETAILERS: 38 CAUSES: 25, mix of large national causes like the American Red Cross and community groups like the Aloha United Way. EASE OF USE: So-so. Shoppers need to register. Hard to switch charities. DISCLOSURE: Good. No reference to tax deduction, but the only site to break down how much each retailer pays on different items and to make clear that hard-to-find items yield no commission. HOW THE SITE MAKES MONEY: Says it gives 100 percent of the commission to charity, but sells information about collective buying habits. Says it will not divulge personal information.  WEB ADDRESS: www.charityweb.com. FOUNDERS: Stanford M.B.A. and wife in Mountain View, Calif. NO. OF RETAILERS: 4 CAUSES: 20, mostly community groups, including a day care center, which the founders' child attends. They share all proceeds unless shoppers email other instructions. EASE OF USE: Good. Shoppers need not register. DISCLOSURE: Good. No reference to tax deduction, but provides some detail about how the site is able to send money to charity. HOW THE SITE MAKES MONEY: Keeps half of all referral commissions.  WEB ADDRESS: www:greatergood.com FOUNDERS: Seattle venture capitalist. Management team boasts one heavy hitter: an ex-president of the National Wildlife Federation. NO. OF RETAILERS: 24 CAUSES: 14, mostly large national charities like Big Brothers, Big Sisters and the Humane Society. The site has contracts with all 14. Write-ins accepted. EASE OF USE: Good. Shoppers need not register but write-in process cumbersome. DISCLOSURE: Poor. No reference to tax deduction and little detail about how the site is able to send money to charity and how it makes money. HOW THE SITE MAKES MONEY: Keeps half of all referral commissions.  WEB ADDRESS: www:igive.com FOUNDERS: Software entrepreneur in Evanston, Ill. NO. OF RETAILERS: 27 CAUSES: 4,300, mostly community groups like the Aldrich School P.T.A. and the Pennsylvania Ferret Rescue Association. Write-ins encouraged. EASE OF USE: Poor. Shoppers need to register. Sign-in can be confusing. Hard to switch charities. Shoppers must email proof of purchase or their charity gets nothing. DISCLOSURE: Good. No reference to tax deduction, but provides updates on how much has been raised. Site carries disclaimer that despite best efforts, in some instances causes may not collect the money. HOW THE SITE MAKES MONEY: Keeps half of all referral commissions.  WEB ADDRESS: www.mycause.com FOUNDERS: A research librarian, a Ph.D. candidate and a computer science guy from Ithaca, N.Y. NO. OF RETAILERS: 5 CAUSES: 275,000 tax-deductible groups of all sizes, including pension plans and associations. Says it will include others at its discretion. EASE OF USE: Good. Shoppers need not register. DISCLOSURE: So-so. While the site makes clear not to expect a tax deduction, and informs shoppers how much has been raised for each cause, it does not make clear how much of the commission it keeps. HOW THE SITE MAKES MONEY: Without providing specifics, the site says it is sustained by an additional commission paid by our affiliate retailers for the referral service we provide.  WEB ADDRESS: www.shop2give.com FOUNDERS: University of Southern California M.B.A. in Los Angeles. Worked as a sales manager of a concrete-cutting equipment manufacturer. NO. Tells shoppers not to expect a tax deduction but holds out hope that the site is actively working on finding a solution that can accommodate tax benefits. Was unclear about own role in transaction. title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Pepsi Bottling is a giant offering that could well fail to excite investors fixated on Internet stocks.
body: IN another environment, the initial public offering of the Pepsi Bottling Group might be one of the hottest stock deals of the year, driven by an international brand name and a consumer franchise with great opportunity to expand abroad. But in the year of the Internet, investors have been rather uninterested in offerings by companies lacking "dot-com" in their names. Add to that the announcement late Monday by the Coca-Cola Company that its sales, measured in cases, took an unexpected drop in the first quarter, and the result could be a tepid reception for the Pepsi Bottling offering. The company, which is the largest manufacturer, distributor and seller of Pepsi-Cola beverages, provided the details of its long-awaited separation from Pepsico late yesterday. It is selling 100 million shares of common stock for $23 a share, raising $2.3 billion before expenses -- the fifth-largest initial public offering by an American corporation, according to the Securities Data Corporation. And if Pepsi Bottling exercises its option to issue an additional 15 million shares, it could rise as high as No. 3, behind only last year's offering by Conoco and the 1996 issue of Lucent Technologies. The price, though, is at the bottom of the $23-to-$26-a-share range that the company had previously said it was considering, most likely reflecting caution after Coca-Cola's surprise announcement. Investors sold shares of several beverage companies yesterday following the Coca-Cola news, with Coke shares falling $1.5625, to $63.25. Shares of Pepsico, which after the offering will own 35 percent of the bottling company's common shares and 43 percent of the voting power in all classes of stock, fell 81.25 cents, to $39.875. Shares of Coca-Cola Enterprises, Coke's largest bottler and the company whose structure most closely reflects that of Pepsi Bottling, fell $1.8125, to $31.50. Some analysts played down any connection between Coca-Cola's weakness and Pepsico's largest bottler. Roy Burry, an analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman, noted that Coca-Cola's loss of market share presumably meant a gain for Pepsi, which would be good news for the bottler. In addition, the only area in which Coca-Cola eked out a sales gain in the first quarter was North America, meaning that the domestic soft-drink market might not be as weak as in the rest of the world. About 92 percent of Pepsi Bottling's case volume is sold in North America, and the company handles about 55 percent of Pepsi's unitedstates volume. "It's tough to look at Coke's volume numbers and deduce how they will affect Pepsi," said Richard Joy, an analyst at Standard & Poor's equity group. Pepsi Bottling could still see some weakness in the small part of its business that is overseas: 8 percent of its sales volume, measured in cases, comes from Spain, Greece and Russia. Russia has been an extremely weak market for multinational corporations like Coke and Pepsi ever since last year's devaluation of the ruble. Spain offers a potential base for expansion into neighboring European Union countries, but that market is not growing very rapidly itself. Greece, meanwhile, offers relatively little opportunity for regional expansion, given its proximity to the war-torn Balkan nations. All that said, Pepsi Bottling has certain attractions. For one, it is likely to trade at a lower valuation than Coca-Cola Enterprises. Standard & Poor's, in its Emerging and Special Situations newsletter, calculated that at the midpoint of the projected price range, Pepsi Bottling would trade at about nine times earnings before noncash charges like depreciation. Coca-Cola Enterprises trades at about 10 times that earnings measure. And since Pepsi Bottling is pricing at the low end of the range, the discount grows that much larger. With its offering, Pepsi is following the trail blazed by Coke and Coca-Cola Enterprises -- a surprising fact given that a number of analysts and customers of the bottler have questioned just how independent those two companies are. But the offering will give Pepsi Bottling the financial strength to expand its vending operations and to continue an overhaul of its manufacturing and distribution network. Those combined efforts could help the company's profit margins in the years ahead. Investors should not expect the shares, which begin trading today on the newyork Stock Exchange under the symbol PBG, to replicate the sharp rise recorded by recent offerings like that of Priceline.com, which rose $53 yesterday, to $69, from its initial offering price of $16. Neither is it preordained, though, that Pepsi Bottling will draw as little interest as the February offering of Del Monte Foods, which went public at $15 a share and closed yesterday at $11.75. Investors with long-term horizons, and a thirst for Pepsi over Coke, might find the offering has some appeal.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Venture Planned For E-Commerce
body: America Online Inc., the world's largest Internet services company, and the computer maker Sun Microsystems Inc. said yesterday that they would develop a unified set of electronic commerce products by early next year. In a statement, America Online and Sun outlined their strategy for the collaboration between the two companies, which they refer to as the Sun-Netscape Alliance. The companies said they planned to develop a unified set of new products, while maintaining support for the current set of products offered by both companies. The alliance said it would develop products for messaging and collaboration over the Internet, as well as directory and security features for safely navigating and doing business on the Web. The companies also sketched plans to develop what they described as packaged electronic commerce software applications that would offer companies seeking to do business on line the means to exchange products, procure inventory, and sell and bill for those products. The alliance said it planned to ship its first collaborative product by the first quarter of the year 2000. The stock of America Online jumped $12.125, or 9.2 percent, to $144.50, on the newyork Stock Exchange, while Sun was up $1.4375 a share, at $125.9375, in Nasdaq trading. http://www.nytimes.com

title: $200 Million Wireless Deal Is Reported
body: MCI Worldcom Inc., seeking advanced wireless Internet links, is investing about $200 million in what is incongruously known as the wireless cable business, executives close to the plans said yesterday. MCI Worldcom is the No. 2 long-distance phone company, after AT& T, and the No. 1 Internet carrier. Even so, it has become frustrated in trying to use lines owned by the Bell local phone companies to connect to its customers. The Bells must lease their lines to other companies that want to use them, and the Bells say that process is easy. The Bells' competitors, including MCI Worldcom, almost invariably contend that the process is arduous and expensive. So, the executives close to the transactions say, MCI Worldcom is buying the shares and bonds of four so-called wireless cable operators: CAI Wireless Systems Inc., CS Wireless Systems Inc., the People's Choice TV Corporation and Wireless One Inc. Control of those companies could allow MCI Worldcom to avoid using the Bells in some places. CNBC, the cable television channel, first reported the plans yesterday. It said the company might have already spent as much as $300 million to $400 million, but executives close to the deals said MCI Worldcom had committed only about $200 million to the initiative. MCI Worldcom declined to comment. The companies in which MCI Worldcom is said to be investing have tried to use wireless technology to transmit signals from television stations that most consumers view using cable. Though direct-broadcast satellite systems have proved effective, the land-based technology embraced by these operators never proved broadly cost-effective for transmitting television signals. But MCI Worldcom apparently believes that the spectrum owned by the operators could be used efficiently to transmit Internet data. CS Wireless, People's Choice and Wireless One are all in financial trouble, and control of those companies may lie in their bonds, rather than in their shares, allowing MCI Worldcom to accumulate control through the traditionally secretive corporate debt market. As for CAI, executives close to the deals said securities regulations would soon force MCI Worldcom to disclose a large investment in that company's stock. Trying to gain control of the wireless cable carriers cheaply and quietly would be a move typical of Scott D. Sullivan, MCI Worldcom's chief financial officer, who has developed a strong financial reputation in the telecommunications industry for his swift seizing of opportunities and his delivery of consistent earnings. http://www.nytimes.com

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Dow Closes Above 10,000, Reflecting Strong Economy After nearly two weeks of thrust and parry, stock traders pushed the Dow Jones industrial average above 10,000 and kept it there until the end of the day's trading. The Dow closed at 10,006.78, up 184.54 points, or 1.9 percent. Although 10,000 on the Dow was little more than a psychological hurdle for investors, the market's move is significant in what it reflects: unparalleled strength of the economy and American corporations' dominance of the world stage.  Page A1. Almost lost in the shuffle of the Dow's record-setting day was a solid performance by broader gauges. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index rose 27.37 points, or 2.1 percent, to 1,310.17, while the Nasdaq composite index jumped 73.67 points, or 3 percent, to 2,492.84.  C11.  Microsoft Reorganizes Into 5 Units Microsoft's president, Steven Ballmer, announced the reorganization of the company into five divisions that he suggested would act with some independence. Brad Chase, left, and Jon DeVaan will run a newly created consumer and commerce group that includes the Microsoft Network. The other new units are the Business and Enterprise Division, the Consumer Windows Division, the Business Productivity Group for "knowledge workers" like telecommuters, and the Developer Group.  C2.
