title:
STATE OF THE ART;
Listen To This Browser
body: Pop quiz for the generation that has grown up with the Internet: Name the information appliance that used to be the focal point for family entertainment before the personal computer, and even before television. (Yes, there was life before television.) Now, name the newest and most entertaining feature of the Microsoft Corporation's new Internet Explorer 5.0 Web browser, which is available for downloading starting today at www .microsoft.com/ie. No, you young whippersnappers, not the telegraph or the Victrola, (pre-Internet equivalents of email and MP3 music files). The answer to both questions is "radio." By adding radio to its Web browser and the multimedia tools to go with the the browser, Microsoft is giving a clear signal of its vision for the future of the Internet. Internet Explorer 5.0 has been turned into a tool not just for searching for and viewing information on the Internet's World Wide Web or a local hard disk, but also for listening to talk and music, and for watching video clips downloaded from the Net. The Internet is evolving into an entertainment network, augmenting its already established roles as a global information, communications and electronic commerce network. The PC is the primary vehicle for exploring this new medium, and Explorer 5.0 is the dashboard, complete with a new set of radio buttons. At first glance, the updated browser looks pretty much like Version 4.0, which is comforting to those of us who have already invested a few million precious brain cells learning how the earlier version works, instead of employing them on something more profitable, like dreaming up creative tax deductions. But on closer examination, Microsoft has streamlined and refined this new edition of its browser in lots of small but significant ways. Streamlined is a relative term. The new browser -- for Windows-based machines only, at this point -- still consumes about 100 megabytes of hard disk space for a full installation, slightly more than its predecessor. But once the browser is in action, it is much more nimble and elegant. Gone, or at least hidden, are the annoying "channels" that Microsoft included in earlier versions of Internet Explorer, in a dubious effort to make it easier for users to get information from their favorite Web sites. Instead, the new browser has a better system for making and organizing bookmarks, shortcuts to favorite sites. Microsoft has made lots of improvements in Version 5.0 that make the browser easier to use. For example, a new Go button has been added to aid people who could not figure out that they should push the Enter key after typing a Web address. And if a user mistypes a Web address, a new feature in the updated browser can often fix the error automatically. Microsoft has added a variety of automated features in the new version, which makes it easier to revisit favorite Web sites, to fill out forms and to conduct searches for information on line. Searching has been organized with buttons specifically for finding people, finding Web sites, finding news groups, finding maps and so on. A Next button enables the user to cycle through different search engines if the first pass does not yield the desired results. A search button has even been added to the "history" list of previously visited Web sites. There are many times I can remember seeing a nugget of information somewhere on a Web site I have visited, but cannot remember which one. By entering a key word, one can search through just the previously visited sites. Very handy. Microsoft also borrowed a clever feature from Netscape Navigator, the ability to search for related links. For example, if I'm viewing this newspaper's Web site at www. nytimes.com, and click on Show Related Links under the Version 5.0 tools menu, I get a list of sites belonging to other major newspapers. Although the updated version has lots of new productivity enhancements, the radio features are the most fun. Computers cannot do as good a job with radio as radios can, and a television set is still better at showing video. But computers do have special skills, like pulling in radio stations from halfway around the world or downloading movie clips to watch over and over again. By clicking on Version 5.0's new radio toolbar (click Views, then Toolbars, then Radio), I was able to choose from an eclectic assortment of radio stations from around the world, most of which delivered their signals as streams of digital bits over the Internet, which were then converted to analog sounds pumped through my computer's stereo speakers. Not all of the preset radio links worked, a problem Microsoft promised would be fixed by today, and woe to the Internet user whose favorite stations, like mine, include such overlooked gems as WOI-FM in Ames, Iowa. I also used Explorer 5.0 and the Windows Media Player to listen to old radio dramas -- the kind where, in our imaginations, the villains neither sounded nor looked anything like Bill Gates, Microsoft's co-founder and principal owner. In the current Federal antitrust trial, Mr. Gates is being portrayed by the Government as the villain who sought to crush little Netscape, a competitor, by making Internet Explorer a seemingly inextricable part of the Windows operating system, thereby unfairly leveraging its Windows monopoly to gain market share for its browser. Microsoft argues that Internet Explorer and other utilities merely add value and convenience for its customers. And now Microsoft is adding more value at an even deeper level, inside the browser that itself is inside the operating system. Clicking on Explorer 5.0's radio buttons brings up Microsoft's Windows Media Player. And by assembling the lists of radio stations, Microsoft has invaded the turf of Internet radio and video companies like Broadcast.com, thus generating instant rivals. And so it goes. The browser is becoming the operating system of the Internet age, and it, too, will inevitably become bloated with built-in search engines, security tools, electronic payment systems, text translators and whatever other new utilities become important as the Internet grows. From a consumer perspective, having these tools tightly integrated, and free, in the operating system and browser makes computers easier and more enjoyable to use. The nice thing is that one is also free to choose other tools like Navigator, Real Player, Quicktime, and Broadcast.com. For regulators, the challenge is to make sure that the companies that make the rival tools have a fair chance to compete. Internet radio is not new, of course. What is new is the easy listening that Explorer 5.0's new radio buttons allow. However, to take advantage of the radio functions, the user must install the Windows Media Player, a free utility that launches automatically when the browser sucks down a multimedia file. It also helps to have a fast Internet connection, like the cable modem I'm lucky to have. When I tried listening to radio stations via a 28.8 kilobit-per-second modem, it was slow death. The stations that were loud and clear on my fast desktop machine were wretched on the slow connection. A 56-kilobit modem is almost a minimum requirement. Even if one never uses Explorer 5.0 for radio, it is still worth getting, especially because it is free. I've been using a nearly final copy of it for a couple of weeks without any serious (i.e. harmful) glitches. But it is a new program, after all, and bugs are bound to surface even though it has been tested for months by tens of thousands of Microsoft's human laboratory mice. As with any new software, be sure to back up your important files before loading it. Microsoft and its chief rival Netscape (soon to be a part of America Online) have been playing leapfrog with their respective Web browsers for several years, a competition that has been of particular interest to the Justice Department in recent months. From a consumer perspective, the competition has been a boon. Netscape's latest version, Navigator 4.51 (www.netscape.com) is quite good and has some unique features, like Instant Messenger 2.0 , which allows Web users to type real-time messages back and forth with friends who are on line at the same time. Netscape is planning to release its own Version 5.0 browser in a few months, so Microsoft's current advantage may be only temporary. As of today, however, the new Internet Explorer is the top frog. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: They've Got Mail, and Game; Chess Fans Make Their Move
body: WHILE slick on-line games like Baldur's Gate and Half-Life are attracting plenty of players with their intense action and glorious graphics, there is another group of gamers on the Internet that is just as passionate. "Chess game anyone? If you would like to play, I am white and my first move is 1. e4," reads a posting in one of the Usenet chess newsgroups. In fact, Usenet, the worldwide bulletin board system, has a forum called rec.games.chess.play-by-email that is devoted to long-distance competitions. No longer do players have to rely on the post office and mailing lists to take on faraway competitors. "I'm not a serious chess player, but I play a decent game if I'm not rushed," Chris Cooper of Silverton, Ore., said via email. "email seemed to be the way to go. Spending 20 to 33 cents a postcard or letter per chess move does not make any sense to me." Working on one's endgame by email is nothing new. But now chess-heads can get a bit more graphic than sending a message that reads "1. Ng1-f3." With Hasbro Interactive's Grand Master Chess program, (which also includes checkers and backgammon), a player can send, via email, an animated color chessboard to an opponent that displays that kingside knight making his first move. The game is part of Hasbro's email Games series of CD-ROM's, which also include two other board-game staples, Battleship and Scrabble. The company plans to release more games in the series this spring, including football, golf and poker. email Battleship comes with explosive noises and digitized fireballs that appear on the game-board grid when you score a hit on the enemy fleet. Scrabble's distinctive letter tiles move just as easily on screen, and having them in digital form relieves the secret fear (especially for parents) of losing all the vowels under the couch over the years. To participate in the games, a player needs to be running Windows 95 or 98, have Internet access and run an email program that allows the sending and receiving of file attachments. Only the player initiating the game needs to have the CD-ROM. Player 1 starts a game and sends the first move to Player 2. The email is routed through Hasbro's game server, and it takes about five minutes for each move to go from Player 1 to Player 2. Player 2 gets the email message and clicks on the attachment to download and install the game. Then Player 2 can make a move, write a message and send the game back to Player 1. Each title in Hasbro Interactive's email Games series costs $14.95, and all are available for purchase on line at www.emailgames.com or in retail stores. People who want to try before they buy can download a free 10-move game demo from the Web site. "I'd say it is pretty good," Mr. Cooper said of Hasbro's chess game. "I like not having to read chess notation. Now I have a reason to look forward to my email." The email games seem to be gaining popularity. Although the games have been out for only a few months, there is already a fan Web page devoted to them: Bill & John's email Games Player's Directory at pages.prodigy.net/n2netsurfn/pbem. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: REPLY REQUESTED -- Players of Hasbro Interactive's email chess game see opponents' moves on an animated color board.

title:
TURF;
Multiple Listings Come to Manhattan. Sort of. - Correction Appended
body: THIRTY-THREE of newyork City's real estate companies have adopted a new coordinated computer system for selling apartments -- a system that, even before it is operating, is the subject of a debate about the city's selective way of selling real estate. After five years of planning, the Lex system -- which will go into operation in June -- will speed the way new listings are sent from one real estate company to another. Lex is "the closest newyork City has ever gotten to a multiple listing service like they have in the rest of the country," said Frederick W. Peters, the president of Ashforth Warburg, and a crucial player in the advent of Lex. The old system involved sending piles of paper faxes between brokerage companies, which then had to be entered into each agency's computer system -- a process that could take days. The proponents of Lex say the new system will offer a benefit to apartment hunters: the latest sales and rental listings will be instantly available, making it possible for them to go and see the apartments more quickly in this lightning-fast market. The apartment profiles delivered through the Lex system will also offer more information than is currently available; each listing will come with a color photograph and a floor plan. The computer software was distributed just two days ago to participants, who must be members of the Real Estate Board of newyork and pay $10,000 each for the privilege. But before Lex even starts operating, the system is being criticized by a number of agents. They complain that the new system merely continues newyork City's entrenched policies of exclusion by sending the listings only to selected brokers and not allowing the general public to view them directly, as they can at various Web sites. Several sites already exist that show listings in newyork City. At one of them, www.gabrielsrex.com, any licensed broker who pays $100 a month can advertise sales and rental listings for a nickel a day apiece; apartment hunters pay nothing to browse. One man who owns a small real estate company -- he spoke on the condition of anonymity because he does business with many of the people involved in Lex -- criticized Lex's founders for not creating a comparable Web site, available to everyone. With the Internet services, most of the apartments are still listed through a broker, who must be called if anyone wants to show the apartment. So, why don't the agents like the idea of a multiple listing service on the Internet? In newyork City, the largest agencies -- as well as some of the small ones -- want to choose exactly who they will share listings with. "Yes, it is exclusionary," said Dexter Guerrieri, the president of Vandenberg Real Estate, who still has not decided whether to sign up with Lex. "But it's the way we do business here." Christopher B. Costello, Lex's technical director, said that was one reason Lex took five years to set up: the affiliated companies had written into the binding guidelines establishing the system that it would "never be a central repository," available to every company. Even in the new system, brokers can still decide to hold back a listing or to share it -- even with brokers outside the system and not necessarily with all 33 members of Lex -- protecting the kinds of options that exist almost nowhere outside newyork City. Throughout the country, brokers generally share their listings or face stiff penalties imposed by their trade groups. That way, a buyer can see every property available in the area. In newyork City, however, brokerage companies do not always share (a process called co-brokering). Especially in a hot market, the temptation for the agents is to try to hold on to a new listing and sell the apartment themselves in order to retain the entire commission, usually 6 percent of the selling price. (For their part, agents argue that the sellers are better served by limiting the number of agents tramping through an apartment, and that only hand-picked agencies have the experience to guide buyers through certain co-op boards.) Many brokers who question the time spent developing Lex see an Internet site as the place for real estate companies to share listings. "The Internet is a great big swimming pool, and you can jump in and jump out," said the company owner who spoke anonymously. "With Lex, they're trying to build the swimming pool from scratch." JoAnne Kennedy, the partner in Coldwell Banker Hunt Kennedy who headed the Lex group at the Real Estate Board, admits there are limitations. But she bridled at the talk about excluding other brokers. "In no way is this meant to exclude the little guy," she said. Mr. Guerrieri, the company owner who is taking what he called a "wait and see" attitude toward Lex, nevertheless has put down a $5,000 deposit to hold a spot for his company on the system, so he will not be, as he said, out of the loop. "Manhattan is really still in the dark ages," he said. "We're very provincial as far as multiple listings. Lex is the version we're easing into." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article on page 14 of the House & Home section today about a computer system that will be used to share listings among some real estate agents in newyork City misstates the eligibility rule for participants. They must be licensed real estate brokers; they need not be members of the Real Estate Board of newyork. Correction-Date: March 18, 1999, Thursday

title:
WHAT'S NEXT;
Signing On With Your Fingerprints
body: WHILE people continue to repeat the newyorker cartoon tag line that no one knows you're a dog on the Internet, the computer industry is working diligently to sort out the sheep from the goats. Anonymity may offer a bit of excitement to chat rooms and keep us safe from stalkers we meet on line, but careful industries like banks and investment houses continue to look for better technology for identifying people. Some of the latest solutions on the horizon are devices for reading people's fingerprints. A number of companies are making relatively inexpensive gadgets that can capture an image of a fingerprint so that it can be compared against a database. The products are not in widespread use yet, but the field of biometrics -- authentication techniques that rely on measurable physical characteristic -- is prompting a lot of interest, and a number of companies have hopes that the fingerprint scanners will catch on. American Biometric, a Canadian-based concern, offers a device called a Biomouse for about $250 that reads fingerprints into a PC and compares them with a database. Sony is shipping similar devices, and the California-based company I/O Software is selling a Sony device packaged with its Secure Suite software for about $350. While these devices might be a bit too expensive to make it into every PC, they are priced low enough for some business applications. Among the places fingerprint scanners might be used are bank teller windows and time clocks. Each of these devices takes an image of a fingerprint and converts it into a file known as a template. The file records the locations of the unique parts of each fingerprint: whorls, arches, ridges, valleys and loops.  Fingerprints can be compared and matched by looking at these locations. But keeping fingerprints on file concerns privacy advocates because such information can be susceptible to abuse. While bank customers may use different passwords on different accounts, for example, their fingerprints remain the same. An unscrupulous programmer at a bank could easily use data records to impersonate a client. "The fingerprint identification raises the difficult tension between security and privacy," said Marc Rotenberg, director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center in Washington. "Security gives more authentication, and that's good because it means that the person using an A.T.M. is who they say they are. But on the privacy side we create the risk of a new global identifier." Both American Biometric's device and the package produced by Sony and I/O Software come with a touch-sensitive screen. The amount of pressure applied by a finger on the screen makes a big difference in producing a machine-recognizable image, and in a test by Circuits, it took several tries to do so consistently. It is also important to place the finger in the same position each time an image is taken, because small shifts can affect which features appear. If the machine can't find the right whorls and loops, it won't recognize you. Both packages come with software that adds security to a computer. I/O Software's Secure Suite package includes a tool that lets the user log onto a computer by checking the fingerprint. While it took several tries in the Circuits test to successfully program the system with a fingerprint, it worked fairly well afterward. The true effectiveness of these devices is hard to judge. Stealing passwords is relatively easy to do, hard to defend against and difficult to detect when the password is taken. Fingerprints, on the other hand, can't be stolen by looking over someone's shoulder but they can be found on water glasses and other smooth-surfaced objects. Both products try to screen out forgeries. Both have touch-sensitive screens that can detect dry-paper pictures of fingerprints. In the Circuits test, neither would accept a laser-printed version of a right thumb print, even after the addition of some moisture to activate the touch-sensitive screens. Steve Borza, a vice president of American Biometric, said the only consistently successful way demonstrated in the company's labs to fool the fingerprint reader has been to use a plaster cast of a finger. Most latent fingerprints left in everyday use, he said, are smudged by tiny rotations of the moving fingers. Researchers who try to use a copy of a print picked up from a wine glass or a car door run into trouble. Even print cards taken at police stations are often distorted. The company is also selling a product known as the Biomouse Plus, which comes with a built-in reader for so-called smart cards, identification cards often used for security. "You essentially need the smart card and the finger," Mr. Borza said. "It's a two-factor authentication. Just having a 'severed digit' isn't going to get you in." He may have been referring to a favorite, apparently apocryphal, story among security people about the mugger who, faced with an A.T.M. that used fingerprint-identification security technology, simply chopped off his victim's finger. Bruce Schneier, the president of Counterpane, a computer security company, said: "Biometrics are secure if you have an armed guard watching the biometric reader. Otherwise it can be fooled." They may work at a bank teller's window but couldn't be trusted if installed on a home PC. Mr. Schneier pointed out that all biometric devices are susceptible to a "replay attack" if an intruder is able to make a copy of the description of the legitimate user's body part. This description is not supposed to change over time, so the intruder may be able to get the system to replay it. This would require some access to the software or the network connection, however, making home PC's much more vulnerable than installations at banks. Mr. Borza argued that endless cycles of counter-engineering and counter-counter-engineering for security purposes have diminishing returns. Citing the classic Mad magazine comic strip, he said, "At some level it becomes 'Spy vs. Spy' and it's hard to justify it.' " http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Mary Ann Smith)

title: Giuliani Says Diallo Shooting Coverage Skewed Poll
body: Mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani blamed partisan politics and an "obsessive media concern" yesterday for the results of a newyork Times poll released this week that showed a sharp drop in his job-approval rating and a widespread belief among the city's black and Hispanic residents that the police routinely use excessive force against them. Speaking at a news conference at the Waldorf-Astoria, he suggested that the numbers were skewed because of the way the news media and various black leaders have responded to the shooting death last month of Amadou Diallo, an immigrant from West Africa. Four white police officers killed Mr. Diallo, who was unarmed, with a flurry of bullets while he stood in the vestibule of his Bronx apartment building. Black leaders immediately denounced the shooting as indicative of a Police Department that too readily assumes that black people pose a threat. After some sporadic demonstrations, the leaders recently began to stage daily protests of civil disobedience. This week alone, former Mayor David N. Dinkins, the Rev. Al Sharpton and Representative Charles B. Rangel were arrested, all to intense news coverage. The Mayor characterized statements by the protesters about police attitudes as inaccurate and partisan, and he said the statements were repeated in a "media frenzy" that distorted reality and affected the perceptions reflected in polls. That is why, Mr. Giuliani suggested yesterday, The newyork Times poll showed his job-approval rating plummeting to 42 percent, from 63 percent only five months ago. That is also why, he said, the poll indicates that fewer than a quarter of all newyorkers think that the police treat blacks and whites in an equally fair manner; that nearly 90 percent of black residents think that the police often engage in brutality against blacks and that one of every three blacks has felt danger in the presence of a police officer. As he has since the Diallo shooting, Mr. Giuliani emphasized that statistics have demonstrated a sharp reduction in incidents of excessive force among the city's police officers, to the point that the department is among the most restrained in the country. "If 70 or 80 percent of the people believe that police officers in newyork City are brutal too often, that's a misperception," the Mayor said. "That's a false perception. It is driven by a very effective partisan political campaign, and the fact that there's been an obsessive concern in the media about it." Mr. Giuliani then sought to put the Diallo shooting in a larger context, saying: "Since the time of Mr. Diallo's tragic death, which was a horrible thing and a terrible thing -- which I have expressed great remorse for and have done everything to try to rectify -- there also have been 60 other murders in newyork City since then, including a substantial number of murders in the minority community that I have to have an equal amount of concern about, and that I need this Police Department to interrupt, prevent and to work on in order to protect people against the more realistic way in which they face danger in this city." He used the Waldorf, where a guest was killed last weekend, to illustrate his point about the "obsessive media concern" -- a phrase he repeated -- that has been shown to the police shooting of Mr. Diallo. "Look, we're in a hotel that two days ago, three days ago, had a horrible murder take place," he said. "A horrible, vicious, awful murder. If you spent the next five weeks covering that murder, you would convince people that there was a murder problem in the city of newyork, even though murder is down by 70 percent. "Just think about that for a moment," he continued. "If you spent the next five weeks -- spent as much time on the murder that took place in this hotel for the next five weeks -- had it on Channel 2, Channel 4, Channel 7, Channel Everyone, and all the newspapers for the next five weeks, you'd have people running around this city, 70 percent, believing that we had a significant murder problem in the city, even though murder is down 70 percent. "That," he said, "is essentially what has happened here." http://www.nytimes.com

title: The Arrogant Ascent to 10,000
body: With the Dow Jones industrial average on the verge of closing over 10,000, I can't get my mind off a strange stock picker known as Tokyo Joe. Tokyo Joe -- a.k.a. TokyoMex, a.k.a. Joe Park -- is a 40-year-old South Korean immigrant who, according to a recent article in Money magazine, used to run a string of burrito restaurants in Manhattan. A few years ago, he became obsessed with the stock chat boards on the Internet. On several of them, he became a dominant figure; other investors began investing in small-cap stocks on his say-so. Soon he had gravitated to day trading, where he claimed to be making a small fortune buying in and out of stocks in the space of a day -- or more likely, an hour. Finally, Tokyo Joe set up a proprietary Web site, where he charges $100 a month for access to his stock picks. He is, without question, one of the most influential stock pickers on the Internet. Sixteen years into the greatest bull market in American history, it no longer surprises when an amateur investor like Tokyo Joe decides to "go pro." No, the real twist here is his investing philosophy. He believes that company fundamentals, which have guided investors from time immemorial, are for saps, and that long-term investing is for losers. (He proudly calls himself a "speculator.") He thinks there's nothing wrong with touting a stock to make it move, and then selling into the run-up. ("Otherwise what am I? A charity?") And he thinks that if you have a problem with any of this, well, too bad. "We're the new blood, man," he exulted to the writer from Money. Here's the sad part. He might be right. Just check out the chat boards these days. They're filled with people who are day trading and speculating and trying to pump up stocks for a quick and easy gain. And to me, they suggest what is truly significant about Dow 10,000. It is not merely that this is the latest, greatest milestone in this astonishing bull market. It is that, unlike 1987 when the Dow Jones average hit 2,000, or even 1995, when it breached the 5,000 barrier, the stock market in 1999 has become a different kind of place, populated by a different kind of investor. At the heart of this change is the Internet. Without question, the new medium has "empowered" investors -- offering them tools that have put them on a more equal footing with the smart money boys on Wall Street. The proliferation of cheap on-line trading has made it easy for investors to make their own instantaneous buy-and-sell decisions, instead of having to rely on brokers. And on, and on. But along with this empowerment has come an extraordinary bullishness that borders on arrogance. In the view of many Internet investors, stocks move up because, well -- who cares why they move up? That's what they've always done. That's the natural order of things. It doesn't matter that many of their favorite stocks -- Internet stocks especially -- don't have earnings or well-tested business models. That old-fashioned stuff is for fuddy-duddies, people who are out of touch with this wondrous new stock market. As it happens, I'm one of those fuddy-duddies. So is my friend Herb Greenberg, who last year left his job as a stock columnist at The San Francisco Chronicle to join TheStreet.com, a Web site that reports on the stock market (and of which The newyork Times Company is the third-largest shareholder). Herb's stock in trade are stories that look closely at things like phony earnings and accounting gimmickry -- and at the kind of fundamentals that used to matter. But in bringing his kind of skeptical reporting to the Web, he's gotten nothing but grief. "I feel like I'm whistling in the wind," he told me recently. That's how I feel, too. But I also feel unnerved by what's happened in the market in the past few years. To me, when a character like Tokyo Joe arrives on the scene, it's a sure signal that the end of the bull market is near. But I'm not sure I have the nerve to say that out loud anymore. I've been burned too many times these past few years. It's tough to believe in fundamentals when the market no longer seems to care. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place -- Trading onE*Trade's Success;
Chief Has Aggressive Plans to Expand Internet Broker - Correction Appended
body:
If a computer glitch kept thousands of customers unsatisfied, wouldn't any company be embarrassed? Not E*Trade, the brash Internet stock brokerage company. Indeed, it ended its shareholder meeting last week with an elaborate video montage of the news coverage of its three days of trading halts in February. While Christos M. Cotsakos, the company's chief executive, acknowledged that E*Trade had to prevent such problems from recurring, he used the video mainly as a rousing affirmation of E*Trade's success. "Other companies have had systems issues, but we were the only company to get worldwide coverage in virtually every media," Mr. Cotsakos said in an interview last week. "The degree to which we have been recognized as a leader in this space is unequaled. And that is something we should be very proud of." That is typical bravado from Mr. Cotsakos, who likes to say he is not simply running a company but rather leading a "revolution that is turning into a movement" as on-line trading grows to account for one in every seven stock trades in the country. Now, Mr. Cotsakos wants his revolutionaries to charge from the stock exchange to the shopping mall and the television station. E*Trade, he said, is becoming a "digital financial media company" that will offer financial transactions, information, advertising and electronic shopping over the Internet, cable television and even wireless hand-held devices. In effect, he wants to marry the media aspirations of Internet portals like Yahoo with the dream of building a financial supermarket. Oh, yes, Mr. Cotsakos also wants E*Trade to foment this movement in more than 30 countries. Yet by fighting on so many fronts, Mr. Cotsakos risks giving up the ground that E*Trade has already won in the brokerage business, where competition from Charles Schwab, Fidelity and Merrill Lynch is growing more intense. He has even sacrificed E*Trade's position as one of the few profitable Internet companies in order to spend as much as $150 million on an extravagant marketing blitz meant to attract a million new customers the next year. "Christos has the most expansive vision of what an on-line trading company can become," said Bill Burnham, an analyst with Credit Suisse First Boston. "But that kind of aggressive attitude, being willing to try stuff that other people don't think is completely baked, is a double-edged sword. They could be throwing money down a black hole." Investors certainly found the timing of the marketing plan half-baked.  It was announced last summer just as a market slump raised fears that volume at stockbrokers would dry up. E*Trade's shares fell to $6 in October, adjusted for a recent 2-for-1 split, from $17.25 in August. Mr. Cotsakos readily acknowledges he has had some selling to do, but that is what he is good at. "If you are making money, how do you convince shareholders that by losing money you will increase value in the long run?" Mr. Cotsakos asked in an earlier interview. "With absolute, sheer fundamentalist dedication, I said the only way we would be successful was to take big bold risks and to move very quickly." Now the company's stock has bounced back, buoyed by the surging market and some early positive return on the marketing campaign. The shares closed yesterday at $54.125, giving E*Trade a market value of $6.2 billion -- now larger than that of Paine Webber, a more conventional brokerage firm. Perhaps more important, investors have come to realize that Mr. Cotsakos's plan to lose lots of money to finance rapid growth resembles the strategy of highly valued Internet companies like Amazon.com. "Christos has turned E*Trade from a brokerage play to an Internet play," noted Julio Gomez, who runs a consulting firm focused on electronic trading. Not all investors are convinced. "Christos rubs institutional investors one of two ways," Mr. Burnham, the First Boston analyst, said. "Some are caught up in the vision. Others are turned off and say he's a self-promoter who doesn't know anything about the blocking and tackling of the brokerage business." Still, even some competitors acknowledge that so far E*Trade has been able to deliver on most of its grandiose promises. "They have thrown the long pass and then to my surprise, they have run forward to catch it every time," said the head of a major on-line brokerage operation who spoke on the condition of anonymity. When Mr. Cotsakos, who is 50, joined E*Trade just before its initial public offering in 1996, he knew nothing of Wall Street. But he brought a passionate leadership style, built on his experience as an Army squad leader in Vietnam and honed by his failure to make it as an actor. After his acting career stumbled, he signed on as a $3-an-hour package handler at Federal Express. He worked his way up rapidly and was assigned to run the company's operations in Continental Europe in 1988. In 1992, he was hired to run the European operations of A. C. Nielsen, the big market research company. He rose to become president but left the company just before its owner, Dun & Bradstreet, took it public. "Nielsen was not successful when Cotsakos was there," said James D. Dougherty, an analyst with Paine Webber who has long followed the company. "He banked all the company's future on whiz-bang silver-bullet software that just never worked." (Mr. Cotsakos said Dun & Bradstreet would not invest the money needed to realize his plans.) At E*Trade Group, based in Palo Alto, Calif., Mr. Cotsakso draws from both his military and theatrical experience to practice what one employee calls "management by revival meeting." He eschews formal meetings for what he calls "swarms," more informal sessions in which employees buzz briefly about dealing with a problem. And he will surprise his executives with sudden changes in strategy, such as replacing E*Trade's somber gold-and-black logo last year with a hip and decidedly unfinancial green and purple model. "He will take your breath away," said Lisa Nash, a vice president for marketing. "That's part of his management style." Mr. Cotsakos hired a management team drawn largely from outside financial services, and it has brought some unconventional ideas. Debra J. Chrapaty, who was recruited from the National Basketball Association, has built a computer system based on a network of dozens of small work station computers -- unusual in finance services, which typically relies on mainframes to keep customer data secure. The company's marketing is in the hands of Jerry Gramaglia, who was recruited from Sprint. Last week, he hired Omnicom Group's Goodby, Silverstein & Partners, the advertising agency that produced the "Got milk?" campaign, to create a successor to E*Trade's long-running "Someday we'll all invest this way" campaign. That campaign began when E*Trade's standard $20 commission level, now as low $14.95 for some stocks, differentiated it from its more expensive competitors. But now competitors like Fidelity and Schwab have lowered their prices. And deep discounters have emerged, like Datek and Ameritrade, with commissions under $10. Full-service firms like Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette and Merrill Lynch, meanwhile, are offering research and advice along with on-line trading. And Schwab, which has become the leading on-line broker despite $30 commissions, is devoting considerable effort to offering advice and hand-holding to lure customers from firms like Merrill. E*Trade does not fear being caught in the middle as the leader in neither price nor service. "Schwab's position is that most people who come on line are clueless and need a broker as a security blanket," Mr. Gramaglia said. "That is not whom we target. We believe that most customers are smart enough and capable enough to control their own investments once we give them the same tools that brokers have." An expanded tool kit is the centerpiece of the company's expensive new strategy: Destination E*Trade. It has refashioned its Internet site to offer casual visitors as well as customers all sorts of up-to-the-minute information, research, bulletin boards and other investing tools, at a cost to E*Trade of several dollars a month for each "member." It is modeled on the popular finance channels of Yahoo and the other portals, where E*Trade was advertising at ever increasing prices. "We were being held hostage to someone else's distribution channel," Mr. Cotsakos said. "It was getting very costly if you didn't own your own distribution." The results from E*Trade's refurbished Web site have so far been mixed. In the last three months of 1998, E*Trade spent $41 million in marketing, including the cost of the site, TV commercials and inducements like $50 rebates for people who opened accounts. That has brought in 500,000 members and 97,000 new brokerage accounts (excluding the low-margin corporate options business), according to Mr. Burnham, the First Boston analyst. That works out to a cost of $404 to lure each new core brokerage account. Since Mr. Burnham estimates that the average account will produce only $526 in profits over the life of the customer, E*Trade may have little to show for its efforts. E*Trade, however, says it can make two or three times that by finding other ways to profit from an affluent customer base. It will expand its own site with banking, mutual funds and other services. And it will sell advertising and generate commissions from referring customers to other on-line merchants. So far, the move into advertising has been disappointing, Mr. Cotsakos acknowledges, bringing in less than $200,000 in the most recent quarter. But he argues that ad revenue will grow quickly, now that the company has expanded its sales force. Mr. Cotsakos also wants to offer a greater range of products to corporations and institutions. The company has invested in E-Offering, an investment bank backed by Sanford Robertson, to compete with Wall Street investment bankers in initial public offerings. And it plans to attract big institutional investors with a service combining electronic stock trading with the sort of data provided by Reuters and Bloomberg. E*Trade has also franchised its name and its systems for use by brokerage firms in 33 countries. Currently, its affiliates have opened in Canada and Australia. The company expects Britain, Japan and a few others to follow this year. It took six months and a revived but still wobbly market in Internet stocks for E*Trade to regain the confidence of investors. But Mr. Cotsakos promises even more changes. "We will morph again in a year," he said. It will start a new "asterisk channel" after E*Trade's logo that will be a combination of CNBC and a sort of financial home shopping network. "To me, the game from here is about interactive multimedia," he said. "It's not the Internet. It's how you take the convergence of video, voice and data on wireless phones, computers and television to give people what they want." For E*Trade, however, to be any more than an asterisk in the history of finance, investors and analysts say it will also have to pay attention to the basics, making sure that last month's computer problems do not happen regularly again. "I'm impressed by the breadth of stuff they are talking about doing," Mr. Burnham said, "but I hope that someone remembers to complete the trades." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  A chart in Business Day on Tuesday, summarizing the approaches of Internet stock trading companies, showed an erroneous screen to illustrate E*Trade. The screen belonged to a different company, known as e-trade. That section of the chart, corrected, appears today on page C2. A chart in Business Day on Tuesday, summarizing the approaches used by Internet stock trading companies to attract customers, referred incorrectly to Waterhouse Securities Inc. It is a large nationwide discount brokerage firm, not a regional brokerage firm.

title: Vulcan Ventures Is Buying A Major Stake in Go2net
body: Vulcan Ventures Inc., the investment company controlled by Paul Allen, the co-founder of the Microsoft Corporation, agreed to buy a major stake in Go2net Inc. for as much as $750 million to link his cable television holdings with a growing Internet search directory. Vulcan, the seventh-largest unitedstates cable company owner, purchased $165 million of Go2Net's convertible preferred stock today and plans to buy $135 million more after receiving Go2net shareholder approval. That represents about a 26 percent stake in Go2net, which is based in Seattle. Go2net shares rose $26.375, to $113.375. Vulcan also agreed to buy 1.4 million shares of common stock from Go2net executives and directors at $90 a share, and will begin a tender offer to buy as much as 3.6 million more Go2net common shares from public shareholders at the same price. That amounts to a 3 percent premium over Friday's close of $87. If Vulcan buys all the common and preferred shares that it is seeking, it would have a 54 percent stake in Go2net. Vulcan plans to make the Internet search directory, or "portal," a source of interactive content for its cable companies such as Charter Communications and the Marcus Cable Company, which have the capability to offer high-speed access to the Internet. Go2net operates a network of Web sites that range from Internet games to the investment site Silicon Investor, and gets about 1.5 million unique users a day. The company has grown steadily by making about one acquisition a quarter. Strategically, the transaction is similar to the At Home Corporation's January acquisition of the Internet search service Excite Inc., which combined a company that provides high-speed Internet access over cable lines with a Web content provider. Go2net, though, is far smaller than Excite. Vulcan, based in Bellevue, Wash., is betting consumers will begin to demand interactive content from their TV sets, rather than just their personal computers. "We think people will want to do more with their remote controls than just change channels," Bill Savoy, the president of Vulcan, said. The all-cash transaction is a departure from many of the recent Internet mergers and alliances. Most have been stock deals, similar to At Home's $6.7 billion agreement to buy Excite. "We're putting real money into the company," Mr. Savoy said. "We think it will increase the value, and we want to be a meaningful owner." For Go2net, the transaction represents an infusion of cash that it said it would use to continue to try to keep pace with its larger competitors on the World Wide Web, like Yahoo Inc. and Excite. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
DIGITAL COMMERCE;
The uproar over the USA Networks-Lycos deal may start a rethinking of the portal concept.
body: WHETHER or not shareholders ultimately bless or curse the proposed merger of Lycos with Barry Diller's television shopping company, USA Networks, the deal may well have catalyzed a long-overdue rethinking of the business of Internet portals, those launching pads from which millions of Web surfers rocket onto the Internet each day. Until the announcement of the USA-Lycos deal sent the stock of both companies plummeting, Internet portals -- most of which used to be known by the nerdier term "search engines" -- were the darlings of Internet-happy Wall Street, stratospheric in their valuations. But even with most portal stocks holding their value, the leaders of some of these companies now say their business needs redefinition. The original idea was that the sheer numbers of visitors to portals would draw advertisers, who needed to drive traffic to their sites so that they, in turn, could sell advertising based on traffic. As demand for ad space outstripped the available number of Web pages at their sites, portal companies started bulking up with news and contests, stock quotes and product promotions, shopping, custom home pages and free email -- just about anything they could think of that would both create advertising space and keep the largest number of users coming back. But now many portal executives are afraid the portal may become the "network television" of the Internet by appealing to the lowest common denominator. As a result, they are beginning to question the value and the proper roles of content and services as audience magnets. Some are also beginning to agree with early critics who predicted that advertising would not be a viable long-term business strategy for the Internet. They are even stepping up early to narrow the grandiose expectations that electronic commerce -- like portals, part of a long lineage of solutions in search of a problem -- will finally kick the Internet into the high-gear global money machine we keep waiting for. Search engines were of inestimable value in the early days of the Web because they were the only way to find anything on the Internet. Everybody used them; virtually all were free and heavily trafficked. The portal concept was born, says Chan Suh, the chief executive of Agency.com, when "America Online did this brilliant thing -- they got Internet access and content, but all the links led to things inside AOL." Opening a door into America Online, instead of onto the global network, created a huge, measurable audience for advertisers in search of eyeballs and made America Online the most valuable commercial real estate in cyberspace. But Mr. Suh now asserts that portals have already seen their best days. Like Mr. Suh, at least one portal executive believes that the business is beginning to veer perilously close to the ways of a dying medium. "Our biggest fear is becoming like TV networks, a commodity," George Bell, the chief executive of Excite Inc., said at a recent industry conference. "How do we avoid being seen as a commodity distributor? How do we become more than a little bit of everything?" He added, "We're taking generic content and reorganizing it" under Excite's brand, but that idea is certainly not proprietary. Nor is it proving particularly valuable to users, said Linda McCutcheon, president of Time Inc. New Media. "We're describing assets, not consumer benefits," Ms. McCutcheon said of most portals' attitudes about content. "It's like getting in your car and saying, 'Honey, it's a beautiful day. Let's drive through the Lincoln Tunnel.' " If questioning the value of content were not heretical enough, some portal purveyors are also sure that advertising itself, as it is practiced today, is on its way out as a significant revenue stream. "Advertising won't carry the freight, because there's no reason it should," Mr. Bell said. "The Web does something different. It interacts, and interactivity begets data. We should focus on direct marketing, driven by personalization and away from the retail chain." This may prove trickier for portals like Excite, which does not own anything it can sell, than it has been for sites like Time Inc.'s Pathfinder and Viacom's MTV Online. Through the eyes of these companies, which sell their own products through their portals, it is even clearer that traditional Web advertising may have seen its day. "If the audience is there, we will be able to monetize them," said Matt Farber, president of MTV Online, using one of today's favored buzzwords for turning a customer relationship into cash. "Advertising becomes E-commerce." The bottom line, Mr. Suh said, is that "portals are dead." Search engines and generic advertising and content, he said, are nearly irrelevant. "The idea that a lot of people had in the beginning of the Web revolution is finally starting to gel a little bit," he said. "People are inventing their own content -- on discussion boards, stock chat areas, family picture and discussion sites. They've invented content in ways they couldn't have before, and that is going to be the most important thing for portals." Which means the Web is in fact not a mass medium, but a medium for the masses, who are already well along in the process of making it their own. Although Mr. Bell, Mr. Diller and many others are already devising new marketing stratagems to take advantage of this shift, it will be fascinating to see who is willing to participate. Will people inventing their own content welcome personalized marketing? Or will most folks simply say, "Monetize this"? http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title: Independent Booksellers Plan to Open On-Line Store
body: Facing intensifying competition, the nation's trade association for independent booksellers is creating its own national on-line store, Book Sense, to stave off fierce competition from Amazon.com and Barnesandnoble.com. The on-line venture, which is scheduled to open for business this summer, is the most ambitious element in a series of countermeasures to promote independent bookstores by the American Booksellers Association, the dominant trade group for a beleaguered fraternity that has seen its share of the popular consumer book market shrink to about 17 percent today from 32 percent in 1991. Those pressures have continued to intensify with competition from superstore chains and on-line bookstores, prompting some store owners to abandon the business with bitter complaints that they are under siege. The electronic bookstore and a planned national marketing campaign are the first collective efforts of an ordinarily disparate group of independents. The goal is to compete against some of the forces that have reduced the association's membership to about 3,300 from 5,200 in 1992. "We're not trying to knock off the Goliaths -- I don't want to look naive," said Hut Landon, a bookstore owner in Mill Valley, Calif., and the executive director of the Northern California Independent Booksellers Association, which developed the pilot concept last year. "All we're trying to do is retain our market share. We recognize that we've got to do this in this day and age. We can't just be quaint little booksellers in our community asking how the kids are." The association has already organized a series of 12 customer focus groups along with the development of the electronic bookstore. In its initial stages, the store will feature all the standard functions of popular on-line sites, including a search engine, a stock of 1.5 million titles, credit card fulfillment, gift wrapping, distribution services and a best-seller list. But it will also allow individual stores to tailor Web pages to reflect their individuality with store reviews and features. "What we're really trying to do is find the different ways that we can do what our competitors are doing," said Michael F. Hoynes, the association's newly hired marketing officer. He said initial interest in the program was enthusiastic because booksellers have been asking for a collective approach. The booksellers' association, based in Tarrytown, N.Y., will begin its first national marketing campaign in May for the Book Sense brand, which in some ways is inspired by the example of the independent hardware stores that promote themselves under the True Value label. So far, the association plans to spend about $2 million to develop the electronic bookstore and about $2 million more on the marketing campaign -- money that comes in part from its half-share of $25 million that the association won from Penguin Group U.S.A in a dispute over favorable discounts that were given to large retail bookstore chains. In Northern California, where there is a strong and active group of independent booksellers, the regional association has also spent about $100,000 to promote a common identity under the name Book Sense. The brand and a slogan, "Independent Bookstores for Independent Minds," are already appearing in newspaper advertisements and on decals, posters and plastic shopping bags in the Bay Area, where more than 200 bookstores have signed up to participate in the pilot program. But the collective approach envisioned by the national association is broader in scope, conceivably allowing customers to order books on line with the freedom to pick them up or return them at any participating Book Sense store. The association is already in discussions with a national wholesaler, Baker & Taylor, to provide distribution services, a critical element for an on-line service that caters to customers with swift delivery. It is also considering expanding the electronic title base to include out-of-print books. At this point, the pricing system is still being determined, although individual bookstore owners will have great flexibility to offer discounts on their templates, said Len Vlahos, the association's spokesman. Within the next few months, the association will start signing up members to participate in the electronic project, which would cost bookstore owners monthly development fees expected to range from $175 to $450. Several technology analysts said that the move was a vital step to protect the booksellers' eroding turf, and noted that the independents may be able to capitalize on unique strengths in ways that Amazon.com and Barnes & Noble cannot. David Brodwin, an associate partner with Andersen Consulting who follows electronic commerce, said the Book Sense venture would draw on the loyalty of customers who prefer local bookstores to corporations. "Independents will feature locally relevant information -- travel, restaurant guides, local history -- with a degree of sophistication and connoisseurship that the nationwide players may have trouble matching," Mr. Brodwin said. He cautioned, though, that associations often move slowly. That could present problems for success in electronic commerce, which requires decisiveness and speed. Kate Delhagen, the director of on-line retail strategies for Forrester Research Inc., a technology research company, said that independent booksellers had no choice but to act because customers' shopping habits are changing. Forrester projects that almost $1.2 billion in book purchases will be made on line this year, she said. Spending will rise in 2003 to almost $3 billion, or about 18 percent of the book market, she added. "The book lover in me is thrilled to hear about this for the independents," Ms. Delhagen said. "Banding together and forming a network is the only way. This is a huge opportunity for them to survive, because long term, they're getting eviscerated. There is an option now rather than shuttering their stores. This development presents them with an opportunity to say, 'I'm sticking around, and we're not letting Amazon and Barnes & Noble run us out of town.' "  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Swindles Start to Flourish on Worries Over Year 2000 Problems
body: While many consumers have worried that Year 2000 computer problems will cripple the banking system, bankers and law enforcement officials have been warning that the bigger financial risks may come from scam artists and thieves playing on such fears. Last week, news reports and rumors began emerging of the kind of problems the authorities had in mind. Frost National Bank in San Antonio sent a warning to other banks after it learned of an incident that sounded like the opening gambit of a fraud scheme. A spokesman for Frost said a man had phoned the bank to report receiving a call in which he was told it would be necessary to move his money to a special "bond" account as part of the bank's work to prepare computers for the Year 2000. He was then asked for personal information, including account numbers, which he declined to give. The Canadian Bankers Association said it had received reports of similar episodes from several provinces in the last week. And the Bank Administration Institute, an industry research group in Chicago, said that a Nebraska bank it declined to identify reported that an employee at the bank's advertising agency got a call almost identical to the one received by Frost National's customer. Similar reports were posted on the Internet, and one such recounting was picked up and widely circulated last week in corporate and police email networks. According to that Internet tale, the unidentified consumer used caller identification to trace the call to the Detroit area. "My mother would believe this, so beware," urged Judy N. Gilleland, a Frito-Lay Year 2000 expert, in an email in which she passed on the Internet posting to all of the snack food giant's information technology employees. So far, none of the reports tell of a consumer falling for the scam. The reports say the unidentified callers have hung up when asked which bank they are calling from or for other verification of their identity. Banking officials say that the general rule -- never give out personal or account information over the phone to a stranger who calls you -- holds for Year 2000-related calls. Other Year 2000 financial scams are also emerging. Barry Elliott, a detective in charge of the Phonebusters hot line of the Ontario Provincial Police, which monitors telemarketing scams, said the hot line had been getting reports from Canadians saying they had received suspicious calls from people identifying themselves as agents of Visa International, the credit card group. According to these accounts, the supposed Visa agent says that the card organization needs to confirm credit card numbers as part of its Year 2000 work. Mr. Elliott said that telemarketers are also apparently trying to obtain credit card account numbers by calling with offers of insurance against false billing or loss of credit card account information as a result of the Year 2000 transition. Visa itself has not received reports of such attempts to gain access to credit card numbers, according to Ryan Nicollaset, a Visa spokesman.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Investing Success Breeds Unlikely Troubles
body: Is CMGI an Internet company or a mutual fund? On its face, the question seems almost absurd. The company owns roughly a dozen Internet start-ups, which offer specialized marketing services to companies that want to do business over the Internet. CMGI had revenue of $90 million in its last fiscal year, ended July 31, and $76 million in the first six months of the current year. But in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last month, CMGI notified investors that because of its highly successful investments in Lycos, Geocities and other Internet-related companies, it meets the characteristics of a mutual fund under the Federal securities laws. The company, which steadfastly states that it does not want to be a mutual fund, has until October to rectify the situation. If it succeeds, CMGI's shareholders will be no worse for the experience, although investors in the companies that CMGI owns could feel a downdraft from CMGI's selling of those securities. And if the company cannot revamp in time, its shareholders could face huge tax burdens. According to the Federal securities laws, a company that owns investment securities with a value exceeding 40 percent of its total assets, excluding cash and government securities, is an "investment company," subject to the Investment Company Act of 1940, which governs mutual funds, closed-end funds and other investment pools. By investing in Internet start-ups through a series of venture capital pools, CMGI's investment assets have grown far more quickly than its underlying direct marketing business. At the end of January, CMGI owned $1.6 billion worth of stock in publicly traded companies. Roughly 60 percent, or $957 million, of that is in companies in which CMGI owns less than 20 percent of the shares. The remainder is in "affiliates," with stakes of more than 20 percent but less than half the total shares. All told, those investments account for a huge portion of CMGI's assets. Just how much, the company will not say; it is scheduled to release those details later this month. But it is likely that it amounts to more than half of CMGI's total assets. At the end of the company's first fiscal quarter, which ended Dec. 31, noninvestment assets were worth about $120 million. The CMGI board instructed the company's management to make sure it was not considered a mutual fund. By Oct. 31 of this year, when the one-year grace period allowed under Federal securities laws will expire, the company's management must take one of two actions: First, CMGI could buy the rest of one of the companies like Lycos in which it already owns substantial stakes. That would change the status of those holdings from investments to continuing business operations. Alternatively, CMGI could sell enough of its investments so that they account for less than 40 percent of assets. But Andrew J. Hajducky 3d, CMGI's chief financial officer, said that was "a last resort" that would generate big tax liabilities for CMGI, since most of the investments were made at far lower prices. Selling is not a particularly attractive option. Besides the tax implications, the company has been banking on the Internet investments to provide its direct marketing business with information about people surfing the Web. By selling some of those investments, "anticipated synergies between our core businesses and disposed assets may never arise," the company said in a recent S.E.C. filing. Unlike most young Internet companies, CMGI does not have losses on its books to offset the capital gains it is reaping from its investments. In the six months ended Jan 31, the company earned net profits of $52.6 million, or $1.04 a share; the company's gains on its investments in the period totaled $134 million, or roughly double its revenues from the marketing businesses it operates. CMGI could also avoid having to buy or sell more businesses by reorganizing as an investment company. (Technically, CMGI would be a closed-end fund rather than a mutual fund, because it has a limited number of shares that trade on an exchange.) But that, a highly unlikely move, would create some unpleasant results. As a fund, CMGI would be forced to distribute to shareholders all of the capital gains from each year's sale of investments. Last year, the company reported $101 million in such gains, and in the first six months of this fiscal year, another $95 million. Together, those would have resulted in taxable capital gains of nearly $4 a share for stockholders. http://www.nytimes.com

title: The Great Campus Goof-Off Machine
body: Conventional wisdom says that computers are a necessary tool for higher education. Many colleges and universities these days require students to have personal computers, and some factor the cost of one into tuition. A number of colleges have put high-speed Internet connections in every dorm room. But there are good reasons to question the wisdom of this preoccupation with computers and the Internet. Take a walk through the residence halls of any college in the country and you'll find students seated at their desks, eyes transfixed on their computer monitors. What are they doing with their top-of-the-line PC's and high-speed T-1 Internet connections? They are playing Tomb Raider instead of going to chemistry class, tweaking the configurations of their machines instead of writing the paper due tomorrow, collecting mostly useless information from the World Wide Web instead of doing a math problem set -- a host of other activity that has little or nothing to do with traditional academic work. I have friends who have spent whole weekends doing nothing but playing Quake or Warcraft or other interactive computer games. One friend sometimes spends entire evenings -- six to eight hours -- scouring the Web for images and modifying them just to have a new background on his computer desktop. And many others I know have amassed overwhelming collections of music on their computers. It's the searching and finding that they seem to enjoy: some of them have more music files on their computers than they could play in months. Several people who live in my hall routinely stay awake all night chatting with dormmates on line. Why walk 10 feet down the hall to have a conversation when you can chat on the computer -- even if it takes three times as long? You might expect that personal computers in dorm rooms would be used for nonacademic purposes, but the problem is not confined to residence halls. The other day I walked into the library's reference department, and five or six students were grouped around a computer -- not conducting research, but playing Tetris. Every time I walk past the library's so-called research computers, it seems that at least half are being used to play games, chat or surf the Internet aimlessly. Colleges and universities should be wary of placing such an emphasis on the use of computers and the Internet. The Web may be useful for finding simple facts, but serious research still means a trip to the library. For most students, having a computer in the dorm is more of a distraction than a learning tool. Other than computer science or mathematics majors, few students need more than a word processing program and access to email in their rooms. It is true, of course, that students have always procrastinated and wasted time. But when students spend four, five, even ten hours a day on computers and the Internet, a more troubling picture emerges -- a picture all the more disturbing because colleges themselves have helped create the problem. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Matthew Martin)

title:
POSTINGS: The City's Rules Are on the Web;
Zoning Code In Cyberspace
body: What's to stop a sign from being erected on a rooftop in a commercial district? Section 32-657 of the Zoning Resolution. What's to say that pedestrian circulation areas along the waterfront are to be open to the public from dawn to dusk? Section 62-624. The Zoning Resolution is a useful Rosetta stone to newyork City's land-use regulations. But until this year, it was also a heavy lift: $450 for a two-year subscription, plus $30 for shipping. Now, the City Planning Department has made the zoning text and accompanying zoning maps available without charge to anyone with access to the Internet, at www.ci.nyc.ny.us/html/dcp/html/zonetext.html. (The most recent version of Adobe Acrobat Reader is required, but is available at the Web site free.) "The kinds of questions we get are: 'What's the zoning on my block? What does R7 mean?' " said Joseph B. Rose, director of the agency. "To be able to log on and get the answers will make life easier." Amendments to the text will be on line within a month of approval by the City Council. So why pay $480 any more? For one thing, the paper version is the official text. For another, consulting the resolution means looking up many cross references, something that is still easier to do with bound volumes. "Being on the Web won't make it less complicated, it will make it more available," Mr. Rose said. "Now, all we have to do is make it intelligible." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
The Way We Live Now: 3-14-99 -- The Ethicist;
Pity for the Plagiarist
body: 'A college student called last week to say his "friend" had visited my Web page, lifted something I wrote and turned it in as her own work. Suspicious, her professor plans to search the Web; if he finds the paper was plagiarized, he'll recommend expulsion. The student implored me to take that paper off my site, lest her "friend's" academic career, and possibly her life, be ruined. What do I do?' Properly assigning credit is delicate business. If I sign Rembrandt's name to my work, it's forgery; if I sign my name to Rembrandt's work, it's plagiarism. There's just no pleasing some people. But what's astonishing here is not the expropriation; it's the request that you cover it up. Presumably, if this woman had stolen your stereo, she'd ask you for a lift to her fence. When the penalty is severe enough, however, a wrongdoer's appeals for mercy are not entirely ludicrous. It would be hard not to relent, say, if the Taliban planned to topple a wall onto her. (Though if she survived, I believe she'd automatically ace the semester.) Expulsion from college is not such a case. Even if she receives the worst possible punishment -- by no means a certainty -- it's unlikely to wreck her life. A young woman with her low level of moral inhibition and high level of chutzpah should flourish in modern America. She might be lucky enough to one day find herself in a nice Federal minimum-security prison, where she can make professional connections that will set her up forever. Or perhaps she'll get a job at Cliffs Notes, giving a new generation of kids a legitimate way to crib their way through college. Even if your heart goes out to the young plagiarist, you're not at liberty to drop the charges, since you're not the victim of this crime. You can, however, call the professor and appeal for leniency. But destroying evidence is definitely the wrong way to go. If you don't believe me, check out a 1976 movie called "All the President's Men." I won't spoil it for you by giving away the ending. "My fun-loving friend Frank is celebrating his birthday next week with a tour of New Jersey's topless (and bottomless) bars. It sounds like a lot of fun (more for anthropological than prurient reasons -- no, seriously), and I'm determined to go, but what do I tell my girlfriend? How do I convince her that I'm doing it for a friend?" Convince her? You haven't even convinced me. In any case, does doing it for a friend alter the essential act? Is the phrase "bottomless bar in New Jersey" already so far beyond the pale that there's little more to say? And might there not be a more evocative way to describe Frank than "fun-loving?" Were your objections merely esthetic, you should of course accommodate your jaunty pal. But if instead you or your girlfriend are discomforted by the moral implications of the festivities, then taking along some buddies is a feeble justification. Nor am I persuaded that there's a meaningful distinction between "anthropological" and "condescending." So there's no point in convincing your girlfriend that you're going for Frank's sake. If you're comfortable with the plan, your task is to convince her that it's O.K. to go at all, at least once. Perhaps this will help. Invited by the Marquis de Sade to a second orgy, Voltaire declined, although he'd quite enjoyed the first. "Once is philosophy," he said. "Twice is perversion." To send Randy Cohen your own question about ethics, write to: ethicist@nytimes.com or The Ethicist, The newyork Times Magazine, 229 West 43d Street, newyork, NY 10036. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
Cheap Air Fares: Bidding on the Web
body: A newyork tour operator and airline-ticket consolidator has opened a Web site to accept bids on domestic and overseas tickets, and the owner says that no bid -- not even $1 -- is too small to start. Many of the fares have limited windows of availability; others, particularly for students, offer a round trip to anywhere in the unitedstates to be used in a wide period of time. The company, Magical Holidays at 501 Madison Avenue, set up www.skyauction .com with no minimum price for any air ticket, package tour or hotel stay. Registration to bid is free, with payment by credit card or check. The president, Michael Hering, said that Magical Holidays was begun in 1981 and, like other consolidators, has contracts with most major airlines to sell tickets below advertised prices when seats are not filling up at regular rates. The Web site, which has a student section with domestic tickets and overseas tickets for long stays, opened Feb. 17. Among the brands identified in the auctions are Virgin Atlantic, Continental, United and Alitalia. One couple won an auction of two tickets to South Africa on Virgin Atlantic for $685 each, plus tax, as against $1,299, plus tax, for a 21-day advance purchase quoted by the airline. Bids can be canceled by email to the company, support@skyauction.com. There is a hypertext line on the site. Skyauction bids can be based on how much has been bid -- bids in the ball park are posted -- and how many tickets are available. In each sale, the price necessary to get a ticket at a given moment is posted, and others that qualify are listed. Most auctions go on for a week, but some of the offers, Mr. Hering said, represent deals that airlines provide for particular dates that are selling badly. These may last only a day. Some winning bids are a loss for his company, Mr. Hering said, in that he pays the airline more for them than they fetch. http://www.nytimes.com
