title:
NEWS WATCH;
From Poetry to Newspapers, MP3 Fare for the Literary Set
body: The use of the MP3 format to download audio files from the Internet has taken on a literary twist. Selections from James Bond novels, Emily Dickinson poetry and daily selections from The newyork Times and The Wall Street Journal are among the works available for downloading in MP3 format from a company called Audible Inc. (www.audible.com). Many of the Web site's offerings are free, making this the first time that books not in the public domain are legally available for download in MP3 format. The MP3 format has generated controversy because it is not encrypted; that enables Web users to download and trade files. Music companies, in particular, have expressed concern that Web users will simply download music free rather than pay for it. In the case of Audible.com, however, the company's founder, Donald Katz, said the idea was not to promote free and illegal distribution of copyrighted content but just the opposite. Mr. Katz said the company hoped to entice people to use books on MP3 format so they would be willing to buy audio files when an encryption standard was eventually set. Mr. Katz said his company had the full backing of the book and magazine publishers to give the content away. "They really want to promote the spoken-word category," he said. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Safer Web Playgrounds Are Aimed at Kids (and Paying Parents)
body: A FEW years ago, Alan Rothenberg was a frustrated parent. He was tired of buying educational CD-ROM's at $45 a pop, only to have his children become bored and abandon them after a couple of hours. Sure, the World Wide Web had plenty of sites with children's games, but he wasn't impressed with their educational content and he was reluctant to let his young children roam on the Internet, where they might end up in a seedy corner. Like many parents, he thought, "If only there were an Internet just for them." So he made one. This month his company, Junior Net (www.juniornet.com), begins what it says will be the first safe on-line service just for preteen-agers. After purchasing Junior Net software and using it to log on, members can access only approved links, trade messages only with approved friends and post only approved postings. Several other companies, some still in embryonic stages, plan to follow with similar pay services in the coming months. They are jumping on what has become a marketing bandwagon that is aimed at signing up parents made wary by scary news reports about the Internet -- or by what they have seen with their own eyes. These services, which are becoming known as "subscription-based virtual private environments for children," say they are like roped-off portions of the Internet, where youngsters can get their feet wet with the ways of the Web without swimming into dangerous waters. "It's a safe playground that's being monitored by people you trust," said Parry Aftab, the author of "A Parents' Guide to the Internet" (SC Press, 1997). "This is where it's going." "What we did for the longest time was say, 'You can't go here and you can't go here,' instead of saying, 'These are the places you can go,' " Ms. Aftab continued. "We were taking the slipper away from the puppy and not giving them anything else to play with." One attempt by lawmakers to keep out the "bad stuff," the 1998 Child Online Protection Act, has been delayed by court challenges every step of the way, said Stephen Valerie. He is the founder of Kids On-Line America (www.kola.net), a service for students, teachers and parents that he hopes will be up and running by the end of the year. "Time and time again, the courts are not going to enforce any kind of censorship," Mr. Valerie said. "Again the private sector is the one that's going to have to come to the floor." In fact, his small company, based in San Francisco, is banking on that. In a survey released in June 1998 by Jupiter Communications in newyork, 53 percent of parents said they would be willing to pay for an on-line service for their children. Mr. Rothenberg said almost 4,000 parents had signed up to test an early version of his Junior Net. A CD-ROM provides access to the service for subscribers and allows them to download stories, activities and games to their hard drives. The content comes from sources like the publications Ranger Rick and Highlights for Children. (Mr. Rothenberg said he had looked at the magazines that littered his children's room for inspiration.) The Junior Net service has no links to other Web sites, but it does aim to be an Internet community and offers email and bulletin boards. Messages to and from people not on the parents' approval list will be automatically bounced, and messages for bulletin boards will be screened by Junior Net employees before they are posted. One selling point pushed by some subscription services is that they will provide safety not only from cesspools of pornography and lurking predators, but from a constant barrage of Internet advertisements. "There's a whole strategy to use kids to get money out of their parents' pockets," said Gerry Bishop, editor of Ranger Rick magazine. He called his publication and Junior Net "refuges from that assault" because neither accepts outside advertising. Established companies are starting to pay more attention to their younger consumers. America Online, which has always had a roped-off area of the Internet pool, has revamped its Kids Only section. Disney's Blast Online (www.disney.go.com) has memberships for children, complete with parental controls for email and chat groups. To try to jump ahead of the competition, the newest services are asserting that their security measures are even more strict. Kola says it plans to protect its community through "registration validation." Members join through schools, community organizations (like the Boy Scouts) or partner corporations that can verify that a 12-year-old girl is really a 12-year-old girl, not a 40-year-old man. Another service, Safe-Site, which is not yet available, plans to be so exclusive that a regular computer cannot get access to it. For $100 to $150, parents can buy the Electronic Learning Aids sold by Safe-Site's parent company, Oregon Scientific. These toy laptops dial up www.safe-site.net directly, where children can compare game scores and trade greeting cards. A Safe-Site modem ($50) and Internet Service Provider ($15 a month) are also required. "It's a safe harbor type of thing," said Jean Armour Polly, whose Net-Mom Web site (www.netmom.com) has links to 100 "mother approved" sites. The whole industry is making a move toward accentuating the positive, she said, not just screening out the negative. To that end, software filters, which were first developed to search for objectionable words and block access to sites containing them, now often work from a list of approved sites. But site addresses have a way of changing overnight, Ms. Polly pointed out, so any services that link to sites outside their own system leave a potential door ajar to something creepy from the Web. Mr. Valerie said, "You'll never hear me saying we are the 100 percent safe solution." His Kola service will have outside links. At the same time, even services, like Junior Net, that promise to provide their young clients with endless new material can offer only a shadow of the wonders of the Web, said Barry Fagin, a founder of Families Against Internet Censorship. "There is also a lot of really great stuff on the Net that children's on-line networks would never capture," he said. It is up to parents to decide whether these services, some of which use filters themselves, are better than such leading filtering software as Surf Watch and Cyber Patrol. Enclosed communities are good for busy parents who might not have time to scrutinize their children's computer use, Mr. Fagin said, but "there is no substitute for parental involvement, and it would be a mistake to become too complacent." For three years, Marney Morris, an interactive-software designer, has worked on creating such a closed environment for an educational service called Sprocket Works. "Then we said, you know what? That's not the spirit of the Web," Ms. Morris said. "And we got feedback from parents, too, who said, 'We don't want our kids restrained.' " Instead, anyone can visit the Web site, www.sprocketworks.com. The site has plans for email and other services, but, for now, it mostly encourages parents to order educational CD-ROM's from the company. Seema Williams, an industry analyst with Forrester Research, predicts that scholastic networks that help teachers pull the Internet into the classroom will soon make it into the home. Good educational content, she said, is what will sell parents on the idea of plunking down $10, $20 or $30 a month. "That's the real challenge for these guys right now," she said. "Are they able to offer enough of extra value that is not available free on line?" http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: CHILD'S PLAY -- Alan Rothenberg, here with his son Joel, is starting what he calls the first safe on-line service for preteen-age children. (Rick Friedman for The newyork Times)

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
A Bevy Of Bovine Tributes
body: COWS and computers go together like, well, milk and cookies. The Gateway computer company uses the familiar Holstein black-and-white pattern in its advertisements and packaging. Nullsoft's Winamp, an MP3 music player for Windows, allows the user to change the on-screen look of the program by adding different "skins," one of which is the Moo Amp, a festive cow pattern. Another feature of the Moo Amp is the Ecowlizer -- a digitized stereo equalizer display that replaces pulsating L.E.D. lights with tiny cow heads bouncing up and down. And cows also turn up in the darnedest places in the South Park Nintendo game. Perhaps cows have become so popular because of their ubiquitous and comforting presence in the American consciousness. Or maybe it has something to do with the fact that many highly regarded computer-science programs are located at universities in the middle of cow country -- the state universities of Illinois, Wisconsin and Texas, and Purdue University, to name a few. Or perhaps the subliminal influence of Ben & Jerry's ice cream is having an effect. Long before the World Wide Web and its fancy graphics went on line, there was a sense of bovine inspiration on the Internet, specifically in the form of simple ASCII art. For those who do not remember computer visuals before GIF's and JPEG's, popular image formats that are Web standards, users would create rustic graphics by carefully arranging alphanumeric text characters. Links to samples of the great works can be found on a Yahoo page that is devoted to collections of ASCII cow art (at www.yahoo.com, follow the trail from Arts to Visual Arts, Computer Generated, ASCII ART, Cows). As you might expect, cows have also stampeded the World Wide Web. Moocow.com (www.moocow.com) greets its visitors with a large winking cow picture and an opportunity to click on one of its hundreds of Random Cow Links. In addition to many pictures and a collection of book titles about cows, the site maintains its own long list of links to cows on the Web: the Super Moo Web Pages Index. Cows on the Web are far from sacred. The Cow Tipping Home Page (members.xoom.com/toch) lets Web surfers participate in that infamous rural prank of shoving over sleeping cattle -- albeit in a much safer, humane and tongue-in-cheek way. The page gives you several cows to choose from, and with one click, Bossy is upside down with a startled, indignant "Moo!" One of the Web's most popular shareware sites, Tucows.com (www.tucows.com), naturally features a couple of cows on its home page. Tucows, which is an acronym for the Ultimate Collection of Winsock Software, has expanded its collection to include Macintosh and some Java applications. A search of the Tucows site will reveal a collection of cow-related software, just in case you need the Moo Amp skin for your Winamp player or that handsome cow screen saver. And for comfortable computing wear, the Ben & Jerry's Blue Moo shirt is available at store.benjerry .com/benjerry1/bluemootshirt.html. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
Foreign Affairs;
KillingGoliath.com
body: I recently wrote a column about Lyle Bowlin, who, for about $150 a month, had managed to put together a Web site that could compete with Amazon.com for selling books. Mr. Bowlin was underselling Ama zon.com (and making a profit!) while running the whole operation out of a spare bedroom in his home in Cedar Falls, Iowa. Well, the column elicited the usual range of skeptical responses from experts, who argued that Mr. Bowlin's operation was just a fluke, or that he wasn't calculating his costs properly, or that Amazon.com would soon crush him and all other would-be little-guy competitors. Well, to all of you I say: YOU'RE WRONG. You think the Internet is overrated. It's underrated. Here's the email I got from Mr. Bowlin two days after the column ran, both in The Times and on line on www.nytimes.com: "Dear Tom, I thought I would just fill you in on the impact the column has had. We had over 142,000 hits between 11 P.M. Thursday night when the column first appeared on the Web and 2 P.M. Friday afternoon from 40 different countries, before the software that tracks hits gave up and crashed. I have personally responded to over 1,400 emails." The email messages fell into three broad categories. One group was people who were interested in the charitable-donation arrangement Mr. Bowlin offers, whereby 10 percent of the purchase price of any book can be dedicated to an I.R.S.-certified charity. Another group was small-business people around the world -- particularly craft makers -- who were interested in competing against the big boys from their spare bedrooms at home, just like Mr. Bowlin, and wanted to know how to get started. "There are a lot of people out there who have a passion for selling different things, and if they all start doing it over the Web as a hobby, it is going to have an impact on the big retailers," argues Mr. Bowlin. What intrigued me most, though, was the third group. "There is a whole group of people out there," says Mr. Bowlin, "who like the idea of the 'little guy' competing against Amazon.com. People see Amazon.com as this big impersonal thing. Whereas they like the idea of dealing with a person they know actually exists. Even though their contact with me is over the Web, and it is through email, they know when they contact me the answer is coming from a real person, with a real name. I'm a real person, not a virtual person. If someone sends me an order and forgets something or makes a mistake, I will send them a message and say, 'Didn't you mean this?' " In other words, there is still a deep hunger out there for that old-style, Main Street feeling, built on human contact. This suggests that the really successful retailers in the Internet Age will be those who can combine the efficiency of cyberspace with the intimacy of the backyard barbecue. Mr. Bowlin's experience underscores another point: If you think globalization is overrated, you're also wrong. You ain't seen nothin' yet. As Lyle Bowlin can tell you, the minute you start to do business on the Web, you now have to think globally. You have to think about your customers as global, your competitors as global, your readers as global, your suppliers as global and your partners as global. "There has never been a commercial technology like this in the history of the world, whereby from the minute you adopt it, it forces you to think and act globally," argues Robert Hormats of Goldman, Sachs. Mr. Bowlin got offers last week to go into partnership with local booksellers in both London and Singapore. Whereas before he was doing at best $2,000 a month in business, since the story about him appeared on the Web he is now doing $2,000 a day from around the globe. This is enabling him to make improvements to his site -- www.positively-you.com -- that will make it even more competitive with Amazon.com. In particular, he is now able to afford a search engine, so his customers can easily search the 500,000 titles offered by his main wholesalers. The only downside to his sudden expansion, says Mr. Bowlin, is that he can no longer compete against Amazon.com from his spare bedroom. It's not big enough anymore to serve as his headquarters. "I've had to move the whole operation into the downstairs formal dining room," he said. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Siemens Buys2 Companies To Enter Data Networking
body: Siemens A.G. of Germany became the latest European maker of traditional telephone equipment to push into the market for data communications gear when it announced yesterday that it had acquired two private unitedstates companies and invested in a third. Siemens said it would fold the two acquisitions and parts of its existing unitedstates operations into a new subsidiary called Unisphere Solutions Inc., based in Burlington, Mass. Siemens said it would initially commit $1 billion to the venture. Makers of traditional telephone systems are rushing to meet the fast-growing demand for data-networking equipment, which is being fueled largely by the Internet. Last week, Alcatel of France, one of Siemens's traditional European rivals, said it had agreed to buy two unitedstates data communications companies, the Xylan Corporation and Assured Access Technology Inc., for more than $2 billion. Senior data-networking executives said yesterday that Ericsson of Sweden could be the next to attempt a big data-networking splash, potentially within a week. Ericsson declined to comment. As expected, Siemens said it had acquired Castle Networks Inc., a private data-networking company based in Westford, Mass., and Argon Networks Inc., a private data-networking company based in Littleton, Mass., and that it had made an equity investment in Accelerated Networks Inc., a private company based in Moorpark, Calif. Siemens did not disclose the terms of the deals. When asked about the terms at a news conference in newyork yesterday, Anthony T. Maher, a director of Siemens's information and communication networks group, said, "the best source is The newyork Times," referring to an article published last week. Last week's article cited executives close to Siemens's planning as saying that the company had agreed to pay about $300 million for Castle, about $240 million for Argon and had agreed to invest $30 million in Accelerated. The executives also said in the article that Siemens was in preliminary discussions with the 3Com Corporation about paying $1.2 billion for the 3Com unit that sells advanced networking equipment to telephone companies. Mr. Maher said at the news conference that that contention "wasn't entirely accurate." 3Com declined to comment. In forming Unisphere, Siemens is trying to combine its strengths as one of Europe's largest manufacturers with the agility of a small independent company. To run the unit, Siemens hired Martin C. Clague, formerly general manager for global network computing solutions at I.B.M. Responding to potential criticism that as a 33-year I.B.M. veteran he may not be well suited to running a small, nimble operation, Mr. Clague said, "There is nothing like experience in managing a matrix and in managing an organization." Referring to the evolution of data communications, he added: "I've been in this Internet space for three years and it was network computers before that and client-server before that. So I know this space." Mr. Clague and Mr. Maher said Unisphere would consider additional acquisitions. Jeff Matros, a former senior Siemens executive, said that even if Siemens's new strategy did not pan out, at least someone would benefit. "I think it was very positive," said Mr. Matros, who until June was vice president for marketing and business development for Siemens's data communications group and who is now a general partner at Walden International Investment Group, a venture capital firm, "certainly for the entrepreneurs in Massachusetts, having another large traditional telecom company with lots of cash to burn on the prowl in the Boston area."  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Journalist Sentenced to 18 Months in Internet Pornography Case
body: A veteran journalist who said he had been researching an article on child molesters was sentenced today to 18 months in prison for distributing child pornography over the Internet. The journalist, Larry Matthews, an editor for National Public Radio and a former reporter for Washington radio stations, pleaded guilty last year to Federal charges of transmitting and receiving child pornography over the Internet after a judge refused to let him defend himself by saying he was acting as a journalist. In sentencing Mr. Matthews today, the judge, Alexander Williams Jr. of the Federal District Court in Greenbelt, Md., said: "I believe Mr. Matthews crossed the line. I also believe that it was immoral." Mr. Matthews's indictment in 1997 made him the first journalist to be prosecuted for receiving and transmitting child pornography over the Internet under Federal child pornography laws, according to the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, a nonprofit organization that provides legal advice to journalists. The laws were passed just months before he was indicted. His case also became one of the first to test the limits of the First Amendment on the Internet for journalists. The Reporters Committee, the American Civil Liberties Union, the Radio and Television News Directors Association and other groups filed friend-of-the-court briefs in his support, urging Judge Williams to allow Mr. Matthews to use a First Amendment defense. In ruling on the defense issue, Judge Williams wrote, "The law is clear that a press pass is not a license to break the law." Beth Farber, a public defender in Baltimore who is representing Mr. Matthews, said she planned to file an appeal by Tuesday, on the ground that Mr. Matthews should have been allowed to offer the defense. Ms. Farber described Mr. Matthews as "very disappointed" over the sentencing but insisted that her client had "not wavered one iota from the position that he did not do this for prurient reasons." She said searches of Mr. Matthews's home after he was charged and a recent psychological examination produced no evidence that he was a pedophile or that he suffered from any sexual problems. Mr. Matthews, 55, who lives in Howard County, Md., was originally charged with 11 counts of receiving and 4 counts of transmitting "visual depictions of minors" engaged in "sexually explicit conduct." The Internet trade occurred in 1996. After Federal agents searched his home computer and discovered images of children in sex acts, Mr. Matthews claimed that he was researching an article on child pornography, a subject he had investigated years before, leading to a three-part series on WTOP-AM, a radio station in Washington, in 1995. He told prosecutors that conventional research methods for his latest project, like posing questions as a journalist in open chat rooms, were unsuccessful and that to delve deeper, he needed to assume the persona of a trader in child pornographic images. That appeared to work. Jane E. Kirtley, executive director of the Reporters Committee, said that to gain credibility and establish a relationship with people he wanted to learn about, Mr. Matthews had to trade pictures. One of the traders, Ms. Kirtley said, turned out to be an undercover agent. Judge Williams said he would recommend that Mr. Matthews serve his sentence in a halfway house and gave him 60 days to surrender. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Lycos Board Member Quits to Protest Deal
body: Pressing his campaign to block the proposed deal between Lycos Inc. and USA Networks Inc., David S. Wetherell, who controls the largest block of Lycos stock, has resigned from the Lycos board. Mr. Wetherell is the chairman of CMGI Inc., a technology investment fund that owns 18.5 percent of Lycos. Last month, Lycos, the Internet search service, agreed to a complex transaction in which it would gain control of the Home Shopping Network and Ticketmaster units of USA Networks, the media and electronic-commerce company, which is based in newyork. It would also acquire Ticketmaster Online Citysearch, a public company mostly owned by USA. In return, USA would gain control of 61.5 percent of Lycos's shares. Mr. Wetherell voted in favor of the proposal when it came before the Lycos board. But he started to voice doubts as Lycos shares fell sharply; they have now lost more than a third of their value since the deal was announced. In a statement, Mr. Wetherell said yesterday: "After further consideration, it is my opinion that the terms of the USA/Lycos transaction are inadequate for Lycos shareholders. As such, I am resigning from the Lycos board in order to be free to explore the best options available to Lycos shareholders, including the possibility of Lycos remaining independent." William White, the president of CMGI's Internet unit, declined to say whether Mr. Wetherell had proposed any alternative transactions. "The goal is to get the maximum return for Lycos shareholders including CMGI," Mr. White said in an interview last evening. "There is no specific proposal we can talk about." He said that CMGI did not object to a combination of Lycos with Home Shopping Network and Ticketmaster, but its position was that Lycos shareholders should own a larger share of the combined company. Mr. Wetherell met with Barry Diller, the chairman of USA, shortly after the deal was announced. And he has had frequent conversations with Robert J. Davis, the chief executive of Lycos, Mr. White said. Investment bankers said Mr. Wetherell's opposition was a blow to the proposal but hardly a fatal one. Many shareholders who did not like the deal have already sold their holdings to lock in their profits, they said, and thus much of the stock is already in the hands of investors who want to own the combined company. Lycos shareholders are to vote on the deal in three or four months. Executives of Lycos and USA did not respond to phone messages left at their offices last night. CMGI has roots in the direct mail and software industries and has evolved into one of the savviest investors in Internet companies. http://www.nytimes.com

title: U.S. Eases Up on Security Software Exports
body: The Internet security software maker Verisign Inc. said today that the unitedstates agency that controls software exports would allow the company to ship its high-security products to a broader set of overseas customers. Verisign stock surged after news of the expanded unitedstates export approval, rising $14.75, or 14 percent, to $119, in Nasdaq trading. The company said it had won approval from the unitedstates Department of Commerce's Bureau of Export Administration to expand the sale of its 128-bit Global Server identification digital certificates. The software, which is used to authenticate the identity of individual computer users and thus pave the way for commercial transactions, uses 128-bit encryption, considered a virtually unbreakable code against hacker attacks. Verisign said expanded sales authorization now includes on-line merchants, health care and insurance organizations and overseas units of unitedstates corporations. Previously, such customers had to make do with weaker 40-bit encryption because of Government export limitations on more powerful encryption technology, which the Government regulates under laws designed to keep advanced munitions from slipping into enemy hands. Encryption software supporters see the sale of such software overseas as crucial to the unitedstates computer industry's competitiveness; critics see the software as a potential threat to national security. http://www.nytimes.com

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Cable Deregulation Raises Specter of Higher Rates Cable television, one of the last industries to have its prices controlled by the Government, is set to become almost completely deregulated this month. But while the prospect of competition was supposed to drive prices down, the opposite has happened. Cable rates continue to rise, with many companies announcing increases for this year averaging 5 percent, more than twice the projected inflation rate. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 assumed the cable industry would be facing far more competition from satellite broadcasters and telephone companies. But that has not happened, raising deep concerns that cable companies unshackled from price controls and not threatened by competition will continue to impose big rate increases.  Page A1. title:
Compressed Data;
New Device for Playing Music From the Internet
body: The recording industry's recognition that the Internet is changing the music business is coming none too soon. At the newyork Music and Internet Expo on Saturday, Creative Technology Ltd., long the leading seller of audio circuitry for personal computers, showed off a line of products to help meet the pent-up demand for devices that can retrieve and play music from the Internet. The devices use the MP3 software format, which is the most popular way to transmit audio files. Creative, a Singapore company with unitedstates operations based in Milpitas, Calif., said that it would start selling its portable MP3 player this spring for less than $200, roughly the same price as the Rio MP3 player from Diamond Multimedia. Like the Rio, which was announced in October to much fanfare along with a lawsuit from record companies, Creative's device, called the Nomad, is about the size of a pack of cigarettes and holds as much music as an audio CD. Creative's announcement came a week after a group of recording and technology companies, which have formed the Secure Digital Music Initiative, announced a leader and an ambitious timetable for their effort to create a technical standard for the copyrighted sale and digital delivery of music over the Internet. The group's effort is an implicit attack on MP3, which has no copyright protections and is the popular choice of Internet music pirates. So far, the main business opportunity for MP3 appears to be the hardware for playing the music. The Recording Industry Association of America went to court last year in an attempt to block Diamond from selling the Rio. But the judge sided with Diamond, paving the road for other companies, like Creative, to enter the MP3 filed. Samsung Electronics of Korea has announced plans to bring a device called the Yepp MP3 player to the unitedstates market sometime this year. Several other consumer electronics companies are also said to be well along in MP3 development, even as they worry that the devices could cannibalize sales of their own portable cassette and CD players. Creative brings an established brand name to the digital music market. Its Sound Blaster audio card for use in PC's has been among the most popular computer peripheral products of the decade. And its Inspire music Web site (www.creativeinspire.com) already has a large following.   LAURIE J. FLYNN http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: Criteria Are Set for Applicants To Join Internet Name Registry
body: Companies wanting to compete with Network Solutions Inc. and its current monopoly in the lucrative business of registering Internet domain names can begin applying for consideration next Monday. Criteria for registration were approved last week in Singapore by the new nonprofit corporation appointed by the Clinton Administration to take over administration of the Internet from the unitedstates Government and to introduce competition into the system of assigning the Internet addresses known as domains. Accreditation guidelines called for applicants to have $100,000 in liquid capital, $500,000 in liability insurance, a proven computer infrastructure and at least five employees. Esther Dyson, interim chairwoman of the group's board, said the board would allow exceptions to some of the standards. The criteria were among the first policy decisions made by the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, or Icann. Tackling other issues, the board also forged a structure for the body that will ultimately recommend how and when to add new top-level domains -- the three-letter suffixes like .com and .org -- to accommodate demand for new Internet addresses; adopted a conflict-of-interest policy, and established procedures for reviewing its staff decisions. "We made some major progress toward creating a truly competitive environment in the .com, .net and .org domain naming system," Ms. Dyson said. "We also showed the consensus process in operation by changing our initial proposals." Although the creation of Icann and just about everything the board has proposed have stirred opposition and controversy around the globe, nothing has been more contentious than its refusal to hammer out policy decisions in public. Ms. Dyson said the board had also relaxed its requirements for companies that wanted to compete with Network Solutions, until now a Government-protected monopoly. It is currently the exclusive registrar for the most popular top-level domains -- .com, .net and .org. International complaints about the company's lucrative monopoly led the unitedstates last year to create Icann and to move administration of the Internet from Federal contractors to the new private corporation. "You can either meet that criteria or you can prove to us that you don't need to," Ms. Dyson said. "You can say, 'Hey, I've got only two guys, but we're total Net heads, we've been in business five years, we've never had any complaints. We don't need five employees.' " Icann's goal is to introduce five competitors to the domain registration business by May 1. About two months later, Icann plans to let an unlimited number of companies around the world participate. Applications for those initial five will be taken beginning next Monday. The Icann staff will pick the first five companies from those applicants. After that, Ms. Dyson said, Icann will lower the threshold. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Concern Plans System for Small On-Line Transactions
body: Cybergold Inc., a company that pays consumers to pay attention to World Wide Web sites, now plans to let consumers make on-line purchases for as little as 25 cents. The new approach, which Cybergold intends to announce on Monday, is the industry's latest attempt at a so-called micropayment system for the Internet -- a way to pay for information or services whose price may be too low to warrant the expense of a credit card transaction. Cybergold already operates the on-line Earn and Spend Community, which has 1.5 million members and enables consumers to earn money by responding to advertisements or commercial offers. The amounts, which are credited to a subscriber's account and can be converted to cash or used as cybercurrency, range from 25 cents for filling out a form for the on-line car buying service 1StopAuto to $3 for purchasing a subscription to Rolling Stone magazine. Currently the highest fee that a Cybergold member can earn is $25 for signing up for a Visa card. The new system would employ electronic accounts from which members could make on-line purchases of as little as 25 cents. The approach is supposed to be simple enough that an individual author, for example, could offer a document for sale on the Cybergold Web site. Each time someone decided to purchase and download that document, the price would be transferred from the reader's account to the author's account. Other possibilities might be downloading digital audio files in the popular MP3 format, which would enable musicians to sell their own recordings directly. Cybergold would take a fee of 10 to 15 percent for each transaction. "This is publishing for the rest of us," said Nat Goldhaber, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur, who founded Cybergold in 1996. "I believe that there is an audience for content that has a smaller constituency." Separately, the Microsoft Corporation announced an "electronic wallet" system last week, to be known as Microsoft Passport and intended to let computer users pay for purchases made via the company's MSN Web portal. Microsoft is trying to attract small businesses to set up electronic storefronts on its Web site. Micropayment systems, which are intended to supplant traditional currency systems on the Internet, are expected to be the means for completing 8 of every 10 on-line transactions -- though only about 25 percent of the total revenue -- by the year 2002, according to Jupiter Communications, a newyork-based market research firm. There have been various attempts to create micropayment systems on the Internet, including efforts by Cybercash Inc., Digicash Inc. and the First Virtual Corporation. But so far, none of these efforts have yet been widely adopted. They have failed, Mr. Goldhaber said, at least in part because their systems required users to download large software files, which then limited the consumer to using the PC on which the software was installed. In contrast, the Cybergold system is based on standard Web software and can be used from virtually any computer with an Internet connection. Mr. Goldhaber said the Cybergold system was still growing rapidly, with 175,000 new members signed up in February. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Media Talk;
Rush Limbaugh Brings His Show to the Internet
body: For the last few years, Rush Limbaugh, the blustery conservative radio talk show host, has resisted bringing his radio show to the Internet, even though an increasing number of syndicated radio programs were being sent on line to homes and offices throughout America. That is, until last Monday, when his show began broadcasting -- or "streaming," as a technophile would say -- over the Internet at Broadcast.com, a Web site that broadcasts audio and video over the Internet ranging from radio and television programs to full-length compact disks and audio books. Mr. Limbaugh said that he had waited to begin streaming his show to protect the more than 600 radio stations that carry his program -- affiliates in the industry lexicon -- from losing listeners to the Internet, which transmits his show without the local commercials carried by the affiliates and the advertising dollars that pay for them. But, Mr. Limbaugh said that there had been "such a public demand" to hear his show from people who "cannot get a radio signal in an office building," that he and the producers of his show, which is owned by the Premiere Radio Networks unit of Jacor Communications, decided it was the right time to move to the Internet. He noted that many of his affiliates were now streaming programs on the Internet anyway. But as part of his efforts to protect his affiliates, listeners will not be able to download his show and listen to it at any time, as they can with many other programs. The "Rush Limbaugh Show" will only be available live, from noon to 3 P.M., Eastern time. Michael Harrison, the editor of Talkers, a talk radio trade publication, said that while Mr. Limbaugh might be one of the last big name radio hosts to begin streaming a show -- Dr. Laura Schlessinger's program, another widely followed syndicated radio show, has been available on the Internet for almost two years -- the medium is still in its nascent stages and the number of Internet listeners is minuscule compared with the estimated 20 million people Mr. Limbaugh's radio show draws every week. "It's a new technology and there was no reason for him to jump in early," Mr. Harrison said. "But it's become apparent that, eventually, this is where people are going to be, and he knows that."   MATTHEW J. ROSENBERG http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Rush Limbaugh comes to the Web. (Associated Press)

title: Musicians Want a Revolution Waged on the Internet
body: Visionaries, hopefuls, hucksters and self-described geeks mingled over the weekend at the first newyork Music and Internet Expo, a convention held at the newyorker Hotel. While Web pages flickered on monitors and cellular phones beeped, musicians and computer entrepreneurs swapped business cards and ideas about how the Internet could revolutionize the music business. Optimists, in the majority, saw it as a force that would inevitably democratize the market, a way to bypass recording companies and radio stations and offer music directly to listeners. "The Internet has made it possible for people to get consistently what they want, their way, without censorship," said Steve Zuckerman, a former music journalist who organized the event and plans to produce another one in Los Angeles on Aug. 7 and 8. "Artists, for a change, have hope. The people here all want something similar: creative control of their products and their companies." Chuck D, the rapper who leads Public Enemy, gave a keynote speech and predicted that there would be "a million artists out there and 500,000 labels or more." He added, "Major labels will not be obsolete, but they're going to have to learn how to share." It was a convention aimed at the grass roots. The Internet expo cost $15 a day to attend and $700 for exhibitors, considerably less than more established and expensive events like the CMJ Music Marathon. Mr. Zuckerman estimated that 2,000 people would come to the two-day event. Speakers included musicians, software and equipment makers and Web site operators. Absent were representatives of most major labels or their trade group, the Recording Industry Association of America, which is playing catch-up with the Internet. It is working to set a standard for digital distribution of music that will prevent unauthorized copying. The National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences, which presents the Grammy Awards, had a booth to promote its programs for emerging musicians. Michael Robertson, the chief executive of the Internet site and company MP3.com, said: "We think the music industry is broken, no matter how you look at it. We need to change the whole business of music." Mr. Robertson's company, and many other Internet sites, offers music in the form of MP3 files, which can be sent quickly over the Internet and copied at will. Because delivery via the Internet eliminates the need to package, manufacture and distribute a CD, it allows musicians to send their latest work out immediately. "An artist can have a creative urge at 2:30 A.M., upload it at 3:30 and have it on the Web at 4:30," Mr. Robertson said. Established stars have begun giving away music on the Internet to promote themselves. Last Monday, Tom Petty made a new song available free on the MP3.com site; during the three days it was available, it was downloaded 157,699 times. In return, Mr. Petty and his recording company have a marketing tool: email addresses for fans, who can be reached when his next album is released. Alanis Morissette made a new song available through AT&T's a2b Music (www.a2bmusic.com), which does not allow copying; the free song was downloaded 285,000 times, while links to the song sold 22,000 tickets to her concert tour. Last year Public Enemy made songs available as MP3 files, but was stopped by the threat of legal action from its label at the time, Polygram, which owns the master recordings. Now, Public Enemy's contract with Polygram has expired, and it has a new MP3 song, "Swindler's Lust," on its Web site, www.public-enemy.com. Chuck D said that in future contracts, Public Enemy would keep its rights to master recordings and enter joint ventures with companies to release the material on disks and tapes. "I'm an Internet presence first, and everything else follows from that," he said. Public Enemy's next album would be available in digital form on the Internet before appearing as a CD, he added. Mr. Robertson said that distributing music through the Internet could restructure the recording business. In a typical recording contract a label finances and promotes an album, and the performer receives a 10 to 15 percent royalty after costs are recouped -- $1 to $2 for each album sold -- while the label owns the master recording. Musicians who finance their own recordings and distribute them through the Internet could receive more for an album, making a profit without blockbuster sales. "The record deal up to now has just been the engine that drives the tour bus," said Ken Hertz, a partner in the law firm Hansen, Jacobson, Teller & Hoberman who represents Ms. Morissette, Hole and others. A few skeptics warned that the unchecked distribution of music on the Internet could rob musicians of income from recordings. "Today everyone's happy and everything's beautiful and everything's free," said Francois-Xavier Nuttall, whose company, Audiosoft, makes software to track copyright and royalty information. "But in the future we will need an economic model." Other panelists noted that the sound quality of music transmitted over the Internet was inferior to CD's. "It's a lot easier for people to make records now," said Joe Alexander, a producer. "I might be able to do it on a wristwatch in a taxicab. But it's not the same as going in and taking the time to make the sound you've worked a lifetime to develop. Don't let this technology lower the standards." Other speakers insisted that appearing in cyberspace was no substitute for hitting the road, and that most of the free music on the Internet was not worth hearing. "A lot of people envision this friction-free future, where everybody has access to everything immediately," Mr. Hertz said. "But if you have to spend your whole day figuring out what's good, you're not going to have time to listen to it." He predicted that filtering -- sites and formats that winnow the choices, as recording companies and radio stations do now -- would be a profitable Internet service, paid for through advertising or subscription fees. For musicians, meanwhile, the promise of the Internet was simpler. "We just want our music out there," said Ricky Byrd, a songwriter. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The rapper Chuck D at the Internet Music Conference. (Rahav Segev) (pg. E7)

title:
TECHNOLOGY: E-Commerce Report;
Internet retailers are attracting lots of window shoppers. Now the push is on to turn those shoppers into buyers.
body: INTERNET shoppers may be at the vanguard of a retail revolution, but as with anyone on the front lines, they are a jittery bunch. Those who shop on the Internet abandon one-half to two-thirds of the purchases they begin, industry executives and analysts say.  One way that sites can measure the dropouts is through "shopping cart" technology, which, as the name suggests, allows users to gather items at a site for a one-stop checkout. The problem is that on-line shoppers often start filling a cart, but then leave the site without buying anything. Tired of such almost-sales, E-commerce sites have begun looking at the problem and are feverishly devising methods to convert these browsers into buyers. "Is there widespread concern in the industry about this?" said Arno Harris, vice president for marketing at 911gifts.com, whose site has seen 45 percent of its potential transactions abandoned before checkout. "I think there is." Of those who bail out, Mr. Harris said, 30 percent drop off at the first page of the billing process. "We're still in the early phase of E-commerce adoption, so a lot of people just get into the process and panic," he said. Industry executives cite various reasons that customers bail out. First, some consumers are just trying out the on-line shopping experience, without intending to make a purchase. Others abandon the process when confronted with often-hefty shipping and handling charges at the end of the transaction, or with registration forms that ask for personal information, like a home address, email address or phone number. Finally, a significant -- but diminishing -- number of users remain unsure about giving out their credit card information on line. Matt Hyde, vice president of on-line sales for REI.com, an outdoor goods retailer, conjectures that many Internet users are simply playing with sites that have E-commerce capabilities, just as people try out anything new before seriously considering spending money on it. "I put stuff in the cart all the time and then leave, don't you?" Mr. Hyde said. "I did it three times on Saturday." But Ken Cassar, an E-commerce analyst for Jupiter Communications, a newyork-based research firm, said a big problem was shipping and handling costs, which many sites do not disclose until late in the buying process. "It's sticker shock," Mr. Cassar said. "A lot of people just aren't willing to pay what is essentially a 30 to 40 percent markup." Mr. Cassar and other analysts said that security was less of an issue than it was last year, when many in the industry were predicting that such fears would slow the growth of E-commerce. To date, there have been few actual reported instances of on-line credit card fraud. And many consumers have chosen to shop on line at sites operated by established companies, perhaps further reducing security concerns. More Internet retailers are also designing their Web sites to convey the image of a secure store, with an abundance of credit card logos and other seals of approval adorning many companies' home pages. Though some shoppers still balk at using their credit cards on line, Mr. Cassar said that many more were put off by registration forms. William Bryant, chairman of Qpass, a company that has developed a billing system for E-commerce sites, understands consumer resistance to registering. "Imagine going to a 7-Eleven to buy a can of Coke, and having to fill out a registration form that asks you about marital status," he said. But don't expect registration forms to disappear any time soon. Internet companies love them, because they help retailers refine their marketing efforts and aim advertisements on the site more precisely (and thus charge more to advertisers). Even so, on-line merchants are exploring ways to make registering less of a hindrance, such as systems that would let users register one time for multiple Web sites. Excite, for example, lets users type in their credit card information once and then shop at a number of merchants within the network. Andy Halliday, vice president for Excite's commerce division, said the system not only eliminated registration redundancies, but also gave shoppers fewer opportunities to abandon a purchase. That is particularly important, he said, because the Internet has been a medium for impulse spending. "You have to make a consumer's purchase decision as slippery a slope as possible," referring to the speed with which sites should finalize sales. Mr. Harris, of 911Gifts.com, said that his company recently started a similar system and that he expected it to reduce the number of lost purchases at his site. "Now that people have pretty much figured out the economics of getting customers to their sites, the focus is on conversion," he said, noting that E-commerce sites typically convert less than 2 percent of their visitors into customers. "This is a really critical way merchants can improve economics without spending a lot more money," he said. Perhaps the most aggressive approach to the problem is represented by Cybershop, an on-line department store that actually pursues shoppers who abandon large purchases. Jeffrey Tauber, Cybershop's chief executive, says that even when a shopper fills and flees, the company can still "capture a pretty good level of information" about who the consumer was. "And if it's a nice-size order, we'll call or email them and try to close the sale," Mr. Tauber said. About 15 percent of the customers the company pursues ultimately complete the sale, Mr. Tauber said. No doubt the best antidote for shopping jitters is, simply, more practice. Industry executives and analysts predict that if the Internet's flagship merchants continue to provide positive shopping experiences, fewer customers will hesitate about making a purchase. In other words, if the industry is going to get past its abandonment issues, companies will have to allay customers' concerns. The E-merchants, meanwhile, will also have to stock up on the one commodity rarely found in cyberspace: patience. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Trolling for Scuttlebutt on the Internet
body: James Alexander is the bearer of bad news for hundreds of corporations. And now, Mr. Alexander's clients can take heart that he intends to bring them more negative tidings more quickly than ever. Mr. Alexander, 30, and his brother, Charles Lukaszewski, 32, are co-founders and operators of Ewatch, a company that scours the Internet on behalf of corporate clients who want to know what the rest of the world is saying behind their backs. "The chairman is a pedophile; the chairman is arrested; the chairman has checked into a hospital under an assumed name," Mr. Alexander said, rattling off recent examples of false rumors from the dark corners of cyberspace. Corporations have long paid so-called clipping services to monitor their appearances in the conventional news media. But Ewatch and its competitors have taken the practice on line and a step further. This new generation of monitors goes beyond news publishers and instead trolls for rumor and innuendo in the Net's virtual back alleys -- in thousands of chat rooms and discussion forums where, Ewatch executives say, unchecked scuttlebutt can damage corporate reputations and stock prices. These brothers grim -- Mr. Lukaszewski a programmer by training and Mr. Alexander a former television producer -- started Ewatch in 1994 from their home offices in Minneapolis and newyork, respectively. With help from friends and family, they spent days searching the Internet for venom spewed against corporations, trying to convince potential clients of the need for on-line rumor detection and control. But bad news for corporate America meant good public relations for Ewatch. After O. J. Simpson's acquittal on murder charges in October 1995, for example, a false rumor -- first reported on the tabloid television show "Hard Copy," and then spread on the Internet -- said that Mrs. Field's Cookies had underwritten a party for the jurors. The company's sales dipped, Mr. Alexander said, and Ewatch was hired to help Mrs. Fields find on-line discussion groups where the rumor had appeared, and then post corrective messages. Cookie sales soon returned to normal levels, Mr. Alexander said. Since then, as cyberspace has grown, so have Ewatch's methods. As its client list expanded, the company scrapped manual monitoring for automated "spiders" -- search tools that scour chat groups for key-word phrases. And earlier this month, Ewatch began a more fundamental overhaul, upgrading its software and server computers to quadruple the speed at which they scan and process information. The company also replaced its home-brewed search engine with search software from Excalibur Technology, which will be coupled with a new Oracle data base management system. "The Internet is experiencing uncontrollable growth, and we have to be prepared for it," said Mr. Alexander, who also said that the upgrade would cost $2 million. Each day, Ewatch combs through more than 250,000 postings from the sprawling on-line discussion forum known as Usenet. It also monitors thousands of other postings from the financial chat rooms on leading Web sites, including Yahoo and Motley Fool, while also scanning discussion areas on the leading proprietary on-line services like America Online. Besides the challenge of keeping apace of Internet growth, Ewatch has another concern: competition. Among the handful of competitors offering monitoring services are Cybercheck, a Denver company that says it can search for key words in 150,000 on-line sources, and Cyveillance, an Alexandria, Va., company that scans the bit stream for rumors, trademark infringements and E-commerce developments that might affect its corporate clients. But Louis M. Thompson, president and chief executive of the National Investor Relations Institute, a trade group based in Vienna, Va., said that among Internet monitoring companies, Ewatch "seems to be the big one on the block." Ewatch serves about 130 clients full time, including U S West, H. J. Heinz, Owens Corning and Northwest Airlines. It is no longer independent, having been acquired by Wavephore Inc., a publicly held data broadcasting company based in Phoenix. But it is still operated by the brothers, with Mr. Alexander overseeing marketing from newyork and Mr. Lukaszewski operating the technology side from Minneapolis, where the brothers were raised. Mr. Thompson said that corporations had come to realize that the same attributes that make the Internet a valuable commercial medium -- such as the ability to quickly and cheaply spread information to the masses -- can be a liability, too. That is especially true as the rising popularity of on-line stock trading has placed a fast-twitch premium on corporate information, often with little regard to its accuracy. And yet, as more companies come to recognize the perils of the electronic grapevine, Ewatch and other monitoring agents are finding that their real competitors are often their would-be clients. Many companies use in-house resources to monitor the Internet, or ask their public relations firms to do the work. Even if companies acknowledge that Ewatch may have superior surveillance capabilities, they may not always be convinced that the $13,000-a-year service is worth the cost. Take the Itex Corporation, a small, publicly held financial record-keeping company in Portland, Ore., which has filed a lawsuit against several people whom Itex accuses of making defamatory remarks against the company in a Yahoo chat room. The burden of trolling the Internet for corporate gossip is being borne by the company's assistant general counsel, Stephen C. Pearson. He said the small public company -- which was recently delisted from the Nasdaq stock market after the Securities and Exchange Commission said Itex had failed to submit its annual report on time -- could not afford the likes of Ewatch. "We looked at Ewatch in particular and did a brief analysis of their systems," Mr. Pearson said. "We came to the conclusion that it was pretty expensive." Some of Ewatch's bigger clients say the service has proved valuable, though. "There's a loose and free exchange of information on the Internet," said Tom Pinto, spokesman for the giant pension system TIAA-CREF, which manages more than $250 billion in assets. "Anything that is inaccurate or harmful, we want to know immediately about it and respond." One day last October, for example, a visitor to a Compuserve discussion room wrote that a TIAA-CREF pension fund called Global Equities held 25 percent of its assets in Asia. In fact, the fund held only 5 percent of its assets in the region, and it was a potentially devastating error, coming amid the Asian economic crisis. Had the rumor spread, Mr. Pinto recalled, it might have caused investors to flee the $6 billion pension fund. The next day, an Ewatch report landed on Mr. Pinto's desk. Two days later, the TIAA-CREF manager of media relations sent email to the mediator of the chat group, who posted a correction. With hundreds of thousands of messages posted daily to tens of thousands of Internet message boards, it might seem humanly impossible to patrol even a fraction of cyberspace. But Ewatch relies on its search spiders and computers to do most of the culling, before handing off to the half-dozen people Ewatch employs to do the final winnowing before passing along the information to clients. Sometimes, Ewatch clients are not necessarily looking for bad tidings, but simply any news or discussions that might be relevant to the company. Owens Corning, based in Toledo, Ohio, instructs Ewatch to search not just for its name, but also for the words "fiberglass," "insulation" and "asphalt," Jim Worden, an Owens Corning spokesman, said. Such searches, he said, help the company stay abreast of consumer sentiments. Soon, Ewatch will be offered for an extra fee to subscribers of Wavephore's primary product, Newscast, which gives corporations tailored news feeds from thousands of sources like Dow Jones, Reuters and PR Newswire. And Ewatch subscribers, in turn, will be given access to Newscast Lite, a significantly slimmed-down version of Newscast. Eventually, Mr. Alexander said he would like to create a service that would help a company analyze the combined impact of Internet rumors, media coverage and the client's own public relations efforts. Although he acknowledged that plenty of details still need to be worked out, he envisions the day when a client could type in a natural-language query like "Why are sales lagging in Minnesota?" and receive reports about marketing, media and mendacity that might help explain the problem. And on the assumption that no news is not necessarily good news, the company plans eventually to monitor not only for gossip and innuendo, but for the absence of chatter. "If you're a company that's spent $100 million on a launch campaign and no one's talking about you -- why is that?" Mr. Alexander said. "If there's nothing about you on line, isn't that valuable information to know?" http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: James Alexander of Ewatch, a company that scans the Net for rumor and innuendo.

title: It's @786. Do You Know Where Your Computer Is?  - Correction Appended
body: WHEN Gustavo Carreno received an email message at his Lisbon office last week asking for an appointment to talk about universal time, an old concept recently repackaged by the Swatch Group, the world's largest watch maker, he sent the following response: "Well the thing is, I'm not that good on converting time but I think there is a -5 hour of difference between Portugal/Lisbon and newyork, meaning that you'll have to add 5 hours to your local time to get my time. So the best thing to do is to say that I'll be available at my work fone from @416 'till @791." So it was that at @786, or about one hour after the sun was overhead in newyork City, or 0552 Greenwich Mean Time, Mr. Carreno, 29, a computer consultant, explained his enthusiasm for what Swatch is calling "Internet time." This way, when he meets with friends and colleagues on-line, they "have an understanding," he said. "It's @786 all around the world." The Swatch scheme, which divides the day into 1,000 "swatch beats" equivalent to 1 minute and 26.4 seconds, is unabashedly commercial. The system's meridian is located, conveniently enough, over the Swatch building in Biel, Swizterland, where midnight strikes @000 beats. Swatch will begin selling a $70 watch that tells Internet time, among other things, in the unitedstates this month. The product is already for sale in Europe. But the company has also made software that displays Internet time on a computer screen available free from Swatch's site on the World Wide Web. About 45,000 people downloaded it in January. Perhaps it is not surprising that the notion of a world without time zones strikes a chord even among some of the more gimmick-weary Internet users. With its capacity to collapse distance, the computer network has already managed to alter the physics of space. And whether or not Internet time a la Swatch catches on, the Internet seems to be responsible for an increasing impatience with time as it has been kept thus far. "There is something screwed up about our sense of time," said Danny Hillis, a computer scientist who is spearheading an effort to build a clock that will strike once every 10,000 years. (He wants to encourage a longer view of the future.) "Our classical notion of time that we've inherited from the industrial age doesn't fit with the way we live now," he said. "Time zones made a lot of sense when we stayed in one zone. Now I find I'm living on CNN time rather than my local time. I can call you back at the end of the hour, but I have no idea which hour it is." In the unitedstates, cities set the time by the sun until the late 1800's, when time zones were invented by the railroads to coordinate schedules and avoid collisions. In the 1960's, after the vibrations in a cesium atom were found to be a more reliable measure that the rotation of the Earth, universal time became based on a a calculation done in Paris of the average of atomic clocks. (Most people still look to Greenwich, England, for the universal time, established in an 1874 treaty.) But the Internet may already have warped the way its frequent users experience time. In the technology industry, "Internet time" has come to mean something like dog years, denoting the ever-accelerating speeds of microprocessors, data transmission and startup companies going public. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology's business school, for instance, recently buried an Internet time capsule -- to be opened in five years. So now there are concerns that Internet time means abandoning biological rhythms in favor of 24-hour computer clocks synchronized to the nanosecond. But it has also increased the demand for the correct time. The guardians of the Network Time Protocol, which allows computers on the Internet to adjust their clock within milliseconds of Greenwich time, say requests for the correct time have doubled in the last six months. For Nicolas Hayek, the founder and chief executive of the Swatch Group, that is all the more reason why people will want to buy Swatch's first Internet time watches. "The Internet has made human beings more globally conscious of being on a small planet where we are all really equal," Mr. Hayek said. "Internet time is the perfect measuring stick for this era." Judah Levine, a physicist at the time and frequency division of the National Institute for Standards and Technology in Boulder, Colo., is not so sure. After all, he notes, they're still sleeping in China when newyorkers are having breakfast, even if it's @430 in cyberspace. "They have the same problems with the Earth going around the sun as we always did," Mr. Levine said. "The Internet can't change that." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article last Sunday about new interest in creating a universal time scheme for the Internet misstated a time measurement using the 24-hour clock; 5:53 P.M. is 1753, not 0553. Correction-Date: March 14, 1999, Sunday Graphic   Diagram: "Beyond Time Zones" The increasing use of the World Wibe Web has raised interest in a universal system of time that breaks the day into 1,000 units each equivalent to 86.4 seconds. After a meridian is established, a unit is then converted into local time. Diagram shows3:00 P.M. displayed on a 24-hour clock and the equivalent in universal time -- @625. (Sources: universal-time.org; Swatch)

title:
PRIVATE SECTOR;
On-Line Stock Advice From the Junior Set
body: Nowhere is it written that a stock guru has to be old enough to vote. But in the age of the Internet, where anyone with a modem can dispense financial wisdom and shift market tides, there are other questions raised about people like Daniel Miller, 15, who maintains a stock-advice Web site. Propelled by a CNBC appearance last month, as well as a couple of stellar picks, his following has been growing so quickly that he is soliciting advertising for his site and considering charging admission. Mr. Miller ducks into the computer room or the library at the Frisch Yeshiva School in Paramus, N.J., where he is in the ninth grade, to post his observations on line. One day last month, he dashed off this note, typo and all: "2/23/99 -- FSOL is my pick . . . I havbe class will explain later." The day before, shares in Filtered Souls Entertainment Inc., a small hip-hop record label in Canada, had risen 92 percent. And that, perhaps, was evidence of Mr. Miller's influence: He had discussed the company on the Silicon Investor site before he actually recommended it on his own. He later told a reporter that he had heard about Filtered Souls through an anonymous email tip and then read more about it on the Business Financial Network site, which was paid a fee for its positive report. Ian Lambert, president of Filtered Souls, said he had never heard of Mr. Miller before, but was "just happy with the publicity." The publicity pleases Mr. Miller less. His father, Leon, has temporarily curbed interviews -- but not before his son could ask a reporter, "Is this story going to be positive or negative?" Anyone charging for investment advice needs to register as an investment adviser, said Duncan King, a spokesman for the Securities and Exchange Commission. But the First Amendment, he said, protects the average citizen or stock tipster, who, for no payment, simply wants to get up on his Web-based soapbox.   LISA NAPOLI http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Daniel Miller

title: Computer Hackers Are Stopped; Pentagon Networks Were Victim
body: Military security analysts uncovered and stopped computer hackers who had discovered a new way to attack open Pentagon networks on the Internet, Pentagon officials said today. In testimony before Congress last week, John J. Hamre, the Deputy Secretary of Defense, said in a closed-door hearing that this new method had been uncovered by analysts at the Naval Surface Warfare Center in Dahlgren, Va., Defense Department officials said. The specialists at Dahlgren found a method to thwart those low-level probes that differ from the more frequent brutal assaults on security systems and alerted all the military services to the new problem and a remedy for it. "There are literally hundreds of attempts weekly to break into the computers," a Pentagon spokesman said. "It's constant because there's a certain cachet to getting into the Pentagon system." The Pentagon has estimated that 99.95 percent of computer hackers fail to penetrate beyond the open networks, which contain unclassified material, and so pose no national security concern. The most notable example of hackers using this new method occurred in January when a military computer server near San Antonio was probed for two days from foreign Web sites. These probes reached only the open military networks connected to the Internet and it was unclear whether the probes originated overseas or were merely routed through those sites. "These hackers try to cover their tracks by initiating the intrusions through an overseas site that has nothing to do with where the hackers actually are," the Pentagon spokesman said. In the last year, each armed service has installed new programs to detect hackers and to protect sensitive material. As the number of surveillance programs have increased, so has the number of detections. These new military computer security officials have said they are fighting a "cyberwar." "To them it's a war, but it's like the war on crime or the war on drugs -- it's the information security guys' war," said William Arkin, author of "The U.S. Military On Line." "But it's not a real war." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
HOME VIDEO;
Catalogue Sellers Thrive on Line
body: As video sales on the Internet rise, it's good to see old-line purveyors -- those with paper catalogues in the two-to-three-pound range -- holding their own, not only between covers but on the Web as well. To be respectable in video mail order these days, one needs at least 40,000 titles. Movies Unlimited, a large Philadelphia distributor, packs that many in a fat catalogue that can now be found on the Internet at www.mostmovies.com. Like other sites, this one has specific strengths. Built over 20 years, the collection at one time or another has gotten into every nook and cranny of a genre or career, at least as it exists on video. Search John Wayne, for example, and you come up with more than 200 entries from feature films to television commercials. Another virtue of the large older mail order operation is that over the years it has accumulated a wide assortment of titles that are no longer in distribution and probably never will be again. If you've been told a film isn't available, perhaps Movies Unlimited has a copy available. For example, "Absolute Beginners" (1985), a look at the London fashion world of 1958 (with a soundtrack by David Bowie and others), is $35.99, which is a representative price for these few-of-a-kind videos. That's $35.99 used, it should be added. Many of the cassettes were in rental circulation years ago. The company says that tapes are in very good shape unless otherwise stated. Prices vary according to a title's past popularity, present rarity and condition. "The American Friend" (1977), Wim Wenders's highly regarded film noir starring Dennis Hopper and Bruno Ganz, is $53.99 used, another typical price. But choice obviously recommends a catalogue or Web inventory. Perhaps the most unusual selection belongs to Facets International, a Chicago distributor. Last week Facets issued its very large (10-by-15-inch, 625-page) paper catalogue. Jump into it at random, and there is Victor Sjostrom's "Secret of the Monastery" (1919), and Henry Jaglom's "Babyfever" (1995) and Jack Arnold's "Tarantula" (1955). The catalogue can also be found at the Facets site, www.facets.org, where this week the noted selections include Mitchell Leisen's 1934 comedy "Death Takes a Holiday" and George Romero's second film, "There's Always Vanilla" (1971). The catalogue is edited by Milos Stehlik, Facets' video director. "The Internet has helped people become aware of these films," he said. "That leads to sophisticated specialized collecting." Another hopeful sign for a broader selection, he said, is increased activity by smaller independent distributors like Fox Lorber, First Run, Kino, Water Bearer and Home Vision. All are putting out more high-grade independent and foreign films, like Abbas Kiarostami's acclaimed "Taste of Cherry," an Iranian film about a man's search for someone to go to the cemetery and bury him after he has committed suicide. Home Vision is to release the movie next month. It was shown at the newyork Film Festival in 1997 and made a brief theater appearance. "People are looking to video for these kinds of films," Mr. Stehlik said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Among the independent and foreign films coming to video is "Taste of Cherry," from Iran, which is to be released next month by Home Vision. (Zeitgeist Films)

title: Microsoft to Sell Business Internet Software
body: Projecting a vision of a world in which most buying and selling takes place between machines, the Microsoft Corporation yesterday announced its electronic commerce strategy, a range of software products and services designed to automate business. Although Microsoft has generally been perceived to be trailing in Internet commerce systems, the company yesterday offered Biztalk, a new language, or a set of conventions, that it said would help draw together disparate business practices and electronic commerce technologies via the Internet. "The Internet is the ultimate market," said William H. Gates, Microsoft's chairman and chief executive. "It's great news for businesses because they can reach out to more customers than ever before." The new approach will offer businesses the ability to configure electronic systems for retail or business-to-business commerce in a "Lego block" approach, Microsoft executives said. But they did not announce specific product availability dates or prices, saying only that they would be available shortly after the company's much-delayed Windows 2000 operating system, the successor to Windows NT, which is scheduled to be released before the end of the year. Microsoft also announced Commerce Server version 3.0, a software program designed for Windows 2000. As part of its new initiative, Microsoft also announced a variety of new business partnerships and the acquisition of Comparenet, a comparison-shopping Web site that it intends to integrate into its MSN Web portal. Microsoft is trying to turn MSN into a marketplace by offering services that will make it easier for small businesses to build an on-line store. Industry analysts said that although Microsoft was late and trailed competitors like I.B.M. in the electronic commerce space, the software company's new strategy appeared to be a systematic approach. "They're definitely late; it's a me-too strategy compared to companies like Yahoo and America Online," said Michael Putnam, a business and technology analyst at Forrester Research Inc., a market research firm in Cambridge, Mass. He added that the strategy was a good one but suggested that Microsoft might run into resistance from competitors and from its own customers and business partners in its attempt to evangelize a broad standard with the Biztalk language. "I don't think Biztalk is a good thing," he said. "Standards are critical for the growth of Internet commerce, but this is like General Motors making the traffic rules." Microsoft executives predicted yesterday that the accelerating pace of electronic commerce would shortly begin to transform some products that have been sold as physical objects into digital information. Speaking in defense of what he has called "friction free capitalism," Mr. Gates said that products like music and books would increasingly be purchased in electronic form. "A lot of products that today are in physical form will become digital," he said. Industry analysts were skeptical that Microsoft would be able to achieve meaningful dominance in electronic commerce markets, because it will have difficulty harnessing broadly used Internet standards to its proprietary software. The company has chosen to build its Biztalk "framework" around an industry Web standard known as XML, which is being used to connect data bases to the Internet. "If they're not using industry-standard XML, they're out of luck," said Kimball Brown, a computer industry analyst at Dataquest, a San Jose, Calif., market research firm. "Microsoft is going to have to play by industry rules."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Merrill Enters Trading World Of the Internet
body: Merrill Lynch & Company, the country's largest brokerage house, dipped its toes into Internet stock trading last night. Now, it has to show it can swim. In the evening hours, Merrill's technicians switched on the firm's long-awaited Internet trading option for a select group of customers, allowing them for the first time to buy and sell listed stocks without calling one of the firm's 15,000 brokers. Merrill will soon give those clients the ability to invest in mutual funds and to buy certificates of deposit as well as stocks. And if the early foray goes well, Merrill plans to soon extend on-line stock trading to more clients, including those who pay full commissions to trade with Merrill, senior executives there said. The firm's Internet offering is too limited -- and the fees Merrill charges for its services too high -- to offer immediate competition to the Internet stock brokerage firms that have begun luring clients away from the established Wall Street firms. But Merrill's main task is not to lure low-end customers away from on-line brokerage firms, but to keep its own eight million clients, and their $1.4 trillion in assets, on board. The idea is to combine the advice from its full-service broker with all-hours stock trading for clients who want to do it themselves.
