title:
USER'S GUIDE;
Virtual Fridge Door, Minus Magnets
body: LAST Saturday, I forgot that my 7-year-old daughter was supposed to go to a birthday party. I am at a loss to explain how I forgot because the invitation was prominently displayed at eye level on the refrigerator door. It was between my second grader's most recent spelling test ("100++ -- excellent!") and a photo of the baby getting a kiss from a jelly-faced friend, and it was barely covered by the corner of the school cafeteria's monthly menu, on which someone had scrawled "Bring lunch from home!" next to "Feb. 22 -- Pork sausage parmesan." The next morning I phoned the parents of the birthday girl and apologized. "I can't explain it because I also had the time and date written in my schedule book," I said. "Of course, I'm not sure where I left the book." "I understand completely," the mother said. "Last fall, I totally forgot about a meeting at work. Missed it. For no reason." There is a good reason, at least in my case. With my family of five, I would need the choreography skills of Balanchine to execute gracefully all the steps needed to complete my competing obligations: the after-school Web Page Club, the dentist, the working lunches and the (increasingly frequent) pit stops at a local Starbuck's. But after I found a coffee-stained scrap of paper covered with the inscrutable message "Friday, 11 A.M., IMPORTANT," I realized that things were out of hand. It was time to clean up the whole mess -- to solve the mystery of the missing schedule book, to liberate the refrigerator and to enter all the flotsam of our lives onto a master calendar that I could check daily. And never misplace. For me, the best place for such a calendar would be the Internet, a place I visit religiously after the rest of the household disperses to various schools, offices and morning naps. Since I was already on line to check email and my favorite Web sites, it would make sense to add the ritual of checking a daily calendar based on the Web. To test my theory, I went to a site called www.familyshoebox.com. This site, which is operated by Koz Inc., offers a number of free services designed to streamline family life. Its easy-to-use templates let you do things like creating an umbrella site, linking an extended family's various Web pages, publishing an on-line newsletter and organizing threaded discussions. I decided to start slowly, by registering for a free family calendar. After choosing a member name and password, I was almost instantly assigned a Web headquarters for my family. Next, I clicked on Calendar, and a divided page appeared. The left side displayed a one-month calendar for February 1999. If I clicked on any specific date, that day's schedule would appear on the right side of the screen. When I clicked on Update, editing tools appeared. I decided to enter "Ella's piano lesson, 4:30," using a pull-down menu to decide whether it would be a one-time event or should be entered as a daily, weekly, monthly or even annual event on my family calendar. Knowing Ella, I chose "one-time only." Next, the site prompted me, with easy-to-complete forms, to enter a description of the event, the location and the time it was to start and end. The site enabled me to enter far more details about an event than would fit in my date book. After I clicked on Save, the site entered the information under the correct date on my calendar. I was pleased -- until I realized that entering a single event had used up roughly 30 seconds of my time. With 54 more events to enter for the remainder of February, this project might consume enough time to conflict with the day's scheduled 3:30 P.M. pickup at school. Suddenly I flashed back, recovering an unpleasant memory from the early 1990's of an attempt to enter my household financial information into the Quicken software program. I aborted the effort before I was even halfway through my checkbook register. To avoid admitting defeat again, I took a cleansing breath and decided there must be some way to speed up the process. I phoned Koz for advice. Instead of entering and saving events one at a time, could I, for instance, click on a date and then type in all the day's events in a single entry? "That suggestion has been brought up before," said Doug Patton, a Koz product manager. "It's in the queue -- not a hard thing to change. It's an enhancement that we're working on." In the meantime? I returned to my calendar, entering such vital events as "pick up vacuum from repair shop" and "Hebrew school -- car pool," but I found the process too tedious. I then went over to www.yahoo .com to check out that site's free calendar service. While the design was remarkably similar and the event-entry process only slightly faster, I preferred two other Yahoo features greatly. One was the To Do list that appeared under the monthly calendar, making it easy to lump mundane chores like the vacuum cleaner expedition together in one place instead of entering each separately. Also, the Yahoo calendar can communicate with a Palm Pilot or a Microsoft Outlook 97 or 98 schedule, enabling you to trade information back and forth. None of that would help me, however, because I don't own a Palm Pilot (I would just lose it) and I don't use Microsoft Outlook. Will either calendar organize my life? Not totally. But there was a nice side benefit to the attempt. When I was looking for the vacuum cleaner receipt, I found my date book -- on top of the refrigerator. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Margaret Riegel)

title: U.S. Hammers At Microsoft's Browser Deals
body: A senior Microsoft official acknowledged in Federal court today that the company's contracts had prohibited Internet service providers from offering its browser on the same Web page as its main competition because Microsoft executives "thought we would lose in a side-by-side choice." The admission clearly pleased David Boies, the Government lawyer who elicited it from the witness, Cameron Myhrvold, a vice president in the Microsoft Corporation's Internet Customer Unit division -- so much so that Mr. Boies asked the same question four different ways and got the same answer each time. "Was it true you were trying to prevent Internet service providers from presenting Netscape and Internet Explorer side by side so users could choose?" he asked at one point. Internet Explorer is the name of Microsoft's browser; the Netscape Communications Corporation's Navigator is its principal rival. "We thought we would lose in a side-by-side choice," Mr. Myhrvold answered, because Netscape was already so firmly established in the market. In all, it was another bad day in court for Microsoft in its antitrust battle with the Justice Department, which charges that the software giant used a monopoly in personal computer operating systems to achieve a dominant position in Internet software. Hour after hour, Mr. Boies chiseled away at Mr. Myhrvold's testimony, forcing him to acknowledge incorrect assertions, misleading omissions and deceptive statements. Mr. Myhrvold repeatedly acknowledged that he made misstatements in email memos. He also testified that he disagreed with Microsoft employees whose memos contradicted his own assertions. As he completed his testimony this evening it was clear that Mr. Myhrvold's appearance had not helped Microsoft's case. In fact, as Microsoft's defense reached its midpoint this evening, none of its first five witnesses had proved particularly effective advocates of the company's position. Mr. Myhrvold, a brother of Nathan Myhrvold, Microsoft's chief technology officer, is in charge of the Microsoft division that negotiates agreements with Internet service providers, the companies that give computer users access to the Internet. The Government charges that Microsoft's restrictive contracts with these companies are anticompetitive and illegal. Mr. Myhrvold tried to make the case that the contracts were largely ineffective or benign. Many of these companies have agreements to be listed in the Internet Referral Service in Microsoft's Windows operating system, which enables users to subscribe to an Internet service posted there. On Tuesday, Mr. Myhrvold insisted that the Government's assertion that these companies had to favor Explorer over Navigator to be included in the service was "absolutely wrong." But under further cross-examination by Mr. Boies today, Mr. Myhrvold admitted that in most cases the companies had been required to ship Explorer to at least 75 percent of their customers. Mr. Myhrvold added that they were free to stop shipping the Microsoft product if they wanted, in which case they could be dropped from the Windows referral service. "It's a fairly subtle point," Mr. Myhrvold acknowledged. Similarly, in his written direct testimony, Mr. Myhrvold pointedly noted that several Internet service providers in the referral service were not shipping Explorer as required, and yet the company had decided not to enforce the contracts. For example, he wrote, "of the copies of Web browsing software shipped by Concentric," a reference to Concentric Networks, a small Internet service provider, "only 17 percent were Internet Explorer." But those figures were for 1997. Mr. Boies entered into evidence a Microsoft document showing that by the first quarter of 1998, 100 percent of Concentric's browser shipments were Internet Explorer. Mr. Myhrvold repeatedly noted that Netcom, a Internet service unit of ICG Communications Inc. that has a contract with Microsoft, made no real effort to switch customers to Internet Explorer, testifying that one point in 1997 -- when 10 percent of Netcom's customers were getting the Microsoft product -- was "the high-water mark." But Mr. Boies then displayed a Microsoft document showing that in early 1998 the percentage had risen to 40 percent. Then Mr. Boies offered another Microsoft document showing that Netcom was actually able to control the browser choice of only a small percentage of the people who signed up for its service; most customers were handed to Netcom by computer makers, or by Netscape. That same document showed that Microsoft won an agreement with Netcom that 90 percent of the customers Netcom did control would switch to Internet Explorer. To that, Mr. Myhrvold said only that the author of the Microsoft document "was a pretty good salesman." Later, in response to a question from a Microsoft lawyer, Mr. Myhrvold denied a Government assertion that his staff had offered a British division of Uunet, an Internet service owned by MCI Worldcom, $500,000 to switch to Internet Explorer. He said he told his staff that "it would not be appropriate to tie payments to shipments of Internet Explorer." Moments later, Mr. Boies displayed still another email that Mr. Mhyrvold had written to a subordinate in Britain in which he said, "I think tying the payment to their shipping of IE is a great idea, though I would not do this formally." Mr. Myhrvold explained that the message had not meant what it said, and he had called the subordinate later to tell him not to tie the two. There was no record of that call, he conceded. On Thursday, Brad Chase, another Microsoft executive, takes the stand. In his written direct testimony, which was made public today, he defends Microsoft's contract requiring America Online to switch its customers to Internet Explorer. Mr. Chase writes that "nothing in the license requires AOL's subscribers to choose Internet Explorer." But a Microsoft memo introduced today suggests the cross-examination Mr. Chase is likely to face. In it, a Microsoft executive writes that "the typical AOL user is a novice." And as a result, AOL uses "the force-feed approach. They force feed the upgrade at log off," meaning that America Online automatically downloaded Internet Explorer to users when they logged off the service. An America Online executive testified earlier in the trial that very few users bothered to switch from Internet Explorer to Navigator, even though they were allowed to, because finding and installing the Netscape browser was too difficult.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Amazon.com Plans to Revise Its Ad Program
body: Faced with email rebukes from its customers, Amazon.com, the on-line bookseller, yesterday revised its advertising policy, pledging to disclose when book publishers pay the company to feature titles. The company said it was still figuring out the mechanics of the new policy, but it will take effect March 1. In the meantime, Amazon has expanded its book-return policy as a way to demonstrate its faith in its recommendations; in a company statement, Amazon's chief executive and founder, Jeff Bezos, said that it will accept a title from a dissatisfied customer "no matter how dogeared or worn it is." On Monday, The newyork Times reported that Amazon had fashioned an "E-merchandising" program for book publishers; in exchange for advertising fees of as much as $12,500, the program provides featured treatment of titles in categories that range from "What We're Reading" to "Destined for Greatness." Amazon, which did not disclose the advertising fees to its customers, contended that its sites were not for sale because its staff editors screened and vetted books worthy of highlighting. Yesterday's change in policy signaled a recognition that with its reviews, recommendations and friendly interaction with customers, Amazon is a hybrid -- both electronic bookseller and adviser, somehow different from bookstore chains or supermarkets that commonly sell shelf space for products. "We're always listening to our customers and it was clear that our customers had a higher expectation for us than the physical bookselling world," said Bill Curry, a spokesman for the company, which is based in Seattle. Mr. Curry said that customers had sent Amazon electronic mail expressing surprise at its advertising program. Mr. Curry said that Amazon would continue to offer the advertising program to publishers, but that it would create a system indicating which features are paid for. Amazon started the program last June and then expanded its scope and prices in January, attracting money called "cooperative advertising allowances" from many major publishers including Random House, Simon & Schuster, HarperCollins, Warner Books and Penguin Putnam. About 20 to 50 publishers were offered the program, and Amazon planned to extend the same opportunities to more publishers later this year. The program drew a mixed response from publishers: some smaller presses feared they would not be able to afford to participate, while larger publishers considered the promotions equivalent to the front table space or shelf-end caps offered for co-op advertising dollars by bookstore chains. For instance, Random House, now owned by Bertelsmann A.G., paid Amazon for featured treatment of Peter Jennings's best seller, "The Century." Simon & Schuster, a unit of Viacom Inc., backed titles on Amazon ranging from Stephen King's "Bag of Bones" to a seasonal Valentine's promotion for "Best American Erotica." The most expensive category for promotion was computer books, critical placement that resulted in significant sales increases for IDG Books Worldwide. Yesterday, Laurence J. Kirshbaum, chairman of Time Warner Trade Publishing, which includes Warner Books and Little, Brown & Company, called Amazon's new policy of openness "a sensible step" that will only enhance the credibility of the on-line bookstore and publishers. Time Warner had paid to feature more than a dozen of its titles, some of which experienced significant sales increases, including Roy Blount Jr.'s photo book of dog poetry, "If Only You Knew How Much I Smell You: True Portraits of Dogs," and Tom Grace's first novel, "Spyder Web." But Mr. Kirshbaum said he did not believe that Amazon's change in policy would have an impact on future promotions that are subsidized with advertising dollars. "I think the customers will respond to the new system because the publishers can muster very effective advertising concepts that will appeal to them," Mr. Kirshbaum said. "All we really want as publishers is a chance to display our wares and this will give it." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Jeff Bezos, chief executive of Amazon.com, the on-line bookseller. (Suzanne DeChillo/The newyork Times)(pg. C5)

title: Cellular Companies Agree To Make NetworksCompatible
body: Two groups of cellular telephone companies and equipment makers agreed today to make wireless networks that use competing digital technologies work together. The agreement would primarily affect networks in the unitedstates and Europe. The Universal Wireless Communications Consortium and North American G.S.M. Alliance groups represent such companies as the AT&T Corporation, SBC Communications Inc., the Omnipoint Corporation, Lucent Technologies Inc. and Ericsson A.B. As wireless service prices have fallen, customers are using their telephones more and demanding that telephone companies increase their coverage to make the phones work anywhere. Today's interoperability agreement will let about 225 million wireless customers worldwide use their telephones on every continent. "It dramatically expands the coverage area for members of both organizations," said Bob Stapleton, president of the Western Wireless Corporation, a member of the North American G.S.M. Alliance. The agreement applies to networks that use digital technologies known as time-division multiple access, or T.D.M.A., and global system for mobile communication, or G.S.M. T.D.M.A. is used by companies like AT&T and SBC in the unitedstates, while G.S.M. is found in Europe and is used by Omnipoint and Western Wireless in the unitedstates. T.D.M.A. phones do not work on G.S.M. networks and vice versa. The groups also plan to support each other's proposals for next-generation networks that will include Internet access, email and other data services to the International Telecommunications Union. The extended reach could make wireless services as ubiquitous as traditional telephone services, one industry executive said. "This opens up an increasingly competitive market between wireless and wireline," said Bo Dimert, who heads Ericsson's North American operations. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Lycos Deal Meets the New Internet Math
body: Events yesterday provided further proof that Internet investors prefer fantasy to reality. That proof came when Lycos Inc., the Internet portal service, said it would merge with the electronic shopping units of USA Networks Inc., including the Home Shopping Network, Ticketmaster and the partly independent Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch. The deal means that Lycos shareholders will go from owning 100 percent of a company with $75 million in revenue to owning 30 percent of a company with $1.5 billion in 1998 sales. Which is better? If this were a fourth-grade math problem, the right answer would be that having a smaller piece of a much bigger pie is clearly superior. But the new Internet math is different. Shares of Lycos fell 26 percent yesterday, to $94.25. That was a huge drop even on a day when the whole Internet sector fell. America Online was down 7 percent at $147.9375 and Yahoo dropped 11 percent, to 140.75. Indeed, the market was in such a sour mood that news announcements that would have pumped up stocks in giddier times were ignored. For example, America Online said yesterday that it had signed up a million new members in the first five weeks of the year, its fastest million ever, for a total of 16 million subscribers. But the even sharper drop in Lycos shares reflected the deflating of hopes by investors that all or part the company would be bought at a premium to its already inflated share price. The deal essentially was the reverse. Lycos is buying the assets of USA Networks and Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch by issuing many more of its own shares. Indeed, Lycos can be seen as paying a premium to USA Networks, which is the main reason that USA Networks' shares increased nearly 10 percent, to 41.625. But there is a more fundamental issue for Lycos's investors: even the best reality cannot compete with fantasy. Suddenly, the stakes in a small, rapidly growing company with seemingly infinite potential have become shares in a finite and measurable enterprise. The new company, which is to be known as USA Lycos Interactive Networks, will have 7,000 employees, 2,900 ticket outlets, and warehouses stocked with 18,000 items for sale. Robert J. Davis, the chief executive of Lycos, who will become the president and chief executive of USA Lycos Interactive Networks, argued that the stock market should still value the new enterprise as an Internet company. Home shopping, he said, should not be seen as a mature business but one at the vanguard of electronic commerce. "I have the ability to be the dominant portal in the world but also the dominant E-commerce entity," Mr. Davis said in an interview yesterday. Thus, he said, the new company should be valued the same way as the old one, at 30 times its projected 1999 revenue. By that yardstick, the combined company would be worth $45 billion. And the Lycos shareholders would see the value of their holdings double. Paul W. Noglows, an analyst with Hambrecht & Quist, agrees that the new USA/Lycos deserves a high Internet multiple. "No matter how you cut this, Lycos is worth more as a part of this venture than it was last night," he said. "It's an electronic commerce powerhouse, spanning television and the Internet." But investors saw it differently. The value of the new company, based on the Lycos share price, fell from $22 billion at Monday's close to $16 billion at yesterday's. And David Simons, an analyst with Digital Video Investments, says that other companies with both Internet and traditional businesses have not been accorded such relatively high stock prices. Indeed, several, including Barnes & Noble, Ziff-Davis and Creative Computers, have spun out their Internet activities to create independent stocks with the higher Internet multiple. "You are merging an Internet business with a traditional business," he said. "The question is, to what extent does this hybrid maintain its Internet valuation?" This is a question that investors will increasingly have to grapple with, said David B. Readerman, an analyst with Thomas Weisel Partners, as Internet operations are, quite logically, combined with television and other traditional media and commerce companies. The Lycos-USA Networks combination "is based on sound judgment, even though USA's assets are in lower-margin businesses than Lycos," Mr. Readerman said. "There may not be any pure Internet companies any more without some media involvement," he added. Mr. Davis of Lycos complained that this talk of lower valuation was unfair and perverse. "The value of Internet businesses has been based on the premise that we will build big, sustainable businesses with high growth rates and high revenues," he said. "I've done that now. It doesn't make sense for the market to say that now that I've done what it asked me to do, it should punish me." But then again, this is the Internet. It doesn't have to make sense.   http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft's Miscues
body: For all its economic and technological prowess, Microsoft is tone-deaf when it comes to public relations. Last week, in the latest of a string of fiascoes, the company was embarrassed at its antitrust trial by a video demonstration that turned out to have been clumsily doctored. But the question before Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson in Federal court is not images. It is whether the Justice Department is correct in arguing that Microsoft has illegally used its monopoly power to punish rivals and partners and expand its software business in other areas. So far the trial has demonstrated that the company faces a tough time challenging the Government's case. The original focus of the Microsoft trial was on whether the company illegally combined its own Internet Explorer browser with its basic Windows software in order to muscle aside the rival browser made by Netscape. It has expanded into a larger Government argument that Microsoft engaged in predatory conduct with rivals. Microsoft argues that it is not a monopoly because of the fiercely competitive and fast-changing environment in computers. Yesterday Microsoft repeated its line that special deals with Intuit and other companies are no different from various exclusive licensing arrangements throughout the industry. As for tying its operating software to a browser, Microsoft argues that doing so is defensible as long as consumers get a better product out of it. In the last few weeks, now that Microsoft is presenting its own case in the trial, several of its witnesses have tried to show that consumers do indeed benefit from fully integrated computer and software products. The Justice Department has repeatedly argued, on the other hand, that the chief advantage gained from product integration is to Microsoft itself, and that Microsoft tried to transform its operating system chokehold into a club, forcing competitors and consumers to choose products they might not otherwise want. Microsoft has a few more weeks to buttress its case. But what is interesting about the trial is the extent to which the economic and technological landscape outside the courtroom has changed even since proceedings began last year. Microsoft's argument that it is not a monopoly at present seems questionable. Most experts find that a 95 percent market share in personal computer operating systems is a monopoly. On the other hand, many of these same experts speculate that in a matter of years there may be other products offering access to the Internet for consumers. It may soon be possible to pick up a telephone, turn on a television or flip on a hand-held device to get on the Internet, without using Windows at all. But that is not the real world yet. Right now, the Justice Department is right to demand that Microsoft not use its current monopoly to restrict consumer choices. Microsoft has had many miscues in this trial, not least the videotaped testimony of Bill Gates in which he seemed to dodge about in a performance worthy of Bill Clinton. All the same, it is best not to see the drama as one of villains and heroes but rather one of competitors using every advantage to go after the competition. The Federal Government, applying antitrust principles more than a century old, has a constructive role to play in insuring that certain basic ground rules of fair competition are observed. In a rapidly changing environment, the entire industry benefits from unfettered competition and basic fairness. http://www.nytimes.com

title: More Peril for Microsoft With Videotape
body: The Microsoft Corporation once again today found itself in trouble with a videotaped demonstration in Federal court. And while even the Government lawyer who discovered the problem conceded, "I don't mean to imply that this is terribly critical," it adds to a growing body of evidence that the Justice Department is using to throw Microsoft's credibility into doubt. Last week, Microsoft played a videotape intended to demonstrate the advantages of integrating a World Wide Web browser with its Windows operating system. But over several days, the Government's lead trial lawyer, David Boies, pointed out so many problems and inconsistencies with the tape that Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson declared that he could not view it as reliable evidence. Today, Microsoft played another tape to demonstrate how much easier it was for a customer to sign up for Internet service on a computer running Windows 98 than it had been on a computer running the older Windows 3.1. On the Windows 98 machine, the sign-up was quite simple and took only about five minutes. On the older system, it took about 17 minutes, including long delays while Internet software was loaded onto the computer. Microsoft's new witness, Cameron Myhrvold, a vice president in the Internet Customer Unit division, supervised the production of the videotape. As soon as his cross-examination began, Mr. Boies pointed out that the Windows 98 computer in the video was using a faster modem, giving the newer system an unfair speed advantage. Mr. Myhrvold acknowledged the difference, but added that while using a faster modem "would have been a factor" on the Windows 3.1 machine, "most of the time was spent loading the software." After the court had adjourned for the day, Microsoft executives scoffed at Mr. Boies's question. Mark Murray, a company spokesman, acknowledged that the Windows 98 machine had used a modem running at 33.6 kilobytes a second, while the other computer used a modem running at 28.8. Of the 12 minutes difference between the operating systems, the modem speed accounted for only 22 seconds, he said. William Neukom, the Microsoft senior vice president for law and corporate affairs, declared, "The difference in the speeds of the two modems is meaningless, academic." Earlier in the day, when a Microsoft lawyer got a chance to question a previous witness, William Poole, a company vice president, he suggested that a key charge in the Government's antitrust suit was insignificant since it merely dealt with whether customers get to see a dancing Mickey Mouse when they visit a Web page. Cross-examining Mr. Poole on Monday, Mr. Boies entered into evidence Microsoft's contract with Intuit Inc., the maker of Quicken, the popular personal finance software, which set out the terms for Microsoft's agreement to carry an Intuit advertisement on the opening screen of Windows. A condition, Mr. Boies pointed out, was that Intuit and other companies signing these contracts had to agree that some Web pages would present a significant "degradation in appearance" for visitors using Netscape Navigator, the rival Web browser. In court today, Mr. Poole said that the Walt Disney Company had been the only company to honor the requirement and that Microsoft had made no effort to enforce the stipulation while the contracts were in place. And the only difference in content on the Disney site, he said, was that a Mickey Mouse cartoon danced across the opening screen for users of Microsoft's Internet Explorer while Netscape users saw no mouse. The judge chuckled and shook his head on hearing that. Later, however, Mr. Boies forced the witness to admit that even this enhancement was important to Microsoft. The company had been arguing that features like this would win millions of new customers.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Schwab Lands Feet First on Net;
Broker Leap-Frogs Rivals to Front of On-Line Trading
body: There are many brand-name banks and brokerage houses battling on the front lines of American investing. Only one of them, the Charles Schwab Corporation, has made peace with the Internet. Schwab, the quarter-century-old discount broker that has long cast itself as a Wall Street outsider, has converted most of its brokerage business to the Internet with an ease few analysts predicted. Moreover, it has quickly come to dominate the booming business of trading stocks on line. Its giant computing center in Phoenix handles almost a third of all Internet trading -- meaning that one in 20 stock trades in America passes through the Schwab system. All this has come while its rivals struggle with the new medium. Merrill Lynch & Company, the country's biggest retail broker, will begin a limited on-line trading service soon, but like other full-service firms has been slow to embrace the Internet. E*Trade, a leading on-line competitor, has suffered a streak of embarrassing trading shutdowns. Nearly all other Internet stock-trading companies talk of "earnings before marketing expenses" instead of profits. Schwab stands practically alone: It has made the wrenching transition -- and made money from it, too. But even as it becomes known as the Houdini of finance for its ability to squeeze profits out of difficult situations, it is undertaking an even trickier make-over. Schwab is trying to convert itself into a full-service brokerage firm for the Internet age. The idea is to use the Web to challenge -- more directly than ever before -- the retail arms of Merrill, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company, Citigroup's Salomon Smith Barney and others. It plans to offer more advice, research, analytics and even hand-holding to customers. Schwab is also fighting to distinguish itself from well-financed on-line trading competitors like E*Trade, Ameritrade and Waterhouse Securities that are clawing at its on-line dominance and offering lower prices. The transition will be closely watched by Schwab's competitors. All are trying to figure out how Americans will invest early in the next century, what role the Internet will play and how investment advice will be distributed. Schwab intends to hog the middle of the road, somewhere between Merrill on the full-service side and E*Trade on the discount side. But it will need sharp elbows to keep that space for itself. "Our mission now is to create a new model of a full service brokerage firm," said David S. Pottruck, Schwab's co-chief executive. "We are not a discount firm anymore." But Mr. Pottruck was careful to distinguish his vision from that of the existing full-service brokerage firms. "I mean a new kind of full-service firm," he said. "Not the kind that sells its own load funds and gives brokers free trips to Hawaii." Mr. Pottruck is a burly native of Levittown, N.Y., who wrestled and played football at the University of Pennsylvania. He had a brief stint on Wall Street before joining Schwab 15 years ago. Promoted to share the executive reins with the chairman, Charles R. Schwab, a year ago, he has made his message resonate: Schwab intends to go after the big Wall Street firms, which control much more of America's investment money than discount firms do, and it will use the Internet as its weapon. A visit to the company's San Francisco headquarters is like dropping in on a West Coast consultants' convention. The dress is Gap casual, the carpets are earth tone and the fixtures gray stone -- no marble or mahogany. And the nouns are all semiotic: segmentation, alignment, high-tech, high-touch and empowerment. But the mission is in many ways the logical extension of the idea that first prompted Mr. Schwab, the 61-year-old founder, to pioneer discount brokerages in the 1970's: distrust of Wall Street. Schwab began as a refuge for investors who felt they were burned by brokers who got commissions each time a stock was bought or sold. Schwab did trades for less and paid its brokers in salary and bonus, not commissions. Now, it is starting to give its customers many of the tools full-service brokers and professional money managers have at their disposal, but for a fraction of the cost. Using the Web, Schwab thinks it can make the desktops of its 2.2 million on-line customers resemble a broker's. Its site has industry research from Standard & Poor's, insider-trading reports from Vickers, live interviews with chief executives from Briefing.com, stock research from Credit Suisse First Boston and Hambrecht & Quist and a proprietary stock screening service that can pinpoint equities that meet an investor's customized criteria. Many are free, though investors with less than $100,000 in assets pay fees for research and some other services. Schwab is also working out the kinks in an email service that it says will make "warm calls" and "hot calls" to existing clients, as opposed to cold-call solicitations. The automated system is designed to monitor clients' portfolios and give them an electronic heads-up if the price moves up or down significantly or if a new equity or mutual fund comes closer than an existing holding to meeting investment goals. email is also seen as a way of knitting together the old and the new Schwabs. The old Schwab has 275 branch offices, places where customers still go to conduct transactions or open accounts. The new Schwab plans to expand those centers and build at least 200 new ones to form what Mr. Pottruck calls the "social fabric" of investing. They will hold seminars and training sessions. A client who sets up a child's trust, say, might get an email invitation to a live discussion on custody accounts and estate planning. "The way Barnes & Noble should compete with Amazon.com is not to offer books at lower prices but to create links between on-line and local services," Mr. Pottruck said. "How do you tie the two together and build relationships? That's the next phase on the Internet business." Schwab is also moving the line in the sand between itself and Wall Street investment banks, which typically work for companies that sell stock as well as customers who trade shares. That is a role that Schwab has often criticized as leading to conflicts of interest. Schwab still does not underwrite securities on its own, avoiding becoming investment bankers for companies. But it has agreed to join investment banks that act as lead underwriters in offering Schwab customers a chance to buy new issues, recognizing that it cannot compete across the board with the big brokerages without giving customers access to some hot initial public offerings. For the first time late last year, Schwab's name appeared on the cover of a prospectus for an initial offering. The company joined Hambrecht & Quist -- it has also reached stock distribution agreements with J. P. Morgan and First Boston -- to find buyers for the public offering of the Select Comfort Corporation, a Minneapolis-based maker of air-mattresses. Not a sexy high-technology issue, but Schwab added a dollop of data base marketing: It was able to find 250,000 of its clients who own a mattress from the company. Many were eager buyers of the shares. But perhaps the biggest initiative is its "signature services." The plan is to retain more wealthy customers, especially those who park more than $500,000 in assets. Many will get a team of perhaps eight designated consultants to help manage their portfolios. And though the company does not plan to advertise it, the wealthiest, if they choose, will be able to have a single broker monitor their investments. Much of this high-end push is part of Schwab's unstated goal to remove Merrill from atop the hierarchy of retail investing. Schwab acknowledges that the people it loses to full-service firms tend to be the wealthiest clients who say that they have graduated from Schwab's do-it-yourself ethic to a full-service broker. Part of the answer is Schwab's network of fee-based investment advisers. Through these 400 advisers so far, the firm refers customers who do not want to manage their own money to professionals who invest for them through Schwab. But for those who do not want to rely on advisers, Schwab's latest initiative is to convince wealthy customers that they can control their own money and get the help they need. "We want our customers to feel we can help them to trade out of a 20,000-share position without losing a point," Mr. Pottruck said, referring to the difficulty clients have making large trades electronically at predictable prices. "We will offer everything Merrill does and many things you can never get at Merrill." Merrill, whose nearly $1.5 trillion in customer assets is about triple what clients invest through Schwab, intends to be a major player on line as well as in its traditional business, said Jim Wiggins, a spokesman. "We have over 400,000 clients with $300 billion in household assets who already use Merrill on line to actively manage their accounts, and we are just scratching the surface," Mr. Wiggins said. "Anyone who thinks that Merrill Lynch won't be using the Internet to magnify the value we deliver to clients is making a major miscalculation." In fact, Schwab still often acts like an underdog, perhaps because some of its good fortune could easily be short lived. Schwab will surely face more competition from full-service firms in coming months, even though many of them face pressures from their brokers not to lure clients on line. Moreover, 20 or so low-cost on-line trading companies are nipping at Schwab's heels. Julio Gomez of Gomez Advisors, an Internet consultancy that rates on-line trading firms, ranks Schwab's Web service as No. 8 out of 20, in part because its $29.95 fee for each trade is at the top end of an industry where $8 trades are no longer unusual. E*Trade; DLJ Direct, a unit of the investment bank Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette, and Morgan Stanley's Discover Brokerage, among others, also offer some research. Schwab's 28 percent share of the on-line trading business is slipping, Mr. Gomez said. But Mr. Gomez also points out that Schwab is perhaps the only on-line broker to have grown out of its capacity problems. It can now handle 88,000 on-line customers at one time. E*Trade, by contrast, had three days within the last week when its trading system crashed, and Ameritrade had a costly shutdown early this week. Schwab, unlike its cut-price competitors, also has healthy profits to sustain marketing campaigns and capacity upgrades. But perhaps the sharpest arrow in Schwab's quiver is its willingness to cannibalize its business if it sees the market is changing direction. Take its transition to the Internet. Early last year Schwab stopped discriminating against on-line traders and gave them access to all services that its higher-paying clients had, even while lowering the cost of on-line trades. Mr. Pottruck estimated that pretax earnings would take a $150 million hit. In fact, Schwab's Internet integration did dampen earnings early last year because of reduced trading commissions and technical glitches. But by year-end, surging volume was more than compensating for declining commissions. And in a tough year for Wall Street, Schwab's revenues jumped 20 percent, and its net profits rose 30 percent, to nearly $350 million. Those numbers have made Schwab the envy of Wall Street, where the San Francisco firm was not long ago dismissed as a self-righteous pipsqueak. "Chairman Greenspan said buying Internet stocks is like a lottery ticket," said Michael Freudenstein, a finance industry analyst with J. P. Morgan, referring to the Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan. "Well, this is a lottery ticket with an earnings stream attached." Asked what some executives at the blue-chip investment bank Goldman, Sachs & Company were pondering when they debated strategy recently, a banker there answered with one word: Schwab. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Schwab's Web site can handle 88,000 customers at a time. Charles R. Schwab, left, and his co-chief executive, David S. Pottruck, are challenging bigger firms on line. (L. Lauterborn/Schwab)  Graphs: "Pumping Up the Volume" While many brokers have been slow to embrace on-line trading, Charles Schwab has shifted much of its business to the Internet with more success than predicted.  The graph shows that the revenue per trade may be lower . . . and Schwab's Average Commission since 1997  Another graph shows . . . but more people are trading on line, and what the Internet trades as a share of all trades at Schwab since 1997  A third graph shows . . . contributing to strong profit growth. And the growth of Schwab's Net Income since 1997. (Source: Charles Schwab)

title:
THE MARKETS;
N.A.S.D. Chief CautionsFirms About Internet Trading Risks
body: The head of the parent organization of the Nasdaq stock market says that the frenzy for trading stocks over the Internet may be creating an increasingly risky environment for investors, which could undermine the public's confidence in financial markets and perhaps even create greater regulatory scrutiny of brokerage firms. Frank G. Zarb, chairman of the National Association of Securities Dealers, which oversees Nasdaq and regulates its member firms, said last week in a letter to the chief executives of the organization's more than 5,000 members that the "frenetic" activity in the marketplace this year was posing greater problems for the industry. He suggested that the turbulence could have a "lasting impact on self-regulation." Mr. Zarb's letter came amid growing concern that the explosive growth of on-line trading in volatile Internet and high-technology stocks was creating a risky and unhealthy environment for small investors who regulators say may be naively trying to trade their way to fast riches. The Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulates the nation's financial markets, says it has been flooded with complaints about poor service and execution of on-line trades in recent weeks. The Attorney General of newyork, Eliot L. Spitzer, said last week that he would investigate the Internet trading industry. And two weeks ago, Arthur Levitt, the chairman of the S.E.C., cautioned investors to approach on-line investing with greater care. In the letter, which was issued last Thursday but posted on the N.A.S.D.'s Web site yesterday, Mr. Zarb said he was also responding to a growing number of complaints from investors about poor service and the execution of on-line trades. He said he was also concerned about customers' borrowing to trade in risky stocks, about advertisements and promotions' creating "unrealistic expectations" about making money trading on line as well as promises of instantaneous access to the market, even during volatile times. Mr. Zarb also said that some brokerage firms, including day-trading firms that house and train traders to speculate aggressively in the hopes of making a quick profit, were inappropriately extending credit to traders, pooling customer money and lending it to traders to use to try to make larger profits. Whether a speculative day trader or an on-line trader who may, for example, trade actively from home, Mr. Zarb suggested that member firms become more scrupulous in dealing with the problems arising from on-line trading. "Today's conditions suggest an increased responsibility for regulators -- for us and for state and Federal authorities -- to be extra vigilant," he wrote. "But nothing can help more than investor education." Officials at some of the largest on-line brokerage firms said that they were well aware of Mr. Zarb's concerns but that they were not trying to seduce investors into risky trading. "We are very concerned about acting responsibly," said Lisa Nash, a spokeswoman for E*Trade, which had technical problems last week that left many investors unable to trade. "We let our customers know about the risks and rewards of investing on line. We think they understand that risks have always existed before there was an Internet and after." Some day-trading officials, however, are disturbed by all the scrutiny being directed at day traders and the suggestions that day traders are creating volatile and risky markets. "They need a scapegoat," said Harvey I. Houtkin, president of All-Tech Investment Group in Montvale, N.J., a company that trains and houses day traders. "Why is this happening? Because the big boys are losing a lot of money to electronic trading." He added, "The real problem is with on-line brokers who can't execute trades, not with direct-access traders."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
Nasdaq Falls 3.9% in Broad Market Selloff
body: Stock prices were battered yesterday in a broad-based selloff that hit not only high-flying technology and Internet issues but also blue chips and small companies. The decline was most pronounced among Nasdaq stocks, which so far this year have posted the biggest gains. But the Dow Jones industrial average fell to its lowest level since Jan. 22, a performance that erased its gains last month and left the index below where it started the year. The Standard & Poor's 500 index, which had been held aloft by the stellar performance of a handful of stocks, also plunged, leaving it in negative territory for the year. The Russell 2000 index of small-company issues, which has badly lagged behind the performance of other market indexes, slumped. Internet stocks, under heavy selling pressure for the last few sessions, were hammered again yesterday. Still, a key index of Internet stock performance is well ahead for the year. The sharp drop in prices was not the product of frantic trading: volume on the newyork Stock Exchange was a relatively modest 736 million shares. And it was not caused by unexpectedly bad news. Analysts attributed the market's behavior to what they called the need for a correction after the sharp ascent by market averages since October. "This is healthier than the alternative, which is that the market's valuation becomes twice as large as the country's gross domestic product," said William Meehan, the chief market analyst at Cantor Fitzgerald. "The pullback we are seeing is still well within what many bullish people call a moderate correction." By the close of trading, the Nasdaq composite had shed 94.13 points, or 3.9 percent, to 2,310.79. It was the worst drop for the index in four months and its third-biggest point decline ever. Since it peaked on Feb. 1, the Nasdaq composite has declined by 8 percent. Still, it rose so much in January that it is up 5.4 percent for the year. The Dow average lost 158.08 points, or 1.7 percent, to 9,133.03. Of the 30 stocks that make up the index, only three -- J. P. Morgan, Coca-Cola and United Technologies -- rose in price yesterday. For the year, the Dow is now down a half percent. The Standard & Poor's 500 index, which for some time has been sustained by highfliers like Microsoft, Intel, Cisco Systems and Dell Computer, fell sharply, as prices of those issues plunged. The index closed at 1,216.14, down 27.63, or 2.2 percent. Since it peaked on Jan. 29, the index has declined 5 percent. It is now down 1.1 percent for the year. As the year began a number of analysts were predicting a comeback for small-company shares. Compared with the prices of large- cap stocks, they looked inexpensive. Thus far, that forecast has been inaccurate. The Russell 2000 index, a broad proxy for small-company stocks, fell 8.20 points yesterday, or 2 percent, to 403.13. For the year, the index is now down 4.5 percent. And then there are Internet stocks. Many forecasters labeled the sharp run-up in Internet stocks over the last few months a mania, and said they were looking for a sharp correction. That may be what is happening. Yesterday, Thestreet.com's index of 20 leading Internet issues fell 48.59, or 9.6 percent, to 456.26. Since its peak on Jan. 11, the index is down 22.5 percent. Still, for the year the index is up 12.2 percent. "What you are seeing is a correction of the leadership stocks of December and January, technology and the Internet," said Marshall Acuff, an equity strategist at Salomon Smith Barney. "That is happening because prices of these stocks had gotten way ahead of themselves" relative to their earnings' prospects. In recent weeks, a number of analysts have said the decline in Internet issues would be touched off by a sharp increase in the supply of stock in these companies. Network Solutions, a company that has the exclusive right to assign Internet addresses, was the victim of that phenomenon yesterday. The company announced that 4.58 million of its class A shares were sold at $170 each in a secondary offering. The increase in supply encouraged many to sell, and Network Solutions fell 26 1/8, to 148. The market's high valuation on Lycos, the No. 3 Internet search directory, did not stand up yesterday. Lycos, which since the start of the year has been the market's 10th-best performer, was pummeled yesterday after USA Networks, a media company, said it had agreed to buy Lycos in a transaction that implied a far lower market price for Lycos. Lycos fell 33, to 94 1/4, after USA Networks valued the combination at $22 billion, an amount analysts said implies a price of $91 a share for Lycos. "The Lycos deal was the dominant factor in what was a very poor day for Internet stocks," said Paul Cook, the lead portfolio manager for Munder Capital's NetNet fund. "That was why a lot of players decided to move out of a lot of these companies." Among other leading Internet stocks, Yahoo fell 17 7/8, to 140 3/4. And Amazon.com lost 9 1/8, to 100. Stocks of much bigger companies that have profited from their exposure to the Internet also fell back. AT&T dropped 3 5/8, to 87 3/8. Cisco Systems fell 6, to 95 15/16. And Microsoft declined 5 3/16, to 160 1/16. Among Dow stocks, Merck was the biggest loser, falling 4 1/2, to 145 3/8. And I.B.M. declined 4 1/4, to 162 3/4.  Treasury Prices Rebound Treasury bond prices rose for the first time in seven sessions yesterday as yields near three-month highs attracted buyers. Gains were limited, though, as the Treasury sold $15 billion of five-year notes, the first of its three-part quarterly debt auction. The price of the 30-year Treasury bond rose 20/32, to 99 9/32. The bond's yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, fell to 5.30, from 5.34 percent on Monday. title: Criteria Proposed for Issuing of Internet Addresses
body: Companies wanting a piece of the lucrative business of issuing Internet addresses will need at least $100,000 in the bank, $500,000 in liability insurance and a proven computer infrastructure, under mininum requirements proposed today by the nonprofit corporation that has been tapped to take over administration of the Internet. Until now, "domain registration," as the issuing of Internet addresses is known, has been the Government-sanctioned monopoly of Network Solutions Inc., a Virginia-based company that grew rich on the business. Coincidentally, Network Solutions priced a new stock offering today. In the more than a year that it has taken the Clinton Administration and the nonprofit Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers to open the business to competition, Network Solutions has set up an international network of partners to administer its domain registration business around the world. The proposed guidelines were announced just as Network Solutions completed what is expected to be the largest secondary stock offering ever by an Internet company. The offering of 4.58 million shares was priced today by J. P. Morgan & Company to open Tuesday on Nasdaq at $170 a share. The sale is expected to bring in about $780 million for Network Solutions' parent company, the Science Applications International Corporation, which will reduce its ownership in the company to 45 percent. Since 1993, Network Solutions, based in Herndon, Va., has had the exclusive worldwide right to assign Internet addresses that end in .com, .net and .org, charging $70 to register a domain name for two years. The result has been phenomenal growth, with net income in the first nine months of 1998 growing threefold, to $7.5 million. Although 1998 revenues have not yet been reported, analysts have predicted they could hit $90 million, compared with $6 million, $18 million and $45 million, respectively, in the previous three years. Today, the nonprofit corporation, known as Icann, also posted competing sets of proposed bylaws for the supporting organization being formed to help the nonprofit corporation decide when and how to add new "top-level domains" -- the three-letter suffixes of Internet addresses, like the popular .com. The guidelines and bylaws have been posted for public comment. Final versions are expected to be approved by Icann's board of directors at its next meeting, to be held in Singapore March 2 through 4. Icann's initial goal is to introduce five competitors to Network Solutions by the end of April. That test is expected to last about two months. Then Icann plans to let an unlimited number of companies around the world participate in the registry. But the board first must decide a number of other issues, including how it will pick the first five companies and how much they will have to pay Network Solutions for its operating of the main registry, the worldwide list of addresses that directs Internet traffic around the globe. Last month, Esther Dyson, interim chairwoman of Icann, said the board would likely hold an international lottery to pick the five test companies. That option, however, is being reconsidered because of opposition from a number of groups, including the European Union, which fears that domain registration will not be geographically balanced. Ms. Dyson said the board wanted to insure that the first five included a variety of big and small companies from different parts of the world. The guidelines say the primary criteria for selecting participants for the test phase "would be the applicant's technical and business capabilities to support the test and its willingness to commit the resources and to collaborate closely." Secondary considerations "include the extent to which the applicant's participation would promote early robust competition, wide geographic availability of domain name registration services, and accommodation of alternative business models and types." The proposed guidelines are outlined by Icann in a 30-plus page document posted on its Web site after the stock markets closed today. In addition to minimum technical, operational and financial issues, the criteria also deal with protections against fraud and infringement of intellectual property rights; data security, privacy and special technical requirements to protect Internet stability and operational integrity. Icann has proposed that applicants who want to compete in the test phase pay a $2,500 application fee. That would drop to $1,000 when competition is opened to an unlimited number of competitors. Companies would then be required to pay an additional $3,000 to $6,000 accreditation fee, and would give Icann $1 a year for each domain name registered. Network Solutions last year registered about 1.9 million new domain names. The monetary requirements are likely to raise a firestorm of protests from smaller Internet groups who fear that Icann is being driven by large corporate interests. However, Ms. Dyson said that the board was trying to "make it pretty easy to be one of these people." "We recognize that implementing changes in the domain name system will be a contentious issue," she said. "The point is to make the transition fair and the results fair. As long as everyone knows the rules and can play on the same terms, we will have achieved that. As the initial board considers comments on the guidelines, we will work hard with the Internet community to develop guidelines that strike everyone as reasonable, sound and transparent." Chris Bura, the president of a Pleasant Hill, Calif., company that plans to apply to be a test registrar, Alldomains.com, said the guidelines and capital requirements looked "doable." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Leading Recording Companies To Test On-Line Digital Sales
body: The five major recording companies said yesterday that they would, for the first time, begin to test selling albums as digital information transmitted over the Internet. A new system to be tested this spring is intended to sell authorized recordings in a medium where most of the music, legitimately copied and otherwise, is now available free. The system was announced yesterday in newyork by I.B.M., which created the software, and the five major recording copanies -- Sony, Time Warner, the Universal unit of the Seagram Company, EMI Group and Bertelsmann Music Group. The system would let consumers pay for an album by credit card, download it with a cable modem in less than 10 minutes, and play it back through computer speakers or record it on tape, digital minidisks, recordable compact disks or other devices now on the drawing board. A booklet would also be downloaded, to be printed on a color printer. The test, to begin between April and June, will involve 1,000 subscribers to Time Warner's Roadrunner cable modem service in San Diego. Initially, 1,000 album titles and several hundred singles will be available, the companies said; the number of selections is to more than double in the six to nine months the test will be conducted. The companies have not announced their pricing for the digital products. A growing number of music recordings are already available on the Internet free, as files that have been copied without permission from CD's in a format called MP3. Music companies have scrambled to find a way to sell legitimate copies of their products on line in what they call a "secure" format. In this test, they will employ a digital watermark containing information on where the music came from and who owns the rights; the data will be encrypted so that only a legitimate user can play it back. The music companies also want the on-line music to be "copy protected," enabling them to determine the number of digital copies a consumer could make. In December, recording and technology companies said they would collaborate on the Secure Digital Music Initiative, a uniform standard for codes to be included with music transmitted digitally. The San Diego test does not supplant the initiative, which is intended to set standards for a new generation of digital players. The MP3 files now found on the Internet can be copied freely, but are of unpredictable quality. "How do you compete with something that's free?" said Larry Kenswil, executive vice president of the Universal Music Group. "Obviously you can't compete on price. Instead, you have to offer higher quality, customer service and ease of use." The recording industry is counting on the spread of cable modems and other high-speed, or "broadband," connections, because conventional dial-up modems receive information too slowly to make digital distribution practical. Mr. Kenswil predicted that in five years, 20 percent of American homes would have broadband connections. In fact, he said, digital distribution of music would be an incentive for consumers to subscribe to cable modem systems. Paul Vidich, executive vice president of Warner Music Group, said that the industry "most enthusiastic about this, second only to the music industry, is the cable industry." The recording companies have no intention of abandoning plastic disks. They plan to announce specifications soon for DVD Audio, a CD-sized disk that will offer multichannel sound and be encoded to prevent digital copying. DVD audio disks will hold considerably more music than audio CD's, making them very hard to transmit over the Internet even at today's fastest speeds.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Executive Ends The Day Mostly Unscathed
body: At the Microsoft trial today, the biggest news was what did not happen: For the first time since the company began presenting its defense against Federal antitrust charges last month, a major company witness did not leave the courtroom with his head on a platter. All through the Government's presentation of its case against the Microsoft Corporation last year, company executives counseled patience. When their time came, they promised, they would present a robust, effective defense. But David Boies, the Government's lead trial lawyer, has forced the first three significant Microsoft witnesses to make damaging statements or to admit embarrassing mistakes, throwing serious credibility questions before Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson, who is hearing the case without a jury. Today's witness -- William Poole, senior director of business development for the company's Windows operating system -- managed to hold his own, though Mr. Boies did leave him mumbling and stammering and even backpedaling a few times. When he returns on Tuesday, he will try to hold his ground while Mr. Boies tries to push him back further. Mr. Poole oversaw the negotiation of contracts in which Microsoft required Internet companies to limit business dealings with the Netscape Communications Corporation, maker of Navigator, the Web browser that is the chief competitor to Microsoft's Internet Explorer browser. In exchange, Microsoft awarded the companies advertising space on the opening desktop screen of Windows. Under questioning, Mr. Poole acknowledged that Microsoft had estimated in 1996 that it could earn about $100 million a year by selling that advertising space but decided to charge nothing. Instead, the companies had to sign binding contracts to promote Internet Explorer and to cease all significant dealings with Netscape. Mr. Poole said one major company, Intuit Inc., maker of the popular personal finance program Quicken, had approached Microsoft "and asked us to let them use our browser" instead of Netscape's. Quicken uses links to Web pages for many of its services. But that testimony contradicted earlier testimony of Intuit's chief executive, William H. Harris. And Mr. Boies displayed an internal Microsoft email from 1996 that told another story. In it, William H. Gates, Microsoft's chairman, summarized for Brad Chase, another senior executive, a conversation with Intuit's chairman at the time, Scott Cook. "I was quite frank with him that if he had a favor we could do for him that would cost us something like $1 million, to do that in return for switching browsers in the next few months, I would be open to doing that," Mr. Gates wrote. But Mr. Cook was reticent, he said. A few weeks later, Mr. Chase reported back to Mr. Gates: "I talked to them again today. I just don't think they are prepared to jump this hurdle. I suggested that at least they ship both browsers." Mr. Poole said he had never seen the email exchange, even though it was entered into evidence in the trial many weeks ago. "Your lawyers didn't show this to you?" Mr. Boies asked. "I don't remember seeing it," Mr. Poole said. A Microsoft spokesman later said the company had issued a new and improved version of Internet Explorer between the time Mr. Gates negotiated with Intuit and when Mr. Poole worked out a contract. With some help from the judge, Mr. Boies also got Mr. Poole to admit that the restrictive contracts with Intuit and others were not standard practices for the company or the industry, as Mr. Poole had asserted in his direct, written testimony. After Mr. Boies repeatedly posed the question, only to get rambling, off-point responses, Judge Jackson finally interrupted, shaking his head as Mr. Poole set off again, saying: "No, No, No. Try to answer, Mr. Poole. Yes, no or I don't know." Mr. Boies was in the middle of asking his final question as court ended for the day, challenging Mr. Poole's assertion that "only 4.7 percent of users surveyed stated that they first became aware of a Web site that they now frequently visit through a pre-configured browser setting or start page." The issue is important because Microsoft and Netscape both ship their browsers with links already pre-loaded to important, money-earning Web pages. Judge Jackson adjourned court before Mr. Poole could find the reference he needed in the survey data. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Big Technology Issues Bolster Advance of S.& P. 500
body: Stock prices were mixed yesterday as bellwether technology issues rebounded after falling last week, but blue-chip securities and shares in small companies, including Internet stocks, slid. Traders and analysts said the market's performance was impressive in light of the sharp run-up in prices since October and several new pressures that could lead to a sharp selloff. "This is a pretty orderly way to digest a good run," said Michael Clark, head of unitedstates stock trading at Credit Suisse First Boston. "I still believe that while inflows are fairly strong, a bit more attention is being paid to valuation, so people are starting to take some profits," he said. "I think this is a healthy way to slowly let a little of the air out of the market." On the newyork Stock Exchange, a big drop in United Technologies helped to push the Dow Jones industrial average down 13.13 points, or a tenth of a percent, to 9,291.11. But the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index, led by rebounds in the technology giants Microsoft and Intel, gained 4.37, or nearly four-tenths of a percent, to 1,243.77. Led by technology companies, the Nasdaq composite index rose 31.30, or 1.3 percent, to 2,404.92. The Russell 2000 index of smaller companies fell 1.39, or 0.3 percent, to 411.33. And Thestreet.com's index of 20 Internet companies slumped 26.67, or 5.2 percent, to 504.85. Volume on the Big Board was 705.4 million shares, the slowest day so far this year. On the Nasdaq, just fewer than 883 million shares changed hands. Mr. Clark and others suggested that the threat of higher interest rates and a spate of new and secondary stock offerings would most likely constrain market indexes for some time. "New supply will hold the market back," said Michael Molnar, a managing director in retail sales and trading at Salomon Smith Barney. "But interest rates are clearly the biggest deterrent" to higher prices, he said. "If the Fed were to pop the liquidity bubble by either tightening monetary policy or changing their bias toward tightening, that could do it. No one has questioned the interest rate environment for months." Among individual stocks, Microsoft was the biggest gainer in the S.& P. 500, rising 5 1/4, to 165 1/4, after it said it would develop wireless Internet services with British Telecommunications. Intel, which was hammered last week, rebounded yesterday, rising 4 7/16, to 132. United Technologies was the biggest loser of the Dow stocks, falling 5, to 120. But big bank stocks also sustained losses. J. P. Morgan, a Dow stock, fell 2 7/8, to 99 1/4. And Chase Manhattan dropped 3 5/16, to 73 1/8. Shares of Internet-related companies and on-line brokerage firms also fell. America Online dropped 5, to 159. Yahoo lost 14 1/8, to 158 5/8. And Amazon.com declined 6 3/4, to 109 1/8. Ameritrade Holding fell 15 1/2, to 80, after its Internet and touch-tone trading services crashed for nearly half an hour yesterday morning. JB Oxford Holdings, another on-line broker, fell 3 9/16, to 8 3/16. And Siebert Financial fell 7 5/8, to 27 1/2. Elsewhere, Executive Risk, a specialty insurer, rose 21 1/8, to 65 1/8, after Chubb announced that it would buy the company for $71.71 a share. Chubb, the nation's 14-largest property and casualty insurer, fell 2 5/8, to 55 7/16. AMR, the parent of American Airlines, fell 2 15/16, to 57. The airline was forced to cancel 22 percent of its flights yesterday after pilots failed to show up for work in a dispute over AMR's purchase of Reno Air. And Boeing fell 1 1/16, to 36 3/8, after it was reported that China had ordered a freeze on new aircraft purchases and postponed aircraft deliveries. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average, since January 1998. title: USA Networks Said to Be in Deal With Lycos
body: USA Networks Inc. has agreed to take control of Lycos Inc., the fourth-most-popular network of Internet sites, people close to the deal said yesterday. The complex deal, which is expected to be announced today, would create a company valued at $18 billion and called USA Lycos Interactive Network. It would combine Lycos, which offers Internet search services, information and on-line communities, with USA Networks companies that sell goods on line, on television and over the telephone. These include the Home Shopping Network, Ticketmaster Online-Citysearch and ISN First Auction. Barry Diller, the chairman of USA Networks, would be chairman of the new company, and Robert J. Davis, the chief executive of Lycos, would be president and chief executive. The transaction is a bet that the best way to profit from the huge audience that sites like Lycos have built is not by selling advertising, as they have done so far, but by selling goods directly to Internet users. As users of Lycos searched for information about fashion, for example, they might see cubic zirconium offered by the Home Shopping Network. Local news could be accompanied by offerings of concert tickets from Ticketmaster. "There is a new convergence of entertainment, information and direct selling," said a person close to the deal. For USA Networks, the deal moves shopping properties that mostly do business over the telephone rapidly into the Internet age. "Electronic commerce has enormous wind at its back," this person said. "And notwithstanding what people say about the crazy valuations, over the next two or five years, we will find something that has a very real base." Until late last week, Lycos had been in negotiations to sell a stake to NBC, which is owned by General Electric, in return for on-air promotions. However several people close to the discussions said that the talks had begun to falter. Talks between Mr. Diller and Mr. Davis began in earnest last week, and Lycos was negotiating with both companies for a while before striking the deal with USA Networks. The deal is unusually complex because USA Networks has spun off a partial interest in its Ticketmaster-Citysearch unit to the public. Lycos will acquire the part of Ticketmaster that USA does not own from the public for 8.5 percent of the shares in the combined company. And Lycos will trade a 61.5 percent interest in return for the Home Shopping Network, ISN First Auction and USA Network's stake in Ticketmaster. USA Networks will have about 96 percent of the voting rights in the new company. Lycos and Ticketmaster shareholders will also receive warrants that would give them the right to increase their stake in the company by 6.25 percent, but only if its stock market value soars to the astronomical level of $45 billion. Based on Lycos's closing share price of $127.25 yesterday, the new company would have a market value of $18 billion. Though the Seagram Corporation owns 45 percent of USA Networks and could have blocked the deal, its three board members voted for it. One of several sites that started by helping people search the Internet, Lycos has moved to keep its audience from surfing away by offering ever more services from news to chat rooms to electronic mail. Now known as portal sites -- because they serve as gateways to all sorts of Internet activities -- Lycos and its competitors, Yahoo, Excite, Infoseek and others, have become attractive to big media companies. Last year, the Walt Disney Company bought half of Infoseek and incorporated it into its new Go portal. NBC bought a stake in Snap, a small portal. And earlier this year, Excite was bought by At Home, a service that offers high-speed Internet access over cable television wires. And Yahoo, the leading portal, bought Geocities, the largest collection of personal home pages. Lycos has been on an aggressive acquisition spree, buying a series of smaller Internet sites to expand its audience. In December, Lycos was the fourth-most-popular network of Internet sites, reaching 26 million people, according to Media Metrix. The most visited was America Online, followed by Microsoft and Yahoo. Yet Mr. Davis, the chief executive of Lycos, had said that the company wanted to sell a partial interest to a media company in order to receive the sort of promotion that Disney was providing to Infoseek. USA Networks has also been on an aggressive acquisition binge over the last two years, merging with Ticketmaster in 1997 in a deal valued at $800 million. It subsequently merged on-line operations with Citysearch, an on-line city guide, and sold 40 percent to the public. The Ticketmaster on-line business has a market capitalization of $4 billion. Last year, the company, then known as HSN Inc., also swapped 45 percent of its equity for Seagram's Universal Television, the USA Network and the Sci-fi Channel in a deal valued at $4.1 billion. The company then changed its name to USA Networks. USA Networks is effectively spinning off assets that represent 62 percent of its sales and will retain the Sci-fi Channel, Universal Television and the company's 16 television stations. The businesses contributed by USA Networks represent sales of $1.5 billion and cash flow of $562 million. Lycos had 1998 sales of $56 million. In general, media companies have moderate to high debt levels, while Internet companies have little debt. The newly combined entity is a hybrid in that it will have earnings, unlike may Internet companies, but will carry no debt. Mr. Davis will have a new five-year contract, and the company will keep its headquarters in Boston. The investment banking firm of Wasserstein Perella represented Lycos; Allen & Company and Lazard Freres represented USA Networks, and Goldman, Sachs represented Ticketmaster. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Barry Diller, the chairman of USA Networks, bets on a bright future for electronic commerce. (Reuters)(pg. C8)

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Shake-Up at BMW Stirs Speculation of Takeover The dismissal of two top executives at BMW on Friday will prompt renewed interest by other auto makers in buying the German maker of sporty coupes and sedans, but it remains unclear whether the controlling Quandt family wants to sell, auto executives said. Volkswagen and Ford both let BMW know last autumn that they were interested in buying the German auto maker, executives said in recent interviews. But BMW rejected both overtures without ever entering into formal negotiations because the Quandt family refused to consider a sale.  Page C10. Long Articles in Shorter Pieces The narrative newspaper series, with its focus on individuals, their trials and their emotions, is gaining converts, but it demands a large chunk of a reader's time. One solution is to make each piece shorter and let the narrative run for weeks.
