title: For Sale: On-Line Bookstore's Recommendations
body: The E-commerce pioneer Amazon.com strives for a clean look for its on-line bookstore. That is why executives consider it unnecessary to clutter its World Wide Web pages and pithy book recommendations with notices that publishers are starting to pay to have titles featured as "New and Notable" or "Destined for Greatness." The rapidly growing company began charging publishers modest fees last summer in a limited experiment. But this year, Amazon increased the offerings to publishers so that now $10,000 is the price tag for a premium package for a newly released computer book -- consideration that includes the top slot on the computer home page, an author profile or interview and "complete Amazon.com editorial review treatment." The practice -- which involves using money from publishers called cooperative advertising allowances -- is a sign of Amazon's growing power in the book industry, which appears eager to pay tribute to promote titles ranging from John Grisham's new novel, "The Testament," to Roy Blount Jr.'s photo book of canine poetry, "If Only You Knew How Much I Smell You: True Portraits of Dogs." It is a rather delicate move for Amazon, which has distinguished itself with its thoughtful editorial voice and its staff of editors, whose recommendations are featured prominently in terse, one-paragraph blurbs on its home pages for a variety of topics. From its crowded Seattle offices, Amazon has sought to create a community of book lovers, who have responded to the bookseller's advice about "What We're Reading" with grateful testimonials lauding the company for avoiding hype. Amazon's executives insist that their virtual territory is not for sale because the company reserves the right to reject books that do not meet their standards of quality. And they stress that they still feature a majority of titles without charge, frequently turning down submissions from publishers. However, several participating publishers said that the titles backed with advertising dollars were rarely rejected. "We don't take real estate on our home page and sell it," said Mary Morouse, Amazon's vice president for purchasing. "I can't just let anybody believe that you give us a check and we're going to put it up there." Yet the new program has evoked a variety of responses from publishers. Some are reluctant to discuss the blurring line between editorial and advertising. Others view the practice as an exciting opportunity that is no different from the terrestrial custom of selling display space in bookstore chains and supermarkets. And then there are the doubting publishers who view Amazon's move as an ominous signal that the David in the competitive Internet book wars is starting to lumber like Goliath. "Amazon does have this kind of karma, as if it were a big independent store, and now they're putting that at risk," said Daniel Simon, publisher of Seven Stories Press in Manhattan. "They're booksellers, but in some respects they're like a book review, with people turning to them to see what's good. They have a very special relationship with their readers and you think they should recognize that they're putting it up for sale." Amazon's fierce No. 2 competitor, Barnesandnoble.com, is also preparing to offer cooperative advertising this year to publishers although it has not publicly released any details. Its new chief executive, Jonathan Bulkeley, promises clear distinctions between editorial material and advertising, possibly by graphically separating advertising from editorial text. "There are areas of editorial that are never for sale at any price," Mr. Bulkeley said, adding that Amazon is "messing with the consumer's brains if they're trying to play both sides, but maybe they can execute it." "But it will always be a question in my mind: Is this 'destined for greatness' or is this paid for?" he said. At Amazon, there was considerable discussion about how to design the program that the company labels "E-merchandising." Mrs. Morouse said that a critical concern "was that we might have a perception that we're selling placement," but she said that the company believed it had resolved that issue by giving editors the power to reject books that were nominated by publishers. The company is also experimenting with a cooperative advertising program for videos and compact disks, which it also sells on line. Asked to list the specific benefits available to publishers, Mrs. Morouse declined, saying that the material is "confidential" for competitive reasons. However, internal price documents obtained by The newyork Times indicate that Amazon has increased the scope and price of its cooperative advertising program since it started offering opportunities last June. The company does not accept advertising dollars for its basic listings of books, which include information about the price and various reviews from critics and readers. With its expanded merchandising program, it offers packages that include a wide variety of features such as its email alerts to customers about not-yet-published books or placement in the "What We're Reading" slots of category pages for cooking or mysteries and thrillers. In the early experimental stages of its cooperative advertising program, Amazon listed a price of $500 to put a title on a list labeled "What We're Reading" for two to three days. With its new price list for the first half of the year, it can cost as much as $5,000 a title to promote a children's book in the program, which offers coverage in the "Destined for Greatness" slot on a Web page devoted to best sellers or a top position in Amazon's Kids Superstore home page. For a popular adult trade book, $10,000 is the price of a "Tier 1" premium package that among other things includes an author profile, feature coverage in the "Destined for Greatness" category and announcements on the home page touting the book's on-sale date. Simon & Schuster sought such treatment for its marquee author, Stephen King, whose novel of haunted love, "Bag of Bones," was also promoted as part of the package with "Bestsellers Delivers" email alerts to thousands of customers. Typically, publishers are more generous with money for well-known authors because they have larger marketing budgets to spend on best-selling writers like Mr. King or John Grisham. In coming months, John le Carre's new novel, "Single & Single," will be featured in a similar fashion. Such promotions do not contain any notice or visual clue to indicate that publishers have backed the recommendations with advertising dollars. During the development of its merchandising program, Amazon decided not to include tags because executives believe that they can provide adequate protection for customers through screening of books by experienced editors, who specialize in particular subject categories and often sign their names to email messages suggesting worthy books. "I think it would be more distracting to have a book tagged," Amazon's Mrs. Morouse said. "I think that would clutter it up. The customer experience is really clean and I want to keep it clean." Thus far, Amazon's advertising opportunity has been limited to about 20 to 50 publishers, many of them large companies like Random House, Simon & Schuster, Penguin Putnam, HarperCollins, IDG and Warner Books. But Amazon has plans to expand its offerings to the next tier of 500 publishers and expects to promote the program at the book industry's trade convention in April. The program is as much of an experiment for publishers, who are also trying to determine the effectiveness of this approach. IDG Books Worldwide, in Foster City, Calif., is so pleased with the results of its participation that it is increasing its on-line marketing. For $2,500, it placed its "Tax Guides for Dummies" on a special seasonal tax center Web page and watched its sales increase 56 percent after it was posted Jan. 15 and highlighted in the "Amazon.com Recommends" feature, which lauded the title as one of a handful of "bellwether" guides. The Dummies tax guide also appeared in the "New and Notable" category of Amazon's business and investing Web page. "In a virtual world, placement is critical," said Steven Berkowitz, president of IDG, who said the company had paid to feature at least 20 titles and would continue to do so. The program works well, he said, because customers feel "the titles are recommended." Warner Books and its sister company, Little, Brown & Company, are still evaluating the best strategies for advertising on line after promoting more than 15 books through the program, according to Sarah Ford, who manages on-line accounts for Warner. They paid to feature Roy Blount Jr.'s book of puppy poetry ("What does that mean 'expensive shoe?' I ate it because it smelled like you." ) in Amazon's gift center during the holiday season and saw sales soar to 1,000 copies a week from about 100.  Amazon's reviewer had advised readers, "You'll never be able to resist this entertaining and affectionate look at our canine friends." Ms. Ford said results were also significant for an on-line promotion of "Spyder Web," a techno-thriller from Warner Books that appeared in the "What We're Reading" and "New and Notable" slots of Amazon's mystery and thriller home page. In its review, Amazon lauded "Spyder Web," for its "cool, careful structure" and the promise of its first-time author, Tom Grace, who may represent "the next generation of Tom Clancys." Other critics were more reserved; Kirkus Reviews, which also appeared on an Amazon listing, labled the book "a spirited if clunky techno-thriller." Amazon's reviewers also praised other books placed by Warner and Little, Brown. They called Michael Connelly's "Angels Flight" "another masterwork" and featured it on its mystery and thriller page under the heading "Amazon.com Recommends." They also commended "Toyer," a featured title placed by Little, Brown, as a "driving (sometimes melodramatic) suspense novel." The newyork Times Book Review panned the same title, about a lunatic who disables a series of female victims with a gruesome surgical procedure, as a "macabre first novel" that is "stunning at first glance, but hollow at the core." The merchandising of featured books can come at a cost, but Amazon stresses that there are still books worthy of highlighting without charge. For example, it gave prominent placement free to "Careless Love," the second volume of Peter Guralnick's biography of Elvis Presley, and to the novel "Amy and Isabelle" by Elizabeth Strout. "With our home page, the overwhelming majority of featured books in a given month do not have co-op dollars behind them," said Bill Curry, a spokesman for Amazon, who noted that Amazon's list of top 20 titles last Friday contained at least nine that were featured without advertising support. That assurance, though, is not entirely comforting to smaller publishers who lack large advertising budgets to back their books. "It's terrible, because I've been in love with Amazon," said John Oakes, the publisher of Four Walls Eight Windows in newyork. "They're very efficient. They really do a good job. You can't tell me that they would pick the same books. If they went to people and said, 'We've chosen these books,' there's obviously no independent publisher who's going to pay 12 grand." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "Selling More Than Books" Amazon.com sometimes sells editorial placement and treatment to publishers without telling consumers that this prominence has been bought. title: Internet Auction System Set For Pricing Stock Offerings
body: William R. Hambrecht, the longtime Silicon Valley investment banker, plans to introduce a system for underwriting initial public stock offerings through the Internet. While other firms have given on-line investors an opportunity to get in on the ground floor of new stock offerings, Mr. Hambrecht's approach would have a new wrinkle: through an on-line auction. The new approach is to be announced today by W. R. Hambrecht & Company, the investment banking boutique he started last year after leaving Hambrecht & Quist, which he co-founded in 1968. His new firm intends to cater to the current fashion among small technology companies of selling stock to the public on line. E*Trade, the on-line broker, recently took a partial interest in a new on-line investment bank, E*Offering, that is backed by another Silicon Valley banker, Sanford Robinson. Wit Capital, currently the leader in offering new shares via the Internet, has participated in several dozen initial stock offerings by big Wall Street houses, making a portion of the shares available to investors on line before public trading begins. And Wit has attracted competition from a number of other firms including Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette and Charles Schwab. But Mr. Hambrecht wants his system to be more than an adjunct to traditional new offerings, in which the initial price is set by a big brokerage firm and most shares are allocated to its favorite customers. Mr. Hambrecht intends for the price and allocation of shares to be set completely on line through what is called a Dutch auction. Potential investors in a planned stock would log into the firm's system and indicate the highest price they would be willing to pay for a given number of shares. The offering is set at the highest price at which there is enough demand to sell all the shares. Anyone who bid at that price or higher is allocated shares at that price. Everyone else is out of luck. The first market test of the system would be with an offering for Ravenswood Winery, the Sonoma County, Calif., maker of a well-regarded zinfandel. Ravenswood, which filed its offering with the Securities and Exchange Commission last Friday, hopes to raise about $11 million. Compared with a traditional offering, this approach would probably mean higher prices when going public and, therefore, more money for the company issuing the shares. Mr. Hambrecht also contends that the approach will mean less frenzied trading by investors in search of a quick buck. "We want to put the issuer together with the people who want to own the stock for the long term," he said. Mr. Hambrecht plans to charge the companies issuing stock a fee of 4 percent of the capital raised, compared with 7 percent charged by a typical Wall Street underwriter.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Joint Venture Aims to Help The Internet Go Wireless
body: In what is being billed as the next giant step in the Internet revolution, the Motorola Corporation, the maker of wireless communications products, and Cisco Systems Inc., which provides Internet equipment, plan to form an alliance that would build the world's largest wireless Internet system. The project is the most ambitious effort yet to build a global network that would enable businesses and consumers to have high-speed Internet access to email and faxes without the burden of wires, cables or even walls. The plan, which is expected to be announced Monday at a cellular telephone conference in New Orleans, makes Motorola and Cisco Systems the latest communications and networking giants to join forces in an attempt to capitalize on the increasing popularity of the Internet and the rapid growth of wireless communications products. Over the last year, several telecommunications companies have announced plans to offer new services or upgrade their wireless communications operations so that businesses and consumers may have some access to the Internet. The AT&T Corporation, for instance, is already offering wireless service that taps into electronic mail and Internet information. The race to transform communications through the Internet has also led to several giant mergers that could result in greater wireless access. In June, Northern Telecom Ltd. of Canada, one of the largest makers of telecommunications gear, said it would acquire Bay Networks Inc., a large data networking company. And just last month, Lucent Technologies, the former research arm of AT&T, announced its acquisition of Ascend Communications, a leading provider of Internet equipment. Executives at the Microsoft Corporation, Apple Computer Inc. and Qualcomm Inc., the wireless communications outfitter, have also expressed an interest in developing products related to wireless Internet access. "This is part of a trend," said Roberta Wiggins, a wireless communications analyst at the Yankee Group in Boston. "People have been saying: 'There are all these people with cell phones and all these people accessing the Internet, and at some point people are going to put these two things together.' " While Ms. Wiggins and other analysts say that developing a wireless system could be costly and cumbersome -- with competing and incompatible systems trying to transmit bulky data and video into wireless units -- officials at Motorola and Cisco say their vision of a world where automobiles could get tuneups by wireless signals and sales executives could obtain company information from a remote place is just beyond the horizon. "This extends the Internet to a world without wires," said Don Listwin, executive vice president at Cisco, based in San Jose, Calif. Over the next four or five years, Motorola and Cisco say they plan to invest more than $1 billion to create a system capable of transmitting voice, data and video over existing cellular telephone stations directly to wireless telephones, laptop computers and other devices. The system would create a new line of products for Motorola, a new generation of wireless networking gear for Cisco and perhaps even signal the convergence of several existing communications products, like pagers, cellular telephones, televisions, radios and computers. "The goal is that instead of having four or five communication devices in your briefcase, you'll have one or two," said Doug Wills, a spokesman for Cisco. The two companies also plan to open four jount research and development centers, two in the unitedstates and two abroad. A critical piece of the puzzle, Motorola and Cisco say, is that the wireless transmissions would be delivered using an Internet Protocol platform would be compatible with all wireless formats. Unlike analog or current digital platforms, the companies say that the Internet Protocol, or IP platform, will be able to more effectively deliver and bundle voice, data and video feeds through cellular stations. What is novel about the effort, the companies say, is that they plan to adopt an "open" standard. In other words, they plan to create a wireless industry standard that could be adopted by any company that wants to develop different or competing products. Such an open standard, officials say, would be different from other wireless Internet efforts now under development. The new IP framework will be published this spring in a "white paper," the companies said. For Motorola, which has stumbled of late in the world of wireless communications, the deal with Cisco is an attempt to help resurrect its reputation as an innovative company. After two years of earnings shortfalls and market share losses tied to its line of wireless telephones, Motorola has been on an aggressive path to new wireless ventures. The company, which is based in Schaumburg, Ill., and had sales of $29 billion in 1998, has a huge stake in Iridium, a satellite venture that offers voice and paging systems. In May, when sharp cuts were being made in its work force, Motorola abandoned a plan to spend $13 billion to build what it called its Internet in the Sky project, a satellite network capable of delivering high-speed data communications anywhere in the world. Instead, Motorola said it would invest about $750 million in Teledesic, a low-orbit satellite venture that also intends to deliver high-speed access to the Internet, beginning in 2003. The new wireless venture with Cisco, officials at Motorola say, is different but would be compatible with Iridium and Teledesic, which was founded by William H. Gates, the chairman of Microsoft, and Craig McCaw, the cellular telephone pioneer. Now, company officials say, they have hit upon a revolutionary scheme. "With this system you can get Internet information any time, anywhere," said Bo Hedfors, senior vice president at Motorola. As for Cisco, executives say the new venture will strengthen its move into the telecommunications equipment market, where it is battling companies like Lucent and Nortel. By forming an alliance with Motorola, Cisco -- which among other things sells networking gear to telephone service providers -- is staking out firmer ground in its efforts to persuade global companies to use its equipment and the Internet to transfer information. Though some analysts insist that Motorola and Cisco face many hurdles in creating a wireless Internet system, including the prospect of transmitting bulky video feeds over a wireless network, the two companies say the framework they have outlined has already won strong support from big telephone service providers like Sprint, Nextel and Airtouch Communications.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Microsoft Is Starting Web Site Aimed at Big Audience: Women
body: The Microsoft Corporation is set to introduce a Web site for women today, hoping to capture what many feel is the largest and fastest-growing market on the Internet. Called Women Central, the site will feature content from Women.com, the largest on-line publisher of women's material, as well as original material, including Microsoft's own Underwire on-line magazine. The company has signed the Unilever Corporation as the site's primary sponsor. The new site will be a channel on Microsoft's revamped MSN network, the fledgling Web site that started out as its own on-line service three years ago and has since undergone several transformations. Microsoft would not disclose how much it was spending on the new site. With Women Central, Microsoft hopes to tap into what Jupiter Communications, a new-media research company, calls the fastest-growing audience on the Web, a market expected to grow to 65 million in 2002 from 45 million today. Last year, according to Jupiter, 55 percent of newcomers to the Internet were women, up from 50 percent in 1997. In designing the new site, Microsoft hopes to help women do what they do best on line: stay put, said Michael Goff, MSN's director of programming. Men tend to surf the Web and jump from site to site, Mr. Goff said, but women are likely to visit fewer sites for specific tasks like joining on-line discussion groups or buying something. Microsoft is hoping Women Central will become a so-called portal site for women, where they can find most of what they want on the Web, including shopping and on-line discussions. But while women may represent the fastest-growing segment on the Web, the market is already crowded, and whether the company will find the right formula is anybody's guess. In November, NBC bought a stake in iVillage, another site aimed at women. And just two weeks ago, the Hearst Corporation announced a joint venture with Women.com. Through the deal, Women.com gained distribution rights for Cosmopolitan, Good Housekeeping and Hearst's other women's magazines.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Plan for Free PC's Has a Few Attachments
body: The personal computer, already dropping precipitously in price, may in some cases become free -- with a few strings attached. In a variation on a popular cellular telephone business model -- sign up for service and pay nothing for the phone -- a Southern California start-up, Free PC Inc., plans to announce today that it will give away Compaq personal computers and a free Internet connection, too. The catch: Users of the computers must accept advertisements that will constantly be displayed on the 15-inch screen, whether the person is on the Internet or operating the computer off line. Not only that, but consumers who want to register for a free PC will have to answer some 20 questions about themselves, involving income, education and the like. The company will then decide who actually gets a free computer, based on who best fits the demographic profiles that advertisers are seeking. "The price of hardware and a connection has come down dramatically," said Donald S. La Vigne, chief executive of Free PC. "There are a lot of people who still aren't participating and a lot of marketers who want to get at those people." There could be a chicken-or-egg complication: applying for a free computer will require visiting the company's Web site, www.free-pc.com, where Free PC intends to start registering applicants today. Free PC, based in Pasadena, Calif., plans an announcement today at the Demo Conference, a technology industry gathering in Indian Wells, Calif., near Palm Springs. Free PC is the brainchild of Bill Gross, the chairman of Idealab, a Pasadena-based Internet business incubator and venture capital firm. Other investors include the media executive Barry Diller. Mr. La Vigne declined to give details about several key aspects of the business. He said the PC's were ones that might normally retail for around $600, for example, but he declined to specify their power and processing speed. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Prospectus;
Can a computer program figure out the market? A former analyst and a mathematician are betting that theirs can.
body: SILICON ALLEY in newyork is known for many things, but not as a hotbed for advances in computer science. Mention genetic algorithms or artificial intelligence, common parlance among computer scientists, and eyes may very likely roll among even the most respected new- media executives in newyork. In fact, an almost Luddite attitude toward hard technology seems to prevail in Silicon Alley, where Bikini.com, "the world's biggest beach party," is an example of the cutting edge. On the fringes of Silicon Alley, though, can occasionally be found a company like the Intelligenesis Corporation, which was founded in early 1997 by Ben Goertzel, a mathematician, and Lisa S. Pazer, a former Wall Street economist and analyst. Intelligenesis is trying to change the way people measure business risks or make buying decisions by combining, in a software program called Webmind, elements of the Internet with artificial intelligence technology or "machine learning," by which the software can, for example, "remember" who Alan Greenspan is and why he matters. The technology is the brainchild of Dr. Goertzel, who received his Ph.D in mathematics at age 22 from Temple University, then did research at the University of Western Australia and later taught mathematics, computer science and psychology at City University of newyork. "For a long time, I had been designing an architecture for artificial intelligence, but didn't have the machine to do it on," said Dr. Goertzel, now 32. "When I started using the World Wide Web, I realized it was a metaphor for the brain -- that the Web could be a mind." Webmind gathers and processes what it perceives as "human intelligence" data from text documents, like news articles -- whether on the Internet or corporate networks -- to help users spot trends or make predictions. The results, which can be presented as numbers, a chart or perhaps eventually even a sentence, are meant to complement rather than replace traditional mathematical modeling -- to help analysts, in a sense, to read between the lines. Ms. Pazer herself left off trying to outguess Mr. Greenspan, the Federal Reserve chairman, and quit Wall Street in 1993 to write a novel. But after coming across Dr. Goertzel's research on the Web, she put aside her fiction project to start Intelligenesis, which she now serves as president and chief executive. Here is how she explains Webmind: "If you want to try to determine whether Greenspan is likely to raise interest rates, Webmind can query news archives for Greenspan's comments over the last six months. Because it understands aspects of natural language, it can give a qualitative answer by building a graph giving weight to each of his comments and showing how he reacted in the past in relation to his comments. You don't search for documents; you search for answers." At full throttle, the software is supposed to be able to answer specific queries that depend on establishing relationships, like "How much money did the unitedstates give to Russia in 1998?" Ms. Pazer contends that Webmind has far-reaching applications. "The financial market is our proving ground," she said. "We can measure risk and volatility. But the technology could be used by anyone trying to evaluate risk or isolate trends." The list of potential users ranges from risk managers at insurance companies to market researchers to political strategists. But Webmind is still in its infancy. Intelligenesis is currently testing the software with potential customers and has a demonstration for qualified users at its Web site, www.intelligenesis.net. "We have to prove to them that the technology works," Ms. Pazer said. If they do that, Dr. Goertzel and Ms. Pazer hope to develop partnerships, supplying Webmind to financial news services or other on-line information providers, in a revenue-sharing arrangement. As the Webmind brand becomes more established, Ms. Pazer would look for such partnerships to give way to straight licensing deals. Though the business viability of Intelligenesis's product remains to be seen, the company has attracted the involvement of some influential people. The vice chairman, for example, is John B. Evans, a co-founder and chairman of another Alley-based company, Biztravel.com. Danny Hillis, co-founder of the supercomputer company Thinking Machines, who is now vice president of research and development in the Walt Disney Company's department of imagineering, recently joined the Intelligenesis strategic advisory board. Among others who are watching the progress of Webmind is Alexander Chislenko, a researcher at the Media Lab at Massachusetts Institute of Technology who has followed Dr. Goertzel's work for some time, because it complements some of his own. "I think it's a credible technology, and the approach is promising," Mr. Chislenko said. He predicted that Webmind would prove valuable in modeling some parts of the financial market that other technologies cannot. But Mr. Chislenko cautioned, "No technology can predict the whole market." Backed solely by private investors so far, Intelligenesis employs nearly 30 people, with a heavy mix of programmers trained in the social sciences -- some working from the company's office on Lower Broadway, others commuting by way of the Internet from Norway, Russia, Brazil and Australia. Dr. Goertzel and Ms. Pazer contend that all the really significant predictions and decisions that people make are, in the end, based on human psychology. And Webmind, they say, can use artificial intelligence to translate the multitudinous outpourings of human psychology into valuable data. "When you think about Webmind, think about being at a cocktail party," Ms. Pazer said. "Think if you could process not just the conversations you had, but all the conversations in the room." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (P. C. Vey)

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
One Man's Dream to Spin a Faster Web
body: As Alan Huang sees it, the key to the Internet's future may lie in a simple card trick. In a restaurant here recently, Mr. Huang, a 50-year-old former Bell Labs data network designer, used a new deck of playing cards to help explain how an esoteric branch of mathematics known as group theory offers a simple solution to the coming explosion of Internet traffic. He separated the cards into three piles, then reassembled them into a single deck, which he riffled with a flourish to show that they were in seemingly random order. After several more times of separating them into three piles and reassembling the deck, he uttered, "Abracadabra." As if by magic, the cards had been reordered into the original sequence and suits of the new deck. Mr. Huang offered the card trick, well known among magicians as the Grand Tour, as a simple demonstration of a type of mathematics called group theory -- in which it is possible with a given set of numbers to change their sequence and then reorder them by repeatedly sorting them by using a specific mathematical function known as a generator. But more to his business point, Mr. Huang presents the card trick as a symbol for the new method -- an efficient generator -- he says he has discovered for sorting out the welter of data that often collides at the Internet's bottlenecks. Whether theory can translate to practice, though, remains a very open question. Despite some impressive credentials in computer-networking circles, so far he has found no backers and has depleted most of his life savings in an effort to keep his technological dream alive. If his technique does work, there would seem to be great demand for it. Almost everyone agrees that greater Internet efficiency will be crucial as vast new torrents of data pour onto the network through new voice and video communications services. What is still subject to debate is how best to accommodate this traffic. Industry leaders like Cisco Systems Inc., the biggest maker of so-called router hardware for directing network traffic, insist that the only way to increase the current Internet's carrying capacity is to build bigger, more expensive routers. But Mr. Huang, card deck and group-theory mathematics in hand, contends that he has conceived a novel way to string together the kind of less-expensive routers already widely used on the Internet to expand its data-carrying capacity. And yet, if the prevention of Internet traffic jams is as deft as Mr. Huang's card trick suggests, why have no big companies or rich investors been willing to give him table stakes? Deaf ears are hardly the reception that one might expect for a researcher with Mr. Huang's credentials. As an AT&T Bell Laboratories researcher in 1982, he was the co-inventor of a traffic-routing approach to computer networks called Batcher Banyan switching, one of the first prototype data networks intended to carry both voice and video. For several years it held the world speed record for a data network of its type. Then, in 1990, while still at Bell Labs, Mr. Huang grabbed national attention when he led a research team that built the world's first optical processor -- an information traffic controller for data conveyed as laser light. Though the invention has yet to make its way into a commercial product, many researchers still think that optical switching will become an essential component for the data networks of the future. But as Mr. Huang now seems to be finding out the hard way, theoretical research does not necessarily translate into the practical ideas that investors and manufacturers are willing to bankroll. "We looked at his idea and it was solid research," said Mike Volpi, vice president of business development for Cisco Systems. "But what is lacking is a practical implementation." In other words: What may work in the ivory tower of academic research may not prove viable in the chaotic real world of the Internet. For Mr. Huang, the Bell Labs ivory tower was shaken by AT&T's decision in 1995 to break into three companies and to split the Bell Labs team between two of them -- the remaining AT&T communications company and the new Lucent Technologies equipment company. At the same time, Mr. Huang was hearing the Internet's entrepreneurial siren song. And so in 1995 he headed back to Silicon Valley, where he had been an electrical engineering graduate student at Stanford University years earlier. Mr. Huang set up a company, Terabit Routers, that initially pursued the idea of building a super-router based on optical switching. But after about a year, while reading the literature of group theory, a branch of mathematics credited to Evariste Galois, the early 19th-century French mathematician, Mr. Huang had an epiphany. Maybe bigger and more complex was not the answer to Internet routing. Maybe there was a way to draw upon the mathematics of group theory and create the order from seeming chaos that might let data networks operate much more efficiently -- so much so that clusters of cheap off-the-shelf routers could be harnessed into acting as a new, faster, more powerful type of router. Since working his router ideas out on paper three years ago, Mr. Huang has diligently solicited Silicon Valley's venture capitalists, hoping to convince someone that his idea deserves financing. But he is finding that esoteric and high-risk technology concepts can be more difficult to sell to venture capitalists at a time when simple get-rich-quick ideas for Web commerce seem much more in vogue. "If you have to have mastered advanced physics, it's harder to understand some technologies than the idea of selling wedding stuff on line," said John Shoch, a venture capitalist at the Asset Management Corporation in Palo Alto, Calif. But Web wedding sites are not Mr. Huang's only obstacle. He contends that his ideas also run counter to Silicon Valley's infatuation with "big iron" -- ever more complex and powerful routers for coping with the coming deluge of Internet traffic. "The good news is that this will accelerate the growth of the Net dramatically," he said of his approach. "But this is just about math, and Silicon Valley is used to building faster chips. It's not used to faster math." Despite Mr. Haung's so far disappointing search, his prospects have begun to improve recently. Late last year he received a patent covering his concept for hooking together computer routers, which he refers to as a Galois network, in a tip of the hat to the French pioneer of group theory. And lately, Mr. Huang has found interest and even enthusiasm in some quarters of the industry. He said that British Telecommunications was looking closely at his concept and was planning an experiment to test his theory. "We've sat down with Alan in some fierce seminars," said Peter Cochrane, head of research for British Telecom. "The common sense underlying his ideas kind of scream out at you." Still, Mr. Huang faces a daunting task in trying to catch up with the giant Cisco, which today makes the world's highest-performance router, the GSR 12000. Moreover, there are already three startup companies -- Avici Systems, Nexabit Netorks Inc. and Pluris Inc. -- all shooting for the market for the next wave of networking. Yet, being late is not always a disadvantage, said Farrokh Billimoria, a research analyst at Hambrecht & Quist in San Francisco who was the co-author of a recent report on the future of the routing business. "If you have a unique idea and you start six months behind, sometimes it's an advantage," he said. "You can start behind and catch up." Which is precisely what Mr. Huang, shuffling his deck, is betting on. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Alan Huang, a former Bell Labs data network designer, holds his model of a multidimensional array of routers, which he says would help ease Internet bottlenecks. (Annie Dowie for The newyork Times)  Chart: "Traffic Control" As the Internet has grown, the specialized computers needed to link it together -- called routers -- have grown more powerful and complex. One researcher, Alan Huang, contends that more powerful routers can be assembled from an arrays of routers that are less complex and less expensive. His idea is based on an area of mathematics called group theory. Here is an explanation.  HOW THE INTERNET WORKS All data travels in packets, through routers. Each router has several pathways along which it can receive or forward packets. A packet can pass through several routers before it reaches its destination. A packet may travel over any of several different paths to reach the same destination. THE BOTTOM LINE: As the Internet grows, it will either be necessary to add more routers, or make the routers more powerful.  THE NEW APPROACH One way to create a more powerful router is to link several less powerful ones together into an array. This array can handle many more packets of information. This makes it possible for the packets to get to their destina-tions quicker and with less disruption. THE BOTTOM LINE: The network costs less to set up and can be built with today's technology.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Was the Victoria's Secret show a Web failure? Hardly. There's no such thing as bad publicity.
body: IF a fashion show is Webcast on the Internet and most people who try to see it cannot, does it still make a splash? You bet. New-media case study: the flaunting of Victoria's Secret spring collection, held live in Manhattan Wednesday evening and simulcast on line for the masses. The lingerie company, a unit of Intimate Brands Inc., spent $1.5 million on one 30-second television spot during the Super Bowl broadcast and $4 million afterwards to advertise the fashion show in newspapers internationally, yielding a bonanza of ink, video, bits and watercooler chat worth exponentially more. Some news reports focused not on the event's success but on the fact that some of the millions of would-be viewers were closed out of the World Wide Web site during the live show. There was also much ado that many who did manage to establish contact received audio and video that sputtered under the Web-surfing deluge. Critics chided both Victoria's Secret and Broadcast.com, the company that delivered the event over the Internet, for not being prepared for this flood of visitors to the site. They wrote the whole thing off as one giant publicity stunt. No kidding! Publicity is exactly what Victoria's Secret wanted. And it got the last laugh, orchestrating what might go down in the textbooks as shrewd multimedia manipulation. The company reports that a million people logged on to its Web site in the hours after the spot appeared during the Super Bowl; a full two million turned up on the day of the fashion show. That would seem to be an example of the cross-media "convergence" that industry pundits have been breathlessly promoting as a benefit of the Web, and which has happened only a few times previously in the medium's short history. Few advertisers using any other combination of media and subject matter could hope to amass the kind of reach and frequency that Victoria's Secret did with such a one-shot campaign. "It's no longer about advertising per se or marketing per se, but about branding, and using all this multi-dimensional media," said Allan Mottus, publisher of The Informationist, a beauty industry newsletter. "Fashion ain't Paris anymore, and it ain't newyork, and it's not Victoria's Secret's 800 stores. Now, every household that has an Internet connection is a fashion store." The Super Bowl spot, the newspaper ads and the Web site were the work of Resource Marketing, an agency in Columbus, Ohio, with an estimated $75 million a year in revenue; its other clients include Cisco Systems, Hewlett-Packard and Netscape Communications. While those in marketing looked at the Victoria's Secret ploy with awe or envy, people more interested in the Internet's infrastructure expressed frustration over this latest example of the continued shortcomings of the Web as a mass medium. Invariably, each time a Web event draws huge crowds, some piece of technology fails, leaving a certain number of would-be viewers in the dark and giving the naysayers grounds to declare that the medium is not ready for prime time. Victoria's Secret was not the only company caught by an overwhelming response. Another first-time Super Bowl advertiser, Hotjobs.com, was unprepared to accommodate the onslaught of visitors drawn to its job-hunters' site after seeing its commercial, a spot on which the company spent half of its annual revenue. And in another recent football-related example of a convergence promise that went awry, ABC canceled promotions for a special Web site offering player statistics and biographies and an on-line play-along game during the Jan. 4 Fiesta Bowl, after the site reached 100,000 users just minutes into the broadcast. Executives at ABC, a unit of the Walt Disney Company, later acknowledged that they had no idea the offering would prove so popular. Even those who did manage to log on to the live Victoria's Secret fashion show did not see anything near the video quality of the glistening, bouncing, full-motion Super Bowl promotional spot. Dave Dadekian, a digital video consultant in newyork, called the Victoria's Secret Webcast a "disservice" to the state of the Webcasting art. No Web organization, Mr. Dadekian said, can handle the big numbers lured to the fashion show. And he also criticized the fashion show's production values. "You can't put dark pictures, a couple of spotlights, a far-away camera, on the Web; it may look great for television, but you can't do that for streaming video," he said, referring to live video on the Internet. Such fretting may miss the point. The Internet doesn't have an endless capacity to accommodate every potential viewer of a live show, as TV does. But aside from the occasional traffic jam, the Internet can give viewers what they're looking for when they want it. Now that the rubberneckers are gone, the shoppers -- and gawkers -- can turn to the Victoria's site any time and see the show at their convenience. Victoria's Secret was able to reach customers in countries where the company doesn't have stores or doesn't distribute the 350 million catalogues that it mails annually -- that's the value of the Web. So are the company's early numbers indicating that men seem more willing to buy on line than in Victoria's Secret stores. "The goal is not to mimic television," said Mark Cuban, president of Broadcast.com. "If you wanted to buy television, you would just buy television. "We weren't trying for perfection," he added. "We were just trying to help Victoria's Secret reach their goals. This is very much a perception-and-momentum business, and all of a sudden they're the talk of the industry." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: An on-line Victoria's Secret show incurred many technical problems. (Associated Press)

title:
MARKET WATCH;
The Net: ACongenial Spot for Touts
body: WHILE the Dow industrials hardly budged last week, shares of a group of lesser-known companies, including J. B. Oxford Holdings and Siebert Financial, were moonshots. Traders watched the stocks double or more in the course of a day on no news whatsoever. What or who was behind the moves? The "what" is the Internet. Siebert Financial, a discount brokerage firm in newyork, and J. B. Oxford, a rival in Los Angeles, got hot because they are both on line. Siebert ran from $19.125 on Monday to $49.50 on Wednesday, then dropped back to $35.125 at week's end. J. B. Oxford, which is, by the way, under investigation by the Securities and Exchange Commission for possible market manipulation, closed on Wednesday at $12 and on Thursday made a high of $25.75 before ending the week at $11.75. More interesting is the "who" behind the activity. It seems to be "Merlin," a man posting stock picks in an Internet chat room called trading-places.net. Outside of cyberspace, Merlin is a Scotsman named Chris Rea, 45; he is pictured on the Web site aboard a yacht. Mr. Rea said on Friday that he founded Trading Places last September. It is a Web site for day traders, the histrionic types who furiously buy and sell stocks through the day. He calls the company a "facilitator of trader training and trader communications on the Internet." In less than six months, Mr. Rea said, he has drawn 817 members to his site who pay $279 a month to get instruction in day trading and access to Merlin's stock picks. But Mr. Rea's reach also extends to thousands of people who learn of his picks indirectly, from friends or other traders. Net watchers say that helps explains the violent moves in stocks he pushes. Before the market opened on Friday, Mr. Rea said, he recommended Omega Research, a Miami maker of financial analysis software. The stock was at $5.25. "Within half an hour, it ran to $10," he said. Never mind that the stock fell back to $7. "Right now we're promoting IMON," Mr. Rea added on Friday morning. That's the ticker symbol for Imaginon Inc., a small software maker in Greer, S.C. "We made it rock," Mr. Rea said. The stock rose 25 percent that day. On-line investing is rife with dubious characters, Mr. Rea said; by contrast, he added, "we see ourselves as being the white knight in this industry." Still, one member of his site who is a professional trader says that the enthusiastic Mr. Rea rarely tells people when to sell -- a problem, given that the stocks inevitably fall after their spikes. Mr. Rea declined to discuss his background, other than to say that he was a trader for years in London, moved to Spain and then came to the unitedstates 10 years ago. Five years ago, he was in the business of designing and producing mailers for car dealerships. He is not a registered broker. As essentially a publisher of financial information, he is generally exempt from regulation. Only if he were found to be buying ahead of his customers or taking money from the companies whose shares he recommends would he be subject to regulators' wrath. He says he does neither. And indeed, Trading Places is filled with effusive testimonials to Merlin's magic. So this is the way we live now. Thousands of people from all over the nation buy stocks on the advice of a stranger known only by his alias and a blurry picture. Strange days. Strange days, indeed. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: "Merlin's Magic" plots high, low and closing stock prices for J. B. Oxford Holdings, since Dec. 1998.

title:
PERSONAL BUSINESS;
Electronic Middleman for Mortgages
body: NEVER before had William Ikley enjoyed much leverage when applying for a loan, especially a mortgage. But this time, Mr. Ikley, 36, a butcher who lives in Eldersburg, Md., had a firm deal just one business day after logging on to the Priceline.com Web site. And he, not a lender, was in charge. "It's been a real easy experience," he said. "There wasn't any pressure, doing it from home." In fact, he applied while in his pajamas. And he expects to have a check in hand tomorrow, 10 days after initiating the name-your-price mortgage. Priceline.com made its name by letting consumers offer bids on airline tickets -- then hotels and, in newyork City, cars. The vendors can then accept or reject the offers.  Now the company has extended this method for more complex transactions: mortgages. The new program might not be such a smooth process for everyone. Mr. Ikley needed only a small second mortgage, a $5,000, five-year home equity loan. He was knowledgeable enough to do without the guidance provided by mortgage brokers, who stand to lose business to this potentially less expensive electronic middleman. And as Mr. Ikley learned, Priceline's lenders are not exactly giving money away. He will be paying 8.17 percent rather than the 6.9 percent he had optimistically proposed. Still, his transaction represents another stage in the evolution of what Priceline calls buyer-driven commerce, which harnesses the Internet's speed and vast scope. The Tower Group, a consulting firm in Needham, Mass., estimates that by 2001, 10 percent of first mortgages in a $1 trillion-a-year market will involve the Internet. Many Web sites and institutions already match borrowers and lenders, but Priceline's is the first program that lets the consumer initiate the terms. "We put the customer more in control," said Richard S. Braddock, a former senior executive at Citicorp who is now chairman of Priceline. THE mortgage process, conducted in partnership with Lendingtree, an on-line loan originator, is fairly straightforward. A loan seeker can apply to finance a particular house, condominium or co-op or to qualify before choosing a property. The borrower visits www.priceline.com and specifies a type of financing (like 15- or 30-year, fixed rate or adjustable), an interest rate, points and a desired closing date. A monthly payment may also be proposed. The applicant also supplies income and other information that a lender can use to evaluate creditworthiness. A $200 deposit is charged to a credit card. Any response from among Lendingtree's 15 lenders, including the Dime Savings Bank of newyork, Greenpoint Financial and the Money Store, must arrive within two business days. If a lender accepts, the deal is struck and the deposit is applied to the usual fees, like the appraisal. Or the lenders can submit counteroffers. If the borrower rejects them, the application dies and the $200 charge is erased. The charge is not refunded if the customer walks away from an accepted bid. Unlike Priceline's other businesses, its mortgage service relies on applicants who have already done enough homework to know what they want and what terms they can reasonably expect. At Priceline.com, borrowers cannot browse through an array of rates and terms without risking a commitment. "It doesn't really allow for shopping," said James P. Punishill, an analyst at Forrester Research of Cambridge, Mass. Other on-line services -- Web sites of individual lenders or the dozens of so-called aggregators like E-Loan or Quicken or Lendingtree itself -- do allow borrowers to survey the financial landscape. Armed with information, though, Priceline customers will gain great flexibility, according to Theodore Iacobuzio of the Tower Group. They will probably save money, too, unless they can strike a deal with, for example, a local bank that throws in a free checking account or other services. Brokers, for their part, are taking this new mortgage-market refinement in stride, said A. W. Pickel 3d of Lenexa, Kan., co-chairman of the technology panel of the National Association of Mortgage Brokers. "There's definitely a place for it," he said, but he contended that he and his colleagues, many of whom have Web sites of their own, would not suffer much, because consumers need the hand-holding that brokers provide. Priceline is not as free of added costs as borrowers might think, Mr. Pickel said, because lenders must add to their rates or points the fees they pay to Priceline but which the service does not disclose. Mortgage brokers collect fees in similar ways. Though Mr. Iacobuzio thinks the on-line mortgage business has "a very big future," he said it would be many years before paperwork disappears and transactions can be conducted electronically end to end. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: William Ikley, above, at work at Giant Food in Laurel, Md., obtained a home equity loan by way of Priceline's new Web site, left. He offered to pay 6.9 percent interest; one business day later, he had a deal at 8.17 percent. (Marty Katz for The newyork Times)

title:
PRACTICAL TRAVELER;
Agents Reckon With the Web
body: ON a Saturday afternoon in October, I sat in a dimmed seminar room at the Los Angeles Convention Center with 22 travel agents facing 12 computer terminals. Using a big screen, Ray M. Greenly, then vice president for member services for the American Society of Travel Agents, was unraveling the Web for one session of Internet 101, six oversubscribed training sessions at the agents' annual convention. Other training sessions at the convention included designing Web sites, desktop publishing, managing databases and one called "Start Your Engines," focusing on five major services that search for information on the Web: Alta Vista, Yahoo, Excite, Hotbot and Lycos. Travel agents in the unitedstates are straining to catch up as the electronic medium gnaws at their business. They are also being squeezed by a reduction in airline commissions, initially in September 1997 for domestic tickets, and since then for overseas tickets and Amtrak. For years they sold tickets at the same price as the airlines, getting a 10 percent commission out of the airlines' gross. Now the airlines are taking back part of that cost, and as a way of staying afloat, more than half the agencies in the country are charging their clients for some services, perhaps $10 for an airline ticket and $50 for trip planning. A further blow to agents came last month when Delta Airlines said it would charge $1 extra for each component -- a round trip is two components -- that was sold any way but through its Web site. This included all travel agent sales and its own sales by phone or over the counter. Two weeks after this step, sharply criticized by the agents' society, Delta canceled it. Agents' electronic competition came on fast. Three years ago airlines latched onto the Internet as a way to sell directly to the consumer: Alaska Airlines was the first, beginning Dec. 27, 1995. Cruise lines, tour operators, limo agencies -- all the agents' normal suppliers -- opened electronic shops; Web addresses joined phone and fax numbers on business cards. Computer experts started creating cyber travel agencies, allowing consumers to comparison shop and buy tickets with credit cards at home 24 hours a day. In these boom times, travel agencies are selling more but making less. In 1998, 2,116 full-service agencies shut up shop, according to the Airlines Reporting Corporation, the clearinghouse for agency sales. Although new agencies were being started, they did not offset the losses. The total number of active agencies reported by the clearinghouse at year end was 28,807, a net loss of 5.23 percent from December 1997, and the smallest total since 1986.  Two Surveys Confirm Trend There were 5,000 delegates at the agents' convention, and all but on-line agency people clearly felt acutely vulnerable. What is the future for the places that are becoming known in the trade as bricks-and-mortar agencies? How often do experts think clients will shift to the electronic sales window, where the line is never busy, and the "agent" is always in? Estimates inevitably disagree on how many people buy travel on the Internet, either from airlines or from on-line agencies like Travelocity, which links to Sabre, a travel-agent reservations system; Expedia, an offshoot of Microsoft; the Internet Travel Network, or 1travel.com, a two-year-old discount agency. But two recent consumer surveys give a snapshot of what is happening: The people who spend more money on travel also spend more time on the Web, and are more likely to buy on line than just to window-shop. One study was issued by the Travel Industry Association, which makes monthly phone surveys. In September it carried out 1,200 interviews as a sample of the 199.8 million adults over 18 in the 48 contiguous states. It checked interest in the new technology among all adults, then among travelers -- defined as people who traveled away from home 100 miles or more, one way, in the last year -- and then among frequent travelers, those who made five or more 100-mile trips in the year. The total of "current users" of the Internet or any other on-line service, including email, was extrapolated to be 76.6 million. As for purchase of travel on the Internet, 6.7 million American adults, or 9 percent of "current Internet users," had booked and paid for an airline ticket, hotel room, rental car, package tour or other travel need. This was up from 5.4 million in 1997. Although use of the Internet is growing faster than the rate at which people are making bookings on line, the booking rate is also leaping ahead: the percent of all adults -- not just Internet users -- in the 48 states who made reservations on line rose from 3 percent in 1997 to 4 percent in 1998.  Using Web for Research The other survey was made by International Communications Research of Media, Pa., for Phocus wright, a research company specializing in Internet travel. The survey was also sponsored by on-line agencies: Expedia, the Internet Travel Network, Preview Travel and the Sabre Group. Philip C. Wolf, the president of Phocuswright, said that 10,000 calls were made randomly to adults in the contiguous 48 states to identify 2,500 people who had flown a commercial airliner in the last year and had "visited a Web site in the last month." These were defined as "wired travelers," and 500 of the 2,500 were selected for the survey, Mr. Wolf said. Since Americans make the huge majority of their trips by car, this was a narrower universe than that interviewed by the Travel Industry Association. Further, as Mr. Wolf pointed out, the heaviest use of the Web is for email, and his survey limited its respondents to those who had visited a Web site. Among the "wired travelers," about a fifth, 18 percent, used the Internet to buy travel, the survey found. Of the "wired travelers" who take vacations, only 10 percent usually buy air tickets on line, but 68 percent research travel on line. Phocuswright said "frequency of Web usage" was a good predictor of on-line buying. Among those who used the Web less than weekly, only 23 percent have bought on line; of those who used it just about daily, 56 percent have. "Most nonbuyers express a reluctance to jump into E-commerce anytime soon," the company said. "A hefty 75 percent say they are not likely to buy anything on line in the near future. They worry about credit card security (82 percent), personal privacy (79 percent) or would rather speak to a knowledgeable salesperson.Travel agents are a big reason why travelers resist on-line services. Among the vast majority (82 percent) of 'wired travelers' who have not bought travel on line, nearly half (48 percent) say it's because they have a travel agent they know and trust." The company, from its electronic viewpoint, said that having a travel agent was a "significant barrier" to buying travel on line, but not an "insurmountable one."  Research by Clients, Too Most of the agents in the Los Angeles class were learning to use the Web as a way to research resorts, spas, ski areas, tours and other suppliers' wares. In many cases, they were acutely aware that their clients had already shopped these Web sites and now wanted corroboration of their choice, or reservations. Most of the class was apparently working where the computers they use for access to the airline reservation systems -- Amadeus, Galileo, Sabre and Worldspan -- do not necessarily have connections to the Internet. But some agencies have embraced technology, either setting up their own Web sites or becoming all-electronic agencies that sell on line. Stratton Travel in Oakland, N.J., characterizes itself as a travel management company. It serves 350 clients that are virtually all corporations. It has a Web site where an employee of a client company may look and even reserve a flight at any hour, but the flight can be sold and ticketed only by Stratton. Brian Harmes, director of information technologies for Stratton, said that this moves information directly into the hands of clients -- no telephone tag, no waiting for the agent to check flights, no need to wait for resort brochures. However, it leaves the agency, as the client's travel manager, in control of policy: business class vs. first class, American vs. British Airways, and so forth. Mr. Harmes said, however, that he had some clients who still were not at ease even with fax machines. He thinks sometimes older clients are slower to shift, and he says Stratton wants to avoid giving the idea it is forcing clients to change their ways. They get the personal phone calls they want, but the company works on shifting them over to email or electronic booking, pointing out the time to be saved and the reduction in service fees that is possible. More than embracing the Web, 1travel.com in Zionsville, Pa., is a child of the Web. It began as a Web site three years ago and in a year became an on-line agency, developing software to let the public see the information travel agents have when using reservation systems. The company, with 40 employees, has headquarters in a barn on a sheep farm. Sally Lewis, the marketing director, said that the company itself sold the "down and dirty," air tickets and car and hotel reservations. For spas, tours and other travel requiring consultation, on-line customers are put in touch with specialists, 450 companies that have pages accessible through the Web site. When Mr. Greenly dispatched his novice Web students in Los Angeles, he urged them not to put their notes away, but to noodle around on the Web when they got back to their agencies, or use home personal computers to become at ease with the new research tool. One student, Raschinna Findlay of the Travel Stores branch in Beverly Hills, Calif., said she had not been on line since the course. Much of her time since then has been spent traveling to look at the things she sells. Only some of the computers in her office have phone connections for the Internet. In the next few months, she said, the Travel Store plans to put in new equipment and hookups to the Web. About 50 percent of her business is leisure, which she said was "very upscale," representing Beverly Hills and other wealthy areas around Los Angeles. For these clients, she specializes in cruises and spas. Her clients shop around the Internet a lot, she said, and frequently ask her for things they notice. "Often I have to tell them that the hotel is not in a good area," she said, "or that it is just not up to par. I know what kind of cruise they will enjoy, and they rely on me to know these things." Ms. Findlay is almost quintessentially Phocuswright's "significant barrier" to buying travel on line. Her clients want advice and personal attention. And she will certainly stay in business as long as she is more savvy than the Internet about places they both know. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Michael H. Thomas, president of 1travel.com, an on-line agency, at work on his Pennsylvania sheep farm. (Photographs by Brad C. Bower for the New York Times)  Graphs: "Buying on the Web" Annual amount spent on travel services over the Internet by th 6.7 million people who used it to make travel reservations. Based on survey taken in September 1998. (Source: Travel Industry Association)(pg. 27)  "Seeking Advice for a Trip" The graph shows the percentage of different information sources used in the past five years. (Source: Travel Industry Association)(pg. 27)

title:
PRIVATE SECTOR;
An Investor Who Shops for Spunk
body: AS investment pundits warn about an Internet bubble and Bill Gates of Microsoft wonders where the mania for Internet stocks will end, Michael S. Egan is quietly keeping his chips on the virtual table. Mr. Egan, 58, knows something about building companies. He made a fortune by turning around the Alamo rental-car company and selling it to Republic Industries in 1997 for $625 million, with his stake worth about $587 million. Then he started an investment company, Dancing Bear Investments, and looked for promising businesses. About that time, he was becoming infatuated with cyberspace. "I started doing a lot of business electronically with the airline reservation systems and the Internet," he said in an interview. "It was quite apparent that it was going to be the major economic revolution of the world since maybe the printing press or currency." But Mr. Egan wasn't about to invest in a company just because it had dot-com in its name. He was looking for a startup nobody else had heard of and true grit in the people in charge. "They had to have a high, high work ethic," he said. "They had to be able to suffer a blow." Mr. Egan, an alumnus of Cornell University, mentioned to the university's president one day that he was looking for a "media play on the Net." Perhaps, he was told, he should check out a company called Theglobe.com that a couple of recent graduates, Todd Krizelman and Stephan Paternot, had started while still in college. Theglobe.com calls itself an Internet "community" that offers its users entertainment, information and shopping opportunities. Mr. Egan liked the concept and flew to Ithaca, N.Y., to have lunch with the two men. After five hours, he made it clear he wanted to buy into their venture. In February 1997, he dispatched Edward Cespedes, a Dancing Bear executive, for follow-up talks. "Ed was told that he couldn't leave the office until the negotiation was done," said Mr. Krizelman, now 25, one year older than his partner. "He lived on our couches in the office and shared meal after meal of Chinese food with us." Six months later, Mr. Egan paid $20 million for a 51 percent stake in the company. The payoff came last Nov. 13. In its first day of trading, the stock of Theglobe.com rocketed 606 percent, from $9 to $63.50, the biggest first-day run-up of any initial public offering. "It was an adrenaline day if there ever was one," Mr. Egan said. His stake of roughly six million shares is now worth $382 million. Mr. Egan has made other smart investments, most notably a controlling stake in Nantucket Nectars, a Massachusetts juice maker, that he sold last year to Ocean Spray for an undisclosed profit. Even for this low-tech venture, his enthusiasm was boundless. Tom First, one of the founders, recalled a conversation on a private jet: "He starts talking about how the company would be a $200 million company within five years while I'm concerned that on our one van in Boston the shocks were blown out." Mr. Egan has used some of his wealth to lead the life of a country squire, building a $12 million mansion in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., for temporary shelter while he renovated his main spread nearby, and assembling a Nantucket vacation compound of 15 houses, a dining hall, a movie house and a baseball diamond for a family that includes five children and three grandchildren. But his fears after selling Alamo -- that he would "dry up and blow away" -- proved groundless. As he looked for investment leads, he says, he heeded a lesson he learned when he was 15 and was helping to build a family amusement park in his native Wisconsin. He was having trouble managing a work crew of a dozen Native Americans and hired a middle-aged chief named White Cloud as his assistant. White Cloud got instant results, making him realize that "it's the people around you who get the job done for you." As a young man, Mr. Egan at first pursued a career in tourism. But a "humbling" job in food service, followed by a low-paying stint in academia, cooled that ambition, and he jumped at the chance to run an old friend's family business. Sitting in the cluttered Silicon Alley office of Theglobe.com recently, he looked more like an artist than an investor with his snowy white hair, black pullover sweater and black trousers. But he talked like an investor as he dismissed fears about an Internet stock bubble. "There's a very good reason a lot of capital is pouring into the Internet," he said. "Fifty million or 100 million data bases being joined with three billion users." In other recent deals, Mr. Egan bought and sold AutobyInternet Inc. and bought a majority stake in Inteletravel, a privately held Internet travel company. He plans to take public his own start-up, Certified Vacations, a travel company, at the end of this year. Last Monday, Theglobe.com announced its first acquisition, the expected purchase of Azazz.com, an Internet retailer. What drives Mr. Egan? He says he wants to help young entrepreneurs make their way. The other day, he says, he had breakfast with the two founders of Nantucket Nectars, both in their early 30's. "You see the enthusiasm for life in their eyes and hear it in their voices," he said. "Maybe I'm trying to recapture my youth." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Michael Egan leans on "Horn Blower," a sculpture by Eduardo da Rosa, at the offices of Dancing Bear Investments, in Fort Lauderdale, Fla. Mr. Egan's passion is building companies. (Susan Greenwood for The newyork Times)

title: Sites to Get You There
body: WEB sites for would-be, armchair and actual travelers are proliferating faster than you can say "dotcom," with so many links that it's easy to lose your way. Following are 44 useful, informative or intriguing sites that can help you find or reach your destination. Portals To travel on the Web you should have a home, a place where you pick up themail or chat with friends. If you belong to one of the big on-line services like America Online or Compuserve, you already have one, with links both to their proprietary sections and to the Web at large. But they also have homes, called portals, on the Web proper that are stripped-down versions of their commercial services; other portals were born on the Web to begin with. All offer such facilities as email, news, calendars and shopping, and all have versatile search engines for finding travel sites. You can narrow your search at the beginning by going into their travel subsections. America Online, www.aol.com. This is a very crowded page and not as homey as the regular A.O.L. site. But the travel section is filled with categories covering destinations, reservations, business travel, travel news, weather, and airline, cruise, hotel and rental car directories. Compuserve, www.compuserve.com. Not as dull-looking as the regular Compuserve site, the travel section is slim, with seven recommended Web sites, including Barnes & Noble, presumably because you can buy travel books there. The Microsoft Network, www.msn.com. Microsoft keeps trying. Clicking on "travel" takes you to Expedia, Microsoft's dedicated travel site. Yahoo, www.yahoo.com. This is my favorite home on the Web, with a fairly well-organized travel subsection you can bury yourself in. Excite, www.excite.com. This is my home away from home. I usually begin by reading my horoscope to see if taking a trip is a wise notion.  On the Town MSN Sidewalk, www.sidewalk.com. For a guide to entertainment and shopping in any of some 75 unitedstates cities, plus Sydney and Melbourne, this is a good first stop. There are also sports scores, white and yellow pages, and airline tickets. City Net, www.citynet.com. Lodgings, restaurants and entertainment in 31 unitedstates cities, a full plate of travel news, and reservations through Preview Travel, as well as email and chat rooms. Newsdirectory, www.ecola.com. Primarily a source for English-language newspapers and magazines, but if you click on Travel Planner under the Bonus heading you get a list of visitors centers in the 50 states by town and area code. Fodor's, www.fodors.com. Fodor's has been a name in travel for as long as most of us can remember, and its Web site is rich with resources for making your own miniguide for a journey. Events Worldwide, www.eventsworldwide.com. This is a reference site for festivals, carnivals, arts, sports and other events. Eventseeker, www.eventseeker.com. An international business and leisure events database catalogued by date, location and type of event. The San Jose Mercury News, www5.mercury center.com. A huge guide to travel, news, and everything else in northern California, and wherever else Knight Ridder publishes newspapers. The newyork Times, www.nytimes.com. This site carries articles from the Travel section, and the companion site, newyork Today (also reachable directly at www.nytoday.com) can guide visitors to the city.  Booking Sites Preview Travel, www.previewtravel.com. Many other services, such as City Net, call on Preview Travel for reservations. You can go to it direct, for information as well as reservations. Expedia, www.expedia.com. Microsoft's broader travel site, where you can plan a trip to practically anywhere, and buy airline tickets and make hotel and car reservations. Travelocity, www.travelocity.com. This is one of a handful of front ends for the Sabre reservations system that professionals use, with some 420 airlines, 40,000 hotels and 50 car-rental companies. It will even send you an email message if a price changes in your favor. Travel Facts, www.travelfacts.com. Travel Facts calls itself a research tool. Provides access to airline, rental car and hotel Web sites, a travel-agent database, all kinds of links, a chat room and feature articles. Priceline, www.priceline.com. You make a bid for an airline seat or a hotel room, and if the establishment is willing to accept it, Priceline lets you know. (Of course, if you know where you are going and how you want to go, every airline has its own Web page.)  Maps to Anywhere The Perry-Castaneda Library Map Collection, www.lib.utexas.edu/Libs/PCL/Mapcollection/world cities.html. All the services offer different combinations of such tools as currency converters, weather forecasts and maps. If getting a map is a first priority, however, a good place to look is the Perry-Castaneda Library at the University of Texas at Austin. The endless list of maps of continents, regions, countries and cities, mostly produced by the State Department, runs from Abidjan to Zagreb. In the event that you can't find your map in Austin (Austin, for instance, is not one of the maps), the collection is linked to other map sites. Worldwide Brochures, www.wwb.com. Here are maps, as well as guides and brochures, more than 15,000 of them. They cost nothing, usually come by snail mail and, since they are promotions issued by the countries, cities, or establishments themselves, are hardly objective sources of information.  Favorite Places Caribbean Tourism, www.caribtourism.com. A guide to weather and events in 36 Caribbean destinations, prepared by the Caribbean Tourism Organization. Paris France Guide, www.parisfranceguide.com. Paris sites are all over the Web. Here are exhibitions, entertainment and food, of course, in clear English from a print publisher of magazines, books and maps. Hidden America, www.hiddenamerica.com. Places to go off the Interstates, and such events as cowboys reciting verse in Nevada. Disney, www.disney.com. Disney's site is first rate if you are interested in making reservations at Disney World or Disneyland, or taking a Disney cruise. Ski-Guide, www.ski-guide.com. Snow, lodging and dining, transportation and events at 570 ski areas in the unitedstates and Canada. Includes most of the famous names, as well as Hound Ears Club, N.C.; Adventure Mountain Lions, Mich., and Lynx Creek, N.H.  On the Cheap Shoestring Travel, www.stratpub.com. Tips, tales and deals on traveling inexpensively, contributed by its users. It is fun even if you are not going anywhere. The Mining Company, www.miningcompany.com. This site "mines" the net to produce concise suggestions in a dozen categories, including travel. Although that category contains the usual suspects, there is a commendable emphasis on such things as camping, eco-tourism, bed-and-breakfasts, and traveling with children. The Web sites are picked by a real person with a name, not by committee or robot. Economy Travel, www.economy travel.com. Economy is an international travel consolidator with contracts with airlines for discounted prices. The seats that go to a consolidator have not been sold through the more usual channels, so it is often possible, or even necessary, to make last-minute arrangements. You fill out a form on screen and, if a flight meets your requirements, book it. Most of the familiar airline names are on the list, as well as ones you might not think of, like Biman Bangladesh, Ukraine International and Jersey European. A.A.R.P., www.aarp.org. The Web site of the American Association of Retired Persons has a travel section with a few articles about destinations, travel articles, and lists of hotels and cruise lines that give discounts to members.  It's Official Centers for Disease Control, www .cdc.gov/cdctext.htm. Government-provided health information you may not know you need for travel, particularly international.
