The State Department, www .state.gov. Voluminous information: travel warnings, addresses of embassy and consulate Web sites, a host of telephone numbers. The passport subsection has an exhaustive compilation of information, downloadable passport applications and addresses of the 3,609 unitedstates places where you can get a passport. Parknet, www.nps.gov. The site of the National Park Service, with information about fees and making reservations, and many maps. You can search for a park by region, state, theme or name. There is also a park of the month (North Cascades Complex, in the Pacific Northwest, when I looked) and several travel features.  Fellow Travelers Traveldog, www.traveldog.com. As the old bumper sticker says, "Children are for people who can't have dogs." Traveldog lists accommodations and amenities for the pooch, including camps, day care, parks and pet sitters. A click on its Travel Agent button links to the agency Stiles in Travel, which will make arrangements after you fill out a form on the screen and email or fax it, or simply phone the company. A.S.P.C.A., www.aspca.org. A page of tips for traveling in a car with your pet. "A strong wire-mesh crate is preferable for car trips because it provides more ventilation," is one piece of advice. Line the bottom of the crate with towels or, if the pet is a cat, a small litter box. At www.avma .org, the American Veterinary Medical Association gives safety tips for "making flying friendly for you and your pet."  Specialties All Aboard Cruise Center, www .flashnet./aacruise. This company says it represents all cruise lines. You can search for specific lines or destinations or consult lists of such specialty cruises as seniors, millennium and family. Golf Travel Online, www.gto.com. Here is a database of travel for golfers; the trips can be reserved on line or by telephone. There are additional services, such as booking flights and rental cars, and getting travel insurance. Special packages are highlighted, like Bordeaux-Biarritz or Provence-Riviera golfing vacations. Swimmers Guide Online, www .lornet.com/sgol. An international database of "publicly accessible, full-size year-round pools." If you can't find a place to swim in 5,509 pools in 67 countries you're not trying. In Andorra, try the Centro Deportivo Els Serradella. Island Scuba, www.islandscuba .com. If plain swimming isn't good enough, drop in here to plan and book scuba-diving, including group trips, in the Caribbean. Both offshore and river diving, and many classes. Rail-to-Trails Conservancy, www .railtrails.org. This is a nonprofit organization devoted to converting former rail lines to trails for walkers and bicyclists. It is an advocacy group and much of the site is dedicated to its cause, but it does include information about 700 rail-trails in the unitedstates, with links to weather, bed-and-breakfasts, tourism centers and maps. Spafinders, www.spafinders.com. You can search for spas by region or interest -- "supreme pampering," for example, or "fasting." There's also a booking function, a list of featured getaways and a day spa finder. Weathernet Weathercams, cirrus .sprl.umich.edu/wxnet/wxcam.html. A directory of live weather cameras in North America offers a chance to see whether it's cloudy or clear in more than 800 destinations. The on-line pictures are usually refreshed every few minutes.  Cash Flow Mastercard, www.mastercard .com. Visa, www.visa.com. When traveling in strange places, you sometimes need an A.T.M. more than another rich meal. Both Mastercard and Visa have sections to locate one of their hundreds of thousands of handy automatic tellers. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A sampling of gateways to vacations, either virtual or real. Directly above is the State Department's passport application site.

title: The Cybercompanion
body: JOHAN REINHARD called a friend in Texas recently to chat from near the top of the world. A high-altitude anthropologist whose explorations in the Andes and Himalayas often appear in National Geographic, Dr. Reinhard was standing at the summit of a 20,000-foot mountain in Peru, using a new kind of telephone that beams conversation from virtually anywhere on earth to a constellation of low-orbit satellites and back down to terrestrial wired and wireless phone networks. Had he wished to (and had he the stamina to carry all the gear up the mountain), he could have snapped a picture of himself with a digital camera, attached it to a lightweight portable computer, and sent the image halfway across the planet as electronic mail via satellite phone over the Internet -- an instant, electronic postcard from the new era of travel. Technology is transforming travel not just for explorers in remote corners of the world, but also for families packing the minivan for a drive to Grandma's house, and for the travel industry itself. Technically savvy consumers have been able to research travel destinations and make airline reservations from home for more than a decade using personal computers and early on-line information services such as Compuserve. But since the mid-1990's, declining computer prices and the rapid growth of the Internet have caused an almost unimaginable proliferation of on-line travel information sites and services, all available from the comfort of home. Computer chips allow people to research trips, shop for the lowest fares, reserve airline tickets, look inside hotel rooms from thousands of miles away, get detailed maps, check train schedules, chat electronically with other travelers familiar with the destination, order travel guides, create custom itineraries, buy luggage, watch video travelogues on a VCR, check detailed weather reports, compare exchange rates, research restaurants, peer through remote cameras to see what the weather is like right now in Seattle or Antarctica, study a foreign language and book tickets to local cultural and sporting events. Taking a trip never sounded so exhausting. Like the telegraph and telephone before it, the Internet was supposed to reduce the need to travel. As technology makes the world a smaller place, people are traveling more, not less. This is partly because technology makes travel more convenient, but also because it stirs the user's imagination. "The most important difference about cyberspace is that there is no distance between two points," said Paul Saffo, a director at the Institute for the Future in Menlo Park, Calif. "The Internet gives people these marvelous electronic seven-league boots that can drop them into Katmandu, and once they visit Katmandu electronically, it is going to make them curious. When people visit somewhere electronically, they want to go there on purpose." The travel industry is helping to push consumers toward computers and Internet services. Last month, Delta Air Lines imposed a $2 round-trip surcharge on domestic tickets not purchased through its Web site. (The surcharge, sharply criticized by travel agents, was withdrawn two weeks later.) In a slight variation, American Airlines, to name one, occasionally gives discounts on tickets purchased via computer. Alaska Airlines and Horizon Air recently imposed a $10 surcharge for mailing paper tickets. Other airlines have been studying similar inducements, to the consternation of travel agents and some travelers without Internet access. The airlines contend that the shift to Internet reservations and ticketing will help them cut costs by reducing staff and increasing productivity, although such pronouncements often do not mention the need to hire more highly paid programmers and Web designers. The Internet offers the airlines, which have been cutting commissions to travel agents in recent years, a way to further reduce commissions and the cost of distributing tickets. In any event, Delta announced record profits the week after imposing the surcharges. Depending on whom one asks and how one counts, travel is the biggest, or one of the biggest, categories of spending by on-line consumers. Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass., estimates that total spending for on-line travel bookings last year, counting airlines, hotels, rental cars, tours and cruises, was $3 billion. Estimates of future bookings vary, but Fiona Swerdlow, a digital commerce analyst at Jupiter Communications in newyork, said the research company predicted in April that on-line leisure travel spending by consumers would rocket to $11.7 billion by the year 2002.  The figure does not include business travel booked through corporate travel agencies, and the increased presence of cruise and tour companies offering bookings on the Web recently may make the total even higher, she said. Travel-specific sites on the World Wide Web are reporting surges of visitors, as consumers become more comfortable researching trips, buying tickets and reserving rooms on line. According to NPD Online Research, a division of NPD Group in Port Washington, N.Y., nearly 70 percent of Web users -- and there are more than 70 million in America alone, according to some studies -- say they have visited a travel-related site at some time. Among computer users who travel frequently, the Web is already as indispensable as a suitcase and a toothbrush. One site, Travelocity (www.travelocity.com), reports that it has more than five million registered users. Preview Travel (www.previewtravel.com) claims six million. Microsoft's Expedia (www.expedia.msn.com), which recently reported more than $10 million in weekly travel sales -- car, air and hotel only -- claims more than four million registered users in the unitedstates and Canada. America Online, with more than 15 million subscribers, is adding a new section for business travelers later this month. Leisure travel is already one of the most popular topics among AOL's subscribers, said Pam McGraw, a company spokeswoman. There are hundreds of smaller Internet sites and on-line information services. Many of them are maintained as hobbies or public services by travel enthusiasts, but in the past two years corporate behemoths have been willing to spend tens of millions of dollars on elaborate sites and E-commerce systems in the belief that profits will eventually accrue. So far, spending is still outpacing revenue, services like Expedia and Travelocity say. The allure of such sites is that they give the traveler direct access to the same information available to travel agents. Like most travel agencies, these on-line services are free -- other than the cost of the Internet connection. While it is true that the personal relationship with a travel agent is lost, there are other compensations. Some automated systems today can notify travelers by pager the minute a flight schedule or gate is changed, or by electronic mail when special fares appear for favorite airline routes. A Web-savvy younger generation and others who have embraced the new technology relish fending for themselves. As a result, some analysts anticipate that the traditional travel agency will eventually become an endangered species. Smart virtual agents, perhaps overseen by smart human travel agents, will someday roam the Internet armed with a dossier of a client's personal and price preferences, said Andrew B. Whinston, a professor of information systems at the University of Texas at Austin, whose expertise is electronic commerce. The software agents, Mr. Whinston said, could quickly construct a comprehensive and complex itinerary of air tickets, hotels, rental cars, restaurant reservations, theater tickets, shopping discounts, sightseeing schedules, reading lists, baby-sitting services, and so on -- all for a predetermined budget. Anyone who has been trapped in an endless loop of a voicemail system, trying to connect with a human, knows that technology often does not work as well as it could, and could definitely be made easier. The Web is no different. In a separate NPD survey, conducted in October with five major airlines, only 18 percent of the airline site visitors polled said they could always find the information they sought. Microsoft and other major travel site operators are scrambling to make their services more convenient, by reducing the number of mouse clicks needed to get a fare quote, for example. Computerized baggage handling, ticket-taking and freight-routing systems installed at some new airports (Denver, Hong Kong) and train stations (Berlin) in recent years have caused more delays initially than they have prevented. Car-based navigation and mapping systems occasionally lead drivers into dead ends, or, in the case of an unfortunate German couple traveling in a rental car at night, to bridges that are not there. (They got wet.) On general Internet sites like America Online or Yahoo, clicking on the "travel" button on screen will present the user with hundreds of topics, often organized into specific groups and sometimes focused with astonishing specificity: travel information for seniors, for backpackers, for motorcyclists and so on. On a site maintained by the travel book publisher Rough Guides (www .roughguides.com), a recent topic was proper etiquette for being thrashed with twigs by friendly strangers in a Finnish sauna -- not the typical information one would get from a local travel agent. Many of the sites offer chat services and bulletin boards. Chat services allow the user to converse on screen with one or more people, anywhere in the world, at the same time. Bulletin boards are used to post questions or comments that others can read and respond to at any time. Some of the commentary is banal, but occasionally the exchanges yield valuable, first-hand (if unsubstantiated) information -- avoid hotel X, don't miss restaurant Y, and Z is the cheapest place to rent gear. It is not unheard of for people to forge friendships in such forums. Although fax machines still appear to be more popular in some parts of the world -- typically where the postal systems are unreliable -- the Internet is invaluable for making reservations. Electronic mail is not a slave to time zones, and in preparing for a recent trip to Italy I discovered that my fractured Italian translated better in electronic mail than it did over the phone. The scope of the Internet surprises even technology aficionados like me. A small hotel where I vacationed in the remote Cinque Terre region of Italy, a place largely inaccessible by automobile, not only has Internet access but also its own Web page. Once in my room, however, I also discovered that while the hotel staff might have E-mail, the concept of allowing guests to have access to personal E-mail is still somewhat foreign. Hooking a personal computer to the phone system in other Italian hotels I visited was either impossible or more trouble than it was worth. On the next trip I'll leave the computer home, and look for cafes that serve Internet access along with gelato and cappuccino. For hikers, bikers and others who take the roads less traveled, satellite technology makes it more difficult to get lost. The planet is now circled by a necklace of Global Positioning System (G.P.S.) satellites that, when signaled by a hand-held receiver anywhere on the globe, can provide the traveler's exact position, velocity, speed and altitude. With a CD-ROM or DVD drive in the computer, the traveler can carry libraries' worth of information on a few shiny disks. Are these gadgets passing fads? The form and function of the devices will certainly evolve, the computer and consumer electronics industries have taught us, but the underlying idea of ubiquitous and enhanced communication through computers is clearly here to stay. Airlines are beginning to install power outlets in their craft to accommodate gadget-laden travelers, initially in the first-class sections, but eventually throughout the cabin. Airborne gambling, shopping and videoconferencing may all be ubiquitous in the future. Hotels are trying to get smarter too, technically speaking, offering automated check-in and check-out and an array of in-room amenities for the connected traveler. The Westin Century Plaza Hotel and Tower in Century City, Calif., in 1996 established a "cybersuite" with an electronic butler that responded -- erratically, some visitors reported -- to voice commands asking it to turn on the stereo, open the drapes, draw a bath, and adjust the room temperature. The butler, named Alexander, was removed last year after requiring almost constant maintenance. But of course any system that relies on technology is subject to disruption, and a widespread technology failure can disrupt travel as much as a winter blizzard. The infamous Y2K bug, a programming glitch that is expected to affect millions of computers and embedded microprocessors in less than a year, is certain to disrupt transportation systems when the calendar flips to Jan. 1, 2000. While the Y2K issue may dampen the enthusiasm of travelers hoping to spend New Year's Eve away from home, only a small number of extremists believe that it will cause more than a temporary disruption. Meanwhile new technologies will inevitably emerge. Once people establish communications with other people and places, physical travel follows. "If you hate airplanes, kill your computer," said Mr. Saffo, the futurist. "The simple fact is that over the past half century or so, travel miles and telecommunications minutes have chased each other upward. If you talk long enough, it is going to lead to face-to-face meetings, and that usually means traveling. Then you continue the conversation electronically between meetings."  The credit-card hurdle When consumers consider typing their credit card numbers into their computers, sending them off through virtual hinterlands to buy something from a Web site, many still freeze. Surveys generally show that one of the main reasons people are reluctant to buy, say, a plane ticket over the Internet is concern about security of their card numbers. It's one of the biggest obstacles the travel industry faces in trying to meet projections by the Travel Industry Association of America that travel-related bookings on the Internet will grow from $827 million in 1997 to $8.9 billion by 2002. Executives in the travel industry typically say, however, that credit card fraud on the Internet is rare, and that they know of no such instance resulting from a travel-related purchase. Nevertheless, they are going to great lengths to ease consumers' fears. Since late last year, Travelocity (www.travelocity.com) has guaranteed that if a credit card number is stolen, it will reimburse the $50 deductible that consumers are sometimes required to pay credit card companies for purchases made with their stolen cards. Many other travel sites have also adopted this policy. The Better Business Bureau is also being used as a marketing tool by some travel sites to relieve doubts about security. Some sites, for example, post the logo BBBOnline to signify that the company that administers the Web site has met standards set by the Better Business Bureau for Internet security. Many Internet sites and Web browsers also use the latest encryption software to scramble credit card data while it is traveling over the Internet, and offer explanations of how the technology works.   ADAM BRYANT http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawings (Kathy Osborn)(pg. 13); (Kathy Osborn)(pg. 18)

title: Where, Oh, Where On the Web . . .
body: SEX. Money. Food. News. Real Estate. Thomas Paine. Ukrainian festivals. Pomeranians. You name the subject -- you can almost certainly find a Web site. Westchester is just like the rest of the wired world. When its name is entered into a computer search engine, the result is a glut of Web sites -- or a bouquet, for those who prefer a prettier image. There are, of course, the expected links to local and county government, like Westchester in Touch, site name: www.co .westchester.ny.us. And it is easy to find local businesses both large -- what's larger than I.B.M.? (www.ibm.com) -- and small, like the Wine Connection, a Pound Ridge shop that specializes in rare and fine vintages (www.wineconn.com). It is also not hard to find someone building a business on E-commerce. In some cases, the Web links a basket of existing services, as it does at the Gold Standard, a marketing communications business in Katonah (www.thegoldstandard.com). "Web site development is one of the fastest growing segments of our practice," Nancy Gold, the company president, said. "Clients are extremely interested in getting up on the Web." In some cases, the business would not exist without the Web. Rebecca Walkley of South Salem, a former I.B.M. programmer, has been operating Westchester Web (www.westchesterweb.com) since 1997. Her one-woman operation produced about 30 local sites, a process that requires artistic, technical and marketing skills. "I think that Westchester County has finally reached critical mass of Internet users," she said. "It is a very sophisticated population that has grown to expect the businesses that they are dealing with to have a Web site." A cruise through Westchester Web sites can tell you where to go, quite literally. Historic River Towns of Westchester (www.hudsonriver .com/rivertowns) offers a weekly calendar of events, plus information about historic sites, dining, lodging, river cruises, recreation, shopping and the seasonal trolley that serves the towns. Each of 11 communities from Peekskill to Yonkers has a page devoted to its own attractions. Geoffrey Haynes of Hudson Valley Web Services in Croton-on-Hudson designed the Rivertowns site as part of a larger Web site (hudsonriver .com), which he has developed for the entire Hudson Valley. "Our goal is to provide Internet users worldwide with a wealth of information about the Hudson Valley, and the Rivertowns site does that in a very colorful and engaging way," he said. But you don't have to have a specific destination in mind when you rev up your search engine. Dave Barry once wrote that the Web consists mainly of 14 million interlinked home pages created by college students who want to tell the world what they look like, how they feel about various rock bands, what snack foods they eat, whether they prefer briefs or boxers. He was wrong -- there are almost certainly more than 14 million. And one of them is run by Melissa Carroll, a Mount Kisco resident and SUNY Binghamton psychology major. Besides her own personal pages, she has set up a site (www.jibboo .com/beatles/linda) devoted to Linda McCartney, the late wife of Paul McCartney, and her days growing up in Scarsdale. Ms. Carroll's site includes a link to a Scarsdale Inquirer article on Ms. McCartney's life and death as well as pictures featuring her from the 1959 Scarsdale High School yearbook. "I also dug up a 1995 version of the Scarsdale High School alumni directory," she wrote on the home page. "I looked up Linda Eastman and was referred to Linda McCartney. It listed her old address and phone number from when she was living in Tucson and named simply 'Paul' as her spouse." "Linda died shortly after I made the site, and it began getting a lot of attention," Ms. Carroll said in an email interview. "I've received quite a few letters from graduates of Scarsdale High School who have additional information or just wanted to send their compliments on the page. I'm surprised by the attention it has received because I really didn't intend for it to be a major -- or even very useful -- site." Not all the fan sites are for the famous or even the human. There is Mamie's Page (www .users.cloud9.net). Follow the prompts to get to the customers' personal homepage and (dlp D.Poe), purportedly the work of Mamie herself, a 2-year-old Pomeranian. "I was born in Florida and moved to newyork when I was just a puppy," Mamie writes. "My original humans couldn't keep me, so they put an ad in a local newspaper -- that's how I came to live with my current (and favorite) human! I've been living with her since I was 6 months old. I've got lots of toys. Most of them are the fuzzy kind (my teeth are very sharp and I can chew through a plastic or rubber squeaky toy in about three minutes). My absolute favorite toy is my tennis ball! I have chewed off nearly all of its yellow covering; it's time for another one. I also love to chew on bones. My favorite actors are canines. I really admire Verdell the Brussels Griffon in "As Good as It Gets" , the Taco Bell Chihuahua and Spuds McKenzie, and I've heard that Puffy's performance in 'There's Something About Mary' should receive an Academy Award nomination. By the way, I can do many tricks: sit, shake hands, beg, lie down, roll over, dance and play dead. At right, I'm doing my Little Red Riding Hood impression. Hollywood casting agents, my email address is MizMamie@aol.com." Mamie's owner is Debbie Poe, 37, an assistant to a financial manager who lives in Bronxville. "The reason I set up a Web page for my dog was mainly because I was bored one night and thought my dog could use a page of her own," she said. "I've had other dogs in the past, but Mamie is the sweetest, most lovable dog of them all (and the cutest one, too), and I thought it would be nice to put some photos of her on the Internet." Ms. Poe (dlp@cloud9.net) said Mamie has received perhaps a dozen emails, mostly from other Pomeranians who wanted to say hello and to declare their love for her. "A few messages wanted to know if Poms were a good breed to own, and one message wanted to know how I trained Mamie to roll over," she said. If that isn't trivial enough, there is also a site produced in Westchester County devoted to the history of the golf tee (www.whackswell.com/ tee.html). Did you know that before the invention of the wooden golf tee, golfers placed the ball on a small mound of sand? And that the first patent for a wooden tee was granted in 1898 to Dr. George Grant, who was, by the way, the first black dentist to graduate from the Harvard School of Dental Medicine? His golf innovation did not win wide acceptance, but one developed by another dentist, Dr. William Lowell, did take off. His invention, patented in 1924, was called the 'Reddy Tee,' named for its color and handiness. Actually, the tee site is just a page in a larger site set up by two Westchester dentists who have started a company, Whacks-well, selling specially made tees to replace the built-in rubber ones at driving ranges. In the last two months, they have had only a few orders, but that does not deter them. "It's like a brochure," one of the dentists, Dr. Evan Wetzler of Briarcliff Manor, said. "If we get sales, great." He and his partner, Dr. Jay Wagner of Yorktown Heights, spent about $2,000 and two months setting up their site; they also pay a monthly fee of about $70. "It's just the way the world works now," Dr. Wetzler said. "You have to have a site." Once you have your golf tee, you can find out where to golf by visiting (www.co.westchester.ny.us/parks/ golf.htm) for information about the five courses owned and operated by the county. Some private clubs have sites as well. Besides golf, the list of sites devoted to interests and organizations is almost endless. Click here for a look at some interesting places you can go and people you can meet in Westchester County. For bird-watchers there is (www.audubon.org/chapter/ny/ sawmillriver), the Saw Mill River Audubon Society's list of popular birding sites in the county. History buff? There is the Thomas Paine National Historical Association in New Rochelle with the archived works of the revolutionary and journalist (www.mediapro.net/ cdadesign/paine). Want to trace your family's roots? There is the Westchester County Genealogical Society (http://pages .prodigy.com/HFBK19A/wcgs.htm). Other sites include Westchester County Genealogical Resources (http://pages.prodigy.com/ HFBK19A/wcgsrs01.htm), which lists libraries operated by the churches of the Latter Day Saints, the Westchester County Historical Society, the Westchester County Genealogical Society, the Guild of Genealogical Research in Westchester County, the Scarsdale Family History Center, the county's public libraries and the Lower Hudson Conference, which is a nonprofit consortium of historical agencies in the six counties of the lower Hudson region -- its Directory of Historical Agencies lists historical societies, museums, historic houses, libraries and town historians in those counties and the Bronx. The genealogy site also has information about Quaker records (members of the Society of Friends were early settlers in the county). For the Westchester County Airport try (www.squid-ink.com/hpn/ index1.htm), a very graphics-intensive site, which offers everything anyone would want to know about the airport, which is so much more convenient for Westchester County residents than La Guardia or Kennedy International or Newark. Now, if only more flights left from there . . . White Plains Rugby (www.ziplink .net/wprugby/history.html) is a site for fans and players sponsored by the White Plains Rugby Football Club. The Taconic Opera? Try (http:// members.aol.com/taconicop). Yes, there is opera in Westchester County -- in Yorktown Heights. The site, however, is almost as difficult to understand as a libretto in Italian. For the German Language Institute of Westchester (http:// 208.31.60.11/gli). Learn German or Japanese at this center in White Plains and Mount Kisco. Personal Connections, a site that links up with the personals advertisements in dozens of publications, including a newspaper that serves Westchester, The Journal News, is at (www.datemaker.com). The Ukrainian Heritage Festival can be found at (www.brama.com/ yonkersukrainianfest), offers information on the annual festival in Yonkers, including photographs of traditional cuisine like the dumplings called varennyky. Sandy's Old Homestead, a bar and restaurant in Port Chester that caters to gays and lesbians, is found at (www.cynergistics.com/sandys/ sandymain.html). . Cybersmith, a cyber cafe in The Westchester mall in White Plains, has this lengthy address: (http:// magneto.cybersmith.com/inside/ whp.html). The Hermit's Grave is where to find Johann W. Stolting (1810-88), the only person in a marked grave in Irvington. (Others are buried elsewhere.) Click on (www.oswego.edu/ yasinsac/hermit.html). http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos

title:
GOLF;
L.P.G.A. Head Takes Job With an Internet Company
body: In an unexpected move, Jim Ritts resigned as commissioner of the Ladies Professional Golf Association Tour today after only three years to become chief operating officer of an Internet company. Ritts will be replaced in 45 days by Ty Votaw, the tour's 37-year-old vice president for business affairs. As recently as November, Ritts was planning to remain as commissioner for at least another three years. But Ritts said he could not pass up the opportunity to work with Digital Entertainment, a corporation based in Santa Monica, Calif., which delivers television-quality programming to the Internet. "I believe we are in the beginning stages of a communications revolution, and it's exciting to have an opportunity to become involved in that," Ritts said from his car phone on his way to the Orlando, Fla., airport. "This is a day of mixed emotions for me. I'm happy about the opportunity, but sad to be leaving the L.P.G.A." Almost everyone within the L.P.G.A. was caught off guard by Ritts's decision. Dottie Pepper, one of the tour's most prominent players, said nobody suspected Ritts might be leaving during last month's players meeting. "I'm shocked," Pepper said. "He had just gotten a contract extension. The L.P.G.A. can keep leaks from getting out better than the Clinton Administration." Pepper said Ritts still had strong support from the players, and she said she believed that the tour would remain in good hands with Votaw, who has been with the L.P.G.A. since 1991, working for Ritts and the former commissioner Charlie Mechem. "Between Jim and Charlie, they really groomed Ty for the job," Pepper said. "Jim's strength was marketing and television, while Charlie had great business savvy." Ritts, 45, made a strong impact during his tenure. Televised events have increased from 19 events in 1994 to 33 this year. The tour has grown from 36 events in 1995 to 43 this year, while this year's total purses are $36.2 million, a 50 percent increase from three years ago. With young stars like Annika Sorenstam, Karrie Webb, and Se Ri Pak to promote, the L.P.G.A. has the potential for more growth. However, Pepper wondered if some of the tour's 43 events would have trouble attracting enough big-name players. "Ty is going to have to listen to the sponsors and to players," Pepper said, "because with 43 events, there's a chance for some weak fields." Meanwhile, many companies within the golf industry are suffering through tough economic times. Attracting strong sponsorship will continue to be one of the tour's biggest challenges. Some of the tour's most prominent players did not have their equipment contracts renewed this year because corporations are cutting back. "We're going to have to reach out to nongolf companies and establish those relationships," Votaw said. "Jim did a great job, and I see no reason why this will not be a smooth transition. The players know me, and my experience with the tour will be invaluable. It's an honor to take this new position, and I'm looking forward to the challenge." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNET REVIEW;
A Sex Metaphor, by Victoria's Secret
body: Maybe this is really what sex is all about. Squinting at a commemorative-stamp-size picture sent through cyberspace by the much-hyped Victoria's Secret's fashion show on Wednesday night, one could make out a bit of flesh peeking above a strip of lacy red. Then the image jerkily churned into a smear of ocher and burgundy: it looked as if a sheet had been pulled out of a copier too soon. And of course there was the inimitable sound: an otherworldly groan slipping into garbled murmurs, then violently erupting with hints of Carl Orff, house music and nightclub bacchanals gone bad. Ah, the glories of Internet broadcasts! So sexual in their teasing incompleteness, their unpredictable tumescences, their latex-garbed sound! In a few years, with appropriate advances in speed and data processing, the Web will provide an experience as seamlessly Lycra-like as television; it may even replace television. But in the meantime, most Internet connections allow only stuttering moving images to be seen in tiny windows. Thousands of dollars of silicon and software are proudly used to present bottled-sounding radio broadcasts, stop-and-start film clips and even a thumb-size video version of the President's grand jury testimony. It looks as if the Victoria's Secret enterprise has eclipsed all events that have ever been broadcast exclusively on the Internet. According to the company that provided access, Broadcast.com, there were more than two million attempts to log on to the show, its previews and its reruns on Wednesday evening, exceeding the audiences for some television broadcasts. Access was often clogged and transmissions distorted even beyond low Internet standards, but it hardly mattered. Peering through that small, smudged window on the computer screen almost made one feel like Jimmy Stewart gazing across the courtyard with oversize binoculars in "Rear Window." That may have been part of the point. Maybe the folks at Victoria's Secret knew precisely what they were doing when they spent $5 million promoting the live Webcast of their "Spring Fashion Show" at Cipriani's on Wall Street. This mail-order and mall-staple company spent three years designing its Web site (www.victoriassecret.com), which comes with sample videos and an interactive bra salon. The company's $1.5 million Super Bowl commercial led to a million visits to their Web site within an hour. Those visitors were more than voyeurs: daily sales doubled or tripled. Then came the full-page ads for Wednesday's Webcast in national newspapers, including The newyork Times, promising a high-toned coupling of high tech and high fashion along with a "seat on the virtual runway." There was even a bit of foreplay: pink ribbons were displayed at the newyork Stock Exchange on Wednesday; Stephanie Seymour, one of the catalogue's stars, rang the closing bell. A seat on the exchange, a seat on the runway, a seat at the computer: money, sex and technology in happy communion. The 20-minute clip is now archived and is available for continuing visits, but why such a fuss in the first place? What was the appeal of high tech and high fashion when the Web already offers so much high tech and low fashion? Why turn to barely visible images of models in white teddies, when G-strings and bras are so quickly shed on other Web sites? Well, there is the obvious: we are obsessed with undergarments -- they certainly played fascinating props in the current drama in Washington -- and the Web, catering to popular taste, is right at home with such matters. The medium has met the message: delay, provocation, unpredictability, furtive flickers of something hidden -- these elements of the Webcast are also part of the appeal of Victoria's Secret. Gazing at this Webcast was like watching a striptease through a keyhole, catching glimpses of a fuller world that one squints at, trying to imagine in fleshy glory. Even the fashion show's camera work -- jumpy, skewed, jarringly shifting perspective -- never let the gaze settle too clearly on anything. This Webcast was, like so much else, media lingerie: teasing garb for an event one could only dream about. With all its awkward crudities, it kept a Web audience captivated as people hit the reload button on their browsers hoping to see through or past or under or beyond. Sex as partial disclosure: sounds like Victoria's secret. http://www.nytimes.com

title: MCI Worldcom to Start Internet Service
body: MCI Worldcom Inc., the No. 2 unitedstates long-distance company, confirmed yesterday that it would start a new Internet access service using information and content from America Online's Compuserve unit. The new service allows MCI Worldcom to re-enter the consumer Internet business that the MCI Communications Corporation exited last year. MCI sold its Internet operations to gain regulatory approval for its $40 billion acquisition by Worldcom Inc. last September. The new MCI Worldcom Internet service is available to MCI Worldcom long-distance subscribers for $16.95 a month for the first 150 hours of local access. MCI Worldcom will send customers one bill for the long-distance and Internet services. Customers using just the Internet service will pay $19.95 a month. Compuserve will provide MCI Worldcom's service with access to news, weather, favorite links and Instant messenger, a pop-up window that allows on-line users to chat with one another. MCI Worldcom dissolved a previous alliance with the Internet search engine Yahoo when MCI sold off its Internet business to Britain's Cable and Wireless for $1.75 billion and closed its merger with Worldcom. MCI Worldcom said it did not anticipate any regulatory problems with the new service. It noted that its relationship with Compuserve was not exclusive. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
System C rash Doesn't Hurt E*Trade Stock
body: Internet stock traders are known, with some justification, as a hair-trigger lot, bidding up the shares of companies on the slightest hint of good news and dropping them with scorn at the first dimming of otherwise glowing prospects. So why wouldn't E-vestors be bailing out of E*Trade Group after two days in which the on-line broker's trading system was down for hours at a time? If that wasn't enough, Eliot L. Spitzer, the Attorney General of newyork, said yesterday that he would investigate the Internet trading industry after his office received complaints about delayed orders and unavailable trading systems. Yet E*Trade's stock hardly flinched. Sure, it fell $1.75 a share yesterday, to $53.50. But given the usual volatility of Internet companies, that is essentially unchanged. And that still leaves E*Trade's market value of $6 billion higher than more established, and decidedly more profitable, firms like Paine Webber,Bear, Stearns and Lehman Brothers. Investors -- a good number of whom use E*Trade and its on-line rivals -- have apparently concluded that the company's problems and the cloud of complaints above the entire industry will not ultimately rain on the parade of on-line investing. "Every other big broker in the space has also had problems and system outages," said Stephen C. Franco, an analyst with Piper Jaffray. "Investors accept that the brokers use cutting-edge technology that doesn't always work perfectly." Mr. Franco released a report yesterday that indicated the number of on-line brokerage accounts last year doubled to 7.3 million, with total assets of $420 billion. This growth has hardly slowed, even at brokers that have had well-publicized system failures. Mr. Franco said, for example, that Ameritrade was forced in the fourth quarter to pay $3.1 million to compensate customers whose orders were mishandled. Even so, only 3 percent of its clients closed their accounts during the quarter, he said. "It is so difficult to move a brokerage account that people rarely do it," he said. Of course, the usual crop of lawyers sprouted yesterday, threatening to file class-action suits to recover the losses E*Trade customers say they incurred from the unavailability of service. Legal experts, however, said that winning such cases would be difficult, either as class actions or as individual suits. "We can't hold people liable for every honest mistake," said Lewis Lowenfels, an expert in securities fraud with Tolins & Lowenfels in newyork. To win a case, he said, an investor would have to prove a broker with a system problem committed the financial equivalent of malpractice. A more difficult challenge for on-line brokerage firms is posed by investors who placed orders to buy initial public offerings that were first priced at, say, less than $20 a share, then filled at closer to $100 a share. Technically, the law provides little protection for investors who place market orders, which are filled at the best available price, rather than limit orders, which specify a maximum share price. Mr. Lowenfels, though, said some brokers might be vulnerable to complaints they violated rules requiring them to make sure investments are suitable for their customers. If a broker knew that a customer who placed an order to buy 1,000 shares of a stock at $20 would not have the resources to buy the stock if the best available price was $100 but executed the trade anyway, that client might have a case, he said. Maryann A. Waryjas, a lawyer with Jenner & Block in Chicago, argues that such laws have not been adjusted to take into account brokers that are machines, not people. "Historically, your broker would call you back and tell you the I.P.O. had gone way up and that you couldn't get it for the offering price," she said. "The technology has gotten ahead of the rules." As for E*Trade, its contract with its customers states that the company, which is based in Palo Alto, Calif., is not liable for system problems. But Lisa Nash, an E*Trade spokeswoman, said that it would still compensate customers who had legitimate claims that they were harmed. "Rather than hiding behind what the legal agreement says, we will try to do what is right," she said. "We have a virtual brand. If people don't trust us, it weakens the power of the brand." She declined to say how much the company expected to pay in compensation, but she said that fewer than 10,000 customers were affected. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Investors seem to have shrugged off bad news concerning E*Trade, an on-line brokerage firm whose corporate offices are in Palo Alto, Calif. (Associated Press)(pg. C7)

title: AT&T Finds Internet and a Crowd of Critics
body: As the AT&T Corporation aggressively enters the cable business, with plans to offer high-speed Internet connections to millions of American homes, a growing group of rivals and consumer groups has begun a nationwide lobbying effort to force the telephone giant to open its system to Internet competitors. The fight pits AT&T, which has struck cable deals in recent months that will give it access to nearly half of the nation's homes, against a coalition led by America Online, the world's largest internet service provider, with 15 million customers. It has also drawn a large group of companies that are the Internet gateways for millions of Americans, as well as some prominent former Washington officials who are now lobbyists working for the telephone industry, the cable industry and the Internet service providers. "This is the biggest issue in the whole technology communications realm," said Charles M. Brewer, chairman and chief executive of Mindspring Enterprises Inc., an Internet service provider with about 340,000 subscribers that joined with America Online, U S West, MCI Worldcom and others today in formally unveiling their anti-AT&T coalition, called Open Net. AT&T is expected to receive approval from Federal regulators as early as this month to complete its $31.8 billion acquisition of Tele-Communications Inc., the second-largest cable company, with 14 million subscribers. By providing high-speed Internet service over cable systems on a broad scale, AT&T will be able to offer millions of consumers the ability to navigate through the World Wide Web at speeds up to 100 times faster than the typical connection through ordinary telephone lines. But there is a catch. AT&T intends to require that any customer who subscribes to its high-speed cable modem service must also pay the monthly fee of $40 or so for Internet access provided by the At Home Corporation, of which AT&T will be the largest shareholder when it completes its acquisition of TCI. That has prompted protests by other Internet providers that fear they may be frozen out and complain that AT&T will control the computer standards on the Internet for video, audio and other transmissions. Both sides say the outcome of the battle -- which is just beginning before regulators and Congress here, and in courts and municipalities around the nation -- may determine whether the Internet will continue to be a free-wheeling technology or will be dominated by a handful of large corporate interests. And both say the fight will determine which companies survive the shakeout of the industry and which profit the most as the Internet matures. "The Internet would not be happening but for the fact that consumers can now choose their service provider in an unimpeded way," Mr. Brewer said. "If we had to rely on the owners of the last mile of transmission, it's unquestionable that the Internet would not have developed as it has." Executives at AT&T and the cable companies respond that America Online and other competitors are trying to muscle in and make use of technological improvements to the cable systems that are requiring investments of billions of dollars. Executives at AT&T and the cable companies say there will be plenty of other providers of high-speed access to the Internet, such as digital telephone technology and satellites. Moreover, they say, customers will still be able to make use of America Online and other Internet providers -- though they will still have to pay the At Home fee. The AT&T and cable executives contend that revenues from At Home will help to defray the huge capital costs associated with upgrading the cable system and that the cable companies did not undertake such an investment simply to provide what they call a "dumb pipeline" for competitors to take advantage of. "There's a certain arrogance to their position, which confuses what's good for AOL with what's good for the Internet," said James W. Cicconi, general counsel and head of government relations at AT&T. "It's certainly disingenuous and borders on hypocrisy to say for years that the government should stay out of regulating the Internet and then suddenly invite the government in when their business interests change. This is just a very big competitive player trying to disadvantage a smaller player that came up with a better idea." Earlier this week, AT&T reached an agreement with Time Warner for access to 12 million of that company's customers to provide local phone service through cable lines. While AT&T executives indicated that they did not anticipate competing with Time Warner's own high-speed Internet service, rivals questioned whether the agreement could ultimately lead toward AT&T's offering some kind of service over Time Warner's cables. While scores of companies are trying to develop higher-speed Internet service through telephones and satellites, some experts say cable modems ultimately hold the greatest promise of making the World Wide Web much faster, and therefore much more attractive to computer users and businesses. At least 350,000 homes -- some estimates run as high as 700,000 -- have some kind of high-speed Internet service, according to a study released today by the Federal Communications Commission. But analysts such as Forrester Research Inc. estimate that by the end of 2002, 16 million American households will have high-speed computer connections to the Internet, and nearly 80 percent of those will be through cable-based providers like At Home and its top competitor, Road Runner, a unit of Time Warner. Although some analysts and executives involved in the fight believe the regulatory war is simply a sideshow to a possible commercial settlement, both AT&T and America Online are prepared to spend millions of dollars for lobbying and legal expenses and have retained some of the biggest lobbying and press relations firms in Washington and around the nation. The fight is being waged on four fronts: in Congress, at the Federal Communications Commission, before local cable regulators in cities around the country, and in the Federal courts. Consumer groups have lined up with America Online, contending that AT&T and the cable companies are trying to control the content of what passes through their wires, just as they tried to control what programs appeared on their channels before that practice was prohibited by an act of Congress. "They are doing what Microsoft is accused of doing: building a system where they say you can't separate the transmission from the actual content," said Gene Kimmelman, co-director of the Washington office of Consumers Union, referring to the Government's antitrust suit filed against the software company. "They're saying if you want AOL, we'll let you have it but you have to pay At Home first. This is precisely what telephone companies can't do. The request from our side is let's open up access to cable wire the same way we require them to open up for programming." In recent days, the Federal Communications Commission has declined to step into the fight, but has said it will watch the situation closely. Officials there say they do not want to do anything that might impede the progress of upgrading the cable lines. But cable regulators in a growing number of cities, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle, have held hearings and vowed to consider the issue as franchise licenses are renewed this year. And one city, Portland, Ore., has blocked AT&T's cable venture from moving in without first opening its proposed new broadband pipeline to rival gateways like America Online. The move by the city's cable regulators recently prompted AT&T to file a lawsuit in Federal court there.  Local Phone Alternative WASHINGTON, Feb. 3 (Bloomberg News) -- MCI Worldcom Inc., the No. 2 long-distance phone company in the unitedstates, will immediately begin offering local phone service to residents in newyork State by leasing the Bell Atlantic Corporation's local phone network. MCI Worldcom will offer flat-rate pricing for a local phone line at about 5 percent below Bell Atlantic's service. In the newyork City metropolitan area and surrounding counties, it will also offer customers a basic local phone line and 100 phone calls a month for about $14.99 a month. MCI Worldcom has offered local service to residential customers in some markets, including newyork City, by leasing the complete phone service of the regional phone companies at a discount and reselling it. It discontinued that resale service last year, saying the discounts given by the regional carriers to rivals were not steep enough to be able to make a profit. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
ESSAY;
He'll Take His Web Pages Straight, With No Java Jive - Correction Appended
body: EVERYWHERE I turn, there's another story or advertisement about the Net. The copy is frequently illustrated with an enviably attractive person sitting in front of a screen from which she has just received masses of intensely satisfying information.  The impression given, if never fully stated, is that most of this red-hot stuff does not arrive in text but in pictures, numbers, sound effects -- a new Ur data for which the tiresome old ABC's are rarely employed. Conceived by President Eisenhower's Pentagon as a system for linking Government computers, the Internet (nee Arpanet) has been called the most significant Federal investment since the Louisiana Purchase, but I'm still from Missouri. All this hoopla reminds me of the A. A. Milne story in "Winnie the Pooh": "In Which Eeyore Has a Birthday and Gets Two Presents." Eeyore is thrilled with the empty honey jar Pooh gives him. "I believe my balloon will just go into that pot," he says. The news bulges with stories about dispensing therapy on the Net, doing business on the Net, trolling for unsuspecting sexual prey on the Net. Not on this computer. Most of what I do on the electronic superhighway is write and read letters, and if it did not involve the elimination of envelopes and a certain parallel loosening of style, the process would be similar to the one that once involved lambskins and sharpened feathers. Putting the fabulous Net to such base service may be the equivalent of dropping a burst balloon into an empty honey jar, but like Milne's old donkey, I am delighted. Admittedly, if it weren't for graphical user interfaces (G.U.I.'s), I probably wouldn't be able to figure out how to get my email. I know this and am thankful. But when it comes to streaming video, downloading music and all the other ways the Web is supposed to deliver images glorious to behold, I'm not all that interested. What's wonderful to me is the happy marriage of hard science and self-expression. And it happened so fast. That the Web would enhance communication -- via text -- was apparent early on to some people, like James P. Girard, a novelist who is a friend and email correspondent. He worked at newspapers as a reporter and later as a computer guru. "Like most people," he told me in an email message, "I thought of computers as number machines, right up until the day I applied for a job on The Wichita Eagle in late 1977 and discovered that the copy editors were working at computer terminals. These are word machines, I thought. I gotta have one of these. I think I was the third person in Newton, Kan., to own one, and I had to go all the way to Kansas City to buy it. The guy I bought it from threw in a membership to The Source and a modem -- 300 baud. I think there were maybe a couple of hundred people on The Source." Most of the early Source correspondents had handles, Jim recalled. " 'The Insane Chicken,' he wrote, "was a very bright 9-year-old girl from Boston, using her father's account (he never used it himself), who pretended for a while -- quite successfully -- to be a woman of 25. There was a highly respected programmer, named John something-or-other, who everyone spoke of with a kind of reverence and deferred to on software issues. (The Source had a built-in programming language, which actually allowed users, if they knew how, to modify the environment and introduce new capabilities; John was one of the most active, and, as far as I know, invented a number of things that are standard now.) It turned out he was a 15-year-old kid from Palo Alto. "You didn't really know any of the usual things you know about people -- age, gender, race, etc. You were really just dealing with another human intelligence, through language, and the rest of that stuff, when you did learn it, often turned out to be a kind of disappointment. People were trying to make for themselves an on-line persona that they liked better. I think that impulse, if nothing else, is likely to boost linguistic skills tremendously over the next couple of generations." Katherine McNamara is another email friend and the widow of Lee Goerner, the editor Jim and I shared at Atheneum. In 1997, she started Archipelago, a serious literary journal on the Net. In an interview for the 1997 Dictionary of Literary Biography, she spoke of the Web as providing a publishing opportunity for people with limited capital. "Even though what's called literature or writing on the Web has incited a great deal of self-indulgence and youthful experimentation," she was quoted as saying, "it has also made it possible, I find, to distribute the best work you can find." Archipelago (www.archipelago.org) is one of the sites I visit (and contribute to). Sometimes I do shop, at other sites, but even then it's usually at Amazon.com, and what I buy is books. I turn off the graphics. In my thirst for pure text, I seem not to be alone. "Readers admire our graphics," said Cyrus Krohn, managing editor of Slate magazine (www.slate.com), "but what they really admire is fine writing. A month ago, we began delivering articles via email several times a day. We're delivering to In boxes around the world with no art. The readers appreciate not having to wade through the pulp to get to the juice." There is plenty of text on the Net. I found a Blake Web site. He was described as a multimedia poet, which I think is a stretch, but it is Blake nevertheless, annotated. If one characteristic of the Net is a flood of sites that are chiefly cherished by this writer for their texts, another is that the Net is wildly democratic. Amazon.com has reviews by professional critics, but it also has reviews written by anybody. In an interview conducted by Jacob Weisberg for Slate, the novelist Tom Wolfe described the on-line community as "a virtual Haight-Ashbury." He added, "The users are kind of virtual hippies; they sense they're discovering a wonderful community and they feel high." Which does not always make for a clear head. I visited a virtual writers' club once and found many virtual writers. Many of them were poets, blank verse having become the medium that requires an awe-inspiring proficiency, or none at all. Never, or rarely, has the artist's feeling of stark and dismal alienation been so widely shared. For his AOL screen name, my son, now 12, chose "stranger." Dozens of others had already picked it, so he had to add a number to the end -- a very high one. If you're going to be alienated, though, isn't it better not to be alone? I used to spend a half-hour every morning writing in my journal. "I'm depressed," I'd write. Now I send email to a half-dozen close and articulate friends. "I'm depressed," I write. "Me, too," they holler back, and we all feel better. Or at least I do. Once or twice, I've been betrayed when somebody sent me a picture, but I'm the forgiving sort. Mostly they send me words.  Sometimes happy, sometimes despairing, often precise. It's astonishing what you can do with those little things. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article in Circuits on Thursday about the lure of words on the Web misstated the source of a quotation from Tom Wolfe. He described the on-line community as "a virtual Haight-Ashbury" in an interview by Steve Hammer for Nuvo Newsweekly, not in an interview by Jacob Weisberg for the on-line magazine Slate. Correction-Date: February 8, 1999, Monday Graphic   Drawing (Charlene Potts)

title: Fund Reels as USA Talks.com Tumbles
body: The WWW Internet Fund slashed the value of its shares in USA Talks.com by 50 percent after the Securities and Exchange Commission halted trading in the Internet telephony company, said Lawrence York, the fund's co-manager. USA Talks.com shares last traded Thursday at $52.25. The fund now estimates the shares are worth $26.125, Mr. York said. At that price, USA Talks.com would lose $650 million of the $1.3 billion market value it commanded on Thursday, the day before the shares were suspended. "We've asked the S.E.C. to tell us what to do," Mr. York said in an interview, adding that no reply had been received. On Friday, the S.E.C. ordered a two-week halt in trading of USA Talks.com. because of questions that were raised regarding the accuracy and adequacy of public information on the company. Mr. York said his fund invested $200,000 in USA Talks.com. He declined to say how many shares it owns or what percentage of the $15 million mutual fund they represent. On Monday, the fund's share value registered the largest one-day percentage decline in at least three months after it cut the valuation of its USA Talks.com investment. The fund shares plunged 5.9 percent, or $1.29, to $20.68, while the Interactive Week Internet Index was unchanged. On Tuesday they fell slightly to $20.53. USA Talks.com on Tuesday dismissed Trendmark Inc., a marketing company that provided most of the 2,300 customers for its start-up Internet telephone service, because of poor sales. It also canceled its agreement to acquire Trendmark, a privately owned company based in Memphis. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
MAKING BOOKS;
Count the Ways: How, Not Why - Correction Appended
body: Yes, one can surely buy the poems of Emily Dickinson and Shakespeare's sonnets this Valentine's Day from any bookstore or on-line bookseller, but publishing has nonetheless turned the holiday of a thousand and one romances into an exercise in the utilitarian. The fuzzy and lyrical, the twisted skeins of lies and sighs that make up so much of the romantic novel are not as popular as the real and practical. How to make love, rather than why. Has it always been thus? Not really. Book publishers, who one supposes are as sentimental and dreamy as anyone else in the faraway spaces of their imaginations, seemingly have gotten caught up this year in the increasingly popular self-help genre. So for Valentine's Day it's refining sex and defining relationships, without the flowers and chocolates. Which may be a bit of a risk since Valentine's Day and Mother's Day are generally the only times of the year in which "women's fiction," as publishers loosely call it, can find its away to the front of the bookstores (with the exception, of course, of the mega-selling female authors). This is either because book makers feel these are the two special days worth spending the money to buy such positioning or the sellers themselves feel it might be good business. Publishers, like other retailers, are driven by their ambits of opportunity, like Christmas, Thanksgiving, etc. Typically this year, for instance, Amazon, the on-line bookseller, has on its Valentine's Day gift list "The Kissing Companion: Secret Technique of Over 500 Exotic Kisses," by Stephen Jarvis and Elaine Edwards, and "10,000 Ways to Say I Love You," by Gregory J. P. Godek. For the outwardly rigid but secretly incontestably romantic buyer there is "Recruiting Love: Using the Business Skills You Have to Find the Love You Want," by Jessica B. Freeman. Barnes & Noble's on-line service is touting, among many others, "The Art of Spooning: A Cuddler's Handbook," by Jim Grace, and "101 Nights of Great Sex," by Laura Corn. And since the celebration is surely about nostalgia, HarperCollins has issued what it calls the "all new" 30th-anniversary edition of "Everything You Always Wanted to Know About Sex (but Were Afraid to Ask)," by Dr. David Reuben, and Pantheon has reissued "The Technique of the Love Affair," by Doris Langley Moore, originally published in 1928 but updated this year by Norris Epstein. That book is almost high art in the lineage of such work, far beyond the liaisons hinted at in the greeting cards, a work of such apparent transcendental importance in the genre that Dorothy Parker said of it that if only she had been privy to its secrets "maybe I could have been successful rather than successive." Probably the most graphic book to capture the quality of this year's celebration is "Sex Tips for Straight Women From a Gay Man," by Dan Anderson and Maggie Berman on Regan Books. Now none of the above is entirely fair to book publishers. There are in fact plenty of lusty romantic fictions in the stores aimed to flutter the hearts of the Valentine's Day buyer, although Irwyn Applebaum, president and publisher of Bantam Books, said: "Many booksellers have the old Erich Segal syndrome: 'Madison County,' 'Message in a Bottle.' They are more into those romances than ones written by women." (Nicholas Sparks's "Message in a Bottle" was published in hardcover last summer, but Warner Books has gotten a huge gushy best-selling paperback pop out of advertising for the movie, which opens two days before Valentine's Day.) But no such manly hangup for Mr. Applebaum. He hopes to make Valentine's Day a bank day for two novelists who are women. In the alchemy that is book publishing, Bantam is printing nearly 500,000 copies of a paperback original by Jane Feather -- her 12th book -- cleverly, if not obviously, titled "A Valentine Wedding." "It combines two certain attention getters -- the word 'valentine' and the word 'wedding' -- and we get a one-two punch," he said, sounding about as happy as a candy maker this time of the year. Bantam also hopes to surf the high emotional tide of the Valentine celebration with Luanne Rice's "Cloud Nine." Mr. Applebaum describes this as "adult fiction in its best sense" by which he means it combines the complex themes of love, remission from cancer and a surprise romance with an unexpected man. He is betting 50,000 copies, hardcover, for a first printing. "There are many meanings to the title," Mr. Applebaum said rhapsodically. "It's the name of the shop the character runs, in which she sells comforters, and of course, dare I say it, she's on cloud nine with pleasure." You see, titles are all important. Over at Warner Books, along with "Message in a Bottle," the publisher has great hopes for Katherine Stone's "Thief of Hearts," a novel of "heart-wrenching betrayals and unforgivable pain." Still John Aherne, the associate editor, said, "It's interesting to see how more and more the prescriptive books are breaking out, along with the fuzzies that come out on the 14th." He has high hopes for Joyce Marlow's "Country Ways: Secrets for Finding and Keeping a Country Man," aimed at those women who, as with Lady Chatterley, are apparently searching for a gamekeeper. "We've found that the books that tend to work for us are practical advice," Mr. Aherne said, adding that he was particularly prideful about what he called an anti-Valentine's Day book, "The Breakup Book," by Monica Sheehan. "It's for people who could use all the advice they could get after the bitter reminder that it doesn't always work out," he said. So what about Mother's Day, the next great celebration of love? Bantam is gearing up "Hot Sex: How to Do It," by Tracey Cox, advice for Mom and Dad on the hot tin roof. http://www.nytimes.com Correction  The Making Books column yesterday, about books promoted around St. Valentine's Day, misstated the given name of the writer who recently updated Doris Langley Moore's 1928 book "The Technique of the Love Affair," reissued this year by Pantheon. She is Norrie Epstein, not Norris. Correction-Date: February 5, 1999, Friday Graphic   Photo: In love: "A Valentine Wedding."

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Vast Riches and Rude Vagaries of Internet Trading
body: There is perhaps one good thing to say about the exuberant frenzy in Internet stocks: It is opening up the Silicon riches beyond the young boys' club that has hoarded them until now. The latest Internet billionaire, for example, is not some lucky Stanford graduate student or nocturnal Seattle programmer barely past shaving age. Yesterday's billion-dollar lottery ticket was in the hands of Muriel Siebert, a veteran of breaking through glass ceilings for four decades. Mickey Siebert, as she is known to those old enough to remember when electronic trading meant calling your broker on the telephone, caused quite a few waves in 1967 as the first woman to buy a seat on the newyork Stock Exchange. Later, she was the first woman banking superintendent of newyork State. Yesterday, the shares of the Siebert Financial Corporation, the holding company for Ms. Siebert's brokerage firm, soared $23.50, or 90.4 percent, to $49.50. A week ago, the shares traded at $11. The stock's ascent places Ms. Siebert's paper wealth slightly over $1 billion. Siebert Financial has benefited from investors' fascination with on-line trading, which has turned out to be the hottest business on the Internet. In the fourth quarter of 1998, one in every seven stock trades in this country was entered over the Internet, according to Bill Burnham, electronic commerce analyst and trading guru at Credit Suisse First Boston. And in January, he estimates, on-line volume rose by a third. As a result, the shares of any company that offers stock trading on a World Wide Web site has been surging. Even shares of JB Oxford Holdings, a Beverly Hills brokerage firm being investigated on charges of market manipulation, rose 153 percent yesterday, to $12. Never mind that the electronic trading business is hardly easy. The E*Trade Group, despite a $100 million investment in technology, suffered significant system problems yesterday and was unable to accept trades in two periods during the day. Analysts say E*Trade will suffer no long-term damage from the incidents because most of the other on-line firms have also had occasional computer glitches. "It's like handing out speeding tickets at the Indy 500," Mr. Burnham said. "You can pull over whoever you want to." In this fast field, Siebert Financial had been something of an also-ran. The brokerage firm has offered on-line trading for the last several years. But Mr. Burnham says it is a minor player in this market, with no more than a few thousand on-line trades a day. Moreover, the firm hardly has a blue-chip pedigree. It went public in 1996, not through a traditional offering, but by buying a defunct Brooklyn furniture company, a tactic looked down upon by Wall Street. But that hasn't stopped stock traders from seizing on Siebert as potentially a cheaper way to bet on electronic brokerage than by buying the expensive leaders: E*Trade, Ameritrade and Charles Schwab. It's not that many people actually believe that Siebert will be the next E*Trade, but that enough people are willing to bet that someone else will think so. "There is a group of marauding traders who are doing this with their eyes wide open," Mr. Burnham said. "There is talk in the chat rooms; then there is takeover speculation, and finally the stock starts to move, bringing in the momentum players." But there are only 710,000 shares of Siebert Financial that the public can trade, as Ms. Siebert owns 92 percent of the company. Since 10.4 million shares of Siebert Financial traded on the Nasdaq stock market yesterday, the average share changed hands seven times during the day. (Nasdaq counts each trade twice.) What that means, of course, is that the real price of Siebert Financial, should Ms. Siebert choose to sell it, will likely be far less than the value ascribed to it by the market yesterday. "I have no intention of selling any of my stock," Ms. Siebert said in a terse telephone interview. "We've been in business for a long time." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph: "Two Faces On Line" Internet trading has helped Siebert Financial, but technical problems that shut down E*Trade for parts of yesterday, gave the stock a hit.
