title:
Trying to Get in Tune With the Digital Age;
Recording Industry Seeks a Standard For Distributing Music on the Web
body: For the music business, it was a harbinger. A Scottish rock band, the Jesus and Mary Chain, played at Irving Plaza during last summer's Intel newyork Music Festival, and two hours later their live performance of "Virtually Unreal" was on the Internet for the group's fans worldwide to download and listen to on their computers. Commercially speaking, it was small potatoes: a technology demonstration by an alternative-rock band with a devoted following but not a mass public. Yet the uploading of "Virtually Unreal" presaged a day when most recorded music will be available as digital information, distributed not on disks and tapes that have to be manufactured and shipped, but as data files that can be zapped instantly across the Internet. The Jesus and Mary Chain gained valuable publicity from their World Wide Web demo. But just as significantly, the band and its label, Sub Pop Records, received not a dime from the thousands of fans who grabbed the song off the Internet. No wonder the record industry is worried. It is easy to give music away on the Internet. In fact, thousands of songs now circulate freely in a technical format known as MP3, an easy way to swap recordings, authorized and unauthorized, as computer files on line. The question now facing the music business is how to sell recordings as profitable pieces of data. The $12-billion-a-year recording industry is trying to catch up to the Internet era. Just before Christmas, the major companies announced what they wanted under their trees for the 1999 holiday season: a uniform, industry-wide standard for digital distribution of music. And this month, a task force of recording companies, software programmers and consumer electronics makers intends to begin work on music's version of the Star Wars missile defense program. The project, named the Secure Digital Music Initiative, aims to make recordings available as pure digital information while letting only the copyright owners choose how the information can be disseminated. It would be, in other words, an attempt by the major recording labels to stake out retail territory in the one part of the music business they do not control, even as their power is being challenged on the Internet by home-recorded musicians, independent labels and countless mouse-wielding music fans. "All we're trying to create here is the structure by which the content would be labeled in a consistent fashion, to serve whatever business model emerges in the future," said Cary Sherman, a senior vice president and general counsel for the Recording Industry Association of America, which represents labels that account for 90 percent of the unitedstates market. European and Asian recording industry trade groups support the initiative, along with hardware and software companies including Microsoft, I.B.M., America Online and AT&T. To avoid antitrust problems, any standards adopted would be voluntary. Howard Singer, chief technical officer of A2B Music, an AT&T unit that produces digital distribution software, acknowledges the pressure is mounting. "Every day that ticks by, there's good news and there's bad news," he said. "The good news is that the potential client base for secure digital distribution is growing. The bad news is that they're also getting used to not paying." Despite the urgency, some participants predict the process could drag out past next Christmas. "These are all highly charged, very competitive companies," said Gerry Kearby, chief executive of Liquid Audio, which makes its own software for encoding and playing back music on the Internet and has already amassed a large catalogue of digitally distributed music. "We won't be surprised if the process takes a little longer than announced." The labels, of course, are already using the Internet to sell conventional products -- compact disks and cassettes -- through on-line retailers like CD Now, N2K and Amazon.com. That business is expected to exceed $280 million this year, according toJupiter Communications, a new-media research company. But the Secure Digital Music Initiative is planning for an era when many consumers will be buying music as downloaded computer files rather than prerecorded disks and tapes. With a uniform standard, embodied in computer codes that all the major recording companies would use, consumers could receive best-selling music directly through modems and play it back using one kind of software. Once the labels agreed on a standard, a fan could jump to a top band's or a label's Web site, bill the purchase through a credit card, and download a song or an album, saving it to the computer's hard drive, recording it onto a CD or transferring it to a memory chip in a portable player. (One such portable device is already on the market.) In turn, the recording company would know where the music was sent, could specify whether or how often it could be copied, and could tabulate royalties and sales. Until such a standard is developed, the labels that own the rights to recordings by everyone from Madonna to the bluesman Robert Johnson are unlikely to make their catalogues available for digital distribution. But while the major labels have hesitated, many of their holdings are already traveling the Internet as files compressed into manageable size via MP3. This software format -- whose name is shortened from an engineering designation known as MPEG-1, Layer 3 -- makes it practical to send full songs relatively quickly over the Internet. Independent labels and individual musicians have made their music available in the MP3 format, but the major labels are alarmed by MP3 because the files can be copied without restriction, even sent as email. The vast majority of MP3 songs circulate free of charge. Some musicians encourage this practice. Others shrug and tolerate it. "MPEG's of my music are all over the network," said the rock songwriter David Bowie. "Things that are embarrassingly cringe-making, things that I swore never would see the light of day, they're completely available." Mr. Bowie has founded his own Internet service (www.davidbowie.com), whose members have on-line access to rare Bowie music and videos. He said that he was now considering making some new music available for downloading as MP3 files, but that he had a recording contract with Virgin Records, which he said was "ambivalent" about the idea. And Mr. Bowie is ambivalent about the industry's Secure Digital Music Initiative. "I'm not sure about uniform standards," he said. "They've never appealed to me. And however much they try and move in that direction, it ain't going to work. Quirkiness and decentralization are what define the Internet, and the idea of trying to formalize it and police it is abhorrent. The Internet is so volatile and idiosyncratic that whoever tries to police it will be beaten."  Seeking Control By Standardization The recording companies are intent on developing software coding standards that would specify what consumers can do with the music they download. Some songs may be available to be copied at will, or copied once, or not at all; some may be listened to for a day, or a week, or forever. Other codes would direct royalties to the appropriate recipients -- a particularly tricky process when the global Internet meets contracts that change at national borders. Various pieces of such technology exist, but in an unruly assortment of incompatible systems. So-called streaming software, offered by Real Networks (www.real.com) and others, lets music be heard through the computer like a radio signal, but it is not stored. Other software companies like Liquid Audio (www.liquidaudio.com) and A2B Music (www.a2bmusic.com) do incorporate the kinds of controls the recording business wants. But the two systems are incompatible. Other companies, including Audiosoft, are adapting MP3 files. As they seek technological security, the recording companies want to avoid costly battles between competing formats, like Betamax versus VHS videos or eight-track cartridge tapes versus cassettes. "Almost anything we achieve will be better than the status quo," Mr. Sherman said.  "The status quo is simply fragmentation of the market. Different technology providers will attempt to encourage different recording companies to make their content available by offering different kinds of secure systems that are incompatible. A consumer would need multiple players, or multiple devices, in order to hear all of the different artists that they want." Currently, for example, songs by the hard rock guitarist Billy Squier are available for sale as direct downloads from J-Bird Records through AT&T's A2B Music. Fishbone offers a song for sale through Liquid Audio. Songs by Frank Black, formerly of the alternative-rock band the Pixies, are for sale as MP3 files sold by Goodnoise (www.goodnoise.com), which prices its MP3 files at 99 cents for a song and $8.99 for an album. Each of these three formats requires the listener to have different software for playback, although Liquid Audio recently announced it would make the next version of its player software compatible with MP3. "The process for the next five or six months is not going to be pretty," said Nicholas DiGiacomo, the senior vice president and general manager for electronic markets of the consulting firm Scient, and an adviser to the Recording Industry Association of America, the trade group. "But if there's going to be a big market, they're all going to have to play together."  Authorization: Now or Never For now, digital distribution is still impractical for the vast majority of consumers. Conventional home modems cannot download information quickly enough to make the process convenient. Even with a 56-kilobit-a-second modem, downloading a high-fidelity song takes at least twice the playing time of the song. But faster computer connections that are already available, particularly on college campuses, make it possible to send and receive music almost instantly. And, with cable modems as well as high-speed services from some telephone companies, those faster connections are becoming available in a growing number of households. "If we don't do this now, it's a lost opportunity," Mr. Sherman said. Unauthorized copying has long worried the music business. When cassette tapes became popular, the recording industry association began lobbying for a royalty on blank tape, as compensation for the sales believed lost to unauthorized copying. The Audio Home Recording Act of 1992 levied a 2 percent royalty on the wholesale price of digital recorders and a 3 percent royalty on blank digital tapes and disks. Even with those royalties, the recording companies refused to release prerecorded tapes in the DAT, or digital audiotape, format, fearing the spread of high-fidelity digital copies. As a result, DAT is used largely by musicians and journalists, not in home audio systems. Labels had refused to release prerecorded DAT's to protect the CD format, which has been a boon for the music business. The CD helped the gross sales of recorded music grow to $12.2 billion in 1997, the most recent year for which statistics are available, from $3.8 billion in 1983. But for those worried about copying, the CD turned out to be a grand strategic error. That is because every CD is a digital master copy that can be duplicated ad infinitum. Recording and technology companies, still hammering out the specifications for the new generation of disks, DVD audio, are hoping to limit the potential for copying. For now, though, much of the music circulating on the Internet has been converted directly from CD's to MP3 files, which in turn can be recorded on CD-ROM's. Some executives predict that a public already used to this free flow of aural bits may resist the industry's effort to clamp down. "Why would I buy into a system that give me less control than I have now with a CD?" said Michael Robertson, chief executive of MP3.com, which makes MP3 songs available from independent musicians and labels. "You have to give people more value if you want to charge the same price, or you have to charge a lower price. All the talk about security is nonsense. The major labels are circling the wagons to preserve their current business model, the CD. But scarcity-based models do not work on the Net." Eventually, digital distribution will have larger implications for the music business. Well-known musicians, with their reputations already established, would no longer be as beholden to the major labels and their manufacturing and distribution capabilities. More musicians might then follow the example of the well-traveled songwriter Todd Rundgren, who sells $25 annual subscriptions to his music, downloadable from his Web site (www.tr-i.com). Music would not have to be packaged in the conventional forms of albums and singles, but in any bundle the musicians chose. And with store shelf space no longer defining the limits of choice, many more selections could find their way to the market at an array of prices. Musicians might also choose to make their songs available free or cheaply, build fan bases, then make their money touring or selling merchandise. "What should we do," Mr. Bowie mused, "give the music away, and sell the T-shirts? Maybe we'll become salarymen again." Whether the companies in the music business make their Christmas deadline or not, the digital clock is ticking. "The notion that music could be free is really something we have to contend with," Mr. Bowie said. "If not, like King Canute, we're just sitting by the sea and forbidding it to roll in." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Recordings by the guitarist Billy Squier can be received over the Internet using software from A2B Music. A2B's Howard Singer, at the keyboard, says the potential customer base is growing, but he frets that people may get used to free music. (James Estrin/The newyork Times)(pg. C1)  Illustration (Illustration by John Hovell)(pg. C1)  Chart: "His Master's Bits" The music industry is working to create a standard for distributing music on-line. Here are the issues that the recording labels, along with software and hardware companies, want to address.  Encryption -- Insures that only the person who is entitled to download the music can play it back.  Identification -- Create a so-called digital watermark for music distributed on-line with imbedded information about who sent it, who wrote it, who performed it and who owns the rights to it.  Copy Protection -- Prevents unauthorized copying of on-line music or limits how long a downloaded recording can be stored. (pg. C1)  "Music Channels" Sales of music over the internet still make up a tiny fraction of all music sales, but that is expected to change in the next few years.  1997 MUSIC SALES BREAKDOWN Wholesale total = $12.2 billion  Record stores -- 51.8% Other stores -- 31.9% Tape and record clubs -- 11.6% Mail order -- 2.7% Internet -- 0.3%  (Source: Audit Bureau of Circulation)(pg. title:
A DIRECTORY OF CRUISES WORLDWIDE;
Through data ports of call on the Web
body: THE building boom in the cruise industry has been matched by the proliferation of cruise-related Web sites. And while navigating the Internet is often called surfing, the term does not quite capture the spirit of trying to work through all the cruise-related sites available. There is, after all, a lot of territory to cover -- the Yahoo search engine found 43 categories and 2,373 sites for "cruises." If nothing else, there is certainly some entertainment value to seeing through the Internet just how splintered the industry has become, with cruises to match every taste, or mix of tastes. The Norway is sailing on Feb. 13, for example, on a Bluegrass Music Caribbean Celebration (www.cruise-eta.com). And what better reason for a floating vacation than to get a jump on New Year's Eve celebrations with a Pre-Millennium Caribbean Cruise in March (www.cruise-eta.com/millen.html)? Or wait until next year for what will presumably be called the Post-Millennium Caribbean Cruise. If your interests tend to be more conventional, the Internet can offer some help in guiding you through myriad choices, though the limitations of the medium may eventually prompt a call to a trusted travel agent or friend who has sampled life aboard a few different ships. Most cruise lines have Web sites that offer details you would typically find in a glossy brochure, and a bit more. You can often call up a detailed map for each deck of a ship, for example. The sites also contain information about destinations, itineraries and special deals. Some try to help find a trip that suits your needs and desires. The Cunard site, www.cunardline.com, has an on-line "cruise consultant." Instead of the flowery greeting-card language that is found so many cruise sites, this electronic Cunard consultant is all business: "I am the virtual cruise consultant," it states. "I will find all cruises which meet your criteria." Some sites offer virtual tours of their ships, but these often require software that must be downloaded from the Internet. That can take time, and if your computer is at all temperamental, it may not be worth all the trouble. For more guidance and suggestions, try Fielding's Cruisefinder, www.fieldingtravel.com. It offers ratings of ships -- 12 receive its highest rating, six stars -- and summary descriptions of the experience. From the site you can learn about their judgment of the popular Carnival Cruise Lines: "While they're not to our own particular cruising taste -- we find it hard to spend more than three or four days aboard before the color, lights and pinging slot machines get to us -- most Carnival passengers think they've died and gone to heaven." There are a number of places to find passengers' comments, though many complaints sound as if they resulted from a mismatch of expectations. And glowing reviews sometimes sound as if they were submitted by loyal ship employees. The sheer volume on these sites can be overwhelming, but they are worth a look, and in some cases you can seek opinions on cruise ships from other Web browsers. Some of these sites include www.cruiseopinion.com, www.stutt.com/ rtc/home.htm, and www.travelpage.com. For a more official opinion on a cruise ship, you can go to the Web site for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, at www.cdc.gov/nceh/programs/ sanit/vsp/scores/scores.htm. The agency regularly conducts sanitation tests of the ships, and makes available its database of scores. It even offers photographs showing an inspector conducting tests aboard a ship, in case you were curious about what sausages resting in a kitchen pan looked like. After many hours with your hand on the electronic tiller of your computer, you may decide that you want to talk to someone in person and see some glossy brochures. The Cruise Lines International Association (www.cruising.org) has a search service for travel agents who specialize in cruises. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
INVESTING: AT THE GATE;
A Test Case Of Internet Exuberance
body: WITH share prices inevitably soaring after the initial public offerings of just about any business related to the Internet these days, it is no surprise that a flood of upstart Internet companies have joined the rush. Most are blank slates. But instead of repelling investors, a lack of profits, past performance or history of any kind appears to be an enticement these days, many befuddled longtime Wall Streeters say. Even the recent volatility of Internet stocks and persistent warnings of a bubble aching to burst have not stanched the flow of new offerings. Among the next crop of initial offerings is one that some financial analysts say could provide a litmus test of just how exuberant Internet investors are: Prodigy Communications. Investment bankers say the company hopes to raise as much as $120 million by going public at a price of $12 to $15 a share the week of Feb. 7. Prodigy and its underwriters declined to confirm the details, citing Securities and Exchange Commission regulations. If the stock explodes from the gate, as so many others have, it will not be because there is much of a chance of substantial growth or profits anytime soon, according to a wide array of Internet and financial analysts. And unlike most of the other new offerings, which are unencumbered by history, Prodigy has to overcome a bleak track record, they add. Even so, that does not mean it won't fly when it hits Wall Street. "If the Prodigy I.P.O. goes off, then it might tell you that people will just pony up for Internet anything," said Peggy O'Neill, an analyst at Dataquest in San Jose, Calif. "This is not a company with a new technology or a new focus that's trying to solve a new problem, which is what a lot of the other Internet stocks are doing." Prodigy is, indeed, the antithesis of a nimble upstart start-up. It has been around since 1984, far longer than most people have owned PC's. It was a pioneer in the on-line business, going nationwide in 1990 and reaching two million subscribers at its 1993 peak, luring them with a friendly realm -- a closed, proprietary on-line service -- loaded with chat groups, encyclopedias and shopping services. Its original owners -- I.B.M., Sears, Roebuck and, early on, CBS -- poured more than $1 billion into the company before selling it in 1996 for a tiny fraction of that amount. It has continued to lose money: net losses ballooned from $3.1 million in 1995 to $132.8 million in 1997. For the first nine months of 1998, losses were $47.9 million. According to Prodigy's prospectus, its subscriber base shrank to just 633,000 paying customers last September, about 200,000 of whom use its old on-line service, Prodigy Classic. It has been trying to shift all of those users to its newer Internet service, begun in 1997, but has not had much success, and it stands to lose a lot of them in October when it phases out Prodigy Classic, analysts say. According to a Merrill Lynch research report, Prodigy needs 1.5 million customers just to break even. Prodigy plans to focus on expanding its role as an Internet service provider, both for individuals and businesses. The company plans to aim at the Hispanic market here and abroad, according to a filing with the S.E.C. The focus on building a Spanish-language market will be helped by Prodigy's links to its biggest current holder, Mexico's Carso Global Telecom, which controls Telefonos de Mexico S.A. and will directly and indirectly control 69.1 of Prodigy after the offering. The chief problem is that there is not a lot of Spanish-language content on the Internet -- at least compared with what is available in English. One of Prodigy's strengths is its network, which covers more than 600 cities in 50 states, allowing about 83 percent of the population to get Prodigy's services with a local telephone call. Its customers rarely get a busy signal, though this is partly because of Prodigy's dwindling customer base. Another plus is its size. Even though Prodigy is tiny compared with its giant rival America Online, it is one of only a few Internet service providers with enough subscribers to lure advertisers and commerce. Although most members of Prodigy's new management team are relatively unknown, its president and chief operating officer, David C. Trachtenberg, gained a solid reputation as director of on-line marketing at MCI Worldcom. Still, analysts who have studied the prospectus say there is little in it that they find exciting. "I would fall off my chair if this has real pop," Gail Bronson, a senior analyst in Palo Alto, Calif., for the research firm IPO Monitor, said of Prodigy's offering. The field of Internet service providers is already crowded, she said, and on-line services are dominated by AOL. "The way that you assure yourself success at this point in the I.P.O. calendar is to come out with an exciting story," she added. "That usually requires good branding and distinctive products: the first Internet ad play of the year, the first women's content play of the year, the voice recognition play of the year." In contrast, she said, "Prodigy is dragging a tin can along behind it." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo  Chart: "Prodigy Communications"  Headquarters: White Plains Business: Internet access Number of shares to be offered: 8 million Lead underwriter: Bear, Stearns Expected price per share: $12 - $15 Sales: $134.2 million  Year ended Dec. 31, 1997 Loss: $132.8 million  Year ended Dec. 31, 1997 Loss per share: $7.66  Graph: "Who's on Line?" title:
MARKET INSIGHT;
Confidently Riding the Technology Bubble
body: IT is pretty easy to be excited and amazed about exciting and amazing technology stocks. It is equally easy to be scared to death of them. Last year, the 250 stocks that make up Hambrecht & Quist's technology index rose 55.4 percent, the biggest annual gain ever. And the gains have not stopped; for 1999 through Friday, the index, which does not include Internet stocks, was up 13.7 percent. The firm's Internet index is up 48.6 percent so far this year. All good things, of course, come to an end. And expectations are high and rising that sooner rather than later the bubble will burst, particularly for Internet stocks. But from his office in Half Moon Bay, Calif., Michael Murphy, editor of the California Technology Stock Letter, took some time last week to share his views on why technology stocks are likely to remain white-hot.  Q.  Last summer, technology stocks stumbled badly, along with everything else. You don't think that selloff was justified, do you?  A.  No, I don't. There was a real fear last summer and early fall that personal computer sales were not growing and communications and semiconductor sales were never going to pick up. It was utterly wrong. At the time, we were in the process of seeing accelerating sales, which have continued into this year. On the communications side -- hardware, routers and switches -- there never was a slowdown. Semiconductor pricing bottomed in May or June, and now we are hearing that there is a real imbalance of supply and demand for certain, mostly higher-valued, chips. And that has translated pretty quickly into orders for semiconductor equipment. So the business looks like it may be approaching a year of normal growth in 1999. And 2000 may be a boom year.  Q.  Why is that?  A.  There are three legs to technology: communications, computing and biotech. All three are having very strong positive product cycles. It is those product cycles that drive the business, not the economy. At the semiconductor industry's forecasting meeting in Monterey earlier this month, they were talking about sales growth of 7 percent for 1999, but with sales exiting the year at a 20 percent growth rate, which is a tremendous amount of momentum. At the end of this year, we will get Windows 2000 from Microsoft, which should further personal computer spending. The Internet will continue its build-out, which will further communications spending. In biotech, we had 50 new drugs approved last year, almost double 1997, and this year we expect that 80 new drugs will be approved. There are 10 profitable biotech companies today. That number will probably double this year.  Q.  How do you think this forecast will play itself out in the stock market?  A.  For the last 18 to 24 months, we have had a very strong rally in the big technology stocks, the Microsofts, the Dells, the MCI Worldcoms. If this move is going to continue, it will spread out to the smaller-cap issues. If it doesn't, I think the rally will die. For example, Oracle is selling at or close to an all-time high, but Informix is selling at half its previous all-time high. Cisco Systems is extremely overpriced, but Premisys, another data communications company, is underpriced. There are lots of mid-cap, second-tier companies that are selling at big disparities to the leaders.  Q.  Speaking of overpriced stocks, what is your opinion of Internet shares?  A.  We are short most of the Internet stocks. My theory has been that you can pop a bubble like this without taking the rest of the market down. The Internet bubble has to pop because the supply of stock is so large. Investment bankers are filing as many offerings as they can, and lots of stock is beginning to unlock from I.P.O.'s done last year as insiders are allowed to sell their shares.  Q.  Has Internet mania inflated prices of issues that are not pure Web plays?  A.  The Internet has infected the rest a lot more than I thought it would have. Cisco, for example, has gotten an extra run because people believe the overwhelming demand will spread out.  Q.  What do you tell people who own shares in companies you consider overpriced or fully priced -- the Microsofts, Intels, Ciscos and Lucents of the world?  A.  I tell people that companies like these are core holdings, that even if in the short term they go down, don't buy them so you can trade the shares. There are none I would run out and buy this minute, but none I would sell right now because they are grossly overpriced. I think people should have 30 percent to 50 percent of their portfolio in these kinds of stocks. If you don't already own them, start dollar cost averaging into them over a six-month period. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Michael Murphy

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK UP CLOSE;
At Last, Printing of the Green for City Hall
body: Attention bureaucrats, reporters, community leaders and assorted fighters of City Hall: the new Green Book has arrived, better late than never. Last week, nearly 40,000 copies of the city's official directory were delivered from the printer, though some were rushed out on New Year's Eve, allowing city officials to announce they got the 1998-99 edition out on time, technically speaking. (Never mind that there was no 1997-98 edition.) A Dec. 31, 1998 press release from the Department of Citywide Administrative Services, which publishes the book, said the edition "celebrates the centennial of greater newyork," without noting that there were but a few hours left to celebrate. The Green Book is an exhaustive listing of city agencies and employees, and many state and Federal offices and officials, too. A dog-eared copy can usually found on the desk of anyone who deals regularly with the government. "They are now as available as they can be," said Patrick Muldowney, a spokesman for the department. "Some came in the last week of December, but now all 40,000 copies are here." Mr. Muldowney said officials had hoped to get the new book out early last fall, "but all these changes kept coming in personnel throughout various agencies." "People kept asking us to hold off the printing to the point where the printer didn't want to be bothered with us until we were absolutely sure we were ready." Even now, he said, addendums are being prepared. "City government is a constantly changing environment." Then there were the late December snowstorms in Grand Rapids, Mich., the site of the printing company. "They wiped the guy out," Mr. Muldowney said. "He could print all right, but he couldn't get anyone to work." The weather, he said, delayed delivery by another few weeks. The Green Book costs $15 and is available at the City Stores at One Centre Street near City Hall and at the Times Square Visitors Center on Broadway between 46th and 47th Streets, or can be ordered by calling 212-669-8246. The latest edition is more cyberfriendly than before, with information about NYC LINK, the city's official Web site, Web site listings for city agencies, and email addresses for some employees. "We've discussed putting the whole thing on the Web," Mr. Muldowney said. "But not everyone is on line." So for now, a search for the Green Book on the Internet isn't likely to yield much about the official city directory. A recent try using the Yahoo search engine found nothing about it, but did turn up a site featuring the complete text of the Green Book by Libya's leader, Col. Muammar el-Qaddafi.   DAVID KIRBY http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Nearly 40,000 copies of the city's official directory arrived last week.

title: Inflated Stocks Cushion Pitfalls Of Net Mergers
body: A handful of leading companies will come to dominate cyberspace. That snippet of rhetoric has become all the analytical underpinning there is to justify the unprecedented stock market values of the prominent Internet companies like Yahoo, America Online and Amazon.com. On the face of it, that well could be true. On the other hand, the Internet may make it easier for new competitors to constantly challenge the leaders. Yet one of the byproducts of the irrational exuberance in Internet stock prices is that the prophesied greatness of certain companies becomes self-fulfilling. Their huge market values allow them to grow by acquisitions. Look at the $3.6 billion purchase announced yesterday by the investors' darling Internet site, Yahoo, of Geocities, the leading creator of electronic communities organized around people's hobbies, passions and peccadilloes. Geocities is, in fact, an extreme example of the sort of tantalizing potential implicit in many Internet companies. It is the fifth- most-trafficked Web site, on which 3.5 million people have created home pages that were viewed 53 million times a day in December. Geocities has the right to put advertising on or next to all of those pages, but in all of 1998, its revenues totaled a meager $18.4 million. (Profits? Nah. It lost $19.8 million last year, double the loss of a year before.) Those modest (to be generous) fundamentals did not stop investors from valuing Geocities at $2.2 billion on Wednesday, before the acquisition was announced. With that price tag, Geocities was essentially too expensive for any company, no matter how big, for which traditional rules of finance applied. But Yahoo, which has a market value of $38 billion, an infinite multiple of its just more than break-even earnings, was easily able to exchange its shares for those of Geocities without breaking a sweat. Indeed, Yahoo's offer of stock worth $113.66 for each Geocities share, was a 52 percent premium over the company's share price Wednesday. Nonetheless, because Yahoo's value is so high -- and the price it paid represents only about 10 percent of its shares -- Yahoo is telling investors that the deal will have no effect on its per-share earnings after it closes in the second quarter. Indeed Yahoo is promising that it can turn around Geocities and make it add to earnings next year. As is usual with Internet stocks, investors leaped at any sign of motion. Yahoo's stock surged by $31.875, to $367.75. Normally, companies' stocks fall when they announce expensive acquisitions. Thus the market is in many ways encouraging the big companies like Yahoo to buy up other Internet companies. The same economics has been behind the other Net deals recently, including the purchase of Excite by At Home and of Netscape by America Online. And many analysts expect Amazon to make some big acquisitions, as well. But while the mystical multiplication of the stock market limits Yahoo's risk from buying Geocities, the potential rewards from turning the site's huge audience into profits will come much harder. "Yahoo's plans to seek incremental revenue from Geocities are difficult to see," said Brian C. Oakes, an analyst at Lehman Brothers. "If I have a Web page that says I love the newyork Jets, who will want to advertise there if they don't control the content?" Yahoo does have a bigger advertising sales staff than Geocities does and has technical resources that can cut that company's costs. Moreover, Jeff Mallett, Yahoo's president, says the company sees two areas beyond advertising on the home pages for growth at Geocities. First, it hopes that people who publish home pages will include links to related stores on their pages. For example, a page on cooking would have a link to a kitchen supply site, which in turn would pay a commission on any sales that would be split by Yahoo and the creator of the site. In addition, Yahoo sees Geocities as a great source of information about the interests of both the creators of the home pages and the people who look at them. It hopes to use this information to expand the profiles it is creating about people's interests -- profiles it uses to send people electronic mail with advertising customized to their particular interests. Yet whether or not Geocities ever produces much in incremental profits for Yahoo, the acquisition may well pay for itself simply by bolstering Yahoo's perceived "leadership" in the market. Most important, Geocities will substantially strengthen Yahoo's position in the highly watched Media Metrix rating of how many people visit a Web site at least once in a month, a measure they call reach. Yahoo's sites now rank third, reaching 48.2 percent of the Internet audience. All of America Online's properties combined reach 54.5 percent of the audience, while Microsoft's sites reach 48.4 percent. Geocities, by itself, reaches 33.4 percent of Web users. Though Yahoo's reach has mostly been flat, Lycos, another Internet service known as a portal because it is a gateway to other on-line services, has been climbing the rating charts. The main reason is that it has been buying up other sites including many of the community sites that compete with Geocities. All of the Lycos sites in December had a reach of 46.5 percent of the audience. Even amid constant speculation that Lycos will soon be acquired, it is worth $5.3 billion, a huge number but a small fraction of the value of Yahoo. Many Lycos investors, as well as its management, were hoping that if it were able to surge past Yahoo, it might well gain some of the market value accorded to leaders. "You can never have too much cash or too much reach," said Chris A. Kitze, the chairman of Xoom.com, a community site that competes with Geocities. No such luck, Lycos. With Geocities, Yahoo says its reach will increase to 58 percent of the Web audience, an undisputed top position, for now. And that will allow the magic multiplication of Internet stock values to keep working and let the company make even more acquisitions, just maybe allowing it to fulfill the prophecies of its cyber-dominance. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "The New Cybermath" The substantial value placed on Internet companies by investors --despite the scarcity of profits in the industry -- has fueled a spate of mergers among the most popular sites. Yesterday, Yahoo agreed to buy Geocities for $3.6 billion. Last week, At Home agreed to pay $6.7 billion for Excite. And late last year, America Online agreed to pay $4.2 billion for Netscape. title: Privacy Advocates Ask F.T.C. To Force Recall of Intel Chips
body: Privacy advocates who object to the Intel Corporation's plan to put identification numbers in its next generation of computer chips went to the Federal Trade Commission today to seek a recall of the Pentium III's. The meeting with the commission followed a visit by Intel executives to the Capitol Hill offices of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, an on-line advocacy group. On Monday, the group and two other organizations called for a boycott of the world's largest chip maker, saying the new technology would compromise the privacy of computer users. In response to the boycott threat, Intel said the company would alter the software that turns the identification feature on and off. But the privacy groups said that solution was inadequate. So Intel executives flew to Washington for a meeting today at which they defended the alteration, saying it gives consumers both choice and control. "They met with us for almost two hours," said Marc Rotenberg, director of the privacy center. "We decided after the meeting that we would actually extend the boycott." Mr. Rotenberg said the privacy advocates wanted Intel to remove the processor serial number from any future Pentium III chip, and to recall all processors that had been shipped with the processor serial number already enabled. The privacy advocates then headed to the trade commission to plead their case for a recall of the chip, which Intel confirmed was already being shipped to computer makers. The trade commission confirmed the meeting with the privacy advocates, but declined to comment further. The commission has been calling for stronger privacy protections on the Internet. Last year, it won passage of a law requiring sites on the World Wide Web to obtain parental permission before collecting personal information from children. The commission has vowed to push Congress to impose tough new laws protecting adults on line if Internet companies cannot prove this year that they have made significant improvements in notifying consumers about what information they are collecting and how that information is used. Privacy advocates are concerned that Intel's chips, which were designed to enhance the security of electronic commerce and safeguard against software piracy, would make it easy for governments and on-line marketers to follow computer users around the Internet and build profiles about their Internet habits. Chuck Mulloy, a spokesman for Intel, said the team that met with the privacy group included a security expert, a public relations executive and an employee in the company's Washington office. "We were grateful for the opportunity to explain our view of the program," he said. Mr. Mulloy said Intel believed its solution gave "consumers both the choice and control over whether or not to use processor serial numbers." Intel is the world's largest computer chip maker, with $26.2 billion in sales last year. Today, it announced a 2-for-1 stock split effective April 11, news that moved the company's stock up $4.4375, to $137.1875, on the Nasdaq stock market. The Santa Clara, Calif., company, which makes about 85 percent of the world's computer processors, unveiled the Pentium III chip containing the so-called processor serial numbers at a trade show in Silicon Valley last week. On Friday, Representative Edward J. Markey, the senior Democrat on the House Consumer Protection Committee, wrote Intel's chief executive, Craig Barrett, asking that the company reconsider its plans to "better balance" commercial and privacy objectives. Over the weekend, a coalition of privacy advocates began discussions about a boycott of Intel. On Monday, as the protest was announced, the company said it would alter software in the system so that the serial number was disabled unless the computer user turned it on. Originally, the feature would have been activated automatically and it would have been up to the user to disable it. But the privacy advocates refused to end their protest, saying the software patch was an unacceptable solution. Among other things, they questioned whether it would protect against intruders breaking in and switching the setting, even though Intel says that is not possible.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS;
Asked About Internet Issues, The Fed Chairman Shrugs
body: He has made a habit of worrying in public that stock prices are getting out of hand, but when Alan Greenspan, the Federal Reserve chairman, was asked today about the highest-flying investments of all, Internet companies, his answer was tinged as much with fascination and even enthusiasm as with caution. Mr. Greenspan hardly suggested that he had become a day trader, one of a new breed of investor who goes on line to trade technology stocks on rumor and whim. He left no doubt, though, that he sees more good than bad in a phenomenon that has driven the market value of America Online higher than that of General Motors and pushed the share price of a new company like Ebay from $18 to more than $300 in just four months. The upward march of Internet stocks continued again today. Reaction to better-than-expected earnings from America Online, the dominant Internet access provider, and an announced acquisition by Yahoo, the largest World Wide Web search engine, of Geocities, the biggest provider of personal Web pages, pushed technology indexes and many company shares to new highs. Asked during a Senate Budget Committee hearing this morning by Senator Ron Wyden, Democrat of Oregon, about the attention surrounding Internet stocks, Mr. Greenspan cited not irrational exuberance but the very real prospect of success for at least some companies. "First of all, you wouldn't get hype working if there weren't something fundamentally sound under it," Mr. Greenspan said. "The issue really gets to the increasing evidence that a significant part of the distribution of goods and services in this country is going to move from conventional channels into some form of Internet system -- whether it's retail goods or services or a variety of other things." The potential market is so big, he Greenspan said, that there are "pie in the sky" growth opportunities for many companies. "And undoubtedly some of these small companies, which have stock prices going through the roof, will succeed and they very well may justify even higher prices," Mr. Greenspan said. "The vast majority are almost sure to fail. That's the way the markets work in this regard." Lest he come across like an analyst promoting a hot sector, Mr. Greenspan quickly added that he viewed the entire Internet-stock phenomenon as another example of human willingness to bet on a long shot. He compared buying Internet stocks to playing the lottery. For centuries, he said, people have been willing to pay more for a lottery ticket than their chances of winning would justify, simply because they are captivated by the possibility, however remote, of a big score. "What that means is that when you are dealing with stocks -- the possibilities of which are it's going to be valued at zero or some huge number -- you get a premium in that stock price which is exactly the same sort of price-evaluation process that goes on in the lottery," Mr. Greenspan said. There has always been a certain dissonance between Mr. Greenspan's libertarian faith in the market and his fretfulness about the ability of investors to gauge risk. And there has been a disconnect of late between Mr. Greenspan's concerns that Wall Street could be in for a downturn and the policy of interest-rate cuts he pursued last fall, probably the single biggest factor in the market's latest rise. But today Mr. Greenspan sounded downright sanguine. "Of course, there's some hype," he said, but the securities markets seemed to be doing a good job of funneling capital to promising ideas even if they had not yet proved profitable. "That's good for our system," Mr. Greenspan said. "With all of this hype and craziness, that is something that at the end of the day probably is more plus than minus."  Durable Goods Orders Rise WASHINGTON, Jan. 28 (Bloomberg News) -- Factory orders for big-ticket goods increased in December for the sixth time in seven months as demand for industrial hardware, electronics and electrical equipment accelerated, the Commerce Department said today. Total orders for durable goods rose 1.9 percent, more than expected, to $192.68 billion last month. In November, orders rose a revised three-tenths of 1 percent, to $189.08 billion. For 1998, orders rose 3.5 percent after increasing 7.1 percent during 1997, the Commerce Department said. That was the smallest annual gain since 1991, when the economy was emerging from recession. In another report today, the Labor Department said wages and salaries in the fourth quarter grew at their slowest pace in two years. The employment cost index -- the broadest measure of wage, salary and benefit costs -- rose seven-tenths of 1 percent in the fourth quarter, less than the third quarter's rise of 1 percent. In addition, first-time jobless claims fell 15,000 in the week ended last Saturday to a seasonally adjusted 301,000, the lowest level in more than a month. The four-week moving average, a less volatile measure of claims, fell to 333,250, from 351,000 a week earlier.   http://www.nytimes.com

title: As On-Line Trading Increases, So Do Complaints
body: One of the millions of small investors who have recently flocked to cyberspace placed an order through his on-line brokerage account for a hot new Internet stock, Theglobe.com, thinking it would cost between $15 and $25 a share. His order was filled for 2,300 shares, at a price of $90 a share and a bill of $207,000 -- nearly $150,000 more than he expected. Another investor placed an order on his personal computer to sell 30 shares of a different company, never got an electronic confirmation, and so placed the sell order again, winding up selling 60 shares, twice the amount of shares he had held. A third investor tried to cancel an order to buy 45 shares of a stock and received an acknowledgement that his cancellation order had been received. But the sale went through anyway, and the investor wound up purchasing the stock. The three are among hundreds of investors who have recently complained to the Securities and Exchange Commission, which reported today that the record amount of on-line trading -- now 25 percent of all retail trading and growing fast -- has also brought a record number of complaints. Most commonly, investors report sharp discrepancies between the prices they see on their PC screens and the prices they wind up paying. As of Sept. 30, the number of complaints had risen 330 percent from the previous year, to 1,114. In more recent weeks, with new issues of volatile Internet and technology stocks coming to market at prices that are seducing new investors into trying to get rich quick, S.E.C. officials report that the complaints are coming in faster than they can be processed. The growing problems prompted Arthur Levitt, the S.E.C. chairman, to caution small investors who have swarmed onto the Internet to approach on-line investing with care. In addition to keeping the fundamentals of investing in mind, he said, investors should take such precautions as placing limits on the prices of buy and sell orders to avoid the recurring kinds of problems that are plaguing the emerging group of small traders called cybervestors. "Investors need to remember the investment basics, and not allow the ease and speed with which they trade to lull them either into a false sense of security or encourage them to trade too quickly or too often," Mr. Levitt said. "Some of the issues raised specifically relate to on-line trading, others are generic to all investing. The majority of them can be addressed through better education and investors insuring that they have done their homework." By the end of this year, 10 million brokerage accounts are expected to be able to trade on the Internet, nearly twice the number now. The stunning growth of on-line trading has already transformed Wall Street, sharply cutting commission costs, increasing the speed of trading and making stock trading more accessible than ever before. But like the proliferation of sport utility vehicles, the explosion of on-line trading has prompted a certain complacency that can be dangerous. The flood of complaints hitting both the securities firms and regulatory agencies comes in large part from angry investors who had mistakenly thought that the ability to trade almost instantaneously through their PC's put them on an equal footing with seasoned Wall Street traders. Yet in part the problems being encountered demonstrate that technological advances in PC's and the Internet trail the advances made at the stock exchanges. For example, the stock price that consumers see on their screens may bear no resemblance to the actual real-time price at the exchange -- particularly when the stock is volatile or during periods of heavy volume. Those lags have become common with hot new Internet issues, whose prices can soar or plummet in a matter of seconds. Mr. Levitt said in an interview today that some problems were rooted in investor misunderstandings about the new technology. Other problems have been caused by the growing number of neophyte traders, many caught in the speculative fever of recent months. Through the new technology they are able to buy and sell in an instant, without any understanding of the risks associated with such highfliers. The more than 100 brokerage companies now on the Internet have taken different approaches to resolving client complaints. In certain circumstances some companies have been willing to undo the trades, but standards vary greatly from firm to firm and are highly dependent upon the specific circumstances -- and status of the client. And the wave of filings at the regulatory agencies demonstrates that in many cases the companies are not reimbursing customers. Instead, to reduce the problems and also try to insulate themselves from possible liability, many brokerage firms post warnings about trading problems on their World Wide Web sites that may be caused by stock volatility and high volume. Those statements were posted even before the National Association of Securities Dealers issued a notice on Tuesday recommending that the firms begin to educate investors and tell them of possible delays and other potential problems. Mr. Levitt warned small investors that since the stock prices they see on their computer screens may not necessarily reflect the real-time market prices, they should consider the advantages of placing orders that limit the price for a trade to be executed. He also cautioned investors not to forsake the basic principles of investing and understand that as much as the new technology has provided important benefits it can also have shortcomings. Nancy M. Smith, director of investor education at the S.E.C., said that the most common complaints concerned investors who bought securities at prices significantly higher than the prices on their screens. Other complaints, she said, came from investors who had moved with a few mouse clicks into securities that, upon reflection, they should never have been purchased. Still others thought they had canceled purchases before those orders had been executed, only to learn they had not.  Investor Rules of Thumb, and Mouse  The National Association of Securities Dealers offers some basic warning flags for investors when they open an account with an on-line brokerage firm:  DELAYS -- High trading volumes can delay the execution of an order, which may mean that a stock's price is significantly different than when the order was placed. Clients should ask their firms how orders are handled, particularly in a volatile market.  TYPES OF ORDERS -- Clients should seek an explanation of the difference between market and limit orders. A market order is done by a brokerage firm regardless of a stock's price. Limit orders are executed only at a specified price or better.  ACCESS -- Clients may have difficulty gaining access to their accounts in periods of heavy Internet traffic and may have difficulty reaching their broker on the phone in periods of high volume. They should ask for an explanation of their firms' procedures for responding to these access issues. http://www.nytimes.com

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Ford Said to Be in Deal For Volvo's Car Business Ford Motor plans to announce today that it will acquire the passenger car operations of Sweden's Volvo for $6 billion to $7 billion, people close to the talks said last night. Ford's deal, which beat a rival bid from Italy's Fiat and strengthens its position as the No. 2 auto maker in the world, marks the latest step in the consolidation of the global automotive industry. Car makers worldwide are rushing into deals because they fear a coming shakeout in the industry, in which the only survivors will be the lowest-cost producers with the greatest economies of scale. title: Keeping Tabs on Flu Outbreaks
body: SICK of all those persistent warnings about viruses on line? Here's one that is certified by bona fide medical doctors: the on-line Flu-o-Meter, which indicates the prevalence of influenza state by state. The meter, a creation of Intelihealth, uses information from the Federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and is part of the www.intelihealth.com Web site. When a visitor passes the cursor over each state in a map of the unitedstates, the meter lights up in one of four different colors to indicate the prevalence of flu cases in the state in question. (That is for surfers who are Java-enabled. Another version is available for those who aren't.) Doctors at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore oversee the editorial content of Intelihealth, which is a collaboration between Aetna U.S. Healthcare and the university. The site also includes information about how to avoid the flu and who needs flu shots (which are best to get in October). The site says flu kills 10,000 to 40,000 people in the unitedstates each year. It also discusses the symptoms and complications. "This is what people want to know if they're suffering the symptoms they feel might be flu," said Dr. Jay Rosan, a family practitioner and executive vice president of Intelihealth. "Is that really what I'm suffering from, or is it just a virus?" he added. "So I can look at my state, and ask is my state really having a flu epidemic or not?" Bob Pringle, president of Intelihealth, said the site might help with prevention. "At least you can know that if you're going into an area with the flu, you should be careful and wash your hands more frequently," he said. Information from Intelihealth, based in Blue Bell, Pa., is distributed by more than 500 partners on the Internet. Intelihealth is an anchor tenant of America Online, which means that it has a prominent position on one or more of AOL's primary channels, and it is the exclusive health channel on Alta Vista. It also appears in Web sites of hundreds of newspapers of various sizes, like The Washington Post and The Dodge City Post in Kansas, Mr. Pringle said. The site received 150,000 hits on one day last week, Mr. Pringle said. The C.D.C.'s flu site is at www.cdc.gov/ncidod/diseases/flu /weekly.htm. A number of states put flu information on the Web, including Massachusetts (www.state .ma.us/dph/flu98-99.htm) and Virginia (www.vdh.state.va.us/epi /flu9899.htm). According to the Flu-o-Meter, there have been scattered outbreaks so far in newyork, Georgia, Arizona and elsewhere. According to the newyork State Department of Health, which does not track individual cases of influenza, there have recently been seven outbreaks in newyork City nursing homes -- three in the Bronx and four in Queens. Anyone trying to stay healthy for the rest of the flu season, which usually lasts until March, is advised to scrub up. "The simplest, oldest method of avoiding spread of infection is frequent hand washing, preferably with antibacterial soap from a sanitary dispenser," the site says. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The Intelihealth Web site offers information and advice for flu sufferers. (George M. Gutierrez)

title: Lost in Cyberspace: How to Hold On to Your Address
body: I TOOK the existence of email and my 6-year-old email address for granted until I found out last month ago that my Internet service provider was discontinuing my address. The change came because my old provider, Digital Express, had merged with several other providers to become a company known as Intermedia. In an effort to harmonize the brand names and create one service, Digital Express informed its customers, the new company was discontinuing the old email addresses ending with digex.net. My new address, if I wanted to keep the service, would end with iamdigex.com. I didn't want that address, though, and so I was cast into confusion. At first glance, changing an email address looks like a problem that can be handled by several hundred electronic notes to friends and relatives. It is often, however, much more complicated than that -- especially if mailing lists, stationery and other software packages are involved. My old address, pcw@access.digex.net, is locked away in archives and Web sites around the world, and no bulk email is going to change all of them. The more immediate problem was to find a new, more stable address that could not be tossed away at corporate whim. That was not going to be easy. There is more flux in email addresses than you might expect. Ben Pritchard, a spokesman for Digital Express, said: "The whole dial-up business is being coordinated and consolidated into one service. The effects on folks like you and other folks who have been around for a few years is more negative than we would have wanted." Some companies have stepped in to try to solve the problem -- and make some money at the same time. Among them is an email provider called Bigfoot. Lenny Barshack, the company's chief executive, said Bigfoot had started out trying to become a comprehensive directory of email addresses throughout the Web. Then company officials noticed that each year, 40 percent of the email addresses in the directory were changing, as people switched jobs or service providers. So Bigfoot began offering a permanent forwarding service for email accounts. The accounts are free, but Mr. Barshack said the company hoped to make money by offering additional services like smart forwarding, which will forward to several addresses. The problem is a serious one for me, because I am self-employed. As a freelance writer of books and magazine and newspaper articles who is also a programmer, I have a small business that is widely scattered. Being quickly accessible to the people who might want to hire me, and to readers, is very important. The most permanent examples of my email address are printed at the end of magazine articles I have written and in the front of my books. They still generate about one or two letters a week. Electronic versions are contained in archives of computer discussion groups I take part in, like the Risks Digest, about computer crashes and technology problems. While the electronic documents, at least, could, in theory, be changed, it is often practically impossible to do so. While I don't have printed business cards or stationery with the email address as many other people do, the address is practically everywhere else. I am luckier than most because my name is not too common and people should be able to find me with search engines. Others, with more common names, are bound to experience some trouble. Gregory Watson, another longtime Digital Express customer, said his email address was in countless places throughout the world. "I'm actually the ringing master of the Washington Ringing Society and the contact person for that," he said about his hobby of organizing people who make music by ringing bells. "I've changed my address on three pages in Britain and Australia, but I can't locate every other Web page that's out there." When Intermedia originally wrote to inform customers on Nov. 10th that the email addresses were changing starting on Dec. 1 -- short notice -- the company said it would forward email from the old addresses for three months. After that, it said, we would be on our own. After many customers complained, the company announced a new plan: it will forward mail for up to a year -- as long as people sign up for the new service plan. After that, the old addresses will be toast. In the end, I went for the one-year plan, but I also decided to search for something more permanent. Here are some of the options for others who may find themselves in similar situations: * Choose a big provider. America Online, for example, is not very likely to merge and change its name to form a new corporate image. In cases where AOL has merged, it is the other company that usually changes its identity to AOL, although in many cases, AOL maintains the old company's separate name and brand. Compuserve customers, for instance, still have Compuserve addresses. But Trish Primrose, a spokeswoman for AOL, points out that the AOL service agreement says only that "AOL provides you with a limited, nonexclusive license for no more than the term of your membership to use the screen name." * Go back to school. Many schools offer alumni permanent addresses because to do so costs little and ties users together and to the school. These addresses are probably much more stable than those of the big service providers. The only downside is that big schools with long histories often end up with several students with the same name. * Check out the various email services on the Web. All of them promise free email and forwarding. Of course, promises aren't necessarily permanent in an ever-shifting corporate world. Hotmail, Yahoo, Geocities, Bigfoot and Netscape are just some of the more stable Web-based email sites. Providing the service is relatively inexpensive for them, and the companies can often make money selling advertisements that they show you when you read your mail. * The best solution is to gain control of your own domain name. Steven King, a programmer, is another former Digital Express customer who also must worry about disappearing on the Web among the many references to the writer of the same name. He told me he doesn't worry as much about his email because he now largely uses an address tied to a domain name he controls. Still, he had been having all his mail forwarded to his Digex address. "Now I have to look for a new dial-up provider," he said. "It's going to cost me about $300." Many people own the domain associated with their last name. Ralph Merkle, a cryptographer and nanotechnologist, controls merkle.com. Pete Loshin, an author and former Byte magazine editor, controls loshin.com. Unfortunately for me, wayner .com is already owned by someone else. Moreover, this solution is not inexpensive. Network Solutions, the company that controls the registration of domain names ending in .com or .org, charges $70 for two years of service. Other countries around the world are running competing services. And once you own the domain name, you must arrange for some computer to answer all requests for that domain. There are already many companies offering what is known as domain hosting for fees that range from $5 to $50 a month. Most of these plans are aimed at companies that need a place for their Web site, but they usually include email as part of the package. The fees are often determined more by how many people visit your Web site than by how many email messages you get. Since I already control a few domain names, I have moved my email address to one of them, flyzone.com, which I created after signing up with Digex, and I have also registered a name at Bigfoot. Assuming no major changes are afoot for the domain system, you can reach me at pcw@flyzone.com. I hope. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Mary Ann Smith)

title: Microsoft Official Defends Company's Strategy at Trial
body: A senior executive of the Microsoft Corporation delivered a forceful defense of the company's actions in the Internet software market today, saying it had acted mainly in the pursuit of a "Holy Grail of software development" by making its products more powerful, easier to use and seamlessly integrated. The executive, James Allchin, the second company official to appear as a witness at the Microsoft antitrust trial, also argued that other software makers have done what the Government says is anticompetitive in Microsoft's case and presented a detailed history of his company's product plans for the Internet. In his 139-page written testimony, Mr. Allchin repeatedly struck the theme that the Justice Department and the 19 states suing Microsoft are making an ill-advised effort to tamper with innovation and product design in a leading high-technology industry. "I am not a lawyer or an economist," Mr. Allchin wrote, "but I do not understand how a company's efforts to improve its products can ever be 'anticompetitive.' " The testimony of Mr. Allchin, a senior vice president in charge of the technical development of the company's Windows operating system, is a salvo in Microsoft's legal fight with the Government over how the lawsuit is framed, which is crucial to the outcome of the case. Microsoft says its decision to bundle its Internet Explorer browser with its industry-standard Windows operating system and give the browser away free was a straightforward product-design decision that benefits consumers. But the Government contends that those moves represent the abuse of Microsoft's monopoly power to thwart competition. Most antitrust experts say that Microsoft's strongest defense is to frame the case as a debate over its product decisions. Indeed, in a related case, a Federal appeals court ruled last June that Microsoft had the right to bundle its browser with Windows, warning of "the undesirability of having courts oversee product design." But the Government views Microsoft's bundling decision as simply one step in a pattern of what it regards as predatory business practices intended to stifle competition. The prosecution case, according to antitrust experts, is strengthened by framing the courtroom debate around Microsoft's business practices and contracts. At the trial today, the Government kept that focus in its third day of cross-examining Microsoft's first executive witness, Paul Maritz, trying to show that the company pressured the Intel Corporation to stop developing technology that conflicted with Microsoft's plans. Intel is mainly a producer of the microprocessor chips that serve as the "electronic brain" of most PC's, but it also develops software. Microsoft's conflict with Intel in 1995 centered on Intel's work on multimedia software called "native signal processing," or N.S.P. Intel wanted to distribute its N.S.P.  software to PC makers, but it pulled back after protests from Microsoft. The Government contends that Microsoft muscled both Intel and the computer makers not to adopt any software that conflicted with Microsoft's plans. Microsoft replies that Intel stepped back on its own, after realizing that there were problems with its N.S.P. software. The Justice Department pointed to internal Microsoft email to try to show that the big software maker did pressure Intel and the industry. An Oct. 18, 1995, email to Mr. Maritz, written by William H. Gates, the Microsoft chairman, said that Intel felt PC makers were resisting Intel's software because of "our N.S.P. chill." Later, Mr. Gates added, "If Intel is not sticking totally to its part of the deal, let me know." "Did you ask Mr. Gates: 'What bargain are you talking about? What deal are you talking about?' " David Boies, the Justice Department's lead trial lawyer, asked Mr. Maritz. Mr. Maritz, the senior executive in charge of most software development and marketing at Microsoft, replied that he had not. But he maintained that Intel ultimately abandoned N.S.P. because it was technically flawed and would not work with recent versions of Windows. In what Mr. Boies portrayed as another example of Microsoft's attempting to co-opt or pressure potential competitors, he also questioned Mr. Maritz about the company's investment in Real Networks Inc., a developer of software that allows audio and video to be transmitted over the Internet. Mr. Maritz acknowledged that executives from Real Networks, then known as Progressive Networks, told Microsoft in 1997 that if Microsoft invested in the company, it would shift its business to other kinds of software and services to avoid competing. But Mr. Maritz noted that Real Networks continues to compete with Microsoft nonetheless. A Real Networks spokesman said yesterday that the company never agreed to get out of the streaming media business. Microsoft is in the process of selling its 10 percent stake in Real Networks. http://www.nytimes.com

Blue Chips Decline 124.35 In a Profit-Taking Session
body: Stocks fell for the first time in three sessions yesterday as investors took profits before Congressional testimony by Alan Greenspan, chairman of the Federal Reserve. Selling was particularly pronounced in computer and bank shares. But it was another good day for Internet stocks, which were lifted by better-than-expected earnings reports from Amazon.com and Ebay. After the market closed, America Online released fourth-quarter figures that also beat estimates. Still, two stocks fell in price for every one that rose on the newyork Stock Exchange. On the Big Board, volume was 894 million shares. The Dow Jones industrial average gave back all its gains from Tuesday, falling 124.35 points, or 1.3 percent, to 9,200.23. Declines in I.B.M., J. P. Morgan and Chevron were the biggest negative influences on the blue-chip index. Computer-generated sell programs were responsible for virtually all the Dow's decline. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index slipped 9.14, or seven-tenths of a percent, to 1,243.17. And the Nasdaq composite index, which has been on a torrid pace this year, declined 26.27, or 1.1 percent, to 2,407.14. The Russell 2000 index of small-company stocks fell 4.21 points, or 1 percent, to 421.12. But Thestreet.com's index of 20 Internet stocks gained 14.51, or 2.8 percent, to 534.60. Despite the broad-based selloff, analysts said the decline was orderly and understandable. "The market is at price levels that concern me, but there is no sense that this is anything beyond profit-taking and hesitancy ahead of Mr. Greenspan's remarks and what people are certain is going to be a strong report on the economy on Friday," said William Meehan, chief market analyst at Cantor Fitzgerald. This morning, Mr. Greenspan is scheduled to testify before the Senate Budget Committee. And on Friday, the Commerce Department is expected to release its first report on fourth-quarter economic growth. "It was a great day for Internet and some technology stocks and not much else," said Karl Mills, executive vice president at Junka & Voyles, a firm based in Oakland, Calif., with $5 billion under management. It was a particularly good day for Ebay, the on-line auction company. Ebay, which reported its fourth-quarter results after the market closed on Tuesday, soared 82 5/8, to 303 1/2. The company said it earned 7 cents a share in the fourth quarter, comfortably beating consensus estimates of 4 cents a share. It also said it would split its stock 3 for 1. But the session was a dismal one for First Union and other bank stocks. First Union led bank shares lower after it said higher expenses and an accounting change would cut into its profits this year. The stock fell 4 7/8, to 52 3/16, after the report. BankAmerica lost 2 13/16, to 62 1/8. J. P. Morgan slipped 4 3/16, to 100 1/16. And Mellon Bank fell 2 3/16, to 64 15/16. I.B.M. and Compaq Computer led computer shares lower. I.B.M. lost 7 5/16, to 178 5/16. And Compaq, which has seen its stock price more than double since early October, fell 1 3/4, to 47 1/2, despite posting fourth-quarter results that were better than expected. title: Yahoo Said to Be Buying Geocities in Union of Top Sites
body: In a move meant to defend its position as the world's leading site on the Internet, Yahoo Inc. has agreed to buy Geocities, another popular site, financial executives briefed on the deal said last night. Late yesterday, Yahoo scheduled a conference call with analysts for today. But Diane Hunt, a spokeswoman for Yahoo, declined to comment on the call's topic last night. Geocities executives did not return calls last night. The executives would not comment on the price that Yahoo will pay. But analysts said that the transaction would most likely be similar to the At Home Corporation's recent agreement to buy Excite, one of Yahoo's chief competitors. In that all-stock deal, At Home paid a 40 percent premium over Excite's average stock price in the 30 days before the deal. Geocities has a market value of $2.3 billion, and thus a 40 percent premium would value it at about $3 billion. Shares of Yahoo fell $15.375 yesterday, to $335.875; Geocities rose $4, to $75. Yahoo is the top-rated of the Internet sites that have come to be known as portals because they serve as gateways to a wide range of information and on-line services. But most of its competitors have recently been bolstered through acquisitions. At Home is starting to offer fast Internet services over cable television wires. Netscape, with its Netcenter portal, was bought by America Online. Infoseek, another portal, was partially bought by the Walt Disney Company and folded into its new portal, the Go Network. The Microsoft Corporation has redoubled its efforts to promote its MSN portal. And just this week, the Compaq Computer Corporation announced plans to expand and partially spin off its Alta Vista portal service. "Given the acquisition of Excite last week, the perception was that Yahoo had to do a deal," said Paul W. Noglows, an analyst at Hambrecht & Quist in San Francisco. "Geocities would not only give them incremental traffic but also the most significant player in the community space." Geocities is the leading service that creates electronic communities of people who share various interests. It mainly allows people to set up their own home pages on the Internet on any topic from family photos to sports-car collecting. With more than three million members, it is among the most popular sites on the Internet. In December, Geocities.com was the third-most-visited Web site, with 19 million unique visitors, according to Media Metrix. The top-rated site was America Online's site, Aol.com, with 28 million visitors. Yahoo was No. 2 with 27 million. Geocities hopes to profit by selling advertising that appears on these home pages. But its revenue growth has been slower than other Internet companies because many advertisers are shy about placing their messages on pages that Geocities does not have direct control over. Such community features, however, are increasingly being folded into the broader array of services offered by portals. Infoseek, Lycos and Excite have all bought smaller community-oriented services. Yahoo tried to buy Geocities last year but was rebuffed when Geocities chose to make an initial public offering instead. Yahoo already has a small stake in Geocities, and the Softbank Corporation of Japan has investments in both. Increasingly, the venture capitalists who have backed a variety of specialized Internet start-ups are encouraging the companies in their portfolios to combine into larger entities. For example, Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers has major stakes in both Excite and At Home. The executives briefed on the transaction said that Geocities would most likely remain an independent unit of Yahoo, retaining its brand name, its management and its offices in Santa Monica, Calif. Yahoo is based in Santa Clara, Calif., in Silicon Valley. http://www.nytimes.com
