title: Protecting Bidders on Line
body: For the moment, Internet auctions are no better -- or no worse -- than giant electronic garage sales, in which thousands of potential buyers can look at a photograph of an item but cannot inspect it, or consult an independent expert to verify the item's quality or authenticity. Nonetheless, people buy and sell things on line every day, from toys to Lincoln artifacts, especially on the largest Internet auction service of its kind, eBay, whose site is at http://www.ebay.com/. But eBay functions only as a sort of electronic middleman between buyers and sellers. An item listed yesterday as "Ghurka Warrior Dagger -- NEAT! PIC" was posted with a disclaimer: "Seller assumes all responsibility for listing this item. You should contact the seller to resolve any questions before bidding." Sotheby's, in return for commission fees, employs a staff of art, jewelry, furniture and other experts to authenticate and assess items it puts up for bid. Under the planned auction system for Sotheby's, buyers will be able to make multiple, successive bids in real time, similar to a live auction. Bidding would be made through secure servers, meaning a computer network resistant to hackers' mischief like the theft of credit-card data. Each item for bid would feature a photograph, a description and a fixed period of time for bidding. Dealers could also continuously "upload," or list, new items for bid. For the time being, said Susan L. Solomon, chief executive of Sotheby's site, Internet auctions will only be by computer and will not be combined with live auctions. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Virtual Sky's the Limit for On-Line Auctions at Sotheby's Web Site
body: If the hottest auction market in the country right now is in cyberspace, why shouldn't Sotheby's get in on the action? Taking its cachet and gavel onto the Internet, the newyork auction house said yesterday that it would spend $25 million on a site called sothebys.com, where the public will be able to bid on art, antiques, jewelry and collectibles like sports memorabilia. On-line auctions have already taken the Internet by storm, and consumer watchdogs have said that the emerging practice has produced more complaints than any other Internet category because of problems like shoddy merchandise and fraud. But Sotheby's officials sought to distinguish their site from competitors. For instance, the merchandise to be offered on sothebys.com beginning in July will come only from the auction house itself or reputable art dealers, said Susan L. Solomon, a former Sony executive who was named the chief executive officer of the Internet site. Just as buyers will be assured that the item has been checked for authenticity, the auction house will also be protected from frivolous consumers. Bids will be accepted only from customers who have registered their charge card numbers with the auction house. Sotheby's entry into the world of on-line auctions comes after other companies have already established a presence in the business, including Ebay, which sells a huge range of products, from Furbys to firearms. Responding to a request for comment, Brian Swette, senior vice president of marketing at Ebay, said through a spokeswoman, "Sotheby's announcement validates Ebay's model and our business approach." Yesterday, investors signaled their approval of the venture, sending Sotheby's stock up by almost 25 percent yesterday to close at $39.875, up $7.75. At first, Ms. Solomon said, the estimated value of the items on the virtual auction block will range from a few hundred dollars to $10,000. Costlier items will go on line when the imaging technology improves, making it easier for would-be buyers to inspect the goods from several angles. "There's no point in having a fuzzy image of a $100,000 item," she said. But she did not rule out the possibility that one day collectors would be able to buy multimillion-dollar old masters over the Internet, paying $9 million, say, for a Rembrandt, as the casino executive Stephen A. Wynn did earlier this year. "I do see that happening," Ms. Solomon said, "but I'm not going to say when." Industry analysts said the Internet site would allow the auction house to broaden its market geographically and in terms of price. Mark R. Miller, an analyst at Merrill Lynch, said many people think of Sotheby's as out of their reach when in fact 80 percent of the items or sets listed in the catalogue are auctioned off for less than $5,000. Last month, Merrill Lynch warned in a report that Sotheby's might risk offending its "high-end clientele" by going after Internet users, but Mr. Miller said the company had alleviated that concern by promising to maintain quality control over the merchandise. Ms. Solomon described on-line auctions as "a natural evolution of the business," and compared it to newspapers and others going on line. She said the company would save an enormous amount of money on handling costs because items would not have to be moved from place to place. "It costs as much for us to handle a $1,000 item as a $1 million item," she said, "and now every item is handled between 5 and 10 times." For its first major Internet auction, Sotheby's will be offering baseball memorabilia from the huge collection of Barry Halper, a limited partner in the Yankees. Some of the 80,000 items will be sold at a weeklong live auction, probably beginning in July, Ms. Solomon said. The on-line sale might go on for several months, giving prospective bidders an opportunity to study the items just as they would at a preview at the auction house's salesrooms in newyork or London. They will also be able to request an email copy of a report describing the condition of the item. Where Sotheby's goes, its chief rival, Christie's, is likely to follow. Taggerty M. Patrick, a spokeswoman for Christie's, said the company had no immediate plans for on-line auctions, but it is exploring that possibility. "Nothing will replace the magic of attending a live auction," she said, "but we are developing a strategy that looks at various collecting categories that might be appropriate for on-line transactions." How will collectors react to this latest evolutionary step in the art market? Steve Shane, a newyork anesthesiologist who owns 400 pieces of art, said that he never misses a preview of a contemporary art auction at Sotheby's or Christie's. For him, he said, collecting is almost as much a social experience as an esthetic one. "The previews are extremely important in my life," he said. "I'll change my vacation plans to be able to go to one. I wouldn't want to wind up staying home with my computer." Ms. Solomon said it was difficult to estimate how many bidders Internet auctions would attract. But she noted that one of the most famous auctions ever held -- the Jacqueline Onassis estate auction in 1996 for $35 million -- involved only 660 bidders in person and on the telephone. "It's very early days, but we expect significant interest on the Internet," she said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Sotheby's home page. Starting in July, the public will be able to bid on line. Advance registration is required. The first auction is to feature baseball memorabilia.

title: Internet Service Is Planning $6 Billion Deal to Buy Excite
body: At Home Network, a high-speed Internet service aimed at cable television subscribers, is expected to announce on Tuesday that it is acquiring Excite Inc., a leading Internet destination, in a transaction valued at about $6 billion, according to a person involved in the deal. If completed, the deal would be one of the biggest in a flurry of recent Internet acquisitions, exceeding even the $4.2 billion purchase of Netscape by America Online announced two months ago. The boards of both companies met tonight to work on last-minute issues, with an announcement planned in newyork before the opening of the stock market. Any deal would require the approval of the shareholders of both companies. It is also possible that a last-minute snag could delay the agreement, but most of the details have been worked out. At Home refused to comment on the reports about negotiations, and Excite officials did not return phone calls requesting comment. The deal would strengthen At Home's position in the competition for destination sites, known as portals, that is increasingly defining the commercial Internet. It would also sharpen the position of AT&T, which is now concluding its acquisition of Tele-Communications Inc., At Home's major shareholder. Under the terms of the agreement, Excite shareholders would receive about 30 percent of At Home in a stock transaction involving the issuing of new shares. The resulting company would be named At Home, and George Bell, Excite's chief executive, would become an At Home board member as well as take an executive position in the combined company. The value of At Home's outstanding shares is about $10.4 billion, while Excite's are at about $3.5 billion. Excite's stock closed Friday at $67.50, up $2.375, while At Home closed at $102, down 62.5 cents. At $6 billion, the proposed deal values each share of Excite at more than $116, more than 72 percent above its Friday closing price of $67.50. At Home now has more than 330,000 customers for its service, which provides high-speed Internet data via cable networks. The deal would give it access to both Excite's users -- it is the sixth most heavily trafficked site on the Internet -- and to the company's content development capabilities. Excite is attractive to At Home as a potential vehicle to market its high-speed cable modem network to those dialing in with conventional modems through telephone lines. In addition, Excite offers a popular Internet brand name as well as the nucleus of an expanded content development capability that would become the heart of a future At Home service. Both At Home and Excite are based in Redwood City, Calif., at the northern edge of Silicon Valley. Mr. Bell and Tom Jermolak, At Home's chief executive, negotiated the deal by walking the short distance between their offices, which are separated by a parking lot. The urgency to strike an agreement was heightened in recent weeks because several other companies were interested in bidding for Excite, including Yahoo, a competing large portal and search engine, and Microsoft, according to people close to the negotiations. A report of a possible At Home acquisition of Excite appeared today in The San Jose Mercury News. The purchase would represent the biggest play yet in the rush to combine Internet access with portals, the starting point for millions of users. In the last year, portals have evolved by mergers and acquisitions of Web directories, or search engines, and content providers, including everything from traditional forms of printed news to audio and video entertainment, email and on-line discussions. In addition to the recent acquisition of Netscape Communications by America Online, Snap, an Internet provider partly owned by NBC, today announced a high-speed Internet service with partners including Bell Atlantic and SBC Communications. For AT&T, the At Home-Excite deal could ultimately help shape its strength in a wide range of Internet services, including dial-up access via its AT&T Worldnet service; the At Home offering, which will permit it to offer both high-speed Internet as well as local telephone services; and a new Excite brand that could serve as both a portal and an important content brand to rival other major Internet players such as Microsoft, Disney and America Online. From a business standpoint, the object of a portal is to offer a starting point to millions of Web users and then attract advertisers to place banner ads on the Web pages those users see. And as America Online has proved by attracting more than 15 million members, providing a combination of access to the Internet and content that will keep users hanging around the portal's pages rather than moving out to other parts of cyberspace is a winning strategy. Since its inception, At Home has followed that formula. The difference is that its users are all accessing the Internet at blazing speeds over cable modems -- in many cases faster than the access they have over high-speed telephone lines at work. At-Home's cable modems can deliver data to home PC's at speeds in excess of 3 million bits a second. At Home has developed a portal that takes full advantage of that access speed, offering colorful, animated pages packed with multimedia content that other portals would not dare offer their users, the vast majority of whom are using dial-up modems at speeds less of than 50,000 bits a second. http://www.nytimes.com

title: New Service for High-Speed Net Users
body: Snap, an Internet company partly owned by NBC, has developed a service that is tailored for the small but growing number of users who have high-speed connections to the World Wide Web. An announcement is expected today. The high-speed service, called Cyclone, has lined up partners including telecommunications carriers like Bell Atlantic, GTE and SBC Communications and on-line programmers offering a variety of information on travel, personal finance and entertainment. High-speed connections promise television-style video and high-fidelity audio over the Internet, but fast communications links have so far been expensive and scarce, confined mainly to corporate users. At the end of last year, roughly 500,000 households had high-speed cyberspace connections using cable modems or the telephone technology known as asymmetric digital subscriber lines, or A.D.S.L. Snap is now an also-ran among the so-called Web portals that offer everything from search functions to email to a wide range of on-line programming. Yet though it trails well behind such leaders as America Online, Yahoo, MSN, Netscape and Excite, Snap has tripled its reach since NBC, a unit of the General Electric Company, bought a 19 percent stake last June from Snap's parent company, Cnet Inc. Snap has forged close relations with some major phone companies, and it is hoping to get a lift as the phone companies increasingly offer customers connections 50 to 200 times as fast as is possible using conventional phone lines. In the industry, high-speed links are often called broadband. "We're making a heavy commitment to broadband because we think this is the year broadband becomes real," said Halsey M. Minor, chief executive of Snap and Cnet. "We want to be there first." All the major Web portals are working on developing high-speed services, which are expected to be offered sometime this year. But analysts say that Snap's Cyclone, which plans to begin this quarter, is an early stake in the high-speed niche of the Internet service market. Last week, America Online announced an agreement offering high-speed connections to its subscribers who are customers of Bell Atlantic for an additional $20 a month. By 2000, about 2 million of the nation's 100 million households will have high-speed connections, according to projections by Forrester Research Inc. "As a mass market offering, broadband is still on the fairly distant horizon," said Kate Delhagen, an analyst at Forrester. "But things like the America Online announcement could speed up the adoption rate." Howard Anderson, managing director of the Yankee Group, estimates that it may take five years to enroll eight million American households in the use of high-speed services. "But afterward, usage will really jump quickly," he added. The big regional phone companies have ambitious plans for offering households high-speed connections. SBC, for example, plans to offer high-speed service to 8.2 million residential customers, mainly in the Southwest, by the end of this year. Bell Atlantic, the local phone company in New England and the mid-Atlantic states, says its own high-speed service should be available to 7.5 million homes by the end of this year and reach 14 million by the end of 2000. Today, the most common benefit of high-speed access is not having to wait so long for Web pages to appear. But with a service tailored for high-speed users like Snap's Cyclone, Mr. Minor said that consumers could get such things as video clips of travel destinations or video previews of an evening's television programs, delivered over the Internet. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Philips and Sony Set a Venture With Sun Mi crosystems
body: The world's two largest consumer electronics companies will announce today an alliance with Sun Microsystems Inc. to create a generation of networked entertainment devices and appliances that will communicate with each other and with humans via the Internet. Royal Philips Electronics N.V., the Sony Corporation and Sun will announce plans to link two developing software standards to forge a global computer network that stretches from the living room to the corporate computing center. Virtually any kind of electronic device built with the combined standards, including televisions, stereo receivers and videocassette recorders, will interoperate with and be controlled by the network. Sun's technology, known as Jini, is based on the company's Java programming language for Internet applications. A new kind of computing environment, Jini (pronounced JEEN-ee) enables programmers to develop software for an entire network of dissimilar machines rather than for just a single computer. It is a "distributed" design, meaning that each device on the network can contribute processing power to the network and can participate in the distribution of information and instructions to all the other attached devices. Under the agreement, Jini will be combined with the Home Audio Visual Interoperability, or HAVI, architecture, developed by a consortium of consumer electronics companies led by Sony and Philips. The resulting network, a new kind of computing platform for the anticipated post-PC era, might make it possible, for example, to program a VCR while away from home or to seamlessly route a television program to a computer disk drive or recordable DVD for later playback. "This is a very good marriage," said Mike Clary, who heads development of Jini, which Sun announced last year and plans to introduce formally next Monday. "It will make possible a wide range of new commercial services." The link between the two consumer electronics giants and a leading developer of Internet computing equipment also represents an alliance strong enough to take on the Microsoft Corporation in a standards battle for the consumer market. Microsoft, which controls the personal computer market with its industry-standard Windows family of operating systems, has made aggressive moves into new consumer markets. At the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas earlier this month, Microsoft introduced a new alliance built around its Universal Plug and Play standard. Major personal computer makers, including Compaq Computer, Dell Computer and Hewlett-Packard, have already announced support for the standard. Microsoft has also tried to forge an alliance with the Intel Corporation and a variety of consumer electronics companies to push a standard known as Home Application Program Interface, or Home A.P.I., which is intended to create links between the personal computer and consumer electronics world. Both the Sun Jini initiative and the new Microsoft Universal Plug and Play alliance appear to be attempts to do roughly similar tasks: make it possible to control myriad devices in the home and office, ranging from digital cameras and entertainment devices to ventilation and lighting. The two technologies, however, also represent deep philosophical differences. Microsoft and the personal computer makers are developing standards for a P.C.-centric vision of the home of the future, in which a personal computer controls everything from energy efficiency to telephone messaging and video delivery. In contrast, the Jini-HAVI alliance is a radical decentralized approach to computing in which control is spread throughout a network with no central point. In the Jini-HAVI vision of the world, the consumer could control all the appliances in a networked home from a personal computer but could also use a television or even some all-in-one infrared remote control device. "With HAVI and Jini, we are laying the foundations for new applications and, secondly, creating ways for consumers to control their appliances the way that they want to," said Eddy Odijk, Philips's general manager for systems architecture. The first pitched battle between personal computer makers and consumer electronics companies for control of consumer devices will probably be for control of the next generation of cable set-top boxes.  Tele-Communications Inc., the nation's largest cable television company, wants to start delivering interactive television services later this year, and Microsoft, Sun and Sony are all competing for inclusion of their software in the standard adopted by TCI for its set-top box. Sony's executives said the company was focusing its development efforts on the ability to move audio and video through home networks with its HAVI standard. "We've been very tied to streaming audio and video media through the home," said Roger Lea, a vice president at Sony's distributed systems laboratory in San Jose, Calif. "Now, that is being expanded to the entire world." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
Titans Race to Do the Policing For the Electronic Roadway
body: No policies were brokered and no deals were done, but the all-star lineup at the first meeting of the Global Business Dialogue on Thursday was enough to convey the group's basic message: The rules of electronic commerce will not be made by governments alone. Convening on the 44th floor of the Bertelsmann Music Group building in Times Square -- far from Washington or any other world capital -- the assembled captains of the media and technology industries vowed to prevent conflicting governmental regulations from obstructing business in cyberspace. Instead, they plan to devise their own united policies on such issues as on-line privacy and taxation under the umbrella of the new organization. Among the chief executives attending what one of their number, Bertelsmann A.G.'s Thomas Middelhoff, called the first global convocation at such a high level were Gerald M. Levin of Time Warner, Steve Case of America Online, Louis V. Gerstner Jr. of I.B.M. and James Barksdale of Netscape. France Telecom and Fujitsu and Toshiba of Japan were also represented. "The Internet is big enough to matter and still small enough to be shaped," Mr. Case said. "A patchwork of policies will slow the Internet and gut its potential." Mr. Middelhoff said, for example, that many members of the Global Business Dialogue do not look favorably on a European Union privacy regulation that went into effect last fall. Itprohibits any company doing business in Europe from transmitting personal data to any country that does not guarantee comparable privacy protections. The group plans to announce its privacy proposal within a few weeks. To what extent the world's governments will heed the proposals of the united business elite is unclear. But consumer advocates said such initiatives raised concerns about protecting the public interest. "One of the great crises in our move toward electronic commerce is the parallel movement toward governance without government," said James Love, director of the Consumer Project on Technology. "Because as awkward and imperfect as governments are, there's still this idea that they're responsible to the people in a way that companies are not."   AMY HARMON http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Meeting to head off regulation of electronic commerce were, front row from left, Gerald M. Levin of Time Warner, Michio Naruto of Fujitsu and Steve Case of America Online.

title: Holiday Use Sours a Few Consumers on Web Shopping
body: Amid post-Christmas giddiness about the stellar holiday drawing power of Web merchants like Amazon.com and portals like America Online, a survey to be released today found that while record numbers of Americans tried Internet shopping, they were not always happy with their experiences. Consumers who expressed satisfaction with their on-line shopping excursions dropped by 14 percentage points from six months earlier, although the vast majority -- 74 percent -- still considered it a positive experience, according to the survey, which was conducted by Jupiter Communications, a new-media research company in newyork. Jupiter's results are based on a questionnaire filled out by 2,369 households that use the Internet. In about 44 percent of those households, someone bought something on line during November and/or December. The households were selected from a group of 4,000 homes randomly chosen by Jupiter's research partner, National Family Opinion, to reflect the total on-line population in the unitedstates. The margin of sampling error was plus or minus two percentage points. The data strongly suggested that the Web had evolved in consumers' perception from an exciting novelty to an alternative means of shopping, with benefits and problems all its own. Still, the No. 1 reason consumers voiced dissatisfaction was a problem as old as retailing: the product they desired was out of stock. Unhappiness about high shipping costs was a close second. By contrast, concerns about merchants protecting credit card numbers, previously the single largest concern about purchasing merchandise on line, ranked fourth among reasons for survey participants' unhappiness. Similarly, discontent with on-line merchants' return policies and their communication problems with customers ranked in the bottom half of the list of consumer complaints. Shoppers were also surprisingly tolerant of technical mishaps. Asked whether poor performance affected their site use, 51 percent responded "no," and only 9 percent said that such glitches would cause them to stop using a site permanently. When a site had problems, however, 28 percent said that they then sought out an alternative, which they continued to stick with. Nicole Vanderbilt, a senior analyst with Jupiter, said on-line merchants should view these deserters as "a warning sign." "There has been a lot of hype about immense growth on the Web," Ms. Vanderbilt said. "What retailers need to be careful of now is taking that for granted. Nineteen ninety-eight brought in a lot of new dollars, but they are going to have to play the game very carefully to maintain their momentum." Several other research firms have also recently released studies on consumer Internet purchasing patterns during the holiday season. Infobeads, a unit of Ziff-Davis Inc., the publisher of PC Week magazine, conducted telephone interviews with 1,000 adults selected at random. Aaron Goldberg, the company's executive vice president, said his firm found that of those users who had actually bought something, 55 percent rated the experience as "easy" and 43 percent said that they had saved money while shopping on the Web. But a not-yet-published survey suggests still another potential area of concern for on-line merchants. Tomorrow, Ernst & Young will release a survey of 1,300 consumers and 125 on-line retailers, which found that 57 percent of consumers were visiting Web sites only to research products. They did their actual buying later in a store or by phone or fax. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Market Place;
Anything.com Likely to Be Hottest Issue In Class of '99
body: You want Internet companies? We'll give you Internet companies. That's the message Wall Street is sending investors in the first quarter. The Class of '99 introduces a new crop of Internet-related companies with initial public offerings that will surely test investors' hunger for anything that hints at the World Wide Web. The first of these, Marketwatch.com, came roaring onto the market Friday. And at least 15 more Internet initial offerings are expected within the next few weeks and months. But after a frenzied run on Internet stocks, a run that has sent the shares of dozens of as yet unprofitable ventures to dizzying heights this winter, Wall Street analysts are warning that investors could suffer huge losses by eagerly chasing these hot and volatile issues. Speculators bent on riding Internet stocks higher may be distorting the true value of these start-up companies, some analysts say. They also warn that with the huge number of offerings coming to market this year, investors' willingness to go after anything with a "dot com" in its name may make it difficult to distinguish companies with solid prospects from companies simply trying to cash in on the market's exuberance. "This is what's called a herd mentality -- everyone's going in the same direction not knowing what they're going after," said David Menlow, the president of the IPO Financial Network, a company in Millburn, N.J., that rates public offerings. "How do you stop to determine what a quality company is when Internet companies are trading on vapors?" The first signs of a frenzy this year came Friday with the start of trading in shares of Marketwatch.com, a financial news Web site partly owned by the CBS Corporation. Wall Street underwriters had priced the initial offering at $17 a share. But the stock soared as high as $130 a share in early trading before closing at $97.50, up $80.50, or 474 percent, for the day. That price run-up was not too different from the pattern that emerged last year, when Internet stocks like Broadcast.com, Theglobe.com and Ebay rocked Wall Street with some of the fastest opening-day sprints in history. Theglobe.com, for instance, soared a record 606 percent in its first day of trading. The Internet enthusiasm has been further fueled by the recent surge of Amazon.com and other electronic commerce stocks. As a result, Wall Street analysts say that underwriters have been besieged by Internet-related companies seeking to go public. "There's a pipeline chock-full of deals," said Henry Blodget, an Internet industry analyst at CIBC Oppenheimer. "The market is willing to fund anything right now." Among those in the pipeline: Ivillage, a Web site that caters primarily to women 25 to 49 years old; Healtheon, a business-to-business health care information company founded by James Clark, who is one of Netscape's founders, and Priceline.com, an Internet auction site that enables consumers to bid for airline tickets, automobiles and hotel rooms. While many leading Internet companies are preparing public offerings -- including Barnesandnoble.com, the on-line operation of the bookseller Barnes & Noble Inc. -- some investment bankers say that the quality of many prospective offerings is dropping. "There's a lot of low-quality merchandise in the pipeline, and a lot of companies with just 'dot com' on the back of their names," said Scott Ryles, head of the technology investment banking group at Merrill Lynch & Company. But there are also high-quality ventures coming public, he said, including a growing number of companies involved in business-to-business activity on the Internet. Investors should be forewarned that a majority of the offerings still come from money-losing ventures. Almost every offering prospectus reads as if the underwriters hit a computer key that was programmed to spit out the words, "The company expects to incur losses for the foreseeable future." Priceline.com, for instance, has had cumulative losses of $41 million; Ivillage has lost $65 million in three and a half years, and Healtheon has had losses of $73 million since 1995. Start-up losses, however, have not prevented Internet companies from winning over investors. The Class of '98 demonstrated that Internet companies are hot, regardless of their profitability. Initial public offerings of Internet companies gained an average of 119 percent last year, according to Richard Peterson, a spokesman for the Securities Data Corporation in Newark. A great deal of the activity came late in the year when a cool market for initial public offerings quickly heated up after media reports on the soaring popularity of the Internet and the rush of retail business done over the Internet during the holidays. "There's just huge mass media attention focused on the Internet," said Bill Burnham, an Internet industry analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston. "It's like a magnifying glass focusing the sun on one little spot." Day traders, who often trade in and out of stocks to ride price trends and buying momentum, saw the rising demand for Internet shares and pushed the volume of Internet trades to record levels. Analysts warn that the speculative frenzy has driven Internet stock prices to irrational levels. As a result, they say, many investors have lost considerable sums chasing volatile offerings, whose prices have occasionally fluctuated wildly on their first day of trading, as Marketwatch.com did on Friday. Charles Schwab & Company, the nation's largest on-line brokerage firm, has decided to restrict the trading in some Internet offerings, including Marketwatch.com and Pacific Internet, which is preparing to go public this week. "The trading in some of those Internet stocks that go public is totally irrational," said John L. Steffens, vice chairman of Merrill Lynch.  "Some of the companies going public have been in business two years and they're valued 10 times higher at the end of the public offering; it doesn't make sense. Some of these issues will have to come home to roost." No one disputes that the Internet offers promising business possibilities or that many of these companies may eventually turn out to be profitable. But everyone from Wall Street investment bankers who take companies public to everyday investors gleeful about big stock market profits are questioning the soaring values of these young companies. "This isn't fictional growth or tulips; these companies are growing," Mr. Blodget, of CIBC Oppenheimer, said. "But these valuations are problematic. I don't think there's a sector in history that's been valued at these heights. It's totally frightening." Part of the problem, analysts and traders say, is that there are so few Internet stocks available to eager investors, and so much demand for those that are available that trading imbalances abound. One measure of the supply-demand imbalance is the huge amount of daily trading volume in comparison with the total number of shares available. Nearly 10 million shares of Marketwatch.com changed hands Friday, for example, even though only 2.75 million were issued. With a large new crop of Internet companies preparing to go public, analysts say that the supply-demand imbalance may ease, and that could lead to softening stock prices as money chases many more issues. Analysts say investors may also alter their habits. "Investors are going to become more selective," said Lawton Fitt, an investment banker at Goldman, Sachs & Company. Analysts are also concerned about a surge in the number of company insiders who sold their shares in the fourth quarter of 1998, which some see as a sign that insiders believe the stocks are near a peak. "We continue to marvel at a veritable explosion of insider selling at the Internet-related or E-trade companies," said Bob Gabele, the president of CDA Investnet, a company that tracks insider selling. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Chart: "WWW.Going Public" The sky-high stock prices of publicly traded Internet companies are proving an irresistable lure for the Internet companies that are still privately held. title:
Patents;
It may be 'big, really big,' but an on-line airline ticket discounter is also being challenged.
body: A WASHINGTON patent lawyer is challenging a fundamental patent issued last summer to Priceline.com Inc. The lawyer, Thomas Woolston, contends that he filed for a patent about 16 months before Priceline applied for its patent in September 1996 covering an on-line auction system that allows consumers to bid for items like airline tickets over the Internet. Mr. Woolston's patent, which was issued in December, in part covers a computerized marketplace that enables "the purchaser to speculate on the price of collectibles in an electronic market for used goods while assuring the safe and trusted physical possession of a good." Indeed, Mr. Woolston, a baseball fan, first thought of his invention as a way to buy and sell baseball cards over the Internet. Although that is very different from the business that Priceline conducts -- it advertises widely, with the actor William Shatner concluding "I told you Priceline was going to be big, really big" -- Mr. Woolston contends that his patent covers the buyer-driven auction model of doing business on the Internet. His start-up venture, Mercexchange, is at this point little more than a company name and a board in search of venture capital. "We're defining our markets right now," Mr. Woolston said. Priceline.com operates a system under which users go to an Internet site and name the price they are willing to pay for airline tickets, hotel rooms or other items. Priceline then tries to find an airline or other company willing to accept that price. Jay S. Walker, vice chairman and founder of Priceline, dismissed Mr. Woolston's challenge. "When you have a landmark patent, you have to expect, as we did, that all kinds of people are going to come out of the woodwork to claim that the Patent Office made a mistake, and that they really invented it first," he said. "Our patent is no exception." Mr. Woolston said that he discussed working with Priceline.com to develop the auction technology but that the talks failed because the company "expressed no serious interest in cooperation." Mr. Woolston has requested that the Patent Office conduct a proceeding known as an interference. It could be months before the agency decides whether to initiate such a review, which could then take several years. Normally, such disputes over issued patents must be fought out in the courts. But for technical reasons, Mr. Woolston is able to challenge the Priceline patent through the Patent Office -- a far less costly way to challenge a patent. Mr. Walker said it was "not inconceivable" that the Patent Office would grant the interference, but expressed confidence that the patent given to Priceline.com would survive such scrutiny. Priceline was assigned patent 5,794,207. Mr. Woolston received patent 5,845,265.  Truth in Labeling, With a View to Safety Frank C. Sadlo, a substitute high school teacher in Louisville, Ky., received a patent last week for what he contends is a way to encourage the practice of safe sex. Mr. Sadlo's idea? Sell condoms that fit to size. "If you walk by the condom rack at the drugstore, you'll see that there are just two sizes -- regular and medium," Mr. Sadlo said. Class A condoms are 7.1 inches in length, according to Mr. Sadlo, while class B condoms are 6.3 inches. "But medical research of the male anatomy shows that the length of an erect penis ranges from about 3.5 inches to 13 inches," he said. "Clearly, one size cannot fit all." Further, Mr. Sadlo said, 15 percent of men are unable to use the latex condoms on the market because their circumference is too small for the condoms to stay put. "There are a lot of people that the condoms just aren't going to fit," he said. "For lots of men it's too long, so there's an unrolled portion at the base which can have a tourniquet effect and restrict neurological and vascular functioning. And if it's not long enough, it's going to have a tendency to pull off or break." Mr. Sadlo has patented a system of selling condoms that vary in length and width. Men could pick up a measuring strip at the drugstore and then take their measurement at home in privacy, he said. When they returned to the store, they would consult a coded chart for the appropriate size. The chart would be similar to, but a bit more complicated than the weight-and-height charts that women consult when they buy pantyhose at a store. But Mr. Sadlo said the size of the condom would not be evident on the package. "It would be coded, so you would pick out say, a J-M," Mr. Sadlo said. "The actual condom package would not indicate any length on it." Mr. Sadlo said he hoped to license his invention. "It can be a real funny subject," he said. "But it can help save a lot of lives because it will be a lot more reliable and comfortable, so a lot more people will be willing to wear them." Mr. Sadlo received patent 5,857,466.  A Trapdoor of Sorts For Discarded Cutlery It can cost a cafeteria thousands of dollars a year to replace flatware that has accidentally been thrown away. Richard E. Edwards has come up with a solution: a trash can with an electronic metal detector. The can described in his patent features a chute at the top. If garbage passing through the chute contains a fork or a knife or a spoon, an alarm sounds and a spring-loaded door closes the base of the chute. Once the metal has been retrieved, the chute opens again. Mr. Edwards, of Long Beach, Calif., received patent 5,797,497. Patents are available by number for $3 from the Patent and Trademark Office, Washington, D.C. 20231. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY: Digital Commerce;
To win and keep customers in a wired world, companies must provide value. Most haven't figured that out, though.
body: IN the early days of the Internet's commercial ascendancy, back in 1996, Jeffrey P. Bezos, founder and chairman of the Internet's retail whale, Amazon.com, made a simple observation that should have signaled problems ahead for technology companies that assumed that the information age would be business as usual. "I hear a lot of people talking about business models, but I don't hear much about customer value," Mr. Bezos said. If value was indeed going to be the key, a lot of business models were going to have to change -- most notably the telecommunications industry's, on which the Internet was being built. But instead of clanging like a gong in the heads of telecommunications executives, the cautionary logic of those words apparently continues to fall on deaf ears. Few industries have gorged themselves on digital commerce with greater appetite than the telecommunications companies. But the result has been a wired world that to many customers seems like a cross between the best-known works of Edvard Munch and Jean-Paul Sartre: we scream, but there is no exit. Telephone services provide a sharp and unfortunate contrast to on-line retailers like Mr. Bezos, who realized early on that keeping customers is a lot easier than losing them to substandard service and continually enticing new ones into the fold. It is a rare consumer today who has only one horror story to tell. Some engage in regular battle with cellular telephone duopolies and their arcane and incomprehensible pricing structures, which sometimes even charge for calls that their own networks are incapable of delivering. Others are continually confronted with pager services with sporadic delivery that charge by the alpha-numeric character and employ operators who apparently have no schooling in even the basics of abbreviation. Still others are engaged in conflicts -- which now involve the Federal Communications Commission -- over so-called casual customer rates for long-distance calls, socking consumers with the functional equivalent of $28 for a $1 gallon of gasoline. What is more, the telephone is the most common bridge to cyberspace, and as Internet and other on-line service providers reach a broader and less sophisticated market, the Internet revolution is in danger of becoming a latter-day Boston Tea Party as customer complaints mount about responsiveness and overcharging. Customer satisfaction rates for companies that were once blue chips in the telephone industry are sinking, said Nick Donatiello, president of the consumer research firm Odyssey L.P. "AT&T's image, for example, has rebounded somewhat, but it had been declining steadily for the past few years," Mr. Donatiello said. The phone giant was rated "very good" by 63 percent of unitedstates households in 1994 but dropped sharply, to 37 percent, in 1997 in Odyssey's surveys before rebounding to 55 percent last year. "Still, it's not nearly what it was," he added. Why are these companies, so central to the continued growth of the digital universe, so apparently intractable about providing value to customers? "The problem," Mr. Donatiello said, is that "virtually everyone in the telecom industry has had the luxury of treating their customers like garbage for a very long time, first because they had a monopoly -- and some still do -- while others have geographic oligopolies." As a result, he says, they are in a position not to care very much whether customers are satisfied with the quality or value of the services they sign up for. One of the most profound differences between on-line retail and the business of providing telecommunications, for example, is that customers find it a simple task to compare the prices of a book from several vendors. In contrast, telecommunications providers -- cellular and long-distance, especially -- seem to take pride in making it almost impossible to do so, with complex rates that vary by day of week, time of day and sometimes, it seems, the phases of the moon. The ability to comparison shop is one reason consumers are moving to support the trend toward flat-rate services, Mr. Donatiello said. "Americans don't like to have the meter running on anything that has to do with entertainment, information or communication," he said. "That's why we saw such a huge uptick in the adoption curve of on-line services when America Online went to its flat-rate model," now $21.95 a month. The single-price model may also account for the popularity of AT&T's Digital One plan, which offers customers in certain cities a flat rate of $90 a month for 600 minutes of cellular calls to or from anywhere in the unitedstates. The popularity of that plan, in turn, is setting off a frenzy among other wireless providers to offer their own flat-rate plans. But consumer attitudes suggest that may not be enough. Increasingly, people want to simplify the enormous complexity of their wired lives by buying all their telecommunications-- local phone service, long distance, cellular, cable television and Internet connections -- from a single provider. And though AT&T again says it is leading the charge with its purchase of the cable television giant Tele-Communications Inc., Mr. Donatiello says consumers apparently do not hold out much hope that even moves this bold will make their lives easier to understand or manage. "The bottom line is that consumers don't think any kind of company would do a good job" providing a full range of services, he said. "Their No. 1 choice was a long-distance company, and only 37 percent of U.S. households said they would do a good job." Local phone companies got a 36 percent confidence rating as potential one-stop providers, while cable television companies scored only 21 percent, and Internet service providers a paltry 17 percent. So in the end, consumer attitudes signal trouble ahead for acquisitive telecommunications companies like AT&T, despite the benefits it promises from its TCI merger and deals with high-speed Internet services like At Home. "It's worse than the blind leading the deaf," Mr. Donatiello said. "The bad has married the ugly, and somehow they expect the children to be the good. Lip service alone won't get you there -- the first thing they still have to prove is that they're worthy of their customers' business." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title: At Last, a New Strategy for AT&T
body: THE future of the AT&T Corporation is not hard to find -- if you can read a floor plan. It is in Room 4430G2 at AT&T's sprawling headquarters in Basking Ridge, N.J. There are five PC's in Room 4430G2, a big-screen television and a bunch of phones. Nothing special in any of that. What distinguishes the setup is what's missing: telephone wires. All the key equipment links to the outside world through a single cable television line. And the line is providing lightning-quick Internet connections, crisp video images and, of course, a dial tone. Simple as it seems, that ribbon of coaxial cable represents what may prove to be the most important strategic shift in decades at AT&T, the nation's biggest communications company and its most widely owned stock. Fifteen years after the break-up of the Bell System severed AT&T's hard-wire link to unitedstates consumers, its pending acquisition of Tele-Communications Inc., the No. 2 cable operator, will allow AT&T to again reach out and directly touch millions of homes. And trying to re-create AT&T's glory days, the company's new chairman, C. Michael Armstrong, wants AT&T to be the only communications provider its customers need. Is that a pipe dream in an arena teeming with competition -- wireless companies, long-distance companies and local phone companies, not to mention Internet providers and satellite TV services? Maybe not. Three thousand miles from Basking Ridge, dozens of technicians in Fremont, Calif., are preparing to move Mr. Armstrong's vision out of Room 4430G2 and into the living rooms of paying customers. Soon after the merger closes, as soon as this spring, the TCI brand will start to disappear in Fremont, a middle-class suburb of San Francisco, and Mr. Armstrong's operators will be calling consumers to offer AT&T's new wares. The pitch will go something like this: "Hi, this is AT&T. Did you know that we can now offer not only long-distance phone service but also four lines of local service with call-waiting and Caller ID? And may we interest you in our high-speed Internet service, called At Home? It lets you download from the Internet at speeds as much as 100 times faster than you can today -- and at prices comparable to what you're already paying." The salesperson will pause to catch a breath, and then continue: "If you don't want high-speed access, how about a more traditional Internet service, like AT&T Worldnet? And a wireless phone that includes nationwide calling for as little as 10 cents a minute? Oh, yes, we can provide all of these services on a single bill with one number to call if you have questions." But AT&T's proposition to consumers will be about more than a simple variety of services; it will be about the extra perks that come from becoming a full member of the AT&T family. So the closer will be along these lines: "By the way, if you use any three of our other services, we would be happy to add HBO and the Disney Channel to your basic cable package for no additional charge." By the end of 1999, AT&T intends to offer this integrated package of communications services not only in Fremont but also in another, undisclosed community in the San Francisco area as well as in Chicago, Dallas, Pittsburgh, Seattle, Denver, Salt Lake City, Portland, Ore., and St. Louis. By the end of 2000, the company intends to expand its competition against its progeny, the Baby Bells, by offering local phone service in most of TCI's other markets. It is one of the biggest gambles in AT&T's 114-year history -- a test of technology, of financial might and of regulatory flexibility. For Mr. Armstrong, it is the ultimate test of managerial prowess: whether he can reshape one of the country's most hidebound corporations to his vision of a lithe competitor in some of technology's fastest-moving sectors. If he succeeds, AT&T will again be not just big, but also dominant, a mantle it lost because of competition from the likes of MCI Worldcom, Sprint, SBC Communications and Bell Atlantic. If he fails? The critics will say he failed to gauge adequately the difficulty and cost of upgrading TCI's somewhat antiquated cable systems. That he did not understand the complexity of the local phone business. That he reached too far, too fast. AT&T declined to comment, citing a "quiet period" mandated by regulators before shareholders vote next month on the TCI merger. And for now, the critics are lying low. That is because Mr. Armstrong has already seemed to make a huge change in an organization that long had seemed to be inertia's captive. Though it lost its monopoly on phone service in 1984, AT&T never seemed able to shake off its monopoly mindset. Well into the 1990's, under Mr. Armstrong's predecessor, Robert E. Allen -- whose entire career was spent at AT&T -- the company continued to rely on the regulatory process to protect its core long-distance business and to keep potential competitors off balance. "The shared belief in the company was that the single most important entity that affected their future was the Federal Government and the regulators," said Richard S. Bodman, who was AT&T's chief of strategy and business development for most of the 90's and who is now managing general partner of AT&T Ventures, a venture capital firm backed by AT&T. "That was a contest that maybe they couldn't win, but it was a contest in which they felt they had pretty good skills and tools to play the game adequately well." ARRIVING in November 1997, after Mr. Allen's choice as heir, John Walter, quickly lost the board's confidence, Mr. Armstrong saw things differently. At Hughes Electronics, he had presided over the transformation of a military contractor into an entrepreneurial dynamo, building its Direct TV satellite business. And under him, AT&T has begun to shed its reputation as a company that would rather lobby than compete. "From the time that MCI was created in the 60's until Mike Armstrong, AT&T was essentially a defensive and reactive company," said Reed E. Hundt, who stepped down as chairman of the Federal Communications Commission just as Mr. Armstrong joined AT&T. "Since he arrived, the company has been pro-active, creative and aggressive." John T. Nakahata, who resigned as chief of staff for Mr. Hundt's successor at the F.C.C., William E. Kennard, late last year, said: "It seems that AT&T has realized that they need a business solution, not a regulatory solution, to their business problem, which is that they have not had a way to touch the customer in the local market." Of course, even as its share of the long-distance business slid and its earnings gains came to rely mostly on cost-cutting, the company always had ideas about how to grow. Some proved disastrous, like its $7.4 billion foray into the computer business by buying the NCR Corporation in 1991, a debacle reversed five years later at an additional cost of $2 billion. Others were inspired, like the acquisition of McCaw Cellular for $12.6 billion in 1993, making AT&T a national player in wireless communications, and the spinoff of AT&T's equipment operation as Lucent Technologies in 1996. Indeed, the seeds of every major move that AT&T has made in Mr. Armstrong's 14-month tenure were planted long before his arrival. His achievement has been in getting those plans off the drawing board -- or out of the dust bin -- and into the marketplace. TCI ACQUISITION -- The most important strategic move of Mr. Armstrong's tenure, the TCI deal is meant to give AT&T a high-capacity pipe into millions of homes and a leg up in striking deals with other cable companies. AT&T had been talking to cable operators, including TCI, about various sorts of joint ventures since at least 1991. But for years those talks never went anywhere, partly because, in its arrogance, AT&T refused to promise that it would not go into competition with the cable companies by jumping into the "content" business, whether by buying cable television networks, for instance, or even a movie studio. It was not until 1997 that AT&T agreed to curb its media ambitions, thereby bringing the cable companies back to the table. Around Christmas that year, AT&T began having serious joint-venture discussions with carriers including TCI, Comcast, Cablevision, Cox and Time-Warner, the No. 1 cable company. Boldly, Mr. Armstrong made the key decision to acquire TCI rather than simply form a joint venture. AT&T is now close to joint-venture deals with Time Warner and wants to sign agreements with the other big cable carriers by midyear. Together, these deals could give AT&T a line into more than half the nation's homes.  TELEPORT ACQUISITION -- Just as the TCI deal gives AT&T a wire into homes, the $11.3 billion deal for Teleport Communications last January gave AT&T entry into the business of providing local voice and data communications to corporate customers. This deal was loaded when Mr. Armstrong arrived. But he pulled the trigger, adding a unit that is expected to provide billions of dollars in revenue.  OVERSEAS DEALS, WITH LIMITS -- Mr. Armstrong led AT&T into a $10 billion joint venture with British Telecommunications P.L.C. All their international communications behemoth needs now is a big Asian partner -- and a chief executive. But in some ways the deal highlights one of AT&T's toughest choices. When the company decided that a big part of its future lay in the huge investments it would make to get into the domestic local phone market, it had no choice but to limit its international aspirations and rely on strong partnerships. Previously, AT&T had been negotiating investments in Germany and France -- and had been thinking about investing in Italy or building a network in Shanghai -- even as it participated in loose overseas ventures. Fittingly, Room 4430G2, where AT&T now demonstrates its ambitions for local communications services, used to be a reception area for visiting foreign executives. NATURALLY, the rich benefits that AT&T stands to reap if its new strategy succeeds are threatened by a commensurate set of daunting challenges. Foremost is the competition -- both from the Bells and AT&T's long-distance rivals. As a group, the Bells -- seven of them when AT&T was broken up in 1984, now consolidated to five -- have more money, more customers and arguably more influence in Washington than AT&T has. Whether the Bells or AT&T emerge as the most powerful players in communications depends on timing and technology. Both AT&T and the regional Bells know that whatever competitor is first to offer customers an integrated package of local and long-distance service in a given market stands a good chance of holding on to that customer for the foreseeable future. The problem for the Bells is that none has yet convinced the F.C.C. that, as required by the Telecommunications Act of 1996, it has opened its local phone networks to competition enough to win entry to the long-distance market. Even as AT&T introduces local service over TCI's cables, the Bells will still have to face that test. Bell Atlantic, the regional Bell serving 13 states from New England to Virginia, thinks it can put together a winning application sometime before the middle of this year. That would be later than originally anticipated but could still give Bell Atlantic a head start on AT&T in the lucrative Northeast. Even then, the technology that Bell Atlantic would have to use -- providing high-speed Internet access over standard copper telephone wires -- appears to some analysts as less developed than the cable technology that AT&T plans to employ. (Bell Atlantic was one of the first companies to have the vision of delivering a full array of communications services over cable lines. But its proposed merger with TCI fell apart in 1993, the victim of regulatory uncertainties and concerns over the costs of upgrading TCI's systems.) The flip side of Bell Atlantic's problem, though, is that AT&T's most cost-efficient technology for delivering phone calls over cable wires -- one that uses Internet systems -- is itself at least a year away. In Fremont and its other initial markets, AT&T plans to start out delivering phone calls using an older technology that could cost as much as $900 a house (though the company is counting on that figure being $550). The Internet option, however, could cost as little as $350 a house. The costs of delivering local services to all of TCI's 10 million customers could total as much as $6 billion, and those costs will be absorbed by AT&T's shareholders. Most analysts expect the TCI acquisition to dilute AT&T's earnings for at least three years. Just as important, AT&T faces big technical challenges in getting TCI's systems to work with its own -- and big human-resources challenges in getting TCI's sales force to work with its own. Complicated new computer systems will be needed, both to connect AT&T's old long-distance network to TCI's cable systems and to provide integrated bills for the company's millions of customers. There is no chance, meanwhile, that MCI Worldcom and Sprint, AT&T's two big rivals in the long-distance business, will stand still. Sprint has already unveiled its own plan to offer a bundle of local services, though how the company will reach large numbers of consumers remains unclear. Sprint has tried to make deals of its own with big cable companies. But in that competition, AT&T may have an edge. For one thing, once AT&T acquires TCI it will be part of the club with the other big cable operators. For another, Sprint has already worked with some of the major cable carriers in forming the Sprint PCS wireless joint-venture -- and that relationship did not go as smoothly as it could, because the cable operators were expecting a higher, quicker return on their investments. MCI Worldcom runs the biggest Internet service provider, Uunet, and one of the Bells' biggest competitors in local phone service, MFS. Both those units, however, are geared to business customers, and it is unclear how MCI Worldcom means to make a big splash in local consumer markets. FOR years, AT&T was a burr in the hide of the Federal regulators whose power still plays a big role in how competition unfolds in the communications world. In consummating the TCI deal, however, Mr. Armstrong and AT&T seem to have a special friend: the F.C.C. From the moment AT&T's deal with TCI was announced, Mr. Kennard, the commission's chairman, has not seemed able to say enough good things about it. And it isn't hard to understand why. For Federal regulators, the main issue of the last few years has been the fostering of competition in local telephone markets. AT&T's strategy promises just that. Mr. Kennard, however, wants to make sure that AT&T follows through, and not just for wealthy people able to afford the full panoply of 21st-century services. "The AT&T-TCI merger holds pro-competitive promise because it's a long-distance company joined with a cable company to compete against the local phone companies," Mr. Kennard said. "That's what all the hoopla is all about. But we need to make sure there's a commitment to deploy these networks to all residential consumers -- not only the affluent but to everybody, not only in the suburbs but also in the inner city." More grave could be challenges to AT&T's plans to limit access to its speedy new cable pipelines. Unlike local phone companies, cable TV operators do not have to open their systems to all comers. TCI, for instance, is under no obligation to let America Online offer direct high-speed access over its lines. That ability to use cable lines exclusively -- while the local phone companies have to open their systems -- is a cornerstone of AT&T's plan. But together, the Bells and leading Internet companies like America Online are challenging the disparity, on both the Federal and municipal levels. That puts the regulators in a tough spot, because AT&T -- on which the regulators are counting to create competition for local phone service -- will say it makes no sense to build advanced networks in the first place if it must open them to still other competitors. Nonetheless, the consensus -- both in the industry and on Wall Street -- is that by moving boldly to deliver his basket of services, Mr. Armstrong has given AT&T a new lease on market leadership. Investors have bid up the company's shares 73 percent since his hiring was announced, including a 29 percent increase since the announcement of the TCI deal in June. IF he succeeds, Mr. Armstrong-- who once longed to run I.B.M., another giant that needed stiff medicine -- will make good on his bid to become a corporate icon. "There is no guarantee that 20 years from now the AT&T's of the world will even survive," said Mark S. Fowler, a chairman of the F.C.C. in the 1980's. "What Armstrong recognizes is that they will have to take some very bold decisions in terms of changes of direction, committing capital, changing the culture within the company. Or they may not be around." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Since taking over late in 1997, C. title:
BUSINESS;
Click for Customer Service. Then Wish You Hadn't. - Correction Appended
body: IF on-line retailers steamrolled their way into the spotlight during the past holiday season, one thing is clear: They crushed a few toes along the way. Consumers have long lamented the state of customer service on line, but perhaps never as vociferously as in the last two months. Stories abound of vendors that shipped products late, sent the wrong item and then ignored complaints, or that required customers to pay the cost of returning goods and then tacked on restocking charges. And then there's the loathsome email "auto response," with advice on everything but what the customer asked about. Asked to summarize on-line customer service in a word, David Cooperstein, senior analyst with Forrester Research, an Internet consulting firm, responded: "Pathetic." Web sites have the powerful advantage of making companies seem accessible and easy to interact with. It's an appearance that all kinds of companies, not just retailers, can have trouble living up to.  Brightware, an email software company, reported in a study released on Thursday that when it tried to reach the 100 largest American public companies by email, 26 either did not accept email or made it so difficult to find the email forms on their Web sites that the surveyors gave up trying. Of the remainder, only 15 responded within three hours; 10 didn't reply at all. Matthew Garelick of Somerville, Mass., knows the frustration of unrequited email.  In early December he ordered the movie "Out of Sight" on DVD from Bigstar Entertainment, an on-line retailer. Between Dec. 28 and Dec. 30, Mr. Garelick sent email to Bigstar three times, asking why the movie hadn't arrived. "I would've been fine with an auto response," said Mr. Garelick, who eventually received the disk in January. "I just wanted an assurance that they were at least working on it. From now on, I'm not doing business on line with anyone who doesn't have a phone number." Having a number to call was small comfort to Duke Nguyen of Cincinnati. Mr. Nguyen said he ordered three items from the Internet site of Intuit in early December and then tried to change his order by phone. "Every time, after 20 or so minutes of waiting, I gave up," he said. He tried faxing in his order change. But, he said, the original items were delivered. "Finally, I called and just put on my speaker phone while I waited," he said. After an hour someone answered and he was able to arrange a return.  But then Intuit credited him for less than the full value of the goods, he said. He tried a new email button on Intuit's site but got an automated response suggesting, among other things, that he call customer service. "I'm computer literate," Mr. Nguyen said. "But when it comes to service, these things scare the heck out of me." Analysts and industry leaders say problems often occur because companies rush to get products and prices onto their Web sites while underestimating the time and resources needed for customer service. But David Levipsky, executive vice president of Bigstar, said that wasn't the case with his site. The company had anticipated a holiday rush by installing a "very cutting-edge" email system, he said, adding, "So it's surprising to me that this happened." As for Intuit, Larry Wolfe, senior vice president for the company's tax software division, said the company does the best it can. "Often in December and January, there are times when people wait longer than we'd like them to wait," he said. "But we take it very seriously, and we work very hard to keep call times down." Analysts say poorly designed Web sites draw complaints. "If a site is designed well, most of the complaints don't happen," said Mr. Cooperstein of Forrester, noting that many sites fail to offer enough information so that customers can help themselves. THE good news for consumers, analysts say, is that Internet merchants are learning two lessons: that ignoring email is the best way to turn customers into enemies, and that improving Web sites is more cost effective than dedicating battalions of employees to answer complaints. "The email deluge everybody was worried about we looked at as a total gift," said Matt Hyde, director for on-line sales at REI, a retailer of outdoor goods. "We've made hundreds of changes to our site based on customer service data." A result: The ratio of email to orders at REI dropped sharply, he said, and so did payroll costs for customer service. Dell Computer uses both software and employees to answer most of its 10,000 weekly emails within a day of receipt, said Manish Mehta, a senior on-line support manager. Its Web site features self-service information like technical support tips. Shoppers are becoming less tolerant of poor service from on-line retailers. "Consumer expectations have definitely grown, because certain sites have set a high standard," said Jakob Nielsen, a site design expert and publisher. "Fair or unfair, other sites have to live up to that standard." Perhaps so. But Kent Krueger, co-founder of the Sitstay GoOut Store, said sites that are honest with consumers can weather service problems. Sitstay, which sells specialty products to dog owners, was the only Web site to get a five-star rating for customer support among 500 rated in December by Bizrate, a market research company that surveys on-line shoppers. "We started selling doormats with little Yorkies on them and got a huge number of orders that we weren't prepared for," Mr. Krueger said. "So we got in touch with everyone and told them who we were, what had happened, and we were working on it." As a result, he said, no customers canceled orders. "The fact is, if you're honest and have a little fun, people will have a good attitude," he added. "But it could also be that dog owners are just a different breed." http://www.nytimes.com Correction  An article last Sunday about Internet retailers misspelled the surname of an executive at Bigstar Entertainment. He is David Levitsky, not Levipsky.
