title:
FILM;
The Newest Wave: Made-for-the-Internet Movies
body: IN the upper left-hand corner of the computer screen, a young woman materializes murkily in a patch of moving image, pauses to gather her thoughts and begins to recite an ode to the ecstasy of love. As she talks, the fuzzy image on the screen shifts and pulsates as if it were liquid. She is standing under a bridge, but on screen the scene is so dark and indistinct it is hard to tell where she is, not that it matters much: her words and body language are the point of the piece. Suddenly her rapture turns to incredulity over the nastiness with which love can end. And at that point so does the film, "1,000 Moons," a five-minute digital short designed for the Internet and one of four movies now being screened at a site called The Bit Screen (www.TheBitScreen.com). It's hazardous to make statements about who is or isn't doing what on the Web, but it would appear that the site is, if not unique, then most unusual. The movies aren't intended for showing on the theater screen or on video. Films like "1,000 Moons" are conceived and created to arrive by modem and be shown solely on a computer screen. Started last year by Nora Barry, a Philadelphia-area specialist in interactive media, The Bit Screen shows several films at a time, changing them every other month. Most are made by experienced creators of material for disk and the Web. Editing by computer, they continually manipulate their work. Movies can be remade after they are finished, and sometimes even while they are being shown. Occasionally viewers are invited to participate, as with other kinds of interactive programming on the Net. For Ms. Barry, these films recall Louis Lumiere, the inventor of the Cinematographe, who in 1895 devised a claw to pull still images along in a strip and a month later turned out "La Sortie des Usines Lumieres," a very brief short showing workers leaving a factory. Ms. Barry has seen Lumiere films that run from 30 seconds to maybe two minutes. "Bit Screen films run anywhere from two to seven minutes," she said, "but within that time frame each pushes the boundaries of the technology and expands or changes the way the story is told." Makers of the shorts (full-length features aren't feasible yet) would likely agree, but as the technology stands, it's arguable whether most viewers would understand what she means. For one thing, poor picture quality can hinder the most creative efforts. Movies on digital video disk are crystal clear on computer screens, but images arriving from the Net via modem haven't yet been smoothed and spread across the screen. Images were dark and cramped in Lumiere's time, of course, but back then who knew better, or cared, given the originality of the invention? Today on the Internet, dark little squares of jerky movement had better have some readily identifiable reason for being. Net moviemakers are full of cinematic concepts that they say can be realized only on the Web. For example, nowhere else can a film's elements be remixed as the movie is being watched. So it's too bad the poor image is such a distraction because the ideas go beyond that to explore some intriguing possibilities for the future use of film. On The Bit Screen, which is put on-line by the large cable company Comcast, images are streamed, a step that avoids downloading by playing back information as soon as enough has been gathered. When the image pauses, it is because more information is being collected. Such interruptions may make a shambles of the picture, but Net moviemakers try to use these limitations to their advantage. In "Positively Negative," an animated short now on The Bit Screen, whirling wheels and sunbursts of design constantly change shape as they work to establish a theme. Made by John Serpentelli, a Philadelphia fine arts animator, "Positively Negative" is intended to define computer animation in its infancy. "My approach was not to imitate Hollywood but aim for low-tech appeal," said Mr. Serpentelli. "I intentionally made it very graphic, black and white, something that would hold up, kind of like simplifying and boiling down a movie." If standard linear movies are made for watching, Web films also encourage participation. "What's so much fun about this genre is that we can do things you can't do in conventional filmmaking," Ms. Barry said. For example, the maker of a film scheduled for The Bit Screen later this winter will use a computer to shuffle audio and visual tracks and reassemble them to tell a different story each time. "Employing technology in that way turns the Internet into a 'shanachie,' or storyteller," Ms. Barry said. "Maybe have one per son start the story and have someone else pick up the threads and tell the next segment, add a few images of their own. It's how stories were told for hundreds of years: they were kept fresh in the retelling. With digital technology, we can do the same with film." Many viewers would rather just watch movies passively. But, Ms. Barry said, on the Web, film is to be used as much as watched. In that respect it's as much for the creator as it is for the spectator. Echoing Ms. Barry, Craig Johnson, who made "1,000 Moons," said Web movies are for "imagining the display monitor as the technological hearth, like storytelling around a campfire designed for the constraints of the Net." He calls his film a "digital haiku." His descriptions of what he's after are complex, but, simply put, the object is to use the digital format to manipulate images and their effect so that the woman's story becomes an experience that one takes part in rather than simply watches. In "1,000 Moons" the camera is fixed and the speaker, Thea Chaloner, "choreographs" her body movements as she wishes. The idea is to entice viewers to decide what they see in the piece rather than simply to present images to them. "You're an active audience because your imagination is evolving the imagery," Mr. Johnson said. If after watching the film you aren't responding accordingly, remember that at this moment on the Web, the beauty may be more in the eyes of the makers than the beholders. "I'm just trying to create a sympathetic magic," Mr. Johnson said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Thea Chaloner, in "1,000 Moons," a five-minute digital short film conceived and created solely for the Internet. (Art Tribe Inc.)

title:
INVESTING;
Newcomers That Faltered May Find Their Legs in '99
body: EBAY, up 1,240 percent. Ubid, up 611 percent. Broadcast.com, up 325 percent. Call the roll of the red-hot Internet stocks that made their initial public offerings in 1998, and you might think it was a great year for I.P.O.'s over all. You'd be wrong. According to the Securities Data Company, the research firm in Newark, 191 of the 373 stocks first offered for public trading in 1998 finished the year below their offering prices. Yes, the Bloomberg IPO Index, which measures new issues one year from their offering, returned 12.8 percent last year, versus 28.6 percent for the broader market, as measured by the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index. And the average new offering had an 18.7 percent gain. But toss out Internet stocks, and that declines to 6.1 percent. Eliminate all technology offerings, and it declines to an average loss of 2.5 percent. "We had a year of Internet blockbusters sprinkled with insanity.com," joked John E. Fitzgibbon Jr., editor of the IPO Reporter, an investment newsletter. The upshot is that last year's loser bin holds a bundle of cheap stocks, many of them solid companies with good growth prospects. "With the exception of Internet stocks, there's definitely more value within the I.P.O. market now than a year ago," said Robert Gardiner, manager of the Wasatch Micro-Cap fund, which often buys new issues. Why the underperformance? Take your pick of reasons. Many of last year's losers came to market in July, just as the markets started to wobble, said Gail Bronson, an analyst for IPO Monitor, a Los Angeles research firm. It was also a year of investor disinterest in small- and medium-capitalization stocks, which form the lion's share of I.P.O.'s, said Edgar Larsen, chief equity officer at AIM Management Group, a Houston fund company. Some offerings were too expensive to start with. "That left very little on the table for investors," said Linda Killian, a portfolio manager at Renaissance Capital, an investment firm that specializes in I.P.O.'s. As the new year begins, the bargains even include some Internet stocks. One of Ms. Bronson's favorite stocks is Pilot Network Services, which offers security services for commerce over the Internet. The company has strong management and a strong business model, she said, yet the the stock has fallen from its offering price of $14 in August to $8.9375 on Dec. 31 and $12.75 on Friday. Why did Pilot suffer? Ms. Bronson said she thought it was left behind in the rush to sexier Internet stocks. The fact that some people have trouble understanding how its business works didn't help, nor did the overshadowing of Pilot by a rival, Network Associates, which garnered attention with a string of acquisitions. Steelcase Inc., the office furniture company, is one of last year's losers that has puzzled some I.P.O. experts. The company went public in February at $28 per class A share and rose to $38.375, but closed on Friday at $16. Ms. Killian figures that Steelcase is simply a good company that went public at a bad time, when the cyclical demand for office furniture had slowed. She likes the company's valuation, now less than 11 times next year's estimated earnings. Mr. Larsen said his firm is expanding its holdings in Rainbow Rentals Inc., which leases furniture, appliances and computers. Rainbow went public at $10 a share in June, finished the year at $9.875, and closed Friday at the same price. He estimates that earnings will grow 15 percent to 20 percent annually over the next few years. The stock trades at just 13 times estimated 1999 earnings. Mr. Gardiner's fund is also expanding its position in Rainbow Rentals, as well as in Marinemax, a power boat retailer that trades at less than 10 times estimates of 1999 earnings and has earnings growth of 20 percent annually. "With this bunch, you don't have to buy any problem companies," he said. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph shows Bloomberg initial Public Offering Index, since 1998.

title:
PRACTICAL TRAVELER;
Older Travelers Turn to Internet
body: ELDERHOSTEL and Interhostel, which offer travel for vigorous older people, have entered cyberspace, putting their catalogues on Web sites. And in November, Elderhostel began taking registrations electronically through its site. Just as the elderly have discovered that email is the ideal way for the sleepless to communicate with the world, they have also apparently found that the Internet is an efficient way to shop. Since Elderhostel began Internet registration in November, a spokeswoman said, 1,000 clients, or 5 percent of those signing up in the period, took the electronic option, plus 50 who used it to change earlier registrations. This is out of Elder hostel's estimate of a total of 325,000 "older learners" who signed on in 1998. Electronic registration is expected to grow, but the process will never be as zip-zip-zip as ordering socks through the Web: One trip does not fit all. People who have traveled with these organizations know what to expect: dormitory rooms or cabins, bathrooms shared with a battalion, meals at cafeteria tables, lots of walking and carrying of one's own bags. But the Internet may pose problems for the uninitiated. Spokeswomen for both organizations said that phone discussions with applicants were frequently necessary to be sure that they realized that air fare is or is not included, or that they have not neglected to read notices that special menus are not available, cobblestones are hard to navigate and applications by frail people are discouraged. There are plenty of warning flags in the paper catalogues, but using Web sites, it is easy to sign up before reckoning with the realities. Those without computers should know that they have not been betrayed in the race for spots in popular Elderhostel courses: the thousands of listings in each fat newsprint catalogue -- or on the Web -- all have a single date for a lottery for registration spots. Until then, all applications -- mail, fax, phone and electronic -- go into the hopper. The lottery for places in Elder hostel's first spring-summer international listing was held in November, and for domestic courses, Jan. 5. Programs in these listings that still have space are open to registration, first come, first served. In this situation, once you have an Elderhostel identification number, registration through the Web on a business day between 9 A.M. and 9 P.M. Eastern time, is supposed to bring immediate confirmation if there is space.  Age Limits The principal registrant for Elderhostel programs must be at least 55; there is no age limit for an adult companion. This organization's "intergenerational" programs usually involve a child or grandchild under 25, and the program descriptions usually indicate what age is appropriate. These adult-child programs can be picked out on the Web site through the use of a search engine there, and they are separately indexed in the paper catalogues. Since Elderhostel stopped using Social Security numbers for identification, catalogues normally arrive with randomly assigned identification numbers. If there is no number, one may be obtained through the Web during business hours. People getting their initial information off the Web can also get a number electronically. An Elderhostel spokeswoman, Heather Baynes, said employees could help applicants on the toll-free number, (877) 426-8056. All applications by Internet, fax and phone require the use of a Visa, Mastercard or American Express card. Interhostel, which usually offers only foreign travel, has distributed its early summer catalogue with 26 programs. Later listings, for July into fall, will bemailed by the end of this month; the information will also be on the Web site. These programs are open to people over 50 and to their companions of at least 40. This organization breaks out its adult-child offerings into a separate Familyhostel catalogue for summer, which has been mailed. The intended age for children here is 8 to 15; adults may be parents or grandparents, but there must be at least one child and one adult in each registration. There are 10 programs in this catalogue, plus the organization's first domestic trip, a New England Sampler, with a base at the organization's home, the University of New Hampshire, in Durham. This one is offered from July 11 to 18. Interhostel has no lottery for places, but accepts registrations as it goes along. The Web site has a place to enter registration information, including the number of the applicant's Visa, Mastercard, Discover or American Express card. But people submitting this material electronically should not assume that they are registered until they get a phone call back from the Interhostel office. According to Carol Bense, a spokeswoman, the organization does not assume that applicants have read all the rules and caveats until there is direct discussion.  High Plains to High Art Here is a sampling of trips listed in the catalogues. Space was still available in the first week in January. * From April 25 to 30, Elderhostel at the Coastal Retreat Center on the Isle of Palms near Charleston, S.C., is offering courses on family history, Martin Luther and "Diaries From Dixie" from the Civil War period, which covers the journals of Mary Boykin Chesnut and two others. The cost is $420. * In newyork, the American Institute of Banking and the South Street Seaport are offering an Elderhostel course called "Navigating Wall Street: Institutions at the Epicenter of World Finance." This is offered May 6 to 11 and June 3 to 8. The students stay in a hotel at the financial center; the fee is $575. * In Montana from June 6 to 26, an Elderhostel program is offered at the Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center in Great Falls: "Lewis and Clark: Explorers at the Portage" and "Agriculture on the High Plains." "Strenuous program," the note on the explorers' sessions says, "the equivalent of two courses." The fee is $425. * Interhostel is offering a new program, the Villas of Rome and Florence, from May 14 to 28, through the auspices of the Lorenzo de Medici Institute. Five nights are spent in Florence, four in Viterbo and four in Tivoli, with a one-day trip to Rome. With air fare from Newark, meals and double-occupancy hotel rooms, this costs $3,285. * A new Familyhostel trip is "Spain and France: Basque Country and Paris," offered June 29 to July 9 under the auspices of the American University of Paris. The hotel in the Basque area is on the beach at St.-Jean-de-Luz, and there are excursions into Bilbao and San Sebastian. With air fare from Newark, the price for one of two in a room ranges from $2,595 for a child 8 to 11 to $2,895 for an adult. Interhostel, University of New Hampshire Continuing Education, 6 Garrison Avenue, Durham, N.H. 03824; (800) 733-9753, fax (603) 862-1113, www.learn.unh.edu. Elderhostel, a nonprofit educational organization, is at 75 Federal Street, Boston, Mass. 02110; (877) 426-8056, toll-free fax (877) 426-2166, www.elderhostel.org. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Leann Johnson)

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
CYBERSCOUT
body: Here are three independent sites on the World Wide Web, each of which intends to be your main or only stop for arranging travel. They all succeed, at least to some extent; they also all fail, to some extent. They are all worth a look.  ON-LINE PLANNING www.travelscape.com "Architected to fully automate and indiv idualize personal travel planning," as it promotes itself, Travelscape is crammed with just about everything needed to arrange, or "architect," a journey. There are sections devoted to cities, hotels, booking, "hot deals," vacations, free trips and, happily, help. If the on-screen help is not good enough, there is a toll-free telephone number "for further assurance of travel integrity." On the opening page, a few packages are spotlighted. If you know where you want to go, you can fill out a form for the service to check rates and schedules for flights and hotels, either together or separately. I said I wanted to leave Newark on Feb. 13, fly to New Orleans, and return Feb. 17. In the time it took to pour a fresh cup of coffee, a new screen had appeared with three flight options, two of them from La Guardia Airport rather than Newark, and five hotels in New Orleans. The free trip, a kind of sweepstakes, was from Los Angeles to Kauai, Hawaii, but to enter the contest you must provide such personal information as name and address and are encouraged, but not required, to contribute additional infor mation. ("How many vacations do you take per year?" None of your business.) The "hot deals" were for rooms at five "luxury-level hotels" in New Orleans, ostensibly at 15 percent to 50 percent below the usual rates. Even though I was booking more than a month before my trip, none of the hotels had any hot-deal rooms available. Travelscape is still worth a look, and maybe even a stay.  LINKS GALORE www.tripspot.com Tripspot, a self-styled "travel sweetspot," has little original content. It offers links to scores of other Web sites, some relevant but many not. It is certainly easier to find an airline, hotel or cruise here than to ride out on the wild wild Web without a scout. And, as with more and more sites, you can shop here, too; the so-called unclaimed baggage center sells books, music, videos, electronic gear, clothing and so on. The "library" is heaped with travel books and other publica tions. It is too easy to get distracted in Tripspot. I ended up in a site full of dumb quotations, which was fun but had nothing to do with arranging a trip. A sample: Duffy Daugherty, the late college football coach and sports analyst, about a player: "Not only is he ambidextrous, but he can throw with either hand."  CHEAT SHEETS www.previewtravel.com Preview Travel says it gives you free access to the same information travel agents use. There is a destination guide (from Fodor), hotel, air and car reserva tions, and vacation and cruise packages. Separate sections are farefinder and car finder, emphasizing low prices, and a business-travel subsection with maps, weather forecasts and a currency conver ter, where you can create a cheat sheet to carry on a foreign trip. There are two long lists of currencies, alphabetically from the American dollar to the Venezuelan bolivar, and the program converts from the curren cy selected in the left-hand list to the currency selected in the right-hand list.   L. R. SHANNON http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: Ebay to Offer Free Insurance and ID System
body: Ebay Inc., the Internet auctioneer, said today that it would offer free insurance and a user-identification system to increase users' confidence in the security of its on-line trading network. Ebay, which holds auctions for small businesses and individuals, said it would begin in March to provide users with insurance through Lloyd's of London for transactions from $25 to $200. The company has asked Equifax Inc., the largest unitedstates consumer-credit reporting service, to start a verified-user program in March in which consumers can register their Social Security number, driver's license number and date of birth for $5. Equifax will verify the data by comparing it with information from other sources and award users with a special icon appearing next to their name on the Ebay site. Details of the plan were first reported in The Wall Street Journal today. The cost of the free insurance program should not affect profit margins at Ebay, the company said, adding that it would not see gains from the verified-user program because it would offer it at cost. Ebay said it averaged about 27 complaints of fraud for every million auctions, or about 257 total complaints in the third quarter, when it had about 9.5 million auctions. The National Consumers League's Internet Fraud Watch has noted that person-to-person auctions account for the greatest incidence of fraud on line, with buyers sending money but failing to receive the merchandise. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Stock Rockets 474% In Initial Offer
body: In an indication that investors remain manic for new Internet stocks, the price of Marketwatch.com, the operator of a popular financial news site on the World Wide Web, rose more than 474 percent yesterday, its first day of trading. Much of that advance came on the first trade. The 2.75-million-share issue, offered to investors through an underwriting group led by BT Alex. Brown Inc. and the Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corporation, was initially priced at $17 a share, slightly above the expected $14 to $16. When the shares were reoffered, their first trade was at $90 a share, an increase of 429 percent. Of recent initial offerings for Internet companies, only Theglobe.com had a bigger percentage gain on the first trade from its initial price, rising 605 percent on the opening when it was offered to investors last November. The move was just the latest illustration of a voracious appetite for Internet stocks that has become almost commonplace in the last few months. Since November, seven new Internet stocks have seen their opening prices shoot up 100 percent or more above their initial offering prices, said Francis Gaskins, editor of Gaskins IPO Desktop, an on-line service based in Los Angeles. Of those, six finished the first day with gains of 100 percent or more. The stock rocketed still higher, peaking at $130. It closed at $97.50, up $80.50, on the day. Trading volume in the stock was more than 9.6 million shares, which means that each share sold changed hands more than three times during the day. The sale, which represented 22 percent of the company, raised $46.75 million for Marketwatch.com. But when the dust had settled at the end of yesterday's trading session, the company's market capitalization was more than $1 billion. "We knew this was going to be a hot deal, but the opening was a surprise to everyone," said Peony Kao, an analyst at the Renaissance Capital Corporation in Greenwich, Conn. Marketwatch.com has no dearth of on-line competitors, including financial news Web sites created by organizations like Dow Jones, CNN and CNBC; general on-line services like America Online and Microsoft, which provide access to financial and business news and services, and Web sites aimed at satisfying business, finance and investing needs, like Thestreet.com and Motley Fool. But in large measure, Marketwatch.com, which was created last year, generated enthusiasm because of its original owners, the CBS Corporation and the Data Broadcasting Corporation. Prior to yesterday's offering, CBS and Data Broadcasting each owned half of Marketwatch.com, and each retained a 38 percent stake. "With its parent companies, it has great leverage," Ms. Kao said. Unlike most fledgling companies on the Web, Marketwatch.com has a commitment from CBS to provide it with $30 million worth of marketing on CBS-owned media from now through October 2002. "The advertising deal is invaluable," said Paul Cook, lead portfolio manager of Munder Capital's Netnet Fund. "The ability to cross-pollinate the two media is remarkable, particularly in sports and financial news." In addition to the marketing agreement, Marketwatch.com is licensed to use the CBS name and logo, as well as its news content. The company has more than 40 journalists. And its Web site is attracting visitors. In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company said there were nearly 2.2 million visitors to the site in October, up from 785,000 in March. But profitability is something that has not yet been achieved. Marketwatch.com lost $3.6 million in the quarter ended Sept. 30 on revenue of $1.8 million. For a day at least, financial data and balance sheets were immaterial, as far as investors were concerned. "I recognized that with the small number of shares being offered there would be an imbalance between supply and demand," Mr. Cook said. "But I thought $50 a share would be a really good reception, and that I could pick it up in the aftermarket at $25 to $30. At $97.50, I am going to wait for a better price to get in." http://www.nytimes.com

title: As Snow Shuts Schools, Computer Users Boot Up
body: Hang up the sled. Put Scrabble back in the box. Surfing is the new snow day activity of choice. That would be surfing on the World Wide Web, of course, not the water (unless you want to try the moving waves on Go Surf, www.geocities.com/TheTropics /4271/gallery.html). With industry experts estimating that more than five million children nationwide have Internet access, a day of canceled classes means clogged chat rooms and crowded cartoon Web sites. Internet service providers estimate that use jumps more than 10 percent during the winter, and Bell Atlantic, whose phone lines connect people to the Internet, reported swollen activity throughout newyork State yesterday, with the system logging its average daily volume of 120 million calls by 5 P.M., barely two-thirds of the way through the day. Some of that surge is probably from increased phone calls and more adults working from home, two phenomena often associated with stormy weather. But experts also believe it is partly because when dozens of school districts in the newyork region declared a day off yesterday, thousands of children scrambled to their desks at home to click the day away. Adam Mele, 15, a sophomore at Fairfield High School in Connecticut, spent about three hours playing Half Life, a three-dimensional interactive shooting game. Lisa Kravitz, 13, an eighth grader at Pelham Middle School in Westchester County, N.Y., went to www.gurl.com and looked up her horoscope. And a New Jersey teen-ager whose America Online screen name is Styli63857 scrolled the love-life advice boards and exchanged instant messages with her friends, some of whom live just down the block. Cindy Berry of Darien, Conn., who has two sons, said, "When you and I were kids, we would talk to our friends all day at school and then call them when we got home; they email each other." Her sons, Nicholas, 8, and Christopher, 11, exchanged computer messages with friends yesterday morning to plan their snow-shoveling business. "It is nice to know that they're using their minds," Mrs. Berry said. "A lot of these games are pretty hard. I think there's educational value on line. If there's no school, they're certainly still using their writing skills and communication skills, and hopefully picking up some education along the way." America Online's Ask the Teacher feature typically collects about 6,000 homework questions a day. But email is the top on-line activity for children younger than 13, according to a survey by Jupiter Communications, an Internet research company. Games and surfing the Internet ranked second and third, and homework was fourth. "You can't really get frostbitten" on line, said Lisa Kravitz, who built a snowman yesterday morning before clicking on the computer. "You can't really get to many places" in the snow, she said, "and the Internet's right here, and you can go all around the world." On Teen People on Line, a popular site for children that can be accessed through America Online, the "Daily Buzz" yesterday bore the headline, "Snowed in? Get Surfing." It suggested cuddling up to the computer with a mug of cocoa and checking out sites to color with virtual crayons (www.kidalex.com/index.html), get movie reviews (www.girlson film.com/film/navigation), and climb Mount Everest -- virtually (www.everest.mountainzone .com/98). Karen-Kristie Prior, community manager of Teen People On Line, said the normal peak period for her Web site is from 3 P.M. to midnight. But in the winter, there are days with thousands of postings between 9 A.M. and 3 P.M. "We'll say, 'Oh my God, why aren't they in school?' Then we'll say, O.K., they're on snow days," Ms. Prior said. "I think the reason that it's popular is kids, they want to talk to one another," Ms. Prior said. "If they're not in school, they're missing that social outlet. They pop on line, and they've got this whole other scene going on." Sure enough, many children and teen-agers interviewed by telephone and email said they spent their snow day doing nothing more exotic than chatting with friends on the computer. "I actually like talking to my friends on the computer more," Christopher Berry said. "I just do. It's good because I can play computer games while I'm talking to them on the Internet." Styli63857, a 15-year-old who declined to give her name over the Internet, said it was a question of volume. "The computer just lets me talk to my friends all at the same time, since you can only talk to one person at a time on the phone," she explained in a flurry of messages. "I just talk to my local friends. I actually think it's corny to make friends on line. Because who knows? They could be fake." Many of those interviewed said they had spent part of the day on sleds and then warmed up inside with the computer. Games, email and other Web sites helped pass the long, slow hours that have always been the cloud surrounding the silver lining of a snow day. "It helps pass time," said Nora Wolf, 13, an eighth grader at Pelham Middle School. When Nora checked her favorite Web sites yesterday, there were "more people than when I go on after school," she said. "They're happy. Bored, but happy." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Left to right, Matt Sara, Christopher Berry and Max Marion of Darien, Conn., all 11, roamed the Internet on their snow day. (A. J. Wolfe for The newyork Times)

title: Delta Sets a Fee for Not Using Its Web Site
body: Starting this week, there are two new classes for Delta Air Lines passengers: wired and unwired. Citing the rising cost of conventional booking methods, Delta is imposing a surcharge -- $1 one way, $2 round trip -- on domestic tickets purchased anywhere but on the airline's own Internet site. No other airline has yet followed suit, though United Airlines, a subsidiary of the UAL Corporation, said yesterday that it was studying such a move. While travel agents acknowledge that the surcharge will not fall on them directly, they contend that the airline's long-range strategy is to further weaken travel agents, whose commissions have been sharply cut by the carriers since 1995, by weaning customers away altogether. "Here the airlines are making more money than they've ever made," said Diane Hanmer, the owner of Diane's Travel in Bartlesville, Okla., "and they're penalizing the people who can't afford a computer and the older generation, who aren't real familiar with using it." Delta declined yesterday to discuss the surcharge policy, though it said that slightly less than 2 percent of its ticketing is now done through its Web site (www.deltaairlines.com). United (www.ual.com) said its Web site's share of its bookings was 1.5 percent, while American Airlines (www.aa.com), a unit of the AMR Corporation, said its Internet bookings were just under 2 percent and growing by 25 percent a year. Over all, Jupiter Communications, a market research firm in newyork, has forecast that air travel bookings through the Internet will grow to 8 percent ($7 billion) in 2002, from 2 percent in 1998. And as the electronic share of bookings grows, many agents and travel industry officials say the major airlines are determined not to yield that business to such Internet travel agencies as Expedia, Preview Travel, Travelocity and Internet Travel Network, whose sale of airline tickets is increasing steadily. The Microsoft Corporation, for example, said last week that its MSN Expedia service (on MSN.com) posted sales of $250 million last year -- mostly airline tickets -- a 150 percent increase over 1997. While that is minuscule compared with the airline industry's $79.45 billion in revenues in 1997, the last year for which figures are available, the Internet agencies' sales are expected to continue growing. "Airlines have been cutting commissions to travel agents for years, long before on-line travel came on the scene," Suzi LeVine, a product manager at MSN Expedia, said. "This is another step in that direction and ultimately against customers' ability to gain access to a broad set of choices." The airline industry has consistently denied any such intent. The two-tier Delta policy is reminiscent of Citibank's policy in the early 1980's, in the early days of the automated teller machine, of requiring a $5,000 minimum balance for customers at some branches to be served by human tellers. At the same time, it follows a trend in other services -- notably stock trading -- in which on-line customers are offered lower rates. At the Satellite Airlines Center on East 59th Street in Manhattan yesterday, Dr. Wilbur Bowne, who was booking a Delta flight to a meeting in New Orleans, called the surcharge "unfair to the customer." But he also said that in the future he would use the Internet. Ken Ward, a travel agent in Atlanta, Delta's corporate backyard, said: "I've been surprised by the groundswell of resentment toward Delta. Two dollars for a round trip isn't much, but to a lot of customers it's a lot like creeping taxes." In Delta's message to travel agents on Monday, advising them of its new policy, effective immediately, the company said its cost of distributing tickets had increased more than 280 percent since 1990, to more than $1 billion in the fiscal year 1998, while revenue had grown just 50 percent over that same period. Moreover, it added, three of the four computer reservation systems used by most airlines and travel agents had already announced fare increases effective early this year. It said it would not apply the surcharge to tickets from its Web site because it was the least expensive way of issuing tickets. The expense of traditional ticketing has led the airlines in recent years to encourage another electronic innovation, the paperless ticket. But all tickets purchased through Delta's Web site, whether traditional or paperless, will be exempt from its new surcharge. The Travel Industry Association of America said that the number of people who booked airline, hotel and rental car reservations on the Internet increased 24 percent last year to 6.7 million, from 5.4 million in 1997.  With sales of $816 million, according to Jupiter, travel is the second-largest on-line industry, trailing only PC hardware and software sales ($836 million). While slow to merchandise their own Web sites, airlines are going all-out now to reap its presumptive riches. In the last two years they have been adding not just bargain fares available only on their Web sites, but discounts for hotels and rental cars. They often give bonus frequent-flier miles to customers who book on their Web site and frequent fliers can pay for certain bargain flights for a nominal fee plus frequent-flier miles. Thus Continental Airlines recently posted round-trip flights between Houston and Newark and between Seattle and newyork for $29 plus 17,500 miles. Many who book on airline Internet sites appear to be younger passengers who have flown only infrequently in the past, the airlines say, and have rarely if ever dealt with a travel agent. United said that 81 percent of its sales last year came through travel agents. Nevertheless, travel agents contend that booking directly with airline Web sites will ultimately hurt consumers. "They will inevitably pay more," said Joe Galloway, the president of the American Society of Travel Agents, "since they won't have the comparative fare and schedule options -- provided by travel agents -- that can help them save hundreds of dollars, as shown by every independent study."  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Foreign Affairs;
We're All One River
body: There are some who will tell you that 1999 will be remembered as the year of Clinton, Starr and Lewinsky. Wrong. This remarkable year will be remembered a decade from now as the year of the Amazon -- the cyber-river and the real river, Ama zon.com and Amazon.country, also known as Brazil. Those two rivers are flip sides of the same coin, and the coin is globalization. The incredible run-up in the stock price of Amazon.com and the incredible run-down in the stock markets of Amazon.country, i.e., Brazil, are both reflections of investors trying to figure out what companies and countries will be worth in this new era of globalization. In the case of Amazon.com, which sells books and CD's over the Internet, some people think it's worth $5 a share and some think it's worth $500. How can that be? Well, investors who have rushed to buy Amazon.com stock (personally, I own none) have the basic trend right. And the trend is that the Internet is going to define how we communicate, how we invest and how we conduct commerce. As a result, I believe there are going to be just two kinds of companies -- Internet companies and anti-Internet companies. Internet companies will be those whose business can be conducted over, or greatly enhanced by, the Internet. This is everyone from booksellers to consultants. Anti-Internet companies will be those whose businesses either cannot be conducted on the Internet -- giving haircuts or making steel -- or those whose businesses will benefit from the fact that the more people are home alone with their Internet, the more they will want to get out and touch something, smell something, feel something, taste something and soak up some community. This includes Starbucks, movie theaters, amusement parks and shopping centers (stock I do own). But while the buyers of Ama zon.com have the general trend right, whether Amazon.com is actually worth $148 a share before it's ever made a dime of profit depends on how you see the future. The Amazon.com bulls believe that there is a huge race going on right now for everyone's credit card. The race is between a number of major on-line retailers -- AOL, Amazon, Yahoo, Excite, etc. The assumption is that all of these sites will eventually become full-service on-line shopping centers that will sell everything, and that you will give your credit card number to one or two of them -- where you will do most of your shopping -- but to fewer than five of them. Therefore, if Amazon.com is one of those winning sites, its profits will be enormous. It will be an on-line shopping mall for the world. The Amazon.com bears, and I'm one, believe that the problem with on-line retailing is that the barriers to entry are so low -- with $100,000 I could start a rival Amazon.com tomorrow -- that there will always be one too many competitors making sure that Amazon's profit margins never get as big as people project. Amazon.com offers 30 percent off almost every hardcover. So Barnes andnoble.com matches that, and then Buy.com comes along and offers best sellers at 50 percent off. Buy.com's founder told USA Today he has no intention of ever making money selling books, but just wants to build up volume to sell ads. As for Amazon.country, Brazil, it's been trying to cut its budget and streamline its economy to make itself an attractive site for global investors. Brazil wants to be a major economic power but it doesn't have the savings or the technology to reach the first rank, so it needs the global markets. But to make Brazil attractive to global investors requires some painful internal reforms and a shrinking of the country's social safety net, which is proving politically explosive. And Brazil knows that if it doesn't do what the global herd demands, the herd will just move to Thailand.country or Mexico.country. What Amazon.com and Ama zon.country are telling us is that the next phase of globalization is going to be a real bear. It's going to squeeze the profit margins of every company that does business over the Internet, which will be great for consumers and a terror for producers. And it's going to squeeze the politics of developing countries even tighter, which is going to be tough on their citizens and a terror for their politicians. Yesterday's 228-point drop in the Dow, because of the economic turmoil in Brazil, is just a small reminder that life on the real Amazon still matters, and it can, and will, affect life on the banks of Amazon.com. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Internet Company Has a Strong Share Sale
body: Marketwatch.com Inc., which runs a popular World Wide Web site covering financial news, raised $46.8 million in an offering to institutional investors today. The San Francisco-based company sold 2.75 million shares, a 23 percent stake, at $17 each. That was $1 more than the top of the expected range of $14 to $16, which had been raised from $10 to $12 on Wednesday by the lead underwriters BT Alex. Brown and Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities. The sale gave Marketwatch.com a market capitalization of $199.8 million. Based on the rise in the sale price and strong investor demand before the sale, the shares are expected to increase sharply when public trading begins on Friday. The institutional sale follows three days of declines for most Internet stocks and broad market indexes. The Dow Jones industrial average has fallen 5.2 percent since Monday, led by concerns that Brazil's economic problems will hurt profits at many unitedstates companies, while the Interactive Week Internet index fell 9.3 percent on concern that Internet stocks are overvalued. The expectations that shares of Marketwatch.com shares will soar have caused the stock price of the Data Broadcasting Corporation to more than triple in the last month. Data Broadcasting, which sells financial market data to individuals via satellite and cable, owns Marketwatch.com with the CBS Corporation, and will own 38 percent of the Internet company after the sale. Shares of Data Broadcasting fell $1.4375 today, to $31.1875; those of CBS fell $1, to $34.125. http://www.nytimes.com

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Lucent Deal for Ascend Comes With Little Fanfare In announcing its $20 billion acquisition of Ascend Communications, Lucent Technologies called it the "largest technology merger ever" and "a leap rather than a step," but there was an unmistakable whiff of ho-hum in the air. The high-technology marriage is a stock swap of 0.825 share of Lucent for each share of Ascend, a 19 percent premium over Ascend's market value when trading ended on Tuesday. The deal would have been dramatic had it occurred a year ago, but by the time it was done it seemed inevitable and perhaps even overdue to many analysts and customers.  Page C2. 2d Year for Wall Street Project Senior executives from several dozen blue-chip corporations will gather in newyork today with hundreds of their counterparts at minority-owned companies for the second annual economic conference organized by the Rev. Jesse L. Jackson's advocacy initiative, the Wall Street Project. Mr. Jackson will use the occasion to exhort corporate America to expand its "trade relationships" with the "emerging markets" in inner cities and rural backwaters, but he will also be trying to demonstrate that the Wall Street Project is operating with a broader mandate and a clearer focus than it demonstrated at its debut conference last year.
