title: For Surfers, the World's a Stage
body: AS William Shakespeare observed in "As You Like It," all the world's a stage -- but these days it helps to have some idea of exactly where to find the good stuff. The American Theater Web (www.americantheaterweb.com) is helping people do just that, providing links and listings in one place for more than 1,000 theaters nationwide. The site's goal is to list as many Web sites from American nonprofit performing arts groups as possible. Web surfers in the mood for a little drama can search for playhouses by either an alphabetical listing of theater names or by city and state. For each entry on the site, there is a summary of the theater company's work and productions, along with a link to that theater's own Web site for more detailed information. The range of organizations found on the site is impressive -- everything from small community theaters in Utah to the Arena Stage in Washington. Although the big commercial houses of Broadway are not on the site, links to several dozen nonprofit drama companies in newyork City are listed. The American Theater Web, which now averages 175 hits a day, went on line last fall and has been growing steadily. The site's creators are constantly on the lookout for new links, and one or two theaters a week have been sending in the U.R.L.'s for their home pages for inclusion. Using keywords, the American Theater Web site can be searched according to a user's tastes. It also has monthly groupings of shows going up nationwide, and many theaters also list all their productions for the current season. A message board for theater professionals and other interested parties to exchange notes, ideas and information is also a popular area of the site. The American Theater Web was created as a nonprofit venture, but its creator, Andrew Propst, said he was looking for a corporate sponsor to help enhance it. "Should this sponsorship be gained," he wrote by email, "the first expansion that we would like to have take place is the creation of a server where smaller theaters can place their Web pages." Many smaller theaters use free Web space on America Online or Geocities, but the Web addresses tend to get a bit unwieldy. "A U.R.L. of 'http://americantheaterweb.com /publictheater,' provided free of charge, we believe would be much more valuable for the theater as it attempts to reach new audiences through the Web," Mr. Propst said. Already, the site is offering to design Web pages, at no charge, for a limited number of nonprofit theaters that need them. As the sponsorship search continues, the site is growing and adding new features. In addition to more theaters submitting their Web addresses for inclusion, the American Theater Web has a new section called "American Theater in the News," devoted to feature articles and reviews of productions from newspapers with on-line sites, as well as stories of general interest to theatergoers. With this site, all the Web's a stage. And if by any chance your appetite has now been whetted for a performance of "As You Like It," the site lists forthcoming versions, including the Alabama Shakespeare Festival's production running from March 9 to July 25. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Andrew Propst, creator of the American Theater Web site. (Dith Pran/The newyork Times)

title: GTS and Flag to Build Phone Cable System
body: Global Telesystems Group, a telecommunications company backed by the billionaire George Soros, and the Bermuda-based Flag Telecom said today that they planned to build a $1 billion telephone cable system to carry high-speed data across the Atlantic. The joint venture will offer a high-speed direct link between newyork, London and Paris, with connections to other cities in the unitedstates, Europe, the Middle East and Africa from next year, GTS said. The venture comes as carriers struggle to cope with demand for Internet and other data traffic, which uses up more telephone cable capacity than voice traffic. The system will carry Internet and video traffic across the Atlantic at speeds of up to 1.28 terabits a second, or 25 times the capacity of current trans-Atlantic cable technology. "One of the drivers is the explosive growth of Internet traffic between the U.S. and Europe," said Dave Scott, a spokesman for GTS Carrier Services. GTS shares fell $1.75, to $59.875. Some forecasts predict that over the next four years, the amount of Internet traffic between Europe and the unitedstates will grow as much as 4,300 percent, Mr. Scott said. The network will be able to carry up to 100 hours of digital video a second, or 15 million simultaneous phone calls. France's Alcatel S.A. will supply some of the equipment for the network. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
LIBRARY/VIRTUAL NATURAL HISTORY MUSEUMS;
Far From the Madding Crowd, Dinosaurs Await
body: WHEN a Tyrannosaurus rex shows up on your computer screen, your spine doesn't tingle as it does when the giant beast dwarfs you at a museum. On the other hand, when you read on line about how dinosaur eggs were discovered in Patagonia, you are not likely to be bashed in the shin by errant baby strollers. Natural history and paleontology museums are exploring new ways to use the Internet to complement exhibits and enhance science education. The results so far have been promising for curators and visitors. Museum scientists can use the Internet to offer new windows into paleontology. Many museums have vast collections but limited space for displaying their artifacts, and financial restrictions can also limit the size and style of exhibits. The Internet is also a good place to see specimens that are too delicate to display openly and others that are barely visible to the naked eye but are captivating when magnified. Museums are also beginning to experiment with the Internet as an education tool that can attract children and adults who might otherwise feel alienated from science. Science textbooks, even those for college students, provide little insight into the real working life of scientists, but on-line exhibits can easily present such details. Paleontologists realize that many people find dinosaurs fascinating and enjoy fossil hunting. Many museum-based educators are responding to this interest by showing enthusiasts what is involved in paleontology research. Taking advantage of the Internet, they help people learn about the kinds of questions paleontologists ask, the kinds of tools they use to look for answers and the process in which new answers lead to new questions. Exploring a museum Web site does not replace the experience of roaming through the actual galleries, but it can enhance the on-site experience. Previewing a museum Web site before your actual visit can help you identify the displays you want to visit. After your visit, a look at the Web site may give you additional information about the exhibits you saw firsthand. Such Web sites can whet one's appetite for information. Since exploring the paleontology museum Web sites, I've made several trips to the American Museum of Natural History in newyork to gaze at the myriad fossils. I got my first newyork Public Library card in order to explore paleontology more deeply, and I am midway through two terrific books: "Taking Wing: Archaeopteryx and the Evolution of Bird Flight" by Pat Shipman (Simon & Schuster, 1998) and "Wonderful Life: the Burgess Shale and the Nature of History" by Stephen Jay Gould (W. W. Norton & Company, 1989). My virtual explorations of paleontology on the Internet led me to many Web sites, including those described below. Among others, I toured the Royal Tyrrell Museum in Canada (www.tyrrellmuseum.com), where I learned about museum-sponsored digs for the general public. Now I'm saving my money to go on a real fossil hunt. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Reuters)

title:
LIBRARY/VIRTUAL NATURAL HISTORY MUSEUMS;
Museum of Natural History Puts the Desert at Your Doorstep
body: AMERICAN MUSEUM OF NATURAL HISTORY www.amnh.org DEEP within the Gobi Desert, Michael Novacek, a paleontologist, had just completed an on-line interview with his colleagues back home at the American Museum of Natural History in Manhattan. Soon after, he got an email message from a boy in New Delhi asking whether he had found a velociraptor skeleton that day. "Here we were, in one of the world's most deserted places," he said recently. "Suddenly I felt more in communication with the population of the planet than I ever did in my life." Dr. Novacek, senior vice president and provost for science at the American Museum of Natural History and co-leader of the museum's Gobi Expedition, relishes the museum's role in turning cyberspace into an interactive showcase for paleontology. For the past two years, the museum has used the Internet to link the world to its scientists on the Gobi fossil hunt. Paleontologists on the 1998 trip gave interviews that people could hear through live Webcasts and submitted nightly email dispatches, which were immediately posted on the Web site. The results reflected life on a dig. Some days were thrilling, while others were hot, tiring and boring. The thrills came in many forms -- new fossil discoveries as well as torrential hailstorms. A History in the Desert, written by the team's co-leader, Mark A. Norell, accompanies the dispatches. This narrative describes the Gobi locale, which contains the most extensive finds to date on animals from the dinosaur age. Links to other sites point to drawings of fossil animals found on this expedition. The daily Web dispatches from the Gobi expedition are only one creative way in which the museum uses electronic media. Nancy Hechinger, director of the museum's National Center for Science Literacy, Education and Technology, noted that the museum's Internet projects extended, rather than imitated, the features provided at the museum. Another area, Dinosaur Discoveries in Patagonia, on the Web site details another of the museum's famous expeditions. A team leader, Luis M. Chiappe, provides clear narratives about the discovery in 1997 of dinosaur eggs containing embryos, skin and all in Patagonia, a remote part of Argentina. To complement this text, the Web site contains pictures of the fossils embedded in rock. As the viewer moves around the frame, the fossil is highlighted against the rock background. The fossil skull exhibit allows an interactive approach. Here you can compare the skull of a modern human with the skulls of several close primate relatives. Moving the mouse within the frame rotates each pair of skulls left or right, or up or down. A visit to the site's Fossil Halls display reveals another example of effective electronic media. In the Hall of Vertebrate Origins, users learn how scientists constructed the vertebrate family tree. The page features a simple tree, called a cladogram. Take care to let the program download, then move your mouse to the Expedition Guide panel at the left. Click on the Vertebral Column and Braincase, and you get a diagram and text explaining that the backbone and braincase were the first features that distinguished vertebrates from other animals. By bookmarking the Electronic Newspaper address found in the site's Fossil Halls, you can easily return for more paleontology news. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
LIBRARY/VIRTUAL NATURAL HISTORY MUSEUMS;
With Minimalist Approach, Paleontology Is Brought to Life
body: UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA MUSEUM OF PALEONTOLOGY www.ucmp.berkeley.edu THE richness of this on-line museum is not found in state-of-the-art interactive features. The museum team elected to keep dynamic features to a minimum until user-friendly software became available and has begun adding fancier features only recently. Instead, the museum provides text -- sometimes with pictures, and frequently with photographs of exceptional quality -- that tells a lot about paleontologic research. The site, one of the first 50 on the Web, was started in 1993 by some visionary graduate students -- Robert P. Guralnick, P. David Polly and Allen G. Collins -- from the department of integrative biology at the University of California at Berkeley. They recognized early the Internet's potential for showing the outside world the processes and thrills of scientific research. The site now registers about a million hits per week. Readers enter the main hall, Paleontology Without Walls, through one of three interlinked portals: Phylogeny presents the Family Tree of Life, Geologic Time shows who shared the earth with whom during each geologic era, and Evolutionary Thought describes the work of major evolutionary biologists, paleontologists and geologists. Brief essays tell the history that led to Charles Darwin's theory of the origin of species and describe the controversy that followed. The Family Tree of Life lets the reader meander through exhibits of the domains of life, from microscopic bacteria to extinct creatures like the quagga. One important side trip explains cladistics, the technique used for figuring out how organisms, both living and extinct, are related to one another. The site's Special Exhibits include Dinobuzz, which covers current dinosaur research. It answers such questions as, How fast did dinosaurs move? While Hollywood films like "Jurassic Park" may show dinosaurs running at a cheetah's pace, Dinobuzz presents the real evidence. The distance between the fossil imprints of dinosaur feet, along with the absence of tracks from their large tails, help answer the question about dinosaur speed. The evidence suggests that some of these beasts could lope along at 26 miles per hour. The Special Exhibit on Vertebrate Flight shows how scientists develop hypotheses, then look for evidence to support or to refute them. Did the ancestors of birds first fly by gliding from the treetops, or did they run fast along the ground and jump into the air? The current wisdom now favors the ground-up idea rather than the trees-down) hypothesis. As you read on, you learn how scientists study flight in modern birds and look at fossil remains to learn how bird flight evolved. The museum's director, David Lindberg, said the Web site was as much an encyclopedia as a virtual museum. The museum staff is currently designing interactive Internet-based programs for teaching the process of paleontology in middle school and high school. New programs will include both tours and interactive laboratory research modules. Judy Scotchmoor, the museum's education and outreach director, showed me the first research module, which is near completion. It draws on a real field study in Montana that museum researchers are conducting and will let students and their teachers study fossils from the Cretaceous/Tertiary (or K/T) boundary, which marks the end of the dinosaur era. Users will be able to take a virtual journey to the field to collect specimens then return to a Berkeley laboratory to sort and classify them. Using the interactive tools, students will learn how to do things like distinguishing teeth from tiny bone fragments and inspecting the teeth to determine their source. Students will record their findings in on-line journals, then submit hypotheses about the ancient environment they are studying. Each class can send a report to the museum and receive a response from graduate students and faculty researchers. The modules are being created in a novel way by museum scientists and graduate students in collaboration with middle school and high school biology teachers. After seeing the interactive research module, I left with the feeling that these Internet pioneers were exploring exciting territory. They are making the process of paleontology come alive. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Want Your Own Talk Show? You Can Get One, on the Net
body: It only seems as though everyone and her grandmother has a radio talk show. Soon, however, everybody might. The catch is that the shows won't take place on the radio, but on the Net. A Silicon Valley company, TalkNetRadio.com, plans to provide Internet users with the technology to start their own talk shows on any topic under the sun (minus hard-core pornography and hate speech). In other words, users who want a half-hour of air time to pontificate on baking, or chat about the state of dental hygiene, will soon have a format. The talk show hosts will speak into microphones from their home computers. The computer will digitize the sound and send it over the Internet to TalkNetRadio.com in Santa Clara, Calif., which will in turn make it available for listeners to download in real time. Listeners can send their responses to the host via email. TalkNetRadio.com has begun registering aspiring on-line talk show hosts on its Web site. But the service will not begin until late summer or so, said the company's chief, Ted Ganchiff. The service is free, with a big caveat. To keep the company's bandwidth costs low, Mr. Ganchiff said, audiences can be no larger than 30 people, making these radio shows more like teleconferences via the Net. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
An Art Book For Browsing The Internet
body: SOMETIMES you have to stare at a work of art for a while before appreciating it. So it is, too, with "Art Information and the Internet: How to Find It, How to Use It," a recently published book from Oryx Press. Written by Lois Swan Jones, whose 1990 book, "Art Information: Research Methods and Resources" (Kendall-Hunt), is a standard reference for educators, students and museum staff members, the new book is also serious stuff. At first glance, it seems useful only to the same audience of researchers. But take time to look deeper and "Art Information and the Internet" turns into a $45 resource that even casual culture lovers can appreciate. "Art Information and the Internet" is a guide to data on the Internet that you never knew you wanted -- but will enjoy once you find it. Consider the sites under "Museums and Libraries: Medieval and Byzantine Collections," in Chapter 10. The Bodleian Library at Oxford University (www.bodley.ox.ac.uk /welcome.html) lets you enter its Map Case and call up a sampling of early maps: the London Docks of 1831, for example. Pick "Early Manuscripts" and you can view several examples up close. Or you can shop in the Bodleian Arcade, check in on the Bodleian's Broadside Ballads Project, which is building a digitized repertory of 30,000 ballads, or try the Toyota City Imaging Project, which offers images of auto ephemera. Have you ever been puzzled by classical paintings, unable to tell Aphrodite from Demeter or Ares from Hades? "Art Information and the Internet" has a section on mythology (in Chapter 12), and one of the listed sites, Classical Myth, may help (web.uvic.ca/grs/bowman /myth/index.html). Besides a timeline of Greek history, it has images and texts for each Olympian god. Classical Myth's links include the Perseus project (www.perseus .tufts.edu), a digital library of resources for studying the ancient world that includes texts and translations, maps and art images from more than 70 museums. You can also, for example, take a walk around ancient Athens (click on Starting Points, then on Sites and click on any triangle to see a photograph from that vantage). Animals can also be artistic symbols, but the Internet references in this category will not help. The Butterfly Site, at www.mgfx.com /butterfly, is charming, however, with illustrated information on the butterflies of every state and other places, plus links to sites-in-the-making on hummingbirds, birds and dragonflies. The book's Chapter 10, on art historical periods, offers many good sites. In one example, readers are directed to an ancient-art site maintained by the University of Wisconsin's art history department. And if you backtrack to the department's main site (www.wisc.edu/arth) and look under "course materials" for various classes, not just ancient art, you will find Assyrian, Renaissance, French and Asian art images. Better yet is the department's "Find an Image" section, which lets you sample the work of an artist, architect, period or site around the world. And there are other sites covering early civilization to the present. It would be a real aid to find information about contemporary artists on line since they are by definition less known. "Art Information on the Internet" first sends readers to galleries, then suggests Worldwide Books on Line (www.worldwide .com). But you will find little to see here. Go to "Artist Index" and you can browse the names of some 6,000 artists, with not much more than a roster of books or their catalogues. Using the Extended Search option will bring up a description of the book, but no images. Another section of the book, "Pronunciation," in Chapter 11, looked promising, perhaps the key to finding out at last the correct way to say Ingres or Caillebotte. Alas, no; it recommends a CD-ROM. Still, the section does direct readers to a French-English dictionary that works for single words, but not phrases (humanities.uchicago.edu /formsunrest/FR-ENG.html). And so "Art Information on the Internet" goes, reflecting the spottiness of Web sites themselves. The publisher, however, posts updates to the book on its Web site (www .oryxpress.com/artupdate). http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: Aphrodite, Artemis and Apollo on the Classical Myth Web site.

title: Seeking Speed, America Online Joins Forces With Bell Atlantic
body: In a move to compete with high-speed cable-modem services, America Online and Bell Atlantic yesterday announced a joint marketing effort to sell high-speed Internet access to America Online's customers. The alliance marks a significant step in America Online's effort to retain its leadership as a "portal," or entry point, to the Internet in a market increasingly moving toward high-speed Internet access. The cable-modem business currently has only about 500,000 customers nationwide but is expected to more than double this year. That presents a threat to local telephone companies and to portals, which make their money primarily by selling advertising on sites that millions of Internet users pass through daily. Of the top portals -- which include Yahoo, Netcenter and Go -- America Online, with 15 million members, is the largest. The cable modem business is dominated by At Home and Roadrunner, which are portals as well as technologies for accessing the Internet over TV cables. While America Online and other portals can be used over cable modems, they are not users' first stop in cyberspace. At the same time, local phone companies are eager to compete with cable companies by offering asymmetrical digital subscriber line, or A.D.S.L., technology over existing phone lines. A.D.S.L. service does not require customers to dial in, and connection speeds are about 20 times faster than standard modems. "This deal is part of our plan to beat cable modems," said Amy McIntosh, president of consumer data services for Bell Atlantic. America Online said many of its members in Bell Atlantic's East Coast territory would be able to purchase the service this summer for an extra $20 a month, bringing the total cost to $40 a month. That is in line with the $40 a month charged by cable modem services but about $20 less than Bell Atlantic charges for full Internet service over A.D.S.L. America Online members who have cable modems pay $10 a month, about half the fees charged dial-up members. America Online's president, Robert W. Pittman, said: "Some of our customers are interested in speed, and we want to provide it for them in a package that makes sense." Bell Atlantic said that close to 7.5 million customers would be able to get A.D.S.L. by the end of 1999. "Most people who want high-speed Internet are going to look first to their Internet service provider, not the local cable provider or phone company," Andy Fuertes, a senior analyst at Allied Business Intelligence, a research firm, said yesterday. "So having someone like AOL involved who is more savvy about marketing to the consumer is a big plus." America Online shares fell $7.875 to $145.75 yesterday, while Bell Atlantic rose $1.1875, to $54.9375. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
STATE OF THE ART;
Whoosh! The Next Pentium
body: WHEN Nick built his own personal computer from scratch in 1996, it was the fastest machine in our house. He spent his life savings for components, including a motherboard that contained an Intel Pentium 166 microprocessor. He was 13 years old then. Now he is 16 and in high school, with the keys to my car, and he cannot believe he ever thought a Pentium 166 was cool. Actually, it was cool, for about three months, until it was upstaged first by faster versions of the Pentium chip, then by the Pentium with MMX and then by the Pentium II, all of which came in steadily ascending chip speeds. Today, Nick regards his ancient computer as decidedly lame, but marginally useful and occasionally amusing -- sort of like his parents. The only difference, from his perspective, anyway, is that parents start out old and get older, while computers start fresh and new, only to descend into decrepitude at an abnormally accelerated pace. And now it is happening again. The Intel Corporation is about to introduce the Pentium III, a new generation of microprocessor for consumer and business computers. Or, as Intel's marketing folks call it, the Pentium !!!, with exclamation points replacing the Roman numerals of the old Pentium II chip. Or are they three daggers? They must look that way to anyone who bought a new Pentium II computer just in time for the holidays. For now, the chip ought to be called the Pentium ??? because Intel will not divulge its performance specifications until later, probably during Super Bowl commercials. Computer makers already have the Pentium III systems ready to be shipped. They are waiting until Intel's marketing army is ready to try to convince us, once again, that it is time to upgrade our PC's and downgrade our bank accounts. At some point, most PC owners question whether they are suckers for buying into this constant game of rapid obsolescence. The advance of computer technology has always occurred at a dizzying speed, but the experience of computing seems to slog along at the same old pace. We have been promised for years that as computers get more powerful, they will become easier to use and more useful, allowing us to do wonderful new things. For consumers, however, the most wonderful advances in recent years have been the growth of the Internet and its main applications, including the World Wide Web, email and E-commerce. When it comes to the Internet, a faster modem has probably had more impact on our happiness than a faster processor. In fact, some analysts are now suggesting that we are on the cusp of a new, "post PC" era in which simple, relatively inexpensive information appliances, not complex PC's with fire-breathing microprocessors, will win the hearts of consumers. With the Pentium III, however, Intel is once again promising that great things are just around the corner, including better tools for using the Internet, and that people who do not adopt the newest chip will miss out on exciting new computing experiences. Yes, we've heard it all before. But there are technical and economic reasons to be interested in the imminent arrival of the Pentium III's, even if one has no plans to move up to the new chip. On the technical side, there are two principal things that differentiate the Pentium III from the Pentium II. One is speed. Intel is expected to offer two versions of the new chip at first, one operating at 450 megahertz and one at the milestone level of 500 MHz. A version that is 600 MHz or faster is expected by the end of the year. Chip speed alone is not a reliable measure of computer performance, but all other things being equal, standard software applications will run faster on a 500-MHz machine than on a 400-MHz system. The second and more intriguing difference is something called the Katmai New Instructions, a set of some 70 new multimedia instructions that programmers can use to create applications with better audio and graphics. Katmai was the code name for the Pentium III. The last time Intel added new instructions for its major PC microprocessor line was two years ago, when it introduced the Pentium MMX chip. MMX stands for multimedia extensions, and software developers eventually took advantage of the new hooks to develop software with better graphics and sound. Intel's rivals, including Advanced Micro Devices, Cyrix and IDT, came up with their own version, called 3DNow, which greatly improves the performance of 3-D graphics and has been very popular with game designers. According to people who have worked with it, the Pentium III chip with Katmai New Instructions pushes ahead of both MMX and 3DNow. Intel has been working with software developers for more than a year in preparation for the Katmai introduction, so announcements are likely to come from software makers about their support for the new chip in coming weeks. In practical terms, consumers can expect new software that makes richer use of video, sound, speech and 3-D graphics. Games will get more realistic, with almost fluid motion, better video playback, better sound quality and superior 3-D graphics. But there will also be improvements in streaming video and audio over the Internet, speech recognition as a user interface, video email, DVD-based entertainment, video and sound editing, and other multimedia applications that developers are keeping secret for now. Such enticements typically make people reach for their wallets. Some do so warily because they know that to take full advantage of a Pentium III machine, they will have to buy new software. Others do so enthusiastically because they want to be the first one on the block to have the new technology. Intel will probably reserve the Katmai instruction set exclusively for its Pentium III chips for the next year, at least, before extending it to the rest of the Intel product line. That will create a clear difference between the high-end Pentium III and the low-end Celeron chips. With the introduction last week of 366-MHz and 400-MHz versions of the Celeron, the performance gap between the cheaper Celersons and the Pentium II's is quite narror. Intel officials would not disclose the pricing for its Pentium III chips, and they are prohibiting PC makers from talking about system prices before the Pentium III is formally launched, which might not occur until late February. But analysts say Intel plans to be aggressive in keeping Pentium III prices low because of increasing pressure from companies like AMD. AMD, meanwhile, is preparing to announce in a few weeks its K6-3 Sharptooth microprocessor, which it will promote as a challenger to the Pentium III. And later this year, AMD is scheduled to unveil the K-7, a powerful and fast chip that AMD asserts will finally let the company break free from its usual place a speed bump or two behind Intel. Details of all these future chips are unknown, but one thing is certain. "There is going to be a price war," said Keith Diefendorff, editor in chief of The Microprocessor Report, a newsletter published in Sunnyvale, Calif. "Intel's latest announcements have some pretty impressive prices on the low end, much lower than what they have done before. They are growing tired of AMD taking market share and they are going to put up a fight. That's going to cause AMD to cut their prices. It's great news for consumers." People who just want to do word processing, email and basic Internet browsing will almost certainly be able to buy a very capable low-end machine, with more power for less money. The cost of Pentium II-based machines will come down as the chip is phased out. Cautious PC owners can relax and wait to see whether the new applications written specifically for the Pentium III are really worth the cost of upgrading. And fanatic game players, who perpetually lust after the fastest machine on the block, will soon have a choice of several new high-end machines. The hard part for Nick will be deciding whether to spend his money on petroleum or silicon. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: Anti-Abortion Site On Web Has Ignited Free Speech Debate
body: "The Nuremberg Files: Visualize Abortionists on Trial," proclaims the site on the World Wide Web. With simulated blood dripping from fetus parts, the site leads a cyber-visitor to the "main archive," listing the names of dozens of doctors and clinic workers around the country who provide abortions. For some of the people the site calls "baby butchers," the information includes photographs, home addresses, license plate numbers, the names of their spouses and children. A few doctors, including Barnett A. Slepian of Amherst, N.Y., near Buffalo, who was fatally shot by a sniper last fall, have a line through their names, denoting that they have been killed; those who have been wounded have their names listed in gray. For a Federal court jury here, hearing a civil case brought by Planned Parenthood and several doctors against some of the most militant abortion opponents in the country, the trial will boil down to this question: is the Web site constitutionally protected free speech? The plaintiffs, who are seeking up to $200 million in damages, have brought their case under the 1994 Federal Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act, which makes it illegal to use "force or threat of force" against anyone seeking or providing an abortion, and allows clinics to seek unlimited damages if workers are harmed or intimidated. But as simple as the question before the jury sounds, the legal issues are not. For one thing, this is the first major case brought under the law that does not involve direct personal threats or an actual physical confrontation. While the plaintiffs say the Web site amounts to a solicitation of murder, the defendants contend that it is a legal informational tool. The Web site, which is named for the German city in which Nazis were put on trial after World War II, explains: "A coalition of concerned citizens throughout the U.S.A. is cooperating in collecting dossiers on abortionists in anticipation that one day we may be able to hold them on trial for crimes against humanity. We anticipate the day when these people will be charged in perfectly legal courts once the tide of this nation's opinion turns against the wanton slaughter of God's children." But abortion is legal. And in the climate surrounding the issue -- the National Abortion Federation says there have been 7 killings, 15 attempted murders, 99 acid attacks, 154 arson incidents and 39 bombings involving abortion clinics or workers in the last two decades -- the plaintiffs here say that radical anti-abortion groups are clearly using devices like the Web site to incite more violence and deny women access to abortion services. "Just like bounty hunters of the Old West, the defendants want to stop the doctors by any means -- dead in their tracks," Maria Vullo, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, told jurors. "It's terrorism." In testimony here on Monday, Dr. Warren Hern, of Boulder, Colo., said his life had been turned into a nightmare by the protesters, who have also put his face on their "Deadly Dozen" flier, which looks like a wanted poster and says he and other doctors are "Guilty of Crimes Against Humanity." "It has made me feel a great sense of personal isolation," Dr. Hern told the jurors, explaining that he now wears a bulletproof vest, covers his windows, always sits with his back toward the wall and is leery of any contact with strangers. But the roster of 14 defendants, which includes the American Coalition of Life Advocates, an umbrella group that has been described as too extreme by more mainstream anti-abortion groups, say most of the information they provide could be found in telephone directories. Furthermore, they say, nothing in the "Nuremberg Files" advocates violence against the doctors or clinic workers, although the site does include links to other Web pages that defend killing abortion workers as legally justifiable homicide, and to a letter from prison from Paul J. Hill, who murdered a doctor in Pensacola, Fla., in 1994. In it, he describes "the joy I felt after shooting the abortionist, and still feel today." In opening arguments last week, Chris Ferrara, a lawyer for the defendants, said the case was baseless. "This is a case about the threat to kill or injure, which is simply not there," he said. "Opinions? Yes, sometimes harsh. But no violence." Judge Robert E. Jones of Federal District Court, has turned down requests from the defendants to dismiss the case outright, in effect ruling that the Web site was not automatically protected free speech. In some ways, Judge Jones seems to have signaled that the plaintiffs may have a valid case. Quoting an appeals court ruling in another case, Judge Jones wrote that "alleged threats should be considered in light of their entire factual context, including the surrounding events and the reaction of the listeners." Jonathan Entin, a law professor at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, said the case posed a difficult question of where to draw the line between protected free speech and illegal threats. The basic standard set by the Supreme Court is that speech is protected unless it is directed toward and likely to produce "imminent lawless action," he said. "The problem for the plaintiffs is, the Web site does not explicitly say, it is your moral duty to go out and kill these people or maim them or harm their family," Professor Entin said. "On the other hand, in the context in which this case is being litigated, we know there are people who are out there who are willing to go out and kill people who perform abortions. So the question is, to what extent will people take seriously the implicit message on this Web site, which is clearly that all right-thinking people should use whatever means necessary to stop people from performing abortions?" Other experts said that if the Web site specifically advocated murder, it would almost certainly be found to be illegal, and, conversely, if it did not list doctors' names and addresses, it would almost certainly be considered protected speech. But the question before the jury, where in the middle does it belong? "The issues in this case are very tricky," said David J. Fidanque, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union of Oregon, which has filed a friend-of-the-court brief, arguing that the jury must focus not only on the fear the list may have spurred in the doctors, but also on the intent of the abortion opponents who contributed to it. Though the case happens to represent one of the first major jury trials regarding free speech and threats on the Internet, several legal experts agreed that the core issue would be the same if the abortion opponents had published the list of doctors in a newspaper or flier. The plaintiffs want an injunction from Judge Jones that could essentially force the abortion opponents to cease circulating the files. Among the named defendants are Michael Bray, a minister and author of a book called "A Time to Kill," which argues that killings of abortion doctors can be justifiable, and C. Roy McMillan, director of an anti-abortion group in Mississippi who has said that "it wouldn't bother me if every abortionist in the country today fell dead from a bullet." In testimony this afternoon, another defendant, Andrew Burnett, publisher of Life Advocate Magazine of Portland, defended publishing the names and addresses of doctors on the Web site with the address www.christiangallery.com/atrocity. He said his own address had been published numerous times in The Oregonian, the daily newspaper in Portland, after he was arrested in abortion protests. It was a jarring experience, Mr. Burnett said, but one that made him realize how committed he was to his cause. Of the lists, he said: "It's a legitimate way to have people reconsider what they do for a living." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: A page from an anti-abortion Web site, which, with its list of names and addresses of abortion providers, is at the heart of a lawsuit. title:
Editorial Observer;
What Will the Internet Economy Look Like?
body: The Internet is the wonder of the era, the tool that is expected to change everything. On Wall Street, Internet stocks are superstars. Amazon.com, the bookseller, now trades for more than 50 times the price at which it went public in 1997. Ebay, an auction house, is valued at 13 times what investors paid four months ago. These prices reflect huge amounts of money. Amazon.com is valued at around $26 billion, about the same as CBS and nearly three times as much as Federated Department Stores, the largest department store chain. Yahoo, the Internet search engine that went public almost three years ago, is valued at about $39 billion, nearly 100 times its valuation when it went public and more than Boeing or Anheuser-Busch. There are two possible explanations for those valuations. The market might be telling us that economic activity will soon come to be dominated by the Internet. Or the market moves could be evidence of speculation gone wild, of a great bubble that will inevitably burst. Those two explanations are not mutually exclusive. The Internet could be all that its fans expect, and some stocks could still be ridiculously overvalued. But what would the 21st-century economy look like if only the first explanation proves accurate? Retail activity would increasingly be dominated by Internet sales, to an extent hard to imagine. Federal Express would be an immediate beneficiary, assuming that Star Trek technology -- "Beam me up, Scotty" -- will not be perfected for packages. But while its stock did well last year, FedEx has slipped a bit this year, even as Internet stocks have zoomed. While Amazon.com fell 12 percent yesterday, it is up 53 percent for 1999. Deflation would be likely in the new Internet economy. It is much easier to compare prices on the Internet, a fact that will tend to force prices -- and profit margins -- down on items that are easily comparable. One of the wonders of the performance of Amazon.com is that it specializes in just such products. A book from one store is no different than a book from another. To be sure, service will also count. Getting a great price on something that does not get delivered for months is hardly a bargain. Brand-name images of quality could, if anything, become more important in a world where shoppers cannot examine the item before buying. Some stores no doubt will continue to prosper. Lettuce does not age well, so food stores are an obvious candidate. For clothes, where fit is important, many will prefer to shop where they can try on before buying. No one will want to wait for mail delivery of a new car battery. But over all the demand for stores would fall, creating a glut of retail space and falling rents as Internet sales represent transactions not made in stores. So far, the stock market does not seem to have anticipated that. While companies that own shopping malls have seen their stock prices slip a bit, the falls have been nowhere near the magnitude that would be expected in the Internet economy. Nor has the market anticipated the economic dislocations that would come along with such a huge change. A recession could easily result just from the upheavals created by failing retailers and plunging commercial real estate values. To say the least, the overall level of stock prices now does not reflect a recession risk. The most likely outcome is that the Internet will grow to be a much larger economic force than it now is, but that the stocks of Internet companies will nonetheless prove to be horrid investments for those who buy at current prices. Those who are buying do not really expect such an economy. They are just betting that this mania will not end soon. There is a precedent. In the 1920's, the great speculative stock was Radio Corporation of America, which took six years to rise 100-fold, twice the time Yahoo required. As the bulls forecast, R.C.A. became a dominant player in an industry that revolutionized American life. But those who bought the stock in 1929 still lost nearly all the money they invested. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Report Issued Early Shows Rise in ProducerPrices
body: Prices paid to producers rose four-tenths of 1 percent last month after a record surge in cigarette prices more than offset declines in energy and food costs, the Labor Department said in a report that was posted by mistake on the Internet today, a day early. For all of 1998, the Producer Price Index fell one-tenth of 1 percent; in 1997, the index declined 1.2 percent. This is the first instance since the Government began compiling the data in 1947 that the index has fallen for two consecutive years. Wholesale cigarette prices rose 30.7 percent last month as tobacco companies began passing on the cost of a $206 billion settlement reached with 46 states to cover health care claims. Without those increases, the December index would have fallen four-tenths of a percent. The index's core rate, which excludes food and energy costs, rose 1 percent in December. Producer energy prices fell 2.3 percent, and food prices dropped one-tenth of 1 percent. Without the cigarette price increase, the core rate would have fallen one-tenth of 1 percent. The premature release of the report was the second such recent episode. The Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Nov. 6 that it was reviewing its procedures after some of the October employment figures were accidentally posted on the Internet. Scott Sager, a spokesman for the bureau, said today's report was posted on the department Web site about 2 P.M. because of a computer error. He said the department deleted the information within an hour but later decided to release the data because some people had seen the posting. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Rare for an Internet company, Yahoo reports actual earnings. Not that such things matter.
body: YAHOO INC., a bellwether Internet stock, released earnings yesterday confirming that it had surpassed Wall Street's financial expectations. But does it matter? The recent surge in share prices for Internet companies has analysts wondering whether financial performance is irrelevant for many of the small investors jumping in. "I don't know how people are getting to these valuations," said Paul Noglows, an analyst at Hambrecht & Quist in San Francisco. "What's going on has nothing to do with fundamentals, good or bad." Mr. Noglows considers Yahoo -- a gateway for Web surfers for information, electronic mail, shopping and other Internet services -- one of the stars of his sector. He likes its strategy and management. In normal times, an announcement like yesterday's might lead him to urge investors to buy more shares. Yahoo, based in Santa Clara, Calif., said that earnings in the last quarter of 1998 jumped to $25.04 million, or 21 cents a diluted share, excluding one-time charges -- more than 10 times the $1.91 million, or 2 cents a share, a year earlier, and well ahead of the 16 cents analysts surveyed by the First Call Corporation had estimated. Yahoo's revenues topped $76.4 million, nearly triple the level of a year ago and 40 percent ahead of the third quarter. In addition, the company said it would split its stock 2 for 1. Yahoo also said that its number of registered users had grown to 35 million from 20 million a year earlier; the number of its advertisers rose to 2,225 from 1,700 a year ago, Yahoo said, and those advertisers were spending more and signing longer contracts. But Mr. Noglows is one of six analysts -- about a quarter of those following Yahoo -- who rate the stock as a hold rather than a buy because these are anything but normal times for the Internet companies that trade publicly. Small investors, mesmerized by the rapid growth of Internet use and commerce, have sent shares in a wide range of Internet stocks rocketing to previously unimaginable heights in recent weeks. Yahoo's shares rose more than $72, or 21 percent, on Monday alone. Much of the fuel for the growth appears to come from small investors who trade rapidly, not the kind of long-term buyer willing to wait years for Yahoo or other Internet pioneers to deliver the huge profits implicit in today's valuations. Yahoo is on more solid ground than most Internet start-ups. It has never underperformed analyst expectations in the three years since it went public -- something few other Internet companies, most of which have yet to earn a dime, can say. But can it really be worth more than the Boeing Company, the world's largest aerospace company, or more than twice the value of Caterpillar, the multinational heavy-equipment maker, as current market capitalizations suggest? Yesterday, short-term traders paused to look at what they had wrought; many headed, at least temporarily, for the exits. Yahoo's shares fell $13.375, to $402, in Nasdaq trading, then, despite the strong earnings, dropped another $8, to $394, in after-hours trading. Other Internet stocks fell even more sharply. Amazon.com, the Internet bookseller, fell $21.25 a share, to $163.375. Lycos, the second-most- popular Internet search company after Yahoo, tumbled $26.50, to $104.50. The Netscape Communications Corporation, the Internet browser pioneer, fell $4.4375, to $64.50. With such volatility, some analysts who continue to favor buying Internet companies say that growth themes and performance trends are more important than price targets. "We've given up establishing price targets," said Daniel King at LaSalle Street Securities in Chicago. He rated Yahoo a long-term buy but said he would hesitate to pay current prices. Yesterday's earnings were notable, he said, because the 36 percent operating margins and tight rein on selling and administrative costs provide further evidence that Yahoo's management is keeping a close eye on its operations as well as its longterm vision. The company ambitiously markets itself as "the only place anyone would have to go to find or get connected to anybody." Mr. King also noted that Yahoo was well positioned to grow through acquisitions, with $482 million in cash, and that highly valued stock. Yahoo is for "conservative Internet investors," he said, because it leads its segment, like Amazon in electronic commerce. Still, he conceded, it might be a stretch to suggest that at these prices there is such a thing as a conservative Internet investor.  http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
SharePrices Slump on Profit Taking and Woes Overseas
body: Stocks moved sharply lower in heavy trading yesterday as continued instability in key foreign economies provided a helpful backdrop for traders and investors looking to take profits on issues that have shot higher since the start of the year. Given the steep, almost frenzied leaps in prices, particularly in technology stocks, analysts have been expecting a pullback, if not a full-fledged correction. "Considering how far we have run in the last two weeks, the market needed a little rest," said Ned Riley Jr., chief investment officer at BankBoston. "I am sort of surprised this downdraft was as contained as it has been." The session's steepest selloff was in Nasdaq stocks -- the securities that have run up the fastest. The Nasdaq composite index, which was up 9 percent for the year through Monday, suffered its eighth-worst point decline ever, falling 63.84 points, or 2.7 percent, to 2,320.75. But other important market measures also suffered. The Dow Jones industrial average dropped 145.21 points, or 1.5 percent, to 9,474.68. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index fell 24.37 points, or 1.9 percent, to 1,239.51. The Russell 2000 index of smaller-company stocks lost 5.77 points, or 1.3 percent, to 427.36. And Thestreet.com Internet index, a popular measure of Internet stocks, tumbled 46.12 points, or 7.8 percent, to 542.07. The index had tripled in the last three months. Volume on the newyork Stock Exchange was 800.2 million shares, down from 818.4 million on Monday. But more than 1.1 billion shares changed hands on the Nasdaq market. It was the fifth consecutive session in which volume exceeded a billion shares on Nasdaq. "Given the frothiness we have seen recently, a 5 percent correction might not be a bad thing," said one block trader, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Foreign markets also lost ground. Fears of a potential default in Brazil pushed down prices on the Sao Paulo exchange by more than 7.6 percent. Mexico's Bolsa index dropped 3.7 percent. In Europe, market indexes on all major exchanges moved lower. All but five of the 30 stocks that make up the Dow fell yesterday. The Dow was led lower by I.B.M., which fell 4 3/16 , to 185 1/16 . Nervousness about Brazil hurt financial stocks like American Express, down 3 7/8, to 102 3/8, and J. P. Morgan, which fell 2 5/8, to 111 13/16 . But the session's most spectacular declines were recorded by Internet stocks. Many of these stocks have seen their prices double in a matter of weeks. For a day at least, that trend was reversed. Ebay, which was offered to the public in September at $18 a share, fell 51 yesterday, to 240 1/2. Broadcast.com slumped 62 1/16 , to 223. Amazon.com fell 21 1/4, to 163 3/8. And Yahoo lost 13 3/8, to 402. But not all Internet stocks suffered. E*Trade jumped 12 7/16 , to 100 15/16 , after it said it planned to form an investment bank that would help companies raise capital by selling securities to investors over the Internet.  Big Gain for Bond Market (By Bloomberg News) -- The bond market posted its biggest gain since November yesterday as the highest yields in two months, a stronger dollar, and stock declines in the unitedstates and Brazil made Treasuries more attractive. The rally snapped a three-day slide, sending the 30-year bond up 1 16/32 , to 100 22/32 . Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, fell to 5.20 percent from 5.30 percent. Signs of economic strength drew investors to corporate bonds, meanwhile, because a strong economy makes people more optimistic about corporate earnings. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company, the biggest unitedstates investment bank, sold $2 billion in global bonds, doubling the size because of investor demand. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average, since January 1998.
