title: Internet Issues Continue to Rise As Investor Interest Stays High
body: On a day when investors seemed cool toward other stocks, they continued their love affair with shares of Internet companies. The stock prices of several companies surged, led by Broadcast.com, Yahoo, Shopping.com and America Online, helping the Nasdaq composite index set another closing high. "There are too many people who want to own these stocks and not enough to go around," Paul Cook, portfolio manager of the Munder Net Net Fund, which manages $400 million, said. Shares of companies that do business over the Internet have soared for the last month on investor enthusiasm for surging on-line sales; the number of people using the World Wide Web is expected to rise 28 percent, to 147 million this year, according to the International Data Corporation. Broadcast.com, an on-line broadcaster of sports, news and music, said it would split its stock 2 for 1, which sent its shares up $87.5625, or 44.3 percent, to $285.0625. The split would double the number of shares to 33.2 million. Yahoo, the No. 1 Internet directory, rocketed to a new closing high on investor optimism that the company will be a dominant leader in the Internet industry. The company, which will report its fourth-quarter earnings today after the close of trading, rose $71.75 a share, to $415.375, after earlier touching a high of $445. Shares of Shopping.com jumped $5.40625, to $18.59375, after the Compaq Computer Corporation agreed to buy the company, an on-line retailer, for $220 million to move into electronic commerce. Compaq, the world's second-largest computer company, rose $3, to $48.375. America Online, the leading on-line service, set a closing high, rising $18.625 a share, to $165.125. Lycos, the No. 3 Internet directory, rose $39.25, to $131. Amazon.com, the No. 1 on-line bookseller, rose $24.375, to $184.625, in trading of nearly 19.5 million. Shares of the company have increased 72 percent since the start of the year and have soared about twentyfold in the last 12 months. Cnet Inc., an Internet news company, rose $11.875 a share, to $74.25, while the on-line service Mindspring Enterprises soared $22.625, to $115.75. Excite Inc., the No. 2 Internet directory, rose $21, to $81.  http://www.nytimes.com

title: Amazon Surge May Reflect The New Math Of the Internet
body: For Amazon.com, the best seller that really mattered last week was not a book title, but the company's stock. Whether it was simply more Internet frenzy, or a further sign that on-line commerce may require its own investment calculus, the company's shares had a remarkable run last week. Amazon.com, an Internet bookseller which has yet to report a profitable quarter since going public in May 1997, saw its share price soar by nearly 50 percent in the first trading week of the new year. Since the beginning of December, the stock price has climbed about 150 percent. Some of last week's run-up came in response to news -- a stock split, word of robust holiday sales of the company's books and compact disks, and a deal to acquire a new warehouse. But mainly, optimistic investors seemed willing to buy Amazon.com shares at any price. At one point on Friday, Amazon.com's total stock market value surged past $30 billion, making it worth more than a major industrial company like Texaco Inc. And even after some investors had second thoughts, and the stock retreated sharply from its high point, Amazon.com, with a market value of $25.4 billion, was still worth more than the combined value of two leading retailers, J. C. Penney and Kmart. Shares of Amazon.com closed on Friday at $160.25, up just $1.375 for the day, after trading as high as $199.125 earlier in the session. Some analysts say this unrestrained enthusiasm despite the company's lack of profit may reflect investors' appreciation for Amazon.com's sales momentum and the value of its dominant position as the leading electronic bookseller. Moreover, it comes as many investors seem to be finding the shares of a variety of Internet companies irresistible. On Friday, for example, Broadcast.com Inc., which provides video and audio programs on the Internet, saw its shares soar $65.50, or 49.6 percent, to close at $197.50, after trading as high as $230. In the absence of news that would justify such a surge, Nasdaq officials asked the company to offer an explanation, but Broadcast.com declined to provide one. In such a context, some Internet bears see more greed than logic in the meteoric rise of Amazon.com. "How can you explain this behavior?" said Rick Berry, an analyst in Atlanta with J. P. Turner & Company, who is advising investors to sell Amazon.com's stock. "It is avarice in its most pure form. It's the greater fool theory, which is that someone buys stock in the hope that someone is going to come from behind and buy it for even more." Such concerns may be expressed in a meeting expected today in newyork, where officials of the National Association of Securities Dealers are to meet with securities industry executives to discuss the recent volatility of many Nasdaq stocks. Mr. Berry predicted that last week's market surge in Amazon would probably represent a buying climax, and he said he expected the stock to start falling 30 to 50 percent in the first quarter. But other analysts see an underlying logic, even if it does not conform to conventional investing theory. Amazon.com's stock began booming in the first week of 1999 trading as investors anticipated the 3-for-1 stock split last Tuesday. That same day, the Seattle-based company announced that its fourth-quarter sales had quadrupled, to $250 million. The company's electronic store drew more than a million new customers in the peak holiday season when it started expanding its product lines to include stuffed toys and personal electronics. That expansion impresses Derek Brown, a senior analyst with Volpe Brown Whelan in San Francisco, who said investors were speculating on the prospects for the company's movement into the future. "Amazon sale's have gone from nowhere to $250 million," said Mr. Brown, who noted that their fourth-quarter sales exceeded his expectations by 30 to 40 percent. "They're on a run rate for a billion dollars a year. That revenue used to be going to traditional booksellers. I think Amazon is taking market share and expanding the market, and the question is who are they taking market share from?" The third-place Internet bookseller, the Borders Group, has suffered from the view that the bookstore chain has not invested aggressively enough in the Internet. Its new chief executive, Philip M. Pfeffer, said in late December that the company needed to start doing more to promote its activities on the Internet even as it continued a rapid international expansion of superstores. Last week, Borders said its on-line commerce effort is projected to post a loss of 12 to 14 cents for the year. Barnes & Noble has seen its own electronic store remain lodged in the No. 2 spot and is also losing money. But the rich German media conglomerate Bertelsmann A.G. is its new partner in the venture, and Bertelsmann's new chief executive, Thomas Middelhoff, predicts that barnesandnoble.com will overtake Amazon sometime next year. Last week, Barnes & Noble announced that its on-line sales in the critical seven-week holiday period ending Jan. 2 rose to $17.8 million, nearly quadrupling 1997 sales in the similar period. But can the more traditional booksellers beat the upstart Amazon.com in the publicity wars? "I think one of the biggest reasons behind Amazon's success is the fact that they do have brand momentum -- Amazon gets a tremendous amount of free publicity," Mr. Brown said. "Investors could lose interest in them, but right now they are the dominant E-commerce player and there is little to suggest that they won't be dominant in the future." Certainly last week, there seemed to be no limit to investor enthusiasm for the future of Amazon.com. As of yesterday afternoon, even its No. 3 and No. 5 best sellers seemed particularly apt: "The Motley Fool's Rule Breakers, Rule Makers: A Foolish Guide to Picking Stocks" and "How to Get Started in Electronic Day Trading: Everything You Need to Know to Win in Wall Street's Hottest Game." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
Compressed Data;
Executive Musical Chairs At Shopping.com, Again
body: It sounded drastic -- the third management team in nine months. But for Shopping.com, an Internet retailing company, it was more like business as usual. The company said last week that Randall R. Read, an executive from the packaging industry, would replace Shopping.com's chairman, Frank Denny, who is becoming president and chief executive. Mr. Denny, in turn, was replacing John Markley. According to Mr. Denny, Mr. Markley resigned to spend more time in the family cabinet business. Mr. Markley had arrived in June to replace Robert McNulty, who was president and chief executive before leaving for undisclosed reasons. In this latest shuffle, Mr. Denny, Shopping.com's founder, will take over day-to-day operations. Shopping.com, which sells housewares, sporting goods, computer supplies, electronic gadgets and more, was initially backed by Bill Gross, the financier who has "incubated" dozens of Internet businesses through his company Idealab. Catching the wave of investor enthusiasm for electronic commerce, Shopping.com's initial public offering in November 1997 was an instant success, starting at $9 a share and soon trading as high as $39. But things soured. The Securities and Exchange Commission suspended trading of Shopping.com shares for two weeks in March, though trading resumed after the S.E.C. found no wrongdoing by executives of Shopping.com. But in September, an arbitration panel of the National Association of Securities Dealers fined the company's underwriter, Waldron & Company, on the grounds that it had inflated Shopping.com's stock price. The company, based in Corona Del Mar, Calif., has had trouble filling customer orders, and dozens of customers have filed complaints with numerous consumer protection agencies. Mr. Denny attributes these problems to an overly ambitious marketing campaign that generated more sales than the company could handle. It grew from $40,000 in daily sales in June to $300,000 a day by October. After scaling back, the company now does about $100,000 in sales a day. Shopping.com's shares, having dipped below $1 each last September, closed Friday at $13.1875, up 68.75 cents. Mr. Denny said the company was now intent on rebuilding its daily sales volume, though more gradually than before. "We're trying to build a power center on the Web, a sort of CompUSA, Home Depot and Wal-Mart," Mr. Denny said. But first, given the recent upheavals, he may be busy building a power center in the executive suite.   LAURIE J. FLYNN http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY: Prospectus;
New York'sunsung captains of code would like to remind the world that not all software comes from California.
body: BRUCE BERNSTEIN is a frustrated man. The proprietor of Main Street Partners, a data base application developer based in newyork, he is also a tireless promoter of the city's software developers as president of the newyork Software Industry Association. What frustrates Mr. Bernstein is that newyork's software industry is almost entirely overlooked except when it is related to new media, the industry that has grown up around the Internet. The problem with fusing the identities of the two industries, he says, is that excitement over the evolution of the Internet into a mass medium eclipses his industry and undermines its value. In short, newyork City is known for its content, not its code. "If the software industry is lumped into new media, it hurts," Mr. Bernstein said. "It hurts when people want to make investments here or locate their company here. It hurts when the best programmers don't want to come here." In fact, newyork City, unlike Silicon Valley or Boston's Route 128, is not recognized as a center for software development. It is not the first place venture capitalists look to invest in technology or programmers look for jobs. Citing perhaps the most obvious flaw in the common perception, Mr. Bernstein said, "People forget that newyork City was the home of I.B.M." Bob Fish, a partner in the newyork City office of the venture capital arm of PricewaterhouseCoopers, agrees that the popular perception is a problem. "Traditionally, venture capitalists have invested in proprietary technology, something which will have an ongoing life," he said. "They need to know that the software industry is here and thriving." In newyork, Mr. Fish said, "the software industry has played second fiddle to the hype of new media." But software development, he added, is a true technology industry, "while new media falls more along the lines of entertainment and publishing." Yet, part of the identity problem is that the edges of the two industries blur on the Internet. "Software may not be the best term now for our industry, with all the issues of convergence," Mr. Bernstein said. "We like to think of it as software and information technology." Mr. Bernstein also contends that many new-media companies are really software developers in disguise. For example, in his mind, Doubleclick, an on-line advertising agency that places clients' banners across the Internet and is one of the most successful companies in Silicon Alley, is a software developer. "The engine of its success is software technology," he said. The confusion is understandable. Historically, software came in a box and was purchased at computer stores. It was easy to recognize. "Packaged software is not delivered in a package anymore," Mr. Bernstein said. "It's delivered over the Internet." Or it may be software developed for use on the Internet. Comet Systems, for instance, has developed a software tool for creating customized cursors at Web sites. While a user is visiting a Disney site, the cursor might be mouse ears, while at the N.F.L. site it might be a football. Software? New media? New-media software? According to the association's definition, software companies fall into four categories, divided by product or service: packaged software, custom software, systems integrators or information-technology management consulting. In addition, the association recognizes in-house software groups, academic computer science centers and freelance programmers. "Essentially, if a primary part of a company's revenue comes from writing code, we consider it a software company," Mr. Bernstein said. "Of course, the Holy Grail is to design your own package." The city's software industry has had very little in the way of hard numbers to promote itself. And despite Mr. Fish's concerns, even PricewaterhouseCoopers's own research categorizes software and new media together. When Coopers & Lybrand, now merged into PricewaterhouseCoopers, published its much-cited survey of new-media companies in newyork City in the fall of 1996, it did not distinguish software companies from more media-oriented companies. And at the Web site of the PricewaterhouseCoopers venture capital survey, figures on financing for Internet companies and software companies are listed together. A quick glance at the survey's findings for the last three years, however, shows that nearly half the companies in the newyork metropolitan area that won financing were software developers. The association will soon have a better set of numbers to fall back on. The newyork City Comptroller's office is nearing the end of a study on the software industry, and its report will be released Jan. 21 at the newyork Software Summit and East Coast Summit for Java Technology at the Fashion Institute of Technology. The newyork City Comptroller, Alan G. Hevesi, will present it when he delivers the event's keynote address. "It is important to have good data," David Neustadt, a spokesman for Mr. Hevesi's office, said. "If you want to help an industry, you have to know what they have and what they need. We want to help get people to take the industry more seriously." In a city that brims with industrial variety and that is the world center of several businesses, including broadcasting, finance, publishing and fashion, Mr. Bernstein's battle for identity may be a tough one, and it may be that the software industry will never attract the recognition and influence it deserves. But it will probably be distinguishable from new media in one major way for a long time to come. "Most of the software companies are financing themselves out of revenue," Mr. Bernstein said. "They make money." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title: WB Succeeds By Serving Youth Alone
body: Along with much of the audience and most of the profit, the confidence bordering on arrogance that once characterized the network television business has faded away this season. But it is alive and well in at least one place, TV's youngest, hippest and increasingly only upwardly mobile address: the upstart would-be network known as WB. Pointing to figures that make WB the only broadcast network to demonstrate ratings growth this season, company executives consider themselves already securely established as a legitimate fifth network, on track to turning a profit within two years, and in position to assume complete leadership among the youngest segment of adult TV viewers within five years. And maybe, the two top WB executives said, the network might just even start scheduling more shows from Warner Brothers, the studio owned by its parent company, Time Warner -- if only the studio starts making shows good enough and hip enough to squeeze their way onto the roster that now includes such youth-oriented hits as "Buffy, the Vampire Slayer," "Dawson's Creek" and "Seventh Heaven." "Warner Brothers just has to do a better job" developing shows with the youthful skew that WB requires, said Jamie Kellner, the chief executive of WB. Mr. Kellner and Susanne Daniels, the new president of WB's entertainment division, spoke at a session of the Television Critics' Association meeting here last week and in separate interviews later. For WB, "broadcasting" is increasingly a misnomer because the network is unflinchingly dedicated to never becoming too broad for its own good. The model, as Mr. Kellner put it, is not what NBC has been for the last five years, the dominant network with a wide range of viewers, nor even what Fox would like to become, the leader with the large adult group of viewers up to the age of 49. Radio is attractive as the new model, Mr. Kellner said, because radio companies have done increasingly well on Wall Street despite being highly fragmented and controlling extremely small slices of audience. That looks to be the future of television networks as well, he said, adding, "If it's going to be a fragmented marketplace, make sure the one you're hanging onto is the most valuable one in terms of advertisers." As WB sees it, what advertisers want is youth, more youth and nothing but the youth, and the network is searingly focused on giving them exactly that. Far from looking to expand its reach, to compete for wider segments of viewers, Mr. Kellner said, WB would stick to its youth orientation. "Our goal is to remain with a median age under 30 years of age," he said. "That is the long-term, set-in-stone goal for this network." But at least one other goal when the network was established four years ago by the Warner television studio was that it would serve as the fallback distribution outlet for the programs the studio makes. Warner Brothers was concerned about the increasing effort by the networks that carried its programs, mostly NBC, owned by the General Electric Company, and ABC, a unit of the Walt Disney Company, to fill their schedules with shows they themselves owned. Subsequent schedules from those networks have begun to validate those concerns. Mr. Kellner conceded that "vertical integration is going to happen in television," with networks relying more on shows delivered by the studios with which they are aligned. Does that mean Warner Brothers will soon be restricted to producing shows exclusively filled with characters in their teens and early 20's? Barry M. Meyer, the executive vice president of Warner Brothers, said he did not think so, because he could not envision a time when a network would be totally vertically integrated, locking out shows from any other studio. He conceded that the "landscape has changed a bit," with networks like NBC trying to compel studios to cede ownership to them on every show scheduled. "But we are still producing older shows for CBS and a lot of shows for NBC," Mr. Meyer said. "If there is a major shift in the policies at these networks, then the whole industry is going to have to be re-evaluated." In the meantime, Warner Brothers is more than happy with the success being built by WB, Mr. Meyer said. "How could we not be pleased?" he asked. "I don't think it's too strong a statement that the WB is redefining the business in a way, both in its economic model and the way they have niched themselves." Still, for the moment at least, WB is hardly a conduit for Warner Brothers programs; only a few of its shows, and none of its high-profile hits, are provided by the Warner studio. Instead, WB's schedule is dotted with shows supplied by the Warner Brothers studio's main rivals, like Fox ("Buffy"), Disney ("Felicity"), Sony's Columbia unit ("Dawson's Creek") and Aaron Spelling's Spelling Entertainment Group("Seventh Heaven"). The WB connection has proved to be a windfall for these studios because in recent years shows on WB have sold re-run rights in syndication for very high prices. Ms. Daniels noted that after its first year, "Buffy" sold to the FX network for more than $1 million an episode. Mr. Kellner said WB was under no obligation to favor Warner Brothers shows. The network is a partnership of Time Warner, the Tribune Company television stations group and his own company, Acme Broadcasting. "We're in this together," Mr. Kellner said, adding that if Time Warner and Tribune are unhappy with WB's executives, "they can fire us if they want to," but that while they're in place "we operate the business." He said that "in our first two years we got no cooperation from the studio." Very few of the studio's producers generated programs for WB. Since then, he said, "more effort has been made." But he said, "Maybe there's a hex on us or something like that, but we've not been able to break through yet with Warner Brothers." Mr. Kellner added: "We always said we were going to put on the best shows. It's their job to get some of their shows to be the best shows." Ms. Daniels said she expected more Warner shows to start filtering to WB soon, after existing deals tying some of the best Warner Brothers producers to NBC and ABC run their course. She mentioned the team of Marta Kaufman, Kevin Bright and David Crane, the creators of "Friends"; Bruce Helford of "The Drew Carey Show," and John Wells of "E.R." "The object of the business is to make money," Mr. Kellner said, describing the approach he believed Warner Brothers executives should apply to WB. "The younger you are in terms of the appeal of your programs, the higher the value in syndication." Mr. Kellner contrasted WB's strategy for building a new network with that of Fox, where Mr. Kellner worked during its ascension in the late 1980's and early 1990's. The mistake Fox eventually made, both he and Ms. Daniels said, was to abandon its one-time identity as "the bad-boy network," as Ms. Daniels put it, in a quest to overtake NBC for command of the broader age group favored by many advertisers, viewers between the ages of 18 and 49. Mr. Kellner said the push by Fox, a unit of the News Corporation, to acquire rights to the National Football League was a mistake because it signaled the end of a programming approach characterized by the philosophy "If you can see it somewhere else, it doesn't belong here." Instead, football became hugely costly. "The Fox network is not profitable now," Mr. Kellner said, For Fox, of course, this analysis flies in the face of the growth that acquiring football helped fuel, both in adding stronger affiliated stations and in gaining wider credibility for Fox as a full-fledged network. Still, Mr. Kellner has a growing body of ratings results to back up his arguments. Of the six networks now competing in prime time, only WB has shown increases in viewing this year, about 10 percent for the season. More important for WB, whose early success came largely as a result of enormous viewing by teen-age girls, some of the most significant increases have been among viewers who qualify as young adults, those between the ages of 18 and 34. Mr. Kellner said WB took in about $300 million in advance commitments from advertisers last spring, and he predicted the comparable figure will reach $450 million this year. Movie advertisers, particularly, have flocked to WB shows, looking for the young viewers that form the base audience for so many contemporary films. So confidence -- yes, even arrogance -- is brimming over at WB. "When we are the No. 1 network 18 to 34, we'll probably be the most profitable network in America," Mr. Kellner said. "That's our goal." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
ART/ARCHITECTURE;
Where the Venues Are Virtually Infinite
body: THERE are plenty of unlikely places to see art in the physical world, but for sheer range and pure oddity, terra firma has nothing on cyberspace. The number of museums on line has assumed proportions that only Alice grown 10feet tall could comprehend. According to the listings provided by the authoritative on-line directory, the World Wide Web Virtual Library, the strangely named Elsas Producties site out of the Netherlands tallies links to more than 10,000 museums in 120 countries. Jonathan Bowen, webmaster of the Virtual Library's museum pages, claims that a new museum is added to its own lists on an average of one a day, every day. The directories themselves are spawning like so many baby galaxies: all of the search services, like Yahoo and Lycos, stock ample museum links; and then the specialized directories like the Virtual Library, ArtNet, Musee and World Wide Arts Resources provide immensely broad (though spottily updated) offerings. What is a virtual museum? It can be anything from a homemade collection of images with accompanying texts that focuses on a category of objects -- paintings, restaurant ware, wooden nickels -- to a slickly produced, elaborate summary of a physical museum, with floor plans, descriptions of collections and exhibitions, images, audio, even virtual-reality tours. Of course, as in the physical world, on-line museums dedicated to art are just a fraction of the virtual storehouses displaying everything from the artifacts of science and history to the more florid examples of humanity's full-bore nuttiness. Witness the Air Sickness Bag Virtual Museum or, back in the realm of artworks, the only slightly less twisted Museum of Bad Art, whose slogan is "Art too bad to be ignored" (but we'll try). The dizzying propagation of visual culture on the Web has its bright sides, from the established international institutions (the Metropolitan Museum of Art in newyork, the Pompidou Center in Paris, the Prado in Madrid) to the local (ever visited the National Gallery of Slovenia or the Tokugawa Art Museum in Japan or the Portland Art Museum in Oregon?) to the deeply strange (try the Museum of Jurassic Technology's exhibit of fruit-stone carving). What is apparent is that museums now see the Internet as a supplementary portal of value. The Museum of Modern Art in newyork has an extraordinarily rich site -- perhaps the best of its kind on the Web -- and its numbers are intriguing. In 1997, 1.2 million art aficionados surfed by, rapidly approaching the 1.65 million visitors who passed through its actual doors. (To put the Modern's yearly numbers in perspective, Yahoo, the most trafficked single site on the Web, has more than one million visitors a day.) For artists attuned to the possibilities of such swelling audiences, museums are offering new cyber venues. The Walker Art Center's on-line Gallery 9 features Piotr Szyhalski's provocative interactive pieces "Ding an Sich" and "Harvest." The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art recently purchased a whole collection of Web works called "RSUB" from the digital-design shop Razorfish Studios in newyork. There is much, much more. Galleries? Hundreds. Auction houses and live on-line auctions? Indeed. Art-locating services, advice about collecting? A click away. All of them -- and who knows what else? -- are now playing on a browser near you. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Art on the Web comes from odd sites like the Air Sickness Bag (top) as well as museums like the Modern in newyork, the Tokugawa in Japan and the Pompidou in Paris. title:
Business & Investing;
Buying In to 'Communicopia,' a Rich New Data Landscape
body: ONE week it is a white-hot debut for a new business on the Internet. The next it's a telephone company breaking a taboo by buying a cable network. Last week, a spirited bidding war broke out over a major wireless phone company. Like pixels lighting up one by one on a flat-screen display, these seemingly disjointed events add new clarity and detail to a developing picture of what analysts at Goldman, Sachs seven years ago called "communicopia": an intertwined landscape of data and voice communications, entertainment programming and electronic commerce. But for all its complexity, this world is rapidly converging. More and more of the companies in these industries are doing more and more of the same sorts of things. In a conference call, Richard P. Simon, a managing director and media analyst at Goldman, Sachs, and Oscar A. Castro, co-manager of the Montgomery Global Communications fund, sorted out the investment implications of the latest developments.  Q.  Have these diverse electronic businesses evolved the way you thought they might in 1992? SIMON "Communicopia" sprang from a conversation I had with people at Time Warner, when we started talking about things like band width, twisted pair compression technology and other things outside my traditional industry framework. I walked away from that meeting thinking how lost I was, that there was a broad cross section of knowledge I didn't have. So a group of us at Goldman set out to write about this thing without knowing what it was. But as we explored, we realized there was a significant convergence taking place, and ended up concluding that cable, not the telephone, is the advantage technology to deliver information, because of its broad-band capability. The cost of doing the same thing for telephone companies would be exceedingly high. During the mid-1990's, it looked like our conclusion might be wrong. But things like AT&T's purchase of TCI and Microsoft's investment in Comcast illustrate cable's dominance. Of course, back in the early 1990's, we didn't consider the Internet. CASTRO I have no problem with that conceptual construct. Cable owns the last mile to the consumer. But I am not so enthusiastic about cable companies as investments, because they don't express their goals clearly, and until recently did not seem to be interested in maximizing shareholder value. But there is no doubt that convergence is happening. The model is more advanced in Britain and Australia and has been developing in the same vein in Germany and France. In the unitedstates, we have not been so quick. SIMON Only one of the companies I cover, Time Warner, is a cable company. But over the last two to three years, they have directly focused on building shareholder value. Q.  What difference has the Internet's rise made in the developing picture? SIMON The Internet has broadened and enhanced things. It is taking another product and offering it over the phone lines, but the advantages of offering it over cable are numerous. For one thing, it is easier and faster to use. Also, the Internet has brought in a lot of players, from advertisers to content providers to portal creators, that were not around before. Q.  Without specialized knowledge, how can investors spot companies that can best take advantage of convergence? CASTRO Investors need to be looking at those companies that have the right management, ones who have proven they can execute and are flexible enough to take advantage of opportunities. Worldcom is an example. These guys were basically second-tier long-distance providers who moved on to be competitive access providers and went international. After that they became one of the largest Internet providers. And now they have MCI, a long-distance provider with a very strong Internet position. SIMON Oscar noted earlier he does not like the News Corporation because they do not appear interested in maximizing shareholder value. But Rupert Murdoch has a very clear vision of how to build global distribution and provide content for those distribution platforms. He has that with the Fox network here, B Sky B in Britain and Star TV in the Pacific. He owns a lot of content, whether it is children's cartoons or the Los Angeles Dodgers, which makes him less vulnerable than others. He makes big, long-term bets. At one of our Communicopia conferences a few years ago, John Malone from TCI was asked which competitor he most feared and admired. He said, "Rupert Murdoch." Q.  Last week MCI Worldcom's name came up in connection with the battle over Airtouch. Should they be interested? CASTRO Well, voice communications is definitely moving to a wireless world. But Bernie Ebbers has shown no interest yet in a wireless strategy, and MCI failed to have a clear cellular strategy, so it is outside their core competence. On the other hand, when they identify a business they want to get in to, they buy a company and its management. Q.  If MCI Worldcom isn't interested, which company, Vodaphone or Bell Atlantic, does Airtouch fit best with? CASTRO The best fit is with Vodaphone. If they got Airtouch, they would control a big part of the wireless market. Bell Atlantic bought Nynex and is buying GTE; if it succeeded in acquiring Airtouch, that could create some digestion problems. Also, Bell Atlantic does not have one of our favorite management teams. Q.  AT&T made headlines last week with announcements of a split, a big buyback plan and some new thinking about how to digest its own recent acquisitions. Is its chief executive, C. Michael Armstrong, on the right track? CASTRO Armstrong has definitely established a clear leadership role at the company, and the pickups of Teleport and TCI have been very smart acquisitions. Their agreement to merge international operations with British Telecom surprised a lot of people, but they could be a formidable competitor internationally. The challenge he has now is to deliver on the expectations that have been built up on the Street. Q.  Which stocks in the world of communicopia do you like? SIMON Time Warner and Viacom are two of the stocks I like. However, they have performed very well and are selling at record multiples. So to some degree degree they are dependent on positive developments to push their prices higher. We also like Newscorp, which traditionally has been undervalued versus other media companies. CASTRO We like Global Telesystems, a European company based in Virginia, and Colt Telecom, a British company. We also like Telephonica and Teleitaliana, because they have articulated a clear international strategy. Airtouch is a company we love, but the stock is too rich. Orange, another British company, we also like. And China Telecom. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photos: Under C. Michael Armstrong, AT&T has diversified into cable TV systems and programming by acquiring Tele-Communications. (Ozier Muhammad/The newyork Times); Bernard Ebbers, chief executive of MCI Worldcom, has shown little appetite for cellular properties but may bid for Airtouch. (Reuters); Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation has built strong media content and distribution businesses by making big, long-term bets. (Associated Press); Richard Simon; Oscar Castro

title:
Ideas & Trends;
Measuring Floor Space And Cyberspace
body: NEVER in the history of modern business has there been a class of companies that has spiraled so high, so fast and with so little regard for convention as the Internet companies whose market values have astonished Wall Street in recent months and caused even more surprise last week. Some have shown profits, but many haven't. Some rent space in office parks or old warehouses. They have relatively few employees, no manufacturing plants and little inventory. By almost every traditional way of measuring a company's worth, they don't add up. "I love that we live in a world where Wall Street can't explain why these stocks are going up and where pundits can't explain why Clinton is so popular," said Mark Pincus, the 32-year-old president of Tioga Systems, a software company in Palo Alto, Calif., who sold his Internet company, Freeloader, for $38 million a few years ago. "The fact is, the old world of building a lot of facilities is going nowhere," Mr. Pincus said, "while the value of doing things that are idea-based on the Web is going up exponentially." Under this theory of business, physical assets are liabilities. "It's atoms you're trying to minimize," said Bill Gross, the president of Idealab, a Pasadena, Calif., company that helps Internet startups. "The more neurons you have per dollar the better." It's a "zero-gravity" view of commerce in which "you don't want molecules," he said. "Knowledge moves at the speed of light; molecules move at 600 miles per hour with Fed Ex." Wall Street analysts have a less exotic explanation for the surge in interest in Internet businesses: the potential for tremendous growth. In 1995, there were about 5 million Internet users, but the number is expected to rise to 115 million by 2000. "The reason for this latest run is growth," said Larry Wachtel, a market analyst for Prudential Securities. "And Wall Street loves growth." Broadcast.com would be a textbook example of the new Internet businesses, if a textbook existed. It was founded almost four years ago by Todd Wagner and Mark Cuban, old college friends who were then in their mid-30's. When it went public last year, it had one of the fastest opening-day sprints in Wall Street history, rising nearly 250 percent. The company broadcasts live speeches, conferences, television events and even professional wrestling over the Internet. It has 250 employees who work out of an old warehouse in Dallas that it rents for $4,000 a month. On Friday, almost inexplicably, shares of Broadcast.com rose 50 percent and the company ended the day with a value of $3.4 billion, more than the value of Wendy's International, which has 150,000 employees and 5,391 restaurants around the country. title: Surging Internet Stock's Trading Halted for a Time
body: In the latest twist on highflying Internet stocks, the Nasdaq exchange yesterday temporarily halted trading of Broadcast.com, a Dallas Internet company, after a more than 70 percent jump in the price of its shares -- then allowed trading to resume even though the company declined to comment on what might have caused the surge. "They basically said that they don't comment on unusual market activity, and we didn't see any information out there, so we resumed trading," said Mike Shokouhi, a Nasdaq spokesman. The company also declined to comment when reached by a reporter. Although several analysts said it was unusual for an exchange to accept a no-comment response from a company, Mr. Shokouhi said: "We basically let the markets do what they do. And you know, it seems like it's a brave new world with these Internet stocks." Nasdaq halted trading on Broadcast.com stock at 11:51 A.M. after the stock surged as high as $230.50 for no apparent reason after opening at $131, Mr. Shokouhi said. When trading resumed at 1:20 P.M., it fell as low as $175 but closed at $197.50, up $65.50. In all, 2.7 million shares changed hands -- most in lots of between 100 and 500 shares, indicating the kind of retail buyers who have been fueling the meteoric rise in Internet stocks. The frenzy caused some transaction delays, with one trader reporting canceling an order after waiting 10 minutes for a sell order, during which the price dropped 17 points. The wild ride capped another week of astronomical gains by Internet stocks and preceded a meeting called for Monday by the National Association of Securities Dealers, Nasdaq's board, with securities firms to discuss market volatility in technology stocks, some of which have recently seen 50-point daily swings. Kathy Smith, an analyst with Renaissance Capital Corporation who follows Broadcast.com, said: "The market is crazy over the Internet. But that's a pretty amazing leap in value, so it must be related to something. It's beyond anything the Internet is producing." As for Nasdaq's resumption of trading after the company's refusal to comment, Ms. Smith said, "That makes it all the more interesting." Broadcast.com, which has about 250 employees, transmits over the World Wide Web sound and video of events ranging from sports and news to corporate shareholder meetings. Among other popular Internet stocks that posted $30 gains yesterday were Amazon.com, CGI Group, Yahoo and Geocities. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
Stocks Take A Wild Rise To New Highs
body: The stock market took a volatile ride to new highs yesterday, finishing a week marked by an Internet stock frenzy, a surge in other technology stocks and new economic data that showed the American economy is refusing, so far, to slow down. The Dow Jones industrial average, which seesawed all day, rallied in the late afternoon to gain 105.56 points, or 1.1 percent, closing at a record 9,643.32. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index rose 5.36 points, or four-tenths of 1 percent, to 1,275.09. The technology-heavy Nasdaq index climbed 18.32 points, or eight-tenths of 1 percent, to 2,344.41. Both were also records. While some of the highfliers of the technology sector, including Microsoft, Dell Computer, I.B.M. and Netscape Communications, slipped yesterday, the overall sector rose, lead by Cisco Systems and its promise of a new voice and data modem. The broader market was paced by Alcoa, which accounted for about one-third of the Dow's surge, after the company announced better-than-expected earnings, a stock split and a dividend increase. The S.& P. 500's performance was held back by declines in drug and consumer stocks, including Pfizer, Eli Lilly and Coca-Cola. The Internet frenzy cost some investors a lot of money yesterday. Amazon.com surged 40 1/4, or 25.3 percent, to 199 1/8, and then gave up almost all its gains, finishing up 1 3/8 at 160 1/4. E*Trade, was up 10 13/16, or 16.9 percent, to 74 7/8, before giving back all but 3 9/16 of the day's gain. Still, for the first week of the year Amazon.com was up 49.7 percent and E*Trade 44.6 percent. "Today was a good indication of why you have to be pretty careful," said Henry Blodget, senior analyst at CBIC Oppenheimer. "These stocks are incredibly volatile. They have spiked here massively and if your time horizon is longer than five minutes you are taking an inordinate amount of risk buying in at this level." For some, the technology rally is creating a worrisome two-tier market. Douglas R. Cliggott, unitedstates equity strategist at J. P. Morgan Securities, is positive on technology stocks but concerned about the rest of the market. "We are getting real close to the levels of overvaluation we had in July of last year," he said. "While we are real enthusiastic about tech, we are recommending caution about the rest of the market." He argued that the tech rally, not including the Internet mania, is powered by several credible forces. One is the improvement in expected demand for computer products since last August. Another is the billions of dollars of cash that portfolio managers and retail investors have on hand to invest. The third is that technology stocks seem to fit nicely into the two possible economic outlooks for this year. In one, the economy slows and interest rates fall but the key technology stocks still produce healthy earnings. In the other, the economy fools most forecasters and does not slow. Technology stocks are perfect here also, Mr. Cliggott said. The increase of 378,000 nonfarm payroll jobs in December reported yesterday by the Labor Department supports the idea that the economy remains stubbornly strong, despite many forecasts of a slowdown. The job growth was far stronger than the 200,000 consensus forecast. While the news was welcomed in the stock market, it contributed to weakness in the bond market, where evidence of economic strength often hurts prices. The Treasury's 30-year issue lost 21/32, to 99 24/32; its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, rose to 5.27 percent from 5.22 percent -- its highest in nearly two months. For the week the Dow was up 5 percent. However, for the last four weeks, the Dow was up 9.3 percent while the S.& P. 500 was up 9.3 percent. And the Nasdaq beat both, rising 15.5 percent. But the real sign of the market's torrid pace -- and why a breather may be in store -- was the surge since the lows in 1998. The Nasdaq was up 65.2 percent since its Oct. 8 low, while the Dow gained 27.9 percent since Aug. 31 and the S.& P. 500 advanced 33.2 percent since the same date. But the story of the week was Amazon.com, On Tuesday, it announced that it still had not made a penny in profit. In fact, losses are expected to rise to 18 cents a share in the fourth quarter report, three times the losses a year ago. That makes no difference, apparently to investors. They are betting the on-line book and music seller is going to be a big winner in the future. So all they cared about in Tuesday's announcement was the projection that fourth-quarter sales would jump to $250 million, well above forecasts of $175 million. But those who got in last year have nothing but profits. From the bottom of the technology selloff on Oct. 8, the Nasdaq 100 index, which includes the biggest of the technology heavyweights, has soared 74.8 percent. But Amazon.com was up 457.8 percent. "The frenetic buying of Internet stocks is going to make the tulip buyers of the 17th century look like value players," said Rick Berry, director of equity research at J. P. Turner & Company in Atlanta. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average, since December 1997 . title:
PUBLIC LIVES;
Pen With Meaning
body: Ordinary Parker Vector rollerball pens retail for $7.95. But they do not have little white letters on the side that say "unitedstates Senator." The Parker Vectors handed out as senators signed their names in the "oath book" at the beginning of the impeachment trial yesterday did. Not that the lettering makes much difference. "The Parker Vector is nothing special, I can tell you," said GEOFFREY BERLINER, a pen dealer in Manhattan. "They're giveaway pens, so they're not going to give away very expensive pens. Would this be a valuable pen? I don't think so, unless you're somebody who's into, I don't know, tawdry sexual items associated with Presidents, and this isn't even that." Pens matter in official Washington, where every loop and line at a Presidential bill signing is done with a different pen, the better to create mementos that can be given to political allies. And since the Senate trial of the President is the first such proceeding in 131 years, the Parker Vectors acquired instant historical value. Or, depending on one's view of the proceeding, infamous historical value. "I'm prouder of the pen I received when I was sworn in as a Senator," said SENATOR CHARLES E. SCHUMER, Democrat of newyork. An aide said he had talked about framing the swearing-in Vector, but not the impeachment-book Vector. Senator Strom Thurmond of South Carolina wants his pen to go to the Strom Thurmond Institute at Clemson University in his home state after he leaves the Senate.  "But he wants a case built to display it in the office until then," a spokesman, JOHN DE CROSTA, said.  Drudge Lite From time to time this week, rumors spread that the Internet gossip columnist MATT DRUDGE was about to break a big story. Computer users tried to point their Internet browsers to his Drudge Report. Some got the Drudge Retort, a send-up of Mr. Drudge's breathless style. They did not mean to. But the addresses are confusingly close. The Drudge Report is at www.drudgereport.com. The Drudge Retort is at www.drudge.com. The Drudge Retort began last spring, when ROGERS CADENHEAD, who writes a syndicated newspaper column about computers and the Internet called "Ask Ed Brice," noticed that the www.drudge.com domain was available. "Whoever owned it before me didn't pay the bill," he said. "It was released to the public, and I was the first to register it. Then it seemed like it would be a shame not to use that to put up a parody of the Drudge Report." Where Mr. Drudge trumpets a big story as a world exclusive, with those words in capital letters, the Drudge Retort heralds a "universal exclusive, except for Uranus and the moon of Io." Last month the Drudge Retort reported on a resignation speech supposedly drafted for President Clinton to deliver after the House voted to impeach him last month. "We've been trying to see if satire can keep up with reality," Mr. Cadenhead said, acknowledging that it has not been easy. "I don't know if there's anything we've come up with that is any more farfetched than what reality's coming up with on a regular basis," he said. Not everything on the Drudge Retort site is made up. Mr. Cadenhead said the logo for the on-line bookseller Amazon.com and the links to that site were real and were "helping to defray our server bills." "I have a feeling Matt Drudge is making a lot more money," he said. Maybe, maybe not. But even Mr. Drudge has been checking the Drudge Retort, which has been drawing 25,000 visitors a day. "I go there when I can't get into my own Web site because mine's so popular," Mr. Drudge said.  Reunion Catalyst The well reported reunion of YOGI BERRA and GEORGE M. STEINBRENNER was sparked by an offhand remark from ROSE CALI, who bought YOGI BERRA'S house in Montclair, N.J. ("He left cases of Yoohoo around" when he moved out, she said.) She is now the president of the board of the Yogi Berra Museum, and as such had a chat with officials from WFAN-AM, the sports-talk station. "I said, 'The time is so right now for this kind of thing to happen. There's a mellowing process, and George keeps making noises and Yogi keeps leaving this little opening,' " she recalled yesterday. "Yogi had to be ready to accept this. I felt the way it could happen would be to have George come here. Rudy Giuliani made the trek. Why couldn't George?"  200 Left Feet First there were the elaborately produced videos that served as invitations to the birthday party for SEAN (PUFFY) COMBS, the rap impresario. Now there are the broken-in, spray-painted shoes. Belgo Nieuw York -- the Manhattan outpost of a Belgian restaurant chain that will have an entryway decorated like a huge, iridescent mussel -- sent out 200 as invitations to its opening-day party on Jan. 27. Accompanying the footwear was a card that said guests would be admitted only with the shoe. One (spray painted an eye-popping yellow) was a size 10 Joan & David pump that had clearly been broken in. Another was a well-worn 8. "They were able to get a bargain" on the shoes, said ROBERT BARR, a publicity agent who is coordinating the guest list. "They were not bought at retail."   JAMES BARRON http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: YOGI BERRA

title:
ESSAY;
Net Presence: If No One Sees a Web Site, Is It Really There?
body: HOMESTEADING on the World Wide Web can be a lonely proposition. I learned this the hard way, when a book I wrote caught the attention of a stranger named Greg O'Brien. First, Mr. O'Brien sent me fan email. One thing led to another, and before long, Mr. O'Brien, a software consultant in Marlborough, Mass., who is well versed in the Web, was volunteering to build a Web site for the book. I couldn't have been more pleased. The book -- "The House at the Bridge" (Scribner, 1995), a nonfiction work about Germany in the wake of reunification -- had long since disappeared from Books in Print. A Web site might be just the way to give it new life. By coincidence, not long after Mr. O'Brien entered my life, the on-line retailer Amazon.com started a new program for out-of-print books in which an author or small publisher, armed with cartons of unsold copies, could become the distributor, shipping books in batches as small as two or three for Amazon to sell when ordered. The Web site, Mr. O'Brien and I decided, would feature a link to Amazon.com. After a month or so of working in his spare time, Mr. O'Brien created a rich, visually engaging Web site, complete with sketches, photographs, prose from the book, a bibliography and links to other sites. I expected that dozens of scholars, students and anyone with a more than casual interest in modern Germany would come to the site every day, using it as an efficient source of information and perhaps even buying the book through Amazon.com. That is not what happened. The problem with erecting a virtual shrine to your out-of-print book, unpublished novel, love of border collies or anything at all is that the mere existence of the site does not mean anyone will go there. If Yahoo, with more than a million visits daily, is as visible a destination as the Eiffel Tower, then home-brewed sites like mine are like so many identical trees in the woods. In other words, don't count on people stumbling across your site. They will find it only if they are looking for it. Knowing exactly how many people were visiting the site was easy. Soon after the site went up, in May 1998, Mr. O'Brien devised a way to monitor traffic, through a service called Nedstat (usa.nedstat.net). Nedstat not only tells you how many visitors, or page views, your site gets each day; it also breaks down the statistics into page views per hour and page views per week and presents the results in colorful bar charts. Mr. O'Brien pointed me to the Nedstat link on a day last fall. When I went there, I found a prediction for the day's traffic. "Forecast for today: nine page views." That was sobering news, especially considering that several of the page views came from Mr. O'Brien himself as he walked the virtual grounds of his creation. The high point came on Nov. 9, the anniversary of the fall of the Berlin wall: 25 visits. Traffic on www.thehouseatthebridge.com needed a boost. For months I had been receiving junk email from various companies offering to increase Web site traffic. The most persistent entreaty came from an outfit called Traffic Accelerator. The offer was difficult to refuse: for $39.95 my site would be submitted to 900 search engines and directories. I perused the site (which is no longer functioning under that U.R.L.) -- and began to surrender my credit card information. As I clicked through the sign-up process, the service tried to goad me into buying the far more expensive $159.95 option, which promised to resubmit the site repeatedly over several months. I resisted, and stuck with the $39.95 one-time service. I asked Mr. O'Brien to help me monitor the results. Yes, he had heard of these submission services, he told me. I wondered aloud if the server he used for the site would be able to withstand the increase in traffic. Mr. O'Brien, a taciturn man to begin with, went dead silent. Finally, he said gently, "Don't be disappointed if it doesn't amount to much." He said he had already submitted the site to several of the major search sites and directories, like Yahoo, Alta Vista, Lycos and Infoseek. But surely the 896 others would yield some new traffic. A few days after buying the service, I called up the Nedstat page. Traffic had not risen that day. In fact, it had reached an all-time low of six visitors. The traffic that did increase was my email. A few messages came from sites that must have received my submission because they were writing to invite me to visit the link they had created. But when I went to look for it, I found nothing. Further, the sites I visited -- devoted to direct marketing and country music -- had no discernible connection to Germany, modern or medieval. More unsettling, many of the sites looked unsavory. Still worse, for the next couple of weeks, I was spammed with email from dozens of other submission services. Traffic on my site, in the meantime, held steady at about 10 visits a day. Despondent, I called my friend Nate Saal, who runs a Web-based software updating service in Palo Alto, Calif. When I explained my problem, Mr. Saal told me, almost apologetically, that his site got tens of thousands of visitors each day. He offered this advice: "You need to narrow down the market so that people who might be interested in your topic find out about your site." He suggested that I find other sites devoted to the Berlin wall and offer to create a reciprocal link. Mr. Saal also stressed word-of-mouth advertising. "Create a means and a reason for people to tell others," he said. Mr. Saal, for instance, had created a "tell a friend" page on his site, making it easy for people to tell friends about the site and giving them a chance to win a T-shirt. I rejected the T-shirt idea but took his advice about reciprocal links and sent email to people whose Germany and Berlin wall pages were prominently featured in search engines, offering to link to them in exchange for a link to me. I heard nothing in reply. I continued, compulsively you might say, to call up the Nedstat page, thinking there might be a delayed effect from the submission service. No such luck. Next, I called Evan I. Schwartz, a writer whose book, "Webonomics" (Broadway Books, 1997), is closely tied to his Web site, Webonomics.com. If anyone could give me tips for cross-promoting a Web site and a book, Mr. Schwartz could. "How do people know about your Web site?" I asked. Mr. Schwartz replied: "The U.R.L. is on the book. It's in big red fluorescent letters on the back." In the case of my book, published a good year before U.R.L.'s started showing up on dust jackets, that was a moot point. Mr. Schwartz also offered his opinion about search engines. "I'm a firm believer that people don't find things through search engines," he said. He explained that tens of thousands of sites contained any of my key words and phrases -- Berlin wall, modern Germany, Potsdam, World War II. "You're a needle in a haystack," he said. While I was on the phone with Mr. Schwartz, an email message arrived with "Link Request" in the subject line: "Hi. I am Larry Steele and I just visited your site at http://vancouver-webpages.com /global-URL-list.html and thought we might help each other. Your prospect is similar to mine; someone interested in his or her appearance. Would you consider putting a link on your site to mine at http://www .logsdons.com/hair? We have a very special video called 'No More Bad Hair Days.' Here is copy of our advertisement to help you." Sure. Why not? http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Drawing (Nurit Karlin)

title: Microsoft Presses Its View About Rivals' 3-Way Deal
body: In its antitrust trial today, the Microsoft Corporation made its most concerted effort yet to convince a Federal judge that the recently announced deal that brings together three of its rivals -- America Online Inc., the Netscape Communications Corporation and Sun Microsystems Inc. -- seriously weakens the Government's case. In a three-way deal announced in late November, America Online agreed to buy Netscape for $4.2 billion and made a side agreement to buy and jointly develop technology with Sun. Last month, Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson, who will decide the outcome of this nonjury trial, expressed the view that the deal "might be a very significant change in the playing field as far as this industry is concerned." During today's cross-examination of the Government's last witness, Franklin M. Fisher, an economist, Microsoft's legal team presented as evidence comments made by executives of the three companies who characterized the deal as sure to strengthen their competitive muscle in software used to browse the World Wide Web, in electronic commerce and in Internet technology -- all areas of head-to-head competition with Microsoft. A Microsoft lawyer, Michael Lacovara, repeatedly tried to get Mr. Fisher to concede that the triumvirate of rivals with ambitious plans for the future did indeed pose a genuine threat to Microsoft's dominance in the personal computer software business. At times, Mr. Fisher would give an inch or two, saying, for example, that moves planned by the three companies were a "hopeful sign" that they might some day be a counterweight to Microsoft. But each time he was challenged, Mr. Fisher returned to his view that Microsoft has a monopoly in the personal computer operating system market with its Windows family of products and that it has illegally used its market power to defend that monopoly. "None of this," Mr. Fisher replied at one point, "affects my conclusions." Mr. Lacovara prodded Mr. Fisher repeatedly to admit that the emerging technology championed by the group -- the combination of Sun's Java software, an Internet programming language, and Netscape's Web browser -- could pose a serious challenge to Microsoft in the long run. Mr. Fisher allowed that it was difficult to predict what might happen. Yet any such challenge will not come soon, he said, adding, "I don't think it will happen at all if Microsoft is permitted to go on as it has." Microsoft insists that the America Online-Netscape-Sun deal fundamentally changes the competitive landscape and undermines a linchpin claim in the Government's case: that Microsoft has a resilient monopoly. "This deal was the shot heard around the world, in the industry, by the public and in this courthouse," said William H. Neukom, the Microsoft senior vice president for law and corporate affairs. Today, Judge Jackson gave another signal that he is weighing the impact of the three-company deal on the case. He interrupted the cross-examination of Mr. Fisher to directly ask his opinion about a column this morning on the Op-Ed page of The Washington Post by David Ignatius, based largely on an interview with Stephen M. Case, the chairman of America Online. In it, Mr. Ignatius quotes Mr. Case as saying that the deal is not intended to mount a challenge to Microsoft's mainstay, the Windows operating system, which controls the basic operations of more than 90 percent of personal computers sold today. "AOL's merger with Netscape has no bearing on the Microsoft case, as nothing we're doing is competitive with Windows," Mr. Case was quoted as saying. "We have no flight of fancy that we can dent in any way, shape or form what is a monopoly in the operating system business." After reading the quotations, Judge Jackson asked Mr. Fisher if he agreed with that view of the deal. "I certainly do," Mr. Fisher replied. Judge Jackson then asked lawyers for both Microsoft and the Justice Department whether they planned to call Mr. Case as a witness. Another America Online executive, David M. Colburn, has already appeared as a witness for the Government. Mr. Case is not on the 12-person witness lists for either side, but he could be called as one of the two additional witnesses allowed to each side after Microsoft presents its defense, which is expected to begin early next week. Both Microsoft and the Government told the judge that they would wait until Microsoft had presented its defense, expected to last six to eight weeks, before naming their two so-called redirect witnesses. Later, on the courthouse steps, David Boies, the lead trial lawyer for the Justice Department, made no commitment, but he said Mr. Case would be a "useful witness" for the Government. "He's very knowledgeable," Mr. Boies said, "and Microsoft is pinning a lot of hopes on the effect of that merger." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Vanity, Thy Name Is (Insert I.S.P.)
body: Die-hard fans of the band Kiss can do more to show devotion to their rock idols than just buy CD's. They can now join Kissonline.net, the official Internet service provider of the band. The service offers unlimited Web access for $19.95 a month, which is no great deal, but it has perks like access to members-only content and an affinity email address. "AOL and Earthlink cater to the general populace. If you're a Kiss fan, you want an I.S.P. that caters to you," said Mike Brandvold, Webmaster for Sony Pictures, a Sony merchandising company that organizes content for the Kiss site and I.S.P. Kiss is on the cutting edge, but the band is not out there alone. David Bowie, the heavy-metal band Megadeth, the Ohio Society of Certified Public Accountants, the alumni association of the University of South Florida and the Vanguard Group, a financial services company, are among many organizations that have recently sponsored private label I.S.P.'s. On the information superhighway, these I.S.P.'s are vanity license plates. These bands and businesses do not operate the services themselves; they contract out the technical side to one of several providers that coordinate access to a national network of dial-up numbers and furnish technical support. For instance, Laser Link Communications, based in Media, Pa., provides all the back room and technical operations for Megadeth.net, and Ohio-CPA.net, among several others. It is up to the sponsors, like Megadeth, to do the marketing and provide extra content for their official sites. It is now possible to establish these special services because it is more economical and less complex to operate a national I.S.P. Much as Visa and Master Card do with their affinity charge cards, companies like Laser Link create a generic product, then let the sponsors stamp it with their own brands. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
Q & A;
When a Site Won't Load
body: Q. My Web browser crashes when I try to look at a certain page. Every other page I want to look at loads fine, so is something wrong with the page?  A. A number of things could be causing the problem, so try to eliminate some possibilities. Try to call up that Web page on another computer (or ask a friend to try) and see if it will load properly. If the page won't load on different computers, it's very likely that something is wrong with the page file. If the page loads for someone else, check your own system. Make sure you have enough RAM to meet the minimal system requirements for the browser program. Many Web pages are designed with more than just the basic HTML (hypertext markup language) coding. Java applets and browser plug-ins like Flash are some of the newer technology used to animate and spice up Web pages. Older browsers -- early versions of Netscape Navigator, Microsoft Explorer or America Online's browser -- can't support some of these newer features. If possible, upgrade your browser to the most current version and make sure that you have all the popular plug-ins. If your computer can't handle the newer, more RAM-hungry browsers, consider switching to a low-cost, low-RAM alternative like the Opera browser (www.operasoftware.com), which can run on even a 386 processor.   J.
