title:
USER'S GUIDE;
Web Lust: More Money, More Stuff
body: A PERSON can live blissfully for 37 years without a coffee table, then one day suddenly look at the big empty area in the center of the living-room rug and realize: it's all wrong. This epiphany occurred at a party recently, as I watched my guests awkwardly balancing plates of food on their knees. Soon after, I embarked on a search for the perfect coffee table with the sort of zealous fervor usually associated with a religious convert. I dragged home two tables from a secondhand furniture store, but one proved too small, the other too red. I returned them. From an antiques store, I borrowed a table with a more expensive price tag of $350; it was rickety. For a while, a round one with a glass top was promising. But the baby crawled under it, got stuck and flailed on her back like a specimen in a petri dish. The universe of available coffee tables suddenly seemed small. Luckily, the Internet can provide a Big Bang. While questions may remain about the original cosmic explosion, I can attest that the on-line version has more than once expanded my choices miraculously. So I went to www.hotbot.com to search for Art Deco furniture. This is how I ended up at www.modernism.com, belonging to a furniture dealer in Coral Gables, Fla. On the site, I saw a snapshot of, well, the most beautiful coffee table in existence. Not too big, not too small, not red at all. Eagerly, I sent a polite email inquiry. The prompt response came on Nov. 25. "Dear Michelle, the price is $4,500, which includes packing, insurance and shipping within the continental unitedstates." I read that repeatedly, trying to process the fact that a piece of wooden furniture, 44 inches in diameter, cost roughly as much as my first car. Quickly I replied, declaring the table to be beyond my budget. But over the next few days, as I hauled home and later returned a sharp-cornered, orangish $50 table on which the baby managed to cut her lip, I kept returning to my computer to stare at the very, very expensive coffee table. Have I mentioned that it was constructed of African rosewood (whatever that is)? The impulse that led me to the Internet in the first place -- the fact that I hate to be thwarted -- had now planted a dangerous idea in my head: I had to get that table. On a practical level, I realized that even toying with the idea of throwing away my children's college funds was a severe indictment of my character. But I no longer cared. They can get scholarships, I thought. Meanwhile, I will entertain beautifully. But first, I needed to rationalize the purchase. So I went to Moneyminded (www.moneyminded.com), a Web site whose goal is to help women get control of their finances. My covert goal: persuading this Web site to convince me that my finances were in better shape than they appeared to my accountant. The site has a nice selection of quizzes that allow you to plug in figures like household income and projected investment returns to determine if you are headed for retirement-on-a-yacht commercials or for a broken, penniless old age. I was taken aback when a quick scan of the site yielded no "Should you buy that expensive coffee table?" quiz. However, I lingered for a while on the amusing "How Much Should That Home Repair Cost?" calculator. There I learned that a plumber charges, on average, $72 to fix an overflowing toilet. In the newyork area, add 32 percent. Amusing, yes, but not what I needed. It occurred to me then that a house without the perfect coffee table could be considered a broken house, in need of repair. If one applied the plumbing equation to a broken house, it would be necessary to factor in an hourly labor rate for time spent fretting over a coffee table. (I think $100 an hour would be fair, $150 if it occurs when you should be asleep.) Figuring, conservatively, that there was one hour of fretting, that's $150 right there. And this is to say nothing of the cost of cleaning up spilled party food ($3.99 for carpet fluid), the broken plate ($6), plus a modest $1,000 settlement for pain and suffering endured by the owner of the broken home. This would bring the average cost to $1,159.99, plus a 32 percent differential in the newyork area: a grand total of $1,531.19. Clearly, this method of calculation was flawed, because the total came nowhere near the cost of the rosewood coffee table. But elsewhere on the Moneyminded site, I could ascertain the general state of my household's financial health. To see if I was saving enough for retirement, I entered annual income, number of years until retirement, savings and investments, and then pressed the key. I had anticipated the response: "Wow, you've been diligent. So go out and treat yourself to that coffee table." Instead, I got: "Caution! You need to get serious about saving for retirement and simply can't afford to wait any longer." The Web site advised me to increase my retirement savings by $8,000 a year. Panicky, I reviewed my answers, and then hit on a solution: What if I changed them? What if I projected a 15 percent annual return on retirement investments? And increased the number of years left until retirement from 30 to, say, 50? After all, my husband and I are writers, not professional athletes. Why would we ever have to retire? It worked. The new response: "Take it easy! You may be saving for retirement too aggressively." It recommended saving $0 a year for the rest of our lives -- instantly freeing up valuable coffee table funds. Now that I fully understood the state of my household finances, I realized I was a rich woman. I could afford the coffee table. I peeked at its image again and realized . . . I no longer wanted it. But I do have my eye on a $9,800 mirror-paneled night table that recently caught my eye. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Illustration (Margaret Riegel)

title: AT&T Wins At Home Deal and a Foothold as a Data Carrier
body: Advancing its aspiration to become a major carrier of Internet data, the AT&T Corporation has won a long-term contract to provide the At Home Corporation, the nation's largest provider of cable modem service, with 15,000 miles of high-speed fiber optic lines. The companies intend to announce the deal today. At Home connects consumers to cyberspace using cable television systems, but it uses long-distance telephone systems to transmit huge amounts of data to local cable operators around the country. AT&T is the nation's biggest communications company, but it has lagged in offering the high-speed data links used by Internet providers. C. Michael Armstrong, AT&T's chairman since 1997, is trying to change that. So while the deal with At Home is marginal in immediate financial value for AT&T -- worth up to $100 million, according to analysts and to executives close to the deal -- it is a big leap strategically. The executives said the deal's financial value could increase if At Home exercised options to expand it in the future. "This is a blue-chip Internet reference account for AT&T, which has not been an especially visible player in making backbone wholesale deals with new-age Internet companies," said Christopher Mines, an analyst for Forrester Research, a consulting firm in Cambridge, Mass. The deal is also a big technical step forward for At Home. Using the AT&T systems, At Home intends to become one of the first major data communications companies to connect Internet routers directly to fiber optic lines. That could give At Home an especially fast and advanced network. Until now, At Home has mostly used systems provided by the Sprint Corporation that incurred a cost to At Home for each unit of data transmitted. Under the AT&T deal, however, At Home will essentially own an entire communications pipeline. "They probably just bought themselves a 5 percent increase in their operating margin," said Richard A. Bilotti, an analyst for Morgan Stanley Dean Witter. He estimated that those margins now are between 25 and 30 percent for At Home's residential business. According to executives close to the deal, At Home asked long-distance companies to submit bids for its business last June, and other bidders were Sprint, Qwest, Level 3, Frontier, Williams and IXC. But not all the bidders were on an equal technical footing when it came to winning the At Home contract, and that is not just because some of the new carriers have not yet completed their fiber optic networks. At Home wants to connect Internet routers directly to a sort of fiber optic transmission gear known as wave-division multiplexing, or W.D.M., equipment. It is suited to systems that carry only data but also to those that carry voice traffic. Some telecommunications equipment companies, primarily Northern Telecom of Canada, tend to build into their W.D.M. gear another sort of fiber optic technology known as Sonet, which facilitates voice traffic but costs more. At Home, which only transmits data, did not want to pay for the use of Sonet, so carriers like Qwest, which uses a lot of Northern Telecom equipment, found themselves at a disadvantage, according to executives close to the deal. Tele-Communications Inc., the big cable television company that has agreed to be acquired by AT&T, is also the largest shareholder in At Home. But Milo Medin, At Home's chief technical officer, said that was not a factor in its choice of AT&T. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
BITS AND BYTES;
Shopping for Groceries in Electronic Aisles: A Revolution at Hand
body: THE idea of doing the week's marketing at a computer screen used to be the stuff of science fiction. But the number of American households shopping for food on the Internet may reach almost seven million by 2002, a projection of Emarketer, which tracks business on line. While specialty foods are becoming a presence on the Web, most of those households will be buying groceries from a few sites like www.peapod.com. Peapod, whose services have been available in the Chicago area (where it is based), on the West Coast and in Texas and Boston, has opened a distribution center, its first, in New Hyde Park, N.Y. Until now, Peapod has teamed up with supermarkets, where uniformed Peapod workers pick the goods from the shelves, check them out and pack them for delivery by white temperature-controlled vans with Peapod logos. The new center eliminates the market in the middle. But because Peapod sells perishable goods like dairy products and meat, the newyork operation so far serves customers only in western Nassau County and eastern Queens. Prices are similar to those in a supermarket, but there are three purchasing plans, ranging from $9.95 for each order to $19.95 for all orders for one month as long as they are over $60 ($5 surcharge for any order less than $60). Peapod's Net shoppers are largely dual-income suburban couples pressed for time, said Mary Wade Kiscaden, a spokeswoman. Some order for elderly parents. What they ordered most between Thanksgiving and New Year's was the humble banana. With Peapod's downloaded software, shoppers can buy, for instance, eight bananas, four ripe and four green. Among other products, it sells 83 choices of spaghetti sauce. Another national site is www.netgrocer .com, with headquarters in New Brunswick, N.J., which sells only big-brand dry goods and ships by Federal Express. It offers coupons on line. Click, instead of clip, and they're subtracted at checkout. Netgrocer has now branched out into electronic goods, books and CD's. A local service for newyork and southern Connecticut, www.yourgrocer.com., will deliver perishables (minimum orders, $50). Two services available only in New England are www.shoplink.com and www .streamline.com. Shoplink also has software to download. It offers more than groceries: dry cleaning, shoe repair and video rental. Streamline provides much hand-holding for new customers and will set up a special refrigerator in the garage for deliveries. Shoppers for specialty foods have a new discriminatingly stocked site, based in Seattle: www.chefshop.com. It sells products that chefs use, like Frontera salsas, Torrefazione Italia coffee, Rustichella d'Abruzzo pasta and Scharffen Berger chocolate. Many of these are handmade by small producers. The Rustichella pasta, for instance, which Chez Panisse in Berkeley, Calif., and Union Square Cafe in newyork both serve, is made with Italian stone-ground wheat and cut with antique bronze dies. It is rough textured, which keeps sauces from slipping off the surface. The pasta is sold in a sampler of spaghetti, fettuccine, penne rigate and orecchiette, a total of 3 pounds 11 ounces (3.5 kilos) for $19.95, as well as in a collection of 15 bags, adding fusilli col buco, twice as long as spaghetti and hollow inside, for $75.95. An older specialty-foods site that operates in partnership with the Culinary Institute of America, www.digitalchef.com, boasts that it offers "the best selection of gourmet food and cookware available anywhere -- on line or off." But most of its fare can be found in good grocery stores. The chefs' gadgets it sells include the excellent Bron mandoline for cutting and slicing vegetables ($150), but also run-of-the-mill tools like a $16 cheese cutter and a $12 pizza cutter.  'Almond Paste' to 'Zester' What's the difference between fusilli and rotini? If you don't know, you just might need www.flavorweb.com. This site aims to inform its users about food and drink in plain and fancy forms, in hopes of sending them by links to commercial sites. But you don't have to click on those links, and if you do, you don't have to buy anything. For a start, click on Food, Wine, Beer, Spirits, then on Glossary of Cooking Terms. There are entries as elementary as "baste" and "fry," but also useful discussions like those on confit, ham and Pavlova, the national dessert of Australia and New Zealand (a meringue bedecked with whipped cream and fruit). The entry for creme fraiche is a recipe. Under "casein" (the milk protein and foundation for cheese) or "rennin" (the coagulating enzyme used in cheese making), click on Cheese for a primer by types of cheese and a few words on eggs. All the way through, there are links to recipes. The site devotes pages to fruits, nuts, vegetables, herbs and spices, beef, fish, dessert wines, sparkling wines and brandy. And it has a recipe index and also a weights and measures link to convert Centigrade to Fahrenheit and grams to ounces. For the ins and outs of penne and orecchiette, click on "pasta shapes" (that link is deep within the Glossary, under "farfalline"). As for fusilli and rotini, they are both names for corkscrew-shape pastas.  A World of Coffee Anyone who likes to sip coffee while surfing the Net will want to know about www.shoppingplace.com/coffee /links1.html. It is a list of links, an electronic skeleton key to 200 sites that sell coffees, among them Hawaiian Kona and Jamaican Blue Mountain. Click on any name to turn the key. Hawaiian Express, for instance, offers five varieties of Kona at per-pound prices, shipping included, from $24 to $31 (for small-bean Kona Peaberry), as well as Maui, Kauai, Molokai and organic Hawaiian coffees. They're all available as whole beans or ground. The Jamaica Blue Mountain Coffee site sells one-pound burlap bags: roasted whole beans, $25.90; roasted ground, $23.80; green beans, $17.50. Shipping is extra. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: NOODLE NEWS -- Can't tell one type of pasta from another? An Internet glossary may help. (Ian O'Leary from "Ultimate Pasta" by Julia Della Croce DK Publishing )

title: Pricing at Issue As U.S. Finishes Microsoft Case
body: The Government called its last witness in the Microsoft trial today after presenting 110 pages of his written testimony that amount to a summation of -- and economic justification for -- the Justice Department's sweeping antitrust suit against the software giant. Much of the testimony by the witness, Franklin M. Fisher, an economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, was a detailed review of major allegations in the Government's case. But he also sought to advance the case and strengthen the argument for strong sanctions against Microsoft with his analysis of Microsoft's pricing tactics. Mr. Fisher asserts that Microsoft commits predatory pricing by giving away its Internet Explorer browser. The doctrine of predatory pricing -- defined as a monopolist selling goods below cost -- has been generally rejected by courts in recent years on the theory that it is difficult to prove both the practice and any resulting harm to consumers. But Mr. Fisher argued that Microsoft decided to give away its browser software only to thwart the threat to its dominance posed by its main rivals in Internet software, the Netscape Communications Corporation, developer of the Navigator Web browser, and Sun Microsystems Inc., creator of the Java programming language. Besides, he added, the tricky matter of trying to determine if a price is below some technical definition of its cost to produce does not apply because "Microsoft distributes its browser at a zero price," though it has spent more than $100 million a year since 1995 on browser development. "Classifying Microsoft's pricing as predatory and anti-competitive," he stated, "does not require reaching the difficult questions that are usually faced in predatory pricing cases." Mr. Fisher also provided a pre-emptive rebuttal to an M.I.T. colleague and former student, Richard Schmalensee, who will testify next, as Microsoft's expert witness on economics. In his own report to the court, which has not been released, Mr. Schmalensee argues that the price of Microsoft's industry-standard Windows operating system is too low for Windows to be legally classified as a monopoly. The comparatively low price of Windows -- less than 5 percent of the total cost of an average personal computer -- has been cited by many economists as inconsistent with the Government's allegation of an enduring monopoly. But Mr. Fisher contends that such analysis means only that Microsoft's management is taking the long view of monopoly. "The proper conclusion from Schmalensee's argument cannot be that Microsoft lacks monopoly power," Mr. Fisher wrote in his testimony. "If any conclusion can be drawn, it would be that Microsoft is not maximizing its short-run profits." Microsoft's product pricing, Mr. Fisher testified, should be viewed as part of a "broader campaign to eliminate Netscape's browser and Java as sources of potential competition to Microsoft's operating system monopoly -- a campaign characterized by actions by which Microsoft lost money in order to raise rivals' costs and exclude them from the market." In court today, a Microsoft lawyer, Michael Lacovara, opened his cross-examination of Mr. Fisher with more than an hour of detailed challenges to the methodology Mr. Fisher used to determine the market shares of competing Web browsers. Mr. Lacovara also introduced criticisms of Mr. Fisher by judges in previous cases in which he appeared as an expert witness. Mr. Fisher, an assertive, 64-year-old economist, has testified in dozens of antitrust cases in the computer industry -- though he was on the other side the last time, as the chief economic witness for the International Business Machines Corporation in its marathon antitrust confrontation with the Justice Department, a case the Government dropped in 1982 after 13 years. Microsoft's lawyers say the company is being attacked by Mr. Fisher for being much the kind of company I.B.M. was when he was defending it. "Monopoly profits are earned through high prices and inferior products," Mr. Fisher wrote in a 1983 book about the I.B.M. case. "The notion that acts showing a pattern of lower prices and better products are the behavior of a monopolist is a confusion of the workings of competition with its opposite -- monopoly." Microsoft said in a statement that "Professor Fisher's testimony would give readers of his 1983 book whiplash." This morning, Microsoft ended the cross-examination of William H. Harris, the chief executive of Intuit Inc., which makes the industry-leading personal finance software, Quicken. The Government also played excerpts from the taped deposition in which William H. Gates, the chairman of Microsoft, was questioned last August about the company's dealings with Intuit. Though Mr. Gates professed no knowledge of any of the interactions with Intuit that are at issue in the case, the Government introduced email messages in which employees had briefed him on the negotiations in exhaustive detail. Shown one such message and asked if he had been informed of its subject, Mr. Gates said, "In the sense that one of the emails that may have come into my mailbox might have related to that, I don't doubt it." Much of the questioning of Mr. Harris had centered on Intuit's interest in becoming an even larger player in Internet commerce. Microsoft's lead trial lawyer, John Warden, asked him about America Online's proposed purchase of Netscape, a deal that Microsoft argues is proof of healthy competition in the software industry. "Doesn't that change the entire landscape of the Internet industry?" Mr. Warden asked. "No, I don't believe so," Mr. Harris said. "There's a great deal of merger activity in this industry. Microsoft is rumored to be in discussions for acquisitions. I don't think the AOL-Netscape deal will be the last one we hear of." http://www.nytimes.com

title: Chattanooga Times Publishes Final Issue
body: The Chattanooga Times, the newspaper that Adolph S. Ochs took over 120 years ago with borrowed money and the same stubborn confidence that later led him to buy The newyork Times, published its final edition yesterday as control passed from Ochs's 13 great-grandchildren to the owner of its evening rival, The Chattanooga Free Press. The two newspapers fought pitched battles against each other in the 1970's. Although the hostility was muted after a joint operating agreement took effect in 1980, they retained distinct personalities. The Times featured a liberal editorial page and analytical coverage; The Free Press fought back with scrappy, locally oriented coverage and a deeply conservative viewpoint. Today, the two newspapers become one, carrying the nameplates of both. But while Chattanooga becomes a one-newspaper town, it will keep two editorial voices. The 70,000 or more subscribers to the merged newspaper will have the chance to read two editorial pages, -- The Times's opinions on the left-hand side, The Free Press's on the right. The alternative to the sale -- an expensive battle between two newspapers with daily circulations of just over 40,000 and profit margins in the single-digit range -- was favored by neither the Ochs descendants nor Walter E. Hussman Jr., who bought The Free Press 10 months ago. As the chief executive of Wehco Media Inc., the 52-year-old Mr. Hussman controls lucrative cable and broadcast properties in Arkansas and Louisiana and had emerged victorious from a fierce newspaper war in Little Rock eight years ago. The Chattanooga Times and a small printing operation are separate from The newyork Times Company, whose controlling shares are also owned by Adolph Ochs's descendants. In national terms, the loss of The Chattanooga Times further cuts the ranks of towns with more than one newspaper. Among large cities, newyork, Chicago, Denver, Boston and Seattle stand almost alone as cities with more than one newspaper. The 13 great-grandchildren of Mr. Ochs, who owned The Chattanooga Times, were among the bidders for The Free Press when its owners, the McDonald family, put it up for sale about a year ago, Mr. Hussman said. "It doesn't make economic good sense to have two newspapers in this city, especially two that were in full-fledged battle," said Ruth S. Holmberg, the chairman of The Chattanooga Times, who is one of Mr. Ochs's four grandchildren. Nonetheless, Mrs. Holmberg said, "yesterday was a very hard day." Yesterday's final edition of The Times included a cartoon of Adolph Ochs with a tear on his cheek. Michael Golden, a son of Mrs. Holmberg and an owner of The Chattanooga Times, said of the sale: "It was a very emotional decision. This is where our roots came from. This is where Adolph Ochs developed his instincts and his feelings about journalism that blossomed so well here and in newyork City." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
On-Line Giant May Link To CBS News
body: CBS News will announce a deal with America Online Inc. later this week to become the exclusive broadcast news provider for the on-line service, executives involved in the agreement said yesterday. The deal lacks only some final details, the executives said. When completed, it will mean that CBS will replace ABC News as the provider of news in text, video and audio on America Online. For CBS, the move to American Online has the potential to jump-start what has been a lackluster presence on the Web. By wide consensus, CBS News has lagged far behind the other news networks in terms of what it has offered to users of the Internet. For America Online, a deal is likely to mean a more favorable financial arrangement than the service had with ABC, one executive said. The exact terms of the deal were not available yesterday, but one executive involved in the negotiations said that it would be along the lines of "promotion for promotion." The deal was reported in the Hollywood Reporter yesterday. Executives from CBS, America Online and ABC, declined to comment on the record. An America Online spokeswoman, Wendy Goldberg, labeled it "a rumor and we don't comment on rumors." Gil Schwartz, the chief spokesman for CBS, said, "We don't have anything to announce." Michelle Bergmann, a spokeswoman for the ABC News on-line service, said, "It's our standing policy not to comment on contractual arrangements." The America Online contract is known to be near an end. An executive involved in the CBS deal said it would include America Online's affiliated services, AOL.com and Compuserve. That will give CBS access to America Online's 15 million subscribers, by far the biggest number on the Internet. The Internet services of the other network news organizations have been far ahead of CBS. CNN's Web site and MSNBC.com, which NBC operates with the Microsoft Corporation, are among the most heavily trafficked sites on the Web. Recently, CBS had been in talks with CNN about a merger of news-gathering resources. That arrangement might have required CBS to pay for access to CNN's news material. The CBS chairman, Mel Karmazin, said in December that he was looking instead for a way to generate revenue from CBS's news product. CBS does have a promotion-for-pay arrangement with the on-line services that use its Sportsline and Market Watch products. And CBS had already established a relationship with America Online last fall in a promotion campaign for its new fall prime-time entertainment lineup. That promotion was regarded as highly successful by CBS executives. An executive involved in the America Online-CBS negotiations said that American Online was also concerned with competitive Internet moves being made by the Walt Disney Company, the parent of ABC, which recently started an Internet portal, the Go Network. http://www.nytimes.com

title: New York Investigation Firm Plans to Buy Internet Consultant
body: Anticipating an era in which fighting computer crime will be as big a business as Internet commerce, the Kroll O'Gara Company, a private security and investigation company in newyork, said it would announce today that it was acquiring Securify Inc., a Silicon Valley computer security firm, for $55.2 million in stock. Securify is among the small but rapidly growing consulting firms that have sprung up as tens of thousands of corporations connect to the Internet. Its acquisition by Kroll shows that security companies are beginning to recognize the rapidly increasing risks in cyberspace. The deal, which was finalized after the close of the market on Thursday, the last day of trading in 1998, will permit Kroll to expand its small business in computer security consulting and computer crime and fraud prevention. Kroll O'Gara will acquire Securify in exchange for 1.4 million shares of stock, totaling $55.2 million. As part of the deal, an additional 211,000 shares will be used as incentives to persuade Securify employees to stay with the company. Kroll executives said the company had explored a large part of the computer security industry before settling on Securify, based in Mountain View, Calif. "We're very familiar with that community," said Jules B. Kroll, the chief executive of Kroll O'Gara. "We felt the credentials and bona fides of the people at Securify are a combination of intellectual and academic as well as those who have been out there doing it in the cyberstreets." Over the last decade, he said, Kroll's traditional business of investigating business fraud has become increasingly computer-oriented. Securify was founded earlier this year by two computer security experts, Tahar Elgamal and Dan Kolkowitz. Mr. Elgamal had been the chief scientist at the Netscape Communications Corporation, where he helped create Internet security standards widely used in commercial transactions on line. Mr. Kolkowitz has computer security experience at several companies. Securify has focused both on auditing companies' hardware and software for potential risks and on assisting those who have been victims of either outside electronic intruders or insider computer fraud. The complexity of today's Internet-based financial systems has left many companies unable to adequately assess risks, Mr. Kolkowitz said. For example, many companies are creating so-called virtual private networks, which allow different branches to communicate through the Internet. However, this does not entirely secure a company's computer network activities, which may remain vulnerable to insider fraud, the largest type of computer crime. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
OUTLOOK 1999: MEDIA & TECHNOLOGY;
A Surge in Popularity of Software That Unlocks the Code
body: The seers of 1997 had the computing trends of 1998 pretty much nailed down -- the Justice Department's antitrust challenge to the Microsoft Corporation, panic over the Year 2000 bug and Wall Street's infatuation with Internet stocks. Unforeseen, however, was one of the year's most striking developments: the surging popularity of what has been called open-source software -- probably because it had long been regarded by the industry's most powerful players as more of a political ideology than a way to make money. Open-source software provides every computer user with free access to the software's source code, the actual lines of commands that the programmers wrote to create the software. Publishing this code offers users who are programmers the chance to examine it, to fix bugs or inefficiencies or to suggest improvements. Once widely denigrated by commercial developers as chaotic programming by committee, open source is now expected to come into its own this year as a business model, with potentially far-reaching consequences for developers and consumers of computer software. Some analysts predict that the growing availability of open-source software will push industry prices down. Others forecast higher quality by both proprietary and open-source products, driven by a new competition. "At the start of 1998, the question was would there be an economic model that would sustain the success of this open-software movement, and I think that question has been answered," said Robert F. Young, chief executive of Red Hat Software, which provides services and support for a free computer operating system called Linux. "The question for this year is how rapidly is this going to deploy?" Open software programs like Linux, (rhymes with "cynics") a variant of the Unix operating system, are not owned by any company or individual. Instead, a global network of programmers and users manage and upgrade them, typically without being paid directly to do so. Their motivations vary. Many have built formidable reputations with their contributions to open-source programs, and those reputations can translate into lucrative job offers. Others profess an almost moral commitment, arguing that open-source development simply works better than the traditional closed, proprietary environment of commercial programming. Linux, the star of the open-source movement, is seen as a competitor to Windows NT, Microsoft's industrial-strength operating system. Indeed, perhaps the most persuasive evidence of the potential of open source to rattle the balance of power in the computer industry came recently from Microsoft itself. In two internal memorandums that found their way to the Internet, a Microsoft engineer described Linux as a "mind-share threat" and suggested ways to compete with and co-opt open-source development. Open-source has its roots in venerable programs like Sendmail Inc.'s software that Internet servers around the world use to relay email to its intended destination, and Perl, the programming language that was used to fashion many of the the World Wide Web's interactive features. The growth of the Internet has fostered such projects, broadening the universe of potential contributors and allowing for nearly instant distribution of constant upgrades. Open source began to gain support last year from blue-chip technology companies. I.B.M., for instance, became a major contributor to Apache, an open-source program for creating Web pages used by the vast majority of Internet service providers. In a new commercial twist on the theme, Sun Microsystems Inc. agreed to make its popular Java source code available to developers who license it. Sun is also retaining PricewaterhouseCoopers to audit the process of who determines which new functions can be added to the language. Perhaps the most widely publicized move in this trend was when the Netscape Communications Corporation released the source code to its Navigator Web browser. America Online Inc., which plans to acquire Netscape, has pledged to support its open-source initiatives. The moves are driven in part by a common interest in supporting alternatives to Microsoft. But they also reflect the emergence of a new emphasis on making money through software services and support rather than from the software itself. Mr. Young of Red Hat Software, which last year received investments from Intel and Netscape, predicts that the top 10 manufacturers of personal computers will offer Linux by the end of this year. Although I.B.M. and Compaq Computer's Digital division sell operating systems, each has announced plans to make some of their software work with Linux. The idea is that they will make money on hardware sales and consulting fees. "The real challenge for open-source software is not whether it will replace Microsoft in dominating the desktop, but rather, whether it can craft a business model that will help it to become the Intel Inside of the next generation of computer applications," wrote Tim O'Reilly, whose company publishes dozens of books about open-source programs, in the November issue of the industry newsletter Release 1.0. "Otherwise," Mr. O'Reilly warned, "the open-source pioneers will be shouldered aside by someone who understands precisely where the current opportunity lies." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
OUTLOOK 1999: MEDIA & TECHNOLOGY -- INTERNET COMPANIES;
The Small Get Big And the Big Get Bigger
body: A year ago, the choice for Lycos, then a struggling Internet search engine, was to make acquisitions or become irrelevant. "We reached 14 percent of the Internet users," recalled Robert J. Davis, chief executive of Lycos Inc. Yahoo Inc. was at 47 percent. "We were never going to grow into a powerhouse," he said. "We had to buy our way to being a powerhouse." And that is exactly what Lycos has done. It has bought five companies, for more than $300 million in stock, in the last year, increasing its audience to 38 percent of Internet users and giving itself a somewhat better chance of staving off irrelevancy. This year, Internet executives and investment bankers agree, the pace of deal-making by Internet publishing and retailing companies is likely to accelerate as more and more of the concerns that have started in recent years realize that they need to grow in order to survive. "On the Internet you have to get bigger fast," said Mark G. Shafir, the head of Merrill Lynch's technology merger practice in San Francisco.  "It's going to be the land of the titans pretty quickly." The trend toward consolidation began last year, when many deals were driven by the desire of smaller companies to end grueling battles for market supremacy. Most notably, CD Now and N2K, the two leading on-line music stores, agreed to merge in order to fight off impending competition from Amazon.com. And Media Metrix, a privately held company that measures the audience of Internet sites, bought its archrival Relevant Knowledge. The existing titans, meanwhile, moved to extend their dominance. America Online Inc., the biggest Internet company, used acquisitions to reach new audience groups in addition to its core of chatty teen-agers and their technology-challenged parents. It bought Mirabilis, the Israeli creator of the chat service called ICQ that appeals to an international audience. And America Online plans to acquire the Netscape Communications Corporation to get Netscape's World Wide Web site, which appeals to business users, as well as its on-line server software. Similarly, the Microsoft Corporation bought Hotmail, a free email service, to funnel users to its own revamped MSN portal service. And Amazon.com bought Junglee, a service that searches for products for sale around the Internet, as a way to transform itself from a book and music store to a vast electronic mall. The surging prices of Internet stocks will help create a handful of new Internet titans as both big traditional companies and smaller start-ups struggle to keep up. Take Yahoo, rated at the top among search engines, or portal services, as they are now called because of the role they try to play as the front doors to people's Internet journeys. Yahoo now has a market value of $23 billion, about as big as that of CBS Inc. That makes Yahoo simply too expensive for any company (save perhaps Microsoft) to buy. But it's easy for Yahoo to use its highly valued shares as currency to make acquisitions of its own. "You have to use your paper while you have it," said David Braunschvig, a managing director at Lazard Freres. "It costs you nothing to get big." While Yahoo and Amazon have, so far, made relatively small acquisitions, their market values will give them the opportunity to make even bigger deals this year, investment bankers contend. Meanwhile the rise in Internet stock values creates nothing but headaches for traditional retailers competing with companies like Amazon and for big media companies competing with Yahoo. These companies cannot pay as high a price for acquisitions, nor can they offer their employees high-flying stock bonuses. "If you are a big company, you won't be able to keep your engineers for a long time if they see all their buddies at small public companies become very rich from the stock options," Mr. Braunschvig said. The solution for an existing company is to take a part-interest in a publicly traded Internet company. The prototype of his arrangement is the Walt Disney Company's purchase of 43 percent of Infoseek, another struggling search engine company. But rather than paying cash, Disney exchanged Starwave, an Internet production company it owned, and only $90 million in cash for Infoseek stock worth $900 million. In addition to providing financial benefits, such deals help the bigger companies keep up with the frantic pace of Silicon Valley. Merger experts predict that media companies will make alliances this year with the remaining independent portal companies, including Lycos, Excite, Alta Vista and maybe even Yahoo. Ironically, for all the appeal and wealth of the publicly traded Internet startup company, and all the high-profile initial public offerings last year, statistics show that small technology companies are less likely to go public than ever before. There certainly will be more public offerings this year, like those last year of Ebay and Broadcast.com. Coming up early this year is the offering for iVillage, a female-oriented Internet service. Later, most likely, will be an offering for Buy.com, an ambitious on-line store that has grown rapidly by selling computer products at cost in hopes of making money on advertising. Yet statistics compiled by Broadview, an investment bank, show that last year, for the first time, there were fewer initial public offerings of small technology companies than there were acquisitions of them by bigger companies. Stock can be sold more easily and with less notice when it's in a larger company than when a founder bails out of his own company's stock. Holding onto stock in one's own company after going public, however, has not proven to be prudent. "Half the companies that have gone public since 1991 are trading below their I.P.O. value," said Alec L. Ellison, a managing director of Broadview. So for those companies that don't see their way to being titans, a quick sale to a more established operation may be both easier and more lucrative than going it alone and risking irrelevancy. "By going public," Mr. Ellison said, "they may not get the strategic resources that a sale to Big Brother would provide." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
OUTLOOK 1999: MEDIA & TECHNOLOGY -- PUBLISHING;
A Marriage Maelstrom Industrywide, as the High-Technology Plot Thickens
body: After a year of page-turner mergers and major deals with unexpected plot twists, the book industry is preparing for still more radical changes that could come with further consolidation, expanded on-line sales and increased clout for the nation's leading bookseller, Barnes & Noble Inc. "It's fair to say that we probably have experienced as an industry more change in the last 12 months than in any period in the history of the business," said Jack Romanos, president of Simon & Schuster. "It's changed in every respect, from the mergers and acquisitions activities on the publishing and distribution side to the creation of the behemoth publishing company," added Mr. Romanos, whose own company was recently split up by its parent, Viacom Inc., and its educational division sold to the British media conglomerate Pearson P.L.C. Last year was the season for whale watching, with behemoths swallowing behemoths: the German media conglomerate Bertelsmann A.G. announced in March that it would buy Random House; then in October it formed a partnership with Barnes & Noble in its on-line venture, Barnesandnoble.com. A few weeks later, the bookstore chain announced that it had agreed to buy the leading book wholesaler, Ingram Book Group, a deal that seemed to roil the book industry in the unitedstates more than any other deal. David R. Brodwin, an associate partner at Andersen Consulting, the management consulting firm, said that behind the scenes it was already apparent that some of the major publishers were starting to explore counter moves. There is also the possibility, he said, that one of the major Internet portal -- or Web gateway -- companies will use its overvalued stock to invest in or buy a publisher. "We know that there are conversations taking place to put together a consortium of some sort to counter the concentration of power that the Ingram and Barnes & Noble combination represents," Mr. Brodwin said. Although he declined to name the companies, he did say they might be considering a purchase of the second-largest wholesaler, Baker & Taylor. "The publishers have lost power over recent years as retailing has consolidated," Mr. Brodwin added. "And to the extent that the consolidation continues, the publishers will lose or are threatened with further erosion of their market power, which could be reflected in further price increases and pressures on terms of trade such as credit." The urge to consolidate has hit the entire book market -- from regional distributors that are buying smaller independent publishers to foreign media conglomerates that are forming alliances across borders, including German acquisitions in the unitedstates or moves by the largest French publisher, the Hachette Livre unit of Lagardere Groupe, to acquire a majority stake in a British consumer book company, Orion Publishing Group. In this frantic chess game, the unglamorous side of the business -- distribution -- has become critical for publishing companies trying to deliver double-digit profits for their corporate owners in a sluggish market for popular books. From 1996 to 1997, consumer book purchases grew by less than 1 percent, failing to keep pace with population growth, according to the Book Industry Study Group, a nonprofit research organization based in newyork, in its most recent report on purchase patterns. With sales growing slowly, distribution has become a critical element for publishers and booksellers. It is particularly important in the book fight that has gripped the leading on-line booksellers, Amazon.com Inc. and Barnes & Noble, which are trying to cut costs and speed delivery to customers. Thomas Middelhoff, the chief executive of Bertelsmann who personally negotiated the deal to buy a 50 percent stake in Barnes & Noble's on-line site, said he had set a goal of overtaking the market-leading Amazon.com by the year 2000. Most publishers and analysts expect on-line sales to increase this year. Such competition is causing some trepidation among independent booksellers, a group whose share of the market amounts to 17 percent. Large chains make up 25 percent, but today most books are sold outside traditional outlets, in discount stores, warehouse clubs and book clubs, and through on-line retailers. "Internet book-selling will grow significantly," said Albert N. Greco, an associate professor of business at Fordham University, who tracks the publishing industry. "The speed, convenience and availability of on-line retailing will overshadow traditional bookstores and cut into their margins." The electronic retail war has helped to push some of the bigger alliances that have taken place, including the Bertelsmann-Barnesandnoble.com-Ingram linkage. Such alliances are raising broader questions about what the ultimate impact will be on the diversity of literature in the future. "The overriding issue is increasing concentration," said William Petrocelli, co-owner of Book Passage, an independent bookstore in Corte Madera, Calif. "I view it as a major threat to writers and readers, as well as to independent booksellers. It seems to me that as fewer and fewer people are making critical decisions along the chain of distribution for books, the more likely it is that diversity, quality and innovation will suffer." < http://www.nytimes.com

title:
OUTLOOK 1999: MEDIA & TECHNOLOGY -- TEL ECOMMUNICATIONS;
2 Industries Unite to Pave the Way for High-Speed Internet Access
body: Anyone who has used the Internet at both work and home knows that those are vastly different experiences. Whatever the metaphor they choose -- jack rabbit and tortoise, water and molasses, heaven and hell -- most people who access the Net from home via dial-up modems miss a big part of what cyberspace ought to be all about: high-speed, low-hassle access to text, graphics, audio and video. The problem, of course, is that typical modems are simply not able to do the Internet full justice. And most consumers have no other economically realistic options for connecting. But if the telecommunications and cable television industries have their way, that will start to change in a big way this year, beginning a process that could bring quick Internet connections from the office to the living room just as Henry Ford brought the automobile from the mansion to the middle class. Coupled with the advent of truly low-cost personal computers, the mass deployment of cheap, reliable, high-speed Internet links for residential consumers could have an impact as deep as Ford's. After all, it was not until cars became less of a novelty for the rich than a necessity for the rest that it made sense to actually pave roads. Likewise, the broad availability of high-speed cyberspace connections could foster the development of new sorts of applications that make today's Internet look like a rutted cart path. That, at least, is the bet that many of the nation's largest telephone and cable television companies have made or are getting ready to make. And 1999 will probably be the year that those two industries, with their vastly different financial, regulatory and cultural dimensions, join their battle to control the future of how the nation's consumers enter cyberspace. "This is the biggest single opportunity that exists in all of communications," said Howard Anderson, the managing director of the Yankee Group, a high-technology consulting firm in Boston. "It will get very serious and this, 1999, is the year that we will see competition." The cable television and telephone industries are trying to use radically different technologies to deliver huge amounts of data to homes, but the financial opportunity for each of them is impressive. Even the most aggressive projections peg the number of homes that had high-speed Internet access at the end of last year at something less than 750,000 (a vast majority of those using cable modems rather than the telephone technology known as asymmetric digital subscriber line, or A.D.S.L.) Over all, somewhere around 45 percent of the nation's 100 million homes have computers, and only about half of those, or around 22.5 million, are on line at all. U S West Inc. has been the most aggressive of the Bell local phone companies in deploying A.D.S.L. technology, planning to sign up as many as 25,000 customers by the end of last year. Michael Rouleau, a U S West vice president for marketing, estimated that about 10 percent of cyberspace-using homes would pay extra for high-speed access. Thomas A. Jermoluk, the chairman of the At Home Corporation, the cable-modem venture backed by many of the nation's large cable system operators, said his company's business plan was to win 20 percent of any given market's on-line homes as customers after four years. Split the difference at 15 percent and the potential market today -- at $40 a month a home, which is roughly what both the telephone and cable companies are charging -- comes to about $1.6 billion. In the communications world, that is not a large number. Mr. Anderson of the Yankee Group, however, believes that fully half of the on-line homes would pay $40 a month for high-speed Internet access. If that were true, and if, in a few years, the proportion of unitedstates homes that had computers rose to 60 percent and if the proportion of on-line homes also rose to 60 percent, then the market opportunity would be a much more significant $8.7 billion. But even that is just the entrance to the potential gold mine. That $40 a month just covers basic access to cyberspace. What the telephone and cable companies may try to do is to leverage that relationship with users to sell them additional services, ranging from email to clothing shopping to video games. Of course, standing in the way of such incremental revenue are some very daunting fixed costs. It generally takes around $700 to upgrade each phone or cable line to provide high-speed data access. (Additional options, like offering Internet-based phone service over a cable line, cost even more.) So, for instance, because At Home's affiliates serve about 60 million customers, Mr. Jermoluk said, it would cost a staggering $42 billion to get all of them on line using cable modems. And so the deployment goes slowly. Other than competition between each other, however, the biggest force pushing the cable and telephone companies to deploy high-speed data systems may not be consumers, but the computer industry. In this day of 450-megahertz processors and video cards with as many transistors as Pentium chips, the biggest bottleneck in the computer system is the link to other computers. If the connections do not increase in speed, the prospect of buying a new computer every year or two becomes less compelling. That is why companies like Compaq Computer and Microsoft are perhaps more eager for widespread high-speed data connections than even the most intense Internet surfer. For the local phone and cable companies, the Internet is the future. For the computer companies, it is now. < http://www.nytimes.com

title: A Rural Town Takes On Obstacles to Internet Ties
body: Even unimaginative futurists predict that some not-so-distant day, geography will barely matter. Humanity's web of electronic connections will trump it utterly. That will be particularly nice for isolated spots like this long-depressed former mill and factory town, cupped in the Berkshire Mountains in the remotest corner of Massachusetts. But here is the transitional rub: Sometimes the places that most need to overcome geography have the hardest time doing it, because they are handicapped by their distance from the nearest access point to the long-distance carriers that offer Internet connections. In other words, words used by members of Berkshire Connect, a task force formed by local civic and business leaders with state help to address the problem, high-speed Internet connections like T-1 lines are too expensive here. Connections often cost double, triple or more what a user would pay in Boston or Springfield, Mass., because of the distance-sensitive telephone charges to reach the far-off big carrier. Telephone companies say that with the region's sparse population, local demand is not sufficient to justify laying new lines that would cut the cost. So the electronic road to the rest of the world can sometimes seem as annoyingly narrow as the winding local Mohawk Trail. That hinders the region's hopes, just beginning to be realized, of replacing its dead mills with engines of the new information economy: high-tech start-ups, new media businesses and other companies that project their presence on the Internet. Berkshire County is not alone in its problem, said Donald Dubendorf, a Williamstown lawyer and head of Berkshire Connect's action committee. "Lots of rural counties find themselves disconnected and presenting too small a demand profile" to prompt telephone companies to improve and thus cheapen Internet connections, Mr. Dubendorf said. "There are parallels in history -- rural electrification in the 30's, 40's and 50's." Mr. Dubendorf also found a parallel in history for what Berkshire Connect is trying to do: the cooperatives that Western farmers formed when the new intercontinental railroads asked too much to bring their goods to market. They pooled their produce and sought ways to buy or build railroad spurs, he said. About a century later, Berkshire Connect appears about to settle on information-age equivalents of the farmers' tactics. The group is about to issue business and technological plans, and members say they are expected to involve some laying of fiber optic cable. In a very 90's economic development tactic, the group is expected to call for drawing the millions needed from public and private money. For decades, Berkshire County residents have been at odds over improving road connections to the Massachusetts Turnpike. With no consensus over routes, nothing has been done. But, task force members say, there is no not-in-my-back-yard attitude about better telephone lines. Everyone seems to want them. Especially two forces: a handful of tech upstarts, most of whom have come from Williams College and into Williamstown, down the road from here, in the last five years; and the high-tech Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art, scheduled to open in May in North Adams. The young founders of Tripod, one of the most visited sites on the Web, do not complain about the high telephone rates. The machines that handle their Internet traffic are based in New Jersey anyway, at a company that specializes in baby-sitting for such servers. And the higher connection cost for their Williamstown office is offset by their rent on a sprawling former factory floor: $2.50 a square foot. Per year. Bought by Lycos last year for $58 million, Tripod is not hampered by connection costs and has been increasing its staff from 40 last year to 80 now, to perhaps 150 by the end of the fiscal year, said Bo Peabody, 27, Tripod's president. Still, said Kara Berklich, 26, Tripod's director for communications, it is cheering on the push for better connections because one of its goals is to help bring jobs to the region. Matthew C. Harris, a classmate of Mr. Peabody and Ms. Berklich at Williams and a venture capitalist who seeks to lure more information-age companies to the region, said the price of Internet connection was not a deal breaker when he tried to bring companies here, but it was a liability. "The problem is for marketing, that it labels us a backwater," said Mr. Harris, managing director of The Berkshires Capital Investors in Williamstown. It is a disadvantage, Mr. Harris said, of about the same magnitude as high property or electricity costs. He said he tried to counter it by saying, "You're going to pay more than in Boston, but your rent will be 10 percent what it would be there, and your salaries 20 percent lower because cost of living is lower." The problem looks more serious in neighboring North Adams at the Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art. Known hereabouts as "MASS MoCA," the institution will offer performing arts as well as exhibitions, and aims to be a "creative campus" with an emphasis on the intersection of art and technology. The museum already offers a technology center that allows people to use computers and take courses on them free; it also plans to rent offices in its 700,000-square-foot abandoned mill complex to technology-related companies. It plans to offer prospective tenants as "smart" a building as possible, with video teleconferencing and more. But to do that now would cost an estimated $35,000 a month, more than twice what it would cost in Boston, said Brett McDowell, the museum's information and media technology director. "If Berkshire Connect succeeds in building its own line, the cost would be the same as Boston or newyork." For now, when a company reaches the point that it needs a T-1 line here, Mr. McDowell said, its manager often ends up protesting: "You're telling me that just to access the Internet at the rates I need is five times more expensive than my rent?" That, Mr. McDowell said, "is when the six-man new media company moves to Boston." One MASS MoCA tenant, Kleiser-Walczak Construction, a film special-effects and animation company, pays about $7,000 a month to keep in touch with its other offices in newyork and Hollywood, said its president, Jeff Kleiser. "To be here, we have to pay the price," Mr. Kleiser said. Still, he added, the price brings admission to a "once-in-a-lifetime experience:" watching the museum and economic changes help North Adams metamorphose "from a post-industrial wasteland to a new high-tech-connected art community." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: The cost of Internet connections concerns the Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art, which is under construction in North Adams. (Keith Meyers/The newyork Times)

title:
BLACKBOARD: WEB SITES;
Matchmaker, Matchmaker
body: More new terrain for the Web: college recruitment. The Scholastic Registry, an on-line repository of resumes, aims to connect college admissions directors with college-bound students. The service (www.scholastic registry.com) works like this: Students create an academic profile and promote their talents in registries for specialties like performing arts, computers and sports. Directors of admissions browse the profiles for candidates. "Say a college has had their entire orchestra graduate and needs a trumpet player and an oboe and someone to play the sax," said George J. Bednar, who began the service about a year ago. "An admissions director can just click on the music registry and, boom, there's their band. "There's also an increased need for diversity at schools," he said. "This helps schools create that." While the service has been endorsed by the National Association of Secondary School Principals, it is not entirely altruistic. A student pays a $50 enrollment fee to post a profile. Mr. Bednar says several thousand have posted their curriculums vitae, and about 200 colleges, from Carnegie-Mellon to Northwestern to Yale, are registered with the site. The jury is still out on how well the registry works. Stacy Zagar, the director of undergraduate marketing at Stephens Institute of Technology, in Hoboken, N.J., noted a few kinks, such as the system's one-sidedness. "You don't know if the students you're contacting are interested in your school," she said. But she has sent more than 40 letters and brochures to students on the site. "It's a good way to get students from geographically diverse areas," she said. "Right now we only travel in limited ways outside New Jersey. I can reach someone in Idaho who might not know about Stephens." JESSE McKINLEY http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
Business;
Playing 'The Price Is Right' With Windows
body: IF the Microsoft Corporation is the predatory monopolist that the Government claims it is, why isn't the price of its monopoly product -- its industry-standard Windows operating system -- higher? That question is a central focus of a new study of Microsoft and the Government's antitrust suit against the company by Robert E. Hall, an economist at Stanford University's Hoover Institution. Mr. Hall helped draw up the Justice Department's 1995 consent decree with Microsoft. The 48-page paper, "National Policy on Microsoft: A Neutral Perspective," written with Mr. Hall's son, Chris Hall, an independent software developer, is being published this week and will be available on the Internet at www.netecon.com. The paper says the Government's evidence puts it on solid ground in challenging some of Microsoft's contracts as violations of Section 1 of the Sherman Act, which condemns contracts that restrain trade. In an interview, Mr. Hall pointed in particular to Microsoft's pacts with America Online and other Internet service providers. These contracts require the service providers to guarantee that 75 percent or more of their customers use Microsoft's browser software, crimping the opportunity for its main rival in the browser market, Netscape Communications. For a company with so much market power, a clause like that "shows that Microsoft really does push the limits," Mr. Hall said. On the pro-Microsoft side of the ledger, the Halls find little merit in the march of Government witnesses confidently proclaiming that operating systems and browsers are distinct products, and that Microsoft fused them only to squelch competition. "Given the complete malleability of software," the authors wrote, "this is a debate at about the intellectual level of trying to decide if the Gulf of Mexico is part of the Atlantic Ocean." The Halls' paper focuses most sharply on the contentious subject of Windows pricing. They say "the low price of Windows looks nothing like a monopoly price," amounting as it does to less than 5 percent of the total price of a personal computer. The "low" price of Windows is a theme that will be forcefully presented by Richard Schmalensee, an economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, when he takes the stand as a witness for Microsoft. Mr. Schmalensee has been making the argument since the early 1990's, when he prepared a paper expounding the low-price thesis for the Federal Trade Commission, which investigated Microsoft before the Justice Department did. The Windows-pricing issue is crucial to the outcome of the case and, if the Government wins, to the remedies it can seek from the court. A narrow victory under Section 1 of the Sherman Act would probably yield merely a court order that Microsoft must make its contracts less restrictive. The Justice Department did not sue Microsoft to accomplish so little. But to win a broader, Section 2 victory, the Government must prove, among other things, that Microsoft has a monopoly, that its exclusionary conduct against potential rivals like Netscape has a "dangerous probability" of preventing a challenge to its monopoly and that its conduct has caused substantial harm to consumers. Only then will stronger remedies -- including, perhaps, breaking up Microsoft -- move onto the agenda. TO try to show gouging of consumers, the Government produced in court an internal Microsoft document showing that from 1990 to 1996 the average price it charged personal-computer makers for licensing Windows rose to $49.40 from $19.03. Its share of the PC's total price grew fivefold, to 2.5 percent. The Justice Department also produced an email written on Dec. 16, 1997, by Joachim Kempin, a senior Microsoft executive, to William H. Gates, the chairman, and other company executives on the subject of Windows prices charged to PC makers. "While we have increased our prices over the last 10 years," Mr. Kempin wrote, "other component prices have come down and continue to come down." The Justice Department says Microsoft's ability to raise Windows prices is strong evidence that the company is overcharging. The Halls are not convinced. Given Windows' 250 million users and market share of more than 90 percent, the authors wrote, PC makers would want it even if it cost "twice or even 10 times as much." Microsoft contends that the Windows price is restrained by a sense that some competitive threat, though not yet in sight, is behind the next corner -- a fearful perspective that is all over parts of the December 1997 memo. In it, Mr. Kempin wrote that a big manufacturer like Compaq Computer, or a coalition of PC makers, could finance development of a competing operating system. Or, he wrote, if the chip maker Intel enters "our business, it will get ugly." (Compaq, incidentally, is sending an executive to testify in Microsoft's defense.) For his part, Mr. Hall does not believe that the seemingly low price of Windows is explained by competition, real or feared. Instead, he suggests that the Windows price is part of Microsoft's broader strategy of making Windows PC's as cheap as possible, hooking new users and making them steady repeat buyers, not only of future generations of Windows but also of higher-priced Microsoft products like its Office suite of word processing, spreadsheet and data base software. "The Government has to make an argument as to why Microsoft keeps the price of Windows low as part of its monopoly strategy, which harms consumers over all," Mr. Hall said. "It's possible, but the Government hasn't done it yet." http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: An economist's report says Microsoft's prices for the Windows operating system do not appear abusively high. (Associated Press)  Graph: "Is It a Whip Hand?" Much of the Government's antitrust suit against Microsoft turns on whether the company has monopoly power over the price of its operating system. Evidence in the trial can be interpreted to support either side's case.  The Government's argument Microsoft has a history of dictating higher prices.  "...While we have increased our prices over the last 10 years other component prices have come down and continue to come down. ..." The graph shows the revenue per computer as compared to the percent of the total cost.   Microsoft's argument Our prices are low, and the risk of future competition keeps them that way. I am convinced they have been thinking about this for some time." Excerpt from Microsoft memo  The price of Windows is low Daily cost at best available prices, from a Microsoft briefing paper.
