title:
NEW YORK ON LINE;
Where the Lions Stand Guard, a Mouse Can Explore
body: Nothing will ever replace a visit to the newyork Public Library, where the big news last year was the reopening of the Main Reading Room in November after a renovation that took 16 months and cost $15 million. But the next best thing to a visit, for scholars, students and the lay public, is an electronic sojourn at the library's Web site, which was also renovated recently.  WHAT YOU SEE -- There are four main sections, covering catalogues, electronic resources, Internet search tools and, most intriguing, digital library collections, which include still images and video and audio clips from the library's more than 40 million research items. The catalogue of most interest for scholars is Catnyp (which stands for catalogue of the newyork Public Library), which focuses on materials that do not circulate outside the library. These include not only books and periodicals, but manuscripts, maps, microfilms, music scores, prints and photographs. If you type "medieval illuminated manuscripts" into Catnyp it will tell you that the library has 39 related titles, including the Chichester Cathedral Prayer Book, which was illuminated, or decorated, in England by a Lancastrian scribe and artist during the Episcopate of Reginald Peacock (1450-1457). For books and other materials that circulate to the public at the branch libraries, there is LEO (Library Entrance Online), which requires a library card and special software to use. LEO allows card holders to survey available books and to reserve books at their nearest branch library. Then there is "Electronic Resources," a collection of 11 data bases like "Books in Print," which, despite its name, is a list of 1.9 million books both in and out of print. "Search the Internet" directs visitors to staff-recommended Web sites, like "The Catapult Museum Online," which looks not only at the ancient "katapultos," Greek for a weapon known as as a "shield piercer," but an airplane-launching catapult developed by the Wright Brothers (http://www.nzp.com/02contents.html). "Digital Library Collections" is a growing group of video and audio clips from the library. "African American Women Writers of the 19th Century," for example, includes the text of an 1861 biography, "Louisa Picquet, the Octoroon: A Tale of Southern Slave Life." One of the most intriguing parts of the site is the Louis Armstrong Jazz Oral History Project, a series of filmed interviews with jazz figures describing their art. McCoy Tyner, the pianist, plays disciplined, elegant music, in contrast to the nervous energy and unfinished sentences of his filmed interview. "I use the piano to write, to hear my instrument in my ear," he says, his hands chopping the air. "I think that it inspires me to write, because you hear all the voices, and hear everything there."  LINKS -- Thousands.  WHAT YOU GET -- A work in progress that already yields many rewards.   ANTHONY RAMIREZ  newyork Public Library Online http://www.nypl.org/online.html http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title:
Private Sector;
Down for the Count, a Stock Becomes a Net Heavyweight
body: For George Horowitz, chairman of the Active Apparel Group, reviving his small clothing company's dead-in-the-cellar share price often seemed like the name of his line of active wear, "The Grind." The thinly traded stock wallowed around at $1.25 a share as recently as Monday. Then, Mr. Horowitz, 48, discovered the Internet. When he announced that his company's retail Web site had started operations, Active Apparel became an instant darling of the Internet stock-trading community. Never mind that it had yet to peddle a single pair of its Everlast boxing trunks electronically. The stock hit $19 by Tuesday. Mr. Horowitz's stake surged from $758,000 to $10.8 million. Since then, investor ardor has cooled and the stock has slipped to $8.125, but it still managed a 550 percent gain for the week. "Such big changes are a little unnerving," Mr. Horowitz said. In fact, the volatility has taken a toll. Mr. Horowitz said he felt "a little under the weather from all this running around," including appearances on CNBC and CNN. "I just hope that when all this settles down, we hold some of the premium. We should, I think, because investors are just beginning to realize the value in our company."   JOSEPH KAHN http://www.nytimes.com

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Notes From Cyberclass
body: Adult education, the concept, has never much appealed to me. Volunteer for more school? No thanks. I was quite pleased, more than 20 years ago, when it was done with the first time. Every now and then I still have that dream about being unprepared for a final exam. (For some reason, the exam is always in French.) There's something about entering a classroom that feels like a withdrawal from the actual business of the world, participation in which I'd earned by virtue of enduring two degrees' worth of pedagogy. I'm not one of those people who get nostalgic about college: I like to get paid for my work, not graded on it. Nonetheless, augmenting one's education isn't anything you can really be against, and I decided to go back to class, via the Internet, spurred by an interest in exploring cyberspace and an instinct that self-improvement wouldn't feel so burdensome if it were a little more convenient. Indeed, by many measures, going to school on line is convenient. You can go undressed. You can go in the middle of the night. You can go in Kansas City. You can participate in discussions to whatever extent you choose, sounding off overbearingly or keeping smugly silent, without having to observe the ordinary etiquette of classroom decorum. You can, in other words, construct your own private experience. Interestingly, this ends up having its burdensome side. For convenience, you pay with responsibility and accountability. On-line school is a venue for self-starters, which may be one reason that, though 10 people enrolled in the class I took, only half were ever heard from after the first few weeks. The first problem any prospective student faces is simply deciding what school to attend. The global reach of Internet technology obviates geography and transportation as considerations in making such a choice. From my home in Chicago I could get to class at the University of California as easily as at the New School for Social Research in newyork, or to any of the hundreds of places that now offer Internet classes. Any thorough perusal of on-line catalogues is so time-consuming as to be daunting. I gave up rather quickly, choosing the New School (www.dialnsa.edu) after checking out only one or two others because it offered the class I wanted -- a playwriting workshop -- and because it was familiar. Until a year or so ago, I lived in newyork, not far from the campus. Call me homesick. Of the nine other people who enrolled in the same class, all but one were newyorkers. The exception was Angela Davis, a Federal prosecutor in Los Angeles. Ms. Davis, whose contributions to the class documents were as voluminous and thorough as legal briefs, told me that she chose the New School because she was impressed by the resume of the instructor, Robert Montgomery (particularly that he had attended Yale Drama School and had had a play of his own produced at the Joseph Papp Public Theater), and because she wanted a drama class taught in newyork, which is, after all, the center of drama. "I was delighted that I had the opportunity to take this 'newyork' class from my home in Los Angeles," she wrote to me in an email message. The second problem is one of access. In one way, real school is a passive experience. You show up in class, the curriculum gets flung at you and maybe, if you're not asleep, it sticks. Cyberschool is a bit more active; you find your classroom and negotiate around it. There's a facility to be learned -- the deft burrowing of a computer mouse, not necessarily a natural thing for a middle-aged man who is habitually behind the techno-curve. It took me about an hour to get comfortable with the mechanics of going to school. (O.K., not as onerous as settling into a dorm room.) How it works at the New School is this: after on-line registration -- and payment via credit card (the nine-week class costs $450 for a non-credit student) -- I was sent a set of passwords that granted me access to the on-line campus, which is essentially a set of Web sites. A handful of them are accessible to all students, no matter what classes they are taking. One is an orientation site, where tips for efficient campus travel are dispensed. One is a student lounge, where students can mingle, posting messages either for general consumption or for individual correspondents. (The tone of the conversation was distinctly eager and friendly -- "Hi everybody! This is my first on-line class and I'm really psyched!" -- much like what I remember freshman orientation to have been so many eons ago. Some things transfer to cyberlife undisturbed.) For some reason, there is also a room set aside specifically to discuss movies. Finally, there is a separate site for each class for which a student has registered, and inside that site is another set of sites set up by the professor. In the playwriting class, Mr. Montgomery had his own "podium," as it were, from which he gave "lectures," providing, about once a week, disquisitions on elements of playwriting -- things like story, character, dialogue -- mostly tips for us students to keep in mind as we composed our own scenes. Each of us had our own site as well, in which we were to post our work for the consumption of our classmates and in which Mr. Montgomery and our classmates could post commentary. Since we all had access to all sites, we were able to keep tabs on our mutual progress. Once I got the hang of it, I found it remarkably efficient and ingenious. There were some obvious drawbacks. Any classroom certainly is meant to take advantage of social intercourse and the dynamic that develops when people are in actual contact with one another. On line this is lost, by definition, but in a playwriting seminar what is also lost is the opportunity for the writers to hear their work read out loud, which it is, of course, meant to be. "The presence thing, that's what's missing," Mr. Montgomery, who also teaches playwriting in "real space" at the New School, told me in a phone interview after the course was over, when I announced my intention to write about the class. "As a playwright you have to know how to include it, the presence of an actor, in your work." Nonetheless, the semblance of a writing seminar became quite persuasive; the discourse involved healthy doses of both insightful criticism and self-serving blather, just what aspiring writers sound like when they gather in person. And because people are forced to write out their reactions, the communication was relatively lean. In writing, the speaking-to-hear-yourself-speak impulse is curtailed. There's no blurting. People take care to say what they mean, not just what has crossed their minds, so even when someone had something silly to say, it was clearly expressed. (For that alone, gratitude is in order.) Writing focuses thought; I've rarely found that illustrated so acutely as I did during this class. And, in a funny way, even without the familiar interaction in a classroom, the human dynamic asserted itself. Personalities became evident. People were supportive mostly, testy occasionally. Alliances were formed. And a general allegiance to Mr. Montgomery was forged, even though none of us ever laid eyes on him. (In four years of teaching on line, he told me over the phone, "this is the longest conversation with a student I've ever had.") Mr. Montgomery, 52, who has taught playwriting for 20 years, is the author of several produced plays, including "Subject to Fits," a musical takeoff on Dostoyevsky's "Idiot," which featured Ben Kingsley when it was produced in London in 1972. He proved to be a careful, diligent reader and critic, offering firm but gently worded suggestions that were both conceptual and quite specific (for instance, line cuts and phrasing changes). I have a terrible time beginning things, but something Mr. Montgomery wrote early on -- that each scene is like a play in microcosm, with the characters wrestling with conflict and moving to resolve it -- helped me decide that my play should start with the two main characters already angry at each other. Otherwise, I'd have had them dithering around, trying to make each other mad, but only frustrating the audience as they frustrated themselves. My classmates -- a diverse bunch and distinctly adult, with several, like me, in their 40's -- included an actress-turned-hospital administrator, two massage therapists, a nurse and an executive with a finance company. They were all, at least the ones who stuck around, serious about writing for the stage. I had wanted to take playwriting because it is a skill I admire, and because I write about the theater as a journalist. It couldn't hurt to get a little closer to my subject. But it was daunting to hear about the projects the others were working on, most of which were more ambitious than my own, an ostensible comedy about two old friends in a battle over a cheap Manhattan apartment. Ms. Davis had already made considerable progress on a historical drama set in 16th-century England. Another was adapting Dickens's "Christmas Carol" with gay characters in a contemporary Manhattan setting. A third was writing about a man who, unhappy in love, was getting nighttime visitations and advice from the ghosts of historical figures like Lord Byron, who spoke to him in rhymed couplets. The hospital administrator was working on a play about Anna Mae Aquash, an American Indian activist whose 1976 murder in South Dakota has never been solved. Naturally, some of the writers were more polished than others, but overall the reading was absorbing. That was a blessing, as there was a lot of it. Those taking the course for credit were required to produce 15 finished pages, and even with half the class falling by the wayside, several people proved to be prolific revisers. (I'm a prolific procrastinator myself, and by the end, I'd only offered an opening scene of four pages. The verdict was that they were promising. Yeah, yeah.) But more than the actual scripts, what also had to be read was the ongoing discussion, and herein lies the main difference between real school and on-line school. The latter may be more user-friendly than the former, but inattention costs more. Though there are no occasions to show up for, that doesn't mean there are no classes; rather, what it means is that the course is one continuous, semesterlong session. In real school, if you cut a class, it is gone, over, unreclaimable. On line, however, you never miss anything. Whatever commentary is offered by the teacher or by classmates is recorded, and whenever you sign on and check in, it is all there, a linear record of what has gone on in your absence. Which means that if you don't check in for a week, a week's worth of discussion is there to be perused. Once, when I didn't sign on for 10 days, there were nearly 200 entries waiting for me when I returned, well over 100 pages of reading before I could begin crafting any of my own responses to my classmates' work. "The interesting thing is that people think an on-line course is going to be easier than a classroom course, but I've spent a lot more time with this one than with the others I've taken at the New School," said Joseph Carman, 42, one of the massage therapists, who is finishing a degree at the New School, both on line and in class, that he left incomplete at Fordham University more than a decade ago. "It takes an awful lot of time, logging on, and then deciding where to go first, and reading other people's work and making a thoughtful response." Mr. Carman, who said he signed into class about four times a week, finished two long scenes during the semester and said he was going to re-enroll so he could finish a draft of his play. His was the one with the Byronic couplets. "It would be interesting to get everybody in a room without identifying ourselves," he said, "to see if we could pick out who's who." I'm thinking about re-enrolling myself. I'd only managed to sign on for class about once a week, and I'd only managed to produce those four pages. My classmates reacted to me accordingly. In the end, my Web site had less activity than any of the others. The salient point, I realized, is that whatever I got out of the class, I earned. Which may be the ultimate definition of adult education. http://www.nytimes.com

title:
VIEW;
Going, Going, Gone on Line
body: I JUST bid $180 for a Donna Karan black cashmere sweater I've never seen. It's supposed to be new, but for all I know it has spent the last three years locked in a closet with bulimic moths. Until very recently I had assumed that anyone foolish enough to buy anything through an Internet auction had too much time, money or both. But today, I find myself eager to shell out $100 for a used scarf. How did this happen? Over the last few months, most of my friends have gone berserk over Ebay, the on-line auction house offering everything from Corvettes to Furbies. Ebay is like a flea market with a potentially limitless number of booths -- and an all-important time limit on the bidding. You can send in your maximum bid and hope for the best or be a jockey and neurotically track the item's progress minute by minute. One friend said she knew she had gone overboard when a dealer sent her an email beginning, "Hello, Darling." Everyone I knew was urging me to join the fun. I resisted. Which wasn't hard. I hate shopping -- that mad-dog look in everyone's eyes, the doctor's-office feeling of taking off my clothes behind a curtain. And I especially hate the overabundance of choices: too many Fendi bags in one place and I hyperventilate.  For years I've strong-armed my best friend, who was approximately my shoe and dress size, to accompany me on every shopping expedition so she can try on stuff that might fit me. But recently, she lost weight and I gained. So it's perhaps not surprising that she was the first one to suggest I try Ebay. She used the one argument guaranteed to get me to the Web site: Ebay, she promised, would help me realize my ultimate goal of never having to leave my apartment. There are several reasons why Ebay can make a rabid shopper out of someone like me. First, the system allows you to limit choices. Sure, you could get waylaid if you're not careful -- which is how I found myself craving a blood-red evening dress yet bidding on a blood-pressure gauge after typing in "blood" and "read" by mistake. But if you're careful, Ebay can target the object of your desire with the precision of a cruise missile. Typing the words "Chanel" "shoes," "size 10" means I never even have to think about Guccis, about Ferragamos, or about whether Chanel 9's might fit. For that matter, who knows whether a Chanel 10 in this particular style will fit: but if it's a great bargain, if it's Chanel and if I can capture it for me, me, me -- I become possessed. And who knows what new merchandise tomorrow will bring? That's why one can't afford not to check in with Ebay once a day. Twice. O.K., 23 times -- but who's counting? Ebay also has its literary pleasures -- and I don't mean just the used-book auctions. (A signed first-edition Anita Brookner was mine for $27!) Many Ebay sellers seem to be frustrated philosophers. My favorite is a seller of vintage clothing who goes by the name enoki. Apparently, enoki sees old cheerleader outfits, deb evening gowns and the like as her chance to comment on the human condition. A recent typical entry, offering a pair of boys' cowboy boots: "Back in the 50's, boys were encouraged to be 'boys,' complete with little Western outfits and capguns. Nowadays, Mommy is so worried about raising a serial killer that she encourages little Andy to play with A B C blocks and leave the guns to the Marines." Take that, J. Peterman. Also undeniably piquant, even to a full-time nonshopper, is the covert market for fetishistic goods hidden among the wholesome designer fashions. I found this out -- quite accidentally, of course -- when I typed in "Calvin Klein" and discovered ads for used underwear amid the jeans, jackets and eyeglasses. "Help a college kid continue with his education" runs an ad for three pairs of pre-owned briefs. On Ebay, my polite and timid department-store persona vanishes. I am not a lumpy size 10 hoping the dressing room has those very special skinny mirrors. Invisible and anonymous, I am a bronzed beach bunny who'll look just fabulous in that vinyl halter mesh-chain dress. But of all its advantages over other forms of shopping, the real selling point is that Ebay allows for -- indeed, encourages -- the consumer version of road rage. If I go to a normal sale, I am far too genteel to elbow anyone out of the way for that last Escada winter-white double-breasted jacket. And real-live auctions leave me exhausted and anxious -- loathing myself for being so grasping and loathing everyone else more for being greedier and richer than I. On line, I am a shopping warrior, able to vanquish every foe with a click of my mouse. You say $80 for that Hermes scarf with the galloping horsies? Die, Earthlings! I've read the tales of fraud and disappointment on Ebay. I understand that the $60 Ralph Lauren square-hoop earrings I just bought for $15 might not be Lauren at all and that the gently worn blue Versace jacket I'm furiously bidding on might not even fit. Maybe there are shills, friends of the sellers' bidding up items. Maybe I'm the shill. (One time I upped the ante on the highest bidder -- only to discover that the ID of the previous highest bidder was mine.) Who cares? I am hooked. It was the final evening of bidding for the Donna Karan cashmere sweater, size L. The auction, which had been going on for six days, was ending at 1 A.M. Someone could (and usually does) swoop in during the last few minutes to beat the highest price. I had to be at a party, and the hostess did not have a computer. I considered bringing my laptop as I saw another Ebay devotee do during this busy holiday season. Instead, I asked a friend to bid for me. At the party, I got into a long obsessional discussion with another Ebay groupie. His habit was 1939 World's Fair memorabilia. I confided to him about the sweater. Would I get it? I had instructed my friend to bid up to $250. But it might not be enough . . . Should I call him, just to see how things were going? Another guest leaned over and gently patted my arm. "I want you to know," she said, "you'll be O.K. without the sweater." She was right, of course. I perked up. Who needed yet another black cashmere sweater? I scorn such nauseating displays of consumerism in others, and I laugh at the country's obsession with overpriced designer goods. As it turned out, I never had to face the future without this sweater. The bidding stopped at $220. Let's see -- that's $30 less than I'd planned to spend. Just enough to start the bidding on that adorable pair of Prada ankle boots. http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo

title: Customers in Cyberspace
body: On-line shopping jumped dramatically this holiday season, and when preliminary estimates indicated that 1998 Christmas sales more than tripled the figures for 1997, investors flocked to buy shares in Internet retailers. Stock prices -- fueled by dreams of mass marketing on line -- soared even though actual sales on the Internet are still tiny compared with sales in the bricks-and-mortar world. Even a tripling of sales is not terribly surprising given how limited on-line retailing has been. One extremely optimistic forecast pegs total Internet-based retail sales in 1998 at about $13 billion, a trivial amount when compared with $2.6 trillion in annual retail sales in the unitedstates, and a fraction of the $118 billion transacted annually in Wal-Mart stores alone. It may be several years before E-tailing comes close to the volume of sales done through mail-order catalogues. But growth in E-commerce is certain, and even traditional retailers sense they cannot ignore the Internet for long. This year, some of their customers might just decide to stay home and click on that little shopping cart icon. Speed and convenience are the obvious lures -- no more waiting in the check-out line or on hold for a customer service agent to take your catalogue order (though back orders can be a big problem in cyberspace, too). Oddly enough, though, some surveys suggest that traditional retailers may be best positioned to take advantage of on-line growth if they are nimble. Companies with stores, catalogues and Web sites -- multichannel retailers -- account for nearly 60 percent of all Internet sales. It turns out that many customers will research products on line, then phone in their orders or even visit the store. Fears about sending a credit card number over the Internet may be a factor. But a lot of consumers obviously think that talking to a sales clerk is an indispensable part of the hassle. At least for now, most of them prefer a live human to an electronic mouse. http://www.nytimes.com

title: Politics a Hot New Internet Investment
body: Though Gov. George W. Bush of Texas has never declared himself a Presidential candidate, at least 39 pieces of prime Internet real estate have already been claimed in his name. Yet only two of those addresses for sites on the World Wide Web -- Bush2000.org and GeorgeWBush.com -- belong to people officially affiliated with Governor Bush. Most of the rest were snatched up by a small group of speculators who have been grabbing politicians' names like mining claims in the Old West. Their motive is financial, not political. The speculators, who paid $70 for each Internet address, or domain name, hope to sell their cyber-claims to the highest bidders, even if the buyer happens to be a political opponent of the potential candidate in question. The leading player in this game is Alex Goldstein, 25, of Los Angeles, who has spent at least $10,000 on domain names. Mr. Goldstein, a Long Island native who worked for a few years as a bond trader in Chicago and now works for an Internet marketing firm in California, owns 9 variations of Governor Bush's name, 5 for the magazine publisher Steve Forbes and at least 15 for the former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, among others. "I was looking for any major national political figures who had left useful names open," Mr. Goldstein said. Politicians, he said, are good targets for domain name investment because they cannot trademark their names. Speculators who tried to grab corporate names in recent years found their claims thwarted by lawsuits claiming trademark infringement. Obtaining a domain name is otherwise not difficult. A $70 registration fee is paid to Network Solutions Inc., the Herndon, Va., company that has handled domain registrations for the last five years under an exclusive contract with the Federal Government. Mr. Goldstein, who describes himself as nonpartisan, said that whether the bidders for his names were supporters or opponents of a candidate was irrelevant. "I personally don't really care who controls these names," he said. In the 1996 elections, political operatives quickly learned the value of publishing Web sites under names that would attract an opponents' supporters. For example, when supporters of Bob Dole, the Republican Presidential nominee, pointed their browsers to dole96.com, they found content that ridiculed and belittled their candidate. Like many other cyberspace speculators, Mr. Goldstein expressed surprise that so many politicians had failed to learn from the 1996 campaign and had left themselves open to the potential for opponents to create sites under Web addresses similar to those of official campaign sites, which candidates use for biographical information, text of speeches and fund-raising. He predicted that in six months, the going rate for such names would be five figures for each. But several political consultants said that while candidates could be hurt by their ignorance of the ways of the Internet, speculators like Mr. Goldstein could get soaked by their ignorance of the ways of politics. Tom Hockaday, president of Campaign Solutions, a Republican consulting firm in Alexandria, Va., that specializes in direct mail, telemarketing and Internet services, predicted that campaign managers were "not going to be held up by highway robbery." "Should they be really worried? Not really," Mr. Hockaday said. "Should they do better promoting of the official site? Absolutely." In the 1998 elections, very few campaigns bothered to promote their Web sites on brochures or television advertisements. But that may change as candidates face the prospect of a field of "look-alike" sites, Mr. Hockaday said. Of the presumed candidates, Governor Bush's name has proven to be the most popular among the speculators, with at least 39 variations having been registered. For most of the domain names bought, no sites have been built. Other potential candidates who have been attracting domain-name speculators are Vice President Al Gore (at least 20 addresses), Mr. Forbes (21) and Representative Richard A. Gephardt, Democrat of Missouri (19). Eight names each have been registered for possible candidacies by Senator Paul Wellstone, Democrat of Minnesota, and former Senator Bill Bradley, Democrat of New Jersey. In those cases, the candidates' own organization had generally registered only one or two of the domain names. But few political consultants see the need to buy a bloc of Web addresses to protect their candidate. "You only get troubled over things over which you have control," said Karl Rove, an Austin consultant to Governor Bush. "If people are interested in good information on a candidate and they find a site that's just a rant about a candidate, they'll pass it by." But advisers to former Gov. Lamar Alexander of Tennessee disagreed. Mel Lukens, a former aide with Mr. Alexander's political action committee in Nashville, strategically bought six variations of the name to block opposition sites. "For every positive site," Mr. Lukens said, "there's a multitude of people who want to get negative information out." There are also strategic issues to be considered when potential candidates or their agents register domain names. To secure one name for a campaign Web site is cautious, for example, but to register 15 names is tantamount to a declaration of candidacy. "You have to do a dance before you're a declared candidate," said Michael Cornfield, a professor at the Graduate School of Political Management at George Washington University who specializes in on-line politics. "You don't want to tip your hand to the Federal Elections Commission and to the other candidates." On the other hand, Professor Cornfield said, the lack of defensive domain name registrations also evinces widespread ignorance among political organizations of the growing importance of the Internet as an information medium. "The elites in the political consultancy world are television people," he said. "They just don't get it." The emerging class of Internet political consultants -- who would invariably advise candidates to buy blocks of Web addresses -- "don't have the access to the inner circles," the professor said. A few people who bought domain names based on potential candidates in 2000 said they planned to create sites opposing the candidate whose name they had registered. Among this group is David Crump of Boston, who runs adult Web sites for a living and bought three variations on "AlbertGore2000." Mr. Crump, a Libertarian, said he might establish parody sites under the Vice President's name that direct traffic to the Libertarian Party's Web site. Of course, he allowed, if someone were to offer him money for the names, he would sell them. Earl Walker, a rent collector in St. Louis, registered four addresses based on Mr. Gephardt's name. Mr. Walker, who had volunteered for the Congressman's campaigns in the past, said he would donate the names to the campaign if anyone asked for them. Mr. Walker said he had never used the Internet but when he heard that people were registering addresses to build opposition sites against candidates, he acted to protect Mr. Gephardt. Brian Rodgers, a real estate broker in Austin, Tex., registered the domain name GeorgeBush2000.com because, he said, "I don't want George Bush to be President." Mr. Rodgers, who describes himself as "neither Republican nor Democrat -- just frustrated," said he had no intention of selling the name. Still, profit potential is by far the most popular reason for registering a domain name. Four Web addresses registered under variations of Vice President Gore's name are already hawking political memorabilia. Vollie Goehring, the systems administrator for the political consultant to Governor Bush, said he received daily email from people offering to sell campaign-related domain names. To Joe Moorman, the domain game is part of the democratic process. Mr. Moorman, a 28-year-old Libertarian programmer in Birmingham, Ala., owns George Bush2000.org and GeorgeBush2004.com. Mr. Moorman said that he might set up parody sites but that he would be willing to sell the names, "especially if I could recoup all those taxes the politicians keep raising on me." Still, Mr. Moorman wonders, in the face of all the speculating, whether the domain name registration process will remain democratic for long. "What I fear," he said of politicians, "is that they're going to try to rewrite the laws -- because they're in control -- and take them from us." http://www.nytimes.com

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
2 Peoples Separated By Ocean, Not by Borders
body: The Borders bookstore version of the Tower of London stands four stories tall, with such vast space devoted to words, chilled chardonnay and house blend coffee that at least one British author felt the acute need to retreat to the new gleaming restrooms for refuge from a panic attack. The superstore, on the eastern side of London's busiest shopping district on Oxford Street, is part of the grand strategy of Borders Group to expand its reach outside of the unitedstates, a feat no other major bookseller in the world has tried. In the last two years, Borders, based in Ann Arbor, Mich., has opened a total of five stores in Britain, Australia and Singapore to headlines declaring a "U.S. Invasion" and a "War of Words." And in the coming year, the bookstore chain, the second-biggest in the unitedstates, is poised to speed up its global expansion in English-speaking countries, with plans to open as many as 10 stores. It also appears to be nearing a deal to buy a stake of nearly 20 percent in Paper Chase, a chain of 14 stationery stores in Britain. While its fierce American rivals, Barnes & Noble and Amazon.com, battle over the so-far unprofitable spoils of the Internet, Borders is clearly investing in terra firma, an approach that has cheered some investors. But the expansion of stores has also raised questions whether the chain has moved too slowly to invest in the electronic commerce of books, which with software are the most popular products sold on the Internet. Borders shares, which hit a 52-week high of $41.75 in July, have fallen sharply since, in part because of a perception that the company was not enthusiastic enough about Internet commerce.  On Thursday, the stock closed at $24.9375, down 20.36 percent for the year. "It's not that Border's stock is doing all that poorly, it's just that the company is not enjoying the Internet lift that goes to the first mover and then to a prominent second competitor, but after that trails off conspicuously," said Mary A. Tolan, global managing partner for the retail operating unit of Andersen Consulting. "However, Borders is pursuing international expansion more aggressively than its competitors. Once investors get as excited about global expansion as they are about the Internet, Borders will be much better positioned." Since his arrival in November, the new chief executive, Philip M. Pfeffer, has said that the company should probably do more to promote its Internet activities, noting that Borders upgraded its Web site in December and plans further improvements in January. But there is no doubt that the company's interests are cemented in bricks and mortar. Mr. Pfeffer said that the company was committed to adding 40 more superstores in the unitedstates next year and actually expects to speed up its international growth because sales at 'some of these stores have been remarkable." Although he declined to disclose the revenues of the new international stores or to comment on profitability, Mr. Pfeffer said that three of the international stores rank among the top five performers of all its nearly 250 superstores. That is not unexpected given that Borders has started its new stores in dense, heavily trafficked areas of the world that are estimated to be three times more expensive than its sites in the unitedstates. (Its other British stores are in Glasgow and in Brighton, on England's south coast.) Ranked in that elite is the Oxford Street store, which in the final days leading to Christmas was so busy that clerks were ringing up sales at nine registers while a line of 40 waiting customers wound around the maple bookshelves. Given its expensive site, Borders is never satisfied; it has tried to entice even more customers with every conceivable notion, short of resurrecting Shakespeare himself. Its cafe is open for business at 8 A.M., serving a menu of sandwiches to a busy lunchtime clientele, who surprised the American managers by actually expecting to eat more than sugar with their cappuccino. At night, the soft strains of a baby grand piano serenade cafe drinkers mixing latte and literature. The bistro tables are littered not only with discarded napkins, but with the books that diners sampled while drinking a glass of chilled Australian white wine. And while Borders has cut back on its familiar price discounts in the unitedstates, it has not stinted on the frenzied schedule of events that make Borders seem more like a cruise liner than a bookstore. For the store's opening in August, Stephen King made his first personal appearance in England in 17 years to promote his novel "Bag of Bones," an event so crowded that autograph seekers were limited to 1,000 ticket holders. Anne Rice paid a visit, and so did the Scottish author of "Trainspotting," Irvine Welsh, who read from his latest novel, "Filth." A British rock singer, Julian Cope, also came to the store, signing three autographs to promote his new book, "The Modern Antiquarian," before locking himself in the men's restroom, with a sudden attack of agoraphobia, or a fear of public spaces. "Accessible sophistication," is the image that Borders is trying to promote in Britain, said Philip Downer, the chief of operations for Borders Ltd., the British subsidiary, who added that style means that in the children's section, "we actively encourage children to trash the place." "We don't get upset if people bring in children who make noise," he said. To achieve that style, the British and American managers of the international stores have strived to mesh two cultures and corporate styles. In the fall of 1997, Borders spent an estimated $65 million to acquire Books Etc., a chain of more than 20 London bookstores started by Richard Joseph, who is now chief executive of the Borders bookstores in Britain. "Integrating two companies is quite a difficult job anyway, but even though we are separated by a very large ocean, I think we have managed rather well," Mr. Joseph said. On the advice of the British employees, Borders brightened the lighting, creating larger signs to direct customers, and painted the walls in bolder colors of yellow and red. And in turn, the British employees adopted the more relaxed dress of the American managers, including Mr. Joseph, who shifted from suit to open-necked shirt, casual slacks and black loafers -- though he draws the line at blue jeans. It was Borders' goal to acquire a company that could give it the instant experience and keen cultural knowledge to enter a foreign market where its buyers could recognize, for instance, the commercial appeal of "Bluff Your Way at Cricket," or "Dress to Kill," a book by Eddie Izzard, the British comedian known for wearing makeup and often-flamboyant dress. Such knowledge is vital in a market with such keen competitors as W. H. Smith and Waterstone's, which earlier this year merged with another rival, Dillons, to form the HMV Media Group and the country's largest bookstore chain. Shortly before the Borders grand opening in London, Waterstone's announced that it would open a bigger store on Oxford Street just a few doors away, and that it would feature 165,000 titles.  Since then the battle has intensified with Waterstone's declaration that it planned to open a seven-story bookstore in a former department store in London. The British market became attractive to price-conscious American booksellers in 1995, when an industry agreement that barred retailers from selling books at discounts was eliminated. Borders also entered Singapore because of liberal copyright laws, which allowed it to ship in most of its book inventory from the unitedstates , eliminating the major costs of setting up local distribution. "The next phase would be to go into non-English-speaking countries -- a large cosmopolitan country with a large population of English speakers," said Vincent Altruda, the president of the international stores division at Borders. "'That's the next logical thing to do, but we'll do it on a city-by-city basis." Started as a used bookstore in Michigan in 1971, the Borders chain is clearly feeling the limits of the domestic borders of the unitedstates, where analysts have been predicting for some time that the expanding market of superstores could reach saturation after 2000. In addition, the chain started its own electronic Web site this spring in third place after Amazon.com and Barnes & Noble, making it an expensive prospect to catch up with the leaders. "If they succeed internationally, they can say we generated higher returns than Barnes & Noble generated on line, but it's so early that you can't say with any certainty that they can be successful overseas," said Craig Bibb, managing partner at Jasper Funds in New York. "Maybe if they pull it off, they'll have the last laugh. I think you can see from the stock price that it's hurt them. They placed their bet, and they said it's going to be international." Danielle Turnof Fox, an analyst with J. P. Morgan Securities, said the company could still prove its mettle. "Because of Borders' strong track record the company has a lot of residual good will on Wall Street," she said. "If the company has strong holiday sales, is able to reassure investors that its growth rate is sustainable at around 20 percent and takes a more aggressive stance on the Internet, I think we could see the stock recover further." In Britain there has been considerable speculation that Borders is the pioneer, whose trail will naturally be followed by the leading American bookseller, Barnes & Noble. And indeed, one publisher said that Barnes & Noble's representatives had quietly approached some of the major British publishers for advice and had also spoken with Books Etc., which ultimately was acquired by Borders. But for now, Barnes & Noble has ceded the rest of the terrestrial world to Borders. "We have so many stores to open here in the unitedstates, we just can't seem to make sense enough of a market for us to want to jump out," said Leonard Riggio, the chief executive of Barnes & Noble. "We look at it from time to time and we may jump in, but I don't think there's going to be any global push for typical bookstores. But you can never say never. Wouldn't it be nice to have a great American bookstore in Paris?" http://www.nytimes.com Graphic   Photo: At the Borders bookstore on Oxford Street in London, the books and browsing can be accompanied by house blend coffee and a snack. (Photos by Carlos R. Lopez Barillas for The New York Times)(pg. C3)  "Spreading the Words" The Borders Group, the second largest American bookseller, is the first to expand outside the unitedstates. Graph tracks the company's total sales and net income/loss, since the beginning of 1997. It also tracks the stock price of Borders Group the beginning of 1998. (Source: Bloomberg Financial Markets)(pg. C1)

title: AT&T Passes Hurdle in Plan To Buy TCI
body: The Federal Government took a big step toward redefining the Internet today when the Justice Department approved the proposed $31.8 billion acquisition of the cable giant Tele-Communications Inc. by AT&T. The deal, announced in June, still cannot be closed without the consent of the Federal Communications Commission, where officials said today that the agency's staff was still more than a month away from finishing its review under different standards and laws than those considered by the Justice Department. After the staff review and recommendations, the five commissioners would have to decide whether the deal was in the public interest or, as critics have argued, that it would give AT&T the power to sharply limit access to the Internet by other telephone companies and access providers. Nonetheless, today's decision by antitrust regulators removed a significant potential obstacle and moved the two companies closer to becoming a vast new telecommunications conglomerate. That conglomerate would offer a big new artery of higher-speed access to the Internet through TCI's cable lines. Executives say that would more easily enable computer users to transfer data, hold clearer conversations and receive TV-quality video. In a separate regulatory action, the Federal Trade Commission approved the $52.4 billion acquisition of Amoco by British Petroleum P.L.C.  Page C2. The agreement announced today with the Justice Department was not without conditions. Because both AT&T and TCI hold substantial interests in wireless telephone services, officials approved the deal only on the condition that TCI divest itself of its interests in that business. The company will have five years to sell its 23.5 percent interest in Sprint PCS, one of the nation's leading providers of digital wireless telephone service. Antitrust officials had raised concerns that the proposed merger could affect the price of wireless service because AT&T, with about nine million customers, is the nation's largest provider. "In the past few years, increased competition in mobile wireless services has produced lower prices, higher quality and millions of new subscribers," said Joel I. Klein, the Assistant Attorney General in charge of the Justice Department's antitrust division. "The settlement reached today will insure that the merger will not blunt the move toward a more competitive market in wireless services and that customers continue to reap the benefits of that competition." Under the agreement with the Justice Department, if the deal closes before TCI sheds its interest in Sprint, then the Sprint stock must be placed in a trust until it is sold. Executives at AT&T and TCI have said that the merger will enable consumers to get one-stop shopping for their local and long-distance telephone service, cable TV and access to the Internet and data services. TCI and its affiliated systems reach more than 14 million customers representing about one-third of the nation's homes. Since the breakup of the Bell telephone network in 1984, AT&T has not had direct access to most homes. But the proposed deal with TCI, made possible by the sweeping deregulation of the telecommunications industry two years ago, would change that. James Cicconi, AT&T's general counsel, said the decision was good news for consumers. "We are now one step closer to finalizing a transaction that will ultimately give residential customers broader choices for local telephone service and other advanced services and products," Mr. Cicconi said. "We think it is especially significant that the only subject of today's consent decree is the ownership interest TCI currently holds in the cellular business of Sprint." But other telephone companies have maintained that the deal is fundamentally anticompetitive. They have expressed fears that it will prevent them from using TCI's lines to offer access to the Internet. That issue is now one of the central ones before the F.C.C. The AT&T-TCI deal is one of three large proposed mergers in the telecommunications industry that are awaiting approval from regulators in Washington and a variety of states. Officials are also considering SBC Communications' $56 billion purchase of Ameritech and Bell Atlantic's $52 billion purchase of GTE.

title: Cartoonists Old and New Are Drawn to the Net
body: PETER SINCLAIR began writing and drawing his comic strip, "Alex's Restaurant" in 1990. The strip details the life of a restaurant run by a rat-race dropout, Alex, and peopled by a crew of holistically minded, slightly batty regulars. These include Cranbrook, a soup-dropping, wild-haired waiter who explains the more obscure items on the menu (like the three-day fast), and Dr. Andy Vial -- a thinly veiled, respectful lampoon of Dr. Andrew Weil, the nationally known dispenser of medical advice -- who stops by the restaurant to promote books like "You Never Know, It Might Help" and "Hooked on Colonics." Syndication once brought Mr. Sinclair's strip to about 50 papers in 1990. But the syndicate lost interest, and the strip was dropped. "Many editors were nervous about its radical content," Mr. Sinclair wrote in a self-published collection of his strips that appeared in 1998. After stints as a nurse and a paramedic, Mr. Sinclair began drawing the strip again in 1995 because a friend convinced him that the Internet offered a good way to reach readers. He opened a Web site that year (www.alexsrestaurant.com). Mr. Sinclair said: "The whole message that the Internet is giving people is, Here's the audience -- it's there to be had. But you have to make it happen." Newcomers like Mr. Sinclair are not alone in using the Web as a way to break into newspapers. Now even some veteran cartoonists with millions, or even hundreds of millions, of daily newspaper readers are also turning to the Internet. They, too, see the Web as the thin edge of the wedge for increasing their circulation in newspapers as well as for generating a wider buzz for their efforts by tapping directly into their most dedicated audience and exposing people to their strips in areas where it does not appear in local papers. The Nando Times, a media Web site (www.nando.net/nt/comics/alex/today), picked up Alex's Restaurant for publication over a year ago and features a link to the strip on its home page. Mr. Sinclair's own site gets a few thousand visitors every day. Mr. Sinclair has garnered praise from sources as varied as Yahoo Internet Life magazine and the Tel Aviv newspaper Ha'aretz, which proclaimed him one of the top five Internet cartoonists. While that might not have quite the same ring to it as the Reuben, the award newspaper cartoonists have traditionally coveted, the praise is still evidence of both Mr. Sinclair's talent and the growing presence of cartoons on the Internet. Like other Web-based cartoonists, however, Mr. Sinclair is not content to limit his work to the Net -- if only because he would like to make a full-time living solely from the strip. Instead, he wants to use his Internet popularity to help gain a stronger foothold in newspapers. Web sites generate negligible revenue for most cartoonists, but each additional newspaper that a cartoonist picks up can bring in anywhere from a few hundred dollars a year to several thousand. Mr. Sinclair said that he had recently fielded an offer from a syndicate but that he prefers to retain as much control as possible over his work and to build his audience through self-syndication to The Nando Times and to the few daily newspapers in which the strip already appears. So far, the comic strip has been providing Mr. Sinclair with only a modest income, which he supplements with illustration and Web-design work. "I'm gaining readers one by one," he said. Another Web-based strip that has achieved some prominence is "Helen, Sweetheart of the Internet" by Peter Zale. "Helen" (www.peterzale.com) follows a Greek-American geek named Helen who cares more about computers than her social life or drop-dead gorgeous looks. Mr. Zale posts about six new strips every two weeks; the everyday grind didn't mesh well with his day job as an art director and computer system administrator at a Midwestern advertising agency. But he considers a Web site critical for the credibility of the strip -- and not just to give it a boost into newspaper syndication. "It was the topic of the strip, Helen being involved with the Internet, that made it necessary for the strip to have a Web site," he said. The lure of improving circulation in newspapers is not the only thing that has made the Internet a daily (or even hourly) part of many cartoonists' professional lives. email has changed cartooning from perhaps one of the loneliest professions into one in which some cartoonists have direct day-to-day contact with fans -- for better or worse. The first cartoonist to put an email address in a comic strip -- in tiny letters just larger than the copyright notice -- appears to have been Scott Adams, creator of the wildly successful "Dilbert." An extensive "Dilbert" Web site was built a few years after that (www.dilbert.com). Mr. Adams credits the rapid spread of "Dilbert" in newspapers to the Web tie-in. He started with about 50 papers in 1989 and had grown to about 150 when he added the email address in 1993. By the time Mr. Adams opened his Web site in 1995, "Dilbert" reached about 400 papers. Of course, Mr. Adams's use of the Web was not the only reason for his success. His rise coincided with Bill Watterson's decision to stop drawing the popular "Calvin and Hobbes," leaving a hole in many daily newspaper comics pages. "When a newspaper was planning to add a cartoon, they'd already have unsolicited letters" asking the paper to run Dilbert, Mr. Adams said. Mr. Adams's reach has now extended to 1,900 papers. And with a "Dilbert" television show in the works and books consistently on the best-seller list -- making him the envy of his peers and aspiring new cartoonists -- Mr. Adams finds himself at the center of a small industry. "Somebody's going to be Walt Disney," Mr. Adams said, "and it would be nice if it were me." Mr. Adams gets help from his syndicate to keep on top of his email. But the demands of email have overwhelmed some cartoonists. Bob Thaves, for instance, has been drawing "Frank and Ernest" for more than 25 years. The strip, which appears in more than 1,200 newspapers, was one of the first widely distributed strips to include an email address (www.comiczone.com/ comics/franknernest/ab.html). Almost immediately, Mr. Thaves began receiving thousands of email messages. "We were totally unprepared for that," said Mr. Thaves, whose son and daughter help handle the strip's correspondence. But, he added, it was "one of the first chances for people to communicate with a strip's creator." Gary Delainey, who writes the daily strip "Betty," distributed to more than 600 newspapers, said: "Cartooning, like writing, is very lonely. You sit isolated doing your stuff in a vacuum." Mr. Delainey sounds almost wistful about life before he was on the Net. "I was free to do whatever I wanted," he said. "I had the feeling that nobody was reading it, anyway." The hundreds of email messages that regularly come in to Mr. Delainey and the strip's illustrator, Gerry Rasmussen (www.comiczone.com/comics/betty/ ab.html), have put the lie to that. Mr. Delainey now knows for certain that readers really do care about what happens to the characters in his strip. "We've had some interesting relationships develop with certain readers," he said. "It opens up a sort of dialogue." But while these cartoonists encourage responses from readers, others, like Bill Amend, creator of the popular "Foxtrot," (www.foxtrot.com) resist that kind of exchange. "I've got a strip that may have 20 million readers," Mr. Amend explained, "but there's one of me." Mr. Amend has even spoofed the on-line success of "Dilbert." One "Foxtrot" strip had a character in the foreground praising Mr. Adams's early use of a "Dilbert" newsletter distributed through email while another character "offstage" pumped Mr. Amend's latest collection of strips, "Camp Foxtrot," holding up a sign with the first few digits of the book's ISBN number. (Mr. Adams nonetheless expresses admiration for Mr. Amend, calling him the "world's smartest cartoonist.") Even though Mr. Amend discourages a give-and-take with readers, he has made use of the lobbying power of his dedicated Net readers, which numbered 30,000 one recent month, to influence comic-page editors to run his strip. For comic-strip artists, the future of on-line cartooning is still the day after tomorrow. The current audience and offerings just scratch the surface of what is likely to come in the next few years. Most cartoonists interviewed are working on some multimedia component. Mr. Thaves's Web site, for example, features a virtual reality experience with Frank and Ernest, while Mr. Amend's site sports some simple games. Mr. Delainey's "Betty" site may involve a little animation in the near future. And Mr. Sinclair already draws an animated strip every Sunday for The Nando Times. For now, cartoonists, other than those who already have large print audiences, are still wondering whether they will be able to make a living from the Internet. "There are very few realistic opportunities for the aspiring cartoonist," Mr. Amend said. The Internet, he said, has "broken that model, given everybody their own printing press. Now, whether they're attracting audiences is a different question."  And Don't Forget . . . title:
GAME THEORY;
At Game Site, Chat Fans Find Their Voices
body: THE Internet is an orchard of unintended consequences. The network itself, with all its content and clamor and chaos, is an unintended consequence of Pentagon research. And like some kind of magic-realist garden plot, it is a place where every seed, whether carefully planted or heedlessly strewn, sprouts into a different species, blossoms into yet another species and bears unexpected mutant fruits. People bend it into shapes you wouldn't expect. And particularly gamers. "I'll never forget one day, about three months after we launched the service, I went into this room and suddenly Van Halen started coming out of my speakers," said Brian Moriarty, co-founder and chief visionary of Mpath (www.mplayer .com), a digital playpen for two million on-line gamers. "It turned out that one guy had decided that he wanted to play music while people were text-chatting, and so he turned on the CD and jammed his mike up against the speaker. "Little did I know what this was going to turn into." From its inception, Mpath had built voice capability into its service so people could hurl epithets across the Internet as they decimated each other on Quake. But most game manufacturers weren't interested in using their limited available bandwidth for carrying voice data. It was more important to pump up the graphics or deliver more accurate positional information about bullets. Audio capacity was all but ignored in the game space. But it wasn't long before someone figured out how to use it in the chat rooms. "There was a point," Mr. Moriarty said, "when suddenly some kind of critical mass was achieved. You began to see a kind of chat regime. Maybe two talkers instead of one, or maybe three, and then the talkers started to outnumber the typers. Then social pressure began to be felt by these people because everyone was in on this conversation and the typers felt left out. So it snowballed very quickly, in a matter of a few months. And now, when you go in there, most of the users have got to have that microphone. If you go into the public chat areas, it's rare to find someone that doesn't have a microphone. In fact, a lot of users, when they create a chat room, it says, 'Mikes only.' " Unlike Internet telephony, which has yet to find its feet, Mpath's voice chat spread in weedy profusion because the technology is cheap (the company's downloadable software is free, the service is free, and headset microphones sell for less than $40) and easy to set up, and because everyone was doing it. And because there is a richness in the human voice and its capacity for nuance: age, sex, social class, regional origin, cadences, rhythm, volume, tension, laughter. A sense of human presence. All of these subtleties, even the intake of breath, are amplified at a distance when you can't see, when all you can do is listen. That's why radio theater was so compelling. That's why the telephone is so compelling -- perhaps more compelling than a face-to-face conversation -- and why videophones are invariably disappointing. As Orson Welles said, the ear is more imaginative than the eye. Of course, people do some of the things one might expect. There are plenty of private chat rooms on Mpath with only two people in them. But there are also channels where far-flung relatives convene conference calls. And there is a sizable religious contingent of armchair preachers. "They sit around and create their own Christian theme chat rooms and talk Christian and sing Christian and preach," Mr. Moriarty noted. "On a good evening, you'll see three or four Christian rooms in chat." And then there's the singing. "This is the fascinating thing that really caught us by surprise," Mr. Moriarty said. "We have average Middle American kind of folks in the Southeast and into Texas who have discovered that Mplayer.com is a great way to get on line and sing. Hillbilly John is one of the ringleaders of the country singing group. He goes in there and organizes these live jamborees. Then there's this guy named Conway, and he runs a karaoke radio station on the service, pretty much every day as far as I can tell, and he sings a lot of Elvis in his own radio format. "It kind of fell on us. All we did was give people the connection, and they discovered it. And now they're going crazy with it." Of course, a lot of the singing is horrible. But it is compelling in its horribleness. It is considerably more compelling than a personal home page, several times more compelling than any customized portal interface, and orders of magnitude more compelling than the whistles and bells of the media behemoths. The horrible singing is compelling because it is human. Because when someone gets up to sing, even in the dark, it involves a degree of risk, and it implies trust. "Even when you hear people singing badly," said Brian Apgar, Mpath's co-founder and chief evangelist for chat, "you can hear in their voice that they're trying. You can hear the feelings and emotions they're trying to communicate. And it makes you feel connected to them. It makes you feel for them. Because they're getting up there and expressing themselves. It's not phony, canned stuff from some major Hollywood conglomerate. It's coming out of somebody's trailer." No matter how fast the modems get, nothing in the overdesigned corporate infoglut can evoke the raw empathy of a butchered karaoke tune -- or "Auld Lang Syne," for that matter. Because of all the fantastic things the Internet has on demand, the best thing it can deliver to us is one another. Happy New Year. title:
NEWS WATCH;
Internet Providers Feel The Holiday Crush, Too
body: On-line retailers urge shoppers to buy on line to avoid big crowds, slow traffic and long lines. But during the holiday shopping season, it seems that the virtual shopping experience had some analogous drawbacks: longer waits to log on and more frequently dropped calls. New research data shows that call-failure rates for the 25 top Internet service providers rose sharply in November and December. In the summer, 5 out of every 100 calls to those I.S.P.'s were dropped in mid-connection; that figure rose to 8.5 per 100 in November and in preliminary December results, according to Inverse Network Technology, an Internet research company in Sunnyvale, Calif. Chris Roeckl, research manager for Inverse, said the rise was partly because of the colder weather, which keeps more people indoors and logged on, but he attributed the bulk of the dropped calls to growth in E-commerce. "People are dialing in longer, staying on longer and clogging up the Internet," Mr. Roeckl said. Call failure rates rise as more people log on and stay logged on because they hog the limited number of modem ports I.S.P.'s have available for their subscribers. On-line shopping keeps at least one advantage, though: There is little chance of facing sharp elbows and fisticuffs to get that last Furby on a virtual shelf.

title: Rival Warns That Microsoft Could Control Web Trade
body: The president of Intuit Inc. stated yesterday that the Microsoft Corporation could use its market power to gain control over "major areas" of Internet commerce and asked the courts to give Microsoft's rivals equal access to its Windows operating system and desktop screen. The 47-page written testimony of William Harris of Intuit, maker of Quicken personal finance software, brings two new issues into the Microsoft antitrust trial -- Microsoft's potential impact on the fast-growing field of Internet commerce and possible steps to curb Microsoft's power. Both issues have been much debated outside the courtroom. The Government's case against Microsoft focuses mainly on its use and alleged abuse of the market power derived from its dominant position in the market for operating system software for personal computers. Microsoft, the Justice Department says, has used its Windows monopoly to try to thwart the challenge posed by software used to browse the World Wide Web, pioneered by the Netscape Communications Corporation, and by Java, an Internet programming language developed by Sun Microsystems Inc. Most of the computer industry witnesses for the Government have testified on the tactics Microsoft used to undermine the Netscape-Sun challenge -- namely, that Internet software could weaken Microsoft's grip on personal computer software. In his testimony, Mr. Harris, who is scheduled to take the stand on Monday, does deal with one such episode involving Intuit in 1997. To obtain prime placement on the Microsoft desktop, Mr. Harris said, Intuit had to agree to bundle Microsoft's browser with Intuit's on-line personal finance software and not bundle Netscape's browser. The arrangement was negotiated for placement on a feature of Microsoft's Internet Explorer browser called Active desktop. Microsoft, Mr. Harris said, wanted Active desktop to be "a new user interface for Windows" that would "provide a choice of Internet Web sites that could be directly accessed from the desktop." Intuit, he said, was prepared to pay "a substantial fee" for this desktop real estate. "But," Mr. Harris added, "Microsoft offered us this placement instead in return for our agreement to forgo future business dealings with Netscape." The Government points to such testimony as evidence that Microsoft has used its market power from Windows, which runs on more than 90 percent of personal computers sold, to unfairly hamper Netscape. Microsoft replied in a statement that Intuit chose Microsoft's Internet Explorer browser over Netscape's Navigator because by 1997 its software was superior. In fact, in his testimony Mr. Harris wrote, "The recommendation of our technical team was to use the Internet Explorer." But he added that it was Intuit's judgment that Netscape could deliver the browser capability Microsoft had, though a bit later. And Mr. Harris said he preferred to work with Netscape because it was not an Intuit competitor -- Microsoft's Money competes with Quicken -- and at the time Netscape's browser was used by many more computer users than Microsoft's browser. Yet Mr. Harris goes beyond the Internet software market by arguing that Microsoft can use its operating system dominance to influence or control Internet commerce and programming. With Windows 98, the operating system upgrade introduced in June, Microsoft has closely integrated Internet Explorer with Windows. As a result, Mr. Harris said, Microsoft's start-up page -- an all-purpose Web site, or portal, with links to many other sites -- will "become the default portal in the Windows operating system." A featured spot on that start-up site, now called MSN.com, is regarded as prime real estate by Web sites offering everything from news to travel services to personal finance information, according to Mr. Harris. Based on his assumption about the importance of the operating system as a "choke point," and its growing importance in the future, Mr. Harris called on the Federal court to impose a sweeping sanction on Microsoft that he terms "operating system neutrality" -- essentially a guarantee that the company enjoy no advantages in new software or Internet commerce markets from its operating system monopoly. In the Microsoft case, the subject of remedies will be taken up only if Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson rules against Microsoft -- and then there will be a separate hearing. What weight, if any, the views of Mr. Harris would have is uncertain. Microsoft called the remedies section of his testimony "an entirely new and irrelevant concept." Industry analysts have also noted that Microsoft's Active desktop initiative proved a failure because people did not use it that much. Its failure has led many analysts to suggest that placement on the Windows desktop, while useful, may not be as important for Internet commerce and programming sites as Microsoft had hoped or rivals like Intuit had feared.  Microsoft Wins Skirmish BRIDGEPORT, Conn., Dec. 30 (Bloomberg News) -- The Microsoft Corporation won a round in an antitrust fight with closely held Bristol Technology Inc. when a Federal judge denied the small software company's bid for access to the software leader's technology. unitedstates District Judge Janet C. Hall refused to issue an order in the suit brought by Bristol, which claims to be a victim of anticompetitive practices by Microsoft. Bristol sought a preliminary injunction forcing Microsoft to provide source code for its Windows NT operating system to let Bristol make compatible software.

title: States in Fine Fiscal Health, But a Revenue Threat Looms
body: Cautious spending and a robust national economy have left virtually all the states in solid financial condition for the fifth year in a row, according to a fiscal survey released today. The healthy economy has allowed the states to give taxpayers the largest projected aggregate tax cuts in five years, $7 billion for the 1999 fiscal year. Twenty-nine states have reduced one tax or another. But the authors of the report, the National Governors' Association and the National Association of State Budget Officers, warned that important challenges loom. In addition to citing an uncertain national economy, they amplified the warning of many state officials, saying that states are confronting the projected loss of billions of dollars in tax revenues to the sale of goods via themail and the Internet. "The revenue loss is not huge now," Raymond C. Scheppach, executive director of the governors' group, said today at a news conference where he discussed the latest Fiscal Survey of the States, a report that is published twice a year. "But it is growing very, very rapidly. If we don't correct the problem, it will virtually lead to the collapse of state sales taxes." Sales taxes account for as much as 40 percent of all state revenues, with the rest coming largely from personal income and corporate taxes. Stymied by courts and Congress in their effort to collect taxes from Internet sales, states have been pushing back, saying that their revenue base is threatened. In comments today, the officials who produced the budget report tried to project how significant that threat might be. Tax revenues from consumer goods and services are eroding as the convenience of shopping by catalogue and, more than ever, computer gains in popularity, Mr. Scheppach said. Measuring how popular is difficult.  A recent survey of consumers by a subsidiary of the Interpublic Group of Companies, an advertising group, estimated that on-line sales this year could reach $5 billion, more than twice merchants' expectations, although still well under 1 percent of total American retail sales. But Bob Chatham, an electronic commerce analyst with Forester Research in Boston, said Internet sales projections for 2000 could exceed four times the amount of 1998 Internet sales. But going far beyond estimates by anyone else in business or government, Mr. Scheppach predicted that by 2002, sales over the Internet could reach $300 billion. If that proves true, it could translate into $20 billion in lost revenues for the states and local governments. But with Internet sales a relatively new phenomenon, no one really knows how high sales might reach or how deeply they could affect states as they try balancing their budgets. "Is this a huge problem in 1998? I don't think so," said William F. Fox, a professor of economics at the University of Tennessee and past president of the National Tax Association, a nonpartisan policy group. "But if the future estimates I've heard are anywhere in the ball park, then yes, there could be a significant and growing problem that states need to worry about." The states, of course, are eager to recoup the losses, but their aspirations have been stymied in some instances by Congress and the Supreme Court as well as the difficulties states have in collecting taxes they would otherwise be entitled to. In October, Congress passed the Internet Tax Freedom Act, which in an effort to nurture fledgling Internet-related businesses declared a three-year moratorium on taxes from on-line sales. The legislation provided for the creation of a 19-member commission to study electronic commerce and recommend solutions to any tax inequities. But squabbles over the makeup of the commission have delayed the start of its work, discouraging Government and business officials who were hoping for answers sooner rather than later. "You always have hope," said Walter Hellerstein, a law professor at the University of Georgia who specializes in state tax laws. "Realistic expectations are much different." The Supreme Court has visited only the issue of catalogue sales, ruling in 1967 and 1991 cases that sellers are not required to collect a tax on goods unless the company has a physical presence in the state of the purchaser. In theory, much of the revenues are there, just waiting for the states to collect them. In the 45 states that have sales taxes -- the exceptions are Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon -- purchasers are supposed to be liable for the taxes, no matter how merchandise is bought. But few citizens voluntarily provide information that would increase their tax liability, and states cannot require sellers to collect taxes on catalogue sales because the Constitution bars states from interfering with interstate commerce. The overall health of the states, as reflected by the survey report, derives in part by a conclusion that governors are making prudent economic and political decisions, by holding down the increase in spending and cutting taxes. The report estimates that states increased spending by 5.7 percent for fiscal 1998 and 6.3 percent for fiscal 1999, a rate that is slightly below the 6.5 percent national average of the last two decades. That combines the overall tax cut of $7.02 billion, much of it in personal income tax. Overall, it represents about 1.6 percent of the states' revenues. Over the last five years, states have cut taxes by $22 billion. The states that enacted the largest cuts were California ($1.38 billion), newyork ($1.10 billion), Massachusetts ($789 million) and Ohio ($780 million). All had Republican governors at the time, but Mr. Scheppach said that the economic health was evident in states with Democratic governors, as well. Six states raised taxes for 1999, led by New Jersey, which budgeted for $200 million in revenues from new cigarette taxes. The others with increases are Florida, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana and South Carolina. The report said that almost all the states reported a surplus for the 1998 fiscal year, but in addition to tax cuts, they used the extra money for investment projects, like schools and roads. Almost half the states, including newyork, New Jersey and Connecticut, used some of the surplus to bolster the state rainy day account.
