title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
Dow Retreats for First Time in Nine Trading Days
body: The stock market ended lower yesterday for the first time in nine trading days, weakened by investors who sold to secure some profits from a 1998 rally that accelerated at year-end. Merck & Company, up 40 percent for the year; Lucent Technologies Inc., up 172 percent, and the Microsoft Corporation, up 115 percent, led the decline. "Stocks have moved up so dramatically that money's being taken off the table," said James Margard, chief equity strategist at Rainier Investment Management in Seattle, which manages $5 billion. "Investors have recognized that some large stocks may be overvalued." The Dow Jones industrial average fell 46.34 points, to 9,274.64, after having gained 530 points since Dec. 16. The Standard & Poor's 500 index declined 9.88 points, to 1,231.93. The Nasdaq composite index dropped 14.82 points, to 2,166.95. Advancing issues slightly outpaced those declining on the newyork Stock Exchange. With one day left in 1998, the S.& P. 500 index has soared 27 percent for the year, on track for an record fourth consecutive year of gains exceeding 20 percent. The Nasdaq composite index is up about 38 percent, and the Nasdaq 100, an index of the market's largest shares, is up 83 percent, the best year in its 14-year history. "The market's had a tremendous run," said Peter Coolidge, senior equity trader at Brean Murray & Company, a newyork brokerage firm. "There's no catalyst pushing us higher." With many investors and traders on vacation for the year-end holidays, trading has been light this week. Monday and Tuesday's levels were about 20 percent below last week's, and 604.92 million shares changed hands yesterday, compared with a three-month average of 726 million shares. Merck fell 2 1/4, to 148 13/16 ; Lucent dropped 3 7/16 m to 108 5/8m and Microsoft fell 1 1/2m to 139. Internet shares fell after posting spectacular gains in recent days on optimism that commerce conducted on the World Wide Web will boom. Charles Schwab, the No. 1 on-line broker, fell 3 1/16 to 56 3/8. Earlier this week, Schwab's stock market value surpassed that of Merrill Lynch & Company, the largest brokerage firm. Now, Schwab's market capitalization is down to $22 billion, below Merrill's market capitalization of $24 billion. Ubid Inc., an on-line auctioneer, fell 24 1/2, to 119; Skymall Inc. fell 13, to 27 3/4, and America Online Inc. dropped 7 1/16 , to 147 9/16 . The Internet directory company Yahoo fell 25 3/8, to 244 5/8. Genesis Direct Inc. soared 2 13/16 , to 9 7/8, after themail-order catalogue company said it would sell some merchandise through Excite Inc., the second-biggest Internet directory. Genesis was the second-most active stock. Amoco fell 3 1/4, to 54 3/4, and British Petroleum's American depository receipts fell 6 3/4 , to 83 3/16 , as B.P. received unitedstates approval to acquire Amoco. Amoco ceased to be a member of the S.& P, 500 index as of today so money managers who mimic the index must sell the stock. Most strategists are still confident about the outlook for stock markets.  Laszlo Birinyi, president of Birinyi Associates Inc., said he expects the Dow average to reach 12,000 by the end of 1999. Mr. Birinyi studies "money flow," which examines the number of shares traded every time a stock goes up or down, and is considered a gauge of the conviction behind the price move. Mr. Birinyi said in an interview that money flow analysis indicates that International Business Machines, Ford Motor and America Online are likely to rally in 1999. Investors reduced the amount of money they added to equity mutual funds by 28 percent this year, and almost tripled their purchases of bond funds. Still, in the week ended Monday they added $3.16 billion more to stock funds than they redeemed, according to Trimtabs.com, a research firm. By any measure, the bull market in stocks is still under way. The Wilshire 5000 index, the broadest indicator, is up 22 percent for the year.  Still, small and mid-capitalization shares continue to lag. The benchmark Russell 2000 index is off 6 percent this year, after being down as much as 31 percent. In the bond market yesterday, Treasuries rose for the third consecutive day, reflecting investor expectations that inflation will remain low next year. The 30-year bond rose 6/32 , to 102 18/32 . Its yield, which falls when the price rises, declined to 5.08 percent from 5.09. Two-year notes rallied amid optimism generated by stronger-than-expected demand at the Tuesday auction. The yield on the new note fell to 4.53 percent, down 16 basis points from the auction rate. With one day left in 1998, 30-year Treasury bonds have handed investors returns of 18.7 percent, when price gains and reinvested dividends are taken into account. That is the best result since 1995, when long-term Treasuries returned 34.7 percent. Volume yesterday was 25 percent below the average for a Wednesday in the last month, according to Govpx Inc., a bond pricing service. title: To Sail Data Across the Web, Computers Seek the Best Routes
body: BILLIONS of times a minute, computers reach out into the maze of machines and connections that form the Internet to find other computers. A bit of magic? Not quite. Computers connected to the Internet need not know exactly how to reach every other computer. They require only a few simple pieces of information to have their requests or messages wind up at the right machine. Each computer needs to know what its unique number is and how to reach the rest of the Internet. Everything else derives from that. An Internet Protocol, or I.P., address gives the computer its unique location. The I.P. address, four sets of digits separated by periods (like 192.168.0.1), uniquely identifies both a particular machine and its local network. A local network is simply a place where all the machines start with the same few numbers. For instance, an address of 192.168.0.1 means that the network is 192.168.0 and that the machine's number is 1. The first one to three sets of numbers define the local network. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology has a comparatively ancient Internet network and uses 18 as the first number for many of its machines. M.I.T.'s Web server lives at 18.181.0.31, which means network 18 and address 181.0.31 within that network. A relative latecomer like Yale University must use two sets of digits (130.132) at the beginning of the I.P. address for each computer. Newer Internet service providers may have to use three sets of digits, like 192.168.5. I.S.P.'s maintain pools of I.P. numbers that they typically assign at random when a user dials up via modem. Every computer connected to the Internet has to have an I.P. number, just as every person who wants to receive telephone calls needs a phone number. Unlike the phone system, though, the Internet has no directory assistance that lists all machines. Instead, each computer knows how to find the others on the Internet. A computer can turn a host name, or Web address, into an I.P. address by using the domain name system, a built-in part of the Internet. If you type in a name like www.apple.com, your computer automatically asks a computer called a domain name server to translate that Web address behind the scenes into an I.P. address. Any request for a Web page or mail server that has an I.P. address that starts with numbers that differ from those identifying the computer's local network has to be sent somewhere else. Each Internet-connected computer knows to send all of such requests to the local network's router. A router is a specialized computer that handles the task of sending data among networks. These networks can be local, like two Ethernet networks in the same building, or they can be far away, like a network on a high-speed digital phone line coming in from another state on one hand, and a local Ethernet network on the other. A router routes data around the Internet along physical pathways made up of high-speed digital phone lines linking different phone companies and I.S.P.'s. Small and medium-size businesses often use a simple router that knows how to send data only up a chain of routers to an I.S.P. or regional or national network. Corporations, major networks, and large I.S.P.'s use high-level routers that keep hundreds of thousands of pathways in their memories at all times, taking up megabytes of RAM. These high-level routers process millions or even billions of transactions a second as they pass information back and forth across networks. Every high-level router knows exactly how to reach every other high-level router, often through multiple paths or routes. Unfortunately, inaccurate routes can throw the whole system off kilter. In April 1997, a small company in Virginia misconfigured its own router so it appeared that all routes on the Internet led to it. When the company's router started feeding out that information, and other routers on the Internet spread the error, it caused a cascade of failures for much of the Net. System administrators across the country had to clear out the mistake, and it took more than two hours to restore the Internet's connections. Some safeguards were added, and the problem has not occurred again. Computers split data into smaller chunks to share the conduits that make up networks more efficiently. Instead of sending a long, continuous Web page, for instance, the computer breaks up the information into smaller, numbered pieces called packets. Each packet is labeled with the addresses of the sending and receiving computers. A 50,000-byte Web page, for instance, might be split into about 100 packets of around 500 bytes each. Each packet contains the I.P. address of the machine that is sending it, the address of the machine it is bound for, some housekeeping details about the size and type of data, and the information itself. The packets are handed off one at a time to a router, which holds on to them until it is ready to hand them off to another router or the intended recipient. It's tempting to think of one machine finding another in this vast network as one fellow yelling, "Hello? Bob Johnson?" in San Francisco and Mr. Johnson replying, "Yes?" in Boston. But the process is closer to the way mail gets delivered by the Postal Service. You may have no idea where Times Square in newyork is, and neither may your mail carrier, but once your mail enters the post office's hubs, the ZIP code speeds it quickly to its destination. Graphic   Diagram: 1. THE STARTING POINT A computer linked to the Internet via a dial-up connection or a router on a local area network knows how to send out packets destined for machines elsewhere. It does not know the physical location of the computer it is trying to reach or what path the data should take to reach the destination, but it does know the destination computer's unique Internet Protocol, or I.P., address, and it knows where to hand off these packets to send them on their way.  2. INTERNET SERVICE PROVIDER An Internet service provider, or I.S.P., network may have several internal routers that help balance the load among the different companies and individuals it serves. Local and regional I.S.P.'s generally have many connections to higher-level networks run by major network providers, like MCI/Worldcom, Cable and Wireless P.L.C. and AT&T.  3. HIGH-LEVEL ROUTERS High-level routers at I.S.P.'s and major networks constantly update multimegabyte lists of end-to-end paths linking all the networks on the Internet. These routers also maintain separate lists of the most efficient routes around their own local networks, like MCI/Worldnet's national network. The best route may not be the shortest or fastest; it is the route involving the fewest networks.  4. CHOOSING A PATH High-level routers choose a set of networks for packets to travel across from start to finish. A router on each network receives the packet, then uses the local network's list of routers to hand it off within that network and send it on to the next network on the route. Based on the list it maintains, Router A determines that the packet should cross MCI/Worldcom's network and move through a network exchange point to Cable and Wireless, then to Apple's network. MCI/Worldcom's routers determine, for instance, that the best path from A to G is through B and D. The whole path from end to end is described as A-B-D-G-L-P-Q.  5. NETWORK INTERCHANGE Regional and nationwide networks rent space and put in routing equipment at several locations around the country, called network access points, or peering points. Different networks have different policies; they generally allow all networks of the same size to exchange packets of data at no charge at these points but sometimes restrict smaller regional or local I.S.P.'s from having direct access. Many I.S.P.s create private peering points by buying connections from several nationwide networks, allowing them to bypass these sorts of bottlenecks. Larger networks also band together in private exchanges.  6. THE DESTINATION The packets reach their destination, www.apple.com, through a high-level router at Apple's Web servers. Because Apple gets so much traffic, it operates routers, just like an I.S.P. or national network, to help speed traffic to and from its site without intermediaries.  (Sources: Nik Mouat, Conjungi Corporation: Computer Networks by Andrew S. Tanenbaum, 3d Edition (Prentice Hall, 1996))

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Technology Stocks Lead Nasdaq to Strong Year
body: The Nasdaq composite index, long home to the market's hottest technology stocks, is on track for one of its best years ever. Through yesterday, the index had risen nearly 39 percent, far ahead of the 28 percent gain in the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index and more than double the 18 percent gain in the Dow Jones industrial average this year. The reason for the surge is both a large number of Internet stocks, which have been the object of investors' lovesick affections -- and, according to one estimate, account for one-fifth of this year's gain in the overall market -- and a dearth of cyclical companies, whose values have been crushed by the collapse in commodity prices. Even a surge in oil and agricultural prices, however, would have trouble getting investors as excited as they have become by big Internet companies like Yahoo, Amazon.com and Netscape. Those stocks, which have recorded three- or four-digit percentage gains this year, plus smaller companies like Ebay, Mindspring Enterprises and Infoseek, which have recorded similar gains, have put the Nasdaq in line for its third-best performance since it was begun in 1971. There are other differences as well. The 10 largest stocks in the Nasdaq index account for more than 39 percent of its value, nearly double the weighting of the 10 largest stocks in the S.& P. 500. The effect of those differences is that movements in the value of the biggest stocks, like Microsoft, Intel and Cisco Systems, have a greater impact on the Nasdaq index than on the S.& P. 500. That effect can especially be seen in the performance this year of the Nasdaq 100 index, a subset of the composite, comprising, as its name suggests, the 100 largest Nasdaq companies. The Nasdaq 100 index has gained 84 percent this year, a blazing performance that is unmatched in its history, which dates to 1985. Nasdaq and the American Stock Exchange, which merged earlier this year, will soon try to capitalize on the success of the Nasdaq technology stocks by offering a new product that tracks the Nasdaq 100. The new product, a unit investment trust, is similar to the Amex's popular Spiders, Diamonds and Webs unit trusts, which, respectively, track the S.& P. 500, the Dow industrials and a variety of foreign stock indexes. But in designing the Nasdaq unit trust, the exchange has changed the way it calculates its 100-stock index, restricting the influence of technology stocks and thus removing some of the fuel that has thrust the index to such historic heights. Whether that dampens investors' reception of the new product remains to be seen. Judging by their willingness to pay virtually any price for Internet stocks, however, it is easy to imagine that investors will care not a whit. Consider some numbers. Wilshire Associates, which manages money for institutions and also compiles a series of stock indexes, recently measured the contribution of Internet-related stocks to the performance of the Wilshire 5000 index, a yardstick that includes all of the 7,400 publicly traded companies based in the unitedstates. For that purpose, Wilshire defined as Internet-related any company whose busi- ness would be materially affected if the Internet ceased to exist -- a broad definition that included some giant companies like Microsoft, but not others, like Dell Computer. Wilshire found that through last Wednesday, 4.1 percentage points of the 21.8 percent gain in the Wilshire 5000 -- or roughly one-fifth of the total -- came from Internet-related stocks. In that time, the value of those Internet stocks climbed to 6 percent of the overall market from 3 percent. It is only logical to assume that the effect of Internet stocks on the Nasdaq composite index is as large or larger. At the beginning of 1998, Yahoo, the 65th-largest stock traded on Nasdaq, accounted for only about two-tenths of a percent of the Nasdaq composite index. By the end of November, it had grown to eight-tenths of a percent of the index -- a fourfold increase that placed it among the 10 largest Nasdaq companies. And since the end of November, Yahoo has climbed even further. Nasdaq is betting that individual investors, in search of a piece of that action, will snap up shares of the Nasdaq 100 unit trust, just as they have the Spiders, Diamonds and Webs. But Nasdaq ran into a problem. For tax and other reasons, Nasdaq had to adjust downward the influence of the biggest stocks in the index -- Microsoft, Intel, Cisco, MCI Worldcom and Dell Computer -- which together accounted for more than 60 percent of the Nasdaq 100. Before the adjustment, Microsoft alone made up 25 percent of the index. Now, those five stocks account for about 40 percent of the index. In the future, the index will be reassessed quarterly, and if the biggest stocks grow to account for more than 48 percent, they will again be scaled back to 40 percent. Similarly, Microsoft now measures about 15 percent of the index; if it grows to 24 percent, it will be cut back to 20 percent. Sound complicated? Think of it as selling the portfolio's winners. If investors continue to favor large technology stocks, as they have this year, the Nasdaq 100 index, and therefore the trust, will be forced to scale back those stocks. Diane Garnick, an equity derivatives strategist at Merrill Lynch, says the reconfiguration is in fact a good development because it makes the index less of a sector product and therefore more attractive as a general equity-market benchmark. Gaining weight are sectors that are not traditionally associated with Nasdaq -- like consumer cyclicals, which feature companies like Costco, the operator of wholesale warehouses. The cyclicals went to 8 percent of the index from 4 percent, Ms. Garnick said. And over all, technology stocks make up about 67 percent of the index, compared with 76 percent before the adjustment. The question is whether investors are looking for another general market index -- or worse, whether Nasdaq's attempt to reduce the influence of technology stocks on its new index product portends an end to the technology stock boom. Either way, the index has far outpaced other benchmarks, thanks to its heavy weighting of technology stocks. title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Preliminary Reports Show Brisk Sales on Internet The first reports on holiday sales for Internet retailers showed results that surpassed even what earlier this month had seemed to be hyped-up preseason predictions. The increases came despite glitches that forced consumers to suffer indignities like access denial to Web sites and despite holiday gifts that did not arrive on time as promised. The figures are preliminary, and even the most optimistic prediction would be far less than 1 percent of the $2.6 trillion in retail sales in the unitedstates for the year, leading many analysts to remain skeptical about the wave of euphoria generated by the data.  Page A1. Internet Stocks Surge, Too The burgeoning use of the World Wide Web for shopping and stock trading lifted shares of Internet-related companies. The Nasdaq composite index, which is heavily weighted toward technology stocks, rose 17.27 points, or eight-tenths of a percent, to 2,180.30, its fourth record in six sessions. The Dow Jones industrial average rose 8.76 points, to 9,226.75, and the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index fell eight-tenths of a point, to 1,225.49.  C6.  Prices of Treasuries Rebound Bond prices posted their biggest gain in four weeks as month-high yields and expectations for low inflation in 1999 attracted buyers. The yield of the benchmark 30-year bond fell to 5.15 percent from 5.21 percent on Thursday.  C6.  Social Security Cleared for 2000 President Clinton called the Year 2000 challenge "a stunning problem" for computer programmers but said the Social Security Administration had fixed its computers so that elderly people would receive their monthly benefits without interruption in 2000. He did not address the situation at other agencies judged by the White House to be inadequately prepared for the year 2000, including the Pentagon, the Energy Department and the agency that runs Medicare and Medicaid. title: Estimates for On-Line Shopping Exceed the Most Bullish Forecasts
body: Holiday sales figures for Internet retailers released yesterday showed a huge season -- stronger than even the most bullish predictions of a month ago. While the data were preliminary, they sent many electronic-commerce stocks soaring as the market got a glimpse of the Internet serving a mass retail market. The increases came despite glitches that forced consumers to suffer such indignities as being denied access to retailers' World Wide Web sites and explaining holiday gifts that did not arrive on time. The most optimistic estimates of holiday sales came from a subsidiary of the Interpublic Group of Companies, an advertising group, whose survey of 1,000 consumers suggested that on-line sales would reach $5 billion. That would be four times the total sales last year on the Internet between Thanksgiving and Christmas and twice expectations for this year of $2.3 billion in sales. The Boston Consulting Group and Shop.org, the industry group for electronic retailers, said that year-to-year sales grew more than threefold for the holiday season that just ended. Apparel sales were particularly strong, reaching $300 million, from less than $100 million in 1997, the consulting group said. In addition, the average order was $55, up 6 percent over last year's average. Still, all these projections were very preliminary -- most retailers will not release actual sales figures until mid-January -- and even the most optimistic would be far less than 1 percent of the estimated $2.6 trillion in retail sales in the unitedstates for the year. To put yesterday's electronic commerce estimates in perspective, Wal-Mart Stores, the world's largest retailer, had $118 billion of sales in 1997 -- more than 23 times the most optimistic estimate of all holiday retail sales on the Internet this year. Those facts led many analysts to remain skeptical of the wave of euphoria generated by yesterday's data. "There is not enough evidence to justify" Interpublic's $5 billion estimate, said James McQuivey, a senior analyst at Forrester, an independent market research firm that specializes in Internet commerce. Moreover, the strong showing did not exactly cause jaws to drop. If an established company like the International Business Machines Corporation, with billions of dollars in sales, had reported such increases, it would have been the business equivalent of an Elvis sighting. But Internet sales have been experiencing phenomenal growth all year. Julie Wainwright, chief executive of Reel.com, an on-line video store that was recently purchased by Hollywood Entertainment, said: "Our business is up seven times from last year. But that is not a surprise really. December is up 25 percent from November, and November was up 40 percent from October." What is more, examining just percentage rates of growth can be misleading because on-line retailers started with such a small revenue base compared with their brick-and-mortar peers. Still, the numbers, the first of the post-holiday season, clearly confirmed strong Internet shopping growth and the Web's potential for further expansion. Seizing on the data, investors snapped up shares of more Internet companies yesterday, sending them to new heights. Skymall Inc., for example, an in-flight catalogue and Internet retailer, announced yesterday that on-line sales of $1 million for the fourth quarter of 1998 would be triple its sales in the 1997 period. Its shares jumped $23, to $35.5625, after touching $48 earlier in the day on heavy trading, of 24.6 million shares. That brought its market value to $302.8 million. Shares of Amazon.com, the giant on-line bookseller, jumped $27.125, to $351.9375. But while the shares of electronic retailers appeared to rise broadly, it was unclear whether small electronic merchants benefited from the holiday on-line frenzy experienced by the largest Internet retailers. Boston Consulting Group, for example, tracked only the leading electronic retailers in 17 gift categories. "The seasoned merchants had room to shine," said Wendy Brown, America Online's director of electronic commerce. Of most significance to potential investors and electronic commerce watchers was the increase in new on-line shoppers. Ms. Brown said that a review of America Online's holiday figures showed that "at any given point, 20 percent of the people on line are there for the first time." Female shoppers also made a strong showing. An Interpublic subsidiary, the Marketing Corporation of America, found that while women still trailed men in total number of Internet purchases, they were 9 to 11 percent more likely to make multiple purchases, spending, on average, $168 a month during the holiday season, versus $125 spent by men. The significant shift in the demographics of Internet shoppers -- from male, typically technologically savvy users to a mass market -- may have its own price tag, however, in the form of higher expectations. "Mass-market users are far less forgiving of technology-related glitches," said Nicole Vanderbilt, senior analyst of digital commerce for Jupiter Communications, a newyork-based market research firm. The as-yet unanswered question is whether on-line retailers this season provided the kind of pleasant and convenient shopping experience that would make first-time experimenters come back for more. "This Christmas was a make-or-break period," said Joe Kraus, senior vice president and co-founder of Excite, a portal and search engine. "It's like the first time you go to a restaurant. If the food and service were good, you'll come back. If the food is cold and the waiter is rude, you'll never go there again." For some, the Internet clearly provided convenience as promised. "I have a newborn baby, so I couldn't leave the house," said Deborah Kamali, a gynecologist in Princeton, N.J.. "I could be in my pajamas, breast-feeding a baby and still go shopping on line." She ended up buying her son a video from Amazon.com and her husband a leather jacket from J. Crew and a cellular phone from AT&T. The Internet, she said, provided all the satisfaction of walking the aisles of a well-stocked store. "It's great," she said. "You can spend hours searching for movies and disks and books." But Jupiter's Ms. Vanderbilt said that, already, "there have been some missteps by retailers during this critical period." She added, "And we are just starting to hear the rumblings about what went wrong." Several sites, including barnesandnoble.com and Macys.com, had trouble processing customers' orders because of heavy traffic. Perhaps worse, several retailers, including Amazon.com, failed in their promises to deliver gifts by Christmas. To make a splash with consumers, 800.com Inc, an on-line electronics, music and video store, offered three movies or CD's for $1 as a promotion in November. Suddenly, the site was swamped. It has received some one million visitors so far this month -- 400 percent over its target, said the company's president, Greg Drew. The result was a two-day period during which the site had trouble processing orders. Mr. Drew estimated that some 50 percent of the CD's and movies ordered were delivered to customers after Christmas. "We thought it was better to have people wait a week or two than be disappointed," Mr. Drew said. Graphic   Photos: The Lands' End "Your Personal Model" World Wide Web site allows shoppers to type in their hair color, weight and size. The site then creates a computerized model to "try on" clothes for them. Margeurite Smalls did some Christmas shopping via the internet last Tuesday from the desk in her office in Bethesda, Md. Last-minute shoppers, meanwhile, were frantically crowding the malls. (Associated Press)(pg. C17)

title: Physicists Discover Another Unifying Force: Doo-Wop
body: The arcane language of physics is not exactly the stuff of song lyrics, but the Cernettes, billed as the world's first particle physics rock band, have hit the Internet. Even if nonphysicists fail to get their musical jokes, the Cernettes count on a growing audience of admiring scientists. The Cernettes take their name from CERN, the acronym for Europe's pre-eminent high-energy particle laboratory straddling the French-Swiss border near Geneva, with which all the singers are associated. Membership in the four-woman amateur singing group and its band changes from year to year, but the Cernettes' songwriter-lyricist, Silvano De Genarro, constantly provides material to keep his group up to par at the many physics meetings and celebrations where they perform. On the job at CERN, Dr. De Genarro, a computer scientist, uses virtual reality to manipulate the virtual counterparts of battleship-size particle detectors that must fit into cramped niches in the laboratory's 17-mile circular accelerator tunnel. But in his spare time he writes songs of the doo-wop style popular in the 1950's and 60's. "The average physicist around here was growing up in those years," Dr. De Genarro said in an interview, "and they get a nostalgic kick out of my tunes." Some of his songs involve the Large Hadron Collider, or L.H.C., nearing completion in CERN's circular accelerator tunnel spanning the border between Switzerland and France near Geneva. Here is a typical verse from Dr. De Genarro's lament "Collider": I gave you a golden ring to show you my love, You went to stick it in a printed circuit To fix a voltage leak in your collector You plug my feelings into your detector You never spend your nights with me You don't go out with other girls either You prefer your collider You only love your collider. Celebrating the L.H.C., which will be a Mecca for American as well as European high-energy physicists, the Cernettes have renamed themselves "Les Horribles Cernettes," or L.H.C. for short, and they have posted some songs on their Web page: http://sgvenus.cern.ch/musiclub/ cernettes. Owners of computers with sound cards can hear the Cernettes (who often emulate the Supremes) croon catchy tunes like "Strong Interaction" ("You quark me up, you quark me down, you quark me top, you quark me bottom"), "Antiworld," "Surfing on the Web" and "Microwave Love." Since its birth in 1954, CERN's achievements have included monumental discoveries in particle physics, a succession of Nobel prizes and the construction of a proton collider that may yield enough energy to discover the elusive Higgs boson -- a theoretical particle supposedly responsible for endowing all matter with mass -- and a magazine read by physicists around the world. But for ordinary people, CERN's most memorable achievement was to invent the World Wide Web as a way to organize and find information on the Internet. The laboratory originally used its Web system as a communication network for physicists, but it grew as the Internet became as universal as the world's postal system. As the Web outgrew the laboratory, CERN cast off its creation, which is now administered by others. Mr. De Genarro, an Italian, writes his songs entirely in English "because English is the universal language of physics." But this has created something of a language barrier between the CERN laboratory and the French and Swiss people outside it. Most of CERN's neighbors do not understand the jokes in his songs. "Our concerts are more popular in France than in Switzerland," he said, "because the Swiss seem to think we're too noisy." The Cernettes are not the only performers specializing in physics songs. In the unitedstates, Dr. Lynda Williams -- a former go-go dancer who teaches physics at San Francisco State University, has become a smash hit at physics conferences. Her on-stage gyrations and clever allusions to physics keep audiences of specialists roaring with laughter. One of the theories she tackles is "supersymmetry." Many physicists believe this theory will eventually unite the realm of the ultra large (as described by relativity) and the ultra small (governed by quantum mechanics). The idea is that for every particle of matter there may be an unseen supersymmetric particle of some force carrier, and that for every known force carrier (photons of light, for example) there is an unseen particle of supersymmetric matter. Such particles are called "sparticles," "squarks," and so on. Dr. Williams's song, to the tune of George Gershwin's "S'wonderful," pokes fun at the Government's cancellation in 1993 of the Superconducting Supercollider (S.S.C.), which would have been the largest accelerator in the world: S'quantum dream, squandered it, Bad publicity. A'awfully sad, S'could of had Our own S.S.C. But where did the funding go? Must be hiding with the higgsinos S'wonderful, s'marvelous There's still the L.H.C! Graphic   Photo: With a computer scientist their Sondheim, the Cernettes sing catchy songs about supercolliders and quarks. (CERN)

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
Schwab, for Now, Bests Merrill on Strength of On-Line Trading
body: As recently as a few weeks ago, it seemed like America's corporate giants need not worry too much about the Internet. After all, if upstart companies that specialize in on-line commerce were ever to realize investors' much-hyped expectations for future profits, Fortune 500 members could always just buy them. Not anymore. The recent explosion in share prices of companies linked to the on-line world has been so spectacular that their market value is rapidly eclipsing that of more established competitors, even when the on-line companies still lag far behind in terms of profits and revenues. Yesterday, the Internet passed another such milestone, this time shaking some core assumptions in the finance industry. The market value of the Charles Schwab Corporation, the discount broker based in San Francisco, reached $25.5 billion. That puts it in the No. 2 position, ahead by a nose of the industry standard-bearer and Wall Street heavyweight, Merrill Lynch & Company, which investors now say is worth $25.4 billion. Market value can change drastically day to day, and investors still value one big investment bank, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company, above Schwab. But Schwab's helicopter-like ascent is unheard-of in speed, analysts said, and perhaps in its challenge to the way Wall Street treats the on-line craze. Consider that just two weeks ago, the market was awash with unconfirmed rumors that Merrill might consider buying Schwab to give it a presence on line, a possibility that now seems far-fetched given the huge increase in Schwab's stock price. "Merrill has to be concerned about this," said Richard Strauss, a securities industry analyst for Goldman, Sachs. "There is significant value in Merrill for many reasons. But the Internet is clearly something that they have to make a top priority." Schwab has been swept up in the Internet stock frenzy, which has inflated the share prices of some new on-line companies well beyond competitors that trail them in selling goods electronically. America Online, perhaps the best-known Internet entertainment and commerce company, recently surpassed Disney in market value. Amazon.com has a market value well above the combined value of two leading book-selling rivals, Barnes & Noble and Borders. Investors value Ebay, the new Internet auction company, at more than five times Sotheby's, the old-world benchmark. Schwab's rise is attributable to the fact that, unlike Merrill and other rivals in the finance industry, it has transformed itself from a traditional retail broker, albeit one that specialized in discounted fees, into a company that does most of its business on line. Merrill, meanwhile, has delayed plans to offer a limited on-line trading service to some customers until early next year. Morgan Stanley and Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, Wall Street houses that like Merrill have a more diverse array of businesses than Schwab, have substantial on-line operations. But only a small part of their revenue is Internet-related. Schwab, moreover, dodged a bullet from rivals like E*Trade Group Inc. and the Ameritrade Holding Corporation, services that focus exclusively on cut-rate, on-line stock trading. Even as on-line trading has soared as a percentage of total stock trading, Schwab has maintained its market share of 30 percent, analysts said. The company has watched the revenue it derives from each trade it handles slide as investors switch to less expensive trading through its Web site. As recently as late last year, it earned $63 on every trade it handled, and now that average has fallen to $53. But a sharp increase in the quantity of trades has more than made up for that loss, and profits are rising at a rapid clip. "Schwab did a great job turning the Internet to its advantage when it could easily have become a victim," Bill Burnham, an on-line commerce analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston, said. "Now, any fears that they will be superceded by the Internet have subsided. They are the leader." Many analysts warn that the lopsided valuations placed on companies with the suffix ".com" has the classic symptoms of a financial bubble and will probably prove fleeting. Some say the same about Schwab's sudden rise, and indeed its valuation by some traditional measures seems extraordinary. Schwab, whose shares closed yesterday at $63.625, up $3.25, now trades at 65 times its projected profits next year, a ratio more familiar to the speculative Internet world than the brokerage community. Merrill, which closed yesterday at $70.75, down $1.0625, trades at 16 times its forward earnings. Merrill manages $1.4 trillion in client assets, three times what Schwab manages. Merrill's revenues in the last year totaled $17.5 billion, seven times Schwab's. "It just does not make that much sense for Schwab. These lofty multiples get applied to Internet companies that are not mature and are thought to have an enormous growth path ahead of them," said Guy Moszkowski, a brokerage stock analyst at Salomon Smith Barney. "I don't see how you apply that kind of thinking to Schwab. It has been around for 25 years and has a more mature business." Likewise, officials at Merrill say they are not about to overhaul their strategy because of daily changes in stock prices. "We have a long-term strategy that is global, that has been very successful in growing clients' assets, revenues and market share," Jim Wiggins, a Merrill spokesman, said. "We are sticking to it." Even if Merrill chose to do so, it might have a hard time mimicking Schwab's heavy Internet focus. Schwab has always sought to provide brokerage services at a low cost. That makes the company more vulnerable to competition from purely Internet companies than full-service brokers like Merrill, which compete on providing advice and financial planning services to customers. Moreover, Merrill has a network of 14,000 brokers who would probably resist any move by Merrill management to shift a large proportion of the firm's business on line. "Just from a structural position, it's incredibly difficult for Merrill to rush into the Internet business," Mr. Burnham said. "They would have a huge political issue." title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Another Big Day for Issues Connected to the Internet
body: Stocks were mixed yesterday as the growing use of the World Wide Web for shopping and stock trading lifted such Internet retailers as Skymall and sent Charles Schwab, the No. 1 on-line brokerage firm, past Merrill Lynch in market value. Traditional retailers, like Wal-Mart Stores and Sears, Roebuck, fell. Electronic commerce "is a legitimate avenue of growth for many companies," said Trent May, manager of the $1.2 billion Invesco Growth Fund. Mr. May has 3 percent of his fund -- which has returned 41 percent this year -- invested in America Online. The Nasdaq index, which is heavily weighted toward technology stocks, rose 17.27 points, or eight-tenths of a percent, to 2,180.30, its fourth record in six sessions. The Dow Jones industrial average rose 8.76 points, to 9,226.75, for its seventh straight advance, matching the longest string of gains this year. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index fell eight-tenths of a point, or less than one-tenth of a percent, to 1,225.49. About eight stocks fell for every seven that rose on the newyork Stock Exchange. Stocks pared gains with an hour left in the trading session amid selling by "momentum" investors -- professionals and individuals who chase rising stocks looking for short-term gains. "There is a lot of fear surrounding Internet stocks and what will happen when the market comes back to reality," said Tim Ghriskey, a senior portfolio manager at the Dreyfus Corporation, which oversees $95 billion. A little more than 531 million shares changed hands on the Big Board, well below the daily average of 729 million shares for the last three months. Trading is expected to be slower than usual all week, as it typically is in the week between Christmas and New Year's. That could mean stocks will move erratically as the year-end maneuvering of money managers has a disproportionate effect. Skymall, the nation's largest in-flight catalogue retailer, soared 23, to 35 9/16, after doubling on Thursday and was the most active stock in unitedstates trading. The company estimated that its Internet sales rose sevenfold in 1998 as more people shopped on line. Schwab rose 3 1/4, to 63 5/8. The company now has a market value of $25.5 billion, more than the $25.1 billion for Merrill Lynch, the biggest unitedstates securities firm by number of brokers. Merrill fell 1 1/16, to 70 3/4. "A lot of people did their Christmas shopping on line this year," said Ryan Crane, who follows Internet stocks for AIM Advisors Inc., which oversees $100 billion and owns CDW Computer Centers, an on-line computer seller, and Infospace.com, an Internet directory. "Those same Internet-savvy people that are shopping on line are probably the ones that are buying these stocks." Traditional retailers declined. Wal-Mart slumped 1 1/4, to 79 7/8. Sears fell 7/8, to 41, May Department Stores dropped 5/8, to 60 1/16, and J. C. Penney lost 1 1/16, to 47 5/8. Professional investors began cutting the amount of money they put into general retail stocks like Wal-Mart in late November, according to money-flow statistics from Bloomberg Analytics. The money-flow data measure the amount of money institutional investors put into a stock each time the price rises compared with the amount they take out when it falls. Of the 20 most active stocks yesterday, 18 benefit directly or indirectly from the Internet's growth. Active Apparel Group soared 10 1/4, to 11 1/2, after the sportswear maker said it created a Web site to sell its clothes, marketed under the brand names Everlast, Converse All Star and MTV's the Grind. The company's market value surged to $29 million yesterday from $3.1 million. E*Trade Group climbed 11 3/4, to 56 3/4, after the No. 2 on-line broker said its new Web site had signed up more than 500,000 members since September, when E*Trade began a $100 million marketing campaign to add new accounts. Amazon.com, the on-line retailer, jumped 27 1/8, to 351 15/16. America Online, the No. 1 on-line service, jumped 20 5/8, to 157 1/4, and Yahoo gained 28 3/8, to 275 1/2. Netscape, the Internet software company, rose 9 1/2, to 68 3/16. The surge in Internet stocks for months has been driven by individual investors, who have been "day trading" -- buying shares in the hopes of selling them minutes or hours later at a profit. With many professionals out of the office this week, the effect of individuals will be even more pronounced, analysts say. "All these Internet stocks are going to run this week," said Bill Burnham, electronic commerce analyst with Credit Suisse First Boston. "There are no institutions in the market, they're all on vacation, and all these people sitting at home after having their turkey dinner are going to move the stocks." title:
COMPRESSED DATA;
Greeting Cards At Your Fingertips
body: Felicia Lindau wants to help everyone whose new year's resolution is to "be a better friend" and, in the process, make a viable business.  Amid this year's holiday bustle, she opened Sparks.com, which she bills as the "world's largest greeting card store." She does not fancy Hallmark as her competition. Rather, Ms. Lindau would like to be the Amazon.com of cards. Her store is a Web site, and it allows would-be senders of cheer, and other sentiments, to browse through an on-line selection of more than 5,000 cards from hundreds of publishers. In contrast, industry data show that the typical neighborhood card store carries 300 to 600 cards, usually from one major publisher. Variety, Ms. Lindau says, guarantees nuance. As evidence that no occasion is too uncommon and no late 20th-century family iteration too obscure for the greeting card, she cites a holiday card for a Christian woman and her Jewish husband. Staff members wearing rubber gloves at a San Francisco warehouse pluck cards from shelves and mail them to the Web site's customers.  For an additional 75 cents a card, they sign them (by laser printer or staff scribe) and post them on the buyer's behalf. While the 17 minutes, on average, that a typical customer spends browsing a card store might not be reduced by on-line shopping, Ms. Lindau said, at least it can be done on the shopper's timetable, or in pajamas. In this age of the ubiquitous digital communique, and with hundreds of free electronic cards available on the Web, is it counterintuitive to sell traditional paper cards on the Internet?  Before heading to the venture capitalists, she posed that question to focus groups and found that "there's very little overlap." "The electronic card is good for novelty," she said, adding that it gets you "half credit" if you have missed a birthday. But "getting something in themail just feels so good." Apparently, that sentiment is widely shared. The Greeting Card Association, an industry trade group based in Washington, predicts a $1.2 billion rise in card sales from 1995 -- the first full year of the Web's existence -- through 1998, when sales are expected to reach $7.5 billion in the unitedstates, a 19 percent increase. Still, Marianne McDermott, executive director of the association, sees the Internet as a threat -- not to card sales but to penmanship. "The subject of discussion isn't whether the Internet is going to do away with paper," she said, "but rather that young people aren't writing anymore because they're on the computer.  We're hoping that young people don't lose the art of writing and communicating with handwritten notes."   LISA NAPOLI Graphic   Photo

title:
Digital Commerce;
The boom in on-line shopping adds a twist to the old quandary of how to tax interstate purchases.
body: EVEN before the final sales numbers were tallied last week, it was clear that on-line holiday sales would shoot well past all expectations. And according to one recent study, the fact that buyers could make their purchases without paying state or local sales taxes or use taxes was a strong incentive for shopping on the Internet. Those who successfully pushed for passage in October of the Internet Tax Freedom Act, which declared a three-year tax moratorium for on-line sales, have reason to cheer. But the long-term implications could be troubling. Although the potential revenue is still too small to pose a serious problem in the immediate future, what happens a few years down the pike, when states see as much of as one-third of their revenues circling the drain? "Right now, sales tax is the most important source of revenue for states, so the moratorium is something they're clearly aware of and worried about," said Austan Goolsbee, an economics professor at the University of Chicago Graduate School of Business. Prof. Goolsbee, who recently completed a study of the purchasing habits of on-line consumers, said his research showed that the number of on-line shoppers and the dollar amounts they spend would drop by 25 percent and 30 percent respectively if they were charged sales tax on their purchases. Despite the hue and cry that taxing Internet sales is "unfair" to a budding new form of commerce, the Internet in fact only intensifies a problem that has been brewing for decades in themail-order business. Simply put, the legal issue is how to tax purchases that cross state lines. A state's sales tax, per se, can only be collected when both buyer and seller have a physical presence in the state -- meaning that either there must be a face-to-face transaction or an out-of-state seller must have an outlet somewhere in the state where the buyer lives. Until a few decades ago, this arrangement worked fine. When mail-order sales started to pick up steam, state governments decided they had better impose a "use" tax on people who bought items through catalogues (so called because they used their purchases in the state). Although virtually no one pays such a tax and virtually no state enforces it, consumers are supposed to voluntarily pay the equivalent of sales tax on these out-of-state purchases. Sellers cannot be required by states to collect these use taxes from their customers, as they collect sales tax, because of constitutional provisions banning the states from interfering with interstate commerce. Although catalogue and Internet buyers benefit from this tangled web, even legendary tax opponents like Arthur Laffer, the supply-side guru of the Reagan Administration, are concerned about the implications. "A lot of government is at risk here," Mr. Laffer said. "Sales tax funds virtually everything in the state," including police and fire departments, welfare, roads, schools and mass transit. "It is probably the single best tax the state has, because it has the broadest base and the lowest rate to collect large sums of money to fund government services," Mr. Laffer said. The situation is something of a political football, says Walter Hellerstein, a law professor at the University of Georgia who specializes in the application of constitutional law to state taxes. Despite the fact that state governments derive at least a third of their revenue and often more from sales tax, Mr. Hellerstein says, neither the Supreme Court nor Congress wants to be responsible for the havoc that would be created if the physical presence rule were rescinded. "Mail-order sellers, since before 1967, have made billions of dollars in sales and have never collected use tax or filed a tax return," he said. "Because of that, the statute of limitations is open" and, theoretically, sellers could be required to pony up huge sums of dollars in back taxes, a situation that would put most of them out of business. Other economists are recommending even more radical action. The Center for Community Economic Research at the University of California, Berkeley, warned in a paper in August 1995 that "state and local government finances are becoming road kill on the information superhighway." In making its policy recommendations, the center noted that commerce was increasingly conducted nationally and globally, rather than locally. Thus, it said, state and local taxes should be scaled back or even eliminated and replaced with a national tax that is disbursed back to the states. Stating that "study after study has shown the regressive nature of sales tax as a revenue source," the paper said sales and use taxes on mail-order (and, it would follow, Internet) purchases have more impact on the poor, the disabled and the elderly than on anyone else. Tell that to the advisory commission on electronic commerce that was mandated by President Clinton, after the passage of the Internet Tax Freedom Act, to come up with a solution to the taxation problem. The commission, which was to be made up of equal numbers of industry and government representatives, is already being berated by local government agencies like the National Association of Counties for being lopsided in favor in industry -- with powerhouse companies on board, including Time Warner Inc., Charles Schwab & Company, the Netscape Communications Corporation and MCI Worldcom Inc. Government agencies are not the only ones incensed by the composition of the commission. "This does not pass the smell test," said Charles McLure, a senior fellow at the Hoover Institute at Stanford University and the economist who wrote the basis for the Tax Reform Act of 1986. "This is, 'We're going to build a fence around the chicken coop -- but let's not put any chickens on it; let's put some wolves.' " Whatever the commission's final composition may be, one hopes its deliberations will be shaped by larger societal concerns and not just the convenience or power of the fortunate few. "Everyone thinks they have a constitutional right to buy tax free when they buy mail order," Mr. Hellerstein said. "At some point, there's going to be revenue shortfall, and then I don't know what will happen. Right now, everyone's flush and all they can think about is some other way to cut taxes." title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
A Quiet Year in the Internet Industry. Right? Right.
body: Had a celebrant dozed off last New Year's Eve and not come to until today, he might woozily take a look at the Internet business and conclude that it had been an uneventful year. After all, the leading on-line service is still America Online, the most popular site on the World Wide Web is still Yahoo, and people are still transacting the most electronic commerce through Amazon.com. All of these companies are growing briskly, as on-line use increases, just as they were a year ago. But what if our Net van Winkle were to groggily dispatch a series of emails to Internet investors and financiers, asking what he had missed? At first, of course, he might be flamed by those incredulous that anyone could sleep through all that ruckus. Internet stocks soared early this year before stalling and then plunging in a terrifying free fall in October, only to pull out and zoom even higher than before. Meanwhile, initial public offerings by Internet companies were exploding into the firmament like fireworks. For all the bombast, though, a look back at the year's events indicates that our sleepy celebrant's initial observation might be fairly accurate. In the Internet business, the forces propelling the leading companies like America Online, Yahoo and Amazon.com remained the same -- even if the pace picked up faster than anyone might have expected. And yet the tumultuous year does seem to yield at least five lessons about the Internet industry and the stocks associated with it: The big get bigger and the small fade away. At first glance, the Internet seems to favor David over Goliath, as any upstart can open an on-line store or an electronic publication. But it appears that the first capable pipsqueak to shoot a slingshot in any given area may grow to giant size so quickly than any new challengers have been kept at bay. "Some very powerful franchises have been built on the Internet in an incredibly short time," said Fred Wilson, a principal with Flatiron Partners, a newyork venture capital firm. "Some of these companies will be the leaders of the economy in the next millennium." The best example is Amazon.com, which continues to widen the gap between itself and its better-known book-selling competitor, Barnes & Noble. And in the year's third quarter, Amazon.com's first full quarter selling compact disks, it became the country's leading on-line music retailer. (It's not an accident that the two other leading music stores CD Now and N2K have chosen to merge to try a new assault on the emerging Amazon.com giant.) "Being a successful Internet company is not as easy is it might appear," said Derek brown, an analyst with the investment bank of Volpe Brown Whelan & Company. When investors spot a category leader, there is no limit to what they will pay to own the stock. The main lesson of 1998, said Keith Benjamin, an analyst with BancBoston Robertson Stephens, is "just don't fight the tape." It's fruitless, Mr. Benjamin has concluded, to try to find rational explanations for the astronomical Internet stock prices sliding across the ticker. The fact that, in the stock market, America Online is worth almost as much as Walt Disney and that Yahoo is more valuable than CBS is simply not relevant, he said. "The market opportunity here is big enough that that is what we should be focused on for any given segment," he said, "and competitive position is the most critical factor in judging these stocks" Such judgment, of course, involves far more forethought than many investors may be applying when they blast buy orders into E*Trade every time an Internet company issues the most inconsequential press release. Yet, while much of the upward pricing pressure has come from individual investors, increasingly the big boys have started to compete for the relatively small number of shares in circulation for the leading Internet companies, and that has pushed prices ever higher. "Institutional portfolio managers learned to 'embrace' Internet stocks in the second half, for a simple reason," said David B. Readerman, an analyst with Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities. "The stocks were going up, and their relative performance suffered by not owning enough of them." Everybody wants to be an Internet company. Imagine the frenzy if someone introduced the antigravity diet, where no matter how much you ate, the scale would still register you as weightless. That is the equivalent of what the stock market has offered to Internet companies, which are not penalized for gluttonous spending far in excess of their meager incomes. So it's no surprise that all sorts of other companies, weary of weighing in every quarter with the traditional measure of profits or losses, would want to belly up to this brave new training table. Witness the lighter-than-air feat of K-Tel International's stock, when the company -- best known for hawking music compilations late at night on UHF television stations -- announced it was moving onto the Web. K-Tel's stock quadrupled in two weeks, and even now is up 80 percent from its pre-Web days, closing last Thursday at $12.5625. "The public is in love with the Internet and believes that Internet stocks are the way to play the future," Mr. Wilson said. "But the public is not particularly adept at picking the good ones from the bad ones." Even old-fashioned companies like Fingerhut, the catalogue merchant, have hired publicists to convince investors that their various Web sites qualify their stocks for Internet-style valuations. Investors are very selective in accepting initial public stock offerings, (except when they'll buy anything.com). After the sharp drop in Internet stocks at the end of the summer, when most companies gave up much of their gains for the year, there was nearly a month when no initial public offerings were brought to the market. Finger-wagging financiers warned that it would be very difficult for any but the very best Internet companies to go public. Then the market devoured offerings from Broadcast.com, the leading Internet audio service, and Ebay, the leading Internet flea market. And suddenly, all sorts of companies were going public that were hardly leaders in anything. One such offering was for Theglobe.com, an on-line chat service that has far fewer users than many of its competitors, but still saw its shares jump from $9 to $97 on the first day of trading in October. It now lingers at $38. One sign that the death of outrage, much noted in Washington, is equally applicable on Wall Street is that Zapata, a fish oil processor, has just resurrected its much-ridiculed plan to transform itself into an Internet service under the name Zap.Com. Zapata's shares nearly doubled in price last Wednesday, when the company issued a news release announcing its comeback. The shares closed last Thursday at $12.375, down $1.875. The power is in the portals. Reading his email, Net van Winkle wouldn't know what anyone meant when they wrote of "portals." A year ago, services like Yahoo and Excite were known as search engines, although they had already started to offer other portal services like news and shopping guides, to keep their vast audiences on their sites longer. This last year, these companies and others doing business as portal sites, along with America Online, were the main beneficiaries of all the money that was pumped into Internet public offerings. How come? Because all of the emerging commerce sites, like Ebay, and on-line communities, like Geocities, spent millions of dollars to buy advertising and other promotions on the popular portal sites. "It was the Tom Sawyer phenomenon, where all of the neighborhood kids paid Tom Sawyer in order to paint the fence for him," said Michael K. Parekh, an analyst with Goldman, Sachs & Company. "One-third to one-half of the money raised by Internet I.P.O.'s was immediately given to the portals." So what about next year? Would these lessons become all the more evident after another 52-week nap? They could. But then again, 1999 might be the year when even some of the Internet giants are toppled. Maybe Walt Disney's new Go network will steal some of the the thunder of Yahoo. Or the upstart Buy.Com, which sells books and computer products at a loss so that it can make money on advertising, could surge past Amazon. Or maybe Congress will figure out how to impose sales taxes on Internet purchases, slowing the growth of electronic retailing. With expectations and many Internet stock prices at such giddy heights, it might not take much of a disappointment to set off a major, negative mood swing. "Valuation is the risk in 1999," Mr. Readerman, the analyst, said. "When the stocks stop performing, the herd who rushed in could just as easily reverse course, as everyone tries to get out first." And that kind of a crash could be a little harder to sleep through. Graphic   Graph "Gauging the Internet Market" tracks several internet-related stocks since January 1998. (Sources: Securities Data Company; Bloomberg Financial Markets)(pg. C7)

title:
BUSINESS: DIARY;
For Niche Food Makers, Some Unlikely Hits
body: You never know what is going to take off in the world of specialty foods, or how. For years, Trappist monks have turned a tidy dollar for their abbey in Gethsemane, Ky., by selling fruitcake, cheese and bourbon fudge they make. Their kitchen methods are steeped in tradition, but they have tried to keep their sales practices up to date: They added order-by-fax to their mail-order operation a few years ago, and this year they ventured onto the Internet. In came the flood. By early December, their site on the World Wide Web, www.monks.org, had attracted 1,600 orders, far more than the 75 brothers of the Abbey of Gethsemani could keep up with working four and a half hours a day each -- practically every minute they are not sleeping, reading or praying. "They don't hire outside people and they have a limited capacity," said Ray Schuhmann, president of the Kinetic Corporation, which operates the Web site for the monks. "We're out of food," said Brother Anselm, head of the abbey. The monks have unplugged the fax machine and stopped taking orders on line. Internet sales, however, cannot explain the public's surging appetite for Flutie Flakes. In a time when cold-cereal sales are usually flat or falling, sugar-coated Flutie Flakes are flying off the shelves of discount and grocery stores in the Northeast. Boxes of the cereal bear the likeness of Doug Flutie, the star quarterback for the playoff-bound Buffalo Bills football team, and a portion of sales proceeds are donated to a foundation Mr. Flutie established to study and combat autism, which afflicts his son, Doug Jr. The team said it has filled mail orders from fans in all 50 states and overseas, and a new Flutie Flakes candy bar is selling well.

title: Long Island Retailers Discover The Selling Power of the Web
body: CRISTINA SAGUIN navigated a long distance to buy her husband, Patrick, the perfect Christmas gift this year. Determined to surprise him with a custom fishing reel, Ms. Saguin of Anchorage scouted all the shops around her home town. No luck. Then, with the shopping days counting down, Ms. Saguin did what many consumers have done this holiday season. She went shopping on the Internet. After 15 minutes of surfing the Web one afternoon, she struck gold: The Fly Fishing Store, situated -- approximately 3,450 miles from Anchorage -- in Bohemia. It not only stocks, but it also manufactures, the Bill Ballan Heirloom Classic reel that caught her interest. Within one week, she received the $390 order. "It was very convenient," Ms. Saguin said. As the number of on-line consumers continues to swell, more Long Island retailers are setting up shop or increasing their presence on the Internet. What they've found is that it typically costs relatively little to reach audiences way beyond their suburban doorsteps. In 1998, 8.7 million households in the unitedstates will have spent $7.8 billion on-line on travel services and retail goods, other than automobiles, according to Forrester Research, a Cambridge, Ma., research company. By 2003, on-line commerce is expected to involve 40 million households and generate $108 billion, or 6 percent of total retail sales in the unitedstates. "More small retailers are getting on line primarily because they're hearing so much about it," said James McQuivey, an analyst in on-line retail strategies at Forrester. Richard DiSilvio, president of Digital Vista, a graphic and Web design company in Massapequa, is seeing more interest among companies. "As time goes by, they're getting more serious about it," he said. "They see that it's here to stay." Adding to the appeal is tumbling Web design prices. In general, a Web site can cost as little as $1,500, Mr. DiSilvio said. When Bill Ballan, owner of the Fly Fishing Store, tackled the Web in 1995, sales were flat at his 3,100-square foot store next to Connetquot River State Park. So he set his eyes on customers outside this fly fisherman's paradise. "A small retailer today just can't survive on local traffic," said Mr. Ballan, a fishing buff who opened his store six years ago. "You have to be innovative to increase sales." He took computer training and spent about $8,000 for someone to construct the site (the site is www.flyfishingstore.com). It includes details and photos of rods and reels and a bulletin board for enthusiasts to swap information and used goods. Thanks to the Internet and the strong economy, sales rose 10 percent his company's first year on the Internet; 20 percent in year two, and 38 percent in year three. In 1998, Mr. Ballan traces $100,000 of $600,000 in total revenues to the Web, including orders from Florida, Mexico, Ireland, and Japan. Other retailers here also have experienced surprising results. Some are good, some problematic. The owners of the Capezio Dance Theater Shop in Rockville Center had not really thought about the Internet when Pagelinx, a Web designer in Patchogue, solicited them two years ago. Although store revenues were steady, they figured it would be a good way to advertise and "fun," said Lisa Spagnola, who is co-owner of the store with her mother, Linda. They paid $2,500 and spend $3,600 annually for Pagelinx to maintain the site. Day one, orders filtered in. The site (www.capeziorvc.com), which displays 500 items, from $6 tights to $62 tap shoes, draws customers worldwide. The home page even plays classical music. Hot spots are the Midwest, where selection is limited, and Japan, where, Ms. Spagnola said, "I heard a $20 leotard here is $80 there." Items sell for 20 to 25 percent below retail. Ms. Spagnola said that the cost usually evens out for walk-in customers because of a 10 percent discount and no shipping charges. These days, Ms. Spagnola is holed up in a back room, responding to emails and readying orders for shipment. The site captures 4,000 to 7,000 hits a month, and 3 to 12 orders a day. Internet sales compose about $100,000 of its $500,000 in annual revenues, generating enough profit to cover store overhead and then some. At the Ski Stop Warehouse in Plainview, the Internet has not proven "a real selling tool," said Al Weisinger. The site (www.skistop.com) draws about $3,000 in orders annually, accounting for a mere 2 percent of total revenues. According to Mr. Weisinger, a major stumbling block is that many of his manufacturers have enforced dealership contracts that prohibit merchandise sales outside one's market. "That's putting a crimp in my sales," he said. Still, Ski Stop is remaining on the Web because it is a "great informational center" and entices local residents who want "to touch and feel" to come in, Mr. Weisinger said. George Lang, a former computer consultant and owner of the Good News Book Store and Religious Gifts in East Northport, blames two factors for the mediocre performance of a folksy Web site (www.goodnewsbooks.com) he created four years ago. First, he believes the majority of his target market are not computer users. And he has barely advertised the virtual store. Then there's the trust factor in cyberspace. At the Fly Fishing Store, sales don't always come easy, Mr. Ballan said. He noted that Internet shoppers ask a tremendous amount of questions. He makes four replies to a customer for every sale. "It's kind of hard to build up the rapport," he said. Diane Clark-Pitura, a dance educator in Bedford Hills, N.Y., shopped on the Capezio Dance Theater Internet site only after the owner of a defunct local dancewear store said she had heard of the retailer. "I wasn't raised in the computer generation," said Ms. Clark-Pitura, who has since opened a dance boutique because of the easy access to inventory through Capezio Dance Theater. "This is a whole new world to me, so there is always a little bit of hesitation." One big question merchants face is whether to make local customers aware of the Web sites. One Long Island retailer intentionally keeps his year-old Web site a secret from the community in which he has operated a home improvement and design product store for 30 years. For that reason, he spoke only on the condition of anonymity. "I am not looking to cannibalize local retail business with a Web presence," he said. He said he can afford to sell products on the Web at 20 percent to 40 percent below retail because of lower overhead and it is not as sales- and people-intensive. Despite his secrecy, some local customers have stumbled upon the site. In those cases, he will honor the lower prices. "It has not become an issue yet," he said. Meanwhile, Internet sales are growing at a rate of 5 percent a month. Graffiti, a clothing retailer, does not consider the Web a separate entity. It wants to reach girls worldwide who do not have access to similar fashion merchandise, plus those who frequent its stores in Commack and Dix Hills. So it features its Web address (www.graffiti-online.com) on business cards and marketing material. The Web accounts for 30 percent of sales. Adam Herman, the company's controller and Web manager, figures residents will visit the stores anyway to avoid shipping costs. But making them aware of Graffiti on-line builds customer loyalty. "When the girls go away or go away to school, they will take this store with them via the Web,' he said. Now, some companies that initially tested the Internet are moving forward more aggressively. Mr. Lang, for example, said he soon plans to market his bookstore's site. Graffiti is adding contests and a chat room where teen-agers can discuss styles or get fashion advice. When computer-savvy Tracey Gera of Gera Gardens in Mount Sinai designed the store's Web site (www.geragardens.com) two years ago, for about $500, it only provided limited information and did not accept orders. Now realizing the Web's power, Ms. Gera -- an addicted cyberspace shopper herself -- recently hired someone to upgrade the site for $1,000. The revamped pages will display about 40 percent of the store's lawn furniture, fountains and garden ornaments, and will be encrypted to accept credit card purchases. Tom Jakab and Todd Morena are reversing the traditional retail-to-Internet path. In a cost-saving move, Mr. Jackab, a graphic artist, and Mr. Morena, a personnel executive, went on the Internet in November 1997, to introduce their product -- socks that snap together to avoid lost sock syndrome. It is linked to quirky sites, like the Bureau of Missing Socks. SnapSock (www.snapsock.com), run out of Mr. Jakab's garage in Merrick, averages $700 to $1,000 in weekly revenues, or 140 pairs of socks, from the Web and a toll-free number. Bolstered by this success, the entrepreneurs plan to open a store in Nassau County this spring. Mr. Morena expects some local customers to swap on-line orders for shopping the old-fashioned way. But, he said, "It doesn't matter which way the sales come in, as long as they come in."
