title:
Compressed Data;
One Trademark Lawsuit That Microsoft May Avoid
body: Bob Kerstein, a former McCaw Cellular Communications executive who is now an Internet entrepreneur in Falls Church, Va., says he has no interest in tangling with Microsoft over use of the term "Windows 2000." But there are plenty of people who want to help him try. After the trade publication Client Server News disclosed last week that he had both the trademark Windows2000 and the domain name www.windows2000.com, Mr. Kerstein received more than 100 messages in one day from people congratulating him and, in many cases, offering to help him capitalize on the name. "People keep telling me I've won the lottery," Mr. Kerstein said. The presumed payoff stems from the fact that the Microsoft Corporation announced recently that Windows 2000 would be the name for the next version of its Windows operating system. (Unlike Mr. Kerstein's trademark, Microsoft's product name will use a space between Windows and 2000.) Earlier this year, Microsoft reportedly paid $5 million to settle a claim brought against it by a small Internet developer called Synet, which had sued over rights to the name Internet Explorer that Microsoft uses for its Web-browsing software. But Mr. Kerstein says he has no plans to take action against Microsoft, even though a Microsoft spokesman, Adam Soan, said Microsoft has no intention of changing its plans to use the name. Mr. Kerstein holds what is known as a common-law trademark on Windows2000 by dint of having been the first to start using the term commercially in early 1996. He operates a Web site that offers a series of live camera views from around the world, including the Eiffel Tower and the Wailing Wall in Israel and a glimpse of Antarctica. Mr. Kerstein said that he was not in the business of "domain name blackmail" and that he had been put off by the number of people encouraging him to try prying money out of Microsoft. But he said he might someday consider offering services related to Windows 2000 software to people who happen to stumble upon his site.   LAURIE J. FLYNN

title: Investment Maverick Navigates the Internet
body: He seemed to be where all the new-media financial wannabes would want to be. But last April, Robert H. Lessin quit his successful career as a vice chairman of one of the country's bigger investment banks to devote his time and money to the Internet -- and to the many new companies he believes it can still spawn. Perhaps the best-known Wall Streeter to make such a dramatic change, Mr. Lessin, 43, left his lofty perch at Salomon Smith Barney Inc. and within days became chairman of the Wit Capital Corporation, (www.witcapital.com) a tiny two-year-old private investment company with offices above the Strand bookstore on Broadway in Greenwich Village. With about 65 employees and some $11 million in capital -- and a couple of slow elevators to its rather dowdy sixth-floor offices -- Wit is seeking to make itself the conduit of choice for individuals interested in investing in young fast-growing companies, most of them ventures related to the Internet. And just this week, Mr. Lessin said, Wit expects to get a further capital infusion of several million dollars from a group of outside investors. Wit caught the eye of the investment community in 1996 when it became the first company to sell stock directly to investors over the Internet, in an initial public offering for the Spring Street Brewing Company (www.witbeer.com). Wit is the brainchild of Andrew D. Klein, 37, a former associate at the law firm of Cravath, Swaine & Moore, who set up the investment firm to finance Spring Street. Now, under Mr. Lessin's guidance, Wit aims not only to invest in the Internet economy, but to use the Internet to help change the economics of investing. "We want to empower the individual in the capital-raising process," Mr. Lessin said. Traditionally, Mr. Lessin said, getting in on the ground floor of initial offerings has tended to be a privilege available only to insiders, investment bankers and big institutional investors. Wit's aim, Mr. Lessin said, is to bring individual investors into the game by using the Internet to build a community of investors. The focus, he said, is not so much on stock trading and brokerage services, but on building and maintaining an on-line capital-raising franchise for individual investors. So far, in a succession of 31 initial public offerings that was halted by the August downturn in the stock market, Wit has raised about $50 million from individuals for start-up companies. The offerings in which Wit has participated, along with other underwriters, include Micro Strategy, an information technology consultant; 24/7 Media, an on-line advertising sales company, and Cyberian Outpost, an electronic commerce site for technology products and services. Some big investors, meanwhile, have taken stakes in Wit itself, including the Mitsubishi Capital Corporation, a subsidiary of the Japanese financial giant, and the Silicon Valley venture capital firm Draper Fisher Jurvetson. And some established names in finance have taken their place on the Wit board, most notably Joseph Hardiman, the former chairman and chief executive of the National Association of Securities Dealers, and Edward H. Fleischman, senior counsel at Linklaters & Paines and a former commissioner of the Securities and Exchange Commission. Mr. Klein, Wit's founder, now plays the role of strategist for the company, which has also brought in Ronald Readmond, a former executive vice president at Charles Schwab, as its vice chairman and president, as Wit seeks to win acceptance among Wall Street's established firms. Yet, promising as this all may sound, skeptics note that until Wit takes a bigger part in more initial offerings larger than its biggest to date -- an undisclosed portion of the $600 million offering for Capstar Broadcasting, the radio properties sold off by Hicks, Muse, Tate & Furst -- Wit's promise remains just that. What is more, the summer turmoil in the stock and bond markets, most analysts agree, has curtailed much stock-issuing activity for months, if not years, to come. "It'll take a long time to happen, longer than they think," said Tom Taulli, a market analyst in Newport Beach, Calif., who works for Silicon Investor, an on-line financial site in Seattle. And whatever Wit's talk of empowering individuals, Mr. Taulli cautioned that a little power can be a dangerous thing. Mr. Taulli, who is writing a book on initial public offering investing for individuals, said "when you open markets, you have to be very careful how you educate investors." Initial public offerings are particularly risky investments, Mr. Taulli said: "Every research study shows I.P.O.'s underperform the market. Most of them don't do well." Mr. Lessin, who readily conceded that Wit has not yet had time to prove its model, said the recent stock market turmoil nevertheless was "a net positive" for his firm -- because it has allowed Wit to demonstrate that it had placed shares into steady hands that would not sell at the first sign of trouble. Of the stock placed by Wit, 85 percent remains with the original investors two months after being issued, a proportion that compares favorably with much of mainstream Wall Street, he said. And, should there be any doubt about his commitment to the Internet as an investment opportunity, Mr. Lessin said he had sunk millions of dollars -- more than $15 million, by some estimates -- of his own money into tens of different Internet-linked ventures. These bets, placed separately from Wit, include budding, still private companies like Culture Finder, (www.culturefinder.com) an on-line source about cultural events around the country; Inns and Outs, (www.innsandouts.com) an on-line bed and breakfast site, and the Main Xchange, (www.mainx.com) which Mr. Lessin described as "the leading teen-age oriented on-line stock exchange site." Mr. Lessin, meanwhile, devotes about one-quarter of his time to Dawntreader, an investment fund that is separate from Wit but that shares his services as its chairman. Dawntreader, which aims to invest at much earlier stages in start-up ventures than would Wit, has so far put money into Watch World, (www.watchworld.com) a retail business selling watches that now is expanding onto the Internet, and Sports Cappers, (www.sportscappers.com) a fee-based on-line business with tips for sports bettors. If Mr. Lessin's plate-spinning act sounds frenetic, it belies the assumption by some on Wall Street that it was the serious stroke he suffered in 1994 that led to his decision to forgo the stress of the financial big leagues for the whimsical pursuit of Internet start-ups. Mr. Lessin, who had returned to work at Smith Barney in a wheelchair within weeks of his stroke, said his leap into cyberspace was anything but an escape. Instead, he described it as a logical move made after analysis of the pending societal changes he summarized in a book "The Middle Chapter: Musings of an Investment Banker," that his employers at Smith Barney published in 1997. In the book he enthused that "the Internet is replicating in five years the superstructure of retailing (distributors, wholesalers, boutiques, malls, superstores, catalogues, etc.) that developed over centuries." After writing that, he said, it would have been hypocritical not to follow his own advice by staking his future on the Net. To some on Wall Street, Mr. Lessin and his new path seem rather outre. "He's very bright, but very strange," said one former investment banking colleague, speaking on condition that he not be identified by name. "Sometimes, he'd turn up to work in chinos and no shoes." Mr. Lessin disputed that account, saying he had always worn shoes to work. And while he may on occasion have shed such formal wear as coat and tie, he noted, he always wore the mandatory business suit for meetings with Fortune 500 companies. That said, he conceded, "No one has ever accused me of being normal." Yet, until his sudden move to Wit, Mr. Lessin, in many ways epitomized the Wall Street establishment. A native of Lexington, Mass., and a graduate of Harvard, Mr. Lessin, the son of a college teacher, followed a well-beaten path to Morgan Stanley & Company after he earned his M.B.A. at Harvard Business School in 1978. A sportsman who loves to ski and play tennis, he met his wife, Naida S. Wharton Lessin, through his passion for ballroom dancing. The couple, who live in Englewood, N.J., have three children. In 1993, along with his mentor Robert F. Greenhill, and other Morgan Stanley bankers, Mr. Lessin left for Smith Barney where he and his colleagues tried, with only limited success, to power that firm into the top echelon of investment banking. Now, after raising billions of dollars for the biggest companies in the country, Mr. Lessin -- laptop computer and HP620 personal organizer in hand -- now busies himself with small start-up companies that may be long on promise, but often are struggling to make even a few thousand dollars in profits. While Wit has suffered significant losses in the recent carnage in the securities markets, and particularly in the market for initial public offerings, it is now seeking to negotiate a capital infusion that would push the capital invested in it to over $25 million, Mr. Lessin said. The biggest challenge to Wit's business model remains the fact that the vast majority of initial offerings still are handled by traditional brokerage houses. And Internet investors account for only an infinitesimally small fraction of one percent of all investment in new stock offerings. "It's certainly small, very small," Mr. Lessin said, "but I intend to make it much larger." Toward that end, Wit has in recent months affiliated itself with a loose collection of companies that calls itself the E-group -- whose members also include Waterhouse Securities, Quick & Reilly's on-line brokerage operation, Datek Online and some 10 other firms that, together, account for about 30 percent of the on-line investing market. The plan is to band together to participate as a group in I.P.O. underwritings involving bigger, conventional brokerage houses. Graphic   Photo: Robert Lessin left the security of a top position at Salomon Smith Barney to head Wit Capital, a tiny investment company. (Joyce Dopkeen/The New York Times)

title:
NEW YORK ON LINE;
With a New Grand Central, Memories of the Old
body: Want to memorialize your personal recollections of Grand Central Terminal for all to see on the World Wide Web? Then hasten to the station, where -- through this Thursday -- the Municipal Art Society is co-host of a multimedia exhibition that will let you do just that. Located in Vanderbilt Hall, the erstwhile waiting room just inside the 42d Street entrance, "The Triumph of Grand Central" consists of a wall of television monitors and a group of three glowing otherworldly-looking orange globes, each more than 6 feet wide and 10 feet tall, with silver exhaust-pipe-like tubes protruding from their sides. These are used to transmit sound from the video screens girding the spheres, which also house large montages of photographs depicting great moments in the station's past. The globes also contain computer terminals where representatives of Excite, the Internet search engine company and the other project co-sponsor, stand ready to assist you in typing in your memories of Grand Central. They will also take your picture or scan in photos that you bring, with everything then posted to a Web site also titled "The Triumph of Grand Central." "We are creating an on-line community," said Michael Kosturos, Excite's man in charge of getting passers-by to commit their recollections to cyberspace. Hundreds of people have participated since the exhibition opened on Oct. 23, he said, and many feel "very strongly" about the station. "It's amazing," he said, "especially among those who lived through World War II and remember seeing people off from here."  WHAT YOU SEE -- From the home page you can go either to a six-part illustrated history of Grand Central or to a site offering 360-degree views of the newly renovated station. You can also choose the community site, which, under "Discussions," contains several rubrics within which project participants have recorded their thoughts about the station, mostly anonymously. These include "What is your favorite memory of Grand Central Station?" ("I remember riding on a train with many sailors," one participant, now 62, noted about the war) and "First Encounter." ("In 1925 my parents took me through Grand Central Station," says another, now "79+" years old. "It was the most overwhelming place I ever saw!") The "Photos" section, also accessible from the community site, displays pictures of the people who have come by the station and recorded their reminiscences, among them a man who used to buy Wendell Willkie political buttons there and a young woman dressed in a cheerleader's uniform advertising Visa credit cards. "There are people from all different cultures," she writes about the terminal.  LINKS -- Just one, to a list of other Excite-sponsored "communities," or discussion groups, which have topics varying from autos to games (http://www.excite.com/communities/directory).  WHAT YOU GET In a busy place in a busy city, those who take the time to participate offer an anecdotal, largely unverifiable and occasionally surreal look at a newyork institution.   BERNARD STAMLER  THE TRIUMPH OF GRAND CENTRAL http://www.excite.com/events/grandcentral Graphic   Photos.

title: Judge in Microsoft Case Tries to Cut Through Jargon as He Questions Witness
body: Exhibiting increasing frustration with the slow pace of the antitrust trial against the Microsoft Corporation, and with the sometimes incomprehensible techno-jargon, the presiding judge stepped forcefully into the courtroom proceedings today, repeatedly rebuking Microsoft's lawyer and then asking the witness, an Apple Computer Company executive, a long series of questions that went directly to the heart of the case. Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson of unitedstates District Court is both judge and jury in this case, and he has made clear over the course of the trial that he is not a technophile. He has also shown impatience with Microsoft's long and often tedious cross-examination of Government witnesses. The witness on the stand this week, Avadis Tevanian Jr., a senior vice president of Apple, is the first witness to testify who is an engineer, not a businessman, and Judge Jackson took the opportunity to ask for explanations on several key points. Microsoft's lawyer, Theodore Edelman, was nearing the end of his cross-examination of Dr. Tevanian this afternoon, when Judge Jackson stepped in, asking first that Dr. Tevanian explain the difference between bundling software with an operating system and fully integrating it into the operating system. The Government accuses Microsoft of wielding the monopoly it has achieved with its Windows operating system to disadvantage its principal competitor in Internet software by the way in which it has combined its Internet Explorer Web browser with Windows. Microsoft argues that Internet Explorer is a fully integrated and inseparable part of the operating system, not simply a "bundled" product that can be removed. To take the browser out of Windows, Microsoft says, would "break" Windows. Apple makes Mac OS, the only major operating system for personal computers that competes with Windows, and for a while Apple included its own Web browser, Cyberdog, with Mac OS. Mr. Edelman was trying to demonstrate that Apple, like Microsoft, saw advantages in combining the browser and operating system, when the judge interrupted and asked, "From a technological perspective, what are the technical advantages of integrating a browser, as opposed to bundling it?" Dr. Tevanian said Apple had made a study of this question, had tried integration instead of bundling but had found that it resulted in "confusion, extra overhead, and there were easier ways to do it." The judge asked, "You don't think there is a benefit in any way, and there may even be a detriment?" Dr. Tevanian responded: "That's right. We have found that we are able to achieve what customers want by bundling browsers." As Judge Jackson continued his questioning, Dr. Tevanian testified that Apple could remove the browser from Mac OS without harming the operating system. The questions and answers cut to the heart of Microsoft's key defense. Dr. Tevanian is a Government witness, so it was not surprising that he gave answers that supported the Government's case. But he is also a top executive of the only company other than Microsoft that makes a commercially viable operating system and thus the only other company with experience in combining operating systems and browsers. Mr. Edelman stood by silently as Judge Jackson's questioning capped a day marked by increasing friction between the lawyer and the court.  Several times during the day Judge Jackson criticized Mr. Edelman for asking "misleading" questions and "mischaracterizing" what Dr. Tevanian was saying on the stand. Once, when Mr. Edelman tried to question Dr. Tevanian about a complex technical document that the witness had never seen, a Government lawyer objected, and Judge Jackson told Mr. Edelman, "I think you'd better go on to something else." As the day ended, Microsoft introduced testimony to rebut one of Dr. Tevanian's allegations, namely that Steven Decker, a senior executive of the Compaq Computer Corporation, had told another Apple executive that Compaq would not license Apple's popular multimedia player, Quicktime, because "that would upset Microsoft." Mr. Edelman played part of a videotaped deposition in which Mr. Decker said that Compaq had decided not to license Quicktime simply because Apple wanted to charge too much for it. The subject of Microsoft never came up in the discussions, Mr. Decker said. Earlier in the day, Dr. Tevanian elaborated on his charge that Microsoft tried to force Apple to stop developing its Quicktime software for use on Windows computers. He said that Microsoft had bluntly described this demand as "knifing the baby." This threat, he said, was made in a meeting in August 1997, when two Apple executives met with two executives from Microsoft. Dr. Tevanian said this was merely the most graphic expression of Microsoft's efforts to use its market muscle to dominate the fast-growing market for the multimedia software used to play audio and video transmitted over the Internet. Mr. Edelman repeatedly portrayed Apple's allegations of Microsoft's threats as vastly overstated. To support that, Microsoft introduced internal Apple email and strategy documents showing that Apple had hoped to try to get Microsoft to adopt Quicktime as a standard for Windows. "The email record shows that Apple wanted Microsoft to adopt its technology, which is what the Government is accusing Microsoft of doing as an illegal act," said Mark Murray, a Microsoft spokesman. With all three of the Government witnesses who have testified so far, Microsoft has introduced evidence intended to suggest that the three companies they represented -- the Netscape Communications Corporation, America Online and Apple -- all employed complaints to the Justice Department's antitrust division as a competitive tactic against Microsoft. To that assertion, Dr. Tevanian testified: "When someone is threatening to use monopoly power against you, it is a perfectly reasonable recourse to go to the Department of Justice. Our goal was to get Microsoft to play fair." The conflict between the two companies over multimedia software continued even after they had reached an agreement in 1997 that included settlement of a patent dispute, a $150 million investment in Apple by Microsoft and Apple's adoption of Microsoft's Internet Explorer as the preferred browser on Macintosh computers. The subject was still a sore point on Feb. 3, when Steven P. Jobs, Apple's acting chief executive, emailed William H. Gates, Microsoft's chairman. Even with the improving relationship between the two companies, Mr. Jobs said "there is one thing that threatens to be quite divisive" -- the behavior of Microsoft's multimedia executives. "They are really going out of their way," Mr. Jobs wrote, "to say that they intend to kill Quicktime, and they are being quite threatening and rude about it." Mr. Jobs added that he hoped Apple's "honest and proper effort" to make Quicktime competitive did not meet with "down and dirty tactics" from Microsoft.

title: On-Line Broker Will Offer Its Own Funds
body: E*Trade Group Inc., a brokerage firm that allows customers to trade stocks over the Internet, plans to sell its own mutual funds. The company, based in Palo Alto, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission late Wednesday to start E*Trade Funds. The company's first in-house fund will be one that mimics the performance of the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index. E*Trade is trying to become the brokerage world's equivalent of the bookseller Amazon.com Inc. and the music retailer CDNow Inc., companies trying to compete with established marketers by using the Internet as a cheaper and more targeted shop window and sales counter. "They're in a position to steal share" from Charles Schwab, Vanguard Group and Fidelity Investments, said Neil Bathon, president of the Financial Research Corporation, a Boston mutual fund research group. Moving into mutual funds is the "right step," he said. Its stock rose $1.3125, or 6.7 percent, to $21, its highest since Aug. 27. In the last three years, E*Trade's revenue has risen tenfold as customer trading volume sextupled. Its market value has almost quadrupled, to $1.19 billion, since its August 1996 initial public offering. E*Trade will compete with more than just Schwab, the largest unitedstates discount brokerage firm and the company with the biggest market share in on-line trading. Vanguard, the No. 2 mutual fund manager, plans to start on-line trading by year-end. Fidelity, the biggest fund manager, has the fourth-largest on-line brokerage firm. E*Trade has also added insurance, mortgage and financial planning information and services to its World Wide Web site.

title:
PUBLIC LIVES;
At 29, an Elder Statesman of Internet Erotica
body: HE is the president of his industry's trade group, a well-known Internet pioneer who has floated above the red ink that has drowned so many other entrepreneurs, but Mark Tiarra still asks that a reporter not mention the northern New Jersey town where he conducts business. "It's a stuffy place around here," he said. "A lot of people wouldn't understand." So let it simply be said that Mr. Tiarra works most days in a nondescript building in Bergen County, not far from Ridgewood, producing, marketing and carefully manipulating the most popular commodity on the World Wide Web: adult entertainment. And as a measure of how rapidly that industry has grown, Mr. Tiarra, who has been in the business only about four years, has become one of its elder statesmen, a highly sought-after guru who is now making plenty of money as a consultant to aspiring Webmasters of cyberporn. He is 29 years old and has the interview spiel down pat. "There's nothing wrong with basing a business on human sexuality," he said, relaxing in front of an enormous computer monitor. "Of course, we don't even do that many hard-core sites. There's nothing wrong with it, but it just doesn't appeal to my tastes. Our sites try to cross the line between art and erotica." He is mildly dismissive of the thousands of coarse, tumbledown Web sites that fail to surround their flesh pictures with the proper graphical environment, but for Mr. Tiarra, the president of the United Adult Sites, there is a limit to condescension. The nonprofit organization, formed in 1996, is the trade association of adult Web sites. It has established a code of ethics for its 500 members and lobbied in Washington against restrictions like the Child On-Line Protection Act, signed into law last month by President Clinton and challenged by Internet professionals. "The Justice Department doesn't even know how it's going to enforce it," he said. "If I were the Supreme Court, I'd be insulted that they passed it." The law penalizes commercial Web sites that fail to keep "harmful material" out of the hands of minors. With his long, limp black hair and faint beard, Mr. Tiarra looks more like the musician and record producer he says he would prefer to be than the pornography industry authority he has become. But he is immensely knowledgeable and utterly straightforward about the details of his work, and though he has no business background, others in the industry say his marketing abilities are remarkable. "Mark is known as a genius at directing traffic," said Fay Sharp, who runs the XWebexpo, a trade show held twice a year for the adult Web industry. "Someone sets up a site and they need to have traffic into the site or they die. So they call Mark and they buy traffic from him, and it's not yucky traffic -- it's people who pay." TRAFFIC, for the uninitiated, refers to the number of people who look at a Web page, and ideally, give out their credit card numbers for a peek at password-protected photos. (According to several industry estimates, more than half the Internet's bandwidth, or capacity, is taken up with traffic in adult material.) By setting up carefully manipulative advertisements on his own popular sites, Mr. Tiarra can send his traffic to other sites, charging them for the privilege. About a year ago, he realized that thousands of people had read about the gold rush of profit possibilities in cyberporn and were trying to enter the industry with no knowledge or ability. So, just as in the mainstream computer world, he began selling his knowledge to new Webmasters, and is now offering complete packages to entrepreneurs with cash. The basic package starts at $3,499, for which a buyer gets two galleries of photos, several completely designed Web pages and a month of consulting advice. The "platinum package" goes for $34,999 and includes a huge gallery of photos, live video feeds, credit card processing, advertising and three months of consulting. His company, Tiarracorp, now has seven full-time employees and 60 or 70 contractors around the world who design the sites. This, of course, is where the big money is. Thousands of inexperienced adult Webmasters have gone under with the increasing competition, but his company has made several million dollars for the last three years, and his telephone continues to ring as newcomers seek out an honest reputation in a rough trade filled with swindlers. Until a few years ago, he had never seen the Internet, coming late to the industry. He grew up in Bergen County, the son of a data-processing executive. He was allowed to play with an Apple 2C and a guitar in high school. He took music in college and later worked in a printing business until a friend asked him to design a Web site for a band. He studied the Internet and by 1994 realized there was only one likely way to make money with it, appealing to a very old-fashioned instinct. His Web sites range from the grandiose ("All the Beauty That Is Woman") to the crass ("The Girls of Tiarracorp"), but every evening, they are seen by thousands of Web surfers, many with credit cards. "I've got a 2-year-old son, and I don't want him seeing these sites until he knows the difference between love and sex," Mr. Tiarra said. "Nobody wants kids on their sites. They cost you bandwidth, and they don't have a credit card to buy anything you have." Graphic   Photo: Mark Tiarra sells his expertise on setting up profitable adult Web sites. (Librado Romero/The newyork Times)

title: Sprint Offers Monthly Plan for UnlimitedLong-Distance Calls
body: For decades, consumers have paid a little more with each passing minute they spent on the phone making a long-distance call. This weekend that will begin to change. Breaking with longstanding practice in the $80 billion long-distance market, the Sprint Corporation introduced an all-you-can-eat pricing plan yesterday that allows consumers to make unlimited long-distance calls on the weekend for $25 a month. The marketing wars in the long-distance business are among the fiercest in any industry, with Sprint, AT&T and MCI Worldcom each spending millions each year to win the ears and mouths of consumers everywhere. The new Sprint Unlimited plan seems sure to give Sprint, the No. 3 long-distance carrier, a big boost in that battle. If the plan proves both popular with consumers and profitable for Sprint, it could usher in a time when people could elect to pay a flat charge for unlimited long-distance calls all week, eliminating the cringe factor when the phone bill arrives. Internet users have enjoyed unlimited-use plans for years. Most people -- except those in much of newyork City, of course -- can make unlimited local phone calls without incurring additional charges. Most cable television channels offer unlimited viewing for a flat monthly fee. But pricing plans in the long-distance business have remained resolutely a la carte. Even as the long-distance giants have started offering special calling plans that eliminate different rates based on geographic distance, those charges have remained resolutely per-minute. "The whole notion that a caller can get on the phone and not worry about how long they are on the call is pretty revolutionary," said Rebecca Sachs, a spokeswoman for the Telecommunications Research and Action Center, a nonprofit research group in Washington. "It is consistent with attitudes people have about the Internet. You don't think about sending email to people in Asia or how long your message is." But do not try to send email with Sprint's new plan. The catch in the program is that Sprint intends the service to be used only for voice calls and will try to ferret out those who use the plan for modems, fax machines or other data services. "It's not available for data usage, Internet connections, because of the usage profile that would be associated with ongoing data connections," said Tim Kelly, a Sprint vice president for marketing. In other words: people spend so much time on line that if they used the Sprint Unlimited plan to make long-distance calls into the Internet, Sprint could end up having a hard time making money on the program. The problem for Sprint is that the new program could end up being highly attractive to cyberspace denizens and fax users. The America Online phone lines in your area are jammed or cranky? Try California. Want to send faxes to a few hundred friends? Wait until Saturday. "We'll monitor the network to identify that," Mr. Kelly said. "We have ways of tracking it." He added that Sprint would not monitor calls but would instead analyze use patterns to figure out whether consumers are making unauthorized use of the program. Customers who use a modem could be kicked off the plan. MCI Worldcom already offers a 5- cent-a-minute rate on Sundays and AT&T offers a 5-cent-a-minute rate all weekend. That means that users would have to make about two hours of calls every weekend to make the Sprint plan economical. The Sprint plan is available nationwide and allows users to make unlimited calls to anywhere in the country on the weekend. During the week, calls cost 10 cents a minute. Mr. Kelly said that the plan would have a positive effect on Sprint's financial results. But Eric Strumingher, an analyst for Paine Webber, estimated that Sprint must pay about 5.5 cents a minute to local phone companies for beginning and ending long-distance calls. That means that the program could potentially hurt Sprint's financial performance if many of its customers signed up for the program and then switched a lot of their calling from the week to the weekend. An MCI Worldcom spokesman said his company had no plans to offer an unlimited-use plan. AT&T said that it would consider such a plan if its customers asked for it.

title:
THE MARKETS;
Agency Tangled in Web By Early Release of Data
body: In an embarrassing blunder that illustrates the pitfalls facing the Government in the Information Age, the Bureau of Labor Statistics inadvertently posted part of its closely guarded jobs report on the Internet a day before the report's scheduled release. As a result, some investors got an advance peek at the economy's performance in October. "We have procedures in place," Katharine Abraham, the bureau's commissioner, said. "They obviously didn't work." By the end of the day, Ms. Abraham said she would not be able to explain what went wrong until today at the earliest. Monthly job data are normally released on a Friday, usually the first one of the following month. The main concern about security involves the circulation of information within the Government. The bureau normally releases manufacturing employment figures to the Federal Reserve two days before the official report is released so that the central bank can use it to estimate industrial production. On Thursday night, it provides a complete report to the Council of Economic Advisers, which briefs the President's economics team and passes the data along to the Treasury and the Fed. Yesterday's glitch was not the first involving the bureau's four-year-old World Wide Web site. Two years ago, a report on producer prices was posted the night before it was scheduled for release. Unlike yesterday, though, bureau staff almost immediately discovered the mistake and retrieved the report. This time, a full 24 hours before the jobs report was scheduled to be released, a table reviewing job increases and declines by industry was mistakenly posted on the bureau's Web site (www.bls.gov). It was a background table prepared for internal use that had only recently been added to the charts the bureau makes available with its jobs report. Raymond Stone, head of the Stone & McCarthy brokerage firm, was one individual who found it while browsing the site. Mr. Stone alerted the bureau -- but also shared the report, which showed that job growth in October was much softer than had been expected, with his clients. "Some people use the Web to make vacation plans, some people use it to buy a new car," he said on CNBC yesterday. "I go look at economic data." The leak did not particularly rattle financial markets. "We're lucky that markets are fixated on other things and that they're paying much less attention to economic data," Bruce Steinberg, chief economist at Merrill Lynch & Company, said. "It's a pretty shocking event, and it had an impact, but it didn't have the impact it could have had." Lawrence Katz, an economist at Harvard University and a former chief economist at the Labor Department, said he assumed the leak had been an innocent mistake. "In the past, even when there have been rumors of a leak, it's been taken very seriously," he said.

title: U.S. Delays Decision on Traffic Data Fees
body: Federal regulators are putting off a decision on whether telephone companies have to continue paying one another fees for carrying data traffic to America Online and other Internet service providers. The Federal Communications Commission planned to address the matter on Friday, but now it is not expected to take action for at least two weeks, commission officials said today. The delay will give the F.C.C. time to consult with state regulators, who are meeting next week in Florida, the officials said. The F.C.C. is expected to propose phasing out these fees -- which total hundreds of millions of dollars -- once companies' current contracts expire in the next two years. The commission also plans to ask for public and industry comment on how carriers should compensate one another in the future. The decision would depend on a finding by the F.C.C. that data traffic destined to Internet service providers and from there to the Internet, is interstate communication. That would make it not subject to these fees because they can be imposed only on traffic deemed local. The compensation issue has pitted major local phone companies including the GTE Corporation and the regional Bells against other phone companies called competitive local exchange carriers, like ICG Communications, e.spire Communications Inc. and MCI Worldcom. GTE and the Bells pay these and other phone companies millions of dollars more in fees than they take in.

title: Browser Memos Pose Challenge To Microsoft
body: The Microsoft Corporation was so worried about the Netscape Communications Corporation's lead in Internet software last year that its senior executives wanted to delay an upgrade of the Windows operating system to gain an edge in the browser battle, according to internal Microsoft documents released this week by the Government. The linchpin of Microsoft's defense in its antitrust trial is that its Internet Explorer, or I.E., browser is a seamless feature of Windows -- not, as the Government contends, a separate product bundled with Windows in an effort to give it an unfair advantage against Netscape. The origins of its product strategy, Microsoft asserts, date back more than four years to a meeting of its executives in April 1994. But internal Microsoft electronic-mail messages released this week by the Justice Department seem to cast doubt on these defense arguments. Microsoft, however, argues that the email mostly supports its legal case. "It shows that they regarded browsing functionality as part of Windows and were willing to delay an upgrade schedule to deliver a superior product," said Mark Murray, a Microsoft spokesman. Still, an email exchange between two senior Microsoft executives in January 1997 -- more than a year after the company first introduced its software for browsing the World Wide Web -- talks of competing with Netscape as "pitting browser against browser" and refers to "browser market share as job 1." The exchange suggests that at that late date, within Microsoft, the browser and the operating system were not viewed as a single, seamless product. In an email on Jan. 2, 1997, James Allchin, a Microsoft senior vice president, writes to Paul Maritz, a group vice president and the most senior Microsoft executive scheduled to appear as a witness in the trial, "I do not feel that we are going to win on our current path." Later, he adds, "I am convinced we have to use Windows -- this is the one thing they don't have." In response, Mr. Allchin urges Mr. Maritz, "If you agree that Windows is a huge asset, then it follows quickly that we are not investing sufficiently in finding ways to tie I.E. and Windows together." The more tightly Internet Explorer can be entwined in the next upgrade of Windows, Mr. Allchin writes, "the more Netscape will be cut off." Defeating Netscape, the email suggests, was such a priority at Microsoft that it was seen to outweigh the impact a delay of Windows would have on the computer industry. Sales of new personal computers, hardware add-ons and software all typically surge in the wake of an upgrade of Windows, part of the central nervous system that controls more than 90 percent of personal computers sold today. Delaying Windows to embed the browser, is "the only thing that makes sense even if O.E.M.'s suffer," Mr. Allchin wrote, referring to "original equipment manufacturers," jargon for computer makers. Mr. Maritz shared that view. In a response on the same day, he wrote that he saw "little option" but to fully integrate the browser in the operating system, "even if it means missing the O.E.M. window" -- the delivery time frame that would allow computer makers to install the upgrade on machines for the 1997 year-end sales season. Microsoft's Windows upgrade, code-named Memphis, was initially scheduled to be released in August or September 1997. But its arrival was delayed until June of this year, and it is called Windows 98. In early 1997, Microsoft started hinting to software developers and analysts at industry conferences that Memphis might be delayed. "It was never the reason given in public, but industry insiders believed that the real reason Memphis was being delayed was to totally integrate the browser and help Microsoft in its life-and-death battle with Netscape," said Richard Doherty, president of Envisioneering, a research firm in Seaford, N.Y. "This email does seem to be proof of what Microsoft's intentions were back then." Memphis was delayed even more than Microsoft had thought in early 1997, partly as a result of Microsoft's $425 million purchase in April 1997 of Web TV Networks, an Internet-via-television service. Afterward, Microsoft also decided to include Web TV software in Memphis. Internet Explorer is fully embedded in Windows 98, but the company released a stand-alone version of its browser, Internet Explorer 4.0, in October 1997. In its defense, Microsoft has also said that it became company policy after a meeting in April 1994 to "make a big bet on the Internet." Though few concrete plans were made that day, Microsoft says, there was agreement that Windows should have built-in access to the Internet, which eventually became its browser strategy. The meeting occurred a couple of days after Netscape was founded and suggests, Microsoft says, that its main intention in the browser battle was to improve its operating system -- not to crush Netscape, as the Justice Department contends. Yet in an email written on June 10, 1994, Steven Sinofsky, a Microsoft executive who helped organize the April meeting, portrays a company ambivalent about the Internet and not yet planning a browser of its own. "I must admit," Mr. Sinofsky writes, "that the thought of 'Internet evangelism' is a little like evangelizing water to Noah." He describes Microsoft's plans for Windows 95 as including "all the plumbing you need to connect to the Internet," mostly software protocols for communicating on the network. Later, Mr. Sinofsky wrote, "We do not currently plan on any other client software, especially something like Mosaic." Mosaic was the name of the browser developed by the programmers at the University of Illinois, most of whom went on to help found Netscape. Even so, Mr. Sinofsky added that Microsoft was "investigating possibilities."

title:
LIBRARY/INTERNET RADIO;
Approach Is Eclectic and Hip
body: WWW.MACRORADIO.NET THE name sums up the Eclectic Radio Company, producers of the Macro Radio Network. Based in Boulder, Colo., this hip, home-grown network plays host to four alternative niche stations: Eardrum World Music Radio, Go Ga Ga Brand Radio, Amino Radio and Radio M. The network certainly doesn't suffer from variety, but it does suffer from broken links to play lists and occasionally from delayed transmissions. Each sponsor-supported station has a lively design and plays some of the best music in its area. The format is like that of a traditional radio station, with scheduled shows run by deejays. "We're trying to take advantage of the editorial style of traditional public and community radio and bring that to the commercial opportunities of the Internet," said Joe Pezzillo, founder and general manager. For virtual globetrotters, Eardrum (www.eardrum.com) offers a solid selection of international music with programs like Global Taxi, Rootsworld Radio and Sacred World Music. While the station does not offer detailed information about an artist during the time a song is playing, it offers a special feature on a different artist's or country's music every week. In addition, the Eardrum Compass section leads to a page with links to interesting facts about various countries. Clicking on the flag of Brazil, for example, will take you to a page that includes facts like the country's capital, population, official languages and traditional recipes, as well as a map and a live picture from a Web camera. Some of the country links offer archival radio shows of music exclusively from that country. There are also bulletin boards to post messages, reviews and recommendations. Amino Radio (www.aminoradio. com) plays an assortment of shows for devotees of the techno beat. "Solid Steel," a popular London show, is now available on the station. Other shows, like DJ Ivy's Nu Skool Neurotix and Nitro's Noise Makers, offer a mix for ravers who are into jungle, trance and house techno. There is also a section with interviews of record producers and deejays and an area that offers a schedule of raves around the world. The Aminomatic lets you create your own CD from a selected list of techno artists. For people who want long shows devoted to a specific genre, Radio M (www.radiom.com) presents a diverse mix. Shows include a hip-hop program called Radio Bums, a surf music show called Club Baja and Reggaelution, in which a Jamaican deejay, Donovan Makha, plays his favorite reggae artists. The Krazy Kooter Rockabilly Show plays swing music, and Avant Gardening plays modern serious music by composers like John Cage and Fred Frith. Listening to this show and clicking through the Radio M link to the Accuweather Web site makes for a strange listening experience. The one problem is that the show schedule is not always accurate. Go Ga Ga Brand (www.gogaga. com) radio is made up of idiosyncratic shows that reflect their deejays' tastes and styles. The Music for Cubicles show offers "music to ward off the management." While listening to things like soul music and polka, you can take a goofy quiz about your work cubicle in which you answer questions about its color and size and your favorite decorating techniques. Another show, Infinite Spins, offers "diverse freeform music just like Mom used to hate," and Alt-X Audio plays "the best in hyperliterary audio art and streaming word dub." Each week The Edition delves into the life and work of an artist, like the jazz musician Mose Allison, or a particular genre, like voodoo music of Haiti.

title:
LIBRARY/INTERNET RADIO;
Network Has Less Glitz, Fewer Glitches
body: WWW.NETRADIO.COM WITH its retro logo, the Net Radio Network conjures up ghosts of early broadcast radio. Operating from Minneapolis, it has been broadcasting since 1995 and provides more than 150 music and information channels. The Net Radio Network doesn't offer personalization options or the ability to scroll through songs, but you run into fewer technical glitches than on some other networks. On the home page, there is a list of genres that include Kidz Hits, Electronica and Christian Hits. Within each category, there are niche channels. For example, in Cafe Jazz there is an Acid Jazz channel, a Big Band channel and a Divas channel. While you listen, you can also choose to read news about the artists or to scan through a list of featured CD's. Every week, each channel spotlights one artist. In Christian Hits, there are channels devoted to Urban Gospel and Christian Rock. The Kidz Hits channel includes educational songs about Vitamin C and hits from the kid rockers Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen, the twins who starred in the sitcom "Full House." Songs are often interrupted with jokes from Earl, a goofy-sounding Webcaster with a infectious giggle. On a channel called Kidz News, Earl will explain a mundane but interesting phenomenon, like why you get hotter in darker colors or why some people are left-handed. There is also a page of links to Web sites for children. The network also broadcasts daily news that is conveniently divided into channels devoted to topics like health, hockey, rock and celebrity news. A channel called Infojunkie combines news reports from all the categories. At the Broadband Point, Net Radio combines some its most popular channels into a high-bandwidth stereo channel called Channel One. It is meant to give people with higher bandwidth (ISDN or above) the ability to listen in broadband 40K stereo without taxing other listeners' bandwidth. The network offers a schedule of times that specific channels play on Broadband Point. Graphic   Photo

title:
LIBRARY/INTERNET RADIO;
Web Radio Expands Listening Horizons
body: I WAS taught not listen to the radio while I worked. One of the fastest-growing Internet industries, Web radio, is based on breaking that very rule. There are two kinds of Web radio, both of which can be heard via streaming-audio technology. One kind is really ordinary radio that is heard over the Internet. The Web now makes it possible to tune into an out-of-state baseball game or listen to your favorite college radio station without leaving town. The other kind of Web radio was created exclusively for the Internet. Together, traditional broadcasters and Internet-only start-ups offer more than 1,700 audio channels that you can listen to through your computer. "It's a critical mass of choice," said Larry Magne, editor of the original edition of "Passport to Web Radio" (International Broadcasting Service, 1997), which describes stations from Texas to Taipei. (An updated edition, edited by David Walcutt, appeared earlier this year.) Web sites like www.broadcast.com and the BRS Radio Directory (www.radio-directory.com) act as portals to thousands of traditional and Web-only stations. Mr. Magne said that in traditional broadcast markets, many genres, like classical, are losing out to programming that draws better advertising. The Web provides a broader range of choice. For example, Mr. Magne said that Radio Beethoven, a tiny classical station that broadcasts from Santiago, Chile, is one of the best classical radio stations around (www.beethovenfm.cl/RealAudio/ index.html). Many Web-only radio stations were founded on the idea of countering a trend toward less broadcast diversity. Web technology allows stations to offer niche programs. Some are homespun pirate stations or stations devoted to only one band, like www.deadradio.com, which exclusively plays the Grateful Dead. In addition to the many independent stations, there are larger Internet-only networks that offer multiple channels of music and talk. Three of those reviewed here -- Imagine Radio, Netradio and Spinner -- have eliminated audio advertisements and disk jockey chatter. They offer a wide variety of programming and, in the case of Imagine, personalizing programming. But personalized programming has made many record labels and the Recording Industry Association of America worry that Web radio will threaten CD sales. The Digital Millennium Copyright Act, which was recently signed into law, further secures copyright protection on line. While all Web radio stations are required to pay fees to artists through Ascap and BMI, this new legislation will force Web radio stations to pay a licensing fee to record labels as well. The act says customized stations must negotiate individual contracts with all the labels whose artists they play, and it forbids stations to play more than two songs in a row from a single artist in a three-hour period. "Record companies don't yet understand the power of user customization," said John Adams, director of programming for Imagine Radio. "They have to realize that it can expose new artists and increase record sales." To listen to Web radio, you need Real Player, a technology developed by the Real Networks Corporation that enables an audio signal to be "streamed" over the Internet. Real Player is available free at www.real. com and takes between 10 and 20 minutes to download. It can also be found through most Web radio portals and networks. If your modem uses dial-up access, Web radio will eat up half your bandwidth, and on any connection slower than an ISDN line, Web broadcasts are accompanied by an AM radio-style buzz. But if choice and control are more important, and if you like the retro charm of the AM buzz, then Web radio can be a listening adventure. Graphic   Photos: COZY MUSICAL CORNERS -- To satisfy various tastes, whether Beethoven or Jerry Garcia, the Net puts more than 1,700 radio channels within reach. (Associated Press)

title: Microsoft Defends Tactics In 1997 Talks With Apple
body: The Microsoft Corporation argued in court today that it had every right to tell Apple Computer last year that it would stop producing word processors and other software for Macintosh computers unless Apple adopted Microsoft's Internet browser as the default choice on all its computers. "Suppose Microsoft simply decides not to offer a product," said Theodore Edelman, a Microsoft lawyer. "Do you have a problem with that?" "Yes," replied Avadis Tevanian Jr., the Apple senior vice president who was being cross-examined today in the Government's antitrust suit against Microsoft. "I have a problem with them doing it when they are using it as a threat to get us to do something we didn't want to do." In his direct, written testimony, made public on Friday, Dr. Tevanian contended that Microsoft had threatened to stop producing a new Macintosh version of Microsoft Office unless Apple reversed its position and favored Microsoft's browser, Internet Explorer, over Navigator, the market-leading browser of the Netscape Communications Corporation. Several email messages written by Microsoft executives disclose that the company intended to use the threat as "a club," as one message put it, to force Apple into line. Microsoft Office is so dominant -- it has more than 90 percent of the market for business applications suites -- that Apple executives worried that their company would be crippled if their customers could not buy it. In the end, Apple gave in and made Microsoft's Internet Explorer the default browser and agreed not to promote Navigator, which had been the default browser on Macintosh computers. Dr. Tevanian disclosed in court today that at Microsoft's insistence, the Netscape browser is not even installed on Macintosh computers when an owner first loads a new computer with software from the installation CD-ROM -- unless the new owner chooses a custom installation option. Hardly anyone does that, Dr. Tevanian said. Apple's agreement to make Internet Explorer its preferred browser was part of the deal in which Microsoft agreed to produce its Office suite for Macintosh customers, invested $150 million in Apple and settled several longstanding patent disputes. Mr. Edelman, a partner in the Sullivan & Cromwell law firm, argued that however Dr. Tevanian chose to describe Microsoft's bargaining tactics, the company had every right to decide which products to develop -- and which to drop. Among other attempts to impeach Dr. Tevanian's testimony, Mr. Edelman suggested that Apple brought a threat of its own to the negotiations last year, saying that it would file a $1.2 billion lawsuit contending that Microsoft had infringed on Apple patents. "Didn't you personally tell Microsoft that if no deal was reached, Apple would sue Microsoft for more than $1 billion?" he asked. No, Dr. Tevanian said, Apple had told Microsoft that it owed Apple $1.2 billion in royalties but had not said anything about filing suit. As Microsoft did with a previous witness, from America Online, Mr. Edleman tried to show that a user could easily install Netscape's browser on a Macintosh computer, even if the computer came with Internet Explorer as the default. On video monitors in the courtroom, Mr. Edelman showed seven sequential photographs of the Macintosh screens a user would have to navigate to change the default browser. As he did that, Dr. Tevanian found himself in the position of having to criticize his own company's product to support his testimony. He told the lawyer that the process was not really as simple as he was making it seem. The menus were counterintuitive, Dr. Tevanian said; it would be easy to get confused. In fact, when Mr. Edleman finished, Thomas Penfield Jackson, the unitedstates District Court judge who is hearing the case, remarked: "It certainly doesn't tell me how to do it."

title: Microsoft Said to Pursue On-Line Deal
body: In a further refinement of its on-line media efforts, the Microsoft Corporation plans to acquire Linkexchange Inc., a closely held Internet-advertising firm, in a stock deal valued about $250 million, according to people close to the companies. Linkexchange, based in San Francisco, has become one of the best-known Internet-advertising networks, a class of new-media companies that sell banner promotions on World Wide Web sites to reach the largest possible audience. Linkexchange alone places ad banners on about 400,000 Web sites, though many of those sites are obscure personal home pages. Under terms of the deal, Linkexchange is to be integrated into the Microsoft Network, or MSN, group. The acquisition could give Microsoft a much stronger position in on-line media. The company has dropped plans for entertainment-oriented sites in favor of services like its Expedia on-line travel agency, Carpoint automobile catalogue and Hotmail, a free electronic-mail offering, and has grouped them under the MSN brand. That strategy is increasingly pitting Microsoft against more established Web portals such as Yahoo Inc. and Excite Inc. Linkexchange, founded in 1996, allows member Web sites to advertise free on other sites throughout the Linkexchange network -- provided they agree to return the favor. Linkexchange then makes money by selling some of the ad space on its member sites to paying sponsors.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Can't Program That VCR? Just Click for Help
body: If a New Jersey Internet company has its way, the telephone will no longer be the only means for seeking assistance from corporations' technical support or customer service lines. The IDT Corporation is marketing a new service called Click 2 Talk that uses the Web to dial into various companies' telephone banks. To place the call, a user merely clicks on a Click 2 Talk icon on a company Web site; the call is placed over Internet lines while, at the other end, a service or support employee receives the call as if it were placed via telephone. The caller then conducts the question-and-answer session by speaking into the PC microphone and listening to the computer's speakers. So far, 70 companies have signed up with Click 2 Talk, including 1-800-Flowers and some Sheraton hotels, said Yonah Lloyd, director of the Click 2 Talk business at IDT. But what was wrong with using a telephone in the first place? Besides, isn't it tough enough to get technical support without having to rely on a computer and an Internet connection -- which seems more fragile than reliable old Ma Bell? Mr. Lloyd said the service offered several advantages, notably that it eliminated long-distance tolls, enabling callers to make contact from anywhere in the word. "We're trying to educate people that they can universalize and globalize their business at no cost," he said.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Get It Wholesale on the Net: A Web Site for Coupon Clippers
body: Note to fans of the coupon: it's time to fire up the printer. Val Pak Direct Marketing Systems, one of the nation's largest distributors of coupons, whose familiar fat blue envelopes periodically arrive in mailboxes nationwide, has gone digital. The company, based in Largo, Fla., has started an ambitious site to put thousands of coupons on the Internet. Visitors to the site (www.valpak.com) can type in their ZIP codes and the types of businesses they are interested in, and Val Pak will spit out a list of related coupons in their geographic areas. Then the coupon surfers can print out the coupons -- as many of each as they please. Val Pak, which circulates 12 billion coupons a year the old-fashioned way, is a bit late in arriving on line. It joins a growing number of services and individual merchants already offering coupons on the Internet, and analysts project explosive growth for the concept. Todd Leiser, vice president for Internet technology services for Val Pak, said one reason the company had taken its time in going on line was to make sure that it had enough participating advertisers. The site now has 30,000 coupons from some 22,000 advertisers, including national chains and numerous mom-and-pop operations in local communities, Mr. Leiser said. Some hesitation on the digital front isn't surprising, given that coupon clippers can print unlimited supplies of digitally delivered discounts. But Mr. Leiser said tests of the concept had shown few, if any, people engaging in rampant redeeming. Mr. Leiser said businesses were careful not to offer certain types of coupons on line, like "buy one hamburger, get one free" offers that could be gobbled up in big numbers. Whatever the reaction to the on-line coupons, Val Pak will not stop sending the familiar blue envelopes via snail mail. "We have no plans to cut back or change that," Mr. Leiser said.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
On-Line Shoppers' Attitudes: A Case of Bahhumbug.com?
body: On-line shoppers evidently haven't grasped the concept that it is better to give than to receive. A new survey by Jupiter Communications, a market research company in newyork, projects that on-line shopping will hit $2.3 billion during this holiday season, up from $1.1 billion a year ago. But the survey also finds that only 16 percent of the purchases will be gifts; the majority will be for the shoppers themselves. What happened to the holiday spirit? Has the Net turned otherwise nurturing souls into self-gratifying surfers? Jupiter says there is a "large source of untapped revenue" for companies that can persuade on-line shoppers not just to purchase for themselves, but to take a chance on a gift. Another recent Jupiter survey indicates that retailers can fuel the growth of electronic commerce simply by offering lower prices or very attractive specials. Nicole Vanderbilt, director of the digital commerce practice for Jupiter, said that not long ago, the biggest hindrance to on-line shopping was the fear that transactions would not be secure. Now, she said, a greater obstacle appears to be that people are not finding the bargains they want. "This marks the next phase of consumer adoption of the on-line channel," Ms. Vanderbilt said. "If we did this survey two years ago, the focus would've been on security. Now it's on incentive."

title: The O.E.D. Adds the Web to Its Lexicon
body: FILED carefully away in the offices of the Oxford English Dictionary are millions of handwritten index cards, many dating back to James Murray, the master lexicographer who presided over the dictionary's first edition at the turn of the century. For decades these cards, which document the appearance in English literature of words from abacination to zumbador, were the raw material from which the dictionary was made. The cards, six million or seven million at last count, are still used in the continuing work of revising and updating the dictionary. But they now compete for office space with a dozen Sun Microsystems servers, 80 Sun workstations and a battery of PC's running Windows NT. The dictionary's lexicographers, in turn, are assisted by a team of systems engineers. In the last few years, the O.E.D., the esteemed lexicon that conjures up images of paper, ink and a heady dust, has gradually entered the silicon age. "We're still straddling the electronic world and the paper world," said Royalynn O'Connor, the on-line product director for Oxford University Press, which publishes the O.E.D. First there was a CD-ROM, which was released in 1992 and contained the entire second edition of the dictionary. Then came a home page on the Web (www.oed.com), featuring history, newsletters and a Word of the Day. Now the O.E.D. is undertaking its most ambitious electronic project to date: next year, the entire dictionary is scheduled to be placed on the Internet as a searchable database. And with the recent publication of the best-selling book "The Professor and the Madman," by Simon Winchester, about a highly regarded contributor to the O.E.D. who also happened to be a deranged murderer, public interest in the dictionary is keen, Ms. O'Connor said. But before the O.E.D. can be put on line, it must overcome a host of technical challenges, some common to all electronic dictionaries, others resulting from the singular and unwieldy nature of the O.E.D. itself. In short, the dictionary's editors and technicians must take a 20-volume, 22,000-page reference work containing some three-quarters of a million entries and turn it into an electronic database that can be searched rapidly by machine and be read comfortably on a 15-inch computer monitor. The dictionary's staff is currently field-testing a prototype of its on-line edition with invited groups of scholars, researchers and librarians around the unitedstates. In January, Ms. O'Connor said, an outside contractor will be hired, after bids are submitted, to create the on-line edition and its search engine according to Oxford's minutely detailed specifications. "Most publishers let their vendors design," said Ms. O'Connor, whose office is in newyork. "We're designing it first because it's so critical and so complex." The idea of on-line publication grew out of a major revision to the dictionary that has been under way since the early 1990's. The O.E.D.'s first edition, shepherded by James Murray, was published in 10 volumes between 1884 and 1928. In the years that followed, various supplements were issued. In 1989, Oxford published the second edition, which comprised the first edition, the supplements and about 5,000 new words, in 20 volumes. Now, besides adding contemporary words (Ruthian, hyperlink), editors are revising the entire content of Mr. Murray's dictionary for the first time, updating Edwardian-era definitions, adding new bibliographic citations and correcting etymologies, based on advances in linguistic research. Work on the revised edition, which is expected to run to at least 30 volumes, is scheduled to last until 2010. The incentive to go on line was twofold, Ms. O'Connor said. "One is, we are making discoveries about the English language that it would be very unfair to ask people to wait until 2010 to read." The other motivation was economic. Throughout its history, the dictionary has never been profitable; the current revision alone is budgeted at $55 million. "There's some sense of, 'Can we get a return before 2010?' " Ms. O'Connor said. "We have to pay the lexicographers." The on-line edition, which is scheduled to be available to the public by the end of 1999, will be accessible for a fee through the O.E.D.'s home page. It will consist at first of the dictionary's second edition, plus some revised entries and new words. As the revisions to the dictionary progress, new entries will be added quarterly, complementing but not replacing the earlier ones. "This is one of the things we get loud and clear from our market research," Ms. O'Connor said. "Say a new entry comes up for 'restaurant.' People still want to see what the old entry was." For every electronic dictionary, there are two paramount considerations: it should be easy to search and easy to read. Open the O.E.D. to any page. Each entry contains certain standard elements: the word itself, its variant spellings and etymology and -- the dictionary's defining characteristic -- citations of the word as it has been used in English literature through the centuries. In the on-line O.E.D., users must be able to search for each of these elements independently. Someone researching words with Basque in their pedigree, for example, should be able to summon up on line a list that includes anchovy, jingo and jai alai. The text of the O.E.D. has actually existed in electronic form since the late 1980's, when it was put into Oxford's computers, a task that took 120 typists a year and a half. (The profusion of special characters in the dictionary made it impossible to scan using optical-character recognition.) The text was then tagged using SGML, a markup language designed to encode and organize large documents. Some institutions, including academic libraries and the Bloomberg News Service, purchased copies of the SGML text on magnetic tape, added their own search engines and offered the result to users as a computerized O.E.D. "In the past few years, universities have been in essence publishing the O.E.D. on line," Ms. O'Connor said. "The problem with it is the cross-references don't work. There isn't the kind of consistency Oxford University Press would want." To make their dictionary fully searchable, the O.E.D.'s editors must standardize a tangle of inconsistencies left over from Mr. Murray's day. Suppose you want to search for words quoted from "Treasure Island." The dictionary currently renders the book's title as Treasure Island, Treasure Isl., Treasure Is., Treas. Isl. and Treasure I. Until those entries are standardized, a search engine cannot easily retrieve them all together. "We have a fairly large process of normalizing this bibliographical data," said John Simpson, the chief editor of the O.E.D., in a telephone interview from Oxford, England. "In the old days, it didn't really matter if you gave a different short title for a text in Volume 1 as you gave in Volume 11 because the reader knew what it meant. But now there's a requirement that people can search for what they want and get the appropriate matches." Another challenge is representing the welter of special characters that appear in the dictionary text. There are more than 600 in all, including letters of the Greek alphabet, diacritical marks, mathematical symbols and the signs of the zodiac. (The CD-ROM came with special fonts that the user had to install, something the O.E.D. editors want to avoid for the Internet edition.) Not only do these characters have to be legible and printable, they must be searchable as well. "Making sure you have a display that is configured so that it can be handled by that many computers operated by that many people in a consistent way is a huge task," said Kara Noble, director of electronic product development for Merriam-Webster, whose Collegiate Dictionary, 10th edition, is published on the Web (www.m-w.com/dictionary.htm). "It's easy for a schwa to look correct on my computer here in the office and totally different on your computer where you're sitting." On the printed page, an O.E.D. entry is a crowded affair. But what readers can tolerate in a book will not always work on a computer monitor. As a result, the overall design of the O.E.D.'s screen display is crucial. "It's important that on first glance it has to look elegant, which isn't necessarily that first thing you think about with a dictionary," Mr. Simpson said. "The O.E.D. has a reputation for being elegant. It mustn't put the reader off by having so much information compacted together that it's difficult to read." To unclutter the screen and reduce the need for scrolling, Oxford is experimenting with allowing features to be switched on and off within each entry. In an early version of the prototype, for example, small buttons labeled S and D represent a word's spelling and derivation, respectively. Call up the entry for the word merchant and click on the S, and up comes a list of variant spellings recorded over the centuries, including marchaund, marchande, mayrchand, maircheant, mairchantt and marchawn. The list can be hidden with another click. Clicking on D reveals the word's derivation, or etymology. To streamline the display even more, the O.E.D. is shunning the electronic bells and whistles common to many Internet sites, like video streaming, audio clips and even illustrations. "There won't be a multimedia aspect to this," Ms. O'Connor said. "Because the entries are so complex, we're really aiming for something very simple." As the specifications for the on-line edition are being finalized, the huge task of revising the century-old printed dictionary continues. As in Mr. Murray's time, the O.E.D. maintains a stable of outside "readers" in England and the unitedstates who scour libraries -- and these days, literature databases as well -- for bibliographic citations. In many cases, their labor has uncovered far earlier citations for words than were previously known. (Mr. Simpson was delighted to report that "market-basket," first cited in 1807 in the O.E.D.'s second edition, has been antedated to 1585.) Today, the readers send in their findings by modem, using what Mr. Simpson calls "the electronic equivalent of index cards" -- specially prepared database shells installed on their laptop computers. As in the past, lay people are also encouraged to contribute. And while some of these lay lexicographers still send in quotations the old-fashioned way, using pen and paper or even mailing in pasted-up pages torn from books (not recommended), many more, Ms. O'Connor said, now transmit their findings via E-mail or the guest book section of the O.E.D. Web site. The site maintains a list of words for which editors need additional citations (glatt kosher before 1973, grandkid before 1948). There is still no decision on how much it will cost to use the O.E.D. on line and what kind of access first-time browsers will get, Ms. O'Connor said. "Is it free one weekend?" she wondered aloud. "Is it free on Sunday? Can you use it for two weeks? Can you look up 30 words? We have to decide, and that's one of the fun things about the Web -- you can do all of those things. It's a fun way to give away information without giving away the whole store." As the O.E.D. lumbers genteelly into the new millennium, it is heartening to note that however vital its computers have become, they can never fully replace the work of its pencil-wielding, flesh-and-blood staff. "An awful lot of it will remain having to be done by the individual editors," Mr. Simpson said. "The actual defining, for example. You can't ask a computer to define for us." And the O.E.D.'s file cards, too, seem assured of a place in the 21st-century life of the dictionary. "It's actually quite efficient to use the index cards," Mr. Simpson said. As he spoke, he riffled through a small batch on his desk containing words beginning with the letter M. "You can put them into little piles," he said. "I wouldn't want to denigrate them."
