title:
Compressed Data;
Coming This Week: A Web Hair Transplant
body: From the company that brought the first live broadcasts of childbirth and open-heart surgery to the World Wide Web comes the latest opportunity for medical rubbernecking: a live Webcast of a hair-transplant operation. No telling how many people will decide to tune in for the event (www.ahn.com), which will take place on Wednesday at Baptist Hospital in Nashville. Despite the sometimes poor picture quality and frequent busy-server signals, nearly a million people managed to log in at some point during the morning of June 16 to see a 40-year-old woman named Elizabeth giving birth to a 7-pound, 8-ounce boy. And in August, nearly 600,000 people caught part of a live Webcast of a 48-year-old Texas woman's quadruple-bypass surgery. Officials from America's Health Network, the cable TV company based in Orlando, Fla., that produces the shows, insist that the Webcasts are not merely aimed at raising brand awareness for the network but are also intended to educate the public. Tod Fetherling, the network's president, said he hoped the hair-transplant show would appeal to some of the 30 million people -- nearly a third of them women -- who he said had some degree of so-called male pattern baldness. "The Internet," he said, "offers people a confidential way to watch the procedure and ask questions about hair transplantation -- often a very sensitive subject." During the procedure, the network's physician-turned-color-commentator, Dr. Walt Larimore, will call the action as a Nashville plastic surgeon removes a patch of skin from the hairy part of the patient's head and then inserts more than 1,000 hair grafts in the bald part of his scalp. The operation will take four to five hours, accompanied by an on-line chat session in which viewers can discuss the surgery and ask questions. America's Health Network intends to make medical Webcasts a monthly event. October will bring an on-line breast-cancer surgery and November an eye operation.   LAURIE J. FLYNN Graphic   Drawing. (P. C. Vey)

title:
Compressed Data;
Real Networks in Pact With America Online
body: It seemed a risky step when Rob Glaser, chairman of Real Networks Inc., appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee in July, joining a chorus of Microsoft bashers. He complained that some of the Microsoft Corporation's latest software refused to work properly with his company's so-called streaming programs, which deliver audio and video over the Internet. Mr. Glaser is no garden-variety Microsoft adversary. He is himself a former Microsoft executive, and Microsoft holds a 10 percent stake in his fast-growing Seattle company. Yet his public dispute with Microsoft has certainly not hurt Mr. Glaser's business so far. There are no signs of retaliation from his giant neighbor, former employer and investor in Redmond, Wash. Meanwhile, people in increasing numbers -- now more than 30 million -- are using his software. And today, Real Networks plans to announce that America Online Inc., the on-line leader, has chosen its technology as the main way for users to play streaming media on the new version of the service, AOL 4.0. That word comes as America Online begins its own marketing drive today for AOL 4.0 -- not only an upgrade for its 13 million current subscribers, but also an effort to lure the millions of other people who will be sent America Online disks in themail. The America Online agreement is a marketing coup for Real Networks. "It is piggybacking on AOL's powerful distribution network," said Jae Kim of Paul Kagan & Associates, a research firm. The Internet, in Mr. Glaser's view, is on its way to becoming a mainstream mass medium for receiving the recorded voice and television-style videos. Already, 85 percent of the Web sites that offer streaming media make use of the technology from Real Networks. And if anything, he says, the spat with Microsoft over his Senate testimony seemed to help, with the volume of daily downloads from the company's site (www.real.com) rising by nearly 20 percent immediately afterwards. "People heard and read about streaming media," Mr. Glaser said, "and wanted to see what all the hubbub was about."   STEVE LOHR Graphic   Photo: Detail from Real Networks site.

title: Potentially Big Security Flaw Found in Netscape Software
body: A potentially serious security flaw has been discovered in the programming language used in the Navigator and Communicator software of the Netscape Communications Corporation, with the defect possibly allowing an outsider to read information on a personal computer user's hard disk. The weakness, which was disclosed in Usenet on-line discussion groups on Friday by Dan Brumleve, a 20-year-old independent computer consultant in Sunnyvale, Calif., can be exploited by the Javascript programming language, which is widely used by World Wide Web page developers for a variety of common tasks. Mr. Brumleve said that he had tested the attack on a range of Navigator and Communicator programs, up through the most recent test version of Communicator, 4.5, and found the flaw in all of them. The vulnerability does not affect the Microsoft Explorer browser and email program, Mr. Brumleve said. He was able to take advantage of the vulnerability by writing a 30-line piece of Javascript code that is able to capture and copy information automatically from the so-called cache, or temporary storage area, on a PC's hard disk. The captured information can reveal which Web sites a computer user has recently visited. The captured information could also include data that a computer user might have created when communicating with a Web site -- including personal data typed in when registering at a site or conducting a retail transaction. Credit card information, however, would not be revealed, because it is protected by seperate security software. "It concerns me, because it means that a high-traffic Web site might use this to find out what other Web sites their visitors are going to," Mr. Brumleve said in a telephone interview today. He said that the flaw could also be used by an employer to see if employees were searching for pornography, for example. Although there is no evidence that the security flaw has actually been exploited by someone with harmful intent, the gravity of the threat was noted by other computer security specialists. They noted that a user's vulnerability extends beyond visiting a hostile Web site that might exploit the flaw. The flaw could also be exploited through email received using Netscape's software, they said, by sending an intended victim an email message that would secretly force the user to run an illicit Javascript program. "This is pretty scary," said Richard M. Smith, president of Phar Lap Software Inc., a Cambridge, Mass. software development company. "In some sense the cache on your computer tells a lot about your life." Privacy of personal information on the Internet has become an increasingly sensitive issue in recent years as many Web sites have begun systematically collecting demographic information on Internet users. But this newly discovered flaw could enable an unscrupulous person or organization to basically read a person's full Web history. "This is a huge privacy issue and it goes directly to the current lack of adequate technical standards to protect privacy on line," said Marc Rotenberg, director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a public policy group in Washington. "There's even a question of a company like Netscape might be liable for the improper disclosure of private information." Netscape said today that it was still assessing the problem. "We're taking a look at the bug, which appears to have privacy implications," said Eric Byunn, a Netscape product manager. He said that the company would make an announcement soon about its plans for responding to the flaw.

title: The Post-Lewinsky Winner Is the Web
body: Longtime users of the Internet often laugh when mainstream media talk about "defining moments for the Net." To them, it was defined long ago. But over the last few weeks the Internet has done more than promote discussion and information about a big news event, as it did during last summer's Mars Pathfinder exploration or in the aftermath of the death of Diana, Princess of Wales. It has played a pivotal role in news events -- the release of the Starr report and President Clinton's videotaped testimony before a grand jury. Each medium has created its own dynamics, its own archetypes and behavior. Movies led to the cult of the movie star and the movie buff, radio to the news broadcast, television to the couch potato and the talking heads. What hints of the future lay in the coverage of the Lewinsky matter on the Internet?  Television Transcends the Den Video of the President's grand jury testimony appeared on World Wide Web sites, creating a hefty new audience: the workplace.  Adam Clayton Powell 3d of the Freedom Forum in Arlington, Va., said, "Think of all of the workplace desks that have PC's but no TV's, and you begin to appreciate a very large potential audience." The Web sites of several cable channels claim wider on-line viewership than their televised components. The Clinton testimony underscored that the biggest concern for employers may soon not be the time-wasting employee who makes personal phone calls. And computer connections are usually faster at the office than they are at home -- making it easier, for example, to watch the Clinton testimony on line from the office desk than from the den. As the power of the traditional networks continues to erode and competition for viewers increases among cable channels, media brands are seeking alternate ways to keep their names in the public eye. The Web is just one of them; CNN Interactive, for instance, just renewed its deal to provide news headlines to Pager Net, a beeper provider that has 1.4 million subscribers.  Citizen as Editor So you didn't kill four hours watching the Clinton testimony -- either on the television or on your personal computer. Perhaps you actually had something more important to do. Perhaps you couldn't stand the commentary.  So, in the dark of night, you signed on to the Web and went to your favorite source. It might have been a site from a traditional news organization. Or maybe it was America Online. And you downloaded the bits and pieces you wanted to see. On the Alta Vista search engine, you could even type in a key word or phrase and search the entire four-hour video for it. "Now," promises the site, "you don't have to watch the entire four hours of testimony or depend on others to spoon-feed you sound bites." With tools proliferating on the Net that allow users to pick and choose sports scores, stock quotes and stories that are of interest, the individual has greater control over news consumption -- and particularly over the time when the consumption actually takes place. All this draws attention to the pressure of the 24-hour news cycle. Tutored by CNN in the early 1980's, viewers learned to expect news more on their own timetables. The Internet intensifies the process. Television networks are no longer competing against only one another, but with expanding offerings on their own and others' Web sites, including those of newspapers. Newspapers must now grapple with how to unload information in the course of the day, rather than hoarding it until the next morning.  The Digital Water Cooler Once the cultural Zeitgeist was reflected in the previous night's Johnny Carson monologue or a "Saturday Night Live" sketch from the weekend. Now, office chit-chat has been enhanced by digital jabs and jokes that arrive in the email in-box. Faster than you can say "Office of the Independent Counsel," jokes about the Presidential liaison, in particular, have been darting across the Net. Some of the recent notables include a song that mixes Mr. Clinton's confessional speech on Aug. 17 with an updated version of an Elton John song; a photograph from what was described as an "actual parade in Germany" in which a float depicts a giant Clinton figure grabbing the breasts of a buxom Statue of Liberty, and a video file of Mr. Clinton's nose growing, Pinocchio-style, as his campaign promises are recounted to the tune of "My Favorite Things." Once cartoons were clipped from the daily newspaper and pinned on the cubicle wall. Today jokes spread farther and wider by simply pressing the forward button. "Look at how much people are depending on the Net for news," said Bob Hirschfeld, a satirist who posts jabs daily on his Web site. "The same thing is happening with topical humor." The Web also proves itself as a great place to spread disinformation. Last week a flurry of emails quoted Kenneth W. Starr as saying on a "60 Minutes" broadcast in 1987, "Public media should not contain explicit or implied descriptions of sex acts." The message was a hoax.  Defining Sex Internet publishers scratched their heads about how to deal with the salaciousness of the President's testimony. It raised the larger questions of how -- or whether -- to regulate the content of the Net and what role news organizations on line must play. One interesting episode: MSNBC took flak for bleeping out one section of the testimony involving the now-infamous cigar -- not on its cable station, but on its Web site. Yet, after the live broadcast, a Web surfer could log onto the site and pull up the entire speech, unedited. Why was it all right to provide the salacious material in one setting but not the other? Governing what gets said on line has been a political hot potato since the birth of the Net, but the Starr report and the Clinton testimony may strengthen efforts in Congress to pass bills that would fine even a news organization for posting content deemed objectionable. Of course, what did most people read of the Starr report? The dirty stuff. One ratings service found that more people read the sections about sex than those about perjury.  Vox Populi More each day, it often seems, the media culture mirrors the surreal universe presented in the movie "Network." There is no vein-popping Howard Beale commanding disgusted television viewers to throw their television sets out the window, but that is because with the growing popularity of on-line chat rooms, who needs Howard Beale? For that matter, who needs to wait on the phone to ask a question on "Larry King Live" or rant on a local radio talk show? As the President's speech rolled, chat rooms on America Online were filled to capacity and bulletin boards allowing expressions of opinion there and on news Web sites overflowed. Not every event elicits such passion, of course, but this one firmly establishes the Net as the soapbox -- and barroom -- of our times.  Triumph of the Nerds Keep these players in mind: Broadcast.com and Real Networks, new kinds of media creatures that work on the assumption that a network is not needed to broadcast video. They present and aggregate video and audio events happening on the Web, and they also provide technical help to the networks' Web sites in times of great demand. The quality of live video on the Net is still primitive at worst and unreliable at best, yet its sheer availability to anyone with the proper gear is important. Wall Street clearly thinks so: Broadcast.com's stock rose 22 percent on the day of the President's taped broadcast.  The Rise of the On-Line Journalists Since January, when the one-man-band pundit and gossip Matt Drudge disclosed that Newsweek was sitting on the Monica Lewinsky story, journalists have watched in amazement as he has gained power. Now the host of his own television show on Fox News, Mr. Drudge brags on his Web site that his name came up six times in the Clinton testimony. He quotes the President: "Well, I had a little anxiety the next day, of course, because of the Drudge Report." The on-line magazine Salon, meanwhile, took heat for publishing a report of an extramarital affair more than 30 years ago involving Representative Henry J. Hyde, chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, who is in charge of preliminary action toward impeachment proceedings against the President. Salon's staff members had to evacuate their offices because of a bomb threat, and they suffered a new type of political vengeance. Protesters waged a "fax attack," barraging the magazine's machines in an effort to break them. And thousands of emails from angry protesters clogged Salon's servers. Graphic   Photo: The Internet showed its power as a medium for breaking news when the Starr report and President Clinton's testimony were released. Television got the news out even to a bicycle messenger in Times Square, and tapes were soon available. But computer users had access almost immediately to text and video over their own PC's.

title: Libraries Using the Net to Lure the Public
body: WHILE attending the East Northport Festival earlier this month, Aviva Guttmann and her son, Benjamin, 9, decided to stop for some cool drinks. But instead of heading for a deli or ice cream parlor, they stepped into the public library on Larkfield Road. "I'd read about the cafe here, so I decided to stop in and get some refreshments," said Ms. Guttmann as she ordered soft drinks. "We're from Smithtown and we don't have anything like this in our library. It's an excellent idea. I'd go to the library more often if we had one. I like the cafes in bookstores, but this is better because you don't have to buy the books." Public libraries on Long Island are going to unusual lengths to keep customers coming in. At the Patchogue-Medford Library they're even offering free fishing tackle, loaned just like books to anyone with a library card, in hopes that young Huckleberry Finns might just check out a book on one of their visits. But in most cases, these gimmicks are not the actions of librarians desperate to drum up business. Attendance at most libraries is up, and the biggest new drawing card is not doughnuts or fireplaces, but Internet access. The libraries have it, and most of them will share it with you, free of charge. The introduction of computers with their databases and connections to the Internet has been a boon to libraries, many of which "have trouble having enough computer work stations" to meet the demand, said James Nichols, director of the Suffolk Cooperative Library System. With Internet access, library users no longer even have to go to the library, Mr. Nichols said. "Book circulation may be down in some libraries, but activity is up in all of them because of the electronic resources," he said. "When you combine electronic usage with book circulation, our usage has skyrocketed. In July 1995, we had fewer than 200 people log on to our home page. In July 1998, we had more than 100,000." Mr. Nichols said his is the only county in the unitedstates in which all the public libraries offer residents free access to the Internet. Mr. Nichols said his organization began offering the Internet to its 54 member libraries four years ago. Computer connections produce other benefits for libraries. Stephanie Heineman, director of the Northport-East Northport Public Library, said that library patrons check out fewer magazines because they can find the articles on the Internet or on research databases the libraries maintain. That has meant that libraries no longer have to set aside storage rooms for stacks of magazines going back 10 or 20 years, she said. Mary Jane Schmidt, director of the Half Hollow Hills Community Library, said that libraries are able to reallocate their resources because they no longer have to buy microfilms of newspapers and other periodicals available on the Internet. "The demand for information is up," she said, noting that there are about 10 Internet stations between the library's two branches, Melville and Dix Hills. "They're busy all the time." Mr. Nichols said a big reason most of Suffolk's libraries have been able to readily accommodate the new technology is because of the library building boom this decade. Since 1990, 30 of the libraries have built or are in the midst of erecting new buildings, or renovating and expanding existing ones. The price tag: $80 million. The Floyd Memorial Library in Greenport expects to complete a two-year, $1.5 million building project at the end of the year. It will have built an addition and renovated its original building, according to its director, Lisa Richland. "Within the last four or five years, we have moved from a card catalogue to five computer catalogues," she said. "Our collection has grown by 25 percent and our circulation has doubled to 90,000 items per year. The community has not grown, but the use of the library has. We're marketing it and providing good reference services. "We're excellent by virtue of the cooperative library's ability to bring the Internet to this outpost," Ms. Richland said. "We're the farthest east on the North Fork, and yet because of the cooperative nature of the library system, we can offer the same high-quality service." The coordinator of computer support services for the Nassau Library System, Debbie A. Jaszcar, said the libraries in Nassau offer free Internet access on site either for patrons or for librarians seeking to assist patrons. And since March, 50 of the 54 libraries in Nassau began offering free Internet service for home-computer operators who call up the local library's web site. Once connected to the library's home page, patrons can also access a full-text database that contains countless articles from periodicals. A total of 5,800 users have been registered for the Nassau service; in Suffolk, a similar service is scheduled to begin on Oct. 1. Registration is as simple as being assigned a library card, a log-in user name and a password. Ms. Jaszcar said the Nassau Library System's office in Uniondale has a central computer to serve the library system and that recently the number of phone lines connected to it was doubled to 120. "In the last month we had almost 66,000 connections to the server," she said. Ms. Jaszcar said the free Internet access from home increases patrons' connections with the library. "Libraries are saying that people call asking for help to find sites on the Internet," she explained. "Our reference staff is participating in ongoing training in how to use it because we see the Internet as just another reference tool." To help patrons go on line, Ms. Jaszcar added, libraries are distributing free software. In addition, the Nassau Library Service maintains a free help line to assist those with technical questions. After Internet access, the free fishing poles and other such programs seem like window-dressing. But they too are raising the profile of libraries across the Island. William D. Cicola, director of the Copiague Memorial Public Library, said he makes it a point to get videocassettes of hit movies the moment they are released and to promote their upcoming release with notices in the library. On Sept. 1, the day "Titanic" was released, his library began loaning eight copies. "We're one of the few libraries that reserves movies, and we have 131 people on a waiting list for 'Titanic,' " he said. "Movies are one of our most popular services." Another attraction is the library's cafe, called Books and Bytes. "It's very popular," said Mr. Cicola. "There are constantly people in there having ice cream, coffee, bagels, pastry and cookies. I moved all of my magazines in there. Mothers who bring their children in for story hour go there and talk with their neighbors over a cup of coffee." The cafe in East Northport has a large gas fireplace that is lit throughout the winter. Twice a month, the library holds Fireside Fridays, featuring either a one-hour poetry reading or musical performance in front of the fireplace. "It's the community's living room," Ms. Heineman said. Ms. Heineman said cafes were installed in the East Northport library, which opened last October, and in the renovated Northport library, which reopened last month. Copiague opened its cafe in January. Ms. Heineman said her cafes are particularly appealing to youngsters who come to the library after school. "We have the 'homework helper' -- hot chocolate and two big cookies for about $1.50," she said. "It's really great. Kids love it." Access to the web pages of libraries in Nassau County can be obtained through www.nassaulibrary.org; those in Suffolk may be obtained through www.suffolk.lib.ny.us Graphic   Photo: At the Northport-East Northport library, patrons can buy a cup of coffee and enjoy it at the fireside lounge or take advantage of the computers to surf the Internet. Oh, yes: there are books for borrowing. (Maxine Hicks for The newyork Times)

title:
The Nation;
Danger: Tangled Web of Taxes
body: MICHAEL O. LEAVITT was visiting California from Utah a few months back, and while staying at a beach house used his laptop computer to shop over the Internet. He accessed a website, made his selections and charged the bill -- $44.50 plus $2.49 for shipping -- to his credit card. But he did not pay sales tax. That bothered him because, as Governor of Utah, Mr. Leavitt is acutely aware of how reliant states are on sales taxes. And he has given considerable thought to the looming problems -- for states, the economy and consumers -- of relying on traditional tax systems in a world in which Internet commerce is starting to change the way people shop. "Which states could logically and reasonably have argued that they should receive the benefits of that tax?" Mr. Leavitt asked about his purchase. "California? I was sitting in California when I made the transaction. newyork? newyork was where the home page was resident and where the company was located. But the goods were packaged and shipped from a warehouse in New Jersey, and they were shipped to Utah, where I used them."  Great Potential Governments have long grappled with how, if at all, they should regulate the global flow of images and information over the Internet, seeking to balance concerns about free speech, for example, with those about pornography. But only recently have policy makers in Washington, in state capitals and around the world begun to confront the economic implications of a new retail marketplace that recognizes no political or geographical boundaries. Almost by the day, the new medium is showing its potential for rapid growth. At Amazon.com, the online bookseller, the latest chapter in President Clinton's woes led to a surge of orders for the book version of Kenneth W. Starr's report to Congress and then for the video of Mr. Clinton's grand jury appearance (both briefly topped Stephen King's latest on the company's best seller list). Catalog companies are increasingly giving customers the option to place orders over the Internet. "You have a major economic force here," said Ira Magaziner, who heads the Clinton Administration's Internet policy team. "It's just beginning to reach the consumer, and it's going to be huge. The question is, how do we create an environment that will allow it to flourish and also will take care of all the side effects that will arise?" The issues are sweeping. Where does a transaction take place when buyer and seller can be defined to be in multiple locations? Will the borderless nature of the Internet force governments further down a road that has already led them to drop trade barriers, harmonize tax policies and form currency unions? On a more immediate level, many governors and state legislatures are convinced that such commerce will present in greatly magnified form the same problem they have faced for years with the L. L. Beans of the world that sell by phone and mail from catalogues: Although consumers are technically liable for sales taxes, companies have to collect taxes only in states where they keep a physical presence. Although some merchants collect the tax even where they are not required to do so, most do not. Barnes & Noble's barnesandnoble.com, another online bookseller, automatically adds sales tax to orders being shipped to newyork, where it has its corporate headquarters; New Jersey, where it has its distribution center, and Virginia, where its computer operation is based. Orders elsewhere go untaxed. The lost revenue for states is relatively trivial now, but could mount substantially in coming years as the volume of business on the Internet grows. Though estimates vary widely, some analysts see the electronic market growing to hundreds of billions of dollars annually within the next decade from next to nothing a few years ago.  Billions Lost By early in the next decade, states could be losing up to $12 billion a year, according to the National Governors' Association. That would be a big chunk of state sales tax revenue, which last year totaled $150 billion, and would be three times what states say they lose each year because of out-of-statemail-order purchases. The states are also under pressure from traditional retailers, who see their Internet competitors as operating in a tax-free zone that will draw customers away from Main Street and the mall. From the perspective of technology companies and on-line service providers, the issue is whether they will become a tempting target for new taxes, or the object of discriminatory policies intended to benefit traditional retailers. A tax free-for-all, they and their supporters warn, will stifle the new marketplace and deny its economic benefits to the country. "It is incumbent upon us to get it right so that we do not allow a feeding frenzy by state and local tax collectors across the world to turn the information superhighway into an empty 21st-century toll road," said Senator Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon. Some experts suggested the problem can be solved by an agreement among the states to levy taxes based on residence and then creating software that would automatically add the appropriate amount to any Internet purchase as part of the credit card billing process. Such a system could also automatically route the tax to the proper state. But getting the balance right between nurturing the new medium and not hurting states and traditional retailers is no easy proposition. In Congress, the Senate is debating a bill cosponsored by Mr. Wyden that would establish a two-year moratorium on any new taxes that would treat Internet commerce differently from traditional retailing, while establishing a commission to sort out the sales tax issue. A similar bill passed the House in June.  Wary of Washington Washington's increasing interest has made the states nervous. Some governors fear that the growth of Internet commerce will encourage the Federal Government to create and administer a consistent sales tax system. "The I.R.S. will say, we'll collect it, and Congress will say, we'll appropriate it," said Mr. Leavitt, a Republican. "We'll have taxes now collected and spent by local governments collected and spent by the Federal Government. That's a massive shift in power." Another concern in the technology industry and in Washington is that other countries could slap duties, tariffs or other trade barriers on international Internet transactions, either to raise revenue or protect their domestic industries, and create new taxes for transactions within their borders. The Clinton Administration has already raised the issue at the World Trade Organization. "Governments around the world are beginning to understand the power of this medium, and it's something a lot of people are wrestling with," said Ben Boyd, a spokesman for barnesandnoble.com. "It's a new medium and you need to look at everything through new lenses." title:
Editorial Observer;
What Monica Has Wrought in the Opinion Biz
body: Perhaps it was inevitable, or at least handy, that a new kind of Presidential scandal would turn up as a test case for what the new media age would do to the workings of politics and public opinion. Right off, we have seen that this scandal is not like Watergate, when the commentators and Congressional sages served as instructors in the necessary level of public outrage. This White House saga has been available in excruciating detail in the people's media -- in particular, the new cable talk channels and the World Wide Web. On the most basic level, which is where the politics of this matter tends to loiter, this is a perfect human drama for these new outlets. Nothing is particularly complicated. This is not Whitewater, not Iran-contra. We know what this President did. We know what Ms. Lewinsky did. Ditto faux friend Linda Tripp and Special Prosecutor Kenneth Starr and Judiciary Committee chairman Henry Hyde. Even the legalisms, the hairsplittings, are not so difficult that most citizens need a commentator or a member of Congress to explain how these everyday weasel words were concocted by the White House to cover a workaday sin. This public expertise, after a season of bewildering leaks to the big media in Washington, comes with the raw, unfiltered data that are now available not merely to Tim Russert or Cokie Roberts but to the rest of the wired world. The Starr report was shoveled out to the real people on the Web in real news time. As Candy Crowley read the allegations to CNN's audience, the operators of over four million computers were jamming on to their favorite Web sites on Sept. 11 to see it for themselves. By that night, computer chat rooms were clogged with debate about whether this President had committed enough sin to be de-elected by Congress. The next morning, email messages including only the dirty bits were exploding exponentially through cyberspace. Most major newspapers printed the report the next day, providing a spike in Saturday's usually lower circulation figures. Many readers soon opted for quickie books, which became instant best sellers. Then came the four hours of Presidential sweating before a grand jury's video camera, a media event that logged daytime television audiences reminiscent of O. J. The cable networks that aired the President's long national discomfort boosted viewership to nine times normal. CNN won its highest day rating for the year. For the broadcast networks, President Clinton's steamy tale even bested some of the nation's most seductive soap operas. Moreover, at least six million people saw the video on the Internet that day -- which is not yet a particularly satisfying way to watch moving pictures. In short, this must be the most democratically reviewed Presidential misstep so far in American history. It is Newton Minow's famous electronic acropolis finally morphing into reality. The public interest in the details may also help explain the gap between the Washington media pundits and the polls. For months now, the prognosticators have been suggesting that this President is a goner. Over 140 newspaper editorial pages have called for his resignation. The general public, so far, has said let him be. These polls showing support for the President could change any afternoon, of course. Those who have been predicting that this is such a volatile mixture that another drop would supersaturate the country with slime could finally, finally, be correct. But failing that, those media executives who are now celebrating a huge audience of readers and viewers courtesy of this Presidential debacle should take note: The public can now look at the same evidence as the media, and the two can come to different conclusions. All those talking heads may not be connected to the body politic.

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Markets Decline as Fears Of Additional Losses Grow The $3.5 billion rescue of a large investment fund verging on collapse unnerved many markets around the world, raised a clamor for a Government investigation and created fear that other losses might surface. Rather than contain the problem and bring stability, the cash infusion late Wednesday by a consortium of banks and brokerage firms to salvage Long-Term Capital Management only seemed to rattle investors.  Page A1.  The Swiss bank UBS said it expected to report a third-quarter loss as high as one billion Swiss francs -- $721 million -- related to losses in emerging markets, equities and the near-collapse of Long-Term Capital Management. Its charge for an equity stake in and derivatives transactions with Long-Term Capital Management was estimated at $685 million.  C4. Russia Warns of a Further Default Aleksandr Shokhin, Russia's Deputy Prime Minister of financial affairs, took a harsh line with the International Monetary Fund and other creditors, warning them of a potential default on its long-term debt if more Western aid is not delivered.  A10.  Lehman Brothers won a court order freezing the British bank accounts of two big Russian banks. It contends the two banks defaulted on $110 million of obligations to it and its clients. Other foreign creditors are scrambling to recover whatever they can from their Russian holdings.  C18.  Shares of an Internet I.P.O. Surge Shares of Ebay, an Internet auction house, closed at $47.375 yesterday, after climbing $29.375 from its offering price. The first initial public offering in nearly a month was priced at $18, opened around 12:15 P.M. at $52, but fell later in the day. Market Place.  C6.  Economic Data Show Strong Growth Two Government reports indicated that the nation's economy remains strong. Gross domestic product grew at a 1.8 percent annual rate in the second quarter -- from the 1.6 percent estimated a month ago, but still well below the growth rate of 5.5 percent in the first quarter. In another report, orders for durable goods jumped 1.6 percent in August.  C2.  Income Higher for Most Americans The Census Bureau said the proportion of Americans living in poverty declined last year, mostly because of reductions in poverty among black and Hispanic families. The data reflected three consecutive years of growth in income, which have restored household incomes and poverty to the levels recorded in 1989, just before the last recession.  A1.  Look Under 'H' for Hostile Bid Day Runner, a manufacturer of personal organizers, made an unsolicited £47.9 million, or $80.5 million, bid for Filofax, maker of the leatherbound diary that became a 1980's accessory, but has since lost ground to electronic organizers.  C3.  TV Networks Faulted on Labels One year after the television networks revised their movie-style ratings code to add labels alerting parents to sexual or violent content, a study has found that the networks are not regularly adding those labels, like V for violence or S for sexual content, to the ratings in printed listings and on screen.  A20.  Profits Off at Luxury Goods Makers Falling profits were reported by LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton, the Gucci Group and Diageo, Europe's leading producers of luxury fashion goods.  C5.
