title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
The debut of an on-line auction house reminds investors of the glories of initial offerings gone by.
body: NOW we know what it takes to shake Wall Street's I.P.O. blues: Beanie Babies and lots of them. In the first initial public offering in nearly a month, shares of Ebay, an Internet auction house, jumped from the offering price of $18 to close at $47.375. In an electronic variation on classified advertising, Ebay lets people auction off whatever is in their attics or, for that matter, their vaults. It has attracted a cult following among fans of various collectibles, including the little bean-bag dolls. Indeed, the 714,792 items for sale on the site yesterday included no fewer than 35,608 Beanie Babies, some with prices as high as $400. The inventory also included 2,979 autographed baseballs, 849 marbles and 501 paperweights. Ebay charges sellers 25 cents to $2.50 to list their items, and it collects a commission of between 1.25 percent and 5 percent on completed sales. "Their business model is great," said Mary Meeker, the Internet stock analyst at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter. Ms. Meeker took the unusual step of issuing a report recommending the shares of Ebay, even though the stock underwriting was managed by Morgan's archrival, Goldman, Sachs & Company. Ms. Meeker said she likes the company because it is attracting a large and growing audience and sales volume while its costs are low. Ebay even turns a small profit, a rarity among Internet companies. She suggests that the company's market potential is huge, since in the traditional markets, people spend $17 billion a year to buy classified advertising, $80 billion in auctions and $103 billion on collectibles. The Internet, she argued, makes matching buyer and seller much easier than traditional markets do. What about the stock price, which values Ebay at $1.9 billion, or 25 times Ms. Meeker's estimate of its 1999 revenues? (Never mind that the price is 306 times her estimates of Ebay's 1999 profit.) "Valuation is always an issue for Internet companies," she said with some understatement. "It's a great company with extraordinary growth potential." Even some Internet bulls, however, are shying away from Ebay. Mark S. Basham, the investment officer of Standard & Poor's small-capitalization stock service, rates Ebay a stock to avoid, even though he recommended Geocities and Broadcast.com, two of the summer's hottest Internet stocks. Mr. Basham said he did not believe that Ebay would be able to increase its revenue enough to justify the current valuation. "I don't buy the argument that margins on the Internet will be much higher than any other business," he said. "Over time, competition will drive down margins." Indeed, Mr. Basham said that Ebay already had potent competitors from search services like Yahoo and Excite, as well as from the traditional players in classified advertising, newspapers. "It's a great idea," he said. "It's just that everyone can have the same idea." Beyond classified advertising, the issue most on people's minds in much of Silicon Valley is the initial public offering. And investment bankers said the success of the Ebay offering would be of little help in opening up the market for the dozens of other companies that have been waiting to go public. Ebay, after all, is profitable, and it is for now the clear leader in its category. Many other Internet companies waiting to issue shares are neither. For example, TheGlobe.com and Xoom are two "community" Internet services that have filed to go public on the heels of Geocities, the No. 1 company of that sort. "The I.P.O. market is fairly closed," said Suzanne N. Richardson, the head of corporate finance for technology companies at Friedman Billings & Ramsey. "Just because one transaction is priced doesn't mean you will see a flood of deals." Standards have tightened for now, she said. "Those companies that are larger, have longer operating histories and stronger backing will have access to the public markets," Ms. Richardson said. James M. P. Feulle, the head of investment banking at Volpe Brown Whelan, a San Francisco brokerage firm, said the fate of public offerings was dependent on the overall market for small-capitalization stocks. "If the market is trending upward and every stock in investors' portfolios starts to work, then they get more confident and will take a little more risk," he said. Since most small-cap funds are down for the year, investors are now especially cautious, he said, adding, "People get overly depressed in the dry periods and overly excited in the good periods." Investment bankers might consider buying up those 35,608 Beanie Babies and sending them out to cheer up the rest of the technology investors.

title: Destroyed German Synagogues Return to Life on a Web Page
body: HISTORY repeats itself. Haunted by that prophecy, Marc Grellert, a professor at Darmstadt Technical University in Germany, started a project that is bringing back to virtual life German synagogues that were destroyed during World War II. The project serves not only as "a memorial to German history," Mr. Grellert said by telephone from Darmstadt, which is near Frankfurt, but also to "admonish" Germany for erasing from the historical record sacred buildings that once contributed to the country's culture. Since 1996, the project's recreated synagogues have been prominently displayed on the Web site of the university's architecture department. Visitors to the site (www. cad.architektur.tu-darmstadt.de) can view three-dimensional images of the synagogues and read about the architectural and cultural history of each. Three Frankfurt synagogues, situated about 20 miles from Darmstadt, have been completed and are displayed on the Web. Mr. Grellert said his class planned to add sketches of 15 more synagogues by the year 2000 to commemorate Kristallnacht, the outburst of anti-Semitic violence that presaged the Holocaust. Mr. Grellert wants the class to concentrate on rebuilding synagogues destroyed in such large cities as Berlin, Dresden, Dusseldorf and Hamburg. He said that way he hoped to draw more attention to the exhibits. Mr. Grellert said an arson attack by neo-Nazis on one of the few remaining synagogues in the German city of Lubeck in 1994 was a catalyst for setting up the site. As a frightening reminder of the past persecution of Jews, Mr. Grellert said, it was an impetus for the university's pilot CAD (computer-aided design) architecture project to reconstruct on the Web several German synagogues that could have remained buried in the rubble of history. Mr. Grellert said he discovered that there was a startling lack of information available in books and records about the architecture of German synagogues. Few buildings in Germany escaped destruction during World War II, but synagogues were made targets by the Nazis, who left no trace of their existence, Mr. Grellert explained. Expanding beyond Germany's borders, during Kristallnacht, or "night of broken glass," in November 1938, Nazis set fire to more than 35 synagogues in Bohemia and Moravia, now part of the Czech Republic. Twenty-five German synagogues were destroyed after World War II in arson or bomb attacks. Markers at the original sites of many synagogues are the only signs of their existence, Mr. Grellert said. Under the guidance of Prof. Manfred Koob, the project's director and chairman of Darmstadt University's CAD department, the synagogues were reconstructed from preserved blueprints and photos and from the recollections of people who once worshipped in the buildings. But the virtual reconstruction of the main synagogue, just outside Frankfurt, was not easy. Few pictures of the exterior existed; there was only one photograph of the interior and one floor plan. It is particularly critical to record these memories while they are still vivid for Holocaust survivors, who are advancing in age, Mr. Grellert said. The Judengasse Museum in Frankfurt had preserved some models, which helped the students construct the synagogues' facades. In 1995, using CAD software, Mr. Grellert built a town-planning model of eastern Frankfurt, placing the synagogues at the sites where each once stood. In 1995, a seminar class of eight students and seven professors began the project using the Speedikon CAD program on Unix computers to build two-dimensional computer drawings, which provided the framework for ground plans. Though CAD software programs render highly detailed, three-dimensional images, the user first has to put the structural models into the program. These models are constructed by compiling detailed information about the building's architecture. Though he is not Jewish, as a student of architecture, Mr. Grellert "wanted to show the contribution of the Jewish community to German society." Since the exhibition serves, in this sense, as a tribute to the contribution of German Jews to the country's architecture, the project's organizers said they will not accept money for their project from German Jewish organizations. The project's expenses to date have come to about $75,000, Mr. Grellert estimated, which includes stipends for the university's staff, and hardware and software expenses. The German Government has provided nominal financing for the project. The university has received financial support from the Judengasse Museum in Frankfurt as well. The Judengasse Museum also displayed the images in its September 1996 exhibition "Fragments and Reconstruction." Each synagogue was selected for its distinctive architecture, Mr. Grellert said. The Borneplatz Synagogue, burned down by the Nazis on Nov. 10, 1938, was known as the "red synagogue at Borneplatz" because of the color of the sandstone used in its construction in 1882. The synagogue once stood as one of four synagogues silhouetting Frankfurt. The exterior shape of the synagogue was influenced by Italian Renaissance architecture. An Orthodox synagogue, it was built so men could enter through a door close to the tower on the southern facade, while women entered through an additional building to the north. A gas station and a flower market now stand on the site. The facade of the main synagogue, the first one to be virtually created, was originally constructed with red stone from a nearby river region. The Oriental and Gothic architecture reflected the bold self-confidence of the Jewish community of the 19th century. Mr. Koob emphasized the importance of remembering the past. "Perhaps it has become more important again, to cultivate the common spiritual site and to preserve it," he said. By reaching out to a wider audience than the history books have, Mr. Koob said the digital processing of information aids "the transmission of the cultural knowledge of humankind" to a third generation. Historical preservation via the Internet is making history more accessible. "When you do things in print and video, you have to sell the information in a package, a unit," said Michael Declun, creator of Cybrary of the Holocaust, a Web site he began in 1995 to provide links to information about the Holocaust. Cybrary of the Holocaust reaches more than 30,000 people a month (www. remember.org). Darmstadt University's progress on the 15 additional synagogues will be updated on its Web site. The project also includes an online video that simulates a walk through the Frankfurt synagogues. Graphic   Photos: Two of the buildings rendered on the Darmstadt University site are the old main synagogue of Frankfurt, above, and the Borneplatz Synagogue, below.

title: House Hunting With Cursor and Click
body: SHOPPING for an apartment in newyork City while living in the Netherlands could be difficult -- particularly in a hot market in which properties often sell as soon as they come on the market, sometimes for more than the asking price. But Gary Ensana and David Vickrey found a way to bridge the intercontinental divide. They bought their apartment in the Murray Hill neighborhood without setting foot in it, after a virtual walk-through courtesy of digital pictures provided through email by Scott Moore, a Corcoran Group real estate agent. "It's not a substitute for being in newyork and being able to go on a moment's notice," said Mr. Ensana, noting that he and Mr. Vickrey had been familiar with the building where they eventually bought an apartment. "But given the fact that we were on the other side of the ocean, it at least made it possible to shop for a place." While most home buyers still step through the front door before putting their life savings into a home, the Internet is changing the way real estate is bought and sold. Real estate sites, still in the early stages of development, have become an invaluable source for sorting through information ranging from how to pick a neighborhood and a property to how to get the best mortgage. "It has great potential," said Andy Sernovitz, president of the Association of Interactive Media, a nonprofit trade association for businesses that use the Internet. "What the Web can deliver matches what you have to do anyway, but it does it better." As a result, potential house buyers are gaining more control of the house-hunting process. At the heart of the change is where consumers look for real estate listings and how they approach the task of shopping for a new home. For the people who do much of their research before setting foot in a real estate office, the days of going out with a real estate agent and driving around neighborhoods to look at houses chosen by the realtor are largely gone. Real estate services on the Web are highly competitive. They became even more competitive in July when Microsoft entered the market with its multifaceted Home Advisor site (www.homeadvisor.com). That site can be seen as a direct competitor to Realtor.com (www.realtor.com), the Web site of the National Association of Realtors. Realtor.com has more than 1.2 million listings, generally regarded as the most on the Internet. "Microsoft scares the daylights out of everybody," Mr. Sernovitz said. "It's assumed that if Microsoft gets into your business, you're in big trouble." But Mr. Sernovitz said he saw it as a good sign. "Every time Microsoft gets into something, they add credibility to that genre as an on-line medium." Realtors need to look only at the sales of airline tickets on line-- and the ways the travel agent business has changed as a result -- to become concerned about what the future holds. "The big issue in the marketplace today is who is going to be the point of control in any transaction," said Ron Lipstone, a realtor with Sotheby's International Realty in Los Angeles and a director of the combined Los Angeles/Westside Multiple Listing Service. "Is it going to be the agent? Is it going to be the lender? Or is it going to be Microsoft?" While realtors ponder those kinds of issues, newspapers and magazines, which carry real estate listings, are looking at the threat to their market. Facing the loss of billions of dollars nationally, newspapers have taken their listings on line and are creating alliances with companies holding similar interests. The Village Voice, for example, has turned its classified listings into a daily service, putting advertisements on line as they come in. Its Web site, www.villagevoice. com, allows viewers to search for real estate by specifying the number of bedrooms, geographic area and price range sought. "I live in a paranoid way," said David Schneiderman, publisher of The Village Voice and president of Stern Publishing, which owns seven papers across the country. "We can't afford to lose this. There are so many different options and players, you don't even know who you're competing with half the time." By some estimates, the Internet may have as many as 200,000 real estate sites, which include Web pages put up by individual realtors and by real estate companies and associations as well as classified advertisements posted by publications. Some sites list descriptions of homes, dimensions and photographs (or, in a few cases, a 360-degree virtual walk-through of the property), details on realtors and mortgage rates. Others present information on property tax rates, schools and town amenities and include calculators that allow you to figure out how much house you can afford. Such listings are "a great facilitator," said Paul Purcell, executive vice president of Douglas Elliman in newyork. "It's amazing." The wider access to information can be disconcerting for realtors. "The realtor of yesterday was totally in control of basic information," said George Stephens, chairman of the Houston Association of Realtors. "Today the consumer is basically controlling the information." Realtors are increasingly running into people like Barbara Nicholson, who did not turn to a realtor until she had found the house she wanted to buy. Ms. Nicholson, who used the Internet extensively for her move from Boston to Syracuse two years ago, said her first instinct had been to "get on the Net." "It's quicker, easier and more cost-effective and time-efficient," she added. Beyond scrutinizing listings on the Internet, she went to a number of related sites, investigating mortgages and calculating cost-of-living differences. She checked out jobs, found the best price from a moving company and even located a company that would help her send address-change notifications to publications and credit-card companies. While Ms. Nicholson doesn't view house hunting on the Internet as a substitute for getting out and seeing houses and neighborhoods in person, she said it had saved her time by letting her narrow down her choices. "I never had an agent until I found the house I bought," she said. "In fact, I think the real estate agent was a little dismayed he didn't have to do anything. I think he thought he hadn't earned his fee." Ms. Nicholson began her shopping on line two years ago by calling up a search engine and typing in "real estate." While that provided her with an overwhelming number of sites, few sites at that time offered anything in Syracuse. The process was also time-consuming because it required following a number of links. While Ms. Nicholson had the most success with Realtor.com, numerous sites have been added since then. And there are now many ways to search for a home, tailoring the listings according to the desired city, price range, house size and special features, like fireplaces and swimming pools. But sorting through those options can be mind-boggling. "It's like a pile of clutter," said Barbara Corcoran, founder of the Corcoran Group real estate company in Manhattan. Speaking of the company's Web site, she said: "We build bridges everywhere we can. The more bridges we have, the more traffic we have." To attract and retain visitors to the Web site, Ms. Corcoran relies on what she calls "bells and whistles" -- 360-degree virtual-reality walk-throughs, for example, a feature that is generally available only for a handful of more expensive properties. One useful feature of Corcoran's site is its inclusion of addresses (but no apartment numbers) for most properties it advertises on the Net. But many real estate agents disapprove of that practice, saying it could jeopardize homeowners' security, and do not list addresses on Web sites. Ms. Corcoran has seen her company's Internet-related sales -- sales that followed an initial contact with the company through email -- grow to $60 million in 1997 from $4.9 million in 1995, when the site began. The company has also found that its Web site helps many customers find what they want more quickly. A survey of Corcoran buyers found that the clients who had used the Internet had spent only a quarter as much time house-hunting as had other clients. The clients who did not use the Web spent about four months with a realtor, on average, and looked at about 21 homes, while the "Webheads," as the survey called them, spent an average of only one month with a real estate agent and saw only 5 properties before buying. The Web can make brokers and sales agents more visible. At Corcoran, Sarah Bond, a vice president at the company, made a valuable contact with a British client who saw a profile of her on the Internet and selected her because she rode a vintage bicycle. Bob Frankovic, an associate broker with Windermere Real Estate in Spokane, Wash., has taken on the persona of Garlic Bob on his Web site. Mr. Frankovic, who was forced to eat garlic sandwiches as a child in the hopes of keeping polio at bay, now grows acres of the stuff. His Web site includes a photograph of him on an old red tractor, and he will happily provide information on garlic as well as on real-estate listings. "It's a goofy picture," he said. "But even if you don't like me, you'll remember me." MR. FRANKOVIC's site was among a dozen that attracted Larry Barnes when he was looking for a new realtor to sell a house he had left 350 miles behind in Spokane after moving to Whidbey Island, outside Seattle. Faced with the option of driving back to Seattle or calling long distance to find a realtor, Mr. Barnes turned to the Internet, narrowing his search by state and city and then looking at his options. "Had I not been on Realtor.com, he would not have found me," Mr. Frankovic said, noting that his commission on the house had been well worth the less than $1,000 he spends a year to operate his Internet site. Realtor.com, which has been in operation for more than two years, has the backing of the National Association of Realtors. Many of its listings come directly from multiple listing services. Michael Keller, vice president for marketing at Real Select, which operates the Realtor.com site, says it has a vast database and takes a direct approach. "What we're really about is convenience," he said. "You go to the grocery store more often than not to pick up milk. That's what we're about, milk." While a variety of companies have top-notch sites, most observers see a battle shaping up between Realtor.com and Home Advisor, which at this point is lagging behind in listings. Ian Morris, the lead product manager for Home Advisor, the Microsoft site, played down the fact that the site is behind Realtor.com in listings, pointing out that Home Advisor opened with a preview only in July. He said Microsoft was providing a comprehensive guide to home buying that helped consumers figure out how much they could afford and offered neighborhood information and loan and closing assistance. Mr. Morris said Microsoft was in the business to generate money from loan origination fees paid by mortgage brokerage companies associated with the service. "It allows us to provide a great service to consumers for free," he said. With such competition, the bottom line seems to be that realtors can jump in or face being left out. "Things are changing," Mr. Frankovic said. "The Internet is the way people like to do business. It's the way I like to do business. You don't have to go knocking on doors." Graphic   Photos: (Illustration by Mary Ann Smith)(pg. G1); VIRTUAL SHINGLE -- Many realtors find that the Internet is a good way to get new customers. One such real-estate agent is Bob Frankovic of Spokane, Wash., who also grows acres of garlic and presents himself as Garlic Bob on his Web site. A SATISFIED CYBERSHOPPER -- Barbara Nicholson used the Internet extensively when she moved from Boston to this house in Syaracuse two years ago. She said the Net was "quicker, easier and more cost-effective and time-efficient" for finding prospective properties, and she even found a good deal with a moving company by searching for such services on line. (Michael Okoniewski for The newyork Times)(pg. G5)

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Tractor Fans on Line
body: IT looks like an ugly hunk of iron. Its machinery shares space with wasps' nests and an occasional skunk. It has more rust than the Titanic. But it's the same model your father drove, or the same one you supported your family with. Or maybe it's just one you've always heard about. And what keeps you working on it through the cuts and bruises is the knowledge that -- unlike the family car -- its parts are usually designed to be fixed easily. It's an old tractor, and restoring, collecting and showing them is very popular. It's very American. It's also very understandable in places where you live by, and on, your tools, where recycling is necessity, not ecology, and where people open antique stores instead of throwing stuff out. The first stop on any Web tractor tour should be Roger Welsch's home page (www.micrord.com/rogerwelsch). Mr. Welsch, a former professor and the sage of Dannebrog, Neb., is the host of the "Postcards From Nebraska" reports on television for "CBS Sunday Morning," and the author of many books, including "Old Tractors and the Men Who Love Them" (Motorbooks International, 1995). He is to tractor restoration, and the Allis-Chalmers WC in particular, what Thoreau was to the lakeside cabin. For details, you can buy his books, but his Web site will put you in the right mood. "Just as tractors kind of exploded on me, so did the Web," Mr. Welsch wrote by email. "Now I haunt the Web and use it hourly. For tractors, too. There are two sites I like and use -- the A.T.I.S. site (www.atis.net/) and any of the multiple sites (including my tall-tale site) at agriculture.com." The A.T.I.S. (Antique Tractor Internet Services) site -- its motto is "Plow the 'Net" -- calls itself "the largest, oldest and the original antique tractor Web site on the planet, bar none." It gets as many as 1,000 visits a day, and the numbers appear to be climbing. It began operation in 1993 as a nopnprofit site but became so popular that it soon became a business. It still says it is a "community of friends," but besides voluminous listings of shows, discussion groups, links and freemailing lists (which the site refers to as a "support group"), it sells advertisements, acts as a host for Web pages and offers electronic mailboxes and a fine assortment of fashion accessories, among other services. Its Frequently Asked Questions include "What Implements Do I Need?" and "Does Tractor Restoration Require a Mechanical Background?" One FAQ page talks about "How to Transport Your Tractor." "Show tractors should be as close to the original as possible," the site notes. Of the 707 members in the site's database profile, only 33, or 5 percent, call themselves as commercial farmers, and another 44, or 6 percent, say they are in a farm-related profession, said Jim Poole, the profile administrator. ("He works for free T-shirts and hats," said the site's owner, Spencer Yost.) The states with the most profiled members are Texas, California, Pennsylvania, Ohio and newyork. John Deere and International Harvester are virtually tied for the most common tractors in the database, with Ford and Allis-Chalmers runners-up. Something is going on here that transcends machinery, of course. "Since A.T.I.S.'s inception, it has been my goal to create a true human community on the Internet, complete with decency, civility, real friendships backed up with face-to-face meetings (we have annual gatherings) and a willingness to help and to uplift each other," Mr. Yost, founder of A.T.I.S., wrote by email. Mr. Yost grew up in a suburb of Atlanta and, as a child, imagined himself riding the rusty machines in the field next door. A stint in the Forest Service acquainted him with a number of north Georgia mountain farmers who used antique equipment. He started A.T.I.S. as a mailing list in 1993 because he had bought himself a 1946 Farmall A and wanted an easy way for him and others to get technical information. The site grew like Iowa corn. Mr. Yost now owns several tractors and says he likes Massey Harris the best. "Yes, there are extremely rare tractors," he wrote, "such as a 730 LP (liquid propane fuel) High Crop (the tractor is taller for higher crops) that sold recently for $56,000 (John Deere Expo auction, 1998)." But unlike other collectors, he said, tractor buffs are motivated less by rarity and investment value than by sentiment, utility and fun. "Antique tractors," he says in the site, "are simply a touchstone we use to understand and find our place in history, in our own lives and within the greater community of mankind." "Ageless Iron" (www.agriculture.com/sfonline/archive/sf/ageless/ agiindex.html), a Web page from Successful Farming magazine, offers photos of tractors from the Ageless Iron Art Gallery, and tractor trading cards. Dean Vinson's Farm Life page (www.geocities.com/ Heartland/Acres/4901) evokes rural Americana as well as hints for newcomers and special advice on buying or selling the Farmall M model. Chuck Bealke of Dallas has a site (web2.airmail.net/bealke/rollagshow.htm) devoted to the 1997 Labor Day steam thresher show in Rollag, Minn., that is worth seeing just for the pictures and the people. Mr. Bealke, who uses expressions like "Dream of Steam" and "Lust for Rust," also has a compact index of tractor museums by state (www.atis.net/museums.html). His main Web page, Chuck's Tractorstuf (web2.airmail.net/bealke/tractors.htm) is a comprehensive and warmly written complement to the A.T.I.S. pages, with many links. "For me," Mr. Bealke wrote by email, "the people in this endeavor are just as much fun as the tractors.  I just got back from three A.T. shows in Ohio and met several fine fellows I would like to live up the road from." Graphic   Photo

title: The Lure of the Underground
body: THE lure of secret and mysterious underground places has always had a hold on some people. For all the on-line Indiana Joneses out there, the Web offers plenty of places, from ancient to modern, to poke around in without getting too grimy or chased by angry guards. For those who want an early historical start, the Christian catacombs of Rome are featured in a Web site (www.catacombe.roma.it/ welcome.html) that takes visitors on an informative tour filled with pictures and text in six different languages. The catacombs were the underground cemeteries of Rome's early Christians, from the second to the fifth century. They contain miles of crypts and tombs, but the Web site points out that the catacombs were not used as secret hiding places for persecuted Christians. "This is only a fiction taken from novels or movies," the text says. It notes that the catacombs were sometimes used for the clandestine celebration of the Eucharist. The word "catacombs" may call to mind Paris and its enormous burial caverns near the Denfert-Rocherau stop on the Metro. Formerly stone quarries and underground galleries, the French catacombs -- much younger than the Roman ones -- are less than 200 years old. The Catacombs (www.mygale.org/11/ houze/english/presentation.html) offers a nice mix of history and anecdotes on the place and is also available to read in French. Thrill seekers and party hounds have begun hanging out in the Parisian necropolis, and a small Web page (www.mygale.org/01/lafouine/ kata/htmleng.intro.htm) celebrates these "Cataphyles." Places that were once used as shelter by the homeless and members of the French Resistance during World War II are now the site of a subterranean subculture (complete with art, social gatherings and graffiti) that has been evolving over the last 15 years, the Web site says. The Paris police play cat to the Cataphyles' mouse. An adventure with the Cataphyles is told on Paris Underground in a first-person narrative by Murray Battle with plenty of pictures to illustrate the journey, crawling through the Catacombs (www.infiltration. org/catacomb.htm). If modern archeology with a little chutzpah appeals to you, Infiltration's main site (www.infiltration. org) offers to take you through several off-limits areas around the world. Proclaiming itself "the zine about going places you're not supposed to go," Infiltration concerns itself with urban exploration, providing surreptitious virtual trips through passageways found in Toronto's subway system and several buildings around town. There's also a fascinating section devoted to roaming through steam tunnels on college campuses. Infiltration includes a link to the College Tunnels page (members.tripod.com/ tunnels/tunnels.html), which educates its readers about the hobby but warns them, "Tunneling is a very dangerous activity and you do so at your own risk." For those who are curious, the page offers links to information on tunnels at 52 major universities. Graphic   Photo: Virtual tours of buried worlds like the Paris catacombs are on line. (David Babinet/Sygma)

title:
USER'S GUIDE;
Web Shopping? Not for the Picky
body: ON days when life is under control in our household, either my husband or I will take the baby to shop at a friendly family-owned grocery. We all benefit from such leisurely outings. Clementine always gets a cookie (iced) from the owner, who also remembers to ask us how our older daughters are liking school so far this year. We bask in the amazing luxury of checkout clerks who cheerfully insist on bagging all the groceries. But more often, our household suffers shopping emergencies. Alerted by the baby sitter that the premises are devoid of some absolutely vital item, I will jump up from my desk to rush out to buy, say, diapers. In theory, that pattern should make me an ideal candidate for on-line shopping -- at least for mundane, nonperishable provisions. After all, I could conveniently arrange for the delivery of whole truckloads of diapers -- and avoid unduly interrupting my work or appearing in public in my lucky writing sweatpants (paint-spattered on one leg). But in reality, I am as reluctant as the next shopper to tinker with my habits. That's because shopping isn't really about shopping. It's about defining ourselves through the acquisition of goods, the items that tell the rest of the world about our wants, needs and tastes, including our willingness to eat generic-brand corn niblets. So as I browsed through on-line shopping sites recently, I realized that I would need an incentive to make an actual purchase, some prize or reward. Something like---- hey, a chance to earn free movie tickets. I had arrived at www.freeride.com, one of a growing number of marketing Web sites that award prizes to on-line shoppers. The more you buy from Freeride partners like www.netgrocer.com, www.books.com or www.magmall.com, the more points you earn. Freeride users who accumulate enough points can redeem them for a $20 gift certificate at Tower Records (1,000 points), a $5 gift certificate at Red Lobster (275 points) or even a Playboy T-shirt (800 points). Me? I opened a Freeride account with the relatively modest goal of getting a free ticket for "There's Something About Mary"(460 points) before it left town. There is nothing new about Freeride's brand of marketing, of course. Today's on-line techniques borrow heavily from the same marketing efforts that led to the trading stamp craze that began throughout the unitedstates and Canada at the turn of the century, according to David Monot, a historian and author of "Store Wars: Shopkeepers and the Culture of Mass Marketing 1890-1939" (University of Toronto Press, 1996).  In those days, the tedium of routine shopping was replaced by the excitement of earning stamps for purchases, then pasting them into books. Full books could be redeemed for prizes. The trading stamp era ended in scandal after some unscrupulous stamp companies didn't pony up the rewards they had promised shoppers. But after I called Freeride's founder, Jordan Stanley, I was confident that Freeride was a legitimate business -- and not just because I learned, coincidentally, that Mr. Stanley lived in the same town I do. And not because every time I go to the Little League fields, I practically drive by his house, which would make it really convenient to knock on his door to complain if free movie passes failed to arrive promptly in themail. No, what endeared Mr. Stanley to me was that he gave me tips for earning Freeride points without actually buying anything. How I love to beat the system. By filling out surveys Mr. Stanley told me about, I earned 55 points. By clicking on any of thedesignated shopping sites promoted on the Freeride site, I could earn 5 more points. Mr. Stanley even told me how to set up a second Freeride account to get around paying a $4.99 shipping fee that Netgrocer wanted to charge me to get six cases of 48 diapers delivered to my door by Federal Express. "We just started a new promotion -- it waives the shipping," Mr. Stanley said. "Go to www.att.net, click on the Freeride ad that rotates on that site, then set up a new Freeride account in your husband's name and go to Netgrocer," he said. But even with the head start given me by Mr. Stanley, I wavered. The real problem was one of choice: On the day I shopped, Netgrocer's best value in the category of diapers was 48 Pampers Baby Dry Stretch Size 4, packaged in a green bag, for $13.49: about what I would pay at the store (once the shipping was waived). But our regular brand is Huggies Ultratrim Girls Size 4, in a pink bag, which would cost $14.58 for the same number of diapers, a dollar more than I would pay at the store. I felt paralyzed by indecision: Should I get the price I want or the diapers I want? I phoned Daniel Miller, a British anthropologist, for guidance, and he made me feel much better. "Shopping isn't just about defining yourself," Dr. Miller said. "It's really about defining your relationships to the people closest to you, in this case, your infant." Dr. Miller, who spent a year studying the shopping habits of North London families for his new book, "A Theory of Shopping" (Cornell University Press), was confident that my crisis was a common case of "infant obsession." That syndrome is characterized by the creation of a largely fictitious list of the infant's likes and dislikes. "Parents develop strong views about the particular nature of their infants," Dr. Miller explained. "That comes out with items of clothing -- what an infant supposedly likes to wear or doesn't like to wear -- and with particular foodstuffs." In case I might have thought that Dr. Miller was being too critical of obsessed parents, he added, "It's a way of expressing love." He was right, of course. Anyone can see that my baby is the sort who likes to wear diapers that come in a pink bag, not green, and it makes more sense to buy them at the store than over the Internet, at least for now. With that problem solved, I logged off, never earning the points I needed for a movie ticket. But we continue to reap the rewards of off-line shopping. Both Clementine and her father came home from the store yesterday licking icing off their fingers. Graphic   Illustration (Mary Ann Smith)

title: Eyes for the Mouse, Wheels for the Joystick
body: Two prominent Internet pioneers have founded a company to create a way of navigating the Internet with maps that portray the relationships between computers and information as three-dimensional space. The company, Invisible Worlds Inc., based in Silicon Valley at Redwood City, Calif., is the brainchild of Carl Malamud and Marshall Rose, both Internet software developers who are credited with helping to create some of the most widely used technology components of the global computer network. The idea underlying the new company is that the current generation of Internet navigation tools -- portals, search engines and directories -- make it difficult for users to visualize dimensions of cyberspace, the virtual universe that has resulted from the emergence of the Internet and on-line services. "We think you should be able to take your mouse or joystick and drive around the Internet," Mr. Malamud said. "One of the reasons the Web seems so chaotic is there is no way to see it visually." Though there are already a number of so-called virtual worlds and 3-D Internet standards such as Virtual Reality Modeling Language, or VRML, Mr. Malamud said this was the first commercial effort to build the tools to map the entire Internet. When it is made available sometime next year, the company's set of visual rules, known as the Blocks protocol, will make it possible for computer users to examine locations of and relationships between Internet computers and network connections much as they would peruse a map or an atlas. Initially, users will view the interactive maps using a standard Web browser. But Mr. Malamud said he hoped someday to see the development of map-viewing software with more powerful visualization features. One benefit of a standard mapping protocol for the Internet will be the possibility of creating many different maps based geography, subject or almost any other concept. For example, the new company is planning to create two demonstration maps, one focusing on financial information and the other on music and media. However, in addition to selling advertising or possibly even renting metaphorical space in the areas it maps, Invisible Worlds is hoping that its new protocol will create a market for tools, service software and map-viewing programs. Neither Mr. Malamud nor Mr. Rose is a novice at creating Internet standards. Mr. Rose is the author of the Post Office Protocol, or POP, the standard that is used by millions of Internet computer users for sending and receiving email. Mr. Malamud has developed a number of nonprofit projects including Internet Talk Radio, the first on-line station, in 1993. He is probably best known for his campaign to persuade the unitedstates Government to publish public records on the Internet. By posting both the entire text of all Security and Exchange Commission documents and much of the Patent Office data base, he created public demand that in turn forced those agencies to make documents publicly available on line at no cost. Trained as an economist, Mr. Malamud, 39, said that the idea of mapping the Internet came to him in 1991 while he was working with the Internet and using computers and routers dispersed around the globe. Because the concept of geographic distance is irrelevant in cyberspace, which is formed of instantaneous connections, Mr. Malamud began searching for a way to provide the kind of rich, spatially oriented view of the Internet that maps afford of the physical world. Although science fiction writers such as Vernor Vinge, Neal Stephenson and William Gibson, who coined the term cyberspace in his 1984 novel "Neuromancer," have all envisioned electronic worlds emerging from computer networks, Mr. Malamud said they did not inspire the concept. "I don't read a great deal of science fiction," Mr. Malamud said. But he did trace his inspiration to the work of writers such as Thomas Pynchon, whose most recent novel, "Mason & Dixon," celebrated the role the cartographer can play in defining uncharted territory. Vinton Cerf, who invented Internet protocol, the set of communications rules that made the Internet possible, said mapping the Internet was an extremely difficult undertaking that had no certain outcome. "Both Carl and Marshall are among the most creative network citizens that we have," said Mr. Cerf, now an executive at MCI Worldcom. He said he had abandoned his own experiments with mapping multiple dimensions of information into a three-dimensional representation, finding the problem too daunting. What Mr. Malamud found daunting was searching for support. His three-year odyssey took him from the unitedstates to Japan and Amsterdam, and he said he settled on a for-profit venture only after his bids to form a nonprofit enterprise to create an Internet atlas failed to win supporters. Mr. Malamud said he decided to come "home" to Silicon Valley, where he has settled into a small office space near several other start-up companies.

title:
HOT SPOTS/SILICON ALLEY;
Putting a Funky Face on Wall Street
body: TWO men in ponytails and a woman with a bleached-blond crew cut were hanging out in their sparsely decorated Internet consulting firm at 11 Broadway in lower Manhattan. Their upstairs neighbor, the president of an Internet company had just stopped by. He had sideburns to his chin. "We were comparing notes about people in the building," explained Mary Olson of Transition Networks, as Paul Guzyk, the president of Infohouse, which provides access to the Internet as well as networking services, headed back to the ninth floor. "We do that sometimes." Just two years ago, Transition Networks didn't exist, Infohouse was operated from an East Village bedroom and 11 Broadway was almost empty. But these days they are all thriving, thanks, in part, to Plug 'n' Go, a program that has put 151 new-media entrepreneurs into 400,000 square feet of cheap, well-wired offices in six buildings south of City Hall. Industry experts credit the program with giving a funky, creative edge to Wall Street, where nose rings and chunky shoes are now seen among the Brooks Brothers suits, and with helping the growth of Silicon Alley, a loosely defined area downtown that has been popular with new-media companies for the last few years. The newyork Media Association, a trade group, estimated that there were 2,600 new-media companies in 1997. "I think Plug 'n' Go is one reason the industry is doing so well here," said Brian Horey, the association's director. "I would like to see it expanded." But Plug 'n' Go has not been the only impetus to luring new-media contenders to the end of Manhattan, others say. "Silicon Alley happened despite government, not because of it," said Tom Watson of @NY, an on-line news service catering to local new-media businesses. "Plug 'n' Go was a reaction to what was already happening." The program was started in February 1997 by the Alliance for Downtown newyork, a nonprofit business improvement group, with help from the city and landlords. It was designed to help that part of newyork recover from the loss of about 100,000 jobs in the early 90's, which left commercial buildings in the Wall Street area only a quarter full. Sharon Greenberger, who manages the program, said the only business that had been growing downtown was information technology. So the Alliance tried to encourage young new-media companies, the Internet and other computer-related services to move in. "These companies needed three things," Ms. Greenberger said, "cheap rent, easy connection to the Internet and short-term, flexible leases." So Ms. Greenberger persuaded the owners of six semivacant buildings to offer small spaces at $15 a square foot (20 percent below market rate then) and to wire the offices for computers and T-1 lines and contract with an Internet provider. Mr. Guzyk said the program has helped Infohouse, which began with two employees in 1995, to grow to 10 employees and a yearly gross of $1 million. "We can do things in this building much easier than if we were in a typical midtown building," he said. Graphic   Photo: Lurking behind this staid facade on lower Broadway are some Internet start-ups. (John Sotomayor for The newyork Times)

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: TV Networks Are Heading For Toughest Fall Fight Yet The new fall television season officially opens tonight, and executives of the six broadcast networks are expecting their bloodiest battle yet for ratings as they squeeze 36 new shows into an already crowded prime time. Indeed, there is a sense of desperation in the industry, because the risks are so great and the stakes so high. That desperation is reflected in deals like the $13 million an episode that NBC will pay for "E.R.," TV's biggest hit. And the networks are anxiously shuffling their schedules to seek an edge on specific nights; Fox, for example, is moving its animated series "King of the Hill," above, to Tuesday.  Page C7. title:
Compressed Data;
What's in a Web Name? Sometimes, Mistaken Identity
body: Jeff Woods, the owner of an Internet service provider to Raleigh and Durham, N.C., has discovered that using an address, or domain name, that people associate with a well-known company may not be worth the free publicity that comes with mistaken identity. He owns delta.com, a domain name he chose in 1993 for his company, Deltacomm Internet Services. Trouble is, nearly everyone who comes to his Web site (www.delta.com) is really looking for the site of Delta Air Lines -- sometimes as many as 10,000 people a day. Over the years, as traffic on the World Wide Web has meant more and more mistakes, Mr. Woods has tried to sell the address to Delta Air Lines. But the airline, which does business on the Web as www.delta-air.com, has repeatedly rejected his asking price as too high. Mr. Woods said he had lowered the price, to a "five-figure amount," which he contends will barely cover the cost of reprinting brochures and manuals and changing his customers' email addresses to a new domain. Because he pays another Internet company to carry his Web site's traffic, Mr. Woods says, he is incurring extra costs to redirect Delta's traffic. And he says he gets no extra advertising value from most of the people who visit in search of the airline because his business serves only customers in the Raleigh-Durham area. Delta Air Lines disputes Mr. Woods's economics. "His asking price is much higher than his cost to migrate his customers," a spokesman, Kip Smith, said. "We don't feel that Delta should subsidize his business interests." And besides, Mr. Smith said, Delta Air Lines has a recognized Web address that has been in place since December 1995. "We're really not interested in pursuing it, although we are always open to discussion," he said. Evidently. The airline recently acquired another Web site name, www.deltaairlines.com from Dennis Toeppen, a speculator in Internet names, who had originally registered it along with 100 or so other corporate names. Delta would not comment on the terms of that deal. After one conversation with Delta that did not go to his liking, Mr. Woods removed all links to Delta Air Lines' official site. But he soon received so many complaints that he restored the link. To goad Delta, he also stuck in a link to its main rival, American Airlines, with a free testimonial that reads, "If you're looking for an airline, try American Airlines, the frequent-flier airline the owners and staff of Deltacomm Internet Services flew 100,000 miles on in 1997."   PETER WAYNER Graphic   Photo: An Internet access service, not an airline.

title: F.T.C. Surfs the Web and Gears Up to Demand Privacy Protection
body: After more than a year of heated debate within the Government, the Federal Trade Commission has all but decided it will part company with the Clinton Administration over the contention that business can regulate itself when it comes to Internet privacy. "We are losing patience with self-regulation," David Medine, an associate director in the commission's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in an interview. "It's too bad, but I think industry has lost the opportunity to show that they will do it on their own." What was the last straw? Within the F.T.C., they code-named it the Big Surf. Last spring, dozens of lawyers trooped into special training rooms equipped with personal computers and high-speed Internet connections. For two weeks, they trolled the World Wide Web, searching for privacy problems. Their intention was to find Web sites that collected personal information from visitors but neglected to post any notice about how that information would be used. The assumption was that many of the companies sold the information -- some of it highly personal data on health, income and personal preferences -- to Internet list brokers, merchants and advertisers. The F.T.C. Web surfers had no idea what they would find; no one had ever dedicated the time and manpower needed for this sort of targeted survey of the vast, tangled, largely unfathomable network that is the World Wide Web. But the effort produced startling results published in a report this summer. More than 90 percent of the roughly 1,400 sites examined collected personal information from visitors, but only 14 percent of them disclosed how that information would be used, convincing the F.T.C. that formal regulation would probably be necessary. For more than a year, the White House had been saying that businesses using the Internet should be allowed to regulate themselves. "If there's ever an arena that should be market driven, this is it," Ira C. Magaziner, President Clinton's adviser on Internet issues, said as the White House announced its Internet policy last year. But while its strategy was being formulated, a few blocks away at the F.T.C -- an independent Federal regulatory agency -- officials were conducting hearings and workshops on Internet privacy, listening to complaints from members of Congress and interest groups. They were also installing up-to-date computer equipment so the agency could carry out its examination and add the Internet to the list of business arenas subject to F.T.C. scrutiny and enforcement. Now with the results from the campaign and the industry's reaction to it in hand, several senior F.T.C. officials said, the agency will give industry just a few more months to respond to the recommendations in its report by demonstrating it is effectively regulating itself. Mr. Medine said he would expect the industry to conduct its own survey and hand over the results. If, as most F.T.C. officials expect, industry does not provide such proof, the commission will draft a bill calling for clear Internet privacy standards and ask Congress to pass it. As an independent agency, the commission does not have to get the Clinton Administration's permission to do this. And given repeated statements in Congress of concern about Internet privacy, a bill would probably get the votes needed to pass. "It's not our intention to overregulate," said Jodie Bernstein, director of the agency's consumer protection bureau. "We don't want to chill new technologies." But, she added, Web sites must begin "telling consumers if they are collecting personal information, what they are going to do with it, and how the consumers can get out of it if they want to." Generally, that means posting a privacy statement that answers these questions. But since the F.T.C.'s survey results were published in June, commission lawyers have begun to think that some Web sites are choosing not to post privacy statements. "There's now a perverse, reverse incentive," said Ori Lev, an F.T.C. official involved in Internet enforcement. "If you don't post a privacy policy, we can't go after you." That became clear last month, after the commission reached a settlement with Geocities, a popular site on the Web that the commission had accused of lying to its two million subscribers. Geocities offered a privacy statement that promised not to give out personal information collected during registration without permission. But the commission found that Geocities was selling the information anyway. That supposed deception was the basis for the Government's case. If Geocities had not promised to keep the information private, then it would probably not have run afoul of the F.T.C. As a result, Mr. Medine said, "clearly there are a lot of corporate lawyers advising their Web clients not to do anything now" -- not to post a privacy statement or anything else. Connie LaMotta, a senior vice president with the Direct Marketing Association, calls that idea nonsense. "It's a very bureaucratic way of thinking," she said. "It's upside down. Businesses want to post privacy statements to establish good customer relationships and customer service. Industry is stepping up to the plate on this." Ms. LaMotta said she and others in the industry agreed with the F.T.C.'s stated Internet privacy goals. But Ms. LaMotta added that she was certain that businesses could accomplish the task on their own. "It's our experience that when you tap them on the shoulder, change happens. They say: 'Oh, gosh. O.K.' " With just a few minutes' effort, most anyone can find a Web site that collects personal information from visitors, in registration or order forms, without disclosing how the data will be used. But how those sites respond when asked about this can differ markedly. A site called Soccer Patch (www.soccerpatch.com) is a trading post for soccer-playing children who want to trade team patches. It lists the names, email addresses and in some cases the hometowns of children who want to trade patches. That was a red flag for F.T.C. enforcers. They worried that child molesters could use the information to find children. As soon as a reporter asked Philip Rubin, president of Edge of Chaos, the company that manages the site, about this, he promised to change the policy. And a few days later, he did. "We now require all contributors to provide us with signed permission letters before email addresses and/ or names can be posted," he said. "Contributors under the age of 18 must provide a form signed by their parents or guardians." And the Soccer Patch site posted the form so that it can be printed out and mailed. Rosenthal Honda, a Washington area car dealer, had a different approach. The company, like many car dealers, posts a prequalification form for auto loans, requesting a variety of personal information, including income, debt load and the amount of rent or mortgage payments. Nowhere on the site does it say how that information will be used. And when asked about that, the dealership issued a statement saying, "We will look at the issue with our Web developer." Asked two weeks later what had come of this, Rosenthal Honda did not respond. F.T.C. officials say they are investigating other Web sites and will almost certainly file charges against other companies. Dean Forbes, 31, a commission lawyer, found the Geocities problem and spends most of his time working on Internet privacy issues. "Generally we get ideas from reading the trade press," he said, as well as from "looking at who is linking up with list brokers; we get tips from interest groups, usenet news group postings and complaints." Mr. Forbes disagrees with the idea that a Web site can escape trouble if it simply decides not to post a privacy policy. "If you don't make a visible statement," he said, "that does not mean there isn't an implied claim." But while his agency and others in the Government figure out whether to push for new rules on Web privacy, Mr. Forbes sees a bit of improvement on the Web. "I'm not saying everything's great," he said. "But there is movement." Graphic   Photo: An F.T.C. lawyer, Dean Forbes, searching for Web site privacy abuses. (Carol T. title:
Industry View;
The stock market's gyrations are causing anxiety among Silicon Alley start-ups that are planning to go public.
body: IN contrast to politics, in the world of entrepreneurs, going public has fabulously positive connotations. Many founders of start-ups set their sights on taking their companies public before even filing their incorporation papers. Going public is how their investors make back their money -- and, hopefully, then some. It is how entrepreneurs achieve real wealth, if only on paper. It is how they will be judged for years to come. It is the consummate measure of business success or failure. So consider the anxiety of Silicon Alley entrepreneurs like Jack Hidary, Todd Krizelman, Stephan Paternot and Alan Andreini. All four run high-profile Internet companies that filed papers in the summer with the Securities and Exchange Commission to go public. All have, to this point, capitalized on the innovation and excitement of the Internet and helped to define the amorphous newyork new-media industry that has come to be known as Silicon Alley. But as the stock market continues to vacillate, all these men face a quandary: to go or not to go. They have arrived at the dance only to find that the band is taking a break. In all, six new-media companies in the newyork area have filed for public offerings, including Mr. Hidary's Earthweb, Mr.  Krizelman's and Mr. Paternot's theglobe.com and Mr. Andreini's Interworld, plus two newyork companies, Multex and Net Grocer, and All-Tech Investment Group of Montvale, N.J. Under the S.E.C.'s quiet-period rules, the executives of those companies are prohibited from discussing their situations, but speculation in the Alley has been rampant. "Those that are in registration now will wait if they can do so," predicted John Siracuse, vice president and head of East Coast Internet banking for Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities. "They don't want to be the first to test the market." Further complicating the go/no-go question, Mr. Siracuse observes, is that the window of opportunity is diminishing as the holiday season approaches. "It's difficult for small-cap companies to get the investors' attention between Thanksgiving and Christmas," he said. If companies wait until the new year to go public, he continued, they will have logistical issues, like having to update their prospectuses, but more important, they will have to wrangle with the perception that they were not ready to go public. "Perception is reality," he said. "And there will be the perception they couldn't get the deal done." Jonathan Cohen, head of Internet research at Merrill Lynch, believes many companies will turn to mergers and acquisitions. He notes that mergers and acquisitions have been increasing in the last 6 to 12 months anyway. And while there have been virtually no technology offerings in the last few weeks, Mr. Cohen said, "The landscape for Internet I.P.O.'s has shifted, but the window is still open for high-quality companies with compelling business models -- models such as community and E-commerce." "Investors want to see properties with components of high functionality and high intellectual property," he said, saying that theglobe.com is an example of a community site where users create a wealth of intellectual property. Venture capitalists see the recent correction in technology stocks as a much-needed dose of reality. Tom Hirschfeld, a principal at Patricof & Company Ventures Inc., which has interests in Alley-based Medscape Inc. and New Jersey-based Audible Inc., says that the current market has not diminished his firm's interest in the Internet and new-media start-ups. But, he added, "It does have an impact on price negotiations." The drop in the market, Mr. Hirschfeld says, brings a sense of sanity to private market valuation. But it also leaves pre-public Silicon Alley companies in a precarious position. If they are hard-pressed for cash, they may have to turn to their original investors or go for a private placement. They may have to pull their public offerings altogether. Mr. Siracuse adds that delayed public offerings can cause another problem. "Employees who have other opportunities may decide to leave the company," he said. A big issue for Silicon Alley is the fact that it is still being judged by the number of successful public offerings. Each one is tallied as younger companies continue to try to lure venture capital from the West Coast, and to garner the respect of Wall Street. Mr. Siracuse agrees with Mr. Cohen that while the outlook may not be peaches and cream, neither is it liver and onions. "There is still an appetite for Internet stocks," he said. "What the market needs is a high-profile Internet stock to go out and do well." The stock needs to sell out at its offering, Mr. Siracuse said, and then continue to sell well in the after market. As for those companies that had already gone public, many star-struck entrepreneurs and their option-holding employees found out what their investors already knew: what goes up must come down. Double Click Inc., an Internet advertising network and an Alley favorite, watched its stock drop from more than $50 a share in July to $23 last week. It closed Friday at $19.69. Double Click's chief competitor, 24/7 Media Inc., went public in mid-August, opening at $18.50 and closing at $20.25. Last week, its stock was selling below $12. It closed Friday at $11.56. Among other Alley stocks that saw their share prices drop into single digits were N2K Inc., the owner of Music Boulevard, and Cyber Shop Inc., an on-line mall. Even so, Mr. Cohen, who has been following Silicon Alley companies for the last three years, first as an analyst at Salomon Smith Barney, then at the Union Bank of Switzerland, remains optimistic. "Silicon Alley has come to be populated with good companies and intelligent people and will continue to be a source of investment ideas going forward," he said. Music to the ears of newyork's high-technology entrepreneurs. Graphic   Drawing (Randy Jones)

title:
Media Talk;
A Forbes List Maker Makes the List
body: Take a look at Forbes ASAP's annual listing of the 100 wealthiest people in technology, which will be published today, and you will learn some of the secrets of getting rich quick these days. They include selling technology for the Internet and selling things on the Internet. And then there is marrying into Internet wealth. One of the 28 Internet executives on this year's list happens to be the husband of the list maker. Nancy Rutter, a senior editor at Forbes ASAP, who was in charge of this year's list and the accompanying articles, is married to Jim Clark, the 54-year-old co-founder of the Netscape Communications Corporation. He is No. 28 on the list, with total assets of $412.4 million. Ms. Rutter, 44, met Mr. Clark in 1989 while he was still running Silicon Graphics Inc. and she was editor of Upside Magazine. They married in 1990. She is now a part-time staffer for ASAP, a bimonthly supplement to Forbes magazine, working from the couple's homes in Silicon Valley and Palm Beach, Fla. Ms. Rutter, whose job includes editing most of the magazine's "list" stories, says she no longer writes the kinds of in-depth industry articles she used to because of the potential for conflicts of interest. And she said the magazine is careful not to involve her in stories even remotely related to any of her husband's businesses. The "Technology's Wealthiest" list is an exception, she said, because the facts speak for themselves. "I'm very happy to be married to No. 28 on the list," Ms. Rutter said in an interview from her California home. "It's not a bad position for a reporter to be in." Topping the list that Ms. Rutter compiled are the industry's old guard, led once again by William H. Gates of the Microsoft Corporation, with a net worth of nearly $59 billion, and his co-founder, Paul Allen, with $16.98 billion. Among executives of Internet companies, Jeffrey P. Bezos, of Amazon.com Inc., joined the billionaires' club at No. 9 with $2.14 billion, along with David Filo of Yahoo, No. 15 with a little over $1 billion. While the Internet may be hot, it should be noted that the Forbes ASAP list was calculated on Aug. 3, well before the market's huge slide.  As of last week, the net worth of the group of 28 Internet executives was down $1.8 billion since the calculations were made. And, yes, that means Ms. Rutter's net worth is down, too.   LAURIE J. title: Studies Differ on Internet's Impact on TV
body: So, are eyes starting to wander? With tens of millions of people using the Internet every day, more and more advertisers and media executives are starting to wonder whether active surfers are watching less television. Indeed, several surveys have found that heavy Internet users say their time on line eats into their television viewing more than any other activity, although they also say they read, talk to friends and sleep less, too. One widely reported study by Nielsen Media Research for America Online last month found that households that had Internet access watched 15 percent less television than those that did not. But the America Online study stopped short of proving that Internet use was the cause of the lower television use. And a lot of other research appeared to show the opposite -- that people were still watching more television even as they increasingly surfed the Internet. Such research indicates that many people perform both activities at the same time. A new study scheduled for release today, commissioned by Discovery Networks, the operator of science-oriented cable television channels and a unit of Discovery Communications Inc., takes the side of those who contend that net-surfing does not cut down on the time devoted to channel-surfing. The Discovery study, which probed deeper into the same Nielsen data that America Online used, concluded that as households began to use the Internet, television use by teen-agers dropped but use by everyone else increased. That was consistent with a study commissioned by MTV Networks, a unit of Viacom Inc., and released in June. "We see media consumption leading to more media consumption," said Betsy Frank, executive vice president for research at MTV Networks. "People don't quit watching television because they go on line. They do more of both." The MTV study asked 25,000 people to keep diaries of their media use. Those who said they were heavy Internet users also said they watched more cable television than average and read more books than the average respondent. In fact, many studies are now finding an increase in what has become known as multitasking -- surfing the Internet, watching television, cooking dinner and talking on the telephone, all at the same time. Ms. Frank said this phenomenon was confirmed on May 14, the night of the last episode of "Seinfeld." That evening the television audience surged, but Internet use increased as well, according to measurements by Relevant Knowledge, an Atlanta research firm. Other seeming threats to television use -- the videocassette recorder and video games, for example -- have been found not to reduce the amount of network and cable television that people watch. People use VCR's to record TV programs they otherwise would miss, enough so to offset whatever decline in television watching that may come from people watching prerecorded movies, said Paul Lindstrom, a vice president of Nielsen. The effect of video games was even more surprising: they increase the number of televisions in a household as well as viewership. "Before video games, kids would watch "The Flintstones" or whatever after school in the family room," Mr. Lindstrom said. "When a family gets a video game, they often buy a television set for the kids' bedroom. That means the kids can watch TV whenever they want to and the parents can watch what they want in the afternoon, too." The stakes in such findings are high for the television networks, for the Internet services and for the advertisers who must choose where to place their messages. Television, after all, has proved to be the most powerful medium in history for selling products. And the idea that the rapid growth of the Internet might pull people away from their sets is frightening to many commercial interests, especially since advertisements on line have yet to prove effective for sales of many consumer products. Internet use is certainly taking a big chunk of Americans' time. The 13 million members of America Online, for example, log an average of 45 minutes daily. That is why the America Online study that showed lower television use in Internet homes received such attention. But many media experts said it glossed over important demographic variables. "The Internet user base is more upscale than the rest of the population," said Lynn Bolger, senior vice president for media at APL Digital, a unit of the Interpublic Group of Companies. "And traditionally that is a group that is not a heavy viewer of television." America Online concedes that its study was limited. "I think on-line time is eating into television time," said Marshall Cohen, the senior vice president for brand development of America Online. "If you say prove it, I say the definitive study has not been done." The best study, of course, would monitor people's use of television before they signed up for the Internet and then after they started to go on line. So far, that research has not been done, but the Discovery study with Nielsen came close. In October 1996 and again in October 1997, it measured television use in 2,218 homes that are part of Nielsen's continuing television rating panel. Nielsen did not ask participants whether they had Internet access in 1996, so the study could not differentiate longtime Internet users from those homes that signed up for the Internet for the first time between the two measurements. Still, since Internet use was increasing nationwide during that period, Discovery estimates that 40 percent of the people who had Internet access in 1997 first went on line after the 1996 measurement. Households that told Nielsen in 1997 that they had access to the Internet increased their television use by 1.8 percent over the previous year, compared with a 1.3 percent increase over all for the whole sample. "It wasn't a perfect measure," said Steve McGowan, Discovery's research director. "But if the Internet was taking time away from television, you should have seen viewership decline, but in fact it went up." Discovery did find that sort of decline for viewers between the ages of 12 and 24. In homes with Internet access, television use by those younger viewers declined by 6.8 percent from 1996 to 1997. Television use by young people without Internet access remained constant. Graphic   Chart: "Which Screen Wins Out?" America Online and Discovery Networks commissioned studies by Nielsen Media Research on television viewing habits and Internet usage. But because they analyzed the sampling differently, they drew contrasting conclusions about the Internet's impact.
