title:
THE TESTING OF A PRESIDENT: THE INTERNET;
Access to Clinton Data Aids E Pluribus Unum in the 90's
body: Tim Ericson was not one of the millions of Americans scrolling through the report by the independent counsel Kenneth W. Starr in cyberspace last week. He read it in his local paper. Nor does he plan to waste bandwidth downloading the video of President Clinton's testimony when it is made available this week. But Mr. Ericson, a 33-year-old graphic designer from St. Paul, has spent hours composing and absorbing a flood of email about the report from an on-line discussion group of about 400 fellow-Minnesotans. "People have very different opinions, and I haven't seen anyone giving way too much," Mr. Ericson said. "But it's only been a week. Our debate over carrying concealed weapons has been going on heavily for months." Congress's decision last week to release Mr. Starr's report over the Internet was seen as a defining moment for the global computer network, a test of both its technical infrastructure and its ability to play a critical role in the political process. In many ways, the ad hoc experiment in electronic democracy was a success. The extraordinary run on government and news sites -- by one count, 20 million Americans had read parts of the report on line within 48 hours of its release -- reflected a public thirst for instant, unfiltered information driven in part by the technology itself. The sprawling web of chips and fiber strained under its heaviest load ever but did not snap. But as part one of the stampede for the Starr report abates and Webmasters brace for part two -- the expected release of the videotape on Monday -- the real test of the Internet as a tool of citizenship lies in politics beyond scandal and lurid details. "I don't know if we'll see millions of people downloading Social Security reform legislation, but we could," said Jonah Seiger, co-founder of Mindshare Internet Campaigns (www.mindshare.net), a political consulting firm based in Washington. "This event on the Internet is changing the way people perceive their role in our political system." The Internet, invented as a communications network for scientists and academics and financed by the Department of Defense, has had plenty of other milestone moments in the last three years as it evolved into a mass medium and a global platform for everything from electronic commerce to dating. When Diana, Princess of Wales, died in a car crash last year, people the world over convened in cyberspace to mourn. When NASA published Pathfinder's first pictures from Mars last summer, millions logged on for a glimpse of the red planet. And when the stock market took a nosedive last month, traffic surged to record highs at some financial Web sites. Now, for the first time in an unfolding national political crisis, the Internet has become a place to turn both for information and debate. From the rumors of President Clinton's affair with an intern, first reported in January on the Web site of the Internet gossip columnist Matt Drudge, to the revelation last week by the on-line magazine Salon of Representative Henry J. Hyde's extramarital affair 30 years ago, the Internet has played a central and controversial role in informing the public about the Presidential sex scandal. And at least for the moment, the medium seems inseparable from that particular message. "Newspapers go out with the recycling," said Jonathan Zittrain, executive director of the Berkman Center for Internet and Society at Harvard University. "Once it's on the Web digitally, your sister-in-law can send you the best parts by email. It forces a level of engagement with the primary material there's no way you would have had otherwise." For Marilyn Lyon, 54, of Mission, Kan., who read Mr. Starr's report on the Internet the day it appeared, there is another advantage. "The news today is so loaded with emotion and opinion that it irritates me." Ms. Lyon said. "This way I can read it without commercials popping in all the time." Yet on-line activists warn that surfing the Web for alternative news sources is very different from using the Internet to forge political consensus over an issue as fraught with emotion as the impeachment of a President. Access to raw data may make for a more informed electorate, but not necessarily a more united one. "Democracy means more than just reading a document," said Steven Clift, chairman of Minnesota E-Democracy, the group that runs the email list that Mr. Ericson subscribes to. "What will determine how the Internet does is what happens in the next few months as we move from the reading phase to the discussing phase." Some longtime "netizens" argue that many Americans have formed an Internet political habit that will extend beyond the current scandal -- and beyond the Internet. Others argue that to exploit the democratic potential of the medium, legislators will have to do more than just publish the occasional high-profile document on line; they may actually have to interact in cyberspace with their constituents. "It sure would be nice to see Congress come out on the Net a bit and talk to people about these things," said Mr. Clift. He noted that the Web site where the House of Representatives published the Starr report has no area for discussion. Still, in private email, on Web forums and chat rooms and in voluntary on-line polls, Americans have found a way to type their politics into the ether in record numbers. On Thursday, Mr. Clift tried to direct his discussion list back to its regular diet of Minnesota politics, with only limited success. It was a phenomenon not unique to Minnesota: As of Friday morning, subscribers to America Online had posted more than 400,000 messages in the area set aside for discussion of the President's affair with Monica Lewinsky. "Conversations over the dinner table are fleeting," said Barry Schuler, America Online's president for interactive services. "With message boards, what you have is a real-time member-published journal. Especially with a topic where there's so much dissonance, it helps to have an ongoing dialogue that's taking shape over time." Typically, part of the Internet's appeal is that it resonates with an American political ideal of unfiltered, unmediated communication. Now, at a time when national political participation has been at one of its lowest ebbs -- turnout in the November election is expected to be sparser than ever -- there is some hope among the politically and digitally inclined that expanded access to the Internet will encourage a more activist electorate. "What I find most interesting about all of this is the way in which the Internet has changed our expectations," said Jeffrey Eisenach, president of the conservative Progress and Freedom Foundation. "It makes people expect information about government and everything else to be available instantly and at almost no cost." But the recent events in Washington have been exploited for commercial purposes as well. Already, marketers have used the Starr report in mass emailings known as spam as a way to tempt consumers to read advertising pitches.

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
CYBERSCOUT
body: The trouble with traveling on the World Wide Web is that after a while you may crave a home there, a place where you pick up your mail, chat with friends, trade gossip and information or just hang out. On the Web, you can wander from site to site, searching for rooms and restaurants, booking air fares, seeking sights to see and places to play. But it is like staying in a different hotel every night of a vacation; eventually you forget where you are, and you never talk to anyone. Consequently, a dozen or so Web sites have gotten more homey lately. Until the early 1990's, the brave souls who sought information and socialization on line joined such services as America On Line, Compuserve, Prodigy, GEnie, Bix, eWorld and hundreds of others. Only the bravest of the brave tried the Internet, a vast collection of cybertext scattered around the world, accessed by arcane commands and intended for the technologically sophisticated. Some of these services still exist, but since the beginning of the World Wide Web, a friendlier subsidiary of the Internet, many people have gone straight to the Web, usually via a search engine, a kind of index.  HOME ON THE WEB www.yahoo.com Yahoo has long been my search engine of first choice, partly because of its rich selection of sites -- there are 47 sub categories in the travel section alone -- and partly, no doubt, from force of habit. Now news headlines have been added, with links to a variety of journalistic establishments, as well as stock quotes, free email, and a personal calendar to remind you of anni versaries, birthdays and other important dates. You can set up your Yahoo page to suit yourself, with the kinds of news, weather, scores and stock prices that you are interested in. I set mine up to watch for Travel (with the key words New England, inn and budget) and Air Fares (with the key words air fares, airline fares, unitedstates and North America). With those person alized changes, which took place imme diately, Yahoo would watch for news in those categories. There are "rooms" where you "chat" with other people about travel, television, investments, sports, science fic tion, cyberdating and whatever -- all on bright, colorful screens that are not so bright and colorful that they take forever to download.  BROWSING THE WORLD www.excite.com Excite tempts me. The opening page, spiffier than Yahoo's but not excessively so, offers email and chat rooms, top news events, technology, business, sports news and scores, stock quotes, weather (you enter your ZIP code or the ZIP code of a place you are planning to visit) and even a horoscope. As with Yahoo, the content can be customized. Excite offers a profusion of travel sites, in broader categories than Yahoo's: reservations, destinations, busi ness travel, cruises and tours, family travel, frequent flier and adventure. There are car rental sites, restaurant guides and a map on which you click to browse the world. Nice.  VIRTUAL HOUSE HUNTING I have dipped into many other portals, as Web homes are coming to be called, and Yahoo and Excite struck me as the leading ones. But a virtual home, like a real home, is a highly personal choice. America On Line, www.aol.com; Compuserve, www.compuserve.com; and the Microsoft Network, home.microsoft.com, have Web pages distinct from, and not nearly as comprehensive as, their proprietary extra-cost services, which are promoted on their Web sites; both AOL and the Microsoft Network have travel categories you can click on. Compuserve does not, and its site seems largely a promotion for their main service. If you are virtual house hunting, you might also check Altavista, www.altavista.digital.com; Geocities, www.geocities.com; Infoseek, www.infoseek.com; Lycos, www.lycos.com; Netcenter, home.netscape.com; Planet Direct, www.planetdirect.com; and Snap, www.snap.com. (Thanks to the Sept. 1 issue of PC Magazine for the list.) It's house-hunting time. L. R. SHANNON Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: Unchained
body: RESCUING PROMETHEUS By Thomas P. Hughes. Illustrated. 372 pp. newyork: Pantheon Books. $28.50. Pathbreaking mega-engineering and technology projects have been hallmarks of our history. The Erie Canal, the transcontinental railroad, the Tennessee Valley Authority complex, the Manhattan Project -- these are just a few of the achievements reflecting America's genius for inventing and building. In "Rescuing Prometheus," Thomas P. Hughes, a professor of the history and sociology of science at the University of Pennsylvania, focuses on the cold war years, a particularly exciting era when rivalry with Moscow caused Washington to finance vast technological innovation, when collaboration between the Pentagon and companies like IBM and universities like the Massachusetts Institute of Technology reached its zenith and when the country's finest talent opted for careers in science and engineering rather than banking and marketing. Writing simply and directly, if a bit dryly, Hughes makes an important contribution to an understanding of the history, politics and culture of big science-based projects in that era. Hughes begins by discussing the early development of air defense systems, which led to the first computers that could assimilate and analyze astronomical amounts of information in order to monitor and control complex military operations. He then turns to the building of the Atlas intercontinental missile, involving over 18,000 technical experts and 200,000 suppliers. From here he moves to the construction of Boston's Central Artery and Tunnel Project, America's largest urban transportation project. And finally he discusses the project called Arpanet (because it was financed by the Pentagon's Advanced Research Projects Agency), which connected networks of computers across the country and became the forerunner of the Internet. His concern is the challenge of managing highly complex projects rather than the importance of the technological breakthroughs themselves. He assumes that scientific knowledge exists or can be discovered, but maintains that it was the application of far-reaching managerial innovations that constituted America's most impressive technological achievement. In the search for an antimissile defense system, for example, he dwells on the struggle for effective cooperation between the Pentagon and research universities, and the difficult task of integrating frontier thinking from experts in engineering, physics and economics. In the Atlas project he underlines two managerial advances: eliminating the old system of prime contractor in favor of a neutral "project czar," and applying new statistical techniques to quantify and monitor every component of a complex process. And in the story of the Arpanet he points to the evolution of a new organizational ethos that anticipated the nonhierarchical, flexible management teams of Intel and Microsoft. Hughes is enamored of leaders who can orchestrate complex systems. He emphasizes techniques of "systems engineering" and "operations research" that allow managers to link the many moving parts of a megaproject and to understand so deeply the many interfaces of a project that they can anticipate adjustments throughout the system required by any change in any part. A particularly intriguing chapter deals with the effort, during the Kennedy and Johnson Administrations, to adapt management processes developed in the military arena to solve great domestic problems. "The techniques that are going to put a man on the moon," Vice President Hubert Humphrey said, "are going to be exactly the techniques that we are going to need to clean up our cities." Hughes shows how Pentagon-supported research organizations like the Rand Corporation or defense contractors like TRW were enlisted in civil projects, and analyzes why such attempts ultimately failed. The four case studies move quickly, and Hughes skillfully explains how lessons learned in one were applied to the next. He is at his best in providing texture by describing the backgrounds and personalities of some of the key figures -- like Jay W. Forrester, who led M.I.T.'s team to create a modern computer for missile defense; Gen. Bernard Schriever, the Air Force combat pilot and engineer who was a power behind the Atlas project; and Frederick Salvucci, an engineer and savvy mediator among special political interest groups in Boston. In all four projects he deftly describes both the political setting and the internal politics of the projects. His enthusiasm for the era is contagious. The book has some shortcomings. There are almost no memorable anecdotes, and the few quotes cited stem from secondary sources. At times Hughes is a bit too breathless in his claims for unprecedented progress. No doubt the development of computers, missiles, the Internet and major transportation systems required new forms of management. But so did the building of the Panama Canal and the construction of the newyork subway system -- both in the early part of this century -- and the interstate highway project begun in the Eisenhower era. Hughes hangs a lot of his enthusiasm on dramatic breakthroughs that "systems engineering" brought, but he could have been more convincing if he explained more lucidly what such techniques really entailed, how they worked and especially why they differed so much from the past. Nevertheless, "Rescuing Prometheus" implicitly contains a powerful message. Throughout our history, great technological advances -- including the radio, the telegraph and the airplane -- have had a strong push from the military. For the last half-century, in particular, it is difficult to think of any major scientific breakthrough in America that cannot be linked to Federal subsidies to universities or to guaranteed Pentagon purchases of technology from private companies. But in recent years Government support for key areas like advanced electronics has been declining. The portion of American students going into hard sciences or engineering is also shrinking, and because of outsized compensation opportunities a growing percentage of graduates are going into private industry and not research universities. Absent a national threat, or a powerful new vision backed by substantial financing from Washington, America's technological base will rest increasingly on the activities of companies whose prime interest is the price of their stock. Anyone reading this book -- with its uplifting description of what this country has achieved over the last few decades -- cannot help worrying about this trend.

title: Happy Birthday, Your Team Won, Your Stock Crashed - Correction Appended
body: WEEKDAY mornings for Jessica Nierenberg, a 23-year-old research manager at a market research company in San Francisco, usually begin with a dash to her neighborhood bus stop for a 30-minute ride to her office in the city's financial district downtown. By 8:30 she is at her desk, pouring herself a bowl of breakfast cereal and firing up her computer for a glimpse at what the planet has wrought while she slept. What greets her on her computer's screen is selected and displayed by My Yahoo, a free service by Yahoo, the giant Internet information company based in Santa Clara, Calif. My Yahoo shows Ms. Nierenberg how many email messages she has waiting to be read and a sampling of news headlines -- she can decide to call up any of the articles on domestic, political and international news for a more detailed look. Weather forecasts for her area and for Boston, her hometown, are parked in a corner of the screen. That wake-up dose of Internet offerings is, more or less, created specifically for Ms. Nierenberg, who, while computer savvy, doesn't consider herself a computer nerd (she does not have a computer at home, for instance). What she gets is a tailor-made collection of information that she has informed Yahoo she wants to get regularly. "It definitely saves me time," said Ms. Nierenberg, whose work requires her to be on a computer for at least eight hours a day. "It's nice to be able to push one button whenever I log on and to get all of this." The process that delivers all of that daily digital data to her and millions more is called personalization, the newest wave washing over the ever-changing shores of the Internet. After years of shaky starts, personalization promises to re-emphasize the personal in personal computing. Without a "personalized page," as she likes to call it, Ms. Nierenberg would have to resort to laboriously searching the Internet herself, plowing through more than 650,000 sites on the Web alone. One of the chief ideas driving personalization, many Internet experts say, is that the Internet, a victim of its own success, has become too voluminous for most people to handle comfortably and efficiently. If you're not using personalization, said Joe Kraus, senior vice president and co-founder of Excite, "you are not taking advantage of the medium." The thinking behind personalization goes something like this: What if your computer "knew" you, had a reasonable sense of your on-line interests and preferences and could respond to them? Forcing the computer to conform to your information needs rather than forcing you to conform to the computer's requirements is a step, many agree, toward realizing the vision that Nicholas P. Negroponte, director of the Media Laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, calls "the daily me." Services like My Yahoo, My Excite and even the set-top Web cruiser My Web TV (like other personalized features offered by America Online and the Microsoft Network, it is part of a service that requires a monthly fee) are increasingly fetching the kinds of content that their users say they want: specific types of news, weather forecasts, sports scores and schedules, stock quotations, horoscopes, television schedules, movie show times and state lottery results, for example. Many of these services also feature lists of users' favorite Web sites, chat rooms and message boards, along with daily health tips, travel alerts and on-line reminders of occasions like anniversaries and birthdays of relatives and friends. "It is empowering," said Steve Boxer, a computer consultant who owns Pachyderm Consulting in Brooklyn, speaking of his experience with personalization. "It really molds your computer to your interests." The first personalization service from a major on-line company was the Microsoft Network, or MSN. When it began in the fall of 1995, it offered users a relatively primitive capacity to customize the kinds of information they received. In January the following year, Excite created My Excite, which was followed that summer by My Yahoo. In July, Netscape, the leading Internet browser company, started offering My Netscape. While America Online offers its members very limited personalization with My AOL, a company spokesman said AOL will begin a much more fully featured service called My News in the next few weeks.. Competition among the companies offering personalization is intense, resembling at times the browser wars between Netscape and Microsoft. Refinements by one are often followed quickly by similar refinements by the others. Representatives of the personalization services refused to disclose just how many dollars each company has poured into creating and continually tweaking its service. But Mr. Kraus did say that his company, Excite, had spent a "significant investment in terms of manpower, money, hardware and engineering time" in creating its version of personalization, called My Excite. Nor will the companies reveal the number of subscribers for each service. "It has exceeded some expectations," said Henry Sohn, a senior producer for personalization for Yahoo. "Part of that is due to the overall growth in the Internet with each quarter. But it is clear that personalization services are really popular." THE promise of personalization had been on the lips of computer visionaries for years, even while the Internet struggled to find its identity. In the mid-1990's, software makers began selling off-the-shelf products like Pointcast Network that automatically log on to the Net, download categories of information broadly defined by users and then log off. These products, known as "push" technologies, began falling out of favor because they tended to be resource hogs and to deposit overwhelming amounts of information on computer hard drives. As many began to complain that push information was not selective enough, some users started looking for something that could pull from the Internet more specific information that matched their interests. "Back then, people didn't know what they wanted, so they wanted things pushed at them," said Rob Bernstein, a senior editor at Yahoo Internet Life, a monthly magazine about Net use. "The Net pretty much rejected that idea. Pull it down. That is the idea of personalization." But the idea of personalization, some experts acknowledged, has been difficult to sell. Part of the problem, said David Sze, vice president for network programming and content at Excite, is that personalization is hard to describe. The concept, he noted, tends to "come off very soft, vague." Using personalization is hardly automatic. First, you must register for it. (Many of the companies offering personalization, including Excite, Yahoo and MSN, have been trying to entice potential users by including very visible links from their popular home pages to their personalization pages.) Registration also means filling out an on-line questionnaire that can take anywhere from a few minutes to a half-hour to complete. (My Excite goes another step, giving brief descriptions of why it requests certain information. It says, for example, "Your birth date is used to provide your horoscope.") Designers of personalization services noted that the more information users provided about themselves, the more personalized the service would be. The My Yahoo form is much more tedious when it asks users to choose the information they want and how it is to be displayed. Each user enters preferences for a front page and pages for subjects like health, entertainment, business, chat and message boards. Each subject page has a dozen slots, and each slot holds a pull-down menu offering 36 choices of content, like sports scoreboards, information about vitamins and herbs, and news headlines. A user may choose one menu item for each slot. Each selection leads to that categories of information being displayed and updated whenever the personalized pages are viewed. My Yahoo goes even further, pressing for even more detail about a user's "specific interests." The categories there, like news, life styles, music and shopping, are more finely tuned. The answers may very well determine whether the Epicurious Web site for fine cooking appears on your finished page rather than Gamespot, which is popular among computer twitch gamers. "It helps us in a number of ways to offer a service that users find more relevant," Mr. Sohn at Yahoo said of the questionnaire. Once the services have an idea of what users want, they extract the information from various sources. To do that, they use relationships with news operations and other partners as well as their own powerful search engines. In most cases, as with My Yahoo, My Excite and My Netscape, the information is stored in central databases. When someone goes on line and types in a user name and a password, a cookie -- an identifying tag stored on the user's computer -- tells the personalization service who is requesting information. Based on what is in the cookie (for My Netscape it is a 16-digit number) the information is unlocked from the database and sent in a fraction of a second to the user. Most of the services regularly update their information and use both machines and people to match the right streams of information with the right users, personalization managers say. Just how these services actually work depends on closely held proprietary technologies, but many personalization operators agree that the services have been made possible by advances in database hardware and software in the last several years, by high-speed user-indentification systems and by the capacity to generate pages on the fly over the Internet. "Making it easy for people is our overarching design point," said Eckart Walther, product manager for My Netscape. "It makes information come to you rather than you going to the information." Nathan Beckord, a 26-year-old research associate for an investment bank in San Francisco, uses My Yahoo to check his stock portfolio and to glance at news about his investments. "For each portfolio, I have it customized to display what I want, quote the volume, and below that it shows the news," he said. Mr. Beckord also has the service set up as his default page, so it is the first thing he sees when he goes on line at work or at home. Users like Mr. Beckord are very useful to Internet companies, which is why the companies invested in personalization. The detailed information users give them about exactly what they want to see on line serves as a kind of survey. The information helps personalization managers decide what kinds of content to add, maintain or remove from their offerings. More important, many of the same managers said, the information makes it possible to match the advertising to users' interests and needs. Much as sporting goods manufacturers know that they have a better chance of reaching their market by advertising on ESPN, the national cable sports network, rather than with general-interest programs, advertisers are looking for much of the same result by having their advertisements sent over the Internet to people whose declared interests identify them as likely customers, explained Mr. Sze, of Excite. Mr. Sohn, of Yahoo, offered an example. "If we know someone is not interested in travel," he said, "then we are not likely to display an ad from an airline or travel agency." And the better his company is able to aim advertising, he added, the more it can charge for that advertising. But Mr. Sze said the use of personalization as an effective advertising tool had just begun. "The true value of this is not being realized the way it is going to be," said Mr. Sze, adding that on a scale of 1 to 10, personalization's use of advertising was in the 3-to-5 range. But, he said, Excite is preparing to step up its use of targeted advertising on the Internet. Mr. Walther also noted that personalization made good business sense because it was a way to capture more users, people who are approaching the Internet differently from their early-adopter predecessors. "We are seeing a lot more practical use of the Web," he said. "A lot of people don't go on the Web to just have fun." He said people tended to care more about how much time they were on the Internet and how much they accomplished. Personalization, he said, especially speaks to such users. And, added Mr. Boxer, the New York computer consultant, many new Internet users start with personalization services and keep returning to those companies. "Everyone has to start someplace," he said, "and the people who control the starting place hold some very valuable real estate." Because personalization requires the user to give a series of very specific preferences, there are growing concerns about what companies will do with all this new information. Mr. Sohn and other personalization service operators said the industry followed strict guidelines to protect users' privacy. Many of the companies' policies regarding privacy are clearly stated on line and linked to the questionnaires. "We care very deeply about privacy," Mr. Sohn said. "We go overboard to make users aware that we don't sell usage information to anyone." Another objection to the current personalization services is that they simply do not go far enough. Walter Bender, associate director of the M.I.T. Media Lab, said he would like to see additional levels of integration between, for example, on-line information and personal on-line calendars. The result, he said, would be more sophisticated services that would not only deliver tailored content but would also match that information with what a user was actually doing. You're taking a business trip to the Caribbean? Your computer would start delivering news, weather and travel information about the Caribbean as your departure date approached. Nonetheless, many Internet experts say, personalization is expected to be the buzz on the Internet for years to come, as it is tweaked and refined along the way. "It's not going to go away," Mr. Sze predicted. It is simply a matter of Internet destiny, others say. "This is the only medium," Mr. Kraus said, "that is inherently personalizable." Correction  An article in Circuits on Thursday about Web personalization services referred incorrectly to the one offered by the Excite search engine. Excite offers its personalization service on its home page (www.excite.com), not as a service called My Excite. The service began in January 1996 as Personal Excite, not as My Excite. In April 1997 it was renamed My Excite, but it is no longer called that. Correction-Date: September 21, 1998, Monday Graphic   Photo: HIS WAY-- Steve Boxer of Brooklyn is among the users of Web personalization services. (Andrea Mohin/The New York Times)(pg. G8)

title: Net Is Not Enough: Books on Starr Report, Too
body: BY midafternoon last Friday, modems and and laser printers were laboring mightily, dishing out the report by the Whitewater independent counsel, Kenneth W. Starr, as quickly as the Web-using public could devour it. Some six million people read the report in cubicles, home offices and living rooms around the world, according to Relevant Knowledge, a Web-usage tracking service. They saved it on disks and loaded it into their Palm Pilots. The following morning, several newspapers around the nation carried the entire text of the report, which detailed President Clinton's relationship with Monica S. Lewinsky. Who, then, will want to buy one of the insta-books that have just arrived at booksellers? The three publishers who rushed their paperback editions of the report to bookstores seem to think that a lot of people will. "Even if you were to download it and print it out, would you rather have 400 loose sheets or stick it in your pocket?" said Gene Taft, a spokesman for Public Affairs, a new publishing house. "A book is just a lot more convenient." Public Affairs printed 300,000 copies in 72 hours and began shipping the books on Monday. Its edition, priced at $10, includes commentary from Washington Post writers and the White House's initial rebuttal. Pocket Books, a division of Simon & Schuster, printed and shipped 650,000 books, priced at $5.99, and went back to press yesterday for an additional 100,000. The third publisher, Prima Publishing, based in Rocklin, Calif., initially printed 155,000 copies and is printing 65,000 more. Pocket Books and Prima had books ready to be shipped by Sunday. Interestingly enough, the on-line booksellers appear to be showing some of the biggest early successes for "The Starr Report," as all three publishers have titled it. The books soared to the top of the best-seller lists at both Barnesandnoble.com and Amazon.com last Friday afternoon through advance orders alone and have remained there, to the surprise of some executives. "My hypothesis was that it would be No. 1 for about an hour," said David Risher, Amazon's senior vice president for marketing and product development. "Everyone would read it in The newyork Times and then it would fall from there because it was free on the Net. But it's stayed at the top." On Monday, Jeff Bezos, chief executive of Amazon, directed his editorial staff to post a notice on the company's Web site to tell shoppers that the report was free on the Web, lest they think that Amazon was pulling a fast one. Still, sales have continued to climb. There have been previous books published from political documents, like Oliver North's testimony in the Iran-Contra affair. But the buyers of one of the instant Starr report books will probably have already read most or all of the report on the Net or in a newspaper or magazine. Buying it in book form, then, is "almost a commemorative impulse," said Paul Elie, an editor at Farrar, Straus & Giroux, a newyork publishing house. Liz Hartman, vice president and director of publicity for Pocket Books, says she believes that the Internet actually stimulated interest among book buyers rather than dampening it. Mr. Bezos said he had bought the Public Affairs edition for himself, even after reading the report on the Net and printing much of it out. "Even though I had printed it, I sort of wanted the thing in book form," he said. "It's easier to keep around." Moreover, he noted, the Net-produced versions have hidden costs. "Add up the toner and printer paper, and it ends up costing about five cents a page to print it," he said. Rick Simonson, a book buyer at Elliott Bay Book Company in Seattle, said his store had ordered the book in modest quantities. "It's almost more a form of magazine publishing, or newspaper publishing, albeit with a different binding," he said. He said he doubted that the book would remain a best seller for long. Rick Warne, a music store owner in Cotati, Calif., said he had no plans to buy the book. If Ms. Lewinsky wrote her own book, he'd be interested. "I'd love to see what Monica has to say in a tell-all book," he said. "It wouldn't be just what she said under oath. And it wouldn't be in the legalese that the Starr report is in."

title: Netscape and Qwest Plan To Announce Web Alliance
body: Forming perhaps the deepest alliance yet between a big Internet content provider and a long-distance company, the Netscape Communications Corporation and Qwest Communications International Inc. plan to announce a far-reaching strategic alliance today. The deal will link Netscape, a company whose browser software for navigating the World Wide Web made it synonymous with the Internet, to Qwest, a well-financed start-up that is building one of the most advanced fiber optic communications networks. The intent of the venture, to be known as Netscape Contact, is to enable consumers to manage voicemail, email and fax communications through a single site on the Web. Under intense competitive pressure from the Microsoft Corporation, which distributes its Web browsing software free, Netscape recently moved away from selling consumer software. It has instead focused on building its Netcenter Web site into an aggregation of information and communications services that generates revenue through advertising and direct sales. The Qwest deal will allow Netscape to broaden its Web offerings while also helping to insulate Netcenter from Internet traffic jams. For Qwest, securing an alliance with Netscape could prove a marketing coup. Along with IXC Communications Inc., the Williams Companies and Level 3 Communications Inc., Qwest is among a new breed of long-distance carriers that are building national networks based on Internet technology rather than on traditional phone technology. "This is a great distribution channel said Joseph P. Nacchio, Qwest's chief executive. "The Netcenter customers are more educated, more computer-centric and higher spenders." Mr. Nacchio said he expected the venture to generate between $150 million and $175 million in revenue over the next 18 months. Qwest will pay Netscape for the right to share the branding on Netscape Contact. In return, Netscape will pay Qwest for access to its network. In the end, Netscape expects to make about $25 million net over three years on the deal. Netscape now mainly employs the Sprint Corporation and the MCI Communications Corporation to provide Netcenter with high-speed, high-capacity access to the Internet. Those relationships are not endangered by Netscape's deal with Qwest, Mr. Homer said. Netscape will use Qwest's network for additional capacity, he said. Over the summer, Netscape added a search engine and email to its Web site in an effort to compete against so-called Internet portal companies like Yahoo and Excite. Working with Qwest, Netscape intends to begin selling long-distance phone service for 9 cents a minute any time of the day and to offer an integrated "in box" for voicemail, faxes and email. On Monday, Qwest announced that it had agreed to buy a rival Internet service provider, the Icon CMT Corporation, in an all-stock transaction valued at $185 million to attract corporate customers to its new super-fast Internet access. As Qwest expands into the Internet service market, it intends to sell Netscape software. Some of Netcenter's main competitors, including Yahoo, Infoseek, Lycos and Excite, have already made deals with long-distance phone companies. None of those agreements, however, appear as ambitious as Netscape's pact with Qwest.

title:
Q & A;
Plug-Ins Offer A Richer Slice Of the Internet
body: Q. When I try to look at a video clip with my Web browser, I get a message saying I need a particular plug-in. What is this, and what should I do? A. Plug-ins are small programs that you can download and install on your computer. They work within your browser, helping it handle certain types of audio, video and document files you might find on the Web. After your browser has a plug-in installed, it can display any file requiring that plug-in. Because plug-ins work within a browser, they differ from helper applications, which are external programs that can be configured to activate whenever the browser needs some help with a particular kind of Web file. When you get a message telling you that you need a certain program, examine all the options in the dialogue box carefully. It will often offer to take you to the appropriate Web page to get the plug-in. Read the information on the Web page carefully and make sure that you have enough RAM and system resources to handle the software. Some plug-ins require that you allocate more memory to your browser. If you decide to download the plug-in, make sure you choose the version for your particular operating system and follow the instructions for installing the plug-in on your computer. The next time you open your browser and return to the page where you encountered the alert, the multimedia or document file should open right in your browser window. Some of the most-used plug-ins include Acrobat Reader from Adobe, which lets you view, download and print documents, and Shockwave from Macromedia for interactive multimedia files.   J. D. BIERSDORFER

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Gilbert and Sullivan: Information Galore
body: FOR many theater lovers, personal participation in show business reaches its pinnacle in a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta. Once bitten, one is likely to be forever entranced by the Victorian wit, period costumes and certainty that the cast will be happily paired off by the final curtain. The Web is perhaps more suited to devotees of the collaborations of William S. Gilbert (1836-1911), the dramatist, and Sir Arthur S. Sullivan (1842-1900), the composer, than to any other group of Victorian fanatics, with the possible exception of the Baker Street Irregulars. And Holmes and Watson don't sing and dance, or shouldn't. The Gilbert and Sullivan Archive (diamond.idbsu.edu/GaS/GaS.html) bills itself as "the premier Internet light opera site." It includes access to what it calls the first Web operas: the complete lyrics, dialogue and music of three of the most popular operettas -- "H.M.S. Pinafore," "The Mikado" and "The Pirates of Penzance" -- and three others. They are MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) files and can be heard on PC's with a MIDI-capable sound card. There are librettos and a discography for all 14 Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, as well as information about the works of Gilbert without Sullivan and vice versa. For performers and audiences, there are links to Gilbert and Sullivan performing-group Web sites, an international calendar of events and a list of Gilbert and Sullivan societies, as well as librettos and extensive information about staging. Savoynet, the Internet Gilbert and Sullivan discussion group that is linked to the archive (www.cris. com/oakapple/savoynet), forwards to its subscribers 50 to 100 messages a day about the partners, their works and related matters of musical theater and British culture. Its Opera of the Week discussions amount to an in-depth study of each work, a resource for amateur theatricals. Elsewhere on the archive, historians will discover short and long biographies of both men and many of their associates, bibliographies and "An Illustrated Interview With Sir Arthur Sullivan" from The Strand magazine in 1897, a detailed account of the composer's mind at work. There is also a history of the D'Oyly Carte Opera Company and capsule biographies of famous Savoyards. (The name comes from the Savoy Theater in London, where Richard D'Oyly Carte produced the original G & S operettas.) Needless to say, the Gilbert and Sullivan Archive is based in -- Boise, Idaho? "It is a neat example of the global village," Alex Feldman, an associate professor in the mathematics and computer science department at Boise State University, wrote by email. Mr. Feldman, who put the archive on the Internet five years ago this month, added, "One fellow wrote that he was going to give us a 'Best of Britain' award until he noticed we weren't in Britain." The entire nonprofit site is assembled by volunteers the world over and is maintained on a Boise State Web server. "Gilbert and Sullivan totally transformed the English operetta scene," Jim Farron of Springfield, Va., the archive curator, wrote by email. "They introduced clean entertainment for the entire family, and for the first time the librettist was an equal to the composer; Gilbert strongly insisted on this. "And the G & S world has a holy grail -- the score for 'Thespis,' the first G & S work. I don't know if any copies still exist, or if they will ever be found, but the possibility certainly gives G & S enthusiasts something to talk about and look forward to." The archive currently has more than 40 librettos and 200 MIDI files, said Mr. Farron, whose day job is being the Webmaster for the unitedstates Office of Personnel Management. The Gilbert and Sullivan archive gets 3,000 to 4,000 visitors a week, and the section that draws the most comments, he said, is the Web operas, particularly "The Pirates of Penzance." He is especially proud of the archive's many lesser-known works, other than the 14 operettas, connected with Gilbert, Sullivan or the Savoy Theater. The archive will add a special treat in a few weeks. "This will be the first operetta score written specifically for the Internet," Mr. Farron said. "This score, which is now pretty well complete, is being written to accompany one of the Savoy companion pieces for which the music has been lost. We think that there may well be considerable interest in this work, especially for performance in the schools, as the requirements for putting it on will be pretty simple." No Gilbert and Sullivan archive would be complete without parodies. One, "I am the very model of a heroine barbarian," is sung by Xena, letter-perfect with the beat and rhyme of the original, on the linked parody archive (www.cs.cmu.edu/ valkyrie/parody). "The Ruddigore Hillbillies," in eight verses, is another; another is called "I Am the Very Model of an Oldbie on the Internet." "Even though much of the humor was topical, it was based on universal themes that are just as valid today as they were then," Mr. Farron said. "The music is beautiful, the jokes funny and original, and these operas are loads of fun to both perform in and watch. I am convinced that the G & S operas are timeless and will still be played a hundred years from now and a thousand years from now." Graphic   Photo: A moment from "The Mikado." (Carol Rosegg/Martha Swope Associates)

title:
The Choices;
Finding the Service Right for You
body: At first glance, the on-line personalized services might all look the same, but don't be fooled by the hypertext. They're not. Here are thumbnail descriptions of some of the pros and cons of a range of these eager data gatherers. MY EXCITE: www.excite.com Getting started: Once users complete a simple on-line questionaire, My Excite automatically becomes the home page for the general-purpose Excite Web site. Advantages: Most of the news articles on the daily list are provided by Reuters and United Press International, with often intriguing links to related stories from more than 250 other on-line sources. The local events finder, a new feature, is helpful in tracking and displaying forthcoming concerts, festivals, plays and the like. An optional word processor, the very basic Notepad, comes in handy for jotting down a Web address or observation. Disadvantages: The layout of My Excite's personalized pages -- crammed with boxes, banners and fine print -- is busy and not always easy to follow. MY YAHOO: www.yahoo.com Getting started: To get the most from My Yahoo, users must fill out an exhaustive series of questionnaires, mostly in the form of pull-down menus, each offering 36 choices, like lottery results and favorite chat rooms. Advantages: The most expansive personalization service, My Yahoo offers 11 major sections on a task bar stripped across its top front page. Each section can contain mountains of information along with on-line applications, like an international currency converter, as well as a useful on-line map maker. A handy bookmark box stores Web sites. Visual clutter, including banner ads, is kept to a minimum. My Yahoo can be set up as default browser page. Disadvantages: For true data addicts, My Yahoo is very likely to be deliciously overwhelming. For practically everyone else, its very richly stocked pages of information and services might be too much. MY NETSCAPE: www.netscape.com Getting started: Only basic information, like name, email address, sex and age range, is required. Users then select the information they want from a handful of choices in three categories: News, Information and Tools. Advantages: Efficient, fast and simple for users who want to see the world at a glance. During setup, each selection is linked to an example of what the information would actually look like if it was included. The layout is clean and logical. For those using the Netscape Web browser, My Netscape can easily be set up as the home page. Disadvantages: A newcomer to personalization, My Netscape is considerably more modest than other services. title:
USER'S GUIDE;
A Second Look at AOL, the Refurbished Ellis Island of the Net
body: EVERY society has its own class system, and so it is with the Internet. So, of course, the people who were first on line -- the early settlers who can reminisce about the good old days of the Arpanet -- get the most points for snob appeal. They are the on-line equivalent of those who claim that their ancestors were on the Mayflower. It is this class system that explains the simmering resentment among early adopters toward America Online. That on-line service has long been a kind of wired Ellis Island, a gateway through which the great unwashed arrive on the Internet shore. I felt no gratitude to America Online for easing my own on-line arrival a few years ago because I, too, wanted desperately to be mistaken for the kind of blueblood who had been on line since the early days, a charter member of the Daughters of the Internet Revolution. It never occurred to me to applaud the service for creating a painless gateway with its easy installation and setup process and its See-Dick-Run interface. As soon as I could, I traded in my place on AOL's crowded network (where I might as well have been michele43333759329602349-579873493@aol.com) for an email address with more cachet. Around the end of 1995, I abandoned AOL altogether, complaining about the clunky nature of the service's proprietary browser, the paucity of sophisticated email features and the relentless stream of advertisements that greet the masses upon logging on. Only in recent weeks, as America Online began with great fanfare to roll out the new 4.0 version of its software, have I looked inside my soul and wondered, Was I too quick to judge? After all, the service has attracted more than 13 million customers, a number that keeps growing. The only fair thing to do would be to test the 4.0 version -- as objectively as possible, given my social-climbing tendencies -- to see if the AOL software could meet my needs. Truthfully, I did not think I would be interested in many of the new features that AOL was most proud of, like the new design that mimics a browser or even a channel guide that makes it easier to navigate through such topics as Sports, News or Lifestyles. Even the new feature that enables users to change screen names without logging off held no appeal for me: I don't use aliases, nor do I allow my daughters to use my account. The only on-line activities I engage in regularly are email and Web browsing. No gaudy welcome screen greets me when my modem connects. Instead, I rely on a tiny, tasteful icon depicting two linked computers. Could AOL do better than my current minimalist setup? First, I had to download AOL 4.0 from www.aol.com. Although the final version for Windows was released at the end of July, production is still under way on the CD-ROM's. AOL expects to start mailing millions and millions of the disks within the next month, however, just in time for my cranky friend Ron Reason to continue his annual Halloween tradition of handing them out to unsuspecting trick-or-treaters in his South Florida neighborhood. (The Macintosh version will lag by a few weeks, an AOL spokeswoman said.) In the meantime, I was surprised that downloading the 4.0 version -- which warned that it might need as much as 17.5 megabytes on my hard drive -- seemed to take forever. Assuming that the process would end quickly, I sat at my desk, waiting. I flipped through the entire autumn Pottery Barn catalog. I phoned the toll-free number to get some information about velvet drapes. Still downloading. Called back to order the drapes. Still downloading. Worried drapes would be wrong color. Phoned to request complete set of drapery fabric swatches (free). Rebuffed in attempts to get Pottery Barn saleswoman to confirm whether this year's "plum" differs from last year's "plum -- 1198134." Still downloading. Composed frosty letter in my mind to Pottery Barn. Luckily for the people at Pottery Barn's customer service department, the download was completed before I wrote the letter. I phoned Jeanie Ryan, a spokeswoman for America Online, to accuse her of forcing me to purchase unnecessary window treatments. "One hour? That's not bad -- you're on the good end," Ms. Ryan said. She explained that Microsoft's Internet Explorer was integrated with the new AOL software so users who have not already installed the browser could wait for up to three hours for the packgage to download. "We thought people would run away screaming," Ms. Ryan confided. (Or at least just wait to go trick-or-treating!) "Yet millions of people have sat through it, and we're like, oh my gosh." The good news was that installation and setup took me just three minutes more. Although determined to ignore the bright colors of the welcome screen, I had to admit that AOL 4.0's newly designed toolbar across the top of the screen was very helpful. Click on any of the three buttons on the left to use email. Click on My AOL, then Preferences, then Marketing to speedily cancel all those "valuable product and service offers" that AOL and its partners serve up via email, phone solicitation, the Postal Service and pop-up on-screen windows. And AOL 4.0 eliminates many of the tedious delays found in earlier versions. To start surfing the Net instantly, type a Web address in the space right under the icons. If you prefer another browser, it is easy to minimize the AOL window and open Netscape Navigator in its place. But the main thing that bothers me about AOL was that the email features are still not robust enough. Unlike my Eudora email program, AOL has no function that allows me to sort messages by date, sender, status, priority, label, size -- or even by various shades of plum. Nor does it allow me to attach a preconfigured signature file -- you know, the kind that gives my name, phone number and a quote from Descartes. "We're working on that," Ms. Ryan said. I won't trade in my current setup for AOL yet. But, amazingly, I did manage to snag the simple and understated slatalla@aol.com as my new email address. I'll be proud to give it out, even to my snootiest Internet friends. Graphic   Photo (Mary Ann Smith)

title: Voting on the Web: Not Around the Corner, but on the Horizon
body: MARC STRASSMAN first began thinking about Internet voting in 1995. Mr. Strassman, a 50-year-old entrepreneur, political activist and occasional Congressional candidate, was in the process of starting a business, and he wanted to file a legal notice on line. He soon discovered that an Internet posting didn't satisfy the legal requirement, but the episode got him thinking about the role of the Internet in democracy. "So I said, 'Why aren't we voting on the Internet?' " he said. "That seemed logical." So, two summers ago, Mr. Strassman spent his days at a food store in Los Angeles collecting signatures to place his Virtual Voting Rights Initiative on the California ballot as a plebiscite. He needed 400,000 signatures. He collected about 6 an hour. Despite the lack of enthusiasm for Mr. Strassman's efforts that summer, Internet voting is a subject of keen interest to policy makers in state legislatures, election offices and even the Pentagon. Plans are under way to start testing systems by 2000. The Department of Defense is sponsoring a program whose success or failure will dictate the near future of Internet voting. The system under design would allow the six million Americans overseas, both military and civilian, to cast ballots by using the Internet. Five states -- Florida, Missouri, South Carolina, Texas and Utah -- will participate in the Pentagon's pilot project, which is scheduled to take place in the 2000 general election. Under current plans, voters will be able to use the voting system on their own computers and on terminals provided at unitedstates installations. Election offices in the participating states will be given Government computers to receive the ballot transmissions. Lessons from the Federal pilot project will help state election officials decide whether they want to offer Internet voting to residents at home. Thomas Wilkey, executive director of the newyork State Board of Elections, said that election officials had a responsibility to find ways to make voting as easy as possible but that he was taking a cautious approach to Internet voting. "You have to get up on the horse and get comfortable in the saddle before we can take a ride," Mr. Wilkey said. "I think every state has a long way to go." In Florida and California, election officials are moving ahead. Paul Craft, a computer audit analyst for the Florida Division of Elections, said Internet voting systems might be ready for testing in Florida as soon as next year. After studying on-line security, he said, he concluded that the Internet was "a very viable technology" for transmitting ballots. "My initial reaction was, 'That's a stupid thing to do,' " Mr. Craft said. "I ended up becoming a leading proponent of it." Now he talks in detail about the ease of using digital signatures to verify voters' identities, about protecting voters privacy by making sure no one could found out how any person voted and about setting up multiple control points to make audits easy. Mr. Craft argues that the Internet could make elections cheaper. Electronic voting machines cost $5,000 to $7,000 apiece. With electronic ballots created for Internet use, the cost of each machine needed to retrieve the ballots would be about $600. While Florida officials are pursuing the issue through their election office, California's Secretary of State, Bill Jones, is setting up a panel to study the issue. He said that when the panel completed its report, perhaps next year, he would send the Legislature the findings. In 1997, the Legislature passed a bill to finance a study of on-line voter registration and voting, as well as the use of digital signatures on the Internet for signing petitions for ballot initiatives, but Gov. Pete Wilson vetoed the bill. Along with the promise of lower costs and increased access, Internet voting raises many questions as well, particularly about security. Polli Brunelli, director of the Federal Voting Assistance Program, said the transmission of votes through the military's pilot program would be protected by an encryption system created at the Department of Defense. Also, the system that is being developed must provide a way for an individual to log in with a unique identity and password, but, to protect the right to a secret ballot, it must make it impossible to match an individual with the vote cast. "At no time during that process would we be able to see how any person voted," Ms. Brunelli said. In his veto message, Governor Wilson cited concern about security as the reason for vetoing the Internet voting bill. "The use of such a system will compromise voter confidentiality and generate significant opportunities for fraud," he wrote. "Although current encryption technology is making advances in providing a more secure environment to prevent tampering by third parties, no one can yet guarantee a completely safe, tamper-proof system. Without such a guarantee, a study is premature." The vetoed bill resembles in some respects the Virtual Voting Rights Initiative that Mr. Strassman circulated in Los Angeles in 1996. "I was flattered that the Republicans were concerned enough to try to kill the bill," he said. On the issue of Internet voting, Mr. Strassman has found that he is not so far ahead of his time as he has been: in 1980, he ran for Congress in Silicon Valley with a slogan of "Compute, don't commute." He lost. He has also learned some of the hard math of California politics. After hours of collecting signatures, Mr. Strassman found that the backers of initiatives often spent $1 million to collect enough signatures to get a measure on the state ballot. So he decided to put the Internet to the test by placing a copy of the voting initiative on the Web for people to sign. The results were not encouraging. In the course of several months, only one person, a Berkeley resident, found it, printed it out, signed it and mailed it. title: Intel Agreement Indicates a Rift With Microsoft
body: In an agreement to be announced on Wednesday, the Intel Corporation will license its advanced video compression software to Real Networks Inc., a Seattle-based developer of programs that deliver audio and video over the Internet. Beyond the expectation that Intel's technology will improve the performance of Real Network's software, the deal is seen as further evidence of growing cracks in the so-called Wintel duopoly, the cooperative relationship under which Intel's microprocessors and the Microsoft Corporation's operating systems have long dictated the direction of the personal computer industry. In the Real Networks deal, Intel is sharing its technology with a Microsoft competitor in an area that is thought to be crucial to the future commercialization of the Internet. Real Networks says that about 30 million people now use its software. That is believed to give it a substantial lead over Microsoft, which developed a competing technology, known as Netshow, then later hedged its bets by paying tens of millions of dollars for an equity stake in Real Networks. Although the Intel-Real Networks deal does not include an Intel investment, both companies are calling it "strategic." Intel will license its compression technology for use in the newest version of Real Networks' multimedia software, Realvideo GE, which is now in testing. Real Networks' "streaming" software delivers audio or video in a stream of bits as it is being heard or watched. That makes it more like television or radio than were early multimedia technologies that required a user to download an entire file from an Internet site before it could be played. Intel's compression software squeezes a lot of data into a tiny file so that it can be sent more quickly over the Internet, resulting in fewer dropped sounds and smoother videos. In addition to improving the quality of videos, Intel's compression technology will reduce the computing power required to translate video images into a digital format. Intel executives said that while in the past multiple computers had been needed to encode live video, the new technology would create video files on a computer running Intel's top-of-the-line 450-megahertz Pentium II microprocessor. The videos can be played back on standard personal computers at rates ranging from 5,000 to a million bits a second, depending on the speed of the user's Internet connection. "You can use this technology to scale up to full-screen video," said Pat Gelsinger, Intel's vice president and general manager of desktop products. Mr. Gelsinger also insisted that the agreement with a Microsoft competitor was not a break with Intel's earlier strategy. "This is business as usual for us," he said. "We've been developing technology for years, and we've worked with industry leaders. Our strategy is no way affected by these issues." The video compression technology was developed at Intel Architecture Laboratories, the Oregon development site of several earlier programs and other technologies that touched off quarrels between Intel and Microsoft. In the past, Intel has attempted to put forward a variety of hardware and software technologies intended to add new features to personal computer design. The company's strategy has been to create market demand for more powerful computer hardware by persuading computer users to adopt new functions. However, Microsoft has frequently opposed Intel initiatives that it believe threatens its control over software design through the Windows operating systems. Rob Glaser, Real Networks' chairman and founder and a former Microsoft employee, said of Microsoft and Intel, "The two companies are becoming more independent as we move more toward a consumer electronics world." The Intel technology is referred to as a codec, a shortening of the term compressor-decompressor. Such programs, which can be created as either hardware circuits or software routines, compress and then decompress digitized audio, video or images.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
A former television executive enters a deal to provide content for Web-faring women.
body: IN a bow to advertisers marketing products to women, America Online said yesterday that it had agreed to sell three of its women-oriented services to a new venture formed by Geraldine B. Laybourne, the former head of cable television operations for the Walt Disney Company and ABC, who will develop them for the on-line service's new Women's Channel. Ms. Laybourne, long considered one of the most successful women in the television industry, left Disney/ ABC in May to form Oxygen Media, a company devoted to creating programs for women and children, both on line and on television. Before joining Disney/ABC, she built up Nickelodeon, the children's cable network. The terms of the deal were not disclosed. But a person close to both companies said that America Online would retain an equity stake of about 10 percent in Oxygen and would receive millions of dollars in cash. In return, Oxygen will get three content services: Electra, a service aimed at women; Moms Online, which is for parents, and Thrive, a service devoted to health issues. Under terms of the deal, these sites will be displayed prominently on America Online's new Women's Channel and other places on its service and on its World Wide Web site, AOL.com. Thrive was part owned by Time Warner Inc., but America Online bought out that stake before selling the service to Oxygen. Similarly, Moms Online had several other investors, which Oxygen bought out. The deal attests to the growing importance of women to on-line marketers. According to America Online, about 51 percent of its 13 million users are women, up from only 16 percent in 1994. "The traditional media have missed the boat with modern women," Ms. Laybourne said. "There is nothing that serves women the way ESPN serves men or Nickelodeon serves kids. We want to create a brand on both television and the Internet that brings humor and playfulness and a voice that makes a women say, 'You really understand me.' " Oxygen and the other women's services hope they can sell ads to makers of the sort of package goods that have typically been promoted on soap operas and other women-oriented television programming. America Online, for example, has an extensive deal to develop new forms of advertising for Unilever, the maker of Wisk detergent and Lipton tea. Some of the Unilever ads are expected to be placed on the services being sold to Oxygen. "Eighty five percent of purchases are made by women," Ms. Laybourne said. "We can be a real facilitator of commerce." The move also represents yet another flip-flop for America Online on the question of whether it wants to create its own programming or rely on outside companies for what the Internet industry calls "content." Initially, America Online was dependent on outside publishers for content. Then it began taking partial stakes in content companies, including iVillage Inc., another service aimed at women. About a year ago, it began to bring some content more directly under its control. It created Electra as its own women's area, competing directly with iVillage. One reason for the latest about-face is a longstanding professional relationship between Robert W. Pittman, the president of America Online, and Ms. Laybourne. Having hired Ms. Laybourne 20 years ago when he was an executive of MTV Networks, which started Nickelodeon, Mr. Pittman called her the day her resignation from Disney/ABC was announced to explore potential deals. Moreover, America Online has now decided it wants to pull back from operating its own content areas, in part because it has discovered that it can exact multimillion-dollar payments from content companies to display their services prominently to its members. As a result, the service would rather offer a menu of a handful of featured content areas in each topic. "Our audience tells us they want us to do the hard work of finding the best content on line and putting a context around it," said Barry Schuler, president of America Online's interactive services unit. "We need to own the top level, but when it comes down to the hard-core editorial stuff, we think that's a game of consolidation and critical mass, and we don't need to own all of that." While America Online now calls Oxygen the "centerpiece" of its Women's Channel, the company also has relationships with most of the other players in programming for women. It is the largest shareholder of iVillage, with a stake of just under 20 percent. And its service also has links to Women.com Networks, the Hearst Corporation's Homearts service and the on-line complements of the Oprah and Rosie O'Donnell talk shows. "Competition is healthy for the marketplace," Mr. Schuler said. "Our audience wins when there is more than one strong player out there." Candice Carpenter, the chief executive of iVillage, agreed. "It's crazy to think that what may be the biggest category on line will only have one player," she said of women's programming. "I'd rather have a few good competitors who will develop the space intelligently and aggressively." Ms. Carpenter denied industry reports that the relationship between iVillage and America Online had become strained. "AOL has been fabulous," she said. "They called me the day that this deal was discussed the first time. And I've signed a lot of big deals with AOL's competitors, and they have given me no flak for it." Moreover, she added, "We were offered Electra and Moms Online, and we turned them down." At this stage, it is hard to discern much difference between the strategies of the two companies. Ms. Carpenter said that iVillage was designed to have more places for advertising than the existing Electra and Moms Online services. And iVillage is less interested than Oxygen in pursuing television programming, she said. Ms. Laybourne said the deal with America Online would be the first of many partnerships Oxygen would forge with big media and on-line companies. In the coming months, she said, she will decide whether to create television programs for an existing network or make the high-stakes bet on forming a new cable network. Oxygen is also already selling sponsorships to companies that seek to sell goods to women.

title: PUBLIC LIVES - Correction Appended
body: Political Portent A lot has happened since DONNA RICE was photographed on Senator GARY HART's lap on the yacht Monkey Business. He dropped out of the 1988 presidential race. She modeled No Excuses jeans. Now married and using the name DONNA RICE HUGHES, she is the vice president for marketing and public relations of an organization called Enough Is Enough. It is a nonprofit group whose goal is making the Internet safe for children, a cause she took up after her 14-year-old sister disappeared in 1996. In her new book, "Kids Online: Protecting Your Children in Cyberspace," Mrs. Hughes writes that her sister vanished after meeting with a man she had met in an Internet chat room; he, too, disappeared. Mrs. Hughes writes that her sister was found and the man apprehended after the case was described on the Maury Povich Show. So where was Mrs. Hughes on Friday, when the report from KENNETH W. STARR was released? At her computer, reading the report. "I like to say, 'Hey, if I didn't have to read it for my job, I wouldn't read it,' " she said. "The organization I work for has been working for four years to make the Internet safe for children, protecting them from pornography and sexual predators. This doesn't fall in that category, but it does raise awareness about information that would be inappropriate." She had expected as much, she said. "I believed, after I heard the request by Ken Starr asking Congress to keep some of the more graphic details of the report confidential, that it certainly had material that would not be appropriate, even for the general public," she said. "I agreed with him, once I read it." Does she see parallels between 1987 and the current scandal? "The situation with me was entirely different from this situation," she said without elaborating. A moment later she steered the conversation back to her work. "I sometimes stop myself," she said. "I'm back in the limelight, and I never wanted to have anything to do with politics or the media again."  Military Support In the 1970's ZACHARY FISHER championed the U.S.S. Intrepid, the aircraft carrier that became a floating museum from a war in which he was not allowed to serve. He failed his Marine Corps physical in 1942. The reason was a knee that had been hurt in a construction-site mishap when he was a teen-ager. Mr. Fisher went back to building buildings, which was the cornerstone of the Fisher brothers' fortune. Over the years Mr. Fisher, 86, has lavished money on military and veterans projects, giving more than $25 million to the Intrepid Museum. He also set up a foundation that sent $10,000 checks to relatives of the 241 victims of a 1983 bombing of a Marine barracks in Beirut. Yesterday PRESIDENT CLINTON presented Mr. Fisher with the Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest award for a civilian. Secretary of Defense WILLIAM S. COHEN, Mayor RUDOLPH W. GIULIANI and Police Commissioner HOWARD SAFIR were also on hand. "The President mentioned my caring about the military so much, more than any civilian he knew," Mr. Fisher said. "I told him I appreciate the acknowledgment of me as a patriot." There was not a word about the Starr report. "This was a graceful and a loving time," Mr. Fisher said. "No mention of anything like that." Of the President, he said, "I love the guy." Then, referring to HILLARY RODHAM CLINTON, who also attended the ceremony, Mr. Fisher said, "I like her very much. She's very caring."  All in the Family Kiss, kiss, darling. SIRIO MACCIONI, the owner of the restaurant Le Cirque 2000, gave a 25th-anniversary party last night and invited a few friends. The guest list stretched to 2,000 names -- including Mayor Giuliani, who proclaimed "Le Cirque 25th-Anniversary Day" -- and the two-story restaurant on Madison Avenue was filled with air kisses. "The family wanted to thank everyone," Mr. Maccioni said, "because in newyork, 25 years doesn't seem like the easiest thing." To celebrate his quarter-century, Mr. Maccioni, 64, hired clowns and jugglers from the Ringling Brothers and Barnum & Bailey Circus. And he said that his three sons, who already run Osteria del Circo on West 55th Street, would be doing some juggling of their own. The eldest, MARIO MACCIONI, 33, has moved to Las Vegas to oversee the new Le Cirque at the Bellagio Hotel, which is scheduled to open next month. MARCO MACCIONI, 30, and MAURO MACCIONI, 26, will be involved in restaurants planned for Paris and London. "I wanted my three sons to do something respectable with their lives," Sirio Maccioni said straight-faced, "but they have all come into the restaurant business."   JAMES BARRON with Glenn Collins Correction  A brief report in the Public Lives column on Tuesday about Donna Rice Hughes and her book "Kids Online: Protecting Your Children in Cyberspace" referred incorrectly to a passage on the disappearance of a 14-year-old girl who had met an older man in an Internet chat room. The passage referred to the sister of a woman named Tracey, not Mrs. Hughes's sister. Correction-Date: September 17, 1998, Thursday Graphic   Photos: DONNA RICE HUGHES; ZACHARY FISHER
