title:
Compressed Data;
Internet Phone Calls Face First Fee Challenge
body: It was like waiting for the other shoe to drop. Ever since April, when the Federal Communications Commission reported to Congress that telephone calls made from one phone to another using the Internet could become subject to network access fees, the industry has been waiting for a test case. BellSouth, the Atlanta-based regional telephone company, has now provided the test. The company has written to a half-dozen Internet service providers in its region saying that, in November, BellSouth will start levying access fees for voice conversations the Internet companies transmit. The fees are the same sort that local phone companies like BellSouth charge to long-distance carriers like AT&T and MCI for connecting calls to the local network. Internet traffic, under a longstanding F.C.C. exemption for data communications, has never been subject to such fees -- which is one reason that phone calls by way of the Internet are usually much cheaper than regular phone calls. Though the F.C.C. has not yet changed its rules, the agency's signal to Congress prompted BellSouth, for one, to test the boundaries. BellSouth intends to use electronic monitors to determine when customers are dialing into an Internet company's voice-network access lines, and then charge the company access fees for all such calls. But the Internet telephony companies are not ready to give in. James A. Courter, president of the IDT Corporation, said that if BellSouth sent his company a bill in November, he simply would not pay it. Access charges are "still an open question," Mr. Courter said. "The issue is going to be decided by the F.C.C. or Congress and not by BellSouth." In some ways, BellSouth's move may be largely symbolic, since most Internet voice traffic so far involves attempts to avoid the high charges for international long-distance calls, in which local access fees are a relatively minor part of the price. And yet, BellSouth is trying to close what many in the telephone industry have seen as a loophole in network pricing regulations. As a document on BellSouth's Web site (www.bellsouthcorp.com) puts it, "If it functions like a phone and rings like a phone -- it's a phone." But regulations are only part of the issue. Down the road, many experts expect an increasing amount of voice traffic to be carried by Internet technology, which transmits information in tiny packets that can commingle with other conversations over the same circuit. Though sound quality may still be subpar, Internet telephony is a much more efficient use of the public network than conventional telephone calls, which require a dedicated circuit for each conversation. Already, some long-distance telephone companies, including AT&T, have begun offering their own Internet telephony services.   LAURIE J. FLYNN

title: Hacker Group Commandeers The New York Times Web Site
body: A group calling for the release of Kevin Mitnick, the imprisoned computer criminal, commandeered The newyork Times site on the World Wide Web for several hours yesterday, forcing the newspaper's electronic edition to shut down at a time when traffic was particularly heavy because of the release on Friday of the independent counsel's report over the Internet. Instead of The Times's opening screen, some visitors to the site at www.nytimes.com early yesterday saw a logo marked "HFG" with images of nude women and a diatribe posted by the hackers that included attacks on The Times's past coverage of Mr. Mitnick, who has been in prison since he was arrested by the Federal Bureau of Investigation in February 1995. Officials of The Times's electronic media division shut down the site at 10:20 A.M. after the break-in was discovered. They did not restore service until about 7:30 P.M. after taking steps to secure the site's computers. Joseph Valiquette, an F.B.I. spokesman, said the agency's computer crime squad in newyork had opened an investigation into the break-in. Martin A. Nisenholtz, president of The newyork Times Electronic Media Company, said late yesterday that the company did not yet know how the hacker organization, which called itself HFG -- or Hacking for Girlies -- had breached its security. But he speculated that the attack was timed to coincide with the increased traffic to the site and to cyberspace in general in the wake of electronic publication on Friday of the report to Congress by Kenneth W. Starr, the independent counsel. "This is a much more destructive weekend to be doing this than normal," Mr. Nisenholtz said. "We were running 35 percent above normal on Saturday, and typically Sunday is twice as big as Saturday." A typical Sunday would see about 150,000 visitors to the Times site. The attack on the Times site appears to be the first time that hackers have penetrated the Web site of a major news organization. But computer security experts noted that attacks on high-profile targets are by no means rare. Other targets have been sites operated by the Pentagon, the Department of Justice, Coca-Cola, a Fox TV affiliate in Chicago, Germany's Free Democratic Party, and President Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico. The incident seemed to underscore the fragility of the global computer network during a period when governments, corporations and individuals are increasingly relying on it as a source of instant news and information. Several large Internet service providers reported record traffic volume over the weekend as people logged on to read the Starr report, which Congress put on the Web before it was made available elsewhere. Lance Hoffman, a computer science professor at George Washington University and director of the nonprofit Cyberspace Policy Institute in Washington, said it was fortunate that the attack was not more malevolent. Even so, "the material posted by the hackers is offensive, childish, threatening and chilling," Mr. Hoffman said. "It's a good example of why we have to bring accountability to the Internet." The approaching trial in January of Mr. Mitnick, a convicted computer criminal who has been imprisoned since he was arrested on charges of parole violation and several Federal felony counts in early 1995, also appears to have galvanized some members of the computer underground. The group that took over the Times site directed some of its comments at John Markoff, a reporter for The Times who covered Mr. Mitnick's arrest. Earlier this year, Yahoo, the biggest Internet search engine site, was hacked by a group proclaiming its support for Mr. Mitnick. And in July, the hacker magazine 2600 led a small protest outside the newyork offices of Miramax Films, which is producing a movie based on the book "Takedown" (Hyperion, 1996) by Tsutomu Shimomura and Mr. Markoff, which details the pursuit and capture of Mr. Mitnick. "Once the trial date comes closer, we're going to be seeing a strengthened effort in hacking Web sites to get the Kevin Mitnick name known," predicted John Vranesevich, founder of Antionline, a Web site at www.antionline.com that tracks hacker activity. Members of the group that claimed responsibility for attacking the Times site have for several years been engaged in a war of words on the Internet with Carolyn P. Meinel, an author who writes about the computer underground. The counterfeit Web page posted on the Times site included text that could be read only by examining the underlying computer code, which revealed an attack on the writings of Ms. Meinel, author of "The Happy Hacker" (American Eagle Publications, 1998). The group took issue with her comparing computer break-ins to terrorism. "If we find the time and effort to hack a few pages, labeling us 'terrorists' will only further annoy us and provoke us," the group's text stated, "since it is absurd to make such parallels between two disparate groups. The real reason we put any blame on Carolyn Meinel is because of her obtuse over-dramatizations of our actions." Ms. Meinel said in an interview yesterday that last month a group identifying itself as HFG attacked the computers of Rt66, an Internet service provider in Albuquerque, N.M., on which she has an account. Mark Schmitz, Rt66's co-founder, said the company was working with the F.B.I. and the local authorities to identify those responsible for the attacks on his site, especially one in which several customers' credit card numbers were stolen. Ms. Meinel also said that she had been the victim of another attack by a group she suspects may be linked to HFG, based on on-line interactions she has had with a person who seems to be involved with both groups. In that attack, made on several Internet users simultaneously, including Ms. Meinel and Mr. Markoff, the attackers subscribed the victims to tens of thousands of Internet mailing lists in an effort to disrupt their electronic mail service. Ms. Meinel said she was writing a second book, to be titled "The Hacker Wars." "These people are desperate for fame," she said. "These are the kids who used to make stink bombs. Now they have the Internet."

title:
Technology;
Critics are picking apart a professor's study that linked Internet use to loneliness and depression.
body: ROBERT KRAUT, a co-author of a new study linking depression with Internet use, sounded a bit depressed himself last week. "I thought I was finished with this," Mr. Kraut, a professor of social psychology and human-computer interaction at Carnegie Mellon University, said with a sigh. He was alluding to the flood of attention -- and criticism -- that his study, titled "Home Net," had received since it was published two weeks ago. Starting in 1995, "Home Net" researchers gave PC's and free Internet accounts to 169 people in 73 families in the Pittsburgh area. After monitoring their on-line behavior, in some cases for more than two years, the researchers concluded that spending time on the Internet was associated with statistically significant increases in depression and loneliness. Critics assert that the study has fatal flaws that neutralize its findings and that they are appalled at the authors' far-reaching conclusions about the impact the findings might have on Internet policy and technology development. Donna L. Hoffman, a Vanderbilt University professor and outspoken critic of Internet research design, was unequivocal about the "Home Net" study. "Speaking as an editor, if this had crossed my desk, I would have rejected it," said Ms. Hoffman, who edits the journal Marketing Science. "The mistakes are so bad that they render the results fairly close to meaningless." Among those mistakes, she said, were the absence of two standard safeguards: a control group and random selection of subjects. "With 'Home Net,' we don't know for sure what led to their results," Ms. Hoffman said of the lack of a control group, "because we don't know what happened to people who weren't using the Internet." In addition, the study recruited people from high schools and community service organizations, instead of selecting people randomly from a large area. Random selection is crucial to building a truly representative sample of a population -- in this case, residents of the unitedstates. The study found that one hour a week on line led to small but measurable increases in depression and loneliness and loss of friendships. While those measurements might well be statistically significant, critics assert that without a random sample, they are meaningless outside the group that was studied. "The assertions have no statistical relevance to any population of Internet users beyond those in the study population -- even in principle," declared Charles Brownstein, a former director at the National Science Foundation, now an executive director at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives in Reston, Va. Although research studies do not always have to use control groups or randomly chosen participants to be valid, Ms. Hoffman said, those safeguards become imperative "when you're doing a study that claims causal relationships and that these relationships hold in the larger population." The "Home Net" team clearly made such claims. For example, the news release stated that "Carnegie Mellon Study Reveals Negative Potential of Heavy Internet Use on Emotional Well Being," and even suggested that parents move PC's out of teen-agers' bedrooms and into shared family rooms. Mr. Kraut was quoted extensively in the release, with such statements as, "We were surprised to find that what is a social technology has such anti-social consequences.' Also: "Our results have clear implications for further research on personal Internet use. As we understand the reasons for the declines in social involvement, there will be implications for social policies and for the design of Internet technology." Last week, Mr. Kraut wearily defended his study. "In 1995, we did start with a control group, but it was very hard to keep it, with little in the way of incentives for them to continue to fill out questionnaires," he said. "And we couldn't use a random sample because of the nature of the study's design -- we wanted to be able to include groups who already had social connections with each other so we could observe some shifting, if it was going to occur, between existing social relationships." And despite criticism of the researchers' methods, he said that the study was widely applicable. "We have changes big enough that they aren't likely to have occurred on the basis of chance," Mr. Kraut said. "There is something here to explain." But critics like Ms. Hoffman look askance at such results, given her experience debunking other Internet studies, including one from Neilsen Media Research in which she participated in 1996 and another in 1995 in which Marty Rimm, a graduate student in Carnegie Mellon's College of Engineering, published a study purporting to show that the Internet was overrun with pornography. The impact of Mr. Rimm's study, though based on false premises and quickly discredited, was profound. The resulting furor in the media and in Congress helped bring about the Communications Decency Act, which the Supreme Court ruled was a violation of the First Amendment. Critics fear that the "Home Net" study might end up having a similar effect. "It's easy to imagine the results of this study being used to influence policy decisions about Internet access, especially in controversial funding decisions for schools and libraries," Ms. Hoffman said. But in the end, Ms. Hoffman said, protecting the Internet itself is not the point. "We're trying to protect the standard of research," she said. "This isn't obscure ivory-tower stuff that never sees the light of day. It has an impact on people's lives. If we're going to the trouble to study the Internet, at least we should make sure we're doing it right." Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Watch what the Internet asks children, sponsors are warned, or see the government step in.
body: ADVERTISERS and agencies involved in aiming on-line sales pitches at children are being exhorted to toughen their policies for protecting privacy or suffer the consequences of growing demands from parents and government officials for restrictive regulation. Those stern warnings were heard on Friday at a daylong conference at the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan that was described by its organizers as a "guide to safe harbors and sound practices on line." The conference, the third of its kind, was sponsored by the Children's Advertising Review Unit, an organization that is a crucial part of Madison Avenue's longtime efforts to resolve disputes about advertising without outside intervention. "We've done a pretty good job so far," Elizabeth Lascoutx, vice president and director for the children's unit, said in her opening remarks to the 85 people at the conference. "But we have a long way to go." Concerns about privacy in cyberspace are intensifying as sites for children proliferate on the World Wide Web. There are increasing consumer perceptions that many marketers are reluctant to address problems like the overzealous collection of personally identifiable information from young computer users and the porous handling of such data. "One site is asking kids for their Social Security numbers," Parry Aftab, a lawyer who specializes in interactive issues, said in her keynote speech. "How frustrating is that?" Those involved in the children's Internet market ought to be "joining forces and writing a privacy page so kids know what to give out and not give out," said Ms. Aftab, the author of "A Parents' Guide to the Internet . . . And How to Protect Your Children" (SC Press, 1997). "We need to find a workable solution," she added, "or we'll lose the wonderful wealth of creativity and content that sites can offer." The advocacy of self-regulation by the children's unit had been echoed enthusiastically by the Clinton Administration, which sent Ira C. Magaziner, the President's Internet adviser, to the 1997 conference to applaud efforts to establish voluntary guidelines to police on-line peddling to youngsters. But in June, a report from the Federal Trade Commission said legislation might be required because violations of children's privacy on line were discouragingly frequent and safeguards were woefully absent. "I'm not suggesting the advertising industry attracts none but the truly altruistic," said Walter J. O'Brien, president of the National Advertising Review Council, which administers the children's unit along with the Council of Better Business Bureaus and three industry organizations. "But it's enlightened self-interest to make a commitment to ethical advertising, particularly to children under 12." And last month, the F.T.C. accused Geocities, a company known for offering members access to so-called virtual neighborhoods, of ignoring the privacy policy posted on its site and engaging in misleading practices that included disseminating information gathered from children. "You don't have to look very far to see a fundamental mistake there, a mistake we cannot make anymore," said John Kamp, senior vice president at the American Association of Advertising Agencies. "In legal terms, it's called fraud," he added with a smile. "In general terms, it's called 'Do you know what you're doing?' " "The more our customers trust us, the more we succeed in developing the relationships with them that make our Web sites work," Mr. Kamp said. "Privacy is the great opportunity to distinguish ourselves from our competition." Mr. Kamp's organization is one of the three involved with the children's unit; the others are the American Advertising Federation and the Association of National Advertisers. The F.T.C. "has been very supportive of self-regulation in children's advertising," said Toby Milgrom Levin, a lawyer with the commission who worked on the Geocities case. "We recognize that the advertising industry did rise to the occasion and develop conventions to protect children from deceptive and overreaching ads." But the belief that advertisers are dawdling about the Internet is likely to lead Congress to act, she said, and "there may well be hearings by the end of the month" on a bill that "authorizes the F.T.C. to prescribe regulations to protect the privacy of children under 16." To forestall legislation, "you can make privacy a front-burner concern," Ms. Levin advised, especially among top management. "The Webmasters are not in a position to make privacy happen," she added. Clearly, more of those involved in putting up Web sites are becoming sensitized to privacy matters. "Privacy is in the forefront of all our programming decisions," said Tina Sharkey, vice president and general manager of the C.T.W. Online unit of the Children's Television Workshop in newyork, which plans to introduce today a redesigned site called the C.T.W. Family Workshop (www.ctw.org). "We don't collect information from children under 13," she added, at areas on the site that are sponsored by marketers like the Ford Motor Company and the Kellogg Company. "And parents are told everywhere they can sign up that they can opt out with a 'click here.' " More than one speaker referred to the timing of the conference, coming as it did while computer users caused some Internet gridlock in searching for the report on President Clinton by the Whitewater independent counsel, Kenneth W. Starr. "If any group in this country understands the danger of private information going public and having an impact on their lives," said Dan Jaffe, executive vice president at the Association of National Advertisers, "it's our politicians."

title: The Real Internet Action Is Local
body: Forget all the talk about the global, freewheeling Internet. Nearly two years after the first on-line city guides appeared, many companies are still betting that the real action on the Internet is in such local on-line markets. From its start, the business of producing locally oriented Web sites that offer everything from concert listings and restaurant reviews to commuter traffic reports and school lunch menus, has been one of the Internet's fiercest battlegrounds. Some cities boast as many as half a dozen full-blown Web sites clamoring for a share of local advertising, media support and loyal users. The lure is tempting indeed. Local businesses in the unitedstates will spend a total of $70 billion on advertising this year. Of that, says Jupiter Communications, the Internet research firm in newyork, $700 million will be spent on line, a figure that analysts say will almost double in 1999 and will continue to rise well into the next century. Clearly, not all the local Web guides that have sprung up can survive in markets crowded with nearly indistinguishable competitors. Already, the business has shown signs of cracking. Earlier this year, the Microsoft Corporation was forced back to the labs for a new approach to its network of local guides, laying off a quarter of its editorial staff in the meantime. Likewise, America Online's Digital City has regrouped in a process that cut 80 staff members. "It's one of those areas where you have too many people doing close to the same thing," Patrick Keane, an analyst at Jupiter Communications, said. So far, there have been few real casualties, and new partnerships are leading to new sites and new business strategies every day. Most recently, for example, Citysearch, a pioneer in the city guides, merged with the Ticketmaster unit of USA Networks with the idea of more closely integrating event listings with the ability to sell tickets immediately to the events. With the Citysearch/Ticketmaster union, someone interested in seeing "Titanic" on the big screen would be able to find out where it was playing and then instantly buy a ticket. Eventually, consumers will also be offered many related transactions at the same time, like the opportunity to buy Titanic memorabilia and make reservations at a restaurant near the theater. Though services like these have long been promised by local guides, no company has yet delivered all the pieces. Citysearch, of Pasadena, Calif., is in a quiet period as it prepares to go public, so executives were not able to comment on their strategy. But the merger with Ticketmaster last month is perhaps the best signal yet that on-line guides are quickly moving from simply providing information to performing transactions. Perhaps the most notable local on-line activity recently has been in the newspaper business, where an aggressive upstart, Zip2, has managed to forge partnerships with 160 papers around the country. Twenty of those deals have led to full-scale city guides, said Elon Musk, chairman and founder of Zip2, which is based in Mountain View, Calif. The remaining deals have produced local guides within newspapers' Web sites. Among the full-scale guides is newyork Today, a result of a partnership between Zip2 and The newyork Times. One of the primary things Zip2 provides newspapers is an on-line Yellow Pages with links directly into store listings and reviews. Zip2 also offers a personalization feature, calendar listings and free email. Through a deal with Zip2, The Boston Globe, a newyork Times Company newspaper, offers event and local information as a part of Boston.com, the regional Web site it created in 1995. Most analysts agree that local newspapers could have an inherent advantage in the local on-line market because they can tap material they already develop for print and use the strength of their brand to attract both advertisers and customers. "We've always said it's the newspaper industry's battle to lose," said Mr. Keane of Jupiter. Citysearch has also linked up with newspapers, including The Los Angeles Times, which is owned by the Times Mirror Company, and Time Out newyork, a weekly arts and entertainment magazine. The Toronto Star, owned by the Torstar Corporation, is working with Citysearch and Tele-Direct, a local phone company that supplies Yellow Pages listings. Likewise, in the crowded newyork market, Microsoft Sidewalk licenses entertainment listings from The Village Voice. The most innovative newspaper effort may be the Real Cities network started a year ago by Knight Ridder, publisher of a chain that includes The Miami Herald, The Philadelphia Inquirer and The San Jose Mercury News. The idea is to give on-line media buyers a network for placing local Web ads, while giving the Web sites access to editorial material and tools like the News Hound program, which delivers news personalized to the needs of each user. Knight Ridder's strategy is similar to that of Cox Enterprises, which last year opened a series of Web sites based on its newspaper and television properties. But perhaps the greatest competitive threat comes from one of the Internet's oldest properties, Yahoo, which offers links to local content and has become the front door for millions of Internet users. Though Yahoo's half-dozen local sites do not offer much in the way of original content, they do carry brand recognition and an already-captive audience, which might prove crucial in the long run. "We think the real battle is with Yahoo and AOL to become a local portal," Mr. Musk, of Zip2, said. "They're building down to the local level, whereas we're building up to it." Yet, Microsoft and America Online, despite their perceived missteps, appear to be gearing up for the fight again. Microsoft Sidewalk, now published in nine cities, is readying Version 3.0 of its service for roll-out by the end of the year. The idea is to offer a national version in which much of the content will be identical from one city site to another but will be supplemented with local information about restaurants, performances and retailers and will carry a combination of local and national ads. The new Sidewalk will place a greater emphasis on helping consumers shop, including the addition of Yellow Pages, said the service's product manager, Gayle Troberman. Peter Atkins, Sidewalk's general manager for advertising sales and marketing, said, "More and more merchants want to come on line and reach people right when they want to buy." Anecdotal evidence would suggest that local businesses are indeed coming on line, selling everything from clothing and computers to hotel rooms and vacation packages, and realizing a decent return on their investment. Sal Patel, reservations manager at the 70-room Union Square Hotel, says his monthly listing in Citysearch San Francisco typically pays for itself within a day or two. But analysts predict the pace of development of new on-line city guides will probably not last long. Despite all the interest from advertisers, no city guide has consistently shown a profit. "We're seeing isolated incidents where these sites are making money," said Peter Kraslinsky, an analyst at Arlen Communication, a research company that studies interactive transactions. "But mostly they're spending with minimal returns." Many producers of on-line guides acknowledge that the effort has proved a more expensive proposition than they expected. Mr. Musk says by hooking up with major media players, Zip2 expects to be profitable sooner than the companies that try to do the bulk of the editorial work themselves. Though the demand for local information and services is huge, it is anybody's guess just how many competing services each market can support and whether the services can turn investments into profits. Lisa Allen, a new-media analyst at Forrester Research, said, "Becoming a media operation and making money at it are a lot easier said than done." Graphic   Chart/Photos: "Let Us Be Your Guide" The market for on-line city guides is growing rapidly, with, it seems, just about everyone putting together a site on the Web. Here are a few national sites' guides to newyork City.  AOL DIGITAL CITIES (July visitors: 2.7 million) Mistakes led to layoffs of 80 people, but it has great brand recognition. title:
EUROPE: FALL/WINTER: STEPPING FORWARD AND INTO THE PAST;
Vienna: A change of pace from chandeliers and Strauss
body: In a few discreet places, Vienna sheds its revered cloak of classical taste in music, fashion and food. The locals find these redoubts first and often secure them for themselves. The latest is Rhiz, a bar featuring electronic music (heavy on drums and bass) and disk jockeys who take turns as presenters. The crowd is mostly young, though not uniformly so, mostly Viennese with occasional foreigners, and the mood high pitched but not frenetic; there is some dancing but not much. Since its spring opening, patrons have been talking, drinking, moving to the music and, heaven forbid, enjoying a cigarette. The dress is as varied as the backgrounds of the clientele: black T-shirts and comfortable pants mingle with sassy skin-hugging dresses and platform shoes. There are few investment bankers here, but plenty of designers, computer programmers and creative directors. One of the most striking aspects of Rhiz is its decor -- no traditional Viennese touches like chandeliers or red lacquered walls.  Large wooden entrance doors from old Vienna and original red brick interior walls give way to a newly installed 1990's green plastic bar. The bar is laid out within the support arches of a tram station designed by Otto Wagner, the Viennese Art Deco designer. Huge ventilation tubes of shiny steel extend the length of the barroom ceiling. Mirrors and a flat-screen computer with access to the Internet add to the contemporary look. Bar stools with black seats and metal legs and white chairs arrayed around green tables send a 1940's message. A black juke box hangs on a wall and when the DJ's have a night off, patrons choose from a selection of electronic, modern rock and hip hop. The fare? Hard alcohol, beer, soft drinks and coffee at reasonable prices. A melange (Vienna's version of a cappuccino) is about $2.35. A large draft beer, $3.25; a glass of good Austrian wine, $2.65; and a shot of the best whisky, $4. To complete the idea that Vienna can be as high-tech as other European capitals, a Web cam films the inside of the bar from 10 P.M. to 3 A.M. The images are shown on the Internet homepage: www.rhiz.org. Rhiz Bar Modern, 1160 Wien Llerchen feldergurtel, 37/38 Stadtbahnbogen, telephone (43-1) 409-2505, is open daily, 11 A.M. to 4 A.M. Take the U6 subway line to the Josefstadterstrasse station. Graphic   Photo: The bar at Rhiz in Vienna is laid out between the support arches of a tram station. (Daniele Mattioli/Anzenberger, for The newyork Times)

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
Going Green on Screen
body: In olden times -- say, before 1995 -- you had to go to a museum to visit its collection or to a garden to see its blossoms. Nowadays, of course, all that has changed; every cultural institution worth its salt has an Internet presence. In newyork, that includes the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, which has been on line for the last two and a half years, according to the editor of its Web site, Jim Santo. Charged, like the garden itself, with the dual purpose of entertaining and educating the public and furthering the garden's scientific mission, the Web site is like many of its institutional counterparts, full of information and enticements for prospective members. But it comes with a bonus that some of its peers lack: designed by Array Technologies, a Manhattan firm, in conjunction with Anne Garland, the designer for the garden's publications, it's actually pretty to look at, "very graphically oriented," Mr. Santo said. "What is a garden but a place to delight the senses?" he asks. "Shouldn't its Web site do the same thing?"  WHAT YOU SEE -- More than 1,900 pages of data on activities, plants, birds and gardening, most accompanied by drawings or photographs. You can take a virtual stroll of the garden itself (soon to be enhanced to allow viewers to see the plants from every angle, "like a bird," in Mr. Santo's words), order gardening books, volunteer or even apply for a fellowship. A section titled "Beguiling Blooms" offers photographs of flowers in season, together with descriptions, while another, called "Gardening, Naturally," provides gardening tips excerpted from the garden's publications. If you are of a scientific bent, you can also check the status of the newyork Metropolitan Flora project, which was begun in 1990 to document all plants growing within 50 miles of newyork City. With the aid of the Metropolitan Plant Encyclopedia and on-line questions and answers, you may even be able to identify that mystery plant growing in your yard or out of the cracks in your sidewalk.  LINKS -- Under the rubric "Metropolitan Green Pages," approximately 50 Web sites offering "botanical or environmental" information are listed, including those of the Cornell Plant Science Center, the American Society of Plant Taxonomists and the Horticultural Society of newyork. All are said to have been evaluated by the scientific staff of the Brooklyn Botanic Garden to insure that visits will be worthwhile.  WHAT YOU GET -- The self-proclaimed "greenest site on the Web."   BERNARD STAMLER  Brooklyn Botanic Garden http://www.bbg.org Graphic   Photos

title:
TESTING OF A PRESIDENT: THE INTERNET;
Tangled Web Tangles Up the World Wide Web
body: The downloads were slow, the error messages were many, but in the first experiment in electronic communication between the unitedstates Government and its citizens on a massive scale, millions of persevering Internet users were devouring the Starr report yesterday within hours of its release. Across cyberspace, the response ran the gamut: "Impeach the hypocrite!" demanded the subject line of an America Online message board. "Keep this President!" came the immediate reply. Many readers simply quoted the most salacious details, and at length. But political activists who have been promoting the Internet as a tool for more participatory democracy said the release of the report on line was a watershed whose implications went beyond the current scandal. "There's a whole universe of information waiting for the public to discover on the Internet," said Kim Alexander of the California Voter Foundation. "Maybe this will lead people to realize that this is a way to become more engaged and involved in public life in this country." Many sites on the World Wide Web reported huge spikes in traffic as people who had been listening to pundits and politicians speculate about the investigation for months stampeded the Internet to find out for themselves what the special prosecutor had to say. MSNBC, one of the leading news sites on the Web, said two million users had visited the site even before the report was published, double its previous record, set when President Clinton testified before the grand jury on Aug. 17. Traffic doubled again once the report was posted. The Washington Post's Web site reported that its traffic had tripled by late afternoon. Despite preparing for logistical nightmares -- news organizations did not know until Friday morning what format the report would be delivered in or whether it would need to be scanned from paper -- the electronic publication process appeared to go smoothly. Yahoo, a popular gateway to the World Wide Web, received the report from Congress through the Internet at 2:50 P.M. and published it five minutes later. Five minutes after that, its message boards were flooded with comments. "So, let me get this straight, you went through the report and thought this was the most damning and critical evidence against Clinton?" demanded one Yahoo user in reply to another who had posted a passage about Monica S. Lewinsky's testimony regarding oral sex. "Ahahahah. But it isn't about sex??" Indeed, one refrain in the on-line debate was whether the report was about sex or substance. "Surprise, surprise, surprise, it's all about sex and covering it up," wrote an America Online user. "Is this what all you Republicans were waiting for?" But others had a different take: "YOU THINK YOU ARE ABOVE THE LAW," another America Online denizen shouted a message to the President in all caps. "WE GAVE YOU A JOB TO DO AND YOU HAVE LET US ALL DOWN." But as Americans across the country tried to participate in this unprecedented kind of electronic town hall meeting, many were shut out because of the overload on the computer network. Keynote Systems, a company in San Mateo, Calif., that monitors Internet traffic, said that half of those who tried to connect to the major news sites received error messages yesterday afternoon. On Thursday, the Library of Congress's Thomas Web site had an average access time of 10 seconds and 98 percent of all requests for pages were successful. On Friday morning, Thomas started out with a 55-second response time and only 13 percent of people's efforts to connect were successful, the San Mateo company said. Still, Internet advocates noted that many of the other events that had caused Internet traffic jams had little to do with politics. The death of the Princess of Wales, the Olympics, the Mars Pathfinder mission and, most recently, the stock market's gyrations have slowed the network. "This shows that the Internet is now the choice medium for distributing information to the public," said Jerry Berman, chairman of the Center for Democracy and Technology. "One benefit is that the Internet is unmediated. There's no one interpreting the material, so citizens can make their own interpretations. On the other hand, the material does require context, and what we're going to have to look at is whether it can provide that, too, and allow people to make intelligent judgments." Although some 100 million people worldwide are now believed to have Internet access, the publishing of the Starr report raises thorny questions about inequality of access -- just who has it, and to what do they have access. Several Internet rating and filtering services said yesterday that the Starr report would be blocked to minors under their family-content criteria. And a recent Department of Commerce report found a "digital divide" based on race and income that appeared to be increasing. And then there is the long-term effect that the Starr report might have on a populace already disenchanted with the political process. "We can put all the information we want on the Internet," said Ms. Alexander of the California on-line advocacy group. "But if people are so cynical and apathetic that they have no incentive to look at it, it's not going to make politics better." Graphic   Photos: STARR'S CASE. The report was released to the press on CD's. FUTURE LAWYERS. Students at Columbia Law School gathered in a computer laboratory yesterday to call up the Starr report on the Internet. (Edward Keating/The newyork Times)

title:
TESTING OF A PRESIDENT;
Web Sites Fear Busy Signals on Report
body: Distributing the Whitewater independent counsel's report on the World Wide Web on Friday might cause an electronic traffic jam that could leave many readers with the Internet's equivalent of a busy signal. Speaker Newt Gingrich's staff members answered questions today from nervous managers of Web sites, including America Online. Their fear is that a deluge of Web surfers will descend on a few Web sites in an effort to be among the first to view the report. Even worse, the report could be released in the afternoon, a peak period for use of the Internet. Tentative plans called for the initial release of the report to a Web site that can be seen only in Congressional offices, then distribution an hour later to a variety of Web sites than can be viewed by the public, including these four Government sites: http://www.house.gov/icreport (House Information Resources); http://www.house.gov/judiciary (House Judiciary Committee); http://thomas.loc.gov/icreport (Library of Congress), and http:// www.access.gpo.gov/congress/icreport (Government Printing Office). Copies will also be made on CD-ROM for use by Web sites and the news media. By placing copies around the country, Web managers hope to prevent Internet traffic jams. Mr. Gingrich's staff members said they were trying to determine if the document came in electronic form, and if it came as page images -- essentially photocopies of each page -- or smaller and more efficient text files, such as the kind produced by word processors. Page images can bloat files so much that they become costly or time consuming to view or download except by Web surfers with expensive high-speed Internet connections.

title: Appalachian Trail Sites Offer Virtual Walks on Wild Side
body: HIKING the entire Appalachian Trail is a daunting task. Walking 2,160 miles in the woods in six months while carrying a heavy pack can make one feel far removed from modern conveniences, like showers, television and computers. But nothing escapes the Web. There are sites catering to "through hikers," those who attempt to walk the entire trail, usually going from south to north, and to the less ambitious day hikers. This year's successful through hikers, who started in February or March, will be finishing in the days and weeks ahead. Brian Vaughan, 18, of Dedham, Mass., began at the start of the trail, at Springer Mountain, Ga., on Feb. 24 and finished at Mount Katahdin, Me., on Aug. 17. His progress on the trail was charted on a Web site, geocities. com/pipeline/dropzone/1840/, maintained by his mother, Valerie McKay. Every week or so, Mr. Vaughan called home with news, and Ms. McKay updated the site. Ms. McKay exhaustively chronicled what and how much her son was eating, and even proudly reported that he had gained weight on the trail. She described herself as "panic-stricken" when she had not heard from her son for a couple of weeks. About 17,000 visitors checked in during his hike. Ms. McKay said she had been shocked by the attention. She even received some "gently irate" email from Web surfers who were impatient for the next update, she said. A few strangers sent packages to post offices where they learned that Mr. Vaughan would be stopping for supplies; one sent granola bars, and another sent $5. At one point in the middle of the woods, Mr. Vaughan, who will be a University of Massachusetts freshman this fall, was stopped in Virginia by a passing hiker who asked: "Are you Brian Vaughan? I saw your Web site." Still on the trail are Jonathan Griffith and Dawn Wood, whose progress is being tracked at www.umit.maine. edu/jonathangriffith/AT. The two 21-year-old college students, who are boyfriend and girlfriend, began their walk on May 16 and expect to finish in mid-October. In addition to offering regular updates on their progress and photographs taken on the trail, the site has links to descriptions of what they have passed along the way. So it provides an overview of the trail for those who do not find the idea of hiking up and down mountains every day for half a year very appealing. Ms. Wood, of Stetson, Me., and Mr. Griffith, of Hudson, Me., were in North Adams, Mass., on Sept. 4. Ben Griffith, Jonathan's older brother, who helps maintain the site, said he had expected those following the pair's progress to be mostly friends and relatives. But the site has been getting about 300 hits a week from readers who have been treated to the drama of a meeting with a rattlesnake in the Smoky Mountains (neither hikers nor reptile was hurt) and news of the nagging troubles with Ms. Wood's boots. ARMCHAIR hikers can also get an overview of the trail at the Appalachian Trail site (www.fred.net/kathy/at.html). The site includes history, advice for hikers and plenty of links to descriptions of the trail's highlights. A central gathering point for through hikers is the www.trailplace. com site. About 2,500 try to hike the entire trail each year, but only a few hundred succeed. The site offers bulletin boards where hikers, using their trail nicknames, can offer advice on what to buy, carry and eat. The Appalachian Trail is kept in shape by hundreds of dedicated volunteer trail managers. Their site is www.atconf.org. Graphic   Photos: A volunteer nonprofit group maintains the Appalachian Trail footpath.

title:
Every Dog Has Its Data;
The Web Has Pets the Way Pets Have Fleas, and There's No Leash Law
body: JUST what is the World Wide Web made of? Tips and tails and puppy-dog sales, if you know where to look. Need a set of tarot cards for your dog? Advice on feline midwifery? Troubled because you have a Belgian Tervuren with reverse sneezing? Trolling through the Internet (if you're not easily repulsed by the human tendency to dote on other species), you can find homeless hairless cats awaiting adoption, sanitary-napkin belts for dogs (one brand is called Fancy Fannies) and home pages for any breed of hound imaginable. And there is plenty to learn about the care and feeding of birds, snakes, fish and assorted furry creatures, from the lowly boa constrictor to the arboreal Australian sugar glider, a five-inch-long marsupial that humans have taken to carrying around in their breast pockets (www.herpeton.com/pet.html). Pet-related sites can have a certain sideshow quality to them. Write to Theophilus, the cat with his own email. Learn the amazing technique by which Bubba the fish learned to swim through a hoop. Meet Pete, the cat who looks like Hitler. Where else could you find Czarina Oksana Borzoi Diva Dog Needlenose of MuffinTush, the Ann Landers of canine expatriate nobility, who answers questions that borzois and other dogs instruct their human servants to email to her? These pressing questions include, "Why do my humans think that decorating is more important than my needs?" and, "Has Your Regalness attended an agility trial?" She regales her readers at members.aol.com/MuffinTush/Pages/Opage.html with tales of her new boy toy, Dylan, who is "not much in the brains department" but "quite a Renaissance dog for a Lab." But the Web offers more than yuks for the pet set. Jibralta Merrill of Studio City, Calif., who types for Oksana, has been able to consult with other borzoi experts about a recent health concern Oksana faced (though in true aristocratic fashion, neither wished to discuss the particulars). Her Web page friends sent more than 50 messages of support. And through the Ask Oksana and borzoi rescue sites, Ms. Merrill was able to find a new home -- in just 36 hours -- for a rambunctious borzoi about to get the boot. A close reading of the Web on a topic as potentially resonant as the silent, forgiving companions asleep by the hearth gives a glimpse of the real life of real people, like the neighbors' nighttime noises, overheard through open windows. For pet lovers, it can be moving to read about Bubba, the double yellowhead parrot whose owners, Paul and Jean Dennis, readers of the on-line Fort Worth Star-Telegram, taught him to sing "You Are My Sunshine" and wave bye-bye. And a prayer written by Bob Deeds for the late Lakota, a wolf-dog hybrid, hits home to anyone who has lost a pet: "Let her spar with Zeiko and Becky so she won't miss Bo and Ced. (For they miss her very much.) Let her howl at her heart's content! Not a melancholy lonely howl, but one of joy and peace." That appeared in www.star-telegram.com/interact/forums/petmemo.htm, The Star-Telegram's popular page for pet memorials. (The paper will even scan in photos free.) The site features an homage to "my first rat, Morpheus Brian," who "left us nine children -- Enga Mircalla, Titania Sophia, Oberon Orpheus, Lulu Winter, Jolly-ette, Homeo, Corpse, Julian El Nino, and Hecubus." A 1996 Gallup poll found that 63 percent of dog owners and 58 percent of cat owners gave their pets Christmas presents. Thirteen percent of dog owners and 10 percent of cat owners talk to their pets on telephones or answering machines. Many owners carry pet pictures in their wallets; 12 percent of dog owners and 9 percent of cat owners, according to the survey. The Web is becoming a place for pet owners to meet and shop. The American Pet Association, a group for pet owners, attributed 9 percent of its membership growth in 1997 to its Web site (www.apapets.com). Many Internet sites are selling pet-related goods, including one that says it acts as a personal shopper for pets (www.rwoof.com/ rwoof/index.html). Many pet-related sites are seeing high volumes of visitors, including a site run by Karen Pryor, author of "Don't Shoot the Dog," (Bantam paperback, 1985), who is a strong proponent of training animals, including llamas and fish, with positive reinforcement by using clickers, those little toys with a noisy, flexible tab of metal on the back. "The Internet has really been the soul of this business, also the soul of the clicker movement," Ms. Pryor said. She said her Web site, which goes by dontshootthedog. com or clickertraining.com and offers information, books and videos, gets 100,000 hits a month. "The month it went up, the site doubled our business, and since then we've been growing at 5 percent a month," Ms. Pryor said. Small groups of clicker-trainers in Finland, Croatia and Australia, as well as larger groups in North America, can keep up to date on various topics (like teaching a dog to ride a skateboard) via the Web site. "It erases time so you don't have to worry about waking someone up at 6 A.M. with a question," she added. "You can make little Manhattan Projects out of your own interests." You can even get Internet help to name your pet. At homearts.com/depts/pastime/ petnam16.htm, enter the species, sex, preferred first letter and up to three categories (arts and literature, biblical/mythologicaland sports, for example) for a name, and you get back a list of possibilities. A request for "insulting" cat names somehow yields the following: Alimony, Dog, Ego, Gore, Hog, Pooper, Trog and Wisenheimer. For those looking to choose and train a dog, the Web offers many suggestions. There is a handy puppy aptitude test available at www.rahul.net/hredlus/pat1.html that allows a prospective dog owner to gauge its temperament on a numerical scale, based on what it does in certain situations, like being rolled over onto its back and held there for 30 seconds. Information on crate training, which gives pets den-like boxes as their own private space, safe from dangers and temptations in the house, can be found in a Frequently Asked Question page called www.cis.ohio-state.edu/ hypertext/faq/usenet/dogs-faq/crating/ faq.html. While the Internet can let you rub shoulders with people you might not want to stand behind in a grocery line -- watch out for what can come up in a search for "naked mole rats" -- the pet lovers appear to be a well-meaning bunch. For instance, the Dog Hause Web ring, a pack of connected dog sites found at www.doghause.com/ links.html, awards an I Care icon to sites that display a graphic about spaying and neutering if said sites are run by people whose pets are spayed or neutered (certified via an email saying they are). The site called www.rwoof.com is a sponsor of PAWS (Pets are Wonderful Support), which helps people with AIDS care for their pets, while a pet supply site, www.sitstay. com, donates 10 percent of its profits to animal rescue efforts, groups that find homes for animals. A number of sites aim to reunite lost pets with their owners, like www.missingpets. com, which lists descriptions of lost and found pets from all over the country, ("lost, St. Gabriel, Louisiana, golden long-hair chihuahua, green eyes; answers to Bean") and missingpet.org, which lists tips for finding lost pets, like distributing Missing Dog Trading Cards. Sherlock Bones, at www.sherlock.com, offers hints on making effective Lost Pet posters and can mail out postcards with pictures of a missing pet in the neighborhood where it disappeared. Tales of happy endings can be found on these sites. But as anyone who has ever fished a bale of cat fur out of a mouse knows, computers and pets aren't always simpatico. The Web is full of sites listing the classic 20 Reasons Why Dogs Don't Use Computers, which includes: 20. Can't stick their heads out of Windows 95. 18. Hard to read the monitor with your head cocked to one side. 16. Can't help attacking the screen when they hear, "You've got mail." 6. Smell U-Smell Me still in beta test. THE POETRY OF BULLDOG X-L www.well.com/user/marebon/xlpoem.htm Looking for bulldog-related poetry? How about: My bully's a joy to behold/ I love every wrinkle and fold? title:
LIBRARY/PRESCRIPTION DRUG SITES;
Places to Check Out the Pills for Your Ills - Correction Appended
body: IF you are like most Americans, your medicine cabinet is packed with a pricey assortment of pills and potions, evidence that we, as a country, like to feel good. And some of the newer pills -- say, Viagra and Prozac -- can make even others feel good about you. Americans are the largest consumers of prescription drugs in the world, spending some $94 billion for them last year, according to IMS Health, a health care consulting company. This year's tally should be ever higher, thanks especially to Viagra, a treatment for impotency, which is expected to rack up a record $1 billion in sales in its first year on the market. Stockholders in the world's pharmaceutical companies have come to expect blockbuster sales, so the companies have been forced to churn out blockbuster remedies faster than before. This year, Merck & Company, the nation's largest pharmaceutical company, released five new drugs that treat everything from migraines to asthma. And there are plenty more on the way. Within a year, Lipha Pharmaceuticals, a German subsidiary of Merck, expects to release Campral, a drug to help alcoholics wean themselves from drinking, in the unitedstates. For people who cannot knock off at night, American Home Products will soon roll out Sonata, a sleeping pill that the company says has fewer groggy after-effects than some of its competitors. It is easy to get buried in the drug avalanche, unable to distinguish the side effects of antihistamines like Claritin and Allegra. If the unthinkable happens and you become impotent, what are Viagra's advantages over Caverject? It makes a difference -- one is a pill and one is a shot. "Within the last several years, the entire process of pharmaceutical research has sped up," said Dr. Jeffrey Adelglass, a Dallas physician. "With some of the pharmaceutical sites now available on the Web, I can get medical information as fast or faster than anyone else in the country." Several sites can help you find out how a drug should be taken, while others blow the whistle on the inaccuracy of some of the drug makers' advertisements. The Food and Drug Administration, which regulates the sales and advertising of prescription drugs in this country, seldom requires a company to correct an error in its marketing. But it does have a site with information on drugs' safety records and Government reprimand letters about advertising campaigns (www.fda.gov/cder/ drug.htm). For those interested in what prescription drugs are under development, sites like www.centerwatch.com list clinical trials for pharmaceuticals and medical treatments being developed. There are other on-line drug information resources, like the National Library of Medicine, which has put Medline, its extensive database of medical information on the Web at www.nlm.nih.gov. Merck & Company, publisher of the drug encyclopedia called The Merck Index, has put The Merck Index of Diagnosis and Therapy on its corporate home page (www.merck.com). The Merck Manual is a more general source of medical information than the Index (which is sold on CD-ROM). It is used extensively by doctors and nurses nationwide. Correction  Because of an editing error, an article in Circuits yesterday about prescription drug Web sites referred incorrectly to Lipha Pharmaceuticals. Lipha is a subsidiary of Merck K.G.a.A., a German company; it has no relationship to Merck & Company, an American drug manufacturer. title:
Mutts by the Megabyte;
Helping to Save a Few Good Doggies From Death Row
body: SAUCER-SIZE brown eyes gaze longingly from the computer screen. His name is Harry, and he was on Death Row. With that exaggerated underbite and those crossed eyes, he looks a little like a gargoyle, and he may be a biter. On the plus side, he's affectionate, neutered and housebroken. He just needs love -- who doesn't? -- but time wasn't on his side. Harry is a 2-year-old, 15-pound Shih Tzu-terrier mix who was listed recently with Pet Finder, a pet adoption center on the Web (www.petfinder.org). The Pet Finder has a searchable database of more than 1,800 adoptable animals from New Jersey, newyork, Connecticut and other areas. In late August, the Pet Finder site added listings from two shelters in Missouri, one in Minnesota, two in Virginia, seven in Pennsylvania and one in Kansas. Being listed with Pet Finder may well have given Harry his best chance at a new life because on any given day, as many as 900 people visit the site, its founders say. Pet Finder was started in January 1996 by Betsy and Jared Saul. Ms. Saul, a 30-year-old agricultural assistant in New Jersey, is an animal lover who has worked with rescue shelters since she was 12. Her husband, 28, is a hospital radiology resident. They made a New Year's resolution to develop a page for animals needing homes. Ms. Saul said Pet Finder was the nation's first statewide Internet adoption site and the first to join on one site any two shelters that were not affiliated in any way. Before that, individual shelters listed their animals individually, as did adopt-a-pet sites linked to specific breeds. "We were frustrated at how few nonprofit organizations were using the full potential of the Internet," Ms. Saul said. "We wanted to design the perfect Web site, where pictures would make a huge difference." Volunteers scan photos of the animals and update the lists regularly. The volunteers get their information by visiting the shelters or taking reports from other volunteers; pets can also be listed for adoption -- without pictures -- by individuals. After some initial reluctance by animal lovers, Ms. Saul said, "eventually they realized that Internet adopters are pretty cool people. They tend to be highly educated and to have more money to take care of pets." While there is no substitute for snuggling with Fido before inviting him into your home, adopting through the Internet has its advantages. Dogs may be purebreds, obedience-trained and housebroken. Cats, rabbits and even ferrets may be neutered and litter-trained. Then there are descriptions of the animals' personalities, like the "2-year-old dwarf rabbit that will run circles around legs while making happy clicking-bunny sounds." Possible problems are pointed out. The site says a 6-year-old English springer spaniel "may bark at ducks." "People can search for pets in the emotional safety of their own living rooms, and the whole family can be involved," Ms. Saul said. That avoids the situation in which people visit shelters and adopt a sad-looking pet out of pity, and the adoption doesn't work out, she added. And how's Harry? He is alive and well now in Spring Valley, N.Y. Harry is now roaming on an acre of land. He belongs to a family with two girls, 10 and 13 years old. Ilana Perles, who adopted Harry, said: "He's adorable. A real sweetie." title:
NEWS WATCH;
PC Data Tries to Catch Up With Web Tracking Survey
body: Web surfing has become a spectator sport -- one that companies are willing to pay to observe. PC Data, based in Reston, Va., has become the latest market research firm to enter the fray. It now offers financial incentives to Internet users in exchange for getting to track not just their every move in cyberspace, but also which hardware and software products they use. Participants in the survey, called @PC Data, download software that sits on their home computer and monitors their computer and Internet use patterns. In exchange, PC Data provides discounts on Internet service, and, for those who stay on as guinea pigs for six months, frequent-flier miles and telephone calling cards. While this might sound novel, PC Data is playing catch up. Its competitors, including Media Metrix, Relevant Knowledge and Net Ratings, have offered similar programs for some time, acknowledged Frank Catalano, acting managing director for Internet monitoring at @PC Data. Mr. Catalano said PC Data could still be on the "bleeding edge" of monitoring software usage, which the company's software also measures. He added that the market would continue to grow in size and importance as advertisers and Web designers, among others, clamored for reliable data about Internet use patterns.

title: In Silicon Valley, Big Swings In Share Price Are Ho-Hum
body: With all due respect to Main Street investors who grew a bit faint when the Dow Jones industrial average plunged 6.4 percent in a day last week, the young workers riding their stock options on Silicon Valley's roller coaster have a message: really, that's nothing. Here at Onsale Inc., an on-line auction house where, as at many ventures in the Internet field, virtually every employee has a package of stock options that may (or may not) be a big part of the employee's net worth some day, wild swings in the company's stock price go with the territory. Just in the year and a half since the company went public, the stock has been as low as $4.625 a share and as high as $36.8125, with plenty of dips and rises along the way. In the last week alone, it careened from a low of $13.875 to a high of $21, finally closing at $16.75. "You get used to it after a while," said 30-year-old Jack Herndon, a marketing director at Onsale, a cyberauction house that sells an eclectic array of goods, mainly computer equipment but also items like rattlesnake meat and a human-shaped inflatable rubber device used for boxing practice known as the Slam Man. "I came here from a company that went from an all-time high to an all-time low in a matter of months," Mr. Herndon said. "One day it went from 42 to 24 overnight, then down to 11. I watched in 36 hours a significant amount of money not yet in my wallet burn before my eyes. It happens." More than in almost any other industry, stock options have fueled the boom in Silicon Valley and in other regions of the country where high-technology and Internet businesses are congregated, allowing start-up companies to pay smart, ambitious workers a relatively low salary -- along with the promise of great riches if their sweat and creativity help these ventures succeed. Along the way, that phenomenon seems to have ignited a singular brand of investment psychology that can be gleaned from talks with employees like those at Onsale, each of whom describes his or her own method of coping with the kind of volatility that might turn the stomachs of the most hardened investors. "Honestly, O.K., I do check the price at least once a day, just to see where it is," said 29-year-old Debbie Rodriguez, a customer service supervisor. "But, I don't calculate what it's all worth when it goes down. I calculate it for its potential, what I think it's really worth because I know how hard everybody at this company is working, and that helps." And, said Stefanie Elkins, a manager of investor relations, also 29: "The swings are all a part of the gamble, the whole Silicon Valley mentality. I think there's a whole, almost pioneer attitude, especially with Internet companies -- it's, 'Let's try this, let's see if we can get it to work, let's see if we can get it to a point where the stock options are really worth something.' There's a thrill in trying. If it doesn't work, you move on." Robert Petrossian, a vice president for engineering at Onsale, said short-term swings in the stock market are not the best way to measure the true value of a company in a fast-changing field like the Internet. "Being human, I do watch the stock price," Mr. Petrossian said. "It's a way to see how other people value your work externally. But I'm at this company for the long term, and I have my own way of valuing the stock. And from day one, in terms of the fundamentals, nothing has changed." Many employees insisted that stock options were not the main attraction of the company for them. "The roller coaster is fun and it's interesting, but it's really not the reason I'm here," said John Dean, a 39-year-old vice president in charge of a new division offering travel products, including weekly time-shares in a Mexican beach condominium for which the bidding starts at as low as $9. (Auctions at Onsale are carried on just as at more traditional ones, where bidders raise their hands. In this case, though, bidders click on an icon to bid, or leave secret instructions as to how high they are willing to bid.) For Mr. Dean, the real thrill comes when he can watch a last-minute bidding war erupt during Onsale's "Going . . . going . . . gone" feature, a fast-paced affair that means fast profits for the company. "When those bids go up," he said, "it's exciting. It's better than watching the World Series." Stock options, which essentially represent an agreement by a company to make shares available to an employee for a specified price in the future, can yield great profits when the company's stock soars, or be worth nothing if it plunges. While not commonly offered in many industries, they are virtually standard in places like Silicon Valley. "The Internet companies have grown up in an environment where this idea is a part of the culture," said Matt Ward, chief executive of Westward Pay Strategies Inc., a San Francisco-based firm that develops incentive compensation packages for many Silicon Valley companies. "I'm not sure you could even get people to work in this field in a situation where you're not giving them a piece of the action." Said Jerry Kaplan, a founder and chief executive officer of Onsale: "I like to say that Silicon Valley has perfected many of the principles laid out by Karl Marx. In his terms, workers control the means of production. In our terms, every employee is an owner of the company." For Onsale workers whose options entitle them to buy stocks at just a few dollars a share, the wild price changes of recent weeks could translate into tens of thousands of dollars in lost or gained wealth. Of course, low-level workers in the 200-employee company have just a fraction of the share options of a founding executive like Mr. Kaplan. Still, with even those employees generally having options on at least a few thousand shares, the potential rewards are great, and many workers here say it builds camaraderie that would not exist if everyone were on straight salary. The fluctuations in stock price for Onsale are by no means atypical, especially among Internet companies. But partly because stock options take effect over a set period of time, typically four years, worrying over today's price swings is a bit like worrying about the weather. There's no point to jumping out of windows when the stock plunges, or burning $1,000 bills when it soars -- what counts is what the stock will be worth the day an employee sells it. "Really, you don't hear employees talking a lot about changes in the stock price, and you don't have a lot of people clicking the refresh button on the browser all day to see what the latest trade is," said Diane Hunt, a spokeswoman for Yahoo Inc., the company based in Santa Clara, Calif., that markets a popular Internet search engine. In the last year, Yahoo stock has swayed from $17.0625 a share to $103.75. But, Ms. Hunt said: "You don't focus on it. Everyone here knows that if you run a good business, with sound fundamentals, and you stick to your plan, the stock price will take care of itself." Here at Onsale, many people said outside shareholders seemed to be more concerned about stock-price swings than those inside the headquarters, a drab two-story building in an industrial stretch of Menlo Park, where many workers are so busy they lack time to even decorate their office walls. Anytime the stock drops, said Brian K. Fawkes, vice president for corporate communications: "I get dozens of calls from shareholders, who want to know why is the stock going down and what are you going to do to make it go up? But not once has an employee come to me and asked why." Both Mr. Fawkes and Mr. Kaplan usually say that such swings are common and that the company and its workers remain focused on long-term growth. Once in a while, though, says the convivial Mr. Kaplan, author of "Start-Up: A Silicon Valley Adventure," a book about a prior, unsuccessful bid of his into pen-based computers, Onsale employees cannot resist offering callers a more basic explanation for why the stock price dropped: "There were more sellers than buyers today." Onsale is one of the main competitors in the rapidly growing on-line auction field, a sort of cyberbazaar in which visitors to the company's Web site (onsale.com) are offered a chance to bid on items (including, in a recent charity event, a date at Spago's in Los Angeles with Ms. California) while spectators on the site ("lurkers," in company lingo) watch the action. Many buyers type in comments along with their bids. "Stop bidding -- it's refurbished!" and "Please, let me have it -- need to get this for Grandma's birthday" were two recent entries. While the company is both a pioneer and current leader in on-line auctions, how it will fare in a competitive field where some experts expect annual sales to climb to $1 billion remains unclear. But even that is part of its appeal to employees. "It just seemed to me like a lot of really exciting things were happening with Internet companies," said Kristin Westland, 29, a human resource manager, who came here two years ago after spending several years as a struggling actress in Los Angeles (she did manage to land a bit part in a "Seinfeld" episode). "I was very tired of L.A., the insecurity of all that, the multitude of jobs, never knowing if a break was going to happen," she said. So she gave it up for the insecurity and the never knowing if a break is going to happen of Silicon Valley. Like many workers at the company, Ms. Westland has no children. Even as she described the excitement of trying to help make Onsale a dominant business in the auction field, she paused when asked whether she would feel the same way if she had a family to support. "Kids?" she said. "I don't know. Wow. You're really mortgaging your future at that point. I don't know. Kids would make it a whole new ball game." Still, for now, Onsale's employees seem very happy to put in 12- to 14-hour days for a lower salary than they might otherwise get -- as long as they retain the chance to strike it rich down the line. "When I first came here, I was like, 'Hey! Stock options!" said Ms. Rodriguez, who came to Onsale from a job selling compact disks and videos in a local store. "This is new to me, this is a first. I actually have stock options in something."
