title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
A New Twist on Air Mail For Unplugged Travelers
body: IN a few short years, email has become the pulse of the workplace and a tool that is often most missed when an Internet connection is unavailable. A wireless email service answers that need by enabling business travelers to send and receive electronic messages almost anywhere in the unitedstates. Pagenet, a leading paging company, last month introduced its Two-Way service built around the Page writer 2000, a palm-size 6.7-ounce device made by Motorola that opens like a clam to reveal a tiny screen in the upper shell and a keyboard below. The Pagewriter has no external antenna, no modem and no telephone jack, yet it sends and receives email almost instantly, and it does so from deep within steel-and-concrete buildings where cellular phones cannot receive a signal. No one is going to write a doctoral dissertation using this Lilliputian device, but it does offer a remarkable set of features and a lot of processing power, considering its size. In addition to sending and receiving Internet email, it includes an address book that can be used independently to store telephone numbers, addresses and personal identification numbers for other pagers that are capable of receiving text messages. It can also send faxes and is designed to be upgraded with more storage capacity and extra programs, including a calendar application and games. The basic model comes with one megabyte of flash memory, which is a type of memory that is used instead of a disk drive, and 256 kilobytes of RAM for a total of 1.25 megabytes, about one-eighth the memory of a typical palm computer but still enough to store dozens of messages and several hundred address-book entries. It comes with a docking station that doubles as a battery charger and connects the Pagewriter to a standard computer to transfer data between the two machines. That feature could not be tested for this review because, as of last week, the software for the personal computer end of the connection was not yet available. The nickle metal hydride battery is rated to last for seven days of standby, that is, waiting to receive a message. After its first charge, the battery in the model tested went dead at the end of three days. But performance improved with each charging; after the fourth, it lasted about five days, during which it was left on continuously and was used to send and receive several dozen messages a day. The Pagewriter uses Motorola's own operating system, called Flex, which cannot run programs written for other handheld devices. Still, the overall design is well-conceived and easily learned. A single home button returns the user to the Pagewriter's main menu of functions. The interface is point-and-click, although in place of a mouse, the device uses a pancake-shaped button called a "Navdisc" that, like a joystick, moves the cursor around the screen. The tab key jumps the cursor from function to function and can be used to cycle quickly through menus. With a little practice, navigation becomes second nature. The ultra-tiny keyboard -- about 3.5 inches by 2 inches -- is very difficult to get used to. But a user eventually discovers that the secret is to avoid the natural inclination to push the keys with the index finger of the right hand while holding the Pagewriter with the left. It is much more efficient, and surprisingly more comfortable, to punch out messages with two thumbs while holding the device with both hands. By necessity, the keyboard has the standard arrangement for letters but nonstandard placement for almost everything else. Yet the functions are logically designed. For example, with so little room, it would take the dexterity of a surgeon to hold the shift key while simultaneously depressing any other key. So the shift key has been designed to produce the uppercase character of the next key that is pressed. Another useful feature for email on the go, and a bit of compensation for the keyboard, is a list of 16 stock responses that pops up whenever the user replies to a received message. These range from a simple "yes" or "no" to "Can this wait?" and "On my way." The user can add custom responses to the list. For safety reasons, the Page writer can be turned off completely when boarding aircraft (required by Federal law) and can be set to receive-only mode for hospitals, clinics and other environments in which radio transmissions can interfere with sensitive equipment. When the Pagewriter is turned off or is unable to receive signals, the Pagenet system stores incoming messages, then delivers them as soon as the pager is turned back on or its signal is restored. The price for this convenience is relatively high. The Pagewriter 2000 costs about $360, although it can also be leased to own for $19 a month for two years. The Pagenet service plans are based on the number of characters sent and received. They range from $24.95 a month, which includes 8,000 characters (a little longer than this column) plus 12 cents for every character over that limit, to $129.95, which includes 60,000 characters plus 4 cents per 10 characters. This is more expensive than it seems because all messages are rounded up to the nearest 10 characters; thus, sending a simple "yes" counts as 10 characters against the monthly limit. Because this product is built around paging technology, each user's email address is his paging number -- minus the 800 -- plus "pagenet.net." This is a convenience in terms of remembering one's own address but is generally annoying to other people, since it is typically easier to remember an address built around a person's name than around a seemingly random seven-digit number. This is exacerbated by a major drawback to the Flex email system -- its inability to use any identification other than the email address of the user in the "From" field of the message header. Thus, instead of getting a message from, say, Fred Klein, the recipient gets a message from someone identified only as 5551234@pagenet.net. Nor can the user send a "subject" line, which might be used to note his or her identity. In a corporation that adopts this system, employees are going to find themselves staring at in-boxes full of messages from senders identified only as numbers. Still, that is a relatively minor flaw. Of greater concern is that on two occasions email sent to the device bounced back to the sender with a notice that no such email account existed. For all the convenience this system offers, reliability is far more crucial to business users, especially at the price of this service. Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: Santa Monica Seeking a Return To On-Line Civic Forum of Yore
body: When Santa Monica City Hall first offered on-line forums nine years ago, the major topic in this upscale community was the homeless. Donald Paschal, who was logging on from a public terminal, offered advice from a unique perspective. He would like to get a job, Mr. Paschal wrote, but he was dirty, he had nowhere to wash his clothes and nowhere to store his belongings. He was, in fact, homeless. People were astonished. They organized to help their on-line compatriot. Soon, they created a program called Swashlock, for showers, washers and lockers. That was in 1989. It was the first major civic initiative of the on-line group, officially known as the Santa Monica Public Electronic Network, or PEN. It was an experiment in electronic democracy that after nine years has become a widely studied model for scholars and municipal officials searching for ways to use on-line tools to foster citizenship. PEN started as an electronic bulletin board, a pre-Internet technology that allowed owners of computers with modems to read material posted by others and to send and receive text messages. The rapid spread of the Internet since 1994 expanded those early efforts. These days, however, local officials are struggling to recapture the enthusiasm that surrounded the network in its early days and to stimulate dwindling on-line discussions. They have a strong incentive: Santa Monica lost a major public forum last March, when the Copley Newspapers chain shut down The Outlook, the only daily newspaper in this city of 90,000 people. Santa Monica, city officials say, is uniquely suited to fill that void with on-line forums. Fifty percent of the households here have Internet access, and nearly 1 in 10 residents is a registered user of PEN. "Everyone in Santa Monica politics got up first thing in the morning and read The Outlook's letters to the editor," said City Councilman Ken Genser. Discussion also faded in PEN partly because the city's forums became plagued by personal attacks and ranting. City officials announced a test solution on Sept. 1. They said the League of Women Voters had agreed to moderate the PEN forums on candidates and issues through the November election. The next step, city officials say, depends on what happens with the moderated forums. Many residents say they hope that interest in the city election will revive the on-line forum. Its early successes in creating equal access to policy makers on line have not been forgotten, nor has the homeless man who so influenced PEN's early days. Mr. Paschal left the city years ago and became a cable talk-show host, but in 1995, he logged on and left a message on PEN for his old friends in Santa Monica. "Just call me EX-homeless," it said.

title:
Compressed Data;
Seeking Compromises On Internet Domain
body: With the Clinton Administration planning to end Federal financing for the management of Internet domain names on Sept. 30, the disparate forces struggling to constitute the global network's first legitimate governing body remain divided on issues trivial and profound. As negotiations continue behind the scenes, the Berkman Center for Internet and Society at Harvard University has canceled a planned compromise session for next weekend that had been set at the behest of one coalition that has sponsored a series of international meetings on the subject this summer. "We're not convinced it's a productive thing to do," said Joe Sims, a lawyer who is advising Jon Postel, the man who has handled the administrative end of the Internet's address system for the last 30 years under the auspices of the federally financed Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, or IANA. To replace IANA, Mr. Postel has proposed a new administrative body that would balance the interests of trademark holders, domain name registrars, national governments and individual Internet users -- and still allow engineers to keep the addresses straight. His approach has been embraced by the Internet's technical community. But Network Solutions Inc., the company based in Herndon, Va., that currently holds an exclusive contract with the U.S. Government to allocate the most popular domains -- including addresses ending in ".com" -- has declined to sign on. So has the International Trademark Association. Among the points of dispute are whether the new group would be likely to favor adding many more domain names, which trademark holders oppose, or to impose regulations on registrars -- something Network Solutions opposes. Still, Ira Magaziner, the senior White House adviser on Internet issues, said he was optimistic that a compromise would be reached soon. "In any negotiation," he said, "if you get things down to two factions you can lock them in a room and push them to have an agreement."   AMY HARMON Graphic   Photo: IANA oversees on-line addresses.

title: In-House Competition From Web News Team
body: The next time Michael Jackson rumors start to swirl, word spreads of a Hollywood murder-suicide or Matt Damon changes his hair style, E! Entertainment will probably dispatch not one, but two teams of Hollywood news hounds. One will come from the cable channel, the other from its sister Web site, E! Online, and company executives will not mind seeing the hounds race to get the exclusive. "They're trying to scoop each other all the time," said Lee Masters, president and chief executive of E! Entertainment. "It keeps everybody on their toes." Mr. Masters said he did not intend the E! site (www.eonline.com) to compete with the network so much as to complement it, but he does intend for the on-line entity to have its own identity. Unlike some Internet sites that are linked to television programs or even entire networks, Mr. Masters wants E! Online to be something more. Whereas E! Entertainment has sought to build its television programming on a shoestring budget, the company has spent more freely to build up the Web site, Mr. Masters said, though he declined to discuss specific figures. Companies that want to stake a claim on the Internet need to do so aggressively, and immediately, he said, and that costs money. "You have to have mouth-watering content and you have to have an incredibly seductive environment," Mr. Masters said. "You have to stake out that territory now." He is less effusive about E! Online's revenue, which he declined to disclose though he concedes that like most Internet companies, it is losing money. E! went on the Web in August 1996 in a partnership with Cnet, a new-media company based in San Francisco. The partnership ended a year later, when E! paid a reported $10 million for Cnet's 50 percent of the venture. At the time, Cnet said it wanted to focus on its core businesses and E! decided it wanted to own its own brand on the Internet. Today, 55 full-time E! employees work on the site, 40 of whom are producing the content -- a daily helping of Hollywood, including updated news, gossip, Webcasts of movie premieres, and features like "Stalkers," a three-part article on fans who stalk celebrities. To be sure, not all the Hollywood scoops are exactly the stuff of the Lehrer Newshour. "We identified that Matt Damon was hot back in 1996," one staffer said, touting the site's accomplishments. "We broke the fact that Blues Traveler was leaving the Horde Festival." The site appears to be getting heavy traffic, with roughly two million visitors a month, according to @plan, a Gallup Organization unit that tracks on-line traffic. And a June 1998 survey by Relevant Knowledge Inc. ranked E! Online as the 23d most heavily trafficked news and entertainment site over all, placing it above ABC.com and MTV.com, and ahead of its direct competitors, which include Entertainment Weekly (www.pathfinder.com/ew), the News Corporation's TVgen.com site, and Entertainment Asylum (www.asylum.com). E! Online is also one of the anchor entertainment tenants on America Online and offers entertainment programming for broadband Internet services that provide access and content over television cable lines, including At Home Network. Mark Mooradian, a group director at the Internet research firm Jupiter Communications, said one of E! Online's strengths was its ability to complement the E! Entertainment cable channel. E! Entertainment cites figures from @plan indicating that nearly two-thirds of the visitors to its Web site also watch its TV programs. That gives Mr. Masters confidence in his long-term plan to make E! a player in the industry's oft-predicted convergence of television and cyberspace. "We want to get our grubby little paws on every aspect of this business that we can," he said.

title: Witness Lists Suggest Moves By Microsoft And the U.S.
body: With the filing of witness lists on Friday night, the Government and the Microsoft Corporation offered the first glimpse of their courtroom strategies in the historic antitrust trial scheduled to begin later this month. The Government will portray Microsoft as an information-age monopolist with anticompetitive practices that are wide-ranging and that began long before anyone heard of the Internet. Microsoft plans to mount its defense by putting eight top executives on the stand, but with one conspicuous absence -- William H. Gates, the Microsoft chairman, who is not on the witness list. The 12-person witness list for the Justice Department and 20 states suing Microsoft suggests a broadening of the evidence it intends to marshal to make its case. Its industry witnesses include executives from the Intel Corporation, the International Business Machines Corporation and the Boeing Company, all of whom are expected to offer evidence of what the plaintiffs say are Microsoft tactics that unfairly curb competition. None were mentioned in the complaint filed in May by the Government and states. "With this witness list, the Government is trying to point to a broader pattern of anticompetitive behavior over many years and to put that long history in the record," said Robert Litan, a former senior Justice Department official who is now at the Brookings Institution. "This is an effort to lift the court's nose out of the details and look at the broader picture." To help fill out that broader picture, the Government will call John Soyring, vice president of personal software products at I.B.M. His history with Microsoft goes back nearly a decade, when he was a manager on I.B.M.'s OS/2 operating system. At the time, the two companies were ostensibly partners in the operating system market with an early plan calling for Microsoft's Windows being developed as a basic system and I.B.M.'s OS/2 evolving into a high-performance operating system. The partnership broke up, the two companies became rivals and Microsoft prevailed. Another industry witness for the Government is Steve McGeady, an Intel vice president. He was present at meetings in 1995 when Mr. Gates reportedly pressed Intel to curb its development of multimedia and Internet software, and to limit its support for the Netscape Communications Corporation, the early front-runner and Microsoft's main rival in the market for software used to browse the World Wide Web. To further broaden its evidence, the Government wants to show the court that Microsoft can press big companies to not purchase software from its rivals. To provide the perspective of a big corporate customer, the Government plans to call a Boeing executive, Scott Vesey. The other industry witnesses for the Government and states include James Barksdale, the president of Netscape, whose battle with Microsoft in the browser market is the central focus of the antitrust case; David Colburn, a senior vice president of America Online Inc., and William Harris, president of Intuit Inc., the personal finance software maker. In the America Online and Intuit cases, the Government contends that Microsoft unfairly used its market muscle to get both companies to choose Microsoft's browser over the Netscape offering. A Justice Department official characterized his side's witness list as a "Who's Who of America's technology leaders." But the Microsoft view is that the Government and states' witnesses are a "sign that they are running away from their original case," said Mark Murray, a company spokesman. A central accusation in the case filed in May, Mr. Murray noted, was that Microsoft's licensing contracts with personal computer makers were anticompetitive. The contracts, the Government said, limited personal computer makers in purchasing software from rival software companies and denied them the freedom to select what Internet services were featured on the desktop screens of the machines they sold. "But the Government did not call a single PC maker as a witness," Mr. Murray said. One witness on the Government's list works for a major PC maker, I.B.M., but the I.B.M. executive is expected to testify mainly about Microsoft's tactics in the software business. An industry witness for Microsoft is an executive for a major personal computer maker, John Rose, a senior vice president for the Compaq Computer Corporation, who is expected to testify that his company's contracts with Microsoft do not hinder its business. Absent from the Microsoft witness list is Mr. Gates, known as a brilliant and energetic executive who is involved in every important decision made at the company. Mr. Gates was omitted from the witness list, Mr. Murray said, because the eight executives included were those on the "front lines of each of the issues raised in the Government's case; Bill Gates was not as directly involved in these issues." Yet the Justice Department and states contend that Mr. Gates is the central figure in Microsoft's strategy in the Internet software market, and his memos and email correspondence are a key part of the evidence in the case. One person who was present at the recent videotaped deposition of Mr. Gates said that Microsoft's lawyers might have determined that putting him on the stand could hurt them more than it helped. "He's so argumentative and contentious," this person said, "that Gates kind of took himself out of contention." During the deposition, Mr. Gates not only professed to many memory lapses but, this person said, disputed seemingly innocuous facts like definitions of computing terms that appeared in Microsoft's own documents. Mr. Gates, this person said, also professed not to know the level of Microsoft's sales and profits and to not know the share of the operating system market held by Microsoft's Windows. In addition to industry witnesses, both sides will call economic and technical experts. On the Government side, the technology experts include David Farber, a University of Pennsylvania computer scientist and an Internet pioneer; Edward Felton, a computer scientist at Princeton University, and Glenn Weadock, president of Independent Software Inc. Its economic experts include Franklin Fisher, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist who was a witness for I.B.M. in its antitrust confrontation with the Government; David Sibley, a University of Texas economist, and Frederick Warren-Bolton, a former chief economist of the Justice Department's antitrust division. For Microsoft, its economic witness will be Richard Schmalensee, an M.I.T. economist, and its technical expert will be Michael Dertouzos, director of M.I.T.'s computer science laboratory.

title:
Hey New York: Listen Up! 12 Ideas From (Gasp) Out of Town;
Weaving More Threads Into the Web
body: Adam L. Barsky, the director of the Mayor's Office of Operations, is proud of newyork City's on-line efforts. "We are really the model for the country when you look at what we've done with technology," Mr. Barsky said. Enter the city's official Web site (www.ci.nyc.ny.us), and you'll be greeted by a photograph of lower Manhattan taken by none other than Mayor Giuliani. The site provides information about the Mayor's office and city agencies, updates on city events and attractions, schedules of public hearings, traffic advisories and the like. There are also complaint forms that let visitors to the site gripe on line to appropriate officials about everything from cable television to pay phones to street lights. Want to nominate a city landmark for historic preservation, pick up a voter registration form, apply for a dog license or adopt a highway? You can get the forms on the Web site, print them out and mail them in. But advocates for efficient government say newyork could learn a lot from other cities that have found new ways to use the Internet to expedite delivery of services. "There are certain things newyork does reasonably well with their on-line approaches, but they certainly don't lead the field in this," said Richard Delaney, president of the Delaney Policy Group, a research and consulting company in Washington that recently did a study for the Citizens Budget Commission on high-tech revenue collection in various cities across the unitedstates. What newyork does well, Mr. Delaney said, is provide information on line. "What they don't do well," he said, "is to respond to the interactive possibilities of the Web." The study found that newyork could save up to $10 million a year by collecting taxes, fees and parking fines and issuing business licenses and building permits on line. Last March, Indianapolis began accepting credit card payments for parking tickets on line. Since February 1997, Houston has allowed on-line filing of building permits. In Kern County, Calif., a private company hired by the county has put a data base of property-tax assessments on the Web. If taxpayers want to challenge their assessments, they can use the data base to compare their properties with others. newyork City does operate 40 kiosks around the city that provide information about tax collection procedures and allow residents to pay parking tickets and real estate taxes with a credit card. But will the city consider offering some on-line conveniences available elsewhere? Mr. Barsky, who said he found the Citizen Budget Commission report "useless," observed that the city had already been looking into several ideas suggested in it. For example, he said, newyorkers will soon be able to pay parking tickets on line.   NINA SIEGAL

title:
THE MARKETS IN TURMOIL: THE I.P.O. MARKET;
Many Newcomers Are Grounded by Turbulence
body: A PEEK at the Equity New Issue Calendar on a Bloomberg terminal last week read like a departure monitor at a fogged-in airport. "Postponed." "Delayed." "Canceled." Indeed, as stocks struggled to climb back after Monday's selloff, not one company ventured onto the public markets last week. "Right now I would say the window is closed," said Andy Kessler, a co-founder of Velocity Capital Management in Palo Alto, Calif. John E. Fitzgibbon Jr., editor of The IPO Reporter, a newsletter, agreed. "What's going on in this market?" he asked. "Nothing, absolutely nothing. The hurricane shutters are down." Four companies that postponed planned stock or units offerings last week were Datalink, a maker of data storage devices; Galacticomm Technologies, an on-line communications software maker; Gary Player Golf, a golf club marketer, and Sunbelt Automotive Group, a car retailer. Datalink, Gary Player and Galacticomm said late last week that they would wait until the second half of September before considering an initial offering. A spokeswoman for Sunbelt did not say when it would reapproach the market. In fact, last week's shutdown follows a month of dismal fortune for I.P.O.'s. The Securities Data Company said that only 19 came to market in August, raising a total of $1.33 billion. By contrast, there were 49 in August 1997, raising $2.86 billion. And even as recently as July, 46 companies managed to break out of the gate, raising $3.89 billion. Prices for recent offerings are grounded, too. According to Mr. Fitzgibbon, as of Aug. 31 only two of the I.P.O.'s in the month were trading over their offering prices: Jenkon International, a software concern, and Geocities, the Internet company that helps individuals create their own Web sites. Mr. Fitzgibbon said the 19 stocks that went public in August lost 20.4 percent of their value by month's end, on average, with the worst performance turned in by Pilot Network Services. That company, which provides secure Internet access services for on-line businesses, was initially priced at $14 on Aug. 11, opened at $13 and closed on Friday at $6.875. "August was a blood bath," Mr. Fitzgibbon said. And even those lucky holders of Geocities and Jenkon were put through the wringer. Geocities jumped to $37.3125 from its offering price of $17 on Aug. 11, peaked at $51.375 the next day and closed on Friday at less than half that amount. Jenkon rose to $5.53125 on Aug. 11 from its offering price of $5, hit a high of $6.375 on Aug. 26 and closed at $5.75 on Friday. Among the biggest losers in the current selloff are investors who signed so-called lock-up agreements, agreeing that they will not sell their holdings for 180 days. Many who did saw their holdings rise and then were forced to sit on their hands as their positions collapsed in the last few months. "All private-round investors are being asked to sign these agreements these days," Mr. Kessler said. But when markets tumble, he added, the lock-ups can cause newly issued stocks to sink out of sight once anxious investors flee. "In the current market, anyone who's locked up is going to be out of luck," he said. So what does September hold for prospective I.P.O. investors? The period after Labor Day has traditionally been popular for initial offerings, and until recently, the calendar for the fall looked full. At the end of August, for example, The IPO Reporter had more than 70 offerings on its September list. Mr. Kessler, however, said he believed half of those prospective I.P.O.'s would be postponed. The current lineup, meanwhile, is weighted heavily toward very small companies, with scant operating histories, trying to take their stocks public without the backing of large, well-known underwriters. Underwriters' support can be crucial in determining an offering's success. I.P.O. experts still see a number of high-profile, potentially well-grounded deals on the horizon. But they say it is unlikely that any one deal will lift the I.P.O. market out of its doldrums. And that includes the much-anticipated proposed offering by Goldman, Sachs & Company. The offering is expected to bring in $2.5 billion or more, although details are still being worked out. A spokesman for Goldman said the firm's plans remain unchanged. Mr. Fitzgibbon predicted that Goldman, Sachs "is going to be a class act onto itself." Of course, if the market picks up significantly this month, the I.P.O. outlook will likely follow suit, regardless of what Goldman does, analysts say. Mr. Fitzgibbon, for one, thinks a new round of internet companies will be going public in the coming months. Indeed, such offerings have fared better than those of other companies in the market's downturn. But don't hold your breath. A survey of the top 15 underwriters by Bloomberg Financial Markets showed that none of them planned I.P.O.'s for this week. title:
VIEWPOINT;
More Proof for the Dow Theory
body: ON Aug. 5, early in a frenzied month for the stock market, there were no apocalyptic headlines heralding the significance of the 299-point drop the previous day in the Dow Jones industrial average. But there should have been. That was the day when the Dow theory -- arguably the oldest market-timing system still in use today -- flashed a sell signal, announcing that a bear market had begun. To those who were alert to it, that signal looked awfully good as the August correction went deeper and deeper. And during the 512-point plunge last Monday, the theory looked positively brilliant. Its followers, prominently including subscribers to Richard Russell's Dow Theory Letters and Chuck Carlson's Dow Theory Forecasts, both market newsletters, have spared themselves a decline (so far) of nearly 1,000 points in the Dow industrials. The theory is named for Charles Dow, a founder of Dow Jones & Company. But it was his associate, William Peter Hamilton, who struggled in a series of Wall Street Journal editorials between 1902 and his death in 1929 to codify the idea and use it to time market gyrations. As Hamilton formulated it, the Dow theory is a trend-following system that focuses on the Dow industrial and Dow transportation averages, which reflect important but distinct segments of the economy and often diverge. He believed that investors should not bet on the market's direction unless it was confirmed by trends in both averages. There are many trend-following systems out there. What sets the Dow theory apart is the way it negotiates market reversals. To know if a bull market had ended, for example, Hamilton would pay close attention to the averages' behavior after each significant correction. (Unlike modern analysts, Hamilton did not insist that a decline exceed 10 percent to earn that label; the gentle decline from April to June this year would qualify.) A sell signal would be generated if two conditions were met in the weeks after a correction. The first condition: At least one of the two averages must fail to surpass its pre-correction high. This requirement was met this past July.  The industrials were reaching record highs, but the transports were still below their April peak. The second condition: Both averages must then sink below their lows in the previous correction. This requirement was satisfied on Aug. 4, when the industrials fell below their mid-June correction low. The transports had done so on July 29. Even before its recent success, the Dow theory was beginning to receive some grudging new respect in academic circles. A number of finance professors have discovered, to their amazement, that it seems to work. One reason that academics of years past so readily dismissed the theory is that it was subject to endless interpretation and revision. How long and deep a correction is necessary to set up the conditions for a sell signal? How much time should the averages be given to surpass pre-correction highs? Unfortunately, Hamilton wrote in editorial-page prose, not detailed explanatory text.  Academics dismissed the theory as no more helpful than tea leaves. THIS deficiency was overcome recently by Stephen Brown of newyork University and William Goetzmann and Alok Kumar of Yale. They utilized neural networks -- artificial-intelligence software adept at pattern recognition -- to analyze Hamilton's work, examining chart patterns of the industrial and transportation averages before each of his buy and sell signals between 1902 and 1929. Then the professors analyzed the averages since 1929 in Hamiltonian terms to see where his buy and sell signals would have fallen if he were still alive. The results, published in the summer issue of the Journal of Finance, are astounding. A portfolio that followed the theory's signals from 1929 until today, buying and selling shares in a hypothetical index fund with no transaction costs, would have outperformed a simple buy-and-hold strategy by about two percentage points a year. But there's more. The theory-guided portfolio would have incurred one-third less volatility, or risk, than the market itself. That's a particularly potent combination. All well and good, but what if you can't load the latest artificial-intelligence software on your PC? Don't despair: Several investment newsletters are good at the pattern recognition needed to apply the theory. Mr. Russell's Dow Theory Letters has the best record among devotees of the theory tracked by the Hulbert Financial Digest. Mr. Russell's timing lagged behind a buy-and-hold system over the last 18 years by an average of 2.6 percentage points a year. But his advice was so much less risky than the market itself that, on a risk-adjusted basis, he actually beat a buy-and-hold strategy. Granted, trailing the market by 2.6 points a year may not seem all that alluring. But Mr. Russell's experience is right in line with what the professors found in their 70-year test: The Dow theory beats the market by the greatest margin during bear markets and shows least favorable results during bull markets. The theory is quite conservative -- willing, essentially, to leave a bit of money on the table in return for not getting caught holding the bag. How long will this bear market last, and how deep will it go? Alas, Hamilton himself said his theory was silent on that issue. But Mr. Russell is willing to venture that this one could be very severe indeed. "Every primary bear market in history has wiped out at least half of the preceding bull market's gains," he said. "I mark this great bull market as having started in 1974 at Dow 577, with the recent high this year at Dow 9,337. If the Dow was to wipe out just half its 1974-98 gains, the Dow would decline to 4,960 or lower." Those would be sobering words coming from any adviser. They're especially so coming from Mr. Russell, who has been editing his newsletter since 1958 -- longer than many mutual fund managers have been alive. And his warning becomes especially compelling now that the Dow theory enjoys newfound academic respectability.

title: John Mortimer, Times Executive, And Wife, Hilda, Die in Crash
body: John Mortimer, 75, a former senior vice president of The newyork Times for personnel and industrial relations, and his wife of 22 years, Hilda, 69, died in the Swissair plane crash on Wednesday. They lived in Stamford, Conn. They were on their way to a vacation in France, their family said. Howard Bishow, a retired senior vice president of The newyork Times for operations, said yesterday that Mr. Mortimer played the dominant role on behalf of the newspaper in negotiations before and during every strike while he was with The Times during the 1960's and 70's. Mr. Mortimer was born in Bronxville, N.Y. He served in the Army Air Force in the South Pacific during World War II and graduated from Williams College in 1948. After working in industrial relations at The Daily News, he joined The newyork Times in 1962 as industrial relations manager and held a succession of industrial relations and personnel positions. From 1973 to 1981, he was senior vice president for personnel and industrial relations. He later held other positions, including senior vice president and assistant to the general manager of the newspaper and, finally, assistant to the president of the newyork Times Company before retiring in 1983. His first wife, the former Harriet Watson, died in 1974 after more than 20 years of marriage. Mr. Mortimer's survivors include two daughters, Claire Mortimer of Berkeley, Calif., and Katherine Mortimer of Albany, Calif.; a son, Stewart of Tucson, Ariz.; a brother, Donald, of Riverside, Conn.; and a sister, Mary Hillegas, also of Riverside. Mrs. Mortimer, the former Hilda Barnes Belcher, divorced Robert S. Huffman in 1972. Mrs. Mortimer's survivors include a daughter, Susan Parker Boal of Salisbury, Conn.; a son, Philip B. Huffman of Williston, Vt.; four sisters, Marjorie S. Belcher of Washington, Elizabeth B. Rogers of Champaign, Ill., and Helen C. Belcher and Ruth S. Belcher, both of Plymouth, Mass.; and a brother, Edward L. Belcher of Rochester, N.Y. Mr. and Mrs. Mortimer are survived by seven grandchildren. title: Desperately Seeking Susan OR Suzie NOT Sushi
body: IF the World Wide Web ever adopted a theme song, it could do worse than picking "I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For." Searching the Web is the most popular on-line activity -- and often the most frustrating. In June, more than half of the top 10 most-visited domains were Web search sites, according to an Internet metering service, Media Metrix. But how many of the people visiting those sites found what they were looking for right away? Not most, according to Karin Rex, whose Pennsylvania-based company Computer Ease conducts Internet search classes. "Most people type in words and get a bazillion hits," Ms. Rex said. "Some of the ones on the first page may pertain to what they're looking for, but most of them won't." On the surface, it ought to be simple. You're looking for Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, you enter those three words, and assuming it's somewhere on the Internet (and that's a pretty safe assumption), the search site gives you a list of relevant Web pages. Right? Not so, Ms. Rex said. "You'll get sites about the Lincoln Continental and vacations in Gettysburg, and real-estate sites listing addresses," she said, "but often, nothing about Lincoln's Gettysburg Address." Danny Sullivan, editor of the Search Engine Watch newsletter, agrees. His publication and Web site (www.searchenginewatch.com) monitorthe world of Web searching, and despite improvements over the past two years, he said, he still sees problems. "They've gotten better, faster and easier to use, but search engines have got a long way to go," Mr. Sullivan said. "They're poor for people who are doing really basic searches. Enter 'Disney' or 'travel,' and it's a crapshoot whether they'll get the Disney site or any good travel sites." One search site could provide 10 top results of pure gold, while another serves up either nothing or dross. Why is there a difference in results? Because there are three basic components of all search engines, and while there is often a lot of overlap, no two engines are exactly the same. One element is the index of Web sites or Web pages that your search roots through; each search site collects its information and updates its database differently. Each site's search function works differently, too, and the order in which the results are sorted is usually based on a proprietary algorithm that no company would be willing to share. To make things harder, search sites generally do not do a good job of explaining how they work. Few people understand, for example, that Yahoo is fundamentally different from search sites like Hotbot, Alta Vista and Infoseek. Yahoo is not really a search engine but rather a Web directory, compiled by humans who classify Web sites under headings. The others are Web search engines, which use software agents called crawlers or spiders to index the contents of individual Web pages, then follow links to other pages. Web directories like Yahoo and Web search engines may look the same, but each type of site is good for finding different types of information. The first step in creating more effective searches is picking the right search site for the job. "If people are doing a general search," Mr. Sullivan said, "they should start off at Yahoo or a Yahoo-like directory like Snap or Look Smart." A directory-style search provides two ways to research broad topics: dive through a list of broad topics by clicking on the appropriate links or fill out a search box to find listings. But directory searches are less effective when looking for specific information -- things like the author of a book, the complete text of the Declaration of Independence or research on drug treatments for a medical condition. For this kind of information, search engines like Hotbot and Alta Vista are the way to go. Because they search an index of keywords drawn by spiders from millions of Web pages, the chances are greater that they will find obscure terms in obscure Web pages. There's a third kind of search site, one that includes popular sites like Metacrawler, Ask Jeeves and Dogpile. These sites -- also called metasearch tools -- don't maintain any kind of index of their own but instead issue search requests to fistfuls of other Web search sites. When Yahoo, Hotbot, Alta Vista and the like return their results, the metasearch site collects them onto a single Web page for display. Because no two search sites index exactly the same set of Web pages, metasearch tools give you a wider scope of results -- but it's worth remembering that more does not necessarily equal better. What really counts is relevant results that are sorted in a relevant order. And that's the rub. Simply picking one of two or three types of sites to search from is no guarantee of good results. Brad Hill, the author of "World Wide Web Searching for Dummies" (IDG), says most search sites deliver too much information. "Search engines do a good job on indexing," he said. But because of that, they deliver more than you want. So when you're faced with several hundred thousand results over dozens of pages, what should you do? "Don't go past the first page of results," Mr. Hill said. "If it doesn't have something of interest, you've probably entered the wrong search string." Most people could get much more relevant results with a few simple tricks for constructing a search "string" -- the words you enter in the search box. The most obvious is to type in several relevant words instead of just one or two. In general, the fewer words you enter, the more general your results will be. But not every search engine returns the most relevant results first -- which leads to lots of pages about Lincoln Continentals instead of Lincoln's most famous speech. To give a search engine more instructions, it helps to master a site's instructions, which search techies call "operators." "Search operators tell a search engine how to interpret your key words," Mr. Hill said. "Words like 'and' or 'not,' and quotation marks can really narrow down search results." And it's narrowing the results -- giving fewer, better pages -- that really counts. "The simplest techniques, like using quotes around a phrase, help the most people," Ms. Rex said. The result of slapping quotation marks around two or more words is remarkable. Type in "Gettysburg Address," with quotation marks, and you tell the search engine to look for a phrase instead of two separate words -- knocking irrelevant vacation sites and real-estate listings out of your top 20 results. That trick works in many search sites, including Yahoo, Alta Vista, Hotbot, Excite and Infoseek. Not all search sites use the same rules for making better searches. Most will let you exclude some terms from your results -- which is great if you're trying to search for, say, the gross national product of Jordan and keep getting sports sites about Michael Jordan. Exclude the word Michael, and you'll trim a few hundred thousand irrelevant results right away. But how you exclude words from a search depends on the search site. In the regular search forms at Yahoo, Excite and Alta Vista, for example, you put a minus sign before the word (-Michael). But in Hotbot, you click on the More Search Options button and select Must Not Contain in the Word Filter section. It is hardly surprising that many people find Web searching confusing and inefficient. So how are you supposed to know which rules apply to which search site? Karin Rex includes a simple piece of advice in lesson one of her Internet search class. "Read the instructions," she said. "The only way to learn the inner workings of each site is to read the help files or frequently asked questions document. Most people don't even realize there are help files, so they'll never be able to take advantage of advanced features." Sage advice though this is, search sites tend to use jargon that's not easily understood by the uninitiated. A single mention of Boolean operators is enough to send many would-be searchers into a tailspin. (Named for a 19th-century British mathematician, George Boole, Boolean operators are words like AND, OR and NOT that many advanced search sites use to make searches more precise.) But in truth, Boolean logic is not hard to learn -- and in many cases, search sites label it with easy-to-understand phrasing like "search for ANY of these terms" or "search for these terms as a phrase." There are options for sufferers of Boolean anxiety, though. One site with a novel approach is Ask Jeeves. When you enter a vague query, Ask Jeeves will throw back a series of questions. From the single-word query "travel," for example, it comes back with 10 possible interpretations of what you might be looking for, including "Where can I rent a cellular phone in a foreign country?" and "Where can I get tourist information about foreign countries?" Another approach is to reduce the scope of your search. Searching the entire Web for a highly specialized piece of information isn't always the best way. For one thing, many Web search engines index only Web pages in HTML format, and many Web pages are generated from databases that search engine spiders can't penetrate. To uncover information from these databases, you usually need to use the search engine provided at the database's Web site. There are literally thousands of these highly specialized Web search tools across the Web. So how can you find these specialized search tools? About 3,000 of them are listed at Internet Sleuth (www.isleuth.com) in Yahoo-style directories. But unlike Yahoo's directories, Internet Sleuth's include only searchable sites and include the search form to issue a query right away. No matter what advice you get, however, you discover the best search techniques by experimenting. Danny Sullivan of Search Engine Watch uses all the major search sites frequently, and refuses to name his favorite site. His reason? "Judging the results is subjective," Mr. Sullivan said. "If your friend raves about a site and you don't like it, try another. Use whatever you find gives you the answers." Graphic   Photo: A TOUR GUIDE -- Karin Rex teaches classes on how to conduct searches on the Internet. (Sal DiMarco Jr. for The New York Times)(pg. G7)  Charts: "A Field Guide to Web Search Sites"  Yahoo www.yahoo.com A human-compiled directory of Web sites, Yahoo doesn't help you search for the contents of individual Web pages. It's excellent for researching broad general topics, but tends to return too many results, many of them irrelevant.  Hotbot www.hotbot.com This is the search site of Wired magazine, whose search engine Inktomi also powers Snap.com's and Yahoo's Web searches. It is an excellent tool for finding specific information. In addition to a thorough and up-to-date index, it provides an easy interface for constructing precise search queries -- but this requires extra effort up front.  Alta Vista www.altavista.net Another excellent tool for exhaustive and precise searches, Alta Vista makes it harder than Hotbot does for beginners to construct precise queries, but once you've mastered its search syntax, it's quick and easy to use. Its results, however, can include many duplicates.  Excite www.excite.com Good for searches on broad general topics, Excite adds interesting extras like a simultaneous search of the Web, news headlines, sports scores and company information -- and groups the relevant results on a single page. Some reviewers have complained that the search results aren't always relevant.  Infoseek www.infoseek.com When searching for Web pages, news stories and Usenet postings, Infoseek produces very accurate and relevant results. But according to Search Engine Watch (www.searchenginewatch.com), it has a much smaller index of Web pages than many others.  Lycos www.lycos.com Lycos provides a good selection of advanced search capabilities, like the ability to search for specific media types (JPEG files, Java scripts and so on). Its advanced search, Lycos Pro, provides even more options. But general Web searches can produce checkered results. Also, Lycos's index of Web pages is small.  Metacrawler www.metacrawler.com This is a metasearch site, simultaneously searching Yahoo, Excite, and five other search engines, then aggregating the results. It's excellent for getting a quick hit of what's out there. But if you don't see what you want in the results, its limited search options make it tough to issue really precise queries.  Dogpile www.dogpile.com This metasearch site can go through 13 Web search engines, more than two dozen on-line news services or other types of sources, and sorts the results by the search engine that found them. While this is not the most useful presentation if you just want the facts, it's a good way to check which search engine works best for you.  Ask Jeeves www.askjeeves.com An excellent beginner's site that's also good for anyone's general queries, Ask Jeeves leads you through questions to help narrow your search, and also simultaneously searches six other search sites for relevant Web pages. Its ability to interpret natural language queries makes it easy to learn but also makes constructing precise queries difficult.  Northern Light www.nlsearch.com In addition to its index of Web pages, Northern Light also searches through pay-per-view articles from periodicals and books not generally available on the Web. It sorts its results into topic headings, which can prove very useful.  Internet Sleuth www.isleuth.com Internet Sleuth is a 3,000-strong collection of specialized on-line databases, which can also simultaneously search up to six other search sites for Web pages, news and other types of information. It's excellent for highly specialized searches in any subjects in its detailed directory -- but the metasearch results aren't sorted intuitively.  PHILIPPE KAHN President, Starfish Software My Favorite Search Engine: Excite and Yahoo I usually use Excite or Yahoo when I have a good idea about the category: I think that Excite's relevance ranking is very good. I use Yahoo as much as Excite, though. It's really a tossup. When it comes to an extensive keyword search, I tend to use Alta Vista or Hotbot.  DYLAN TWENEY Net Prophet columnist for Infoworld, a management information journal My Favorite Search Engine: Hotbot I used Alta Vista for a while, then it seemed to be returning too much stuff. Now I favor Hotbot. It's fast and its results seem more up to date. Also if you want to fine-tune your searches, it has some great search options.  RON WHITE Net Kahuna columnist for PC Computing and author of How Computers Work (Que, 1998). My Favorite Search Engine: Web Compass (Quarterdeck, $49.95) I don't use search engines so much as software on my PC that searches all the engines. Web Compass searches places I would never have thought of, like Brazil Online and Mr. Showbiz and places I've never heard of. It handles Boolean searches pretty well, and I get back a database I can search on my own PC. Another thing I've been experimenting with is Copernic 98. It's shareware that does the same thing, but it divides the searches into categories like news events, so you can concentrate your searches while spreading the scope.  KARIN REX Technology trainer and author of Internet Search Techniques (Ziff-Davis Education, 1998) My Favorite Search Engine: Alta Vista Alta Vista is my favorite search engine because I have studied its help files and I understand how to use some of its more advanced search techniques. Therefore I usually can find what I need. If I can't find what I am looking for, I then turn to a metasite search engine. Dogpile, for example, sends your query to 25 different Internet search tools.  ROGER EBERT Film critic and Yahoo Internet Life magazine's "Critical Eye" columnist My Favorite Search Engine: Metacrawler Why start there? Because I can search them all at once, natch -- Alta Vista, Infoseek, Excite, Yahoo -- all with one query. Or I may go to Northern Light, which organizes the findings into folders and is therefore easier to use than engines with a long list of hits.  BRAD HILL Author, "World Wide Web Searching for Dummies" (IDG, 1997) My Favorite Search Engine: Yahoo I'll go to different engines according to my needs, but I start with Yahoo. I consider it the most valuable site on the Web. Yahoo doesn't do any editorializing and hand-holding -- the results you get from it are more of an overview. It can be overwhelming, but it's a good place to start.  "Steps to Smart Searching"  PICK YOUR SITE No one site is good for every search. Search directories like Yahoo and Lycos's Top 5% are good for researching general topics. Search engines like Hotbot and Alta Vista are better for very specific information. Metasearch sites like Dogpile and Metacrawler cast the net a little wider on searches for specific information by using more than one search engine.  PICK YOUR WORDS Most search engines do a poor job when seeking out a single word. Increase the number of words to increase the scope of your search. And pick the words well -- many search engines ignore common words like 'the,' 'and' and 'Web.'  USE THE PHRASE THAT PAYS Enter the two words Strawberry Fields in a search box, and you could get results as diverse as W. C. Fields and strawberry shortcake. Yahoo, Alta Vista, Hotbot and others recognize words in quotes -- Strawberry Fields -- as a phrase. Metacrawler and others provide phrase searching as an option.  TAKE ADVANTAGE OF THE OPERATORS Most search sites use code words or symbols called operators to make searches more precise. The operators vary from site to site, but the common ones are AND, OR, NOT, quotation marks and the plus and minus signs (see the table below for details on how to use them).  USE BROWSER CLICK TRICKS When checking out results, view them in a new browser window so you can quickly return to the results page without clicking the browser's Back button. In most browsers, you can open a link in a new browser window by holding down the Shift key while clicking on the link. And if a page fails to load the first time you click on a link, try clicking again.  CHECK YOUR SPELLING Many Web sites are riddled with spelling errors, but for the ones that are worth finding, correct spelling helps. Ask Jeeves and Infoseek provide spelling help for the orthographically challenged. Also, vary the styling of terms, so that a search for CD-ROM, for example, will also turn up CDROM or CD ROM.  COVER ALL THE BASES If you're looking for gardening tips, for example, you may need to account for several different words -- garden, gardens, gardening, gardener and so on. Infoseek and Lycos handle plurals and word stems automatically. Alta Vista uses a different approach, the wildcard character. Enter garden* and you'll get results on all the different options. Search sites that don't recognize word stems or wildcards need you to think up variants by yourself and search for them all (e.g., garden OR gardening OR gardens).  ASK FOR DIRECTIONS Not every search site works the same way, but all of them provide a help section and tips. A couple of minutes spent checking the help pages can pay dividends later.  DON'T STICK AROUND If you don't find what you're looking for in the first couple of results screens, either go back and enter a different set of search terms or move on to another search site.  How Operators Work " "-- (quotation marks) enclose words to search for a phrase: "Strawberry Fields Forever"  AND connects two or more words, all of which must appear in the results: Strawberry AND Fields AND Forever  OR connects two or more search words, any of which may appear in the results: Strawberry Fields OR Strawberryfields  NOT excludes the word after it from the results: Strawberry Fields NOT W.C.  - (minus sign), like NOT, excludes the word that follows it: Strawberry Fields -W.C.  + (plus sign) precedes a word that must appear: +Strawberry +Fields  Note that it's possible to string together several operators to construct a very precise query. To exclude certain cover versions of a certain song, for example, you could try: Strawberry Fields AND The Beatles NOT Sandy Farina NOT Nashville Superpickers (pg. G7)  Illustration (Illustration by Seymour Chwast)(pg. G1)

title: Internet Child Pornography Operation Is Raided in U.S. and Abroad
body: The police in 22 states and a dozen countries late Tuesday and early today swept down on scores of homes belonging to young and old, professional people and factory workers, all suspected of belonging to a huge Internet club trafficking in child pornography. Several dozen people were arrested, but officials said they expected more than 100 to be charged as law-enforcement officers with expertise in computers downloaded the contents of hard drives and disks that were seized. "The volume is enormous," Ray Kelly, the Commissioner of the unitedstates Customs Service, said today, noting that the investigation had turned up a database of more than 100,000 sexual photographs of naked boys and girls, some younger than 2, some engaged in sexual acts with adults. Mr. Kelly said the material went far beyond anything that could remotely be called art, and a British police official agreed. "It's stomach-churning," said Detective Superintendent John Stewardson, who led the British phase of the operation. Police officials in the unitedstates and Britain called the operation one of the largest against the spreading netherworld of child pornography in cyberspace. The suspects were believed to belong to the Wonderland Club. A membership requirement, police officials said, was possession of pornographic photographs of children and a willingness to share them. The raids in the unitedstates took place in places as diverse as Brooklyn, Salt Lake City, Dallas, Kennebunk, Me., West Orange, N.J., and Norcross, Ga. They yielded a half-dozen arrests and a treasure trove of computer equipment that will be used as evidence, Mr. Kelly said. One of those arrested was a University of Connecticut teacher seized at his home in New Britain, said an official familiar with the operation. Another raid, in Missouri, turned up a cache of weapons as well as child pornography in a heavily fortified trailer, this official said. The Customs Service, which coordinated the unitedstates raids in connection with local authorities, did not release the names of the arrested. The accused face Federal child-pornography charges that could bring up to 10 years in prison, said a Customs agent, Bill Anthony. They could also face local charges, he said. In some instances, Wonderland Club members are believed to have posed their own children for pictures, Mr. Anthony said. In other cases, he said, parents may have taken money to let their children be used. What happened to the children is among the questions that investigators are agonizing over and will be for weeks as the inquiry unfolds, officials said. Mr. Kelly said law-enforcement's knowledge of the Wonderland Club grew out of a 1996 investigation in San Jose, Calif. In that case, 16 people in the unitedstates and abroad were charged with taking part in an on-line pedophilia club. Mr. Kelly and Mr. Anthony said some implicated in the 1996 case cooperated with investigators. The information thus gleaned proved invaluable, especially when it was shared with British detectives, who earlier this year discovered pedophiles downloading child pornography. Over months of looking into the Wonderland Club, investigators learned how its members communicated by code and on some occasions were able to follow cybertrails, Mr. Kelly said. Mr. Anthony said the raids were timed to minimize the risk of Wonderland members' warning one another. They began around 5:30 A.M. today in Britain, when it was late Tuesday on the East Coast of the unitedstates. Homes in Australia, Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Norway, Portugal and Sweden were also raided. Bob Packham, the deputy director general of the National Crime Squad in Britain, was pleased afterward, saying, "I am unaware of another police operation that has ever pulled together so many law-enforcement agencies worldwide to effect simultaneous raids and arrests."

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Heavy Weather: Hurricane Bonnie a Big Draw
body: In addition to taking its toll on the Atlantic Coast States, Hurricane Bonnie did a number on the Internet server of Weather.com, the Web site of the Weather Channel cable network. When Bonnie was at her mightiest last week, traffic volume was sky high at Weather.com. Todd Walrath, vice president for on-line services at the Weather Channel, said the Web site received some 40 million page views. Those included 10 million on Aug. 26, when Bonnie swept into North Carolina. That compares with three million page views on a typical day, Mr. Walrath said. As a result, some visitors faced slow download times as they tried to get information from the overwhelmed servers. Weather.com was not the only such site with heavy traffic. A study by Relevant Knowledge, an Atlanta-based market research business, found that the number of visits to seven major weather sites was 123 percent higher from Aug. 24 to Aug. 26 compared with the same period a week earlier. In all, the study found aggregate traffic on those sites to be 3.3 million visitors, compared with 1.5 million the previous week. "This is another endorsement that the Web is becoming a primary source of instant information," said Ted Hawthorne, vice president for research and client information at Relevant Knowledge. title:
NEWS WATCH;
No More Paper Chasing For One Business School
body: Applicants to the Sloan School of Management at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology had better know their way around the World Wide Web. If not, the admissions staff will not be admitting them. In fact, the staff won't even look over their applications. That's because Sloan is apparently the first graduate business school in the nation to accept only applications submitted over the Internet. Sloan officials said their motivation to do so was not so much to make sure that applicants would be tech-savvy as to save space and money. "In our traditional application process, we printed and mailed 30,000 applications," said Rod Garcia, Sloan's director of admissions, in a statement available on the Sloan Web site (web.mit.edu/sloan/www). He called the new system a "significant step" in eliminating "all the paper waste and postage and mailing costs." The on-line application program, effective for the fall class of 1999, works through a process called Grad Advantage. Developed by John Pyrovolakis, an M.I.T. graduate, the process allows an applicant to set up a password-protected folder and fill out the forms a little at a time. The applicant can submit the final application when ready and also use the basic information to apply to any of the other 40 participating graduate schools, without having to retype the data (www.gradadvantage.org). At least one part of the process is still old-fashioned. Decisions on applications will be sent through regular mail, so applicants will still have to sweat it out by themailbox for the good (or not so good) news. Graphic   Photo

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Many Sites To Confess One's Sins
body: THE Internet may be the world's largest confessional. Its paradoxical combination of anonymity and intimacy provides fertile ground for admissions that might never be aired in "real" life. Even when real names are known, the medium -- a step removed from physical contact and thus, perhaps, from perceived consequences -- somehow evokes a closed-curtain, hush-toned closeness that draws people out in occasionally astonishing ways. Anyone who frequents a newsgroup, email discussion group or chat room will eventually be privy to a confession -- of a lie, a vice or even a crime. In a recent striking example, a regular participant in a Net support group for alcoholics admitted that he had killed his daughter in North Dakota, and was arrested after several members notified the police. In August, the man, Larry Froistad Jr., was given a 40-year sentence with 10 years suspended as a result of a plea agreement in the case. There are also Web sites that display or collect confessions. In these sanctuaries, the act of confession is emphasized. The audience is secondary. At Confess.net (www.confess. net), a simple, spare site with a somehow soothingly straightforward address, only the confession of the last visitor is displayed until a new one is added. No identifying data are required, and the site has no other content. This is the confessional as streamlined application. Tane Langton, a New Zealander and Web designer now living in Prague, said he posted the site a few months ago for no other reason than "it's the kind of thing I'd like to use myself because it's anonymous and public at the same time." A site that alternately allows all archived confessions to be viewed is being collected as part of an event called Surpu Masu, which is to take place tomorrow at the Burningman art festival in the Black Rock Desert in Nevada. Surpu Masu will involve the burning of a 13-foot wooden "sacrificial scapegoat" stuffed with printouts of the sins confessed to the Web site (www.serv.net/jmurphy/ anunaki/sm.html). A Seattle resident, Wally Glenn, one of the site's creators, describes it as "a mix of ancient mythology and a bit of showmanship" that borrows liberally from Sumerian, Chaldean and Semitic cultural symbolism. At the opposite extreme of the public nature of Mr. Glenn's site is the Ten Nines (www.fred.net/turtle/ journal/tellme.html), a personal confessional, for lack of another term, on the home page of a person who goes by the on-line handle The Turtle. The site's name is taken from John Brunner's cult sci-fi novel "The Shockwave Rider," which describes an untappable, untraceable phone confession line reached by dialing the number 9 ten times. The Turtle's version of the Ten Nines provides an open text box where visitors can type a confession to him and him alone, but the results are not posted on the site. The Turtle does keep his own open Web diary called "My Head Talking" that is linked to the Ten Nines. As a result, visitors may feel they can use him as a "disinterested sounding board," as he put it, because he's so open about his own life. He wouldn't quote directly from any of the dozens of postings he said he had received, but said: "It's pretty amazing the range of things that people will say when they're pretty sure that no one can throw it back in their face. People have confessed to crimes. People have told me stories of infidelities, revenge, fetishes and perversions." Some may be reluctant to take the Turtle at his word, since there's no way to review the messages he has received. In fact, that goes for the confessions that are openly posted at various other sites; there is no way to tell a true confession from a false one. But surely cabdrivers and bartenders, favored confessors of the pre-Internet era, would confirm that people will tell strangers the most amazingly personal things. With the ease -- and sense of removal -- provided by technology, is it any surprise, as Mr. Glenn said, that "people want to confess and will use whatever means possible"?
