title: Strange Things Happening? Blame Your Biorhythms
body: YOU oversleep and walk in late and un-ironed for your Big Meeting, plus you're limping from tripping over the curb on the way in. Mama said there'd be days like this, and now she can call up a Web-based biorhythm calculator on her laptop and warn you ahead of time -- all in good fun, of course. The pseudoscience of biorhythms, sometimes thought of as on par with astrology -- except that the fault, dear Web surfer, lies within you instead with the stars -- has been around for a century, and the Internet offers many sites that will let you plot your own. All you need is a birthdate and a browser. Two popular sites with biorhythm calculators are Web-O-Rhythm (www.qns.com/html/weborhythm) and Life Sines (www.lifesines.com), but there are plenty more out there. Just do a search for "biorhythms," and you'll probably score a few hits for sites offering similar programs for downloading. The notion that biological rhythms affect emotions, alertness and readiness to mate, among other things, was developed from about 1897 to 1932 by medical doctors in Paris, Berlin and Vienna as well as Philadelphia and other cities. The basic biorhythm chart has three undulating lines crossing a horizontal line. The wavy lines represent the physical, the emotional and the mental, or intellectual, cycles of a person over a period of time. On a basic biorhythm chart, which is based on one's birthdate, the physical cycle lasts 23 days, the emotional cycle 28 days and the mental cycle 33 days. The first half of each cycle, falling above the chart's horizontal line, is considered to be positive, while the second half, below the line, is thought to influence those particular aspects negatively. The days on the chart when each cycle crosses the line are said to be "critical." When two or more cycles hit the same critical day, bad things will happen, believers say, but these days are easy enough to predict, supposedly, with the aid of mathematics. "The actual curves are generally plotted as sine waves of the appropriate length," said Jeff Jetton, a programmer with a biorhythm program for the Pilot (www.mindspring.com/ jetton/pilot). "Who said you'd never use trigonometry again?" While certain circadian rhythms (like digestive timetables, the sleep-wake cycle and hormone activity) have been shown to exist in all sorts of organisms, the human biorhythms described above are thought to be mere whimsy by most scientists. One of the main reasons cited is that natural rhythms in living organisms approximate regular cycles but vary in exact cycle lengths due to environmental and other factors and could never maintain the rigidly precise period lengths described in the biorhythm hypothesis. Scientific papers addressing biorhythms, but not supporting the biorhythm concept, have been published in The New England Journal of Medicine and The Journal of Safety Research. "Personally, I haven't come across any experimental evidence, which is not to say that there isn't any out there, so I remain a skeptic," Mr. Jetton said. "Still, it's a fun theory," he added, "and very useful for giving an excuse for locking your keys in the car or blowing off your workout." Graphic   Photo: Web users can make their own biorhythm charts at a number of sites.

title: Telnet: Old Friend Offers High Speed
body: YOU log onto the Internet one day, and it's blazingly fast; no more World Wide Wait. Pulling up Web pages is instantaneous. Your email soars by more quickly than you can read it. Information is at your fingertips with hardly a pause. A dream of the future? No, it's telnet, a tool of the Internet of yesterday: no graphics, no fancy software, simply unformatted text in an 80-character-by-24-line window. With a few bits of knowledge in hand, you can gain access to the World Wide Web, your email, terabytes of file archives and other Internet resources using telnet, a piece of Internet technology that has been aged to perfection over the last 30 years. It's fast, efficient and hardly subject to the vagaries of regularly changing bells and whistles. Telnet is a method of typing text on your own computer, which gets sent over the Internet to another computer, whether on the next desk or on the next continent. Through text commands, just like those found in MS-DOS, you can operate this other computer. This can amount to something as simple as listing the files in a directory or as complex as reading email or Web browsing -- all without pictures, buttons or clicking. Working over the Internet, telnet connects a computer using a program that runs on, for example, a PC with Windows 98, to another machine that can handle several users at once, like a mainframe or a server computer. (The server is typically running the Unix operating system, but Microsoft Windows NT and other computer systems can handle telnet as well.) After connecting, you can execute programs on that separate machine, just as if you were typing on a keyboard directly connected to that machine. To run a program, type the command and hit enter; this is why it is called a command-line interface -- as opposed to the graphical user interface, with icons and mouse movements, that describes both the Macintosh and Windows operating systems. The server runs the software you specify and displays the results. There are no images. In real terms, let's say you are on vacation overseas, with your laptop far behind, and you want to read your email. Find any computer with an Internet connection, no matter how slow, and you can connect to your Internet service provider or your company's computer with little fuss. Millions of people still use telnet every day around the world to handle their email, write software, search library collections and create documents -- all without a graphic in sight. For this reason, telnet is often favored by programmers and the visually impaired. Speed is also a benefit: because it is text-based, even the slowest possible connection still seems perky. Telnet was developed in the early 1970's, when the collection of networks that would later come to be called the Internet first allowed university researchers to connect to machines all over the country without directly dialing into a modem connected to those machines. Telnet evolved as a way to operate those distant machines while taking advantage of the nascent network. Scientists and military personnel were the original audience; many computer scientists still rely on it as their primary tool. Telnet's original purpose was to mimic older machines that had a single function: sending and receiving text through a wire connected directly to a mainframe computer. The first of these devices, the teletypewriter, or tty, was just a typewriter and a roll of paper. Later advances brought a monitor-and-keyboard combination called a video-display terminal, or VDT, but users still exchanged only text. Graphics required too much computer horsepower, and the connection speeds were far too slow. Not every server or mainframe will allow someone to telnet in. Some corporations and other institutions have firewalls, or software that acts as a protective barrier between machines inside the institution and those outside. These firewalls often prevent outside users from using telnet via the Internet if they are outside of the corporate network. Secure versions of telnet that exchange encrypted information may be used in these cases. So why use such an ancient mechanism, aside from the geek appeal and the desire to impress friends and colleagues with your technical elan? For one thing, it works almost everywhere; for another, a text-only connection can be extremely fast. There are also some services you can't gain access to any other way. Many libraries spent a lot of money in the 80's and early 90's providing dial-up connection and telnet access to their catalogues and related information. Most of those services remain active and updated -- and not on the Web. The Seattle Public Library, for instance, maintains a full searchable catalogue via telnet at spl.lib.wa.us. Seattle library patrons can also request books on line and have them transferred to branches near them throughout the city, or get put on a waiting list for the next available copy. The Library of Congress has long maintained a telnet service (locis.loc.gov) for searching its vast information base and now offers the same searching on the Web (www.loc.gov).  Two Examples The Seattle Public Library's catalog via telnet at spl.lib.wa.us. LYNX IS A WEB BROWSER that runs on the computer you connect to, retrieving the pages you request and displaying only the text of those pages. You navigate by using the arrows keys, and Tab, space and Enter keys to move around and select links on the pages. Many Web sites offer text-only versions of their sites, which are somewhat easier to navigate with Lynx. Graphic   Chart: How to Do It" Getting the telnet software  WINDOWS: Windows 95, 98 and NT have a stripped-down version of telnet software that is installed along with the Internet software. More elaborate telnet programs are available as freeware or share-ware, or commercially. Dave Central, an index to resources on the Web, lists 47 telnet programs (www.davecentral.com/telnetclnt.html).  MACINTOSH: NCSA Telnet, formerly the most widely used telnet program, has not been updated since 1995. Better Telnet, a more recent adaptation of that original software, is available free from Sassy Software (www.cstone.net/rbraun/mac/telnet). For other choices for Macs, see www.macatawa.org/mthomas/telnet.html.  Connecting  Connecting via telnet is simple: ENTER THE FULL NAME of the remote machine or its INTERNET PROTOCOL (I.P.) NUMBER. For example, subscribers to Panix, a large Internet service in newyork, connect to either panix.com or 166.84.1.66; the name and address are interchangeable. Before using telnet to connect to a machine, YOU NEED A USER ACCOUNT on that server computer. Getting a user account is like getting a room in a hotel; you can wander the halls at will, but without the key to your suite, you can't get in to use the phone or watch a movie. Many I.S.P.'s used to include these accounts as part of the service. Few nationwide providers now offer it, but many regional ones still do. You can also get an account at a nonprofit community network or local freenet. These FREE OR INEXPENSIVE ACCOUNTS often include limited telnet access to run software like Lynx. With an account, you connect and ENTER YOUR USER NAME AND PASSWORD as prompted. Some systems provide a menu of programs or services. Others connect you directly to the equivalent of an MS-DOS prompt, at which you type the name of the software, like "lynx." A bit of warning: many servers, for security reasons, set off internal alarms when someone connects via telnet, even when the server computers automatically rebuff the attempt. To avoid a problem, or even prosecution, connect only to services you signed up for, or publicly advertised ones like library catalogs. A NICE TEST DRIVE for your newfound knowledge that does not require a user account is the Library of Congress catalog. (Note that many parts of the catalog are unavailable late at night and in the wee hours.) Always press Enter after typing in text at each step below.  1. Connect to the Internet in whatever way you normally do (or none at all if you're always on line).  2. Start your telnet program (this varies depending on your software. With Windows 95, 98 and NT, from the Start menu, select Run. At the prompt, enter "telnet" and hit Enter). If you're given a chance to select a "terminal type" -- the kind of old hardware that telnet will behave like -- select vt100, which acts as a standard least common denominator.  3. Enter the name of the Library of Congress Information System server. Different telnet programs prompt you for the name in different ways: in the built-in Windows telnet program, select Connect from the File menu; in NCSA Telnet for Macintosh, select Open Connection from the File menu. In the field labeled Host Name in either program, enter the server name:  4. Text will appear on the screen, giving you access to different collections. To browse the library's catalogue, enter:  5. At the next screen, to search books catalogued since 1975, enter:  6. The library's catalog has many somewhat cryptic commands, but here is a sample search to get you started. Below the "ready for new command" text, to browse ("b") for books by or about Bill Gates, enter: (For other commands type help.)  7. To retrieve listings representing that set of found books, enter:  8. To read one of the bibliographic entries, enter:  9. To leave, type QUIT and then 12 at each of the next two prompts. Then close your telnet program.

title:
USER'S GUIDE;
Do-It-Yourself Travel With a Load of Guilt
body: I HAVE avoided taking infants on airplanes ever since the mashed peas incident of 1990. On a nonstop flight from Phoenix to newyork, my 11-month-old daughter smeared a handful into the hair of a sleeping woman in the row ahead. The next three hours were as suspenseful as any Hitchcock movie; what if the passenger woke? She slept. But next time I might not be so lucky. Plus, now we're a family of five, counting the current infant. Air fare to Arizona to visit my parents in December would cost roughly as much as a cruise missile. For that kind of money, shouldn't we head to a tropical resort instead? "But you said you wanted to visit your relatives," said Diane Bacigalupo, the assistant manager of Village Travel in Huntington, N.Y., where I live. She looked up from a screen full of air fares to see me biting my nails nervously. I admit that I have some idiosyncrasies when it comes to travel. Could any travel agent know enough about my quirks to create the perfect itinerary? Maybe I needed to be my own travel agent, a role the Internet has made possible in recent months with a proliferation of on-line sites where travelers can confirm room rates and air fares, book reservations and read reviews of hotels and restaurants. A half-hour later, I was at my home computer, ready to pit the machine against the real-life travel agent. I would start small, by comparing the cheapest round-trip air fare that Ms. Bacigalupo had found -- $486 a person, including an $8 travel agent's commission -- to the rates on three Web sites. I logged onto Travelocity (www.travelocity.com), Microsoft's Expedia (www.expedia. com) and the Internet Travel Network (www.itn.com). It took less than five minutes for even a novice like me to figure out how to compare dozens of possible itineraries by entering the time and date of the trip, the number of people traveling together and destinations. But other on-line features were worrisome. For instance, Expedia was the only site where I could specify that I would be traveling with an infant on my husband's lap. At the other sites, my group was identified as four passengers. I feared that this could lead to problems later; in the past, reservations clerks have always wanted to know ahead of time if an infant was accompanying me. The three sites rely on different computerized reservations databases, but each quoted an identical low fare: $478. Such details as airlines, connections and flight times differed slightly, but not enough to matter. And I could shave off the $8 commission. But Ms. Bacigalupo had spent an hour listening to me whine -- er, talk -- about my concerns. Guilt overtook me. Next, where to stay near my parents' house? None of the sites' resort or hotel databases had information on the dude ranches that Ms. Bacigalupo had pinpointed. With her leads, I conducted fruitful keyword searches at www.hotbot.com and quickly found encyclopedic listings at www.duderanches.com and www.ranchweb.com. I sent email to the owner of the Kay El Bar Ranch. But before I received a reply, Ms. Bacigalupo phoned: the Kay El Bar was fully booked. Besides, she pointed out, these dude ranches were pricey. Would my family get its money's worth? Now that she mentioned it, I remembered Arizona as being too chilly and windy in December for long rides in the desert. After wrestling with these questions for three days, I went on line again -- and was shocked to learn that I could now fly the same route on the same days for less money. This time, the three sites' fares differed, ranging from $442 to $464. I phoned representatives of the three Web sites to ask why prices were fluctuating. "The airlines make one million changes in their inventories every day," said Lois Shore, vice president of marketing at the Internet Travel Network. "There could be a drop in price, an increase, a change in time, in routing." Why the different air fares? Although the sites' databases are similar, my method of searching was slightly different at each. At one, for instance, I requested nonstop flights. That volatility in price might be a comfort to an unencumbered solo traveler who could take advantage of last-minute deals. For those free spirits, the Internet Travel Network has a low-fare ticker that flashes tempting fares like "San Francisco to Boston, round trip $273." Just click on the ticker to book the flight. But I was getting so frustrated that I was ready to mash peas into my own hair when the phone rang -- Ms. Bacigalupo again. "Why don't you fly to Phoenix, stay a night with your family, then fly from there to the Baja Peninsula?" she said. "It's warm and costs less than a dude ranch." At that point, I came clean. "I've been checking out some on-line travel sites," I admitted. "So I can also check out air fares." For the next 10 minutes, we tested itineraries simultaneously. The best fare she found was $1,141. But Expedia quoted $811. Even odder, when I changed the parameters of my multiple-destination search slightly to eliminate any mention of Phoenix on the return trip, Expedia quoted $685 for an identical itinerary. "I'm not getting that rate," Ms. Bacigalupo said. "What should I do?" I asked. "Reserve it," she said. "Quick." Neither Ms. Bacigalupo nor a spokeswoman for Expedia could explain the disparity. "It reminds me of a TV show a while back where they went onto a plane and asked all the passengers how much their tickets cost," said Suzi LeVine, a product manager for Expedia. "They were all different." But by bypassing Ms. Bacigalupo, who had helped me so much, I felt as if I had cheated her out of the $32 commission. "You have a moral dilemma," Ms. LeVine observed. If so, we are all going to lose in this particular battle of computers vs. humans. No, I will pay Ms. Bacigalupo the commission anyway. Technically, the machine won this contest; no wonder Ms. Bacigalupo said she worried that the Internet's ability to blithely reshape industries overnight would transform real-life agents into "dinosaurs." But maybe not. Without help from both quarters, I would have stayed home. Graphic   Drawing (Mary Ann Smith)

title:
THE MARKET TURMOIL: ON LINE;
Fewer Delays Than Selloff In October '97
body: Market Plunge 2.0, it seems, may be quite an upgrade for Internet stock brokers. It was only last October when the first billion-share trading day on the newyork Stock Exchange tested Wall Street, as many of the new Internet trading services failed. Customers found that their brokers' Web sites had ground to a halt and phone lines were clogged. Over the last two days, with volume surging to a new record of 1.21 billion shares on the Big Board yesterday, the Internet brokers have handled the business with very few reported problems. The reason, the brokers say, is that they have made big investments to increase their capacity. "Last October was a wake-up call for this industry," said Joseph A. Konen, president of Ameritrade Holdings, which mainly operates on the Internet. "We have invested $15 million over the last year and have increased our capacity by 10 times." Alexander D. Stein of Gomez Advisers, a research firm that studies on-line trading, said, "The whole industry is doing dramatically better," adding, "This time, we haven't heard of any failures." Gomez Advisers conducted a test to see how long it took for an Internet user to load the main page of various on-line brokers. On Monday, the average time was five seconds, a vast improvement over last year. While investors may have had few problems, the brokers have been busy, making margin calls -- the industry practice of demanding that customers who borrowed money secured by their investments pay off their loans or put up new collateral. "Yesterday and today will be a record for the number of new margin calls," said Thomas J. O'Connell, executive vice president of Discover Brokerage Direct, the Internet trading service of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter. "There are customers that are losing money, and that's never good for business. But it's all going relatively smoothly." About one-third of the service's accounts have some margin borrowing. He said most people had been relatively cautious in the use of borrowed money to increase their potential return, and their risk. "When you get down there with the common people and look at what they do with their own money," he added, "you'll see them being much more conservative than you might expect." Another reason the brokers are not in such trouble is that volume spikes have not been as sharp as last year. Ameritrade handled 35,000 trades Monday, about 1.7 times its average volume. Last October, its systems bogged down when trading peaked at 2.5 times daily volume. Mr. Konen said customers did have to wait "a few minutes" to talk to a broker on the phone, but the wait was far less than the 15 minutes last October. Christos M. Cotsakos, chief executive of E-Trade, said clients might have found trading a bit sluggish because market makers had been busier than usual, but E-Trade's systems had not had delays. "Because access to information was a lot faster, there wasn't the panic selling we saw last year," he said.

title: U.S. Faults Depositions of Microsoft Executives
body: In a court document made public today, the Justice Department accused top executives of the the Microsoft Corporation, including its chairman, William H. Gates, of "an astonishing lack of recall" when they were questioned under oath for the Government's antitrust suit against the software giant. That assertion, plus several pieces of new evidence to support the Government's case, were submitted to Federal District Court here as part of the Justice Department's response to Microsoft's request that the case be dismissed. "Executives who are stated to be the author of documents claim not to remember writing them," Government lawyers wrote. "Executives who are the stated recipients of documents claim not to remember receiving them. And both authors and recipients claim not to know what the documents mean." The Government's new evidence was gathered by the Justice Department in recent weeks in preparation for the trial, which is set to begin on Sept. 23. It includes allegations that Microsoft tried to bully several competing companies that until now had not been mentioned in court proceedings. Among them are the Intel Corporation, Apple Computer, Real Networks, which makes video and audio software for the Internet, and the Intuit Corporation, maker of the Quicken accounting software. In the depositions of Microsoft executives, which are still under way, the Government said that Mr. Gates "displayed a particular failure of recollection," even though "he is placed at the center of key events by numerous documents." The brief provides the first look at the Government's view of the depositions of senior Microsoft leaders in recent days. The questioning was to have been taken in public, but an appeals court accepted Microsoft's request that the depostions proceed in private. Mr. Gates' three-day deposition is to end on Wednesday. Mark Murray, a Microsoft spokesman, said of the Government's lawyers, "It's unfortunate that they have lost faith in the substance of their case and have resorted to this kind of name calling." He noted that Mr. Gates receives hundreds of pieces of email every day and so cannot be expected to remember every one of them, especially those dating back several years. The Justice Department brief also accuses Mr. Gates and other Microsoft executives of "attempting to rewrite history" in their pretrial testimony. The antitrust suit, filed in May, accuses Microsoft of trying to persuade or force a competitor, the Netscape Communications Corporation, to give up part of the market for browsers, the software used to navigate the World Wide Web. It also accuses Microsoft of illegally integrating its browser, Internet Explorer, with the Windows operating system and then claiming that the browser and Windows were never intended to be separate products. In its brief, the Government says that effort has now gone so far that Microsoft executives no longer even utter the word browser "except when they slip." "Although browser is a term used throughout Microsoft's documents and licenses, the industry literature, and even in the dictionary Microsoft publishes for software professionals," the brief says, "in the interest of Microsoft's litigation arguments it becomes a nonword. Witnesses claim they don't know what a browser is. What used to be browsers are now simply 'bits of browsing technologies.' " The brief also says that Microsoft's supposed effort to reduce or elimate competition from Netscape "is part of a pattern that includes similar discussions" with other companies, including Apple and Intel. Lawyers involved in the case say that the Justice Department intends to use this new evidence to show that the initial evidence offered to support its claims against Microsoft is standard practice for the company. Some of the new evidence has been the subject of news articles in recent weeks, but this is the first time the Justice Department has indicated that it intends to use the accusations as evidence in the trial. The 89-page brief contends that Microsoft tried to persuade Apple "to withdraw its 'Quicktime' software from competition with Microsoft's 'Netshow' software." Both products are used to receive audio and video information from the Internet. The brief said that Apple refused the request and added that Microsoft also tried to coerce Apple to stop offering Netscape to its customers. Microsoft makes a verson of Internet Explorer for Apple's Macintosh line of computers. Since Apple computers use the Mac OS operating system, not Windows, the Government argues that Microsoft's dispute with Apple demonstrates that the browser is obviously a stand-alone product, not a fundamental part of the operating system. "Microsoft's determination to restrict the support and distribution of Netscape's browser by Apple is particularly telling since Apple represents the main alternative to desktop PC's running Microsoft's Windows," Justice Department lawyers wrote. "Whatever the relevance of Microsoft's arguments about why it wanted Windows users also to use Internet Explorer, those arguments cannot apply to Internet Explorer use by Apple users." The charges concerning Real Networks are not as well defined because some information in the document was deleted before it was made public, and the department declined to elaborate. Real Networks, whose chief executive, Robert Glaser, is a former Microsoft executive, also makes software that enables personal computers to receive radio-style audio and television-style video over the Internet. The Government brief asserted that Microsoft tried to "coerce Real Networks" to get out of the multimedia software business and to withhold its technology from Microsoft's competitors. In the case of Intuit, the brief said, "Microsoft succeeded in getting Intuit to agree not to support Netscape, but only after tying Intuit's access to valuable placement on the Windows desktop to Intuit's agreement to abandon Netscape." The "desktop" is the Windows main screen. The Government also asserted that Microsoft pressed Intel into agreeing that it would no longer write software intended to enhance the performance of Intel's microprocessors. To all of this evidence, Mr. Murray said: "In every case, the Government is misrepresenting Microsoft's business relationships with other companies. We meet with hundreds of companies to make them aware of our technology plans and to promote the tools in our operating system and to insure that our products and their products work well together. Microsoft has never tried to divide any market, period."

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
Phone Companies Create Traffic Jam on Road to Internet
body: THE next high hurdle for the personal computer industry is keeping many a chip maker and computer manufacturer awake at night, because after 15 years of building ever faster and more powerful machines, the wizards of silicon increasingly find themselves at the mercy of local phone companies. The hurdle is the capacity of a channel to carry signals from one point to another, known as bandwidth. The channel in question is the local telephone network, and as the future of computing comes to rest more and more with the Internet, the phone companies represent a serious bottleneck. No matter how much faster the microprocessors and memory chips, no matter how much more efficient the architecture of the machines, the finest computer technology dead-ends with the phone jack in every consumer's wall. Computer technology gave us the Internet; telephone technology gave us the World Wide Wait. The reason for this is rooted in vast differences between the two industries. Dealing in microscopic distances, the chip makers have grown accustomed to improving performance continually and exponentially by finding ways to reduce the lengths of paths that electrons must travel within silicon wafers while at the same time multiplying the number of paths within the chips and between components. The net result has been an enormous increase in bandwidth -- and in power. Intel Corporation's 8088 microprocessor, the brains of the original I.B.M. PC, could carry out about 750,000 instructions per second at a speed of 8 million cycles per second, or megahertz. Today's Intel Pentium II processor can carry out 855 million instructions per second at a speed of up to 450 megahertz. Things have not moved so fast in the world of telephones. True, digital switches and fiberoptic cables have greatly expanded the total number of calls that can be placed at any one time. But the capacity of the typical phone line in a typical home is virtually the same today as it was in the 1960's. Only so many electrons can be squeezed through a copper wire. The computer industry has long struggled to compensate for this weakness. The first breakthrough came in the late 1970's when Ward Christensen, an engineer with the International Business Machines Corporation and an early personal computer enthusiast, invented an error-correction technology and released it to the public domain. Until then, modems -- devices that enable computers to communicate over telephone lines by converting digital signals into sounds on one end of the call and from sounds back to digital signals at the other end -- were largely useless because phone lines were so noisy that the receiving modem often failed to differentiate signal from noise. Since then, modem makers have made enormous strides in error correction and in pushing ever more information through standard phone lines. First the Hayes Corporation and later USRobotics led the way in accelerating data transmission from 300 bits per second in the early 1980's to 1,200, then 2,400 and on up to today's 56K modems, which can theoretically receive 56 thousand bits per second. But 56K modems are limited by Federal telephone rules to 53,000 bits per second. And the erratic quality of local phone service limits them even more. For example, a state of the art USRobotics 56K modem can achieve a speed no greater than 26,400 bits per second in many of the most densely populated areas of the East Coast, including big parts of Manhattan and New Jersey, because the local phone company, Bell Atlantic, has not upgraded its cables and switches to the demands of high-speed data. In fact, in many instances, it has installed technologies that compress bandwidth in order to carry more voice calls, which coincidentally reduces the capacity of its lines to carry data calls. A Bell Atlantic representative informs an inquiring consumer that the company is not obligated to carry high-speed data calls, so unless the customer is willing to buy a special modem and fork over a hefty installation fee plus high monthly charges for an I.S.D.N. (integrated services digital network) line, he or she will be living with a maximum speed of 26,400 bits per second, or less, for the foreseeable future. Local phone companies respond that they cannot keep up with the demand as families order separate lines for children, fax machines and modems. But critics say this has more to do with the corporate culture of a regulated monopoly than with telephone technology. The computer industry knows that pointing fingers accomplishes nothing; at the end of the day, a lot of computer power is still dammed up behind the modem. So the industry has begun wooing the local phone companies with incentives. The carrot is a standard for A.D.S.L. (asymmetric digital subscriber line), a technology that offers simultaneous voice and data calls at speeds up to 8 million bits per second over standard copper wires. This technology and other flavors of digital subscriber lines have been around for a long time, but the phone companies have quarreled bitterly over a standard. So earlier this year, Compaq, Intel and Microsoft helped to form the Universal A.D.S.L. Working Group and anointed a standard known as G.lite. Yet the phone companies have not yet ratified G.lite, so the first modems will not be available until at least well into next year, and it could take decades for this technology to reach all American homes. Thus the stick: building specific circuitry, known as ethernet, into its machines to allow them to connect directly to cable modems without a special installation. The most recent example of this is the Apple iMac, a home-market computer that has built-in ethernet circuitry. Ethernets are the standard networks used in businesses, but the only use for such technology in the vast majority of homes is to connect the computer to the phone companies' most dangerous competition in data bandwidth -- cable television companies that offer high-speed Internet access. And just in case that fails to get the local phone companies' attention, Microsoft's chairman, William H. Gates, earlier this year invested $1 billion in the Comcast cable television network, one of the most aggressive marketers of cable modem services, while the Bells' progenitor, A.T.&T., is buying TCI, the nation's largest cable television operator and the largest stockholder of At-Home, the leading cable modem service. If the local phone companies fail to make A.D.S.L. widely available soon and at a competitive price, the computer industry is poised to quickly embrace cable or other alternative channels. And many of those channels will one day offer local and long-distance phone services. Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
THE MARKET TURMOIL: INVESTORS ON LINE;
Misery Loves Cybercompany but Has Little Sympathy for Market Losers
body: Heavy Internet traffic slowed many on-line investment sites yesterday as fearful investors mobbed cyberspace, checking their stock prices and then sticking around to commiserate. "All the bears are patting themselves on their backs now, saying 'We told you so!' But they don't really care, do they?" demanded one investor on a Yahoo discussion forum called Follow the Yellow Brick Road. "I'm back to where I was sometime in the middle of January. I'll go slit my wrists now." The sense of calm expressed amid market chaos by many of middle America's typical mutual fund investors was nowhere in evidence in Internet forums and chat rooms, where participants tend to be active investors and where emotion is never quite as tempered as it is in other environments. On America Online, where chat room convention usually dictates a cheery tone, yesterday afternoon it had turned decidedly somber. Investors kept one another up to date on what analysts were saying on CNBC. ("Shoot the jerks on CNBC," one said, "nothing but bears, one after another.") A typical exchange went like this: ROWNAROWNA: -- Hiya Cohen --- how are you doing? CohenInvGr: -- Not good. Bleeding. ROWNAROWNA: -- We all are. Fozziebare, the screen name of another regular in the America Online investor forums, complained, "can no longer afford my AOL subscription." David Gardner, co-founder of the Motley Fool, one of the oldest investment sites in cyberspace, said that among the most popular discussion groups on the site yesterday was one titled Living Below Your Means. Another was the Communion of Bears. Mr. Gardner said of regulars in the bear forum: "In the past what characterized that conversation is they had to team up together because they were so marginalized. Now they're just calling for blood." Indeed, sympathy for the market losers did not run deep on several popular message boards yesterday. "I have told you people for some time now Dell is going to the dogs!" a participant known as FantomBoy wrote in a discussion group about Dell Computer. "Dell lost all its recent gains, and you folks call Dell bullett proof! BAWHAHAHAHAH." Dell's stock, which had held out until yesterday, suffered a 16 percent decline. The rout for technology stocks was particularly hard felt by on-line investors who had remained optimistic amid the market tumult of recent weeks. "If this isn't a free fall for for the markets, and Dell, then I don't know what a free fall is," wrote Stock Bull, a previously bullish investor. "Wish I had a parachute on." David Zgodzinski, who writes a column for the SiliconInvestor Web site based on what people are saying in the discussion forums said on-line investors had been harder hit because they typically owned stocks in individual companies, rather than in mutual funds. "In general, the reaction is shock," Mr. Zgodzinski said. "These people are more enthusiastic and more tuned in, and they're feeling the loss more personally. The man on the street hasn't had the perception of how bad the drop has already been." One participant in a SiliconInvestor forum called the Big Kahuna drew on the immortal words of Dr. McCoy of "Star Trek" to convey his feelings: "They're dead Jim, they're all dead. Japan, Russia and now China and hongkong. ANY BUYERS OUT THERE??" A relatively new investor on a Yahoo discussion group wrote: "Gotta love this investment language. I figured I'd need to learn about Fibonacci sequences and 10-K's. Instead, I end up with catching falling knives and dead cat bounces." Still, the cybergloom cleared occasionally yesterday as investors reassured one another that this was a buying opportunity and that they were in it for the long haul. The Motley Fool's "post of the day" was an impassioned exhortation from a Dell investor to look on the bright side: Subject: Self Fulfilling Prophecy Author: rj610w With all due respects to those on this board who are so far above me that I can't see the light of the sun coming over their heads, let me sound a note of concern. I am concerned that the bottom doesn't have to fall out from under us less we beat ourselves into believing it's coming and stampede in fear. Once the panic starts, we will have no one to blame but ourselves. I think a lot of our future is in our own hands and how it turns out is up to us. A little more encouragement and a little less scare talk may serve everyone better."

title:
Compressed Data;
Software Engineer Tests Law on Encryption Code
body: Charles Booher was hardly surprised last month when two agents from the Department of Commerce knocked on his door in Silicon Valley and handed him a Federal subpoena. In fact, he had been expecting it ever since he first made his data-encryption program available on the Internet in the summer of 1997. The Commerce Department is investigating whether Mr. Booher's software, which is called Secure Office and is intended to protect the privacy of computer files by scrambling the data, violates unitedstates export law. The rules require Americans who distribute encryption software internationally to obtain an export license; making software available on the Internet is considered international distribution. Mr. Booher acknowledges that few people have downloaded the software from his Web site at www.filesafety.com. But a big number of users was not his real goal. Mr. Booher, a software engineer at the Phase Metrics Corporation in Fremont, Calif., who wrote the encryption program in his spare time, said he posted the program to challenge the export rules. Encryption has been a hotly debated issue in Washington lately, with the Commerce Department, the F.B.I. and other agencies arguing that powerful data-scrambling programs put high-technology espionage tools in the hands of criminals, spies and terrorists. But Mr. Booher is among the software developers who contend that their right to write encryption code is protected by the First Amendment and that the technology is already easily available overseas. "The issue is not whether this stuff is going to exist," Mr. Booher said, "but who will develop it." Monika Wasiewicz, the Commerce Department agent in charge of the case, declined to comment. Mr. Booher was supposed to testify to a Federal grand jury in San Jose, Calif., last week, but the session was canceled because too few jurors showed up. Mr. Booher's testimony is supposed to be rescheduled for this week.   LAURIE J. FLYNN Graphic   Photo

title: Few Federal Web Sites Observe U.S. Privacy Guidelines
body: When it comes to on-line privacy, it seems that the Clinton Administration has not been practicing what it preaches. Only a handful of the Administration's sites on the World Wide Web post the kinds of privacy guidelines that the Federal Trade Commission recently criticized businesses for failing to post, and none of the Administration's sites offer the special protections for children that the Government recommends for commercial sites. Even the White House Web site does not meet the standards recommended by the Federal Trade Commission and endorsed by the Administration. For example, the White House site collects email addresses -- and in some cases, home addresses -- through links that allow visitors to send electronic messages to President and Mrs. Clinton and Vice President Al Gore and Mrs. Gore. Yet, it does not provide any notice about how that information will be used by the White House. Nor does the site ask visitors to its special children's pages to consult their parents before divulging personal information, as the Administration has recommended. In June, the F.T.C. released a survey of commercial Web sites along with a report that was highly critical of industries that gather information on line and, without notifying the visitors to their sites, use or sell the data for marketing purposes. The report's findings, particularly with respect to children, prompted the F.T.C. to recommend that Congress pass a law requiring that on-line businesses and Web site operators obtain parental permission before gathering email addresses or other information from children under age 13. Unlike operators of commercial sites, Federal agencies do not collect or sell personal data for marketing purposes. The issue, critics say, is more one of leading by example. "It's really a matter of practicing what they preach," said David Banisar, senior policy analyst and staff counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a public interest research group in Washington. "They have been pushing notice and consent and they can't even do it themselves. They really have a dismal record on this." Mr. Banisar also pointed out that while the White House might not be using the information for marketing purposes, the data could be transferred to the Democratic National Committee or used for other political ends. The Administration has endorsed child-protection legislation that was introduced in response to the F.T.C. report. It has also endorsed new self-regulation guidelines and enforcement procedures recently proposed by the Online Privacy Alliance, a coalition of businesses and associations that aims to foster privacy protections. Those guidelines call for all Internet businesses to clearly post policies concerning the use and collection of personal information, and they require Web site operators to obtain parental approval before gathering data from children. Yet, despite the Administration's support for these measures, the White House Web site collects information from children without parental notification. Within a special children's section on the site, a White House tour led by cartoon caricatures of the "First Pets," Buddy the dog and Socks the cat, ends with an invitation to send email to President Clinton, Hillary Rodham Clinton or Vice President Al Gore. The electronic form asks for the sender's name, age, email address, grade at school, the school's name and, from those visitors who want a response, a home postal address. The site does not advise children to ask their parents before divulging that information. Likewise, the Federal Emergency Management Agency has an area for children, like that of the White House site, that offers the opportunity to send an email message, yet does not display a privacy policy or request that children seek parental permission before giving out email addresses. The White House Web site provides links to 70 Web sites of Federal agencies, Cabinet departments and White House offices and commissions. Of those 70 sites, only 12 had posted privacy policies as of Friday afternoon. That amounts to 17 percent of the sites surveyed, only slightly better than the 14 percent of commercial sites that, according to the F.T.C.'s report, had clearly posted privacy policies earlier this year. The White House, the Vice President's office and Mrs. Clinton's press office did not respond directly to questions about the Web sites' lack of a posted privacy policy. But Administration officials stressed that in May, President Clinton ordered the Office of Management and Budget to conduct an agency-by-agency review to insure that new technologies were not violating the Privacy Act or otherwise eroding privacy protections. A spokeswoman for the Office of Management and Budget said that the agency was drafting guidelines for Federal Web sites. Mr. Clinton's top adviser on Internet issues, Ira Magaziner, said on Thursday that the Administration was working "to get its own house in order." He also noted that unlike the private sector, Government agencies are bound by the Privacy Act to protect personal data. "There are privacy principles being followed," Mr. Magaziner said. "And we are taking steps to insure that Government agencies are in fact in a more visible way confirming that." Government agencies must comply with the Privacy Act, which establishes controls over personal information collected by the Federal Government. The act requires that each agency that maintains records on individuals inform the person whose data are being collected, by notifying the individual of that fact either on the form that is used to collect the information or on a separate form that the person can keep. Ari Schwartz, a policy analyst for the Center for Democracy and Technology, a Washington advocacy group, said, "When they collect specific information about people, they have to give notice." "It is a technical violation of the law," he added. "They should be posting privacy policies." The White House is exempt from the Privacy Act, but Federal departments and agencies are not. Kathryn Montgomery, executive director of the Center for Media Education, said that "where government is concerned, we need to be very, very careful about data collected on line." But she also emphasized that she saw a clear distinction between commercial and noncommercial Web sites. "One issue is whether we would make a distinction between commercial enterprises that are collecting data, selling it and coming back with exploitive personal advertisements, and noncommercial uses of the Internet," said Ms. Montgomery, whose nonprofit organization has been pushing for legislation to protect both adults and children on line. For the most part, the White House has taken a hands-off approach to Internet commerce, saying that industry should police itself on issues like consumer privacy. In that arena, the Administration has encouraged on-line merchants and marketers to post clearly how the information they collect from consumers is used and to adopt mechanisms to enforce stated privacy policies. Not surprisingly, the Federal Trade Commission has the most prominent privacy policy of all of the Federal Web sites. The agency declined to comment on the lack of clearly posted policies by other agencies, saying its jurisdiction -- and its survey -- covered only commercial sites. Mr. Schwartz of the Center for Democracy and Technology, who helped write a report on Federal Web site privacy policies a year ago, said the Government "generally has been better" than the private sector in keeping private information confidential. And most Government Web sites that take applications for things like volunteers and disaster relief, he said, do post privacy policies. "But there's a question of whether all sites in general that collect personally identifiable information should have privacy policies," he said. As for the Administration, Mr. Schwartz said, "They should lead by example." title: Going From the Corporate World to Silicon Alley Can Prove Tough
body: Lon Otremba has a rare advantage among top executives in newyork City's Silicon Alley high-technology industry: a track record as an executive who took an Internet company from ground zero to a respectable public stock offering. A member of the original management team of the on-line publisher Cnet, Mr. Otremba is now the chief operating officer of Iname, a start-up that offers permanent and personalized email accounts. In an industry that has very little history and thus a dearth of experienced, successful executives, he is already on Round 2. The scarcity of experienced managers in technology industries is especially acute in newyork. Unlike Silicon Valley, Northern California's hotbed of high-technology start-ups, or Dallas, the hub of the telecommunications industry, Silicon Alley has only a handful of executives who have actually built a company from the ground floor. "It's going to be an ongoing problem to attract senior management and build a board," said Michael Flannery, president of the newyork-based executive search firm Redwood Partners. Although successful initial public offerings by a handful of Silicon Alley companies have made the industry more attractive to experienced executives and have thus eased the problem a bit, more recent start-ups are still struggling to find and lure top managers, he said. Given the tiny pool of second-generation entrepreneurs, recruiters must turn to the corporate world, he said, and gamble that an executive hailing from an established corporation can drive a start-up to success. Mr. Flannery, who also manages a small venture capital fund and is in need of managers for his own portfolio of companies, says there is no sure formula for determining who can make the transition. "It's a tough call," he said of finding the right executive. "I really put them through the drill. I take them down the road, painting a picture of what it's like to run a start-up; making payroll; constantly raising capital; building a model. I watch their facial expressions. Sometimes, after I'm finished, they say, 'You're right, Mike. I don't want to do this.' " The executive candidate is gambling, too. When Mr. Otremba joined Cnet in 1993, for example, he was leaving a comfortable position as publisher of PC Magazine, a Ziff-Davis publication. In his job at Ziff-Davis, he could see the Internet coming, so when Cnet's founders, Halsey Minor and Shelby Bonnie, approached him with their idea for a company that would produce television and Internet programming about computers, he understood the potential. Even so, with his proven track record in traditional publishing, high marketability and a wife and two children to consider, Mr. Otremba, who was then 36, had a lot of options. In addition, the job would require him to commute weekly to San Francisco. "I had no doubt the idea was a good one," he said in a recent interview. "Still, I had to do a lot of soul-searching to decide if it was the right time to join a start-up. Finally, I realized I wouldn't be starving if the whole thing imploded." The upside was an equity stake in Cnet and the opportunity to create a corporate culture and be part of a technology revolution. On the other hand, he had to create the company from scratch and sacrifice many amenities. "It was a big deal for me when I could arrange for car service to the airport, when I got my corporate credit card and could hire an assistant," he said of the growth of Cnet. Mr. Otremba stayed with Cnet three years, until he was fully vested, helping take the company from 10 employees to 600. Then he was ready to do it again. "People read the registration statement, so they knew exactly when my vesting was up," he said. "I started getting calls immediately." At the time, Mr. Otremba was commuting weekly from newyork to San Francisco, so when he ran into the founders of the newyork-based Iname, he was ready to talk. "I was available for a second run while it was still early" in the development of the Internet, he said. Recruiting firms have recognized the challenge and are setting up special efforts to find executives for new-media start-ups. Among those specializing in Silicon Alley companies is Cara Erickson, a partner at the search firm of Accord Group/Johnson, Smith & Knisley who has placed executives for companies like Classified Ventures, based in Chicago, and Microsoft. She is now seeking a chief executive for TheStreet.com an on-line financial news service whose founder, James Cramer, already runs a hedge fund. Compensation is often not the issue, Ms. Erickson said, because the industry has matured enough that many start-ups, particularly those with solid venture backing, can compete with the high-end salaries of the established corporate world and are not deterred by the price tag for seasoned executives. But finding the right executive can take time. Ms. Erickson says she looks for problem solvers who fit into the management team puzzle -- that is, a chief executive, chief financial officer and chief operating officer who complement one another in skills and experience. "You're never going to find one person with all the elements necessary to help build a company," she said. "You have to look at the management team as a whole. If you have a C.E.O. who has never taken a company public, then you need to have a C.F.O. who has." Start-ups often find themselves in a chicken-and-egg quandary. Without good management they cannot find financing, but without financing, they cannot afford good executives. Consider the case of Lisa Church, who turned down the opportunity to run a start-up to take a lower-level job at a more established company. Like Mr. Otremba, Ms. Church found herself in newyork City with a unique resume that included helping to build a technology company from the ground up. As vice president of marketing and new-business development for Advent Software of San Francisco, she was responsible for building the company's East Coast presence. She joined Advent, which specializes in portfolio management software, in 1985 when the company had six employees and sales in tens of thousands of dollars. When she left last year, the company employed more than 300 and revenues were approaching $50 million. Knowing that it was time to move on, Ms. Church took stock of her opportunities while observing and, eventually, participating in the evolution of Silicon Alley. She spoke seriously with several Alley companies and came close to joining a newyork software firm as chief executive. But she turned down that opportunity to join Decalog, a Boston-based, Israeli-backed software company, as vice president of North American sales and marketing. "The lure of the new-media business is that it's a new technology and a new industry," Ms. Church said. "It's fun and exciting, but there are the financial realities of life. I've got a family and a mortgage." In the end, she said, she took the Decalog job because it promised to be equally exciting, but more stable. "The company's just more established," she said, adding that she still hopes to work with a start-up in the future. Venture capitalists face similar decisions in finding the right company, said Ed Sim, senior vice president of the venture-capital firm Dawntreader. "Eight of the 10 companies we speak to need management," Mr. Sim said. "Part of the deal has to be we can either bring in a new C.E.O. or C.O.O. to complement the founder. We get resumes in every day, so the tricky part is to identify the right person." What his group can offer potential executives is "the wealth factor" and a long-term relationship with the firm. "We tell them that if the company doesn't work out for market reasons, we'll drop them in another one of our companies," Mr. Sim said. "So then it's a portfolio risk versus a single company." Among an executive's biggest fears when contemplating joining a start-up, he said, is failure. "In fact, a company might fail through no fault of the C.E.O.," he said. "We mitigate their fear by pointing out that every company is developing an Internet strategy, so their experience will be invaluable, that it's still early, and people like wounds and scars." Even some executives who emerged from start-ups are intrigued but ultimately put off by culture shock when stepping into the world of Silicon Alley start-ups. For example, Peter Kestenbaum resigned recently as director of North American field marketing for Sun Microsystems after 13 years with the company. Having joined Sun a year before the company went public, he was already familiar with the grueling hours and guerrilla tactics of start-up life. And having witnessed the birth of Silicon Alley, he decided that the time was perfect to try some start-up companies on for size. His first experience was less than perfect. "Everyone was in shorts and sandals," he said. "There was no receptionist, so I just wandered to the back looking for the person I was there to meet. But the clincher came when I went to use the bathroom. There I was, standing in my $1,000 suit, and the urinals were filthy. It was like a gas station. I thought, 'I can't do this.' " Mr. Kestenbaum has decided to look for a position with a more established company. Perhaps the hardest part of finding the right executive is finding someone with a passion for the product, not just the money. Mr. Otremba agrees: "When you join a start-up it's like joining a family. All the stock options in the world don't amount to anything if the business doesn't interest you. There has to be a passion."
