title:
Patents;
An Internet search systemis said to respond to queries phrased the way that people really talk.
body: SEARCHING the Internet is inevitably an exercise in information overload. Type in a single word and you are likely to get thousands of hits, only a handful of which are pertinent to your actual field of interest. Adding an extra search term can often make things worse -- instead of narrowing your search, you can end up with even more hits. But what if you could pose a question to the search engine in plain English, in the same way that you might pose a question to the research librarian at your local library? And what if the search engine could understand the question, and respond to it precisely, just as an all-knowing librarian would be able to reach for the right book on the reference shelf? Kathleen Dahlgren, a computational linguist, and her colleague, Edward Stabler, contend that they have built exactly such a search engine, which they recently patented. The system, dubbed Inquizit, is based on natural-language searching, which means that it retrieves and stores information in much the way that people talk. The system is built in part on a set of principles Ms. Dahlgren laid out in her 1988 book, "Naive Semantics for Natural Language Understanding." "We model the way people interpret the meanings of a word -- through context," Ms. Dahlgren said. "We search on meaning by using grammar and structure and semantics. Every word has associated with it a set of beliefs." Thus, Ms. Dahlgren said, a query such as "What kinds of wood are bats made of?" would probably yield documents having to do with baseball bats and hickory. On the other hand, a query using identical key words with vastly different meanings -- "Do bats live in the woods?" for example -- would yield documents about species of bats who live in trees. But don't other search engines, like Ask Jeeves (www.askjeeves.com), already rely on natural-language retrieval? Ms. Dahlgren contends not. "With these pseudo-natural-language searches, you write the sentence and they throw away the little words and then do a standard Boolean search, possibly with some statistics thrown in," she said. "But they are essentially all pattern matchers. Since they don't actually figure out what the query means, they end up with enormous over-retrieval." During a recent visit to the askjeeves.com site, the query "What kinds of wood are bats made of?" turned up 10 sites, including 3 devoted to the actor James Woods, 2 that sold golfing equipment and encyclopedia entries on "bat," "bats" and "wood." The query "Do bats live in the woods?" turned up six hits, including a site selling softball and baseball equipment, a site that features Major League batting average records, and a link to the Death Clock site, "the Internet's friendly reminder that life is slipping away." Ms. Dahlgren acknowledged that others, like Microsoft, are trying to develop true natural-language programs. But she said the difference between her approach and that of Microsoft was that she and Mr. Stabler had hand-built their vast linguistic dictionary -- an undertaking that took nearly 15 years. "Microsoft is trying to write dictionaries automatically by searching machine-coded dictionaries," she said. "We actually built the dictionary by hand, as opposed to throwing a machine at the problem so we wouldn't have to sit down and write up all these linguistic rules." Microsoft declined to comment on Inquizit's technology or on Ms. Dahlgren's assessment of its own approach. Thus far, Inquizit has been financed by an Army research grant, private investors and "sweat equity," according to Ms. Dahlgren. So if Inquizit has discovered the Holy Grail of search engines, why hasn't it been gobbled up yet by a Microsoft or Yahoo? "We're talking to companies whose names you would recognize," said Taylor Hawke, director of marketing for Inquizit. He said the company planned to license its technology but that it was considering setting up its own Internet search engine. Inquizit, which is based in Santa Monica, Calif., received patent 5,794,050.  A Bra for Women After Heart Surgery Mary K. Whisman had open-heart surgery a few years back, as did her daughter and her daughter-in-law. "I realized that women have this terrible problem that men don't have," Mrs. Whisman said. "Store-bought brassieres push terribly on the place where they put the wire in after they open up your sternum." So Mrs. Whisman has patented a brassiere for postoperative open-heart surgery patients. Its main feature is a roll of soft padding that sits underneath the breasts, and which keeps the bra from pressing directly against the sternum area. The bra, which opens in front, holds each breast in a separate cup and features wide, padded straps, according to Mrs. Whisman. Mrs. Whisman, who lives in North Vernon, Ind., said she hoped to license patent 5,782,670.  System to Prevent Fake Videotapes Finally, a way to verify whether those videotapes of alien spaceships are authentic. Harlan J. Brothers, of Branford, Conn., has patented a video camera encryption system that employs Global Positioning System satellite receivers to encode videotape with the time and place it was taken. The tape is then played back on special equipment that decodes and displays the time and place information. "In the case of U.F.O.'s, you would be able to know whether the tape was doctored in any way," Mr. Brothers said. "Of course, that doesn't stop anyone from staging an event." Mr. Brothers, who is looking to license patent 5,799,083, said the technology had more pedestrian applications, such as documentation for insurance purposes. Patents are available by number for $3 from the Patent and Trademark Office, Washington, D.C. 20231.

title: Sad, Lonely World Discovered in Cyberspace
body: In the first concentrated study of the social and psychological effects of Internet use at home, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University have found that people who spend even a few hours a week on line experience higher levels of depression and loneliness than if they used the computer network less frequently. Participants who were lonelier and more depressed, as determined by standard questionnaires at the start of the two-year study, were no more drawn to the Internet than those who were originally happier and more socially engaged. Instead, Internet use itself appeared to cause a decline in psychological well-being, the researchers said. The results of the $1.5 million project ran completely contrary to expectations of the social scientists who designed it and to many of the organizations that financed the study. These included technology companies like the Intel Corporation, Hewlett Packard, AT&T Research and Apple Computer, as well as the National Science Foundation. "We were shocked by the findings, because they are counterintuitive to what we know about how socially the Internet is being used," said Robert Kraut, a social psychology professor at Carnegie Mellon's Human Computer Interaction Institute. "We are not talking here about the extremes. These were normal adults and their families, and on average, for those who used the Internet most, things got worse." The Internet has been praised as superior to television and other "passive" media because it allows users to choose the kind of information they want to receive, and often, to respond actively to it in the form of email exchanges with other users, chat rooms or electronic bulletin board postings. Research on the effects of watching television indicates that it tends to reduce social involvement. But the new study, titled "HomeNet," suggests that the interactive medium may be no more socially healthy than older mass media. It also raises troubling questions about "virtual" communication and the disembodied relationships that are often formed in the vacuum of cyberspace. Participants in the study used inherently social features like email and Internet chat more than they used passive information gathering like reading or watching videos. But they reported a decline in interaction with family members and a reduction in their circles of friends that directly corresponded to the amount of time they spent on line. At the beginning and end of the two-year study, the subjects were asked to agree or disagree with statements like "I felt everything I did was an effort," and "I enjoyed life" and "I can find companionship when I want it." They were also asked to estimate how many minutes each day they spent with each member of their family and to quantify their social circle. The subjects were given standard questionnaires used to determine psychological health. For the duration of the study, the subjects' use of the Internet was recorded. For the purposes of this study, depression and loneliness were measured independently, and each subject was rated on a subjective scale. In measuring depression, the responses were plotted on a scale of 0 to 3, with 0 being the least depressed and 3 being the most depressed. Loneliness was plotted on a scale of 1 to 5. By the end of the study, the researchers found that one hour a week on the Internet led, on average, to an increase of .03, or 1 percent, on the depression scale, a loss of 2.7 members of the subject's social circle, which averaged 66 people, and an increase of .02, or four-tenths of 1 percent, on the loneliness scale. The subjects exhibited wide variations in all three measured effects, and while the net effects were not large, they were statistically significant in demonstrating deterioration of social and psychological life, Professor Kraut said. Based on these data, the researchers hypothesize that relationships maintained over long distances without face-to-face contact ultimately do not provide the kind of support and reciprocity that typically contribute to a sense of psychological security and happiness, like being available to baby-sit in a pinch for a friend, or to grab a cup of coffee. "Our hypothesis is there are more cases where you're building shallow relationships, leading to an overall decline in feeling of connection to other people," Professor Kraut said. The study tracked the behavior of 169 participants in the Pittsburgh area who were selected from four schools and community groups. Half the group was measured through two years of Internet use, and the other half for one year. The findings will be published this week by The American Psychologist, the peer-reviewed monthly journal of the American Psychological Association. Because the study participants were not randomly selected, it is unclear how the findings apply to the general population. It is also conceivable that some unmeasured factor caused simultaneous increases in use of the Internet and decline in normal levels of social involvement. Moreover, the effect of Internet use varied depending on an individual's life patterns and type of use. Researchers said that people who were isolated because of their geography or work shifts might have benefited socially from Internet use. Even so, several social scientists familiar with the study vouched for its credibility and predicted that the findings would probably touch off a national debate over how public policy on the Internet should evolve and how the technology might be shaped to yield more beneficial effects. "They did an extremely careful scientific study, and it's not a result that's easily ignored," said Tora Bikson, a senior scientist at Rand, the research institution. Based in part on previous studies that focused on how local communities like Santa Monica, Calif., used computer networks to enhance civic participation, Rand has recommended that the Federal Government provide email access to all Americans. "It's not clear what the underlying psychological explanation is," Ms. Bikson said of the study. "Is it because people give up day-to-day contact and then find themselves depressed? Or are they exposed to the broader world of Internet and then wonder, 'What am I doing here in Pittsburgh?' Maybe your comparison standard changes. I'd like to see this replicated on larger scale. Then I'd really worry." Christine Riley, a psychologist at the Intel Corporation, the giant chip manufacturer that was among the sponsors of the study, said she was surprised by the results but did not consider the research definitive. "For us, the point is there was really no information on this before," Ms. Riley said. "But it's important to remember this is not about the technology, per se; it's about how it is used. It really points to the need for considering social factors in terms of how you design applications and services for technology." The Carnegie Mellon team -- which included Sara Kiesler, a social psychologist who helped pioneer the study of human interaction over computer networks; Tridas Mukophadhyay, a professor at the graduate business school who has examined computer mediated communication in the workplace, and William Scherlis, a research scientist in computer science -- stressed that the negative effects of Internet use that they found were not inevitable. For example, the main focus of Internet use in schools has been gathering information and getting in touch with people from far-away places. But the research suggests that maintaining social ties with people in close physical proximity could be more psychologically healthy. "More intense development and deployment of services that support pre-existing communities and strong relationships should be encouraged," the researchers write in their forthcoming article. "Government efforts to wire the nation's schools, for example, should consider on-line homework sessions for students rather than just on-line reference works." At a time when Internet use is expanding -- nearly 70 million adult Americans are on line, according to Nielsen Media Research -- social critics say that the technology could exacerbate the fragmentation of American society or help to fuse it, depending on how it is used. "There are two things the Internet can turn out to be, and we don't know yet which it's going to be," said Robert Putnam, a political scientist at Harvard University whose forthcoming book, "Bowling Alone," which is to be published next year by Simon & Schuster, chronicles the alienation of Americans from each other since the 1960's. "The fact that I'm able to communicate daily with my collaborators in Germany and Japan makes me more efficient, but there are a lot of things it can't do, like bring me chicken soup." Professor Putnam added, "The question is how can you push computer mediated communication in a direction that would make it more community friendly." Perhaps paradoxically, several participants in the Internet study expressed surprise when they were informed of the study's conclusions. "For me it's been the opposite of depression; it's been a way of being connected," said Rabbi Alvin Berkun, who used the Internet for a few hours a week to read The Jerusalem Post and communicate with other rabbis across the country. But Rabbi Berkun said his wife did not share his enthusiasm for the medium. "She does sometimes resent when I go and hook up," he said, adding after a pause, "I guess I am away from where my family is while I'm on the computer." Another possibility is that the natural human preference for face-to-face communication may provide a self-correcting mechanism to the technology. The rabbi's daughter, Rebecca, 17, said she had spent a fair amount of time in teen-age chat rooms at the beginning of the survey in 1995. "I can see how people would get depressed," Ms. Berkun said. "When we first got it, I would be on for an hour a day or more. But I found it was the same type of people, the same type of things being said. It got kind of old."

title:
LIBRARY/TENNIS SITES;
Advice for Playing Better Plus Lots of Gear and Gab
body: WWW.TENNIS.COM WATCHING or reading about tennis professionals chasing a ball from one side of the court to the other can certainly be entertaining, but it provides a limited view of the sport. Among the Web sites offering a more complete version is the one created by Tennis Magazine. The site devotes considerable coverage to teaching average players how to improve their tennis strokes, strategy and fitness. Of course, there is no guarantee that incorporating such advice into one's game is easier when gleaned from the Internet than from a magazine, book or a live tennis lesson. Like Tennis Magazine, the Web site rates the quality of new racquets and shoes. But readers of the electronic magazine can offer their own evaluations and ask questions about equipment in a chat room dubbed "gear gab," found in the "bbs central" section. Indeed, this free site has many other features not found in the monthly magazine, which requires a paid subscription. Among them are daily updates from the pro tours, weekly rankings, instructional tips and more chat areas. (Many of the postings seemed to be the work of adolescent minds, given the number of expletives and exhortations of "Sampras rules.") Tennis.com is planning extensive coverage of the U.S. Open, with photographs and daily stories about matches and the ambiance. Visitors to the site can also get TV broadcast times, ticket information and match schedules. This site is probably the slickest and most mass-market oriented of all the tennis magazines on the Web. For people with time to browse only one publication, it is a good choice. Graphic   Photo: Tennis Magazine has a slick site.

title:
LIBRARY/TENNIS SITES;
As U.S. Open Nears, It's Everything Tennis
body: THE world's top tennis players will not be the only ones sweating, lunging and sprinting when the U.S. Open championships start on Monday in Queens. Thousands of the nation's computers will be doing the electronic equivalent, as their owners put them through their paces in the name of tennis enthusiasm. The two weeks of the U.S. Open are among the busiest times for many of the hundreds of tennis-oriented Web sites on the Internet. Not only do people want to know such details as how easily Martina Hingis squashed an opponent on a given day, but they also are inspired to learn how to improve their own wristy forehand and speed up their lazy feet. According to I.B.M., which creates the official Web pages for all four of the major tennis championships (the Australian Open, the French Open, Wimbledon and the U.S. Open), the U.S. Open site usually gets the most traffic. Last year, the site measured 63.7 million hits, according to Jeff Ramminger, who lead the design of the U.S. Open site. Many of those hits come from tennis enthusiasts like Cheryl Hand, a nurse from Birmingham, Ala., who browses the Internet, not just during the big tournaments but nearly every day. In fact, she spends more time reading on-line tennis magazines and checking results on the professional tours than she does on the court improving her own game. "Like the other day, I was watching Pete Sampras play on television and I saw him lose because of a bad line call on match point," Ms. Hand said. "I looked on the Internet to see what he said about the call afterward because he was a little vocal about it on the court." Indeed, Ms. Hand eventually logged onto the official Pete Sampras Web site and sent an email expressing her sympathy about what she saw as poor officiating. "That call just really upset me, so I felt that I had to give my 2 cents," Ms. Hand said. She has yet to get a response from Mr. Sampras, nor does she expect to get one. One of the easiest ways to find information about the game is to go to a site like Yahoo (www.yahoo.com) and click on its recreation and sports subject heading. Browsing among the offerings opens a window into the diversity of the Web's tennis subculture. Visitors can experience tradition at the Wimbledon Championships site (www.wimbledon.org), community at the Gay and Lesbian Tennis Alliance (www.glta.org), and levity at Alt.Tennis, an instructional site that promises "explicit, uncensored, alternative ways to play tennis" (www.alttennis.com), which includes between-the-legs shots and faking out your opponent. And visitors can see for themselves how tennis on the Web, perhaps like no other sport, is driven as much by Hollywood-style glamour as by talent. For example, Anna Kournikova, a teen-aged Russian tour player who has never won a professional championship but still draws considerable attention with her starlet looks and midriff-baring outfits, is listed as the subject of more than 20 sites on Yahoo. In contrast, Jana Novotna, of the Czech Republic, this year's winner of the Wimbledon women's title, perhaps the most prestigious in the game, has just four Yahoo-listed sites to her name. Indeed, many of the general tennis bulletin boards on the Web appear to be filled with postings about personalities: which pro is better, more polite, more attractive. However, discourse on the specialized sites is typically more elevated, particularly when it comes to asking questions about the quality of equipment. One feature that some may find especially advantageous about the Web is the multitude of tennis equipment for sale on line often at cheaper prices than those in sporting goods stores. With locations like www. tennis-warehouse.com and their vast stocks of equipment, a tennis enthusiast may never have to step into a pro shop again. Graphic   Photo (Suzanne DeChillo/The newyork Times)

title:
LIBRARY/TENNIS SITES;
Focusing on Fundamentals
body: WWW.TENNISSERVER.COM IF THERE is an equivalent of the neighborhood tennis club newsletter on the Internet, the Tennis Server could be it. The site has little in the way of impressive graphics and video clips, but it does feature extensive coverage about the fundamentals of the game. Names like Michael Chang and Venus Williams are only occasionally mentioned here. Instead, the site focuses on what is relevant to weekend-playing amateurs, with columns about mental toughness (the writer has a Ph.D. in psychology), improving strokes and fitness. Much of the writing is in the form of personal experience as if it were being offered by the local club pro. The quality of advice appears to be good and often unique, at least to someone who has taken a few hundred tennis lessons during his lifetime. There is also a guest column that seems to deal with whatever is on the mind of that month's author. A writer in a recent issue, for example, told a story about how his tickets to the U.S. Open were stolen by a pickpocket. Even a novice player who can barely hit a forehand will probably feel comfortable here. Information is available on such basics as the rules governing tennis, tennis clubs and organizations around the country, and how to store tennis racquets. Two often neglected groups that this site serves are junior and senior players. There is a column that takes turns addressing these two groups: one month, how to better develop junior talent; the next month, protecting yourself from skin cancer while on the court. Graphic   Photo

title: Mystery Sites Easy To Deduce - Correction Appended
body: MARISA BABJAK laughs when she thinks about the noose pin she sold to the judge in Florida, but she has other, more serious things on her mind now. Like visiting the Orange County, Calif., morgue on a slow night to take a look at a few toe tags. She thinks the toe tags will lend themselves nicely as a stern message to friends and loved ones, as in, "You're dead meat if you don't write." Unpleasant reality filtered through humor sells well for Ms. Babjak, 39. She markets mystery-related items by catalogue and through her Web site, Femmes Fatales (mall6.register.com/femfatal). There you can scroll through a limited list of gift items, like the Mad Mother Shower Curtain, police patches from the former Soviet Union, T-shirts and all manner of pins -- guns, hatchets, thumb prints. Femmes Fatales opens a window on hundreds of mystery-related Internet sites where people have taken up residence to chat, read about their favorite authors, buy gifts and books, solve whodunits and answer trivia questions. There are other Web pages dedicated to Agatha Christie and Arthur Conan Doyle, and modern authors like Sue Grafton and John Grisham. Links to many of those can be found at Mysterious Strands (www.idsonline.com/userweb/cwilson/ mystery.htm).The sites tend to leave trails, or links, to other sites, making iteasy to find a slew of others. There are true-crime sites, like Black Dahlia (www.bethshort.com), and other reality-based fare, like the Smoking Gun page (www.thesmokinggun.com). For a serving of rock-and-roll and mystery, there's www.paulisdead.com, which invites you to solve the drowning of a fictional rock star, Paul Lomo. Jiro Kimura, 49, of Kanazawa, Japan, writes a regular column on the Internet mystery scene for Hayakawa's Mystery Magazine and opened the Gumshoe page in January 1996 (www.nsknet.or.jp/ jkimura). "I usually write in Japanese to make money," she said in a recent email exchange, "but I wanted to write something in English too for non-Japanese mystery fans. I thought the Web site would be the best way." At the site, which is impressive in its simplicity, she describes what's new and lists some of her favorite bookmarks. "The Internet is just another means by which mystery fans communicate with one another," Ms. Kimura said in her email. Often that communication leads to a face-to-face visit at the many mystery conventions held each year. At Partners & Crime, an independent bookstore in Greenwich Village (www.crimepays.com), email correspondents who have been at the shop's site looking for first-edition copies or original art make a point of stopping at the store when they are in Manhattan, said Kizmin Reeves, a partner in the store. "There's a huge world out there and it's really quite diverse," said Patty Suchy, who runs Novel Explorations (www.erols.com/ novelexp), a travel company based in Columbia, Md., that this winter held a mystery-theme vacation cruise. "People become more aware to the possibilities on the Internet," she said, where they can find like-minded groups and other places to go. For those with a particular interest in Sherlock Holmes, there is the Sherlockian Holmepage (watserv1.uwaterloo.ca/ credmond/sh.html), created in 1995 by Chris Redmond, author of "A Sherlock Holmes Handbook." The idea, he said, was to have a page pointing to all things about Sherlock Holmes on the Web. "Sherlockians have always been great at letter writing and newsletters," he said. "A lot of that has shifted on the Web." Susan Dahlinger, a writer in Secaucus, N.J., has signed onto two mailing-list sites for mystery aficionados, mostly to do research, she said. One is by invitation only, she said. The other, Hounds of the Internet (www.bcpl.lib.md.us/lmoskowi/hounds/ hounds.html), is open to anyone. Many authors and publishers are using the Internet to publish the first couple of chapters in their books to get fans hooked. Ms. Babjak, who lives in Lakewood, Calif., said her Femmes Fatales catalog and site grew out of her hobby of making and selling gift items to mystery fans at conventions.  Femmes Fatales (French for "deadly women") was created with the help of her husband, Jim, in 1995 to broaden her business and her love of mysteries. New morbid items may show up for sale at Femmes Fatales. Customers like police officers, coroners and an entomologist Ms.  Babjak has nicknamed "Maggot Man" keep requesting more unique items. When you think about it, she says, when's the last time you saw a T-shirt for a bug guy? Correction  An article in Circuits on Aug. 27 about Web sites for mystery fans referred incorrectly to Jiro Kimura, who runs the Gumshoe site (www .nsknet.or.jp/jkimura). Jiro Kimu ra is a man, not a woman. Correction-Date: September 16, 1998, Wednesday Graphic   Photo: Marisa Babjak, whose Femmes Fatales site sells mystery-related gift items. (Ed Carreon for The newyork Times)

title:
NEWS WATCH;
A Different Type Of Computer Monitor
body: Better watch what you type. A new generation of software is emerging to permit employers to record not just which Web sites employees browse, but also which programs they use, memos they write, emails they send -- in short, every keystroke. Win What Where, a software company in Kennewick, Wash. (www.winwhatwhere.com), released its entrant into the field this month, a program called Win What Where, which costs $285 for each desktop computer in which it is installed. The company says its software keeps a record of every keystroke, mouse click and command. In June, Tech Assist of Largo, Fla. (www.toolsthatwork. com), began distributing Desktop Surveillance in North America, a comprehensive computer-monitoring program by the British company Omniquad. The software costs $55 per computer and has been on sale in Europe for about eight months. Desktop Surveillance is being marketed as the "software equivalent of a video surveillance camera on the desktop." It permits third-party observers to view, in real time or in playback, exactly what tasks a user is performing and what keystrokes he or she is entering. Each program lets employers hide the fact that the software is running on an employee's computer. Desktop Surveillance even allows a record of the employee's activities to be emailed to a supervisor without an employee's knowledge. Officials from both Tech Assist and Win What Where said they saw a demand from employers concerned about employees' wasting time on their computers. They also said that employers wanted a record in case the employees sued or were sued. Still, Richard Eaton, president of Win What Where, said his company had struggled with whether to produce software that could be used to invade employee privacy. "There was a lot of turmoil internally about monitoring keystrokes," Mr. Eaton said. "It just seemed like too much, but it was the No. 1 request from our customers." Julie Allen, senior product manager for Tech Assist, said Desktop Surveillance could be set only to record an employee's actions when certain off-limits activities occurred, such as when an employee visited a sex-related Web site.  "Companies have proper use policies for computers and the Internet," she said. "This is just an enforcer of those policies." Graphic   Drawing

title:
NEWS WATCH;
University Takes Magazine To Task on the Internet
body: Stanford University believes it has a thing or two to teach U. S. News & World Report about accuracy. The magazine counters that Stanford needs a lesson in objectivity. The dispute surrounds the magazine's college rankings issue, which reached newsstands on Monday and is typically its best-selling issue. Stanford is using the Net to press its several-year-old stand against the rankings, asserting that they mischaracterize the experience at various institutions. On its Web site (www.stanford. edu/home/statistics/index.html), the university has posted data about Stanford that it says more accurately reflects the Stanford experience; it also has posted a report by PricewaterhouseCoopers, which audits the universities' data. U. S. News's report (www.usnews.com) does not disagree that Stanford's own internal findings are accurate, but the magazine says its own rankings offer prospective students a more objective look because U. S. News does not favor any particular institution. Indeed, a magazine spokeswoman, Celeste James, said that the publication was well accustomed to hearing criticism from colleges that did not necessarily agree with how the rankings portrayed them. "We are an independent source," Ms. James said. "When someone selects their own data, it is inherently subjective." A Stanford spokesman, Terry Shepard, countered that the university was not complaining about its rank, which consistently has been in the top six. Instead, he said, Stanford believes that U. S. News and World Report overly generalizes and reaches unsupportable conclusions. For example, he said, the magazine unfairly seeks to measure student satisfaction partly by determining what percentage of alumni donate to the school. "They count what's countable rather than what's accurate," Mr. Shepard said, adding that Stanford would like to see the rankings abolished and might decide not to provide information for the survey next year. The current U. S. News & World Report annual survey, its 12th, ranks more than 1,300 institutions based on questionnaires sent to college officials. On at least one point, the magazine agrees with Stanford. It notes that students should not base their decision solely on the rankings. Graphic   Photo

title:
Q & A;
Messages That POP
body: Q. I need an Internet provider that offers POP3 capabilities. How can I find one? A. For those who need a little background: POP stands for Post Office Protocol, a method that email applications use to download messages to the computer from email servers on the Internet. Once the message gets to the email server, the user can dial in to his or her Internet service provider and download the message. A POP3 server, if you've ever wondered about the term (you may have seen it in your email program's settings box or as an occasional flash on-screen as the program checks your mail) is where incoming email sits until you log on to download it. In addition to the popular POP3, there is IMAP, the Internet Message Access Protocol. With the right settings and email program, POP3 is useful for people who want or need to retrieve their messages from any computer that has Internet access, although the IMAP standard is often considered better at handling mail from different workstations. Some on-line services use their own proprietary software, so call the prospective company's tech-support line and ask whether it uses POP3. If you already have on-line access, explore the support area of your provider's Web site.   J. D. BIERSDORFER Circuits invites questions about computer-based technology, by postal mail to Questions, Circuits, The newyork Times, 229 West 43d Street, newyork, N.Y. 10036-3959 or by email to QandA@nytimes.com.

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Batches of Butterflies Can Be Bought On the Web, or Just Studied From Afar
body: THE World Wide Web captures everything in its sticky threads, including just about anything anyone would ever want to know about butterflies. Flitting from link to link can yield serendipitous citings and other drops of nectar. At www.holeinhand.com, for example, the site for a butterfly farm in Hazelton, Pa., you can discover how to purchase live butterflies to release at "weddings, graduations, corporate events, divorces, anniversaries, grand openings, births and funerals." Before shipment, all butterflies are hand-fed and exercised to guarantee health, according to the site, though the concept of butterflies doing calisthenics stretches the imagination. The Butterfly Web Site promotes the releasing of butterflies at events as "more ecologically sound than rice or balloons," though make sure to release lepidoptera that are native to your region, so as not to disturb the gene pool (butterflywebsite.com/ series.htm). The site discusses how butterfly farms can be started on just a windowsill or desktop. Under frequently asked questions, there's a listing of how to say butterfly in 51 languages, including Indonesian (kupu-kupu), Malaysian (rama-rama) and the Australian aboriginal tongue, Wiradjuri (buuja-buuja). The Butterfly Web site also has a bulletin board section, where you can join the three dozen others who have read postings with headings like "Butterflies in my coneflowers." For a listing of pictures and natural history of the butterflies by state and other parts of North America, see butterflywebsite.com/articles/ npwc/butterflychecklist.htm. This site is as good as some nature guides, where one learns that in Washington the Bramble Green Hairstreak lays its eggs singly on the flower buds of its host plants. And take a look at www.discovery.com/area/science/ micro/butterfly.html to see a butterfly wing magnified 650 times. You can also trace or help report the progress of the annual migration of monarch butterflies, through the Journey North site (www.learner. org/jnorth/current.html). And at the same site, classrooms in the unitedstates and Canada can pair up with those in Mexico to send symbolic butterflies south for the winter. "Mexican students will watch over them -- and return them next spring as the real monarchs journey north," the site says. Butterfly-related volunteer opportunities can be found on the Web, too. Amateur and professional butterfly watchers are needed to monitor trends in butterfly populations for five consecutive days or five years, (www.cfe.cornell.edu/oneshots/ butterfly.html). You could also find how to purchase "Flights of Fancy," a 24-by-36-inch, $2,350 collage made with real butterfly wings (www.butterflycreations.com/orderEntry.html). Not to worry about the carnage, though: "All of the butterflies used for Butterfly Creations are bred on butterfly farms, primarily in South America. In these enclosed plantations they flourish in their natural surroundings and they die naturally. We do not capture or kill any of the butterflies we use for display and none are an endangered species." You can also find chat sites with postings like the following: "I am a translator (Dutch to English) and have been having some trouble with names of butterflies. The one I'm currently stuck with is 'vliervlinder,' which I have found referred to as 'ourapteryx sambucaria.' It will be a European butterfly. Does anyone know an English common name for it?" Perhaps the most intriguing page is not simply about butterflies, but about the myths and superstitions humans have concocted about them, like those found at www.insects. org/ced4/symbollist3.html). One example given says that according to Funk and Wagnalls' Standard Dictionary of Folklore, Mythology and Legend, "to get a new dress all a girl need do is to catch a butterfly of the desired color and crush it between her teeth while muttering a magic formula," and "Some say that if a butterfly is put in a gun, it is impossible to miss the target." And for those who wondered why some angels were pictured with butterfly wings in medieval times, and even for those who did not, the site explains: "The Serbians look on the butterfly as the soul of a witch and believe if they can find her body and turn it around while she is asleep, the soul will not be able to find her mouth and re-enter, and the witch will probably die." It may sound odd, but after all, the Greeks used the same word for both butterfly and soul. Graphic   Photo

title: The Art of Driving Is All the Rage
body: ONCE you have come to terms with the number of computers inside your car, try looking at the number of cars on your computer -- Web sites devoted to just about all aspects of the automotive experience. And when it comes to popular driving topics on the Web, road rage is all the rage. Road rage, the phenomenon of agitated drivers' becoming aggressive, dangerous and potentially lethal to other drivers, has triggered a number of sites set up to record license plates and automotive offenders on the Web. Yahoo keeps a comprehensive index of recent news stories and Web pages about the topic (headlines.yahoo.com/ FullCoverage/US/RoadRage). Two rage pages in particular take vastly differing views on the subject. The Principles of Driving Psychology (www.aloha.net/ dyc/ch11.html) is a paper published on the Web by Dr. Leon James that explores attitudes and moral implications concerning transportation manners among individuals. A lengthy treatise on human behavior behind the wheel, the page also offers a test called What's Your Moral Driving IQ? (Sample yes-or-no question: "When I encounter road-hugging pedestrians, I feel like pushing them out of my way.") If you are in the mood for more rage than road, try the scathing site How to Drive Like a Moron (members.aol.com/doggiesnot). Decorated with illustrations and animations that bring to mind the look of Comedy Central's crudely animated "South Park" cartoon, the site sarcastically compiles just about every possible bad-driving habit as part of its instruction in the art of idiot behavior. In the Shopping Center Parking Lots area, for example, the site suggests: "Always park on the lines, taking up as many spaces as possible. Diagonal parking is preferred." Because of its size and traffic congestion, the newyork metropolitan area most likely has more than its share of angry drivers. For those wanting to know what they're getting into before leaving the office, there's the Metro Commute site, which will let you check a number of local regions for accident alerts, construction areas and traffic warnings and posts an illustrated map regularly (www.metrocommute.com). If you've finally made it home and find yourself locked in the Web's slow lane, you can even check out the Internet Traffic Report (www.internettrafficreport.com) to see how much congestion the Net is under. And remember, whether you're driving a Jeep Cherokee or a Dell Pentium, let's be careful out there. Graphic   Photo: TAKE MY LICENSE -- PLEASE -- This Web site, which humorously catalogues bad driving habits, is one of many sites inspired by the culture and psychology of the roadway.

title: Virtual Virtuosos of the Holler
body: The Internet is not just a place for crass commercialism, vapid flirtation and the homogenization of American life. It is a timeless storehouse of priceless, rare, indigenous oral tradition. Honest. If you don't believe it, head on over to sunsite. unc.edu/hollerin/hollerin.htm and get a load of grown folks hollerin' their hearts out. It's a hoot. Don't try this at work. The vocal samples, all in streaming (more like screaming) Real Audio, sound like Tarzan's first yodeling lessons or a cross between an apoplectic elephant and a submerging submarine. But they're virtuosic, the brightest and best of the National Hollerin' Contest, held each June in Spivey's Corner, a hamlet in North Carolina. According to the Web site, hollering is thought to be one of the earliest forms of human communication and falls into four categories: functional, communicative, pleasure and distress, with the last known for its "falsetto and a sense of urgency," though nearly all hollering might be said to fit that description. Folklore researchers have found hollering to be most prevalent in black communities of the Southeast, though on this site and in Sampson County, N.C., home of the competition, most hollerers are white. The art form's roots reach back to the 1700's, the site says, when men transporting logs by river from Sampson County developed a system of hollers to avoid bashing into one another and to call for help if they ran aground. Hollers can be heard up to three miles away and were used on isolated farms to find lost children and summon help in case of house fires. A skilled hollerer could call in his or her hogs, cattle, sheep, dogs, children or spouse, and the art was particularly handy for separating animals grazing on common land. The contest began in 1969 with the help of Ermon Godwin, 70, whose grandfather Bud Godwin "was a hollerin' man" and whose 9-year-old granddaughter appeared on David Letterman's show as the junior hollerin' champion. He figures he can identify, just by their hollers, all 30 contest champions. "It has brought a sense of feeling to our people here in Spivey's Corner, especially for the young people," Mr. Godwin said. "We have something unique to give to the world, though we're just a little crossroads community of 49." You can hear hollerin' quartet versions of "Amazing Grace," "Old Gray Goose" and "The Lion Sleeps Tonight," as presented by Suzie Bolotin, in audio and video, with arpeggios that could challenge a violinist reared on Vivaldi. And where else can you hear the North Carolina Agriculture Commissioner Jim Graham do a hollering impression of a mule, with high, eerie overtones and alarming similitude? The Web site is a project of Paul Jones's class in cyberpublishing and cybercasting at the University of North Carolina School of Journalism. His students were surprised when they taped Ms. Bolleton. "They thought they were going to get 15 seconds and they got 3 minutes 50 seconds," he said, not to mention having a hollerin' champion who is a Klezmer singer who won with a Zulu song. Graphic   Photo: The hollerin' site offers pictures and sounds of champion vocalists.

title: Bits and Bytes
body: Flavors of the Caribbean In the Air (and on the Web) In the summertime, when the tropics try to migrate to Hudson Bay, the Caribbean seems awfully close to these northern latitudes. And just now the flavors of the West Indies -- a medley of fruits, spices, grains, roots and tubers -- are much in the air. If the motto "When in the tropics, cook like the tropics" appeals to you, help is at hand on the Internet. An extremely well stocked site is Recipes From Guyana and the Caribbean, run by Wayne Moses, a Guyanese (www3.nbnet.nb-.ca/wmoses/recipes.html). He offers recipes for island classics like callaloo jumble (salt fish, bacon, beef or pork, shrimp, the spinachlike callaloo and a few other good things, all served on rice); mango fly (a drink); banana fritters, and curried hassars a la Courantyne, which calls for four wirri-wirri peppers. Mr. Moses thoughtfully supplies much vital information: just click on "frequently asked questions." You can learn there that a hassar is a black catfish about six to eight inches long with a tough shell, and that wirri-wirri peppers are edible cherry bombs, like habaneros but less incendiary. Spiciness is a fact of Caribbean cookery, with its curried dishes and the omnipresent habanero, or Scotch bonnet, the world's hottest pepper, which is native to the region. But why do hot countries favor hot foods? The most widely accepted answer is that they set off the body's own refrigeration system: a curry legendarily isn't hot enough until it makes you break out in a cold sweat. Another site, West Indian Recipes (www.chrisevelyn.com/WIrecipes.htm), is part of the unofficial Internet voice of St. Kitts and Nevis, founded last year by Christopher Evelyn. The recipes section has a grilled jerk chicken that calls for 10 pureed Scotch bonnets (serves four); curried goat, but also a vegetarian curry; banana bread, and black cake, a Christmas specialty, made with a cup of rum. ("For best results," the directions say, "let the cake remain in the pan while you are sprinkling it with rum for three days.") Windows on Haiti (www.geocities.com/ Heartland/Pointe/5200), run by Guy Antoine, is the hub of an on-line Haitian cultural center, with pages on art, books and songs of Haiti. Click on "recipes" for dishes like Ti-Malice sauce, a hot sauce that accompanies many Haitian fish and meat dishes, and pain patate, a potato bread made from sweet potatoes. There are also chicken with peas (poulet pois France), and rice and beans, both staples of the Haitian diet. The recipes on these sites come from many experienced cooks, who are by and large not professional cookbook writers. They usually assume that anyone who will cook from their recipes knows in advance what the dishes are. Some of the directions can be sketchy or might reflect the conditions of island life. For instance, a recipe might ask you to grate a coconut for coconut milk, instead of suggesting you buy a can.  Think Cold Soup Soup of the Evening, Beautiful Soup (www.geocities.com/NapaValley/6188/ hpsoup.html) owes its mellifluous name to the Mock Turtle's song in "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland." Nor do its literary associations end there; by clicking on "food tales" at this site, for instance, it's possible to learn what Samuel Johnson thought of cucumbers (not much). But for the main reason to know about this site as summer clings, click on "cold soups." The menu of tempting recipes includes vichyssoise, of course, but also Czech blueberry soup (it calls for 1 1/2 cups sour cream, but substituting yogurt would make it lighter); lime-cucumber soup with a kick (from tequila); golden gazpacho (made with cantaloupe, yellow peppers and yogurt), and strawberry balsamic soup (it includes a quart of strawberries, orange and lemon zest, Grand Marnier and balsamic vinegar). Unfortunately, when you call up this site with Netscape, a pesky rectangular window of advertisements pops up with it. Just swat it on the "X" in its upper right-hand corner. Whatever you do, don't minimize it, or it will fall to your tool bar and multiply. As for Samuel Johnson, he said, "A cucumber should be well sliced and dressed with pepper and vinegar, and then thrown out, as good for nothing."  Recipes of the Spas Many people who try the spa experience find it transformative, teaching them to slow down, appreciate nature and eat more healthfully. The Web site of Spa Finders magazine (www.spafinders.com) makes the immodest claim that spa chefs have changed the way Americans eat (click on "magazine"), by bringing dishes low in both fat and calories into the mainstream. To see what all the crowing is about, there's a recipe section compiled by the International Spa and Fitness Association (click on "spa cuisine" and then "recipes"). The bill of fare includes pesto risotto di mare; red lentil chili, and grilled mahi-mahi with herbed couscous and three-bean salad with orange vinaigrette. Evaluating these recipes, Margaret Pierpont, the co-author with Diane Tegmeyer of "The Spa Life at Home" (Longstreet Press, 1997), commented by email: "Spa chefs create meals that are highly nutritious, which is why there are many creative ways of serving fruit and vegetables, beans and whole grains in this collection." She also noted that when meat, fish or poultry is included, the amounts are small. The recipes are generally for tablefuls of diners and need to be scaled down. Ms. Pierpont, who collected and tested recipes from spas all over the country for her book, also faced this problem. For soups, chilis and breads particularly, she recommends making the amount called for and refrigerating or freezing the rest. The site's main activity is finding spas to match a spa seeker's needs and budget. Graphic   Drawing (Bob Scott)

title: U.S. INVESTIGATING MICROSOFT'S ROLE IN INTEL DECISIONS
body: The two companies are so intertwined, so seemingly mutually dependent for their extraordinary success that the Microsoft Corporation and the Intel Corporation are often referred to as a single entity -- "Wintel" -- in recognition of the degree to which Microsoft's Windows operating system and Intel's microprocessors dominate the technology of personal computing. But the Government is investigating whether Microsoft has used its market muscle to force even Intel, its only real peer, to shelve new technology efforts that conflicted with Microsoft's ambitions. Federal and state investigators appear particularly interested in an August 1995 meeting between Intel executives, including Andrew S. Grove, the chairman, and executives of Microsoft led by William H. Gates, its chairman. At the meeting, Mr. Gates made "vague threats" about supporting Intel competitors, according to one of many internal Intel memos that the company was required to hand over to investigators. Mr. Gates, according to a memo written by an Intel executive who attended the meeting, was "livid" about Intel's "investments in the Internet, and wanted them stopped." In the last few weeks, Federal and state investigators have been taking depositions from four Intel employees, including Mr. Grove, people close to the investigation said. The investigators are pursuing additional evidence that might be included in the sweeping antitrust case against Microsoft filed by the Justice Department and 20 states. The Government and the states accuse Microsoft of using unfair business practices to protect its monopoly in operating systems and to extend that monopoly into the new markets for Internet software and commerce. The case, scheduled to go to trial on Sept. 23, focuses mainly on Microsoft's tactics in the market for Internet browsing software for navigating the World Wide Web. The depositions of Intel employees could strengthen the case if the evidence suggests a pattern of Microsoft's abusing its monopoly power. The Justice Department and the states say that in addition to thwarting competition, Microsoft has the power to control the pace of innovation in computing, which is the focus of the investigation of Microsoft's dealings with Intel. The public policy implication of Microsoft's power, the Government says, is that technology makes its way into the marketplace at the pace that is best for Microsoft instead of what is best for the economy and for consumers. Microsoft replies that the antitrust suit is misguided, and that the company is a champion of innovation, enriching not only itself but also much of the high-technology economy, and benefiting consumers. In the Intel case, and others, Federal and state investigators are trying to portray routine business meetings as attempts to forge an anti-competitive conspiracy, Microsoft says. "Business partners like Intel and Microsoft occasionally have minor disputes, and the fact that the Justice Department and the states are apparently trying to shoehorn this into their case at the last minute shows how desperate they are," said Charles F. Rule, a partner at the Washington law firm of Covington & Burling and a former senior Justice Department official who is an adviser to Microsoft. The Justice Department would not comment on its investigation of Microsoft. The meeting between executives of Microsoft and Intel in early August 1995 came only weeks before the introduction of Windows 95. Microsoft was already well along in its plans for the Internet, though it would not announce them until December 1995. This was none too soon, for by early August 1995, the Netscape Communications Corporation, the pioneer in browser software, was a hot start-up about to sell shares to the public, setting off an Internet mania on Wall Street. On Aug. 2, 1995, Mr. Grove met with Mr. Gates on Intel's corporate campus in Santa Clara, Calif., according to the Intel documents. The three-hour session in a windowless second-floor conference room was attended by several executives from each company. It was mainly a confidential exchange of product plans and market strategies -- not only for Microsoft's operating systems and Intel's microprocessors but also including areas like multimedia software and the Internet. There was a heated discussion of software, according to Intel documents, but it was software that had been developed by Intel rather than by Microsoft. Though its business is making microprocessor chips, Intel also works on software, just as Microsoft does research and development work on hardware. Intel's silicon microprocessors are typically called the electronic brains of personal computers, while Microsoft's operating system is referred to as the central nervous system. Just as the brain is part of the central nervous system, the line separating the fundamental hardware and software technology of computing is often blurred. Software instructions can be programmed into chips, and hardware functions can be emulated in software. "Silicon is simply frozen software," Intel's Mr. Grove once said. Intel's software work has long been done at the company's research center in Hillsboro, Ore., the Intel Architecture Labs. Intel has mainly developed the software that sits between the operating system and the microprocessor -- under-the-hood programs that enhance the performance of advanced tasks like Internet communications, video or audio. Typically, Intel gives such software to developers, including Microsoft, which has often added Intel-developed enhancements to its operating systems. This kind of software development makes business sense for Intel because the more people want high-performance computing for work or games, the more they need powerful new computers -- about 85 percent of which are powered by Intel microprocessors. But at times, Intel's software development conflicts with Microsoft's plans. At the August 1995 meeting, Mr. Gates expressed concern about Intel's software work in two areas -- a layer of multimedia software called native signal processing, or N.S.P., and the possibility that some of Intel's Internet software development might be at odds with Microsoft's strategy. The differences between Microsoft and Intel over N.S.P. technology were widely reported in the trade press in 1995, but the memos now disclose that the two companies were also at odds over Intel's plans for developing support for Internet features and a software engine for Java, a programming language created by Sun Microsystems Inc., a Microsoft rival. A microprocessor that supported Java would have enabled programs written in that language to run on any operating system -- a serious threat to the dominance of Microsoft's Windows. According to an internal memo written by an Intel executive who attended the meeting, Mr. Gates left no doubt that he wanted the software development at the Intel Architecture Labs, or I.A.L., curbed. And at the same time, he publicly announced that Microsoft would share technologies and spend up to $100 million to train engineers to develop and service products on a version of Windows written for a competitor's microprocessor. "Gates didn't want I.A.L.'s 750 engineers interfering with his plans for domination of the PC industry," the Intel memo stated. "Gates made vague threats about support for other platforms, and on the same day he announced a major program to support Digital Equipment's Alpha microprocessor, an Intel competitor. Gates was livid about I.A.L.'s investments in the Internet, and he wanted them stopped." The subject of Netscape also came up at the meeting and, according to Intel documents, Mr. Gates said it was fine for Intel to support Netscape to the degree it would support any company developing software for the Wintel technology. But the Intel documents also say that Mr. Gates clearly delivered the message that he wanted the most and closest cooperation for Microsoft. How evidence about the meeting might be used in the case against Microsoft is not clear. At this point, the Government can add evidence only if it mirrors charges already in the suit filed in May. In that complaint, the Government contends that during two meetings in June 1995 between Microsoft and Netscape executives, Microsoft tried to persuade Netscape to divvy up the browser market instead of competing. Microsoft denies the allegation. In any case, Netscape says it declined the offer. Still, Government lawyers could argue that the Microsoft-Intel meeting was an effort to limit competition -- Intel's freely distributed software, in this instance. "At the least, this potentially reinforces the Government's argument that Microsoft is a monopoly -- if it can even push Intel around," observed Robert Litan, a former senior official in the Justice Department's antitrust division who is now at the Brookings Institution. Whatever the legal implications, industry analysts say that Microsoft exercises considerable control over the pace of innovations in computing. For another company's hardware or software to work, it must conform to Microsoft's operating system. That power, industry analysts say, cuts both ways. "Somebody has to set standards for everything in your computer to work, and Microsoft has assumed that role," said Richard Doherty, president of Envisioneering, a research firm in Seaford, N.Y. "But it is also true that when Microsoft can't yet see a way to gain some proprietary advantage from some new technology, it is in Microsoft's interest to stall its introduction -- and it does. In all sorts of ways, Microsoft can create a weather storm in the industry, so the ships will not leave port." After the August 1995 meeting, Intel pretty much followed Microsoft's lead on Internet and multimedia software. In later meetings, Intel made it clear it would back off on the technology initiatives Microsoft found objectionable, according to Intel documents. In a September 1995 meeting with Intel, Paul Maritz, a senior Microsoft executive, told the Intel group, according to an Intel memo, that it was "imperative we are in lock step on the Internet." Intel shifted course, presumably, for pragmatic reasons -- its relationship with Microsoft was too important to jeopardize. And the outcome of the dispute over Intel's multimedia program, N.S.P., sheds some light on the business logic involved. In 1996, in a long dialogue between Mr. Grove and Mr. Gates, published in Fortune magazine as "A Conversation With the Lords of Wintel," the two men discussed the matter. Mr. Gates said, "Intel deserves a lot of credit for stepping back." Mr. Grove replied: "We didn't have much of a choice. We basically caved." Mr. Gates objected to that characterization, but Mr. Grove stuck to his line. "We caved," the Intel chairman said. "Introducing a Windows-based software initiative that Microsoft doesn't support . . . well, life is too short for that." Mr. Grove declined to comment for this article. And Intel itself faces a Government antitrust suit; the Federal Trade Commission charges that the company has abused its dominance in microprocessors by retaliating against corporate customers and competitors, withholding information on Intel technology needed to make other products. title: Gregg Burge, 40, Choreographer And Dancer on Stage and Screen
body: Gregg Burge, a dancer and choreographer on Broadway and in films, died on July 4 at Piedmont Hospital in Atlanta. He was 40 and had homes in Atlanta and newyork. The cause was complications from a brain tumor, his mother, Thelma, said. A friend of Mr. Burge's reported his death to The newyork Times. Nominated for two Tony awards and two Drama Desk awards, Mr. Burge had a distinctive style that blended a glittering, crackling stage presence and virtuoso tap dancing with the aristocratic manners, lightness and ground-skimming speed of a classical ballet performer. He began performing professionally on television and on the stage while a teen-ager. His first major stage role was as the Scarecrow in the Broadway musical "The Wiz." He was also featured on Broadway in "Sophisticated Ladies," "Song and Dance" and "Oh Kay!" In a newyork Times review of "Sophisticated Ladies" in 1981, Frank Rich described Mr. Burge as "a lithe fellow with an insouciant grin" and as a "standout tapper." Mr. Burge's lead film roles included Richie in "A Chorus Line" and Virgil in Spike Lee's "School Daze." He appeared on numerous television specials. He also performed in one-man shows. In a review of Mr. Burge's act at the Ballroom in 1990, Stephen Holden of The newyork Times described his dance solos as "spectacular." Born in newyork City and raised on Long Island, N.Y., Mr. Burge was inspired at an early age to become a song-and-dance man after seeing Sammy Davis Jr. perform on the Ed Sullivan show. At age 7, after four years of nagging, he persuaded his parents to enroll him in tap classes at the Red Slipper Dance Studio in Merrick, N.Y. Three years later he began winning local talent shows and soon after emerged a three-time winner on "The Ted Mack Amateur Hour" on television. By 13, Mr. Burge was earning $30,000 a year. Television commercials followed, along with a job as a regular on "The Electric Company" and, at 13, a stint in the Off Broadway musical "Bojangles." There he learned dance history firsthand, appearing with tap stars like Chuck Green, Rhythm Red and Mabel Lee, who taught him to improvise rather than simply dance steps. Mr. Burge received formal training in ballet and tap from the High School of the Performing Arts and the Juilliard School. Mr. Burge was assistant choreographer and director to Donald McKayle and starred in "One More Time" in Israel. He was a lead performer in "Evolution of the Blues" at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington. He choreographed the Steel Pulse "Reaching Out" video, directed by Mr. Lee, and Michael Jackson's "Bad." He also starred for two years as the Easter Bunny in the Easter show at Radio City Music Hall, and represented the unitedstates and Atlanta as a featured performer in and co-choreographer of the closing summer Olympics in Barcelona. Mr. Burge received two Fred Astaire Awards, for his performances in "Song and Dance" and "Oh Kay!" In addition to his mother, he is survived by his father, Fred; two brothers, Frederick Daryl Burge and Christopher Lance Burge, and his grandmother, Mary. title:
Media Talk;
Fate of Journal Reporter Adds to Soul-Searching
body: Has journalistic rigor gone too far? Are news executives going overboard? Those questions, first asked when The Boston Globe cracked down on its columnist Mike Barnicle for borrowing jokes without attribution, returned with renewed force last week after James S. Hirsch lost his job as a Boston correspondent for The Wall Street Journal. Mr. Hirsch, 36, and The Journal parted company Tuesday after he reported erroneously that The newyork Times Company had "declined to comment" on The Globe's Aug. 11 decision to rescind its demand for Mr. Barnicle's resignation. The Times Company owns The Globe. Mr. Hirsch, who said in an interview that in nine years The Journal "has sent me all over the world and let me cover some of the most important beats," acknowledged last week that he had not called The Times that day. He said he had been on a tight deadline and had believed, based on earlier interviews with The Times's spokeswoman on issues related to The Globe, that her response would be, in effect, a "no comment." On the day of Mr. Barnicle's reprieve, Nancy Nielsen, the spokeswoman, gave reporters who inquired this prepared statement: "The newyork Times Company has a policy that all of its media properties have editorial independence and autonomy. In keeping with our policy, we support The Globe's right to make its own decisions, just as we would with any of our other media properties." Ms. Nielsen confirmed last week that after she saw Mr. Hirsch's article, she wrote to The Journal's managing editor, Paul E. Steiger. On Tuesday, Mr. Steiger's deputy informed Mr. Hirsch that he had committed "a firable offense," Mr. Hirsch recalled. "The question is proportionality: Is it fair or not fair?" Mr. Hirsch asked. He continued: "It was an error, and it shouldn't have happened. But it had no bearing on the story. And it certainly wasn't journalistic malice or deception." Karen Miller Pensiero, a spokeswoman for Dow Jones & Company, The Journal's parent, said that the Globe incident alone would justify termination. "There are few, if any, more serious violations of journalistic norms than knowingly printing a falsehood," she said. Ken Martin, the grievance chairman of the union that represents Journal reporters, the Independent Association of Publishers' Employees, said last week that a grievance filed Tuesday contended that Mr. Hirsch was "terminated without just and sufficient cause."   FELICITY BARRINGER

title: Mergers and Year 2000 Slow On-Line Banking
body: Earlier this decade, bankers and software developers looked ahead eagerly to 1998 and 1999 as the period when electronic banking would evolve from a niche business to a ubiquitous service, saving financial institutions millions of dollars in transaction costs. Instead, it is proving to be the era of megamergers and millennium preparation, two issues that have distracted software and system developers and have, for the time being anyway, delayed consumer banking via personal computers. "We would have expected more activity at this point in our evolution," said Scott Wallace, director of marketing for Integrion Financial Network L.L.C., a leading developer of electronic banking software. "But the rapid consolidation diverts the attention of institutions. It takes a long time to integrate two different systems." Original estimates that 15 percent of banking customers in the unitedstates would be on line by 2000 have now been pushed back two years. Currently, about 6 percent of customers nationwide have electronic banking available, said Ian Rubin, senior analyst at the Tower Group in Newton, Mass. The main distraction has been the greatest rush of bank mergers in history -- more than $200 billion in the first half of this year alone. In each case, a merger requires a melding of different and sometimes stubbornly incompatible computer systems. And as the millennium approaches, solutions that the merging banks have adopted to fix the year 2000 problem must also be made compatible. In some cases, banks that saw themselves as takeover targets halted further development of electronic-banking initiatives, Mr. Rubin said. Even so, there has been a bright side to the delay. A new generation of consumer electronic banking, based on Internet connections, promises to replace today's myriad bank-specific and incompatible software programs that offer access by direct dial-up connections to a bank's computer. Bank analysts predict that improved systems using Internet browser-based software will draw millions of new customers to on-line banking as merger frenzy slows and prices for the services decline. Citibank introduced its Internet-based system, the latest incarnation of its Direct Access electronic banking service, last October after upgrading to the most robust encryption security available, said a spokeswoman, Maria Mendler. The bank has offered various versions of Direct Access since 1984, when forecasters were predicting a personal computer on every kitchen table by 2000, Ms. Mendler said. Today, the bank has about 300,000 electronic-banking clients and those using the older software will be moved to the Internet-based version by the end of this year. Customers, she said, are motivated by cost more than technology. "We saw a real jump in 1995, when we eliminated the fee," Ms. Mendler said. The industrywide shift to Internet-based systems has come at the expense of personal financial management software like the Microsoft Corporation's Money, the Intuit Corporation's Quicken and Meca Software's Managing Your Money. All three had been widely used by banks on the consumer end of direct dial-up systems. But such software has serious drawbacks. If a customer changes banks, for example, he usually has to switch software as well, because no two bank systems integrate a program in the same way. In contrast, browser programs for navigating the World Wide Web offer customers and banks a universal interface on almost any computer system and eliminate problems that customers often encounter installing proprietary software. Foremost among the open systems is a package developed by Integrion, a Philadelphia-based consortium of 17 banks, the International Business Machines Corporation and Visa USA. Integrion created a platform for banks to interact with customers for a range of retail services using the Internet, direct dial-up software or a telephone. "In the last six months," Integrion's Mr. Wallace said, "the Web has become more important, and banks that might not have focused on a transactional Web site now are doing that." At the same time, mergers have also sometimes accelerated electronic banking. Mr. Rubin, the Tower analyst, points to two examples of this: the combination of NationsBank and Florida's Barnett Bank and the acquisition of the Corestates Financial Corporation by the First Union Corporation. In both cases, he said, a smaller, regional bank that had been slow to offer on-line banking was forced to change plans once it was purchased. "Institutions were slower to introduce Internet banking than we thought," Mr. Rubin said. "Of the top 100 banks, only about 30 have a transactional Web site. Another 30 to 40 more are planning to offer it this year." At the same time, he added, so-called virtual banks, which were created to exist solely on the Internet, have reluctantly had to acknowledge the need for face-to-face interaction with customers for products like loans and have opened conventional brick-and-mortar branches. The oldest of these, Atlanta-based Security First Network Bank, was created in 1995. It opened its first branch -- it calls it a "city office" and the staff "customer assistants" -- in January 1997, said Eric Hartz, the bank's president. Security First also has a software division that competes with Integrion, and dozens of banks now use its Internet-based system. Security First was acquired earlier this year by Royal Bank of Canada, which has said it plans to spin off the software division as a publicly traded company. Mr. Rubin projects that banks in the unitedstates will spend $336 million this year for on-line initiatives, and accelerate that process at an annual growth rate of 29 percent for the next four years. Original estimates were off base, he said, because the banking industry looked at the explosion of Internet use in 1994 and 1995 and predicted a similar pattern for electronic banking. Instead, banks found themselves limited by systems they had built around personal finance software, which required the user to buy frequent upgrades and limited the design of the overall service. Internet-based systems do away with those issues and offer other strengths as well: questions can be answered quickly via email, applications for accounts and services can be transmitted electronically, and a bank can more closely track a customer's account, which in turn enables it to market products or services like insurance, credit cards and auto and home loans. Consumers had any number of reasons for not quickly embracing electronic banking. The software was expensive, the service was often unreliable, technical support was limited, and the security of financial data was unproved. In addition, Integrion's Mr. Wallace said, the services were not well designed. Bill payment, for example, often cost a hefty monthly fee for not much added convenience. Internet-based systems now emerging enable utility, phone, credit card and other companies to bill customers electronically; customers, in turn, can approve payments by emailing instructions to the bank. Still, even with the newest software and best system designs, many questions have to be answered before banks start closing branches and eliminating staff thanks to electronic banking. Don Kunz, manager of electronic banking for PNC Bank of Pittsburgh, said that it was anyone's guess when the bank might see real savings from the Web-based system it introduced in June. "We're still struggling with 'What does the customer want to do?' and 'As a bank, have we created a redundant way of doing business?' " Mr. Kunz said."Our biggest criteria for success will be customer usage. We need to figure out whether it adds revenue or just additional expense." Weiner for The newyork Times)  Chart: "Growing, Not Booming, on Line" The banking and computer industries anticipated huge growth and cost savings with the increased availability of electronic banking. But consumers have not been so quick to embrace the service.
