title: Surfing the Web for the News In a Blockbuster News Week
body: Traffic to news sites on the World Wide Web soared last week, suggesting that more people than ever turn to the Web to follow breaking news stories -- particularly from the workplace, where television sets can be scarce. Indeed, on both Monday afternoon, while President Clinton was testifying, and Thursday afternoon, when he was announcing military strikes on terrorist targets, record numbers on news sites were reported. "There's no doubt that our busiest times are during the U.S. business day," said Kerrin Roberts, a spokesman for CNN Interactive. For Monday, the site reported a 31 percent increase over its previous busiest day, which occurred in April. Relevant Knowledge, a measurement firm in Atlanta, reported a nearly 43 percent increase in traffic to 11 news sites -- including MSNBC, ABCnews.com and The newyork Times on the Web, as well as the Drudge Report, which was included because of its role in reporting on the brewing Monica Lewinsky matter back in January. While the quest for the latest information is part of the attraction of the Web, many of those who went on line did so to do what the Web allows for best: the expression of personal opinion. Opinion was something that was not in short supply during the week's news events. "The promise and the expectation of the Internet is the ability to reach out and touch everyone," said Jim Schulte, editor of the on-line edition of USA Today. "That's the whole strength. Everyone gets their 2 cents in." More people posted messages to bulletin boards on America Online about the Clinton-Lewinsky relationship than in the aftermath of death a year earlier of Diana, Princess of Wales. That could be as much a reflection of the growth of the on-line medium as it is the nature of the news reports involved, experts said. "It is building as more and more people get on line," said Adam Clayton Powell 3d, vice president for technology at the Freedom Forum, a free-speech advocacy group based in Arlington, Va. He foresees a day when the primary sources of news will be on line. "Each time we have one of these big events, it's another big boost up," he said, "and each time the peak is a little higher. The thing that's hard to predict is where it all starts to plateau."

title:
THE MARKETS: Market Place;
In a volatile economy, newspaper stocks closely echo the rise and fall of the market.
body: IN a volatile economy, analysts say, newspaper industry stocks tend to be like the canary in the mine, singing their hearts out while the air smells sweet, and keeling over at the first couple of sniffs of toxic economic fumes. This spring and summer have tended to bolster that notion. The stock market peaked on July 17; the Standard & Poor's index of newspaper stocks peaked on July 14. Since those peaks, S.& P.'s index of 500 stocks has dropped more than 10 percent; its newspaper index has dropped more than 13 percent. Newspaper companies whose stock prices had flourished in 1997 and the first half of 1998, from the Gannett Company to the Times Mirror Company to The newyork Times Company, saw those prices dip with the market around the time that second-quarter earnings reports came in -- even though the companies' earnings were on target. By Friday, of the largest newspaper companies, only the stock prices of the Washington Post Company (up 6.5 percent since Jan. 1, closing Friday at $517.9375) and the Tribune Company (up 8.9 percent, closing Friday at $67.8125) were ahead of their level when the year began. Gannett's stock price, which closed at $61.375 on Friday, is down seven-tenths of a percent since Jan. 1. Times Mirror, $60.9375 on Friday, is down nine-tenths of a percent; The newyork Times is down 7.2 percent, closing at $30.6875 on Friday; Knight Ridder, which closed Friday at $48.125, is down 7.5 percent. Over all, the Standard & Poor's index is up 11.4 percent since 1998 began. "The two things that appear to be overhanging the newspaper stocks are concerns about the economy -- because classified is a more important component of the profits -- and newsprint prices," said Gracia Martore, Gannett's treasurer and vice president for investor relations. Lauren Rich Fine, an analyst with Merrill Lynch, agrees that newspapers' increasing reliance on high-margin classified advertising to power revenues and earnings reports is giving investors pause. "The biggest reason for changes on the newspaper side is the classified advertisements -- help wanted, real estate and auto," she said. "During an economic expansion that's the line item that gets most leverage on the way up. And then it has the highest height from which to fall." Classified advertising, she said, "is a higher portion of revenues today than it's ever been." She continued: "Most newspapers get about 75 to 80 percent of their revenues from advertising; of that 45 to 50 percent is classifieds. About 35 to 40 percent of the overall revenues come from classifieds." This advertising, she said, has proved sensitive to regional factors -- and newspaper companies are nothing if not regional businesses. For instance, she said, companies that own large newspapers in high-technology centers, like The Los Angeles Times of Times-Mirror and The San Jose Mercury of Knight Ridder, are finding that high-technology companies are cool to the idea of placing job advertisements in newspapers. They prefer to use venues like the Internet, she said, adding that "high-tech advertisers have realized they are not getting the return from newspapers." While newspapers have been concerned for years about the potential impact of new electronic media on their revenue stream -- and have joined together in many cases to try to harness Internet-based classified advertising to their own existing classified ad operations -- the threat has not shown itself to be serious. Over all, according to Steven N. Barlow, an industry analyst with Credit Suisse First Boston, investors are particularly skittish about newspapers right now, but he expects them to calm down shortly. "I think we have another month or so for a little bit of indecision here, in terms of whether or not investors believe that the economy is going to be strong," he said. "I think newspaper stocks are getting overly penalized in this market," Mr. Barlow added. "I'm not worried about earnings estimates for the rest of the year." He predicted 1998 annual earnings growth would run between 12 and 15 percent for the major newspaper companies. Both analysts also cited investor concerns about a continuing strike at Abitibi-Consolidated Inc., the Canadian paper company that supplies newsprint, which is one of the biggest costs for the industry. Ms. Fine said that newspaper companies have recently received letters from other newsprint suppliers suggesting that current prices -- which vary from about $575 to $595 a ton -- would be pushed to $610. But, Ms. Fine said, the drop in demand for newsprint in Asia probably means the newspaper companies will be able to resist the price increase. While Gannett, whose market capitalization of $17.6 billion is the highest in the industry, depends on classified advertising for just 25 percent of its overall revenue, it has also been hurt, Ms. Martore said, by the loss of advertising brought on by the General Motors strike. The newyork Times Company's stock price, which grew more robustly than that of much of the industry in the last year, dipped more sharply than its peers when the markets began to wobble last month. In a letter to the company's employees earlier this month, the company's chairman, Arthur Sulzberger Jr., and its president and chief executive, Russell T. Lewis, noted the general industry trends and added that the earlier performance of the stock may have attracted "momentum players," who "are now taking their profits and moving on to other opportunities." The company, though, sees the lower share price as an investment opportunity. Last Thursday, the Times Company board authorized a buyback of up to $575 million -- or roughly 10 percent -- of the company's class A shares. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- Selling Soap Without the Soap Operas;
Mass Marketers Seek Ways to Build Brands on the Web
body: Mr. Whipple, where are you now? That seemed to be the big unanswered question during two days of high-powered industry talk, as some of the most practiced dream merchants in America assembled here at the headquarters of the Procter & Gamble Company to ponder the Internet. P.& G. grew to be the nation's largest consumer products company in large part by grasping the storytelling power first of radio, then of television, and by using those media to tell the company's own 30-and 60-second stories, like the constant battles of Mr. Whipple to find time to Squeeze his Charmin in peace. And often, those narratives were inserted into 30- and 60-minute stories of a serial genre that Procter helped create just for that purpose: the soap opera. Whether heartwarming or annoying, these product parables worked their way into the back of shoppers' minds so that they would reach for the Charmin, or for other Procter brands like Crest or Tide, while rolling their carts down supermarket aisles. But now that the Internet has become the first medium to actually reduce the viewership of television -- and World Wide Web surfers have shown little interest in serial storytelling -- Procter is trying to figure out how to sell soap without soap operas. That is why the company convened a two-day "summit" meeting that brought together some 400 top executives from Internet and consumer marketing companies, including America Online and Agency.com, Coca-Cola and Sears, and even Procter archrivals like Unilever and Philip Morris's Kraft Foods unit. While much of the discussion centered on technical matters, participants struggled with issues like whether Web sites, so-called banner advertisements and other on-line vehicles can ever achieve the emotional resonance of a little boy in a Crest television commercial bounding up to say "Look, Ma! No cavities!" "I can't think of one slogan developed on the Net that everybody knows," says Seth Godin, the chief executive of Yoyodyne, an Internet promotion company. "It's not a medium for the Great Big Idea." Many of the Internet executives who attended the meeting argued that P.& G., in fact, was asking the wrong question. The Internet, these experts said, might not be so much about mass-market brand building as about providing detailed information about brands consumers already recognize from other media, the way Ford Motor does with its automobiles, or for selling things directly, as Amazon.com does with books. Though often vaunted as the first medium that enables marketers to interact with consumers one to one, the Web has yet to reveal itself as a means for mass marketing the communal dreams in which a box of detergent or a can of soda comes to symbolize a way of life. Part of the problem may be the current limitations in bandwidth, or network carrying capacity, that make the Web better suited to text, still images or simple animation than high-fidelity sound and full-motion video. John Sculley, the former president of Pepsico and former chief executive of Apple Computer, who is now an investor in various Web-related ventures, said in a recent interview that today's Internet simply cannot be used to create the sort of hip imagery employed by Pepsi in the early 1960's and 70's. "When we created the Pepsi Generation, we needed to make Pepsi a drink that says something about the people who drank it," Mr. Sculley said. "The Web isn't ready for that emotion yet." Yet Procter and others insist that they can, indeed must, find ways to use the Internet to peddle packaged goods like dish-washing liquid, diapers and soap -- items that might fall into the purgatory of who-cares commodities, without marketing's holy trinity of product differentiation, brand recognition and unique selling proposition. Right now, many Web sites for consumer products emphasize information -- like recipes or health facts -- rather than the emotive aura that is favored by many television commercials. But one of P.& G.'s goals for the summit meeting was to press reluctant Internet companies to offer bigger, more elaborate advertisements that can pull in the audience the way the best television commercials can. At the same time, the company and others contend that the Internet may prove to be a catalyst for a broader change -- away from a focus on products and toward services and experiences better suited to delivery on line than via any other medium. So far, P.& G. and other consumer products companies have been doubtful enough of the payoff to have contributed only a small fraction of the nearly $1 billion spent for on-line advertising last year. The Internet, for example, represents only four-tenths of 1 percent of Procter's $3 billion annual advertising budget. Unable to measure any discernable sales attributable to their initial Internet efforts, consumer product companies have so far shown themselves unwilling to spend more. Most on-line advertising today takes the form of banner ads -- the wide, shallow rectangles often seen at the top or bottom of Web pages, which if clicked with a mouse take the user to the advertiser's Web site. But these banners were widely disparaged at the P.& G. summit meeting as being too small, too ineffectual and simply too ignorable to perform the hard work of building brands and selling products. Evan Neufeld, an analyst with the research firm Jupiter Communications, presented data at the conference that underscored these concerns. In a Jupiter survey, 21 percent of Internet users polled said they never clicked on banner ads and another 51 percent said they clicked only rarely. Such doubts notwithstanding, some big packaged-goods companies have decided that they should take a leap of faith by stepping up their on-line efforts. For example, Unilever, the company behind brands like Popsicle, Lipton and Ragu, has signed a deal with America Online that calls for experiments ranging from banner ads to the creation of new on-line areas devoted to food, health, cleaning and grooming. "It appears you can sell automobiles and books on line, but I don't know if it will be a good place to sell detergent," Richard A. Goldstein, the head of the North American unit of Uniliver, a British-Dutch company, said in an interview. Still, "you can't sit back and wait to see what happens," Mr. Goldstein added. "You have to get involved and experiment." Unilever's Ragu spaghetti sauce was an Internet pioneer in 1995 when it set up Eat.com, featuring a tongue-in-cheek site about Italian cooking and culture, labeled Mama's Cucina, which Unilever's Lipton Inc. food unit has continued to update. Procter & Gamble, meanwhile, has put most of its on-line marketing budget behind brands like Always panty liners, Tampax tampons, Pampers diapers, Cover Girl makeup and Olean fat substitute. (So far, there is no Charmin.com.) "Those have a narrow target audience with a more personal subject matter," said Denis Beausejour, P.& G.'s vice president for advertising. The company, for example, has turned Pampers.com into the Pampers Parenting Institute, addressing various issues of concern to new or expectant parents. And it is by no means the dry reference library it might appear to be at first glance. "Our site lets a woman who is pregnant explore what will happen to her in private, so she doesn't have to ask stupid questions," Mr. Beausejour said. "That's as emotional as you can get in that context." Some companies have tried to put entertainment on their sites to attract wired children and teen-agers. Unilever's Popsicle.com site offers games, and Warner-Lambert's Certs.com site enables users to send electronic greeting cards to people with whom they want to get cozy. But what about products with even less emotive potential than breath mints? "There really is a big challenge with selling soap on the Internet," said Rex Briggs, vice president of Millward Brown Interactive, a company that tests the effectiveness of advertising. "Right now the brands that do well are those that the consumer is already pretty interested in. There isn't a lot of excitement surfing a site about shampoo." Indeed, it is because some products are so inherently unexciting that Procter has been so insistent that Internet publishers allow it to offer more attention-getting advertising. The company and other advertisers would like to see bigger ads than the standard banner -- especially those called "interstitials," which are screens that pop up to interrupt Web surfing the same way television ads are inserted into breaks in programming. And Procter wants more sites to accommodate advertisements that use techniques known as "rich media," which can enable both banners and bigger ads to include animation, sound and even full video. IPSOS/ASI, another research firm, released a study at the conference indicating that larger, more complex types of advertising are remembered more and are more likely to prompt users to click on them. Many Internet publishers, however, complain that interruptions by interstitials and the surfing slowdowns caused by rich-media ads will scare off their audiences. "The basic methodology of advertising since I've been alive has been breaking and entering," said Meyer Berlow, the head of sales for America Online. "I jump in front of you, amuse you a little, give you a piece of information I hope will change your behavior." But "that's a brain-dead model," Mr. Berlow said of the in-your-face approach. "It worked when there were only three channels and the bathroom. Now the consumer has a million choices." For packaged-goods companies, like all manufacturers, the capabilities of the Web raise the question of whether they will start selling goods directly to customers rather than, as they now typically do, indirectly through wholesalers and retailers. While big-ticket items like computers or cars, or even less costly products like books, may be conducive to direct sales, the cost of packing and shipping a single tube of toothpaste or a lone jar of spaghetti sauce makes direct sales of individual items impractical. "I'd be hard pressed to see the potential of selling our products to consumers one to one," Mr. Goldstein of Unilever said. Of course, there are a number of companies, led by Peapod (www.peapod.com) and Netgrocer (www.netgrocer.com), that are seeking to replace conventional supermarkets by taking on-line orders for a full load of groceries and shipping them to consumers. For the packaged-goods companies, the aim would be to continue making their brands the ones consumers place in their virtual shopping carts. Unilever, for example, has struck a deal with Netgrocer to use pop-up ads to promote its products as people shop on line, much as Unilever works with supermarket chains to create in-store promotions. In the same way that demographic shifts and the rise of the female work force has changed the audience for daytime television soap operas, the Internet is a medium affected by and reflecting societal trends. In the case of the Web, this may mean less emphasis by packaged-goods purveyors on individual products and greater attention to service. Mr. Goldstein says, for instance, that the average household now spends an average of 20 minutes a day shopping for and preparing dinner -- down from two and a half hours 30 years ago. That may require food combines to sell not mere food but "meal solutions," which may include a package of ready-to-assemble ingredients supported by on-line information and help. Procter & Gamble is looking at using the Internet to sell products with far more variations than could be sold through traditional supermarket chains. It has already designed an on-line ordering system for its Millstone premium coffee brand, for example, that lets consumers create their own blends, which are then shipped to them monthly. "We can ask you 20 or 25 questions and blend a blend of Millstone that you will find vastly superior to the coffee you drink today," Mr. Beausejour said. "We can do things on the Internet that are not possible today in a big scale." Soap advertisements through the years were the subject of a display at the conference, which attracted marketing and Internet executives. (Photographs by Mark Lyons for The New York Times)(pg. D7)  Table: "Big Spenders, Except in Cyberspace" The leading consumer product companies spent billions of dollars last year trying to sell their products, but on-line advertising was not a high priority.   (Sources: Competitive Media Reporting; Intermedia Advertising Solutions; Ford Motor; Johnson & Johnson)(pg. D1)  Chart: "Ads for a Web Generation" As the Internet, particularly the World Wide Web, has become a more important source of information and entertainment, advertisers have been trying to figure out how to use it to reach consumers. The search has led to the development of several categories of interactive advertisements, as well as an attempt to create some technical standards. Here is a guide to advertising on the Web.  BANNER ADS -- These are the most common, and simplest type of ads. Guidelines for ad sizes were developed several years ago by the Coalition for Advertising Supported Information and Entertainment and the Internet Advertising Bureau, two groups supported by the advertising industry. The standards are voluntary, but most advertisers follow them. Sizes are measured in pixels, the smallest individual picture elements on a computer screen.  INTERSTITIAL ADS -- When someone is trying to go to a Web site, these ads will flash in the browser window for several seconds before the site is loaded. Clicking on the ad takes users to the advertiser's site.  POP-UP ADS -- These are very similar to interstitial ads, but instead of appearing before a Web site is loaded, a pop-up ad opens a new browser window with the advertiser's message in it. To get back to the destination Web site it is necessary to close the pop-up window.  TRANSACTIONAL ADS -- A new and increasingly popular type of ad. Instead of asking users to go to the advertiser's Web page, these ads let users request information or buy something without leaving the Web page on which the ad appears.  RICH MEDIA ADS -- These are not really a type of ad as much as a description of how the ads are designed. Rich media refers to ads that move, talk, beep or flash. Banner ads, interstitial ads, pop-up ads and transactional ads all can be rich media ads. As communication lines improve and transmission speed becomes less of an issue, these type of ads are becoming more popular. (pg. D7)

title:
ART;
Real Exhibitions, Experienced Virtually
body: FROM the Nezu Institute of Fine Arts in Tokyo to the Louvre in Paris, from the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan to the Exploratorium in San Francisco, museums, galleries and individual artists around the world are giving rise to a virtual wave of art on the World Wide Web. Those in New Jersey are no exception. The quantity of art exhibited on the Internet from web sites in the state has increased greatly in recent years, said Randolph Black, registrar and collections manager of the Montclair Art Museum. "It's not surprising to see 200 to 300 percent increases in information relating to art collections on the Internet," he said. "Just a few years ago, only the big guns had art on the Net, and they didn't always provide for extended viewing. Now, small-to-medium museums and companies can load up with hundreds of images." Mr. Black has worked on the museum's Web site since its inception in 1995, when it consisted only of text. The site, expanded last year, now shows more than 20 images at a time to highlight American and Native American works from the permanent collection. A baby carrier, circa 1890, made of buckskin, beads and fabric is one of seven pieces displayed under the on-line Native American category. The paintings category ranges from a 1783 portrait, "Gen. George Washington," by Charles Willson Peale, to Arshile Gorky's 1937 "Abstraction With Artist's Materials," an Abstract Expressionist ode to the tools of the trade. Other categories include works on paper and sculpture. But the scope of these categories, added last year, will seem rudimentary as the museum puts up a virtual gallery, which is to showcase 150 images by fall and eventually expand to 500. This gallery is to include a data base in which on-line visitors will be able to view and download particular artworks. The museum also plans to use sound -- narrative and music -- to highlight exhibitions with their own pages on the site. Wheaton Village in Millville is already linked to a virtual gallery. A series of prompts leads from the home page to the three-dimensional web site of J. Kenneth Leap's studio on the village grounds. From the studio's main menu, Internet users may read Mr. Leap's resume, view a portfolio of his commissioned work, tour his recent retrospective at the Museum of American Glass, or explore "New Jersey: A 360-Degree View," the 1,500-piece skylight Mr. Leap made for the annex of the State House in Trenton. Visitors may enlarge any of the skylight's 24 square sections to investigate details. Mr. Leap's retrospective on the web -- the real one closed on March 22 -- is composed of a virtual museum with three-dimensional rooms. Visitors may use the scroll bar at the bottom of the computer screen to travel through the exhibition. The black-walled rooms are illuminated and given dimension by black-and-white images that are either hanging on walls or positioned on floors. When a visitor clicks on any image, a blown-up color version of the work with explanatory text fills the screen. Last month, Grounds for Sculpture in Hamilton announced the opening of its Web site, which displays sculpture by about 25 artists. Each piece is accompanied by text describing the artist and the work. In a virtual stroll through the grounds, one might see Mel Kendrick's "Black Trunk," a cast-bronze sculpture originally carved from a partly decomposed tree trunk, or the gargantuan "Garden State," a 75-ton, 16-foot-tall sculpture by Isaac Witkin made of black granite from Zimbabwe. This site may prove particularly helpful for potential visitors to the 22-acre park, who can use it to pinpoint areas of interest before they physically make the trip. Digital art, in which the computer is not just a means of display but the primary medium, is showcased by the Williams Gallery in Princeton. It displays the work of dozens of traditional and digital artists, making this Web site perhaps the most extensive among galleries in New Jersey. From the home page, visitors may view and buy works from the gallery's on-line catalogue, which includes digital art as well as paintings, drawings, original prints, photography and sculpture. Visitors may also get details on local exhibitions in other galleries, read art reviews, tour the gallery or use the "art links" page as a launching pad to continue exploring art on the Internet. The site is linked to the Williams Gallery's showroom in Hollywood, Fla., the Bock Gallery, and to its virtual West Coast branch, which began operating in March primarily to show the work of contemporary West Coast artists. Individual artists are also using the Web. Peter Jacobs, a collagist and a professional photographer from Montclair who specializes in reproducing images for catalogues and art books, made a deal with an artist and AT&T master programmer who needed transparencies of his work. Mr. Jacobs traded his services in photography for lessons in HTML, the language of the Internet, and since then he has created his own site. The site includes information about his professional studio, Fine Arts Photography; an on-line gallery of his work; an artist's statement, and a resume. The on-line gallery has five virtual walls (not in 3-D) that display two works each. All the works are dense, protean collages that seek to "challenge the viewer's concept of visual perception," Mr. Jacobs says. It is possible to enlarge the images to the extent that viewers with standard-sized computer screens must use side bars to see a particular work in its entirety. Particularly striking is "Sacred Cow," a photo collage with the foreground made of images of women outlining the head of a horned cow, and the rest split between cascading concrete structures and abstract, earthy terrain. Another photo collage, "Florence," appears to probe into the art, architecture and daily life of the Italian city. Mr. Jacobs said the Internet was a great marketing tool for artists; his on-line gallery has attracted more than 3,000 hits and made him one sale. "Artists are realizing the value of the exposure that the Internet can provide," he said. "Anyone can look at an artist's work from anywhere in the world." An email message that Mr. Jacobs recently received attests to the reach of this exposure: "Dear sir, I'm very glad to have see the paintings on the page. I'm an artist of China . . . We will be good friends, I thought."  http://www.wheretofind.art  Here is a sampling of New Jersey galleries and artists exhibiting on the Internet. title:
DINING;
Ordering In: Everything From Raw Materials to Really Home-Cooked Meals
body: AUGUST heat is one good excuse. A few months from now, the winter's cold will be another. And then there's lack of time, or lack of transportation, or physical disabilities, or (for those of us not too proud to admit it) just plain laziness. Some days, even the most dedicated shopper and cook doesn't feel like making the effort. When that day comes, fortunately, average New Jerseyans can take advantage of a variety of services that transcend basic takeout to bring the elements of good eating -- from raw materials to multi-course meals -- to your door. Here's a sampling. Internet Grocers Everything from plane tickets to pantyhose is sold over the Internet these days, so why not pasta? Netgrocer dispatches nonperishable groceries by Fedex from a warehouse in North Brunswick. A trip to the web site brings up a list of departments, which lead to "aisles," which call up pictures of specific products (featuring current "best buys") with information on size, price and unit price (i.e., price per pound). A click on "buy" adds the item to your shopping cart. Traveling through the aisles, which are really menus, tends to be slow, but using the shopping-list option speeds up the process. The selection of items and brands is limited; what you see on the menu is very much what you get, so expect to do supplementary in-store shopping. A $40 test order this month brought two large boxes -- filled with extra-virgin olive oil and arborio rice, chicken broth and cat litter -- to my door within three days. The items were packed as carefully as any professional mover would do the job, with individual items swaddled in thick brown paper, a plastic foam cushion on the bottom of the box and an invoice on top. Netgrocer says its prices are up to 20 percent lower than those in most supermarkets, and the statement held true for most items on my order: $2.49 for a three-pack of Bumble Bee chunk white tuna in water, compared to $3.50 or more, and $2.08 for 10 pounds of Johnny Cat, rather than $2.89. Shipping by Fedex, with arrival within four business days, costs $2.99 for orders up to $50 and $4.99 for more than $50. Coming soon to New Jersey is Peapod Inc., based in Skokie, Ill., and now serving more than 104,000 customers in seven metropolitan areas. Peapod has announced plans to begin operating in the newyork market, starting on Long Island in late 1998 and expanding early next year to North Jersey, which will be served from a warehouse in New Hyde Park, N.Y. Unlike Netgrocer, Peapod can deliver meats, vegetables, dairy products and other perishables because it works in partnership with local retailers, in New Jersey's case Giant Foods and Edwards. "It's much like a milkman coming to your door," said Mary Wade Kiscaden, Peapod's public relations manager. "You can do things like order six bananas, three green and the rest ripe. If things are not to your liking, you can send them back and take care of it right there."  Netgrocer, http://www.netgrocer.com. Peapod, http://peapod.com.  Produce by Phone Fresh fruits have long been sold by mail; seasonal gift catalogues for Harry and David in Oregon and a multitude of Florida citrus growers should be arriving in mailboxes any day now. Now, the market has extended to everyday items like lettuce and carrots. Door to Door Organics, based in Ivyland, Pa., near Philadelphia, offers "certified organic fruits and veggies, delivered to your door." It buys from co-operatives, distributors and individual farmers, including some in New Jersey, that are inspected by independent testing organizations like the Northeast Organic Farming Association. "The farm must be chemical-free for at least four years," said Alan Tizer, a partner in the business. He added, "We like our vegetables to be as local as possible." The company delivers throughout New Jersey, by United Parcel Service or its own trucks as far north as Princeton. Each box contains a variety of fruits and vegetables, in sizes ranging from about 12 pounds ($33) to 36 pounds ($71), with an "All Veggie" option "for our macro friends." There is a one-time processing fee of $20 (waived for single try-out orders), with a two percent discount for pre-payment of 10 boxes to be delivered as often as the customer wants. Orders go out on Monday afternoons and should arrive at most New Jersey locations the next day. A test order for the smallest box, placed on Aug. 4, was shipped the following Monday and arrived on Wednesday, a day after the projection. It contained a week's ample supply of produce for a single person: a large bunch of kale leaves, a very large head of romaine lettuce, three white peaches, five plum tomatoes, two large green peppers, eight plums, more than a pound of red seedless grapes, three small but unusually flavorful bananas, three ears of sweet corn, one bunch of slender carrots, one cucumber and three summer squash (along with a recipe for cream of summer squash soup). The produce came, mostly loose, in a box lined with plastic foam and two Polar Packs, with several plastic bags thoughtfully added for storage at home. About half the romaine had turned yellow or worse, and some other pieces had blemishes, but that is to be expected with organic produce, which contains no chemical preservatives, especially after two August days in transit. Orders may be faxed using a form that can be downloaded or printed from the company's web site. (Mr. Tizer said the company hoped the web site would be offering more than 300 organic products by October.) But a telephone call will put you in touch with a human being who will gently ask your preferences. (Kale or no kale? Arugula instead?) My box arrived marked "no kale -- sub 3 plums"; it contained both. Never mind. The kale was very fresh, and delicious.  Door To Door Organics, (888) 283-4443 or http://www.LifeEnrichment.com/organics.htm.  Takeout Pickup Restaurant deliveries are a way of life in Manhattan, but elsewhere the menu is too often limited to pizza or Chinese. In some parts of New Jersey, though, a variety of restaurants participate in third-party delivery services, in which the crucial ingredient is not culinary flair, but a car. Takeout Taxi, based in Herndon, Va., is "a food court on wheels," said Avigdor Orr, a franchise holder based in Edison. "We're basic takeout and not so basic. We can deliver anything from a $2.50 sub to a chateaubriand on an hour's notice." Many of the participating restaurants in the state are well-known chains (Pizzeria Uno, Houlihan's, Chili's), but they include local Italian, Indian, Korean and other ethnic restaurants as well. The minimum food order is $10 to 15 at dinner and $20 to 25 at lunch, depending on the area, with a basic service charge of $4.50 for one restaurant and an extra $4 for each additional restaurant. In the Montclair area, Kitchen to Kitchen is a network of independent drivers who deliver from 20 restaurants in its delivery guide. In theory, you can put together a dinner (operating hours are 5 to 9 P.M. daily) from the various restaurants -- say, an appetizer of rock shrimp arabbiata from La Couronne, an entree of goat vindaloo from Natraj Palace and, for dessert, fallen chocolate souffle cake from the Shubox Cafe. But most people stick to one restaurant, said Chris McKinnie, Kitchen to Kitchen's president. The minimum is $15, with a service charge of $4.50 an order and a note that drivers work mainly for gratuities.  Takeout Taxi: for Bergen County, (201) 612-9400; East Brunswick, Sayreville, Old Bridge, and central and north Middlesex County: (973) 227-5550; Wayne, Parsippany, the Caldwells, Montville and Fairfield: (973) 227-5550. Kitchen to Kitchen, (973) 744-8200.  Personal Chefs The ultimate luxury, of course, would be to have someone come into your home, cook a delicious dinner, set a glittering table and vanish. Even better would be to have a week's worth of menus in your fridge or freezer, neatly bagged, with instructions for reheating. That's the M.O. of the unitedstates Personal Chef Association, based in Albuquerque, N.M. "We're more of a personal chef service for middle Americans, not wealthy families," said David E. MacKay, its executive director. With his wife, Susan P. Titcomb, a former restaurant chef who in 1987 retreated to her home kitchen to become a personal chef, Mr. MacKay has created a network of 2,000 chefs in the unitedstates and abroad, including about 65 throughout New Jersey. The chefs work not in their homes but in the clients', arriving on a scheduled day with all the necessary ingredients and utensils. Recipes are selected in part for how well the food holds up in storage; generally, Mr. MacKay said, chefs start out using the association's recipes but soon learn to adapt their own. Special diets and individual preferences can also be accommodated. Chefs' charges vary, but the nationwide average for "20 plates" -- 10 dinners for two people -- ranges from $175 to $300, "depending on how restrictive the diet is, cuisine styles and sometimes location," Mr. MacKay said.  unitedstates Personal Chef Association, (800) 995-2138 or http:// www.uspca.com. title:
INVESTING IT;
Books Did It for Amazon, but What's Next?
body: MANY an eye, on Wall Street and Main Street alike, is trained on the Internet, seeking signs that its much-hyped promise as a channel of retail commerce is beginning to be realized. The big breakthrough so far, the bookseller Amazon.com, demonstrated that ordinary products not composed of chips and bits can be successfully retailed over the Internet. And, perhaps more important, it showed that investors see no need to wait for consistent operating profits before betting heavily on a company that may have found the key. So the old question of whether Internet retailing can work is giving way to a new question: In which retail categories will the next Amazons emerge? Forecasters say the stakes are high. Forrester Research, a market research firm in Cambridge, Mass., expects the on-line retail market to mushroom from $4.8 billion in sales in 1998 to more than $17 billion in 2001. But Forrester expects 86 percent of that trade to be in just five categories, all of them already established on line: Computers, software, entertainment, books and travel. "Those industries that are most susceptible to on-line retailing are already obvious," explained David Alschuler, an electronic-commerce analyst at Aberdeen Group, a consulting firm in Boston. The best candidates are those where consumers do a lot of research before buying and want information that traditional sales channels have a difficult time supplying, he said. Still, Internet experts have already spotted opportunities for a new round of on-line retailers. One company that may have its toe on the escalator is Etoys, a year-old on-line toy retailer still in the venture-capital stage. It sells about 3,000 products, according to Kate Delhagen, director of on-line retail strategies at Forrester. "Etoys has built up a good, customer-friendly front end of the business," Ms. Delhagen said. "And they've done a good job matching inventory to logistics." Another category that analysts are calling ripe for Internet retailing is consumer electronics. Tim Bajarin, president of Creative Strategies Inc., a consulting firm in Campbell, Calif., sees Amazon's recent deal to acquire the Junglee Corporation as giving it an important leg up in the field. For comparison-shopping on the World Wide Web, Junglee offers consumers a powerful search engine, one of the few ways to research consumer electronics prices. The demographics certainly seem right. Consumer electronics shoppers tend to be men with relatively high incomes -- among the people most likely to use the Internet. But traditional electronics retailers like Circuit City and Best Buy have so far been slow to step into cyberspace. And Nicole Vanderbilt, director of digital commerce at Jupiter Communications, an Internet consulting company in newyork, said start-ups have a difficult time breaking in because they lack the buying power of larger retailers and must deal with a raft of distributors. So despite the large volume of computer products now sold on line, "no one yet has come forward and positioned themselves as a category killer" in other consumer electronics, Ms. Vanderbilt said. Some electronics retailers are moving ahead. In mid-June, Tops Appliance City linked up with Cybershop International, a publicly traded on-line retailer of luxury merchandise like Coach bags and Mikasa tableware, to develop a new Web site. Mr. Bajarin saw rich opportunities for retailers of cameras. "There's an amazing amount of comparison-shopping among photography shoppers," he said, yet Web sites are often so primitive that consumers must phone for prices. Discount buying clubs are another area that analysts say can do well on the Internet. The leader so far is Net Market, a Cendant subsidiary. But a competitor, Value America, has attracted attention with heavy advertising; in July it filed a registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission to go public. Industry experts also see apparel as gaining momentum on line, despite clothing manufacturers' traditional slowness to adopt new technology. Ms. Vanderbilt said one company with an early, interesting niche is Pivot Rules Inc., formerly a maker of golf clothing. In May it switched gears and began developing a Web site called Bluefly, offering designer apparel at deep discounts. The company's chief executive, Kem Seiff, said the off-price apparel business frustrated many consumers with hit-or-miss excursions to stores full of chaotic clothing racks. And catalogue companies struggle with the unpredictable availability of off-price apparel. ANALYSTS are divided over the prospects for selling mundane items like groceries over the Internet, offering widely divergent revenue forecasts. "We think it will grow into billions of dollars eventually, but not soon," said Ms. Delhagen of Forrester. "And that's because there's a very powerful dynamic at work. Even though we say we hate grocery shopping, it's still very easy to do" and typically does not require a lot of research, she said. Analysts say Peapod Inc., a publicly traded pioneer in on-line grocery sales, may expand nationwide only gradually because so many of its wares are perishable. By contrast, Net Grocer Inc. concentrates on longer shelf-life products and is expected to gain momentum. In mid-July, America Online agreed to make Net Grocer the exclusive supermarket delivery service for its customers in exchange for a $15 million fee over the next three years, a share in ad and transaction revenues and warrants to buy Net Grocer stock. Net Grocer has also filed plans to go public. It's a short leap from groceries to drugstore sundries, and, so far, the best-capitalized on-line entry seems to be Drugstore.Com, a privately held company founded by a former Microsoft executive, Peter Neupert. Ms. Vanderbilt of Jupiter thinks on-line sales make sense for basic supplies that consumers often need to restock, like toilet paper and soap. But drugstores' best profits are from goods that are hard or impossible to sell on line: prescription drugs and impulse purchases like cosmetics. Wal-Mart and Net Grocer already offer some drugstore items on line, Ms. Vanderbilt said, but the selection is limited, and, in Wal-Mart's case, not heavily promoted. "We think there's an opportunity here for a category killer like Amazon," she said.
