(Source: Forrester Research)

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORTS: NEW YORK UP CLOSE;
Trying to Keep Library Computers Smut-Free for Children
body: As the start of school approaches, some City Councilmen are hoping that rumblings about budget cuts will prompt the city's libraries to limit children's access to pornographic materials on the Internet. In the past year, several Republican Council members have said they were considering legislation that would cut funds to libraries that did not install pornography-filtering software on Internet terminals used by children. But last week, James S. Oddo, legal counsel to Thomas V. Ognibene of Queens, the Council's minority leader, said plans to propose such legislation had been "put on hold" because of what Mr. Ognibene views as serious exploration by the city's three library systems into limits on Internet access. "Legislation would be a last resort," said Mr. Oddo, who said he had recently received indications that all three library systems had quickened the pace of their reviews of filtering software. He said a Council meeting on the issue in April, as well as statements to the press by Mr. Ognibene and Councilmen Marty Golden and John A. Fusco of Brooklyn, had served to "bring this to a boil." Mr. Oddo said meetings to discuss two software products -- for which he expressed salesmanlike enthusiasm -- had been arranged for next month with Norman Holman, director of the branch libraries at the newyork Public Library, and Martin Gomez, executive director of the Brooklyn Public Library. A report was expected from Gary E. Strong, director of the Queens system, he added. Library officials did not directly link their activities to any threat of financing cuts. But Caroline Oyama, a spokeswoman for the newyork Public Library, confirmed that Mr. Holman would meet with Mr. Oddo and others "to talk about our findings." Linda Locke, a spokeswoman for the Brooklyn Public Library, said she had no information about such a meeting with Mr. Gomez. And Joanne King, a spokeswoman, said Mr. Strong of the Queens system intended to review the recommended products "as part of an ongoing process." Currently, all of the newyork Public Library's 85 branches have Internet terminals, as do all 63 Queens library sites, while the Brooklyn Public Library plans to have all its 60 locations on line by October. In all three systems, filtering software has been under review for some time, but none is in use, the spokeswomen said. The Queens system "makes an effort to guide children" by using special "kids' links" computer displays in children's areas, Ms. King said. Ms. Locke and Ms. Oyama said librarians carefully monitored children's computer use. Ms. Oyama added that inappropriate computer use by children was rare. "There are obviously First Amendment issues related to filtering," she said. "Children's librarians are trained in handling kids and defusing situations. They're doing it without filtering at this time." But, she added, "That is not to say that won't change."   MARCIA BIEDERMAN Graphic   Photo: Children as well as adults connect to the Internet at the Brooklyn Public Library on Grand Army Plaza. The access is causing some concern. (Michelle V. Agins/The newyork Times)

title:
SPENDING IT;
Information Age? Maybe Not, When It Comes to Prices
body: EVEN as the Internet has given consumers a powerful tool for learning what things cost, sizable chunks of American business seem determined to make price comparisons hard, sometimes frustratingly so. Consider the Oreck Corporation, which boasts that its compact XL vacuum cleaner has been embraced by luxury hotels and that the XL's four-pound supplementary vacuum is so powerful that it can pick up a 16-pound bowling ball. Oreck promotes these products heavily on radio and television, on fliers accompanying credit-card bills and in such mass-market publications as Parade magazine. But the prices of these marvels are not divulged: The potential buyer must mail or phone a request for an "information kit" to learn them. A consumer may also be frustrated when banks post or orally quote mortgage rates but refuse to actually make agreements on these terms until he plunks down cash to "lock in," typically hundreds of dollars. "This sure discourages comparison-shopping," contended Stephen Brobeck, executive director of the Consumer Federation of America, which has mounted a campaign against the practice. Then there is America Online, which was luring new subscribers with offers of free time but without specifying the costs at the end of the trial period. The company agreed this spring to explain its charges more clearly as part of a broad settlement with 44 state attorneys general. Except in financial services, there are few laws or regulations requiring sellers to disclose prices to prospective buyers, whether the item in question is a house or car -- both usually subject to negotiation anyway -- a box of cereal or even the product widely considered to serve as the economy's most visible barometer, a gallon of gasoline. For the most part, the Government just polices advertising to keep it from being false or misleading. "Our interest gets piqued if it's a way to restrain competition or if there's consumer deception involved," said Willard K. Tom, deputy director of the Bureau of Competition of the Federal Trade Commission. (In a recently settled case over competition issues, the F.T.C. had contended that a group of farm-equipment dealers in Kentucky and Indiana had withheld advertisements from an industry journal after it published ads by other dealers featuring prices lower than those offered by the group members. The F.T.C. had also contended that the journal later agreed to stop accepting ads that included prices.) One obvious reason that consumers are often left to guess at prices is that manufacturers and retailers know that general American prosperity has reduced the need for many people to watch how they spend each nickel and dime. But there is more to it than that, marketing and advertising specialists say. Generally speaking, marketers say they are finding an emphasis on price to be a poor, often self-defeating strategy. It tends to erode consumer perceptions of product quality, and also eventually loses impact even with shoppers whose primary consideration is price. That's because the bargain-hunters wait to buy only during the inevitable sales. The notion of buying goods at sale prices "becomes an entitlement," said Tom Lawson, managing partner at Arnold Communications, an advertising agency in Boston. Just as important, others say, is a desire not to unnecessarily intensify competition. "Marketers aren't pushing prices because they don't want to get into wars," said Audrey Guskey, professor of marketing at Duquesne University in Pittsburgh. And manufacturers see little to gain by parading before Wall Street their current inability to raise prices in a minimum-inflation climate. Asked about his strategy of deferred price disclosure, David Oreck, the chief executive of the vacuum cleaner company, said it was a matter of practicality. "We have several different models and there's just so much you can say in an ad," he said. Perhaps, the specialists suggested, the Oreck strategy is to concentrate on prospects who are motivated enough to request price information, at the risk of losing some potential customers who assume that Oreck cleaners are priced beyond their means. The products, which Mr. Oreck calls "kind of mid-range," average $300 to $400. It is clear, though, that the rapid proliferation of Internet technology has complicated marketing strategies. "A whole new source has emerged for price information that wasn't there before," said Joseph Plummer, director of brand strategy at McCann-Erickson Worldwide. Some sellers, though, avoid electronic commerce "for fear that people would go on the Internet and comparison-shop," perhaps unfairly penalizing goods that should command premium prices, said Frank Torres, a spokesman for Consumers Union. YET according to a study by researchers at Pennsylvania State University's Smeal College of Business, consumer sensitivity to price "tends to be lower on line" than in stores, particularly when the sales pitch describes a product's other attributes, like nutritional value of a food product. In some cases, of course, the lack of a price tag is pure snob appeal, its absence intended to suggest that the product "is for the kind of people who don't have to worry about the price," said Diane Cook-Tench, director of the Adcenter at Virginia Commonwealth University. Or, as has been said about yachts, if you have to ask what one costs, you can't afford it. Graphic   Drawing (Jane Sanders)

title: The Internet's Growth: History Isn't Repeating
body: To the Editor: Re "In Radio's Past, a Hint of the Internet's Future," by Alfred Balk (From the Desk Of, Aug. 16): The problems associated with the growth of radio had to do with two problems, both intractable: the limitations of bandwidth and the inability to ascertain who was responsible for a particular broadcast at a particular frequency. The Internet is different in that there are no bandwidth problems, and sites on on the World Wide Web generally have easily identified sets of people responsible for them. While it is possible that the sheer numbers of packets being thrown out onto the Internet could someday cause capacity to become an issue, it seems doubtful in light of the exponential growth in the capacity of data networks. And the fact that I need only seconds to do a search to find the sources behind a Web site, where its offices are, and even its email address and phone number, suggests visibility far beyond that found in any medium ever. The Internet's development shares the democratic and egalitarian nature of the telephone system but also the richness and one-to-many potential of print, radio and television. It has already changed millions of lives and will radically change the way people live in the 21st century. There are growing pains, of course, as there are with any life-changing technology. Let's hope that legislators who are unable to understand the Internet do not stifle its progress.  VAN GARRETT Manhattan, Aug. 17

title: Access Fees and the Internet
body: A Federal appeals court decision this week should benefit Internet users and the fast-growing electronic information industry by holding down connection costs. The decision upheld the authority of the Federal Communications Commission to exempt Internet service providers from interstate access charges paid to local phone companies. The issue was raised in a lawsuit by telecommunications companies challenging Federal regulations intended to deregulate the industry. The lengthy decision by the unitedstates Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit allows the agency to get on with that task without dampening growth in the electronic information sector. The local phone companies have argued that Internet services should have to pay the same access fees that long-distance carriers pay for using the local phone lines. But the F.C.C. contends that Internet services are not equivalent to long-distance carriers and do not use local systems in the same way. Imposing access fees would very likely have caused on-line services to raise their rates, and perhaps abandon the flat-fee structure that has attracted millions of customers to on-line services. The F.C.C. policy was created in 1983, recognizing that the nascent electronic information industry needed breathing room to develop. Last year the F.C.C. decided that keeping the access fee exemption for on-line services was still appropriate to avoid disrupting the still-evolving industry. The agency also is not convinced that Internet services impose uncompensated costs on the local phone companies or that congestion on local phone lines warrants the imposition of new charges. That judgment may change in the future, but it is one for the agency to make without judicial interference.

title: Boston Globe Columnist Resigns Over Authenticity of 1995 Story
body: Eight days after salvaging his career at The Boston Globe, the star columnist Mike Barnicle resigned yesterday, at the newspaper's request, when editors could find no evidence that two young cancer victims he described in a 1995 column had ever existed. Mr. Barnicle told his editors on Tuesday that he had been given the story by a nurse whose name he could not recall. He also said he had never tried to speak with the boys' families. The Globe's editor, Matthew V. Storin, said in a statement yesterday: "In light of his failure to follow the most basic reporting requirements as well as the duplicitous way in which the story was written, it is clear that Mike Barnicle can no longer write for The Boston Globe. Therefore we have asked for and received his resignation today." The abrupt end of Mr. Barnicle's quarter-century career at The Globe, owned by The newyork Times Company, was another chapter in a wrenching summer at the newspaper, which in only nine weeks has lost two of its most popular metropolitan columnists, Patricia Smith and now Mr. Barnicle, to accusations of fabricating. Mr. Storin was alerted to the Barnicle column at issue by Kenneth Y. Tomlinson, a retired editor of Reader's Digest, on Monday. Mr. Tomlinson, whose own son had survived a spinal tumor, was moved when he read the column, published on Oct. 8, 1995, and sought to reprint it soon afterward. But the fact-checkers at Reader's Digest, who spoke with various cancer societies and with Children's Hospital in Boston, where by Mr. Barnicle's account the boys had been patients, could find no evidence of their existence. Eventually, Mr. Tomlinson said yesterday, he decided that the column had been fabricated. In a statement that was by turns gracious and resentful, Mr. Barnicle said yesterday that he felt consumed by a "media feeding frenzy," with his work of 25 years -- some 4,000 columns -- under scrutiny. "Just in the last 24 hours," he said, "I was asked to explain circumstances and columns written in 1973, 1981, 1986 and 1995 and was given 24 hours -- a single day's news cycle -- to rebut all the allegations at once. "Frankly, this is not what I want to do with my life. And it is hurting the paper I love. This burden has made it impossible for Matt Storin and the editors of The Globe to publish the terrific product they put on the street each day." Asked in a telephone interview how he had come to write the column on the young cancer victims, Mr. Barnicle said, "That story was told to me by a nurse who had told the story to someone else at The Globe -- a telephone operator," who then told him. "I believed the story to be true," he said, "and I wrote it after talking to the nurse." The telephone operator, Rose Berry Devine, an old friend of Mr. Barnicle, agreed with his account yesterday, saying she remembered that a call had come in from a "nurse's aide" who has since died. The column told of a friendship that had developed between the two boys -- one black, one white -- while they were hospitalized together. It reported details like the downsizing that had cost the black youngster's father his job at a high-technology company, and began with a passage in which that child's mother received a $10,000 check from the white family: "She opened the letter as she strolled up the driveway from themailbox. As she finished the first paragraph, she stopped in her tracks, unable to focus because of the tears in her eyes. "After a few seconds, she lifted her head toward the perfect sky and, for a brief, wonderful moment, she could hear her son singing his favorite song." The column went on to quote her husband as saying, "There really is a God." Aside from the questions raised by Mr. Tomlinson -- who said he was now writing an article about the column for The Weekly Standard, a Washington magazine -- The Boston Phoenix, the city's alternative weekly, has prepared an article, posted yesterday on its Web site, showing strong similarities between A. J. Liebling's biography of former Gov. Earl Long of Louisiana and a 1986 column by Mr. Barnicle. Asked yesterday why he had not alerted The Globe to his suspicions back in late 1995, Mr. Tomlinson said the reason was in part that he had planned to have one of his own reporters write an article on how a column can be fabricated. "At one point I assigned a colleague to do a piece on the fabrication of a column," he said. "I couldn't get a lot of interest going. It was one of those good ideas that fell by the wayside." When he read about the forced resignation of another Globe columnist, Ms. Smith, in June, and the paper's decision then to review some of Mr. Barnicle's past work, "I thought, 'Any examination by The Globe will turn this up.' " But that examination of Mr. Barnicle's work since January 1996 turned up no problematic columns, Globe editors said. Then, Mr. Tomlinson said, two weeks ago, when The Boston Herald disclosed the similarities between Mr. Barnicle's Aug. 2 column and jokes in a 1997 book by the comedian George Carlin, he thought Mr. Barnicle's career would surely be over. "I thought it was a foregone conclusion he was going down and his sins had caught up to him," Mr. Tomlinson said. "I couldn't believe the massive pressure brought to bear on The Globe to keep him," Mr. Tomlinson added, referring to the support of the popular radio talk-show host Don Imus, prominent journalists, a major Globe advertiser and hundreds of Globe readers who deluged the newspaper with phone calls of protest. Only after Mr. Storin had reversed his initial decision to ask for Mr. Barnicle's resignation for misleading The Globe about the Carlin situation did Mr. Tomlinson send a fax to Mr. Storin questioning the cancer-victim column. Mr. Barnicle's resignation caps a period of troubles and embarrassment not only at The Globe but for journalism more broadly. In addition to the episode involving Ms. Smith, others have included the discovery of wholesale fabricating by Stephen Glass, a writer for The New Republic, and the CNN-Time retraction of a report that a small American force used nerve gas in a Vietnam-era assault in Laos. In The Globe's newsroom, where there had been a wave of complaints in recent days about Mr. Barnicle's standards, the mood lightened perceptibly yesterday afternoon. "I think by and large the staff feels better than they've felt in two months," Mr. Storin said in a telephone interview. When he read his statement to the staff, the final words -- "I'm glad we can now move forward with everyone operating from the same ethical page" -- provoked a smattering of applause and some nervous laughter from relieved journalists, said two people present. Joseph Williams, an assistant metropolitan editor, said: "One of the other reporters in the newsroom said if someone asked him to describe the mood in a single word, that word would be 'catharsis.' We're happy it's over with. But it's hard to feel pleased about a columnist whose career ends up this way. It's never a happy thing." News of Mr. Barnicle's resignation came to the city of Boston in a report from the ABC-TV affiliate, WCVB, whose program "Chronicle" features him as a curmudgeonly commentator. Paul A. LaCamera, the station's general manager, said yesterday that Mr. Barnicle would remain an occasional contributor there. Asked what he would do now, Mr. Barnicle, who has seven children ranging in age from 5 to 34, said: "I don't know. Tomorrow is my precious boy's 14th birthday. My job is to make sure that he knows that everything will be O.K." While The Globe's newsroom was recovering from the Barnicle episode, the newsroom of The Wall Street Journal was getting word that James S. Hirsch, a Journal reporter who had covered the controversy, was no longer working for that newspaper. Mr. Hirsch wrote last week, erroneously, that The newyork Times Company had declined to comment on Mr. Storin's decision then to keep Mr. Barnicle on the staff. The Journal published a correction on Tuesday noting that The Times Company had not been asked for comment. Richard Tofel, a spokesman for Dow Jones & Company, The Journal's parent, said that the reporter "knew that that sentence in the story was not true" and that "the reporter has been disciplined for that." A moment later, Mr. Tofel added, "I can confirm that he doesn't work for us." When Mr. Tofel's remarks were relayed to Mr. Hirsch, he replied, "That's not right." But he declined to elaborate. Graphic   Photo: The Boston Globe reporting Mike Barnicle's resignation in today's issue. (pg. A16)

title: Internet Service Providers Victorious on Access Fees
body: Internet service providers won a major victory yesterday when an appeals court upheld the Federal Communications Commission's decision to exempt them from paying local phone companies the access fees the phone companies are allowed to charge long-distance carriers. The ruling was a blow to the Baby Bells and other local telephone companies, which had argued that Internet service providers use local phone lines to connect users to global networks as long-distance companies do and thus should have to pay the same fees. Moreover, the Bell companies argued that on a per-customer basis, Internet users tend to be a greater drain on local phone networks than long-distance callers are because Internet connections often last for hours, while most long-distance calls are measured in minutes. The decision on local access fees was handed down by the unitedstates Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit in St. Louis as part of a broader opinion ruling on a number of issues stemming from portions of the 1996 Telecommunications Act in which Congress tried to encourage cuts in long-distance rates. In another setback for the local phone companies, the judges also upheld F.C.C. regulations intended to reduce the $23 billion in access fees from long-distance carriers by $1.7 billion. The commission estimated that the savings would be worth about $2 a month to the average long-distance customer. The exemption for Internet service providers was especially controversial because so much had changed since it was put in force. More than a decade ago, the F.C.C. defended the exemption from access charges for what was then the fledgling data communications industry on the grounds that assessing the same fees exacted from long-distance companies would stifle the young industry's growth. In a brief filed in the case that was ruled on yesterday, the BellSouth Corporation and the Bell Atlantic Corporation -- two of the many telecommunications companies involved in the suit -- argued that times and the industry had changed. Describing the exemption as a "new, implicit and discriminatory subsidy" for the Internet service providers, they said the rise in Internet use was taxing their systems and forcing them to make huge investments in additional capacity. Phone networks were originally designed to handle only 10 percent usage, meaning that no more than 1 in 10 phones would be in use at any one time. With the increasing growth of Internet users who spend infinitely more time on the lines than traditional telephone callers, local phone companies maintain they are the ones shouldering the burden. The three-judge panel said that the F.C.C.'s exemption did not discriminate in favor of Internet service providers because they did not use the services of the local phone companies "in the same way or for the same purposes as other customers who are assessed per-minute interstate access charges." Unlike long-distance companies, which charge users by the minute, most Internet service providers offer unlimited access for a flat monthly fee. Analysts had predicted that if the local phone companies were to prevail, on-line services would have to raise their rates and might be forced to abandon the flat-rate pricing that had helped propel the rapid growth of the Internet. "This ruling maintains the status quo," said Scott Cleland, a telecommunications analyst in Washington for the Legg Mason Precursor Group. Referring to Internet service providers, he added, "This is a win for I.S.P.'s." America Online, the largest Internet provider in the country, declined to comment. Local phone companies argued that the access fees subsidized phone service for low-income people or people living in rural areas or other places where the cost of building and maintaining a telephone infrastructure would otherwise be prohibitive. Long-distance carriers maintained that the reduced access charges were still too high because they "are set at billions of dollars more than what it cost the Bells to provide the service," said Peter Lucht, a spokesman for MCI Communications. Still, he said, "the F.C.C.'s decision last May to reduce access charges was at least a step in the right direction, and the court was right to uphold it." In the ruling, the court also upheld an F.C.C. decision to increase the federally mandated "subscriber line charge" for businesses and residences with multiple phone lines.

title:
LIBRARY/CUSTOM-CD SITES;
Big Names but So-So Titles
body: WWW.MY-CD.COM THIS site's magic moment occurred just as Tyler Peppel was thinking about how Oompala, his software company, might use the Internet to personalize entertainment. "Around that time, my assistant's boyfriend gave her a CD he recorded for her with only one special song on it," Mr. Peppel recalled from his San Francisco office. Inspired by the romantic gesture, Mr. Peppel pitched the custom-disk idea to financial backers, and MY-CD Inc. was born as a separate enterprise. Edward A. Bennett, former president of VH1, was brought in to run the newyork company. The site was opened in May and already offers 16,000 cuts. It is especially strong in jazz and blues. The rock music area has some star-studded acts, including Fleetwood Mac and Santana, but their major-label hits are noticeably absent. Track annotation is sparse, so listening to the audio samples is essential to insure that the version of a song you have selected is the original you truly want. The MY-CD site was recently overhauled, but some bugs still need to be worked out. As I tried to compile a collection, the software lost my order every time I tried to go back a page to review it. The company vowed to fix this soon. Ultimately, I did succeed in creating a custom disk, combining all the tracks from the avant-samba composer Arto Lindsay's "Mundo Civilizado" with 9 of the 11 cuts from his "O Corpo Sutile" album for about half the price of the two CD's bought separately. In the bargain, I lost the song-lyric translations and original cover art. Disks from MY-CD cost $16.99 and are limited to 25 tracks or 70 minutes. With shipping, the total for the Lindsay disk was $19.48. All of the custom-CD sites hope to reach the same level of success as Mr. Peppel's assistant and her beau. The couple, he reported, is "living happily ever after." Graphic   Photo: Recently overhauled, the MY-CD site has a few bugs to work out.

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Harnessing the Energy Of Psychics via Modem
body: WONDERING if you'll get that new job? Meet that special someone? See the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in the Super Bowl? Every day, legions of seekers take their questions, however mundane, to legions of psychics: on the street, on the phone, on TV and, increasingly, on line. Sammye Souder of Raleigh, N.C., who works as a psychic on line, had been practicing for years off line when a friend suggested she see clients over the Web. Now one of her primary marketing tools is a site through America Online. Like most Web psychics, she offers traditional phone appointments, plus personal email readings (not to mention selling her homemade barbecue sauce). Customers fill out an on-line form with their credit card numbers, birth dates and questions. Sammye, as she is known professionally, responds in a couple of days. A true clairvoyant, she said in an interview, need not perform a session in person. "I have the capacity to tune in to people when they send me email," she said. "Their message has their energy because they sent it; I can pick that up." Michele Anderson, another on-line psychic, says she believes email or on-line chat can interest clients who might not ordinarily seek out psychic guidance. "The Web does not have the same warmth as a personal meeting," she said, "but it offers anonymity to someone who might be concerned about a serious issue." One of Ms. Anderson's clients, Zachary Stuart, a newyork actor, said not all Web psychics are created equal. While he said he's satisfied with Ms. Anderson, "I had a couple experiences on line that were really quite the joke," he said in an email message. "The connection the psychic made with me and the things I was told had absolutely nothing to do with who I was whatsoever. It was humorous how 'wrong' my first couple readings were. It seemed so very generic I requested refunds." Exchanging metaphysical energy over the wires isn't cheap. The Psychic Internet charges customers by the word length of the psychic's reply: $35 for what's called a "quick hit" reading of 200 words to $175 for an 1,800 word "email Comprehensive." One customer wanted to find a job in biotechnology sales. According to the Tarot Cards' answer, part of the Psychic Internet site, the job seeker was talented, but suffered from a Type A personality and needed therapy. (This customer is in luck: there are plenty of on-line therapists.) Not everyone has to pay for a premonition. Many free sites are harnessing the power of age-old and new-age oracles. Ouija boards abound on the World Wide Web Ouija; players rest their fingers on the mouse, telepathically sliding the cursor over the letter board on screen. Since 1993, the World Wide Web I Ching has brought the ancient Chinese "Book of Changes" into the digital era. To simulate the throwing of the three yarrow sticks, surfers type in a question, then click a button on screen. The resulting hexagram reading is revealed with a traditional explanation under each heading. Michael Gamson, an avid I Ching user, likes the immediacy of the on-line version. But it doesn't quite evoke the mystical experience he conjures off line, which includes candles and incense, he said. "The process leading up to receiving an oracle is as important as the oracle itself," he said. "It is a period of clearing the mind similar to meditation. You simply can't get that by watching the Web browser load the next page." Also, he noted, "It's essentially just a random number generator." In fact, random generator programs, which spit out responses each time a button is clicked, inform a sublegion of psykitsch sites. Dozens emulate the erstwhile Magic 8 Ball. The creator of Kurt Cobain's Magic 8 Ball promises that the Punk Poet of Grunge is standing by on the other side, ready to help you tackle the big questions. Visitors type in queries, then click on Kurt for a response. Using random sound files from old Nirvana interviews, the site answers with casual obliqueness: "Yes, no, maybe so, kind of, sort of." Just how dependable are on-line psychics? When asked, a pudgy automated psychic called The Dack Head had this to say: "could you rephrase the question in a way that would make me care?"  They're Awaiting You For those who need to know the future, here are links.  SAMMYE: members.aol.com/ sammyes/donna.htm  THE PSYCHIC INTERNET: www.wholarts.com/psychic/  WORLD WIDE WEB I CHING: www.facade.com/attraction/ iching/  WORLD WIDE WEB OUIJA: www.math.unh.edu/black/ cgi-bin/ouija.cgi  KURT COBAIN'S MAGIC TALKING 8 BALL: www.xworld.com/ cobain/index.html  ASK THE DACK HEAD: toybox. asap.net/shockmon/ dackpage.html  MICHELE ANDERSON: newvision-psychic.com/ Graphic   Photo: Michele Anderson, a psychic, chats on line with her clients. (Larry Pierce for The newyork Times)

title: Netscape Results Beat Forecasts
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation, the leading maker of Internet browser software, reported third-quarter earnings today that exceeded Wall Street estimates. Netscape now gives away its browser but competes in the market for corporate communications software and derives substantial revenue from its Web site, Netcenter, which offers directory services and sells advertising. "On the revenue side, they did a little bit better than Street expectations," said David Readerman, an analyst with Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities. "They are both selling license software and services and on the Netcenter side generating sponsorship and advertising revenues." Netscape, based in Mountain View, Calif., reported its results after the market closed. In Nasdaq trading, shares of Netscape rose $1.8125, to $32.125. For the quarter ended July 31, Netscape earned $88,000, or break-even on a per-share basis, in constrast to a loss of $44.7 million, or 53 cents a share, in the quarter ended June 30, 1997. Revenue rose 10 percent, to $150.2 million. Analysts had expected Netscape to report a loss of 2 cents a share. The results were not a direct comparison because Netscape changed to a fiscal year from Nov. 1 to Oct. 31 from a calendar year to better align itself with the buying patterns of corporate customers.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Procter & Gamble calls Internet marketing executives to Cincinnati for a summit meeting.
body: AN advertising behemoth is gathering hundreds of executives for a one-of-a-kind conference with an ambitious goal: improving the Internet as a marketing medium by hastening the discovery of solutions to the panoply of problems that now vex cyberpeddlers. The meeting, which begins tomorrow, stems from the increasing frustration of its sponsor, the Procter & Gamble Company, at what is widely perceived as the poky pace of efforts to eliminate the difficulties confronted by marketers using on-line media to pitch products. P.& G. spends $3 billion a year on advertising but has been recently spending only $3 million a quarter on interactive ads. The conference is significant because P.& G. -- the packaged-goods powerhouse that sells such omnipresent brands as Tide detergent, Crest toothpaste and Bounty towels -- is considered a leader among mainstream marketers in such realms as building brands, developing products and cultivating longterm relationships with agencies. "There's no question that if you get a call from a Procter & Gamble, you're going to pay attention," said Wenda Harris Millard, executive vice president for marketing and sales at Doubleclick in newyork, a Web advertising network. "The buzz among Internet companies is 'Are you going?' " said Ms. Millard, who was invited to attend. "Nobody even says 'To what?' " Asked if she would indeed go, Ms. Millard replied, laughing, "Have you ever heard me so excited about going to Cincinnati in August?" The meeting is significant for another reason: P.& G.'s well-known reputation for media innovation. Indeed, the company's early enthusiasm for radio was so ardent that soap operas still bear that name in tribute to their initial sponsor's brands of soap and soap flakes like Ivory, Oxydol, Duz and Dreft. "It's a very savvy move on P.& G.'s part because it puts a company that carries an immense amount of weight at the forefront of an evolving medium," said Evan Neufeld, practice director for on-line advertising at Jupiter Communications, the Internet consulting company in newyork. Mr. Neufeld, who is scheduled to address the meeting, said: "P.& G. is telling us 'We know this is important, but if you want our money you have to be part of the solution and not part of the problem.' Three years from now, we might look back and say that it all began to make sense after the FAST forum." His reference was to P.& G.'s formal name for the meeting, the Future of Advertising Stakeholders. Plans for the meeting were announced in May at Adtech, a digital marketing conference in Chicago. "If packaged-goods companies like P.& G. start moving ad dollars into the Net, it could change the dynamics of all media," said Chuck Martin, who was the chairman of the Adtech conference and has written books about interactive marketing including the forthcoming "Net Future: The Seven Cyber Trends that Will Drive Your Business, Create New Wealth and Define Your Future" (McGraw-Hill, 1998). The meeting is set to discuss the impediments to such investments of ad dollars. They range from inconsistent standards of measurement to incomplete data on effectiveness to infighting among the advertisers, agencies and media. Some who will attend the meeting say they hope the agenda will be expanded beyond those concerns. They note that 50 years after Milton Berle first put on a dress, the ratings system that measures television audiences remains fiercely disputed -- but that has not kept TV from becoming the biggest ad medium. "People are trying to get the Holy Grail of all media measurement from the Web," said Chan Suh, chief executive of Agency.com, an interactive agency in newyork, who is to participate in a panel on Friday. "But it's so 1996 to fixate on that. I hope we can get out of the meeting not only a 'state of the nation,' but also where we go from here." Topics to be considered at the meeting are to include measurement standards, advertising formats like banners, consumer acceptance of on-line advertising (including privacy issues) and making on-line media easier to buy. In addition to the executives mentioned above, P.& G. invited to the meeting about 400 representatives of such companies and agencies as the AT&T Corporation, the Clorox Company, the Coca-Cola Company, the Kraft Foods unit of the Philip Morris Companies, Levi Strauss & Company, the McDonald's Corporation, the Modem Media.Poppe Tyson unit of True North Communications, the Ogilvy One Worldwide unit of WPP Group P.L.C. and Unilever. "Industry conferences are always for the usual suspects," said Rich LeFurgy, chairman of the Internet Advertising Bureau in newyork, which represents more than 300 cyberplayers. "This will be the unusual suspects, and that in and of itself is very important." "The news here is that this is the first time within the Internet industry that traditional advertisers, on-line media companies, interactive agencies and service infrastructure companies are coming together," said Mr. LeFurgy, who plans to attend the meeting. "It's an opportunity for us all to check our agendas at the door and speak to the higher good of advertising on line."

title:
National News Briefs;
Woman Sues to Nullify On-Line Gambling Debts
body: A woman who lost more than $70,000 gambling on line has filed a lawsuit in an effort to avoid paying her credit card bills on the ground that wagering on the Internet is illegal. The woman, Cynthia Haines of Marin County, was sued by Providian National Bank, based in San Francisco, for not paying her credit card bills. Ms. Haines used a dozen cards to cover on-line losses incurred while playing craps, blackjack and other games since 1997. She then sued Providian, Visa International, Mastercard International and 50 on-line gambling operators last month. Her suit seeks to bar the credit card companies from collecting gambling debts owed by California consumers, since gambling is illegal in the state and on-line wagering is illegal in the unitedstates. Carolyn Brestchneider, a Visa International spokeswoman, said, "A consumer's financial responsibility in the real world is the same as in the virtual world." Ms. Haines's lawsuit, if successful, could cause the collapse of the Internet gambling industry, which brings in $600 million in wagers annually, said I. Nelson Rose, a law professor at Whittier College and an expert on gambling law. He said credit card accounts were the key to betting at Internet casinos, which are based outside of the unitedstates.

title:
Personal Computers;
Windows 98 Feature Combines TV, Terminal and the Internet
body: FOR all the recent media noise about the paucity of new features in Windows 98, surprisingly little has been written about WebTV for Windows, an intriguing addition to the operating system that foreshadows both the promise and the growing pains of mixing television with the personal computer. In its most basic form -- running on a standard PC connected to the Internet -- WebTV for Windows acts as a sort of electronic TV Guide that automatically gathers programming information for the user's local broadcast area, cable system or satellite television service. This information, plus brief descriptions of each program, is delivered over the Internet and presented in a grid covering about 72 hours of programming -- generally, the current, previous and following days. The guide is searchable by word or phrase, enabling the user to hunt for a special program, character, actor, etc., without having to read the entire guide, which can run to more than 100 channels on some cable and satellite services. The object of the search does not have to be in the program's title. Entering "Mary Tyler Moore" on Thursday, for example, brought up two time slots for "The Dick Van Dyke Show" on Nickelodeon and "Ordinary People" on the Movie Channel. In this basic configuration, WebTV for Windows is sort of useful but no more so than TV Guide's TVGEN Web-based service or Gist, the Web-only television guide. But WebTV for Windows gets a lot more interesting on a computer with both an Internet connection and a TV tuner card, which allows viewers to watch broadcast, cable or satellite programming on the computer screen. In this configuration, the lines separating television, computer and Internet begin to dissolve. The electronic program guide melds with channel selection, a preview window and the interactive television/Web technology that was created for the original WebTV system. The inclusion of this last feature is a rich irony, since the original WebTV was designed by a small company of the same name as a sort of antidote to the computer. By offering people email, Web access and other Internet features through their television sets, the company hoped to attract customers who did not own -- or did not want to bother with -- a computer. WebTV was arguably the first of an entire category of devices known as "Internet appliances" that were intended as alternative gates to cyberspace. When Microsoft acquired the WebTV company last year for $425 million, many industry analysts saw it as a defensive move, since people who did not want or need computers obviously did not need Microsoft. But increasingly, the acquisition is looking like an astute offensive move as the company builds a platform for interactive digital television on the WebTV foundation. In January, Microsoft sealed a deal to provide key elements of WebTV technology to Tele-Communications Inc., the cable giant acquired last month by AT&T. Like all the major cable players, TCI is eager to sell customers more products, many requiring a new generation of set-top boxes that can meld cable television and Internet access into a seamless, interactive information and entertainment system. In June, with the release of WebTV for Windows as part of Windows 98, Microsoft demonstrated an eagerness not only to play in the digital television market but to formulate the rules. This is nothing new; Microsoft has tried to dictate the rules in every industry it enters. But it does not always get its way. One of its major losses came after an aggressive attempt in the last 18 months to dictate standards that would have made digital television sets compatible with computer monitors at the expense of high definition. Even so, it is the only company offering a product that not only melds the Internet and television but offers a rudimentary form of that long-promised but elusive Holy Grail of the cable industry, interactive television. And it is not a bad attempt at that. No, WebTV for Windows will not provide video on demand, but if a cable provider carries the interactive portions of programming that have been enhanced for WebTV -- not all do -- consumers can click their way through some extra interactive features of a particular show. For example, a viewer could call up a pitcher's earned run average while watching a game, open a chat window to compare notes with other investors during a financial report or download recipes while watching a program about cooking. Steve Guggenheimer, who oversees development of WebTV for Windows as Microsoft's group product manager for digital television, said last week that he was not surprised by -- or worried about -- consumer confusion about WebTV, which he called "the first integration of television and Internet infrastructure." The technology will continue to advance, he said, and will eventually be added to Windows CE, for hand-held devices, and Windows NT, the industrial-strength version of the operating system. "People think that Microsoft is trying to force everyone to watch television on their PC's," Mr. Guggenheimer said. "That's not true. We're working to integrate two information platforms. The PC is an information appliance, and television is another form of information. There are many ways they can be used separately or in combination." The goal, he said, is to develop an information machine that offers enough flexibility so that each user can take from it what he or she needs, whether it is Mr. Guggenheimer's watching a Sonics game in the corner of his screen on nights he works late or students in a classroom using interactive educational television with the Internet for enriched instruction. Not surprisingly, that enthusiastic vision is shared by the companies that manufacture TV tuner cards for personal computers. Andrew Morrison, product development manager of ATI Technologies Inc., the Toronto-based market leader in both graphics and TV cards, said the company had seen "a very large increase in demand and sales" in the few weeks since the release of Windows 98. And, while it is too early to know for certain how much of that can be attributed to WebTV for Windows, he says he is certain that consumers will eventually share his enthusiasm as they begin simultaneously surfing channels and the Web. "First Microsoft added a Web browser to Windows," he said last week. "Now they've added a cable browser and, really, a lot more." Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
Beyond Boosterism in the Alley;
New York's Web Industry May Be Outgrowing Its Image
body: The restless clan of chic geeks and entrepreneurs who populate newyork's new media industry may not be anywhere near as rich as their West Coast counterparts. But in the pages of Jason McCabe Calacanis's monthly Silicon Alley Reporter, they emerge far more glamorous. "The industry here is driven by people," Mr. Calacanis, 27, lectured a magazine job applicant recently over breakfast at Balthazar's. "On the West Coast there are a handful of celebrities -- Bill Gates, Larry Ellison," Mr. Calacanis said, referring to the chairman of the world's two largest software companies. "Those people are boring. They don't take good pictures." Mr. Calacanis's irreverence is either refreshing or hopelessly sophomoric, depending on one's point of view. Yet his shameless boosterism of Silicon Alley -- newyork's downtown multimedia hub -- has helped create the aura of community and even home-team spirit for a disparate group of colleagues and competitors who otherwise might have little more in common than being located in Manhattan and trying to find some sort of profitable business on the World Wide Web. Certainly Mr. Calacanis's application of celebrity journalism to the world of newyork new media has earned him a certain measure of success. In less than two years the Silicon Alley Reporter has grown from a few photocopied sheets to 116 glossy pages, on the strength of advertising sales and revenue from the periodic industry conferences Mr. Calacanis has organized like last month's "Rising Tide Summit," which attracted more than 200 registrants who paid $500 each to attend. And yet, there is a growing sense in some quarters that the community identity that Silicon Alley Reporter has worked so hard to sell may no longer be the way many members of that community want to see themselves -- or be seen by the larger business world. Although there are some holdouts, notably the on-line magazines Feed and Word, increasingly, the definition of "new media" in newyork seems to be moving away from artsy, underfunded Web sites like Stim, a Prodigy pop-culture project that fell by the wayside, or the interactive soap opera The East Village. The new media seem to be maturing instead into on-line extensions of the old-line Manhattan media -- whether in advertising, marketing, publishing or broadcasting. And as venture-capitalized start-ups evolve into I.P.O.-financed corporations, some industry executives are concerned that Mr. Calacanis' unflagging promotion of an image evoking artists' lofts and SoHo may be at odds with the businesslike demeanor that will play well in boardrooms and on Wall Street. "He is a hypester in an industry that could do with less hype," said Kyle Shannon, co-founder of Agency.com. The company's major shareholder is the giant advertising holding company the Omnicom Group, which, through a series of acquisitions, has become the largest agency devoted to creating advertising on the Internet. "There are two Silicon Alleys -- the one where people go to the parties and the one where people actually do the work," Mr. Shannon said. To be sure, many of the citizens of Silicon Alley are not yet ready to go completely corporate -- to stop dressing in black or bleaching their hair blonde or, among the men, raising goatees. "We have to work very hard to balance the kind of accountability we have to have now with the creative risk-taking that brought us to where we are," said Nicholas Butterworth, president of Sonicnet, an Internet broadcaster acquired last year by the cable giant Tele-Communications Inc. "We have to move to new office space, and I'm scared," said Mr. Butterworth, whose company has been located in a loft. "One of the terrible and great things about Sonicnet is we have no walls. What happens if we put up walls?" Mr. Butterworth said he reads the Silicon Alley Reporter because Mr. Calacanis, a former gossip columnist from Brooklyn, manages to tell it mostly like it is. "Is it balanced? No. It's partisan. But it delivers the goods." Few would fault Mr. Calacanis for not speaking his mind -- although he seems to save his rants for subjects beyond the borders of downtown Manhattan. Born of a new-media column that he was writing for Paper magazine, the first issue of Silicon Alley Reporter carried the headline "Microsoft Alienates Alley." And in his daily email feed last week, Mr. Calacanis' critiqued Texas-based Zapata's Internet acquisition strategy as "over-simplistic 1995 thinking." Other characteristic fixtures of Mr. Calacanis's magazine include a controversial map that highlights a revolving -- some say random -- bunch of new media firms below 57th Street. Then there's the monthly feature labeled "Digital Dim Sum: They lead the charmed life so you don't have to," which presents paparazzi-style photographs of aspiring Silicon Alley business leaders. "Jason's challenge will be to figure out what his focus is as the industry fragments into its logical genres," said Josh Harris, co-founder of the online research firm Jupiter Communications and now chief executive of an Internet television venture. "I look at my contemporaries and we've all been through the war and we all know it's never going to be the same. It's like after my freshman year, it's time to leave the dorm." At last month's conference, for instance, some attendees grumbled at the hour devoted to interviewing the Belgian anarchist who won notoriety earlier this year by throwing a cream pie in the face of Microsoft's chairman, Bill Gates. "Jason doesn't represent Silicon Alley," said one attendee, who insisted on anonymity because he didn't want to risk retribution in print. "This is someone who is busy being flip and glib when the industry is really about serious people who are running serious businesses." But such criticism may also belie a certain defensiveness about the industry's lingering immaturity, even as it struggles through adolescence. "What people try to avoid saying about Jason, and it's not really about Jason but about the industry in newyork, is that it's small-time," said Michael Wolff, the newly appointed media columnist for newyork magazine and author of "Burn Rate," (Simon and Schuster, 1998) a book about the rise and fall of his own newyork new media company. "The point about newyork is we have not had a defining business here," Mr. Wolff said. The Alley's derivative nickname first caught on in 1995, with the explosion of Web and the conviction that its "content" -- the techie catch-all for magazines, newspapers, music, movies, TV, advertising and various vaguely defined interactive stuff -- would be produced in the world's media capital. But of all of those things, only advertising has shown a propensity to make money on the Web. Moreover, the truly successful Web content -- at least this month -- appears to be the information tools or "portals" aggregated by major search engines like Yahoo, Excite and Snap, which are all located on the West Coast. Still, newyork partisans are quick to point to the initial public offering of Doubleclick, an advertising services firm, which went public last winter at $17 a share and closed Friday at $43. City officials cite a survey conducted by Coopers & Lybrand that shows that by mid-1997, the number of new media jobs and companies had doubled to 105,771 and 4,881, respectively, in a mere 18 months. And on Friday, shares of 24/7, another Web advertising firm, rose 45 percent to close at $20.25 in its first day of trading. Two more newyork companies, The Globe, an on-line community Web site and Earthweb, an interactive services firm, also recently announced their intention to go public. By most accounts, the disadvantage of being across the continent from Sand Hill Road where Silicon Valley's venture capitalists hold court is not as sharp as it once was, as East Coast investors like Flatiron Partners take up some of the slack. Yet, in the insular new media community, the fact that Joanne Wilson, wife of a Flatiron partner, Fred Wilson, sells advertising for the Silicon Alley Reporter has raised eyebrows in some circles. Mr. Calacanis denies critics' contention that the companies Mr. Wilson invests in get special editorial consideration. A black belt in karate who put himself through Fordham University repairing electronic equipment, Mr. Calacanis makes no pretense to vaunted journalistic objectivity. "It's no secret I'm a fan of this industry," he said. "We write about every failure. We cover it. We don't obsess over it." After graduating with a degree in psychology, Mr. Calacanis landed a job in technical support for the Sony Corporation's legal department. A habitual hustler, he managed to talk his way into a ride on the corporate jet to chat about the Internet with Sony's then-president, Michael P. Schulhof. A project for America Online that he developed after leaving Sony did not take off, but in the winter of 1996, Mr. Calacanis took the modest sum America Online paid him for his efforts and started Silicon Alley Reporter, which he initially wrote, produced and distributed almost entirely himself. Now, with a staff of eight helping him put out the magazine, Mr. Calacanis is growing up and branching out. Forsaking neighborhood loyalties for the prospect of a new market, he has been spending a lot of time in Los Angeles lately and has begun running a "Digital Coast Reporter" insert in the magazine, appropriating the appellation a group of Southern California new-media entrepreneurs recently bestowed on the region. Back home, meanwhile, to compete with a local on-line news service, @NY, Mr. Calacanis recently started a daily email news feed. And he has entered into a partnership with Gordon Gould, 28, who has put more than $100,000 into the magazine -- its first investment. On behalf of the magazine, Mr. Gould also organized a conference last month at the newyork Historical Society, where Palm Pilot-toting new-media executives dined on sushi and were invited to think beyond their business concerns to the social implications of the Web and related media. David Bunnell, a West Coast technology publishing veteran who attended the conference, said he came away bullish on the newyork new-media enclave and on The Silicon Alley Reporter. "What good magazines do is identify some kind of audience and provide the members of that audience with a sense of membership and belonging; and they've done that remarkably well," said Mr. Bunnell, who runs the trade publication Upside. "What they lack in resources they make up for in enthusiasm." And as with the industry Mr. Calacanis covers, maturity shows signs of tempering raw enthusiasm One evening last week, dressed in black with sunglasses atop his head, Mr. Calcanis made an appearance at a SoHo courtyard party held by the Web ad-tracking company I-Traffic. Six months ago he might have been carrying a camera to snap the faces of his favorite entrepreneurs and their hangers-on. But this time he said there would be no party report in his magazine. "I have other things to do; I have to write an analysis of the Ticketmaster-City Search deal," he said, referring to last week's announcement of a West Coast new-media merger. "I have to get the daily out. I have work to do." Graphic   Photos: Jason McCabe Calacanis, top, has helped create the artist's loft aura of Silicon Alley, but that image may become outdated. For example, Sonicnet, above, was bought by Tele-Communications Inc. last year and will move to new, perhaps more corporate, offices. (Carrie Boretz for The newyork Times); "There are two Silicon Alleys--the one where people go to the parties and the one where people actually do the work," said Kyle Shannon, left, who founded Agency.com withy Chan W. Suh. (Rahav Segev for The newyork Times); (Frances Roberts for The newyork Times)(pg. D1)  Chart: "The New Media Capital" Silicon Alley is rapidly becoming an important part of the economy of newyork City and its surrounding area, particularly in southern Manhattan where most of the businesses are located. Chart shows the amount, in thousands, of new media employment, in billions, of new media revenues, and new media payrolls for the newyork Metropolitan Area. (SOURCE: COOPERS & LYBRAND)(pg. D6)  Table: "A New Media Sampler" Unlike California's Silicon Valley, which has become a magnet for developers of computer software and hardware, newyork's Silicon Alley has built its reputation on providing content and services for the World Wide Web. So far, no company has established itself as the pre-eminent player in this market. Instead, several companies have sprung up to cater to different niches. title:
Compressed Data;
Gracious Concession On Internet 'Spam'
body: For several years, the company stood by as Internet users turned its Spam brand name into a derisive label for unwanted junk email. But now the Hormel Foods Corporation is looking to the Net as way to enhance the brand's image. Hormel, which makes its highly processed pork luncheon meat in Austin, Minn., has just launched the official Spam Web site (www.spam.com). One might have expected that the company would be forced to pay dearly -- or even fight -- to acquire the domain name spam.com, given all the domain-name speculators on the prowl. But Hormel officials said they seized control of spam.com years ago, along with hormel.com, hormelfoods.com and other monikers. In the past, Hormel could be defensive about Spam's pejorative use, and the company even attempted last year to stop Sanford Wallace, the self-proclaimed king of unsolicited email, from using the word "spam" to promote his business. But courts have had little sympathy for companies' efforts to prevent trademarks from entering common usage -- as Lucas Films found when a Federal judge refused to intervene when "Star Wars" became standard slang for President Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative. Besides, the zeitgeist seems to be working against any hope of Hormel officials to limit of limiting the usage of "spam" on the Web. There are dozens of spam-related sites, including spam limericks, spam sonnets and spam haiku (which can be found at http://pemtropics.mit.edu/jcho/spam/limericks.html). And so with its new Web site, Hormel Foods appears to have decided to have some fun with the brand name, selling a line of Spam-logo clothing that includes boxer shorts and baseball caps. There's also a Spam history that starts with the product's debut in 1937 and commences with these words: "Every once in a while, something comes along that changes the course of history. So it is with Spam Luncheon Meat."   LAURIE J. FLYNN Graphic   Photo

title:
Compressed Data;
Let Your Least Favorite Know What You Think
body: A cure for the boring date, writes Nick Usburne, a marketing consultant, is to imagine that date with a fork in his or her head. From that kernel of an idea grew the notion of forkinthehead.com, a place on the World Wide Web where surfers can "fork" sites they deem boring, cumbersome, or otherwise unsuitable. Cathie Walker, a partner in the venture and the creator of the notorious Web time-waster the Center for the Easily Amused, said the fork site is partly for fun and partly a front for a nascent consulting business. "People love it because there's never been a way to let Web site owners know they need a little help," she said. Giving such feedback to offending site owners is easy: Critics fill out fork forms that are sent as email. Forks can be issued for shortcomings like bad content ("poor spelling and lousy grammar"), baffling navigation ("I can't find what I want!") or poor design ("nasty background pattern!"). But no anonymous thrusts are allowed. "If you're going to do it, you might as well introduce yourself," she said. "It's just polite." And for those who really want their opinion to count -- or at least be counted -- there are the newly conceived Mud Brick Awards (http://www.netstudio.com/muddies/), which aim to be to the Web what the Worst Dressed Awards are to Hollywood. Here, surfers are encouraged to nominate "the worst of the Web; sites only their creators could love." Early entries reportedly include the City of Fresno (www.fresno.gov), California Public Utilities (http://www.cpuc.ca.gov/), and the Defense Internet Service Provider of the Netherlands Armed Forces (http://home.mindef.nl). From among the nominees, a panel of judges, including the computer industry luminaries Esther Dyson and John Dvorak, will select the worst of the worst. The winning loser will receive a free consultation from the awards' creator, Netstudio -- which, not surprisingly, makes software for the creation of Web pages.   LISA NAPOLI Graphic   Photo

title:
Compressed Data;
P.G.A. Earns Points With Internet Broadcast
body: Give the Professional Golfers' Association credit for perseverance. Five months after the final half of the AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am tournament in California was rained out, the tour plans to complete the event today. Denied the customary media exposure, the tour will broadcast the event on the Web. The rain delay has lasted since March because after watching the tournament's final Saturday and Sunday disappear under water, there was no confidence that Monday, when it would normally be completed, would be any drier. With many of the tour's players returning to the West Coast over the weekend for the P.G.A. Championship outside Seattle, today was the first convenient date. In light of the effort of insuring that the final day of play would happen at all, setting up a broadcast on the Internet may not have seemed particularly daunting. But for Charles F. Schmitt, the executive producer of www.pgatour.com, the tour's official Web site, today's broadcast will be his biggest challenge yet. That is because, unlike most golf tournaments, the AT&T is staged on three courses at once: Pebble Beach, Spyglass Hills and Poppy Hills. CBS, which held the television rights, declined to move the equipment necessary for a live broadcast back to the Monterey Peninsula. "Technically, it's much more complicated," Mr. Schmitt said in a telephone interview from the tour's headquarters in Jacksonville, Fla. "Take the challenge of doing it on one course and multiply it by three." But don't expect to use the Internet to actually watch anyone play golf. The broadcast, set to begin at 1 P.M. Eastern daylight time, will have audio coupled with still photos of the holes and updated scoring. In addition to pgatour.com, the broadcast will also be available through www.cbs.sportsline.com, the site of CBS Sportsline. For golf fans, the final day of action features some marquee names. Tom Watson shares the lead with Tim Herron. Tom Lehman, Phil Mickelson, Davis Love 3d, Paul Azinger and Jim Furyk are each within two shots. The players will have to be content with an estimated audience of 200,000, rather than the roughly five million viewers that the tournament's final day drew on television last year. But the purse of $2.5 million may provide some consolation.   SETH SCHIESEL

title:
Media Talk;
'Burn Rate' Author Getsa Media Column
body: How does an erstwhile journalist and failed entrepreneur become a media critic? In the case of Michael Wolff, whose media column has its debut in the current issue of newyork magazine, his new status as enfant terrible of media culture old and new is a result of his recent book, "Burn Rate: How I Survived the Gold Rush Years on the Internet" (Simon & Schuster). The book recounts Mr. Wolff's escapades, raising and spending money in the early days of the World Wide Web in the mid-1990's, as the publisher of Netguide, a series of books about the Internet. Though "Burn Rate" has been acclaimed for its candid, behind-the-scenes glimpse at the frenzy of the early on-line world, it did not endear its author to the many people whose blunders in their race for money and power he details. Since early summer, Mr. Wolff has been critiquing the on-line media for the Industry Standard, an Internet trade publication. His newyork magazine column will focus on the traditional media. Mr. Wolff finds his sudden stature as pundit "funny" because he ended up where he is because he got out of journalism in the first place. (He had written for magazines and had two books published before moving on to Netguide.) "It is an irony that I giggle at every day," Mr. Wolff said. It was not until a story about the book appeared in newyork that the notion occurred to the magazine's editors that Mr. Wolff might be a candidate for the media critic job, which had been open since Rich Turner left for Newsweek last year. The Wolff column, according to Caroline Miller, newyork's editor, will be "written from his personal perspective, from his experiences and considerable relationships with people." Mr. Wolff described his approach to writing as "there is no 'off the record.' " "Media is filled with people who are always spouting off at each other," he said. "So much of the information that moves around in the business is information people feel they can't report. The nice thing about a column is it's my space and I can report that."   LISA NAPOLI Graphic   Photo: Michael Wolff, media critic. (Chang W. Lee/The newyork Times)

title:
TECHNOLOGY: DIGITAL COMMERCE;
As long as software code is kept secret, Internet security is at risk.
body: THE trade secrets of commercial software vendors are threatening the security of the global Internet -- and that threat extends to the future of electronic commerce as well. This was not the conclusion that most people would have reached over the last two weeks as significant security flaws were disclosed in several popular email packages, including Eudora, Microsoft Outlook and Netscapemail. Instead, most of the focus was on how users could get their hands on patches, the additional bits of software code that would spackle over the holes in their vulnerable email programs. Nonetheless, network security experts are adamant that the roots of the problem are fundamental and widespread. They think that the Internet's structure as it exists today -- the open, freely available Internet protocols, with overly bulky and/or proprietary software running atop them -- is impossible to secure because only the software vendors know what is in their code. Consider the recently exposed email flaw that would enable an intruder to send an electronic message containing a program intended to damage or steal data. How could a company release software that would allow such a thing to happen? "The problem is these gigantic, 10-megabyte Web browsers," said Mark Seiden, chief network consultant for Veriguard Inc., a computer-security concern in Menlo Park, Calif. "Nobody knows what flaws are in them. Nobody even knows, really, everything that they do." Yet, he said, we install them without thinking. "Or worse," Mr. Seiden said, "you have no choice but to install them because, in the case of Internet Explorer, they're part of the operating system. Then there are all the things which are part of Windows which haven't been looked at, with an eye toward security, by anybody other than the vendor." Any software company that, for example, develops software for Windows has to trust whatever security defaults Microsoft has chosen to use, yet "the developers have no idea what's in them," Mr. Seiden said. "There's no way to find out the Windows source code." Until a few months ago, the same was true of Netscape. But earlier this year, Netscape published its source code to encourage its use by third-party software developers. Apparently, developers have not had sufficient time to discover all its flaws. What this means in the end is that the network infrastructure created by popular Web browsers from the Netscape Communications Corporation and the Microsoft Corporation -- and from the scores of other companies that produce software to work with them -- has not been subjected to the same rigorous peer review that went into the design of Internet protocols, the rules that are continually scrutinized by some of the world's best software engineers. As a consequence, Mr. Seiden said, there is always the possibility, however remote, that "any of the stuff that's on your desktop can be gotten to by hostile programs." For today's on-line consumers, that means exposing bank accounts, password files -- anything that is in a file on a hard drive connected to the Internet. But for companies conducting business on the Internet, that means exposing trade secrets, intellectual property, product designs, customer data bases, marketing strategies and more. Mr. Seiden recommends encrypting sensitive information on a vulnerable machine by using code embedded on a computer chip, rather than encryption software. But even if a company follows that recommendation, the incentive to steal corporate data appears to be increasing at an alarming rate. According to the 1997 Global Information Security Survey, conducted by Ernst & Young in conjunction with Information Week magazine, 38 percent of respondents in the unitedstates said their networks had been compromised for purposes of industrial espionage, up from 6 percent in 1996. Those reporting malicious acts by outsiders increased to 42 percent in 1997 from 17 percent in 1996. Although there is no known instance of any intruder actually exploiting the email security flaws disclosed this month, this increasing vulnerability alarms security experts. "Corporate espionage is the fastest-growing sector of the computer crime business," said Thomas Noonan, chairman and chief executive of Internet Security Systems, an Atlanta-based supplier of security management systems. "Flaws in the infrastructure are inevitable, a fact of life," Mr. Noonan said. "But if electronic commerce is about the ability to trade ubiquitously in all corners of the globe, one of the huge challenges for business is how to protect the security and integrity of my information, which is now the basis of my competitive advantage." Mr. Noonan, whose clients include some of the world's largest companies, says corporate information officers realize that commercial software is "the source of their vulnerabilities." But though they spend millions of dollars on software every year, "they feel their hands are tied." "I really think that unless these vendors provide their customers with a much higher level of comfort for managing security risks, then a lot less software will be sold, and electronic commerce will gain a lot less traction than it could have," Mr. Noonan said. If Mr. Noonan is right, the industry's very tentative steps toward open source code -- a la Netscape and the Linux version of the Unix operating system -- become even more attractive. When a program's code is open to inspection by everyone, bugs are fixed and quality improves much more quickly because an entire industry of engineers is working on them at once. Maybe one day, the software industry will have to embrace the truth of the old Psychology 101 adage: You're only as sick as your secrets. Graphic   Drawing (Randy Jones)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Cisco Systems Plans National TV Campaign
body: After carving out its niche as the the No. 1 maker of Internet communications equipment, Cisco Systems Inc. is taking on another medium by introducing its first national television campaign. A series of four television commercials, created by Goldberg Moser O'Neill in San Francisco, Cisco's agency since 1992, takes a winsome, humanistic approach in an effort to expand its consumer audience, demystify technology, communicate the power of the Internet and emphasize Cisco as an Internet leader. "One of our goals is to convey Cisco's key role in this new Internet world and convey the urgency and opportunity behind this change," said Keith Fox, vice president for corporate marketing at Cisco. The spots, which carry the theme, "Empowering the Internet generation," are scheduled to begin Aug. 24 in several major cities in the unitedstates and will be expanded later across North America. Spending was estimated at $30 million for the 60-second and 30-second spots, which will run on sports, news and prime-time network programs and business and technology shows. Mike Massaro, executive vice president and chief operating officer of Goldberg Moser, said that most high-technology advertising focused on products, technologies or services. "We wanted to focus on the power of the Internet and to evoke a real sense of humanity," he said. The warm-and-fuzzy ads, which were filmed in London, Spain, Vietnam and New Orleans, pose the question "Are you ready?" In one spot, children offer tidbits such as "The Web had more users in its first five years than the telephone did in their first 30," and "A new population the size of the United Kingdom joins the Internet every six months." A sneak preview of the spots will be broadcast on the Internet at www.cisco.com this week. A print and on-line advertising campaign will also be introduced to complement the television spots.

title: Big Web Sites to Track Steps of Their Users
body: Some of the largest commercial sites on the World Wide Web have agreed to feed information about their customers' reading, shopping and entertainment habits into a system developed by a Massachusetts company that is already tracking the moves of more than 30 million Internet users, recording where they go and what they read, often without the users' knowledge. The agreement calls for the participating Web sites to track their users so that advertisements can be precisely aimed at the most likely prospects for goods and services. But while this system guarantees the anonymity of individual users, the underlying technology disturbs privacy-rights advocates, who have long worried about the growing ability of on-line companies to collect and store personal data about people who use the Web. Many individual Internet services have begun to amass detailed records of who uses their sites and how they use them. But this new industry cooperative represents the most ambitious effort yet to gather disparate bits of personal information into a central data base containing digital dossiers on potentially every person who surfs the Web. Participating sites will include the Lycos-Tripod site, which was visited by 14.8 million people in July, according to Relevant Knowledge, a market research firm, and the Geocities on-line community of more than two million personal Web sites that attracted 14.2 million visitors last month. The system's proponents extol its promise for delivering precisely directed, sometimes personalized, ads. For example, an Internet user who looks up tourist information about England on a travel site in the network might be fed ads for airlines flying into Heathrow Airport and for hotels in London as he checks sports scores. "If someone comes to your bookstore the first time, you can find out if they are interested in mountain climbing, organic gardening and tennis; you can present them books related to their interests immediately," said David S. Wetherell, the chief executive of the company behind the Internet system, CMG Information Services of Andover, Mass. In addition to a few large sites, CMG has attracted a host of smaller participants like NBC Videoseeker and Ticketmaster. CMG's system and a dozen other similar efforts under development are rooted in the same marketing needs that have prompted direct-mail companies to assemblemailing lists using nearly every publicly available scrap of information on people, from their auto registrations to their vacation habits. But whilemailing-list companies are limited to identifying people for mailing lists by broad interests -- for example, subscribers to fishing magazines -- Internet-based systems can find a person who reads articles about fishing even if the Web page he is visiting is part of a general news or recreation site. The Internet systems can also tighten their focus by, say, sending an ad from a charter operator to someone who has spent time reading about deep-sea fishing. Mr. Wetherell argues that CMG's system, known as Engage, protects people's privacy in ways that mailing-list companies never can. In particular, he says, Engage does not record the name, street or email address or credit card numbers of the people it profiles. Instead, it places a unique identifying number on the computer hard drive of every person who visits one of the participating sites. That way the system can keep track of all the sites visited by that computer, regardless of the identity of its user. "We took the highest road you could possibly take with respect to privacy," Mr. Wetherell said. "We think you can learn a lot more about someone from their behavior than from their name and address." Moreover, a user can choose not to have his or her surfing observed by visiting the company's Web site (www.engage.com) and selecting an option that will remove the identification number, known in the language of the Internet as a "cookie," from their computer. Users can also set their Web browsers not to put any cookies on their computers, but this can complicate access to some sites. Some privacy advocates agree that Engage's promise of anonymity could help protect Internet users from hackers and commercial or government snoops.
