title: Campaign Contributors Are Listed on the Internet
body: In a milestone in the effort to inform the public about the political process, the newyork City Campaign Finance Board unveils a new feature today on its Internet site that allows users to search a list of campaign contributors. Visitors to the Web site can examine the names of donors and the amount they gave to the campaigns of more than 175 candidates who ran in the 1997 city elections, from Mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani to losing contenders for the City Council. The records for candidates who plan to seek office in the next city election, in 2001, are also available at the site (www.cfb.nyc.ny.us). Since it was established in 1988, the board has required most candidates who take part in the city's voluntary campaign finance system to submit their disclosure records on computer disk. Members of the public were then able to obtain copies of the records on disk or view them at a terminal at the board's offices. But the board had not put the records on its Internet site. The new feature includes information on the names, occupations and employers of contributors, as provided by the campaigns. It also includes the date when the donations were received. "By visiting the board's Web site, the public can now follow the money that funds newyork City campaigns right from their own homes, 24 hours a day," said the board's executive director, Nicole A. Gordon. "No other jurisdiction in the country offers all the public disclosure resources that the Campaign Finance Board now provides." Candidates in the city's campaign finance system obtain money from the city treasury for their campaigns in return for agreeing to limits on their fund raising and spending, as well as increased disclosure rules. The state does not disseminate information on computer for the finances of campaigns for state offices. It plans to change that after the elections in November, when it begins a new disclosure system that is supposed to be similar to the one in the city, with information available at an Internet site.

title:
Compressed Data;
A New Watchdog Against Internet Fraud
body: The Securities and Exchange Commission is beefing up its cyberpatrols with the creation of a new office to combat investment fraud on the Internet. John Reed Stark, an eight-year member of the S.E.C.'s enforcement division, has been named to lead a new unit, the Office of Internet Enforcement. Mr. Stark, formerly the commission's special counsel for Internet projects, said that creating the office would formalize efforts that had already resulted in the prosecution of 30 cases. Those have involved virtually every type of investment scam, including phony offerings, market manipulations, frauds that aim at a particular ethnic or religious group, and so-called pyramid and Ponzi schemes. "Internet access is ubiquitous and coming down in price," Mr. Stark said. "Hardware is cheap. A lot of software is free, so it is spreading across the planet. At the same time, we are experiencing the greatest bull market in history. Put the two together and you have more people gambling instead of investigating their investments." The S.E.C. already maintains a Web site (http://www.sec.gov/enforce/comctr.htm) where people can lodge complaints. Mr. Stark said he received about 120 complaints via email a day. "They are the same scams that we've had over the last 65 years -- just on the Internet," he said.   JERI CLAUSING Graphic   Photo: John Reed Stark will investigate on-line fraud. (Paul Hosefros/The newyork Times)

title:
Compressed Data;
A Way to Find Out What a Job is Worth
body: Dagwood Bumstead made a career of asking for a raise he never seemed to get, but he might have had better luck had he been armed with data from a new World Wide Web site, the Salary Zone (http://www.ioma.com/zone). The site lets surfers, from clerks to chief executives, determine their value in the marketplace by asking for comparable salaries based on several factors: sex, region, management responsibility, size of company and level of education. "All over the world you can find out what you're worth in a way that wasn't possible before," said Kathie Fitzgerald, the Webmaster for the site, which is run by the Institute of Management Administration, a business management publisher. The group surveys professionals in a variety of fields twice a year and publishes 34 newsletters, like Shipping Manager's Report and Controlling Law Firm Costs. "A human resources professional would pay $199 a year for a subscription to one of our publications," Ms. Fitzgerald said. "But if you're a job hunter, that would be ridiculous." Instead, visitors to the site can pay $40 and wait 24 hours for a verdict on their worth in the open marketplace. The institute's parent company, the Bureau of National Affairs, based in Washington, collects similar data on a wider group of professions, and the two groups merged their data bases for this Web site. Ms. Fitzgerald said there was a growing interest by individuals in using the Web for career development. "People looking for work and people looking for talent are using the Internet more and more," she said.   LISA NAPOLI Graphic   Photo: The home page for the Salary Zone.

title:
Compressed Data;
One Expert's Buzz Is Another's Target
body: There are two main paths to credibility in the world of professional technology experts. One is to champion new trends, making sweeping judgments and pronouncing ways in which the latest technology could make all nonbelievers obsolete. This is called preaching to the chat room. The other is to debunk new trends, poking holes in the assumptions that others have made and throwing cold water on the preachers. This is called being a calculated contrarian. Both techniques seem to work when it comes to selling reports for thousands of dollars. But the two strategies will go head to head this week as two of the more prominent high-technology consulting firms publicize reports on the convergence of voice and data traffic in the nation's communications networks. In its report on the market for telephone calls that use Internet technology, Abhi Chaki of Jupiter Communications calls the consolidation of voice, video and data information onto unified networks an "inescapable reality." The firm says that will fuel the adoption of Internet-style phone calls. Over the last year or so, the views of people like Mr. Chaki have taken on the patina of conventional wisdom. But what is really inescapable after reading the report is the feeling that Jupiter, based in newyork, is congenitally friendly to the Internet. The calculated contrarian, Forrester Research, based in Cambridge, Mass., is as in tent on tearing down the concept of network consolidation as Jupiter is in promoting it. In its latest report, Forrester says that businesses will not bother with unified voice-data networks and that multiple networks will live on. "What we try to do is demystify hype," Maribel Lopez, the Forrester analyst behind the report, said in an interview. "The buzz, a lot of it has to do with data guys looking to sell the next router upgrade." But in the interest of demystification, it should be made clear that Forrester made an early copy of the report available to a reporter in an effort to create some buzz of its own.   SETH SCHIESEL

title: Deal to Create The Largest Interactive Ad Agency
body: In a combination that will create the largest agency devoted to creating advertising on the Internet, Agency.com has agreed to buy Eagle River Interactive. This deal, which is expected to be announced today, is the latest in a mad game of Pac Man, in which the dozens of small agencies founded by young entrepreneurs are racing to gobble each other up. Behind the scenes in many of these transactions is the Omnicom Group, the huge advertising agency holding company, which has taken stakes in several of the most prominent start-up interactive agencies. Omnicom owns 40 percent of Agency.com, which is based in newyork, and all of Eagle River Interactive, based in Chicago. The terms of the deal have not been disclosed, but Omnicom's stake in Agency.com will increase to just under half as a result of the deal, said Chan Suh, Agency.com's chief executive. In recent months, Agency.com has also bought Online Magic, Spiral Media, Ketchum Interactive and Interactive Solutions. The later two were also owned by Omnicom. Interactive agencies provide a range of services, including helping companies set up their own sites on the World Wide Web and placing "banner" advertisements on other sites to bring in traffic. While this business incorporates the sort of writing and design skills used by conventional advertising agencies, much of the work of the interactive shops more closely resembles such detailed computer programming typically provided by technology companies. "An interactive company is one part creativity, one part technology and one part business strategy," said Felice Kincannon, who looks after Omnicom's interactive holdings through a unit called Communicade. Indeed, technology companies have been expanding into this field. Both the International Business Machines Corporation and the Electronic Data Services Corporation have set up big interactive design departments as an adjunct to their business of building elaborate Internet sites for companies. And two of the most aggressive acquirers of interactive agencies -- U S Web in Santa Clara, Calif., and iXL in Atlanta -- have been buying both technology and design companies. Still, the conventional advertising companies have the greatest ties to the existing Interactive agencies, with True North Communications, Grey Advertising and the Interpublic Group all owning stakes in at least one of the top 15 agencies. Omnicom, however, has been the most aggressive, with stakes in 4 of the top 15 ranked by Adweek magazine, including Agency.com, now tied with iXL for first place; Think New Ideas, the fifth-ranked agency; Organic Online, No. 7, and Eagle River, No. 14. In total, its six agencies have 1,500 employees and revenues of $180 million. That represents about one third of what Jupiter Communications estimates is a $500 million market this year. "Instead of picking one horse to ride, Omnicom has spread its bets and has watched how the race turned out," said Seth Alpert, a senior adviser to Ad Media Partners, a newyork investment bank that specializes in media companies. "So far, they have done a pretty good job. As it has with conventional advertising agencies, Omnicom has been able to buy into the younger interactive agencies by offering to act as the friendly, but unintrusive, big brother. "They are not backseat drivers," Mr. Suh said, adding that Agency.com had few client referrals from other Omnicom agencies. But it has been able to ask executives of the holding company questions from time to time. "It's like having your own consulting company on call," he said. Yet Omnicom has subtly encouraged the strongest of its flock to absorb the laggards. In February, it flew the top executives of all of its interactive companies for a retreat in Miami. While Omnicom did not play explicit matchmaker, the flirtation was as heavy as on a college spring break. "It was a courting thing," said Kevin Rowe, the chief executive of Eagle River. After a first date of a joint project for Compaq Computer, Eagle River and Agency.com decided to get hitched. As a result of the combination, Agency.com will have 575 employees in 10 offices and 1998 revenues of about $80 million. Founded in 1995, Agency.com's largest clients include British Airways, GTE and Metropolitan Life. Eagle River, a descendant of a company that placed billboards on Colorado ski slopes, serves clients that include Sprint and Disneyland Paris. Many advertising industry executives expect that Agency.com is trying to grow quickly in preparation for an initial public offering. Mr. Suh declined to comment on any potential offering. Yet others wonder whether many of these young companies are expanding faster than they can handle. "I get worried for a company like Agency.com," said Gene DeRose, the president of Jupiter Communications. "I think they have to be careful about how they integrate their acquisitions." Mr. DeRose pointed to the example of CKS Group, one of the first publicly held interactive agencies, which has found melding its many acquisitions harder than it expected. CKS's stock trades at less than half of its 52-week high of $64.25, reached last September; the shares closed at $19.3125 Friday, off 12.5 cents, in Nasdaq trading. Others point out that the acquisition prices for interactive agencies is vastly higher than for conventional ad agencies, which typically are sold for about the total of their annual revenues. The high water mark for pricing was recently set by ICC Technologies, a Hatboro, Pa., maker of humidity control systems, which recently moved onto the Internet by buying Rare Medium, a small newyork agency for $45 million, more than 11 times its revenues. Many other more traditional buyers are turning up their noses at those prices. "We recently met with a foreign agency who said they were looking for an Interactive shop in this country," Mr. Alpert of Ad Media Partners said. "We told them they would have to pay four or five times revenue, and they were aghast and went home."

title:
Industry View;
Internet journalists are beginning to gain respect in an area once seen as a stepchild by established media companies.
body: The Internet has created lots of jobs for journalists. But how about career opportunities? After a few years of print and broadcast reporters moving on line, we're starting to find out. Two years ago, when I left my reporter's job at Smart Money magazine to help start an independent on-line financial publication, TheStreet.com, the Internet was not exactly viewed as a clear step up career-wise. A leap over a black hole was more like it. At least that's how naysayers saw Web journalism. The Net's anarchic, everything-goes image turned off print and broadcast stalwarts. With Web publishing technically easy -- any high school student could put up a site -- doubters questioned the caliber, not to mention credibility, of on-line work. They saw the virtual world as a journalistic Wild West, lacking the ethical rigor of a conventional newsroom. Writers, in particular, preferred sticking with a medium that would give them their portfolio of "clips," as though the paper their articles was printed on counted more than their words. Then there was the circulation myth. Why go to an Internet site with readership un known, when you could work at a magazine or a national TV news show and know that your work would be seen by millions? The Internet stigma was even worse within established media companies, thanks to the so-called stepchild syndrome. Even when the conventional media companies lent their brand names to Internet ventures, for fear of being left behind, the backing didn't always come with critical corporate support -- financial, or perhaps more important, psychological. And often, as companies proceeded with on-line plans, the staffers at their flagships continued to see the Internet start-up not as a cool, new-media sibling, but as the ugly stepchild. "It's hip in the reverse," said a writer at a business magazine. "From the magazine's perspective, anyone working on the Internet is like being in Siberia. Here in magazines, print journalism rules." This respect factor was not lost on those making a go of it. Wendy Nelson, who used to be a local editor and producer at New Jersey Online, the World Wide Web outlet for The Newark Star-Ledger and two other papers owned by Advance Publications and a television station partly owned by Advance, recalls sending email to her colleagues on the print side and getting no response. "Some of the newspaper people didn't see us as particularly important," Ms. Nelson said. "They just didn't feel it was relevant to what they were up to." She left the site in April to edit two print trade publications for physicians. Despite these hurdles, many journalists with good jobs in print and broadcast news were excited by the prospect of creating something new and being able to play the kind of leading roles that might not be available to them in the established media until much later in their careers. Two years ago, for example, Nicholas Ascheim left his job at ABC News at age 26 to help start what is now Fox News Online. "I was a producer, and I got to do very interesting stuff at ABC, but I was still a lower man on the totem pole" Mr. Ascheim said. The Fox job "was an opportunity to get in at the ground level, not just in the company but in the medium." Mr. Ascheim left his job as editorial director of Fox News Online last month to go to Harvard Business School. In time, many more journalists, both established and fledgling, flocked to the Net. Among the notables in business journalism was Jim Jubak, an editor and columnist at Worth magazine who now writes for Microsoft Investor, and Herb Greenberg, the nationally known Wall Street columnist from The San Francisco Chronicle who joined TheStreet.com. With the arrival of such writers, the initial stigma began to fade. The pioneers helped bring to on-line journalism the training they learned off line, showing doubters -- both peers and readers -- that this seemingly anarchical medium could adhere to the toughest traditional standards. (Which is not to say that all on-line writers are pillars of the profession; the Web gossip writer Matt Drudge might be a must-read among journalists but he's far from a model.) "We think of ourselves as journalists first and then as people who can adapt to the potential of this medium," said Bob Arnold, a former Business Week magazine editor who has been editor of Business Week Online since 1994. "Half of us were on the magazine for a decade or two. We bring the same standards of quality, good reporting, good writing." Qualms about readership have also receded. A national magazine might flaunt an official circulation in the millions, but its writers could toil for years without ever knowing who, if anyone, actually read their work. Net writers know what readers think within minutes, thanks to email feedback. And on-line work is having an impact. Adam L. Penenberg, writing for the on-line Forbes Digital Tool, was responsible for breaking the news that Stephen Glass, a New Republic writer, had fabricated an article in the magazine -- only one of many fabrications, The New Republic subsequently discovered. Finally, while by no means a consistent trend, some major media companies now seem to be treating their on-line publications as more than just brand extensions. Last November, the News Corporation put its electronic publishing ventures into a separate company: News America Digital Publishing, which includes Fox News Online. Among other things, Mr. Aschiem said, the change meant "our resources were our resources, nothing was a hand-me-down." At The Wall Street Journal, a small group from the print publication recently came to staffers of The Wall Street Journal Interactive Edition complaining that they hadn't been asked to contribute more material to the on-line service. "That is a good sign that people are saying 'We want to participate in on line -- get us involved,' " said Neil Budde, editor in chief of the Interactive Edition. "When we first started, it was like we were going out and trying to recruit people." And Business Week now considers a staffer's contribution to its Web site when the magazine's managers conduct performance and pay reviews. All of these shifts point to potential career rewards for on-line risk takers. But as my colleague Dave Kansas, a former Wall Street Journal reporter who is editor in chief of TheStreet.com, points out, the conclusive evidence is not yet in. "The real validation," he said, will come when on-line journalists move "to prominent jobs at newspapers, and movement back and forth becomes transparent." Mr. Ascheim, who plans to return to the media -- "something digital," he said -- after business school, is also looking to the future: "The opportunities for 28-year-old editorial directors are already gone. I think it will be a much more competitive and, I'm loathe to use this word, much more legitimate industry in two years." Two years, though, is an eternity in Internet time. By then, whatever the conventional media elite may think, on-line journalists might have decided that they're already arrived -- and are happy to stay right where they are. title: Power Companies Embrace the Internet
body: There's a new power in the Internet access business: your utility company. A growing number of electric companies -- once slow-moving, government-regulated monopolies -- are getting into one of the most rapidly changing businesses. At least 100 utility companies offer Internet access, including more than 30 of the nation's biggest electricity providers, and dozens of others may follow suit. At the larger end are the likes of Arizona Public Service, whose Phoenix-based subsidiary, Cyber Trails, has grown into one of the top 10 Internet service companies in the state. At the other end of the spectrum is Plumas-Sierra Rural Electric Cooperative, a power provider nestled in the Northern Sierra Nevada mountains that also serves about 2,000 dial-up Internet customers. Large or small, electric companies are moving into the Internet business because of utility deregulation. Eighteen states have opened their power industries to some form of competition, and most others are expected eventually to do so as well. That means the utilities not only have to learn to compete, they have more reason to seek new sources of revenue. Moreover, many power companies already have the telecommunications infrastructures that their Internet subsidiaries could use to serve outside customers. So more than 100 utilities have turned to telecommunications, including long-distance, wireless and local phone service, cable television access, home security systems and, now, Internet access. "We have another business in this building, another way to pay rent," said Robert Marshall, general manager of Plumas-Sierra and its Internet access subsidiary, Plumas-Sierra Local Net. "It will help us hold our own in the big wide world when electricity deregulation hits." The power companies are joining a host of other businesses in trying to own a piece of the ground floor of cyberspace. Aspiring Internet access providers range from mom-and-pop operations to giant long-distance carriers like AT&T, MCI Communications and Sprint, and radio and cable television stations. Even while there has been some consolidation among large and regional Internet service providers, their overall number has exploded to 4,850 from 1,500 in the last five years, according to Boardwatch Magazine, an industry trade journal. The growth and diversity of Internet service providers means "you can't even recognize what an I.S.P. is anymore," said Jack Rickard, editor of Boardwatch. For their part, power companies say providing Internet services is a natural move for them. Across the country, many of the 180 large, investor-owned utilities own large fiber-optic networks that they built for internal communication across states and among power plants and field offices. They used only a portion of the capacity, however, eventually leasing it out to telecommunications businesses. Now, they are developing their own telecommunications businesses, including Internet access, said John Castagna, a spokesman for the Edison Electric Institute, an electric industry trade group. Mr. Castagna said 30 to 40 major utilities were offering Internet access and others were considering it. Further, the power companies say they understand other crucial aspects of the Internet business: billing, customer service and computer networking. "You already have expertise on the communications and you already have expertise on the computer networking," said Ben Preusser, business manager for Cyber Trails in Phoenix. "All you need to do is drop a line to the Internet." Of course, it is not quite that easy. Since the utilities themselves are regulated, any costs from the Internet business cannot be passed on to power customers in the form of higher rates. So the Internet subsidiaries must pay fees for using the utilities' telecommunications infrastructure, and the start-up costs are the responsibility of the utilities' parent companies and their shareholders, not the utilities' rate payers. Arizona Public Service invested more than $2 million to get its Cyber Trails subsidiary up and running, Mr. Preusser said. This involved buying modems, routers -- which route Internet traffic to the proper destination -- and establishing a high-speed line into the backbone of the Internet. Cyber Trails also leases data lines from U S West and from Arizona Public Service. Cyber Trails, which began offering Internet access in March 1997, has 6,000 dial-up customers, adds 20 new ones a day, and has one of the 10 largest subscriber bases in the state, Mr. Preusser said. He said the company had marketed aggressively, going after rural areas that national Internet service providers had ignored, and also had contracts to provide access to several Indian reservations. Mr. Preusser said the new business was helping Arizona Public Service learn about the challenges of moving into a new business in a competitive marketplace -- knowledge that should prove beneficial as the utility heads into a deregulated and much more competitive electricity marketplace. "It's a different set of skills," he said. "It turns out that just leveraging your existing technology doesn't work all that great." Carol A. Heiberger, an energy and telecommunications consultant in Philadelphia, has a similar view, noting that the relatively low cost of offering Internet access gives utilities the chance to experiment with a new business model. "They're practicing running a competitive business to see what it looks like," she said. But Ms. Heiberger, who has written extensively on the efforts by utilities to offer Internet access, said there was no guarantee that power companies could succeed in this business. On the one hand, she said, they have infrastructure, marketing, brand recognition and customer service experience; on the other, they are not accustomed to the fast-moving world of technology. Still, the potential problems did not discourage Carolina Power and Light, which serves 1.1 million residences with electricity, from entering the Internet business. In January, it acquired Interpath Communications, a company that provides consulting, Web page hosting and design, and Internet access to 4,500 businesses in North Carolina, as well as surrounding states. The experience of Carolina Power and Light also highlights an approach taken by dozens of utility companies entering the telecommunications business: rather than building from scratch, as in Arizona, they are buying existing Internet companies or signing joint ventures with major telecommunications providers. A year ago, for example, a subsidiary of the Potomac Electric Power Company, which serves Maryland and the District of Columbia, pledged to spend $150 million to develop long-distance, cable television and Internet services in partnership with the RCN Corporation, a major telecommunications provider. There are other reasons some utilities turn to the Internet. Warren Dunn, director of communication for the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, said that at least 60 of the nation's 1,000 rural cooperatives offered Internet access, in part because they consider it part of their charter to serve their communities. Mr. Marshall, the general manager of Plumas-Sierra, said the utility cooperative felt it had a responsibility to provide Internet access in a region others were ignoring. Before the electric company started its Internet subsidiary in the fall of 1995, residents of the area had to place a long-distance call to get Internet access. "We felt advanced technology would not be available unless we stepped up to do the job," Mr. Marshall said. title: Senate Panel Would Reduce Tax Moratorium onInternet
body: A proposed six-year moratorium on taxes in cyberspace would be reduced to only two years under the version of the Internet Tax Freedom Act approved by the Senate Finance Committee. The committee also voted last week to force states and local governments that tax Internet access to end these taxes, but left untouched claims for millions of dollars in taxes that America Online did not collect from customers and may now have to pay at its own expense. The Finance Committee's version of the bill differs significantly from those passed by the House and by the Senate Commerce Committee. The House version calls for a three-year moratorium, while the Senate Commerce Committee's version would keep the six-year moratorium. Both the House and the Senate Commerce Committee versions would block states from citing the presence of computer servers to establish a company's physical presence within a state. The Senate Finance Committee's version is silent on this issue. Until most of these and other differences are worked out, the bill is unlikely to reach the Senate floor for a vote. The Senate is in recess until the end of the month. The Internet Tax Freedom Coalition, the leading electronic commerce group lobbying to make cyberspace free of taxes and tariffs, contends that confusion about taxes is hampering the growth of commerce in cyberspace. That argument was rejected by Senator John H. Chafee, Republican of Rhode Island, and Senator Bob Kerrey, Democrat of Nebraska, both members of the Finance Committee. Senator Chafee, citing testimony by America Online that electronic commerce will grow to $20 billion by 2000, said a two-year moratorium was enough to determine how to tax cyberspace transactions properly. Senator Kerrey dismissed the arguments of industry lobbyists that taxes are crippling electronic commerce. "This is no infant industry in swaddling clothes," he said, citing 30 percent growth a month in retail sales on the Internet. "Wall Street can't throw money at Internet companies fast enough." The 19-to-1 vote by the Senate Finance Committee to approve its version of the bill came last Tuesday, the same day that the Commerce Department issued a report showing a growing disparity in access to the Internet among various income groups. People making more than $75,000 a year are seven times as likely to have access to the Internet as those making $15,000 to $20,000 a year and more than twice as likely as those making $35,000 to $50,000. The concept of making the Internet a tax-free zone was criticized by Michael Maserov, a senior policy analyst with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. "This is just one more tax break for the affluent at the expense of the poor," he said. The Senate Finance Committee rejected, on a 10-to-10 tie vote, a proposal by Senator Kent Conrad, Democrat of North Dakota, that would have allowed states that tax Internet access and data sold over the Internet to continue those levies. Senator Conrad, who was formerly his state's elected tax commissioner, said he saw no compelling reason for the Federal Government to interfere with state tax policies. The "ability of states or local governments to collect tax" on transactions before July 29 would not be affected by the Senate Finance Committee's version of the bill, according to the committee's chairman, Senator William V. Roth Jr., Republican of Delaware. That provision is a serious setback for America Online, the nation's largest Internet service provider, which collects sales taxes on behalf of foreign governments but has refused to collect the same taxes when they are required by the states and local governments.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: DIGITAL COMMERCE;
The Internet, whose reason for being lies in open standards, is snagging on free-market appetites.
body: WHEN does the term "commercial Internet" become an oxymoron? Perhaps it is when powerful corporations use their market strength to impose technical standards -- intended to further their own interests and improve their bottom lines -- at the expense of universal access to on-line goods and services. The browser war between Microsoft and the Netscape Communications Corporation already threatens a truly global marketplace that is fully accessible with any browser on any computer platform. And this threat is growing with the continuing push toward unilateral standards that will dictate how consumers will one day interact, for example, with on-line video programming or World Wide Web pages. In some cases, this trend merely reflects companies' attempts to differentiate their products -- an axiom of capitalism -- in the chaotic Internet market. But in other cases, it stems from an unrestrained appetite to control the flow of electronic commerce. Such appetites ignore that the Internet exists in the first place because its technical protocols are open standards, freely available for use by everyone. Standards were the reason for its rapid adoption by the commercial world: the network itself became exponentially more valuable as its popularity avalanched and more companies and users tumbled to the benefits of being on line. The Internet's ultimate seduction was that no matter what kind of computer one used, its standardized protocols would smooth out the rough spots and give the user as uniform and predictable an on-line experience as possible. But the World Wide Web browser war that erupted in 1996, when Microsoft launched the market equivalent of a thermonuclear attack on Netscape's Navigator, brought that fairy tale to an abrupt end. Almost overnight, notices started appearing on various Web sites, declaring that the sites had been "optimized" for one browser or the other: "Best viewed with Internet Explorer," or "Navigator required to display this page." Such practices annoyed users, who until then could view virtually everything that was on the Web no matter what computer or browser they were using, and infuriated Web pioneers. They saw browser battles as turf wars, the first step toward Balkanization of the Internet -- a step that, if you believed the power of the network to be collective by nature, would ultimately defeat the purpose. More recently came the so-called portal, a thinly veiled advertising strategy that purports to draw Web users into the wonderful world of Disney, say, or Netscape or Yahoo, and keep them there. But of course, the trend for companies to establish their proprietary identities atop the open Internet protocols did not stop with software. Take, for example, the "optimized content" initiative sponsored by Intel. So blatant it is almost endearing, the initiative encourages Web developers to "optimize" Web sites so they look noticeably better running on a Pentium II-based computer. This means, conversely, that they look noticeably worse if you happen not to own a Pentium II -- which is the precise situation that Intel hopes to remedy. Of course, none of these companies can really be expected to do anything but mess around with the open standards of the Internet. They are just following the laws of the free-market jungle. But an industry analyst notes that standards are also used as a club by market leaders, thus stifling innovation. William Gurley, an analyst and venture capitalist with Hummer Winblad Venture Partners in San Francisco, took on the issue of standards in a recent article, saying that they actually run counter to the interests of small, innovative companies. "Open is a euphemism for commodity," Mr. Gurley wrote. "In commodity markets, people differentiate with production or distribution prowess and not with innovation." And the companies with production and distribution prowess are generally the market leaders. So, he says, although everyone believes that "open" is really good for innovation -- especially in the Internet economy -- actually "open" is the most reliable way to preserve the status quo. The Internet is today's hottest commodity, and an industry announcement last week serves as a model for Mr. Gurley's point. The new Advanced Television Enhancement Forum, a coalition of media and technology giants spearheaded by Intel, said it had defined a modification to the standard Internet language, HTML, that will govern the digital distribution, via the Internet, of television programs with data added. And of course, the specification also includes new computerized products for consumers to buy, devices that are designed to display the hybrid data. The group -- whose members include CNN, Disney, Microsoft, NBC, Sony and Warner Brothers -- said that it intended to submit its new rules to a variety of standards bodies, including W3C, the World Wide Web Consortium, but that it would not wait for the group's approval before promoting the standard to the industry. Mr. Gurley says it will be impossible for any start-up not to support a standard from such a powerful series of market leaders. If he is right, the Advanced TV Forum has, then, already trumped any competing technical innovations that may be in the pipeline. However, it also sloughs off vast numbers of existing Internet users who may never have the proper equipment. Why would these entertainment and media companies make such a huge investment in a tiny fraction of the Internet market -- which is already a fraction of their existing markets for movies and music -- in a genre where there continues to be no compelling interactive applications, or income? If differentiation is indeed the only way to succeed in business, then it is clear that the Internet as it was designed -- global, two-way and largely accessible by anyone -- is going the way of all flesh. Yet the question remains: Is there some point at which differentiation kills the goose that laid the golden egg? Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title: Banks' Obligations
body: To the Editor: As banking becomes less localized and large institutions focus on a national base, the notion of placing a particular lending focus on the community that surrounds a brick-and-mortar branch seems almost quaint. The problem is even more acute when the law is applied to the growing number of "virtual banks" that operate only through phone lines or over the Internet. These banks have no branches and draw deposits and make loans without regard to location. Banking regulators are struggling with this issue, and their decisions will have a profound effect. If a virtual bank's community is deemed to be the area surrounding its base office, there will be tremendous incentive to locate such banks in areas without significant neighborhood needs. If a virtual bank can satisfy its responsibilities by lending in any lower-income area, the direct community involvement so prized by neighborhood groups will be lost. One possible solution is to provide credit under the Community Reinvestment Act to a virtual bank that establishes operations in a lower-income neighborhood. This would be a logical extension of the credit already afforded to banks that support activities to promote lower-income job creation. Virtual banks that choose not to locate in lower-income areas could adopt a specific lower-income community from which their responsibilities would flow.  WARREN W. TRAIGER Manhattan, July 6  The writer, a principal in the law firm of Butler, Fitzgerald & Potter, advises banks on Community Reinvestment Act issues.

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
A Work in Progress From the Met
body: When the Metropolitan Museum of Art first went on line in October 1995, the site was more a way to encourage its 17 curatorial departments, overseeing some two million works of art, to think creatively about the Internet than to help its more than five million annual museumgoers find their way through one of the world's biggest museums. "It was primarily a way to engage the curators and staff here," said Arthur G. Tisi, the Met's chief information officer. Now the Met is in the midst of a wholesale rethinking of its site, which is not as extensive as sites at other major museums, like the Louvre (Mus'ee du Louvre, http://mistral.culture.fr/louvre/) or the Museum of Modern Art (http://www.moma.org/). During the next six months, the Met wants to find ways to help peoplenavigate through the actual museum when they visit, enhance those visits with information found in the "virtual" Met, and sell products on line from the gift shop and other merchandising operations, Mr. Tisi said. A virtual visit to the Met's American Wing on the Web, for example, might have links to books or other items from the gift shop. So far, the Met's model is the Web site for Federal Express, the package-delivery service (http://www.fedex.com/). "They have a mission and they reflect that mission on the Web," said Mr. Tisi. WHAT YOU SEE -- The present site has a floor map of the museum with links to the collections. Click on European Paintings on the second floor, for example, and there are four paintings with explanatory text. They include Vermeer's "Young Woman with a Water Jug" (early 1660's), with a computer image that can be downloaded from the Web to a viewer's hard drive. Under Education, the site provides a look at recent exhibits that a Web viewer might have missed. It includes "The Private Collection of Edgar Degas," which closed in January, one of the few instances of a first-class artist who was also an art collector of rare verve and breadth of interests. Under "Looking at Art," portraiture is discussed with eight examples, including a 16th-century African pendant mask from the royal court of Benin. The mask's oval face has a decorative band of coral beads, a material so precious it could only be owned by a king, or oba. Around the perimeter of the head and below the chin are the bearded faces of Portuguese traders who were associated with the sea god Olokun because they arrived by sea carrying coral. LINKS -- Scores, under Selected Internet Resources in the page for the Thomas J. Watson Library, the Met's research library of 400,000 books and other documents. The outside links include hundreds of downloadable images of medieval illuminated manuscripts from the Biblioth'eque Nationale de France (http://www.bnf.fr/enluminures/aaccueil.shtm). WHAT YOU GET -- A work in progress. "We're going to continually add functionality," Mr. Tisi said.   ANTHONY RAMIREZ  The Metropolitan Museum of Art http://www.metmuseum.org Graphic   Photo.

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Easy Degrees Proliferate on the Web
body: Ira Doreen Donovan, an elementary school teacher in Miami, was 31 credits shy of a master's degree in special education when she saw an on-line advertisement for Columbia State University. After sending $800 as the first payment on a $2,000 degree, Ms. Donovan received a textbook to summarize and send back for grading. Believing this was the first step of several, she was shocked when shortly after, a certificate not only for a master's but a doctorate arrived at her home. Along with the degrees came transcripts awarding her a 3.9 grade point average for classes never taken and credit for a completed thesis and dissertation. "I called the school and told them if this degree isn't worth the paper it's printed on, I don't want to pay for it," Ms. Donovan said. "This degree mill made me look like a fool." Columbia State returned her money, but others say they have not been so lucky. After investigating 36 complaints, including one from Norway and one from Malaysia, the Louisiana Attorney General's office has filed for a preliminary injunction against Columbia, charging that it violates the state's Unfair Trade Practices Act and consumer protection laws. Last month the State of Illinois also filed suit seeking an injunction and restitution for consumers and the state. Repeated calls to Columbia's office in Metairie, La., seeking comment were not returned. The Internet has "rekindled the old-fashioned diploma mill," said Michael Lambert, the executive director of the Distance Education and Training Council, a recognized accrediting agency that has approved 65 on-line and home-study schools. "The Internet is a haven for these places." Surfing the Web these days is like flipping through a virtual college catalogue. With its interactivity and accessibility, the Internet has sparked new interest in home-study programs, offering actual courses on line or just information. Although many distance-learning schools have solid reputations and graduation requirements, hundreds of Web sites have popped up for schools charging between $200 and $7,000 for sheepskin that requires little or no work from students. Columbia, for instance, promises degrees within 27 days. Elaborate home pages make schools look credible, Mr. Lambert said. The schools can operate in the anonymity of cyberspace, sometimes listing just an email address or post office box. And on line, they can reach a global audience for minimal cost. Eugene Sullivan, co-author with David W. Stewart and Henry Spille of "External Degrees in the Information Age," the American Council on Education's guide to correspondence programs, defines a diploma mill as an "organization that sells degrees without an academic base and without requiring sufficient academic achievement." While perfectly legitimate schools might have an element or two of a diploma mill (say, credit for work experience), experts say there are multiple defining characteristics: * The school emphasizes credit for work or life experience without appropriate mechanisms for assessing that experience in terms of college-level learning. * Degrees are obtained in far less time than would be required at a legitimate institution. (A bachelor's degree typically takes four years of full-time course work, a master's one to two years, a Ph.D. dissertation several years to research and write.) * Tuition and fees are on a per-degree basis instead of per semester or course. * School brochures list faculty members who neither teach nor provide other services, and there is virtually no interaction with faculty members. * The school is not accredited by an agency approved by the Department of Education, the Council for Higher Education Accreditation or other legitimate institutions. Accreditation, however, is voluntary. "From my experience it's not the blatantly fraudulent schools that are the real threat," Mr. Stewart said. "It's the academic frauds that have a little substance that are the problem." He was referring to schools that require students to perform some academic exercises like writing a paper or taking an exam -- and some students might invest considerable effort -- but their degrees are unacceptable to established colleges and universities and unimpressive to prospective employers. But experts admit that most such institutions cater to people who know exactly what they are getting into. "Many people are well aware of what they are doing," Mr. Sullivan said. "They want a credential and they want to get it quickly. But others are busy people or foreign students who don't know much about higher education. They see these places as programs that fit their needs." Joe Joyal of Atlanta said he had worked as an engineer for 20 years without a degree and applied to Columbia State for a joint bachelor's/master's degree in mechanical engineering. He received both degrees in under six months after summarizing two textbooks. He said he suspected the degree was worthless but nonetheless listed it on his resume. Later he had second thoughts and took it off. He is pursuing a degree from an accredited distance-learning program. Columbia State claims in Internet advertising that it is accredited by the International Accrediting Association, a "fictitious school accrediting agency," according to the Louisiana Attorney General's complaint. The owner of Columbia, Ronald Dante, was sentenced in February in Los Angeles to five-and-a-half years in prison for operating fraudulent schools in California. He jumped bail and is being sought by unitedstates marshals, according to Michelle Muth, a spokeswoman for the Federal Trade Commission. Columbia continues to operate. Perhaps the largest crackdown on schools took place from 1981 to 1991, when Operation Dipscam (for diploma scam) put 50 out of business on charges ranging from mail or wire fraud to conspiracy. "Sometimes we'd find phony accreditations or that we were able to negotiate a degree for a lower price," said Allen Ezell, a former agent with the Federal Bureau of Investigation who oversaw Dipscam. "Some schools sent transcripts and diplomas to students for courses never taken." States like newyork and Illinois closely regulate academic institutions, requiring that they be authorized to operate. But many don't. Mr. Ezell said investigations often start by looking into schools incorporated in the states with the weakest laws, like Hawaii, Utah and Louisiana. Hawaii has been wrangling with a few unaccredited schools lately. Its department of consumer affairs has sued Pacific Western and American State Universities, two distance-learning schools with offices there, for not making clear in advertisements that they are unaccredited. After agreeing to a settlement, American State decided to close. "The penalties were too substantial," the school's lawyer, Evan R. Shirley, said, specifically citing the requirement that every ad disclose its unaccredited status. "My client never explicitly expressed wrongdoing," he added, "but a conclusion could be rationally made that there was wrongdoing." Pacific Western's case is pending. Calls to its office and lawyers were not returned, but in answer to the complaint filed in circuit court in Honolulu, it denied allegations that it misleads consumers about its accreditation or suggests it is "somehow accredited or approved by the State of Hawaii to award academic degrees." Another area of dispute that has caused considerable legal wrangling has been the similarity in names between accredited and unaccredited schools. An unaccredited school called Washington University, which has an office in Bryn Mawr, Pa., but is incorporated in Hawaii and the British Virgin Islands, settled a suit in June filed by the more established Washington University of St. Louis. The suit charged that the unaccredited school infringed on its trademark and engaged in unfair competition. The details of the settlement are confidential, but the consent judgment entered by the court told the school to come up with a new name, and one that separated the words "Washington" and "University" with a word of at least 10 characters. Yil Karademir, who owns the unaccredited school, chose Washington International University. (Unaccredited schools tend to favor the word "International," as well as "America," "United" and "Pacific.") The St. Louis school had complained that it had received inquiries from prospective students and alumni who were confused when they saw the other school's ads -- not to mention being the target of protests from human-rights activists after a businessman linked to Myanmar's military dictatorship bought an honorary doctorate. "What they do bears no resemblance to the education we provide," said Lori Fox, the associate general counsel for Washington University in St. Louis. "Are they a diploma mill? You'll have to draw your own conclusions." Mr. Karademir said he is not running a diploma mill. "We are a young university," he said. "We didn't even know about them when we chose the name three years ago. They're not exactly Harvard. Calling us a degree mill is hitting below the belt in order to belittle and discredit us." Mr. Karademir said his school is made up mostly of international students who are given academic credit for life experience, though he plans to add on-line courses in the fall. Washington International's Web site is extensive and promises to grant degrees in one year. "The academic comunity sic find our degree programs to be OUTSTANDING!" the Web site declares. "All Washington International University degrees are ATTESTED and sealed for authenticity by a Government appointed NOTARY!" Costs range from $2,850 for a Bachelor of Science in business administration to $7,400 for a combination bachelor's and master's degree. Meanwhile, the Pennsylvania Department of Education is investigating complaints about the school, according to Michelle Haskins, a department spokeswoman. Last year, the Illinois Attorney General succeeded in shutting down an on-line school, Loyola State University, for violating consumer protection laws by confusing students into thinking it was Loyola University of Chicago. Patricia Kelly, division chief of consumer protection in the Attorney General's office, said that Lorie LaFata, who ran the school, created dummy transcripts with fictional class names, codes and grades. Students would receive diplomas after paying $2,800. "We were able to see she was not offering what she promised," Ms. Kelly said. In her settlement with the Attorney General's office, which had filed suit against her, Ms. LaFata agreed to pay restitution to the state and not to conduct business on the Internet for five years, including having a Web site. "The state and I came to a good understanding," said Ms. LaFata, who offered that she had been a Columbia State student. "I did have to admit to wrongdoing. It was an awful time for me. I hope to leave that behind." Richard Mitchell, president of the New Orleans Better Business Bureau, advises prospective students to do their own investigating before signing up with a distance education school. "Do some intelligent things like checking out a school with agencies that can give you more information," he said. "Don't just jump into a school because they have an impressive Web site. If you take time and do your homework, you can avoid a problem." Mr. Lambert said it was easy for unsophisticated applicants to be fooled. "In mixing dollars and dreams," he said, "it's many of the true innocents that get trampled on."  How to Check School Credentials Surfing the Web for a home-study school? The Department of Education suggests that thr first step is to check a school's accreditation - a process in which courses are reviewed, students surveyed and campuses inspected. For a list of agencies approved to accredit schools, write: Department of Education Accreditation and Eligibility Determination Division, 6000, Independence Ave., S.W., Washington, D.C. 20202-5244; (202) 708-7417; www.ifap.ed.gov/scb.html/agenc.htm. The Council for Higher Education Accreditation, an organization of colleges and universities, also approves accrediting agencies. Write: One Dupont Circle, N.W., Suite 854, Washington, D.C. 20036-1110; (202) 955-6126; www.chea.org. Graphic   Photo: The home pages of two on-line schools that offer quick degrees, left. Ira Doreen Donovan's doctorate.

title:
YOUR HOME;
Visiting Neighborly Web Sites
body: IN times past, residents met in the town square to exchange ideas, information, and the experiences that defined their lives. In the last couple of years, however, a new town meeting place has emerged on home computer screens. It is in the form of electronic bulletin boards, which that provide a focal point for neighborhoods ranging in size from the area around a strip mall to communities defined not by physical boundaries but by the bonds of common interests and ideals. Welcome to the virtual town center of the global virtual village known as the Internet. "What we're seeing now flies in the face of what everyone thought computers were going to do to us," said Kenny Greenberg, the creator of LICWeb (www.licweb.com), an Internet site that provides information and interaction for residents of Long Island City, Queens. "People thought computers were going to isolate us. But the ability to communicate with my neighbors electronically over the Internet has made my life richer instead." Among the free services provided by the site are links to the Long Island City Virtual Mall, where local artists and musicians can post notices of future appearances and businesses and professionals can tack up electronic business cards. There are also on-line tours of Socrates Sculpture Park and of Long Island City by Jack Eichenbaum, a local historian. While the informational portion of the site is clearly useful to residents, Mr. Greenberg said, what was surprising to him was the way local residents immediately responded to the electronic bulletin boards accessible through the site. "I figured the boards would be popular," Mr. Greenberg said. "But they seem to be expanding at an alarming rate." He pointed out that in July alone the site logged more than 30,000 "hits" -- the term used to indicate the number of times visitors visit the site. The most popular bulletin board -- for Queens West, the huge waterfront development site -- accounted for nearly 75 percent of the total visits to the site. Others include a board named "Astoria, Sunnyside, etc.," and one called "Citylights," a board within the Queens West board that is accessible, by means of a password, only to tenants of the first apartment tower on the Queens West site. Another community site accessible from LICWeb via a hyperlink is GoSteinwayStreet (www.gosteinway.com), a site dedicated to a neighborhood surrounding a strip mall in Queens. "The mall itself is seven blocks long but the neighborhood is 17 blocks square," said Zarrar Sheikh, an Astoria, Queens, resident who helped create the site along with Cyberpoint, an Astoria web-design company. Mr. Zarrar said he was in the process of creating a bulletin board for interaction among residents. "Somebody had to represent the area sooner or later," he said. At the other end of the spectrum is "HV/ Net" (www.hvnet.com), a Web site that provides a wide range of information about the towns and hamlets that make up the Hudson Valley, from Westchester to Albany. "HV/Net is a huge site," said Ed Szamborski, president of American Digital, the online service provider that hosts the site on its computers. "It has more than 8,000 pages that cover just about every town in the Hudson Valley." Starting from the HV/Net "front page," visitors can link to pages about historic points of interest in towns along the Hudson River; take virtual tours of Hudson Valley wineries and make reservations in hundreds of hotels, motels, bed-and-breakfasts and small inns throughout the area. In addition to such visitor-type information, the site also provides minutely-detailed information about towns and villages in the valley. Other sites that area residents might find useful include the TownLink Network,(www.townlink.net), which provides information about community organizations and municipal services in most Westchester County towns; and Westchester In Touch(www.co.westchester.ny.us), a site hosted by the Westchester County government itself. "Westchester didn't have many town centers even in the old days," said Norman Jacknis, chief information officer for the county and webmaster for the site.  "So we've made arrangements with the Westchester library system to use their Internet service to make as much information available to the public as we can." The link to the library site provides schedules for local flea markets, farmers' markets, arts and crafts fairs and historic events, Mr. Jacknis said. It also contains information about government services available to county residents. And soon, Mr. Jacknis said, the Westchester In Touch site is expected to provide visitors with access to important documents drafted by the county's Board of Legislators; geographical information, including location and condition of area watersheds and tens of thousands of deeds, mortgages and related documents filed in county offices. "It's the modern way of providing a community service," Mr. Jacknis said. A number of commercial sites offer community services to individuals and groups registered with the site. For example, Interclubs (www.interclubs.com), allows individuals with similar interests to form their own "clubs" and then invite others to join. The site allows for either public or private clubs, with the latter being accessible by a special password given only to those who have been invited to join. Another site, Koz (www.koz.com), also offers public and private "mini-networks," but with an emphasis on community-based information and services. The site allows groups of 50 or less to set up their own "Koz community" free of charge. Larger groups pay a fee for the service. Other sites that provide varying combinations of services to groups -- services like homepage publishing kits, email, chat rooms, bulletin boards, calendar services and online space for group information -- include Xoom (www.xoom.com), GeoCities (www.geocities.com), and a newyork Times web site, newyork Today, (www.nytoday.com). newyork Today provides noncommercial groups the ability to publish events in an online calendar, and is testing a service that would allow community groups to establish mini-networks on the site on which information would be posted that would be accessible only to members. America On-Line (www.aol.com) is also developing plans for a service it calls Hometown AOL, aimed at members with common interests. Those interested in finding out whether there are Internet sites that provide information or community services for residents in their area should enter the name of their county, town or neighborhood -- perhaps adding modifying phrases like "community," or "local government services" -- to limit the number of "hits" returned. The results might be surprising. Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title: Gore Outlines Privacy Measures, but Their Impact Is Small
body: The Clinton Administration announced a new privacy initiative today intended to protect children and medical patients, among others. But while the proposals were ambitious, the Administration can enforce few of them without the consent of Congress or private industry. Calling privacy in the age of electronic commerce "a basic American value" that "must be protected," Vice President Al Gore made public a list of a dozen or so new initiatives that seek to tighten the security of financial and medical records and to protect the privacy of children who use the Internet. Many of the proposals are simply endorsements of bills being considered by Congress. Others require new Congressional action that is, in some cases, uncertain at best. But the Administration chose not to offer any broad new ideas for protecting the privacy of adults on line. Mr. Gore announced instead that, for now, the Administration would leave industry to regulate itself. The Government's privacy rules are of special concern now because the European Union plans to enforce a new electronic privacy program in October and has threatened to stop doing business with companies in other countries that have looser rules. In Congressional testimony earlier this week, Commerce Secretary William M. Daley said the Administration's new proposals would bring the unitedstates into compliance. But some experts in privacy law disagree. The Administration can enforce only a handful of the initiatives proposed today, including two that would tighten the security of medical and banking records. The White House said the Department of Health and Human Services would propose a rule next week to enhance the security of electronic medical records, but offered no details. And Federal bank regulators will strengthen the enforcement of a law that sets limits on how easily banks can share information about their customers and their accounts with related business, like insurance companies, according to a senior Administration official. Many of the other proposals are just that -- ideas that are up to others to implement. For example, Mr. Gore said he wanted to discourage "profiling" -- the practice by some companies of building dossiers on the activities of private citizens using a variety of databases and then using or selling that information to other businesses. "We are working with the Federal Trade Commission to issue a new challenge to companies that use information technology to piece together personal profiles of American citizens and then sell those profiles for profit," the Vice President said. "And here is the message to them: If you don't find a way quickly to effectively regulate your own industry, we will take actions to make you protect the privacy of all Americans." Similarly, the White House urged Congress to pass pending legislation that would enforce criminal penalties for "identity theft" -- stealing someone's Social Security number, credit card numbers or other identifiers and using them to commit a crime, like credit card fraud. Mr. Gore also urged Congress to approve legislation that would forbid companies running sites on the World Wide Web to collect information about children under 13 visiting the sites without permission from their parents. Some experts found few new ideas in the White House initiative. David Sobel, general counsel for the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a private research group based in Washington, said, "We didn't hear much here that we haven't heard before, and the gaping hole in their policy continues to be Internet privacy" for adults. Evan Hendricks, editor of the Privacy Times newsletter, said: "In form and ceremony, it's a great day. But in substance this leaves a lot wanting." Mr. Sobel also said the proposals "still leave us out of step with Europe."

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
France to Sell Up to 30% Of Thomson Multimedia
body: The French Government agreed today to sell as much as 30 percent of Thomson Multimedia, one of Europe's largest consumer electronics makers, to industrial partners including the Microsoft Corporation, which is expected to use the investment to expand its push into delivering Internet services via television. The Government said that Microsoft and the DirecTV unit of the Hughes Electronics Corporation, which is part of General Motors, along with the NEC Corporation of Japan and Alcatel S.A. of France, would each be allowed to buy 7.5 percent of the state-owned Thomson Multimedia, which has been losing money for years. The financial terms of the sale were not disclosed. For Microsoft, the Thomson investment is the latest of several intended to encourage the television industry to adopt its technology for enabling people to tap into the Internet from television sets. Along with the investment, Microsoft will provide Thomson with the software to display text and images from the Internet on television, using Microsoft's Windows CE operating system. And Thomson will license and sell set-top boxes, using Microsoft's WebTV technology, under the Thomson brand in Europe and the RCA brand in the unitedstates. The sale is part of the French Government's efforts to sell state-owned assets to end decades of bailouts and help reduce its budget deficit before the 1999 introduction of the euro, Europe's planned single currency. France tried to sell the unprofitable television maker to the Daewoo Electronics Corporation of South Korea in 1996 but reneged amid protests that it was giving away one of France's industrial jewels. The move comes as Thomson Multimedia, one of the biggest unitedstates color-television makers, battles to return to profitability after years of losses. The company received an 11 billion franc bailout from the state in 1997, helping to make it attractive enough to sell. The parent company, Thomson S.A., traded its medical division and $800 million for RCA consumer electronics, then part of the General Electric Company of the unitedstates, in 1987. "The protocol agreement signed with each of the partners will help reinforce Thomson Multimedia's industrial and marketing strategy," the Government said in a statement. Microsoft has been pushing aggressively to develop interactive television and set standards for the emerging industry. It is moving into enhanced television sets that allow consumers to surf the Internet, receive email and shop. This spring, Microsoft teamed with the Intel Corporation to work on the technology and already offers Internet service on television sets through WebTV. "Microsoft is betting that the TV set and the computer will meld together over time into one instrument that provides the consumer with all his communications needs," Frederick Moran, an analyst at ING Barings Furman Selz, said. Thomson S.A. also owns the state's stake in Thomson-CSF, Europe's biggest military electronics business. Microsoft's chairman, William H. Gates, agreed during a visit in February to work with the French Government to find ways to cooperate on research and promote the use of the Internet in France.

title: Anyone Can Dial In for Your Dollars
body: TO most people, few things are more private than their money -- how much they have and where they keep it. But with only the help of a touch-tone telephone, just about anyone can learn the approximate balance of a checking account at some banks. Using a decades-old system reserved for small businesses, called merchant check verification, someone with enough curiosity and determination can simply call a bank's customer service line, put in the customer account number printed at the bottom of a check and enter a dollar amount. (Some banks require a check number, as well; some don't.) The system tells the caller whether the amount is in the account. After a half-dozen or so inquiries involving different amounts, a caller can learn approximately how much money is in the account. A sampling of a handful of banks, with the consent of the accounts' owners, proved how easy it was to do. The automated system at Chase Bank, for example, asks for a check number, but from there it was easy to guess other check numbers and request verification of other amounts. Within a few minutes, it was learned roughly how much money was in the account. Bank of America's merchant check-verification system was equally easy to manipulate, as was that of Wells Fargo Bank. It proved more difficult to get the same information through the merchant check services of a credit union because a customer representative handled the call. To some privacy rights advocates, automated check-verification practices are just one example of a system in dire need of better controls. One concern is that manipulating such a system will become even easier as banks move more of their consumer operations on line. Eventually, someone could conceivably write a program to check the balance of an account automatically. "I find it quite bothersome because how much money you have is one of the most private things," said Brad Templeton, a board member of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a civil liberties group based in San Francisco. "And then to find out it's not really a secret at all." Edmund Mierzwinski, consumer program director for the unitedstates Public Interest Research Group, a consumer watchdog group based in Washington, said he thought that merchant check-verification systems could add better controls, like automatically shutting down after someone made more than one entry. "Certainly, companies have the right to reduce their risk," Mr. Mierzwinski said. "But it should be a 'go/no go' thing." Not all privacy advocates view the merchant check system with alarm. Marc Rotenberg, director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a privacy rights group in Washington, said he thought that the system adequately protected privacy rights because it gave merchants the least amount of information available. Trying to manipulate it by putting in multiple check numbers, he said, was "a little like trying all possible combinations on a lock on a suitcase." A spokesman for Wells Fargo Bank in San Francisco said that its phone-in system was being replaced by point-of-sale technology that automated the check-verification process. In the meantime, he said, the bank is not aware of misuse of the system, which it has used in some form for nearly 20 years. Others, however, say the current state of check-verification systems illustrates the need for better privacy controls in banking. "That's just one of the flaws in the banking system," Mr. Mierzwinski said. "This is where things are headed."

title: Forget Joyce; Bring on Ayn Rand
body: LITERATURE has certainly come a long way since it really mattered. Consider the example of the Modern Library, which recently published its list of the 100 best English-language novels of the 20th century, starting with James Joyce's "Ulysses" at No. 1 and ending with Booth Tarkington's "The Magnificent Ambersons" at No. 100. Forty years ago, critics and intellectuals would have dismissed a list like this one as a cheap marketing ploy. Today, critics celebrate the marketing smarts behind the Modern Library list but confess that they cannot be bothered to read the great works anymore. Once, we loved literature and scoffed at the list; now, we love the list and laugh at "Ulysses." The Modern Library list has uncovered one place, apparently, where books still matter, and that is the Internet. Concurrent with its publication of the list, Random House, Modern Library's parent company, established a readers' poll, where on-line visitors could vote for their favorite works of fiction at www.randomhouse.com/modernlibrary/ 100best. If the Modern Library list represents the middlebrow sensibility, the poll, which runs until September, gives a snapshot of the literary tastes of the on-line community, what could be called netbrow. As might be expected, the poll has yielded a few predictable trends, like a predilection for science fiction and fantasy, a bizarre affection for Ayn Rand, who has four books in the top 30, including "Atlas Shrugged" at No. 1, and a few mysteries, like who is Charles de Lint and how did he get four books among the top 50? But the readers' poll does have its virtues, especially when placed beside the Modern Library list. Readers who also use the Internet, for example, seem less afraid of experimental fiction, like Thomas Pynchon's "Gravity's Rainbow" (No. 8) and less ashamed of big, historical crowd pleasers like "Gone With the Wind" (No. 48) and "Bonfire of the Vanities" (No. 95), all of which failed to make the Modern Library list. While most of the Modern Library entries were written before 1950, many readers' poll books were written in the last 20 years. Only nine of the Modern Library books were written by women. The readers' poll list, helped along by Ayn Rand, has 24. The Modern Library list has also been attacked for being too American. The Internet list is, if anything, too Canadian, with books by Margaret Atwood, Robertson Davies, various Tek War novelizations from the Modern Library reject William Shatner and the four entries from Charles de Lint who, it turns out, lives in Ottawa. And the readers' poll, however its voting may be stacked, is free of the taint of self-interest. The Modern Library, after all, has published many of the titles on its list and would like to sell more. The bulk of the readers' list could be bought at the local 7-11. The real sport of the readers' poll site is found in the forum, where readers defend their choices, attack other people's choices and murmur darkly about Random House's attempt to filter out votes for Howard Stern. (An unsuccessful attempt, apparently: "Private Parts" was as high as No. 20 at one point.) In the forum is the kind of passion for literature that Random House must have hoped to inspire with its Modern Library list. Internet readers tend to be cranky, argumentative, a little perverse and full of resentment toward the crushing weight of history and good taste -- the attributes that were once ascribed to modern literature.
