title: Senate's Internet Legislation Under Fire
body: By the beginning of July, a number of the Internet bills had been languishing in Congress for months, their sponsors unable to muster the necessary support for floor debates on what could become precedent-setting laws covering free speech and content in the digital age. Then one-by-one, in a three-day period last week, the proposals were quietly attached to a Senate appropriations bills, in most cases without debate. Although the bills must still pass the House and make it through a conference committee to become law, civil liberties groups are crying foul, questioning whether senators understand or gave responsible consideration to complicated issues that could have long-term impacts on the global network. It started on Tuesday when Senator John McCain, the Arizona Republican who is chairman of the Com merce, Science and Transportation Committee, offered as an amendment to the $33 billion spending plan for the Departments of Commerce, State and Justice a bill requiring filtering software on computers in schools and libraries that get Federal funds for Internet hookups. Attached to that was a measure that has been dubbed the Communications Decency Act II, a bill by Senator Daniel R. Coats, Republican of Indiana, that would make it a crime for commercial Web sites to distribute or display to minors any material that could be "harmful" to children. The original Communications Decency Act, which outlawed the general distribution of material harmful to minors, was struck down last year as unconstitutional. Then on Wednesday came an amendment by Senator Lauch Faircloth, a North Carolina Republican, to give the Federal Bureau of Investigation access to the customer records of Internet Service Providers in investigations of pedophilia without an order from a court or grand jury. Finally, on Thursday, another Arizona Republican, Senator Jon Kyl, added a bill that would ban gambling on the Internet, in part, Senator Kyl argued, because Internet gambling is "accessible by minors." While all the bills are presented as measures for protecting children, opponents argue that they raise complicated free speech, privacy, censorship and regulatory questions that could have long-term impacts on civil liberties. "The technology is racing ahead of policy makers, and the policy makers are stumbling to catch up," said Ron Weich, legislative consultant to the American Civil Liberties Union. "The Congress has not begun to consider the important constitutional and practical considerations of these bills." Senator Kyl's gambling bill was the only one of the Internet bills debated on the floor. Although Mr. Weich criticized the process as sloppy legislating, Mark Buse, policy director for the Commerce Committee, defended the procedure. Senator McCain, he said, had been working for weeks to get his bill scheduled for floor debate. "There were certain Democrats fronting for the A.C.L.U. who would not allow us to bring the bill up for debate," Mr. Buse said. "We had no choice but to offer it as an amendment." Lisa Dean, director of the Center for Technology Policy at the Free Congress Foundation, said Republican lawmakers were"dealing with a medium here that defies control, and they are trying to control it."She said of the gambling bill, for example: "It sets a precedent to restrict other habits later on. "Whether or not you are in favor of gambling is immaterial." Civil liberties advocates have vowed a court fight, if necessary, over the constitutionality of both the Coats and the McCain bills. The Coats bill, they say, would unconstitutionally restrict free speech on the Internet. They oppose filtering mandates because the software often blocks Web pages that provide information on subjects like AIDS, breast cancer, even debates on free speech issues. Dave Farber, a professor of computer science at the University of Pennsylvania and a board member of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, said that Congress was in a panic, passing bills on issues they did not understand or that they know will eventually be struck down as unconstitutional. "It is an election year coming up, and let's be kind and say they like to put on a good face to their community, even if they do things that damage their community in the long run, which these do," he said. "But there are nicer ways to protect our children than doing things that take away their rights when they grow up."

title:
Shopping for Toys Without the Kids;
Virtual Stores Give the Big Retailers A Foothold Against On-Line Upstarts
body: First virtual toys, now virtual toy stores. With toy makers and sellers catching up with the computer age and making a big push into Internet retailing, shoppers can now buy everything on line -- from Tamagotchi virtual pets to Teletubbies plush dolls. The hope is that these stores-without-walls will attract parents with modems and motivation, people either too busy or too impatient to deal with the big chain stores' huge, warehouse-like retail outlets. So, well ahead of the 1998 critical year-end selling season, toy companies are racing to become the Amazon.com of their industry. Some of the on-line players include Noodle Kidoodle Inc., Toys "R" Us and the leading upstart company, Etoys, a unit of Idealab. Some manufacturers, including Mattel Inc., which has a Barbie Web site, www.barbie.com, are also experimenting with on-line marketing. Having had one of its best years in a decade last year, thanks to a healthy economy, and hoping for a repeat performance this year, the toy industry is in an expansive, experimental mood. Though on-line retailing still accounts for only $13 million of the $22 billion annual unitedstates toy market, the virtual toy shop is the industry's attempt to find new or additional sales among the households that are most likely to value time-saving efficiency and to have the discretionary income to pay a premium for such convenience. Nearly 20 million Americans now shop on line, according to the Web measurement company Media Metrix Inc. But the industry's move on line is not without risk. The big retailers face the same sort of internal conflicts that the bookseller Barnes & Noble does in trying to counter Amazon.com -- how to respond to the on-line upstarts without cannibalizing the brick-and-mortar franchise. Toy makers must venture carefully into cyberspace, lest their direct-sales activities rankle the retailers they rely upon to move their merchandise. For their part, the on-line upstarts, despite the cost advantages of not having to invest in stores, warehouses and big inventories, may find themselves struggling to match the marketing muscle of big established retail brand names. Then there is the question of whether the touch and the texture of toy shopping can translate as readily to the digital realm as some other consumer activities that have taken hold on line, like booking airline seats or trading shares of stock. "One of the big strengths of toy retailing is the in-store excitement, merchandising and the personal touch," said Frank Reysen Jr., editor of Playthings, a toy industry publication. "There is a danger of that getting lost in the web of technology. The initiatives, attitude and approach have to be a virtual representation of the store itself, and that's not an easy thing to do." The toy merchants are undaunted, though. The large retailers say they will win the Internet game because their well-regarded names and vast resources give them an in with consumers that should spill over into on-line selling. For customers, the companies say, those strengths will translate into low prices, quick response to orders and a better chance of finding limited-edition items -- like Mattel's popular Share a Smile Becky doll, a wheelchair-bound friend of Barbie -- that smaller toy sellers may have trouble obtaining in large volume. But the small, niche operators say they have the upper hand because they offer many of the must-have items and also specialty products -- like Schylling's make-your-own chewing gum kit -- that tend to sell in such small numbers that the big guys find them not worth stocking. And whether large or small, the companies say they can offer on-line consumers the advantage of not having to traipse around in search of the last Beanie Baby in town. Longer term, toy merchants envision that this type of retailing will become the modern equivalent of that more traditional form of direct-to-consumer marketing -- catalogue shopping. Like catalogue sales, which rely on mailing lists assembled from consumers' past buy-by-mail habits, the data bases created by electronic commerce would enable toy makers to observe the shopping habits of computerized households and use discounts and other enticements to keep them coming back for more. It is a way for merchants to get to know their customers' preferences to an extent not possible when a person goes into a store and pays cash for a Sing and Snore Ernie. All of the industry's behind-the-scenes strategizing for her money and loyalty is just fine by Chana Wilson, a housewife and mother of two boys, ages 3 and 12, who was in the market recently for an ant farm for her out-of-state nephew. "I knew I had to buy a toy, wrap it up and ship it to Houston," said Mrs. Wilson, who lives in Beckley, W.Va., and ranks shopping at toy stores right up there with visiting the dentist. Trying to avoid "all that rigamarole," Mrs. Wilson, whose husband, Derric, is a supervisor at a prison, went on line and found Etoys, where she bought an Uncle Milton ant farm for $19.95 plus $4 for shipping and $3 for gift wrapping. "That saved me time and money and a major headache with my 3-year-old," Mrs. Wilson said. "You just don't want to take a 3-year-old shopping for other kids' toys." It is just this sort of shopper that the big conventional retailers are going after. Toys "R" Us, the nation's largest toy retailer, started a Web site last month that it intends to heavily advertise on the Internet as well as on television and through home delivery circulars later this year. So far, the site has about 2,000 items, compared with about 15,000 stocked in Toys "R" Us stores. Tens of thousands of Internet users have already visited the site, though the company declined to say how many had bought anything. Visitors to www.toysrus.com, are assured that shopping is "fun and fast." Say, for instance, someone is clueless as to what to buy an 8-year-old girl. The shopper need only choose a category, like dolls, click on the child's age and the target price. Seconds later a suggested list of merchandise appears, including Baby Pick Me Up, which sells for $14.97 plus shipping and handling. Just like a theater operator who tries to drum up concession sales by piping in the smell of freshly popped corn, Toys "R" Us is using its personalized suggestion feature also to get shoppers to consider buying items they may not have intended to. Those looking for dolls, for instance, are also shown a Barbie Disc Girl CD Player for $16.99. Call it an electronic hard sell. Prices are typically the same for toys bought on line or in stores. But the convenience of Internet shopping does mean having to pay shipping rates, which are about $5 for a $25 order and around $9 for a $100 purchase. The companies insist, though, that the cost is more than worth the convenience. "People are more strapped for time, and they are looking for new ways of shopping," said Joel Anderson, vice president of Toys "R" Us Direct. "There is a new medium out there that is emerging, and it is an area we need to be in." The toy maker Hasbro Inc. is feeling the same need. The company, which has been dabbling in on-line product marketing for more than a year, recently hired a specialist in Internet commerce to develop a plan to advertise further and sell selected items like collectibles directly to the consumer (www.hasbro.com). The executive, Wendy Riches, had managed the interactive advertising unit of WPP Group's Ogilvy & Mather agency, as part of her role as chairman and chief executive of the Ogilvy One North America division. One potential problem is that Hasbro sells mainly to retailers, some of whom may frown on any form of added competition. This sort of conflict has also been a problem for computer makers, like Compaq, which has a well-established network of distributors who have been wary of the company's plan to expand into on-line direct sales. Already, some toy retailers are raising concern about Hasbro's intentions. "This is the manufacturer cutting out the middle man," said Shane Igoe, new media manager at F.A.O. Schwarz, which was one of the first toy sellers to go on line when it started www.faoschwarz.com nearly two years ago. Toys "R" Us is less concerned, saying Hasbro's Internet appeal will be limited because it will offer only its own brands and not Barbie, Beanie Babies and other popular toys made by its competitors. For its part, Hasbro says its on-line selling efforts are not meant to put it in competition with Toys "R" Us or any other retailer. Rather, the company says, it is seeking to augment what retailers are already doing, even listing store locations where shoppers can find certain items. "We look at this as a partnership with the retail trade," said Adam Klein, Hasbro's head of global marketing. "Each one of our key retailers is going at this thing a different way. We have to have our own in-house expertise to both work with them and, where there are gaps, to be able to recognize them and go after these opportunities." Hasbro also says that, at least initially, it will limit its toy selling to items not available in retail stores. The company, which has not determined when it will begin selling on line beyond the interactive products like the Yahtzee CD-ROM it already offers, was fuzzy on whether consumers would have to pay retail prices for toys bought directly from the manufacturer. Mr. Klein said only that "the idea is not to compete with the retail trade, and this is part of everything we are going to be looking at." With Hasbro and other industry giants edging in on its domain, Etoys, a year-old company based in Santa Monica, Calif., that has about 3,000 items listed for sale on its site, www.toys.com, may need a Star Wars laser to fend them off. But the company says its strength is in the range of playthings it provides. "What we do is have the popular products and also have a lot of cool products like kits to make your own chewing gum, products you never see in Toys 'R' Us," said Toby Lenk, chief executive of Etoys. "A big retail buyer can't buy six of something. It's too inefficient for them so they buy in bulk and can't test on a smaller scale." Etoys also knows it will have to rev up its marketing machine to avoid getting overshadowed by the competition. Without discussing precise amounts, the company said it planned to triple its multimillion-dollar marketing budget for the next six months. If people like Mrs. Wilson, the mother in West Virginia, are any indication, the on-line toy market is up for grabs to anyone who can make toy shopping effortless without significantly adding cost. But won't she miss an intrinsic part of the toy-buying experience by buying a lovable baby doll without first giving it a squeeze or without reading product information on a box of building blocks? "Heavens, no," Mrs. Wilson said. "I could care less. I already know what a box of Legos looks like. I wish I'd found this before last Christmas." Graphic   Photos: (Frank C. Dougherty for The New York Times)(pg. D1); The leading upstart on-line toy company, Etoys, a unit of Idealab, features a page on Barbie dolls and other types of dolls on its Web site. (pg. D2)

title:
Technology;
As Web search engines mutate into portal sites, the idea is to get and keep your selective attention.
body: INTERNET business models, like the technologies that drive them, mutate faster than a flu virus. A case in point: the "portal," a scheme whereby a handful of mostly money-losing enterprises band together to form a mega-Web site that combines searching, content, email, chat and other services. The portal, its defenders insist, is a whole greater than the sum of its parts because people who come for one service will discover another and stick around. Advertisers and investors have demonstrated that they love this sort of reasoning. Still, the logic of the portal concept is lost on some. For one thing, there are amusing contradictions to the portal fad. Not the least of these is the spectacle of hundreds of new-media geeks who spent years painting America Online as the trailer park of cyberspace now scrambling desperately to be . . . well, America Online, the original, and some would say, only authentic portal. Beyond simply creating a hip version of America Online, the idea is to make the portal site so enticing that World Wide Web users will make it their first stop and so seductive that they will not want to stray elsewhere. Among the first to be seduced were Wall Street and a few big media companies. All told, many billions of dollars have been invested in enterprises that with two notable exceptions have yet to make a profit. Why? Because advertisers have been drawn to portals at a level that defies all reason. According to "The Great Portal Shakeout," a recent report by Forrester Research, the top nine portals -- those of Alta Vista, America Online, Excite, Infoseek, Lycos, Microsoft, Netscape, Snap and Yahoo -- account for a mere 15 percent of all Internet traffic. Yet they attract 59 percent of all advertising revenue on the Internet, an extraordinary 293 percent premium. Network television, in contrast, attracts 67 percent of all viewers and 84 percent of advertising, for a 25 percent premium. Yet despite this enormous bonus, only the two largest portals, America Online and Yahoo, have so far managed to eke out a net income. This reality, said Chris Charron, the analyst who was the lead author of the Forrester report, makes the infant portal industry ripe for a shakeout that will leave only three or four winners dividing at most 20 percent of Internet traffic by 2002. "Something has to give," Mr. Charron said. "The pie is advertising, and the pie that's available, we think, will be $8 billion in five years, with 30 percent of that going to portals -- about $2.4 billion." And of that $2.4 billion, he added, "AOL and Yahoo will grab half." The business concept is simple on its face: If you can stuff enough services and content into a single Web address, you will, in the ugly parlance of the industry, "aggregate eyeballs" -- that is, bring a lot of people with disparate interests and needs to the same place so that the owners of the portal site can sell advertising priced on a certain dollar amount for every 1,000 pages viewed. If this algorithm seems vaguely familiar, it may be because it is the basic programming plan of network television. And that is precisely the problem, said Michael Wolff, whose book "Burn Rate" (Simon & Schuster, 1998) chronicles the origins and quixotic meanderings of many of the companies that are now either portals or the anchor tenants of portals. While a television audience is attracted to a network by the program playing at any given moment, when it comes to a portal, Mr. Wolff argues, "there really is no natural reason why the audience is there." Except, of course, to get somewhere else. "The audience isn't there for unique content or for a partiality to the experience or really for any self-selected reason," he said. "You are there for the same reason you might find yourself on a highway interchange or in an airport." How would the same people who have enthusiastically invested in a portal react if the Department of Transportation were to design a huge Federal highway interchange with the sole objective of having drivers continuously circle a row of billboards? Yet such a comparison is not all that far-fetched. Cyberspace is its own reality. Even so, following the why-am-I-here question to its logical answer suggests that the true essence of a portal is a sort of parlor-trick illusion. The anchor tenant of each of the portals is what used to be known as a search engine or Internet directory service. These services -- Yahoo, Excite, Infoseek, etc. -- were designed to do one thing: help people find what they are looking for on the Web. To various degrees and in different ways, they all do this well. But the metamorphosis from search engine to portal is something of a paradox, since one is the antithesis of the other. Search engines are intended to point you to your desired destination in the increasingly complex terrain of cyberspace. Now, they are becoming tools in a scheme to keep you in one place. If you actually go where they point you, some other site may get your attention and the few micro-cents your attention is worth. In the words of another Forrester analyst, Kate Delhayn, "Most portals have transitioned from intersections on the Internet to sticking points." Obviously, most consumers will not appreciate the discovery that someone has lined the hallway with flypaper. So the portal has to keep up at least the illusion of movement. It continues to send users to a destination just as before. Only now, the deck is stacked in favor of destinations that are owned by the portal itself or by its partners or advertisers -- at least, there is very real danger that consumers will perceive things that way. "Once a portal becomes captive to any one source of content, or is perceived to be captive -- Snap, for example, being seen simply as an outlet for NBC to the exclusion of other content -- it runs the risk of turning away consumers who are looking for an open gateway to the Internet," Mr. Charron warned. Which, he is quick to point out, is just about everyone. Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
3 Advertisers Select Agencies for Accounts
body: hree advertisers have named agencies to handle accounts after reviews in which the other participants were not disclosed. Hotbot, the Internet search engine owned by Wired Digital, named Goodby, Silverstein & Partners in San Francisco as the first agency to create a local and national brand-building campaign in traditional media, which is intended to broaden Hotbot users beyond "Webheads" to a wider audience. Andrew de Vries, marketing communications director at Wired Digital in San Francisco, said an initial campaign would begin in early October, adding that spending in the first year was planned at $10 million to $15 million. Goodby, Silverstein, part of Omnicom Group, was chosen after an informal review, Mr. de Vries said. The on-line component of the adver tising would be created in-house using material from the Goodby, Silverstein campaign, he added. The Aon Corporation, an insurance services company in Chicago, named McCann-Erickson Worldwide Advertising in newyork as the first agency to handle worldwide advertising. Billings were estimated at $10 million. McCann, part of the McCann-Erickson World Group unit of the Interpublic Group of Companies, was awarded the account after a two-month review. And Madison Square Garden Networks, which includes the MSG network and Fox Sports newyork, selected Kirshenbaum Bond & Partners in newyork to handle its integrated advertising and branding account, which had been handled by various agencies on a project basis. Billings were not disclosed. Kirshenbaum Bond was awarded the account after a brief, informal review. Madison Square Garden Networks in newyork, part of Madison Square Garden L.P., is majority owned by the Cablevision Systems Corporation.

title: High Tech for Elderly
body: SOME graduates at the Fairview Greenburgh Community Center are seniors in more ways than one. They are older than 55 and members of Seniornet, a national nonprofit computer training organization that teaches computer technology and the Internet to more than 23,000 older people a year. But like graduates everywhere, each has a different reason for choosing to take the 8-week, 16-hour course at the center. Betty Flanagan, a retired social worker at the Blythedale Children's Hospital in White Plains, received a computer as an 80th birthday gift. Explaining why she was learning what she called a "terrifying machine," she quoted from Oliver Wendell Holmes, "It is required of a man that he should share the action and passion of his time at peril of being judged not to have lived." Al Goldstein, 71, of Tuckahoe, a mechanical engineer who says he still does some work, wants to use a computer-aided design program, which will enable him to see changes made by architects. Stanley Fensterman, 78, of North White Plains, a retired accountant for the Internal Revenue Service, plans to use the computer to keep current financial records and make stock transactions. Ruth Fensterman, 68, his wife and fellow student, foresees using her new knowledge to keep the financial records of her Hadassah organization electronically instead of manually. Using the Internet is a goal of all who want to stay in touch through email and do any research. The programs for the elderly in the Greenburgh-White Plains area and Ossining were set up largely by two companies, Bell Atlantic of Valhalla and International Business Machines of Armonk. The companies contributed funds for the program, provided the computers and chose the sites. They also contacted retirees to find teachers and coaches.  Aided also by support from the towns in which the centers are situated, the county and private philanthropy, the program participants pay $30 for their course plus $35 to join Seniornet. That organization provides a curriculum, which "takes the mystique out of computer technology," said Rai Cockfield, vice president for market development at I.B.M. Older people are a logical choice for intensive computer training since most completed their education before computers were widely used. In their personal lives, too, they have managed for more than 55 years without a computer, but, as Richard P. Biondi, regional director for public affairs at Bell Atlantic, observed: "More and more in our everyday life we're asked to convey information via the computer. Some people can no longer use a pen or pencil because of rheumatism. They have to learn to adopt and adapt to new technology." Michael Negrelli of Yorktown Heights, a volunteer who shares coordinating and teaching computer technology at the Town of Ossining Senior Center with Marian Picarelli of Ossining, said, "As a senior, too, I know the most frustrating thing can be a brilliant young person who does things so quickly mature adults can't learn from him." And there are many things that are completely new, like using a mouse. Bill Langenstein of South Salem, who is co-coordinator with Barbara Niles of Hartsdale of the Seniornet program at the Greenburgh center, said that his students often have initial difficulty using a mouse because of a lack of dexterity, but once they practice, they are able to use it efficiently. Despite any physical limitations and a tendency to feel intimidated by the new technology, the elderly have shown enthusiasm for joining the programs. Almost 250 people have called the Fairview Greenburgh Community Center about the Seniornet course. They are admitted first come first served, and so far 40 have graduated from the course in which 11 computers are available. A graduation ceremony for a class of 11 students found the participants reluctant to turn off their machines for the presentation of computer-generated certificates of completion. "Diplomas," which were wrapped and rolled and tied with a ribbon to resemble scrolls, were actually guides on how to buy a computer. Elderly people who are computer literate are a growing market, and Seniornet offers a special package at reduced cost, including an I.B.M. computer, to its members. At the Town of Ossining Senior Center, Fran Anderson, the director, said she considered her center "lucky to have been chosen" as a site for the program from which 54 have graduated. That program has been increased to 14 hours of instruction. People older than 55 interested in taking courses and individuals who wish to volunteer may call Mrs. Anderson at 762-8953, Mr. Langenstein at 763-5190 or Ms. Niles at 761-3911. Graphic   Photo: Hope Williams at computer at Fairview Greenburgh Community Center. (Richard Harbus for The newyork Times)

title: Net Worth
body: Burn Rate How I Survived the Gold Rush Years on the Internet. By Michael Wolff. 268 pp. newyork: Simon & Schuster. $25. Few Americans who have witnessed the riches to be made from the Internet can be immune to the thought that they, too, could wake up one morning and be worth tens, even hundreds, of millions of dollars. Particularly following the Netscape Communications Corporation's initial public offering, which saw the browser company's stock more than double on the day trading started, it all looks so easy: come up with an idea, cobble together a business plan, attract investors, stir up a frenzy on Wall Street and watch the market react. In "Burn Rate: How I Survived the Gold Rush Years on the Internet," Michael Wolff, a journalist and the founder of Wolff New Media, chronicles his relatively brief flirtation with great wealth. Ostensibly, "Burn Rate" is the story of Wolff's search for capital to keep his small company afloat. The title refers to a term venture capitalists use to describe the amount of money a start-up is spending in excess of revenues. Wolff New Media was apparently in the business of what the Net community calls "content," in the form of books and a Web site, although Wolff remains curiously vague about its daily operations. Then again, it hardly seems to matter, as Wolff's own, rather vanilla start-up is only the vehicle for telling a larger, far more interesting story about what makes the Internet industry and those who invest in it tick. The narrative follows a series of meetings, with the occasional business-class flight thrown in for good measure. In less capable hands, such a book would hold little appeal for the average reader. But Wolff, a nimble writer with a knack for spotting colorful details, moves the story along at movie-of-the-week pace. Wolff started his Internet adventure in the early 1990's, and in 1994 he published "Net Guide," a book about interesting spots on the Internet, just before the World Wide Web popularized the Net beyond anyone's imagination. Three years later, Wolff's company had expanded almost twentyfold. At the same time, its burn rate was more than half a million dollars a month. Wolff, who possesses something of an anti-Midas touch, was desperate for solid investment. Ameritech, the regional telephone company, was interested at one point, as was the Washington Post Company, but those prospects and others fell through. Wolff handles the material deftly. In the process of telling his own story, he adroitly drops in gossipy tidbits about other, better-known Net figures: Louis Rossetto and Jane Metcalfe, the founders of Wired magazine, whom Wolff met in Amsterdam when both were still unknown, starry-eyed expatriates; Walter Isaacson, now the managing editor of Time, who started Pathfinder, Time Warner's Web site; and Robert Maxwell's children, who ventured into the Internet business with a search engine company called Magellan. Wolff makes it clear that in this business principles are often cast to the wind. And he himself is no exception. The most astonishing illustration of this comes halfway through the book, when he and his lawyer, Alison Anthoine, who is also his wife, strike a lucrative deal with a computer magazine publisher whose executives are so eager for a slice of the Internet action that they fail to see that they are paying handsomely for what amounts to nothing. Wolff and Anthoine are only slightly contrite at their caper. In fact, they seem to congratulate themselves for having got away with something so bold. Wolff also gives an incredible account of negotiations with America Online, and with one anonymous AOL executive in particular, who strings him along with promises of substantial investment and partnership. Wolff calls AOL "the most dysfunctional company in America." After a series of bizarre meetings and endless promises from the AOL executive, the deal evaporates. Wolff spares no feelings. He casts such an unforgiving eye on the people around him that his tone often smacks of vendetta. He depicts his cohorts as fakes and blowhards, arrogant and clueless. He is locked in a hate-hate relationship with one of his main investors, who Wolff believes is out to double-cross him. Wolff portrays his partner as a wealthy, simpering venture capitalist wannabe, and makes disagreeable sport of deceiving him. It is this dark figure who eventually strips Wolff of control of his own company. Wolff describes the Internet business as founded on nothing but bravado and lies. "Mendacity is a system that we live in" were Brick's words in "Cat on a Hot Tin Roof," but they suit the world Wolff describes to a T. Contrary to his assertions, however, the fact is that many of the people in this industry, like those in any other, are honest, straightforward and hard-working. But acknowledging such a thing would introduce shades of gray into a tale that Wolff seems intent on telling as black and white. SOME of Wolff's most trenchant observations come tacked onto the end of a vignette, almost as an afterthought. Of one fellow floundering entrepreneur whom Wolff watches make the fatal error of admitting to a group of investors that he will not be able to meet his next week's payroll, Wolff writes, "And while that was true of his business and of every other business in the new Internet industry and while everybody knew it was true -- that is, that cash was just being consumed at a rate and with an illogic that no one could explain, much less justify -- you must never, never admit it." Therein lies the genuinely unsettling truth about the Internet, which "Burn Rate" lays bare. Mind-boggling sums have been sunk into start-ups, many of which have had hugely successful public stock offerings. At the same time, few have actually succeeded in generating substantial revenues. Still fewer have managed to turn a profit. Ultimately, Wolff failed as an entrepreneur. He left a stack of unpaid bills behind. One of his three public relations companies sued him to recover the money. He now writes a column in The Industry Standard, a new business magazine focusing on the Internet, in which he rails against the industry, including the public relations firms that did not get him sufficient ink. So Wolff has gone out and produced some ink of his own.

title:
SPENDING IT: FOCUS ON AIR TRAVEL;
Name That Fare! (And Other On-Line Challenges for Travelers)
body: JUST because August is around the corner and you still haven't planned your summer vacation, don't despair. The Internet can help book a quick -- even bargain-priced -- getaway. Priceline.com has generated a big buzz since its start-up in April, when it kicked off a multimillion-dollar advertising campaign, promoting a "name your own price" service for buying discounted plane tickets. Priceline's on-line auction, though, is only one of the most recent additions to the Internet's fare deals. Depending on how nimble a traveler you are -- and how much inconvenience you can endure -- various travel opportunities are only a click away. Each week, the World Wide Web sites of individual airlines post deeply discounted fares for travel that weekend. Other sites gather and update information on inexpensive fares from several sources. Still, Priceline has made a sizable impression in a relatively short time. Jay Walker, chairman of the company, based in Stamford, Conn., said it had already sold 40,000 tickets, generating revenues of more than $10 million. Though Priceline has satisfied some customers, its lengthy list of requirements has frustrated others. And most major domestic airlines do not cooperate with the service, since they promote their own specials on line to fill their empty seats; this limits Priceline's offerings. To use the service, customers make a ticket request on its Web site, saying where and when they want to travel and how much they are willing to pay. (Travelers without Internet access can bid by phone.) If a bid is much lower than published fares, it will be rejected. To determine a reasonable price, customers should research the standard range of fares on the desired route. Once a bid is submitted, Priceline sorts through the airline seats at its disposal. It says it can notify customers within an hour whether a bid for a domestic flight has been accepted or rejected -- 24 hours for international flights. In submitting bids, customers also provide their credit card information. If a bid is accepted, a ticket is automatically issued and the credit card is billed; if the bid is rejected, travelers can submit other bids using different airports or different dates, but cannot re-bid with higher amounts using the same itinerary. There are other restrictions: tickets are not refundable or exchangeable and are not eligible for frequent-flier miles. Priceline's services are free for travelers using electronic tickets, which are generally available only on domestic flights; if travelers require a paper ticket, they pay a $12.50 overnight delivery fee. And those are just the rules for getting tickets. The flights themselves may challenge an individual's notion of ease and comfort. Travelers must be willing to leave anytime between 6 A.M. and 10 P.M. on their selected date if flying domestically, or any time if flying overseas. Flights may also require a stop or a connection en route. A potentially bigger obstacle is that the auction site seems to have the cooperation of only a few domestic airlines. Eight of the 10 major unitedstates airlines -- Alaska, American, Continental, Delta, Northwest, Southwest, United and U S Airways -- say they have chosen not to work with Priceline. The other two -- America West and Trans World Airlines -- declined to comment, though industry executives say they do work with the service. That is not to say you can't get tickets on the major carriers through Priceline's auctions. As a licensed travel agency, the company offers discounted seats on major airlines through the Worldspan computerized reservations system and its inventory; Priceline also sometimes resells the wholesale seats offered by consolidators. Mr. Walker, though, said that less than 5 percent of the tickets Priceline sells are through Worldspan or consolidators. Mr. Walker declined to identify which major unitedstates carriers worked with his company, saying only that a total of 15 unitedstates and international airlines are offering Priceline seats to sell. The limits on inventory can stymie bidders, as Michael Spohn, a 21-year-old student at the University of Missouri, has discovered. Since late May, Mr. Spohn, an intern in the retail advertising department of The Des Moines Register, has placed bids with Priceline nine times to fly from Omaha, Des Moines or Cedar Rapids, Iowa, to his hometown, St. Louis. Each time, he said, he has bid three or four days before he wanted to travel and set a price $10 to $15 above the lowest available published advance-purchase fare; in his research, he also found that seats were still available on these routes. Yet each bid was rejected; he suspects that Priceline simply had no seats to sell on those routes. "I don't understand why they can't do it," he said, "especially if you offer bids above the airlines' lowest fare." Mr. Walker said Priceline could not offer seats in all markets, acknowledging that it had "no lift in small cities that have no lift." "You need to be willing to drive to a bigger city," he said. Priceline has its fans, including George Miller, 54, artistic director of the Theater Outlet in Allentown, Pa. Several weeks ago, Mr. Miller bought two roundtrip tickets, at $550 each, to fly on Aer Lingus from Newark to Dublin for his honeymoon, which is to begin today. The lowest published fare offered by the airline for the same date was $598. Mr. Miller said he found Priceline to be "very prompt and very courteous." Ashita Patel, 34, a pharmacist from Edison, N.J., is also happy: Earlier this month, she bought four roundtrip tickets, at $300 each, for her family to fly on United from Newark to London for a September wedding. United's lowest published fare for that time was $788. (Prices do not include tax.) She said she was "shocked that they could do it so fast. It only took 12 hours." OTHER Web sites also offer deeply discounted tickets; in some cases, they can arrange for cheap hotel rooms and car rentals, too. Most major unitedstates airlines offer special weekly Internet fares, usually for travel that weekend; prices are much lower than their cheapest advance-purchase fares. The drawback, of course, is that destinations are limited: You have to go where they want to take you. On-line travel agencies including Preview Travel, Expedia and Travelocity have special features that help track low fares. Preview offers low fares and announcements of airlines' latest specials. Expedia, owned by Microsoft, and Travelocity, controlled by AMR, the parent of American Airlines, send regular email to travelers listing the lowest published fares on the routes of their choice. Travelocity also posts a list of each day's lowest fares. Cheaptickets.com, a consolidator based in Honolulu, sells published and unpublished discount fares for flights on domestic and foreign airlines; Michael J. Hartley, its president, said it obtains the unpublished discounts from established carriers. Travelers must provide credit-card information before they can conduct a fare search; requests result in a choice of 25 fares, which the customer can accept or decline. Another site, Bestfares.com, based in Dallas, has sections with general access to rate information and others only for subscribers, who pay $60 a year to get more detailed travel data and more deals. A site operated by 1travel.com, a Zionsville, Pa., travel agency, provides another path to discounts. It publishes all airlines' weekly Web specials and will send email lists of them, customized to the traveler's requirements. It also provides data on deeply discounted international tickets sold by several large consolidators. Graphic   Photo: Michael Spohn, an intern at The Des Moines Register, has had no success with Priceline.com, an on-line service that lets users bid for air fares. He says it has rejected each of his nine bids for a ticket to St. Louis. (Steve Pope for The newyork Times)  Chart: "Wings on the Web" The Internet has become one of the best places to find discounted airfares, with travel agencies and the airlines themselves competing on line to deliver cheap tickets.
