title:
YOUR HOME;
Selling Without A Broker
body: WHEN eager buyers outnumber anxious sellers -- as is apparently the case in much of the newyork metropolitan region today -- an increasing number of "For Sale by Owner" signs sprout up on residential lawns. The possibility of making sales in such a fashion is becoming increasingly attractive as sellers now extend their front lawns into cyberspace by placing "For Sale" signs on the Internet. But there are pitfalls along the way. "The biggest blunder most people make is getting into the F.S.B.O. process with a complete and utter lack of preparation," said Jim Edwards, author of "Selling Your Home Alone," a primer for selling a home without a real estate broker. Mr. Edwards, a real estate agent in Norge, Va., who also maintains an F.S.B.O. Internet Web site at http://www.fsbohelp.com, said that the most important considerations in trying to sell a home without a broker are preparing the house for sale and then getting the broadest exposure possible. "People expect your home to be immaculate," Mr. Edwards said, explaining that if it is not, sellers will probably see a lot of prospective buyers come and go before one stays long enough to look below the grit and clutter. At the same time, he said, the value of exposing the house to as many potential buyers as possible is something many such sellers underestimate. Mr. Edwards said that the best way for a seller to market his home is to blitz prospective buyers with information. For example, he said, sellers should distribute fliers containing information and a picture of the house as widely as widely as possible. In addition, he said, classified ads should be paired, if feasible, with a more detailed description of the house on the Internet. "Using the Internet gives you a way to tell a whole lot more about you house than you can in a classified ad," he said. There are an ever-increasing number of Internet sites -- including individual postings, and regional and national databases -- that list "For Sale By Owner" homes. (A search of the term "for sale by owner" using the Alta Vista search engine produced no fewer than 20,000 hits.) Some larger sites include the For Sale By Owner Network (http://www.f-s-b-o.com); Real Estate For Sale By Owner, USA. (http://www.webbrowsers.com) and the For Sale By Owner Real Estate Listing Service (http://www.fsbolistings.com). Peter Bell, chief executive officer of Balch Buyers Real Estate, a "buyers only" real estate broker in Mamaroneck, N.Y., said that a common mistake made by F.S.B.O. sellers is failing to establish the correct sale price. "It's very common to see F.S.B.O.'s greatly overpriced," Mr. Bell said, adding that overpricing can cause two problems for sellers: First, an overpriced house is much more difficult to sell, and second, even if a buyer can be found there is a good chance that the buyer will have difficulty obtaining a mortgage if the lender's appraisal comes in for less than the sale price. As a result, Mr. Bell said, it is wise for sellers to ask two or three real estate brokers to do a market analysis for the house in order to determine the appropriate sale price. He pointed out that sellers should be candid with the broker and explain that they are going to be using the analysis to market the house themselves, at least for a time. "Most brokers won't mind because they figure that you'll give them the listing if there hasn't been any action on the house a couple of weeks down the road," he said. Mr. Bell pointed out that a significant element missing from many sales by the owner is the ability of the seller to assess the ability of the buyer to go through with the deal.  Most experienced real estate agents, he said, will "pre-qualify" a buyer to determine how much house the buyer can afford. In sales by owners, however, sellers -- and frequently buyers as well -- have no idea whether the buyer will qualify for the necessary mortgage, Mr. Bell said.. In this regard, access to the Internet again proves valuable in that there are an increasing number of web sites that can provide buyers with pre-qualification letters. Sites such as Intuit's Quicken Mortgage (http://www.quickenmortgage.com) permits prospective buyers to apply for a mortgage on-line by electronically submitting an application, which is then distributed to the site's 12 participating lenders. If qualified, prospective buyers can then print out a pre-qualification letter on the lender's letterhead and then give it to the seller when making an offer. But what is a seller to do when a buyer actually bites? "Get it in writing and get a check," said William Selsberg, a Stamford, Conn., real estate lawyer. To get the offer in writing, Mr. Selsberg said, sellers should talk to a lawyer before they start marketing their homes to provide a simple binder they can use to formalize any offer they receive. The binder Mr. Selsberg faxes to clients, which is later used as a framework for a more formal contract, has spaces for the names of the parties, the address of the property, the price, deposit, the amount of the mortgage sought, the date by which the mortgage commitment must be obtained and a list of items included or excluded from the sale. The check, Mr. Selsberg said, should be for 1 percent of the purchase price and should be made out to the seller's lawyer, as trustee. "Every deal needs some glue to hold it together," he explained. Generally, the driving force behind most sales by owners is the desire to avoid paying the standard 6 percent commission. By bypassing the broker, the seller of a $200,000 house can save $12,000. In real life, however, it doesn't always work that way. "From the buyer's perspective, if the seller isn't paying a commission, the savings should be passed along to the buyer," said Frank Struck, owner of Realty Network Better Homes and Gardens in Rutherford, N.J. As a result, he said, a sale by owner may hardly be worth the time and effort expended by the seller if the buyer ends up with the savings. In addition, Mr. Struck said, sellers should also be aware that while the Internet may provide a vast audience of potential buyers, the multiple listing systems in place in most areas generally result in a more focused sampling of more serious buyers. As a result, Mr. Struck said, sellers should be open to cooperating with real estate agents with qualified buyers in tow. "If a broker can produce a seller for the best price and the best terms, why turn him away?" Mr. Struck said, adding that in such a case, the seller would only be required to pay the commission earned by the buyer's broker. "And commissions are always negotiable." Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title: Ally or Foe? A Complaint On Microsoft
body: The chairman of a young, fast-growing software company testified at a Senate hearing today that the Microsoft Corporation had introduced a competing product that crippled his company's most recent technology. Competitors commonly complain that Microsoft business practices are unfair. But this complaint appears particularly intriguing because it comes from a company with close ties to Microsoft -- and one that is engaged in a promising niche of the Internet software market in which the Government is investigating Microsoft tactics. The complaint was made by Robert Glaser, a former Microsoft executive. Microsoft holds a 10 percent stake in his Seattle company, Real Networks Inc., and licenses Real Networks technology. After his appearance before the Senate Judiciary Committee, Mr. Glaser said, "I loved my 10 years at Microsoft and, even after today, I think I have friends there." Mr. Glaser's company is the leader in the emerging field of so-called streaming software, which is used for sending recorded voice and television-style video over the Internet and receiving such multimedia programming on personal computers. Mr. Glaser's appearance before the committee included a computer demonstration of how the latest version of Microsoft's software for receiving streaming media, Windows Media Player, cannot play Internet multimedia programming that is based on the latest Real Networks technology. Mr. Glaser also read excerpts from an email exchange with William H. Gates, Microsoft's chairman, starting on July 6. Mr. Glaser said he first became concerned about the problem caused by Microsoft's new program, and the potential effect on his company, in May. By July, Mr. Glaser said, he was growing increasingly alarmed. Senator Orrin G. Hatch of Utah, the chairman of the Judiciary Committee, had been in touch with him about testifying in Washington, and Mr. Glaser sent Mr. Gates an email saying that he might go. In his testimony, Mr. Glaser suggested that the communication with his old boss was a final effort to settle his dispute instead of voicing it publicly. According to Mr. Glaser's account, Mr. Gates seemed in no mood to reach an accommodation. Mr. Glaser said that Mr. Gates had said he was "not very familiar with our business relationship" and later added that he found it "interesting" that Mr. Glaser felt he had no choice but to go to Washington. Mr. Gates closed his last email to Mr. Glaser with what seemed to its recipient a chilly dismissal. "While you're in Washington, I suggest you visit the National Gallery and the Smithsonian," Mr. Gates wrote, according to Mr. Glaser. Microsoft vigorously denies Mr. Glaser's version of the recent conflict between the two companies. Microsoft officials say the software breakdown that seemed to be so convincingly shown by Mr. Glaser's computer demonstration in the Senate hearing room applies only to a test, or beta, version of Real Networks' software that was posted on its Web site for downloading only a week or so ago. "This smoking gun turns out to be a water pistol," said Mark Murray, a Microsoft spokesman. "That demonstration was something of a misleading stunt." According to Microsoft, Mr. Glaser was mainly using his Senate appearance as a negotiating ploy. And Microsoft was able to present that view forcefully before the committee, thanks to its allies in the Senate. At the hearing, Senator Robert G. Torricelli, a New Jersey Democrat, introduced an affidavit of Paul Maritz, a group vice president at Microsoft. The affidavit said Mr. Glaser called Mr. Maritz Wednesday afternoon and said that he was prepared to "negotiate all night if that's what it takes" to come to terms with Microsoft. The Maritz affidavit added, "Mr. Glaser said that if the negotiations he proposed for the night of July 22 resulted in an agreement between the two companies, he would not testify the next day before the Senate Judiciary Committee." In an interview after the hearing, Mr. Glaser said his call to Mr. Maritz was merely a courtesy call. At the time, Mr. Glaser said, he was in Washington and on his way to speak to Senator Hatch before appearing today. The Maritz affidavit, Mr. Glaser said, "is simply not true." "I was locked, loaded and ready to testify," Mr. Glaser said. The committee hearing comes prior to a trial of the Justice Department's antitrust case against Microsoft, which is scheduled to begin on Sept. 8 in Federal District Court in Washington. The Government contends that the company is unfairly using its near-monopoly of the market for desktop personal computer software to dominate the new market for Internet software. Microsoft executives characterized Mr. Glaser's allegation as an inexplicably overwrought reaction. "We are still willing to have our engineers sit down with the engineers of Real Networks and work these problems out," said Mr. Murray, the spokesman. Still, agreement among the engineers might be difficult as well. Wednesday night, after six hours of software testing by its programmers, Microsoft had concluded that the problem was Real Networks'. "It is a bug in their program, not ours," said Yusuf Mehdi, an executive. Graphic   Photo: Robert Glaser testified that Microsoft had crippled his company's most recent technology. But he also said, "I loved my 10 years at Microsoft and, even after today, I think I have friends there." (Associated Press)(pg. D3)

title:
AUTOS ON FRIDAY/Technology;
Net-Savvy Car Takes Computer For a Ride
body: WHAT'S the next big thing? To judge from many of the concept cars at this year's auto shows, it is an on-board computer that would allow a driver or passenger to log onto the Internet to read or send email, check stock quotes or get traffic reports. The Chrysler Corporation wants to give customers a chance to surf the World Wide Web, too, but it has come up with a bring-your-own approach to computing. One of Chrysler's showcase concepts this year, the Dodge ESX2, has drawn attention for its lightweight body, which could be made of polyethylene terephthalate, or P.E.T., the material used for plastic soda bottles, and for its hybrid powertrain, which combines a diesel engine and an electric motor. The ESX2 also takes an unusual approach to on-the-road computing: Instead of permanently installing a computer with Internet access, as other manufacturers have done, Chrysler built in a docking station for a small, portable computer. A user would plug in his or her own computer, then use it to call up, say, real-time traffic reports. In the ESX2, a hand-held Hewlett-Packard 620LX sits on a small shelf in the center of the dashboard, secured by Velcro. In the back of the computer is a Motorola module that uses an infrared interface, similar to a television's remote control, to link the computer to the car. Once the computer is docked in the car, the driver can display menu choices that include the audio and climate controls, traffic information, weather forecasts, Internet and cellular phone connections and software that would give customers remote control over devices at their homes, including appliances, lights, sprinklers and security systems. A diagnostics option would help to pinpoint any problem with the vehicle and provide step-by-step instructions for simple repairs, like replacing a flat tire. The driver selects choices from the menu by touch, though computers like these will eventually be operated by voice commands. Chrysler's approach has several advantages over the permanent installation of a computer in a vehicle, Steve Buckley, an electronics specialist for Chrysler, said. For starters, it helps to hold down the cost of an Internet-capable car, because built-in computers and modems add hundreds of dollars, perhaps more than $1,000, to the purchase price. Chrysler says the docking station would cost no more than $100. Hand-held computers, which have become increasingly popular mass-market products, cost from $500 to $1,000. Most of these do not currently come with modems for connecting to the Internet, which add another $200 to $700. Flexibility is increased because the hand-held computer can do double or triple duty: in the car, at the office, at home. Chrysler's docking station is compatible with various computer sizes and brands that use Microsoft's Windows CE operating system. And because the computer is not built in, the car would not spend much of its useful life with an obsolete gadget imbedded in the dashboard -- the digital equivalent of an eight-track tape deck. The hand-held computer can be removed and replaced, its software can be updated and features can easily be added long before the vehicle itself is replaced. Pointing out how quickly computer technology changes, Mr. Buckley said that within the 10 months he spent developing the ESX2's docking station, he used three generations of hand-held computers. Voice-recognition software was unavailable when he started; it is now available and can be added on, which would provide a boon to drivers who will be able to surf the Net without looking away from the road. "I'm personally on my third home computer, but I can't afford to buy a new car every time the computer technology becomes obsolete," Mr. Buckley said. Chrysler plans to use the ESX2 to gauge consumer interest in the in-car docking stations for hand-held computers. The module that would make this kind of communication possible in existing production cars and trucks could be installed as an after-market option within two years, Chrysler said. The devices could be made available through the company's dealerships. Graphic   Photos: Any of various hand-held computers could be plugged into a docking station inside the Dodge Intrepid ESX2. (Mark Stehrenberger)

title: Microsoft Describes a Successful Year and Talks of More
body: Confident Microsoft executives today outlined for industry analysts a string of successes suggesting momentum throughout the computer industry in markets as diverse as home computers, business desktop machines, engineering work stations and the giant computers that connect entire corporations and serve up World Wide Web sites on the Internet. To maintain this momentum, the company said it planned to increase research and development spending to $3 billion a year from $2.5 billion in the fiscal year that ended on June 30, and to pump almost $200 million a year more into technical and customer support. As Microsoft officials here were laying out some of the most impressive results recorded by a major American corporation this year, in Washington the Senate Judiciary Committee was hearing complaints from executives of several competing software companies that Microsoft uses predatory marketing practices to squelch competition. Among those testifying was Robert Glaser, a former Microsoft employee who is now chairman of Real Networks, a Seattle-based maker of software that enables users to receive live audio and video on their Web browsers. Mr. Glaser told senators that Microsoft had developed a new version of its media player for the Windows 98 operating system that undermines his software. A Microsoft lawyer, Brad Smith, assured analysts that any problem Mr. Glaser had encountered was unintended, adding that "we'll keep working with them" to resolve it. However, at a time when the company's business practices are under attack by the Justice Department, several Congressional committees and 20 states and the District of Columbia, and under investigation by European governments, Microsoft executives gave no indication of abandoning the aggressive strategies that have made it one of the world's most successful and feared corporations. In fact, while citing increasing market share against its strongest rivals, including Sun Microsystems, Novell and Oracle in applications as diverse as operating systems, data bases and Internet commerce software, the company sought to play down any possibility that the Justice Department's antitrust suit would have a negative effect on its profit. Indeed, Jeff Raikes, its sales chief, suggested that Justice Department investigators had misinterpreted a corporate sense of humor as a strategic intention to eradicate competition. To demonstrate this corporate humor, Mr. Raikes played a music video that the company had produced to motivate its sales force. In the video, a spoof on the movie "Men In Black," Mr. Raikes plays the role of a rap singer wearing wrap-around dark glasses. His lyrics include, "We're the first, last and best line of defense against the worst scum in the industry," and, referring to Lawrence J. Ellison, the chairman of Oracle, "Ellison is a loser." In particular, Microsoft officials expressed satisfaction with advances in their share of several markets and with sales of Windows 98, which they said was on track to match the first three months' sales of Windows 95, the best-selling software ever. "That has surprised a lot of people, including myself to some extent," Mr. Raikes said. There were other areas where the company acknowledged it had made less progress than it expected. Novell had proved to be a tougher competitor than was expected in the network service market. But Microsoft executives asserted that they had taken five to eight percentage points of market share away from Novell in the last year, and Mr. Raikes said he would be disappointed if Microsoft's market share did not grow an equal amount next year. As he does every year, Microsoft's chief financial officer predicted that the company's growth would decline substantially in the coming year because many of its products are mature and are reaching the saturation point in the market. He also expressed fear about the Asian troubles, adding, "In fact, there is evidence it's getting worse." Each year Microsoft appears to zero in on one company for attack, and analysts who attended today's meeting said the next focus would be on the corporate data base business that Oracle now dominates. Mr. Ellison was in Washington today, testifying against Microsoft's business practices.

title: Protecting Digital Copyrights
body: Traditional copyright concepts that have served this nation well for centuries should guide the debate on copyright in the digital universe. As Congress fashions ways to protect commercial interests in the digital realm, it must be careful also to protect the larger public interest in broad access to information. Digital copyright legislation, required to institute two international treaties that would protect movies, music and other intellectual property from piracy, passed the Senate and the House Judiciary Committee this spring. But controversy continues to swirl around a provision in the legislation that would make it a crime to circumvent encryption used to control access to digital material or to manufacture or sell devices that could be used to circumvent protection measures. Movie and music producers argue that making circumvention illegal is the only way to prevent consumer theft of on-line movies, recordings and other products. But libraries and schools believe that the prohibition is so broad that it could greatly limit access to electronic information that copyright law would otherwise allow. Existing law assures producers the right to profit from their creative works. But the law does not allow a creator to control who looks at the material or prevent the material from being circulated or lent to others. It specifically allows the "fair use" of copyrighted materials for commentary, criticism, teaching, news reporting, scholarship and research under certain circumstances without permission from the copyright owner. Thus a library can purchase a book, allow hundreds of patrons to borrow it and let teachers make copies of material in it for classroom use, all without infringing the copyright. Preserving these user rights is important in the digital world where copyright owners, with the right technology, could limit or prevent access to information. The content producers dismiss fears that the Internet could become a strictly pay-for-use world as unrealistic, but neither they nor Congress can predict how the Internet will develop. That is why legislation needs to be flexible enough to deal with rapid evolution in technology and electronic commerce. A prudent compromise approved by the House Commerce Committee last week would delay the anti-circumvention rule for two years while the Commerce Department and the Federal patent and copyright offices study the effect of the prohibition on users. The Commerce Secretary could waive the rule for any class of works where technological shields were impeding the lawful use of copyrighted matter. The situation would be reviewed every two years. Both the content producers and the libraries and schools are willing to accept this more fluid approach. Congress should adopt this plan in the final version of the digital copyright legislation.

title:
GAME THEORY;
Web Sales Fill Gap Left by Software Stores
body: ONE argument against buying books on line: Shopping for books is a pleasant experience. There are lots on the shelves. You can flip them open and browse. If you go to a small independent bookseller, you will find articulate salespeople. If you go to a megastore, you will find comfy seats and cappuccino and young urban singles trolling for mates. It's not a bad way to kill an hour. The same cannot be said for video games. Shopping for them falls somewhere between tax returns and a Quake death match on the stress continuum. Selection is extremely limited and blockbuster-heavy, particularly with regard to computer games. If you're not looking for Lara Croft, Warcraft, hunting and fishing titles, or the latest offering from Id software, you're generally out of luck. You can't open the boxes, and there aren't many games on display. When the holidays roll around, the video game section of Toys "R" Us turns into a hallucinatory nightmare for parents -- a disorienting maelstrom of sound and light where everything is back-ordered. Video games, it would seem, are begging for on-line commerce. And on the Internet, no consumer itch goes unscratched for long. Witness Gameserve.com, a site with more than 10,000 console, PC and Mac titles, a full line of game hardware and more than 1,000 joysticks, action pads, steering wheels and other play-enhancing accessories at up to 20 percent off their suggested retail prices (money saved by not maintaining brick-and-mortar stores is ostensibly passed on to the customer). A search engine pulls up product descriptions for curious browsers and wary parents. There are strategy guides, a game maker's directory, a chat room and a forthcoming filtering feature to recommend games based on what you already like. Everything you decide to buy goes into a virtual shopping basket to be taken to an on-line checkout counter, charged to your credit card and shipped within 48 hours. (For customers drooling in anticipation, Gameserve emails a package-tracking number so you can follow your order's every turn -- or answer the question, "Mom, when will it get here?") An affiliate program pays Web mavens a commission for selling games off their own sites. This is the Amazon.com of video games. And in fact, Gameserve .com's parent company, Speedserve, began as an on-line bookseller. "Our first storefront, Bookserve .com, came out around the same time Amazon did," said Michael Mason, 28, Speedserve's chief executive. "We tracked really great with those guys for a while. And then we made some mistakes. Our technology was sort of homespun technology, and we couldn't scale quick enough. So as more customers came into our store, we weren't able to serve them." Having stubbed its big toe on infrastructure, Speedserve underwent a complete back-office overhaul in 1997, replacing its own technology with I.B.M. E-commerce software. But by the time Bookserve.com was ready to race, Amazon.com and BarnesandNoble.com had already crossed the finish line. There wasn't room to compete as an electronic book retailer. So Speedserve reinvented itself as an Internet movie merchant, Videoserve.com, and opened the world's largest on-line video game store, Gameserve.com. After two months, 8,000 visitors a day were hitting the site. It remains to be seen whether digital entertainment and bound books will follow the same trajectories on line. In a marketplace where Amazon.com has yet to turn a profit, Gameserve.com may have the last laugh. Unlike the publishing business, the computer game industry is growing prodigiously: according to the Interactive Digital Software Association, video games and computer games were a $5.1 billion business in 1997, up 38 percent from the previous year. Forty percent of American homes have computers, and one out of 10 packaged software purchases is a game. Sony just announced the sale of its ten-millionth Playstation in North America. Every year a new crop of video game customers surges up from the schoolyard to join millions of game fans in their teens, 20's, 30's and 40's. Unfortunately, places to buy games are not multiplying as fast as the number of people who want to buy them. The checkout counter remains a bottleneck for this industry because book retailing and software retailing are very different creatures. A bookseller can order a thousand copies of a book, sell a hundred and return the rest to the publisher, who eats the cost. To a large extent, this return policy defines the book-buying experience -- acres of space and endless variety -- because bookstores bear no risk for this embarrassment of riches. In the video game world, retailers bear all the risk. Inventory is bought and paid for, and it's extremely difficult to return. Hence the small selection of sure-fire sellers. "Distributors often have copies of old games that they can't do anything with," Mr. Mason said. "Yet they keep them because they've paid for it. So they have standing inventory. We can take advantage of that. And that's completely different from the way we have to operate on the book and video side of things." Under these circumstances, Gameserve is at a distinct advantage because the physical world is failing consumers and because Gameserve carries no inventory whatsoever. Everything is shipped directly from the distributor to the customer, an expedient arrangement. Speedserve's major backer is Ingram Entertainment, the unitedstates' largest distributor of video games and home videos, which holds a majority interest in the startup. There is a family legacy as well. Mr. Mason's father, who now works in the insurance industry, was once the president of Ingram Books, a 900-pound gorilla of distribution in the publishing world. So what does the old man think of this electronic game-brokering business? "He likes it," said the second-generation media salesman. "He came over and checked out our little fulfillment center and kind of chuckled and had a good time. He doesn't know anything about games. But he likes it." Graphic   Photo: AIMING HIGH -- With more than 10,000 game titles and lots of hardware, Gameserve aims to be the Amazon.com of computer games.

title: Initials on a Tree, Web Style
body: WATSON and Crick have nothing on Smit and Kinkhorst when it comes to unraveling the mysteries of life. Smit and Kinkhorst? Matthijs Sypkens Smit and Thijs Kinkhorst are two men from Utrecht, Holland, whose Love Calculator on the World Wide Web (www.lovecalculator.com) brings a bizarre -- some might say completely perverse -- mathematical rigor to matters of the heart. Simply type in two names, and after a brief calculation, up pops a percentage, indicating a couple's chances for romantic success. Lest you doubt the reliability of the Love Calculator, consider the evidence: Bruce Willis and Demi Moore: 45 percent. Woody Allen and Mia Farrow: 38 percent. Mr. Allen and Soon-Yi Previn? 79 percent. Romeo and Juliet: 98 percent (Remember: The Love Calculator measures compatibility. Fate does not compute.) Are Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman really that happy together? According to Dr. Love -- they scored 99 percent -- they are. O.K., so it's not infallible. Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton scored a predictable 18 percent. But Liz Taylor and Richard Burton: 82 percent. Mr. Smit and Mr. Kinkhorst, who together are Dr. Love on their Web site, offer somber words with each calculation, like this: "Dr. Love thinks that a relationship between Tristan and Isolde has a reasonable chance of working out, but on the other hand, it might not. Your relationship may suffer good and bad times. If things might not be working out as you would like them to, do not hesitate to talk about it with the person involved. Spend time together, talk with each other." Obviously, then, Mr. Smit and Mr. Kinkhorst rely on years of accumulated wisdom. Or do they? Now 18 years old, the two computer science students were both 16 when they first put the Love Calculator on the Web. Alas, wisdom plays no role in Dr. Love's prognoses. It's all arithmetic. The calculator uses an algorithm familiar to elementary-school children and math teachers around the world. It starts by looking for the number of times the letters L, O, V, E and S occur in the two names; then, through a series of addition sequences, it produces the percentage.  For example: Bill Clinton and Hillary Rodham. L: 5, O: 2, V: 0, E: 0, S: 0. Write those numbers down and you get 52000. Then add up the individual numbers -- 5+2, 2+0, 0+0, 0+0 -- and you get 7200. Keep doing the same addition of individual numbers for each sum. If you add the numerals in 7200 in the same way, you get 920 (7+2, 2+0, 0+0). Do the addition on 920 (9+2, 2+0) and the result is 112. Once again with 112 (1+1, 2+1), and you get down to two numerals, which gives you the chance of a successful relationship: 23 percent. The system makes perfect sense, to a third grader. Mr. Smit said the Web site had received about 2.5 million hits since it first went up. He and Mr. Kinkhorst have received email from around the world, thanking them for the service they have done for romance in the late 20th century. Wrote a grateful calculatee from Brazil: "I have put my name and my first wife's and I have gotten 0 percent; the incredible thing is: we got divorced 15 years ago! On the other hand I got 97 percent with my second wife, and we have been together for 12 years!" Wrote another: "On the eve of our fourth date (the day before Valentine's Day), a friend called me to tell me that she had entered my name and my date's in the love calculator -- we got 97 percent. Strangely enough, we fell madly in love and are now engaged to be married. Are we your first Love Calculator wedding?" Disgruntled visitors, Mr. Smit said, also send email. "When people get a low score and react to it, they most often use offensive language or say it's all a big fake," he said. Graphic   Photo: Romeo and Juliet get a high compatibility score on the Love Calculator.

title:
Metro Business;
Mistake Drives Up Stock
body: Shares of the Cityscape Financial Corporation, a lender that plans to file for bankruptcy protection, increased more than sixfold in a week after investors mistook the company for Citysearch Inc., an Internet company that plans to use the same stock ticker symbol. Shares of Cityscape were worth less than a nickel at the start of last week. They rose as high as 27 cents yesterday, then slumped back to 12.5 cents as more than 1.9 million shares changed hands. More than 2.7 million shares traded during the last two days, the first activity since July 9. The fervor surrounding shares of new Internet companies, many of which have more than doubled in their first days of trading, may have accidentally driven up shares of Cityscape, which is based in Westchester County. Citysearch, based in Pasadena, Calif., plans to sell four million shares in an initial public offering in the coming months, at a price of more than $11, according to recent filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company produces Internet city guides with information on local events and news. Citysearch has designated CTYS as the symbol for its shares -- a symbol Cityscape used until January, when it was kicked off the Nasdaq National Market. Cityscape said yesterday that investors may be confused about the identities of the two companies. "Investors interested in Citysearch are urged to take all appropriate steps to insure that any investment they wish to make in Citysearch is made in Citysearch and not in Cityscape," the company said in a press release. Cityscape told shareholders in June that it planned to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, after selling its profitable British lending unit and a unitedstates loan servicing business.

title: Bills Curbing Minors' Web Access Pass Senate
body: The Senate today approved two proposals for controlling children's access to pornography on the Internet, endorsing without debate one measure that would make it illegal for commercial Web sites to distribute adult material to minors and another that would require software filters on computers in libraries and schools that receive Federal Internet subsidies. The measures, which had been introduced as separate bills, were added by voice votes to the $33 billion appropriations bill for the Commerce, Justice and State Departments. Civil liberties groups vowed to fight the measures, saying they infringed on free speech. The filtering proposal, sponsored by Senator John McCain, the Arizona Republican who is chairman of the Commerce Committee, would require schools and libraries to install filtering technology on computers used by students if they receive financing for discounted Internet hookups from the Federal Communications Commission. "Children should not be allowed to enter school or a public library and gain access to material that their parents would never allow them to see," Mr. McCain said, "and that most in society believe is inappropriate for those who are not yet adults." The other amendment, sponsored by Senator Dan Coats, Republican of Indiana, would make it a crime for commercial Web site operators to distribute material harmful to minors. Violators would be subject to fines of up to $50,000. Civil liberties groups said they would fight the proposals in court. "Free speech on the Internet was ambushed today," said Barry Steinhardt, president of the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Marc Rotenberg, director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said he thought both bills raised constitutional questions. But because they are intended to protect children, he said, they will "be hard for members to vote against." Civil liberties groups say they have opposed filtering mandates because many filters block access to more than just inappropriate sites, preventing computer users from getting information on subjects like breast cancer. When the bills were before the Commerce Committee, the privacy information center, the American Civil Liberties Union and the Center for Democracy and Technology argued that the Coats bill's standard of regulating material "harmful to minors" would unconstitutionally restrict free speech on the Internet. Mr. Steinhardt said the bill would apply to any commercial distribution of information on the Internet. The House has yet to act on its version of the spending bill, which an appropriations committee approved last week. Senate and House versions would have to be reconciled before final action. A provision similar to Mr. McCain's filtering proposal has been added to a House appropriations bill.

title: Microsoft's Chief Salesman Named Second in Command
body: Steven A. Ballmer, the combative chief salesman of the Microsoft Corporation, was named the company's president yesterday. The promotion is a formal acknowledgment of what has long been an accepted fact within the company -- that Mr. Ballmer is Microsoft's second in command and that he is the natural successor to William H. Gates, the 42-year-old chairman. With Mr. Ballmer becoming president, Mr. Gates will hand over some of his day-to-day management chores, spending less time on operations and having fewer executives report to him. In a conference call with journalists, Mr. Gates emphasized that the management change was mainly intended to allow him to spend more time on long-term technology and product issues. "I'm not backing off at all in terms of my commitment to Microsoft," Mr. Gates said. "I want to get in there and work with our software developers. I want to spend more time to help drive our breakthroughs." In an email memo to Microsoft workers, Mr. Gates explained the management shift as a move to bolster the company as it worked to defend its lucrative franchise and set out to conquer new markets in Internet software and electronic commerce. In the future, he said, electronic devices like intelligent telephones and televisions, all connected to the Internet, will outnumber personal computers. Many personal computers, he predicted, will become "tablet-sized" machines, while Microsoft's desktop software will be able to tackle computing challenges that are now the bailiwick of the most powerful mainframe systems. When people use the Internet to pay bills, buy cars and plan vacations, Microsoft wants a slice of the business. Its new-product goals, Mr. Gates wrote, "require breakthrough work." Mr. Gates's email is an ambitious call to arms to Microsoft's 25,000 workers, admonishing them to prepare for a "new phase -- one that finds us with greater opportunities and challenges than ever before." The internal email, posted on the Microsoft Web site later in the day, was also intended to send a message to the larger audience in the computer industry and among investors. To some degree, it was meant to deter the inevitable speculation that Mr. Gates was easing up. Because Microsoft's success is so closely associated with Mr. Gates, any shift in his duties is a subject of scrutiny. In his email, Mr. Gates did not mention the Government's antitrust pursuit of the company as being among the challenges faced by Microsoft. By contrast, in a February message to Microsoft employees and shareholders, Mr. Gates wrote, "We have dealt with many challenges in Microsoft's short history, but few as important as the issues we're facing in Washington, D.C., today." After a Federal appeals court last month struck down a temporary injunction against the company, Microsoft seems to have more confidence that it will prevail against the Justice Department, industry analysts say. A trial is scheduled to begin in September in the Government's major antitrust case against Microsoft. Indeed, the 42-year-old Mr. Ballmer has been the company's most unqualified critic of the Justice Department's antitrust scrutiny. Mr. Ballmer's appointment as president is "certainly not an effort to make Microsoft a kinder, gentler company in response to the Justice Department suit," said Richard Sherlund, an analyst at Goldman, Sachs & Company. By now, Mr. Ballmer is famous in the computer industry for his animated style and his aggressive business tactics. He gets so excited praising Microsoft or excoriating its rivals that he has been known to cut himself, when an errant hand gesture hits his face. He has, according to one industry executive, sent Christmas cards to the children of Microsoft competitors, just to unnerve them about how much he knows about his adversaries. As the executive vice president in charge of sales and support, Mr. Ballmer has taken the lead in convincing corporate customers to buy Microsoft products. "Ballmer is a hard-line, take-no-prisoners competitor," said David Coursey, editor of Coursey.com, an industry newsletter. "He has probably been more important to the day-to-day success of the company over the last couple of years than Bill Gates." Naming Mr. Ballmer president also conveys the message, well known in the industry, that "Microsoft is far more than Bill Gates," noted Esther Dyson, editor of Release 1.0, a technology newsletter. "But this move is not surprising, given how long and closely these two have worked together." Mr. Gates and Mr. Ballmer played poker together at Harvard University, where Mr. Ballmer stayed on to graduate while Mr. Gates dropped out to start Microsoft. Mr. Ballmer went to work for Procter & Gamble and earned an M.B.A. from Stanford University, before joining Microsoft in 1980 to make his fortune. Today, he owns 4.9 percent of Microsoft, worth about $13 billion.

title: N.Y.U. Sues Web Site Operator, Saying Photos Are Not From Dormitory
body: Contending that its name had been tarnished by falsehoods on the Internet, newyork University has filed a lawsuit against the operators of a sexually explicit Web site that claims to offer a secret camera to spy on women students at the university who "romp for your enjoyment in their own dorm room." Photographs on the Web site depict scantily clad women in rooms that are supposed to be university dormitories, the suit says. The women in the photos are shown wearing tank top shirts with the N.Y.U. insignia, and the rooms are decorated with the university's pennants and bumper stickers. "Five girls are currently living in the dorm," the Web site says, adding that subscribers can view them through an "NY University Dorm Cam." University officials said they first learned of the Web site and its unauthorized use of the school's trademarked name and symbols -- including the school's color, violet -- after being asked about it recently by a reporter for The Daily News. "This site has about as much connection to N.Y.U. as the M.T.A. does to snowfall in the Himalayas," said John H. Beckman, an N.Y.U. spokesman. The university's housing director was called in, and quickly ascertained that the rooms shown on the Web site were not at the school. "There is no 'N.Y.U. Dorm Cam' installed in any N.Y.U. dorm room" the suit says, and pictures of "alleged N.Y.U. coeds romping" in a dormitory are fakes. In the lawsuit, the school said that it had been harmed not only by the X-rated pictures but also by the text, "which describes an entirely false scenario represented to be true: that N.Y.U. students will parade around in their dorm rooms, posing in various states of undress for paying customers" of the Web site. The lawsuit, filed last Friday in Federal District Court in Manhattan, seeks an injunction as well as compensatory and punitive damages. The university said that it sued only after the Web site's operator refused to stop using the university's name and symbols and instead added new pictures. The defendants include Frank Monte, who is described as the site's operator and owner of Monte Investigation Group in Manhattan. Mr. Monte did not respond to two messages left on his answering machine. Mr. Beckman said the school would move aggressively to block the Web site, adding, "This fellow appears to want to try and ride the rocket to Internet riches on N.Y.U.'s good name, and we're not going to let him do it."

title: Back on Line: The Word According to Bowe
body: WHEN it was born three years ago, the literary Web magazine Word was widely praised as an example of how good Internet content could be, a kind of hip, lo-fi newyorker magazine for a new generation. It attracted well-known authors like Mary Gaitskill, who wrote about her first sunburn, and David Foster Wallace, who excerpted a chapter of his novel "Infinite Jest." The magazine won awards, and its hard-working, low-profile editor, Marisa Bowe, even ended up with her picture in Esquire, one of its "women we love." The only problem? Like other worthy endeavors in the still unmapped world of Internet commerce, Word made no money. Its corporate parent, Icon CMT, which once dreamed of fast profits in Web magazines, closed it last March without so much as a courtesy call. ("They walked in at 5 and said, 'Be out of here by 7,' " Ms. Bowe recalled.) But now, after months of dire "content is dead" predictions from Web watchers, Word is being reborn. Its unlikely savior is a Houston company that was founded as an oil business in the 1950's by a young George Bush but that now focuses on processing protein extracted from fish. This summer the company suddenly announced that it would become a major player on the World Wide Web, though it had no experience in the Internet business. The company, Zapata, controlled by the Glazer family of Rochester, then changed the name of its Internet division to the more cybercool Zap. Like a lonely heart looking for a date, it began advertising in newspapers across the country to buy Web sites. It is a turn of events that Ms. Bowe says can sound like a parody of the Internet business, something Word itself might have published. The staff members now call a Louisiana fish meal company, one of Zapata's holdings, when they have questions about their health plan. ("They're really sweet," Ms. Bowe says of her new personnel department.) And the editors count among their new corporate colleagues the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, a team also owned by the Glazers. "It's all kind of nerve-racking," Ms. Bowe said one morning last week before meeting with her staff, "but that's the Internet business itself." She said that when she first heard about Zapata she "pictured some egomaniac Texan with a big hat going, 'Hey, I want to get into the content business.' " But whatever worries remain, her new backers have assured her not to worry about one thing: Word can continue to pursue its defiantly nontraditional vision without interference. It will still have no celebrity profiles and no reviews. It will continue to publish funny, raw, sometimes disturbing and mostly first-person articles about subjects ranging from sex to getting stabbed. In other words, it will continue to have a slim chance of raking in a lot of money. AVRAM GLAZER, Zapata's chief executive, seems not to mind. "We didn't buy them because we wanted People magazine," he said, adding that, besides, he finds Ms. Bowe "witty and easy to work with." The magazine is a creation that Ms. Bowe, 39, has been cultivating, almost unwittingly, for a long time. Growing up in Minneapolis, where her father worked for the Control Data Corporation, she would roam around a precursor to the Web developed by the Defense Department. In high school, she used the early technology mostly to flirt on line with male programmers. "So my first primal experiences with computers were all sexy, fun, social," she said.  Then came the second part of her education, in which she developed what she calls a populist's passion for the unadorned and unrehearsed in American culture. There was the job as a trainee lumberjack, then as a cocktail waitress and a taxi driver, all in Minneapolis ("my mini-Jack-Londonette trip"). She got involved in the city's punk scene, which meant mostly that she "chased the boys in the bands and got dressed up in cool clothes." Moving to newyork 13 years ago, she finally graduated from college, Columbia University, with a degree in modern European history. She became involved in a "Marxist guerrilla video collective" that produced angry public access television programs and then she managed an on-line interactive bulletin board. All of that left her with a distinct yearning to create a Web publication for "people turned off by the incessant glare of publicity and promotion and gloss and perfect people using perfect things." But one that was more funny than preachy. (A good sense of the tone can be gained by reading an editor's letter that Ms. Bowe posted at Word's Web site -- www.word.com -- which will become active again in September. Betraying a broad smirk, she asks loyal readers to remember that the magazine is "erudite, aggressively avant-garde, trenchant and metastasizing ergonomically," which is not always easy because it also tends to be hermeneutical and "ur-echt-gestalt-schadenfreude-y," which loosely translated means taking pleasure in pointing out American society's defects). Ms. Bowe said that the magazine world is filled with niche publications aimed at small groups of readers, like, for example, baking enthusiasts. "Word is for people with a certain kind of a sensibility," she said. "There are probably more of them out there than bakers." She added, smiling nervously, "But maybe not." title: Group Proposes Voluntary Guidelines for Internet Privacy - Correction Appended
body: In a continuing effort to head off new laws governing how companies can collect and use personal information gathered on the Internet about consumers, an industry coalition today proposed a voluntary enforcement program to certify World Wide Web sites that comply with privacy guidelines. Under the plan offered by the Online Privacy Alliance, Web sites that comply with the group's guidelines could display a seal of approval. While privacy advocates said the measure fell far short of the level of enforcement that is needed, the Clinton Administration, which has been critical of the electronic commerce industry's initial progress in policing itself, applauded the proposal. "I think the enforcement mechanisms that they are putting in place are what we have been calling for," said Ira Magaziner, Mr. Clinton's top adviser on electronic commerce. "Now what we need to do is monitor it to see that it really happens." The proposal was shown privately to Administration officials today. It will be publicly disclosed on Tuesday at a Congressional hearing on on-line privacy. Several recent polls have indicated that privacy is the No. 1 concern for Internet users. The proposed enforcement policy calls for appointing a third party to monitor compliance with the guidelines, which, among other things, require that consumers be told in advance what information is being collected and what it will used for. It would also establish a system to resolve consumer complaints. Christine Varney, a former Federal Trade Commission member who is working with the coalition, said, "To increase consumer confidence in cyberspace, companies need to have an independent and trusted third party validate compliance with clearly stated policies and confirm that companies are engaged in credible self-regulation." But some privacy advocates said the proposal did not go far enough. "We have concerns that the whole process of the alliance is voluntary, that it is a self-selecting pool of Web sites willing to engage in fair marketing practices," said Jeff Chester, spokesman for the Center for Media Education, a nonprofit children's advocacy organization in Washington. "This scheme does not protect all consumers." The F.T.C. earlier this year surveyed 1,400 Web sites and issued a report that found private-sector initiatives seriously lagging, especially regarding information collected from and about children. In its report, the commission recommended that legislation be passed to protect children from on-line marketers. Several bills have emerged, including a proposal by Representative Ed Bryant, a Tennessee Republican, that would give the F.T.C. the authority to write and enforce rules for protecting children on the Internet. While support for mandatory protections for children is almost universal, business and privacy groups are divided over whether laws are needed to cover adults. The Online Privacy Alliance, representing 50 companies and marketing groups, is leading the push for self-regulation. Last month, it released a set of privacy guidelines on the eve of a meeting called by the Department of Commerce to assess self-regulation efforts. The Commerce Department is drafting a report for President Clinton on whether self-regulation is working. Commerce officials lauded the alliance's goals but chastised companies for not having self-enforcement plans in place. Today's proposal attempts to answer that concern. The program would include periodic reviews of companies' practices and a complaint resolution system for consumers. Correction  An article in Business Day yesterday about voluntary guidelines on Internet privacy proposed by an industry coalition misidentified the author of a bill intended to protect the privacy of children on line. He is Senator Richard H. Bryan, a Nevada Democrat, not Representative Ed Bryant, a Tennessee Republican. Correction-Date: July 22, 1998, Wednesday

title: Broadcast.com Faces Risks After Strong Initial Offering
body: Take a piece of twine and run it between two empty dog food cans, and you have a sound transmission system with the approximate quality of many audio broadcasts over the Internet. Cover the stage of Carnegie Hall with 10 million $100 bills and you would see the amount of money that investors have poured into Broadcast.com Inc., a company devoted to putting radio and television programs on the Internet. Investors are apparently willing to overlook the current technical limitations of Internet broadcasting. On Friday, the first day of trading after Broadcast.com's initial public stock offering, the company's shares opened at $68, nearly four times higher than its $18 offering price. That was the biggest initial jump in the history of stock offerings in the unitedstates. The shares shot up to as high as $74 before closing at $62.75. At that price, Broadcast.Com has a total market value of $1.06 billion. The company was founded in 1995 by Todd R. Wagner and Mark Cuban, who began by putting the broadcasts of a Dallas radio station onto the Internet through a computer in a friend's bedroom. Mr. Cuban, 39, had run a computer consulting firm and a technology investment fund. Mr. Wagner, 37, is a lawyer and a certified public accountant. On paper, Mr. Cuban's share of the company stock is worth more than $350 million. Mr. Wagner's stake exceeds $200 million. Broadcast.com executives were unavailable for comment because the company is in its Government-mandated quiet period. Broadcast.com, which is based in Dallas and recently changed its name from Audionet, now offers transmissions of 345 radio stations, flickery images from 17 television stations, games from 350 sports teams and other talk and music programs. In return for helping broadcast stations extend their reach, Broadcast.com receives some on-air commercial time slots to sell to advertisers. It also can sell audio advertising that Internet listeners hear before joining the program of their choice. The company also sells on-screen ads that the audience members can view while they are listening. Broadcast.com also has a second business, broadcasting corporate presentations, like meetings for analysts, over the Internet, offering a lower cost alternative to telephone and video conference calls. Fans of the company say that as the technology for Internet broadcasting improves, Broadcast.com is in a prime position to capitalize on a medium that could be far more compelling than the text-based Internet is today. But analysts point out that the risk in its plans are at least as great as the opportunity. To start with, the company is small, and spending nearly twice as much money as it is taking in. In 1997, it lost $6.5 million on revenue of $6.9 million. And the company's prospectus filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission says it expects the losses to continue indefinitely. What is more, there appears to be little the company can do to defend against competition. "Anyone can do what they're doing," said David Simons, managing director of Digital Video Investments, a research service. "Net investors are impervious to the notion of competition." Yet both ESPN Sportzone and CBS Sportsline have their own Internet broadcasting service that competes with Broadcast.com's sports services. And Broadcast.com has exclusive Internet rights to only some of its programming. Other programs can be carried by its competitors. Broadcast.com does have some programs that it will probably not have to fight to keep, though. It runs a site called www.policescanner.com, for example, which transmits the emergency service radio broadcasts from newyork, Los Angeles and Dallas. Not only is that programming free -- it is supposed to sound like it is coming in on two dog food cans and twine.
