title: Survey Finds TV Is Major Casualty of Net Surfing
body: MOST of us know that Internet use is up. But what is down? With only 24 hours in a day, is cyberspace stealing time from sleeping, stepping on the Stairmaster, watching television or working? The answer, according to a new survey, is all of the above. The activity taking the biggest hit is television- and VCR-watching, according to the survey by Strategis Group, a Washington-based research firm that studies patterns in telecommunications use. Nearly 65 percent of 500 Net users surveyed said they had sacrificed time in front of the TV for time in front of the computer monitor. Forty-eight percent said they spent less time reading, and 29 percent said they slept less. The survey results, issued at the end of June, seemed to validate a trend reported in a similar poll last year by a newyork research company, Cyber Dialogue. It found that in addition to spending less time with their television sets, 22 percent of Internet regulars were also spending less time making long-distance phone calls. Cyber Dialogue further found that 16 percent of Net surfers were spending less time reading newspapers; an identical percentage spent less time reading magazines. Now for the more difficult question: What do these data mean? John Zahurancik, director of Internet and telephony at Strategis Group, said the findings that the Internet was stealing time from other media meant that the Net was sharing their stage. "The Net is becoming a mainstream medium," he said. "It is a competition to all these other traditional sources of entertainment." But scratch beneath the surface and the lessons are not so obvious or clear-cut, said Stuart Gibbel, director of marketing for Cyber Dialogue. Mr. Gibbel said it might be years before it is known what activities will suffer, diminish or even die because of the new medium. For instance, Mr. Gibbel said, a computer user may go on line to reinforce outside interests, like checking out a Web site for background on a favorite television show or ordering a book. Doug Milford, who owns a newyork art-management software company, Artsystems, and is an inveterate Net surfer, said that when he first encountered cyberspace, it was a black hole. "The Internet took from everything, including reading books, a social life, sleep," he said. "It's such a deep lake." Still, Mr. Milford says the Net now saves him time because it helps speed information gathering and other tasks, and that time can be spent on other activities. Further, Mr. Milford, who is 39, says he has mastered the art of simultaneously watching television and surfing the Net. Television executives are seeking to capitalize on this sort of crossover viewing. NBC, for example, hopes to use its television network to steer Net surfers to its Web site, and vice versa, according to Edmond Sanctis, senior vice president and general manager of NBC Digital Productions. In other words, if NBC is going to lose viewers to the Net, it wants to lose them to its own Web pages, where visitors can also be directed back to NBC. "This is a profound opportunity," he said. One thing that is certain is that the Web is being rapidly adopted by Americans. Allen Goldberg, vice president for business development at Relevant Knowledge, a research company based in Atlanta, noted that it took 40 years for radio to gain 50 million domestic listeners and 13 years each for television and cable television to each acquire 50 million domestic viewers. While acknowledging that the population is larger now, Mr. Goldberg said it was nonetheless noteworthy that it has taken only four years for the World Wide Web to reach that same plateau. Editor and Publisher magazine recently noted that people were going on line more frequently, with 61 percent of Internet users surfing the Net at least twice a week, up from 53 percent last year. However, that may not mean that people are spending more time on the Net. Cyber Dialogue found that the total time spent on line each week -- five hours -- did not change from the beginning of 1997 to the beginning of 1998.

title:
USER'S GUIDE;
Bumps in the Road With Netcasts
body: I AM still trying to repress memories of my own aborted attempt to use the Internet as a broadcast medium. Back in 1996, I was the host of a weekly on-line show called "Web Whirl," the goal of which was to take the audience along on a tour of a dozen or so Web sites. The show didn't work because most home users were at the wrong end of an information bottleneck. Relying on fickle modem connections, their on-line forays resembled uneasy games of Russian roulette. Would they connect on the first try? Or even the second? Would their connections fail in the middle of downloading a Web page? After a few months, the show was canceled. So when I heard that the Intel Corporation was planning to broadcast the live performances of 300 bands on line this week and call the adventure a "music festival," my first reaction was skepticism. After all, not much has changed in the past two years to erase the obstacles that doomed "Web Whirl." Today, with most home users still relying on finicky modems, will the so-called streaming video clip from a concert arrive instead as herky-jerky niblets of image? I hoped not. But my first glance at the Web page for the festival (which began last night and will run through Saturday) did not reassure me. The broadcast site at www.intelfest.com instructed me to download the software tool Real Player from Real Networks so I could hear and see the on-line performances. But my first two attempts failed because somewhere between the computer where Real Player was archived and my own desktop, the connection failed. With 300 bands playing live in 20 newyork City clubs for the four-day period, Intel faces an even greater technical challenge. For each band, the club sets up a microphone to capture vocals and the softer instruments like flutes and violins, mixing those sounds at a main sound desk. Another microphone supplied by Intel picks up other instruments, like drums and guitars. Then the feeds from both microphones are mixed and prepared for on-line broadcast on a personal computer that encodes the sound and translates it into digital bits. Intel broadcasts the digital transmission through two dual-Pentium II 333-megahertz servers, which in turn distribute the signals over the Internet. Performances at five clubs are also being broadcast in a simultaneous video feed. The home users with the best chance of enjoying the performances are those with newer equipment. While you might technically be able to connect to the festival's Web site on a poky old 486 machine, I doubt that you could enjoy the experience with anything less than a microprocessor that runs at 166 megahertz and employs MMX technology to enhance audio and video. As for modem speed? Well, frankly, there is no dial-up modem that pushes sound and video across the Net reliably enough -- or fast enough -- to satisfy me. "So why bother?" the curmudgeon in me wondered. The whole venture sounded like a flashback to the early days of radio or TV, with the broadcasters relying on an uneasy combination of prayer, spit and willpower to overcome inevitably choppy transmissions. But then, those early broadcasts, imperfect though they may have been, were exciting partly because of the unknown limits of raw technology. The roughness was fraught with endless possibility. So maybe I was being unfair to the Internet -- and to Intel -- by expecting too much too soon from this nascent medium. Why not give everyone points for trying? During a similar festival that Intel sponsored last year, 125,000 computer users tuned in, er, connected -- five times as many as attended the live performances. Weren't those numbers an indication that the experiment was at least somewhat successful in increasing people's access to music? A closer look at the schedule on the festival Web site also swayed me. The musicians in that eclectic group of 300 bands, whose sounds include rock, punk, rap, jazz and folk -- would surely not have agreed to participate in this endeavor if they felt that the medium failed to convey their message. There must be benefits from playing to an on-line audience that would outweigh the apparent lack of intimacy between performer and listener. I decided to ask a singer, Victoria Williams, who was scheduled to perform in the festival live (and on line) at the Bowery Ballroom last night. A few days before the performance, I spoke on the phone to Ms. Williams to tell her that I had just been listening to the folky, lyrical stories she sang on "This Moment in Toronto With Victoria Williams," recorded live in 1995. "Do you think that you will interact differently with an on-line audience?" I asked. There was a moment of silence on the phone that lasted just long enough to make me wonder if the connection had failed. "I had no idea that this is an on-line concert that I'm doing," Ms. Williams said. "I thought it was a live concert." I explained about the computers that would transmit her performance across the Net. "You mean that people are going to be able to watch it on their computers, but it will sound kind of broken up, with herky-jerky video?" she asked. I told her I wasn't sure whether the Bowery Ballroom was one of the five clubs that would transmit simultaneous video. (I quickly tried to check the Web site for her, but my connection stalled.) But Ms. Williams sounded so unhappy about the possibility that I felt bad for her. "Maybe it will all work fine," I said, trying to sound as if I had not lived through the broadcast disappointment of "Web Whirl." After all, I went on, here was a medium that might have the power to propel her music to a whole new audience -- to millions of people around the world who could not physically attend her concert. Maybe the Internet would prove to be as potent a broadcast tool as television had been in 1964 when Ed Sullivan introduced the Beatles to 73 million viewers. "Wouldn't that be great?" I said cheerily. "I've just never seen it like that, but it would be incredible," Ms. Williams agreed. She paused again. "Or maybe the band and I could just walk kind of herky-jerky in the club, and shuffle our feet a bit, to give the live audience the Internet experience." Graphic   Drawing. (Margaret Riegel)

title: Videoconferencing's Killer App May Be Sex
body: VIDEOPHONES add a new dimension of anxiety to the familiar problem of the phone ringing while you are in the bathtub. It turns out, however, that thousands of people actually look forward to video calls while they, and their callers, are undressed. In fact, as is typically the case with a new technology, early adopters of videoconferencing have discovered that the so-called killer app is sex. From Kansas to Kiev, Internet users are enthusiastically embracing Net-based videoconferencing that allows them to play show-and-tell with other uninhibited souls. The Microsoft Corporation and other companies that make videoconferencing products say that while sex-related applications are a very visible use of the new technology, the most common applications are indeed for business: conducting meetings, collaborating on work projects and telecommuting, for example. But there are also some people -- thousands, actually -- who use the technology to exhibit themselves, in real time, without clothes and to watch others doing the same. All it takes is a recent-model personal computer, an Internet connection, conferencing software, a microphone and a video camera. For voyeurs, even less equipment is needed. Thousands of commercial sex sites on the Internet offer live video to customers. But for two-way video and audio, it gets a bit more complicated. One of the most popular software packages for Internet videoconferencing is Net Meeting, which is free from Microsoft. To make it easy for software users to find one another, Microsoft has set up a half-dozen Internet Locator Server computers. There are probably 200 public locator servers on the Net. There may be thousands more on private networks. On one morning this week, the Adults Only directory on a server run by Microsoft was fully populated with users who had registered their home countries as Canada, China, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Taiwan, Korea and Turkey, among others. Users from the unitedstates accounted for about half of the connections. Net Meeting users register to be included in a directory that displays names, email addresses, home locations and special interests. On the Adults Only directory, very few people use their real names or email addresses. Tom Laemmel, a product manager for Net Meeting, said Microsoft did not encourage the use of its products for what he called risque activities. "We're looking for technology to solve the problem," he said. But he added, "We're not in the business of trying to police the stuff." Mr. Laemmel said users could screen out other directory entries and get an unlisted number. "I use Net Meeting with my mom all the time, and frankly, it could be embarrassing if she saw all the directory listings," he said, but they bypass the directories and call each other directly. "Luckily, she never even logs on to the Internet Locator Server."

title: Web Hears You Knocking But You Can't Come In
body: FOR anybody who wonders what the neighborhood would look like from the viewpoint of a low-flying aircraft, Microsoft's Terra Server -- a database of aerial and satellite images -- may provide an answer. But many who tried to visit the site after it went on line recently saw absolutely nothing (www.terraserver.microsoft.com). Nothing, that is, except for an hourglass or a spinning ball, occasionally followed (with some browsers) by "403.9 Access Forbidden. Too many users are connected." Some futurists (and now, apparently, the cable giant TCI and the telephone giant AT&T, which intends to take over TCI) may believe that the World Wide Web and television will one day be indistinguishable, but it looks as though some work needs to be done first. While television programs have always been available to all who tune in, Web pages too often are not. The reasons why you may not be able to get to a Web site are numerous, and the "explanatory" phrases that appear on the monitor are cryptic at best, useless at worst. Like the Long Island Expressway, the Web often has trouble getting travelers to their destinations because of heavy traffic. And even when Web surfers manage to get to a page, many may find the door slammed in their faces because thousands of people are trying to squeeze simultaneously through the same narrow entranceway into the site's computer servers. "When people can't access sites, it's usually not the PC's or the phone line's fault," said Igor Shindel, vice president of technology for Time Inc. New Media, operators of Time Warner's Pathfinder site (www.pathfinder. com) and linked areas, which include Time, Fortune and People. "The problem typically lies in the general load on the Web, or the load on the actual server farm." Requests for a site's material must go to a server, a computer (or a chain of them) that stores the information. The www.pathfinder. com site keeps its Web pages on eight Sun Microsystems multiprocessor computers running Solaris 2.6 and maintains five copies of the pages to protect the site from crashes. The 300,000 pages of the Microsoft Web site (www.microsoft.com) are held on 58 Compaq computers, each with 4 processors. Each of these $25,000 behemoths contains a 30-gigabyte hard drive and 512 megabytes of RAM. Duplicate (or "mirrored") information is held in similar sites in Tokyo and London, said Tim Sinclair, Microsoft.com's editor in chief. Like someone getting a busy signal when trying to make a phone call, a user who cannot get into a Web site should keep trying. Every person who ends a connection instantaneously makes room for another. Sites that offer software for downloading can get tied up for even longer periods. While viewing a Web page requires just a few seconds of connect time, downloading the latest version of Internet Explorer could require 20 minutes to 3 hours on line, limiting the number of people who can get to the servers. Even the large capacities of the more popular Web sites do not mean easy access. A site may go down for many reasons, like a lost connection with an Internet service provider or a decision by the site's administrator to remove it from the Net temporarily to update its pages. If a smaller site goes down, the reason could be even more quirky -- a child might have run behind his mother's desk and tripped over the server's electrical cord. Sites may also appear to be unavailable when they are actually just loading at a snail's pace. Pages with lots of graphics will load slowly, causing some users to hit their browser's Stop button in the mistaken belief that nothing is happening. Sometimes your browser will tell you in a small window at the bottom of the screen just what it is trying to do -- getting in contact with the host's server or downloading material, for instance. Typing the wrong Web address (the U.R.L., or uniform resource locator) -- even if it is off by only one letter or digit -- will also block access to the site. (Some Web site providers, especially those with pornographic sites, take advantage of misspellings by registering site names that are just one letter away from the spellings of popular ones, so unsuspecting users will go there by accident.) Or you may click on a link from a home page or Internet search engine like Yahoo or Alta Vista but wind up going nowhere because the page is no longer there, even though there is still a record of it. According to a recent survey by the All Things Web site (www.pantos.org/atw), which explains how to set up Web sites, Internet pages are getting bigger, and the number of missing links, pointing to nonexistent pages, has ballooned in the past year. Today, the average page weighs in at 61 kilobytes, up from 44 a year ago, while the incidence of missing links has increased by almost 40 percent. Today, 23 percent of all pages have at least one dead link. A consortium is trying to find ways to eliminate many of the problems with gaining access to Web sites. It is working on Internet 2, a next-generation service that will increase the size of the electronic road to Web sites (the bandwidth), making it 10 to 100 times as large, said a consortium member, Mario Gerla, a professor of computer science at the University of California at Los Angeles. The plan calls for an Internet that will sense when multitudes are trying to gain access to a particular site and will automatically copy that site's pages to another local server. Now if only someone can figure out how to keep that child from running into the computer power cord. Graphic   Graph: Here are the most common types of connection messages and what you can do to avoid some of them. The actual wording of the messages may vary, depending on the Web site.  The Server Does Not Have a DNS Entry After you type a Web address, your Internet provider looks up its numeric Web equivalent; this message indicates that it cannot find one. Sometimes you have done nothing wrong, and trying again with the same address solves the problem. Sometimes the address was typed incorrectly. And sometimes there is a problem with the server.  Spinning Hourglass or Beach Ball A connection is being made. If the hourglass or ball persists, "an Internet router somewhere along the path to your site is down," said Tim Brady, executive producer of the Yahoo search engine. Try again.  404-Not Found You have arrived at the correct server, but the exact page you are looking for cannot be found. If you have not mistyped the address, the page probably no longer exists or has been moved. Sometimes it helps to back up: remove every part of the address to the right of the first single slash. That way, you will see if the site is still active, and you can try to search within the site for the page you want. If the address ends in .htm, try .html, or vice versa.  503-Service Unavailable . . . . . . Too much network traffic, service temporarily overloaded, network connection was refused by the server, gateway timeout: these are variations on the theme of site overload -- too many people are trying to get into a site at the same time. The only solution is to keep trying.  401-Unauthorized and 403-Forbidden You have either failed to enter a password or the one you entered is wrong. Or the site may be available only to users from a particular Internet domain, like microsoft.com for Microsoft employees.  Drawings.

title: www.HowSmartAreYou.quiz
body: BORED with chat? Tired of shopping on the Web? Sick of email from your relatives? How about taking a test? That's right, a test. The World Wide Web has become a breeding ground for psychometricians, professional and otherwise, who are filling cyberspace with thousands of tests that you can administer to yourself. It is difficult to log on these days without being collared by someone with just a few questions that purport to test your intelligence, your emotional well-being or your predisposition to depression, alcoholism, hypochondria, diabetes or attention deficit disorder. The odd thing is that people seem to like to take these tests. In a world in which children spend years suffering through tests, why adults would take them for fun is a mystery. But there is something alluring about an optional quiz, with its promise of ranking you in terms of your lovability or likelihood of having a heart attack. Just look at the number of quizzes in magazines, on television and radio, and now, in spades, on the Web. Aptitude tests with actual relevance to the workaday world are still hard to find on line. Someday, certainly, it will be possible to take the SAT on the Net. But not yet, because the College Board, which administers the test, still considers the Net insufficiently secure. But late at night or on a rainy day, the Net offers a chance to quiz yourself silly, to find out how you rank in every imaginable context. And on the Web, there are no visible proctors or stopwatches, and no one to raise an eyebrow at your response to a question about sexual habits. For instance, you might scoff at Mensa, the organization of self-anointed geniuses, but it is hard to turn down the chance to spend three minutes on a test to see if you would be admitted. "I love the idea of being able to confront your deepest fears in private," said Jim Goldberg, a 51-year-old management consultant in Sonoma, Calif., who took the Mensa test. "And it's comforting to know that even if I do score like an intellectual and emotional misfit, it can remain my own little secret." Mr. Goldberg is one of a small group of people recruited by Circuits, in a purely unscientific fashion, to explore the Web's variety of tests. The group included a doctor, a lawyer, a British civil servant, a writer, a consultant, a German freelance journalist and an Internet project manager. Members of the group recently chose from a dozen or so Web-based tests -- including a test that promised to gauge I.Q., an emotional quotient test and a karma calibrator -- and sampled whatever struck their fancy. By day's end, all had discovered that they were geniuses but also emotionally dysfunctional karmic failures. But it is difficult to know how private an on-line test really is, or what kind of data the test is collecting -- particularly when it starts out by testing knowledge of your name, address and telephone number. The first stop for Robert Wallich, 39, an earnest civil servant in London, was the Karmometer. The test can be found on the Random House page for Laura Esquivel's novel "The Law of Love." It promises to tell you how karmically evolved you are, as well as your chances of finding your soul mate in your current lifetime. The test includes this question: "It is the Golden Age of Spain and you are a valiant captain in Cortez's army. You are rewarded for your bravery in the conquest of Mexico with a house atop an ancient pyramid of great religious significance." Your choices: (a) Accept the house. You deserve it. (b) Offer it back to the aboriginal people. (c) Keep the house but free your slaves. "Karmically challenged" was the verdict for Mr. Wallich, who chose (a) when the karmically correct answer was presumably (b). (The Karmometer's creators do not supply the correct answers, preferring perhaps for test-takers to divine them.) Regine Wosnitza, on the other hand, a 39-year-old freelance journalist in Berlin who is a firm believer in reincarnation and the powers of karma, was disappointed in the Karmometer for a different reason. "The questions themselves, I thought, had nothing to do with real karma theory," she said. Like Mr. Wallich, Ms. Wosnitza was told that she would have to wait until her next lifetime to find her soul mate. "I am not too happy about that," she said. Neither Ms. Wosnitza nor Mr. Wallich thought to purchase Ms. Esquivel's novel from the Random House site. Susan McCarthy, 43, a science and humor writer in San Francisco, tried her hand at a New Age I.Q. test. Her score: Very Good. "This score was despite my refusal to agree that alien spaceships landed at Roswell," Ms. McCarthy said. "I said it was a high-altitude weather balloon, and they told me that was wrong. I have references, but there was nobody there to fight with." Few could resist the emotional intelligence quiz. This test, which is offered on the Utne Reader's Web site, was written by Daniel Goleman, who covered behavioral science for The newyork Times for a number of years. Not surprisingly, it is based on Mr. Goleman's best-selling book, "Emotional Intelligence." The test includes such stumpers as this: "Imagine you're an insurance salesman calling prospective clients. Fifteen people in a row have hung up on you, and you're getting discouraged. What do you do? (a) Call it a day and hope you have better luck tomorrow. (b) Assess qualities in yourself that may be undermining your ability to make a sale. (c) Try something new in the next call and keep plugging away. (d) Consider another line of work." Scoring well on that question -- the "correct" answer is (c) -- and most others on the test isn't easy. The median score of the volunteer group was 60 out of a possible 200. That could lead a cynic to wonder if the test is aimed, ever so subliminally, at suggesting to people that they bolster their emotional wherewithal by reading the book. Handily enough, the book is available straight from the Utne Web site, through a direct link to Amazon.com. Many of the wandering test takers complained about the thinly disguised effort at marketing. Dr. Kirk Neely, an endocrinologist who lives in Portola Valley, Calif., is an easygoing 44-year-old whose happy domestic life -- he has been married for more than 18 years -- is something to which many of his friends aspire, but he flunked the emotional test with a score of 80. "I was honest," he said. "When I went back and answered the way sincere self-improvers would probably want you to behave, I got a 180." Intelligence tests on the Web are something else altogether. The widely adopted, if also controversial, Wechsler and Stanford-Binet I.Q. tests are hard to find on line, if they are there at all. Still, dozens of Web sites say they offer a test of basic intelligence, and those tests appear to be enormously popular. One cottage purveyor of I.Q. tests says he gets more than 200 email messages each day regarding his tests. This kind soul, who administers his tests from his home in China, reminds his visitors, in large type: "LOW POINTS DO NOT NECESSARILY MEAN YOU ARE NOT SMART." One particularly easy test that supposedly gauges intelligence can be found at www.iqtest.com, where several of those smarting from a slap from Mr. Goleman's test found salve for their psyches. In contrast with Mr. Goleman's workout, this test is hard to flub. "The early questions were at the level of my 9-year-old," Dr. Neely said. "The later ones were more subtle and thus more satisfying. The following slowed me down: 'Does an inside-out left-handed glove fit a right hand?' and 'Can your niece be your aunt?' I kept thinking, from the odd groups I've seen, it must be possible." Dr. Neely reported scoring a remarkable 158, which put him, he said, "between Plato and Darwin." When a couple of stragglers clicked on the I.Q. test site, they were startled to see that it had been hijacked by a hacker threatening (with many misspellings) to "reveal the I.Q. scorez of all the pplz I hate," including President Clinton, Monica S. Lewinsky and all French people. About 24 hours later, the site was restored, leaving no trace of the hacker. Such are the potential hazards of an idle traipse through cyberspace. Stephen Tobias, 54, a lawyer in Oakland, Calif., turned to the Web site of the newyork University psychiatry department, where he found a test to screen for attention deficit disorder. "It told me that my procrastination was a possible symptom of attention deficit disorder that perhaps should be evaluated by a psychiatrist," Mr. Tobias said. Dr. Neely and Mr. Goldberg were told the same. "Procrastination and disorganization are my major faults," Dr. Neely said. "If my major faults indicated A.D.D., 70 percent of the adult population would be on Ritalin." But Dr. Lenard Adler, director of the newyork University Hospital for Joint Diseases' Attention Deficit Disorder Center, which sponsors the test, cautioned that the Web-based test is "not in any way, shape or form meant to be diagnostic." Mr. Tobias noted that the psychiatry department offered a phone number for referrals -- to the Attention Deficit Disorder Center. He said: "The Web is an interesting place for an A.D.D. screen. When I first encountered it, I thought Web surfing itself might be symptomatic." Not all the recruits enjoyed the tests. Mr. Tobias recommended against Web tests: "Don't bother. The tests I took struck me as simple-minded, commercial or both." But Jon Lebkowsky, 49, "the Internet guy" for the Whole Foods Market in Austin, Tex., enjoyed the tests. "I now know that I am truly an excellent person," he said. "However, my stomach's still growling, my deadlines are still hanging over my head, and I'm still prone to the same anxieties and depressions. Now what?" Mr. Lebkowsky might consider pointing his browser toward the newyork University depression screening test. Or perhaps he should quit while he's ahead and log off.  SITE-SEEING: QUIZZES Here's a sampling of Web sites with self-tests:  EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE: www.utne.com/cgi-bin/eq BRAIN TEASERS, RIDDLES AND OTHER TESTS: www.puzz.com  NEW AGE I.Q. TEST: www.salemctr.com/iqtest.html  THE KARMOMETER: www.randomhouse.com/lawoflove/karm.html  MENSA: www.canada.mensa.org/mensa/workout.html  AN EASY I.Q. title: Taking a Step Toward Converting The Home Into a Supercomputer
body: For more than 25 years, computer scientists have been working to develop a technology known as distributed computing that would put the processing power of a supercomputer in the hands of average users. For scientists and others who need enormous computing power, distributed computing holds out the promise of increasing the power of a standard laptop exponentially. But for the average consumer, it will eventually produce smart gadgets such as cars that avoid traffic jams and phones that know not just the telephone number of every listed person in the unitedstates but their addresses, ZIP codes and the names of their family members. In short, distributed computing promises to endow consumer appliances -- from telephones, televisions and stereos to kitchen appliances and cars -- with an infusion of borrowed intelligence by connecting them, with or without wires, to a computer network. On Wednesday, Sun Microsystems will unveil the first consumer version of this technology, a product called Jini, which uses Sun's Java programming language to harness the power of potentially millions of computers, ranging from giant mainframes to tiny palm-sized devices. "We now have all the ingredients to build a distributed computing fabric which approaches science fiction," said David Farber, a University of Pennsylvania computer scientist who pioneered distributed computing in 1971. "You will be able to sit with your laptop, and it will be able to reach out across the network. And for the moments you need the power, it will become the largest supercomputer in the world." It could also shift the balance of power in the computer industry. At a time when worried governments on three continents are struggling to restrain the Microsoft Corporation's iron grip on computing and its ambitions on the Internet, distributed computing could level the playing field by shifting growth in high-technology industries to the millions of consumer appliances that increasingly contain powerful embedded processors. Indeed, Microsoft itself is known to be working on a system similar to Jini, known as Millennium. But Sun, among Microsoft's fiercest competitors, has an early advantage in this race because of the nature of its Java programming language, which is designed to move chunks of computer code from machine to machine. Jini uses this ability in ways that allow computers and other devices to cooperate, sometimes by sharing instructions or information, sometimes by actually dividing a program into parts and spreading the computation work across several computers. In addition, Java has already achieved widespread distribution -- thanks, in part, to Microsoft, which ships it with its Internet Explorer browser for navigating the World Wide Web and with Windows 98. Although Sun is suing Microsoft for making unauthorized changes to Java, the Microsoft version of the language will support Jini. If all goes according to Sun's plans, over the next 18 months, a number of companies that make computer hardware and consumer gadgets will begin incorporating Jini, allowing each of these devices to talk with each other and to share processing power. Among the first of these will be the Quantum Corporation, a disk drive maker based in Milpitas, Calif., that intends to commercialize the Jini technology to make drives that have built-in office network connections. Today, such connections are controlled by the operating system and are difficult to configure. "There is definitely going to be a dramatic leap in ease of use," said Paul Borrill, vice president and chief architect at Quantum. Over the next few years, advocates of distributed computing predict, today's desktop computer will evolve from a self-sufficient machine that must hold all the memory, storage and processing power it needs for any job into a social machine that will automatically interact not only with other computers but also with myriad consumer devices. Microsoft, potentially, has the most to lose from such a change since it would make the operating system incidental to the power and control wielded by a networked computer in a distributed system. For that reason, Microsoft would hold no obvious advantage over competitors in marketing a distributed computing technology. Unlike its competitors and computer scientists, who view distributed computing as the antithesis of an operating system, Microsoft prefers to think of it as the operating system of the future. In a recent paper on its Millennium product, a Microsoft research team wrote: "We argue that advances in hardware and networking technology enable a new kind of operating system to support tomorrow's applications. Such an operating system would raise the level of abstraction for developers and users, so that individual computers, file systems and networks become unimportant to most computations in the same way that processor registers, disk sectors, and physical pages are today." Processor registers, disk sectors and physical pages are all elements of hardware that today are controlled by an operating system. But there is a catch to all of this: The technology at the heart of this evolution is the network, and all the assumptions about the future of distributed computing are based on the belief that computer networks will be ubiquitous -- and, in most cases, wireless. On a large scale, such networks are now being deployed by cellular telephone companies and by computer industry groups working on new standards for wireless office networks. Once these technologies are available to consumers, beginning later this year, the stage will be set for a fundamental change in personal computing. It is the network, which can range in size from a group of linked household devices to the global Internet, that is the foundation upon which the new distributed computing will be built. The essence of distributed computing is the ability to divide a large set of computer instructions into multiple small parts, each of which is processed by a different machine within a network of computers. Until now, each generation of computers -- mainframes, minicomputers and personal computers -- has been built on a foundation of centralized control wielded by an operating system, a single, monolithic program that performs the combined role of a traffic cop, butler and secretary. But the recent proliferation of high-speed and wireless networks and the melding of computing and telecommunications technologies driven by the Internet has encouraged developers to proceed on the assumption that every home, car and other personal environment will eventually be part of -- and empowered by -- a universal network. For that reason, it is sometimes known as "ubiquitous computing." Distributed computing foresees a world in which millions of small programs, called objects, seamlessly flit back and forth between tens of thousands of devices that have been enabled to recognize and be recognized by the network. For example, in a world of cars equipped with distributed computing devices linked by a wireless network, each car would be delivering and receiving information from every other car, or to and from aggregated traffic reports, along the route being driven. This kind of networking could significantly reduce traffic congestion by alerting drivers to accidents, congestion and weather conditions. In such a world, the traditional operating system, say advocates of distributed computing, becomes an ungainly encumbrance, akin to asking a baton-wielding maestro to conduct a jam session of jazz musicians. Moreover, in such a distributed world, the boundary lines between individual computers blur as thousands or even millions of computers are harnessed to particular tasks as exotic as predicting the weather or as mundane as controlling the heating and lighting in a building. "The trend is very clear," said William Joy, a co-founder of Sun Microsystems and the chief designer of Jini. "We are moving toward a world in which it will be possible to move software codes that act as our personal agents between many different computers in a global network." Advocates of distributed computing envision a computerized world in which each person will be surrounded by a web of hundreds of small computers embedded in everything from smart cameras, to pagers, to cell phones and hand-held computers that will exchange messages and data without the intervention of a centralized computer. Sun's Jini is scheduled to be publicly described for the first time on Wednesday on Sun's Web site. It will be marketed in September under the name Java Tone, an analogy to the ubiquitous nature of the telephone dial tone. Sun says it is now working with more than 30 companies, ranging from the Federal Express Corporation to the giant software maker Computer Associates, to develop Java Tone products. For the last decade Mr. Joy, who co-founded Sun after dropping out of graduate school at the University of California at Berkeley, has holed up in a small laboratory in the mountains of Colorado where he has been attempting to reinvent modern computing by exploiting the concepts of distributed computing. Four years ago, Mr. Joy's small group of researchers decided to put into effect the ideas of David Gelernter, a computer scientist and author from Yale University who invented a computing language called Linda that was intended to enable the writing of programs that could utilize the power of many computers simultaneously. Mr. Gelernter's original vision was a vast distributed computer to simulate much of the surrounding social and physical world. He called his vision "Mirror Worlds" and described it in a 1992 book by that name (Oxford University Press). "The guts of an operating system have always been an ensemble of small programs, but that aspect has always been suppressed in favor of the monolithic desktop," Mr. Gelernter said. "Sun is breaking the news to the user that an ensemble is a simple and natural and straightforward computing model." Graphic   Photo: William Joy, a co-founder of Sun Microsystems, is the chief designer of Jini, which would endow common appliances with borrowed intelligence available from powerful computer networks. (Thor Swift for The New York Times)(pg. D4)  Diagram: "The Network Becomes the Computer" Sun Microsystems' new Jini system would vastly increase the computing power available to ordinary users by allowing all devices that speak the Java programming language -- computers and, potentially, an array of consumer products from cameras to air-conditioners -- to communicate and cooperate with one another. Below, how the system compares with current personal computers.  CURRENT SYSTEM Printers, scanners, data storage drives and (with some difficulty) consumer devices are attached to the computer and controlled by its operating system and specialized software. To get a digital camera to print out an image, for example, the computer must download the image and then issue commands to an attached printer.  The computer is linked by cables to its peripheral devices.  JINI SYSTEM Each device can communicate directly with every other device so that many tasks are handled independent of a computer. So a computer can monitor and adjust the thermostat on an air- conditioning system while a digital camera prints a photograph directly to a printer and a stereo saves a recording to a data storage device, which may not even be in the same building.  The network is made up of high-speed cable or wireless connections, either local or remote.  (Source: Sun Microsystems)(pg. D4)

title: Cuban Exiles Say Times Articles Are Baseless
body: The Cuban-American National Foundation today dismissed as "baseless" a series of articles that have appeared in The newyork Times in recent days about ties between leaders of the group and a Cuban exile who has acknowledged carrying out a series of bombings in Cuba last year. The foundation said there was "no truth to any of the allegations made in the story." At a news conference here this afternoon at which he was flanked by leaders of the organization, Jorge Mas Jr., a son of the late founder of the group, described the articles as part of an effort to weaken the foundation in order to end the American economic embargo against Cuba. He also questioned whether an interview with the exile commando leader, Luis Posada Carriles, had taken place at all. In an interview with a Spanish-language television station in Miami today that was later broadcast at the news conference, Mr. Posada confirmed that he had talked with The Times about his relationship with the foundation and its leaders. But he denied that foundation leaders had ever supported him financially or that he served as the armed wing of the movement. The Times article said that Mr. Posada agreed to about six hours of tape-recorded interviews in which he said his efforts were supported financially for more than a decade by leaders of the foundation. "I don't represent the armed wing of any exile organization and I don't belong to the foundation," he said in the television interview. "I am an independent man, which is why I call myself Solo." He added, "I make a living from my work, from the sale of my paintings and my books."

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Canadian Ruling Unmasks a Company's Internet Critics
body: In a ruling that may impose new limits on some on-line discussions, a Canadian court has unmasked several pseudonymous critics that attacked an Ontario-based recycling company on an Internet message board. While the company, the Philip Services Corporation, has not yet sued for libel, it contends that it has been defamed by comments posted in a finance forum on Yahoo, a popular World Wide Web site. Last month, a court in Toronto ruled for the company, ordering 12 Internet service providers to turn over the names of subscribers who used aliases in expressing their often-vituperative opinions. At least one Internet service provider complied with the order last week. Recent Internet postings about Philip included personal attacks on its executives, with racial slurs and threats, said Lynda Kuhn, a company spokeswoman. "A couple of posters began making remarks and all of a sudden it was open season," Ms. Kuhn said. "We believe that laws that apply to any form of communication should also apply to this one." The case underscores the fact most Internet communications are not truly anonymous. Although many Internet service providers have policies protecting the privacy of their subscribers, they have frequently turned over records, including subscribers' real names, to law enforcement authorities. Some critics said the ruling could have a chilling effect on Internet communication, at least in Canada. Indeed the ruling has set off a heated debate about the balance between anonymity and accountability. In an editorial on the case yesterday, The Toronto Globe and Mail cited Emile Zola's defense of Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish officer in the French Army falsely accused of treason, in urging Internet users to remember that "a real name adds conviction, credibility and moral authority to a denunciation." "Libel is still libel, even on the World Wide Web," the editorial said. Based in Hamilton on the west end of Lake Ontario, Philip has had a hard few months. A copper trading scandal and the departure of many of its senior managers have contributed to a recent steep drop in its stock. Many of the Internet critics insist they were simply relaying important information that the company would rather not have had publicized. One participant on Monday pointedly posted a quote from a former Canadian Prime Minister on the Canadian Bill of Rights: "I am a Canadian, free to speak without fear." Legal experts said one question posed by the case was whether anonymous accusations carried enough weight to be considered defamatory. That may become more important as Internet users realize that the anonymity they have now is by no means ironclad. "The Constitution protects anonymous speech, but that doesn't matter if Internet service providers don't provide it," said Mike Godwin, author of "Cyber Rights," published last month by Random House. If consumers demanded it, Mr. Godwin said, technology now available that would provide true anonymity so that service providers would have no information to turn over, even if ordered to do so by a court, would be more widely used. John Gallagher, 49, an active poster on the Yahoo board whose identity was made known to Philip last week by his service provider, Weslink Datalink, said he felt justified in using an alias. A former Hamilton City Council Representative, Mr. Gallagher said he had been publicly involved in various controversies and wanted to protect his privacy. "People have a right to know what this company is doing," Mr. Gallagher said. But he acknowledged that the pseudonymous communication allowed the discussion at times to become "aggressive."

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
MCI Reported To Be Near Full Internet Sale
body: The MCI Communications Corporation is close to an agreement to sell its entire Internet business to Cable and Wireless P.L.C. for $1.5 billion to $2 billion in cash, executives close to the negotiations said yesterday. A deal between the companies could be announced this week, the executives said, adding that minor negotiating points remained unresolved yesterday. The executives speculated that the only possible development that could scuttle a deal would be the existence of separate, secret talks between MCI and another buyer. The deal would clear the way for the Justice Department to approve the $37 billion acquisition of MCI by Worldcom Inc. While the Federal Communications Commission would also have to rule on the MCI-Worldcom deal, few people in Washington or on Wall Street expect the commission's review to be onerous for the companies in the way the Justice Department's antitrust analysis has been. Justice Department officials, along with antitrust regulators from the European Union, have been concerned that a combined MCI and Worldcom could dominate the Internet business. Worldcom's Uunet operation is the biggest Internet service provider, while MCI is also a major Internet carrier. Opponents of the deal have said that the combined company could control as much as 70 percent of the market for wholesale access to cyberspace. MCI has tried to allay those concerns before. In May it announced that it had sold its wholesale Internet business to Cable and Wireless, an international communications company based in Britain, for $625 million. The unit that MCI initially agreed to sell served smaller Internet companies that in turn sold services to consumers. At the time, MCI said that deal would be sufficient to answer the antitrust questions of regulators. "By divesting MCI's Internet backbone, we have eliminated any overlap with Worldcom's Internet business," Bert C. Roberts Jr., MCI's chairman, said. "We have formed an agreement that addresses antitrust concerns with the MCI-Worldcom merger." The regulators did not agree. As the GTE Corporation led the lobbying effort against both of MCI's pending deals, the American and European antitrust officials maintained that MCI would have to sell its units that offer cyberspace services directly to businesses and consumers in addition to the wholesale division. Any new deal between MCI and Cable and Wireless would include those divisions. The antitrust officials and GTE would have preferred that Worldcom sell Uunet, but Worldcom refused. The $1.5-billion-to-$2-billion negotiating range would include the $625 million that Cable and Wireless already agreed to pay MCI, executives close to the talks said last night. Like MCI's original deal with Cable and Wireless, any subsequent agreement would also make the sale contingent on MCI's being acquired by Worldcom, the executives said. MCI, Cable and Wireless and the Justice Department all declined to comment yesterday. People close to MCI and the Justice Department said that the department had all but agreed to approve the MCI-Worldcom deal if MCI struck an additional deal with Cable and Wireless that included the units that sell Internet services to consumers and business customers. When MCI first explored selling parts of its Internet business, Justice Department officials told the company that GTE and the Sprint Corporation would not be acceptable buyers. GTE and Sprint are big Internet companies, and the officials were concerned that a sale to either of them would fail to refashion the industry's competitive landscape. Cable and Wireless was of interest to both MCI and the regulators because it is a hungry, hefty company that is not a huge-scale communications competitor in the unitedstates.  Sale to Italians Is Off LONDON, July 13 (Dow Jones) -- Cable and Wireless said today that it would withdraw from a deal to sell its 20 percent stake in Bouygues Telecom to Telecom Italia S.p.A. and would instead sell it to shareholders of the French mobile phone operator. Cable and Wireless also said it was now unlikely that Telecom Italia would acquire a direct interest in its subsidiaries in North America and the Caribbean in the foreseeable future. But it confirmed that talks on both a global alliance and a possible investment by Telecom Italia in its unitedstates and Caribbean businesses were continuing. The announcement represented a big step back from an agreement reached in April, under which Telecom Italia was to have bought Cable and Wireless's stake in Bouygues Telecom for $743 million in cash. The Italian phone company was also to have acquired as much as 20 percent of the West Indies unit of Cable and Wireless and 5 percent of its North American business. Telecom Italia noted that it remained in discussions with Cable and Wireless, but declined to comment further.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
A Marketing Pact; A Strategy Pact
body: Two sets of companies announced agreements yesterday without disclosing their terms. Quantum Leap Communications, part of Leap Group in Chicago, signed an Internet marketing agreement with Broadvision Inc. in Redwood City, Calif. Broadvision makes software that enables businesses to build custom Internet sites for electronic commerce, customer service and delivery of interactive content. The two companies will jointly sell Web-based marketing and commerce software, using Broadvision applications and content from Quantum Leap. After the agreement was announced, Leap shares more than doubled in price, closing on Nasdaq at $7, up $3.78125. And two design firms -- Deskey Associates in newyork and Raymond Loewy International Ltd. in London -- have formed a strategic alliance. The alliance is meant to promote Loewy's expansion in the unitedstates and provides Deskey with broader access to clients in Asia, Europe and the Middle East. The companies will serve worldwide clients together and market their combined resources as well as work independently on existing assignments. Deskey works for clients like Black & Decker, I.B.M., Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble, while Loewy works for clients like Barilla, Exxon and Nestle.

title:
Compressed Data;
Trying to Interpret An Error Message
body: Conspiracy or bad choice of words? An Internet service provider in Vancouver, British Columbia, says an error message in Microsoft's Internet Explorer 4.0 is advising his customers to take their business elsewhere. The message appears in a dialogue box that pops up when something goes wrong. It says, "You might want to try selecting 'other Internet provider' from the list of Internet service providers." The error message affects only certain Explorer users who have built Web pages with Microsoft's Front Page Express. As a result, customers of MDI Internet Inc. are calling the company's customer service line for help. The messages "just totally confuse your customers into believing there's got to be something wrong with your company and to choose a different one," says Shiloh Costa, MDI's senior system administrator. What it also means, he said, is that Microsoft is trying to get his company to move from the Unix operating system to Microsoft's Windows NT and its server software. A Microsoft spokesman, Adam Sohn, conceded that the message was confusing but insisted it was an innocent mistake. "It was never our intention to advise people to go out and find another I.S.P.," he said. The company plans to issue software to fix the problem on its Web site and will change the message in future versions of Internet Explorer. In fact, Mr. Sohn said, the message is not even referring to Internet service providers like MDI but to the transmission protocol used for sending and receiving data. He said the company would change the wording to "Please choose another transmission protocol" or something like it. Not everyone believes the mistake was so innocent. "Its an old trick," said Ken Wasch, president of the Software Publishers Association in Washington. Microsoft, he said, has in the past included error messages in its applications that encourage users to take certain actions that promote other Microsoft products, like error messages saying a product is not compatible when it is.   LAURIE J. title: Real Networks Hopes New Streaming Software Will Open Up Medium
body: The streaming technology that allows music and video to be sent over the Internet to personal computers is still a curiosity as a medium and a puzzle as a business. But Real Networks Inc., the leader in streaming software, is making announcements today that represent steps toward developing both the medium and its business model further, industry analysts say. The company is releasing a test, or beta, version of its desktop and network server software that employs a new standard for streaming technology, Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language, or SMIL (pronounced smile.) In the industry, the hope is that the new format, recommended by the World Wide Web Consortium, a nonprofit arbiter of technical standards for Internet software, will open the way for a flood of streaming-media programming -- as did agreement on Hypertext Markup Language, or HTML, the document format for the Web. SMIL should allow Web programmers to put video, audio, text and charts into an integrated presentation that can be broadcast live or on demand to Internet-connected personal computers. Until now, streaming technology has tended to be used to send standard radio or television programming over the Internet, like video of a sports event. "But Real Networks' deployment of SMIL is an important step toward moving streaming technology to become a real new media," said Jae Kim, an analyst for Paul Kagan Associates, a research firm in Carmel, Calif. Real Networks' latest version of its desktop software for receiving streaming media, Real Player G2, has "channels" to link users to Internet broadcast sites of more than 60 media companies including CNN, ABC, Fox, ESPN, CBS Sportsline, Sony CMPnet and The Wall Street Journal. Real Player is distributed free from the company Web site. The channel feature is the Seattle-based company's effort to become a gateway, or portal, for steering users to other programming. The steering strategy, if successful, will bring in added revenues and advertising. Real Networks software is used on more than 80 percent of the Web pages with streaming media, and it said it had more than 26 million registered users, up from 7 million in April 1997. "After the Web browsers, we have by far the largest base of users," said Rob Glaser, chairman of Real Networks. The Microsoft Corporation bought a 10 percent stake in Real Networks last July, before the company went public in November. Under securities law, Microsoft has to hold onto its shares for a year, meaning it can sell at the end of this month. Mr. Glaser declined to comment on whether Microsoft, whose Netshow product competes with Real Networks, might sell off its holding. Real Networks' stock closed last week at $34.75 a share, compared with its initial public offering price of $12.50. The company will lose $10 million on revenues of $54 million this year, estimated David Readerman, an analyst at Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities. By 2000, he projected, the company will earn $12 million on revenues of $100 million.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Ammirati Puris Lintas stakes its claim to cyberspace with a new unit, APL Digital.
body: A GIANT agency is forming a division to specialize in interactive marketing. The agency is Ammirati Puris Lintas, one of four worldwide networks owned by the Interpublic Group of Companies. Ammirati Puris, with billings estimated at $4.4 billion, has opened a division named APL Digital, which will seek to harness the new media "to bring brands closer to consumers," said Martin Puris, the chairman, chief executive and chief creative officer at Ammirati Puris in newyork. Given that the Internet began to assume prominence along Madison Avenue three or four years ago, it would not be surprising if people were to ask, to paraphrase a line from an old commercial, "Ammirati Puris, what took you so long?" An in-house group, Ammirati Puris Lintas Online, has given the agency "interactive capability since the beginning of 1995," said Brian Cauley, president at APL Digital, "so it's not as if we've just discovered it." But about three weeks ago, he added, the Ammirati Puris worldwide operating board decided "to formally set up an Internet capability and subbrand it as APL Digital." APL Digital is the "first subbrand ever for the Ammirati Puris Lintas network," Mr. Cauley said. "That's an indication of how important this move to digital communications is." APL Digital has 140 employees in offices in hongkong, London, newyork and Sydney, Australia; plans call for offices to be opened in additional cities before the end of the year. The formation of APL Digital is indicative of the growing ardor among traditional agencies to stake a claim to cyberspace. But many involved in interactive advertising, electronic commerce and the Internet continue to disparage the digital efforts of the Madison Avenue mainstays, asserting that they are not as nimble or skilled as the crop of fledgling independent agencies that were founded recently to specialize in digital communications. "That's baloney," Mr. Cauley said. "We all know what the Web is about: commerce, customer service and a more efficient distribution of information." "Now the game is who's going to do those things better," he added. Mr. Puris took issue with the widespread belief that Madison Avenue is, to quote the headline on an article last month in the trade publication Brandweek, "Missing the E-Boat." "We know it represents a fundamental change," Mr. Puris said. "And we've been in pitches with the independents -- and we've won." Still, Mr. Cauley acknowledged, "there is some truth" to assertions that more than a few traditional agencies had tarried in dedicating resources to the interactive realm. "Those of us who work in new media are always a little bit 'Come on, let's move faster,' " he added. APL Digital is doing worldwide work for two clients, the Compaq Computer Corporation and Iridium L.L.C. In this country, the interactive unit is handling assignments for Aetna Inc., the Ameritech Corporation, Lego Group, the Nickelodeon cable television network owned by Viacom Inc., Unilever and United Parcel Service of America. In a staff memo last week announcing the promotion of Mr. Cauley, 39, to president at APL Digital from executive vice president and managing director, Mr. Puris projected the unit's revenue at $10 million; Mr. Cauley estimated billings at $20 million to $30 million. Mr. Cauley, as part of his promotion, joins the newyork management committee of Ammirati Puris and the worldwide operating board. Other top officers of APL Digital include Mark Avnet, senior vice president and director for production and technology; Lynn Bolger, senior vice president and media director, and Bruce Ledbetter, principal technical strategist. About two-thirds of what APL Digital does "is hard core Web site development," Mr. Cauley said. Examples include a 12-language site for Iridium (www.iridium.com) and an E-commerce initiative for Compaq (www.directplus.compaq.com). The remaining APL assignments are centered on ads for Web sites. The timing of the announcement of the formation of APL Digital came a month after Compaq, a big technology account of Ammirati Puris, moved the creative and media portions of its account, with billings estimated at $250 million to $300 million, to DDB Needham Worldwide in newyork, part of Omnicom Group. Ammirati Puris retained the direct marketing and interactive parts of the account. "Our Internet clients at Compaq tend to be different from our advertising clients," Mr. Cauley said. Whatever manner in which interactive marketing is handled, Mr. Puris said, one verity remains: "You still have to go on the Internet with an idea. Without one, it doesn't work any better than a billboard outside of La Guardia Airport."

title:
The Neighborhood Business;
Geocities' Cyberworld is Vibrant, but Can It Make Money?
body: Rick Brown did not set out to be anyone's hero. Simply wanting to learn a little more about the Internet, he signed on two years ago with Geocities, a service that gives people free space to publish their own pages on the World Wide Web. Some people use their Geocities sites to show the world their children, their poetry or their model train collection. Mr. Brown built a tribute to Monty Python, the British television comedy troupe. His Web site started slowly, but Mr. Brown, 34, a grocery store merchandiser who lives in Bridgeport, Conn., kept adding Python memorabilia, sound clips, scripts and pictures. Soon the site took on a life of its own, and Geocities began promoting it as one its "landmark" pages. By June, when he had a falling-out with the service over a promotion effort, his site had attracted more than 100,000 visitors. Mr. Brown's experience exemplifies the paradox of Geocities: The service is attracting an impressive and growing number of members and visitors, yet as it moves toward a public stock offering, it is struggling to formulate a credible image as a viable business. The founder of Geocities, David Bohnett, says that the sheer scale of the service's operation and popularity would have been unimaginable when he started experimenting with the Internet in 1994. As of June, more than two million members had created personal Web sites consisting of more than 15 million pages about nearly every imaginable topic. Organized into 40 virtual "neighborhoods" at www.geocities.com, these sites add up to the third-most-visited domain on the Web, attracting 14 million viewers in April, the most recent month for which figures are available. The audience for Geocities has been growing at twice the speed of the average Web site, according to Media Metrix, which measures traffic on the Internet. Now the company, based in Santa Monica, Calif., is going public. The investment bankers promoting the initial public offering hope investors will be drawn to the potential of Geocities' vast audience and to the low overhead of publishing a site created by millions of volunteers. They also hope that investors will not be discouraged by financial statements that suggest only the weakest vital signs of a going concern. Of course, as the company begins its road show over the next few weeks, it will probably talk of many plans to build its audience, to sell more advertising and to extract fees from at least some members for certain services. But it is not clear whether the service can build its business without alienating its members. For example, it was a promotional effort known as a watermark that set off the feud with Mr. Brown. The watermark is a translucent image of the Geocities logo that hovers in the lower right hand corner of the pages of its members, like the "ghost" logos that identify television channels. The watermark's purpose is to encourage people entering one Geocities site to try other sites on the service. But many Geocities members complained that the watermark made their pages load more slowly on visitors' browsers, cluttered their screens and obfuscated links. So using the very tools that Geocities had given them to build their Web sites, some members created anti-watermark pages, chat rooms and mailing lists. When Mr. Brown turned the front page of his Monty Python site black in protest, Geocities stopped featuring his page. Other members got wind of this and turned his case into a rallying point for the anti-watermark campaign. The whole situation, Mr. Brown said, reminds him of Monty Python's infamous sketch in which a pet store patron tries to return a dead parrot. "The customer has a valid complaint, and the management uses every trick available to avoid facing that fact," Mr. Brown said. Such are the promise and the peril that come with trying to build a business by giving a megaphone to millions of people. Geocities is one of a growing number of "on-line communities" -- sites or services that allow people to publish Web pages and communicate with one another by chatting, sending email and so forth. Such community sites now make up 6 of the 20 most-popular sites on the Web. Geocities is the largest, followed in descending popularity by Tripod, Anglefire, Hotmail, Switchboard and Xoom. Some advertisers are wary of placing their product next to chat that as likely as not will turn sexual -- or on a page that today is an affable tribute to Monty Python and tomorrow is a diatribe against the host service. "What gives us a nervous twitch is the fear that if a user has a bad experience they will think negatively on our clients," said Jonathan Adams, a media buyer for Ogilvy One, the on-line agency for Ogilvy & Mather. "Even if 99.9 percent of the sites are squeaky clean, it's that tenth of 1 percent that will wind up in the C.E.O.'s lap." Mr. Bohnett, who has championed the right to free expression of minorities as a board member of the Gay and Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation, says that playing censor in chief for two million people weighs heavily on him. "A lot of what I'm doing has to do with being gay and part of a minority that has not had an equal voice in society," Mr. Bohnett said in an interview in March. "But we have to balance freedom of expression with commercial viability. Otherwise all of this will go away." Mr. Bohnett has declined to comment on the watermark or any other matter recently because Geocities is in a required "quiet period" related to its planned stock offering. In May, Mr. Bohnett hired Thomas R. Evans, the publisher of U.S. News & World Report, to be Geocities' chief executive. Mr. Bohnett remains chairman. The impulse that created Geocities was more expressive than commercial. In the spring of 1994, Mr. Bohnett took a break from a career in software marketing after his longtime companion died of AIDS. Intrigued by the Internet, Mr. Bohnett and a friend, John Renzer, bought a $5,000 computer powerful enough to serve up Web pages and published a little site with a live picture of the Intersection of Hollywood and Vine and a few other locales. Within a year, they seized on the idea of giving users free home pages and organizing them into "virtual" cities, arranged loosely by topic. Thus, when a new "homesteader," in Geocities' lingo, wants to set up a page, he or she selects a lot in a particular city. Those who are interested in cars move into Motor City; jazz fans choose Bourbon Street. The most heavily populated of the 40 cities are Silicon Valley, about computers, and South Beach, a vast spring break-style party. But the most popular destination among visiting Web surfers is Hollywood, the home of most of the fan pages, including Mr. Brown's Monty Python page. Most of the sites are simple, even hokey affairs, offering photos of pets, love poems, pie recipes and other matter that lived between the refrigerator and a magnet in the past. But some are much more elaborate. "If you're a bank clerk by day and a Smashing Pumpkins fan by night, this gives you an opportunity to express yourself," Mr. Bohnett said. Once they expose themselves to the world, Geocities members closely watch the count of how many visitors their sites attract, and they express glee at receiving an email from a far-off place. "I was a ham radio operator in high school," Mr. Bohnett said. "It was exciting to collect postcards from people you talked to around the world. That is a lot of what the Web is about." Even more surprising, people started sending email to their virtual neighbors to comment on their sites and offer help. Mr. Rezner, now the company's chief technical officer, said, "People actually go out of their way to become block captains, to join welcome wagons and to monitor chat rooms so they can have a neighborhood that is safe and clean." Indeed, Geocities now has 1,500 volunteer community leaders who help other members and watch out for offensive behavior. "The community leader program is the perfect environment for folks with a 'helper complex,' " said Sherri Kaufmann, a housewife in rural Minnesota. She originally joined Geocities to show off pictures of her 10 children. Now she spends an hour a day on the computer in her kitchen watching over her corner of the "Picket Fence" neighborhood. "We truly are a community of neighbors who help each other out," Ms. Kaufmann said. "I have made many friends here. Recently, my father became ill, and I was overwhelmed by the letters from the friends I have made at Geocities." But even more powerful than the common human urge to help a neighbor, however virtual, is the sexual urge. Much of the time of the volunteers and of Geocities' small staff is spent rooting out pornography that sprouts constantly on members' pages, as well as other illegal or objectionable material. "We've gone through seemingly endless debates about content guidelines," Mr. Bohnett said. And, still, its rules are uncomfortable compromises: Political opinion is O.K.; hate speech is not. You can have a page about sex but no pictures of naked people, unless they are classic artworks or on pages about nudism as a life style. Most members can criticize Geocities on their pages somewhat, but community leaders cannot. Similarly, Geocities has been in a constant battle with its members about how much of their pages it controls for advertising and promotion. Other protests arose when the service began superimposing advertisements over members' pages. Geocities has not been able to fill the ad space that it does have. Last year, the company had only six advertisers. Now, after a reorganization of its sales force, it says it has more than 100. But its members' pages are only about 25 percent sold. Now, with a new management team drawn from larger media companies, Geocities is trying to find ways to turn its audience into cash. It has tinkered with the design of the site to create more places for ads and to keep surfers longer at Geocities, especially on those pages that attract ad rates with a high cost for every thousand visitors, like pages about cars and other expensive items. And it is coming up with other sources of revenue. There are deals with on-line merchants like Amazon.com, which will sell books recommended on member pages, paying commissions to both the member and Geocities. There are services that for a fee let the most dedicated members build more ambitious and complex sites. And for those who want to set up business in cyberspace, it has started a program called Geoshops to display on-line storefronts for which it charges monthly fees starting at $25 a month. Taken together, Geocities hopes all these initiatives will quadruple its revenue from $4.6 million last year to a range of $20 million to $25 million this year, Mr. Bohnett said in March. Stephen L. Hansen, the company's chief financial officer, said in March that he expected Geocities to break even next year. But this rush to make money is leaving some members behind. "Right now, I feel they are pushing commercialism a little too much with all the home pages inundated with ads and links to ads," said Sharyn Gleaves, who has built an elaborate site devoted to drumming around campfires. Indeed, Mr. Brown says he is about to move his Monty Python site to another service. Yet Mr. Rezner, the co-founder, argues that making money is just another aspect of Geocities' virtual vision. "Everything in the real world should be mirrored in Geocities," he said. "What do you do? You go to bars. You talk to people. You find a date. But you also go shopping, and you have a job." And, for that matter, there are virtual protests, boycotts and heroes as well.
