title: Caught in the Net
body: AND THAT'S THE WAY IT WILL BE News and Information in a Digital World. By Christopher Harper. 255 pp. newyork: newyork University Press. $24.95. Why are many journalists so afraid of the Internet? Early in "And That's the Way It Will Be," Christopher Harper quotes Walter Cronkite's assessment of the new medium as a "frightful danger to all of us." Cronkite offered this alarm after Pierre Salinger claimed to have unearthed new evidence about the T.W.A. Flight 800 crash. It turned out that Salinger's "fresh" documents had circulated on the Internet for weeks -- and had been discounted. The incident demonstrated the Internet's power to disseminate -- and discredit -- unsubstantiated rumor. It also illustrated the dangers the new medium holds for those who forget to pack their skepticism when they venture on line. For journalists, fear of the Internet seems mostly to be a fear of the unknown. That terror should dissipate as more reporters come to view it as simply a new research tool and an alternative mechanism for delivering information. Harper argues, intelligently, that journalists had "best get used to the new medium," but "And That's the Way It Will Be" is apparently aimed at those still wary of the Net. There are thousands of journalists already at work on the Internet, serving a public of millions; yet Harper writes about it as if surveying some inaccessible, inhospitable terrain from afar. This veteran television newsman (now a professor at Ithaca College) provides a casual and haphazard survey of his subject, less a systematic study than a slapdash assemblage of the kind of information nuggets you might find on a shoddy Web site. The book hops from an examination of why people are becoming disenchanted with newspapers and television news to brief profiles of "digital journalists" to disconnected quotations from experts on the future of the Internet. Harper provides some outright misinformation ("electronic mail may be the easiest way for you to get a virus") and some well-meaning but impractical and probably unconstitutional recommendations (Internet providers should "ban" people from "providing information that emphasizes racism and hate"). And he deals only cursorily with the commercial forces at work as the news media migrate to our computers. Harper pictures the Internet mostly as a publishing medium, a kind of digital-age printing press, and misses that it's also a communications medium, like a party line. Web sites are easy to build, email lists cheap to set up; while it's still hard to assemble a crowd of millions, it's easier than ever before for Joe Public to reach tens of thousands. And that turns out to be a valid reason for journalists to fear the Internet. By letting virtually anyone distribute information cheaply and widely, it does threaten journalists' exclusive role, while simultaneously unraveling the business that pays their salaries (by, for example, stealing newspapers' classified-ad revenue). Harper views the Internet from the narrow vantage of the existing news industry, mostly ignoring the Net's homegrown press -- like the controversial gossip columnist Matt Drudge. Drudge has gathered a wide audience for his sometimes unreliable scoops while denying that he is a journalist at all; his readers seem to understand that he's to be taken with a grain of salt. In fact, as the new medium matures, many Internet news junkies are quickly learning to shoulder some of the old journalist's job of evaluating sources. Such Internet-inspired changes in our news-consumption habits fail to draw Harper's notice. Instead, he wonders whether the Internet -- by making reporters more accessible and letting readers customize their news diet -- can come to the rescue of a news profession that seems to be losing the public's trust. He asks, "Can digital journalism change the image of the media?" Certainly it can. But in the meantime, the Internet is likely to change journalism itself so drastically that the question becomes moot.

title:
EARNING IT;
Surfing the Web and Snaring an Owed Pension
body: NEARLY 1,400 Americans are collecting pension benefits because they found their names on an Internet site created by the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, the Federal agency that insures pensions. The agency posted the names of about 8,600 people who have not applied for benefits due to them from plans the agency now administers. "The vast majority of the people entitled to pensions receive their full pension, but sometimes people move or forget to inform past employers of their new address," said David M. Strauss, executive director of the agency. "The pension search helps us find workers owed benefits who couldn't be located when their pension plans are closed." A total of more than $4 million in benefits has been paid to nearly 1,400 people since the agency started its Pension Search Directory on the Internet 18 months ago, he said. The remaining 7,200 or so are owed nearly $13 million in benefits. The pension beneficiaries who have been located through the directory live in 40 states; 113 of them are from newyork and 309 are from California. The average value of those recovered benefits, if paid immediately in a lump sum, was $4,100, though most people will get monthly annuity checks. Benefits range from a few dollars to more than $100,000. Most of the accounts were for closed pension plans in which the former workers could not be found, Mr. Strauss said. Others were participants in pension plans that the agency took over because they did not have enough assets to pay all promised benefits. The agency guarantees pensions up to about $34,000 annually. "We are continuously striving to insure that workers receive every dollar of their hard-earned pensions," said Labor Secretary Alexis M. Herman, who is chairwoman of the Pension Benefit Guaranty board. The Internet directory lists workers who have pension money coming to them from terminated defined-benefit pension plans. The directory address is http://search.pbgc.gov. As of Friday afternoon, 98,358 name searches had been made, said Judy Welles, the agency's senior spokeswoman. The directory contains nearly 1,000 companies owing pension benefits. They are concentrated in the transportation, machinery, retail trade, apparel and financial services industries. Individuals who find their names on the Internet list must supply additional information to verify their identities, a process that typically takes four to six weeks, officials said. Monthly checks start to arrive about two months later, they added.

title:
INVESTING IT;
Thinking Rationally As the Web Goes Wild
body: IT was a wild week on Wall Street for Internet stocks. But because many of these fledgling companies may be years away from actually making money, the sight of their stocks skyrocketing one day and plummeting the next is enough to make investors wonder if the Internet is paved with gold or just a high-technology version of the tulip craze. There is not much doubt that people who have been riding the wave this year have done well. The Interactive Week Internet Index, a group of 50 companies, has risen 46 percent this year. After hitting a record last Monday, the index retreated but still ended the week up 1 percent. Internet stocks have been good for managers like Paul Cook, a former director of information technology at Munder Capital Management in Birmingham, Mich., who now runs the Munder NetNet fund, which invests in companies engaged in research, design, development and manufacturing related to the Internet. Since it began in August 1996, this fund, with a maximum 5.5 percent load, or initial sales charge, and $33 million in assets, is up more than 57 percent on average per year. So far this year, it has risen more than 37 percent, excluding the load. During a business trip last week to the Research Triangle of North Carolina, Mr. Cook took some time to talk about the current mania.   KENNETH N. GILPIN  Q. What has been driving the big moves in these stocks? A. I think a lot of it is driven by speculation about who will be the next company to get snapped up by a much bigger company from another medium as a way of buying their way on to the Internet. Also, I think there has been a bit of a short squeeze on some of these stocks. And there are momentum players who are involved. I hear that this is a retail phenomenon, but I don't believe it. If it is, there are some awfully big retail players out there. Q. Those sorts of conditions have pushed prices for a number of these stocks to very high levels. What do you say to an investor who either owns or is contemplating a purchase of a stock like Yahoo, for instance? A. I think Yahoo is overvalued and has been overvalued for a while. But I would not short it. Anyone who did that in the last couple of months has gotten creamed. Q. You own 50 stocks out of what you see as a universe of 600 companies. Are there really 600 Internet companies out there? A. I would guess there are only about 25 pure Internet stocks, companies like Onsale, Inktomi, Doubleclick and Gravity. But the fund is not a pure Internet fund. What we are looking for are beneficiaries of the Internet. Q. What is your biggest holding currently? A. Microsoft. And we also own companies in areas like finance, where companies like Charles Schwab, E-Trade and Ameritrade are giving their customers the opportunity to buy and sell stocks over the Internet. Q. What other groups do you see as beneficiaries of the Internet? A. Security firms who ward off hackers or insure that a transaction works. Hardware companies like Sun Microsystems, as well as anyone else making servers, like Cisco Systems. Content providers like Cnet. And consulting companies like Forrester Research, Medigroup and the Gartner Group. Those companies will be important in helping others construct their best Internet strategy. We also like so-called portal stocks like America Online, a stock that has done extremely well. But we also like Worldcom and MCI. These stocks are pretty frothy, but I don't think they are fully valued yet. Q. Your opinion on Amazon.com? A. I own Amazon. I used to be overweight in the stock. Now I am underweight. But I think they have a real opportunity to leverage their brand to sell not only books and CD's but cigars and wine, to become the supermarket of the Internet. Q. There are an awful lot of companies that are putting an awful lot of what they sell in other ways onto the Internet for free. When they start to charge customers for the information, isn't there a risk that customers won't pay the freight? A. There is the risk that people will not buy what Internet companies are selling. But I think that over the long term, as more and more companies start building their own Internet presence, you will get a critical mass of customers. Q. Much of the growth in the Internet has occurred during extremely good economic times. What happens when the unitedstates economy turns down? A. I think the digital economy is decoupling from the regular economy. The price of entry to get on the Internet is coming down. In my view, the forces for the digital economy will survive better than other sectors of the economy in a recession, because it is in the process of ramping up, with its own evolution. Q. What advice would you give investors who are interested in sinking money into some of these stocks? A. A lot of information about these companies is flying around out there, and a lot of it is rumor. I would stay clear of rumors. Try to make informed decisions. At the moment, I don't know how many investors are doing that. I think a lot of investors are just chasing these stocks up, and that scares me. But at this stage it is too hard to pick winners and losers, which makes it difficult to pick one or two names. You should either create your own basket of stocks or buy a fund. That is why we created ours. Graphic   Photo: Paul Cook runs a Munder fund that invests in Internet stocks.

title: Dow Jones Profit Rises Before Charges
body: Dow Jones & Company said yesterday that its second-quarter operating profit rose 11 percent, before charges and losses at its former Telerate unit, while earnings from print publishing fell because of revenue shortfalls stemming from the Asia crisis and higher newsprint costs. Profit before the previously announced Telerate charges and other losses rose to $54.7 million, or 56 cents a diluted share, from $49.5 million, or 51 cents, a year earlier. Earnings at the company's print publishing business, which includes The Wall Street Journal and Far Eastern Economic Review, fell 5.4 percent, to $69.7 million, in significant part because of lessening demand in the Asian advertising market and higher newsprint prices, Dow Jones said. The company's shares fell $1.4375, to $57.0625. Still, Dow Jones profit beat second-quarter consensus estimates of 46 cents, the average estimate of analysts polled by the First Call Corporation. Including operating losses at Telerate and a $98 million charge reflecting a loss on the $510 million sale of Telerate to Bridge Information Systems Inc. in March, the company posted a net loss of $51.7 million, or 54 cents, compared with net income of $34.9 million, or 36 cents, a year earlier.

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Dow Retreats 85.19 as Investors Scramble for Profits
body: The Dow Jones industrial average ended lower yesterday after a market leader, DuPont, and other companies issued surprise earnings warnings that sent investors scrambling to grab some profits. The Dow was off 85.19 points, or nine-tenths of a percent, at 9,089.78. The Nasdaq composite index posted its second consecutive record close, rising 4.43 points, or two-tenths of a percent, to 1,939.82. The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 7.82 points, to 1,158.56. "When the Dow did not have much momentum on the upside from yesterday, some traders decided to take profits," said Alfred Kugel, senior investment strategist at Stein Roe & Farnham. "I don't think it's significant, and it's still only a question of time before we surpass the old highs in the Dow." DuPont fell 7, to 70 1/8, after saying its second-quarter earnings would fall as much as 15 percent below levels a year ago as a result of weak oil prices and the effects of the General Motors strike. The retailer J. C. Penney was down 5 13/16, to 65 5/8, after issuing a warning on its quarterly results. Sears, Roebuck, a Dow component, was off 2 7/16 at 59 5/16, while Wal-Mart Stores rose 5/16, to 63 1/8. Hershey Foods fell 3/4, to 66, also on an earnings warning. "It's an earnings-driven market and it looks like earnings will keep a wet blanket on the market," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown & Catherwood. Record profits and revenues at General Electric failed to counter the gloom brought by earnings warnings. G.E. was up 13/16, to 94 1/8. First Call, a firm that tracks analysts' earnings forecasts, said Wall Street expects the earnings for the Standard & Poor's 500 companies to grow 4.3 percent from the corresponding quarter last year. Profit growth in the second quarter is expected to be little better than the first quarter, which was the weakest in more than six years. Oil producer and services stocks were also weaker amid gloomy expectations for their earnings because of weaker crude prices. Chevron ended off 2 3/16 at 81, while the Exxon Corporation shed 1 7/16, to 71 3/4. Internet stocks zigzagged, gaining early after Yahoo Inc. came out with quarterly earnings that soundly beat Wall Street estimates before staging a late retreat on profit taking. Yahoo ended 2 3/16 lower at 184 after racing to a record high of 204. Other Internet stocks fell. Infoseek was off 2 1/16 at 32 7/16 and Excite dropped 9 1/8 at 82 1/4. But America Online was a gainer, rising 3 1/8, to 113 7/8, while Zapata rose 7/8, to 17 1/4. Zapata recently said it would split into two companies, separating Internet operations from its marine protein and food packaging businesses. Navarre soared 3, to 7 3/16. Navarre won a deal to supply Barnes & Noble Inc.'s on-line Web site with consumer software. It already supplies software products to Barnes & Noble retail stores. title: Can the Internet Cure the Common Cold?
body: ONE Sunday afternoon last March, a 9-year-old boy, Robert Lord, fell from a rope ladder in the backyard of his home in San Diego. His neck snapped. As he lay unable to move, he told his little sister to run for help. The next day, a doctor told Robert's parents that the injury was so severe that there was a strong possibility that their son would not regain the use of his body below his arms. Desperate, Robert's father, Stephen, said he called a researcher he knew at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minn., and got the advice, " 'Look on the Web -- that's your best chance.' " Mr. Lord logged onto the World Wide Web and typed the words "spinal cord injury" into a search engine. After several hours, Mr. Lord came upon a report about an experimental drug, GM-1 ganglioside. When given within 72 hours of a spinal cord injury, the drug seemed to improve the chances of recovery, the report said. Mr. Lord told his son's doctor immediately. It was 78 hours after the accident when the boy took the drug. On the following day, he could move his arms, and on the day after that, feeling began to return to his legs. Eleven weeks after the accident, he left the hospital, using a walker, a result that could be part of the boy's normal recovery or could be linked to the drug. The Lords will never know for sure. While the Lord family's experience was unusual, patients have been finding ways to be better-informed and have been acting as their own best advocates for some time. AIDS and breast cancer patients have helped publicize research issues concerning those two diseases, and managed care has forced health care consumers to take medical matters into their own hands as never before. But the sheer quantity of information available on the Internet -- more than 10,000 sites with information from experts, amateurs and quacks on diseases ranging from common complaints to the more unusual, like Lou Gehrig's disease -- combined with instant accessibility is bringing about an unparalleled shift in the way doctors and patients interact. "Being a highly involved patient was possible before, but only for the most dedicated, committed people," said Dr. Tom Ferguson, editor and publisher of The Ferguson Report, a newsletter about on-line health information based in Austin, Tex. "Now all the information is available to anyone with an Internet connection." At its best, the Internet elevates a doctor-patient relationship into a partnership and even saves lives. At its worst, information found on line is misleading or inaccurate. Reliance on the Net can waste a doctor's time, dash a patient's hopes and put a life in danger. "I'm sure there's good information on the Internet, but there's got to be an increase in people's skepticism because it's so easily retrievable," said Dr. John Renner, a family doctor in Independence, Mo., who is president of the National Council for Reliable Health Information, a nonprofit watchdog group. "People turn off their reality checkers because they desperately want to find something that will help them be young forever or be healthier or better-looking." Of course, Robert Lord's case included not only useful information but also a positive combination of people, circumstances and good luck. The boy's father was able to work as a team with the boy's pediatric neurosurgeon, Dr. Hal Meltzer, who sent faxes to the Food and Drug Administration to ask permission to use the drug on a "compassionate use" basis. Mr. Lord grappled with the logistics of transporting the medicine to San Diego from the pharmaceutical company's office in Washington. As soon as the package arrived at the airport, Mr. Lord was in his car rushing it to the hospital. While such cases are not common, more people than ever are turning to the Internet for health advice. According to a recent survey conducted jointly by the Institute for the Future in Menlo Park, Calif., and Princeton Survey Research Associates, nearly two-thirds of the people who use the Web seek medical information and referrals. Doctors generally say they welcome a more educated patient. Dr. Michael Tedford, an ear, nose and throat specialist in Minneapolis, said he first became aware of the volume of information his patients were able to find on line when someone came to him three years ago for a second opinion on an unusual ear condition. Not only had the patient used the Internet to investigate his problem, but he was also able to discuss it in minute detail. "My job was a piece of cake," Dr. Tedford said. "All I had to do was sit there and nod." Dr. Tedford said he had welcomed the level of knowledge the patient possessed. "It moved us more quickly through the most time-consuming part of my job, which is patient education," Dr. Tedford said. "Then I could talk about his options for treatment, with his values and priorities guiding his choice." Dr. David Teitel, a professor of pediatrics and chief of pediatric cardiology at the University of California at San Francisco, agreed. "It's a phenomenally powerful thing when you're not just sitting down and drawing pictures about the plumbing," he said. Dr. Ferguson, who has worked extensively in the area of on-line health information and its effect on the doctor-patient relationship, said that while a doctor must be familiar with hundreds of different diseases and conditions, a patient becomes a specialist in one condition -- his or her own -- and its effect on daily life. "Sometimes your patients think they know more than they do, but sometimes they know more than you do," Dr. Ferguson said. Such was the case with Robert Lord, a situation in which the openness of the doctor played a crucial role. Dr. Meltzer said that although he had been aware of the ganglioside experiment, it wasn't until the boy's father presented him with greater detail and a strong desire to try it that he had seriously considered it. "In 1998, no one person can know every single medication, every trial and all that's on the Internet," Dr. Meltzer said. "Here we have a situation where a child is very severely injured and you'd like to do anything you can to help out." Since dangerous side effects did not appear to be a risk, the question was whether the drug worked. "If the family was willing to accept the risk, and the Government was willing to provide the medication, then I said, Let's go for it," he said. Still more unusual was the way Mr. Lord found out about the drug. In his all-night search of the Net, after hours of clicking on reports with bleak scenarios, Mr. Lord found a report about the ganglioside drug in a paper written by a high-school senior for her English class. Only the Internet would have produced such a link. "I think this is part of the information age," Mr. Lord said. "The connections aren't logical any more in any real sense. It's not a matter of calling some medical data bank." Dr. Meltzer cautioned that it was impossible to know whether Robert had regained his mobility because of the experimental drug he was given, the surgery he had to help speed his healing, the standard medication he had taken or a combination of the three. Or the boy might have recovered on his own, he said. The more collaborative approach to medicine stands on its head the tradition in which a doctor gives orders and the patient obeys. And that makes some doctors nervous. "It's hard for physicians because once you get the education out of the way, you can get to more depth of humanity, and a lot of physicians have never had discussions like that before," said Dr. Richard Rockefeller, president of the Health Commons Institute, a nonprofit organization in Falmouth, Me., that promotes the use of computerized information tools in clinical settings. Many doctors warn against relying too heavily on information found on the Internet, as it can be difficult to distinguish between amateur medicine, even chicanery, and valuable data. According to another Institute for the Future survey, this one a poll of doctors done with Louis Harris & Associates, 67 percent of those surveyed said that patients came in with information they had found on the Internet but that only 12 percent referred patients to the Internet for information. "People are finding information their doctors may not have seen, and sometimes it is welcomed and sometimes it is not," said Dr. Jerome Kassirer, chief editor of The New England Journal of Medicine. "The issue is the validity of the information." There is a danger in turning to the Internet as a virtual Lourdes, particularly when it comes to life-threatening illnesses. The explosion of interest in alternative medicine and holistic approaches to health has brought with it plenty of Web sites promoting nutrition, vitamins and herbs to remedy everything from chronic fatigue to cancer. The temptation to diagnose diseases oneself also worries doctors. Dr. Laurel Warner, an infectious-diseases specialist in Santa Rosa, Calif., said a patient who had been looking up his symptoms on the Internet had shown up convinced that he had Lyme disease. After examining him, Dr. Warner said, she doubted that he had the disease, but he insisted on blood tests anyway. When the test results were negative, she added, he remained unconvinced and told her that according to what he had found on the Internet, false negatives when testing for Lyme disease were common. It wasn't until his symptoms eventually disappeared on their own that he finally believed her, she said. Dr. Warner said she grew still more frustrated when people came to her with information about, say, an experimental drug. "Someone comes in with information about a new drug for Parkinson's or Alzheimer's, and it's very sad because you really have to sit people down and burst their balloons a little bit," Dr. Warner said. "At the same time, you don't want to discourage the dissemination of information. I just wish there were a better way to filter the information." Dr. Teitel, of the University of California, agreed. "I spend a fair amount of my time saying, 'Well, that's very interesting, but it was a test done on pigs, not humans.' People take everything off the Net as gospel." Separating gospel from prayer has become something of a specialty for Hamilton Jordan, chief of staff in the Carter Administration. Mr. Jordan, 53, has educated himself on and off the Internet through three different bouts with cancer. Mr. Jordan said he was now free of the disease and had turned to helping others with cancer. When Gayle Reinsch, the employee of a friend of Mr. Jordan's, turned to him in early 1997 after she was found to have small-cell lung cancer, an especially virulent cancer, Mr. Jordan went to the Net. His search quickly turned up an experimental vaccine program at the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center in New York, and he told Ms. Reinsch about it. Her doctors at the cancer center where she was being treated were not enthusiastic. But Ms. Reinsch, 50, stopped being passive and spoke her mind to her doctors. "I said: 'You have a reputation for being Midwestern, middle-of-the-road and conservative. Well, I don't want that,' " she recalled. She enrolled in the Sloan-Kettering program. Eighteen months after the diagnosis, Ms. Reinsch's cancer remains in remission. "Information may not save us all, but it will give more of us a chance," she said. Mr. Jordan said the Internet had played an important role in his willingness to help a stranger. The search took him 10 minutes. "If I'd had to get in the car and drive to a university library, left to my own devices, I'm not sure I would have done it," he said. Some doctors, still a distinct minority, are going well beyond simply welcoming their patients' input. More doctors and nurses are logging on as moderators of, or participants in, on-line health discussions. Dr. John Mangiardi, chief of neurosurgery at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York, said he had had no inkling that his patients were so upset about unsightly incision scars until a few years ago, when he began logging onto discussion groups and heard patients complain among themselves. Since then, he has tried to keep incisions less noticeable, even making them behind patients' eyebrows. More doctors and nurses are communicating with patients through E-mail. "It creates greater intimacy in a bounded relationship," said Dr. Beverley Kane, chairwoman-elect of the American Medical Informatics Association Internet Working Group, who has helped establish the association's guidelines for such E-mail. "But the main problem is that it adds uncompensated time to the doctor's day, and it's hard to know whether it requires more time than it saves." Experts estimate that just 1 percent of doctors use E-mail to talk with patients, and still fewer participate in on-line discussion and chat groups, but Dr. Kane and others expect that number to increase as a generation of doctors weaned on computers supplants its elders. Most doctors are careful not to offer E-mail diagnoses, but Dr. Renner, of the National Council for Reliable Health Information, said he was surprised by the number of doctors verging on giving specific medical advice to individuals, not just general information, via E-mail. "I thought physicians would be a lot more cautious than what some of them have turned out to be," he said. Despite the problems, reliable medical information is becoming easier to find on the Net, as the bad is filtered from the good. Many commercial Web sites now help guide people to accurate health information. "Right now the Internet is a huge gusher of an oil well," Dr. Rockefeller said. "We're just beginning to build the refineries." Graphic   Photos: (Andy Chen for The New York Times; photograph by David Corio for The New York Times)(pg. G1); Stephen Lord, left, searched the Web before choosing a treatment for his son, Robert, in consultation with Dr. Hal Meltzer. Robert, now 10, was 9 when he injured his neck. title:
COMPANY REPORTS;
Yahoo Reports Strong Earnings For 2d Quarter
body: Yahoo Inc. reported second-quarter earnings yesterday that were sharply higher than analysts' expectations. The results and the announcement of a 2-for-1 stock split sent Yahoo's already stratospheric stock price surging even higher in after-hours trading. Yahoo runs the most popular sites on the World Wide Web, and unlike most Internet companies it has begun to earn a small operating profit. In the last month, its share price has increased by more than 70 percent, giving the tiny company a market value of nearly $9 billion. Other Internet companies have seen similar run-ups. Amazon.com, for example, the money-losing on-line bookstore, now has a market value that is $5.3 billion more than that of Barnes & Noble and Borders Group, the two largest bookstore chains, combined. Yesterday, shares of Yahoo, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif., closed at $186.1875, down $4.8125, on the Nasdaq stock market. Yahoo released its earnings after the market's close; in after-hours trading, its shares rose as high as $202. Excluding a one-time charge, Yahoo earned $8.1 million, or 15 cents a share, in the second quarter. Analysts had expected Yahoo to earn 9 cents a share. With the $44.1 million charge, related to its acquisition of Viaweb Inc., which runs Web sites for small businesses, Yahoo lost $36 million in the second quarter. Revenue increased to $41.2 million, from $30.2 million in the first quarter and $14.1 million a year ago. Analysts said Yahoo continued to show that it was among the strongest Internet companies, with its advertising income rising faster than its costs. But Keith Benjamin, an analyst with BancAmerica Robertson Stephens, said that despite the good news, Yahoo's shares could well fall 10 percent to 20 percent in the next few months. "This news perfectly supported the bullish case on Yahoo," Mr. Benjamin said. "But there was nothing that a rational person would see in this release that should make the stock go up." He said that using the most bullish assumptions, he could not justify a price of more than $150 a share. Much of the activity in Yahoo's stock has come from small investors, analysts said, as larger institutional investors have been afraid to commit to the stock at these prices. The stock split, effective Aug. 3, is likely to encourage retail investors by making it easier to buy shares. In recent weeks, several other Internet companies, including Lycos and Excite, announced stock splits, prompting their shares to jump. Another force pushing up the price of the stock, analysts said, is the admission of defeat by investors who bet that Yahoo's stock would fall by selling its shares short. In a short sale, an investor sells borrowed shares, hoping to buy them later at a lower price. If the stock price then goes up, as Yahoo's has, the short-seller has to live with the prospect of increasing pain or buy back the stock at a loss. This buying back often drives prices higher. In what could be seen as an endorsement of its high valuation, Yahoo also said yesterday that it had sold $250 million worth of stock to the Softbank Corporation of Japan at about $183 a share. The deal increases the stake of Softbank, already Yahoo's largest shareholder, from 29 percent to 31 percent. The company said it wanted the extra cash as a reserve to use for potential acquisitions or other expansions, but it said none were planed yet. If the company does not spend the money, analysts said, the interest alone will increase its earnings by about 10 percent. Yahoo said it did not plan major expenditures on television ads or other marketing efforts to counter the increased exposure that two of its competitors will receive as part of recent linkups with big media companies. General Electric's NBC unit has agreed to take a controlling interest in Snap, and the Walt Disney Company took a 43 percent stake in the Infoseek Corporation. Both deals involve substantial network TV promotion for the search services. "We anticipate that the media companies will spend a lot of money and stir up the market," said Jeffrey Mallet, Yahoo's chief operating officer. "That will drive new users to the Web, and if we do our job right we will get our share of them." The rise in Yahoo's shares is forcing many traditional investors to rethink their long-held views about how to look at stock prices. "None of the old ways of valuing companies make sense anymore," said Peter J. Tanous, the president of Lynx Investment Advisory, a money management consulting firm. In some ways, he said, the Internet has all the hallmarks of past investment fads. "Forty years ago there was a frenzy about the miraculous effect of chlorophyll, then all the chlorophyll companies went bust," he said. Yet Mr. Tanous conceded that there might be something to all the boasts that the Internet would really change the world. "I've got this lingering fear that the Internet stocks are for real," he said. "I just don't know what to do about it." Graphic   Table: "Yahoo Inc. title:
LIBRARY/ON-LINE MUSIC STORES;
Amazon's Musical Offerings
body: WWW.AMAZON.COM AMAZON.COM has been selling books on the Web since 1995, but its music site is the new kid on the block, appearing just last month. Unlike its well-developed literary counterpart, the music area remains very much a work in progress. The look is simple, the recommendation system is in its early stages, and plans for a classical section are still being drafted. At the moment, the site also has the dinkiest selection, a mere 125,000 titles and 225,000 clips. Shipping is $2 per order, plus 95 cents per item, and taxes are levied on residents of Washington State (the company is based in Seattle). Amazon.com deserves praise for its search engine, which yielded a recording by the Three Baritone Saxophone Band that other sites did not when queried with the word "baritone." Similarly, the site's song-title search is also the most effective, a useful feature for those who are unable to identify a tune heard on the radio -- you know, the one with the chorus that goes "something, something, mmm, hmm . . . baby!" Only on the Amazon.com site did a search on "corner" lead to Creedence Clearwater Revival's "Down on the Corner." Besides providing review excerpts from about a dozen publications, Amazon.com allows visitors to sound off about recordings. While these comments are rarely illuminating, they can be entertaining, as in this analysis of a new release by Master P: "Could've been better, but could've been much worse." Graphic   Photo: Visitors to Amazon.com are now able to browse more than books.

title:
LIBRARY/ON-LINE MUSIC STORES;
Flea Market Offers Surprises
body: WWW.GEMM.COM WHEN a friend's romantic relationship ended recently, she lost more than a beau. A treasured CD by Timbuk 3 also vanished from her life. The disk was not available at several music sites on line, but rather than scour the used-CD bins, she searched the Global Electronic Music Marketplace's listings. Six entries popped up, ranging in price from $7.95 to $35.66. The credit goes to Roger Raffee's mom. When Mr. Raffee decided to unload his vinyl LP's in 1994, his mother suggested that he meet with Jim Hall, a programmer, about cataloguing the collection on a PC. Over dinner, the pair hatched a plan for an open marketplace on the Internet. Born as a bulletin board system, GEMM hit the Web that fall. It has become a huge on-line flea market with 1,500 retailers selling everything from old 45's and posters to new-release CD's and concert videos. The GEMM database has an astounding 2.7 million items, although entries from different merchants for the same title do pad that count. "I'm pretty sure we've got everything CDnow, Amazon and all the other music sites combined have -- and a heck of a lot more," Mr. Raffee said. Despite its unrefined appearance, GEMM's functions are quite polished, enabling users to customize their searches by filtering out, say, older disks, imports or any item that costs more than $12. Buyers can order through the site, operated from San Diego, or get in contact with the seller directly, possibly avoiding a commission of up to 15 percent that GEMM sometimes collects. GEMM's site is devoid of news, commentary and audio clips, although there are easy-to-follow links to noisier locales, and the text-heavy look derives too clearly from the site's bulletin-board roots. Mr. Hall promised a graphics update soon. But the blend of used CD's, vintage vinyl and unusual memorabilia is a collector's dream. Mr. Raffee said he regularly received email messages of thanks for fulfilling decades-old desires, like an unused ticket from a Beatles concert at Shea Stadium. Because GEMM is not the actual retailer, it monitors sellers to make sure that transactions actually take place. Mr. Raffee said only five vendors had been banned from the site. "Seduced by Money," a power-pop CD by the Thieves, has long been on this writer's wish list, but GEMM did not have it. Ever mindful of the vagaries of data entry, I tried again after reversing the middle vowels in "Thieves." The out-of-print disk was delivered Monday, a week after it was ordered. On a lark, I also tried the site's "best price" filter to look for the same three chart-topping titles I had used to test the other sites. GEMM directed me to a site that beat all the others (www.cdcellar.com).

title:
LIBRARY/ON-LINE MUSIC STORES;
Variety and Prices Draw Music Fans to Web
body: JIM AUMAN has stopped wolfing down his lunch. He used to spend his meal break in the music marts of Raleigh, N.C., hunting for hard-to-find compact disks by Yes and the other progressive-rock bands he enjoys. Now, instead of scarfing a sandwich on the run, Mr. Auman, a 28-year-old network administrator, munches in front of his computer while shopping at CDnow, a huge music boutique located solely on the World Wide Web. "The Blockbuster Musics and Wal-Marts have billions of copies of whatever is in the Top 40, but I'm usually going for the more obscure stuff," said Mr. Auman, who figures that 10 percent of the 500 CD's in his collection have been ordered from CDnow. He is not alone in turning to the Internet to satisfy his musical needs. While music sales nationwide through on-line retailers will reach only $81 million this year, according to Jupiter Communications, a new-media research company in newyork, they are expected to grow to $1.1 billion in 2002. On-line music retailers are essentially mail-order vendors who post interactive catalogues on the Web. Those catalogues are searchable databases attached to distribution and credit-card billing systems; orders may also be placed by phone. Mr. Auman occasionally pays extra for overnight delivery so a hot new release can be delivered to his desk before Raleigh's stores open. On-line music stores can offer a vast selection, long lists of CD's that would dwarf most real-world inventories. The entries are often supplemented with song titles and cover art. Even ardent fans may be surprised by the availability of imported recordings and other rarities by their favorite performers. Another benefit can be price: the time spent waiting for music to arrive in themail is often offset by attractive Web prices. An informal survey of eight music retailers, four on line and four off line, showed that a trio of chart-topping disks bought from CDnow, Music Boulevard or Amazon.com was as much as 4 percent cheaper than the same albums purchased at the lowest-cost chain store, once shipping charges and sales taxes were factored in. But every music vendor's prices fluctuate regularly, especially with sales on current hits. It pays to shop around: choose several sites and open a browser window for each site, then register at each, pick identical items and choose the store with the lowest price. The options include Sound Stone (www.soundstone.com), Tower Records (www.towerrecords. com), Total E of Columbia House (www.totale.com) and Tunes.com (www.tunes.com). Virtual merchants also capitalize on the Web's multimedia capabilities by offering hundreds of thousands of 30-second song snippets that encourage you to sample before you buy. Mr. Auman said he had been inspired to buy a John Wetton album -- a disk he would never have found at a Tower Records listening station -- after sampling its tracks on the Web. In on-line music catalogues, as in any database, accuracy is critical for conducting searches. An errant keystroke can alter results -- is that band's name Figdish or Fig Dish? (It is the latter.) Nor should the data necessarily be trusted; two sites list "Some Girls," a 1978 Rolling Stones album, as having been released in 1994. Sometimes a database by itself is valuable, as is the case with the Global Electronic Music Marketplace (www.gemm.com), a clearinghouse for used, out-of-print and esoteric recordings that is little more than an enormous text-based registry. Other on-line retailers routinely decorate their shops by adding digital bells and whistles, typically including album recommendations meant to spur further buying. Shoppers truly seeking guidance should turn to specialty retailers like Descarga, a Latin-music purveyor in Brooklyn that opened its Web site (www.descarga.com) in June. Or they might consider returning to the real world. Chicago Compact Disc in Evanston, Ill., had the highest prices of the eight sites participating in the informal survey. But its owner, Michael Bernard, has been selling used CD's to this collector for nearly a decade. Asked to suggest a new disk he thought I might like, he immediately volunteered a recently reissued Miles Davis title. "I don't even have to think about it," Mr. Bernard said. He was right. Graphic   Photo. (Sara Krulwich/The newyork Times)

title:
LIBRARY/ON-LINE MUSIC STORES;
Visually Rich, but Slow, Site
body: WWW.MUSICBLVD.COM MUSIC BOULEVARD is a nice ride if you are willing to tolerate the speed limit. With its colorful graphics and glossy black backdrops, the site creates a visually appealing environment, a Barneys among two Bloomingdale's and a Kmart. The trade-off is the wait while the graphics-rich pages load. Started in 1996, Music Boulevard carries 260,000 titles and provides 350,000 audio clips. On-screen annotation comes from the All-Music Guide, among other sources, but large amounts of original content can be found by following the links to Classical Insites, Jazz Central Station and Rocktropolis, genre-specific sites also operated by N2K, Music Boulevard's parent, based in Manhattan. One oddity: despite the company's attention to classical music, the search function does not permit hunting for compositions by name. Music Boulevard offered a few more sound samples and consistently lower prices -- this week, anyway -- on an offbeat array of 10 titles, like NRBQ's "Tapdancin' Bats." Shipping is $2.49 for the first item and 49 cents for the next, but a total of only 99 cents for three or more. Taxes are assessed in Pennsylvania, California and newyork. Repeat customers are rewarded with a free CD after buying 10. Good customer service is essential for on-line retailers. When a CD arrived with a cracked case, I wrote to Music Boulevard via email. Just as when I placed my order, my message was immediately acknowledged. Four days later, the company informed me that a replacement had been shipped; three days after that, it was delivered. I also got an explanatory note intended for another customer. Mr. Wild, I hope your problem was solved, too. Graphic   Photo: Music Boulevard offers 260,000 titles, frequently at attractive prices.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
My People, Your People: Contact Managers Go on Line
body: The Web is normally associated with surfing, not syncing, but Puma Technology has teamed up with Planet All to change that. The beneficiaries are those people who use personal information database software, commonly known as contact manager programs. Planet All is a contact manager that, unlike others, is Web-based and self-updating. That means that the user's information is linked with that of his or her regular contacts, and users are automatically notified of any changes in one another's contact information. Puma, one of the market leaders in synchronization software, has a new package that synchronizes a customer's existing contact database with the Planet All database, allowing users to have access to their contact lists from any Web browser. That allows people to use their contact managers from borrowed computers without having to copy a particular application and database to the computer. Brad Rowe, president of Puma Technology, said that synchronizing a database to the Web and sharing selected parts of it was a good way to keep people who talk to each other up to date.  "This uses the Internet as a tool to stay in touch without much effort," Mr. Rowe said. Another version from Puma uses Orchestrate, a Web-based universal in-box for faxes, email and voicemail. That version allows a user to retrieve messages from Orchestrate and respond to them using their computer.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
New Barter Site on the Internet For Unloading White Elephants
body: Auctions successfully moved from the auto lot to the Internet, and now the barter system is going to give it a try. Ubarter.com is scheduled to start July 20, giving consumers a chance to trade unneeded items for something they deem a bit more important. (There were already barter sites for corporations.) "Our guess is that people have things around the yard or business that they don't need," said Steven White, president of International Barter, Ubarter's parent company. Ubarter will take a 2 percent to 3 percent fee for helping to set up the transaction. Since it is barter, the fee is determined by the value listed on the item listed. Ubarter will have 10 categories, focusing on things like electronics, vehicles, vacations and home furnishings as well as several business-related groups. Users will be able to post an item, along with its value, in a category. They will also list what they would like in return. ("Exercise bike. Never used. $450 new. Will trade for concave mirror or convertible."). Other people can look at the list and see if there is a match for a trade. ("Sideshow sell-off. Closing House of Mirrors, opening health club.") Ubarter also opens up the opportunity for cross-trading, in which a series of swaps are used to get people the items they want. "In an auction, the highest price gets the item," Mr. White said. "With us, the right product gets it." The site will recommend that traders use an on-line escrow service or a local lawyer to insure that products will be as advertised. Mr. White expects that his company will be paid by credit card, although in the spirit of the enterprise, "Ubarter dollars" are on the drawing board.

title: On-Line Polling Is More Business Than Science
body: MCI issued a press release last week declaring America's Internet literacy on the upswing. Touting the results of a survey, MCI heralded baby boomers, Generation X-ers and residents of Delaware as among the most Net-savvy segments of the population. Here's the catch: The survey did not test the population at large, but only regular Web surfers and visitors to the MCI site, who were presumably already fairly Internet-literate. MCI did not claim otherwise, but it used a bit of sleight of hand to overstate the survey as a basis for "the American public to gauge their 'Net know-how,' " prompting several news outlets to report the findings. The company said it did not mean for people to misinterpret the findings as comprehensive. "The survey is not scientific in any way," conceded an MCI spokeswoman, Mary Matalobos. Cyberspace is filling up with surveys and polls. In fact, news junkies can participate in dozens of polls posted on line on any given day. Last Monday, for instance, ABC News polled visitors to its site on whether they worried about on-line privacy. CNN's on-line quick poll asked if Netizens supported an anti-flag-burning amendment to the Constitution (as opposed to the "in-depth" CNN poll, which asked about China and democracy). ESPN queried visitors about who would make it to the finals of the World Cup; a daily survey by the search engine Excite asked, "What's gone wrong in fighting Florida's fires?" and Time magazine's Web page posed a question about trust and the news media: "Whom can you believe anymore?" All of which raises another question: Which, if any, of these polls can be taken seriously? The answer to that is not many, some polling experts say, because for the most part, the polls are marketing ploys designed to attract traffic. Getting more poll participants means more page views and that, in turn, can produce advertising revenue, said Dan Murphy, director of research and analysis for Relevant Knowledge, a market research company in Atlanta. "When they create polls, they create page views," Mr. Murphy said, referring to the number of Web pages that visitors call up. "It's methodical. It's a business model." Generally, the sites do not present their polls as anything more than an unscientific sampling of opinion. The CNN site, for instance, plainly states that its "poll is not scientific and reflects the opinion of those Internet visitors who have chosen to participate." Besides, the polls' creators say, the polls are meant to be fun. Scott Woelfel, editor in chief of CNN Interactive, said CNN's polls gave people the opportunity to express themselves and to see where other people stand. Tens of thousands participate in CNN's more popular polls, he said. Mr. Woelfel also said that CNN had taken steps to prevent virtual ballot-box stuffing by making it possible for each individual to vote only once. That effort took on new importance after an advocate of nuclear testing by India overwhelmed a CNN poll on the subject and made it seem as if testing had widespread support. Another example of skewed results followed an effort by the radio broadcaster Howard Stern, who urged visitors to the People Magazine site to vote for "Hank the Angry Drunken Dwarf" as the most beautiful person of the year. Hank crushed Leonardo DiCaprio. "Now, it's one person, one vote," Mr. Woelfel said. Although the Internet presents significant challenges to prospective pollsters, it offers certain advantages, too. Indeed, some scientists and polling organizations are seeking to capitalize on some of the inherent advantages of conducting surveys in cyberspace, like the medium's wide reach and affordability. Harris Black International in Rochester, N.Y., the publisher of the Harris telephone polls, says that on-line polling, if done correctly, can be statistically valid. In the last six months, Harris has begun using the Internet to conduct popular-opinion polls. Leonard Bayer, chief scientist for Harris, said the company believes that understands the population on the Net well enough to find samples that are representative of the population at large. The company is creating a sampling pool of five million email respondents, which Mr. Bayer said would be far larger than most off-line pools. He said it was easier to find rare subsets of the population using the Net because there were so many people to draw from. "If we need to reach 10,000 people with a particular medical condition, say multiple sclerosis, we can do so virtually overnight," Mr. Bayer said. Previously, he added, "it was unaffordable." But Mr. Bayer and others emphasize that there was a major difference between a study that sought to survey a representative sample and a mere popular opinion poll. "You can't just hang out a couple of questions, say, about which university has the best fight song and expect it to be representative," he said.

title:
Site-Seeing: Medical Information;
Sorting Health Facts From Fiction on Line
body: SUPPOSE you just found out that you have diabetes or high blood pressure, or someone in the family has asthma or cancer, and you need to learn about it. Search engines provide thousands of hits for a word like asthma with no evaluation of the information. Where can you turn? For people who want basic information from sources deemed reliable by the Government medical establishment, www.healthfinder.gov is a good way to start. The site, created by the Federal Department of Health and Human Services, lets users search by subject and provides links to information from Government health agencies, public health and professional groups, universities, support groups, medical journals and some news sites. The Healthfinder site also gives information about enrolling in clinical trials for cancer and AIDS. Healthfinder covers an impressive array of topics, including common illnesses and some uncommon ones like leprosy, the Ebola virus and mercury poisoning. But the search engine can be stumped: it produced nothing in response to queries about pinworms, tapeworms, hookworms, common asthma medications, swimmer's ear or popular supplements like echinacea and ginkgo biloba. And it has its quirks: it blanked on the phrase "Cesarean section" but responded to just "Cesarean." Similarly, "bee sting" and "St. John's wort" led nowhere, but "sting" and "wort" got results. Another searchable site, Medscape (www.medscape.com), answered all the queries that Healthfinder did not. Med scape, which carries advertising, offers access to journals, news and other links relating to medical specialties and drugs. It has a medical dictionary and a link to Medline, the medical database at the National Library of Medicine. Med scape offers technical material for doctors and a special section geared to lay people, but it does not bar ordinary folks from the technical information. For people who want to search medical journals, two of the best-known offer nonsubscribers limited access to their contents on the Web. The New England Journal of Medicine (www.nejm.com) and the Journal of the American Medical Association (www.ama-assn.org) post abstracts of their research papers. The New England Journal also posts complete versions of some material, like letters, editorials and book reviews, but charges nonsubscribers $10 for the full text of an article. Another general medical journal, Annals of Internal Medicine, posts the full text of current and past articles (www.acponline.org/journals/annals/annaltoc.htm). Dr. Tom Ferguson, who publishes a newsletter about on-line health information called the Ferguson Report, said the real value of the Internet emerged when people got beyond the generic information found on most sites and started to talk to one another via support groups, chat rooms, news groups and mailing lists. People with the same illness can compare notes about treatment and sometimes consult doctors who join on-line groups. "That's where things are headed," Dr. Ferguson said. Many such groups, he said, "contain a high proportion of health professionals interested in that topic." Dr. Ferguson's site (www.healthy. net/selfcare) helps guide people to self-help groups and other sources of information. To find on-line groups, the doctor also recommends www.dejanews.com. Although Dr. Ferguson's own site includes his email address, he said he did not practice medicine and cannot answer personal medical questions. An alternative-medicine advocate, Dr. Andrew Weil (www.drweil.com), does answer some email questions. At the other extreme is www.quackwatch.com, run by Dr. Stephen Barrett, a longtime scourge of alternative medicine. The site www.childrenwithdiabetes. com, created by the parents of a diabetic daughter, has a volunteer staff of 16 doctors, nurses and other health professionals who answer medical questions.

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Slide in Oil and Internet Shares Helps Stall Summer Rally - Correction Appended
body: A summer rally stalled yesterday as concerns about stock valuations caused investors to sell shares that had strong gains in recent weeks. Recent high-flying Internet shares and oil producers, weakened by falling crude oil prices, were at the center of the declines. After climbing as much as 59 points, the Dow Jones industrial average closed down 6.73 points, to 9,085.04, with Chevron among the average's leading decliners. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index fell 2.67 points, to 1,154.66, and the Nasdaq composite index slipped 1.36 points, to 1,908.11. The Nasdaq composite index was weighed down by sizable declines in several Internet-related issues. Lycos, which soared 20 1/2 on Monday after the company announced plans for a 2-for-1 stock split, plunged 14 9/16 yesterday, to 85. The stock had more than tripled this year, to 99 9/16 on Monday from a low of 33 1/8 on Jan. 9. Other Internet shares, including America Online, Yahoo, Doubleclick and Earthlink, fell sharply. The shares had been rising recently on speculation about potential acquisitions or combinations. Amazon.com, the Internet bookseller, fell 17 3/8, to 122 1/8. Still, the stock has risen more than 300 percent this year. As a result of such lofty gains, said Charles Pradilla, chief investment strategist at Cowen & Company, Amazon and other Internet shares were poised to fall as investors expressed skepticism about whether the stocks had become too expensive. "I'm very nervous about it," Mr. Pradilla said about the gains. "Some of these companies are two years away from making money." But there were some notable gains yesterday. Merrill Lynch rose 3 5/16, to 104 5/16, a 52-week high. The shares moved higher amid speculation that the company would split its stock, which would allow more individual investors to buy shares. Merrill officials declined to comment. Merrill last split its stock on May 30, 1997. General Electric rose 3/4, to 92 5/8 -- a new high -- as it became the first American company with a market capitalization of more than $300 billion. Its market capitalization, or the value of its outstanding shares multiplied by its stock price, stood at $301.7 billion at the end of trading yesterday. So far this year, G.E. shares have gained more than 26 percent. Such gains underscored the belief of some analysts that yesterday's declines would be short-lived and that the summer rally would soon resume. "I don't think the summer rally is over yet," Mr. Pradilla said. His confidence is grounded in the current low interest rates and expectations that corporations will report strong second-quarter earnings. James M. Griffin, senior vice president in charge of investment strategy at Aeltus Investment Management, said, "We're in a moment of everything going right, and the real risks to this balance are everything overseas" in Asia. Some analysts, however, think American companies may have already felt the worst sting from Asia. "I think the third quarter will be an important psychological turning point," said Thomas Galvin, chief investment officer at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "Beginning in August and September, people will start to value stocks based on 1999 earnings." And by September, the effect of economic measures enacted by the Japanese Government earlier this year should be apparent, he added. "By the third quarter, we should have more answers than questions," Mr. Galvin said, "and if investors just think that we've started to hit a bottom, that's all we need to improve. Uncertainty is usually the worst side of the market." In addition, shares of large domestic banks fell sharply during the fourth quarter of 1997 because of their exposure to Asia. That drag on profits should not happen again this year, he said. title:
Foreign Affairs;
Mideast Future Shock
body: The big talk in Israel last week was that three young Israeli software designers, and their venture capitalist backer, just sold their two-year-old company -- Mirabilis -- to America Online for $287 million. Mirabilis is an Internet communications tool that allows users to talk and exchange computer files while on line. Israel is now second only to the U.S. in the number of computer-related start-up companies spawned in the 1990's. Meanwhile, up north, Syria is still debating whether to allow in the Internet. A Palestinian businessman from Bethlehem who had just returned from trying to do business in Damascus complained to me: "If I go to Syria and I don't have fax, cell phones or Internet, what do I do? These are my tools." Question: What does it mean for the future of the Middle East that Syria is still debating whether to get on the Internet and Israel is already designing the next generation of the Internet? I think it means a lot. This widening tech gap between Israel and her neighbors -- Israel's G.D.P. is roughly equal to that of Egypt, Jordan, the West Bank and Gaza, Lebanon and Syria combined -- will simultaneously make Israel much less vulnerable to Arab political pressures, terrorism, boycotts and the ups and downs of the peace process, while making Israel much more vulnerable to conventional or unconventional warfare. There are several reasons. First, in the old days Israel grew oranges, Morocco grew oranges, Spain grew oranges. So if importing countries were upset with Israel they could easily punish it by buying someone else's oranges. But what happens when there is only one Mirabilis? What happens when an Israeli company near Tiberias is the only one in the world that makes a key Ethernet switching chip? What happens when Israeli companies start to dominate a key tech sector like on-line tools for Internet security, which are built around algorithms developed in the Technion and Israeli Army? What happens is that everyone comes courting Israel, no matter where the peace process is. Japan, which always shied away from Israel fearing Arab retaliation, is now the second-largest venture capital investor in Israel, after the U.S. Japan is weak in software design and has been gobbling up Israeli software companies. China now has 52 scientists doing research at Israel's renowned Weizmann Institute. India also has 52. "If you have the technology people want," an Israeli business writer told me, "no one cares if you are suppressing Palestinians." In the 1970's the Arabs had what the Japanese needed most to fuel their economy -- oil. Now Israel has a raw material that others covet almost as much -- information technologies. Another reason Israel is less vulnerable to low-level pressures is that knowledge investors are sophisticated. They understand, unlike tourists, that when a shooting happens in Luxor, Egypt, it is nowhere near their software-design center in Haifa, so they don't run easily. Moreover, high-tech knowledge exports tend to be very light and not easy to disrupt. Some are exported by modem. Also, Israel's high-tech exports go, not to its neighbors, with whom it is in tension, but to faraway markets in Asia, the E.U. and the U.S. Finally, high-tech investment is in people, not factories, which can be easily destroyed. But it is precisely this last point that underscores Israel's vulnerability as well. Israel is developing a knowledge economy, but knowledge workers are very mobile and they like to live in nice places. If the key knowledge workers in Israel decide that the situation has reached an intolerable point -- because they cannot abide the rising influence of the ultra-Orthodox in political life, or the unresolved conflict with the Palestinians or Prime Minister Netanyahu's mounting attacks on Israeli intellectual elites -- then knowledge people will leave. Also, while Israel's economy today might be able to absorb more pain without economic costs, there is one thing it cannot absorb, and that is a new war with the Palestinians. With a $17,000 a year per capita income, Israel today has a standard of living close to England's. The Mirabilis kids are the new role models in Israel, where there are now long waiting lists for every engineering school. If the political situation here deteriorates, and Mr. Netanyahu has to call on Israeli boys to go back and recapture the West Bank and Gaza, the Israeli middle class will be infuriated, and some will be out the door. Israelis will never begrudge Mr. Netanyahu for bargaining hard, but they will not accept a new war of attrition. There is one more vulnerability -- that Israel will get so far ahead of its neighbors that one of them will, out of humiliation or frustration, lash out in some unconventional manner and try to level the playing field -- and Israel. Those who can't make a bomb will buy a bomb. Those who can't export software will export rage.

title: Radio Writer Pleads Guilty In Child Pornography Case
body: A veteran radio reporter pleaded guilty today in Federal court to violating the nation's child pornography laws, saying he did so to hasten his appeal that he was trafficking in lewd photos of minors on the Internet as part of his First Amendment right to research an article on the subject. The reporter, Larry Matthews, a freelance journalist who works for National Public Radio and public television in Maryland, was scheduled to go on trial in suburban Maryland on Tuesday on 15 counts of using his computer to trade images of under-age girls engaged in various sexual acts with other minors and adults. But Mr. Matthews's lawyer, Michael V. Statham, said a ruling by the trial judge last week dealt a fatal blow to his client's chances and made it pointless to go to trial. The judge, Alexander Williams Jr. of Federal District Court, ruled that Mr. Matthews could not use the First Amendment's guarantee of an unfettered press as a defense. "A press pass is not a license to break the law," Judge Williams ruled, adding that Mr. Matthews would not be allowed even to suggest to the jury that he was a journalist whose motive was to expose aspects of the child pornography trade on the Internet, not to break the law or to satisfy any personal interest. Mr. Matthews has been a reporter for various radio stations, and in 1995 he had broadcast a three-part series on the subject of Internet child pornography on a Washington radio station. He said in court papers that he had hoped to use the information he was acquiring to write a magazine article although he did not offer evidence that he had communicated with any publication about arranging to sell such an article. Mr. Statham said, "After the judge's decision, he had no defense left." Mr. Matthews, 54, pleaded guilty to one count of receiving lewd images of minors and one count of transmitting such images; the plea came in agreement with prosecutors that allowed him to appeal. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Dec. 11, after which his lawyers may seek to have Judge Williams's ruling overturned by a Federal appeals court. "The reason we decided we had to do it this way was because it allowed us to appeal more quickly the judge's decision." Mr. Statham said. Mr. Matthews's lawyers had argued that the only way for their client to penetrate the secretive world of fanciers of child pornography was to pretend to be one himself. Many transactions in that world, they argued, occur in private Internet chat rooms where people are hard-pressed to win the confidence of suspicious players. But Judge Williams said there were ways to scrutinize the world of child pornography without breaking the law, including interviewing law-enforcement officials. Mr. Matthews's lawyers had argued that such a method would only provide a government-approved version of the story. Throughout the second half of 1996, Mr. Matthews engaged in a brisk trade of child pornography over the Internet. As often happens in such cases, one of the people with whom Mr. Matthews corresponded was not a child pornography trader as advertised but a Federal agent trolling cyberspace to snare people violating the Federal law against such traffic. Mr. Matthews, then under investigation, declared he also was not what he seemed. He was, he said, just researching an article he hoped to write about whether child pornography was as easily available as its critics contended and how well it was policed. The Justice Department said that such an explanation did not matter, and Mr. Matthews was indicted in July 1997. Moreover, the prosecutors in suburban Maryland asserted that they were convinced that Mr. Matthews was not researching a news article but was just using that as an excuse to send and receive illicit materials. Mr. Matthews operated under such Web names as Mr. Mature and Dd4SubFem. When agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation raided his home in Silver Spring, Md. in December 1996, they found two images of pre-pubescent girls on his computer's hard drive. They then subjected his computer to a sophisticated search and found many more such images he had tried to delete. The Federal child pornography laws are themselves an unusual exception to traditional First Amendment theory and practice that generally allows people to possess and consume any information no matter how offensive it may be to the Government or others. In the case of child pornography, however, the Supreme Court has ruled that there is a legitimate Government interest in outlawing its possession because it creates a market that inevitably requires the exploitation of children. In a 1982 ruling upholding a newyork State law, the court raised the possibility that there might be legitimate exceptions of "serious literary, scientific or educational value."
