title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Web Offers Wide Menu For Sports
body: IN the days before the Web, few fans of baseball or football felt as if they were missing anything. After all, newspapers, magazines and television provided ample coverage of their favorite sports. But fans of rowing, swimming, cycling and other less popular sports had to make do with the occasional paragraph, if they were lucky, or maybe just a monthly newsletter. Fans of the biggest American sports have certainly benefited from the explosion of information provided by the Web. But it has probably made the greatest difference to enthusiasts of lesser-known sports. Now even devotees of billiards, rounders and korfball can find something for themselves on the Web. Korfball? More on that later. Surely one of the less extensively covered sporting events is the World's Strongest Man competition. An event seen on ESPN and ESPN2 late at night, it features burly Icelanders and others lifting barrels and dragging anchors in races against the clock. When Bill Henderson, an 18-year-old college student in Ewing, N.J., posted some information about the competition on his personal Web site, he had no idea what was in store. Soon he was deluged with mail from other enthusiasts and, later on, from some of the entrants themselves. Eventually ESPN and Transworld International, which televises the competition in Europe, recognized the page as the event's official site. Mr. Henderson said his Web site (www.strongestman.com/magnus. html) filled a void. The site includes results dating from the first competition in 1977, profiles of the competitors and photographs. One highlight is the extensive collection of sound files, enabling the curious browser to hear the American strongman O. D. Wilson boast: "There is nobody stronger than me, nobody. I'm the strongest man on this planet," or John Pall Sigmarsson of Iceland declare, "I am a Viking." The site gets about 1,300 hits a week, and Mr. Henderson, who answers questions about the competition on a site bulletin board, gets 50 to 70 emails a week from fellow fans. In recent years, bicycle racing, especially each summer's Tour de France, has attracted more press attention. Die-hard fans subscribe to Velonews, a 50,000-circulation magazine, for more complete results year-round. Now Velonews has a Web site with daily reports from races around the world (www.greatoutdoors.com/ velonews/index.htm). Most people think of tug-of-war as a friendly pastime at a picnic or fair. But there is also international competition in the sport, which used to be an Olympic event. In addition to world championship results, www. tugofwar.org devotes much of its space to the rules: the eight pullers on each team are allowed to apply resin on their hands only, and spikes and nails in the shoes are not allowed. Once every four years, Olympic viewers watch men and women slide down a refrigerated chute on their backs. The rest of the time, luge fans can turn to www.luge.com for results of non-Olympic competitions, world rankings and tips on technique. Bandy is a winter sport with a profile even lower than luge's. Essentially it is hockey played on ice the size of a soccer field with a ball rather than a puck. Although most popular in Europe, it has a North American following, as well. A Canadian site, www.escape.ca/gbgre, is realistic about the sport's popularity. The page begins, helpfully, by answering the question "What is bandy?" It offers links to other bandy sites, including the results of the 1997 world championships (won by Sweden) and a history of the sport. For a good all-in-one site, there is www.sportcal.co.uk, with schedules of events and links for 180 sports like dragon boat racing, Canadian five-pin bowling, underwater rugby (there was a competition June 20 in Slovakia) and, yes, korfball. Korfball, a nearly 100-year-old sport, is a form of basketball with teams of four men and four women. "Korf" is Dutch for basket, and the Netherlands won the European championship in April. The Dutch also win the prize for best korfball Web site: www.knkv.nl/english/ index.html. Graphic   Photo: Devotees of world-class tug-of-war can follow their sport on line. (Steve Munday/Allsport)

title: The Blossoming of Internet Chat
body: SINCE the first time someone went on line and thought to type in a question like "What are you wearing?" to an unseen stranger in cyberspace, computer chat has had a somewhat shady reputation. At its best, chat has been a way to waste time, the equivalent of being a teen-ager on the telephone but with a dozen chums at once. At worst, chat has been about cybersex, and lots of chat rooms have been seedy locations, virtual back alleys where pedophiles and sexual predators lurked. But chat is changing, maturing, diversifying. "Until now, chat was something my aunt used to talk to her friends about making doll-house clothing," said Marty Focazio, director of strategic services at Spiral Media, an Internet development company based in newyork. "But I use it basically for fast, tactical communication, whether I'm in or out of the office." Chat is being used in business, education and consumer service. It is turning out to be a way to promote television and movie stars and to provide a forum for authors to talk to their readers. It is also being renamed "real-time customer interaction" and labeled an "Internet collaboration tool." "Right now, chat is the easiest and most reliable way to communicate over the Internet in real time," said James P. Tito, president and chief executive of Eshare Technologies, a major provider of chat technology to companies like Merrill Lynch, 1-800-Flowers, Mail Boxes Etc. and AT&T Worldnet Services. The company, based in Commack, N.Y., also provides chat services to 100 universities, including Yale and Cornell, so they can stretch physical classrooms into virtual ones by offering distance education. "It's a way that most people can use the Internet," Mr. Tito. "You don't need any specific equipment or special browser or special plug-ins." Mr. Tito estimates that of the 107 million people who use the Internet worldwide, at least 40 million to 50 million of them use chat in some fashion, including the more recent innovations of one-on-one chat pioneered by America Online's Buddy List and Instant Messenger systems. AOL, which, with 12 million users, is the largest on-line service in the unitedstates, recently found that its users spent 19 percent of their time in on-line chat rooms, 2 percentage points more than the time they spent combing the Internet. Doug Hirsch, a senior producer at Yahoo (www.yahoo.com), described chat as a ubiquitous "everyman's tool" that "can be used in any way anyone would want to use it." Yahoo, an Internet media company, itself schedules at least 100 chat events a month, Mr. Hirsch said. At The Globe, an Internet site that encourages its users to build on-line communities (www.theglobe.com), about 30 percent of its more than five million users chatted on line, said Stephan Paternot, the company's president and co-founder. Not that chat has gone completely sober and serious. Consider this recent exchange with Gena Lee Nolin, the actress who plays the "Baywatch" bad gal Neely Capshaw. Dandeanie asks: Does it scare you knowing that people out there on the Net obsess over you? Nolin: Do they obsess over me? Oh, that flatters me! I didn't know they obsessed over me, though. Wow. CoolKiss84 asks: I want to be an actress. How do I get an agent and a manager? Nolin: Well, where do you live? If you live in L.A. or N.Y. (you should be based there) you need to get photos taken and have some sort of acting experience. The conversation was made possible by Big Star Entertainment (www.bigstar. com), an on-line movie store that arranges regularly scheduled chats in a partnership with Yahoo. Ms. Nolin only had to talk on the telephone from her home in Los Angeles while Big Star's staff read questions to her and had her answers typed and dispatched into cyberspace. In all, some 5,500 questions buzzed across the Internet to Ms. Nolin in the 30 minutes before the chat officially began and during the hour it lasted. She answered as many as she could, or cared to (she ignored questions about whether her figure had been surgically enhanced). Computer chat, practically born with the Internet almost 30 years ago, is a simple, sometimes bumpy, means of immediate on-line communication in which people type live messages over computer networks. People can chat one on one or in groups. The responses are live also, so a conversation among several people can make about as much sense as the babble when a group of people in a room all talk at once. One way to talk on line is to enter a chat room, or forum, by following the directions at America Online or Microsoft Networks to one of their chat rooms or by logging on directly to a chat site on a Web page like Big Star's or the one offered by Ivillage: The Women's Network. Conversations there are wide-ranging, touching on topics like health, careers, relationships and rearing children (www.ivillage.com). Another way to chat is through instant messages. AOL members have long been able to send instant messages to other members that flash on the screen -- if the recipient is on line -- no matter what that person is doing. And other programs like Ding make it possible to send instant messages on the Web. As with many other aspects of the Internet, what was once a means for people to connect with one another has become a commercial tool. Chat is certainly a natural way to promote entertainment figures. "Everybody is doing chat now," said Jerry Shandrew, the publicist for Ms. Nolin and a number of other stars and supermodels he has nudged to chat on line. "It's the Internet, so you can reach an audience all over the world, and you can put people directly in touch with someone. That's exciting and personal." A spokeswoman for America Online, Wendy Goldberg, agreed, noting that a chat in May with some of the stars of ABC's popular Friday night sitcoms had drawn 117,000 people, AOL's largest chat audience. But chat is by no means limited to Hollywood. Almost at the same time as the chat with ABC stars, a collection of international scientists and business leaders met in a chat forum to discuss biotechnology and its implications. This month, a California computer game maker is starting a chat room for toddlers, while all sorts of groups, like computer manufacturers and the Internal Revenue Service, are exploring chat as a way to improve customer service while lowering costs. "You hear a lot of times that people don't communicate anymore," Ms. Goldberg said. "But people are communicating a lot more now." She said her 78-year-old aunt and her mother, who lives in Massachusetts, frequently used AOL's Instant Messenger service, which opens a chat window between two computers linked to AOL. Sometimes, Ms. Goldberg said with a chuckle, her mother will go on line and notice that Ms. Goldberg is on line and working late in AOL's corporate office in Reston, Va. Using chat technology, Ms. Goldberg's mother sends her daughter instant messages that urge her not to work so hard and to get to bed. David Phipps, a lawyer in a Los Angeles suburb who is a volunteer host for a technology chat room on the Microsoft Network, said chat helped make sense out of the chaos that often rules the Internet. Computer chat makes communicating with many people almost as easy as communicating with one. "Most people can't talk and listen at the same time because our own voices drown out all others," Mr. Phipps said. "In an Internet chat room, many people can talk at once. The computer sorts it all out and displays everyone's statements in order." Well, most of the time. While the speed of computers and Internet connections have surged in recent years, some longtime computer users like Laura Balsam, a computer consultant in newyork, are not overly impressed with chat technology. "In general," she said, "chat rooms are so slow. You type something and five minutes later, someone responds to you." On the other hand, Ms. Balsam said she liked instant chat, those message windows that, unlike open chat rooms, link only those who know one another. "It's like walking down the street and sometimes running into a friend," she said. "It's a spontaneous kind of thing." It is precisely that kind of comfort with chat that Richard Dym, vice president of marketing for Tribal Voice of Scotts Valley, Calif., is counting on as he tries to broaden chat's reach into more homes, offices and classrooms with Pow Wow, he said. Pow Wow, he explained, is a software program that lets users create their own chat rooms. Room can be entered only with keys, which can be given to up to 800 people, far extending the usual chat-room limit of 25. The program, like Ding by Activerse of Austin, Tex., offers instant messaging and the ability for users to see quickly if users in the lists they create are actually on line. Pow Wow and Ding also offer Internet telephony, the ability to transmit instant voice messages over the Internet. In fact, Mr. Dym said, just as chat is expanding, its end may be in sight. He said full Internet telephony would overtake and mostly replace text-based chat in a few years. Many disagree with Mr. Dym's forecast, especially on-line chatters who say they enjoy a level of anonymity that text-only chat provides them. "Text-based chat is probably always going to be there in some shape or form," said Mr. Tito, Eshare Technologies' president. "No matter what you do, it is very difficult for 50 people to actually talk all at the same time." Randal Vaughn, a professor of information systems at Baylor University in Waco, Tex., said he used Pow Wow's chat system -- without telephony -- to extend his reach to his students, who are extremely computer literate. He said his three undergraduate classes tended to be large, each with about 50 students. Dr. Vaughn said computer chat had helped him reach more students, extending his office hours by allowing him to meet with many of them on line. He recalled how one of his students had recently encountered a problem while working as a Web developer 10 miles off campus. By using chat, the student and the professor found a solution together. Another advantage of chat, Dr. Vaughn said, is that students using a crowded computer laboratory can confer with him in his office without leaving their seats and losing their turns with the computers. "It's all voluntary," he said, adding that his classroom chats were also popular. Many businesses are also turning to chat. Eshare Technology is setting up chat-based customer service for 1-800-Flowers that is expected to begin later this month. Mr. Tito said it would permit people to use their Internet connections to not only communicate in real time with a company representative but also to see and choose flower arrangements on line. On the lighter side, many Internet multiplayer game services use chat rooms as meeting places for players to choose sides, discuss strategies or simply brag about their prowess. Multitude, a computer game company in Burlingame, Calif., is testing Fire Team, an Internet collaborative game that is played in squads in which players are linked through voice chat so they can speak and listen to one another through headsets as they coordinate their play. And this month, Gizmo Gypsies, a children's computer game company in Santa Clara, Calif., is starting the Little Wizard Activity Center, which features an Internet chat room for children 3 to 8 years old. The baby chatters will appear as cartoon bugs with their names attached to them. The child simply clicks on a picture of a gesture along the screen's lower edge and the bug waves, jumps, dances or squawks, among other things, in bugspeak. "At the moment, the kids just go into rooms and experience other bugs and the kids," said Mike Hayes, the company's chief executive. "We also want to provide them with the opportunity to maybe get into a room with a grandparent or mom or dad." Mr. Hayes said the bug chat room, called Bugville, would break new ground and help children prepare for communicating on the Internet. "They are getting the benefit of starting to understand that there are other people in this world," Mr. Hayes said. "And that they are totally unpredictable."  Site-Seeing: Chat Rooms So there's all this chatting on the Internet and you want to join the big conversation. Where do you begin? An easy way to get started is to enter the chat rooms of on-line service providers like America Online and the Microsoft Network. These chat rooms are simple to use and are organized in categories like arts, entertainment, news, sports, finance and romance. On the Web, major Internet information services like Yahoo and Excite offer a broad range of free chat rooms. One of the largest chat offerings is on Internet Relay Chat, though connecting requires special software like MIRC, a shareware program that can be downloaded at www.geocities.com/mirc. But caution is warranted. Some of the hundreds of I.R.C. chat rooms are sexually oriented and not subject to the rules against vulgarity that most on-line services have. title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Easing of Worries on Japan Helps the Dow Top 9,000
body: The Dow Jones industrial average closed above 9,000 yesterday for the first time in three weeks as concerns about Japan eased and Federal Reserve officials left interest rates unchanged. The index of 30 blue-chip stocks rose 96.65 points, to 9,048.67, a gain of 1.1 percent. The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 14.72, or 1.3 percent, to 1,148.56, another record. "I don't think it was any surprise," said Alan Skrainka, chief market strategist at Edward Jones & Sons, referring to the Fed's decision to leave rates unchanged. "You cannot fight what you cannot see, and right now we don't see any signs of inflation on the horizon." Today, Japan's leaders are expected to disclose steps to tackle bad bank loans in a bid to restart their economy. This would help drag Asia out of its slowdown, analysts said. "The market is reacting today to the rally in Japanese stocks, and the sense that Japanese political leaders are no longer in denial and will do something to spur the economy," Mr. Skrainka said. Stocks in Japan jumped 3.4 percent overnight, the second day of strong gains, bolstered by a rising yen and optimism about Government plans to deal with the banking crisis. In Washington, the Fed, the nation's central bank, left interest rates unchanged after a two-day meeting. Investors' hopes that the worst of the second-quarter profit warnings were out of the way also bolstered sentiment. In the broader market, advances beat declines by better than 2 to 1 on active newyork Stock Exchange volume of 701.6 million shares. The Nasdaq composite index, weighted with technology stocks, rose 19.72, to 1,914.46. Smaller stocks also rallied, with the Russell 2000 index of small issues adding 2.46, to 459.85. Internet-related stocks were particularly strong on speculation that AT&T, America Online, CBS and others are shopping for Internet partners. Netscape Communications rose 8 5/8, to 35 11/16, in Nasdaq trading. Doubleclick jumped 14 5/16, to 64; Yahoo gained 12 3/8, to 169 7/8, and Earthlink Network rose 10 1/4, to 87. These and other Internet stocks rallied in recent weeks after the Walt Disney Company bought 43 percent of the on-line directory Infoseek. The At Home Corporation surged 6 3/16, to 53 1/2, after the Internet content company said it had reached agreements with Jones Intercable to offer high-speed Internet service over cable television lines in the Washington area. Nike gained 3 3/8, to 52 1/16, after the footwear company reported fourth-quarter profit of 4 cents a share, a penny above estimates. Analysts at several brokerage firms raised their rating on the stock. Hambrecht & Quist Group, a San Francisco investment bank, slumped 2 5/16, to 34, after Credit Suisse First Boston said it had hired Deutsche Bank Securities' three most productive investment bankers. Hambrecht had surged 22 percent Tuesday on speculation that Credit Suisse First Boston would make a takeover offer. Graphic   Graph tracks the Dow Jones industrial average, since June 1997. title:
USER'S GUIDE;
Digital Bread Crumbs Through the Forest
body: FOR a long time, I thought that it was my fault that I could never find the information I wanted on the Web. My search method -- typing one or two words hastily into a query box -- rarely yielded worthwhile results. So imagine my relief to learn that my approach is typical. A recently published study of one million queries conducted in a single day in 1997 on the Excite search site found that only one in nine users embrace the nuances of Boolean logic to concoct sophisticated queries. The rest of us "are basically entering one or two search terms in the query box," said Amanda Spink, one of the study's authors and an assistant professor in the School of Library and Information Sciences at the University of North Texas. Since there is no evidence that users can be persuaded to change, search sites have begun to mold their tools to fit our habits. The challenge is to improve the search results even if users do not improve their search techniques. The Excite search site has been the most innovative so far, taking the first steps toward what Chris Charron, an analyst at Forrester Research, describes as "adding real intelligence to the search function." What Excite (www.excite.com) has done is try to guess what a user is seeking -- the specific bit of information the user wants to know even when typing a general query -- and then to use that assumption as a starting point for search results. Here is how it works: If you type a single keyword in the query box on the Excite home page -- try "orioles," for example -- you will see that Excite's staff has made the assumption (based on users' past patterns) that you want information about the Baltimore Orioles baseball team. The search results will be about the team but will not be limited to relevant Web pages from Excite's index. You will also get information culled from other databases -- including those of current publications, for example -- giving you game scores, the team's schedule and recent news articles. All that information will appear on the first screen of the search results. Excite's co-founder Joe Kraus describes this approach as creating "channels" of information. It also takes into consideration the fact that some users who type "orioles" will not be looking for information about the sports team. For them, the search results page displays a prominent link to sites relevant to other meanings of the word. Excite has organized information about public companies into channels, as well. So if you type "Microsoft" in the query box, the search results will display the information that past users have sought most frequently: the company's phone number and address, as well as recent news articles, culled from 350 publications, and the stock price (updated every 20 minutes). When I tried out Excite's system, searching suddenly seemed fun. Not since the long-ago day when I finally mastered the intricacies of the Dewey Decimal System had I felt so empowered by the giddy knowledge that vast troves of valuable facts were mine for the asking. I felt, for a moment, as if the Web could live up to the so-far-mythical promise of organizing the world's information in a coherent and accessible fashion. Here was proof of the value of such a dynamic medium, where facts are in flux -- things like sports scores and stock prices change from minute to minute -- and the latest bits of data are just a click away. It was easy to get spoiled, but reality brought me up short. It turns out that Excite has so far organized only a fraction of its available information into channels. So if you are searching for something other than information about a sports team or a public company, no channels for you. Back to the old search results, lists of Web sites that might or might not be relevant to the query. That frustrated me at first. Why was Excite discriminating against users who wanted to search for "applesauce recipes" or "Chesapeake Bay retrievers"? Were we not entitled to, say, the most recent articles published on those topics? But Mr. Kraus calmed me with the news that Excite will expand the scope of its intelligent search function, with plans in the next few months to create a number of other channels on topics like health, cities and celebrities. These channels are likely to appeal to a broad cross-section of users; Ms. Spink's analysis found that users often searched for information about a specific person or place. Unfortunately, it is impossible to organize all information into channels, Mr. Kraus said. "If you want to know something very specific -- say, the effects of sleep deprivation on heart disease in men on the East Coast -- we won't ever be able to program a channel to answer that query," he said. "That's what we call a needle-in-a-haystack query." To increase the success rate for those kinds of searches, some sites have borrowed a technique that off-line information retrieval systems have been using for decades: improving the relevance of search results. Infoseek (www.infoseek.com), for instance, determined from search patterns that when most users searched for "airlines," they wanted search results that included the home pages of major airlines. So search results now include those pages. Another search site, Cnet's Snap (www.snap.com), uses a recipe for finding relevant results to make searches more successful. When a user types a keyword query, the site's software automatically assesses the potential relevance of all the sites in its index, assigning a weight to each site's Web address, description and content, then using those weights to rank sites. To supplement its method, Snap has human editors assign keywords to specific documents to give them added weight. "We can quickly improve relevancy by responding to seasonal trends, news and current events," said Katharine English, the site's executive producer. How relevant are the results? In my own unscientific experiments, I conducted searches on both sites to try to answer my 7-year-old daughter's question about the average life span of a house cat, and the results indicated that the technology still has a long way to go. It took me about 10 minutes of clicking on unlikely search results to learn that the answer is probably 15 years (according to a source who identified herself only as Cat Lady in a message she posted on the cat health bulletin board of Acme Pet). Of course, the search results suggested that I might also find the answer at a link called "Stupid threatened Snakes Don't Deserve to Live." But at least I no longer think that's my fault. title: Differences Over Privacy On the Internet
body: Differences between European nations and the unitedstates over how to protect consumer privacy have led to a clash over technologies endorsed by the world's two leading makers of browsing software for navigating the World Wide Web, the Microsoft Corporation and the Netscape Communications Corporation. The differences between Europe governments, which favor enacting laws to protect consumer privacy on line, and the Clinton Administration, which prefers to let electronic commerce industries regulate themselves, could delay the much-anticipated evolution of the Internet into a huge international supermarket of goods and services. At issue are two proposed standards: the Privacy Preferences Project, or P3P, and the Open Profiling Standard, or OPS. Both are technologies intended to make it possible for individual computer users to determine how much personal information they are willing to make available to various Web sites. Both proposals are being considered for possible international implementation by an Internet standards group, the World Wide Web Consortium. But earlier this month, a committee of the European Union issued a tough report attacking both proposed standards as inadequate and possibly in violation of European laws designed to protect consumer privacy. The report states that P3P and OPS, which will be built into browsers made by both Microsoft and Netscape, clash with the European Privacy Directive, which restricts the ability of businesses to collect private information about individuals without their permission. When it goes into effect this October. the directive is expected to toughen national laws of 15 European governments whose privacy standards are already more stringent than those of the unitedstates. The European laws require that corporations get people's permission before collecting demographic or marketing information about them. "This is significant, because the Europeans are saying this mechanism might not work," said Joel Reidenberg, a law professor at Fordham University in newyork City and an expert on international privacy law. The European Union's committee, the Working Party on the Protection of Individuals' Personal Data, issued its draft opinion on June 16. In addition to criticize the technology itself, the report stated that "a technical platform for privacy protection will not in itself be sufficient to protect privacy on the Web." Gerard de Graaf, First Secretary of the European Commission delegation in the unitedstates, said, "We believe technology has a role to play in enhancing privacy protection, but we have some concerns about seeing technology as the magic bullet." The committee's report said that such a technology for privacy protection would still need to be applied within a framework of enforceable laws if it was to protect privacy. The committee also said there was a risk that the P3P standard would mislead European companies into believing that they had met their legal obligations by offering the software. There is added risk that European computer users would come into contact via the Internet with Web sites that do not meet European data protection standards, according to the report. It warns that the current P3P does not require, or even allow for, the providing of information about sanctions or remedies to users, a violation of European laws. Finally, the report states that Internet users are unlikely to alter the so-called default settings that are preconfigured with each browser. The committee warns that the software will be of minimal privacy protection value if the browsers are not set by default to the highest privacy protection possible. "This is a shot across the bow," said Evan Hendricks, publisher of Privacy Times, a privacy policy newsletter, which reported the European Union criticism of the P3P standard earlier this week. "If the Europeans enforce their own standards, then the U.S. is now headed on a collision course over the Directive." Until recently, the Clinton Administration has pressured unitedstates industries to arrive at strong self-regulatory standards that would avoid the necessity of enacting new laws to protect personal information in the information age. However, in recent weeks that position has appeared to weaken as critics -- including the unitedstates Commerce Department -- continued to point out areas in which self regulation is failing as corporations rush to take advantage of the Internet as a new medium for marketing and commerce. "This could be a flash point," said Marc Rotenberg, director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a Washington, D.C., privacy organization. European approaches have tended to encourage systems that permit anonymity, he said, while American companies have been building systems that encourage users to provide personal information. In April, Microsoft acquired Firefly, a Cambridge, Mass., Internet start-up company that develops technologies that support P3P. Microsoft declined to comment today on the European Union report. Officials of the World Wide Web consortium said today that they had been in discussions with members of the European Commission and that they believed that the technology could be modified to meet the European privacy concerns. But they also acknowledged concerns that the technology might become embroiled in a political war between Europe and the unitedstates. "If there's a middle ground it's going to take some time to find it," said Joseph M. Reagle Jr., a policy analyst at the consortium. "I'd hate to see it used as a political straw man anywhere. While P3P isn't perfect, it is a step forward. Issues related to the harmonization of data protection regulations and extraterritorial claims of jurisdiction on the Web will take many years to resolve." Mr. Reagle disputed the report's assertion that there were shortcomings in the basic P3P vocabulary that notifies computer users of their privacy options. In fact, he noted, the system can be easily tailored for any set of privacy guidelines. The European Commission report follows a similar, but less strongly worded report by the International Working Group on Data Protection in Telecommunications, a group of privacy officials from various governments. The group, which met in hongkong in April, stated in its report: "Technology cannot in itself be the solution for securing privacy on the Web. It needs to be applied according to a regulatory framework."

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
Networks for Super-Linked Families
body: AS the planet becomes increasingly networked, shrinking the globe and redefining age-old concepts of community, all this digital connectivity has so far bypassed our most fundamental social unit, the family. Now, a rapidly emerging new industry is betting that the next "killer app" will be a network in your home. Already, according to the Dataquest research firm, two or more computers are being used in some 15 million American households, a number that is expected to more than triple by 2002. The assumption that people will want all those computers to talk to one another, from bedroom to den to living room, kitchen, deck and patio, has touched off a race for a chunk of a what Wedbush Morgan Securities of Los Angeles estimates will be a $4 billion market within four years. My own family contributed a few hundred dollars to the beginnings of that market last month when it became clear that installing a home network would cost a lot less than buying modems, Internet access and printers for each the four computers accumulated by three students and two increasingly Net-dependent adults. The deciding factor, though, was the introduction of a cable modem into the household. Always connected and delivering incoming data at better than 60 times the speed of today's fastest modems, it quickly made the Internet the children's primary reference library as well as a social and entertainment hub. But there was a bottleneck. The cable modem is connected to the same multimedia PC that runs the color printer, the scanner and, most importantly, a CD-ROM changer with an encyclopedia, an atlas, a dictionary and other reference books. In other words, the vast majority of our digital resources were available only to the family member who happened to be using that one machine. Simple efficiency, not to mention domestic harmony, demanded that they be shared. That, says John W. Todd, Wedbush Morgan's vice president for research, is a typical set of reasons for installing a home network. "It's definitely shared Internet access that will drive the home networking market," said Mr. Todd, who recently released an investment analysis on the subject. "But in addition, people are quickly realizing that they can't afford to equip every computer in the house with a complete set of peripherals." Rapidly falling prices for network cards and ethernet hubs, the equipment needed for the kind of high-speed network typically used in corporate environments, now make it possible to connect two home computers for less than $200 -- but only if both machines happen to be in the same room. The biggest expense faced by would-be home networkers today is the cost of running ethernet cables through walls, floors and ceilings. Wiring a typical home can easily cost several thousand dollars. I took this route because I am comfortable doing my own wiring, but by the end of this summer, consumers will have a choice of several easier, less costly alternatives. The best features of all these new schemes is that they will require no new wiring and most will configure themselves -- a significant breakthrough, since setting up a network is a more than daunting challenge for most weekend warriors. While none of these new systems will deliver the 10 to 100 megabits per second bandwidth of a cable-connected ethernet (at least not yet) they will offer speeds up to 1.6 megabits per second, about 30 times faster than today's fastest modems. They will arrive in three basic flavors: wireless, phone-line systems and power-line systems. Wireless networks use a high-frequency radio signal to connect computers equipped with tiny two-way radios, or transceivers. While these are prone to interference from other radio sources, they will be by far the most attractive options when the technology is mature. One system is already on the market, but faster, more reliable systems will be introduced later this summer. For the foreseeable future, systems that use a home's existing telephone lines -- without interfering with normal telephone use -- will be the most dependable and among the fastest and lowest cost. The most developed of the home network technologies, they inspired the creation earlier this month of the Home Phoneline Networking Alliance, a standards group that includes industry giants like A.T.&T., Compaq, Hewlett-Packard, I.B.M. and Intel. Significantly, it also includes 3Com, Lucent Technologies and Rockwell Semiconductor Systems, indicating that these three companies learned a hard lesson when their years of sparring over a standard all but destroyed the market for 56K modems. Systems that use existing electrical wiring employ the oldest technology and, to date, are the more expensive and least dependable of the home networks under development. But they are also the most promising because of the ubiquitous nature of electrical wiring in every room in most homes. Look for systems of this type by the end of the year. None of these systems is likely to be really mature and glitch-free for several years, but even in their primordial stages, they will nurture the emergence, for better or worse, of the super-connected family. title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: How Malone Did So Well On AT&T's Takeover of TCI John C. Malone, the chairman of Tele-Communications, made a lucrative deal for himself when he agreed to sell his cable company to AT&T. The class B shares he owns will receive 9.7 percent more a share in AT&T stock than TCI's class A shares will get. Mr. Malone will also retain control of Liberty Media, TCI's programming company, and can sell a handful of key assets to AT&T, and if Liberty is ever sold, Liberty's shareholders, not AT&T shareholders, will get the profit. title:
Compressed Data;
Backing for Bill To Shield Children
body: An Oklahoma Congressman won preliminary support last week for legislation that would require public schools and libraries to use filters on their computers as a way to keep children from seeing sexually explicit material on the Internet. The proposal by Representative Ernest Istook Jr., a Republican, was added to an $81.9 billion budget bill pending in the House Appropriations Committee to cover education, labor and health and human services. The bill is expected to be sent to the full House after lawmakers return from the July 4 recess. Since the Communications Decency Act was overturned by the Supreme Court last year, lawmakers have sought more narrowly tailored legislation to shield children without violating the First Amendment. "The appropriations bill is a must-pass bill, so it is very dangerous that the provision has been added to that bill," said Ron Weich, a legislative consultant to the American Civil Liberties Union, which successfully challenged the Communications Decency Act. An aide to Mr. Istook said the amendment stirred no controversy among members of the subcommittee that approved it. "There was no opposition," the aide said. "It was a 14-0 vote." A similar bill, sponsored by Senator John McCain, an Arizona Republican, has passed the Senate Commerce Committee. But it is narrower, applying only to schools and libraries that receive Federal financial assistance in obtaining Internet access.   JERI CLAUSING

Compressed Data;
I.R.S. Redesigns Form On Tax-Exempt Status
body: The nation's tax collectors are planning a surfing safari on the Web to hunt for nonprofit groups that are really commercial enterprises in charitable camouflage. The Internal Revenue Service is redesigning the application form for organizations that seek tax-exempt status. The existing application form asks for examples of brochures and other printed materials, which I.R.S. officials use to evaluate applications. More than 1.5 million organizations have won tax exemption from the service. The new form, expected to be released by fall, will add a box for a would-be nonprofit to list its Web address. "We're bringing ourselves up to 21st-century technology," said Don Roberts, an I.R.S. spokesman, "and realizing that a lot of these organizations have Web sites, as well as printed materials, will help us evaluate applications." KPMG Peat Marwick, the accounting firm, tells clients in its June newsletter that having a list of nonprofit Web sites will also help agents quickly check whether a tax-exempt organization is straying too far into commercial activities. Nonprofits are allowed to engage in business activities like operating museum gift shops if the activities are related to the organization's core purpose. But if the venture is unrelated to that mission, the group must pay taxes on any profits. Not yet on the I.R.S. agenda for the 21st century: on-line application for tax-exempt status.   DAVID CAY JOHNSTON

title: Investment Site Co-Founder Is at Home on the Internet
body: On a white board in the newsroom of TheStreet.com, an investment news service published on the World Wide Web, employees keep a running list titled the "self-importance meter." The entrants vary, but, inevitably, somewhere in the ranking is the name James J. Cramer. Mr. Cramer happens to be the service's co-founder, as well as one of its marquee columnists. He writes three bombastic missives daily, dispatched via email to 18,000 subscribers, under the rubric "Wrong!" His reach extends well beyond the computer terminal and this has made Mr. Cramer a kind of Zelig of the information age, cutting across all media and raising the issue of his own involvement in the market as the manager of a $350 million private investment firm. Mr. Cramer, 43, appears as a commentator on "Good Morning America" on ABC, as a guest co-host on CNBC and in print with regular columns in GQ and The newyork Observer; he also has alliances with on-line ventures including America Online and Yahoo. It is the Internet, he said, that provides immediacy to match his frenetic pace, and That of the financial markets he covers. "I've been waiting for this medium to be built all my life," he said. From the offices of his investment fund on Wall Street, he monitors the markets from a bank of computer terminals that proffer data and news, zipping off email between trades in an environment which makes a typical newsroom appear sleepy. "I'm not capable of thinking of anything in terms other than stocks," he said. He described a meeting with an executive at Disney, which owns ABC and whose Web site TheStreet.com supplies with financial news; he also recently did a television pilot for the company. "All I could think about was, "Disney's stock is down today," he recalled. Mr. Cramer is betting on the notion that the rapid ups and downs of the stock market make for compelling Internet fare, matching the rapid-fire pace of the new medium. Mr. Cramer is hoping that the growing sector of home investors, as well as the financial professionals, who comprise 60 percent of the customers who pay $9.95 a month for his wisdom, will translate into a publishing success. Those who follow the world of on-line business news said it would be a difficult market to win. "You've got a huge number of competitors and some of them are extremely well funded, everything from The Wall Street Journal Online, to brokerages that are looking at ways of putting content on line," said Mike Gazala, an analyst with Forrester Research in Boston. He expressed doubt that TheStreet.com, with a staff of 30 and little brand recognition, could amass a large enough audience to succeed. "Beyond Jim Cramer, I don't think there's much there," Mr. Gazala said. "If you took away Jim Cramer, you wouldn't have too many people visiting that 'street.' " Clearly, Mr. Cramer remains the allure. Recently, he and his co-founder, Martin Peretz, the owner and editor in chief of The New Republic, received $10 million in venture capital financing from a syndicate led by the investment firms Flatiron Partners, Chase Capital Partners and Softbank Technology Ventures, who are now minority stakeholders in the business. "This is a very important trend," Jerry Colonna, co-founder of Flatiron Partners, said of the quest for investment information on line. He said Mr. Cramer's cantankerous, shoot-from-the-hip style of presentation was a big reason for the investment. Dave Kansas, editor of TheStreet.com, conceded that Mr. Cramer's involvement as manager of an investment firm presents an editorial challenge. Some prospective employees have been concerned, he conceded, that Mr. Cramer's dual life as a money manager and journalist sullies the credibility of the financial news service. "We've had people we've tried to hire who said they're not comfortable with the perception," Mr. Kansas said. When he first conceived of TheStreet.com, Mr. Cramer said, he approached the Securities and Exchange Commission to ask advice on how to set up the business to avoid conflict. The issue of conflicts of interest is not a new one for Mr. Cramer. In 1995, while a contributor to Smart Money magazine, Mr. Cramer was widely criticized for an article that he wrote recommending the stocks of several small companies in which he owned large stakes. The article did not make note of those holdings. As a result of the incident, Smart Money changed its policies, restricting contributors from writing about stocks in which they own large positions or which are thinly traded and adding disclosures about the stock holdings of contributors. At TheStreet.com, rules were instituted under which Mr. Cramer would not have any editorial control beyond his column. All his columns, writings and television appearances are accompanied by disclaimers of some kind. That does not mean he skirts controversy, however. In January 1997, Mr. Cramer, through his fund, bought up 1.1 million shares of Dow Jones stock, and was one of three big stockholders using their investment to push the company to sell Telerate, its financial information business. He sold off most of his shares five months later when it became clear the sale would not happen. (Mr. Cramer said he took great pleasure in the fact that Dow Jones ultimately did sell Telerate earlier this year.) For Mr. Kansas, the scrutiny of the medium in which he publishes is a bigger issue than critics of Mr. Cramer's possible conflicts. "To me, " he said, "the mainstream medium likes to harp on the potentially scary issues relating to the Internet. We have to work very hard to rise above that." Conrad/The newyork Times)

title: Media Convergence - Correction Appended
body: Billions of dollars and a bold high-technology vision are fueling the AT&T Corporation's plan to buy Tele-Communications Inc. The merger, announced last week, is the latest in a rising wave of corporate deals sweeping up telecommunications, cable television and media companies as these industries become increasingly dependent on the digital technology of computing. The business logic behind the trend is that companies now face a once-in-a-corporate-lifetime choice of getting in early to become leaders in the new markets of the information age or being relegated to also-ran status. Earlier this month, two major media companies -- the Walt Disney Company and the NBC unit of the General Electric Company -- applied that logic in making significant investments in popular sites on the Internet's World Wide Web. Whether any of these deals make sense, or make money anytime soon, will depend largely on the economic behavior of people like Charles Vandagriff of Oakland, Calif. Mr. Vandagriff, his wife and two daughters are the kind of well-off, technologically fluent family earmarked first by phone, media and computer companies in their consumer marketing campaigns. Someday, AT&T wants families like Mr. Vandagriff's to turn to the company for one-stop shopping for not only all of their telephone and cable television services but new information services as well. And AT&T's purchase of TCI, the nation's second-largest cable television company, is seen as a big step toward realizing AT&T's vision of becoming an all-in-one digital delivery system. The 49-year-old Mr. Vandagriff is a furniture designer, and his wife, Kathy Sinsheimer, is a psychotherapist. Their household has three personal computers, four phone lines, a cellular phone and two pagers. There are 16 million such wired families in America, typically with incomes of $70,000 or more, at least one PC and often more than one telephone line, according to the Yankee Group, a research firm. "No new technology or technology marketing plan will succeed if it doesn't succeed first with families like that one," observed Howard Anderson, the Yankee Group's managing director. By acquiring TCI's cable-television system, AT&T gets a higher-speed network for sending telephone, video and Internet services directly into consumers' homes, including 1.3 million TCI customers in the San Francisco area like the Vandagriffs. It was this vision of a phone-entertainment-Internet supercarrier that C. Michael Armstrong, AT&T's chairman, and John C. Malone, the chairman of TCI, were extolling last Wednesday when they announced their $31.8 billion deal. Mr. Vandagriff remains skeptical. "I'm sure these companies are trying to think ahead, but it's not clear to me what they are going to try to sell us really," he said. "I have so many services now -- Internet, cable, phone, cellular and pagers -- that I can't imagine I want any more. I'll wait for the future to arrive." Telecommunications and media companies do not believe they have the luxury of waiting. The rapid advances of technology, they say, are forcing them to act now. The main engine is the spread of digital technology that enables text, sound and video all to be expressed and distributed in the form of the elemental building blocks of computing, the electronic 1's and 0's called bits (short for binary digits). Though all forms of information can be reduced to bits, text requires the fewest bits, while sound and video consume many more. One letter in a word can be rendered in eight bits, while a few seconds of movie-style video may require millions of bits. Most of the new services companies hope to market eventually -- from video phones to movies on demand -- are expected to be multimedia offerings that require high-speed connections into homes. So today, companies are puzzling over both how to carry more bits into homes and how to package those bits into new entertainment, information or shopping services that people may actually want. In simple terms, telecommunications companies can be thought of as the pipes and media companies as the programmers. It will be costly and time-consuming to upgrade the existing bit-delivery mechanisms. Phone lines are skinny pipes, but they are two-way networks that can both send and receive data; cable systems offer fat pipes, but must be converted from one-way to two-way systems. It will, for example, take AT&T nearly five years and $9 billion to upgrade the entire TCI network, the Yankee Group estimates. As with most new technologies, from the telephone to the personal computer, companies will be able to pay for high-speed Internet service first, before costs come down to make it common in homes. The impact, many experts predict, will be sweeping. Nicholas Negroponte, director of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Media Laboratory, insists that for all the attention the Internet has received, the power of the technology is still not understood. "The Internet is wildly underestimated," Mr. Negroponte said. "It will grow to be the enabling technology of all media -- TV, radio, magazines and so on." A longtime Internet enthusiast, Mr. Negroponte advises many of the nation's leading media and telecommunications companies. What gives his counsel added weight, though, are the recent trends in household computer and Internet use. By January 1998, the share of American households with personal computers had reached 42 percent, up from 31 percent in 1995, according to Odyssey L.P., a research firm in San Francisco. Over the same three-year span, the percentage of households on line has increased to 23 percent from 7 percent. "A few years ago, the Internet was a geek network," noted Kate Delhagen, an analyst at Forrester Research Inc., a technology research firm. "Now, the Internet equals consumer network, something that is increasingly part of day-to-day life." As more people go on line, the Internet attracts more advertisers, increasing the potential for electronic commerce. For example, on-line purchases of airline tickets, hotel rooms and other travel services tripled last year to $654 million, Forrester estimates. By 2001, it projects on-line travel sales will reach $7.4 billion, as the number of on-line shoppers increases fourfold to 43 million people. With new-media startups beginning to attract large audiences to their sites on the Internet's World Wide Web, the established media companies are taking notice, starting to move beyond experiments to make sizable investments. Two weeks ago, for example, Disney announced that it would buy 43 percent of the Infoseek Corporation, an on-line directory service, in a deal worth about $900 million. The most popular properties on line, from the Yahoo directory service to America Online Inc., are likely takeover candidates, industry executives say. Indeed, AT&T did talk to America Online recently, though the overture was rebuffed. The Internet media business is expected to follow the pattern of cable television, where entrepreneurs created CNN, ESPN and MTV and were later bought out by Time Warner Inc., Disney and Viacom Inc., respectively. "It's inevitable that you will see increased concentration in the new-media field as it matures, just as you did in every other media business in history," said Mike Slade, chief executive of the Starwave Corporation, the Web developer that built Disney's ESPN and ABC News sites. Someday, people will look back on the recent telecommunications and media deals as either shrewd or premature depending on how quickly the anticipated new business develops. History, both recent and more distant, suggests some caution is in order. In December 1992, Mr. Malone of TCI declared that as early as 1994 his company would install digital compression technology enabling customers to receive as many as 500 channels on their televisions and many of the interactive shopping and information services that people are today saying will be delivered via a supercharged Internet. Back then, television was declared the engine of the so-called information highway. "Television will never be the same," Mr. Malone said. "Our ability to deliver program services is limited only by our imagination." Following a slightly different avenue of technology, Mr. Malone may be proved correct, though his timetable was overly optimistic. Over the years, the technologies that have truly transformed the way people live required some time to spread. For example, it took 70 years from the first consumer sale of a telephone in 1876 to the year when half of the nation's households had phones, in 1946, according to a study by Technologic Partners, a research firm in New York. It took the automobile 29 years, from 1895 to 1924, to reach half of American families, while it took the television only 8 years, from 1946 to 1954. "Unless you keep some technology history in mind, you are setting yourself up for disillusionment," said Richard Shaffer, a principal of Technologic Partners. Mr. Shaffer's own guess is that it will be 5 to 10 years before most Americans will find that communications or media offerings have changed markedly. In the meantime, analysts expect that combinations like AT&T-TCI will focus on consolidated marketing of existing services. Such telecommunications supercarriers want to offer local and long-distance phone and cellular service, cable TV and Internet access -- all on one bill with a price discount for buying all these services from one company. Now that is an innovation that intrigues Mr. Vandagriff in Oakland. "If they could simplify all this, put it on one understandable monthly bill and then offer me a discount of 20 percent or so, I'd say, 'O.K., you've got my attention,' " he said. In January, according to a survey by Odyssey L.P., 40 percent of American households had cellular phones and 23 percent had on-line services.
