title:
TECHNOLOGY;
The battle for Internet supremacy is shifting to the companies that sell the connections to users.
body: WHEN America Online rebuffed AT&T's merger flirtations last month, it could hardly have known that the long-distance giant would soon marry what may be the on-line service's most potent long-term enemy: the At Home Corporation. At Home, in which AT&T will get a 42 percent interest as part of its $31.8 billion acquisition bid for Tele-Communications Inc. last week, markets a high-speed Internet service over cable television wires. It is hardly a force today, with only about 100,000 subscribers. America Online says it has 12 million customers, more than half of the homes in the unitedstates that have on-line access. Still, a new front is opening in the Internet wars with the development of so-called broadband services like At Home that offer transmission speeds 20 to 100 times as fast as traditional modems. That is fast enough to offer rich graphics, live video feeds and an end to the finger-tapping delays that most on-line users endure today. Right now, the most visible battles in the broadband world are among various technology providers -- for example, between cable-modem systems and a new standard of high-speed Internet access over telephone wires called digital subscriber lines. And the cable industry itself is divided: one group backs At Home, and another supports Time Warner's cable-modem service, Road Runner. But a much more intense clash is brewing over whether access to broadband lines will be open to America Online or any other on-line service or will be closed to all content except that chosen by the system operator, just as cable systems now choose which channels to carry. Not surprisingly, both At Home and Road Runner want to use their wires to promote their own on-line news, information and entertainment. Why does this matter? For the same reason that media giants like the Walt Disney Company and General Electric's NBC have been buying Internet directory services: It is clear that whoever controls the front door that people use to start their Internet surfing -- a "portal" in industry jargon -- will control the biggest share of advertising and shopping revenues. And whoever sells the connection to the Internet, as America Online and At Home both do, controls the portal. Just hours after the AT&T-TCI deal was announced, America Online's chairman, Steve Case, issued a statement challenging At Home's exclusive deal to provide high-speed programming over TCI's cables and challenging AT&T to let his service offer high-speed cable-modem access under its own brand. This did not sit well with At Home. "The thought that AT&T or TCI will become a dumb pipe and turn over the portal service to AOL is just ridiculous," Thomas Jermoluk, At Home's chairman, said in an interview last week. "AOL is paranoid about keeping exclusive control of the portal. But in the new broadband world, the facilities provider wants to participate in the revenue stream when users see ads and buy things." The stakes are compounded for At Home, which has a minority of its shares trading publicly. The company's stock has soared to a value of $4.2 billion despite huge losses because of the perceived potential of its exclusive contracts with TCI and other cable systems. To be sure, even if At Home controls the first screen its users see, any At Home user with only a modest technical ability could use the cable modem to gain access to America Online or any other Internet service at high speeds. That is no different than the ability of a current America Online user to jump right to Yahoo or any other Internet site. But experience shows that most people use whatever pops up on the first screen they see. At Home, however, does not want simply to depend on inertia. It has been developing attractive content that takes advantage of its service's speed. Its news and information screens, for example, have much bigger, brighter color graphics than other Web-based services. And it offers a wide range of short video clips from sources like CNN. Mr. Jermoluk says that one measure of the allure of these flashy offerings is that half of At Home's first customers were America Online members and that most of them dropped the on-line service once they got used to the cable offering. America Online, he said, will have to give up its dream of being the exclusive portal in a broadband world. "We have the access to the home," he said. "If AOL wants to get there with broadband, they will have to work with us." Robert Pittman, America Online's president, insists that despite the protests over the current cable lockout, he is not worried. "Broadband is just not ready for prime time," Mr. Pittman said. As much as consumers may want faster access, broadband will not take off, he said, until its price comes down from the current $40 a month and customers can hook themselves up easily without technicians visiting their homes, as the current technology requires. More important, Mr. Pittman argues that for the foreseeable future, the most likely customer for broadband services is someone who is already on line at slower speeds. Thus, America Online offers the biggest pool of broadband prospects in the world. So the cable companies and the phone companies will all eventually trip over themselves to cut deals with the on-line service. "Since we have so many subscribers," he said, "we have big buying power already." Moreover, Mr. Pittman argues that AT&T's strategy of selling telephone, cable and Internet services in one package will ultimately prove ineffective. "They talk about bundling, but what's missing is someone to sell the bundle," he said. "The only thing TCI can sell is cable TV. AT&T has 80 million customers, but it was only able to get one million customers for Worldnet," the Internet service AT&T introduced two years ago. He said that America Online has fared better on AT&T's turf, selling long-distance telephone service since last year through a carrier called Tel-Save Holdings. "We have an interactive relationship with our consumers," he added, "so when we started offering long distance we converted one million lines in six months." Graphic   Drawing. (Tom Bloom)

title:
We, the People Of the Internet;
Cybercitizens Debate How to Form On-Line Union, Perfect or Otherwise
body: These are the times that try a cyberpatriot's soul. Consider Jon Postel, who has served as the unflaggingly serene citizen-sentry of the Internet's address system since he began keeping track of it on a piece of notebook paper in 1969. But Mr. Postel is weary these days, and a little bit grumpy -- and not because the Internet has doubled in size yet again in the last year. It is because Mr. Postel, a University of Southern California researcher, has recently been anointed a founding father of the network's nascent political structure -- a move toward Internet "self-governance" that is being propelled by various governmental, commercial and social forces. For nearly three decades, Mr. Postel's work has been supported by a combination of contracts from the Federal Government and consensus by the Internet's ad hoc technical community. But now, as a de facto delegate to what is shaping up as a constitutional convention in cyberspace, Mr. Postel suddenly finds himself accused of seizing illegitimate power, threatened with lawsuits and bombarded in email wars. His critics include Jim Dixon, president of Euro Internet Service Providers Association, a trade group of 600 Internet companies in Europe. "You have a small group of people asking that they be given a large amount of power simply because they've been there for a long time," complains Mr. Dixon, noting that Europe wants more say in how the Internet will be run. His concerns are shared by many Internet industry leaders outside the unitedstates, who have made their feelings known to Mr. Postel and the unitedstates Government via email. Mr. Postel cannot help but feel besieged. "I'd rather be doing the technical stuff," he said recently with a sigh. "But there are so many questions that need to get answered. How do we form a representative board? How do we make it international? How do we find enough agreement to move forward?" Far from being Mr. Postel's private agony, these are among the questions that are bound to be debated at a meeting near Washington this week, at another in Geneva later in July and at various other caucuses, conferences and on-line sessions this summer. The partisans of the Net are working toward a Sept. 30 deadline for the unitedstates Government to hand over control of a key portion of the Internet to an as-yet-unformed nonprofit international group. Even for many Internet users who do not care much about the specific job at hand -- determining who gets to register whom for which types of Internet addresses -- the need to create a governing system for that task has been given a sense of urgency and common cause to representatives from the Government and industry, as well as the libertarian technologists who have historically supervised the Internet. Though they may have competing goals, all share a belief in free-flowing communication and in the value of electronic commerce, which the Department of Commerce recently reported was growing twice as fast as the rest of the economy. While no one is sure how it should work, the idea is that a uniquely participatory medium like the Internet -- one that transcends national borders and whose fast-evolving technology can be shaped to fit social policy -- ought to be able to come up with its own semiofficial political structure. Regulation by more traditional means, the thinking goes, would stifle electronic commerce and the free flow of ideas. The stakes are sufficiently high to elicit a recent emotional appeal from David Farber, a professor of computer science at the University of Pennsylvania, who is a widely respected email pamphleteer with nearly 25,000 subscribers. "If we blow it, the result will be governance by Governments with all the negatives that holds for the future evolution of the net," Professor Farber recently wrote to his email constituents. "What do we do. We could act grown up!! We could coordinate the meetings and make it appear like we are organized. I wonder if the net establishment is indeed willing to be grown up, or will they fight till there is nothing left." His recent missive was a cry from the heart. "This is a defining moment," Professor Farber said in an interview. "If we can't pull it together on something like this, governments are going to get together and decide this is too important to their economic health to leave in the hands of chaos. They'll start writing treaties, and we'll end up with a very slow mechanism." Mr. Farber is himself an Internet founding father. He was Mr. Postel's thesis adviser in 1969 and assigned his student the task of cataloguing Internet addresses. That academic exercise eventually became a full-time job as the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, financed by the Department of Defense. While Network Solutions Inc., a Reston, Va., company, has had an exclusive Government contract to register addresses under the most popular domains -- the suffixes on Internet addresses like ".com," ".net" and ".org" -- Mr. Postel has been responsible for insuring that each address corresponds to a unique string of digits that all of the Internet's computers can recognize. And now Mr. Postel finds himself being swept toward that Sept. 30 deadline -- the date the Clinton Administration recently set for handing over control of the distribution of Internet addresses to whatever international nonprofit group has formed by then. The Administration's report on the matter earlier this month prompted the announcement of at least two meetings by competing factions, with others rumored to be in the works. One, to take place in Reston, Va., begins on Wednesday. The other, in Geneva, will start July 21. With the Administration and industry seeming to have more faith in technology and market forces to regulate cyberspace than legislation, the effort to supervise Internet addresses has become the first test of the self-governance movement. The parties with cross-cutting interests include large trademark holders, who want to limit the number of domains -- ".com," ".net" and ".org" -- to reduce the opportunities for others to co-opt their brand names. It is one thing for Coca-Cola (www.coke.com) to make sure no one is trying to do business as www.coke.org. It might be far harder to police dozens of domains, to ferret out coke.web or coke.store, for example. But small businesses and individuals would like to see more domains created to increase the odds of obtaining their own preferred addresses. Meanwhile, there are many entrepreneurs intent on making a profit out of registering domain names -- and perhaps just as many domain democrats who would rather see registration be a strictly nonprofit enterprise. To some extent, the struggle is also between the old-guard technical wizards like Mr. Postel and the new commercial interests that have begun to assert themselves as the Internet expands. Tamar Frankel, a law professor at Boston University who has taken a leading role in organizing this week's conference in Reston, has been accused by some Internet traditionalists of being an interloper with no credentials -- or worse, a promoter for Network Solutions Inc., a unit of the Science Applications International Corporation, which assigns the domain names that Mr. Postel helps catalogue. To such criticism, Ms. Frankel replies: "The issues now before the Internet are not technical. They are political, they are structural, they are organizational. What I find is that people who are tremendously sophisticated in the technical workings of the Internet are not necessarily knowledgeable in how to create an organization -- especially one that has no clear model." But a growing number of academics, industry and Government officials and so-called netizens who are not entirely convinced that a new electronic order will emerge on its own have begun to seek a clear structure for the process. Today, for example, Martin Bangemann, the European Union Commissioner for Industry, is convening a conference in Brussels for industry representatives to discuss his proposal for an international charter to coordinate Internet regulation of electronic commerce. Next month, the faculty of the John F. Kennedy School of Government at Harvard will discuss the subject. "The Internet overlaps with geographical governments, but it also floats above them," Joseph Nye, dean of the Kennedy School, said. "So trying to work out governance is quite difficult, and no analogy quite fits." Ira Magaziner, a senior White House policy adviser, was the chief architect of the recently issued hands-off policy on domain names. "What we believe is the ideal kind of coordinating structure of the Internet is not to have an intergovernmental organization, but to have a number of private nonprofit international groups that have specific charters," Mr. Magaziner said. But so far private industry has made little progress in self-regulation. Some critics say that even an effective industry effort would not necessarily safeguard the principles of democracy. "My fear is that there won't be any accountability," said Andrew L. Shapiro, a fellow at the Center for Internet and Society at Harvard. "Your common Internet user doesn't know diddly about Internet domain name registration, and those people need to be represented. It runs the risk of being intensely skewed toward private, for-profit interests." But some proponents of self-governance argue that the participatory nature of the Internet will allow a bottom-up approach to decision-making that has little precedent in the world of parliaments and industrialists. David R. Johnson, director of the Internet Policy Project at the Aspen Institute in Washington, points to Mr. Farber's call for peace as an example of what he calls the Internet's tendency toward natural "self-ordering." After Mr. Farber sent out his appeal he received vows of cooperation from many sides. There is talk of a series of meetings around the world, to which various factions would send delegates. "See, one of our senior moral leaders calls on the Net to grow up and there's already progress in that direction," said Mr. Johnson, a lawyer who was influential in drafting the Government's domain-name policy. Drawing on recent research at the Santa Fe Institute and elsewhere that holds that any complex system, whether technological or biological, will spontaneously order itself, Mr. Johnson predicts that the Internet will produce its own social order -- one that, because it arises from the network itself, will have its own legitimacy. Such an order would not rely on the delegation of state power to representatives, but rather on contractual agreements between Internet users who would then be responsible for their own decisions. "Some people mean by self-regulation a small number of industry players adopting voluntarily or even under duress some codes that match what the Government could legislate," Mr. Johnson said. "What I think the Net holds out as a possibility is a very different mechanism." Graphic   Photos: Jon Postel. A technical wizard, he now finds himself helping organize a political structure for the Internet. (Chris Pizzello for The New York Times); Tamar Frankel. A law professor, she sees the need for new kinds of expertise for Internet governance that go beyond mere technical know-how. (Even Richman for The New York Times); David Farber. An email pamphleteer, he has called on rival Internet factions to unite in the spirit of self-governance. (Tim Shaffer for The New York Times); David Johnson. A lawyer-philosopher, he believes the Internet, if left to evolve naturally, will create its own social order. (Amy Toensing for The New York Times)

title: Internet Is New Pet Issue in Congress
body: The Internet, with its influence on everything from commerce and national security to privacy and crime, has become an issue as politically alluring to many lawmakers as cutting taxes, educating children and locking up criminals. It seems that not a week goes by on Capitol Hill without a hearing, a meeting or a gathering about one of a bevy of Internet-related issues confronting Congress. When revenue-hungry governors threatened to tax the Internet, Congress got busy drafting legislation to keep levies at bay, a bill that passed the House this week. When parents expressed fears about pedophiles stalking their children on the Internet, the House passed legislation to help prosecutors chase them down. And when Hollywood voiced deep concern about copyright piracy in cyberspace, House members began studying the question of how to protect software and movies. Lawmakers have also grown fond of making speeches about the subject. Just listen to Representative Thomas J. Bliley Jr., Republican of Virginia and chairman of the Commerce Committee, who recently delivered remarks to the Computer and Communications Industry Association trade group, praising its members' ingenuity. "The digital and information revolution in which many people in this room are front-line soldiers is truly liberating," Mr. Bliley said. "You should be proud of your contributions. So much has been done in a few short years. Congress can be proud as well, of some of the work it is doing. And since there is an election coming up, I will claim credit for most it." Just two years ago, the term "chat room" conveyed nothing but a cozy hideaway office in the Capitol to most Senators and House members. And only 14 of them boasted Web sites. So what changed? Millions of voters have discovered the Internet. An estimated 23 million people in the unitedstates now log on to the Internet, a figure that grows tremendously every day, and profits continue to skyrocket, including sales figures for goods that are bought and sold on line. This growth dovetailed with another crucial change in the high-technology industry. Once loath to lobby Congress, executives of the industry have discovered Washington's relevance the hard way -- watching Microsoft take a pounding, for example -- and have started paying regular visits to influential members of Congress. Two weeks ago, Bill Gates, Microsoft's chairman, huddled with lawmakers and Justice Department officials to discuss the encryption of data on the Internet. For politicians, a breed perpetually in search of fresh battles and causes, the Internet offers a freshly minted take on old but sprightly issues. It gives lawmakers a new theme on which to stump, one that remains virtually wide open and unmarked. Senator Jon Kyl, Republican of Arizona, has taken his opposition to gambling in the real world to the next level, gambling on line. His legislation would ban it. Two weeks ago, Republicans and Democrats joined forces in combatting pedophiles who stalk children on line. And Senator Dan Coats, Republican of Indiana, is working to try to stamp out on-line pornography. Congress tried to do that in 1996 in its first real effort to deal with the Internet, but that law was struck down by the Supreme Court last year. There are new issues as well. The scourge of junk email, or spam, was the topic of a recent Senate subcommittee hearing at which Senator Frank H. Murkowski, an Alaska Republican and one of the more senior members of the Senate, could not help but reminisce about the old days. "I don't know if you recall the first time I ran into Spam," he told the assembled senators and witnesses, with a chuckle. "I do. It was as a youngster during World War II. It was rationed. A can of Spam and a cigarette." The Senate passed a plan to combat junk email earlier this year.  The House has not taken up the issue. In the coming months the Senate is expected to consider the tax moratorium, children's protection and copyright privacy on the Internet. For years, Vice President Al Gore and his Democratic allies in Congress had a near lock on the subject of cyberspace, at least in the view of most Americans. The Republicans had Speaker Newt Gingrich, who was equally smitten with high technology. But now other Republicans have started to make in-roads on the information highway, framing themselves as natural allies of the libertarian-minded high-technology community industry, with which they share a fondness for laissez-faire governance. Several prominent senators, including John McCain, Republican of Arizona, have taken to speaking often, and with intelligence, on the Internet's impact on society and the economy. Lawmakers sense what pollsters know. Many of the legions of Internet devotees hopscotch just as easily from one party to another. "The real group up for grabs in the future are the libertarians," said Kellyanne Fitzpatrick, a Republican pollster who has queried lawmakers and the public about the Internet and has found a substantial rise in interest. "Some call themselves liberals and some call themselves conservatives." Now, with both sides engaged, these cyber issues are beginning to acquire the traditional partisan gloss of election-year politics. Most recently, Republicans lashed out at the Clinton Administration when they discovered that an effort to hook up every classroom in America to the Internet, something Congress endorsed in 1996, is resulting in heftier telephone bills for some taxpayers. They have dubbed it the "Gore tax." And it seems that not a day drifts by without someone somewhere on Capitol Hill admonishing Mr. Gore for the dreaded year 2000 problem, which is shorthand for the devastating consequences that could be suffered if computers are not reprogrammed to recognize 00 as 2000 instead of 1900. More often than not, however, these cyber issues, which are mostly nonpartisan in nature, tend to draw together hostile forces. Senator John Ashcroft, Republican of Missouri and one of the most conservative members of Congress, has teamed up with Senator Patrick J. Leahy, Democrat of Vermont and a longtime liberal, over the issue of data encryption. The same sort of bond was cemented between Representative Christopher Cox, a California Republican, and Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, for the moratorium on Internet taxes. "The Internet is relatively new, and the technology has changed so rapidly that it's not in a well-worn partisan rut," said Mr. Cox, who added that he works routinely with Ira Magaziner, the Administration's Internet guru. "There isn't a partisan lock on this.' These members have forged these alliances around a common interest: staving off regulation, a position wholeheartedly supported by the industry. Representative Rick White, a Republican who is from Microsoft territory in Washington, describes the mission of Congress as establishing "rules of the road," a basic framework. Mr. Leahy and the others fear that the Internet is becoming too popular a topic too quickly in Congress, and leading too often to "bumper sticker politics," especially when it comes to privacy. "Those that want short-term political gains are closing out the possibility of real long-term benefits," Mr. Leahy said. The consensus today, Mr. White said, is "we better not move too fast." But, he added, "the pressure is continuing to build." Sensing that pressure, the industry is also beginning to act. At the behest of lawmakers and the Administration, two industry organizations submitted plans this week to address the outcry over the violations of consumers' privacy on the Internet. Many people fear giving out their Social Security numbers on the Internet, feeling that that is like Big Brother. But some lawmakers maintain that legislation is needed to safeguard the privacy of people who conduct business on the Internet. In the past year, members have tried to educate themselves and each other about the Internet. For example, Representative W.J. (Billy) Tauzin, Republican of Louisiana, the chairman of a subcommittee, held a series of what he called "tutorials" on the impact of electronic commerce. He said that lawmakers were beginning to realize that the old legislative framework did not necessarily apply to the Internet. "The difference today is that if you are not prepared to deal with a new paradigm of virtual stores and boundaryless commerce, where brick and mortar is not relevant, then you will be a dinosaur," Mr. Tauzin said. "We are just beginning to be prepared."

title:
Q&A/Allan H. Weis;
Contest Helps Internet Work for Students
body: AS someone who was involved at Ground Zero with the start of the Internet, Allan H. Weis cringes when he encounters news accounts of the bad aspects of the Web for children, including pornography and lack of content. As president and chief executive officer of the Armonk-based Advanced Network and Services and with a lot of extra money on hand, Mr. Weis and his company decided to do something to change that. Three years ago, Advanced Network began its yearly Thinkquest contest, where students 12 through 18 are invited to form teams that design Web pages and are eligible for $1 million in prizes and scholarships. The top prize is $25,000 a student on the winning team, $5,000 for the coach and $5,000 for a designated school or library. About 2,000 teams of two or three students each and a coach are completing entries for the August deadline of what has become an international competition. Further information about Thinkquest -- or the company's newest contest for younger students, Thinkquest Junior -- can be found at its Web site: www.advanced.org/thinkquest/. The site also has a library of contest submissions from previous years. Mr. Weis, who has lived in various places in Westchester but now lives in Greenwich, worked for International Business Machines for 30 years before retiring and starting Advanced Network and Services. From 1990 through 1995 the nonprofit company helped build the Internet. In 1995 that part of the company's business was sold to America Online for what Mr. Weis says was "quite a bit of money." As a company dedicated to advancing education by accelerating the use of computer networking applications and technology, it looked for a way to spend the money appropriately. Here are excerpts from a recent conversation with Mr. Weis: Q. Why did you start this contest? A. We sat down several years ago and said, What do we want this company to do? We're fortunate enough to have quite a bit of money. We struggled with the question for a long time and came up with: we want to advance education through the use of computer networking technology and applications. Once we decided that, we asked, how will we get the greatest leverage to do that? Q. What was wrong with what was out there in the way of educational software? A. I took a look at what the power of Web and the Internet could really bring to education, and there wasn't a lot there. There wasn't a lot of content out on the Web that students and teachers could use in their everyday classroom for a variety of subjects. And the content that was out there -- most of it was built by adults with the mindset of adults rather than the mindset of a kid. Students think differently than adults. They play computer games. They explore. They learn through exploration. They learn through a combination of hand-eye coordination and doing things. And I wanted to get some of that thought and learning process into learning tools. And I thought there was no better way to do that than have the students do it. I was also a little concerned that students from some of the better schools were moving faster than students that were lower on the informational technology ladder. So I wanted to see if we could couple students across schools on the informational technology ladder into teams so they could help each other, learn from each other. We decided to use a contest as the format to create a library -- and we have a wonderful legacy of what the students have done there, which is very heavily used worldwide. Q. Are people other than contestants visiting your library of home pages? A. Absolutely. Some days we have had almost two million hits. It's used regularly in the schools around the world. For example, if you want to learn the computer programming language C++, there is no better tool anywhere in the world than the page done by one of last year's winners. It's used by companies such as Lockheed. The Air Force Academy uses one of the entries to teach economics. Our pages are used all around the world not only in high schools but in industry to teach a variety of subjects. These kids really have developed very good language tools. And there is another legacy in that the teachers who have acted as coaches have really been exposed to a whole new way of learning. And this is really good. All too often you read the bad things about the Internet. Very rarely do we see that this is a very powerful tool for students to use as a research tool, as a development tool, to give them the ability to sort of be more competitive in their lives in a dozen ways. Q. How much does it cost your company to run these contests? A. Take Thinkquest and Thinkquest Junior and that's about $1.5 million in scholarships and cash awards. But there are several additional million dollars behind it. We help teach the teachers so they're not afraid to bring the technology into their classrooms. We give out hundreds of thousands of CD-ROM's to schools all around the world that contain some of the entries and good software for development of entries. And we run the server, which is a very large job when you get so many hits a day. We spend on K-through-12 programs pretty close to $5 million a year. Q. Your judging criteria include extra points for co-ed teams from different school districts, different countries, different ages. Why? A. That's how we fine-tune the contest. We wanted more women to be involved, that's why we put the gender in. We wanted to encourage international teams. But we didn't want to encourage those things to the point of hurting the original goal of making sure there were high-quality educational tools. So we just give it little points for these things. Still the way you become a winner is you get every point. One of the teams last year that won first place in the Sports and Health category had a student from Virginia, another from Alaska and the third one from Russia. Q. The judging must be so hard. A. We use the Internet Society, and they do a spectacular job for us. They have hundreds of people who spend hundreds of hours on this. And many of them do it out of their heart, because they absolutely love being involved and love seeing what the students do. Each entry is looked at three times before it makes the semifinals and then a couple of times before it makes the finals. And then the judges sit with the students at the finals and talk to them for about an hour, going through their entry. They look at the codes the students have written and ask questions why they did it one way and not another way. The judges continue to be amazed by the students, and the students continue to be impressed with the judges. Q. Have the judges been impressed with the depth of the topic or how the Web page was built? A. The thing that impresses me the most about the winners is their imagination. They've really picked good topics, and they have good reasons to pick the good topics. For example, the students who did C++ said that was a language that was so important to learn and it wasn't being taught in schools. So they wanted to create a tool that was useful to other students. And if you pick up a book and try to learn C++ the first thing you have to do is read the book, and then you may have to go out and get the software and install it on your computer. What they did was make it so if you have a computer you can get to their tool, and it will teach you and let you write a program and it will execute that program for you and see if it works. So it was really a brilliant implementation with great ideas and great motivation behind it. We've had other wonderful topics: the Himalayas, diseases, music. We have such a rich library of different subjects. It's really wonderful. Q. What do you think participants get out of this contest? A. I've talked to students who say, I can build a home page, and they build a home page and they say, Gee I want to make it look better, so they learn Java. And they say, I can't do everything I want with this, what I'm going to do is learn the programming language C, and then I'm going to learn this and I'm going to learn that and all of a sudden they've learned a lot about computer science, and they're interested in computer science. And they have something they can make a lot of money with during the summer. I think it has really helped bring a lot of students new jobs and maybe even a new outlook on life. It has been the most rewarding program I've ever worked on in my life. Graphic   Photo: Allan H. Weis, president and chief executive officer of Advanced Network and Services, in his Armonk office. (George M. Gutierrez for The New York Times)

title: A Mistaken Microsoft Ruling
body: One month after the Justice Department filed its sweeping antitrust suit against Microsoft, a Federal appeals court has issued a deeply flawed ruling that may weaken the Government's case. The three-judge panel seemed to adopt Microsoft's arrogant claim that it has the right to incorporate its browser, or any other software, into its Windows operating system as long as doing so offers certain advantages to consumers. But if the thinking behind this decision prevails, it could permit Microsoft to use its monopoly power to crush competitors throughout the Internet. The Justice Department thus needs to mount a vigorous counterattack invoking the full force of antitrust laws. The Justice Department can argue that the appeals court ruling need not determine the outcome of its larger antitrust case against Microsoft. That is because it was based on a narrow case brought by the Justice Department last year, when it charged that Microsoft violated a 1995 consent decree affecting the marketing of Windows 95. In that decree, Microsoft agreed not to condition its sale of Windows to computer makers on the sale of other software, but could improve Windows by integrating other functions into it. In December a Federal district judge ordered Microsoft to split off its browser, the software used to navigate the World Wide Web, from Windows 95. Now the appeals court has said the browser can be included, because with it Windows became a new and improved integrated product. The problem with the appeals court's reasoning is that virtually any new form of software can be integrated into the basic Windows system, arguably improving it. Right now, Microsoft is expanding into myriad Internet businesses, including news, entertainment information, banking, financial transactions, travel bookings and other services. Since consumers have no choice but to buy the Windows operating system when they buy personal computers, Microsoft is in a position to give such a big advantage to its own software that any other software maker would not be able to compete. Because the court of appeals ruling was based on the meaning of the 1995 consent decree, the Justice Department has a chance to reverse its thinking in its larger case against Microsoft, which is to come to trial in September. In that case, the judge will be asked to look beyond the consent decree to the broad principles of antitrust law, and to look as well at Microsoft's predatory practices. The department has assembled impressive evidence that Microsoft deliberately used its monopoly in Windows to crush its rival Netscape, which was selling a browser that many consumers preferred to the one made by Microsoft. The appeals court's decision referred to the general "undesirability of having courts oversee product design." Judge Patricia Wald, in her dissent, correctly warned that the decision "would seem to permit" Microsoft to incorporate "any now-separate software product into its operating system by identifying some minimal synergy" as a result. It is not healthy for the courts to grant Microsoft a permanent chokehold over the entire expanding world of the Internet.

title:
COMMUNICATIONS GIANT: THE REGULATORS;
Early Reviews Look Positive; Close Scrutiny Is a Certainty
body: While Federal regulatory officials expressed initially favorable views of the AT&T Corporation's proposed acquisition of the cable television giant Tele-Communications Inc., they said today that they would closely examine the impact the deal would have on creating competition in local phone markets and increasing home access to the Internet. "I'm looking forward to learning more about this transaction," William E. Kennard, chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, said in a speech this afternoon.  "But if it means that these companies will make a real commitment to building facilities to bring residential voice and high-speed Internet service to America's homes, then this merger is eminently thinkable." F.C.C officials said the commission could be expected to grant approval if the two companies showed that their merger increased competition. The Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission, the two agencies that share responsibility for enforcing antitrust laws, have not yet decided among themselves which agency will handle this case. But both generally apply the same test: If competition is harmed, the merger receives critical scrutiny. Most mergers, by their very nature, reduce competition. But in some ways, the officials said, this one could be different. Through TCI, AT&T intends to introduce significant new competition in the telephone and Internet service markets. In a few small markets, cable companies have been offering local telephone service. But once it acquires TCI, AT&T plans to move aggresively into that business, giving the local telephone companies their first significant competition since the breakup of AT&T. Mr. Kennard indicated he would like to see that happen. Greater competition in local telephone service could also open up long-distance competition. The regional Baby Bell telephone companies have tried to move into the long-distance market but have been rebuffed because they face so little competition locally. "If all of this happens as is being discussed," a senior F.C.C. official said, "this could take some of the issues off the table that have prevented the Baby Bells from moving into long-distance services." Meanwhile, the cable-television industry has been slow to offer Internet services, even though using cable modems gives customers far faster access to the Internet. But AT&T is a major Internet server and is expected to ramp up TCI's presence in that market -- bringing a significant new competitor into that business too. Senior members of Congress with responsibility in this area said they were grappling with the same questions. Ken Johnson, an aide to Representative Billy Tauzin, the Louisiana Republican who is chairman of the House Telecommunications subcommittee, said: "We're going to take a good hard look, but I think a lot of good could come from this. It will give consumers one-stop shopping for the Internet, cable and telephone services. But we do have to see what impact this will have on cable-TV competition." Senator John McCain, the Arizona Republican who is chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, complained that the 1996 Telecommunications Act was supposed to increase competition, thereby reducing the need for mergers. "This approach ignores marketplace realities and forces companies that are forestalled from competing to take the simpler route of merging," Mr. McCain said. Graphic   Photo: William E. Kennard, F.C.C. chief, says the deal looks "thinkable." (Amy Toensing for The newyork Times)

title:
COMMUNICATIONS GIANT: THE STRATEGY;
Hooking Up The Nation
body: A telephone giant agrees to acquire the cable company Tele-Communications Inc. in a bold move that promises to redefine the communications landscape. Sound familiar? It should. Nearly five years ago, another big phone company, Bell Atlantic, struck a merger agreement with the same cable giant. But that deal, which soon unraveled, was based on the vague plan of transforming telephone and cable networks into an "information highway" with 500 channels of interactive television -- something no one could be certain consumers even wanted. So what is different now that would prompt AT&T to spend $31.8 billion to buy TCI? The Internet. Rather than chasing an elusive vision, AT&T and TCI are scrambling to keep pace with a race to use phone networks, cable networks and other means to provide consumers and businesses with connections to the Internet -- a race that involves not only other cable titans like Time Warner and ambitious phone companies like a merged Worldcom and MCI but also competitors like America Online that were barely visible five years ago. By agreeing to merge, AT&T and TCI are not so much gambling on a vague vision of the future but betting they can help satisfy the proven public demand for high-speed connections to the Internet. Though few would have predicted it back in 1993, the Internet and its multimedia World Wide Web have become that vaunted information highway -- and the main vehicle for driving it is not a television set but an increasingly TV-like computer. These days, tens of millions of households are regularly surfing the Web to download text, images, sound and video clips and to chat on America Online or other Internet access services. So important has the Internet become to so many people's lives, in fact, that the average amount of time Americans spent watching television declined for the first time last year since television's invention. And for the first time, more messages were sent by email than through the post office. "Nobody wanted 500 channels," said Eric R. Paulak, a telecommunications analyst for the Gartner Group. "Today, what people do want is Internet access." Indeed, even as AT&T began serious negotiations with TCI last Tuesday, the phone company was still trying to arrange a merger with America Online, which decided to remain independent -- at least for the time being. "Just as the home computer caused a whole lot of changes over the last 10 years, there is going to be a new revolution in telecommunications," said Barry Schuler, the president of creative development at America Online. "When you are chatting with someone on AOL, you will be able to click a button and your phone will ring and you can talk to them by voice," he said. AT&T, primarily a long-distance carrier, with 90 million customers, and TCI -- still mainly a cable company, serving 10.5 million homes -- already dabble in Internet service. AT&T's Worldnet Internet access service has attracted about one million customers on the strength of its brand name and an initial offering of a year of free service. TCI owns about 40 percent of At Home Network, which is developing technology and information and entertainment content for high-speed Internet access over television cables. While phone networks can route traffic virtually anywhere on the system, cable networks have a much higher carrying capacity -- which translates to higher speed on the Internet. Yet both companies know the network future lies not in today's telephone-network or cable-system technologies but in providing consumers and businesses with high-speed network access based on Internet technology -- whether for data transfers, voice conversations or, eventually, even TV-quality video. While Internet traffic can flow over phone wires or cable lines or even radio waves, the Internet employs a transmission format that is far more efficient and flexible than conventional telephone or cable systems and seems destined eventually to render those conventional systems obsolete. "There is going to be no difference between local and long distance, between voice and data, between voicemail and email," said Howard Anderson, managing director of the Yankee Group, a telecommunications consulting firm. Indeed, such a network is so flexible that everything from thermostats to refrigerators to door locks are being designed to be linked to the Internet so that they can be remotely controlled by the owners. But the many billions of dollars that will be required for the communications industry to update to a future all-Internet format must come from the revenues of current customers. That is why the first battles in the long war over who provides Internet access to the home will probably be fought over local telephone service. After all, nearly every household, whether it subscribes to cable or even has a personal computer, requires phone service, which remains the surest way to establish a direct relationship with a household. AT&T has not had a direct line into most consumers' homes since it was banished from the local telephone business by the breakup of the Bell System in 1984. But the company, freed to return to the local phone business by the Telecommunications Act of 1996, now hopes to offer customers a complete package that includes local, long-distance and wireless telephone service along with cable television and Internet access all on one monthly bill. Even before the TCI deal, AT&T has been assembling pieces of that capability. In January, it agreed to pay $11.3 billion for the Teleport Communications Group, which provides local phone and data services, mainly to businesses. It has also been trying to develop an affordable wireless system for local calls from the home that would bypass the local telephone companies by tapping into and the vast cellular network it bought in the $12.6 billion purchase of McCaw Cellular in 1993 and has been expanding and modernizing ever since. And in the local markets in which TCI operates, the deal announced yesterday would give AT&T direct wires into consumers' homes. There is no guarantee that AT&T and TCI will succeed in their quest, of course. The competition is simply too fierce to predict the winners as players in all areas of the telecommunications industry move rapidly into one another's markets. America Online, in an effort to fend off phone company competition, for example, has signed up one million people for its low-cost long-distance service offered through Tel-Save Holdings. Local telephone companies, meanwhile, are creating technology that would enable them to offer high-speed Internet connections over conventional phone lines. And the long-distance company Sprint, already a big provider of Internet services to other network operators, has spent $2 billion to reconfigure its network to use Internet-format technology rather than traditional phone-network circuitry. And all the while the industry urge to merge grows stronger on the assumption that victory ultimately will go the companies with the greatest size and geographic reach. Thus Worldcom has a pending deal to acquire MCI, SBC Communications has agreed to buy Ameritech, and so on. All of which has put pressure on AT&T to respond. "The Worldcom-MCI deal will make the resulting company the most important worldwide supplier of communications," said Jerry Michalski, a computer industry consultant. "AT&T had to do something in order to avoid slipping out of contention as the major platform for worldwide, integrated communications." It is only when a company can offer a full range of services that it can hope to recoup the cost of building an advanced, Internet-ready network. "It will cost $500 to $600 per house to offer Internet, telephone and cable services," said David Dorman, the chief executive of the Internet company Pointcast and a former top executive of Pacific Telesis, one of the original regional Bell companies. "If a household spends $100 to $200 a month for all those services, it doesn't sound like a terrible payback." But as Mr. Paulak of the Gartner Group points out, only the affluent will be able to afford these offerings. "At $100 a month for telephone and high-speed Internet access, that rules out the half of the population that earns less than $35,000 a year," he said. "And it will mainly benefit the 12 percent who earn more than $100,000." What is more, TCI, lumbering under a huge debt burden, has been much slower than its competitors to modernize its network. "TCI is big hat, no cattle," said Mr. Anderson of the Yankee Group, who estimates that AT&T will have to invest $10 billion in TCI's network to be able to deliver all the new services it is promising. And AT&T better start writing big checks immediately, Mr. Anderson added, because the winner in the market will be declared early. "The first person to provide high-speed Internet access with voice and data wins," he said, "because if customers are satisfied, they are never going to switch." Graphic   Photo: C. Michael Armstrong of AT&T, left, and John C. Malone of TCI created a communications giant. (Ozier Muhammad/The New York Times)(pg.
