title: Huge Microsoft Photo File Is Part of a Bigger Picture
body: NEED an aerial picture of your house or your business or even the Great Wall of China? There's no need to ask the Government for a satellite photo; just get on the Web and ask the Microsoft Corporation, which unveiled an on-line database this week granting access to satellite and aerial pictures of nearly half of the unitedstates and some foreign sites. While Microsoft says that its database (www.terraserver.microsoft. com), called Terra Server, is the largest database available on line, there appears to be some dispute about that. In any case, the project not only marks the creation of one whopper of a digital scrapbook, it also says something very big about Microsoft's effort to enter the database business, using as an opener a venture that can capture the public imagination. Microsoft's strategy is to use Terra Server to prove that its software and operating system are suited to massive databases. Business strategy aside, the mechanics of the database are impressive. A 45-foot-by-25-foot Compaq computer in Canyon Park, Wash., holds satellite images of the unitedstates and Europe and aerial photographs of the unitedstates. The aerial photographs come from the unitedstates Geological Survey; the satellite pictures are distributed by Aerial Images, which in turn obtained them through a branch of the Russian Space Agency. Two years in the making, the project offers access to images previously unavailable to the public -- at least not without much more time, effort and bureaucracy. The images are useful, according to Microsoft, for farmers, academics and businesses needing survey information, as well as for ordinary Netizens who want to peruse their surroundings. There are also pictures from on high of such landmarks as the Great Wall of China and Central Park. The test site got four million hits on Tuesday, the day after it was first publicized nationally. The U.S.G.S. pictures can be downloaded for free. The photos from Aerial Images cost $7.95 to $24.95. In all, the database contains 178 million photos covering 45 percent of the unitedstates and portions of Europe. Within two years, the creators hope to have images of the entire contiguous 48 states. "We hope that you'll be able to start at Barstow, Calif., and move the cursor east until you get to the Atlantic Ocean," said John Hoffman, president of Aerial Images. There is a handful of publicly available databases offering even more than Microsoft's one terabyte of data, which is enough information to fill two million books taking up 15 miles of shelf space. A site from the Dialog Corporation offers about 2.5 terabytes listing unitedstates patents and images; an I.B.M. site that also includes patents is 1.5 terabytes. Not surprisingly, I.B.M. -- a clear competitor for Microsoft in its effort to collect database business -- has some opinions about the Terra Server's size. "It's not the world's largest database on line," said Jeff Cross, an I.B.M. spokesman. Mr. Cross added, "We've been at this for a while. It's good to see other companies learning to put large databases on the Internet." In fact, Microsoft's original goal was to create the database not for consumers but as a showcase for technology. It considered creating a database of major league baseball statistics, or of every trade in the history of the newyork Stock Exchange, but neither project provided enough data to suit its goals. It is not surprising that Microsoft wants to play in this industry, known as enterprise computing. The database software business is a $10 billion market, according to Richard Winter, president of the Winter Corporation, a Boston consulting firm that specializes in large databases. The industry is dominated by names like I.B.M., Oracle, Sybase and Informix. Microsoft is not a player at the very high end. Many of today's multiterabyte databases are used inside companies. By making Terra Server accessible over the Internet, Microsoft is trying to show that its software can also be used inside companies, where storage and retrieval demands are less severe. "It's an interesting statement from Microsoft," Mr. Winter said. "It says, 'Sit up and take notice. We're going after the big database market.' "

title: Internet Venture in SoHo Runs Afoul of Fire Codes
body: Josh Harris has made a name for himself in newyork City's Silicon Alley -- first by founding a new-media consulting company, then by holding large parties in a SoHo loft that evoked comparisons to Andy Warhol's Factory, and most recently by producing video programming for the Internet through a company called Pseudo Programs. Mr. Harris, who said he employs 45 people and provides an outlet for independent producers, would like the city to offer incentives for start-up Internet ventures like his. Instead, he said, he has been awakened in the middle of the night by gun-toting fire marshals in bulletproof vests over complaints, mostly from neighbors, that he stages his Internet programming in front of live audiences. "The whole tone and tenor of them showing up that way is to intimidate us from holding the events," Mr. Harris said. As city fire officials see it, however, Mr. Harris is violating the fire codes that are required of social clubs and other places where more than 75 people congregate. After receiving 11 complaints about Pseudo Programs, the Fire Department's Social Club Task Force inspected its studio six times and ultimately issued a summons against Mr. Harris in January for failing to provide lighted exit signs, maintain his sprinkler system and meet other fire codes, said Louis F. Garcia, the chief of fire investigations. Fire marshals are required by law to wear bulletproof vests and carry firearms, he added. "I don't think he's being persecuted," the chief said. Under the summons, Mr. Harris faces a $10,000 fine or six months in jail or both. Mr. Harris said he had already spent $50,000 to bring his studio up to code. Pseudo Programs was established in May 1994 as a content provider for the Internet service Prodigy. At the same time, Mr. Harris said, he began throwing huge parties, often attracting as many as 2,000 performance artists, musicians and other creative people. From these events, Mr. Harris said, he developed the contacts and ideas for the niche programming that the company began producing about a year ago. Today, Pseudo offers 45 one-hour programs a week on subjects from hip-hop music to skateboarding. But Pseudo has also annoyed some neighbors by regularly inviting what Mr. Harris describes as 75 "movers and shakers in the hip-hop business" to his Wednesday night webcast from his sixth-floor studio. As he acknowledges, some of his guests hang around afterward in front of a Pottery Barn store at street level and occasionally leave graffiti behind them. "Our storefront is covered with graffiti," said Susanna Somogyi, a manager of the Pottery Barn in SoHo. She said that a few times -- most recently, last week -- people believed to be guests of Pseudo have also tried to break into the store. Both Mr. Harris and his lawyer, John Johnson, said they felt that Pseudo was a target of the city's Multi-Agency Nightclub Enforcement Task Force. That unit, which is headed by Deputy Mayor Rudy Washington, was formed in 1996 to address problems of noise and illegal activities at bars and nightclubs. But Mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani's office said that the nightclub task force had not been involved in the case against Pseudo. The social club task force, which sometimes participates in investigations by the nightclub task force, operates independently under the Fire Department. It was formed after a 1990 fire that killed 87 people at the Happy Land Social Club in the Bronx. Chief Garcia said that an Internet company with a live studio audience had the same obligation as, say, David Letterman had with his "Late Show" to conform to fire codes. "We don't want to wind up with another fire in another unprotected location and wind up with a lot of people dead," he said. But Mr. Johnson said that since Pseudo did not have the resources of CBS, the city should work with him to help him meet the fire codes. "My big bone of contention with the city is that they should tell them what they need to get done and try to help them with interim measures so they could still operate and be within the law," he said. A hearing on the summons is set for July 28.

title: Literary Site Offers More Than Words
body: THERE is no frigate like a book to take us lands away," Emily Dickinson wrote. Of course, she died in 1886, decades before anyone conceived of the Internet. Anyone who sympathizes with Dickinson and has access to the Web should set aside a hefty block of time and hie to a site called Literary Locales. It is listed on a page maintained by the English department at San Jose State University (www.sjsu.edu/ depts/english). With a click, you can visit 122 places that figure in the lives or the works of nearly as many writers (some have more than one site). There are, of course, links to Shakespeare and the Globe Theater, Proust's Combray, the West Yorkshire hills that the Brontes called home, Dickens's Kent and many more places that undeniably figure in the literary canon. There are also links to such lesser-known authors as Flannery O'Connor, Anais Nin, Raymond Chandler and Langston Hughes. With so many options, it was hard to choose where to go first. That decision grew harder, not easier, because each site turned out to be totally different from the others, which only heightened the sense of exploration. Chaucer's Canterbury seemed intriguing -- and it was. Up popped a map of the town today, with several roads highlighted in yellow. You decide where you want to go, what you want to look at, from a fish-and-chips shop to the Norman castle. After this introduction, look above the map and click on the box marked "Canterbury Web." Find and click on "Canterbury Tales," then on "The Chaucer Pages." The scene-setting music you hear is "Bring a Torch, Jeannette Isabella," and you can now choose among quotes from Chaucer, a list of his works, a biography, essays on him and additional sources and books. But tarry on this page a little longer: at the bottom is a link to the "Anthology of Middle English Literature," which takes you to similar offerings on Sir Gawain, Everyman and other medieval plays and lyrics, each with an early music accompaniment ("Sumer Is Icumen In" for Gawain). The "Canterbury Web" page has many more options, including a list of local hotels, restaurants and other tourist information for those who want to make a real visit (which turned out to be not untypical for these sites). For a total change of mood and sound, go back to the main list and try "Edgar Allen Poe's Favorite Haunts," which lists links to Poe's cottage in the Bronx, his house in Baltimore and his national historic site in Philadelphia. The best is the Poe museum in Richmond, where your arrival is met with crashing thunder. You can tour the museum's rooms, and you can access (under "A Poe Pourri") samples of his works, a biography and so on. Poe enthusiasts will then want to move to "Poe's Virtual Library" back on the main page, which lists links to bibliographies, biographies, clothing, courses, movies, comics, plays, family ties and you-name-it about Poe. A. A. Milne has two sites. "Cotchford Farm" in East Sussex, where Milne vacationed and which he used as a setting for "Winnie-the-Pooh" and "The House at Pooh Corner," offers background and a nice picture of Poohsticks Bridge, but its real value is as a link to other Pooh sites. Back on the Literary Locales menu, the site called "A. A. Milne's Ashdown Forest" covers that ground and more, with more pictures of the bridge, the surrounding area and scenes from the books, like Roo's sandpit. It was time for something more exotic: Palermo, Argentina, known here as "Jorge Luis Borges's Childhood Home." Almost a homage, this site begins with a gallery of photographs of Borges. Then it moves on to a serious examination of him, with a biography, a compendium of critics' views of his works, an outline of his influence on other authors and a collection of quotations, including "I have always imagined that Paradise will be a kind of library." This site, by the way, also has a section in Spanish. And so to the Middle East. For many people, Naguib Mahfouz -- his Nobel Prize notwithstanding -- does require an introduction. "Naguib Mahfouz's Cairo" provides one, Cliff Notes-style: a biography, an analysis of his development as a novelist, the beginning and ending passages of "Palace of Desire" and "Adrift on the Nile," a few one-liners lifted from reviews and an anthology of his works, with brief synopses of 8 of his more than 30 novels. Half a world away, there is "Yukio Mishima's Home," a Victorian house in Tokyo that requires only a brief stop. Click on his name to call up an illustrated page giving a little summary of his life and listing the works of Mishima, thought by some to be one of Japan's postwar literary stars. Mishima committed suicide in 1970 and will soon be honored with a museum near Mount Fuji; construction is to begin in the fall. For a preview, click on "Mishima Cyber Museum." One listing, the history of his life, is available only in Japanese, but others are in English. If you click on Proust's Combray, you will land in the village in central France once called Illiers, but renamed Illiers-Combray after Proust used it as the setting for the vacation home in "Remembrance of Things Past." The page offers a description and a few pictures, but scroll to the bottom for the best part: icons depicting Proust himself. Click and you are in the realm of a newsletter called "Proust Said That," in which you will find that Proust "ate little, surviving on a diet of cafe au lait toward the end of his life," and that, when he was 13, in response to a party question 'Who would you have liked to be?' he answered, 'Since the question does not arise, I prefer not to answer it. All the same, I should very much have liked to be Pliny the Younger.' " There's more, of course, including a recipe for bouillabaisse. Sometimes, the sites offer more in the way of scene setting than they do about an author. "Langston Hughes's Lawrence," for example, provides the basics of his life, illustrated by photographs of his home and schools in Lawrence, Kan. But the site, including links, tells more about local history and about Kansas than about Hughes. Others are simple and simply literary. "Dylan Thomas's Fern Hill" provides just the text of that poem, pictures of the Welsh farmhouse in question and a nearby creek, and a brief recounting of a local tale about the farm. Tours are popular. "D. H. Lawrence's Eastwood," which follows the blue-line trail through Nottinghamshire, past homes he lived in, is typical. Some sites proved disappointing. "Bronte Country" seemed all too commercial, designed to lure tourists and sell merchandise more than to slake the thirst of devoted readers. And "Samuel Beckett's Fermanagh" is a link to the official site of the Northern Ireland Tourist Board, which doesn't even mention Beckett. Likewise for "James Herriot's Yorkshire," which gets you to the Yorkshire Tourist Board. Only trial and error will tell you which Literary Locale is evocative and which is perfunctory, which site to bookmark and which to dismiss. Consider the sites devoted to William Wordsworth. Click on "Wordsworth's Tintern Abbey" and you see a gorgeous view of the abbey, a field of purple flowers in the foreground and four interior views of the medieval structure. Go to "Lines," and there is the poem he wrote in 1798. You can leave quickly or linger on his artistry, no distractions. Now try "Wordsworth's Lake District" and you get an album of pictures of the area, perhaps a dozen altogether, and links to walks in the Lake District that William and Dorothy Wordsworth walked. On to the second listing of "Wordsworth's Lake District" and you have 222 additional photographs, plus links to a glossary of Lake District terms ("bield," meaning a shelter, and "gill," meaning a small ravine, to name two), more suggested walks, local weather information, a screen saver to download and more. You could be here for hours. Then again, a fourth site, "Wordsworth's Alfoxden," might beckon -- especially given its links to Coleridge. No wonder that, from now on, you are on your own. Graphic   Photos: WRITERS' HAUNTS -- The Literary Locales site offers glimpses of the venues of literary works and their creators. Clockwise from top left, Shakespeare's Globe Theater, A. A. Milne's Cotchford Farm, Dylan Thomas's Fern Hill and Jorge Luis Borges's childhood home.

title: NEWS WATCH
body: SELECTIVE SCREEN -- Just what the Web needs -- another filtering program. But this two-in-one product looks like a good one. SOS Kidproof, from Sterling Strategic Solutions, filters inappropriate Web sites and protects PC's from accidental or intentional tampering. And the company says it can distinguish between a Web site containing "breast of duck" and one with questionable pictures. The $29.95 package is expected to be in retail stores next month. MAKING ROOM ON LINE -- According to a report issued jointly earlier this week by two research outfits, International Data Corporation and Relevant Knowledge, the number of home Web users in the unitedstates will increase to nearly 102 million by 2002 from roughly 30 million. IDC reports that the percentage of those users who purchase items on line will grow to almost 50 percent from 36 percent, with overall spending increasing to more than $54 billion in 2002 from $4.3 billion in 1997.  SHOP TALK -- Speaking of shopping, Compare.net (www.compare.net), the on-line shopping guide, announced deals with Classifieds 2000 and Deja News, the Internet discussion group search and archive service, to allow its shoppers to search classified ads and get access to discussion groups for peer opinions on products like washing machines and used Corvettes.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
On-Line Medical Aid for China
body: Timed to coincide with President Clinton's visit to China this week, American and Chinese doctors plan to perform a live consultation over the Internet tonight to discuss two severely ill children in China. It will be the first real-time medical consultation between China and the unitedstates over the Internet. The event is less a practical medical move than a show of diplomacy. Members of the Clinton Cabinet are expected to be on hand with doctors at the Medical University in Xian, a city in central China, as they consult pediatricians at the Lucile Packard Children's Hospital at Stanford University about a 12-year-old girl with inflammation of the heart and a newborn with brain damage. The consultation will take place using standard Internet tools for audio and video, as well as a "white board" feature that enables participants to share text, images and sketches. "When there's direct interplay, you get more from it," said Dr. David Teitel, chief of pediatric cardiology at the University of California at San Francisco, who will be participating. "They can respond, and you can respond more quickly." There have been other experiments with telemedicine in China, relying mainly on email among doctors. Several hospitals in China, including Peking Union Medical College Hospital, have acquired sophisticated video-based teleconferencing systems, but such systems are not available for the rest of China's population. "Everyone in the world has satellite links to Beijing, which is not a very real test of medicine to China," said John Reuling, director of information technologies at Stanford University's School of Medicine. Mr. Reuling said the group had chosen to use widely available Internet tools rather than state-of-the-art video-conferencing systems because they wanted to focus on what was actually available to doctors in Chinese cities outside the capital. High-performance computers provided by Sun Microsystems will be left in Xian so further exchanges between doctors from both countries can take place. The consultation was organized by Bridge to Asia, a nonprofit group.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Web Surf With Disney
body: Disney Online, a three-year-old unit intent on bringing all the fluff and pink that is Disney to cyberspace, yesterday opened Disney's Internet Guide, a Web search and directory site for children and families. Dubbed Dig (www.dig.com), the new site is designed to compete with Yahooligans, Yahoo's popular kids' directory. And in a sign that the company is wasting no time capitalizing on its new partnership with Infoseek, the site will also soon serve as the kids' directory on Infoseek. Like Yahooligans, Dig contains eight wholesome categories, like Animals and the Outdoors, Stories and Comics, Games and Toys, and Arts and Entertainment. Each of the Dig categories, which, according to the company, "collectively represent what Disney Online considers to be the best of the Web for kids and families," have been picked by Dig team members and will be reviewed every few days. "It really comes back to our overall Disney Online mission, to provide a gateway to the Internet," said the president of Disney Online, Richard Wolpert. Mr. Wolpert said Disney Online had been working on development of the new site for a year. Disney Online has lagged behind its competition. According to a rankings list maintained by Media Metrix, Disney Online barely registers among the top 20 Web sites. The new partnership with Infoseek, in which Disney acquired a 43 percent stake in Infoseek, is expected to help, but analysts are skeptical of Disney's overall prospects of displacing others as a so-called portal site -- the Web site Internet users see when they first log on. "If you're using Yahoo now, particularly if you're an adult, there's no way you're going to switch to Infoseek and Disney, not in this life," said Keith Benjamin, an Internet analyst with BancAmerica Robertson Stephens. A link to the new site will also be available on the Disney home page (www.disney.com). Dig is Disney's fourth Web site. In addition to Disney.com, the company maintains Family.com and Disney's Blast Online, a paid subscription service for children.

title: Prime Real Estate on the Web: Portals
body: IN the past, Internet insiders liked to use the phrase prime real estate to describe the places on line where people liked to congregate. The new catch term is portal, which is often invoked when talking about the on-line plans of companies like Netscape, Infoseek, Lycos, Yahoo and Microsoft. Each of them wants to be the entryway to the Net, the place where users pause and look around before deciding where else to go once they have logged on. The word emerged as Internet developers realized that cyberspace could have places equivalent to town squares, business districts or malls by providing places where people could turn first by force of habit. A portal is a place that people look for information. People might turn to particular portals first because they are fairly certain that they will find the information they want there. Yahoo, for example, has become a popular portal because it provides reliable and comprehensive listings of things on the Net. Netscape has built a big portal business simply by programming its browser to open at its home page by default. Users could set a different first page or start with a blank one, but many stay with Netscape. At first thought, being the first Web page that pops up on a viewer's screen each day doesn't seem to be particularly valuable for the company providing the page. People use the verbs browse and surf to describe the way they move around the Internet, so most users will probably not hang around that first page for long. Unlike a mall, the Internet allows browsers to jump from a portal to any other place on the Web, including another portal. So stores and sites without prime real estate are not as hard to reach as they might be in a large mall or the center of town. But even persuading Internet users to pause at a portal can be quite valuable. The portals carry advertising, and revenue from that already reaches into the millions of dollars. Companies like Netscape and Microsoft quickly realized that these revenue streams might be more valuable than sales of the browser programs themselves. Netscape gives away its browser, but it says Excite paid $70 million for a premium spot on Netscape's page for two years. Excite will also share advertising revenue with Netscape. The banner advertisements that float across the top of pages can be an ideal way to place brand names and announcements in front of computer users. Advertisements for products are also common. Microsoft is a major advertiser, for instance, of its serious products like Windows NT. Of course, Microsoft also plays the portal game. The company caught the eye of the Justice Department with its plan to grant spots on its opening Windows screen, on the so-called channel bar. This bar, one of the major new features of Internet Explorer 4.0, appears on the desktop in an easy-to-reach position. It displays a number of icons for Web sites like the Walt Disney page and The newyork Times on the Web. Parceling out this real estate raised questions about whether Microsoft was using monopoly power to gain control of popular content on the Internet. The channel bar, however, has not gathered as much steam as other portals, and Microsoft announced plans in March to drop the bar from the 5.0 version of Internet Explorer around the same time that the Senate began inquiries into contracts between the company and the companies with space on the channel bar. Other portal owners are succeeding by looking for ways to make money by steering people to preferred merchants. The Alta Vista search engine, another popular site, offers people a chance to jump immediately to Amazon's Web site and search for books related to their Alta Vista searches. That integration is valuable enough for Amazon to pay fees to Alta Vista. Don Bradley, a spokesman for Compaq, the company that bought Alta Vista when it bought Digital Equipment, said that Alta Vista would get a commission for steering a customer to Amazon even when the customer did not buy anything until a return visit later. Portals like Infoseek, Excite and Lycos began mainly as search engines, and the search software can also be designed to make money for a company. A search may return thousands, if not millions, of hits -- lists of sites related to a given topic -- and each search engine has some way to sort its findings. Alta Vista offers a service that, for $40, allows a person or company to register a word, like Titanic, and arrange for a special Web site to come to the top in a separate section of search results when someone searches for that word. In this case, a search for Titanic takes a browser to www.titanicmovie.com, a site that promotes the movie. Advertising does not affect the order of the rest of the sites found in the search. The latest rounds in the portal wars include adding new information -- news, sports scores and other items -- intended to draw people into the page and keep them coming back. Games are also frequently offered as a lure. Internet-based games are burgeoning, and some portals are giving them away as Java applets. Yahoo, for instance, offers poker game software that allows people to play against others in the country. Netscape's new version of its Netcenter portal, still in beta testing, will present multiple pages with content tailored to different markets. One, for instance, will offer a mixture of business news and features for small businesses. The Netcenter developers are redesigning the site in much the same way that newspapers or magazines work to identify and attract potential readers. If the readers show up, the advertisers will follow. Still, many people wonder what it will take to create large portals that many people will want to visit on the Web. Many users continue to enjoy the fragmented, eclectic and very homespun nature of the Web. Several Web pages run by a single writer, like Matt Drudge, are very popular and thus fairly powerful. But none have the concentration of viewers that the major networks and newspapers still have. Of course, the most clever new portal may be the four buttons on the new Compaq keyboards. If you push the Search button, the computer will take you to the Alta Vista site, which brings in advertising dollars to Compaq. That sort of mutual back-scratching means that the world of real estate on the Web is starting to gain the flavor of land deals in the real world. It may be only a matter of months before someone remakes "Chinatown," the movie about real estate double-dealing in Los Angeles, and substitutes characters from Silicon Valley. Graphic   Photos: Gateways to the Net -- Portals like Alta Vista, above, and Yahoo, below, entice Web browsers by offering news and directions to various areas as well as search engines. Attracting lots of users makes the spots more attractive to advertisers. Default Launching Pad -- Netscape has programmed its browser to open at its portal, called Netcenter, which generates a great deal of traffic. But users can go to the Edit menu to tell the browser to open at another portal.

title: Ruling on Microsoft Shows a Fault Line In Antitrust Theory
body: To the Microsoft Corporation, a Federal appeals court ruling in the company's favor on Tuesday was a gratifying triumph of sweeping importance for its long-running antitrust battle with the Government. To the Justice Department and 20 states pitted against Microsoft, it was merely a bump in the road as they head to court again in September with a broader antitrust case against the leading computer software company. Yet antitrust experts said yesterday that the split decision by the three-judge panel -- a majority opinion written by a conservative and a partial dissent by a liberal -- was both a big victory for Microsoft and a reflection of the wider debate over how antitrust doctrine should apply to high-technology industries. The majority ruling, they say, echoes the hands-off approach championed by Microsoft, while the dissent mirrors the Justice Department's philosophy. "This is a landmark antitrust opinion," said Stephen M. Axinn, a leading antitrust litigator. "It deals with a classic fault line in antitrust -- when a court can second-guess a company's product decisions. The majority opinion, at least for the moment, moves the law further toward a noninterventionist stance, especially in high-tech cases." Investors viewed the opinion as a critical victory for Microsoft and a green light to buy Microsoft stock, which rose 5.15 percent Tuesday and a further 4.16 percent yesterday to $104.9375, a record. Justice Department officials and state attorneys general yesterday pointed to reasons why the impact of the ruling might be limited. The appeals court struck down a ruling last year by a Federal judge who had ordered Microsoft to offer its Windows 95 operating system and Internet Explorer browser program separately. The injunction by Federal District Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson was intended to preserve competition in the market for browsers, software used to navigate the Internet's World Wide Web. In the case, the Justice Department had maintained that by bundling its browser with its industry-standard Windows operating system, Microsoft was violating its 1995 consent decree with the Government. Tuesday's majority opinion, Justice Department officials said, applied to the consent-decree case and not necessarily to the Government's broader antitrust case against Microsoft. The broader monopoly case, based on a far more extensive Federal investigation, contains several additional charges against Microsoft. But a pivotal argument in the case -- and one sharply criticized by the appeals court majority opinion -- is that by tying new software programs to its Windows operating system, Microsoft is unfairly squelching competition in new markets, like Internet software and commerce. Microsoft insists that it, and it alone, should be the arbiter of what new software is bundled into its Windows operating system, the equivalent of the central nervous system on 90 percent of personal computers. Besides, Microsoft contends, its Internet browser is not a separate product, as the Government asserts, but an "integrated feature" of Windows. The appeals court majority sided with Microsoft, saying "the limited competence of courts to evaluate high-tech product designs and the high cost of error should make them wary of second-guessing the claimed benefits of a particular design decision." The appeals court, legal experts say, could have merely struck down Judge Jackson's injunction with a brief ruling. Instead, it presented detailed views on antitrust law and high-technology markets. The majority opinion, legal analysts say, is clearly intended as a warning to the Government, the states and Judge Jackson, who will hear the broader antitrust case starting Sept. 8. "The opinion is very applicable to the broader case," said Joe Sims, a partner at Jones Day Reavis & Pogue, who is a former senior official in the Justice Department's antitrust division. "It's a first indication that this court believes that the conceptual approach of the Justice Department is a stretch legally." The appeals court majority ruling must figure into the preparations for the broader case, Justice Department officials and state attorneys general acknowledged, by suggesting where more facts must be marshaled to strengthen its arguments. "This is very definitely a bump in the road," said Richard Blumenthal, the Attorney General of Connecticut, "but it doesn't knock the wheels off our wagon." Thomas Miller, the Iowa Attorney General, emphasized that the appeals court setback would not prompt the states to reconsider proceeding with its broader case. "It's full-speed ahead -- no thought of the opposite," Mr. Miller said. Several states filed a friend-of-the-court brief in the Justice Department's consent-decree case. Though Justice Department officials said no tactical decision had yet been made on appealing the ruling, it is unlikely to try to appeal to the Supreme Court -- saving that option, if necessary, for the broader case. The majority opinion reflects the more conservative approach termed "judicial restraint" by its advocates. Its author was Judge Stephen F. Williams, a Reagan appointee and self-described adherent of the doctrine of judicial restraint. The conservative approach leans hard on the notion that if a company, like Microsoft, can show a discernible consumer benefit to its tying together of products or features, such bundling should be permitted under antitrust law. The Government contends that other factors, especially the potential harm to competition and innovation, should also weigh in the balance. Conservatives tend to shun judicial "balancing" in antitrust cases. Judge Williams wrote, "Courts are ill equipped to evaluate the benefits of high-tech product design, and even if they could place an evaluation on one side of the balance, the strength of the 'evidence of distinct markets,' proposed for the other side of the scale, seems quite incommensurable." Judge Patricia M. Wald, a Carter Administration appointee, took issue with the majority opinion in some key respects. The majority view, she wrote in her dissenting opinion, seemed to mean Microsoft could bundle anything into its Windows operating system merely by "identifying some minimal synergy associated with such 'integration.' Judge Wald suggested that balancing consumer benefit versus economic harm was, at times, something courts should do. "By no means do I endorse routine judicial intervention in the details of product design," she wrote. "But I also do not endorse (as the majority comes close to doing) judicial abdication in the face of complexity. The courts are certainly capable of determining whether a particular integration offers any synergistic benefits at all or whether these benefits are minimal, significant or great." Eleanor M. Fox, a professor at the newyork University Law School, observed: "The majority opinion is one possible interpretation of antitrust law, but it's a very laissez-faire interpretation. Judge Wald's interpretation is much closer to the Justice Department's argument."

title: U.S. to Release Patent Data On a World Wide Web Site
body: In a new plan for making Government information freely available over the Internet, the Clinton Administration will announce today that it will make the full data base of the nation's patents since 1976 and trademark text and images starting from the late 1800's available on the World Wide Web beginning in August. The project, which will create the largest Government data base on the Internet, is to be announced by Bruce A. Lehman, Assistant Secretary of Commerce and Commissioner of Patents and Trademarks, in a speech to the American Bar Association's section on intellectual property law in Williamsburg, Va. The decision to make the data base freely available is a result of a fierce debate that has gone on for years between public interest advocates who argue that Government information should routinely be made available on the Internet and companies that purchase the data from Government agencies to resell. Indeed, the Clinton Administration's action came less than a week before a deadline imposed by Carl Malamud, an independent Internet pioneer, who in May said he planned to purchase the data from the Patent and Trademark Office and make it publicly available if the Government failed to act. After imposing the deadline in a letter to Vice President Al Gore Jr. and the Commerce Secretary, William M. Daley, Mr. Malamud said that he had received an anonymous donation to support his project and that he was developing his own system of patent and trademark records. Mr. Lehman, however, said that his agency had already made a commitment to Mr. Gore to make the data base available as part of the Vice President's "reinventing government" program. Mr. Malamud said today that he had decided to shelve his plans. "Our site was a backup in case the Administration refused to budge," he said. "We very pleased with the outcome of this five-year struggle. The American public gets the data they deserve, and the Clinton Administration has shown real responsiveness by reversing its earlier policy." In January 1994, Mr. Malamud's group, the nonprofit Internet Multicasting Service, posted the full text of filings made by corporations to the Securities and Exchange Commission and several years of the patent data base over the objections of the S.E.C. and the Patent and Trademark Office. His organization later added data bases from the General Services Administration, the Federal Election Commission, the Federal Reserve Board and the Government Printing Office. In a telephone interview, Mr. Lehman said that it had long been his intention to make both data bases available on the Internet but that he needed first to meet a range of technical and policy criteria. "Creating a 1.3-terabyte searchable data base is a big technical feat," he said. A terabyte is one trillion characters of information, equivalent to about a million copies of "Moby Dick." First, he said, such a system requires tight security provisions to isolate it from the Patent and Trademark Office's internal computer network. In addition, he said, his agency had to perform an economic analysis on how the decision would affect both the Patent and Trademark Office and the information industry. "We have no interest in competing with the private sector," he said, adding that his agency's analysis had shown that the private-sector offers added value beyond the patent and trademark documents. The new data bases will be available at the Patent and Trademark Office's Web site beginning in August, when trademark text will go on line. Trademark images and patent text will follow in November. Patent images linked to the text of the patents will be made available by March 1999, he said. The data base of more than two million patents will be searchable by key word, as will more than 800,000 registered trademarks and 300,000 pending trademarks. The entire data base will be made up of 21 million documents. Currently the Patent and Trademark Office makes abstracts of patents available, a system that is already providing users with more than three million pages of patent material a month. The Patent and Trademark Office received 237,045 patent applications in the most recent fiscal year -- a 14.9 percent annual increase -- and approved about 114,000 patents. Trademark applications grew by 11.8 percent, to 224,355. The new data base on the World Wide Web is a significant step forward, Mr. Lehman said, adding that his plan calls for completely automating the nation's patent system by 2003.

title: AT&T IS NEAR DEAL FOR NO. 2 COMPANY IN CABLE TV IN U.S.
body: The AT&T Corporation is close to an agreement to acquire the nation's second-largest cable television operator in a deal that could sharply expand AT&T's ability to provide Internet access and local telephone service. The deal between AT&T and Tele-Communications Inc. is expected to be worth at least $25 billion in stock. A final agreement had not been reached late last night, but a deal could be announced as soon as today, an executive close to Tele-Communications and an official who had been briefed on the talks said last night. AT&T is seeking to acquire only Tele-Communications' cable properties, which connect to homes, not its programming unit, which creates television programs, said a person close to Tele-Communications, known as TCI. Tele-Communications' programming unit, Liberty Media, already trades as a separate stock. Its ultimate fate is unclear. AT&T is prepared to pay about $50 for each share of Tele-Communications' stock, the person said. That would represent a premium of more than 28 percent to Tele-Communications' closing stock price of $38.6875 yesterday. Any deal between the two companies is likely to face a rigorous review by regulators including the Federal Communications Commission. If the deal wins approval it will firmly put the stamp of C. Michael Armstrong, AT&T's new chairman, upon one of America's most venerable corporations. A merger between AT&T and Tele-Communications would be the biggest sign yet that trying to deliver high-speed access to the Internet and other advanced services is one of the strongest imperatives in today's business world. In recent years, the Internet has emerged as a new sort of media that could rival radio and television in its impact on the nation's economy and culture. The technological bottleneck that has kept cyberspace from becoming a true mass media has been the difficulty in transmitting large amounts of digital data to everyday homes. Consumers gain access to the Internet at speeds a mere fraction of those available to people in modern offices. That has kept the process of linking to cyberspace a relatively awkward procedure in some ways akin to using a ham radio. But by acquiring Tele-Communications, which serves 14.4 million customers, AT&T would gain direct access to homes and apartments for the first time since the leading long-distance company spun off its local telephone operations in 1984. The importance of the Internet to AT&T became clear last week when news emerged that the company had engaged in preliminary discussions to merge with America Online Inc., the nation's biggest provider of access to cyberspace. AOL rebuffed AT&T, though the two could still strike a marketing alliance. Although new telecommunications carriers boast more advanced networks, AT&T retains a vast capacity to transmit information of all sorts from coast to coast at lightning speeds. By merging with Tele-Communications and gaining its many wires into homes, AT&T would acquire an ability to bypass its own ornery progeny, the Baby Bell local phone companies. That could allow AT&T to create an end-to-end network that would allow the company to deliver not only Internet data but also everyday phone calls. With their control of the copper telephone wires that stretch into most every home and apartment, the Bells have appeared to have an advantage in some ways over long-distance companies like AT&T and MCI Communications. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 cleared the way for the Bells to enter the long-distance market once they convinced regulators that they had opened their local networks to potential competitors. Likewise, long-distance telephone companies won the right to compete in local markets. The Bells have not yet won approval to offer long-distance service, but were they to gain the go-ahead, they could be expected to win large chunks of the long-distance market away from traditional long-distance carriers by buying long-distance capacity in bulk and reselling it at a profit. Long-distance companies like AT&T, however, would face the huge cost of building elements of local networks on their own. Indeed, AT&T agreed in January to acquire Teleport Communications Group Inc., a competitive local phone company, for $11.3 billion in a bid to jump-start that effort. Speculation about a possible alliance between AT&T and a major cable company has been rife in the industry for months and caused cable stocks to rise sharply yesterday. The cable industry has been spending billions of dollars to upgrade its lines to offer more data options at faster speeds. TCI in particular has been busy upgrading the capacity and speed of its cable systems. TCI is one of the leading companies behind At Home, the cable industry's broadest venture to offer high-speed Internet access to consumers. The telephone and cable television industries have been locked in a battle over which sector would be first to provide high-speed Internet access to consumers. In some ways an AT&T-Tele-Communications deal would represent a return to a strategy tried by Tele-Communications' chief executive, John C. Malone, in 1993, with a proposed merger with the Bell Atlantic Corporation. That deal later collapsed as visions of cable companies' delivering phone service and telephone companies' delivering movies into living rooms failed to take shape. In many respects TCI is responsible for the evolution of the nation's cable system into what it is today. The company traces its roots to 1956, when Bob Magness, a Texas Panhandle rancher, sold some cattle to build his first cable TV system. Nine years later Mr. Magness, who died in 1996, moved the company to Denver to serve small towns in the Rocky Mountains and hired John Malone, a 32-year-old executive at General Instrument, to help him expand. The effort grew into a company with more than $7.5 billion in annual sales and cable television operations in more than 40 states, Argentina, Brazil, Britain, France, Germany, Japan, Mexico and Spain.

title: House Bill Protects Internet From New Taxes
body: Hoping to throw cold water on the frenzy to tax the Internet, the House today passed a bill that would bar state and local governments from imposing new Internet taxes for three years. Framing the measure as a "pre-emptive strike" on taxes during a period of rapid Internet growth, including the on-line sale of goods, the House approved the measure on a voice vote after months of negotiations by state governors, businessmen and the Internet industry. The Senate wants a six-year moratorium on taxation, and is expected to take up its bill sometime this year. The House bill would also stave off taxes on sales that would ordinarily not be taxed if they had taken place over the telephone or by mail. With an eye on the three-year deadline, the bill would create a commission to study the issue of Internet taxes and make recommendations. For months, the National Governors' Association has opposed the measure, saying it would infringe on the right of state and local governments to levy taxes. The opposition stemmed mainly from the possibility of taxing goods sold on the Internet. By some estimates, Internet sales are expected to reach $200 billion to $500 billion by 2002. For the support of the governors' association, the Internet study group's mission was expanded to include recommendations on a uniform way to tax out-of-state customers.

title: Ruling Unlikely to Affect Windows 98 Release
body: For all the dust kicked up in the legal battle over the Microsoft Corporation's right to include Web browsing software in its Windows 95 operating system, a ruling by an appeals court today in the software giant's favor will have almost no impact on the imminent release of Windows 98, a new version that integrates the browser even more tightly. What the ruling and the suit have managed to do is focus a lot of public attention on a product that has been playing to widespread yawns in computer industry publications. In recent weeks, even Microsoft has been playing down revenue expectations for Windows 98, which is scheduled to go on sale at retail outlets on Thursday. Moreover, the software publisher appears to have generated even less enthusiasm for Windows 98 among corporate computer buyers, where a consensus appears to be emerging that this upgrade should be skipped in favor of Windows NT, a more powerful and robust version of the operating system designed for large networks of computers. "The message is clearly that NT is the future in the corporate market," said Mike Elgan, the editor of Windows magazine, a computer industry news weekly. The Case Corporation, a maker of agricultural equipment, based in Racine, Wis., is representative of many corporate buyers who have decided to forgo upgrading their entire company to Windows 98. "Our strategy is to, in an evolutionary fashion, migrate to NT," said James Hatch, Case's chief information officer. "We haven't evaluated Windows 98, and we don't see a compelling need to orchestrate a mass change." Where today's ruling might have an impact, analysts said, is in emboldening Microsoft to adopt a tougher stand in its contractual dealings with computer makers and Internet service providers. In the last three weeks, several computer makers have announced that they will ship their products with Windows modified so that it opens with a customized screen that either identifies the brand or offers icons that link to sites on the Internet chosen by the manufacturers. This was a practice that Microsoft had forbidden in its contracts in recent years but did not fight after the Justice Department included the company's restrictive contracts in the antitrust lawsuit it filed in May. "This means that Microsoft will have more muscle to reapply the screws," said Jessie Berst, editorial director of AnchorDesk.com, a Internet publication of the Ziff-Davis Corporation. "Recently, we've seen large manufacturers such as NEC Corp., Compaq and Gateway become emboldened by the Justice Department's pressure. This gives Microsoft the court sanction to reinstitute its previous business practices. The court ruling will also put new pressures on the Netscape Communications Corporation, which created the commercial Web browser market with its Navigator software only to lose much of that market to Microsoft in the last year. Earlier this month, Netscape executives sketched out a new business strategy: to transform its home page into a "portal," an industry buzz word used to describe huge World Wide Web sites that attract heavy Internet traffic with a mixture of search engines, Web directories, news, on-line shopping and entertainment. Such sites are becoming lucrative in attracting advertising and steering Web users into the expanding world of Internet commerce. However, while NBC and the Walt Disney Company both invested in portal sites this month, analysts have remained cautious about the revenue prospects for such a strategy by Netscape, which has no search technology or content of its own. The popularity of its home page rests primarily with the fact that it is the first site that people see after they install the Navigator browser. As the market shifts toward Microsoft's browser, Netscape's on-line traffic could well sink. In addition, Netscape suffered two setbacks this week. The first involved server software, the programs that run on the large computers that are hosts to Web sites. Since competition with Microsoft in the browser market forced Netscape to give Navigator away free, server software has been a main source of revenue. On Monday, I.B.M. announced that it would begin supporting Apache, a free Web server that competes against Netscape's server product. Then, today, the appeals court ruling meant that Microsoft can continue to include its Explorer browser with about 90 percent of all computers sold in the foreseeable future. "Netscape has gotten a one-two punch, and it's only Tuesday," said David Readerman, a financial analyst at Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities in San Francisco. After competition with Microsoft forced Netscape to stop charging for Navigator, its revenues from browser sales fell from $17 million in the quarter that ended in December to zero in the quarter ending in April, Mr. Readerman said. In contrast, Mr. Readerman is estimating that Microsoft will realize $2.24 billion in revenue from sales of Windows 98 to computer makers and retail customers in its first year. Microsoft executives acknowledge that they are doing far less to promote the upgrade than they did with Windows 95. Industry analysts say the company is spending only about $10 million on marketing versus almost $200 million for its introduction of Windows 95. "It's hard to say we're ratcheting back," said Yusuf Mehdi, director of Windows marketing at Microsoft. "In fact, outside of the Department of Justice coverage -- which has been extensive -- I think that Windows 98 has been an under-hyped product." The attention to Windows 98 in the news media's coverage of the antitrust suits has been "bittersweet," Mr. Mehdi said, because while it brought the issue of browser integration to the public's attention, it did so in a negative context. But at least one retail chain sees the impact differently. CompUSA, the nation's largest computer retailer, will open its doors at midnight on Wednesday in an effort to make the release of Windows 98 a "marketing event," said Larry Mondry, an executive vice president at CompUSA. "I don't know what Microsoft spent," he said. "The Government gave them so much free advertising they probably didn't have to spend as much. There is much more interest now than there ever would have been."

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Europe Approves MCI-Worldcom Merger Deal
body: The European Union agreed today to approve Worldcom Inc.'s proposed $43.7 billion purchase of the MCI Communications Corporation, the No. 2 unitedstates long-distance company, after MCI said it would sell its Internet business. Negotiations among MCI; Worldcom, which is No. 4 in the unitedstates long-distance business, and European officials ended after MCI addressed concerns that the combined company would dominate the Internet. Stefan Rating, a spokesman for Karel van Miert, the European Union's competition commissioner, declined to provide details of the agreement. The European Commission will issue its formal approval of the deal on July 8, and American regulators are expected to give their clearance soon after. MCI is likely to wait until it officially gets the regulatory approvals before disclosing a buyer for the Internet operations. Cable and Wireless P.L.C. of Britain is a likely buyer of the MCI Internet business, analysts said. Worldcom and Cable and Wireless said they were still talking after an initial agreement did not go far enough toward satisfying regulatory concerns that the combined MCI-Worldcom would dominate the Internet. Cable and Wireless agreed last month to buy MCI's wholesale Internet business, which carries traffic for other Internet service providers, for $625 million in cash. MCI and Worldcom expect to complete the deal this summer. It would create the second-largest unitedstates phone company, behind the AT&T Corporation.

title:
Compressed Data;
Conference Takes On Internet Privacy Again
body: If the Commerce Department's weekly conference calls are any indication, the chief result of its summit meeting on Internet privacy in Washington this week will very likely be frustration on all sides. With nearly 75 representatives from government, industry and civil liberties groups burning up the phone lines during marathon sessions recently on such topics as children's privacy and legislative alternatives to self-regulation, the dialogue has followed a distinctly predictable pattern. "Industry says, 'This is what we're doing to protect privacy; we say, 'It's not enough,' " Mark Rotenberg, the director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center in Washington, said in an interview. "It's kind of a nightmare actually." Arguing that the growth of the Internet and electronic commerce depends on the Government's staying out of the way, the Clinton Administration has advocated a policy of self-policing to address widespread concern by Internet users over their personal privacy on line. But in the wake of a Federal Trade Commission report that found the on-line industry had taken virtually no steps over the last year to insure consumer privacy, that position is getting harder to defend. Still, the agenda for this week's privacy conference is chock-full of industry panels with titles like "Evaluating the Effectiveness of Self-Regulation." And a group of about 50 companies and associations is set to announce the creation of an "on-line privacy alliance," whose members will have to take a pledge to participate in "effective and appropriate self-regulatory enforcement activities and mechanisms." Following the summit meeting, the Commerce Department is supposed to submit its own report to President Clinton next month evaluating the state of on-line privacy. "Do I expect that on the first of July we'll be able to say effective self-regulation is in place; no, absolutely not," said Becky Burr, the Assistant Secretary of Commerce. "But somebody told me U.S. businesses often rally in the last few minutes of the game."   AMY HARMON Graphic   Drawing.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: DIGITAL COMMERCE;
A commercial code revision tries to take on the task of legislating the Internet.
body: IN a climate where any regulation of the Internet in its commercial infancy is considered high treason, many law experts are dismayed at the tidal wave of restrictive legislation -- governing everything from software filters to digital copyrights and public domain information -- being drafted and enacted by states and the Federal Government. Currently these experts find themselves battling yet another "solution in search of a problem" in the form of a far-reaching revision to the Uniform Commercial Code -- the body of law, mostly common to all 50 states, that governs a broad range of commercial transactions, including the sale of goods. The revision, a 200-page epic called Article 2B, would legislate on the sale of virtually all kinds of digital information, including data, text, images, sounds, computer programs, software and data bases. When work on 2B began in the early 1990's, "our primary concern was software," said Gene Lebrun, the president of the National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws (www.nccusl.org). The conference is a volunteer group responsible for revising and updating the code in conjunction with, and monitored by, the American Law Institute (www.ali.org). "But as technology changed," Mr. Lebrun said, "we figured that eventually software would go the way of the 78-r.p.m. record, and the law would probably be outdated." So instead, he said, "we started working on contracts governing all copyrighted information." And that, many critics say, was the first step down the wrong path. Article 2B is so overbroad and complex, the critics say, that it threatens to bury in legalese the very electronic commerce industry that it was created to encourage. As its foundation, the Article supports the controversial "shrink wrap" license, used for years by software companies, which asserts that consumers do not "buy" a software product, but merely buy a license to use the software in limited ways. Most courts have refused to uphold these licenses for many reasons -- not the least of which, they say, is that buyers cannot be held to a contract that they only see after they have already paid for the product. Even so, the enormously complex Article 2B was built around the shrink-wrap premise. It renames this shrink-wrap license a "mass-market contract" -- a term that many lawyers consider an oxymoron, since one party to the contract, the buyer, is not free to negotiate its terms in advance. What is more, it details a complex legal and technical infrastructure for governing and enforcing these contracts for all digital information sold. As a result, some legal scholars assert there can be little argument that Article 2B is bound to run into trouble as the commercial Internet continues its chaotic development. For example, jurisdictional problems abound. The Uniform Commercial Code's provisions become law in any given state only after they are adopted by that state's legislature. So what happens when an information product -- software, music, whatever -- is purchased in a state that has not signed on to Article 2B but was sold in a state that does? And how does one apply the rules when a single purchase buys both information and more traditional goods -- say, for example, a WebTV system? What parts of the law apply to which parts of the same transaction? As it is written today, Article 2B is so convoluted that even those who are intimately involved have difficulty answering such questions. "What does the text say? It is difficult to follow in many respects," said Geoffrey Hazard, the director of the American Law Institute and a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania. "When I'm talking to you on the telephone, for example, we're exchanging information -- we're even doing it electronically. Is that governed by this law? They say no, but I say why not? It's not clear." Article 2B even tries to legislate in territory that does not yet exist. For example, it would make legally binding any transaction made by an "electronic agent" that acts on behalf of a buyer. Such a law seems more than premature when this kind of "agent technology," although anticipated, has not yet made a successful foray out of the laboratory. Yet those who support Article 2B are convinced that new laws are necessary. "Understanding and resolving some of these issues is essential to making the Internet work," said Holly Towle, a partner with Preston Gates & Ellis L.L.P., who was hired to represent the Business Software Association on the Article 2B committee. (The association's guide to 2B is at www.softwareindustry.org/issues/guide/index.html.) "You have to solve some of these things or companies will be reluctant to put their information onto the Internet." But her point of view has some powerful opposition. "Contract law that's stated in terms of regulating information is just unfeasible and therefore undesirable," Professor Hazard said. "I do think changes could be helpful in defining electronic contracting. I think there's potential in governing software to some extent. Beyond that, I'd like to feel that I understand the text of the Article. And we're still engaged in that process." Such strong sentiments seem to be having an effect. The final draft of Article 2B was scheduled for consideration by state law commissioners at their annual meeting in July; instead, the group will keep hearing opposing arguments and working with Professor Hazard to modify Article 2B. "People say to us, 'Don't you know how important this is?' We say, 'You bet we do, and that's why we won't support a statute that will create a lot of problems,' " Professor Hazard said. "This legislation would govern an enormous amount of commerce, and a set of difficult-to-understand rules of uncertain scope wouldn't be helpful. We'd be back to square one." Graphic   Drawing (Randy Jones)

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
A Site That Gets Lots of, Well, Hits
body: The Yankees have the best record in baseball, winning three out of four games so far this season. But Paul Gomez, a veteran Yankee fan, takes the long view. "In my lifetime," he said, "I've had my ups and downs with the team." Mr. Gomez turned 18 last week. Whatever his perspective, Mr. Gomez has developed one of the liveliest Yankee Web sites on the Internet, called, with disarming simplicity, "Paul Gomez's Yankees Page." Mr. Gomez is a child of the Internet. His freshman year in high school in 1994 coincided with the popularization of the Web. The son of an electrical engineer (also a Yankee fan), Mr. Gomez remembers looking, at the age of 3, at his father typing on a Tandy TRS-80, one of the first laptops. At the age of 8, Mr. Gomez began writing simple game programs on the family's Tandy 1000. "I learned how to type because of that computer," he said. WHAT YOU SEE Besides the usual game statistics, the highlight of Mr. Gomez's site is his two bulletin boards, or what he calls "bullpens." One is devoted to the Yankees and the other is devoted entirely to Derek Jeter, the star shortstop. In April 1997, Mr. Gomez had to set up the Jeter board. That was because so many 10-year-old girls, fans of Mr. Jeter's, had been writing in and then clashing with other, usually male, fans of Mr. Jeter's, sometimes over the ballplayer's reported romances, most recently with the singer Mariah Carey. Mr. Gomez now requires a (free) password before signing on to the Jeter board, which has helped reduce the traffic, at one point more than 100 posts a day, to a more manageable volume. The exchanges are still spirited. On Tuesday, for example, someone signed Alisha reported about a Michigan television show that had toured Mr. Jeter's newyork apartment. The kitchen "counters are white and the tile is white," she wrote. "All of the appliances are white. He said something really funny when they were in the kitchen. He says, 'That's the stove . . . I think. I never use it.' . . . I have to go to softball practice. But later today I tell ya what his bedroom looks like and anything else I may have forgotten since I am typing this in a hurry." Someone named Michelle2 seemed less worshipful. She replied to Alisha, "We know that Derek's a momma's boy, so how much of the decorating do you think his mom did?" And on the subject of Mr. Jeter and Ms. Carey, "Derek's Princess" is frustrated. She wrote earlier this month, "O.K. I am like so sick of this. First, they say, 'No, we are not together,' then they are like 'no comment,' then they are like 'yeah we are together,' now it's like 'no comment' again. I'm so sick of this. I mean come on, Derek, if you're gonna date her admit it! I'm sorry, guys, but this is upsetting me big time. What's your intake on this?" LINKS Eleven, including "Behind the Bombers," another fan Web site but with live chat rooms (http://www.behindthebombers.com/). WHAT YOU GET Celebrity worship, but with a fair amount of baseball.   ANTHONY RAMIREZ  PAUL GOMEZ'S YANKEES PAGE (http://www.intercall.com/gomez1/YANKEES/index.htm) Graphic   Photo

title:
SUNDAY: JUNE 21, 1998: THE INTERNET;
con.com
body: Steve Castillo is about as locked-down as they come. An inmate at the Pelican Bay State Prison in Northern California, he has spent the past four years in maximum-security confinement because prison authorities have judged him to be "a gang associate." Graham Noyes, his San Francisco lawyer, thinks the perpetual confinement is a bit much, so he's turning Castillo's plight into a cause. This being the 90's and all, one of his tools is a Web site, Virtual S.H.U. (ncal.verio.com/lazlo), which provides a virtual tour of Pelican Bay's darkest innards. (The home page is pictured below left.) Prison-oriented sites like this are increasingly common; almost always maintained by sympathetic outsiders or prison buffs, they can be serious, silly, rah-rah, grotesque and, of course, scary. Here's a look. MARKS OF CAIN: Prison tattoos -- called "tats" or "ink" -- are a big part of prison life for many, whether they're vulgar (nudes), sentimental (bouquets and Mom), tribal (tattoos often identify racial cliques) or philosophical (like "13," a formula for how one lands in jail: 12 jurors + 1 judge + " a chance). The Convicts Homepage (mypage. direct.ca/b/berzerkr) gives a basic primer on tattoo taxonomy. BIG "GOOD" JOHN: For his many crimes, John Gotti is roosting forever in the maximum-security Federal penitentiary in Marion, Ill. The pseudonymous keeper of the John Gotti Tribute Page (gotti.com) still thinks he's innocent. She's Ravenna Angelini, a vivacious young Californian who is deep into Gotti, Vegas and "Alpha males," and who hates "rats," RICO and prosecutors. A click on the "Kinder Gentler Gotti" button takes you to a rundown of Gotti's alleged good works. FREE THE PERUVIAN: 1! Many pages are devoted to political prisoners hailing from the far left, including the ubiquitous Leonard Peltier and a slightly less familiar name: Lori Berenson. Convicted by a Peruvian military court of helping the Tupac Amaru guerrillas with a plan to take the Peruvian Congress hostage, Berenson is serving a life sentence in a harsh mountaintop prison in Peru. Her supporters' page (geocities.com/ CapitolHill/9968/) includes everything from the latest wire dispatches to the reports of Amnesty International. CHARLIE'S ANGEL: Press the wrong button and you're greeted by an infamous glare: Manson! Access Manson (www.atwa.com) bills itself as the "real source for Manson thought." Unfortunately, the thoughts include 1) Manson is innocent and 2) Manson should be set free. At this site and a related link (revolting.com), you get to hear from the man himself, via reprints of his deep thoughts on the power of the Web. "The Web is my mind," Manson declares, "I brought the Web into play. The Web is my church." EXPRESS YOURSELF: Check out the PrisonZone (prisonzone.com) for a comprehensive look at works ranging from cartoons and caricatures to legitimately talented oil work to stuff best suited for motel velvet. Of the many con artistes, one who seems the most "ripe for hanging" is Anthony Papa, a harshly angular stylist whose on-line gallery contains such make-no-mistake-about-it works as "Mandatory Minimum Sentencing," "Radiological Detection Search," "Forced Strip Search" and "Body Cavity Search." Papa's gentler, more reflective side comes out -- sort of -- in canvases like "Hudson River Landscape From Sing Sing." Graphic   Photos

title:
YOUR HOME;
Web Sites For Co-ops And Condos
body: WHEN the pool at Hampton Commons in Hampton Township, N.J., opened last month, residents of the 300-unit condominium association were reminded that only unit owners whose maintenance charges were current would be admitted. Bathers in arrears, the board noted, could be fined $25. Not only did the Hamptons Common board tack up the announcement on the bulletin board, but it also went a little further: It posted a "news flash" on its Web site. "The Web site is an extremely valuable tool for getting the word out to our homeowners," said Thomas Gaines, secretary of the condominium association. "A lot of the people who live here commute to somewhere else for work. That means there's not always a lot of time or energy left for going to meetings." Hampton Commons appears to be on the leading edge of a trend in community relations -- providing residents with information and interaction over the Internet as a supplement to the more traditional ways of communicating with them. "A growing number of condominium, co-op and homeowner associations are using the World Wide Web to communicate with residents," said Donna Reichle, director of media relations for the Community Associations Institute in Alexandria, Va., a trade organization for co-ops and condominiums.  "And the homeowners are really responding." Since 1996, Ms. Reichle said, her organization has maintained a Web site that residents, board members and co-op and condominium managers can turn to for up-to-the-minute information about community living. The site, http://www.caionline.com, is a central repository for publications, articles, "how-to" advice, court rulings and real-life experiences of residents and board members dealing with just about every conceivable aspect of co-op and condominium ownership and management. Increasingly, boards are discovering that what the Community Associations Institute Web site does for its members, individual buildings can do on a smaller scale for their unit owners. Hampton Commons, for example, posts on its Web site the minutes of every board meeting, reports prepared by committees and notices that range from who may use the pool to when shrubs displaced by sewer line work will be replaced. In addition, the board also posts bylaws, rules and regulations and other information relating to the finances of the association.  And, like most Web sites, the Hampton Commons site also provides links to other Web sites like local schools, governmental agencies and, of course, the Community Associations Institute which, in turn, provides links to hundreds of other related sites. "We've found that one of the biggest benefits for unit owners is when the Web site is used as an on-line service desk," said Ms. Reichle. "Instead of having to get someone on the phone at the management company, a resident who has access to a computer and the Internet can send in an email message any time of the day or night." Some co-ops and condominiums, Ms. Reichle said, post electronic forms on their Web sites so that when residents want to apply, for example, for permission to make repairs or alterations, they can complete the forms on-line and file them electronically.  Other buildings, she said, use the Web site as a marketing tool for potential purchasers -- posting pictures, financial reports and other details about the building and its amenities. "Buyers can look at pictures of an apartment, check the financials and even get a feel for the community without even leaving their desk," Ms. Reichle said. While establishing a presence on the Internet is neither technically difficult nor excessively costly, there are at least two issues that must be addressed by any co-op or condominium board contemplating such a project. The first is that not every unit-owner owns a computer or has access to the Internet. And second, it takes more than just a rudimentary understanding of computers to establish an internet address, create a "home page" for the site, add content and links to the site, and then keep that information up-to-date and accurate. The first issue, it seems, is quickly taking care of itself. "An estimated 28 million households have Internet access today," said Ms. Reichle, adding that in addition to being able to access the Internet from home computers, many individuals are able to gain such access from computers at work, school and even from public libraries. The second issue -- creation and maintenance of the site -- is also becoming increasingly easy to address. At Hampton Commons, for example, a computer-savvy resident, Bonnie Venable, volunteered her time and expertise to construct the association's site and keep it current. And for co-ops and condominiums in newyork, the Council of newyork Cooperatives recently began providing member buildings with the ability to establish a professionally designed site at minimal cost. "It is no longer a luxury to have a Web site," said Mary Ann Rothman, executive director of the Manhattan-based co-op and condominium organization. "We have nearly 2,000 member associations in newyork City and its environs and this is our way of helping our members make the transition into the 21st century." She said the council's Web site (http://www.cnyc.com) has had nearly 16,000 "hits," or visits by web surfers since it was established about two years ago. In addition, she said, the council has received an increasing number of requests from other Web sites to share mutual links with those sites. As a result, she said, the council last month established CNYCSites, a web site design and maintenance service for member buildings. Lloyd Chrein, president of Chrein.com, the company that designed the council's Internet site, said that buildings that sign up for CNYCSites will have a site designed for them that will be linked directly with the council's existing site. "We're trying to make the process as simple, painless and inexpensive as possible," Mr. Chrein said, explaining that the basic site design being offered to member buildings consists of two "pages." Each page, he explained, can contain virtually any information that can be stored and displayed on a computer. At present, Mr. Chrein said, the basic package being offered by CNYCSites allows members to choose from three predesigned templates into which individual buildings can insert whatever information they choose. Generally, Mr. Chrein said, the first page -- the home page -- contains information about the building, pictures or illustrations, and links to other Internet sites. The second page, he said, usually contains a bulletin board for listings of meetings, activities and events and for posting apartments for sale or sublet. Additional pages can be added so that other information -- including building bylaws, proprietary leases and rules and regulations -- can be instantly accessed by clicking on a link to the desired page. "We've already gotten about 250 hits on the CNYCSites page," Mr. Chrein said. "And we've sent out a few dozen application packages to member buildings." For members of the Council of newyork Cooperatives, he said, the one-time charge for designing a two-page site is $400. In addition, Mr. Chrein said, member sites can be updated monthly for an annual fee of $175. Additional information may be obtained by calling CNYCSites at (212) 787-3462.
