title:
USER'S GUIDE;
In Sex-Role Tangle, A Woman's Search
body: DO women search for information differently from men? I never thought so myself -- and in fact, found the notion rather sexist on its face -- until the other day when I stumbled across an unusual Web search site called Look smart that is particularly popular with women. During the first five months of this year, Looksmart attracted a higher percentage of women than the other top search sites, according to statistics compiled by Craig Ruskin, a research analyst with Relevant Knowledge, which measures Web traffic. While other sites' audiences tended to reflect the male-centric face of the Web (only 44 percent of Web users are women), Looksmart (www.looksmart.com) consistently attracted a higher proportion of female users, more than half in three of the previous five months. When Evan Thornley and Tracey Ellery designed the site three years ago, they were not trying to target women. "We started out to target professional families, busy people, a highly educated group of folks," Ms. Ellery said. "Our vision was to reach a mainstream audience on the Web. It turned out that a large proportion of that audience is women." That intrigued me because I have been disappointed by most of my attempts to find useful information on the Web. No matter what search site I try -- Yahoo, Excite, Infoseek, Lycos, Alta Vista, Hotbot and the list goes on -- I usually end up frustrated, wading through screen after screen of long lists of sites unrelated to what I was searching for, like sites written in German or reams of personal home pages. But now I had hope. Perhaps the problem all along was that I was a woman searching for information in a man's environment. I admit that it sounded a little odd and even self-serving. But Looksmart has a higher percentage of women users, so it must be doing something that appeals to them. I mean, us. When I went to Looksmart to investigate, I noticed a difference. Although Looksmart offered the usual opportunity to type in a keyword to conduct a search, the design of the site nudged me in a different direction. Looksmart was clearly encouraging me to browse. Along the left side of the screen was a prominent list of 12 tempting categories like Travel and Vacations, Business and Finance, and Shopping and Services. I could click on any of these to begin broad searches. Idly, I chose Shopping and Services, and that produced a list with more specific subcategories. To narrow my search, I clicked again, delving deeper into such subcategories as Clothes and Accessories and then Women's Wear. I arrived within seconds at a list of sites labeled rather inelegantly as Footwear. Skeptical of any site that would use such an unevocative label for the glorious subcategory of shoes, I clicked on the list. Was I about to be confronted by page after page of socks? Instead, I found myself happily examining images of actual pairs of shoes by companies like Kenneth Cole, Steve Madden and Hush Puppies. The Hush Puppies site even flashed this message: "Browse our shoes!" There are no three sweeter words in the English language. After about a half-hour of comparing heel heights, prices and options for summer sandals, I tried to make sense of the experience. I believed that I had been randomly experimenting with the search site. But when I phoned Mr. Thornley and Ms. Ellery and described my journey, I learned that the pattern of my search had been no accident. "You ended up using the site to shop," Mr. Thornley said. "This is not unusual, and it is not unlike what people have observed. Women on average shop in a more browsing context. Men tend to be more hunters, searching for a specific item." "Does that mean that when women are searching for information, they're really in effect shopping for facts?" I asked. "It's important not to overstate the generalizations," Mr. Thornley cautioned. "But what we appear to see is that on average, women are more disposed toward a category approach to searches." Looksmart is certainly more disposed toward that approach. While most search engines rely primarily on software to sort sites automatically, Looksmart employs a staff of 30 real people to review each site, write a brief description of it and categorize it. "This is how we give a much more hands-on approach to sifting through the information," Mr. Thornley said. "Yahoo is the only other site that really does the same thing." But each has an idiosyncratic way of organizing information in its database. Yahoo's categories (www. yahoo.com) were very different from Looksmart's. To arrive at a list of Yahoo's shoe sites, I had to follow a route that was, to my mind, less intuitive. I clicked first on Business and Economy, then Companies, then Apparel, then Footwear, then Women's, then Brand Names. Although Yahoo's database of sites is more than twice as large as Looksmart's database of 400,000, I preferred browsing on Looksmart. Since my opinion of browsing was based on personal taste, I enlisted the aid of Gary Arlen, who heads Arlen Communications, a company that has studied on-line shopping patterns. He readily agreed to act as a sort of scientific control. He and his wife had been pricing bedding the day before, and he was willing to do some comparison shopping. But Mr. Arlen's experience on Looksmart was vastly different from mine. He narrated his search over the phone in real time: "I'm starting at Shopping and Services, then going to Decor and Design, then searching for bedding, and here's a list for some appropriate sites. But wait, by the time I get to the sixth or seventh site on the list, I'm at something called Eco-Baby, and it sells natural diapers, breast pumps, a whole list of things I'm not interested in. Oh, wait, -- the last item is bedding." Mr. Arlen was disappointed that he had been compelled to wade through stuff he considered extraneous. "I'm not convinced browsing is better," he said. But then, he is a man. Of course, the real difference in search techniques is based not on sex but rather on what you need to find. I enjoy browsing as much as the next, er, person when I am shopping. But when I am looking for specific information, like the answer to a question my 7-year-old recently posed -- "How many babies can a horse have at once?" -- I can find the answer much faster by searching with the keywords "horse" and "facts" on Yahoo than by using Looksmart. (The answer is usually one foal, but sometimes two.) Believe me: even after hours of browsing, I can still type as fast as any man. Graphic   Illustration. (Margaret Riegel)

title: Virtual-Classes Trend Alarms Professors
body: ABOUT 850 professors at the University of Washington have signed an open letter to Gov. Gary Locke to say they are worried about the enthusiasm he and one of his advisers are showing for instruction via CD-ROM's and the Internet. The teachers worry that Washington State will be too quick to embrace the idea of the virtual, on-line university to cut costs and jobs. They say they see some disturbing national trends in that direction, citing the results of a roundtable of university professors and presidents brought together by the consulting arm of the Coopers & Lybrand financial services company. A white paper issued after the conference in July said that "instructional software could easily substitute for campus-based instruction or at least be a substantial part of the delivery system" and that the creation of only 25 on-line courses could serve about 80 percent of the undergraduate enrollment in core courses. The faculty members' letter, which they plan to deliver next week, urges Governor Locke to "support learning as a human and social practice, an enrichment of soul and mind, the entitlement of all citizens in a democracy, and not a profit-making commodity to be offered on the cheapest terms to the highest bidder." College professors are facing great upheaval as policymakers talk about using the Internet to modernize academia. With the arrival of the World Wide Web, video streaming, multimedia CD-ROM's and computer-assisted research, students now have easy access to more facts than scholars a few decades ago ever imagined, and those changes have made some administrators and taxpayers view a classroom lecture as an inefficient mode of imparting knowledge from one brain to many. A speech by Wallace Loh, the Governor's policy director, to the University of Washington Law School in May worried many professors. In that speech, Mr. Loh said telecommunications would be especially useful for teaching adults returning to school. "Technology is likely to be the much more common method of delivering the learning they need, at home or in the workplace for them, simply because they're place-bound," he said in an interview. Younger students would be more likely to attend traditional colleges or universities, he said. The professors do not oppose all Internet instruction. "Under certain circumstances, distance learning is a wonderful option for people who are incapable of getting to a campus," said Lauren Goodlad, an assistant English professor who signed the letter. "The faculty is just concerned that this would be economically foolhardy because in point of fact, high-quality teaching, whether done on a distance-learning basis or on a campus basis, requires contact." Many professors did not like what Mr. Loh called the "brave new world of digital education." But others believe that high technology could free up time for instructors to advise or tutor students and pursue more research. Already schools can circulate lectures and video clips of top professors electronically, and professors can get short-answer tests graded by computers.  One of the main proponents of the letter acknowledges that technology has helped streamline academic life. "We're happy to use it and are all using it, but when they basically want to replace people with computers, that's where we draw the line," said Galya Diment, an associate professor in the department of Slavic languages and literatures and president of the University of Washington chapter of the American Association of University Professors, which helped circulate the letter. She noted that 95 percent of the signatures on the letter had been gathered via email. "We don't want to go back to the caves or even to typewriters," she said. "What we objected to were the extreme views, like beaming an image of professors to students and thinking that would be a satisfactory way of replacing face-to-face education." Alan Borning, a professor of computer science and engineering, joined a dozen other teachers in his department in signing the letter. "A lot of education happens through the interaction of faculty and students in a variety of departments," he said. He described studies in computer graphics at the university that successfully bring together art, music and computer scholars. "If you have people learning from CD-ROM's off in their garage, this sort of thing is not going to happen." Earlier this year, Governor Locke, a Democrat, created the 2020 Commissionand told it "to rethink and re-invent higher education from the ground up." Some at the University of Washington have criticized the selection of commission members -- whom Governor Locke called "a group of this state's smartest people"-- because the panel includes many from the business community but no professors from any college or university. The commission's recommendations to the Governor are due in September.

title: Microsoft and Compaq to Buy 10% Stakes in Road Runner
body: The Microsoft Corporation and the Compaq Computer Corporation said yesterday that they would each invest $212.5 million for 10 percent stakes in Road Runner, the high-speed cable-modem joint venture of Time Warner Inc., Time Warner Entertainment/Advance-Newhouse and the Mediaone Group. Analysts said the deal reflected the interest of Microsoft and Compaq in fostering the growth of high-speed Internet connections for home users. For most users, the Internet experience is limited by the amount of information that can be squeezed through a telephone line. Until the current bottleneck in this information plumbing, or bandwidth, can be opened, consumers will find little performance gained in buying more powerful computers or new software. Cable modems and a competing telephone line technology known as A.D.S.L., for Asymmetrical Digital Subscriber Link, promise to break through this traffic jam. Under optimal circumstances cable modems and some configurations of A.D.S.L. can pump about 4 million bits a second from the Internet into a PC, compared with a maximum speed of fewer than 56,000 bits a second from the fastest dial-up modems. Microsoft, Compaq and other leaders in the personal computer industry are investing in both cable modems and A.D.S.L. technology in the hope that high-speed Internet connections will increase sales of higher-speed computers and associated software. To that end, they are spreading their bets. Last year, Microsoft bought a $1 billion stake in the Comcast Corporation, a major cable company that owns a small interest in the At Home Network, a provider of cable Internet services. But Microsoft, Compaq and the Intel Corporation are also founding members of the A.D.S.L. Forum, a group promoting high-speed data connections over telephone lines. "The bottom line for both of these companies is it is in their best interests to accelerate the arrival of high-bandwidth services to consumers," said Michael Harris, an analyst with Kinetic Strategies in Phoenix. "Given the glacial pace at which the telcos move, they're probably better off pushing the cable companies," Mr. Harris added. "But they are really agnostic; they just want more bandwidth to the home no matter how it gets there." The Road Runner venture, which was announced late last year but officially closed yesterday, says it has more than 90,000 subscribers, compared with At Home's 110,000 users. As part of their effort to accelerate the delivery of broadband services over cable modems to consumers and small businesses, Microsoft will provide the new venture its expertise in Internet, client, server and application software, while Compaq said it would deliver PC's with pre-installed cable modems to the market by the end of the year. "The real objective here is to make high-speed cable access the dominant technology," said Doug Holmes, executive vice president for strategy and business development of Mediaone, the broadband and cable unit of the U S West, which split last week. "To that extent, we and At Home are complementary. We expect to collaborate with At Home." Thomas A. Jermoluk, At Home's president and chief executive, cast the deal with Compaq and Microsoft in a similar light. "It's good to have them investing in cable," Mr. Jermoluk said. "We don't compete with Road Runner; there's no overlap. Any technology they develop in their partnership with Road Runner will only help us." At Home has not worked with Compaq, but has joined with Microsoft to improve server software for its Internet service. Microsoft's chairman and chief executive, William H. Gates, said in a statement, "This venture brings the right combination of technology and Internet access to make high-speed Internet connectivity a reality for consumers." Microsoft's Internet Explorer is currently the standard Web browser offered with Road Runner's service, but users can change to Netscape Navigator or other programs as they wish. At Home users now get a highly customized version of Navigator but will soon be able to choose between Navigator and Explorer at the time their service is installed. Ownership of Road Runner on a fully diluted basis will break down as follows: Microsoft and Compaq each will have 10 percent; Time Warner Inc. will have about 9 percent; Time Warner Entertainment (through its Time Warner Cable division), in which Time Warner Inc. and Mediaone Group are partners, will have about 20 percent; Mediaone Group will have about 25 percent, and Time Warner Entertainment/Advance-Newhouse will have about 26 percent. Advance/Newhouse is a partnership of the Advance Communications Corporation, a subsidiary of Advance Publications, Inc., and the Newhouse Broadcasting Corporation.

title: More of MCI Internet Unit Said to Be for Sale
body: Continuing to try to win regulatory approval of its $37 billion acquisition by Worldcom Inc., the MCI Communications Corporation has offered to sell additional components of its Internet business, people close to the negotiations between MCI and regulators said yesterday. It was unclear how precise MCI had been in its offer, but the people close to the discussions said MCI had offered to sell parts of its Internet business that were not included in the $625 million deal that MCI struck with Cable and Wireless P.L.C. last month. Both the Justice Department and antitrust regulators from the European Union are weighing Worldcom's planned takeover of MCI, which was announced last fall. The regulators are concerned that the combined MCI-Worldcom could wield dominant power in the Internet industry. MCI, the nation's No. 2 long-distance telephone company, is also one of the country's largest Internet carriers. Worldcom's Uunet operation is the world's biggest Internet service provider. MCI made a big gamble last month when it announced a deal to sell to Cable and Wireless the wholesale part of MCI's Internet business, but not the units that provide data services directly to consumers and big business customers. Before the deal was made public, MCI tried to win assurances from regulators that the Cable and Wireless arrangement would be sufficient to allay antitrust concerns about MCI-Worldcom, but the regulators refused to sign off on either deal. In the apparent hope that it could present the regulators with a fait accompli, MCI announced the Cable and Wireless deal anyway. "By divesting MCI's Internet backbone, we have eliminated any overlap with Worldcom's Internet business," the chairman of MCI, Bert C. Roberts Jr., said at the time. "We have formed an agreement that addresses antitrust concerns with the MCI-Worldcom merger." The regulators did not agree. Karel van Miert, the European Union's competition commissioner, has made no secret of his intention to oppose MCI's deal with Worldcom unless the companies sell additional Internet assets. The European Union has said it may not make a formal decision on the MCI-Worldcom merger until July 15. But an influential advisory committee is scheduled to meet on Friday and Mr. van Miert will make a recommendation to the committee before then. The Justice Department has not set a formal timetable for its deliberation, but the department is working closely with the European officials. The regulators hold significant bargaining power in their talks with MCI and Worldcom. If the MCI-Worldcom deal does not win all of the necessary regulatory approvals by the end of the year, MCI can demand $1.6 billion in cash from Worldcom along with the right to walk away from the deal. It is clear that the MCI-Worldcom merger would sail through the regulatory reviews were Worldcom to agree to sell Uunet. But Worldcom is not willing to do that. John W. Sidgmore, who runs Uunet, is Worldcom's vice chairman and it is likely that Worldcom would rather see the MCI deal die than sell Uunet. That leaves MCI and Cable and Wireless in an odd position. Cable and Wireless recently sued MCI for the right of first refusal to any additional Internet assets that MCI might sell. That suit was rejected in court last week.

title: Phone Giant To Acquire Bay Networks
body: Grasping for leadership in the market for Internet communications equipment, Northern Telecom Ltd. of Canada, North America's No. 2 maker of telephone gear, announced yesterday that it had agreed to acquire Bay Networks Inc., a leading data networking company, for $9.1 billion in stock. Yesterday's deal was the largest in a recent series of mergers in the telecommunications equipment and data networking sectors. Companies that have thrived making equipment for traditional telephone systems have been trying to jump into the fast-growing market for gear that links computers at high speeds. Meanwhile, small communications equipment makers and foreign companies that have struggled to win business from big unitedstates communications carriers have looked to mergers as a way to enhance their distribution networks. Two weeks ago, Alcatel Alsthom of France, one of the world's biggest communications equipment makers, tried to bolster its presence in the unitedstates when it agreed to acquire the DSC Communications Corporation for $4.4 billion in stock. Earlier that week the Ciena Corporation agreed to be acquired by Tellabs Inc. for $7.1 billion in stock. With yesterday's announcement Northern Telecom made a bold, and expensive, bid for a company with a culture that appears quite different from its own and that has had difficulty in recent years meeting the high expectations of Wall Street and industry experts. As a maker of equipment that routes information between computers, Bay has had some difficulty contending with competition from Cisco Systems Inc., which is three times Bay's size. Many analysts agreed that integrating Bay and Northern Telecom successfully could pose a challenge but said the deal made sense in light of the fundamental direction of the companies' industries. Networks based on Internet technology, known as I.P., for Internet protocol, are gaining in popularity over more traditional circuit-switched networks. While traditional networks in essence force different streams of information to stay within their own digital lanes, networks based on Internet technology can perform more efficiently by allowing packets of information to switch lanes in search of faster paths to their destinations. "It's time to design networks that are designed for I.P. and put the voice over top of that, which is a huge change from the circuit world of the past," John Roth, Northern Telecom's chief executive, said in an interview. Referring to Bay's chairman, Mr. Roth added, "In talking to Dave House, we were looking to put some of their technology in our products. Then we realized the fit was just great." But investors were not so sure of that yesterday. Northern Telecom's shares fell by 15.2 percent after the deal was announced, falling $9.6875, to $54 on the newyork Stock Exchange. Some institutional investors had told Northern Telecom's management that they would not support an acquisition of Bay, which had been rumored for weeks, and they followed through on that promise. Under the terms of the agreement, shareholders of Bay will receive 0.6 share of Northern Telecom for each share of Bay owned. Northern Telecom's shares closed at $63.6875 on Friday, making the deal worth $38.21 for each share of Bay. Investors had speculated that Northern Telecom could acquire Bay for a price in the mid-$30's. Bay's shares closed on Friday at $28.3125, meaning the original premium for Bay's stockowners was about 35 percent. Shares of Bay rose 8.6 percent, or $2.4375 yesterday, to $30.75. Northern Telecom said the deal, which it intends to complete in the third quarter, would dilute the company's earnings this year and add to earnings after that, discounting charges the company will take to pay for the merger. Some analysts, however, said that was an aggressive timetable. Another financial issue that emerged yesterday was that as a Canadian company, and as one that is mostly owned by another company, BCE of Canada, Northern Telecom must use the purchase method of merger accounting, which forces an acquirer to take charges against future earnings to cover the difference between the assessed value of the target and the purchase price. At the end of the last quarter Bay had a book value of $1.5 billion. If Northern Telecom pays $9.1 billion for the company, it could have to take charges of as much as $7.6 billion. Analysts estimated that Northern Telecom would try to write off as much as 80 percent of that as a charge to cover the value of Bay's in-process research and development. Mr. House would become president of Northern Telecom, taking that title from Mr. Roth, but would remain based at Bay's present headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif. That also raised concerns among analysts, because many of Bay's recent problems emerged because of an internal rift between the company's two predecessors, Synoptics Communications, based in Santa Clara, and Wellfleet Communications, based in Billerica, Mass. Synoptics and Wellfleet merged in 1994 to form Bay. "If we take a three-to-five-year horizon, we may well say this was a good deal for Nortel," said Gregory S. Geiling, an analyst for J. P. Morgan Securities. "Near term, though, this is going to be a very difficult acquisition to integrate, from a culture perspective, from a product perspective and from a location perspective, and that's why investors are really beating up Nortel today." Bay was advised in the transaction by Morgan Stanley Dean Witter and by the law firm of Simpson Thacher & Bartlett. Northern Telecom was advised by Deutsche Bank Securities and by the law firm of Cleary, Gottlieb, Steen & Hamilton.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Ziff-Davis is pushing its 24-hour cable television network on computing in a three-front campaign.
body: ZIFF-DAVIS, the high-technology media and marketing company, has introduced a 24-hour cable television network focused on computing and the Internet and is counting on a multimillion-dollar advertising campaign to put it on the map. Ziff-Davis Inc., which is 70 percent owned by the Softbank Corporation, the Japanese computer company, introduced the network, ZDTV, last month. Ziff-Davis is investing $100 million in the network over a two-year period, ending early next year, including an estimated $10 million for the advertising campaign. Ziff-Davis is based in newyork, ZDTV in San Francisco. The campaign, which was developed by Blazing Paradigm in San Francisco, is directed at three audiences: cable affiliates, which Ziff-Davis is wooing to carry the network's programming; potential viewers, whom Ziff-Davis hopes will watch the programming and also ask their cable operators to carry it, and potential advertisers. To date, Ziff-Davis has signed agreements with 17 cable operators in 15 states, most recently with DirectTV Inc., a unit of the Hughes Electronics Corporation, which has more than 3.6 million subscribers. By the end of this month, ZDTV expects to be available in six million homes. The creative work for the ad campaign is largely the same for all three audiences. Written in a somewhat humorous tone with an edge, the advertising "tries to capture the personality and attitude of the channel," said Sam Pond, creative director of Blazing Paradigm. "The ads have to show that it's not a geek pointing to a motherboard, that the channel has the spirit and energy technology has today." A 30-second television spot announces that "as we launch the future of computer entertainment, we'd like to take a moment to reflect on the past," then cuts first to footage of a "Pong" video game, popular 20 years ago, and next to a montage of photos of the new ZDTV shows. All print ads depict television sets floating in empty rooms, with various ZDTV programs on their screens.  One ad asks, "If food gets its own channel, why shouldn't computers?" while another says: "Introducing a TV network all about computing and the Internet. (And to think television used to be called the idiot box.)" Advertisements geared toward cable affiliates and advertisers are running in industry publications. The cable ads will continue, but the advertisers' campaign will run only at the time of the network's introduction. Print advertising for viewers is running through this month on the television listings page of The Wall Street Journal, and in the June and July issues of Wired, Red Herring, Upside and Fast Company. It is also running indefinitely in the 17 Ziff-Davis computer magazines for the unitedstates market, which include PC magazine, Internet Computing and Yahoo! Internet Life. The television ad, also geared toward viewers, is appearing indefinitely on MSNBC. An unusual component of the advertising is a direct response campaign on the company's web site (ZDNet.com) and on the network's web site (ZDTV.com). It asks prospective viewers to have their local cable operator "ZDTV me" by filling out a form and expressing their interest in the network. Ziff-Davis will forward the form to the operator. Greg Jarboe, a company spokesman, said that 17,000 people had completed the form as of early June. Larry Gerbrandt, a senior analyst at Paul Kagan Associates, a Carmel, Calif., consulting firm, who follows the cable industry, said that although "Ziff-Davis has staked out some territory here that's been underserved, right now it's all about carriage." He added, "They've got to get shelf space." He called the company's $10 million budget "a useful amount of money, enough to get them on radar screens." Jim Nail, a senior analyst at Forrester Research Inc. in Cambridge, Mass., called the Ziff-Davis on-line petition initiative superb, saying, "People on the site are exactly the audience for the TV programming." Still, he added, "The big question in my mind is whether instead of watching 'Baywatch,' consumers will watch programs about computers." Other analysts, recalling less than spectacular earlier forays into cable by Ziff-Davis and its rivals, questioned the network's prospects. Ziff-Davis produced a show called "The Site" for MSNBC that the latter canceled last fall after 16 months, when it switched to an all-news format. The Jones Education Company of Denver killed its computer network in 1996, after two years. Andy Holdgate, a spokesman, said that it could not convince enough cable operators to carry it. Halsey Minor, chairman and chief executive officer of Cnet, a San Francisco-based high-technology media company, said: "The question is whether ZDTV will be able to do the programming that delivers on their marketing. They're taking a huge gamble." Cnet, which once considered creating a 24-hour high-technology cable network but ultimately opted not to do so, produces four computer-related television shows shown on the Sci-Fi Channel and USA Network. Scott Kurnit, chief executive officer of the Mining Company, a network of special interest Internet Web sites, and the former president of Viewer's Choice, a pay-per-view cable network, was more sanguine. "The stars line up for me; I think this network is around for the long haul," he said. "They ought to win with their distribution plan because they're giving cable operators a way to position themselves as more technologically savvy."

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Guide to Entertainment Opens on the Internet Today
body: Entering a market crowded with some of the biggest companies in cyberspace, The newyork Times Company said yesterday that it would introduce an Internet service about entertainment, restaurants and shopping in newyork City and its suburbs. The site, called newyork Today, will be available, starting today, at www.nytoday.com. The service will compete with newyork Sidewalk from Microsoft, Digital Cities newyork from America Online and Citysearch newyork from Citysearch, a privately held company. All the companies are seeking a share of the rich market for local advertising, which includes classified advertising, yellow pages listings, outdoor, broadcast and print ads. "Local advertising is the biggest and most profitable market for advertising," said Brian C. Oakes, an analyst with Lehman Brothers who follows newspapers and Internet companies. "It is critically important for newspapers to win the local market, both in print and on line." Newspapers may have an edge over technology companies because of their history and reputation in the cities they serve, analysts said. "One of the problems for all these local arts and entertainment sites is that they all look the same," said Patrick Keane, an analyst with Jupiter Communications, a newyork research firm. "The Times has an established brand, while the others have to build theirs from scratch." Daniel J. Donaghy, the general manager of newyork Today, said that he hoped that the breadth of the news and reviews about newyork events written for The newyork Times would distinguish the site from the competition. But Mr. Donaghy said the company expected that the most important advantage would be technology that allowed each user to customize the service to see both information and advertising related to the user's own interests. The site is designed to look like an appointment calendar, with weather forecasts, arts events and other information listed by date. In one unusual feature, advertisers can have their sales and other promotional events mixed in with the arts and entertainment listings. Users can see a list of these sales and, if they choose, have sales for categories of their choice displayed when they first enter the site. In addition to the calendar listings, newyork Today has a number of other close links between advertising and the site's editorial content. For example, a user who searches the classified advertising listings of The Times for, say, condominiums in Greenwich Village will also see advertisements offering listings of the same type of property from several real estate brokers. That advertising will be marked as such and displayed in red type, while editorial content will be in blue type. Martin A. Nisenholtz, the president of The newyork Times Electronic Media Company, said that such links were a service to users in the long tradition of publishing. "People often buy the newspaper as much to read the ads as to read the news," he said.

title: Critics Contend U.S. Policy On the Internet Has 2 Big Flaws
body: Nearly one year after President Clinton disclosed a list of ambitious goals to foster the commercial growth of the Internet, critics say that the Administration's contradictory policies on data encryption and its slow progress on privacy controls have left the nation's nascent electronic commerce industry adrift on a rudderless ship. And critics contend that two major issues seem particularly in disarray -- a policy for protecting consumer privacy on line, and an export policy on data-scrambling, or encryption, technology. "The whole area of E-commerce is going to come unglued unless we solve the crypto policy, unless we resolve the privacy issue," said David Farber, a professor of computer science at the University of Pennsylvania and a board member of the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Because electronic commerce -- buying and selling products and services on line -- is widely considered the engine that promises to drive commercial activity in the next decade, the stalemates on those two key points have overshadowed an otherwise productive year for the Administration on information-technology issues. Mr. Clinton's senior adviser on Internet issues, Ira Magaziner, in an interview last week declared success in meeting most of the one-year goals that he had set in drafting the President's framework for a tax-free, self-regulated digital marketplace. Most important, he said, the Administration made considerable progress on international accords to keep Internet commerce duty free. Mr. Magaziner also noted that pending legislation would put a moratorium on domestic Internet taxes; that a framework had been developed for making the issuing of Internet addresses a self-governing and competitive system and that Congress was close to putting into effect a treaty to protect digital copyrights in cyberspace. In the private sector, companies and Internet consortiums have developed a variety of filtering products and rating systems to give parents options for controlling where their children can venture on the Net. Those efforts have so far averted new attempts at Government controls over Internet content. "If you had asked me a year ago would we be as far as we are, I would have been cautious about it," Mr. Magaziner said. "I think we have made tremendous progress." Yet, two weeks shy of the White House's own July 1 deadline for initiating an effective code of conduct to protect consumer privacy on line, the Administration is scrambling to address a report issued last week by the Federal Trade Commission. That report, the culmination of more than 10 months of hearings and investigations, paints a dismal picture of the industry's efforts to police itself on privacy issues. It proposes that legislation be enacted to protect children on line -- not just from the usual suspects like pedophiles, but from predatory marketers who gather information about children and their families with no apparent regard for privacy rights. Industry groups generally praise the Administration for staying true to its vow to let the private sector lead. With a little more time, they say, they will have the proper controls in place. But privacy advocates and academic observers say that the Administration has been inconsistent and passive. Worse, they say, it has failed to provide the kind of leadership that would force the private sector into the kinds of cross-industry agreements needed to make self-regulation work. About the only thing everyone, including Mr. Magaziner, agrees on is that the Administration has made no progress in resolving its most glaring policy contradiction: its continued support for Government regulation of encryption technology. Bowing to law enforcement concerns about terrorists and drug cartels using strong data-scrambling technology to conceal their crimes, the Administration has refused to let American companies freely export strong encryption. But the same kinds of computer security that the Federal Bureau of Investigation and other police agencies insist on controlling are exactly the kinds of security that must be in place before credit card and other sensitive transactions can be considered safe from hackers and on-line thieves. "E-commerce cannot succeed without strong encryption to protect people on the Internet," said Robert Holleyman, president of the Business Software Alliance, an industry association whose members include the Microsoft Corporation, the Netscape Communications Corporation, Novell, Sun Microsystems and the nation's other top software developers. In a sign of just how crucial encryption policy is to the computer industry, Microsoft's chairman, William H. Gates, and his top rivals put aside their differences last week and traveled to Washington for a closed-door meeting with Attorney General Janet Reno and the F.B.I. director, Louis Freeh. "It is fair to say this is one area where our policies are not consistent with the rest of the approach, and the reasons are because of the concerns of law enforcement," Mr. Magaziner said. As for privacy, Mr. Magaziner said it was too soon to call self-regulation a failure. Many in the on-line business world agree. "People have to understand that this is a fairly new phenomenon," said Harris Miller, president of the Information Technology Association of America, a trade group. "The technology is still being developed to give people the confidence that their privacy is being protected." What is more, says Henry H. Perritt Jr., dean of the Chicago-Kent College of Law at the Illinois Institute of Technology and president of the Center for Information Law and Policy, if progress on self-regulation is slow, it is the Administration that is to blame. Lending a sense of urgency to that perception is the fact that in October, strong privacy protections take effect in European Union nations and those measures could have a serious impact on American companies doing business overseas. Mr. Magaziner has been globe-trotting for the last few weeks trying to dissuade other nations from following the European model, assuring them that self-regulation will work. An industry-Administration summit meeting to help draft privacy guidelines has been in the planning stages for months. Final dates, June 23 and 24, were set the day that the trade commission issued its dismal findings about children's privacy on line. Graphic   Chart: "A 13-Step Internet Program" Here is an overview and status report on the Administration's proposals and goals for promoting electronic commerce, which were spelled out last July.  ONE YEAR GOALS  Develop rules and solutions for protecting privacy on the Internet -- A Federal Trade Commission report found that private industry efforts have been inadequate. The Commerce Department will hold a conference this month on the subject, just days before a progress report is due.  Secure international agreements to keep the Internet tax-free -- Japan has signed an agreement and it has general support worldwide. The World Trade Organization recently adopted a one-year ban on tariffs on information sold on line.  Reach agreement with state and local governments to keep the Internet tax-free -- Legislation is pending to create a three-year moratorium on taxes on Internet access, on-line services and information traveling across the Internet, at least until a study on taxing electronic commerce can be done.  Ratify World Intellectual Properties Organization treaty on digital copyrights -- The Senate has ratified the treaty. Legislation to put the treaty into effect has passed the Senate and is pending in the House of Representatives.  Make control of Internet domains private and competitive -- Currently, domain names are assigned by Network Solutions Inc. under a Government-sponsored monopoly. The Administration has released a plan for handing governance over to a nonprofit corporation, but the international community still has to reach agreement on who will be on the board.  Develop rules for authenticating electronic transactions -- International discussions are continuing and legislation is pending to adopt a uniform national standard.  Develop Internet rating and filtering systems that can screen content deemed unsuitable for children -- Several technologies are being developed, but their effectiveness is debatable. Legislation is pending to require schools that receive Federal Internet funds to install software to screen content.  Get more involved in electronic commerce -- The Administration wants to expand its GSA Advantage on-line shopping service.  LONGER-TERM GOALS  Create international standards for Internet security -- The Administration remains deadlocked with private industry over controls for encryption technology.  Create a seamless environment for electronic commerce worldwide and insure access for all -- International discussions are continuing.  Update U.S. patent policy to meet the needs of the electronic age and seek worldwide agreements to protect patents -- Work is underway.  Promote private sector development of electronic technical standards and oppose efforts by other Governments to impose standards -- International discussions are continuing.  Monitor developments in electronic payment systems and oppose imposition of restrictions -- Work is underway. (pg. D7)

title:
Validation;
Even if Halsey Minor's NBC Deal Doesn't Insure Success, It Does Give Big-Media Cachet to His New-Media Strategy
body: It is hard for most people, even those who know him, to comprehend the magnitude of Halsey Minor's ambition. But Thomas S. Rogers, the president of NBC's cable and Internet division, got to witness Mr. Minor in the full flush of confidence last Wednesday at Le Cirque 2000 in Manhattan -- a victory lunch to celebrate NBC's acquisition of a controlling stake in Snap, the Internet directory and guide service created by Mr. Minor's company, Cnet. After Mr. Rogers asked Mr. Minor to write his prediction for Cnet's stock price a year from now on a slip of paper, a half-dozen NBC executives around the table jotted down their own guesses of what he had written. Knowing the 33-year-old Cnet founder's lofty regard for his new-media vision, each picked a figure far above the $48 that Cnet shares were trading at that day -- a number that was already a 45 percent jump from Monday, the day before the NBC deal was announced. Even so, when Mr. Minor unfolded his paper, it had a figure much higher than anyone had dared guess. (The price? No one would comment for publication, but more on that later.) Mr. Rogers was surprised by the apparent hubris, he recalled later, for even the most ambitious executives at General Electric, NBC's parent, cloak their aspirations behind at least some false modesty. And in Silicon Valley, near Cnet's headquarters in San Francisco, executives typically sit in torn jeans and talk about how their technology is improving society. (It is only on the sly that they peek at the up-to-the-minute value of their stock options.) But Halsey Minor has always made his aspirations clear: He's not out to save the world; he's going to conquer it. With a preppy appearance masking a pit bull intensity, Mr. Minor is not embarrassed to proclaim his intention to become the first media mogul of the Internet, the Ted Turner or Rupert Murdoch of his generation. Depending on one's viewpoint, Mr. Minor is either a charismatic and passionate visionary or an abrasive, egotistic upstart. Whatever the angle, NBC decided to endorse Mr. Minor's strategic direction. "This is the sign of a guy with a true vision, someone who doesn't mess around and mince words," Mr. Rogers said. "He is very creative, but he's also a businessman with two feet on the ground." In last week's $63 million deal, NBC agreed to acquire up to 60 percent of Snap's technically elegant but money-losing service and to promote it on the air to the 73 million people who watch its programs each week. NBC's seal of approval does not guarantee Mr. Minor's success, of course. But the deal, and other recent evidence that his ideas may be catching on, does at least validate a new-media approach that until now has flouted conventional wisdom. His first Internet services, a series of Web sites about computers that started in mid-1995, gambled that money could be made producing new information for the Internet. Mr. Minor has expanded Cnet's original programming even as the approach has fallen out of fashion because it is expensive. Most of the successful content sites, like CNN.com and Time Inc.'s Pathfinder, so far largely reprint information created for other media or showcase content created by users, as in chat rooms. Then, in an even more controversial move, Mr. Minor diverted 150 people at a cost of $25 million to develop Snap, which was introduced last fall, three years after the introduction of Yahoo, Excite and other competing Web guide sites. So far, its ratings have been minuscule. But Mr. Minor was proved right that Internet guide services would be popular with users and more so with advertisers looking to find people interested in their wares. And he predicted that big media companies would decide that these sites, now known as portals, would be the centerpieces of their Internet strategy. Indeed, before he reached the deal with NBC, which thinks its prime-time promotion can make Snap a top-rated portal, Mr. Minor was close to selling an interest in Snap, according to people close to the negotiations. One interested buyer late last year was Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation. Early this year, he was also close to a deal with the New Century Network, a consortium of newspapers that is now defunct. Things are also looking brighter for the computer Web sites as well. With far less information than its archrival, the computer publishing colossus Ziff-Davis, Cnet's bright, easy-to-use sites have remained the ratings leaders in their category. Its News.com service has become Silicon Valley's leading source of up-to-the-minute information about the technology business. And because people who read about computers tend to buy them, advertisers have been drawn to Cnet's sites, too. Ziff-Davis, fresh from a public stock offering, is trying hard to overtake Cnet on line. And it is beginning a 24-hour television network about computers, which would compete with Cnet's five weekly television shows that appear on some broadcast and cable outlets. Still, with the financial drag of Snap lifted, analysts expect Cnet to become profitable this year. "I was surprised at just how much we were hurt because the market didn't see us as having a chance of surviving," Mr. Minor said last week. "But I believe in the end our strategy has been vindicated." Investors simply have not understood Mr. Minor's long-term prospects, said Brian C. Oakes, an analyst with Lehman Brothers. "The market is very short-term oriented," he said. "Building media brands takes years." For now, Mr. Minor and a newly hired team of experienced media executives will try to give Wall Street the profits it is demanding. Earlier this year, budgets and sales goals were imposed on Cnet's young staff for the first time. But ultimately, Mr. Minor says, the history of the most successful media tycoons is filled with bet-the-ranch deals and Hail Mary passes, not by fastidious attention to quarterly earnings. "Ted Turner never made money, yet he sold his company for $15 billion," Mr. Minor said, somewhat oversimplifying the facts. (Turner Broadcasting was marginally profitable before Time Warner bought it for stock worth $7.5 billion when the deal was announced in 1995.) Mr. Minor was intent on becoming a media baron even before he founded Cnet in 1992. While an undergraduate at the University of Virginia in the late 1980's, he installed four computers in public places to let people search for rental apartments. Later, Mr. Minor, along with Jeff Bezos, then both investment banking trainees at Merrill Lynch in newyork, almost persuaded the brokerage firm to back them in a venture to deliver news electronically to executives. In a cost-cutting move, Merrill killed the project. (Mr. Bezos would go on to start Amazon.com, the on-line bookstore.) Mr. Minor was crushed. "He was hopeless. He was like a colt in the stable waiting for the gate to open for a big race," recalled Russell S. Reynolds Jr., the well-known head hunter, who interviewed Mr. Minor for a position as his executive assistant a few months after he left Merrill. Looking for a smart aide to carry his bags and write speeches, Mr. Reynolds offered this deal: If Mr. Minor worked for two years, Mr. Reynolds would help him develop a plan for a new business. The ideas were flowing from the start. "One day he came in with a stack of PC magazines, $279 worth, that was three feet tall," Mr. Reynolds said. "Halsey said, 'Get it: People are spending money on this stuff.' " But after his two indentured years, and despite introductions from Mr. Reynolds, Mr. Minor's plan for Cnet was rejected by most of the leading venture capitalists. Only after a year of living off money from friends and credit cards did Mr. Minor attract $5 million from Paul Allen, the billionaire co-founder of Microsoft. Suddenly, Cnet was in business, with an ill-formed plan to start a cable network about computers and do something on line as well. Mr. Minor set up a studio in some unused squash courts in a health club in the North Shore district of San Francisco, not far from many advertising agency offices. In April 1995, Cnet began a half-hour weekly program on the USA Network cable channel. In June of that same year, the company began Cnet.com, its first Web site, a sort of electronic computer magazine with product reviews, news and helpful tips. (Today, Cnet's four weekly television shows operate at a break-even level and are meant mainly to promote its Web sites.) It was a heady time as Mr. Minor began to hire a handful of experienced computer journalists and armies of eager young workers, all excited by the promise of inventing a new medium. "There is nothing sexier than a C.E.O. who has a passion for his product," said Christopher Barr, a top editor of PC World magazine who quit to join Cnet in March 1995. Mr. Minor obsessively surfed Cnet's sites and those of its competitors, looking for flaws and opportunities. As developers worked, they would talk of the "H-factor" -- the likelihood that Mr. Minor would bawl them out for missteps. "People think I have an uncanny ability to find anything that is broken," Mr. Minor said. "I would say to the programmers, 'If you can't do it, I'll write it myself.' I'm no expert, but I can make a credible threat." Some of the threats, accompanied by notorious temper tantrums, have been too credible. And several senior editors, along with a raft of junior staff members, have left Cnet in recent months. Yet it was his decision in 1996 to slow Cnet's momentum by building Snap that drew the most criticism to Mr. Minor inside and outside the company. People said he was simply too late. But Mr. Minor believed the game was only beginning. "When I was in college, I read a lot about Michael Dell," he said. "I felt it was too bad I wasn't as smart as he was and the PC game was already over. But at the same time I was going through that agony, Ted Waite was starting Gateway 2000." Still, Mr. Minor found only limited success in his initial strategy -- offering Snap as a home page to Internet service providers so that they could appear to offer their customers as much content as America Online. The on-line service Prodigy, for example, ultimately chose a deal with Excite rather than Snap, even though Prodigy's chief executive, Russell I. Pillar, is another friend from Mr. Minor's stint at Merrill. "My ears still ring," Mr. Pillar said of the conversation in which he told Mr. Minor he had decided to link Prodigy to Excite rather than Snap. "Halsey likes to win at all costs." And indeed, in order to get the deal done with NBC, Mr. Minor had to confront the true cost of success. Initially, he did not want to give up more than half the ownership in Snap. But NBC would not do the deal if it could not own at least 60 percent, and Mr. Minor conceded. "Ultimately, we said we would rather own 40 percent of No.1 than 50 percent of No. 3," Mr. Minor said. NBC has the option to buy the 60 percent stake for $39 million. It has also bought 4.99 percent of Cnet's stock for $26 million. Most important, NBC will provide extensive on-air promotion of Snap. Mr. Minor says the value of that air time will be far higher than the $100 million over three years that CBS traded for a stake in the Sportsline Web site. So what was the stock price prediction that Mr. Minor wrote on that piece of paper? Neither he nor Mr. Rogers will say, citing laws against promoting stocks. But Mr. Minor is happy to explain his thinking. "Yahoo is worth $5 billion," he said. "With NBC's backing, we can get as big as Yahoo within five years, so our 40 percent turns into $2 billion." And beyond that point, it is hard to comprehend the magnitude of Halsey Minor's ambition. D1)  Chart: "A New-Media Model" When Halsey Minor founded Cnet, few could have foreseen that he would build it into a new-media company with a stock market value of $665 million. Here is a look at the pieces of the company.  CNET COMPUTER WEB SITES The cornerstone of Cnet's business. It has nine Web sites, including cnet.com, news.com and computers.com, which offer everything from news to games to search engines to a computer comparison shopping service. title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
Jewish Museum Appeals To Eye, Ear and Taste Bud
body: Unlike most museum Web sites, which tend to be little more than brochures on a computer screen, the Jewish Museum's site takes advantage of many of the visual, audio and interactive capabilities of the Web; all this and recipes, too. The museum, at 92d Street and Fifth Avenue in Manhattan, was founded by the Jewish Theological Seminary in 1904. It expanded its rudimentary Web site last November with the help of the Antenna Tool and Die Company, a Manhattan Web site developer. The museum's director of marketing, Grace Z. Rapkin, said it had tried to learn from some of the best museum and gallery Web sites, like the Exploratorium in San Francisco (http://www.exploratorium.edu/), the Art Gallery of Ontario (http://www.AGO.on.ca/) and the Museum of Modern Art (http://www.moma.org/). "We wanted a taste of what's available here so people would want more when they came to visit," she said, "but we wanted a big enough taste so that people would know something if they didn't visit at all." The site features, for example, several paintings from the much-anticipated Chaim Soutine exhibition, open through Aug. 16 and the first major show of the artist's work in newyork in nearly 50 years. WHAT YOU SEE The Permanent Exhibition pages feature such unexpected paintings as John Wesley Jarvis's 1815 portrait of Solomon (Steamboat) Isaacs, whose copper mill provided the boilers for Robert Fulton's steamboats. Last year, some of Mr. Isaacs's descendants saw the painting at a special exhibition and were thrilled to discover that the clan's distinctive eyes and eyebrows came from "Uncle Sol." The Contemporary Artist Project pages feature art available only on the Web, like Kristin Oppenheim's "Untitled, Landscape Series, 1997." It is a photograph of trees against a cloud-filled sky, as Ms. Oppenheim, in a breathy, Jacqueline Kennedy-like voice, sings, "Black bird, black, where are you now?" The artist said the blackbird is an allusion to mythological birds in Jewish folklore. The cabalists, Jewish mystics, believed that birds were divine instruments by which God revealed His intentions. "Live at the JM!" features sound excerpts from popular lectures, like the March 1997 performance by Jonathan Katz, the humorist who helped create "Dr. Katz: Professional Therapist" on the Comedy Central cable television channel. "I had dinner with Boutros Boutros-Ghali," he says. "I had the couscous. It was so-so." At "Dining at the Jewish Museum," there are recipes for potato pancakes and Hometown Hamantaschen, cookies traditionally eaten at Purim. Go ahead, fress a bissel. That's Yiddish for "Try it, you'll like it." LINKS None, but several soon, including the National Foundation for Jewish Culture, an advocate for Jewish cultural preservation (http://www.jewishculture.org/). WHAT YOU GET A look at Jewish culture that employs the most commonly used plug-ins, or special application programs, so even the novice can enjoy the latest in Web wizardry.   ANTHONY RAMIREZ  THE JEWISH MUSEUM http://www.jewishmuseum.org/ Graphic   Photo

title: House Passes Bill to Crack Down on Pedophiles Exploiting Internet
body: The House today unanimously approved a bill to crack down on pedophiles who use the Internet to entice children sexually, making prosecutions easier and toughening prison sentences. The bill passed 416 to 0, reflecting Congress's growing concern with cyberspace as the number of children who use the Internet continues to boom while pornography and pedophilia grow along with it. The legislation now goes to the Senate. Embraced by all sides -- Republicans, Democrats and the Clinton Administration -- the bill would prohibit "contacting" a minor through an on-line service, like the Internet, or engaging in sexual activity and would establish a three-year minimum sentence for using a computer to do so. Under current Federal law, prosecutors must prove that a pedophile persuaded or forced a child into a sexual act, a situation that has made convictions difficult. The bill would also make it a crime to transfer obscene materials knowingly to a minor over the Internet. "Individuals who seek children to sexually exploit and victimize them are also a mouse click away," said Representative Bill McCollum, the Florida Republican who worked with the Justice Department to draft the bill. "Cyberpredators often cruise the Internet in search of lonely, curious or trusting young people." The House vote comes at a time when law-enforcement officials are recognizing the popularity of the Internet as a vehicle to commit crimes, are stepping up their efforts to combat fraud, pornography and pedophilia in cyberspace. So far in Federal courts, there have been 450 convictions of people who have used the Internet to solicit children to engage in sexual activity or to post pornographic images, according to statistics from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. Cyberspace poses a particular threat to children because they often sign on to the Internet unsupervised and can enter chatrooms, where computer users hold typewritten conversations. Although there is no way to know how many children are contacted by pedophiles or are exposed to pornography through the Internet, law-enforcement officials say it is a growing problem. By using the Internet, pedophiles can remain anonymous and hidden from view, making it easier to seduce children and set up meetings. Internet-savvy children can also easily access on-line pornography. The word "sex," typed into a search engine, can summon numerous listings. And while commercial sites usually require the use of a credit card, some pornography sites offer free photographs to lure customers. The bill also cracks down on serial rapists and on those who attack the elderly and the disabled.

title: Keep Internet Funding for Schools
body: With the Internet becoming increasingly important in commerce and education, the Federal Government should be redoubling its efforts to help disadvantaged communities get on line. Instead, some in Congress want to pull the plug on a modest program that is critical for thousands of schools and libraries around the nation that cannot afford to pay for Internet access on their own. The "e-rate" program, created by the 1996 Telecommunications Act, provides subsidies to poor schools and libraries to pay for wiring and telephone costs. The cost of computers, software and teacher training are not covered. Most of the funding comes from big long-distance companies that pushed for passage of the act, which allowed them to pursue new lines of business. Now those companies are pressuring Congress and the Federal Communications Commission, which administers the program, to cut the subsidies. More than 30,000 schools and libraries have applied for subsidies totaling $2.02 billion, an amount less than the annual spending limit of $2.25 billion set by the F.C.C. So far only $625 million has been collected for the first half of the year. Today the F.C.C. is expected to decide whether to collect $1.3 billion in the second half of the year, as planned. Any significant reduction would be irresponsible given the needs of schools and libraries. The political pressure on the F.C.C. has been intense, with opponents deploying several different arguments. Congressional critics warn that e-rate collections will cause long-distance companies to raise their rates. The carriers, by putting a separate e-rate charge on telephone bills, are threatening to pass the cost on to consumers, when in fact they should be absorbing that cost. House Speaker Newt Gingrich plays to that strategy by labeling the e-rate subsidy a "tax." The e-rate program is a public obligation that the carriers agreed to and are required to finance under the 1996 law because they stand to reap enormous financial benefits from deregulation. Access charges that long-distance companies pay to local phone companies have been cut significantly as a direct result of the 1996 act. Should the F.C.C. decide to trim the program, it will be capitulating to company greed at the expense of communities all over the country.

title:
PUBLIC LIVES;
Readying the Slingshot for a Modern Goliath
body: DAVID BOIES is the former Cravath, Swaine & Moore superstar trial lawyer in the cheap suits and stretch limousines who has defended some of the biggest legal game of the last 30 years: I.B.M. in its 13-year fight with the Government, CBS in the libel suit brought by Gen. William C. Westmoreland, and the nation's failed savings-and-loans against Michael R. Milken. Now he is the Government's chief lawyer in the snazziest antitrust lawsuit of the 1990's: unitedstates v. Microsoft. Tough case? "Not really," he said. "To be honest." Mr. Boies (pronounced BOYZ) has been called an eccentric genius, a prima donna, wry and amusing -- but never modest. He said in an interview on Wednesday that the Microsoft case would be over by October (the trial is set to start on Sept. 8 in Washington), and that he was pleased with the judge's decision on Tuesday to limit each side to 6 to 12 witnesses. He also said the Government's best evidence against Microsoft was Microsoft's own documents, used in the Government's complaint. "We didn't sort of hold back the best," Mr. Boies said. Microsoft responded to Mr. Boies's manueverings with its own. "That's useful information for us," William H. Neukom, Microsoft's senior vice president for law and corporate affairs, said about the documents. Mark Murray, a Microsoft spokesman, said yesterday that the Justice Department was deliberately withholding the documents it was using against Microsoft to "hamstring" the defense. And so forth. The heart of the case is this: The Government says Microsoft used its monopoly in its Windows software to illegally crush competitors in another market -- Internet browsers -- in favor of Microsoft's own browser, called Internet Explorer. Microsoft counters that Internet Explorer is an "integrated product" with Windows. Things were sunnier two days ago, when Mr. Boies talked in the study of his very large red-brick house on 10 acres in Armonk, in northern Westchester County. There were a pool, a tennis court, a few dogs, the noises of children (Mr. Boies has six from three wives). It might have been a pleasant scene from the life of a country squire, were this country squire not distracted by five phone lines and clients like Gary Shandling, the actor, who is suing his manager in what is Mr. Boies's most time-consuming case right now. Mr. Boies, 57, had the body language of a harried man who was just passing through his home en route from Washington to the office in Armonk. But he sat still for an hour, in black sneakers and a $160 suit from Macy's, and dismissed the idea that as a onetime I.B.M. lawyer against the Government he can now bring tricks to the Government side. "You've got to be sure you don't fight the last war," Mr. Boies said. Naturally, he said that he was on the right side both times, and that "I.B.M. did not engage in the kind of practices" that Microsoft did. HIS main lesson from I.B.M.? "Speed," he said. It took the I.B.M. case five years to get to trial; eight years after that the Justice Department dropped the case because it was technologically irrelevant. Last month, it was Mr. Boies who pushed for the early Microsoft trial date. He grew most engaged when he talked about the Sherman Act -- the 1890 law passed to control the robber barons and now being used against Microsoft. "You're applying antitrust principles to software," Mr. Boies said. "It's interesting, and it's important. But it's not that difficult." He sees a "re-emergence" of antitrust enforcement in the 1990's, after a trough during the Reagan Administration, and says antitrust laws "are what make free markets possible." It is probably impolite to point out that Mr. Boies has grown rich from the antitrust laws -- he was making about $2 million a year when he left Cravath in 1997 -- especially since he is charging the Justice Department a bargain-rate $250 an hour for his services. Mr. Boies's normal fee is $600 an hour. He expects his total bill to the Justice Department will be $100,000, although if it were a corporate client, he said, "I would have added at least a zero." Mr. Boies was hired by Joel I. Klein, the Assistant Attorney General in charge of the department's antitrust division. Mr. Klein said yesterday that his division had not handled major antitrust cases for a number of years, and he needed a lawyer with long-term experience. "There's no substitute for that many years of orchestrating litigation," he said. "It's a high art form." Mr. Boies was asked what inspired his career choice. "Perry Mason," he said. "Seriously." Mr. Boies grew up in Orange County, Calif. His father was a high school history teacher; Mr. Boies thought for a time about getting a doctorate in American history. Instead he married his girlfriend right after high school, and worked on a construction crew and as a bookkeeper before graduating from Northwestern University and then Yale Law School. He joined Cravath in 1966, made partner in 1972, and left last year to represent such clients as George M.  Steinbrenner 3d, whose interests collided with some of the giant companies the firm represents. (Law firms may not represent competing clients.) He now has his own firm, Boies & Schiller, with 23 lawyers and clients that include CBS and the French Government. He has been married to his third wife, Mary, since 1982. He has a famous fly-paper memory, and loves to gamble in Las Vegas. Graphic   Photo: David Boies is the Government's lawyer in its suit against Microsoft. (Librado Romero/The newyork Times)

title: Sailor Victorious in Gay Case of On-Line Privacy - Correction Appended
body: In a victory for gay rights, with implications for the millions of people who use computer on-line services, both the Navy and America Online have reached settlements with a highly decorated sailor who was investigated by the Navy after he posted a message in which he described himself as "gay." Under the Navy agreement, the 36-year-old sailor, Master Chief Petty Officer Timothy R. McVeigh, will retire from the military with full benefits and with tens of thousands of dollars to pay his legal fees. The Navy had originally sought to discharge Mr. McVeigh without any benefits, despite 18 years of unblemished service, after he posted a note on the on-line service in which he identified himself as "Tim," whose marital status was "gay" and whose email address was "Boysrch." The Navy's settlement with Mr. McVeigh, who is no relation to the man convicted of bombing the Federal Building in Oklahoma City, is expected to be announced on Friday. In a separate settlement, America Online, the nation's largest on-line computer service, with 12 million users, has apologized to Mr. McVeigh for violating his privacy and has agreed to pay him damages. The company acknowledged that it had confirmed to a Navy investigator that Mr. McVeigh was "Tim." Under the settlement, both sides agreed not to reveal the amount of money paid to Mr. McVeigh by America Online. As a result of the case, the company has also announced new policies intended to guarantee the privacy of its users. The policies will require that all of the company's nearly 5,000 customer-service representatives be provided with special "scenario training" to insure that they do not give out private information about users without the user's consent or without a court order. The company has also rewritten its privacy policy to make it far clearer, and has made the new policy available on line to all users. "I'm happy that this case has been resolved on my terms," Mr. McVeigh said in a telephone interview today from his home in Honolulu. "I think that all sailors can take comfort from this. I hope it sends a message that the rules and regulations that are in place need to be followed by the military." The Navy said it would withhold comment on the settlement until the terms were made public. Mr. McVeigh, who normally would not have been eligible for retirement for another two years, said he felt some sadness in leaving the Navy. "It's a job that I've been doing for 18 years, that I'm good at, that I like, but I'm ready to move on to bigger and better things," he said. "I think this opens a much broader opportunity for me." Mr. McVeigh's lawyer, Christopher Wolf of Washington, said the settlement with the Navy was a very significant victory. "It shows what we alleged at the outset, that Mr. McVeigh's electronic privacy rights and his rights under the military's 'don't ask, don't tell' policy were seriously violated by the Navy," Mr. Wolf said. "It is the first time, as far as I'm aware, that the Navy has let stand a court decision that it has broken the law in this area. Obviously it has a precedent that can be relied on in the future." Last January, Judge Stanley Sporkin of Federal District Court in Washington ordered the Navy to halt its efforts to dismiss Mr. McVeigh and ruled that the Navy's investigation into his sexual orientation was a clear violation of the military's five-year-old "don't ask, don't tell" policy. The policy was intended to allow gay service members to remain in the military so long as they were discreet about their private lives. Judge Sporkin also appeared to side with lawyers who suggested that the Navy and America Online had violated a 1986 Federal law that bars computer service companies from releasing confidential information about customers without the person's permission or a court order. Mr. Wolf said that under the settlement with the Navy, the Defense Department would not appeal the judge's ruling. The case dates to September, when Mr. McVeigh sent an email message to the wife of a fellow crewman aboard the nuclear-powered submarine Chicago about a Christmas toy drive for the crew's children. Navy officials said the woman was disturbed by the return address on his email -- "Boysrch," which apparently referred to "boy search" -- and she consulted the customer profile listed under the return address on America Online. The profile identified the user as Tim of Honolulu, whose hobbies included "collecting pictures of other young studs." The information was passed on to a Navy investigator, who contacted America Online. Without identifying his ties to the Navy, the investigator asked for the full name of Tim. America Online acknowledged this year that a customer-service representative had violated the company's in-house rules and confirmed to the investigator that Tim was Master Chief Petty Officer McVeigh. In interviews, Mr. McVeigh, who was described in recent performance evaluations as "an outstanding role model" and "the embodiment of Navy core values," has declined to discuss his sexual orientation, saying it was irrelevant to a case that should be focused instead on the possibility of misconduct by the Navy. A spokeswoman for America Online, Tricia Primrose, said the settlement between the company and Mr. McVeigh was reached several months ago but was not announced at the time. "In our review of the situation, we recognized that we had made a mistake as a result of human error, and that we absolutely regretted it," Ms. Primrose said. "We've taken responsibility for this action and satisfactorally resolved it with Mr. McVeigh." As a result of the case, she said, America Online will require all of its customer-service representatives to undergo "scenario training, in which we give them examples of the ways in which they could be misled" into turning over confidential information to unauthorized callers. The representatives, she said, will also be required to read and sign a copy of the company's privacy policy every six months, with the understanding that violations of the policy "will be sanctioned all the way up to and including termination." She said the company had also recently rewritten its privacy policy to make it clearer, and had made it available on line. "We wanted to make this easier to read, written in plain English," she said. "It was a big overhaul to make this document understandable to us mere mortals." The policy opens with a statement that America Online is "committed to protecting your personal privacy" and that "we understand that for you to take full advantage of the benefits of this interactive medium, we must do everything we can to insure that your privacy is secure." Correction  An article on Friday reported settlements by the Navy and America Online with a highly decorated sailor who was investigated by the Navy after he posted a computer message, under an anonymous email address, in which he described himself as gay. America Online, which divulged the sailor's real name to the Navy, agreed to pay him damages for violating his privacy. Under the Navy's part of the agreement, the 36-year-old sailor will retire with full benefits and with tens of thousands of dollars to pay his legal fees. The first paragraph of the article described the settlements as a "victory for gay rights." That phrase was supplied in editing. It failed to take the Navy's view into account. And it did not reflect any opinion expressed by the sailor, Master Chief Petty Officer Timothy R. McVeigh, whose lawyer has commented only on the privacy aspects of the episode. The Navy, which withheld comment at the time, now says the settlement was in no way a victory for gay rights, since the service was achieving at least part of what it wanted: the departure of Mr. McVeigh, because of what appeared to be a declaration of homosexuality.
