title: Language Called Java Transcends Barriers
body: IT'S a familiar name with many meanings -- an ancient kingdom in what is now Indonesia, slang for a cup of coffee and one of the most important developments in the short life span of the Internet. Java, a programming language for applications used on networks, is being heralded, at least by Scott McNealy, chairman of Sun Microsystems, which developed and licenses Java as the next great thing, ready to change the nature of computing. Not everyone is quite as optimistic, but Java's growth and success so far is clear. Created in 1991 by James Gosling and his associates at Sun Microsystems, Java (originally called Oak, after a tree outside Mr. Gosling's window) began as part of an effort to make a consumer-oriented home control unit (a device to start the coffee in the morning, regulate the temperature in the house, operate the VCR, etc.). The device never took off, but the ascendance of the Internet three years later opened unforeseen channels for Sun's new language. Most often associated with the whirring and spinning elements on a favorite Web page, Java has uses far beyond that. It has become ubiquitous to the point that its name is no longer just a noun but also an adjective used to describe all sorts of devices, virtual and physical, Mr. McNealy said at a recent conference at Harvard University. What distinguishes Java from other programming languages is that applications, or programs, written in Java can run on any computer operating system, be it Windows, Mac OS or Unix. Applications written in Java are also unique in the way in which they take advantage of computer networks. The Java programming on your computer goes out to the Internet to retrieve bits of computer code from other computers to do specific tasks. Applications of the new language range from the grand (Home Depot uses Java-based applications to track inventory across its 560 stores) to the minor (the various flashing advertisements on innumerable Web pages are small programs written in Java known as applets). And as networks become more sophisticated and allow more data to be carried more quickly, Java-related applications will become more commonplace. But, of course, reliance on a network does have its limitations. As Rob Currie, vice president of engineering at Marimba, a company that develops business applications using Java-based programming said, "When you're connected, great," but when you're not, "then you really want the whole program there with you." Graphic   Chart: One way to think about how Java works is to imagine a functioning application, or a software program, as an orchestra playing a concert. In reality this might be the computer solving math problems, drawing maps, showing video or doing some other activity. The Java language allows the writing of applications as a collection of small chunks of programming language called objects. Object-oriented programming has been around since the early 1970's, but Java added a new wrinkle by allowing a computer to download the program in parts.  THE JAVA VIRTUAL MACHINE The key to all of this is something called the Java Virtual Machine, a piece of software that orders up needed bits of other software from the Net, translates the code and insures that it works in whatever real machine it is in. In verifying and translating the code, it also screens the code for viruses.  The Main Object Provides the framework for the rest of the application and often includes the information about where to get pieces of code for various functions.   1. When the computer user starts a particular application, the main object is downloaded and will then act with the J.V.M. in much the same manner as a conductor.  2. For the music to begin, the conductor calls on each section of the orchestra, like the violins (another piece of the program). So the Java Virtual Machine searches to see if each piece was brought down with the Java program. The J.V.M. requests the objects it needs from the network, and the browser downloads each piece.  3. Once found, each needed object downloaded. Through the the J.V.M., it is linked to the rest of the application and responds to the conductor's commands.  Another way The non-Java way is to write an application is to have all the computer code -- all the software instructions -- be specific for a particular chip. The code tends to be in bigger chunks. That way of writing an application is a powerful method, but it may contain parts of the application that may never be used.  Other Java Devices  Cell Phones and Pagers Developers hope to transform these items into more all-purpose information devices. Java will enable people to use these to read email and browse Web pages, and the devices will act as calculators and perform other tasks, all through through a cellular connection to a network.  Televisions The same cable that brings your favorite programs into your home will deliver Java-enabled applications. People will be able to use their sets to browse Web pages, bank and shop from home or register for school classes with just a few more clicks of the remote control.  Smart Cards Meant to replace cash eventually in our society, these universal identification cards can digitally store money in an embedded microchip. Java's cross-platform compatibility allows these cards to be interchangeable despite the variety of companies and formats involved.  The Java Ring A favorite of Scott McNealy, chairman of Sun Microsystems, this has an embedded chip that can store one's authenticated ID. It could be used to allow access to a secure home or to interact with an A.T.M. or another information device to get access to accounts or read email.

title: Suit Against MCI In Internet Unit Sale
body: Cable and Wireless P.L.C. of Britain said yesterday that it had filed a lawsuit seeking to require MCI Communications to comply with a $625 million agreement to sell its wholesale Internet business to Cable and Wireless. The suit comes a week after the European Union competition commissioner, Karel van Miert, said the sale was not enough to guarantee that MCI's $41.8 billion combinanation with Worldcom Inc. would not dominate the Internet market. The suit, analysts said yesterday, is an effort by Cable and Wireless to protect its position should MCI make other concessions -- instead of the sale to Cable and Wireless -- to appease antitrust regulators. In a statement, Cable and Wireless said it had filed the suit in Federal District Court in Washington to "protect its position." The Internet sale agreement, the company said, required the companies to negotiate "modifications needed to secure approval by the U.S. Department of Justice and the European Commission." The company declined to comment further. MCI said it was surprised by the suit, adding that it had not changed the terms of the sale agreement. Worldcom, meanwhile, said earlier yesterday that it was confident it would not have to sell its Uunet Technologies Internet unit to allay European Union antitrust concerns. Mark Weeks, a spokesman for Worldcom in London, said Worldcom and MCI were in daily talks with European Union antitrust officials and were trying to convince them the proposed MCI sale eliminated all overlap between the two companies. He did not rule out the possibility of MCI's making a further offer.

title:
Journal;
Bob Hope Lives
body: Contrary to published reports, the Internet didn't kill Bob Hope. The real culprit was Congress, whose members took to eulogizing the still-living comic from the floor last Friday on the basis of an advance obituary accidentally posted on an Associated Press web site. Had anyone in the House actually looked at the computer printout that cued the funeral oratory, he would have seen a patently dummy news story shot through with long strings of xxxxxxxxx as space holders. But why let the facts ruin a touching impromptu memorial service being beamed by C-Span to the voters back home? All the way around, it was human error, not computer error, that led to this gallows comedy of errors. And there may have been no one who enjoyed the farce more than Matt Drudge, the Internet's self-styled Walter Winchell and every commentator's favorite poster boy (me included) for journalistic impropriety in the new media age. On his site, Mr. Drudge made fun of ABC News, which had broadcast Mr. Hope's "death" on its radio network. "In January," Mr. Drudge wrote with deadpan irony, "ABC News Nightline devoted a show to the perils of speed Internet reporting and the danger of false information being circulated online without fact-checkers and editors." ABC's gaffe hardly clears Mr. Drudge of his own egregious errors, one of which has led to a ferocious libel suit. But about at least one thing, one big thing, he has been right, and he was right long before most of the rest of us recognized it: The Internet, speed and all, is shaking up the coverage and dissemination of news as has nothing else in the half-century since the proliferation of television. It may one day even eclipse TV, much as TV long ago downsized radio. A new Pew survey released on Monday talks in very unpollster-like language of the "astonishing rate" of increase in the Internet news audience. In 1995, only 14 percent of Americans surfed the net for news; now, just three years later, 36 percent do. In recent years the audience for print journalism has remained stable while the number of Americans who rely exclusively on TV's nightly broadcast news has fallen from 30 to 15 percent. The same survey also showed that most Americans cite accuracy as by far the most important component of news, and that they distinguish clearly between credible brands like The Wall Street Journal (which 81 percent rate as largely accurate) and the National Enquirer (which only 7 percent do). Would these news consumers be turning to Internet news sources if they believed them to be intrinsically inaccurate? Hardly. If anything, you could argue -- as Mr. Drudge slyly did when addressing Washington's National Press Club last week -- that it is the non-Internet media that have made the most notorious journalistic errors of late: the bogus eyewitness account of a Monica-Clinton tryst, the incrimination of Richard Jewell, the digital capping of Bobbi McCaughey's teeth, the serial publication of plagiarized and fictional stories in The New Republic and, just three days after the Drudge speech, Bob Hope's "death." It's past time to retire the Internet as a scapegoat for journalistic ills; it's a medium, not a message, and it can be used as irresponsibly or as honorably as a printing press or a TV network can. Americans will surely distinguish between credible and tabloid news on the net just as they do in other media. When Matt Drudge runs an inaccurate, unsubstantiated story, he pays -- if not in court, then in how his audience perceives him. His undeniably entertaining site could end up as widely read as the Enquirer -- and just as widely disbelieved. Or he could turn himself with unassailable scoops into the net's Horace Greeley. At this embryonic moment in Internet news history, Media Metrix, a company that counts web-site visitors, reports that msnbc.com (rated #5), an aggressive and rarely inaccurate chronicler of Clinton scandals, dwarfs drudgereport.com (#228) by twelvefold. "The Internet is going to save the news business," Mr. Drudge declared at the Press Club. It's hard to fault him for striking back with such hyperbole at his critics within the journalistic establishment. Their reports that he and his new medium would kill the news business have proved as inaccurate as those of the death of Hope.

title: NBC Buying A Portal To the Internet
body: Venturing into the most competitive area of the Internet, NBC said yesterday that it had agreed to buy a controlling stake in Snap, an upstart search and directory service, from its creator, Cnet Inc. The television network said it was also buying a nearly 5 percent stake in Cnet itself. NBC, a unit of the General Electric Company, is endorsing the view that Internet directory companies, or search engines, like Yahoo and Excite are emerging as the cornerstones of profitable on-line ventures. Such portals, as the directory sites have come to be called, have started charging large fees from World Wide Web sites to which they direct Internet users. In addition, portal sites, taking a page from the success of America Online, are beginning to offer their own versions of services like email and chat rooms as a way of engaging users of Web pages on which the portals sell advertisements. The deal, which could total $39 million by the time it is completed, represents the first time a broadcast network has entered the Internet portal market, although all the networks have built or acquired various sites that offer content like news, sports or entertainment. NBC, for example, is already a co-owner with the Microsoft Corporation of the MSNBC network, which is available on both cable and the Web. At the same time, a range of companies, including the Netscape Communications Corporation and Microsoft, are building their own portal services. And big companies including Walt Disney and Time Warner have been exploring buying part or all of the various directory services. The most popular of these are Yahoo, Excite, Infoseek, Lycos and Alta Vista, a Digital Equipment Corporation unit -- each of which is among the most frequented sites on the Web. Yahoo is consistently the Internet's most popular site, according to Relevant Knowledge, a company that measures Web traffic. "Media companies now realize that the Internet is important and that they have to be there," said Brian C. Oakes, an analyst with Lehman Brothers. For Cnet, the deal vindicates its decision to build Snap, which had been widely criticized by investors. Cnet's first business, television programs and Internet sites about computers, has been the most successful original programming on the Internet. But many saw Snap, which ultimately cost the company $25 million to build, as an expensive distraction that was far too late to catch up with the likes of Yahoo. Cnet's stock has floundered over the last year, rising only 15 percent through Monday, a period in which Yahoo's stock quintupled. But yesterday, Cnet's shares surged nearly 37 percent to close at $45.125. "This has saved Cnet's bacon," said David Simons, managing director of Digital Video Investments, a research firm. "Snap was not gaining the sponsorship or the franchise it had anticipated." NBC said it was not deterred by Snap's low ratings. "Snap is a first-class service that is ready to handle millions of users," Robert C. Wright, the president of NBC, said at a news conference. "It is not as well known as it could be, and our job is to make it more well known." Indeed, NBC's strategy appears to have been to buy the least successful of the portal sites and build it through constant promotion on the television network. The aim is to build Snap's name recognition among the 80 percent of unitedstates residents who are not yet using the Internet, so that when they venture into cyberspace it will already be familiar to them. NBC has agreed to pay $5.9 million for 19.9 percent of Snap and has a three-year option to buy a further 40.1 percent of the service for $32 million. The rest of Snap will be owned by Cnet. From the start, a majority of Snap's board will be NBC executives, although Halsey M. Minor, Cnet's chief executive, will stay on in the near future. Separately, NBC has purchased 4.99 percent of Cnet's stock for $26 million, or $32 a share. To turn a $25 million investment into a company valued at $60 million would be a good return in any other industry, but it is hardly the magic multiplication that many Internet companies have come to expect. Analysts said that the most positive aspect of the deal for Cnet was that it would no longer be responsible for Snap's continuing losses, which have been running at $1.2 million a month. "The single most important moment in the life of an Internet company is when it starts to make money, said Keith E. Benjamin, an analyst with BancAmerica Robertson Stephens, long a fan of Cnet's stock. "This will let them turn a profit in the third quarter." For NBC, the deal offers a relatively inexpensive way to enter the Internet portal business. The publicly owned search companies range in value from $850 million for Infoseek to $5.5 billion for Yahoo. Of course, all those companies have far greater audiences than Snap does. But that was integral to NBC's bet. "With the enormous valuations these other companies have, it's hard to structure a deal," said Tom Rogers, president of NBC's cable and Internet group. "Snap didn't have all the traffic yet that creates the valuations." While NBC expects to build Snap's audience through extensive promotion on its television programs, network executives declined to specify the amount of air time they would give such promotions. "Nobody will miss the fact, regardless of what day part you look at, that there's something out there called Snap as a key starting point to the Internet," Mr. Rogers said. The companies said they had not decided whether to use the NBC brand name on the Snap service. NBC executives said that the company's goal was to run Snap as a stand-alone business, not to use it mainly to promote its other television and Internet programs. The venture will be kept at arm's length from MSNBC, which network executives said would probably provide news to both Snap and Microsoft's new portal service, Start. Meanwhile, Snap will be free to draw content both from other NBC affiliates and other competing sources of programming. Similarly, Cnet will continue to produce programs for the USA and Sci-Fi cable networks, although it may explore television ventures with NBC in the future. Eventually, NBC and Snap executives said they would consider selling part of Snap to the public in a stock offering. Having publicly traded shares, at the high prices Internet companies now fetch, would make it easier for Snap to acquire related Internet companies. News of NBC's acquisition helped buoy the stock yesterday of most other Internet portal companies, which have lagged in recent weeks. Yahoo's shares, for example, jumped $8.50 to close at $117.875. Some analysts argued that NBC's deep pockets and vast reach could turn Snap into a potent competitor. "Investors have the infinite-sum, unlimited-possibility syndrome," said Mr. Simons of Digital Video Investments. "What they miss is that the promotion costs for everyone will go up. This is the beginning of the great Internet marketing wars." While such pressure may press the portal companies and other big media corporations to explore more such deals, analysts said they might be frightened off by the market valuation of the top portal businesses. "Snap was the safest play for a traditional company because it is the weakest player," said Mr. Oakes of Lehman. "The other companies may not be bought until one of them stumbles." title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS & BONDS;
Many Internet Shares Rally, but Major Indexes Are Mixed
body: A three-day rally in stocks fizzled yesterday and left major market indexes mixed, illustrating Wall Street's renewed concerns about the corporate earnings outlook and some wariness about the near-term prospect for interest rates. But a rally among some Internet-related shares pushed technology stocks higher, as the Nasdaq composite index closed above 1,800 for the first time since May 22. Falling energy prices pushed up transportation stocks, and news concerning prescription drugs continued to buoy pharmaceutical shares. Blue-chip issues bore the brunt of the declines, with the Dow Jones industrial average falling 19.68 points, to 9,049.92. Financial services companies like American Express, J. P. Morgan and Wells Fargo, as well as some multinational companies such as McDonald's, which had been higher in recent days, had some of the largest retreats. Concerns about today's Congressional testimony of the Federal Reserve chairman, Alan Greenspan, also helped weaken blue-chip issues, analysts said, as investors expressed some concern that the Fed could still raise interest rates sometime soon. "The consensus seems to be that rates will not be going higher," said Charles W. Johnson, a managing director and head equity trader at Blaylock & Partners. "But there is that nervousness in the marketplace that maybe the Fed sees something that we don't," which would justify an interest rate increase, he said. A continuing flow of earnings warnings from companies is keeping investors worried about the outlook for corporate profits, analysts said. Yesterday, Billing Concepts, a billing agent for the telecommunications industry, warned that earnings could fall below expectations in its third and fourth quarters because of a decline in demand. Arrow International, a maker of disposable medical products, said fiscal third-quarter sales are likely to increase less than expected because of slowing international orders. A decline in oil prices pushed the stocks of companies like Chevron and Exxon lower after the Paris-based International Energy Agency forecast a decline in Asian demand for oil. However, the oil-price drop lifted stocks of transportation companies, particularly airlines. Gains in such carriers as Alaska Air Group and US Airways Group lifted the Amex airline index 4.1 percent and the Dow Jones transportation average 3.11 percent, its biggest one-day gain this year. Led by a 4-point rise in Pfizer, the Standard & Poor's 500 index inched up 2.69 points, to 1,118.41. Pfizer soared to 112 7/16 on news that the Food and Drug Administration said the company's impotence-treatment drug, Viagra, did not directly cause the deaths of 16 users. The Nasdaq composite index gained 12.99 points, to 1,800.76, pulled higher by a broad rally in Internet stocks on news of a deal between General Electric's NBC and the struggling Web service Cnet, which shot up 12 1/8, or 37 percent, to 45 1/8. Lycos, Yahoo, America Online, Netscape Communications and Earthlink Network all rose. Lycos also gained after receiving a patent for its "spider" search technology. But some Internet-related shares that had caught investor attention in recent weeks are now languishing. K-Tel International, which soared to 33 15/16 after the company announced in April that it would sell music on the Internet, fell 33/64, to 11 1/4. Other prominent losses yesterday included Chromatics Color Sciences International shares, which fell about 49 percent before partly recovering to close at 6 1/2, down 2 5/16. The company develops technologies to scientifically measure skin color in order to detect jaundice in infants. Asensio & Company, a firm that bets that stocks will go down, recommended selling the stock yesterday. Asensio said that Chromatics' principal product had no sales and licensing potential and that irregular trading activity might have occurred in the stock among owners, including two Dreyfus micro-cap mutual funds that have sizable holdings in Chromatics. A Dreyfus spokesman called the allegations "unsubstantiated." And Darby Macfarlane, the chief executive of Chromatics, said the company was "working diligently to put out a detailed report" to counter the Asensio claims.  Bonds End Little Changed By Bloomberg News Treasury prices were little changed yesterday for a second consecutive session as investors awaited today's Congressional testimony from Alan Greenspan, the chairman of the Federal Reserve. While few expect him to signal any change in monetary policy, many investors remained cautious, knowing that his remarks have the potential to cause big price swings. The price of the 30-year Treasury bond fell 2/32, to 104 27/32, leaving the bond's yield unchanged at 5.78 percent for a second day. Trading was lighter than usual. About $53.8 billion in Treasury securities were traded as of 3 P.M., 30 percent below average, said Govpx, a bond pricing service. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING -- ADDENDA;
Acquisitions By Three Companies
body: Three agency companies have made acquisitions for undisclosed financial terms. The New Paradigm Corporation, an Internet company in newyork, acquired a majority interest in Schoen, Kapelus & Cipriano in Harrison, N.Y., an agency that specializes in travel, tourism and hospitality accounts. Schoen, Kapelus, which is being renamed SKC Advertising, has 10 employees and estimated billings of $3 million from clients like Kemwel Holiday Autos. Milton Kapelus, 61, president of Schoen, Kapelus, will head SKC as president. Agency.com in newyork, which had owned a majority stake in Spiral Media, an Internet and digital media communications company in newyork, acquired the remaining shares to give it 100 percent ownership. Spiral will operate as a subsidiary of Agency.com under the name Spiral Media, an Agency.com Company. Art Williams, 31, chief executive at Spiral, was named to the additional position of executive vice president for operations at Agency.com. Spiral has 35 employees and billings estimated at $7.5 million from clients like AT&T and Unilever. The deal was the third in recent days for Agency.com. And Research International Group in London, a custom research consulting company that is part of WPP Group P.L.C., acquired another custom research company, Conway/ Milliken & Associates in Chicago. Conway/Milliken has 90 employees and annual revenue of more than $12 million; it will operate as a division of Research International USA under present management.

title: America Online to Buy Internet Chat Service for $287 Million
body: With all the frenzy over the Internet, entrepreneurs have been able to create and sell companies for huge sums without ever earning a dime. But in what may be a record of financial weightlessness, America Online said yesterday that it would pay at least $287 million for a company that has never taken in a penny in revenue and has no plans to start charging money. What the company, an Israeli concern called Mirabilis Ltd., does have is users, 12 million of them who spend an average of more than an hour a day on its Internet chat service. Ultimately, America Online hopes to put advertising on the chat service and sell its members products and services. "When you talk about making money on the Internet, no one is doing more than America Online," said Robert W. Pittman, the company's president. He compared the Internet today to the early days of cable television. MTV, which Mr. Pittman helped start, took in only $500,000 in revenue its first year. Mirabilis is highly regarded among savvy Internet users for its chat service, known as ICQ (shorthand for "I seek you"), which enables them to detect when fellow users are on line and to communicate instantly with them. With no promotion other than word of mouth, it has already achieved something of a cult status, growing at more than 50,000 subscribers a day. ICQ is attractive to America Online because it appeals to a much younger and more technologically sophisticated audience than the mainstream America Online brand. "If this were 1980, think underground album-oriented rock radio," Mr. Pittman said. Moreover, he said, ICQ users spend an average of 75 minutes a day on the service, compared with fewer than 10 minutes a day for highly touted search and directory services such as Yahoo and Lycos. Many Internet stock analysts praised the deal as an inexpensive way for America Online to increase its customer relationships. The company's shares rose $1.50 yesterday, to $84.75. But there is some skepticism that chat services, no matter how popular, will turn into big money makers. "email, chat and instant messaging are not good advertising platforms," said Bo Peabody, the chief executive of Tripod, an on-line community service recently bought by Lycos. "When you chat, you look at what you are writing, not what other people are writing," he said. Moreover, advertisers worry that their advertisements will be associated with content that they do not control and may be embarrassing. As a result, chat services that do take ads receive the lowest rates of any type of Internet service. That has not stopped other companies from buying similar services. Most notably, Microsoft paid a reported $400 million for Hotmail, which offers free email services. (Unlike ICQ, Hotmail had started to sell advertisements.) Mirabilis also helps America Online's efforts to expand overseas. About 40 percent of ICQ's members are in the unitedstates, 40 percent are in Europe and the rest are spread elsewhere. Mirabilis was founded two years ago by four Israelis in their early 20's. With a few million dollars in backing from local investors, it has built one of the most popular services on the Internet. Yossi Vardi, the Mirabilis chairman, said the company had been in discussions with a number of suitors since last August. But they were initially put off by the price the company wanted. "People were quite amazed with our growth and it took them a while to come to grips with that," he said. America Online agreed to pay $287 million in cash up front and up to $120 million in additional payments starting in 2001, depending on the performance of Mirabilis, which will continue to be run as a separate subsidiary in Tel Aviv. America Online's own Internet chat service, AOL Instant Messenger, will continue to be a separate product mainly to allow Internet users to communicate with those on America Online's service. America Online will also provide some technical support to Mirabilis. Mr. Peabody of Tripod said that since America Online now controlled the two largest chat services it should embrace an open standard that would allow the user of any chat service to send an instant message to a user of a competing service, much as electronic mail works now. "Now that AOL has a monopoly on the instant messenger space, I'm hopeful they will open the market to everyone," he said. Tripod hopes to offer its own message service and such a standard would help it break into the existing market. Tricia Primrose, a spokeswoman for America Online, said that there were no standards for instant messages now, but that "historically AOL supports open standards that gain critical mass and acceptance by consumers."

title:
SOCCER: NOTEBOOK -- WORLD CUP;
Live From France On World Wide Web
body: With all 64 games of the World Cup finals being broadcast live in the unitedstates by a combination of ABC, ESPN, ESPN2 and the Spanish-language Univision, it will be difficult for a hard-core fan to miss much of the tournament. The competition starts tomorrow in France when Brazil, the defending champion, plays Scotland at 11:30 A.M. Eastern time. And therein is the potential problem: with the six-hour time difference between the East Coast of the unitedstates and France, all of the games will have ended by 5 P.M. Eastern time. So unless you have got your days free, it may be hard to follow the tournament live on television. Enter the Internet and the World Wide Web. There are a plethora of Web sites to slake the thirst of even the most avid fans. Some will offer live broadcast of matches via the Internet (www.broadcast.com/sports/worldcup98/english/); daily updates, complete rosters, schedules and souvenirs at the World Cup's official Web site (www.france98.com), and movies of all the tournament's goals (www.tin.it/rete/). The newyork Times Web site (www.nytimes.com/worldcup) will publish reports from its reporters in France, which will be posted on the Web site hours before the newspaper version goes to press. A year-old magazine in headquartered in the unitedstates, Match Day (www.matchdayusa.com/worldcup), is taking an interesting approach. The magazine will feature the work of 35 photographers stationed in 22 countries around the globe to chronicle how the world watches and reacts to the World Cup. A kind of Day in the Life of the World Cup.  W-LEAGUE The unitedstates men are rated as a 150-1 shot to win the World Cup, but it is the American women who are the team to beat in the world. The unitedstates has developed some of the best female players in the world; they finished second in the last Women's World Cup and won the gold medal at the Atlanta Olympics in 1996. The unitedstates will play host to the Women's World Cup next summer, but there is no need to wait if you want to see some of the best female soccer players around. There is the two-tier W-League, a collection of 33 teams in 22 states that is playing under the auspices of the United Systems of Independent Soccer Leagues, the outfit that also runs the minor league A-League, the D3 League and the Premier Development League. The W-League's newyork franchise is the defending league champions, the Long Island Lady Riders, who play their home games at the North Hempstead Town Park in New Hyde Park, N.Y. The Lady Riders play in the 15-team W-1, or elite league. (There are 18 teams in the W-2 league; no affiliation with the Internal Revenue Service.) The Lady Riders are undefeated four games into their 1998 season and are tied with Boston in the North division after having defeated Buffalo by 5-0 on Saturday before a franchise-record crowd of 1,500.  MAJOR LEAGUE SOCCER The league will carry on during the monthlong World Cup and could actually ride the tournament's coattails. No Major League Soccer games will be played in direct conflict with matches in France. In addition, the league will reduce its schedule by about one game a week during the tournament. In all, there are 21 M.L.S. players participating in France, with 16 playing for the unitedstates national team. The Columbus Crew has been the hardest hit, losing five players, four to the unitedstates team (Brian McBride, Juergen Sommer, Brian Maisonneuve and Thomas Dooley). The MetroStars are without the services of two American players (Alexi Lalas and Tab Ramos) and the club's Chilean international (Marcelo Vega). Yesterday, the struggling Tampa Bay Mutiny (3-12) dismissed John Kowalski and named Tim Hankinson as the club's coach. Until the appointment, Hankinson, the league's director of player development, had been the coach of the unitedstates Pro-40 Select team. That squad had been playing in the A-League. The Western Conference-leading Los Angeles Galaxy (12-2) continues to roll. Fresh off an 8-1 rout of Dallas last week, the Galaxy drew a crowd of 38,383 to the Rose Bowl on Sunday for the home debut of the former Mexican star Carlos Hermosillo. The home team didn't disappoint its fans, defeating New England by 5-1. The Galaxy is the league's top-scoring team with 49 goals, 11 more than D.C. United, which is second in scoring.   JACK BELL

title: A New Executive-Recruiting Service on the Web
body: For many companies, recruiting executives is like looking for needles in a haystack. The Wall Street Journal and Korn/Ferry International, a leading executive search firm, hope to use the Internet to get the needles to emerge on their own. The two companies plan to announce today a national rollout of "Futurestep," a service that seeks to recruit midlevel managers via the Web and match them with prospective employers. There is a second high-technology twist: Futurestep automates the cumbersome recruiting process by using software designed to match a person's skills and interests with job types. The service is free to prospective employees, who fill out a questionnaire at www.futurestep.com, listing background and job interests. The software then grades the responses; it is capable of determining what job and corporate culture an employee best fits, said Man Jit Singh, the chief executive of Futurestep. Prospective employers who have submitted job openings to Futurestep will receive a list of potential candidates selected from the data base -- along with a videotaped interview of the top prospects. If a company hires a candidate, it pays Futurestep 30 percent of the first year's cash salary, a standard executive recruiting fee. The concept is aimed at reducing the time it takes to find midlevel managers -- who typically make between $75,000 and $200,000 -- and thus make the process cost effective, said Michael Boxberger, chief executive of Korn/Ferry. For its part, The Wall Street Journal, a unit of Dow Jones & Company, hopes to capitalize on the success of its executive recruiting classified advertising, which presently is the single largest classified category in the print version of The Journal, said Mike Wilson, the company's director of classified advertising. The Journal plans to make Futurestep a component of its Wall Street Journal Interactive Edition career site, www.careers.wsj.com. The Journal will also seek to entice its print-based advertisers to participate. The advertisers can put the Futurestep Web address on their advertisements then have Futurestep sort incoming resumes.

title: Dropping an Internet Hot Potato
body: The Clinton Administration called it "A Proposal to Improve the Technical Management of Internet Names and Addresses." But the report released on Friday by the Commerce Department was much more than that. It had been long awaited by the Internet community -- which these days means everyone from multinational corporations to sandals-and-socks computer programmers to grandmothers on America Online -- as the Government's first real attempt to specify a system of governance for the informally organized global computer network born in Federal laboratories nearly three decades ago. But after a year of intense study, peering into issues of technology, trademark law, international politics and competition, the Government turned to the Internet community and said -- Here, you do it. The Government said it had decided to turn the management of Internet domain names -- and thus the management of the Internet itself -- over to an as-yet-unformed private corporation, representing various Internet interests. That organization will be responsible for fixing the escalating problem of assigning Internet domain names -- the chaotic scramble for coveted cyberspace addresses that was the impetus for the review in the first place. Domain names and addresses are the computer network equivalent of phone numbers, street addresses and trademarks, all rolled in one. Each of the millions of computers connected to the Internet requires a unique address, which enables electronic mail to get to its intended destination and World Wide Web pages to be found in what is rapidly becoming the world's main library. Each computer's formal address is expressed as a series of numbers, for example, 199.181.172.241. But to make the addresses easier to use, companies and individuals can ask to assign a name to the numbers, like nytimes.com. The ".com" part of the address is called a top-level domain, and it is roughly the equivalent of a telephone area code. The current top-level domain system -- seven generic top-level domains like .com and .org and .edu, plus a couple of hundred two-letter country codes -- was created when there were just a few hundred computers connected to the Net. Nobody anticipated the phenomenal growth of the Internet as a global network used by millions for electronic commerce, communications and entertainment. Today, the domain set aside for commercial activity -- .com -- is the largest and fastest growing. With more than 100,000 new commercial domain-name registrations being added each month, the Internet is headed toward a traffic jam that makes the overcrowding of phone area codes look benign. Rather than try to fix the problem by adding more top-level domains, which it proposed doing in an earlier, much-criticized draft of the report, the Administration called for creation of a private not-for-profit international corporation whose job it would be to find a solution to the domain-name problem. If all went according to plan, the new corporation would assemble an international board of 15 directors from the private sector (the report did not even specify how the board would be chosen, leaving even that matter to the Internet community) and would begin tackling the most fundamental questions about the future of the global network by October. People hoping for more immediate action were left unsatisfied. "If they were going to do that, they could have done it a year ago," said Carl Oppedahl, a patent and trademark lawyer in Colorado, who has been a critic of the current system, which has no formal structure for resolving domain-name trademark disputes. "I feel badly about the time delay. The Internet has not benefited from having all these months go by." The Government reserved the right to overrule whatever choices the private sector makes. And, while repeatedly professing its desire to get out of the Internet oversight business, the Government left open the possibility that it might retain that option until well into 2000. The Government's proposal was bad news for those looking for relief from domain congestion or seeking some improvement of the current trademark dispute morass, and for dozens of domain name registry businesses that had hoped to become rich selling names in proposed new domains like .web, .inc, or .sex. But the Government's network solution was good news for Network Solutions Inc., the Virginia company that five years ago was awarded an exclusive Government contract to administer the .com, .org and .net domains. When Network Solutions got the contract, there was no fee to register names. Soon after, it got permission to begin charging $50 for each name (recently reduced to $35). Network Solutions' contract is supposed to expire on Sept. 30, but the new report opens the possibility that the company will continue to have a monopoly on the lucrative ".com" franchise until the new corporation comes up with an alternative -- something that everyone agrees will be no easy task. As a result, Network Solutions' stock soared on Friday, up $6.75, to $39.25. Viewed one way, the Administration's decision to not make any decisions was a vote of support for the Internet's old guard, which has long argued that the Internet is capable of regulating itself without government interference. "I have to read it as a victory for self-governance, a victory for the Internet and a demonstration that the Government has developed a profound understanding of the way the Internet works," said Don Heath, president of the Internet Society, a trade association. Viewed another way, the Government looked at all the hulking issues now pressing in on the Internet and punted. Critics say that by essentially freezing the domain-name situation in its current form for an indeterminate time, the problems facing the new board will be even tougher when it convenes. Time was rarely a concern as the Internet grew organically from its origins in the 1960's and 1970's. Keeping track of all the new computers on the network, and all of the technical issues of the emerging medium, was largely a volunteer effort. But in the early 1990's, when restrictions against commercial uses of the Internet were relaxed, the environment changed. Today, millions of companies are investing billions of dollars in Internet-related ventures. Millions of email messages cross the network every day, and it is rapidly becoming a conduit for much of the world's telephone calls. Universities, grade school students, farmers, scientists, lonely singles, traveling salesmen, busy families, small businesses and giant corporations have come to depend on it. Husbands and wives battle over domain names in divorce court, companies pay six-figure amounts for rights to "business.com" and "internet.com" and million-dollar legal fees are increasingly common in domain-name trademark disputes. With such large issues at stake, many people want a more defined structure for the Internet -- not just an ad hoc group of volunteers, albeit very diligent ones, running the show, as is currently the case. The domain name issue is just one of many decisions that need to be made quickly. Others include: Who is responsible for making decisions?  What parts of the structure are best left to the marketplace, and what parts are best left to government interests? In the latter case, whose government? Trademark law is based on geography, while the Internet is the antithesis of geography. How to reconcile? These are among the questions that the Clinton Administration expects a new, unformed, untested, international corporation of indeterminate composition to answer as quickly as possible. "The process is going to have to be accelerated because the demand for domain names is astronomical," said Ken Stubbs, chairman of the executive council of CORE, the Council of Registrars, a group of more than 80 companies that handle domain-name registrations for businesses and individuals worldwide -- and that all must funnel registrations to Network Solutions. "If domain names were "800" numbers or cell phone numbers, and someone announced that there would be no more phone numbers issued for 12 to 18 months, there would be concern."

title: Poll Shows Cable News Catching Up
body: Following a pattern seen in entertainment viewing, Americans now watch news programs on cable television networks about as regularly as those on broadcast networks, according to a survey by the Pew Research Center for the People and the Press. The researchers also found that the number of people who get their news from the Internet is rising rapidly and they estimated that almost as many people use the Internet on a typical weekday as spend time reading a magazine. About 20 percent of American adults, or an estimated 36 million people, get news from the Internet at least once a week, the survey found, compared with 6 percent, or about 11 million, two years ago, when Pew conducted a similar survey. Those who use the Internet for news are disproportionately younger, better educated and more affluent, the survey said. As for television, more than half of those surveyed said they watch the news with a remote control in their hands, poised to change the channel. "It's a quixotic audience," said Andrew Kohut, director of the Washington-based Pew research group. "Post-cold war, people say local news is much more important to them than national or international news. We found that in the survey and in focus groups afterward, too." The percentage of Americans who watch the network evening news and local news only on broadcast television has fallen to 15 percent, from 30 percent five years ago, according to the telephone survey of 3,002 adults conducted April 24 to May 11. In the survey done two years ago, Mr. Kohut said, "We found all news viewership going down, but this time the slide is limited to broadcast networks and to a certain extent CNN." Fully 40 percent of Americans said they regularly watched one of the leading cable news networks (CNN, CNBC, MSNBC or Fox News Channel), while 57 percent said they watched the major broadcast networks' morning, evening and prime-time news programs regularly. When the Weather Channel and ESPN's Sports Center program are added, the cable figure grows to 60 percent, the survey said. These responses may seem inconsistent with Nielsen ratings, which show most cable news networks getting minuscule figures. Gregory Flemming, one of the survey's directors, said this was because Nielsen measures actual viewership by program or time period, while the survey's tally of viewers who say they watch "regularly" might include people who watch only one show a day (but almost every day) or people who tune in for a few minutes several times a day. Only 38 percent described themselves as regular viewers of the ABC, CBS or NBC evening news broadcasts, compared with 60 percent five years ago. An obvious advantage for the cable news networks is that they have news around the clock, unlike the broadcast networks. Most Americans said they would turn to cable channels first if a big news event broke. Indeed, 46 percent of Americans surveyed said they only follow national news when a major event is occurring, and 67 percent said that is the only time they follow international news. The survey found the average American spends an hour a day absorbing news -- whether from television, radio or newspapers -- but the amount of time varies widely with age. Older people watch and read more news than younger people. Predictably, young people are the most likely to go on line to get news, and even though they pursue news less often, large numbers of young people said they enjoyed having the wide variety of choice in news sources that is available today. In a separate Pew survey about the credibility of news organizations, conducted May 7-13 among 981 adults, CNN ranked highest in "believability" among broadcast and cable television sources, with CBS's "60 Minutes" second. The syndicated tabloid television show "Inside Edition" ranked lowest, with National Public Radio second lowest. The survey broke down respondents by age, income and whether they were occasional, moderate or frequent news viewers. Information about the survey may be obtained from the Pew Center for Research on the People and the Press, 1150 18th Street, N.W., Washington, D.C. 20036, or on the Internet at http:// www.people-press.org. (Source: Pew Research Center Biennial News Consumption Survey)

NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
Kids, Don't Try This at Home
body: Never ask Fred Kahl whether he really can swallow a sword because, without a word, he will slip the four-inch stylus from his electronic organizer deep up his right nostril. Then, pointing to a photograph of himself -- arms outstretched, head back, an 'ep'ee buried to the hilt down his throat -- he will shrug, as if to say, "Same idea." Until he is asked, he does not remove the stylus. For six summers until he retired last year, Mr. Kahl was the Great Fredini in a Coney Island sideshow. But in his other incarnation, Mr. Kahl, 33, is a project manager at Funny Garbage, a Silicon Alley Web site designer. Last summer, he developed a site about Coney Island U.S.A., a nonprofit group that operates the sideshow where Mr. Kahl learned his skills, as well as a museum at 12th Street and Surf Avenue on Coney Island. The son of two college administrators from Albany, Mr. Kahl still swallows swords 30 to 40 times a year in shows, but he couldn't support his growing family on a performer's meager income. (His wife, the former Kiva Shliuger, performs regularly as a fire-eater known as Combustible Kiva, the Queen of Kerosene.) Unlike his friend Michael Wilson, the Illustrated Man, who is tattooed head to foot, Mr. Kahl said he was not "visually arresting" enough to make the "big money" from private parties, television appearances and music videos.  WHAT YOU SEE -- One of the most striking pages is Mr. Kahl's paean to his art, the Great Fredini's CyberSideshow (http://fargo.itp.tsoa.nyu.edu/'fredini/index.html). The site includes an X-ray movie of a man (not Mr. Kahl) swallowing a sword, as well as a version of Mr. Kahl's master's thesis in applied computer technology at newyork University. And it has panoramic shots of Coney Island performers and a soap opera-like narrative. "I think of it as Coney Island Meets Twin Peaks," he said. Another page is about Melvin Burkhardt, Mr. Kahl's predecessor as the Human Blockhead. Now in his late 80's, he still performs in his hometown, Gibsonton, Fla. Mr. Burkhardt was able to shmooze with audiences for minutes or hours, and Mr. Kahl presents some of Mr. Burkhardt's carny patois. ("I'm the Human Blockhead. I have here a common ordinary ice pick that I will jab into my head, but I'm not going to drop dead.") On the same site, Whirl-i-gig, another Web site developer, has done the pages for the 16th Annual Mermaid Parade on Coney Island. It is set for June 27, with David Byrne, the rock musician, as king of the parade. The photo album of past parades is a delight, even without Mr. Kahl's deadpan narration. "And here," he said, clicking his mouse, "are mermaid biker chicks."  LINKS -- More than 30, including "World of Coasters" (http://www.rollercoaster.com), which has a roller-coaster glossary (TPM, for example, means "theme park mentality," referring to roller coaster operators' rules that are seen by buffs as overly strict.)  WHAT YOU GET -- An engaging and technologically sophisticated site that may frustrate some Web viewers because it works best with a host of "plug-ins," or special application programs.   ANTHONY RAMIREZ  Coney Island U.S.A. http://www.coneyislandusa.com/ Graphic   Photo.

title:
POP/JAZZ;
(Even) Jazz Makes the Leap to Cyberspace
body: COMPUTERS speak in many different voices, but the one coming out of the PC on Bret Primack's desk is likely to startle even the most jaded of Web surfers. Low, amused and overcareful, it sounds suspiciously like a man who has just taken a good-size shot of heroin, and not without reason: the speaker is Charlie Parker, jazz's best-known junkie. "I had the pleasure to meet Miles for the first time in St. Louis when he was a youngster," says the digitized Parker, referring to Miles Davis, the subject of www.milesdavis.com, an interactive Web site designed by Mr. Primack that opened for public viewing two weeks ago. Milesdavis.com is not the first site devoted to the legendary trumpeter -- there are at least 20 others -- but it is the only "officially sanctioned" one, meaning that it has been authorized by Davis's estate. In addition to the voice of Parker, it contains numerous audio and video clips of Davis, interviews with musicians who knew him, and an elaborate multimedia biography written by Mr. Primack that will be rolled out in 12 monthly installments. Visitors can also purchase CD's by Davis and books about him, which is the whole point of the exercise, since milesdavis.com is produced by Jazz Central Station (www.jazzcentralstation.com), by far the largest and most ambitious of the many jazz-related sites currently accessible on the World Wide Web. Jazz is big -- very big -- on the Web. Jazz Central Station and similar enterprises like Jazz on Line (www.jazzonline.com) and All About Jazz (www.allaboutjazz.com) are among the 300-odd Web sites devoted to jazz, the number of which is growing daily. Many of these sites are difficult to locate on search engines, but if you know where to look, you can find everything from serious scholarship to heartfelt tributes posted by avid fans. Want to know who played bass on Bill Evans's 1962 recording of "Funkallero"? A quick visit to the Bill Evans Jazz Resource (www.34skid.com) reveals that it was Ron Carter. Looking for nightspots in Azerbaijan? According to Jazz Clubs Worldwide (www.jazz-clubs-worldwide.com), there are two in Baku. Some jazz sites are commercial in nature: Jazz Central Station, for example, is part of the Music Boulevard Network, a group of genre-specific music channels linked to an on-line retail "store" (www.musicblvd.com) that offers more than 200,000 CD's for sale at the click of a mouse. Most jazz record labels now have their own promotional sites (too many, alas, top-heavy with graphics and thus time-consuming to access with a normally equipped computer), which usually include artist biographies, tour itineraries and updates on new releases. But jazz on the Web is just as often the work of individuals willing to pay the modest price of maintaining a site (a couple of hundred dollars a year is all it takes) in return for the privilege of paying public homage to their favorite artists. To be sure, the coverage is spotty and arbitrary: a recent search turned up no full-scale site devoted to Count Basie and no Dizzy Gillespie site of any kind. Moreover, the typical jazz Web site is amateurish-looking -- homemade graphics and painful misspellings abound -- and enthusiastic to the point of hysteria. Yet the Web can also be used effectively as a research tool. A few sites, including the Benny Carter Web Site (www.lpb.com/benny), have been designed by noted scholars, who view them as an adjunct to their conventionally published work. Several scholarly discographies are now available on the Web, and some are equipped with their own search engines: Miles Ahead, the best of the unofficial Miles Davis sites (www.wam.umd.edu/losinp/music/ahead.html), can tell you in a matter of seconds when, where, what and how many times Davis recorded with a particular sideman. The ubiquity of jazz-related Web sites may come as a surprise to those who see jazz as a tradition-oriented music chiefly appealing to middle-aged fans. In fact the jazz audience, whose members tend to be better educated than the average CD buyer, has turned out to be full of what the industry refers to as "early adopters" -- including countless younger musicians who have been surfing the Web for much of their lives, many of whom are now starting their own sites as a means of inexpensive self-promotion. Kendra Shank, a protegee of Shirley Horn, markets her own singing and her debut CD, "Afterglow" (Mapleshade), through a Web-based home page (www.speakeasy.org/nwjazz/kendra.html). "I've only got a very basic page, with some sound bites from my CD," Ms. Shank says, "but I still get between 300 and 400 hits a month. At my gigs, I always invite people to sign up for my mailing list -- both snail-mail and email -- and I announce all my gigs by email. I get a lot of email from Web surfers, and I hear from DJ's, who want me to send them the CD for airplay. Not long ago, I was contacted by a Web jazz magazine in France, which interviewed me for one of their issues." Self-marketing seems likely to become one of the Web's most popular jazz-related applications, especially when bandwidth -- the amount of traffic that can be carried on the Internet -- increases to the point at which recorded music can be downloaded at very high speeds. Frustrated musicians unable to attract the attention of major record labels have long been attracted to the idea of starting their own "kitchen table" labels, but they were never before able to find a simple and effective way of distributing their product. Digital on-line music delivery will make it possible for such musicians to make their own recordings and sell them directly to Web surfers, a technological development of particular significance for middle-aged artists currently regarded as unmarketable by the youth-conscious major labels.  "We're finally going to be able to cut out the middlemen," says the pianist Roger Kellaway, "and go straight to the listeners." Such applications are not a pipe dream of starry-eyed computer geeks: N2K Inc., the parent company of Jazz Central Station, is already selling downloadable music singles via emod, its proprietary on-line music delivery system. Mr. Primack estimates that within three to five years, most computer owners will have modems fast enough to make digital on-line music delivery both feasible and convenient. For now, though, jazz on the Web remains the preserve of early adopters like Ms. Shank, and few as yet have done more than merely scratch the surface. "So far," she admits, "I've done nothing to encourage people to look at my page, and I haven't used it to solicit gigs -- for example, sending a bulk emailing to festivals suggesting they check out my page and consider booking me." Still, the potential of the World Wide Web as a marketing tool is already clear. One figure alone tells the story: 200,000 different computers log on to Jazz Central Station every month. Such numbers are unlikely to impress record producers who specialize in mass-market pop, but for jazz musicians wondering where their next gig is coming from, 200,000 sounds as sweet as Miles Davis playing "My Funny Valentine."  JAZZ SPOTS ON THE WEB  JAZZ is big oon the Internet: some 300 Web sites are devoted to the music, and the number is growing. Here are 10 sites worth visiting.   TERRY TEACHOUT  JAZZ CENTRAL STATION (www.jazzcentralstation.com) A one-stop "virtual community" for jazz fans: bulletin boards, news and reviews, profiles and discographies, instant polls, a retail CD store, and much more. DESIGN: Cluttered, but makes sense once you get used to it. SPEED: Sometimes sluggish HIGHLIGHT: milesdavis.com, among the best interactive jazz sites on the web  FANTASY RECORDS (www.fantasyjazz.com) Information on new Fantasy jazz releases (including biographies and itineraries for selected artists), plus a CD catalogue. DESIGN: Clear and to the point SPEED: Fast, especially for a record-label site HIGHLIGHT: Quick access to complete track listings for all Fantasy CD's  BLUE NOTE HOME PAGE (www.bluenote.net) All about newyork's fanciest jazz club, from the schedule to the menu. DESIGN: Nondescript SPEED: Slow HIGHLIGHT: Live closed-circuit telecasts of selected performances  KANSAS CITY JAZZ AMBASSADORS MAGAZINE (www.kansascity.com/kcjazz) A comprehensive guide to the jazz scene in Kansas City, including feature stories, club schedules, and links to 638 Web sites by or about local musicians, past and present. DESIGN: Attractive and easy to use SPEED: Fairly fast HIGHLIGHT: "A Virtual Visit to Charlie Parker's Grave in Kansas City"  JAZZ CLUBS WORLDWIDE (www.jazz-clubs-worldwide.com) Information about clubs in more than 40 countries, from Azerbaijan to the Unites States. DESIGN: No-nonsense SPEED: Very fast HIGHLIGHT: Links to club Web sites and email addresses  JAZZ CORNER (www.jazzcorner.com) A commercial service providing home pages for more than 60 "independent" jazz musicians, including Ben Allison, Joanne Brackeen, Robin Eubanks, Dave Holland, Jonny King, and renee Rosnes. All pages are designed in-house and contain biographies, itineraries, sound bites, discographies, and email addresses. DESIGN: Garish but effective SPEED: Fast HIGHLIGHT: Ideal for computer-illiterate musicians interested in using the Web as a promotional tool  BENNY CARTER WEB SITE (www.lpb.com/benny) The story of the master alto saxophonist-trumpeter-composer, as told by the Carter scholars Ed and Laurence Berger. Definitely a fan's site, but useful nonetheless.
