title:
POSTINGS: Fannie Mae Approvals on the Internet;
A Mortgage In Four Minutes
body: Mortgage approval in as little as four minutes is now available on the Internet. Dan Rawitch, chief executive officer of Finet Holdings Company, a mortgage lender in Walnut Creek, Calif., said that last month, Finet, working with Fannie Mae, the nation's largest source of residential mortgage funds, began iQualify.com (http://www.iQualify.com) -- the first on-line mortgage application service that provides Fannie Mae pre-approvals. Mike Williams, a senior vice president for Fannie Mae in Washington, said that by linking Fannie Mae's computers with Finet's and then allowing homebuyers to hook up to Finet's computers on the Internet, it is possible for Fannie Mae to provide a mortgage approval directly to the customer. Mr. Williams said that borrowers need to enter just 30 "data points" of information -- name, address, income, mortgage amount, etc. -- while connected to Finet's Web site. The information is transmitted to Fannie Mae's computer, which crunches the numbers, orders electronic credit reports and reports back to the customer via email, often in as little as four minutes. Mr. Rawitch said his company could issue a mortgage check within 48 hours of Fannie Mae's approval. But customers are not required to deal with Finet -- they can go to other lenders with their Fannie Mae approvals. The fee for an on-line mortgage application, Mr. Rawitch said, is $39 and can be paid by credit card.

title: Tangled Web
body: SPEEDING THE NET The Inside Story of Netscape and How It Challenged Microsoft. By Joshua Quittner and Michelle Slatalla. 323 pp. newyork: Atlantic Monthly Press. $25. A fascinating story lies behind Justice Department-embattled Microsoft's trouncing of the Netscape Communications Corporation, the scrappy software start-up whose groundbreaking Navigator program helped popularize the World Wide Web. Unfortunately, that tale doesn't begin until at least halfway through "Speeding the Net," an expert but long-winded account by the husband-and-wife team of Joshua Quittner and Michelle Slatalla. The book's first half details the rise of Marc Andreessen, Navigator's pudgy primary programmer. He and his workaholic hacker friends make entertaining, if cliched, characters. Their cars are filled with greasy fast-food wrappers. They rail in email flame wars. They spend weeks at their keyboards with little in the way of showers, exercise or items from the fruit-and-vegetable food group. Both Quittner and Slatalla are computer columnists: he writes for Time magazine, and she is a contributor to the Circuits section of The newyork Times. They do their best to enliven this protracted prologue, writing in a colloquial, thriller-like style and striving to turn software demos into drama and buttoned-down executives into emotion machines. While this technique may have worked in their previous nonfiction collaboration, "Masters of Deception: The Gang That Ruled Cyberspace," the story this time isn't about on-line skulduggery; at its heart, "Speeding the Net" is about boardroom meetings, stock options and the fundamentally boring process of typing computer code. As a result, the excitement often has a tacked-on, hyperbolic ring. The Microsoft Corporation's relatively easy ride to Web dominance is called "one of the great corporate battles of the century." The Internet itself -- a forum actually frequented by only a minority of Americans (and even smaller populations elsewhere) -- is billed as "a ubiquitous cultural and economic phenomenon." When Netscape itself finally appears, the authors hit their stride. Conflict, in the form of Bill Gates, triggers a chain of events that merits the novelistic prose. Over the course of four desperate years, Netscape scrambles to resist Microsoft's onslaught. James L. Barksdale, Netscape's C.E.O., sics the Justice Department's antitrust investigators on Microsoft. The Netscape board gives away stock to its employees as a motivator to improve flagging sales. Finally, hoping to diversify itself out of a Web-browser showdown with Microsoft, Netscape spends millions to acquire other software companies. The authors clearly sympathize with the panicked crew at Netscape, yet they ignore the possibility that the company may have brought about some of its own problems. In tacking its acquired software onto Navigator, for example, Netscape bloated its crown jewel and may have spread the company too thin. Nor do the authors consider that Netscape lost the war because Microsoft simply created a better product: Microsoft's browser, Internet Explorer, was stable, fast and free, whereas Netscape's $49 Navigator program was buggy. THE book ends with Netscape's March 1998 last-ditch ploy, in which the company released the source code for Navigator to the public. The slim hope is that independent programmers will refine the software, extending its life in the marketplace despite Microsoft's dominance. Aside from painting Microsoft as the villain, the authors offer no analysis; "Speeding the Net" is an exercise in pure reporting. At their best, they deftly demystify both the technology and the forces -- legal, economic and personal -- that drive the software business. But by the time the tale is over, the reader is left feeling like Netscape's college-kid programmers: depressed that Microsoft has seemingly squashed yet another innovator, and not quite sure what went wrong.

title: Cuts Are Urged In Internet Fund Clinton Praises
body: While President Clinton was speaking enthusiastically yesterday in favor of a program to help schools and libraries connect to the Internet, the Federal Communications Commission, under pressure from Congress, was preparing to scale back the program, officials close to the commission and to Congress said yesterday. Some 30,000 schools and libraries have submitted applications for Internet grants totaling $2.02 billion. But under the plans being considered by the commission, the program would almost certainly get less than $1.7 billion this year, and possibly less than $1.4 billion, the officials said. Big long-distance phone companies contribute most of the money that goes into the program. The commission and lawmakers are concerned that fulfilling all the applications from schools and libraries could lead to higher long-distance telephone rates. But while some members of Congress want to cut off funds to the program completely, F.C.C. officials want to shrink the program more modestly. Negotiations among commission, Congress and White House officials are expected to continue through the weekend. Still, the commission is not expected to agree to stop collecting money for the program altogether, as has been urged by four powerful members of Congress. The AT&T Corporation and the MCI Communications Corporation have said they intend to make charges for the program explicit on customers' bills. That move has led to pressure on lawmakers to eliminate the charges, even though the F.C.C. has given long-distance companies new savings to compensate for the new fees, and rates have fallen partly as a result. Referring to the school and library program by its Washington nickname, Mr. Clinton said yesterday, "I say we cannot afford not to have an e-rate." "Thousands of poor schools and libraries and rural health centers are in desperate need of discounts," the President said, giving a commencement address at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. "If we really believe that we all belong in the Information Age, then, at this sunlit moment of prosperity, we can't leave anyone behind in the dark." The President has set a goal of connecting every classroom to the Internet by 2000, and he said yesterday that by this time next year "we will have connected well over half our classrooms, including 100 percent of the classrooms in the nation's 50 largest urban school districts." The F.C.C. collected $625 million for the schools and libraries program in the first half of the year. If the commission does not vote to change the program by Tuesday, the F.C.C. will collect an additional $690 million in the third quarter and as much as $705 million in the fourth quarter. That would meet all of the grant applications. The commission must vote by Tuesday because the third quarter begins on July 1 and the commission has said that phone companies must know their obligations by next week in order to prepare and modify their billing systems. But few people at the F.C.C. believe that the commission will allow the schools and libraries fund to grow to meet the outstanding demand. That is partly because the commission, led by William E. Kennard, a Democrat, as chairman, has insisted since last year that the schools and libraries program not increase the price of phone calls for consumers. To achieve that goal, the commission has pegged the long-distance companies' contributions to regulated reductions in the charges, known as access fees, that the companies pay to local phone companies to begin and end calls. Some of the access fee reductions are meant to flow through to consumers in the form of lower rates, and the major long-distance companies say they have done so. But AT&T and MCI are also about to begin telling their customers that the Government is making consumers pay more to support schools and libraries. "People's bills have stayed at, say, $20," an F.C.C. official said. "But instead of $20 they see $19 plus $1, and they focus on the plus $1." The commission is scheduled to create $700 million to $800 million in additional annual access charge reductions on July 1. That works out to $175 million to $200 million in quarterly savings. The commission collected $325 million for the fund in the second quarter. If that rate was increased to reflect the July 1 access fee reduction, the F.C.C. would collect for the rest of the year at a rate of $500 million to $525 million a quarter. In fact, a majority of the five-member commission had agreed on a plan to collect $524 million a quarter at least until the end of the year, people close to the commission said yesterday. That would have yielded a total budget for the calendar year of $1.67 billion. On Thursday, however, the four high-ranking members of Congress wrote to Mr. Kennard urging the F.C.C. to stop collecting for the program altogether, destroying the $524 million consensus. The schools and libraries plan, which has its origins in the Telecommunications Act of 1996, is part of a larger program that also supports telecommunications service in poor and rural areas, known as universal service. "The commission's efforts to implement the universal service provisions of the act have been a spectacular failure and -- more importantly -- a raw deal for consumers," wrote the four members of Congress: Representative Thomas J. Bliley Jr., a Republican from Virginia who is chairman of the House Commerce Committee; Representative John D. Dingell, a Democrat of Michigan who is the ranking minority member of that committee; Senator John McCain, the Arizona Republican who is chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, and Senator Ernest F. Hollings, Democrat of South Carolina, the ranking minority member of that committee. Although an F.C.C. spokeswoman declined to confirm it, people on Capitol Hill said yesterday that the commission was floating a plan to collect $375 million for the fund each quarter, for a 1998 total of $1.38 billion. In a statement, Mr. Kennard said: "Ending this effort is not in the best interest of the American people. We need to find a way to insure that this effort continues. I am committed to this."

title: U.S., in Shift, Drops Its Effort to Manage Internet Addresses - Correction Appended
body: The Clinton Administration renounced the last vestige of control by the unitedstates Government over the Internet's basic structure yesterday, acknowledging that the computer network had grown too big, too global and too commercial to be overseen by any one nation. That last vestige is the distribution and management of Internet addresses, an issue that has become the focus of increasingly heated debates and litigation as companies, institutions and individuals found that the land rush to cyberspace was being slowed because all the best addresses had already been snapped up. In a long-anticipated policy paper, the Administration said it would turn over the management of the Internet's address system to an international nonprofit group that could represent a range of constituencies from large corporations struggling to protect their trademarks and market their products on line to Saturday night Web surfers. The final policy dispenses with many of the more controversial Government mandates that had produced widespread opposition to early drafts of the report. Instead, adopting a plan that could become a general model for Internet self-governance, the Government will abdicate the sticky task of building a consensus across national boundaries, private and public sectors, and big and small businesses to the as-yet-unformed group. While governments are not soon likely to abandon attempts to control aspects of the Internet within their territories that violate moral or cultural values -- pornography, pedophilia, gambling and invasion of privacy are the most popular targets -- the ultimate futility of localized efforts to place limits on a global network is widely expected to result in more Internet self-regulation. The question of who gets what address on the Internet does not strike at the core values of any one group or culture, but it has become an increasingly contentious issue. That is because while real estate in cyberspace is theoretically unlimited, the Government has only authorized the use of a handful of "top-level domains," the suffixes at the ends of Internet addresses that are supposed to denote what type a site is. The ".edu" domain, for example, is restricted for use by schools and universities, while ".gov" is available only to governments, and ".mil" can be used only by the military. In addition, ".org" is supposed to denote nonprofit organizations, and ".net" is given out only to Internet service providers. That leaves everyone else, from the largest corporations to your Aunt Mae, vying for a domain address that ends in ".com," which the Government introduced in 1990 to denote commercial sites. That was before the World Wide Web, and no one dreamed that demand for Internet domain addresses would be so great. In a frantic electronic land grab that began about three years ago, those seeking to stake out an on-line identity have rapidly scooped up many of the most desirable domain addresses. This has already resulted in wild speculation. Last week, it was reported that Shopping.com had paid $750,000 in cash and stock to buy its domain name from the person who had registered it for $70. The yet-to-be-established oversight group would have the authority to designate dozens of new top-level domains -- like ".web" or ".store," for instance -- and would arbitrate disputes between address-seekers. But Internet analysts said that the process itself represented a significant first step toward the creation of a governing body for the Internet independent of governments, trade associations or international bodies like the United Nations or the World Trade Organization. Although it makes some traditional policy makers nervous, self-governance is a model that is gaining support from a broad spectrum of Internet users, including Ira C. Magaziner, the senior White House adviser who oversaw the rocky evolution of the domain name policy articulated in yesterday's report. Last week, America Online's chairman, Steve Case, called for the formation of an "Internet Alliance" to "avoid outrageous local and national laws that would strangle the growth of the medium." And the European Union Commissioner, Martin Bangemann, has proposed an international charter to deal with issues like data encryption. Advocates of self-governance argue that the network is changing too fast to be effectively monitored by governments and is too far-flung to be constrained by them. "We think it is in the best interest of the Internet and the best interest of the unitedstates for this medium to grow and become ubiquitous," Mr. Magaziner said. "And the Government's getting out of the way of its management is the best way to achieve that." Hatched almost 30 years ago by the Defense Department as a closed conduit for military and academic communications, the network, under various names, has spawned prodigious progeny. Today, the Internet is a global nervous system linking 30 million host computers and an estimated 102 million users, according to Matrix Information and Directory Services in Austin, Tex. And while the unitedstates has long dominated the Internet, its fastest growth is now in countries like the Netherlands and Brazil. The Administration's earlier plan drew criticism that despite its assertions to the contrary, the unitedstates was seeking to exert too much control over the Internet. But some of the plan's harshest critics were pleased with the Commerce Department's final report. "This clearly shows the U.S. Government heard the international community and listened to them," said Don Heath, president of the Internet Society, which oversees the technology of the network. "They showed they understood the dynamics of the Internet, the need for bottom-up, grass-roots consensus building. This is a victory for the Internet and a victory for self-governance." The Government has been withdrawing from the Internet since the network began its exponential growth in the early 1990's. In 1992, the Government agreed to let commercial traffic use the Internet's main pathway, known as the backbone. In 1995, it relinquished the administration of the backbone to commercial entities. But it has always retained control of the critical function of assigning addresses. Under a five-year contract with the National Science Foundation, all registrations for the major Internet domains are currently performed exclusively by Network Solutions of Herndon, Va., which charges first-time registrants $70. Network Solutions is a unit of Science Applications International. When the Commerce Department issued a draft domain name policy in January, many would-be competitors complained that it protected Network Solutions' monopoly. Under the new plan, such companies could compete with Network Solutions when its contract expires on Sept. 30. In the interim, the feuding over addresses continues, often in strange ways. In one recent case, the Prema Toy Company, which owns the trademarks on the claymation character Gumby and his horse, Pokey, sued a 12-year-old Web designer whose parents had registered "pokey.org" because the boy's nickname is Pokey. Correction  Because of an editing error, a front-page article on Saturday about the management of Internet addresses misstated the year that the suffix ".com" was introduced for commercial enterprises. It was 1985, not 1990. Correction-Date: June 9, 1998, Tuesday

title: Europe Official Cites Concern On Worldcom-MCI Merger
body: The top European regulator reviewing Worldcom Inc.'s proposed $37 billion acquisition of the MCI Communications Corporation said yesterday that MCI's proposed sale of part of its Internet business might not allay his antitrust concerns. MCI announced last week that it had agreed to sell its wholesale Internet unit to Cable and Wireless P.L.C. for $625 million in cash. European regulators and the Justice Department had made clear to MCI and Worldcom a concern that the combined company could unfairly dominate the Internet and that the regulators would require the companies to sell off some cyberspace assets. Foes of the deal, led by the GTE Corporation, which lost in its attempt to acquire MCI, have been pushing Worldcom to sell its Uunet unit, the leading Internet service company. But Worldcom has refused. Instead, MCI agreed to sell part of its Internet unit to Cable and Wireless. MCI told Justice Department officials about the Cable and Wireless deal more than a week before it was publicly announced, in the hope of winning the department's blessing. But the department refused to assure MCI that the Cable and Wireless deal would be sufficient to remove its concerns. Yesterday, Karel van Miert, the European Union's competition commissioner, also refused to give such an assurance. "I'm not sure that what has been offered will be good enough," Mr. van Miert told a news conference in Washington. Mr. van Miert said he had notified each affected company of his concerns and said the companies would each have a chance to make additional suggestions. GTE welcomed Mr. van Miert's comments, saying they" clearly indicate that MCI's recent attempt to create the appearance of a divestiture through partial sale of some minor Internet assets are not going to fool the E.C."

title: Guidelines Are Sought for Internet Privacy
body: Civil liberties advocates and children's groups urged the White House today to abandon its hands-off stance to Internet privacy regulation after a Federal Trade Commission report painted a dismal picture of the effectiveness of companies' self-regulation, especially in regard to children. "It's clear that the Clinton Administration policy has been an abysmal failure," said Jeff Chester of the Center for Media Education, an electronic media public-interest group. After the F.T.C. report was released this morning, the agency's chairman, Robert Pitofsky, called its conclusions "disappointing" but declined to call self-regulation a failure. "I still believe that the best way to deal with this is self-regulation rather than heavy-handed government," he said. The F.T.C., which surveyed 1,400 Web sites, found that a year after the agency had warned businesses of the need to adopt strong privacy guidelines to avoid Government regulation, 92 percent of all Web sites collected personal information from users and only 14 percent disclosed how the data were used. Most troubling to the F.T.C. was the finding that 89 percent of the children's sites surveyed collected personal information. Of those, only 23 percent told children to seek parental permission and less than 10 percent provided for parental control over the collection and use of the information. At one Web site, the agency said, children were asked to give their names, addresses, email addresses, ages and whether they ever received gifts of stocks, cash, savings bonds or certificates of deposit. Also troubling, the report said, was the amount of data collected by interactive public areas like chat rooms, which are accessible to everyone. "These activities enable children to communicate freely with strangers, including adults," the report said. Investigation by the F.B.I. and the Justice Department, it said, "has revealed that on-line services and bulletin boards are quickly becoming the most powerful resources used by predators to identify and contact children." The report recommends that Congress pass legislation to require that Web sites collecting personal information from children younger than 12 notify parents and obtain consent to collect the information. The F.T.C., Mr. Pitofsky said, will continue to evaluate the broader issues of Internet privacy and make recommendations later this year on whether protections are needed for adults. Jerry Berman, executive director of the Center for Democracy and Technology, an on-line advocacy group, called on the F.T.C. to ask Congress for authority to immediately adopt rules to protect children. "Punting this issue to Congress without taking this first step may result in a political nightmare for the Internet community, with controls on content and moves to a national identification scheme for the Net," he said. Marc Rotenberg, director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said the F.T.C. report failed to address all of the critical issues. "We wanted to see them make a clear statement on the need for protecting the anonymity of people on the Internet," he said. Mr. Rotenberg added, "The people who really need to do something are the people in the White House." He said Ira Magaziner, President Clinton's Internet adviser, had been "traveling the world telling everyone that self-regulation works. The message is clear: self-regulation has not worked." Mr. Magaziner was traveling today and could not immediately be reached for comment. But Commerce Secretary William M. Daley was critical of the progress made by industry to police itself. "There has to be a critical mass of the companies to make self-regulation work, and we haven't seen that yet," Mr. Daley said. The Commerce Department is supposed to make a full report to the White House in July on whether self-regulation is working. Business groups insist it is and are pleading for more time to prove it. The Direct Marketing Association, for example, has endorsed privacy policies similar to those recommended by the F.T.C. and is working to educate businesses of the need to follow the guidelines. The association said its own survey in May of the top 100 children's Web sites showed that 70 percent posted privacy polices, compared with 38 percent in January.

title:
PRO FOOTBALL;
Giants' Back Optimistic in Cancer Fight
body: Giants running back LeShon Johnson smiled when he referred to his wife of six weeks as "a computer geek." "She can get on the Internet and find out anything," Johnson said today of Nalani, whom he married April 27. "She can fly in and out of all those web sites." For the last 10 days, Nalani has been doing research on a totally unexpected subject. It is non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, the type of cancer that has stricken her husband and will be treated with six months of chemotherapy beginning next week. "She's been finding out all she can and then filling me in," LeShon said today at Giants Stadium. This, too, brought a smile to Johnson's face. "I'm very lucky to have her," he said. Staring down between the cowboy boots on his feet, he added: "We're going to beat this thing and get on with life." Today was the day Johnson met with reporters and teammates, preparing for the next, unexpected stage in his life: the one after cancer. He has been examined and tested. "I've been poked so much I feel like a human pin cushion," he said. He has had long, emotional telephone conversations with his mother, father and brothers back home in Oklahoma. And he has come to face a new reality. "I thought you had to be old to get cancer," said Johnson, signed by the Giants just three months ago as a free agent."I thought I was a healthy 27-year-old football player." Today, standing on a makeshift podium next to the Giants practice field, Johnson listened as the Giants' trainer, Ronnie Barnes, read off a new set of statistics for this football player. "LeShon has non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, B cell," Barnes said. "CAT scans have isolated the tumor above his waist. It is eight millimeters in size. The doctors tell me they are very encouraged and optimistic that the lymphoma is localized and treatable. He will start his chemotherapy treatments next week." Johnson will be treated by Dr. David J. Wolf, an oncologist at newyork Hospital-Cornell Medical Center who also treated the former Giants lineman Karl Nelson in the late 1980's. Nelson, like the hockey star Mario Lemieux, had Hodgkin's lymphoma, which is generally considered easier to treat than non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. But as Dr. Marc Lippman, the director of the Vince Lombardi Cancer Research Center of Georgetown University, said in a telephone interview from Washington, there are about 15 different types of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. "The 10-year survival rates for these lymphomas can range from 10 percent to 90 percent," Lippman said. "It all depends exactly what subtype of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma he has." The Giants, although questioned on the subject, were not specific about Johnson's lymphoma type. "The fact is some lymphomas are completely curable and most can be put into remission," Lippman said. "If he goes into remission, he can play again, and most likely he will." Lippman added that it was a good sign that Johnson had no symptoms before the tumor was detected by a routine chest X-ray last month. It was also a good sign that Johnson's doctors are saying the lymphoma was detected at an early stage. Asked if Johnson could play while undergoing chemotherapy, Lippman said: "Some people go through chemo with only a few setbacks and some people get kind of beat up. Let's just say he certainly wouldn't be on top of his game." On the podium today, beneath a brilliant sun, Johnson nodded at the Giants' practice field. "It's my goal to be back out there before my six months of treatments are over," he said. He thanked the Giants for making him feel so at home and welcomed in just three months. "I was speechless when they told me," Johnson said of the diagnosis. "I was scared and nervous. But I know I have a lot of people praying for me."  Exhibition Games on Grass The Giants and Jets will test the durability of a grass surface in several exhibition games at Giants Stadium this season. The teams and the New Jersey Sports and Exposition Authority, which operates Giants Stadium, announced yesterday that the Giants' game against Cincinnati on Aug. 8, the Jets-Baltimore game on Aug. 15 and the Jets-Giants game on Aug. 20 will be played on the grass-tray surface now used by the MetroStars soccer team. The Giants' preseason finale against Baltimore on Aug. 28 will be played on the stadium's AstroTurf 12 field.

title: A Small Card Maker Finds Itself Atop the Web
body: THE appearance of the site www.bluemountain.com at the top of various lists of popular sites has left Web watchers scratching their heads. Blue Mountain Arts is a small greeting card company based in Boulder, Colo., and known for its sincere if slightly treacly sentiment. But on the net, the Blue Mountain site is beating out big names like Disney Online, the bookseller Amazon.com and the Hotmail free email service. The site, which attracted more than 5,085,000 individual visitors in April, offers electronic personalized greeting cards commemorating everything from first holy communion to the death of a pet. For those occasions when you care enough to click the Send button, you can send messages that can include a picture and room for a personal sentiment, some animation and music. "It just goes to show how different the Web is from anything else before it, in terms of business," said Stacie Leone, marketing and communications manager at Media Metrix, a newyork company that measures Web audiences and recently found Blue Mountain to be the most popular shopping Web site. "A site like this that doesn't advertise and doesn't make any money out of its Web site can skyrocket to the top." Media Metrix found the site ranked 13th among home computer users and 15th among people using their computers at work. Relevant Knowledge, an Atlanta company that tracks a panel of Web users, ranked it 17th most popular among all domain names in April. To send greetings to friends who have email accounts, senders pick designs and messages, or write their own, fill out address labels and send the completed greetings to another part of the company's Web page. Recipients automatically get email announcements, including a Web site address and a message number. Go to the Web site, plug in your number, see the picture and message, and consider yourself duly greeted. James McQuivey, an analyst of on-line retail strategies for Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass., explained part of the site's success. "They have this little secret going for them," he said. "When you use one of their cards and send it to a friend, he or she has to log into the site to receive it," thereby doubling the number of visitors. Blue Mountain, which also sells cards on paper, has been able to find a market for electronic cards for Waitress Day, World Environment Day, the Jewish holiday of Shavuot and Eid Norouz, the Persian holiday. "In the physical greeting card industry, you don't have the market there, but on the Web, it's not like those cards are taking up retail real estate," said Jared Schutz, Blue Moutain's director of business development. "We can offer cards for holidays we wouldn't necessarily offer in a store." Blue Mountain's competitors include Greet Street, which charges 50 cents per greeting (greetstreet. com); the card is sent directly to the recipient's email address. Another site, 123 Greetings (123greetings. com), offers messages grouped into categories like Kisses, Cats, Pizzas, Virtual Money (missives with pictures of bills; you choose the denomination) and Cuddly Tuddly, a collection of alarmingly cute stuffed animals. The site is slow, requiring the sender to go through nine screens to send a message. Hallmark (www.hallmark.com) charges $2.50 for on-line greetings featuring animation and sound. The site requires customers -- even those ordering the free, lower-tech virtual greetings -- to sign in with a mailing address and password. The form asks, "Would you like to receive information about Hallmark products, services and events?" Not surprisingly, the default answer, Yes, is already checked. (This is not the first instance of Hallmark's losing out to Blue Mountain Arts, which in 1986 successfully sued Hallmark to keep it from producing a line of cards copied from Blue Montain's line.) Another site, based in hongkong (www.icard.com.hk), allows senders to add their own photos and sound files to greetings. An alphabetical listing of electronic postcards, from Angel Winks Heavenly Postcards to the Zodiacal Zephyr Card Shop, is available at www.wp.com/annag/ ecards.htm. And check out the Amstel site there (www.amstel.nl/cam2.htm), with sendable views from a live camera in Amsterdam. What better way to say: "Having a wonderful time. Wish you were here"? title: F.T.C. to Call for Laws to Protect Children on Line
body: Amid mounting public concern about the abuse of personal data in an increasingly digital world, the Federal Trade Commission is expected to censure the Internet industry today in a report to Congress for doing virtually nothing to insure adequate consumer privacy protection on line. In a departure from the Clinton Administration's hands-off approach to the Internet, the agency will call for legislation that would require sites on the World Wide Web to obtain parental consent before collecting personal information from children, according to the report. The commission said it would make recommendations on privacy for other Web users this summer. "Children are told by parents not to talk to strangers whom they meet on the street, but they are given a contrary message by Web sites that encourage them to interact with strangers in their homes via the Web," the report says. Representative Edward J. Markey, Democrat of Massachusetts and the ranking minority member of the House telecommunications subcommittee, said, "This is a historic benchmark that changes forever the discussion of the protections which children need in a cyberera." In a study of 1,400 Web sites in March, the commission found that 85 percent collect personal information but only 14 percent provide any notice about what they do with the data. Only 2 percent provide such notice with a comprehensive privacy policy, the report said. "Those numbers are frightening," Mr. Markey said. "If privacy protections are not built into Internet commerce, then a vast majority of Americans will never trust the Internet." Although few had seen the long-anticipated report yesterday, news leaks about it added fuel to a heated debate among industry leaders and privacy advocates about how to address privacy concerns. Several companies and trade groups rushed to blunt the effect of the report with announcements of new policies. Technology trade groups representing more than 10,000 companies sent President Clinton a letter asking for a chance to allow self-regulation to work. And the Direct Marketing Association touted its own study, which showed that 70 percent of the top 100 children's Web sites publish a privacy policy. The group, which has lobbied against legislation, said late yesterday that it had adopted a new policy to seek parental consent for on-line marketing involving children younger than 13. "This is business stepping up to the plate, moving in the direction that it needs to, and that is how self-regulation works," said Connie Heatley, senior vice president of the association. For many companies trying to do business on the Internet, the entire promise of the medium rests on the ease with which it allows the collection of information for focusing advertising and marketing. Based on forms that consumers fill out when they first visit a site, or on simply tracking which areas of a site they visit most frequently, Web site owners can, for example, determine which advertisements to show them. "If it's not customized and personalized, it might as well be television," said David Card, a senior analyst at Jupiter Communications, an on-line consulting operation in newyork. "I'm nervous that we'll get stuck with a law that would eliminate the technical ability to do that." Still, consumers have continually expressed fears about what happens to information that they provide in cyberspace. Anxiety about the use of of medical and financial information on line is one of the top reasons people do not use the Internet, according to several recent polls. And some companies have decided that electronic commerce would be more helped than hurt by ending such practices. America Online, which has been much criticized for privacy lapses, said yesterday that it would not use the information that it gathered about what members did on line for any marketing purposes. "This can be extremely valuable information in the marketplace," said Jill Lesser, the on-line service's deputy director for law and public policy. "The ability to target consumers is extremely valuable. But you have to strike a balance." Ms. Lesser added: "It's hard to fault the F.T.C. for calling a spade a spade. Hopefully this will be a catalyst for companies to look at privacy protection as a business imperative." But Government action is needed, privacy advocates said, because children have never been more more vulnerable to commercial exploitation. "We're creating a new children's culture, and if we don't set ground rules for how that's done, we could see a whole set of very egregious, manipulative practices that could do a lot of harm to kids," said Kathryn C. Montgomery, president of the Center for Media Education, a child advocacy group. The problem with many sites aimed at children is that they make divulging information seem like a game, Ms. Montgomery said. For example, the Popsicle Web site, published by the Good Humor-Breyers Ice Cream unit of Unilever, asks children to choose whether they want to be commanders or passengers. Just one catch: Commanders have to fill out their age, sex, favorite TV show and favorite popsicle before blasting off. And in case anyone was inclined to just go along for the ride, the passenger option cautions: "Sure, you can ride in the big stuffed chair, but you'll miss out on the chance to win free Popsicles. Plus it's really cold in outer space without a Spaceship. Why not be a commander?" Popsicle's privacy policy says that it does not release the data it gathers to third parties.
