title:
NEWS WATCH;
Can the Internet Be Addictive, Or Is the Problem Elsewhere?
body: The results of a small new study cast some doubt on the notion of Internet addiction as a psychiatric problem. The report, presented earlier this week at the annual meeting of the American Psychiatric Association in Toronto, suggests that people who seem unable to curtail the number of hours they spend on the Internet may suffer from a raft of other psychiatric disorders. The researchers, at the University of Cincinnati, interviewed 14 people who had spent so much time on line that they were facing problems like broken relationships and job loss. The most striking finding of the survey, the researchers said, were the other psychiatric problems that turned up. Eleven of the 14 people had diagnoses of bipolar disorder, commonly known as manic-depression. The study's authors said it was unclear whether the Internet problem should be considered an addiction; a symptom of something else, like manic-depression, or a disorder caused by faulty impulse control, similar to compulsive shopping, or trichotillomania (a compulsion to tear your hair out). The small number of study subjects has generated skepticism. "Based on 14 cases, I don't know that we'd conclude much of anything," said Malcolm Parks, an associate professor of speech communication at the University of Washington. "The question is, could you find 14 people equally weird who didn't use the Internet?"

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
6 Degrees of Networking
body: SIX degrees of separation, the theory that everyone on the planet is connected by a chain of only six people, carries the grace of logic and the tantalizing lure of being impossible to disprove. The idea of six degrees of separation was advanced by Guglielmo Marconi, the inventor of the wireless telegraph, and popularized in the 1990 play of the same name by John Guare. It has fueled countless conversations pondering connections to the famous and infamous, the dead and living. It has also come to the Web in the form of a networking site called Six Degrees (www.sixdegrees.com). Six Degrees, which has 675,000 members and adds 3,000 more every 24 hours, uses the standard tools of the Internet -- email, bulletin boards and search engines -- to offer links to friends and friends of friends. What makes Six Degrees different from other public on-line services is that a member has a connection to all the other people on the site through a series of mutual acquaintances. A participant can either sign up at the Six Degrees Web site or join by responding to a member's email invitation. Participants choose an initial circle of friends (the first degree), and they in turn recruit their friends (the second degree), who can repeat the process. Members control who can see their personal information. As with similar networking tools at other membership-based sites like Geocities (geocities.com), Six Degrees offers an opportunity to ask people with shared interests for information. So, reaching into a network for a car repair shop, a chiropractor or a good place to go birding in eastern Pennsylvania can yield useful recommendations. One of the enjoyable features at Six Degrees is being able to look up the path of acquaintances between yourself and another member. The resulting "I know her through Mr. Barker at the printing shop and his cousin Trisha" list is reminiscent of those conservations about how you are connected to Warren Beatty. David Barton, a systems engineer in Stockholm, Sweden, the country with the highest per-capita membership in Six Degrees, recruited several members after he joined. "I use the site to keep track of my friends and business contacts," he said. The owner of the site, Macroview Communications of newyork, promises not to sell members' names to marketing businesses, though it does sells banner ads for the site and demographic statistics based on the site's membership. The company has also formed partnerships with sites like Job Direct (www.jobdirect.com) and College Beat (www.collegebeat.com). If a member registers with Six Degrees through one of these sites, his or her personal information belongs to both partners. According to the company, half the site members joined Six Degrees because friends had invited them, but they never do any networking. One such member is Derek Whiteside, a software engineer from Corvalis, Ore., who uses other on-line sources for getting advice and parts from owners of American Motors cars, which he collects. Only two of his friends joined Six Degrees when he listed them in his initial circle,and he said he is not comfortable pushing membership. "The site has the feel of a multilevel marketing thing," Mr. Whiteside said. "Before you can reap the benefits, you have to get others to join." Even though Six Degrees was inspired by a theoretical connection among six people, there is a limit to how far into the network a question can be distributed. Users can communicate via email only within their first or second degree. Still, if Marconi's theory is true (and if everyone on the planet joins the site), it may be possible one day to get email from Warren Beatty. Graphic   Photo: Six Degrees' 675,000 members have at least one thing in common.

title: The Great Domain Name Hunt
body: "YOU filthy-minded little pervert! The Kingdom of Tonga admonishes you. Now go back and think of another name that you wouldn't be embarrassed to say to your mother." Oh, the shame, being scolded by a computer. But more about that later. All I wanted to do was to get an Internet domain name of my own. The problem is that Lewis is a very common name, and lewis.com was already taken. So, like millions of Internet users before me, I began looking elsewhere for a domain I could call home, the Internet equivalent of 40 acres, where I could grow electronic mail, raise a small herd of Web pages and maybe someday open a little electronic cottage industry of my own, all with my own unique electronic brand. Lewis dot something. Lewis dot anything. It used to be technically difficult for average computer users to get their own personal, second-level Internet domain names -- the part of an email address to the right of the "@" and the part of the World Wide Web address that typically follows www. But if you could figure out how to do it, registering a domain name was free, and good names were plentiful. No more. The Internet is now the world's fastest-growing economy, and the commercialization of the Internet has created a feeding frenzy for domain names. A combination of greed, government bureaucracy, technical jingoism and wild consumer speculation has thrown the Internet addressing system into chaos. This week, after months of debate and policy wrangling, the Clinton Administration is expected to issue its revised proposal for turning the management of the Internet domain naming system over to a private nonprofit international organization. If all goes according to plan, individuals and businesses alike will find it easier to register and begin using a domain name. With 100 million people on the Internet, domain names are already a precious commodity. An Internet domain name is not just the equivalent of a telephone number and mailing address but also a status symbol, a powerful marketing tool and a vanity license plate. Last year, someone in Texas was reported to have paid $150,000 for the name business.com. Although alternatives will soon abound, nearly everyone agrees that no other Internet address carries the cachet of a personal "dot com" domain, the equivalent of a 212 area code for a phone number or a Fifth Avenue address. It is the largest top-level domain on the Internet, with more than two million unique secondary domains (like nytimes.com). More than 100,000 new "dot com" domains are added each month. "There are still good dot-com names available," said Doug Wolford, senior vice president for marketing and sales at Network Solutions, a for-profit company that for the past five years has had a virtual monopoly on registering .com domains because of an early agreement with the National Science Foundation, the original Internet overseer. Network Solutions, known as N.S.I., is a case in point. Someone else nabbed the address nsi.com before N.S.I. did, so the company took the less intuitive netsol.com. And now, facing the end of its Government-mandated monopoly on Sept. 30, the company has been marketing itself as "The Dot Com People" (www.thedotcompeople.com). I tried to be creative. Peterlewis .com had been registered by a fire-and-brimstone Christian group in Kansas called the Friend to Friend Foundation (www.friendtofriend. com) that apparently finances its ministries by registering Internet domains and releasing them to others in return for donations. Pete.com already belongs to a guy named Pete in Hawaii. Peter.com was taken by a chap named Jimmy in England. Phoenix Home Life got to my initials before I did, so I had to scratch phl.com. As expected, lewis.org and lewis. net -- .org and .net being arguably the two most desirable top-level domains after .com -- had been snatched already. Lewis.edu belongs to Lewis Middle School in San Diego, which has a dandy Web site. Lewis. gov and lewis.mil are available, but since I have neither my own Government bureaucracy nor an army, I don't qualify. So, like my Irish and Welsh forebears more than a century ago, I began looking for a virtual homestead in another country. Using the "whois" command (neatly automated for novice computer users at rs.internic.net/cgibin/whois), I quickly scratched from my list Sweden, Denmark, South Africa, Switzerland and New Zealand, all of which had been electronically homesteaded by Lewises, or pretenders, before I got there. But the world is a big place, and the Internet is spreading. More than 200 countries offer Internet domain registrations under their own two-letter country codes, like .jp for Japan and .uk for Britain. The .us for the unitedstates is used mostly by state and local governments. More than 70 of these 200-plus countries have no local residence requirement (most require merely some sort of local presence) and, shall we say, relaxed concepts of trademark law. Some have policies that allow any paying customer to register names on a first-come, first-served basis, allowing any swift and unscrupulous entrepreneur to register microsoft.xx or mcdonalds.xx. In fact, Turkmenistan's country code, .tm, might be mistaken for a trademark notice, which has made it very popular. Turkmenistan is one of many unlikely countries trying to capitalize on the demand for Internet domain names and generate some income. In recent months, domain registries have been marketing little pieces of Bhutan (.bt), the Cocos Islands (.cc), Tuvalu (.tv), Congo (.cd), Niue (.nu) and American Samoa (.as), among many others. Many of these burgeoning Internet paradises have no meaningful communications infrastructure, at least in terms of the big-bandwidth demands of the Internet, so they form partnerships with Web-savvy companies in major cities like newyork, San Francisco and London. The all-important name-server computers, which keep track of all the names and addresses of all the clients in the given domain, are often tethered to high-capacity phone lines thousands of miles away from the namesake country. Alas, I was beaten to lewis.tm by just one day, by someone in England named Jones. Another British rival had registered lewis.cc, from the Cocos. Even the microscopic island of Niue had already issued lewis.nu to someone else. So I raced through the global Internet Packet network to the South Pacific island of Tonga, only to discover that the same Mr. Jones, who fittingly lives on Robin Hood Street in Gloucester, had also snatched lewis.to just ahead of me. An information superhighwayman, indeed. In frustration, I tried to register the first word that came to mind -- one that cannot be printed in this newspaper -- prompting the stinging rebuke from the Tongan computer. Tonga and its Internet overseer, His Royal Highness Crown Prince Tupouto'a, are extremely proud of the island's Christian heritage and ban pornography and foul language. Turkmenistan recently suspended all new domain registrations after it discovered that people were registering obscene and unholy words. At this point I resolved to find the most remote speck in the ocean, where the fame and prestige of the Lewis clan has not yet spread. I picked Christmas Island, a territory of Australia in the Indian Ocean, with fewer than 900 residents. Surrounded by sharks, it is home to one television station, one AM radio station, one casino and several million scuttling crabs. But to me, the island's most interesting resource was -- at last! -- an unclaimed spot for lewis.cx. A search of the domain's official records revealed the welcome news that Christmas Island's domain is administered by four name-server computers in London. With the end of my search so tantalizingly near, and with no desire to navigate a foreign technical bureaucracy, I decided to use a domain name agent. One of the best is Netnames USA (www.netnamesusa. com), which is based in newyork and boasts that it can easily and painlessly, if not exactly inexpensively, register secondary domain names almost anywhere on the globe. Netnames typically charges a onetime fee of $75 to set up each .com, .net or .org domain and $249 to set up a national domain. National domains also charge their own registration and annual fees, which vary widely. The customer can also hire the agent to administer the domain, in effect renting the use of the agent's name servers. The arrangement can be temporary (until the domain name is transferred to a local Internet service provider) or long-term. Netnames allows the user to set up as many as five email accounts on the new domain without charge. Mail sent to pete@lewis.cx, for example, assuming I get the name, will automatically be forwarded to my preferred email account. Similarly, requests sent to  www.lewis.cx would be automatically forwarded to the humble Web site that my preferred I.S.P. provides free -- but now I won't have to use a Web address that contains lots of squiggles and dots and dashes and slashes. So for the bargain price of $249, I bought a piece of Christmas Island. My application will be evaluated by the Christmas Island domain administrator and will be operational as soon as I am determined to be a good citizen, electronically speaking. And if I'm rejected, well, there can't possibly be many Lewises in Antarctica or Tajikistan. Graphic   Map of Indonesia: END OF RESEARCH -- Staking a claim for a Christmas Island domain name.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
Three new acquisitions and affiliations reflect the quickening pace in the world of interactive ads.
body: THE pace of deals involving interactive advertising accelerated yesterday as three acquisitions and affiliations were announced. In one deal, 24/7 Media Inc. in newyork acquired Cliqnow Sales Group, the Internet advertising sales representation division of K2 Design Inc. in newyork, for $1 million in cash and $3 million in convertible preferred stock of 24/7. Cliqnow, which K2 started in 1996, has 10 employees who handle ad sales for 75 Web sites including those of The Associated Press, PR Newswire and the Women's Forum. Cliqnow will operate as an autonomous unit of 24/7 with sales staffs in Chicago, Los Angeles, newyork and San Francisco, and the Cliqnow sub-networks, offering computer users content on topics like finance and travel, will operate separately from the 24/7 network. Though Cliqnow has been successful, said Matthew de Ganon, president at K2, "we need to focus specifically on our core interactive advertising and media business." The sale, he added, would enable K2 to concentrate on that "and pursue aggressive growth." Scott Paternoster, 32, president at Cliqnow, and Joe Apprendi, 31, executive vice president, will continue in those roles and also become senior vice presidents at 24/7. The second deal involved Double Click Inc. in newyork, an interactive advertising network, and Ad Knowledge in Palo Alto, Calif., which provides tools for Internet media planning and buying and campaign management. The two companies have formed a strategic partnership; financial terms were not disclosed. The goal of the affiliation is to integrate the technologies of the two companies to create standard industry platforms for Web ad management that would help make buying and selling on-line advertising more efficient and effective. Ad Knowledge will now focus primarily on operations intended to help advertisers and agencies buy ads on the Internet while Double Click will support the Ad Knowledge operations focused on selling ads on the Internet. For instance, customers of Click Wise, the Ad Knowledge Web site ad management software, will now be able to use the Double Click DART service, a proprietary technology, offering ad server, reporting and tracking abilities. "As the on-line ad industry continues to expand, there is significant benefit to creating uniform standards for site publishers and advertising agencies," said Kevin O'Connor, chairman and chief executive at Double Click. "With the standardization that this partnership represents, we believe that on-line advertising will improve industrywide. And, by consolidating our efforts with Ad Knowledge, we believe we can expand DART's reach and market penetration." Scott Kauffman, president and chief executive at Ad Knowledge, said, "We believe DART provides the best solution for Web site publishers and we are confident our Click Wise customers will benefit tremendously from the power of Double Click advanced technology." Both Mr. Kauffman, 41, and Mr. O'Connor, 37, will continue in their respective roles. The third deal involved Interactive8, an on-line marketing agency in newyork, which acquired Tuckett/ Parshall Interactive in newyork, which specializes in interactive advertising aimed at black consumers. Financial terms were not disclosed. Tuckett/Parshall, which will be renamed as the TPI division of Interactive8, has estimated billings of $500,000 from clients like Essence magazine, Motown Records and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Company. TPI will be headed by Lawrence Tuckett, 43, founder and partner at Tuckett/Parshall, who also becomes creative director, and Michael Waite, 30, partner, who becomes executive producer. The acquisition "puts us at the forefront of urban on-line marketing and will greatly benefit companies expanding into the African-American consumer demographic," said Bill Markel, partner at Interactive8. Interactive8 has 37 employees and estimated billings of $4.9 million from clients like the AT&T Corporation, the Citibank unit of Citicorp and the M&M/Mars unit of Mars Inc. The quickening pace of deal-making in cyberspace is echoing the frenzied deal-making among traditional agencies as well as reflecting how the dynamics of interactive advertising and marketing are changing rapidly as the industry grows. Other Internet-related deals in the last month included two acquisitions by Agency.com in newyork; the purchase of Digital Cafe, a digital media agency in St. Paul, by Campbell Mithun Esty in Minneapolis, which is majority owned by the Interpublic Group of Companies; the acquisition of Circle Interactive L.L.C. in Boston by Arnold Communications, a unit of Snyder Communications in Boston, and the expansion of the on-line career services of TMP Worldwide in newyork through the purchase of two Web sites, About Work and Student Center, from Ivillage in newyork for $1.7 million in cash.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Disney Official Hired For Post at Comcast
body: The Comcast Corporation named a Walt Disney Company executive head of its cable television unit today as it moves toward selling digital television service and Internet access through cable lines. Steven Burke, 39, has been president of Disney's ABC Broadcasting division with its 10 television stations and radio group. He helped found the chain of Disney Stores, led the revamping of Euro Disney S.A. and was considered by some analysts as a possible successor to Michael D. Eisner as chief executive. His departure may revive questions about how much freedom Mr. Eisner, 56, gives his executives and whether he is grooming a replacement. A string of executives have recently left, among them the chief financial officer, Richard D. Nanula, who resigned in April to run the Starwood Hotels and Resorts lodging and gaming business, and Disney's cable chief, Geraldine B. Laybourne, who left last week to form her own company to produce Internet and television content for women and children. Comcast will soon be the nation's third-largest cable provider but was known in recent years for its financial transactions. It has led the push to use cable as a conduit to the Internet and in the process attracting a $1 billion investment a year ago by the Microsoft Corporation.

title: Dow Jones Decides to Buy Back Shares
body: Dow Jones & Company plans to buy back as much as $300 million of its shares and take a $98 million second-quarter charge as it completes the sale of its financial information unit to Bridge Information Systems Inc. The charge is to cover costs related to the $510 million sale, and it follows a $922.5 million fourth-quarter charge to write down the value of its initial $1.6 billion purchase of the unit, which was once known as Telerate. Dow Jones, whose main business is The Wall Street Journal, said in March that it would sell the unprofitable unit to Bridge after criticism from investors that it was weighing down the company's share price. The share repurchase is an effort to increase shareholder value, the company said. The number of shares involved amounts to about 6 percent of those outstanding. The newyork-based Dow Jones last bought back stock in 1996. Under the terms of the sale to Bridge, Dow Jones will receive $360 million in cash and $150 million of five-year, 4 percent preferred stock that is convertible into 10 percent of Bridge's equity. Bridge is owned by Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe, a closely held investment firm. The purchase made it the second-largest provider of financial news and analytical information, behind Reuters.

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
The High Price of Getting Something for Nothing
body: ONE of the most appealing aspects of the Web is getting something for nothing, not counting connection fees. One short-term no-cost offering is Outlook 98, the latest version of Microsoft's ambitious calendar, email and address book package. The software (not to be confused with the very different email-only Outlook Express program that comes with Internet Explorer) is available free for the downloading at www.microsoft.com/outlook/ until June 30; a CD-ROM can be ordered for $9.95. On July 1, the official price goes up to $109 except for registered users of Office 97, Outlook 97 or Exchange Server. Something for nothing often ends up incurring subtle costs. First surprise: If you already have Microsoft Office 97, you may first need to install the Office 97 Service Release 1 Patch, also known as SR-1. This is a collection of repairs for several unfortunate gaffes, including the one in Word 97 that refused to save files correctly in the prior Word format despite what the program claimed on the screen. SR-1 also repairs one of my favorite demonstrations of Microsoft's emphasis on quality, the Outlook calendar that put Thanksgiving on Tuesdays and Wednesdays over the next few years, but never on Thursday, not even in the year 2000. Since the SR-1 fixes must be in place before you can use a forthcoming SR-2 patch, which includes another hunk of code that repairs potential errors in Excel's spreadsheets, installing SR-1 is a good idea. Most recent versions of Office already include the SR-1 fixes, but it can be impossible to tell until you have installed the program. The clue: When you run a repaired version and click the "About" item under the Help menu, the rubric "SR-1" will appear after the program's name. Retail copies sold today should contain the updated code, but a CD with the defective version came with a new Micron computer that I tested a month ago, and other computer makers may still be shipping the unfixed version. Things get stranger. If you need to reinstall Office 97 or one of its programs, you will need to run the patch again. Worse, if you need to install a smaller component, you will need to uninstall Office in its entirety, reinstall it, and then run the patch program. The details in all their stupefying glory are available at the hard-to-find www.microsoft.com/office/office97/servicerelease/ sr1readme.htm page. So one expense of getting Outlook 98 for nothing is your time. Microsoft's Web site informed me that the 7-megabyte patch download would take a minimum of 35 minutes over a 28.8 kilobit-per-second modem. It actually took a lot longer. Two successive attempts to grab the file from Microsoft's own site and one in California stalled halfway through. A site in New Zealand actually worked. The final round started with the Internet Explorer 3 announcement that the estimated download time was 36 minutes, which swelled to 40, then an hour, then more before ending with a series of countdowns that claimed 11 seconds remaining, then 7,5,4,1 and -- whoops! -- 1 minute, 2 seconds. Including the false starts, the whole process took two hours. When I finally got to install the thing, a dispiriting message warned that "the patch can take up to 45 minutes to finish depending on your hardware," but on a fast new machine it took only 5. If you fail to check out the system requirements for Outlook 98, you might miss an essential point. The program requires Internet Explorer 4.01 and installs it for you unless it is already on your machine. That wipes out any previous version, even if you happen to prefer it, but you do get to enjoy IE 4.01's many bugs and anomalies and a reduction in disk space, and you can still use Netscape Navigator if you want to. On my machine, which already had Outlook 97 and Internet Explorer 3 installed, the "standard" installation grabbed 54 megabytes of disk space for itself despite omitting some potentially useful optional components. The official download estimate was three to four hours; in the interest of sanity I cheated and used a CD-ROM. And once Outlook 98 was finally up and running? Well, it can do all sorts of things you may have never even considered, like turning an electronic message into a calendar entry or a to-do item simply by dragging it from one place to another. It can present a concise one-page summary of the day's appointments, ongoing tasks and unread mail. It can keep an automatic record of how you have been spending your time with Office applications and quickly launch that file you were working on last Thursday. It can color-code your messages so the ones from the boss appear in red and the ones from duck salesmen turn up in teal. But trying to figure out just how to do these things, or even simpler ones, can be infuriating. Although the program has been modestly improved since its first release, new users will cry out for a tutorial, a book or, better still, a complete redesign. The program's many capabilities will be overkill for most people, because its quirky, unfinished, inconsistent interface buries them under a mound of puzzling options and tricky gizmos that conceal what you are trying to find. Like its competitors, it fails to shift grunt work from human to machine by learning from what you do. Time and again, Outlook's features fail to work the way you expect them to. Yellow on-screen notes are described as "the electronic equivalent of paper sticky notes," but they disappear from the screen the moment you open something on top of them. The monthly calendar cannot display a week with Sunday first, even if you set up your workweek to begin on that day. And in a throwback to the past, Outlook 98 cannot always close itself when you tell Windows to shut down. You have to do the job for it, sometimes while facing down Windows error messages. You can get along with Outlook 98 if you are willing to work at it, but most users are likely to be more comfortable with simpler email software like Outlook Express and personal information managers like Sidekick or the software that comes with the Palm computer. As something for nothing, Outlook 98 turns out to be too much and not enough. Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: An On-Line Critic Tackles the Big Papers
body: Scott Shuger is paid to do what most readers do free: rant about -- and at -- the nation's major daily newspapers. Every night, working from his home office in Los Angeles, he consumes the next morning's front pages, writing a report of what made news and what didn't, tweaking reporters and editors for missed details and placement of articles. He then dispatches his analysis, simply called "Today's Papers," to the 20,000 subscribers of the electronic magazine Slate. Nonsubscribers can read it free on the magazine's home page. "One of the things he is supposed to do is educate people about how to read the newspaper," said Michael Kinsley, the editor of Slate, which is owned by the Microsoft Corporation.  "It's always interesting that USA Today and The newyork Times have different views about what's going on in the world. One will lead with a story on page one and the other will have it buried on D24. Both of those judgments can't be right." Mr. Shuger worked as a Navy intelligence officer, an editor at The Washington Monthly and a book reviewer for Amazon.com. He said his column was not about what is right or wrong: I'm not trying to preach as much as wonder what the papers are doing," he said. Here are some of his impressions: How he sees the newspapers (The Wall Street Journal, USA Today, The Washington Post, The Los Angeles Times, The newyork Times.) All are very good to excellent papers. The fact of the matter is you don't get everything you need from every one of them. USA Today is the least affected of the papers; it doesn't write for the people who fly business class. It doesn't have the class or money orientation. This is probably one of my most politically incorrect judgments, but I think it's an effective national newspaper. It has something that I'd love to see the other papers pick up on: the routinization of the news. The press is too crisis-oriented, the stories too breathless. Patterns in the way articles are displayed. I don't think the patterns are hard and fast. Some of the differences are clearer than others. USA Today is very good expository reporting, more of a briefing paper. It's rare you pick up a story and don't know what happened. There are many times I've read a newyork Times story where sometimes they're so strong in explanation and context that you actually lose sight of what happened. It's like a wealth of information. That's not the same as burying its lead. The L.A. Times tends to bury its leads. I am likely to go much deeper into an L.A. Times story without knowing what the point of it is. Ten years ago I would have said The Washington Post was demonstrably stronger on domestic political angles. Now, The newyork Times Washington bureau has gotten hip to the nuances of D.C. The L.A. Times, in political stories, isn't much behind. It weaves domestic political elements pretty effectively. Why he feels he is qualified to critique daily newspapers. I've never worked for a daily newspaper. I was on a paper in high school. I used to be in the military, an intelligence officer in the Navy. I had a good job -- I didn't get killed and I learned a lot. I served in aviation, on a carrier overseas. People say you have no idea what the pressures are on a daily reporter. I say I used to brief admirals. What readers say. As soon as I heard the idea for this column, I thought of the morning briefing prepared by the staff in the Pentagon. I knew people would want it if it was done well. There's a base motive: people like to see the media brought down. Readers do really feel like communicating. I've always found letters really interesting. I love knowing the readers can click on my name and send memail. If people write me and they've not understood me, I feel this tremendous need to take the time to explain it to them. A lot of people define things left, right, liberal. I basically ignore people who are ranting at me from a very doctrinal point of view. Graphic   Photo: Scott Shuger at home and work in Los Angeles, immersed in newspapers -- the grist for his mill. (Kim Kulish for The newyork Times)

title: Businesses Explore Cyberauctions
body: When Mark A. Weimer talks about Internet auctions, both delight and frustration play in his voice. For six months, his Del Ray Beach, Fla., company, INXS Inc. -- pronounced "in excess," an apt name for a dealer in surplus and used equipment -- has been selling slow-moving microscopes and accessories, even old gas chromatographs, on an on-line auction run by Labx Technologies Inc. He has cleared about $15,000 for items he had been ready to throw out, and had an absolute ball doing it. "It was such a kick, watching guys electronically beat each other up, raising their bids by $1 a pop," Mr. Weimer said. So why the frustration? Because he cannot forget the items he did discard. "I figure I could have gotten $2,000 each for machines I threw out," he said. "Now, I throw nothing away without checking Labx first." Chalk up another convert to the brave new world of business-to-business Internet auctions. They are already growing common for commodities like oil and gas. And now, a whole new industry is forming around the idea that business people are as likely to bid electronically for machine tools and computer parts as consumers are to bid for sneakers and personal computers. "Auctioneers without Internet auctions will be out of business in five years," said Michael Brader-Araje, chief executive of Open Site Technologies (www.opensite.com), which sells auction software. It sounds self-serving, but the numbers are on his side. Forrester Research Inc., which analyzes the impact of technology, estimates that $8.7 billion worth of business-to-business goods will be auctioned on line this year, growing to $52.6 billion in 2002. The growth is no surprise. This is a low-cost, low-risk business for all sides. Sellers pay nothing if their products do not move. Buyers can stop payment on checks if the goods are not as advertised. And the auctioneer's costs, limited to software and advertising, plummet once it has a solid base of buyers and sellers. Then there is the fun factor. "This is a novel way to buy things that adds real entertainment value to some stodgy industries," said Scott Andrews, president of Sciquest Inc., which will soon auction laboratory equipment on the Net. The list of auctioneers hawking business wares is growing fast. Labx already auctions lab equipment, while Fast Parts Inc. auctions surplus electronic parts. Next Monday, Norman Levy Associates, a huge industrial equipment auctioneer, will hold its first Internet auction. Next month, H. K. Equipment, which sells used vacuum furnaces and other laboratory items, will start auctioning them on the Net. And before year-end, Internet Liquidators International, a consumer cyberauction company, will test two auction formats: one for diverse wares from a single source -- say, a corporate liquidation; the other for similar wares from different vendors -- say, agricultural equipment or used cars. "There's so much custom-made equipment that gets sold for scrap, because no one realizes that it fits perfectly for a project being done half a world away," said Paul Godin, president of Internet Liquidators. Cyberauctions are not problem- free. Although vendors post descriptions and photographs of their goods, bidders are really buying blind. The anonymous nature of most auctions -- bidders show up on the screen as, say, Paddle 7 -- makes it hard for sellers and buyers to gauge negotiating styles or form relationships. And it presumes that all potential buyers are comfortable surfing the Web. "I don't even have a computer, so how could I bid?" asked Charles N. Yanoff, president of Pattern Metals Company, a steel distributor. There are other problems in the wings. Anyone with the software and a Web page can run an auction, and auctioneers worry that fly-by-night operators will crowd the field with shoddily run sales. "Let's face it, Internet software is a dime a dozen," said Bob Kafuto, president of Labx. And the novelty of on-line bidding can attract mischief-makers, who clog the process with bogus bids. Although most auctioneers do a cursory check of each bidder's legitimacy, most acknowledge that a determined prankster can get through. "There's still the small problem of, are the buyers real, will they pay, will they pick up the equipment on time?" said Stuart I. Feldman, director of the I.B.M. Institute for Advanced Commerce. Most cyberauctions work like this: Bidders key in their bids, and are told immediately, either on screen or by email, if their bid is topped. There are official closing times, but the electronic gavel rarely comes down until at least two minutes go by without a bid. At that point, the auctioneer puts the winning bidder in touch with the seller, takes a commission from both, and bows out. But there the similarities end. Some auctions last an hour, some a week. Some auctioneers hold separate auctions for each item; others hold regularly scheduled auctions of assorted items. Still others hold auctions only when they have enough wares to draw a big bidding crowd. At least one, Freemarkets Online, holds reverse auctions -- companies describe what they want to buy, and vendors bid for the contract. "We provide a level field, where a small company gets the same data as General Motors," said Glen Meakem, chief executive of Freemarkets. Kent L. Brittan, vice president for supply management at United Technologies, has bought numerous plastic parts, machined items and the like through Freemarkets. "We've saved at least 10 percent on everything, and we've met suppliers that we'd never have known of," he said. Indeed, since bidders can participate without leaving their desks, and since business cyberauctions often operate round the clock, their potential audience is huge. "When you're holding a live auction at 4 P.M. in Detroit, it's rough for someone in Paris to bid," said Robert Levy, Norman Levy's president. Aficionados of cyberauctions list other pluses: *The auctions let companies push older models off their shelves and off their books. "When we need inventory space, auctions are our first choice," said Steven C. Miles, sales manager of Analtech Inc., a maker of laboratory equipment. *They obviate the need to transport equipment to a live auction. "I'll happily take a lower price for the convenience," said William C. Nagy, president of Technik Machine Tool Inc., which hopes to sell surface grinders at Norman Levy's auction. *They let equipment dealers buy and sell goods without moving them to their own warehouses. "I can buy equipment in Vermont once our auction is up," said Peggy Skelly, a sales representative at H. K. Equipment, in Wilmington, Mass. *They let companies unload excess parts anonymously. "No one wants to tell the world they lost a big order," said Kristine McCusker, marketing manager for Fast Parts. *They help companies that have closed or modernized plants place unneeded tools. "Used-equipment dealers just never give you full value," said Gary Lyons, a plant manager of Chanute Manufacturing Company, which just switched to numerically controlled drills, and will soon auction off its manual ones. Even Mr. Yanoff, the self-described computer illiterate, is putting a metal-forming machine into the Norman Levy auction. He expects to get $65,000 for it. "We don't use it anymore, but I hadn't tried to sell it," he said. "It would be hard to get what it's worth by just advertising locally." Graphic   Photo: William Nagy, president of Technik Machine Tool Inc., hopes to sell surface grinders at an on-line auction. (Frank C. Dougherty for The newyork Times)  Chart: "Where to Go" The number of Web sites offering auctions of industrial and scientific equipment, and of electronic parts, is growing exponentially. Here are a few that are up already, and a few that will soon be.  FastParts Inc., Elmhurst, Ill. Auctions off electronic components, chips, and memory modules. http://www.fastparts.com  Internet Liquidators International, Inc., Toronto Will soon test two auction formats: one for diverse wares from single sources, like corporate liquidations, the other for similar wares -- say, used cars -- from different vendors. http://www.internetliquidators.com  FreeMarkets Online, Pittsburgh,Pa. Runs a buyer's auction -- companies say what they want to purchase, vendors bid for the contract. http://www.freemarkets.com  SciQuest, Inc., Research Triangle Park By fall, will be auctioning scientific equipment. http://www.labdeals.com  Labx Technologies Inc., Winnipeg, Canada Auctions scientific equipment and materials http://www.labx.com  Norman Levy Associates Inc., Southfield, Mich. Will hold its first industrial equipment cyberauction on June 8. http://www.nlainc.com  H.K. Equipment, Wilmington, Mass. Will soon start auctioning used vaccuum furnaces and laboratory equipment. http://www.hkequip.com

title: Creating a Silicon Valley in the Washington Area
body: In the new-media business, there is a palpable sense of regional competition among the centers for Internet commerce and content. Silicon Valley in Northern California, Silicon Alley in newyork and the recently named Digital Coast of greater Los Angeles all lay claim to a share of status as places where start-ups prosper, venture capital flows and the sky's the limit in the digital future. And then there is Washington, and the surrounding area from Baltimore down through northern Virginia. It has no fancy nickname. It does not yet enjoy a hip reputation among the wired set. But it does have more than a thousand Internet-related start-up companies, a generation of technology business experience and growth, and a ready market for digital services in the Federal Government and all the political entities eager to exploit the reach and promise of the Net. And it also has Mario Morino. The 54-year-old is the guiding light and financial patron of an ambitious effort to make the Washington area a model for entrepreneurial success in new media. Mr. Morino has some experience with start-ups. He founded a small software company in northern Virginia, built it relentlessly, and walked away with $80 million when the Legent Corporation was purchased by Computer Associates in 1995. He used the money to start the Morino Institute, which finances programs in youth advocacy and services, entrepreneurship, social networking and community services. In 1995, the Institute founded the Potomac Knowledgeway Project, which aims to promote growth in "knowledge-based" business in the region. Last year, it started a spinoff, the Netpreneur program, which is aimed at building the wired business community by getting digital entrepreneurs together, on line and off. While the Knowledgeway Project is expected to have only a five-year existence, Mr. Morino and his team believe the Netpreneur program can be self-sustaining and lead to a model that can be used throughout the country. All of these efforts have two things in common: they are financed by Mr. Morino to the tune of what he terms "seven figures" a year. And they are all based on Mr. Marino's belief that a newly networked society combined with opportunity for small-business growth can lead to social change. His heady goals for the region include 2,000 new start-up companies, 50,000 new jobs and $2.5 billion in new income. He also hopes to establish "greater Washington as the top U.S. location for knowledge-based companies and entrepreneurial activity." Netpreneur (www.netpreneur.org) sponsors conferences, offers a data base of business plans for companies looking for investors, and plans a full-scale survey of the Washington region's new-media economy, similar to those commissioned by the newyork New Media Association of Silicon Alley. Netpreneur's "Coffee and DoughNets" gatherings bring business people together in informal settings, hooking up start-up companies with potential investors, and large companies with small ones. "I just love the start-ups," Mr. Morino said, adding that the region's big-business past had not encouraged start-ups until recently. "I have tremendous empathy for that kind of person, and I think what I have to offer resonates well with kids in the game right now." The "kids" seem to agree. Mr. Morino's rapid-fire delivery and no-nonsense business advice for start-ups resonate among the small shops popping up from downtown Washington to Reston, Va. "He's great at the end of meetings," said Eric Loeb, 35, co-founder of the Washington-based Net Capitol, a new-media services and applications company that serves public affairs organizations. "It's an impromptu business lesson and it's very compelling, like a little sermon." Mr. Loeb said one particular piece of advice from Mr. Morino -- "your goal is to dominate your niche" -- helped Net Capitol better focus its efforts. Of course, the Washington region has several things going for it besides a patron with deep pockets. For one, it boasts one of the largest concentrations of Internet service providers in the world, companies like UUNet, Digex, America Online, MCI and PSINet. And it has a ready source of customers for Internet design, services and consulting businesses: the Government and its many tentacles. "What's unique about Washington is that we have representatives of every special interest group and every country in the world, and they all want to be on the Web," said Chris Casey, 32, the chief technologist for the Senate Democratic leadership's Technology and Communications Committee. Mr. Casey built the Senate's first World Wide Web page, for Senator Edward M. Kennedy, the Massachusetts Democrat, in 1994, and is the author of a book, "The Hill on the Net: Congress Enters the Information Age." He said Washington's Internet community was relatively tight knit, though geographically dispersed. Michael T. Hernon, 42, chief technology officer for the District of Columbia, agreed. "It's not as organized as in newyork or Boston yet, but it's happening," said Mr. Hernon, who moved to Washington last year after three years as Boston's chief technology officer. "Every major technology company has a presence here, and on the Web development side, there is much more activity than I thought I'd find." Indeed, the Netpreneur program has identified more than 1,000 new Internet-related companies in its data base. Among the companies is Sync, a small Internet broadcasting company based in College Park, Md. It specializes in "Webcasting" (the digital equivalent of sending video live over the Web) and Internet broadcast consulting. In addition, it has produced or sponsored events ranging from Congressional hearings and speeches by Vice President Al Gore and Attorney General Janet Reno to independent films and the mildly controversial "Jenni Show," based on the voyeuristic Jenni Cam, a Web site on which a young woman keeps a camera in her bedroom to capture much of her life, which sometimes includes nudity and sex. Thomas Edwards, president and chief executive of Sync, said that while newyork's new-media sector benefited from having the advertising industry resident in the city, and Los Angeles could claim the entertainment industry, Washington and the surrounding area was experiencing new-media growth because of the Government. "We're already a leading new-media center, and people don't realize it," he said. "It's much harder to find programmers now, people you used to able to get at $40,000, you now can't get for $80,000. That's a sign of real business." Graphic   Photo: Mario Morino, a software entrepreneur in Virginia, is financing youth advocacy programs and the growth of digital businesses in his region. (Carol T. Powers for The newyork Times)

title:
Long Boom or Bust;
A Leading Futurist Risks His Reputation With Ideas on Growth And High Technology
body: Peter Schwartz is a professional marketer of big, brow-furrowing ideas. By 2020, he says, the internal combustion engine will probably have gone the way of the dodo bird as conventional automobiles are replaced by hybrid cars powered by fuel cells that mostly use hydrogen. A telecommunications revolution, Mr. Schwartz believes, is coming even sooner. Thanks to big satellite projects, connections for high-speed Internet, telephone and video will be commonplace in six years or so. The world will be wired, inexpensively. By 2005, teen-agers in villages in developing countries will be chatting on video phones as they surf the Net. By 2010, Mr. Schwartz predicts, breakthroughs in biotechnology and gene therapy may enable science to reverse aging and extend life. The prospect here, he insists, is not merely a prolonged old age but living for decades in one's biological 40's. Yet these are mere ingredients of Mr. Schwartz's biggest idea, which he calls the "Long Boom." Its thesis is that the world is witnessing what Mr. Schwartz calls "the beginnings of a global economic boom on a scale never experienced before," driven by waves of fundamental technological change and free-market economics. The Long Boom, which he sees running through about 2020, is a vision of almost unabashed technological optimism about the future from Mr. Schwartz, a leading futurist and chairman of the Global Business Network, a research and consulting firm. His manifesto first appeared as a cover story last summer in Wired magazine, whose pages generally celebrate the virtues of technology. Ever since, he has found himself at the center of a spirited debate about technology and the future. Bearded, affable and articulate, Mr. Schwartz is a skillful salesman who has won supporters for his ambitious idea, but he has been roundly criticized as well. In March, a loose-knit group calling itself the "Technorealism Project" emerged. Among the tenets proclaimed on its Web site at www.technorealism.org is the assertion, "The Internet is revolutionary, not utopian." Andrew L. Shapiro, a fellow at the Harvard Law School's Center for the Internet and Society and a founder of the Technorealism Project, said, "We're just skeptical of the kind of sheer boosterism that Peter Schwartz is promoting." Mr. Schwartz recently debated the merits of the Long Boom with Daniel Yankelovich, the public opinion analyst and president of Public Agenda, a research organization, at a conference in San Diego. In Mr. Yankelovich's view, the Long Boom betrays a "remarkable naivete" not only about technology but also about the working of market economics. "The market is great at distributing economic goodies," Mr. Yankelovich said, "but it doesn't have all these moral virtues that Peter Schwartz attributes to it." Such reactions, Mr. Schwartz says, are precisely why he wrote the Long Boom. It has provoked thought and, he insists, changed the debate about the future. The Long Boom, he asserts, represents "a better vision of what could be if we make the right choices; it is what I think could and should happen." As a futurist, Mr. Schwartz has impressive credentials. An alumnus of the Stanford Research Institute, now SRI International, he led a planning team at the Royal Dutch/Shell Group in London from 1982 to 1986. One of three possibilities drawn up in 1982 by Mr. Schwartz and his team was that oil prices would collapse. That possibility was taken seriously by Shell's senior management, which piled up cash to prepare. After prices fell precipitously, Shell began a $3.5 billion buying spree in 1986, buying oilfields and locking in a long-term cost advantage over most of its rivals. The Shell legacy gave Mr. Schwartz and four colleagues a head start in attracting corporate clients when they founded the Global Business Network in 1988. "Everybody wanted the Shell magic," he recalled. The Global Business Network, known as GBN, is no ordinary consulting firm. Based in Emeryville, Calif., where it occupies a converted factory in the shadow of the Bay Bridge, GBN is eclectic if not eccentric. Its character is evident in the backgrounds of its five founders. Besides Mr. Schwartz, they are Jay Ogilvy, a former philosophy teacher at Yale University who headed values and life styles research at SRI International; Napier Collyns, who spent 30 years in Shell's planning group; Stewart Brand, creator of the Whole Earth Catalog and a founder of the Well computer network, and Lawrence Wilkinson, former president of Colossal Pictures. Today, GBN is a small but thriving specialist firm. Compared with mainstream consultants like McKinsey & Company or Andersen Consulting, GBN is minuscule. Its revenues are running at $10 million a year, about double the level in 1994, while its staff has also doubled, to 55 people. (McKinsey says it has 4,500 consultants in 81 countries.) GBN has roughly 100 clients, about half of which sent executives to the company's four-day annual conference in San Francisco last month. The client list is as eclectic as the firm, ranging from I.B.M. and AT&T to the Pentagon, the Government of Singapore and the National Education Association. The conference concluded with an advance screening of the Dreamworks SKG movie "Deep Impact," which has since become a box-office hit. GBN worked with Dreamworks on developing the film, and Mr. Schwartz and a few other GBN members are mentioned in the film's credits. The narrative spine of "Deep Impact" is how people behave in the months after they learn that a comet is going to collide with Earth. The movie, in essence, illustrates the fulcrum of scenario building -- a what-if question. And creating scenarios is GBN's specialty. At the San Francisco conference, four scenarios for the next decade were presented as narratives for the participants to read and debate. They ranged from crisis and decline to an equivalent of the Long Boom, all rendered in imaginative detail. In the gloom-and-doom scenario, for example, the year 2000 computer bug and global warming are culprits in the tailspin. The European Union is shattered, the Middle East has water shortages, oil prices surge and inflation is ignited. In 2003, the scenario said, "the Dow plummeted from 10,000 to 6,000 in a matter of months." In Mexico, the economy crumbles, South American drug cartels move in, guerrilla wars flare and refugees flood north. "In 2010," the scenario asserted, "President Wilson sent in the U.S. Army to establish order in Mexico." Certainly provocative and undoubtedly more entertaining than most business reading, but what use is this kind of thing to corporations? Most companies say the GBN scenarios -- whether broad ones, like those presented at the San Francisco conference, or ones tailored for specific industries or nations -- are useful mainly as complementary planning tools. The scenarios are built upon in-depth research of demographic, political and technology trends. Daniel McGrath, a business strategy consultant at I.B.M., said the scenarios then sketched out "causative chains that stretch your imagination and broaden your thinking." GBN tries to broaden its own thinking through a network of about 100 people in diverse fields. They include Francis Fukuyama, the political scientist; Bruce Sterling, a science fiction writer, and Donella Meadows, an environmentalist. Yet the membership roster is heavy with technophiles including Danny Hillis, a computer scientist and research fellow at Walt Disney; Esther Dyson, an author and newsletter publisher, and John Gage, chief scientist at Sun Microsystems. Another GBN member is Kevin Kelly, the executive editor of Wired. Both GBN and Mr. Schwartz personally were original investors in Wired, a fact not mentioned in the magazine when it published Mr. Schwartz's Long Boom article. "It's very incestuous in some ways," Mr. Schwartz allowed. For $35,000 a year, corporate clients get to join the GBN network members on the company's private Web site to discuss all sorts of subjects, from the future of the car to computing's millennium bug. In addition, clients aremailed two books a month, selected by Mr. Schwartz and Mr. Brand. "We've basically solved the problem of executives' reading guilt," Mr. Schwartz observed. Recent selections include "Remaking Eden," about cloning by Lee M. Silver, and "The Commanding Heights," a history of the triumph of free-market policies, by Daniel Yergin and Joseph Stanislaw. GBN has prospered in recent years, partly because so many corporations, observing developments like the end of the cold war to the rise of the Internet, sense that change is accelerating. Divining traits of an uncertain future, more than ever, seems an essential corporate survival skill. But GBN has also done a deft job of marketing its mainstay business of scenario building. "Scenarios have become the leading tool in thinking about the future, and GBN is the best at it," noted Michael Marien, editor of the Future Survey, a monthly newsletter. A central tenet of the discipline, Mr. Schwartz wrote in his 1991 book, "The Art of the Long View," is that "scenarios are not predictions. "It is simply not possible to predict the future with certainty," he wrote. "Rather, scenarios are vehicles for helping people learn." Scenarios are typically presented in groups of three or four, not alone. Yet the Long Boom concept appears to be more a prediction than a scenario. And Mr. Schwartz, planning experts say, is taking a real risk with his reputation by championing the Long Boom. Professionals in the field of forecasting will talk cautiously about reducing uncertainty, while predictions suggest the hucksterish world of crystal balls, soothsayers and shamans. "I think you are moving down a dangerous slope in this business if you become identified with one view of the future," said Paul Saffo, a director for the Institute of the Future, a research organization. Mr. Schwartz acknowledges that risk, but he feels it is worth taking. "I wanted to influence the future," he said. And Mr. Schwartz is an inherent optimist -- a trait reinforced by his personal life and his professional experience. His parents were survivors of Nazi concentration camps. Mr. Schwartz was born in a refugee camp in 1946, outside Stuttgart, Germany, and lived until he was 5 in a Norwegian refugee camp. His family then immigrated to New Jersey, living in one room of a brownstone. His father, Benjamin, a self-trained engineer, quickly became a model of postwar upward mobility, steadily increasing his skills and income. He ended up designing advanced computer systems, and the family moved to a wealthy suburb of Philadelphia. Professionally, Mr. Schwartz said, he has missed trends most often because of a failure to grasp the forces behind positive outcomes. In the early 1980's, he said, he consistently misread the outlook for the American economy because he failed to imagine the entrepreneurial effect of new industries led by the personal computer business. "It was a big miss, and that was a real learning experience for me," he said. Graphic   Photo: Peter Schwartz, chairman of the Global Business Network, has set off a spirited debate about the future. (Jenny Thomas for The New York Times)  Charts: "Some Visions' Peter Schwartz foresees a long boom of growth driven by technology. Here are some of its ingredients:  By 2005, phone and high-speed Internet access for everyone. By 2010, gene therapies to reverse aging. By 2015, simultaneous language translation, made possible by computer chips 100 times more powerful than today's. By 2020, the death of the internal combustion engine. Cars are powered by hydrogen fuel cells.  "Some Stumbles" Though often prescient, Peter Schwartz has also misread the future:  In 1981, he was an author of a book that assumed oil prices were on their way to $85 a barrel. In the early 1980's, he was too gloomy about the prospects for the American economy. He failed to understand the entrepreneurial impact of the PC industry. In 1994, he missed the Mexican financial crisis. He was the host of a conference on Mexico's future a few weeks before, but did not consider the possibility.

title:
Technology;
For Internet stocks, the fall of overvalued companies can hurt strong companies as well.
body: WHEN the stock of a distributor of 30-year-old music soars after it announces that it plans to sell compact disks directly over the Web, there is more at risk than investors' capital. Obviously, the people who bid up the stock of that distributor, K-Tel International, know they are risking their money, let alone any gain, if the current fascination with all things Internet wanes. In the case of K-Tel, for example, that fascination soon wore thin and the stock fell back to much-less-lofty levels. But what many investors may not realize is that the phenomenal stock surges of companies either only remotely associated with the Internet, or those with questionable long-term business capabilities, threaten the underpinnings of the broader Internet industry, as well. Full disclosure: As an investor in privately held Internet companies, I am benefiting along with my colleagues from the run-up in Internet stocks. A number of the companies we've invested in, for example, are in various stages of planning for public offerings. Still others have been sold for a very nice return on investment. But we can also see the powerful -- and often negative -- effect that illogical overbidding can have on the companies seeking capital and their investors. This is not simply a complaint about escalating valuations. Yes, the public's appetite for the Internet has rippled throughout the private side of investing. Yes, I have sat across the table from a 22-year-old chief executive who told me with a straight face that his nine-month-old company was worth $20 million. Annoying as that can be, the fact is the 22-year-old had a point: as long as the stock market holds, you can profit from a high-priced investment when you sell it. The problem is, in a market like the current one, Internet companies are going public that have no business being public. Many recently public companies have substantially weaker balance sheets -- as well as less-promising prospects -- than those of the companies that preceded them. These differences seem lost on many investors. The real problem occurs, of course, when the poor fundamentals catch up with the company and it fails to meet Wall Street's projections for earnings or revenues. Then, stock prices throughout the industry nose-dive, hitting the strong companies as hard as the weak. Of course, the public is not entirely to blame for the valuation roller coaster. In many ways, the public market mania for Internet companies has been fueled by the succession of mind-boggling stock-for- stock transactions. For example, late last year, Microsoft bought a small company called Hotmail for $400 million in stock. Hotmail is a provider of a free, advertising-supported email service. The company's service allows anyone with a standard Web browser to send and retrieve email using a Hotmail account. At the time of the deal, Hotmail said it had more than nine million email accounts. Of course, no computer users are paying for those accounts, many people have multiple accounts, and the ability to aim advertising at those users is a bit unpredictable. But when a company like Hotmail, with no real revenue to speak of, is sold for $400 million, other companies may feel like failures in comparison -- even when they are sold for three to five times the amount their investors put into them. In the pre-Internet days, a return of five times invested capital would have been terrific. But venture capitalists like myself will be judged not only by the absolute dollars we return to our investors, or the internal rate of return on the capital invested, but against our peers, many of whom have seen $2 million investments turn into $1 billion in value in three to five years -- thanks to those runaway stock prices. This unrealistic comparison threatens the foundations of one of the most remarkable constructs of a capitalist economy. The business of venture capital, providing growth financing to entrepreneurs in exchange for equity in fledgling or semi-established companies, can be a superb engine of economic growth, creating an enormous number of jobs and fueling an entrepreneurial spirit essential to a healthy economy. But when a company with no visible means of support, let alone a plan to generate revenue, sells for $400 million, even normally sharp-witted venture capitalists lose their minds. In a mad scramble, they start outbidding each other to provide capital to what they hope will be the next Hotmail. So what? Who gets hurt? The entrepreneurs. I know one chief executive who has worked day and night for three years to build his Internet software company. He has suffered through all of the dysfunction and pain of nurturing a start-up. This year, in the first full year of selling his product, his company is the No. 1 or No. 2 player in the market (depending on which research report you believe), he has more than 1,200 customers and has expected annual revenues of $3.5 million to $4 million. And, he may turn cash flow positive sometime in the fall. Not bad by anyone's measure, right? Wrong. He thinks he has failed. Given the economics of the software industry, the likely exit scenario for this company is a sale to another software company. The likely price will be somewhere just below $50 million. But if that happens, the chief executive told me, he will have failed. And so will his investors. After three or fours years of work, he will walk away with "only" $2 million to $3 million. And the investors will see a return of "only" 200 percent to 300 percent. So to avoid the perceived failure, he will probably choose to hang on longer than he should in pursuit of a market that simply may not be big enough to support his enterprise as a stand-alone company. And he and his investors, instead of cashing in, will sit at the table too long and possibly walk away with nothing. John Doerr, a much better-known and wealthier venture capitalist than I, is often quoted as saying that the Internet represents the greatest legal creation of wealth in history. So far, Internet stocks seem to be proving him right. For my part, I just hope he is not the yardstick against which we will all be measured. Graphic   Drawing (Tom Bloom)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS: ADVERTISING;
A big World Wide Web site by Time Inc. New Media is devoted to the 1998 soccer World Cup.
body: TIME INC. NEW MEDIA is introducing what the company is calling its first big worldwide on-line project, a Web site devoted to the 1998 soccer World Cup. The site, which went up last week, is being presented under the aegis of Time magazine; the home page of the site (www.time.com/worldcup) carries the logo "Time Reports World Cup '98." Four multinational advertisers have agreed to sponsor the site: the Hewlett-Packard Company, the American computer marketer; Nokia, the Finnish telecommunications company; the Dutch company Royal Philips Electronics N. V., and Varig Brazilian Airlines. The Web site is intended to offer computer users comprehensive coverage of the tournament, which will take place in France from June 10 to July 12. Content will include scores, features, analysis and historical highlights. There will also be links to the home pages of the 32 participating teams and the 10 cities where the 64 matches will be played. The project is emblematic of the increasingly ambitious efforts by marketers to capitalize on the fervent international interest in the World Cup, which is the quadrennial championship competition of the world's most popular sport. "The World Cup is the Olympics, the N.F.L. and the N.B.A. all rolled into one monthlong event," said John Voelcker, director for electronic custom publishing at Time Inc. New Media in newyork, a unit of Time Warner Inc. "It's a project we can do with a built-in appeal to everyone in the world." Along with the Time site sponsors, the advertisers striving to become closely identified with the 1998 tournament include the Coca-Cola Company, Electronic Data Systems, Mastercard International, Nike Inc. and Reebok International Ltd. For instance, Coca-Cola and its bottlers will spend an estimated $200 million on advertising and marketing campaigns -- about what they spent during the 1996 Summer Olympics. "This is the first time we have done anything like this," Dennis de Poorter, Internet coordinator for Philips in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, said of his company's participation in the site. "Being a main sponsor of the World Cup itself, we also wanted to provide all lovers of the game good coverage via the Internet," he added. "Sponsoring this, from our perspective, helps to advocate our 'Let's make things better' theme line," which appears in advertising for Philips. The Time Web site is also indicative of the growing ardor among worldwide media titans in developing interactive communications aimed at sports fans, who are considered among the most ardent and involved Netizens. Advertisers are particularly keen on finding ways to reach sports fans because many of them are younger men, who typically watch less television than other demographic groups. "The Internet is the most global medium," Mr. Voelcker said. "If any event makes sense for the Internet, it's the World Cup." Among the media powerhouses with Web sites devoted to sports are the CBS Corporation, with CBS Sports Line (www.sportsline.com); the Walt Disney Company, with ESPN Sports Zone (www.espn.com or www.sportszone.com), and the News Corporation, with Fox Sports Online (www.foxsports.com). Time Warner already has a Web site dedicated to sports, CNNSI, (www.cnnsi.com), which teams up the CNN cable television network and Sports Illustrated magazine. The decision was made to present the World Cup site under the Time name because of its worldwide circulation and recognition, said Graham Cannon, communications director at Time Inc. New Media, compared with the lesser global presence of Sports Illustrated. Sports Illustrated and CNN are "American-centric," he added, whereas Time Inc. New Media wanted a "global perspective" for the site so that "a Brazilian, a South Korean, a Canadian, can each get what they see as unbiased coverage." That is also why the site is being branded as a Time project rather than a project of the Pathfinder Network (www.pathfinder.com), the aggregate World Wide Web site of Time Inc. magazines like Entertainment Weekly, Fortune, Money, People and Time. Mr. Cannon and Mr. Voelcker valued the cost of the sponsorship for the four advertisers at $500,000. There are also promotions related to the site. For example, Hewlett-Packard emblazoned the U.R.L., or address, of the site on five million CD-ROM's distributed in Europe. "We hope this serves as a prototype for other, similar projects," Mr. Voelcker said, "albeit you don't get a World Cup every six months."

title: Defendant In Internet Torture Case Gets 15 Years
body: Ending a trial that gained attention because the victim met the defendant on the Internet, a State Supreme Court judge sentenced Oliver Jovanovic to a minimum of 15 years in prison for kidnapping and sexually abusing a young woman he met in a computer chat room. After a three-week trial that ended in April, a Manhattan jury found that Mr. Jovanovic, 31, had imprisoned the young woman and tortured her over two days in November 1996. The defense had claimed that the encounter between the two was consensual. Yesterday, Justice William A. Wetzel of State Supreme Court in Manhattan said that Mr. Jovanovic, a Columbia University graduate student, had a sense of superiority and believed that "nothing in the world could stand in the way of his intellect and its promise." "The defendant now must live a life in which his intellect is not a particularly prized commodity, his academic achievements of no great value, and his relationships will be face to face, not mediated by the Internet," Judge Wetzel said. "He will have to look people in the eye and let them know who and what he is, day to day. His exploration of the nature of good and evil will be practical, not philosophical." Judge Wetzel sentenced Mr. Jovanovic to 15 years to life in prison for kidnapping, along with concurrent sentences for lesser charges including assault and sexual abuse. Mr. Jovanovic had faced a maximum sentence of 25 years to life in prison. Mr. Jovanovic, extremely pale and dressed in a blue suit, made a brief statement before the sentencing. "I am innocent," Mr. Jovanovic said. "I could not plead guilty to something I did not do." The young woman, who was 20 at the time and attended Barnard College, testified that she agreed to go to dinner with Mr. Jovanovic after she had met him over the Internet and after extended correspondence by email. The woman, whose identity has been withheld because of the nature of the crime, testified that after bringing her to his Washington Heights apartment, Mr. Jovanovic tied her to a futon frame and tortured her for more than 20 hours. During several days of testimony and cross examination, the young woman said Mr. Jovanovic bit her, burned her with wax and struck her with a baton. At the sentencing yesterday, Gail Heatherly, the prosecutor, praised the woman's courage and said she agreed to testify because she knew that "Oliver Jovanovic was going to do this to someone else." "This is a very dangerous person," Ms. Heatherly told Judge Wetzel before the sentencing. Ms. Heatherly said prosecutors were not allowed to introduce email from Mr. Jovanovic's computer during the trial. She said the email, and other evidence, showed that Mr. Jovanovic was a "controlling, manipulative sexual sadist." Jack Litman, the defense lawyer, told Judge Wetzel that the defense was also prevented from introducing evidence during the trial and said he would appeal the case. "What occurred on that night was a consensual activity between two consenting adults," Mr. Litman said. During sentencing, Judge Wetzel criticized Mr. Jovanovic's supporters, defense lawyers and some members of the news media. "If there is anything unique about this case, it is the fact that each and every witness, each and every assistant district attorney involved in the case, as well as many others, has been the object of unwarranted, vicious, personal attacks," he said. "No witness went unscathed, whether it was the victim, a detective, an eyewitness, or even a medical examiner." During the trial, Judge Wetzel, who kept a tight rein on proceedings, frequently clashed with Mr. Litman, who is noted for his aggressive defense tactics. Yesterday, the judge criticized the defense for conduct inside and outside the courtroom. "Criminal cases should be tried in a courtroom, not on the steps of the courthouse, not at press conferences, and not on the Internet," he said. "While some would expect this behavior to influence the sentencing judge, I can assure you, Mr. Jovanovic, that true to my oath I have not taken it into account in determining the appropriate sentence in this case."
