title: Head of German Web Sentenced for Pornography
body: A judge in Bavaria sentenced the former head of Compuserve Deutschland to two years in jail on charges of spreading pornography, but suspended the sentence. It was the first time in Germany that the manager of a provider of Internet access had been held legally responsible for images reached through its service. The manager, Felix Somm, was indicted in April 1997 on 13 counts of distributing pornography involving children and animals in 1995 and 1996. The indictment raised an outcry among advocates of free expression and among experts who argued that it was technically impossible to block access to the material. Legislation approved after the indictment largely exempts providers from legal responsibility for material beyond their control. Under those laws, Mr. Somm's supporters said, it would have been difficult to bring him to trial. Indeed, even in Mr. Somm's case, both the defense and the prosecution in Munich argued today in favor of his acquittal. But the judge, Wilhelm Hubbert, responded, "Even on the Internet, there can be no lawless zones." German authorities have set up police units to seek out Web material they consider to be illegal, including child pornography, bestiality, replication of Nazi symbols and material deemed to "endanger youth," like violent games. But because many such sites are managed from other countries, they have had no recorded success. The ruling today made little immediate difference in the accessibility of pornographic sites by German computer users. One computer operator said he had been able to obtain sexual material involving children and animals through a variety of providers today.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
MCI to Sell Wholesale Internet Unit to Cable and Wireless
body: The MCI Communications Corporation announced yesterday that it had agreed to sell its wholesale Internet business to Cable and Wireless P.L.C. for $625 million in cash. The sale was widely perceived as an attempt to placate antitrust regulators who are reviewing the planned $37 billion acquisition of MCI by Worldcom Inc. But it was also a reflection of just how testy relations between MCI and the Justice Department have become. Along with the European Commission, the Justice Department is evaluating Worldcom's acquisition of MCI primarily with an eye toward the power a combined MCI Worldcom would wield in the Internet industry. Worldcom's Uunet unit is the largest provider of Internet service, and MCI has a significant presence in cyberspace. Ever since it was reported last week that MCI had solicited bids in the $500 million range for the Internet unit, it has been clear that regulators are demanding that MCI and Worldcom sell part of their combined Internet business as a condition of approval for their merger. But executives involved in yesterday's announcement said the deal between MCI and Cable and Wireless had been sealed even before news of the solicitation first emerged. The executives said MCI had explained the deal to lawyers and economists at the Justice Department and had waited for the officials to indicate whether the sale to Cable and Wireless would allay the Government's antitrust concerns. That indication was never given. Instead, Justice Department officials told MCI that they could not evaluate the effect of the Cable and Wireless deal without discussing it with MCI's competitors, the executives said. That concept was unacceptable to MCI, so the company went ahead and announced the deal yesterday. The Justice Department said yesterday only that it was still considering the Worldcom-MCI deal and that the sale to Cable and Wireless would be part of that consideration. MCI, which was built on confronting regulators, used yesterday's announcement as a pre-emptive strike against the Justice Department. The company has appeared to grow increasingly frustrated with the department's handling of the merger. "They have explicitly refused to explain their reasoning about the Internet backbone issues," a person close to yesterday's deal said. But the Justice Department did explain one important thing. Department officials told MCI that any sale of Internet assets to companies that already had a big presence in the Internet business would fail to alleviate the antitrust concerns, people close to the talks between the department and MCI said yesterday. The Justice Department saw MCI's willingness to sell part of its Internet business as an opportunity to increase competition generally in the cyberspace industry. The department's thinking held that selling MCI's Internet units to established carriers would do little to shake up the competitive landscape. As big Internet companies, the GTE Corporation and the Sprint Corporation were essentially anathema to the Justice Department, people close to the talks said. The AT&T Corporation, which is trying to join the top rank of Internet providers, "was in a gray area," one person said. None of the three were invited to bid for the unit that Cable and Wireless agreed to buy. Executives close to yesterday's announcement said that MCI would have liked to explore selling the unit to British Telecommunications P.L.C., its erstwhile merger partner, but they said that MCI feared that such a deal could have appeared improper. Worldcom has already agreed to pay British Telecom more than $7 billion in cash for its stake in MCI when Worldcom's acquisition of MCI is completed. The Williams Companies and IXC Communications Inc., two new but well-financed long-distance carriers, were also bidders for the unit. For MCI's purposes, however, Cable and Wireless was in some ways the perfect partner for the deal. Cable and Wireless, based in London, is already a big long-distance carrier in the unitedstates and an even bigger telecommunications presence overseas; the companies can argue that MCI's Internet assets are going to a company that can use them. But Cable and Wireless is not so strong that it could threaten MCI's business. And, as a bonus, Cable and Wireless is a European company, which could help assuage European regulators. AT&T declined to comment on the deal yesterday. Sprint and GTE described it as inadequate to remove antitrust concerns. The unit that MCI agreed to sell to Cable and Wireless provides wide pipes to cyberspace to more than 1,300 smaller Internet service providers. GTE was disappointed that MCI did not also agree to sell its unit that provides Internet service to residential customers and businesses. Shares of MCI climbed $1.40625 yesterday, to $53.9375; Worldcom rose 93.75 cents, to $45.625.

title: FOOTLIGHTS
body: NEWS Ca Change The Comedie Francaise may trace its origins to 1680, but that doesn't mean it can't adapt to the age of the Internet. Beginning next month, the troupe, the state theater of France, will maintain an English-language Web site where browsers will be able to read the history of the company and to reserve tickets. The address will be http://www.comedie-francaise.fr. Troubled Times In the final years of Frederic Chopin's life, one of his closest friends and confidants was Count Woychek Grzymala, a Polish emigre who lived as a dilettante in Paris. To him, Chopin wrote of his love for George Sand, the tuberculosis that was to take his life, his travels and his distaste for his life in London. "I have to go around in society circles every evening until late," he wrote. "I am not strong enough for such a life. If only it brought money." On June 26, at Sotheby's newyork, 14 of these handwritten letters will be sold at auction. Sotheby's estimates that they will fetch $250,000.  Onstage When the winners of this year's Tony Awards are announced on June 7 at Radio City Music Hall, they will receive their honors from presenters including Helen Hunt, Alec Baldwin, Marisa Tomei, Nathan Lane, Angela Lansbury, Annette Bening, Liam Neeson and Bebe Neuwirth. With Rosie O'Donnell as the host, a dozen awards will be handed out in ceremonies broadcast on CBS from 9 to 11 P.M., including live production numbers from seven nominated musicals. Another 10 awards will be announced between 8 and 9 P.M., when PBS broadcasts "Broadway '98: Launching the Tony Awards," a look back at highlights of the 1997-98 season. That program will include scenes from various productions, film of Paul Simon at work on "The Capeman" and interviews with Tony Award nominees like Julie Taymor, Terrence McNally and Brian Stokes Mitchell.  In Harmony From the earliest days of movies, music has been the ideal accompaniment. At 8 P.M. tomorrow at Alice Tully Hall, music will be in the forefront of that happy pairing when the Concordia Orchestra presents "A Night at the Movies -- A Montage of Classic Hollywood and Music." While films as diverse as the romantic "Humoresque," the gritty "On the Waterfront" and the Tom and Jerry cartoon "Sufferin' Cats" are projected on a screen behind the ensemble, Marin Alsop will lead the Concordia in a performance of their scores with the violinist Nadja Salerno-Sonnenberg, the pianist Leslie Stifelman and the vocalist Janis Siegel as soloists. The music is by such composers as Dvorak, Wagner, Rimsky-Korsakov, Bizet, Franz Waxman, Cole Porter, George Gershwin, Richard Rodgers and Leonard Bernstein.   LAWRENCE VAN GELDER Graphic   Photos

title:
LIBRARY/WEB-SITE SOFTWARE;
Templates With Humor And Beauty
body: NET OBJECTS FUSION 3 Net Objects; $295; Windows 95 and NT, Macintosh.) IF professional Web developers were ever to imagine themselves as Picassos, passionate about creating something new in cyberspace each day, then Net Objects Fusion 3 would be not only the palette and brush but an extension of the artists' thoughts as well. Of course, few Web designers would admit using a prefabricated template on a site, but the magnificence of the designs included on Fusion 3 indicates the care and precision with which the program was developed. The templates -- there are almost 60 -- are beauties, showcasing the distinct art and marketing value that a well-designed page can offer consumers and businesses alike. (An update of the Mac version will be available later this year.) The templates include the humorous Joe's Diner, with bacon-strip-shaped buttons to click, and the funky, tastefully primitive Surf's Up site, with its surfer hanging 10. Fusion 3 shows what is possible -- and what will amaze -- on a well-composed site. Of course, depositing all this information onto a hard disk requires about 100 megabytes of free space. Fusion 3 is not, however, a bloated program with useless features. Its blue tool bar offers you various views of your site-in-progress. In Site View, you plan and create the site's overall architecture. In Page View, you lay out individual pages and add content. In Style View, you create and manipulate the site's text, banners and buttons. In Publish View, you can generate HTML code and upload your site to the Web server. With Fusion 3, HTML programmers can generate what Net Objects calls Everywhere HTML, so every piece of code will look the same in every version of Internet Explorer and Netscape Navigator. It also allows clean, top-notch production of DHTML-based pop-up menus and animated navigation controls. Various buttons let you add content like pictures, video and database records, but some of these buttons are hard to find on the screen, making you hunt for them. Obviously, a more demanding program like Fusion 3 requires more effort. The program comes with two hefty manuals, separate HTML editor software, a calling card-like tech-support card that offers only three free calls to the company, and a demo version of Bazaar Analyzer, which lets you track how people use your site and how they move once they are on your stretch of cyberspace. Fusion 3 is worth the effort; it is satisfying software for the intermediate consumer and the pro as well.

title:
LIBRARY/WEB-SITE SOFTWARE;
Tools to Help You Stake a Claim on the Web
body: AS the World Wide Web threatens to become as beguilingly popular as television, more viewers are being captivated by the slick presentation and intriguing animation on sites like Hotwired and Shockrave (at www.hotwired. com and www.shockrave.com). And because the Web is still a do-it-yourself medium, many might start to think, "Gee, I want to do that, too." Making a web site can be exhilarating, like creating your own magazine or making your own movie. There are now dozens of Web-site development tools, ranging from products for simple personal sites to products for the spectacular, data-rich sites for Fortune 500 corporations. As is the case with many profitable software niches, upgrades seem to arrive daily. For professionals, the cost of a full tool box rife with extravagant software can reach into the thousands of dollars. For the inspired amateur, three of the four products reviewed here will hold your hand through the process. They are similar to prefab houses: you choose a plan from the models each program offers, then add your own touches: you don't even have to mess around with programming languages if you do not care to. The easiest software to use is priced under $100 and allows you to post a functional Web site in less than a few hours. For slicker pages or pages with animation, you will need to learn some programming languages, like HTML (hypertext markup language), Dynamic HTML (DHTML) or Java, and to apply what you have learned in the more complex Web design programs like Dreamweaver. Sites like Web Monkey (www.webmonkey.com) and Project Cool (www.projectcool.com) offer design tips for those who have mastered programming basics. Just be patient: after all, you learned how to use Windows 95. You can learn this, too. Whatever your level of experience, follow this simple rule: Before you begin designing, outline what kind of information you want to put on the Web. You will also need your own acre in cyberspace to build on; many Internet service providers offer sites. Once you have designed and built your site, you can upload it to the Web. The four software packages reviewed here were tested on a 300-megahertz Pentium II machine with 64 megabytes of RAM and an 8-gigabyte hard drive. But all the programs will run with a lower-end Pentium 90 processor and 32 megabytes of RAM. The good news is that all the makers of these programs offer free trial versions, downloadable from their Web sites. These versions expire after 30 days -- 45 days for Microsoft Front Page 98 -- but they give you time to decide whether a tool suits your needs. Graphic   Photo. (Milan Trenc)

title: Lucent Extends Its Reach to Internet Technology
body: Extending its reach further beyond the traditional telecommunications equipment industry, Lucent Technologies Inc. yesterday announced a new set of products that transmit digital information using Internet technology rather than older network systems. The announcement pushed Lucent's share price up $2.625, or 3.8 percent, to $72.375. One of the main trends in the high-technology industry is the convergence of voice and data networks. Companies including Lucent and Northern Telecom of Canada, which have thrived as builders of traditional phone systems, are expanding into the business of data networking. Conversely, data networking giants including Cisco Systems Inc. are developing technologies to transmit voice conversations over advanced data networks. Many analysts and industry executives believe that networks built around Internet technology can be more efficient than older networks, for both voice and data traffic. While traditional networks in essence force different streams of information to stay within their own digital lanes, networks based on Internet technology allow packets of information to switch lanes in search of faster paths to their destinations. "If there has been a question mark raised in people's mind over the past several years, it's been, 'Can Lucent get with the new program, get with the set of revolutionary changes that are happening in the industry?' " said Carleton S. Fiorina, president of Lucent's unit that sells products to big communications carriers. "What this announcement says is, 'Yes, we get it.' " Lucent announced two sets of products yesterday. One product uses Internet technology essentially to replicate an advanced telephone switch, allowing carriers to combine data and voice traffic. Northern Telecom, Lucent's main rival, announced a similar product last week. "Lucent probably has a broader product line with this announcement, and Nortel are really the only people who are close," said Michael Arellano, an analyst with Degas Communications Group, a high-technology consulting firm in newyork. The second product announced by Lucent is meant to route Internet information between different points at high speeds and appears aimed at competitors like Cisco. Lucent said its new product could transmit 2.5 gigabits of information, or the equivalent of about 70 volumes of an encyclopedia, a second. Cisco says it will begin shipping a 2.5 gigabit Internet switch in the third quarter. Ms. Fiorina said Lucent's new Internet products would become generally available in the third quarter or early in the fourth quarter.

title: Microsoft Gives A Freer Hand To Gateway
body: Gateway Inc. offered yesterday a glimpse of the future that the Government is seeking in its antitrust suit against the Microsoft Corporation: more freedom for personal computer makers, and less control by Microsoft over precisely what people see on their computer screens. After months of prodding, Gateway, a large personal computer maker, was able to gain through negotiations the kind of freedom the Government wants to impose by law. Microsoft relented only after the Justice Department became curious. Indeed, Microsoft's resistance to Gateway's requests until two weeks ago figures into the Government's suit, in depositions Justice Department investigators took from Gateway executives. Still, Gateway finally got approval to make a few changes in the Microsoft-ordained regimen for how users move from its Windows operating system out onto the Internet. To do that, Microsoft altered its contract with Gateway, easing the screen restrictions. And yesterday, Gateway demonstrated the result of its new freedoms -- including the ability to offer users an equal choice between Microsoft's Internet Explorer software for browsing the Internet or the rival Navigator from the Netscape Communications Corporation. That choice appears one click away from the start-up Windows screen for Gateway owners who have signed up for the company's Internet access service, gateway.net. "Microsoft allowed us to do this, but we don't think we should have to ask permission every time we want to make some minor software modification," said Ted Waitt, the chairman of Gateway. "Windows is an operating system, not a religion." The Justice Department is intent on loosening Microsoft's contract restrictions and giving personal computer makers more freedom to determine what appears on screens of the machines they make. In its antitrust case filed last week, the Government argued that empowered personal computer makers, once freed from Microsoft's shackles, would work to foster increased competition in the markets for Internet software, shopping and entertainment. They will do this, according to the Government's theory, on behalf of consumers. But so far, most PC makers -- all of whom remain dependent on Microsoft's industry-standard software -- have been ambivalent about the new powers they would inherit if the Government wins its antitrust suit. Lewis E. Platt, chairman of the Hewlett-Packard Company, a major PC maker, said, "If we get more freedom, that will be fine. If we don't that will be fine. We have a very close relationship with Microsoft." Microsoft executives said that the Gateway experience was proof that contrary to the Government's claims, the computer makers that distribute Windows have plenty of freedom. "We're flexible with the PC makers and we have been for some time," said Rob Bennett, a group product manager for Windows. The essential issue for Microsoft, the company said, is to make sure that the essential look-and-feel of Windows is consistent. To accommodate Gateway, Microsoft did have to revise its contract with the company. But the freedom Gateway wanted stopped short of asking for a layer of software that covered the main Windows screen. These so-called "shell" screens were offered by some PC makers until a few years ago, when Microsoft tightened its contract restrictions, industry executives say. Microsoft, industry executives say, feared that the shells could undermine the value of Windows by becoming an "alternative interface" that users see first and could be used to start programs like word processors, spreadsheets and games. In 1994, one industry executive said, Compaq had the consulting firm, McKinsey & Company, study the potential for shell programs -- a development that alarmed William H. Gates, the Microsoft chairman, when he heard of it, the executive said. With the rise of the Internet in the last couple of years, the business potential -- and threat to Microsoft -- of an alternative interface increased sharply, either as a shell provided by a PC maker or a browser like Netscape's Navigator. The personal computer has become the means people use to the new markets of Internet commerce. And much of the Justice Department's case centers on how Microsoft fought this perceived threat from Netscape. One step Microsoft had taken in the last couple of years, the Justice Department contended, was to tighten its contract restrictions on PC makers. In its court papers, the Justice Department stated that these restrictions thwart the PC makers' "abilities to differentiate their products by highlighting competing Internet software or service offerings, as they did before Microsoft imposed its screen restrictions." Then, citing a deposition taken on April 30, from James Von Holle, director of software products at Gateway, the Government said the company "wishes to define its own Internet software and service partners and arrange direct business relationships with them in order to offer its customers additional options. Microsoft's restrictions, however, have prevented it from meeting what it perceives to be consumer demand." On the eve of settlement talks between Microsoft and the Justice Department that began on May 15, Microsoft informed Gateway that it was willing to grant Gateway the freedoms it needed to make yesterday's announcement. "They were asking for flexibility, but not an alternative interface," one Microsoft executive said. The settlement talks broke down on May 16, over the issue of Microsoft's control of its main screen. The Government said it agreed to the settlement talks because Microsoft said it was willing to discuss control of the desktop screen. Yes, replies Microsoft, but never to the point of allowing alternative shells that hide the Windows desktop. Even if the Government does win its suit, it remains uncertain how much the desktop would change. "Most customers want PC manufacturers to be able to make some modifications, but they do not want a huge variation in the desktop from one PC company to the next," said Richard Shaffer, principal of Technologic Partners, a research firm. "Good, bad or indifferent, Windows is the standard that people are familiar with and they don't want to relearn another desktop language."

title: Wanted: Web-Site Addresses That Won't Twist the Tongue
body: IT'S a question of syllables. The letter W has too many -- three times the number of every other letter, to be precise. And that's three too many for Dave Yost. Mr. Yost is on a quixotic mission to simplify perhaps the most inelegant aspect of the Web: its addresses. Inelegant in terms of the spoken word, that is. Spitting out http:// www.youraddress.com is annoying at best. Listening to radio announcers recite a U.R.L. -- the abbreviation for uniform resource locator, as Web addresses are called -- can lead to violence. Most people drop the http:// when saying a Web address. But Mr. Yost, a software designer and classical pianist in Los Altos, Calif., isn't satisfied with that shortening. He despises www, an abbreviation that, he takes pains to point out, has three times as many syllables as the phrase it stands for -- World Wide Web. Mr. Yost has been running a one-man campaign to get sites to replace their U.R.L.'s "double-you-double-you-double-you dot" with "web-dot," as in web.youraddress.com. By doing that, Mr. Yost is addressing a linguistic frustration that dates from the Web's early days, when various pundits suggested triple-ya, trip-dub and even wuh-wuh-wuh as preferred pronunciations of www. "I'm passionate about improving the user experience in software -- and all other human endeavors," Mr. Yost said. "We really don't have to take this lying down." The home page of the Webdot Campaign (web.yost.com/misc/ webdot.html) lists about 60 examples of sites using web-dot addresses, typically in addition to, rather than replacing, their www addresses. These include schools (web.mit.edu, web.reed.edu) as well as companies (web.aimnet.com, web.games4girls. com). And there are signs that Mr. Yost is gaining ground: a spot check with two major search engines found 150,000 to 200,000 U.R.L.'s that begin with web-dot. Does a web-dot address work the same way as a traditional one? Yes, if your Internet service provider is willing to allow it to act as an alias, though it might cost you extra. Mr. Yost's page does mention one other alternative to web-dot: aaa, as in aaa.wraithspace.com. But another check using the two search engines revealed fewer than 1,000 pages using it. Note that "triple a" has three syllables. One of Mr. Yost's favorite examples of a web-dot address is that of the publisher W. W. Norton & Company (web.wwnorton.com), for whom his addressing method appears tailor made. Still, Kirsten Miller, the Webmaster at Norton, said the company no longer advertised that U.R.L., even though visitors would reach the site if they typed it in. "We made the change simply because it's the standard, and we wanted to make it easy for people to find us by trying a conventional domain name," she said. The primary Norton U.R.L. is now www.wwnorton.com -- in Mr. Yost's words, "a true travesty." Graphic   Photo: Dave Yost, a computer and music fan, wants Web addresses that sing. (Steve Castillo for The newyork Times)

title: You Can't Always Judge a Domain by Its Name
body: AS one might expect, the Web site www.ringlingbrothers.com featured stories of elephants, but it did not focus on the amazing and heartwarming feats of circus pachyderms. Instead it claimed that Ringling Brothers and Barnum & Bailey Circus degrades, chains up and even hastens the death of elephants. That was because the site was posted not by the circus but by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, an animal rights group that had registered the Ringling domain name in February expressly to lodge its protest. But in early May, PETA folded its tent. Faced with a threat of a trademark infringement lawsuit from Feld Entertainment, the parent of Ringling Brothers, PETA surrendered the domain to the circus. (The circus's site is www.ringling.com.) PETA had reason to fear a trial's outcome. In a growing number of disputes, courts and regulators have forced individuals and organizations to hand over domains to major corporations that own trademarks bearing their name. Almost overnight, it has become clear that big commercial interests dominate the domain game. The shift may seem technical, but it underscores a debate that goes to the very heart of how the Internet will be defined. The medium that began as a wondrous new form of mass communication has also morphed into a medium of mass commercialism. And that means the two interests may increasingly conflict. "Courts as a whole are bending over backward to respect trademark rights," said Sally M. Abel, a lawyer in Palo Alto, Calif., and a member of the board of directors of the International Trademark Association. The courts, she added, "appear to have accepted that this is a commercial medium." But not everyone is going along with the program. A few organizations and individuals are registering domain names to make political statements, contending that the foundation of the Internet is communication, not just commerce. They argue that courts are eviscerating the true essence of cyberspace. "The Internet is the greatest form of communication ever created," said Mikki Barry, the president of the Domain Name Rights Coalition, which advocates the rights of small domain-name holders. "These people want to make the Internet safe for trademark holders to the detriment of free speech and communication." On the Web site, PETA had posted a page stating it was not affiliated with the circus. It then detailed instances in which the Government has found Ringling out of compliance with animal care regulations. Ingrid Newkirk, president of PETA, said the idea was to counter the circus's own claims that it has an "unblemished" record regarding its treatment of animals, noting that the circus has been accused of numerous violations by the unitedstates Department of Agriculture. Ms. Newkirk was unapologetic about luring people with the ringlingbrothers.com domain name. Citing trademark law, Ringling officials countered that while PETA may have a right to express its views, it should not be allowed to confuse people and "deceive" them about the nature of the site. The company accused PETA of using Ringling's "good name" to attract people to the site. Ultimately, PETA did not concede the point, but said its official position was that it couldn't afford the court fight. PETA is continuing its effort at another Web site, www.circuses.com. Two recent court decisions indicate that for PETA, the money wouldn't have been well spent anyway. One case took place last year when a Federal judge ordered Richard L. Bucci, the host of the "Catholic Radio" program broadcast from Syracuse, N.Y., to stop using the site address www.planned parenthood.com to send his anti-abortion message. What made the case so clear-cut, said trademark lawyers, was that Mr. Bucci presented the site as the Planned Parenthood Federation of America home page. Trickier issues were posed by the Web site www.jewsforjesus.org, which was posted by Steve Brodsky, an Orthodox Jew from New Jersey. Mr. Brodsky's site stated plainly that it was not affiliated with Jews for Jesus, a religious organization that teaches Jesus is the Messiah to Jews. The site said, "The answers you seek already exist within your faith," and was linked to a site for an organization called Jewish Outreach. "This is false advertising," said David N. Brickner, the executive director for Jews for Jesus, which is based in San Francisco. Mr. Brickner said the site misled potential supporters of Jews for Jesus, which uses the Web address www.jews-for-jesus.org. "We believe people who are looking for us should be able to find us without confusion," he added. Judge Alfred J. Lechner Jr. of the unitedstates District Court for the District of New Jersey agreed. In March of this year, Judge Lechner issued an opinion saying that Mr. Brodsky had "intended to intercept, through the use of deceit and trickery, the audience sought by" the religious organization. The ruling is being appealed. For the time being, Jews for Jesus is using the jewsforjesus.org domain name. To forestall similar problems, it has spent $1,000 to register 10 other domains, including jews4jesus.org and jewsforjesus.net. Some legal observers contend that the courts and corporations are using trademark law, which is meant to balance commercial interests, in a fundamentally noncommercial dispute. These critics note, for example, that Mr. Brodsky was not selling a product on his site but was expressing an idea and spurring a debate. Furthermore, the critics say that visitors to his site would have been misled only momentarily. The court disagreed, stating that a sophisticated Internet user is not necessarily sophisticated about religious organizations and that such "a user may find his or her way to the defendant Internet site and then be confused." In their appeal, Mr. Brodsky's lawyers said simply that the site does not require sophistication to figure out but that "it requires the ability to read." They are calling for Congress to intervene. "People are using trademark law to stifle free expression, which wasn't meant to be," said Ronald D. Coleman, a lawyer with Pitney Hardin Kipp & Szuch, a New Jersey firm that represents Mr. Brodsky. "Congress should step in and say so." The PETA case is paradoxical because the group was once on the other side of a domain name dispute. In 1996, the organization petitioned Network Solutions Inc., a governing body for the registration of domain names, to prevent a man named Michael Doughney from using the domain peta.org, which he registered to publish his parody "People Eating Tasty Animals." Network Solutions took the domain name from Mr. Doughney and now precludes both him and PETA from using it. The punch line: Mr. Doughney was so upset that he founded the Domain Name Rights Coalition, the organization now speaking out on PETA's behalf against Ringling. While these cases do illustrate a controversial new wrinkle, not all the recent domain conflicts are as ideological. Many corporations and organizations have commandeered Web sites or threatened lawsuits against domain name holders. The reasoning is that when people surf on the Internet, they should be able to find a famous corporation or product easily by typing in the logical domain name. "A common way for people to find out about the company is to assume that a domain name is the same as the trademark name," said David Quinto, a lawyer for the label-making company Avery Dennison. The company was recently successful when it sued to retrieve avery.net and dennison.net, both of which had been registered by a Canadian entrepreneur who was licensing the domain names to individuals with the last name Avery. Graphic   Photo: A NEW REFUGE -- An animal rights group posted this site after it lost a court battle.

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: Supporting Cast Figures In Microsoft Complaint While Netscape, Microsoft's rival in producing Internet browser software, is mentioned scores of times in the Government's antitrust complaint against Microsoft, and the Justice Department's case focuses mainly on the browser market, another bitter Microsoft competitor, Sun Microsystems, makes a few cameo appearances in the court papers filed last Monday. Quoting internal Microsoft email messages tinged with profanity and hostile intent, the filings discuss Microsoft's plans for blunting the success of Sun's Java programming language.  Page D4.  Microsoft's Media Are Watching By almost any measure, it is remarkable how much of the coverage offered by Slate, the Microsoft-owned on-line magazine, and by MSNBC, the cable network and World Wide Web site in which the software giant is a partner, has been about Microsoft.  D4.  Inside Look at Gates A new behind-the-scenes book about Microsoft, rushed into print last week, presents an unflattering picture of its chairman, William H. Gates. In depicting Mr. Gates as profane and belligerent, the book runs counter to the official line maintained by Mr. Gates's publicist -- who happens to be the author's mother.  D4.  Unconventional Internet Pitch There is more to the Virtual Pet Cemetery, where bereaved pet owners post eulogies to pets past, than might be apparent on first encounter. The quirky Web site actually serves as an imaginative come-on for Lava Mind, a small computer game maker seeking to expand its retail sales.  D5.  Game Giants Face Off in Atlanta The computer-gaming industry will convene in Atlanta this week for the Electronic Entertainment Expo, the annual battle of the gaming titans. This year, that mainly means a face-off between Nintendo, creator of Nintendo 64, and Sony, creator of Playstation, which has come from nowhere three years ago to take almost 60 percent of the market.  D5.  Designers Get a Bit More Exposure Harper's Bazaar, the glossy, Hearst-owned fashion magazine, has begun identifying the designer who dressed the model or celebrity who appears on its cover each month. The practice, which began in February, appears to set a precedent, and not every editor is comfortable with the development.  D6.  Gay Paper Loses Printer A small daily newspaper owned by Gannett has reversed its earlier decision to print the largest gay newspaper in the South after a group of ministers encouraged parishioners to cancel subscriptions and advertising. The publisher of The Times in Gainesville, Ga., said that scheduling press time had become too complicated.  D6.  Color Woes at The Daily News Eighteen months after The Daily News spent hundreds of millions of dollars and installed nine state-of-the-art Goss Newsliner presses -- named for the newspaper with which the technology is making its maiden voyage -- full-color images are nowhere in sight in The News, except on Sundays. Publishing.  D6.  Inventors Head for the Altar Weddings are big business, and several inventors are hoping to carve themselves a slice. Their offerings include a kit to design bridal gowns, interchangeable collars to add color to the standard tuxedo, and even a system that lets guests use credit cards to make those always-appropriate gifts of cash right at the reception. title: Netscape Plays It Cool as Rival Is Sued
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation has done a lot of crowing in the last week. It announced it had won a big contract to supply Citibank with software for electronic commerce. It outlined details of its new strategy to turn itself into a Web-based information service in competition with America Online and Yahoo. And, oh yes, the Justice Department and 20 states filed antitrust suits against its archrival, the Microsoft Corporation. The lawsuits, if successful, could significantly help Netscape over the long run, company officials acknowledge. Despite that, and despite years of complaining that Microsoft was competing unfairly, Netscape officials greeted the filing of the lawsuits with studied indifference. The Government lawsuit, "is not an asset or liability of the company," James L. Barksdale, Netscape's president and chief executive, said today in his first interview since the suits were filed Monday. "We're off to many other bigger things right now." The stock market reaction was also subdued. Netscape shares fell 68.75 cents on the day the suits were filed. Part of the reason for caution is that it is not yet clear whether or what the Government will win and how long it will take. "The suit could take months, if not longer," said Michael K. Parekh, an analyst at Goldman, Sachs. But Netscape, the one-time Internet superstar that has fallen on hard times, needs to move faster than that to right its business, he and others said. There is also a complex politics of perception at work. Netscape officials do not want to be perceived as "whiners," Mr. Barksdale said. That would play into Microsoft's contention that the lawsuits will not help consumers but will merely bail out a handful of competitors that cannot hold their own in the marketplace. The Justice Department's suit seems highly focused on what it says are Microsoft's attempts to use its near-monopoly in computer operating systems to promote its Internet Explorer Web browser at the expense of Netscape's Navigator. As a remedy, Justice wants Microsoft to either stop bundling its browser with Windows or include Navigator. Netscape and the Justice Department say the suit looks at Netscape's plight only as a case study of broader practices by Microsoft. Still, the perception is spreading that Netscape needs the Government. "There is an increasing perception in Silicon Valley that Netscape is the computer equivalent of a welfare mother, totally dependent on government intervention," said Roger B. McNamee, general partner of Integral Capital Partners, an investment group in Menlo Park, Calif. That could make the company complacent when, he said, its destiny is actually in its own hands. An even more unfavorable perception, raised in numerous industry publications, is that Netscape might not be able to survive on its own. Calling attention to a Government lawsuit that quotes a Microsoft executive vowing to "cut off the air supply" to Netscape could scare off big corporate customers, which are generally reluctant to depend on software from a company they fear will not be around for the long haul. The Justice lawsuit "is good for us from a factual standpoint," Marc Andreessen, the company's co-founder and technology guru, said in an interview at the company's Silicon Valley headquarters. "From a perception standpoint, it's as much negative as positive." To some extent, Netscape sympathizers say, the Federal suit's focus on the browser business is too late. It is like the police responding to a report of a robbery in progress two years late, after the property is long gone. That is because to maintain its market share, Netscape began giving its browser away in January, killing what had been a $180 million business in 1996. "I don't have any browser business," said Mr. Barksdale, who tends to talk about the company in the first person. "It was half my revenues a year ago; it's none now." The company now has two businesses. One, with revenues of about $100 million a quarter, is selling software that allows corporations to manage their Web sites and internal operations. The other business, with revenues of about $25 million a quarter, is to sell advertising and services on its Web site. The Justice Department suit will not restore the lost browser revenues. Netscape could file a private antitrust suit against Microsoft seeking damages but says it has no plans to do that at this point. "It takes a lot of resources -- time, money and energy" said Roberta Katz, the company's general counsel. Still, some of this playing down of the Justice Department suit is a bit disingenuous. Netscape did its share of complaining against Microsoft and hired its share of high-powered lobbyists and lawyers. And while it might not get revenues directly from its browser, the product is still key to its business. "Browser share is a very significant strategic issue, not necessarily a monetary issue," said Marc S. Usem, an analyst with Salomon Smith Barney. This is particularly true in Netscape's effort to make its home page into a "portal," a jumping-off point to the Web, providing everything from news to job listings to financial services. Netscape's site, called Netcenter, is one of the three busiest Web sites along with those of America Online and Yahoo, which are already well established as portals. With such traffic, Netscape can sell advertising and charge fees to companies that want to provide services on its site. But a substantial chunk of Netcenter's traffic comes from the fact that 50 percent of the 70 million users of its browser use Netcenter as their home page by default. So getting its browser bundled with Windows could provide a huge boost. "We are leveraging the browser," said Michael Homer, Netscape's executive vice president in charge of Netcenter. The company is moving to further integrate its browser and its Web site. Registered users of the browser, for instance, will automatically receive email accounts on Netcenter. And users who press the search button on the browser will increasingly be directed to Netcenter's search service rather than to outside providers. Such "seamless integration" is, in a sense, what Microsoft is accused of doing by Netscape and the Justice Department -- integrating Windows with Internet Explorer and Microsoft's own on-line services. Such tying of products is generally not illegal unless one of the products is a monopoly. Netscape can argue that it does not have a monopoly in browsers but, arguably, Microsoft does in Windows. The browser is also important to Netscape's business of selling corporate software. "That's my brand recognition," Mr. Barksdale said. Moreover, some analysts say, if Microsoft were to gain complete control of the browser market, it would give it an advantage in selling the software used by corporations to create Web sites. Competition from Microsoft's browser, which some reviewers rate more highly than Netscape's, has clearly hit the smaller company hard. Netscape lost $115.5 million in 1997 on revenues of $534 million. The company's stock, as high as $59 early in 1997 is now at $24.875, although it has recovered somewhat from a 12-month low of $14.875. Netscape officials say the company has adjusted amazingly rapidly to the loss of revenue from its main product. But the quick changes in course, which Netscape officials see as adaptability, have been interpreted by analysts as a lack of focus. "When you keep changing the strategy, that's a confusing message," said David M. Smith, research director for Internet strategy at the Gartner Group. And some analysts question the latest portal strategy. "They are more programmers than media moguls," said Kathey Hale, principal analyst at Dataquest, a market research firm. Netscape counters that it will be mainly distributing content and services for others, not making its own. There are positive signs. With the browser now free, the erosion of Netscape's browser market share has leveled off at about 55 percent and has even shown a tiny uptick, according to the company's figures. Excite, a Web search service, recently agreed to pay $70 million to provide searches and other services on Netcenter. Concrete data on how the company is coping will come on Tuesday when it announces its latest financial results. Analysts are expecting another loss, but the situation is somewhat complicated. Netscape is shifting to a fiscal year ending in October rather than December, so it will announce results for both its second quarter, ending in April, and for a first quarter consisting of only one month. Netscape is expected to use that one-month quarter to take some further charges against earnings. Netscape officials say the market has underappreciated the company's accomplishments. "Somehow we've built a $500 million business in four years," Mr. Andreessen said. "It's worth $2.5 billion to $3 billion in the stock market. The Government hasn't helped us at any step of the way." And, he added, "To double our business, the D.O.J. doesn't have to do anything." Graphic   Photo: James L. Barksdale, chief executive of Netscape Communications. (Steve Castillo for The New York Times)(pg. D4)  Graph: "Shrinking Share" tracks the percentage share of Web browsers in use, worldwide, from 1995 through the third quarter of 1997. (Source: Dataquest)

title: Quirky PC Games Try to Find Market Niche in a Virtual Pet Cemetery
body: The Virtual Pet Cemetery (www.lavamind.com/pet.html) is one of the more oddly compelling Webside attractions to have sprung up along the Internet. A million or so visitors find their way there each year to gawk at the eulogies posted in loving memory of Misty the Brown Mutt or Moretta and Her Kittens. Most are probably unaware that they have been flagged down by a larger-than-life roadside attraction, like a Paul Bunyan statue. Once there, perhaps the tourist will stop by the gift shop and make a purchase. At least that is the hope of Steven Hoffman and Naomi Kokubo, a husband-and-wife design team in their early 30's who operate the pet cemetery as a come-on for Lava Mind, their home-based company in San Francisco. Lava Mind is best known for a series of zany CD-ROM business simulation games for personal computers, including Gazillionaire and Zapitalism, which generally receive high marks from game reviewers for sheer fun and pliability, and from educators for instructional value. (In Gazillionaire, players putter from planet to planet in funky space ships buying and selling oddball commodities in an effort to outwit alien competitors. Zapitalism is a more advanced variation on the same theme, played out in a tropical archipelago complete with monks and pirates.) Despite the games' popularity, selling them has required its own creativity in the last few years, as the CD-ROM game industry has consolidated around a handful of big publishers and shoot-'em-up action titles like Quake from Id Software. Small publishers like Lava Mind with niche titles like Gazillionaire have been all but squeezed out of retail stores. "It's impossible these days for a small, self-published game to get shelf space, no matter what the genre," said Elizabeth Crocker, publisher of Happy Puppy, a game-review and resource Web site. So Lava Mind, which had been struggling with its retail-distribution network, decided to shift to a marketplace with infinite shelf space: the Internet. This year so far, sales on the World Wide Web, averaging about $6,000 a month, have been their primary source of income. "It gives us a good feeling to know if somebody really wants to get our game, they can," Mr. Hoffman said. Though it is difficult to gauge how much of their game sales can be attributed to click-through traffic from Virtual Pet Cemetery, it is worth noting that the pet site receives roughly three times the traffic of the Lava Mind home page itself. Whatever the leaping-off point, customers who have discovered Lava Mind through the Internet include prison inmates and a parochial middle school in Albany, Ga., which recently ordered 14 copies of Gazillionaire for a class in personal finance. And when the authors of a top-selling introductory college business text, "Understanding Business," fell in love with Zapitalism earlier this year after stumbling upon it on the Internet, their publisher, Irwin/McGraw-Hill, bought 1,000 copies to send to professors to gauge their interest. The response was favorable enough that Irwin/McGraw-Hill is considering bundling the CD-ROM with the book. "What got me excited was the combination of good business sense and their sense of humor," Susan McHugh, co-author of the textbook, said of Zapitalism and its creators. "I tried it out on my own kids last fall and they're still playing with it. They came in the other day and said, 'Mom, it tricked us. We're learning about business.' " Ms. Kokubo, a graduate of the International Christian University in Japan, first worked at Morgan Stanley's Tokyo office as a financial analyst and then held a variety of positions ranging from interpreter to production coordinator for the Leo Burnett advertising agency in Japan. Mr. Hoffman, who has a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the University of California and a master's in film and television production from the University of Southern California, worked on entertainment software projects for companies that included Lucasfilm Ltd. and Sega Enterprises in Tokyo. Early in 1994, having been married for four years and having built up a cushion in their savings account, they quit their jobs in Tokyo to make a go of it on their own in the unitedstates. What appealed to them most about working on a shoestring-budget CD-ROM from their two-bedroom row house in the Sunset district of San Francisco was that they could create the game they wanted without waiting for someone else's approval or financing. Nine months and $30,000 later, Gazillionaire was born. They released a shareware version of the game over the Internet, which proved so addictive to members of the quality assurance department at Spectrum Holobyte, a Bay area software distributor, that the company bought the rights to distribute it in the unitedstates. Lava Mind estimates that 150,000 copies of the original Gazillionaire and two repackaged versions, Gazillionaire Player's Choice, and Gazillionaire Deluxe, have been sold. The more advanced simulation, Zapitalism, was released last year. Although Ionos Inc., a small company based in Scottsdale, Ariz., agreed to distribute it, Ionos had trouble negotiating shelf space and Lava Mind has yet to receive any royalties from the company. Rather than sit back frustrated and broke, the couple switched their energies to promoting their products over the Internet, which enables them to keep 100 percent of the average $40 sales price, compared with just a few dollars for each disk sold through traditional channels. So while they are seeking a distributor for their third business simulation game, Profitania, they are already offering it for sale on their Web site. Ms. Crocker of Happy Puppy predicted that more and more niche game developers would resort to direct Web promotions. "The Internet is definitely providing a medium for small developers to end-run the monopoly the big publishers and distributors have on the retail market," she said. Still, repeating the Lava Mind model may be difficult, in the view of Regina Joseph, an interactive media analyst at Jupiter Communications. "They came up with good ideas like the Virtual Pet Cemetery that people could connect with emotionally before anyone else and got a lot of traffic on word of mouth alone," Ms. Joseph said. "If you're not as lucky or talented as they are, you're going to have to spend money to advertise and publicize your product. That can get very expensive." Graphic   Photos: Steven Hoffman and Naomi Kokubo, holding their son, Zachary, quit their jobs in Tokyo to start Lava Mind, the publisher of CD-ROM business simulation games in San Francisco. The games are popular among college professors and children. (Photographs by Sam Morris for The newyork Times)

title: Still Another Adversary for Microsoft
body: Netscape, Netscape, Netscape. The Microsoft Corporation's rival in the browser market is mentioned 130 times in the Government's antitrust complaint and a supporting memorandum. Yet while the Justice Department's case focuses mainly on the browser market, another bitter Microsoft competitor makes a few cameo appearances in the court papers filed last Monday -- Sun Microsystems Inc. Quoting internal Microsoft email messages tinged with profanity and hostile intent, the Justice Department papers discuss Microsoft's plans for blunting the success of Sun's Java programming language. These plans, the Government contends, are pertinent to the antitrust case because Java includes technology that makes it easier for software developers to write programs that run on a variety of computer systems. This so-called cross-platform capability means that Java technology has the potential to loosen the grip of Microsoft's Windows operating system -- the technology standard to which most desktop applications are written today. The Justice Department argues that Microsoft's tactics in the browser market have served to deflect the Java threat. This is because the Netscape Communications Corporation incorporates Java technology in its Navigator browser, so thwarting Netscape in the browser market serves to choke off Java's main distribution channel. Microsoft also licensed Java from Sun in 1996, but later began adding modifications to the code. The resulting Microsoft version of Java is tailored to run only on Windows, which negates the cross-platform purpose of Java. Sun has a civil suit pending against Microsoft on this issue, charging contract violation and unfair business practices. In the court memorandum, the Government quotes a June 1996 email message sent by Paul Maritz, a Microsoft group vice president, in which he stated, "No matter what happens, we have to slow Netscape's ability to drive new protocols or standards down." Mr. Maritz went on to explain that it was "necessary to fundamentally blunt Java momentum" in order "to protect our core asset Windows." Adding its own commentary, the Justice Department memo stated, "In short, Microsoft feared and sought to impede the development of network effects that cross-platform technology like Netscape Navigator and Java might enjoy and use to challenge Microsoft's monopoly." Referring to another internal Microsoft planning document, the Government memorandum said, the goal cited under the heading "Strategic Objective" was to "kill cross-platform Java by growing the polluted Java market." In a footnote, the memo states, "As used in Microsoft documents, the term 'polluted' appears to refer to Java implementations that can only work with Windows." A September 1997 email message, sent by a Microsoft official identified as P. Sridharan, is quoted as saying: "Let's move on and steal the Java language. That said, have we ever taken a look at how long it would take Microsoft to build a cross-platform Java that did work? Naturally, we would never do it, but it would give us some idea of how much time we have to work with in killing Sun's Java." William H. Neukom, Microsoft's senior vice president for legal affairs, has characterized the Justice Department's practice of plucking quotes from many thousands of documents that Microsoft supplied to the Government as "trial by excerpt." When Microsoft presents its side of the case later, Mr. Neukom said, comments that seem inflammatory when taken out of context will be shown to be workaday business communications with a company renowned, and respected, for its competitive drive. As for Microsoft's version of Java, Mark Murray, a company spokesman, said it is simply a faster, more powerful variant of Sun's technology. Much of the computer industry, Mr. Murray added, is realizing that cross-platform programming does not work as well as Java written for a specific operating system, like Windows. As for Sun's suit against Microsoft, he said, it is "nothing more than Sun trying to rewrite a contract through a lawsuit." Sun Microsystems sees things quite differently. Lloyd R. Day Jr., a partner of Cooley Godward, a Palo Alto, Calif., law firm representing Sun, said that Microsoft had engaged in a "longstanding scheme to fragment and hijack the Java technology." Now that the Government has disclosed some of the Java-related documents in its antitrust case, Sun plans on Tuesday to ask the unitedstates District Court in San Jose, Calif., to unseal the court papers in its suit against Microsoft. However the suit is resolved, software-industry analysts say that Microsoft has apparently done a good job of slowing the advance of Sun's Java. "Microsoft has been very successful in engendering a degree of doubt about Java among corporate customers," Scott Winkler, an analyst at the Gartner Group, a research firm, said. Graphic   Chart: "The Microsoft Case" For readers who want to go beyond the news media coverage, these three Web sites contain documents from the Federal and state antitrust suits against Microsoft -- and the company's response.  The Justice Department's filings -- the Sherman Act complaint, supporting papers and the expert declarations of two economists. http://www.usdoj.gov/atr/cases3/micros/msindex.htm  The suit by 20 state attorneys general and supporting papers. title:
Technology;
'Baby Softs'? Envisioning A Breakup Of Microsoft
body: Now that the Justice Department and the Attorneys General of 20 states have filed long-threatened antitrust suits against the Microsoft Corporation, the question remains why the most obvious, and perhaps cleanest, solution has yet to be put on the bargaining table: the breakup of Microsoft into its component businesses. Many analysts and industry executives have noted that the complex, arcane lawsuits filed last week are probably too closely tied to the software giant's current products and business strategies to have any lasting effect. Demands regarding Windows 98, for example, or even specific concessions to Microsoft competitors like the Netscape Communications Corporation will probably be outdated in a matter of months as technology continues to change at its usual breakneck pace. But perhaps most important, the challenges to Microsoft's monopoly do not address the more fundamental issue of how to insure a truly competitive environment in which software code is the currency upon which a new digital economy is increasingly based. Microsoft's iron-fisted control of the market for operating-system software is the keystone of its continuing efforts to dominate applications programs, new media and other businesses -- a degree of control that has prompted speculation about a breakup for years. Most recently, a Silicon Valley research institute, SRI International, offered a hypothetical model in which Microsoft eventually becomes five separately owned and operated companies, which SRI called the Baby Softs. According to SRI, these Baby Softs would consist of the following: *An operating-systems company that sells all versions of Microsoft's Windows operating system. *An applications-software company that invents, acquires and sells classical productivity applications like word processors, spreadsheets, data bases and Internet browsers. *A content media company, taking as its genesis today's Microsoft Network, that would acquire, promote and sell access to on-line and traditional media products. *A networking company that includes network technology assets like the recently acquired WebTV Networks. *A company that oversees the holdings of Microsoft's chairman, William H. Gates, and anything else that does not fit into the other companies. The logic of such a setup becomes apparent when viewed against the specific demands of the lawsuits filed last week. Most of the demands in the suits are intended to stop Microsoft from using its operating-system monopoly to force personal computer makers and consumers to accept the company's applications and World Wide Web links. To preserve competition for Internet browser software, Government officials have asked that Microsoft either decouple its Internet Explorer browser from Windows 98 or include Netscape's browser. Yet, this demand might provide an unnecessary entitlement for Netscape, and it still does not provide for what happens when Microsoft ships future versions of the operating system like Windows NT or Windows 2000 -- which, like Windows 98, will incorporate Microsoft's browser in such a way that it appears to be an integral part of the operating system. The Justice Department has various other goals, including forcing Microsoft to let computer makers distribute rival browsers and modify their opening "boot up" screen if they so choose -- something the company has contractually forbidden manufacturers to do in the past. The states, in their lawsuit, want to stop Microsoft from linking the sales of its Microsoft Office application suite to sales of Windows for computer makers. Breaking up Microsoft into separate operating-systems and applications companies, with a clear definition of those two categories, would eliminate the need for all these demands. Leaving Microsoft intact fails to address the original impetus for the antitrust suits: the need to create an environment in which competition can flourish. In any case, in seeking to re-establish a competitive market, the definition of an operating system versus an application is perhaps the most crucial component of any legal action against Microsoft. This is a contentious area, and one in which Microsoft has to date been intractable. It is none of the Government's business, the company says, to decide what it will build into its operating-system software, including applications like browsers. But the malleable nature of software is such that when lines between operating systems and applications blur -- as they have so fully to date -- the ability of Microsoft's competitors to provide innovative applications, and the ability of consumers to buy those products, is all but eliminated. The argument that an operating system is whatever Microsoft or anyone else says it is has purely technical merit. But one can imagine that the AT&T Corporation felt the same way about what constituted a telephone network in 1974, when the Government first filed suit against the telephone monopoly for keeping competitors out of the now fiercely competitive long-distance and telephone-equipment markets. In the end, defining the components, and the boundaries, of the software industry will be necessary to level the playing field for Microsoft's competitors and to create a foundation for the future of digital commerce. Rather than cutting incremental deals with Microsoft about specific products and practices, the Government should ask: In what areas are there companies that want to compete? Where are competitors being unfairly stopped by an existing monopoly -- or where might that monopoly unfairly stop them in the future -- and where and how do we draw the line? "The worst thing would be a settlement agreement with Microsoft," said a prominent Silicon Valley lawyer who contends that the Federal and state governments have not gone far enough in their lawsuits. "There needs to be a bright line drawn that can't be interpreted through wordsmithing," he said, speaking on condition of anonymity. "If there are ambiguities on a piece of paper, Microsoft will just do what they want and argue later about the paper. The Government needs to say: 'These are the places where you cannot go. Don't go there!' " Under that reasoning, a true challenge to Microsoft's monopoly would require that the Government set new definitions and standards not only for operating systems but also for all the product lines and business strategies by which Microsoft and its competitors conduct themselves in the future. Certainly, it would be no picnic for the Government to enter a definitional debate with Microsoft in an attempt to draw that bright line separating its operating system from other software products. But by not addressing these fundamental issues, the Government could squander a crucial opportunity to build a firm and lasting foundation for fair competition in the digital age. title: Web Coverage Of Microsoft By Microsoft
body: They were born to be incestuous. But even so, it is remarkable how much of the coverage offered by the Microsoft-owned on-line magazine Slate and by MSNBC, the cable network and Web site in which the software giant is a partner, has been about the Microsoft Corporation. That coverage has been hard to avoid, with the Justice Department's filing on Monday making Microsoft's business practices the focus of the most sweeping antitrust charges in a generation. MSNBC devoted several segments to the case on Monday and Tuesday; its Web site featured the antitrust issue as its lead report on Monday, though by Tuesday afternoon it had dropped deeper inside the Web site, leading the business page and not being featured on the home page. Still, "we've written more about our parent than any other news organization," said Merrill Brown, the editor of MSNBC's site on the World Wide Web. And while Slate's coverage has not been as copious as MSNBC's, it brings the same wry tone to its critiques of its parent company as it does to its coverage of the Clinton Administration in general and the Justice Department in particular. "In crafting its suit against Microsoft, the Justice Department made two smart public relations decisions and one serious blunder," wrote William Saletan, a Microsoft contributor, in a piece posted Tuesday of last week, the day after the long-discussed and debated antitrust suit was filed. "But it isn't clear," he added, "whether Microsoft can transcend its martyr complex and self-absorption to take advantage of the error." The Justice Department's blunder, he said, was insisting that Microsoft's new operating system, Windows 98, offer Netscape's World Wide Web browser software to consumers along with the Microsoft rival product, Internet Explorer. Microsoft, Mr. Saletan writes, "foolishly frames this as an assault on its own freedom, welfare, and dignity" when "this misses the more lethal point: that the free ride benefits a particular company." This may not be stinging criticism, but it is hardly the Microsoft party line. That lies a few hyperlinks away, at Microsoft's own site, where its long press release was featured, along with a transcript of the news conference given Monday by the company's chairman and chief executive, William H. Gates. The professionally produced pages on the Microsoft site, in fact, felt little different in their appearance and ease of access as the pages of the Microsoft news organizations. Indeed, what reason would Microsoft have to pressure its editors to skew their coverage, when in the newsstand that is the Web, Microsoft's own press releases look just as newspaper-like as the news organizations' Web sites? On Tuesday, under the headline "Microsoft Will Vigorously Defend Principle of Innovation; State, Federal Lawsuit Will Hurt Consumers, Software Industry and U.S. Economy," the company's press release looked for all the world like another news article. It began: "Redmond, Wash., May 18, 1998 -- The Microsoft Corporation said today that a lawsuit filed by the U.S. Justice Department and several State Attorneys General is without merit and will hurt consumers and the American software industry, a leading contributor to the U.S. economy. Microsoft said it will vigorously defend the freedom of every American company to innovate and improve its products, a principle that lies at the heart of this case." One short click away was the text of the news conference; there was also a long essay by Mr. Gates, though this was at best tangentially related to the antitrust issue. And, while it is impossible to determine how many readers went to Microsoft's site instead of the sites of news organizations, it was certainly one frequently consulted source of information in the days just before and after the suit was filed. According to Relevant Knowledge, one of the companies that measures traffic on the World Wide Web, the Microsoft site was among eight destinations that 550,000 Web-based consumers of Microsoft news turned to during the weekend before the long-expected suit was filed and the first two days after the filing. (The others included CNN, CNNfn, MSNBC, The newyork Times on the Web, and the Web sites of The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal.)

title: For Women and Girls, a Global Forum for Navigating the Web
body: ALISON BERKE'S desk is a mess. Stacks of papers are piled up in front of her computer screen. She brushes them aside and makes a few deft strokes on her ergodynamic keyboard. Quickly, the 33-year-old website designer accesses electrolysis applications, listings for summer shares on Fire Island, Emmy-award nominations and business profiles of women on the fast track. From the tiny spare bedroom of her rented Great Neck home overlooking the Manhasset valley, Ms. Berke is building a virtual domain.  Hers is a career for the millenium, a home-based, high-tech small business with a worldwide reach and a volunteer outreach stint on the side.  Achieving on the cutting edge of new media is a matter of strategic chat room connections. What else could a suburban female entrepreneur ask for? Factor out commuting, leave the talk show blasting on the television in the next room and don't even bother getting dressed. A Looney Tunes crewneck, jeans and stocking feet will do just fine, thank you. As president of Webgrrls, Long Island, the local chapter of a global networking forum for women and girls interested in new media technologies, Ms. Berke is encouraging women to grab the joystick. Technology, contrary to what many prepubescent females seem to think, does not a geek or nerd make, she feels, and stay-at-home moms need not be afraid of the Internet. "Unfortunately, no matter how you look at it," said Ms. Berke, "girls are intimidated in the computer classes with the boys. It's the usual girl-boy thing. They will stand back and let the boys take over the joystick and play the games." Sifting through the hundreds of emails she receives daily, Ms. Berke posts job requests for technical writers looking for assignments. She queries whether any of the 300 Webgrrls on her group list has a sublet available for a web designer relocating from California and asks for troubleshooting advice from the 10,000 female forum members worldwide. Who knows? The answer she is looking for might come from a downsized bank vice president working in New Zealand or Japan. Sisterly support, transmitted on a 17-inch screen, counters the isolation of the self-employed businesswoman. The Internet forum has given women with a modem like Ms. Berke the ability to swap business cards, find solutions to technical glitches, connect with mentors and ease re-entry into the work force with cyberspeed. Working the net, they find, is less intimidating with a network of women. Sometimes it's easier for a mother who is not computer savvy to begin with to learn from another woman. Logging on to the Internet is the next step. But Ms. Berke had to call her "guy friend," Anthony Spira, the "computer genius," to coach her through the more complicated procedures. Ms. Berke has competition from 13-year-old boys, who have a knack for building web sites between baseball practices. Despite the competition, Ms. Berke said women were well-suited to computer work because they are well-organized and creative. y Alona Berzups of Glen Cove worked for a television station for 18 years before starting her own business selling audiobooks on tape through an Internet website. "As a woman in business," she said, "it's a lot tougher to get your foot in the doors, dealing with distributors or publishers. You have to prove yourself a lot more. You have to talk to see what other women have done, that really helps." Ms. Berzups said she turned to Webgrrls to hook up with other women in technology. "It was important to me that it was a woman's group. I belong to a lot of associations and other networking groups on Long Island that were mixed. The collaboration was different. With Webgrrls, it's a whole different feeling. It's more intimate. If I have a need, I don't feel embarrassed about saying I don't know how to this, can somebody help me? I'm a lot more comfortable. We've met with similar obstacles so it's easier to share or to say I have a particular problem. Women understand better. They may have experienced it themselves." Plugged into Webgrrls, 62-year-olds grapple with design skills that might lead to a promotion and college women scan opportunities in a male-dominated industry that produces computer games, CD-ROM's and graphics for the World Wide Web. There are about 160 new media companies on Long Island and 35 internet service providers, of which at least 35 percent are owned by women, said Tyler Roye, president of Longisland.org., a trade association for new media businesses. "The Internet is a place where men have not assumed control like in other businesses," said Diane Sivertsen, who felt empowered by the online women's network to start NetSavvy, a Greenlawn consulting firm that specializes in teaching other mothers about the Internet. "It's a wonderful way to get women involved in this new medium.", Two million women surf online, but "a lot of women don't know much about it, she added. "Kids have access to it in school. They can use it as a resource. For moms, it depends if they work or not. Fathers are exposed to computers more at work." Safety is another concern. Parents worry about children cruising the Internet. Four Webgrrls are part of the Suffolk County District Attorney's task force on Internet safety. "It's the parent's responsibility as well as the child's to use the Internet in a safe manner," she said. "Have your computer located in a family room, the kitchen, any place it's heavily trafficked. Have it pointed towards middle of the room so you can see the screen, as opposed to having it in the child's room." "It's very easy to get into the wrong place. Even though there are not as many violent or pornographic areas as we may think, they are easy to get to if you don't have any kind of control. Kids need to know that people who could potentially harm them may be in these chat rooms posing as other teenagers." Parental controls and blocking software can be installed to keep X-rated and violent material off the screen, she said. Webgrrl's computer link ties other local women's and trade groups together. Ms. Berke is uploading a website for Women on the Fast Track, an Oceanside- based national professional and business women's networking organization in which small groups of non-competing women from masseuses to lawyers share ideas, resources, contacts and experiences. The website of the Long Island Women's Network for Female Executives is accessible from Ms. Berke's Internet development company's bworks.com homepage. Ms. Berke entered the world of multimedia five years ago, armed with $250 and her father's old computer. After briefly studying film in college, she dropped out and worked as a stock trader, then dabbled in computer-generated graphic design while creating presentations for her father's equipment leasing and finance business. As her self-honed computer skills improved, she started troubleshooting for home businesses and teaching people in their homes. "I was waiting for the Internet to be invented," she joked. "The Internet didn't exist at the time. I was playing around and working my way up. When it came, I had the business experience, computer experience and marketing experience behind me from the other things that I had been doing." Webgrrls offers Internet and HTML programming language classes. Ms. Berke also teaches four Internet courses in the Adult Program of the Great Neck public schools. The bworks.com homepage from Ms. Berke's Internet development company also links to the website of the Long Island Women's Network, a female executive group, and Longisland.org, a local trade association for new media businesses. Through a Webgrrls contact, Ms. Berke connected with the National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences and designed their local website. Additionally, she runs Internet directories with ferry schedules, restaurants and rentals for Fire Island and home pages for the Great Neck Chamber of Commerce. She is designing websites for a cruise line, lawn service and a company that manufactures wind baffles for convertible automobiles. Once connected to the World Wide Web, Ms. Berke and a friend created a chiropractic referral directory. It didn't take long before Ms. Berke was an on-line junkie. She taught herself HTML, the web design language, researched Internet service providers, search engines, listservs, file transfer protocols and website hosting. Soon after, Ms. Berke met another web designer, Aliza Sherman, founder of Webgrrls, on a pay telephone line at a trade show in Manhattan. The two techies became fast friends. Ms. Berke started planning cybergatherings for a Long Island forum, one of more than 110 chapters worldwide. Ms. Berke's mission has expanded from teaching women not to be afraid of technology to Internet education. Recently, she was selected as the small-business woman of the year by the Nassau Council of Chambers. She is working with the Suffolk County District Attorney's task force on Internet safety. And the women's group is working with the Nassau County Girl Scouts to get girls on line. The bottom line, Ms. Berke said, is just to get on the Web. "You don't even need a purpose," she said. "For business, for work, for pleasure, for getting in touch with family, for homework, for finding out about vacations, for relaxation, for medical information. Everything's out there."
