title:
PRACTICAL TRAVELER;
States Embrace The Web - Correction Appended
body:
THE information superhighway now runs through all 50 states and the District of Columbia. For generations, travelers have written to state capitals to get maps and event calendars, plus thick bunches of motel brochures and discount tickets to amusement parks. But now this sort of travel information that was requested by mail and sent by the same route is findable on the Worldwide Web. The Travel Industry Association of America even has a Web site, www.tia.org, that provides a list of the state Web sites in hypertext, which means that most states' Web pages can be called up from a central site. For those with access, the Web is almost instantaneous, and particular interests -- a ranch, a water park -- can be pinpointed at once. There are a few potholes in the road. First, state highway maps, the old basic offering, can be printed out from a computer screen but they are too dinky, at 8 1/2 by 11. Material on a Web site can be out of date, and sometimes is inaccessible, too. There are many dead ends in Web addresses that states confidently give out. But anyone who wants to demonstrate the radical shift from using paper to distribute information to doing it electronically need look no further than the promotion efforts of state tourism departments.  Moving Beyond Mail This department last undertook the project of writing to all the states for information in 1993. A reader, Carlos G. Munoz of newyork, recently wrote to say that the '93 address list appeared out of date: he had sent an inquiry to the Mississippi address in Jackson, and it was returned "Moved, not forwardable." Mississippi has given a contract for its fulfillment operation to a company in Ocean Springs, according to Steve Martin, assistant manager in the state tourist agency. The shift was made because requests reached 60,000 to 85,000 a month. When the '93 survey was made, to see what the states sent and how long it took to get to a private address in newyork (The Times was not mentioned in the request), it was clear they were already moving beyond themail in-mail out system. They were often using 800 telephone numbers to take requests. The states now all have 800 numbers, frequently using devices like Mississippi's "800 WARMEST" or Virginia's "800 VISIT VA." Mr. Martin said that Mississippi's contractor had 17 operators to answer questions and send out material. But a phone-request system has problems, too. It may be in another state, or even in a state prison. In such circumstances, it can be futile to ask questions about what is across the street from a particular historic site or how hard it is to get from one place to the other.  Updating the Lists The list of Web sites below was compiled and corrected from the material on several lists, including a flier of 800 numbers sold by the Federal Government. The list of state Web sites given at www.tia.org under "Discover America" has some glitches that seem to indicate it may be more out of date than the list mentioned above, although the Travel Industry Association prepared both lists. For example, the hypertext link under Kansas, apparently provided by a school, proved to be a dead end. The address on the list below, obtained by phone, produces Kansas sunflowers in golden profusion and appropriate information. To get the leaflet with a full list of state and territorial 800 numbers, 14 Web addresses and a few mail addresses, send 50 cents to Consumer Information Center, Department 363E, Pueblo, Colo. 81009. This is called "Discover America," but so is a free list with all the 800 numbers, plus the street addresses and local (toll) numbers but no computer links. The free "Discover America" list is found on the Web by going through a Government site, www/pueblo.gsa.gov, and selecting the entry "travel and hobbies." It prints out easily in nice big type. Every state has a Web site at an address in a standard format that uses its two-letter postal code. For example, for South Dakota, it is www.state.sd.us. Since tourism is a major consideration for a state, it is not hard to find a way to the tourism button from one of these pages. newyork State tourism leaps out easily once you pass a picture of the Governor and other introductory features. Many states, California, for one, use a free program, Adobe Acrobat, as a way to pull out maps and graphics. To load this program into a personal computer go to the Acrobat logotype on the screen, click and follow the instructions. A computer must have these specifications to use Adobe Acrobat: An I.B.M.-style personal computer should be at the 386 level or better, have a Windows 3.1 or Windows 95 operating system, 8 megabytes of random access memory and 5 megabytes of disk space. A Macintosh should be an Apple system 7 or later with a 68020 processor and 3.5 megabytes of random access memory.  Wheelchair Access For those needing it, few things are more essential than information about places that accommodate wheelchairs. Virginia and New Mexico, both sponsors of printed guides to accessible hotels and attractions, do not have this information fully on the Web. North Carolina published "Access North Carolina" in 1990. It is out of print, although Jim Thompson, a spokesman for the state, said the data had been compiled for a new edition, and he hopes the book will be put on the Web site. Information about Virginia is available largely because of the efforts of one couple, Sheryl and Bill Duke, who needed accommodations for their son, a wheelchair user. They published a guide in 1988, updating and republishing it in 1989. A big third edition was published last year, with financing from the state and corporations. The book, a 212-page paperback, is available free to those calling (800) 742-3936. The Virginia book is not on the Web, but at the Virginia site, www. virginia.org, a list of places will appear if one selects "search by category," then "special interest" and, finally, "handicap." If "search by word" is used, "disable" brings up only one entry, but "handicap" brings up a number, including a golf page. Of such uncertainties are Web pages created. Martha Stager, a spokeswoman in the Virginia tourism agency, says a revamped version of the site is expected in July. @compuserve.com. title:
MARKET PLACE;
Zapata Finds Its Internet Bid Is Not Taken Seriously
body: You can't blame the executives of the Zapata Corporation for trying. Zapata, a Houston oil-and-gas company turned fish-meal producer, announced last month that it was changing its name to the much zippier Zap and planning to enter the Internet world in a big way. The mere mention of an Internet strategy has sent stocks zooming in recent weeks. Just witness K-tel International, which reached dizzying heights after saying it would sell musical recordings over the Internet. Zapata's announcement last month did give its stock a small lift. But yesterday morning, it made a bold move. The company, whose market capitalization is only about $250 million, announced that it was interested in buying Excite Inc., a major Web search company, for $1.68 billion. Zapata offered the equivalent of $72 a share, a 20 percent premium over Excite's closing price the day before, in newly issued Zapata shares. Excite promptly issued a statement rejecting the offer, which a company representative called "frivolous." "It is really a publicity stunt," said Greg Klaben, Excite's vice president of investor relations. That skepticism was shared by people outside the company. "Excite is too big a fish for a fish-oil company to swallow as a way to get into the Internet," said J. Neil Weintraut, a partner in 21st Century Internet, a venture capital firm in San Francisco. "It is amusingly backward." Two of Excite's biggest shareholders, Intuit Inc., the software outfit, and Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers, a venture capital firm in Menlo Park, Calif., were also not taking the offer seriously. "I'll buy my fish oil somewhere else," said Vinod Khosla, an Excite director who is also a general partner at Kleiner Perkins. "I can't believe they're serious about it." Even normally excitable investors seemed restrained. Zapata's shares fell 87.5 cents, to close yesterday at $10.50. Investors also proved in no hurry to bet on the takeover: Excite's stock rose only 81.25 cents, to close at $61. The chief executive of Zapata, Avram Glazer, cannot understand why he is not getting more respect. In an interview yesterday, he pointed to his family ties. His father, Malcolm, who is also Zapata's chairman, has built a sizable fortune by amassing stakes in various businesses in real estate, nursing homes, fish processing, restaurants and food equipment. He bought the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the football team, a few years ago for $200 million, and the team is now believed to be worth several times that amount. "If you look at my family's history, we have a history of going in on new things," the younger Mr. Glazer said. "We've been very, very successful." Zapata's own stock has gained 150 percent over the last year. "We are very disappointed that Excite did not give the proper time to study our proposal and mischaracterized our resources and proposal," said Mr. Glazer, who had said Zapata would only pursue a friendly takeover. He argued that Zapata would help bring Excite financial stability and keen investment vision. But the financial power that Mr. Glazer boasts of is not immediately evident. To be sure, the Glazer family has a lot of money -- although Mr. Glazer would not give an actual dollar amount. Forbes estimated his father's net worth at some $300 million a few years back. Zapata itself, founded as an oil company in 1953 by George Bush, has $126 million in cash. The company owns about $275 million in stock in two companies: the Omega Protein Corporation, of fish meal and oil fame, and Envirodyne Industries, which makes sausage casings, among other products. It recently spun off a minority stake in Omega in an initial public offering, raising $77 million. "We have a lot of financial options available to us," said Mr. Glazer, who refused to be more specific about his plans to provide capital for Excite. Still, Excite is hardly without its own resources. The company, based in Redwood City, Calif., recently announced that it plans a secondary offering of 1.4 million shares. "They are only raising exactly what they need," said Henry Blodget, an analyst with CIBC Oppenheimer. "They could raise anything they want." If Excite wanted to find someone with deep pockets, it would not be without choices, agreed Jonathan Cohen, an analyst at Merrill Lynch.  Analysts say a huge media company like a Time Warner or Disney would be logical partners. For what it is worth, Zapata got its 15 minutes of fame. The company has run advertisements in newspapers, including The Wall Street Journal and The newyork Times, saying that Zapata will buy Web sites. While investors and Web companies looking for a partner may now have heard of Zapata, they don't know a lot more about the company's plans after yesterday's events. "We're continuing to explore a broad number of acquisition possibilities," Mr. Glazer said. So far investors don't seem to be biting. Graphic   Chart: "Zap, It's A New Company" 1953 -- Zapata was formed from the merger of Bush-Overby, an oil company owned by George Bush, and another independent oil firm.  1993 -- The company shifts focus to natural gas by acquiring Cimarron Gas, Stellar Energy and Energy Industries.  1994 -- Zapata buys a 31 percent share of Envirodyne, a food-packaging manufacturer.  1997 -- Zapata sells the last of its energy holdings and purchases two fish processing companies.  1998 -- Zapata announces that it will change its focus to the Internet. (Source: Hoover's)(pg. D6)

title: After Windows 98: The Future According to Microsoft
body: THE fight between the Microsoft Corporation and the Department of Justice has placed Windows 98, the upgrade to the Windows 95 operating system, under a microscope. But in the fast-paced world of software development, Windows 98 is already yesterday's news -- it may be shipping now, but it went into development nearly three years ago. At a news conference on Monday, the day the Government filed an antitrust lawsuit against the company, Bill Gates, the Microsoft chairman, defended his company's "right to innovate on behalf of consumers" while vowing to "continue to create great software." So what is Microsoft working on? What it decides to pursue will depend on how it sees the future. For instance, whether personal computers will stick around, or whether they will merge with television or telephone or automobile technology, will affect the future of the so-called first screen, which computer users see when they boot up a computer. The content of the first screen is hotly disputed between Microsoft and its adversaries, the Justice Department and the state attorneys general -- will a Microsoft first screen enable the company to control access to the Internet? But the issue will take an entirely different shape if, say, PC's are eventually supplanted by small mobile devices, a market where Microsoft currently has no particular stronghold. The future comes quickly, and any company like Microsoft has to look beyond today's issues. The company is planning many products, some that are directly involved with Internet access and others that go far afield. In consumer electronics, Microsoft is working hard to reach a simple goal: putting its technology everywhere. Products designed to help the company attain that goal include dashboard-mounted computers for cars, interactive stuffed animals and computers that can see. Some are on the market now. Others are expected in coming months. Still others are at least a decade away -- if all goes well, and it often doesn't. To develop new technologies, Microsoft has reached into its deep coffers: a cash balance of $12.3 billion. The company has acquired companies with promising technologies, bought a significant stake in others and recruited some of the world's leading researchers. The company is pulled in two directions: toward selling operating system software for PC's and toward following consumers as they move away from the PC into new areas like television-based Web surfing. Microsoft has good reason to defend Windows, an operating system that runs on 92 percent of the new PC's sold. In the Microsoft fiscal year that ended last June 30, the company's so-called platforms business, which includes the core operating system sales, generated $5.97 billion in revenues, more than half of the company's total revenues of $11.4 billion. "Operating systems are what the company was built on," said David Readerman, an analyst at Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities. "It's the foundation of the company." At the same time, very fast, inexpensive microprocessors and wireless data networks are making it increasingly clear that there is little reason for a user to be chained to a desk by a bulky PC. For more than two years, Microsoft has sought to translate its dominance of the PC market into control of gateways to the Internet. Such control would give Microsoft the upper hand in the rapidly growing area of Internet commerce. In many of Microsoft's research efforts, even those that range far from the desktop, the company's blending of operating system software with Internet access is evident. Part of the company's strategy calls for expanding the distribution of its software to various low-cost devices like its Web TV set-top box, which delivers Internet services on a television screen. "We're trying to create a computing world that complements the traditional PC," said Craig Mundie, a Microsoft senior vice president who runs what he called the company's "non-PC" division. Future versions of the $200 Web TV box, for example, are expected to contain a consumer-electronics version of Windows, called Windows CE, that has already made its way into handheld computers and is beginning to show up on still smaller palmtop devices like the Philips Nino and the Everex Freestyle. Microsoft is also locked in a battle with Sun Microsystems over the software for interactivity and Internet access that will reside in television cable boxes. Sun is the developer of Java, a programming language primarily intended for use with the Web. Java represents a threat to Microsoft because programs written in Java can run on different kinds of machines. Windows-based programs, on the other hand, must hew to the demands of the Microsoft operating system. For devices running Windows CE, Microsoft circumvented Sun and licensed software to run Java programs from Hewlett-Packard. In the PC market, Microsoft has created its own, slightly mutant version of Java. Sun says both moves undermine its control of the language. For the hour each day that the average American driver spends in a car, Microsoft is developing the Auto PC, which will allow users to listen to their email messages and surf the Web as they drive. The safety concerns surrounding such systems have placed a premium on research into technologies like speech recognition, a favorite topic of Mr. Gates's these days. Using voice commands, the driver can get email, dial a cellular phone or get directions to a restaurant. Of course, the product runs on Windows CE. The Auto PC, available from the Clarion Corporation of America this fall, will also include a voice-operated CD player and AM-FM radio. Nissan and Ford are looking into incorporating Auto PC technology into cars. Of course, just how well these systems work, and whether drivers actually want such a thing in their cars, remains to be seen. Microsoft's blue-sky projects are less sharply focused on the Internet. The company spends some $150 million a year on six-figure salaries for a legion of research scientists. That is just a fraction of the $2.7 billion the company spends annually on research and development overall. But in recent years, Microsoft has quietly built a basic research laboratory to rival the Bell Laboratories of old. The company has hired 300 top researchers from universities and corporations around the world and plans to hire an additional 300 by the end of the decade. Their fields range from computer graphics to more obscure, theoretical disciplines like statistical physics. The work of many of these scientists offers no immediate apparent gain for Microsoft, but the company is looking well beyond short-term benefits. Mr. Gates has often said the company's goal is to build computers that see, listen and learn. "We're working on a whole variety of problems and a whole variety of time scales," said Nathan Myhrvold, Microsoft's chief technology officer and the person who oversees Microsoft research. High on Microsoft's list of research priorities is teaching computers to see. Computer vision and image recognition are technologies that computer scientists have worked on for years. It is only relatively recently that companies like Microsoft have begun to think about computer vision for consumer applications. "If you can have the computer sense its surroundings in a reasonable way, there's an awful lot you can do," Dr. Myhrvold said. For example, the company is working on prototypes of video game technology that can help determine a player's mood. Furrowed brows (frustration, perhaps?) or wandering eyes (boredom?) can cause the game to change its behavior. "It can't tell directly what you're thinking, but it can tell when someone is getting bored in a video game and pick up the pace," Dr. Myhrvold said. Vision systems can also track a user's eyes and fill a screen first in the spot where the eyes are focused. Of course, these plans may well not come to fruition. They are areas of interest, not guaranteed to lead to products ready for sale. For all the money Microsoft spends on research, it has yet to produce breakthroughs as remotely revolutionary as, say, Bell Labs' invention of the transistor. The company has, in fact, fallen behind others in speech recognition, and outsiders question the usefulness of technologies like image recognition. In a lengthy memorandum he wrote seven years ago, Dr. Myhrvold outlined a plan for a wireless digital wallet that would act as, among other things, a communications device, fax machine, scheduler, pager, notepad, credit card, checkbook and personal ID. It did not materialize. If he had that memo to write over again, he said, acknowledging his misplaced optimism, he would date the predictions 2004. Simplicity is another byword at Microsoft these days. At the news conference on Monday, Mr. Gates pointed to the company's work on simpler ways to use computers, saying it was a high priority. Simplicity is a concept seldom associated with Microsoft, yet the company recently assembled a team to build a prototype operating system, based on the Windows NT system, that will "dramatically simplify" PC's, said Jim Allchin, a Microsoft senior vice president and the company's new simplicity czar. Up to now, Windows NT has been sold to corporate users, but the company is working on a version of the operating system aimed at consumers. Then there is tomorrow's generation of PC users, those who are still toddling today. In the past year, Microsoft has produced a line of stuffed dolls called Actimates. Based on popular public television characters like Barney, Arthur and Arthur's little sister, D. W., the dolls talk, play games and sing when prompted. Press Barney's toe, and he sings one of 17 songs in his repertory, including the dreaded "I Love You." Squeeze D. W.'s foot, and she starts a counting game. The toys also react to television programs, mimicking an actual couch companion by singing and counting along with the program and making chirpy side remarks like "That's a big orange carrot!" Although the toys, which sell for about $100, try the patience of many parents, they have aroused the interest of child development experts who see them as a leap forward in interactive play. The Actimates are fascinating for the glimpse they offer into Microsoft's approach to new technology design. First, they represent a new kind of user interface -- the dolls are the interface. "People have asked about 3-D interfaces for a long time," Dr.  Myhrvold said. "These things truly are a 3-D interface." Erik Strommen, a developmental psychologist who headed the design team for the Actimates, said they also signaled a new way of building computers. For years, Dr. Strommen said, engineers have approached the computer as a tool. The new approach, which has emerged in the last five years, represents what Dr. Strommen and others call a social approach to building computers: the technology as a partner or collaborator in the work, rather than a tool. If more devices like the interactive Barney begin to emerge, Microsoft's operating system would become more invisible to consumers. A sticker saying "Microsoft Inside" might become necessary if the software became packaged out of sight in things like plush dolls or electronic organizers. Such credit is important to the company, said Tom Rhinelander, an analyst at Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. While the 3Com Corporation wants consumers to know about its Palm Pilot, "it doesn't care if you don't know about the Palm OS," he said, but the opposite is true of Microsoft. At Microsoft, he explained, "they want everybody to know about their operating system." But at this point, given the unwanted attention the Government has given to Windows 98, a less visible operating system might not seem like such a bad thing after all. Graphic   Chart: "Microsoft's Road Ahead" Windows 98 is the focus of attention but, given the pace of change in software and hardware development, its time will soon be over. Looking ahead, here are the research and development projects that Microsoft is pursuing.  1. Windows NT -- The company is now working on Windows NT 5.0, which will supersede other Windows products in the business market.  2. Windows CE -- Introduced in late 1996, this is Windows Lite, designed to run on small mobile devices such as handheld PC's, which are becoming more and more popular.  3. Auto PC -- Seeking to capitalize on the hour a day many Americans spend in a car, Microsoft is planning a computer that includes everything from email to music and navigation.  4. Actimates -- This line of plush dolls for kids offers a fascinating glimpse into what Microsoft is thinking about the future of user interfaces.  5. Speech recognition -- Microsoft has fallen behind in dictation software, but has made a $45 milion investment in Lernout & Hauspie.  (pg. G7)

title:
DOWNTIME;
Cable Modems: For a Few, Real Speed
body: SWITCHING her home Internet access from a fast dial-up connection to a cable modem has made Dana Chee much more popular around her house. "I used to be the dragon lady, kicking the kids off the Internet to keep the phone bill down," she said. "Now it doesn't matter. We're always connected, it's fast and it's cheap." The Chee family, of Maplewood, N.J., is in a small but growing world of people with high-speed Internet access in their homes. Until recently, such access was limited to corporations, universities and people lucky enough -- or wealthy enough -- to have a T-1 phone line at home. The rest of the world was limited to far slower dial-up access, with busy signals, long connection processes and frequent disconnections. Mrs. Chee was already lucky because she had an I.S.D.N. line, a digital phone connection that is about four times as fast as an average modem and telephone line at carrying data. She was even luckier to get a cable modem, a technology that carries information over cable television lines at a rate that is 8 to 10 times as fast as I.S.D.N. Cable modems are rapidly supplanting I.S.D.N. as the connection method of choice for the home user when they are available. And the cable companies intend to push the technology strongly to keep the upper hand over a competing technology: the digital subscriber line, or D.S.L., that is coming soon from the telephone companies. D.S.L. usually runs about as fast as a cable modem but can cost about 30 percent more.  It can, however, be faster and even more expensive, though still far less expensive than a T-1 line's 1.5 megabits per second, which can cost several thousand dollars. Cable modems are still a rarity, with about 250,000 to 275,000 users in the country, said Bob Arick, president of CATV Cyberlab, a research company in St. Petersburg, Fla. But the lure of a constant, high-speed connection for about $40 a month is pushing the demand. Those lures were enough to make Cheryl Currid, president of Currid & Associates, a technology consulting company in Houston, consider renting an apartment in a building down the street from her office, although in the end she did not. Cable modems are not available in her office building, but tenants in the apartment building down the street can sign up for them. "We use I.S.D.N. and it's nice, but faster would be better," Ms. Currid said. "It used to be the right side of the tracks people worried about, but now it's the right side of the bandwidth. You either live in the right neighborhood or you don't." Most people are not in the "right" technology neighborhood. Gregory Wester of the Yankee Group, a technology research firm, said he expected only about 10 percent of the people who connect to the Internet to have access to cable modems by 2000. Once hooked up, cable customers have a constant connection to the Internet. That is more important to many of them than speed or cost, and it changes the way they use the Internet and their computers. Dan Bricklin, a developer of Visicalc, an incredibly popular spreadsheet in the early 80's, likened the ever present access to the Internet to having a well-stocked library at his fingertips. "The thing that gets everybody is that you're always connected," said Mr. Bricklin, a beta tester for cable modem service offered by Media One, a large cable company, during its trial two years ago. "We've taken an equivalent of the best library and moved it into our house. You want to go to a circus or get the schedule, you just look it up and get it. It's like taking a book off the shelf. The book is already there. You don't even have to start the browser." Mr. Bricklin also said that having Internet protocols in the house opened up a host of possibilities for wiring houses and controlling things. Mrs. Chee has taken the first step toward that, installing what Ms. Currid calls a TAN, or teeny area network. The Chee house was wired for a TAN, with cables to every room. The cable modem is hooked to a firewall that separates the TAN from the outside world; that allows everybody to use individual computers without hogging phone lines or bothering one another. "It is kind of strange, though," Mrs. Chee said. "My daughter uses it to go into chat rooms and talk with the kids two doors down the street." That chat room behavior may look odd to her mother, but Charles Moldow, vice president of media development at the cable network called At Home, said chat was the most popular of the four major areas of usage among cable-access customers, or Internet users in general. He said the typical uses were for email and chat; finding information and downloading software, and entertainment. Mr. Bricklin and other users said the constant connectivity meant that they used the computer more, but for shorter times at each session. Because it takes no time to connect -- if the computer is running, it is connected -- people use the computer for things that used to be done on the phone or elsewhere. "Now I have the computer in a closer spot, not just in an office, and use it for more things," Mr. Bricklin said. "I don't have to keep all that written stuff around." At Trellix, a software company in Waltham, Mass., where Mr. Bricklin is the chief technology officer, other employees have also embraced cable access. Winslow Kelly, a developer for Trellix, said that it made telecommuting much easier. "I need high-speed access to machines or I will need an entire development environment at my fingertips," Mr. Kelly said. "I now have a higher speed connection on my end than at work." This access has allowed Mr. Kelly to change the way he works. "I can sit at home and do demos at the office," he said. "And when I'm at work, I can get information I need off my computer at home." It has also changed the way his family uses the computer, allowing his son to look up information about the Stanley Cup playoffs and player statistics quickly and letting family members dig up a recipe. "As a family, we just don't think about it any more," Mr. Kelly said. "The computer is always on, so we just go to the Web and look it up." Lori Golden, a nurse in Fremont, Calif., with cable Internet access, said she now looked up traffic reports and checked the highways before heading to work. She also looks at movie clips when trying to choose a movie, something that was painful with her dial-up connection. Linda DiCiccio, of Orange County, Calif., who was identified by the At Home network as its 100,000th subscriber, seemed quite pleased when asked about her service. Ms. DiCiccio, formerly an America Online user, said she had been frustrated by freezes and slow speed and had often been disconnected. "Now I find myself renting cars, checking weather forecasts and shopping on the Internet," she said. "It is absolutely wonderful, and I will never go back to a dial-up service."  Buying Internet Access A Look at Rivals' Costs and Services THE I.S.D.N., or integrated services digital network, line was the first high-speed connection available to consumers and, at up to 128 kilobits per second, is only about four times as fast as most home modems. It can get quite pricey, with a combination of flat fees and per-minute charges. The members of Dana Chee's household, in Maplewood, N.J., paid $250 to $325 a month, depending on usage, for I.S.D.N. access as well as fees to their Internet service provider. "The kids would get real upset when I disconnected them," Mrs. Chee said. "But those minutes can really add up." The Chees now pay $35 a month for cable modem service that is always on and far faster, at roughly one megabit, or more, per second. The price to install I.S.D.N. and cable modem service is comparable, about $150; discounts are often available. I.S.D.N. usually requires a visit from a technician, and ordinary modems do not work with I.S.D.N. Cable Internet access also requires a visit from a technician and a special adapter instead of an ordinary modem. Although I.S.D.N. is more common than cable Internet access, it is hardly ubiquitous. Service is still unavailable in many areas. The phone companies and some major players in the computer world are pushing D.S.L. (digital subscriber line). GTE said in April that it would roll out D.S.L. to more than 30 locations beginning in June, but standards are still being set and pricing looks to be higher than what cable companies are charging. Cable companies themselves have a few things to overcome: a reputation for reliability problems and a network that was designed for one-way distribution of a signal from a central office to numerous end points. The cable companies are attacking those issues by guaranteeing quality service and rewiring networks. Some cable companies have said they are considering offering a second tier of additional services and guaranteed reliability for telecommuters and businesses, but very few systems can handle multitier service.   STEVEN E. BRIER Graphic   Photo: A cable modem has meant much lower Web-access bills for the Chees: from left, Ty, Allison, Dana and Devin. (Norman Y. Lono for The New York Times)

title: How Servers Find Needle In Haystack Of the Net
body: THE Defense Department created the Internet and so the nature of its offspring should come as no surprise -- it's a vast hierarchy with redundancy added in case of war. That is most evident in the conventions for creating Web addresses like www.nytimes.com, which are, of course, aliases for the strings of numbers that computers use for addresses. The addresses are called domain names; they are converted into numbers known as I.P. (for Internet protocol) addresses. I.P. addresses come as sets of four numbers, like 199.181.172.241. The domain name system, or D.N.S., is the Internet telephone book that allows computers to convert names into numbers. Of all the computers that make up the Internet, the machines that are ultimately responsible for keeping track of all the names are called the root servers. The pieces of site names fall into a hierarchy. To parse a name in descending hierarchical order, you start at the right. Americans are most familiar with addresses that end with .com, the designation for commercial ventures. That is called a top-level domain. Other top-level domains are .org for groups like nonprofit organizations, .gov for government agencies, .edu for educational institutions, .mil for military sites and .net for companies that are more closely related to providing Internet services. Outside the unitedstates, the top-level domains are usually related to a country. For instance, many addresses in the United Kingdom end with .uk. Some addresses in the unitedstates also end in .us, but they are less common. Top-level domains are just the beginning, even though they come at the end of addresses. Computers decode addresses by examining them from right to left. The machine running the top-level domain answers questions about the smaller domains in the address, and these smaller domains may be broken up even more. The Web addresses most known to Americans have three levels, but ones with four or even five levels are quite common. For instance, nytimes-gw.customer.ALTER.NET is the name of a machine that helps provide network access to The newyork Times. The machine belongs to a company named Alternet, which uses four levels to name its computers. Most companies stick their Web servers in the third-level domain and name it with www. This is not a requirement. Some of my Web pages are parked on a machine called www.access.digex. net. The Web server does not have to be named www; treesaver.nytimes.com would have worked just as well. The hierarchy gives computers a clue about how to convert domain names into numbers. Each D.N.S. server is responsible for answering questions about all the machines a step down in the hierarchy. Consider how a computer might look up the www.nytimes.com address. First, it goes to a root server that maintains the list for the top-level domain at the end of the name, in this case, a .com server. It asks for the address for nytimes, then goes to that address and asks for the www address. WHAT happens when the root server suffers a glitch? Is all the Internet frozen if someone trips over the plug to this machine? No. There are actually nine root servers for the .com domain and more for others. If a computer cannot find the right answer from one, it asks the others. It should be immediately clear how valuable it can be to control this first step in looking up an address. One glitch in the database can make someone disappear or send that person's traffic to someone else. The power of this location has caused great political turmoil lately because a single company, Network Solutions, controls the information going into the root servers for some of the most popular top-level domains, like .com and .org, and charges fees -- $50 a year to list a name -- that have been criticized as unfairly high. Network Solutions runs the primary top-level server for the .com domain. Each day around 3:30 A.M. Eastern Daylight Time, that primary server takes its master list of names and I.P. addresses and converts it into a database that is then copied to the eight other servers. Many people are offering proposals for how to reorganize the root servers. Some are pushing for the creation of new top-level domains like .firm, which will provide competition for companies like Network Solutions and reduce the concentration in one major database like .com. Others have already started running their own servers with extensions like .xxx. Not all computers recognize these addresses because most are programmed to start with only the standard top-level domains. Some proposals would even make it easier for people to control which root servers they use. That would provide the most competition, but some people are uneasy about that idea because it could fragment the Internet. A used-car lot might not want to advertise on a site named like-new.used.car unless every computer was programmed to recognize the .car root server. The role and future of root servers already has the attention of government officials in Washington and abroad. Governments view this job as one role they can serve in cyberspace. Other people, however, say that market-based solutions, where people are free to list with and use the root servers they like, can be just as effective, if not better. Graphic   Diagram: "Roots and Branches Of a Web Address" To the uninitiated, Web addresses seem like a jumble of letters, numbers and punctuation. But it does not take long to discern order in the chaos. Most addresses begin with http://, which reflects how computers on the Web trade information: a method called hypertext transfer protocol. That may be followed by www and may end in one of five suffixes: com, org, net, mil, edu or gov. In between are names identifying the desired site. Most Web addresses follow this hierarchy so the root servers keeping track of each Web site's location can find it quickly when a user goes looking. Here's how those servers work.  1. Request When you type the address of a Web site into your browser, your computer asks other computers, known as servers, for directions.  2. com The first stop is actually the last part of the Web site's name. Nine computers, which are called root servers and are located around the country, keep track of the location of every Web address that ends in com.  3. The root server directs you to another computer, nytimes, which acts like a telephone operator forwarding requests to yet another server owned by The newyork Times.  4. www is the last stop the request makes. The www server will bring up the requested Web page. If, instead, the request had something to do with email, it would have traveled to either themail or pop servers.  "Finding Each Site"  Old Way The request for a Web page used to go first to the root server called "A" and work its way around to the one called "I" until it found the right address.  New Way Now, most Web browsers re-member which of the root ser-vers gave them the response most quickly the last time the question was asked, and they ask that root server first.  Updating Addresses The "A" root server keeps a master list of every Web address, and each night the master list is copied onto the other root servers.  Illustration by Gorka Sampedro; Kris Goodfellow/The newyork Times

title: Information Highway Maps Speed Traps
body: DID a momentary lapse on the road ever leave you at the mercy of a radar-equipped, revenue-hungry highway patrol officer with a pack of speeding tickets? Well, what the asphalt highway may take away, the information highway may give back. The WWW Speedtrap Registry (www.speedtrap.com) lists regular speed patrols in every state, town by town. Separate pages list foreign speed traps, updates on state laws and information about police radar. "Thankfully, opinion has been just about the same from the general public and law enforcement," said Andrew W. Warner, Speedtrap's 22-year-old founder. He called the response "overwhelmingly positive." Speedtrap, which Mr. Warner founded three years ago when he was a student at Vanderbilt University, has about 17,000 listings, many of them by ticketed drivers. He said it had roughly 100,000 visitors a month, peaking before holiday weekends. Its information is unofficial and unverified, but Mr. Warner said the public quickly corrected errors. Many items, he said, are sent in by the police. The information is practical on a number of levels. In the newyork State listing, for example, the reader learns: "Binghamton is by far the worst place on 81 as far as speed traps go, but also a word to the wise as far as college students and out-of-state plates -- NYS troopers HATE you!" For the international traveler or surfer, the listings of international sites bring information -- and personality -- not to be missed. In the listing of Israeli speed traps, the writer includes this comment: "On the Ramot Road toward Jerusalem, at the bottom of the hill, before the final ascent to the city. I've been stopped here a few times (and never seem to learn!)." On the site listing speed traps in Andorra, a principality nestled in the eastern Pyrenees between Spain and France, it says that the police photograph speeding cars to document their license plates but that some residents "report a degree of success by using a high-gloss hair spray on the license plate, which creates, at least in theory, a reflection which may blur some of the numbers." In Finland, the site says, "the ticket was for about $495 and is based on your admission of income, number of dependents and ability to pay." Mr. Warner tries to keep off the site any references to the police as "pigs" and other vitriol. The site also advocates patrols on dangerous roads. It does not list sobriety checkpoints -- "I am not going to make it easy for drunk drivers," Mr. Warner said. Despite these considerations, the site is not universally welcomed. "The newyork State Police have the most sophisticated practices and policies in traffic enforcement in the nation," said Lieut. Jamie Mills, director of public information for the State Police. "If people feel they can speed or drive aggressively by merely locking in on the Web site, they are sadly mistaken." But Sgt. Al DellaFave, a spokesman for the New Jersey State Police, said: "We have no problem with it at all. If anything, it just helps us advertise." But he warned that people should not rely on it. "The troops aren't always in those areas, and those areas change from day to day," he said. "It's just like radar detectors. They aren't foolproof." Radar is a favorite topic of Web ire. A listing for Scottsdale, Mesa and Tempe, Ariz., contends that their use of photo radar units "constitutes the most serious cluster of speed trap activity in North America." From St. Petersburg, Fla.: "City police pose as 'homeless,' sitting on drink coolers at side of road with cardboard sign which holds radar gun." But local departments have defenders. A Brusly, La., resident wrote: "It is a shame to consider our town a speed trap when the officers will give you at least 13 m.p.h. over the zone most of the time." In Fair Lawn, N.J., Police Director Robert Martin chuckled at Speedtrap's warning to avoid Route 4 late at night: "Watch out for Unit 908. It is occupied by a large cop who was definitely trained by the German Army because he never will give you a break." Mr. Martin said, "I think probably from a safety standpoint, it's a great idea." Mr. Warner said his motive was safety, not libertarianism. "The reason most people speed," he said, "is they're running late or they're simply out to speed. If they're simply out to speed, there's nothing I can do to slow them down." But for the drivers who value the law, their health and their time, he said, "They're going to heed the warnings, and it really can be useful for them." Graphic   Photo: A Web site is aimed at helping drivers avoid speeding tickets. (Chet Gordon, 1992)

title:
USER'S GUIDE;
Joys of Hanging Out On a Virtual Corner
body: THE other day, as I was scrolling down a ranking of the most popular Web sites, I found myself stifling a yawn as I was confronted with the usual suspects: Yahoo (been there), Netscape (done that), America Online (ho-hum), Microsoft, Lycos, Excite (yeah, whatever), Mirabilis. . . . That one woke me up. In April, Mirabilis had more than two million visitors. That was certainly curious news because Mirabilis does not fit my idea of the kind of site that should be wildly popular. It isn't a search engine, after all, or a place where I can go to download a browser or the on-line headquarters for some mammoth on-line service. Nor does it run banner advertisements on other sites. Instead, Mirabilis is a software company, based in Tel Aviv, whose main product is a free chat and messaging program called ICQ (pronounced I Seek You). "We're not really sure how to characterize it," agreed Doug McFarland, senior vice president of Media Metrix, which ranked Mirabilis 29th in March among the 5,300 sites home users visit most frequently. ICQ is reported to be the most popular Internet software downloaded from the Net. Intrigued, I went to the Mirabilis site (www.mirabilis.com). From all appearances, the main thing it offered was the opportunity to download yet another free software tool that promised to let me communicate with other people on line. Now, don't get me wrong. No one is more excited than I am about the Net, the most revolutionary communications medium of the century. But excuse me for thinking that email had already licked the problem of how to talk to one another on line. And a wide array of other tools is available, including Internet Relay Chat, which has long been popular; mailing lists, and personal home pages that let you sign a guest book. Certainly, there is nothing new about the concept of an on-line chat format or instant messaging. America Online pioneered both services long ago. But on closer inspection, I realized that Mirabilis's ICQ software offered something most others didn't. ICQ is a single program that enables a user to chat on line while simultaneously having instant messaging. Here's how it works: I went on line and opened my browser, which allowed me to run ICQ and hook up to one of Mirabilis's servers. Then I searched among ICQ's 11.5 million registered users to create a personal list of "contacts." Random searches revealed that at least a half-dozen friends and relatives, including my mother-in-law, were registered users. My list of contacts appeared in a discrete window on the screen while I browsed the Web and checked my email. ICQ notified me when one of my contacts came on line. I then had a choice: I could correspond with my contact by sending an instant message -- a little window opened in the middle of my screen, where I could type text and then click on a Send button -- or by going to a private chat room that I could create within seconds. In either case, the ICQ software relayed messages back and forth within seconds -- much faster than standard email. But ICQ and similar software programs are still more a gimmick than a utility. ICQ will not replace email for the simple reason that its universe is limited to registered users. That is not to say that ICQ is not compelling, even addictive. I got so carried away by the novelty that I was feverishly engaging in multiple simultaneous conversations, using both the chat format and instant messages. That is when I had an epiphany about why ICQ is so popular. The program transforms Net surfing from an essentially solitary endeavor into a social activity. One moment, I was sitting alone in my dark office, typing away at 2 A.M. Then ICQ informed me that one of my brothers (using the pseudonym Braveheart -- what is that all about?) had come on line. Physically, my brother was nearly 1,000 miles away, in his house in a Chicago suburb. But at that instant, we might as well have stumbled across each other on the way to the corner store. We could wave hello (metaphorically) with an instant message before we continued on our separate ways. Or we could stop on the corner and catch up on our lives, via an extended chat. On the Net, the buzzword "community" gets tossed around quite a bit. It is no secret that on line (as well as off), people want to connect to one another in ways that make them feel less lonely, or simply less alone. ICQ has been able to tap into and satisfy that hunger. "What we have done with ICQ is to position the product not as a software product but as a social product," said a company founder, Yossi Vardi. Of course, there is still a major limitation to instant messaging and chat software: you can communicate only with people who happen to be on line with ICQ open. So conversation tends to be serendipitous. While you can send a message to an ICQ user who is not on line at the time and specify that it be sent later, there is no guarantee that the recipient will open ICQ anytime soon. So if you really need to talk to one of your "contacts" right now, you might be reduced to employing the old-fashioned method: pick up the phone, dial and say into the receiver, "Uh, Braveheart, would you mind logging on? I think we need to talk." AMERICA ONLINE'S INSTANT MESSENGER: www.aol.com -- You do not have to be an AOL member to use this instant messaging service. Download it free from this home page. In either case, you can set up a list of friends from the more than 20 million users who have registered for the service and send them instant messages.
