You can also find a separate chat program offered by Yahoo there and download it.  Drawing (Margaret Riegel)

title:
U.S. v. MICROSOFT: THE CASE;
Separating Fixations From Fixes
body: Many analysts predict that the Government's attempt to protect the Netscape Communications Corporation's Navigator browser from the onslaught of the Microsoft Corporation's Windows operating system and its Internet Explorer browser will prove futile. Larry Dietz, vice president of Zona Research, a Northern California company that conducts market research on Internet use, reflects a common view when he observes that individual computer buyers want a browser "that is fast, easy and cheap." "For 9 of 10, that will mean Microsoft," he predicts. Yet, even if Netscape's share of the browser market shrivels, the Government's proposed legal remedies will not necessarily be in vain. For even though the Justice De partment focused on Netscape in its announcement on Monday, the remedies it seeks range far beyond one product or one manufacturer. Their overriding purpose is to shift control over some features of the operating system from a single software company to numerous computer makers. By stripping Microsoft of some of its monopoly power, the Justice Department hopes to create room for companies that sell services over the Internet to compete with Microsoft. It also hopes to create room for Netscape or any other company to create a software program someday that would have wide appeal as an alternative to Windows. Computer makers are expected to begin installing Windows 98 on new units next month. Though Microsoft has interlaced computer code for its browser with the code for the rest of the operating system, it will still be possible for manufacturers to hide Internet Explorer and feature Netscape's browser on the main Windows screen, or desktop. Indeed, if the Justice Department gets its way, the courts will insist that Microsoft allow the manufacturers to make any number of changes to the desktop if that is what they think their customers want. But many analysts predict that very few individual consumers -- business customers are another story -- will want anything other than Microsoft's default desktop and Internet Explorer running on Windows. A common logic behind that assumption is better customer support. Buyers might prefer Microsoft's Internet Explorer because it takes only one call to diagnose software problems. Consumers who use Netscape's Navigator with Windows risk having technicians at Microsoft and Netscape each blame the other's company for a problem or direct users to the other's customer service department with questions. This is a complaint commonly voiced. In fact, customer service is often cited for the success of Microsoft's other programs, like word processors and spreadsheets. If that reasoning is correct, Netscape's market share -- now about 55 percent -- cannot be saved. But beyond browsers, the remedies sought by the Government are mostly intended to preserve competition in Internet commerce and to preserve the possibility that some company can someday create and market a program that gives computer users an attractive way to run applications without relying on Windows. To that same end, the Government also asks the court to prohibit Microsoft from writing exclusionary contracts that effectively discourage competition. And it asks the courts to wrench some control over the design of Windows from Microsoft and hand it over to computer manufacturers. Specifically, Microsoft's contracts now prohibit computer makers from substantially redesigning the appearance of the Windows desktop.  First appearances may seem trivial.  But to Microsoft's competitors, the desktop can be all important. Microsoft litters the desktop with icons that take users to Web sites on which the company and its partners sell services. In the future, that could include real estate, travel, banking, news, entertainment and many other products and services. That offers Microsoft a huge advantage, because for consumers to link up with non-Microsoft Web sites, they must engage in time-consuming searches. Microsoft insists that it is legal for it to advertise its wares. Besides, it says, companies in every industry piggyback marketing for products on the backs of other products. But the Justice Department argues that under antitrust laws, business practices that are routine for ordinary companies are not legal if they are used by monopolists to trample competition from potentially superior products. Besides, the Government is not ready to declare the browser war over. The Justice Department intends to use the antitrust laws to preserve the possibility that a company can design and market a product that consumers might find an attractive alternative to Windows. The Government's seeming fixation on Netscape's browser flows not from a judgment that browsers are in themselves especially important. But as a technical matter, they might some day serve as a substitute operating system -- a platform on which word processors, spread sheets and other applications programs run. If so, they could eliminate the importance of Windows or any other operating system. For that reason, browsers pose a threat to Microsoft, which explains its previous attempts to write exclusionary contracts that prohibit its partners from promoting Netscape's Navigator. Whatever the outcome of the suit, the Government cannot micromanage software markets. It cannot know if Netscape's browser has a future. But it does not have to know. The point of antitrust laws is not, as some of the Government's statements and remedies may wrongly suggest, to give a specific competitor a helping hand. Rather, antitrust principles are solely designed to preserve the possibility that a smart company has a fighting chance to flourish in a market. The remedies of the Justice Department may wind up doing nothing for Netscape, but the test is whether they provide opportunities for anyone else. Graphic   Photo: William H. Gates, the chairman of Microsoft, shown here at a news conference on Monday, has proved himself to be a master of metaphor in trying to explain his company's antitrust dispute with the Government. (Dan Lamont for The newyork Times)

title:
Business Travel;
American Airlines to offer new discount fares for weekend getaways over the Internet.
body: AMERICAN AIRLINES, emboldened by the response to the discounted fares for last-minute weekend getaways it offers in weekly email messages sent free to more than 1.5 million subscribers, is now offering another round of last-minute mini-getaways to selected destinations. But these offers are for $39 plus frequent-flier miles -- 75 percent fewer frequent-flier miles, in some cases, than are normally required for a free flight. For example, among the offers scheduled for posting this morning on American's website (www.aa.com), and good for travel after 7 P.M. this Friday with return next Monday or Tuesday, are: Washington to Dallas/Fort Worth, 13,000 frequent-flier miles plus $39; newyork to Albany, 6,000 miles plus $39; Hartford to Chicago, 7,000 miles plus $39. Destinations will change each week.  Checking Bags Passengers aboard a recent Continental Airlines flight from Los Angeles to Newark may have wondered what was going on when they were required to check all roll-on luggage, even that of the size suitable for overhead bins. But contrary to appearances, Continental said it had not changed its policy. What must have happened, the airline said, is that the flight attendants knew this particular aircraft had some restrictive dimensions in the overhead bins, which vary from plane to plane, and based on their experience, they realized that the roll-ons could prove troublesome on a crowded flight. "But that flight was just an anomaly," said Dave Messing, a Continental spokesman. "In fact, we're in the process of re-outfitting many of our planes with specially configured overhead bins," to accommodate roll-on bags.  Airline News Hoping to attract more business travelers, Frontier Airlines -- the Denver-based carrier whose destinations include newyork, Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles and San Francisco -- plans to add first class to its planes this fall. Through Friday, Alaska Airlines is offering discounted fares for summer travel between the Pacific Northwest and California, Arizona and Nevada. Restrictions apply.  Knopf City Guides First came the Knopf Guides, lavishly illustrated guidebooks to England, France and many other countries. Now it is Knopf City Guides, hip-pocket-sized books of about 170 pages with 600 full-color drawings and photos. The first titles, just recently shipped to bookstores, are of newyork, London, Paris, Madrid, Milan, Lisbon and Berlin.  Insuring a Cruise Robert M. Jarvis, a professor of law at Nova Southeastern University in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., said that the Titanic disaster was a good example of why cruise passengers should buy trip insurance. Before 1936, if a ship sank, its owners' liability was zero, said Professor Jarvis, who is also editor in chief of the Journal of Maritime Law and Commerce. Following the sinking of the Morro Castle in 1936, a minimum liability for death or injury was established at a rate of $60 per ship's ton, then raised to $420 in 1984. "Although $420 sounds like a substantial sum," Professor Jarvis said, "some quick math shows why it is not. The biggest cruise ships today weigh 100,000 tons, thus a shipowner would have to establish a fund of at least $42 million for such a ship. But because such ships are designed to carry an average 2,000 passengers, the fund works out to just $21,000 per claimant." By contrast, he added, relatively inexpensive trip insurance, depending on the policy, covers not only injury or death, but also trip cancellation, interruption or delay, lost or stolen baggage and medical emergencies.

title: MCI Said to Be Soliciting Bids For a Division
body: Trying to placate regulators who are weighing its $37 billion sale to Worldcom Inc., the MCI Communications Corporation has quietly solicited bids for part of its fast-growing Internet business, people close to the negotiations said yesterday. The unit should fetch around $500 million, and British Telecommunications P.L.C. is among the companies expected to be involved in the bidding, the people close to the talks said. Small new long-distance carriers including IXC Communications Inc. and the Williams Companies Inc. were also invited to participate, the people close to the talks said, and the GTE Corporation could play a role. But MCI had not solicited bids from its main competitors, the AT&T Corporation and the Sprint Corporation. By declining to solicit bids from AT&T and Sprint, MCI appeared to be trying to insure that the Internet unit it was considering selling could not be used by its most formidable foes. The companies declined to comment yesterday. By weighing the sale of a big portion of its Internet unit, MCI is moving to allay fears by regulators in Europe and the unitedstates that a combined MCI Worldcom would dominate the market for long-distance, or "backbone," Internet capacity. The Internet backbone can be likened to the nation's interstate highways, while the retail Internet market, which includes companies like America Online Inc., is more akin to the roads that feed such highways. Consumer groups and some rival companies that oppose MCI's proposed merger with Worldcom and some independent analysts have estimated that a combined MCI Worldcom would control as much as 70 percent of the Internet backbone, a figure both companies dispute. The Justice Department's antitrust lawyers have focused on the Internet issue. Regulators from the European Commission were also examining the merger. MCI is considering selling its domestic wholesale business, which provides broad cyberspace on ramps to smaller Internet access providers, and its trans-Atlantic Internet business. MCI would not sell its retail Internet unit, in part because MCI and Worldcom do not stand accused of having the potential to dominate the consumer Internet business in the same way they could control wholesale pricing. America Online, for instance, is the largest on-line service, with 11 million customers, providing ample competition in the retail market. But its Internet communications network is owned by Worldcom. By divesting itself of much of MCI's Internet business, the combined company would strengthen its case for being allowed to hold on to Uunet Technologies Inc., the largest Internet backbone supplier. Worldcom acquired Uunet in 1996 when it agreed to acquire the MFS Communications Company, a big competitive local telephone company, for $14 billion. MFS completed its $2 billion acquisition of Uunet only weeks before MFS itself agreed to be acquired by Worldcom. John W. Sidgmore, Uunet's president, is now vice chairman of Worldcom. GTE asked European regulators last week to force Worldcom to sell Uunet as a condition for approving Worldcom's acquisition of MCI, people close to the companies said. One of the odd twists of the current solicitation process is that both British Telecom and GTE were involved in the original battle for MCI last year. British Telecom had agreed to acquire MCI for $24 billion before renegotiating the price to $19 billion, opening the door for Worldcom. GTE offered $28 billion in cash for MCI shortly after Worldcom made its initial $30 billion stock bid last October but GTE did not or could not keep pace when Worldcom made its second, and winning, proposal of $37 billion in both cash and stock. British Telecom has agreed to support MCI's merger with Worldcom, partly because British Telecom would receive $7.3 billion in cash for its 20 percent stake in MCI. But GTE has adopted an aggressive lobbying position that has seen it fight the deal at every turn, including in the courts. The European Commission has said that it will rule on the proposed merger by July 15, while the Justice Department has not outlined a definitive time frame.

title: United States v. Microsoft
body: In their sweeping antitrust suit against Microsoft, the Justice Department and 20 state attorneys general have made reasonable demands to preserve competition in the world of computers and the Internet. Bill Gates needs to respond with something better than disingenuous countercharges that his company is being punished for its success. Instead of forcing a protracted court battle over remedies, Microsoft should work with Federal and state lawyers to reshape the marketplace to help consumers obtain the products they may want. A sense of history was in the air as Joel Klein, director of the Justice Department's antitrust division, stepped forward in Washington, D.C., to charge Microsoft with engaging in predatory conduct to choke off its rivals. Within hours, Mr. Gates and his phalanx of lawyers in Redmond, Wash., warned that the Government was in danger of destroying innovation and enterprise in the country's most dynamic business sector. He made no concession to the idea that Microsoft had used its monopoly in personal computer operating systems to force computer makers to favor its other software products. Much will now depend on whether the Justice Department and attorneys general can prove their charges of illegal anti-competitive conduct. One of the most explosive charges disclosed yesterday was that Microsoft first tried to cut a deal with Netscape, makers of the main rival to its Web browser, to carve up the browser market. Only when that approach failed, said the department, did Microsoft shift tactics and try to muscle Netscape out of the market, fearing that its success on the Internet would supplant Microsoft's dominance in the operating system business. In response, Microsoft says that its conversations with Netscape were innocent and that every one of its decisions was a legal effort to serve its customers. For all its heated language, the Justice Department stepped back from trying to block the shipment of Microsoft's Windows 98 operating system, probably because it would be hard to prove serious and irreparable damage. Instead, the Government wants Microsoft to unbundle its own browser, Internet Explorer, from Windows 98 or to include the rival Netscape browser along with it. The Government also wants Microsoft to stop giving preference to its own software products on the screen that first comes up when customers turn on their computers. Microsoft maintains that everything it is being asked to do is impractical. That is for the courts to decide. But Mr. Gates must know better than to assert that the Government's demands are the equivalent of asking Coca Cola to include cans of Pepsi in all its six-packs. Coca Cola is not a monopoly, but Microsoft's operating system is. It would be better if Mr. Gates recognized that reality and stopped behaving as if his company were still a struggling upstart. As he said yesterday, the world awaits an era of accelerating change in computers, with undreamed-of products in voice recognition, artificial intelligence and Internet commerce. The Justice Department and the attorneys general are right that the inventors of products in these areas must be allowed to market them to consumers free of a stranglehold by Microsoft.

title:
U.S. V. MICROSOFT;
Excerpts From the Lawsuit Filed by 20 State Attorneys General
body: The following are excerpts from the complaint filed yesterday against Microsoft by 20 state Atorneys General in the unitedstates District Court for the District of Columbia. The Internet browser is a separate product which competes in a separate product market from the PC operating system. Microsoft itself has consistently offered, promoted, and distributed its Internet browser as a stand-alone product separate from Windows, and intends to continue to do so after the release of Windows 98. No other product duplicates or fully substitutes for the functionality of an Internet browser. Internet browsers that work with one operating system will not work with another operating system without significant modification. The geographic market for Internet browsers is worldwide. The Internet browser has the potential to enable "platform independent" applications. Internet browsers can be, and have been, developed to run on the major desktop operating systems. If an application is written to run on the browser, it can be platform-independent in the sense that it does not depend on compatibility with an underlying operating system. Rather, it depends on compatibility with the Internet browser and associated technologies. By offering the possibility of a "middleware" layer which would, in essence, permit applications to run on any operating system, the Internet browser threatens Microsoft's Windows monopoly. If an application's ability to run no longer depends on the use of a particular operating system, consumers will no longer be required to purchase the dominant operating system in order to ensure access to a wide portfolio of desired applications. Accordingly, customers would no longer see any particular operating system as having intrinsic value simply by virtue of its ubiquity. This would, in turn, facilitate entry of other operating systems into the competitive market. Thus, while not itself an operating system, the Internet browser poses a significant potential challenge to Windows. In its current form, the Internet browser does not threaten to eliminate the Microsoft operating system, but to "commoditize" it. . . . Through the actions described above, Microsoft has illegally attempted to prevent competition to its software products, with the following anticompetitive effects: Actual competition between Microsoft and actual and potential competitors in the markets for Internet browser and related software, office productivity suites, and first screen and boot up access has been or is threatened to be curtailed and foreclosed; OEM's (Original Equipment Manufacturers) have been denied, or are threatened with denial of, the benefits of a free, open and competitive market in the sale of licensing rights for Internet browsers and related software, office productivity suites, and first screen and boot up access; Consumer purchasers of personal computers pre-loaded with software have been denied, or are threatened with denial of, the benefits of a free, open and competitive market for Internet browsers and related software, office productivity suites, and first screen and boot up access; Barriers to entry into the markets for operating systems and office productivity suites have been raised and reinforced, tending to forestall the development of actual competition in those markets; and The states general welfare and economies have been injured through prevention of free and open competition in each of the States' economies. Plaintiff states and their citizens will be subject to a continuing, substantial and immediate threat of irreparable injury to the general welfare and economy and to competition in their states unless Defendant is enjoined from its illegal conduct..  . . . Microsoft has monopoly power in the market for PC operating system software. Through the actions complained of in this petition, Microsoft has willfully and illegally used its monopoly power to maintain and extend its monopoly in this market in violation of Section 2 of the Sherman Act. 15 U.S.C. 2. . . . Microsoft has attempted to monopolize the market for Internet browsers through the acts and practices described above in violation of Section 2 of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. 2. Microsoft has specific intent to achieve monopoly power in this market, and in furtherance of this intent has engaged in the exclusionary conduct described above. There is a dangerous probability that Microsoft can and will achieve a monopoly in the market for Internet browser software through the actions complained of by the plaintiff states.

title:
U.S. V. MICROSOFT: THE COMPANY;
On TV, a Defiant Gates Faults Tactics by U.S.
body: A defiant William H. Gates took to a television studio stage today on the Microsoft Corporation's campus to defend his company's business practices and to assert that by filing broad antitrust lawsuits against his company, the Government and a group of state Attorneys General were threatening the pace of technological innovation in the personal computer industry. "Federal and state regulators have taken the unprecedented step of intervening in America's most successful and growing industry by trying to design software," a stern-looking Mr. Gates said to a group of reporters in the studio and others watching around the world. Yet despite the stark terms in which Mr. Gates cast his company's confrontation with the Government, he and other senior executives took pains to play down the impact of the battle on Microsoft and on the almost 16,000 people who work for the software maker in this Seattle suburb. "The mood of the company is really quite positive," said Geoff Raikes, group vice president for sales. "This is an exciting time for us and most of the company is really quite focused on our products." Indeed, besides responding today with broadsides to the Government lawsuits, the company began shipping the first master copies of the product that is at the heart of the dispute, its new operating system for personal computers, Windows 98. During his prepared statement and in several minutes of taking reporters' questions, Mr. Gates also sought to sweep aside any suggestion that the legal battle was the culmination of a personal confrontation with Joel Klein, the head of the Justice Department's antitrust division. "I wouldn't say this is personal," Mr. Gates said. At the same time, though, he expressed bafflement that Federal and state officials had singled him out in a news conference in Washington several hours earlier.  "They kept using my name," he said. "Why would they do that?" In two weeks of negotiations with Government officials, Mr. Gates said, Microsoft had made numerous compromise offers. But, he added, the Government had chosen to ignore its efforts to reach an accommodation. Mr. Gates was vague, however, on the terms of any compromises that might have been made to negotiators. "We were very creative," he said, noting that one possibility had been to include a link to the Netscape Navigator web site on the main Windows 98 screen, known as the desktop. The Navigator, made by the Netscape Communications Corporation, is the main competition to Microsoft's Internet Explorer Web browser. The Government had demanded, he said, that the company either include the Navigator browser itself on the desktop or remove its own browser from the screen. In building Microsoft from a tiny software publisher for hobbyist personal computers into the world's most powerful information age corporation, Mr. Gates has used his company's control of the personal computer operating system as his key weapon against competitors. Those tactics were defended today by William H. Neukom, Microsoft's senior vice president for law and corporate affairs, who likened Microsoft's bruising business tactics to those of a team in a football game. He said that antitrust law offered the company broad latitude in employing those tactics. "We are free to continue to compete as aggressively as the little guy as long as we compete according to the rules," he said. "If the competitors are bruised, that's the nature of competition." The dueling news conferences here and in Washington seemed to be an occasion for dueling metaphors as well. Microsoft executives repeatedly reacted with indignation to the Government's effort to force the company to include the Netscape Navigatorin its Windows 98 software. "It's a little like asking us to include three cans of Pepsi with every six-pack of Coke," Mr. Gates said. For his part, Mr. Klein of the Justice Department suggested that Microsoft's control of what was included with the operating system was akin to the manufacturer of compact disk players dictating which CD's could be heard on its system. In an effort to counter the Government's contention that it was locking computer makers into selling their machines with the same start-up desktop, known as the "first boot" screen, Microsoft executives today turned the news conference into a PC showroom. Mr. Gates demonstrated five different personal computers from four companies -- Compaq, Packard Bell, Hewlett-Packard and Sony -- showing how the companies were permitted what he said was wide latitude to include their own features as well as software made by others. In two cases, he showed examples in which the computers came pre-loaded with the Netscape Navigator browser. He also showed how it was possible for computer owners to remove both the icon for Microsoft's browser and the web browser "channel bar" feature, which Microsoft has hailed as an innovation. The channel bar, which has been part of the most recent version of the Internet Explorer browser, allows the user to put together a selection of Internet web sites, much like channels on a television. Mr. Gates made an effort to show that the Government litigation would do little to disturb the company's business efforts. Indeed, the only aspect of the case that appeared to draw his anger was the allegation that Microsoft had once approached the then-infant Netscape with an offer to divide the Internet market. "That's an outrageous leak and an outrageous lie," he said. Microsoft had licensed the original core technology for its browser from Spyglass, another Internet browser company, he said, and did not need Netscape's help. Microsoft had met several times with Netscape executives at their request, he said. Microsoft had planned to add its browser as an operating system feature even before Netscape was incorporated, he added. Moreover, Mr. Neukom challenged the Government's use of Microsoft internal documents and statements by its executives as "trial by excerpt." In the Government's news conference, Mr. Klein made reference to a statement by a Microsoft group vice president, Paul Maritz, "to cut off the air supply" from Netscape by giving away products in every business in which the company, based in Mountain View, Calif., had revenue. Microsoft executives said that after delaying the initial shipment of Windows 98 on Friday because of last-minute talks with the Government, it released the "gold disk" for the software today to about 100 computer makers and to the company's manufacturing plant in Puerto Rico. The company said that it is on target for a June 25 commercial release of the product, which is intended to offer such new features as support for digital video disks and easier integration with peripheral equipment via a new high-speed hardware interface known as a Universal Serial Bus. Mr. Neukom said that he did not believe that the litigation would interfere with Windows 98, even if the case is settled before the release of the program in late June. He argued that the Government faced several difficult challenges in its lawsuits. He also cited a recent ruling in Microsoft's favor by the Federal appeals court in Washington in the Government's pending case against the company over its licensing practices relating to Windows 95. The ruling involved Microsoft's alleged violation of a 1994 consent decree growing out of that case. The court, he said, had pointed out in its ruling that judges and juries should not be put in the position of designing operating systems.

title:
U.S. V. MICROSOFT: THE INDUSTRY;
No Sympathy for Gates in Parts of Silicon Valley
body: The Microsoft Corporation's many dependents offered a muted reaction to today's suits by the Department of Justice and state Attorneys General, but the software maker's outspoken adversaries called the action a major step toward dismantling its dominance. The most forceful reaction came from Lawrence J. Ellison, chairman and chief executive of the Oracle Corporation, who ridiculed Microsoft's chairman, William H. Gates, for calling the lawsuits harmful to American innovation. "Bill's call for an opportunity to innovate is the big lie theory," Mr. Ellison said. "His idea of innovation is to take other people's technology, copy it, put it into the operating system, and then raise the price of the operating system. Who's kidding who?" Mr. Ellison called the lawsuits a "wonderful first step." Mitchell Kertzman, chairman and chief executive of Sybase Inc., said he hoped the Government would expand its action beyond Internet browsers and desktop computing to include Microsoft's business practices in the broader market. "They are leveraging their monopoly in desktop applications to sell their back office suite," he said, referring to corporate software applications. He called it "virtually the same tactic" Microsoft uses to sell other products and services. Both Netscape Communications Inc. and Sun Microsystems Inc., the two companies with perhaps the most to gain from any action against Microsoft, praised the Department of Justice and the states. "This is a serious case they have brought, and it has the potential to address some serious competitive imbalances in our industry," said Michael Morris, Sun's general counsel. He said the action differed substantially from a 1994 antitrust settlement agreement Microsoft reached with the Government, which "attacked a practice that had already done its dirty work." In a statement, Netscape executives called the legal action an "initial step in loosening the choke-hold the Microsoft monopoly has on the computer industry." "Given its pervasiveness and role in our lives, the personal computer simply has to be a flexible tool, one that can be adapted to a wide variety of personal uses and preferences," Netscape said. "If we all are required to use the same software, meaning the software selected for us by Microsoft, the tool will become ever more a blunt, dull and oppressive instrument, and consumers will lose a basic right -- the right to exercise choice of goods and services -- that has always been fundamental to American commerce." Many more companies declined to comment. Some computer makers did not appear eager to take steps that the Government's legal actions, if successful, would allow, such as creating alternative start-up screens and loading Netscape's browser software. Others were more cautious in their appraisal of the lawsuits and the possible outcome, partly because of Microsoft's enormous leverage. "I view it as an interim step; it really isn't a solution," said Gary Reback, a lawyer with the Silicon Valley law firm of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosetti, who has represented several of Microsoft's competitors. "It's hard to know whether there are additional steps or what they are and how to evaluate those steps." Some computer manufacturers who would comment said they were in no hurry to offer alternative start-up screens or browsers, which the lawsuits would permit. The I.B.M. Corporation declined to comment, and calls to Micron Electronics, Packard Bell and Gateway were not returned. "Our plans haven't changed," said T. R. Reid, a spokesman for the Dell Computer Corporation, which plans to ship machines loaded with Microsoft's Windows 98 on June 25. "We felt that our customers are happy with what comes up at this time, and we're happy with the current arrangements we have with Microsoft regarding that," said Jim Finlaw, a spokesman for the Compaq Computer Corporation. "We do see that there's merit in having commonality there. We're happy that our customers will get Windows 98 on time and we're fully scheduled to deliver on June 25," he said. Compaq has no plans to offer Netscape's browser at this time, he said. Although the Government did not seek to block shipments of Windows 98, any uncertainty about its shipping date could ripple through software and hardware sales, some analysts and executives said. "I certainly think there's a significant risk of delaying peoples' purchases," said Gordon Eubanks, president and chief executive of the Symantec Corporation. "Innovation is always proceeding in this industry, and the pace of innovation is very different from the pace of the Department of Justice. So it's not clear to me that this is going to end up pursuing anything of any real benefit to consumers." But companies that compete with Microsoft, whether in the field of Internet browsers or in the development of alternatives to Windows, say the company is unfair.
