CHOICES -- Allow computer manufacturers to pick which browser or browsers they want to include on their machines and to alter the first screen users see from the one designed by Microsoft.  BEYOND BROWSERS -- The states also demand that other Microsoft products, like word processors and spreadsheets, be separate from Windows 98.

title:
U.S. V. MICROSOFT: THE ISSUES;
Stopping a Monopoly from Begetting Others
body: Some monopolies are good -- or at least inevitable. When the Department of Justice and 20 state Attorneys General filed antitrust suits against the Microsoft Corporation yesterday, the issue was not whether the company's industry-dominating Windows software operating system constituted a monopoly. With Windows serving as the command-and-control system for approximately 90 percent of all new personal computers, monopoly power is assumed -- and there is nothing illegal about that. The problem, according to Joel I. Klein, the Justice Department's antitrust chief, is that Microsoft is "illegally leveraging its Windows monopoly" in an attempt to squash competition and extend that monopoly to the market for Internet browser software for viewing the World Wide Web. The antitrust laws do not outlaw monopoly or the profits that flow from market power. The various versions of Microsoft's operating systems over the years, including the current version, Windows 95, came to dominate the PC industry by legal means. Not only has the company been a remarkably effective marketer, but consumers tend to like having a single operating system because it guarantees that programs running on one person's computer will also run on almost everyone else's. And computer makers have catered to that customer preference by making Windows a de facto standard. Having come by its monopoly through legal means, Microsoft is not the easiest of prey for an antitrust challenge. But public policy has often held that the best monopoly is usually the most carefully curtailed monopoly. There are often good reasons to pare monopolies down to size. In the early 1980's the Federal Government broke apart AT&T's nationwide Bell System, creating a competitive company to provide long-distance service and limiting the regional telephone monopolies to local service. In the 1990's, some states have broken apart electric utility companies, setting generating plants to compete on their own and limiting the monopolist who has the wires to distribution. And so, too, are yesterday's suits by the Federal and state governments seeking to chisel Microsoft's monopoly to its essential core. For although the antitrust rules do permit monopolies, the laws do not allow companies to exploit a monopoly in one product to crush competitors in another market. And that is what the Justice Department contends that Microsoft sought to do to its main competitor for Internet browser software, the Netscape Communications Corporation. "Microsoft -- from Bill Gates on down -- quickly realized that Netscape's Internet browser, Navigator, held a real threat to Microsoft's Windows monopoly," Mr. Klein said at the news conference announcing the lawsuits. And so Microsoft pursued a strategy designed "to cut off Netscape's air supply," Mr. Klein said. Specifically, the Government wants to give computer manufacturers the ability to choose Netscape's browser over Microsoft's. The suits also want to keep Microsoft from dictating what screen computer users see when they first turn on their machines, so that the company cannot use its Windows monopoly to automatically promote its other products or to unfairly promote the Web sites of companies with which it has struck exclusive deals. Finally, the Justice Department wants to prohibit Microsoft from writing contracts that prohibit Internet services from promoting the wares of Microsoft's rivals. No law prevents Microsoft from selling a superior browser that ends up dominating the market. No law keeps Microsoft from offering Web sites for selling cars, real estate, travel services or other offerings that are so superior that rival Web sites go out of business. What yesterday's suits do seek to prevent is Microsoft's driving better products and services out of the market because the Windows monopoly never gives competitors a fair chance to reach customers. Microsoft contends that its restrictive contracts and cross-marketing deals are common throughout the economy. That is true. But the antitrust laws hold monopolists to a higher standard. Exclusive contracts among companies that possess no market pose no threat to consumers because they can always flee to other vendors. But the Justice Department and the state Attorneys General maintain that consumers cannot easily flee Microsoft. Microsoft executives said yesterday that the suits were "without merit." And indeed, as the Federal District Court in Washington begins considering these lawsuits, the Justice Department and the states will need to overcome ambiguities in the antitrust laws that could work to the company's advantage. The laws prevent Microsoft from any practice whose sole purpose is to harm competitors. But if the company's marketing contracts or the design of its products -- such as embedding its browser deep inside Windows -- can be demonstrated to provide consumers some benefit, however minor, then the law is unclear as to whether Justice and the states have grounds for intervening. Here's where legal and policy issues can clash. The Justice Department, following the advice of many economists, wants to pursue a balancing test -- prohibiting practices that do more to throw barriers in front of Microsoft's competitors than to benefit consumers. Microsoft's lawyers say the antitrust laws call for no such balancing. It could take years of rancorous negotiations and litigation to determine which view will prevail.

title:
U.S. V. MICROSOFT: THE JUDGE;
A Courtroom Disciplinarian Who's Unintimidated by Technology
body: Skeptical of the Microsoft Corporation's insistence that its Internet browser could not easily be separated from its Windows 95 operating system, unitedstates District Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson decided on his own one day to embark upon a simple experiment. With the help of a court technician, he clicked a computer mouse about half a dozen times and, in less than three minutes managed to remove the browser icon from the main screen without disabling the operating system. The outcome, presented to an astonished courtroom a few days later, helped exert pressure on Microsoft, which then faced the possibility of a contempt-of-court citation, into agreeing to offer computer manufacturers a version of Windows 95 without the Internet Explorer browser. Judge Jackson, 61, will continue to wield considerable influence over Microsoft, and the computer industry, as he supervises the sweeping antitrust cases brought today by the Justice Department, 20 states and the District of Columbia. Not since Judge David N. Edelstein in newyork oversaw the long-running I.B.M. antitrust action has a Federal judge faced such an important antitrust contest. And like Judge Edelstein, Judge Jackson has shown a marked preference for the arguments made by the Government lawyers over those put forward by the company. Yet after years of litigation and nearly daily battles between Judge Edelstein and the defense lawyers from Cravath, Swaine & Moore, I.B.M. ultimately prevailed. While Judge Jackson has consistently leaned in favor of the Government since he got the first Microsoft antitrust case last October, he has shown little of the hostility to defense lawyers that marked Judge Edelstein's treatment of the I.B.M. legal team. Judge Jackson was given the case today at the request of the Justice Department. Technically, the department said that the case was related to the earlier proceeding, but it was also clear that Government lawyers had been pleased with his earlier rulings. Judge Jackson was appointed to the bench in 1982 by President Ronald Reagan, after serving as a Republican precinct leader in Maryland and a trial lawyer at the firm co-founded by his father, Thomas Searing Jackson, a prominent member of the Washington Bar for decades. Although legal publications have noted that he generally runs a slower docket than many of his colleagues, he has moved the earlier Microsoft proceedings along at a faster tempo. He is known for control over his courtroom, a grip so tight that it has occasionally provoked rebukes from the Court of Appeals. One of his best-known cases was the perjury and cocaine trial of Washington's Mayor, Marion S. Barry Jr., seven years ago. Judge Jackson tried to bar from the trial the Rev. Louis Farrakhan, leader of the Nation of Islam, and the Rev. George A. Stallings Jr., leader of a black Catholic congregation that had broken from the Roman Catholic Church. Both men had maintained that the Barry case was an effort by white prosecutors to unseat a black leader. A Federal appeals court reversed Judge Jackson on this, ruling that he could not keep the two men out just because their presence might send a message to jurors. Ultimately, the jurors convicted Mr. Barry on one misdemeanor count of possessing cocaine and acquitted or deadlocked on 13 other, more serious counts. A few days after handing down the maximum sentence of six months, the judge infuriated Barry supporters at an appearance at Harvard Law School, his alma mater. He said he believed that four of the jurors were biased and "obviously did not tell the truth" during voir dire, the process of examining prospective jury members, that they "had their own agendas" and "would not convict under any circumstances." He also said he had "never seen a stronger Government" case against a defendant. At the time, he did not know two reporters were present. Judge Jackson has had other important cases. Last year, he ruled that the Presidential line-item veto law was unconstitutional. The Supreme Court reversed him, finding that the lawmaker plaintiffs had not been personally injured and therefore had no standing to sue. A different judge has since struck down the law, and the case is before the Supreme Court again. In 1994, he dealt a mortal blow to the political career of Senator Bob Packwood of Oregon, when he ordered him to turn his diaries over to the Senate ethics committee. The committee's investigation ultimately led to Mr. Packwood's resignation. And in 1987, Judge Jackson presided over the trial of Michael K. Deaver, a top Reagan aide, who was convicted of lying under oath during an investigation of whether he was involved in improper lobbying of former White House associates. The judge tried to close part of the jury-selection process to reporters and the public, but was instructed by an appeals court that he could not do so. After Mr. Deaver's conviction, Judge Jackson decided against sentencing him to jail, saying that he had found Mr. Deaver's lobbying and influence-peddling distasteful but indicated that he had been swayed in part by Mr. Deaver's statement that alcoholism contributed to his predicament.

title:
U.S. V. MICROSOFT: THE OVERVIEW;
U.S. AND 20 STATES FILE SUITS CLAIMING MICROSOFT BLOCKS COMPETITION OVER INTERNET
body: The Federal Government and 20 state Attorneys General filed two broad, aggressive antitrust suits against the Microsoft Corporation today, launching the most concerted government attack on a single company in a generation. The suits accuse the world's most powerful software company of using its monopoly in personal computer operating systems to win control of the Internet and software products, particularly browsers, which are necessary for viewing and interacting with the World Wide Web. What is more, the Justice Department suit accuses Microsoft of having once approached its then-infant rival, the Netscape Communications Corporation, with an offer to divide the Internet market. As Attorney General Janet Reno announced the filing of the suits this afternoon, with Attorneys General from Connecticut, Iowa and newyork standing at her side, she said that Microsoft's business practices had "restricted the choices available for consumers in America and around the world." In a meeting with reporters at Microsoft's headquarters in Redmond, Wash., this afternoon, Microsoft's chairman, William H. Gates, said, "This is a step backward for America, for consumers and for the personal computer industry that is leading our nation's economy into the 21st century. "How ironic," Mr. Gates added, "that in the unitedstates -- where freedom and innovation are core values -- that these regulators are trying to punish an American company that has worked hard and successfully to deliver on these values." The Justice Department and Attorneys General asked the unitedstates District Court for the District of Columbia to issue a preliminary injunction to stop the practices described in the suits immediately. But in a curious twist in their decision to take on the company that epitomizes the supremacy of the nation's high-technology industry, they stopped short of asking the court to block the release of Microsoft's latest version of its operating system, Windows 98. Even as the lawsuits were being filed, Microsoft began shipping the product to computer manufacturers, and it announced that it was on schedule to sell Windows 98 in stores beginning June 25. Joel I. Klein, the Assistant Attorney General for antitrust, said that the Justice Department would not try to block Windows 98 because the Government wanted to "create options, not restrict them, so we will not try to stop the shipment of the software." With the final version of Windows 98 already shipped, it was clear that many consumers were likely to get the new operating system without the limits and remedies being sought in the lawsuits. But Mr. Klein also made it clear that his goal was not to block one piece of software but to force Microsoft to change its way of doing business. "What cannot be tolerated -- and what the antitrust laws forbid," Mr. Klein said, "is the barrage of illegal, anticompetitive practices that Microsoft uses to destroy its rivals and to avoid competition." In a decision that pleased the Justice Department, the case was assigned to District Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson, who issued a ruling favorable to the Government in the antitrust case filed against Microsoft last October. That suit charges Microsoft with violating a 1995 consent decree by forcing computer manufacturers to accept the company's browser, Internet Explorer, as a condition of licensing its Windows 95 operating system. The new Federal and state suits would require Microsoft to sell a version of Windows 98 that does not include Internet Explorer -- or to package Netscape's Navigator browser, the principal competing product, with Windows 98. The state suit also asks that Microsoft be forced to include a third Web browser of Microsoft's choice unless Internet Explorer is removed from the operating system. Microsoft maintains that Internet Explorer is now part of the Windows operating system, not a stand-alone product, and therefore cannot be removed. Dennis C. Vacco, the newyork Attorney General, whose office will head the states' litigation team, said, "Our action today aims to protect consumers from a single power controlling and dominating an information infrastructure that one day may be our primary link to communications, commerce and information." A senior Justice Department official noted that there were precedents for requiring a company to carry its competitors' products. Long-distance telephone companies, for example, have been required to allow competitors to use their lines, and one airline's reservation system has been required to carry the flight information of competing airlines. But Mr. Gates said that neither of the alternatives described in the suits was acceptable. "I don't think asking us to ship a competitor's product is an appropriate solution," he said. "And if they want us to re-engineer Windows to take these new features out, we'll have to turn to the courts." The Federal and state suits also try to stop Microsoft from requiring that computer makers set up new computers so that consumers see Microsoft's main Windows screen, or desktop, when they first turn on their machines. This requirement is important to Microsoft -- and to the Government -- because the desktop can now serve as a gateway to the Internet and to every other service and piece of software available. "At stake here," said Richard Blumenthal, the Connecticut Attorney General, "is whether Microsoft's control over gateways could throttle Internet commerce -- and indeed commerce itself." In a statement, Microsoft said: "Consumers who purchase a new PC and see the Windows desktop as the first screen are assured of the product's quality, simplicity and reliability. Once that first 'boot-up' takes place, consumers can customize the desktop in any way they like." That may be true, Mr. Klein said, but he added that it was "quite clear" that most consumers maintained the basic desktop they were given. And a senior Government official said that the prosecutors saw the first-screen requirement as Microsoft's way of maintaining its operating system monopoly. Without it, Mr. Klein said, computer manufacturers would be able to bring their own "interesting, challenging opportunities to consumers." The state and Federal suits also seek to end "exclusionary contracts with providers of Internet and on-line services" that are intended to make them favor Microsoft products and services. During negotiations between prosecutors and Microsoft lawyers over the weekend, that was one area where the company initially expressed some flexibility. But the talks foundered over other issues, so no agreements were reached. Today, Microsoft said: "Like virtually all companies in the software industry and many other industries, Microsoft has entered into various cross-promotional agreements in which Microsoft agrees to help promote and distribute a company's products and services in exchange for promoting Microsoft's technology. These agreements are legal and commonplace." The suit filed by the state Attorneys General follows the lines of the Federal suit in most areas but adds charges of its own. For example, the states charge that Microsoft is using predatory pricing strategies to gain monopolies in other software products, including word processors and spreadsheets that are packaged in office "suites," including the market-leading Microsoft Office. The states' suit says that Microsoft offers steep discounts only if the company's office suite is purchased for installation on a manufacturers' entire line of computers. The manufacturers "cannot afford to pay the significantly higher royalties for per-copy licenses, because their profit margins are very narrow," the suit says. "As a result of that pricing strategy," the suit goes on, "Microsoft Office has attained monopoly power in the field of office productivity suites. By calendar year 1995, Office accounted for over 85 percent of all sales of office productivity suites, and its share of sales has increased since that time." That pricing strategy, the suit charges, has made it "economically impractical for manufacturers to offer competing office productivity suites for preinstallation on their PC's." In his remarks this morning, Mr. Gates said the company's products had been successful "because we did a better product." The state suit also accuses the company of trying to take control of the E-mail software market by bundling Outlook Express, the company's E-mail program, with Windows 98. The suit does not, as some state officials predicted last week, challenge Microsoft's inclusion in Windows 98 of WebTV for Windows, an electronic program guide that shows what is on television and on certain Web sites. Still, the suit clearly leaves the door open so that new charges can be added if more states join the effort and bring their own concerns. The Attorneys General said they were acting to protect consumers -- and aspiring entrepreneurs -- in their states. Iowa's Attorney General, Tom Miller, chairman of the Antitrust Task Force for the National Association of Attorneys General, said, "We are taking this action to give a fair shake to competitors and free choice to consumers in one of the most crucial industries in the nation." Scott Harshbarger, Attorney General of Massachusetts, said the intent of the suit, from his point of view, was to make "an opportunity for Massachusetts companies to compete with Microsoft on a fair and level playing field. "It could mean new jobs, new innovations and new choices for consumers," he said. The states collaborating on the lawsuit are California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, newyork, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Utah, West Virginia and Wisconsin. The District of Columbia, represented by the unitedstates Attorney, also joined the action. Graphic   Photos: Joel I. Klein, ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL FOR ANTITRUST (Stephen Crowley/The newyork Times); William H. Gates, MICROSOFT CHAIRMAN. (Agence France-Presse)

title: A Video Middleman as Shopkeeper, Too - Correction Appended
body: Now, the revenge of the middlemen. Since the advent of on-line retailing, doomsayers have predicted failure for companies in the middle of the retail food chain -- wholesalers that distribute products to local stores. Now one such company -- at the risk of a revolt among its retailing customers -- has moved into its own on-line storefront so it can sell directly to consumers. Ingram Entertainment, the largest wholesale distributor of recorded videocassettes, disclosed last week that it had quietly bought a controlling interest in Speedserve, which sells videos and books over the Internet. The deal would appear to violate an unwritten rule for wholesale distribution companies in most industries: they do not compete directly with the stores they sell to. Such traditional arrangements, however, are being shaken up by the Internet, which is enabling companies of all sorts to build direct relationships with consumers. Bertelsmann A.G., for example, the German media conglomerate, is creating a store to sell its books directly on line. "On-line retailing is more like distribution than it is like retailing," said David Ingram, president and major shareholder of Ingram Entertainment, a division of the privately held Ingram Industries of Nashville. "It doesn't involve having goods on the grounds and bricks-and-mortar stores. It's more about having good systems and a good back office." Indeed, many on-line stores never take possession of the goods they sell. Rather, they arrange with a distributor to ship the products directly from the wholesale warehouse to the customer -- an arrangement known as drop shipping. Ingram Entertainment, which supplies about one-third of the videocassettes for sales and rentals at local video stores, hopes to offer drop-shipping services to other on-line video companies and to Speedserve. The market for videocassettes bought over the Internet is far less developed than for books or music, because people are more likely to rent movies than to buy them. Moreover, many of the $8 billion in videocassettes that are purchased each year are bought as impulse items in chain stores and supermarkets. As a result, Speedserve's Videoserve store is one of half a dozen companies hoping to become a leader in the category, as Amazon.com leads in on-line book sales. These include start-ups like Reel.com and Bigstar.com and traditional players like Borders and Blockbuster, which is owned by Viacom Inc. Ingram's plan to be both friend and foe to video stores may be difficult. Hollywood Entertainment, Ingram's largest customer, has decided not to buy videocassettes from Ingram for its own Internet store because of the Speedserve investment, said Mark. J. Wattles, chairman of Hollywood Entertainment. "If Ingram is in the business of selling directly to consumers, we would not be interested in having them ship cassettes to our customers, as well," he said. For now, Hollywood will continue to buy videos from Ingram for its stores. But Mr. Wattles noted that Mr. Ingram had tried to smooth the ruffled feathers of the video stores by inviting them to participate in the Speedserve venture. Hollywood, so far, has declined to do so, Mr. Wattles said. "David has risk in entering a business where he is competing with people who he is currently selling product to," Mr. Wattles said. "But I think he understands and is trying to mitigate that risk." Mr. Ingram played down the potential conflict. "We sell a lot of stuff to retailers that compete with each other," he said. "I don't see a problem if we sell to another on-line retailer that we happen to have a majority interest in." Yet the sensitivity of the topic can be seen in the secrecy with which Ingram has treated its Speedserve involvement. Ingram Entertainment actually bought a controlling interest in the company in 1996, but had not disclosed that investment until now. Mr. Ingram said the secrecy was needed because Speedserve was still improving its computer systems. "You don't want to make an announcement that will drive people into the store if you are not ready to handle the business," he said. Speedserve has always been seen as very close to the interests of the Ingram family, which owns Ingram Entertainment and the larger Ingram Industries. Speedserve was founded by Michael and David Mason, the sons of Steven Mason, a longtime executive in Ingram Industries. Correction  Because of an editing error, an article in Business Day on Monday about Ingram Entertainment's plans to distribute videocassettes on line misstated the ownership of the company. It is an independent company; it is no longer a division of Ingram Industries. Correction-Date: May 20, 1998, Wednesday

title: From Oil to Fish to the Internet: Zapata Tries Another Incarnation
body: Alice Bradley sits at a desk in the very office in midtown Manhattan from which she was laid off months ago, back at her job as the editor of the on-line sports magazine Charged. When the publication, and its culture-watching sister, Word, were shut down by the owner, Icon CMT, in March, hopes were slim for finding a buyer to revive the Webzines. "I didn't ever think I'd come here again," Ms. Bradley said. That was before an unlikely white knight emerged: the Houston-based Zapata Corporation. Avram Glazer, Zapata's 37-year-old president and chief executive, announced late last month that the company would not only acquire the two popular but unprofitable magazines, but redirect Zapata's entire focus to matters Internet. To boot, he said, Zapata -- founded as an oil business in 1953 by a young George Bush, retooled in 1994 as a food processing business under Mr. Glazer -- planned to change its name to the more digitally hip Zap. The company will become a major player in the Internet and electronic commerce, Mr. Glazer predicted in an interview. "We want to have a global network of sites," he said. To find the pieces of that network, Mr. Glazer is conducting a national talent search. Last week, he began running advertisements in newspapers, including The Wall Street Journal and The newyork Times, proclaiming, "Zapata Will Buy Your Web Site." His email address and phone number are listed in the ads, which have generated a "tremendous response," he said, declining to elaborate further. It might all sound like cyberhype, were Zapata not an established company with reported profits of $6.5 million on revenue of $30 million in the quarter that ended March 31 and a stock that has been trading in the $11 range lately after languishing below $5 most of last year. Still, Mr. Glazer has disclosed little detail about how he intends to achieve his E-commerce goal. Nor would he comment on a more recent announcement that Zapata had secured three addresses on the World Wide Web -- instantwinner.com, internetnames.com, and betaworld.com. "Their names sort of speak for themselves," he said vaguely. He did say that he planned to transform Zapata's corporate Web site into a "gateway to all our sites." "At the end of the day, what we want is a network," he said. Internet industry analysts are confounded by the company's interest in the notoriously unprofitable Internet content business. "I think they have more money than sense," said Regina Joseph, senior analyst at Jupiter Communications, a new-media research firm in newyork. "So many people have invested so much money, and gotten badly burned. How can they jump into the fray? I seriously question their due diligence and their intent." But Mr. Glazer comes from a family that has often dared to enter new territory. Through a patchwork of investments, his father, Malcolm, 69, amassed a fortune estimated by Forbes magazine at $300 million. Starting more than 40 years ago as a watch salesman in Rochester, the elder Mr. Glazer parlayed his profits into diverse holdings that include real estate, a local television station in Laredo, Tex., nursing homes, junk bonds, restaurant chains, fish processing and professional football. He controls most of those holdings through his privately held First Allied Corporation. "Going in a new direction is something a lot of people won't or can't do," said the younger Mr. Glazer, who since earning a law degree from American University in 1985 has managed his father's investments, including a controlling stake in Zapata acquired in 1993. Two of his brothers, Bryan and Edward, sit on the Zapata board, as does his father, while two other brothers and his sister are active in other parts of the Glazer empire. The publicity-shy family had drawn scant attention before 1995. But that year, the Glazers' purchase of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the National Football League team, for $192 million (a league record at the time), thrust them into the glare of the news media. As newcomers to the sporting world, they provided endless fodder for Tampa Bay-area journalists, who chastised the Glazers for renaming the stadium after the Houlihan's Restaurant Group (whose stock they controlled), even though there was no Houlihan's restaurant in the area. It is not the only time the Glazers have drawn criticism for their links to Houlihan's, which they now have a contract to sell to the Scoggin Group, a restaurant holding company. In October 1996, the family's plan for Zapata to acquire Houlihan's was abandoned after Zapata shareholders sued to block the deal -- which would have paid Malcolm Glazer $29 million in cash for his 73 percent stake in the restaurant group. An earlier transaction, in which Zapata bought stock in another company controlled by Malcolm Glazer, Envirodyne, is the subject of pending litigation. "To me it's a ridiculous lawsuit," Mr. Glazer said of the Envirodyne dispute. "We bought the stock at $4.50 and now it's trading at $8. Most of these lawsuits filed are just nuisances." (Envirodyne's shares, which traded above $8 earlier this month, closed at $6.75 on Friday.) The Glazers "have been absolutely maligned and tarred and vilified," said Joe Von Rosenberg, a former director of Zapata and now the president of its Omega Protein unit, a fish-protein processor, which raised $130 million for Zapata in an initial public offering of stock in April. "But they have an uncanny ability to pick investments that do well," he said. "They look at a set of numbers and see things people don't see." Yet even a Zapata fan, Tim Ramey, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, which was an underwriter of the Omega Protein offering, is reserving judgment on Avram Glazer's current plan. "Who knows if the Internet strategy can work or not?" Mr. Ramey asked. One apparent winner from the acquisition of Word and Charged is the previous owner, Icon CMT, which had operated the two publications as loss leaders for Icon's Internet hardware and technology businesses. In exchange for the on-line magazines, Icon received a promise of $2 million in business from Zapata. "People forget that the Internet is tiny as a medium," said Scott Baxter, Icon's president. "But in five years, it's going to be a completely different story. They understand that it's a growing market." But Ms. Joseph, the new-media analyst, predicted that Zapata stockholders might not be so patient. "If, after a period of time, Word and Charged are drains, Zapata will come to the same conclusion as Icon," she said. "It's a stay of execution for them, but only a temporary one." Still, Mr. Glazer plans to give the two Webzines resources that Icon did not -- including an advertising sales staff. And he offered jobs to all 12 employees whom Icon had dismissed, including Word's editor, Marisa Bowe, and Ms. Bradley, who is busy preparing for the re-introduction of Charged. "He's told us to do whatever it takes to create the best publication possible," Ms. Bradley said of Mr. Glazer. "He has yet to say, 'That's too much,' " she said of spending. Graphic   Photo: Avram Glazer, Zapata's 37-year-old chief executive, plans to make a pair of World Wide Web magazines the seeds of an on-line empire. (Michael J. Okoniewski for The newyork Times)

title: I.B.M. Is Close to Deal On Phone Service Over the Internet
body: Throwing its weight behind the nascent business of Internet telephone calls, I.B.M. has agreed to promote the cyberspace phone service of the IDT Corporation, according to executives close to the negotiations. The companies plan to announce the marketing agreement this week, the executives said. The IDT service will be offered on I.B.M.'s growing Internet access network. The support of I.B.M. represents a big vote of confidence for new technologies that transmit phone conversations over the Internet rather than over traditional telecommunications networks. Although calls over the Internet sometimes have a poorer sound quality than conventional phone calls, differences in technology and regulation mean that Internet phone providers can typically offer lower prices than can traditional long-distance companies. IDT, a small Internet access provider in its own right, with 80,000 subscribers, already offers the voice service, called Net2Phone, to its own Internet customers -- and to anyone else who cares to use it with any other Internet provider. IDT, which is based in Hackensack, N.J., also markets its voice service through Singnet, an Internet service provider in Singapore. But the deal with I.B.M. would be the first Internet phone pact with a major international service provider. Under the agreement, the Net2Phone software will be included with I.B.M.'s standard Internet access kit. IDT's program allows users to place long-distance calls to normal telephones from computers equipped with a microphone. I.B.M. will also place a button on its Web site at www.ibm.net enabling users to download IDT's software. I.B.M.'s Internet service has about 750,000 customers. Calls they make using IDT's service will travel over I.B.M.'s extensive international network. Neither company will pay the other an upfront sum as part of the deal, executives close to the companies said. Instead, they will share revenue generated by I.B.M. customers who begin to use IDT's service. America Online Inc. charged Tel-Save Holdings Inc. $100 million last year for the right to sell long-distance service to America Online's customers. But that was basically a joint-marketing deal for conventional phone service -- not Internet calls. Though few in number, companies that use Internet technology to carry long-distance calls have been shaking up the telecommunications industry with prices as low as 4.9 cents a minute for calls to anywhere in the unitedstates at any time. Government rules that are meant to promote the development of cyberspace allow Internet phone companies to price their offerings below those of traditional carriers, primarily by waiving the fees that most long-distance carriers must pay for connecting to local phone networks. The Federal Communications Commission has taken the first steps toward closing that loophole. Even so, transmitting calls with Internet technology is more efficient than traditional telephone networks, which means lower costs. In fact, some experts predict that Internet-style phone calls may one day replace most conventional telephone calls. Perhaps the best sign that Internet phone companies are emerging as a new force in the industry is that established long-distance companies are beginning to try the technology for themselves. Last week the AT&T Corporation, the No. 1 long-distance carrier, began offering Internet calls on a trial basis in Boston.

title:
MEDIA TALK;
As Print Revenue Ebbs, www.juneplaymate.com?
body: The on-line version of Playboy, with 25,000 paying customers, is not going to obscure the magazine's 4.5 million subscribers worldwide anytime soon. But the Internet business was the only bright spot in an otherwise dismal quarterly report this month. The magazine publishing group reported minuscule earnings last quarter and a 30 percent decline in newsstand revenue compared with the corresponding quarter in 1997. Advertising revenue was down 11 percent. The World Wide Web site, a mixture of advertising and subscriber-supported content from the magazine, as well as a catalogue of Playboy-brand merchandise for sale, showed 84 percent growth, to $1.42 million from $772,000. What does Christie Hefner, chairwoman and chief executive of Playboy Enterprises Inc., the empire started by her father in 1953, make of this? In a statement, Ms. Hefner said she thought Playboy could become "the first true global multimedia brand and do so with a much lower investment in marketing than is needed by other Internet companies." Besides the brand, analysts say, the on-line service has another thing going for it: its content. "Adult revenue is one of the very few areas where people are willing to pay, and that opens a whole new revenue stream that The newyork Times or ABCNews.com does not have available to it," said Bill Bass, an analyst with Forrester Research in Boston. Purchased each month on the newsstand, Playboy magazine costs $61.40 a year. On line, it is free -- unless you choose a premium subscription service called Playboy Cyberclub, which offers additional features like chat rooms and archives of every Playmate and cover in the magazine's 45-year history. That costs $60 a year.   LISA NAPOLI

title: New Plan for Junk email Is Dividing Internet Camps
body: Legislation quietly passed last week by the Senate to control spam, the annoying junk email that has increasingly been flooding the Internet, has driven a wedge between two camps of Internet activists -- free-speech advocates and anti-spam crusaders. The measure was added as an amendment to a bill that prohibits long-distance phone companies from "slamming," or switching customers' long-distance carriers without their consent. The bill, passed on Tuesday night, would require that all unsolicited commercial email contain the actual name, postal address, email address and phone number of the sender. It would also obligate senders of junk email to honor recipients' requests to be removed from mailing lists. The Federal Trade Commission would have authority to investigate complaints and to impose civil fines of up to $15,000. The anti-spam wording was a compromise between Senators Robert G. Torricelli, a New Jersey Democrat, and Frank H. Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, who filed competing bills last year. They are now working with Representative W. J. Tauzin, a Louisiana Republican who has a similar bill pending in the House. Committee hearings are scheduled on that measure next month. Some opponents of spam favor an outright ban, although the different sides have been working together for almost a year to reach consensus on some form of control. Free-speech advocates, concerned that proposals for an outright ban would go too far in regulating Internet speech and commerce, say the Murkowski-Torricelli measure is a good beginning. "We still have some concerns about making sure that this doesn't affect the right to anonymous political speech, but we're pretty confident that is going to be worked out," said Daniel Weitzner, deputy director of the Center for Democracy and Technology, an on-line civil liberties group based in Washington. "I think what Senators Murkowski and Torricelli did is very important in moving toward a comprehensive solution to the issue." Mr. Weitzner said, "I think the solution to spam is going to require a combination of legal and technological measures, and this is a good first step." But passionate opponents of spam say the Murkowski-Torricelli bill is worse than no legislation at all. "This is a dark day for the Internet community," said Scott Hazen Mueller, chairman of the Coalition Against Unsolicited Commercial email, a grass-roots group that says it represents more than 10,000 Internet users. "This bill appears to have been written by big-money marketing interests instead of by people who want to help the Internet thrive." The problem with the amendment's approach, Mr. Mueller said, is that senders of junk email would each get one free shot at sending their advertisements to Internet users, who would then have to get in touch with each sender, asking to be removed from his mailing list. John Mozena, a member of the coalition's board, added: "Since this bill legitimizes junk email, we can expect to see a lot of companies that had been held back by the string of court rulings that found spam to be analogous to trespass, starting to use junk email as a component of their marketing campaigns. Imagine what happens when every company that buys newspaper ads, that buys radio spots or direct postal mail begins to spam. You'd never get yourself removed from every mailing list." The coalition is backing a bill by Representative Chris Smith, a New Jersey Republican, that would ban spam in much the same way that fax advertising is prohibited. Mr. Weitzner, however, said he thought such a bill would be unconstitutional. "What we like about this," he said of the Murkowski-Torricelli bill, "is we think it enhances the ability for users to control what comes into their mailbox. It's that user control that I think ultimately will be the solution here."

title:
TECHNOLOGY;
Alternative doorways to the Internet are popping up in the spirit of free-flowing information.
body: THERE were only a few snickers last week at a new-media conference in Chicago when someone asked a group of executives from Web-search companies which of them would be the first to buy a major television network. It was a sign of just how quickly the likes of Yahoo, Lycos, Excite and Infoseek have grown, how grand their mass media dreams have become and how much their original vision of the World Wide Web has changed. No longer content to direct a user to the Web sites most relevant to the individual's interests and tastes, the former search services are intent on creating "portals" to the Internet, complete with dial-in service, free email and personal Web pages, paging and messaging, customized news, local weather and stock tracking. The aim: get the suckers under the tent and keep them there. That's a radical departure from the original business model of catching the customer's eye on the way to other sites. The original search model was deeply steeped in the Internet ethos -- the idea that information and traffic flows freely from site to site and value is added by serving that urge, not resisting it. It is an ethos that favors entropy over organization, an open range of Web publishing compared with the stockyard chutes of the portal sites. And it is an ethos that for many in the Web business still endures -- despite the portal fad. "There are between 5 and 10 million content areas on the Web, and in many ways the Internet is more like print publishing," observed Brewster Kahle. Mr. Kahle is an Internet pioneer whose 1989 invention, the Wide Area Information Server -- or WAIS -- was a pre-Web system for searching distant data bases on the Internet. He later sold his on-line and software publishing company, WAIS Inc., to America Online. The main portals are following a model that mimics the control and distribution of cable television networks. But Mr. Kahle thinks that is the wrong model. "There are 16,000 journal publishers in print, real diversity. And everyone's experience is different. Do we need a TV Guide? I think we need something a little more sophisticated." Certainly the current search services are far from exhaustive. A study released last month by the NEC Research Institute of Princeton, N.J., indicated that even the most thorough service, Hotbot (www.hotbot.com), has indexed only 34 percent of the Web's estimated 320 million pages. But Mr. Kahle is hardly a disinterested observer. He is the president and co-founder with Bruce Gilliat of Alexa Internet, a two-year-old start-up company based in San Francisco. Their product is Alexa, part Web browser, part navigation service. Users download the software from www.alexa.com free, after which Alexa manifests itself as a thin toolbar under the regular Web browser -- whether the PC is using the Netscape Navigator or Internet Explorer from Microsoft. Alexa offers quick access to information on each site visited (who owns it, how much traffic it gets, and how Alexa users rated its content), provides links to other similar sites and, lately, tiny advertising messages keyed to the user's browsing selections. About 350,000 copies of the program have been downloaded and there are 100,000 regular users, according to Mr. Kahle. Alexa is a geeky end-run around the sleek mass media dreams of the search engine companies. While Excite, Yahoo, Lycos and Infoseek are adding as many features as possible to keep users on their sites for as long as possible, Alexa encourages wide and frequent grazing by recommending sites wherever the user's interests may lead, based on the person's past preferences -- and based on the preferences of other users who have frequented the same sites. Mr. Kahle calls this approach "contextual navigation." The more users in Alexa's data base, the better the similar-preferences software works -- and the more precisely that Alexa can tailor its ads to individual users. In other words, the more that users surf outside the main portals, the better Alexa's revenue stream. Alexa is named for the library of Alexandria, the ill-fated attempt of the ancient Greeks to amass all of the literate world's printed knowledge. And in keeping with this ideal, Alexa brings the emphasis in Web navigation back to content -- not just a reader's digest of the Web. And yet, in choosing to name his venture after an ambitious idea that ultimately fell short, Mr. Kahle is implicitly conceding that the sheer size, growth, and second-to-second mutability of the Internet makes it almost impossible to amass the collected works of the Web. The reason the current search services consistently rank among the most popular Web sites is that many people presumably do want some winnowing. But the mass-market model need not be the only portal approach. "We believe that people are more in need of filters than catch-alls," said Rufus Griscom, co-founder of the artily erotic on-line magazine Nerve (www.nervemag.com). That is why Nerve, which bills itself as "literate smut," has created its own, more narrow portal: a directory of sexually oriented Web sites. And Nerve it is not alone in providing a narrower doorway to the Web. Alternative portals are everywhere, including Razorfish's "Disinformation" search engine (www.disinfo.com) that provides links to various subculture sites, and "John Skilton's Baseball Links" (www.baseball-links.com), perhaps the most complete guide to baseball on the Web. These alternate portals are evidence of the Internet ethos that refuses to conform to a mass media structure. In their race to emulate mainstream media giants like Time Warner, CBS and Disney, the search engines may be forgetting the very phenomenon that brought them into being: the Internet is a medium of creators as much as it is a medium for consumers. title: Antitrust Talks With Microsoft Are Called Off
body: Negotiations between the Microsoft Corporation and state and Federal officials collapsed today after the company's chairman, William H. Gates, ordered lawyers to withdraw earlier concessions, and Justice Department officials said they intended to file a sweeping antitrust suit on Monday. A senior representative of the state Attorneys General who were also involved in the negotiations said 20 states would file their own suit on Monday unless Microsoft offered significant new concessions before then. In a statement issued late today, the Justice Department said that discussions between Microsoft and representatives of the Justice Department and the Attorneys General ended today without a resolution. "At this point they are not expected to resume," the department said. Microsoft, in its own statement, said the company had "engaged in serious discussions with Federal and state officials to resolve this matter and avoid a protracted and expensive lawsuit." In the statement, Mr. Gates said: "This impasse is disappointing. We worked hard to resolve this, but the Government demands went too far with no basis in law, and most importantly were not in the interests of consumers." The Federal and state Governments had planned to file their antitrust suits last Thursday. The suits, which are described as being similar, assert that Microsoft has used predatory pricing policies and contract restrictions to extend its monopoly in computer operating systems to other areas of the computer industry, particularly the Internet. They also challenge Microsoft's practice of bundling applications programs, especially its Internet Explorer browser for viewing the World Wide Web, with its Windows operating system, because they say it leaves companies that make similar programs with no way to compete. Greg Shaw, a company spokesman, said Microsoft was expecting to be sued on Monday. Microsoft also announced that, on Monday, it would begin shipping Windows 98, its updated operating system, to computer manufacturers. Throughout last week, Microsoft had been negotiating with the Justice Department and Attorneys General while also carrying out an ambitious lobbying and public relations campaign to stave off litigation. At the last minute on Thursday, as state and Federal officials gathered in Washington to announce the filing of their suits, Microsoft offered new concessions that won the company a short reprieve. Principal among those concessions was an offer to negotiate whether computer makers would be allowed to determine what appears on the computer screen when it is first turned on. Now Microsoft requires that Windows come on the screen when it is turned on. In return for a delay in the filing of the lawsuits, Microsoft delayed shipments to computer makers of Windows 98, its updated operating system, until Monday. The company had planned to begin shipping the software on Friday. It is scheduled to be sold by retailers beginning June 25. Talks opened at the Justice Department on Friday and continued today in the offices of Microsoft's Washington law firm, Sullivan & Cromwell. Two senior Government officials who were involved with the talks said that Microsoft, on order of Mr. Gates, had retracted some of the concessions from the day before. One official said the talks fell apart "because Microsoft didn't put anything of substance on the table." "They said that, on reflection, Bill Gates had expressed an unwillingness to do what they had said they were willing to do before," one of the officials said. Another said: "We were told that Bill Gates talked it over with some other people within the company and decided he didn't want to do it." Microsoft, on the other hand, said it had made "extremely far-reaching concessions in the area of contracts with Internet service providers." Mr. Shaw of Microsoft said: "Negotiations are fluid; proposals are put on the table and taken off the table. And when we saw their demands, it became clear to us that they were intended to benefit a competitor, not the public." The principal offer withdrawn was the company's willingness to negotiate whether Windows appears the first time the computer is turned on. "This is very important to us," Mr. Shaw said. "We have felt that PC users prefer to have the Windows experience out of the box. The Government wanted to change that, and in essence, allow computer makers to take bids from software companies to win the right to that first screen." A government official denied that assertion but said that Federal and state governments did want to break Microsoft's hold on the default desktop. "We want to give computer manufacturers and consumers a choice of what appears on their screens," the official said. Entering the talks, Microsoft had also said it was willing to negotiate some alterations in the terms of its contracts with computer manufacturers, primarily those that force manufacturers to take other Microsoft products along with Windows, the operating system that runs about 90 percent of all personal computers. Microsoft did make offers in those areas, the company said, but an official involved with the talks called them "not terribly significant." Microsoft's statement also charged that "Federal and state lawyers asserted that making Windows work well with the Internet is somehow illegal." Mr. Shaw added that the prosecutors "demanded that Microsoft give up its right to display a Web browsing functionality that is a core part of Windows, thereby making it hard for consumers to use these technologies." Alluding to Netscape Communications Corporation's Navigator browser, the Microsoft statement said that the Justice Department had "also demanded that Microsoft include Netscape's competing browsing software in every copy of Windows." Mr. Shaw called that idea "simply outrageous, over the top," adding that including Navigator with Windows "would be like telling Coke that they have to have three cans of Pepsi in every six pack." Government officials said that including a copy of Netscape's browser with Windows was just one of several options offered to open up competition in the Web browser market. "We discussed a number of ways that Microsoft's unlawful, monopolisitic practices could be remedied," said one official. "That was one of them." The Justice Department's original complaint against Microsoft, filed last October, charged that the company had violated a 1995 consent decree by requiring computer makers to take its Internet Explorer browser as a condition of licensing Windows 95, thereby putting Netscape, Microsoft's principal competitor in the browser market, at a severe disadvantage. Internet Explorer is even more closely integrated into Windows 98. In the lawsuits to be filed on Monday, state and Federal prosecutors also are intent on preventing Microsoft from continuing to bundle all manner of additional programs with Windows, including the company's new electronic program guide called WebTV for Windows, which allows computer users to see what's on television and certain Web sites. The lawsuit prepared by the state Attorneys General urges the court to separate this program, among others, from Windows 98. At the negotiating table, Microsoft's lawyers refused to budge on the bundling issue. A senior government official who was briefed on the discussions said: "Some of the Attorneys General got the feeling that Microsoft was just fooling around, trying to learn as much as possible about what we planned to do. They really failed to make any substantive offers. And we're not in the mood to be jerked around anymore."

title:
Many Customers Still Balk At Push-Button Banking;
Skipping A.T.M.'s for Tellers and Passbooks
body: In an age of money machines, on-line banking and the quicksilver transfer of cash via computer, Maria Russo, a 38-year-old typist, is holding fast to another age. Hers is the gentle -- some might say fusty -- world of teller windows, withdrawal slips and passbook savings accounts. "I never use the automated teller machines, because you never know who's lurking behind you," Ms. Russo said, passbook in hand, as she paused recently beneath the soaring ceiling of the Flushing branch of Queens County Savings Bank. "And I prefer the passbook. I have to be able to see each entry that goes in there." For many baby boomers the passbook is a quaint relic of childhood, when the concept of earning interest on money made from mowing the neighbor's lawn was new and thrilling. But passbooks, those passportlike booklets that document the ebb and flow of one's savings, did not go the way of camera flashbulbs and stereo turntables. In fact, Ms. Russo is one of a sizable number of holdouts who have simply refused to get with the program. At savings banks in newyork City, 40 percent to 60 percent of customers still use passbooks. Their very existence may surprise those who think nothing of zapping money from one stock fund to another before breakfast. But when considering the fees that customers are sometimes charged to use automated teller machines, the hassle of correcting electronic mistakes and the temptation that round-the-clock access to money brings, old-time banking is not without its merits. Rather than try to convert customers clinging to an earlier era, some banks seem happy to allow them to remain fiscal dinosaurs because they can be so profitable, parking money in savings accounts yielding less than 2.5 percent at a time when the stock market is showing annual gains of more than 20 percent. These customers prefer thrift institutions, which offer the option of a passbook (as opposed to a monthly statement). They visit the same branch every week to deposit their paycheck, withholding enough cash to carry them through to the next payday. They hurl verbal darts at A.T.M.'s, accusing them of being unsafe, confusing and prone to error. And they relish the face-to-face contact at the teller's window. "It's a very serious thing for people who have sacrificed greatly to know that the person handling their money is a good person," said Joseph R. Ficalora, president of Queens County Savings Bank, where well over half of the 41,500 customers still use passbooks. "They want to look you in the eye." Some customers go a step further, wanting to look George Washington, Alexander Hamilton and Andrew Jackson in the eye. "We get tremendous lines of people manually depositing their paychecks and bringing their passbooks to be stamped," said Charles J. Hamm, chief executive officer of Independence Savings Bank in Brooklyn. "Some of them even withdraw the money to make sure it's there. They want to see it, smell it, feel it. And then they'll get back on line and redeposit the cash." To a large extent, the customers who bank the old-fashioned way fall into one of two groups. They are either new immigrants skittish about the security of financial institutions who may not have enough command of English to navigate the electronic superhighway, or they are older people who may have had direct experience with stock market crashes and who are comfortable with lifelong routines. But banking experts say young customers are also in the mix. "That's one of the myths, that it's a function of age," said Ed Furash, chairman of Furash & Company, a banking industry consulting firm in Washington. "It's an attitudinal thing, and there are many young people who are technophobes." At the Bensonhurst branch of Independence Savings Bank, however, most of the passbook holders there on a crystalline spring day were longtime residents, like Elizabeth Minacapelli, a 77-year-old retired dressmaker. Mrs. Minacapelli said it never occurred to her to switch from her navy blue passbook to a monthly statement. "You look at it, and you know what's there," she said. As for the automated teller machines, she does not need extra cash after bank hours. "I'm from the old school, I guess," she said. Joseph Cotugno, another customer at the same branch, where there is no Plexiglas distancing the 22 teller windows from the customers, gave similar reasons for not getting an A.T.M. card. "I come once a week to take out $100, and I'm never out at night anyway," he said. A retired mechanic with newyork City Transit, Mr. Cotugno has banked at the Bensonhurst branch since 1953 and now, at 73, has his life savings -- $83,000 -- on deposit there, mostly in conservative savings vehicles like one-year certificates of deposit. The branch welcomes its elderly customers with a large sitting area near a special window from which a teller calls out, "Next." "A lot of the money that actually resides in the banking system belongs to this more traditional group, and the last thing you want to do is to alienate them," said David S. Berry, director of research for Keefe, Bruyette & Woods, an investment bank that specializes in financial institutions. Although many passbook holders also have money in the stock market, Mr. Berry said, "There are people who leave a shocking amount of money in what are fairly low-interest savings accounts." All that money has helped savings banks reap profits through mortgage lending and refinancing. Mr. Ficalora, the president of Queens County Savings Bank, said the bank had "far more money on deposit by people who do not use A.T.M.'s than by people who do use A.T.M.'s." Savings banks profit from such customers by taking the money on deposit in their savings accounts -- generally earning less than 2.5 percent -- and lending it out at a rate of about 7.5 percent. The spread may not be as wide as that realized by commercial banks from credit card accounts and commercial loans, but the default rate on residential loans is lower. Queens County Savings Bank, with $1 billion on deposit, is now the 10th largest multifamily housing lender in the nation. Since the bank started to trade publicly in 1993, the stock has split four times, its value rising 800 percent. By comparison, an index of the nation's 24 largest commercial banks rose 329 percent during the same period. Banking consultants say Brooklyn and Queens are hubs in the newyork region for the more traditional banking customer, reflecting the demographics of age, ethnicity and income. Although savings banks have a disproportionate share of such customers, even a large commercial bank like Chase Manhattan reports that about a third of its three million branch customers in the region do not use cash machines. But passbooks have been kept alive in only a half-dozen of the bank's 500 branches, mostly in Chinatown, in lower Manhattan, and in immigrant neighborhoods in Queens. "It's not a technology issue in those branches," said Ken Herz, a bank spokesman. "It relates to the fact that in their home countries there's a tremendous lack of confidence in the banking system." But technology is an issue with many customers. "I will not use an A.T.M.," said Carl Meyer, a 64-year-old sales executive in Manhattan, as he left the North Fork Bank branch at Avenue of the Americas and 37th Street. "I don't think they're safe, and I'm concerned about errors." Even some bank officials are empathetic. David R. Jones, chairman of the board of Carver Federal Savings Bank in Harlem, said he watched as his 11-year-old daughter tried to withdraw $200 from a machine in another bank. Distracted by music, she hesitated a few moments when the money slid forward. "I saw the money being sucked back into the machine," Mr. Jones said. He spent the next two and a half months trying to get his $200 from the bank, since the withdrawal had been recorded on a computer. "People say the elderly are not willing to get with it," he said. "But this is not silliness. It's not irrational. The machines are, in many cases, very difficult and are not very forgiving." Yet banks say they are noticing a shift toward more modern ways of banking on the part of technophobes. "Even older, more conservative customers are finally coming around and doing more and more business through A.T.M.'s," said John Adam Kanas, president and chief executive officer of North Fork Bank. "But it has probably taken 15 years for them to break down those barriers." North Fork Bank, a commercial bank with headquarters in Melville, N.Y., has systematically bought up seven savings banks in the last 10 years, including Eastchester and Home Federal, increasing its customer base to 700,000 and expanding its number of branches in the newyork area to 110. The bank is soon to open a second Manhattan branch at Amsterdam Avenue and 72d Street. Mr. Kanas views the high-maintenance customer base the bank has acquired as an asset. About half of his customers do not use the automated teller machines, while about half still have passbook accounts. "A lot is made in our industry about the cost of our delivery system -- that is the branch," he said. "But very little is discussed about the fact that these types of traditional customers are willing to leave deposits with thrift institutions at lower-than-competitive interest rates. So it more than makes up for the cost of the delivery system." Graphic   Photos: Like many bank customers, Elizabeth Minacapelli has held on to her passbook. (Andrea Mohin/The newyork Times)(pg. 27)

title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
CYBERSCOUT
body: ON-LINE PLANNING Vacations With Children www.miningco.com Teresa Plowright, who lives with her husband and three sons on Bowen Island, near Vancouver, British Columbia, has "hauled three children around the globe," she says, and been a computer addict since the days of punched cards. So she is a natural choice to operate the Travel With Kids area of The Mining Company's Web site. The Mining Company, mentioned here in March in connection with its honeymoon destinations, uses real people and not software "agents" to make its selections. The Travel With Kids section is particularly rich. There were articles on great garden-parks, highlighting, when I first looked, Jurong Bird Park in Singapore and the Royal Botanical Gardens at Kew; Airfare Deals on the Web; Kid Cruises; Florida Family Vacations, and How to Afford to Travel With Kids. The How to Afford sub-subsection suggested such air fare strategies as traveling when the children are very young and can take advantage of low or no fares, and how to best use frequent-flier plans and other discounts. "The Internet is awash in sites that offer you discount travel fares," Ms. Plowright points out, adding that "there's a lot to be said for local travel agents, and the usefulness of on-line sites will vary widely." There is a bulletin board where people can ask questions and hope to get answers. Christine, who asked on Jan. 29 for "suggestions for keeping my 6-year-old daughter amused during long car trips" had received no replies by early April; as parents know, there are no ways to keep a 6-year-old amused on a car trip of more than five minutes. Shar, whose daughter became ill with a virus on a cross-country flight and acted very badly on the return trip, after she had presumably recovered, got a medically dubious reply from MamaBunny: "Could it be that your daughter had an underlying ear infection?" MamaBunny also independently contributed a suggestion to pack a can of club soda on automobile journeys to clean up children's messes. Other people asked for suggestions about portable cribs, fighting kids, and trips with grandparents. Rita was looking for cheap, safe hotels for two adults and three children in midtown Manhattan. Ms. Plowright recommended a half-dozen, and provided the addresses of other Web sites. Not all questioners are so specific. "I do get a surprising number of emails asking me for cheap fares to, say, Los Angeles," Ms. Plowright said in an on-line interview, "but the person doesn't tell me where they live."  Sites Galore There are countless resources on the Internet for people traveling with children. Travel With Kids itself offers links to at least dozens of related Web sites. Once you get started, you'll be hooked. There's the Family Travel Forum; the travel section of Family.com; Kids Cruises; Traveltime; the Great Outdoors Recreation Pages, known unappetizingly as GORP; A Zoo's Who's; Seattle: Indoor Playgrounds, for rainy days; Home Swaps, and on and on. Traveltime's Kids in Tow offers the Parents Survival Guide; Eat and Run; Play It Safe, and Road Scholars. The Parents Survival Guide alone has 14 subsections; Just Stay Home was the one that drew me: "If you find yourself needing a vacation, but dreading the preparation required, you might consider taking a vacation at home this year." Eight ground rules are given, from "start with a clean house, and then forget about it" to "home vacations are a good time to explore all your local parks, museums, zoos and wildlife sanctuaries."   L. R. SHANNON Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: Gore to Announce 'Electronic Bill of Rights' Aimed at Privacy
body: Vice President Al Gore will announce on Thursday a new "Electronic Bill of Rights" to help insure the privacy of consumers' medical records, Internet transactions and other computerized personal data, Administration officials said. In an address to graduates of newyork University, the Vice President is expected to detail several steps designed to respond to growing uneasiness among consumers that they have lost control of once-confidential information about their medical histories, children, income, reading habits and shopping preferences. The actions represent one of the broadest Federal responses to privacy concerns in the digital age and an admission that private industry has been slow to act to safeguard the confidentiality of individuals' records. Mr. Gore will define privacy as a basic American value, protected by the Constitution and numerous Federal laws, according to officials who have worked on the speech and on the policies. But he will note that the reach of the Internet and the power of computerized databases have combined to threaten Americans' privacy as never before. Alarms have been raised in recent years about the sale of computerized drivers' license information to marketers and the electronic capture of Web surfers' Internet travels for commercial purposes. Children who visit Web sites with alluring cartoon characters often find themselves deluged with unsolicited advertising pitches in themail or on their family's email accounts. "As you look at privacy in an increasingly complex world, it is necessary to constantly evaluate to see that we are doing everything we can to provide consumers with the ability to control information about themselves," said an Administration official involved in writing the new policy. "That is a task not for a day or a week or a month; rather, it is a continuum of activities that starts with making sure the Government does everything it can to insure meaningful and enforceable rules that protect consumers." According to White House aides, Thursday's speech has four central elements: a call for Congress to pass legislation protecting the privacy of medical records; establishment of a Web site that will make it easier for consumers to delete their names from direct mail and telemarketing lists; creation of a privacy officer in each Federal department and agency to insure compliance with existing laws, and announcement of a privacy conference in June to be sponsored by the Commerce Department. Mr. Gore plans to prod Congress to meet the demand of the 1996 Kennedy-Kassebaum health care bill to pass a law insuring that patients' medical records are kept confidential. Congress has heard testimony about pharmacies selling individuals' prescription records to drug companies and health insurers sharing medical data with marketers, violating consumers' medical privacy. If Congress fails to act, Mr. Gore is expected to say, the Administration plans to use its authority to enforce medical privacy by regulatory fiat. "He will be using medical privacy as a signal to the public and a stick to industry to say that we have a history of abuse in this area and the Administration wants to do something about it," said Janlori Goldman, director of the health privacy project at Georgetown University Medical Center. "I'm encouraged by this step," Ms. Goldman added. "This Administration has been singing the praises of self-regulation for some time now, but this is an acknowledgment that there are significant limits to what the private sector will do on its own." Mr. Gore will also announce that President Clinton will issue an executive memorandum directing every Cabinet department and major Federal agency to appoint a senior officer responsible for insuring compliance with privacy laws and regulations. That person will review pending or proposed legislation affecting the agency to make certain that it does not erode individual privacy. "We're certainly pleased at the high-level attention this issue is getting," said Deirdre Mulligan, staff counsel at the Center for Democracy and Technology, an electronic privacy advocacy group. "We hope that it starts the high-level dialogue that needs to occur if we're going to get a good policy on privacy."

title: Net Metaphors Stretch to Fit The Evolution Of Data Flow
body: THE long stretches of fiber optic cable carrying large volumes of data have been known as "backbones" for a long time by folks inside the data shipping business. Internet consumers are starting to hear the term as well, thanks in large part to Internet service providers who tout the speed of their backbones. The word probably emerged because the structure of computer networks looks a bit like the human nervous system. Most computer networks are set up as long stretches of fiber that carry big loads, with tendrils branching off to carry smaller and smaller loads. Just as the human spinal cord carries the command "kick" from head to leg, backbones aggregate all the traffic going across the country. A message from newyork to San Francisco may travel through local wires until it reaches a major backbone that traverses the country. The word backbone also carries the meaning of supporting the weight of a system and defining the shape of an animal. Both ideas are relevant to an Internet backbone. But the metaphor of the information superhighway, illustrated at right, also fits. A good Internet backbone means the faster transmission of messages. The tendrils are much slower. Companies providing Internet service brag about their backbones' size and speed because that gives an indication of their ability to carry traffic. An MCI customer on the East Coast who calls up a Web page of an MCI customer on the West Coast will exchange messages through MCI's backbone. The larger the capacity of this data pipeline (the need to define complex reality means that these metaphors multiply like rabbits with 400 MHz processors), the better the chances that the data won't be delayed or lost. Of course, the unitedstates isn't just bicoastal, with people only in newyork and Los Angeles. Just as the interstate highway system looks like a web, with many interconnections, backbones are not so simple. A big company like MCI or Sprint may have many branches in its main network, while a smaller company may have only one long run across the country. Companies link their networks together by using their own fiber optic networks or leasing capacity from other networks. The shape and structure of these networks depends upon the number and location of customers and patterns of data flow. A company with many customers in newyork and Chicago may put together a high-capacity channel between those two cities with a smaller channel to the West Coast. The speed of these connections is measured with shorthand terms like T-1 (1.5 megabits per second), T-3 (45 mbps), OC-3 (155 mbps) or OC-12 (622 mbps). Right now, most large service providers have OC-3 channels carrying data across the country, and the major networks are aiming to upgrade to OC-48 (2.4 gigabits per second). Does a high-speed backbone, also known as a fat pipe, mean that Web pages pop up faster? Nothing is certain. If the user and the Web site share the same company, then the traffic will travel along that company's network, and the bigger pipes mean less chance of a backup. But delays could still happen in the smaller segments at either end as well as at the Web server itself. If the user and the Web site use different companies, everything gets more complicated. The Internet uses what is known as hot-potato routing, a system in which each company gives up carrying each piece of data as soon as possible. If an MCI customer on the East Coast, for example, sends a request for a Web page from a Sprint customer on the West Coast, MCI hands off the data to the nearest interconnection to Sprint, perhaps in newyork. Then Sprint carries the data the rest of the way. Balance is preserved because the pieces of data will take a different route on the way back. Sprint hands them off as soon as possible, and MCI carries them back. That is why transactions often follow different routes as they travel between two locations in different directions. In this example, both companies traded data because they are "peers" -- they have negotiated a relationship in which they say, "You carry my customer's data for nothing and I'll do the same for you." Smaller companies have trouble entering these relationships with larger companies because the larger companies often end up doing more of the work. The negotiation of peer relationships between companies is a hot topic that blends business savvy with engineering common sense. The smaller company usually makes up for the imbalance with money. The major companies, which all have peer relationships with one another, refer to themselves as the first tier. Smaller, local Internet service providers are in the second tier. Some companies with hefty local backbones are often called tier 1.5 because they have some local peer relationships but end up buying connections to handle nonlocal traffic. There are several companies that serve the newyork-to-Washington corridor with their backbones but buy service to cover the rest of the country. But new, high-bandwidth networks will soon emerge from the wireless world. Companies like Teledesic, Ellipso, Motorola and Skybridge are working hard at creating a satellite data network, and that network will compete with ground fiber optic cables. If these plans are successful, they may change the marketplace for data traffic (and jeopardize the metaphors of backbone, highway and pipe). These satellites will form a whirling constellation overhead, and each user will switch satellites every several minutes. A piece of data will be routed among the satellites in space until it finds the right satellite to beam it back to Earth. The effect will be closer to a fast-passing, unselfish lacrosse or basketball team unfolding complicated plays than to transmission through a backbone. Perhaps the information highway might come to be called the information carousel, or circus. That word might be suitable in some ways even now.

title: NEWS WATCH
body: GOT A TV TUNER CARD? -- According to a recent survey of Internet surfers in the unitedstates, 51 percent of them are expected to curb their on-line cruising for a while tonight to watch the on-air series finale of "Seinfeld."
